units.la: I DIVINVS SCRIPTOR, LVCAS EVANGELISTA, nihil praeter officium fecit, quando historiam aeterni Filij Dei Iesu Christi, quam in communem totius Ecclesiæ vtilitatem conscripsit, nominatim Theophilo dedicauit: nemo cordatus opinor mihi vitio verterit CHRISTOPHORE Princeps illustrissime, quod meas in illum Lucubrationes sub felicibus tuæ Clementiæ auspiciis in lucem exire volui. Fuit enim Theophilus vir illustris & in publica authoritate constitutus, cuius multa in Ecclesiam beneficia extitisse credibile est: certè non vulgaris fidei & pietatis argumentum censeri debet, quòd solus fere inter sui loci & ordinis homines illo tempore inuetus sit, qui causam hanc odij & periculi plenam suscipere ausus fuerit. Similem huius nostro seculo Deus excitauit parentem tuum, Illustrissimum Principem FRIDERICHVM, Electorem: quem & ipsum non puduit puriorem Ecclesiarum Christi doctrinam, quam alij communi Veritatis odio accensi; alij ignorantia falsinati aut decepti, persequebantur, propius cognoscere, & cognitam amplecti: etiamsi non ignoraret, quantam ea res inuidiam, & quam multa quamque grauia pericula ipsi paritura esset. Fuit ea pietas grata admodum multis fidis Christi cultoribus, quibus apud se asylum tutissimum aperuit, sibiipsi vero laudem & gloriam immortalem acquisiuit. Te vero CHRISTOPHORE Dux, paternæ virtutis vt hæredem, ita imitatorem acerrimum esse omnes prædicant; qui tecum aliquando familiarius versati sunt. Ego certè cum ab hinc biennio hac transfires, non obscura præclaræ pietatis semina in te deprehendisse mihi videbar: quæ ab eo tempore vnà cum ætate non pœnitendis incrementis aucta esse; amici testantur, quibus ego fidem derogare neque possum neque debeo. Mihi autem tunc in primis probabatur grauis illa facilitas, qua te mores & sermones tuos ita moderari videbam, vt nihil tanti parentis filio indignum faceres, grauitatem vero illam non minus festiua quàm mirifica erga omnes affabilitate condires. Placuit ea nostris hominibus quàm maxime, apud quos tui memoriam & iucundam & honorificam reliquisti: me vero eius recordatio sic mouet, vt nihil non mihi de tua benignitate pollicear, & sperem te nunc ad te venientem Lucam nostrum eo vultu acceptururn esse, quo tunc me qualemcunque Christi ministrum domi meæ conuenire & alloqui dignatus es. Nec enim illorum peruersis iudiciis moueris, sat scio, qui dona literaria ad principes viros pertinere negant, indignissimum autem facinus esse arbitrantur, si quis apud eos de sacris verba faciat, aut eorum lectione illos occupari velit, quæ ad Scripturæ Sacræ interpretationem faciunt. Quia enim eo parente natus es, qui tibi viuum omnis virtutis exemplar in semetipso præfert, & ab ineunte ætate sub doctissimis piissimisque præceptoribus institutus es, denique (quod de Timotheo suo Paulus dicebat) à puero sacras literas nouisti: non potes ignorare, nihil principe dignius; nihil reipublicæ vtilius esse syncero & ardenti verae religionis studio, quae nos cum Deo omnis boni authore conciliat, vt inter infelicis mundi horribiles motus sub illius alis tuto & feliciter degamus. Mirum autem est inter Christianos homines inueniri, qui vt apud Principes bonam gratiam ineant, ea persuasione eorum animos imbuere audent, quae illos praecipua suae gloriae & dignitatis parte spoliat, & eorum authoritatem, qua in primis armatos esse oportet, quam maxime labefactat. Quid enim in illis reliquum erit quod authoritatem mereatur, si religionis existimationem ab eis auferas? Num sapientia? Atqui hae non omnes instructi sunt, eadem autem in multis inuenitur, qui vulgo contempti & obscuri sunt. Num iustitia? Sed & haec multis deest, qui sibi quod libet licere putant. Num potentia? At si haec per se aestimetur, maior est apud populum, qui illos multitudine & viribus vincit. Num generis nobilitas & praeclara maiorum virtus? Sed ne haec quidem sola sufficit. Est quidem non poenitendum Dei donum, ex familia illustri & maioribus vere generosis progenitum esse, qui virtutum exemplis & factis heroicis clari habentur: quantum item momenti ad Regnorum conseruationem & pacem publicam afferat legitima Principum successio, quos antiqua stemmata & hereditaria virtutis existimatio commendant, Regni luda cum Israelitico diligens collatio abunde docet. Veruntamen apud degeneres, ne haec quidem gloria perpetua est, & plerunque maiorum fiorum exemplis damnantur, qui relictis eorum vestigiis, vitam in ignavia aut vitiis turpem transigunt. Sola igitur religio reliqua manet, quae magistratum gerentibus authoritatem conciliat, dum docet, eos a Deo institutos esse & Dei seruos, quibus obedientia debeatur, non tam supplicij metu, quam propter conscientiam, ne Dei iram in nos provocemus, sicut Paulus graviter testatur. Quis ergo sanae mentis homo Verbi Dei & religionis studium ad principes pertinere negauerit? Quanto rectius olim Poetae, qui Reges θεογενεῖς, id est, Diis genitos dixerunt? Quem honore etsi post eris temporibus multi nimium seruilis ingenij homines adulatorie magis quam serio tyrannis quoque impuris & crudelibus detulerint, primi tamen illi, quos & propria eruditio, & priscorum temporum gravitas commendat, altius quid & sublimius spectauerunt. Etenim hoc omnibus persuasum esse cupiebant, magistratus siue principatus ex Deo esse, ideoque non vulgarium hominum loco, sed pro Dei filijs aut Semideis eos esse habendos, qui in illo dignitatis atque potentiae fastigio constituti sunt. Idem praeterea tanti nominis splendore Reges non arroganti aut stulta praesumptione inebriari voluerunt, sed potius sui officij admonere, vt suae dignitatis memores, Deum audiant, & huius ingenium atque mores referre studeant. Ita denique insedit omnium Regum atque Principum animis haec sententia, vt quotquot inter gentes sapientiae & iustitiae existimatione claruerunt, religionem aliquam non vulgarem simulare, & legum suarum originem ad aliquam Deorum referre soliti fuerint: quod viderent, illis non vlla alia ratione authoritatem solidam & stabilem conciliare posse. Zoroastes certe, qui Nini temporibus apud Bactrianos & Persas regnauit, legum quas ferebat authorem fecit Oromazonem, vel Meforomasdem (quod nomen ei Plutarchus tribuit) quem illi Deorum optimum & omnis boni authorem esse credebant. Mercurius autem ille Trismegistus, hic Aegyptijs dictus, quod & philosophos omnes sapientia, & sacerdotes omnes religione, reges autem omnes potentia superare crederetur, leges se a Mercurio auo suo accepisse, populo persuasum voluit. Minos, qui Cretensibus leges dedit, se cum Ioue familiarius conuersari, & huius διαιτη se esse finge-bat, vt illis inde pondus maius accederet. At Charondas, Carthaginensium Legislator, Saturnum legum suarum conditorem nominabat. Lycurgus, vt suas Lacedaemonijs commendaret, eas ab Apolline primum aeditas esse testabatur. Simili ratione Solon & Draco adducti suas sub Minervae nomine promulgauerunt, quam apud Athenienses suos in summo honore & pretio esse sciebant. Quid Numam referam, qui vt Romanos in armis enutritos legum disciplinae assuefaceret, nocturnos sibi cum Ægeria Nympha congressus esse simulauit? Sed quid istos commemorare attinet, quos sapientiae & eruditionis politioris studium perspicaciores fecit, quando barbarus ille Xamolxis, Scytharum Rex, efferam & immanem gentem non aliter quam numinis reuerentia cicurari posse vidit, & proinde legibus absolutis authorem fecit Vestam? Taceo infelix illud diaboli mancipium, Mahumetem, qui Alcorani fuit, quo fabulas & commenta non minus impia quam pudenda complexus est, authoritatem nullam fore intellexit, nisi illius authorem faceret Gabrielem archangelum, quem secum familiarius colloqui mentiebatur. Et haec quidem olim finxerunt, quos veri Dei ignorantia apud homines aequè ignorantes, existimationis & dignitatis suae praesidia vndequaque conquirere coegit. Nos autem ista commemoramus, non quòd nugatorum eiusmodi fabulae nobis probentur, sed vt nostrorum hominum stultitiam arguamus, qui religionis curam atque studium Principes viros minus decere arbitrantur. Hi vt ne de humanis quidem recte iudicare possunt: ita nescium, quanto praestantior felicior-que fit Christianorum principum conditio, quos ad commenta eiusmodi recurrere nequaquam est opus: quando constat eos reuera θεoγενεῖς, aut ex Deo genitos, & potestate diuina armatos esse, à Deo denique ipso leges accepisse, quas sequi vt illis tutissimum, ita toti populo & Reipublicae saluberrimum fuerit. Cur enim de generis aut natalium nobilitate dubitent, qui non minus ad se quàm vulgus Christianorum pertinere sciunt, quod de verae illius θεογονίας ratione Ioannes Euangelista tradidit, de aeterno & vnigenia Dei Filio, Iesu Christo, sic scribens: Quotquot eum receperunt, iis potestatem siue dignitatem dedit, vt filij Dei fierent: nem pe iis, qui credunt in nomen eius: Qui non ex sanguine, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo geniti sunt. En ex Deo genitos & Dei filios dicit Apostolus omnes eos, qui credunt in nomen Iesu Christi, id est, qui Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, agnoscunt promissum illum humani generis vindicem atque seruatorem esse, quem pater ex aeterno decreto vnxerit oleo laetitiae, vt eum Ecclesiae suae Regem & Sacerdotem constituerit. Quòd si Dei filij sunt Christiani omnes, quis Dei filios esse negauerit Reges & Principes, qui eadem fide praediti, Filium illum Dei aeternum osculantur & reuerenter colunt? Vel num diuina potestate armatos esse dubitabimus, quos ipse Deus in hoc fastigium euexit? quos ex suo nomine Deos dici voluit? quos denique suae Ecclesiae, qua nihil in terris pretiosius habet, nutritios fecit, vt Isaiae verbis vocantur? Quis vero Legum & iuris publici authoritatem contemnat, qui iudicium omne Domini esse nouit, & Ecclesiam ex Spiritus Sancti mandato seu suggestione precari audit: Deus iudicia tua Regi da, & iustitiam tuam filio Regis: vt ius dicat populo tuo ex iustitia, & afflictis tuis in iudicio? Haec consideratio principes in primis decet, & ijsdem quàm maximè necessaria est: quia vt authoritatem veram illis conciliat: ita in periculis, quae ipsis multa & grauissima impendent, efficacissimè consolatur, & simul eosdem in officio continet, ne caeca potentiae suae fiducia ebrij cupiditatibus prauis indulgeant, aut impotenti affectuum libidine abripi sese patiantur, dum quid possint volunt ostendere. Meminerint ergo, authoritatem qua illos Deus armauit, tunc demum ipsis saluam fore & stabilem, si officium diligenter faciant, & illum animo toto honorent. Itaque occinant sibi ipsis frequenter, quae in Scripturis Spiritus Sanctus illis loquitur. Est inter ea cumprimis mcter, quae in Scripturis Spiritus Sanctus illis loquitur. morabile, quod in Psalmo secundo apertis quidem Iesu Christi hostibus dicitur, sed ita dicitur, vt simul omnibus quoque ijs conveniat, qui in populo Christianorum potiuntur. Sapite(inquit) o Reges, erudimini iudices terrae: Seruite Domino in timore, & exultate cum tremore: Osculamini Filium, ne irascatur, & amittatis viam: Breui exardescet furor eius: Beati omnes, qui sperant in eum. Pauca verba, sed plus quam aurea vel gemmea, & digna, quae in portis, in compitis, in foro, in curijs, in palatijs & cubiculis principum omnibus, in primis autem cordibus eorum inscribantur. Non iubet diuinus Psaltes, vt abiecto sceptro & positis Regni insignibus vitam priuatam viuant (quod hodie Anabaptistae, fanaticum & seditiosum hominum genus, exigere audent, quasi nemo simul & magistratum gerere & Christianum agere possit) sed vt intelligentes sint iubet, & vere sapiant. Quia enim in populo capitis instar sunt, in quo oculi corpori vniuerso prospiciunt, aures omnibus membris audiunt, cerebrum ipsdem simul omnibus reminiscitur, cogitat, ratiocinatur, sapit, os denique cibum acceptum ad stomachum transmittit, vt illic digestione facta alimentum in omnes corporis partes distribuatur: haec eadem principes reipublicae toti & singulis in ea agentibus praestare debent. Primi ergo pericula providere, primi afflictorum querelas audire, earundem recordari, & tam de publica totius populi quam priuata singulorum ciuium salute cogitare & consilia suscipere debent. Est hoc magni laboris opus, & quod serio consideratum facile animos torpentes excitare, otium ignauum procul expellere, & illicitarum voluptatum studia prohibere poterit. Plutarchus author est, Persarum Regibus ex more veteri cubicularium fuisse, qui diluculo cubiculum regium ingressus clamaret: ἀνάστα ὦ βασιλεῦ, καὶ τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἡμέρας, ὧν σε ἐργάτην ἐποίησεν ἡ θέλησις. Id est, Surge, o Rex, & negotia cura, quae te curare voluit Mesopromasdes. Quo loco idem author subiicit: At erudito prudentique Principi intus in animo adest, qui semper idem dicet & iubeat. Nam cum in singulas horas occurrant, quae illum de functionis suae difficultate & quae hanc comitantur, periculis admonent, facile videbit sapientia singulari sibi opus esse neque aliquem otio aut secordiae locum dari posse, nisi & seipsum & suae fidei creditum populum in discrimen extremum adducere velit. Quod probe obseruans Solomon, cum quiduis postulandi copiam a Deo sibi factam audiret, non vitam longaeuam, non immensos opum thesauros, non hostium suorum animas, sed cor intelligens & sapiens sibi dari petiit, vt populo ius dicere, & salutem publicam tueri posset. Quae postulatio tantopere Deo placuit, vt incomparabili sapientiae, qua eum donabat, diuitias simul & gloriam adiiceret, quibus omnes orbis terrarum Reges longe superarent. Caeterum quia tanti momenti res est, vt Principes sapientia vera atque solida instructi sint, Dauid eos non solum sapere iubet, sed insuper, vt sese erudiri patiantur, grauiter monet. Erudimini (inquit) iudices terrae. Est quidem sapientiae author vnus Deus, cui soli in corda & animos hominum ius est: sed is per organa agit, inter quae primus locus Verbo eius debetur. Ad huius ergo disciplinam principes remittuntur, cui nisi se subiecerint, nunquam vere sapient, neque quid facto opus sit intelligent. Viderunt quidem olim gentes quoque, quantum hic posset institutio, & ideo Plutarchus apud Principes cumprimis philosophandum esse docuit, vt eorum animi curentur, quos pro multis solicitos esse, multis item sapere & multis ius dicere oporteat. Sed & Reges potentissimi aliqui illustres viri plerunque filijs suis Praeceptores dederunt philosophos, sibi quoque frequenter eos accersiuerunt, quos eruditione & rerum vsu prae aliis excellere videbant. Sic Anaxagoram Periclii, Dioni Platonem, Italiae primatibus Pythagoram, Athenodorum Augusto Caesari, familiares fuisse legimus. Et Philippus Macedo Alexandrum filium ab Aristotele, institui voluit: Scipio autem Aphricanus praeceptorem habuit Panaetium, cuius hodie etiam celebratur sententia ista, quam Principes viri perpetuo meditari debent: Vitam hominum ex improuiso assidua & prope quotidiana periscula ferre; ad quae cauenda animo semper intento esse oportet, ut sunt athletae: Sicut enim illi in certamine caput manibus oppositis, quasi vallo praemuniunt: ita animus sapientis aduersus petulantiam iniuriarum; ictúsque fortunae debet esse erectus; arduus, septus, ne qua in re repentina incursio imparatis & improtectis nobis oboriatur. At rectius hic quoque sui populi Regibus Deus consuluit, quando ut Legis suae librum semper penes se habeant, & in eius lectione quotidie exerceantur iussit. Ea enim cum voluntate diuina rationes quoque efficacissimas proponit, quibus ut recte sentiant & faciant homines permouentur. Et constat felicissime regnasse eos, qui fidos Legis interpretes, Prophetas reuerit sunt: infelicissimos autem fuisse eos, quotquot se ab his admoneri aut coerceri noluerunt. Exempla, quae plurima extant, non commemorabo, quando unus Ioas nobis suffi cere potest: Qui ut per Iehoiada Sacerdotem seruatus & in regnum euectus fuit: ita feliciter rebus praefuit, quam diu eodem monitore & consultore vsus est: postea autem tam se ipsum quam alios perdidit, postquam excussi disciplinae diuinae iugo, Zachariam, Iehoiadae filium, plus quam parricidali ingratitudine crudeliter necauit. Hoc ergo illud est, quod principum filijs commendatissimum esse debet, ut a teneris annis Verbo Dei obedire discant, nec cum aetatis progressu disciplinam tandem excuti debere arbitrentur. Ideo enim huius iugo iuuenes assuescere debent, ut tunc quoque se Deo obedientiam debere intelligant, quando iam in multos alios habent imperium. Et ne tunc in inani & otiosa cognitione acquiescant, semper in mentem illis venire debet, quod tertio loco Dauid subiicit: Seruite Domino cum timore; & exultate in tremore: Osculamini Filium, &c. Vt enim in quauis scientia cum θεωρίᾳ πράξιν coniungi necesse est, quando sine hac nullus illius vsus erit: sic coelestis illa sapientia & disciplina tunc demum fructum vtilem & salutarem feret, si factis & opere seipsam declarauerit. Sunt autem Regum atque principum opera plurima, quae singulatim enumerare longum foret, nec vt id fiat necesse est, quando summam & Colophonem omnium Dauid uno verbo complectitur, dum eos Domino seruire iubet. Haec enim vera illa sapientia est, haec summa Regum dignitas & gloria; ex qua regnorum quoque felicitas omnis dependet. Gaudent principum seruitio, qui his se charos esse featiunt, & gloriosum putatur in magni Regis aula locum aliquem honoratiorem tenere. Quanta igitur maior ipsorum principum gloria, quos pro seruis suis Deus agnoscit, quorum opera in sui Regni administratione vtitur? Etenim qui mundo seruiunt, aut affectum libidini seipsos sponte subiiciunt, ij non rerum domini, sed herorum turpissimorum, imo (vt Sophocles de libidine Venerea dicebat) agrestium atque furiosorum mancipia sunt. At Domino seruire, ea demum libertas vera & iucunda est, quando vt id faciamus fieri non potest, nisi a peccato & huius authore diabolo prius manumisi simus: quam manumisionem comitatur spontaneus ille & voluntarius spiritus, qui iucundos nobis facit labores omnes, quos in Christi seruitio subire debemus. Id vero etsi omnibus Christianis commune sit, vt nimirum quisque pro suae vocationis ratione Deo sponte seruiat, maxime tamen ad principes pertinet; & latissime extenditur. Nec enim audiri debent, qui illos tunc officio suo defunctos esse sentiunt, si ius dicant, & rebus huius seculi fideliter praesint: Nam & religionis cura ad ipsos praecipue pertinet, neque Dei serui fideles dici merebuntur, si illam negligant, quae sola nos ei obstringit. Regum itaque est doctrinam Veritatis tueri, cultus illicitos abolere, superstitiones tollere, cultum verum propagare, Dei hostes coercere, blasphemos punire, pijs autem & sanctis Dei cultoribus adesse, vt pace & libertate conscientiarum diuinitus data possint frui. Negarunt quidem olim Donatistæ ad Reges pertinere Ecclesiæ & religionis negotia, & illorum vestigijs nostro sæculo Anabaptistæ insistunt. Sed graviter illis omnibus ex huius Psalmi verbis Diuus Augustinus ad Bonifacium Epistola quinquagesima respondet, inter alia sic scribens : Quomodo Reges Domino seruiunt in timore, nisi ea quæ contra Domini iussa fiunt, religiosa seueritate prohibendo atque plectendo ? Aliter enim Rex seruit, quia homo est, aliter quia etiam & Rex est. Quia homo est, ei seruit viuendo fideliter: quia vero etiam Rex est, seruit, leges iusta præcipientes & contraria prohibentes concinenti vigore sanciendo. Et quod dicit, ibidem Ezechiæ, Iosiæ, Regis Niniuitarum, Nabuchodonozoris denique & Darij exemplis confirmat. Non est ergo quod fanaticorum istorum clamoribus moueantur Christiani principes, aut se falcem in messem alienam mittere putent, si quid ex Dei Verbo de religione statuunt. Hæc enim cura proprie ad eos pertinet, neque officium aliud Deo magis gratum aut iucundum præstare possunt. Estq; hoc loco dignissimum obseruatu, quod duas animi affectiones inter se diuersissimas Spiritus sanctus coniungit. Iubet enim Reges seruire Domino in timore, & exultare in tremore. Quomodo autem quis simul gaudeat & timeat? simul exultet & tremat? Sed probe ista conuenire sentiunt Principes, qui vere Christiani sunt. Nec enim seruitus illa eiusmodi est, quæ animo aut conscientiæ molestiam & labores exhibeat; sed cum gaudio, cum exultatione, cum tripudio coniuncta est. Gaudent enim, quod se Dei seruos esse sciant; qua nulla homini dignitas maior potest obtingere. Exultant, quod sua efficia Domino grata esse norint, & ab eo retributionem expectent. Idem intra animos suos tripudiant & iubilant; quod illum ipsum, cui seruiunt, iam sibi adesse, iam ipsos tueri, & ipsorum consilia, dicta, facta gubernare sentiunt. Et cur non toto corde exultet & gaudeat, qui in semetipso Dei omnia gubernantis imaginem totius mundo propositam esse sentit, & cuius faciès serena (vt Solomon ait) vita est, & gratia eius velut nubes imbris serotini? Horum consideratio certe non potest non excitare Reges, vt animo alacri & exultabundo functionem suam obeant, & Deo debitum obsequium præstent. At illi ipsi simul timent & tremunt, quoties sui muneris difficultatem, dignitatis suæ excellentiam, donorum Dei immane pretium, cum sua infirmitate, & quam cum reliquis hominibus communem habent, naturæ vitiositate conferunt. Tunc enim illud Apostoli ipsis succurrit, se thesaurum hunc pretiosissimum in vasis fictilibus aut testaceis portare, cuius iactura vt maxima, sic fere irrecuperabilis est. Timent item, quoties cogitant errores & delicta sua non in ipsis solis hærere, sed ad populum simul omnem & Rempublicam ac deoque ad innocentissimos quosque redundare. Adhæc solicitos reddit vulgi ingenium, quod plerunque cæco affectu abreptum iusta imperia excutere conatur, leges intolerabiles putat, consultoribus fidis pessimam gratiam refert, & ipsdem nequicquam reluctantibus in proprium exitium ruit. Timent ergo sibi ipsis optimi quique principes, ne vel ignorantia, vel negligentia, vel affectu praue deceptí aliquid designent, quod ipsos Deo parum fidos, aut etiam ingratos esse arguat. Timent item populo, ne eum perdant aut perire sinant, de quo olim Deo rationem reddi oportere intelligunt. Timent denique vt parentes pij liberis suis, quos multa inepte & pueriliter, multa imprudenter, multa cum periculo præsenti coniuncta tentare vident. Etenim quomodo securus esse possit inter tot rerum discrimina Christianus princeps, quem vt summi numinis metus & reuerentia coertia coercet, ita populi & reipublicæ amor totum regit & gubernat: quando inter Ethnicos olim reperti sunt, qui dicerent, boni principis esse, magis timere ne quid mali faciat, quàm ne quid mali ipse patiatur? Et memorabile est Plutarchi sententia: Hic principis metus est & humanus & verè generosus, vt his quibus imperat metuat, ne quid se insciò lædantur. Idem canibus generosis similes dicit Reges, quium in septis custodiam agentibus, qui simul atque feram appropinquantem audierint, timent non sibi, sed his quæ custodiunt. Exemplum huius timoris præclarum olim fortissimus ille Thebarum imperator, Epaminondas, præbuit: quando Thebanis in ludos quosdam festos & compotationes solutis, solus armis sump-tis mœnia obibat, dicens, se sobrium esse & vigilare, quò alijs copotare & dormire liceret. Et hoc illud est, in quo inter Reges & tyrannos ingens discrimen appa-ret. Qui enim veri Reges sunt, timent ijs, in quos habent imperium: è contra tyranni eos ipsos timent, metúmque eorum auget aucta potentia, & quò pluribus imperant, eò plures metuunt.
units.tr: The divine writer Luke the Evangelist did nothing but his duty when he dedicated by name to Theophilus the history of the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, which he wrote for the common benefit of the whole Church. I think no sensible person will hold it against me, most illustrious Prince Christopher, that I have wished my labours on that history to come out into the light under the happy auspices of your Clemency. Theophilus was an illustrious man, placed in public authority, and it is credible that many benefits to the Church came from him. Certainly it must be counted no common proof of faith and piety that he was almost the only man of his place and rank at that time found bold enough to take up a cause so full of hatred and danger. In our own age God has raised up a like parent of yours, the most illustrious Prince Frederick, the Elector. He was not ashamed to come to know more closely the purer doctrine of the Churches of Christ, which others, kindled by a common hatred of the truth, or deceived and misled by ignorance, were persecuting, and, having come to know it, to embrace it, although he was not unaware how great the envy, and how many and how grave the dangers, that this would bring upon him. That piety was most pleasing to many faithful worshippers of Christ, to whom he opened a most secure refuge in his own domain, and he won for himself praise and immortal glory. And of you, Duke Christopher, all who have been closely acquainted with you declare that you are, as heir of your father's virtue, so also his most eager imitator. As for me, when I passed through here two years ago, I seemed to myself to have detected in you no obscure seeds of an excellent piety, and my friends, whom I cannot and must not doubt, testify that these have since grown together with your age, to no regrettable degree. What I especially approved then was that grave affability by which I saw you so moderate your manners and speech that you did nothing unworthy of so great a father's son, and you seasoned that gravity with a courtesy no less cheerful than remarkable toward all. My people, among whom you left a pleasant and honourable memory of yourself, were very pleased with this. And the recollection of it moves me so that I promise myself nothing but kindness from you, and I hope that when you now come to see us you will receive our Luke with the same countenance with which you deigned to meet and address me, such as I am, a minister of Christ, in my own house. For I am sure you will not be moved by the perverse judgements of those who deny that literary gifts belong to princes, and who think it a most shameful thing if anyone speaks of sacred matters before them or wishes to occupy them with reading those works that bear on the interpretation of Holy Scripture. For since you were born of that father, who sets before you in himself a living pattern of every virtue, and since from your earliest years you have been instructed by most learned and most pious teachers, and finally (as Paul said of his Timothy) have known the sacred letters from childhood, you cannot be ignorant that nothing is more worthy of a prince, nothing more useful to the commonwealth, than a sincere and ardent zeal for true religion, which reconciles us to God, the author of every good, so that amid the dreadful upheavals of this unhappy world we may live safely and happily under his wings. It is, however, a strange thing that there should be found among Christian men those who, in order to win favour with princes, dare to imbue their minds with that persuasion which strips them of their chief part of glory and dignity, and most greatly weakens their authority, with which above all they ought to be armed. For what will remain in them that deserves authority, if you take away from them the esteem of religion? Wisdom? But not all are endowed with it, and yet it is found in many who are commonly despised and obscure. Justice? But this too is lacking in many, who think they may do whatever pleases them. Power? But if that is valued in itself, the people, who outnumber them in multitude and strength, have greater power. Nobility of birth and the splendid virtue of ancestors? But not even these alone suffice. It is indeed a gift of God not to be regretted to have been born from an illustrious family and forebears truly noble, who are regarded as famous for the examples of their virtues and their heroic deeds. And how much weight the lawful succession of princes, whom ancient pedigrees and the reputation of hereditary virtue commend, brings to the preservation of kingdoms and public peace, the careful comparison of the kingdom of Judah with that of Israel teaches abundantly. Yet among degenerate men even this glory is not lasting, and they are commonly condemned by the examples of their ancestors, who, having abandoned their footsteps, spend their lives in idleness or in shameful vices. Religion alone therefore remains, which wins authority for those who bear the magistracy, while it teaches that they have been instituted by God and are servants of God, to whom obedience is owed, not so much from fear of punishment as for conscience' sake, lest we provoke the wrath of God upon ourselves, as Paul solemnly testifies. Who then of sound mind would deny that the study of the Word of God and of religion belongs to princes? How much more rightly did the poets of old speak, who called kings theogeneis [θεογενεῖς], that is, born of the gods? Although in later times many men of too servile a disposition, flattering rather than serious, bestowed this honour even on impure and cruel tyrants, those first poets, whom their own learning and the dignity of early times commend, looked to something higher and more sublime. For they wished it to be persuaded to everyone that magistracies or principalities are from God, and therefore that those who are placed on that height of dignity and power are not to be held as ordinary men, but as sons of God or demigods. Moreover, those same men, by the splendour of so great a name, wished that kings should not be puffed up by arrogant or foolish presumption, but rather reminded of their duty, so that, mindful of their dignity, they should listen to God and strive to reflect his character and his ways. So at last this opinion took root in the minds of all kings and princes, that all who among the nations have shone in the reputation of wisdom and justice were wont to feign some uncommon religion and to refer the origin of their laws to some god. For they saw that in no other way could they win solid and stable authority. Zoroaster certainly, who reigned among the Bactrians and Persians in the time of Ninus, made Oromazes, or Mithromazes (which name Plutarch gives him), the author of the laws he brought, whom they believed to be the best of the gods and the author of all good. And that Mercurius Trismegistus, so called in Egypt, because he was believed to surpass all philosophers in wisdom, all priests in religion, and all kings in power, wished it to be persuaded to the people that he had received the laws from Mercury, his grandfather. Minos, who gave laws to the Cretans, pretended that he conversed rather intimately with Jupiter and that he was the diaite [διαιτη] of him, so that greater weight might thereby accrue to his laws. And Charondas, the lawgiver of the Carthaginians, named Saturn as the founder of his laws. Lycurgus, in order to commend his laws to the Lacedaemonians, testified that they had first been issued by Apollo. In a similar way Solon and Draco, led by the same purpose, promulgated their laws under the name of Minerva, whom they knew to be in the highest honour and esteem among their Athenians. Why should I mention Numa, who, in order to accustom the Romans, reared in arms, to the discipline of laws, pretended that he had nocturnal meetings with the nymph Egeria? But why do I recall these men, whom a keener wisdom and the study of a more refined learning made more perceptive, when that barbarian Zamolxis, king of the Scythians, saw that a savage and monstrous nation could be tamed in no other way than by reverence for the divinity, and therefore, having set forth his laws, made Vesta their author? I pass over that unhappy minion of the devil, Mahomet, who, in the Alcoran, which he composed, wove together fables and inventions no less impious than shameful; he understood that it would have no authority unless he made the archangel Gabriel its author, whom he lied that he conversed with more intimately. And these men indeed of old invented such things, whom the ignorance of the true God, among men equally ignorant, compelled to seek from every quarter the defences of their reputation and dignity. We, however, mention these things not because such fables of triflers are approved by us, but in order to expose the folly of our own men, who think that the care and zeal for religion is less fitting for princes. These men cannot even judge rightly about human affairs; and they do not know how much more excellent and happier is the condition of Christian princes, who have no need at all to resort to inventions of this kind, since it is established that they are truly theogeneis, or born of God, armed with divine power, and have finally received laws from God himself, which to follow is as safest for them as it is most healthful for the whole people and the commonwealth. For why should those doubt about the nobility of their birth and origin who know that what John the Evangelist taught about the true theogonia [θεογονίας] belongs no less to them than to the common run of Christians, concerning the eternal and only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, writing thus: "As many as received him, to them he gave power, or dignity, to become the sons of God: namely to those who believe in his name. Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." Behold, the Apostle calls all those who believe in the name of Jesus Christ born of God and sons of God; that is, those who acknowledge that this Jesus, who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, is that promised redeemer and saviour of the human race, whom the Father from eternal decree anointed with the oil of gladness, that he might appoint him King and Priest of his Church. But if all Christians are sons of God, who will deny that kings and princes are sons of God, who, endowed with the same faith, kiss and reverently worship that eternal Son of God? Or shall we doubt that they are armed with divine power, whom God himself has raised to this height? Whom he wished to be called gods from his own name? Whom finally he made nursing fathers of his Church, which has nothing more precious on earth, as they are called in the words of Isaiah? And who would despise the authority of laws and of public right, who knows that all judgement is the Lord's, and hears the Church praying, by the command or prompting of the Holy Spirit: "God, give your judgements to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, that he may judge your people in righteousness and your afflicted in judgement"? This consideration befits princes above all, and is most necessary for them. For just as it wins them true authority, so in the dangers that hang over them in great number and of the gravest kind, it most effectively consoles them; and at the same time it keeps them in their duty, lest, drunk with a blind confidence in their power, they indulge their wicked desires, or allow themselves to be carried away by the unbridled lust of their passions, while they wish to show what they can do. Let them therefore remember that the authority with which God has armed them will be safe and stable for them only if they perform their office diligently and honour him with their whole heart. Let them therefore often sing to themselves what the Holy Spirit speaks to them in the Scriptures. Among these there is one especially remarkable passage, which in the second Psalm is spoken to the open enemies of Jesus Christ, but is spoken in such a way that it simultaneously applies to all those who hold power among the Christian people. "Be wise," he says, "O kings; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish from the way; soon his wrath will burn. Blessed are all who put their trust in him." Few words, but more than golden or jewelled, and worthy to be inscribed on the gates, the crossroads, the forum, the courts, the palaces and bedchambers of all princes, and above all on their hearts. The divine Psalmist does not bid them, having cast aside the sceptre and laid down the insignia of their kingdom, to live a private life (which the Anabaptists today, a fanatical and seditious kind of men, dare to demand, as if no one could at once bear the magistracy and act as a Christian), but he bids them be intelligent and truly wise. For since they are in the people as the head is in the body, in which the eyes watch over the whole body, the ears hear for all the members, the brain together for all remembers, thinks, reasons and is wise, and finally the mouth passes on the food received to the stomach, so that after digestion the nourishment is distributed to all parts of the body, so princes ought to render these same services to the whole commonwealth and to each of those who act in it. They must therefore first foresee dangers, first hear the complaints of the afflicted, remember them, and take counsel and think upon both the public safety of the whole people and the private safety of each citizen. This is a work of great labour, and one that, if seriously considered, will easily be able to rouse sluggish minds, drive far away idle leisure, and restrain the pursuit of forbidden pleasures. Plutarch is the authority that among the Persian kings, by ancient custom, there was a chamberlain who, entering the royal bedchamber at daybreak, would cry out: "Rise, O King, and attend to the business of the day, to which the will of Mithromazes has made you a labourer." [ἀνάστα ὦ βασιλεῦ, καὶ τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἡμέρας, ὧν σε ἐργάτην ἐποίησεν ἡ θέλησις.] That is: "Rise, O King, and take care of the affairs which Mesopromasdes wished you to take care of." In the same place the same author adds: "But in the mind of the learned and prudent prince there is within him one who will always say and command the same thing." For since at every hour there occur things that remind him of the difficulty of his office and of the dangers that accompany it, he will easily see that he needs singular wisdom, and that no place can be given to idleness or to sloth, unless he wishes to bring himself and the people entrusted to his faith into extreme peril. Solomon, observing this well, when he heard that he had been granted by God the opportunity of asking for anything, did not ask for a long life, nor immense treasures of wealth, nor the lives of his enemies, but asked that an understanding and wise heart be given to him, so that he might be able to render justice to the people and guard the public safety. This request so greatly pleased God that he added to the incomparable wisdom with which he endowed him riches and glory at once, by which he surpassed far all the kings of the earth. But because the matter is of such weight that princes should be furnished with true and solid wisdom, David not only bids them be wise, but also earnestly admonishes them to allow themselves to be instructed. "Be instructed," he says, "you judges of the earth." God alone is indeed the author of wisdom, and to him alone belongs right over the hearts and minds of men; but he works through means, among which the first place is owed to his Word. Princes are therefore sent back to the discipline of this Word, and unless they submit themselves to it, they will never truly be wise, nor will they understand what needs to be done. The nations of old also saw how much instruction can accomplish, and therefore Plutarch taught that above all philosophy must be pursued by princes, so that the minds of those should be cared for who, as they must be anxious for many, be wise for many and render justice to many. Indeed, the most powerful kings and illustrious men have often given philosophers as teachers to their sons, and have frequently summoned to themselves those whom they saw to excel others in learning and experience of affairs. Thus we read that Anaxagoras was intimate with Pericles, Plato with Dion, Pythagoras with the chiefs of Italy, and Athenodorus with the emperor Augustus. And Philip of Macedon wished his son Alexander to be educated by Aristotle. Scipio Africanus had Panaetius as his teacher, whose saying is still celebrated today, which princes ought to meditate on continually: that men's lives suffer unforeseen and almost daily dangers; and to guard against them the mind must always be intent, as athletes are. For just as they in the contest protect the head with their hands opposed, as if with a rampart, so the mind of the wise man ought to be raised against the wantonness of injuries and the blows of fortune, lofty and fenced about, lest any sudden assault arise in any matter upon us unprepared and unprotected. But God has also here cared more rightly for the kings of his own people, when he commanded that they always keep the book of his Law with them and exercise themselves in reading it daily. For with the divine will it sets forth also the most effective reasons by which men are moved to think and act rightly. And it is established that those reigned most happily who were faithful interpreters of the Law, and who revered the prophets; but those who would not allow themselves to be admonished or restrained by them were most unhappy. I will not recount the many examples that exist, since one Joash can suffice for us: who, saved by Jehoiada the priest and raised to the kingdom, governed well as long as he used that monitor and counsellor; but afterwards he destroyed both himself and others, when, having shaken off the yoke of divine discipline, he cruelly slew Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, with more than parricidal ingratitude. This therefore is what ought to be most strongly commended to the sons of princes: that from their tender years they learn to obey the Word of God, and not think that discipline may finally be cast off as they advance in age. For young men ought to be accustomed to this yoke, so that they understand that they owe obedience to God even then, when they already hold dominion over many others. And lest they rest in an empty and idle knowledge, what David adds in the third place should always come into their minds: "Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son," etc. For just as in any science contemplation (theoria [θεωρίᾳ]) must be joined to practice (praxis [πράξιν]), since without this there will be no use of it, so that heavenly wisdom and discipline will at last bear useful and salutary fruit only if it reveals itself by deeds and by work. Now the works of kings and princes are very many, and it would be long to enumerate them one by one, nor is it necessary to do so, since David embraces the sum and crown of all in one word, when he bids them serve the Lord. For this is true wisdom, this is the highest dignity and glory of kings, on which all the happiness of kingdoms also depends. Those who find themselves dear to great kings rejoice in their service, and it is thought a glorious thing to hold some more honourable place in the court of a great king. How much greater, then, is the glory of princes themselves, whom God acknowledges as his servants, and whose works he uses in the administration of his kingdom! For those who serve the world, or who willingly subject themselves to the lust of the flesh, are not masters of things, but, as Sophocles said of carnal desire, slaves of the most shameful masters, indeed of savage and raging ones. But to serve the Lord is the true and sweet freedom, since this cannot be done unless we are first set free from sin and from its author, the devil; and this manumission is accompanied by that spontaneous and willing spirit which makes pleasant to us all the labours we ought to undertake in the service of Christ. This indeed, though it is common to all Christians, namely that each should serve God willingly according to the calling of his vocation, pertains nonetheless especially to princes, and extends most widely. For those should not be heard who think that they have discharged their office if they administer justice and faithfully preside over the affairs of this age; for the care of religion belongs to them especially, nor will they deserve to be called faithful servants of God if they neglect that, which alone binds us to him. It is therefore the duty of kings to defend the doctrine of truth, to abolish unlawful worship, to remove superstitions, to propagate the true worship, to restrain the enemies of God, to punish blasphemers, and to stand by the pious and holy worshippers of God, so that they may enjoy the peace and freedom of conscience divinely given. The Donatists indeed once denied that the affairs of the Church and of religion pertain to kings, and in our age the Anabaptists follow their footsteps. But the divine Augustine, in his fiftieth letter to Boniface, answers all of them gravely from the words of this Psalm, writing among other things thus: "How do kings serve the Lord in fear, unless by a religious severity they forbid and punish those things that are done against the commands of the Lord? For a king serves in one way because he is a man, and in another because he is also a king. Because he is a man, he serves by living faithfully; but because he is also a king, he serves by enacting with fitting vigour laws that command what is just and forbid what is contrary." And he confirms this from the examples of Hezekiah, Josiah, the king of the Ninevites, Nebuchadnezzar finally, and Darius. There is therefore no reason why Christian princes should be moved by the clamours of those fanatics, or think that they are putting a sickle into another's harvest if they decree anything about religion from the Word of God. For this care belongs properly to them, nor can they render any other duty more pleasing or agreeable to God. And it is worth most careful observation here that the Holy Spirit joins two affections of the mind that are most opposed to each other. For he bids kings serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in trembling. But how can someone at once rejoice and fear, at once exult and tremble? Yet princes who are truly Christians feel that these agree well together. For that service is not of such a kind as to cause trouble and labour to the mind or conscience, but it is joined with joy, with exultation, with triumphant delight. They rejoice, because they know that they are servants of God, than which no dignity can come to a man greater. They exult, because they know that their works are pleasing to the Lord, and they expect a recompense from him. Within their own hearts they also leap for joy and shout, because they feel that he whom they serve is now present with them, now protecting them, and now guiding their counsels, words and deeds. And why should not someone who feels within himself the image of God governing all things, set before the whole world, and whose face is serene (as Solomon says) is life, and whose favour is like a cloud of late rain, rejoice and exult with his whole heart? Certainly the consideration of these things cannot fail to rouse kings to discharge their function with a cheerful and exultant spirit, and to render the obedience owed to God. But those same men fear and tremble at once, whenever they weigh against their own weakness and the natural frailty which they share with other men, the difficulty of their office, the excellence of their dignity, and the immense price of the gifts of God. For then that saying of the Apostle comes to their aid, that they carry this most precious treasure in earthen or clay vessels, the loss of which is as great as it is almost irrecoverable. They also fear whenever they consider that their errors and offences do not cling to themselves alone, but spread to the whole people and the commonwealth, and indeed to the most innocent of all. Besides, the nature of the common crowd makes them anxious, which, carried away for the most part by a blind passion, tries to shake off just commands, thinks laws intolerable, repays faithful counsellors with the worst thanks, and, though they resist in vain, rushes to its own destruction. Therefore the best princes fear for themselves, lest through ignorance, or negligence, or being deceived by a perverse affection, they decide upon something that shows them to be little faithful to God, or even ungrateful. They also fear for the people, lest they destroy it or allow it to perish, for which they understand that an account must one day be rendered to God. Finally they fear as pious parents fear for their children, whom they see attempting many things foolishly and childishly, many imprudently, and many with present danger attached. For how can a Christian prince be secure amid so many dangers of affairs, whom the fear and reverence of the supreme Deity restrains as a bridle, and whom love of the people and the commonwealth wholly directs and governs? For among the Gentiles of old there were found some who said that it is the mark of a good prince to fear more lest he do any wrong than lest he himself suffer any wrong. And the saying of Plutarch is memorable: "This fear of a prince is both human and truly noble, that he should fear lest those whom he rules be harmed without his knowledge." The same author compares kings to noble dogs that keep watch in the pens, who, as soon as they hear a beast approaching, are anxious not for themselves but for those they guard. A notable example of this fear was once given by that most brave commander of the Thebans, Epaminondas, when, the Thebans having given themselves over to certain festive games and drinking parties, he alone, taking up arms, went round the walls, saying that he was sober and watchful, so that the others might drink and sleep. And this is the point in which a great difference appears between kings and tyrants. For those who are true kings fear for those over whom they have dominion; on the contrary, tyrants fear those same people, and their fear is increased by their increased power, and the more people they rule over, the more they fear.

units.la: S E D vt ad Dauidis verba redeamus, hæc præcipua principum cura esto, vt eum sibi omnium studiorum & laborum finem propositum habeant, quem ille monstrat, quando Filium osculari iubet. Loquitur autem de æterno & vnigena Dei Filio, Iesu Christo, quem Regem regum & Dominum dominantium Scripturæ vocant. Osculantur hunc, qui eum Dominum & Seruatorem suum esse agnoscunt, eundem venerantur, colunt, obseruant, qui denique fide vera & constanti se totos illi subjciunt. Est hoc proprium eorum munus, qui in terris imperant. Quia enim omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra Christo data est, nullum imperium vel legitimum vel iustum fuerit, quàm quod sibi ab illo collatum esse principes intelligunt, quodq; ita gerunt, vt se aliquando illi rationem reddituros esse meminerint. Est autem osculum hoc vt sanctissimum, ita maximorum bonorum mater fœcundissima. Nam communionem spiritus Christi parit, iram Dei restinguit, in via salutis & pacis dirigit, adhæc spe bona plenos vera & æterna beatitudine donat. Quod Dauid intelligens, doctrinam istam epiphonemate lætissimo & dulcissimæ consolationis pleno concludit: Beati omnes qui sperant in eum.
units.tr: BUT to return to David's words: this should be the chief concern of princes, that they keep before them as the goal of all their studies and labours the one he points to when he bids them kiss the Son. He is speaking of the eternal and only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom the Scriptures call the King of kings and Lord of lords. They kiss him who acknowledge him as their Lord and Saviour, who honour, worship and obey him, and who at last submit themselves wholly to him in true and steadfast faith. This is the proper duty of those who rule on earth. For since all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, no government is lawful or just unless princes understand that it has been conferred on them by him, and conduct it in such a way that they remember they will one day give him an account. This kiss is as holy as it is the most fruitful mother of the greatest blessings. For it brings forth fellowship with the Spirit of Christ, quenches the wrath of God, directs us in the way of salvation and peace, and gives those who are full of good hope the true and eternal blessedness. David, understanding this, closes his teaching with a most joyful epiphonema, full of the sweetest consolation: "Blessed are all who put their trust in him."

units.la: Opponit autem dictum hoc omnium, qui de Regum & Principum conditione perperam sentiunt, iniquis iudicijs: ne his moveantur qui suam functionem fideliter obeunt. Nam etsi multi in ipsos ingrati, multi iniusti sint, multi etiam aduersus eos seditiose tumultuentur, non fallet tamen eos, quam in Domino collocatam habent, spes & fiducia, quò minus omnibus periculis & laboribus superiores facti, tandem pace fruantur, & simul potentia atque gloria illustres sint. Pertinent enim ad huius dicti expositionem, quæ in Psalmo septuagesimo secundo de Rege iusto & sancto dicuntur: Ferent montes pacem populo, & colles iustitiam. Iudicabunt pauperes populi, seruabit filios pauperis, & confringet calumniatorem. Timebunt eum dum Sol & Luna lucebunt in omne æuum. Descendet sicut pluuia super defectam herbam, sicut imbres stillantes super terram. Florebit in diebus eius iustus, & multitudo pacis, donec non sit Luna. Dominabitur à mari vsq; ad mare, & à flumine vsque ad terminos terræ. Coram illo procident habitatores deserti, & inimici eius terram lingent. Reges maris & insularum munus afferent, Reges Scheba & Saba honoraria adducent. Et incuruabunt se ei omnes Reges, omnes gentes seruient ei. Et rursus: Erit pugillus frumenti in terra fatus in capite montium, & contremiscet sicut Libanus fructus eius, & germinabunt è ciuitate sicut herba terræ. Erit nomen eius in sæculum, quàm diu fuerit Sol, propagabitur nomen eius: & benedicent se in eo omnes gentes, & beatum dicent eum, &c. Dicuntur hæc quidem magna ex parte de Rege regū, Iesu Christo; at quia in eodem boni principis exemplar absolutissimum proponitur, ad hunc quoque referri debent, quae de Regni eius felicitate, ac beata eorum qui ei subsunt, conditione Spiritus Sanctus pollicetur. Nec est quod de eo aliquis dubitet, quando exempla patrum occurrunt, quae promissionibus istis possunt fidem facere. Inter quae merito primus locus ipsi Davidi datur, cuius Regni initia prorsus talia fuerunt, qualia in Psalmi secundi principio describuntur. Quia autem vere sapuit, & Verbi Dei disciplinam patienter tulit, Domino denique in timore ingenuo, alacri item laetoque animo seruiuit, per omnia discrimina non minus feliciter quam fortiter eluctatus, populo suae fidei credito pacem optatam peperit, posteris autem suis Regnum reliquit tutum atque amplissimis Dei promissionibus confirmatum, quodque per petuum esse poterat, nisi degeneres quidam illud sua impietate labefactauissent. Poterant huius generis multa adduci ex Veteri Testamento, & in Ecclesiastica historia Constantinum Magnum habemus cum Theodosio aliisque similibus, qui cum Dei timentes fuerint, in Regni quoque administratione felicissimi fuerunt. Quibus si eos opponere libeat, qui procul abiecto Dei timore, omnia pro sua libidine facere ausi sunt, in immensum crescceret oratio. Tales enim fere veritatis spiritu Deus inebriat, qui ut libidines vagas & effrenem scelerum omnium licentiam parit: ita hanc consiliorum incertitudo insequitur, quibus seipsos & populum vniuersum implicant. Sed quo feror CHRISTOPHORE, Princeps Illustrissime? Abripuit me profecto doctrinae Davidicae consideratio, ut longius quam instituieram, progressus sim. Veruntamen tua Clementia fretus, spero non iniucundum tibi fore istorum commemorationem, vel potius repetitionem, quae a doctissimis Praeceptoribus, in primis autem a parente tuo Illustrissimo, FRIDERICHO Romani Imperij Septemuiro dignissimo, multoties audiuisse fatscio. Nec me prorsus extra oleas (quod dici solet) cucurrisse arbitror; quando hoc mihi argumentum orationis propositum fuit, ut ostenderem, me nihil a meo officio alienum, vel tuae illustris Clementiae praestantia indignum facere, dum tibi meos in Lucam Euangelistam labores nuncupo. Hic enim totius Scripturae Sacrae, & in primis quidem Euangelicae historiae, finis atque scopus est, ut omnes homines in Deo sperare, eidem seruire, & Filium eius Iesum Christum exosculari, id est, fide vera amplecti discant, sicque in eo vitam atque salutem aeternam consequantur. Quae cum Principibus viris Spiritus Sanctus tam graviter commendet, eorum in primis fuerit, diligentius ea cognoscere, quae ab Ecclesiae ministris in Scripturarum explicationem scribuntur. Quod autem ex multis te potissimum delegi, Illustrissime Princeps CHRISTOPHORE, cui prae aliis Lucam hunc nostrum dedicarem, non vna, neque leues me causae moverunt. Extant Palatinae familiae multa in totam Helvetiorum gentem, maxime autem in Tigurinam Rempublicam beneficia & praeclara merita. Quia enim ex illa progeniti Principes vt iuris & aequi, sic pacis quoque & concordiae semper amantissimi fuerunt, non semel eorum operam sibi vtilem & salutarem experti sunt maiores nostri, quando aut ipsi inter se bellis ciuilibus commissi, aut ab exteris hostibus armis petiti sunt. Inter ea cumprimis memorabile est, quod cum ante annos circiter centum viginti bellum illud Sociale exarsisset, quo nullum inter nostros homines crudelius & maiori animorum contentione gestum est, & quo Tigurini toto decennio grauissime iactati sunt, inter primos fuit Ludovicus, Palatinus Elector, qui de pace inter confoederatos instauranda consilium coepit: & cum plerique alij per legatos agerent, ille neque sumptuum neque laborum magnitudine se abster reri passus est, quin Constantiam vsque cum illustri comitatu veniret, nec inde priusreuerteretur, quam pacis, quae mox secuta est, fundamenta iecisset. Fuit beneficium istud Heluetiæ totî saluberrimum, quæ utrinque exarserat, vt vix aliqua ratio appareret, quæ bello Ciuili finem posset imponere: tam gratum vero fuit maioribus nostris, vt non multo post, cùm FRI-DERICHVS, qui Ludouico fratri in Septemuiratu successerat, à Romano Pon-tifice Pio II. excommunicatus, vicinorum Principum armis peteretur, Tiguri-ni complures duce VValdmanno (cuius virtus postea in bellis Burgundicis elu-xit) in eius auxilium venerint atque præclaram operam nauarint eo prælio, quo ille lætam de Papæ coniuratis victoriam retulit, & tres Imperij principes cœpit. Ita vero tunc nostrorum hominum virtus FRIDERICHO probata fuit, vt quingentos ex illis Carolo Burgundo transmitteret, qui eodem tempore cum Lu-ouico XI. Francorum Rege bellum gerebat. Simile erga nostram gentem stu-dium Philippi Palatini Electoris, Ludouici illius, cuius modo meminimus, filij extitit. Nam cùm Maximilianus Imperator turbulentorum quorundam consilijs persuasus, totius Imperij Germanici vires contra Heluetios excitauisset, ille bel-lo eo quàm maximè feruente, pacis consilia tractare cœpit: quibus etsi nihil tunc efficeretur propter eorum importunitatem, qui optimum Imperatorem ad arma extimulabant, gratissima tamen maioribus nostris fuit Philippi voluntas, & ad-huc in Annalibus nostris magna cum laude prædicatur. Possem his multa alia ad-iicere, quæ Illustrissimi Palatini Comites in totam Germaniam contulerunt be-neficia, quorum pars aliqua ad nos quoque non semel redundauit. Sed sufficiat nobis nunc eorum commemoratio, quæ non obscurè docent, summam iam olim inter Palatinos Principes & nostram gentem animorum coniunctionem fuisse, ideoque me simul & boni ciuis & grati hominis officium facere, dum eam fami-liam colo & obseruo, ex qua tot Heroes, communis patriæ & publicæ pacis vin-dices acerrimi, prodierunt. Quòd si Illustrissimi parentis tui, FRIDERICHI Se-ptemuiri, virtutes & egregia in Ecclesiam Christi merita commemorare velim, dicendi exordium citius, quàm finem inuenero: sed neque ea exponere nunc in-stitui, neque vt id faciam opus est, cùm bonis omnibus notissima sint, & ne ab iis quidem illius pietas atque probitas reprehendi aut negari possit, qui ei pro-pter puriorem fidei & Veritatis professionem minus fauent. Quod autem is merebatur, publicum mei erga ipsius Celsitudinem studij testimonium, ide-o in te CHRISTOPHORE Princeps Illustrissime transferre volui, & hoc officium vtrique non iniucundum fore confido, cùm ille te ardenter ac merito diligat, tibi autem à curis publicis adhuc libero plus otij sit nostra hæc legendi, teque ipsum in iis exercendi, in quorum usu & præxi ille iampridem ita profecit, vt paucos sibi pares habeat. Tuam verò Clementiam rogo Illustrissime Prin-ceps, vt quod pie & magno cum piorum omnium applausu cœpisti, forti & con-stanti animo perficias, & hunc gloriæ immortalis colophonem esse tibi certò persuasum habeas, si quod dixeris re ipsa præstes: id est, vt Christum, à quo nomen tibi indi-tum est, toto animo conceptum vita & moribus referas. Lucam verò nostrum nullo præconio operosiori Clementiæ Tuæ commendo, quia etsi meis Lucubrationibus multum desit, sarcit tamen defectum omnem argu-menti amplitudo & diligentius considerata diuini scriptoris virtus, meis quo-que aliquid lucis afferre poterit. Me autem Tuæ Clementiæ magno tuo meri-to obstrictum putabo, si illas qualecunque meæ erga te obseruantiæ testimo-nium esse patiaris. Deus, Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, te Illustris-sime Princeps, cum pijssimo parente, cum fortissimis fratribus, Ludouico & Ca-simiro, cum toto denique domo Palatina seruet ad sui nominis gloriam, & sua in vobis omnibus dona augeat. Amen. Datæ Tiguro primaria Heluetiorum vrbes
units.tr: But this saying is set against the unjust judgements of all who think wrongly about the condition of kings and princes, so that those who faithfully perform their office may not be moved by them. For although many are ungrateful towards them, many are unjust, and many even rise up against them in sedition, the hope and trust they have placed in the Lord will not fail them. So, raised above all dangers and labours, they will at last enjoy peace and be made illustrious both in power and in glory. To the explanation of this saying belong the things said in Psalm 72 about the righteous and holy king: "The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the hills righteousness. He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and break in pieces the oppressor. They shall fear you as long as the sun and moon endure, throughout all generations. He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass, like showers that water the earth. In his days shall the righteous flourish, and abundance of peace, until the moon be no more. He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Those who dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. All kings shall fall down before him; all nations shall serve him." And again: "There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon, and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth. His name shall endure for ever; his name shall continue as long as the sun; men shall be blessed in him, and all nations shall call him blessed," and so on. These things are said for the most part of the King of kings, Jesus Christ. But since in him the most perfect pattern of a good prince is set forth, they must also be referred to him, namely what the Holy Spirit promises concerning the happiness of his kingdom and the blessed condition of those who are subject to him. Nor need anyone doubt this, when examples of the fathers occur which can give credit to these promises. Among these the first place is rightly given to David himself, whose beginnings as king were altogether such as are described at the beginning of the second Psalm. Because he truly had wisdom, patiently endured the discipline of God's Word, and at last served the Lord with a sincere fear and a ready and joyful heart, struggling through all dangers no less happily than bravely, he won the desired peace for the people entrusted to his faith, and left to his descendants a kingdom made safe and confirmed by the great promises of God, which could have remained perpetual had not certain degenerate kings weakened it by their impiety. Many examples of this kind could be brought from the Old Testament, and in ecclesiastical history we have Constantine the Great, with Theodosius and others like them, who, being God-fearing, were also most fortunate in governing their realm. If it pleased us to set against them those who, having cast off the fear of God, dared to do everything according to their own lust, the speech would grow to an immense length. For God usually deludes such men with a spirit of falsehood, which begets wandering lusts and an unbridled license for every crime; and uncertainty of counsel follows, in which they entangle both themselves and the whole people. But where am I being carried, most illustrious Prince Christopher? Certainly the consideration of David's teaching has carried me off, so that I have gone further than I intended. Nevertheless, trusting in your clemency, I hope it will not be unwelcome to you to hear a recollection, or rather a repetition, of these things, which I know you have heard many times from your most learned teachers, and above all from your most illustrious father, Frederick, most worthy Elector of the Roman Empire. Nor do I think I have run entirely outside the olive grove (as the saying goes), since my purpose in this discourse was to show that I am not acting contrary to my office, nor doing anything unworthy of the excellence of your illustrious clemency, in dedicating to you my labours on the Evangelist Luke. For this is the end and aim of all Holy Scripture, and especially of the Gospel history: that all men may learn to hope in God, to serve him, and to kiss his Son Jesus Christ, that is, to embrace him in true faith, and so obtain life and eternal salvation in him. Since the Holy Spirit commends these things so earnestly to men in princely station, it is especially fitting for them to examine carefully what is written by the ministers of the Church in explanation of the Scriptures. As for why I have chosen you above many others, most illustrious Prince Christopher, to whom I should dedicate this our Luke, I was moved by more than one reason, and not slight ones. The Palatine family has many benefits and distinguished services to the whole Swiss nation, and especially to the Zurich commonwealth. For the princes born of that house have always loved justice and equity, and likewise peace and concord; more than once our forefathers have found their help useful and wholesome, whether when they themselves were set against one another in civil wars or when they were attacked with arms by foreign enemies. Among these, one thing especially is memorable: about one hundred and twenty years ago, when that war between the confederates broke out, which was waged with no more cruelty and greater contention of spirits among our people, and in which the Zurich people were most grievously harassed for a whole decade, the first to take up the work of restoring peace among the confederates was Ludwig, the Palatine Elector. While most others acted through envoys, he did not allow the size of the expense or of the labour to keep him back, but came as far as Constance with a distinguished retinue, and did not return from there until he had laid the foundations of the peace which soon followed. That benefit was most wholesome for the whole of Helvetia, which had been inflamed on every side, so that hardly any means appeared by which an end could be put to civil war. And it was so pleasing to our forefathers that not long after, when Frederick, who had succeeded his brother Ludwig in the electorate, had been excommunicated by the Roman Pontiff Pius II and was attacked by the arms of neighbouring princes, several Zurich men under the leadership of Waldmann (whose courage later shone forth in the Burgundian wars) came to his aid and performed a distinguished service in that battle in which he won a joyful victory over the Pope's conspirators and captured three princes of the Empire. Indeed, the valour of our people was so proved to Frederick at that time that he sent five hundred of them to Charles of Burgundy, who was at the same time waging war with Louis XI, King of the Franks. A similar goodwill towards our nation was shown by Philip, Elector Palatine, the son of that Ludwig whom we have just mentioned. For when the Emperor Maximilian, persuaded by the counsels of certain troublemakers, had roused the full strength of the whole German Empire against the Swiss, Philip, while that war was at its hottest, began to negotiate for peace. Although nothing could be achieved then, on account of the obstinacy of those who goaded the excellent Emperor to arms, Philip's goodwill was nevertheless most welcome to our forefathers, and it is still praised with great honour in our annals. I could add many other benefits which the illustrious Palatine Counts have conferred upon all Germany, some part of which has more than once flowed back upon us as well. But for now it is enough to recall those things which clearly show that there was long ago the greatest union of spirit between the Palatine princes and our nation; and so I perform at once the duty of a good citizen and a grateful man in honouring and revering that family from which so many heroes, the fiercest defenders of the common fatherland and of public peace, have sprung. But if I wished to recount the virtues of your most illustrious father, Frederick the Elector, and his outstanding services to the Church of Christ, I would find an end to my beginning sooner than an end to my praise. Yet I have no intention of setting these things out now, nor is there need to do so, since they are most well known to all good men, and his piety and uprightness cannot be blamed or denied even by those who favour him less because of his purer profession of the faith and of the truth. Since he deserved this, I wished to transfer to you, most illustrious Prince Christopher, this public testimony of my devotion to his Highness, and I trust this duty will be welcome to both of you: to him, because he loves you ardently and deservedly, and to you, because you are still free from public cares and have more leisure for this reading of ours, and for exercising yourself in those things in whose use and practice he has long since advanced so far that he has few equals. I ask your Clemency, most illustrious Prince, to carry through with a brave and steadfast spirit what you have begun piously and with the great applause of all the godly; and be firmly persuaded that this will be the crowning achievement of immortal glory for you, if you make good in deed what you say: that is, that you express in your life and conduct Christ, from whom your name has been given you, conceived in your whole heart. I commend our Luke to your Clemency with no more laborious eulogy, for although my own commentaries lack much, the greatness of the subject and the virtue of the divine writer, more carefully considered, will be able to bring some light to my own work as well. I shall count myself bound to your Clemency by a great debt of gratitude if you allow these labours, however slight, to serve as a testimony of my devotion towards you. May God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, keep you, most illustrious Prince, together with your most godly father, your most valiant brothers Ludwig and Casimir, and with the whole Palatine house, to the glory of his name, and increase his gifts in you all. Amen. Given at Zurich, the chief city of the Swiss.

units.la: IN EVANGELIVM IESV CHRISTI SECVNDVM LVCAM, RODOLPHI GVALTHERI TIGVRINI HOMILIAE. CAPVT I.
units.tr: IN THE GOSPEL OF JESUS CHRIST ACCORDING TO LUKE, HOMILIES BY RUDOLPH GWALTHER OF ZURICH. CHAPTER I.

units.la: HOMILIA I.
units.tr: HOMILY I.

units.la: QVONIAM multi aggressi sunt componere narrationem earum rerum, quarum plena fides nobis facta est, prout tradiderunt nobis, qui à principio spectatores ipsi & ministri fuerunt sermonis: Visum est etiam mihi omnia altè repetita penitus consecuto, ordine de illis ad te scribere praestantissime Theophile, ut agnoscas eorum, quae auditione accepisti, veritatem.
units.tr: Since many have undertaken to draw up a narrative of those matters which have been fully established among us, just as those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning and ministers of the word handed them down to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced everything carefully from the start, to write them down in order for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of those things you have been taught.

units.la: DIVVM Lucam ex septuaginta duorum discipulorum Christi numero fuisse, Epiphanius non uno loco testatur: sed huius sententiae palàm repugnat, quòd ipse historiam rerum à Christo Iesu gestarum se ab apostolis, ceu testibus oculatis & verbi huius ministris, accepisse scribit. Ex Antiochia autem oriundum fuisse unanimi consensu veteres perhibent, & professione Medicum, quo titulo illum Paulus quoque in epistola ad Colossen. exornat. Ubi verò ad Christi fidem conversus fuit (quod non multo tempore post illius ascensionem factum fuisse constat) Paulum prae aliis comitatus est: non quidem privato consilio aut affectu motus, sed ex ecclesiarum consilio, quae ipsum illi peregrinationum periculosissimarum comitem esse voluerunt. In quo officio tanta fide & constantia versatus est, ut post infinitos labores terra marique perpessos captum quoque Romam usque secutus sit, ubi omnibus aliis vel deficientibus turpiter, vel ad sua dilabentibus, solus illi induulse adhaesit. Et quia ei Paulus laudem eximiam tribuit in evangelio, non dubium est, quin in praedicando quoque diligens & assiduus, multos Christo adduxerit, multos item in fide confirmarit. Tandem ex Spiritus sancti suggestione libros duos scripsit: quorum altero Iesu Christi historiam complexus est, quod ideo Evangelium dicitur: alterum de Apostolorum actis, quo ecclesiae & regni Christi progressum ad Neronis tempora deduxit, docens, ut fides & religio Christiana per orbem terrarum propagata sit, quibus augmentis creverit simul atque floruerit inter labores & undiquesurgentia pericula. Et quae praecipua historici laus est, in utroque opere veritati & perspicuitati ita studuit, ut res gestas non tam narrare, quàm suis coloribus depictas omnium oculis proponere videatur: unde apud multos pictoris nomen obtinuit. Qua occasione Satan fabulam commentatus est de Christi & Mariae virginis imaginibus ab illo pictis, quarum nonnullae in hunc usque diem à superstitiosis magna cum religione asseruantur. Fuit autem hoc astutissimum hostis nostri stratagema, quo incautos & superstitiosos decepit, ut circa imagines pictas & sculptas occupati, veram viuamque Iesu Christi imaginem in Evangelio expressam negligerent. Sed quia istorum error totius scripturae consensu & sanctorum omnium exemplis abundè confutatur, in illo refellendo non opus est nunc insistere.
units.tr: That the divine Luke was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, Epiphanius testifies in more than one place. But this opinion is plainly contradicted by the fact that he writes that he received the history of the things done by Christ Jesus from the apostles, as eyewitnesses and ministers of this word. The ancient writers, however, report with one voice that he was a native of Antioch and by profession a physician, a title by which Paul also honours him in his letter to the Colossians. When he was converted to the faith of Christ, which is known to have happened not long after Christ's ascension, he accompanied Paul above others. He did so not moved by any private plan or affection, but by the counsel of the churches, which wished him to be Paul's companion on his most dangerous journeys. In this duty he so persevered in faith and constancy that, after enduring endless labours by land and sea, he followed Paul even when he was taken prisoner to Rome, where, when all the others had either shamefully failed or deserted to their own affairs, he alone clung faithfully to him. And because Paul pays him singular praise in the gospel, there is no doubt that he was also diligent and assiduous in preaching, and that he brought many to Christ and strengthened many in the faith. Finally, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he wrote two books. In one of them he embraced the history of Jesus Christ, and for this reason it is called the Gospel; the other concerns the acts of the apostles, in which he carried forward the progress of the Church and of Christ's kingdom down to the times of Nero, teaching how the faith and religion of Christ were spread throughout the world, and by what increases it grew and flourished amid labours and dangers rising up on every side. And, which is the chief praise of a historian, in both works he so pursued truth and clarity that he seems to set forth the deeds not so much narrated as painted in their own colours before the eyes of all; for this reason he has gained among many the name of painter. On this occasion Satan devised the fable about images of Christ and of the Virgin Mary painted by him, some of which to this day are preserved with great reverence by superstitious people. This was indeed the most cunning stratagem of our enemy, by which he deceived the incautious and superstitious, so that, busy with painted and sculpted images, they would neglect the true and living image of Jesus Christ expressed in the Gospel. But since the error of these people is amply refuted by the consensus of all Scripture and by the examples of all the saints, there is no need to dwell on refuting it now.

units.la: Observari autem debet in his Dei bonitas, qui ut filium suum unigenitum pro nobis tradidit: ita scriptores quoque excitauit, qui quaecunque ille fecit aut passus est, scriptis mandarunt, ut certa nobis esset omnium, quae ad nostram salutem pertinent, cognitio. Estque haec Dei bonitas eò memorabilior, quod libros istos, quibus Christi historia continetur, inter assiduos persecutionum ecclesiae motus & impios immanissimorum tyrannorum conatus in hunc usque diem mirificè conseruauit, & eosdem in omnes fere linguas transferri curauit: tam multis interea clarissimorum scriptorum monumentis amissis aut in perpetuas tenebras demersis, in quorum conseruatione Reges potentissimi omne studium impenderunt. Debet nos consideratio ista ad diligentem illorum lectionem & cognitionem excitare, ne tantum spiritus sancti thesaurum ingrati aspernemur. Soletur praeterea nos ne impiorum minis & machinationibus terreamur, qui hodie Euangelij doctrinam extinctam volunt, & in huius libros ferro atque flamma grassantur. Obseruatu quoque dignissimum est hoc loco Dei consilium, qui filij sui Iesu Christi historiam non ab Apostolis modo, Matthaeo & Ioanne, conscribi voluit, sed his eorundem discipulos, Marcum & Lucam quoque coniunxit. Ita enim cauere voluit, ne quis spiritum sanctum soli Apostolorum collegio alligatum esse putaret: & ne qua esset perfidae collusionis suspicio. Quae etiam mihi causa esse videtur, ob quam non ijsdem verbis Euangelistae vtuntur, & saepe in speciem inter se dissident, cum tamen dissensio plane nulla sit, si res ipsas diligentius & propius inspiciamus. Priusquam vero ad Lucae verba accedamus, de Euangelio quoque aliqua dicenda erunt, quo nomine librum hunc inscriptum esse ante diximus.
units.tr: Now in these matters we ought to observe the goodness of God, who, as he handed over his only-begotten Son for us, so also raised up writers who committed to writing whatever he did or suffered, so that we might have certain knowledge of all things that pertain to our salvation.
