This goodness of God is the more remarkable because, amid the constant movements of persecution against the Church and the impious attempts of most savage tyrants, he has wonderfully preserved these books, in which the history of Christ is contained, down to this day, and has caused them to be translated into almost all languages; meanwhile many monuments of most distinguished writers have been lost or plunged into perpetual darkness, although the most powerful kings devoted every effort to preserving them. This consideration ought to stir us to diligent reading and knowledge of these books, lest we ungratefully despise such a treasure of the Holy Spirit. Let us also take comfort that we should not be terrified by the threats and schemes of the impious, who today want the doctrine of the Gospel extinguished and who rage with sword and fire against its books. It is also most worthy of notice here what counsel God had, who willed that the history of his Son Jesus Christ be written not only by apostles, Matthew and John, but also joined to them Mark and Luke, the disciples of the same men. For he wished to guard against anyone thinking that the Holy Spirit was bound to the college of the apostles alone, and against any suspicion of treacherous collusion. This also seems to me to be the reason why the evangelists do not use the same words, and often seem to disagree with one another, although there is in fact no disagreement at all if we look more carefully and closely at the things themselves. Before we come to Luke's words, something must also be said about the Gospel, by whose name we have said before that this book is entitled.

units.la: Euangelij vox Graeca bonum laetumque nuntium significat, et interdum pro praemio etiam, quod laeta nuntianti dari solet, accipitur. At cum nuntiu pro rerum diuersitate multa & varia sint, hic rem de qua agitur ante omnia inspicere oportet, vt ex ea veram Euangelij definitionem colligamus: quod facilius & certius fiet, si ipsos Apostolos de toto hoc negotio audiamus loquentes. Ioannes in epistolae suae Catholicae exordio testimonium dicit de Christo, quem ipsi coram viderint, audierint atque contrectarint. Paulus sermonem reconciliationis & gratiae appellare consueuit. Et idem cum ad Romanos dixisset, se segregatum esse ad Euangelium Dei, mox subiecit: Quod is promiserat per Prophetas suos in scripturis sanctis de Filio suo, qui genitus fuit ex semine Dauid secundum carnem, qui declaratus est Filius Dei cum potentia secundum spiritum sanctificationis, ex eo quod resurrexit ex mortuis. Dicitur praeterea Euangelium regni Dei aut caelorum. Est ergo Euangelium testimonium gratiae Dei, nobis exhibitae in Iesu Christo, vero & aeterno Dei filio, qui vt olim Deus promiserat & futurum praedixerant Prophetae, homo factus, suae mortis & resurrectionis virtute atque merito nos ex peccati & diaboli seruitio mortifero redemit, & patri suo reconciliatos eidem per fidei obedientiam consecrauit, vt is in nobis regnum obtineat, nosque cum eodem in caelis aeternum regnemus. Est definitio haec plena, & omnia comprehendit, quae ad Euangelij cognitionem pertinent.
units.tr: The Greek word euangelion means good and joyful news, and sometimes it is also taken for the reward that is usually given to one who brings glad tidings. But since the kinds of news differ greatly, here we must first look at the matter in question, so that from it we may gather a true definition of the Gospel; this will be done more easily and more surely if we hear the apostles themselves speaking about this whole business. John, at the beginning of his Catholic epistle, bears witness to Christ, whom they had seen with their own eyes, heard, and handled. Paul is accustomed to call it the word of reconciliation and grace. And when he had said to the Romans that he had been set apart for the Gospel of God, he immediately added: which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of holiness, by his resurrection from the dead. Moreover, it is also called the Gospel of the kingdom of God or of heaven. The Gospel, therefore, is the testimony of the grace of God, given to us in Jesus Christ, the true and eternal Son of God, who, as God had long ago promised and the prophets had foretold that he would come, was made man, and by the power and merit of his death and resurrection redeemed us from the deadly bondage of sin and the devil, and reconciled us to his Father and consecrated us to him through obedient faith, so that he may hold his kingdom in us and that we may reign with him eternally in heaven. This definition is full and comprehends everything that pertains to the knowledge of the Gospel.

units.la: In his autem singulari diligentia obseruari meretur, quod testimonium est gratiae & reconciliationis cum Deo. Id enim bifariam facit ad Euangelij commendationem. Primo doctrinam hanc certam & fide dignam esse docet. Vulgo enim ijs credi solet, quae testimonijs idoneis confirmantur: imo leges tam diuinae quam humanae credere iubent testibus, qui legitime producuntur. In ore duorum aut trium testium (inquit Moses) stabit omne verbum. Deut. 19. Quanto magis igitur credendum est testibus Dei, quos hic verbo simul suo & miraculorum virtute instructos emisit, vt de rebus per Filium gestis testimonium ferant? Qui deniq, quod verbis & signis testati sunt etiam sanguine suo obsignarunt? Etenim quicunque his fidem adhibere dedignantur, ij non in Apostolos modo, sed in ipsum Deum contumeliosi sunt, quem mendacij insimulant, & impostorem fingunt, qui causam regni sui falsis testimonijs stabilire voluerit. Id vero non nos primi dicimus, sed dicti huius authorem habemus Ioannem, dilectum illum Christi discipulum, qui in epistola sua Capit. 5. sic scribit: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem fecit eum, &c. Est ergo peccatum hoc atrocius, quam vt huic describendo verba vlla sufficiant: at idem (proh dolor) vulgare nimis est, & vtinam non multa alia accederent, quae illud grauius & atrocius reddunt. Quam multos enim est inuenire, qui non contenti Euangelium falsi accusasse, illud insuper haereticum, seditiosum & bonis moribus inimicum esse clamant? Quod vnum nos de malis huius seculi admonere poterat, quibus infelix hic mundus grauissime premitur. Quid enim aliud faceret Deus, quando nos illum tam atrocibus iniurijs afficere non cessamus? Deinde fructum quoque Euangelij nobis denotat spiritus sanctus, quando testimonium gratiae & reconciliationis cum Deo dicit. Ergo nos de gratia Dei certos reddit, & animos scelerum conscientia miserè fluctuantes placat atque serenat. Est hoc inter praesentis vitae bona omnium praestantissimum, sine quo inutiles sunt opum thesauri, honores, voluptatum illecebræ, & quæcunque alia sunt huius generis: sicuti in ijs est videre, qui euangelicarum consolationum ignari vel circa superstitiosos cultus fatigantur, vel ad desperationem inclinant. Euangelium ergo audiant, qui salutis suæ consulcum volunt. Qui vero hoc persequuntur, ij & propriæ & publicæ salutis hostes sunt.
units.tr: Now in these things we ought to observe with special care that it is a testimony of grace and of reconciliation with God. For this serves in two ways to commend the Gospel. First, it teaches that this doctrine is certain and worthy of belief. For things are commonly believed when they are confirmed by competent testimonies; indeed, both divine and human laws order that witnesses who are duly produced be believed. "By the mouth of two or three witnesses," says Moses, "shall every word stand." (Deut. 19.) How much more, then, ought we to believe the witnesses of God, whom he has sent forth, equipped with his word and the power of miracles, to bear witness to the things done by the Son? And finally, what they attested by word and sign they also sealed with their blood. For whoever disdains to give faith to these men insults not only the apostles but God himself, whom they accuse of lying and whom they make out to be an impostor, who would seek to establish the cause of his kingdom by false testimonies. We do not say this first; we have the author of the saying in John, that beloved disciple of Christ, who in his epistle, chap. 5, writes thus: "He who does not believe God has made him a liar," etc. This sin is therefore too monstrous for any words to describe it adequately; yet (alas!) it is only too common, and I wish that many other things did not add to it, making it more grievous and monstrous. For how many are there who, not content with having accused the Gospel of falsehood, also loudly declare it heretical, seditious, and hostile to good morals? This alone might warn us of the evils of this age, by which this unhappy world is most heavily oppressed. For what else would God do, when we do not cease to load him with such outrageous wrongs? Next, the Holy Spirit also points out to us the fruit of the Gospel, when he speaks of it as a testimony of grace and of reconciliation with God. It therefore makes us certain of the grace of God, and calms and quiets minds that are wretchedly tossed by consciousness of sins. This is the most excellent of all the goods of the present life, without which the treasures of wealth, honours, and the allurements of pleasures, and whatever else is of that kind, are useless; as may be seen in those who, ignorant of the consolations of the Gospel, are either worn out by superstitious cults or inclined to despair. Let those, then, who wish to take care of their salvation hear the Gospel. But those who persecute it are enemies both of their own salvation and of the public good.

units.la: Porrò partes quoq; Euangelij nouisse oportet, vt quomodo prædicari debeat intelligamus. Vbi obseruabis quod in definitione de Christo dictum est: Quòd vt olim Deus promiserat, & futurum prædixerant Prophetæ, homo factus, suæ mortis & resurrectionis virtute atque merito nos expectati & diaboli seruitio mortifero redemit, et patri suo reconciliatos eidem per fidei obedientiam consecrauit. Itaq; euangelicæ prædicationis prima pars est ipsa historia de Christo Iesu, qua quid ille propter nos fecerit narratur. Quia sine horum cognitione illum pro redemptore & seruatore nostro nunquam agnoscemus. Ideò historiæ illius scriptores κατ' ἐξοχὴν Euangelistæ dicuntur. At quia historia vsus nullus est, nisi fructum quoque eius teneamus, secundus in Euangelij prædicatione locus illi tribui debet, qui in pœnitentia et remissione peccatorum consistit, ex quibus universa nostræ salutis ratio dependet. Et has quidem prædicationis illius partes ipse Christus nobis constituit, quando ex mortuis resuscitatus discipulis dicebat: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati & resurgere à mortuis tertio die, & prædicari in eius nomine resipiscentiam et remissionem peccatorum apud omnes gentes. Et eundem etiam Apostoli testantur Dei dextera exaltum esse principem & seruatorem ad dandam resipiscentiam Israeli & remissionem peccatorum. Quo loco admonemur, qui nam Euangelium vere & recte prædicent, & quibus inter docendum fides haberi debeat? Ijs nimirum, qui primò quidè historiam omnē de Iesu Christo fideliter proponunt, deinde vero omnes eius partes ad hæc capita reuocant: Vt demonstrent, omnes homines peccatores et ideo morte dignos esse, qui & pœnitentia & gratuita peccatorum remissione opus habeant: vtrunq; vero in vno et solo Iesu Christo haberi docent: qui & peccata nostra mortis suæ merito expiauit, & mortem resurrectione vicit, & in se credentes ex verbi sui semine spiritus virtute regenerat, vt noui homines fiant, & toti Deo patri suo consecrentur. Hoc verum Euangelium est, quod in omnes gentes Christus prædicari iussit: & hæc vnica atque vetustissima redemptionis nostræ ratio est, in qua sancti patres omnes iam inde ab origine rerum omnem salutis suæ fiduciam collocarunt. Falsi ergo doctores sunt, qui hominis dignitatem & liberi arbitrij vires extollunt, qui peccatis blandiuntur, aut eorundem remissionem alibi quam in vno Iesu Christo commonstrant. Vbi videt quid de toto Papatu iudices, in quo maxima sermonum ecclesiasticorum pars ex fabulosis Sanctorum legendis (vt ipsorum verbo vtar) et ineptis decurtati Euangelij fragmentorum postillis constat: doctrina vero omnis ad operum nostrorum merita remittit, et salutem in frigidissimis ceremonijs ostendit, quæ nulla alia quam humanarum traditionum authoritate confirmantur.
units.tr: Moreover, we must also know the parts of the Gospel, so that we understand how it ought to be preached. Here you will observe what was said in the definition of Christ: that, as God had promised long ago and the prophets had foretold, he was made man, and by the power and merit of his death and resurrection redeemed us, who were lost and enslaved to the deadly service of the devil, and by the obedience of faith consecrated us, reconciled, to his Father. Therefore the first part of evangelical preaching is the very history of Christ Jesus, which narrates what he did for us. For without knowing these things we will never acknowledge him as our redeemer and saviour. For this reason the writers of that history are called, preeminently, Evangelists [κατ' ἐξοχὴν Euangelistae]. But since history is of no use unless we also hold its fruit, the second place in the preaching of the Gospel ought to be given to that which consists in repentance and remission of sins, on which the whole reasoning of our salvation depends. Christ himself set out these parts of preaching for us, when, raised from the dead, he said to his disciples: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations." The apostles likewise testify that God's right hand has exalted him as prince and saviour, to give repentance to Israel and remission of sins. At this point we are reminded who truly and rightly preach the Gospel, and whom one should believe when teaching: namely, those who first faithfully set forth the whole history of Jesus Christ, and then refer all its parts to these heads, so as to show that all men are sinners and therefore deserve death, and that they need both repentance and the free remission of sins; and who teach that both are to be had in the one and only Jesus Christ, who by the merit of his death expiated our sins, by his resurrection overcame death, and regenerates by the power of the Spirit, from the seed of his word, those who believe in him, so that they become new men and are wholly consecrated to God his Father. This is the true Gospel, which Christ commanded to be preached to all nations; and this is the one and most ancient ground of our redemption, in which all the holy fathers from the beginning of things placed all their confidence of salvation. Therefore they are false teachers who extol the dignity of man and the powers of free will, who flatter sins, or who show the remission of them anywhere other than in the one Jesus Christ. Here you see what you may judge of the whole Papacy, in which the greater part of ecclesiastical sermons consists of fabulous legends of the saints (to use their own word) and of postils made from fragments of a mangled Gospel; and whose teaching all refers to the merits of our works, and shows salvation in the coldest ceremonies, which are confirmed by no other authority than that of human traditions.

units.la: Reliquat postrema definitionis pars de fine Euangelij, qui est, vt Deus in nobis regnum obtineat, nosq; cum eodem in cælis æternum regnemus. Nisi enim in nobis suo spiritu Deus regnet, tunc neq; filei obedientia consistere poterit, neq; nos illi consecrabimur. Ideo vt regnum Dei adueniat, ex Christi mandato oramus. Et idem inter docendum clamabat, regnum Dei iam appropinquauisse. Quia enim ad destruendum diaboli regnum ille venerat, eadem opera simul Dei regnum in nobis instaurat. Quod vt in hac vita inchoatur, dum illi locum damus: ita continuo progressu confirmatur quoad in fide perseueramus, perficitur autè, quando animæ corporis huius vinculis soluta ad Christum colliguntur, qui olim corpora quoque in vitam resticuta ad se recipiet. Sunt hæc nobis ideo obseruanda, vt discamus, quales eos esse oporteat, qui Euangelium cum fructu audire volunt. Sciant illi ante omnia, carnis mortificatione opus esse, vt ad regni cælestis possessionem regenerentur. Inde vero Euangelium attente audiant, & ab illo se nullis vel mundi huius illecebris, vel vitæ & fortunarum periculis auocari patiantur. Cur enim vel hæc metuant, vel illis capiantur, qui mundum hunc & eius formam omnem transfire, et huius seculi afflictiones momentaneas esse nouerunt? Accedant hisce studijs preces, in quibus veros Dei cultores semper assiduos & diligentes fuisse constat.
units.tr: The last part of the definition remains, concerning the end of the Gospel, which is that God may obtain his kingdom in us, and that we may reign with him for ever in heaven. For unless God reigns in us by his Spirit, then obedience of faith cannot stand, nor shall we be consecrated to him. Therefore we pray, by Christ's command, that the kingdom of God may come. And he himself, while teaching, cried out that the kingdom of God was now at hand. For since he came to destroy the kingdom of the devil, at the same time he restores God's kingdom in us. This is begun in this life while we give it place; it is confirmed by continual progress as long as we persevere in faith; but it is perfected when souls, loosed from the bonds of this body, are gathered to Christ, who will also receive into himself the bodies, raised again to life. These things must be noted by us, so that we learn what sort of people ought to hear the Gospel with profit. Above all, let them know that the mortification of the flesh is needful, so that they may be regenerated to possess the heavenly kingdom. Then let them listen attentively to the Gospel, and not allow themselves to be drawn away from it by any allurements of this world, or by dangers to life and fortune. For why should they fear these things, or be caught by those who know that this world and all its form pass away, and that the afflictions of this age are momentary? Let prayers accompany these studies, in which it is agreed that the true worshippers of God have always been constant and diligent.

units.la: His præmissis ad Lucam nostrum accedamus, qui operi suo præfationem præfigit, quatria o-mnino agit. Primò causam indicat, quæ ipsum ad scribendum impulit. Deinde quid scripturus sit doceet: postremò finem sui scripti ostendit. Ad primum pertinet, quod multos huic laborem aggressos esse ait, vt rerum Christi narrationem contexerent. Poterat hoc prima fronte sic accipi, quasi ab exemplo argumentum petat, vt demonstrari et sibi idem licere, quod multi alij hucusque fecerint. At si argumentum hoc valeret, nullus esset scribendi finis, & quo plures historiam Euangelij conscripsissent, eò plures ad scribendum fuissent excitati. Potius ergo eos perstringit, qui opus istud aggressi minus præstiterant quàm debebant, & inde colligit, necessarium omnino esse, vt ipse singula verius & plenius perscribat. Erant enim iam tunc, qui sua figmenta obtrudebant ecclesijs, & falsis narrationibus imperitos & rudes circumducebant: quales fuere, qui Euangelium secundum Nazaræos, Matthiam, Nicodemum, Bartholomæum & Iacobum finxerunt. Epiphanius certè Cerinthum & Merinthum à Luca perstringi scribit, & idem Euangelij cuiusdam Ægyptij meminit, quo Sabelliani hæretici multos deceperunt. Est enim mirifica admodum & indefessa diaboli in obscuranda veritate industria & astutia. Itaque viventibus adhuc apostolis hoc ausus est, & quidem in eo argumento, cuius veritas multis notissima erat, & testes habebat oculatos. Nemini ergo mirum & insolens videri debet, si posteris temporibus sub patrum orthodoxorum titulis ecclesiæ libellos obtrusit putidissimos & à religione Christiana prorsus alienos: quorum authores fere fuerunt Monachi non minus indocti quàm impudentes. Excitent autem nos exempla vetera, vt vigilemus, & in probandis spiritibus diligenti examine utamur, secundum illud Pauli: Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. 1. Thess. 5.
units.tr: With these things premised, let us come to our Luke, who prefixes a preface to his work, which in all handles four things. First he indicates the cause that moved him to write. Then he teaches what he is about to write. Last, he shows the end of his writing. As to the first, he says that many have undertaken this labour, to compile a narrative of the things of Christ. At first sight this could be taken as if he were drawing his argument from example, to show that he too may do what many others have done hitherto. But if this argument held, there would be no end to writing, and the more who had written a history of the Gospel, the more would have been stirred up to write. Rather, he censures those who undertook that work and accomplished less than they ought, and from this he concludes that it is entirely necessary for him to write each thing more truly and fully. For even then there were those who foisted their own fictions upon the churches and led the untrained and ignorant about with false narratives; such were those who forged the Gospel according to the Nazarenes, and the gospels of Matthias, Nicodemus, Bartholomew and James. Epiphanius indeed writes that Cerinthus and Merinthus were censured by Luke, and he also mentions a certain Egyptian gospel, by which the heretical Sabellians deceived many. For the devil's industry and cunning in obscuring the truth is truly remarkable and tireless. So Luke dared this while the apostles were still living, and indeed on a subject whose truth was very well known to many and which had eyewitnesses. Therefore no one should think it strange or unusual if in later times, under the titles of orthodox fathers, books utterly foul and wholly alien to the Christian religion have been thrust upon the Church, whose authors were mostly monks no less ignorant than shameless. Yet let the old examples rouse us to be watchful, and to use diligent scrutiny in testing spirits, according to that saying of Paul: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." 1 Thess. 5.

units.la: Sed proponit Lucas, quid ipse scribere decreverit: Narrationem nimirum rerum à Christo gestarum certam ex ordine, & quidem altius repetito principio. Et ne illa quoq; suspecta esset, ea modo se scripturum dicit, quæ ex iis habeat, qui sermonis illius testes oculati & ministri fuerunt. Quod de solis Apostolis dici, non est dubium. Hinc verò colligitur, Lucam nihil eorum omisisse, quæ nobis ad Christi & salutis æternæ cognitionem necessaria sunt. Præmisit enim quæcunque de præcursore Iesu Christi, Ioanne Baptista, dicenda erant, vt maior esset testimonij, quod is de Christo tulit, authoritas. Inde ab ipsa Christi conceptione exorsus, illum Deum verum et æternum, simulq; postea ex virgine hominem factum esse docet. Doctrinam item & facta eius miraculosa prolixè recenset. Mortis verò & resurrectionis eius historiam ad ascensionem usque in cælos deducit. Quòd autem nonnulla præter hæc alij tradiderunt, id Lucæ dignitati & fidei nihil derogat, sed potius eius narrationem confirmat, quando eiusdem argumenti sunt omnia, & ad eundem scopum diriguntur. Deinde historiam hanc fide dignissimam esse, verba ista indicant, eò quòd ab ipsis Apostolis sit tradita. Ne quis tamen ex eo colligat, Euangelium suam fidem & authoritatem ab hominibus accepisse, Apostolos ab officio describit, ostendens, eos non in hominum vulgarium ordine censendos esse, cùm ab ipso Christo ad hoc delecti fuerint, vt rerum ab ipso gestarum oculati testes, & sermonis euangelici ministri essent. Quapropter Euangelio sua authoritas ex seipso constat, quia verum Dei æterni verbum est: neque audiendi sunt, qui illud Ecclesiæ calculo confirmari oportere contendunt. Id enim perinde est, ac si populus bonis & iustis Legibus parere recusef, eò quòd ipse suo testimonio illas nondum approbarit. Olim quidem adulterina & supposititia euangelia à veris discerni oportuit per Apostolos & viros apostolicos. At quia hoc illi iam pridem fecerunt agunt quicunque hoc ipsum adhuc hodie fieri oportere contendunt ab illis, qui ecclesiæ titulum & potestatem omnem sibi solis vendicant. Qui nisi ex Euangelij verbo renascantur, & huic se totos per fidei obedientiam subijciant, indigni sunt, qui vel postrema & vilissima ecclesiæ membra dicantur. Seruit præterea locus hic ijs quoque confutandis, qui traditiones, nescio quas, Apostolorum nomine venditant, quas multùm ab ea doctrina dissentire constat, quam illi literis mandauerunt, &c.
units.tr: But Luke sets out what he himself has resolved to write: a narrative of the things done by Christ, certain and in order, and indeed traced back from the beginning. And so that this too might not be suspect, he says he will write only those things which he has from those who were eyewitnesses and ministers of that word. There is no doubt that this is to be said of the apostles alone. From this, however, it is gathered that Luke omitted nothing of those things which are necessary for us to know of Christ and of eternal salvation. For he set out first everything that had to be said about the forerunner of Jesus Christ, John the Baptist, so that the testimony which he bore to Christ might have greater authority. Beginning from the very conception of Christ, he teaches that he was true and eternal God, and at the same time, afterwards, made man of a virgin. He also recounts at length his teaching and his miraculous deeds. But the history of his death and resurrection he carries down to his ascension into heaven. Now, that some things were related by others besides these detracts nothing from Luke's dignity or faith, but rather confirms his narrative, since all of them concern the same subject and are directed to the same goal. Furthermore, that this history is most worthy of belief, these words indicate, because it was handed down by the apostles themselves. Lest anyone, however, gather from this that the Gospel received its faith and authority from men, he describes the apostles by their office, showing that they are not to be counted in the order of ordinary men, since they were chosen by Christ himself for this purpose, to be eyewitnesses of the things done by him and ministers of the evangelical word. Wherefore the Gospel's authority rests on itself, because it is the true word of the eternal God; nor are those to be listened to who contend that it must be confirmed by the vote of the Church. For that is just as if a people should refuse to obey good and just laws because the people itself has not yet approved them by its testimony. Formerly, indeed, adulterated and spurious gospels had to be distinguished from true ones by the apostles and apostolic men. But since they did this long ago, those do it again who contend that this must still be done today by those who claim for themselves alone the title of Church and all its power. Unless they are born again by the word of the Gospel and submit themselves wholly to it by the obedience of faith, they are unworthy even to be called the lowest and most contemptible members of the Church. Moreover, this passage also serves to refute those who peddle certain traditions, I know not what, under the name of the apostles, which are well known to differ greatly from that doctrine which they committed to writing, etc.

units.la: Postremùm, finem & scopum instituti sui Lucas indicat: Visum est (inquiens) ad te scribere præstantissime Theophile, vt agnoscas eorum, quæ auditione accepisti, veritatem. Fuit autem Theophilus hic (vt ex titulo apparet) vir illustris & in publica authoritate constitutus, quales omnibus seculis Deus excitauit, vt suæ ecclesiæ tutores essent & nutritij. Et quidem magnæ fidei & intrepidæ constantiæ virum fuisse oportet, qui hoc passus sit, vt ipsius nomini publicè inscriberentur libri de fide Christiana, quam Romani Imperatores hostiliter oppugnabant. At hodie multos ministrorum Euangelij pudet, & iniuriam sibi fieri putant, si ipsis dedicentur libri, quibus fidei & religionis mysteria exponuntur. Quoad vero Lucæ scriptum, nō obstat dedicatio ista, quò minus illo omnes ad suam institutionem vtantur, qui Dei amantes & salutis studiosi videri volunt. Et hic quidem totius scripturæ scopus & vsus est, vt in vera Iesu Christi cognitione instituamur, & per fidem in hunc vitam consequamur æternam. In primis tamen hic obseruari debet, quòd Theophilo ista scribit, quem in Christi doctrina iam ante informatum & institutum esse non ignorabat. Habet enim fides sua incrementa, & prodest nos de ijs sæpius admoneri & plenius instrui, quorum aliquam cognitionem degustauimus. Itaq; nulla doctrina & admonitio superuacanea est. Nam tentatur sub inde fides nostra, et caro frequenter nos officij immemores reddit, vt ad priora eius studia aut etiam illis deteriora relabamur. Exempla eius cum priuata tum publica passim occurrunt, & multa huius generis in nobisipsis experimur. Sunt ergo ingrati nimis & simul infelicissimi mortalium, qui quasi ipsi sibi sufficiant, doceri & admoneri nolunt. Nostrum est Dei bonitatem agnoscere, qui tanta suo rum seruorum industria nos quotidie instituere dignatur. Studeamus autem indies proficere in cognitione Iesu Christi, vt hac confirmati vitæ huius certamina vincamus, & tandem regni cælestis cum illo simus hæredes: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, Luke sets out the purpose and aim of his work: "It seemed good to me also," he says, "to write to you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of those things which you have received by hearing." This Theophilus was (as the title shows) an illustrious man holding public authority, the kind of men whom God raised up in every age to be guardians and nurturers of his Church. He must have been a man of great faith and fearless constancy to allow books on the Christian faith, which the Roman emperors were attacking with hostility, to be publicly dedicated to his name. Today, however, many ministers of the Gospel are ashamed of this, and think they are being wronged if books expounding the mysteries of faith and religion are dedicated to them. As for Luke's writing, this dedication does not prevent anyone who wishes to be seen as a lover of God and eager for salvation from using it for his own instruction. Indeed, this is the whole aim and use of Scripture: that we be instructed in the true knowledge of Jesus Christ and, through faith, obtain eternal life. Yet here it must above all be noted that he writes these things to Theophilus, whom he knew had already been informed and instructed in the doctrine of Christ. For faith has its increases, and it profits us to be admonished about these things more often and to be taught more fully in those matters of which we have tasted some knowledge. Therefore no teaching or admonition is superfluous. For our faith is continually tested, and our flesh often makes us forgetful of our duty, so that we slip back into our earlier pursuits or even into worse ones. Examples of this occur everywhere, both private and public, and we experience many instances of this kind in ourselves. Those therefore are exceedingly ungrateful and at the same time the most unhappy of mortals, who, as if they were sufficient for themselves, are unwilling to be taught and admonished. It is our duty to acknowledge the goodness of God, who daily deigns to instruct us by the diligence of his servants so great. Let us strive, then, to make daily progress in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, so that, strengthened by it, we may overcome the struggles of this life, and at last be heirs with him of the heavenly kingdom: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILY II.

units.la: Fuit isti diebus Herodis illius regis Iudææ Sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias, ex vice Abia: vxor autem illius erat ex filiabus Aaron, & nomen eius Elizabet. Erant autem iusti ambo in conspectu Dei, incedentes in omnibus mandatis & constitutionibus Domini inculpatè. Nec erat ipsis proles, eò quod esset Elizabet sterilis, & amboprouecti iam essent ætate.
units.tr: In the days of Herod, that king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. And they had no child, because Elisabeth was barren, and both were now advanced in years.

units.la: Diuus Lucas hoc libro historiam Iesu Christi narrare instituit, quæ Euangelium dicitur, quia lætum nostræ redemptionis nuntium & Dei nobiscum reconciliati testimonium continet. Vt autem historia hæc perfectior sit, non ab eius in carnem aduentu ordiri voluit, sed ea quoq; commemorat, quæ hunc proximè præcesserunt. Cùm enim Christus Rex sit potentissimus & gloriosissimus, & vt scriptura loquitur, Rex regum sit & Dominus dominantium, aduentus eius minimè obscurus esse debuit: & ideo à prophetis olim prædictum erat, anteambulonem aut præcursorem illi fore, qui homines de aduentu eius admoneret, & ad illum digne excipiendum præpararet. Ab huius ergo descriptione narrandi initium facit Lucas vt maior sit testimonij eius authoritas, quo ille Christum toti populo commendauit. Itaq; ne quid intermittat, in præsenti de tempore, quo hic natus est, deq; eius parentibus disserit.
units.tr: Saint Luke set out to write a history of Jesus Christ in this book, which is called the Gospel, because it contains the joyful news of our redemption and the testimony that God has been reconciled to us. So that this history might be more complete, he did not wish to begin with the Lord's coming in the flesh, but also recorded the things that immediately preceded it. For since Christ is the most powerful and glorious King, and, as Scripture says, the King of kings and Lord of lords, his coming ought not to have been obscure. Therefore the prophets had foretold long ago that a forerunner or precursor would go before him, to warn men of his coming and to prepare them to receive him worthily. Luke therefore begins his narrative with this man's description, so that the authority of his testimony, by which he commended Christ to the whole people, might be greater. And so, lest he omit anything, he speaks first about the time in which he was born and about his parents.

units.la: A tempore orditur, primùm quidem ad declarandam rei gestæ certitudinem, vt minus suspecta sit narratio. Ita enimferè solent historici, eò quod veritas historiæ vix alio argumento facilius & certius cognoscitur. At simul altius quid & quod maioris momenti est, in hac temporis notatione Lucas spectauit, Prophetarum oracula nimirum, vt Christum eum esse euincat, quem illi venturum esse prædixerunt. Extat enim Iacobi patriarchæ vaticinium, qui promissum illum Schilo, id est, seruatorem siue sospitatorem tunc nasciturum monuit, quando sceptro à Iuda translato, Iudæorum gens alieno imperio pareat. Conuenit huic Isaias, qui germen illud benedictum ex trunco Isai oriturum scribit, ita innuens, proditurum quidem ex Dauidis familia, sed quam prius ex regio fastigio deijci, & ad vilem atq; humillimam conditionem deprimi oporteat, qualis sub Isai olim fuit, quem hominem plebeium & pecuarium fuisse scimus. Quibus addendum est, quòd Messiæ aduentum Daniel in Quartam Monarchiam vsque extendit, quam Romanorum esse constat. Atqui his omnibus conuenit, quod Lucas scribit, ista regnante in Iudæa Herode Rege facta esse. Fuit enim Herodes Antipatri hominis Idumæi filius, qui cùm Iulio Cæsari in bello Ægyptiaco præclaram operam nauauisset, in Romanorum amicitiam sese insinuauit, & ea occasione filium Herodem ad honores & imperium euehere studuit. Qui cùm Iudæa iam pridem à Pompeio deuicta in Romanorum potestatem venisset, ab Antonio primùm Iudææ tetrarcha factus est: postea autem ex Senatus decreto Regis titulum accepit, & medius inter Augustum & Antonium in Capitolium deductus est, ut regnum a sacris solennibus auspicaretur. Inde cum Hierosolymam vi occupasset, multa crudeliter & nefarie fecit, & ut tutius regnaret, Machabaeorum posteros & totam sacerdotalem prosapiam e medio sustulit, Davidicae autem familiae hostis fuit infensissimus: quod ex ea Regem Iudaeis nasciturum audiuisset, qui rebus afflictis salutem afferret. Ergo haec quoque maxima ex parte deleta esset, reliquiae autem parvae admodum ad extremam inopiam redactae (ut in Mariae virginis historia audiemus) sola paupertate et contemptibili sua specie tutae fuerunt. Fuit ergo iam praeforibus tempus illud fatale, quo Messias nasci debuit, cum Ioannis natiuitatem Sacerdoti Zachariae angelus praedixit. Ista autem sic fieri oportuit, ut & Iudaicae gentis confidentia deprimeretur, qua illi gentes reliquas contemnere solebant, & simul omnibus constaret, totum Iesu Christi atque nostrae redemptionis negotium ex nulla hominum dignitate sed mera Dei gratia & misericordia pendere. Adhaec consolationis plenum est, quod olim quoque populum Dei exterorum tyrannide oppressum, & sanctissimos homines sub impiis tyrannis vixisse audimus. Ut enim hoc illis non fuit impedimento, quo minus sub Dei tutela essent, & salute promissa tandem frueretur: ita neque nostrae saluti istud obstabit, siquidem illorum fidem atque constantiam imitemur. Quod vero Christi Iesu negotium, quo de hic agitur, apparet hoc certum, firmum & ab omni fraude vel impostura alienum esse. Ut enim tempus incarnationis & adventus eius cum veteribus prophetijs conuenit: ita locus quoque natalis, parens virgo, opera miraculosa, mors, resurrectio, regni eius inter omnes gentes propagatio ab ijsdem olim praedicta fuerunt, de quibus singulis suo loco plenius dicetur. Nobis autem istorum vsus sit, ut in fide Christi constantes simus & intrepidi, neque nos ab eius confessione vllis sive periculis sive mundi nobis arridentis blanditijs dimoueri patiamur. Ut enim momentanea sunt omnia, quae in hoc seculo habentur, ita sibi ipsi semper constat Christus, & nunquam nos fallet, quae illo nititur aeternae salutis fiducia.
units.tr: He begins with the time, first indeed to establish the certainty of the events, so that the narrative may be less open to suspicion. For historians usually do this, since the truth of a history is scarcely known more easily or more surely by any other evidence. But at the same time, Luke, in this dating of the time, looked to something higher and of greater importance, namely the oracles of the prophets, so as to prove that he is the Christ whom they foretold would come. For there is the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, who declared that Shiloh, that is, the Saviour or Deliverer, would be born at the time when the sceptre had been transferred from Judah and the Jewish nation was subject to foreign rule. Isaiah agrees with this, who writes that the blessed shoot would spring from the stump of Jesse, thereby implying that he would indeed come from the family of David, but that this family must first be cast down from royal dignity and brought to a lowly and humble condition, such as it was under Jesse, who we know was a common man and a shepherd. To these must be added that Daniel extends the coming of the Messiah to the Fourth Monarchy, which is known to be that of the Romans. Now all these prophecies agree with what Luke writes, that these things happened while Herod was reigning as king in Judea. For Herod was the son of Antipater, a man of Idumaean descent, who, having rendered distinguished service to Julius Caesar in the Egyptian war, insinuated himself into the friendship of the Romans, and on that occasion strove to raise his son Herod to honours and power. When Judea, which had been subdued long before by Pompey, had come under Roman power, Herod was first made tetrarch of Judea by Antony; afterwards, by a decree of the Senate, he received the title of king, and was led up to the Capitol between Augustus and Antony, so that his reign might begin with sacred solemnities. Then, having seized Jerusalem by force, he did many cruel and wicked things, and in order to reign more securely, he removed from the midst the descendants of the Maccabees and the whole priestly lineage. He was most bitterly hostile to the family of David, because he had heard that a King would be born of it for the Jews, who would bring salvation to their afflicted affairs. Therefore this family too was almost entirely destroyed, and the very small remnants, reduced to extreme poverty (as we shall hear in the history of the Virgin Mary), were kept safe only by their poverty and their contemptible appearance. So the fateful time, in which the Messiah was to be born, was now at the doors, when an angel foretold to the priest Zacharias the birth of John. Yet these things had to happen in this way, so that the confidence of the Jewish nation, by which they were accustomed to despise the other nations, might be broken down, and at the same time it might be plain to all that the whole work of Jesus Christ and of our redemption depends not on any human dignity but on the pure grace and mercy of God. Moreover, it is full of consolation that we hear that the people of God, too, was once oppressed by the tyranny of foreigners, and that the most holy men lived under impious tyrants. For just as this was no hindrance to them, so that they were not under God's protection and did not at last enjoy the promised salvation, so this will not stand in the way of our salvation, provided we imitate their faith and steadfastness. As for the work of Jesus Christ of which we are speaking here, it is clear that it is certain, firm, and free from all fraud or imposture. For just as the time of his incarnation and coming agrees with the ancient prophecies, so too the place of his birth, the virgin mother, the miraculous works, his death, his resurrection, and the spread of his kingdom among all nations were foretold long ago by the same prophets, and each of these will be discussed more fully in its place. For us, let the use of these things be that we may be steadfast and fearless in the faith of Christ, and not allow ourselves to be turned away from his confession either by any dangers or by the flattering allurements of the world. For all the things that are had in this age are momentary, but Christ is always consistent with himself, and he will never disappoint us, the trust in eternal salvation that rests on him.

units.la: Caeterum ad parentes Ioannis describendos transit Lucas, ne quis obscurum erronem fuisse dicere t. Fuerunt illi Zacharias & Elizabet, vterque ex tribu Leui, & haec quidem ex Aaronis posteris oriunda. Erat autem nobilis omnino & praeclara Leuitica tribus dignitas, eo quod illam Deus sibi ex peculiari gratia delegisset, cui sacrorum & cultus sui curam committeret. Vnde factum est, ut inter hanc & regiam tribum Iuda, ut & inter ipsos Reges & Sacerdotes magna semper coniunctio fuerit. Neque contemni debet generis nobilitas vera, cum hanc inter huius seculi bona non postremum esse constet. Nam etsi ex vno Adamo omnes homines originem ducant, Deus tamen omnibus prope seculis aliquos certo consilio & gratia singulari ad res maiores destinauit, & eosdem donis quoque peculiaribus & indole generosiori instruxit, ut rebus illis gerendis sufficerent. Tales olim fuerunt Abraham, Ioseph, Dauid, & inter Iacobi filios Iudas & Leui. Et inter prophanas quoque gentes nonnullos ad res praeclaras natos fuisse legimus, qui postea familias suas illustribus factis & omni virtutum genere nobilitauerunt. At hic meminisse oportet, inutilem esse prorsus natalium splendorem, nisi posteri maiorum virtutes imitentur. Docent hoc infinita exempla, in quibus fratres germanos aut veterinos multum inter se diuersos fuisse videmus, ut alij quidem Deo probati fuerint, alij vero vitijs immersi, a gratia omni exciderint, & tam seipsos quam gentem suam turpiter dehonestarint. Ex quorum numero Cain & Abelus, Ismael & Isaac, Esauus & Iacob fuerunt. Et inter Aaronis filios, qui inter Leuitas primam dignitatem obtinebant, numerantur Nadab & Abihu, qui cum in officio suo negligentiores essent, igne caelitus immisso conflagrarunt. Et si exteras historias cum ijs, quae quotidie fiunt, probe inspiciamus, patebit, eos qui a maiorum virtute degenerant, non sibi ipsis solum infelices & miseros esse, verumetiam plerunque reipublicae grauissimarum calamitatum esse authores: cuius mali exemplum memorabile in coniuratione Catilinaria Romani scriptores proponunt. In quorum consideratione vtinam hodie multi diligentius versarentur. At plerique, qui nobiles dici volunt, quasi generis nobilitas & maiorum egregie facta sufficiant, de virtute nunquam cogitant. Imo dum nobilitatem in externo splendore, stemmatum ostentatione & immunitate quadam, vel potius impunitate, consistere arbitrantur, nihil non sibi licere putant, & proiecta quaeduis audendi licentia in omne scelus ruunt, neque se Legum vinculis coerceri patiuntur. Neq; inter privatos homines hanc pestis sese continet, sed ad Rempub. quoque serpit, & causa est, ut plerique maiorum victorijs & virtutibus super-biant, interim verò sublata omni morum disciplina ciuitates & terras suas omni scelerum genere dehonestent.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke turns to describe the parents of John, lest anyone should say that he was some obscure fellow. They were Zacharias and Elisabeth, both of the tribe of Levi, and she indeed was descended from the posterity of Aaron. The tribe of Levi was indeed altogether noble and distinguished, because God had chosen it for himself out of special grace, to entrust to it the care of his sacred rites and worship. Hence it came about that between this tribe and the royal tribe of Judah, and between the kings and the priests themselves, there was always a great close bond. Nor should true nobility of birth be despised, since it is agreed that it is not the least among the goods of this age. For although all men derive their origin from the one Adam, God has nevertheless, in almost every age, destined certain people for greater affairs by a settled purpose and singular grace, and has also equipped them with special gifts and a more noble disposition, so that they might be fit to carry out those tasks. Such were Abraham, Joseph, and David of old, and among the sons of Jacob, Judah and Levi. We also read that among the profane nations some were born for distinguished deeds, who afterwards ennobled their families by illustrious actions and every kind of virtue. But here we must remember that the splendour of birth is utterly useless unless the descendants imitate the virtues of their ancestors. Countless examples teach this, in which we see brothers, whether full or half-brothers, very different from one another: some have been approved by God, while others, plunged into vices, have fallen away from all grace and have shamefully disgraced both themselves and their nation. Among those of this sort were Cain and Abel, Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob. And among the sons of Aaron, who held the first dignity among the Levites, are numbered Nadab and Abihu, who, because they were more careless in their office, were consumed by fire sent down from heaven. And if we carefully examine foreign histories along with what happens every day, it will be clear that those who degenerate from the virtue of their ancestors are not only unhappy and wretched for themselves, but very often are also the authors of the most grievous calamities for the commonwealth. The Roman writers set forth a memorable example of this evil in the conspiracy of Catiline. Would that many people today would think more carefully about these matters! But most who wish to be called noble behave as if the nobility of birth and the splendid deeds of their ancestors were enough, and never think about virtue. Indeed, while they suppose that nobility consists in outward show, in the display of pedigrees and a certain immunity, or rather impunity, they think nothing is not allowed to them, and, once they have cast off all restraint, they rush into every crime, and do not allow themselves to be restrained by the bonds of the laws. Nor is this plague confined to private men, but it creeps also into the commonwealth, and the cause is that many take pride in the victories and virtues of their ancestors, while meanwhile, with all discipline of morals removed, they disgrace their cities and lands with every kind of wickedness.

units.la: Atqui nihil huius in Ioannis parentibus, Zachariâ & Elizabeta, Spiritus sanctus notat, sed generis splendori illos probè respondisse docet, dum conditionem, vitam & mores eorum diligen-ter describit. Fuit enim Zacharias non ex Leuitarum otiosorum numero, quales tunc temporis multi erant, sed sacerdos fuit de vice Abia, quam in ordine sacerdotali, per Dauidem constituto, octauam fuisse constat. Qua autem diligentia vices suas obierit, in sequentibus dicetur. Deinde vxorem habuit ex filiabus Aaronis, legitimo connubio sibi coniunctam. Quod non vulgaris pietatis & obedientiae argumentum censeri potest, quando constat, illo tempore iam coepisse tribuum confusionem, & plerosque in coniugijs maiorem libidinis & auaritiae, quàm Legum diuinarum, rationem habuisse. Atqui mirum hoc nonnullis videri poterat, Zachariam & sacerdotem simul & vxoratum fuisse. In Papatu certè istud nouum & insolens habetur, in scripturis autem, quae Ecclesiam Dei nobis depingunt, non item. In veteri enim Testamento Leuitis & sacerotibus non modò per-missum fuit vxores ducere, sed Leges etiam peculiares datae sunt, qualem Sacerdos vxorem sibi copulare debeat: filiam nimirum de populo suo, non exteram aut alienigenam, non repudiatam, non viduam, sed virginem. In noua autem Testamento Paulus diserte iubet, vt episcopus vnius vxo-ris maritus sit. Neque hoc aliquis mirari, aut illo offendi debet. Quod enim per se sanctum est, id ne-minem polluit aut prophanum reddit. At coniugij conditionem sanctissimam esse, ex eius institutio-ne patet, cuius origo ad Deum authorem refertur, qui illud in paradiso, priusquam peccatum vllum esset, instituit, simulque hanc Legem omnium animis insculpsit, vt coniugium honorabile & thorum coniugalem impollutum esse intellexerint. Ideo coniuges fuerunt sanctissimi quique Dei cultores, patriarchae, Moses, Aaron, prophetae, apostoli denique, qui (vt Paulus in priori ad Corinthios te-statur) vxores secum in suo comitatu habuerunt, cùm Euangelium inter gentes praedicarent. Ne-que vlla in sacris literis Lex extat, quae alicui generi hominum coniugij legitimi vsum prohibeat. Antichristo autem inter alia hoc quoque Daniel tribuit, quòd nullam amoris legitimi mulierum rationem habiturus sit. Et Paulus inter daemoniorum dogmata recenset leges eas, quae matrimo-nia & ciborum aliquorum vsum prohibent. Tentarunt quidem nonnulli in Niceno Concilio ad coe-libatum astringere Ecclesiarum ministros: sed illorum institutio grauiter se oppo-suit Pæphnutius, cuius summa erat propter synceram fidei confessionem & quae in corpore suo gestabat Christi stigma ta authoritas, & effecit, ne quid huius decerneretur. Secutus est autem post annos ab eo tempore sexaginta Syricius Romanus Episcopus, cuius decretum in Iure Canonico extat, quo Ecclesiarum ministris coniugio interdicitur. Non tamen obtinere potuit quod volebat, & reperti sunt posteris diebus, qui & coniugij dignitatem & Ecclesiae libertatem acriter defenderent. Tandem Gregorius VII. maiori audacia rem aggressus, primum quidem in Italia coelibatus Legem tulit, quae il-lic facilè recepta est. Cùm verò eandem Germanis quoque episcopis obtrudere conaretur, ea res turbas dedit grauissimas, quae bellorum quoque ciuilium causa fuerunt. Extat etiam adhuc ante illa tempora scripta Diui Huldrychi, qui Augustae Vindelicorum Episcopus fuit, epistola ad Rom. pontificem, qua causam hanc graviter tractat, & ex qua satis apparet, quantis difficultatibus Pon-tifices impuri coelibatus decretum Germanis veteribus obtruserint. Quò magis dolendum est, hodie adhuc in illa gente Pontificum fautores inueniri, quando nemo non videt, quàm turpes & foedi-tyrannidis istius effectus fuerint.
units.tr: Yet the Holy Spirit does not note any such thing in the parents of John, Zacharias and Elizabeth. On the contrary, he shows that they lived up well to the distinction of their family, since he describes carefully their condition, their way of life and their character. For Zacharias was not one of the idle Levites, of whom there were many at that time, but was a priest of the course of Abijah, which, as is clear, was the eighth in the priestly order established by David. How diligently he discharged his turns of duty will be told in what follows. Next, he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, joined to him in lawful marriage. This can be regarded as no ordinary proof of piety and obedience, since it is clear that at that time the confusion of the tribes had already begun, and that most men in their marriages paid more regard to lust and greed than to the divine laws. Yet this may have seemed strange to some, that Zacharias was both a priest and a married man. Among the Papists this is certainly regarded as new and unusual, but in the Scriptures, which set out for us the Church of God, it is not so. In the Old Testament, not only was it permitted to Levites and priests to take wives, but special laws were also given as to what kind of wife a priest should take to himself: namely a daughter of his own people, not a foreigner or alien, not one who had been divorced, not a widow, but a virgin. In the New Testament, however, Paul expressly commands that a bishop be the husband of one wife. Nor should anyone wonder at this or be offended by it. For what is holy in itself does not defile anyone or make him profane. But that the married state is most holy is evident from its institution, whose origin is traced to God as its author, who instituted it in paradise, before any sin existed, and at the same time impressed this law on the minds of all, that they should understand marriage to be honourable and the marriage bed undefiled. Therefore the most holy worshippers of God were married: the patriarchs, Moses, Aaron, the prophets, and finally the apostles, who (as Paul testifies in his first letter to the Corinthians) had wives with them in their company when they preached the gospel among the nations. Nor is there any law in the sacred writings that forbids any class of men the use of lawful marriage. But Daniel ascribes to Antichrist, among other things, this also: that he will have no regard for the lawful love of women. And Paul counts among the teachings of demons those laws which forbid marriages and the use of certain foods. Indeed some attempted at the Council of Nicaea to bind the ministers of the Churches to celibacy; but Paphnutius opposed their proposal vigorously, whose authority was very great on account of his sincere confession of faith and the marks of Christ which he bore on his body, and he brought it about that nothing was decreed on this. Sixty years after that time, however, Siricius, Bishop of Rome, followed, and his decree forbidding marriage to ministers of the Churches is found in the canon law. Yet he could not secure what he wanted, and in later days there were men who vigorously defended both the dignity of marriage and the freedom of the Church. At last Gregory VII, attacking the matter with greater boldness, first indeed enacted a law of celibacy in Italy, which was there readily accepted. But when he tried to impose the same on the German bishops also, this matter gave rise to most serious disturbances, which were also the cause of civil wars. There also survives, from before those times, a writing of the blessed Huldrych, who was Bishop of Augsburg, a letter to the Roman pontiff, in which he treats this cause seriously, and from which it sufficiently appears with what difficulties the impure pontiffs of celibacy forced their decree upon the old Germans. It is all the more to be lamented that even today supporters of the Pontiffs are found in that nation, when everyone sees how shameful and foul were the effects of that tyranny.

units.la: Sed ad sanctos hosce coniuges, Zachariam & Elizabetam, redeamus, qui exemplo suo do-cent insuper, qualia piorum coniugia esse debeant. Vbi ante omnia finis spectandus est, quem Deus ipse constituit: Vt nimirum procreandae sobolis ergò contrahantur, vt quisque sibi vitae sociam querat, qua cum & honestè viuat, & vitae huius labores facilius vincat. Deinde nihil fiat legi-bus diuinis contrarium, quae vt olim tribus Israeliticas confundere noluerunt: ita certos cognationis & affinitatis gradus ostendunt, quos incestis nuptijs violare nefas est. At quia eosdem sui lucri causa longius extenderunt Pontifices, moderationem adhibeant Christiani magistratus, vt & libertas sua pijs salua maneat, & publicae honestati consulatur, ne cui simus offendiculo. In primis autem cauendum fuerit, ne imparibus coniugijs fideles cum infidelibus aut idololatris miscceantur. Prohibuit hoc olim Deus admodum seueriter, & periculum ostendit, quod incurrant, qui ab eiusmodi connubijs non abstinent. Et Paulus non temere monuit, ne iugum ducamus cum infidelibus. Quantum enim malorum inde oriatur, infinita exempla docent, inter quae cumprimis memorabilia sunt, quod de primi mundi hominibus, qui ante diluuium vixerunt, & de Solomone in scripturis narratur. Neque desunt nostri seculi exempla, quae pios & cordatos terrere poterant. Imo, si verum fateri libeat, quia in coniugijs minima religionis cura est, plerunque vero auaritia, ambitio & libido in consilium adducuntur, infelices fere sunt illorum exitus, & vix nobis aliqua melioris sortis spes affulget, &c.
units.tr: But let us return to those holy spouses, Zacharias and Elizabeth, who by their example teach moreover what the marriages of the pious ought to be like. Here the end God himself appointed must above all be kept in view: namely that marriages be contracted for the sake of begetting offspring, so that each may seek a companion of life, with whom he may both live honourably and more easily overcome the labours of this life. Next, nothing should be done contrary to the divine laws, which, just as they would not allow the tribes of Israel to be confused, so also show the fixed degrees of kinship and affinity, which it is unlawful to violate by incestuous marriages. But because the Pontiffs have extended these degrees further for the sake of their own gain, Christian magistrates should apply moderation, so that the freedom of the godly remains safe and public decency is looked after, lest we become a stumbling block to anyone. Above all, care must be taken that the faithful are not mixed in unequal marriages with unbelievers or idolaters. God forbade this of old very severely, and showed the danger which those incur who do not abstain from such marriages. Nor did Paul give this warning without reason, not to be yoked together with unbelievers. For the infinite examples teach how much evil arises from this, among which the most memorable are those told in the Scriptures about the men of the first world, who lived before the flood, and about Solomon. Nor are there lacking examples from our own age which might terrify the pious and the wise. Indeed, if it is right to speak the truth, since in marriages there is very little concern for religion, and for the most part greed, ambition and lust are taken as counsellors, the outcomes of these are almost always unhappy, and scarcely any hope of a better lot shines upon us, etc.

units.la: Caeterum a vita quoq; & morum integritate Zacharias & Elizabeta commendantur. Erant iusti (inquit) ambo in conspectu Dei, incedentes in omnibus mandatis & constitutionibus Domini inculpatè. Coram Deo iustos fuisse dicit, vt ostendat non fuisse hypocritas, qui coram hominibus inani iustitiae fuco se palliarint, quales tunc erant pharisaei & qui horum doctrinam sectabantur: sed in hoc potius fuisse, vt (quod in foedere cum Abrahamo facto iubemur) coram Deo ambularent, & illius iudicio probarentur. Sunt ergo nimium inepti & curiosi, imo scripturis sacris vim faciunt, qui ex hoc loco & similibus operum nostrorum iustitiam & nostri arbitrij vires stabilire conantur. Conuincuntur hi totius scripturae consensu, qui docet, omnes homines natura peccatores esse, & gratuita Dei misericordia opus habere, qui nobis nihil huius meritis iustitiam & salutem in Christo offert. Adhaec ipsius Zachariae peccatum, de quo mox agetur, illorum errorem confutat, & quod in praesenti per expositionem additur: quod nimirum incesserint aut ambularint in omnibus mandatis & constitutionibus Domini inculpatè, id est, ita vt nemo hominum de illis iure posset conqueri. Et Dei mandata hominum traditionibus opponuntur, quas tunc plerique observabant, vt maior esset harum quam praeceptorum Dei authoritas. Mandatis vero constitutiones coniungit, vt sub illis quidem morum & vitae praecepta, sub his autem ceremonias & sacros ritus comprehendat. At si praecepta & constitutiones Legis omnes excutias, praecipuus omnium scopus est, quod ad Christum deducunt, & hunc fide recipiendum esse docent. In hunc ergo, quem venturum certò credebant, Zacharias & Elisabeta intenti, ex fide iustificati sunt coram Deo, iustitiae autem eius fructus fuere obedientia, vitae integritas, innocentiae studium, quibus suam fidem & pietatem publicè testati sunt. Minime ergo confundi debet causa cum suis effectis, sed spiritus in scripturis loquens audiri debet, qui ita distincte de his disserit, vt iustitiae & salutis causas nobis in sola Dei gratia per Christum commonstret, simul autem eiusdem effecta & fructus commendet, ne nosipsos aut alios in ni specie fallamus. Docet igitur hic locus, eam demum veram esse iustitiam, si in Dei mandatis & constitutionibus incedamus. Vbi ante omnia fide in Christum opus est. Nam vt Ioannes ait, hoc est praeceptum aut mandatum Dei, vt credamus nomini filij eius Iesu Christi, & diligamus alij alios, sicuti nobis mandauit. Etenim cum omnes promissiones vnü Christum praedicent, illis autem omnino credendum sit, neque iusti neque Deo grati aut accepti erunt, quicunque a fide in Christum alieni sunt. Parit fides haec dilectionem Dei, ex qua serium obedientiae studium & proximi dilectio enascuntur. Ad obedientiam vero non solum morum praecepta pertinent, verumetiam quae de sacris caeremonijs & vero Sacramentorum vsu habentur, quae nunquam negligent ij, qui per fidei obedientiam se totos Deo consecrauerunt.
units.tr: Besides, Zacharias and Elizabeth are also commended for the integrity of their life and conduct. "They were both righteous," he says, "before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly." He says they were righteous before God, to show that they were not hypocrites, who cloaked themselves with empty pretences of righteousness before men, as the Pharisees then did and those who followed their teaching; but rather that, as we are commanded in the covenant made with Abraham, they walked before God and were approved by his judgment. Therefore those are far too foolish and curious, or rather they do violence to the sacred Scriptures, who from this passage and similar ones try to establish the righteousness of our works and the powers of our free will. They are refuted by the agreement of the whole of Scripture, which teaches that all men are sinners by nature, and have need of the free mercy of God, who offers us in Christ righteousness and salvation, not on account of any merits of ours. Moreover, the very sin of Zacharias, of which we shall speak shortly, refutes their error; and so does what is added in the present passage by way of explanation: namely that they walked, or went on, in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly, that is, in such a way that no one could justly complain of them. And the commandments of God are set against the traditions of men, which many then observed, so that the authority of these might be greater than that of God's precepts. Moreover, he joins ordinances to commandments, so that under the former he understands the precepts of conduct and life, and under the latter the ceremonies and sacred rites. But if you examine all the precepts and ordinances of the Law, the chief aim of all is that they lead to Christ, and teach that he is to be received by faith. Therefore it was on him, whom they firmly believed was to come, that Zacharias and Elizabeth were intent, and were justified before God by faith; and the fruits of his righteousness were obedience, integrity of life, and zeal for innocence, by which they openly bore witness to their faith and piety. Therefore the cause must in no way be confused with its effects; rather the Spirit speaking in the Scriptures must be heard, who discusses these things so distinctly that he shows us the causes of righteousness and salvation solely in the grace of God through Christ, and at the same time commends the effects and fruits of the same, lest we deceive ourselves or others in any way. This passage therefore teaches that that is true righteousness if we walk in the commandments and ordinances of God. Here faith in Christ is above all necessary. For, as John says, this is the precept or commandment of God, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he has commanded us. For since all the promises proclaim Christ alone, and since they must be wholly believed, those who are alien from faith in Christ will in no way be righteous, nor pleasing or acceptable to God. This faith brings forth love for God, from which an earnest zeal for obedience and love of neighbour are born. Yet obedience pertains not only to the precepts of conduct, but also to those things concerning the sacred ceremonies and the true use of the Sacraments; those who have wholly consecrated themselves to God through the obedience of faith never neglect these.

units.la: Porrò his dictis descendit Lucas ad natiuitatis Ioannis historiam, quam miraculo clariusse often dit, dum Elizabetam sterilem, & simul ambos iamProuectae aetatis fuisse scribit. Ex eo enim sequitur, praeter naturae cursum singulari virtute Dei factum fuisse, vt quae in iuuentute sterilis fuerat, iam senior ex marito grandaeuo conciperet & pareret. At quia de hoc postea pluribus dicetur, nunc obseruemus, hoc tam sanctum coniugium non caruisse sua molestia. Nam vt suo loco audiemus, sterilitas probro erat inter Iudaeos, eo quòd inter promissiones Dei non postrema erat, quae de seminis & posteritatis multiplicatione habetur. Tentabatur etiam non leuiter sterilium fides, quòd a Dei promissionibus excluši viderentur, vt pote, cum illas per ipsas impleri Deus nollet. Qua causa pias & sanctas matronas, Saram, Rahelem, Annam & similes mouerunt, vt de sterilitate conquereren tur. Ita vero videmus sanctis nunquam deesse crucem, & in primis hanc esse coniugij sortem, vt curas & molestias sentiant varias, qui in hoc viuunt. Habent illæ originem suam ex peccato, ut in Dei verbis esse videre, quibus primos parentes nostros in paradiso corripuit. Et expedit nobis illud vitæ genus aduersis & molestijs condiri, ut & fidei coniugalis vinculum hac quasi necessitate arctius constringatur, & minus in nobis possit libidinis æstus, in quo ferè petulantia effreni & nimis impudenti modum excedunt, qui nulla crucis molestia coercentur. Agnoscant ergo pij coniuges Dei consilium, & quas hic illis imponit molestias patienter ferant, atque earum acerbitatem mutua dilectione molliant aut temperent, quæ ipsis leuia & iucunda reddet, quæ prorsus intolerabilia esse videbantur. Ante omnia verò meminerint, liberos à Deo dari, & ideo illos ad huius gloriam æducari & instituì curent. Peccatur in hoc plurimum hodie, quando pauci cogitant, liberos sibi ex Dei benedictione datos esse. Quæ causa est, quod vel laborem omnem in illis æducandis impatienter ferunt, vel iam adultos negligunt, aut etiam indulgentia nimia eos male perdunt, dum relicto pietatis studio in hoc vnum intenti sunt, ut illos opibus & honoribus augeant. Et si verum fateri licet, plus hodie studij opulentiores in equis, canibus & accipitribus, rustici verò in reliquo pecore alendo & gubernando impendunt, quàm plerique hominum in liberorum æducatione adhibeant. Quid ergo miramur, si & turpius viuant postea, & tam sibijpsis quàm parentibus probro sint, qui ab ineunte ætate pessimis moribus imbuti fuerunt? Itaque Zachariæ & Elizabetæ exemplum imitentur coniuges, quoad coniugij vsum: simul verò omnes alij ita viuant, ut coram Deo pro iustis habeantur propter fidem in Iesum Christum, qui ut nobis à patre iustitia factus est, ita vnicus quoque omnis boni author est: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Having said these things, Luke goes on to the history of John's birth, which he shows to be made more remarkable by a miracle, since he writes that Elizabeth was barren and that both of them were already advanced in years. For it follows from this that, beyond the course of nature, by the singular power of God, a woman who had been barren in her youth conceived and bore a child from her elderly husband in his old age. But since this will be discussed at more length later, let us note now that this holy marriage was not free from its own distress. For, as we shall hear in its place, barrenness was a disgrace among the Jews, because the promise of a multiplied seed and posterity was not among the least of God's promises. The faith of barren women was also sorely tested, since they seemed to be shut out from God's promises, as if God were unwilling to fulfil them through themselves. This is why pious and holy matrons, Sarah, Rachel, Hannah and others like them, complained about their barrenness. Indeed we see that the saints never lack a cross, and above all that this is the lot of marriage: that those who live in it feel various cares and troubles. These have their origin in sin, as can be seen in God's words, with which he rebuked our first parents in paradise. It is also useful for us that this way of life is seasoned with adversities and troubles, so that the bond of conjugal faith is drawn tighter by this kind of necessity, and the heat of lust has less power over us, since those who are restrained by no trouble of the cross often go beyond measure in unbridled and excessively shameless wantonness. Let pious spouses therefore acknowledge God's counsel, patiently bear the troubles he lays upon them here, and soften or temper their bitterness by mutual love, which will make light and pleasant what seemed utterly intolerable to them. Above all, let them remember that children are given by God, and therefore take care that they are brought up and instructed for his glory. Much sin is committed in this today, when few consider that children are given to them as a blessing from God. This is why people either bear all the labour of bringing them up impatiently, or neglect them once they are grown, or even ruin them by excessive indulgence, while, having abandoned the pursuit of piety, they are intent on this one thing alone: to increase their wealth and honours. And if it is permitted to speak the truth, today more care is spent by the wealthier on feeding and training horses, dogs and hawks, and by country people on the rest of their livestock, than most men devote to the upbringing of their children. Why then do we wonder if they live more disgracefully afterwards, and are a shame both to themselves and to their parents, when they have been steeped in the worst morals from their earliest age? Let married couples therefore imitate the example of Zechariah and Elizabeth in the use of marriage; and let all others likewise live so that they are accounted righteous before God on account of faith in Jesus Christ, who, as he has been made righteousness for us by the Father, so is also the one and only author of every good: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILY III.

units.la: Factum est autem cum is sacerdotio fungeretur, in ordine vicis suæ ante Deum, secundum ritum functionis sacerdotalis, sortitus est munus suffimenti faciendi, postquam ingressus esset in templum Domini. Et tota multitudo populi foris precabatur tempore suffitus. Visus autem est ei Angelus Domini, stans ad dexteram altaris suffitus. Et Zacharias eo viso turbatus est, & pauor incidit in eum.
units.tr: Now it happened that, while he was serving as priest before God in the order of his course, according to the custom of the priestly office, he was chosen by lot to offer incense, after he had entered the temple of the Lord. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of the incense. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. When Zacharias saw him, he was troubled, and fear fell upon him.

units.la: Lvcas Euangelista non temere tanta diligentia parentes Ioannis Baptistæ, & quæ ad eius nativitatem pertinent, describit. Quia enim redemptoris nostri Iesu Christi præcursor & testis esse debuit, magnam eius authoritatem esse oportebat, ut plus fidei mereretur testimoniu, quod Christo perhibuit. Exposuit ergo hucusque parentum eius genus, conditionem & mores atque studia, in quibus præcipuum est, quod coram Deo iusti fuerunt, & in huius præceptis atque constitutionibus ambularunt. Habuit tamen coniugium hoc tam sanctum suas quoque molestias, cum prole carerent, quod illo tempore pijs molestissimum erat propter promissionem Abrahamo factam, de qua nuper diximus. Sed ita voluit Deus, ne quod vitæ genus ex omni parte beatum fit, cuius eos cum primis meminisse oportet, qui in coniugio viuunt, ut huius curas atque molestias patientius ferant. Cæterum ad commendandam Zachariæ iustitiam hic quoque locus facit, quo narratur, ut commissum sibi sacerdotalis functionis munus obierit. Nec enim satis est, si quis in genere iustitiæ studeat, ut & neminem lædat & suum cuique reddat, sed simul suam vocationem singuli sectari debent, & in eo exequendo diligentes esse & strenui, ad quod illos Deus destinauit. Quod Zachariam probè & fideliter præstitisse audiemus. Meretur autem eo diligentiorem consideratione locus iste, quod simul exemplum aut formam sacrorum cœtuum continet, in quibus non minima pars religionis siue externi cultus consistit. Videamus ergo quid Zacharias, quid item populus fecerit, & quis verum studij tam sancti fructus fuerit.
units.tr: Luke the evangelist did not describe the parents of John the Baptist, and the things that pertain to his birth, with such care without reason. For since John was to be the forerunner and witness of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, it was necessary that he have great authority, so that the testimony he bore to Christ would deserve more faith. So far Luke has set out the family, condition, character and pursuits of his parents, and the chief point is that they were righteous before God and walked in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. Yet this marriage, so holy, had its own troubles, since they had no children. In those times this was most distressing to the godly, because of the promise made to Abraham, of which we spoke recently. But God willed it so, so that no way of life should be wholly happy. Those who live in marriage especially ought to remember this, so that they may bear its cares and troubles more patiently. Moreover, this passage also serves to commend the righteousness of Zacharias, in that it tells how he discharged the priestly duty entrusted to him. For it is not enough for someone to aim at general righteousness, so that he harms no one and renders to each his due; each person must also pursue his own calling and be diligent and vigorous in carrying out that to which God has appointed him. We shall hear that Zacharias performed this well and faithfully. This passage deserves closer consideration because it also contains an example, or pattern, of holy assemblies, in which no small part of religion, or of outward worship, consists. Let us see, then, what Zacharias did, what the people did too, and what was the true fruit of so holy a practice.

units.la: De Zacharia primùm in genere dicitur, quòd sacerdotio functus sit in ordine vicis suæ ante Deum, secundum ritum functionis sacerdotalis. Ergo quàmuis summam obtineret authoritatem, non tamen turbauit ordinem sacerdotij, qui tunc ex veteri instituto seruabatur. Fuit hoc eximium pietatis & animi religiosi argumentum, si illorum temporum mores spectemus. Quia enim (vt alibi diximus) pleriq; sacerdotes ex sece vulgi ad eam dignitatem ab Herode euecti fuerant, & inter hos auaritia & inanis gloriae studium regnabat, summae modestiae fuerit oportet Zacharias, qui intra suae vicis ordinem se continuit, neque insolenter abusus est prærogatiua, qua præ aliis omnibus eminebat. Hanc vero modestiam in illo peperit pietas & seriurn conseruandi purioris cultus studium, quod simul auaritiam & ambitionem omnem ex animo eius exclusit. Debet exemplum hoc diligenter obseruari, quia ad Ecclesiae aedificationem hoc plurimum facit, vt omnia cum ordine legitimo & decenter fiant, & ideo de hoc praeceptum quoque peculiare olim dedit Apostolus 1.Cor.14. Et quid ordinis Ecclesiastici turbatores maneat, exempla cumprimis horrenda docent, quae in illos Deus edidit. Nam Coran cum suis coniuratis & fortunis omnibus terra absorbuit, vt viui ad inferos descenderent, qui Dei Ecclesiam in terris turbare ausi fuerant. Et Vziam regem lepra percussum esse legimus, quod non contentus regia dignitate sacerdotalis quoque functionis partes invaderet. Quo exemplo Deus ostendit, indignos esse qui in ecclesiae societate feratur, quotquot ab ipso institutum ordinem priuato affectu labefactare audent. Paulus item eos abscindi optat, qui ecclesias turbare non verentur. At quod de ecclesia dicimus, ad Rempub. quoque referri debet, in qua ni si inter proceres & subditos ordo seruetur, & singuli in suo gradu se contineant, res diu salvae esse non possunt, sicuti olim Menenius Agrippa humani corporis Apologo Romanum populum aduersus patres tumultuantem monuit. Debet hoc ipsum priuatim etiam in re domestica obseruari: quae tunc demum salua erit, si certo ordine paterfamilias, vxor, serui, liberi, ancillae officium faciant. Vbi vero aliqui suo officio neglecto, in aliorum munera inuolant, rerum omnium dissipatio nascitur.
units.tr: First, it is said of Zacharias in general that he served as priest before God in the order of his course, according to the rite of the priestly office. Therefore, although he held the highest authority, he did not disturb the order of the priesthood, which was then kept according to ancient institution. This was a striking proof of piety and of a religious mind, if we look at the morals of those times. For, as we have said elsewhere, many priests had been raised from the common people to that dignity by Herod, and among these greed and the desire for empty glory reigned. Zacharias, who kept himself within the order of his own course and did not insolently abuse the prerogative by which he stood out above all others, must have had the greatest modesty. This modesty was produced in him by piety and by a serious concern to preserve purer worship, which at the same time drove out of his heart all greed and ambition. This example ought to be carefully noted, because it contributes greatly to the building up of the Church that everything be done in lawful order and decently. For this reason the Apostle also long ago gave a special precept on this matter in 1 Cor. 14. And the most dreadful examples show what awaits those who disturb ecclesiastical order, the examples God displayed against them.
