For the earth swallowed up Korah with his fellow conspirators and all their goods, so that those who had dared to disturb the Church of God on earth went down alive to hell. And we read that King Uzziah was struck with leprosy, because, not content with royal dignity, he invaded also the functions of the priestly office. By this example God shows that those who dare by private inclination to overthrow the order he has instituted are unworthy to be borne in the fellowship of the Church. Paul too wishes that those who do not fear to disturb the churches be cut off. But what we say of the Church must also be applied to the commonwealth. In it, unless order is kept between the leaders and the subjects, and each keeps to his own rank, affairs cannot long remain safe. Menenius Agrippa once warned the Roman people, who were rising up against the senators, by the fable of the human body. The same must be observed in private, domestic affairs too, which will then be safe only if the head of the household, the wife, the servants, the children and the maids each perform their duty in fixed order. But where some, neglecting their own duty, rush into the functions of others, the dissolution of all things arises.

units.la: Sed ad Zachariam redeamus, in quo certa quoque cultus diuini species exprimitur, cui vacauit, quando de filio Ioanne sibi nascituro promissionem accepit. Sortem enim illi obuenisse ait, Lucas, vt templum Domini ingressus suffimentum faceret. Quod vt rectius intelligatur, nonnulla de templo & tota cultus Leuitici ratione dicenda erunt. Legis doctrinam in tota Iudaeorum gente prædicari voluit Deus, & in eum vsum per oppida & vicos celebriores Synagogae extructae erant, in quibus coetus sacri habebantur, & populus a Leuitis (qui eam ob causam potissimum in omnes tribus erant dispersi) in Legis Domini notitia erudiebatur. Templum vero totius gentis vnicum fuit Hierosolymis, ad quod ceu ad communem parochiam omnium tribuum homines diebus festis conueniebant, & in quo solo externus cultus exercebatur, qui in sacrificiis & suffimento maxima ex parte consistebat. Ita autem Deus in eadem religionis forma omnes continere voluit, & simul fidem in promissum Seruatorem, Iesum Christum, omnibus commendare, qui suo tempore Hierosolymis pro peccatis totius mundi victima fieri debebat. Et templum quidem in partes tres distinctum fuisse legimus. Prima adytum erat, quod vulgo Sanctum sanctorum dicebatur, eo quod inde oracula edebantur, & totius templi pars esset sanctissima, & ipsos caelos, aeternae beatitudinis sedem, adumbraret. In ea erat arca testamenti, diuinae praesentiae symbolum, & in hanc quotannis semel duntaxat non sine sanguine ingrediebatur Summus Pontifex, vt Christi typum gereret, qui (vt ad Hebraeos scribitur) semel mortuus, cum proprio sanguine caelum conscendit, vt perpetuo in conspectu Dei appareat pro nobis. Secunda pars Sanctum dicebatur, quam a Sancto sanctorum velum ingens pretiosum dirimebat. In illius parte australi stabat mensa aurea cum panibus propositionis, ex opposito in meridionali latere candelabrum aureum, in medio autem utriusque ante velum erat altare aureum thymiamatis aut suffimenti. Et haec templi pars Sacerdotibus proprie erat destinata. Tertiam partem occupabat atrium, in quo magnum altare aeneum erat pro holocaustis faciendis, & in quo populus ad sacrificandum & ad audiendum Legem Domini, ad preces item publicas conueniebat. Vt autem quotidie duo agni immolabantur, alter quidem matutino tempore, alter vero sub vesperam: ita quotidie bis quoque vnus ex Sacerdotibus quem sors destinauerat, templum ingressus thymiama seu suffimentum incendebat super altare illud aureum, quod inter mensam & candelabrum collocatum fuisse diximus. Erat altare illud Christi Iesu typus, suffimentum vero illud preces adumbrabat, quod non obscure Dauid docuit, dicens.
units.tr: But let us return to Zacharias, in whom a definite form of divine worship is also expressed, to which he was devoted when he received the promise of the son John who was to be born to him. For Luke says that the lot had fallen to him, that he should enter the temple of the Lord and offer incense. So that this may be understood more correctly, some things must be said about the temple and the whole system of Levitical worship. God willed that the teaching of the Law be preached throughout the whole Jewish nation, and for this purpose synagogues were built in the more important towns and villages, in which sacred assemblies were held, and the people were instructed in knowledge of the Law of the Lord by the Levites, who for this reason had especially been scattered among all the tribes. But there was one temple for the whole nation, at Jerusalem. To it, as to a common parish, the people of all the tribes gathered on the festival days, and in it alone the outward worship was carried out, which for the most part consisted in sacrifices and incense. God willed to hold all in the same form of religion, and at the same time to commend to all faith in the promised Saviour, Jesus Christ, who at his appointed time was to be made a sacrifice at Jerusalem for the sins of the whole world. We read that the temple was divided into three parts. The first was the inner sanctuary, commonly called the Holy of Holies, because oracles were given from it, and it was the most sacred part of the whole temple, and it foreshadowed heaven itself, the seat of eternal blessedness. In it was the ark of the covenant, the symbol of the divine presence, and into it the High Priest entered once a year only, and not without blood, so that he might bear the type of Christ, who (as is written to the Hebrews) having died once, entered heaven with his own blood, so that he might appear before the face of God continually for us. The second part was called the Holy Place, and a great precious veil separated it from the Holy of Holies. On its south side stood the golden table with the bread of the presentation; opposite it, on the south side, the golden lampstand; and in the middle, in front of the veil, between them, stood the golden altar of incense or fragrance. This part of the temple was properly set apart for the priests. The third part was occupied by the court, in which stood the great bronze altar for burnt offerings, and where the people gathered to sacrifice, to hear the Law of the Lord, and likewise for public prayers. Each day two lambs were offered, one in the morning and the other toward evening. Likewise twice a day one of the priests, whom the lot had designated, entered the temple and burned the incense, or fragrance, upon that golden altar which, as we said, was placed between the table and the lampstand. That altar was a type of Jesus Christ, and the incense represented prayers, as David clearly taught when he said:

units.la: Num 16. / 2. Par. 16. / Gal. 5. / De templo & cultu Leuitico. / Psal. 141. cens: Dirigatur oratio mea tanquam incensum in conspectu tuo, elevatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum. Sacerdos vero, qui peracto sacro ad suffimentum faciendum ingrediebatur, Christi mediatoris personam sustinebat, utpote ex officio quasi medius inter Deum & populum constitutus. Erat itaque haec actio plena mysteriorum, & monebat, in Ecclesia preces assiduas fieri debere, eas autem uno & soli Deo offerendas esse, qui tunc demum acceptas sibi & ratas habiturus sit, si per Christum offerantur, qui nobis ab illo Mediator factus est, & qui solus patris iram placavit. Ideo neq; plura altaria thymiamatis extruere, neque thymiama illud (cuius compositio singularis à Mose describitur) in alios usus transferre licebat. Sacerdotem vero interea dum suffimentum fiebat, populus foris expectabat, donec illo rursus egresso cum benedictione solenni dimitteBatur. Haec paulo fusius dicere libuit, quia ad totam Zachariae historiam illustrandam faciunt, & quod frequens apud Evangelistas occurrit templi & coetuum sacrorum mentio. Nunc vero observemus, Zachariam hic etiam non aliud fecisse, quam quod Lex fieri iubebat: & est hoc novum pietatis & modestiae eius argumentum, quòd vt in reliquis non turbauit ordinem ecclesiae, ita neq; ad suffimentum faciendum prorupit, priusquam se per sortem postulari videret. Habent ergo in eo exemplum egregium ministri ecclesiastici, in cuius imitatione illos diligentes esse conuenit. Ante omnia ergo ipsi quoque vocationem & missionem legitimam expectent. Quia enim, vt Paulus monet, ex nobisipsis ne ad congradiendum quidem idonei sumus, quomodo praedicabunt, qui non mittuntur à Domino? Equidem exempla docent, eos qui temere sese ingerunt, velignauos & mutos canes esse, vel in periculis qualibuscunque turpiter succumbere, cùm de Dei auxilio nihil certi sibi polliceri possint, cuius vocationem expectare noluerunt. Ideo olim ab Apostolis forte deligebantur Euangelij ministri (vt in Matthiae electione patet) vt & sua constaret ministerio authoritas, & plus animi illis esset, qui se ad illud diuinitus vocatos esse sciebant. Deinde si cui legitima vocatio obtigit, is officium strenuè faciat docendo, monendo, hortando, increpando, consolando, precando item & intercedendo pro publica totius populi salute. Quoad vero ordinem docendi & administrandi sacramenta, nihil temere mutet, quod à Christi institutione non omnino alienum est; & quod salua pietate & religione fieri potest. Vt enim leuis quidem, sed inconsiderata humorum & sanguinis commotio in corpore bene constituto fere morbos parit grauissimos: ita crebræ & temerariæ mutationes in Ecclesia infirmos in fide offendere solent, & sæpe subitis dissensionibus uniuersam religionis causam suspectam reddunt. Plurimum autem ministris proderit, si Ecclesiæ dignitatem sæpe animo suo considerent, quam Dei Filius sanguinis sui pretio redemit, vt illam sibi desponsaret, simulque meminerint, se coram Domino ministrare, cui olim suæ functionis rationem sint reddituri. Et hæc quidem de Zachariæ dicta sint.
units.tr: Num. 16. / 2 Par. 16. / Gal. 5. / On the temple and Levitical worship. / Ps. 141. Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice. The priest who entered to burn the incense, after the sacred rite was done, bore the person of Christ the Mediator, since by his office he was set as it were in the middle between God and the people. This action, then, was full of mysteries, and it taught that continual prayers ought to be made in the Church, and that these must be offered to one God alone, who will then receive them as acceptable and valid if they are offered through Christ, who was made our Mediator by him and who alone appeased the Father's wrath. Therefore it was not permitted to build more altars of incense, nor to turn that incense (whose special composition is described by Moses) to other uses. Meanwhile the people waited outside for the priest while the incense was being burned, until he came out again and they were dismissed with the solemn blessing. I have wished to say these things a little more fully, because they help to illustrate the whole history of Zacharias, and because mention of the temple and the sacred assemblies occurs frequently in the Evangelists. But now let us observe that Zacharias here also did nothing other than what the Law commanded. This is a new proof of his piety and modesty: just as he did not disturb the order of the Church in other matters, so he did not rush forward to burn the incense until he saw that he was summoned by the lot. Therefore ministers of the Church have in him an outstanding example, and it is fitting for them to be diligent in imitating it. Above all, then, let them also wait for a lawful calling and sending. For, as Paul warns, we are not of ourselves even sufficient to think anything as of ourselves; how shall they preach who are not sent by the Lord? Indeed, experience teaches that those who thrust themselves in rashly are either lazy and dumb dogs, or basely give way in any dangers, since they cannot promise themselves anything certain about the help of God, whose calling they were unwilling to wait for. Therefore in former times the ministers of the gospel were chosen by lot by the Apostles (as is clear in the election of Matthias), so that the authority of their ministry might stand firm, and that those who knew they had been called to it by God might have more courage. Then, if anyone has obtained a lawful calling, let him perform his office vigorously: teaching, admonishing, exhorting, rebuking, comforting, and also praying and interceding for the public welfare of the whole people. As for the order of teaching and administering the sacraments, let him change nothing rashly, provided it is not wholly alien to the institution of Christ and can be done without loss of piety and religion. For just as a slight but ill-considered disturbance of the humours and blood in a well-constituted body often produces very grave diseases, so frequent and rash changes in the Church are wont to offend the weak in faith, and often by sudden dissensions make the whole cause of religion suspect. Ministers will benefit greatly if they often consider in their minds the dignity of the Church, which the Son of God redeemed at the price of his own blood, so as to betroth her to himself, and at the same time remember that they minister before the Lord, to whom they will one day have to render an account of their office. And let these things suffice concerning what was said of Zacharias.

units.la: Videamus nunc quid populus in sacro coetu fecerit? Tota multitudo populi (inquit Lucas) foris precabatur tempore suffitus. Vbi primùm obseruabimus, quòd totam multitudinem nominat. Ex eo enim apparet, illos in coetibus eiusmodi frequentes fuisse, in quibus cultus diuini pars non postrema consistit. Vt enim Deus charitatem passim præcipit, & Christus suos vnum esse vult: ita coetibus suorum maximè delectatur, qui externum sunt eius vnionis testimonium. Ideo in Lege maxima festorum pars populi congregatione constabat, imo in eum finem præcipuè festi dies instituti erant, vt aliquando in vnum conuenirent ad cultus diuini exercitia, qui hinc inde dispersi habitabant. In Euangelio autem Christum quoque in Synagogis frequentem fuisse legimus, vt suo exemplo doceret, non temere deferendos esse eos, qui ad audiendum Dei verbum & preces publicas conueniunt. Adhæc promissionem dedit, quòd præsens adesse velit ijs, qui in suo nomine conueniunt, & quòd illorum preces pater exauditurus sit. Et ne quod esset excusationis effugium, vnum & idem Euangelium omnis loci & ordinis hominibus prædicari, vno baptismo omnes tingi, ad eandem mensam omnes accedere voluit, vt vnionis studium sibi sequendum esse omnes intelligerent. Nimium ergo imprudentes sunt, qui intempestiuis excommunicationibus communionem Ecclesiasticam scindunt, & de dissipando potius quàm colligendo grege dominico solicité sunt. Impios autem & contemptores omnis religionis esse constat eos, qui à templis omnino abhorrent, & cœtus sacros deuitant, vnà cum exercitijs illis sacris, quibus nos in fide Dominus vult confirmari. Discant ergo ecclesiarum ministri, officij sui esse, vt populum colligant, cœtus sacros & eorum disciplinam diligenter conseruent, curent denique, ne quid hic peccetur ipsorum incuria vel negligentia. Debent etiam in re tam sancta & necessaria suam authoritatem magistratus interponere, quando multos esse inuenire, qui ministrorum admonitionibus & adhortationibus se moueri non patiuntur. Et huc pertinet, quod Assyriaci belli tempore Ioel sacerdotibus & principibus dicebat: Clangite tuba in Zione, sanctificate ieiunium, indicite coetum, congregate populum, sanctificate coetum, congregate senes, colligite paruulos, &c. Neque audiendi sunt, qui cum Dauid Christi populum spontaneum fore praedixerit, neminem cogendum aut vrgendum esse putant. Manet enim in electis quoque carnis reliquiae, qui illos saepe negligentiores & cunctatores faciunt; & constat multos mitescere, vbi verbum audiunt & coetibus vel inuiti intersunt, qui si suo arbitrio permitterentur, tandem omni freno excusso misere perirent. Adhaec non ferenda sunt exempla eorum, qui sua petulantia & manifesta secessione vel emansione, omnem ecclesiae disciplinam conuellunt.
units.tr: Let us now see what the people did in the sacred assembly. "The whole multitude of the people," Luke says, "was praying outside at the time of the incense." Here we should note first that he says "the whole multitude." This shows that those people were regular attenders at gatherings of this kind, in which a not inconsiderable part of the worship of God consists. Just as God commands love everywhere, and Christ wills that his people be one, so he takes great delight in the assemblies of his people, which are the outward testimony of that unity. For this reason, under the Law, the greater part of the festivals consisted in a gathering of the people, and indeed the festival days were instituted chiefly for this purpose: that those who lived scattered here and there might at times come together to exercise the worship of God. In the Gospel we also read that Christ himself was a frequent attender of the synagogues, so that by his example he might teach that those who gather to hear the Word of God and to offer public prayers are not to be lightly scorned. Besides, he promised that he would be present with those who gather in his name, and that the Father would hear their prayers. And so that there should be no pretext for excuse, he willed that the one and the same Gospel be preached to people of every place and rank, that all be baptized with one baptism, and that all come to the same table, so that everyone might understand that the pursuit of unity must be followed by them. Those therefore are far too imprudent who rend ecclesiastical communion by untimely excommunications, and who are more anxious to scatter than to gather the Lord's flock. It is plain that those are impious and despisers of all religion who utterly shun the churches and avoid the sacred assemblies, along with those holy exercises by which the Lord wills us to be confirmed in the faith. Let the ministers of the churches therefore learn that it is their duty to gather the people, to preserve diligently the sacred assemblies and their discipline, and finally to take care that nothing is sinned here through their carelessness or negligence. In a matter so holy and necessary, the magistrates too ought to interpose their authority, when they find many who do not allow themselves to be moved by the admonitions and exhortations of the ministers. To this belongs what Joel said to the priests and princes in the time of the Assyrian war: "Sound the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the people, sanctify the congregation, gather the elders, collect the little children," and so on. Nor are they to be heeded who, because David foretold that Christ's people would be willing, think that no one should be compelled or pressed. For remnants of the flesh remain even in the elect, which make them often negligent and hesitant; and it is certain that many grow milder when they hear the Word and attend the assemblies even unwillingly, and who, if they were left to their own judgment, would at last, with every bridle thrown off, perish wretchedly. Moreover, the examples of those who, by their wantonness and open secession or staying away, tear up all church discipline are not to be tolerated.

units.la: At non modo frequentes foris expectarunt, verumetiam interea precati sunt. Minime ergo eorum similes fuere, qui hodie in templis nugantur, fabulas inter se conferunt, vel etiam ludos agunt, aut si quae longior mora ferenda est, animi impatientiam fremitu & murmure, pedum strepitu & in decoris gestibus produnt. Quin potius, quia suffimentum illud quod Zacharias offerebat precum typus erat, ipsi cum illo preces suas coniungunt, ne interea rem a sacris alienam faciant. Quod ipsum Zacharias quoq; inter suffiendum fecit, sicuti ex Angeli verbis suo loco apparebit. Quo exemplo docemur, quid in sacris coetibus fieri debeat. In his praecipuae partes Dei verbo debentur. Hoc igitur ministri praedicent, & in illo audiendo populus sese attentum & diligentem praebeat, ne vel infelices illae aues, de quibus in euangelio Dominus loquitur, semen hoc ex animis auferant, vel cupiditatum spinae succrescentes illud opprimant & suffocent. Dum vero Sacramenta administrantur, animi ijs, quae tunc aguntur, intenti sint, & quae illic nobis obsignantur Dei beneficia considerent, promissionum diuinarum meditatione fidem exerceant atq; confirment, simulq; cogitent ad quae officia nos Sacramentorum vsus obstringat. Fuit ergo laudabilis admodum veteris ecclesiae mos, quo in Coenae Dominicae administratione ministri populo dicebant, Sursum corda; illo vicissim respondente, Habemus ad Dominum. In primis autem precibus hic opus est, quando sine Dei gratia neq; verbum in animis nostris germinat, neq; Sacramenta aliquem fructum ferunt. Atqui hodie in his omnibus peccatur. Verbum Dei oscitanter pleriq; audiunt, multi interea somno indulgent & ad hunc capessendum sese dedita opera componunt, plurimi quoq; solis symbolis externis intenti de mysteriis fidei vix cogitant, & salutem in externa actione consistere arbitrantur. Deniq; ij fere mores nostro tempore in coetibus sacris visuntur, quos Dominus apud Ezechielem cap.33. in Iudaeis reprehendit. Non mirum ergo fuerit, paucos ex illis meliores redire.
units.tr: But they not only waited outside in great numbers; in the meantime they also prayed. They were therefore far from resembling those who today trifle in the churches, chat with one another about trivial things, or even play games, or, if some longer delay has to be endured, betray their impatience by grumbling and murmuring, by the stamping of feet and by unseemly gestures. Rather, because that incense which Zechariah was offering was a type of prayers, they joined their own prayers with his, so as not to make the matter alien to the sacred rite in the meantime. Zechariah himself also did this while offering incense, as will become clear in its place from the words of the angel. From this example we are taught what ought to be done in sacred assemblies. In these the chief place belongs to the Word of God. Therefore ministers should preach it, and in hearing it the people should show themselves attentive and diligent, lest those unhappy birds of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel snatch away this seed from their minds, or the thorns of desires, springing up, choke and suffocate it. While the sacraments are being administered, let minds be intent on what is then being done, let them consider the blessings of God that are sealed to us there, let them exercise and strengthen faith by meditating on the divine promises, and at the same time let them think to what duties the use of the sacraments binds us. The custom of the ancient Church was therefore very praiseworthy, by which in the administration of the Lord's Supper the ministers said to the people, "Lift up your hearts," and they in turn answered, "We have them lifted up to the Lord." Above all, prayer is needed here, since without the grace of God neither the Word sprouts in our minds nor do the sacraments bear any fruit. Yet today wrong is done in all these things. Most people hear the Word of God carelessly, many in the meantime indulge in sleep, and many more, being intent only on the outward signs, hardly think about the mysteries of faith, and suppose that salvation consists in an outward action. Finally, those are almost the customs seen in our time in sacred assemblies, which the Lord rebukes among the Jews in Ezekiel, chapter 33. It is no wonder, then, that few of them return better.

units.la: Restat vt fructum huius coetus tam pie & sancte instituti videamus. Apparet Zachariae Angelus stans ad dexteram altaris suffitus, ea autem nuntiat (vt in sequentibus audiemus) quae non ad solum Zachariam, sed ad populum vniuersum pertinebant, & quibus non obscura continentur salutis mox futurae praeludia. Veram ergo experiuntur promissionem, quae in templi dedicatione Solomoni data fuit, & quam Christus nobis instauravit, quando se praesentem ijs adesse velle dixit, qui in suo nomine congregati fuerint. Occurrunt huius generis exempla passim in scripturis, & multa nos quotidie experimur, quae docent, preces piorum nunquam irritas esse, & in primis magnum pondus eas habere, quae in publicis coetibus pia quadam vi (vt Tertulliani verbo vtar) & impressione in Deum fiunt. Debet horum consideratio nos excitare, vt ecclesiae coetus frequenter accedamus, & in precibus assidui simus, quae proprium sunt fidei verae exercitium.
units.tr: It remains for us to see the fruit of this assembly, so piously and holily instituted. The angel of the Lord appears to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense; and he announces (as we shall hear in what follows) things that pertained not only to Zechariah but to the whole people, and which contain the unmistakable prelude of the salvation soon to come. They therefore experience the true promise that was given to Solomon at the dedication of the temple, and which Christ restored for us when he said that he would be present with those who have been gathered in his name. Examples of this kind occur everywhere in the Scriptures, and we daily experience many things that teach that the prayers of the godly are never in vain, and that above all those prayers have great weight which are offered to God in public assemblies with a certain holy force (to use the words of Tertullian) and impression. The consideration of these things ought to stir us to come often to the assemblies of the Church, and to be constant in prayers, which are the proper exercise of true faith.

units.la: Porro Zacharias Angelo visso turbatus est, & pauor incidit in eum. Est hoc infirmitatis humanae exemplum, quam in sanctis quoque locum habere constat. Manent enim in his carnis reliquiae, quae diuinae & coelestis gloriae splendorem atque vim sustinere non poterat. Ita Danielem olim angeli conspectu & voce consternatum fuisse legimus, vt vires in ipso nullae reliquae essent. Et tres discipuli similiter examines quasi iacuerunt, quando Christi clarificati speciem & cum hoc Eliam atque Mosem illis videre contigit. Et idem postea iterum passus est Ioannes quando Angelum conspexit, qui ipsi futura ecclesiae fata reuelabat. At dies me deficeret, si omnium exempla commemorare
units.tr: Furthermore, Zechariah was troubled at the sight of the angel, and fear fell upon him. This is an example of human weakness, which is known to have a place even in the saints. For remnants of the flesh remain in them, which could not bear the brightness and power of divine and heavenly glory. Thus we read that Daniel was once so dismayed at the sight and voice of an angel that no strength remained in him. And the three disciples likewise lay as if half-dead when it was their lot to see the glorified Christ and with him Elijah and Moses. And John afterwards suffered the same again when he saw the angel who was revealing to him the future fates of the Church. But the day would fail me if I wished to recount the examples of all those who have experienced this in themselves.

units.la: Apoc.1. morare velim, qui hoc in semetipsis experti sunt. Sunt haec nobis observanda, ne fidem facilè apud nos inueniant fanatici impostores, qui visionibus crebris gloriantur, & quasi otiosi spectatores diu fuerint, de regni caelorum mysterijs differunt. Nam hoc uno argumento satis se ipse produnt, quòd à sanctorum ingenio & moribus alienissimi sint. At si sancti angelorum conspectum & splendorem ferre non possunt, quid miseris nobis fiet, si suae iustitiae rigorem & diuinae maiestatis radios ad nostram contumaciam retundendam Deus exerat? Quam igitur stulti & infelices sunt, qui suis viribus & propria dignitati confidunt, cum vnius angeli vox nobis consternandis sufficere possit? Interim magno nostro bono rem ita instituit Deus. Quia coram Deo nunquam cum aliquo fructu apparebimus, nisi ad eius conspectum trepidemus, & verbo eius audito intra animos nostros percellamur. Notum enim est illud Domini apud Isaiam dicentis: Quem respiciam? pauperem & contritum spiritu, & qui ad verbum meum contremiscit. In horum consideratione nos hodie frequenter versari conueniebat. Instant undique pericula omnis generis, & in omnibus prope mundi partibus irati Dei indicia apparent. Intonat idem ille verbo suo, quo & scelera hominum increpat, & poenas graviores minatur. Tempus ergo est, ut ingenuum Dei timorem animis nostris concipiamus, & sub eius manu humiliati totis cordibus conteramur, spem verò salutis incocussam seruemus in illius misericordia & bonitate, cuius nobis Mediator est Iesus Christus; cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Apoc. 1. Let us note these things, so that fanatical impostors, who boast of frequent visions and, having been idle spectators for a long time, discourse about the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, may not easily find credence among us. For by this one argument they sufficiently betray themselves, that they are most alien from the disposition and manners of the saints. But if the saints cannot bear the sight and brightness of the angels, what will become of us wretches, if God should display the rigour of his righteousness and the rays of his divine majesty to crush our stubbornness? How foolish and unhappy, then, are those who trust in their own strength and their own dignity, when the voice of a single angel can suffice to terrify us! Meanwhile God has arranged the matter so for our great good. For we shall never appear before God with any profit unless we tremble at his sight, and are struck to the heart on hearing his Word. For that saying of the Lord in Isaiah is well known: "On whom shall I look? On the poor and contrite in spirit, and on him who trembles at my word." It was fitting that we should often dwell on this consideration today. Dangers of every kind press on us from all sides, and signs of the wrath of God appear in almost every part of the world. That same God thunders with his Word, by which he both rebukes the sins of men and threatens heavier punishments. It is time, then, for us to conceive in our minds a genuine fear of God, and, humbled under his hand, to be crushed with our whole hearts; but let us keep our hope of salvation unshaken in his mercy and goodness, of which Jesus Christ is our Mediator, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 4.

units.la: Dixit autem ei Angelus: Ne time Zacharia: nam exaudita est deprecatio tua, uxorque tua Elizabetha gignet tibi filium, & vocabis nomen eius Ioannem. Et erit tibi gaudio & exultatione, atque multi super eius nativitate gaudebunt. Erit enim magnus in conspectu Domini, & vinum siceramque non bibet: & spiritu sancto implebitur etiam ab utero matris suae: multosque filiorum Israel conuertet ad Dominum Deum ipsorum. Et ipse praecedet in conspectu eius cum Spiritu & virtute Eliae, ut conuertat corda patrum in filios, & rebelles ad prudentiam iustorum, ut paret Domino populum instructum.
units.tr: But the angel said to him: "Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great in the sight of the Lord, and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, and he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to prepare a people fit for the Lord."

units.la: Quemadmodum in uno Iesu Christo habentur quaecunque ad salutem & conseruationem humani generis faciunt: ita omnium, quae scripta sunt in sacris literis, hic proprius finis & scopus est, ut in veram Christi cognitionem adducamur; & in ipsum credendo vitam assequamur aeternam. Debet ergo ad hunc finem quoque referri tota Ioannis Baptistae historia. Quia enim hic Iesu Christi praecursor, adeoque primus noui Testamenti minister fuit, eius natales, educatio, vitae genus & quaecunque ab illo gesta sunt, ideo ab Euangelistis describuntur, ut maior sit apud nos doctrinae eius, & testimonij, quod de Christo tulit, authoritas. Et in natales quidem illius duo inciduntur in primis memorabilia. Primum, quòd ex matre sterili natus est: ex quo apparet, ipsum à Deo ex peculiari gratia datum fuisse, ut olim Isaacum, Samsonem, Samuelem, & similes, quorum opera & ministerio Deus adres praeclaras vsus est. Alterum, quòd eius conceptio & nativitas praedicitur ab Angelo: vnde rursus colligi potuit, hominem fore non vulgarem. Sed praestat Angelum loquentem audire, cuius oratio duabus omnino partibus constat. Priori consolatur Zachariam, quem subita illius apparitione consternatum fuisse nuper audiuimus. Altera de Ioannis dignitate & officio disserit.
units.tr: Just as all things that serve the salvation and preservation of the human race are found in Jesus Christ alone, so the proper end and aim of all that is written in the sacred letters is that we be brought to the true knowledge of Christ, and by believing in him attain eternal life. The whole history of John the Baptist must therefore also be referred to this end. Since he was the forerunner of Jesus Christ, and so the first minister of the New Testament, the Evangelists describe his birth, upbringing, manner of life, and all that he did, so that the teaching and the testimony he bore concerning Christ may carry greater authority with us. Concerning his birth, two things in particular are worthy of note. The first is that he was born of a barren mother. From this it appears that he was given by God through a special grace, as once Isaac, Samson, Samuel and others like them were, through whose work and ministry God accomplished illustrious things. The second is that his conception and birth are foretold by an angel, from which again it could be gathered that he would be no ordinary man. But it is better to hear the angel speaking, whose address consists of two entirely distinct parts. In the first he consoles Zechariah, who, as we heard recently, had been dismayed by the sudden appearance of the angel. The second part deals with the dignity and office of John.

units.la: Consolationis propositio & summa est, Ne time Zacharia. Dum timere vetat, simul vt animum spe bona & gaudio impleat iubet. Quia tamen hominis mens timorem aliqua graui causa conceptum non facile excutit, rationes profert, quibus territum & timentem confirmet. Prima exilis est, quòd deprecationem eius exauditam esse dicit à Deo. Id verò Dei nobis propitij argumentum est certissimum, & cur sibi ab aliquo metuant, qui Deum sibi fauere norunt? Interim debet hinc doctrina generalis peti, preces nimirum nostras à Deo exaudiri, siquidem ex fide promanent, & ea petamus, quæ ad illustrandam Dei gloriam & ad salutem nostram faciunt. Sunt de hac re promissiones, in quibus non fallet nos Deus, qui ipsissima est Veritas. In die tribulationis (inquit) invoca me, & liberabo te. Item: Fiet, vt priusquàm invocent, ego respondeam: & adhuc illis loquentibus, ego exaudiam. Et in Euangelio Christus ait: Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, dabit vobis pater. Neque nos ideo desperare oportet de Dei fide, si aliquandiu opem promissam differat, & non statim ea largiatur quæ petimus. Nostro etenim bono hoc facit, quorum fidem exercet ac probat, & quibus interdum crucis disciplina magis quàm liberatio necessaria est. Tunc autem nos soletur, quod dum opem ille differt, fidelis tamen est, neque nos supra vires tentari finit, sed interea spiritus sui gratia nos suffulcit, vt ijs ferendis sufficiamus, quæ nobis ab eo imponuntur. Exaudit verò & liberat, quàm primùm hoc nobis salutare fore videt. Nostrum ergo fuerit illum expectare constanti fide & cum silentio, vt Dauid loquitur: non quidem quoad preces, in quibus nos assiduos & indefessos esse conuenit: sed ne morae impatientia superati murmuremus, & illius accusemus iudicia.
units.tr: The proposition and summary of the consolation is: "Do not be afraid, Zechariah." While forbidding fear, he at the same time bids him fill his mind with good hope and joy. Yet because a man's mind does not easily shake off fear conceived from some serious cause, he offers reasons by which to strengthen the one who is terrified and afraid. The first is slight: he says that his prayer has been heard by God. Yet this is the most certain sign of God's favour toward us, and why should those fear anyone who know that God is favourable to them? Meanwhile a general doctrine should be drawn from this, namely that our prayers are indeed heard by God, provided they proceed from faith, and we ask for those things which serve to illustrate God's glory and our salvation. There are promises on this matter, in which God, who is very Truth itself, will not deceive us. "In the day of trouble," he says, "call upon me, and I will deliver you." Likewise: "It shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear." And in the Gospel Christ says: "Whatever you ask in my name, the Father will give it to you." Nor ought we on that account to despair of God's faithfulness if he delays the help promised for some time and does not at once grant what we ask. For he does this for our good, whose faith he exercises and proves, and for whom at times the discipline of the cross is more necessary than deliverance. Then this should console us: while he delays help, he is nevertheless faithful, and he does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but in the meantime sustains us by the grace of his Spirit, so that we are equal to bearing what he lays upon us. He hears and delivers as soon as he sees that this will be salutary for us. It is therefore our part to wait for him with constant faith and in silence, as David speaks; not indeed as regards prayer, in which we ought to be constant and untiring, but lest, overcome by impatience at the delay, we murmur and accuse his judgments.

units.la: Admonet præterea nos hæc Angeli apparitio, quanta cum religione & modestia nos inter precandum versari deceat. Nam etsi non semper nobis etiam specie visibili angeli appareant, certum tamen est, illos nobis præsentes adesse, vt nos tueantur & obseruent. Castrametatur (inquit Psaltes) Angelus Domini circa eos, qui ipsum timent & eripit eos. Orantibus autem potissimum adesse angelos, Paulus quoque credidit, & ideo mulieres monet, vt in cœtibus sacris honestè velentur, idque propter angelos, si minus apud ipsas valeat honestatis publicæ ratio. At quid de angelis dicere opus est, quando ipsum Dei filium precantium cœtibus medium interesse, ex illius promissione constat, quam nuper adduximus? Vtinam verò huius meminissent, qui superbo vestitu, fastuoso incessu & gestibus indecoris templa ingrediuntur, & ita agunt, vt libidini potius suæ quàm pietati studere videantur. Qui principem supplices adeunt, ijs maxima cura est, ne illius oculos vel aures aliqua re offendant: Et nos impudenter & effronti proteruia in Dei conspectum ruimus, qui si vno momento suam nobis gratiam subducat, toti perimus?
units.tr: Moreover, this appearance of the angel admonishes us with how much reverence and modesty we ought to conduct ourselves while praying. For although angels do not always appear to us in visible form, it is nevertheless certain that they are present with us, to guard and watch over us. "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them," says the Psalmist. Paul also believed that angels are especially present to those who pray, and for this reason he admonishes women to be decently veiled in sacred assemblies, and that on account of the angels, if the consideration of public decency has less weight with them. But why speak of angels, when it is clear from the promise we recently cited that the Son of God himself is present in the midst of the assemblies of those who pray? Would that those would remember this who enter the churches in proud dress, with haughty bearing and indecorous gestures, and so act that they seem intent on their own lust rather than on piety! Those who approach a prince as suppliants take the greatest care not to offend his eyes or ears in any way. And we rush shamelessly and with brazen insolence into the sight of God, who, if he withdraws his grace from us for a single moment, we perish utterly?

units.la: Sed pergamus in Angeli verbis, qui alterum quoque consolationis argumentum profert, dicens: Vxor tua Elizabet gignet tibi filium. Et vxoris quidem diserte meminit, ne hac sublata & defuncta (quam procul dubio charissimam habebat) filium ex alia sibi nasciturum putaret. Indicant autem hæc Angeli verba, quid inter alia potissimum postularit à Deo Zacharias. Pro publica quidem populi totius salute illum cumprimis orauisse, non est dubium. Hoc enim inter Sacerdotum officia non postremum numeratur, quos Christi mediatoris personam sustinuisse scimus. Simul tamen cum publicis precibus priuatas quoque coniunxit Zacharias, vt pro prubum sterilitatis abs se & vxore dilecta Deus removeret. Licet ergo pijs à Deo temporaria quoque bona petere, qualia sunt, bona valetudo, victus sufficiens, famæ integritas, commoda conjux, proles ingenua, honestum publicæ pacis otium, & quæ alia sunt huius generis. Tenenda tamen in his omnibus est regula, quam nobis Christus in orationis ab ipso præscriptæ formula & proprio exemplo commendauit: vt nimirum vota ista Dei voluntati subijciamus. Nec enim nobis certò constare potest, num ista dare velit Deus, aut num ea accipere nobis tutum & bonum sit. Admonet etiam nos hæc Angeli promissio, liberos à Deo dari, neque ex hominum voluntate & arbitrio illorum procreationem pendere. Nam is est, qui (vt Dauid olim dicebat) sterilem efficit matrem, quæ liberis gaudeat. Agnouit hoc ipsum Iacob patriarcha, qui Rahel cum stomacho dicenti, Da mihi liberos, alioqui morior: pia ira succensus respondit: Num Dei loco sum ego, qui prohibet ne parias? Prodest autem hoc tenere, vt inde discant parentes, patienter ferendos esse labores, qui in liberorum educationem incidunt, & eosdem Deo adduci & consecrari debere, qui nobis illos dedit. Est hoc non postremum verae pietatis officium, & Abrahamum hoc etiam nomine potissimum commendat Deus, quod suos in ipsius cognitione & timore instituere t.Vide Gene.18.
units.tr: But let us proceed with the words of the angel, who gives a second argument of consolation, saying: "Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son." He mentions the wife expressly, lest Zechariah should think that a son would be born to him from another woman, once she was taken away and dead, whom he undoubtedly held most dear. These words of the angel also indicate what, among other things, Zechariah had especially asked of God. That he had prayed above all for the public salvation of the whole people is not in doubt; for this is counted not the least of the duties of the priests, who, as we know, bore the person of Christ the Mediator. Yet together with public prayers Zechariah also joined private ones, that God would remove from him and his beloved wife the reproach of barrenness. It is therefore lawful for the godly to ask of God also temporal goods, such as good health, sufficient food, integrity of reputation, a pleasant spouse, well-born children, the honourable quiet of public peace, and other things of this kind. Yet in all these things the rule must be kept which Christ commended to us in the form of prayer he prescribed and by his own example: namely, that we subject these wishes to the will of God. For we cannot be certain whether God wishes to give these things, or whether it is safe and good for us to receive them. This promise of the angel also admonishes us that children are given by God, and that their procreation does not depend on the will and choice of men. For it is he who (as David once said) makes the barren mother to rejoice in her children. Jacob the patriarch also acknowledged this, who, when Rachel said to him in anger, "Give me children, or else I die," answered, moved by pious wrath: "Am I in God's place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?" It is useful to hold this, so that parents may learn to bear patiently the labours which fall upon the upbringing of children, and that those whom God has given us ought to be brought to God and consecrated to him. This is no small duty of true piety, and God especially commends Abraham for this, that he taught his own in the knowledge and fear of him. See Gen. 18.

units.la: Sequitur altera orationis Angeli pars, qua filium ex Elizabeta nasciturum describit. Et à nomine exorsus, Vocabis (inquit) nomen eius Ioannem. Huius autem admonet, cùm vt fidem fadem faciat ampliorem promissioni, tum ut magis consoletur territum. Ioann-es enim nomen He-braeis a gratia deducitur, & gratiosum significat. Neque temere sic dictus est, qui primus in no-uo Testamento sub Christi aduentum gratiae praeco esse debebat. At hic simul obseruabimus, quam curae sint Deo res mortalium, quando hunc nominum quoque nostrorum rationem cer-tam habere videmus. Quod enim hic fit, id ipsum saepe aliàs factum esse legimus. Abraha-mi certè & Sarae nomina Deus ipse mutauit. Et Cyri nomen Isaias praedixit annis circiter du-centis priusquam ille nasceretur. Christum praeterea discipulis nonnullis nomina noua impositi-se Euangelistae testantur. Quanto magis ergo nostra corpora, vitae dies, valetudo, animarum sa-lus & reliqua diuinae prouidentiae consilio aeterno dispensantur & reguntur? Vidit hoc olim Da-uid, quando dicebat: Oculi tui me viderunt Domine, cum essem foetus informis, & in libro tuo vniuersa descripta fuerunt, quae longo post tempore formarentur, &c. Et Christus pilos capitis no-stri numeratos dicit, & idem Dei prouidentiam ad passerculos, pullos coruorum & floscul-os in agris nascentes extendit. Debet nos istorum consideratio consolari, ne facile desperemus in tentatio-nibus & periculis. Cur enim animarum nostrarum salutem negligat, qui corporibus tam liberali-ter prospexit? Aut qua ratione eorum, qui iam sunt, curam deponat, qui nos priusquam essemus & vitae nostrae dies atque fortunas omnes descripsit? Negant hoc quidem Epicurei, & qui ex suo arbitrio res suas pendere arbitrantur: qui ideo vel excusso omni Dei timore in omnem li-centiam ruunt, vel incertis consiliis semetipsos deludunt, & tandem in grauioribus periculis despe-ratione infelici absorbentur: cum interea ad omnem euentum parati & in quouis casu intrepidi & inuicti consistant, qui in aeternam Dei prouidentiam intenti, huic se & res suas omnes subijce-re didicerunt.
units.tr: The second part of the angel's speech follows, in which he describes the son to be born of Elizabeth. Beginning with the name, he says: "You shall call his name John." He admonishes Zechariah of this, partly to make the promise more credible, and partly to comfort him more, since he was terrified. For the name John is derived in Hebrew from grace, and means gracious. Nor was he rightly so named by chance, since he was to be the herald of grace at the coming of Christ in the New Testament. But here we shall also observe how much God cares for human affairs, since we see that he keeps an exact account even of the reasons for our names. For what is done here, we read has often been done at other times. Indeed God himself changed the names of Abraham and Sarah. And Isaiah foretold the name of Cyrus about two hundred years before he was born. Moreover, the Evangelists testify that Christ gave new names to some of his disciples. How much more, then, are our bodies, the days of our lives, our health, the salvation of our souls, and the rest, dispensed and governed by the eternal counsel of divine providence? David saw this long ago, when he said: "Your eyes saw me, Lord, when I was an unformed embryo, and in your book all things were written which were to be formed over a long time, etc." And Christ says that the hairs of our head are numbered, and he extends the providence of God to the sparrows, the young ravens, and the little flowers growing in the fields. The consideration of these things ought to console us, so that we do not easily despair in temptations and dangers. For why would he neglect the salvation of our souls, who has so liberally cared for our bodies? Or by what reasoning would he lay aside the care of those who now exist, he who, before we existed, has described both the days and all the fortunes of our lives? The Epicureans deny this, and those who think that their affairs depend on their own judgment; these either, having cast off all fear of God, rush into every license, or deceive themselves with uncertain plans, and at last, in graver dangers, are swallowed up by unhappy despair. Meanwhile those who, intent on the eternal providence of God, have learned to submit themselves and all their affairs to it, stand ready for every outcome and steadfast and unconquered in every case.

units.la: Caeterum ipse Angelus nominis istius rationem aliqua ex parte reddens, addit: Et erit tibi gaudio & exultationi, atque multi super eius natiuitate gaudebunt. Fuit hoc addendum necessa-rio, quia multi filij parentibus dolorem afferunt, quod interdum sanctissimis quoque Dei cultori-bus accidere videmus, & olim hanc calamitatem passi sunt Abraham quoad Ismaelem filium, Isaac quoad Esauum, Iacob item & Dauid, quorum filij incestibus, parricidijs & omni scele-rum genere se polluerunt. Quod autem de Ioanne dicitur, mox in eius natiuitate impleri coepit, quae parentibus & toti cognationi gaudium & exultationem peperit, ut suo loco audiemus. Ma-ior tamen postea exultatio secuta est, quando regnum Dei iam appropinquans annunciare coe-pit, & promissum diuque expectatum humani generis redemptorem digito monstrauit. Tunc enim totis animis gauisi sunt, qui prius peccatorum conscientia & malis undique incumbentibus pres-si gemebant. Etenim non alia maior & iustior gaudij causa pijs offertur, quam ex Christi praedi-catione, in quo Deum sibi reconciliatum & aeternae vitae thesauros repositos esse intelligunt. In-terim sibijpsis exemplum Ioannis applicare debent omnes iuuenes, ut sui officij esse meminerint parentibus gaudij & laetitiae materiam praebere. Iubet hoc Lex naturae, quae ut gratias dignas be-nefactoribus referamus praecipit. Et quia liberi cum dolore procreantur, & eorundem educa-tio a pueris curarum, laborum & molestiarum plena est, nimium profecto ingrati, & vitae hu-ius vsu indigni sunt, qui iam adulti parentibus nouas molestias & dolorem acerbiorem exhibent, dum effreni contumacia illorum senectam contristant, aut sceleribus suis toti familiae infamiam & ignominiam pariunt. Punit ingratitudinem istam Deus admodum gravibus supplicijs, ut mul-torum exempla testantur, & plerunque fit, ut qui tales sunt, vel immatura morte pereant, vel summo cum dedecore et infamia vitae dies prorogent. Facile autem sibi cauebunt, si verae sapientiae studeant, cuius principium est timor Domini. Tunc enim vitam omnem ad Dei praescriptum in-stituent, & morum honestate omni, virtutum genere illustres erunt, atque Dei benedictione ver-rima fruentur. Itaque parentibus quoque honori sunt & ijsdem gaudium ferunt exoptatissimum. Hocigitur maxime spectauit Solomon, cum diceret: Filius sapiens exhilarat patrem, at stultus fi-lius moeror est matri suae, Proverbiorum decimo. Peccatur in hoc multum hodie, & quod maxi-me dolendum est, fere parentum culpa peccatur. Zachariae gaudio fuit Ioannes, quod eum Deo con-secratum & fidelem Iesu Christi seruum fore audiret. Et si vitam ei tam diu concessit Deus, non dubium est, quin ex illo summam voluptatem caeperit, quando ille suo officio tam probe functus est. At hodie plerosque pudet minister evangelici, & filios malunt diabolo consecratos esse, qui opibus per fas nefasque partis superbiant, & apud mundum in pretio sint, quam qui praedicatione verbi Dei sibi ipsis odium & invidiam multorum accersant. Sunt ergo digni, qui poenas dent, & qui ipsi quoque ex liberis fructum nullum percipiant, quos ad Dei servitium destinare noluerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the angel himself, giving some account of the name, adds: "And it will be a joy and gladness to you, and many will rejoice at his birth." This had to be added, because many sons bring grief to their parents. We see this happen even to the most holy worshippers of God. Abraham suffered this calamity with regard to his son Ishmael, Isaac with regard to Esau, and Jacob and David likewise, whose sons polluted themselves with incest, murder and every kind of wickedness. What is said of John began to be fulfilled at once at his birth, which brought joy and gladness to his parents and to all their kin, as we shall hear in its place. A greater joy followed later, when he began to proclaim the kingdom of God now at hand and pointed with his finger to the Redeemer of the human race, who had been promised and long awaited. Then those who had previously groaned, oppressed by consciousness of their sins and by evils pressing on them from every side, rejoiced with their whole souls. For no greater or more just cause of joy is offered to the godly than the preaching of Christ, in whom they understand that God has been reconciled to them and the treasures of eternal life have been laid up. Meanwhile, all young people ought to apply the example of John to themselves, remembering that it is their duty to provide their parents with a source of joy and gladness. The law of nature commands this, which requires us to return thanks worthy of benefactors. And because children are born with pain, and their upbringing from infancy is full of cares, labours and troubles, those who, once grown, bring fresh troubles and more bitter grief to their parents, by their unbridled obstinacy saddening their old age or by their crimes bringing disgrace and dishonour on the whole family, are truly most ungrateful and unworthy of the use of this life. God punishes such ingratitude with very severe penalties, as the examples of many attest, and it often happens that such people either perish by an untimely death or spend their days of life with the greatest shame and infamy. They will guard themselves easily, however, if they devote themselves to true wisdom, whose beginning is the fear of the Lord. For then they will order their whole life according to God's rule, and will be distinguished by every kind of moral integrity and variety of virtues, and will enjoy the truest blessing of God. Thus they also are an honour to their parents and bring them the most desired joy. This is what Solomon especially had in view when he said: "A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is a grief to his mother," Proverbs 10. Today this is sinned against a great deal, and what is most to be lamented, the sin is mostly committed through the fault of the parents. John was a joy to Zechariah because he heard that his son would be consecrated to God and would be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ. And if God granted him a long life, there is no doubt that he drew the greatest pleasure from him when he discharged his office so well. But today most people are ashamed of a minister of the gospel, and prefer their sons to be consecrated to the devil, who swell with pride in wealth gained by right or wrong and are held in esteem by the world, rather than to those who bring upon themselves the hatred and ill will of many through the preaching of the Word of God. Therefore they deserve to be punished, and they themselves will receive no fruit from their children, whom they were unwilling to dedicate to the service of God.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Angelum, qui quod de Ioanne in genere dixerat, diligentius exponit, & ita paulatim descendit ad officii sui, quo functurus erat, descriptionem. Erit magnus (inquit) coram Domino: nimirum propter dotes eximias, & quod ipsdem bene utetur ad Dei gloriam propagandam. Quia vero coram Domino magnum fore dicit, non obscure docet ea locutione, eam demum veram gloriam esse, si Dei iudicio magni sumus. Mundi enim gloria incerta & instabilis est, ut quae leui momento in extremam ignominiam convertitur: ut in eorum exemplis est videre, qui olim Magni dicti sunt. Inter quos primus fere nominatur Alexander Macedonum Rex: qui etsi victorijs amplissimis hoc nomen sibi acquisuisset, subita tamen morte abreptus vitam una cum gloria finiuit, & haeredibus nihil praeter infelicem bellorum civilium materiam reliquit, quibus maxima orbis terrarum pars aliquandiu laboravit. Inter Romanos autem Magnus dictus fuit Pompeius, qui paulo post urbe profugus, & in acie victus in Aegyptum confugit, & illi bili lethi genere occubuit. Quid autem de Fabio dicemus, qui cum Maximi titulum meruisset, Scipioni, iuvenili audacia ferocienti, cedere coactus fuit, & cum huius potentiam patriae aliquando periculosam fore putaret, ideoque successorem ei substituendum esse sentiret, magnam sibi apud omnes invidiam conflauit, quasi morosus & invidus esset, & iam affecta aetate Hannibalem timeret? Et quod de his dicitur, hoc idem de multis dici potest, & similem fortunam in multis quotidie cernimus, qui dum altius conscendere indies conantur, mox praeter omnium expectationem praecipites ruunt. Longe alia est piorum conditio, qui dum in paruo fideles sunt (ut Christus ait) super multa constituuntur, & tandem in gloriam herifui ingrediuntur, quae ut nullis hominum iudicijs subiacet, ita sibi ipsi semper constat & aeternum durat. Confirmatur hoc Ioannis exemplo, quem etiamsi sacerdotes & scribae contemptui habuerint, Herodes item in carceribus ignominiose nimis occidi curarit, coram Domino tamen magnus fuit, & immortali gloria inter pios florebit quoad mundi huius machina superstes fuerit.
units.tr: But let us return to the angel, who, having said in general what he had said about John, now explains it more carefully and so gradually descends to the description of the office he was to fulfil. "He will be great," he says, "before the Lord": clearly on account of his outstanding gifts, and because he would use them well to spread the glory of God. But because he says that he will be great before the Lord, he teaches, in that manner of speaking, not obscurely that true glory is that by which we are great in God's judgment. For the glory of the world is uncertain and unstable, since in a short moment it turns into utter disgrace, as can be seen in the examples of those who were once called "Great." Among them, the first to be named is almost always Alexander, king of the Macedonians, who, although he had won this name for himself by very great victories, was nevertheless carried off by a sudden death, ending his life together with his glory, and left his heirs nothing but the unhappy cause of civil wars, by which the greatest part of the world laboured for a long time. Among the Romans, Pompey was called "the Great," who, shortly afterwards, fleeing from the city and defeated in battle, took refuge in Egypt and perished by a base kind of death. And what shall we say of Fabius, who, although he had earned the title of "the Greatest," was forced to give way to Scipio, who was boiling over with youthful audacity, and who, thinking that the power of this man would one day be dangerous to his country, and feeling that a successor should therefore be appointed to him, brought upon himself great hatred from everyone, as if he were a sullen and envious man, and as if, in his advanced age, he feared Hannibal? And what is said of these men can be said of many others, and we daily see a similar fortune in many who, while they strive to climb ever higher day by day, soon fall headlong beyond everyone's expectation. Far different is the condition of the godly, who, being faithful in small things (as Christ says), are set over many things, and at last enter into the glory of their lord, which, since it is subject to no human judgments, always remains consistent with itself and endures for ever. This is confirmed by the example of John, whom, although the priests and scribes held in contempt, and Herod too shamefully saw to it that he was put to death in prison, nevertheless he was great before the Lord, and he will flourish among the godly with immortal glory for as long as the frame of this world endures.

units.la: Porro vitae etiam genus describitur, quod Ioannes securus sit, & hoc una quasi nota designat Angelus, dicens: Et vinum siceramque non bibet. Sicera Hebraeis a Schachar dicitur omnis potus, qui inebriandi vim habet. Notatur autem hac locutione genus vitae asperum & durum, quale Nazaraeorum fuit, quibus inter alia vini quoque & siceræ usus interdictus fuit. Itaque verborum istorum sensus est, Ioannem sic consecratum fore Deo, ut omnia caveat, quae ipsum vel ab officio revocare, vel contemptum facere possint. In primis autem vinum & siceram nominat, non quod his uti impium sit (ut olim Encratitae haretici sentiebant) sed quia in horum usu fere intemperantia peccatur, et ebrietate nihil nocentius est ijs, qui ad res magnas sunt destinati. Nam ut in Hosea dicitur, scortatio & vinum sive siceram auferunt cor hominis, ut & officij sui prorsus sit immemor, & ea designet, quorum ipsum postea vehementer pudet, & quae apud omnes contemptissimum reddunt. Exemplo nobis esse possunt Noa et Lothus, quibus vinum intemperantius sumptum imposuit, ut turpissime peccarint, & sibi ipsis doloris nunquam finiendi causa fuerint. Sed exemplis veteribus minime opus est, quando multa horum similia quotidie fiunt, quae ebrietatis odium omnibus conciliare poterant, nisi plerique iampridem cum pudore & ratione sensum quoque omnem exuissent. Hoc unum si hodie omnes diligentius expenderent, non mirarentur eorum fere omnium authoritatem concidisse, qui sua prudentia & consilio alijs praeesse debebant. Quid enim aliud fiat, quando apud viros principes, urbium magistratus, iudices, praefectos, patresfamilias item & non paucos ecclesiarum ministros atque pastores ebrietas regnat? Solebant olim Spartani servos vino multo ebrios in publicum producere, ut indecoris illorum gestibus & moribus visis Iuniores ebrietatem fugere discerent. At hodie spectacula talia nobis passim exhibent, quos virtutis exempla esse decebat, & ex illis voluptatem capiunt, quorum erat disciplinam meliorem in republica & ecclesia constituere. Non ergo mirum est, si omnia in peius ruant.
units.tr: Furthermore, the manner of life of John is also described, namely that he will be abstinent, and the angel marks this with a single sign, saying: "And he will not drink wine or strong drink." Among the Hebrews, every drink that has the power to intoxicate is called schachar [שכר] (here, "Schachar" as transliterated). By this expression is indicated a harsh and austere way of life, such as that of the Nazarites, among whom the use of wine and strong drink was forbidden, among other things. The meaning of these words, therefore, is that John would be so consecrated to God that he would avoid everything that could either call him back from his office or make him contemptible. He names wine and strong drink in particular, not because it is wrong to use them (as the heretical Encratites of old held), but because intemperance is almost always committed in their use, and nothing is more harmful than drunkenness to those who are destined for great things. For, as is said in Hosea, fornication and wine or strong drink take away the heart of a man, so that he becomes utterly forgetful of his office, and does those things of which he is afterwards greatly ashamed and which make him utterly despised by all. Noah and Lot can serve us as examples, whom too immoderately drunk wine led into the most shameful sins, and who became for themselves a cause of grief that never ended. But there is no need of ancient examples, since many similar things happen every day, which might have won everyone's hatred of drunkenness, unless most people had long since cast off with shame and reason all sense of decency. If only everyone today weighed this one thing more carefully, they would not wonder that the authority of almost all those who ought to preside over others by their wisdom and counsel has collapsed. For what else can happen when drunkenness reigns among princely men, magistrates of cities, judges, governors, heads of households likewise, and not a few ministers and pastors of churches? The Spartans used once to lead their slaves, made drunk with much wine, into public view, so that the younger men, seeing their unseemly gestures and manners, might learn to flee drunkenness. But today men who ought to be examples of virtue exhibit such spectacles to us everywhere, and take pleasure in them, when it was their duty to establish better discipline in the commonwealth and the Church. It is no wonder, then, if all things are going from bad to worse.

units.la: Ac ne
units.tr: And lest

units.la: At ne quis Ioannem ista ex semetipso habituram putaret, causam efficientem horum omnium indicat Angelus his verbis: Et Spiritu sancto implebitur etiam ab utero matris suæ. Cuius prodigi missionis specimen infra videbimus, quando sex mensium fœtus in utero matris adhuc delitescens exilijt ad occursum Mariæ virginis, quæ Spiritus sancti virtute impregnata Dei filium concepérat. Nos autem Ioannis exemplo docemur, ex Deo manere ea omnia, quæ nos magnos & rebus arduis atque præclaris idoneos reddunt. Nam si ad nostram originem descendas, nihil præter deploratissimam naturæ corruptionem invenies. In peccatis siquidem concipimur & nascimur, & figmenta cordis nostri prava sunt ab ineunte ætate. Quo fit, ut Paulo teste, ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, nisi nos singularis spiritus sui gratia Deus dignetur. Et ideo de semetipso idem ille dicebat: Gratia Dei sum quod sum. Quod ipsum omnes alij senserunt, qui in scripturis propter fidem & pietatem commendantur. Sunt ergo nimium vani & insolentes, qui suas vires iactant & meritorum suorum fiducia superbiunt. Quid enim habent, quod non acceperint? Imo si eos propius inspiciamus, fere alijs infirmiores sunt, qui tam magna sibi ipsis de sua virtute pollicentur. Est præterea Ioannis exemplum hoc etiam nomine diligentius observandum, quod in eo apparet, infantes quoque Spiritus sancti & donorum eius capaces esse, & proinde neque à fide neque à regni Dei communione alienos censeri debere. Nam etiamsi peculiaris quædam spiritus gratia in Ioanne eluxerit, de reliquis tamen minime putandum est, quòd Spiritu sancto in vniversum careant. Etenim credentium infantes quoque fædere salutis contineri notius est, quàm ut demonstratione opus habeat, & ideo ijdem ex Dei instituto circuncidi & in ecclesiæ societatem recipi solebant. Paulus vero de imparibus coniugijs fidelium cum infidelibus loquens eos infantes sanctos vocat, qui ex alterutro solum parente fideli nascebantur. Atqui sanctius nemo fuerit absque spiritu Dei, qui ut nos huc consecrat, ita fidem & omnis generis bona in nobis operatur. Superat tamen hæc omnia Christi testimonium, qui parvulos in se credere dicit, & ut eos ipsi adducamus præcipit. Quod si autem nos non possumus intelligere, quomodo fides in illis locum habeat, non tamen ideo falsi accusandus est Christus, cùm infinita alia fieri certò constet, quorum rationem & modum ipsi non percipimus. Seruiunt hæc confutandis Anabaptistis, qui infantibus baptismum negant, & eosdem ab Ecclesiæ communione arcent, & ita noui Testamenti conditionem deteriorem faciunt quàm veteris fuerit. Furiosum planè et contumax hominum genus, qui dum pietatem summam simulant, neq; Dei gratiam agnoscunt, neque Ecclesiæ vnionem conseruare student, quam ille in primis saluam manere vult.
units.tr: And lest anyone think that John would have these things from himself, the Angel names the efficient cause of all of them in these words: "And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb." We shall see below a sample of this extraordinary mission, when the six-month-old foetus, still hidden in its mother's womb, leapt at the approach of the Virgin Mary, who had conceived the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit. But from the example of John we learn that all those qualities which make us great and fit for difficult and distinguished tasks come from God. For if you trace our origin, you will find nothing but the most desperate corruption of nature. We are conceived and born in sins, and the imaginations of our heart are evil from our earliest age. Hence it follows, as Paul testifies, that we are not even fit to think, unless God deigns to favour us with the singular grace of his Spirit. And so the same man said of himself: "By the grace of God I am what I am." All the others also felt this, who are commended in the Scriptures for their faith and piety. They are therefore excessively vain and arrogant who boast of their own powers and swell with pride in their confidence in their merits. For what do they have that they have not received? Indeed, if we look at them more closely, they are almost weaker than others, who promise themselves such great things about their own virtue. Moreover, John's example is to be observed more carefully for this reason too, that in him it appears that infants also are capable of the Holy Spirit and of his gifts, and therefore should not be counted as strangers either to faith or to fellowship in the kingdom of God. For although a peculiar grace of the Spirit shone forth in John, we must not think that the rest are entirely without the Holy Spirit. Indeed, that the infants of believers are also contained in the covenant of salvation is too well known to need demonstration, and for that reason they were circumcised by God's appointment and were accustomed to be received into the fellowship of the Church. Paul, however, speaking of the unequal marriages of believers with unbelievers, calls holy those infants who were born of only one believing parent. Yet no one can be holier without the Spirit of God, who, as he consecrates us here, so also works faith and every kind of good in us. Christ's testimony surpasses all these things, however, when he says that little children believe in him, and commands us to bring them to him. But if we cannot understand how faith has a place in them, Christ is nonetheless not to be accused of falsehood, since it is certain that countless other things happen whose reason and manner we do not perceive. These things serve to refute the Anabaptists, who deny baptism to infants, exclude them from communion in the Church, and so make the condition of the New Testament worse than that of the Old. They are a plainly frantic and obstinate kind of men, who, while they pretend the highest piety, neither acknowledge the grace of God nor strive to preserve the unity of the Church, which he above all wishes to remain safe.

units.la: Sed omissis vafanis Ecclesiæ turbatoribus, ad Angelum reuertamur, qui de officio Ioannis apertius differere incipit, docens primò cui rei ipsum Deus destinarit, deinde quomodo commissum sibi munus sit obiturus, tandem functionis eius effectum exprimit. Officij aut muneris huius summam his verbis comprehendit: Multos filiorum Israel conuertet ad Dominum Deum ipsorum. Ita vero munus prædicandi verbi Dei definit, in quo præcipuum est, ut homines Deo adducantur. Sunt hi natura ab illo alieni, & vel circa superstitiones & idololatriam, vel circa peccandi licentiam & manifesta scelera occupantur. Et quia ipsi sua sponte non redeunt in viam, adhæc Dei conspectum horrent, cuius voluntatem cum suis studijs pugnare sentiunt, ab alijs conuertantur & reducantur oportet. In eum ergo finem Verbi sui præcones seu administros Deus instituit, qui pœnitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum prædicatione (quibus partibus Euangelij doctrina absoluitur, ut Lucæ vltimo Christus docet) homines conuertant. Id vero illo tempore tunc in primis factio opus erat. Nam etsi Iudæorum populus Dei veri cognitionem atque cultum profiteretur, illum tamen pleriq; ignorabant, cum neglecto redemptore patribus promisso, hominum traditiones sequerentur, qui salutem in legalium operum meritis monstrabant. Imò qui sub vno Deo eiusdem fidei & religionis vestigijs incedere debebant, in sectas diuersas erant scissi, quas sub Ioanne Hircano annis ante natum Christum circiter centum triginta exortas fuisse alibi diximus. Et hic quidem præclara operam nauauit Ioannes, quando & peccata grauiter accusauit, & ad pœnitentiam omnes hortatus est, simulq; peccatorum remissionem in vno Christo monstrauit, quem agnum illum Dei esse docuit, qui peccatum mundi tollat. Et hæc illa doctrinæ forma est, quam in Ecclesia constanter retinere debent, qui homines saluos volunt; simulq; confutantur huius loci authoritate, qui auditores suos aliò remittunt, quàm ad vnum Deum, quem prophetæ & apostoli prædicauerunt. Clamant hodie aduersarij, redeundum nobis esse ad Romanam ecclesiam: at nos ecclesiam nullam nouimus, quàm quæ Dominum Deum patrem nostrum agnoscit, & hunc per fidem Iesu Christi colit in spiritu & in veritate. Ab hac quia nos minimè defecisse scimus, nulla nobis conuersione opus est: pœnitentia autem & vitæ emendatione, & vt in fide indies proficiamus nobis opus esse fatemur, & libenter omnibus ijs gratum obsequium præstabimus, qui nos suo studio & industria iuuare poterunt.
units.tr: But, leaving aside those crafty disturbers of the Church, let us return to the Angel, who begins to speak more plainly about John's office, teaching first for what purpose God appointed him, then how he is to discharge the duty entrusted to him, and finally expresses the result of his function. He summarises the sum of this office or duty in these words: "He shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God." Thus he defines the function of preaching the Word of God, the chief part of which is that men be brought to God. They are by nature alienated from him, and are occupied either with superstitions and idolatry, or with licence to sin and manifest crimes. And because they do not return to the way of their own accord, and moreover shrink from the sight of God, whose will they feel to be at odds with their own pursuits, they must be converted and led back by others. To this end God has appointed heralds or ministers of his Word, who by preaching repentance and the forgiveness of sins (which are the parts by which the doctrine of the Gospel is summed up, as Christ teaches at the end of Luke) convert men. And this work was especially needed at that time. For although the people of the Jews professed the knowledge and worship of the true God, most of them were ignorant of him; neglecting the Redeemer promised to the fathers, they followed the traditions of men, who showed salvation in the merits of legal works. Indeed, those who ought to walk in the footsteps of one God, of the same faith and religion, were split into diverse sects, which we have elsewhere said arose about one hundred and thirty years before the birth of Christ, under John Hyrcanus. Here John indeed performed an excellent work, when he both accused sins severely and exhorted all to repentance, and at the same time showed the forgiveness of sins in Christ alone, whom he taught to be that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. This is the form of doctrine which those who wish men to be saved ought constantly to retain in the Church; and at the same time this passage refutes those who send their hearers anywhere rather than to the one God, whom the prophets and apostles preached. Today our adversaries cry out that we must return to the Roman Church. But we know no church other than that which acknowledges the Lord God as its Father, and worships him in spirit and in truth through faith in Jesus Christ. Since we know that we have by no means departed from this, we have no need of any conversion; but we confess that we need repentance, amendment of life, and daily progress in faith, and we shall gladly render a grateful service to all those who can help us by their zeal and diligence.

units.la: Secundo loco modum & rationem indicat Angelus, quam in obeundo munere suo Ioannes sit secuturus. Præcedet (inquit) in conspectu eius (nimirum præconis aut præcursoris instar) cum spiritu & virtute Eliæ. Vbi ante omnia euidens & irrefragabile diuinitatis Iesu Christi argumentum obseruabis. Nam paulò ante de Domino Deo Israelis dixerat Angelus, ad quem omnes conuerti oporteat. Nunc Ioannem ante eius faciem præcessurum dicit. At præcessit ille in conspectu Christi: ergo hic Deus verus & æternus sit oportet, quem vetus Israel coluit. Frustra igitur nobis oblatrant Seruetani canes, qui infelicem Arianismum instaurare satagunt, & nescio quem Deum fingunt essentiatum, atque suo figmento ipsa Christianæ fidei fundamenta conuellunt. Quoad vero huius loci statum, cum Malachiæ vaticinio consentiunt Angeli verba. Ille enim de Messiæ aduentu differens, inter alia dixit: En ego mittam vobis Eliam prophetam, priusquam dies Domini magnus & terribilis veniat. Is reducet cor patrum in filios, & cor filiorum in patres, &c. Quem locum Iudæi vulgò de Elia Thesbite, sub Messiæ aduentum redituro, intellexerunt. Sed de Ioanne intelligendum esse, non solùm Angelus docet, verumetiam Christus apud Matthæum vnde cimo & decimoseptimo capite. Itaq; Ioannes non quidem Elias ille Thesbites est, sed Eliæ spiritu & virtute instructus ea præstitit, quæ olim ab Elia facta fuerunt. Et sanè omnia inter vtrumque probè conueniunt.
units.tr: In the second place the Angel indicates the manner and method which John is to follow in discharging his office. "He will go before him," he says, "in the sight of him (namely, like a herald or forerunner), with the spirit and power of Elijah." Here, above all, you will observe a clear and irrefutable proof of the divinity of Jesus Christ. For a little earlier the Angel had spoken of the Lord God of Israel, to whom all ought to be turned. Now he says that John will go before his face. But he went before the face of Christ; therefore the one whom old Israel worshipped must be the true and eternal God. In vain, then, do the Servetan dogs bark at us, who labour to revive the wretched Arianism, and invent I know not what God of a created essence, and by their fiction overthrow the very foundations of the Christian faith. As for the state of this passage, the words of the Angel agree with the prophecy of Malachi. For he, speaking of the coming of the Messiah, said among other things: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. He shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to the fathers," etc. The Jews generally understood this passage of Elijah the Tishbite, who was to return before the coming of the Messiah. But that it is to be understood of John, not only the Angel teaches, but also Christ in Matthew, chapters eleven and seventeen. Therefore John is not indeed that Elijah the Tishbite, but, furnished with the spirit and power of Elijah, he performed those things which were once done by Elijah. And indeed all the points of comparison between the two agree well.

units.la: Vt enim Eliæ tempora multis modis corruptissima fuerunt, quoad Dei cultum & publicos mores, eò quòd sub impio rege Achabo & sanguinaria Iezabele Baalis mysteria dominarentur: Ita non minor inter Iudæos religionis simul & disciplinæ publicæ corruptio fuit, cùm penes Herodem, hominem impium & sanguinarium, summa rerum potestas esset, scribæ verò & sacerdotes doctrinam vnà cum externo cultu fœdè corrupissent.
