Vt autem Elias admirabili constantia sese omnibus opposuit, & pœnas à Deo impijs destinatas prædixit: Ita Ioannes inuicta animi fortitudine Dei causam egit, & pœnitere nescijs exitium minatus est, quod non multò post secutum fuisse constat. Et vt Eliæ hostes acerrimi fuerunt Achab & Iezabel: ita Ioannes non alios grauiores hostes habuit, quàm Herodem & Herodiadem, cuius dolis tandem interfectus est. Debent autem vtrunque exemplum sibi ipsis ob oculos ponere ecclesiarum ministri, vt ipsi quoque fortes in Domino non cedant impiorum conatibus, & verum Dei cultum cum vitæ etiam periculo instaurare studeant. Quia enim causa, quam agunt, non ipsorum sed Dei est, facile illam hic tuebitur, licet illos periclitari, vel etiam in hoc certamine mori contingat.
units.tr: For just as the times of Elijah were in many ways most corrupt, both as regards the worship of God and public morals, because under the impious king Ahab and the bloodthirsty Jezebel the mysteries of Baal held sway, so there was no less corruption of religion and of public discipline among the Jews at the same time, when supreme power in affairs rested with Herod, an impious and bloodthirsty man, while the scribes and priests had foully corrupted doctrine together with external worship. And just as Elijah with admirable constancy set himself against everyone and foretold the punishments which God had destined for the impious, so John, with an unconquered strength of spirit, pleaded the cause of God, and, threatening those who would not repent with the ruin which it is clear followed not long after, did the same. And just as Ahab and Jezebel were the most bitter enemies of Elijah, so John had no more serious enemies than Herod and Herodias, by whose wiles he was at last killed. Now the ministers of the churches ought to set both examples before their own eyes, so that they too may not give way, being brave in the Lord, to the attempts of the impious, and may strive to restore the true worship of God even at the risk of life. For since the cause which they pursue is not their own but God's, he will readily defend it here, even though it should happen that they are put in danger, or even die in this struggle.

units.la: Restat effectus & finis ministerij aut prædicationis Ioannis, de quo sic loquitur Angelus: Vt conuertat corda patrum in filios, & rebelles ad prudentiam iustorum, vt paret Domino populum instructum. Corda patrum in filios conuersurum dicit, eò quòd in hoc fuit totus, vt maiorum fides, religio & pietas in posteris eluceret, omnesque ad eam fidem conuerterentur, quam prisci patres tenuerunt, quos omnes (vt de Abrahamo Christus testatur) in promissum illud semen mulieris respexisse cobstat. Et hæc vera illa & laudabilis fidei vetustas est, cui eos studere decebat qui hodie veteris & antiquæ religionis titulo gloriantur. Deinde conuertet (inquit) rebelles aut contumaces ad prudentiam iustorum: Vt nimirum rectius sapiant, & veris Dei cultoribus, quos ille solos pro iustis agnoscit, se accommodent. Denique hoc aget, vt Domino præparet populum instructum ad excipiendum redemptorem, cuius aduentus præ foribus adest. Fecit ista Ioannes partim pœnitentiæ doctrina, qua omnes ab erroribus & peccandi licentia ad mentem meliorem reuocauit: partim quòd de Christo luculenter testatus est, in quo vno veritas & vita inuenitur. Rursus autem hic officij sui admonentur pastores & ecclesiarum ministri. Debent illi hoc agere, vt omnes in veteri fide patrum conueniant. At hic non de patribus sermo est, quos plerique in ore habent, & qui à seculis aliquot proximis vixerunt: sed priscis illis, quorum fides in scripturis commendatur. Princeps horum facile est Abraham, quem ante Legem latam & priusquam circunci-deretur. deretur, propter solam fidem in Iesum Christum iustificatum fuisse scribit Paulus, postea vero circumcisionis signum, ut sigillum iustitiae fidei accepisset, ut pater esset omnium credentium, tam eorum qui ex gentibus sunt, quam eorum qui ex Iudaeis prodierunt. Adhuius ergo fidem omnes adducant, neque aliquem (quantum in ipsis est) circa superstitiones inutiles & noua opiniorum figmenta vagari patiantur. Hic vero magno animo & inuicta constantia opus erit, qua se contumacibus & rebellibus opponendo Christi in ipsis loquentis experimentum praebeat: ut hi quoque tandem discant rectius sentire. Finis autem omnium hic esto, ut singulos idoneos & instructos reddant ad excipiendum Iesum Christum, extra quem nihil habetur, per quod homines seruari possint. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains to consider the effect and the aim of the ministry or preaching of John, of which the angel speaks thus: "To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the rebellious to the wisdom of the just, so as to prepare for the Lord a people made ready." He says that he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, because his whole task was that the faith, religion and piety of our forefathers should shine forth in their posterity, and that all should be converted to that faith which the ancient fathers held, all of whom (as Christ testifies of Abraham) undoubtedly looked to that promised seed of the woman. This is the true and praiseworthy antiquity of faith, which those ought to pursue who today boast in the title of an old and ancient religion. Next, he says, he will turn the rebellious or obstinate to the wisdom of the just: namely, that they may think more rightly, and accommodate themselves to the true worshippers of God, whom alone he acknowledges as just. Lastly, he will bring it about that he prepares for the Lord a people made ready to receive the Redeemer, whose coming is at hand. John did these things partly by the teaching of repentance, by which he called all back from errors and from licence to sin to a better mind; partly because he bore clear witness concerning Christ, in whom alone truth and life are found. Again, here the pastors and ministers of the churches are reminded of their duty. They ought to bring it about that all agree with the old faith of the fathers. But here the discussion is not about those fathers whom most people have on their lips, and who lived in the last few centuries; rather it concerns those ancient ones whose faith is commended in the Scriptures. The chief of these is easily Abraham, of whom Paul writes that before the Law was given, and before he was circumcised, he was justified by faith alone in Jesus Christ; but afterwards he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith, so that he might be the father of all believers, both of those who are of the Gentiles and of those who have come from the Jews. Therefore let all bring people to this faith, and let them not allow anyone (so far as it lies in them) to wander about in useless superstitions and new fabrications of opinions. Here indeed great courage and unconquered constancy will be needed, by which, opposing themselves to the obstinate and rebellious, they may show in themselves the proof of Christ speaking; so that these too may at last learn to think more rightly. Let this be the aim of all: that they make each person fit and prepared to receive Jesus Christ, outside of whom there is nothing by which men can be saved. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA V.
units.tr: HOMILY V.

units.la: Et dixit Zacharias ad Angelum: Quo argumento istud noscam? Ego enim sum senex, & vxor mea profecta est aetate. Et respondens Angelus dixit ei: Ego sum Gabriel, qui adsto in conspectu Dei, missusque sum vt te alloquar, & haec tibi laeta nuntiem. Et ecce silebis, nec loqui poteris ad eum vsque diem, quo haec fiant: eo quod non credidisti sermonibus meis, qui implebuntur tempore suo.
units.tr: And Zacharias said to the angel: By what sign shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is well advanced in years. And the angel answering said to him: I am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God, and I am sent to speak to you and to bring you these glad tidings. And behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.

units.la: EXpositu hucusque Lucas apparitionem Angeli, qui Zachariae annuntiauit, quod ipsi ex Elizabeta vxore, quae antea sterilis fuerat, filius Ioannes nasciturus esset, simulque huius officium diligenter descripsit. Proponitur illic euidens bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui filij sui aduentum in carnem minime obscurum esse voluit, quo facilius ab omnibus agnosci & recipi posset. Qua bonitate cum etiam hodie vtatur, nostrum fuerit nos illi accommodare, ne ingrati tantae gratiae contemptores deprehendamur. His autem duo cumprimis memorabilia subijcit Lucas, peccatum videlicet Zachariae, & eiusdem supplicium, de quibus ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Up to this point Luke has set out the appearance of the angel who announced to Zacharias that a son, John, would be born to him from his wife Elizabeth, who had been barren before. At the same time he has described carefully the angel's office. Here is a clear demonstration of God's goodness, who wished the coming of his Son in the flesh to be by no means obscure, so that he might more easily be recognised and received by all. Since God still shows this same goodness today, it is for us to adapt ourselves to him, lest we be found ungrateful despisers of so great a grace. Luke then sets out two things especially worth noting: the sin of Zacharias and his punishment. We shall speak of them in order.

units.la: Ad peccatum illius pertinet, quod Angelo post diligentem diuini consilij & promissionis expositionem respondet: Quo argumento istud noscam? Ego enim sum senex, & vxor mea prouecta est aetate. Quibus verbis idem dicere videtur, quod paulo post Maria Angelo filij Dei incarnationem pollicenti respondit: Quomodo erit istud, quoniam virum non cognosco? At si rem ipsam diligentius inspiciamus, magnum discrimen apparebit. Maria enim de promissionis veritate non dubitat, sed quia insolens & nouum erat quod promittebatur, de modo & ratione quaerit qua paritura sit ipsa, quae viri congressum nunquam experta fuerat. Interim illam Dei verbis credidisse, Elizabetae, verbis & toto sermonis contextu abunde probatur. Zachariae autem verba incredulitatis plena sunt, & ita ab Angelo exponuntur, imo ipsa satis docent, eum diuinae promissioni non credidisse. Primo enim aduersus Angelum argumentis agit, & dum suam senectam et vxoris aetatem iam ad pariendum non amplius idoneam adducit, non obscure ostendit, se ad vulgarem naturae cursum potius quam ad Dei verbum respexisse: quod a fidei ingenio alienissimum esse, Abrahami exemplo probat Paulus. Deinde signum petit, quod merae incredulitatis esse, infinitis exemplis poterat demonstrari. Et eo minus excusationis Zacharias habet, quod etsi promissio Angeli cum naturae legibus pugnaret, tamen neque noua erat neque insolens omnino, cum eius exemplain Sara, Rahele, Anna Samuelis matre, & similibus praecessissent. Imo Abrahami exemplum nouisse debebat, qui in simili casu, non ad corpus suum effaetum, neque ad emortuum Sarae vterum, sed in vnum Deum respexit, quem & veracem & omnipotentem esse credebat. Itaque etsi non devota aut impia malitia peccarit Zacharias, quoad tamen factum ipsum, idem fecit quod Israelitae in deserto, qui Deum tentauisse dicuntur, eo quod post infinita diuinae bonitatis & potentiae exempla, tunc demum se credituros dicerent, si carnes illis daret & mensam lautiorem ipsis instrueret. Est autem peccatum hoc gravius quam vulgo putetur. Eo enim non modo bonitas & potentia in dubium vocantur, verum etiam veritas Dei, & ita omnis eius honor atque dignitas, quantum in nobis est, proculcatur. Atqui viro bono & honesto nihil intolerabilius videtur, quam si quis ei hominis vani & menda-
units.tr: To his sin belongs the reply he gave the angel, after the angel had carefully explained the divine counsel and promise: By what sign shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years. These words seem to say the same as Mary said a little later, when the angel promised her the incarnation of the Son of God: How shall this be, since I do not know a man? Yet if we look more closely at the matter, a great difference appears. Mary does not doubt the truth of the promise; but because what was promised was unusual and new, she asks about the manner and means by which she, who had never known a man, was to conceive. That she believed God's words is amply proved by Elizabeth's words and by the whole context of the story. Zacharias's words, however, are full of unbelief, and the angel so interprets them; indeed they themselves sufficiently show that he did not believe the divine promise. First, he argues against the angel, and by alleging his own old age and his wife's years, no longer fit for bearing children, he clearly shows that he looked to the ordinary course of nature rather than to the word of God. Paul proves from the example of Abraham that this is most alien to the nature of faith. Then he asks for a sign, which could be shown to be nothing but plain unbelief by countless examples. And Zacharias has even less excuse, because although the angel's promise ran counter to the laws of nature, it was neither new nor wholly unusual, since similar things had gone before in Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah, the mother of Samuel. Indeed he ought to have known the example of Abraham, who in a similar case did not look to his own worn-out body or to Sarah's dead womb, but to the one God, whom he believed to be both true and almighty. So although Zacharias sinned not from a devout or wicked malice, nevertheless, as far as the deed itself goes, he did what the Israelites in the desert did, who are said to have tempted God, because after endless examples of divine goodness and power they said they would believe only if he gave them meat and set a richer table before them. This sin, however, is more serious than is commonly thought. For by it not only God's goodness and power are called into doubt, but also his truth, and so, as far as we are concerned, all his honour and dignity is trampled underfoot. Yet nothing seems more intolerable to a good and honest man than for someone to brand him with the mark of a vain and lying man.

units.la: Zachariae peccatum incredulitate. cus notam inurat. Et nôs nobis licere putabimus, vt Dei promissiones pro vanis & irritis accusemus, cuius verbum in aeternum manet.
units.tr: The sin of Zacharias: unbelief. And shall we think it lawful for ourselves to accuse God's promises of being empty and void, when his word endures for ever?

units.la: Atqui passim hodie regnat istud peccati genus. In ijs certè quae ad religionem & fidei causam spectant, multi etsi scripturae aperta testimonia audiant, & fidei Christianae doctrinam olim signis stupendis & evidentibus miraculis confirmatam esse non ignorent, tamen nova signa à nobis etiam requirunt; & se tunc creduros aiunt, si nunc quoque ab Euangelij ministris caecorum oculos aperiri, surdorum aures patefieri, mutorum linguas solui, leprosos purgari, claudos & mancos restitui, daemonia eijci & mortuos excitari videant. Et ista hodie audiuntur, non à Turcis & Iudaeis solùm, aut iuratis Christiani nominis hostibus, verùmetiam abijs, qui Christiani dici volunt, & scripturarum authoritatem se agnoscere profitentur. Sunt ergo Pharisaeorum similes, qui cùm Christus singulis prope momentis miracula aederet, quibus suam diuinitatem & doctrinae suae certitudinem afferebat, adhuc tamen signum postulabant è coelo, quo se diuinitus missum esse probaret. Si enim illi scripturis credunt (quod nisi faciant, Christiano nomine indigni sunt) habent vtrique signa, quibus olim prophetae, deinde Christus & Apostoli doctrinam nostram confirmauerunt: neque illa ad nos pertinere negare possunt, cùm non alia doceamus, quàm quae in scriptis Apostolicis continentur. Qua ergo ratione signa noua postulant, cùm doctrina nostra non nova sit, & cùm inter eos praedicemus, quibus illa noua & insolens videri non debet? Vel si non sufficiunt illis quae olim facta sunt, cur non in praesentem mundi faciem oculos intendunt, vt videant hodie etiam miracula fieri, quibus Deus sui verbi authoritatem tuetur? Quod enim signum excogitari potest euidentius & diuinum magis, quàm quod in medio hostium suorum Christus dominatur? quòd ecclesiam inter persecutionum fluctus subinde conseruat? quòd oues suas inter medios lupos pascit? quòd per homines nullius pretij (si mundi iudicium audias) potentissimorum Regum consilia dissipat, vires debilitat & arma confringit? quòd spem hostium toties eludit? quòd per crucem in suis perpetuò triumphat? Potuit olim Gamaliel videre pro diuino negotio agnoscendum esse, quod non sponte sua tandem ruit. Quàm ergo illi stupidi sunt, qui diuinum esse non vident, quod in medijs periculis saluum manet; imò inter ignes & gladios nouis quotidie incrementis surgit atque propagatur? At non solùm in hac causa peccari solet, verùmetiam in ijs, quae ad corpus spectant, victu nimirum, amictu, valetudinis cura, publica pace & similibus. Extant de his omnibus promissiones, quibus liberalissimè pollicetur Deus, quaecunque nobis necessaria sunt. Et quò minus dubitemus, Christus nos ad aues in aere vagantes, ad coruorum pullos & flores in agris nascentes remittit, vt inde colligamus, multò magis nos curae esse Deo, qui haec omnia propter nos condidit. Accedunt his exempla, quibus promissioni suae fidem facit, dum mirificè eos seruat, quorum vita & salus omnino desperata putatur. Nihilominus tamen in his omnibus solicitudo ethnica regnat, neque plus fidimus Deo, quàm sensus nostri percipiunt. Audiuntur equidem passim eorum voces, quos non pudet dicere: Quo argumento nos camus nos sub Dei cura & protectione esse, qui esurimus, algemus, sitimus, exules vagamur, ex morbis diuturnis decumbimus, multorum odia & persecutiones perpetuas sustinemus? Et haec fere causa est, quòd ad carnis praesidia conuertimur, & fere ad media illicita, quae cum fide & iustitia atque charitate Christiana pugnant. Alius enim ex vsuris ditescere studet, alij furantur & rapiunt, alij vindictae cupiditate superati seditiones mouent, multi in morbis & periculis grauioribus ad incantationes, exorcismos, fortilegia & daemoniorum opem confugiunt. Omnes vero ipsi simul Deo praescribere & eius fidem atque bonitatem tentare solent, dum quid sibi fieri volunt audacter postulant. At quod de Pharisaeis dicit Christus, hoc ipsum de illis etiam dici debet, quòd generatio sint prava & adultera. Si qui ergo Dei filij dici volunt, procul abiectis carnis dubitantis rationibus, patrem credentium Abrahamum imitentur, qui in Dei veritatem & potentiam respiciens tunc quoque sperauit constanter, cùm in humanis spes omnino nulla reliqua esset. Hinc vera fidei obedientia enascitur, quae vt nos ad omne obsequium promptos, ita etiam in omni casu fortes & intrepidos reddit.
units.tr: Yet this kind of sin reigns everywhere today. In matters that concern religion and the cause of faith, many people, although they hear the plain testimonies of Scripture and do not doubt that the doctrine of the Christian faith was once confirmed by astonishing signs and evident miracles, nonetheless still demand new signs from us. They say they will believe only if they now see, through the ministers of the Gospel, the eyes of the blind opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, the tongues of the dumb loosed, lepers cleansed, the lame and maimed restored, demons cast out, and the dead raised. And such things are heard today, not only from Turks and Jews or the sworn enemies of the Christian name, but also from those who wish to be called Christians and profess that they acknowledge the authority of the Scriptures. They are therefore like the Pharisees, who, although Christ performed miracles almost every moment, by which he proved his divinity and the certainty of his doctrine, still demanded a sign from heaven to prove that he had been sent by God. For if they believe the Scriptures (and unless they do, they are unworthy of the Christian name), they both have the signs by which the prophets of old, and then Christ and the Apostles, confirmed the doctrine we hold. Nor can they deny that these signs pertain to us, since we teach nothing other than what is contained in the apostolic writings. Why then do they demand new signs, when our doctrine is not new, and when we preach among those for whom it ought not to seem new or strange? Or if what was done long ago is not enough for them, why do they not turn their eyes to the present face of the world, to see that miracles are still wrought today, by which God maintains the authority of his word? For what sign can be devised more evident and more divine than that Christ rules in the midst of his enemies? That he keeps the Church safe amid the waves of persecution? That he feeds his sheep among the wolves? That, through men of no worth (if you listen to the judgement of the world), he scatters the counsels of the most powerful kings, weakens their forces, and breaks their arms? That he so often mocks the hopes of his enemies? That through the cross he always triumphs in his people? Gamaliel was able to see that what fell of its own accord was not of God, but what remains safe in the midst of dangers should be recognised as divine. How stupid, then, are those who do not see that what is divine is what stays safe amid perils; indeed, what rises and spreads with new growth every day amid fires and swords? But this sin is committed not only in this matter, but also in things that concern the body: namely food, clothing, care of health, public peace, and the like. There are promises about all these things, in which God most generously pledges whatever we need. And so that we may doubt less, Christ sends us to the birds wandering in the air, to the young ravens and to the flowers growing in the fields, so that we may conclude from them that God cares for us much more, since he made all these things for our sake. To these are added examples by which he makes good his promise, for he wonderfully preserves those whose life and safety are thought wholly hopeless. Nevertheless, in all these matters ethnic anxiety reigns, and we trust God no more than our senses perceive. Indeed, everywhere voices are heard of people who are not ashamed to say: By what sign can we know that we are under God's care and protection, when we hunger, freeze, thirst, wander as exiles, lie sick for long periods, and endure the hatred and constant persecution of many? And this is largely the reason why we turn to the defences of the flesh, and mostly to unlawful means, which clash with faith, justice, and Christian love. One man strives to grow rich from usury; others steal and plunder; others, overcome by a desire for revenge, stir up sedition; many in serious illnesses and dangers flee to incantations, exorcisms, charms, and the help of demons. Indeed, all of them together are accustomed to prescribe to God and to test his faithfulness and goodness, while they boldly demand what they wish to have done for them. But what Christ says of the Pharisees must be said of these people too: that they are a wicked and adulterous generation. If therefore any wish to be called sons of God, let them cast aside the reasonings of doubting flesh, and imitate Abraham, the father of believers, who, looking to the truth and power of God, hoped steadfastly even when no hope remained in human affairs. From this is born true obedience of faith, which makes us ready for every service and also bold and fearless in every circumstance.

units.la: Apparet autem in Zachariae exemplo, quanta sit carnis nostrae infirmitas, quando haec in sanctis quoque & iustis locum inuenit. Iste certè non in ijs Dei legato obloquitur, quae factu difficilia vel auditu molesta erant; sed in eo quo nihil ei iucundius magisque gratum poterat accidere. Et sanè sane multa admiratione dignum est, quòd qui paulò ante prolem sibi dari orauerat, nunc illam pro-mittenti Deo non credit. Sed hæc est naturæ nostræ corruptio, vt non modò aduersorum casuum difficultate, verumetiam promissionum Dei magnitudine & excellentia superati, fidem nostram siu stuare & labascere sentiamus. Si enim in rebus temporarijs & vulgaribus frequenter non credi-mus ea, quæ maximè vellemus vera esse, quid miramur, si in ijs diffidamus Deo, quæ nostri ingenij captum longè superant? Ita Dauid auditis amplißimis promissionibus de Messia ex suis posteris nascituro exclamabat: Quis ego sum, & quæ est domus patris mei? &c. Et Petrus: Exi àme Do-mine, quia homo peccator sum. Quò magis nos anniti decet, ne nostro sensui locum demus, quando de Dei promissis & æternis regni cœlorum mysterijs agitur.
units.tr: Zachariah's example shows how great the weakness of our flesh is, since it finds a place even in holy and righteous men. He certainly does not object to things that were hard to do or unpleasant to hear, but to something that could have been most pleasing and welcome to him. And it is truly remarkable that a man who a little before had prayed for a child now does not believe God when he promises one. But this is the corruption of our nature: we feel our faith wavering and faltering, overcome not only by the difficulty of adverse circumstances but also by the greatness and excellence of God's promises. For if in temporal and ordinary matters we often fail to believe what we most wish were true, why should we be surprised if we distrust God in things that far exceed the grasp of our intellect? So David, on hearing the most ample promises about the Messiah who would be born of his descendants, cried out: "Who am I, and what is my father's house?" etc. And Peter said: "Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man." All the more should we strive not to give place to our own sense when the promises of God and the eternal mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are in question.

units.la: Obseruari etiam debet hoc loco, cur eiusmodi sanctorum lapsus aut delicta nobis scripturæ pro-ponant, et vt nos exemplis illorum vti debeamus. Constat enim illis multos abuti, vt sceleribus suis patrocinentur, & peccandi licentiam seu impunitatem inuchant. Sic ebriosi Noam & Lothum ad-ducunt, vt suam intemperantiam excusent, & Dauidis exemplo adulteri stupra sua defendunt. At est hic impius scripturæ sacræ abusus, & in Dei præceptum illi pugnant, quo prohibet, ne eius no-men leuiter & scurriliter vsurpemus. Longè igitur aliud est in his proponendis Spiritus sanctí con-silium. Primò enim vult vt exemplis huiusmodi excitati diligentius vigilemus aduersus carnis de-fideria & diaboli suggestiones, ne nobis quoque nostra vel securitas vel confidentia imponat. Ideo non delicta solùm describuntur, verumetiá pœnæ, quas propter illa de seruis suis Deus grauissimas sumpsit. In quibus semper nobis in animo versari debet Christi Iesu sententia: Si hoc olim factum in viridi ligno, id est, in ijs, qui arbores frugiferæ fuerunt, & dignis fructibus pœnitentiam testati-sunt, quid fiet in nobis aridis truncis, si steriles esse pergamus? Seruiunt etiam exempla ista nostræ institutioni aduersus Nouatianos nostri sæculi & Anabaptistas, qui præcipiti nimis iudicio omnes eos damnant, quos post factam fidei professionem peccare & in aliquod grauius delictum labi vi-dent. Atqui iustus erat Zacharias, nimirum ex fide qua in promissum humani generis redempto-rem respiciebat: attamen peccat, & quidem non leuiter, sed ita vt abijcia Deo meruerit, si iis suum ius contra eum persequi voluisset. Quòdipsum multis alijs accidisse constat, qui tamen in gratiam recepti sunt, et Deo postea fideliter seruierunt. At nostri illi nõ contenti eos damnauisse qui peccant, insuper totas Ecclesias suo iudicio Satanæ tradunt, quæ tales foueant & ad pœnitentiam erudiunt. Est præterea exemplorum istorum hic etiam vsus, vt ex ijs consolationem capiant, qui peccarunt. Vt enim prioribus illis ad se conuersis Deus ignouit: ita nobis quoque propitius erit, si ad ipsum con-uertamur, sicuti promissiones eius passim testantur. Ita exemplis hisce vti docet Paulus, quando Christum ideo sui misertum esse dicit, vt in se primo ostenderet omnem clementiam, vtq exemplar fieret ijs, qui crediturî essent ipsi in vitam æternam. 1. Tim. 1. cap.
units.tr: It should also be observed here why Scripture sets before us the lapses and sins of such saints, and how we ought to use their examples. For it is well known that many abuse them to defend their wickedness and to claim licence or impunity for sinning. Thus drunkards bring forward Noah and Lot to excuse their intemperance, and adulterers defend their debaucheries by David's example. But this is an impious abuse of Holy Scripture, and such people fight against the command of God, by which he forbids us to use his name lightly and scurrilously. The purpose of the Holy Spirit in setting these things forth is therefore quite different. For first, he wishes that those stirred by such examples should watch more diligently against the desires of the flesh and the suggestions of the devil, lest our security or confidence deceive us too. Therefore not only the sins are described, but also the punishments which God, in his great severity, inflicted on his servants because of them. In these things the saying of Christ Jesus should always be in our minds: "If this was done in the green wood, that is, in those who were fruitful trees and showed repentance by worthy fruits, what will be done in us dry trunks, if we continue to be barren?" These examples also serve our instruction against the Novatians and Anabaptists of our own age, who with too hasty a judgment condemn all those whom they see sin after making profession of faith, or fall into some graver offence. Yet Zachariah was righteous, namely from the faith by which he looked to the promised Redeemer of mankind; nevertheless he sins, and not lightly, but in such a way that he would have deserved to be cast off by God, had God wished to pursue his right against him. It is known that this happened to many others as well, who nevertheless were received again into favour and afterwards served God faithfully. But those men, not content to condemn those who sin, moreover hand over whole churches by their judgment to Satan, because they harbour such people and train them to repentance. There is also this further use of these examples: that those who have sinned may take consolation from them. For just as God pardoned those earlier men when they turned to him, so he will be merciful to us too if we turn to him, as his promises testify everywhere. Thus Paul teaches us to use these examples, when he says that Christ had mercy on him so that in him first he might show all clemency, and become a pattern for those who would believe in him unto eternal life. 1. Tim. 1.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad alterum angelici sermonis caput, quo pœnam incredulitatis Zacharia de-nuntiat, & id quidem singulari cum grauitate. Nam initio seipsum describit, vt peccatum eius amplificet. Ego sum (inquit) Gabriel, qui adsto in conspectu Dei, missusque sum vt te alloquar, & hæc tibi læta nuntiem. Gabrielem se esse dicit, quod heroem Dei aut in Deo fortem & robustum si-gnificat. Deinde muneris & functionis suæ meminit, quando se apparitoris instar in Dei conspe-ctu adstare ait, vt nimirum ad accipiendu & exequendum mandata diuina semper paratus sit. Ad-ditur tertiò, quod nunc peculiariter ad Zachariam sit missus, & quidè in eum finem, vt rem lætam diuq ab ipso optatam nuntiet. Sensus itaq; est: Si quis angelus vulgaris, aut etiam homo propheta, ad te missus, ipsius Dei nomine tibi loqueretur, nefas foret, fidem illi negare: & exempla sunt, quàm duriter in illos statuerit Deus, qui prophetis credere noluerunt. Quanto igitur grauius est tuum pec-catum, qui mihi non adhibes fidem, qui ex præcipuis Dei ministris sum, qui à Dei potentia & robore nomen accepi, cuius solius recordatio omnem dubitationem animo excutere debuit: qui denique tibi, qui sacerdos es, ex ijs quæ olim cum Daniele egi, notissimus esse debeam? Si item credendũ est Deo, dum vel pœnas graues minatur, vel increpat, vel etiam noua & priusinaudita pollicetur, tuum e-rat multò magis mihi credere, qui vt rem lætissimam tibi annuntio, ita nihil aliud promitto, quàm cuius exempla in sacris historijs extant, quæ & tibi, homini in scripturis versato, ignota esse non possunt. Est ergo hæc tua culpa grauior, quàm quæ excusationem admittat, aut veniam merea-
units.tr: But let us come to the second part of the angel's speech, in which he announces the punishment of Zachariah's unbelief, and does so with singular gravity. At the start he describes himself, so as to magnify the sin. "I am," he says, "Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God, and have been sent to speak to you and to bring you these glad tidings." He says he is Gabriel, which means hero of God, or strong and mighty in God. Then he recalls his office and function, saying that he stands in God's presence like an attendant, so that he is always ready to receive and carry out the divine commands. Thirdly, it is added that he has now been sent specially to Zachariah, and indeed for this purpose: to announce a joyful thing that Zachariah had long desired. The sense, then, is this: if some common angel, or even a man who is a prophet, were sent to you and spoke to you in God's own name, it would be wrong to deny him faith; and there are examples of how harshly God has dealt with those who refused to believe the prophets. How much greater, then, is your sin, who do not give faith to me, who am among the chief ministers of God, who have received my name from God's power and strength, whose mere remembrance ought to have shaken every doubt from your mind; who, finally, ought to be well known to you, a priest, from what I once did with Daniel? Likewise, if we must believe God when he threatens or rebukes with heavy punishments, or even promises new things never heard before, it was much more your duty to believe me, who, while announcing to you a most joyful thing, promise nothing except what examples of which are found in the sacred histories, and which cannot be unknown to you, a man versed in the Scriptures. Therefore your fault is too grave to admit excuse or to deserve pardon.

units.la: Dan. 8. 9. tur. Hic (inquam) verborum Angeli sensus est, in quibus officium quoq; angelorum & eorundem conditio pulchrè describitur. Vocat hos alibi scriptura spiritus, vt eos à nobis & omni terrena atque crassiori substantia discernat. Ignem quoque flammantem eos dicit, nimirum à celeritate & incredibili omnia penetrandi virtute. Utrumque Dauid vno versu comprehendit, de Deo loquens: Qui legatos suos facit spiritus, & ministros suos ignem flammantem. Ideo quoad officium suum, coram Deo astare dicuntur, non quidem otiosi gloriæ & maiestatis eius spectatores, sed vt ministri. De quo Daniel scribens ait: Millies mille ministrabant ei, & decies mille myriades ante ipsum stabant. Emittuntur autem ijdem, tam vt sanctis seruiant, & eos tueantur, quàm vt impios perdant atq; coerceant. Quod non obscurè in epistola ad Hebræos Apostolus docet, ita de Angelis loquens: Nonne omnes sunt ministratores spiritus, qui ministerij causa mittuntur propter eos, qui hæredes erunt salutis? Exempla huius passim extant. Iacob certè cum àfratre Esauo sibi timeret, turmas angelorum vidit, qui & ipsum tueri, & Esauum cohibere debebant, ne illi manus violentas inferret. Et idem angelus Ægyptiorum primogenita occidit, Israelitarum verò œdibus pepercit, & eis ex Ægypto exeundi copiam impetrauit. Rursus vnus & idem angelus populum Dei deduxit, & ante eos eiecit hostes, vt ipsi terra patribus promissa potirentur. Sic idem angeli Elisæum quidem cum suo famulo defenderunt, Syros autem oculis captos in Samariam adduxerunt. Sed dies me deficeret, si exempla omnia commemorare velim, quæ in historijs habentur, & hodie etiam eueniunt. Nos ex his inuictam Dei potentiam agnoscamus, qui talium ministrorum infinitis millibus stipatur, quorum singuli totis gentibus vno momento perdendis sufficiunt. Exosculemur præterea immensam & plus quam paternam eius bonitatem, qui suos in terris hisce inter omnis generis pericula laborantes tam fido tamq; potenti præsidio munit, vt certò illis cum Elisæo dicere liceat: Plures sunt eorum, qui à nobis stant, quam eorum qui hostium partes tuentur. Nobiscum enim sunt non solùm angeli, verùmetiam angelorum princeps, Iesus Christus, cui omnis potestas data est in cælo & in terra. Quàm verò infelices sunt, qui nihilominus sibi ab hoc mundo metuunt? aut qui vitæ & morum impuritate angelos procul abs se arcent, seq; præsidio hoc tam sancto & necessario spoliant? Non autem ex iis sequitur, angelos vel diuinis honoribus coli, vel in periculis inuocari, aut cùm se nobis præsentes fistūt, adorari debere. Quia enim conserui nostri sunt (quod cum Ioanne agens angelus disertè fatetur) suus honor Deo saluus manere debet, qui in eo non minima ex parte consistit, vt illum solum in omni necessitate inuocemus: qua de re cum sæpius dictum sit, hæc paucula modò sufficere possunt pijs, qui serio gloriæ Dei studio tanguntur.
units.tr: Dan. 8. 9. Here, I say, is the sense of the angel's words, in which the office of angels and their nature are also finely described. Scripture elsewhere calls them spirits, to distinguish them from us and from all earthly and grosser substance. He also calls them a flaming fire, namely because of their swiftness and their incredible power to penetrate all things. David comprehends both in a single verse, speaking of God: "Who makes his messengers spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire." Therefore they are said to stand before God as regards their office, not indeed as idle spectators of his glory and majesty, but as ministers. Daniel writes of this: "Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him." But they are sent out both to serve the saints and protect them, and also to destroy and restrain the wicked. The Apostle teaches this plainly in the Epistle to the Hebrews, speaking of angels thus: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation?" Examples of this are found everywhere. Jacob certainly, when he feared his brother Esau, saw troops of angels, who were to protect him and restrain Esau, lest he lay violent hands on him. The same angel struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians, but spared the houses of the Israelites, and obtained for them the freedom to leave Egypt. Again, one and the same angel led God's people and drove out their enemies before them, so that they might possess the land promised to their fathers. So too the angels defended Elisha and his servant, and led the Syrians, struck blind, into Samaria. But the day would fail me if I wished to recall all the examples that are found in histories and that still happen today. From these let us acknowledge the invincible power of God, who is surrounded by infinite thousands of such ministers, each of whom is sufficient to destroy whole nations in a moment. Let us also embrace his immense and more than fatherly goodness, who fortifies his people, labouring on earth amid every kind of danger, with so faithful and so powerful a protection that they may rightly say with Elisha: "There are more who are with us than those who take the part of our enemies." For with us are not only angels, but also the Prince of angels, Jesus Christ, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth. But how unhappy are those who nevertheless fear this world for themselves? Or who, by impurity of life and morals, keep angels far away from themselves, and deprive themselves of so holy and necessary a protection? Yet it does not follow from these things that angels should be worshipped with divine honours, or invoked in dangers, or adored when they present themselves to us. For since they are our fellow servants (as the angel plainly confesses when dealing with John), their honour must remain safe for God, and this consists in no small part in our invoking him alone in every need. Since this has been said often, these few things may suffice for the godly, who are seriously moved by zeal for the glory of God.

units.la: Obseruemus etiam Angeli verbis, quod etsi de sua conditione magnificè loquatur, in primis tamen mandatum Dei vrget, qui ipsum Zachariæ ista dicere iusserat. Nam nisi quis Dei verbum nuntiet, nullam fidem merebitur, quantumuis splendida & gloriosa fuerit persona, quam sustinet. Ergo non in hominum personas respicere oportet, vt propter has vel credere vel non credere velimus. Fides enim Dei verbo nititur, & qui hoc contemnunt, pœna digni sunt, etiamsi quoad humanum iudicium nullius pretij videatur, qui illud prædicat. Rursus qui ea docet, quæ cum verbi Dei veritate pugnant, anathema sit nobis, quàmuis angelus de cælo fuerit.
units.tr: Let us also observe, from the angel's words, that although he speaks grandly of his own condition, he nevertheless insists first of all on the command of God, who had ordered him to say these things to Zechariah. For unless someone announces the word of God, he deserves no belief, however splendid and glorious the person he represents may be. So we ought not to look at the persons of men, so that we are willing to believe or disbelieve on account of them. Faith rests on the word of God, and those who despise it deserve punishment, even if he who preaches it seems, by human judgment, to be of no worth. Conversely, one who teaches things that clash with the truth of God's word is to be accursed by us, even if he were an angel from heaven.

units.la: Cæterum audiamus, qua pœna Zachariam Deus multauerit. Denuntiat hanc illi Angelus his verbis: Et ecce silebis, nec loqui poteris ad eum vsque diem, quo hæc fiant: eò quòd non credidisti sermonibus meis, qui implebuntur tempore suo. Ergo linguæ & sermonis vsus illi ereptus est, quæ pœna illius peccato optimè respondit. Debebat enim exauditus à Deo, hunc glorificare, & eius promissionem cum digna gratiarum actione excipere. Quod quia non fecit, dignus omnino fuit, qui ad silentium damnaretur, vt ita aduersus Dei verbum disputare desineret. At si hoc Zacharias meruit, quem partim carnis infirmitate, partim diuinæ promissionis excellentia superatum peccauisse nuper diximus, quo non supplicio digni sunt impij, qui Dei verbum conuiciantur? qui æternæ salutis promissiones scurriliter eludunt? qui Euangelium de Iesu Christo hæresEOS accusant? qui sacrosancto Dei nomine ad execrationes, vel ad periuria & omnis generis impostoras abuntur? Sunt hæc nimis vulgaria hodie, & adhuc Dei iram nos punientis admiramur? At quod Zachariæ accidit, hoc vulgo omnibus accidere solet, qui Dei verbo credere nolunt. Carent hi vera Dei & regni eius cognitione, & proinde muti fiunt in diuinis omnibus, ve neque cum Deo per preces pias colloqui, neque cum hominibus de regni cœlorum mystriis differere, aut aliquid afferre possint, quid vel ipsorum vel aliorum ædificationi seruiat. Imò si quid loquuntur, hoc ferè eiusmodi est, vt satius esset, illos pisce magis mutos esse factos. Adhæc generalem doctrinam hoc exemplum continet, quid ingratos omnes maneat, qui Dei donis nolunt vti ad ipsius gloriam. Amittunt ea etiam quæ habent, & ferè inglorij & infelices ex regno Dei eijciuntur, sicut Christus in talentorum parabola docet. Debet hoc ad corporalia simul & spiritualia bona extendi, & exemplis non opus est, quando quotidie videmus, quid ijs eueniat, qui corpris valetudine & viribus, animi prudentia, eloquentia, authoritate & aliis donis abutuntur, aut ea ignauî nimis defodiunt.
units.tr: But let us hear what punishment God imposed on Zechariah. The angel announces it to him in these words: "And behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time." So the use of tongue and speech was taken from him, and this punishment corresponded very well to his sin. For, having been heard by God, he ought to have glorified him and received his promise with due thanksgiving. Because he did not do this, he fully deserved to be condemned to silence, so that he might cease disputing against the word of God. But if Zechariah, whom we have just said sinned partly through the weakness of the flesh and partly overcome by the excellence of the divine promise, earned this, what punishment do the ungodly deserve who revile the word of God? Who mock with buffoonery the promises of eternal salvation? Who accuse the Gospel of Jesus Christ of heresy? Who abuse the most sacred name of God for curses, for perjuries and for every kind of deceit? Are these things now so commonplace that we still marvel that God punishes us in anger? But what happened to Zechariah usually happens to all who are unwilling to believe the word of God. They lack the true knowledge of God and of his kingdom, and so they become mute in all divine matters, so that they can neither converse with God in pious prayers, nor speak with men about the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, nor contribute anything that serves the edification either of themselves or of others. Indeed, if they say anything at all, it is usually of such a kind that it would have been better for them to have been made more silent than fish. Moreover, this example contains a general teaching: what awaits all ungrateful people who are unwilling to use God's gifts for his glory. They lose even those things they have, and, mostly without glory and unhappy, they are cast out of the kingdom of God, as Christ teaches in the parable of the talents. This ought to be extended to bodily and spiritual goods alike, and examples are not needed, since every day we see what happens to those who abuse bodily health and strength, prudence of mind, eloquence, authority and other gifts, or who, being too lazy, bury them.

units.la: Est tamen in his omnibus consolationis plenum, quòd Angelus promissionum Dei nihilominus ratam fore, & suo tempore implendam dicit, quamuis Zacharias ob incredulitatem suam puniri meruerit. Dei enim veritas minimè ab hominum assensu & authoritate pendet. Quid tum enim (vt Pauli verbis vtar) siqui sunt increduli? Num incredulitas eorum fidem Dei irritam faciat? Imò sit Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Quò etiam referri debet, quod alibi dicitur, cœlum quidem & terram transitura, Dei verbum autem permansurum esse in æternum. Exempla in hanc sententiam multa adduci poterant ex veteris testamenti libris. Promiserat Deus, Israelitas suo tempore, post quartam nimirum generationem ex Ægypto educendos esse, vt terram sibi promissam occuparent. Promissionis huius fides apud multos nulla erat, multi etiam illius omnino erant immemores, aut etiam ignari. Attamen ea efficax & rata fuit, cum tempus illud fatale instaret. Idem de omnibus propheta rum sermonibus dicere possumus, quorum tam minæ quàm promissiones suum habuerunt euentum, quamuis plerique illos cum risu exciperent, multi etiam hostiliter insectarentur. Sunt ergo hæc omnibus applicanda, quæcunque Deus vnquam pronunciauit, præceptis nimirum eius, minis atque promissis. Prædictum est olim fore finem mundi, resurrecturos mortuos & ad Christi tribunal sistendos fore omnes homines, vt digna suæ vel fidei vel incredulitatis præmia accipiant. Ridentque multi, & plerique sibi ipsis inter scelera sua delitias faciunt, quod nihil huius euenturum sibi persuadent. Sed sentient illi olim magno suo malo, Dei veritatem stabilem esse, & nullis hominum commentis impediri. Idem de Euangelij promissionibus debet intelligi. Pollicetur nobis in cruce sua gloriam, in morte vitam Dominus Iesus Christus. Videntur hæc absurda multis, qui spem nostram scurriliter ridcnt. Sed non fallet ea nos, & suo tempore ista implebuntur, quando superatis omnibus huius sæculi molestijs vitam & regnum in Christo Iesu possidebimus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet in all these things there is much to console us: the angel says that the promises of God will nonetheless stand firm and be fulfilled in their time, although Zechariah had deserved to be punished for his unbelief. For the truth of God does not depend at all on the assent or authority of men. What then, to use Paul's words, if some were unbelieving? Will their unbelief make the faith of God void? Far from it: let God be true, but every man a liar. To this also should be referred what is said elsewhere, that heaven and earth will pass away, but the word of God will remain for ever. Many examples to this effect could be brought from the books of the Old Testament. God had promised that the Israelites would be led out of Egypt in their time, namely after the fourth generation, to take possession of the land promised to them. Faith in this promise was nonexistent among many; many also were utterly forgetful of it, or even ignorant of it. Nevertheless it was effective and fixed when that appointed time drew near. We may say the same of all the sayings of the prophets, whose threats as well as promises had their outcome, although most received them with laughter and many even attacked them with hostility. Therefore all these things apply to everything that God has ever pronounced, namely his precepts, threats and promises. It was foretold long ago that the world would come to an end, that the dead would rise and that all men would be brought before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive the due rewards of either their faith or their unbelief. Many laugh, and most of them indulge themselves amid their sins, persuading themselves that none of this will happen to them. But they will one day feel to their great cost that the truth of God is stable and cannot be hindered by any inventions of men. The same must be understood of the promises of the Gospel. The Lord Jesus Christ promises us glory in his cross and life in death. To many these things seem absurd, who mock our hope with buffoonery. But it will not deceive us, and these things will be fulfilled in their time, when, having overcome all the troubles of this age, we shall possess life and the kingdom in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: HOMILY VI.

units.la: Et erat populus expectans Zachariam: & mirabantur, quod is tardaret in templo. Ille autem egressus non poterat eis loqui: & cognosuerunt eum visionem vidisse in templo. Nam ipse innuebat eis, permansitque mutus. Et factum est, vt impleti sunt dies ministerij ipsius, abijt domum suam. Post illos autem dies concepit Elizabet vxor eius, & occultauit se mensibus quinque, dicens: Nempe ita fecit mihi Dominus in diebus, quibus respexit, vt auferret probrum illud meum inter homines.
units.tr: And the people waited for Zacharias, and they marvelled that he tarried so long in the temple. And when he came out, he could not speak to them, and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple, for he beckoned to them and remained dumb. And it came to pass, when the days of his ministry were accomplished, that he departed to his own house. And after those days Elisabeth his wife conceived, and hid herself five months, saying: Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men.

units.la: Quamuis Angelus Gabriel ad Zachariam ideo missus fuerit, vt illi rem lætissimam & diu optatam nuntiaret, idem tamen, cùm ille incredulus esset, eius diffidentiam grauiter corripit, & pœnam minatur, qua ipsum multari oporteat. Fuit ea peccato eius admodum conueniens. Quia enim exauditus à Deo, hunc non glorificauit, vt par erat, quin potius aduersus nuntium Dei disputationem instituere ausus fuit, dignus erat, qui linguæ & sermonis vsum omnino amitteret. Est hæc communis omnium sors, qui Dei verbo credere dedignantur. Non percipiunt illi res diuinas & cœlestes, eò quòd hæ sola fide percipi possunt. Ergo de iisdem neque cum Deo neque cum hominibus colloqui possunt. Nam etsi inter precandum (vt de pharifæis Christus ait) multiloqui sint, precandi tamen fiducia destituuntur, cùm spiritu Christi careant, qui solus nos de benigna Dei voluntate certos reddit, vt hunc patris nomine possimus invocare. Adhæc in omnibus quoq; aliis inepti, infantes & rerum incerti sunt, sicuti non in vulgaribus modò hominibus est videre, ve rumetiam in doctoribus bullatis, qui præcipuam summæ eruditionis existimationem sustinent. Nihil igitur homine incredulo miserius & infelicius est, & quo maior videtur eiusmodi hominis authoritas, eò verius in eum conuenit, quod olim proverbio dicebatur, Nullus, magnus, malus, piscis. Quò magis annitimur decet, ne locum demus cæcæ carnis rationibus, quæ fidem nostram labefactare aut euertere possunt. Sed relicto hoc infelici hominum genere, ad huius loci tractationem accedamus, qui primò pœnæ executionem continet, deinde ostendit, vt nihilominus rata fuerit promissio Dei de filio ex Elizabeta & Zacharia nascendo. Vtriusq; autem exempli vsus est egregius ad asserendam Dei veritatem in minis & promissionibus, quæ nobis in verbo eius proponuntur.
units.tr: Although the angel Gabriel was sent to Zacharias so that he might announce to him a most joyful thing, long desired, yet the same angel, when Zacharias proved unbelieving, sharply rebuked his distrust and threatened a punishment by which he must be chastised. This punishment was well suited to his sin. For since he had been heard by God, and yet did not glorify him as he should, but rather ventured to dispute against the messenger of God, he deserved to lose altogether the use of speech and words. This is the common lot of all who disdain to believe God's word. They do not perceive divine and heavenly things, because these can be perceived by faith alone. Therefore they can speak of them neither with God nor with men. For even if, while praying, they are many-worded (as Christ said of the Pharisees), they are nonetheless without confidence in prayer, since they lack the Spirit of Christ, who alone makes us certain of God's kindly will, so that we may call upon him by the name of Father. Moreover, in all other matters too they are foolish, infants, and ignorant of things; and this may be seen not only among ordinary men but also among the bearded doctors, who hold the chief reputation for great learning. Nothing, therefore, is more wretched and unhappy than an unbelieving man; and the greater such a man's authority appears, the more truly does that old saying apply to him, that big fish are bad fish. The more we must strive not to give room to the reasons of blind flesh, which can weaken or overthrow our faith. But leaving this unhappy race of men, let us come to the treatment of this passage, which first contains the execution of the punishment, and then shows that the promise of God concerning the son to be born of Elisabeth and Zacharias was nonetheless fulfilled. Both examples are most useful for establishing God's truth in the threats and promises that are set before us in his word.

units.la: Ad pœnæ executionem pertinet, quòd Zacharias postquam eum diu expectauit populus, tandem mutus exiuit, neque illos pro more alloqui potuit. Et credibile est, alia quoque pauoris indicia in eius vultu ac gestibus apparuisse, ex quibus colligi potuit, ipsum visionem vidisse non vulgarem. Habuit ergo effectum suum Dei sententia, & quidem absque omni mora, eò quòd hoc tota istius causæ ratio exigebat. Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, non deesse Deum suis minis, sed certò euenire quæcunque nobis denuntiat, neq; ea vllis hominum viribus aut consilijs impediri posse. Nam vt Solomon ait, non est sapientia, non prudentia, neque consilium contra Dominum. Debet ergo hoc ad generales illas Dei comminationes referri, quibus iram & maledictionem suam omnibus denuntiat, qui præcepta ipsius impiè transgrediuntur. Sunt enim hæ quoque infinitis exemplis confirmatæ, & quàmuis interdum plagas differat Deus, suo tamen tempore iudicia sua in pœnitere nescios exercet. Idem in peculiaribus quoque minis obseruandum est, equi certus sceleribus & flagitijs suas pœnas decernunt. Maledictus (inquit Lex) qui accipit munus, vt percutiat innocentem sanguinem. Et per prophetam Deus clamat: Væ tibi qui prædaris, & tu non es præda factus: & prævaricanti, cùm in te non sit prævaricatum: Cùm prædari desieris, prædationem patieris, &c. Item: Væ ei, qui ædificat ciuitatem in sanguine. Sed & Christi vox est: Qua mensura metiemini, eadem vobis quoque homines metientur. Ridենt hæc hodie principes, qui bellis non necessarijs orbem tocum implicant, & qui vili pretio conducti illis suam operam locant Cares mercenarij. At si historias euoluamus, miras illas olim suum effectum habuisse patebit in Assyrijs, Babylonijs, Persis, Græcis, Romanis & multis alijs, qui indomito bellandi & prædandi studio flagrauerunt, vt vel imperij sui fines propagarent, vel priuatim opes colligerent. Non est ergo quod dubitemus, quin in illis etiam illas ratas esse velit Deus, qui hodie iisdem studijs occupantur. Ita adulteris & scortatoribus suum iudicium Deus per Paulum denunciat, & quòd eosdem, nisi resipiscant, à regni sui hæreditate excludere velit. Videtur hæc quoque comminatio dura admodum: sed non vanam esse Israelitarum miserabilis clades in deserto, Dauidis infelix casus & periculosæ regnorum potentissimorum mutationes testantur, quas ob stupra factas olim fuisse in historijs legimus. Et vt vetera omittamus, quotidie fiunt, quæ isti comminationi possunt fidem facere, etiamsi ad quorundam nequitiam Deus interdum diutius conniueat. Eadem est vsurariorum & omnium eorum conditio, qui per fas nefasque ditescunt. Clamat aduersus istos Dominus: Væ ei, qui auget non sua. Quod dictum multis fortuitum & in ore prophetæ natum esse videtur. Sed si veteres historias inspicere libeat, & quæ quotidie fiunt attentius obseruemus, nihil ista comminatione verius aut certius esse apparebit. Posset hoc latissimè per omnes peccatorum species diduci, sed ista vberrimam de his cogitandi materiam præbere possunt omnibus, qui serio verbi Dei studio tanguntur. Discant modò singuli, posita virium & consiliorum humanorum fiducia, pœnitentiam agere, neque perpetuam impunitatem sibi ipsis ex Dei indulgentia polliceri, ne is aliquando tarditatem supplicij grauitate compenset, &c.
units.tr: To the execution of the punishment belongs the fact that Zacharias, after the people had waited for him a long time, at last came out dumb, and could not address them as was customary. And it is credible that other signs of fear also appeared in his face and gestures, from which it could be gathered that he had seen no ordinary vision. God's sentence therefore had its effect, and indeed without any delay, since the whole nature of this case required it. From this a general doctrine must be drawn: God does not fail in his threats, but whatever he announces to us will certainly come to pass, nor can it be hindered by any human strength or counsels. For as Solomon says, there is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord. This must therefore be applied to those general threats of God by which he declares his wrath and curse against all who impiously transgress his precepts. For these too are confirmed by infinite examples, and although God sometimes defers the blows, yet in his own time he executes his judgements upon those who know not how to repent. The same must be observed concerning particular threats: God decrees punishments for particular crimes and shameful deeds. Cursed (says the Law) is he who takes a bribe to slay innocent blood. And through the prophet God cries: Woe to you who plunder, and you yourself were not plundered; and to the transgressor, when no transgression was committed against you: when you cease plundering, you shall be plundered, etc. Likewise: Woe to him who builds a city with blood. And the voice of Christ also says: With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again. Today princes laugh at these things, who entangle the whole world in unnecessary wars, and mercenaries, cheap hirelings, who let out their labour to them for a low price. But if we turn over the histories, it will be plain that those threats once had their remarkable effect among the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, Romans and many others, who burned with an untamed zeal for war and plunder, either to extend the boundaries of their empire or to gather wealth for themselves. There is therefore no reason to doubt that God also wills these threats to stand against those who today are occupied with the same pursuits. So too God, through Paul, declares his judgement against adulterers and whoremongers, and that he wishes to exclude them from the inheritance of his kingdom unless they repent. This threat also seems very harsh; but the miserable destruction of the Israelites in the desert, the unhappy fall of David, and the dangerous overthrows of the most powerful kingdoms, which we read in histories were once brought about on account of fornications, bear witness that it is not an empty threat. And to pass over ancient things, there happen every day things which can give credence to this threat, even though God sometimes winks at the wickedness of certain men for a longer time. The condition of usurers, and of all who grow rich by right and wrong alike, is the same. The Lord cries out against these: Woe to him who increases what is not his. This saying may seem to many to be a chance remark, born in the mouth of a prophet. But if we care to look into ancient histories, and observe more attentively what happens every day, nothing will appear truer or more certain than this threat. This could be unfolded very widely through all the kinds of sins, but these things can supply abundant matter for thought to all who are seriously moved by the study of God's word. Let each one only learn, laying aside confidence in human strength and counsels, to repent, and not to promise himself perpetual impunity from God's indulgence, lest he sometime make up for the delay of punishment by its severity, etc.

units.la: Cæterum extra hunc Zachariæ casum, in populo quoque nobis quædam obseruanda veniunt. Inter quæ primum est, quòd illum diutius solito morantem patienter expectant, & neque conuicijs agunt, tijs agunt, neque insano murmure tumultuantur, multò minus sese cum indignatione domum reci-piunt. Fuit igitur in populo aliâs corruptissimo aliquod disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ studium, & suam apud illos authoritatem habuit Lex Dei, qui populum è sacris cœtibus non sine solenni benedictione dimittendum esse constituerat, cuius formula peculiaris habetur: Benedicat tibi Dominus, & custodiat te: illustret Dominus faciem suam super te, & misereatur tui. Attollat Dominus faciem suam super te, & det tibi pacem. At hodie plerique in templis morâ omnes impatientissimi sunt, multi interea dum res sacræ tractantur nugas agunt, & vel de rebus leuissimis differunt, aut animos in cogitationibus vanis & impuris vagari sinunt. Causa huius vitij est, quòd non recte iudicamus de verbo Dei, neque in mentem nobis venit, nos in Dei conspectu esse, vt ea agamus, quæ ad nostram salutem faciunt. Accedimus ergo vt ij, de quibus apud Ezechielem Deus queritur, quòd verbum suum instar cantilenæ nihil ad ipsos pertinentis audiant, & proinde nihilo meliores discedant. Posset malum hoc aliqua ratione excusari, si omnem aliam quoque moram eadem impatientia sustineremus: sed cum circa ludos & res turpes & aut inanes nullius nos temporis aut laboris pigeat, satis apparet, nos natura à diuinis abhorrere, & indignos esse, quos sua gratia Deus dignetur. Longè alij fuerunt veteris Ecclesiæ mores, quando propter insidias & omnis generis pericula noctu ferè Christiani conueniebant, neque illis graue erat totas noctes insomnes ducere, modò animos verbi cœlestis pabulo pascerent, & precibus pijs recrearent. Quàm verò ignauia hæc & impij verbi fastidium Deo displicrant, olim Eutychi exemplo ostendit, qui cùm Paulo concionante interea somno indulgeret, ex fenestra decidit & exanimis factus est. At si in iuuene somnolentiam tam grauiter Deus castigauit, grauius certè supplicium merentur, qui manifesto verbi diuini contemptu peccant, & ludos vanissimos aut etiam cum scelere coniuncta carnis atque mundi studia sacris omnibus præferunt.
units.tr: Apart from this case of Zacharias, certain things in the people also deserve our notice. Among these the first is that they patiently waited for him, though he tarried longer than usual, and did not abuse or insult him, nor did they make an uproar with senseless murmuring, much less did they go home in anger. There was therefore in that people, otherwise most corrupt, some concern for church discipline, and the Law of God had its authority among them. That law ordained that the people should be dismissed from the holy assembly not without a solemn blessing, whose special formula is given: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee: the Lord make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. But today most people in the churches are most impatient of any delay; many, meanwhile, while sacred things are being handled, trifle, and talk of the most trivial matters, or allow their minds to wander in vain and impure thoughts. The cause of this vice is that we do not judge rightly of God's word, nor does it come into our minds that we stand in God's sight, to do those things that serve our salvation. We therefore approach as those of whom God complains through Ezekiel, that they hear his word as a song of no concern to them, and so depart no better. This evil might be excused in some way, if we bore every other delay with the same impatience; but since we grudge no time or labour to games, to shameful or at least idle things, it is plain enough that we are by nature averse to divine things and unworthy that God should deign to favour us with his grace. Far different were the customs of the ancient Church, when, because of plots and dangers of every kind, Christians used to gather almost at night, and it was not hard for them to pass whole nights without sleep, provided only they nourished their minds with the food of the heavenly word and refreshed them with godly prayers. How much this sloth and impious disdain for the word displeased God was shown long ago by the example of Eutychus, who, while Paul was preaching, indulged in sleep, fell from the window and was taken up dead. But if God so severely punished drowsiness in a young man, those surely deserve a heavier punishment who sin by manifest contempt of the divine word, and prefer the vainest games, or even pursuits of the flesh and the world joined with wickedness, to all sacred things.

units.la: Sed vt ad huius populi factum redeamus, non temere annotatur illos non obscuris indicijs deprehendisse, quòd Zacharias visionem aliquam vidisset peculiarem, quæ ipsum diutius solito detinuerat. Fuit ergo multiplex huius pœnæ vtilitas. Zachariæ enim hanc profuisse totius negotij euentus docebit. Nunc verò ad populum quoq; totum eius fructus redundauit. Eius enim consideratione excitati omnes intelligunt in Ioannis natiuitate nihil fortuitum fuisse, & procul dubio maior illius fuit apud omnes authoritas, quòd illum hominem non vulgarem esse, ex tota hac actione iam ante cognouissent. Omnium verò istorum finis fuit gloria Dei, quæ eò clarior & illustrior facta est, quòd in sanctissimo sacerdote incredulitatem non impunitam abijsse viderent. Est eadem ratio omnium afflictionum apud Dei timentes. Quia enim Dei iudicia obseruant, ea quoq; illis adiumento sunt ad bonum, quæ primo intuitu tristia nimis & noxa videbantur. Conuertuntur enim ad illum, à quo se percuti sentiunt, & de illo placando cogitant: quod Zachariam fecisse, suo loco audiemus. Hodie non postrema malorum omnium causa est, quòd ad illicita pleriq; conuertuntur, & per ea sibi consulere studeant, quibus Dei ira magis provocatur.
units.tr: But to return to the conduct of this people: it is not without reason recorded that they perceived, by no obscure signs, that Zechariah had seen some special vision, which had kept him longer than usual. This punishment therefore had many uses. For the outcome of the whole affair will show that it benefited Zechariah. But its fruit also spread to the whole people. For, stirred up by consideration of it, all understood that there was nothing accidental in John's birth, and without doubt his authority was greater among all, because from this whole event they had already known that this man was not ordinary. The end of all these things was the glory of God, which was made clearer and more illustrious because they saw that unbelief in the most holy priest had not gone unpunished. The same reason holds for all afflictions among those who fear God. For since they observe God's judgments, those things also help them to good which at first sight seemed too sad and harmful. For they turn to him by whom they feel themselves struck, and think about appeasing him; which Zechariah did, as we shall hear in its place. Today the not least cause of all evils is that many turn to unlawful things and seek help through those things by which the wrath of God is more provoked.

units.la: Priusquam verò ab hoc loco discedamus, obseruari quoque debet, quod de Zachariæ interfe-ritur, illum videlicet expleto demum sui ministerij tempore domum suam redijsse. Est hoc magnum modestiæ simul & obedientiæ seu pietatis veræ argumentum. Alius enim visionis & promissionis diuinæ excellentia elatus, mox sese ad sua propripuisset, & inani iactantia omnium aures impleuisset. Alius verò supplicio irritatus functionem suam deseruisset, & hoc se non immeritò facere putasset, quando linguæ vsus amissus erat, sine quo multa sacerdotalis functionis officia non poterant peragi. At nihil horum Zachariam mouit, vt ante tempus præfinitum à templo discederet, sed maiorem sui ministerij rationem habuit, quàm priuati affectus. Iubebantur enim sacerdotes in lege eo tempore, quo sacris vacabant, mulierum consuetudinem vitare, & simul à vino & sicera abstinere, nimirum, quòd temperantiæ & castitatis studiosissimos esse oportet eos omnes, qui sacra sua Deo probari cupiunt. At quia vix sibi temperant, qui domi suæ intra priuatos parietes viuunt, non imprudenter institutum fuit, vt ij ad quos sacrorum administrandorum vices redierant, toto illo tempore apud templum residerent, in quem vsum cubicula quædam in templi lateribus ædificata fuisse legimus. Quòd autem ex antiquo sacerdotij Leuitici more argumentum sumunt aduersarij nostri, quo cœlibatum sacrificulorum & monachorum tuentur, quos toto vitæ suæ tempore Deo
units.tr: Before we leave this place, it must also be observed, as is reported about Zechariah, that he returned home only when the time of his ministry was fully completed. This is a great proof of modesty and at the same time of obedience or true piety. For another, puffed up by the excellence of the divine vision and promise, would straightaway have hurried off to his own affairs and filled everyone's ears with empty boasting. Another, provoked by the punishment, would have abandoned his office, thinking he did so not unjustly, since the use of speech had been lost, without which many duties of the priestly function could not be carried out. But nothing of this moved Zechariah to leave the temple before the appointed time; he had a greater regard for his ministry than for private feelings. For in the law the priests were commanded, during the time when they were occupied with sacred duties, to avoid the company of women, and at the same time to abstain from wine and strong drink; clearly because all who wish their sacred service to be approved by God ought to be most diligent in temperance and chastity. But since those who live at home within their private walls hardly restrain themselves, it was wisely instituted that those to whom the turns of performing sacred duties had come back should remain near the temple for that whole time; for which purpose we read that some chambers were built along the sides of the temple. As for what our opponents take from the ancient custom of the Levitical priesthood, by which they defend the celibacy of sacrificing priests and monks, who they say are dedicated to God for their whole life

units.la: c consecratos, & in sacris publicis quotidie uersari oporteat: nimis friuolum & ridiculum est. Quia enim in Christi morte sacrificia Leuitica cessarunt, temerarie nimis ad Euangelij ministerium extendunt, quod propter illa sola fuit institutum. Et Apostolorum exemplo conuincuntur, qui cum euangelizandi causa orbem terrarum circuirent, uxores suas secum duxerunt, sicuti Paulus in priori ad Corinthios testatur. Iniqui etiam nimis sunt, quod hodie apud ecclesiarum & sacrorum ministros perpetuo volunt obseruari, quod olim ad aliquot modo dies obseruabatur, neque humanae infirmitatis rationem habent, quam in hac causa Christus obseruare iubet, quando donum hoc castitatis non omnibus datur. Mirum autem est, egregios illos Leuitici Sacerdotij obseruatores pro solo caelibatu contendere, & non similiter a vino abhorrere, cuius usum prisci sacerdotibus lex prohibebat. Sed durum fortasse hoc visum fuit hominibus ventri gulae deditis, qui interim scie-bant non defore ipsis rationes, quibus caelibatus molestiam leuarent, & illius praetextu ad stupra & vagas libidines abuterentur. Caeterum reliquis impuris illis sponsis Penelopes, in Zachariae exemplo discamus primum, officium sedulo facere in ijs, ad quae nos deflinauit Dominus, neque ullas rationes quantumuis plausibiles & splendidas admittere, quae nos a functione commissa revocare videntur. Deinde temporis rationem certam habeamus, ut omnia suo tempore fiant. Est hac non postrema sapientiae pars, & quia (ut Solomon olim docebat) omnia suum tempus habent, nunquam res suas feliciter agent, qui temporum occasiones negligunt. Debet hoc ad poenitentiae quoque doctrinam referri, ut obseruemus diligenter, quibus signis iram suam nobis denuntiet Deus, nosque ad resipiscendum excitet. Quam enim displiceant Domino, qui nihil huius animaduertunt, ipsius querela apud Ieremiam testatur, qua Israelitarum incurabile socordiam accusans inter alia dicit: Equidem ciconia in aere novit sua stata tempora: turtur, grus & hirundo obseruant tempus professionis suae: at populus meus non agnoscit iudicium Domini. Atq; vtinam non hodie etiam de nostri seculi moribus idem dici posset. Vulgò enim hoc vitium obtinuit, ut in secundis quidem insolenter efferamur, & proterui nimis admonitiones omnes contemnamus, sicut illos facturos Dominus praedixit, quos in nouissimis temporibus eorum similes fore ait, qui Noae atq; Lothi temporibus vixerunt. Quod si vero res aduersae incidunt, iam aut prorsus desperamus, aut poenitentiam agimus hypocriticam & momentaneam, quae ut in externis laruis consistit, ita ad primam peccandi occasionem iterum euanescit. Sed quia haec alterius loci sunt, plura non addemus.
units.tr: consecrated, and must be engaged daily in public sacred duties: that is far too frivolous and ridiculous. For since the Levitical sacrifices ceased with Christ's death, they too rashly extend to the ministry of the gospel what was instituted solely for those sacrifices. They are also refuted by the example of the apostles, who, when they travelled round the world for the sake of preaching the gospel, took their wives with them, as Paul testifies in his first letter to the Corinthians. They are also far too unfair in wanting what once was observed for only a few days to be observed today perpetually by the ministers of the churches and of the sacred rites; and they take no account of human weakness, which Christ bids us observe in this matter, since this gift of chastity is not given to all. It is strange indeed that those distinguished observers of the Levitical priesthood contend for celibacy alone, and do not similarly abstain from wine, whose use the law forbade the priests of old. But perhaps this seemed hard to men given over to the belly and gluttony, who meanwhile knew that they would not lack reasons to lighten the burden of celibacy, and under that pretext would abuse it for fornication and wandering lusts. Moreover, from the example of Zechariah let us learn, in contrast to those other impure suitors of Penelope, first to perform diligently the duty to which the Lord has assigned us, and not to admit any reasons, however plausible and splendid, which seem to call us back from the office entrusted to us. Then let us keep a sure reckoning of time, so that everything is done in its time. This is no small part of wisdom, and since (as Solomon taught of old) all things have their time, those who neglect the opportunities of times will never carry out their affairs successfully. This too ought to be referred to the doctrine of repentance, that we observe diligently by what signs God announces his wrath to us and stirs us to repent. How much they displease the Lord who take note of none of these things, his complaint in Jeremiah bears witness, in which, accusing the Israelites of an incurable dullness, he says among other things: "Indeed the stork in the air knows her appointed times; the turtle-dove, crane and swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people does not know the judgment of the Lord." And would that the same could not be said today of the manners of our own age. For this vice has become common, that we are insolently puffed up in prosperity, and shamelessly despise all warnings, just as the Lord foretold that those would do who, he says, in the last times would be like those who lived in the times of Noah and Lot. But if adverse things befall, then either we altogether despair, or we do penance that is hypocritical and momentary, which, as it consists in outward masks, so at the first occasion of sinning vanishes again. But since these matters belong to another place, we will add no more.

units.la: Transeamus ergo ad alterum huius loci caput, quo narratur, ut non minus rata quoque fuerit promissio Dei, qui Ioannem ex Elizabeta nasciturum esse pollicitus fuerat. Nam sic scribit Lucas: Postquam illos autem dies (Zacharia nimirum domum reuersus) concepit Elizabet uxor eius, & occultauit se mensibus quinque, &c. Ergo (ut alibi diximus) hominum incredulitas Dei fidem non reddit irritam: Imò verax manet Deus, etiamsi omnes homines vani & mendaces fuerint. At si propter incredulitatem nostram Deus promissa sua non reuocat, multò minus fidei infirmitas obstabit, quò minus illorum fructum percipiamus. Debet ergo hinc communis consolatio peti, ne propter fidei nostrae imperfectionem desperemus, sed in Christi bonitate spem firmam habeamus collocatam, qui (ut propheta ait) linum fumigans non extinguit, & calamum quassatum non omnino comminuit. Soletur hoc ipsum nos aduersus aliorum quoque incredulitatem & contumaciam, ne hanc nobis fraudi fore timeamus. Quia enim iustus sua fide viuit, nunquam illi exitialis aut noxia erit aliorum incredulitas. Et potest Deus contumaces & rebelles ita punire, ut interim suorum rationem habeat, & paucos licet in medio nationis prauae conseruet. Ita solû Noam olim cum sua familia Deus seruauit, cum totus mundus diluuij aquis perdi meruisset: & ex Sodomis ereptus est Lothus, cum & regio circumiacens & vicinae vrbes omnes caelestibus flammis arderent. Similiter vniuersalis Israelitarum rebellio non obfuit Iosue & Chalebo, quò minus ipsi terram patribus promissam obtinerent. Et possent huius generis exempla innumera adduci, quorum omnium hic nobis vsus esse debet, ut diuinae veritatis consideratione in fide promissionum eius confirmemur, & in periculis vndique imminentibus spem in Deo nostro habeamus inconcussam.
