units.tr: Let us pass then to the other point of this passage, in which it is narrated that the promise of God, who had promised that John would be born of Elizabeth, was no less sure. For Luke writes thus: "After those days (that is, when Zechariah had returned home) Elizabeth his wife conceived, and hid herself for five months," etc. Therefore (as we have said elsewhere) the unbelief of men does not make the faith of God void: rather God remains true, even if all men be vain and liars. But if on account of our unbelief God does not revoke his promises, much less will the weakness of faith stand in the way of our receiving their fruit. Hence common comfort ought to be drawn, that we may not despair on account of the imperfection of our faith, but keep a firm hope fixed in the goodness of Christ, who (as the prophet says) does not quench the smoking flax, nor wholly crush the bruised reed. This same thing should console us against the unbelief and obstinacy of others too, so that we do not fear that it will be a loss to us. For since the just man lives by his faith, the unbelief of others will never be deadly or harmful to him. And God can so punish the obstinate and rebellious that meanwhile he takes account of his own, and preserves a few even in the midst of a wicked nation. Thus God once saved Noah alone with his family, when the whole world had deserved to perish by the waters of the flood; and Lot was snatched out of Sodom, when both the surrounding region and all the neighbouring cities were burning with heavenly flames. Likewise the universal rebellion of the Israelites did not hinder Joshua and Caleb from obtaining the land promised to their fathers. And innumerable examples of this kind could be brought forward, all of which should be of use to us here, so that by considering divine truth we may be confirmed in faith in his promises, and may have an unshaken hope in our God amid dangers threatening on every side.

units.la: Porrò memorabile in primis est, quòd Elizabeta postquam concepit, se mensibus quinque occultauisse dicitur. Adducunt huius facti rationes alij alias, at mihi hoc pudoris coniugalis argumentum esse videtur, qui ut mulieres in primis decet, ita in Elizabeta plus loci habere debuit, cum iam prouecta proueƈta ætatis esset. Nam etsi coniugalis thorus ab Apostolo impollutus dicatur, & recte olim Phinutius concubitum cum propria coniuge castitatem esse dixerit, constat tamen sanctos in illo temporis & ætatis suæ rationem habere, ne intemperantiores videantur. Quod Saram quoque observasse constat, quando promissionem de filio ex se nascendo cum risu excipiens dicebat: Postquam consenui, & herus meus vetulus est, num voluptati operam dabo? Et non dubium est, Elizabetam ingenuo pudore suffusam fuisse, cum se prægnantem ab omnibus observari sentiret: quando hoc ipsum iunioribus fœminis accidit, quæ honestatis sunt amantiores. Credibile etiam est, Zachariam coniugi sanctissimæ promissionem ab Angelo denuntiatam scripto indicavisse, et hanc eius consideratione impulsam fuisse, ut publica vicinarum commercia vitaret, sed totam precibus & ardentiori studio pietatis adderet, quod omnino requiri intelligebat, cum fatale illud tempus præforibus esse sentiret, quo exoptatus diu humani generis redemptor nasci debebat. Arguit exemplum hoc puellas & mulieres, quæ procul abiecto omni pudore vagantur, & ad impudica desideria spectatores alliciunt, dum libidinis ardorem vestitu, dictis & gestibus falacissimis produnt. damnantur etiam hic coniuges impudici, quos eo usque libido incendit, ut liberis tenellis & totifamiliæ scandalum præbeant, & sæpe intemperantiæ authores sint illis, quos exempli sui gravitate ad mores pudicos & honestos excitare debebant. Peccant hi in naturæ leges, quæ ut partes corporis inhonestiores tegere docet: ita inter animalia ijs, quæ generosa sunt, pudorem indidit, ut generationi operam datum recessum quærant. Elephantes certe in occulto coire scribunt, neque prius ad agmen redire quam vino amne abluti fuerint. E contra proverbio publico notari solet canum in publico et promiscue coeuntium impudentia: quorum non multum abssimiles sunt, qui sanctum et castum per se coniugii usum lasciuia & petulantia turpi impudenter prophanant. Quid vero de illis dicemus fratres, quos suæ libidinis adeo non pudet, ut stupris quoque & adulteriis glorientur, ex eorum commemoratione laudem & voluptatem quærant, adhæc (quod olim impuri poetæ solebant) ea carminibus publicis celebrent? Sunt hi omnes indigni Christiano nomine. Nam Dei Lex est, ne sit scortum in Israel. Et Paulus scortationem & quamuis aliam impuritatem inter Christianos ne no minari quidem vult, & idem ex Christi decreto scortatores & adulteros a regni coelorum communione excludit. Quis ergo Christianos esse dixerit eos, qui in illis sibi placet, quæ a Christi regno sunt alienissima? Sedo infelicitatem nostri seculi, quando eo res redijt, ut qui summum in ecclesia & republica Christiana gradum sibi vendicat, scortationi patrocinentur, lupanaria publica foveant, & ipsi inter stupra & vagas libidines consenescant. Est horum culpa gravior, quam ut verbis explicari possit: pœnam vero eo graviorem merentur, quod pessimi exempli authores sunt, et multos alios trahunt in sceleris societatem.
units.tr: Moreover, the thing to note first is that Elizabeth, after she conceived, is said to have hidden herself for five months. Others give various reasons for this fact, but to me it seems an example of married modesty, which befits women above all. In Elizabeth, who was already advanced in years, this modesty should have had even more place. For although the marriage bed is called undefiled by the Apostle, and Phinutius rightly said of old that intercourse with one's own wife is chastity, it is nonetheless clear that the saints took account of their time and age, so that they would not seem too intemperate. Sarah is known to have observed this as well, when she received with laughter the promise of a son to be born from herself and said: "After I have grown old, and my lord is an old man, shall I give myself to pleasure?" And there is no doubt that Elizabeth, struck by a modesty worthy of a free woman, was ashamed when she felt that she was being watched by everyone as she carried a child. This happens even to younger women, who are more fond of decency. It is also credible that Zachariah, having revealed in writing to his most holy wife the promise announced to him by the angel, was moved by this consideration to avoid the public company of neighbours, but to add to all of it prayers and a more ardent zeal for piety. He understood that this was altogether required, since he felt that the fateful time was at the doors, when the Redeemer of the human race, so long desired, was to be born. This example condemns girls and women who wander, having cast off all shame, and who entice onlookers to shameless desires while they betray the heat of lust by dress, words and most deceitful gestures. Here too are condemned shameless spouses, whom lust inflames to such a degree that they give scandal to tender children and to the whole household, and are often the authors of intemperance to those whom by the dignity of their example they ought to have stirred to chaste and honourable morals. These people sin against the laws of nature, which teaches us to cover the more shameful parts of the body. Among animals, nature has put a sense of shame into those which are noble, so that they seek a withdrawn place for the business of generation. Elephants, indeed, are written of as mating in secret, and not returning to the herd until they have been washed in a river. On the other hand, by a common proverb the shamelessness of dogs, which mate in public and indiscriminately, is usually noted. Not much unlike them are those who shamelessly profane the holy and chaste use of marriage in itself with shameful wantonness and lewdness. But what shall we say of those, brethren, whom shame does not restrain from their lust to such a degree that they even boast of debaucheries and adulteries, seek praise and pleasure from recounting them, and, as impure poets used to do, celebrate them in public songs? All of these are unworthy of the Christian name. For it is the law of God that there be no whore in Israel. And Paul does not even wish fornication or any other impurity to be named among Christians, and the same man, by Christ's decree, excludes fornicators and adulterers from fellowship in the kingdom of heaven. Who then would call Christians those who take pleasure in things most alien to the kingdom of Christ? But I lament the unhappiness of our age, when things have come to such a point that those who claim for themselves the highest rank in the Church and the Christian commonwealth defend fornication, keep public brothels, and themselves grow old amid debaucheries and wandering lusts. Their guilt is too grave to be explained in words, and they deserve a punishment all the heavier because they are the most wicked examples and draw many others into the fellowship of their crime.

units.la: Restat ut Elizabetæ verba quoque audiamus, quibus Dei beneficium celebravit. Nempe ita (inquit) fecit mihi Dominus in diebus, quibus respexit, ut auferret probrum illud meum inter homines. Est hoc quoque animi pij & modesti indicium, quod neque insolenter se iactat, neque æmulis suis amarulenter insultat, sed ad Deum omne hoc referens, hunc omnis boni authorem agnoscit. Vbirursus admonemur, liberos nobis a Deo dari, & proinde patienter ferendos esse labores, qui illis educandis & instituendis incumbunt. Curemus autem in primis, ut ad Deum adducantur, & huic consecrati sint. Turpe enim & iniquum fuerit, nostra negligentia eos a Deo alienari, quos ab illo accepimus. Qui vero steriles sunt, ij se a Deo humiliari cogitent, & orbitatem patienter ferant, quæ etsi sua incommoda habeat, vicissim tamen multis molestijs & curis caret, quibus exercentur, qui liberos habent. Probrum vero, quod ex orbitate nascitur, inter solos homines hæret (sicuti Elizabetæ verba testantur) coram Deo autem nos nihilo inferiores reddit, neque animarum saluti incommodat. Discamus prætera secundum sanctissimæ huius mulieris exemplum, omnis boni authorem agnoscere Deum. Qui id faciunt, ij donis omnibus digne & recte vtuntur, cum fere omnia propter abusum exitio sint ijs, qui quasi nihil a Deo habeant, sua industriæ omnia transcribunt. In primis autem celebremus Dei gratiam, qui infelix peccati & mortis æternæ probrum a nobis abstulit, & gloriæ immortalis atque cœlestis hæredes fecit per meritum filij Iesu Christi. Cui debetur benedictio, bonor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains that we should also hear the words of Elizabeth, in which she celebrated God's benefit. Thus, she says: "The Lord has done this for me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my disgrace among men." This too is a sign of a pious and modest mind, which neither boasts insolently nor insults its rivals bitterly, but refers all this to God and acknowledges him as the author of every good. Here again we are reminded that children are given to us by God, and that therefore the labours which are involved in bringing them up and instructing them must be borne patiently. Above all, let us take care that they are brought to God and dedicated to him. For it would be shameful and wrong, through our negligence, for those whom we have received from him to be estranged from him. Those who are barren, however, should consider that they are humbled by God, and should bear their childlessness patiently. Although this has its own inconveniences, it is free in return from many troubles and cares with which those who have children are exercised. The disgrace that arises from childlessness clings only among men (as the words of Elizabeth bear witness), but before God it makes us in no way inferior, nor does it harm the salvation of our souls. Let us learn besides, following the example of this most holy woman, to acknowledge God as the author of every good. Those who do this use all their gifts worthily and rightly, whereas almost all things are, through abuse, a ruin to those who, as if they had nothing from God, ascribe everything to their own industry. Above all, let us celebrate the grace of God, who has taken from us the unhappy disgrace of sin and eternal death, and has made us heirs of immortal and heavenly glory through the merit of his Son Jesus Christ. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: Homily VII.

units.la: Mense autem sexto missus est Angelus Gabriel à Deo in vrbem Galilææ, cui nomen Nazareth, ad virginem desponsam viro cui nomen erat Ioseph, ex domo Dauidis, & nomen virginis erat Maria. Et ingressus Angelus ad eam, dixit: Aue in gratiam recepta, Dominus tecum, benedicta tu inter mulieres.
units.tr: "In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary. And the angel came in unto her and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women."

units.la: INter Dei opera nullum præstantius & admirabilius est, quàm quòd filium suum vnigenitum, sibi coæternum & coessentialem, in mundum hunc misit, vt verus homo factus, omnes huius vitæ labores atque molestias in terris subiret, & tandem peccata nostra mortis suæ merito expiaret. Nam vt hoc omnem humani ingenij captum longè superat: ita in eodem Deus omnem suam naturam & quæcunque de ipso in scripturis prædicantur, abunde declarauit: iustitiam nimirum, qua pec catis hominum irascitur: bonitatem, qua nostri miseretur, vt nos saluos faciat: veritatem in promissis: sapientiam in inuenienda salutis ratione: potentiam item inuictam, qua per infirmam carnem diabolum & regnum eius omne deuicit. Continetur præterea in hoc Dei facto vniuersa humani generis redemptio atque salus, quam nusquam alibi inueniri apostoli omnes vnanimi consensu testantur. Quapropter communis noster hostis Satan omnibus seculis in hoc fuit, vt aut Iesu Christi historiam totam negaret, aut quæ ad eius incarnationem faciunt, falsis opinionibus aut disputationibus spinosis in dubium vocaret. Olim enim hæreses excitauit per homines contentiosos & rixatores, quorum alij æternam Iesu Christi Deitatem oppugnauerunt, alij eiusdem naturam humanam vellicarunt, & portenta quædam absurdissimarum opinionum commenti sunt, quibus Christianam religionem toti tantumnon mundo suspectam & inuisam fecerunt. Hodie verò non solum veteres hæreses instaurare satagit, sed inter eos, qui de filij Dei diuinitate & incarnationis mysterio non male sentiunt, plerosque virium humanarum & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia ita decepit, vt Iesu Christi meritum omnino euacuent, & illum sibijpsis inutilem reddant, dum in suorum operum meritis salutis spem collocant, quæ in eius solius merito collocata esse debebat. Nihil ergo nobis tam vtile tamen necessarium est, quàm probè tenere filij Dei propter nos incarnati historiam, vt & in fide confirmemur, & aduersus errores atque impias hæreticorum opiniones instructi simus. Est in illius descriptione Lucas præ alijs Euangelistis diligentissimus. Postquam enim de Ioannis conceptione egit, nunc similiter à filij Dei in carne manifestandi conceptione exorsus, hanc ita proponit, vt euidenter doceat, quid de eius cum persona siue essentia tum merito sentire debeamus.
units.tr: Among the works of God there is none more outstanding or admirable than that he sent into this world his only-begotten Son, co-eternal and co-essential with himself, so that he, made true man, might undergo all the labours and troubles of this life on earth and at last expiate our sins by the merit of his death. For although this far exceeds the grasp of the human mind, in it God has also abundantly declared his whole nature and everything that is said of him in the Scriptures: namely his justice, by which he is angry at the sins of men; his goodness, by which he has pity on us, that he may save us; his truth in his promises; his wisdom in devising the way of salvation; and likewise his unconquered power, by which, through weak flesh, he overcame the devil and all his kingdom. Moreover, the whole redemption and salvation of the human race is contained in this deed of God, which all the apostles with one accord testify is to be found nowhere else. Therefore our common enemy Satan has in every age aimed either to deny the whole history of Jesus Christ or to call into doubt, by false opinions or thorny disputations, the things that bear on his incarnation. For of old he stirred up heresies through contentious and quarrelsome men: some of them attacked the eternal Deity of Jesus Christ, others plucked at his human nature, and they devised monstrous opinions of utter absurdity, by which they made the Christian religion suspect and hated by almost the whole world. Today, however, he not only strives to revive the old heresies, but among those who do not think badly of the divinity of the Son of God and the mystery of the incarnation, he has deceived most of them by confidence in human strength and their own righteousness, so that they utterly empty the merit of Jesus Christ and render him useless to themselves, while they place their hope of salvation in the merits of their own works, when it ought to have been placed in his merit alone. Nothing, therefore, is so useful and yet so necessary for us as to hold firmly to the history of the Son of God, incarnate for our sake, so that we may both be confirmed in faith and be equipped against errors and the impious opinions of heretics. Luke is more painstaking than the other evangelists in describing it. For after treating of the conception of John, he now likewise begins with the conception of the manifestation of the Son of God in the flesh, and sets it forth in such a way as clearly to teach what we ought to think of him, both as to his person or essence and as to his merit.

units.la: Rursus autem à circunstantijs narrandi initium facit, vt ostendat non de alio hic agi, quàm qui olim promissus fit, & quem in carnem venturum esse olim prophetæ prædixerint. Et primo quidem tempus notat, mensem nimirum sextum à Ioannis conceptione. Tot igitur mensibus hic Christum antecessit. At hic repetere oportet, quod initio huius libri de regno Herodis & tempore illo fatali dictum est, quando Iudæorum gente à Romanis deuicta & exteri regis tyrannide oppressa, promissus ille humanæ salutis author expectabatur secundum Iacobi patriarchæ & aliorum prophetarum vaticinia. Deinde author totius negotij indicatur Deus, qui Angelum Gabrielem misit, ne quid humano consilio gestum esse, vel alicuius viri operam huic conceptioni inseruisse putemus. Rursus autem Gabrielis nomen exprimitur, quo Dei potentiam aut robur denotari nuper diximus, vt huius consideratione fidem suam confirment, quibus impossibile videtur, filium Dei à virgine concipi & illæsa eius virginitate ex illa hominem nasci potuisse. Adhæc locus conceptionis nominatur, Nazareth, vbi postea æducatum quoque fuisse constat: quod maioris mysterij ergo factum esse Matthæus testatur, vt nimirum omnes intelligerent, Christum verum illum Nazaræum esse, quem veteres illi designarint, & cuius typus olim in Samsone, populi veteris vindice, præcesserat. Postremò matrem Christi ostendit Euangelista, Mariam virginem: ita nimirum innuens, non aliam hanc fuisse, quàm de qua olim Isaias dixit: Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Immanuel. Cui vaticinio etiam promissio primis parentibus facta consentit, in qua semen mulieris dicitur Christus, vt qui ex sola muliere absque viri congressu nasci debuit. Ita vero facto opus erat, ne secundum naturae leges conceptus & natus naturae nostrae vitiositatem in se reciperet, & natales haberet peccati labe pollutos vt reliqui homines, quos omnes in peccato concipi & nasci sacrae literae testantur. Christus itaque ex virgine natus est, vt nostros natales suo merito sanctificaret, & innatae nobis vitiositati mederetur. Quod vtinam hodie diligentius observarent aduersarij nostri, qui de virginitate quidem Mariae multum contendunt (quasi vero hanc aliquis nostrum neget) interim vero eius causam & vsum prorsus negligunt, imo hoc ipsum non obscure negant, cuius causa ipsam virginem esse oportuit. Caeterum virginis Mariae conditionem quoque exprimit Lucas, quando desponsam fuisse ait viro Iosepho nimirum, qui ex Dauidis domo seu posteritate originem ducebat. Desponsam vero fuisse dicit, nondum ad virum adductam, ne virginitas in suspicionem veniret. Ideo Matthaeus scribit, illam praegnantem deprehensam fuisse, priusquam Iosephus illam adse duxisset. Solebant enim Hebraei filias maritis promissas aliquo tempore domi suae detinere, & virginitatis signa asseruare, quae proferre possent, si postea a marito violati pudoris accusarentur. Nominatur autem Iosephi familia, vt inde constet, Mariam quoque eiusdem familiae fuisse. Extat enim Lex, qua prohibetur ne familiae & tribus miscentur, & ne hereditatum confusio fiat. Quam legem etsi illo tempore non ab omnibus observatam fuisse nuper dixerimus, non tamen verisimile est, Iosephum & Mariam in hanc voluisse peccare, cum a iustitia & pietate prae aliis commendentur. Scio nonnullis argumentum hoc infirmum, imo ridiculum videri: sed illi dum in illo confutando ingenij acumen & eruditionem exquisitam ostentant, sibi plus iactantiae & ambitionis quam pietatis inesse probant, dum in dubium vocant id, quod ad confirmandam fidem in Christum facit, neque interim firmiora argumenta proferunt, quibus demonstretur, Christum quoad carnem ex Dauidis familia descendisse. Quod si quaeras, cur id non clarius expresserint Euangelistae, respondeo, illis satis fuisse in rebus omnibus nota eam generis aut familiae notationem ponere, quae tunc apud omnes recepta & in vulgari vsu erat. Quod autem scioli illi de Elizabeta obiiciunt, quae Mariae cognata dicitur, suo loco diluetur. Nunc sufficiat, in Christi natalibus omnia convenire cum promissionibus & prophetijs, & proinde illum esse promissum illum humani generis redemptorem. Priusquam tamen ab hoc loco discedamus, duo nobis consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: Again, he begins the narrative from the circumstances, to show that it is not another who is here spoken of than the one who was promised of old and whom the prophets foretold would come in the flesh. And first he notes the time, namely the sixth month after John's conception. So Christ here comes six months after him. But here we must recall what was said at the beginning of this book about the reign of Herod and that fateful time, when the Jewish nation had been conquered by the Romans and oppressed by the tyranny of a foreign king, and that promised author of human salvation was awaited according to the prophecies of the patriarch Jacob and the other prophets. Then God is indicated as the author of the whole undertaking, since he sent the angel Gabriel, lest we think that anything was done by human counsel or that the work of any man contributed to this conception. Again, the name of Gabriel is expressed, which we lately said denotes the power or strength of God, so that by considering it they may strengthen their faith, for whom it seems impossible that the Son of God could be conceived by a virgin and that a man could be born from her with her virginity unharmed. In addition, the place of the conception is named: Nazareth, where it is also agreed that he was afterwards brought up. Matthew testifies that this was done for a greater mystery, namely so that everyone might understand that Christ is that true Nazarene whom the ancients designated, and whose type had gone before of old in Samson, the deliverer of the old people. Finally, the Evangelist shows the mother of Christ, the virgin Mary, thereby indicating that she was none other than the one of whom Isaiah long ago said: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Immanuel." The promise made to the first parents agrees with this prophecy, in which Christ is called the seed of the woman, because he was to be born from a woman alone, without the union of a man. Yet it was necessary that it be done in this way, lest the conceived and born one, according to the laws of nature, should take on himself the corruption of our nature and have a birth polluted by the stain of sin, as the other men have, all of whom Holy Scripture testifies are conceived and born in sin. Christ therefore was born of a virgin, so that he might sanctify our birth by his merit and heal the corruption innate in us. Would that our adversaries today observed this more carefully, who indeed contend much about the virginity of Mary (as if any of us denied it), yet meanwhile wholly neglect its cause and purpose, and even do not obscurely deny that very thing for which the virgin had to be a virgin. Moreover, Luke also sets out the condition of the virgin Mary, when he says that she was betrothed to Joseph, a man who traced his origin from the house or posterity of David. He says she was betrothed, not yet brought to her husband, so that her virginity might not come under suspicion. Hence Matthew writes that she was found to be pregnant before Joseph had taken her to himself. For the Hebrews used to keep daughters promised to husbands in their own homes for a time, and to preserve the signs of virginity, which they could produce if they were afterwards accused by the husband of violated chastity. Joseph's family is named so that it may be clear that Mary also belonged to the same family. For there is a law forbidding that families and tribes be mixed, and that inheritances be confused. Although we said lately that this law was not observed by all in that time, it is nonetheless not likely that Joseph and Mary wished to sin against it, since they are commended above others for justice and piety. I know this argument seems weak to some, even ridiculous; but while they display the keenness of their wit and their exquisite learning in refuting it, they prove that they have more vanity and ambition than piety, since they call into doubt what serves to confirm faith in Christ, and yet they do not offer firmer arguments by which it might be shown that Christ descended from the family of David according to the flesh. But if you ask why the Evangelists did not express this more clearly, I answer that it was enough for them to set down that designation of descent or family, which was then received by all and in common use. As for what those smatterers object concerning Elizabeth, who is said to be a kinswoman of Mary, it will be answered in its place. For now it is enough that in Christ's birth everything agrees with the promises and prophecies, and therefore that he is that promised redeemer of the human race. Before we leave this passage, however, two things come to be considered by us.

units.la: Primum est, quod nihil hic refertur, quod non cum extremo contemptu & miseria coniunctum sit. Tempus enim hoc toti Iudaeorum genti afflictissimum fuit, sicuti initio huius libri diximus, & vt infra evidentius patebit, vbi Christi natiuitas describitur. Locus vero non obscurus modo & ignobilis fuit, verumetiam infamis, nimirum propter incolarum mores parum probatos. Patet hoc apud Ioannem Euangelistam ex Nathanaelis verbis, qui Philippo dicenti, Invenimus illum, de quo scripsit Moses in Lege & Prophetis, nempe Iesum, filium Iosephi, illum Nazarenum: respondit: A Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse? Quod si Virginem matrem inspicias, pauperculam & viro Pauperi, qui opere manuario victum quaerebat desponsam fuisse videbis. Et quod miserrimum censeri potest, ne pauperibus quidem satis tuto viuere licebat. Constat enim Dauidis familiam Herodi Regi inuisam & suspectam fuisse, eo quod ex ea Regem nasciturum audiuisset, qui populum priscinae libertati vindicaret. At tales voluit Deus esse natales filij sui in carne manifestandi, vt credentes per stultitiam praedicationis, id est, per eorum praedicationem, quae mundo stulta & nullius pretij videntur, salui fierent: vt eq simul constaret, regnum Christi & vniuersam salutis nostrae rationem non constare rebus, quae in mundo hoc eximiae sunt, & externo splendore venditantur. Est hoc multa consideratione dignissimum. Primo enim admonet, de religione & salutis aeternae negotio non ex hominum sensu iudicandum esse, qui multitudinis & mundanae potestatis authoritate ducuntur. Quia enim regnum Christi non est de hoc mundo, nihil etiam nobis ad fidei veritatem & salutis certitudinem hic mundus conferet: sed aeternum Dei decretum nobis spectandum est, quod ille nobis per scripturas propheticas & apostolicas in filio suo reuelauit. Deinde docemur, posito huius mundi fastu humilitati studere. Nec enim stulti modo, verumetiam iniqui & praeposterè ambitiosi sunt, qui gloriam in illis rebus quaerunt, quibus filium Dei, qui Rex gloriae apud Prophetas dicitur, caruisse sciunt. Studeant potius singuli bene vti bonis praesentibus, & propria virtute patriam suam & familiam illustrare, quam alienis plumis sese vestire, dum ex his nobilitatem & nominis splendorem vanantur. Facit praeterea hoc ad consolationem afflictorum, ne se a Deo negligi putent. Nam vt Christus nihilominus fuit dilectus ille Dei filius, etiamsi tota eius vita in terris plena miseriarum & malorum fuerit: ita non obstabunt huius saeculi calamitates, quo minus nos quoque pro suis agnoscat Deus, modo filio suo per fidem insiti fuerimus. Est enim hoc Dei proprium, quod afflictos & miseros maxime respicit. Ideo in Lege & Prophetis viduas, orphanos & peregrinos diligentissime nobis commendat, & se illorum patrem esse profitetur. Et exempli docent, paucis impune cessisse, qui miseros vel inhumaniter neglexerunt, vel illos maioribus malis insuper aggravarunt. Itaque vehementer errant, qui ex huius saeculi conditione de Dei fauore iudicant. Sunt hi mortalium miserrimi, eo quod tunc a Deo, cum ipsis inimico refugiunt, quando ad eius opem in primis recurrere oportebat. Et idem de religione & aeternae salutis ratione nihil certum statuere possunt, cum omnia in hoc saeculo incerta & fluxa sint.
units.tr: The first is that nothing is related here which is not joined with extreme contempt and misery. For this time was most afflicted for the whole Jewish nation, as we said at the beginning of this book, and as will appear more clearly below, where the birth of Christ is described. The place, moreover, was not only obscure and humble, but even infamous, on account of the poorly regarded morals of its inhabitants. This is evident in John the Evangelist from the words of Nathanael, who, when Philip said, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and the Prophets wrote, namely Jesus, the son of Joseph, that Nazarene," replied, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" And if you look at the Virgin Mother, you will see that she was a poor little woman, betrothed to a poor man who earned his living by manual labour. And what can be thought most wretched, even the poor could not live safely. For it is known that the family of David was hated and suspected by King Herod, because he had heard that a king would be born from it who would restore the people to their ancient liberty. Yet God willed the birth of his Son in the flesh to be of such a kind, so that those who believed through the foolishness of the preaching, that is, through the preaching of those things which seem foolish and worthless to the world, might be saved; and so that it might at the same time be clear that the kingdom of Christ and the whole plan of our salvation do not rest on the things that are eminent in this world and boast of outward splendour. This is most worthy of much consideration. For first it warns us that concerning religion and the business of eternal salvation we must not judge by the opinion of men, who are led by the authority of the multitude and of worldly power. For since the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, this world will contribute nothing to us for the truth of faith or the certainty of salvation; rather we must look to the eternal decree of God, which he has revealed to us in his Son through the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures. Next we are taught that, setting aside the pride of this world, we should strive for humility. For those are not only foolish but also wicked and perversely ambitious who seek glory in those things which they know the Son of God, who is called the King of glory by the prophets, lacked. Rather let each one strive to use well the goods at hand, and by his own virtue to make his country and family illustrious, rather than to clothe himself in borrowed feathers while seeking from these nobility and the splendour of a name. Moreover, this serves for the consolation of the afflicted, lest they think that they are neglected by God. For just as Christ was nonetheless that beloved Son of God, even though his whole life on earth was full of miseries and evils, so the calamities of this age will not prevent God from acknowledging us also as his own, provided we have been grafted into his Son through faith. For it is the peculiar property of God that he especially regards the afflicted and wretched. Therefore in the Law and the Prophets he most diligently commends to us widows, orphans and strangers, and professes himself to be their father. And examples teach that few have gone unpunished who have either inhumanly neglected the wretched or have further burdened them with greater evils. Thus those greatly err who judge of God's favour from the condition of this age. Such people are the most wretched of mortals, because they flee from God when they are his enemy, at the very time when they most need to run to his help. And likewise they can establish nothing certain about religion and the reckoning of eternal salvation, since everything in this age is uncertain and fleeting.

units.la: Alterum non minus dignum consideratu occurrit, quod etsi Dei Filium ex virgine hominem nasci oportuerit, ex ea tamen voluit nasci, quae viro iam promissa, & proinde coniugii legibus alligata erat. Fecit hoc quidem ad defendendam virginis famam inter homines, & ad testimonium virginitatis, quod Iosephum ex Angeli oraculo certissimum reddere potuit. At simul exemplum hoc matrimonij dignitatem vehementer commendat. Instituit illud Deus (quemadmodum muper quoque diximus) in paradiso, priusquam parentes nostri in peccatum prolapsi essent. Deinde Legem hanc omnium gentium animis inscripsit, vt coniugium in honore habuerint, & eius violatores quoque supplicio dignos iudicarint. At quasi parum hoc esset, illud ipsum aeterni filij Dei incarnatione sanctificari oportuit, quo melius constaret, illud revera sacrosanctum, & ab omni labe sceleris alienissimum esse. Nemo igitur inter veri Dei cultores vnquam inuentus est, qui non maximi fecerit coniugium: haereticis vero plerisque hoc commune fuit, quod vel impia audacia illius vsum omnem damnauerunt, vel sub huius praetextu in foedissimas libidines effusi sunt (sicuti de Nicolaitis & Gnosticis tradunt scriptores ecclesiastici) vel saltem absque religione in illo versati sunt. De Antichristo autem non obscura vaticinia extant, quae illum prophanatorem coniugalis foederis fore testantur: quā de re cum alibi sit dictum, eadem nunc repetere superuacaneum est. Discant nunc qui Christianum nomen profitentur, non minimam pietatis partem in religiosa fidei coniugalis obseruatione consistere, neq; dignos esse nomine Christiano eos, qui illam impudenter violant, aut eum statum prophanare audent, quem Dei filius salutifera sua incarnatione ornare & sanctificare dignatus est.
units.tr: Another point, no less worth considering, presents itself. Although the Son of God had to be born as a man of a virgin, he nevertheless willed to be born of one who had already been promised to a husband and was therefore bound by the laws of marriage. He did this, certainly, to defend the virgin's reputation among men and to provide a witness to her virginity, which could make Joseph certain through the angel's oracle. But at the same time this example greatly commends the dignity of marriage. God instituted it (as we said just before) in paradise, before our parents fell into sin. Then he wrote this law on the minds of all nations, so that they held marriage in honour and judged its violators worthy of punishment. But as if this were too little, that very institution had to be sanctified by the incarnation of the eternal Son of God, so that it might be clearer that marriage is truly holy and most remote from every stain of wickedness. Therefore no one has ever been found among the true worshippers of God who did not esteem marriage most highly. Among most heretics, however, it was common either that, in impious boldness, they condemned all use of it, or that under its pretext they plunged into most foul lusts (as the ecclesiastical writers relate of the Nicolaitans and the Gnostics), or at least that they engaged in it without any religious regard. Concerning Antichrist, moreover, there are clear prophecies which testify that he will be a profaner of the marriage covenant. Since this has been said elsewhere, it is superfluous to repeat it now. Let those who profess the Christian name learn that a not small part of piety consists in the religious observance of the marriage bond, and that those who shamelessly violate it, or dare to profane that state which the Son of God deigned to adorn and sanctify by his saving incarnation, are not worthy of the Christian name.

units.la: Quia vero Angelum Gabrielem ad Mariam a Deo missum dixerat Lucas, nunc vt idem suae legatione functus sit narrat. Quo loco primum occurrit, quod ad illam ingressus dicitur, in eius nimirum domum aut eam domus partem, quam frequentius incolebat. Ergo non foris vagantem, aut hinc inde discurrentem inuenit, quod lasciuae & petulantes puellae & mulieres facere solent, quae etsi quod foris agant nihil sit, ad quaeuis tamen spectanda prodeunt in publicum, & vt Poeta dicebat: Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur vt ipsae. Est ergo hoc in Maria castae pudicitiae argumentum, qua virgines cumprimis ornatas esse conuenit, vt in sequenti sermone pluribus dicetur.
units.tr: But since Luke had said that the angel Gabriel was sent by God to Mary, he now relates how the same angel carried out his embassy. Here the first thing that meets us is that he is said to have entered to her, namely into her house or into that part of the house which she more often occupied. So he did not find her wandering abroad or running hither and thither, as wanton and frivolous girls and women are wont to do, who, even if they have nothing to do outside, nevertheless come out into public to be looked at, and, as the poet said: "They come to be seen, they come that they themselves may be looked at." This, then, is a proof of Mary's chaste modesty, with which virgins above all should be adorned, as will be said at greater length in the following sermon.

units.la: Nunc salutationem audiamus, qua illam Angelus compellauit, in cuius consideratione nos eo diligentius versari oportet, quod eius occasione omnis generis superstitiones circa Diuae Virginis cultum obortas esse constat, quibus hodie multi ita detinentur, vt vix vllas rationes admittant, quibus illos ad puriorem vnius veri Dei cultum reuocare studemus. Olim quidem in Arabia Collyridianos fuisse legimus, quos orthodoxi patres haeresteos crimine notarunt, quod ipsorum faeminae in honorem Mariae sacra facerent, & huic collyridem (quae placenta species est) offerrent. Neq; in illis hoc solum reprehenderunt, quod faeminae sacrificandi munus vsurparent, & gentilitio more placentā immolarent, sed ipsam adorationem & inuocationem Diuae Virginis damnauerunt. uerunt. Testem habemus eius rei Epiphanium,qui vt Antidicomarianitas, qui perpetuam Ma-riæ virginitatem negabant,grauiter confutauit:ita istorum quoque superstitionem non minori stu-dio oppugnans,inter cætera sic scribit: Reuera sanctum erat corpus Mariæ,non tamen Deus. Re-uera virgo erat ipsa virgo,& honorata,sed non ad adorationem nobis data,sed ipsa adorans eum, qui ex ipsa quoad carne genitus est,de cœlis vero ex sinibus paternis accessit. Et paulo post: Quis prophetarum præcepit hominem adorari,nedum mulierem? Eximium equidem est vas,sed mulier & nihil à natura immutata: verum & intelleētu & sensu in honore honorata, veluti corpora san-ctorum,& siquid amplius ad glorificationem dixerim, sicut Helias ex matre virgo, & sic ma-nens in perpetuum,& translatus, & mortem non conspicatus: sicut Ioannes, qui super pectus Do-mini recubuit, quem diligebat Iesus: sicut Thecla sancta. Et Maria adhuc honoratior hac est propter dispensationem mysterij, qua digna facta est. Sed neque Helias adorandus est, etiam-si in vnius sit: neque Ioannes adorandus, quanquam per preces suas proprias dormitionem suam admirandam effecerit, imò potius ex Deo gratiam acceperit. Sed neque Thecla, neque quisquam sanctus adoratur. Non enim dominabitur nobis antiquus error, vt relinquamus viuentem, & adoremus ea quæ ab ipso facta sunt. Et rursum: Sit in honore Maria: Pater & Filius & Spi-ritus sanctus adoretur, Mariam nemo adoret, non dico mulierem: imò neque virum: Deo debe-tur hoc mysterium. Et aduersus Antidicomarianitas in genere de sanctorum cultu pronuntians idem pater ait: Non conuenit colere sanctos vltra decorum, sed honorare ipsorum Dominum. Et hæc quidem omnia ex Epiphanij scriptis recitare libuit, vt eorum calumniis respondeamus, qui nos noui dogmatis authores & in Diuam virginem & reliquos sanctos contumeliosos esse aiunt, quòd illos diuino cultu & adoratione colendos esse negamus. Cur autem in illos iniurij dicimur, cùm relucentem in illis Dei gratiam agnoscamus & gratis animis prædicemus? Cur nouitatis ac-cusamur,qui idem cum veteri Ecclesia sentimus,cuius sententiam Epiphanius tam diserte expo-suit,neque ab aliquo vnquam est reprehensus? Sed facile est crimen hoc in aduersarios nostros retorquere, qui circa eum Mariæ cultum occupantur, quem multis sæculis demum postea institu-tum, & nouis subinde superstitionibus auctum esse constat. Nam vt à festis exordiamur, inter il-la antiquissimum habetur, quod Purificationis dicunt. At hoc à Iustiniano Imperatore in Christi honorem institutum & festum τῆς ὑπαπαντῆς, id est, exceptionis Christi nimirum per Simeo-nem in templo factæ, dictum fuisse Nicephorus tradit. Posteris demum temporibus mutatum, nomen quoque nouum accepit, vt Mariæ festum esset, quod prius Christi fuerat. Festa verò Af-sumptionis & Natiuitatis Mariæ circa annum Domini 1273. in Lugdunensi Concilio institu-ta fuisse, ex libro Decretorum apparet. Visitationis Mariæ festum Vrbanus Papa Sexus indi-xit sub annum Domini 1380. quo tempore machinas bellicas quoque, quas àsono tonitruum fra-gorem imitante bombardas dicunt, Monachus quidam adinuenit cum incredibili totius generis humani pernitie. Annunciationis autem festum sub Ludouico Pio celebrandum statuerunt in Sy-nodo, quæ Aquisgrani coijt,circa annum à nato Christo 819. Quod autem in Conceptionis Ma-riæ memoriam celebratur, in Concilio demum Basiliensi initium habuit, anno Christi 1439. Et his omnibus postremum tandem accessit festum Præsentationis Mariæ anno Domini 1484. Sunt ergo hæc omnia noua hominum superstitiosorum inuenta,quibus veterem Ecclesiam prorsus caruis-se certò constat ex D. Augustini ad Ianuarium epistola, qui Ecclesiæ annuas ferias enumerans, Christi quidem paucas admodum, Mariæ autem nullas omnino recenset. Quod ipsum de precibus quoque & inuocatione illius dici potest. Nam vt horæ (quas vocant Canonicas) illi quotidie di-cerentur, Vrbani Secundi decretum est, qui Gregorij Septimi, hominis scelestissimi & totius or-bis turbatoris discipulus, adhæc belli sacri author fuit, quo nullum vnquam crudelius & diutur-nius gestum est. Incidunt eius tempora in annum Domini 1090. Adiecit horis istis postea circa annum 1240. canticum illud superstitiosissimum, quod Salue Regina vocant, Gregorius nonus, ipse quoque notus in historia ex virtutibus pontificijs, perfidia nimirum in Imperatores & bel-lus cruentis,quorum faces accendit. Secutus est sub annum Christi 1310. Ioannes XXII. qui sta-tuit, vt sub vesperam campanæ pulsentur, & tunc quisque salutationis angelicæ verba ter reci-
units.tr: Now let us hear the greeting with which the angel addressed her. We ought to dwell on it the more carefully because it is well known that on its occasion every kind of superstition about the worship of the Blessed Virgin has arisen, by which many are now so held captive that they admit scarcely any reasons by which we seek to recall them to the purer worship of the one true God. Indeed we read that long ago in Arabia there were Collyridians, whom the orthodox Fathers branded with the crime of heresy, because their women performed sacred rites in honour of Mary and offered her a collyris (a kind of cake). Nor did they reprove in them only this, that the women usurped the office of sacrificing and offered cakes in the manner of the Gentiles, but they also condemned the very adoration and invocation of the Blessed Virgin. We have Epiphanius as a witness to this matter, who, when he sharply refuted the Antidicomarianites, who denied Mary's perpetual virginity, likewise opposed their superstition with no less zeal, and among other things writes thus: "Truly the body of Mary was holy, but it was not God. Truly the Virgin was a virgin and honoured, but she was not given to us for adoration; rather she herself adored him who was born of her according to the flesh, and who came from the heavens out of the bosom of the Father." And a little after: "Which of the prophets commanded that a man be adored, let alone a woman? She is indeed an outstanding vessel, but a woman, and nothing changed from nature; yet in understanding and in sense she is honoured with honour, like the bodies of the saints; and if I may say something further for her glorification: like Elijah, who, a virgin from his mother, remained so for ever, and was taken up, and did not see death; like John, who reclined on the breast of the Lord, whom Jesus loved; like the holy Thecla. And Mary is more honoured than these because of the dispensation of the mystery for which she was made worthy." But neither is Elijah to be adored, even though he is one alone; nor John to be adored, although by his own prayers he made his falling asleep wonderful, rather he received grace from God. But neither Thecla nor any saint is adored. For the ancient error shall not rule over us, so that we should forsake the living God and adore those things which he has made. And again: "Let Mary be honoured; let the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit be adored; let no one adore Mary, I do not say a woman, but not even a man: this mystery is owed to God alone." And against the Antidicomarianites, speaking generally about the cult of the saints, the same Father says: "It is not fitting to worship the saints beyond what is proper, but to honour their Lord." These things I have been pleased to recite from the writings of Epiphanius, so that we may answer the calumnies of those who say that we are authors of a new doctrine and insulting towards the Blessed Virgin and the other saints, because we deny that they are to be worshipped and adored with divine worship. But why are we accused of injuring them, when we acknowledge the grace of God shining forth in them and gladly proclaim it? Why are we accused of novelty, when we hold the same view as the ancient Church, whose judgment Epiphanius set forth so clearly, and was never rebuked by anyone? But it is easy to turn this charge back on our opponents, who are occupied with that cult of Mary which is known to have been instituted many centuries later and to have been increased by new superstitions from time to time. For, to begin with the feasts, among those the most ancient is held to be the one they call the Purification. But Nicephorus relates that this was instituted by the Emperor Justinian in honour of Christ, and was called the feast of [hypapante] (that is, of the meeting of Christ, namely as made in the temple by Simeon). In later times it was changed, and it also received a new name, so that what had been the feast of Christ became the feast of Mary. The feasts of the Assumption and the Nativity of Mary were instituted about the year of the Lord 1273, at the Council of Lyons, as appears from the book of the Decretals. Pope Urban the Sixth appointed the feast of the Visitation of Mary about the year of the Lord 1380, at which time a certain monk also invented war machines, which they call bombards, imitating the crash of thunder, with incredible destruction of the whole human race. The feast of the Annunciation, moreover, was ordered to be celebrated under Louis the Pious, at the synod which met at Aachen, about the year 819 after the birth of Christ. That which is celebrated in memory of the Conception of Mary first began at the Council of Basel, in the year of Christ 1439. And finally, to all these was added the feast of the Presentation of Mary, in the year of the Lord 1484. These, then, are all new inventions of superstitious men, and it is certain from the letter of St Augustine to Januarius that the ancient Church lacked them entirely; for in enumerating the yearly feasts of the Church, he mentions indeed very few of Christ, and none at all of Mary. The same can be said of prayers and of the invocation of her. For the hours, which they call canonical, were ordained to be said daily by a decree of Urban the Second, who was a disciple of Gregory the Seventh, a most wicked man and a disturber of the whole world, and moreover the author of the holy war, than which none was ever waged more cruelly and for longer. His time falls in the year of the Lord 1090. Afterwards, about the year 1240, Gregory the Ninth, also well known in history for his papal virtues, namely perfidy towards emperors and bloody wars, of which he kindled the flames, added to these hours that most superstitious canticle which they call the Salve Regina. Then, about the year of Christ 1310, John the Twenty-second ordained that the bells be rung at evening, and that then each one should say three times the words of the angelic greeting in honour of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: De consecrat. dist. cap. prou nuntiandum. cet in Mariæ virginis honorem. At Ioannes ille Papa is est, qui fortissimum & pissimum Imperatorem Ludouicum III. primum Helueticæ libertatis confirmatorem, anathemate ferit, & postea multa in totum genus humanum designata facinora hæresim quoque sparsit, animas non videre Deum ante diem nouissimum. Errorum autem & superstitionum istarum omnium mihi præcipua causa fuisse videtur, quod salutatio Angelica à nonnullis precationis loco habita fuit, qui errorem hunc ipsius Angeli exemplo defendi putauerunt, & in illo postea confirmati sunt, cum Romani Pontifices superstitionem istam proprijs nolarum sacrarum pulsibus & indulgentijs consecrarent. Auxerunt interea superstitionem Monachi, qui Rosaria (vt illorum verbo vtar) commenti sunt, & eò rem adduxerunt, vt salutationis istius maior & frequentior quàm Orationis dominicæ visus fuerit, imò hæc inter Christiani nominis professores præ illa quasi vilescere & negle& fit.
units.tr: De consecrat. dist. cap. prou nuntiandum. ...ordered in honour of the Virgin Mary. But that John is the pope who anathematized the most brave and most pious emperor Louis III, the first champion of Helvetic liberty. Afterwards, besides the many crimes he committed against the whole human race, he also spread the heresy that souls do not see God before the last day. The chief cause of all these errors and superstitions seems to me to be that the Angelic salutation was taken by some as a form of prayer. They thought this error could be defended by the example of the angel himself, and they were confirmed in it later, when the Roman pontiffs consecrated this superstition with their own peals of sacred bells and with indulgences. Meanwhile the monks increased the superstition. They invented the Rosaries (to use their own word), and they brought the matter to such a point that this salutation seems greater and more frequent than the Lord's Prayer. Indeed, among professors of the Christian name it is almost held cheap and neglected in comparison with that prayer.

units.la: Sed facile est errorem illum argumentis solidissimis refellere. Si enim oratio colloquium est cum Deo, quo vel petimus quæ nobis necessaria & vtilia esse putamus, vel pro acceptis beneficijs gratias agimus: nimium inepti & sacrarum rerum imperiti sunt, qui orationis loco vtuntur his verbis, quibus neque Deus compellatur (qui vnus & solus inuocari debet) neque aliquid petitur, & quæ gratiarum quoque actionem nullam continent. Deinde ijdem Angelum neglecti cultus diuini insimulant. Si enim orationem hæc illius verba continent, Mariam adorauerit oportet. At hoc ab Angelorum officio alienissimum est, qui vt ipsi à nemine mortalium adorari volunt (sicut ex Apocalypseos vigesimo secundo capite apparet) ita neminem illi quoque, præter vnum Deum adorant. Neque hic illorum obiectionem magni facimus, qui dicunt: Fatemur equidem, precationem his verbis nullam contineri, neque ijs aliquem precationis loco debere vti: at quis prohibebit, quò minus ijsdem verbis Dominam virginem salutem, quibus eam Angelus salutauit? Num quod huic licuit, mihi nefas esse putabitur? At his respondemus, non omnia in exemplum trahi debere, quæ ab Angelis aut Sanctis Dei cultoribus olim facta scribuntur. Salutauit Gedeonem quoque Angelus, dicens: Sit Dominus tecum vir fortissime. Quis verò piorum veteris Testamenti Gedeonem, iam vita defunctum, simili salutatione dignatus est? aut quis eundem in periculis bellicis ideo salutandum putauit, vt victoria facilius potiretur? Qui ergo Mariam hodie salutare solent, ij primò officium alienum inuadunt, dum quod Angelo soli in mandatis datum fuit, ad se transferunt. Deinde nimium ridiculos sese præbent dum absentem compellant, & illi verba faciunt, quæ neque nostrorum negotiorum curis iam occupatur, neque responsa dat vlla, quibus constet, nos ab illa exaudiri. Itaque relictis hominum superstitiosorum ineptijs, preces vni Deo offeramus, & à Christo nobis traditam precandi formulam constanter teneamus: salutationis autem Angelicæ hic nobis præcipuus vsus sit, vt de incarnatione filij Dei certiores facti, salutis spem omnem in illo solo habeamus collocatam, neque priuata temeritate honorem, qui illi debetur, in aliquam ex creaturis transferamus, cum illius vox sit: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Docet deinde Angeli salutatio, quid de Maria iudicari, quidue in illa prædicari debeat. Quæ omnia vt rectius intelligantur, singula verba inspexisse proderit.
units.tr: But that error is easily refuted by very solid arguments. If prayer is a conversation with God, in which we either ask for what we think necessary and useful for us, or give thanks for benefits received, then those are far too foolish and ignorant of sacred things who use in place of prayer these words, which neither address God (who alone ought to be invoked) nor ask for anything, and which contain no thanksgiving either. Furthermore, these same people charge the angel with neglecting the divine worship. For if these words contain a prayer, then he must have worshipped Mary. But this is most alien to the office of angels, who, as they do not wish to be worshipped by any mortal (as appears from Apocalypse 22), so they worship no one else except the one God. Nor do we set much store by the objection of those who say: "We admit that no prayer is contained in these words, and that no one ought to use them in place of prayer. But who will forbid us to greet the Virgin Lady with the same words with which the angel greeted her? Will it be thought wrong for me to do what was allowed to him?" To these we reply that not everything recorded as having been done by angels or by the saints of God is to be drawn into an example. The angel also greeted Gideon, saying: "The Lord be with you, most valiant man" (Judg. 6). But which of the godly of the Old Testament ever honoured Gideon, already dead, with a similar greeting? Or who thought he should be greeted in this way in the perils of war, so that he might more easily win the victory? So those who are accustomed to greet Mary today first usurp an office that is not theirs, while they transfer to themselves what was committed by command to the angel alone. Then they make themselves quite ridiculous when they address one who is absent and speak to her words which, neither occupied with the cares of our affairs nor giving any answer, show that we are heard by her. Therefore, leaving aside the follies of superstitious men, let us offer our prayers to the one God alone and firmly hold to the form of prayer handed down to us by Christ. The proper use of the angelic salutation for us is this: having been informed of the incarnation of the Son of God, we should place all our hope of salvation in him alone, and not by private rashness transfer to any creature the honour that is due to him, since his voice is: "I am the Lord, this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42). The angel's greeting then teaches what ought to be judged and what proclaimed concerning Mary. To understand all of these more correctly, it will be useful to examine the individual words.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum vox Aue, quæ in Græco χαῖρε habetur. Significat autem χαίρειν idem quod gaudere, quod ipsum per Auere etiam interdum exprimitur, eò quod quæ magno desiderio aüemus, id est cupimus, eadem nobis gaudium & oblectationem maximam pariunt. Vulgò autem obtinuit ex vetusto more, vt inter salutandum hoc verbo vtamur: quia tunc amicis omnia precamur læta & fausta. Respondet ergo formula hæc Hebræorum salutationi, qui pacem optant, sub qua omnem hominis salutem comprehendunt. Voluit autem isto verbo vti Angelus, vt Mariam subito ipsius ingressu & aspectu territam siue turbatam consolaretur, ne quid illa triste vel inauspicatum animo conciperet. Commendatur autem nobis Angelorum exemplis publicus salutandi mos, qui vt ad conciliandam animorum benevolentiam multum confert: ita sine manifesta inhumanitatis specie negligi non potest.
units.tr: The first word that occurs is "Ave," which in the Greek is [χαῖρε]. Now χαίρειν means the same as to rejoice, which is sometimes also expressed by "avere" in Latin, because those things which we greatly desire, that is, which we long for, bring us joy and the greatest delight. From ancient custom, however, it has become common to use this word in greeting, because when we greet friends we wish them all things joyful and auspicious. This formula therefore corresponds to the Hebrew greeting, by which they wish peace, under which they comprehend all the welfare of a person. The angel wished to use this word so that he might comfort Mary, who was terrified or troubled by his sudden entrance and appearance, lest she conceive anything sad or ill-omened in her mind. The angels' example also commends to us the public custom of greeting, which contributes much to winning the goodwill of minds; and so, without a clear appearance of inhumanity, it cannot be neglected.

units.la: Deinde titulo proprio illam Angelus dignatur, & vocat κεχαριτωμένη, quod vetus interpres transtulit, Gratia plena: vnde erroris occasio enata videtur apud linguarum imperitos, qui eam eam sic dictam putarunt, quasi fontem gratiæ, ex quo hanc in nos redundare oporteat. At pugnat hic sensus cum fide vera, & Christi merito detrahit, qui solus est fons ille diuinæ bonitatis atque salutis, de cuius plenitudine (vt Ioannes ait) omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia, id est abundantissimam gratiam & novus quotidie augmentis redundantem. Etsi Græci vocabuli etymon spectes, eam significat, quam Deus sua gratia, id est gratuito fauore sic complexus. Ideo Paulus eodem verbo vtitur, quando de omnibus credentibus loquens, Deum illos in Christo in gratiam recepisse ait. Et Angelus hoc ipsum paulo post exponens ait: Ne timeas Maria: inuenisti enim gratiam apud Deum. Quod si vero Mariam gratuito fauore prosecutus est Deus, perperam faciunt, qui in hac colenda aut inuocanda occupantur, & non potius ad fontem gratiæ contendunt, quem in eius filio Iesu Christo nobis pater aperuit.
units.tr: Then the angel honours her with a title of her own and calls her [κεχαριτωμένη], which the Vulgate translator rendered "full of grace." From this an occasion of error seems to have arisen among those unskilled in languages, who thought she was so called as if she were the fountain of grace, from which it must overflow upon us. But this sense conflicts with the true faith and detracts from the merit of Christ, who alone is that fountain of divine goodness and salvation, "from whose fullness," as John says, "we have all received grace for grace" (John 1), that is, most abundant grace, overflowing with new increases every day. Even if you look at the etymology of the Greek word, it signifies that grace with which God has embraced someone by his own favour, that is, by free kindness. For this reason Paul uses the same word when, speaking of all believers, he says that God has accepted them into grace in Christ (Eph. 1). And the angel, explaining this very thing a little later, says: "Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God" (Luke 1). But if God has shown Mary free favour, they act wrongly who are occupied with worshipping or invoking her, and do not rather hasten to the fountain of grace, which the Father has opened to us in his Son Jesus Christ.

units.la: Porro facit ad prioris expositionem quod sequitur: Dominus tecum. Solet enim Deus perpetuo illis adesse, quos semel in gratiam recepit, vt opus suum in illis perficiat, & ne ipsi carnis infirmitate superati sub onere sibi impositio succumbant. Exemplum eius in virgine Maria euidens habemus, quæ etsi postea curis & laboribus assiduis fatigata sit, & postremo indignissimæ mortis filij sui spectatrix fuerit, ea tamen fidei constantia in hisce certaminibus perseuerauit, vt de præsenti Dei auxilio nemo dubitare possit. Debent vero hoc ad se transferre omnes, qui per fidem in Christum Deo reconciliati sunt. Nam his quoq; præsens adest Deus, neq; patietur, vt à gratia sua & salute excidant, quos filij sui pretioso sanguine acquisiuit.
units.tr: Moreover, what follows supports the former explanation: "The Lord is with you." For God is accustomed always to be present with those whom he has once received into grace, so that he may bring his work to completion in them, and so that they, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, may not succumb under the burden laid upon them. We have a clear example of this in the Virgin Mary, who, although afterwards she was worn out by constant cares and labours, and finally was a witness to the most unworthy death of her son, nevertheless persevered in these struggles with such constancy of faith that no one can doubt the present help of God. Yet all who have been reconciled to God through faith in Christ ought to apply this to themselves. For God is present with them too, and he will not allow those whom he has acquired by the precious blood of his Son to fall away from his grace and salvation.

units.la: Addit Angelus: Benedicta tu inter mulieres. Benedictionis nomine Hebræi omnem felicitatem intelligunt, quæ ex Dei fauore ad nos redit. Sic Lex benedictos in exitu & ingressu suo, id est, felices in omnibus actionibus suis pronunciat, qui Dei præcepta obseruant. Itaque huius membri sensus est: Tu es felicissima illa & beatissima, quam Deus ex vniuerso muliebri sexu sibi delegit, & de qua promissiones extant, quod ipsius semen caput serpentis contriturum sit. Tu (inquam) beata illa virgo es, de qua Isaias olim vaticinatus est: Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabunt nomen eius Immanuel. Quod si omnia, quæ verbis hisce Angelus dixit, simul comprehendas, nihil habebis, cuius ergo Maria vel diuinis honoribus coli, vel in periculis inuocari debebat. Quare Dei gratiam potius agnoscamus, quæ in tota huius mysterij dispensatione sese exeruit, & ex eo consolationem certamque salutis fiduciam concipiamus, quod filium suum ex nobis hominem nasci & amissæ salutis instauratorem fieri voluit. Quoad Mariam vero, tribuamus huic honorem debitum, & eam agnoscamus esse κεχαριτωμένην illam, quam singulari fauore Deus dignatus est, vt illæso virginitatis flore filium suum ex Spiritu sancto conciperet & pareret: imitemur autem eius virtutes, humilitatem, patientiam, fortitudinem, obedientiam, & in primis fidem, in qua constantissimè in finem vsque perseuerauit. Ita fiet, vt ipsi quoque Deo grati simus, & felicitatem veram consequamur in filio eius Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The angel adds: "Blessed are you among women." By the name of blessing the Hebrews understand every happiness that comes back to us from the favour of God. Thus the Law pronounces those blessed in their going out and coming in, that is, happy in all their actions, who keep the precepts of God (Deut. 28). So the sense of this clause is: You are the most fortunate and most blessed, whom God has chosen for himself from the whole female sex, and concerning whom promises exist, that her seed would crush the head of the serpent. You (I say) are that blessed virgin, of whom Isaiah long ago prophesied: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (Isa. 7). But if you take together everything that the angel said in these words, you will have nothing on whose account Mary ought to be worshipped with divine honours or invoked in dangers. Therefore let us rather acknowledge the grace of God, which showed itself in the whole dispensation of this mystery, and from it let us conceive consolation and the sure confidence of salvation, because he willed that his Son should be born of us as a man and become the restorer of lost salvation. As for Mary, let us give her the honour due to her, and acknowledge her to be that [κεχαριτωμένη], whom God by singular favour deigned to make, so that with the flower of her virginity unharmed she should conceive and bear his Son by the Holy Spirit. Let us imitate her virtues: humility, patience, fortitude, obedience, and above all faith, in which she persevered most steadfastly to the end. So it will come about that we ourselves also are pleasing to God, and attain true happiness in his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: HOMILY VIII.

units.la: Illa vero cum vidisset, perturbata est super eius sermone, & cogitabat qualis esset salutatio ista. Tunc dixit ei Angelus: Ne time Maria: inuenisti enim gratiam apud Deum. Et ecce concipies in vtero, & paries filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum. Hic erit magnus, & filius Altissimi vocabitur, dabit ei Dominus Deus thronum Dauidis patris ipsius, regnabit super domum Iacob in æternum, & regni eius non erit finis.
units.tr: But when she saw him, she was troubled at his words and wondered what manner of greeting this might be. Then the angel said to her: "Fear not, Mary, for you have found favour with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end."

units.la: Quoniam Deus in Iesu Christo omnia ea complexus est, quæ ad humani generis redemptionem atque salutem faciunt, non tam vtile quàm necessarium fuit, vt de eius incarnatione nobis certò constaret, per quam ille nobis vnitus atque coniunctus est. Ideo in eius descriptione nihil eorum Lucas omittit, quae nos ad pleniorem Christi cognitionem possunt inducere. Hactenus enim circumstantias expositit, quas cum veterum prophetarum oraculis per omnia conuenire vidimus. Subiecit his salutationem Angelicam, qua apud Mariam virginem vsus est, & quae nos excitat, vt hic magnum quid & nequaquam vulgare animo concipiamus. Sequitur nunc plenior omnium, quae ad huius mysterij cognitionem pertinent, declaratio.
units.tr: Since God has embraced in Jesus Christ all the things that contribute to the redemption and salvation of the human race, it was not merely useful but necessary that we should be assured of his incarnation, through which he has been united and joined to us. Therefore Luke omits nothing in his description of Christ that can lead us to a fuller knowledge of him. Up to this point he has set out the circumstances, which we have seen agree in every respect with the oracles of the ancient prophets. He has added the angelic greeting that the angel used with the virgin Mary, which stirs us to conceive in our minds something great and by no means ordinary. Now follows a fuller explanation of everything that pertains to the knowledge of this mystery.

units.la: Primo tamen indicatur, vt Maria Angeli salutatione affecta fuerit. Illa (inquit) cum vi-disset, perturbata est super eius sermone, & cogitabat qualis esset salutatio ista. Primo perturba-tam fuisse scribit, pinimirum partim ob repentinum & improuisum Angeli sub viri specie ad se in-gredientis aspectum: partim ob salutationis insolitae verba magnifica, quae nihil vulgare praesefe-rebant. Deinde non temere & illico respondet, sed penes se diligentius expendit rem, quid salutatio haec sibi velit, & quam responsionem mereatur. Debent enim Dei opera non oscitanter considerari, neq; in illis quicquam praecipitantius est pronuntiandum. Et credibile est eam fuisse Angeli speciem, vt Maria in illo aliquid homine maius agnoscere potuerit, & ideo non stupido pauore, sed religioso metu commota, animum totum ad sanctas cogitationes conuerterit. Indicant autem haec omnia Virginem pudicam & honestatis studio deditam. Quo illud etiam referri debet, quod nuper audiuimus, Angelum illam non foris discurrentem, aut in spectandis ludis occupatam, aut ipsam in vicis ludentem reperisse, sed ad eam ingressum esse, cum se domi contineret, & rebus ad suum officium pertinentibus vacaret.
units.tr: First, however, it is shown that Mary was affected by the angel's greeting. "She," he says, "when she saw him, was troubled at his words and wondered what manner of greeting this was." He writes that she was first troubled, partly on account of the sudden and unexpected sight of the angel entering to her in the appearance of a man, and partly on account of the unusual and lofty words of the greeting, which suggested nothing ordinary. Then she does not answer rashly and at once, but weighs the matter more carefully within herself: what the greeting means for her and what kind of reply it deserves. For the works of God ought not to be considered carelessly, and nothing should be pronounced hastily about them. It is also likely that the angel's appearance was such that Mary could recognise in him something greater than a man, and so she was moved not by stupid fear but by religious awe, and turned her whole mind to holy thoughts. All these things show that the Virgin was modest and devoted to the pursuit of honour. To this should also be referred what we heard recently, that the angel did not find her roaming abroad, or busy watching the games, or playing about in the streets, but came to her while she was staying at home and occupied with the duties that belonged to her.

units.la: Habent ergo hic virgines & matronae exemplum quod imitentur, & inquius consideratione frequentes esse conuenit. Decet has in primis, vt domi se contineant, quando illas publicis negocijs praesse non voluit Deus, sed viris parere iussit. Sunt quidem negocia ad rem domesticam pertinentia, propter quae illas interdum prodire opus est. Tunc vero decori sui meminerint, ne sub honesto praetextu vel otium quaerant, vel vagabunda discurrant, & rebus superuacaneis, aut etiam inhonestis se immiscant. Quam enim periculosum sit huic sexui in publico versari & curiositati indulgere. Dinae exemplo docemur, quae etsi a pijs parentibus procul dubio honeste educata & instituta esset, pudicitiae tamen iacturam fecit, cum iuuenili cupiditate abrepta Sichemiticas puellas & regionis illius mores otiosa spectaret, simulque fratribus suis horrendi sceleris causam praebuit, qui ira & dolore accensi religionis praetextu ad vindictam priuatam abusi sunt, & vrbis illius mares omnes crudeliter occiderunt.
units.tr: Here, then, virgins and matrons have an example to imitate, and it is fitting that they be frequent in considering it. Above all it becomes these women to remain at home, since God did not wish them to preside over public affairs but ordered them to obey their husbands. There are, to be sure, business matters that concern the household, for which they sometimes must go out. Then, however, let them remember their dignity, so that under a respectable pretext they do not seek leisure or wander about aimlessly, nor mix themselves into superfluous or even dishonourable matters. For how dangerous it is for this sex to be seen in public and to indulge in curiosity! We are taught by the example of Dinah, who, though no doubt brought up and instructed honourably by pious parents, nevertheless lost her chastity: carried away by youthful desire, she went idly to look at the Shechemite girls and the customs of that region. At the same time she gave her brothers occasion for a horrible crime. Inflamed with anger and grief, they abused the pretext of religion for private vengeance and cruelly killed all the males of that city.

units.la: Et Bethsabae hoc in primis nocuisse scimus, quod inter lauandum se Dauidi spectandam exhibuit. Extant huius generis exempla plusimi in prophanis historijs, quae commemorare superuacaneum foret, cum quotidie fiant, quae his possunt fidem facere. Recte igitur olim Aegyptij Venerem restudini insistentem pingebant, vt docerent matrem familias in primis decere, vt domus curam gerat, neque vnquam foras prospiciat, nisi quando hoc monet necessitas, idque tunc etiam sic faciat, vt decori sui non obliuiscatur. Obseruauit hoc diligentissime Sara, quae ne in hospitum quidem, qui ad maritum diuertebant, conspectum temere prodire solita fuit, sed circa rem domesticam occupata suo loco se continuit, donec vocaretur. Et hoc est, quod de Maria Lucas quoque annotauit, illam Angeli conspectu turbatam fuisse. Quod ipsum Christianas virgines & matronas cumprimis decet. Quia enim Dei antiquissimum mandatum est, vt mulier virum, ceu caput & dominum suum suspiciat, virorum reuerentia illas tangi, & ad illorum conspectu ingenuo pudore affici conuenit. Nam scimus grauiter a Deo per Isaiam accusari filias Zionis, quod erecto collo incederent, fallaci oculorum nutu & incessu petulanti virorum oculos ad se allicerent, atq; formam suam impudentius ostentarent. Est hoc vitium nimis vulgare nostro seculo, & huius culpa non minima ex parte in ipsis viris haeret, qui cum capitis instar mulieribus praesse deberent, fere omnis rationis simul & officii immemores omnia petulanter & insolenter nimis faciunt.
units.tr: We know that Bathsheba too was harmed chiefly by this, that while bathing she exposed herself to be seen by David. There are very many examples of this kind in profane histories, which it would be superfluous to recall, since such things happen every day and can give credit to these things. Rightly, therefore, the Egyptians of old painted Venus playing the lyre, to teach that it is above all fitting for the mother of a household to look after the home and never look out of doors except when necessity requires it, and even then to do so in such a way that she does not forget her dignity. Sarah observed this most carefully: she was accustomed not to come out rashly even into the sight of guests who lodged with her husband, but, occupied with domestic matters, she kept herself in her place until she was called. This is also what Luke noted about Mary, that she was troubled at the sight of the angel. This is especially fitting for Christian virgins and matrons. For since it is God's most ancient command that a woman should look up to her husband as her head and lord, it is proper that they be moved by reverence for men, and be affected by a modest shame in their presence. For we know that the daughters of Zion were gravely accused by God through Isaiah because they walked with their necks stretched out, and with deceitful nods of the eyes and wanton gait drew men's eyes to themselves and displayed their appearance more shamelessly. This vice is all too common in our age, and the blame for it lies in no small part with the men themselves, who, though they ought to preside over women as their head, almost forgetting all reason and duty, act too wantonly and insolently in everything.

units.la: Pro alijs autem Mariae grauitas laudem meretur, quae priusquam Angelo respondeat, rem ipsam penes se diligentius expendit. Est enim sermo animi index, & quae in respondendo praecipites sunt, eo animum produnt leuem, & plerunque proprijs verbis irretiuntur, vt ea desigent, de quibus ante vix cogitabant. Exemplum huius vitij in Eua cernimus, cui peccati & miserabilis lapsus praecipua causa fuit imprudens & inconsideratum cum serpente colloquium, & quod ad istius interrogata incautius respondet. Et hodie captiosis proprocorum & libidinosorum iuuenum dictis multæ capiuntur, quæ pudicitiæ suæ iacturam numquam facerent, si linguam suam frenare didicissent. Meminerint ergo virgines neque cum omnibus loquendum, neque ad omnium quæstiones aut obiectiones respondendum esse. At hodie ea in hoc sexu passim regnat morum corruptio, ut pleraque non expectato virorum alloquio ipsæ priores procacibus dicteriis illos provocent.
units.tr: Yet Mary's gravity deserves praise beyond others, for before she answers the angel she weighs the matter more carefully within herself. For speech is the index of the mind, and those who are hasty in answering show a light mind, and are often ensnared by their own words, so that they confirm things they had scarcely thought of before. We see an example of this vice in Eve, whose chief cause of sin and miserable fall was an imprudent and thoughtless conversation with the serpent, and that she answered too carelessly the questions put to her. And today many women are caught by the cunning words of suitors and lustful young men, who would never suffer the loss of their chastity if they had learned to bridle their tongues. Let virgins therefore remember that they should speak neither with everyone nor answer everyone's questions or objections. But today such a corruption of manners reigns everywhere among this sex that, without waiting to be addressed by men, many women themselves provoke them first with shameless taunts. "Suitors"

units.la: Sed Angelum audiamus, qui trepidantem & perturbatam iterum alloquitur, & de singulis plenius instruit. Partes orationis tres sunt. Prima consolationem habet paucis verbis comprehensam. Ne time (inquit) Maria. Et mox dicti huius rationem subjicit: Invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum, id est: Es in gratia apud Deum, qui tui misertus te benignè respicit, & fauore singula ri prosequitur. Ita enim hac loquendi formula Hebraei utuntur. Sic Noa gratiam apud Deum inuenisse dicitur, cum omnis caro corrupisset viam suam. Est autem multa observatione dignissimum, quod omnem Mariæ dignitatem Angelus ad gratiam Dei refert, qui illam filij sui in carne manifestandi matrem facere dignatus sit. Etenim in nobis, adeoque tota humani generis massa, boni nihil est, sed mera corruptio, quam in universam posteritatem Adamus propagavit. Bonum verò omne ex patre luminum est, ut Iacobus ait.
