Ab hoc igitur petere conuenit ea, quæ nobis ad salutem necessaria sunt; & simul cauendum est, ne donis acceptis efferamur, aut ea ut propria superbè ostentemus: sed in hoc potius simus, ut iisdem digne utamur ad prouehendam Dei gloriam & multorum edificationem. In primis autem suæ arrogantiæ superbos suorum meritorum ostentatores pudeat. Quid enim illi merebuntur apud Deum, quando Mariæ Virginis dignitas omnis ex gratuito Dei fauore manauit? Obseruemus etiam, quod non alio argumento illam consolatur, & metu omni liberat Angelus, quam quod apud Deum sit in gratia. Id enim iustissima de causa facit: quia Dei gratia sola vero gaudio animos exhilarat, & rerum securos reddit: cum è contra, qui Deum sibi iratum & infestum esse sentiunt, perpetuis conscientiæ terroribus excruciantur, & vita quoque illis acerba & amara fit. Atqui gratiam suam nobis omnibus per Euangelium in Christo Iesu offert, in quo nos gratiam pro gratia, id est, gratiam gratia accumulatam & effusissimè redundantem Ioannes accepisse testatur: & huius arrhabonem habemus Spiritum sanctum, qui & adoptionis spiritus dicitur, & in quo clamamus Abba pater. Quid ergo consternamur, etiamsi undique nos pericula circumstent? Quid doloribus excruciati muliebriter eiulamus, aut de Dei rigore querimur? Quin cogitamus nobis quoque dici, Ne timeatis, invenistis enim gratiam apud Deum. Paulum certè de Satana ipsum infestante conquerentem non alio argumento consolatus est Dominus, quàm quòd illi dicebat: Sufficit tibi gratia mea. Et sanè hæc sola nobis ad omnia sufficit, quia in egestate diuites & forte sua contentos reddit, in infirmitate viribus instruit, in aduersis exhilarat, oppressos erigit, afflictos iuuat, & iam iam succum bentes sub periculorum mole inuictos facit. Quid, quòd ipsæ afflictiones gratiæ & paterni fauoris argumentum sunt? Nam patris instar quos diligit castigat Dominus, ne cum mundo nescio pœnitere condemnentur. Ideo Paulus credentes afflictionibus gloriari dicebat, ut qui in his patientiæ exercendæ occasionem atque materiam inueniunt: & dum hanc exercent, nouam indies Dei bonitatem experiuntur, & in spe promissæ salutis confirmantur, quæ illos minimè fallit, cum Dei dilectione nitatur, quam ille nobis in Christo plus quàm paternam exhibuit. Vnde apparet, eos neque fidei principia tenere, neque gratiam Dei primis labijs (ut aiunt) degustauisse, qui ad quemuis casum attoniti stupent aut animo concidunt.
units.tr: But let us hear the angel, who addresses the trembling and troubled woman again and instructs her more fully about each point. The speech has three parts. The first contains consolation, expressed in a few words: "Fear not, Mary," he says. And soon he adds the reason for this word: "For thou hast found grace with God," that is, you are in favour with God, who, having mercy on you, looks upon you kindly and pursues you with special goodwill. For the Hebrews use this form of speech in this way. Thus Noah is said to have found grace with God, when all flesh had corrupted its way. It is also most worthy of careful observation that the angel refers all of Mary's dignity to the grace of God, who deigned to make her the mother who would reveal his Son in the flesh. For in us, and indeed in the whole mass of the human race, there is nothing good, but only pure corruption, which Adam passed on to all his posterity. Every good gift, however, is from the Father of lights, as James says. It is fitting, then, to ask from him what is necessary for our salvation; and at the same time we must take care not to become proud of gifts received, or to display them haughtily as if they were our own, but rather to strive to use them worthily for the advancement of God's glory and the building up of many. Above all, let those who proudly display their merits be ashamed of their arrogance. For what will they deserve before God, when the entire dignity of the Virgin Mary flowed from the free favour of God? Let us also observe that the angel comforts her and frees her from all fear by no other argument than that she is in grace with God. He does this for the most just reason: because only the grace of God gladdens minds with true joy and makes them secure in all things, whereas, on the contrary, those who feel that God is angry and hostile to them are tormented by constant terrors of conscience, and their life too becomes bitter and harsh. Yet he offers his grace to us all through the Gospel in Christ Jesus, in whom, as John testifies, we have received grace for grace, that is, grace heaped upon grace and most abundantly overflowing. And we have as the pledge of this the Holy Spirit, who is also called the Spirit of adoption, and in whom we cry "Abba, Father." Why, then, are we dismayed even when dangers surround us on every side? Why, racked with pains, do we lament like women, or complain of God's severity? Rather, let us think that these words are said to us too: "Fear not, for ye have found grace with God." Certainly the Lord consoled Paul, when he complained about Satan who was harassing him, by no other argument than by saying to him: "My grace is sufficient for thee." And indeed this alone is enough for us in all things, because it makes the poor rich and content with their lot, strengthens the weak, cheers us in adversity, raises up the oppressed, helps the afflicted, and makes us unconquered even when we are on the point of sinking under the weight of dangers. What of the fact that afflictions themselves are a proof of grace and of a father's favour? For the Lord chastens those whom he loves as a father does, so that they may not be condemned with the world, which does not repent. Therefore Paul said that believers glory in afflictions, since in them they find the occasion and matter for exercising patience; and while they exercise it, they experience the goodness of God anew each day, and are confirmed in the hope of the promised salvation, which does not disappoint them, since it rests on the love of God, which he has shown us in Christ more than fatherly. From this it is evident that those who are stunned and lose heart at every mishap neither hold the first principles of faith nor have tasted the grace of God, as they say, with the first lips.

units.la: Secunda parte summam legationis Angelus exponit, dicens: Et ecce concipies in utero, & paries filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum. Sensus est: Ideo te benedictam inter mulieres esse, & gratiam apud Deum inuenisse dico, quia tu beata illa & prophetarum oraculis decantata virgo es, quam olim Isaias concepturam & filium pariturum prædixit, qui verus sit Immanuel, cuius intercessione Deus nobis reconciliatur. Vtitur autem prophetarum verbis Angelus, ut plus fidei mereatur apud eam, quæ vaticinia illa non ignorabat, cum in meditatione promissæ salutis assiduè versaretur. Arguunt autem eiusmodi Angelorum sermones eorum insolentiam, qui nimium delicatuli scripturarum phrases fastidiunt, & ex prophanorum scriptorum chartis nescio quid audire
units.tr: In the second part the angel sets out the substance of his message, saying: And behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus. The sense is this: I say that you are blessed among women and have found grace with God because you are that blessed virgin, celebrated in the oracles of the prophets, whom Isaiah long ago foretold would conceive and bear a son who would be the true Immanuel, through whose intercession God is reconciled to us. The angel uses the words of the prophets so that he may win more belief from her, since she was not ignorant of those prophecies and was constantly occupied with meditation on the promised salvation. Yet such speeches of the angels also rebuke the arrogance of those who are too fastidious and dainty, scorn the phrases of Scripture, and wish to hear and read some novelty from the pages of profane writers, something that pleases their palate.

units.la: Gen. 6. & legere cupiunt, quod ipsorum palato arrideat. Sunt hi digni, qui pro Angelorum & diuini verbi vocibus porcorum grunnitum aut asinorum alte rudentium clamores fatuos audiant, et magno suo malo poëtarum impurissimorum & futilium phi losophorum nugacibus commentis immorantur, quibus adeo sordet Spiritus sancti facundia. Confutantur hic quoq; qui in salutis causa nouam & prius inauditam doctrinam requirunt, & doctores sibi cœlitus mitti vellent, quibus tuto credere liceat. Atqui cœlitus aduenit Angelus Gabriel, & Maria vniuersum incarnationis filij Dei myste rium expositurus, nihil nouum profert, sed quæ olim à prophetis prædicta fuerunt repetit. Venit prætere a sinu patris Filius ille vnigenitus, imò idem ex mortuis rediuiuus ad suos redijt, qui tamen etiam ipse concionum suarum argumenta non aliunde quàm ex Mosis & prophetarum libris desumit. Debent ergo hæc nobis quoq; sufficere, noua autem & inaudita quærant, quibus perire libet in humanorum figmentorum erroribus.
units.tr: Gen. 6. Such people deserve to hear, instead of the voices of angels and of the divine word, the grunting of pigs or the foolish braying of asses, and to dwell, to their great harm, on the trifling inventions of the most filthy poets and frivolous philosophers, for whom the eloquence of the Holy Spirit is so cheap. Those are also refuted here who seek a new and previously unheard doctrine for the cause of salvation, and who would want teachers sent to them from heaven whom they could trust safely. Yet the angel Gabriel has come from heaven, and Mary is to be told the whole mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, and he brings nothing new but repeats what was foretold long ago by the prophets. Moreover, that only-begotten Son came from the bosom of the Father, and indeed, having risen again from the dead, returned to his own; yet even he takes the arguments of his sermons from nothing other than the books of Moses and the prophets. Therefore these things ought to be enough for us too. Let those who seek new and unheard-of things be content to perish in the errors of human fictions.

units.la: Quia tamen hæc alterius loci sunt, nunc quæ ad præsens institutum faciunt in Angeli verbis consideRabimus. Primùm, Ecce (inquit) concipies in vtero, & paries filium. In vtero concepturam ait, vt ostendat Dei filium ex ipsa Virginis substantia carnem assumpturum esse. Nam etsi ex Spiritu sancto conceptus sit, in vtero tamen fœtus ille sanctissimus suis incrementis creuit, & auctus est, vt & illa grauida esse agnosceretur, & legitimo demum tempore pareret, sicuti Euangelistæ alibi aperte docent. Apud Matthæum enim Angelus Iosepho dicit: Quod in ea genitum est, ex Spiritu sancto est. Et Paulus ad Galatas scribit: Postquàm venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, &c. Et huc pertinent loci illi scripturæ, in quibus semen mulieris, germen Isai, semen item Dauidis & filius hominis dicitur. Et talem quidem fieri oportebat Dei filium, vt & frater nostER esset, & suum meritum optimo vindicis iure nobis communicare posset: vt denique Sacerdotis veri instar à nobis acciperet, quod pro nobis Deo patri suo offerret. Procul ergo valeant Marcionitæ & Eutychiani cùm veteres tum recentes, qui Christi Iesu incarnationem & carnis ab illo assumptæ naturam in dubium vocant: dum illam vel cœlestem fingunt, vel corporis veri proprietatibus spoliant. Videntur illi hominibus imperitis de re non adeò magni momenti contendere: multi etiam omne hoc, quod de Christi corpore dicitur, incertum esse arbitrantur. Sed ipsa redemptionis & salutis nostræ ratio in disputationem venit, quæ consistere non potest, nisi Dei filium veram carnem assumpsisse, & hanc in cœlos subuexisse nobis constet. Nam qui hoc negant, ij neque in illius merito sperare, neque sibi quoad corpus olim in cœlis locum fore credere possunt. Non temere ergo sferi putemus, quod hoc ipsum Spiritus sanctus in ista tractatione subinde repetit, vt deinceps suo loco videbimus.
units.tr: Since, however, these matters belong to another place, let us now consider what bears on the present subject, in the words of the angel. First, he says: "Behold, you shall conceive in the womb and bring forth a son." He says "to conceive in the womb" to show that the Son of God would assume flesh from the very substance of the Virgin. For although he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, that most holy fetus nevertheless grew in the womb by its increments and was enlarged, so that she was recognised to be pregnant, and at the appointed time at last she gave birth, as the evangelists clearly teach elsewhere. For in Matthew the angel says to Joseph: "What is begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit." And Paul writes to the Galatians: "When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman," etc. To this also belong those passages of Scripture in which he is called the seed of the woman, the branch of Jesse, likewise the seed of David and the Son of man. Indeed, the Son of God had to be such that he would be our brother, and could communicate to us his merit with the right of the best avenger, and finally receive from us what he, as the true priest, might offer to God the Father for us. Let the Marcionites and the Eutychians, both ancient and recent, therefore keep their distance, who call into doubt the incarnation of Christ Jesus and the nature of the flesh assumed by him, while they either imagine it to be heavenly or strip it of the true properties of a body. They seem to contend with unlearned men about a matter of no great importance, and many even think that all that is said of the body of Christ is uncertain. But the very ground of our redemption and salvation is brought into dispute, and this cannot stand unless it is certain that the Son of God assumed true flesh and carried it up into the heavens. For those who deny this can neither hope for anything from his merit nor believe that a place in heaven will one day be theirs in respect of the body. Let us not therefore think it is without purpose that the Holy Spirit repeats this very point again and again in this treatise, as we shall see in its proper place.

units.la: Deinde nomen quoque filij ex Maria nasciturj exprimit. Vocabis (inquit) nomen eius Iesum. Ita verò Græci inflexerunt Hebræum nomen Iehoschua, quod Seruatorem significat. Rationem autem nominis huius idem Angelus Iosepho apud Matthæum his verbis exponit: Ipse enim seruabit populum suum ex peccatis ipsius. Est hoc nobis probè tenendũ, vt quid in illo quæri debeat intelligamus. Falluntur enim plurimi turpiter, dum ad Christum quidem magno animo contendunt, nihil autem in eo sublimius, nihil diuinum aut cœleste sperant: sed eo prætextu vel opes ingentes, vel honores, vel etiam quiduis faciendi licentiam & impunè voluptuandi materiam se inuentu- ros esse arbitrantur. Offendunt hi postea ad crucem, quæ perpetua professionis Christianæ comes est, & ex eorum numero sunt, quos ipse Dominus in sementis parabola <bl>ωεσκαιρως</bl> vocat, eò quod subitò ostentant, vt segetes in loco saxoso enascentes, exorto autem persecutionam æstu mox flaccescunt, vt fructus eorum in ipsa herba (vt proverbio dicitur) pereat. Semper ergo animis nostris obuersetur, Christum seruatorem quidem esse, sed non talem, qui quosuis ad se venientes ex egestate, morbis, infamia & aliis huius sæculi aduersis liberet (nam etsi suos interdum in hoc etiam sæculo beatos & felices reddat, hoc tamen non omnibus contingit, neque perpetuum est) sed qui populum suum, id est, omnes in se credentes ex peccatorum laqueis liberet, & in libertatem filiorum Dei asserat. Est hoc beneficium multò excellentius, quàm si huius sæculi bonis nos totos obrueret. Ex illo etenim tota hominis totius felicitas dependet. Qui enim ex peccatis liberati sunt, ij pœnam quoque peccati effugerunt, & (vt Paulus ait) iustificati ex fide pacem habent erga Deum, & liberò ad thronum gratiæ accessu gaudent, atque olim regni cœlestis hæreditatem obtinebunt. Sed & in ad uersis omnibus superiores fiunt Christo duce & protectore, qui oues suas ex manibus suis eripi non finit. Ad hunc ergo seruatorem contendant, qui & in hac vita sibi bene esse, & immortalis atq; cœlestis vitæ gaudijs potiri volunt.
units.tr: Next he also states the name of the Son who is to be born of Mary: "You shall call his name Jesus." The Greeks have indeed given the Hebrew name Yehoshua this inflected form, which means Saviour. The same angel explains the reason for this name to Joseph in Matthew in these words: "For he shall save his people from their sins." We must hold firmly to this, so that we understand what ought to be sought in him. For very many men are shamefully mistaken: while they eagerly press towards Christ, they hope for nothing loftier in him, nothing divine or heavenly, but under that pretext they think they will find either great wealth, or honours, or even licence to do whatever they like and material for sinning with impunity. Such men later stumble at the cross, which is the constant companion of the Christian profession. They belong to the number of those whom the Lord himself, in the parable of the sower, calls temporary [πρόσκαιρος], because they quickly sprout up like the crops growing on rocky ground, but when the heat of persecution arises, they soon wither, so that their fruit perishes in the very grass, as the proverb says. Let it therefore always be before our minds that Christ is indeed the Saviour, but not of the kind who frees all who come to him from poverty, disease, disgrace and the other adversities of this world. For although he sometimes makes his own happy and blessed even in this world, this does not happen to all, nor is it lasting. Rather, he frees his people, that is, all who believe in him, from the snares of sins, and asserts them into the liberty of the sons of God. This benefit is far more excellent than if he were to overwhelm us entirely with the goods of this world. For the whole happiness of a man depends on it. Those who have been freed from sins also escape the punishment of sin, and (as Paul says) being justified by faith they have peace with God and rejoice in free access to the throne of grace, and in time they will obtain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. And in all adversities they are made superior, with Christ as their leader and protector, who does not allow his sheep to be snatched from his hands. Let those, then, who wish both to be well in this life and to enjoy the joys of an immortal and heavenly life, strive towards this Saviour.

units.la: At ne nomen hoc Mariæ filio temere impositum putemus, eundem diligentius describit. Angelus. Et primò quidem Magnum fore dicit, quo titulo aliquos ob victorias & res præclare gestas inter gentes quoque superbiuisse, supra diximus. Et Ioannem quoque Magnum vocauit idem Angelus propter eximia spiritus dona, quibus illum Deus ornauit: Christo autem nomen hoc non proprer aliena dona, sed proprie & optimo iure debetur, siue ipsius diuinitatem siue humanitatem spectes. Quoad illam enim, cum vnum sit cum patre, Deus nimirum verus & æternus, verè vtique magnus, adeoque cœlis atque terris sublimior est. Quoad vero humanam naturam, etsi in ea extremè humiliatus sit, idem tamen in illa manifestatus est per signa & omnis generis opera, quæ illum Dei filium esse declarauerunt. Quibus adde, quod eidem secundum humanam quoque naturam omnis potestas data est in cœlo & in terra. Verè ergo magnus est, & (vt in epistola ad Hebræos scribitur) tanto præstantior factus Angelis, quanto excellentius præ illis sortitus est nomen. Nam cui dixit vnquam Angelorum, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Et rursus: Ego ero ei pater, & ipse erit mihi filius: Item, Adorent ipsum omnes Angeli Dei. Frustra igitur nobis Diuorum & Angelorum excellentiam obijciunt, qui illos inuocant & superstitiose colunt. Quia enim omnibus illis maior est Christus Iesus, eidem quoque cultus ille omnis debetur, ne illum in inferiori gradu collocemus, quando non alium illi honorem impendimus, quàm qui ipsi cum Diuis cœlitibus & Angelis communis sit.
units.tr: Lest we think that this name was rashly given to Mary's son, the angel describes him more carefully. And first he says that he will be great, a title by which some, on account of victories and famous deeds, have also grown proud among the nations, as we said above. The same angel also called John great, on account of the outstanding gifts of the Spirit with which God adorned him; but this name is due to Christ not on account of foreign gifts but properly and by the best right, whether you look at his divinity or his humanity. For as regards the former, since he is one with the Father, he is truly God and eternal, and therefore truly great, and so higher than heaven and earth. As regards his human nature, although he was utterly humbled in it, yet he was nevertheless made manifest in it through signs and works of every kind, which declared him to be the Son of God. To these add that, according to his human nature too, all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth. He is therefore truly great, and (as is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews) he has become as much superior to the angels as the name he has obtained is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did God ever say, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you"? And again: "I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son"; likewise, "Let all the angels of God worship him." It is therefore in vain that they object to us the excellence of the saints and angels, those who invoke them and worship them superstitiously. For since Christ Jesus is greater than all of them, all that worship is owed to him alone, lest we place him in a lower rank, when we give him no other honour than that which is shared with the saints and angels of heaven.

units.la: Deinde, filius Altissimi vocabitur. Facit hoc ad prioris explicationem. Altissimus enim dicitur Deus, quia maiestas eius (vt in Psalmo canitur) cœlis sublimior est. Vocandi autem verbo non inanis titulus, sed res ipsa denotatur. Quia enim Dei proprium est vocare ea quæ non sunt vt sint, minimè inanibus titulis ille ludit, sed vt hi ipsis rebus aut personis respondeant, facit. Vocatur igitur Filius Altissimi Iesus Christus, partim quòd æterna & incomprehensibili generatione ex Deo genitus, illi coæternus et coessentialis est, partim quòd in carne etiam assumpta (vt modo diximus) se Dei Filium esse operibus verè diuinis abundè demonstrauit. Frequenter autem diuinitas Christi asseritur, & multa eius in scripturis testimonia passim occurrunt: quia nisi Deum esse agnoscamus, nunquam in illo certam & solidam habere possumus nostræ salutis fiduciam.
units.tr: Next, "he shall be called the Son of the Most High." This bears on the explanation of the previous point. God is called "the Most High" because his majesty, as the Psalm sings, is higher than the heavens. Now, to be called does not signify an empty title but denotes the thing itself. For it belongs to God to call those things which are not as though they were (Rom. 4.17), and he does not play with empty titles but makes them correspond to the things or persons themselves. Jesus Christ is therefore called the Son of the Most High, partly because, begotten of God by an eternal and incomprehensible generation, he is co-eternal and co-essential with him, and partly because, even in the flesh he assumed (as we have just said), he has amply shown by truly divine works that he is the Son of God. The divinity of Christ is asserted frequently, and many testimonies to it occur everywhere in the Scriptures; for unless we acknowledge him to be God, we can never have a certain and solid confidence in him for our salvation.

units.la: Postremò ad regnum quoque Christi descendit Angelus, quo totum eius officium siue munus continetur, cui illum pater destinauit. Dabit ei Dominus Deus (inquit) thronum Dauidis patris sui ipsius, regnabitque super domum Iacob in æternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Est hæc magnifica admodum promissio, cuius singula verba pondus habent. Nam primùm Dandi verbo regnum legitimum denotatur, in cuius possessionem non violenta aut iniusta vsurpatione, sed optimo iure venturus sit. Et videtur Angelus ad Psalmi secundi verba alludere, vbi sic loquitur Deus: Ego constitui Regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum. Item: Postula à me, daboque gentes vt sint hæreditas tua, & terminos terræ vt sint possessio tua. Ista verò regni huius stabilitatem indicant. Constat enim infirma & quasi momentanea esse regna, quæ per vim, non legitima successione obtinentur. Secundò regnum hoc quasi definit, quando thronum Dauidis vocat, non aliud nimirum fore innuens, quàm quod Dauidi & semini eius olim promissum fuit. Extat promissio illa in primo Samuelis Cap.septimo, vbi per Nathanum sic ait Dominus Dauidi: Cùm exacti fuerint dies tui, dormierisque cum patribus tuis, excitabo semen tuum post te quod egredietur de vtero tuo, regnumque eius firmabo. Is extruet domum nomini meo, & ego confirmabo solium regni eius perpetuò. Ego ero ei pater & ipse erit mihi filius, &c. Quo loco, etsi quædam admisceantur, quæ ad Salomonem & ex hoc progenitos Reges Iuda pertinent, præcipua tamen oraculi huius pars non de alio quàm Iesu Christo exponi potest, cuius typum Reges illi gesserunt. Huc igitur respiciens Angelus simul innuit, Christum fore verum illum Dauidis filium, quem prophetæ regnaturum & populi seruatorem fore prædixerunt. At licet ijdem regnum eius locutionibus ex regnis huius sæculi desumptis describant, non obscurè tamen innuunt, illud non terrenum neque de hoc mundo esse, cùm perpetuum & æternum fore testentur, huius autem mundi regna varijs vicibus subiecta sint, & tandem sua mole ruant, etiamsi nulla vis externa accedat. Regnat quidem in terris hisce Christus, sed spiritu et verbo suo regnat, quod à Dauide etiam sceptrum potentiæ eius dicitur. Vbi rursus admonemur, nihil in illo terrenum aut temporarium quærendum esse, de Euangelio autem longè lateè propagando solicitos esse debere eos, qui regnum Christi prouebere student. Tertiò subditos quoque & ciues regni huius indicat, quando super domum Iacob regnaturum dicit angelus. Ita verò Israelitarum aut Iudæorum gentem dici manifestius est, quam vt demonstrari oporteat. Nominantur isti, non quòd intra Iudææ fines aut populi Iudaici terminos regnum Christi concludi oporteat: sed quòd initium eius in illa gente Deus constituit, vnde tamen illud ad omnes gentes per totum orbem propagandum esse prophetæ prædixerunt. Et Israelitarum nomine omnes promissionus filios, id est, omnes credentes significari, Paulus ad Romanos docet. Ergo ijdem quoque ad regnum illud salutiferum Christi pertinent, & verè Christiani sunt: ab eodem verò excluduntur, quicunque à fide in Christum alieni sunt, & illum Regem atque seruatorem vnicum non agnoscunt. Postremò tempus quoque regni Christi denotatur, vel æternitas potius, quæ nullis temporum spatijs mensuratur. Nam regnaturum ait in æternum, Et regni eius (inquit) non erit finis. Conuenit hoc cum promissione Nathani, quam supra adduximus, & quæ in Psalmo 89. copiosius exponitur. Pepigi fœdus (inquit) cum electo meo, iuraui Dauidi seruo meo. Semen tuum in æternum confirmabo, & stabilia m solium tuum ad omnem posteritatem. Semen eius æternum erit, solium eius coram me vt Sol perstabit: Firmum vt Luna manebit, quæ est fidus in æthere testis. Quò in primis referri debet, quod apud Danielem legitur: Spectabam in visis nocturnis, et ecce veniebat in nubibus cœli quidam, ceu filius hominis, qui vsque ad Antiquum dierum peruenit, eumq; adduxerunt ante illum. Et dominatus est ei traditus & honos, & regnum, vt omnes populi, nationes & linguæ colant eum: cuius dominatus est dominatus æternus, qui non præteribit, & cuius regnum haudquaquam destruetur. Ista autem non minus verè quàm perspicuè dicuntur. Nam in terris hisce regnum continuum & perpetuum habet Christus, dum continua est fidelium successio, qui nequicquam oblustantibus tyrannis fidem profitentur, & Deum verum in spiritu & veritate adorant. Et Christi promissio est: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi. Vbi verò mundi huius finis aduenerit, tunc ad inferos detrusis hostibus suis omnibus ad se suos recipiet Christus, vt secum in cœlis æternum viuant & regnent, qui ipsum in hac vita Regem suum esse agnouerunt. Et hæc quidem in vtriusque testamenti libris varie confirmantur. In præsenti autem nostrae cum consolatione tum institutionis seruire debent: ne vllis tyrannorum minis & machinationibus terreamur, & vt Regi huic fidele præstemus obsequium, regni eius legibus obtemperemus, illi vni fidamus & seruiamus, olim cum eodem in cœlis quoque regnaturi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, the angel descends to the kingdom of Christ, in which his whole office or charge is contained, for which the Father appointed him. "The Lord God," he says, "shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." This is a most magnificent promise, and each of its words carries weight. For first, by the verb "shall give," a lawful kingdom is signified, into the possession of which he is to come not by violent or unjust usurpation but by the best right. The angel seems to allude to the words of the second Psalm, where God speaks thus: "I have set my King upon my holy hill of Zion." Likewise: "Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession." These words indicate the stability of this kingdom. For it is agreed that kingdoms which are held by force, and not by lawful succession, are weak and almost momentary. Secondly, this kingdom is in a sense defined when he calls it the throne of David, clearly implying that it will be nothing other than what was once promised to David and his seed. That promise stands in the seventh chapter of the first book of Samuel, where the Lord says to David through Nathan: "When your days are fulfilled, and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son," etc. In that place, although some things are mixed in that pertain to Solomon and the kings of Judah descended from him, the principal part of this oracle can be explained of no one other than Jesus Christ, whose type those kings bore. Looking to this, the angel at the same time indicates that Christ will be the true son of David, whom the prophets foretold would reign and be the saviour of the people. But although the same prophets describe his kingdom in terms drawn from the kingdoms of this world, they nonetheless indicate not obscurely that it is neither earthly nor of this world, since they testify that it will be perpetual and eternal, whereas the kingdoms of this world are subject to various changes and at last collapse under their own weight, even if no external force intervenes. Christ indeed reigns in this earth, but he reigns by his Spirit and his word, which is why David also calls it the sceptre of his power. Here again we are admonished that nothing earthly or temporary is to be sought in him, and that those who strive to advance the kingdom of Christ ought to be anxious to spread the gospel far and wide. Thirdly, the angel also indicates the subjects and citizens of this kingdom, when he says that he will reign over the house of Jacob. That this means the nation of the Israelites or Jews is more evident than that it needs to be demonstrated. They are named not because the kingdom of Christ must be confined within the borders of Judea or the limits of the Jewish people, but because God established its beginning in that nation, from which, however, the prophets foretold it was to be propagated to all nations throughout the whole world. And Paul teaches the Romans that by the name of Israelites all the sons of the promise, that is, all believers, are signified. Therefore those same believers also belong to that saving kingdom of Christ and are truly Christians; and whoever are estranged from faith in Christ and do not acknowledge him as the one King and Saviour are excluded from it. Lastly, the time of the kingdom of Christ is also denoted, or rather eternity, which is measured by no spans of time. For he says that he shall reign for ever, "and of his kingdom," he says, "there shall be no end." This agrees with the promise of Nathan which we have cited above, and which is set out more fully in Psalm 89: "I have made a covenant," he says, "with my chosen; I have sworn to David my servant: I will establish your seed for ever, and build up your throne to all generations. His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne before me shall stand like the sun; it shall remain firm like the moon, which is a faithful witness in the sky." To this, above all, what is read in Daniel should be referred: "I was looking in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of heaven one like the Son of man, who came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him before him. And there was given to him dominion, and honour, and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed." These things are said no less truly than clearly. For Christ has a continuous and perpetual kingdom on this earth, as long as there is a continuous succession of the faithful, who profess the faith in vain against the threats of tyrants and worship the true God in spirit and in truth. And the promise of Christ is: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." But when the end of this world has come, Christ will then cast all his enemies down into hell and receive his own to himself, so that they may live and reign with him for ever in heaven, those who acknowledged him as their King in this life. These things are indeed confirmed in various ways in the books of both Testaments. For the present, however, they ought to serve both for our consolation and for our instruction: that we may not be terrified by any threats and machinations of tyrants, and that we may render faithful obedience to this King, obey the laws of his kingdom, trust in him alone and serve him, being one day to reign with him also in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IX.
units.tr: HOMILY IX.

units.la: Dixit autem Maria ad Angelum: Quomodo erit istud, quandoquidem virum non cognosco? Et respondens Angelus dixit ei: Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te, & virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi: propterea id etiam quod ex te nascetur Sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Et ecce Elisabeta cognata tua, & ipsa concepit filium in senectute sua: & hic mensis est sextus ipsi, quæ vocabatur sterilis. Quia apud Deum non erit impossibile vllum verbum. Dixit autem Maria: Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Et abiit ab ea Angelus.
units.tr: Mary said to the angel: "How can this be, since I do not know a man?" And the angel answered her: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy child who is born of you will be called the Son of God. And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren. For with God no word will be impossible." And Mary said: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." And the angel departed from her.

units.la: Vemadmodum infelix primorum parentum lapsus & ex hoc dependens humani generis perditio, ex colloquio initiû habuit, quod diabolus sub serpentis specie cû Eua instituit, vt Deû inuidum & hominum osorem esse illi persuaderet: Ita incarnationem filij Dei, quæ nobis redemptionem & salutem attulit, proximè præcessit colloquium Angeli Gabrielis cum Maria virgine, quo Dei bonitas & ardens nos seruandi desiderium euidentissime exponitur. Nam nõ obiter modo filium Dei ex ipsa hominem nasciturum esse denuntiat, verumetiam fructum eius exponit, & ea occasione regnum eius describit, in quo vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio fundatur. Dictum de hoc nuper inter alia, quòd non terrenum, sed cœleste & spirituale sit: & proinde falli eos omnes, qui in hoc carnalia bona quaerunt. Deinde cives huius esse veros Israelitas, qui fide vera & constanti omnibus ijs superiores fiunt, quae ad salutem contendentibus obstare solent: & ideo Christi atque salutis per ipsum partae cõfortes fieri non posse eos, qui non huic vni fidunt, aut qui socordes & ignavi aduersis facilè succumbunt. Praeterea regnum hoc aeternum & proinde inuictum, & inexpugnabile esse audiuimus: quae omnia ad nostram consolationem & institutum mirificè faciunt. Sequitur postrema huius colloquij pars, quae pleniorem totius huius mysterij declarationem continet, quam ex ordine considerabimus.
units.tr: Just as the unhappy fall of our first parents, and the ruin of the human race that depends on it, began with a conversation which the devil held with Eve under the form of a serpent, in order to persuade her that God envies and hates men, so the incarnation of the Son of God, which brought us redemption and salvation, was immediately preceded by the conversation of the angel Gabriel with the Virgin Mary, in which the goodness of God and his burning desire to save us are most plainly set forth. For the angel does not merely announce that the Son of God will be born of her as man, but also sets out his fruit and, on that occasion, describes his kingdom, on which the whole plan of our salvation is founded. Recently we heard, among other things, that this kingdom is not earthly but heavenly and spiritual, and that all those are deceived who seek carnal goods in it. Next, that its true citizens are the Israelites who, by a true and steadfast faith, rise above all those obstacles that usually stand in the way of those who strive for salvation; and that therefore those who do not trust in him alone, or who are slothful and cowardly and easily give way in adversity, cannot become partakers of Christ and of the salvation won through him. Furthermore, we heard that this kingdom is eternal and therefore unconquered and impregnable; all of which greatly serve our consolation and instruction. There follows the last part of this conversation, which contains a fuller explanation of the whole mystery, and which we shall consider in order.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi Maria praebuit, quae Angeli promissioni tam magnificae quaestionem opponit, dicens: Quomodo erit istud, quandoquidem virum non cognosco? Quibus verbis idem omnino dicere videtur quod nuper Zacharias, quem suae incredulitatis poenas dedisse audiuimus. Sed si rem omnem propius inspiciamus, magnum discrimen apparebit. Zacharias enim totum illud, quod Deus per Angelum pollicebatur, in dubium vocat, & disputationem suscipit, in qua senectam suam & ad pariendum non amplius idoneam vxoris aetatem Dei promissis opponit, ad hanc signum sibi dari petit, quae omnia illum à fide tunc alienum fuisse probant. Maria autem fore omnino credit, quod promitti audierat: de solo autem modo quaerit, neque id immerito, cum ille humani sensus captum omnem superaret. Deinde excusationem nullam meretur Zachariae incredulitas, quia promissionem generalem habebat, Deum ex sterilibus quoque matres efficere, quae ex liberis voluptatem capiant: & promissionem hanc exemplis plurimis iam olim confirmatam esse non ignorabat. At Maria nihil huius habuit, praeter vnicum Isaiae vaticinium (quod iam non semel adduximus) & hoc quidem obscurius, cum conceptionis modum in illo nequaquam exprimatur. Praeterea cum iam animo cogiperet, Messiae generationem non vulgarem, & alienam fore à communi generationis modo (nam vt apud Ioannem est videre, vulgo illud ferebatur: Cum venerit Christus, nemo sciet unde sit) sanctissima virgo tanti mysterij consideratione abrepta, quaerit, quis nam generationis istius modus sit futurus: & vt de hoc quaereret, pudicitiae studium monebat, quod in virginibus ardentissimum esse debet. Itaque quaestio ista non diffidentiam arguit, sed piae admirationis argumentum est, quae non poterat non commoueri, cum tantum Dei beneficium in animo suo expenderet. Denique hoc vnum quaerit Maria, cum simul multa alia occurrerent, quae carnis rationi dubia & impossibilia videri poterant, nisi fide fuisset instructa, quae carnis sensum sub verbi obedientiam cogebat. Nam ipsam inter mulieres omnium beatissimam dixerat Angelus, cum pauperculâ esset & ab omnibus derelicta. Ex ipsa item regni Davidis instauratio promittebatur, quae vix propriam vitam in summa rerum angustia sustentabat. Istis tamen fidem adhibet, quam haud dubie iam prius ex Dei verbo didicerat, quo docemur, Deum humiles & afflictos respicere. Ideo non punit illam Deus, sed ita ei per Angelum respondit, vt quaestio haec non tam ipsi, quàm omnibus nobis feliciter cesserit. Nam ista occasione declarantur articuli fidei nostrae, quibus profitemur, Iesum Christum ex Spiritu sancto conceptum & ex Virgine intemerata natum esse. Priusquam tamen de illis dicamus, rursus obseruari debet Virginis castissimae exemplum. Audiuit illa ex Angelo promissiones magnificas & cum humani generis salute coniunctas. Illis tamen non ita inebriatur, vt sui pudoris immemor mox cedat, sed de modo & ratione tanti mysterij diligenter quaerit. Debebant exemplum hoc imitari matronae & puellae omnes: sed in plerisque ea leuitas cernitur, vt non promissa modo quaeuis temere admittant, sed munera quoque à quibusuis, quorum libido satis nota est, recipiant, neq; vllis exemplis terreantur earum, quibus illud infeliciter ceciderit. Dignae sunt ergo, quae infames fiant, & suo malo discant verum esse, quod ex pijs admonitionibus discere nolunt. Sed omissis illis Angelum loquentem audiamus, cuius oratio tribus omnino partibus constat.
units.tr: Mary gave occasion for this discussion, for she raises a question against the angel's so magnificent promise, saying: "How can this be, since I do not know a man?" In these words she seems to say altogether the same thing as Zacharias recently did, whom we heard had paid the penalty for his unbelief. But if we look at the whole matter more closely, a great difference will appear. For Zacharias calls into doubt the whole of what God promised through the angel, and enters into a dispute, in which he sets his own old age and his wife's age, no longer fit for bearing children, against God's promises, and asks for a sign to be given him; all of which prove that he was then far from faith. Mary, however, fully believes what she had heard promised; she asks only about the manner, and not undeservedly, since it surpassed all the grasp of human sense. Further, Zacharias' unbelief deserves no excuse, because he had a general promise that God makes even barren women mothers who take joy in children, and he knew that this promise had already been confirmed by very many examples in the past. Mary, however, had none of this, except the single prophecy of Isaiah (which we have already cited more than once), and that one is rather obscure, since the manner of conception is by no means expressed in it. Moreover, since she was already pondering in her mind that the generation of the Messiah would be unusual and different from the common manner of generation (for, as is seen in John, it was commonly said: "When Christ comes, no one will know where he is from"), the most holy Virgin, carried away by the consideration of so great a mystery, asks what manner of generation this would be; and in asking this, the zeal for chastity, which ought to be most ardent in virgins, admonished her. Thus this question does not reveal distrust, but is a sign of pious wonder, which could not but be stirred when she considered so great a benefit of God. Finally, Mary asks only this one thing, although many other things presented themselves at once which might seem doubtful and impossible to human reason, unless she had been instructed by faith, which brought the sense of the flesh under obedience to the word. For the angel had called her the most blessed of all women, although she was poor and abandoned by all. Likewise, the restoration of David's kingdom was promised through her, though she was scarcely sustaining her own life in the depths of her poverty. Yet she gave credence to these things, which she had doubtless already learned from the word of God, in which we are taught that God looks upon the humble and afflicted. Therefore God does not punish her, but answers her through the angel in such a way that this question turned out happily not so much for her as for all of us. For on this occasion the articles of our faith are set forth, by which we confess that Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the pure Virgin. Before we speak of these, however, the example of the most chaste Virgin must again be noted. She heard from the angel magnificent promises, bound up with the salvation of the human race. Yet she is not so intoxicated by them as to forget her modesty and yield at once, but carefully inquires into the manner and method of so great a mystery. All matrons and maidens ought to imitate this example; but in most of them such levity is seen that they not only rashly accept any promises whatever, but also receive gifts from whomever, whose lust is well known, and are not frightened by any examples of those who have fallen unhappily through it. They are therefore worthy to become infamous, and to learn by their own harm that what they refuse to learn from godly admonitions is true. But, setting those aside, let us hear the angel speaking, whose address consists of three parts altogether.

units.la: Prima modum conceptionis exponit, non quidem vt carnis nostrae curiositati satisfaciat, sed vt animum Virginis inter varias cogitationes fluctuantem ad diuinae virtutis aut potentiae consideratione reuocet. Est hoc optimum & praesentissimum in rebus dubijs remedium, vt non quid nos possimus, aut quid naturae cursus ferat, sed quid Deus velit & possit consideremus; qui (vt propha-[?] ni quoque poetae agnouerunt)nutu suo cælum terramque concutit, & rerum naturam uno momento mutare vel innouare potest. Non minus diligenter autem quàm grauiter Angelus loquitur. Primum ait: Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te. Atqui iam tunc spiritu donatam fuisse Mariam, non est dubium. Sed significatur singularis & efficacissima Spiritus sancti operatio, qua negotium hoc omne confici oportuit. Sic supra Samsonem spiritus Domini irruisse dicitur, quando ille huius impulsu singulare aliquod facinus designauit, quod humanis viribus perfici non potuisset. Et de prophetis eadem locutio usurpatur, quando illos propriori afflatu spiritus impleuit & monuit. Hoc quia nonnulli veterum non obseruarunt, spiritum loco seminis fuisse tradiderunt, ex quo Christus in virginis utero natus sit. Quod dogma ut à pietate Christiana alienissimum est, & salutis nostræ fundamenta labefactat: ita nullis scripturis probari potest, & ab Angeli verbis dissentit, qui de Spiritus sancti operatione & virtute loquitur, non de causa materiali ex qua Dei Filius carnem assumpserit. Imo hanc ille infra in Virgine monstrabit, ut suo loco audiemus. Sed & in præsenti mysterium hoc clarius exponens addit: Et virtus Altissimi obumbrabit te. De virtute ergo diuina loquitur, & obumbrandi verbo partim operationem eius arcanam, partim protectionem & defensionem significat, quam simul præstiturus sit Deus, ne quam suæ pudicitiæ aut virginitatis iacturam patiatur, nihilominus tamen fœcunda fiat & concipiat. Sic sub umbra omnipotentis pium tutum fore Dauid testatur. Et apud prophanos quoque scriptores obumbrandi verbum hoc sensu usurpatur, Metaphora nimirum ab arboribus sumpta, aut etiam scutis maioribus, quibus milites aduersus tela ex alto incidentia defenduntur. Notum est enim illud Vergilianum de Turno, quem aduersus maleuolorum sermones Amatae reginae fauor tuebatur: Magnum reginae nomen obumbrat. Sensus ergo verborum Angeli hic est: Ne timeas quicquam, neq; de tuæ pudicitiæ fama aut honore solicita sis Maria. Nam totum hoc negotium, de quo nunc agimus, Dei est, qui benedictum illud semen & olim Dauidi promissum excitabit: & quia hoc non alicuius viri commixtione, sed Spiritus sancti operatione fiet, nihil carnale aut impurum imaginaberis, &c.
units.tr: The first sets out the manner of the conception, not indeed to satisfy the curiosity of our flesh, but to recall the mind of the Virgin, wavering among various thoughts, to the consideration of the divine power and might. This is the best and most effective remedy in doubtful matters: that we consider not what we ourselves can do, or what the course of nature brings, but what God wills and can do; who (as even the profane poets have recognised) shakes heaven and earth by his nod, and can change or renew the nature of things in a single moment. The angel speaks no less carefully than gravely. First he says: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." Yet there is no doubt that Mary had already been endowed with the Spirit. But what is signified is the singular and most effective operation of the Holy Spirit, by which this whole business had to be accomplished. Thus of Samson it is said that the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, when at his impulse he performed some singular deed which could not have been done by human strength. And the same expression is used of the prophets, when he filled and admonished them with a more special inspiration. Because some of the ancients did not observe this, they taught that the Spirit took the place of the seed, from which Christ was born in the womb of the Virgin. This dogma, as it is most alien to Christian piety and undermines the foundations of our salvation, so can be proved by no Scripture, and it disagrees with the words of the angel, who speaks of the operation and power of the Holy Spirit, not of the material cause from which the Son of God took his flesh. Indeed, he will show this in the Virgin below, as we shall hear in its place. But also, in setting forth this mystery more clearly at present, he adds: "And the power of the Most High will overshadow you." He therefore speaks of divine power, and by the word "overshadow" he signifies partly its hidden operation, partly the protection and defence which God will at the same time afford, so that she suffers no loss of her modesty or virginity, and yet becomes fruitful and conceives. Thus David testifies that the godly will be safe under the shadow of the Almighty. And among the profane writers too the word "overshadow" is used in this sense, a metaphor taken from trees, or even from large shields, by which soldiers are defended against missiles falling from on high. For that Virgilian saying about Turnus is well known, whom the favour of Queen Amata protected against the slanders of ill-wishers: "The great name of the queen overshadows him." The sense of the angel's words, then, is this: Do not fear anything, and do not be anxious, Mary, about the report or the honour of your chastity. For this whole business, of which we are now speaking, is God's, who will raise up that blessed Seed, promised of old to David; and because this will be done not by the union of any man, but by the operation of the Holy Spirit, you shall imagine nothing carnal or impure, etc.

units.la: Afferuntur autem & confirmantur hoc loco (ut supra diximus) articuli fidei nostræ de Filij Dei incarnatione: Conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine. De quibus nos non curiosius disputare decet, ut olim hæretici fecerunt. Quia enim conceptionis modum ipsi Mariæ virgini non aliter exponit Angelus, nefas fuerit in hunc altius inquirere, & nostri ingenij acumine ea scrutari velle, quæ omne humanæ rationis captum superant. Sufficiat nobis, hoc omne Spiritus sancti opus fuisse, qui diuina virtute ex sanctissimæ virginis substantia carnem genuit, & eidem animam humanam indidit, cui eodem momento æternus ille Dei Filius, eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ, coniunctus est in vnam eandemque personam: & ita quidem, ut neque Deus in hominem, neq; hic in Deum conuersus, sed homo à Deo assumptus sit: neque etiam duo sint Christi, quorum vnus Dei, alter Mariæ filius dici debeat: sed vnus sit Christus, verus & æternus Dei Filius in carne assumpta manifestatus, ut vnicus quoque inter Deum & homines Mediator fieret. Hunc conceptionis istius modum & ordinem Angeli verba indicant, & cum eodem scripturæ utriusq; testamenti consentiunt. In eo igitur nos acquiescere conuenit, & quod verè factum esse audimus credere, ne dum tanti mysterij causas & modum curiosius inuestigamus, ea in dubium vocemus, sine quibus salutis nostræ ratio non potest consistere. Cur autem alicui impossibile videatur, Dei filium illæsa Mariæ virginitate in illa conceptum & ex eadem hominem natum esse, cùm olim totam hanc mundi machinam ex nihilo solius verbi virtute productam esse, & in eadem multa quotidie fieri constet, quæ carnis rationi non minus absurda et difficilia videntur, & quorum ratio nequaquam reddi potest? Quin ergo relictis hominum phanaticorum & impurissimorum quæstionibus, conceptionis & generationis huius sanctissimæ vsum obseruemus: qui in hoc potissimum consistit, quòd nostram conceptionem & generationem per illam sanctificari oportuit: Vt enim Adamus cùm à dignitate sua & Dei imagine excidisset, filios suos in imagine sua corrupta nimirum & peccatrice genuit: ita omnes homines in peccato concipi & nasci constat, sicut de semetipso Dauid ingenuè fatetur. En ego (inquit) in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Nam, ut Paulus ait, per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiuit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors transijt, quatenus omnes peccauerunt. Est quidem honorabile apud omnes coniugium, gium, & thorus coniugalis impollutus, quoad Dei institutionem. Quia tamen in liberorum genera-tione affectus & cupiditates carnis concurrunt, & in ijs illi concipiuntur, fieri non potest, quin pec-catricem naturam ab vtero materno secum in hanc lucem proferant, & proinde peccato obnoxij sint. Quod si qui Pelagianorum vestigijs insistentes negare audent, facile ijdem convincuntur mor-tis supplicio, cui infantes quoque subiectos esse constat. Quia enim mors peccati stipendium est, in-fantes autem recens nati a peccato (vt illi aiunt) alieni sunt, iniustus certe erit Deus, qui multos in vtero adhuc delitescentes occidit, multos in ipso partu enecat, multos item in prima pueritia ex-tinguit, priusquam vel bonum vel malum actu designent. Taceo nunc, quod infantes olim octavo die circuncidi oportuit ex Dei mandato, qui ita testabatur, in illis esse, quod purgatione & purga-tione opus habeat. Et cur Christus necesse esse ait, vt homo renascatur, si pura & sancta est, qua ex matris vtero progeniti sumus natiuitas? Itaque vt in illo renasci possemus, & innatae nobis cor-ruptioni remedium afferretur, Dei filium ea ratione incarnari oportuit, vt ex Spiritu sancto con-ceptus, ex Virgine intemerata nasceretur. Ita enim nomen feminis benedicti obtinuit, in quo omnes gentes terrae benedicuntur, sicut olim Abrahamo Deus promiserat. Est ergo firmiter nobis tenen-dum conceptionis & generationis Christi Iesu mysterium, vt ex eo salutis nostrae certiores redda-mur, & consolationem habeamus solidam, qua nosmetipsos aduersus innatam nobis naturae corru-ptionem & ex hac enascentes dubitationes confirmemus. Et hic verus & proprius Virginitatis Mariae vsus est, quem omnino negant & euacuant aduersarij nostri, qui hominis vires & operum merita afferunt. Si enim ea est hominis conditio, vt ἀντεπαίρει & ἀντεξάσει & ipse sibi ad salu-tem sufficiat, quam obsecro causam dabimus, ob quam Dei filium praeter communem naturae ordi-nem, absque viri congressu, & Spiritu sancto concipi & ex Virgine pura atque incorrupta nasci op-portuerit? Volunt illi quidem accerrimi Mariae & virginitatis eius vindices videri, at si reipsam diligentius expendamus, hoc vno dogmate & Christi Iesu meritum & Virginitatis Mariae vsum fructumq; exinaniunt. Neq; ad Christianismum & salutis nostrae negotium sufficit rerum a Chri-sto gestarum historiam tenere, nisi simul vsum teneamus eorum, quae de illo dicuntur, & in eo vno spem omnem salutis collocemus.
units.tr: Moreover, the articles of our faith concerning the incarnation of the Son of God are presented and confirmed in this place (as we said above): He was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. We ought not to dispute about these matters too curiously, as the heretics did of old. Since the angel explains the manner of the conception to the Virgin Mary in no other way, it would be wrong to inquire into it more deeply and to wish to search out with the sharpness of our wit those things which surpass all grasp of human reason. It is enough for us to know that this whole work was done by the Holy Spirit, who by divine power brought forth flesh from the substance of the most holy virgin and infused into it a human soul, and to which at the same moment the eternal Son of God, of the same essence as the Father, was joined in one and the same person. And so it was, that God was not turned into man, nor man into God, but man was assumed by God. Nor are there two Christs, one of whom ought to be called the Son of God and the other the son of Mary; rather there is one Christ, the true and eternal Son of God, made manifest in assumed flesh, so that he might be the only Mediator between God and men. The words of the angel indicate this manner and order of the conception, and they agree with the Scriptures of both Testaments. In this, therefore, we ought to rest, and to believe that what we hear was truly done, lest, while we investigate too curiously the causes and manner of so great a mystery, we call into doubt those things without which the ground of our salvation cannot stand. But why should it seem impossible to anyone that the Son of God was conceived in Mary with her virginity unharmed and was born of her as a man, when it is agreed that this whole machine of the world was once produced from nothing by the power of the word alone, and that many things happen every day in it which seem no less absurd and difficult to the reason of the flesh, and for which no reason can be given? Why then, setting aside the questions of frantic and most impure men, do we not observe the use of this most holy conception and birth? That use consists chiefly in this: that our conception and birth had to be sanctified through it. For just as Adam, when he had fallen from his dignity and the image of God, begot sons in his own image, corrupted and sinful indeed, so it is agreed that all men are conceived and born in sin, as David himself frankly confesses: "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me." For, as Paul says, "by one man sin entered into the world, and by sin death, and so death passed upon all men, inasmuch as all have sinned." Marriage is indeed honourable among all, and the marriage bed is undefiled, as far as God's ordinance goes. Yet because in the generation of children the affections and lusts of the flesh come together, and in these the children are conceived, it cannot but be that they bring with them from the mother's womb into this light a sinful nature, and are therefore subject to sin. But if any who follow the footsteps of the Pelagians dare to deny this, they are easily refuted by the punishment of death, to which it is agreed that infants also are subject. For since death is the wages of sin, and infants newly born are (as they say) free from sin, God would certainly be unjust, who kills many who still lie hidden in the womb, destroys many in the very birth, and extinguishes many also in early childhood, before they have done either good or evil in act. I say nothing now of the fact that infants were once to be circumcised on the eighth day by God's command, who thus testified that there was in them something that needed cleansing and purging. And why does Christ say that it is necessary for a man to be born again, if the nativity by which we were brought forth from our mother's womb is pure and holy? Therefore, so that we might be born again in him, and a remedy might be brought to the corruption innate in us, the Son of God had to be incarnate in this manner: conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the unspotted Virgin. For in this way the seed of the blessed woman obtained its name, in which all the nations of the earth are blessed, as God had once promised to Abraham. We must therefore hold firmly to the mystery of the conception and generation of Christ Jesus, so that we may be made more certain of our salvation, and may have a solid consolation by which we may strengthen ourselves against the corruption of nature innate in us and the doubts arising from it. And this is the true and proper use of the virginity of Mary, which our adversaries, who attribute strength to man and merit to works, utterly deny and make void. For if man's condition is such that he can rise up against sin [ἀντεπαίρει] and hold out against it [ἀντεξάσει] and suffice for his own salvation, what cause, I beg you, will we give, for which the Son of God had to be conceived without the intercourse of a man, beyond the common order of nature, by the Holy Spirit, and born of a pure and uncorrupted virgin? Those men wish indeed to seem the most vehement defenders of Mary and of her virginity, but if we weigh the matter more carefully in reality, by this one dogma they empty both the merit of Christ Jesus and the use and fruit of Mary's virginity. Nor is it enough for Christianity and the business of our salvation to hold the history of the things done by Christ, unless at the same time we hold the use of those things which are said of him, and place all our hope of salvation in him alone.

units.la: Secunda suae orationis aut responsionis parte Christum amplius describit Angelus, cum ex prae-missis infert: Propterea id etiam quod ex te nascetur Sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Quibus ver-bis diserte illum ex communi hominum sorte eximit. Nam quod ex te nascetur Sanctum, inquit, Sanctum ergo fore docet ex ipso matris vtero, cum omnes homines (vt paulo ante diximus) impuri & prophani nascantur. Interim ex Maria nasciturum ait (quod D. Athanasius quoq; diligenter ob seruauit) vt verum Mariae filium, & ex eius substantia natum doceret. Verba Athanasij in epistola ad Epictetum sunt haec: Gabriel plane & certo Mariae nuntium illud laetum exposuit, cum non simpliciter diceret: Quod gignetur in te: ne quis existimaret corpus in ipsam foris introductum: sed Ex te: nempe vt natura fore ex ipsa crederemus quod gigneretur. Sanctus autem dicitur Christus partim quoad seipsum, quia totus purus & omnis labis expers est: partim quoad nos, quos suo me-rito & spiritu sanctificat, vt toti Deo consecrati simus. Ipse enim nobis a patre factus est (vt Pau-lus ait) sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio et redemptio. Itaq; suum illi honorem eripiunt, qui sanctifica-tionem vel suorum operum meritis transcribunt, vel apud Diuos coelites quaerunt, qui cum in terris viuerent, ad vnum Christum omnes remiserunt, & fidem in hunc sanguine proprio sunt testati. Qui vero sanctitatem apud Romanos Pontifices inueniri putant: & his Canonizandi vel inter Sanctos referendi ius tribuunt, ij perinde faciunt, ac si quis in proflibulo inter lenones pudicitiam quaerat, aut in cloaca foetidissima ablui velit. Quae enim illi sanctificabunt, qui ipsi a Deo alienissimi sunt, & se totos turpissimis flagitijs quotidie polluunt, adhaec suos sectatores ab vnius Dei cultu ad creaturas & nugacissima suarum traditionum figmenta remittunt? Deinde repetit Gabriel quod prius dixerat: Filius Dei vocabitur. Quod non modo ad aeternam illius diuinitatem, verum etiam ad incarnationem referri debet. Vt enim quoad diuinam naturam verus & aeternus filius est Christus, ita quoad assumptam carnem quoq; reuera Dei filius dicitur. Nam si homines Dei filios scriptura dicit, ad quos (vt Christus ait) Dei sermo factus est, id est, qui ad munus aliquod peculiare diuinitus destinati sunt, quanto magis nomen hoc Christo debetur, qui vt quoad carnem absq; viri congressu
units.tr: In the second part of his speech or reply, the angel describes Christ more fully, when from what has been said he infers: "Therefore also the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God." By these words he clearly removes him from the common lot of men. For when he says "the holy thing which shall be born of you," he teaches that he will be holy from the very womb of his mother, since all men are born impure and profane (as we said a little before). Meanwhile he says that he would be born of Mary (which Athanasius also carefully observed), to teach that he was the true son of Mary and born of her substance. The words of Athanasius in his letter to Epictetus are these: "Gabriel plainly and certainly announced that joyful message to Mary, when he did not simply say, 'What shall be begotten in you,' lest anyone suppose that a body was brought into her from outside, but said, 'of you,' namely, that we might believe that what was begotten would be of her nature." Christ is called holy partly with respect to himself, since he is wholly pure and free of all stain; partly with respect to us, whom he sanctifies by his merit and Spirit, so that we may be wholly consecrated to God. For he has been made to us by the Father (as Paul says) wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Therefore they take away his honour who transfer sanctification to the merits of their own works, or seek it from the saints in heaven, who, while they lived on earth, referred all men to Christ alone, and bore witness to faith in him with their own blood. But those who think holiness is to be found with the Roman pontiffs, and grant to them the right of canonizing or enrolling men among the saints, act just as if someone should seek chastity in a brothel among pimps, or wish to be washed in a most foul sewer. For how can they sanctify others who are themselves most alien from God, and who daily defile themselves wholly with the most shameful crimes, and moreover send their followers away from the worship of the one God to creatures and to the most trifling inventions of their own traditions? Next, Gabriel repeats what he had said before: "He will be called the Son of God." This must be referred not only to his eternal divinity, but also to the incarnation. For just as in respect of the divine nature Christ is the true and eternal Son, so in respect of the flesh he assumed he is also truly called the Son of God. For if Scripture calls men sons of God, to whom (as Christ says) the word of God came, that is, who are divinely destined for some peculiar office, how much more is this name owed to Christ, who, as to the flesh, without the intercourse of a man

units.la: 1.Cor.ii Spiritus sancti virtute & operatione singulari ex virginis substantia generatus est: ita munus etiam à Patre accepit omnium excellentissimum, ut scilicet populi Dei Rex et Sacerdos æternus, atq; unicus humani generis redemptor sit? Facit igitur huius nominis consideratio ad nostræ salutis certitudinem afferendam, quæ dubia esse non potest, cum eum authorem habeat, qui & verus Dei Filius est, & ut hanc nobis acquireret ex æterno patris decreto in terras venit, & ex Virgine matre hominem verum assumpsit. Continetur præterea hisce Angeli verbis euidés sanctæ & adorandæ Trinitatis testimonium. Nominantur enim diserte Altissimus, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. At quia Deum unum esse scriptura alibi testatur, in eius unitate personas tres agnoscamus oportet, nisi Angelum mendacij arguere, & totum Iesu Christi incarnationis mysterium in dubium vocare libeat.
units.tr: Was he not generated from the substance of the virgin by the singular power and operation of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 2)? So also he has received from the Father the most excellent office of all, namely that he should be the eternal King and Priest of the people of God and the only redeemer of the human race? Therefore, the consideration of this name serves to establish the certainty of our salvation, which cannot be doubtful, since it has as its author him who is both the true Son of God, who came into the earth by the eternal decree of the Father to obtain this for us, and who assumed true man from the Virgin mother. Moreover, the clear testimony of the holy and adorable Trinity is contained in these words of the angel. For the Most High, the Son and the Holy Spirit are expressly named. But because Scripture elsewhere testifies that God is one, we must acknowledge three persons in that unity, unless we are willing to charge the angel with lying and call into doubt the whole mystery of the incarnation of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Restat tertia responsionis Angelicæ pars, quæ confirmationem istorum omnium continet. Etsi enim Deus pro suo iure fidem à nobis exigere posset, nostræ tamen infirmitatis rationem habet, & carnis rationibus, quibus fides nostra tentari solet, argumenta opponit, quibus ea confirmetur. Quæ nos in omnibus eius promissionibus observare decet, ne illius bonitate contemnere videamur. In præsenti autem duo argumenta producuntur. Primum ab exemplo petitur, cuius magna vis est in iis, quæ nova & insolita esse videntur. Ecce (inquit) Elizabet cognata tua, & ipsa concepit filium in senectu te sua: & hic mensis est sextus ipsi, quæ vocabatur sterilis. Ibi quærunt nonnulli, quomodo Elizabet, quæ ex filiabus Aaronis fuisse supra dictum est, Mariæ cognata fuerit, si hæc ex Davidis genere & tribu Iuda originem habuit? Sed facile soluitur quæstio, si observemus, legem de tribuum commixtione non pertinuisse ad Leuitas. Quia enim hi terras proprias non possidebant, nullum periculum erat, ne terræ hereditas confunderetur, etiamsi vel ipsi uxores ex aliis tribubus ducerent, vel suas filias aliis elocarent. Ideo ipse Aaron uxorem ex tribu Iuda oriundam habuit, Elisabam filiam Aminadabi, sororem Naasson: & Iehoidæ sacerdotis coniunx fuit Iehoseba filia Regis Iorami & Ahasiæ Regis soror. Eadem ergo ratione fieri potuit, ut Elizabeta mater ex Davidis stirpe nata Sacerdoti nupserit, & proinde cognatio inter illam & Mariam intercesserit, quàmuis patres ex diversis tribubus essent oriundi. Quod autem Angeli argumentum, non tue hoc fuit aut vulgare. Perinde enim hoc est, ac si dixisset: Ne mireris, quod absq; viri congressu te paritura dico, quæ iuuencula es & ad concipiendum idonea, cum cognata tua Elizabeta, quæ & sterilis semper fuit, & nunc ob senectam ad conceptum minime idonea est, ex Zacharia marito vetulo conceperit, et iam mensem sextum agat, ex quo prægnans facta est. Qui enim senem & sterilem potuit fœcunda reddere, te quoq; absq; viri opera matrem facere poterit. Vel anno maior et efficacior erit Spiritus sancti virtus ex quo te concepturam esse dixi, quàm Zachariæ sit, ex quo Elizabeta concepit? Addit huic argumentum aliud ab omnipotentia Dei petitum: Quia apud Deum non erit impossibile vllum verbum. Id verò absolute pronuntiat Angelus, ut pote generale fidei & veræ pietatis principium, de quo nemini pio dubitare fas sit. Quid enim Deo impossibile sit, qui (ut supra diximus) ex nihilo creauit omnia, & quæ nulla erant, solo verbo ut essent euocauit? Admonent autem ista, ut ipsi quoq; fidem nostram fulcire debeamus. In promissionibus ad Dei potentiam respicere oportet, quod fidei proprium esse, Paulus ad Romanos Abrahami exemplo docet. At ne illa nostro modulo metiamur, et ideo in negotijs difficilioribus dubitemus, simul exempla vetera in mentem revocare conuenit, quæ in omni genere aduersorum plurima occurrunt, & quorum consideratione fides plurimum confirmabitur, si cogitemus, Deum sibi ipsi semper constare, & vires habere inexhaustas, quæ nullis operibus fatigari aut debilitari possint. At hic cauendus est illorum error, qui ex nuda omnipotentia argumentantur de illis rebus, de quibus non constat, an eas perfici velit Deus. Nam quæcunque vult facit Deus, non quæcunq; potest. Nisi ergo de eius voluntate nobis constet, frustra omnipotentiam illius allegabimus.
units.tr: There remains the third part of the angel's reply, which contains the confirmation of all these things. For although God could rightly demand faith from us, he nevertheless takes account of our weakness and sets against the arguments of the flesh, by which our faith is usually tested, arguments by which it may be confirmed. We ought to observe this in all his promises, lest we seem to scorn his goodness. In the present case, two arguments are put forward. The first is taken from example, whose great force lies in those things which seem new and unusual. "Behold," he says, "Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her, who was called barren." Here some ask how Elizabeth, who, as was said above, was of the daughters of Aaron, could be a kinswoman of Mary, if Mary was descended from the line of David and the tribe of Judah. But the question is easily resolved if we observe that the law concerning the mixing of tribes did not apply to the Levites. For since they did not possess their own lands, there was no danger that the inheritance of the land would be confused, even if they took wives from other tribes or gave their own daughters to other tribes. Thus Aaron himself had a wife of the tribe of Judah, Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Naashon; and the wife of the priest Jehoiada was Jehosheba, daughter of King Jehoram and sister of King Ahaziah. By the same reasoning it could happen that Elizabeth, the mother, born of the stock of David, married a priest, and so a kinship arose between her and Mary, although their fathers were descended from different tribes. Moreover, this was not an ordinary or trivial argument of the angel's. For it is just as if he had said: "Do not be surprised that I say you, who are a young woman and fit for conception, will bear a child without the intercourse of a man. Your kinswoman Elizabeth, who was always barren and now in her old age is by no means fit for conception, has conceived by her aged husband Zechariah, and is already in her sixth month since she became pregnant. For he who could make an old and barren woman fruitful, will be able to make you a mother without the work of a man. Or will the power of the Holy Spirit, from which I have said you will conceive, be greater and more effective in the year than that of Zechariah, from which Elizabeth conceived?" He adds to this a second argument, drawn from the omnipotence of God: "Because with God no word will be impossible." Indeed, the angel pronounces this absolutely, as the general principle of faith and true godliness, a thing about which no pious person may rightly doubt. For what could be impossible for God, who (as we said above) created all things out of nothing, and called into being by a word alone things that did not exist? Yet these words also admonish us that we too ought to support our faith. In promises we must look to the power of God, which is proper to faith, as Paul teaches by the example of Abraham to the Romans. But lest we measure these things by our own measure, and therefore doubt in more difficult matters, it is fitting also to call to mind the examples of old, which occur in great number in every kind of adversity, and by considering which faith will be greatly strengthened, if we reflect that God always remains consistent with himself and has inexhaustible strength, which cannot be worn out or weakened by any works. Here, however, we must beware of the error of those who argue from bare omnipotence about those things of which it is not certain whether God wishes them to be accomplished. For God does not do whatever he can, but whatever he wills. Therefore, unless we are assured of his will, we shall argue in vain from his omnipotence.

units.la: Obseruauit hoc probè Maria, quæ cùm de voluntate Dei probè edocta esset, magni ponderis æstimat Angeli argumenta, & ideo respondet: Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Obstabant quidem adhuc multa, quæ carnis rationi dubium mouere poterant: sed proculexplosis illis omnibus, diuinæ voluntati se committit, & ita ex fide concipit, sicuti de Sara in epistola ad Hebræos scribitur. Itaque ab illa quoque mox discedit Angelus, utpote confecto plane negotio, cuius causa ad illam missus fuerat. Habemus autem hic verae fidei exemplum. Proprium illius est, Dei verbo credere, quamuis cum hoc ipsa rerum natura & communis sensus pugnare videantur. Vbi plurimum proderit, si illud æternum esse cogitemus, & tunc quoque ratum fore, quando cœlum & terra dissoluentur. Sequitur ex hoc obedientia, qua se homines totos voluntati Dei subijciunt: quem Euangelicæ prædicationis finem esse, Paulus non vno loco testatur. Sunt ergo à fide alieni prorsus, qui de hijs quoque disputationes instituunt, quæ diserto Dei verbo traduntur: qui item non obtemperant ijs, quæ nobis diuinitus præcepta esse non ignorant. Discamus adhæc ex ipso loco de Maria recte iudicare. Fuit hæc ancilla Domini fidelissima, & ad omne obsequium parata. Eam, vt filij sui in carne manifestandi mater fieret, Deus sibi ex gratuito fauore elegit. Illius ergo fidem & obedientiam imitemur, salutis vero fiduciam in eo collocemus, quem illa genuit, filio nimirum Dei æterno, & humani generis vnico redemptore, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Mary rightly observed this, since, being well taught about the will of God, she valued the angel's arguments at their true weight, and therefore she answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." Indeed, many things still stood in the way, which could raise doubt by the reasoning of the flesh; but, having dismissed all of them, she commits herself to the divine will, and so conceives by faith, just as is written of Sarah in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Thus the angel also departs from her at once, since the business for which he had been sent to her was entirely completed. Here we have an example of true faith. It is proper to it to believe the word of God, although the nature of things itself and common sense seem to fight against it. Here it will be of great benefit if we reflect that this word is eternal, and that it will also remain valid when heaven and earth are dissolved. From this follows obedience, by which men subject themselves wholly to the will of God, which Paul testifies in more than one place is the end of the evangelical preaching. Therefore those are wholly alien from faith who set up disputations even about those things which are plainly delivered in the word of God, and likewise those who do not obey what they know has been commanded to us by God. Let us learn from this very passage to judge rightly about Mary. This handmaid of the Lord was most faithful and ready for every obedience. God chose her for himself out of his free favour, that she might become the mother by whom his Son would be manifested in the flesh. Therefore let us imitate her faith and obedience, and place our confidence of salvation in him whom she bore, namely the eternal Son of God and the only redeemer of the human race, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA X.
units.tr: HOMILY X.

units.la: Cum autem surrexisset Maria in diebus illis, profecta est in montanam regionem cum festinatione in vrbe Iuda. Et ingressa est in domum Zachariæ, & salutauit Elizabetam.
