Et factum est, vt audiuit Elizabeta salutationem Mariæ, salijt fœtus in vtero eius, & repleta est spiritu sancto Elizabeta, exclamauitque voce magna, & dixit: Benedicta tu inter mulieres, & benedictus fructus ventris tui. Et vnde hoc mihi, vt veniat mater Domini mei ad me? Ecce enim vt peruenit vox salutationis tuæ ad aures meas, salijt fœtus præ gaudio in vtero meo. Et beata quæ credidit: quia perficientur ea quæ dicta sunt ei à Domino.
units.tr: And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Juda; And entered into the house of Zacharias, and saluted Elisabeth. And it came to pass, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost: And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy. And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.

units.la: QVamuis in vnigenito Dei Filio, Domino nostro Iesu Christo, omnes diuinæ gratiæ & salutis humanæ thesauri continentur, idem tamen non prodesset, nisi vere cognitus & fide vera perceptus. Ideo illius incarnationem iam inde ab origine rerum Deus multifariam hominibus innotescere voluit, & cum iam illius tempus appropinquauisset, eandem non vno modo manifestauit. Vbi post Angelum Gabrielem primas tenent mulieres, quæ in præsenti producuntur, Elizabeta & Maria Virgo. Differunt hæ ex Spiritus sancti suggestione de mysterio omnium excellentissimo, quod (vt Paulus ait) à temporibus æternis tacitum fuit, & quod omnes gentium philosophi, & quotquot vnquam sapientiæ summæ existimationem sustinuere, ignorauerunt. Superat ergo colloquium hoc sua authoritate omnia Pontificum concilia, qui etsi Spiritus sancti nomen suis decretis prætexant, de fidei tamen & salutis nostræ mysterijs adeo inepte & obscure balbutiunt, vt cordatis omnibus risum mouere possint, si in re tam feria risus vllum locum haberet; rudes vero & imperitos rerum omnium magis incertos reddant. Voluit autem Deus tanto negotio mulieres adhibere, vt certius constaret, muliebrem quoque sexum per Christum restitutum esse: ad quod peculiari demonstratione omnino opus erat. Quia enim mulier primum peccauit, & humanæ perditionis causa fuit præcipua, atque ideo sexum illum Deus variis morborum & laborum molestijs multauit: facilis inter has ad desperationem lapsus esse poterat, nisi peculiares quoque consolationes accessissent, quibus in spe certa salutis confirmarentur. Quæ causa est, quòd ex muliere hominem nasci oportuit Dei filium, vt ex eodem sexu iustitia & vita oriretur, per quem peccatum & mors ingressa fuerant. Et ipse Christus, cum iam in terris ageret, mulieribus adipsum confluentibus familiarissimum sese præbuit, & quidem ijs etiam, quæ libidine & vitijs infames erant: neque Pharisæorum calumnijs abstterreri potuit, quo minus illis pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum offerret. Constat præterea, selectas aliquot mulieres mortis & resurrectionis ipsius testes fuisse, quarum fides ipsis apostolis præstantior fuit, qui tunc metu dispersi erant, & rerum dubij vacillabant. Debent ista animum addere pijs fœminis, vt & certam salutis in Christo exhibitæ spem concipiant, et patientius ferant dolores atque molestias, quæ illis in liberorum educatione & tota re domestica
units.tr: Although all the treasures of divine grace and of human salvation are contained in the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, they would nonetheless profit us nothing unless he were truly known and received by true faith. Therefore God willed from the very beginning of things to make the incarnation of his Son known to men in many ways, and when its time had drawn near, he did not reveal it in only one manner. Among those who showed it, after the angel Gabriel, the first place belongs to the women who are presented in the present passage, Elisabeth and the Virgin Mary. Prompted by the Holy Spirit, they speak of the most excellent of mysteries, which (as Paul says) has been hidden since eternal times, and which all the philosophers of the nations, and all who have ever claimed the highest reputation for wisdom, have not known. This conversation therefore surpasses by its authority all the councils of the Pontiffs, who, though they pretend the name of the Holy Spirit for their decrees, stammer about the mysteries of our faith and salvation so foolishly and obscurely that they could move all sensible people to laughter, if laughter had any place in so serious a matter; and they leave simple and unskilled people even more uncertain about all things. God, however, willed to use women in so great a matter, so that it might be more certainly established that the female sex too has been restored through Christ, and for this a special demonstration was entirely needed. For since woman sinned first and was the chief cause of human ruin, God burdened that sex with various troubles of sickness and toil; among these it could easily have fallen into despair, unless special consolations had also been added, by which women might be strengthened in the sure hope of salvation. This is the reason why it was fitting that the Son of God should be born of a woman, so that righteousness and life might arise from the same sex through which sin and death had entered. And Christ himself, while he was still living on earth, showed himself most familiar to women who flocked to him, and indeed even to those who were infamous for lust and vices; nor could he be deterred by the slanders of the Pharisees from offering them repentance and the forgiveness of sins. Moreover, it is established that certain chosen women were witnesses of his death and resurrection, and their faith was more outstanding than that of the apostles themselves, who at that time were scattered by fear and wavered in doubt about these things. These matters ought to encourage godly women, so that they may both conceive a sure hope of salvation offered in Christ, and bear more patiently the pains and troubles which they must undergo in the bringing up of children and in the whole management of the household.

units.la: Mariæ & Elizabetæ de maximo mysterio colloquium.
units.tr: The conversation of Mary and Elisabeth about the greatest mystery.

units.la: Christus mulierum quoque sexus vindicator. subeundae sunt. Deinde apparet in hac actione mos Dei, qui vt alibi personas humiles & contemptas rebus maximis destinat: ita hic quoq; ad istud colloquium Elizabetam anum & sterilitatis nota in famem, Mariam item pauperculam & contemptam, delegit, cum non deessent, quae dignitate, opibus & externo splendore commendabantur, quas ipsi facile fuisset suo spiritu excitare & ad tanti mysterij tractationem idoneas facere. Sed ita solet Deus, vt huius mundi faslum atque excellentiam confundat, & vt omnibus constet, ea quae inter homines in pretio habentur, ad salutem aeternam nihil conferre, neque nobis aliquam reliquam esse gloriandi occasionem, cum tota illius ratio ex mera Dei gratia dependeat.
units.tr: Christ the vindicator of the female sex too. Next, in this action appears the manner of God, who, as elsewhere, assigns the greatest things to humble and despised persons. So here too he chose for this conversation Elisabeth, an old woman marked with the reproach of barrenness, and likewise Mary, a poor and despised girl, although there were not lacking women commended by rank, wealth and outward splendour, whom it would have been easy for him to stir by his Spirit and make fit for the handling of so great a mystery. But God is accustomed to do this, to confound the pomp and excellence of this world, and to make it plain to all that the things which are held in esteem among men contribute nothing to eternal salvation, and that we have no remaining ground for boasting, since the whole reckoning of it depends on pure grace of God.

units.la: Porro ad rem ipsam accedamus, vbi primum colloquij istius occasio occurrit, quam Maria Virgo praebuit. Haec enim cum ex Angelo didicisset, promissum illum humani generis redemptorem ex ipsa nasci debere, mox in regionem montanam proficiscitur, vt in eam ciuitatem tribus Iuda venias, in qua Zacharias habitabat: quo cum festinanter venisset, illius domum ingressa Elizabetam salutat. Causa profectionis istius fuit, non curiositas aut hinc inde vagandi libido (quibus vitijs fere sexus ille laborat) sed quod Angelus inter argumenta, quibus diuinam promissionem confirmauit, Elizabeta etiam exemplum adduxerat, quae iam anus & antea sterilis vterum ferret, & filium esset paritura. Itaq; quod ex Angelo audiuerat, coram cognoscere cupit, non quod verbis illius diffidat, sed vt in fide confirmetur, & vt mutuo colloquio sese inuicem consolentur. Est enim hoc fidei proprium, quod magno studio ea sectatur, quae nos plenius instituere & confirmare possunt. Ideo qui hac donati sunt, non modo Dei verbum frequenter audiunt, verumetiam in precibus sunt assidui, quibus petunt, vt Dominus ipsis vias suas offendat, spiritu suo fulciat, atque fidem ipsorum confirmet. Et notum est Pauli exemplum, qui hoc nomine Ecclesiam Romanorum inuisere cupiebat, vt ex mutuae fidei collatione vtrinq; consolationem acciperent, & ad huius studium mutuo exemplo excitarentur. Sunt igitur a fide alienissimi, qui & in precibus frigent, & Dei verbum atque sacras conciones negligunt, imo illud tunc quoq; fastidiunt atq; aspernantur, quando hoc illis Dominus offert. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, quibus nullum negotium tam vile, nullum lucrum tam sordidum & exiguum est, quod non coetibus sacris praferant, in quibus verbum praedicatur, & publicae preces fiunt. Arguit hos suo exemplo Maria, quae etsi audisset, se esse benedictam illam in ter mulieres, & iam vtero gestaret aeternum Dei filium, iter tamen longinquum & arduum suscipit, vt maiores in fide progressus faciat. Pudeat ergo istos suae socordiae, & saltem poena terreantur, quam de illis sumit Deus, quando eos in peius proficere sinit, vt tandem fidei totius iacturam faciant, & salutis suae securi nimis misere pereant.
units.tr: But let us now come to the matter itself, where first the occasion of this conversation presents itself, which the Virgin Mary provided. For when she had learned from the angel that the promised Redeemer of the human race must be born from her, she at once set out for the hill country, to go into that city of the tribe of Judah in which Zacharias lived; and when she had come there in haste, she entered his house and greeted Elisabeth. The reason for this journey was not curiosity, nor a desire to wander here and there (vices to which that sex is generally prone), but that the angel, among the proofs by which he confirmed the divine promise, had also adduced Elisabeth as an example, who, though now old and formerly barren, was carrying a womb and was about to bear a son. Therefore she wished to know for herself what she had heard from the angel, not because she distrusted his words, but so that she might be confirmed in faith, and that they might comfort one another by mutual conversation. For it is a property of faith that it eagerly seeks those things which can instruct and strengthen us more fully. Hence those who have been given this gift not only hear the word of God frequently, but are also constant in prayers, by which they ask that the Lord would show them his ways, strengthen them by his Spirit, and confirm their faith. And the example of Paul is well known, who on this account desired to visit the Church at Rome, so that by a mutual comparing of faith they might both receive consolation, and be stirred to pursue this by mutual example. Therefore those are most alien to faith who grow cold in prayer, and neglect the word of God and holy sermons; indeed they then loathe and spurn it, when the Lord offers it to them. There is today a great number of such people, for whom no business is so mean, and no gain so sordid and small, that they do not prefer it to sacred assemblies, in which the word is preached and public prayers are made. Mary shames them by her example: although she had heard that she was blessed among women, and already bore in her womb the eternal Son of God, nevertheless she undertakes a long and arduous journey, so that she may make greater progress in faith. Let them therefore be ashamed of their own sloth, and at least be terrified by the punishment which God exacts from them, when he allows them to go from bad to worse, until at last they suffer the total loss of faith, and, too secure in their salvation, perish miserably.

units.la: Non temere autem Maria in hac profectione festinauisse dicitur. Nam est hoc fidei ardentis argumentum, & quod Dei beneficium magni fecerit. Deinde rursus hoc exemplo Spiritus sanctus virgines officij admonet. Decet has (vt alibi monuimus) domum curare, & quae illic agenda sunt fideliter agere. Quod si quando propter negotia necessaria prodeundum est, current nec in publico vel diutius versentur & moras nectant inanes, vel temere discurrant. Quantum enim hoc mali olim Dinae dederit, supra diximus: & quam periculosum sit puellas vagari, exemplis quotidianis doceri poteramus, nisi iam pridem toti obsurduissemus ad ea, quae nos honestatem & pietatem sectari docent.
units.tr: Nor is it said that Mary hastened on this journey without reason. For this is a sign of a fervent faith, and shows that she held the benefit of God in high esteem. Next, by this example the Holy Spirit again admonishes virgins of their duty. As we have elsewhere taught, such women ought to keep the house, and faithfully do what must be done there. But if at any time they must go out because of necessary business, they should hurry, and not linger in public or stay longer than needful, nor wander about rashly. How much harm this once brought to Dinah we have said above; and how dangerous it is for girls to roam about we could show from daily examples, were we not long ago grown deaf to those things which teach us to pursue modesty and piety.

units.la: Caeterum ad salutationem Mariae Virginis in Elizabetae vtero foetus subsilijt. Quod singulari Spiritus sancti operatione factum fuisse, postea ex Elizabetae verbis patebit. Ita enim declarari oportuit, eum, quem Maria iam conceperat & suo vtero gestabat, esse exoptatum illud sanctorum patrum desiderium: illum (inquam) cuius diem Abrahamus gestiuit videre, & cuius fiducia atque spe gaudisus est. Simul autem denotatur hoc argumento, quanta sit Ioannis praestantia & dignitas, qui cum in vtero materno adhuc delitesceret, officio suo fungi coepit. Nam ad hoc illum a Deo electum & praedestinatum fuisse scimus, vt Christi Iesu anteambulo & testis esset, & ad hunc excipiendum omnes excitaret. Id ergo iam nunc facit, & nondum in lucem hanc aditus insolita exultatione Elizabetam matrem admonet, Mariam foetum illum diu exoptatum concepisse. Vere igitur de illo dixerat Angelus, ipsum Spiritus sancti plenum fore ab vtero matris suae. Nec sine causa de illo postea Christus testatus est, quod inter natos ex mulieribus nemo illo maior & praestantior habea-tur. tur. Hæc autem nos in eum finem obseruare conuenit, non vt (quod superstitiosi solent) Ioannem in uocemus, & honoribus diuinis prosequamur: sed vt eò maior apud nos sit authoritas testimonij, quod de Christo tulit, & proinde hunc agnoscamus esse agnum illum Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi, atq; in illo vno omnem salutis fiduciam collocemus. Et huc facit, quòd hoc ipso argumento constat, Ioannem ex gratia habuisse quicquid insigne & eximium habuit, cuius nomine alijs hominibus præferri meretur. Quid enim illum meruisse dicemus, cùm adhuc in matris vtero conclusus detinereteur? Aut num ipsius proprium opus fuit: quòd & ipse nondum natus Christum nuper ex Spiritu sancto conceptum et adhuc fœtum informem in virginis vtero iacentem agnouit, & de illo testatus est? Dei certè hoc opus fuit, qui vt de illo per prophetas olim vaticinatus fuit, ita eunde priusquam esset elegit & ad hoc munus prædestinauit, vtq; ei sufficere posset, iam inde ab vtero matris donis Spiritus sancti ad illud necessarijs instruxit. Atqui eandē esse omnium hominum rationem, Paulus ad Romanos exemplo Iacobi & Esau probat, qui cùm simul concepti essent, & neuter aliquid vel boni vel mali fecisset, alter tamen à Deo electus, alter reprobatus aut derelictus fuit. Neque ideo Deum vel iniustitiæ vel crudelitatis accusare possumus, cùm nemini quicquam debeat, & neminem immerentem damnet: potius illius bonitatem nos agnoscere & prædicare decet, qui ex corrupta & perdita humani generis massa aliquos eligere dignatur, quos absque omni ipsorum merito salutis æternæ & bonorum suorum cœlestium consortes faciat.
units.tr: Moreover, at the salutation of the Virgin Mary the babe leaped in Elisabeth's womb. That this was done by a singular operation of the Holy Spirit will afterwards become clear from Elisabeth's words. For it was fitting that it be declared in this way that he whom Mary had now conceived and carried in her womb was that longed-for desire of the holy fathers: he, I say, whose day Abraham desired to see, and in whose trust and hope he rejoiced. At the same time, this argument shows how great the excellence and dignity of John is, who, while still hidden in his mother's womb, began to perform his office. For we know that he was chosen and predestined by God for this, to be the forerunner and witness of Christ Jesus, and to stir all men to receive him. So already now he does this, and before he has come into this light, by an unusual exultation he informs his mother Elisabeth that Mary has conceived that long-desired offspring. Truly, then, the angel had said of him that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb. Nor without cause did Christ afterwards bear witness of him, that among those born of women none was greater or more excellent than he. We ought to observe these things to this end: not, as the superstitious are wont to do, that we should invoke John and honour him with divine worship; but that the authority of the testimony he bore concerning Christ may be greater for us, and that we may therefore acknowledge him to be that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and place in him alone all our hope of salvation. This also serves the point, that from this very argument it is clear that John had from grace whatever was distinguished and eminent in him, by which he deserves to be preferred to other men. For what merit shall we say he had, when he was still shut up and detained in his mother's womb? Or was it his own work that, though not yet born, he recognised Christ, recently conceived by the Holy Spirit and still lying as an unformed babe in the virgin's womb, and bore witness concerning him? Certainly this was the work of God, who, as he once foretold about him through the prophets, so chose him before he existed and predestined him to this office, and, so that he might be fit for it, from his mother's womb equipped him with the gifts of the Holy Spirit needed for it. And yet Paul, by the example of Jacob and Esau, proves to the Romans that the reasoning is the same for all men: when they had been conceived together, and neither had done anything either good or evil, one was nevertheless chosen by God, and the other rejected or left aside. Nor for this reason can we accuse God of injustice or cruelty, since he owes nothing to anyone, and condemns no one who does not deserve it. Rather it becomes us to acknowledge and proclaim his goodness, who deigns to choose some out of the corrupt and lost mass of the human race, and makes them partakers of eternal salvation and of heavenly goods without any merit of their own.

units.la: Est præter exemplum hoc plenum consolationis, quòd videmus, infantes, seu fœtus potius, adhuc in matris vtero delitescentes Deo curæ esse: Quod enim de Ioanne Bapt. de Ieremia, Paulo apostolo & horum similibus dicitur, hoc sanctissimi quiq; ad seipsos etiam transtulerunt. Dauid certè, vt seipsum consoletur, non semel exclamat: Ab vtero matris meæ Deus meus es tu. Tu is es, qui me ex vtero matris extraxisti. Itè, Tu possides renes meos, & contexisti me in ventre matris meæ. Oculi tui me viderunt, cùm essem fœtus informis, & in libro tuo vniuersa descripta fuerunt, quæ de inceps formarentur, &c. Hæc vt Dei bonitatem nobis commendant, ita consolatione dulcissimam afferunt prægnantibus, imò parentibus vniuersis, quos cura liberorum & plena laboris eorundem educatio vehementer exercet. Adhæc vitæ & morum institutioni seruiunt, vt memores, nos à Deo creatos & formatos esse, vitam omnē & omnia corporis membra (vt Paulus monet) illius seruitio consecremus, vt tanquam arma iustitiæ ad illius gloriam omnia faciant. Confutantur item exemplis istis Anabaptistæ, qui infantes ab Ecclesiæ consortio excludunt, & eos baptizandos esse negant. At qui infantes quoq; (de credentium infantibus loquor) Dei fœdere cõtineri, Spiritus sancti, & proinde donorum eius, fidei nimirum, remissionis peccatorum & vitæ æternæ capaces esse constat. Quæ ergo iniquitas & temeritas est, illis symbolum externum gratiæ & Ecclesiæ negare, & ab huius societate alienos ducere? Atqui nescimus nos, quomodo ista infantes capiant. Fateor. Num verò nostra insciitia & ignoratia illis fraudi esse debet? Quin potius Christo pro illis stipulati credimus, qui illos in se credere, & regnū cœlorum ad eosdem pertinere testatur, & ideo vult, vt ipsi adducantur. Quia tamen de his alibi commodius dicetur, hæc nunc obiter perstrinxisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Besides this example, which is full of comfort, we see that infants, or rather embryos, still hidden in their mother's womb, are a care to God. For what is said of John the Baptist, Jeremiah, the apostle Paul and their like, the holiest men have also applied to themselves. David, to comfort himself, cries out more than once: "From my mother's womb you are my God. You are he who drew me out of my mother's womb." Likewise: "You possess my reins, and you have knit me together in my mother's womb. Your eyes saw me when I was an unformed embryo, and in your book all things were written which were to be formed," and so on. While these words commend God's goodness to us, they also bring the sweetest comfort to pregnant women, indeed to all parents, whom the care of children and their laborious upbringing greatly trouble. Moreover, they serve the training of life and morals, so that, mindful that we have been created and formed by God, we may consecrate our whole life and all the members of our body to his service (as Paul admonishes), so that they may do everything as weapons of righteousness to his glory. The Anabaptists, who exclude infants from fellowship in the Church and deny that they are to be baptized, are also refuted by these examples. For it is clear that infants too (I speak of the infants of believers) are included in God's covenant, and so are capable of the Holy Spirit and therefore of his gifts, namely faith, forgiveness of sins and eternal life. What iniquity and rashness is it, then, to deny them the outward sign of grace and of the Church, and to treat them as strangers to its fellowship? Yet we do not know how these things take hold in infants. I grant it. But ought our ignorance to be a loss to them? Rather, we believe that we have stipulated with Christ on their behalf, who testifies that they believe in him, that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them, and therefore wills that they be brought to him. But since these matters will be spoken of more fittingly elsewhere, it is enough for now to have touched on them in passing.

units.la: Nunc ad Elizabetæ sermonem accedamus, cuius eò maior debet apud nos esse authoritas, quòd Spiritu sancto repleta fuisse & exclamauisse, id est, voce clara & singulari animi intentione ista pro nunciauisse dicitur. Sunt ergo hæc nō vt aniculæ vulgaris verba, sed vt Dei oracula consideranda, ex cuius inspiratione illa locuta est. Ante omnia verò nobis hoc loco obseruandum est, fidelium & piorum studia nequaquam irrita & inania esse. Quæsuit Maria fidei suæ confirmationem, & vt in mysterio incarnationis filij Dei pleniùs institueretur. Id verò inuenit, & ipsa quoq; paulò post propio spiritus afflatu excitata carmè profundit, quo de toto hoc negotio mira perspicuitate et gravitate disserit, & ipsi etiā Elizabetæ consolationē nouam impertit. Id verò omnibus certò sperare licet, qui serio salutis & gloriæ Dei studio tanguntur. Extant enim generales promissiones: Quærite Dominum, & viuetis. Item: Quærite, & inuenietis. Vt enim Deus seipsum omnibus in Christo filio suo offert, ita etiam apprehendi vult, vt gratiæ & bonorū ipsius communione fruamur. Quòd ergo pauci hodie salutē & veritatis æternæ cognitionē inueniūt, nō Dei hac inuidiose occultantis vitio sed ipsorū culpa fit, qui circa infelicis mundi & carnis impuræ studia occupati, ea securè negligunt, quæ ipsos ad regni cœlorum possessionem prouehere poterant. Porrò sermonis Elizabetæ partes sunt quatuor.
units.tr: Now let us come to Elizabeth's speech, whose authority ought to be greater with us because she is said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit and to have cried out, that is, to have pronounced these things with a clear voice and a singular intensity of mind. So these words are to be considered not as the words of some common old woman, but as oracles of God, by whose inspiration she spoke. Above all, we must observe here that the earnest efforts of the faithful and the pious are by no means vain and empty. Mary sought confirmation of her faith, and to be more fully instructed in the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God. And she found it, and herself, a little later, stirred by the breath of the Spirit, poured forth a song in which she discourses on this whole matter with wonderful clarity and gravity, and bestowed a new consolation even on Elizabeth. Everyone who is seriously moved by zeal for salvation and the glory of God may surely hope for this. For there are general promises: "Seek the Lord, and you shall live." Also: "Seek, and you shall find." For just as God offers himself to all in Christ his Son, so he wills also to be apprehended, that we may enjoy his grace and the fellowship of his good things. Therefore, that few today find salvation and the knowledge of eternal truth is not the fault of God, who hides it out of envy, but of their own, who, occupied with the pursuits of the unhappy world and impure flesh, carelessly neglect the things which could have advanced them to possession of the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, there are four parts to Elizabeth's speech.

units.la: Prima Angeli Gabrielis verba repetit, exclamans: Benedicta tu inter mulieres. Facit hoc ad fidei Mariae confirmationem. Quia enim eadem ex Elizabeta audit, quae prius ipsi Angelus dixerat, facile intelligit, nihil hic ex carnis affectu agi, sed negotium hoc omne divino consilio gubernari. Quod ergo Elizabetae exemplo sese tuentur, qui salutationem Angelicam in preces converterunt, nimis frivolum est. Ut enim verba ista repeteret Elizabeta, tunc suum usum certum habuit, at ut idem hodie fiat, minime opus est. Deinde ineptum est absentem salutare, et perinde eam alloqui, ac si praesens esset. Observatu digna autem est Elizabetae modestia, quae etiam aetate et conditione (utpote Sacerdotis uxor) Mariam excelleret, et in eandem propter cognationem ius aliquod peculiare haberet, in illa tamen Dei dona ingenue agnoscit atque commendat, neque ei dignitatem maiorem invidet, in quam Deus ipsam extulerat. Sunt ab huius sanctissimae matronae ingenio alieni nimis, qui ut soli inter homines emineant, omnibus invident, et quae in aliis conspicantur praeclara Dei dona, omnino sepulta cupiunt, neque gloriae Dei et publicae multorum salutis aliquam rationem habent, quae simul in periculum venit. Est hoc vitium nimis vulgare hodie in repub. et ecclesia, quo fit, ut qui in illis praesunt, multis publice incommodent, et simul proprii honoris non mediocrem iacturam faciant, dum huic ambitiosius consulere instituunt.
units.tr: The first repeats the words of the angel Gabriel, crying out: "Blessed are you among women." This serves to confirm Mary's faith. For since she hears from Elizabeth the very things the angel had said to her before, she readily understands that nothing here is done from fleshly feeling, but that the whole business is governed by divine counsel. It is therefore too frivolous of those who take shelter in Elizabeth's example and have turned the angelic salutation into prayers. When Elizabeth repeated these words, they had their certain use; but there is no need at all for the same thing to be done today. Next, it is absurd to greet someone who is absent, and to address her as if she were present. Elizabeth's modesty, however, is worthy of notice: although she excelled Mary in age and station (being a priest's wife), and might have claimed some peculiar right over her by reason of kinship, she frankly acknowledges and commends the gifts of God in her, and does not begrudge her the greater dignity to which God had raised her. Those who, that they alone may stand out among men, begrudge everyone else and wish every remarkable gift of God they see in others utterly buried, are far removed from the disposition of this most holy matron. They have no regard for the glory of God or for the public salvation of many, which at the same time is brought into danger. This vice is far too common today in commonwealth and Church, with the result that those who preside over them publicly harm many, and at the same time suffer no small loss of their own honour, while they set about looking after this more ambitiously.

units.la: Secunda parte addit: Et benedictus fructus ventris tui. Quibus verbis rationem reddit, cur benedictam inter mulieres dixerit. Quasi diceret: Quia tu promissum illud semen paries, in quo omnes gentes benedici et promissiones de salute humani generis universas impleri oporteat. Docet autem haec causae redditio, Mariam ex Christo habuisse, quicquid eximium habuit, et non alia ratione benedictam illam et omnium mulierum beatissimam dici, quam quod eam ex gratia ad hoc delegit Deus, ut filii sui in carne manifestandi mater fieret. Nam ut alibi diximus, ex Christi plenitudine omnes sancti acceperunt quicquid habent. Nimis ergo praepostere faciunt, qui neglecto Christo in Maria eius matre aut aliis Dei caelitibus haerent, quos no ad hoc destinavit Deus, ut salutis aut gratiae eius authores essent: Agnoscamus nos in illis Dei gratiam, et huius organa illos fuisse fatea mur, adhaec eorum fidem et virtutes alias imitemur; salutem vero nostram in solius Dei gratia quae ramus per Iesum Christum, quem ille inter se et nos Mediatorem unicum constituit.
units.tr: In the second part she adds: "And blessed is the fruit of your womb." With these words she gives the reason why she called her blessed among women, as if she were saying: because you will bear that promised seed, in whom all nations must be blessed and all the promises concerning the salvation of the human race fulfilled. This explanation of the cause teaches that Mary had from Christ whatever excellence she had, and that she is called blessed and most blessed of all women for no other reason than that God by grace chose her for this, that she should become the mother of his Son, to be manifested in the flesh. For, as we have said elsewhere, all the saints have received from the fullness of Christ whatever they have. Those therefore act far too preposterously who, neglecting Christ, cling to Mary his mother or to other heavenly beings whom God did not appoint to be the authors of salvation or of his grace. Let us acknowledge God's grace in them, and confess that they were its instruments; let us also imitate their faith and their other virtues. But our salvation we should seek in the grace of God alone, which we obtain through Jesus Christ, whom he has constituted the one Mediator between himself and us.

units.la: Asseritur autem hoc Elizabeta dicto vera Iesu Christi humanitas. Quia enim fructus ventris Mariae dicitur a Spiritu sancto, qui per illam locutus est, ex Virgine matre carnem acceperit oportet. Consentiunt huic dicto veteres promissiones, in quibus semen mulieris et Abrahami, germe aut surculus ex trunco Isai enasciturus et Davidis filius vocatur. Quae omnia improprie dicerentur, nisi ille ex ipsa virginis substantia veram carnem et sanguinem assumpsisset. Neque ista temere toties inculcantur et repetuntur. Hic enim unum ex praecipuis nostrae fidei et salutis fundamentum latet. Nam quia verus homo ex Maria natus est Dei filius, vere etiam noster frater est, et ad nos pertinet eius iustitia et mortis meritum. Itaque et fidelem pro nobis Pontificem agere potuit, et certa nobis in illo salutis spes esse potest, quod regni caelestis cum ipso coheredes futuri simus. Procul ergo a cessant, qui hoc salutis nostrae fundamentum labefactant, dum Christo corpus aerium aut caeleste tribuunt, quod per Mariam, ceu canalem, in mundum venerit. A quorum delirijs non procul absunt, qui etsi illum ex Maria verum hominem assumpsisse fateantur, corpus tamen eius nunc tale fingunt, quod veri corporis proprietates depositurit, et a Deitate absorptum, adeoque totum caeleste factum sit, ut inter res creatas non amplius censeri debeat. Voluntistimi omnes maiestatis Christi propugnatores videri: at interim illum praecipua sua gloria spoliant, dum meritum eius extenuant, cuius virtus ex hoc potissimum dependet, quod nostram carnem assumere, et eandem in caelestem gloriam subuehere dignatus est, ut ipsi quoque nostris corporibus olim eiusdem consortes efficiamur.
units.tr: By Elizabeth's saying, the true humanity of Jesus Christ is also asserted. For since the fruit of Mary's womb is spoken of by the Holy Spirit, who spoke through her, he must have received flesh from the Virgin mother. The ancient promises agree with this saying, in which he is called the seed of the woman and of Abraham, the shoot or branch that is to spring from the stock of Jesse, and the son of David. All these things would be said improperly unless he had taken true flesh and blood from the very substance of the virgin. Nor are these things so often insisted upon and repeated without reason, for here lies hidden one of the chief foundations of our faith and salvation. For because the Son of God was born of Mary as a true man, he is also truly our brother, and his righteousness and the merit of his death belong to us. And so he could act as a faithful high priest on our behalf, and in him we can have a sure hope of salvation, that we shall be co-heirs with him of the heavenly kingdom. Far from the truth, therefore, are those who undermine this foundation of our salvation, while they ascribe to Christ an aerial or heavenly body which came into the world through Mary as through a channel. Not far from their delirium are those who, although they confess that he assumed a true man from Mary, nevertheless imagine his body to be of such a kind that it has laid aside the properties of a true body, and, swallowed up by the Deity, has become so wholly heavenly that it ought no longer to be counted among created things. They seem to be the most zealous defenders of Christ's majesty; yet in the meantime they strip him of his chief glory, while they diminish his merit, on which his power depends above all, in that he deigned to assume our flesh and to raise it to heavenly glory, so that we too may one day become partakers of the same with our bodies.

units.la: Tertia sui sermonis parte gratia Dei singulare, quam tunc experiebatur, Elizabeta celebrat, dicens: Et unde hoc mihi, ut veniat mater Domini mei ad me? Et ne hoc temere dici Mariae existimet, quid ipsi acciderit, narrat. Ecce enim (inquit) ut peruenit vox salutationis tuae ad aures meas, salijt foetus prae gaudio in utero meo. Quod rursus ad fidei Mariae confirmationem fecit, ut supra quoque diximus. At quod Elizabeta facit, hoc pijs et sanctis omnibus proprium atque commune est: quod nimirum de semetipsis admodum humiliter sentiunt, Dei autem beneficia magnifice extollunt, ut se praeter omne meritum ab illo tam benigne respici testentur. Exempla huius modestiae in Abrahamo et bamo & Dauide alibi ostendimus. Quibus adnumerari debet Petrus Apostolus, de quo infra Cap.5. dicetur, & Centurio ille, cuius fidem præ omnibus Israelitis Christus prædicat. Neque aliter ipsam quoq; Mariam affectam fuisse, in sequenti Sermone audiemus. Arguunt ista Pharisæorum cōsiden tiam, qui suorum operum meritis, quæ nulla sunt, superbi, se quouis honore dignos æstimant. Magni facit Eliz̄abeta Mariæ virginis, Christum adhuc in vtero gestantis, ad se aduentum atq; salutatio nem. At isti, quia se sibijpsis sufficere putant, ipsum quoq; Christum se & meritum suum ipsis offeren tem fastidiose nimis contemnunt, & Deum ipsis nihil non debere sibi persuadent.
units.tr: In the third part of her speech, Elizabeth praises the singular grace of God which she was then experiencing, saying: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Lest anyone think she has said this rashly of Mary, she goes on to tell what happened to herself: "For behold (she says), as soon as the voice of your greeting reached my ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy." She did this again to confirm Mary's faith, as we have also said above. What Elizabeth does is proper and common to all the godly and holy: they think very humbly of themselves, but extol God's benefits magnificently, and bear witness that, beyond all merit, he has regarded them so kindly. We have shown examples of this humility in Abraham and David elsewhere. To these must be added the Apostle Peter, of whom it will be said below in chapter 5, and that centurion whose faith Christ preferred to all the Israelites. And we shall hear in the following sermon that Mary herself was disposed in the same way. These things refute the self-confidence of the Pharisees, who, proud of works that are nothing, think themselves worthy of every honour. Elizabeth values highly the coming and the greeting to herself of the Virgin Mary, who was still carrying Christ in her womb. But those men, because they think they are sufficient for themselves, scorn with excessive disdain Christ himself offering himself and his merit to them, and persuade themselves that God owes them nothing.

units.la: Vt vero in præcedentibus verae incarnationi Christi testimonium tulit Elizabeta: sic in præsen tieiusdem veram & æternam Deitatem asserit. Nam Domini sui matrem vocat Mariā. At qua ratione fœtum in vtero adhuc delitescentem poterat Dominū suum dicere, nisi in illo aliquid homine maius agnouisset? Consentit ergo hoc dictum cum illo Dauidis: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, &c. Verè autem hic titulus Christo conuenit, cui omnis potestas data est in cælo & in terra. Proprie tamen credentium Dominus est, quos sui sanguinis pretio redemit, vt suum sint peculium. Ideo apud Isaiam clamat: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Et eodem Paulus respiciens in priori ad Corinth. scribit: Etiamsi multi sint, qui dicantur domini, nobis tamē vnus est Dominus, Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Quod veteres quoque patres obseruarunt, quando virginem Mariam Θεοτόκον, id est, Deiparam dixerunt. Etsi enim Deitas minimè ex illa nata sit, siue suam originem habuerit, verè tamen sic dicitur illa, quando eum pepe rit, qui cum Deus sit verus & æternus, ex ipsa tamen homine assumpsit, vt in eadem persona Deus & homo inseperabiliter vnirentur. Neminem ergo Iudæorum & Turcarum ludibria moueant, qui nos Deum colere aiunt, qui ex muliere natus sit: neminem quoque impurorum hominum blasphemiæ offendant, qui cum Dei filium ex Virgine natum audiunt, impura & fœda quædam animo concipi- unt. Nā vt reuera Deus æternus est Christus, ita verè ex Maria Virgine homo natus est, & nunc Deus & homo noster apud patrem Mediator est.
units.tr: Just as Elizabeth bore witness to the true incarnation of Christ in what has gone before, so in what is present she asserts his true and eternal Deity. For she calls Mary the mother of her Lord. But on what ground could she call the child still hidden in the womb her Lord, unless she recognised in him something greater than a man? So this saying agrees with that of David: "The Lord said to my Lord," etc. Indeed this title truly belongs to Christ, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth. Yet he is properly the Lord of believers, whom he redeemed with the price of his own blood, that they might be his own possession. Therefore in Isaiah he cries: "I am the Lord; this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." And Paul, looking back to this in his first letter to the Corinthians, writes: "Even though there are many who are called lords, yet for us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." The ancient Fathers also observed this when they called the Virgin Mary Theotokos [Θεοτόκον], that is, Mother of God. For although the Deity was not born of her, nor did it have its origin from her, she is truly so called, since she bore him who, being true and eternal God, nevertheless took his manhood from her, so that God and man are inseparably united in one person. Let no one, therefore, be moved by the mockeries of Jews and Turks, who say that we worship a God who was born of a woman; nor let anyone be offended by the blasphemies of impure men, who, when they hear that the Son of God was born of a Virgin, conceive in their minds some foul and filthy things. For just as Christ is truly the eternal God, so he was truly born a man of the Virgin Mary, and now our God and man is Mediator before the Father.

units.la: Sequitur postrema sermonis Elizabeta pars, qua causam felicitatis Mariæ exponens ait: Et beata quæ credidit, quia perficientur ea, quæ dicta sunt ei à Domino. Neq; dubium est, hoc illam ma gno serio dixisse, vtpote domestico exemplo edočtā, cùm maritū propter incredulitatē silentij pœna multatum esse videret. Ad fidem ergo omne hoc bonum refert, qua Maria oblata sibi promissionem amplexa fuerat. Quòd si quæras, quæ illa fides fuerit, patet ea ex angeli verbis. Promiserat ille, quòd Dei filium paritura esset, promissum illum humani generis redemptorem, & illius regnum descripse rat. Isti promissioni credidit Maria, & proinde de fide in Christū Elizabetæ verba debent intelligi. Ergo eadem fide Virgo mater beatitudinem assecuta est, qua Abrahamum olim iustificatum esse, Paulus ad Romanos docet. Obseruabis autem, quòd ibidem ex Abrahami exemplo doctrinā generā lem Apostolus colligens ait: Scriptum est non propter Abrahamum solum, quòd fides ei adiusti- tiam imputata fuerit, sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est vt imputetur, qui credimus in cum, qui excitauit Iesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis, &c. Quod non minus de Maria dici debet, cuius exemplo doctrina apostolica de iustificatione et beatificatione fidei validissimè cōfirmatur. Si enim illa, quæ inter omnes homines merito gradum supremū obtinet, non aliter quàm per fidem beata fa- ſta est, nimium confidentes & in Deum ipsum imperiosi sunt, qui sibiipsis nouam salutis cōsequenda rationem fingunt, & suorum operum meritis cœlos conscendere conantur. Habet præterea locus hic aliam quoq; doctrinam, Dei nimirum promissiones non nisi credentibus impleri. Est quidem Deus verax, neq; illius promissis nostra incredulitas siue diffidentia quicquam derogat. Sed vt fides orga- num est vnicum, quo promissiones eius nobis applicamus: ita incredulitas illas respuit, & nos indi- gnos facit, quibus Deus promissa præstet. Et quia ille ea conditione nobis sua bona pollicetur, vt nos illi morigeros & fideles præbeamus, nihil nobis in eius promissiones iuris est, si nos incredulos & ino bedientes præbeamus. Debet hoc applicari omnibus promissis, tam iis quæ ad salutem æternam spe- ctant, quàm quæ de bonis temporariis habentur. Vbiq; enim illud Christi ratū erit: Fiat tibi secundum fidem tuam. Quia ergo hodie fides in terris rara est, non mirū videri debet, pauciores esse, qui promis sionū Dei fructu fruantur. Itaq; procul exclusa diffidentia & omnibus carnis incredulæ rationibus, euangelium de Iesu Christo attentis animis audiamus, ipsum verò fide constanti ampleƈtamur, & in ipso beati erimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows the last part of Elizabeth's speech, in which, setting out the reason for Mary's happiness, she says: "And blessed is she who believed, for those things shall be accomplished which were spoken to her by the Lord." There is no doubt that she said this with great earnestness, since she had learned from a domestic example, seeing her husband punished with the penalty of silence for his unbelief. She therefore refers all this good to faith, by which Mary embraced the promise offered to her. But if you ask what that faith was, it is plain from the words of the angel. He had promised that she would bear the Son of God, the promised redeemer of the human race, and he had described his kingdom. Mary believed that promise, and so Elizabeth's words must be understood of faith in Christ. Therefore the Virgin Mother attained blessedness by the same faith by which Paul teaches in his letter to the Romans that Abraham was once justified. Note, however, that there the Apostle, drawing a general doctrine from Abraham's example, says: "It was written not for Abraham alone, that faith was imputed to him for righteousness, but also for us, to whom it is to be imputed, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead," etc. This must be said no less of Mary, by whose example the apostolic doctrine of justification and of the blessedness of faith is most strongly confirmed. For if she, who rightly holds the highest rank among all men, was made blessed in no other way than through faith, those are overconfident and presumptuous towards God himself who devise for themselves a new way of obtaining salvation and try to climb to heaven by the merits of their works. Moreover, this passage contains another teaching, namely that God's promises are fulfilled only for believers. God is indeed true, and our unbelief or distrust takes nothing from his promises. But just as faith is the one instrument by which we apply his promises to ourselves, so unbelief rejects them and makes us unworthy of receiving what God has promised. And since he offers us his good things on the condition that we show ourselves obedient and faithful to him, we have no right to his promises if we show ourselves unbelieving and disobedient. This must be applied to all promises, both those that concern eternal salvation and those that are held out concerning temporal goods. For everywhere that saying of Christ will hold good: "Let it be done to you according to your faith." Since faith is therefore rare on earth today, it ought not to seem strange that fewer enjoy the fruit of God's promises. Let us therefore, with distrust and all the reasonings of unbelieving flesh cast far away, hear the gospel of Jesus Christ with attentive minds, and embrace him with steadfast faith, and in him we shall be blessed. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XI.
units.tr: HOMILY XI.

units.la: Et ait Maria, Magnificat anima mea Dominum, & exultauit spiritus meus super Deo seruatore meo. Quia respexit ad humilitatem ancillae suae. Ecce enim ex hoc me beatam praedicabunt omnes generationes. Quia mihi fecit magnifica potens ille. Et sanctum est nomen eius, & misericordia eius in omnes progenies timentibus ipsum.
units.tr: And Mary said: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. For he that is mighty hath done to me great things, and holy is his name. And his mercy is on them that fear him from generation to generation."

units.la: O Vemadmodum Deus adiuuandum propensus est, & suam gratiam nobis sponte & liberaliter offert: ita ut nos ipsi gratos praebeamus postulat. Et sane cum gratitudinem nobis ipsa natura lex commendet, quae illius exempla in brutis quoq; animalibus praclara proponit: nulla venia digni fuerint, qui Deo ingrati sunt, cui nosipsos & omnia nostra debemus. Etsi vero gratitudo haec maxime in obedientia & praeceptorum Dei obseruatione consistat, simul tamen publica quoque acceptorum beneficiorum & gratiae Dei praedicatio exigitur: Ipsius enim praeceptum est: In die tribulationis tuae invocame, & liberabo te, & tu me glorificabis. Id autem Deo acceptius esse Dauid testatur, quam si quis iuuencum cornibus & unguliis praestantem ipsi offert. Nec enim (ut ipse ait) boum carnibus vescitur, neq; hircorum sanguinem bibit: delectatur autem laude & gratiarum actione, non quidem ut ambitiosi solent, quibus nulla Musica dulcior est, quam qua laudes suas decantari audiunt: sed quod per illam, si publice fiat, plures alij in ipsius cognitionem adducantur, & ad cultum eius verum excitentur: multi vero, qui in afflictione constituti sunt, illis auditis exhilarentur, & cum consolatione certam suae etiam salutis spem concipiant. Ideo hic mos inter pios & sanctos Dei cultores obseruatus est omnibus saeculis, ut singularia Dei beneficia carminibus & publica gratiarum actione celebrarint. Exempla vetustissima habemus in Mose & Aarone, qui Israelitican gentem ad hoc adsuefecerunt: quos postea imitata est Debora, cum eundem populum Deus ipsius opera ex hostium tyrannide vindicauisset. Priuatim vero hoc fecerunt Anna Samuelis mater, Jonas, Ezechias, & in primis Dauid, qui ut in grauioribus periculis nō aliud Domino vouit, quam cantica eucharistica: ita liberatus illa praestitit, & toti populo decantanda proposuit, ut suo exemplo quam plurimos erudiret. Imitatur hos in praesenti Maria Virgo, cum immensam & exemplo carentem Dei bonitatem experta esset. Audiuerat enim ex Angelo, se esse benedictam illam mulierem, ex qua Dei filium & unicum humanae salutis authorem hominem nasci oporteat. Didicerat item conceptionis & generationis huius modum fore nouum & cum primis gloriosum, ut nimirum illa sa virginitate conciperet & pareret. Iam vero per Elizabetam nouis promissionibus & signo memorabili confirmata & ab ipso Spiritu sancto beata dicta fuerat, eo quod Dei promissis fide habuisset. Sunt haec eiusmodi bona, quae ut captum humanum superant, ita cum publica omnium hominum salute coniuncta sunt, & proinde singularem gratitudinē merebantur. Quod ergo pro illis reprendit Domino Maria? Hoc unum, quod ex Spiritus sancti impulsu in Dei laudes erumpit & carmē profundit vere diuinum & magnificum: quo primum eam Dei benignitatem & misericordia commendat, quam ipsa experta erat: deinde eiusdem potentiam & iudicia non minus iusta quam seuera in genere praedicat: postremo omne hoc ad causam praesentem accommodat, & illic de redemptione populi Dei disserit, quam olim promissam nunc praeforibus adesse videbat. Voluit autem Spiritus sanctus carmen hoc, cuius ipse author fuit, à Luca scriptis mandari, quia generale & consolatiouis plenam doctrinam continet, qua praecipuae Dei virtutes illustrantur, Bonitas nimirum & misericordia, qua nos miseros & indignissimos mortales dignatur: Potentia item & iustitia, quibus in coercendis impijs & afferendis suis vtitur: & veritas, qua felicissime praestat, quaecunq; pollicetur. Quarum omnium consideratio diligens, ut homines in officio continet, ita fidei confirmandae in primis seruit. Est ergo carmen hoc dignissimum, cuius singulas partes ex ordine consideremus.
units.tr: Although God is ready to help us and offers his grace to us freely and generously, he nonetheless requires that we show ourselves thankful to him. Indeed, nature itself, which presents remarkable examples of this even among the brute animals, commends gratitude to us as a law. Those who are ungrateful to God, to whom we owe ourselves and all that we have, deserve no pardon. Yet although this gratitude consists chiefly in obedience and in keeping God's commandments, the public proclamation of the benefits we have received and of God's grace is also required. For it is his command: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me." David testifies that this pleases God more than if someone offered him a bullock with horns and hoofs. For, as he says, he does not feed on the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats. Rather, he delights in praise and thanksgiving. Not, indeed, in the way that ambitious men do, for whom no music is sweeter than hearing their own praises sung. Rather, it pleases him because, if it is done publicly, many others are led to know him and are stirred to his true worship. And many who are in affliction are cheered on hearing it and conceive with comfort a sure hope of their own salvation. For this reason, the custom has been kept among the pious and holy worshippers of God in every age, that they celebrated God's singular benefits with songs and public thanksgiving. We have the most ancient examples in Moses and Aaron, who accustomed the Israelite people to this. Deborah afterwards imitated them, when God had delivered the same people from the tyranny of their enemies by her work. Privately, Hannah the mother of Samuel did this, and Jonah, Hezekiah, and above all David. In greater dangers David vowed nothing to the Lord but songs of thanksgiving, and when he was delivered he rendered them, and he set them forth to be sung by the whole people, so that by his example he might instruct very many. Now the Virgin Mary imitates these in the present case, since she had experienced the immense goodness of God, which had no equal. For she had heard from the angel that she was the blessed woman from whom the Son of God and the only author of human salvation was to be born as a man. She had also learned that the manner of this conception and birth would be new and especially glorious, namely that she would conceive and bear while remaining a virgin. Moreover, through Elizabeth she had been confirmed by new promises and by a memorable sign, and she had been called blessed by the Holy Spirit himself, because she had believed God's promises. These are the sorts of blessings which, as they surpass human understanding, so they are bound up with the public salvation of all people, and therefore deserved singular gratitude. What then did Mary render to the Lord for them? This one thing: that by the impulse of the Holy Spirit she burst into praise of God and poured out a song truly divine and magnificent. In it she first commends that kindness and mercy of God which she herself had experienced. Next she proclaims in general his power and his judgments, no less just than severe. Lastly, she applies all this to the present cause, and there she speaks of the redemption of the people of God, which she now saw standing at the doors, having been promised long ago. The Holy Spirit, who was himself the author of this song, willed that it be written down by Luke, because it contains a general doctrine full of consolation, in which the chief virtues of God are set forth: his goodness and mercy, by which he deigns to regard us wretched and most unworthy mortals; his power and justice, which he uses in restraining the wicked and in bringing help to his own; and his truth, by which he most faithfully performs whatever he promises. Careful consideration of all these things both keeps people in their duty and serves above all to confirm faith. This song is therefore most worthy of attention, and we shall consider its individual parts in order.

units.la: Principio proponit rem omnem his verbis: Magnificat anima mea Dominum, & exultauit spiritus meus super Deo seruatore meo. Magnificandi verbo pro Hebraeorum more vtitur, quibus illud idem significat, quod celebrare aut laudibus eximijs atq; magnificis vehere. Animae autem & spiritus vocabulis omnes hominis facultates comprehendit, intellectum, rationem, voluntatem, quæcunq; alia ex his dependent. Itaq; sensus est: Quanta quanta sum, tota in Dei laudes effundar, & quicquid in me est virium cum corporis tum animi, illud omne impendam, vt Deus per me glorificetur: neq; id inuita aut coacta faciam, sed cum spiritus exultatione, qui totus mihi gestit ad hoc officium Deo præstandum. Conueniunt ergo ista cum Dauidis verbis, quibus ille interdum sese ad Dei laudes excitat: Paratum est cor meum ô Deus, paratum est cor meum, & psallam: Expergi- scere ô gloria mea, expergiscere nablum & cithara, &c. Item, Propterea canet tibi gloria mea, & non silebit. Vbi gloriæ nomine omne id intelligit, quod in se gloriosum & eximium habebat, & quod gloriæ Dei celebrandæ seruire poterat.
units.tr: At the beginning she sets forth the whole matter in these words: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." She uses the word "magnify" in the Hebrew manner, for which it means the same as to celebrate or to extol with exceptional and splendid praise. By the words "soul" and "spirit" she comprehends all the faculties of a person: understanding, reason, will, and whatever depends on these. The sense, then, is: "However great I am, I will pour myself out wholly in the praises of God, and whatever strength I have, of body as well as of mind, I will spend it all, that God may be glorified through me. Nor will I do this unwillingly or under compulsion, but with exultation of spirit, since my whole spirit longs to perform this duty to God." Thus her words agree with those of David, by which he sometimes rouses himself to the praises of God: "My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise. Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp," and so on. Likewise: "To the end that my glory may sing praise to thee, and not be silent." By the name of "glory" he understands everything that was in him glorious and excellent, and which could serve to celebrate the glory of God.

units.la: Obseruabis autē in Mariæ exemplo, quis effectus sit fidei, qua illa præditam fuisse, nuper audi- uimus. Nititur hæc vno Deo, & proinde huius gloriæ vnice studet, & hanc promotam cupit. Nam vt bonæ indolis filij de parentum gloria vehementer solliciti sunt, & ab ijs omnibus abhorrent, quæ parentibus dedecori fore nouerunt: ita qui per fidem Dei filij facti sunt, illius gloria nihil antiquius habent, & huic promouendæ se totos impendunt. Parit hoc studium publicam fidei confessione et cum gratiarum actione coniunctā gratia in Iesu Christo exhibitæ prædicatione. Cur enim illos Christi pu deat, in quo vitam & salutem suam omnem repositā esse nouerunt? Vel cur fidem suā dissimulent, qua sola Christus apprehenditur, qui nobis à Deo patre sapientia & iustitia factus est? Neq; verbi solum Dei gloriā prædicant, sed vitam quoq; omnē ita instituunt, vt propter ipsos Dei nomen apud alios quoq; glorificetur, qui nondum in plena eius cognitione peruenerunt. Potest hoc infinitis exemplis probari eorū, quorū fides & pietas in scripturis commendantur. Sunt ergo à fide alienissimi, quos nulla gloriæ Dei cura detinet, & qui ita viuunt, vt propter ipsos verè Dei cultus & tota religio Christiana male audiant, & ipsorū exemplo multi abterreantur, quo minus ad Christū accedant, quem licentiæ huius & proteruiæ authorem arbitrantur, quā in illis cernunt. Est horū infinitus numerus hodie inter eos, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, vt iam de illis nihil dicā, qui ineptissimis super stitionibus & publico idolorū cultu Christianum nomen Turcarum & Iudæorum ludibrijs exponunt.
units.tr: In Mary's example you will observe what effect faith has, the faith with which, as we have just heard, she was endowed. This faith rests on the one God alone, and therefore it strives for his glory alone and desires that this be advanced. For just as good children are anxious about the honour of their parents and shrink from all those things which they know would bring shame on their parents, so those who have become children of God through faith hold nothing more dear than his glory, and devote themselves wholly to advancing it. This zeal brings forth a public confession of faith, joined with thanksgiving, and the proclamation of the grace that has been shown in Jesus Christ. For why should they be ashamed of Christ, in whom they know all their life and all their salvation to be laid up? Or why should they conceal their faith, by which Christ alone is laid hold of, he who has been made to us by God the Father wisdom and righteousness? They not only proclaim the glory of God in words, but also so order their whole life that because of them the name of God is glorified among others too, who have not yet come to full knowledge of him. This can be proved by countless examples of those whose faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures. Those, then, are most alien to faith, whom no care for the glory of God holds back, and who so live that because of them the true worship of God and the whole Christian religion come under a bad report, and many are deterred by their example from coming to Christ, whom they take to be the author of that licence and wantonness which they see in them. Of these there is today an infinite number among those who profess the doctrine of the Gospel. I say nothing yet of those who, by the most absurd superstitions and by the public worship of idols, expose the Christian name to the mockery of the Turks and the Jews.

units.la: Admonemur item hoc loco, vt Deus laudari debeat: Nimirum non obiter, sed anima & spiritu. Quia enim ex illo habemus quicquid sumus, merito idē nos totos sibi vendicat, & proinde sacrilegij species erit, si quam nostri partem ab illius cultu & obsequio alienemus. Monet hoc ipse, cum in lege requirit, vt ipsum diligamus ex toto corde, & ex tota anima et omnibus viribus nostris. Nihil ergo ad verum Dei cultum faciunt, qui illi ore appropinquant, & eum labijs honorant, corde autē procul ab eo absunt. Erant tales olim inter Iudæos, quos per Isaiam Deus grauiter reprehendit: & horum similes sunt hodie, qui psalmos vel non intellectos, vel saltem non bene consideratos demurmurant, aut publicè decantant, & in cantu illo præcipuā cultus diuini partem collocant. Sunt hi potius profanatores nominis Dei, quando de illo nō honorificentius sentiunt, quàm quòd illū eiusmodi vlula tu placare posse putant. Adhæc cum ecclesia nimis scurriliter ludūt, dum populi aures inani verborū non intellectorum sono pascunt, imò fatigant potius, & eos inutiliter detinent in templis, quos sana verbi Dei doctrina ædificare debebant. Cæpit hoc vitiū Apostolorum temporibus, vt in Corinthijs est videre, quos linguarum peregrinarum ostentatione superbiuisse Paulus scribit: sed idem illos grauiter corripit, & cùm ipse linguarum dono præ multis alijs excelleret, malim tamen (inquit) quinq; verba loqui, quæ et ipse intelligam, et quibus alij informentur, quàm decem millia verborum linguis peregrinis profundere. At non eadem est hodie cleri papistici sententia, cuius potentia atq; tyrannis populi ignorantia potissimum fulcitur & confirmatur.
units.tr: We are also reminded here that God ought to be praised, and not carelessly but with soul and spirit. For since we have from him whatever we are, he rightly claims us wholly for himself. Therefore it would be a kind of sacrilege if we withheld any part of ourselves from his worship and service. He himself reminds us of this when in the law he requires that we love him with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with all our strength. Those therefore do nothing for the true worship of God who draw near to him with their mouth and honour him with their lips, while their heart is far from him. Such people there were of old among the Jews, whom God sharply rebuked through Isaiah. Like them are those today who mumble or publicly chant psalms that they do not understand, or at least have not properly considered, and who place the chief part of divine worship in that chanting. Such people are rather profaners of the name of God, since they think of him no more honourably than that he can be appeased by such empty noise. Moreover, they play the fool with the Church too much, while they feed the ears of the people with the empty sound of words they do not understand, or rather weary them, and keep them uselessly in the temples, when they ought to have been built up by the sound doctrine of God's Word. This fault began in the times of the Apostles, as can be seen among the Corinthians, whom Paul writes were made proud by showing off foreign tongues. But the same Paul sharply rebukes them, and although he himself excelled many others in the gift of tongues, he says: "I would rather speak five words that I may understand, that I may instruct others, than ten thousand words in foreign tongues." But the opinion of the Papist clergy today is not the same, and their power and tyranny rest mainly on, and are confirmed by, the ignorance of the people.

units.la: Est autem in Mariæ verbis inter alia maximè obseruatu dignū, quod ait: Exultauit spiritus meus super Deo seruatore meo. Est hæc causa prioris, quo se Deum magnificè celebraturā dixerat: in Deo seruato re suo. Nec enim id faciunt, nisi qui & illum suū seruatorē esse agnoscunt, & in illo salutis spem certā collo carunt, qua fit, vt in illo gestiant & exultent. Equidē mirabitur Mariæ dictū humana ratio, si hoc ab ea dici cogitet, quæ paupercula & non vno modo misera erat, quoad huius seculi conditionem. Sed quia fides animos altius euehit in eorū bonorum consideratione, quæ nobis in Deo repositā sunt, non mouentur huius mundi casibus & periculis fideles, quò minus tunc in Deo exultent & tripudient, quando omnia deploratissima videntur. Intelligunt enim crucē & aduersa adeò nihil derogare felicitati veræ, vt potius in his ferendis Christi Iesu socij efficiamur, & proinde artius quoq; cum Deo vniamur, in quo omnis nostra felicitas & beatitudo consistit. Itaq; vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit, ipsis etiâ afflictionibus gloriantur. Nam præter id quod modò diximus, videt in illis sibi materiam patientiæ propositam esse: quam qui præstant Deo, ij huius gratiam et bonitatem quotidie maiorem experiuntur: ex eo autem spem indies maiorem concipiunt, quæ illos minimè frustratur, cum dilectio nis Dei testem habeant locupletissimum, spiritû sanctum, qui certus & minimè fallax salutis arrha bo est. Vnde apparet, side nondum rectè præditos esse eos, qui ad primum aduersæ fortunæ assultum concidunt, & non solum eiulatu muliebri suam diffidentiam produnt, verumetiam Dei iudicia audacius accusant, dum eius rigore nimio, vel etiam negligentia quiritantur, quasi suos minus curet. Est autem hæc præclara fidei laus, quòd sola hoc nobis impetrat, vt inter media pericula & in medijs calamitatibus possimus in Deo exultare. Nesciunt huius virtute infelices huius mundi filij, & ideo in opibus, dignitatibus, sæderibus & sociorum potentia exultant, quando longius absunt pericula. Vt primum vero his propius vrgentur, & se neq; diuitijs, neq; honoribus, neq; amicorum & sociorum viri bus vmquam sentiunt, omni simul spe destituti succumbunt, & se omnibus modis miseros et infelices esse clamant: & quiæ vere, cum illo careant, qui vt solus seruator est, ita solus in periculis intrepidos & constantes reddit. Quanto autem omnibus his infeliciores sunt, qui in nequitia sua exultant, et tunc sibi beati videtur, quando ipsis impunè belluari, scortari, mœchari, ludere & quæuis alia pro suo arbitrio facere licet? Sunt hi ex potentum illorum numero, quos Dauid in malitia gloriari ait. Sed dissipantur ijdem in æternum, & abradit eos Dominus de tabernaculo suo, neq; illos radices agere sinit in terra vere viuentium. Discant ergo quicunq; sibi bene esse volunt, in vno Deo gloriari & exultare, qui cristitiam omnem in gaudium conuertere, & in medijs aduersis seruare potest.
units.tr: Among the words of Mary, the most noteworthy point is what she says: "My spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour." This is the reason for the earlier phrase, in which she had said she would magnify God as her Saviour. People do not rejoice in God unless they acknowledge him as their own Saviour and place their certain hope of salvation in him. Human reason will be astonished at Mary's words if it considers that she was poor and in many ways wretched, as far as the condition of this world goes. But faith lifts the mind higher, to consider the good things that are laid up for us in God. So believers are not moved by the misfortunes and dangers of this world to hold back from rejoicing and exulting in God, even when everything seems utterly hopeless. For they understand that the cross and adversity take so little from true happiness that, on the contrary, by bearing them we become companions of Christ Jesus and are joined more closely to God, in whom all our happiness and blessedness consists. Thus, as Paul writes to the Romans, they glory even in their afflictions. Besides what we have just said, they see that affliction sets before them a field for patience, and those who exercise patience towards God experience his grace and goodness growing greater every day. From this they conceive a greater hope day by day, which never disappoints them, since they have as their most abundant witness of God's love the Holy Spirit, who is a sure and never deceptive pledge of salvation. Hence it is clear that those are not rightly endowed with faith who collapse at the first assault of adverse fortune. They not only betray their distrust with womanish wailing, but also accuse God's judgments more boldly, complaining of his excessive severity or even his negligence, as if he cared little for them. This is the outstanding praise of faith, that it alone wins for us the ability to exult in God in the midst of dangers and calamities. The unhappy sons of this world do not know this virtue, and so they exult in riches, honours, alliances and the power of their allies, while the dangers are still far off. But as soon as these press closer, and they feel that riches, honours and the strength of friends and allies are of no help to them, they give way, stripped of all hope, and cry out that they are wretched and unhappy in every way. And rightly so, since they lack him who alone is Saviour, and who alone makes people fearless and steadfast in dangers. But how much more unhappy than all these are those who exult in their wickedness, and seem blessed to themselves when they are free to revel, whore, commit adultery, gamble and do whatever else they please with impunity? They belong to that number of the powerful whom David says glory in their malice. But these very men will be scattered for ever, and the Lord will pluck them from his tabernacle and will not let them take root in the land of the truly living. Let all who wish to be well off therefore learn to glory and exult in the one God, who can turn all sorrow into joy and preserve them in the midst of adversities.

units.la: Sed ad Mariam redeamus, quæ his præmissis primam suæ gratiarum actionis partem aggreditur, quæ diuinæ bonitatis & misericordiæ commendationem continet. Primò autem eam gratiam celebrat, quam ipsa in præsenti experiebatur, & ait: Quia respexit ad humilitatem ancillæ suæ. Quo loco ineptis & superstitiosis Mariæ cultoribus imposuit Humilitatis vox, qua illi virtutem illius commendari, & hanc ab ea quasi meritum quoddam adduci putauerunt, cuius causa Deus tantâ dignitatem illi contulerit. At in Græco nõ ταπεινωσις habetur, quæ animi humiliter de seipso sentientis modestiam significat, sed ταπεινωσις, qua humilis et vilis siue abiecta hominis alicuius conditio denotatur. Neq; tamen negamus Mariam vt reliquis virtutibus, sic etiâ animi modestia præclarè ornatâ fuisse, sed hac illam minimè gloriatam fuisse dicimus hoc loco, vbi Dei potius bonitatem, qua is sese ad nos vsq; demittit, quàm seipsam prædicare voluit. Itaq; verborum sensus est: Cùm pauperula essem & ab omnibus contemnerer, imò cum familiam meam Herodes crudeliter persequeretur, & nihil in me inueniretur quod aliquê splendorem præ se ferret, Deus me respexit: Deus (inquam) me vilem ancillam respexit, non ego illum suspexi: ille mei misertus est, non ego quicquam apud eum merui, &c.
units.tr: But let us return to Mary, who, having set these things before us, takes up the first part of her thanksgiving, which contains a commendation of divine goodness and mercy. First she celebrates the grace she was experiencing at that moment, and says: "Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid." Here the word "lowliness" has misled foolish and superstitious worshippers of Mary, who thought that her virtue was being commended, and that it was put forward as a kind of merit on account of which God had conferred such dignity upon her. But the Greek is not ταπεινοφροσύνη [tapeinophrosynē], which signifies the modesty of a mind that thinks humbly of itself; it is ταπείνωσις [tapeinōsis], by which the humble, lowly or abject condition of a person is denoted. Nor do we deny that Mary, like the other virtues, was also adorned with modesty of mind. But we say that she was by no means glorying in this here, where she wished rather to proclaim the goodness of God, by which he lowers himself even to us, than to proclaim herself. So the sense of the words is: "Although I was poor and despised by all, indeed when Herod was cruelly persecuting my family, and nothing could be found in me that showed any splendour, God regarded me. God, I say, regarded me, a worthless handmaid; I did not look up to him. He had mercy on me; I had deserved nothing from him, and so on."

units.la: Rursus autem admonemur, nos dum Dei beneficia celebramus, in primis quàm viles & indigni nos simus spectare debere. Nisi enim hoc fiat, facile efferimur, vt Deum ex nostris meritis illa nobis debere putemus, quò fit, vt nobis exitio sint, quæ ille in nos confert, & ex quibus eius bonitatem agnoscere debebamus. At si in nosipsos descendamus, et cum nostris factis primâ quoq; originem nostram consideremus, & quales ex matris vtero nascamur, quot item modis Dei iustissimi et sanctissimi in dictis oculos offenderimus: mox patebit, nobis omnia hæc ex gratia obtingere, & ita de nobis quidem ipsis humiliter sentiemus, Deo autem nos gratos præbebimus. Exempla, quæ hic adduci poterat, alibi commemorauimus, inter quæ primus locus merito Mariæ debetur: à cuius ingenio nimis alieni sunt, qui hodie sua merita apud Deum ostentant, & hunc sibi quasi debitorem faciunt.
units.tr: Again we are reminded that, when we celebrate God's benefits, we ought above all to consider how base and unworthy we are. For unless this is done, we are easily puffed up and think that God owes us these things because of our merits. The result is that what he bestows on us, which ought to show us his goodness, becomes our ruin. But if we descend into ourselves, and consider our origin from the very beginning, what kind of people we are born from the mother's womb, and how many ways we have offended the eyes of the most just and holy God by our words and deeds, it will soon become clear that all these things come to us from grace. Thus we shall indeed think humbly of ourselves, and shall make ourselves pleasing to God. We have mentioned elsewhere the examples that could be brought forward here, among which the first place is rightly owed to Mary. Those who today display their merits before God, and make him, as it were, their debtor, are very far removed from her disposition.

units.la: Id vero euidentius patebit in ijs, quæ sequuntur. Nam pergit Diua Virgo & ait: Ecce enim ex hoc me beatâ prædicabunt omnes generationes. Quasi diceret: Nunc quidem tu Elizabeta me benedictam inter mulieres pronuntiauisti, sed nõ tu sola sic de me iudicas. Fiet enim deinceps, vt quot quot in Christum ex me nasciturû crediderint, idem tecum sentiant, & me mulierum beatissimam prædicent. Qua vero de causa? aut quo meo merito? Num propter meâ virtutem? Non: sed quia mihi fecit magnifica potes ille: Deus nimirû, qui omnibus pro suo nutu & arbitrio imperat. Itaq; Maria felicitatis suæ causam non in ijs constituit, quæ ipsa fecerat hucusq;, sed quæ ipsi fecerat Deus. Etsi enim omni virtutum genere ornatissima fuerit, nihil tamen ex seipsa habuit, quod nõ diuinitus acceperit: et ideo nullũ suum meritũ potuit aut voluit allegare. Quæ autem erant illa, quæ ipsi fecerat Deus? Respexerat humilem & afflictam. Deinde ad hoc illam destinarat, ut filij sui æterni in carne mani festandi mater fieret, & salvo virginitatis flore pareret promissum humani generis redemptorem. Adhæc fide eam donarat, qua promissiones omni captu humani ingenij ampliores posset amplecti. Hæc vere magnifica sunt, & omnem huius mundi dignitatem atq; felicitatem superant. Prædicatur in Romana historia Q. Metellus, ut qui mortalium felicissimus fuerit. Quas vero ob causas? Quod in urbe terrarum principe natus sit: quod parentes habuerit nobilissimos: quod animi dotibus & corporis viribus instructus laboribus sufficere potuerit: quod uxor illi obtigerit pudicitia simul & fæcunditate celebris: quod consulatum et imperatoriam potestatem cum laude gesserit: quod rem pub. & domum propria triumphis speciosissimis ornarit: quod eodem tempore tres filios consulares, unum etiam censorium, duos triumphales, & quartu prætorium videri: quod tres filias nuptui dederit, earumq; sobole suo sinu excepit: quodq; tandem ultimæ senectutis spatio defunctum, & leni genere mortis inter oscula atq; complexus charissimorum pignorum extinctum filij & generi suis humeris per urbem latum rogo impositum. Sunt hæc sane magna & rara, quæ in huius vitæ curricu lo paucis obtingere constat, ut non singula infinitis curis & aduersis casibus interdum turbentur.
units.tr: This will be seen more clearly in what follows. For the blessed Virgin goes on and says: "For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed." As if she were saying: "Now indeed you, Elizabeth, have pronounced me blessed among women, but you are not the only one to judge me so. For it will come about that all who believe in Christ to be born of me will think as you do and will proclaim me the most blessed of women." But for what cause? And by what merit of mine? Is it because of my virtue? No, but because he who commands all things at his nod and pleasure, God himself, has done great things for me. So Mary placed the cause of her happiness not in what she herself had done up to that time, but in what God had done for her. For although she was adorned with every kind of virtue, she had nothing of herself that she had not received from God, and therefore she could allege no merit of her own, nor did she wish to. But what were the things that God had done for her? He had regarded her lowliness and affliction. Then he had destined her for this, that she should become the mother of his eternal Son, who was to be made manifest in the flesh, and that, her virginal bloom preserved, she should bear the promised Redeemer of the human race. Besides, he had endowed her with a faith by which she could embrace promises greater than any human understanding can grasp. These are truly magnificent things, and they surpass all the dignity and happiness of this world. In Roman history Q. Metellus is praised as the most fortunate of mortals. For what reasons?
