Because he was born in the city, the prince of all the lands; because he had most noble parents; because, endowed with gifts of mind and strength of body, he was able to endure labours; because he gained a wife renowned both for chastity and fruitfulness; because he held the consulship and imperial power with praise; because he adorned the state and his own house with most splendid triumphs; because at the same time he saw three sons who were consuls, one also censor, two triumphers, and a fourth praetor; because he gave three daughters in marriage and received their offspring into his bosom; and finally because, having died at the end of extreme old age, by a gentle kind of death, amid the kisses and embraces of his dearest children, he was carried through the city on the shoulders of his sons and sons-in-law and placed on the pyre. These are indeed great and rare things, which, as is well known, few obtain in the course of this life. Yet not one of them is free from being disturbed, at times, by countless cares and adverse chances.

units.la: Attamen omnia hæc temporaria, caduca & vana sunt, neq; aliquid faciunt ad veram felicitatem, quæ ex gratuito Dei fauore dependet, et nec ipsa morte finitur, sed continuatur potius, ut æternum duret. Recte ergo Maria felicitatis suæ causam in gratuitis Dei beneficijs constituit, quæ cum ipsius simul & totius generis humani salute coniuncta fuerunt. Nimium vero inepte (ut ne quid gravius dicam) faciunt superstitiosi eius cultores, qui novis titulis & dignitatibus ita illam ornare & extol lere satagunt, ut quæ Deus in illam vere magnifica & eximia contulit, quodammodo obruant, ne a quoquam digne consideren-tur. Vocant illam portam cæli, spem salutis, reginā cæli, stellam maris, vitam, dulcedinem, & infinita alia congerunt, quæ non minus impie quàm ridicule de illa prædican-tur. Neq; contenti sunt Christi honorem in illam translulisse, dum eam nobis aduocatam faciunt, insuper ei in illum ius & imperium tribuunt, & quod per vbera ab illa rogatus petenti nihil denegare possit. Sunt hæc aliena a scripturis, & ipsius Mariæ testimonio confutantur: neq; maiorem illi iniuriam facere poterant, quàm quod ex ea idolum fingunt, quam in eam dignitatem Deus euexit, ut Christum nobis pareret, cuius solius merito nos ipsi reconciliaremur. Ergo omissis istorum delirijs, ad Mariæ verba redeamus, in quibus hoc etiam non oscitanter considerari debet, quod Dei bonitatem prædicatura, potentiæ quoq; illius meminit. Na fecit, mihi (inquit) magnifica potens ille. Equidem necesse est, ut in Dei bonitate simul eiusdem potentiam quoq; spectemus. Ita enim promissionibus eius credemus, etiamsi hæ nostri ingenij captum vincant, & insuper in fide confirmabimur, certi quòd in posterum quoq; suum fauorem continuare, & omnibus aduersis superiores facere possit.
units.tr: Yet all these things are temporary, perishable and vain. They contribute nothing to true happiness, which depends on God's free favour and is not ended even by death but continues, so that it lasts forever. Rightly, therefore, Mary placed the cause of her happiness in God's free benefits, which were joined with her own salvation and that of the whole human race. Truly foolish (to say nothing harsher) are her superstitious worshippers, who strive with new titles and dignities to adorn and extol her so that they bury under them the magnificent and remarkable things God really conferred on her, and no one can consider them worthily. They call her the gate of heaven, the hope of salvation, the queen of heaven, the star of the sea, life, sweetness, and heap up countless other titles, which are preached about her no less impiously than ridiculously. Nor are they content to have transferred Christ's honour to her, while they make her our advocate; they also give her power and rule over him, so that he cannot refuse anything asked of him through her breasts. These things are alien to the Scriptures and are refuted by Mary's own testimony. They could do her no greater injury than by fashioning from her an idol, when God raised her to that dignity so that she might bear Christ for us, by whose merit alone we are ourselves reconciled. Therefore, leaving aside the delusions of these people, let us return to Mary's words, in which this too must be carefully considered: in proclaiming God's goodness she also remembers his power. For, she says, the Mighty One has done great things for me. Indeed, we must in God's goodness also regard his power at the same time. For thus we shall believe his promises, even if they exceed the grasp of our understanding, and we shall be confirmed in faith, certain that he can continue his favour in the future too and make us superior to all adversities.

units.la: Cæterum ut quod de se dixit Maria, communi omnium institutioni seruiat, hoc ipsa in genere ad omnes extendit. Summa vero omnium, quæ de Deo dici possunt præmittit, sub exclamationis specie dicens: Et sanctum est nomen eius. Vbi obseruabis, Deum nullum habere nomen proprium, ut res creatæ, quæ suis nominibus definiuntur. Quia enim ille immensus & infinitus est, nullum quoq; nomen potest fingi aut inueniri, quod eius naturam atq; essentiam comprehendat. Ideo Iacobo nomen eius quæ-renti dicebat: Cur interrogas de nomine meo? Et Mosi eandē quæstionem mouenti respondit: Sum qui sum. Dicitur ergo Dei nomē quicquid de illo prædicatur, et quo se nobis cognoscendū ille præbet. Itaq; huc pertinet eius attributa omnia, sapientia nimirum, bonitas, misericordia, iustitia, veritas, omnipotentia, & quæcunq; alia sunt huius generis. Sunt hæc omnia per se sancta, id est, veneratione digna & adoranda: adeò ut nihil in illo accusari debeat, etiamsi quæ de illo dicuntur, & quæ facit, non statim rationi interdum minus æqua aut tolerabilia videantur. Quod ut vbique alias, sic maxime in Christi Iesu negotio obseruari debet. In hoc enim virtutes suas omnes Deus nobis ceu in speculo spe-ctandas proposuit, & eidē postea nomen dedit, quod (ut Paulus ait) est supra omne nomē, & in quo omnia genua cum cœlestium, tum terrestrium et eorum qui apud inferos sunt, flecti coeunt. Istud autem Epiphonema hic interseri necesse fuit. Ita enim Diva virgo primùm multis quæstionibus occurrit: Cur filij sui aduentu hucusq; Deus distulerit? Cur ad negotiū hoc puellam delegerit vilem et nullius inter homines authoritatis? Cur filij sui conceptione non aliquo publico miraculo omnibus commen-dauit? &c. Sufficit enim ad hæc omnia respondisse: Sanctū est nomen eius, & nō falli potest Dei sapientia,neq; aliquid praeter aequū & ratione agit, cuius iudicia sunt iustitia & veritas: tu vero quis es, qui ab illo factorum rationem exigas? Deinde superstitioni mederi voluit hoc dicto spiritus sanctus, quam circa Mariae cultum exorituram esse praevidebat. Cum enim Maria in media eorum commemoratione, quae sibi eximia contigerant, ad hunc modum exclamat, simul non obscure omnes homines abs se ad unius veri Dei cultum remittit, neq; vult, ut in ipsa haereamus, aut penes ipsam quaeramus quae apud unum Deum inveniri possunt. Est hoc proprium sanctis omnibus, sicuti Apostolorum, Ioannis & Petri, Pauli item & Barnabae exempla testantur. Angeli quoq; sese adorari non sinunt, sed hominum piorum conservos esse profitentur, ut omnem superstitiosi cultus occasionem nobis praeripiant. Est hoc probe observandum, ut quoties nobis Divorum virtutes homines superstitiosi commendant in eum finem, ut illos invocemus, parata nobis sit responsio: Domini Dei nomen sanctum est, & is solus dignus est, quem omnes colant & invocent.
units.tr: Moreover, so that what Mary said of herself may serve the common instruction of all, she extends it to everyone in general. She first sets out the sum of all that can be said of God, in the form of an exclamation: And holy is his name. Here you will observe that God has no proper name, as created things are defined by their names. For since he is immense and infinite, no name can be devised or found that comprehends his nature and essence. Hence he said to Jacob, who asked for his name, "Why do you ask about my name?", and to Moses, who raised the same question, "I am who I am." Therefore whatever is predicated of God, and whereby he makes himself known to us, is called God's name. To this belong all his attributes: wisdom, goodness, mercy, justice, truth, omnipotence, and whatever else is of this kind. All of these are holy in themselves, that is, worthy of reverence and adoration, so that nothing in him should be blamed, even if what is said of him and what he does does not at once seem reasonable or tolerable. This must be observed everywhere, but most of all in the business of Jesus Christ. For in him God set forth all his virtues for us to behold as in a mirror, and then gave him the name which (as Paul says) is above every name, and at which every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth. But it was necessary to insert this exclamation here. For the Divine Virgin first meets many questions: Why has God delayed until now the coming of his Son? Why did he choose for this task a lowly girl of no authority among men? Why did he not commend the conception of his Son to everyone by some public miracle? And so on. It is enough to answer all these by saying: Holy is his name. God's wisdom cannot be deceived, nor does he act beyond equity and reason, whose judgments are justice and truth. But who are you, that you should demand from him an account of his deeds? Then the Holy Spirit wished by this saying to remedy the superstition which he foresaw would arise around the worship of Mary. For when Mary, in the midst of recounting the remarkable things that had happened to her, exclaims in this way, at the same time she not obscurely refers all men away from herself to the worship of the one true God. She does not want us to cling to her or seek from her what is to be found with the one God alone. This is characteristic of all the saints, as the examples of the Apostles, of John and Peter, and likewise of Paul and Barnabas, attest. Angels too do not allow themselves to be adored, but profess themselves fellow-servants of pious men, so that they may snatch away from us every occasion of superstitious worship. This must be carefully observed: whenever superstitious men commend the virtues of the saints to us in order that we invoke them, let our ready answer be: The name of the Lord God is holy, and he alone is worthy to be worshipped and invoked by all.

units.la: At generali huic doctrinae peculiare divinae bonitatis commendationem subijcit Maria, addens: Et misericordia eius in omnes progenies timentibus ipsum. Id vero non ex suo cerebro fingit, sed in foedere Deum suam fidem et bonitate non soli Abrahamo, sed eius etiam feminis obstrinxisse sciebat. Et nota est omnibus eiusdem promissio, quae in lege habetur, qua se misericordiam facere ait in millia his, qui ipsum diligunt, & praecepta eius observant. Oportuit autem istud hic adiici, ne quis gratiae Dei cursum in Maria substitisse, aut eius fontem tanta in hanc liberalitate exhaustum esse putaret. Etenim probe tenendum est hoc nostrae fidei & verae consolationis principium, quod Scripturae passim tradunt, & quod David nunquam non in Psalmis repetit & inculcat, Misericordiam Domini manere in aeternum, & in omnibus operibus eius eminere supra alias ipsius virtutes. Testatur hoc continuus historiae totius mundi cursus, iam inde a prima origine. Etsi enim patribus, qui diluvium praecesserunt, suam gratiam liberaliter contulerit Deus, non obstitit tamen hoc, quo minus posteris quoq; benefecerit. Imo in medijs scelerum poenis misericordiae suae recordari solet, quae poenas sic temperat, ut ad salutem fere nobis cedant, quae prius exitio fore videbantur. Vicit tamen omnia alia divinae misericordiae opera beneficium, quod in Christo Iesu accepimus. In hoc enim nos priusquam essemus elegit ab aeterno. Eundem praefinito tempore in mundum misit, ut humani generis redemptor esset. Idem toto illo tempore, quo in terris vixit, in miseros mortales beneficetiam omnem exercuit, in docendo & consolando diligens, in miraculis assiduus, quae omnia non ad ostentationem sed ad hominum utilitatem instituta fuerunt. Attamen quasi nihil fecisset unquam, ipse sollicite quaesivit quibus benefaceret, & quasi vinis expansis omnes laborantes atque oneratos ad se invitavit. Denique hostium quoq; miserius, eorum infelicitatem & quod illis imminere sciebat excidium lachrymis minime fictis prosecutus est. Et quod olim fecit, hoc ipsum etiam hodie illum facere videmus, dum per Evangelium quotidie nos ad se vocat, & non quaerentibus salutem benigne offert. Tantus autem est benefi-centiae ipsius fons, ut quemadmodum meriti eius virtus ad primos usq; parentes extenditur (quo nomine agnus dicitur immolatus ab origine mundi) ita in consummatione seculi usq; duret, & omnibus seruandis sufficiat, qui ad ipsum accedunt. Arguunt haec illorum stultitiam, qui cum fonte misericordiae sibi in Christo apertum esse videant, hoc tamen relicto cisternas fodiunt, & circa Dios occupantur, qui gratiam quidem Dei singularem experti sunt, non autem eam ab illo potestatem acceperunt, ut eandem ad nos deriuare possint. Diligenter ergo hoc Virginis Deiparae dictum observuent afflictae conscientiae, quibus hac potissimum ratione Deus consulere voluit, quod in Christo misericordiam illis suam liberaliter offert, ne incertis ambagibus defatigentur.
units.tr: But to this general doctrine Mary adds a particular commendation of divine goodness, saying: And his mercy is on those who fear him from generation to generation. She does not make this up from her own head; she knew that God had bound himself by covenant, with his faithfulness and goodness, not only to Abraham but also to his descendants. The promise is well known to everyone and is found in the law, where he says that he shows mercy to thousands of those who love him and keep his commandments. It was necessary to add this here, lest anyone think that the course of God's grace had stopped in Mary, or that its fountain had been exhausted by so great a generosity towards her. For we must firmly hold this principle of our faith and of true consolation, which the Scriptures teach everywhere and which David never ceases to repeat and impress in the Psalms: that the mercy of the Lord endures forever, and that it stands out above his other virtues in all his works. The continuous course of the whole history of the world, from its very beginning, bears witness to this. For although God freely bestowed his grace on the fathers who preceded the flood, this did not prevent him from doing good to their posterity as well. Indeed, in the midst of punishments for crimes he is accustomed to remember his mercy, which tempers the punishments so that they mostly turn out for our salvation, things which previously seemed destined for our ruin. Yet the benefit we have received in Christ Jesus surpasses all the other works of divine mercy. For in him he chose us from eternity, before we existed. At the appointed time he sent the same Son into the world, to be the redeemer of mankind. Throughout the whole time he lived on earth, he showed every kindness to wretched mortals, diligent in teaching and comforting, constant in miracles, all of which were performed not for display but for the benefit of men. Yet as if he had never done anything, he himself eagerly sought out those he might benefit, and, as if with arms outstretched, invited all who labour and are burdened to come to him. Finally, he lamented even his enemies with tears that were in no way feigned, grieving over their unhappiness and the destruction he knew hung over them. What he did of old, we see him doing today too, while through the Gospel he calls us to himself every day and kindly offers salvation to those who do not seek it. So great is the fount of his beneficence that, just as the power of his merit extends back to the first parents (for which reason the Lamb is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world), so it lasts until the end of the age and suffices for saving all who come to him. These things show the folly of those who, seeing that the fountain of mercy has been opened to them in Christ, nevertheless leave it and dig cisterns, busying themselves with broken ones. They have indeed experienced God's singular grace, but have not received from him the power to pass it on to us. Let afflicted consciences therefore diligently observe this saying of the Virgin Mother of God, by which God chiefly wished to provide for them: he freely offers them his mercy in Christ, so that they may not be wearied by uncertain detours.

units.la: Probe autem tenere oportet, quibus misericordiae huius fructus destinatus atq; paratus sit: Nimirum ijs, qui ipsum timent. Comprehenditur autem sub timore Dei omnis pietas atq; religio. Vbi ante omnia Dei cognitione opus est. Parit haec fidem, ex qua timor atq; obedientia nascitur. Turpis ergo & perniciosus illorum error est, qui Dei misericordia freti in sceleribus pergunt, et ita sibi ipsis thesaurum irae colligunt, neq; cogitant (ut Paulus inquit) Deum sua illa lenitate ad poenitentiam invitare. Calumniantur quidem aduersarij nostri, nos doctrina gratiae & misericordiae Dei hominibus securitatis & licentiae scelerum authores esse: sed ignorant illi, aut saltem ignorare volunt, huius doctrinae usum, & notior est pijs omnibus innocentia nostra, quam ut multa excusatione opus sit. Nos itaque observemus, contineri hoc dicto veram felicitatis consequendae rationem. Pendet haec tota ex eo, ut Deum nobis propitium habeamus, qui unicus omnis boni fons est. Id vero tunc fiet, si illum timeamus, & timorem hunc sancto atq; assiduo obedientiae studio testemur. In hoc ergo publice sint omnes, quando fame, peste, bello aut aliis calamitatibus vexantur. Priuatim quoq; de hoc serio cogitent, qui rem domesticam sibi saluam esse cupiunt. At quae nostri seculi est perversitas, hanc viam pauci ingrediuntur, plerique vero ad media illicita recurrunt, & scelera scelerius accumulant. Quae causa est, quod continuis plagis nos percutit Deus, & quod omnia ea nos indesinenter fatigant, quae nouissimi seculi hominibus olim Dominus comminatus est. Vt tamen ista habeant debent ex hoc etiam loco consolationem petere pij. Etsi enim in illos totus mundus conspiuret, & circum quaq; tyranni saeuiant, Dei tamen misericordia in aeternum durat timentibus ipsum, & idem vindicem habent fidelissimum Iesum Christium, cuius promissio est: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; in consummationem seculi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: It is important to hold firmly to whom the fruit of this mercy is destined and prepared: namely, to those who fear Him. Under the fear of God is comprehended all piety and religion, and for this, above all, the knowledge of God is needed. This knowledge produces faith, from which fear and obedience are born. Therefore the error of those is shameful and deadly who, relying on the mercy of God, persist in their wickedness, and so heap up for themselves a treasure of wrath, and do not consider (as Paul says) that God by His very gentleness invites them to repentance. Our adversaries indeed slander us, claiming that we, by the teaching of grace and the mercy of God, are the authors of security and licence for sins; but they do not know, or at least do not want to know, the use of this doctrine, and our innocence is too well known to all the godly to need much excuse. Let us therefore observe that this saying contains the true way of attaining happiness. All of this depends on our having God propitious to us, who alone is the fountain of every good. This will indeed happen if we fear Him, and bear witness to this fear by a holy and constant zeal for obedience. Let all therefore be earnest about this in public, whenever they are afflicted by famine, plague, war or other calamities; and let those who wish their household to be safe think seriously about it in private as well. But such is the perversity of our age that few walk this way, while most have recourse to unlawful means and pile up wickedness upon wickedness. This is the reason why God strikes us with continual plagues, and why all those things which the Lord long ago threatened to the people of the last age now wear us down without ceasing. Yet the godly ought to draw consolation from this passage even so. For although the whole world conspire against them and tyrants rage on every side, the mercy of God endures for ever toward those who fear Him, and they have as their most faithful defender Jesus Christ, whose promise is: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XII.
units.tr: HOMILY XII.

units.la: Fecit potentiam in brachio suo: dissipauit superbos cogitatione cordis ipsorum. Detraxit potentes e thronis, & extulit humiles. Famelicos impleuit bonis, & divites ablegauit inanes. Suscepit Israel puerum suum, vt memor esset misericordiae: (prout locutus est patribus nostris, Abrahamo & semini eius) in aeternum. Mansit autem Maria cum illa quasi menses tres, & inde reuertit domum suam.
units.tr: He hath shewed strength with his arm: he hath scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart. He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he hath sent empty away. He hath received Israel his servant, being mindful of his mercy (as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed) for ever. And Mary abode with her about three months, and then returned to her own house.

units.la: Etsi homines Deo, summo & aeterno bono, quiq; nullius rei indigus est, pro infinitis, quae in nos quotidie confert, beneficijs dignam gratiam referre nullo modo possint: vult tamen ille, vt ea grata animis agnoscamus, & laudes ipsius publice praedicemus, vt plures alij nostro exemplo illum agnoscere & eidem confidere discant. Fecerunt hoc diligenter omnes ij, quorum fides & pietas in scripturis commendatur: & hoc ipsum Maria quoq; facit, quae ex singulari gratia Deus rebus maximis & ad communem humani generis salutem pertinentibus destinauerat. Pro ijs vero omnibus non aliud, quam Canticum reppendit, quo omnia complectitur, quae nos in veri Dei cognitionem indu cere, inq; eius fide confirmare possunt. Nam primo, quam ipsa experta erat, Dei bonitatem praedicat, simulq; hanc omnibus, qui illum timent, paratam esse docet. Ab hoc autem orditur, vt suo exemplo doceat, omnium beneficiorum Dei causam ad solam eius gratiam atq; misericordiam debere referri, cum nihil in nobis sit, quo aliquid apud illum mereamur. Deinde potentiam Dei celebrat, et ita quidem, vt hanc ostendat cum iustitia coniunctam esse, quae in coercendis impijs, & suis seruandis vtatur. Tandem vero hoc omne ad praesentem causam incarnationis filij Dei accommodat. Et de prima quidem Cantici huius parte nuper dictum est, nunc ergo duas alteras videamus.
units.tr: Although men can never repay in any way the grace that is due to God, the highest and eternal good, who has need of nothing, for the infinite benefits he bestows on us every day, yet he wills that we acknowledge them with grateful hearts and proclaim his praises publicly, so that many others, by our example, may learn to acknowledge him and to trust in him. All those whose faith and piety are commended in Scripture have done this diligently, and Mary too does it, since God, by his singular grace, had destined her for the greatest things, which pertain to the common salvation of mankind. For all these blessings she has returned nothing but this Canticle, in which she embraces everything that can lead us to the knowledge of the true God and confirm us in faith in him. For first she proclaims the goodness of God, which she herself had experienced, and at the same time teaches that this goodness is ready for all who fear him. She begins with this so that by her own example she may teach that the cause of all God's benefits must be referred to his grace and mercy alone, since there is nothing in us by which we may merit anything before him. Then she celebrates the power of God, and in such a way that she shows it is joined with justice, which uses its power to restrain the wicked and to preserve its own. Finally, she applies all this to the present matter, the incarnation of the Son of God. We have already spoken briefly of the first part of this Canticle; now let us look at the other two parts.

units.la: Secunda (vt diximus) de potentia Dei inuicta agit, quam initio in genere proponit, dicens: Fecit potentiam (id est, potenter operatus est) in brachio suo. Brachium autem Deo tribuit, non quod is membris humanis constet (spiritus enim est omnia complens & penetrans) sed vt ostendat illum propria virtute omnia facere, neq; auxilio alieno opus habere. Itaq; locutio est ei similis, quae Isaias cap. 59. vtitur: videt Dominus, & displicet in oculis eius, quod non est iudicium: videt (inquam) quod non sit quisquam, & obstupescit quod nemo intercedit, & salutem operabitur ei brachium suum. Quasi diceret: Etsi nemo sit, qui rebus afflictis opem ferat, non tamen ideo salus omnis desperata est: quia Deus ipsi sibi sufficit, & proprijs (quod aiunt) manibus salutem afferre poterit. Sunt igitur istae locutiones plenae consolationis, & docent, non desperandum nobis esse, etiamsi nullum in humanis auxilium appareat. Non obstat enim hoc, quo minus suum brachium exerat Deus, & eos iuuet, qui ab omnibus derelicti sunt. Imo vt olim Philo Iudaeus socijs ob Cai Caesaris minas consternatis dicebat, necesse est adesse diuinum, vbi humanum cessat auxilium. Quod vt in omni alio casu obseruari debet, ita maxime locum habet in aeternae salutis negotio. Illic vero brachium aut manus Dei dicitur aeternum illud verbum, per quod omnia creata sunt, & cuius virtute omnia gubernantur: Filius nimirum Dei, qui homo factus in mundum venit, & propria virtute atq; merito
units.tr: The second part (as we said) deals with the invincible power of God, which she first sets out in general, saying: He hath shewed strength (that is, he has acted powerfully) with his arm. She ascribes an arm to God not because he consists of human members (for he is spirit, filling and penetrating all things), but to show that he does all things by his own power and has no need of another's help. So the expression is like that which Isaiah uses in chapter 59: The Lord saw, and it displeased him that there was no judgment; he saw (I say) that there was no man, and he wondered that there was none to intercede; and his arm shall bring salvation to him. As if he said: Even if there is no one who brings help to afflicted things, salvation is not therefore utterly despaired of, for God is sufficient for himself and can bring salvation, as they say, with his own hands. These expressions, then, are full of consolation, and they teach us that we must not despair even when no human help appears. For this does not prevent God from stretching out his arm and helping those who have been abandoned by all. Indeed, as the Jew Philo once said to his companions, dismayed by the threats of Gaius Caesar, where human help fails, divine help must be present. This should be observed in every other case, and it holds especially in the business of eternal salvation. Here, however, the arm or hand of God is that eternal Word through which all things were created and by whose power all things are governed: namely the Son of God, who came into the world made man, and by his own power and merit

units.la: Potentia Dei celebratur. salutem humani generis operatus est, dum nemine alio ipsum adiuuante peccatum omne sustulit, mortem deuicit, inferorum portas effregit, & diaboli regnum euertit. In hoc igitur nobis uniuersa salutis spes collocata esse debet, ne dum alia adminicula quaerimus, illius potentiam in dubium vocemus.
units.tr: The power of God is celebrated: he has worked the salvation of the human race, for with no one else helping him he has taken away all sin, conquered death, broken open the gates of hell, and overthrown the kingdom of the devil. In him, therefore, our whole hope of salvation must be placed, lest while we seek other supports we call into question his power.

units.la: Caeterum quia Dei virtutem non semper agnoscunt homines, & quamuis eam in genere fatean tur, non tamen illi in quouis casu confidunt, illam Maria operum aliquot commemoratione illustrat, ut his obseruatis in eius fide confirmentur. Inter haec primum his verbis comprehendit: Dissipauit superbos cogitatione cordis ipsorum. Eos autem intelligit, qui confidenter nimis quiduis se effectu ros putant, et nihil non sibi ipsis de suis viribus atque industria pollicentur. Ab his vero oritur, ut ostendat tantam esse Dei potentiam, ut nihil aduersus illum proficere possint, quicunque aduersus illum suas cogitationes atq; consilia conferunt. Sunt hi revera gigantes illi, quos poetae montes coacervasse & Pelion Ossae impositae fabulantur, ut Iouem e coelo deiicerent. Nam ad eundem modum hi quoque consilia sua et vires congerunt, potentissimos quosq; in foedus & societatem attrahunt, ut quod semel instituerunt, etiam inuito Deo conficiant, adeoque hunc ipsum in ordinem redigant.
units.tr: Moreover, since men do not always acknowledge God's power, and although they confess it in general, do not trust in it in every case, Mary illustrates it by recalling several of his works, so that by observing these we may be confirmed in faith. Among these she first comprises in these words: He has scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart. By this she means those who presume too confidently that they will achieve anything whatever, and promise themselves everything from their own strength and industry. From these she goes on to show that God's power is so great that nothing can prevail against him, however much men pile up their thoughts and plans against him. These are truly those giants whom the poets fable heaped up mountains, placing Pelion on Ossa, to hurl Jupiter from heaven. For in the same way these men also pile up their counsels and strength, draw the most powerful into alliance and fellowship, so that what they have once resolved they may accomplish even against the will of God, and so bring him, too, into order.

units.la: Sed tunc fere fit, quod in praesenti dicitur, & cui per omnia consentiens Dauid inquit: Novit Dominus cogitationes hominum, quod vanae sint. Item: Dominus irritum facit consilium gentium, & cogitationes populorum differt. Consilium autem Domini in aeternum perstat, & cogitationes cordis eius per omnia saecula. Typus huius rei pulcherrimus & euidentissimus in illis praecessit olim, qui ne in totam terram dispergerentur, sicuti Deus constituerat, sibi ipsis nomen facere, & turrim aedificare conati sunt, cuius fastigium coelos contingeret. Qui conatus initio illis pulchre succedere visus fuit, cum & locum aedificio huic commodum, & materiam omnem praeparatam & ad manus habe rent: Sed ecce in medio opere Deus superbas illas cordis ipsorum cogitationes disperdit, & quidem nullo negotio, & quasi per ludibrium. Subito enim linguas diuersas dedit, ut neque se mutuo intelli gere, neque ad quaesita respondere possent: & ita factum est, ut qui sibi ipsis nomen gloriosum parare voluerunt, intermisso hoc opere suo tam ambitioso in omnes terras dispersi sint, et locum illum poena sua nobilitarint, qui ex linguarum confusione illic facta Babel dictus est. Voluit autem eo exemplo docere Dominus, idem omnibus euenturum esse, qui confidentia propria elati cogitationes concipiunt cum ipsius voluntate & decreto pugnantes. Idem ergo posteris temporibus sensit Sennacherib Assyriorum Rex, qui (ut Isaias de illo narrat) regnorum & populorum fines abolere, & gentes omnes vna cum Dijs suis Assyriorum monarchiae subijcere conabatur: sed dispersit eius cogitationes Deus, ut amisso apud Hierosolymae muros exercitu ipse inglorius profugeret, et mox in conspectu Dei sui fi lijs Nisroch a proprijs filijs trucidatus vitam cum imperio finiret. Accidit simile quid postea Balthazari Babyloniorum regi, cuius cogitationes erant: Coelos conscendam, supernè penes stellas Dei exaltabo solium meum, & sedebo in monte congregationis, in lateribus Aquilonis ascendam super altitudinem nubium, altissimo aequalis ero. At idem non multo post vrbe a Persis & Medis capta inter ebriosorum satraparum & meretricum mensas crudeliter occisus, inferis alibus spiritibus (ut idem Isaias testatur) spectaculum praebuit. Eadem quoq; Alexandri Macedonis fortuna fuit, cuius ambitioni ne totus quidem orbis sufficiebat, imo qui diuinitatem affectabat, tandem vero vnius poculi hausfu satiatus cogitationum suarum superbissimarum finem tristissimum inuenit. Sed dies me deficeret, si quaecunque huius generis exempla in historijs occurrunt, commemorare vellem. Neq; illorum commemoratione opus est, cum priuati quoq; homines experiantur verissimum esse, quod Maria canit. Quàm multos enim videmus, qui de opibus et dignitatibus huius seculi consequendis cogitationes concipiunt mirificas, & consilia ineunt, quorum euentu infallibilem fore sibi ipsis persuadent? At ijdem ferè vel subito aliquo infortunio circumuenti ad egestatem extremam rediguntur & infames fiunt, vel improuisa morte abrepti cogitationes quoq; suas simul abrumpunt, priusquam earum fine attingant. Debet istanos coercere, ne incōsulto Deo de rebus nostris statuamus, neq; aliquid tribuamus nostris viribus, sed sub potentis Dei manu humiliemur. Habet praeterea dictu hoc egregiam consolationem qua fide nostram aduersus pericula, quae a tyrannis ecclesiae persecutoribus impendent, confirmemus. Fuerunt enim omnibus seculis, qui ecclesiam Dei excindere, inq; ea relucente veritatis doctrina extinguere, imo huius Regem Iesum Christum e regno suo deturbare conati sunt. Et hodie adhuc fremunt gentes, & inania meditantur populi, reges terrae ire concurrant & consilia sua conferunt principes ad cipes, aduersus Dominum & Vnctum eius. Sed qui in cœlis sedet, ridet, & Dominus subsannat eos, & (vt hic dicitur) dissipat confidentes illas cordis ipsorum cogitationes. Et quod olim Pharaoni, Antiocho, Romanis Imperatoribus & multis alijs accidisse constat, qui in hoc lapide collendo vi-res suas experiri voluerunt, hoc ipsum nostro seculo potentissimus Regibus & populis ferocissimis euenit, vt non modo irritos viderint esse suorum consiliorum euentus, verumetiam mundi totius ludibrium facti sint. Ista ergo nos consolentur & in fide Christi Iesu fortes atque constantes reddant. Nam vt mundus hic ferociat atq; tumultuetur, facile tamen erit Christo eius consilia dissipare, & pusillum suum gregem in medio luporum defendere. Interim ratum firmumq; stabit Dei decretum, qui per Isaiam olim impijs aduersus Ecclesiam suam coniurantibus dixit: Societatem inite o populi, at inferiores eritis: auscultate qui in remotis estis regionibus: accingamini, at inferiores eritis: accingamini (inquam) at inferiores eritis: inite consilium, & fiet irritum: loquimini sermonem, sed non stabit: quoniam nobiscum est Deus. Isa. 8.
units.tr: But what is said here usually comes about, and David, agreeing with it in every respect, says: The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Again: The Lord brings to nought the counsel of the nations, and defeats the devices of the peoples. But the counsel of the Lord stands for ever, and the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation. A most beautiful and clear type of this happened long ago in those men who, so that they might not be scattered over the whole earth as God had ordained, tried to make a name for themselves and to build a tower whose top would reach the heavens. At first their effort seemed to succeed well, since they had a suitable place for the building and all the material prepared and at hand. But behold, in the middle of the work God destroyed those proud thoughts of their hearts, and that with no trouble, almost in mockery. For suddenly he gave them different tongues, so that they could neither understand one another nor answer what was asked; and so it came about that those who wished to make for themselves a glorious name, abandoning this ambitious work, were scattered over all lands, and made that place notorious by their punishment, the place called Babel from the confusion of tongues there. The Lord wished by this example to teach that the same would befall all who, puffed up by their own confidence, conceive thoughts that fight against his will and decree. The same thing, in later times, befell Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, who (as Isaiah relates of him) tried to abolish the boundaries of kingdoms and peoples and to bring all nations, together with their gods, under the monarchy of the Assyrians. But God scattered his thoughts, so that, having lost his army before the walls of Jerusalem, he himself fled ingloriously, and soon, in the sight of his God, was slain by his own sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, and ended his life and rule. Something similar later happened to Belshazzar, king of the Babylonians, whose thoughts were: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; I will sit on the mountain of the congregation, in the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. Yet not long after, when the city was taken by the Persians and Medes, he was cruelly killed at the tables of drunken satraps and harlots, and afforded a spectacle to the spirits below (as the same Isaiah testifies). The same was the fate of Alexander of Macedon, whose ambition the whole world was not enough to satisfy, and who aspired even to divinity, but who at last, sated by the draught of a single cup, found a most sorrowful end to his most proud thoughts. But the day would fail me if I wished to recount all the examples of this kind that occur in histories. Nor is there any need to recall them, since even private persons experience that what Mary sings is most true. For how many do we see who conceive marvellous thoughts about obtaining the riches and dignities of this age, and form plans which they persuade themselves will certainly succeed? Yet these very men, either caught by some sudden misfortune, are reduced to extreme want and become infamous, or, snatched away by an unexpected death, break off their thoughts together with their life before they reach their goal. This should restrain us, so that we do not decide our affairs without God, nor attribute anything to our own strength, but humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God. Moreover, this saying has an excellent consolation by which we may strengthen our faith against the dangers that threaten from tyrants, the persecutors of the Church. For in every age there have been those who have tried to tear up the Church of God and to extinguish in it the shining doctrine of truth, and even to cast Jesus Christ, its King, down from his kingdom. And even today the nations rage and the peoples devise vain things; the kings of the earth set themselves, and the princes take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Anointed. But he who sits in the heavens laughs, and the Lord scoffs at them, and (as is said here) scatters the confident thoughts of their hearts. And what is known to have happened long ago to Pharaoh, to Antiochus, to the Roman emperors and to many others, who wished to test their strength against this stone, the same has happened in our own age to the most powerful kings and the fiercest peoples, so that they have seen the outcomes of their counsels not only come to nothing, but have themselves become the mockery of the whole world. Let these things therefore console us and make us strong and steadfast in the faith of Jesus Christ. For however much this world rages and rushes into tumult, it will be easy for Christ to scatter its counsels and to defend his little flock in the midst of wolves. Meanwhile the decree of God will stand firm and sure, who long ago said through Isaiah to the wicked conspiring against his Church: Join together, O peoples, and you shall be broken; hearken, you who are in distant lands: gird yourselves, and you shall be broken; gird yourselves (I say) and you shall be broken: take counsel, and it shall come to nothing: speak the word, but it shall not stand; for God is with us. Isa. 8.

units.la: Sed aliud adhuc opus Dei commemorat Maria, quo eius potentia illustratur. Detraxit (inquit) potentes è thronis, & extulit siue exuit humiles. Facit hoc ad prioris confirmationem. Ostendit e-nim non eos modo, qui priuata confidentia aduersus Deum consilia ineunt, huius potentia debellari, verumetiam ipsius gubernationi & prouidentiæ illos esse subiectos, qui legitimum inter homines imperium obtinent: adeoq; Deum esse, qui (vt Daniel & Dauid loquuntur) regna mutet & transfe-rat, Reges deijciat à suæ dignitatis fastigio, & humiles atq; pauperes è pulvere & luto extrahat, vt inter populi sui principes collocentur. Probari hæc possunt omnium gentium atque seculorum exemplis. Constat enim Reges potentissimos præter omnem expectationem subitò deiectos & fortunæ ludibrium factos esse, multos etiam vnà cum regnis suis corruisse. Crœsus Lydiæ Rex, cùm regumditissimus esset, & se mortalium felicíssimum putaret, Apollinis ambiguo oraculo delusus in Cyri manus venit, qui regno exutum & bello captum rogo imposuit. At Cyrus post multas victorias Thomiris regina Scythicæ insidijs circumuentus vitam & regnum simul amisit. Dionysium Siciliæ tyrannum diuina vindicta eò usq; persecuta est, vt regno eiectus Corinthi pueros mercede literas doceret. Inter Romanos Imperatores Diocletianus & Maximianus vno die deposita purpura vitam priuatâ agere cœperunt. Taceo nunc septuaginta illos reges, quos Adonibæsek amputatis manuum atque pedum pollicibus canum instar sub mensa sua ciborū reliquias colligere coegit. Licinium verò Valerianum Sapores Persarum rex sibi equū conscensuro scabellum fecit, & tandē viuenti adhuc pellem detraxit. Quid de Nabuchodonosore dicemus, qui amissa hominis ratione instar seræ in sylvis & defertis locis vitam degit, vt suæ insolentiæ pœnas lueret? Sed quid ego ista recensere incipio, quando nullū vnquam regnū in mundo extitit, quòd non innumera huius generis exempla viderit? Nec pauciora sunt eorū exempla, qui ex humili & abiectissima conditione ad supremas dignitates euecti sunt. Inter quos in sacris literis censentur Josephus, Moses, Saul, Dauid, Ieroboam, Hestera: in prophanis autē historijs Cyrus, Romulus, Iustinus maior, Ottomannus & plures alij. Et hæc qui de hominibus à Dei cognitione alienis cæcæ fortunæ ludibria esse videntur, & ideo cū Poeta dicūt: Si Fortuna volet, fies de Rhetore Consul, Si volet hæc eadem, fies de Consule Rhetor.
units.tr: But Mary mentions yet another work of God, by which his power is shown. "He has put down the mighty from their thrones," she says, "and exalted (or stripped) the humble." This serves to confirm what went before. It shows that God's power overthrows not only those who form private plots against him, but that those who hold lawful rule among men are also subject to his government and providence. It is God who, as Daniel and David say, changes and transfers kingdoms, casts kings down from the height of their dignity, and lifts the lowly and poor out of the dust and mire to be set among the princes of his people. These things can be proved from the examples of all nations and all ages. It is well established that the most powerful kings have been suddenly overthrown beyond all expectation and made the sport of fortune, and many have fallen together with their kingdoms. Croesus, king of Lydia, though he was the richest of kings and thought himself the happiest of mortals, was deceived by an ambiguous oracle of Apollo and fell into the hands of Cyrus, who stripped him of his kingdom and, when he had been captured in war, placed him on the pyre. Cyrus himself, after many victories, was trapped by the treachery of Tomyris, queen of the Scythians, and lost both his life and his kingdom. Divine vengeance pursued Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, so far that, driven from his kingdom, he taught letters to boys at Corinth for a fee. Among the Roman emperors, Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the purple on the same day and began to live as private men. I pass over those seventy kings whom Adonibezek, after cutting off the thumbs of their hands and feet, forced to gather the scraps of his food under his table like dogs. And Sapor, king of the Persians, made Valerian a footstool for himself to mount his horse, and at last flayed him while he was still alive. What shall we say of Nebuchadnezzar, who, having lost the use of reason, lived like a beast in the woods and deserted places, so that he might pay the penalty for his arrogance? But why do I begin to recount these things, when no kingdom has ever existed in the world that has not seen countless examples of this kind? Nor are the examples fewer of those who have been raised from a humble and most abject condition to the highest dignities. Among these, in the sacred writings are counted Joseph, Moses, Saul, David, Jeroboam, and Esther; in profane histories, Cyrus, Romulus, Justin the Elder, Osman, and many others. And those who, being strangers to the knowledge of God, think that these things are mere sport of blind fortune, say with the poet: "If Fortune wills, a rhetorician becomes a consul; if she wills the same, a consul becomes a rhetorician."

units.la: At aliter nos docet Spiritus sanctus, qui ista per Dei prouidentiam certo et iusto iudicio administra-ri ostendit. Ita enim fieri oportet, vt omnibus notum fiat, regna & principatus non hominū figmenta, sed Dei instituta esse, & proinde neminem in externo splendore solùm obstupescere debere, aut etiam illo efferri insolentius. Deinde tyrannorum petulantiam & crudelitatem sic punit Deus, & oppressos eripit. Et hoc in præsenti Maria ex peculiari spiritus suggestione obseruauisse videtur, & inter Dei opera huius etiam mentionem ideo fecisse, vt afflictæ Iudæorum genti consolaitonem afferret, & ostenderet Romanorum potentiam, quantùmuis immanem & hucusq; inuictam, non ob stituram esse, quò minus Christus nascatur, & humilis licet quoad carnem, regnum tamen obtineat, & populo suo afflicto opem ferat. Debent interim hæc omnes homines ad suam institutionem atque consolationem accommodare: vt primò quidem non confidant suæ potentiæ, neque magnificis huius mundi dignitatibus superbiant. Quid enim in his firmum aut stabile est? Aut quis ei conditioni fidat, quæ præ alijs omni periculorum generi est obnoxia? Etenim vt fulmina non imas vallet, sed summa montium cacumina & turres altius eminentes feriunt: ita qui in summo dignitatis gradu constituti sunt, pluribus quoq; casibus subiiciuntur, & quo altius ascenderunt, eo gravio-ri lapsu ruunt. Quòd eò citius & maiore ipsorum malo fit, quò confidentius superbiunt. Notũ enim est illud Apostoli: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Deinde discimus, neminem offendi debere impiorum potentia atque successibus. Facile enim illos deturbare potest Deus cum voluerit: & procul dubiò volet (vt modò diximus) si ab illo datis viribus aduersus illum & cultores eius abutuntur. Apparet quidem interdum extra omnem teli iactum consistere illorum conditio, sed reuera (vt Asaph dicebat) in lubrico constituti sunt, & subitò ferè præcipites cadunt, qui perpetuò regnaturi videbantur. Præterea hinc consolationem petant, afflicti, ne se propter huius se culi miserias à Deo derelictos esse existiment. Solet enim hic talium curam potissimum suscipere, quia in illis illustrius lucet eius bonitas atq; potentia. Quod vt in multis alijs, sic in Mariæ exemplo euidentissimè apparet. Hanc enim vulgo contemptam & magnatibus ignotam in filij sui matrem elegit Deus, præteritis tot reginis, & heroinis nobilissimis, quæ tunc in toto terrarum orbe celebrabantur. Quis ergo illam infelicem dixerit? aut quis dubitet, quin in omnibus quoque alijs suam potentiam Deus aliquo singulari specimine posset declarare?
units.tr: But the Holy Spirit teaches us otherwise, showing that these things are administered by God's providence with a certain and just judgment. For it must be so, that it may be known to all that kingdoms and principalities are not the inventions of men but the institutions of God, and that therefore no one should be dazzled by outward splendour alone, or be puffed up more insolently by it. Next, God thus punishes the wantonness and cruelty of tyrants and rescues the oppressed. It seems that Mary, prompted by a peculiar suggestion of the Spirit, observed this in the present case, and mentioned it among God's works so that she might bring consolation to the afflicted Jewish nation, and show that the power of the Romans, however vast and hitherto unconquered, would not stand in the way of Christ's birth, and that he, though humble as to the flesh, would nevertheless obtain a kingdom and bring help to his afflicted people. Meanwhile all men ought to apply these things to their own instruction and comfort: first, so that they do not trust in their own power, nor take pride in the splendid dignities of this world. For what in these is firm or stable? Or who can trust a condition that is exposed to every kind of danger beyond others? Indeed, just as lightning strikes not the low valleys but the highest mountain peaks and towers that rise above the rest, so those who have been placed on the highest step of dignity are also subjected to more accidents, and the higher they have climbed, the heavier the fall they suffer. And this comes the sooner and to their greater harm, the more confidently they are proud. For that saying of the Apostle is well known: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Next, we learn that no one should be offended by the power and success of the wicked. For God can easily cast them down whenever he wishes, and he will surely wish to do so (as we have just said) if they abuse the power given them by him against him and his worshippers. Sometimes their condition appears to stand beyond every range of a missile, but in truth (as Asaph said) they are set on slippery ground, and those who seemed destined to reign forever often fall headlong almost suddenly. Moreover, let the afflicted seek consolation from this, lest because of the miseries of this world they think they have been forsaken by God. For God is wont especially to take care of such people, because in them his goodness and power shine more brightly. This is most clearly seen in the example of Mary, as in many others. For God chose as the mother of his Son this woman, despised by the common people and unknown to the great, passing over so many queens and most noble heroines who were then celebrated in the whole circuit of the earth. Who, then, would call her unhappy? Or who doubts that God could also in all others declare his power by some singular example?

units.la: Videamus nunc tertium diuinæ virtutis opus, quod Maria his verbis celebrat: Famelicos implet bonis, divites autem ablegauit inanes. Factum hoc sæpe secundum literam, & hodie hoc ipsum non raro fieri videmus, vt qui ditissimi sunt, vel ad egestatem subitò redigantur, vel curis edacibus excrucientur, aut morbis lentis contabescant, vt Tantali instar in medijs opibus egeant, dum illis frui nequaquam possunt: Alijs interea vel adopes maximas ex inopia extrema peruenientibus, vel in mediocri fortuna laetis, dum quantum ipsis satis est habent, & bonis sibi à Deo concessis cum honesta voluptate fruuntur. Et hæc quidem exempla nobis proponit Deus, vt eius manu ea etiam, quæ ad victum nostrum faciunt, dispensari intelligamus, & proinde procul abiecta carnis sollicitudine in ipsius benedictionem respiciamus. Etenim vt Paulus dicebat, magnus quæstus est pietas μετ' αὐταρκείας, id est, cum animo sua sorte contento. Et qui hunc sibi pararunt, ij potentissimis quoq; Regibus beatiores sunt. Vidit hoc olim Solon, cui inter septem Græciæ sapientes primus locus datus fuit. Is enim Cræso, Regum sui seculi opulentissimo, quoad veram beatitatem anteposuit Aglaum quendam Arcadem, qui patrij agelli finibus contentus, intra hos in bono pace & honesto atq; tollerabili labore consenuerat. Quò magis damnari merentur, qui cùm Christiani dici velint, se ipsos diuitiarum immodicarum curis excruciant, & dum in summa rerum copia metuunt ne quando egeant, ijs etiam non audent frui, quæ manibus tenent. Caterum quod hic Maria dicit, altiori etiam sensu exponi potest, & in primis locum habet in æternæ salutis negotio, illic enim famelici dicuntur, qui propriæ infirmitatis sensu & peccatorum cognitione presi iustitiam Dei atq; salutem esuriunt atq; sitiunt. Hos Christus saturat & bonis spiritualibus implet. Est enim panis ille vitæ, qui semel perceptus nos postea esurire non finit: est item fons aquæ viuentis, ex quo qui bibit, is in æternum non sitiet. Ardet quidem in credentibus vitæ æternæ desiderium, & dissolui cupiunt, vt cum Christo in cælis viuant: sed procul ab illis abest anxietas illa, quæ desperationem parit: quia salutis suæ certi sunt, et intra animos suos spiritus testimonio atq; arrhabone confirmantur. Rursus divites vocat scriptura eos, qui sibi ipsis tales videntur, & sui arbitrij libertate, proprijs suæ naturæ viribus, adhæc suorum operum meritis & propria iustitia in Dei conspectu superbiunt. Hos inanes ablegat abs se Dominus. Quia enim sibi ipsis sufficere videntur, & suam iustitiam constituere volunt, non recipiunt iustitiam Dei, quam ille nobis in filio suo offert: & quamuis circa multa occupentur, nihil tamen proficiunt. Nam vt Christus ait, qui alibi quàm ex ipso bibunt, sitiunt iterum, imò perpetua animarum fame atq; siti excruciantur. Exempla in vtranq; partem euangelica historia proponit. Venerunt ad Christum meretrices & publicani, quos peccatorum conscientia famelicos faciebat, & illius gratia saturati sunt: at interim propriæ iustitiæ fiducia superbi pharisæi contabuerunt, & tandem ob contemptum Christum grauissime puniti sunt. Et huius generis multa accidunt quotidie, quæ nos admonere debent, ne quid nobis ipsis tribuamus, sed vnius Dei gratiæ fidamus, qui hoc peculiare suæ potentiæ specimen ædidit, quòd filij sui in carne manifestati merito peccatum abo-leuit, & ad hunc confugentium animas vere saturat & tranquillas reddit.
units.tr: Let us now consider the third work of divine power, which Mary celebrates in these words: "He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty." This has often happened literally, and today we often see it happen that the very rich are either suddenly reduced to want, or are tormented by consuming cares, or waste away with lingering diseases, so that, like Tantalus, they lack amid their wealth, since they cannot enjoy it at all; while others, who have come to the greatest poverty from extreme want, or who are content with a moderate fortune, have what is enough for them and enjoy the goods given them by God with honest pleasure. God sets these examples before us so that we may understand that even the things that serve our sustenance are dispensed by his hand, and therefore, casting aside carnal anxiety, we may look to his blessing. For, as Paul said, "godliness with contentment is great gain" [μετὰ αὐταρκείας], that is, with a mind content with its lot. And those who have acquired this are happier even than the most powerful kings. Solon saw this long ago; he was given the first place among the seven wise men of Greece. For he preferred to Croesus, the richest king of his age, as regards true happiness, a certain Arcadian named Aglaus, who, content with the bounds of his ancestral little field, had grown old within them in peace, goodness, and honest and bearable labour. How much more deserving of condemnation, then, are those who, while they wish to be called Christians, torment themselves with the cares of immoderate riches, and, while they fear lest at some time they may be in need amid the greatest abundance of things, do not dare to enjoy even what they hold in their hands. But what Mary says here can also be explained in a higher sense, and it applies chiefly to the business of eternal salvation. For those are called hungry who, pressed by the sense of their own weakness and the knowledge of their sins, hunger and thirst after the righteousness and salvation of God. Christ satisfies these and fills them with spiritual goods. For he is that bread of life which, once received, does not let us hunger afterwards; he is also the fountain of living water, from which whoever drinks will never thirst forever. Indeed, in believers there burns a desire for eternal life, and they long to be dissolved and to live with Christ in heaven; yet that anxiety which breeds despair is far from them, because they are certain of their salvation and are confirmed within their souls by the testimony and pledge of the Spirit. Again, Scripture calls the rich those who seem to themselves to be such, and who take pride before God in the freedom of their own will, in the powers of their own nature, and besides, in the merits of their works and their own righteousness. The Lord sends these away empty from himself. For since they seem sufficient to themselves and wish to establish their own righteousness, they do not receive the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son; and although they are busy with many things, they gain nothing. For, as Christ says, those who drink anywhere other than from him thirst again, indeed they are tormented by a perpetual famine and thirst of soul. The gospel history sets out examples on both sides. Harlots and publicans came to Christ, whom the consciousness of their sins made hungry, and they were satisfied by his grace; but in the meantime the proud Pharisees, confident in their own righteousness, pined away, and at last, because they despised Christ, were most severely punished. Many things of this kind happen every day, and they ought to admonish us not to attribute anything to ourselves, but to trust in the grace of God alone, who has displayed this peculiar specimen of his power: that by the merit of his Son made manifest in the flesh he has blotted out sin, and truly satisfies and calms the souls of those who flee to him.

units.la: Sequitur postrema huius Cantici pars, qua ad causam praesentem propius accedit Maria, & simul Dei veritatem praedicat, qui olim promissam sui populi redemptionem nunc praestare velit. Sic autem ait: Suscepit Israel puerum suum, ut memor esset misericordiae (prout locutus est patribus nostris, Abrahamo & semini eius) in aeternum. Quibus verbis ad Isaiae oraculum alludere videtur, quod Cap. 41. extat, ubi sic loquitur Dominus: Tu Israel seruus meus es, Iacob quem elegi, semen Abrahami amici mei. Quia apprehendi te ab extremis terrae, & a finibus eius vocavi te, dixi tibi: Seruus meus es tu, elegi te, & non abieci te. Ne timeas, quoniam tecum sum ego: ne terrearis, quia ego Deus tuus sum: roboraui te, insuper auxiliatus sum tibi, atque suscepi te dextra iustitiae meae, &c. Suscipiendi verbi autem ad afflictum & infelice populi Iudaici statum refertur, qui eo redactus erat, ut nulla restitutionis spes reliqua esset. Nam Ecclesiae gubernatio penes Pharisaeos erat, qui annis ante Christum natum circiter septuaginta ab Alexandra, Hircani & Aristobuli matre, in summam dignitatem euectii, saniorem legis doctrinam humanis traditionibus obscurarant, & sacra omnia fecerant venalia. Respub. autem sub Romanis erat, qui Herodem ex infestissima Idumaeorum gente oriundum, hominem insuper crudelem & sanguinarium, illis imposuerant, qui & veterem politiam aboleuerat sublato supremo Senatu, qui LXXII. senioribus constabat, & deleta Machabaeorum posteritate omni Dauidis quoque familiam hostiliter persequebatur. Erat ergo hoc ingens & inspseratum beneficium, quod illorum curam Deus tunc suscipiebat. At ne quis eius causam in hominum meritis constitueret, hoc Deum fecisse ait, ut memor esset suae misericordiae, olim patribus promissae, adeoque ut foedus cum Abrahamo & semine eius sancitum confirmaret. Etenim si ipsum Abraham & primam eius vocationem consideremus, nihil illi ex proprio merito accidisse constabit, sed gratuito Dei fauore ad hoc delectum fuisse, ut in ipso instauraretur foedus salutis, quod in diluuio abolitum videri poterat. Promissiones, quarum hic fit mentio, ex ordine commemorare nunc minime opus est, quando in Mose & prophetis passim occurrunt, & omnibus satis notae sunt. Nunc autem probe obseruemus, Deum suae misericordiae memorem esse in aeternum, & proinde veracem quoque esse, neque unquam obliuisci promissionum suarum, quamuis res interdum afflictissimae & omnino deploratae videantur. Et in primis memorabile est, quod promissiones cum misericordia Dei Maria coniungit. Sunt enim, qui hanc quidem nunquam non in ore habent, ei tamen non possunt certo confidere, si quando tentatio aliqua grauior incidit: quia promissiones ignorant, quibus se nobis Deus ex gratia obstrinxit. Itaque ex eius misericordia non plus commodi referunt, quam ex diuitiis opulenti alicuius, qui ipsis nullo iure obstrictus est, & cum quo illis nulla societas aut communio intercedit. Recte igitur Maria promissionum simul meminit, & in has proculdubio omnes illae electorum reliquae respexerunt, ex quibus sub Christi aduentum Ecclesiam instaurandam fore olim prophetae praedixerant. Et multum facit cum ad commendandam nostrae fidei certitudinem, tum ad salutis spem confirmandam, quod utramque non in aliquo nouo hominum figmento, sed in vetustissimis Dei promissionibus fundata esse scimus, quas ad nos etiam pertinere scriptura passim testatur. At hic simul diligenter meminisse oportet, qui nam illi sint, quorum Deus secundum promissiones suas perpetuo miseretur. Maria enim diserte Israelis serui Dei & seminis seu filiorum Abrahami meminit. Sed non omnes (inquit Paulus) qui sunt ex Israel, sunt Israel: neque quia sunt semen Abrahami (secundum carnem nimirum) omnes sunt filij: sed Israelitae & germani Abrahami filij sunt, qui promissiones Dei fide constanti apprehendunt, seque Deo per fidei obedientiam subjiciunt. Non ergo pertinent promissiones istae salutis ad incredulos & superstitiosos, qui extra Christum vagantur: nec item ad rebelles & contumaces, qui aduersus Deum impudenter proteruiunt. Docet itaque huius loci consideratio, qui fiat, quo minus fruamur hodie promissionu Dei fructu? Quomodo enim hunc percipiant, qui promissionibus non credunt? Atqui ut Christus olim praedixit, fides in terris rara est. Nam quoad salutis aeternae negotium, multi caelum cum inferis negant, & religionem inter indifferentia, aut etiam inter res inutiles & superuacaneas numerant. Qui vero Christi nomen profitentur, non hoc uno contenti sunt, sed infinita alia ei coniungunt, quibus meriti ipsius virtus euacuatur. Multi ad quoduis periculum consternati ab illo turpiter deficiunt. Multi vero fidem, quae uno Iesu Christo nititur, & huius sectatores ferro & igne persequuntur. Quod si adres externas transeamus, in illis quoque paucissimi Deo fidunt: sed quasi sua industria ipsis sufficiat, illius beneficentiam plane negligunt. Fit ergo,
units.tr: Now follows the last part of this Canticle, in which Mary comes closer to the present matter and at the same time proclaims the truth of God, who now wishes to bring about the redemption of his people that he promised long ago. She says: "He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (as he spake to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed) for ever." In these words she seems to allude to the oracle of Isaiah in chapter 41, where the Lord speaks thus: "Thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend. For I have taken thee from the ends of the earth, and called thee from the coasts thereof, and said unto thee: Thou art my servant, I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away. Fear not, for I am with thee: be not dismayed, for I am thy God: I have strengthened thee, yea, I have helped thee, and I have upheld thee with the right hand of my righteousness," and so on. The words "he has taken up" refer to the afflicted and unhappy state of the Jewish people, which had been brought to such a point that no hope of restoration remained. For the government of the Church was in the hands of the Pharisees, who, about seventy years before Christ's birth, had been raised to the highest dignity by Alexandra, the mother of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. They had obscured the sounder teaching of the law with human traditions and made all holy things venal. The commonwealth was under the Romans, who had set over them Herod, sprung from the most hostile nation of the Idumaeans, moreover a cruel and bloodthirsty man. He also abolished the old polity, removing the supreme Senate, which consisted of seventy-two elders, and, having destroyed the posterity of the Maccabees, relentlessly persecuted the whole family of David too. This was therefore a great and remarkable benefit, that God then took up their cause. But lest anyone should ground its cause in men's merits, she says God did this so that he might be mindful of his mercy, promised long ago to the fathers, and so as to confirm the covenant sanctioned with Abraham and his seed. For if we consider Abraham himself and his first calling, it will be clear that nothing came to him from his own merit, but that by God's free favour he was chosen so that the covenant of salvation, which might seem to have been abolished in the flood, should be restored in him. There is no need now to recount in order the promises mentioned here, since they occur everywhere in Moses and the prophets and are well known to all. But let us now carefully observe that God is mindful of his mercy for ever, and therefore is also true, and never forgets his promises, although matters sometimes seem most afflicted and altogether hopeless. And in particular it is worth noting that Mary joins the promises to the mercy of God. For there are some who always have that mercy on their lips, yet cannot trust in it with certainty when some heavier temptation falls upon them, because they do not know the promises by which God has bound himself to us out of grace. Thus they gain no more advantage from his mercy than from the riches of some wealthy man who is bound to them by no right and with whom they have no fellowship or communion. Rightly, then, Mary recalls the promises at the same time, and undoubtedly all the remaining elect looked to these, from whom the prophets had long foretold that the Church would be restored at Christ's coming. It greatly helps both to commend the certainty of our faith and to confirm the hope of salvation that we know both are founded not on some new invention of men but on the most ancient promises of God, which Scripture everywhere testifies also pertain to us. Here, however, we must also carefully remember who those are whom God constantly pities according to his promises. For Mary explicitly mentions the servant of God Israel and the seed or children of Abraham. But, says Paul, "not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor, because they are the seed of Abraham (according to the flesh, of course), are they all children; but the Israelites and the true children of Abraham are those who lay hold of God's promises with steadfast faith and submit themselves to God through obedient faith." Therefore those promises of salvation do not pertain to unbelievers and superstitious people who wander outside Christ, nor likewise to rebels and the obstinate, who shamelessly defy God. Thus consideration of this passage teaches why we do not today enjoy the fruit of God's promises. For how can those who do not believe the promises receive that fruit? Yet, as Christ foretold long ago, faith is rare on earth. For as to the matter of eternal salvation, many deny heaven together with hell, and count religion among indifferent matters, or even among useless and superfluous things. Those who profess the name of Christ are not content with this alone, but join to him endless other things by which the power of his merit is emptied. Many, dismayed at any danger, shamefully fall away from him. Many others persecute with sword and fire the faith that rests on Jesus Christ alone, and his followers. And if we pass to external matters, very few even among these trust in God; but, as if their own industry were enough for them, they plainly neglect his kindness. Thus it comes about,

units.la: Promissiones Dei cum misericordia coniunguntur. Dei promissiones ad quos pertineant. vt Reipub. quidem salutem plerique in fœderibus & mundi amicitia consistere putent, & proinde hanc turpi à Christo defectione redimant: rei domesticæ verò incolumitatem in artibus vsurarijs & insatiabili opum augendarum studio collocent: quæ tautæ est, quòdius & æquum violant, charitatis leges impiè negligunt, & tam priuatim quàm publicè omnia turbant. Quis ergo miretur, Deum quasi promissionum misericordiæ suæ immemorem, tot tantaq; scelera vltrici manu & perpetuis plagis punire? Ista emendare necesse est, si mala præsentia effugere, & promissionum Deifrum fructum percipere volumus.
units.tr: God's promises are joined with mercy. To whom God's promises belong. that most people think the safety of the commonwealth consists in treaties and friendship with the world, and so they buy it back at the price of shameful desertion from Christ; while they place the welfare of their households in usurious practices and an insatiable zeal for increasing wealth. This zeal is so great that it violates justice and equity, impiously neglects the laws of charity, and throws everything into confusion, both in private and in public life. Who then should wonder that God, as though forgetful of his merciful promises, punishes such great and numerous crimes with an avenging hand and constant plagues? These things must be amended if we wish to escape present evils and to receive the fruit of God's promises.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci particula, qua Maria dicitur tribus quasi mensibus apud Elizabetam substitisse, nimirum ad partum vsq;, vt & gaudio pio cum illa tunc frueretur, & interea ipsi iam grandæuæ & vterum gerenti inseruiret. Ita verò & religiosæ virginis & piæ cognatæ officio fungitur, dum nullam fidei confirmandæ occasionem negligit, & Elizabetæ suam operam & industriam non negat. Exemplo autem suo iuniores admonet, vt senioribus libenter suum obsequium præstent, & parentum loco eos colant, quos ætate grandiores esse vident. Iubet hoc naturæ lex, cuius occulto instinctu fit, vt omnes senectutem appetant, & eandem honore & reuerentia dignam iudicent. Caeterum euoluto hoc tempore domum redijt Maria, eadem nimirum festinatione, qua prius ad Elizabetam profecta fuerat. Quia verò tempus est, vt ipsi simul dicendi finem faciamus, præcipuus huius loci vsus erit, vt Cantici Mariæ doctrinâ nobis applicemus. Meminerimus ergo Deum nobis quoque salutem in Iesu Christo offerre ex gratia: & ipsum non minus potentem quàm iustum esse, qui superbos suæ gratiæ contemptores puniat, humiles verò & obsequentes benignè suscipiat: ad hæc veracem esse in promissis suis, etiamsi interdum nostri oblitus esse videatur. Huic ergo credamus, eundem timeamus & colamus, vt promissionum eius fructu fruamur in filio ipsius vnigenito, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, in which Mary is said to have stayed with Elizabeth for about three months, namely until the birth, both so that she might share in the holy joy with her and in the meantime serve her, now aged and pregnant. In this way she fulfils the duty both of a devout virgin and of a pious kinswoman, neglecting no opportunity to strengthen faith and not refusing Elizabeth her labour and diligence. By her example she also admonishes the younger to render willing service to their elders and to honour in the place of parents those whom they see to be advanced in years. The law of nature commands this, by whose hidden instinct it comes about that all desire old age and judge it worthy of honour and reverence. Moreover, when this time had passed, Mary returned home, with the same haste with which she had earlier set out for Elizabeth. Since it is time for us also to bring our discourse to an end, the chief use of this passage will be that we apply the teaching of Mary's Canticle to ourselves. Let us remember, then, that God offers us also salvation in Jesus Christ by grace, and that he is no less powerful than just, to punish the proud despisers of his grace, and kindly to receive the humble and obedient. Moreover, he is true in his promises, even if at times he seems to have forgotten us. Let us therefore believe him, fear and worship him, that we may enjoy the fruit of his promises in his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XIII.

units.la: Elizabetæ autem impletum est tempus pariendi, & peperit filium. Et audierunt vicini & cognati eius, quod magnificè sua misericordia erga illam vsus esset Dominus, & ei gratulabantur. Et factum est die octauo, venerunt vt circuciderent puerulum, & vocabant eum ex nomine patris ipsius, Zachariam. Sed respondens mater eius ait: Ne quaquam, sed vocabitur Ioannes. Et dixerunt ad eam: Nemo est in cognatione tua, qui vocetur isto nomine. Innuebant autem patri eius, quid vellet eum vocari. Ipsq; postulatis tabellis scripsit, dicens: Ioannes est nomen eius. Et mirati sunt omnes. Apertum est autem os eius, illico, & lingua eius, & loquebatur benedicens Deo. Ortus est igitur timor omnibus vicinis eorum: & in tota montana regione Iudææ diuulgata sunt omnia verba ista. Et omnes qui audierunt, reposuerunt ea in corde suo, dicentes: Quis nam puerulus hic erit? Manus autem Domini erat cum eo.
units.tr: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had shown her great mercy, and they rejoiced with her. On the eighth day they came to circumcise the little boy, and they wanted to call him by his father's name, Zacharias. But his mother answered and said, "By no means; he shall be called John." They said to her, "There is no one in your family who has this name." Then they made signs to his father, asking what he wanted him to be called. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, "His name is John." And they were all amazed. Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. Fear came upon all their neighbours, and all these words were spread through the whole hill country of Judea. All who heard them kept them in their hearts, saying, "What then will this child be?" For the hand of the Lord was with him.

units.la: VT Deus omnibus seculis aliquos delegit ex peculiari gratia, quorum opera & ministerio in alijs hominibus iuuandis vteretur: ita eosdem singularibus testimonijs & operibus in ipsa ista tim infantia siue pueritia commendauit, quò facilius inter homines fidem inuenirent. Exempla huius rei in Mose, Samuele & multis alijs occurrunt, quorum pueritia peculiaribus factis atque donis illustris fuit. Inter hos autem in primis numerari meretur Ioannes, cui postea Baptistæ nomen ex officio impositum fuit. Quia enim hic promissi Redemptoris anteambulo & primus gratiæ noui testamenti præco esse debebat, quem venturum prophetæ olim prædixerant, ita eum concipi & nasci voluit Deus, vt cordati quique intelligerent hominem fore non vulgarem, & proinde ex eo peculiare quid expectari debere. Conceptum enim audiimus fuisse à matre sterili & iam grandæua. Adhæc conceptionem eius prædixit Angelus. Accessit item miraculum, quòd Zacharias pater sermonis vsu spoliatus fuit, eo quod diuinae promissioni minus credidisset. Itaque non dubium est, quin ista multorum animos suspensos habuerint, qui rei nouae & insolitae euentum cum desiderio expectabant. His ergo nunc descriptionem natiuitatis eius subijcit Lucas, quae etiam ipsa plurima habet, quae obseruationem & admirationem merentur. Omnium vero hic scopus est, vt testimonio Ioannis credamus, quod is de Christo Iesu tulit.
units.tr: As God in every age has chosen some people out of his special grace, to use their work and ministry in helping other men, so he has also commended these same people, even in their infancy or boyhood, by remarkable signs and deeds, so that they might more easily win men's faith. Examples of this occur in Moses, Samuel and many others, whose childhood was made illustrious by extraordinary deeds and gifts. Among these, John deserves to be counted first, to whom the name Baptist was later given because of his office. For he was to be the forerunner of the promised Redeemer and the first herald of the grace of the New Testament, whose coming the prophets had long foretold. God therefore willed that he be conceived and born in such a way that all thoughtful people would understand that he would be no ordinary man, and that something special was to be expected from him. We hear that he was conceived by a mother who was barren and already advanced in years. Moreover, the angel foretold his conception. There was also the miracle that his father Zacharias was deprived of speech, because he had been slow to believe the divine promise. It is therefore no doubt that these events held the minds of many in suspense, as they awaited with longing the outcome of a new and unusual matter. Luke now adds to these events an account of his birth, which itself contains many things worthy of notice and wonder. But the whole aim here is that we should believe the testimony that John bore to Christ Jesus.

units.la: Praemittitur initio natiuitatis huius breuis & simplex narratio. Elizabeta (inquit) simplex tum est tempus pariendi, & peperit filium. Dum temporis impleti meminit, illum secundum naturae ordinem, perinde vt alios homines, natum esse ostendit. Est autem hoc frequens admodum in scripturis, quod dum Sanctissimorum Dei seruorum historiae describuntur, non pudet Spiritum sanctum conceptionis eorum & partus mentionem facere. Facit hoc plurimum ad coniugij & thori coniugalis commendationem, quem Paulus quoque impollutum dixit. Deinde communis illa naturae lex aut ordo nobis ob oculos ponitur, qui eandem omnium hominum sortem & conditionem esse docet, iam inde ex vtero matris. Nam eodem modo omnes concipiuntur & nascuntur, in peccato nimirum, vt defemetipso Dauid fatetur, & praeter corruptam atque vitiosam naturam nihil proprium secum in hanc lucem ferunt. Quoad corpus autem, similiter omnes ex matris vtero nudi & imbelles prodeunt, & sese in lachrymarum vallem prodire miserabili vagitu testantur. Quod vero postea alij alijs excellentiores fiunt, diuinae dispensationis opus est, quae nostri commodi causa diuersos hominum ordines instituit. Debent ergo, qui reliquis hominibus praestant, Dei beneficium agnoscere, & se huic gratos praeberent; non autem natalium suorum splendore superbire, quasi ex illis aliquid reliquis hominibus excellentius habeant. Est quidem non vulgare Dei donum ex parentibus progenitum esse virtute eximijs, & quos res gestae nobilitarunt. Sed quibus hoc contigit, hi meminerint, maiorum gloriam ipsis ignominiae maioris causam fore, nisi eosdem virtute referant, & illorum vestigijs insistant.
units.tr: At the beginning of this birth, a brief and simple narrative is put forward. "Now the time came," it says, "for Elizabeth to be delivered, and she bore a son." By mentioning the fulfilment of the time, he shows that the child was born according to the order of nature, just as other men are born. This is very frequent in Scripture: when the histories of the holiest servants of God are described, the Holy Spirit is not ashamed to mention their conception and birth.
