This serves greatly to commend marriage and the marriage bed, which Paul also called undefiled. Then that common law or order of nature is set before our eyes, which teaches that all men share the same lot and condition from the very womb of the mother. For all are conceived and born in the same way, namely in sin, as David confesses of himself, and they bring into this light nothing of their own except a corrupt and vicious nature. As for the body, likewise all come forth naked and helpless from their mother's womb, and by their miserable wailing testify that they enter this vale of tears. That some later become more excellent than others is the work of divine dispensation, which for our good has established different ranks of men. Those who excel the rest should therefore acknowledge the benefit of God and show themselves thankful for it; they should not be puffed up by the splendour of their birth, as if they had anything more excellent than other men by it. It is indeed no small gift of God to be born of parents distinguished by virtue, and whose deeds have made them noble. But those to whom this has happened should remember that the glory of their ancestors will be the cause of greater shame for them, unless they match them in virtue and follow in their footsteps.

units.la: Habet praeterea locus hic memorabile veritatis diuinae exemplum. Promiserat Deus Zachariae per Angelum suum, quod & filius ipsi ex vxore Elizabeta nasciturus esset, & quod multi eius natiuitate essent gauisuri. Vtrunque vero humanae rationi impossibile videbatur. Erat enim Elizabeta natura sterilis, & huic vitio aetas grandior accedebat, quae fecundas quoque ad conceptum ineptas reddit. Ea autem tunc erat rerum Iudaicarum conditio, vt prudentiores quique, ob nascentes sibi liberos dolere potius quam gaudere deberent, cum nulla (vt nuper diximus) recuperandae libertatis spes reliqua esset. Fit tamen quod Deus promiserat. Parit enim feliciter Elizabeta, & vicini omnes atque cognati gaudium inde concipiunt, quod illis de publica etiam salute melius sperandi occasionem praebet, vt in sequentibus patebit. Debet exemplum hoc omnibus alijs promissionibus applicari, ne de earum veritate dubitemus. Sunt promissiones euangelicae, in quibus iustitiam nobis pollicetur Deus, cum in nobis nihil quam peccatum videamus: pollicetur item suam gratiam & fauorem, cum passim irae eius argumenta in oculos nostros incurrant: pollicetur vitam, & ecce morbis obnoxij tandem morte absumimur. At non ideo de promissionibus Dei dubitare nos oportet. Potest enim ille nos filij sui iustitia donare, potest salutem nostram per ea promouere, quae irae & exitij indicia esse videntur: potest in morte seruare, imo hanc iam pridem in melius mutauit, vt iam felix ex hoc infelici mundo ad vitam aeternam transitus fit, quae prius peccati poena fuit. Eadem est promissionis ratio, qua suam Ecclesiae patrocinium & perpetuam incolumitatem vsq; in seculi huius consummationem pollicetur. Videmus enim Ecclesiam nouis subinde casibus iactari, multis in locis collabi, & passim ab hostibus immanissimis peti. Sed nō deerit suis pollicitis Dei Filius, & tunc nos cogitare oportet, hoc illi proprium esse, quod per crucem triumphat, & in medio suorum hostium dominatur. Sunt praeterea priuatae promissiones de vitu & amictu, quem habituri sint qui regnum Dei & iustitiam eius ante omnia quaerunt. At frequenter illi bonis omnibus spoliantur, a patrijs sedibus exulant & inopes oberrant. Sed tunc meminerimus, non in solo pane hominem viuere, sed quouis verbo, quod egreditur ex ore Dei, & Christum panibus hordeaceis suos pascere, vt tamen saturentur, & in sua inopia regum opulentissimorum thesauros longe superent. Deniq; fidem habeamus Dei promissis omnibus, & hunc haud dubie in illis veracem esse experiemur.
units.tr: This passage also contains a memorable example of divine truth. God had promised Zacharias through his angel both that a son would be born to him from his wife Elizabeth, and that many would rejoice at his birth. Yet both seemed impossible to human reason. For Elizabeth was barren by nature, and her advanced age was added to this defect, which also makes even fertile women unfit for conception. Moreover, the condition of Jewish affairs was then such that the wiser sort ought rather to grieve than rejoice at children being born to them, since (as we said recently) there was no remaining hope of recovering their freedom. Yet what God had promised came to pass. For Elizabeth gives birth happily, and all her neighbours and relatives conceive joy from it, because it gives them an occasion of better hope even for public salvation, as will appear in what follows. This example ought to be applied to all the other promises, so that we do not doubt their truth. There are gospel promises in which God promises us righteousness, when we see in ourselves nothing but sin; he likewise promises his grace and favour, when the signs of his wrath meet our eyes everywhere; he promises life, and yet we, subject to diseases, are at last consumed by death. But we ought not on that account to doubt God's promises. For he can give us the righteousness of his Son; he can advance our salvation through those things which seem to be signs of wrath and destruction; he can preserve us in death, indeed he has long since turned it into something better, so that now the passage from this unhappy world to eternal life is a happy one, which before was the punishment of sin. The same reasoning applies to the promise by which he pledges the protection and perpetual safety of his Church until the end of this age. For we see the Church from time to time tossed by new misfortunes, falling in many places, and attacked on every side by most savage enemies. But the Son of God will not be lacking to his promises, and then we must reflect that it is his proper work to triumph through the cross and to rule in the midst of his enemies. There are also private promises concerning food and clothing, which those will have who seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness above all things. But often such people are stripped of all goods, go into exile from their homes, and wander in poverty. Yet then let us remember that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God; and that Christ feeds his people with barley loaves, so that they are satisfied, and in their poverty far surpass the treasures of the most wealthy kings. Finally, let us have faith in all God's promises, and we shall undoubtedly find him true in them.

units.la: Sed ad institutam Lucae narrationem redeamus, qua docetur, quid Ioanne iam in lucem ediso praeterea sit factum. Audierunt (inquit) vicini & cognati eius, quod magnifice sua misericordia erga illam vsus esset Dominus, & ei gratulabantur. Est ergo hic vetus mos, quo ijs gratulamur, quae felici partu leuatae liberos pepererunt. Neque hoc absque ratione pijs faciunt. Nam per se ingens Dei beneficium est, liberos ex se progenitos videre, in quibus parentes quasi renouiscunt, & qui sua accessione genus humanum augent. Ideo Christus, mulierem, cum peperit, doloris sui non amplius recordari ait, eo quod hominem ex se in mundum progenitum esse videat. Meretur ergo hoc beneficium, vt & Deo gratias agamus, & illis ex animo gratulemur, quibus illud contigit.
units.tr: But let us return to the account Luke has undertaken, in which we are taught what happened next, once John had been brought into the light. "The neighbours and relatives," it says, "heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her." So there is here an old custom by which we congratulate those who, relieved by a happy delivery, have borne children. Pious people do this not without reason. For it is in itself a great blessing of God to see children born from oneself, in whom parents are as it were renewed, and who by their addition increase the human race. Therefore Christ says that a woman, when she has given birth, no longer remembers her sorrow, because she sees a human being born into the world from herself. This blessing therefore deserves that we both give thanks to God and wish joy from our hearts to those to whom it has come.

units.la: Adhaec ipsa rei necessitas requirit, vt simul apud Deum pijs precibus instemus, vt tam nostri quam aliorum liberi recte instituantur, & in ijs proficiant, quae ipsorum saluti & prouehendae gloriae Dei seruiunt. Docet enim experientia, quam procliuis ad lasciuiam sit iuuentus, vt vix vlla parentum & institutorum diligentia sufficiat, nisi nos suo spiritu Deus in hoc opere tam sancto & necessario adiuuet. At in hoc hodie plerique negligentissimi sunt. Seruatur quidem vulgo mos, quo puerperis aut e puerperio primum prodeuntibus gratulamur; at qui de liberorum institutione serio cogitent, paucos est videre. Publica igitur authoritate opus erat, quam hic eos in primis adhibere oportebat, qui Ecclesiae & Reipub. praesunt. Simul vero generalem doctrinam hoc exemplum continet. Agnoscunt vicini illi & cognati misericordiam Dei, cuius magnificum sane specimen erga Elizabetam editum videbant. Itaque quod Dei opus peculiare cernimus, mox in eo illius bonitatem, iustitiam, sapientiam, veritatem & omnipotentiam obseruemus, vt his consideratis nostrae institutioni & aedificationi seruiant, quae prius fortuita videbantur. Qui hoc non faciunt, ij ex eorum numero sunt, quos Isaias hoc nomine reprehendit, quod circa gulae & ventris studium occupati non considerent opus Domini. Deinde ad nos quoque pertinere putemus, quae cum alijs aguntur. Iubet hoc charitatis lex, & de eodem nos communis omnium fors & conditio admonet. Quia enim eiusdem corporis membra & ijsdem casibus omnes obnoxij sumus, aliorum fortuna perinde vt nostra nos affici conuenit. Itaque secundum Apostoli praeceptum gaudeamus cum gaudentibus, quos aliqua peculiari gratia Deus dignatur, ploremus item cum plorantibus, quos aliquis triftior casus exercet. Etenim nimis turpiter peccant inuidi aemulatores, quos aliorum felicitas vrit, & qui perinde faciunt, ac si foli digni sint, quibus benefaciat Deus; neque minor eorum culpa est, qui quasi ipsi extra omnem fortunae casum constituti sint, omnium aliorum calamitates absque gemitu & siccis oculis intuentur. Sunt hi ἀσοροι illi, qui naturalibus affectibus destituuntur, & quales nouissimis temporibus venturos esse, olim Paulus praedixit. Pagnat hoc malum hodie passim, imo tanta est nostri seculi durities, vt non priuatas modo, verumetiam publicas calamitates plerique negligant, modo ipsis in pace & otio voluptuari liceat. Sed sit ferè iusto Dei iudicio, vt proprijs malis tandem doleant, qui alienis condolere nolunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the very nature of the matter requires that we at the same time earnestly pray to God that our children, and the children of others, may be rightly brought up and may make progress in those things that serve their salvation and the advancement of God's glory. Experience teaches how prone youth is to wantonness, so that hardly any diligence of parents and teachers suffices unless God by his Spirit helps us in this so holy and necessary work. Yet today most people are very careless about this. It is indeed the common custom to congratulate women who have just given birth, or who are coming out of childbed; but there are few to be seen who think seriously about the upbringing of their children. Therefore public authority was needed, and it was especially those who preside over the Church and the commonwealth who ought to apply it here. At the same time, this example contains a general teaching. Those neighbours and relatives recognised the mercy of God, whose remarkable proof they had seen in the case of Elizabeth. So when we see a work of God that is special, we should straightway observe in it his goodness, justice, wisdom, truth and omnipotence, so that, having considered these, we may apply them to our instruction and edification, things which before seemed accidental. Those who do not do this belong to the number of those whom Isaiah reproves for this, that, busy with the pursuit of the belly and of gluttony, they do not consider the work of the Lord. Next, let us also think that what is done to others concerns us. The law of charity commands this, and the common lot and condition of all reminds us of the same. For since we are all members of the same body and subject to the same misfortunes, it is fitting that we be moved by the fortune of others just as by our own. Therefore, following the Apostle's precept, let us rejoice with those who rejoice, those whom God honours with some special grace, and likewise let us weep with those who weep, those whom some more sorrowful accident troubles. For those envious rivals sin most shamefully, whom the happiness of others burns, and who act as if they alone deserved that God should do them good; and no less guilty are those who, as though they themselves were placed beyond every chance of fortune, look upon the calamities of all others without a groan and with dry eyes. These are the [ἄστοργοι] of whom Paul long ago foretold that they would come in the last times, people destitute of natural affections. This evil is widespread today; indeed the hardness of our age is so great that many neglect not only private but even public calamities, provided they may take their pleasure in peace and leisure. But it is almost by the just judgment of God that those who are unwilling to grieve with the misfortunes of others should at last grieve over their own evils.

units.la: Porro pergamus in historia, qua narratur, vicinos & cognatos illos die octauo rursus apud Zachariam conuenisse, vt puerum circumciderent. Solebant hoc domi apud parentes facere, nimirum quod Circumcisio non posset sine acerbissimo infantis cruciatu fieri, cui remedium absque mora adhiberi oportebat. Veruntamen videmus, hoc illos non inter paucos, sed in aliqua forma coetus ecclesiastici fieri, adquem vicini & cognati omnes conueniebant. Est hoc probe obseruandum in Sacramentis. Quia enim publica diuinae gratiae sigilla & fidei exercitia sunt, quae toti Ecclesiae Deus tradidit, minime admittendum, est vt priuata fiant, & ab vno atq; altero priuatim vsurpentur. Peccant igitur Papistae, qui vt baptismi administrationem obstetricibus permittunt, ita Coenam quoq; in Missam priuatam conuerterunt, in qua vnus edit & bibit, caeteris omnibus circa nudum & inane spectaculum occupatis. Inter alia autem hic diligenter obseruari meretur, quod Zacharias & Elizabeta filium suum circuncidi curauerunt. Erat Circumcisio signum foederis olim cum patribus initi. Eadem innatae corruptionis admonebat, cum in genitali membro fieret, & recens natis infantibus adhiberetur. Praeterea ad Christum remittebat, qui foederis illius complementum est, quia solus nos ab innata naturae vitiositate & inde enascentibus peccatis emundat. Itaque superuacanea poterat videri Circumcisio in Ioanne. Sciebant enim hunc ex singulari Dei consilio natum, & iam inde ab vtero matris Spiritu sancto esse implerum. Sciebant eum Christi praecursorem fore, & illi iam pridem testimonium tulisse quando ad Diuae Virginis salutationem in matris vtero exilijt. Sciebant bant praeterea iam in foribus adesse tempus illud correctionis, quo novum testamentum impleri, & umbras legales cum veritate commutari oportebat. Attamen non negligunt ideo Circumcisionis usum, quem a Deo tanta cum gravitate mandatum esse noverant: & quidem absque mora eodem die filium circumcidi curant, quem Deus huic Sacramento destinarat. Debent huius meminisse, quicunque verum Dei cultum profitentur. Et quia Christi praeceptum est, ut per baptismum in Ecclesiae suae societatem adoptentur, quotquot ad eam pertinent, coster autem huius membra etiam infantes esse, qui ex Christianis hominibus nascuntur, & hos quoque ad se venire velit Christus, etiam atque etiam curent parentes, ne quid hic negligant aut cunctentur. Etenim graviter peccant, qui baptismum leves ob causas diutius differunt, dum prius domi omnia ad fastum pro ipsorum arbitrio praeparentur, aut convivium instrui possit, quod gulae & ventri sufficit. Fit hoc vulgo hodie, & pleraque leviculum videtur, sed nulla venia dignum scelus est, non sanctius iudicare de Sacramentis communionis, quae nobis cum Christo Iesu intercedit, & ex qua omnis nostra salus dependet. Quid vero de Anabaptistis dicemus, qui ut verbum externum contemnunt, & Sacramentorum usum superuacaneum esse ducunt: ita infantes a baptismo prorsus reiiciunt, & a Christiana societate excludunt? Volunt hi quidem Sacramentorum vindices videri, qui eorum prophanationem vitare studeant, non vident autem, vel potius videre nolunt, quam atrocem iniuriam Ecclesiae Christi faciant, cuius conditionem deteriorem fingunt, quam olim veteris ante Christi incarnationem fuerit. Plus ergo apud nos vetus & receptus ecclesiae mos & sanctissimorum hominum exempla valeant, quam phanaticorum illorum deliria, qui nullis rationibus sese in viam reduci patiuntur, si quid defendendum semel suscepterunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us continue with the story, in which it is related that those neighbours and relatives gathered again on the eighth day at Zacharias' house, to circumcise the boy. They used to do this at home with the parents, doubtless because circumcision could not be performed without the most bitter pain to the infant, for which a remedy had to be applied without delay. Yet we see that they did this not among a few, but in a form of ecclesiastical assembly, to which all the neighbours and relatives came together. This is to be carefully observed concerning the sacraments. For since they are the public seals of divine grace and exercises of faith, which God has delivered to the whole Church, they must by no means be allowed to become private things, to be appropriated privately by one or another person. The Papists therefore sin, who while they allow the administration of baptism to midwives, have likewise turned the Supper into a private Mass, in which one eats and drinks while all the others are occupied with an empty and bare spectacle. But among other things, what is worth observing carefully here is that Zacharias and Elizabeth took care that their son should be circumcised. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant once made with the fathers. It also reminded of innate corruption, since it was performed on the genital member and applied to newborn infants. Moreover, it pointed to Christ, who is the fulfilment of that covenant, because he alone cleanses us from innate corruption of nature and the sins that spring from it. Therefore circumcision might seem superfluous in the case of John. For they knew that he had been born by a singular counsel of God, and that from the womb of his mother he had already been filled with the Holy Spirit. They knew that he would be Christ's forerunner, and had already borne witness to him long before, when he leaped in his mother's womb at the Virgin's greeting. They knew also that the time of correction was now at the door, in which the new covenant had to be fulfilled and the legal shadows exchanged for the truth. Yet they did not therefore neglect the use of circumcision, which they knew had been commanded by God with such solemnity; and indeed they took care that on that same day, without delay, the son whom God had destined for this sacrament should be circumcised. Whoever professes the true worship of God ought to remember this. And since it is Christ's command that all who belong to his Church should be adopted into its fellowship by baptism, and since the members of this Church are infants too, namely those born of Christian people, and since Christ wishes these also to come to him, parents should take the greatest care, again and again, that they neglect or delay nothing here. For those sin grievously who for trivial reasons postpone baptism for long, while at home everything is prepared for show according to their own pleasure, or a feast is arranged that suffices for gluttony and the belly. This is commonly done today, and it seems a rather small thing; but it is a crime deserving no pardon, not to judge the sacraments of the communion that we have with Christ Jesus, on which all our salvation depends, as holy as they ought to be. But what shall we say of the Anabaptists, who, while they despise the outward Word, also think the use of the sacraments superfluous, and so entirely reject infants from baptism and exclude them from the Christian fellowship? These men indeed wish to seem the defenders of the sacraments, who strive to avoid their profanation; but they do not see, or rather do not want to see, what a dreadful injury they inflict on the Church of Christ, whose condition they picture worse than it was of old, before the incarnation of Christ. Therefore the ancient and accepted custom of the Church, and the examples of the holiest men, should count for more with us than the ravings of those fanatics, who will not allow themselves to be brought back to the right way by any reasons, once they have undertaken to defend something.

units.la: Caeterum in Ioannis Circumcisionem contentio incidit memorabilis, & cuius descriptio considerationem diligentissima meretur. Ea de nomine quod infanti imponi debebat, exorta est. Fuit enim hic vetus mos, ut infantibus in Circumcisione nomina imponerentur, ut hodie inter Christianos fieri solet, quando per baptismum in Ecclesiae societatem adoptantur. Ratio eius est, ut quoties nominis nostri recordamur, simul etiam cogitemus, ubi aut quando illud nobis sit datum, & ita simul officij nostri admoneamur, quod in hoc potissimum consistit, ut quoniam in Christi Iesu mortem baptizamur (ut Apostolus scribit) simul cum eo moriamur peccato, & ad vitae novitatem resurgamus: ut denique in Iesu Christi militiam ascripti, eius auspiciis subq eius signo fortiter dimicemus adversus hostes illius, peccatum, mundum, diabolum, & omnia ea, quibus oppugnat regnum illius. Adeo nihil in Ecclesia Christi fortuitum esse voluit Spiritus sanctus, ut certam quoque nominum imponendorum rationem esse voluerit. Atqui constat antiquitus pios patres hoc etiam observauisse, ut suis liberis nomina vel ex prophetica spiritus suggestione, quae de illorum officio aut fine, cui destinati erant, admonebantur, vel ex certo aliquo eventu impositum esse. Sic Iacob a planta aut supplantatione nomen accepit, Samuel ab eo, quod matris Annae preces exaudiisset Deus: & Moses filium sibi peregre agenti natum Gersonem dixit: ut nunc infinita alia huius generis praeteream. At posteris temporibus, ne nullus omnino esset fingendorum nominum modus, hoc a pijs fere observatum fuit, ut ex se natis liberis ea imponerent, quae suae gentis hominibus vsitatissima fuerant sem per, & quae vel maiorum suorum vel veterum beneficiorum Dei memoriam conseruare, aut in memtem revocare poterant. Quem morem istos etiam obseruauisse, ex verbis eorum patet. Et laudem merentur, quod parentis, optimi viri & sanctissimi Sacerdotis nomen huic puero indere voluerunt, neque peregrinum aliquod & insolens quaerunt: ut hodie solent, qui ut eruditionem suam ostentent, aut inani fuco sese venditent, suis liberis nomina velignota prorsus vulgo, vel etiam prophana imponunt, quae ab hominibus sanguinarijs & sceleratis desumunt, quorum memoria pijs merito inuisa esse debebat. Veruntamen pio instituto illi errant, eo quod Dei consilium & praeceptum ignorarent, quod illi per Angelum suum Zachariae dederat. Itaque mater Elizabeta, quae procul dubio per maritum ea de re scripto certior facta fuit, illis contradicit, & Ioannem vult dici. Et magnum animi affectum verba eius referunt, quando ex abrupto exclamans ait: Nequaquam, sed vocabitur Ioannes. Sed huic rursus sese opponunt cognati atq; vicini, & communi more illius institutum confutare volunt, dicentes. Nemo est in cognatione tua, qui vocetur ista nomine. Attamen ne quid insolentius agant in re aliena patris sententiam rescire cupiunt: qui postulata tabella, scribit: Ioan
units.tr: Moreover, a memorable dispute arose over the circumcision of John, and its account deserves the most careful consideration. It arose concerning the name that was to be given to the infant. For it was an ancient custom that infants were given names at circumcision, as today among Christians it is customary when they are adopted into the fellowship of the Church by baptism. The reason for this is that whenever we recall our name, we should at the same time think where or when it was given to us, and so be reminded of our duty, which consists chiefly in this: that, since we are baptized into the death of Christ Jesus (as the Apostle writes), we should die together with him to sin, and rise again to newness of life; and finally, enlisted in the service of Jesus Christ, we should fight bravely under his auspices and by his sign against his enemies, sin, the world, the devil, and all those things by which they assail his kingdom. So much did the Holy Spirit will that nothing in the Church of Christ should be accidental, that he also willed there to be a certain rule for the imposition of names. Yet it is established that the godly fathers of old also observed this, that names were given to their children either by the prophetic prompting of the Spirit, by which they were reminded of the office or end for which they were destined, or from some particular event. Thus Jacob received his name from the heel or supplanting, Samuel from the fact that God had heard the prayers of his mother Hannah, and Moses named the son born to him while he was a stranger abroad Gershom; and I pass over now countless other examples of this kind. But in later times, lest there should be no rule at all for the making up of names, it was generally observed by the pious that they gave to the children born to them those names which had always been most usual among the people of their own nation, and which could preserve or recall the memory of their ancestors or of God's ancient benefits. That this custom was observed by these people also is plain from their words. And they deserve praise because they wished to give this boy the name of his father, a most excellent and holy priest, and did not seek some foreign and unusual name, as those do today who, to show off their learning or to sell themselves with empty show, give their children names quite unknown to the common people, or even profane ones, taken from bloodthirsty and wicked men, whose memory the godly ought rightly to abhor. Yet those people erred in their godly intention, because they did not know the counsel and command of God, which he had given to Zacharias through his angel. Therefore the mother Elizabeth, who doubtless had been informed of the matter by her husband in writing, contradicts them and says that he is to be called John. And her words express a great emotion of spirit, when she exclaims suddenly: "No, but he shall be called John." But the relatives and neighbours oppose her in turn, and wish to refute her decision by the common custom, saying: "There is no one in your family who is called by that name." Yet, lest they should act too presumptuously in another's affair, they want to learn the father's opinion, and having asked for a writing tablet, he writes: "Ioan"

units.la: Ostenditur de Ioannis nomine. nes est nomen eius. Quod etsi illis admirationem moueat, desinunt tamen contra dicere, vt qui ista non sine numine fieri iam demum intelligere incipiant. Atqui mirum alicui videri poterat ista tam diligenter descripsi: sed non mirabimur, si cogitemus, nos hic de rebus cognitu & obseruatu maxime necessarijs admoneri. Primo enim adumbratur, perpetuas lites fore inter praecones gratiae Dei (ex qua Ioannem denominatum fuisse iam ante diximus) & eos, qui Iudaica legalis iustitiae fiducia turgent. Cur ergo contentionibus nostri seculi offendimur, quae circa hoc argumentum maxime versantur, quod alij quidem Dei gratiae, nobis in Christo exhibitae confidunt: alij vero suorum operum & propriae iustitiae meritum stabilire contendunt? Deinde memorabile admodum est, quod in Zacharia et Elizabeta nobis proponitur, obedientiae exemplum. Etenim per se indifferens est, quo nomine appelletur, quando nomina ad hominis salutem nihil faciunt. Sed quia isti certum & expressum Dei mandatum acceperant, nolunt aliquid facere, quod illi aduersetur, quamuis in contrariam partem rationes essent multae & graues. Nam vt vicini dicebant, nemo vnquam in ipsorum cognatione hoc nomine dictus fuerat. Ergo insolens & affectatum nimis poterat videri, filio nomen eiusmodi imponere, quod magnum quid & insolitum portendebat. Adhaec iuniiles nimium & aequo morosiores fortasse videbantur, qui se in re tantilla toti cognationi & vicinitae opponerent. At nihil huius mouet sanctissimos coniuges, qui iam ante didicerant, Dei verbum omnibus argumentis praeualere, quae ex humanae rationis scrinio depromuntur. Et haec illa obedientia est, quam in Lege Deus requirit, monens, ne quod nobis bonum videtur faciamus, neue ab ipsius mandatis vel ad dextram vel ad sinistram deflectamus, id est, ne quid contra ipsius voluntatem vel deuoto ad peccandum animo, vel pia & bona intentione designemus. Debebant exemplum hoc diligenter obseruare, qui hodie veterem ecclesiae morem & multorum seculorum consuetudinem vrgent. Nam vt D. Cyprianus olim dicebat, quae apud quosdam obrepsit consuetudo, minime impedire debet, quo minus Veritas praevaleat & vincat. Nam consuetudo sine Veritate vetustas erroris est. Quae enim obstinatio, quaeue praesumptio est, humanam traditionem diuinae dispositioni anteponere, nec animaduertere indignari & irasci Deum, quoties diuina praecepta soluit & praeterit humana traditio? Frustra igitur qui ratione vincuntur, consuetudinem nobis opponunt, quasi consuetudo maior sit Veritate. Quid vero de consuetudine opus est dicere, quando constat ne ipsam quidem religionem & diuinitus instituta sacra nos ab obedientiae debito eximere, quo nos sibi Deus obstrinxit: sicuti Saulis exemplo docemur, cui Samuel dicebat: Obedire praestantius est sacrificijs, & auscultare praestat arietum adipi? 1. Samuelis 15.
units.tr: It is shown concerning the name of John: "John" is his name. Although this moved them to wonder, they stop contradicting, since they now begin to understand that these things do not happen without the will of God. Yet it might seem strange that I have described these matters so carefully, but we shall not wonder if we consider that here we are reminded of things that are most necessary to know and to observe. For first, it is foreshadowed that there will be perpetual quarrels between the heralds of the grace of God (from which grace John was named, as we have said before) and those who swell with confidence in Jewish legal righteousness. Why then are we troubled by the disputes of our own age, which turn chiefly on this question: some trust in the grace of God shown to us in Christ, while others strive to establish the merit of their own works and their own righteousness? Next, the example of obedience set before us in Zacharias and Elizabeth is very memorable. For in itself it makes no difference by what name a child is called, since names contribute nothing to a person's salvation. But because these two had received a certain and express command of God, they were unwilling to do anything that opposed it, although there were many weighty reasons on the other side. For, as the neighbours said, no one had ever been called by this name in their family. So it might seem strange and too much of an affectation to give the son a name of this kind, which seemed to foretell something great and unusual. Besides, they may have seemed too youthful and perhaps rather too stubborn, to set themselves against the whole family and neighbourhood over such a trifling matter. But none of this moved these most holy spouses, who had already learned that the Word of God prevails over all the arguments that are drawn from the storehouse of human reason. And this is the obedience that God requires in the Law, warning us not to do what seems good to us, nor to turn aside from his commands either to the right hand or to the left; that is, not to devise anything contrary to his will, whether with a mind bent on sinning or with a pious and good intention. Those who today urge the old custom of the Church and the practice of many centuries ought to observe this example carefully. For as Saint Cyprian once said, whatever custom has crept in among some people ought in no way to hinder truth from prevailing and conquering. For custom without truth is the antiquity of error. What obstinacy or presumption it is to set human tradition above the divine ordinance, and not to notice that God is angry and indignant whenever human tradition breaks and passes over divine precepts! Therefore those who are overcome by reason set custom against us in vain, as if custom were greater than truth. But why need we say anything about custom, when it is plain that not even religion itself, nor sacred things instituted by God, release us from the debt of obedience by which God has bound us to himself? We are taught this by the example of Saul, to whom Samuel said: "To obey is better than sacrifices, and to listen is better than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 15).

units.la: Sed non opus est testimonijs aut exemplis alienis agere, quando praesens historia abunde docet, quam delectetur Deus eorum officijs, qui ipsi fidele obsequium praestat. Fuit enim illius obedientiae multiplex fructus, siue Zachariam, siue reliquos spectemus, qui illius negotij spectatores fuerunt. De illo etenim sic scribit Lucas: Apertum est os eius illico, & lingua eius, & loquebatur benedicens Deo. Atqui prius dictum fuit, Zachariae sermonis & linguae vsum ereptum fuisse, eo quod Dei promissis non credidit, & contra illa disputare ausus fuit. Erat haec grauis admodum multa, quod cum publica ignominia coniuncta esset, et malenolus multa in illum dicendi occasionem praeberet. Nunc vero, quia Dei praeceptum constanter vrget, & nullis rationibus sese ab eo dimoueri finit, no modo linguae vsum recipit, sed insuper noua gloria a Deo ornatur, quando in laudes eius cum omnium admiratione erumpit, & insuper plenus spiritu sancto (vt suo loco dicetur) de Christo & regno eius vaticinium contexit plenum consolationis. Ita solet laetissimus esse finis afflictionum, quas pij inter du sustinent: eo quod ad Dominum conuersi resipiscunt atque emendantur. Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, obedientiae esse vnicam rationem, qua poenas a Deo immissas subterfugere & ex afflictionibus elabi possimus. Clamat enim per prophetas Dominus: Conuertimini ad me, et ego conuertar ad vos. Et alibi manuum suam adhuc extensam esse ait ad percutiendum, eo quod ipsi redire nolint ad eum, qui hucusque ipsos percusserit. Quod vnum si hodie omnes obseruarent, minus offenderentur nostri seculi calamitatibus, & non multis disputationibus de via effugij sibi opus esse viderent. At simul eorum officium adumbratur, qui ex poenis liberati sunt. Benedicit Deo Zacharias, & huic iam con secrat linguam, qua prius aduersus illius promissionem disputando abusus erat. Deum ergo glorificare de-
units.tr: But there is no need to appeal to the testimonies and examples of others, since the present history teaches abundantly how much God delights in the duties of those who render him faithful obedience. For there was a manifold fruit of that obedience, whether we look at Zacharias or at the others who were witnesses of that business. For Luke writes of him as follows: "His mouth was opened at once, and his tongue, and he spoke, blessing God." Yet it was said earlier that Zacharias had lost the use of his speech, because he did not believe God's promises and dared to argue against them. This was a very grave affliction, since it was joined with public disgrace and gave the malicious many occasions to speak against him. But now, because he steadfastly holds to God's command and allows himself to be turned from it by no arguments, he not only recovers the use of his tongue but is also adorned with a new glory from God, when with the admiration of all he breaks out into praise of him, and, filled with the Holy Spirit (as will be said in its place), he composes a prophecy full of consolation concerning Christ and his kingdom. So the most joyful outcome usually comes at the end of the afflictions that the godly endure, because, turned to the Lord, they repent and are amended. From this a general teaching ought to be drawn: obedience is the only way by which we can escape the punishments sent by God and get free of afflictions. For the Lord cries through the prophets: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you." And elsewhere he says that his hand is still stretched out to strike, because they are unwilling to return to him who has hitherto struck them. If all people observed this one thing today, they would be less troubled by the calamities of our age, and would not think they needed many disputations about the way of escape. At the same time the duty of those who have been freed from punishments is set forth. Zacharias blesses God, and now consecrates to him that tongue which he had before misused by arguing against his promise. So those who feel that they have been freed by his hand ought to glorify God...

units.la: Isa. 4. 9. tare debent, qui eius manu se liberatos esse sentiunt, sicuti nuper ex Psalmo quinquagesimo docuimus. At non sufficiet hoc verbis fecisse, nisi simul ad prouehendam Dei gloriam nostris facultatibus vniuersis vtamur, quibus contra illum aliquando abusi sumus. Debet ergo hoc transferri ad omnia tam animi quam corporis & fortunae bona, quorum omnium hic demum vsus legitimus est, si eius gloriae seruiant, qui illa nobis dedit.
units.tr: Isa. 4. 9. ...ought to glorify God, as we recently taught from the fiftieth Psalm. But it will not be enough to have done this in words, unless we also use all our faculties to advance the glory of God, the faculties with which we have at some time abused him. So this must be applied to all the goods of mind, body and fortune, of which the only lawful use is this: that they serve the glory of him who gave them to us.

units.la: Caeterum non in solo Zacharia huius obedientiae fructus haeret, sed ad plures alios redundat. Nam primo timor sanctus oboritur vicinis omnibus, qui tantae rei admiratione abrepti videbat a Deo magnum quid & insolitum agi. Deinde in totam regionem finitima rei fama diuulgatur. Ad haec quotquot ista audiunt, simul ea corde suo reponunt, deq; ijs inter se colloquuntur, vt omnium fere communis vox audiatur: Quis nam puerulus hic erit? Et haec quidem causa praecipua est, propter quam haec omnia Deus fieri voluit: vt nimirum opinionem de Ioanne praeclaram omnes animo concipe-rent, & facilius postea crederent testimonio, quod ille Christo perhibuit. Nec dubium mihi est, plu-res qui ista vel tunc viderunt, vel postea ex suis audierunt, plurimum ijs adiutos fuisse, vt doctrinae Ioannis celerius accederent. Et hunc nobis quoque istorum omnium vsum esse debere, initio dixi-mus. Debent autem simili studio obseruari omnia opera Dei singularia, quae propter nos multa quo-tidie fiunt, vt ex illis in ipsius cognitione & pietate vera proficiamus.
units.tr: Moreover, the fruit of this obedience does not cling to Zacharias alone, but spreads to many others. For first, a holy fear comes upon all the neighbours, who, carried away with wonder at so great a matter, saw that something great and unusual was being done by God. Then the report of the thing is spread abroad through the whole neighbouring region. Besides, all who hear these things lay them up in their hearts and talk about them among themselves, so that almost the common voice of all is heard: "What then will this little child be?" And this is indeed the chief reason why God willed all these things to happen: that everyone might conceive in his mind a high opinion of John, and might afterwards more readily believe the testimony that he bore to Christ. Nor do I doubt that many who saw these things then, or afterwards heard of them from their own people, were greatly helped by them to come more quickly to the teaching of John. And we, too, ought to have this use of all these things, as I said at the beginning. Moreover, all the singular works of God, which many times daily happen for our sake, ought to be observed with a similar zeal, so that by means of them we may make progress in the true knowledge and piety of God.

units.la: Additur huic narrationi: Manus autem Domini erat cum eo, puerulo nimirum Ioanne. Id est, Deus illi sua virtute & gratia sic adfuit, vt omnes perspicerent, hic singulare quid agi, & infantem istum in virum non vulgarem aliquando euasurum esse. Id vero futurum Angelus praedixerat. Et est hoc etiam in genere applicandum nostris infantibus. De illis enim pronuntiat Christus, quod Deo patri curae sint, quod ipsorum sit regnum caelorum. Nunquam ergo nobis excidat, Deum esse nostrum ab vtero matris: agnoscamus autem in his illius veritatem, misericordiam, iustitiam & sa-pientiam, quarum virtutum thesauros saluberrimos nobis propositum in filio suo Iesu Christo, domi-no & seruatore nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It is added to this narrative: "And the hand of the Lord was with him," that is, with the little child John. That is, God was so present with him by his power and grace that everyone perceived that something singular was being done here, and that this infant would one day turn out to be no ordinary man. The angel had foretold that this would happen. And this should also be applied in general to our own infants. For of them Christ declares that they are cared for by God the Father, and that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them. Let us therefore never forget that God is ours from the mother's womb; and let us acknowledge in these children his truth, mercy, justice and wisdom, and the most wholesome treasures of these virtues set before us in his Son Jesus Christ, our only Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIIII.
units.tr: Homily 14.

units.la: Et Zacharias pater eius repletus est spiritu sancto, prophetauitq; dicens: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quod visitavit et fecit redemptionem populum suum, & erexit cornu salutis nobis in domo Dauidis pueri sui: prout locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a seculo fuerunt, prophetarum suorum: Salutem nimirum ex inimicis nostris, & e manu omnium, qui oderunt nos. Vt faceret misericordiam erga patres nostros, ac memor esset testamenti sui sancti, & iuriurandi, quod iurauit Abrahamo patri nostro: nimirum se daturum nobis, vt sine metu, e manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, seruiamus ipsi in sanctitate & iustitia coram ipso cunctis diebus vitae nostrae.
units.tr: And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and wrought redemption for his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from the beginning of the world: salvation indeed from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us. To show mercy to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant and the oath which he swore to Abraham our father: that he would grant us that, being rescued without fear from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our life."

units.la: Ioannis Baptistae natiuitate multis argumentis illustrem esse oportuit, vt omnibus constaret, illum a Deo missum esse, & plus fidei haberet testimonium, quod de Christo tulit. Inter alia autem, quae in ea acciderunt, cum primis memorabile est, quod Zachariae, qui initio propter incredulitatem mutus fuerat factus, subito & cum multorum admiratione vsus linguae restituitur, quando ille Dei praecepto constanter obtemperat. Nec enim vulgarem modo sermonis vsum recipit, verumetiam spi-ritu sancto repletus prophetat: & sic quidem, vt non solum vetera prophetarum oracula interpretetur, sed ipse etiam ex peculiari spiritus suggestione vaticinium contexat de toto humanae redemptionis ne-gotio, quod tunc praeforibus erat. Quo exemplo inter alia admonemur, quam liberaliter Deus peccata remittat ijs, qui ad ipsum vere et ex animo converuntur: ita nimirum, vt eos non modo poenis liberet, quibus peccata illorum prius castigauit, sed insuper donis maioribus ornet, & rebus excellentioribus idoneos reddat. Simile gratia Petrus quoq; expertus est, quae post abnegationem facta ad se reuersum & apostolicae functioni Christus restituit, & uberiori spiritus virtute donauit, vt primus ad praedicandu prodiret, & quàm plurimos ad fidem verâ conuerteret. Quod ipsum postea & Paulo accidit, qui ex immani persecutore ecclesiæ eximium & electum Iesu Christi organum factus est, quando illius vocationi se morigerû præbuit. Nemo igitur de Dei bonitate et misericordia desperet, sed hoc nobis persuasissimum sit, illum interdum nostris peccatis prouocatum opus ab ingenio suo quasi alienum (vt propheta loquitur) facere, vt postea nobis ad ipsum conuersis, occasionem habeat, amplioris gratiæ in nos effundendæ. Sed ad Zachariæ vaticinium accedamus, quod Carmine constat, & circa duo potissimum capita versatur. Primò Dei misericordiam & veritatem celebrat, qui salutem olim patribus promissam nunc præstet: et ea occasione de humani generis redemptione sic disserit, vt simul Christi regnum describat, quidq; nobis ex illo sperandum sit, doceat. Altero de filio suo Ioanne vaticinatur, deque eius officio, cui illum destinatum esse, ex Angelo intellexerat.
units.tr: It was fitting that the birth of John the Baptist should be made illustrious by many signs, so that it might be plain to all that he was sent by God, and that the testimony he bore concerning Christ might carry more weight. Among the other things that happened then, the most memorable is that Zechariah, who had been made mute at first because of his unbelief, is suddenly restored to the use of his tongue, to the great amazement of many, when he steadfastly obeys God's command. For he not only recovers ordinary speech, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesies; and he does so in such a way that he not only interprets the ancient oracles of the prophets but also, by a special prompting of the Spirit, composes a prophecy about the whole business of human redemption, which was then at the doors. By this example we are admonished, among other things, how generously God forgives sins to those who truly and from the heart turn to him: namely, that he not only frees them from the punishments by which he had previously chastised their sins, but also adorns them with greater gifts and makes them fit for more excellent tasks. Peter too experienced a similar grace: after his denial, Christ received him back, restored him to the apostolic office, and endowed him with a richer power of the Spirit, so that he came forward first to preach and converted very many to the true faith. The same happened afterwards to Paul, who from a fierce persecutor of the Church became a remarkable and chosen instrument of Jesus Christ, when he showed himself obedient to his calling. Let no one therefore despair of God's goodness and mercy; but let this be most firmly fixed in us: that he is sometimes provoked by our sins to perform a work foreign to his nature (as the prophet says), so that afterwards, when we turn to him, he may have an occasion of pouring out more abundant grace upon us. But let us come to Zechariah's prophecy, which is composed in verse and turns chiefly on two heads. First, he celebrates God's mercy and truth, who now grants the salvation once promised to the fathers; and on that occasion he speaks of the redemption of mankind in such a way that he at the same time describes the kingdom of Christ and teaches what we ought to hope for from it. Second, he prophesies about his son John and about his office, for which he had learned from the angel that he was destined.

units.la: Propositio totius Carminis est: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israelis. Habet ista Epiphonematis speciem, quia ex abrupto et præter omnium expectationem exclamat, Deum illum prædicari & laudari debere, qui Israelem iam inde à prima gentis origine singulari fauore & bonitate complexus sit. Ista autem dicendo negotium hoc omne ad vnum authorem Deum refert, quæ vera est gratiarum actio, quam ille à nobis requiris, quando iubet, vt liberati ex aduersis ipsum glorificemus. Est hoc in omnibus Dei beneficijs diligenter obseruandum, ne quid nobisipsis tribuendo aduersus illum efferamur insolentius, et ab ipso datis bonis turpiter abutamur. Peccauit in hoc olim graviter Nabuchodonosor, & ideo rationis vsu amisso inter feras vitâ egit, vt ita Deum omnis boni authorem esse disceret. Et hodie ad eundem lapidem multi offendunt, qui mihi quodammodo cum ratione insanire videntur, quando inter tot nostræ infirmitatis et corruptissimæ naturæ argumenta adhuc superbire et suis viribus aut meritis aliquid tribuere audent. Non temere autem factum putabimus, quòd Dominum Deum Israelis dicit Zacharias. Num verò Iudæorum Deus solùm? inquit Paulus: Nonne & gentium? Certè & gentium. Israelitarum verò Deus fere dicitur in scripturis, quia illos præ aliis gentibus elegit, vt seipsum & voluntatem suam in illis toti mundo manifestaret. Cum illis ergo fœdus fecit, quo se ipsis obstrinxit; inter illos sui cultus sedem constituit, & quod omnia alia longe superat, filium suum ex illis homine nasci voluit. Et hæc quidem prisci patres diligenter obseruarunt, quibus frequenter in ore fuit Deus ille Israelis, vt maiorem consolationem haberent in tentationibus, quando Deum genti ipsorum peculiariter obstrictum, & se huius peculium esse cogitabant. Hinc vocēs illæ in Psalmis: Notus in Iuda Deus, præclarû nomen eius in Israele. In Salem est tabernaculum eius, & mansio eius in Zione. Nuntiat verbum suum Iacobo, & decreta sua atque iudicia sua Israeli: Non egit ad hunc modum cum vlla gente. Et constat pios ex eo efficacissimam consolationem petijsse, quòd ad se pritatim pertinere crederet promissiones, quibus sese toti genti Hebræorum Deus obstrinxerat. Debent ergo illas etiam ad se transferre hodie, quicunq; per fidem veri Israelitæ facti sunt. Quia enim promissionum omnium complementum est Christus, ad eos in primis illarum fructus pertinet, qui Christo per fidem sunt insiti. Itaque in medijs tentationibus hoc eos maximè consoletur, quòd Deum sciant suum Deum esse, & sibi hanc potestatem ab ipso Christo datam esse, vt illum patris nomine inuocare, & quidem suum patrem dicere possint. At simul officij sui meminerint, quod in eo consistit, vt Deo se totos vicissim consecrent, huic induisse adhæreant, & eundem fide vera colant, ne quando idem quod Iudæi patiantur, quos per incredulitatem & contumaciam suam ab illa dignitate excidisse Paulus testatur. Sequuntur rationes, cur Deus celebrari debeat, & his primum huius Cantici caput absoluitur.
units.tr: The theme of the whole hymn is: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel." This has the form of an epiphonema, since he exclaims abruptly and beyond all expectation that God is to be proclaimed and praised, who from the very first origin of the nation has embraced Israel with singular favour and goodness. In saying this, he refers the whole matter to God as the one author, and this is the true thanksgiving that he requires of us when he bids us, once delivered from adversity, to glorify him. This must be carefully observed in all of God's benefits, lest we, by attributing something to ourselves, become puffed up more insolently against him and shamefully abuse the goods given by him. Nebuchadnezzar sinned gravely in this once, and therefore, having lost the use of reason, he lived among the beasts, so that he might learn that God is the author of every good. And today many stumble over the same stone, who seem to me in some measure to be mad with reason, when amid so many proofs of our weakness and most corrupt nature they still dare to be proud and to ascribe something to their own strength or merits. We shall not think it without reason that Zechariah says "the Lord God of Israel." Is he, however, the God of the Jews only? says Paul; is he not of the Gentiles too? Certainly of the Gentiles too. But in the Scriptures God is commonly called the God of Israel, because he chose them above other nations, so that in them he might reveal himself and his will to the whole world. With them, therefore, he made a covenant by which he bound himself to them; among them he set the seat of his worship; and, what far surpasses all else, he willed that his Son should be born of them as a man. The ancient fathers observed this carefully, and the phrase "the God of Israel" was often on their lips, so that they might have greater consolation in temptations, when they considered that God was bound peculiarly to their nation and that they were his peculiar people. Hence those sayings in the Psalms: "God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. In Salem is his tabernacle, and his dwelling in Zion. He declares his word to Jacob, and his statutes and judgments to Israel; he has not dealt thus with any nation." And it is plain that the godly drew most effective consolation from this, believing that the promises by which God had bound himself to the whole nation of the Hebrews pertained to them personally. Therefore those who have become true Israelites through faith ought to apply them to themselves today too. For since Christ is the fulfilment of all the promises, the fruits of them belong first of all to those who have been grafted into Christ by faith. Hence, in the midst of temptations, this will console them most of all: that they know God to be their God, and that this power has been given to them by Christ himself, to invoke him by the name of Father, and indeed to call him their own Father. But at the same time let them remember their duty, which consists in this: that they consecrate themselves wholly to God in turn, cling to him in true faith, and worship the same God in sincere faith, lest at some time they suffer what the Jews suffered, who, as Paul testifies, through their unbelief and obstinacy fell from that dignity. Now follow the reasons why God ought to be celebrated, and with these the first head of this canticle is finished.

units.la: Primò autem laudandum esse ait, quòd inuiserit & redemerit populum suum. Inuisendi aut visitandi verbo vtitur more Hebræorû, & ad populi statum afflictissimum alludit. Quasi dicat: Fuimus aliquanto tempore mortalium miserrimi, vt à Deo omnino derelicti videri potuerimus, cùm in ecclesia simul & repub. nihil sanû & integrum esset. Sed respexit nos Deus tandè, & quodammodo ad nos redijt, vt redemptionem olim patribus promissam nunc reipsa præstaret. Debet ante ex hoc exemplo generalis doctrina peti, Deum sui populi curâ minimè negligere, licet opem aliquandiu differat. Sinit quidè nos exerceri, quia sic nobis opus est, ne nostri simul et ipsius immemores cū impio & pœnitere nescio mŭdo malè pereamus. Idè tamen, qui nos terrâ & puluerè esse nouit, nostræ infirmitatis memor est, et nos supra vires tëtari nö finit, imò vires nobis interea suffícit, quibus tentationū certamině certamina vincamus. Et quando tempus est, praeter omnem expectationem liberat. Sic olim factum, quando filiorum Israelis res in extremis constitutae erant, ut Deus foederis & promissionum omnium oblitus esse videretur, & Moses ipse apud Madianitas exularet. Tunc enim praeter spem huic apparens dicebat: Videndo vidi afflictionem populi mei, qui est in Ægypto, & audivi clamorem eorum, propter exactores quos habent: quoniam novi dolores eorum, & ideo descendi ut liberem eos de manu Ægyptiorum. Et huic simile exemplum est, quod in liberatione ex Babylone accidisse legimus. Quod autem publice fieri solet, id ipsum frequenter privatim quoque experiuntur, qui Deum ex fide vera invocant, & huius generis exempla quotidie multa cernimus. Visus eorum nobis hic esto, ne in afflictionibus desperemus, sed expectemus Dominum, neque excidat nobis dictum illud prophetae, qui in silentio & spe robur nostrum fore pollicetur. Isa.30.
units.tr: First, he says that God is to be praised because he has visited and redeemed his people. He uses the word "visit" in the manner of the Hebrews, alluding to the most wretched state of the people, as if he said: For some time we were the most miserable of mortals, so that we could seem to have been wholly forsaken by God, since in the Church and in the commonwealth alike nothing was sound or whole. But God at last looked upon us, and in a sense returned to us, so as in fact to bring about the redemption once promised to the fathers. From this example a general doctrine ought first to be drawn: that God by no means neglects the care of his people, although he may defer his help for a while. Indeed he allows us to be exercised, since we need this, lest, forgetful both of ourselves and of him, we perish wretchedly along with an impious world that knows not how to repent. Yet he who knows that we are dust and ashes remembers our weakness, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength; rather, in the meantime he supplies us with the strength by which we may overcome in the contest of temptations. And when the time comes, he delivers us beyond all expectation. So it was once, when the affairs of the children of Israel were at their lowest, so that God seemed to have forgotten the covenant and all his promises, and Moses himself was in exile among the Midianites. For then he appeared, beyond hope, and said: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows, and therefore I have come down to deliver them from the hand of the Egyptians." And a similar example is what we read happened at the deliverance from Babylon. What is commonly done publicly is often also experienced privately by those who call upon God in true faith, and we see many examples of this kind every day. Let their sight be before us here, so that we may not despair in afflictions, but wait for the Lord; and let not that saying of the prophet slip from our minds, who promises that our strength will lie in quietness and hope. Isa.30.

units.la: Sed evidentius docet Zacharias, quomodo populum suum iniuserit & redemerit Dominus. Erexit nobis (inquit) cornu salutis in domo Davidis pueri sui, prout locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a saeculo fuerunt, prophetarum suorum. Sunt haec desumpta ex Psalmo 132. ubi sic loquitur Dominus: Illic cornu David germinare faciam, lucernam paravi unctio meo. Per cornu autem intelligit regnum & robur, metaphora a cornutis animalibus sumpta, quorum vires fere in cornibus existunt. Estque metaphora haec frequens admodum in scripturis, & tam in malam quam in bonam partem sumitur. Nam Psal.75. ait Christus: Confringam omne cornu impiorum, cornua vero iustorum exaltabuntur. Et in Psalmo 112. de viro pio & benefico dicitur: Cornu eius altum erit cum gloria. Quibus addi potest, quod apud prophetas, Danielem in primis & Zachariam, regna huius mundi non uno loco per cornua adumbrantur. Quare verborum istorum sensus est, Deum nunc praestare quod olim promiserit, ut nimirum in Davidis domo regum illud salutiferum constituat, de quo Prophetae, homines sanctissimi, passim vaticinati sint. Promissiones, quae ad huius loci illustrationem faciunt, praeter illam quam ex Psal.132. adduximus, plurimae extant. Inter quas primum locum tenet, quae in posteriori Samuelis libro cap. septimo per Nathanum edita legitur. Exponitur eadem prolixe admodum in Psal.89. Et propheta Isaias de surculo aut germine ex trunco Isai enascituro vaticinatur. Nihil denique frequentius est, quam quod humana redemptio per Davidis regnum describitur, & ipse Christus Davidis nomine insignitur. Quae omnia Zacharias paucis hisce verbis pijs in mentem revocat. Continet autem simul descriptionem regni Christi, quam observasse non parum proderit, eo quod ad fidem confirmandam multum facit. Primo enim dum cornu dicit, illad potentiam & viri sti describitur bus instructum esse docet, quibus & sese tueatur, & adversariorum conatibus resistat. Quod de illo verissime dici, res ipsa testatur, quando et olim omnem adversariam potestatem Christus deuicit, & hodie regnum suum servat neque quicquam adversus illum pugnantibus, qui illud evertere cupiunt. Deinde idem hoc pijs atque credentibus regnum salutis est. Nam sublato & destructo diaboli regno peccata mundi expiavit Christus, iusticiam sempiternam reduxit, patri Deo nos reconciliavit, regni coelestis haeredes fecit, & nos vsque tuetur, ne sibi eripiantur, quos semel in ouiu suarum gregem adoptavit. Non ergo huius mundi regnis simile est regnum Christi. Illa enim subditis onerosa & molesta sunt, eo quod illi Reges suos alere cogantur, ijsdem tributa & vectigalia soluant, pro ijsdem bella gerant, & plerunque vix in conspectu illorum venire possint, si quam causam habent, in qua Regum patrocinio in primis opus erat. At nihil huius in Christi regno inuenitur. Is enim suos alit, & ut hoc posset, carnem & sanguinem suum pro illis tradidit. Idem dona spiritualia & corporalia inter suos liberalissime distribuit, ipse pro sua Ecclesia & singulis eius membris pugnat, & aures suas nobis faciles praebet, adeoque ad se invitat omnes, qui sese grauatos esse sentiunt. Magna ergo mundi huius infelicitas est, qui Regem tam beneficum faslidit, & Antichristum sibi ipsi imponit, quem perditionis filium scriptura dicit, eo quod & ipse perditus sit, & eos perdat secum, qui ipsum sequuntur. Praeterea non nouum est Christi regnum, sed omnium, quae unquam in mundo fuerunt, vetustissimum. Ut enim de illo vaticinati sunt prophetae, sic in aeterno Dei decreto fundatum est, & inter homines tunc coepit, quando salutis promissio primis parentibus data fuit: inde vero novis subinde incrementis confirmatum adhuc hodie durat, et deinceps quoque durabit usque ad consummationem seculi. Faciunt ista ad fidei Christianae & salutis nostrae certitudinem, quam turpiter & pernitiose labefactant, qui eunque prophetarum libros, quasi nihil ad nos pertinentes reiiciunt.
units.tr: But Zechariah teaches more clearly how the Lord has visited and redeemed his people. "He has raised up," he says, "a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old." These words are taken from Psalm 132, where the Lord speaks thus: "There will I make the horn of David to bud; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed." By "horn" he means kingdom and strength, a metaphor taken from horned animals, whose strength lies largely in their horns. This metaphor is very common in Scripture and is used both in a bad sense and in a good one. For Psalm 75 has Christ say: "I will break all the horns of the wicked, but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted." And Psalm 112 says of the godly and generous man: "His horn shall be exalted with glory." To these may be added that in the prophets, Daniel above all and Zechariah, the kingdoms of this world are in more than one place pictured by horns. The sense of these words, therefore, is that God now performs what he promised long ago, namely that he will establish in the house of David that saving kingdom of the kings about which the prophets, most holy men, prophesied everywhere. Many promises that help to illuminate this passage, besides the one we have quoted from Psalm 132, are extant. Among them the first place belongs to the promise given through Nathan, which is read in the seventh chapter of the second book of Samuel. The same is set out at great length in Psalm 89. And the prophet Isaiah prophesies of a shoot or branch that will spring from the stock of Jesse. Finally, nothing is more frequent than that human redemption is described through the kingdom of David, and Christ himself is marked with the name of David. Zechariah recalls all these things to the godly in a few words. At the same time he contains a description of the kingdom of Christ, which it will be no small profit to have observed, since it contributes greatly to the confirming of faith. For first, when he says "horn," he signifies power, and teaches that he is equipped with virtues by which he both defends himself and resists the attempts of his adversaries. That this is most truly said of him the thing itself bears witness, since Christ has at times overcome every adverse power, and today preserves his kingdom, nor does anything avail against those who fight against him and wish to overthrow it. Next, this same kingdom is a kingdom of salvation to the godly and believers. For, after the kingdom of the devil was taken away and destroyed, Christ expiated the sins of the world, brought back everlasting righteousness, reconciled us to God the Father, made us heirs of the heavenly kingdom, and guards us to the end, so that those whom once he adopted into the flock of his sheep may not be snatched from him. Therefore the kingdom of Christ is not like the kingdoms of this world. For those kingdoms are burdensome and troublesome to their subjects, because the kings compel them to support them, pay them taxes and tolls, wage wars for them, and for the most part can scarcely be approached by them, even when they have some cause in which the patronage of the king was above all needed. But none of this is found in the kingdom of Christ. For he feeds his own, and in order to do this he gave up his flesh and blood for them. He also distributes spiritual and bodily gifts most generously among his people, he himself fights for his Church and for each of its members, and he offers his ears readily to us, and so invites all who feel themselves burdened to come to him. Great, then, is the unhappiness of this world, which scorns so beneficent a King and sets up for itself the Antichrist, whom Scripture calls the son of perdition, because he himself is lost and destroys with himself those who follow him. Moreover, the kingdom of Christ is not new, but the most ancient of all those that have ever existed in the world. For just as the prophets prophesied of it, so it was founded in the eternal decree of God, and it began among men when the promise of salvation was given to our first parents; from that time it has been strengthened by new increases, and it endures even today, and will endure hereafter to the end of the age. These things serve to make the Christian faith and our salvation certain, and those who shamefully and perniciously undermine them, rejecting the books of the prophets as though they had nothing to do with us, do the opposite.

units.la: Cap. L
units.tr: Chapter L

units.la: Caeterùm pergit Zacharias, & clarius adhuc describit redemptionem illam, quâ olim Deus per prophetas suos promiserat, nunc autè in Christo velit praestare. Salutem (inquit) id est, liberationem aut redemptionē (sic enim Hebraei Salutis vocabulo interdū utuntur) ex inimicis nostris, & è manu omnium qui oderunt nos. Atqui nō possunt ista intelligi de liberatione ex tyrannide, quâ Iudaei tunc per Romanos & Herodem premebantur. Constat enim illos sub hac deinceps quoq; laborauisse, imò Romanorum armis non multò post excisos & in totū orbē dispersos fuisse, cum increduli et contumaces esse pergerent. Ergo de spirituali liberatione loquitur, quâ totius humani generis salus continetur.
units.tr: Moreover, Zechariah goes on and describes still more clearly that redemption which God had once promised through his prophets and now wishes to bestow in Christ. "Salvation," he says, that is, deliverance or redemption (for so the Hebrews sometimes use the word salvation), "from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us." But these words cannot be understood of deliverance from the tyranny under which the Jews were then oppressed by the Romans and Herod. For it is certain that they laboured under this afterwards as well, and indeed a little later they were cut down by Roman arms and scattered throughout the whole world, since they persisted in unbelief and obstinacy. Therefore he speaks of a spiritual deliverance, in which the salvation of the whole human race is contained.

units.la: Habuit illud & adhuc habet hostes acerrimos & omnium crudelissimos: quorum princeps est Satā siue diabolus, quem Christus in veritate non perstitisse, & iam inde ab initio homicida fuisse ait. Is enim cùm sua culpa ipse à dignitate sua excidisset, invidia stimulante, hominis quoq; primum creati saluti insidias struxit, et effecit, vt Dei mandatū transgrederetur, et ita Dei imagine amissa peccati seruus fieret. Hinc exorta est maledictio, quæ vt terra nobis aduersaria et ad proferendas fruges atq; alia vitæ subsidia difficilem fecit: sic omnes alias huius mundi partes nobis infestas reddidit. Huc ergo debemus quod coelitus demissæ tempestates prouentus agrorum intercipiunt, quòd modò ignem nobis inimicum sentimus, modò aquarum vel inundatione vel penuria perclitamur: quòd aërem nobis noxium experimur: quòd animalia aduersus nos ferociunt: quòd denique nihil tam minutum aut vile est, quod nō sufficiat nobis perdendis: imò quòd ipse homo homini hostis et daemon sit.
units.tr: That deliverance had, and still has, most bitter enemies, and the cruellest of all: the chief of them is Satan or the devil, of whom Christ says that he did not stand in the truth and has been a murderer from the beginning. For when he had fallen from his dignity through his own fault, goaded by envy, he also laid snares for the salvation of man, newly created, and brought it about that he transgressed the command of God, and so, having lost the image of God, became a slave of sin. Hence there arose the curse, which made the earth hostile to us and difficult for bringing forth fruits and other means of sustaining life; in the same way it made all other parts of this world hostile to us. To this we owe it that storms sent from heaven destroy the produce of the fields, that we at one time feel fire as an enemy, at another are endangered by floods or by drought; that we experience the air as harmful; that animals grow fierce against us; and finally that nothing is so small or worthless that it is not enough to destroy us; indeed that man himself is an enemy to man, and a demon.

units.la: Ne tamē in solis corporibus aut fortunis hæc pnities hæreat, nō quiescit interea hostis ille noster diabolus, sed in star leonis rugientis obambulat, & animabus quoq; æternum exitiū struit. Itaq; modò cordibus nostris sese insinuans immanissimorū facinorum nobis author est, modò prophanū Dei contemptū nobis persuadere conatur, modò mundi illecebris nos circūuenit, modò tyrannos et religionis omnis contemptores aduersus nos armat, modò in secundis rebus confidentes & superbos, in aduersis autem impatientes & murmuratores facit. Quid multis? Author est nobis improbus ille, vt omnibus ad nostra pernicien abutamur. Dominabatur ergo ille toti humano generi olim per peccatum & mortem, eoq; infelicior erat nostra conditio, quòd miseriā hanc nulli agnoscerent, perditione autē propria delectarentur, adhæc diabolo seipsos sponte subiicerent, & ei arma præberent, quibus in ipsis debellandis ille uteretur.
units.tr: Yet lest this misery cling only to our bodies or fortunes, that enemy of ours, the devil, does not rest in the meantime, but walks about like a roaring lion, and plots eternal ruin for our souls as well. So, now insinuating himself into our hearts, he is the author of most monstrous crimes for us; now he tries to persuade us to a profane contempt of God; now he surrounds us with the allurements of the world; now he arms tyrants and despisers of all religion against us; now he makes us proud and confident in prosperity, but impatient and murmuring in adversity. What more? That wicked one is the author for us of abusing everything for our own destruction. He therefore once held dominion over the whole human race through sin and death, and our condition was the more unhappy because no one acknowledged this misery, but rather took delight in their own perdition; moreover, they willingly subjected themselves to the devil and offered him the weapons with which he might wage war upon them.

units.la: Fuit ergo deploratissima hominum omnium conditio, neq; salutis spes ulla erat, cùm ipsi homines sese hosti sciētes volentes dederēt, & in proprium ruerent exitium. Et hanc miseriā Paulus alicubi uno verbo explicat, quādo nos potestati tenebrarum subiectos fuisse scribit. Succurrit hic nobis unus Deus per filium suum unigenitum Iesum Christum. Is ex Virgine Maria homo factus in mundū venit, & in domū fortis illius (vt ipse in Euangelio loquitur) ingressus, illū vicit et cōstrinxit, eiusq; vasa diripuit, id est, in libertatem asseruit miseros mortales, quibus ille ceu vasis & armis proprijs adomnem iniustitiā abutebatur. Victoriæ modus fuit, quòd in cruce pro nobis mortuus suæ mortis merito peccata mundi expiauit, deinde ex mortuis resuscitatus suæ resurrectionis virtute mortē deuicit & portas inferorum effregit, ne nos amplius detinere possint. Itaq; ille semen illud mulieris est, quod veteris serpentis caput contriuit, & principem huius mundi foras eiectum omni potestate exuit, vt quāmuis adhuc tumultuetur, nihil tamen possit aduersus ipsum & eos, qui ipsi per fidem sunt insiti.
units.tr: The condition of all men was therefore most desperate, nor was there any hope of salvation, since men themselves knowingly and willingly gave themselves to the enemy and rushed headlong into their own destruction. Paul explains this misery in one word somewhere, when he writes that we were subject to the power of darkness. Here one God comes to our aid through his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ. He, made man of the Virgin Mary, came into the world, and having entered the house of the strong man (as he himself speaks in the Gospel), bound him and overcame him, and plundered his goods, that is, he asserted the wretched mortals into liberty, whom the devil used against all righteousness as his own vessels and weapons. The manner of victory was this: he died for us on the cross and by the merit of his death expiated the sins of the world; then, raised again from the dead, by the power of his resurrection he conquered death and broke open the gates of hell, so that they can no longer hold us. Thus he is that seed of the woman who crushed the head of the old serpent, and he has cast out the prince of this world and stripped him of all power, so that, although he still stirs up tumult, he can do nothing against him or against those who have been grafted into him through faith.

units.la: Et huius redemptionis hic etiam fructus est, quòd nobis placatus pater maledictione aboleuit: quo fit, vt iam nobis omnia adiumento sint in bonum, & nihil vspiam in rerum natura sit, quod nos separare possit à dilectione Dei, quæ nostræ salutis fundamentum est firmissimum, vt mox audiemus.
units.tr: This redemption also has this fruit: the Father, having been reconciled to us, has taken away the curse. As a result, all things now work together for good for us, and there is nothing anywhere in nature that can separate us from the love of God, which is the most firm foundation of our salvation, as we shall hear shortly.

units.la: Nam etsi nos per Legem accusat Satan, & intra conscientias nostras nos peccati conuincat, non tamen (vt Paulus scribit) peccatum nobis dominatur, vt vel totos nos in seruitutem redigat, vel ad mortē imputetur: eò quòd non sumus sub lege, sed sub gratia, id est, non ea est amplius nostra conditio quæ olim, quando Lex suo rigore adhuc armata omnes damnabat, qui vel in minimo deliquissent: sed iam sub regno gratiæ sumus, quam Christus nobis meruit, & qua fit, vt & peccata nobis nō imputentur, & simul in Christo posumus omnia. Sumus ergo verè liberati ex manu hostiū nostrorum, quando neq; peccatum nos damnare potest, neq; in nos ius habet aliquod Satan, neq; mors aut infernus nos detinent, quò minus cum Christo æternum viuamus. Debet autē diligenter obseruari, huius redemptionis authorem vnicum esse Deum, Mediatorem quoq; vnicum Iesum Christum, & proinde non minus pernitiosè quàm turpiter eos falli, qui salutem suam alibi quaerunt.
units.tr: For although Satan accuses us through the Law and convicts us of sin within our consciences, sin does not (as Paul writes) have dominion over us, so as either to reduce us entirely to slavery or to be imputed to us unto death. This is because we are not under the law but under grace. That is, our condition is no longer what it was formerly, when the Law, still armed with its severity, condemned all who had offended even in the smallest matter. Rather, we are now under the reign of grace, which Christ merited for us, and by which our sins are not imputed to us and at the same time we possess all things in Christ. We are therefore truly freed from the hand of our enemies, since sin cannot condemn us, Satan has no right over us, and neither death nor hell can keep us from living eternally with Christ. But it must be carefully observed that the sole author of this redemption is God, and the sole Mediator is Jesus Christ. Therefore those who seek their salvation elsewhere are deceived, and that is no less destructive than it is shameful.

units.la: AsmireAt miretur aliquis quæ causa Deum moverit, vt tantam de nobis curam susciperet: & hic fere eorum error sese prodit, qui salutem suorum operum meritis aut veterum patrum virtuti adscribunt. Sed rectius multò Zacharias tanti beneficij fontes nobis ex spiritus revelatione monstrat, quando Deum ista fecisse dicit, vt videretur misericordia erga patres nostros, ac memor esset testamenti sui sancti, & iurisiurandi quod iurauit Abrahamo patri nostro. Quibus verbis & causas & ordinem salutis simul comprehendit. Primam causam, adeoque fontem ipsum in misericordia Dei commonstrat, qui ita nos dilexit, vt filium suum unigenitum pro nobis dederit. Vere autem hoc ab illo dici patebit, si ad primum parentem nostrum, Adamum, ascendamus. Quid enim ille meruerat, cum præcepti divini immemor peccaret, peccando divinitatem affectaret, & mox audita Dei voce in pedes se conjiceret, vt ab eius conspectu sese occultaret? Quid obsecro illi debebat Deus, qui neque culpam suam deprecabatur, neque ipsius gratiam implorabat, sed potius culpam omnem in ipsum transferre studebat? Atqui talem Deus quæsiuit & vocauit, eidemque ex fuga retracto semen illud mulieris promisit, quod serpentis caput conculcaturum sit, vt eius regno destructo humanum genus vindicetur. Solius ergo misericordiæ hoc beneficium fuit. Idem fateri cogemur, si Abrahamum inspiciamus, quem inter idololatras & Deorum aliorum cultores agente (vt Iosue ait) ex Chaldæa eduxit, & cum eo fœdus salutis ferijt, idque postea iureiurando confirmauit. Similiter nouum quoque testamentum fecit, cum Iudæi sua perfidia prius illud prophanauissent, sicuti apud Ieremiam ipse conqueritur. Quod autem ex gratuito fauore patribus promisit, hoc suo tempore præstitit misso in carnem filio suo, in quo omnes promissiones sunt Etiam & Amen, & qui ipse nouum testamentum in suo sanguine confirmari atque ratum fieri testatur. Concurrunt ergo hic misericordia & veritas Dei, & apparet simul certam & infallibilem esse salutis nostræ fiduciam. Nam vt modo diximus, ex misericordia Dei fontibus illa emanat, quos perennes & inexhaustos esse constat. Eadem Dei veritate confirmatur, quæ & ipsa neque fallit neque fallitur. Nam in æternum manet verbum Domini, & quamuis olim tota hæc mundi machina ruitura sit, ex illo tamen ne iota quidem aut apex unicus peribit.
