His ergo fundamentis nos insistere conuenit firmiter, neque eos audire, qui dum humanæ iustitiæ fulcris salutis fiduciam fulcire conantur, eius certitudinem omnino labefactant, imò funditus euertunt. At hic inter alia obseruatu dignissimum est, quod in Christo nobis exhibitam Dei gratiam ad patres vsq; extendit. Illius ergo merito illi quoque seruati sunt, & alibi hoc nomine agnus ille dicitur, qui immolatus sit ab origine mundi. Admonet id nos dulcissimæ communionis, quæ nobis cum lectissimis illis Dei amicis intercedit, et ita nostra salutis fiducia amplius confirmatur. Possumus etiam ex hoc loco animarum immortalitatem & corporum resurrectionem asserere aduersus Epicureos, qui vt sibi in sceleribus suis blanditias faciant, illa negare solent. Si enim quam in Christo exhibuit nobis Deus misericordia ad veteres etiam patres se extendit, qui iam seculis aliquot hac vita defuncti fuerunt, illi post mortem iam tunc superstites fuerint, oportet. Vixerunt ergo illorum spiritus cum Deo, & eorundem corpora in spe resurrectionis quiescunt, quæ illis salutem omnibus numeris perfectam afferet. Vsus est simili argumento Christus aduersus Sadducæos, vt infra Cap.20. videbimus.
units.tr: But someone may wonder what cause moved God to take such care of us. Here the error of those is revealed, more or less, who ascribe their salvation to the merits of their own works or to the virtue of the ancient fathers. Far more rightly, however, Zechariah, by the revelation of the Spirit, shows us the sources of so great a benefit, when he says that God did these things to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant and the oath which he swore to Abraham our father. In these words he comprehends both the causes and the order of salvation together. He shows the first cause, and so the very source, in the mercy of God, who loved us so much that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. Indeed, it will be clear that this is rightly said of God if we go back to our first parent, Adam. For what had he deserved when, forgetful of the divine command, he sinned, aspired to divinity by sinning, and, having heard the voice of God, immediately threw himself at his feet so as to hide himself from his sight? What, I ask, did God owe him, who neither begged pardon for his fault nor implored God's grace, but rather strove to shift all the blame onto God himself? Yet God sought such a man and called him, and, when he had turned back from his flight, promised him that seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, so that by the destruction of his kingdom the human race might be delivered. This benefit therefore came from mercy alone. We shall be compelled to confess the same if we look at Abraham, whom God led out of Chaldea, where he was living among idolaters and worshippers of other gods (as Joshua says), and with whom he made a covenant of salvation and afterwards confirmed it with an oath. Likewise he also made a new covenant, when the Jews had first profaned it by their faithlessness, as he himself complains in Jeremiah. But what he promised the fathers out of free favour, he performed in his own time, when he sent his Son in the flesh, in whom all the promises are Yea and Amen, and who himself testifies that the new covenant was confirmed and made valid in his own blood. Here, then, the mercy and the truth of God meet together, and it becomes clear at the same time that our confidence of salvation is sure and infallible. For, as we have just said, from the fountains of God's mercy that salvation flows, which are known to be perennial and inexhaustible. It is likewise confirmed by the truth of God, which neither deceives nor is deceived. For the word of the Lord endures forever, and although one day this whole machinery of the world will perish, not even one iota or one little stroke of that word will perish. It is therefore fitting for us to rest firmly on these foundations, and not to listen to those who, while they try to prop up the confidence of salvation with the supports of human righteousness, utterly weaken its certainty, and indeed overturn it from the foundations. But here, among other things, it is most worthy of notice that he extends to the fathers the grace of God exhibited to us in Christ. By his merit, therefore, they too were saved, and elsewhere that Lamb is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world. This reminds us of the most sweet fellowship which we share with those most choice friends of God, and so our confidence in salvation is strengthened further. From this passage we can also assert the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies against the Epicureans, who are wont to deny these things so that they may indulge themselves in their wickedness. For if the mercy of God, exhibited to us in Christ, extends also to the ancient fathers, who departed this life several centuries ago, it must be that they are still living after death. Therefore the spirits of those men live with God, and their bodies rest in the hope of the resurrection, which will bring them salvation perfect in every respect. Christ used a similar argument against the Sadducees, as we shall see below in chapter 20.

units.la: Restat vltimum huius de Christo vaticinij membrum, quo docetur quis redemptionis & salutis huius finis aut scopus nobis esse debeat, quoad vitæ nostræ consuetudinem: Nimirum vt sine metu, è manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, Deo seruiamus in sanctitate & iustitia coram ipso cunctis diebus vitæ nostræ. Continetur his verbis quicquid ad vitæ veræ Christianæ pertinet. Vbi ante omnia obseruare oportet, finem & vsum redemptionis nostræ nequaquam hunc esse, vt gratia Dei ad vitæ & morum licentiam transferamus, & impunè peccemus. Sed vt Dei cultores simus et vitam viuamus Christiana professione dignam. Admonet nos de hoc Christus, quando iubet vt in ipso multum fructum feramus, & vt qui per ipsum loti sunt, quotidie pedes suos abluant. Nisi ergo hoc faciamus, Ioan.13.14. Christi meritum nobis irritum & inutile reddemus, & quod ore profitemur, idipsum factis negabimus. Non ofcitanter autem prætereundum est, quod nos Deo ἀφόβως, id est, sine metu aut timore seruire iubet. Nō enim damnatur hic pius ille & ingenuus Dei timor, quæ sapientiæ vere principium dicit Solomon, & sine quo carnis libidinem refringere non possumus: sed de salutifera illa animi religiosi securitate sermo est, quam in nobis parit certa misericordiæ Dei fiducia, & quæ nos in Dei culcu alacres atque conflantes reddit. Quam nisi habeamus, neque Deo fidere possumus, neque nobis ipsis persuadere, quòd illi grata sint nostra officia, & proinde in eius cultu nimium frigebimus. Ideo Paulus de carnis mortificatione & vitæ nouitate differens, vt infirmis spem faceret, diccbat: Peccatum vobis non dominabitur, quia non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Adde, quòd neque munditi cerriculamentis refisere poterunt, quos non confirmat certa diuinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ fiducia. Vides ergo quid de Scholasticorum dogmate sentire debeas, qui hominem, quoad hic vixerit, de Dei gratia certum fieri posse negant. Dicunt se ita docere, vt segnes ad ardentius pietatis studium accendant. Atquomodo hunc colent ex animo, qui eum sibi inimicum fingunt? Itaque isti homines non solum salutis fiduciam labefactant, sed verum colendi Dei studium quoque in hominum animis restinguunt.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this prophecy concerning Christ, which teaches what the goal or aim of this redemption and salvation ought to be for us, as regards the conduct of our life: namely, that, delivered without fear from the hand of our enemies, we should serve God in holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our life. In these words is contained whatever pertains to a true Christian life. Here we must first of all observe that the end and use of our redemption is by no means that we should turn the grace of God into a licence for life and morals and sin with impunity. Rather, it is that we should be worshippers of God and live a life worthy of the Christian profession. Christ admonishes us of this when he bids us bear much fruit in him, and that those who have been washed by him should wash their feet every day. Unless we do this, we shall make Christ's merit void and useless for us, and we shall deny with our deeds what we profess with our mouths (John 13:14). Nor should we pass over carelessly that he bids us serve God ἀφόβως [afobōs], that is, without fear or dread. For this does not condemn that pious and free fear of God, which Solomon calls the beginning of true wisdom, and without which we cannot restrain the lust of the flesh. Rather, the discourse concerns that saving security of a religious mind, which the sure confidence in God's mercy produces in us, and which makes us eager and bold in the worship of God. If we do not have this, we can neither trust God nor persuade ourselves that our duties are pleasing to him, and so we shall grow too cold in his worship. Hence Paul, when treating of the mortification of the flesh and the newness of life, in order to give hope to the weak, said: "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law but under grace" (Rom. 6:14). Add to this that those who are not strengthened by the sure confidence in divine grace and mercy will not be able to withstand the little trifles of the world. You see, then, what you ought to think of the doctrine of the Schoolmen, who deny that a man, as long as he lives here, can be made certain of the grace of God. They say they teach this so as to rouse the lazy to a more ardent zeal for piety. But how will those who imagine God to be their enemy worship him from the heart? Thus these men not only weaken the confidence of salvation, but also extinguish in the minds of men the true zeal for worshipping God.

units.la: Sed in primis spectare conuenit, quibus rebus potissimum nos Deus sibi seruire velit. In sanctitate (ait Zacharias) & iustitia. Duobus membris vtramq; Legis tabulam complectitur. Sanctitate enim toti Deo consecramur: quod si fiat, iam illum ex toto corde diligemus, in illo vno spem & fiduciam omnem collocabimus, eundem colemus ea forma et ritu, quem ille nobis prescripsit: nomen deinde eius nobis sanctum & venerabile erit, neque aliquid eorum omittemus quæ ad ipsius gloriam faciunt. Iustitia vero ea virtus est, quæ suum cuique tribuit. At quia omnibus hominibus dilectionem debemus, quæ totius secunda tabulæ est completio, nihil in huius præcepta peccabunt, quicunq; iustitiæ veræ studuerint. Cur enim occidant eum, quem vt seipsos diligunt? Vel cur eius vxorem aut filium polluant, vel eius opes diripiant, vel famam lædant, cui se omne officium debere sentiunt? Certe ij, quibus iustitia hæc cordi est, cupiditates quoque frenabunt, ne extra illius limites vagentur. Duobus itaque verbis Zacharias absoluit, quod prophetæ & apostoli in suis scriptis, propter carnis nostræ tarditatem, admodum prolixè tractant. In primis autem ad huius loci explicationem pertinet, quod Paulus ad Titum sic scribit: Illuxit gratia illa Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, vt abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, moderatè & iustè & piè viuamus in præsenti seculo, &c. Non temere autè hic nos admonet Spiritus sanctus, vt coram ipso Deo sanctitati & iustitiæ studeamus, id est, vt meminerimus, nos in Dei conspectu agere, qui nullo fuco aut hypocrisi fallitur, sed ipsos hominum animos inspicit, & proinde sic viuamus, vt eius iudicio probemur. Quid enim iuuabit, nos hominibus sanctos & iustos videri, si Dei sententia nos damnet, cui executio certa coniuncta est?
units.tr: But first it is fitting to consider in what things God especially wishes us to serve him. "In holiness" (says Zacharias) "and righteousness." He embraces the two tables of the Law in two members. For by holiness we are consecrated wholly to God; and if this is done, we will then love him with our whole heart, place all our hope and trust in him alone, and worship him in the form and manner he has prescribed to us; then his name will be holy and venerable to us, and we will omit none of those things which pertain to his glory. Righteousness, moreover, is that virtue which gives to each his due. Now because we owe love to all men, which is the fulfilling of the second table, those who earnestly pursue true righteousness will sin against none of its precepts. For why would they kill the one whom they love as themselves? Or why would they defile his wife or son, or plunder his goods, or harm his reputation, to whom they feel bound by every duty? Surely those to whom this righteousness is dear will also restrain their desires, lest they wander beyond its limits. Thus in two words Zacharias sums up what the prophets and apostles, because of the slowness of our flesh, treat at great length in their writings. Moreover, for the explanation of this passage it is especially relevant what Paul writes to Titus: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, training us so that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age," etc. It is not without reason that the Holy Spirit here admonishes us to strive for holiness and righteousness before God himself, that is, that we remember we act in the sight of God, who is not deceived by any pretence or hypocrisy, but looks into the very minds of men; and therefore we should so live that we may be approved by his judgment. For what will it profit us to be seen as holy and righteous by men, if the sentence of God condemns us, to which certain punishment is joined?

units.la: Ne quid tamen omittat Zacharias, quàm diu etiam nos in hoc Dei cultu & seruitio durare oporteat, admonet: Nimirum cunctis diebus vitæ nostræ. Opus autem fuit, hoc adiici propter eos, qui vel Dei cultum certis diebus astringunt, quibus se totos magna cum animarum deuotione (vt videri volunt) rei diuinæ consecrant, ijs autem transfactis ad effrenem peccandi licentiam redeunt: vel eos etiam, qui vbi res aduersæ & graviora pericula imminent, ad pœnitentiam sese comparant, vt Dei fauorem demereantur; hanc verò momentaneam agunt, & mox in priores mores effunduntur, vbi periculi metus euanuit. Sunt hi ex eorum numero, quibus per Hoseam olim dicebat Dominus: Quid faciam tibi Ephraim? quid faciam tibi Iuda? Pietas vestra est quasi nubes matutina, & vt luti ros mane veniens & abiens. Et tales fere sunt, qui hodie optimi videntur. Quid verò illi aliud agunt, quàm quòd duobus heris simul seruire volunt, Deo nimirum & diabolo? quod fieri impossibile esse Christus docet. Meminerimus ergo, nos (vt Paulus monet) ea conditione ex peccati seruitio liberatos esse, vt nunc Deo mancipati, huic soli seruiamus. Et hæc in primam huius Cantici partem dicta sint, cuius doctrinam nobis commendare debemus, vt Dei quidem gratiam totis animis agnoscamus, eidem verò nos totos consecremus in sanctitate & iustitia, cuius nobis Mediator factus est Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lest Zacharias omit anything, he also reminds us how long we ought to persist in this worship and service of God: "Namely, all the days of our life." This had to be added on account of those who indeed bind the worship of God to certain days, on which they devote themselves wholly to divine matters with great devotion of soul (as they wish to seem), but once those days are past return to an unbridled license to sin; or on account of those who, when adverse circumstances and more serious dangers threaten, prepare themselves for repentance, so that they may win back God's favour; yet they perform this only for a moment, and soon they pour back into their former ways, once the fear of danger has vanished. These are among those to whom the Lord once said through Hosea: "What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your goodness is like a morning cloud, and like the dew that comes early in the morning and passes away." And such, for the most part, are those who today seem most upright. But what else do such people do than wish to serve two masters at once, namely God and the devil? which Christ teaches is impossible. Let us therefore remember that we have been freed from the servitude of sin (as Paul admonishes) on this condition, that, now that we are bound to God, we should serve him alone. And let these things be said concerning the first part of this Canticle, the teaching of which we ought to commend to ourselves, so that we may acknowledge with our whole souls the grace of God, and consecrate ourselves wholly to him in holiness and righteousness, of which Jesus Christ has been made Mediator for us: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XV.
units.tr: HOMILY XV.

units.la: Et tu puerule, propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Præibis enim ante faciem Domini, vt pares vias eius: Et des cognitionem salutis populo ante faciem per remissionem peccatorum ipsorum; Propter viscera misericordiæ Dei nostri, quibus inuisit nos Oriens ex alto: Vt appareat iis, qui in tenebris & umbra mortis positi sunt, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Ipse autem puerulus crescebat, & corroborabatur spiritu, fuitque in desertis ad eum usque diem, quo se ostenderet apud Israelem.
units.tr: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; to give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins, through the tender mercy of our God, whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts until the day of his shewing unto Israel."

units.la: Quàmuis Zacharias hoc Cantico Dei beneficium celebrare instituerit, qui ipsi ex Elizabeta uxore sterili filium dederat, prima tamen eius parte ex Spiritus sancti suggestione de ipso Christo vaticinatur, & ea occasione totum humanæ salutis negotium exponit, quod tribus fere capitibus comprehendit. Primo docet, nos huius virtute & merito liberatos esse ab inimicis nostris, quorum princeps diabolus nos sub immani peccatorum seruitute premebat. Secundo causas redemptionis huius indicat in Dei misericordia & veritate, qui vt olim nostri misertus salutem patribus promiserat, sic eandem misso in mundum filio suo præstitit. Tertio officia vitæ Christianæ tradit, quorum summa est, vt omni damnationis metu excusso, vni Deo seruiamus in sanctitate & iustitia omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ. Sequitur nunc altera huius Cantici pars, qua de filio Ioanne agit, cuius officium primò summatim paucis verbis comprehensum proponit, mox vero idem pluribus exponit. In his autem ferè prophetarum veterum & Angeli verbis vtitur, quod nos obseruare conuenit, vt videamus, quàm bene sibi semper constet Spiritus sanctus, & quòd non eadem sit verbi Dei, quæ humanorum figmentorum conditio, quæ in singula prope momenta pro vanissimorum hominum arbitrio mutantur. Cantico autem Zachariæ æducationem Ioannis subiicit Lucas, quia hæc quoque ad eius institutum faciebat. Vt verò istis omnibus Ioannis fides & authoritas commendatur: ita fidelis præconis aut administri verbi Dei exemplum continent, ex quo de omnibus iudicare possumus, qui in munere Ecclesiastico sunt constituti, aut huius authoritatem sibi vendicant. Est igitur locus hic cognitu & consideratu valde necessarius hodie in tanta iudiciorum varietate, qua de munere illo magna cum contentione animorum pugnatur.
units.tr: Although Zacharias undertook to celebrate with this canticle God's benefit, who had given him a son by his barren wife Elizabeth, yet in its first part, prompted by the Holy Spirit, he prophesies about Christ himself, and on that occasion sets out the whole business of human salvation, which he comprehends under roughly three heads. First, he teaches that we have been freed by Christ's power and merit from our enemies, of whom the chief is the devil, who had oppressed us under the cruel bondage of sin. Second, he points out the causes of this redemption in God's mercy and truth, who, as he once promised salvation to the fathers out of pity for us, has now granted the same by sending his Son into the world. Third, he hands down the duties of the Christian life, the sum of which is that, with all fear of damnation cast off, we serve the one God in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life. There now follows the second part of this canticle, in which he treats of the son John: he first sets out John's office briefly, in a few words, and then soon explains it at greater length. In doing so he uses almost the words of the ancient prophets and of the angel, which we should observe, so that we may see how consistently the Holy Spirit always agrees with himself, and that the word of God is not in the same condition as human fictions, which are changed almost every moment at the whim of the most vain men. After Zacharias' canticle Luke adds the upbringing of John, because this too served his purpose. And so that John's faith and authority are commended by all these things, they contain the example of a faithful herald or minister of the word of God, from which we can judge all who are placed in ecclesiastical office, or who claim its authority for themselves. This passage is therefore very necessary to know and consider today, amid such great variety of judgments, by which that office is fought over with great contention of minds.

units.la: Orditur verò partem hanc Zacharias cum Apostrophe pathetica, & quæ paterni animi affectum pulchrè exprimit. Dicit enim: Et tu puerule, propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Coharent autem ista cum iis, quæ præcesserunt, & sensus est: Etsi nunc puerulus sis tantillus, & nihil eximium præ te feras, in hoc tamen regno tam potenti & salutifico non postremas partes tenebis. Vocaberis enim propheta Altissimi, id est, veri & æterni Dei, quem hic vocat scriptura, quæ cœlis terrisq; sublimior in omnes creaturas imperium habet. Vocandi autem verbo non solum pro communi more Hebræorum vtitur, vt talem reuera fore ostendat, sed vt simul doceat, eum publicè hoc nomine celebrem & insignem fore, vt pro propheta maximo à plerisque agnoscatur. Dicitur autem propheta in sacris literis, non solum qui futura prædicit, sed quisquis voluntatis diuinæ interpres est, & huius doctrinam ad ecclesiæ siue auditorum institutionem, & consolationem aut ædificationem accommodat. Sic enim munus hoc ab ipso Deo apud Ieremiam describitur. Cum enim illi dixisset Dominus, Prophetam gentibus te constitui, mox subiicit: Ecce ego posui verba mea in os tuum, ecce ego constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, vt euellas & extirpes, vt perdas & dissipes, vt ædifices & plantes. Quò Paulus videtur respexisse, cum scriberet: Qui prophetat, hominibus loquitur ædificationem & exhortationem, & consolationem. Et in his quidem sedulum fuisse Ioannem, eius facta abundè testantur, vt suo loco fusius dicetur. Neque hic alicui scrupulum moueat, quod apud Ioannem Euangelistam ipse se propheta esse negat. Illic enim de magno illo propheta agebatur, quem Deus olim per Mosem promiserat, & quem non alium quàm Iesum Christum esse, ex Petri & Stephani interpretatione constat. Vide Actor. 3. & 7. cap.
units.tr: Zacharias begins this part with a passionate apostrophe, which beautifully expresses the feeling of a father's heart. For he says: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest." These words cohere with what has gone before, and the sense is this: though you are now a little child and show nothing outstanding, you will not hold the last place in this kingdom, so powerful and so saving. For you shall be called the prophet of the Highest, that is, of the true and eternal God, whom Scripture calls the one who is higher than the heavens and the earth and has dominion over all creatures. He uses the word "called" not only according to the common manner of the Hebrews, to show that you will truly be such, but also to teach that you will be publicly celebrated and distinguished by this name, so that you will be acknowledged by most people as a very great prophet. In Scripture, however, a prophet is called not only one who foretells the future, but anyone who is an interpreter of the divine will, and who applies its teaching to the instruction, comfort or edification of the Church or of the hearers. For this is how God himself describes the office to Jeremiah: when the Lord had said to him, "I have appointed you a prophet to the nations," he immediately adds, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to pull down, to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant." Paul seems to have had this in mind when he wrote: "He that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." That John was diligent in these things his deeds amply bear witness, as will be said more fully in its place. Nor should it trouble anyone here that in the Gospel of John he denies that he is a prophet. For there the great prophet was being discussed, whom God had promised long ago through Moses, and who, from the interpretation of Peter and Stephen, is known to be none other than Jesus Christ. See Acts chapters 3 and 7.

units.la: Nunc autem nobis paulò diligentius Zachariæ animus inspiciendus erit, qui hoc nomine sibi ipsi potissimum gratulatur, quod diu exoptatum filium Dei prophetam & verbi præconem so-resciret. Potest hoc rationi humanæ mirum & absurdum videri. Sciebat enim munus hoc arduum, adhæc inuidiæ & odij plenum esse. Sciebat quid olim prophetis accidisset, quibus cum popu-li contumacia, cum regibus, cum sacerdotibus perpetuò fuit luctandum: & quod plerique illorum vel patriis finibus eiecti fuerunt, vel in carceribus tetris contabuerunt, vel lapidibus obruti,
units.tr: But now we must look a little more carefully into the mind of Zacharias, who above all rejoices in this, that he has learned that his long-desired son will be a prophet and herald of the Word of God. To human reason this may seem strange and absurd. For he knew that this office was arduous, and moreover full of envy and hatred. He knew what had happened to the prophets of old, with whom there was constant struggle against the obstinacy of the people, against kings and against priests; and that most of them were either driven out of their native lands, or wasted away in foul prisons, or were overwhelmed with stones,

units.la: Ioannes propheta altissimi. Zacharias sibi gratulatur ob filium propheta. Ier. 1. 1. Cor. 14. aut gladio percussi vitam finierunt. Neque meliorem filij sortem sperare poterat, quoad rerum quâ tunc erat conditionem: cum in repub. quidem prophanæ gentes, in ecclesiâ autem pharisæi & scribæ, superstitionum & traditionum humanarum magistri dominarentur. At non ad huius mundi sortem respicit Zacharias, sed rem ipsam secum expendit. Etenim quia præcipuum diuini fauoris argumentum est, quod nobiscum colloqui & nos suæ voluntatis certiores facere dignatur, eximium & diuinum sit munus oportet, quod in eum finem est institutum. Neque hic nos mouere debet, quod eius dignitatem mundus non videt neque intelligit. Dei enim ministri sunt, qui eos amicorum loco habet (vt de Apostolis Christus loquitur) & in medijs periculis tuetur, quoad illorum operam sibi & ecclesiæ vtilem esse nouit. Quia ergo vidit Zacharias, quanto satius sit Deo, quàm mundo impio & ingrato seruire, non potuit non gaudere, quod filium illius seruitio destinatum esse intelligebat. Idem olim Samuelis parentes viderunt, quorum hoc supremum votum fuit, vt filius in Ecclesiastico ministerio suam operam Deo collocaret. Arguitur itaque exemplis infelix seculi nostri corruptio, quando nullum vitæ genus magis contemptum & exosum est, vt plerosque pudeat filios suos Ecclesiæ & verbi Dei ministerio consecrare. Olim quidem cum sub Antichristi regno errorum atque superstitionum tenebræ dominarentur, non pudebat principes viros ex filijs suis Abbates & Episcopos facere, & nulla familia tam nobilis, tam opulenta, tam ampla, vel etiam inops & contempta erat, quæ non aliquos ex suis Ecclesiasticæ functioni, aut Monachorum & Monalium collegijs destinaret. At postquam veritatis lux tenebras illas discussit, & plurimis non solum corporis, verumetiam animarum libertatem peperit, vix quisquam inuenitur, qui filium Christi & Euangelij præconem esse velit. Imò nisi iam inde à pueris aliqui ad munus istud publicis Ecclesiæ impensis educarentur, breui doctrinam omnem cum Ecclesia ruituram videremus. Itaque ad ministerium sacrum soli ij fere veniunt, quos vel sua paupertas, vel familiæ obscuritas contemptos reddit. Qui enim diuitijs abundant, sij filios suos vel ad mercaturam & artes vsurarias destinare, vel principum aulis mancipare, vel ignauo & turpi otio consecrare malunt. Constat ergo hodie à plerisque pluris fieri gloriam hominum quàm Dei, & omnis iudicij inopia turpiter laborare eos, qui ita sentiunt. Nam si instabilem mundi huius conditionem recte expenderent, multò aliter iudicarent. Olim quidem magna fuit Pharaonum, Achabi, Manassis, Zedechiæ, Herodis, Pontificum Iudæorum & Romanorum Imperatorum gloria. At quis non videt hodie sanctionem & laudabiliorem esse memoriam Mosis, prophetarum, apostolorum & martyrum, quos illi iniquis suis iudicijs damnarunt, quos hostiliter persecuti sunt, & infamibus supplicijs extinxerunt? In horum igitur consideratione versentur Ecclesiæ ministri, & simul meminerint, se Dei altissimi prophetas esse, qui & ipsos tueri, & quam hic sustinent ignominiam, æterna gloria compensare poterit.
units.tr: John the prophet of the Highest. Zacharias rejoices for his son as a prophet. Jer. 1. 1 Cor. 14. or were struck down with the sword and ended their lives. Nor could he hope for a better lot for his son, given the condition of things at that time, when in the state the profane nations ruled, and in the Church the Pharisees and scribes, masters of superstitions and human traditions, held sway. But Zacharias does not look to the lot of this world; he weighs the thing itself in his mind. For since the chief proof of God's favour is that he deigns to speak with us and to make us certain of his will, the office that is appointed to this end must be an outstanding and divine one. Nor should it move us that the world neither sees nor understands its dignity. For those who are ministers of God, whom he treats as friends (as Christ speaks of the Apostles), he protects in the midst of dangers for as long as he knows their work to be useful to himself and to the Church. Therefore, because Zacharias saw how much better it is to serve God than the impious and ungrateful world, he could not but rejoice that he understood his son to be destined for that service. The parents of Samuel once saw the same thing; their highest wish was that their son should devote his labour to God in the ecclesiastical ministry. The corruption of our age is thus proved by examples, since no kind of life is more despised and hated, so that most people are ashamed to consecrate their sons to the ministry of the Church and the Word of God. In former times, indeed, when the darkness of errors and superstitions held sway under the reign of Antichrist, princely men were not ashamed to make abbots and bishops of their sons, and no family was so noble, so wealthy, so great, or even so poor and despised, that it did not dedicate some of its members to the ecclesiastical function or to the communities of monks and nuns. But since the light of truth has dispelled those shadows, and has brought freedom not only of body but also of souls to very many, hardly anyone is found who wishes his son to be a servant of Christ and a herald of the Gospel. Indeed, unless some were educated from boyhood for this office at public expense, we would soon see all doctrine falling to ruin along with the Church. Thus almost only those come to the sacred ministry whom poverty or the obscurity of their family renders despised. For those who abound in riches prefer to destine their sons either to trade and usurious arts, or to hand them over to the courts of princes, or to consecrate them to idle and shameful leisure. It is therefore plain that today by most people the glory of men is valued more than the glory of God, and that those who think in this way are shamefully lacking in all judgment. For if they weighed rightly the unstable condition of this world, they would judge far otherwise. In former times, indeed, the glory of Pharaoh, Ahab, Manasseh, Zedekiah, Herod, the Jewish high priests and the Roman emperors was great. But who does not see that today the memory of Moses, the prophets, the apostles and the martyrs is holier and more praiseworthy, whom those men condemned by their unjust judgments, whom they persecuted as enemies and extinguished with infamous punishments? Let the ministers of the Church therefore dwell on the consideration of these, and at the same time remember that they are prophets of the Most High God, who both can protect them, and will be able to repay with eternal glory the disgrace they endure here.

units.la: Sed ad Zachariam redeamus, qui cum filium Ioannem prophetam fore dixisset, mox eius officium diligentius describit, sic dicens: Præibis enim ante faciem Domini, vt pares vias eius, & des cognitionem salutis populi eius per remissionem peccatorum ipsorum. Primò Christi Iesu Domini nostri anteambulonem fore ait, quod de tempore ministerij Ioannis intelligi debet. Vt enim Reges & Monarchæ non subito aduenire solent, sed ex suis aliquos præmittunt, qui & ipsorum aduentum denuntiant, & in hunc præparant quæ illis aut necessaria sunt aut honorifica: Ita Dei filius, æternus ille rex gloriæ, non ignarus omnibus in mundum irrepere, sed Ioanne præcursore & præcone vti voluit, qui de eius aduentu omnes admoneret, & hominum mentes ad illum excipiendum præpararet.
units.tr: But let us return to Zechariah, who, having said that his son John would be a prophet, then describes his office more carefully, saying: "For you will go before the face of the Lord, to prepare his ways, and to give knowledge of salvation to his people through the remission of their sins." First, he says that John will be the forerunner of Christ Jesus our Lord, which must be understood of the time of John's ministry. For kings and monarchs do not usually arrive suddenly, but send some of their own ahead, who both announce their coming and prepare for it whatever is either necessary or fitting for them. So the Son of God, that eternal King of glory, did not wish to creep into the world unnoticed, but chose to use John as his forerunner and herald, who would warn everyone of his coming and prepare the minds of men to receive him.

units.la: Quod ita fore olim prophetæ prædixerant. Apud Malachiam certè ait Dominus: Ecce ego mitto legatum meum, qui purgabit viam ante me. Isaias autem vocis in deserto meminit clamantis, Parate viam Domino, in solitudine planam facite semitam Deo nostro. Atque vaticinia Zachariam respexisse verba eius satis testantur. Est autem hoc magnum diuinæ bonitatis argumentum, quod filij sui aduentum publicè omnibus innotescere voluit: at eodem omnem simul excusationem Iudæis abstulit, qui contempti Christi pænas horribiles merito dederunt, quando eum aspernati sunt, qui tanti præconis testimonio, adhæc docendi dexteritate & proprijs miraculis commendabatur.
units.tr: That the coming would be thus, the prophets had foretold long ago. In Malachi the Lord certainly says: "Behold, I send my messenger, who will prepare the way before me." Isaiah too speaks of the voice of one crying in the wilderness: "Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert a highway for our God." And that Zechariah had these prophecies in mind his words sufficiently testify. This is a great proof of divine goodness, that he willed the coming of his Son to be made publicly known to all; and at the same time he took away from the Jews every excuse, since they despised Christ and rightly suffered terrible punishments for rejecting him, who was commended by the testimony of so great a herald, and also by his skill in teaching and by his own miracles.

units.la: At præcipuum huius loci caput est, quod Ioannis exemplo nos de ministrorum Ecclesiæ officio Spiritus sanctus admonet. Etsi enim Christus in terras hasce non amplius corporali & visibili modo descendat, & proinde anteambulone eiusmodi, qualis olim Ioannes fuit, nimirum opus habeat, est tamen hoc commune & proprium administrorum verbi munus, vt ipsi viam parent, id est, hominum mentes instruant, vt Dominus apud illos locum atq; domicilium inveniat. Hic enim ministerij Ecclesiastici finis est, vt homines cum Deo communionem habeant, quod dilectus ille discipulus in sua epistola his verbis perspicuè docet: Quod vidimus & audivimus id annunciamus vobis, vt & vos communionem habeatis nobiscum: & communio nostra sit cum patre & cum filio eius Iesu Christo. At qua ratione via haec Domino paretur, Ioannes hic nostrer suo exemplo abunde docet. Fecit is docendi initium a poenitentia, quam ita docuit, vt omnis loci & ordinis hominum peccata accusarit, & vt ista emendari oporteat ostenderit. Libertate certè dicendi tanta vsus est, vt neque sacer dotibus & pharisaeis pepercerit, neque Herodi, cùm is quoq; mali exempli & publici scandali author esset. Inde verò Christum praedicavit, & hunc digito commonstrans dixit: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Hunc ergo ordinem etiam hodie ministri omnes tenent. Quia enim peccata nos instar maceriae cuiusdam a Deo separant, nunquam huic, nisi illis sublatis, coniungi poterimus. Et haec sunt ad quae euellenda, diruenda & extirpanda Ierem. missum fuisse supra audivimus. Isaias quoque ex gutture clamare & vocem instar tubae exaltare iubebatur, vt populo peccata sua annuntiaret. Imò Christus a poenitentia doctrina apostolos suos praedicandi initium facere iussit. Nihil ergo praeter officium faciunt, qui hodie peccata arguunt & quosuis ad poenitentiae studium graviter hortantur. Qui enim haec intacta relinquunt, cùm salutis doctores videri velint, perinde faciunt, ac si medicus humores noxios in corpore diffundi patiatur, interim verò valetudinem meliorem aegrotanti promittat. At ne quem in desperationem coniciat poenitentiae praedicatio & acrior scelerum redargutio, aut illius studium nos inani propriae iustitiae fiducia inflet, simul Christum praedicare oportet, qui nobis a Deo patre satisfactio, redemptio & iustitia factus est. Ideoque vehementer errant, qui in increpandis quidem hominum flagitiis & tradenda respiscentia assidui sunt, nullam verò Christi mentionem faciunt, qui solus afflictis conscientiis medicinam veram adhibet. Et hic ille praecipuus error est, qui in Papatu plurimos fallit, quod poenitentiam sine Christo tradunt, & ita vel in desperationis praecipitium miseros adducunt, vel suorum operum fiducia turgentes a salutis via abducunt.
units.tr: But the chief point of this passage is that the Holy Spirit, by the example of John, admonishes us about the office of the ministers of the Church. For although Christ does not now come down to these lands in a bodily and visible way, and so does not indeed need a forerunner of the kind John once was, it is nonetheless the common and proper duty of the ministers of the Word to prepare the way for him, that is, to instruct the minds of men, so that the Lord may find a place and dwelling among them. For this is the goal of the ecclesiastical ministry: that men may have communion with God; which that beloved disciple teaches plainly in his epistle in these words: "What we have seen and heard, we announce to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ." But by what method this way is prepared for the Lord, John, our forerunner, teaches abundantly by his example. He began his teaching with repentance, and taught it in such a way that he accused the sins of every place and rank of men, and showed that these must be amended. Indeed he used such freedom of speech that he spared neither the priests and Pharisees nor Herod, though he too was the author of bad example and public scandal. Then he preached Christ, pointing to him with his finger and saying: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." This same order all ministers hold to today. For since sins separate us from God like a certain wall, we can never be joined to him unless they are taken away. And these are the things which we heard above were sent to Jeremiah to pluck up, break down and root out. Isaiah too was commanded to cry out from the throat and to raise his voice like a trumpet, so that he might announce their sins to the people. Indeed Christ bade his apostles begin their preaching with the teaching of repentance. Therefore those who today denounce sins and earnestly exhort everyone to zeal for repentance do nothing beyond their duty. But those who leave these things untouched, while wishing to be seen as teachers of salvation, act just as if a physician allowed harmful humours to spread through the body, and meanwhile promised the sick man better health. But so that the preaching of repentance and the sharper rebuke of wickedness do not drive anyone into despair, or so that zeal for it does not puff us up with the empty confidence of our own righteousness, we must at the same time preach Christ, who has been made for us by God the Father satisfaction, redemption and righteousness. So those greatly err who are busy in denouncing the vices of men and in delivering repentance, but make no mention of Christ, who alone applies the true remedy to troubled consciences. And this is that chief error which deceives very many in the Papacy: they teach repentance without Christ, and so either lead wretched men into the precipice of despair, or, puffed up with confidence in their works, draw them away from the way of salvation.

units.la: Rectè ergo Zacharias filio Ioanni hoc quoque tribuit, quod in hoc ordinatum air, vt salutis cognitionem det populo Domini. Frustra enim excindentur quae in salutis via nobis occurrunt obstacula, nisi veram huius cognitionem teneamus. At priusquam de hoc plura dicamus, videndum erit quo sensu Ioannes illam dedisse dicatur. Nam si proprie loqui libeat, solus Deus suo spiritu hominum mentes illuminat, vt veram salutis rationem videre & intelligere possint. Docet hoc ipse Christus in Evangelio dicens: Nemo novit filium nisi pater, & nemo novit patrem nisi filius, & cui filius vult revelare. Item: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit ipsum. Et Petro, qui ipsum Dei filium & Christum esse confessus erat, respondit: Beatus es Simon, quia caro & sanguis tibi non manifestavit, sed pater meus qui in coelis est. Quod ergo de Ioanne dicitur, solius ministerij ratione accipi debet, quo Spiritus sanctus vsus est, vt salutis cognitionem in hominum cordibus accenderet. Si enim huius gratiae facultas penes Ioannem fuisset, procul dubio Sacerdotes quoque & scribae, & in primis Herodes, cognitione illa per ipsum fuissent donati. Vt autem Deus opera, quorum ipse in nobis author est, nostra dicit, & eadem ex gratia peculiari tanquam nostra in nobis remuneratur: ita hominum ministerio ea tribuit, quae non illi propria virtute faciunt, sed in quibus conscientiis ipse hominibus ceu organis & instrumentis vtitur. Quo sensu Paulus & Barnabas credentium animas confirmauisse dicuntur, cùm hoc quoq; solius Spiritus sancti opus sit. Et hoc quidem Apostolus ipse diligenter exponit, quando Corinthijs, qui quòd ministris nimium tribuerant, in sectas scindebantur, dicit: Quis est Paulus? quis Apollos? Nonne ministri sunt, per quos credidistis, & vt cuiq; Dominus dedit? Ego plantavi, Apollos rigavit, sed Deus dedit incrementum. Itaq; neq; is qui plantat est aliquid, neq; qui rigat: sed Deus, qui dat incrementum. Est autem haec distinctio probè observanda ad confutandam Episcoporum & sacrificulorum tyrannidem, qui sibi eorum potestatem attribuerunt, quae de solo ministerio intelligi debebant. Quae causa fuit, vt clavium praetextu sibi in hominum animas & conscientias potestatem vsurparint, quasi penes ipsos esset peccata vel remittere vel irremissa tenere. Admonet item distinctio ista, ne ministris numium addicti simus & ita hominum serui reddamur, & quam in Christo obtinuimus libertatem turpiter prodamus. Meminerimus ergo omnes verbi praecones Christi ministros esse, quorum sit, non sibi ipsis sed uni & soli Christo discipulos colligere. Illis ergo credamus, quatenus Dei verbum praedicant, interim vero Iesum Christum agnoscamus unicum Regem & Sacerdotem, cuius nomine nos gloriari, & in eo solo salutis fiduciam habere conveniat.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, Zechariah also attributes this to his son John, that he was appointed in this office to give the knowledge of salvation to the people of the Lord. For the obstacles which meet us on the way of salvation will be cut away in vain, unless we hold true knowledge of it. But before we say more about this, we must consider in what sense John is said to have given it. For if we wish to speak properly, God alone enlightens men's minds by his Spirit, so that they may see and understand the true way of salvation. Christ himself teaches this in the Gospel, saying: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him." Again: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." And to Peter, who had confessed him to be the Son of God and Christ, he answered: "Blessed are you, Simon, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." What is said, therefore, of John must be understood with respect to the ministry alone, by which the Holy Spirit has been pleased to kindle the knowledge of salvation in the hearts of men. For if the power of this grace had rested with John, without doubt the priests and scribes, and above all Herod, would have been given that knowledge through him. But as God calls works which he himself is the author of in us our own, and rewards in us, as our own, those same works by peculiar grace, so he gives through the ministry of men those things which they do not accomplish by their own power, but in which he uses men as organs and instruments for consciences. In this sense Paul and Barnabas are said to have strengthened the souls of believers, although this too is a work of the Holy Spirit alone. The Apostle himself explains this carefully when, speaking to the Corinthians, who were splitting into sects because they attributed too much to ministers, he says: "Who is Paul? Who is Apollos? Are they not ministers through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him? I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase." This distinction, moreover, must be carefully observed in order to refute the tyranny of the bishops and sacrificing priests, who have claimed for themselves powers which ought to be understood of the ministry alone. This was the cause why, under the pretext of the keys, they usurped power over men's souls and consciences, as if it lay with them either to remit sins or to hold them unremitted. This distinction also warns us not to become bound to ministers, and so become slaves of men, and shamefully betray the liberty we have obtained in Christ. Let us therefore remember that all preachers of the Word are ministers of Christ, whose task is to gather disciples not for themselves but for one and only Christ. So let us believe them insofar as they proclaim the Word of God, but meanwhile acknowledge Jesus Christ as the sole King and Priest, in whose name it is fitting that we glory, and in him alone have confidence of salvation.

units.la: - Pergit autem Zacharias, & quae illa salutis cognitio sit quibusq; partibus constet, diligentius exponit, dicens: Ut des cognitionem salutis populo eius per remissionem peccatorum ipsorum: propter viscera misericordiae Dei nostri, quibus invisit nos Oriens ex alto, ut appareat iis, qui in tenebris & in umbra mortis positi sunt, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Comprehendit his verbis omnia capita, in quibus vera & solida salutis cognitio consistit, quae si nobis ob oculos ponamus, facile de quavis doctrina iudicare poterimus, an ex Deo sit, vel num in viam salutis nos dirigat, aut inde abducat. Nam primo docet, in quo nam salus omnis sit sita. Deinde eius fontem atque originem commonstrat. Tertio medium quoq; salutis ostendit. Quarto finem quoq; & fructum tradit, qui inde ad nos redit. De quibus etsi in prima etiam Cantici huius parte multa dixerimus, exigit tamen huius loci tractatio, ut causam hanc iterum excutiamus.
units.tr: Zacharias goes on and sets out more carefully what that knowledge of salvation is and what parts it consists of, saying: "To give knowledge of salvation to his people through the remission of their sins, because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dayspring from on high has visited us, to shine on those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, and to guide our feet into the way of peace." In these words he comprehends all the heads on which true and solid knowledge of salvation rests. If we keep them before our eyes, we can easily judge of any doctrine whether it is from God, and whether it leads us into the way of salvation or draws us away from it. For first, he teaches in what salvation as a whole lies. Second, he shows its fountain and origin. Third, he also shows the means of salvation. Fourth, he hands on the end and fruit that comes back to us from it. Although we have said much about these in the first part of this Canticle, the treatment of this passage requires that we examine the matter again.

units.la: Quoad primum, cognitionem salutis, vel potius salutem ipsam nobis in peccatorum remissione monstrat. Quia enim peccata Deiiram provocant, & (ut supra dictum est) nos a Deo separant, (quae omnis miseriae & perditionis unica causa est) salus certe nulla sperari poterit, ubi peccata regnant, aut adhuc in rationem veniunt. Observabis autem Zachariam, salutem nostram non in hoc collocare, ut peccata in nobis prorsus nulla sint, sed in peccatorum remissione. Quoad enim in carne vixerimus, absq; peccato esse non possumus, cum in eo concepti & nati simus, ut de semetipso David fatetur. Quapropter Apostolus dicebat: Si dicamus nos peccatum non habere, nosipsos fallimus, & veritas Dei in nobis non est, imo Deum mendacem facimus. Quia ergo natura peccatores sumus, peccati vero stipendium est mors, constat utique salutem nostram in eo consistere, ut peccata nobis non imputentur, id est, in eorum remissione gratuita. Ad hunc modum David quoque (sicut Paulus observavit) hominis beatificationem describit. Beati (inquit) quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir, cui non imputarit Dominus peccatum. Est hoc salutis principium probe tenendum, ut agnita peccatorum nostrorum multitudine & gravitate, procul abijciamus pharisaicam & exitialem propriae iustitiae fiduciam, & salutem nostram in remissione peccatorum quaeramus, quae unica nobis iustitia restat.
units.tr: As to the first point, the knowledge of salvation, or rather salvation itself, he shows to us in the remission of sins. For since sins provoke the wrath of God and (as has been said above) separate us from God, which is the sole cause of all misery and perdition, certainly no salvation can be hoped for where sins reign, or where they still come into account. Notice, however, that Zacharias does not place our salvation in this, that sins are wholly absent from us, but in the remission of sins. For as long as we live in the flesh, we cannot be without sin, since we were conceived and born in it, as David confesses of himself. Therefore the Apostle said: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth of God is not in us; indeed, we make God a liar" (1 John 1.8, 10). Since, then, we are sinners by nature, and the wages of sin is death, it is certainly clear that our salvation consists in this: that sins are not imputed to us, that is, in their free remission. In this way David also (as Paul observed) describes the blessedness of man: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin" (Rom. 4.7-8; Ps. 32.1-2). This is a principle of salvation to be firmly held: having acknowledged the multitude and gravity of our sins, we should cast far from us the Pharisaical and destructive confidence in our own righteousness, and seek our salvation in the remission of sins, which is the only righteousness left to us.

units.la: At quae nam (inquis) remissionis istius causa est? Rursus ergo Zachariam audi, qui eam nobis obtigisse ait, propter viscera misericordiae Dei nostri. Ut ergo prius nos debitores esse ostendit, quibus remissione gratuita opus fit, ita hanc in mera Dei misericordia commonstrat. Utque hanc nobis magis commendet, viscera misericordiae nominat, ita nimirum naturales illos commiserationis motus intelligens, quibus parentes erga liberos ex se natos affici solent, quas Graeci σπλάγχνα dicunt, & quarum exemplum in meretrice illa proponitur, quae de filio suo apud Solomonis tribunal contendisse scribitur. Tanta autem harum vis est, ut nunc quoque sese exerant, quando contumaces filios & quovis supplicio dignos in periculo aliquo graviori parentes conspicantur. Recte vero has Deo tribuit Zacharias, eo quod hic se patrem nostrum profiteatur, & apud Isaiam dicat: Num oblivioni tradit mulier infantem suum quo minus misereatur filii uteri sui? Sed esto oblivisca ntur illae, ego tamen tui non obliviscar. Consentit autem cum Zachariae ipse Dei filius, Iesus Christus, Nicodemo dicens: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum pro illo tradiderit, &c. Et Paulus, nos tunc illi reconciliatos fuisse dicit, cum inimici & filii irae, id est, ira & supplicio digni essemus. Quid vero testimonijs pluribus est opus, cum huius generis loci passim occurrant, & omnium patrum exempla iam inde ab origine mundi testentur, eos per solam Dei misericordiam servatos esse? Rursus ergo vanitatis arguitur nostrorum operum & proprij meriti fiducia. Si enim ipsi nobis succurrere poteramus, minime opus erat diuinae misericordiae viscera propter nos commoveri. At hoc non temere factum fuisse Dauid agnoscebat, cum multitudinem miserationum Dei implorarct, qua non minori desiderio omnes etiam ij invocabunt, qui seipsos & peccata sua propius inspexerint. Sed medium quoque videre oportet, per quod nobis Deus salutem attulit. Quia enim ille non solum milium misericors, verumetiam iustus & seuerus scelerum vindex esset, non sufficiebat, illum nostri mi-sertum, sed insuper peccata nostra expiari oportebat, vt ea ratione etiam ipsius iustitiae satisfie-ret. Quod qua ratione factum sit, Zacharias sic docet: Inuisit nos Oriens ex alto. Ita vero nominat æternum Dei filium, Iesum Christum, & alludere videtur ad promissionem, quae apud Malachiam habetur: Orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol iustitiae, & sanitas sine medicina in alis eius. Causam huius nominis Ioannes Euangelista reddit, quando illum dicit lucem illam veram esse, quae suo in mundum aduentu omnem hominem illuminet. Et ipse non semel se lucem mundi esse fa-tetur, quam qui sequuntur, non ambulent in tenebris. Hic Sol (inquit Zacharias) visitit nos ex al-to, id est, Deus filium suum misit, qui se humiliauit, & assumpta carne causam quoq; nostram su-scepit, vt nostrae salutis Mediator fieret, sicq; suis alis aut radijs afflicto hominum generi medicinam attulit, quod illum facturum Malachias praedixit. Ita vero filium Dei humiliari & verum homi-nem fieri oportuit, vt frater noster factus, simul vindex quoq; noster fieret, ad quae nostrae salutis cau-sa iure pertineret. Ita vero hanc egit, vt peccata quidem nostra in se translata mortis suae merito ex-piarit, mortem vero resurrectione vicerit, & inde à nobis assumptam carnem in coelos subuehendo, horum quoq; portas nobis patefecerit, quae propter peccatum prius occlusae erant. Et in his quidem no-strae cum Deo reconciliationis summa consistit, quae omnia cum vnus & solus Christus praestiterit, h:c quoq; vnicus nobis apud Deum Mediator est. Quod ipse non obscure testatur, dicens: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Et huius dicti ipsum patrem suffragatorem habet, qui coelitus clamat: Hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Non temere autem Sol iste ex alto exortus esse, & nos inuisisse dicitur. Ea enim locutione innuit Spiritus sanctus, salutem nostram per nulla huma-na aut terrena media obtigisse, sed negotium hoc totum diuinum & coeleste esse, atq; ex sola Dei mi-sericordia pendere, qui filium suum nobis de coelo seruatorem miserit. Ideo apud Isaiam haec quasi communis credentium & salutem promissam expectantium vox auditur: O si coelum scindas, ac de-scendas, vt montes à facie tua, vt ab igne incendio, colliquescant. Cui & hoc Dauidicum consentit: Attollo oculos meos ad montes, unde nam veniat auxilium meum. Auxilium meum à Domino, conditore coeli & terrae. Psal.121.
units.tr: But what, you ask, is the cause of this remission? Again, then, hear Zacharias, who says that it has been obtained for us because of the tender mercy of our God. Just as he first showed that we are debtors, and therefore in need of free remission, so he here shows that this remission lies in the pure mercy of God. And so that he may commend it to us more, he calls it the "bowels of mercy," understanding of course those natural movements of pity by which parents are wont to be affected towards children born of themselves, which the Greeks call σπλάγχνα [splanchna], and of which an example is set before us in that harlot who is written of as contending about her son before the tribunal of Solomon. The force of these feelings is so great that they still show themselves even when parents see their stubborn sons, who deserve any punishment, in some graver danger. Zacharias rightly attributes these to God, because God declares himself our Father and says through Isaiah: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? But even if those women forget, yet I will not forget you" (Isa. 49.15). The Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, agrees with Zacharias, saying to Nicodemus: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it," etc. (John 3.16). And Paul says that we were reconciled to him when we were enemies and children of wrath, that is, deserving of wrath and punishment (Eph. 2.3). But what need is there of more testimonies, when passages of this kind occur everywhere, and the examples of all the Fathers from the beginning of the world bear witness that they were saved through the mercy of God alone? Again, then, the confidence in our works and our own merit is shown to be vain. For if we could have helped ourselves, there would have been no need for the bowels of divine mercy to be moved on our behalf. Yet David recognised that this had not happened rashly, when he implored the multitude of God's mercies; and all those too will call upon it with no less desire who have looked more closely at themselves and their sins. But we must also see the means by which God has brought us salvation. For since he was not only merciful to thousands but also just and severe as the avenger of crimes, it was not enough for him to pity us; our sins had to be expiated as well, so that in this way the satisfaction of his justice might also be made. How this was done Zacharias teaches thus: "The Dayspring from on high has visited us." He thus names the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, and seems to allude to the promise found in Malachi: "To you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall arise, and healing is in his wings" (Mal. 4.2). John the Evangelist gives the reason for this name when he calls him the true light, which by his coming into the world enlightens every man. And he himself more than once declares that he is the light of the world, and that those who follow him shall not walk in darkness. This Sun (says Zacharias) has visited us from on high, that is, God sent his Son, who humbled himself and, taking on flesh, also undertook our cause, so that he might become the Mediator of our salvation; and so with his wings or rays he brought a remedy to the afflicted race of men, as Malachi foretold he would do. For the Son of God had to be humbled in this way and become a true man, so that, having become our brother, he might also become our avenger, to which our cause of salvation rightly belongs. And he carried this out in such a way that, by transferring our sins to himself, he expiated them by the merit of his death, conquered death by his resurrection, and then by carrying up to heaven the flesh he had taken from us, opened for us the gates of heaven, which had been closed on account of sin. In these things lies the sum of our reconciliation with God; and since the one and only Christ has accomplished all of them, he alone is our Mediator with God. He himself bears clear witness to this, saying: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14.6). And for this saying he has the Father himself as his advocate, who cries from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3.17). Nor is it without reason that this Sun is said to have risen from on high and visited us. For by this expression the Holy Spirit signifies that our salvation has come about through no human or earthly means, but that this whole business is divine and heavenly, and depends solely on the mercy of God, who has sent his Son from heaven as our Saviour. Therefore in Isaiah this voice is heard, as it were, common to believers who await the promised salvation: "O that you would rend the heavens and come down, so that the mountains might melt before your face, as fire melts by burning" (Isa. 64.1). To this the saying of David agrees: "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where shall my help come? My help is from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth" (Ps. 121.1-2).

units.la: Restat vt salutis huius per Christum exhibitae finem & fructum consideremus, qui ex illa ad nos redit. Tradit hunc Zacharias, quando Solem hunc nos ex alto inuisisse ait, vt appareat iis, qui in tenebris & in vmbra mortis positi sunt, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Comprehendi-tur his verbis fructus duplex, quorum alter ad conscientiarum consolationem maxime refertur, al-ter etiam ad vitae totius institutionem pertinet.
units.tr: It remains to consider the end and the fruit of this salvation, brought through Christ, which comes back to us from it. Zechariah sets it out when he says that this Sun has looked down on us from on high, to appear to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, and to guide our feet into the way of peace. In these words two fruits are comprised: one of them pertains above all to the comfort of consciences, the other also to the whole formation of life.

units.la: Primus est, quod iis apparet Christus Solis instar, qui in tenebris & in vmbra mortis sunt po- siti. Meminit huius Isaias quoq; ad cuius vaticinium Zacharias allusisse videtur. Sic enim ille ait: Populus, qui in tenebris ambulat, vidit lucem magnam, & habitantibus in terra vmbrae mortis affulsit lux. Vmbram mortis Hebraica phrasi dixit pro vmbra mortifera & exitiali. Adumbra-tur autem per tenebras & vmbram mortis calamitosa & infelix generis humani conditio, quam temporibus ignorantiae sub potestate tenebrarū (vt Paulus loquitur) sustinuimus, priusquam Chri-stus nobis innotesceret. Vt enim qui per loca ignota et tenebricosa ambulant, exire quidem cupiunt, sed quo se vertant nesciunt: ita qui Dei ignorantia & errorum tenebris excaecati sunt, vellent qui-dem viam salutis inuenire, non vident autem quid agant, aut quo pedes suos dirigant. Imo vt qui in obscuro carcere capitis sententiam in singulas horas expectat, duplici maerore conficitur, dum & mor-tem instantem pertimescit, & tenebris impeditus quid solatij quaerat non videt: ita miseri mortales caecitate mentis & Dei ignorantia ceu carcere aliquo teterrimo, conclusi fuerunt, quae illis vmbra mortis, id est, perditionis & exitij causa fuit, eo quod inde omnis generis errores & infinita peccata emanarunt. Senserunt plerique hanc suam miseriam, & intra conscientias suas grauissime excrucia-ti sunt, cum se quidem à Deo alienos & mortis aeternae nos propria conscientia teste intelligerent, nescirent autem quanam illis ad thronum gratiae & salutem aditus pateret. Exorti sunt hinc cul-tus superstitiosi, qui etsi sectatoribus suis laborum & sumptuum grauissimorum causam praeberent, nunquam tamen per illos effici potuit, quo minus miseris illis peccata simul & horum poenae subinde ob oculos versarentur. At in his angustijs agentibus Sol iustitiae exortus est, Iesus Christus nimirū,
units.tr: The first is that Christ appears, like the sun, to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. Isaiah also mentions this, and Zechariah seems to allude to his prophecy. For he says: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light; and light has dawned upon those who dwell in the land of the shadow of death." By a Hebrew idiom he calls it "the shadow of death" for a deadly and destructive shadow. Now by darkness and the shadow of death is figured the wretched and unhappy condition of the human race, which we endured in the times of ignorance, under the power of darkness (as Paul puts it), before Christ was made known to us. For as those who walk through unknown and dark places wish indeed to get out, but do not know where to turn, so those who have been blinded by ignorance of God and the darkness of error would indeed like to find the way of salvation, but do not see what they are to do or where to direct their feet. Indeed, as one who waits in a dark prison for the sentence of death hour by hour is worn down by a twofold grief, since he dreads imminent death and, hindered by the darkness, does not see where to seek any comfort, so wretched mortals, shut up through blindness of mind and ignorance of God as in some most foul prison, were for them a shadow of death, that is, the cause of ruin and destruction, because from it came every kind of error and endless sins. Many have felt this misery and have been most grievously tormented in their consciences, since they understood, with their own conscience as witness, that they were estranged from God and destined for eternal death, but did not know by what way an approach to the throne of grace and to salvation lay open to them. From this arose superstitious worship, which, although it caused its followers the greatest labours and expenses, could never prevent those wretched souls from having their sins and their punishments constantly before their eyes. But upon those who were struggling in these straits the Sun of righteousness has risen, namely Jesus Christ,

units.la: g qui & Dei veri cognitione salutifera hominum mentes illuminat, & solutis peccati vinculis nos in lucem educit, adhæc in seipso nobis accessum ad thronum gratiæ monstrans, conscientias ante metu & terrore damnationis consternatas incredibili gaudio exhilarat. Cur enim non gaudeant & exultent, qui illum clamantem audiunt: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis præstabo? Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Gaudij certè huius vis tanta est, ut in medijs quoq; afflictionibus nos exhilaret, ut hostibus nostris pia gloriatione insultare nō vereamur, quando nos Christi socios & regni eius coheredes factos esse videmus. Ita Dei electis & nomen eius timentibus aureus ille iustitiæ Sol oritur, qui suis radijs medicinam affert præsentissimā conscientijs sub peccatorum pondere & mortis metu laborantibus.
units.tr: who, by the saving knowledge of the true God, illuminates human minds, and, loosing the bonds of sin, leads us out into the light; moreover, by showing us in himself access to the throne of grace, he cheers with incredible joy consciences previously dismayed by fear and the terror of condemnation. For why should not those rejoice and exult who hear him calling: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Certainly the power of this joy is so great that it cheers us even in the midst of afflictions, so that we do not hesitate to insult our enemies with a holy boasting, when we see ourselves made companions of Christ and co-heirs of his kingdom. So for God's elect, who fear his name, that golden Sun of righteousness rises, bringing with its rays the most ready remedy for consciences labouring under the weight of sins and the dread of death.

units.la: Alter Christi fructus est, quòd pedes nostros dirigit in viam pacis. Pedum nomine affectus & institutum hominis notari sæpe diximus. Et videtur hoc membrum propheta verbis opponi, qui hominum à Dei & Christi eius cognitione alienorum mores describens, inter alia dicit, pedes eorum veloces esse ad effundendum sanguinem. Interim ostendit Zacharias, Christum nobis à patre non modo seruatorem, verumetiam doctorem datum esse, qualem olim Moses quoq; sub magni illius prophetæ nomine descripserat. Recte autem metaphoris & similibus vtitur ab ijs, qui iter faciunt, desumptis, quando constat vitam nostram omnem peregrinationem esse, qua nobis per vallē lachrymarum ad cœlestis patriæ possessionem enitendum est. Est autem peregrinatio illa ut laboris sic etiam periculi plena. Infestat enim nos varie mundus hic et eius princeps Satan: et nī quid periculi desit, ipsi pedes nostri, id est, innati affectus nobis plurimum negotij exhibent, dum nos post errorum auia & peccati illecebras transfuersos abripiunt. Hic ergo duce opus est fido & itinerum perito, quem Christum Iesum esse Zacharias docet, et idem prophetarū quoq; oracula passim testantur. Is nos in viam pacis dirigit, & ita quidem, ut nō solum verbis doceat, verumetiā exemplo proprio præcedat, ut ad sequendum magis exciter, & peregrinatione hanc nobis tutiorem & faciliorē reddat. Pacis autem nomine omnem felicitatē pro Hebræorum more intelligit, ad quam per Christū deducimur. Hic nos patri reconciliat, quod omnis beatitatis principiū est. Docet idem quid nos agere deceat, si in Dei fauore & protectione manere velimus: quo loco fidem nobis commendat, quæ ut nos bonorū cœlestiū consortes facit, ita fructus quoq; sanctissimos parit, pacem conscientiæ, dilectionē Dei & proximi, obedientiæ veræ studium, vitæ innocentiam, iustitiam & sanctitatem. His quicunq; studeant, ij & Deo propitio vtuntur, & cum hominibus quibusuis, quantum in ipsis est, pacificè viuunt, & proinde tam in hoc sæculo quàm in futuro verè felices & beati sunt. Possent hic multis recenseri præcepta Christi ex ordine, quæ ad hanc οδηγίαν seu manuductionem faciunt, sed cum sacra legentibus passim occurrant, & iam plus satis excreuerit oratio, illa consultò prætermittimus.
units.tr: The other fruit of Christ is that he directs our feet into the way of peace. We have often said that by the name of feet the affections and the manner of life of a person are signified. And the prophet seems to set this member against the words of Zechariah, when, describing the morals of men alienated from the knowledge of God and of his Christ, he says among other things that their feet are swift to shed blood. Meanwhile Zechariah shows that Christ has been given to us by the Father not only as Saviour but also as Teacher, such as Moses too had once described under the name of that great prophet. He rightly uses metaphors and comparisons taken from those who travel, since it is clear that our whole life is a pilgrimage, in which we must strive through this vale of tears towards possession of the heavenly fatherland. Now that pilgrimage is full of danger as well as of toil. For this world and its prince, Satan, assail us in various ways; and if no danger were lacking, our very feet, that is, our innate affections, give us great trouble, while they drag us, turned aside, after the pathless ways of error and the allurements of sin. Here therefore we need a faithful guide who knows the roads, and this is Christ Jesus, as Zechariah teaches, and the oracles of the prophets everywhere bear witness to the same. He directs us into the way of peace, and so indeed that he not only teaches us in words but also goes before us by his own example, to stir us more to follow, and makes the journey safer and easier for us. By the name of peace, after the manner of the Hebrews, he understands all happiness, to which we are led through Christ. He reconciles us to the Father here, which is the beginning of all blessedness. The same guide also teaches us what we ought to do if we wish to remain in God's favour and protection; in this place he commends to us faith, which, as it makes us partakers of heavenly goods, so also brings forth most holy fruits: peace of conscience, love of God and neighbour, zeal for true obedience, innocence of life, righteousness and holiness. Those who strive after these things both enjoy God's favour and live peaceably with all men, so far as lies in them, and so are truly happy and blessed both in this age and in the age to come. The precepts of Christ which serve this guidance [οδηγία], or manuduction, could be recounted here one by one at length; but since they meet readers of the sacred books on every page, and since the discourse has already grown more than enough, we deliberately pass them over.

units.la: Et hæc quidem cognitio illa salutis est, quam Ioannes populo tradere debuit. At si eius doctrinam inspiciamus, illum hoc ordine & modo ista tradidisse patebit. Salutem enim in gratuita peccatorum remissione, cuius nobis Christus author est, monstrauit, quando illo viso dixit: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Omnes item homines ad vnum Christum remisit, hunc vnicum salutis Mediatorem esse docuit, & tanto præconio commendauit, ut se indignum diceret, qui corrigiam calceorum eius solueret. Et cum discipulos præpostero zelo accensus Christum æmulari videret, magna cum gravitate ait: Ipsi vos testes estis, quòd dixerim, Ego non sum Christus, sed missus sum ante illum. Qui sponsam habet, sponsus est, &c. Item, Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui. Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit in manum eius. Qui credit filio, habet vitam æternam. Qui non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super illum. Quibus adiecit pœnitentiæ doctrinam, qua omnes homines ad innocentiæ, mutuæ dilectionis & pacis studium excitauit. Discant igitur hoc exemplo omnes de doctrinis iudicium facere. Quia enim Ioannes hic tam in veteri quàm nouo testamento multiplici spiritus sancti testimonio commendatur, deque eodem Christus ipse pronuntiat, neminem illo sanctiorem ex muliere natum esse: nefas fuerit eius doctrinam & quam ille secutus est docendi rationem in dubium vocare. Quisquis ergo ad eius exemplum salutis fontes in Dei misericordia monstrat, eiusque Mediatorem esse docet vnum Iesum Christum, & hunc simul fidei vitæque omnis ducem constituit, is doctoris officio verè fungitur, & neque ipse errat, neque sectatores suos in errorem adducit. Christus enim sibi ipsi semper constat, & unus idemq; est hodie & heri & in omnia secula. At qui aliam viam ingressus ad operum merita, satisfactiones, humanam iustitiam, Diuorum intercessionem, ignis purgatorij lustrationem, Missarum oblationes et alia huius farinæ remittit, quibus & Dei gratia negatur, & Christi Iesu meritum exinanitur: is Euangelium aliud prædicat, præter illud quod apostolorum temporibus prædicatum est, & proinde impostor est, etiamsi angelus de cœlo fuerit. Frustra igitur hodie queruntur multi, se nescire quid credant aut faciant in tanta sententiarum de fide & religione varietate. Si enim Christianus es, Christo ausculta. Si ovis Christi es, vocem eius audi & sequere. Si Dei filius es, patris voce obtempera. Si Christi sponsa es, aut sponsæ eius membrum, huic uni adhære, hunc dilige, & eius monitis te obedientem præbe. Quod si cui ista non satisfaciunt, sed insuper Patrum & Conciliorum decretis atque superstitionibus quotidie novis opus esse putat, & ea mordicus tuetur, quæ nullo scripturarum testimonio probari posse novit, hunc nos suo iudici relinquamus, ut in ipso tandem impleatur quod Christus dixit: Si cæcus cæco ducem fuerit, ambo cadent in foveam. Matth. 15. Et hæc dicta sint in divinum hoc Zachariæ Canticum, quod utinam tam diligenter expenderent monachi & sacrificuli, quàm in illo decantando assidui sunt.
units.tr: And this indeed is that knowledge of salvation which John ought to have handed down to the people. If we examine his teaching, it will be clear that he set these things out in this order and manner. For he showed salvation to lie in the free remission of sins, of which Christ is the author, when on seeing him he said: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." Likewise he sent all men to Christ alone, taught that he is the only Mediator of salvation, and commended him with such high praise that he said he was not worthy to loose the thong of his sandals. And when he saw the disciples, kindled by a misplaced zeal, seeming to rival Christ, he said with great seriousness: "You yourselves are witnesses that I said, I am not the Christ, but I am sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom, etc." Again: "He must increase, but I must decrease." "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand." "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." To these he added the teaching of repentance, by which he stirred all men to the pursuit of innocence, mutual love and peace. Let all therefore learn from this example to judge doctrines. For since John is commended in both the Old and the New Testament by the manifold testimony of the Holy Spirit, and since Christ himself pronounces of him that no one born of woman is greater than he, it would be wrong to call in question his teaching and the method of teaching which he followed. Whoever, then, following his example, points to the springs of salvation in the mercy of God, and teaches that the one Jesus Christ is the Mediator, and at the same time appoints him as the leader of all faith and of the whole of life, he truly discharges the office of a teacher, and neither errs himself nor leads his followers into error. For Christ is always consistent with himself, and is one and the same yesterday, today and for ever. But whoever enters another way, and sends men back to the merits of works, satisfactions, human righteousness, the intercession of the saints, the purging of purgatorial fire, the oblations of masses and other things of that sort, by which the grace of God is denied and the merit of Christ Jesus is emptied out, he preaches another gospel, besides that which was preached in the times of the apostles, and therefore he is an impostor, even if he were an angel from heaven. It is in vain, then, that many complain today that they do not know what to believe or do amid such great variety of opinions about faith and religion. For if you are a Christian, listen to Christ. If you are a sheep of Christ, hear his voice and follow. If you are a son of God, obey the Father's voice. If you are the bride of Christ, or a member of his bride, cling to him alone, love him, and show yourself obedient to his commands.
