But if anyone is not satisfied by these things, and thinks that the decrees of the Fathers and the Councils and new superstitions are needed every day, and holds stubbornly to those things which he knows cannot be proved by any testimony of the Scriptures, let us leave him to his own judgment, so that in him at last may be fulfilled what Christ said: "If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit." Matt. 15. And let these things be said on this divine Canticle of Zechariah, which would that monks and mass-priests weighed as carefully as they are diligent in chanting it.

units.la: Sequitur Ioannis pueritia & institutio, adhæc vitæ totius ratio, quam ad eum usq; diem tenuit, quo impositam sibi à Deo functionem cœpit obire. Ubi paucis verbis rem maximi momenti Lucas absoluit. Ipse autem puerulus (inquit) crescebat & corroborabatur spiritu, fuitq; in desertis ad eum usque diem, quo se offenderet apud Israelem.
units.tr: Next comes John's childhood and upbringing, and the manner of his whole life, which he kept until the day he began to discharge the office God had laid on him. Here Luke concludes in a few words a matter of the greatest importance: "But the child," he says, "grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the deserts until the day when he should show himself to Israel."

units.la: Primo illum creuisse et simul spiritu corroboratum fuisse ait. Ergo ut ætatis progressu corpore crevit, ita spiritus quoque sancti donis indies auctus est, quæ in illo novis quotidie argumentis sese magis atq; magis exeruerunt. Non temere autem ab hoc orditur Euangelista. Ex eo enim apparet, quæ nam virtutum omnium in Ioanne causa atq; origo fuerit: non quidem propriæ naturæ indoles, (nam ut alij homines in peccato conceptus et natus fuit) non parentum meritum (Zachariam enim ob incredulitatem quousque supplicio dignum fuisse audimus) sed Dei gratia, qui sicuti promiserat, illum adhuc in matris utero delitescentem spiritu suo donavit, & huius dona deinde in illo quotidie auxit. Spiritus ergo sancti opus fuit, quod vitam egit Ioannes à communi viuendi consuetudine alienam, & quæ omnibus admirationi fuit: quod veritati testimonium tam constanter perhibuit, quod pœnitentiam tanto serio docuit, & scelera publica tanto ardore & libertate dicendi corripuit, ut ne Regi quidem Herodi parcendum putarit, quin mortem potius crudelem voluerit perpeti, quàm ad flagitium tanto cum scandalo coniunctum consentire. Nam si ista ad nostræ rationis calculum examines, huic impossibile fuerit, pericula tanta spe bonorum cœlestium subire, & propter futuram retributionem præsentis vitæ commoda negligere. Quæ causa est, quod Christus discipulos non ante ab Hierosolymis discedere & ad prædicandi munus prodire voluit, donec spiritum sanctum accepissent, qui rebus agendis idoneos & ad pericula quæuis intrepidos faceret. Debent hoc observare quicunque ad ministerium ecclesiæ vocantur, ut pietati, sanctitati et innocentiæ studeant: quando certum est illos absque spiritu sancti auxilio nihil egregij facturos esse, ille autem cum impiis & impuris commercij nihil habet, neque in animam malignam ingreditur. Orent denique indesinenter, ne spiritum suum illis Deus subducat, sed hunc in ipsis indies confirmet & augeat, ut & stationem suam tueri, & ministerium suum maiori cum fructu obire possint. Excitet illos adventus Domini, qui ut tunc veniet, quando minimè venturus putabitur: sic ab illis suæ functionis rationem exiget, & de illorum manu requiret sanguinem eorum omnium, qui ipsorum negligentia perierunt.
units.tr: First, he says that John grew and was at the same time strengthened in the Spirit. Therefore, just as he grew in body as he advanced in age, so the gifts of the Holy Spirit increased in him day by day, and these showed themselves more and more through new evidence each day. The Evangelist does not begin from this point by chance, for it shows what was the cause and source of all John's virtues: not the disposition of his own nature (for he was conceived and born in sin like other men), nor his parents' merit (for we hear that Zechariah, on account of his unbelief, was for a time worthy of punishment), but the grace of God, who, as he had promised, endowed him with his Spirit while he was still hidden in his mother's womb, and then increased these gifts in him daily. It was therefore the work of the Holy Spirit that John lived a life apart from the common manner of living, a life that was a wonder to all; that he bore witness to the truth so steadfastly; that he taught repentance so earnestly and rebuked public sins with such fervour and frankness of speech that he thought not even King Herod should be spared, and preferred to suffer a cruel death rather than consent to a scandal so great. For if you weigh these things by the reckoning of our reason, it would have been impossible for him to face such dangers in hope of heavenly goods, and to disregard the present advantages of life for the sake of future reward. This is why Christ did not wish his disciples to leave Jerusalem and go out to the work of preaching until they had received the Holy Spirit, who would make them fit for their task and fearless before any danger. Whoever are called to the ministry of the Church should observe this: they should devote themselves to piety, holiness and innocence, since it is certain that without the help of the Holy Spirit they will accomplish nothing excellent, and he has no fellowship with the impious and impure and does not enter a malicious soul. Finally, let them pray without ceasing that God not withdraw his Spirit from them, but confirm and increase it in them day by day, so that they may both keep their post and discharge their ministry with greater fruit. Let the coming of the Lord stir them up; he will come when he is least expected, and so he will require from them an account of their office and will demand at their hand the blood of all who perished through their negligence.

units.la: Deinde in desertis vitam egisse dicitur Ioannes. Vitæ vero rationem Matthæus & Marcus diligentius exprimunt, qui illum pilis camelorum vestitum & zona coriacea succinctum fuisse, mele autem sylvestri & locustis victitasse scribunt. Fuit ergo tota vitæ ratio conformis ei loco, in quo versabatur. Ubi nemo putaverit, exemplo hoc vitam Monasticam aut eremiticam commendari. Nullum enim Dei præceptum extat, quo in solitudinem secedere & hominum consortio nos in vniuersum subducere iubeamur. Quin potius societate & mutuis hominum officijs ex charitate non fucata manantibus Deus delectatur, & quemque in sua vocatione obeunda diligentem esse iubet. Quod ergo Ioannes vitæ genus peculiare à prima pueritia secutus est, id ex singulari spiritus sancti impulsu et ministerij causa fecit, cui ipsum Deus destinauerat. Quia enim Christi praenuntius atq; primus noui Testamenti minister, adeoq; prophetis omnibus excellentior esse debebat, necesse fuit ita eum a pueris educari, ut vulgò omnes viderent, singulare quid de illo sperari debere. Deinde cum per annos circiter quadringentos & quinquaginta (post Malachiam nimirum, qui vltimus veteris testamenti propheta fuit) prophetandi munus cessisset, illud non sine noua aliqua praeparatione instaurari oportuit, ut omnium mentes ad audiendum verbum Domini excitarentur. Praeterea quia Angelus dixerat, Vinum & siceram non biberet, hominum quoq; consuetudinem vitare debuit, ne ea corrumperetur. Exigebat etiam tale quid populi Iudaici ingenium, qui in externis haerere, & ex his de doctoribus iudicium facere solebat. Illis ergo sese accommodare voluit Dominus, ne quam suae incredulitatis & contumaciae excusationem haberent. Ex his vero colligitur, non debere hoc Ioannis factum in exemplum trahi, & nisi ipsi quoq; diuinitus vocemur, non nouam institui debere viam rationem, sed hoc potius curandum esse, ut nostrae vocationi satisfaciamus. Interim discimus, a pueris assuefaciendum esse iis, quae ad functionem, cui destinati sumus, necessaria sunt. Quantum enim possit educatio, in brutis quoq; animantibus cernitur, & olim Lycurgus Spartanos suos duorum catulorum exemplo docuit, qui etsi ex iisdem parentibus nati essent, alter tamen venationi idoneus, alter ignavus culinae custos factus est, cum diuerso modo institui essent. Est vero hoc in primis obseruandum in iis, qui aliquando ad Ecclesiae ministerium accedere debent, cum eorum functio vires humanas superet, & cum eruditione pietatis quoq; studium singulare requirat. Ideo Samuelem olim parentes a pueris apud Eli sacerdotem in tabernaculo institui volebant, cum illum sacro ministerio destinauissent. Et frequens est in Regum historia filiorum prophetiorum mentio, qui in collegijs educabantur, ut in suo tempore ad docendum prodirent. De Timotheo etiam suo Paulus testatur, quod a puero sacras literas didicerit. Apud Amos autem graviter accusantur, qui Nazaraeos, id est, sacris studijs destinatos iuuenes vini nimio vsu & disciplina dissolutiori corrumpebant. Huius vitiam hodie meminissent omnes ij, quorum curae iuuentus commissa est. Sed ut in alijs, ita hic quoq; plurimum peccatur, & ideo infeliciores sunt ta respublicae quam ecclesiae, quod earum gulernaculis ij fere adhibetur, qui a primis annis abs disciplina educati, pessimis moribus assueuerunt.
units.tr: Then it is said that John lived in the deserts. Matthew and Mark describe his way of life more carefully, writing that he was clothed with camel's hair, girded with a leather belt, and fed on wild honey and locusts. So his whole manner of life was in keeping with the place where he dwelt. No one should think that by this example monastic or eremitic life is commended. For there is no command of God bidding us to withdraw into solitude and altogether to separate ourselves from fellowship with men. Rather, God delights in society and in mutual services among men flowing from unfeigned love, and he bids each person to be diligent in carrying out his own calling. So what John followed from his earliest childhood, a peculiar way of life, he did from a singular impulse of the Holy Spirit and for the sake of the ministry for which God had destined him. For since he was to be the herald of Christ and the first minister of the New Testament, and so should be more excellent than all the prophets, it was necessary that he be brought up from boyhood in such a way that everyone could see that something singular was to be hoped for from him. Again, since the office of prophesying had ceased for about four hundred and fifty years (namely since Malachi, the last prophet of the Old Testament), it had to be restored not without some fresh preparation, so that the minds of all might be stirred to hear the word of the Lord. Moreover, because the angel had said that he should drink neither wine nor strong drink, he also had to avoid the customs of men, lest these corrupt him. The temper of the Jewish people also demanded something of this kind, for they clung to outward things and were accustomed to judge teachers by these. The Lord therefore wished to accommodate himself to them, so that they would have no excuse for their unbelief and obstinacy. From these things, however, it is gathered that John's act ought not to be drawn into an example; unless we too are called by God, we ought not to devise a new way of life, but rather take care to satisfy our own calling. Meanwhile we learn that from boyhood men must be trained in what is necessary for the office to which they are destined. How much education can do is seen even in brute animals, and long ago Lycurgus taught his Spartans by the example of two puppies which, though born of the same parents, were made one fit for hunting and the other a lazy guard of the kitchen, because they had been trained in different ways. This above all must be observed in those who at some time are to come to the ministry of the Church, since its office exceeds human strength and requires, along with learning, a singular zeal for piety. Thus long ago parents wished Samuel to be brought up from boyhood in the tabernacle with Eli the priest, once they had dedicated him to the sacred ministry. And in the history of the Kings there is frequent mention of the sons of the prophets, who were educated in colleges so that in their time they might come forward to teach. Paul also testifies that his Timothy had learned the sacred letters from boyhood. But in Amos, those are gravely accused who corrupted the Nazarites, that is, young men destined for sacred studies, with excessive use of wine and a looser discipline. All those to whom the care of youth is entrusted should today remember this fault. But, as in other matters, so here too very much sin is committed, and therefore states are less fortunate than churches, because their helm is commonly given to those who, having been brought up without discipline from their earliest years, have become accustomed to the worst morals.

units.la: Postremo indicatur, quam diu Ioannes in desertis vixerit: Nimirum vsq; ad diem ostensionis suae, id est, ad eum diem vsq; quo a Deo euocatus est, ut docendi munus publice susciperet, seq; ipsum Israeli manifestaret. Vbi apparet, illum etsi donis spiritus sancti instructissimus esset, non tamen confidentiorem fuisse, neque seipsum insolenter ad res magnas & arduas ingessisse. Imo etsi in ecclesia Israelitica summam corruptionem videret, quam ipsi ex animo displicuisse non est dubium, Dei tamen vocationem expectauit, ne quid abs huius auspicijs imprudenter et inconsulto ageret. Est hoc obseruatu dignissimum. Vt enim vnicus in ecclesia paterfamilias est Deus, ita huius mandatum expectent, qui in illa aliquid tentant. Nam constat olim graviter accusatos fuisse, qui nō missi currebant. Quae causa est, quod prophetae & apostoli suae vocationis saepius meminerunt, ut & doctrinae suae authoritatem afferant, & seipsos confirment aduersus hostium minas, qui regnum Dei euersum cupiunt. Peccatur in hoc plurimum hodie ab ijs, qui solius ventris studio ad ecclesiae ministerium aspirant, aut omnes eos ecclesiae obtrudunt, quos non alia ratione victum sibi parare posse vident. Quasi vero ecclesia propter ministros, non autem potius hi propter ecclesiam instituti sint. Sed sunt hi fere ex mercenariorum numero, qui vt viso periculo ecclesiam turpiter deserunt: ita dum res saluae sunt, fere legitimis & fidis pastoribus molestiam exhibent, dum & scandalorum publicorum authores sunt, & illorum authoritatem tam exemplo quam calumniandi libidine labefactant. Est ergo probe consideranda ministris omnibus Ioannis tota historia, vna cum Cantici huius parte, qua de illius ministerio agitur: ut salutis cognitionem vere & fideliter tradant, ne cui perditionis authores sint. Discant praeterea singuli homines de verbi ministris iudicare, ut impostores quidem caueant, fidis autem pastoribus obtemperent, et ita vitam suam omnem instituant, ut salutis aeternae possessionem olim adire possint cum Iesu Christo Domino nostro; cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, it is indicated how long John lived in the deserts: namely until the day of his showing forth, that is, until the day when he was called by God to take up the office of teaching publicly and to make himself known to Israel. Here it appears that, although he was most richly furnished with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he was not for that reason more self-confident, nor did he insolently thrust himself into great and difficult affairs. Indeed, although he saw the great corruption of the Israelite Church, which there is no doubt displeased him heartily, he still awaited God's calling, lest he act rashly and without counsel under his own auspices. This is most worthy of observation. For as God alone is the householder in the Church, so those who attempt anything in it should await his command. It is certain that those who ran without being sent were long ago gravely accused. This is why the prophets and apostles so often mention their calling, both to bring authority to their teaching and to strengthen themselves against the threats of enemies who desire the overthrow of the kingdom of God. Today those most at fault in this are those who aspire to the ministry of the Church out of a desire only for their belly, or who thrust upon the Church all those whom they see cannot otherwise earn a living, as if the Church were instituted for the sake of the ministers, and not rather they for the sake of the Church! But these men are mostly of the number of hired hands, who, when they see danger, shamefully desert the Church; and so, while things are safe, they cause trouble to legitimate and faithful pastors, while they themselves are the authors of public scandals and undermine the pastors' authority, both by their example and by a lust for slander. Therefore all ministers should carefully consider the whole history of John, together with that part of this Canticle which speaks of his ministry, so that they may truly and faithfully hand down the knowledge of salvation and not be authors of destruction to anyone. Let individual people further learn to judge the ministers of the Word, so that they beware of impostors but obey faithful pastors, and so order their whole life that they may one day come to the possession of eternal salvation with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT II.

units.la: HOMILIA XVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XVI.

units.la: FActum est autem in diebus illis, exiit edictu à Cæsare Augusto, ut describeretur vniuersus orbis. Hęc descriptio prima facta est præsi de Syriæ Cyrenio. Ibant igitur omnes ut describerentur, in suā quisque vrbem. Ascendit autem etiā Ioseph à Galilæa, ex vrbe Nazareth, in Iudæam, in vrbem Dauid, quæ vocatur Bethlehē (propterea quod esset ex domo & familia Dauid) vt describeretur cū Maria despōnsa sibi vxore, quæ erat prægnans. Factum est autē cum essent illic, completi sunt dies, quibus ipsa pareret. Peperit igitur filium suum, illum Primogenitum, & fascijs eum inuoluit, reclinauitq; eū in præsepi, eò quod non erat eis locus in diuersorio.
units.tr: Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled. This first enrolment was made while Cyrenius was governor of Syria. So all went to be enrolled, each to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem (because he was of the house and family of David), to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was great with child. And it came to pass, while they were there, that the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.

units.la: ADMIRABILIS quidem & magnus est Deus in vniuersis operibus suis: et nullum inter hæc admirabilius et magnificentius, quàm quod filium suum vnigenitum, sibi coæternum & coessentialem in mundum hunc non minus sceleratum quàm infelicem, imò in carnem miseram & mortalem, misit, & homine fieri voluit omnibus miseriis & æerumnis obnoxium, quibus miseri mortales in terris exercentur. In eo enim opere omnia quæ de illo prædicantur, ita sese exerunt, vt dubium sit quid potissimum admirêre: bonitatem ne et misericordiam, qua humani generis miseriam respexit: an iustitiam, qua peccatum mundi digno supplicio expiari voluit; vel potius sapientiā, quæ hanc redemptionis nostræ viam inuenire potuit, quā & nobis subueniretur, & simul iustitiæ ipsius æternæ satisfieret. Meretur ergo historia hæc, vt in eius consideratione diligenter versemur, quam modò Lucas Ioannis Baptistæ natiuitati subiicit. Repetenda sunt autem hic nobis & probè tenenda, quæ de illius conceptione in primo Cap. dicta sunt: quòd nimirum ex Spiritu sancto verum & æternum Dei filium Maria conceperit, qui ex eius substantia carnem assumpsit, & ex illa verus homo natus est. Itaq; qui hic nobis nascitur, verus Deus & homo est, & proinde Mediator verus inter Deum & homines, adeoq; promissus ille humani generis redemptor est. Quod vt rectius intelligatur, multùm proderit huius loci historiam propius inspexisse. Nam etsi Lucas in ea commemoranda hoc in primis spectasse videatur, vt doceret, qua occasione Maria, quæ Nazarethi in Galilæa domicilium habebat, Bethlehemum, locum Messiæ natalibus æterno Dei decreto destinatum & à prophetis olim prædictum, deuenerit: narrationem tamen illam ita contexit, vt singulæ eius circumstantiæ non obscurè relucentur, Iesum hunc esse Christū, salutis olim promissæ Mediatorem. Nam à tempore exorsus, simul infelicem & miseram, quæ tunc fuit, populi Dei conditionē indicat. Deinde de loco natali & Mariæ atq; Iosephi familia aut genere disserit. Praeterea partus huius ratione siue modū exponit, vnà cum ijs, quæ cum infante recens nato sunt facta. In sunt aut singulis partibus quæ ad fidei nostræ confirmationē et vitæ institutionē plurimum faciunt.
units.tr: Indeed God is wonderful and great in all his works, and among them none is more wonderful or magnificent than that he sent his only-begotten Son, co-eternal and co-essential with himself, into this world, no less wicked than wretched, and even into miserable and mortal flesh, and willed that he be made man, subject to all the miseries and hardships by which wretched mortals are harassed on earth. For in this work all the things that are proclaimed of him so display themselves that it is doubtful what one should admire most: his goodness and mercy, by which he looked upon the misery of the human race; or his justice, by which he willed that the sin of the world be expiated by a worthy punishment; or rather his wisdom, which could devise this way of our redemption, by which both we might be helped and at the same time the satisfaction due to his eternal justice might be made. This story therefore deserves that we dwell diligently upon its consideration, the story that Luke now places after the birth of John the Baptist. Here we must also repeat and firmly hold what was said in the first chapter about his conception: namely, that Mary conceived of the Holy Spirit the true and eternal Son of God, who took flesh from her substance, and was born from her a true man. Therefore he who is born for us here is true God and man, and consequently is the true Mediator between God and men, and so he is that promised redeemer of the human race. To understand this more rightly, it will help greatly to have looked more closely at the history of this passage. For although Luke, in relating it, seems chiefly to have had in view this purpose, to teach by what occasion Mary, who had her home at Nazareth in Galilee, came to Bethlehem, the place destined by the eternal decree of God for the Messiah's birth and foretold long ago by the prophets; nevertheless he so arranges the narrative that each of its circumstances clearly shows that this Jesus is the Christ, the Mediator of the salvation promised of old. For beginning from the time, he at once indicates the wretched and miserable condition of the people of God as it then was. Then he speaks of the place of birth and of the family or lineage of Mary and Joseph. Besides, he sets out the manner or mode of this birth, together with the things that were done to the newborn infant. In each of these parts there are matters that greatly contribute to the confirmation of our faith and the ordering of our life.

units.la: Orditur autem narrationem hanc à temporis considerationē, non solùm pro historicorum more, vt plus fidei mereatur, sed potius propter veterum patrum et prophetarū oracula, vt offendat, tunc tempus illud fuisse, quo Messiam venturū esse illi olim prædixerant. Extat enim Iacobi patriarchæ vaticinium, qui cùm iam moriturus ex Spiritus sancti suggestione filijs suis fausta imprecaretur, et de eorundem & posteritatis totius fatis dissereret, inter alia dixit: Non recedet sceptrum de Iuda, neq; legulator de pedibus eius donec veniat Schilo, id est, felicitatis author, et ad illū gentes confluent. Cuius oraculi sensus est, Iudæorum gentem tunc demum amisso regno alienis principibus & seruitu- ti nunquam finiendæ subijciendæ fore, cùm promissi redemptoris aduentus præ foribus fuerit. Nā etsi prius non semel ab hostibus deuicti, tam peregre quàm domi gentium tyrannidem sustinuerint, semper tamē illis reliqua mansit restitutionis spes, neq; prorsus intercidit regiæ familiæ authoritas, vt sibi non obscurè meliora tempora polliceri possent. Sub Christi verò aduentum ea seruitus cœpit, quæ in hunc vsq; diem durat, & cuius finis, quoad remp. nullus sperari potest. Conuenit Iacobi vaticinium cum tempore Christi.
units.tr: He begins this narrative with a consideration of the time, not only after the manner of historians, so that it may deserve more trust, but rather because of the oracles of the ancient fathers and prophets, so that it may be clear that that was the time in which they had long before foretold that the Messiah would come. For there is the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, who, when he was about to die, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit pronounced blessings on his sons, and spoke about the fates of them and of all their posterity; among other things he said: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come, that is, the author of happiness, and to him shall the nations gather." The sense of this oracle is that the Jewish nation would at last, once its kingdom was lost, be made subject to foreign princes and to a servitude that would never end, when the coming of the promised redeemer was at the doors. For although before this, not once only, they had been conquered by enemies and had endured the tyranny of the nations both abroad and at home, still there always remained to them the hope of restoration, nor did the authority of the royal family altogether perish, so that they could promise themselves better times. But at the coming of Christ that servitude began which lasts to this day, and whose end, as far as the commonwealth is concerned, cannot be hoped for. Jacob's prophecy agrees with the time of Christ.

units.la: Incarnatio filii Dei memorabilis. ticinio, quòd Isaias germen illud benedictum ex trunco Isai nasciturum, id est, tunc venturum ait, quando Davidis familia ad infimam conditionem redacta fuerit, qualis olim sub Isai rustico & homine pecuario erat, adeoque eradicati & excisi trunci instar nullam de se spem præbeat amplius. Daniel autem huius quoque subiectionis aut servitutis tempus & simul filij Dei in carnem aduentum differtè in quarta monarchia monstrauerat, quam Romanorum fuisse, omnium historiarum consensus abunde testatur. Atqui iste vaticinijs pulchrè conueniunt quæ hic ab Euangelista dicuntur. Quia enim ex Cæsaris Augusti mandato orbis totius, id est, omnium prouinciarum, quæ Romano Imperio parebant, census agitur, iam prorsus confirmatam esse oportuit monarchiam, quam Deus ad illam vt hem deuenturam esse prædixerat. Factum est hoc, vt historici docent: sub annum Augusti quadragesimum secundum: quando fractis omnium Imperij Romani hostium viribus, orbis terrarum pacem habuit & Iani templum tertio clausum fuit. Duravit ea pax annis totis duodecim, quòd à prima vrbis origine nunquam accidisse constat. Et hæc hominibus antea bellis perpetuis occupatis causa fuisse videtur, vt prouincias omnes census, & potentiæ suæ experimentum sumere vellent. Et videtur huc referri debere quod Dion scribit, Augustum hoc excogitauisse, vt omnium prouinciarum census ageretur, & ex eo colligerentur pecuniæ ad alendas legiones, quas Romani hinc inde dispositas habebant, vt suo imperio subiectos populos in officio continerent. Et sane incredibile dictu fuerit, quanta pecuniarum vis hac ratione intra paucos mensesv colligi potuerit. In censu enim & capita singulorum describebantur, & secundum cuiusque facultates tributum exigebatur, vt hodie in publicis exactionibus fieri consueuit. Pace ergo fruebantur quidem Romani, sed interim sub tristi seruitutis iugo laborabant reliquæ gentes, quibus insuper omnis libertatis recuperandæ spes adempta erat. Præ alijs autem miseri & infelices erant Iudæi, quorum res tunc afflictissimæ fuerunt. Iam pridem enim à Pompeio Magno deuicti, sub Romanorum ditionem venerant, qui (vt alias diximus) regem ipsis imposuerunt Herodem, hominem libidine & crudelitate infamem, & ex infestissima Idumæorum gente oriundum. Habebant item Romani (vt ex euangelica historia apparet) hinc inde dispositá præsidia, quæ populū ad seditiones procliuem coercerent, & ita sub plausibili pacis prætextu arma in medijs vrbibus dominabantur. Mittitur nunc præses Syriæ Cyrenius, vt censum quoque illorum agat, quod illi populo non potuit non molestissimum & intolerabile videri. Nam & seruitutis atque subiectionis extremæ hoc erat indicium, & cum publica non solum gentis totius, verumetiam religionis ignominia coniunctum erat. Prius enim soli Deo census ex lege soluebatur, qui hoc ita instituerat, vt populum hunc suum peculium, & se solum eius Regem & dominum esse testaretur. Dum ergo censum sibi vendicat Augustus, & hoc fieri Deus patitur, perinde illud erat, ac si hic iuri suo prorsus renunciauisset, & hoc in hominem prophanum atque religionis verae hostem in vniuersum esset translatum. Certè quàm acerbum hoc plerisque fuerit, ex eo apparet, quòd cum Christo vellent summam inuidiam apud populum conciliare, quæstionem de censu Cæsari soluendo proposuerunt. Dauidis autem familia adeò tunc vilulit in extremam miseriam redacta, vt eius posteris Bethlehemi vix in stabulo locus detur. At hic nos simul meminisse oportet, tantæ miseriæ illis causam fuisse ambitionem fratrum Hircani & Aristobuli, qui de Pontificatu certamine inter se suscepto non solum Iudæorum gentem in partes distraxerunt, & bellorum ciuilium fuerunt authores, verumetiam accersitis vtrinque exteris auxiliis, communem patriam cum vrbe regia & templo Romanis occupandam & diripiendam propinauerunt, & eius calamitatis causa exiterunt, cuius finis ne tota quidem gente euersa & dispersa inueniri potuit. Quod exemplum vtinam hodie attentius obseruarent, qui vt affectui suo indulgeant, cum suis gentilibus digladiantur, cum exteris fœdera iungunt, auxilia aliunde adducunt, & dum conciues suos ferre nolunt, barbarorum crudeli & sanguinariæ libidini patriam et posteritatem simul omnem subijciunt. Vidimus iam annis aliquot funesta tanti mali præludia in bellis Turcicis, quæ vtinam non aliquando cum vniuersali orbis Christiani exitio finem suum consequantur, & (quod olim Lactantius prædixit) imperium reuertatur in Orientem, ac rursum seruiat Occidens. Sed hæc præter huius historiæ argumentum.
units.tr: The incarnation of the Son of God is memorable. The prophecy agrees also in that Isaiah says that the blessed branch would spring from the stump of Jesse, that is, that it would come when the family of David had been reduced to the lowest condition, such as it once was under Jesse, a rustic and shepherd, and so, like a cut and felled stump, it would offer no hope of itself any more. Daniel, too, had clearly shown in the fourth monarchy the time of this subjection or servitude and at the same time the coming of the Son of God in the flesh; and that this monarchy was the Roman one, the consent of all histories abundantly testifies. Now these prophecies agree well with what the evangelist here says. For since by the command of Caesar Augustus a census of the whole world, that is, of all the provinces that obeyed the Roman Empire, was being taken, the monarchy, which God had foretold would come to that point, must by then have been fully established. This happened, as historians teach, in about the forty-second year of Augustus, when, the strength of all the enemies of the Roman Empire having been broken, the world had peace and the temple of Janus was closed for the third time. That peace lasted a full twelve years, which, as is agreed, had never happened since the first origin of the city. And this seems to have been the reason why men, previously occupied with perpetual wars, wished to take a census of all the provinces and a trial of their own power. And it seems that what Dio writes should be referred here, that Augustus devised this, that a census of all the provinces should be taken, and from it money gathered to support the legions which the Romans kept stationed here and there, so that they might keep the peoples subject to their rule in obedience. And indeed it would be hard to believe how great a sum of money could be collected in this way within a few months. For in the census the heads of individuals were recorded, and tribute was exacted according to each one's means, as is customary to do today in public levies. So the Romans indeed enjoyed peace, but meanwhile the other nations laboured under the sad yoke of servitude, from which all hope of recovering liberty had been taken away. Above others, however, the Jews were wretched and unhappy, whose affairs at that time were most afflicted. For long before, having been conquered by Pompey the Great, they had come under the rule of the Romans, who (as we have said elsewhere) placed over them as king Herod, a man infamous for lust and cruelty, and born of the most hostile nation of the Idumaeans. The Romans also kept garrisons stationed here and there (as appears from the evangelical history) to restrain a people prone to sedition, and so under the plausible pretext of peace they ruled by arms in the midst of the cities. Now the governor of Syria, Cyrenius, is sent to take their census too, which could not but seem most troublesome and intolerable to that people. For it was a sign of extreme servitude and subjection, and it was joined with public disgrace not only to the whole nation but also to its religion. For formerly the census was paid by law to God alone, who had so ordained that he might testify that this people was his own possession, and that he alone was its King and Lord. So when Augustus claims the census for himself, and God permits this to be done, it was just as if he had utterly renounced his right, and had transferred it to a profane man and a general enemy of the true religion. Certainly how bitter this was to many is clear from the fact that, wishing to win great hatred for Christ among the people, they put to him the question about paying tribute to Caesar. And the family of David was then reduced to such extreme wretchedness that its posterity can scarcely be given room even in a stable at Bethlehem. But here we must also remember that the cause of such great misery for them was the ambition of the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, who, having undertaken a contest between themselves over the high priesthood, not only divided the Jewish nation into factions and became the authors of civil wars, but also, by summoning foreign auxiliaries on either side, offered their common country, with its royal city and temple, to be occupied and plundered by the Romans; and they became the cause of that calamity whose end could not be found even when the whole nation was overthrown and scattered. Would that those who today, to indulge their passion, fight against their own countrymen, join alliances with foreigners, bring in help from elsewhere, and, since they are unwilling to bear with their fellow citizens, subject their country and all their posterity to the cruel and bloody lust of barbarians, would pay closer attention to this example! We have already seen for some years the dismal prelude of so great an evil in the Turkish wars; would that these do not at some time reach their end with the total destruction of the whole Christian world, and (as Lactantius once foretold) that the empire return to the East, and the West serve again. But these matters are beside the argument of this history.

units.la: Nunc iste potissimum obseruari conuenit, quòd ex æterno patris decreto tunc homo nasci debuit Iesus Christus, quando res populi Dei modis omnibus afflictissimæ fuerunt. Conuenit hoc cum more Dei iam multis seculis confirmato, quo fit, ut tunc maxime suam opem ille proferat, quando nulla in humanis spes salutis est{ς} reliqua. Sic olim ex Ægypto populum suum tunc asseruit, cum Pharaonis crudelitas ad infantes vsq; extenderetur, et cuius metu Moses quoq; profugus inter Madianitas lateret. Et simile quid in Babylone accidisse constat, e qua tunc Iudæi liberati sunt, cum tyrannos potius novos & primis crudeliores, quam libertatem sperare possent. Exempla huius rei passim occurrunt, & fiunt huius generis multa quotidie publice & privatim, quæ sepe nostram & fidem confirmare possunt, ne in extremas angustias coacti desperemus. Cur enim periculis quantiscunq; terreantur pij, qui Christum in media etiam morte suos tueri posse norunt, & hunc iampridem nobis meruisse, ut mors iam non amplius peccati pœna sit credentibus, sed felix transitus & hac lachryma- rum vallè ad vitam æternam? Est{ς} autem hoc in primis observandum in æterna salutis negotio. Quo ad enim aliqua in humanis spes est, & nostris sive viribus sive meritis fidimus, salus nobis nulla affulget. Nam quod Iudæis olim accidisse scribit Paulus, hoc omnibus illorum imitatoribus accidere solet, ut dum propriam iustitiam stabilire conantur, à Dei iustitia excidant, quam hic nobis in filio suo offert, & quæ sola nos apud tribunal ipsius tuetur. At ubi de nostris viribus desperare, et ad thronum gratiæ confugere incipimus, mox nobis Christus affulget, & quasi recens natus nova salute mentes nostras exhilarat. Et hæc causa est, quod Euangelij prædicationem à pœnitentiæ doctrina exordiri iubet, ut per hanc intra animos nostros conuictí, gratuito Dei fauore nobis opus esse sentiamus, & ad hunc excipiendum simus promptiores.
units.tr: Here it is especially fitting to observe that, by the eternal decree of the Father, Jesus Christ was to be born as a man at the very time when the affairs of the people of God were in every way most afflicted. This agrees with God's manner, confirmed over many centuries, that he displays his help most of all when no hope of salvation remains among men. So once he rescued his people from Egypt when the cruelty of Pharaoh extended even to the infants, and Moses, a fugitive from fear of him, lay hidden among the Midianites. Something similar is known to have happened in Babylon, from which the Jews were freed when they could hope for nothing but new tyrants, and crueller than the first. Examples of this occur everywhere, and many such things happen daily, both publicly and privately, which can often strengthen our faith, so that we do not despair when we are driven into the greatest straits. For why should the godly be terrified by any dangers, when they know that Christ can protect his own even in the midst of death, and that he has long since won for us that death is no longer a punishment of sin for believers, but a happy passage through this valley of tears to eternal life? This, however, is above all to be observed in the matter of eternal salvation. For as long as some hope lies in human things, and we trust in our own strength or merits, no salvation shines upon us. For what Paul writes happened to the Jews is wont to happen to all their imitators: while they try to establish their own righteousness, they fall away from the righteousness of God, which he offers us here in his Son, and which alone defends us before his judgment seat. But when we begin to despair of our own strength and to flee to the throne of grace, Christ immediately shines upon us, and as one newly born he gladdens our minds with new salvation. And this is the reason why he bids the preaching of the Gospel begin with the doctrine of repentance: so that, through this, having been convicted within our souls, we may feel that we need the free favour of God, and may be more ready to receive it.

units.la: Sed pergamus in propositam narrationem, & locum quoque videamus, in quo Dei filius homo natus est{ς}. Fuit is Bethlehem, quæ in tribu Iuda præ aliis clara & celebris habebatur: nimirum propter Davidis, potentissimi regis & sanctissimi prophetæ, memoriam. Hanc ut antea dictum est, Messiæ natalem urbem esse voluit Deus, idq; olim per Micheam prædixerat, cuius hoc vaticinium habetur: Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata, parvula quidem es, ut sis inter chiliarchias Iuda, ex te tamen mihi prodibit, qui sit dominator in Israele, & exitus eius ab initio, à diebus æternitatis. Neque hoc temere constitutum fuit. Quia enim Bethlehem domum panis significat, voluit huius urbis nomine docere, Christum esse verum illum panem vitæ, qui solus nos pascit ad vitam æternam. Ascendit autem eo Iosephi una cum Maria, quæ iam uterum gerebat, & partui vicina erat, ut illic profiteretur in tribus suæ civitate primaria. Quo loco memorabile habemus diuinæ providentiæ exemplum, qua res omnes præter hominum opinionem ad finem constitutum diriguntur, & qua Deus illorum etiam opera ad res suas conficiendas abutitur, qui nihil minus in animo habent, quam ut ipsi inserviant. Quis enim de Messia Augusto cogitauisse putet, quando edictum de censu agendo promulgabat? Aut quis Iosephum tempore omnium incommodissimo illuc profectum putet contultò, qui procul dubio domi suæ manere maluisset, quam profectionem laboris & molestiæ plenam subire? Sed cogit illum Augusti authoritas, qui suam potentiam apud Dei populum quoq; insolenti edicto ostentare voluit. Idem tamen dum hoc agit, rerum diuinarum inscius Dei minister fit, & ea occasione Maria ex Nazareth o, obscuro Galilææ oppido, euocatur, ut in loco Messiæ natalibus destinato pariat, & eum quidem pariat, qui (ut olim Isaias prædixit) iugum illud oneris & virgam exactoris confringere debuit. Seruiat exemplum hoc nostræ consolationi, ne tyrannorum minis & conatibus nostram fidem labefactari patiamur. Nam (ut Dauid inquit) dissipat Deus consilia gentium, ipsius autem consilium manet in æternum, & plerunq; illorum conatibus promouetur, qui illud impedire volunt.
units.tr: But let us proceed with the narrative proposed, and also look at the place where the Son of God was born as a man. It was Bethlehem, which was regarded as famous and renowned among the other places of the tribe of Judah, certainly because of the memory of David, the most powerful king and most holy prophet. As was said before, God willed this city to be the birthplace of the Messiah, and he had foretold this long ago through Micah, whose prophecy is found thus: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little to be among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to me he who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from of old, from everlasting." Nor was this arranged by chance. For since Bethlehem means "house of bread," God willed by the very name of this town to teach that Christ is the true bread of life, who alone feeds us to eternal life. Now Joseph went up there together with Mary, who was already carrying a child and was near her delivery, so that he might be enrolled in the chief city of his tribe. Here we have a memorable example of divine providence, by which all things are directed to their appointed end beyond human expectation, and by which God makes use of the works of those who have no intention at all of serving him, to accomplish his own purposes. For who would have supposed that Augustus was thinking of the Messiah when he issued the edict for taking a census? Or who would think that Joseph set out to that place at the most inconvenient time on purpose, when he would doubtless rather have stayed at home than undertake a journey full of labour and trouble? But the authority of Augustus compelled him, who wished by this insolent edict to show his power also among the people of God. Yet while he did this, he unknowingly became a minister of God's purposes, and on that occasion Mary was summoned from Nazareth, an obscure town of Galilee, so that she might give birth in the place destined for the Messiah's nativity, and she gave birth to him who (as Isaiah foretold long ago) was to break the yoke of that burden and the rod of the taskmaster. May this example serve for our consolation, so that we do not allow our faith to be shaken by the threats and attempts of tyrants. For (as David says) God scatters the counsels of the nations, but his own counsel stands for ever, and it is often advanced by the very efforts of those who want to hinder it.

units.la: In primis autem hic multa & diligenti consideratione dignum est exemplum Iosephi, qui ut Cæsaris edicto obediat, cum Maria Bethlehemum ascendit. Fuit profectio ista ipsis procul dubio molestissima. Nam ut nihil dicamus de itineris longitudine, de impensis, quæ quantulæcunq; sint, tenuis fortunæ hominibus graues & intolerabiles sunt, de re domestica item, quam interea negligere coguntur, superat hæc omnia, quod Maria partui vicina erat, & ad conficiendum hoc iter minime idonea. Atqui non deerant rationes Deo, quibus consum istum in aliud tempus reijcere, vel illos molestia tanta liberare poterat. Attamen id nunc fieri vult, & illos spiritu patientiæ donat, ne quid cum scandalo coniunctu desiguent. Ita vero non solum ad locum illum destinatum ipsorum pedes dirigit, sed insuper exemplum obedientiæ proponit, quæ magistratui debetur. Et hoc quidem in ipsa Christi imcarnationem proponi vtile atq; necessarium fuit, ad eos confutandos, qui sub Christianæ libertatis praetextu aduersus principes suos tumultuantur, seq; omni obedientiæ debito solutos putant. Transferunt hi libertatem, cuius nobis author est Christus ad carnis licentiam, & non solum contra ipsius exemplum peccant, qui sub censu nasci voluit, verumetiam ipsius doctrinam falsi arguunt, qua monet, vt Cæsari demus quæ huic debentur. Quia enim magistratus à Deo institutus est, minime pure nus filium Dei illum abolere voluisse. Et satis nota est super hac re apostolorum sententia, qui ex Spiritus sancti suggestione omnes hortantur, vt magistratibus suis obtemperent, & vnicuique reddant quod debetur: cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui honor, honorem, &c. Constat deniq; prophanis quoq; hominibus legem hanc diuinitus inscriptam fuisse, vt magistratus suos pro sacrosanctis haberent, & illis debitum obsequium praestarent. Est ergo laude dignissimum Iosephi & Mariæ factum, qui etsi Augustum hominem idololatram & à societate populi Dei alienum, edictum vero hoc iniquum & tyrannicæ insolentiæ plenum esse scirent, & sese excusandi rationes habe rent multas & graues, non tamen aduersus illud murmurant, non publicè de Imperatoris aut præsidum eius iniquitate conqueruntur, neque de iugo illo exeundo consilia seditiosa cum aliquo ineunt: sed in Dei consilium respiciunt, qui populi sui ingratitudinem atq; contumaciam hac virga coercere decreuerat: & quamuis ipsi nihil huius, vt cæteri sceleribus publicis infames, meruissent, com mune tamen hoc flagellum patienter ferunt. Iflos ergo imitentur, quotquot Christiani dici & haberi volunt, & in externis quidem omnibus, quæ corpus & fortunas attinent, principibus suis etiam dura & iniqua petentibus obtemperent: at si quorundam insolentia eò vsq; progreditur, vt illis nō contenti, de religione etiam leges ferant, quibus Dei cultus vel omnino euertitur, vel aliqua ex parte impeditur, tunc apostolici illius dicti meminerint: Oportet Deo plus obedire quàm hominibus. Vide Actor. 4. & 5. cap.
units.tr: Here, however, the example of Joseph deserves to be considered at length and with careful attention: he went up with Mary to Bethlehem in order to obey Caesar's edict. That journey was doubtless most troublesome for them. For to say nothing of the length of the road and the expenses, which, however small, are burdensome and intolerable for people of modest means, and of the household affairs which they were forced to neglect in the meantime, this surpasses all: Mary was near her delivery and quite unfit to undertake such a journey. Yet God did not lack reasons by which he could have put off that census to another time, or freed them from so great a trouble. Nevertheless he wills it to happen now, and he grants them the spirit of patience, so that they do not desert anything that is joined with scandal. And so he not only directs their feet to that appointed place, but moreover sets before them an example of the obedience owed to the magistrate. This was indeed useful and necessary to be set forth in the very incarnation of Christ, to refute those who under the pretext of Christian liberty rise up against their princes and think themselves released from every debt of obedience. They turn into a licence of the flesh the liberty of which Christ is the author, and they not only sin against his own example, since he wished to be born under a census, but also convict his teaching of falsehood, by which he bids us give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar. For since the magistrate is instituted by God, the Son of God would by no means have wished to abolish him. And the saying of the apostles on this matter is well known: they, moved by the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, all exhort us to obey our magistrates and to render to each what is due: "Tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour," etc. It is established that this law was written by God even in the hearts of profane men, that they should hold their magistrates as sacred and render them due obedience. Therefore the deed of Joseph and Mary is most worthy of praise: although they knew that Augustus was an idolatrous man, alien to the fellowship of the people of God, and that this edict was unjust and full of tyrannical insolence, and although they had many and weighty reasons for excusing themselves, yet they do not murmur against it, they do not publicly complain of the wickedness of the Emperor or his governors, nor do they enter into seditious plans for throwing off that yoke; but they look to the counsel of God, who had decided to restrain the ingratitude and stubbornness of his people with this rod. And although they had deserved nothing of this, unlike others infamous for public crimes, they patiently bear this common scourge. Let all who wish to be and to be called Christians therefore imitate them: in all external matters that concern body and property, let them obey their princes even when those princes demand harsh and unjust things. But if the insolence of some goes so far that, not content with these, they also enact laws concerning religion by which the worship of God is either wholly overturned or in some part hindered, then let them remember that saying of the apostles: "We ought to obey God rather than men." See Acts chapters 4 and 5.

units.la: Caeterum quia in Bethlehemi mentione Lucas incidit, clarius quoq; exprimit causam, quæ Iosephum mouit, vt eò ascenderet, & ea ratione maiores etiā Iesu Christi attingit, ex quibus hic, quoad carnem, descendit. Nam Iosephum ex Dauidis domo et familia oriundum fuisse scribit, quod ipsum infra in genealogia eius prolixa enumeratione demonstrabit. Annotatur autem ab Euangelistis Iosephi genus, non quod Christus ex illo genitus sit, sed vt ex more veteri & in Lege recepto doceant, Mariam quoque ex Dauide descendisse: qua de re supra diximus. Saepius autem de hoc nos admonent Euangelistæ, vt certius constet, Iesum hunc exoptatū illud Dauidis semé esse, quod olim Deus promiserat, & in quo salutem humani generis instaurandam fore prædixerant prophetæ. Facit hoc ad afferenda fidei nostræ certitudinem, quando ea non nouo aliquo & patribus ignoto redemptore, sed hoc vno nititur, in cuius aduentu & merito olim sancti omnes suæ salutis spem atque fiduciam collocatam habuerunt. At quia de hoc etiam non semel dictum est, nunc obseruemus, Deum suarum promissionum probè memorem esse, neq; suorum curam vnquam abijcere. Constat enim Dauidis familiam illo tempore non solum ad extremam egestatem redactam, sed etiam in summo periculo constitutam fuisse, eò quòd eam Herodes extinctam vellet, qui Regem & vindicem populi Iudaici ex illa nasciturum esse audiuerat. Itaque videri poterat Deus tam Dauidis & posterorum eius quàm promissionum suarum oblitus esse, neque magni aliquid ex hominibus tam afflictis & abiectis porrò sperari posse. Sed ostendit hic Deus, promissiones suas non ex hominum authoritate & potentia seu splendore pendere, sed se Dominum illum exercituum esse: qui ex obscuris illustres, ex infirmis potentissimos, ex contemptis clarissimos facere, ex tenebris item lucem, & ex ipsa morte vitā elicere possit. Est quidem paupercula & inops Maria, sed eum parit illa, in quo omnes regni cœlorum thesauri sunt reconditi. In gloria & contempta in obscuro Galilæa angulo delitescit: sed ex ipsa nascitur rex ille gloriæ, qui nobis gloriæ cœlestis & immortalis author est. Persecutionis periculo cum tota sua gente subiacet, at vtero suo eum gestat, qui vnica electorū Dei spes, & petra illa inuicta est, ad uersus quam ne inferorum quidem portæ prævalent. Deniq; cùm Dauidis domus in extremo discrimine constituta esset, eum nobis genuit, qui omnes ex illa natos Reges gloria, potentia, victoriis & triumphis in tantum excellit, quantum Dei potentia & maiestas omnem huius mundi potentiā & gloriam superat. Nemo igitur de promissionum Dei veritate desperet, vt carnis rationi res prorsus desperata esse videatur. Nam vt Isaias clamat, est quidem omnis caro fœnum, & gloria carnis flos nihil flos agri, at Dei verbum manet in æternum. Nouit itē suos Dominus, neq; eorum vnquam ob liuisci potest, quos æterno decreto in filio suo elegit, & eiusdem sanguine redemit. Nostrum autem est non præscribere Deo, sed illum expectare in spe & silentio, & (quod de Abrahamo Paulus scribit) in spe contra spem credere.
units.tr: But since Luke has mentioned Bethlehem, he also states more clearly the reason that moved Joseph to go up there, and in this way he touches on the ancestors of Jesus Christ, from whom, according to the flesh, he descended. For he writes that Joseph was descended from the house and family of David, which he will later demonstrate in the lengthy enumeration of Joseph's genealogy. The Evangelists note Joseph's lineage not because Christ was born of him, but in order to teach, in keeping with the old custom received in the Law, that Mary too was descended from David, as we said above. The Evangelists remind us of this often, so that it may be more certain that this Jesus is that long-awaited seed of David, which God had promised long ago and through which the prophets had foretold that the salvation of the human race would be restored. This serves to establish the certainty of our faith, since it rests not on some new redeemer unknown to the fathers, but on this one, in whose coming and merit all the saints of old placed the hope and confidence of their salvation. But since this has also been said more than once, let us now observe that God is mindful of his promises and never casts off the care of his own. For it is clear that at that time the family of David was not only reduced to utmost poverty but was also in the greatest danger, because Herod wished it destroyed, having heard that a king and deliverer of the Jewish people would be born from it. So it might have seemed that God had forgotten both David and his descendants as well as his promises, and that nothing great could henceforth be hoped for from men so afflicted and humble. But here God shows that his promises do not depend on the authority, power or splendour of men, but that he is the Lord of hosts, who can make the obscure illustrious, the weak most powerful, the despised most renowned, and likewise bring light out of darkness and life out of death itself. Mary is indeed a poor and needy woman, yet she bears him in whom all the treasures of the kingdom of heaven are laid up. She lies hidden in contempt in the obscure corner of Galilee, yet from her is born that King of glory, who is the author of heavenly and immortal glory for us. She is exposed with all her people to the danger of persecution, yet she carries in her womb him who is the one hope of God's elect and that unconquered rock against which not even the gates of hell prevail. Finally, when the house of David was in the utmost peril, she bore for us him who surpasses all the kings born from that house in glory, power, victories and triumphs, as far as the power and majesty of God surpass all the power and glory of this world. Let no one therefore despair of the truth of God's promises, as if the matter seemed utterly hopeless to human reason. For, as Isaiah cries out, all flesh is grass, and the glory of flesh is like the flower of the field, but the word of God endures for ever. The Lord also knows his own, and he can never forget those whom he chose in his Son by an eternal decree and redeemed with his blood. It is our part, however, not to prescribe to God, but to wait for him in hope and silence, and (as Paul writes of Abraham) to believe in hope against hope.

units.la: Sequitur nunc, vt huius partus modum & rationem inuestigemus, quod præcipuum huius narrationis caput est. Ex eo enim simul patebit, quis nam Christus sit, quidque ex ipso nobis sit sperandum. Vbi ante omnia in mentem reuocare oportet, quod primo Capite de eius conceptione dictum est, & quòd Maria virginitate sua illæsa peperit, sicut hoc prophetæ olim præduxerant. Itaenim fieri oportebat, vt & nostram generationem sanctificaret, & ipse sanctum & sufficiens esset pro peccatis mundi sacrificium: quem proprium virginitatis Mariæ visum esse alibi diximus. Interim viro eam desponsari oportuit, vt & famæ eius, quoad homines, consuleretur, & simul matrimonij dignitas asseretur contra impuri cælibatus authores, quos nouissimis temporibus exoritu- ros esse, Spiritus sanctus non uno loco prædixit. In primis autem ad partus istius modum pertinet, quòd dies completi fuerunt, quibus illa parere debuit. Facit hoc ad asserendam veram humanitatem filij Dei. Vt enim spiritu ita operante in vtero Mariæ conceptus est, & ex eius substantia carnem veram assumpsit: ita in eodem creuit, & constituto demum tempore, vt in reliquis hominibus fieri solet, in lucem editus. De hoc autem nos diligenter admoneri oportuit, quia hic nostræ salutis certitudo non minima ex parte fundatur. Ex eo enim colligimus, Dei filium fratrem nostrum factum esse, & proinde ad nos pertinere omnia, quæcunque ille fecit aut passus est: imò per hunc nos in filiorum Dei numerum esse adoptatos. Constat præterea, illum nobis fidelem esse pontificem in omnibus quæ apud Deum agenda sunt. Quia enim verus homo factus est, & nostras infirmitates ipse sustinuit, potest vtiq; nobis condolere & compati, neq; verendum est, ne durus & rigidus nimis nos in tentationibus laborantes deserat.
units.tr: It now follows that we should investigate the manner and reason of this birth, which is the principal point of this narrative. For from this it will at the same time become plain who Christ is and what we may hope for from him. Here, before all else, we must recall what was said in the first chapter about his conception, namely that Mary gave birth while her virginity remained intact, just as the prophets had foretold long before. For it had to happen this way, so that he might both sanctify our generation and be himself a holy and sufficient sacrifice for the sins of the world; we have said elsewhere that this was fitting for the virginity of Mary. Meanwhile she had to be betrothed to a husband, both so that her good name might be protected in the eyes of men and so that the dignity of marriage might be affirmed against the authors of impure celibacy, whom the Holy Spirit has foretold in more than one place will arise in the last times. But the manner of this birth pertains especially to this, that the days were completed on which she was to give birth. This serves to establish the true humanity of the Son of God. For just as he was conceived in the womb of Mary by the Spirit's working, and took true flesh from her substance, so he grew in the same womb and, when the appointed time came, was brought into the light as is usual with other men. We ought to be carefully reminded of this, because the certainty of our salvation is founded in no small part upon it. For from it we gather that the Son of God has become our brother, and that therefore all that he did or suffered pertains to us; indeed through him we have been adopted into the number of the sons of God. It is further clear that he is a faithful high priest to us in all matters that must be transacted before God. For because he was made a true man and himself bore our infirmities, he can surely sympathise and have compassion with us, nor need we fear that he, too harsh and rigid, will abandon us when we labour in temptations.

units.la: Porrò diligentius exprimit Lucas, quis nam ille sit, qui ex Maria natus est. Peperit (inquit) filium suum, illum Primogenitum. Primò eam filium suum peperisse ait: eum scilicet, quem ex Spiritus sancti virtute conceperat, quæ vtero gestarat, qui solitis incrementis secundum naturæ leges in ipsius vtero creuerat, vt legitimo tempore in lucem ederetur. Rursus ergo vera Christi humanitas exprimitur: quia Mariæ filius non poterit dici, nisi verum hominem esse fateamur. Sed alio etiā titulo illum ornat Lucas, & Primogenitum dicit. Id verò non (vt olim Heluidius sentiebat) ad Mariam referri debet, quasi hæc postea alios quoq; filios ex Iosepho conceptos peperit, sed ad solū Christum pertinet, & non ordinis, sed dignitatis titulus est. Facile hoc vident, qui Græcæ linguæ periti constructionem verborum obseruant. Nam primogenitum interposito articulo à filio Mariæ distinguit Lucas, quasi diceret: peperit filium suum, qui verus ille Primogenitus est, quæ vetus illa Lex Mosis in primogenitorum prærogatiuis adumbrauit. Nam ex Legis præscripto primogeniti censebantur quotquot (vt scriptura loquitur) vterum aperiebant, etiamsi nulli postea eos nascerentur. Et hi quidem omnes Deo consecrati erant, nisi redimerentur. Deinde ijsdem duplex hæreditatis pars cedebat, & inter fratres primatum obtinebant, adeò vt inter illos regum & sacerdotum loco essent. Fuit ergo hoc dignitatis nomen, cuius quanta authoritas fuerit antiquitus, ex Iacobi & Esaui contentione apparet, quæ illis propter primogenituræ ius intercessit. Docent ergo hæc verba, quid de Christo nos sentire conueniat. Est is verus & æternus Dei filius, & quia idem Mariæ etiam filius factus est, verus Deus & verus homo fit oportet in vna individua persona. Deinde verus ille Primogenitus omnis creaturæ est, vt qui non cum aliis creaturis factus est, sed iam inde ab æterno ex patre genitus. Est præterea (vt Paulus inquit) primogenitus inter multos fratres. Vt enim ipse filius Dei vnigenitus est & naturalis siue germanus (vt ita dicam) sic nos quoq; filios Dei fecit, quando per incarnationem nostræ naturæ consors, & proinde frater noster factus est, & nobis vicissim spiritum suum contulit, qui spiritus adoptionis dicitur. Neque inanis est in illo Primogeniti titulus, sed penes illum est Sacerdotium & Regnum filiorum Dei siue totius Ecclesiæ. Illi enim dictum est a patre: Tu es sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchizedech. Item, Ego constitui regem meum super Zion, montem meum sanctum. Et ista verè de illo dici res ipsa testatur. Nam sacerdotem agit reuera, quando nos docet, nobis benedicit omni benedictione spirituali, peccata item nostra corporis & sanguinis sui sacrificio semel ita sustulit, vt ea nobis amplius imputari non possint: quando denique noster apud patrem intercessor atq; aduocatus est. Adhæc Rex est non minus potens quàm fidelis. Nam ex diaboli potestate nos asseruit, assertos tuetur, & omni bonorum cœlestium genere beat, adhæc iudiciorum suorum exempla quotidie exerit, & olim veniet ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, quando singulis retribuet, pro vt bonum aut malum fecerunt. Hæc igitur in Primogeniti nomine obseruare conuenit, vt illum agnoscamus Sacerdotem & Regem nostrum, eidem fidamus, & præceptis ipsius obtemperemus.
units.tr: Further, Luke expresses more carefully who he is who was born of Mary. She bore (he says) her son, that firstborn. First he says that she bore her son: namely him whom she had conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit, whom she carried in her womb, who grew in her womb with the usual increase according to the laws of nature, so that at the proper time he was brought into the light. Therefore the true humanity of Christ is again expressed, for he cannot be called Mary's son unless we confess him to be a true man. But Luke also adorns him with another title, calling him the firstborn. This ought not, as Helvidius once held, to be referred to Mary, as if she afterwards bore other sons conceived by Joseph; it pertains to Christ alone, and it is a title of dignity rather than of order. Those who are skilled in the Greek language and observe the construction of the words readily see this. For by inserting the article, Luke distinguishes the firstborn from the son of Mary, as if he were saying: she bore her son, who is that true Firstborn which the old Law of Moses foreshadowed in the privileges of the firstborn. For by the prescription of the Law, all were reckoned firstborn who (as Scripture puts it) opened the womb, even if no others were born to them afterwards. And all of these were consecrated to God, unless they were redeemed. Moreover, a double portion of the inheritance fell to them, and they held the primacy among their brothers, so that among them they stood in the place of kings and priests. This name therefore was one of dignity, and the great authority it once had is clear from the contention between Jacob and Esau, who quarrelled over the right of the firstborn. These words therefore teach us what we ought to think of Christ. He is the true and eternal Son of God, and because he was also made the son of Mary, he must be true God and true man in one undivided person. Next, he is the true Firstborn of every creature, since he was not made together with other creatures, but has been begotten of the Father from eternity. Moreover, he is (as Paul says) the firstborn among many brethren. For just as the Son of God himself is the only-begotten and natural, or, if I may so put it, his own true brother, so he has also made us sons of God, since by the incarnation he became a partaker of our nature and therefore our brother, and in turn he has imparted to us his Spirit, which is called the Spirit of adoption. Nor is the title of Firstborn empty in him, but in him reside the priesthood and the kingdom of the sons of God, that is, of the whole Church. For it was said to him by the Father: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek. Likewise: I have set my king upon Zion, my holy mountain. And the thing itself testifies that these words are truly spoken of him. For he really acts as priest when he teaches us, blesses us with every spiritual blessing, and by the sacrifice of his body and blood has once for all so taken away our sins that they can no longer be imputed to us; and finally when he is our intercessor and advocate before the Father. Moreover, he is a King no less powerful than faithful. For he has rescued us from the power of the devil, guards those rescued, and blesses us with every kind of heavenly good; he also daily displays examples of his judgements, and one day he will come to judge the living and the dead, when he will repay each one according as they have done good or evil. It is fitting, therefore, that we observe these things in the name of the Firstborn, so that we may acknowledge him as our Priest and King, trust in him, and obey his precepts.

units.la: Restat post remum huius loci caput, quo narratur, quid cum recens nato sit factum, & quæ filij Dei in carne manifestati crepundia aut incunabula fuerint. Sic autem scribit Lucas: Fascijs eum inuoluit, reclinauitq; eum in præsepi. Et quia hoc absurdum nimis, aut Maria plus æquo negligentior videri poterat, causam huius factifubijcit: Eò quòd non erat eis locus in diuersorio. Factum ergo hoc fuit cum propter inopiam Mariæ, tum propter hominum loci illius inhumanitatem, qui prægnantem & partui vicinam in stabulum detruserunt. Credibile enim est, in magna peregrinorum frequentia, qui propter censum eo confluxerant, hospitia meliora (vt fieri soles) ab opulentioribus occupata fuisse, & loca incommodissima pauperibus cessisse, ex quibus lucrum nullum sperari poterat. Et est quidem multa reprehensione dignißima hæc Bethlehemitarum inhumanitas & ingratitudo, qua in Dauidici generis virginem peccarunt: sed meminisse simul oportet, hoc præludio Christum nos docere voluisse, quæ semper ipsius in bisce terris sors futura fit: ea nimirum, vt qui cœlum & terram condidit, qui omnes pascit & vestit, nullibi fere inter homines locum inueniat. Idem certe in membris & verbo suo patitur, vt nihil de pauperibus dicamus, quos suo nomine nobis commendauit. Cùm enim palàm flagitiosos mundus ferat, cùm ineptissimarum superstitionum inuentores in pretio habeantur, cùm templa & palatia regum occupent, soli Christi cultores in angulis late re coguntur, & vix in siluis, in stabulis & ferarum lustris locum tutum inuenit Euangelij prædicatio. Sed non offendant nos ista, quando Christum non aliud suæ vitæ in terris initium esse voluit. Si mul autem arguitur hoc exemplo mundi ingratitudo, qua fit, vt apud posteros facile intercidat beneficiorum memoria, & fere opti meritorum filijs pessima gratia referatur. Quàm præclara enim & eximia Dauidis, Solomonis, Asa, Josaphat, Ezechiæ, Isaiæ, Zorobabelis & multorum aliorum, qui ex illa domo prodierant, in totam Iudæorum gentem beneficia fuerint, vix longa oratione commemorari posset. Sed ecce eiusdem familiæ puella, nullo crimine infamis, cum sponso, etsi non diuite, honesto tamen & probo: adhæc vterum gestans, & partui vicina, in ipsa Bethlehem, vbi olim Dauidis incunabula fuerant, non aliud hospitium inuenit, quàm quod ei cum pecore & iumentis commune est. Inunc, & de hominum ingratitudine, aut de tuæ sortis iniquitate conqueritor, aut Dei iudicium accusa. Quid enim tibi faciant homines, qui communem suum patrem & creatorem non agnoscunt, & beneficia eius tantum non pedibus calcare non verentur?
units.tr: There remains, after the end of this passage, the chapter which relates what was done with the newly born child, and what the swaddling clothes and cradle of the Son of God made manifest in the flesh were. Luke writes thus: "He wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger." And because this seemed too absurd, or might make Mary appear rather careless, he adds the reason for the deed: "because there was no room for them in the inn." This was done both because of Mary's poverty and because of the inhumanity of the people of that place, who thrust a pregnant woman near her time into a stable. For it is credible that, in the great crowd of strangers who had gathered there for the census, the better lodgings were occupied by the wealthier (as usually happens), and the most unsuitable places were left to the poor, from which no profit could be hoped. This inhumanity and ingratitude of the Bethlehemites, by which they sinned against a virgin of David's line, deserves the strongest reproof. But we must also remember that by this prelude Christ wished to teach us what his lot in this world will always be: namely, that he who made heaven and earth, who feeds and clothes all, nearly nowhere finds a place among men. Certainly he suffers the same in his members and in his word, not to mention the poor, whom he has commended to us in his own name. For while the world openly tolerates wicked men, while the inventors of the most foolish superstitions are held in high esteem, and while they occupy temples and royal palaces, the worshippers of Christ alone are driven into corners far and wide, and the preaching of the gospel scarcely finds a safe place, in woods, stables and the dens of wild beasts. But let these things not offend us, since Christ wished that the beginning of his life on earth should be no other. At the same time, this example condemns the ingratitude of the world, by which it comes about that the memory of benefits easily perishes among posterity, and the best deserts are very often repaid with the worst favour to the sons. For how splendid and remarkable were the benefits conferred on the whole Jewish nation by David, Solomon, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Isaiah, Zerubbabel and many others who sprang from that house, can hardly be recounted in a long speech. Yet behold, a girl of the same family, infamous for no crime, with a spouse who was not rich but honest and upright, carrying a child in her womb and near her delivery, in Bethlehem itself where David's cradle had once been, found no other lodging than that which she shares with the flock and the beasts of burden. Now, complain either of the ingratitude of men or of the unfairness of your lot, or accuse the judgment of God. For what can men do to you, who do not acknowledge their common Father and Creator, and do not hesitate to trample his benefits almost underfoot?

units.la: Sed vt ad filij Dei incarnatione redeamus, subinde nos meminisse oportet, hæc omnia propter nos sic fieri debuisse. Nec enim suipsius, sed nostri causa ille in mundum venit, & ideo nostræ salutis ergo fecit, quicquid fecit. Itaq; hominis filius factus est, vt nos Dei filios faceret. Infans infirmus & imbellis natus est, vt nos in ipso (vt Paulus ait) in virum perfectum adolescamus. Infirmitates nostras ipse suscepit, vt nos viribus nouis instrueret. Fascijs inuolui & ligari voluit, vt nos carnis peccatricis & mortalis vinculis solueret. Pilibus pannis tegitur, vt nos sua innocentia & sanctitate, quæ vera illa vestis nuptialis est, exornet. Pauperrimus & rerum omnium egens nascitur, neq; quicquam in terris proprium habet, vt nos in ipso diuites faciat. Peregrinus est in mundo, vt nobis ciuitatem & patriam in cœlis inueniat. Sub censu nascitur, & ita prophani Cæsaris imperio sese subijcit, vt nos ex diaboli tyrannide liberet. Demittit sese ad pecora vsque, vt nos in gloriæ cœlestis consortium euehat. In præsepi reclinatur, vt animabus nostris pabulum vitæ æternæ exhibeat. Denique peccati reus fieri, & tandem crudele mortis supplicium subire voluit, vt nos eius merito iusti ficati vitæ hæredes efficiamur. Vsus istorum nobis hic esto, vt in illo nobis plenè exhibita esse discamus, quæcunque ad salutem consequendam nobis necessaria sunt, & proinde adipsum vnum confugiamus, vt qui se nostrum pastorem, medicum & vindicem fidissimum esse profiteatur. In primis autem ab eorum superstitione nobis caueamus, qui dum illum iudicem seuerum & immitem fingunt, Diuorum coelitum intercessione atq; patrocinio apud eum sibi opus esse arbitrantur, & in iis praecipuam salutis spem collocant. Faciunt hi Christo iniuriam longe maximam. Quis enim hominum filios ferat, qui post multa paternae bonitatis indicia ipsum ceu iudicem aut carnificem horreant? Et tu Christo rem gratam te facturum arbitraris, si de eius clementia tam inique sentias, & nunc superbum, immitem, difficilem & inexorabilem esse credas, qui nihil non facere & pati voluit, ut sua erga nos benignitatem indulgentissima testaretur? Damnantur communi omnium iudicio, qui ex sordibus egestatis euecti superbiunt & se inhumanos praebent. Cur ergo Dei filium superbum humani generis contemptorem putemus, qui extrema quaeq; pati voluit, ut eum esse sciemus, qui nostris infirmitatibus condolere possit? Agnoscit bos possessorem suum, & asinus praesepe heri sui. Quae ergo stupiditas aut dementia est, homines ratione praeditos non agnoscere suum redemptorem & advocatum fidelissimum, qui nullum unquam morositatis aut nimij rigoris specimen nobis praebuit?
units.tr: But to return to the incarnation of the Son of God, we must keep in mind that all these things had to happen for our sake. For he did not come into the world for his own sake but for ours, and so he did whatever he did for the sake of our salvation. Therefore he became the Son of Man, that he might make us sons of God. He was born an infant, weak and unwarlike, that in him (as Paul says) we might grow up into a perfect man. He took upon himself our infirmities, that he might furnish us with new strength. He willed to be wrapped in swaddling cloths and bound, that he might free us from the bonds of sinful and mortal flesh. He is covered with coarse rags, that he might adorn us with his innocence and holiness, which is the true wedding garment. He is born most poor and destitute of all things, and has nothing of his own on earth, that in him he might make us rich. He is a stranger in the world, that he might find for us a city and a homeland in heaven. He is born under the census, and so submits himself to the rule of a profane Caesar, that he might free us from the tyranny of the devil. He lowers himself even to the beasts, that he might raise us to fellowship in heavenly glory. He is laid in a manger, that he might set before our souls the food of eternal life. Finally, he willed to become guilty of sin and at last to undergo the cruel punishment of death, that by his merit we, being justified, might be made heirs of life. Let the use of these things be this for us: that we may learn that everything necessary for obtaining salvation has been fully provided for us in him, and therefore that we may flee to him alone, since he professes himself our most faithful shepherd, physician and deliverer. Above all, let us beware of the superstition of those who, while they imagine him to be a stern and harsh judge, think that they need the intercession and patronage of the blessed heavenly ones with him, and place their chief hope of salvation in them. These people do the greatest wrong to Christ. For who among men would endure sons who, after many proofs of a father's goodness, shudder at him as a judge or an executioner? And do you think you do Christ a favour if you think so unfairly of his mercy, and believe that he is now proud, harsh, hard to approach and inexorable, he who was willing to do and suffer everything so that he might testify his most indulgent kindness towards us? By the common judgment of all, those are condemned who, raised up from the filth of poverty, grow proud and show themselves inhuman. Why then should we think the Son of God proud and a despiser of the human race, when he willed to suffer the utmost things, so that we may know that he is one who can sympathise with our weaknesses? The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's manger. What stupidity or madness, then, is it for men endowed with reason not to acknowledge their Redeemer and most faithful advocate, who has never shown us any sign of moroseness or excessive severity?

units.la: Deinde exemplo etiam suo nobis praeiuit Dei filius, cuius vestigijs nos per omnem vitae nostrae cursum insistere convenit. Et primo quidem humilitatem & modestiam nobis commendat, ne nos pudeat ea facere, quae proximi commodum aut salutem proebere possunt. Est enim detestabilis & homine Christiano prorsus indigna superbia, qua quidam generis aut conditionis suae splendore elati, proximum quemq; fastidiunt, & iniuriam sibi atrocem fieri putant, si quis ab ipsis fraternae charitatis officium requirat. Quasi vero aliquem Deus ideo donis amplioribus instruat, ut ijs solus fruatur, & non potius nos ea, quae ex ipsius liberalitate accepimus, in commune deferre velit, ut illis multi alij iuuentur? Hos ego Dei filium in praesepi iacentem intueri velim, qui etsi verus & aeternus Deus sit, & quoad carnem ex familia omnium nobilissima & plurimorum Regum atque Prophetarum genitrice prodierit, propter eos tamen se e o vsq; demittere voluit, quos illi tanto cum fastu despiciunt. Deinde paupertatem & omnes alias huius vitae miserias suo exemplo Christus consecrare voluit, ne quis illas divinae irae indicia esse, aut animarum salutem per illa impediri putaret.
