Est hic incarnationis istius fructus non vulgaris. Ut enim natura afflictiones omnes horremus, ita pauperatem & inopiam plerique malorum omnium, quae homini accidere possunt, gravissimum & ipsi etiam Deo exosum esse arbitrantur. Quae causa est, quod & contra Deum murmurant, & ad artes illicitas convertuntur, quibus iugum illud egestatis excutere student. At si ijdem Christi exemplum propius intuerentur, procul dubio rectius iudicarent, & patienter ferrent onus, quod aeternus Dei filius nobiscum commune habere voluit. Imo puderet ipsos multo auro & ostro superbire & deliciis diffluere in conspectu filij Dei, qui nostri causa infimam inter homines fortem sustinuit. Discamus ergo ex his, quae hucusque dicta sunt, Iesum Dei patris & Mariae Virginis filium, esse Christum & salutis humanae vnicum Mediatorem. Huic autem ita fidamus, ut simul eundem vita & moribus exprimamus, neq; aliquid desgnemus a fidei professione alienum. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next, the Son of God has also gone before us by his own example, in whose footsteps we ought to walk through the whole course of our life. And first of all he commends to us humility and modesty, so that we are not ashamed to do those things which can bring advantage or salvation to a neighbour. For that pride is detestable and utterly unworthy of a Christian man, by which some, elated by the splendour of their birth or condition, despise every neighbour and think it a grievous injury done to them if anyone asks of them the duty of brotherly love. As if God furnished anyone with greater gifts so that he alone might enjoy them, and did not rather wish us to bring into common use what we have received from his generosity, so that many others might be helped by them! I would have those people look upon the Son of God lying in the manger, who, although he is true and eternal God, and in respect of the flesh has come forth from the most noble of all families, the mother of many kings and prophets, nevertheless was willing to lower himself even to those whom they despise with such scorn. Next, by his own example Christ willed to consecrate poverty and all the other miseries of this life, lest anyone think them signs of divine wrath, or think that the salvation of souls is impeded by them. This is no common fruit of that incarnation. For as nature makes us shrink from all afflictions, so most people think that poverty and want, of all the evils that can befall a man, are the most grievous and even hateful to God himself. Hence it is that they both murmur against God and turn to unlawful arts, by which they strive to shake off that yoke of want. But if these same people looked more closely at the example of Christ, they would undoubtedly judge more rightly, and would bear patiently the burden which the eternal Son of God was willing to share with us. Indeed, it should shame them to be proud of much gold and purple and to wallow in luxuries in the sight of the Son of God, who for our sake endured the lowest lot among men. Let us learn, then, from what has been said so far, that Jesus, the son of God the Father and of the Virgin Mary, is Christ and the only Mediator of human salvation. Let us trust in him in such a way that at the same time we express him in our life and conduct, and let us not practise anything foreign to our profession of faith. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XVII.

units.la: Erant autem pastores in eadem regione excubantes & agentes vigilias noctis super gregem suum. Et ecce Angelus Domini superuenit illis, & gloria Domini circumfulsit eos, & timuerunt timore magno. Et dixit eis Angelus: Ne timete: ecce enim euangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit toti populo. Quia natus est vobis hodie Seruator, qui est Christus Dominus, in vrbe Dauid. Hoc autem vobis signum erit: Inuenietis infantem fasciis inuolutum, iacentem in praesepi. Et repente affuit cum Angelo multitudo exercituum coelestium, laudantium Deum, & dicentium: Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax, in hominMes beneuolentia.
units.tr: Now there were shepherds in the same region, living out in the fields and keeping watch over their flock by night. And behold, an angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them, and they were terrified with great fear. And the angel said to them: "Fear not; for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign unto you: you shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men."

units.la: Omnes quidem suae gratiae atq; bonitatis thesauros nobis Deus in filio suo, Iesu Christo, propinauit, idem tamen nobis ad salutem consequendam nihil proderit, nisi eum vere cognoscamus, & agnitum fide constanti amplexemur. Ideo illum iam inde à primo mundi exordio patribus promisit, & eundem typis legalibus adumbrauit, imò prophetas dedit, qui ex spiritus revelatione de omnibus, quae ille facturus & passurus erat, concionarentur, ut ita omnibus constaret, quae vera sit & certa salutis consequendae ratio. At postquam idem ille praefinito tempore in mundum venit, & ex muliere (ut Pauli verbis vtar) homo factus est, mox illum omnis loci & ordinis hominibus multifariam manifestauit, ne tantus thesaurus abscondus & ignotus delitesceret. Ita magis in Oriente per fidus caelestem innotescit. Idem stella duce Hierosolymam veniunt, & dum recens natum Iudaeorum regem studio ingenti quaerunt, omnes alios ad eundem cognoscendum excitant: & inter alios Herodem quoq;, qui per Scribas de loco Messiae natali certior redditur. Interea in templo quoque, cum secundum Legem Domino sisteretur, quaedam sunt facta, quae ad illius manifestationem pertinuerunt. Et si historicos audiamus, apud exteras quoq; gentes multa accidere, quae orbis totius mutationem & generis humani restitutionem praeforibus adesse significabant. Nam ut Orosius scribit, Augusto vrbem ingrediente circulus ad speciem arcus caelestis Solem ambijt, fons item olei lar gissimus de taberna meritoria per totum diem fluxit, Augustus vero sub idem tempus se dominum appellari prohibuit, adhaec seruorum triginta millia dominus suis restituit. Et noluit ista in vrbe rerum domina fieri Deus, ut ostenderet, iam adesse verum illum pacis caelestis authorem & gratiae diuinae mediatorem, qui & ipse prae consortibus suis vnctus sit oleo laetitiae, & omnes in se credentes vngat in reges & sacerdotes: cui item soli debeatur Domini nomen, cum vnicus sit humani generis redemptor, quiq; homines primùm sub diaboli tyrannide laborantes domino suo vero restituat, ut à peccato quidem liberati, Deo autem mancipati fructum suum habeant in sanctimoniam. Caeterum inter nati Christi manifestationes prima numeratur, quam in praesenti Lucas describit, & in qua hominibus rerum imperitis atq; fraude dolo; alienis omnia ea luculenter annuntiata sunt, quae nos tam in ipsius Christi quam in salutis per illum partae cognitione instruere possunt. Quo nomine digna plane est historia, quam singulari diligentia consideremus.
units.tr: God has poured out all the treasures of his grace and goodness to us in his Son, Jesus Christ; yet these will profit us nothing for obtaining salvation unless we truly know him and, having known him, embrace him with a steadfast faith. Therefore from the very beginning of the world he promised him to the fathers, shadowed him forth in the legal types, and indeed gave prophets who, by the revelation of the Spirit, preached about everything that he was going to do and suffer, so that it might be plain to all what the true and certain way of obtaining salvation is. But after he came into the world at the appointed time, and was made man of a woman (to use the words of Paul), he at once made himself manifest in many ways to men of every place and rank, lest so great a treasure should lie hidden and unknown. Thus he became more widely known in the East through the heavenly sign. Led by the star, the wise men came to Jerusalem, and while they eagerly sought the newly born King of the Jews, they stirred up all others to know him as well, and among them Herod too, who was informed through the scribes of the place of the Messiah's birth. Meanwhile, in the temple also, when he was presented to the Lord according to the Law, certain things happened that pertained to his manifestation. And if we listen to the historians, many things happened among foreign nations too, which signified that a change of the whole world and the restoration of mankind were at hand. For, as Orosius writes, when Augustus entered the city a circle in the shape of a rainbow encircled the sun; a spring of oil also flowed most abundantly from a tavern for a whole day; and at about the same time Augustus forbade himself to be called lord, and he restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters. And God did not wish mistress of the world to be made in that city, so that he might show that the true author of heavenly peace and mediator of divine grace was now at hand, who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and who anoints all who believe in him as kings and priests; to him alone the name of Lord is due, since he is the only redeemer of the human race, and who restores to their true Lord men who were first labouring under the tyranny of the devil, so that, freed from sin but given over to God, they may have their fruit unto holiness. Moreover, among the manifestations of the newborn Christ, the first is the one Luke describes in the present passage, in which everything was clearly announced to men ignorant of worldly affairs and free from deceit and guile, all of which can instruct us both in the knowledge of Christ himself and in the salvation won through him. For this reason the account is plainly worthy of our careful consideration.

units.la: Orditur hanc Euangelista ab eorum descriptione, quibus Iesu Christi nativitas primis innotuit. Erant (inquit) pastores in eadem regione, Bethlehemica nimirum, excubantes & agentes vigilias noctis super gregem suum. Quibus verbis duo dicit. Nam & conditionem illorum indicat, & quid illo ipso tempore fecerint. Nos de vtroq; ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: The evangelist begins this account by describing those to whom the birth of Jesus Christ was first made known. "There were," he says, "shepherds in the same region", that is, of Bethlehem, "living out in the fields and keeping watch over their flock by night." In these words he says two things: for he indicates both their condition and what they were doing at that very time. We shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Quoad conditionem aut vitae genus, pastores fuisse dicuntur, & quidem (ut ex circumstantiis colligi potest) pauperes, vel etiam mercenarij, cum reliquis dormientibus ipsi nocturnas vigilias apud gregem suum agant. Neque dubium est, illos non multum cordi fuisse opulentis & in authoritate constitutis, qui interea vel rebus saeculi iudicio maioribus intenti erant, vel in mollibus stratis suauiter dormiebant, aut etiam libidini vacabant. At non ideo illos Deus negligit, qui eis filij sui salutiferam natiuitatem primùm denuntiat, & eosdem ad spectaculum euocat, quo nullum vnquam in mundo splendidius & iucundius esse editum. Quo loco docemur, Deum homines pauperes & abiectos minimè fastidire, ut plerunque ij solent, quos mundi gloria & fastus inebriat. Hi enim quia gloriam suam in externo splendore sitam putant, neminem sua amicitia aut fauore dignum iudicant, quem ipsis inferiorem esse vident. At longè aliter Deus, qui etsi in alto residea (ut Dauid inquit) eò vsq; tamen sese demittit, ut omnia inspiciat, quaecunq; in caelo & in terra sunt, & pauperes etiam ex pulueribus & caeno extrahit, ut inter populi sui principes collocentur. Quin nō vno loco se pupillorum patrem, viduarum tutorem, & peregrinorum atq; afflictorum patronum esse profitetur, & hos in primis commendatos esse vult ijs, qui in publica authoritate sunt constituti. Soletur hoc egenos & pauperes, omnes deniq;, qui in hoc mundo molestiam aliquam & calamitatem sustinent, ne tentationum pondere superati, se à Deo negligi arbitrentur, eò quòd in humanis praesidij nihil inueniunt. Discant autem tunc salutis spem in Christo collocare, qui ijs potissimum sese fruendum offert, qui in mundo hoc contempti sunt.
units.tr: As to their condition or way of life, they are said to have been shepherds, and indeed (as can be gathered from the circumstances) poor men, or even hired hands, who, while others slept, kept their night watches with their flock. There is no doubt that they were not much valued by the wealthy and those placed in authority, who meanwhile were either busy with matters that by worldly judgement were more important, or were sleeping comfortably on soft beds, or even given over to lust. Yet God does not on that account neglect them; he is the one who first proclaims to them the saving birth of his Son and calls them to a sight more splendid and delightful than any ever displayed in the world. In this place we are taught that God does not at all despise poor and humble men, as those are wont to do whom the glory and pride of the world intoxicate. For since they think their glory lies in outward show, they judge no one worthy of their friendship or favour whom they see to be beneath them. But God acts quite differently: although he dwells on high (as David says), he nevertheless so stoops down that he looks upon all things that are in heaven and on earth, and he lifts the poor even out of the dust and the mire, so that they may be placed among the princes of his people. Indeed, in more than one place he professes himself the father of orphans, the guardian of widows, and the patron of strangers and the afflicted, and he wishes these to be especially commended to those who are set in public authority. This should comfort the needy and the poor, and indeed all who suffer any trouble or calamity in this world, so that, overcome by the weight of temptations, they do not think they are neglected by God because they find nothing in human help. Let them learn instead to place their hope of salvation in Christ, who offers himself above all to those who are despised in this world.

units.la: Deinde admonet hic simul Spiritus sanctus, Christi cognitionem ad eos in primis pertinere, qui in populo pastorum locum & nomen sustinent, & quorum fidei salus populi commissa est. Inter hos primi fere sunt Ecclesiarum ministri, quos Paulus à Spiritu sancto constitutos ait, ad pascendum gregem Christi, quem hic sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit. At quoniam idem hic summus Ecclesiae suae pastor flor simul & vnicum animæ pabulum est, adhæc fons aquæ viuentis, via ite & ostium, per quod ad communionē cũDeo patre peruenitur: hunc omnino norint oportet, quicunq; gregis dominici pastores esse volunt. Nam si eum ignorent, inani quidem pastorū titulo & insignibus pastoritijs gloriari possunt, at interim non omnes Domini, sed potius seipsos pascent, & stulti illius pastoris similes erunt, què Deus apud Zachar. se missurum minatur, vt populi ingratitudinem & contumaciam puniat. Patet igitur hoc loco, quæ præcipua sit dissipationis causa, quæ hodie in orbe Christiano cernitur: hæc nimirum, quòd qui ad Ecclesiæ ministerium accedunt, vt gregis dominici pastores sint, ij aut omnium rudes & imperiti, aut philosophorum placitis imbuti sunt, & Christum ignorant, in quo vno eos coalescere oportet, qui Deo placere & seruari cupiunt. Deinde non minus oportet Christi cognitione instructos esse eos, qui in magistratu constituti rempub. administrant. Quia enim gregē non solum pascere, ve- rumetiam pedo coercere oportet, ne dissipetur, voluit Deus iudices & principes viros esse, qui publica authoritate populum in officio contineant. His autē Christi cognitio multas ob causas necessaria est: vt intelligant nimirum, cuius peculium sit populus, cui ipsi præsunt, cui item illum adducere debeant, & vt exemplū habeant, quod in tota sua functione imitentur. Quæ omnia cum vnus Christus in se contineat, si qui hunc ignorant, ij mox in tyrannos degenerant, & potestate sua pro libidine abu- tuntur, tandemq; sibijpsis simul & toti populo exitij authores sunt. At qui Christū nouerunt, ij hunc à patre Regem sui populi constitutum esse intelligent, & populum non sui iuris, sed Christi peculium esse sciunt, qui illum sanguinis sui pretio redemit. Norunt item, hunc olim venturū esse ad iudican- dum viuos & mortuos, & quòd tunc ipsos quoq; apud illius tribunal suæ functionis rationem reddere oporteat. Itaq; in Christi verbum & exemplū totis animis intenti, suæ fidei creditos amant, tuen- tur, & in viam pacis atq; salutis publicæ dirigunt. Et ij demum veri ποιμένες λαῶν, id est, pastores populorum & patriæ patres sunt, cum nemini sua libidine graues & molesti sint, omnium autem commodis pro viribus consulant. Potest hoc probari omnium seculorum exemplis, quando ex historijs constat, nullam rempub. vnquam felicem fuisse, nisi cuius principes Christum regem suum agnoue- runt, seq; huius sceptro gubernandos præbuerunt. At hodie pleriq; religionis causam nihil ad se perti- nere putant, & tunc demũ se veré pios arbitrantur, si Ecclesiæ tyrannidi Pontificum subijciant. Itaq; intercedit pasim vera Christi cognitio, augentur vero superstitiones, & crescit in dies personatorum antichristum potentia, quæ tandem toti Ecclesiæ & reipub. Christianæ extremū exitium afferet.
units.tr: Next, the Holy Spirit here also admonishes that the knowledge of Christ pertains especially to those who hold the place and name of shepherds among the people, and to whom the salvation of the people is entrusted in faith. Among these, the first are almost always the ministers of the Churches, whom Paul says were appointed by the Holy Spirit to feed the flock of Christ, which he has acquired here with the price of his blood. But since this same chief Shepherd of his Church is also the flower and only food of the soul, and moreover the fountain of living water, the way, the gate, through which one comes to communion with God the Father, all who wish to be shepherds of the Lord's flock must certainly know him. For if they are ignorant of him, they may indeed boast of the empty title of shepherd and of the pastoral insignia, but meanwhile they are not shepherds of the Lord but rather feed themselves, and they will be like that foolish shepherd whom God threatens in Zechariah that he will send, to punish the ingratitude and stubbornness of the people. It is plain, therefore, in this place, what is the chief cause of the dissipation that is seen today in the Christian world: namely, that those who come to the ministry of the Church, in order to be shepherds of the Lord's flock, are either utterly rude and unskilled, or are steeped in the opinions of philosophers, and do not know Christ, in whom alone all who wish to please God and be saved ought to be united. Next, those who are set in the magistracy and administer the commonwealth ought to be no less instructed in the knowledge of Christ. For since it is necessary not only to feed the flock but also to restrain it with the crook, lest it be scattered, God willed that judges and princes be men who keep the people in obedience by public authority. Now the knowledge of Christ is necessary for these men for many reasons: that they may understand whose possession the people is, over which they preside, and to whom they ought to lead it, and that they may have an example to imitate in their whole office. Since the one Christ contains all these things in himself, those who do not know him soon degenerate into tyrants, abuse their power at will, and at last become the authors of ruin both for themselves and for the whole people. But those who know Christ understand that he has been appointed by the Father King of his people, and they know that the people is not its own but the possession of Christ, who redeemed it with the price of his blood. They also know that he will one day come to judge the living and the dead, and that they themselves must then give an account of their office before his tribunal. Therefore, intent with their whole soul on the word and example of Christ, they love and protect those entrusted to their faith, and direct them into the way of peace and public salvation. These are at last the true "shepherds of peoples" [ποιμένες λαῶν], that is, the pastors of the people and the fathers of their country, since they are burdensome and troublesome to no one through their lust, but for the good of all they look after the common welfare as far as their strength allows. This can be proved by the examples of all ages, since history shows that no commonwealth has ever been happy unless its princes acknowledged Christ as their king and submitted themselves to be governed by his sceptre. But today most people think the cause of religion has nothing to do with them, and they consider themselves truly pious only if they subject themselves to the tyranny of the Pontiffs in the Church. And so the true knowledge of Christ is everywhere impeded, superstitions are increased, and the power of the masked Antichrist grows day by day, which will at last bring utter destruction upon the whole Church and the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Sed ad pastores hosce reuersi, audiamus quibus studijs aut negotijs tunc intenti fuerint, cum il- lis Christi natiuitas annuntiaretur. Solet enim apud istud quoque hominum genus sæpe vel locor- dia, vel nequitia atque lasciuia locum habere, vt officij sui immemores circa res ludicras & scrurri- les occupentur, aut confabulationibus vel cantilenis turpibus & ad libidinem seruientibus vacent. Sed nihil huius de istis dicitur, quin potius excubias & vigilias noctis diligenter egerunt super suum gregem. Admonemur isto exemplo, quales esse conueniat, qui Christum sibi innotescere, & eo ad salutem frui cupiunt. Decet illos ante omnia innocentia & simplicitas, qualis olim inter pa- stores & agricolas fuit, cum dolis & fraudibus, quæ in vrbibus & principum aulis regnat, non- dum assueuissent. Deinde excubijs & vigilantia opus est, idque bifariam: Primum in ijs, quæ ad animarum salutem & regnum Dei spectant, vbi periculorum & insidiarum plena sunt omnia. Ha- bemus enim hostilem publicum & communem, diabolum, qui vt primos parentes perdidit, ita omni um hominum saluti insidiatur, & dies noctesque instar leonis rugientis oberrat, querens quem de- uoret. Aduersus eum vero eò diligentius vigilare & eius insidias obseruare necesse est, quòd no- cendi studium & animum hostilem mirifice dissimulare, & interdum se in angelum lucis trans- formare solet, vt nobis sub veritatis & salutis prouehendæ prætextu imponat. Vestit enim do- los suos miro lenocinio, & peccata quoque manifesta fuco depingit, vt eorum atrocitas minus agno- scatur: imò veneficorum more mortifera toxica & aconita mellitis poculis propinat. Iuuat hunc mundus hic, qui & exemplo publico & infinitis illecebris incautos trahit, vt illum principem se- quantur. Periculum vero omnium maximum & nocentissimum nobis ex propria carne imminet, quæ vt naturali segnitie in omni bono opere torpet, ita ad malum procliuis, facile arripit quicquid prauis ipsius desiderijs respondet. Nullam ergo curam superfluam, nullam industriam nimiam, nullas vigilias vel excubias superuacaneas putare debemus: quando constat, sanctissimos quoqué Dei cultores interdum circumuenìri & decipi, vt in errores et manifesta flagitia pertrahantur. At cedit in his communis et omnibus impositae moriendi necessitas, quam vt nemo hominum effugere possit: ita incerta prosus est hora, qua nobis ex hac vita migrandum est, & plerunque tunc euocamur, quando nobis vitam iucundiorem & magis quietam in multos adhuc annos pollicemur, sicuti in stulti illius parabola Christus docet, quem inspératus anni proventus cõfidentiorem faciebat. Quid vero de nouissimo Christi aduentu dicemus, in quo omnis poenitentiae agendae occasio eripietur, et ad eius tribunal omnes sistemur, vt illic digna accipiamus vitae anteactae praemia? Certè, qui de his nõ ofcitan ter cogitant, videbunt, ita sibi vigilandum esse, vt nullus socordiae & segnitiei locus illis superfit. At non sufficit ista vigilantia, sed quia multae & diuersae hominum functiones sunt, quemq; in sua etiam vocatione sedulum & inductrum esse conuenit, vt quod ipsi iniunctum est officium bona fide obeat. Faciunt hoc pastores isti quos neque intempestanox, neque frigoris rigor, neque alia incommoda absterrent, quo minus gregem suum tueantur, & pro illo diligentes excubias agant. Idem ergo faciant, qui in magistratu constituti pastorum instar sunt, vt nuper diximus. Vigilent pro populi salute, iuuent afflictos, tueantur viduas & pupillos, redimant animas pauperum à fœnore & violentia, & pretiosum sit sanguis populi in oculis eorum. Psal.72. Meminerint item iudicii Dei esse, se autem huius esse ministros, qui verum culum tueri, iustitiam & morum honestatem promouere & plantare debeant. Neque vnquam illis excidat, Deum ipsum in medio iudicum consessu praesentem adesse, & huic olim rationem fore reddendam. Idem faciant ecclesiarum ministri, & sibi diligenter cogitent, quod Dominus sub speculatoris parabola Ezechieli dicit, & quod Paulus Actae episcopis ait: Attendite vobisipsis et toti gregi, in quo vos spiritus sanctus constituit episcopos ad pascendam ecclesiam Dei, &c. Ita patresfamilias cogitent, se gregis sui domestici pastores esse, & proinde vigilent, ne qui ipsorum vel indulgentia vel negligentia deteriores fiant. Excubent item diligenter conjuges, ne diaboli insidijs pateant, & fidem mutuam turpiter fallant. Qui vero caelibes viuunt, eo magis sibi vigilandum esse putent, ne carnis libidine abrepti aliquid praeter officium faciant. Ad eundem modum heri famulorum salutem curae habeant, & vicissim hi quoque fide bona illis seruiant, neque herorum improbitate aut duritia se vinci patiantur. Qui enim pastoribus istis praemium suae fidei amplissimum retribuit, idem remunerator est fidelissimus omnium, qui officio suo probè funguntur, etiamsi homines omnes sui laboris iniquos et ingratos aestimatores habeant. At si ista cum nostri seculi moribus conferamus, non mirabimur raram hodie esse in terris Christi cognitionem, cùm paucissimi sint, qui vel eam sedulò quaerant, vel in concredito sibi officio vigilent & bona fide versentur. Cur enim maiora illis credat Deus, qui in paruo infideles sunt? Sequitur nunc reuelationis aut denuntiationis istius modus, quem ita Lucas describit: Et ecce Angelus Domini superuenit illis, & gloria Domini circumfulsit illos, & timuerunt timore magno, &c. Vt in natiuitate nihil audiuimus, quàm quod vile, humile, abiectum & sordidum cernì poterat, ita hic gloriosa & diuinae maiestatis plena sunt omnia. Vt enim seipsum extremè humiliauit Dei filius, ne diuinus caelestis gloriae splendor nobis miseris terrorem incuteret: ita vicissim huius quoque specimen praeberi oportuit, ne illius humilitate & contemptu specie offenderemur. At hic ante omnia obseruabimus, primum nati Christi nuntium, non hominem, sed angelum fuisse. Respondet hoc Legis promulgationi, quam olim similiter per Angelos factam fuisse Paulus scribit. Erant autem illic omnia terroris & horroris plena. Visebantur enim faces ardentes & vapores densi, audiebantur tonitrua & fulminum micantium fragores, tam horribilis denique erat rerum facies, vt populus illam ferre non posset. Ita vero adumbrabatur, quem in conscientijs nostris Lex excitat, terror, & qui ex maledictionis Dei sensu oritur. In praesenti vero longe aliter res geruntur. Nam etsi pastores quoque isti timorem aliquem concipiunt, eius tamen causa non alia est, quàm innata nobis infirmitas, & quòd Deus verbo suo reuerentiam maiorem conciliare, & illos ad diligentiorem rei consideratio-nem excitare voluit: & mox nuntium auditur plenum consolationis, ex quo gaudium incomparabile concipiunt. Docet autem nos ista comparatio, Christum consolationis & pacis authorem esse, quae Legis terrores discutit, & omnem mundi intellectum (vt Paulus ait) longè superat. Ideo Christus quoque spiritum, quem suis largitur, consolatorem & aduocatum nominat, eò quòd salutis certos reddit, & dit, & monet vt Deum patris nomine inuocemus. In primis autem elucet hoc loco Euangelij Christi Iesu dignitas. Nam vt eius promissiones primas Deus ipse in paradiso primis parentibus, deinde sanctis patriarchis proposuit, postea per prophetas, sanctissimos homines, illustrauit: ita Christo iam nato primum huius nuntium aut praeconem dedit Angelum, qui (vt postea audiemus) se euangelizandi causa venisse ait. Postea ipse Dei filius hoc munus suscepit, seque huius obeundi causa venisse testatur, & in eo diligentissimus fuit. E terris autem discessurus sibi substituit Apostolos, quos amicorum nomine dignatur, & quos ceu peculium aliquod singulare sibi e mundo selegerat. Debent ista ijs opponi, qui euangelium eo nomine contemnunt, quod per homines mundi iudicio obscuros & contemptos praedicetur. Quia enim Dei verbum est, non opus habet vlla hominum fastuosorum commendatione. Quotquot certe illud contemnunt aut negant, ij non in homines modo sanctissimos, Prophetas & Apostolos, sed in ipsum Dei filium contumeliosi sunt, imò (vt Ioannes pronuntiat) Deum mendacij arguere audent, dum quod hic de filio suo tulit testimonium reijciunt. Socij horum sunt, qui doctrinam Euangelij pro suo arbitrio mutant, ei adijciunt aut adimunt, & in illa ludunt perinde ac si humani ingenij figmentum sit. Paulus Angelum Anathema pronuntiat, qui Euangelium aliud praedicauerit. Quae ergo dementia est, hominibus tantum iuris permittere, vt id faciant?
units.tr: But let us return to these shepherds and hear what they were occupied with when the birth of Christ was announced to them. Among this class of people, too, idleness, wantonness and licentiousness often have their place: men forget their duty and busy themselves with frivolous and trifling matters, or give their time to filthy chatter and songs that serve lust. But nothing of this is said of them. On the contrary, they kept careful watch and vigil over their flock by night. This example teaches us what kind of people ought to be, those who desire to come to know Christ and to enjoy salvation through him. Above all, such people should have the innocence and simplicity that once marked shepherds and farmers, before they had become accustomed to the deceit and fraud that reign in cities and princely courts. Next, watchfulness and vigilance are needed, and this in two ways. First, in matters that concern the salvation of souls and the kingdom of God, where everything is full of dangers and snares. For we have a common enemy, the devil, who, just as he destroyed our first parents, lies in wait for the salvation of all people and wanders day and night like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Against him we must watch all the more carefully and keep an eye on his snares, because he is wont to conceal his hostile purpose and his desire to harm in a wonderful way, and sometimes to transform himself into an angel of light, so as to impose upon us under the pretext of promoting truth and salvation. He clothes his deceits in a marvellous allurement, and he paints even manifest sins with a false colour, so that their atrocity is less recognised. Indeed, like poisoners, he offers deadly poisons and aconite in honeyed cups. This world helps him, which by its public example and by countless enticements draws the unwary to follow that prince. But the greatest and most harmful danger threatens us from our own flesh, which, as it grows sluggish in every good work by its natural laziness, so it is quick to evil, and readily seizes whatever answers to its wicked desires. Therefore we ought to think that no care is superfluous, no diligence excessive, no watching or vigil needless, since it is certain that even the most holy worshippers of God are sometimes surrounded and deceived, so that they are drawn into errors and open wickedness. Yet in these matters the necessity of dying, which is common to all and laid upon all, yields to no one, so that no one can escape it. The hour when we must depart from this life is wholly uncertain, and for the most part we are summoned at the very time when we promise ourselves a more pleasant and quieter life for many years to come, just as Christ teaches in the parable of the foolish man, whom the unexpected abundance of his year made more confident. But what shall we say of the last coming of Christ, when every opportunity for repentance will be taken away, and we shall all be brought before his tribunal to receive there the due rewards of our past life? Surely those who often think about these things will see that they must so watch that no place for carelessness and sloth remains for them. But this vigilance is not enough. Since there are many and various offices among people, each one ought to be diligent and active in his own calling, so that he may discharge in good faith the duty laid upon him. Those shepherds do this, whom neither the middle of the night, nor the bitterness of the cold, nor other hardships keep from guarding their flock and keeping diligent watch over it. Therefore let those who are placed in the magistracy, who are like shepherds, do the same, as we said a little while ago. Let them watch for the safety of the people, help the afflicted, protect widows and orphans, redeem the souls of the poor from usury and violence, and let their blood be precious in their eyes (Psalm 72). Let them also remember that judgment belongs to God, and that they are ministers of him, who ought to guard true worship, promote justice and moral integrity, and plant them. Let them never forget that God himself is present in the midst of the assembly of judges, and that an account will one day have to be rendered to him. Let the ministers of the churches do the same, and let them carefully consider what the Lord says to Ezekiel in the parable of the watchman, and what Paul says to the bishops in Acts: "Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God," etc. Likewise let fathers of families think that they are the shepherds of their own household flock, and therefore let them watch lest any of those under them become worse through their indulgence or negligence. Let spouses also watch diligently, lest they lie open to the snares of the devil and shamefully break faith with one another. Those who live unmarried should think that they must all the more watch over themselves, lest, carried away by fleshly lust, they do anything beyond their duty. In the same way let masters care for the salvation of their servants, and in turn let these also serve them in good faith, and not allow themselves to be overcome by the wickedness or harshness of their masters. For he who rewards those shepherds with the greatest reward for their faithfulness is also the most faithful rewarder of all who discharge their duty well, even if all people regard their labour as unjust and ungrateful. But if we compare these things with the manners of our age, we shall not be surprised that the knowledge of Christ is rare on earth today, since there are very few who either seek it diligently or watch over the office entrusted to them and conduct themselves in good faith. For why should God trust them with greater things, when they are unfaithful in small ones? Next follows the manner of this revelation or announcement, which Luke describes thus: "And behold, an angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them, and they feared with great fear," etc. As in the nativity we heard nothing but what could be seen as cheap, lowly, abject and squalid, so here everything is full of glory and of divine majesty. For just as the Son of God humbled himself in the extreme, so that the divine splendour of heavenly glory might not strike terror into us miserable creatures, so in turn it was fitting that a sample of this glory should also be shown, lest we be offended by the appearance of his humility and contempt. But here we shall first observe that the first messenger of the birth of Christ was not a man but an angel. This corresponds to the promulgation of the Law, which Paul writes was likewise once made through angels. There everything was full of terror and horror. For burning torches and thick vapours were seen, thunderings and the crashing of flashing lightnings were heard, and finally the appearance of things was so dreadful that the people could not bear it. Thus indeed was foreshadowed the terror which the Law stirs up in our consciences, the terror that arises from the sense of God's curse. But at present things are done in a far different way. For although these shepherds too conceive some fear, its cause is nothing other than our innate weakness, and the fact that God through his word wished to win greater reverence and to rouse them to a more careful consideration of the matter. And soon they hear a message full of consolation, from which they conceive an incomparable joy. This comparison teaches us that Christ is the author of consolation and peace, who dispels the terrors of the Law and far surpasses every understanding of the world (as Paul says). Therefore Christ also names the Spirit, whom he gives to his own, a comforter and advocate, because he makes them certain of salvation, and he admonishes them to invoke God by the name of Father. Above all, the dignity of the Gospel of Jesus Christ shines forth in this place. For just as God himself first set forth its promises to our first parents in paradise, then illuminated them to the holy patriarchs, and afterwards through the prophets, most holy men, so, when Christ had now been born, he gave an angel as the first herald or proclaimer of this message, who (as we shall hear later) said that he had come for the purpose of preaching the good news. Afterwards the Son of God himself took up this task, and testified that he had come to discharge it, and he was most diligent in it. And about to depart from the earth, he appointed in his place the Apostles, whom he honours with the name of friends, and whom he had chosen out of the world as a special people for himself. These things ought to be set against those who despise the Gospel on the ground that it is preached by men who are obscure and contemptible in the judgment of the world. For since it is the Word of God, it has no need of any commendation from proud men. Certainly all who despise or deny it are insulting not only to the most holy men, the Prophets and Apostles, but to the Son of God himself. Indeed (as John declares) they dare to charge God with lying, while they reject the testimony that he has given concerning his Son. Allies of these are those who change the doctrine of the Gospel according to their own judgment, add to it or take away from it, and play with it as if it were a fiction of human wit. Paul pronounces anathema on the angel who should preach another Gospel. What madness, then, is it to grant men so much right that they may do this?

units.la: Sed Angelum pastoribus loquentem audiamus, cuius oratio haec fuit: Ne timete: ecce enim Euangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit toti populo. Quia natus est vobis hodie Seruator, qui est Christus Dominus, &c. Continetur his verbis prima Euangelij concio, quae post natum ex Virgine Dei Filium habita est, & constat ea quatuor partibus, quas ex ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: But let us hear the angel speaking to the shepherds, whose words were these: "Fear not, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all the people. For unto you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord," etc. These words contain the first sermon of the gospel, delivered after the Son of God was born of the Virgin. It consists of four parts, which we shall examine in order.

units.la: Prima consolationem continet, qua opus erat consternatis. Amicè igitur eos compellans timere vetat: Et mox causam subijcit: Ecce enim euangelizo vobis gaudium magnum. Est ergo euangelium rei laetae & faustae nuntium, quo exhilarantur, qui prius conscientia peccatorum territi in tenebris & vmbra mortis desidebant. Annuntiatur enim nobis Iesus Christus, qui vt peccata nostra mortis suae merito expiauit: ita iustitiam nobis sempiternam reduxit, & patrem placauit, vt per ipsum nobis tutus ad thronum gratiae accessus pateat. Itaque cum terroris causae sublatae sint, gaudium & consolatio sequantur oportet. Docent ista, quo loco doctores illi habendi sint, qui imperitum populum nouis quotidie terroribus vexant, & conscientijs duros & intolerabiles omnino scrupulos injiciunt, quando de gratia Dei dubitare docent, et nos salutis certos fieri posse negant, quoad in hu-ius vitae curriculo laboramus; qui denique iam morituros ignis lustralis seu purgatorij (vt illi loquuntur) minis excruciant. Non sunt illi Euangelicae doctrinae praecones, & proinde audiri non merentur. Fatemur equidem contumaces & poenitere nescios ad Dei tribunal trahendos & publicè etiam arguendos esse. At hic de infirmis & sub tentationum pondere laborantibus sermo est, quibus Euangelium medicinam & consolationem affert, & quos gratiae praedicatione confirmari atque erigi oportet.
units.tr: The first part contains a consolation, which the frightened shepherds needed. Addressing them kindly, the angel forbids them to be afraid, and at once gives the reason: "For behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy." The gospel, then, is a message of joyful and happy news, by which those are cheered who, previously terrified by the awareness of their sins, were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. For Jesus Christ is announced to us, who by the merit of his death expiated our sins, restored to us everlasting righteousness, and appeased the Father, so that through him a safe access to the throne of grace lies open to us. Therefore, since the causes of terror have been removed, joy and consolation must follow. This teaches us what kind of teachers should be regarded as such: those who vex an untrained people with fresh terrors every day, cast hard and utterly intolerable scruples upon consciences, teach men to doubt the grace of God, deny that we can be made certain of our salvation while we labour in the course of this life, and, finally, torment those now about to die with threats of the cleansing fire of purgatory (as they call it). These men are not heralds of the evangelical doctrine, and so they do not deserve to be heard. We admit indeed that the obstinate and those who do not know how to repent must be dragged before the judgment seat of God and also publicly rebuked. But here the discourse concerns the weak, who labour under the weight of temptations, to whom the gospel brings medicine and consolation, and whom the preaching of grace ought to strengthen and raise up.

units.la: Deinde ad quos nam gaudium illud pertineat, docet, & hic totius populi meminit, quo nomine omnes cuiuscunq; loci & ordinis homines comprehendit. Et hoc illud est, in quo fidei cardo potissimum versatur. Sunt enim, qui non negant, Euangelio gaudiũ & salutem praedicari, sed illius promissiones ad se pertinere negant, & ideo nullam ex illis consolationem percipiunt. Cui infirmitati vt mederetur Deus, promissiones illas vniuersales esse voluit, vt singuli eas sibi applicare possent. Abrahamo certè dicebatur: In semine tuo benedicetur omnes gentes terrae. Isaias verò scribit: Omnes errauimus vt oues, at Deus omnium peccata in illum conuenire & ei imputari voluit. Et frequens admodum est sententia illa in apostolorum scriptis, qua negatur personarum respectus apud Deum esse: & ipse Christus omnes qui laborant & onerati sunt ad se inuitat. Idem deniq; Apostolis praecipit, vt Euangelium in toto orbe omnibus gentibus praedicent. Rectè igitur Angelus, gaudium hoc ad omnem populum redundaturum ait, idem verò hoc ipsum ad pastores istos quasi restringens, dicit: Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum. Et mox: Quia natus est vobis Seruator, &c. Ita nimirum monens, vt singuli ad se rapiant priuatim quod Deus in genere omnibus offert, si quando Satan ex nostra conditione aut moribus argumenta petit, quibus nos à salutis cõsortio exclusos esse nobis persuadere conatur. Obseruauit hoc olim probè D. Augustinus, cuius verba, cùm propriũ huius loci vsum & dulcissimam simul consolatione contineant, recitare libet. Ad omnes (inquit) gaudium istud pertinet, quia Christus omnibus venit: nec oportet esse tristitiae locum, vbi est natalis gaudiorum. Nullus arbitretur se ab illa laetitia alienum. Si quis sanctus est, gaudeat: quoniam accipiet remunerationem. Si peccator est, gaudeat: quoniam invitatur ad veniam. Si gentilis est, gaudeat: quoniam admittitur ad salutem. Deniq; si nos ipsos a Christo alienos non facimus, iam in Christo sumus. Ille vero alienum se a Christi consortio efficit, qui se in Christi corpore esse denegarit. Exultate ergo pueri sancti. Exultate virgines sanctae. Virgo peperit vobis, cui sine corruptione nubatis. Exultate iusti, natalis est iustificatoris. Exultate debiles et aegroti, natalis est Saluatoris. Exultate captivi, natalis est redemptoris. Exultate omnes Christiani, natalis est Christi. Exultemus servi, natalis est domini. Exultemus liberi, natalis est liberantis. Haec omnia Augustini sunt.
units.tr: Next, the angel teaches to whom that joy belongs, and here he mentions "all the people," by which name he embraces all men of every place and rank. And this is the point on which the chief hinge of faith turns. For there are some who do not deny that joy and salvation are preached in the gospel, but deny that its promises pertain to themselves, and so they receive no consolation from them. To remedy this weakness God willed that those promises be universal, so that each person might apply them to himself. To Abraham it was certainly said: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." And Isaiah writes: "We have all gone astray like sheep," yet God willed that the sins of all should meet in him and be imputed to him. Very frequent in the writings of the apostles is that saying by which respect of persons before God is denied. Christ himself invites to himself all who labour and are burdened. Finally, he commands the apostles to preach the gospel to all nations throughout the whole world. Rightly, then, the angel says that this joy will overflow to all the people, and yet, as if narrowing it down to those shepherds, he says: "I announce to you great joy," and soon after: "For unto you is born a Saviour," etc. He thus admonishes each of us to seize privately for himself what God offers in general to all, whenever Satan seeks from our condition or manners arguments by which he tries to persuade us that we are excluded from the fellowship of salvation. Saint Augustine rightly observed this long ago, and since his words contain both the proper use of this passage and a most sweet consolation at the same time, I am pleased to recite them. "This joy (he says) pertains to all, because Christ has come for all; nor ought there to be a place for sadness where is the birthday of joys. Let no one think himself a stranger to that gladness. If someone is holy, let him rejoice, since he will receive a reward. If someone is a sinner, let him rejoice, since he is invited to pardon. If someone is a Gentile, let him rejoice, since he is admitted to salvation. Finally, if we do not make ourselves strangers to Christ, we are already in Christ. But he makes himself a stranger to the fellowship of Christ who denies that he is in the body of Christ. Exult, therefore, holy boys. Exult, holy virgins: a virgin has borne for you one to whom you may marry without corruption. Exult, righteous men: it is the birthday of the justifier. Exult, weak and sick: it is the birthday of the Saviour. Exult, captives: it is the birthday of the redeemer. Exult, all Christians: it is the birthday of Christ. Let us exult, servants: it is the birthday of the Lord. Let us exult, free men: it is the birthday of the liberator." These are all the words of Augustine.

units.la: Sed Angelum rursus audiamus, qui gaudij huius causam perspicuè indicat, & ea occasione illius authorem describit. Quia natus est vobis hodie (inquit) Seruator, qui est Christus Dominus, in vrbe Dauid. Quasi dicat: Hactenus quidem salutis verae expertes, et propter peccata (vt & reli qui homines) morti & exitio obnoxij fuistis. Sed nunc natus est Schilo, id est, sospitator ille & vnicus omnis felicitatis author, quem olim Iacob venturum praedixit. Et hic est CHRISTVS ille, id est vnctus Dei, Rex & Sacerdos electorum omnium, in quo vno salus habetur. Natus est autem in ciuitate Dauidis, Bethlehemi scilicet, quem locum eius natalibus destinatum fuisse, no ignoratis. Obseruabis autem tribus verbis filium Dei describi ab Angelo, quibus abunde docemur, quid ex illo sperari debeat. Primo Saluatorem dicit, & huius nominis rationem ipse iam ante reddiderat, Iosepho in somnis dicens: Quoniam seruabit populum suum a peccatis ipsius. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi semel modo nos seruet aut ex peccatorum laqueis eripiat: sed perpetuus suorum seruator est, & eosdem semper tuetur atque defendit. Est enim inuicta illa petra, aduersus quam ne portae quidem inferorum praualent. Pastor item est fidelis et fortis, ex cuius manu oues nemo potest rapere, idemq; se nobis praesentem affuturum promittit, vsque ad finem seculi. Deinde Christum, id est, vnctum dicit, quo nomine Regem & Sacerdotem denotari, non vno loco iam diximus. Et in illo constat plenissimè contineri omnia boni Regis & fidi Sacerdotis officia. Suos enim asserit, iustur, donis caelestibus beat & iudicat. Idem vero docet etiam, seipsum pro nobis sacrificauit, adhaec intercedit pro nobis, & sublata ira Dei benedictionem nobis restituit. Quia vero haec ille praestat, caput quoque suae ecclesiae sit oportet, quem titulum cuiquam alij tribuere scelus & sacrilegium est. Tertiò Dominum vocat, quod nomen relationem habet ad seruos, & ita proprie ille dicitur, eò quòd nos sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit, vt suum essemus peculium. Ideo apud Isaiam clamat: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Habes ergo in hisce Angeli verbis, quid de Dei filio ex Maria nato tibi polliceri debeas. Opus nobis est Seruatore, qui nos ex peccati, mortis & diaboli tyrannide liberet? Est is Christus, qui peccatum omne mortis suae merito expiauit, mortem resurrectione vicit, & diaboli regnum destruxit. Opus est Rege, qui nos tueatur, regat & opibus augeat? At hic etiam Christus est, qui seipsum ad omnia optimi Regis officia sponte taneum offert. Opus sacerdote, doctore, sacrifico & intercessore apud Deum? Ecce ista quoque omnia in vno Christo inuenies. Deniq; Domino opus est, qui te protegat, deq; necessarijs omnibus tibi prospiciat? Sed et hic ad omnia haec Christus vnus sufficit: neq; de eius fide dubitare licet, cum seipsum pro nobis in mortem dederit. Quae ergo stultitia est, hoc relicto post vanissimorum hominum figmenta vagari?
units.tr: But let us hear the angel again, who clearly indicates the cause of this joy, and on that occasion describes its author: "For unto you is born this day," he says, "a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David." As if he said: "Hitherto, indeed, you have been strangers to true salvation, and, on account of your sins (like all other men), you have been subject to death and ruin. But now there is born Shiloh, that is, that Saviour and the only author of all happiness, whom Jacob long ago foretold would come. And this is that Christ, that is, the anointed of God, King and Priest of all the elect, in whom alone salvation is found." He was born, moreover, in the city of David, that is, at Bethlehem, a place which you know was appointed for his birth. Now you will observe that the Son of God is described by the angel with three words, by which we are abundantly taught what ought to be hoped for from him. First, he calls him Saviour, and he himself had already given the reason for this name, when he said to Joseph in a dream: "For he shall save his people from their sins." This should not be understood as if he saved us only once, or rescued us from the snares of sin once and for all; rather, he is the perpetual Saviour of his own, and always keeps and defends the same. For he is that unconquered rock, against which not even the gates of hell prevail. He is also the faithful and strong shepherd, from whose hand no one can snatch the sheep, and he promises that he will be present with us, even to the end of the age. Then he says Christ, that is, the anointed, a name by which we have already said more than once that King and Priest are denoted. And in that name it is fully clear that all the duties of a good King and a faithful Priest are contained. For he claims his own, justifies them, blesses them with heavenly gifts, and judges them. He also teaches that he offered himself as a sacrifice for us, further intercedes for us, and, the wrath of God being removed, restores blessing to us. And because he performs these things, he must also be the head of his Church, a title which to assign to anyone else is a crime and sacrilege. Third, he calls him Lord, a name which has relation to servants, and in this sense he is properly so called, because he has acquired us at the price of his own blood, that we might be his own possession. Therefore in Isaiah he cries out: "I am the Lord, this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." You have, then, in these words of the angel, what you ought to promise yourself concerning the Son of God born of Mary. Do we need a Saviour who frees us from the tyranny of sin, death, and the devil? He is Christ, who by the merit of his death expiated every sin, conquered death by his resurrection, and destroyed the kingdom of the devil. Do we need a King who protects us, rules us, and enriches us with resources? Yet this is also Christ, who of his own accord offers himself as fit for all the duties of the best King. Do we need a priest, a teacher, a sacrifice, and an intercessor before God? Behold, you will find all these things also in Christ alone. Finally, do we need a Lord who protects you and provides you with all necessities? But Christ alone is sufficient for all these things as well, nor is it lawful to doubt his faithfulness, since he has given himself into death for us. What folly, then, is it to leave this aside and wander after the fictions of the most vain men?

units.la: Restat vltima orationis Angelicae pars, in qua signo addito verbis suis fidem facit, vt & minus dubitent pastores, & Christum inuenire atque agnoscere possint. Dicit enim: Hoc autem vobis signum erit, Inuenietis infantem fasciis inuolutum, iacentem in praesepi. Est hoc magnum bonitatis Dei argumentum, quòd qui pro suo iure fidem a nobis exigere potest, nostrae tamē infirmitati se accommodat, et verbis suis signa adhibet, quae & promissiones eius atq; beneficia in mente renouocent, & fidem nostram confirment. Quem proprium & praecipuum Sacramentorum ecclesiae vsum esse constat. Ob seruabis autē signa eiusmodi, quoad externa speciem, fere vilia et contemptibilia esse, vt vix aliquid cum promissionū diuinarū maiestate comune habere videatur. Hic sane cùm de Christo Seruatore & Domino tot seculis expectato cocionatus esset Angelus, nō palatij magnifici, nō purpura, nō quae apud huius seculi principes in usu sunt regalium insignium, sed pueruli vilibus pannis inuoluti & in præsepi iacentis meminit. Obseruauit hunc morem Deus iam inde à prima rerum origine. Quid obse cro unquam in hoc mundo admirabilius & excellentius factum est, quàm quòd Deus ille immensus, infinitus, immortalis, bonus, iustus, sapiens et nullius indigus, cum miseris mortalibus, cum iniustis, stultis & egentissimis hominibus fœdus facere dignatus est, quo seipsum & omnia sua nobis obstrin geret? At quàm vile, quàm contemptibile, imò quàm ridiculum (si humanæ rationis iudicium audias) fuit fœderis signum tenuis pelliculæ, in genitali membro prominentis, resectio? Quid item pretiosius & magis necessarium ablutione peccatorum per Christi sanguinem facta, & adoptione in filiorum Dei aut Ecclesiæ societatem? At tanti mysterij Sacramentum est Baptismus, in quo oculi nihil quàm vilis aquæ asperstionem cernunt. Similiter quid unquam mundus hic vidit stupendum magis, quàm humani generis redemptionem, indigna Filij Dei morte factam, ad cuius conspectum terra tremuit, petræ disilierunt, & Sol radios suos contraxit? Cæterum tanti beneficij memoriam Christus parua panis bucella & vini haustu tenui consecrauit. Miratur hunc Dei more carnis ratio, & nescio quid maius sibi pollicetur, si Sacramenta splendore externo commendarentur. Sed certa est Deo sui consilij & instituti ratio, qui cùm carnis ingenium probè nosset, cauere voluit, ne externis inhærendo in terna salutis mysteria negligeremus, & signa pro rebus signatis acciperemus, quam miserrimam animarum seruitutem Augustinus dicit. Neminem ergo vilis Sacramentorum species offendat, sed pastores hosce imitentur, quos neque stabuli neque præsepis mentio abstrruit, quò minus Christum Bethlehemi quærerent: & procul dubio nos quoque sese & meritum suum nobis offerentem in stulta Euangelij prædicatione & simplici Sacramentorum usu inueniemus. Et hæc quidem in Angeli orationem dicta sunto.
units.tr: Remains the last part of the Angelic address, in which, by adding a sign to his words, he gives assurance, so that the ministers may have less doubt and may be able to find and recognise Christ. For he says: "And this shall be a sign to you: you will find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." This is a great proof of God's goodness, that he who could rightly demand faith from us nevertheless accommodates himself to our weakness and attaches signs to his words, which both bring back to mind his promises and benefits and strengthen our faith. It is well established that this is the proper and chief use of the sacraments of the Church. Yet you will observe that such signs, as far as their outward appearance goes, are almost cheap and contemptible, so that they seem to have scarcely anything in common with the majesty of the divine promises. Here, certainly, when the angel was preaching about Christ the Saviour and Lord, who had been awaited for so many ages, he mentions not a magnificent palace, not purple, not the royal insignia that are in use among the princes of this world, but a little boy wrapped in poor rags and lying in a manger. God has observed this custom from the very beginning of things. What, I ask, has ever been done in this world more wonderful and more excellent than that God, immense, infinite, immortal, good, just, wise, and in need of nothing, deigned to make a covenant with wretched mortals, with unjust, foolish and utterly needy men, by which he bound himself and all his possessions to us? Yet how cheap, how contemptible, indeed how ridiculous (if you listen to the judgement of human reason) was the cutting away of a thin little piece of skin protruding from the genital member, as the sign of that covenant! Likewise, what is more precious and more necessary than the washing away of sins through the blood of Christ, and adoption into the fellowship of the sons of God or of the Church? Yet Baptism is the sacrament of so great a mystery, in which the eyes see nothing but the sprinkling of a paltry water. Similarly, what has this world ever seen more astonishing than the redemption of the human race, brought about by the unworthy death of the Son of God, at the sight of which the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and the sun drew in its rays? Moreover, Christ consecrated the memory of so great a benefit with a small morsel of bread and a slight draught of wine. Human reason, following the way of the flesh, marvels at this and imagines that it knows not what greater thing God promises, if the sacraments were recommended by outward splendour. But God's reasoning concerning his own counsel and ordinance is sure; since he knew the nature of the flesh well, he wished to take care that we should not, by clinging to outward things, neglect the inward mysteries of salvation, and take signs for the things signified, a most wretched bondage of souls, as Augustine calls it. Let no one, therefore, be offended by the lowly appearance of the sacraments; rather let us imitate those shepherds, whom neither the mention of the stable nor of the manger kept from seeking Christ at Bethlehem. And without doubt we too shall find him, offering himself and his merit to us, in the foolish preaching of the gospel and in the simple use of the sacraments. And let these things be said concerning the Angel's address.

units.la: Sequitur postremus huius reuelationis siue annuntiationis Christi nati actus, quo eius maiestas amplius declaratur. Nam repente affuit cum Angelo multitudo exercituum cælestium, laudantium Deum & dicentium: Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax, in homines beneuolentia. Facium hic officium suum angeli, quos in hoc potissimum destinatos esse scriptura testantur, ut Deo seruiat & eius gloriam celebrent. Hymnum vero istum præsenti causæ accommodant, & simul humano generi ob natum in carne Dei filium gratulantur, & incarnationis huius fructum prædicant. Partes illius sunt tres.
units.tr: There follows the last act of this revelation or announcement of the birth of Christ, by which his majesty is declared still further. For suddenly there appeared with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill towards men." Here the angels perform their duty, those whom Scripture bears witness were especially appointed for this purpose, namely to serve God and to celebrate his glory. They adapt that hymn to the present occasion, and at the same time they congratulate the human race on account of the Son of God born in the flesh, and proclaim the fruit of this incarnation. Its parts are three.

units.la: Primam à gratiarum actione exordiuntur, & canunt: Gloria in altissimis Deo. Merito autem gloriæ Dei mentionem faciunt, quando constat, hanc non alio opere magis illustrari, quàm eo, quòd filium suum unigenitum pro nobis hominem & peccati reum fieri, imò propter nos mortem infamem subire voluit. Hic enim (ut nuper quoq; diximus) illius iustitia, bonitas, veritas, sapientia & omnipotentia sic sese exerunt, ut de omnibus istis nemini posthac dubitare liceat. Dum vero gloriam omnem uni Deo transcribunt, simul nos admonent, ut ipsi quoq; omnem humani generis redemptionem ad unum hunc authorem referamus, cùm nihil nobis meriti aut dignitatis sit, cui in hac causa locus aliquis debeatur. Etenim si cælestes illi spiritus in uno Deo acquiescunt, & huic uni gloriam omnem tribuunt, intolerabilis nimium & plus quàm sacrilega confidentia fuerit, si nos illi aliquid negemus, ut id nobis vendicetur.
units.tr: They begin the first part with thanksgiving, and they sing: "Glory to God in the highest." They rightly make mention of the glory of God, since it is plain that this glory is illustrated by no work more than by this, that he willed his only-begotten Son to become man for us, and guilty of sin, indeed to undergo an infamous death on our account. For here (as we said just now also) his righteousness, goodness, truth, wisdom and omnipotence display themselves in such a way that henceforth no one may doubt any of these things. While they ascribe all glory to God alone, at the same time they admonish us that we too should refer the whole redemption of the human race to this one author, since we have no merit or worth which could be owed any place in this cause. For if those heavenly spirits rest in the one God and ascribe all glory to him alone, it would be an intolerable and more than sacrilegious presumption if we were to deny him anything, so as to claim it for ourselves.

units.la: Secunda parte humano generi gratulantur angeli, & præcipuum quod ex Christo nobis obtigit beneficiū prædicant, dicentes: Et in terra pax. Eam vero pacem intelligunt, quæ cum Deo nunc nobis intercedit, qui prius inimici & filij iræ eramus. Fecit hanc Christus, quando peccata, quibus à Deo dirimebamur, expiauit, & maceriam Legis destruxit, quæ nos sua sententia ad mortem æternam damnabat. Quo nomine Paulus illum pacem nostram dicit. Dum vero pacem hanc iam in terris factam esse angeli canunt, simul omnes homines officij admonent, ut & ipsi inter se pacem colant, & concordiæ mutuæ studeant. Turpe enim fuerit, nos propter res ludicras & temporarias dissidere, cùm Deus nobiscum pacem coire voluerit, qui inimicitiarum causas iustissimas & grauissimas habebat. Itaque nimis leuiter hoc Dei beneficium æstimant, vel potius omnino ignorant, quibus adeo leue videtur pacis fraternæ vinculum abrumpere.
units.tr: In the second part the angels congratulate the human race and proclaim the chief benefit that has come to us from Christ, saying: "And on earth peace." They understand by this peace the peace which now stands between us and God, we who were formerly enemies and children of wrath. Christ made this peace when he expiated the sins by which we were separated from God, and destroyed the dividing wall of the Law, which by its sentence condemned us to eternal death. It is by this name that Paul calls him our peace. And while the angels sing that this peace has now been made on earth, at the same time they remind all men of their duty, that they too should cultivate peace among themselves and strive for mutual concord. For it would be shameful for us to quarrel over trifling and temporary things, when God has willed to make peace with us, he who had the most just and most grievous causes of enmity. Thus they value this benefit of God too lightly, or rather they are altogether ignorant of it, for whom it seems so trivial to break the bond of brotherly peace.

units.la: Porrò tertia parte fontem & causam pacis huius indicant adiecta particula: In homines beneuolentia. Debet enim εὐδοκία siue beneuolentia hæc de Deo exponi, ut eius fauorem gratuitum de notari intelligamus, quo is nos complectitur. Causa huius in Christo est. Quia enim æternus ille Dei filius mortali carne vestiri & huius vitæ miseriis subijci voluit, propter hunc ita nobis placatus est pater, vt iam nos quoq; indignos licet & nihil huius meritos, pro gratis & acceptis habeat. Et hoc angelorum dictum ipse interpretatur, quando vocem illam dulcissimæ consolationis plenissimam cantus iucunat: Hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Et eò respiciens Paulus dicebat, placuisse Deo, vt in Christo sibi reconciliarei cum qua in terra, tum quæ in cælis sunt. Procul ergo facessant, qui humanæ iustitiæ meritum extollendo Christi meritum euacuant, & ita pacem & consensum illum cœli & terræ saluberrimum turbant, cuius nobis ille vnicus est Mediator. Nituntur isti ferè patrum & Conciliorum decretis, & hodie multi dissensiones de fide nō aliter quàm Concilij vniuersalis authoritate componi posse arbitrantur. At si patres audire libet, eos audiamus, quorum fides spiritus sancti testimonio in scripturis probatur. Si Conciliorum tanta est apud nos authoritas, quin angelorum Concilio subscribimus, qui simul omnes collecti omnem redempti humani generis gloria vni Deo transcribunt, pacem inter Deum & nos per Christum factam esse docent, & totius negotij istius causam in gratuito Dei fauore monstrant, quo ille nos in Christo complexus est. Vt vero tandem dicendi finem faciamus, agnoscamus charissimi, hunc Dei amorem, qui filiū suum nobis Seruatorem destinauit, & eundem etiam hodie nobis per Euangelium suum quotidie offert. Hunc ergo amplectamur fide constanti, & simul officij nostri memores excubias agamus perpetuas, ne illius merito partam salutem nostra siue incuria siue socordia amittamus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the third part the particle added, "goodwill towards men," indicates the source and cause of this peace. For this goodwill [εὐδοκία] ought to be explained of God, so that we understand it to denote his free favour, by which he embraces us. The cause of this is in Christ. For since that eternal Son of God willed to be clothed in mortal flesh and to be subjected to the miseries of this life, on account of him the Father has been so reconciled to us that he now counts us, though unworthy and deserving nothing of this, as acceptable and beloved. And he himself interprets this saying of the angels, when he sings that voice, full of the sweetest consolation: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And looking to this, Paul said that it had pleased God to reconcile all things to himself in Christ, both those on earth and those in heaven. Let those therefore keep far away who, by extolling the merit of human righteousness, empty the merit of Christ, and so disturb that most wholesome peace and agreement of heaven and earth, of which he alone is the Mediator for us. Such men lean mostly on the decrees of the Fathers and of Councils, and today many think that disagreements about the faith can be settled in no other way than by the authority of a universal Council. But if we are willing to hear the Fathers, let us hear those whose faith is proved from the Scriptures by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. If the authority of Councils is so great among us, why do we not subscribe to the Council of the angels, who, all gathered together, ascribe all the glory of the redeemed human race to the one God alone, teach that peace has been made between God and us through Christ, and show the cause of the whole matter to lie in the free favour of God, by which he has embraced us in Christ. And so, that we may at last make an end of speaking, let us acknowledge, most beloved, this love of God, who has appointed his Son as our Saviour, and who even today offers him to us daily through his Gospel. Let us therefore embrace him with a steadfast faith, and at the same time, mindful of our duty, let us keep perpetual watch, lest through carelessness or sloth we lose the salvation won by his merit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XVIII.

units.la: Et factum est, vt discesserunt ab eis Angeli in cœlum, tum pastores illi dixerunt alij ad alios: Eamus sanè Bethlehem vsque, & videamus factum istud, quod Dominus notum fecit nobis. Venerunt igitur festinantes, & inuenerunt Mariam & Iosephum, & infantem iacentem in præsepi. Cum vidissent autem, diuulgauerunt id quod dictum fuerat ipsis de puerulo illo. Et omnes qui audierunt, mirati sunt ea, quæ ipsis dicta fuerant à pastoribus. Maria autem conseruabat omnia verba ista, conferens ea in corde suo. Et reuersi sunt pastores, glorificantes & laudantes Deum super omnibus quæ audierant & viderant, prout ipsis dictum fuerat.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, that the shepherds said one to another, "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us." And they came with haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger. And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child. And all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

units.la: Præclarum & assidua meditatione dignum est Iesu Christi dictum: Non omnis qui mihi dicit, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum cœlorum, sed qui facit voluntatem patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Nam etsi ille omnia ea in se plenissime cotineat, quæ nobis seruandis seruiunt, idem tamen non omnibus prodest, qui nomen eius atq; fidem in ipsum proficentur, nisi vita simul et moribus professioni suæ respondeant. Quia enim fides non temere concepta opinio siue persuasio est, sed certus firmusq; animi assensus, quo promissiones Dei apprehendimus, & Christo, qui illarum fundamentum atque complementum est, inferimur, fieri non potest, quin qui illa præditi sunt, Christi spiritu animati eundem vita & moribus referant, & per fidei obedientiam voluntati patris cœlestis se accommodent. Vnde rursus colligitur, eos à fide & Christi communione alienissimos esse, qui carnis & mundi illecebris abrepti, obedientiæ officiū negligunt. Non temere ergo spiritus sanctus in scripturis exempla omnis generis proponit, tam eorum qui inani & fucata fidei professione se palliant, & quorum mores nobis cauendi sunt, quàm eorum, qui Christum viua fide amplexi sunt, vt eorum vestigijs insistamus. Inter hæc cumprimis memorabile est, quod in pastoribus hisce proponitur. Vt enim hos præ alijs hominibus dignos iudicauit Deus, quibus salutifera filij sui æterni & vnigeniti incarnatio primis innotescet: ita eorundem exemplo omnes homines docere voluit, vt Dei verbum audire & in hoc se offerentem nobis Iesum Christum excipere atque amplecti debeant. Ideo hanc quoque huius historiæ partem Lucas diligenter describit. Nam primò colloquium exponit, quod post auditas angelorum voces inter se mutuo habuerunt. Deinde ut Christum quaesierint simul atq; inuenerint, narrat. Praeterea quid hoc inuento fecerint, & ut alij etiam homines tantae rei consideratione sint affecti. Postremo quanta cum gratulatione & gaudio pastores ad sua redierint. Et de his quidem singulis ex ordine dicemus, quantum temporis angustia permittet.
units.tr: The saying of Jesus Christ is excellent and worthy of constant meditation: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." For although he fully contains in himself all those things that serve for our salvation, yet he does not benefit everyone who professes his name and faith in him, unless their life and conduct correspond to their profession. For faith is not an opinion or persuasion rashly formed, but a certain and firm assent of the mind, by which we lay hold of the promises of God and are brought into Christ, who is their foundation and fulfilment. It cannot be that those who are endowed with it, animated by the Spirit of Christ, do not express the same in life and conduct, and by the obedience of faith accommodate themselves to the will of the heavenly Father. Hence it follows again that those are most alien from faith and from communion with Christ who, carried away by the allurements of the flesh and the world, neglect the duty of obedience. It is therefore not without reason that the Holy Spirit sets before us in the Scriptures examples of every kind: both of those who cloak themselves in an empty and feigned profession of faith, and whose conduct we must beware of, and of those who have embraced Christ with a living faith, that we may follow in their footsteps. Among these, what is set forth in these shepherds is especially memorable. For just as God judged these men worthy above other men to be the first to learn of the saving incarnation of his eternal and only-begotten Son, so by their example he wished to teach all men that they ought to hear the Word of God and receive and embrace Jesus Christ, who offers himself to us in it. Therefore Luke also describes this part of the story diligently. For first he sets out the conversation which they held among themselves after hearing the voices of the angels. Then he relates how they sought Christ as soon as they had heard, and found him. Besides, what they did after this discovery, and how other men too were moved by the consideration of so great a matter. Lastly, with what great rejoicing and joy the shepherds returned to their homes. Of these things, each in order, we shall speak as far as the shortness of time permits.

units.la: Primam huius narrationis partem hisce verbis Lucas describit: Et factum est, ut discesserunt ab eis Angeli in caelum, tum pastores illi dixerunt alij ad alios: Eamus sane Bethlehem usq; & videamus factum istud, quod Dominus notum fecit nobis. Adumbrantur hoc exemplo mores piorum, qui Euangelium digne audiunt, quid id eos facere deceat, quibus illud praedicatur; quapropter singula diligentius excuti merentur.
units.tr: Luke describes the first part of this narrative in these words: "And it came to pass, when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, that the shepherds said one to another, 'Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us.'" In this example are foreshadowed the manners of the godly, who hear the Gospel worthily, and what it becomes those to do to whom it is preached. For this reason each point deserves to be examined more carefully.

units.la: Hic autem ante omnia occurrit, quod quam primum Angeli ab ipsis discesserunt in caelum (aeternas nimirum beatae immortalitatis sedes) ipsi de negotio eis per illos denuntiato colloqui incipiunt, & serio quidem, non ofcitanter aut iocose, ut in re non magni momenti fieri solet. Ergo nō cum Angelis simul verba quoque eorum ipsis euanuerunt; sed ut illos non inane spectrum putarunt, ita Dei verbum esse agnouerunt, quod ex illis audiuerant. Nam nisi huic ex animo credidissent, multa erant, quibus apparitionem istam in dubium vocare aut eludere potuissent. Ut enim noctis tenebrae ad omne praestigiarum genus cumprimis commodae sunt, & ijs fere ad dolos suos abutuntur, qui rerum ignaris imponere gaudent; ita vix credibile videbatur, rem tanti momenti pauperculis pastoribus primis denuntiari, quos nulla vel publica vel privata authoritas commendabat. Metuendum item erat, ne seipsos omnium ludibrio exponerent, si quid huius effutirent, quod nullis alijs testibus poterat probari. Imo periculosum videri poterat de Messia verba facere, cum Herodes iampridem Dauidis familiam persecutus esset, quod illum ex hac nasciturum audiuisset. Et fere pro seditiosis habebantur, qui de illo liberius differebant. At non mouentur eiusmodi argumentis isti, quorum animos certus fidei assensus afficiebat. Est hoc in primis necessarium: quia nisi credamus Dei verbum esse quod praedicatur, neq; illud vero sensu percipere, neq; serio salutis studio accendi poterimus. Ideo Galatas & Thessalonicenses suos hoc potissimum nomine Paulus commendat, quod ipsum ut angelum Dei exceperint, quodq; sermonem, quem ipse praedicabat, non pro hominum sermone, sed pro Dei sermone (qui & vere erat) agnouerint. Debet enim ad omnes legitimos Euangelij praecones extendi, quod de Apostolis Christus dicit: Qui vos audit, me audit. Item qui recipit eum, quem ego misero, me recipit. Luc. 10. Ioan. 13.
units.tr: Here, first of all, we notice that as soon as the angels had departed from them into heaven (the eternal seat, to be sure, of blessed immortality), the shepherds began to talk with one another about the matter announced to them through those angels, and that seriously, not carelessly or jokingly, as is usual in a matter of no great importance. Therefore the words of the angels did not vanish from them together with the angels themselves; but just as they did not think them an empty phantom, so they recognised that what they had heard from them was the Word of God. For unless they had believed this from the heart, there were many things by which they could have called that appearance into doubt or mocked it.
