Non autē hoc temere fieri putemus, quòd ab his Simeone istum Spiritus sanctus commendat, non autem vllam facit eorum mentionem, quæ mundus hic admirari & commendatione in primis digna putare solet: qualia sunt generis splendor imaginarius, publici honores, trium phi, opes & sexcenta alia, in quibus homines carnis iudicio & desiderijs dediti omnē felicitatem collocat. Ita vero docet, quæ vera laus sit, et vnde nominis aut gloriæ verę perpetuitas sperari debeat. Friuola & caduca sunt, quæcunq; mundus hic suspicit. Omnis caro fœnum (clamat propheta) & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Et vt Apostolus ait, transit mundus hic & quicquid in illo desiderabile est. Æternum autem manent iustitia atq; religio, & proinde nomen quoq; æternum suis parant cultoribus. Intercidunt quidem inter homines interdum hominũ iustorum atq; piorum nomina, sed eadem (vt Christus ait) in cœlis ascripta sunt, & olim in Christi aduentu aperientur libri, vt cum eodem promissa beatitudinis æternæ præmia recipiant. At obseruatu in primis dignum est, quòd iustitiam cum religione coniungit Lucas: eo enim docet nos Spiritus sanctus, virtutes istas sic inter se connexas esse, vt neutra illarum absq; altera consistere possit. Qui enim iustitiam colunt, Deum non possunt negligere, cui timorem & obedientiam deberi, communi sensu docemur. Similiter qui religionis sensu serio tanguntur, ijdem in Deo omnes homines amore digno complectuntur, neq; propter res huius seculi, quas breui perituras esse norunt, iura publica & concordia turbant, quibus Deus quàm maximè delectatur. Arguit hoc eos, qui ciuili quadam iustitia sese venditant, religionem vero prorsus negligunt, imò eius curam nihil ad se pertinere putant. Merentur isti inter homines iustitiæ laudem, sed si rem ipsam spectemus, illos non iustitiæ cultores esse patebit, sed hoc agere, vt commodius viuant, quando constat neq; pacem nobis consistere posse cum quoquam, nisi iudiciorum & legum publicarum vsus obseruetur. Nec minus hypocritarum sanctimonia hic damnatur, qui religionis quidem studium ardentissimum simulant, interim vero sibi soli s viuunt, & humanarum traditionum regulis astricti, ne parentibus quidem propriis debita officia præstant. Quid autem de illis dicemus, qui turpissimis cupiditatibus abrepti in manifesta scelera effrenes ruunt, & vitam viuunt à Christiana professione alienissimam? Et tales hodie vulgò passim conspiciuntur.
units.tr: Indeed, the evangelist fittingly begins the narrative with a description of the person, prefaced by the demonstrative particle "behold", by which he stirs everyone to a more careful consideration of the whole matter. "Behold," he says, "there was in Jerusalem a man named Simeon, and this man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him." He says Simeon lived in Jerusalem. That city, although on account of its ancient religion and as the seat of divine worship it was most famous, could at that time be counted a sink of crimes and a school of heresies. Herod reigned there, and the Pharisees held sway over sacred things; they had long since corrupted both the doctrine and the worship of God by human traditions devised for hypocrisy and gain. Nothing therefore could prevent the Holy Spirit from breathing where he wills, and exerting his power there too, where he seems shut in by impregnable bars. But let us see what sort of man Simeon was. First, he says he was just and devout, that is, one who feared God and was zealous for divine worship. In these two epithets he comprehends whatever is necessary for rightly ordering life. For they answer to the two tables of the Decalogue: religion contains the knowledge of the true God, fear, worship and obedience, while by the word justice are denoted all the duties we owe to our neighbour. We should not think it is by chance that the Holy Spirit commends Simeon for these things, and makes no mention of those things which this world is wont to admire and to think especially worthy of commendation. Such things are the imaginary splendour of birth, public honours, triumphs, riches, and six hundred other things in which men given over to the judgement and desires of the flesh place all their happiness. Thus he teaches what true praise is, and whence the permanence of a name or of true glory ought to be hoped for. Frivolous and fleeting are all the things this world looks up to. "All flesh is grass," cries the prophet, "and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field." And as the Apostle says, this world passes away, and whatever in it is desirable. But justice and religion remain forever, and therefore they also secure an eternal name for their worshippers. The names of just and pious men indeed sometimes perish among men, but these same names (as Christ says) are written in heaven, and at the coming of Christ the books will be opened, so that with him they may receive the promised rewards of eternal blessedness. But it is especially worthy of note that Luke joins justice with religion. By this the Holy Spirit teaches us that these virtues are so connected that neither can exist without the other. Those who cultivate justice cannot neglect God, to whom fear and obedience are owed, as common sense teaches us. Likewise, those who are seriously touched by a sense of religion embrace all men in God with a worthy love. They do not, for the sake of the things of this age, which they know will soon perish, disturb public laws and concord, in which God takes the greatest delight. This condemns those who make a show of a certain civil justice but utterly neglect religion, and even think that its care does not pertain to them. Such men deserve praise for justice among men. But if we look at the thing itself, it will be plain that they are not cultivators of justice; they are working to live more comfortably, since peace cannot exist with anyone unless the practice of judgements and public laws is observed. Nor is the sanctimony of hypocrites spared here. They feign the most ardent zeal for religion, yet live for themselves alone, and, bound by the rules of human traditions, do not even render due duties to their own parents. But what shall we say of those who, carried off by the most shameful desires, rush headlong into open crimes and live a life most alien to the Christian profession? Such people are commonly seen everywhere today.

units.la: Cæterùm nequis in Simeone vulgarem solummodo iustitiam & religionem fuisse putaret, verum omnis pietatis fundamentum indicat Lucas, quando illum consolationem Israelis expectauisse ait. Ita vero dicitur Christus, vel potius in illo nobis exhibitum redemptionis nostræ beneficium, cuius consideratione pij omnes sese inter grauissimas tentationes consolabantur. Ex illo autem appareret, Simeonem fide præditum fuisse, qua promissiones & prophetarum vaticinia de Christo amplexus est. Expectandi autem verbo fidei illius constantia & fortitudo exprimitur, quam non vulgarem fuisse fatebimur, si cogitemus, quæ tunc tempora quisq; rerum inter Iudæos statu fuerit, eiusmodi nimirum, vt propter extrema reipub. simul & Ecclesiæ corruptionem vniuersa salutis spes extincta esse videretur. Et Simeonis verba, quæ mox audiemus, non obscurè testantur expectationem illam suam satis diuturnam & longam fuisse, eò quòd promissionem suam Deus diutius extraheret: nimirum vsque ad punctum temporis illius præfiniti, quo Christus in mundum venire debebat. Variè ergo & graviter tentata fuit proculdubio Simeonis fides, cùm res quotidie in peius ferri, se autem Simeonis descriptio. Iustus & religiosus. Isa. 40. 1. Ioan. 1. Luc. 10. Expectavit consolationem Israelis. iam multa senecta grauem ad vitæ suæ finem appropinquare videret. At hoc proprium illud fidei exercitium est, quo illa Deo maximè probatur. In hoc certè Abrahami fidem eluxisse scribit Apostolus, quòd contra spem in spe crediderit, cum Deus quidem promissa sua differret, multa autem in seipso simul & vxore Sara ille inueniret quotidie, quæ fidem labefactare poterant. Similis fuit in Dauide fidei constantia, quando post acceptam regni promissionem patriæ finibus eiectus, interim fœdissimam Philistinorum gentem sedes & asylum quærere cogitur, neq; tamen de Dei veritate dubitauit, sicuti eius Psalmi testantur. Idem de reliquis patribus dici potest, quoad Christum, in quo illos spem omnem salutis collocauisse constat, quam tunc quoque inconcussam seruarunt, quando sibi per mortem hinc migrandum esse videbant, priusquam ille exhiberetur. Omnium enim illorum eadem fuit sententia, quam Dauid his verbis complectitur: Propono mihi Dominum perpetuo: à dextris enim mihi est, ne nutem. Propterea gaudebit cor meum, & exultabit lingua mea, quin & caro mea in tuto quiescit, &c. Debent hoc ipsum singuli sibi ipsis accommodare. Eadem enim expectationis & spei constantia etiam hodie opus est, quando inter nouissimorum temporum periculosos motus, in postremum illum Iesu Christi aduentum respicimus, qui plenam redemptionem nobis afferet, & ideo dies restitutionis omnium dicitur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone should think that Simeon had merely ordinary justice and religion, Luke points out the foundation of all piety when he says that Simeon was waiting for the consolation of Israel. That is said of Christ, or rather of the benefit of our redemption, which is exhibited to us in him. By contemplating this, all the godly comforted themselves amid the gravest temptations. From this it appears that Simeon was endowed with faith, by which he embraced the promises and the prophecies of the prophets concerning Christ. The steadfastness and fortitude of that faith is expressed by the word "waiting." We shall confess that it was no ordinary faith if we consider what state the Jews were in at that time: so corrupt were the commonwealth and the Church that every hope of salvation seemed to have been extinguished. Simeon's own words, which we shall hear shortly, clearly testify that his waiting was rather long, because God delayed his promise for a long time, namely until the appointed moment at which Christ was to come into the world. Simeon's faith was therefore without doubt tried in various and grievous ways, since things grew worse every day, and he saw himself, now old, drawing near the grave end of his life. But this is the peculiar exercise of faith, by which it is most approved before God. The Apostle writes that the faith of Abraham shone forth in this, that against hope he believed in hope. God indeed deferred his promises, while Abraham found daily in himself and in his wife Sarah many things that could weaken his faith. Similar was the steadfastness of faith in David. After receiving the promise of the kingdom, he was driven out of his country and forced to seek a seat and refuge among the most foul Philistine nation, yet he did not doubt the truth of God, as his Psalms testify. The same can be said of the other fathers with regard to Christ, in whom it is certain they placed all their hope of salvation. They kept this hope unshaken even when they saw that they must depart hence by death before Christ was revealed. For all of them held the one opinion that David expresses in these words: "I have set the Lord always before me: for he is at my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart is glad, and my tongue rejoices; my flesh also rests in hope..." Each of us should apply this to himself. For the same steadfastness of expectation and hope is needed today, when, amid the dangerous upheavals of the last times, we look toward that final coming of Jesus Christ, who will bring us full redemption, and for this reason is called the day of the restitution of all things.

units.la: De Simeone autem nostro tertium quoq; dicit Lucas: Et spiritus sanctus erat super eum. Non loquitur de spiritu adoptionis, quem credentes omnes communem habent, sed de dono spiritus peculiari, prophetia nimirum; & ideo additur expositionis loco: Fuerat, ipsi diuinitus nuntiatum à Spiritu sancto, ipsum non visurum mortem, priusquam vidisset Christum illum Domini, id est, vnctum illum, quem Deus æterno suo decreto Ecclesiæ suæ sacerdotem & regem dedit. Fuit hoc singulare præmium, quo Simeonis fidem Deus remunerare dignatus erat, & quod vniuersa huius seculi bona longè superat. Constat enim videndi Christi desiderio omnes patres supra modum accensos fuisse. Nam etsi de eius aduentu minimè dubitarent, & eius meritum ad se pertinere firmiter crederent, tamen fidei huius ardore abrepti nihil perinde in votis habebant, quàm iam exhibitum videre eum, in quo ipsis spes omnis erat posita. Ideo Christus discipulis dicebat: Vestri beati sunt oculi, quia cernunt: & aures vestræ, quia audiunt. Amen enim dico vobis, quòd multi Prophetæ & iusti desiderauerunt videre quæ videtis, & non viderunt: & audire quæ auditis, & non audierunt. Quo loco non negat quidem beatos fuisse patres, sed quoad huius vitæ conditionem Apostolos illis præfert, qui coram videbant & contrectabant salutis authorem, quem illi eminus fidei oculis solum intuebantur. Fuit autem illo tempore eò maior & ardentior piorum lætitia in Christi aduentu, quod eum rebus iam omnino desperatis salutem optatam afferre viderent. Quare non dubium est, Simeonem istud Spiritus sancti oraculum in summa suæ felicitatis parte habuisse, & ex eo omnem haussisse consolationem, qua inter horribiles illius seculi motus & totius Orientis mutationes seipsum sustentauit. Vt vero nos hodie Christum oculis corporeis videamus minimè opus est, quando illum iampridem exhibitum nobis salutem plenam acquisiuisse scimus. Et ad nos pertinet quod Thomæ Christus dixit: Quia vidisti me Thoma, credidisti: Beati qui non viderunt, et crediderunt. Interim meminerimus adumbrari nobis hoc loco fidei et veræ pietatis præmiū, quo omnes fruentur, qui constanter credunt. Reuelatur illis Christus indies magis atq; magis, qui in huius vitæ palæstra laborantes suo spiritu regit atq; confirmat. Et cùm inter huius seculi pericula totis animis in extremum illius aduentum intenti sint, ipse sua nequaquam fallentur. Nam etsi diem suum prius obeant, olim tamen exmortuis restituti videbunt illum sicuti est, & similes ei erunt, vt æternum cum illo viuant & regnent. Fuit hæc spes sanctorum vnica, quam nos quoq; fide constanti fouere & retinere decet.
units.tr: Of our Simeon, Luke also says a third thing: "And the Holy Spirit was upon him." He does not mean the Spirit of adoption, which all believers share in common, but a special gift of the Spirit, namely prophecy. That is why an explanation is added: it had been divinely revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ, that is, the anointed one whom God, by his eternal decree, gave to his Church as priest and king. This was a singular reward, by which God deigned to repay Simeon's faith, and it far surpasses all the goods of this age. It is well known that all the fathers were burning with an excessive desire to see Christ. For although they never doubted his coming and firmly believed that his merit belonged to them, yet, carried away by the fire of this faith, they had nothing so much in their prayers as to see with their own eyes him in whom all their hope was placed. So Christ said to the disciples: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. For truly I say to you, that many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." In this place he does not deny that the fathers were blessed, but as to the condition of this life he places the apostles above them, since they saw and handled before their eyes the author of salvation, whom the fathers looked upon only from afar with the eyes of faith. Moreover, the joy of the godly at Christ's coming was then all the greater and more ardent, because they saw that he brought the desired salvation to a state of affairs now utterly hopeless. Hence there is no doubt that Simeon held this oracle of the Holy Spirit as the chief part of his happiness, and drew from it all the consolation by which he sustained himself amid the terrible upheavals of that age and the changes throughout the whole East. As for us today, there is no need for us to see Christ with bodily eyes, since we know that he, having been revealed to us long ago, has obtained full salvation. And what Christ said to Thomas applies to us: "Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Meanwhile let us remember that in this passage is foreshadowed for us the reward of faith and true godliness, which all enjoy who believe steadfastly. Christ is revealed to them more and more each day, since he, who rules and strengthens by his Spirit those who labour in the arena of this life, does not fail his own. And although they are intent with their whole minds, amid the dangers of this age, upon his final coming, they will in no way be deceived. For even if they die before their day, yet at length, raised up from the dead, they will see him as he is, and will be like him, so that they may live and reign with him for ever. This was the sole hope of the saints, and we too ought to cherish and hold it with steadfast faith.

units.la: Porrò præmissa Simeonis descriptione occasionem subijcit Lucas, qua ille voti compos factus, Christum non solum vidit, verum etiam vlnis complexus est. Nam duce spiritu eum in templū venisse dicit eo ipso temporis momento, quo Ioseph & Maria puerulum introducebant, vt eum Domino sisterent, eaq; omnia facerent, quæ secundum ritum in Lege præscriptum fieri oportebat. Poterat hoc hominibus prophanis fortuitū videri: sed Deus est, qui non res modò hominū generali quadam prouidentia inspicit, sed singulas quoq; illorū actiones ad finem ab ipso præfixū destinat, & ideo temporum etiā momenta regit. Exempla huius prouidentiæ passim in scripturis habentur. Sic Abrahami famulus ea ipsa hora ad vrbem Nahor venit, qua puellæ aquatum exire solebant, & eodem temporis puncto Rebecca illuc progreditur, ut ea occasione Isaaco desponsetur. Ita Saulem ea hora ad Samuelem deduxit Dei providentia, qua illum hic oraculo prius de eius adventu admonitus expectabat. Similiter Davidem tunc in castra venire oportebat, quando Goliathi consptetu & impia atq; immani ad pugnā provocatione omnes territi trepidabant, ut ipse cum illo congrediendi occasio nem invenires. Sed quid exempla vetera commemorare opus est, cum huius generis multa quotidie fiant, & nunquam non nobis praeter nostram expectationem rerum agendarum occasiones obijciantur? In his nos Dei providentiam agnoscere decet, qui ut omnia videt & novit, sic manum quoque rebus admouet, ne temere ferantur, sed finem suum attingant. In nobis quidem & actionibus nostris contingentia quaedam esse videtur, at si Deum spectes, nihil illic fortuitum, nihil contingens dici potest, ubi certo consilio omnia reguntur.
units.tr: Next, after describing Simeon, Luke supplies the occasion by which, having obtained his desire, he not only saw Christ but also embraced him in his arms. For he says that, led by the Spirit, Simeon came into the temple at the very moment when Joseph and Mary were bringing in the little child to present him to the Lord, and to do for him all those things that, according to the rite prescribed in the Law, had to be done. This might seem to profane men to have happened by chance. But it is God who regards not only the affairs of men under a general providence, but also directs each of their actions to the end set by himself, and therefore governs even the moments of time. Examples of this providence are found everywhere in Scripture. Thus Abraham's servant came to the city of Nahor at the very hour when the maidens were accustomed to go out to draw water, and at that same moment Rebekah came forth there, so that on that occasion she might be betrothed to Isaac. So too the providence of God led Saul to Samuel at the hour when Samuel, having been warned beforehand by an oracle about his coming, was waiting for him. Likewise David had to come into the camp just when all were terrified and trembling at the sight of Goliath and his impious and monstrous challenge to battle, so that he might find an opportunity to engage with him. But why is it necessary to recall ancient examples, when many things of this kind happen every day, and opportunities for doing things are always presented to us beyond our expectation? In these things we ought to acknowledge the providence of God, who, as he sees and knows all things, so also applies his hand to events, so that they are not carried along at random but reach their end. In us and in our actions some things may seem to be contingent; but if you look to God, nothing can be called accidental or contingent there, where all things are governed by a certain counsel.

units.la: Docentur autem Simeonis exemplo senes, quae ipsorum studia & qui mores esse debeant. Spiritum ducem ille sequitur. Eidem ergo ipsi quoque sese regendos & gubernandos praebeant, neque carnis desideriis indulgeant, ut spiritus libidinis, intemperantiae, leuitatis & petulantiae sequantur. Mel minerint satis nimium, satis datum esse iuuenilibus annis, & cum Sophocle sibi ipsis gratulentur, quod heris istis indomitis & saeuissimis tandem liberati sint. Nam ut Cicero aiebat, luxuria cum omni aetati turpis, tum senectuti foedissima est. Duplex enim inde malum est, quod & ipsa senectus dedecus concipit, & facit adolescentum impudentiorem intemperantiam. Quantum vero scelus est, canitiem, quam senii decus scriptura vocat, publicis ludibrijs exponere, dum intempestivae lasciviae indulgemus? Multum vero proderit ad seruandam dignitatem, si in templis & sacris coetibus sint frequentes. Illic enim Christus inuenitur, qui & verbo suos docet, & spiritu suo medius illis inter est, qui in eius nomine congregantur. At quia hodie in utroq; plurimum peccatur, & in senibus fere intemperantia maxime regnat, non mirum est & Christi cognitionem rariorem esse, & omnem morum disciplinam passim intercidere.
units.tr: Moreover, by the example of Simeon, old men are taught what their pursuits and manners ought to be. He followed the Spirit as his guide. Let them therefore also yield themselves to be ruled and guided by the same Spirit, and not indulge the desires of the flesh, so as to follow the spirit of lust, intemperance, levity and wantonness. Let them remember that enough, indeed more than enough, has been given to youthful years, and let them congratulate themselves with Sophocles that they have at last been freed from those untamed and most savage masters. For, as Cicero said, luxury is disgraceful at every age, but most foul in old age. For there is a double evil in this: old age itself incurs disgrace, and it makes the intemperance of the young more shameless. And how great a crime it is, while we indulge in untimely wantonness, to expose grey hair, which Scripture calls the glory of old age, to public mockery! Indeed, it will greatly help to preserve dignity if they are frequent in the temples and sacred assemblies. For there Christ is found, who teaches his own by his word, and by his Spirit is present in the midst of those who are gathered in his name. But since today men sin very much in both respects, and intemperance reigns above all among the old, it is no wonder that the knowledge of Christ is rare and that all discipline of morals everywhere falls into decay.

units.la: Sequitur quid fecerit Simeon, ubi puerulum vidit, & spiritus suggestione hunc agnouit esse Christum, quem tanto desiderio lucusque expectauerat. Primo in vlnas accepit et pectori applicuit, quod animi gestientis & iam optime contenti argumentum est euidentissimum. Deinde benedixit Deo, id est gratias egit pro tanto beneficio. Ita solent sancti, cum sciant se nihil praeterea habere, quod Deo rependant, qui nullius est indigus, neque nostro seruitio opus habet. Postremo ita abripitur salutis iam praesentis consideratione, ut se totum Deo offerat, seq; ad moriendum omnino paratum & voluntarium esse protestetur. Describit ista diligenter Lucas, quia exemplo hoc docemur, quo animo ipsi quoque Christum in Euangelio se nobis offerentem excipere & complecti debeamus. Sed ne diutius meis verbis vos detineam fratres, praestat ipsum Simeonem loquentem audire, ex cuius verbis intelligemus, eum non solum corporeis oculis Christum vidisse, sed eundem fide vera complexum esse, quae sub vili & contemptibili vulgaris & pauperculi infantis specie aeternum Dei filium & promissum humani generis Seruatorem delitescere intellexit.
units.tr: There follows what Simeon did when he saw the little child, and by the prompting of the Spirit recognised that this was Christ, whom he had awaited so long with such desire. First he took him into his arms and pressed him to his breast, which is the most evident sign of a mind that is exulting and already wholly content. Then he blessed God, that is, he gave thanks for so great a benefit. So the saints are accustomed to do, since they know that they have nothing else to repay God with, who lacks nothing and has no need of our service. Finally, he was so carried away by the thought of the salvation now present that he offered himself wholly to God and declared that he was entirely ready and willing to die. Luke describes these things carefully, because by this example we are taught with what disposition we ourselves too ought to receive and embrace Christ when he offers himself to us in the Gospel. But, brethren, lest I detain you longer with my words, it is better to hear Simeon himself speaking, from whose words we shall understand that he saw Christ not only with bodily eyes, but also embraced him with true faith, understanding that beneath the lowly and contemptible appearance of a common and poor infant lay hidden the eternal Son of God and the promised Saviour of mankind.

units.la: Primum exordio abrupto vtitur, sicuti solent, quibus aliquid inspseratum vel etiam diu optatum subito offertur. Nunc dimittis (inquit) seruum tuum Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace, &c. Quasi dicat: Dudum quidem optani, ut ex hoc mortali corporis ergastulo liberatus ad patres meos colligerer. At tu me eo vsq; superstitem fore voluisti, donec diu expectatus vindex & redemptor in mundum veniret: cuius videndi desiderio & spe certa confirmatus, patienter tuli et vici, quae cunque hoc afflictissimo seculo ferenda fuerunt. Et quanquam mora haec mihi longa & molesta visa sit, credidi tamen omnino euenturum quod mihi pollicitus fueras. Neque me spes ista fefellit. Iam nunc enim vident oculi mei, quem diu desiderauerunt videre, neque oculis solum illum video, sed vl-nis meis hoc meum desiderium completor. Quid ergo reliquum est mi Deus, quam ut me ex isto car cere liberes, & huius mortalis vitae faturum ad te recipias; ut salute in hoc Christo tuo promissa fruar? Haec (inquam) & quaecunque alia in istam sententiam dici possunt, paucis hisce verbis pius hic Senex comprehendit. Nobis autem hic inter alia hoc maxime considerandum est, quod eius persona ille suscipit, qui carcere deterrimo diu detentus tandem toto animo gestit, quando exeundi copiam sibi factam videt. Cur enim non totus exultaret, & corporis huius infelix onus reijcere cuperet, qui illum iam mundo exhibitum videbat, cuius merito patefieri & aperiri oportebat viam san
units.tr: He begins with an abrupt exordium, as people do when something unexpected, or even long desired, is suddenly offered to them. "Now you let your servant depart, Lord, according to your word, in peace," and so on. As if he were saying: "I had long desired to be freed from this mortal prison of the body and gathered to my fathers. But you willed that I should survive until the Deliverer and Redeemer, so long awaited, came into the world. Confirmed by the desire to see him and by sure hope, I have patiently borne and overcome whatever had to be endured in this most afflicted age. And although this delay has seemed to me long and tedious, I nevertheless believed that what you had promised me would certainly come to pass. Nor has that hope deceived me. For now my eyes see him whom they have long desired to see, and I see him not only with my eyes, but my desire is fulfilled in my arms. What, then, remains, my God, but that you should free me from this prison and receive me, weary of this mortal life, to yourself, so that I may enjoy the salvation promised in this your Christ?" These things, I say, and whatever else can be said to this effect, this pious old man comprehends in these few words. But for us, among other things, the chief consideration here is that the person he assumes is one who, having been long detained in the most wretched prison, at last exults with his whole mind when he sees the way of exit opened to him. For why should he not exult entirely, and long to cast off the unhappy burden of this body, who saw already revealed to the world him through whose merit the way of the saints ought to be opened and laid bare, that is, the way by which one comes to the heavens and to the full possession of eternal life? Therefore the Holy Spirit, by this example, teaches whence that joyful and holy readiness to die arises, which despises the terrors of death and overcomes all fear of it. It arises, of course, from faith, which...

units.la: [?]lorum,id est eam viam, qua ad cœlos et æternæ vitæ plenam possessionem venitur? Admonet igitur hoc exemplo Spiritus sanctus, unde oriatur lœta illa & sancta moriendi alacritas, quæ mortis terrores spernit & omnem eius metum superat. Ex fide nimirum, quæ Christum nobis præsentem sistit, vt in illo nobis gestire atque exultare liceat. Qui enim hac illuminati sunt, ij se in terris peregrinos, patriam verò & ciuitatem suam in cœlis esse sciunt. Itaque patienter quidem ferunt peregrinationis suæ molestias, quoad Domino visum fuerit. Quando autem hic eos euocat, ad migrandum parati sunt, imò (vt Paulus dicebat) cupiunt dissolui, vt Christo propius coniungantur, cuius coheredes se fore per fidem intelligunt. Etenim si dimitti cupiuit Simeon, quod Christum infantulum adhuc in vlnis haberet, quanto maior in nobis esse debet moriendi alacritas, qui illù peccati, mortis & diaboli iampridem victorem, nunc in cœlis ad patris dexteram considere & omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra accepisse credimus? Qui hoc verè credunt, ijs neque propria mors acerba esse potest, neque de suis quos relinquunt nimiùm sunt anxij. Sciunt enim se quidem ex morte ad vitam transire, suos autem sub Christi tutela agere, qui solus illis seruandis sufficit. Vides igitur, quid de illis iudicari debeat, qui mortem ita horrent, vt eius metu vel fidem abnegent, vel officium fraternæ charitatis prætermittant? Licet quidem illis, quoad homines, Christi cognitione gloriari, at si hanc animus suus concepissent, nunquam sese tam turpes darent in eo, quod omnibus necessariò subeundum est. Interim non minus cauere nos decet, ne præcipiti nimiùm vitæ æternæ desiderio abrepti, dimittere vt limus, priusquam nos Deus vocat. Æquum enim est, vt stationem nostram fortiter teneamus, quoad Domino visum fuerit, & nostra opera ipsi inter homines vtilis esse potest. Simeon certè secundum Domini verbum dimitti vult, vnde patet hoc vnicam voti ipsius regulam fuisse. Et Paulus ad Philippenses ex vinculis scribens ait: Coarctor vtrinque, cupiens migrare et esse cum Christo (nam id longè optimum est) sed permanere in carne, magis necessarium est propter vos. Et hoc confisus nouì quòd mansurus sim, & vnà permansurus cum vobis omnibus ad vestrum profectum & gaudium fidei. Hunc animum nos quoque concipere decet, & ad omnem euentum verè parati erimus.
units.tr: [?]lorum, that is, the way by which one comes to the heavens and to the full possession of eternal life? The Holy Spirit therefore admonishes us by this example whence that joyful and holy eagerness for dying arises, which despises the terrors of death and overcomes all fear of it. It arises, of course, from faith, which sets Christ before us as present, so that we may rejoice and exult in him. For those who have been enlightened by this know that they are strangers on earth, but that their fatherland and citizenship are in heaven. Therefore they bear patiently the troubles of their pilgrimage, for as long as it seems good to the Lord. When he calls them hence, however, they are ready to depart; indeed (as Paul said) they desire to be dissolved, so as to be joined more closely to Christ, whose co-heirs they understand themselves to be through faith. For if Simeon desired to be released because he still held the infant Christ in his arms, how much greater should our eagerness for dying be, since we believe that he, long since the conqueror of sin, death and the devil, now sits in heaven at the Father's right hand and has received all power in heaven and on earth? Those who truly believe this can find their own death no bitter thing, nor are they excessively anxious about those whom they leave behind. For they know that they pass from death to life, while their loved ones are kept under Christ's protection, who alone is sufficient to keep them. Do you see, then, how we ought to judge those who so shudder at death that through fear of it they either deny the faith or neglect the duty of brotherly love? They may indeed glory, as far as men go, in their knowledge of Christ; but had their minds truly grasped it, they would never make themselves so base in regard to that which must necessarily be undergone by all. Meanwhile we ought to take no less care that, carried away by an overly hasty desire for eternal life, we do not, like a clod, let go before God calls us. For it is right that we hold our post bravely, for as long as it seems good to the Lord, and our labour can be useful to others among men. Simeon indeed wishes to be dismissed according to the Lord's word, whence it is plain that this was the sole rule of his desire. And Paul, writing to the Philippians from his chains, says: I am hard pressed on both sides, desiring to depart and to be with Christ (for that is far the best); but to remain in the flesh is more necessary on account of you. And trusting in this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and joy in the faith. Let us also conceive this mind, and we shall be truly ready for every outcome.

units.la: Sed ad Simeonem redeamus, qui tanti gaudij & alacritatis causam clarius exprimit, & ea occasione Christum magnificè prædicat. Dicit enim: Quia viderunt oculi mei Salutem tuam, quam parasti in conspectu omnium populorum, lumen ad reuelationem gentium, & gloriam populi tui Israelis. Primò Christum vocat Salutem Dei. In Græco σωτήριον habetur, quæ vox plus quiddam significat, ipsam nimirum salutis materiam siue authorem, vel serinium potius, in quo salus omnis continetur. Videtur autem ad Isaiæ vaticinium alludere, qui olim dixerat: Nudauit Dominus brachium suum sanctum in oculis omnium gentium, & videbunt omnes fines terræ salutem Dei nostri. Dicitur autem Salus Dei, non quod is salutem aliunde accipiat, sed quòd huius decreto Christus nobis Seruator sit factus. Ideo per expositionem additur. Quam parasti in conspectu omnium populorum. Quibus verbis tria comprehendit cognitu in primis necessaria: Nimirum, quòd in Christo salus certa et omnibus numeris absoluta habeatur. Deinde quòd ad hanc nobis præstandam æterno Dei decreto destinatus sit. Quod ipsum Apostoli quoque docent, quando illum ante iacta mundi fundamenta præordinatum, nosque in illo priusquam hic mundus conderetur, electos esse scribunt. Quod firmiter tenendum est, quia eo potissimùm salutis nostræ certitudo asseritur: quando constat Dei decretis neminem obstare posse, quo minus finem suum attingant. Tertiò Christum hunc communem & generalem omnium populorum Seruatorem esse ostendit, in quo vno seruari oporteat cuiuscunque loci & ordinis homines, qui perire nolunt. Confutantur igitur hoc loco, qui vnumquemque in suis superstitionibus & cultu suo arbitrario seruari contendunt. Pugnant hi aduersus æternum Dei consilium, & eundem stultitiæ & iniustitiæ insimulant, qui salutis humanæ rationem tam difficilem & grauem in filij sui dira morte proponat, cùm quoduis hominis commentum nobis ad illam consequendam sufficere possit. Est ergo illorum impietas maior, quàm vt ferri debeat, sicuti alias prolixè demonstrauimus.
units.tr: But let us return to Simeon, who sets out more clearly the cause of such great joy and alacrity, and on that occasion proclaims Christ magnificently. For he says: Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel. First, he calls Christ the Salvation of God. In the Greek it is [σωτήριον], a word which signifies something more, namely the very matter or author of salvation, or rather the seed in which all salvation is contained. He seems, moreover, to allude to the prophecy of Isaiah, who once said: The Lord has bared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. But he is called the Salvation of God not because he receives salvation from elsewhere, but because by this decree Christ was made our Saviour. Therefore the explanation is added: which you have prepared before the face of all peoples. In these words he comprehends three things especially necessary to know: namely, that in Christ salvation is certain and complete in every respect. Next, that he was appointed by the eternal decree of God to bring this salvation to us. The apostles themselves also teach this, when they write that he was foreordained before the foundation of the world, and that we were chosen in him before this world was founded. This must be held firmly, because by it the certainty of our salvation is chiefly asserted: since it is agreed that no one can hinder the decrees of God from attaining their end. Thirdly, he shows that Christ is the common and general Saviour of all peoples, in whom alone men of every place and rank who do not wish to perish ought to be saved. Therefore those are refuted here who contend that each person is saved in his own superstitions and by his own arbitrary worship. These men fight against the eternal counsel of God, and charge with folly and injustice him who has set out the way of human salvation so difficult and grievous in the cruel death of his Son, when any invention of man could suffice for us to obtain it. Therefore their impiety is greater than it ought to be borne, as we have shown at length elsewhere.

units.la: Secundò Christum Simeon lumen esse ait, ad reuelationem gentium, id est quo gentes illuminari oporteat. Quo loco rursus ad Isaiam alludit, apud quem pater de filio in carne manifestado ait: Dabo te in fœdus populi, in lucem gentibus: vt aperias oculos cæcorum, vt educes è carcere vinctos, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris. Et rursus: Leue sit quòd seruus meus sis ad erigendas tribus Iacob, ad reducendas vastitates Israelis, nisi te dedero vt lux sis gentium, vt sis salus mea vsque ad extre mum terrae. Hæc vt Christi regnum inter gentes propagandum esse docet, ita simul nos pristinæ con ditionis admonent, in qua totus hic mundus constitutus fuit, priusquam Christus manifestaretur. Nam sub tenebrarum potestate detenti homines infinitis erroribus simul & sceleribus implicati fue runt, neque lux aliqua illis affulsit, aut etiam cerni potuit, cùm homo animalis non percipiat ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Venit autem Christus, qui vera Dei cognitione hominum mentes illustrauit, & de pulsis superstitionum & peccatorum tenebris, nos in viam salutis deduxit. Ipse denique lux illa mundi vera & æterna est, quam qui sequuntur, ij in tenebris non ambulant. Nostri autem ossi- cij est, exhibitum nobis in illo Dei beneficium agnoscere, & relictis operibus tenebrarum in luce ambulare. Nimium ergo ingrati diuinæ bonitatis æstimatores sunt, qui tenebras luci præferūt, imò lucem extinctam volunt, quo liberius lasciuire possint: quod hodie multi faciunt, qui Christi nomine gloriantur.
units.tr: Secondly, Simeon says that Christ is a light for the revelation of the Gentiles, that is, by which the Gentiles ought to be enlightened. Here again he alludes to Isaiah, in whom the Father, speaking of the Son to be manifested in the flesh, says: I will give you for a covenant of the people, for a light to the Gentiles, that you may open the eyes of the blind, that you may bring the bound out of prison, and those sitting in darkness out of the house of confinement. And again: It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to restore the ruins of Israel; unless I give you to be a light of the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth. This teaches that the kingdom of Christ is to be spread among the nations, and at the same time reminds us of the former condition in which this whole world was placed before Christ was manifested. For men, held under the power of darkness, were entangled in infinite errors and at once in crimes, and no light shone upon them, nor could be seen, since the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. But Christ came, who illumined the minds of men with the true knowledge of God, and, driving out the darkness of superstitions and sins, led us into the way of salvation. He himself, finally, is that true and eternal light of the world, whom those who follow do not walk in darkness. It is our duty, however, to acknowledge the benefit of God offered to us in him, and, leaving the works of darkness, to walk in the light. Therefore those are far too ungrateful estimators of divine goodness who prefer darkness to light, or rather wish the light extinguished, so that they may indulge themselves more freely: which many do today, who boast in the name of Christ.

units.la: Tertiò gloriam populi Israelitici dicit Christum. Ergo quanquàm regnum eius ad gentes vs- que extendat, tamen peculiare quid tribuit Iudæis, quorum erat adoptio & fœdus. Et sane gloria il- lorum singularis fuit Christus, quia illis præcipuè promissiones de illo datæ fuerunt, & ex illis ipse homo natus est, & priusquam nasceretur, illis maximorum bonorum author fuit, imò illos in peri- culis omnibus defendit, vt apud Isaiam cap.7.8. & 9. est videre. Recte ergo & merito illorum glo- ria dicitur. Etenim si aliis gentibus gloriari licet, quod ex ipsis heroes fortissimi aut legislatores pru dentissimi prodierint, incomparabile profecto gentis Iudaicæ decus censeri debet, quòd æternus Dei filius & vnicus humanæ salutis author ex illis carnem assumere voluit. Quantum ergo est hoc Dei beneficium, qui hanc Israelis gloriam per Euangelium ad nos vsque transferre voluit, qui per fidem nunc Christo insiti, illum totum nostrum dicere possumus? Non agnouerunt olim hanc Dei gratiam Iudæi, ideo propter incredulitatem & contumaciam reiecti & omnium hominum contemptissimi facti sunt. Excitet ergo nos illorum exemplum, vt tanta liberalitate se nobis offerentem Iesum Chri- stum, eadem fidei alacritate, quam in Simeone fuisse audimus, & animis gratis complectamur, vtq; in eius luce ambulantes finem nostræ peregrinationis lætum inueniamus, & huius corporis vinculo soluti colligamur ad eos, qui eadem fide per illum seruati sunt. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Thirdly, he calls Christ the glory of the people of Israel. Therefore, although his kingdom extends to the Gentiles, nevertheless he grants something peculiar to the Jews, to whom belonged the adoption and the covenant. And indeed Christ was the singular glory of that people, because the promises concerning him were given especially to them, and he himself was born of them, and before he was born he was the author of the greatest blessings to them, and indeed defended them in all dangers, as may be seen in Isaiah chapters 7, 8 and 9. Rightly and deservedly, therefore, is their glory spoken of. For if other nations may glory that the most valiant heroes or the most prudent lawgivers have sprung from them, the incomparable honour of the Jewish nation ought surely to be reckoned that the eternal Son of God and the sole author of human salvation willed to assume flesh from them. How great, then, is this benefit of God, who through the Gospel willed to transfer this glory of Israel even to us, so that we, now ingrafted into Christ through faith, can call him wholly ours? The Jews did not in former times acknowledge this grace of God, and therefore, on account of their unbelief and stubbornness, they were rejected and made the most despised of all men. Let the example of them therefore stir us, that we may embrace with thankful minds Jesus Christ, offering himself to us with such generosity, with the same eagerness of faith which we hear was in Simeon; and walking in his light may find a joyful end to our pilgrimage, and, loosed from the bond of this body, may be gathered to those who have been saved through him by the same faith. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXII.

units.la: Porro pater & mater eius mirabantur super iis, quæ dicebantur de eo. Et benedixit eis Simeon, dixitq; Mariæ matri eius: Ecce positus est iste in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel, et in signum cui con tradicatur. Quin & tuam ipsius animam transiciet gladius, vt detegantur ex multis cordibus cogitationes.
units.tr: And his father and mother marvelled at those things which were spoken about him. And Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary his mother: Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against. Yea, a sword shall pierce through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

units.la: QVoniam Dominus noster Iesus Christus in mundum venit et homo verus factus est, vt omnis loci et ordinis hominũ Seruator fieret, voluit eundem Deus, quàm primum natus fuit omnium ordinum hominibus innotescere et diuersæ conditionis hominũ testimonijs publicè commen dari. In quibus commemorandis Lucas diligentissimus est, vt per illa nos quoq; in illius cognitione & fide confirmemur. Audiuimus ex his nuper optimi & piissimi senis Simeonis oraculum, plenum san- ctissimi gaudij, quo ille perfusus fuit, & dulcissimæ consolationis, quo pleraq; continentur, quæ nos in Christo agnoscere & credere oportet, si illum nobis salutiferum esse cupimus. Sequuntur nunc alia, quæ ab eodem Simeone ex spiritus sancti impulsu dicta sunt ad tollendū scandala, quibus fides mul- torum labefactatur, multi quoque impediuntur, ne vnquam ad Christum accedant.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ came into the world and was made a true man, so that he might become the Saviour of every place and order of men, God willed that he should be made known to men of every rank as soon as he was born, and that he should be publicly commended by the testimonies of people of different conditions. Luke is most diligent in recording these, so that through them we too may be confirmed in the knowledge and faith of him. Lately we have heard from this best and most devout old man Simeon an oracle full of most holy joy, with which he was overflowing, and of the sweetest consolation, containing many things which we must acknowledge and believe about Christ if we wish him to be our Saviour. Now follow other things, which Simeon spoke by the impulse of the Holy Spirit to remove the stumbling-blocks by which the faith of many is shaken, and by which many also are hindered from ever coming to Christ.

units.la: Priusquam verò illa proponat Lucas, quædam de Iosepho & Maria interserit, vt nimirum il li Simeonis verbis fuerint affecti. Pater (inquit) & mater eius mirabantur super ijs, quæ diceban- tur de eo. Quo loco Iosephum Christi patrem dicit, non quòd is aliquid ad illius generationem contu- lerit (est enim Christus semen mulieris, & lapis ille, quem Daniel absque manibus reuelli vidit) sed quòd vulgò pater eius esse crederetur propter coniugium, quod ipsi cum Maria Virgine intercedebat. Et ita seipsum postea exponet cap.3. vbi scribit: Iesus incipiebat esse quasi annorum triginta, filius (vt existimabatur) Iosephi, &c. Admirati autem sunt Simeonis tanto gaudio gestientis de Christo puerulo testimonium, non quod quae ille dicebat, ipsis noua aut incredibilia viderentur, sed quod non possent non rapi in diligentem consilij diuini considerationem, quando nouos quotidie accedere videbant, qui infantulum nihil adhuc magnificum praesè ferentem pro Dei filio & hominum redemptore agnoscerent. Quoad enim illius cognitionem ipsi iampridem probè instructi erant. Audierat enim Maria Angelû de totius negotij huius mysterio perspicuè differentem. Ex eodem Iosephus quoq; didicerat, quid de puerulo isto deberet sentire, priusquam in lucem editus esset. Aduenerant deinde pastores, qui quid ex Angelis audissent prolixè narrabant. Quibus non multò post Magi succeßerunt, qui illum donis quoq; regalibus honorauerant. Non ergo nouum & insolens illis videri poterat quod nunc agebatur: sed vt prius de Maria dictum fuerat, eam in animo suo repositsse & contulisse omnia, quae pastores dicebant: ita nunc tam ipsa quàm Ioseph pia & sancta admiratione Dei bonitatem & prouidentiam prosequuntur, cum tam laeta viderent regni Christi initia, & huiusmodi nouis quotidie testimonijs ornari audirent. Admirantur ergo, quia credunt, non admiraturi sed potius risuri & contemptuti haec omnia, nisi vera esse credidissent.
units.tr: Before Luke sets out these words, he inserts some things about Joseph and Mary, namely that they were moved by Simeon's words. "His father and mother," he says, "marvelled at those things which were said about him." In this passage he calls Joseph the father of Christ, not because he contributed anything to Christ's generation (for Christ is the seed of the woman, and he is that stone which Daniel saw cut out without hands), but because he was commonly believed to be his father on account of the marriage which he had with the Virgin Mary. And so Luke afterwards explains this himself in chapter 3, where he writes: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph," and so on. They marvelled, however, at Simeon's testimony about the infant Christ, which he gave in great joy, not because what he said seemed new or incredible to them, but because they could not help being carried away into a careful consideration of the divine counsel, since they saw new people arriving every day who recognised as the Son of God and Redeemer of men a little child who as yet displayed nothing great. For they had long been well instructed about his identity. Mary had heard the angel explain clearly the mystery of the whole matter. Joseph too had learned from the same angel what he ought to think of this child before he was born into the light. Then shepherds came, who told at length what they had heard from the angels. Not long after them the Magi followed, who honoured him with royal gifts too. So what was now happening could not seem strange or unusual to them. Just as it had been said earlier that Mary kept all these things and pondered in her heart what the shepherds said, so now both she and Joseph, with a holy and devout wonder, marvelled at the goodness and providence of God, seeing such joyful beginnings of Christ's kingdom and hearing that it was being adorned daily with such new testimonies. They marvelled, therefore, because they believed; they would not have marvelled, but rather laughed and despised all these things, had they not believed them to be true.

units.la: Nobis autem in illis considerandum venit verae fidei ingenium. Saepius iam eadem dicti audierat Maria, non tamen illa vt superuacanea ridet aut contemnit, multo minus vt trita nimis fastidit, etiamsi fere ab illis toties repeteretur, quos nulla authoritas publica aut externus splendor commendabat: sed in animo repostia fouet & diligenti meditatione tantorum beneficiorum Dei ipsam solatur atque confirmat. Ergo fides non ita satiatur Christi mysterijs et salute per hoc exhibita, vt disceндi fastidium concipiat: sed quia in illo omne salutis fontem contineri nouit, nihil credenti dulcius & iucundius accidere potest, quàm si nouam de illo cogitandi occasionem subinde sibi offerri videat. Quae causa est, quòd qui fide vera instructi sunt, ijdem au diendi Verbi Dei studio flagrant, hoc sanè multo melle stillantibus (vt Dauid olim dicebat) praeferunt, in quo eo dies & noctes meditantur. Quòd si vero aliqua occurrunt, quorum ratio non statim videri aut cognosci potest, tamen ne haec quidem contemptim abijciunt, sed admirantur & fide superant, quod humani ingenij acumine penetrari non posse videt. Quod in Christi mysterijs fieri oportere, olim in agno paschali fuit adumbratum, quae totum comedere iubebantur, ossa autem, quae manducari non possunt igne coburere: hoc nimirum innuente spiritu sancto, Christum totum, quantus et qualis est, apprehendi oportere: quia autem in illo quaedam sese efferunt, quae capru nostro non possunt intelligi, ea fide percipienda, adeoq; concoquenda esse, ne nobis sint obstaculo. Etenim hunc quoque praedicationis euangelicae finem aut scopum esse scribit Apostolus, vt nostros sensus simul atque cogitationes vnà cum affectibus carnis omnibus sub fidei obedientiâ redigat. Sunt haec obseruanda aduersus eos, qui Christianam fidem & aeternae salutis mysteria nostri ingenij sensu metiuntur, & Porphyrium atque Iulianum imitati, scurriliter ridBnt quicquid ipsi intelligere non possunt: quasi vero Dei sapientia ad nostri captus modulum astringi debeat. Proximi his sunt, quibus nuda Christi cognitio sordet, & impatientius ferunt, quòd vnum hunc praedicemus, & tunc demum se in fide profecisse putant, si extra Christum vagando portenta quaedam absurdissimarum opinionum excogitent, in quibus sui ingenij acumen ostentent. Memini fratres, hoc mihi aliquando à quodam extero (cuius nomini & patriae consulto nunc parco) dictum fuisse, se non posse improbare nostrarum ecclesiarum doctrinam, non videre autem quid in salutis & regni Dei cognitione proficere quis possit, quando in concionibus sacris & praelectionibus Theologicis nihil praeter Christum audire liceat. Respondebam ego satis profecisse eum, qui Christum agnoscat, neq; nos plura scire velle quàm Paulum, qui etsi in tertium caelum raptus verba ineffabilia audiuisset, in sola tamen Christi cruce gloriabatur, & se nihil praeter hunc crucifixum nouisse affirmabat. Neque vt in aeternae salutis argumento aliquid praeterea sciamus opus est, quando non aliud nomen sub caelo hominibus est datum, in quo nos seruari oporteat. Sed possumus eiusmodi sciolis Mariae exemplum opponere, quam non piguit ex pastoribus & Simeone plebeio fericulo, & mox ex Anna vetula eadem audire, quae iampridem ex Angeli ore didicerat. Neque superuacanea censeri debet cuiquam millies repetita Iesu Christi praedicatio, quando illius cognitione obiter degustauisse non sufficit, nisi eadem in nobis quotidie nouis auditibus crescat, vt inter tentationum assultus, quibus eam labefactare studet Satan, salua & inuicta consistat.
units.tr: Here we should consider the character of true faith. Mary had already heard these same words many times, yet she does not laugh at them as superfluous, nor despise them, much less find them stale and tiresome, even though they were repeated so often by people whom no public authority or outward show recommended. Instead she cherishes them, laid up in her mind, and by diligent meditation on such great benefits of God she comforts and strengthens herself. Faith, therefore, is not so satisfied with the mysteries of Christ and the salvation shown through them that it conceives a distaste for learning. Rather, because it knows that every fountain of salvation is contained in him, nothing can happen more sweetly and pleasantly to the believer than to see a new occasion for thinking about him continually offered to him. This is why those who are instructed in true faith burn with eagerness to hear the Word of God; they prefer it to honey dripping (as David once said), and they meditate on it day and night. But if some things occur whose reason cannot immediately be seen or understood, they do not cast these aside with contempt either, but they marvel at them and overcome them by faith, seeing that they cannot be penetrated by the sharpness of human intellect. That this is how it must be with the mysteries of Christ was once foreshadowed in the paschal lamb, which they were commanded to eat whole, but whose bones, which cannot be eaten, they were to burn with fire. This clearly signifies, by the will of the Holy Spirit, that Christ must be laid hold of whole, as great and as he is; and because some things in him stand out which cannot be understood by our small capacity, these must be grasped by faith and so digested, lest they become a hindrance to us. For the Apostle also writes that this is the purpose or aim of the preaching of the gospel: to bring all our senses and thoughts, together with the affections of the flesh, under the obedience of faith. These things must be observed against those who measure the Christian faith and the mysteries of eternal salvation by the sense of their own wit, and who, imitating Porphyry and Julian, scoffingly mock whatever they cannot themselves understand, as if the wisdom of God ought to be confined to the measure of our capacity. Close to these are those who find bare knowledge of Christ distasteful, and who bear it with impatience that we preach this one alone; they believe that they have progressed in faith only when, wandering outside Christ, they devise some monstrous and most absurd opinions in which they display the sharpness of their wit. Brothers, I remember that once a certain foreigner (whose name and country I now deliberately spare) said to me that he could not disapprove of the doctrine of our churches, but that he could not see what anyone could gain in the knowledge of salvation and the kingdom of God, since in the sacred sermons and theological lectures one may hear nothing but Christ. I replied that the man who acknowledges Christ has made sufficient progress, and that we do not wish to know more than Paul, who, although he was caught up to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words, nevertheless gloried only in the cross of Christ, and affirmed that he knew nothing except Jesus crucified. Nor is it necessary, as a proof of eternal salvation, for us to know anything further, since there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved. But we can set against such smatterers the example of Mary, who was not ashamed to hear from the shepherds and from Simeon, a plebeian old man, and soon afterwards from the aged Anna, the very things she had long before learned from the mouth of the angel. Nor should the preaching of Jesus Christ, though repeated a thousand times, be considered superfluous to anyone, since it is not enough to have tasted it in passing, unless it grows in us daily through fresh hearings, so that it may remain safe and unconquered amid the assaults of temptations, by which Satan seeks to shake it.

units.la: Sed ad Simeonem accedamus, qui vbi primam sui vaticinij partem absoluit, iam ad Christi pue ruli parentes conuertitur, Mariam in primis, et cum his etiam ea agit, quae ad illos maxime pertine bant. Primo autem illis benedixit. Quod non de solenni benedictione intelligi debet, cuius ministri & internuntij erant Sacerdotes: sed vulgari & ciuili, vt sic loquar. Quare non opus est disputare, quomodo Simeon, homo mortalis & plebeius Christo benedicere potuerit, cum hoc officium ex Legis praescripto maiores minoribus praestare solerent, sicuti Apostolus in epistola ad Hebraeos admonet.
units.tr: But let us come to Simeon, who, when he had finished the first part of his prophecy, turns to the parents of the infant Christ, to Mary first, and deals with them also in those matters which pertained most to them. First, however, he blessed them. This must not be understood of a solemn blessing, whose ministers and go-betweens were the priests, but of an ordinary and civil blessing, if I may so speak. Therefore there is no need to dispute how Simeon, a mortal man and of humble station, could bless Christ, since this office was customarily performed by greater men towards lesser ones according to the prescription of the Law, as the Apostle reminds us in his Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Nam etsi Christum simul hic comprehendere libeat, nihil absurdi fuerit, si Simeonem & parentibus eius omnia fausta laetaque optauisse dicamus, & Christo simul felicem regni Dei per ipsum instaurandi successum fuisse imprecatum. Potest enim pium illud votum etiam sub benedictione comprehendi. Vt ergo Simeon hic quoque fidem & studium suum erga Christum & regnum eius declarauit: ita charitatis officio simul vsus est, quae monet, vt & quibusuis obuijs bene precemur, & vota pia pro illis maxime concipiamus, qui res arduas & cum multorum salute coniunctas aggrediuntur. Facit hoc plurimum ad fouendam mutuam charitatem, in cuius leges vehementer peccant inuidi illi aemulatores, qui aliorum laetis succesibus ringuntur, & suae crudelitatis tantum non ministrum faciunt Deum, quando dira quaeque ijs imprecantur, quorum conatibus fauere debebant. Est horum impietas maior, quam vt verbis nudis reprehendi mereatur, vt alibi copiosius esse dictum.
units.tr: For even if we are willing to include Christ here as well, it would be no absurdity to say that Simeon wished every happy and joyful thing to his parents, and at the same time prayed for the successful establishment of God's kingdom through Christ. For that pious wish can also be included within the blessing. So just as Simeon here declared his faith and zeal toward Christ and his kingdom, he at the same time exercised the duty of charity, which urges us to bless whomever we meet and especially to form pious wishes for those who undertake difficult tasks bound up with the salvation of many. This contributes greatly to fostering mutual charity, against whose laws those envious rivals grievously sin, who are tormented by the happy successes of others, and who, in their cruelty, almost make God the minister of their malice when they call down dreadful things upon those whose endeavours they ought to favour. Their impiety is too great to deserve to be rebuked with mere words, as has been said more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Caeterum benedictioni huic alteram sui vaticinij partem subijcit Simeon, qua Christum describit, quoad diuersos effectus, quibus erga homines vim suam declaraturus sit. Et quamuis sermonem ad Mariam potissimum dirigat, doctrina tamen profert, quae & illo tempore cognitu valde necessaria fuit, & hodie non minus vtilis est ad tollenda scandala, quae in Christi & communis salutis causa no bis obijciuntur. Nam etsi inter Iudaeos nihil vulgarius esset Messiae nomine, & in huius aduentum totius populi animus esset intentus, pauci tamen vel potius nulli erant, qui de illo recte sentirent, & quid in illo sperari aut quaeri debeat, intelligerent. Sciebant quidem regnum eius apud prophetas magnifice describi, & huic a Deo dictum esse: Postula a me, daboq; gentes vt sint hereditas tua, & termini terrae vt sint possessio tua. Sceptro ferreo confringes eos, veluti vasa testacea comminues eos. Ite de regno eius dictum esse noverant: Ferent montes pacem populo, et colles iustitiam. Vindicabit affli ctos in populo, & seruabit pauperes, et violentum calumniatorem contundet. Timebunt te dum Sol & Luna lucebunt, in omne aeuum. Florebunt ipso regnante iusti, multaq; pax erit, donec Luna deficiat. Imperabit a mari ad mare vsq;, & a flumine vsq; ad terminos terrae. Coram illo procumbet accola deserti, & inimici eius puluere lingent. Reges maris mediterranei & insularum munera afferent, Reges Scheba & Saba honoraria adducet. Et adorabunt eum omnes reges, & omnes gentes seruiet ei. Et rursus: Comorabitur lupus cum agno, & pardus cum haedo accubabit, similiter iuuencus, leo & pecus saginatum simul erunt, et puer paruus ducet ea. Vacca cum urso pascetur, simul accubabunt catuli eorum. Leo sicut bos paleas comedet. Delectabitur lactes antro aspidis, cuique fuerit ablactatus, inferet manum suam in spelunca reguli. Non afficient malis, neque vastabunt per omnem montem meum sanctum: plena enim erit terra scientia Domini, perinde ac dum aquae maris inundant. Ite: Fiet & hoc in diebus illis vt apprehendant decem viri ex omnibus linguis gentium, apprehendat (inquam) alam alicuius Iudaei, & dicat: Ibimus vobiscum, quia audiuimus Deum vobiscum esse. Haec & infinita alia huius generis in prophetarum libris extant, quibus illi Christum & per hunc facta humani generis redemptione sub regni terreni & victoriosi similibus describunt.
units.tr: Next to this blessing, Simeon adds the second part of his prophecy, in which he describes Christ with respect to the various effects by which he will show his power towards human beings. And although he directs his speech chiefly to Mary, he nevertheless sets forth a teaching that was very necessary to know at that time and is no less useful today for removing the stumbling blocks that are placed before us concerning Christ and the cause of common salvation. For although nothing was more common among the Jews than the name Messiah, and the minds of the whole people were intent on his coming, there were few, or rather none, who thought rightly about him or understood what ought to be hoped for or sought in him. They indeed knew that his kingdom was magnificently described by the prophets, and that God had said to him: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall break them with an iron sceptre; you shall dash them in pieces like earthenware." They also knew what had been said about his kingdom: "The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the hills righteousness. He shall vindicate the afflicted among the people, and save the poor, and crush the violent oppressor. They shall fear you while sun and moon shine, for all generations. In his days the righteous shall flourish, and there shall be abundant peace until the moon is no more. He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the dwellers in the desert shall bow down, and his enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of the inland sea and of the islands shall bring gifts; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall bring tribute. And all kings shall worship him, and all nations shall serve him." And again: "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the calf and the lion and the fatling shall be together, and a little child shall lead them. The cow shall feed with the bear; their young shall lie down together. The lion shall eat straw like the ox. The suckling shall play over the den of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand into the viper's hole. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea." Again: "It shall come to pass in those days that ten men from all the tongues of the nations shall take hold, yes, take hold of the skirt of a Jew, and say: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you." These and countless other passages of this kind are found in the books of the prophets, in which they describe Christ, and the redemption of the human race accomplished through him, under the likeness of an earthly and victorious kingdom.

units.la: Quae omnia cum Iudaei secundum litera acciperent, illum Regem terrenum fore somniabant, qui euersa Romani imperij Monarchia, quae tunc longe lateque dominabatur, Iudaicam gentem libertati veteri restitueret, et in illa regnum instauraret victorijs, opibus, triumphis illustre, quale olim sub Dauide & Solomone fuerat. Quae sententia omnium animis ita insidebat, vt discipuli post longam consuetudinem, quae ipsis cum Christo intercesserat, imo post triste crucis et mortis indignae spectaculum, adhuc de regno illo quaestiones moueret, & sibi in eo honores et dignitates pollicentur. Et haec praecipua causa fuit, ob quam pleriq; Iudaeorum Christum Iesum aspernati sunt, quod non videre possent, quomodo prophetarum vaticinia in illo loco haberet, in quo nihil praeter inopia, cotem ptum & continua omnis generis afflictionum serie cernere licebat. Quapropter admodum necesse erat, initio statim omnes Iudæos de his publicè admoneri, in primis verò Mariâ, ne communi errore implicita eò grauius postea offederetur, quò propius ad illâ pertinebat dolor, qui ex filij indignissima sorte enascebatur. Et hodie multus & necessarius huius doctrinæ vsus est, quando multi ad Euangelium Christi nō alia spe accedunt, quàm quæ olim Iudæos decepit: dū aut triumphos perpetuos, aut opes ingentes, aut (quod longè turpissimū est) peccādi licentiā atq; impunitatē sibi ex illo pollicetur. Audiamus ergo de Christo cōcionante Simeone, vt quæ de illo semper futura sint hominū iudicia, intelligamus.
units.tr: Since the Jews took all these things according to the letter, they dreamed that he would be an earthly king who, overthrowing the monarchy of the Roman empire, which then ruled far and wide, would restore the Jewish nation to its ancient liberty and establish in it a kingdom distinguished by victories, wealth and triumphs, such as had once existed under David and Solomon. This opinion so possessed the minds of all that the disciples, even after the long companionship they had enjoyed with Christ, and indeed after the sad spectacle of his cross and unworthy death, still raised questions about that kingdom and promised themselves honours and dignities in it. And this was the chief reason why most of the Jews rejected Jesus Christ: they could not see how the prophecies of the prophets applied to one in whom nothing but poverty, contempt and a continual series of afflictions of every kind could be discerned. Therefore it was very necessary, that at the outset all Jews should be publicly admonished about these things, and especially Mary, lest, entangled in the common error, she be more grievously offended afterwards, the closer the grief arising from her son's most unworthy lot touched her. And today the use of this teaching is great and necessary, since many come to the gospel of Christ with no other hope than that which once deceived the Jews: they promise themselves from it either perpetual triumphs, or immense wealth, or (what is by far the most shameful) licence and impunity for sinning. Let us therefore listen to Simeon preaching about Christ, so that we may understand what the judgements of men about him will always be.

units.la: Ecce positus est iste (inquit) in casum & resurrectionē multorum in Israel. Conueniunt ista cum veteribus prophetarum oraculis, quæ in mentem reuocari proderat, vt de alteris illis hucusqueperperam intellectus Iudæi rectius sentire discerent. Alludit autem ad duos Isaiæ locos, quorum alter octauo, alter vigesimo octauo capite habetur. In illo sic de Christo pronunciat: Is erit sanctuarium, & lapis offendiculi, & petra ruinæ duabus domibus Israelis: in laqueum deinde & in tendiculam ei qui habitat Hierosolymæ. Ad quæ multi impingent, corruent, conterentur, irretientur & capientur. Alterum verò vaticinium eiusmodi est: Sic dixit Dominus, Ecce ego fundo in Zion lapidem, lapidem probationis, fundamentum, singularem, pretiosum, solidum fundamentum, credens non festinabit: Vel (vt Paulus interpretatur) non pudefiet. Vtrunque locum prophetæ Simeon duobus verbis complexus est, quando Christum positum, id est diuinitus ordinatum esse ait, vt alijs quidem ad casum vel ruinam, alijs in resurrectionem cedat. Emphasim verò habet singularem, quod ait, In Israel. Quasi dicat, illum non exteris solùm, sed multis in Iudaica gente, cui ille peculiariter promissus fuit, lapidem scandali fore. Quod Ioannes clarius exponens dixit: In sua venit, & sui eum non receperunt. Quid, quòd ab ædificantibus, id est, à Sacerdotibus reiectum iri Dauid præmonuit, qui ecclesiæ architecti haberi volebant? Optimus autem & fidelissimus oraculi huius interpres, adeoque paraphrastes est Petrus Apostolus, qui cùm Isaiæ locum, cuius modò meminimus adduxisset, mox subijcit: Vobis igitur honor est, qui creditis: immorigeris verò lapis, quem reprobauerunt ædificantes: hic factus est caput anguli. Et lapis offendiculi, & petra offensionis: ijs nimirum, qui offendunt ad sermonem, immorigeri, ad quod etiam constituti sunt. In quibus omnibus obseruari debet, in Christo omnibus hominibus salutem & vitam offerri per Euangelium, & officium eius proprium esse seruare et viuificare, sed pro hominum diuersitate diuersos ex illo effectus sequi, vt alijs ruinæ alijs resurrectionis causa fit. Aperte ergo & perspicuè Petrus inter duo illa hominum genera distinguit & hos quidem credentes, illos autem immorigeros vocat. Itaque in casum & ruinam positus est Christus illis, qui sua rebellione & contumacia adillum offendunt, & ita sibijpsis exitium accersunt ex eo, qui verus et proprius salutis author est. Id autē fit bifariā. Sunt enim, qui (vt diximus) in Christo regnum somniant & omnia huius seculi commoda sibi in eo pollicentur. Offendunt isti ad vilem & contemptibilem illius speciem, & quòd huius cultores non solùm in mundo obscuros, pauperes & egenos, verumetiā plerisq; exosos et persecutionibus assiduis obnoxios esse vident. Et hi tantùmo cum pharisæis dicunt: Num quis ex principibus credidit in eum? quin sola turba hæc & sex plebis, quæ non nouit Legem, execrabilis est. Et est hoc scandali genus admodum vulgare, eò quòd plerique religione ex carnis sensu et huius seculi successibus metiuntur. Ideo Christus ipse suos pasim ad crucem vocat, nosq; in hoc mundo afflictionibus perpetuis exercendos monet, & quò minus ijs offendamur, suum exemplum nobis ob oculos ponit, nosq; nimiùm importunos et plus æquo delicatulos fore docet, si nostram conditionem lautiorem esse cupiamus, quàm ipsius fuerit, cùm in terris ageret. Et Paulus Corinthios monebat, ne in externa Christi et ecclesiæ facie hærerent: sed ipsum Christum, Dei potentiam & sapientiam, propius intuerentur, & ita mox intellecturos dicebat, stultitiam Dei sapientiorem esse quàm homines, & Dei infirmitatem omnes hominum vires longè superare. Sed alia etiam ratione ad Christum nonnulli offendunt, quibus nimirum doctrina Euangelij scandalum est, qua omnes hominis facultates deijci, omne operum nostrorum meritum negari, homines denique omnes peccati & mortis reos agi, iustitiā verò & salutem omnem in sola Dei gratia nobis per Christum monstrari audiunt. Offendit hoc eos potissimùm, qui præ alijs iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ titulum sibi vendicant, quales inter Iudæos olim Pharisæi fuerunt, hodie autē Monachi sunt, & qui horum doctrinam secuti salutis spem in suorū operum meritis et propria iustitia collocatā habent. Clamant illi omnes Christum esse socium publicanorum & comessatorum, doctrinam item eius bonis moribus inimicam, legi diuinæ aduersam, deniq; licentiæ & petulantiæ magistram esse. At ijdem dum suam iustitiam (vt Paulus inquit) stabilire volunt, à iustitia Dei excidunt, quam ille nobis in Christo offert, & quæ sola nos apud eius tribunal tuetur. Itaque istis quoque in ruinam & casum positus est Christus, quùm eius meritū ipsi sibi inutile reddant. His ex aduerso opponuntur, qui toti mundo & carniediti ad mortificationis & abnegationis nostri ipsius doctrinam offendunt, & ea exigi arbitrantur, quæ omnem ex mundo amicitiā tollant, et vitā ipsam nobis amaram reddant. Sed quia isti omnes scandalum dedita opera quærunt, & scientes volentes offendunt, neq; etiam admoneri et insti tui volunt, non est quòd eorum exemplis multum moueantur pij, quibus sua salus ex animo cordi est. Ad hos enim pertinet, quòd idem Christus lapis resurrectionis dicitur: pretiosus nimirum lapis ille, quem Zionis, id est, Ecclesiæ fundamentum Isaias dicit, & qui fide vera apprehensus nos ex pecati et errorū seruitio quasi e x mortuis excitat, vt viui lapides efficiamur, ex quibus ædificiū illud sanctum Ecclesiæ totius constuitur, in quo idem ille caput anguli est, quo & inter se connectuntur omnes qui credunt, & spiritu vitæ animantur, vt olim regni cœlestis cum illo cōsortes fiant. Est ergo Christus in se salutis & vitæ author, & (vt ipse apud Ioannem ait) resurrectio simul & vita nostra est: quicunq; autem pereunt, suo vitio pereunt, dum ad illum vel crassa ignorantia, vel etiam manifesta rebellione impingunt, & Euangelium sibi ipsis odorem faciunt mortiferum, ex quo vitæ odorem concipere debebant. 2. Cor. 2.
units.tr: "Behold, this one is set (he says) for the fall and the rising again of many in Israel." These words agree with the ancient oracles of the prophets, which it is worth calling to mind, so that the Jews, who have hitherto understood those other passages wrongly, may learn to judge them more rightly. He alludes to two passages of Isaiah, one in chapter eight and the other in chapter twenty-eight. In the first he speaks thus of Christ: "He shall be a sanctuary, and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of ruin to the two houses of Israel; a snare and a trap to him who dwells in Jerusalem. Many will stumble against these, fall, be broken, be entangled and be taken." The other prophecy runs thus: "Thus says the Lord, Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; he who believes shall not make haste." Or (as Paul interprets it) "shall not be put to shame." Simeon has embraced both passages in two words, when he says that Christ has been set, that is, divinely appointed, so that for some he becomes a fall or ruin, and for others a rising again. The emphasis lies especially in the words "in Israel." As if he said that he will be a stone of stumbling not only to foreigners but to many within the Jewish nation, to which he was promised in a special way. John makes this plainer when he explains: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." And what of the fact that David forewarned that he would be rejected by the builders, that is, by the priests, who wished to be regarded as the architects of the Church? But the best and most faithful interpreter, indeed the paraphrast, of this oracle is the Apostle Peter. When he had quoted the passage of Isaiah we just mentioned, he immediately adds: "To you therefore who believe there is honour; but for the disobedient, the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence." Plainly, to those who stumble at the word, that is, the disobedient, for which also they were appointed. In all these things it must be observed that salvation and life are offered to all men in Christ through the Gospel, and that his proper office is to save and to quicken; but, according to the diversity of men, different effects follow from him, so that for some he is the cause of ruin, for others of resurrection. Peter, then, clearly and plainly distinguishes between these two kinds of men, calling the one believers and the other the disobedient. Christ is therefore set for the fall and ruin of those who stumble at him through their rebellion and obstinacy, and so bring destruction upon themselves from him who is the true and proper author of salvation. This happens in two ways. For there are some who (as we have said) dream of a kingdom in Christ and promise themselves in him all the advantages of this age. These stumble at his lowly and contemptible appearance, and because they see that his worshippers are not only obscure, poor and needy in the world, but also hated by most people and constantly exposed to persecution.
