Such men say, with the Pharisees, "Has any of the rulers believed in him? But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed." And this kind of offence is very common, because most people measure religion by worldly feeling and by the success of this age. Therefore Christ himself everywhere calls his people to the cross, warns us that we are to be trained by constant afflictions in this world, and, so that we may not be offended by these things, he sets his own example before our eyes, teaching us that we shall be too demanding and too pampered if we wish our condition to be more comfortable than his was while he lived on earth. Paul also warned the Corinthians not to cling to the outward appearance of Christ and the Church, but to look more closely at Christ himself, the power and wisdom of God, and so, he said, they would soon understand that the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God far surpasses all human strength. But some also stumble at Christ in another way, namely those for whom the doctrine of the Gospel is a scandal, which teaches that all human abilities are cast down, that all merit of our works is denied, that all men are held guilty of sin and death, and that righteousness and all salvation are shown to us through Christ by grace alone. This offends above all those who claim for themselves the title of righteousness and holiness before others, as the Pharisees once did among the Jews, and as monks do today, and those who, following their teaching, place their hope of salvation in the merits of their own works and in their own righteousness. All of these cry out that Christ is a companion of tax-collectors and drunkards, that his teaching is hostile to good morals and opposed to the divine law, and, finally, that it is a teacher of licence and wantonness. Yet these same men, while they wish to establish their own righteousness (as Paul says), fall away from the righteousness of God, which he offers us in Christ, and which alone protects us before his judgment seat. Therefore Christ is also set for the ruin and fall of these men, since they render his merit useless to themselves. Opposed to these are those who, devoted wholly to the world and the flesh, take offence at the doctrine of mortification and self-denial, and think that things are demanded of them which would strip away all friendship with the world and make life itself bitter to them. But since all these men seek out offence deliberately, and knowingly and willingly stumble, and do not wish to be admonished or instructed, there is no reason for godly people to be much moved by their examples, for whom their own salvation is a matter of the heart. For it is to these that the saying applies, that the same Christ is called a stone of resurrection: that precious stone, namely, which Isaiah calls the foundation of Zion, that is, of the Church, and which, when apprehended by true faith, raises us up, as if from the dead, out of the bondage of sin and error, so that we become living stones, from which that holy building of the whole Church is constructed, in which he himself is the head of the corner, by which also all who believe are joined together, and are quickened by the Spirit of life, so that at length they may become partners with him in the heavenly kingdom. Christ, then, is in himself the author of salvation and life, and (as he himself says in John) is at once our resurrection and our life. But those who perish, perish by their own fault, while they stumble against him either through gross ignorance or through open rebellion, and make the Gospel a deadly odour for themselves, when from it they ought to have drawn the odour of life. 2. Cor. 2.

units.la: Sed aliud addit Simeon, quo docet non solùm multos fore, qui ad hanc petram offendant, verum etiam qui illi contradicant palàm, adeoq; se hostiliter ei opponāt. Nam ecce (inquit) positus est in signum, cui contradicitur. Inest his verbis Metaphora à sagittantibus sumpta, & sensus est: Vt sagittarij signum & scopum habent, quem omnes petunt, & ad quem sagittas suas dirigunt: ita Christus instar scopi erit, quem omnis loci & ordinis homines oppugnabunt, vt eius doctrinam euertant & ab ipso homines abstrahant. Quod quàm verè prædictum sit à diuino hoc Sene, omnium temporum historiæ testantur. Nam vt à Iudæis exordiamur, quàm primùm ille se mundo manifestare cœpit, exorti sunt qui illi contradicerent, & quidem non vulgares homines, sed scribæ, sed sacerdotes, sed pharisæi, penes quos tunc summa erat in sacris authoritas, & qui summam doctrinæ & sanctitatis existimationem sustinebant. Neq; privatim hoc fecēre singuli, sed non semel publica & Ecclesiastica authoritate Concilij illū cum sua doctrina damnauerunt. Imò non contenti doctrinæ eius obstrepuisse, miracula quoque calumniati sunt, quàmuis toti populo vtilia, & simul ab omni fuco & fraude aliena essent. Et ne quis leuem putet illam contradictionem fuisse, non modò nugatorem, sed pestiferum seductorem, seditiosum, Samaritanum & dæmoniacum dixerunt. Quod vt inter Iudæos fieri cœpit, sic idem postea inter gentes factitatum est, cùm inter has Christus prædicaretur. Tunc enim aduersus apostolos & horū successores philosophi insurrexerunt, qui doctrinam de Christo suis strophis in contemptum & dubium vocare conati sunt. Iunxerunt cum his operam suam Regum & Imperatorum ministri, qui falsa insuper crimina Christianis omnibus intentarunt, & nullum tam nefarium tamq; inauditum scelus est, quod non illis obiectum fuerit. Nam & infantes iugulare, & humanis carnibus vesci dicebantur. Neque defuerunt, qui Romanum Imperium saluum fore negabant, nisi illi extirparentur, qui et sacrorum & legum hostes essent, et Deorum iram aduersus totum terrarum orbem excitarent. Itaque quicquid mali publici accideret, mox ad leones, ad rogos, ad remos, ad metalla Christianos arripiendos esse clamabatur. Taceo nunc edicta publica, in quibus Romani Imperatores Christum & Euangelium eius damnauerunt. Et ne exteri soli Ecclesiæ negotiū facerent, inter ipsos Christianos hæretici exorti sunt, qui portentosis simul atq; impijs commentis & plus quàm diabolica obtrectandi libidine linguas suas aduersus Christum & puriorem Veritatis doctrinam soluerunt. Quorum omnium calumnias, fallacias et mendacia si quis enumerare vellet, vix vnquam dicendi finem inueniret. Et quod olim factum est, hoc ipsum hodie etiam fit passim. Perguntenim Christo contradicere Iudæi, & ne nunc quidem eius manum agnoscunt, cuius iusto & gratui iudicio sese premi & in extremas miserias detrusos esse sentiunt. Miscent cum his suas quoque calumnias Mahometani, qui longè maximam orbis partem occupant. Latrant quotidie aduersus æternum patri coessentialem Dei filiū Seruetani canes, et quotquot hodie vel Arij, vel Marcionis, vel Eutychis, vel aliorū hæreses postliminio reuocant. Imò qui Ecclesiæ gubernacula sibi vendicant pontifices & episcopi, se cum rebus suis non posse salvos esse arbitrantur, nisi Christo per Euangelium nobis loquenti contradicant, & illum e solio suo deiiciant. Sub horum deinde signis in lacunis suis coaxant aduersus eundem Monachi, boant sacrificuli, crocitant Purgatoriani corui, noctuae sepulchrales vlulant, serpentum & anguium instar sibilant Moniales & Begutta, rudunt deniq; asini & muli Romanenses: qui simul omnes undique tam nobilium quam plebeiorum turmas atque cohortes excitant, ut crabronum & muscarum instar, vel pungant veros Christi praecones, vel imbelli, clamosa tamen stridore illis obstrepant. Et haec quidem impune passim fiunt inter eos, qui Christi nomine & merito gloriantur. Atqui mirum videri poterat, mundum totum in vno Christo oppugnando consentire posse, qui in caeteris omnibus dissentiunt, & in novas quotidie sectas & diversa scelerum studia scindutur. Sed mirum aut insolens hoc non est, quando constat natura dissidere lucem & tenebras, veritatem & mendacium, iustitiam & iniustitiam. Et iampridem Christum dixisse scimus, quod mundus hic spiritum veritatis percipere non possit. Vehementer ergo falluntur, qui hodie vniuersalem in veritatis doctrina consensum sibi pollicentur, & nihil interea de religione & salutis ratione a quoquam constituendum esse censent. Nec enim ingenium suum mundus mutabit, & quo propius hic ad finem suum accedit, eo magis in illo accendetur contradicendi studium, sicuti Christi vaticinia de nouissimis temporibus abunde testantur. Quare dissidijs et pugnis hisce nemo offendi debet, ea potius constanter teneant pij, quae scripturis traduntur, neque se abstrahi sinant a lapide fundamenti, Iesu Christo, qui & Veritas & lux est, neque eos aberrare finit, qui eius vestigijs insistunt. Solet́ praeterea, quod etsi plerique contradicant Christo, habet tamen ille suos quoq; discipulos, qui portenti quidem instar sunt (vt Isaias dicebat) in hoc mundo, sed in ipsis ille triumphat & regnat.
units.tr: But Simeon adds something else, by which he teaches that not only will many stumble over this rock, but also that some will openly contradict it and set themselves against him in hostility. For, he says, "behold, this child is set for a sign which shall be spoken against." There is a metaphor in these words, taken from archers, and the sense is this: just as an archer has a mark or target that everyone aims at and directs his arrows toward, so Christ will be like a target, which men of every place and rank will attack in order to overthrow his teaching and draw men away from him. How truly this was foretold by the divine old man, the histories of all ages bear witness. To begin with the Jews: as soon as he began to make himself known to the world, there arose men who contradicted him, and not ordinary men either, but scribes, priests and Pharisees, who then held supreme authority in sacred matters and enjoyed the highest reputation for learning and holiness. Nor did they do this only individually; on more than one occasion they condemned him and his teaching by the public and ecclesiastical authority of a council. Indeed, not content with raising an outcry against his teaching, they even slandered his miracles, though these were useful to the whole people and free from every trace of deceit and fraud. And lest anyone think that this contradiction was a slight one, they called him not merely a trifler but a pestilent seducer, a seditious man, a Samaritan and a demoniac. As this began among the Jews, so the same thing was afterwards practised among the Gentiles, when Christ was preached among them. For then philosophers rose up against the apostles and their successors, and tried to bring the doctrine about Christ into contempt and doubt with their sophistries. Servants of kings and emperors joined them in this work, and they brought false charges against all Christians, and there is no crime so wicked or so unheard of that it was not laid against them. For they were said to slaughter infants and to feed on human flesh. Nor were there lacking those who declared that the Roman Empire could not be safe unless those were rooted out who were enemies both of the sacred rites and of the laws, and who stirred up the anger of the gods against the whole world. Thus, whatever public misfortune befell, the cry at once went up that Christians were to be seized and thrown to the lions, to the stakes, to the galleys, to the mines. I say nothing now of the public edicts in which the Roman emperors condemned Christ and his gospel. And lest outsiders alone should give the Church trouble, heretics arose among the Christians themselves, who with monstrous and impious inventions, and with a spite more than diabolical, loosed their tongues against Christ and the purer doctrine of the truth. If anyone wished to enumerate the slanders, deceits and lies of all these men, he would hardly ever find an end of speaking. And what was done of old is still done everywhere today. For the Jews still continue to contradict Christ, and even now they do not acknowledge the hand of him by whose just and merciful judgment they feel themselves pressed down and cast into the utmost miseries. The Mahometans, who occupy by far the greater part of the world, mix their own slanders with these. Every day the Servetian dogs bark against the Son of God, co-essential with the eternal Father, and as many as now revive by postliminy the heresies of Arius, Marcion, Eutyches or others. Indeed, the pontiffs and bishops who claim for themselves the helm of the Church think they cannot be saved with their possessions unless they contradict Christ speaking to us through the gospel, and cast him down from his throne. Under their standards, in their marshes, the monks croak against him, the sacrificing priests bellow, the Purgatory ravens caw, the sepulchral owls howl, the nuns and Beguines hiss like serpents and snakes, and finally the Roman asses and mules bray. All of these together stir up on every side troops and cohorts of nobles and commoners alike, so that, like hornets and flies, they either sting the true heralds of Christ or drown them out with feeble but noisy buzzing. And these things are done with impunity everywhere among those who boast in the name and merit of Christ. Yet it might seem a marvel that the whole world could agree in attacking Christ alone, when it disagrees in everything else, and is split daily into new sects and diverse pursuits of wickedness. But this is neither marvellous nor strange, since it is well established that light and darkness, truth and falsehood, justice and injustice are by nature at odds. And we know that Christ said long ago that this world cannot receive the Spirit of truth. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who today promise themselves a universal agreement on the doctrine of truth, and meanwhile think that nothing about religion and the way of salvation needs to be settled by anyone. For the world will not change its nature, and the nearer it comes to its end, the more its zeal for contradiction will be kindled, as the prophecies of Christ about the last times abundantly testify. Wherefore no one ought to be offended by these disputes and conflicts. Rather let the godly hold firmly to those things which are handed down in the Scriptures, and not allow themselves to be drawn away from the cornerstone, Jesus Christ, who is the truth and the light, nor allow those to lead them astray who walk in his footsteps. Moreover, although many contradict Christ, he has also his disciples, who are indeed (as Isaiah said) a wonder in this world, but in them he triumphs and reigns.

units.la: Porro vt ad Simeonem redeamus vnum adhuc adijcit ille, quod ad Mariam in primis pertinebat: Quin & tuam ipsius animam traijciet gladius, vt detegantur ex multis cordibus cogitationes. Ex quibus verbis mira quaedam de compassione Mariae fabulati sunt Monachi, vt mulierculis lachrymas mouerent, simulq;, eadem facilius pecuniis emungerent. Ideo non contenti verbis picturas quoque produxerunt, in quibus illa multis gladijs circundata fingitur, quorum mucrones omnes ad illius cor diriguntur. Sed sunt haec ineptiora, quam vt inter Christianos audiri mereantur. Adhaec a Simeonis instituto aliena sunt, qui etsi certamina imminere praedicat, illam tamen ad inuictam fidei constantiam exhortari & praemunire vult, quam in illa incomparabilem fuisse, ex passionis historia apparet. Sensus ergo est: Non leues erunt pugnae, quas hic filius tuus subibit: sed eo vsq; exardebunt, vt tu quoq; acutissimos corde tuo dolores sentias, quando illum indigna & infami morte tolli videbis. Quapropter quoad hoc seculum, tibi ex illo non opes, nō honores, non voluptates aut otium polliceberis: sed vt ad certamina haec grauissima te armis fidei & constantiae induas necesse est. Et sane negari non debet, Mariam dolore immenso vulneratam, eiusque fidem grauissimè tentatam fuisse, quando filium flagris antea concissum inter latrones sublimem in dira cruce pendere, & omnium lu dibrijs expositum esse, simulq; Centurionem & armatas militum cohortes vndique circumstrepere videbat. Sed ea illam tunc nimis muliebriter dixisse aut fecisse negamus, quae Monachi finxerunt. Fuit enim in ea fidei virtus maior, quam vt eo vsq; deijci potuerit. Habet autem hic quoq; locus generalem doctrinam, eos qui Christo per fidem insiti sunt, in hoc mundo crucem & omnis generis aduersa manere, neq; tamen in ijs desperandum esse, quasi Dei nobis irati sint indicia. Si enim matrem dilectissimam tam acerbo dolore compungi voluit Christus, nimium nos iniqui erimus, si dolorem omne procul a nobis cupiamus profligari. Hoc ergo nobis certò persuasum sit, nos eo grauiora in mundo passuros esse, quò propius & arctius Christo coniuncti fuerimus. Nam vt mundus ipse nos tanto maiori odio persequetur, & aequum est, vt Deus ad sui nominis gloriam grauioribus certaminibus eos obijciat, quos donis pluribus ornauit. Neq; id nobis durum videri debet, quando nos olim in caelesti regno filij Dei coheredes fore certò scimus.
units.tr: Further, to return to Simeon, he adds one thing more, which pertained especially to Mary: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thine own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." From these words the monks have invented marvellous tales about Mary's compassion, so as to move silly women to tears and at the same time to draw money more easily from them. Not content with words, they have therefore also produced pictures, in which she is depicted surrounded by many swords, all of whose points are directed at her heart. But these things are too silly to deserve a hearing among Christians. Moreover, they are foreign to the purpose of Simeon, who, although he foretells conflicts to come, wishes to exhort and fortify her toward that unconquered constancy of faith which she showed in an incomparable degree, as the history of the Passion makes plain. The sense, therefore, is this: "The struggles which this son of yours will undergo will not be light; but they will blaze so fiercely that you too will feel the sharpest pains in your heart, when you see him taken away by an unworthy and infamous death. Therefore, for as long as this age lasts, you will not expect from him wealth, honours, pleasures or ease, but it is necessary that you arm yourself with the weapons of faith and constancy for these most grievous struggles." And indeed it must not be denied that Mary was wounded by immense grief, and that her faith was most severely tested, when she saw her son, previously torn with scourges, hanging high on the dreadful cross among thieves and exposed to the mockery of all, while the centurion and armed bands of soldiers clamoured on every side. But we deny that she said or did in that moment anything too womanish, such as the monks have invented. For there was in her a virtue of faith too great to be cast down to that extent. This place also contains a general teaching: that those who have been grafted into Christ by faith must remain in this world under the cross and adversities of every kind, and yet they must not despair on that account, as if they were signs of God's anger against them. For if Christ willed that his most beloved mother should be pierced with such bitter grief, we shall be far too unjust if we wish all sorrow to be banished far from us. Let this therefore be firmly persuaded in us: that we shall suffer the more grievous things in the world the nearer and more closely we are joined to Christ. For the world itself will persecute us with so much the greater hatred, and it is fitting that God, for the glory of his name, should expose to heavier conflicts those whom he has adorned with more gifts. Nor should this seem hard to us, since we know for certain that we shall one day be fellow heirs of the sons of God in the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Sed aliam quoq; crucis Christi & membrorum eius causam indicat Simeon: Vt nimirum detegantur ex multis cordibus cogitationes. Est enim cor hominis (vt propheta ait) profundum & inscrutabile, quodq; soli Deo pateat, qui ideo corda & renes nouisse dicitur. Idem tamen abstrusas cogitationes hominum quasi in lucem protrahit, quādo vel Christus purè praedicatur, vel propter eius praedicationem periculā incidunt. Priusquam enim Christus illucesçat, eadem fere hominum de religione
units.tr: But Simeon also points to another cause of the cross of Christ and of his members: namely, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. For the heart of man is (as the prophet says) deep and unsearchable, and it lies open to God alone, who is therefore said to know the heart and the reins. Nevertheless, the Lord brings hidden thoughts of men, as it were, into the light whenever Christ is preached purely or whenever dangers arise because of his preaching. For before Christ dawns, the opinions of men about the

units.la: gione
units.tr: (the end of the word "religion")

units.la: Ioan. 14. ligione sententia, eadem mens & voluntas esse videtur. At quando ille prædicatur, electi quidem pastoris huius vocem agnoscunt & sequuntur, reprobi verò eam non solùm negligunt, sed si fortius vrgeantur, ius animo concipiunt, & aduersus Dei verbum hostiliter insurgunt. Ita fit, vt qui regnan te superstitione sanctissimi putabantur, tunc se apertos Dei hostes et mortalium impiissimos esse prodant. Factum hoc Christi tempore, quando meretrices & publicani illum docentem audiuerunt, & fide vera amplexi sunt, impie aduersus eum pugnantibus pharisæis, qui optimi & sanctissimi prius habiti fuerant. Et hodie hoc ipsum pasim est videre. Quem enim ardenti fide recipiunt multi, qui prius ab omni religione alienissimi erant, eum ferro & igne persequuntur Monachi & horum discipuli, qui prius mundo mortui esse videbantur. Fit idem, si quando inter ipsos Euangelij professores de graviore aliquo dogmate dissensio oriatur. Tunc enim papisticum fermentum in multorum animus adhuc latere deprehenditur, quos prius perfecta Christi notitia instructos esse dixisses. In primis tamen hoc accidit, si quæ grauior tentatio ex persecutione & apertis Christi hostibus oritur. Nam tunc quoq; turpiter deficiunt sæpe, qui Ecclesiæ columnæ & bases videbantur, cum è contra strenuos Christi milites & intrepidos gloriæ eius vindices videas, qui antea vix tyronum loco habebantur. Specimen eius rei in morte Christi luculentissimū habemus: quando Petrus feruentissimus ille fidei propugnator cum alijs discipulis nescio vbi abstrusus latuit, Nicodemus verò et Iosephus noua animi fiducia confirmati Christum è cruce ablatum honorificæ sepulturæ mandarunt. Quid autem de latrone dicemus, qui ex cruce eius innocentiam & diuinam atq; saluificam virtutem publicè prædicat, quem paulò ante Petrus turpiter negarat? Sunt hæc Dei iudicia admirabilia, quorum exempla nobis ideo proponi cogitemus, vt neq; de nobis ipsis temere quid polliceamur, neq; aliquem hominum præcipiti sententia damnemus. Probè autem memores simus eorum, quæ toto suo vaticinio Simeon tradidit, & itanos ad omnem huius vitæ euentū præparemus, vt quando in magno illo die omnium cogitationes detegentur, nos cum vnigenito Dei filio, Iesu Christo, in cœlis æternum viuamus & regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: John 14. (the end of the word "religion"): the opinion, the mind and the will of men seem to be the same. But when he is preached, the elect indeed recognise the voice of this shepherd and follow it, while the reprobate not only neglect it but, if they are pressed harder, conceive hatred in their minds and rise up hostilely against the word of God. So it comes about that those who were thought most holy while they were ruled by superstition then reveal themselves as open enemies of God and the most impious of mortals. This happened in Christ's time, when harlots and tax collectors heard him teaching and embraced him in true faith, while the Pharisees, who had previously been regarded as the best and most holy, fought against him impiously. And today the same thing may be seen everywhere. Those whom many receive with burning faith, people who had previously been most alien to all religion, are persecuted with sword and fire by the monks and their disciples, who had previously seemed dead to the world. The same happens if a more serious dispute over some doctrine arises among the professors of the gospel themselves. For then the Papist leaven is found still to lie hidden in the minds of many whom you would have said were previously furnished with a complete knowledge of Christ. Above all, this happens if some heavier trial arises from persecution and from the open enemies of Christ. For then many, who seemed to be the pillars and foundations of the Church, often fail shamefully, whereas on the contrary you may see strenuous soldiers of Christ and fearless defenders of his glory, who were scarcely regarded as beginners before. We have a most striking example of this in the death of Christ: when Peter, that most fervent champion of the faith, lay hidden with the other disciples somewhere out of sight, Nicodemus and Joseph, strengthened by a new courage of mind, gave Christ, taken down from the cross, an honourable burial. But what shall we say of the thief, who from the cross publicly proclaims his innocence and divine and saving power, whom Peter had shamefully denied a little before? These are the wonderful judgments of God, and we should consider their examples set before us so that we neither rashly promise anything about ourselves nor condemn anyone with hasty judgment. Let us rather be mindful of what Simeon handed down in his whole prophecy, and so prepare ourselves for every outcome of this life, that when on that great day the thoughts of all are revealed, we may live and reign for ever in the heavens with the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXIII.

units.la: Erat etiam quædam Anna prophetissa, filia Phanuelis, ex tribu Aser: hæc processerat in multam ætatem, postquam vixisset cum viro annis septem à virginitate sua. Et cum esset vidua quasi annorum octoginta quatuor, non abscedebat à templo, ieiunijs ac deprecationibus seruiens Deo noctem & diem. Hæc igitur cum ea ipsa hora superuenisset, vicissim confitebatur Domino, & loquebatur de eo omnibus, qui expectabant redemptionem in Hierusalem. At illi vt perfecerunt omnia secundum Legem Domini, reuersi sunt in Galilæam, in ciuitatem suam Nazareth. Puerulus autem crescebat, & corroborabatur spiritu, implebatur sapientia, & gratia Dei erat super ipsum.
units.tr: There was also a certain prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in years, having lived with a husband for seven years from her virginity. And since she was a widow of about eighty-four years, she did not depart from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers night and day. And coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord in turn and spoke of him to all who were waiting for the redemption in Jerusalem. When they had done everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth. The little child, however, grew and was strengthened in spirit, was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.

units.la: Quanquam Iesu Christus, æternus Dei filius & ipsissima Veritas sit, & proinde ab homine testimonium non accipiat, neq; etiam opus habeat, vt hominum testimonijs commendetur: propter nos tamen illum à multis prædicari oportuit, vt facilius ipsum recipiamus, & eum absq; omni personarum respectu ad omnis loci & ordinis homines sciamus pertinere. Et hæc causa est, ob quam Lucas omnis generis testimonia ex ordine commemorat, quæ diuersæ multum conditionis homines illi perhibuerunt. Audiuimus enim Ioannem infantulum adhuc in vtero matris delitescentem de illo testatum fuisse. Fecerunt idem Zacharias sacerdos & eius vxor Elizabet, coniuges sanctissimi, pastores item, homines illiterati & à dolo alieni, Simeon Senex probus & pius, adhæ Magi ex Oriente in hunc finem adducti, quibus ex parte succinuerunt scribæ & sacerdotes ab Herode de eius natali loco interrogati. Potest ℨ his ipsa Virgo mater adnumerari, quæ procul dubio quod ex Angelo audiuerat, Iosepho sponso suo retulit, vt iam de eius Cantico nihil dicamus, quo totum hoc negotium complexa est ℨ. Et Iosephum quoque ab Angelo de re tota edoctum fuisse audiuimus, qui etiam ipse non sibi soli seruauit, quæ ex illo didicerat. At ne quod hominum genus deesset, additur his omnibus vidua quoque, ætate grauis & multa pietate celebris, Anna nimirum, cuius testimonium in prima huius loci parte describitur: cui posteà Iesu pueritiam Lucas subijcit.
units.tr: Although Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God and very Truth itself, does not receive testimony from man, nor has any need to be commended by the testimonies of men, nevertheless it was fitting that he should be proclaimed by many, so that we might more readily receive him, and know that he belongs to men of every place and rank, without any respect of persons. This is the reason why Luke recounts in order every kind of testimony that people of very different conditions gave to him. For we have heard that John, while still a babe hidden in his mother's womb, bore witness concerning him. Zacharias the priest and his wife Elizabeth, a most holy couple, did the same; so did the shepherds, unlearned men free from deceit; so did Simeon, an upright and devout old man; and also the Magi, brought from the East to this end, and, in part, the scribes and priests whom Herod questioned about the place of his birth. To these the Virgin mother herself may be added, who without doubt related to her betrothed, Joseph, what she had heard from the angel; not to mention her Canticle, in which she embraced the whole matter. We have also heard that Joseph was taught the whole business by an angel, and he too did not keep to himself what he had learned from him. Lest any kind of people be missing, a widow is added to all these as well, advanced in age and renowned for great piety, namely Anna, whose testimony is described in the first part of this passage, and after whom Luke adds the childhood of Jesus.

units.la: Rursus autem à persona descriptione orditur, in qua omnia dicit, quæ secundum Rhetorum leges in hominis commendationem dici possunt. Nam etsi Dei veritas minimè pendeat ab hominum authoritate, neque etiam hac nitatur fidei & salutis nostræ certitudo, non dissimulat tamen Spiritus sanctus seruorum Dei virtutes, quo minus habeant calumniandi occasionem impij, & ut doceat simul quibus studijs ipsi quoque fidem nostram Deo & hominibus probare debeamus. Primò autem prophetissam fuisse scribit, quo nomine non vulgaris verbi Dei in scripturis revelati cognitio aut diuinæ voluntatis studium, sed singulare donum Spiritus sancti significatur, quo instructa non solum veteres prophetias intellexit, sed privatim quoque de multis admonita est, quæ illis temporibus cognitu & observatu necessaria erant. Quàmuis enim post Malachiam nullus extitisse legatur, qui munus prophetandi publicum obiret, voluit tamen subinde aliquos extare Deus privatos homines, in quibus veteris doni virtus sese exerceret, per quos & pij privatim in spe & expectatione Messiæ confirmarentur, & quorum exemplo atque authoritate Sacerdotum & Scribarum audacia siue impietas aliqua ex parte coerceretur. Et talis illo tempore Simeon fuit, de quo nuper diximus, talis etiam fuit Anna hæc cum pauculis alijs, quos propter sui populi reliquias Deus donis præstantioribus instruxit. Facit autem hoc in primis ad commendationem testimonij, quod illa de Christo tulit. Quia enim prophetissa fuit, non humanum figmentum censeri debet, aut deliræ anus somnium, quod illa dixit, sed hoc omne ex Spiritus sancti suggestione dictum esse firmiter tenendum est. Deinde natales eius indicat, & filiam Phanuelis fuisse ait, hominis nimirum non obscuri (nam talium nomina apponere ridiculum & superuacaneum esset) ex tribu Aser. Et sane, cum iampridem tribuum confusio cœpisset (ut alibi diximus) non obscuros & abiectos omnino fuisse oportuit eos, quorum genus & maiores certò ostendi poterant. Tertiò pueritiam & adolescentiam vnà cum educatione à primis annis vno quasi verbo comprehendit, quando eam septem annis à virginitate sua cum viro suo vixisse scribit. Ita enim dotet, eam à primis annis pudicè & castè educatam fuisse, ut illæso virginitatis pudore ad maritum, cui legitimè desponsa fuerat, accesserit, & cum eodem annos septem transegerit, ea morum probitate & fidei coniugalis integritate, quæ matronam piam & honestam decet. Quartò conditionem eius, quæ tunc erat, ostendit. Nam viduam annorum octoginta quatuor fuisse ait: ex quo apparet, eam ætate adhuc integra maritum amisisse, quod magnum pudicitiæ singularis argumentum est. Constat enim viduas iuniores plerunque ad libidinem proclives secundas nuptias appetere, et multa facere petulantius, nisi novo coniugij fræno coerceantur. Quod Paulus obseruans tales Ecclesiæ nequaquam obtrudendas, sed remittendas esse monebat, ut nubant, viris obediant & domum administrent. Fuit ergo rara & singularis hæc Annæ virtus, quòd optimam & præstantissimam ætatis partem ad extremam usq; senectam absq; omni publica reprehensione transfigere potuit. Postremò studia quoq; eius recenset, quibus toto illo tempore dedita fuit. Non abscedebat (inquit) à templo, ieiunijs & deprecationibus, seruiens Deo noctem & diem. Putant aliqui eam ex illa rum numero fuisse, quæ totæ Deo sacræ ad ostium tabernaculi excubabant, de quibus in Lege sermo est, & quas olim à filijs Heli corruptas fuisse in historia Samuelis scribitur. Sed cum incertum sit, an mos ille ad Christi aduentum vsque duraret, verisimilius est hoc per Hyperbolem dici, & sensum esse, quòd vitam omnem Deo consecrauerit, seque totam addixerit verè pietatis exercitijs, ut quodammodo nunquam à templo abscedere videretur. Si enim hac rigidius secundùm literam accipere velimus, Lucam sibi ipsi contradicentem fingemus, qui paulo post dicet eam illo ipso temporis articulo superuenisse, cùm Simeon suum de puerulo Iesu vaticinium proferret. Quomodo autem superue nire potuit, si nunquam discedebat? Quo sensu etiam intelligi debet, quòd ieiunijs & deprecationibus Deo seruiuisse dicitur dies & noctes. Nec enim dubium est, quin cibum quoque sumpserit ad vitam sustentandam necessarium, sommo item locum dederit, quando sine hoc nullis laboribus & studijs possumus sufficere. Commendat ergo eam Lucas ab assiduo pietatis studio, & quòd reliquis, quoad eius fieri potest, omnibus alijs actionibus hoc vnum curarit, ut publicè quidem sacris communibus interesset, & Deum precibus communibus placaret, priuatim verò domi cum precibus sobrietatem piam temperantiam coniungeret, ne praui carnalium affectuum motus susceptum pietatis studium turbarent. Fuerunt haec paulò diligentius explicanda, ut maioris apud nos ponderis sit fœminæ tot virtutibus illustris testimonium, & quòd in eius exemplo multa continentur, quæ ad formandos mores & veræ pietatis siue religionis doctrinam plurimum faciunt.
units.tr: Again, he begins with a description of the person, in which he says everything that, according to the rules of the rhetoricians, can be said in commendation of a man. For although the truth of God does not depend at all on the authority of men, and the certainty of our faith and salvation does not rest on it, the Holy Spirit nonetheless does not conceal the virtues of the servants of God, so that the wicked may have no occasion to slander, and so that he may at the same time teach us by what pursuits we too ought to commend our faith to God and to men. He writes first that she was a prophetess, a name which signifies not the ordinary knowledge of the Word of God revealed in the Scriptures, nor zeal for the divine will, but a singular gift of the Holy Spirit, by which she was equipped not only to understand the ancient prophecies, but was also privately admonished about many things that were necessary to know and to observe in those times. For although we read that after Malachi no one arose who discharged the office of prophesying publicly, God nevertheless willed that from time to time there should be some private persons in whom the power of the ancient gift might show itself, through whom the godly might be privately confirmed in the hope and expectation of the Messiah, and by whose example and authority the boldness or some impiety of the priests and scribes might in part be restrained. Such a man was Simeon, of whom we spoke recently, and such also was this Anna, along with a few others whom God, for the sake of the remnant of his people, endowed with more excellent gifts. Now this serves especially to commend the testimony which she bore concerning Christ. For since she was a prophetess, what she said is not to be regarded as a human fabrication, or the dream of a crazed old woman, but all of it must firmly be held to have been spoken by the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Then he indicates her ancestry, and says that she was the daughter of Phanuel, a man evidently not obscure (for to list the names of such persons would be ridiculous and superfluous), of the tribe of Asher. And indeed, since the confusion of the tribes had begun long before (as we have said elsewhere), those whose family and forebears could be certainly shown had to be men not obscure and altogether abject. Third, he summarises her childhood and youth, together with her upbringing from her earliest years, in what is almost a single word, when he writes that she lived with her husband seven years from her virginity. For he means that she had been brought up chastely and modestly from her earliest years, so that, with the modesty of her virginity unharmed, she came to the husband to whom she had been lawfully betrothed, and spent seven years with him, with that integrity of character and that faithfulness of marriage which befit a devout and honourable matron. Fourth, he sets forth her condition at that time. For he says that she was a widow of eighty-four years: from which it appears that, while still of unimpaired age, she lost her husband, which is a great proof of singular chastity. For it is well known that younger widows are generally prone to lust and eager for second marriages, and do many things more wantonly, unless they are restrained by the new yoke of marriage. Paul, observing this, warned that such women were by no means to be enrolled in the Church, but were to be sent away, that they should marry, obey their husbands, and manage the household. This virtue of Anna was therefore rare and singular, that she could spend the best and most excellent part of her life up to extreme old age without any public reproach. Last, he also recounts the pursuits to which she was devoted throughout that whole time. She did not depart (he says) from the temple, with fastings and prayers, serving God night and day. Some think that she was one of those women who kept watch, wholly consecrated to God, at the door of the tabernacle, of whom the Law speaks, and who, as is written in the history of Samuel, were once corrupted by the sons of Eli. But since it is uncertain whether that custom lasted until the coming of Christ, it is more probable that this is said by hyperbole, and that the meaning is that she consecrated her whole life to God and devoted herself entirely to the exercises of true piety, so that in a way she seemed never to depart from the temple. For if we wish to take these words more rigidly according to the letter, we shall be making Luke contradict himself, since he says a little later that she came up at that very moment when Simeon was uttering his prophecy about the child Jesus. But how could she have come up, if she never departed? In the same sense must it also be understood that she is said to have served God day and night with fastings and prayers. For there is no doubt that she also took food necessary for sustaining life, and likewise gave place to sleep, since without this we cannot sustain any labours and studies. Luke therefore commends her for her constant devotion to piety, and because, so far as it was possible, she attended to this one thing in all her other activities: that she took part publicly in the common sacred assemblies and appeased God with common prayers, while privately at home she joined with prayers sobriety, pious temperance, lest the wicked movements of carnal affections should disturb the devotion she had undertaken. These matters needed to be explained somewhat more carefully, so that the testimony of a woman illustrious for so many virtues may carry greater weight with us, and because many things are contained in her example which contribute greatly both to the formation of morals and to the teaching of true piety or religion.

units.la: Occurrit in his primùm, quòd tria vitæ genera Annæ tribuuntur. Nam & virgo vixit, & coniunx fuit per annos septem, & postremò vidua mansit annis quasi octoginta quatuor. Ita autem in gulorum meminit Spiritus sanctus, vt nullû ex ijs reprehendat, imò in singulis ostendat, quod ad illius commendationem facit. Ergo neq; virginitas, neq; coniugium, neq; cælibatus siue viduitas per se aliquam reprehensionem merentur, neq; nos à regno Dei abstrahunt. Vt enim virginitas nobiscum nascitur, & in se bona atq; sancta est: sic coniugium Dei institutum est bonum & sanctum, & idem ille nobis viduitatis author est, quando coniugem nobis aufert. Et cum Anna in omnibus hisce vitæ generibus sanctè et inculpatè vixerit, Deoq; grata et accepta fuerit, non dubium est, quin hoc ipsum omnibus liceat, vt vel virgines maneant, vel coniugij vinculum subeant, vel vidui aut cœlibes ad extremum vsq; viuant, nisi peculiari Dei vocatione aliud iubeantur. Nam quia non est personarum respectus apud Deum, & in Christo non est seruus aut liber, non mas aut fœmina, non princeps aut subditus, sequitur nos quoq; propter nullum vitæ genus, quod per se sanctum & honestum est, illi displicere posse: sed hoc à nobis requiri, vt in Christo Iesu renati et noua creatura facti, sanctè viuamus, & officij probè memores simus, quod in vnaquaq; vocatione à nobis exigitur. Est hoc diligenter observandum propter nimios virginitatis & cœlibatus admiratores, qui hæc duo vitæ genera sic commendant, vt coniugio vix locum aliquem honestum inter Christianos relinquant. Nam quamuis hoc ad humani generis conseruationem necessarium esse fateantur, eos tamen qui coniugio operam dant, in carne viuere aiunt, & proinde Deo placere non posse. Et quia durum atq; impossibile erat omnes homines ab illo reuocare, hoc saltem efficere studuerunt, vt ijs non liceret matrimonium contrahere, qui ad aliquod Ecclesiæ ministerium sunt destinati. Fuit hoc egregium Satanæ stratagema, qui cùm non ignoraret dictum illud Dei, Non est bonum, hominem esse solum: curauit vt sub plausibili castitatis & pudicitiæ prætextu eos stuprus, adulterijs & omni libidinis genere infames & contemptos faceret, qui suo exemplo omnibus aliis pudicitiæ & honestatis magistri esse debebant: imò eadem opera religionem quoq; & vniuersum Dei cultum in contemptum adducere studuit, vt non tam sacris ministerijs destinatos perderet, quàm eos etiam, qui per illos instituebantur. Quod Paulus olim præuidens graviter monuit, dæmoniorum doctrinam esse quæ coniugij vsus prohibetur. Fatemur equidem, quoad præsentem vitam commodius agere eos, qui dono virginitatis præditi nullis coiugij curis & molestijs distrahuntur. At quia donum hoc neq; omnibus commune est, neq; vt illud habeamus in nostro arbitrio situm est, simulq; constat eos qui illo destituuntur graviter viri & turpissimis desiderijs atque cogitationibus turbari; nimis periculosum & iniquum fuerit, aliquem ad hoc capessendû cogere, quod neq; tu ei dare potes, neq; si posses ille accipere potest, nisi singulari Dei gratia iuuetur. Itaq; non minori diligentia nobis obseruandi sunt scripturæ loci, quibus coniugij vsus commendatur, & tenendā semper Apostoli regula: Propter fornicationes, suam quisq; vxorem habeat, & propriùm quæq; virum habeat. Quòd si qui hanc libertatem in nobis damnare volent, meminerint quàso illi, non nos huius primos authores siue vsurpatores esse, sed pro nobis stare Dei institutum, cuius studiosissimos fuisse constat omnes fere eos, qui in vtroq; testamento veræ pietatis nomine commendantur.
units.tr: The first point to notice here is that three kinds of life are attributed to Anna. She lived as a virgin, she was a wife for seven years, and finally she remained a widow for about eighty-four years. The Holy Spirit mentions each of these states without blaming any of them, and in each he shows something that adds to her commendation. Therefore neither virginity, nor marriage, nor celibacy or widowhood is in itself deserving of blame, and none of them shuts us out of the kingdom of God. Virginity is born with us and is good and holy in itself. Marriage was instituted by God as good and holy, and the same God is the author of widowhood when he takes a spouse from us. Since Anna lived holily and blamelessly in all these states of life, and was pleasing and acceptable to God, there is no doubt that all people are free to remain virgins, or to enter the bond of marriage, or to live as widows or unmarried to the end, unless God calls them by a particular vocation to do otherwise. For there is no respect of persons with God, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free, male nor female, prince nor subject. It follows that God cannot be displeased with us on account of any state of life which is holy and honourable in itself. What is required of us is that, being born again in Christ Jesus and made a new creature, we live holily and faithfully remember the duty that is laid upon us in each calling. This must be carefully observed because of the excessive admirers of virginity and celibacy, who so commend these two states that they leave hardly any honourable place for marriage among Christians. For although they admit that marriage is necessary for the preservation of the human race, they say that those who devote themselves to marriage live in the flesh and therefore cannot please God. And since it was hard and impossible to call all people back from marriage, they have at least tried to bring it about that those destined for some ministry of the Church should not be permitted to marry. This was an outstanding stratagem of Satan. Though he was not ignorant of that saying of God, "It is not good for man to be alone," he saw to it that under the plausible pretext of chastity and purity he made infamous and contemptible, through fornication, adultery and every kind of lust, those who ought by their example to be teachers of purity and honesty to all others. Indeed, by the same means he sought to bring religion itself and the whole worship of God into contempt, so that he destroyed not so much those destined for the sacred ministries as those who were instructed through them. Paul foresaw this long ago and warned gravely that it is "a doctrine of demons" to forbid the use of marriage. We grant indeed that, as far as the present life goes, those who are endowed with the gift of virginity live more conveniently, since they are not distracted by the cares and troubles of marriage. But since this gift is not common to all, and it does not lie in our power to have it, and since it is plain that those who lack it are grievously troubled by base desires and thoughts, it would be too dangerous and unjust to compel anyone to take up what you cannot give him, and what he cannot receive unless he is helped by a special grace of God. Therefore we must observe with no less diligence those passages of Scripture in which the use of marriage is commended, and always keep to the rule of the Apostle: "Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband." But if any wish to condemn this liberty in us, I beg them to remember that we are not the first authors or users of it, but that the institution of God stands on our side, and it is certain that almost all those who are commended in both Testaments for the name of true piety were most zealous for it.

units.la: Deinde continet Annæ exemplum omnia per omnes gradus sexus muliebris officia. Primò vir gopudica & casta ad maritum legitimum deuenit. Est hoc præcipuum, quod post religionem & diuini cultus studium in puellis requiritur: vt nimirum pudicitiæ suæ curam atq; ratione habeant diligentem, ne & seipsas turpiter prostituant, & maritos postea primo statim congressu sub sancto coniugij prætextu perfidè fallant. Nam vt hoc ab ea ætate & sexu alienissimum esse Lex naturæ admonet: ita constat Deum graue supplicium impudentibus illis constituisse, quæ illud facere audent. Sic enim Deut.22.ca.loquitur Moses: Si quis vxorem duxerit, & accesserit ad eam, atq; non inuenta fuerint apud ea signa virginitatis, ducent seniores ciuitatis puellā illā ad ostiū domus patris sui, obruentq; illam ciues ciuitatis illius lapidibus, vt moriatur: quia fecit nefas in Israel scortando in domo patris sui, & exures malū è medio tui. Plurimū ergo proderit, si religioni à teneris annis puellæ assuescant, domus amantes sint, loca publica deuitent, à spectaculis turpibus abstineant, omnem deniq; lasciuiæ speciem fugiant, quà impudentiores in vestitu, gestu, sermone & infinitis alijs rebus (vt nihil æquitia esse ingeniosius) vti consueuerunt. Deinde vbi viris connubiali vinculo coniunguntur, meminerint, se iam in virorum suorum ius transfuisse, quibus ipse Deus in vxores imperium concessit. Itaq; viros suos cum reuerentia diligant, fidem illis promissam inuiolatam & sanctam seruent, rem domesticam administrent summo studio, liberos suos sancte educent, & patienter ferant labores & molestias, quibus Deus coniugium propter nos grauauit, vt carnem plus æquo lasciuientem in officio contineat. Et hæc quidem non tunc solum præstanda esse sciant, si mariti illis obtingant comodi, & qui vicissim sui etiam officij memores sint: verumetiam iniquis & duris sese officiosas & obsequentes præbeant. Nec enim laudem merentur, quæ ex alienis peccatis occasionem peccandi arripiunt, sed quæ sua modestia & prudentia virorum morositatem corrigere & vincere satagunt. Probatur quidem in sacris literis Sara, quæ Abrahamum, virum omni virtute ornatissimum, amore fido persecuta est, & eum dominum suum agnouit. At non minor laus Abigaeli debetur, quæ Nabali, hominum ineptissimo & importuno nimis, fidelis fuit, & sui capitis periculo Dauidem illi imminentem placauit. Denique curent vxores, vt maritis suis decori & ornamento sint: quod tunc omnino fiet, si cum fide coniugali induştriam atq; modestiam coniungant. Quod si quæ abstersa pudore in libidinem feruntur, hæ & rem domesticam perdunt, & maritis quidem atq; suis omnibus infamiam, sibiipsis vero cum hac exitiü quoq; accersunt. Nec est, quod eiusmodi mulieres vel formæ, vel generis, vel opum fiducia sese extollant. Fluxa enim sunt hæc omnia, & nisi pietas morumq; probitas accedat, circulus aureus sunt in naribus porci, vt olim Solomon dicebat. Sed idem ille Prouer.cap. 31. prolixè describit vxoris fidæ & industriæ exemplum, quod sibi imitandu proponere debent, quæcunq; tam sibi ipsis quàm maritis suis consultum volunt. At si contingat, vt maritis hac vita defunctis ipsæ superstites sint, licet eis, vt vel ad secundas nuptias animum apponant & alijs viris nubant, vel vt in viduitate maneant. Nec enim eorum sententia admitti debet, qui ex singularibus exemplis eorû, quæ abstq; superstitione in viduitate manserunt, generalem doctrinam colligunt, & secundas nuptias damnant, cum et Dei Lex extet, quæ olim fratri defuncto ex relicta eius vxore semen suscitare iubebat: & Paulus innuptis & viduis omnibus dicat: Bonum & commodum quidem est eis, si sic manserint: sed si se non continent, nubant: nam satius est nubere quàm vri. Et exempla sunt Ruthæ & Abigaelis, atq; aliarum plurium, quæ cum propter fidem & pietatem in scripturis commendentur, viris tamen alijs absq; crimine coniugatæ fuerunt. Si cui verò vita cælebs arriserit, & à nuptijs abhorruerit, ante omnia illam meminisse oportet, se viri quidem legibus non amplius teneri, non autem ideo exlegem esse quoad Deum, quin potius eo magis sibi vigilandum esse, ne carnis lasciuientis cupiditatibus & diaboli illecebris circumuenta aliquid aduersus morum honestatem & Christianam sanctimoniam designet. Ideo Paulus olim monebat: Quæ verè vidua est ac sola, sperat in Deo, & permanet in deprecationibus & orationibus noctem & diem. Quibus addi debet, quòd idem omnibus fœminis iam ætate provectis præcipit, vt in statu qui sanctimoniam decet degant, non calumniatrices sint, non vino dedita, vtq; fœminas iuniores doctrina simul & exemplo ad honestatem instruant. Talem olim Iudith am fuisse legimus, tales Martha & Maria, Lazari sorores fuerunt, siue illæ virgines, siue viduæ fuerint: & talem in præsenti Annam fuisse Lucas scribit. Quarum exempla si quæ imitantur, illæ profectò multa laude dignæ sunt. Cauendum tamen in eo instituto diligenter sit, ne quæ superstitiosa huius status fiducia illas decipiat, aut ne dum maiora viribus suis suscipiunt, satanæ occasione præbeant & pudicitiæ iacturam faciant, vel (quod in primis damnat Apostolus) ne otiosæ domus circuire discant, imò nugaces & curiosæ garriunt quæ non decent. In summa, Annæ exemplum virgines, maritatæ & viduæ sibi applicent, vt ex eo decerpant, quod singularum vocationi conuenit, ne in solo postremo hærentes, quod de eius viduitate dicitur, stulta & præposterra æmulatione peccent, & à Deo sibi creditam stationem deserant.
units.tr: Next, the example of Anna contains all the duties of the female sex at every stage of life. First, a girl who is modest and chaste comes to a lawful husband. This is the chief thing required of girls, after religion and zeal for the worship of God: that they take diligent care and account of their chastity, so that they neither shamefully prostitute themselves nor afterwards deceive their husbands treacherously at the very first meeting under the holy pretext of marriage. For as the law of nature warns that this is most alien to that age and sex, so it is certain that God has appointed a grievous punishment for those shameless women who dare to do it. Moses speaks in this way in Deut. 22: "If anyone takes a wife and goes in to her, and no tokens of virginity are found in her, the elders of the city shall bring that girl to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones, so that she dies, because she has done wickedness in Israel by playing the harlot in her father's house; and you shall purge the evil from among you." It will therefore be of great benefit if girls are accustomed to religion from their tender years, love the home, avoid public places, keep away from shameful spectacles, and finally flee every appearance of wantonness, in which the more shameless are accustomed to indulge in dress, bearing, speech and countless other things (for nothing is more ingenious than wantonness). Then, when they are joined to men by the bond of marriage, let them remember that they have now passed under the authority of their husbands, to whom God himself has granted rule over wives. Let them therefore love their husbands with reverence, keep the faith promised to them inviolate and holy, manage the household with the utmost care, bring up their children holily, and patiently bear the labours and troubles with which God has burdened marriage for our sake, so that it may keep the flesh, which is too prone to wantonness, in its duty. And let them know that these things are to be done not only when their husbands are kind and mindful of their own duty in turn, but also that they should show themselves dutiful and obedient to husbands who are unjust and harsh. For those women do not deserve praise who seize on the sins of others as an occasion to sin, but those who by their own modesty and prudence strive to correct and overcome the moroseness of their husbands. Sarah is indeed praised in Holy Scripture, for she loved Abraham, a man adorned with every virtue, with faithful affection, and acknowledged him as her lord. Yet no less praise is due to Abigail, who was faithful to Nabal, a man most foolish and excessively troublesome, and at the risk of her own life appeased David, who was about to fall upon him. Finally, let wives take care to be an ornament and adornment to their husbands. This will certainly happen if they join industry and modesty to conjugal faithfulness. But if some women, having cast off shame, are carried away into lust, they ruin the household, and bring infamy upon their husbands and all their own people, and at the same time bring destruction upon themselves. Nor is there any reason why such women should exalt themselves in confidence of beauty, birth or wealth. For all these things are fleeting, and unless piety and integrity of character are added, they are, as Solomon once said, a gold ring in a swine's snout. But the same Proverbs, chapter 31, describes at length the example of a faithful and industrious wife, which all women who wish to provide for themselves and for their husbands should set before themselves to imitate. But if it happens that the husbands die and the wives survive them, they may either give their minds to second marriages and marry other men, or remain in widowhood. For the opinion of those should not be admitted who gather a general doctrine from the singular examples of those who remained in widowhood without superstition, and condemn second marriages, since God's law stands, which once commanded that a dead brother's seed be raised up from his widow, and Paul says to all the unmarried and widows: "It is good and useful for them if they remain as they are; but if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn." There are also the examples of Ruth and Abigail and many others, who, though they are commended in Scripture for faith and piety, were nevertheless lawfully married to other men. But if anyone who lives unmarried is pleased with that life and shrinks from marriage, it is above all necessary for her to remember that she is no longer bound by the law of the husband, but she is not therefore free from law as far as God is concerned. Rather, she must all the more watch over herself, lest, deceived by the lusts of the lascivious flesh and the enticements of the devil, she plan something against honesty of conduct and Christian holiness. Therefore Paul once admonished: "She who is truly a widow and alone hopes in God, and continues in supplications and prayers night and day." To this must be added that he also commands all women who are now advanced in age to live in a manner befitting holiness, not to be slanderers, not given to wine, and to teach younger women by doctrine and example alike to be honourable. We read that Judith was such a woman, and Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, were such women, whether they were virgins or widows; and Luke writes that Anna too was such a woman. If any women imitate their examples, they are certainly worthy of great praise. Yet in this way of life care must be taken that no superstitious confidence in this state deceives them, nor that, while they undertake greater things than their strength allows, they give Satan an opportunity and suffer loss of chastity; or (which the Apostle especially condemns) that they learn to go about idle from house to house, and indeed chatter about curious things that are not fitting. In sum, let virgins, married women and widows apply to themselves the example of Anna, so that from it they may take what belongs to the calling of each, and not, clinging only to the last point, which is said of her widowhood, sin by foolish and preposterous emulation, and desert the station entrusted to them by God.

units.la: Habemus præterea in Anna hac veræ religionis & pietatis typum, quem viri quoq;, adeoq; omnis sexus & ætatis homines imitari debent, vt Deo probari possit. Fuit illa Prophetissa, quo nomine et si donum spiritus singulare significetur (vt diximus) quod req; commune omnibus neq; etiam semper necessarium est, simul tamen prophetandi verbo studium scripturæ sacræ & verbi Dei denorari notari scimus, & in priori ad Corinth. prophetare dicuntur tà qui ipsius scripturæ oracula interpre tantur, quàm qui horū interpretes audiunt. Eo autè sensu prophetiæ studiū omnibus necessariū est, quia sine Dei verbo neq; fides nostra cōsistere, neq; cultus aliquis Deo probari potest. Ideo passim illud commendatur, & Christus Marthæ circa multa occupatæ vnum hoc necessarium esse dicebat, quod Maria sibi faciendum delegerat, quùm ad pedes eius considens Dei verbū ex illo audiret. Est ergo religionis & cultus diuini principiū verum verbi Dei studium, à quo quicunq; alieni sunt, ij neq; religiosi dici possunt, neq; salutis vnquam participes erunt. Deinde in templo frequens & assidua fuisse dicitur Anna, quo dicto omnia publica pietatis aut religionis exercitia comprehenduntur, quæ et Dei beneficia nobis repræsentant, et eiusdem promissiones nobis obsignant, nosq; nostri officij admonent, qualia apud veteres sacrificia & solennia festa aliqui ritus sacri fuerunt, hodie autè sacramentorum vsus est, qui ex Christi instituto in Ecclesijs obseruatur. Quæ omnia cum simul ad fidei cōfessionem pertineant, minimè negligi debent ab ijs, qui Dei cultores censeri volunt; quæ de re supra in circuncisionis Iesu Christi historia satis est dictum. Cæterùm non ea fuit apud Annā externi cultus fiducia, vt se omni pietatis officio defunctam putaret, si à templo vix vnquā abscederet, sed huius studio simul alia pietatis exercitia coniunxit. Nam Deo publicè & priuatim, adhæc dies noctesq; seruiuit ieiunijs & deprecationibus. Vbi deprecationū nomine multa simul comprehenduntur. Nam primo his fidem suam publicè testata est, cuius proprium opus esse inuocationem alibi diximus. Deinde non potuit huic supplex fieri, quin ei se totam subijceret atq; consecraret. Hinc ergo vitæ probitas & morum honestas atq; sanctimonia, quæ per omnes ætatis suæ gradus eluxit. Innuit præterea deprecationum vox, quòd infelicem populi conditionē miserata, calamitates quibus tunc passim premebantur deprecata sit, & Deum inuocarit, vt promissionum veterū memor Messiā daret, qui rebus afflictis opem ferret. In quibus omnibus vt feruentior esset, ieiunia coiunxit, quorū hunc vsum scriptura esse docet, non vt suo merito nobis Deum concilient (nam siue editis siue ieiunatis, non mihi sed vobis ieiunatis & editis, inquit ille) sed vt carni ferocienti frænum iniiciatur, vt vel inuita spiritui obtemperet. Ideo non ad aliqua ciborū discrimina, neq; ad certos dies olim ieiunia astrigebantur: sed tunc illa suscipiebant pij, quando vel publica aliqua necessitas preces ardentiores & feruentius pietatis studium exigebat (vt apud Ioelē est videre) vel ipsi priuatim sentiebant carnis affectus disciplina artiori reprimendos esse. Et de hoc Christus admonet, qui ieiunandum tunc esse dicit, quando sponsus à nobis discedit, idest, quādo ipsum minus apud nos posse videmus, et periculū est ne spiritus Christi in nobis per carnis petulantiā suffocetur, quantū in nobis est. In eo autē ieiunij genere omnia ea re mouentur, qui carnis ferociā augere possunt, cibi nimirum delicatiores, vini vsus immodicus, vestes molliores & ad fastū factæ, imò & thori coniugalis vsus, & quæcunq; aliæ voluptates per se honestæ & concessæ sunt. Ita Annam quoq; ieiunasse certū est: & proinde nihil faciunt hypocritæ, qui quoties de ieiunijs in scriptura agitur, de suis illis dici putant, quæ superstitioso ciborū discrimine constant, & certis diebus alligata sunt, & in quibus ipsi meritū boni operis constituunt, imò non postremā salutis fiduciā repositam habent. Scimus quidē non multò post Apostolorū tempora cœpisse ieiunandi consuetudinē solennem: sed non eadē huius ratio vbiq; locorum fuit, neq; legibus necessarijs quisquam piorū astringebatur, sed sufficiebat si quis ecclesiæ, qua cū viuebat, sese accōmodauisset, salua interim aliorū libertate. Nam vt D. Augustus scribit, alij sabbato ieiunabant, alij non item. Et idē D. Ambrosij, cuius sententiam ipse matris nomine requisierat, eiusmodi de hac re respōsum profert: Cùm Romam venio, ieiuno sabbato: cùm hic sum, non ieiuno. Sic etiā tu ad quam forte Ecclesiā veneris, eius more serua, si cuiquam non vis esse scandalo, nec quenquā tibi, & c. Hæc (inquā) piorum libertas fuit olim, quam posteris temporibus homines superstitiosi ineptis traditionibus astrinxerunt, quibus conscientiæ multorum grauiter excruciatæ sunt. Præstat ergo veterē & in scripturis traditum ieiuniorum vsum retinere, & curare vt tota vita sobrietatē Christianam referat, vt omni temporis momento ad omne opus bonū idonei simus. Et hæc illa religio vera & hæc illa pietas est, quam Paulus ad omnia vtilem esse, & tam præsentis quàm futurę vitæ promissiones habere ait.1. Tim.4.
units.tr: We have also in Anna a type of true religion and piety, which men too, and indeed people of every sex and age, ought to imitate, so that they may be pleasing to God. She was a prophetess. Although by this name a singular gift of the Spirit is signified (as we have said), which is neither common to all nor always necessary, we know that the zeal for prophesying also denotes the study of Scripture and of the Word of God. In the first epistle to the Corinthians, those who expound the oracles of Scripture themselves are said to prophesy, as are those who listen to their expositions. In this sense, zeal for prophecy is necessary for all, because without the Word of God our faith cannot stand, nor can any worship be pleasing to God. Therefore this is commended everywhere, and Christ said that Martha, busy with many things, needed only one thing, which Mary had chosen for herself, when she sat at his feet and heard the Word of God from him. So the true study of the Word of God is the beginning of religion and of worship, and those who are strangers to it cannot be called religious, and will never share in salvation. Next, Anna is said to have been frequent and constant in the temple, a phrase which comprehends all the public exercises of piety and religion. These both represent God's benefits to us, and seal his promises to us, and remind us of our duty. Among the ancients these were the sacrifices and solemn feasts and some sacred rites, and today it is the use of the sacraments, which are observed in the churches by Christ's institution. Since all these things pertain together to the confession of faith, those who wish to be counted worshippers of God ought by no means to neglect them; what needs to be said on this matter has been said sufficiently above, in the history of the circumcision of Jesus Christ. But Anna did not have such confidence in outward worship that she thought she had discharged every duty of piety if she hardly ever left the temple; rather, she joined other exercises of piety to her zeal. For she served God publicly and privately, and besides this, day and night, with fastings and supplications. Under the name of supplications many things are comprehended together. For first, by these she publicly testified her faith, and we have said elsewhere that invocation is its proper work. Next, she could not become a suppliant without wholly subjecting and consecrating herself to him. Hence came the integrity of her life, the honesty and holiness of her manners, which shone forth at every stage of her life. Moreover, the word "supplications" implies that, moved with pity for the unhappy condition of the people, she prayed against the calamities by which they were then everywhere oppressed, and called upon God, that, mindful of the ancient promises, he would give the Messiah, who would bring help to the afflicted. To make these prayers more fervent she joined fastings to them. Scripture teaches us the purpose of these: not that by their merit they win God for us (for, as he says, "whether you have feasted or fasted, you have done it not to me but to yourselves"), but that the wild flesh may be bridled and made to obey the spirit even against its will. Therefore in former times fasts were not bound to certain distinctions of food or to fixed days. Rather, the godly undertook them when either some public necessity demanded more fervent prayers and a more earnest zeal for piety (as may be seen in Joel), or they themselves privately felt that the desires of the flesh had to be restrained by a stricter discipline. Christ also reminds us of this, when he says that they must fast when the bridegroom is taken away from us, that is, when we see that he has less power among us, and there is danger that the Spirit of Christ in us will be suffocated, so far as lies in us, by the wantonness of the flesh. In this kind of fasting, all those things are to be set aside which can increase the wildness of the flesh: namely, more delicate foods, immoderate use of wine, softer clothing made for show, and indeed even the use of the marriage bed, and whatever other pleasures are in themselves honest and permitted. It is certain that Anna fasted in this way too. Therefore the hypocrites do nothing when, whenever fasting is discussed in Scripture, they think it refers to their own fasts, which consist in a superstitious distinction of foods, are bound to certain days, and in which they place the merit of good works, or even keep a chief confidence of salvation. We know indeed that not long after the times of the apostles the custom of solemn fasting began, but its reason was not the same everywhere, and no one among the godly was bound by necessary laws; it was enough if someone accommodated himself to the church with which he lived, while the liberty of others was preserved. For, as St. Augustine writes, some fasted on the Sabbath and others did not. St. Ambrose, whose opinion he had asked on his mother's behalf, gave this answer on the matter: "When I come to Rome, I fast on the Sabbath; when I am here, I do not fast. So too you, to whatever church you happen to come, keep its custom, if you do not wish to be a scandal to anyone, nor have anyone be one to you," and so forth. This, I say, was the liberty of the godly in former times, which in later times superstitious men bound with foolish traditions, by which the consciences of many were grievously tormented. It is better, therefore, to retain the ancient use of fasts, as handed down in the Scriptures, and to take care that the whole of life reflects Christian sobriety, so that at every moment we may be fit for every good work. This is that true religion and that piety which Paul says is profitable for all things and has promises of both the present and the future life. (1 Tim. 4.)

units.la: Porrò tempus est, vt testimonii Annæ videamus, quod illa de Christo tulit. Absoluit hoc paucis Lucas, sic scribens. Hæc igitur cùm ea ipsa hora superuenisset (nimirum ita ipsam gubernante Dei prouidentia, quæ vt de Simeone diximus, nihil fortuitum esse finit) vicissim confitebatur Domino, idest, fuecinebat Simeoni, & huius dicta suo testimonio confirmabat: adhæc loquebatur de eo omnibus, qui expectabant redemptionem in Hierusalem, id est, quorum mentes in Christi aduentu inten tæ erant, & promissam in illo salutem cum fide expectabant. At hos paucos numero fuisse vel ex hoc loco patet, cum plerique vel prophano Dei contemptu scripturas negligerent, vel humanis traditionibus in sectas scisi circa inania figmenta vagarentur. Noluit autem spiritus sanctus Annæ testimonii verbotim recitare, quia vt id fieret minimè opus erat, cum non aliud dixerit, quâ quod prius à Simeone dictum fuerat. Obseruari potius debet, quòd non contenta Simeonis oraculo, ipsa quoque spiritu eam agitante idem de Christo testificatur. Facit hoc contra eorû sententiam, qui vt suæ ignauiæ & timiditati aliquam excusationem inueniant, minimè necessarium arbitrantur, vt ipsi ea dicant & palàm proficeantur, quæiam prius à multis alijs dicta sunt. Atqui à singulis hoc requiritur, vt Christo testimonium ferant, & non alia harmonia magis delectatur Deus, quàm quæ fideles ipsius laudes & exhibitum nobis in Christo beneficium vnanimi consensu celebrant. Neque opus est, vt quid noui fingamus, sed in veteri sanctorum Dei, qui olim fuêre, confessione omnes perseuerent, quæ eos falli non sinet. Et hæc quidem fuerunt seruorum Dei testimonia, per quæ Christum infantulum adhuc celebrari voluit Deus, vt de illo omnes spem maiorem conciperent.
units.tr: Now it is time to see the testimony which Anna bore about Christ. Luke finishes this in a few words, writing thus: "And she, coming in that same hour, gave thanks likewise to the Lord" (namely, Providence so governing her, which, as we said of Simeon, allows nothing to be fortuitous), "and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem"; that is, to those whose minds were intent upon the coming of Christ, and who with faith awaited the salvation promised in him. That these were few in number is clear even from this passage, since most either neglected the Scriptures out of profane contempt for God, or, torn into sects by human traditions, wandered about empty fictions. But the Holy Spirit did not wish to recite Anna's testimony word for word, because there was no need for this, since she said nothing other than what had been said before by Simeon. Rather it should be observed that she, not content with the oracle of Simeon, was herself also moved by the Spirit and bore the same witness concerning Christ. This is against the opinion of those who, in order to find some excuse for their laziness and timidity, think it by no means necessary that they themselves should say and openly profess those things which have already been said by many others. Yet this is required of each one, that they bear witness to Christ, and God takes no delight in any harmony more than in that in which the faithful celebrate with one accord his praises and the benefit given to us in Christ. Nor is there need for us to invent anything new; rather, all should persevere in the ancient confession of the servants of God who lived in former times, which will not let them be deceived. And these were the testimonies of the servants of God, through which God willed that Christ, still an infant, be celebrated, so that all might conceive a greater hope concerning him.

units.la: Transit nunc ad describendam pueritiam Iesu, quæ et ipsa non pauca continet, quæ nos in illius cognitione possunt instituere. Interserit tamen de Maria & Iosepho, quòd postquam omnia secundum legem Domini peregerant, reuersi sint in Galilæam, in ciuitatem suam Nazareth. Vbi iam subijci debuisset fuga in Ægyptum, quam Angelo monente Ioseph suscepit, vt infantulum Herodis manibus sanguinarijs subduceret. Sed quia illam historiam prolixè descripserat Matthæus, eandè hîc repeti nõ fuit necesse: & quæ in illa nobis obseruanda sunt, alibi dicentur. Nunc pueritiam Iesu paucis sic describit Euangelista: Puerulus autem crescebat, et corroborabatur spiritu, implebaturq; sapientia, & gratia Dei erat super ipsum. Creuisse illum dicit, nimirum quoad staturam corporis, prout alij infantes solent, cum repente posset magnus fieri. Vt autem corpore creuit, sic etiam spiritu & mente corroboratus est, vt scilicet in puerili etiam ætate maioris indolis specimina apparerent, neq; vitijs illis puerilibus laboraret, qualia sunt leuitas morum, petulantia, iudicij inopia, & si quæ alia sunt huius generis. Addit, Implebatur q; sapientia: vt qui quoad diuinitatem ipsissima sapientia est, hanc in assumpta etiã carne indies magis atq; magis declararet. Et gratia Dei erat super ipsum. Quia enim dilectus ille Dei filius erat, & ex patris decreto homo factus fuerat, fieri non potuit quin assumptum quoq; ab illo hominem pater singulari gratia donaret, quæ illum omnibus gratiosum atq; acceptum faceret. Scio hæc nonnullis absurdiora videri, qui ne quid filio Dei indignum sentire & dicere videantur, hæc omnia per nescio quam dispensationem exponunt, quæ à simulatione & dissimulatione nihil aut parum differt. At si ista de Christo homine non verè dicuntur, non video quid illis responderi possit, qui illum verè in cruce mortuum esse negant. Aut si mortuum esse merito credimus, quæ obsecro religio est ea de illo nolle fateri, quæ cum nulla infamia aut ignominia coniuncta sunt? Nam quòd illi incrementa ætatis & ignorantiam simpliciter inter pœnas peccati numerant, id nulla cum ratione & nimis præcipiti audacia faciunt, cùm alterum secundùm naturæ leges fiat, alterum Angelis quoq; tribuatur, qui nihil peccauerunt. Notum enim est illud Christi, quo Angelos diem postremi sui aduentus nescire affirmat. Sed vt demus ista peccati supplicia esse, num ideo illa in Christo locum habuisse negabimus, qui vt mortem (quæ proprijssimum peccati stipendium est) subiret, in mundum venit atq; homo factus est? Fateamur ergo quod omnis scriptura docet, Dei filium carnem veram assumpsisse, & ita hominem factum esse, vt nostras quoq; infirmitates susceperit, & fratribus (vt Apostolus loquitur) per omnia similis factus sit, vno peccato excepto. In his consistit nostræ fidei atq; salutis certitudo: quia inde colligimus, eius meritum ad nos pertinere, nosq; Seruatorem habere fidelem & perfectum, qui nos quantùmuis corruptos & perditos seruare possit ac velit.
units.tr: He now turns to describe the boyhood of Jesus, which also contains not a few things that can instruct us in knowing him. He does, however, insert a note about Mary and Joseph: after they had done everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city of Nazareth. Here the flight into Egypt ought to follow, which Joseph undertook at the angel's warning so that he might rescue the infant from the bloody hands of Herod. But since Matthew had described that story at length, there was no need to repeat it here, and the lessons to be drawn from it will be given elsewhere. Now the Evangelist describes the boyhood of Jesus briefly, as follows: "The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him." He says that he grew, of course as to the size of his body, as other infants usually do, since he could not suddenly become a grown man. But as he grew in body, so too he was strengthened in spirit and mind, so that even in his boyhood signs of a greater character appeared, and he was not troubled by those childish faults such as fickleness of manners, petulance, lack of judgement, and whatever else is of this kind. He adds, "and was filled with wisdom," so that he who, as to his divinity, is wisdom itself, might display it more and more each day in the flesh he had assumed. "And the grace of God was upon him." For since he was that beloved Son of God, and had been made man by the Father's decree, it could not but be that the Father gave to the man he had assumed a singular grace, which made him pleasing and acceptable to all. I know that these things seem to some rather absurd, and that they, lest they seem to think or say anything unworthy of the Son of God, explain all of this by some dispensation I know not what, which differs little or not at all from pretence and dissimulation. But if these things are not truly said of Christ the man, I do not see what answer can be given to those who deny that he truly died on the cross. Or if we rightly believe that he died, what religion, I beg you, is it to be unwilling to confess those things about him that carry no infamy or disgrace? For as to their claim that the growth of age and ignorance are simply counted among the punishments of sin, they do this without any reason and with excessive rashness, since the one happens according to the laws of nature, and the other is attributed even to the angels, who sinned not at all.
