For that saying of Christ is well known, in which he affirms that the angels do not know the day of his last coming. But granting that these are punishments of sin, shall we then deny that they had a place in Christ, who came into the world and was made man so that he might undergo death, which is the very proper wage of sin? Let us therefore confess what all Scripture teaches: that the Son of God assumed true flesh, and became man in such a way that he took up our infirmities too, and was made like his brothers (as the Apostle puts it) in all things, sin excepted. In these things consists the certainty of our faith and salvation, for from them we gather that his merit pertains to us, and that we have as our Saviour one who is faithful and perfect, who is able and willing to save us, however corrupt and lost we may be.

units.la: In primis autem hîc obseruari debet, Christum omnis ætatis hominum redemptorem esse, quando constat eum & infantem fuisse, & puerum, & iuuenem atq; virum perfectum. Est hoc cognitu valde necessarium quoad infantes et puerulos. Hos enim in peccato concipi et nasci, & hæreditariam illam naturæ vitiositatem, quæ ex Adamo in nos deriuata est, secum ex vtero matris in lucem hac afferre constat. Ne quis ergo eos qui priusquam ad Christi fidem perveniunt, moriuntur, à salute exclusos putet, illius infantia prohibemur. Quia enim Dei filius infantiae infirmitates subire dignatus est, horum quoq; Seruator sit oportet, nisi illum frustra infantê factum fuisse dicamus. Et quia idem agnus ille Dei est, qui omne mundi peccatum tollit, & proinde etiam Originale, nunquam propter hoc damnari poterunt ex Christianis progeniti infantes, qui ex fœdere ad ecclesiæ & salutis in Christo exhibitæ societatem pertinent. Nam quod Abrahamo dictum fuit, Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui: hoc ipsum Christus confirmat, dicens: Sinite pueruulos ad me venire, nam talium est regnum Dei. Quod Paulus obseruans, eos qui in impari coniugio nascuntur, sanctos dixit, eò quòd alterutrū parentem habeant fidelem. Sunt ergo temerarij nimis, qui infantum salutem in dubium vocant, & eos aperte damnant, qui absq; baptismo decedunt: quasi vero id Christi merito aliquid possit derogare. Sed de hoc alibi plura. Nunc exhibitum nobis à Deo salutis beneficium agnoscamus, & tot tamq; præclaris testimonijs commendatum nobis huius Mediatoris, Iesum Christum, vera fide amplectamur, inq; eo viuamus et spiciamus indies. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Here, in the first place, it ought to be observed that Christ is the redeemer of men of every age, since it is certain that he was an infant, a boy, a youth, and a full-grown man. This is very necessary to know with regard to infants and little children. For it is agreed that they are conceived and born in sin, and bring with them from the mother's womb into the light that hereditary corruption of nature which has been derived to us from Adam. Lest anyone therefore think that those who die before they come to faith in Christ are excluded from salvation, we are kept from that view by his infancy. For since the Son of God deigned to undergo the weaknesses of infancy, he must also be the Saviour of these, unless we say that he was made an infant in vain. And since he is that same Lamb of God who takes away all the sin of the world, and therefore also original sin, the infants born of Christians, who belong by covenant to the fellowship of the Church and of the salvation offered in Christ, can never be condemned on account of this. For what was said to Abraham, "I will be your God and the God of your seed," this very thing Christ confirms, saying: "Suffer the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of God." Paul, observing this, called holy those who are born of an unequal marriage, because one of their parents is a believer. Therefore they are too rash who call the salvation of infants into doubt, and openly condemn those who die without baptism, as if indeed this could take anything away from the merit of Christ. But of this more elsewhere. For now let us acknowledge the saving benefit given to us by God, and embrace with true faith this Mediator, Jesus Christ, commended to us by so many and such notable testimonies, and let us live in him and look to him each day. To him belong blessing, honour, glory, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXIV.

units.la: Et ibant parentes eius quotannis Hierosolymâ in festo Pasche. Cùm igitur factus esset annorum duodecim, ascenderunt illi Hierosolymam secundùm ritum festi: peractisq; eius diebus cùm reuerterentur illi, remansit puer Iesus Hierosolymæ: neq; id sciuit Ioseph, neq; mater eius. Existimantes autem eum esse in comitatu, ierunt viam vnius diei, & requirebant eum inter cognatos & inter notos. Et cùm eum non inuenissent, reuersi sunt Hierosolymâ quærentes eum. Et factum est triduo post inuenerunt eum in templo sedentem in medio Doctorum, & audientem eos & eos interrogantem. Obstupescebant autem omnes qui eum audiebant super intelligentia & responsis eius.
units.tr: And his parents went every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast. When the days were over and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. Supposing him to be in the company, they went a day's journey and looked for him among their relatives and acquaintances. When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem to seek him. And after three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.

units.la: Lucas Euangelista perquàm diligenter non solùm incarnationem et natales filij Dei Iesu Christi describit, verumetiam quæ illo iam in carne manifestato acciderunt. Causam huius diligentiæ alibi annotauimus, quòd nihil in illo tam minutum est, quod non plurimum faciat ad nostræ fidei & vitæ totius institutionem. Vidimus hoc in testimonijs, quæ illi reddiderunt Angeli, pastores, Simeon & Anna: quorum omnium hic finis & scopus est, vt doceant illum esse humani generis vindicem olim promissum, in quo vno salus et vita inueniri possit. Idè nos illius pueritia docet. Nam quia infans natus est, & per omnes omnium ætatum gradus adoleuit, aperte satis apparet, illius merito infantes quoq; seruari, adeoq; eum ætatum omnium seruatorem esse. Ne tamen pueritia, quæ per se contempta & ridicula est, authoritati eius aliquid derogaret, dictum est nuper, illum vnà cum ætate et corporis statura profecisse etiam spiritu et sapientia: nimirum vt in puero quoq; aliquid homine maius appareret. Quod ne temere dictum putetur, subijcitur diuinæ illius indolis et sapientiæ specimen, quod tunc edidit, cum annum suæ ætatis duodecimum demum attigit. Et est hoc eiusmodi, vt non obscurè hoc quasi præludio publicè ostenderit se magnum illum prophetam esse, de quo olim Moses Vaticinatus fuit, & quem omnes audire debeant. Cæterum continet simul ista historia memorabile exemplum educationis & institutionis puerorum, quod vt quàm diligentissimè consideretur, nõ solùm dignum huius historiæ verumetiam necessarium est. Nam non sine dolore cernunt pij, quantum in hac re vulgò peccetur: cùm & parentes pauci sint, qui in liberorum educatione verum scopum sibi serio proponant: et pleriq; pueri atq; iuuenes correctionis & disciplinæ impatientes iugum omne impudentissimè & incurabili proteruia excutiat. Fit ergo, vt qui legem peccati ex vtero matris sibi connexã habent, insuper diutina peccandi licentia & consuetudine ita indurentur, vt tandem parentibus suis acerbissimi doloris & ignominiæ, sibijpsis verò exitij authores sint. Itaq; etsi multa de hac re in scripturis tradantur, voluit tamen Deus in filij quoq; sui educatione et pueritia exemplum omnibus numeris absolutum extare, quod nemo sanæ mentis contemnere posset, & quo omnes abundè admoneantur, quid hic factu & obseruatu opus sit. Quæ causa est, quòd historiam hanc Lucas cum singulis suis partibus atq; circumstantijs prolixè describit. Et in præsenti quidè primùm occasio rei gestæ præmittitur, vbi
units.tr: Luke the evangelist describes with great care not only the incarnation and birth of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, but also what happened after he had been manifested in the flesh. I have noted elsewhere the reason for this care: there is nothing in him so small that it does not greatly contribute to the instruction of our faith and of our whole life. We have seen this in the testimonies that the angels, the shepherds, Simeon and Anna gave to him, all of which aim at showing that he is the deliverer of the human race promised of old, in whom alone salvation and life can be found. So his boyhood also teaches us. For since he was born an infant and grew through all the stages of age, it is plain enough that infants too are saved by his merit, and that he is the Saviour of every age. Lest, however, his boyhood, which in itself is despised and laughable, should detract anything from his authority, it was said a little earlier that he advanced in spirit and wisdom along with his age and stature of body, so that even in a boy something greater than a man might appear. Lest this be thought to have been said rashly, there follows a specimen of his divine nature and wisdom, which he gave when he had reached the twelfth year of his age. It is of such a kind that, in this prelude as it were, he openly showed himself to be that great prophet of whom Moses prophesied long ago, and whom all must hear. Moreover, this history contains a memorable example of the upbringing and training of children, which deserves to be considered most diligently; it is not only worthy of this history but also necessary. For the godly cannot see without grief how much is commonly sinned in this matter: there are few parents who seriously set before themselves the true aim in bringing up their children, and most boys and young men, impatient of correction and discipline, shake off every yoke with the most shameless and incurable wantonness. So it comes about that those who have the law of sin bound to them from their mother's womb, and are further hardened by long licence and habit in sinning, become at last the authors of the most bitter grief and disgrace to their parents and of ruin to themselves. Therefore, although much about this matter is handed down in the Scriptures, God nevertheless willed that in the upbringing and boyhood of his own Son there should stand a pattern complete in every respect, which no sane person could despise, and by which all may be abundantly admonished what must be done and observed here. This is why Luke describes this history at length, with each of its parts and circumstances. And in the present passage the occasion of the event is first set forth, where

units.la: Vsus & scopus huius historiæ Iosephi et Mariæ industria et sedulitas indicatur, qua in puero Iesu bene instituendo usi sunt. Narratur deinde, illos nihilominus dolore et molestia non vulgare sustinuisse, etiamsi officio suo minime defessi essent. Quibus primum quasi tyrocinium pueri Iesu subjicitur, quod docet, quæ nam pueritiæ et iuventutis exercitia esse debeant, si quidem et Deo placere velint, et senectutem sibi lætam et honorificam obtingere cupiant.
units.tr: The use and aim of this history is shown in the diligence and earnestness of Joseph and Mary, with which they used to bring up the boy Jesus well. It is then related that, although they were in no way weary of their duty, they nevertheless endured no small grief and trouble. To these things is first added, as it were, an apprenticeship of the boy Jesus, which teaches what the exercises of boyhood and youth ought to be, if indeed they wish to please God and hope for a happy and honourable old age.

units.la: Quoad primum, duo de Iosepho (quem abusive patrem Iesu dici, nuper monuimus) et Maria dicuntur. Alterum, illos quotannis in Paschæ festo Hierosolymam ascendisse; alterum, quod eodem secum duxerint puerum Iesum, quam primum tantæ profectionis laboribus per ætatem sufficere potuit. Utrum autem non pro suo arbitrio fecerunt, sed ut Deo obedirent, qui ita fieri præceperat. Nam Deut. 16. hæc scribitur: Ter in anno apparebit omnis mas coram Domino Deo tuo, in loco quem elegerit: nempe in festo azymorum, in festo hebdomadum, et in festo tabernaculorum. Præcipit præterea Deus, ut liberi quoque, epulo paschali adhibeantur, et ut ipsdem diligens omnium reddatur ratio, ut et Dei vetera beneficia norint, et huic credere atque eundem colere discant. Quod ergo Iosephus et Maria faciunt, vere bonum opus est, cum ex fide et secundum divinæ legis præscriptum illud omne fiat. Ita vero pietatis simul et obedientiæ veræ, quæ Deo debetur, exemplum nobis exhibent. Nam multa erant, quæ illos a profectionibus eiusmodi revocare poterant, si carnis potius rationes quam Dei præcepta audire voluissent. Erat enim iter hoc longum, quod vix aliquot diebus confici poterat. Atqui graves qualiscunque profectio est tenuioris fortunæ hominibus, qui manuum labore victitant. Neque unius diei festum illud erat, sed diebus totis octo durabat, quibus impensæ extraordinariæ faciendæ erant, quibus non poterant non plurimum gravari. Adhæc superuacaneum et tantum non superstitiosum videri poterat ad festum paschæ eos proficisci, qui verum illum agnum Dei penes se habebant, et quem nostrum pascha esse Apostolus testatur. Sed non movent hæc omnia ipsos, quo minus expresso Dei mandato obtemperet. Unde facile colligitur, quam studiose in reliquis omnibus Deum coluerint, qui in re laboris et sumptus plena nihil omittendum esse putarunt. Arguunt ista nostri seculi socordiam. Habemus nos hodie, cum correctionis tempus iampridem advenerit, omnia veteribus illis ritibus præstantiora. Nam in Dei verbo ipse Christus nobis præsens fisitur, et (ut Paulus Galatis dicebat) per Euangelium ita depingitur, ut inter nos crucifixus videri possit. Cœtus item sacros et publicas preces amplissima promissione nobis Christus commendat, quod et illis medius interesse, et preces patri acceptas facere velit. Adhæc non longis itineribus neque impensis magnis opus est, quando Deus iam passim adorari et coli potest in spiritu et veritate. Attamen non movent ista plerosque, quin Deum ipsum et sacra omnia negligant.
units.tr: As to the first point, two things are said of Joseph (whom, as I lately warned, is called the father of Jesus only in a loose sense) and of Mary. The first is that they went up to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the Passover; the second is that they took the boy Jesus with them as soon as he was old enough to bear the labours of so long a journey. Now, they did this not at their own discretion, but in order to obey God, who had so commanded. For in Deuteronomy 16 it is written: "Three times in the year shall every male appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose: namely, at the feast of unleavened bread, at the feast of weeks, and at the feast of tabernacles." God furthermore commands that children too be admitted to the Passover meal, and that a careful account of all things be given to them, so that they may know God's past benefits and learn to believe in him and to worship him. What Joseph and Mary do is therefore truly a good work, since it is all done in faith and according to the prescript of the divine law. In this way they set before us an example of true godliness and of the obedience which is owed to God. For there were many things that could have called them back from such journeys, had they wished to listen to the reasons of the flesh rather than to the commands of God. The journey was long, and could scarcely be completed in a few days. Yet any journey is burdensome for people of modest means who live by the labour of their hands. Nor was that feast of one day only, but lasted a full eight days, during which extraordinary expenses had to be met, which they could not but feel heavily. Besides, it might seem pointless, and not far from superstitious, for those who had the true Lamb of God with them, and whom the Apostle declares to be our Passover, to go up to the Passover feast. But none of these things moved them to disobey the plain command of God. Hence it is easily gathered how earnestly they worshipped God in all other matters, since they thought nothing should be omitted in a matter full of toil and expense. These things shame the slothfulness of our age. Today we have, although the time of reformation has long since come, things far better than those old rites. For in the word of God Christ himself is set before us as present, and (as Paul said to the Galatians) he is so portrayed through the Gospel that he can be seen crucified among us. Likewise Christ commends to us sacred assemblies and public prayers with the most ample promise, that he will be present in their midst and make the prayers acceptable to the Father. Moreover, no long journeys or great expenses are needed, since God can now be adored and worshipped everywhere in spirit and in truth. Yet these things do not move most people from neglecting God himself and all sacred things.

units.la: Sed ut ad huius Sermonis argumentum accedamus, admonentur hoc exemplo parentes, institutionem liberorum tunc recte fieri, si a seipsis initium faciant. Constat enim in quovis doctrinæ et artificij genere nihil efficacius esse exemplis, et hæc eo efficaciora esse, quo magis apud nos in pretio sunt, a quibus illa præbentur. Quia ergo parentum authoritas apud liberos maxima esse debet, et ideo illos ut plurimum amant, etiam atque etiam cavendum erit, ne ipsis alicuius exempli mali authores sint. In primis autem pietati erga Deum parentes studeant, et illa assidua auditione verbi Dei, colloquiis de Deo religiosis et precibus crebris testentur. Ita liberi quoque a primis annis religioni assuescent, qui e contra non possunt non Dei contemptores fieri, si parentes divina ita contemnere et calumniari videant. Post religionem vero proxima pudicitiæ et honestatis cura sit, cuius tam attenti observatores olim Romani fuerunt, ut nefas putarent in eodem balneo simul patrem et filium, aut socerum et generum conspici. In primis vero a verbis aut sermonibus obscænis abstineant. Solent enim hi in puerorum animos altius infidere quam putetur, et notus est poetæ versus, quæ Apostolica authoritate spiritus sanctus commendari voluit. Corrumpunt mores bonos colloquia prava. Quanto magis vero cavendum erit, ne spem coniugale turpiter fallendo liberis occasione præbeat de illa leuius iudicandi, qui proximus ad omnem libidinem gradus est. Accedat his concordiæ coniugalis studium, quæ ut omnes coniugij molestias leues reddit: ita ad liberorum institutionem admodum necessaria est. Si enim inter se dissideat coniuges, mox iurgijs et conuitijs mutuis ita strepunt, quorum non alius fructus est, quam quod omnis illorum authoritas apud liberos intercidit, et idem moribus istis adsuescunt, ut ipsi quoque morosi et intractabiles fiant. Præterea œconomiæ et impensarum certa ratione habeat parentes, ne vel prodigaliores vel æquo tenaciores sint. Nam qui luxu delectatur, iis fere et cibis delicatioribus et vestitu molliori liberos corrumpunt, ut et
units.tr: But to come to the subject of this sermon: parents are admonished by this example that the upbringing of children is rightly done only if they make a beginning with themselves. For it is agreed that in every kind of teaching and craft nothing is more effective than examples, and that these are the more effective the more highly those who provide them are esteemed by us. Since, then, the authority of parents ought to be very great with their children, and since children for the most part love their parents, parents must take the greatest care that they are not themselves the authors of any bad example. Above all, parents should strive for piety towards God, and bear witness to it by constant hearing of the word of God, by godly conversation about God, and by frequent prayers. In this way children too will be accustomed to religion from their earliest years, whereas on the contrary they cannot help becoming despisers of God if they see their parents despising and slandering divine things. After religion, the next concern should be for chastity and decency, which the Romans of old observed so carefully that they thought it an abomination for father and son, or father-in-law and son-in-law, to be seen together in the same bath. Above all, parents should abstain from obscene words and talk. For such things are wont to sink into children's minds more deeply than is supposed, and the verse of the poet is well known, which the Holy Spirit, by apostolic authority, wished to commend: "Evil talk corrupts good morals." How much more, then, must care be taken that parents, by shamefully breaking faith in marriage, do not give their children occasion to judge lightly of that very thing, which is the step nearest to every lust. To this should be added a zeal for marital harmony, which makes all the burdens of marriage light, and is most necessary for the upbringing of children. For if husband and wife disagree among themselves, they soon quarrel and bandy reproaches with each other, and the only fruit of this is that all their authority is lost in the eyes of their children, who in turn grow accustomed to the same manners, so that they themselves become peevish and unmanageable. Furthermore, parents should keep a sure rule in household management and expenses, lest they be either too lavish or more stingy than is fitting. For those who delight in luxury corrupt their children, for the most part with more dainty foods and softer clothing, so that also

units.la: 1. Cor. 15. ut & ipsis vbi adoleuerit, nihil satisfaciat. Qui vero auari nimis officia Christianæ beneficetiæ negligunt, liberis quoq; exemplo sunt, vt inhumani & immisericordes nullis aliorum malis comoueantur, & tandem in raptores & tyrannos degenerent. Postremo plurimum hic proderit, si parentes de iis qui in rep. præsunt, aut ecclesiarum ministri sunt, aut scholarum gubernacula regunt, honorifice sentiant atq; loquantur. Hinc enim fit, vt liberi quoq; hos omnes admirentur, & proinde magistris suis faciliús obtemperent, legum disciplinam non impatienter ferant, & verbi Dei admonitiones atq; increpationes nō scurriliter eludant, sed ijs emendentur. Et hæc præcipua sunt, in quibus parentes liberis suis præire debent, ne proprio exemplo eos offendant & corrumpant, quos ad pietatem et honestatē debebant instituere. Vbi illos semper meminisse oportet grauis illius sententiæ, quam Christus pronuntiauit: Quisquis offenderit vnum ex paruulis hisce, qui in me credunt, præstiterit ei vt suspendatur mola asinaria in collum eius, & demergatur in profundum maris. Væ ei, per quem venit scandalū. At facile in hoc sibi cauebūt, qui quod in Iosepho et Maria habemus exemplū sibi imitandū proposuerint.
units.tr: 1. Cor. 15. so that, once they have grown up, nothing will satisfy them either. Those who are too greedy and neglect the duties of Christian beneficence also set a bad example for their children, so that the children become inhuman and merciless, unmoved by the misfortunes of others, and at last degenerate into robbers and tyrants. Finally, it will help greatly if parents think and speak respectfully of those who hold office in the commonwealth, or who are ministers of the churches, or who govern schools. For in this way the children too will admire all of them, and so obey their teachers more readily, bear the discipline of the laws without impatience, and do not mock the admonitions and rebukes of God's Word with buffoonery, but are amended by them. These are the chief matters in which parents ought to go before their children, lest by their own example they offend and corrupt those whom they ought to be training in piety and honesty. Parents should always remember that grave saying which Christ pronounced: "Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and he be drowned in the depths of the sea. Woe to the one through whom the offence comes." Those who set before themselves the example of Joseph and Mary to imitate will easily be on their guard in this.

units.la: In eo autem cumprimis obseruari debet, quod non ipsi solum cultus diuini causa Hierosolymam ascenderunt, sed eodem secum duxere Iesum, qui duodecimū modo ætatis annū attigerat. Quia enim tenellū adhuc sacris interesse voluerunt, quis dubitet aliquid officij ab illis intermissum esse, quod ad formandā pietatem & morum probitatē facere poterit? Itaq; non sufficit, si ipsi quidē pie sanctèq; vi uamus, sed annitendum simul est, vt ijsdem studijs & moribus nostri liberi à pueris imbuantur. Peccat in hoc plurimi, qui quasi satis sit liberos procreauisse, eos postea secure negligūt. Sunt ij ignauorum agricolarum similes, qui arbores quidem omnis generis magno studio plantant, sed eas dū frutescere sinunt, vt succrescere & fructu sperato ferre non possint. Non temere aut Lucas omissis alijs omnibus hoc vnum narrat, vt Christum Hierosolymam ad Pascha solennitatē secum deduxerint. Eo enim docemur, hunc nobis in liberorum educatione scopum vnicum debere propositum esse, vt illos Deo adducamus, & vt huic seruire atq; eius gloriā prouehere discāt. Exigit hoc primum iustitiæ lex, vt quia liberi nobis à Deo dati & eius quasi depositū sunt, ijdem huic resignentur, vt eius gloriæ seruiant. Deinde cū natura peccatores nascamur, neq; ex nobis ipsis boni aliquid possimus, necesse omnino est, vt tellurīs instar à pueris excolamur ad ferendum fructum Deo, & vt naturæ corruptio diuturniori consuetudine (quam veteres non temere alteram naturam dixerunt) corrigatur. Vt enim canem vel tulum loro assuescere difficile est: ita nunquā postea disciplinæ sanctiori collū subijcient, qui in impietate & prophano numinis contemptu callū obduxerunt. Ideo Solomon rectè & grauiter monet: Initia vel instrue puerū in ore viæ suæ, id est, in ipsa pueritia, dum quasi in biuio constitutus vel ad virtutem vel ad vitiū deflectere solent iuuenes. Tunc (inquit) cura, vt Deo consecretur, & pietatis vitā capessat. Et admonitionis huius causam subijcit: Etiam cum senuerit, non recedet ab ea. Adhæc excitare debet parentes ad hoc studium liberorum incolumitas & salus, cuius omnes homines natura studiosissimi sunt. Atqui constat illam ex hoc in primis pendere, vt Deum nobis propitium habeamus. Et cum præstantior hominis pars sit anima, cuius iactura (vt Christus ait) ne totius quidē mundi vniuersa substantia redimi potest, nimium stulti sunt, qui vt liberis suis quoad corpus & huius seculi honores consulant ringuntur, nihil interim de eo soliciti, an Dei cognitione veram illi habeant, an huic per fidem in Christum coniuncti sint, & an norint in quo animarū salus & æterna hominis beatitas consistat. Placent illi sibi ipsis in sua industria, & quàm probè suis filijs cōsuluerint magnificè gloriantur. At si rem ipsam propius inspiciamus, non plus illi ex se natis conferunt, quàm bruta animalia suis pullis aut catulis conferre soleant, quos illa etiam eò vsq; æducant, vt ipsi sibi victum quærere possint. Et plerunq; fit, vt qui ingentes opum aceruos liberis suis congerunt, ijsdē nihil quàm peccandi materiam & diuinæ maledictionis ignē relinquant, quæ illos & in hoc præsenti & futuro seculo infelicissimos reddit. Multò igitur rectius Abrahamus & patres alij sapuerunt, quorum hoc præcipuum studium fuit, vt liberos in Dei cognitione & timore instituros haberent. Sciebant enim quæstum omnium vberrimum esse pietatem, vt quæ vitæ præsentis & futuræ promissiones habeat.
units.tr: In this matter, the following above all must be noted: they did not go up to Jerusalem for the sake of worship alone, but took Jesus with them, who had only just reached the age of twelve. Since they wished the boy, still tender, to take part in the sacred rites, who could doubt that they omitted nothing of the duty that could contribute to forming his piety and integrity of character? So it is not enough that we ourselves live piously and holily; we must also strive that our children, from boyhood, be steeped in the same pursuits and morals. Many people sin in this way: as though it were enough to have begotten children, they then carelessly neglect them. They are like lazy farmers, who plant trees of every kind with great zeal, but then let them grow wild, so that they cannot grow up and bear the fruit that is hoped for. It is not by chance that Luke, leaving out everything else, relates this one thing: that they took Christ with them to Jerusalem for the solemn feast of the Passover. For by this we are taught that the one aim we ought to set before us in the upbringing of our children is to bring them to God, and that they learn to serve him and to advance his glory. The law of justice first requires this: since our children have been given to us by God and are, as it were, a deposit entrusted to us, they should be returned to him so that they serve his glory. Then, since we are born sinners by nature, and cannot of ourselves do anything good, it is absolutely necessary that from boyhood we be cultivated like the soil, so that we bear fruit for God, and that the corruption of nature be corrected by long-continued habit (which the ancients not without reason called a second nature). For just as it is hard to accustom a dog or a colt to the leash, so those who have hardened their neck in impiety and profane contempt of the divine majesty will never afterwards submit their neck to a holier discipline. Therefore Solomon rightly and gravely advises: "Train up a boy at the entrance of his way," that is, in boyhood itself, while young men, as if standing at a crossroads, are accustomed to turn either to virtue or to vice. "Then," he says, "take care that he is consecrated to God and takes hold of a life of piety." He adds the reason for this admonition: "Even when he has grown old, he will not depart from it." Moreover, the safety and welfare of their children should urge parents to this care, since all men are by nature most eager for these. Indeed, it is certain that safety depends above all on this: that we have God favourable to us. And since the soul is the more excellent part of man, whose loss (as Christ says) cannot be made good even by the whole substance of the world, they are exceedingly foolish who strive to secure honours in this age for their children as regards the body, while meanwhile caring nothing about whether they have a true knowledge of God, whether they are joined to him through faith in Christ, and whether they know in what the salvation of souls and the eternal blessedness of man consist. They are pleased with themselves in their diligence, and boast magnificently of how well they have provided for their sons. But if we look more closely at the matter itself, they contribute no more to those born of them than dumb animals are wont to contribute to their young whelps or chicks, which they nourish only so far as to enable them to seek their own food. And it often happens that those who heap up huge piles of wealth for their children leave them nothing but material for sinning and the fire of divine curse, which makes them most unhappy both in this present age and in the future. Much more rightly, therefore, did Abraham and the other fathers judge, whose chief concern was to have children whom they might instruct in the knowledge and fear of God. For they knew that piety is the most abundant gain of all, since it holds promises for both the present and the future life.

units.la: Debent de iis omnibus diligenter cogitate parentes, ne eorū rationibus se decipi patiantur, qui puerilem ætatem minime onerandam putant ijs rebus aut studijs quæ ad religionem & æternæ salutis negotium pertinent: quia tantorū mysteriorū pueri nondum capaces sint. At qui ita sentiunt, nō modo suorū liberorum salutem negligunt, sed ipsi etiam Deo non leuem faciunt iniuriam: quasi is aliquid inutile aut superuacaneū à nobis exigat. Vel num tu quisquis es ô bone, tibi persuadere audes, quòd puerorū captus tibi melius quàm Deo, qui te illoś creauit, notus atq; perspectus sit? Fatemur equidem cum Paulo, hominem animalem nō percipere ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei: At scimus è contra diuinitus eos illuminari, qui Dei præceptis sese accomodant, & pueros etiam spiritu sancto donari, supra in Ioanne diximus, idemq; multorum aliorum exempla testantur. Sed non multis argumentis aduersus eos opus est, qui sic sentiunt, cùm ipsi proprijs factis, ceu sorices sese prodant. Nam qui pueros religionis et cognitionis Dei nondū capaces esse aiunt, idem fere filios suos vel ad exteros ablegant, vt in tenella ætate linguas addiscant peregrinas, in quibus etiam mirificè proficiunt: vel domi eos instituunt in Arithmeticorum subtilissimis rationibus, in Musices præceptis, in arte gladiatoria, in recitandis poetarum prophanorum versibus & fabulosis narrationibus, aliisq; huius generis rebus, quae sine ingenij acumine & diligenti studio addisci non possunt. Taceo nunc eos, qui puellas nere et texere docent, imò qui ita illas instituunt, vt priusquam literarum elementa norint, cantilenas longas et artificiose ad libidinem excitandam compositas decantare possint. Et hi fere sunt, qui illam ætatem fidei & æternæ salutis cognitione minimè grauandam esse censent, in cuius doctrina nihil perplexum, nihil ambiguum aut inexplicabile continetur.
units.tr: Parents ought to think carefully about all these things, and not allow themselves to be deceived by the reasoning of those who think that boyhood should not be burdened with those things or studies which pertain to religion and the matter of eternal salvation, because boys are not yet capable of such great mysteries. But those who think so not only neglect the salvation of their own children, but also do no small injury to God himself, as if he demanded from us something useless or superfluous. Or, you, whoever you are, my good sir, do you dare to persuade yourself that the understanding of boys is better known and understood by you than by God, who created them? We grant indeed with Paul that the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. But on the contrary we know that those who accommodate themselves to God's precepts are enlightened by God, and we said above, on John, that even children are endowed with the Holy Spirit, and the examples of many others bear witness to the same. But there is no need of many arguments against those who think in this way, since by their own deeds they betray themselves, like mice. For those who say that boys are not yet capable of religion and the knowledge of God are generally the same people who send their sons abroad to learn foreign languages at a tender age, in which they indeed make remarkable progress; or who at home train them in the most subtle rules of arithmetic, in the precepts of music, in the art of fencing, in reciting the verses and fabulous tales of the profane poets, and in other things of this kind, which cannot be learned without a keen wit and diligent study. I say nothing now of those who teach girls to spin and weave; indeed, who so train them that, before they know the elements of letters, they can sing long songs artfully composed to stir up lust. These are generally the people who judge that the age of boyhood should not be burdened with the knowledge of faith and eternal salvation, a doctrine in which nothing is complicated, nothing ambiguous or inexplicable is contained.

units.la: Sed procul dubio aliter sentire discent, qui cogitant sub religione & timore Dei omnia ea comprehendi, quæ ad liberorum institutionem necessaria sunt, & proinde huius quasi compendium facillimum esse religionis doctrinam. Si enim Dei timore imbuti fuerint puerorum animi, ijdem etiam audiendi verbi eius studio ardebunt. Ita vero discent parentes debito honore prosequi, ijsdem obsequium fidum præstare, & iam senio confectos pie fouere atq; alere. Discent etiam obedire magistratibus & omnibus ijs, qui in aliqua publica authoritate constituti sunt. Adhæc iam inde à pueris cupiditates carnis frænare & coercere discunt, quod vitæ piæ & honestæ principium est. Istis vero studijs suam benedictionem Deus coniungit, vt et ipsi feliciter agant, et parentibus suis ornamento sint. Sed ô deploratam nostri seculi socordiam, quando paucos est videre, quibus ista cordi sint. Imò inueniuntur passim, qui puerilem ætatem data opera à religione & diuini cultus studio abstrahunt, ne quando propter hoc in periculum veniant: eosdem vero vel in artibus vsurarijs, vel ad fastum, vel ad libidinem & gulam, vel ad militiam mercenariam & alia huius generis studia instituunt. Qui vero optimi habentur, tunc se omni officio defunctos putant, si pueri ipsorum orationem dominicam & Symboli apostolici articulos ex more recitare possint, quorum tamen sensum & vsum prorsus nesciunt. Istis ergo debemus vniuersalem illam omnium ætatum & ordinum corruptelam & effrænem scelerum licentiam, quæ passim regnat, & cuius causa iram suam in nos Deus tam multis tamq; grauibus & continuis iudiciorum suorum exemplis declarat. Fieri enim non potest, vt vllis legibus aut disciplina coerceantur, qui licentiæ & nequitiæ à teneris annis assuenerunt. Nunquam ergo non nobis ob oculos versetur Mariæ & Iosephi exemplum, qui etsi Iesum Dei Altissimi filium ex spiritu sancto conceptum & absq; omni hereditariæ vitiositatis labe hominē factum esse scirent, ita tamen educandum putarunt, vt puerulum duodennem non sine molestia graui ad festa solennia deduxerint, in quibus cætus sacri & alia religionis exercitia habebantur. Quid ergo non facere nos decet, qui ex nobis natos naturali prauitate infectos & ad omnem nequitiam proclines esse non ignoramus? Equidem quàm minimè superuacanea sit vlla industria, quæ hic adhibetur, idem hoc Mariæ exemplum abunde docet.
units.tr: But without doubt those who consider that everything necessary for the upbringing of children is comprehended under religion and the fear of God, and that therefore the doctrine of religion is, as it were, the easiest summary of this, will learn to think otherwise. For if the minds of boys are imbued with the fear of God, they will also burn with zeal for hearing his Word. Thus they will learn to show their parents due honour, to render them faithful obedience, and to cherish and nourish them piously when they are worn out with age. They will also learn to obey the magistrates and all those who are set in any public authority. Moreover, from boyhood they learn to restrain and curb the lusts of the flesh, which is the beginning of a pious and honourable life. God joins his blessing to these pursuits, so that they themselves may prosper and be an ornament to their parents. But, O the deplorable carelessness of our age, when there are few to be seen to whom these things are dear! Indeed, one finds everywhere people who deliberately draw the boyhood of their children away from religion and the study of divine worship, lest on account of it they come into danger; and then they train those same children in usurious arts, or towards pride, or towards lust and gluttony, or towards mercenary soldiering and other pursuits of this kind. Those who are regarded as the best think they have discharged every duty if their children can recite the Lord's Prayer and the articles of the Apostles' Creed by rote, although they know absolutely nothing of their meaning and use. To these people, therefore, we owe that universal corruption of all ages and ranks and that unbridled licence of crimes which reigns everywhere, and on account of which God declares his anger against us by so many, so grave and so continual examples of his judgements. For it cannot be that those who have been accustomed from tender years to licence and wickedness are restrained by any laws or discipline. Let the example of Mary and Joseph, therefore, never cease to be before our eyes. Although they knew that Jesus was the Son of the Most High God, conceived by the Holy Spirit and made man without any stain of hereditary corruption, yet they judged that he must be brought up in such a way that they took the boy, twelve years old, with no little trouble, to the solemn feasts, in which sacred assemblies and other exercises of religion were held. What, then, ought we not to do, who know that those born of us are infected with natural depravity and prone to every wickedness? Indeed, how far from superfluous is any diligence applied here, this very example of Mary teaches abundantly.

units.la: Sequitur enim non vulgaris cura & dolor, quem ex filij Iesu amissione concepit. Nam cùm finitis festi diebus domum redire constituissent, puer illis nescientibus Hierosolymæ remansit. Id verò neq; ipsius malitia, neq; parentum negligentia factum fuit. Iesum enim iam vrgebat Dei patris vocatio, vt diuinæ virtutis specimen ederet: hi verò illum inter profectionis suæ comites esse arbitrabantur, inter quos plurimi erant ex ipsorum cognatis & amicis. At vbi sub vesperam diuerterunt, & ipse nusquam comparuit, mox totu illud vnius diei iter remensi Hierosolymæ reuersi sunt, vbi diligenter et anxiè quæsitu tandem post triduum demum in templo inter Rabbinos disputantē inuenerē. Quibus ante cogitationibus interea vexata fuerit Maria, quamq; mordacibus, facile intelligunt, quibus simile quid aliquādo accidit. Ipsa certè illas nō dissimulauit, cùm illo inuento dicerēt: Fili cur ita fecisti nobis? Ecce pater tuus et ego cruciati quærebamus te. Etenim vt vulgaria illa omittamus quae in illo casu occurrebat, ne forte in profluente lapsus perijsset, aut relictus comitibus feris praeda factus esset, vel in raptores & plagarios incidisset, qui ipsum aliis venderent, aut saltem inops & fameli cus in locis ignotis oberraret: periculum maximum ex eo timeri poterat, ne Herodianis proditus esset, & à Magni illius Herodis, crudelissimi latronis, filiorum aliquo occisus. Haec certè omnia castissimum virginis pectus vulnerarunt, & singula ei procul dubio ipsa morte fuerunt acerbiora, maximè cum sim mul cogitaret, quis nam esset puer ille, qui iam ipsius incuria amissus videri poterat. Describuntur autem haec tam diligenter, ut omnium parentum consolationi & institutioni serviant. Nam ad consola tionem facit, quando inter educationis suorum liberorum molestias atq; labores cogitant, non sibi so lis multa praeter animi sententiam accidere: sed similia iam olim passos esse sanctissimos Dei ser uos, & inter hos Mariam, & lectissimum illud Dei organum, ex qua Dei filius aeternus carne assu mere dignatus fuit. Ex eo enim mox colligunt, patienter sibi ferendum esse, quod ipsis cum tantis Dei servis commune est. Accedit tamen consolationi huic pondus maximum, si libros (ut ante quoq; di ctum est) Dei depositum esse cogitent, neq; nobis hic aliquam iniuriam fieri, cum haec & alia his gra vior peccatis nostris mereamur. In primis autem admonemur isto exemplo, in liberorum educa-tione nullam curam aut industriam nimiam aut superuacaneam censeri posse. Nam ut ante dixi mus, nulla erat in puero Iesu naturae vitiositas, & idem dilectus ille erat Dei filius, de quo custodien do peculiare mandatum Angeli acceperant, ut in Psalmo 91. scribitur. Accidit tamen in eius educa tione, quod parentibus dolorem et molestiam dedit acerbissimam. Quid ergo de nostris liberis nobis polliceamur, in quorum membris Lex peccati viget, quae in illis vitia omnis generis quotidie pro-creat? Certè etsi in illis instituendis nunquam nostro officio desimus, idem tamen nobis quod agrico lis eueniet. Ut enim illi in terrae cultu labores quidem gravissimos subeunt, non autem possunt obsta re, quo minus illa ex maledictione, cui obnoxia est, vrticas quoq; et spinas & infelix lolium inter ipsas segetes suapte natura proferat: ita etsi nihil studij & industriae parentes intermittant, subinde tamen in liberis suis corruptae naturae germina pullulare videbunt, in quibus eruendis & resecandis noua quotidie cura opus est. Docent hoc ipsum sanctissimorum hominum exempla, quae in Adamo & Caino, Noa & Chamo, Abrahamo & Ismaele, Isaaco & Esau, Iacobo & filijs eius, Samuele item & Dauide & utriusq; filijs, innumeris item alijs proponuntur: ut nunc ea taceam, quae in prophanis historijs extant, quae tam multa occurrunt, ut nō temere olim dictum sit, Herodis filios fere noxas esse. Debent ista parentes omnes excitare, ut nulli industriae & studio parcant: ijdem tamen exemplis illis se consolentur, si suâ operam omnè incurabili liberorum contumacia superari videat. Probabit enim ipso rum studium Deus, dignas autem suae peruicaciae poenas dabunt, qui parentibus doloris authores sunt.
units.tr: Next comes no ordinary anxiety and grief, which Mary felt over the loss of her son Jesus. When the days of the feast were over and they had decided to return home, the boy stayed behind in Jerusalem without their knowledge. This happened neither through his own wickedness nor through his parents' carelessness. Jesus was already being moved by the summons of God his Father to give a sign of divine power, while his parents supposed he was among the companions of their journey, of whom there were many from among their own relatives and friends. But when they stopped for the night and he was nowhere to be seen, they hurried back the whole day's journey to Jerusalem. There they searched for him anxiously and diligently, and after three days at last found him in the temple, disputing among the rabbis. Anyone who has suffered something similar can easily understand what painful thoughts troubled Mary in the meantime. She herself did not hide them when, on finding him, they said: "Son, why have you treated us like this? See, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish." For, to pass over the ordinary dangers that attend such a case, he might have fallen into a river, or been left by his companions and become prey to wild beasts, or fallen among robbers and kidnappers who would sell him to others, or at least wandered about hungry and destitute in unknown places. There was also the great danger that he might be betrayed to the Herodians and killed by one of the sons of that great Herod, the most cruel of robbers. All these thoughts pierced the most chaste heart of the Virgin, and each of them, no doubt, was more bitter to her than death itself, especially as she wondered who that boy really was, whom through her own carelessness she might seem to have lost. These things are related so carefully so that they may serve to console and instruct all parents. For they console when, amid the troubles and labours of bringing up their children, they consider that they are not the only ones to whom many things happen contrary to their wishes, but that the most holy servants of God have suffered similar things long ago, and among them Mary, and that chosen instrument of God from whom the eternal Son of God deigned to take flesh. From this they soon conclude that they must bear patiently what they share in common with such great servants of God. Yet this consolation has a very great weight if they reflect, as was said before, that their children are a deposit entrusted to them by God, and that no wrong is being done to us here, since we deserve this and other things heavier than these for our sins. Above all, this example warns us that in the upbringing of children no care or diligence can be considered excessive or superfluous. For, as we said before, there was no viciousness of nature in the boy Jesus, and he was that beloved Son of God for whose keeping the angels had received a special command, as is written in Psalm 91. Yet in his upbringing there occurred what gave his parents the bitterest grief and trouble. What then can we promise ourselves about our children, in whose members the law of sin is alive, and which daily brings forth vices of every kind in them? Surely, although we never fail in our duty in instructing them, the same will happen to us as to the farmer. For although he undergoes the heaviest labours in cultivating the land, he cannot prevent the earth, by reason of the curse to which it is subject, from naturally producing nettles and thorns and the unhappy darnel among the very crops. So, although parents neglect no study or diligence, they will still see the shoots of corrupted nature sprouting up in their children, and these must be uprooted and cut back with new care every day. The examples of the holiest men teach this very thing: those of Adam and Cain, Noah and Ham, Abraham and Ishmael, Isaac and Esau, Jacob and his sons, likewise Samuel and David and their sons, and countless others are set before us. I say nothing now of what is found in profane histories, which present so many such cases that it was not rashly said long ago that the sons of Herod were almost always harmful. All parents ought to be stirred by these things, so that they spare no diligence or effort. Yet they may console themselves with those examples if they see that all their work is overcome by the incurable obstinacy of their children. God will approve their zeal, but those who are the authors of grief to their parents will pay the penalties their stubbornness deserves.

units.la: Priusquam autem ab hoc loco discedamus, Dei quoque prouidentiam, omnia bene & feliciter administrantem obseruare conuenit. Anxia admodum & solicita hinc inde discurrit Maria, filium amissum quaeritans, nec quid speret aut metuat nouit. Interea autem ille in templo gloriosum suae fun-ctionis, ad quam destinatus erat, tyrocinium praebet magna cum totius populi admiratione. Solent huius generis multa accidere, ut propter ea turbemur & eiulemus, quae ut nostrae saluti & gloriae consulat Deus fieri voluit, & quorum finem nobis tandem utilem & salutare esse experimur. Imo nos afflictione & castigatione dignos esse nostra illa impatientia & querelis iniustis testamur. Me minerimus ergo nos & res nostras omnes Dei prouidentia gubernari, & nihil nobis fortuitum acci dere. Deinde hunc non solum omnipotentem rerum omnium, quae in mundo sunt & fiunt, rectorem esse, verumetiam patrem esse nostri amantissimum, qui nos saluos esse cupiat. Adhaec sapientia aeternam esse, quam nihil latet, & quae falli non potest, quo minus omnia finem ab illo propositum attingant. Eum deniq; esse, qui ex tenebris lucem, ex inopia diuitias, ex morbis vires integras, ex morte vitam elicere potest. Quin ergo huius curae nos permittimus, qui (ut Paulus ait) cum tentatione euentum largitur, neq; nos supra vires tentari patitur. 1. Corinth. 10.
units.tr: Before we leave this passage, however, it is fitting also to observe the providence of God, who manages all things well and happily. Mary runs about here and there, very anxious and troubled, seeking her lost son, and she knows neither what to hope nor what to fear. Meanwhile he, in the temple, gives a glorious first exercise of that office for which he was destined, to the great admiration of all the people. Things of this kind often happen which trouble us and make us lament, though God has willed them to happen for the good of our salvation and glory, and we find by experience that their end is at last useful and salutary for us. Indeed, our impatience and unjust complaints in such troubles show that we deserve affliction and chastisement. Let us therefore remember that we and all our affairs are governed by the providence of God, and that nothing happens to us by chance. Then let us remember that he is not only the almighty ruler of all things which are and happen in the world, but also our most loving Father, who desires us to be saved. Moreover, he is eternal wisdom, which nothing escapes and which cannot be deceived, so that all things cannot fail to reach the end he has purposed. Finally, he is the one who can bring light out of darkness, riches out of poverty, sound strength out of sickness, and life out of death. Why then do we not leave this care to him, who (as Paul says) "with the temptation also makes a way of escape, and does not suffer us to be tempted above what we are able." 1 Corinthians 10.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad postremam huius loci partem, qua narratur, Iesum triduo post à parentibus inuentum esse, & quidem in templo sedentem in medio Doctorum, quos & audiebat & interrogabat, & ipse quoque ad propositas ab illis quaestiones respondebat. Miretur vero aliquis hoc illi licuisse; sed diuinae virtutis opus fuit, quae postea efficacius adhuc se exeruit, quando in Synagogis & tem plo publicè in illorum hypocrisim, auaritiam & dolos inuectus est, adhaec nundinatores sacrorum flagello eiecit, numulariorum mensas euertit, neq; aliquis repertus est, qui se eius conatui opponere auderet. Et eiusdē virtute fit, quòd etiam hodie magni illi Pontifices in suis vrbibus & templis Christo velinuiti locum dant. Poterant etiam hic multa dici, vt Christus quæri debeat, & vt in templo suo, id est, Ecclesiæ, inter Euangelij prædicationem & legitimū Sacramentorum vsum sese nobis inueniendum & apprehendendū offerat: At quia hæc non sunt præsentis instituti, & de illis alibi commodius dicetur, nunc illud obseruabimus, quod ad liberorum institutionem pertinet. Vbi cumprimis memorabile est, quòd Iesus puer non inter cœtaneorum lusus, non in taberna apud ebriosos comessatores, & multò minus in alio loco minusque honesto inueniri voluit, sed in templo, quod doctrinæ & cultui Dei consecratum erat. Docet hoc suo exemplo, à pueris (vt nuper quoque monuimus) ijs studijs assuefscendū esse, quibus Deus colitur eiusq; gloria propagatur. Et simul eos omnes arguit, qui pueros ad concionēs sacras minimè adigendas putant, quando eas per ætatē non possint intelligere. At qui Ioannes Apostolus Euangelij doctrinam, non senibus modò & iuuenibus, verumetiā pueru lis conuenire scribit, quia per hanc in veri patris cognitionem adducantur. Debet ergo exemplum hoc probè obseruare, qui liberos suos ita assuefaciunt, vt eos in templis quærere minimè opus sit, cùm ipsa etiam hora sacrarum concionū per vicos discurrant, et ludis non tam puerilibus quàm scurrilibus occupentur. Quin eò vsq; progressa est parentum indulgentia, vel oscitantia potius, vt pij videri possint, qui liberos eo tempore, quo cætus sacri habentur, domi suæ continent. Solent hi suâ indulgentiā variis rationibus excusare, & modò frigoris immodicum rigorem, modò nimium æstum, et plerunq; vestium inopiā aut aduersam liberorum valetudinē prætexunt. Est enim mire ingeniosus Satan in excogitandis argumentis, quibus piam & sanctā puerorū institutionē impediat. At si illos ipsos propius inspicias, qui rationibus eiusmodi in fouēda liberorū licentia sibijpsis & illis blandiuntur, mox videbis, nihil illorū liberis deesse ad omne nequitiæ genus exercendū. Præcipua ergo culpa in parentibus hæret, quorum corda in gloriā Dei studio frigent, quiq; liberorum salutem impiè negligunt.
units.tr: Let us now come to the last part of this passage, in which it is related that Jesus was found by his parents three days later, sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, whom he both heard and questioned, and he himself also answered the questions put to him by them. Someone may wonder that this was permitted him; but it was the work of divine power, which afterwards showed itself even more effectively when he publicly inveighed in the synagogues and the temple against their hypocrisy, avarice and deceit, and moreover drove out the sellers of sacred things with a whip, and overturned the tables of the money-changers, and yet no one was found who dared to oppose his attempt. It is by the same power that even today those great pontiffs give place in their cities and temples to Christ, though against their will. Many things could also be said here about how Christ ought to be sought, and how he offers himself to be found and laid hold of by us in his temple, that is, the Church, amid the preaching of the gospel and the lawful use of the sacraments. But since these matters do not belong to the present purpose, and will be treated more fittingly elsewhere, we shall now note what pertains to the instruction of children. Here it is especially memorable that the boy Jesus did not wish to be found among the games of his peers, nor in a tavern among drunken revellers, and much less in some other place less honourable, but in the temple, which was consecrated to teaching and the worship of God. By this example he teaches that children (as we lately admonished) ought to be accustomed to those pursuits by which God is worshipped and his glory spread abroad. At the same time he rebukes all those who think that children are by no means to be compelled to attend sacred sermons, on the ground that they cannot understand them because of their age. But the Apostle John writes that the doctrine of the gospel is suited not only to the old and the young but also to children, because through it they are led to the knowledge of the true Father. Therefore those who train their children so that there is no need to look for them in the churches, since even at the very hour of the sacred sermons they run about the streets and are occupied with games not so much childish as buffoonish, ought carefully to observe this example. Indeed parental indulgence, or rather carelessness, has gone so far that some may seem pious who keep their children at home during the time when the sacred assemblies are held. Such people excuse their indulgence in various ways, sometimes pleading the excessive rigour of the cold, sometimes the excessive heat, and very often a lack of clothing or the poor health of their children. For Satan is wonderfully ingenious in devising arguments by which he may hinder the pious and holy upbringing of children. But if you look more closely at those who flatter themselves and their children with reasons of this kind for fostering their children's licence, you will soon see that their children lack nothing for practising every kind of wickedness. The chief fault therefore lies with the parents, whose hearts are cold in zeal for the glory of God, and who impiously neglect the salvation of their children.

units.la: Porrò videamus, quid in medio Doctorum Christus fecerit. Audiuit eos, & interrogauit eos: deinde responsorum quoq; fit mentio, quæ ad quæstiones sibi propositas dedit. Duo igitur de illo dicit Lucas. Primum, quòd docentes audiuerit, & vt solent qui discendi studio tenentur, de nonnullis diligentius interrogarit. Alterū, quòd ad interrogata sic respond��rit, vt eius modestiā & sapientiam omnes admirati sint. At si illum consideremus, qualis est, æternus nimirum Dei filius, qui nobis à patre sapientia factus est, minimè illi opus fuit aliquem audire vel interrogare. Quia tamē propter nos homo verus factus est, noluit Ecclesiæ & verbi ministerium contemnere, quod ad nos instituendum Deus ordinauit; & vt huic sese omnes homines accommodent, suo exemplo docet. Neq; hic opus est quærere, annon absq; doctrina externa Deus mentes nostras veritatis & salutis æternæ cognitione illuminare possit? Nam qui hoc quærunt, perinde faciunt ac si quis interroget, annon absq; cibo & potu, aut saltem absq; laborioso agrorum cultu nos idem ille alere & feruare queat? Quod certè nemo pius negauerit, cùm Moßis & Eliæ, adhæc Israelitarum in deserto exempla extent, quos ita aliquandiu seruatos fuisse constat. At quia diuinitus sic constitutum est, vt vitam victu ordinario sustentemus, eumq; manuum labore quæramus, impium fuerit Deum tentare, & ab illo nouam viuendi rationem exigere. Hoc ipsum in præsenti quoq; causa obseruandum esse dicimus. Spirat certè spiritus Dei vbicunq; vult, neq; ministerio Ecclesiæ virtus eius necessariò alligata est: imò ministros in hominum animis nihil proficere dicimus, nisi Deus incrementum det. Quia verò hunc docendi ordinem Deus instituit, ingratè & impiè arrogantes sunt, qui & illum contemnunt, & se dignos arbitrantur, in quorum gratiam Deus nouī quid instituat. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter sanctissimi quiq;, qui in cœtibus sacris & verbi prædicatione voluptatem summam sibi repositam putarunt, quod non vno loco Psalmi testantur, vt infinita alia scripturæ loca omittamus. At nō sufficit Verbum audiuisse, sed vt hoc attentè & cū iudicio audiamus opus est, ne sub verbi diuini prætextu quis nobis imponat. Ideo Christus Doctores etiam interrogauisse dicitur: nimirum quòd illos humanas traditiones cū Lege Dei miscere & multa perperam docere cerneret. Et Apostoli graviter monent, vt quæ dicuntur probemus ad fidei analogiam & dijudicemus spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Quod cùm pueros etiam facere iubeat Christus suo exemplo, inexcusabilis prorsus illorum socordia est, qui absq; omni delectu quiduis sequuntur, quasi salus ipsorum ab alieno iudicio pendeat.
units.tr: Let us next consider what Christ did in the midst of the teachers. He listened to them and questioned them, and mention is also made of the answers he gave to the questions put to him. Luke therefore tells us two things about him. First, that he listened to the teachers and, as those who are eager to learn usually do, questioned some of them more closely. Second, that he answered their questions in such a way that everyone admired his modesty and wisdom. But if we consider who he is, namely the eternal Son of God, who has been made wisdom for us by the Father, he had no need at all to hear or question anyone. Yet because he became a true man for our sake, he was unwilling to despise the Church and the ministry of the Word, which God ordained for our instruction, and by his own example he teaches all men to submit themselves to it. Nor is there any need to ask whether God could not illuminate our minds with the knowledge of truth and eternal salvation without external teaching. Those who ask this do just as if someone were to ask whether that same God could nourish and preserve us without food and drink, or at least without the laborious cultivation of the fields. No pious person would certainly deny this, since the examples of Moses and Elijah, and also of the Israelites in the desert, exist, and it is known that they were preserved for a time in this way. But because it has been divinely ordained that we sustain life by ordinary food and seek it by the labour of our hands, it would be impious to tempt God and to demand from him a new way of living. We say that this same principle must be observed in the present case too. The Spirit of God certainly blows where he wills, nor is his power necessarily bound to the ministry of the Church. Indeed we say that ministers accomplish nothing in men's minds unless God gives the increase. But since God has instituted this order of teaching, those are ungrateful and impious arrogant men who both despise it and think themselves so worthy that God should introduce something new for their sake. The most holy men have observed this diligently, who thought the highest pleasure was reserved for them in the assemblies of worship and in the preaching of the Word, as many Psalms bear witness in more than one place, to say nothing of countless other passages of Scripture. But it is not enough to have heard the Word; we must listen to it attentively and with judgement, lest anyone impose on us under the pretext of the divine word. Therefore Christ is said to have questioned the teachers too, clearly because he saw them mixing human traditions with the Law of God and teaching many things wrongly. The Apostles also earnestly warn us to test what is said by the analogy of faith and to discern the spirits, whether they are from God. Since Christ commands even children to do this by his example, the sloth of those is wholly inexcusable who follow whatever they are given without any discrimination, as if their salvation depended on another's judgement.

units.la: Ne quis vero actionem hanc puerilem fuisse putet, addit Lucas: Obstupescebant autem omnes, qui eum audiebant, super intelligentia & responsis eius. Quibus verbis totius istius negotij finis & scopus principalis exprimitur. Voluit enim Christus suae vocationis tyrocinium facere (ut diximus) quo doceret, se catholicum, id est universalem illum & vere orthodoxum humani generis doctorem esse, cuius vocem omnes audire, cuius sapientiam omnes admirari, cuius item authoritati omnes obedire debeant. Et quidem a docendo regni sui auspicium fieri voluit, ut hoc non in externo splendore & armorum praesidio, sed in spiritus virtute consistere doceret, quae per Verbum sese potissimum exerit. Quod etsi mundi iudicio puerile & ridiculum videatur, idem tamen hoc omnem mundi sapientiam confundit, & ijs quoq; admirationem parit, qui illi credere & obedire nondum dignantur. Quod enim hic accidi, saepe alias evenisse constat. In Actis certe scribitur, totum Senatum Hierosolymorum ad Petri & Ioannis in dicendo libertatem ita perculsos fuisse, ut quid in ipsorum causa statuendum esset, nō viderent. Et in Ecclesiastica historia saepe indicatur, homines illiteratos, imo iuuenes et puellas, non solum acutissimis philosophis negotium fecisse, sed tyrannis quoq; stuporem & timorem incussisse. Et hoc illud est quod discipulis Christus pollicetur: Ego vobis dabo os & sapientiam, cui no poterunt contradicere neque resistere omnes qui se opponent vobis. Cuius promissionis effectus, cum etiam hodie duret, debent ex ea consolationem petere, quicunque coram hostibus veritatis fidei aut doctrinae suae rationem reddere coguntur. Sed de hoc plura suo loco dicentur. Nunc quoad huius orationis argumentum, meminisse debent parentes, liberos sibi a Deo datos esse, & proinde eosdem huic adduci & consecrari debere. Quod ut maiori cum fructu fiat, non doctrina solum & institutione, sed exemplo illis praeire debent. E contra pueri institutionem admittant, ut Christo Iesu per fidem insiti, in eodem adolescant in viros perfectos, & caelestis regni coheredes fiant. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lest anyone think this action was childish, Luke adds: "And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers." In these words the purpose and chief aim of this whole matter is expressed. For Christ wished to make a beginning of his calling by teaching (as we have said), so that he might show that he is the catholic, that is, the universal and truly orthodox teacher of the human race, whose voice all should hear, whose wisdom all should admire, and whose authority all ought to obey. And indeed he wished the beginning of his kingdom to be made by teaching, so that he might show that it consists not in external splendour and the protection of arms, but in the power of the Spirit, which chiefly shows itself through the Word. Although this may seem childish and ridiculous by the judgement of the world, it nonetheless confounds all the wisdom of the world, and it produces admiration even in those who do not yet deign to believe and obey him. For that this happened here is known to have happened often elsewhere. In the Acts it is certainly written that the whole Senate of Jerusalem was so struck by the freedom of Peter and John in speaking that they did not see what ought to be decided in their case. And in ecclesiastical history it is often recorded that unlettered men, indeed young men and girls, have not only troubled the most acute philosophers but have also struck tyrants with astonishment and fear. This is what Christ promises his disciples: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all who oppose you will not be able to contradict or resist." Since the effect of this promise lasts even today, all who are compelled to give an account of their faith or their teaching before the enemies of the truth ought to draw consolation from it. But these matters will be discussed more fully in their proper place. Now, as to the subject of this discourse, parents ought to remember that children have been given to them by God, and therefore they ought to be brought to him and consecrated to him. So that this may be done with greater fruit, parents must go before their children not only by teaching and instruction but also by example. On the other hand, children should accept instruction, so that, grafted into Christ Jesus through faith, they may grow up in him into perfect men and become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXV.
units.tr: HOMILY XXV.

units.la: Et visus eo fuerunt attoniti, & dixit mater eius ad eum: Fili, cur ita fecisti nobis? Ecce pater tuus & ego cruciati quaerebamus te. Tunc dixit ad eos: quid est quod quaerebatis me? An nescietis, quod in ijs, quae Patris mei sunt, oportet me esse? Sed ipsi non intellexerunt verba, quae locutus est eis. Descendit autem cum eis, venitq; Nazareth, et erat eis subiectus. Et mater eius conseruabat omnia haec in corde suo. Iesus autem proficiebat sapientia & statura, ac gratia apud Deum & homines.
units.tr: And they were astonished at him. And his mother said to him: "Son, why have you treated us like this? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish." Then he said to them: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" But they did not understand the words he spoke to them. Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. And his mother kept all these things in her heart. And Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature, and in grace with God and men.

units.la: Nemo superuacaneum putet, quod Christi pueritia & quae in ea ab illo puero adhuc facta sunt, Spiritus sanctus tanta diligentia per Lucam describi voluit. Quia enim Dei filius propter nos ita hominem assumere debuit, ex aeterno patris decreto, ut puer etiam fieret, aequum & pium fuerit ea nouisse & diligentius considerauisse, quae ad eius puerilem aetatem faciunt: in quibus nihil tam minutum aut contemptibile esse, quod non aliquam doctrinam & consolationem singularem afferat, si attentius a nobis expendatur. Vidimus hoc in proxima huius historiae parte, vbi multa eius generis proponuntur: quae cum in recenti adhuc memoria sint fratres, nolo vos inutili, aut saltem non necessaria eorundem repetitione fatigare. Pergamus ergo ad huius loci, quem modo recitauimus, tractationem. Proponitur in eo primum Mariae virginis ferium & vehemens cum filio Iesu Christo colloquium. Deinde ut hic cum Iosepho & Maria Nazarethum reuersus & ijsdem subditus fuerit, narratur. Quibus tandem praeclarum & eximium fructum subijcit Lucas, qui ad Iesum Christum, quo ad assumptum hominem, ex sancta illa institutione atq; disciplina redijt.
units.tr: No one should think it superfluous that the Holy Spirit wished Luke to describe so carefully the boyhood of Christ and what the boy Christ did at that time. For since the Son of God, by the eternal decree of the Father, had to assume humanity in this way, so that he would also become a child, it is right and good for us to know and to consider carefully the things that pertain to his childhood. In these matters nothing is so small or contemptible that it does not bring some particular teaching and comfort, if we weigh it attentively. We saw this in the earlier part of this history, where many things of this kind were set forth. Since they are still fresh in your memory, brethren, I do not wish to weary you with a useless, or at least unnecessary, repetition of them. Let us therefore proceed to the treatment of the passage we have just read. In it, first, the grave and vehement conversation of the virgin Mary with her son Jesus Christ is set forth. Then it is related that he returned with Joseph and Mary to Nazareth and was subject to them. Finally, Luke adds the remarkable and outstanding fruit: that Jesus Christ, as regards his assumed humanity, grew up under that holy upbringing and discipline.

units.la: Quoad colloquium, constat id partibus duabus. Prima Christum Mariae accusat & reprehendit. Altera Christi responsionem & defensionem continet. Accusatio vel reprehensio Mariae talis est: Fili, cur ita fecisti nobis? Ecce pater tuus et ego cruciati quaerebamus te. Sunt haec verba pauca quidem, sed dura satis & gravia, si cogitemus quo affectu, & in quae dicantur. Nam perinde hoc est, ac si dixisset. Quia filius meus es, dicebat, ut filium bonum agendo me labore & molestia, quam hucusque propter te multiplicem & grauem sustinui, leuares. Sed quantum video, non satis est, me peregre agentem partum doloribus oppressam fuisse, necessarijs omnibus destitutam in stabulo peperisse, inde ut te Herodis manibus cruentis subducerem in Aegyptum profugisse, vbi inter homines superstitio fos & idololatras nihil non malorum passa sum, quae fugam & exilium comitari solent: Quin tu nobis adhuc nouas molestias exhibes & noui doloris iidem es author. Respice quaeso hunc Iosephum, quem sine aetatem eius, sine quam saepe expertus es fidem in te tuendo considereis, non potes non patris loco habere, & me plus satis afflictam matrem tuam, et cogita quam indigne abs te factum sit, quod te clam subducendo nos in terrores grauissimos, in acerbissimum luctum, simulque in labores nouos conieceris, ut totius diei itinere confecto huc redire opus fuerit, vbi te toto triduo no fine summo animi cruciatu quaesiuimus. Quare ita fecisti nobis? Anno aequius erat, ut tu nos abiturientes obseruares, teque nobis coniungeres, quam quod nos in te quaerendo nouum curis & laboribus fatigari oportuit? Quae obsecro ratio sufficere potest ad te excusandum? &c. Haec omnia & alia huius generis multa sub pauculis bisce verbis comprehensa latent. Fuit haec obiurgatio acrior quam decebat, maxime, cum hunc Dei filium esse Maria non ignoraret. Expressit tamen ei illam dolor nimius, ut in iure suo tuendo modum excedat. Accidit hoc nobis frequenter, quae causa est, quod summum ius saepe in summam iniuriam exit, & in bona etiam causa peccemus, dum mediocritatis & aequitatis leges transgredimur, & in nostrum modo ius intenti, non obseruamus quae reuerentia quodam officium illis debeatur, quibus cum nobis res est. Quo magis nos aduigilare decet, & nostra omnia suspecta habere, ne grauius ijs peccemus, quos nostra reprehensione dignos iudicamus.
units.tr: As for the conversation, it consists of two parts. The first is that Christ is accused and rebuked by Mary. The second contains Christ's answer and defence. The accusation or rebuke of Mary is this: "Son, why have you treated us like this? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish." These words are few, but harsh and grave enough, if we consider with what feeling and about what they are spoken. For it is as if she had said: "You are my son; you ought to relieve me, by acting like a good son, of the labour and trouble which I have borne for you until now in great measure. But, as far as I can see, it is not enough that I, while travelling abroad, was overcome by the pains of childbirth, that I gave birth in a stable with no necessities at hand, that to snatch you from the bloody hands of Herod I fled into Egypt, where among a superstitious and idolatrous people I suffered every kind of evil that usually accompanies flight and exile. Rather, you still bring us fresh troubles and are the author of new grief. Look, I beg you, at this Joseph, whom, for his age and for the faithfulness he has often shown in caring for you, you cannot but regard as a father, and at me, your mother, already more than sufficiently afflicted. Consider how unworthily you have acted, in secretly slipping away from us and casting us into the most grievous terrors and the most bitter mourning, and at the same time into new labours, so that after a full day's journey we had to return here, where for three whole days we searched for you with the greatest anguish of mind. Why have you treated us like this? Would it not have been more fitting for you to watch over us as we departed and to join yourself to us, rather than for us to be wearied with new cares and labours in seeking you? What reason, I beg you, can suffice to excuse you? And so on." All these things, and many others of this kind, lie hidden under these few words. The rebuke was sharper than was fitting, especially since Mary did not fail to know that this man was the Son of God. Yet her excessive grief drew it from her, so that in defending her own right she went beyond due measure. This happens to us often, and this is why the highest right often turns into the highest wrong, and why we sin even in a good cause when we transgress the laws of moderation and fairness, and, intent only on our own right, do not observe the respect that is owed to those with whom we have to do. All the more should we be watchful and regard all our own conduct with suspicion, lest we sin more grievously against those whom we judge worthy of our reproof.

units.la: Caeterum quamuis in hoc peccarit Maria, magnus tamen huius exempli vsus est, quoad educationem & institutionem puerorum. Docet enim quod nam ius sit parentum in filios, quodque illis liceat eos non solum blandioribus verbis monere, verumetiam durius corrigere, & prout meruerunt, castigare quoque liceat. Est hoc factu necessarium ad coercendum innatam nobis naturae vitiositatem, quae suos effectus in tenera etiam aetate non obscure profert. Nam ipso etiam Deo teste, figmenta cordis humani iam inde a pueris prava sunt, ideoque multa obseruatione dignissima est Solomonis sententia: Stultitia colligata est in corde pueri, sed ferula castigatrix procul expellit ea. Et ex eo alibi infert: Qui abstinet virgam suam, odit filium suum: qui vero eum amat, mature disciplinam adhibet. Item: Virga & obiurgatio dat sapientiam, & sibi, id est, suorum affectuum libidini relictus puer pudefacit matrem suam. Castiga filium tuum: hoc quiete tibi afferet, deliciasque animo tuo, &c. Nec temere faciet putabimus, quod mortalium sapientissimus, & Regum, quotquot vnquam fuerunt, illustrissimus, Solomon, eo vsque sese demisit, ut de puerorum institutione et disciplina tam multis tamque diligenter egerit. Sciebat enim rempub. diu salua esse non posse, in qua iuuentutis institutio negligitur. Nam vt greges paulatim deficiunt, cuius agni non probe seruantur, vtque de anni proventu spes bona esse nequit, si segetes in herba pereant: ita populus pereat oportet, si pueri (quos reipub. & patriae communis spem veteres dixerunt) aut negligantur, aut praua institutione corrumpantur. Ergo optimi & sapientissimi Regis officio fideliter functus est Solomon, quando huius aetatis diligentem institutionem tam diligenter commendauit. Neque ex suo cerebro ista protulisse videri debet, quando conscribitur: Si quis filium habuerit defectorem seu rebellem, qui vocem patris sui & matris suae audire noluerit, & si castigent eum ipsis obedire nolit: apprehendent eum pater eius & mater eius educentque eum ad Seniores ciuitatis illius, & ad portam eius loci, dicentque ad Seniores ciuitatis illius: Filius hic noster defector est & rebellis, nec vult audire vocem nostram, comessator est & potator: lapidibusque eum obruent omnes ciues illius ciuitatu, donec moriatur, & expurgabis malum de medio tui, vt omnes Israelitae audientes timeant. Est Lex ista non ociter negligenda. Nec enim de filijs periurus, blasphemis, adulteris, raptoribus, parricidis aut alio capitali crimine infamibus hic sermo est: sed de responsatoribus & immergeris, qui comessando, potando, ludendo rem domesticam dissipant & parentibus luctum atque dolorem afferunt, & illis capitis poena statuitur: adeoque ipse quasi gladius parentibus in manum datur, quo tales iugulentur. Neque nuda haec permissio est, sed vt hoc faciant parentes atque iudices, diserte mandatur. Et constat, eos, qui in hoc exequendo negligentiores fueres fuerunt, tandem graues suæ indulgentiæ pœnas Deo dedisse.
