Exemplum eius rei euidens & in primis luctuosum in Elio sacerdote & iudice historia sacra nobis exhibet. Fuit is, vt ex circunstantijs apparet, pius, religiosus & honesti amans: sed in filios suos indulgentior suo iure in illis punien-dis non esset vsus. Cum enim illi sacrilega audacia carnes sacrificantium raperent, stupris & adulte-rijs tabernaculum Domini prophanarent, & sua libidine cultum Dei in contemptum adducerent: verbis quidem durioribus eos corripuit, & Dei irati iudicium minatus esset: at quia contumaces & incurabiles pro patris & iudicis officio non dignis pœnis (sicuti in Lege iubebatur) coercet, suo in il-lum iudicio animaduertit Deus, & per Samuelem puerü pœnam illi denunciat horrendam, quæ non multo post non sine publica totius populi calamitate secuta est. Nam vno eodemq; die filij eius ho-stili gladio cadunt, arca fœderis ab hostibus capitur, & ipse Eli audito tam tristi nuntio e sella supi-nus cadens fracta ceruice tristem vitæ suæ finem attingit. Possent huius generis exempla ex gentiū quoq; historijs infinita adduci. Sed exemplis longè petitus minimè opus est, quando multa quotidie fiunt, quæ his fidem faciunt. Quàm multos enim est videre, qui omne genus nequitiæ in filijs suis pa-tienter ferunt, neq; mouentur si quando illos vel vicinię toti vel multis bonis molestos esse audiant? At ijdem postea, vbi filiorum prouentia ferocior facta est, illos in se quoque tales esse magno cum do-lore sentiunt, quales diu in alios fuerunt. Et peccant quidem tunc admodum graviter filij, sed pecca-tum (vt aiunt) peccati pœna est, & iusto Dei iudicio fit, vt parentes quoq; eum fructum metant ex filijs, quem nimia sua indulgentia seminauerunt. Discant ergo omnes suam authoritatem erga libe-ros tueri, nedum eos indulgentius tractant, ipsi quoque cum eorum sceleribus communicent, & Deo pœnas dignas exoluant. Discant vicissim liberi patienter ferre parentum castigationem & disciplì-nam, ne dum hanc audacius reijciunt, ordinem a Deo institutum magno suo malo turbent. Memi-nerint item nulla venia dignam fore ipsorum contumaciā, si corripi nolint, cùm æternus Dei filius, sanctus ille sanctorum à matre publice reprehensus fit: cui facile erat hoc declinare, nisi nos suo exem-plo officij admonere voluisset. At quia de hoc mox plura dicentur, nunc alteram huius colloquij par-tem audiamus, qua Christus factum suum matri excusat.
units.tr: Yet although Mary sinned in this, the example has great use for the education and instruction of children. For it teaches what the right of parents over their children is, and that it is lawful for them not only to admonish them with gentler words, but also to correct them more sharply and, as they deserve, to chastise them. This is necessary for restraining the innate viciousness of our nature, which shows its effects plainly even in tender age. For, as God himself testifies, the imaginations of the human heart are evil from childhood, and therefore the saying of Solomon is most worthy of close attention: "Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction will drive it far away." And elsewhere he draws the inference: "He who spares his rod hates his son, but he who loves him applies discipline early." Again: "The rod and rebuke give wisdom, but a child left to his own will brings shame to his mother." And: "Correct your son, and he will give you rest, and will give delight to your soul." Nor shall we think that the wisest of mortals, and the most illustrious of all kings who have ever been, Solomon, stooped so low without reason as to deal at such length and with such care with the instruction and discipline of children. For he knew that a commonwealth cannot long be safe in which the training of youth is neglected. Just as flocks gradually perish when their lambs are not properly kept, and just as there can be no good hope of the year's yield if the crops perish in the blade, so the people must perish if the children, whom the ancients called the common hope of the commonwealth and of the fatherland, are either neglected or corrupted by bad training. Solomon therefore discharged the duty of a good and wise king faithfully when he so diligently commended the careful training of this age. Nor should it seem that he put forward these things out of his own head, when it is written: "If anyone has a son who is stubborn and rebellious, who will not hear the voice of his father and his mother, and when they chastise him he will not obey them, then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city, and to the gate of that place, and they shall say to the elders of his city: 'This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious, he will not hear our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.' And all the men of his city shall stone him with stones until he dies, and you shall purge the evil from among you, so that all Israel, hearing, may fear." That law is not to be lightly disregarded. For it does not speak of sons who are perjurers, blasphemers, adulterers, robbers, parricides, or infamous for some other capital crime, but of wasters and gluttons, who by feasting, drinking and gambling squander the household property and bring sorrow and grief to their parents, and for these a penalty of death is laid down. Thus the sword itself is, as it were, put into the hands of the parents, so that they may slay such sons. Nor is this a bare permission; it is expressly commanded that the parents and the judges should do this. And it is clear that those who were more negligent in carrying this out were in the end made by God to pay heavy penalties for their indulgence. Sacred history presents us with an evident and especially sorrowful example of this in Eli the priest and judge. He was, as the circumstances make plain, a pious, religious man who loved what was honest, but he had been too indulgent toward his sons and had not used his right to punish them. For when they, with sacrilegious boldness, seized the flesh of those who offered sacrifice, profaned the tabernacle of the Lord with fornications and adulteries, and by their lust brought the worship of God into contempt, he rebuked them with rather harsh words and threatened them with the judgement of an angry God. But because they were stubborn and incorrigible, and he did not restrain them with the punishments that were not worthy of a father and judge (as the Law commanded), God passed judgement on him for this, and through Samuel announced to him a dreadful punishment for his sons, which not long afterwards followed, not without public calamity to the whole people. For on one and the same day his sons fell by the hostile sword, the ark of the covenant was taken by the enemies, and Eli himself, when he heard such sad news, fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and came to the sorrowful end of his life. Innumerable examples of this kind could be brought from the histories of the nations as well. But there is no need to seek examples from far away, since many things happen every day which bear witness to this. How many are there to be seen who patiently bear every kind of wickedness in their sons, and are not moved even when they hear that these sons are troublesome to the whole neighbourhood or to many good people? Yet afterwards, when the boldness of their sons has grown fiercer, they feel with great grief that their sons are toward themselves just what they had long been toward others. The sons indeed sin very grievously then, but sin (as they say) is the punishment of sin, and by the just judgement of God it comes about that parents too reap from their sons the fruit which their excessive indulgence has sown. Let all therefore learn to maintain their authority over their children, and not treat them too indulgently; and let them not share in their wickedness, but pay the penalties due to God. In turn, let children learn to bear patiently the correction and discipline of their parents, lest by rejecting it too boldly they disturb the order instituted by God, to their own great harm. Let them remember also that their own obstinacy would be worthy of no pardon if they would not be corrected, since the eternal Son of God, that holy one of the saints, was publicly rebuked by his mother. For him it would have been easy to avoid this, had he not wished by his own example to remind us of our duty. But since more will be said of this shortly, let us now hear the other part of this conversation, in which Christ excuses his action to his mother. Thus he answered: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" This reply seems harsher and more arrogant than becomes a son of good hope and promise. For the words sound as if…

units.la: Sic vero ille respondit: Quid est quòd quærebatis me? An nesciebatis, quòd in ijs, quæ patris mei sunt, oportet me esse? Videtur responsio hæc durior & arrogantior quàm bonæ spei & frugis fi-lium deceat. Nam perinde sonant verba, ac si de eorum molestia & dolore non multum ipse sit solici-tus, & quasi illos ignorantiæ & iniquitatis manifestæ accuset. Imò parentes hos suos esse tantùm nõ aperte negat, quando patrem alium nominat, cuius vocationi nunc sit obediendum. At si rem ipsam propius consideremus, facilè patebit, illum nihil præter officium fecisse, neque iunioribus exemplum præbuisse, quo parentibus suis respondere discant. Fuerunt enim graues causæ, propter quas ipsum ma-tri grauius respondere oportuit. Nam primò necesse erat, vt suam tueretur innocentiam, quā Ma-ria doloris effectu abrepta nõ leui labe aut macula asperserat. Accusarat enim ipsum inobedientiæ, & quòd præter officium parentibus molestiæ & doloris maximi author fuisset. Est hoc peccatū, imò scelus ingens, & quouis supplicio dignum. Nec enim temere Sapiens ille dixit: Infamis est desertor patris, & maledictus Domino, qui matri suæ mouet indignationem. Quia ergo impossibile fuisset, Christum pro peccatis nostris sacrificium Deo gratum fieri, si tanto scelere ipse Dei maledictionem meruisset, non tam ipsius honor & gloria, quàm nostræ salutis ratio exigebat, vt suam innocentiam fortiter assereret. Deinde tam matri Virgini quàm aliis hominibus aliquo modo ostendi oportebat, quis nam esset Christus, quod alterum huius historiæ caput esse, nuper diximus. Adhæc simul docere voluit, quo vsque extendi debeat obedientiæ officium, quo parentibus liberi obstricti sunt. Confert enim inter se matris mandatum & patris Dei vocationem. Matris mandatum siue sententia erat, ipsum vnà secum ab Hierosolyma discedere debuisse. At Dei patris voluntas erat, vt in templo do-ceret, et suæ functionis tyrocinium faceret, ne puerilis ætatis contempta et infirma species diuinæ eius sapientiæ & authoritati aliquid derogaret. Pugnabant hæc ita inter se, vt eodem tempore verum simul fieri non posset. Ideo inter illa distinguens diserte monet, sibi necesse fuisse, vt patris mandatum faceret, & proinde non potuisse nunc matri suum obsequium præstare.
units.tr: Yet he answered them thus: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?" This answer seems harsher and more arrogant than a son of good hope and promise ought to give. The words sound as if he cared little for their distress and grief, and as if he were accusing them of plain ignorance and unkindness. He comes close to openly denying that they are his parents when he names another Father whose calling he must now obey. But if we consider the matter more closely, it will readily appear that he did nothing beyond his duty, and gave the younger ones no example of answering their parents back. There were weighty reasons why he had to reply more sharply to his mother. First, it was necessary for him to defend his innocence, which Mary, carried away by the force of her grief, had stained with no slight blemish. For she had accused him of disobedience, and of being the author of great grief and distress to his parents beyond his duty. This is a sin, indeed a great crime, deserving of any punishment. Nor did that wise man speak carelessly when he said: "He who grieves his mother is an infamous deserter of his father, and is cursed by the Lord." Therefore, since Christ could not have become an acceptable sacrifice to God for our sins had he himself deserved God's curse by so great a crime, it was not so much his own honour and glory as the reason of our salvation that required him to assert his innocence boldly. Next, it was necessary to show, in some way, both to the Virgin Mother and to other people, who Christ was, which we lately said was the second main point of this history. Besides this, he wished to teach how far the duty of obedience, to which children are bound towards their parents, should extend. For he sets the command of his mother against the calling of God his Father. His mother's command, or opinion, was that he should have left Jerusalem together with her. But the will of God the Father was that he should teach in the temple and make a beginning of his office, lest his youthful age and humble appearance, despised, should detract from the divine wisdom and authority that was in him. These things were so opposed to each other that both could not be true at the same time. Therefore, in distinguishing between them, he clearly reminds them that he had to do his Father's business, and so could not now render obedience to his mother.

units.la: Debet ex hoc Christi exemplo generalis doctrina aut regula peti, quam in sequenda Dei vocatione obseruemus. Est hæc, ne aliquê mortalium tantæ authoritatis esse putemus, vt in eius gratiam iniunctum à Deo munus negligamus. Nam quæcunq; hominibus debentur officia, ad secundam Decalogi tabulam pertinent, quæ tunc demum rectè à nobis obseruabitur, si prioris tabulæ authoritas apud nos sancta & rata fit, neq; diuini cultus leges temere aut superstitiose violemus. Constat equidem inter homines neminem nobis arctiori vinculo deinctum esse, quam parentes, quibus parem gratiam referri nunquam posse, gentium philosophi non male dixerunt. Illis enim post Deum vitam nostram debemus, cum ab ipsis & geniti & infinito cum labore atq; molestia educati simus. At si illi non contenti ea, quam ipsis debemus, obedientia, illud quoque à nobis requirant, quod salua fide & pietate erga Deum fieri nequit: tunc cessante illa reuerentia, quæ illis debetur, ad Christi responsum nos confugere oportet: An nescitis nos in iis esse oportere, quæ patris nostri cœlestis sunt, cui omnes ex æquo obedientiam debemus? Ita nos ille suo exemplo vti docet, quādo ait: Veni vt diffidere faciam hominem aduersus patrem suum, & filiam aduersus matrem suam. Qui parentes suos magis quàm me diligit, non est me dignus. Imò vt parentes odio habeamus iubet, non quidem impietatem & inhumanitatem præcipiens, sed nos ita sibi addictos esse volens, vt nullius hominis authoritate, & ne naturalibus affectionibus, quas Græci [?] dixerunt, nos ab eius præceptis abduci patiamur. Iis ergo sese tueantur liberi, si quando (vt sæpe fieri solet) à parentibus solicitantur, vt abnegata Christi fide, superstitionibus & idololatriæ sese mancipent, aut sese aliorum scelerum socios atq; ministros illis præbeant. Quia enim parentes in eiusmodi casu iure sibi diuinitus concessso impie contra Deum abutuntur, tunc nobis non parentum loco, sed pro Dei aduersarijs habendi sunt.
units.tr: From this example of Christ a general doctrine or rule should be drawn, which we should observe in following God's calling. It is this: that we must not think any mortal to be of such authority that we neglect a task enjoined by God for his sake. For whatever duties are owed to men belong to the second table of the Decalogue, and these will be rightly observed by us only if the authority of the first table is holy and fixed among us, and we do not rashly or superstitiously violate the laws of divine worship. It is indeed agreed among men that no one is bound to us by a closer tie than our parents, to whom the philosophers of the nations rightly said an equal return can never be made. For after God we owe our life to them, since we were both begotten by them and brought up with infinite labour and trouble. But if they, not content with the obedience that we owe them, require of us also what cannot be done without loss of faith and piety towards God, then, when that reverence which is due to them ceases, we must take refuge in Christ's answer: "Did you not know that we must be about the things of our heavenly Father, to whom we all owe obedience alike?" Thus he teaches us to use his example when he says: "I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Indeed, he bids us hate our parents, not commanding impiety or inhumanity, but wishing us to be so devoted to him that we do not allow ourselves to be drawn away from his precepts by the authority of any man, nor by natural affections, which the Greeks called [?]. Therefore children should defend themselves against these things if, as often happens, their parents urge them to abandon the faith of Christ and give themselves over to superstitions and idolatry, or to become partners and helpers of their parents in other crimes. For when parents, in such a case, impiously abuse against God the right divinely granted to them, then they are to be regarded not in the place of parents, but as adversaries of God.

units.la: Eadem plane est magistratuum quoq; ratio. Sunt hi diuinitus instituti, & Deorum nomen in scripturis obtinent, Deoq; aduersari dicitur, quisquis se illis seditiose opponit. Ita verò illis obedire oportet, vt simul Deo etiam obtemperemus, & huic debitum præstemus officium. Ideo Christus olim dicebat: Date Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris, & Deo quæ sunt Dei. Quod dictū suo exemplo Apostoli egregiè interpretantur. Cum enim Senatus Hierosolymitanus mandaret, ne posthac in Christi nomine docerent, primò modestius respondent: An coram Deo iustum sit vos potius audire quàm Deum, iudicate: quasi dicant: Non equidem vos vel tam imprudentes, vel tam impiè arrogantes putamus, vt maiorem vestri quàm diuini mandati authoritatem esse velitis. At cum illi posteà suum edictum in solentius vrgerent, ipsi quoque liberius aduersus eos pronuntiant: Obedire oportet Deo potius quàm hominibus. Vtrunq; verò hoc responsum communi omnium nomine Petrus dedit, qui in sua epistola Regem honorare & ab hoc institutis magistratibus obedire iubet. Erant hæc ijs consideranda diligentius, qui fidei veræ abnegationem & defectionem ad superstitiones eo potissimum argumento excusant, quòd magistratui obediendum esse dicunt. Fatemur hoc etiam nos, sed vsq; adeo, quod aiunt: Sed ita produnt seipsos illi homines, quòd humanam authoritatem diuinæ præferant, & magis eos metuant, qui corpus solum possunt occidere, quàm Deum, cui in nostra corpora simul & animas plena potestas est. Sed de hoc plura alibi.
units.tr: The reasoning is exactly the same for magistrates also. They are instituted by God, and in Scripture they bear the name of gods, and whoever seditiously opposes them is said to oppose God. Yet we must obey them in such a way that at the same time we also obey God, and render to him the duty owed. Therefore Christ once said: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." The apostles, by their own example, interpret this saying admirably. For when the Senate of Jerusalem ordered them not to teach any more in the name of Christ, they at first answered rather modestly: "Judge whether it is right before God to hear you rather than God." As if they said: "We do not indeed think you so imprudent or so impiously arrogant as to wish the authority of your command to be greater than that of the divine command." But when the Senate afterwards pressed its edict more strongly, they too pronounced more freely against them: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Peter gave this answer in the name of all of them together, and in his epistle he bids us honour the king and obey magistrates set up by him. These matters ought to be considered more carefully by those who excuse the denial of the true faith and the defection to superstitions mainly on this argument: that they say magistrates must be obeyed. We too admit this, but only so far, as they say; but those men betray themselves in this, that they set human authority above the divine, and fear more those who can kill only the body than God, who has full power over both our bodies and our souls. But more on this elsewhere.

units.la: Priusquam vero ad alteram huius loci partem transeamus, hoc quoque excutiendum venit quod dicitur: Sed ipsi non intellexerunt verba, quæ locutus est eis. Atqui non ignorabant ipsum filium Dei esse, & promissum illum populi vindicem, quem vulgò Messiam dicebant. Quæ ergo causa istius ignorantiæ? Ea nimirum quòd cum nondum publicè manifestata esset Dei vocatio, illi de Christi officio non rectè iudicarunt. Itaq; communi Iudæorum errore decepti, Regem sibi finxerunt, qui populo ex Romana tyrannide liberato, regnum in terris constitueret, victoriis & diuitiis illustre. Ad quem lapidem Ioannis & Iacobi matre & simul discipulos omnes postea offendisse constat. Hac igitur opinione parentes etiam adhuc decenti, non possunt videre, quæ nam illa sint patris negotia, in quibus ipsum esse oporteat: cum docendi officio eum fungi viderent, quem ipsi Regem terrenum fore somniabant. Quo exemplo admonemur, quanta sit nostræ rationis cæcitas in iis, quæ ad Dei regnum spectant. Nihil ergo illi nos tribuere decet, neq; eos audire, qui fidei & æternæ salutis mysteria ad nostri intellectus calculum reuocant. Quin potius per fidei obedientiam nos totos Dei verbo subijciamus. Quod qui faciunt, si suo tempore diuinitus illuminati ea intelligunt, quæ prius ipsis incerta & obscura videbantur. Admonet de hoc nos Maria, quæ iterum hæc etiam in corde suo conseruauit: neq; dubium est, quin eadem postea in memoriam reuocarit, cum filium publicè docentem videret, & illorum recordatione plurimùm fuerit confirmata, &c. Accedamus nunc ad secundam huius loci partem, quam his verbis Lucas comprehendit. Descendit autem cum eis, venitq; Nazareth, & erat eis subiectus. Docent ista satis evidenter, Christum priori responsu nõ contumace animum prodidisse, sed ad patris cœlestis vocationem respexisse, quam etiam nunc sequitur. Quia enim in mundum venerat, ut servi formam suscipéret, mox ubi tyrocinium hoc suum ædidit, cum parentibus domum reuertitur, & iisdem cum debita subiectione obtemperat. Completitur autem Euangelista tribus (ut ita dicam) verbis universum illud tempus Christi, quod à duodecimo eius ætatis anno ad tricesimum vsq; effluxit, quo publicum docendi munus suscepit, ut suo loco pluribus dicetur. Toto autem illo tempore Nazarethi vixit (unde & nomen Nazareni obtinuit) & parentibus fuit subiectus. Licet autem ex eo conijcere, quod nam vitae genus in terea secutus sit, aut quo artificio victum sibi parauerit. Nam ex Matthaeo constat, Iosephum fabrum fuisse, & apud Marcum Nazarethani Christum quoq; fabri dicunt. Ergo eodem cum putatitio patre artificio occupatus fuit, neq; eius ipsum puduit, ne parentum inopiam sua inertia magis grauaret.
units.tr: Before we pass to the second part of this passage, this also must be examined, what is said: "But they did not understand the words which he spoke to them." Yet they were not ignorant that he was the Son of God and that promised deliverer of the people whom the common people called the Messiah. What, then, was the cause of this ignorance? Clearly this: since God's calling had not yet been publicly made manifest, they judged rightly about Christ's office. So, deceived by the common error of the Jews, they imagined a king for themselves who, once the people had been freed from Roman tyranny, would establish a kingdom on earth, renowned for victories and riches. It is well known that the mother of John and James, and afterwards all the disciples, stumbled over this stone. Holding this opinion, then, the parents, even still, could not see what those affairs of the Father were in which he ought to be engaged, since they saw him performing the office of teaching, when they had dreamed that he would be an earthly king. From this example we are warned how great is the blindness of our reason in matters that concern the kingdom of God. Therefore it is not fitting for us to attribute anything to ourselves, nor to listen to those who bring the mysteries of faith and eternal salvation back to the reckoning of our understanding. Rather, through the obedience of faith, let us submit ourselves wholly to the word of God. Those who do this, if at their proper time they are divinely enlightened, understand those things which before seemed uncertain and obscure to them. Mary admonishes us of this, for she kept these things also in her heart, and there is no doubt that she afterwards recalled them to memory when she saw her Son teaching publicly, and was greatly strengthened by remembering them, and so on. Let us now come to the second part of this passage, which Luke comprehends in these words: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them" (Luke 2). These words show quite clearly that Christ, in his earlier answer, did not reveal a stubborn mind, but looked to the calling of his heavenly Father, which he still follows even now. For since he had come into the world to take upon himself the form of a servant, as soon as he had made this beginning of his office, he returns home with his parents and obeys them with due submission. The Evangelist, in three words, as it were, sums up the whole period of Christ's life which ran from his twelfth year to his thirtieth, when he undertook the public office of teaching, as will be said more fully in its place. Throughout that time he lived at Nazareth (whence he also obtained the name of Nazarene) and was subject to his parents. From this one may infer what kind of life he followed in the meantime, or by what trade he provided for himself. For it is clear from Matthew that Joseph was a carpenter, and in Mark the people of Nazareth also call Christ a carpenter. Therefore he was occupied in the same trade as his supposed father, and he was not ashamed of it, lest by his idleness he should burden the poverty of his parents the more.

units.la: Docentur hoc Christi exemplo liberi, quae nam suis parentibus officia debeant. Lex Dei est: Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam, ut sis longaeuus in terra, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi. Et quod veteribus dictum fuit, Paulus ad Christianos etiam pertinere docet, imò hoc ipsum Lex naturae omnibus praecipit. Non autem honorem solùm à liberis exigit Deus, qui in externis gestibus, et titulis quibusdam ambitiosis consistit, sed honoradi verbo omnia, quae parentibus debemus officia comprehenduntur. Inter quae primum est obedientia, ita hoc exponente Paulo, qui dicit: Filij, auscultate parentibus in omnibus, hoc enim gratum est Domino. Et notum est illud Solomonis: Fili mi, audi disciplinam patris tui, & institutionem matris tuae ne reijcias. Ea enim gratiam addent capiti tuo, & vice torquis erunt collo tuo. Peccant ergo in praeceptum Dei, qui parentibus respondant, aut quocunq; modo animum rebellem produnt: Nec enim obedientia sua parentes honorabunt, nisi qui voluntarij & ex animo illis obsequuntur. Exigitur deinde, ut vitae etiam subsidia progenitoribus suis liberi subministrent: quod ipsum naturae lex monet, quae ut in omnibus rebus creatis gratitudinis exempla proponit; ita brutis quibusdam hunc sensum indidit, ut parentes senio confectos allant. Et proverbio quoque celebratur Ciconiarum pietas, quae illud prae alijs facere consueuerunt. At quia hic multi nimium duri, & sordidi sunt, multùm proderit diligentius expendisse, quot curis, laboribus atq; molestijs parentes propter nos fatigati sint, & mox intelligemus, illis (quod supra quoq; diximus) parem gratiam referri non posse. Quoties ergo te laborum aut sumptuum piget, cogita te eos alere, vestire, ferre, qui te olim aluerunt, vestierunt, & nullum non fastidij genus deuorarunt, ut tuis fortunis quàm optimè consulerent. Haec olim gentium Legislatores tanta grauitate consideraverunt, ut decernerent vinciendos & perpetuis carceribus mancipandos esse eos, qui parentibus vitae subsidia negant. Et cùm illos longaeuos fore polliceatur Deus, qui parentes honorant, procul dubio aut morte praematura auferentur, aut miseri & infames viuent, quicunq; illos neglexerint, aut etiam tractarint inhumaniùs. Et exempla horrenda sunt in Cham, & in Eli filijs, in Absalomo & infinitis alijs, qui huius impietatis horribiles poenas dederunt. E contra in prophanis historijs multorum fama & nomen in hunc vsq; diem celebratur, qui pietatem in parentes omni officiorum genere, & interdum vitae periculo declarauerunt, quales fuisse legimus Æneam, Amphinoum, Aphricanum seniorem, & horum similes. Estq; hodie eò detestabilior eorum impietas, qui cùm Christiani haberi velint, se ab hominibus ethnicis vinci patiuntur in re, quae naturae legibus commendatur.
units.tr: By this example of Christ, children are taught what duties they owe their parents. God's law is: "Honour your father and your mother, that you may live long in the land which the Lord your God gives you." Paul teaches that this, which was said to the people of old, also pertains to Christians, and indeed the law of nature itself commands it of all. God does not require only honour from children, which consists in outward gestures and ambitious titles, but under the word "honour" all the duties we owe our parents are included. Of these, obedience comes first, as Paul explains when he says: "Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well pleasing to the Lord." And the saying of Solomon is well known: "My son, hear the instruction of your father, and do not reject the teaching of your mother. For they will be a graceful addition to your head and a chain about your neck." Therefore those sin against God's command who talk back to their parents or show a rebellious spirit in any way. Indeed, parents are not honoured by obedience unless it is given to them willingly and from the heart. Children are next required to supply their parents with the means of living. The law of nature itself teaches this. Among all created things it sets out examples of gratitude, and it has put this feeling even into some brute animals, so that they feed their parents when they are worn out with age. The proverb also celebrates the devotion of storks, which are accustomed to do this above others. But since many here are too hard and mean, it will greatly help to consider carefully how much parents have been worn out for our sake by cares, labours and troubles, and soon we will understand that (as we have also said above) an equal return of gratitude cannot be made to them. So whenever you grudge your labour or expense, think of how you are feeding, clothing and supporting those who once fed and clothed you, and endured every kind of discomfort so that they might look out for your welfare as well as possible. Lawgivers of the nations once considered this with such seriousness that they decreed that those who deny their parents the means of living should be put in chains and condemned to perpetual prison. And since God promises long life to those who honour their parents, undoubtedly those who neglect them, or even treat them more cruelly, will either be taken away by an early death or live wretched and infamous lives. There are dreadful examples in Ham, in the sons of Eli, in Absalom and in countless others, who paid the terrible penalties of this impiety. On the other hand, in profane histories the fame and name of many are celebrated down to this day, people who showed devotion to their parents by every kind of duty, and sometimes at the risk of their lives. Such were, as we read, Aeneas, Amphinomus, Africanus the Elder, and others like them. And today the impiety of those is all the more detestable who, while they wish to be considered Christians, allow themselves to be outdone by heathen men in a matter commended by the laws of nature.

units.la: Sed ut ad Christi exemplum reuertamur, non debet ofcitanter praeteriri, quòd cum Iosepho artificium manuariū exercere dignatus est. Quo facto omnes quidem artes mechanicas sanctificauit Dei filius, ne quis se propter eas & laborem, qui illis plerunq; coniunctus est, Deo minus curae esse arbitretur, at simul haec quoq; pars ad institutionem liberorū, de qua agimus, in primis pertinet. Admonentur enim parentes, ne liberos suos in otio inerti et ignauo æducēt: liberi verò ut studio & labori alicui honesto se addicant, ex quo absq; aliorum fraude & damno victum sibi parare possint. Quia enim ocium cupiditates prauas accendit, & sceleribus multis quasi viam sternit, iuuenilis autem ætas natura ad malum procliuis sit, non tam utile quàm necessarium est, ut laboribus assuefiant, quicunq; vel sibi ipsis aliquando utiles, vel communi patriae ornamento esse cupiunt. Peccatur in hoc multùm nostro seculo. Nam inter pauperes quoq; inueniuntur, qui suos liberos mendicando potius victu quae rere, quàm ad laborem aliquem honestum adigi malunt. Augetur ergo numerus ἀτάκτων (vt Paulí verbo vtar) id est, eorum, qui omnis disciplinæ expertes, absq; omni ordine viuunt, & sibi ipsis infamiam accersunt, & communi patriæ graues atq; molesti sunt. Qui verò generis nobilitatem & opes iactant, ij nihil suo statu indignius fieri posse arbitrantur, quàm si filios suos aliquo labore manuario occupatos esse videant. Quo fit, vt nobiliùm artes et studia sint, potare, ludere, scortari: quibus si quando ad inopiam redigantur, ipsis mendicis calamitosiores fiunt. Nam vt improbus ille dispensator in Euangelio dicebat, fodere non valent, mendicare autem erubescunt. Itaq; ad peiora animum applicant, ad imposituras nimirum, rapinas, cædes, bella nō necessaria, quibus seipsos interdū & rempub. innoluunt. Recte ergo olim patriarchæ, qui etsi opes tantum non regias possiderent (vt in Abrahamo cernimus) tamen & ipsi ab ocio alienissimi fuerunt, & suos filios circa agriculturam & rem pastoritiam occupari voluerunt, quò minus ad libidinem et nequitiam animum appellerent. Quorum ve stigijs Ioseph & Maria insistentes, et si ex regio semine genus ducerent, suam tamè inopiam manuū labore subiecuare nē sunt veriti, & Iesum quoq; eidem consecrarunt, quem Dei Filium & Messiam promissum esse non ignorabant. Inter gentes verò hanc curam principes viri et in magistratu constituti ad se pertinere putarunt, & ideo leges tulerunt, quibus ocium prohiberetur. Solon etenim sanxit, ne quam gratiam liberi parentibus deberent, qui illos in nulla arte honesta ad victū parandum instituissent. Apud Athenienses item Areopagitæ singulos cives observabant, qua quisque arte viueret, & in ius trahi curabant eos, qui se turpi & inerti ocio addixissent. Massilienses autem ciuitatis suæ ingressu eos prohibebant, qui artem nullam noverant, qua vitam suam sustentarent. Et ne qui artes vel inutiles vel etiam inhonestas colerent, locum nullum dabant ludionibus, mimis, gelopæis, scurris, circulatoribus, imò ne illis quidem, qui sub religionis prætextu ex alieno viuunt, quales hodie sunt fratres mendicantes, & qui Diuorum reliquias vel Indulgentias Romanas venditare consueuerunt. Quò magis reprehendi meretur nostri seculi socordia, qua fit, vt de re maximè necessaria paucissimi seriò cogitent. Vos autem ego hortor & obtestor iuuenes Christiani, per viscera misericordiæ Dei & nouissimum Iesu Christi aduentum, ne eos audiatis, qui in ocio summam hominis voluptatem & dignitatem collocant, & quibus turpe videtur aliquid negocij certi agere, quo & vobispsis et vestris prospiciatis. Cur enim honestū putetur, quod vitijs omnibus alimenta ministrat? Cur turpe & indignum homini videatur, quod Deus præcepit, Adamo dicens: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum? Cur item pudeat vos eius, quod sanctissimi patres, sapientissi viri & fortissimi heroes tam Græci quàm Latini olim fecerunt? & quod ab ipso Dei filio factitatum fuisse ait dimus? Turpe potius est, tempus, quo nihil in vita hac pretiosius habemus & cuius iactura irrepara bilis est, in ocio terere, vt neq; tibi ipsi neq; aliis sis vtilis. Turpe est ætatem iuuenilibus ijs vitijs inquinare, quorum vos aliquando non posset non pudere. Turpe est relicto honesto labore ysurarijs artibus & quæstuosis numulariorum inuentis vacare, quæ toti populo inopiæ & caritatis rerum omnium causa sunt. Turpe & inhumanū est, vbi tua consumpseris, in militiam mercenariam profugere, ad hominum lanienam, perinde vt ad boues mactandos, pretio conduci, homines ignotos occidere, vastare vrbes, incendere villas, proculcare segetes, viduas & pupillos affligere, ea deniq; facere, quæ in Turcis & Tartaris detestamur. Atò infelices nos, qui in ea tempora incidimus, quando ista laudi ducuntur, & principum authoritate d nduntur.
units.tr: But to return to Christ's example, we must not pass over carelessly the fact that he deigned to practise a manual craft together with Joseph. By this act the Son of God indeed sanctified all the mechanical arts, so that no one should think himself of less concern to God because of them and the labour that is usually joined to them. At the same time, this part also belongs chiefly to the training of children, which we are discussing. Parents are reminded not to bring up their children in idle inactivity and sloth, and children are reminded to devote themselves to some honest study or labour by which they may get their living without fraud or loss to others. For since idleness kindles wicked desires and, as it were, paves the way for many crimes, and since youth is by nature prone to evil, it is not so much useful as necessary that those who wish either to be useful to themselves at some time or to be an ornament to their common country should be accustomed to hard work. This fault is greatly committed in our age. For among the poor too there are some who prefer to seek their children's food by begging rather than have them driven to some honest work. So the number of the disorderly [ἀτάκτων] grows (to use Paul's word), that is, of those who, lacking all discipline, live without order, bring disgrace upon themselves, and are a burden and nuisance to their common country. Those who boast of the nobility of their family and their wealth think that nothing could be more unworthy of their rank than to see their sons occupied with any manual labour. As a result, the pursuits and studies of the nobility are drinking, gambling and whoring; and if at any time they are reduced to poverty, they become more wretched than beggars themselves. For, as that wicked steward said in the Gospel, they cannot dig, and they are ashamed to beg. So they turn their minds to worse things, namely to deceits, robberies, murders and unnecessary wars, in which they sometimes entangle both themselves and the commonwealth. Rightly, therefore, did the patriarchs of old, who possessed wealth hardly less than royal (as we see in Abraham), nevertheless stay far from idleness, and wanted their sons to be occupied with agriculture and the keeping of flocks, so that they would turn their minds less to lust and wickedness. Following in their footsteps, Joseph and Mary, although they descended from the royal line, did not fear to submit their poverty to the labour of their hands, and they dedicated Jesus to the same work, knowing that he was the promised Son of God and Messiah. Among the nations, however, leading men and those set in public office thought this care belonged to them, and therefore they enacted laws by which idleness was forbidden. For Solon decreed that children owed their parents no gratitude if the parents had not trained them in some honest craft for earning a living. Likewise at Athens the Areopagites watched over individual citizens, noting by what craft each one lived, and they took care to bring before the courts those who had given themselves over to shameful and idle leisure. The Massilians, moreover, forbade entry to their city to those who knew no craft by which to sustain their life. And so that no one should practise useless or even disgraceful arts, they gave no place to jesters, mimes, buffoons, clowns, street performers or quacks; nor even to those who live at the expense of others under the pretext of religion, such as the mendicant friars today, and those who are accustomed to hawk the relics of saints or the Roman indulgences. All the more does the carelessness of our age deserve blame, through which it happens that very few think seriously about a matter of the greatest necessity. But I exhort and beseech you, Christian young people, by the tender mercy of God and the coming of Jesus Christ, not to listen to those who place the highest human pleasure and dignity in idleness, and who think it shameful to undertake any sure business by which you may provide for yourselves and for your own. For why should that be thought honourable which supplies nourishment to all vices? Why should it seem shameful and unworthy of a man, when God commanded Adam, saying, "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread"? Why should you be ashamed of what the most holy fathers, the wisest men and the bravest heroes, both Greek and Latin, once did, and what we have said was practised by the Son of God himself? It is rather shameful to waste in idleness the time, which we have nothing more precious in this life and whose loss cannot be repaired, so that you are useful neither to yourself nor to others. It is shameful to stain your age with those youthful vices of which you will one day not be able but be ashamed. It is shameful, having abandoned honest labour, to devote yourself to usurious arts and the profit-making inventions of money-changers, which are the cause of want and of the dearth of all things for the whole people. It is shameful and inhuman, when you have spent your own resources, to flee into mercenary soldiering, to be hired for money like oxen for slaughter, to kill strangers, to lay waste cities, to set villages on fire, to trample down crops, to afflict widows and orphans, and finally to do those things which we detest in the Turks and Tartars. Alas for us unhappy people, who have fallen into times when such things are counted as praiseworthy and are given out by the authority of princes.

units.la: Porrò posteremam huius loci partem ai amus, quæ sic habet: Iesus autem proficiebat sapientia & statura, ac gratia apud Deum & homines. Non possunt hæc aliter, quàm de sola hominis natura intelligi, quam Dei filius assumpsit. Quia enim diuinitati nihil vnquam deest, eadem proficere quoq; non potest, neq; profectu opus habet. Quomodo item in sapientia profecisse dicemus eum, qui ipsa sapientia est? Sic neq; gratiam maiorem apud Deum sibi acquirere poterat, qui iam inde ab æterno vni genitus & dilectus filius est, propter quem nobis quoq; pater placatus est. Itaq; ad solū hominem ista referri debent: qui vt cum ætate quoad corporis staturam creuit, ita quoad animam sapientia et intellectu profecit, simulq; accidit, vt clariora etiam gratiæ Dei indicia in illo indies elucerent, quæ illum hominibus quoq; commendarunt, & omnibus, quibus cum versabatur, magis atq; magis acceptum fecere. Ita locum hunc veteres & orthodoxi patres expo-suerunt, quorum testimonia recensere longum esset, & iam tempus est, vt velis collectis nos in portum recipiamus.
units.tr: Finally, we come to the last part of this passage, which reads: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature, and in grace with God and men." These words can only be understood of the human nature alone, which the Son of God assumed. For since nothing is ever lacking to the divinity, it cannot advance either, nor does it need progress. Likewise, how could we say that he who is wisdom itself grew in wisdom? So neither could he who has been the only-begotten and beloved Son from all eternity acquire greater grace with God, he on account of whom the Father has also been appeased toward us. Therefore these things must be referred to the man alone: who, as he grew in bodily stature with age, so in soul he advanced in wisdom and understanding; and at the same time it came about that clearer tokens of God's grace shone forth in him day by day, which commended him also to men and made him more and more acceptable to all with whom he associated. The ancient and orthodox Fathers have expounded this place in this way, and their testimonies would be too long to recount; and now it is time that, with our sails furled, we bring ourselves into harbour.

units.la: Obseruabis igitur hanc clausulam ijs, quæ præcesserunt, commodissime subijci. Docet enim quis ex pia & Christiana institutione fructus tam ad parentes quàm liberos redeat. Primus est, quòd qui ita instituuntur, sapientia proficiunt. Quia enim (vt supra monuimus) stultitia, quæ in puerorum cor-dibus colligata est, per disciplinam expellitur, fieri non potest, quin hac expulsa sapientiæ locus de-tur. Ideo Solomon rectè ait: Qui diligit castigationem, diligit scientiam: qui verò odit correptionem, obbrutescit. Atqui filius sapiens (vt idem ille inquit) exhilarat patrem, at filius stultus mæror est matri suæ. Nam qui sapientia præditi sunt, ij belluinis carnis affectibus resistere, & vitam ita instituere solent, vt tam sibi ipsis quàm multis aliis vtiles & decori sint, vnde maxima ad eorum parentes gaudendi causa redundat. Sequitur ex hoc alius fructus, quòd tales gratia quoque apud Deum & homines proficiunt. Pollicetur enim ille, se ijs propitium velle esse, qui in eius præceptis ambulant. At si Deus nobiscum, quis contra nos? Sunt enim in Dei manu corda hominum, quæ illi facile est pro suo arbitrio vel mutare vel regere, vt nobis bene velint. Erant hæc nobis cōsideranda quàm diligentissimè. Natura enim sic comparatum est, vt & nosipsos & ex nobis natos apud homines in pretio esse cupiamus. Quæ causa est, vt vel ad diuitias parandas animum adijciamus, qui proximum ad honores gradus esse videtur: vel omnibus morem gerendo nobis amicos quàm plurimos conciliare cone-mur. At qui ita res suas instituerunt, ij multa contra ius & æquum faciunt, & manifesta scelera fouent, dum ijs blanduntur, quos sua authoritate coercere debebant. Itaq; ad tempus quidem apud ple-rosq; in pretio et fauore sunt. Sed non durabilis est fauor ille, neq; diu sibi constat quæ ex eo manat au-thoritas. Nam vt opes fluxæ sunt, ita mutabile vulgus leuissima quauis occasione odisse incipit, quos paulò ante laudibus suis in cælum vsq; euehebat. Et hæc mihi causa præcipua videtur, quòd optimè meritorum filij fere ingratos experiuntur eos, in quos magna & infinita parentum beneficia extant. Quia enim parentes dum multis benefaciunt, non Deo, sed mundo potius seruire student, beneficio-rum quoq; remunerationem non aliunde quàm ex mundo sperare possunt, cuius proprium est, benefa-ctoribus suis pessimam gratiam referre. Habes igitur hoc loco, quod ijs respondeas, qui de collapsa omnium ordinum authoritate queruntur, & malum hoc mundi iniquis iudicijs atq; ingratitudini acceptum ferunt. Atqui non negamus, grauem esse eorum culpam, qui Verbi præcones, magistratus, præceptores, parentes & eos qui parentum loco sunt, improbe contemnunt. At simul singulos in seip-sos descendere oportebat, & mox viderèt, se istius mali præcipuos esse authores. Quotus enim quisq; est inter ecclesiæ ministros, qui non priuatum commodum gloriæ Dei anteponat? Certè pinguiori conditione oblata plerique ecclesias suæ fidei creditas deserunt, neq; in hoc sunt, vt quàm plurimos Christo adducant, sed vt ipsis bene sit, & vt opes accumulent. Inter magistratus vero postrema fere de religione & gloria Dei cura est, quando vt populum aliquo modo in officio contineant, quiduis impune fieri sinunt, quod cum manifesta Dei contumelia coniunctum est. Idem apud plerosq; parentum & apud omnes ordines videre licet. Quid ergo aliud fiat, quàm vt secundum Dei sententiam, contempti & ignominiosi sint, qui ipsum ignominia afficiunt? 1. Samuel. 2.
units.tr: You will observe, therefore, that this closing clause is most fittingly joined to what has gone before. For it teaches what fruit of pious and Christian upbringing returns both to parents and to children. The first is that those who are so brought up advance in wisdom. For since (as we noted above) the foolishness bound up in children's hearts is driven out by discipline, it cannot but be that, once it is expelled, a place is given to wisdom. Hence Solomon rightly says: "He who loves correction loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof grows brutish." And indeed, as the same man says, "a wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother." For those endowed with wisdom are accustomed to resist the brutish appetites of the flesh and to order their life so that they are useful and becoming both to themselves and to many others, whence the greatest cause for joy redounds to their parents. From this there follows another fruit: that such children also advance in grace with God and men. For he promises that he will be favourable to those who walk in his precepts. "If God is with us, who is against us?" For the hearts of men are in God's hand, and he can easily change or direct them, according to his will, so that they wish us well. These things we ought to consider most diligently. For nature has so arranged it that we desire both ourselves and those born of us to be held in esteem among men. This is why we apply ourselves to amassing wealth, which seems the nearest step to honours, or we try to win for ourselves as many friends as possible by humouring everyone. But those who order their affairs in this way do many things contrary to right and justice, and foster manifest wickedness, while they flatter those whom they ought to restrain by their authority. And so for a time they are indeed held in esteem and favour by most people. But that favour does not last, nor does the authority that flows from it long remain consistent with itself. For just as riches are fleeting, so the fickle crowd begins to hate, on the slightest occasion, those whom a little before it had raised with its praises to the very heavens. And this seems to me the chief cause why the sons of very worthy men commonly find ungrateful those upon whom their parents' great and countless benefits rest. For parents, while they do good to many, strive to serve the world rather than God, and so can hope for the repayment of their kindnesses from nowhere but the world, whose proper nature it is to return the worst thanks to its benefactors. Here, then, you have an answer to those who complain of the collapsed authority of all orders, and who attribute this evil of the world to unjust judgements and ingratitude. Yet we do not deny that the fault of those is grave who shamelessly despise the heralds of the Word, magistrates, teachers, parents and those who stand in the place of parents. But at the same time each ought to descend into himself, and he would soon see that he is himself a chief author of this evil. For how few are there among the ministers of the Church who put the glory of God before private advantage? Indeed, when a fatter condition is offered, many desert the churches entrusted to their faith, and they are not concerned to bring as many people as possible to Christ, but that it may go well with themselves and that they may amass wealth. Among magistrates, moreover, the care of religion and the glory of God comes almost last, since, provided they keep the people in some kind of obedience, they allow whatever they like to be done with impunity, even when it is joined with manifest dishonour to God. The same may be seen among many parents and in all orders. What else, then, will happen but that, according to God's judgement, those who bring ignominy upon him are themselves despised and disgraced? 1 Samuel 2.

units.la: Et hæc quidè in Christi Iesu pueritia atq; æducatione hucusq; dicta sunt. At ista dixisse non suf-ficiet, nisi illius exemplo et doctrinæ nos accommodemus. Et quia is omnium ordinum doctor & serua-tor est, singuli ista ad se pertinere serio cogitent. Meminerint ergo principes viri, puerorum & iuue-num cura ab ipsis suscipi debere, & si quos ex parentibus negligentiores esse vident, sua authoritate illos in ordinem redigant. Meminerint scholarum præfecti totius reipub. & ecclesiæ spem ipsorum fidei & industriæ commissam esse, & proinde communis patriæ dissipatores merito eos censeri, qui hic officium non faciunt. Meminerint parentes inanes fore omnes suas curas & labores, quibus in re domestica fatigantur, nisi liberos suos Deo adducant, & in eius timore instituant. Debent causam hanc indesi-nenter vrgere ecclesiarum ministri, cùm ex ea patriæ et reipub. salus potissimum dependeat. Cogitent praeterea pueri & iuuenes vtriusq; sexus, sibi disciplina & institutione in primis opus esse, & proin-de illam patienter ferant. Est res ista maximi momenti, & in ea situm est reformationis Christianæ fundamentum, quam necessariam esse omnes fatetur. Faxit Deus Opt. Max. vt de ea omnes serio cogitent, & idem omnis sexus, ordinis & ætatis homines suo spiritu regat, vt vitam viuant verè Christianam, & olim vitæ cœlestis cohæredes sint cum filio eius vnigenito, Iesu Christo, Domino no-stro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Up to this point these things have been said of the childhood and upbringing of Christ Jesus. Yet to have said these things will not suffice unless we conform ourselves to his example and teaching. And since he is the teacher and saviour of all orders, let each one earnestly consider these things as applying to himself. Let princely men therefore remember that the care of boys and young men ought to be undertaken by them, and if they see any who are more negligent than their parents, let them bring such people back into order by their authority. Let the prefects of schools remember that the hope of the whole commonwealth and of the Church has been committed to their faith and diligence, and that therefore those who do not perform this duty here are rightly judged the squanderers of the common fatherland. Let parents remember that all their cares and labours, with which they are wearied in domestic affairs, will be empty unless they bring their children to God and bring them up in his fear. The ministers of the churches ought to press this cause without ceasing, since the welfare of the fatherland and of the commonwealth depends above all upon it. Let boys and young people of both sexes further consider that discipline and instruction are above all necessary for them, and so let them bear it patiently. This matter is of the greatest moment, and in it lies the foundation of Christian reformation, which everyone confesses to be necessary. May God, the best and greatest, grant that all think seriously upon it, and that he rule men of every sex, order and age by his Spirit, so that they may live a truly Christian life and one day be heirs of heavenly life together with his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT III. HOMILIA XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. HOMILY XXVI.

units.la: ANno autem decimoquinto imperij Tiberij Caesaris, Pontio Pilato praeside Iudaeae, tetrarcha Galilaeae Herode, Philippo autem fratre eius tetrarcha Itureę & Trachonitidis regionis, & Lysania Abilenes tetrarcha: Sub Pontificibus Maximis Anna & Caiapha, factum est Verbum Domini ad Ioannem Zachariae filium, in deserto. Venit igitur in omnem regionem circumiacentem Iordani, praedicans baptismum resipiscentiae in remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John the son of Zacharias in the desert. He went therefore into all the region around the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

units.la: ESCRIPSIT hucusq; Lucas filij Dei, in carne manifestati, natales atq; pueritiam: & paucis complexus est omne illud tempus, quod illi visq; ad tricesimū aetatis suae annū effluxit. Finis & visus eorū omnium hic est, ut intelligamus, Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria Virgine natum est, esse Christū, id est aeternū Dei filium, qui propter nos hominē induerit, ut ecclesiae Dei Rex & Sacerdos, nosterq; apud patrē Mediator, amissam salutem nobis instauraret. Et probatū est hoc quidē aliquot testimonijs, sed quae paucis modò et obscurius proposita videri possunt, si cū densissimis, quae tunc omniū animis incumbebant, tenebris conferantur. Sed & ipse Christus post editū in templo suae functionis tyrocinium, in obscuro Galilaeae oppido vitā privatā agens quasi delite scere voluit, donec tepus illud adesset, quo ex aeterno patris decreto munus sibi destinatū publicè suscipéret. Id autē quando & qua ratione factū sit, hoc Capite Euangelista narrat. Orditur aut à Ioanne Baptista, quem primū noui Testamenti ministrum fore olim prophetae praedixerūt, et de quo ipse Christus idem testatur, dicens: Lex & prophetae vsq; ad Ioannē, ab eo tempore regnum Dei annunciatur, et quiuis in illud vim facit. Quia ergo ille Iesu Christi praecursor fuit, diligenter narratur, ut hic quoq; munus suum coeperit obire, vtq; eū, qui luciferi instar praeibat, mox secutus sit verè aureus ille Sol iustitiae, in cuius alis est salus, & qui nobis iustitiam sempiternā atq; salutem perfectissimā reduxit. Estq; visus historiae Ioannis multiplex. Continet enim instauratae religionis Christianae principium atq; progressus, in quibus cernere licet admirabilem Dei bonitatem, adhaec totam ministerij euangelici rationem, & quaecunque nobis ad aeternam salutem cognitu necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Hitherto Luke has written of the birth and childhood of the Son of God, manifested in the flesh, and has briefly summarised all that time which passed until his thirtieth year of age. The aim and purpose of all these things is this: that we should understand that this Jesus, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is the Christ, that is, the eternal Son of God, who for our sake took on human nature, so that as King and Priest of the Church, and our Mediator with the Father, he might restore the salvation we had lost. This has indeed been proved by several testimonies, but these may seem only slightly and obscurely set forth in a few words, if they are compared with the very dense darkness which then lay upon the minds of all. But Christ himself, after the apprenticeship of his office had been completed in the temple, living a private life in the obscure town of Galilee, wished as it were to lie hidden until that time came when he would publicly take up the task appointed for him by the eternal decree of the Father. Luke relates in this chapter when and how this was done. He begins with John the Baptist, whom the prophets long before foretold would be the first minister of the New Testament, and of whom Christ himself also bears witness, saying: "The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses into it." Because John was the forerunner of Jesus Christ, his story is told carefully, so that it may be shown that he too began to discharge his office, and that he who went before like the morning star was soon followed by that truly golden Sun of Righteousness, in whose wings is salvation, and who restored to us everlasting righteousness and most perfect salvation. The purpose of the history of John is manifold. For it contains the beginning and progress of the restored Christian religion, in which one may discern the wonderful goodness of God, and besides, the whole manner of the gospel ministry, and whatever things are necessary for us to know for eternal salvation.

units.la: Rursus autem à temporis consignatione narrandi exordium facit, & ea quidem diligentissima. Nec enim solius Tiberij Caesaris, penes quem tunc erat orbis terrarum imperium, annum decimum quintū annotat, verumetiā, qui tunc eas terras tenuerint & administrarint, quae olim omnes ad Iudaici populi ius atq; ditionem pertinebat. Nam Iudaea, quam Romani post Archelai mortē Syriae dispensationi adiunxerant, praeses fuit Pontius Pilatus: Galilaeae tetrarcha Herodes cognomento Antipas, Iturae autē & Trachonitidis regionis Philippus (vterq; Herodis magni filius & Archelai frater) Abilenes autē Lysanias, quem Ptolemaei Minaei (qui Chalcidem prope Libanū tenuit) filium fuisse Iosephus docet. Acceperat is tetrarchiā viuente Augusto, & eam adhuc Imperante Tiberio diu tenuit, ut ex hoc loco apparet. Addit his etiā Lucas Pontifices Maximos, Annā & Caiapham, qui cum sacerdotium in suas quasi manus redegissent, illud per annuas vices administrarunt, ut alibi diximus. Non debet autem cuiq; superuacanea videri haec tam diligens temporis consignatio. Quia enim ex veteri more in rebus arduis & magni momenti annus & dies annotari solent, ut quo tempore quidq; gestū sit, certius constet: multò magis hoc in praesenti debuit obseruari, vbi de re omniū maxima agitur: nimirū de religionis Christianae instauratione, quae totius orbis mutationem peperit. Nam etsi eadem fides & religio omnium Dei cultorū ab ipsa mundi origine fuerit, & quidem ea, quae promissionibus de venturo humani generis redemptore nitebatur, & quā hodie Christianam dicimus, attamen huius doctrina intra angustos Iudaici populi fines conclusa erat, & sub legalium ceremoniarum vmbra seu velo quasi latebat, ut paucis vere & perfectè nota esset. At Christo iam manifestato & per Euangelij praedicationē inter gentes diuulgato, dies quidam subitò illuxit, per quem pulsis Iudaicis vmbris & simul dissipatis gentilium superstitionum tenebris tota orbis facies immutata est. Fuit haec maximi momenti res, cuius simile exemplum nullum à condito mundo editum æditum fuit. Æquùm ergo, imò necesse fuit, vt huius reformationis initia sic describerentur, ne quis propter temporis incertitudinem de tota causa dubitandi occasione haberet. Accedit huic causa alia grauioris momenti, quòd sic ostendi oportuit, Christum eo ipso tempore mundo innotuisse, quod olim prophetæ prædixerant, et proinde illum esse verum atq; vnicum humani generis seruatorem, per cuius fidem omnes homines iustificari & seruari oporteat. Nam scimus inter prophetarum prædictiones præcipuam de tempore fuisse, quòd nimirum tunc venturus esset Messias, quando sceptro à Iudæis sublato & Dauidis posteritate ad egestatem & contemptum extremum redacta, Romani (qui per quartam Monarchiam designantur) longè latéq; per orbem dominarentur. Vt ergo tunc ille natus esset, quando Herodes Romanorum beneficio totius Iudææ & finitimarum gentium regnum obtinuit, & Augustus orbis terrarum censum egit: ita nunc per prædicationem & miracula publicè se manifestare incipit, quando per eosdem Romanos terra, quam olim Iudæi tenuerant, in tetrarchias descripta multis regulis paruit, vt nulla libertatis recuperandæ spes reliqua esset. At quia de hoc alibi prolixius diximus, ista nunc sufficiant.
units.tr: Again, he makes a beginning of the narrative by fixing the time, and does so with the greatest care. For he notes the fifteenth year not only of Tiberius Caesar, in whose hands at that time lay the imperial rule of the world, but also of those who then held and governed those lands which had once all belonged to the right and power of the Jewish people. For Judaea, which the Romans had attached to the administration of Syria after the death of Archelaus, was governed by the governor Pontius Pilate; Galilee by the tetrarch Herod, surnamed Antipas; the region of Iturea and Trachonitis by Philip (both sons of Herod the Great and brothers of Archelaus); and Abilene by Lysanias, who, as Josephus tells us, was the son of Ptolemy Mennaeus, who held Chalcis near Lebanon. He had received the tetrarchy while Augustus was still living, and held it for a long time, even while Tiberius was reigning, as appears from this passage. Luke adds also the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, who, when they had as it were gathered the priesthood into their own hands, administered it by yearly turns, as we have said elsewhere. Now this so careful fixing of the time ought not to seem superfluous to anyone. For, following the ancient custom, in matters of difficulty and great importance the year and day are usually recorded, so that it may be more certain at what time each thing was done. All the more ought this to be observed in the present case, where the most important of all matters is treated: namely, the restoration of the Christian religion, which brought about a change in the whole world. For although the same faith and religion of all the worshippers of God has existed from the very beginning of the world, indeed that faith which rested on the promises of a future Redeemer of the human race, and which we today call Christian, nevertheless this teaching was confined within the narrow limits of the Jewish people, and lay hidden as it were under the shadow or veil of the legal ceremonies, so that it was truly and perfectly known to only a few. But when Christ had now been manifested, and spread abroad among the nations by the preaching of the gospel, a certain day suddenly dawned, through which, the shadows of Judaism being driven away and at the same time the darkness of Gentile superstitions dispelled, the whole face of the world was changed. This was a matter of the greatest importance, of which no similar example has been produced since the world was made. It was therefore fair, indeed necessary, that the beginnings of this reformation should be so described, lest anyone should have occasion to doubt the whole matter because of uncertainty about the time. To this is added another reason of graver weight: it was fitting to show that Christ became known to the world at that very time which the prophets had long before foretold, and that therefore he is the true and only Saviour of the human race, through whose faith all men ought to be justified and saved. For we know that among the predictions of the prophets the chief one concerned the time: namely, that the Messiah would come when the sceptre had been taken from the Jews and the posterity of David had been reduced to extreme poverty and contempt, and the Romans (who are designated by the fourth monarchy) ruled far and wide over the earth. So, just as he was born at the time when Herod obtained the kingdom of all Judaea and the neighbouring nations by the favour of the Romans, and Augustus took a census of the world, so now he begins to manifest himself publicly through preaching and miracles, when, through the same Romans, the land which the Jews once held has been divided into tetrarchies and obeys many petty rulers, so that no hope of recovering liberty remains. But since we have spoken of this more fully elsewhere, let these things suffice for now.

units.la: Attamen diligentius nobis consideranda est perdita & omnibus modis corruptissima illius seculi conditio, quam quivis cernere poterit, qui eorum mores vel obiter inspexerit, qui tunc rebus cum politicis tum ecclesiasticis præfuerunt. Nam vt à capite, Tiberio Cæsare, exordiamur, fuit is (vt Suetonius & alij historici de illo tradunt) omni libidinis genere infamis, & tantæ impuritatis homo, vt satius sit de illo prorsus tacere, quam pauca dicendo illius nequitiā extenuare, vel omnia eius flagitia commemorando pias aures offendere. Fuit dignus hoc Imperatore Pilatus, qui vt auaritiæ suam multis facinoribus & sacrilegijs declarauit, ita multarum seditionum inter Iudæos author fuit, & tandem innoxio filij Dei sanguine manus plus satis sceleratas amplius polluit. Quoad verò Herodis filios, Antipam & Philippum, ille quidem incestus nebulo fuit, & legitima vxore repudiata fratris coniugem ad se pellexit: hic verò homo nihili & ignauus iniuriā tam atrocem turpiter neglexit: ex quibus facilè apparet, quæ sub eiusmodi principibus fuerit populi plus satis afflicti conditio, aut quid præsidij in suis periculis boni habuerint apud eos principes, qui tam effræni petulantia & turpi socordia suam authoritatem prostituebant. De Lysania non multa quidem memoriæ prodita sunt, sed vix credibile est virum bonum fuisse, qui Augusto & Tiberio, hominibus impuris & patriæ libertatis oppressoribus, placere potuit. Quod si ad Ecclesiæ administrationem accedas, nominatur hic duo Pontifices, Annas & Caiaphas, quod vnum satis ostendit, ordinem à Deo institutum iampridem tur batam & abolitum fuisse. Voluit enim Deus vnum solum in suo populo Pontificem esse, eò quòd is Summi illius & æterni Sacerdotis, filij sui Iesu Christi typum gereret. Sed Romanorum præsidum auaritia & prophana sacerdotum impietas Sacerdotium venale fecerant, & ita factum est, vt annuæ vices institurentur, vt vtriusq; quæstus esset uberior. Et verisimile est, duos hosce illud diutius tenuisse, cùm alter alterius generi esset, & quàmuis illud per vices administrarent, vtrosq; tamen Pontifices Maximos à populo dictos fuisse, cùm soli istâ dignitatè quasi certa possessione tenerent. Fuit autem hæc non minus impia quàm fœda ordinis diuini peruersio, quæ cum falsa doctrina sacrilegam sacrorum omnium nundinationem inuexit, vt alibi cernimus. Taceo nunc sectas varias, quæ ecclesiæ vnitatem miserè discerpserant, vt iam Pharisæi, aut Sadducæi, aut Esseni dicerentur, qui Israelitæ aut Iudæi dici debebant. Quid autem de populi moribus dicere attinet, qui cùm auita contumacia & ingratitudine laboraret, non potuit nō indies in peius proficere, cùm eiusmodi principes res sacras & politicas administrarent? Quales certè erga Deum fuerint, ex ijs patet, quæ in Iesum Christum designarunt: de reliquis verò illorum studijs crebræ illorum & assiduæ seditiones testantur, vt multa alia extremæ impietatis argumenta nunc omittamus. Est autem hoc ingens diuinæ bonitatis argumentū, quòd istis temporibus tantum pœnitentiæ præconē Deus excitauit, & mox huic salutis æternæ authorem tot seculis olim expectatum, submisit. Vnde colligitur, velle illum homines salvos facere, illos autē sibi ipsis exitij authores esse, dum ex propria malitia peccant, & oblatas sibi salutis occasiones improbè aspernantur. Posset hoc infinitis alijs exēplis demonstrari, si opus esset: sed cùm vetera multa occurrant, & quotidie fiant quæ hïs fidem faciunt, nunc consulto breuitati studemus. Excitent nos ista, ne quā hodie experimur Dei nos amicè monentis longanimitatē contemnendo, eius iram in capita nostra prouocemus. Præterea admonet nos hæc tam desperata illorū tempo-
units.tr: Yet we must consider more carefully the ruined and in every way most corrupt condition of that age, which anyone may see who has looked even briefly at the morals of those who then held office, both in civil and in ecclesiastical affairs. To begin with the head, Tiberius Caesar: he was (as Suetonius and other historians relate of him) notorious for every kind of lust, and such a man of such impurity that it is better to say nothing of him at all than to belittle his wickedness by saying a few things, or to offend pious ears by recounting all his crimes. Pilate was a fit governor under such an emperor: just as he showed his greed by many crimes and sacrileges, so he was the author of many seditions among the Jews, and at last polluted with the innocent blood of the Son of God hands already more than sufficiently wicked. As for Herod's sons, Antipas and Philip: the former was indeed an incestuous scoundrel, who, having repudiated his lawful wife, enticed his brother's wife to himself; the latter was a worthless and idle man who shamefully disregarded so atrocious a wrong. From these things it is easily seen what was the condition of a people already more than sufficiently afflicted under such rulers, or what good protection they had in their dangers from princes who prostituted their authority with such unbridled wantonness and shameful sloth. Not many things have been handed down to memory about Lysanias, but it is hardly credible that he was a good man, if he could please Augustus and Tiberius, men impure and oppressors of the liberty of their country. And if you turn to the administration of the Church, two high priests are named here, Annas and Caiaphas, which alone sufficiently shows that the order instituted by God had long been disturbed and abolished. For God willed that there should be only one high priest among his people, because he bore the type of that supreme and eternal Priest, his Son Jesus Christ. But the greed of the Roman governors and the profane impiety of the priests had made the priesthood a thing for sale, and so it came about that yearly turns were instituted, so that the profit of both might be greater. And it is likely that these two held it for a long time, since each was of the other's party, and although they administered it by turns, both were nevertheless called high priests by the people, since they alone held this dignity as if by a certain possession. This perversion of the divine order was no less impious than it was foul; together with false doctrine it brought in a sacrilegious trade in all sacred things, as we see elsewhere. I pass over now the various sects which had miserably torn apart the unity of the Church, so that they were called Pharisees, or Sadducees, or Essenes, when they ought to have been called Israelites or Jews. And what need is there to speak of the morals of the people, who, labouring under their ancestral obstinacy and ingratitude, could not but grow worse daily, when such rulers administered both sacred and civil affairs? What their attitude toward God was like is clear from what they did against Jesus Christ; of their other pursuits, their frequent and constant seditions bear witness; and we now omit many other proofs of extreme impiety. Yet this is a great proof of the divine goodness, that in those times God raised up only a herald of repentance, and soon after sent to them the author of eternal salvation, who had been long expected through so many ages. From this it is gathered that he wishes men to be saved, but that they themselves are the authors of their own ruin, when they sin from their own malice and wickedly spurn the opportunities of salvation offered to them. This could be shown by countless other examples, if it were necessary; but since many old instances come to mind, and daily things happen which bear witness to them, we now deliberately keep to brevity. Let these things stir us, lest today, despising the long-suffering of God who warns us in friendship, we provoke his wrath upon our own heads. Moreover, this so desperate condition of those times admonishes us that the salvation of which Christ is the author flows from the sheer grace or mercy of God. For who in such a universal corruption of all orders could have deserved that God should deliver up his only-begotten Son for us? It remains, therefore,

units.la: {infelix illius seculi conditio} rum conditio, salutem, cuius nobis author est Christus, ex mera Dei gratia siue misericordia profluere. Quis enim in tanta atq; universali omnium ordinum corruptione mereri potuit, ut filium suum unigenitum Deus pro nobis traderet? Restat ergo, ut quod ille ipse in Euangelio docet, istud omne ad illius dilectionem referamus, qua mundum complexus est. Ioan.3.
units.tr: {the unhappy condition of that age} Salvation, of which Christ is the author, flows to us from pure grace or mercy of God. For who, in such a universal corruption of all orders of men, could have deserved that God should deliver his only begotten Son for us? It remains, therefore, that we refer all this to that love of his by which he embraced the world, as he himself teaches in the Gospel. John 3.

units.la: Porrò subijcitur his vocatio Ioannis, quem supra audiuimus in deserto vitam privatam vixisse vsq; ad tempus illud praefinitum, quando eum prodire & manifestari oportebat apud populum. Sic autem ait Lucas: Factum est verbum Domini ad Ioannem, Zachariae filium, in deserto. Locutione vtitur in prophetis vsitata, ad quos verbum Domini fieri dicitur, quando vel primum vocantur ad suum munus, vel mandatum aliquod a Deo peculiare accipiunt. Exponit illam ipse Christus, apud Ioannem de magistratibus loquens: Si illos dixit Deos, ad quos verbum Dei factum est, id est, qui ad rempub. legitime & illo auspice vocati sunt. Itaq; sensus est, Ioannem non priuato consilio ad docendum prosiliisse, sed a Deo euocatum, qui volebat illum iam ad functionem, cui destinatus erat accedere. Pulchre autem hoc subijcit euangelista mentionem Pontificum, Annae & Caiaphae, vt ostendat idem hic factum a Deo, quod olim saepius eum fecisse constat, quando cessantibus in suo munere sacerdotibus, extraordinarie prophetas excitauit, qui & populum sui officij admonerent, & sacerdotum socordiam atque corruptos mores, vt par erat, reprehenderent. Ita nunquam desunt Domino occasiones & media, quibus verbum suum inter homines annunciari curet, & illi contra id quod vulgo dicitur, facile est ex quouis ligno Mercurium, id est, sua voluntatis interpretem fingere, cum in eius manu sint linguae & corda omnium hominum. At hic in primis memorabile est, quod Ioannes ad munus publicum docendi non accedit, donec peculiari Dei mandato vocetur. Atqui veteres de illo prophetiae extabant, quae illum ad hoc destinatum esse testabantur. Adhaec spiritu suo eum in matris vtero adhuc delicescente Deus donauerat, qui in hunc maxime finem datur, vt ad docendum idoneos reddat, qui ex semetipsis nihil possunt. Fiebant item multa quotidie, quae illum offendebant graviter, & quae emendata voluisset, cum non vulgaria irae Dei exempla passim extarent. Nihilominus tamen Dei vocationem expectat, ne quid hoc incon sulto aggrediatur in re maximi momenti, & in qua absq; Dei auxilio nihil proficitur. Debent exemplum hoc imitari omnes homines, ne vel in ecclesia vel repub. sese temere ingerat, etiamsi sibi satis iustrutti videatur.
units.tr: Next follows the calling of John, whom we heard above living a private life in the wilderness until that predetermined time when he ought to come forth and be made manifest before the people. Luke writes: "The word of the Lord came to John, son of Zacharias, in the wilderness." He uses a phrase common among the prophets, to whom the word of the Lord is said to come, either when they are first called to their office or when they receive some special command from God. Christ himself explains it, speaking in John about magistrates: "If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came," that is, those who have been lawfully called to the commonwealth under that authority. The sense, then, is that John did not leap forward to teach on his own counsel, but was called by God, who wished him now to take up the office for which he was destined. The evangelist rightly adds the mention of the high priests, Annas and Caiaphas, to show that this too was the work of God, just as God is known to have often done before: when priests ceased to perform their duty, he raised up prophets outside the ordinary order, who both reminded the people of their duty and rebuked, as was fitting, the sloth and corrupt morals of the priests. Thus the Lord never lacks occasions and means by which he sees to it that his word is announced among men. And although the common saying holds that it is easy to fashion a Mercury, that is, an interpreter of one's own will, out of any piece of wood, the tongues and hearts of all men are in his hand. Here, however, it is especially worth noting that John did not take up the public office of teaching until he was called by a special command of God.
