Yet there were old prophecies about him which testified that he had been destined for this. Moreover, God had endowed him with his Spirit while he was still hidden in his mother's womb; this gift is given chiefly for this end, that those who of themselves can do nothing may be made fit to teach. Likewise, many things happened every day which grieved him deeply and which he would have wished to see corrected, since examples of God's wrath were to be found everywhere. Nevertheless, he waits for God's call, lest he undertake anything rashly in a matter of the greatest moment, and one in which nothing succeeds without God's help. All men ought to imitate this example, so that they do not thrust themselves rashly into the Church or the commonwealth, even if they seem to themselves sufficiently qualified.

units.la: Quomodo enim praedicabunt (inquit Paulus) nisi cum aliqui fructus, nisi missi fuerint? Et apud Ieremiam graviter illis irascitur Deus, qui cum non mitterentur, ex priuato arbitrio currebant. Equidem qui id faciunt, ij & sibi ipsis & ecclesiis perniciose consulunt. Nam vt sibi ipsis onus imponunt, cui ferendo non sufficiunt: ita si quid grauioris periculi imminet, stationem temere vsurpatam turpiter deserunt, & causa sunt, vt ecclesiae doctoribus in vniuersum destituantur, quando illis quam maxime opus erat. Sunt ergo Thrasonum similes, qui inanis gloriae studio in primam aciem procedunt, & nihil non de sua fortitudine pollicentur, ad hostis vero conspectum abiectis armis fugiunt, & toti exercitui fugae initium faciunt. Quoad vero rempub. multis exemplis docemur, infelices esse illorum exitus, qui vel largitionibus, vel dolo malo, aut per artes seditiosas ad munera publica contendunt. Nam plerunq; aut ignavi officium negligunt, aut potestate male vsurpata peius abutuntur, & publicorum malorum atq; mutationum in repub. periculosissimarum authores sunt. Discant ergo singuli intra suos fines sese continere, & meminerint, se Deo curae esse, qui vt Ioannem in deserto inuenit: ita ipsos minime negliget, si ex re ipsorum & aliorum hominum foresciat, vt ad honores & officia publica euehantur. Quod si illis contingat, tunc ab illo impositam sarcinam animo forti subeant, eius promissis & gratia freti, qui donus quoq; maioribus eos exornat & instruit, quos in suo munere fidos & industrios esse videt.
units.tr: For "how shall they preach," says Paul, "unless they be sent?" And through Jeremiah God is angry with those who ran about on their own judgment when they were not sent. Indeed, those who do this bring ruin on themselves and on the churches alike. For just as they take on a burden which they are not up to bearing, so, if some more serious danger threatens, they shamefully desert the post they rashly seized, and they are the cause that the churches are left entirely without teachers just when they most need them. They are therefore like the boastful soldiers of Thraso, who, from a desire for empty glory, march to the front line and promise everything about their courage, but at the sight of the enemy throw down their arms and flee, and make a beginning of flight for the whole army. As for the commonwealth, we are taught by many examples that the outcomes are unhappy for those who press for public offices by bribery, by deceit, or by seditious arts. For they are mostly either idle and neglect their duty, or, having seized power badly, abuse it all the worse, and become the authors of public evils and of the most dangerous upheavals in the state. Let each therefore learn to keep himself within his own bounds, and let him remember that he is a concern to God, who found John in the wilderness; so God will by no means neglect him, if he knows from the interests of himself and other men that he should be raised to honours and public offices. And if this should happen to them, then let them bear the burden laid on them by him with a brave spirit, trusting in his promises and his grace, since he also adorns and equips with greater gifts those whom he sees to be faithful and diligent in their office.

units.la: Non temere autem loci quoque mentionem facit Lucas, vbi Ioannem Deus inuenit, quando eum ad docendi munus vocauit. Fuit is desertum Iudaeae non procul a Iordane (vt ex aliis Euangelistis colligitur) in quo hactenus ille vixerat, & vbi etiam praedicandi initium fecit. Factum hoc non sine mysterio. Ita enim significare voluit spiritus sanctus, quae tunc esset totius mundi conditio. Deserta non solum inculta & sterilia sunt, verumetiam sylvis et vepretis horrida, adhaec propter feras periculorum plena. Insunt haec omnia mundo, si Christum auferas. Quem enim fructum ferat, qui totus in malo iacet, et lucem veritatis odisse confuenit? Accedunt pericula ex errorum labyrinthis, quos vel ipsi nobis fingimus, vel in quos alij nos abducunt. Oberrat item Leo ille rugiēns Satan, & modò minus, modò apertus periculis, modò plus quàm vulpina astutia vritur, vt à via salutis nos revocet. Et ista quidem omnia tunc vulgò locum habebant inter Iudæos & gentes, ex quibus hæ quidem manifesta diaboli tyrannide premebantur, & totæ (vt Paulus inquit) sub tenebrarum potestate erant, illorum autem infelicior erat conditio, quòd sibijpsis inani ecclesiæ titulo blandirentur, & se miseros esse non sentirent. Magnum ergo divinæ bonitatis argumentum est, quòd tunc lucerna salutis Deus accendit, & in filio suo viam aperuit, quæ miseros mortales per horribile illud mundi desertum ad cœlestem patriam deduceret. Quod autem illo tempore factum fuit, hoc ipsum hodie etiam non vno loco experti sumus, & quotidie experimur. Quàm enim infelix fuerit totius orbis conditio, quando papisticarum superstitionum tenebræ omnium animos occuparunt, ij testari possunt, qui aliquando in illis oberrantes propriæ conscientiæ morsibus & carnificina excruciati sunt, & insuper sibi cum episcoporum insolentia et sacrificis atq; monachis rem esse senserunt, quorum alij dolis & fraudibus, alij aperta etiam vi in miseros perdendis aut perterrefaciendis vsi sunt. At hic quoq; verbi sui faciem Deus accendit, & gratiæ suæ præcones præter omnium expectationem excitauit, qui deserti huius tenebras illustrarunt, & regnum Antichristi magna ex parte labefactarunt, vt iam paucis terrori sint eius fulmina, quibus olim Reges potentissimos debellabat. Agnoscamus ergo ô fratres admirabilem illam & verè paternam Dei bonitatem, & relićtis alijs in veritatis via ambulemus, quam ille nobis in filio suo Iesu Christo aperuit. Sed de hoc pluribus alibi dicemus.
units.tr: Luke does not mention the place where God found John when he called him to the office of teaching without reason. It was the wilderness of Judea, not far from the Jordan (as is gathered from the other evangelists), in which he had lived up to that time, and where he also began to preach. This was not done without a mystery. For the Holy Spirit wished thereby to signify what the condition of the whole world then was. Deserts are not only uncultivated and barren, but also rough with woods and thickets, and besides, full of dangers from wild beasts. All these things belong to the world if you take Christ away. For what fruit can bear one who lies wholly in evil and is accustomed to hate the light of truth? There are dangers too from the labyrinths of errors, which either we ourselves invent or others lead us into. That roaring lion Satan also wanders about, and now with less, now with open peril, now with more than foxlike cunning, he tries to call us back from the way of salvation. And indeed all these things then commonly held sway among the Jews and the Gentiles; of these, the latter were oppressed by the manifest tyranny of the devil, and were all (as Paul says) under the power of darkness; but the condition of the former was more unhappy, because they flattered themselves with the empty title of the Church and did not feel that they were wretched. Therefore it is a great proof of divine goodness that God then kindled the lamp of salvation and opened, in his Son, a way which might lead wretched mortals through that dreadful desert of the world to their heavenly homeland. And what was done at that time we have experienced in more than one place even today, and we experience it every day. How unhappy the condition of the whole world was when the darkness of Papist superstitions seized the minds of all, those can bear witness who once, wandering in them, were tormented by the stings and the torture of their own conscience, and who besides felt that they had to do with the arrogance of bishops and with priests and monks, some of whom used deceit and fraud, others open force, to destroy or terrify the wretched. But here too God kindled the light of his word, and beyond all expectation raised up heralds of his grace, who illumined the darkness of this desert and in large part shook the kingdom of Antichrist, so that now his thunderbolts, with which he once overthrew the most powerful kings, cause terror to few. Let us therefore, O brethren, acknowledge that wonderful and truly fatherly goodness of God, and, having left the other paths, let us walk in the way of truth which he has opened for us in his Son Jesus Christ. But we will speak of this at more length elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc ad Ioannem redeamus, qui Domino vocanti absq; mora obtemperat, & ex deserto in publicum prodiens in tota regione, quæ Iordani adiacet, concionatur. Dicitur autem prædicauisse baptismum resipiscentiæ in remissionem peccatorum. At baptismi nomine totum Ioannis ministerium comprehendi, ex alijs locis constat, maximè ex Christi quæstione, qua Iudæorum antistites interrogat, quid de baptismo Ioannis sentiant, an illum ex Deo aut hominibus esse credant? Et baptismum pœnitentiæ dicit, eò quòd resipiscentiam & vitæ emendationem ab ijs requireret, qui per illum Christo initiabantur. Adhæc dabatur in remissionem peccatorum, non quòd hæc baptismo esset alligata, aut propter resipiscentiam, & vitæ melioris meritum obtingeret: sed quia omnium istorum finis esset Christus, qui & veræ pœnitentiæ in nobis author est, & idem in se credentium peccata expiauit, vt propter ipsum, cui per fidem insiti sunt, remissionem apud Deum inueniant. Tria ergo fecit Ioannes. Primò pœnitentiam siue resipiscentiam docuit, quæ vitæ totius emendationem, imò hominis totius innouationem continet. Secundò huius prædicatione contritis ostendit remissionem gratuitam propositam esse in Iesu Christo. Tertiò baptismum addidit, qui & resipiscentia opus esse docebat, & remissionem peccatorum, quam nobis Christus meruit, externè obsignabat, totosq; Christo consecrabat eos, qui illo tingebantur. Ergo totum Ioannis ministerium duabus omnino partibus constitit, doćtrina nimirum & baptismo. Doćtrinæ capita fuerunt, pœnitentia & remissio peccatorum, quibus Euangelij prædicationem totam comprehendi docet ipse Christus, quando duo hæc in suo nomine prædicari oportere testatur. Vt verò vtrumq; prædicauit, suo loco audiemus. Doćtrinæ verò huic accessit baptismus, qui cùm nouum quid præ se ferret, ex eo Baptistæ nomen accepit. Itaq; Euangelij minister fuit, neq; discrimen vllum inter eius doćtrinam & apostolicam constitui debet: & quia doćtrina eadem est, baptismus quoq; eius idem sit oportet cum eo, quem apostoli postea admistrauerunt. Qua de re nunc prolixius dicere non est opus. Nunc ea modò videbimus, quæ proprie ad loci istius tractationem faciunt, quæ sunt duo numero.
units.tr: Now let us return to John, who obeys the calling of the Lord without delay, and coming forth from the wilderness into public, preaches throughout the whole region adjoining the Jordan. It is said that he preached "the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." That his whole ministry is comprehended under the name of baptism is clear from other passages, especially from Christ's question, by which he asks the chief priests what they think of the baptism of John, whether they believe it to be from God or from men. And he calls it the baptism of repentance because it required repentance and amendment of life from those who were initiated into Christ through it. Moreover, it was given for the remission of sins, not because remission was tied to baptism, or because it was obtained on account of repentance and the merit of a better life; but because the end of all these things was Christ, who is the author of true repentance in us, and who also expiated the sins of those who believe in him, so that, through him, into whom they are grafted by faith, they may find remission with God. John therefore did three things. First, he taught repentance or conversion, which contains the amendment of the whole life, indeed the renewal of the whole man. Second, by his preaching he showed to the contrite that remission, freely offered, is set forth in Jesus Christ. Third, he added baptism, which both taught that there was need of repentance and outwardly sealed the remission of sins which Christ merited for us, and consecrated wholly to Christ those who were washed in it. Thus the whole ministry of John consisted of two parts altogether: teaching, namely, and baptism. The heads of his teaching were repentance and remission of sins, by which Christ himself teaches that the whole preaching of the gospel is comprehended, when he testifies that these two must be preached in his name. How he preached each we shall hear in its place. To this teaching was joined baptism, which, since it presented something new, received from this the name of the Baptist. Therefore he was a minister of the gospel, and no difference at all ought to be set between his teaching and the apostolic; and since the teaching is the same, his baptism too must be the same as the one the apostles afterwards administered. There is no need to say more on this matter now. Now we shall consider only those things which properly bear on the treatment of this passage, and these are two in number.

units.la: Primum est, ministerium Ecclesiæ, in quo necesse est nouisse, quibus partibus illud constet, ne à Deo institutum ordinem turbemus, & priuata temeritate nobis inutile & perniciośum reddamus, quod nostræ salutis ergo Deus instituit. Atqui minimè dubium est, Ioanne, qui primus noui testamenti minister fuit, nihil eorum omisisse, quæ ad ministerium istud pertinent. Idèque nō aliud quàm docuit & baptizauit. Ergo in Ecclesia doćtrina & Sacramentorum vsus retineri debent, in quo duobus hisce ministerijs Ecclesiæ totum consistit. Vtrisq; propter nos opus est. Quia enim nos nostræ rationis acumine non percipimus regni cœlorum mysteria, institutionem nobis adhiberi oportet: hæc autem doćtrinæ formam certam requirit, ne circa quæstiones inutiles & incerta hominum superstitiosorum figmenta vagemur. Comprehendit hanc olim Deus primis promissionibus, quæ homines & officij admonebant, & salutem in femine mulieris monstrabant, per quod diaboli regnum destrui oporte-ret. Clarius deinde doctrinam hanc Deus in fœdere cum Abrahamo facto in certa capita distinctam propositit, vt alibi diximus. Secuta est tandem Lex, quæ singulorum capitum fœderis expositionem plenam & diligentem continet. Huic additi sunt sacerdotes, & hijs cessantibus prophetæ, qui doctrinam hanc rebus præsentibus accommodarunt, & ideo non simplici institutione, verumetiā admonitionibus, hortationibus, minis & increpationibus vsi sunt, vt homines vel in officio continerent, vel in viam reducerent. Nec mutata est in nouo testamento doctrinæ forma, nisi quod exhibita iam luce in Christo Iesu clarius omnia fulserunt, quæ veteribus obscuriora visa sunt. At quia nos pro carnis ingenio externis signis atq; exercitijs maximè ducimur, verbo seu doctrinæ cæremonias coniunxit, quæ vulgò Sacramenta dici solent. Constant hæ non otiosis & mutis signis aut symbolis, sed actionesfunt sacræ, quæ vt secundum Dei institutum peraguntur, ita in eorum administratione Dei verbum semper illis coniungi debet, quo & verus illorum vsus monstratur, & animi ad mysteriorum, quæ sub his latent, consideratione excitantur. Neq; tamen hic subsistit eorum vsus, sed quod his omnibus maius est, Deus promissiones suas illis obsignat, quò minus de earum veritate dubitemus. Et ideo sigilla iustitiæ fidei esse, fidem confirmare, & salutis in Christo exhibitæ nos certiores reddere dicuntur. Vtq; doctrinam certam esse voluit Deus, cui nihil addere vel adimere liceret: ita Sacramenta quoq; certa ipse nobis tradidit, quorum neq; numerum augere vel minuere, neq; formam mutare, multo minus vsum inuertere debent, quicunq; ingenui & germani cultores Dei haberi volunt. Poterant hæc multis demonstrari, si in re omnibus nota demonstratione opus esset. Sufficiat nunc officij pios admonuisse, vt à Deo traditam doctrinam studiosè audiant, Sacramentis item religiosè vtantur, & se Deo gratos præbeant, (qui immensa sua bonitate se nostro captui accommodat) & proinde eius præceptis obtemperent, neq; pro superuacaneis ducant ea, quæ ille propter nos instituit. In primis autem eos caueant, qui humanarum traditionum figmentis vel Verbi diuini doctrinam corrumpunt, vel Sacramenta adulterant & legitimum eorum vsum peruertunt. Frustra enim Deus humanis inuentis colitur, & in Sacramentorum corruptores horrenda exempla omnibus seculis ille edidit, quæ commemorare longum foret.
units.tr: First, there is the ministry of the Church, and in it we must know what parts it consists of, so that we do not disturb the order instituted by God and, by our private rashness, make useful and salutary for ourselves what God instituted for our salvation. Yet there is no doubt that John, who was the first minister of the New Testament, omitted none of those things that pertain to this ministry. Therefore he did nothing other than teach and baptize. Accordingly, in the Church the teaching of doctrine and the use of the sacraments must be retained, and the whole of the Church's ministry rests on these two offices. We need both for our sake. For since we do not, by the keenness of our own reason, grasp the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, we must be given instruction; and this in turn requires a fixed form of doctrine, lest we wander about in useless questions and in the uncertain inventions of superstitious men. God once comprehended this doctrine in the first promises, which admonished men of their duty and showed salvation in the seed of the woman, through whom the kingdom of the devil was to be destroyed. Later God set forth this doctrine more clearly in the covenant made with Abraham, divided into certain heads, as we have said elsewhere. At last the Law followed, which contains a full and diligent exposition of the individual heads of the covenant. To this were added priests, and when these ceased, prophets, who applied this doctrine to present circumstances; and therefore they used not simple instruction only but also admonitions, exhortations, threats and rebukes, so that they might either keep men in their duty or bring them back to the way. Nor was the form of doctrine changed in the New Testament, except that, the light now having been revealed in Christ Jesus, all things shone more clearly which had seemed more obscure to the ancients. But because we, according to the nature of the flesh, are led chiefly by external signs and exercises, God joined to the word or doctrine those ceremonies which are commonly called sacraments. These are not idle and mute signs or symbols, but sacred actions, which are performed according to God's institution; and in their administration the word of God must always be joined to them, by which both their true use is shown and the minds are stirred to consider the mysteries which lie hidden beneath them. Nor does their use stop here; but, what is greater than all these things, God seals his promises to us by them, so that we may doubt less about their truth. And therefore they are said to be seals of the righteousness of faith, to confirm faith, and to make us more certain of the salvation exhibited in Christ. And just as God willed that doctrine should be certain, to which nothing might be added or taken away, so he himself delivered the sacraments to us as fixed, and they ought neither to increase or diminish their number, nor change their form, much less pervert their use, whoever wish to be regarded as genuine and sincere worshippers of God. These things could be shown at length, if the matter needed a demonstration that all know. It is enough now to have admonished the pious of their duty: that they listen diligently to the doctrine delivered by God, use the sacraments devoutly, and show themselves pleasing to God (who in his immense goodness adapts himself to our capacity), and accordingly obey his precepts, and not regard as superfluous those things which he instituted for our sake. Above all, let them beware of those who corrupt either the doctrine of the divine Word with the inventions of human traditions, or adulterate the sacraments and pervert their lawful use. For God is worshipped in vain with human inventions, and he has displayed dreadful examples of the corrupters of the sacraments in all ages, which would be too long to recount.

units.la: Alterum, quod hoc loco considerandum venit, est baptismus què Ioannes primus administrauit, & cuius mysterium minimè ignorare conueniteos, qui Christi cultores & ecclesiæ eius membra haberi volunt. Est enim is Sacramentum, quo in ecclesiæ societate externam ascribimur, & quo nobis ob signatur ablutio peccatorum & regeneratio ad vitam cœlestem, cuius nobis author est Christus. At quia de hoc in Marco nostro diximus, quæcunq; cognitu & obseruatu necessaria sunt, eadè hic nolumus repetere. Interim admonedi sunt Christiani homines, vt meminerint suæ professionis, quâ in baptismo fecerunt. Nam vt Paulus ait, quotquot in Christum Iesum baptizantur, ij in morte eius baptizantur, & per baptismum vnà cum eo in mortem sepeliuntur. Decet ergo, vt quemadmodum ille à mortuis excitatus ad vitam verè diuinã resurrexit, ita nos quoq; mortificata carne & corpore pecacati, resurgamus ad vitæ nouitatem. Etenim ea conditione in album ecclesiæ ascribimur, vt Christo nomen demus, & sub eius signis militemus aduersus carne, mundum & huius principem diabolum. Itaq; quicunq; fidem in Christū profitentur & baptismum sibi ad salutem sufficere arbitrantur, cum vitam à Christianæ fidei professione alienam viuant, ij et baptismum & fidei sacrosanctum nomen prophanant, & olim professionis suæ testimonio damnabuntur. Excitent nos ista, vt exhibita nobis in Christo Iesu bonitate digne consideremus, & eius consideratione incensi, totos nos ei consecremus, eundem vita & moribus referamus. Ita enim & gloriam Dei prouehemus, & olim cum illo regni cœlestis hæreditatem adibimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The second thing to be considered in this place is the baptism which John first administered, and whose mystery those who wish to be regarded as worshippers of Christ and members of his Church ought by no means to be ignorant of. For it is the sacrament by which we are enrolled externally in the fellowship of the Church, and by which the washing away of sins and regeneration to the heavenly life, of which Christ is the author, is sealed to us. But since we have spoken of this in our commentary on Mark, whatever is necessary to know and observe, we do not wish to repeat here. Meanwhile Christians must be admonished to remember the profession which they made in baptism. For, as Paul says, all who are baptized into Christ Jesus are baptized into his death, and through baptism are buried together with him into death. It is fitting, therefore, that just as he was raised from the dead to a truly divine life, so we too, with the flesh and body of sin mortified, should rise to newness of life. For on this condition we are enrolled in the register of the Church, that we give our name to Christ and fight under his standards against the flesh, the world and the devil, the prince of this world. Therefore, whoever profess faith in Christ and think baptism is enough for their salvation, while they live a life alien to the profession of the Christian faith, they profane both baptism and the holy name of faith, and will one day be condemned by the testimony of their own profession. Let these things rouse us to consider worthily the goodness exhibited to us in Christ Jesus, and, kindled by its consideration, to consecrate ourselves wholly to him, and to conform ourselves to him in life and manners. For thus we shall both advance the glory of God and one day with him enter into the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVII.

units.la: Sicut scriptum est in libro sermonum Isaiæ Prophetæ, dicentis: Vox clamantis in deserto. Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas eius. Omnis vallis implebitur, & omnis mons & collis humiliabitur, et quæ curua sunt fient recta via, & aspera vertentur in vias planas. Videbitq; omnis caro salutem Dei.
units.tr: As it is written in the book of the sayings of the prophet Isaiah, who says: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight his paths. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and crooked things shall become straight, and rough places plain. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God."

units.la: Quemadmodū Dominus noster Iesus Christus olim Ioannis Baptistae ministerio vsus est, vt per hunc homines ad illum digne excipiendum praepararentur: Ita hodie nobis etiam multa doctrina & exhortatione opus est, vt in Euangelio ad nos venientē excipere & retinere possimus, ne mala tractatione offensus iterum à nobis abscedat. Non temere ergo Lucas diligenter admodum ea omnia exponit, quae ad Ioannis ministerium pertinent. Nam à vocatione exorsus temporis notationem accuratissimam ponit, quò minus de re tota dubitemus. Deinde locum quoq; no minat, qui ad commendandam Dei gratiam in primis faciebat. Istis mox summam doctrinae eius subiecit, quae resipiscentiam & peccatorum remissionem comprehendit. Doctrinae verò signum addidit Baptismum, qui resipiscentia quidem opus esse docebat, remissionem verò peccatorū monstrabat in Christo, vera illo & æteruo agno Dei, qui mundi peccata tollit & expiat. Et haec illa sunt, in quibus assidui & industrij esse debent, quicunq; ad Ecclesiae ministerium vocati sunt, vt Christo apud homines locum faciant. Quia verò Ioannis doctrinam totius orbis mutatio secuta est, qualis à prima rerum origine nunquam facta fuit, in praesenti veteris Prophetae Isaiae vaticinium adducit Lucas, cuius hic finis est scopus est, Ioannem non temerarium nouatorem fuisse, neq; aliquid fecisse ex priuato consilio siue arbitrio: sed munere sibi diuinitus commisso functu esse, cui illum Deus iam olim praedestinarat. Quod ipsum alij etiam Euangelistae obseruarunt, Matthaeus in primis & Marcus, qui eiusdem oraculi mentionem diserte fecerunt. Vbi nobis ante omnia obseruanda venit Euangelij dignitas & fidei nostrae certitudo. Vt enim in Christi historia cum promissionibus & prophetarū vaticiniis omnia pulchrè conueniunt: ita nihil ab his diuersum inuenitur in toto euangelico negotio, siue primum eius ministrum Ioannem, siue Apostolos spectes, qui illud postea inter omnes gentes praedicauerunt. Sunt ergo nimium ignaui & imprudentes, qui ista nō obseruāt, & proinde de illius veritate perpetuò dubitant: inexcusabilis autem est eorum impietas & malitia, qui cùm ista non omnino ignorent, neq; etiam negare possint, nihilominus argumenta vndique conquirunt, quibus Euangelij doctrinam in dubium vocent, & tam propriam ipsorum quàm aliorum incredulitatem augeant.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ once made use of the ministry of John the Baptist, so that through him men might be prepared to receive him worthily, so today we too need much teaching and exhortation, so that we may receive and hold on to the Gospel as it comes to us, and so that it does not, offended by our mishandling, depart from us again. It is not without reason, then, that Luke sets out with such care all the things that pertain to John's ministry. For beginning from his calling, he gives a most exact note of the time, so that we may doubt the whole matter less. Then he also names the place, which served especially to commend the grace of God. Immediately after these he adds the sum of John's teaching, which comprises repentance and the forgiveness of sins. As a sign of this teaching he added baptism, which taught that there was need of repentance, but showed the forgiveness of sins in Christ, the true and eternal Lamb of God, who takes away and expiates the sins of the world. These are the things in which all who have been called to the ministry of the Church ought to be diligent and busy, so that they may make room for Christ among men. But since a change of the whole world followed John's teaching, such as had never been made since the first origin of things, Luke brings in the prophecy of the ancient prophet Isaiah. The aim of this is to show that John was not a rash innovator, nor did he do anything on his own private counsel or judgment, but discharged a office committed to him by God, for which God had long before predestined him. The other evangelists also noted this, Matthew and Mark above all, who expressly mentioned this same oracle. Here, before all else, the dignity of the Gospel and the certainty of our faith are to be observed. For just as in the history of Christ everything agrees well with the promises and prophecies of the prophets, so nothing different from these is found in the whole evangelical business, whether you look at its first minister, John, or at the Apostles, who afterwards preached it among all nations. They are therefore far too sluggish and imprudent who do not observe these things and so constantly doubt its truth. But inexcusable is the impiety and malice of those who, though they are not wholly ignorant of these things, nor can even deny them, nevertheless seek arguments from every side by which they may call the doctrine of the Gospel into doubt, and increase both their own unbelief and that of others.

units.la: Porrò quoad Isaiae locum, extat is in cap. 40. vbi consolationes instituit propheta, quibus pios confirmet, qui comminatione exilij seu captiuitatis Babylonicae consternati, ecclesiam simul omnem ruituram timebant. Docet ergo, quod etsi populus propter peccata in Babylone abducendus sit, Deū tamen promissionum suarum probè memorem fore, & daturū prophetas, qui afflictos consolentur: imò promittit fore, vt nō solùm cum gaudio, verumetiā magna cum gloria inde reducatur. Et quia huic promissioni multa videbātur obstare, vtpote itineris longitudo, Babyloniorū immanis potentia, gentium aliarū hostiles animi, & in primis diuturna vastitas terrae Iudaicae, quae inculta, inuia & inhabitata per annos septuaginta iacuerat: ostendit non defore Deo media, quibus haec omnia remoueat, & facillima reddat, quae nunc impossibilia putentur. Vtq; magis fidē faciat ijs, quos sciebat in Babylone multis atq; grauissimis tentationibus obnoxios fore, fingit emissos anteambulones seu praecones regios, qui deserta Iudaeae accolis alta voce et cum regia authoritate mandēt, vt Domino, qui populū suum reducturus sit, viam sternant, & impedimenta omnia è medio tollant. Verba prophetae sunt: Vox clamantis (scilicet audietur) in deserto, Parate viam Domino, in solitudine planam facite viam Deo nostro. Omnis vallis exaltabitur, omnis autē mons aut collis humiliabitur, siue deprimetur: quod curuum est, fiet rectum, & prærupta redigentur in planitiem. Reuelabitur enim gloria Domini, videbitq; omnis caro pariter quoniā os Domini locutū est. Et haec quidem, quoad illorū temporū historiā, impleta sunt, quādo Cyrus euerso Babylonico regno, & Monarchia ad Persas et Medos translata, Iudaeis ad auitas sedes redeundi copiā fecit, & publicis quoq; edictis cauit, ne quis vel redeuntibus negotium faceret, vel vrbis & templi ædificationem impediret. Quia verò liberatio ex Babylone eius redemptionis typus fuit, quae postea praefinito tempore toti generi humano obtigit per Christum, qui euersa diaboli tyrannide nos asseruit in libertatem filiorum Dei, imò idem hic veteris quoq; liberationis verus author fuit (Constat enim Deum veteribus quoq; propter vnū Christum, qui ex illis nasciturus erat, & quem vēturū pij sperabāt, propitiū fuisse) non immerito Euangelistae vaticinium istud de Ioanne Baptista & filij Dei in carnē aduentu exponunt, & eidē circunstantiae omnes mirificè conueniūt. Nā vt olim propter immanē Babyloniorū potentiā impossibile videbatur, populū Dei ad sua reditur esse: ita vix sperari poterat, aliqué ex potestate tenebrarū liberari posse. cùm & gentium idololatria et Iudæorũ superstitiones Romani Imperij authoritate defenderentur, cuius vires tunc toti orbi formidabiles erat. Et vt via nulla patebat per infestas gentes & horrida deserta iter facturis ex Babylone: ita nõ aliqua via apparuit, qua Dei filius in mundũ hunc, quouis deserto steriliorem & infeliciore veniret, & rebus afflictis salutē afferret. Præterea, vt regijs Cyri edictis suam authoritatem Deus esse voluit, & præter omnē spem populum auitis sedibus restituit: ita eiusdem spiritu factum est, vt Ioannes Christi anteambulo & præco non sine authoritate & mirifico profectu totum populum excitarit, vt Christo ad templum suum venturo (sicut Malachias prædixerat) viam sterneret: cuius aduentum mox secuta est veri templi & Hierosolymæ cœlestis ædificatio, Ecclesiæ nimirum, quæ ex omnibus gentibus collecta Deo seruit in spiritu & veritate, & salutifera libertate in Christo Iesu fruitur. Itaque hic demum verè impletum est, quod in reditu ex Babylone obscurius adumbratum, & vniuersalis illius redemptionis tenue aliquod (vt sic dicam) præludium fuit: ideoq; quod de voce in deserto clamatura Isaias prædixit, de nemine rectius & verius quàm de Ioanne Baptista exponitur. Porrò videamus, qui præcipui huius tractationis loci sint, quorum obseruatio ad nostram institutionem faciat.
units.tr: Moreover, as to the passage of Isaiah, it stands in chapter 40, where the prophet sets out consolations by which he might confirm the godly, who, dismayed by the threat of exile or the Babylonian captivity, feared that the whole Church would be overthrown at the same time. He teaches therefore that although the people were to be carried off into Babylon on account of their sins, God would nevertheless remember his promises well and would give prophets who would console the afflicted; indeed he promises that they would be brought back from there not only with joy but also with great glory. And because many things seemed to stand in the way of this promise, namely the length of the journey, the savage power of the Babylonians, the hostile minds of the other nations, and above all the long desolation of the land of Judah, which had lain uncultivated, trackless and uninhabited for seventy years, he shows that God would not lack means by which he might remove all these things and make easy what now seemed impossible. And so that he might give more confidence to those whom he knew would be exposed in Babylon to many and very grievous temptations, he imagines royal heralds or forerunners sent out, who would command the inhabitants of the Judean wilderness, with a loud voice and with royal authority, to prepare a way for the Lord, who was about to bring back his people, and to remove all the obstacles from the middle. The words of the prophet are: "The voice of one crying (that is, it will be heard) in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord; make a plain way in the desert for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain or hill shall be brought low, or levelled; what is crooked shall become straight, and rough places shall be reduced to a plain. For the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, since the mouth of the Lord has spoken." And indeed these things, as far as the history of those times goes, were fulfilled when Cyrus, the Babylonian kingdom having been overthrown and the monarchy transferred to the Persians and Medes, gave the Jews the opportunity to return to their ancestral seats, and also provided by public edicts that no one should either give trouble to those returning or hinder the building of the city and the temple. But since the deliverance from Babylon was a type of that redemption which afterwards came to the whole human race at the appointed time through Christ, who, overthrowing the tyranny of the devil, has set us free into the liberty of the sons of God; indeed, this same Christ was also the true author of the ancient deliverance (for it is established that God was favourable to the men of old too, on account of the one Christ who was to be born from them and whom the godly hoped would come): for this reason the Evangelists rightly expound this prophecy concerning John the Baptist and the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, and all the circumstances agree wonderfully with it. For just as it once seemed impossible, on account of the enormous power of the Babylonians, that the people of God should return to their own land, so it could hardly be hoped that anyone could be freed from the power of darkness, since both the idolatry of the nations and the superstitions of the Jews were defended by the authority of the Roman Empire, whose power was then formidable to the whole world. And just as no way lay open for those who were to go from Babylon through hostile nations and dreadful deserts, so no way appeared by which the Son of God might come into this world, more barren and unhappy than any desert, and bring salvation to afflicted things. Moreover, just as God chose to give authority to the royal edicts of Cyrus and restored the people to their ancestral seats beyond all hope, so by the same Spirit it came about that John, the forerunner and herald of Christ, with authority and wonderful success, stirred up the whole people, so that he might prepare a way for Christ who was to come to his temple (as Malachi had foretold). Soon after his coming followed the building of the true temple and of the heavenly Jerusalem, namely the Church, which, gathered from all nations, serves God in spirit and truth and enjoys the saving liberty in Christ Jesus. Thus at last that was truly fulfilled which was dimly foreshadowed at the return from Babylon, and was, so to speak, a slight prelude to that universal redemption; and so what Isaiah foretold about the voice that would cry in the wilderness is explained of no one more rightly and truly than of John the Baptist. Now let us see which are the chief points of this discussion, the observation of which will serve for our instruction.

units.la: Occurrit hic primũ, quòd Christus Euangelij sui & totius negotij salutis nostræ ab Ioannis nisterio initium fieri voluit, qui præconis aut anteambulonis instar ipsi populum præpararet. Ex eo colligimus, præparatione opus esse ijs, qui Christum Iesum ad se accedere optant, aut cum illo coniungi & eo ad salutem frui cupiunt. Ea enim est omnium nostrum conditio, vt nisi toti immutemur, nulla inter nos & Deum communio esse possit. Est iustitia, sapientia, veritas, bonitas, imò ignis consumens est, in cuius conspectum nihil quod corruptum & vitiosum est, appropinquare poterit. Ut si nos speculles, iniustos, stultos & rerum cælestium ignaros, mendaces, malos & ad omnem nequitiam natura proclives esse videbis. Itaq; omnes exclamare cogemur cum propheta: Quis nostrum habitabit cum igne devorante? quis nostrum habitabit cum ardoribus æternis? Vt ergo pharmaca in affectis corporibus locum non habent, nisi eiectis prius humoribus noxijs, qui valetudini obstant: ita neq; salutifera illa animarum medicina, quam nobis Christus propinat, quicquam iuuabit, nisi eijcia tur prius, aut saltem in ordinem redigatur innata nobis natura vitiositas, qua regnante multa quotidie facimus, quæ Deum à nobis arcent, nosq; salute in Christo indignos reddunt. Deinde exigit hoc ipsum Christi maiestas, & bonorum, quæ secum affert, excellentia. Si enim huius seculi Reges, qui à victoria contra hostes redeunt, aut regna sua occupare volunt, vrbes non ingrediuntur, nisi explorati prius & repurgatis per antecursores suos itineribus, & ad omne vsum necessarium probè instructis hospitijs: quanto iustius est, ad Christi aduentum nos præparari, qui Rex Regum est & Dominus dominantium, quiq; nostræ salutis ergo cum hoste diabolo congressus, illum deuicit, & sibi quidem regnum gloriosum, nobis verò pacem, libertatem & vitam æternam acquisiuit? Vehementer ergo errant, qui in illo peccandi licentiam vænantur, & sub plausibili Christianæ libertatis prætextu ea designant, quibus ille non potest non offendi, cùm ad destruenda diaboli opera et ad abolendum in carne nostra regnum peccati venerit.
units.tr: Here first occurs this: that Christ willed that the beginning of his Gospel and of the whole business of our salvation should be made from the ministry of John, who, in the manner of a herald or forerunner, was to prepare the people for him. From this we gather that preparation is needed by those who desire to come to Christ Jesus, or wish to be joined with him and to enjoy salvation through him. For this is the condition of all of us: unless we are wholly changed, no fellowship between us and God can exist. He is justice, wisdom, truth, goodness, indeed a consuming fire, into whose sight nothing that is corrupt and vicious can come near. For if you look into us, you will see us unjust, foolish, ignorant of heavenly things, liars, wicked, and by nature prone to every wickedness. And so we shall all be compelled to cry out with the prophet: "Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?" Just as remedies have no place in diseased bodies unless the harmful humours that stand in the way of health are first expelled, so that saving medicine of souls which Christ offers us will help us in no way unless the natural viciousness innate in us is first cast out, or at least brought into order, a viciousness which, reigning in us, makes us do many things every day that keep God far from us and render us unworthy of salvation in Christ. Next, the very majesty of Christ and the excellence of the good things which he brings with him demand this. For if the kings of this age, returning from victory over their enemies, wish to take possession of their kingdoms, they do not enter their cities unless the roads have first been explored and cleared by their forerunners, and lodgings have been properly furnished for every necessary use. How much more just is it that we should be prepared for the coming of Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and who, having engaged with the enemy, the devil, for our salvation, conquered him, and acquired for himself indeed a glorious kingdom, but for us peace, liberty and eternal life? They therefore greatly err who hunt for a licence to sin in him, and under the specious pretext of Christian liberty set about those things by which he cannot but be offended, since he came to destroy the works of the devil and to abolish the kingdom of sin in our flesh.

units.la: Secundo loco tenendum est, in quo nam præparatio illa consistat? Requiritur hic ante omnia ardens salutis & iustitiæ æternæ desiderium. Nam nisi eo inflammemur, non multùm cœlestia bona cu rabimus, qui per innata carnis desideria ad terrena & mundi voluptates toti abripimur. Ideo Christus passim esurientes & sitientes ad se vocat, eos nimirum intelligens, qui peccatorum pondere depressi & fatigati, totis animis ad salutem æternam aspirant. Nihil ergo hic faciunt: qui cùm se sibi ipsis sufficere putent, sanctam illa esuriem atq; sitim nondum sentiunt, aut se inter media scelera beatos & felices esse arbitrantur. Deinde procul remoueri oportet, quæcunque nos à Deo reuocant, aut illius oculos offendunt, quò minus ad nos accedat. Est hoc (si vno verbo omnia complecti libeat) peccatum. Vt enim primi parentes peccando seipsos à Deo alienauerunt: ita hæc etiam hodie scelerata illa & infelix maceria est, quæ nos ab illo & bonorum eius communione separat. Docet hoc Isaias, quando de nimio Dei rigore & seueritate conquerentibus dicit: Ecce manus Domini non est abbreuiata, quò minus seruare possit, neq; aggrauata auris eius, vt exaudire non queat: sed iniquitates vestræ diuidunt inter vos & Deum vestrum, & peccata vestra abscondunt vultum eius à vobis ne exaudiat. Manus enim vestræ pollutæ sunt sanguine et digiti vestri iniquitate; labia vestra loquuntur men-tur mentur mendacium, &c. At quia multiplex & varia est peccati soboles, non immerito diligenti enume ratione idem Isaias in præsenti vtitur. Nam in capta Metaphora aut similitudine pergens, quæ-cunq; in itineribus occurrunt incommoda exponit, montes nimirū inuios, valles profundas & palu-dibus tetris hiantes, viarum diuersissimarum incerta diuerticula, præcipitia item & quæcunq; alia sunt eius generis: quibus diuersas peccati species & diuersa quæ ex his enascuntur hominum inge-nia denotat. Ita vero simul admonere vult Spiritus sanctus, hoc nō parui laboris opus esse, adeoq; hic serio requiri quod in Xerxe historici reprehendunt, qui Isthmum perfodere, montes transferre, maria pontibus sternere, flumina exiccare, deniq; totam orbis facie mutare conatus est. Sunt enim alij montes & valles, rupes item & præcipitia, paludes, gurgites in ipsa hominis natura, quæ omnia qui suis viribus remouere velit, ipso Xerxe confidentior fuerit, & tamen vt remoueantur omnino opus esC. Per valles enim intelliguntur homines desperabundi, quos scelerum admissorum conscientia de primit, vt oculos ad Deum non ausint attollere. Illos exaltari, id est, erigi oportet, non quidé vt confidenter aduersus Deum insurgant, sed vt de eius gratia & Christi merito certiores facti animum colliгant, & constanti fide diaboli tela eludant, quibus hic in desperatione illos adducere conatur. Est hoc factu in primis necessarium. Vt enim medicum & medicina non admittit, cui nulla valetudinis melioris spes superest: ita Euangelij prædicatione nunquam mouebitur, qui de Dei gratia desperauit, & totus sub peccatorum conscientia succumbit. Itaq; vt prudentes medici ægrotum amice compellant, & ei salutis spem faciunt, ne ex desperatione obortus dolor morbum augeat: ita verbi ministros hoc ipsum facere conuenit apud eos, quos desperatione vinci & quasi in vallem profundam debiscere vident. Montes vero & colles dicuntur, qui huius seculi fortunis & successu ebrij capita attollunt, & disciplinam omnem reijciunt: vel suorum operum & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia elati coram Deo superbiunt, neq; putant sibi gratuita peccatorum remissione opus esse, quæ nobis per Euangelium in Christo Iesu offertur. Est vtrunq; genus hominum frequens valde. Qui enim in opum abundantia & lætiori fortuna Dei beneficentiā agnoscere & huic sese gratos atq; morigeros sistere debebant, plerunq; sibi ipsis placent, & ex eo laudem venantur, quod omnia pro suo arbitrio faciant. Rursus qui inter homines iustitiæ & sanctitatis existimatione sustinent, eadem apud Deum quoq; (vt olim Pharisæi) confidentius gloriantur, & gratiæ prædicationem indignissimè ferunt, quod nimirum omne hoc sibi decedere sentiant, quod Deo tribuitur. Et in hoc albo præcipui sunt Monachi, & quicunq; horum doctrinam sequuntur. Vtrunq; vero genus humiliatione opus habet, & ideo pri-oribus illis incertam & caducam rerum huius seculi conditionē ob oculos statuere oportet, vt illis superbire desinant: alteros autem ad Dei tribunal citare, & Legis speculo eorum non solum aperta flagitia, verumetiā membris inhærente naturæ vitiositatē arguere, vt se miseros & infelices esse intelligat, quibus gratuita misericordia opus fit. Per curua et obliqua omnes errorum atq; superstitionum amba ges intelligé, quibus ferè circunducuntur, qui ex suo cerebro sapere instituunt, & regni cælorum mysteria ad suæ rationis calculum reuocant. Horum omnium sensus atq; rationes ad verbi diuini regulam dirigere oportet, vt ad Christum conuertantur, qui via & veritas est. Sunt item prærupta & aspera multa, sub quibus omnia alia vitiorum genera comprehendi possunt. Prærupta equidem præcipitia sunt libido, gula, auaria, luxuria, odium, invidia, ira, & quæcunq; alia sunt huius farinæ: quæ vt suos sectatores exitio æterno demergunt, ita asperos quoq; & intractabiles reddunt, vt nemo illis sine aliqua iactura aut periculo conuersari possit. Et hi omnes ad excipiendum Christum nunquam idonei erunt, nisi relictis studijs prioribus mollescant, seq; ipsos Dei verbo regendos præbeant. Quæ omnia si cum nostri seculi moribus conferamus, non mirabimur tam paucos esse, qui Christum vere recipiant & in illo feruentur. Constat enim plerosq; hominum superstitionibus delectari, quæ sectatoris suis desperationis causa sunt: aut opibus, honoribus, potentia & mundi huius fauore superbire, aut pharisaica operum suorum fiducia turgere, aut per incertos errores vagari, & eosdem pertinaciter tueri, aut effræni licentia in sceleribus & manifestis flagitijs pergere. Estq; istorum omnium eo infelicior conditio, quod suam infelicitatem non agnoscunt, neq; de istis emendandis cogitant, quæ ipsos à Christo, vnico salutis authore, alienos reddunt.
units.tr: Second, we must consider in what this preparation consists. Above all, an ardent desire for salvation and eternal righteousness is required here. Unless we are inflamed with it, we will hardly pursue heavenly goods, since we are wholly carried off to earthly things and the pleasures of the world by the desires innate in the flesh. That is why Christ calls the hungry and thirsty to himself everywhere, meaning of course those who, weighed down and worn out by the burden of their sins, aspire with their whole souls to eternal salvation. Those who think they are sufficient for themselves, and so do not yet feel that holy hunger and thirst, or who think they are blessed and happy in the midst of their wickedness, do nothing here. Next, whatever calls us back from God or offends his eyes must be removed far away, so that he may not draw near to us. If we want to embrace all of this in one word, it is sin. For just as our first parents, by sinning, estranged themselves from God, so this wicked and unhappy wall is still today what separates us from him and from communion in his goods. Isaiah teaches this when, answering those who complain of God's excessive rigour and severity, he says: "Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither is his ear heavy, that it cannot hear. But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear. For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, and your tongue has muttered wickedness" (Isa. 59). But since the offspring of sin is manifold and various, Isaiah rightly uses a careful enumeration in this passage. Continuing with a borrowed metaphor or comparison, he sets out the hindrances that meet travellers on their journeys: trackless mountains, deep valleys gaping with foul marshes, the uncertain byways of very different roads, and precipices and other things of that kind. By these he marks out the different species of sin and the different dispositions of men that arise from them. In this way the Holy Spirit wishes at the same time to warn us that this is no small labour, and that what the historians blame in Xerxes is seriously required here: he tried to cut through the Isthmus, move mountains, bridge the seas, dry up rivers, and, in short, change the whole face of the earth. For there are other mountains and valleys, crags and precipices, marshes and whirlpools, in human nature itself, and whoever would remove all of these by his own strength would be more over-confident than Xerxes himself; yet for them to be removed completely is necessary. By "valleys" are meant despairing men, whom the consciousness of their committed crimes casts down so that they dare not lift their eyes to God. These must be "exalted," that is, raised up, not indeed so that they confidently rise against God, but so that, made more certain of God's grace and the merit of Christ, they gather their spirits and with steadfast faith ward off the darts of the devil, with which he here tries to drive them into despair. This is above all necessary to be done. For as a physician does not admit a patient who has no hope of better health left, so a man who has despaired of God's grace, and is wholly crushed under the consciousness of sin, will never be moved by the preaching of the gospel. Therefore, just as wise physicians address the sick kindly and give them hope of recovery, lest the pain arising from despair increase the disease, so it is fitting that the ministers of the Word do this very thing among those whom they see overcome by despair and, as it were, gaping into a deep valley. But "mountains and hills" are those who, drunk with the fortunes and success of this age, lift up their heads and cast off all discipline, or who, puffed up by trust in their own works and their own righteousness, are proud before God and do not think they need the free forgiveness of sins that is offered to us through the gospel in Christ Jesus. Both kinds of men are very common. For those who, in abundance of wealth and a happier lot, ought to acknowledge God's kindness and present themselves grateful and compliant to it, for the most part please themselves and seek praise from this, that they do everything according to their own judgement. Again, those who are held in esteem among men for their righteousness and holiness boast all the more confidently before God as well (as the Pharisees once did), and they bear very badly the preaching of grace, because they clearly feel that everything that is attributed to God is taken away from them. Monks, and whoever follow their teaching, are especially prominent on this list. Both kinds of men need humbling, and therefore the former must be set before the eyes of the uncertain and fleeting condition of the things of this age, so that they cease to be proud; the latter must be summoned to the judgement seat of God and, in the mirror of the Law, be charged not only with open crimes but also with the wickedness of nature that clings to their members, so that they understand that they are wretched and unhappy and in need of free mercy. By "crooked and oblique paths" we are to understand all the winding ways of errors and superstitions by which those are led about who set out to be wise from their own brain and call the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven back to the reckoning of their own reason. The thoughts and reasonings of all these must be directed to the rule of the divine Word, so that they may be turned to Christ, who is the way and the truth. There are also many steep and rough places, under which all other kinds of vices can be included. Indeed, the steep precipices are lust, gluttony, avarice, luxury, hatred, envy, anger, and whatever else is of this sort, which, as they plunge their followers into eternal ruin, so also make them harsh and intractable, so that no one can associate with them without some loss or danger. All these will never be fit to receive Christ unless, having given up their former pursuits, they grow soft and allow themselves to be ruled by the Word of God. If we compare all these things with the manners of our own age, we will not be surprised that there are so few who truly receive Christ and are kindled in him. For it is plain that most men delight in superstitions, which are the cause of despair for their followers; or they puff themselves up with wealth, honours, power, and the favour of this world; or they swell with a Pharisaic trust in their own works; or they wander through uncertain errors and stubbornly defend them; or they persist in wickedness and open crimes with unbridled licence. And the condition of all these is the more unhappy because they do not recognise their unhappiness and do not think about amending it, and this is what makes them alien from Christ, the only author of salvation.

units.la: Nouit hanc nostram infelicitatem Deus, & quia nemo sibi ipsi manum admouet, publicum ver bi sui ministerium instituit, & vt olim Ioannem dedit, cuius prædicatione omnium animi ad excipiendum Christum praepararentur: ita ante hunc prophetas, & postea apostolos misit, quorum omnium idem officiu fuisse constat. Imo perpetuum esse vult docendi munus in Ecclesia, ne qui ignorantiam possint suae pertinaciae praetexere. Nam, vt Paulus ad Ephesios scribit, iam nunc quoque Christus dona sui spiritus e coelo distribuit, & alios quidem dat prophetas, alios apostolos, alios doctores, alios pastores, qui Ecclesiam aedificent, & omnes illi quotidie nouas adducant. Est hoc singulare et praeclarum suae bonitatis indicium. Poterat quidem ille suo spiritu hominum mentes immutare, & ab errorum atq; vitiorum auijs abductos illuminare, vt nemine monente ad Christum accederent: sed primo quidem nostrae carnis ingenio sese accommodat, & certam verbi sui doctrinam eiusq; certos ministros esse vult, quo minus locum habeant dubiae & incertae reuelationes, quibus Satan incautos ludere & lactare consueuit: deinde eo honore nos dignatur, vt ipsius sumus auditores siue cooperarij, vt Paulus loquitur. Debent ergo hunc Dei morem diligenter obseruare omnes homines, ne verbum quoddam Dei non scriptum & nescio quas spiritus inspirationes imaginando, sese diabolo seducendos exponant: & vt ij, qui ad docendi munus vocati sunt, suae dignitatis memores commissam sibi provinciam exornent, & olim in magno illo die in gaudium heri sui ingrediantur.
units.tr: God knows this our unhappiness, and since no one lays a hand on himself, he has established the public ministry of his Word, and, as once he gave John, through whose preaching the minds of all were prepared to receive Christ, so before him he sent the prophets, and afterwards the apostles, whose office is known to have been the same for all. Indeed, he wills the office of teaching to be perpetual in the Church, so that men cannot use ignorance as a pretext for their obstinacy. For, as Paul writes to the Ephesians, Christ even now distributes the gifts of his Spirit from heaven, and some he gives as prophets, some as apostles, some as teachers, some as pastors, who build up the Church, and all of them bring in new converts every day. This is a singular and remarkable token of his goodness. He could indeed, by his Spirit, change men's minds and enlighten those led astray from the paths of errors and vices, so that they would come to Christ without anyone prompting them. But first he accommodates himself to the nature of our flesh, and wills that there be a certain doctrine of his Word and certain ministers of it, so that doubtful and uncertain revelations, with which Satan is accustomed to mock and beguile the unwary, may have no place. Then he honours us with this dignity, that we are his hearers or, as Paul puts it, his fellow-workers. Therefore all men ought carefully to observe this custom of God, lest, by imagining some unwritten word of God or some inspirations of I know not what spirits, they expose themselves to be seduced by the devil. And let those who are called to the office of teaching, mindful of their dignity, adorn the task committed to them, so that on that great day they may enter into the joy of their Lord.

units.la: Est ergo omnibus, qui in Ecclesia & verbi ministerio constituti sunt, probe obseruandum, quod de Ioanne dicitur, eum vocem clamantis in deserto fuisse. Nam quamuis ad diu intermissum prophetiae munus propheta respicere videatur, quod noua Ioannis praedicatione Deus instaurari voluit: simul tamen praecipitur clara, ingenua & perspicua dicendi libertas, quae non aures solum feriat, sed ipsos etiam animos auditorum penetret. Requirit hanc ab omnibus prophetis Dominus. Isaias certe vocem instar tubae exaltare & ex guttere clamare iubetur, vt populo scelera sua annuntiet. Ezechiel vero speculatoris instar constitutus esse dicitur, vt diserte moneat eos, quorum ceruicibus gladius Domini imminet. Et eodem facit quod apostolos in tectis praedicare & diuulgare iubet Christus ea, quae in aurem audiuerint, id est, quae ex occultiori spiritus reuelatione didicerint. Paulus item Timotheum suum monet, vt non simpliciter solum doceat, verumetiam moneat, hortetur, increpet, adeoq; instet tempestiue & intempestiue. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter prophetae, sicuti eorum sermones testantur. Et quae Ioannis παῤῥησία siue libertas in dicendo fuerit, suo loco audiemus. Nec enim contentus fuit in genere poenitentiam docuisse, sed doctrinam hanc omnis loci & ordinis hominibus accommodauit, vt neq; pharisaeis, neq; sacerdotibus, neq; ipsi etiam Regi Herodi parceret. Secuti sunt exempla haec apostoli, vt videre est in primis illis concionibus, quas in sanguinaria Hierosolymorum vrbe habuerunt. Idem ergo hodie etiam fieri oportet. Exigit hoc infelix & tantumnon deplorata nostrae naturae corruptio. Blanditijs enim peccati sic capimur, vt hoc vel omnino nō agnoscamus, vel agnitum quoq; non fugiamus. Inuiti igitur ab eo auellimur, & efficaci omnino praedicatione opus est, vt Deum nos ad meliora vocantem sequamur. Scio equidem ministros aliquos segnio res fieri, quod se nihil proficere videant: sed non quantum proficias, sed quid ex officio facere debeas videndum est. Esto enim nihilo meliores fiant, quorum scelera nostro clamore prodimus, non tamen labor hic noster irritus est. Nam sunt interea alij, qui timorem concipiunt, & irae Dei considera tione territi de salute sua magis serio cogitare incipiunt. Multi etiam de sceleribus recte iudicare discunt, & minus offenduntur sceleratorum successibus, aut impunitate quae in hoc seculo interdum vtuntur. Et vt hi quoq; nulli sint, tamen suas animas (vt Ezechieli dicitur) ministri liberant, & proinde studij & fidei suae fructum vberrimum metunt. Debent ista diligenter meditari ministri hisce nouissimis temporibus, quando ea peccandi licentia et securitas passim regnat, de qua nos Christus admonuit, & cui excutiendae vel coercendae ne Ionae quidem minacissimae conciones suffecerint. Ferunt quidem indigne ministrorum libertatem, qui sceleribus iampridem assueuerunt: sed ijdem aliquando grauiora ferre cogentur, quando vndiq; irruentium hostium clamore, cornuum clangore, armorum strepitu, & promiscuo miserabiliq; pereuntium eiulatu illos Deus excitabit. Accidit hoc olim Iudaeis, cum prophetas diu nequicquam clamantes contempsissent, vt postremum cap. secundi Paralip. testatur. Quid vero nobis hodie sperandum sit, facile videt, qui intestina dissidia, simultates, bella ciuilia & inter haec indies sese dilatantem Turcarum tyrannidem non ofcitanter considerauerit.
units.tr: Everyone who has been placed in the Church and in the ministry of the Word must therefore observe carefully what is said of John, that he was a voice crying in the wilderness. For although the prophet seems to look back to an office that had long lapsed, God wished to restore it through John's new preaching, yet at the same time a clear, frank and plain freedom of speech is required, one that not only strikes the ears but also penetrates the minds of the hearers. The Lord demands this from all the prophets. Isaiah is commanded to raise his voice like a trumpet and to cry aloud from the throat, so that he may announce their sins to the people. Ezekiel is said to have been appointed as a watchman, so that he may plainly warn those over whose necks the sword of the Lord hangs. Christ does the same when he bids the apostles preach from the housetops what they have heard in the ear, that is, what they have learned from a more hidden revelation of the Spirit. Likewise Paul warns his Timothy not only to teach but also to admonish, exhort and rebuke, and to press on in season and out of season. The prophets observed this diligently, as their sermons bear witness. What John's freedom of speech [parrhesia] was, we shall hear in its proper place. For he was not content to teach repentance in general terms, but adapted this teaching to people of every rank and station, so that he spared neither the Pharisees, nor the priests, nor even King Herod himself. The apostles followed these examples, as can be seen in those first sermons they delivered in the bloodthirsty city of Jerusalem. The same therefore ought to be done today. This is required by the unhappy corruption of our nature, which is all but beyond hope. For we are so caught by the enticements of sin that either we do not recognise it at all, or, even when we recognise it, we do not flee from it. Being unwilling, we are therefore torn away from it, and we need a thoroughly effective preaching, so that we may follow God as he calls us to better things. I know that some ministers grow sluggish because they see that they accomplish nothing. But the question is not how much you are profiting, but what you ought to do by virtue of your office. For even if those whose crimes we expose with our outcry do not become any better, our labour is not thereby in vain. For meanwhile there are others who conceive fear, and, terrified by the consideration of God's wrath, begin to think more earnestly about their salvation. Many also learn to judge rightly about sins, and are less offended by the successes of the wicked, or by the impunity they sometimes enjoy in this age. And even if there were none of these, the ministers still deliver their own souls (as is said of Ezekiel), and so they reap the most abundant fruit of their study and faith. Ministers must meditate diligently on these things in these last times, when that licence to sin and that security reign everywhere, of which Christ warned us, and which even the most threatening sermons of Jonah were not enough to shake off or restrain. Indeed, those who have long been accustomed to sin bear the freedom of the ministers with indignation; but these same people will sometimes be forced to bear heavier things, when God stirs them up with the clamour of enemies rushing in from every side, the blare of horns, the clash of arms, and the mingled and pitiful wailing of those who perish. This happened once to the Jews, when, after they had despised the prophets who had cried out in vain for a long time, it came about as the last chapter of the second book of Paralipomenon attests. What we may hope for today, anyone can easily see who has considered, not without concern, the internal strife, the enmities, the civil wars, and, among these, the tyranny of the Turks spreading daily.

units.la: Caeterum finem quoq; totius negotij Euangelici Isaias indicat, cum addit: Reuelabitur enim gloria Domini ria Domini, videbitá, omnis caro pariter, quoniam os Domini locutum est. Quæ verba Lucas Græcam interpretationem secutus reddidit: Videbitq, omnis caro salutem siue Salutare Dei, id est, eum in quo ille omnes salutis thesauros nobis proponit, & qui vnicus salutis humanæ author est. Sed in idem sensus recidit. Scimus enim nullum diuinæ gloriæ specimen illustrius à condito mundo ædcitum esse, quàm quòd filiũ suum vnigenitũ misit in similitudine carnis peccati (vt Paulus loquitur) et peccatum condemnauit per eũ, qui pro nobis peccati hostia factus est, vt à Lege peccati & mortis liberemur. Ita enim diaboli regnum destruxit, & suam gloriam magnificè asseruit, quæ prius quasi concultata iacebat. Est autem eò vberior hæc Dei gratia, quòd salutem hanc omni carni, id est, hominibus vniuersis proponit & consentit huic oraculo mandatum Christi, quo Euangelium in toto orbe prædicari voluit in omnes gentes, promittens simul salutem omnibus iis, qui Euangelio credunt, & Ecclesiæ eius societati coniunguntur. Ista autem nos officij admonent, ne quis sibi licere arbitretur, vt Christum reijciat, & ad salutem per alias vias aut rationes contendat. Quia enim hoc vniuersale præceptum est, à nemine contemni poterit absque manifesta salutis iactura. Confirmationis loco additur, Quoniam os Domini locutum est. Sunt ergo hæc firma & rata, neque hominum vanissimorum commenta putari debent. Quia enim æterno etiam Dei decreto niituntur, vt sæpe aliàs dixi mus, nemo illa poterit irrita facere. Agnoscamus ergo hanc Dei bonitatem, & totis animis præparemur ad excipiendum Iesum Christum, vt in illo vitam & salutem consequamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Isaiah also indicates the goal of the whole Gospel enterprise when he adds: "For the glory of the Lord will be revealed, and all flesh will see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." Luke, following the Greek translation, rendered these words: "And all flesh will see the salvation of God," that is, him in whom God sets before us all the treasures of salvation, and who is the sole author of human salvation. Yet both come to the same sense. For we know that no more illustrious display of divine glory has been seen since the world was made than that God sent his only-begotten Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (as Paul puts it), and condemned sin in him, who was made a sacrifice for sin on our behalf, so that we might be freed from the law of sin and death. For in this way he destroyed the kingdom of the devil and vindicated his own glory magnificently, which had lain as it were shaken and cast down before. Moreover, this grace of God is all the richer because it offers this salvation to all flesh, that is, to all men without exception, and the command of Christ agrees with this oracle, by which he willed that the Gospel be preached throughout the whole world to all nations, at the same time promising salvation to all those who believe the Gospel and are joined to the fellowship of his Church. These things remind us of our duty, that no one should think it lawful for himself to reject Christ and strive for salvation by other ways or means. For since this command is universal, no one can despise it without manifest loss of salvation. By way of confirmation it is added: "for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." These things are therefore firm and settled, and should not be thought to be the inventions of most vain men. For since they rest on the eternal decree of God, as I have often said elsewhere, no one can make them void. Let us therefore acknowledge this goodness of God, and prepare ourselves with all our hearts to receive Jesus Christ, so that in him we may obtain life and salvation: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVIII.
units.tr: Homily 28.

units.la: Dicebat igitur turbæ venienti vt baptizaretur ab ipso: Progenies viperarum, quis præmonstrauit vobis vt fugeretis à ventura ira? Ferte igitur fructus qui resipiscentiam deceant, & ne coeperitis dicere apud vosipsos: Patrem habemus Abrahamum. Dico enim vobis, posse Deum etiam ex lapidibus istis excitare filios Abrahamo. Iam vero & securis ad radicem arborum posita est. Omnis ergo arbor non ferens fructum bonum exciditur & in ignem conijcitur.
units.tr: So John said to the crowd coming out to be baptized by him: "You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Bear therefore fruits that befit repentance, and do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones. Indeed the axe is already laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire."

units.la: Diligenter admodum scribit Lucas, quod nam Ioannis ministerium, & quæ eius doctrina fuerit. Primò enim omnibus conflare oportebat, doctrinam hanc, cuius ipse primus in novo testamento administer fuit, non nouam esse, sed eam humanæ salutis rationem continere, quæ æterno Dei consilio nitatur, & de qua olim Prophetæ etiam sint concionati. Deinde cum nobis quoq; præparatio ne opus sit, qua ad Christum excipiendum idonei reddamur, nobis etiam eadem doctrina necessaria est, ne nostræ rationis figmenta secuti nobisipsis remoras obijciamus, quæ nos à Christo & in hoc posita salutis via abducant. Consistit autè præparatio illa non in externis & inutilibus ceremonijs, sed in vera resipiscentia, vt nimirum relictis studijs prioribus nos totos Deo consecremus, & certa bonitatis atque gratiæ eius fiducia freti vitam viuamus nostra professione dignam. Et hæc quidem primùm in genere omnibus prædicauit Ioannes, & auditores suos simul baptismo tinxit, qui eos & ad pænitentiam agendam obstringebat, et in fiducia gratuitæ remissionis peccatorum confirmabat. Se quuntur deinceps conciones aliquot speciales (vt sic dicam) quas pro ratione eorum, qui ad ipsum veniebant, instituit, quales erant præter commune vulgus Pharisæi et Sadducæi, Publicani, Milites: qui cùm diuersa vitæ genera sequerentur, & diuersis quoq; vitijs laborarent, singulis propria doctrina opus fuit, qua sui officij admonerentur.
units.tr: Luke writes with great care about what John's ministry was and what his teaching was. For first of all it had to be made clear to everyone that this teaching, of which John was the first minister in the New Testament, was not new. It sets out the way of human salvation that rests on the eternal counsel of God, and of which the prophets of old also preached. Next, since we too need a preparation that makes us fit to receive Christ, this same teaching is necessary for us as well, so that we do not follow the inventions of our own reason and put obstacles in our own path, which would draw us away from Christ and from the way of salvation laid down in him. That preparation does not consist in external and useless ceremonies, but in true repentance: that is, leaving behind our former pursuits, we devote ourselves wholly to God, and, trusting firmly in his goodness and grace, we live a life worthy of our profession. John preached this first of all in general to everyone, and at the same time baptized those who heard him, binding them to repentance and confirming them in the confidence of the free forgiveness of sins. Then follow several special sermons, as I may call them, which he delivered according to the condition of those who came to him. Such were those addressed to the Pharisees and Sadducees, the publicans and the soldiers, apart from the common crowd. Since they followed different ways of life and suffered from different vices, each needed their own teaching, by which they might be reminded of their duty.

units.la: Præmittitur autem occasio, quòd nimirum populo ad ipsum confluente conciones hasce habuerit. At quod vno verbo dicit Lucas, hoc Matthæus diligentius exponit, vnde nimirum isti omnes aduenerint, docens. Tunc egressa est ad illum (inquit) Hierosolyma, & tota Iudæa, totaque regio vndique finitima Iordani. Ex quibus verbis colligi potest, hoc ipsum tunc factum fuisse, quod & ho die fieri consueuit. Nam sicubi locorum pij saniorisdoctrinæ instauratores exurgunt, qui Euangelium, diu prius occultatum, prædicant, mox confertim omnes accurrunt, mirantur, laudant, seque mutuo ad illud audiendum hortantur. Id vero plerique non veritatis amore aut æternæ salu-tis desiderio, sed potius novitatis studio faciunt, ut aures pascant, vel etiam odio eorum, quos præ aliis perstringi aut palam accusari arbitrantur. Ita tunc quoque noui doctoris fama omnes excitati concurrebant, audiebat docentem, venturi Messiæ desiderio ardebant, multi quoq; baptizabantur: at qui de resipiscentia serio cogitarent, paucissimi erant. Et est hoc mundi ingenium, quo tamen Deus pro sua æterna et imperuestigabili sapientia optime vtitur: vt nimirum periftam occasionem electi simul & reprobi ad audiendum Verbum excitentur, & illi quidem ad salutem instituantur bi vero inexcusabiles fiant. Ita in præsenti quoq; concursus ille plurimum profuit. Ea enim occasione Ioannes de singulorum ordinum officio concionatus est, & quid vnumquenq; pro sua vocatione ratione facere conueniat docuit: & vt Christus postea dicet, ex publicanis et meretricibus multi resipuerunt, quàmuis Pharisæi & Scribæ Dei consilium improbe contemnerent. Quoad vero exemplum Ioannis, admonentur eo omnes ecclesiarum ministri, ne se officio suo per omnia defunctos putent, si Verbum Dei in genere omnibus prædicent & generalia tradant veræ pietatis præcepta, sed meminerint doctrinam illam singulis applicandam esse pro personarum & temporum ratione, vt singuli quid in seipsis emendari opus sit intelligant. Est hoc necessarium valde, quia plerique dum verbum audiunt, non putant de se agi, aut dum communem pietatis Christianæ formam vt cunque sequuntur, ea interim negligunt, quæ ad vocationem ipsorum priuatam pertinent. Ideo Christus à suo illo Oeconomo requirit, vt familiæ suæ cibum suum in καιρῷ, id est, opportunè & prout vnus quisque egit proferat: & Paulus ministrum eiusmodi esse vult, qui verbum Dei recte secet, id est, ita doceat, vt singuli discant quid ipsis maximè sit faciendum.
units.tr: Luke mentions only the occasion, that John gave these sermons while the people flocked to him. Matthew explains more fully, in a single phrase, where all these people came from: "Then there went out to him," he says, "Jerusalem and all Judea, and all the region round about the Jordan." From these words it can be gathered that the same thing happened then as usually happens today. For wherever godly restorers of sounder teaching arise, preaching a gospel long hidden, at once everyone runs together in crowds, marvels, praises, and urges one another to hear it. Yet most do this not out of love for the truth or desire for eternal salvation, but rather from a zeal for novelty, to feed their ears, or even out of hatred for those whom they think are singled out above others and openly accused. So then too, the fame of the new teacher drew everyone together; they listened to him as he taught, they burned with longing for the coming Messiah, and many were baptized. But very few seriously thought about repentance. This is the nature of the world, yet God, in his eternal and unsearchable wisdom, uses it very well: the elect and the reprobate are both stirred by such an occasion to hear the Word, and the former are thereby instructed unto salvation, while the latter are made inexcusable. So in the present case too that gathering was of great benefit. For on that occasion John preached on the duty of each order and taught what each should do according to his calling. And as Christ later says, many publicans and harlots repented, although the Pharisees and scribes wickedly despised God's counsel. As for the example of John, all ministers of the churches are reminded by it that they should not think they have fully discharged their office if they preach the Word of God in general to all and deliver the general precepts of true piety, but they should remember that this teaching must be applied to each person according to the condition of persons and times, so that each may understand what needs to be amended in himself. This is very necessary, because many, while they hear the word, do not think it applies to them, or while they follow the common form of Christian piety in some fashion, they meanwhile neglect those things that pertain to their own private calling. Therefore Christ requires of his steward that he bring forth food to his household in due season [καιρῷ], that is, fittingly and as each one needs it. And Paul wants a minister to be one who rightly divides the word of God, that is, who so teaches that each one learns what he most needs to do.

units.la: Porrò ipsum Ioannem audiamus, qui concionem, quæ in præsenti describitur, ad Pharisæos & Sadducæos potissimum habuit, vt ex Matthæo colligitur, qui sic scribit: Cum vidisset multos ex Pharisæis & Sadducæis venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit illis: Progenies viperarum, &c.
