Lucas simpliciter turbæ, id est, populi promiscui meminit, in cuius corona hæc dixerit. Vnde apparet, illum hos nō priuatim aut occultius, sed in publico & omnibus audientibus increpuisse: de quo postea amplius dicetur. Nunc quia apud Euangelistas frequens est Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum mentio, de illis aliquid dicendum erit. Sunt ergo ista sectarum nomina, in quas illo tempore Iudæi scissi fuerunt, ea omnino ratione, qua Christianum populum sub papatu in diuersos Monachorum ordines finitimum fuisse scimus. Voluit quidem Deus vnam omnium fidem atque religionem esse, & proinde communes quoq; omnibus leges dederat, quæ fidei & diuini cultus adhæc vitæ morumq; præcepta ex æquo ad omnes pertinentia comprehendunt. Vtq; formam religionis vnam tradiderat: ita templum quoq; vnicum esse voluit, in quo solo sacra facerent, ne facile in sectas aut partes scinderentur. Et constat Iudæos veteres, etsi multis vitiis laborarent, externa tamen ecclesiæ vnitate diligenter seruauisse, ne in factiones diuersas abirent, qui in circumcisione vni Deo nomē dederant, & ad eiusdem Legis obseruationem erant astricti. At hostis vnitatis ecclesiæ Satan, vt totius religionis corruptionem & humanarum traditionum figmenta facilius induceret, tandem sectas & partium fluidia circa doctrinam & religionem excogitauit. Itaque annis ante natum in carne Dei filium circiter centum & triginta, sub Ioanne Hircano Simonis F. sectæ tres emerserunt & confirmatæ sunt, quæ vt sententijs ita vestitu quoque & certis ritibus inter se discernebantur. Inter hos primatum facile cenebant Pharisæi, quos Alexandra Hircani & Aristobuli mater in summam potentiam atque dignitatem euexerat, eò quòd præ aliis scripturarum cognitione & morum integritate atque sanctimonia commendarentur. Nam scripturas sedulò explicabant (unde illos nomen accepisse pleraque existimant) res omnes ad Dei prouidentiam, vel potius ad fatū Stoicum referebant, liberum hominis arbitrium afferebant, in ieiunijs, precibus, eleemosynis frequentes erant, neque à republica abhorrebant, in qua fere honoribus primis potiebantur. Error autem illorum præcipuus et maximè pernitiosus erat, quòd suorum operum meritis & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia elati, gratiam Dei non dignè æstimarent, & ita Dei iustitiam reijcerent, dum suā stabilire conabantur. Proximi ab hīs Sadducæi fuerunt, homines nimium politici, vel etiam Epicurei plane, qui etsi à religione minimè alieni esse vellent, & proinde libros Mosis admitterent, interim præcipua fidei & religionis fundamenta negabant, animarum immortalitatem & corporum resurrectionem. Attamen vt respub. & pax inter homines consisteret, iustitiæ studendum esse docebant, non aliqua futuri præmij spe, sed propter ipsam iustitiam. Fuerunt ergo inter hos & Pharisæos perpetuæ lites, potuerunt tamen postea in Christo oppugnando conuenire, vt suo loco dicetur. His tertij accessere Esseni, qui cum Sadducæorum impia placita merito detestarentur, apud Pharisæos autem plus hypocrisis quàm veræ & solidæ pietatis esse cernerent, ab vtriusque secessione facta, nouum vitæ genus secuti sunt, austerum prorsus, laboriosum, frugale & innocuum. Nam agriculturæ intenti nihil præter victum quærebant minimè sumptuosum, seruos possidere nefas putabant, bona omnia habebant communia, à sacris item publicis abstinebant, ne aliorum contagio polluerentur, aut sceleribus alienis communicarent: similes ferè Anabaptistarum, quos partim propriæ sanctitatis persuasio, partim immodica vulgi licentia ad similem errorem inducit. Erant tamen illi numero paucissimi, neque aliqua erat ipsorum authoritas, quòd eorum opiniones ad reipublicæ euersionem facerent, & cum coniugio proprietatem quoque rerum damnarent. Pharisæi autem & Sadducæi eò progressi erant, vt pauci reperirentur, qui non vel horum vel illorum essent sectatores. Habebant tamen vtrique suos principes & antesignanos, qui reliquis authoritate præstabant. Ex his multos ad Ioannis baptismum venisse dicitur, in quos orationem ille habuit, quam in præsenti Lucas describit. Sunt eius partes quatuor, quas ex ordine insp iciemus.
units.tr: Let us now hear John himself, who delivered the sermon described here, chiefly to the Pharisees and Sadducees, as is gathered from Matthew, who writes thus: "When he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: 'You brood of vipers,' etc." Luke simply mentions the crowd, that is, the mixed people among whom these words were spoken. From this it appears that John did not rebuke these men privately or in secret, but publicly and in the hearing of all. This will be discussed more fully later. Now, since the Pharisees and Sadducees are frequently mentioned in the Evangelists, something must be said about them. These are the names of the sects into which the Jews were divided at that time, in much the same way as we know the Christian people under the papacy was split into various orders of monks. God indeed wished there to be one faith and one religion for all, and therefore he gave common laws to all, which comprise the precepts of faith, of divine worship, and of life and morals, applying equally to everyone. And just as he had given one form of religion, so he willed that there should be one temple, in which alone sacrifices were to be offered, lest they be easily torn into sects or parties. And it is well known that the ancient Jews, although they suffered from many vices, nevertheless carefully kept the external unity of the Church, so that they did not fall into different factions; they who had been enrolled in the one God through circumcision and were bound to observe the same Law. But Satan, the enemy of the unity of the Church, in order to bring about more easily the corruption of all religion and the inventions of human traditions, at last devised sects and factions with variations in doctrine and religion. Thus about one hundred and thirty years before the Son of God was born in the flesh, under John Hyrcanus son of Simon, three sects arose and were established, which were distinguished from one another not only by their opinions but also by their dress and certain rites. Among these the Pharisees easily held the first place. Alexandra, the mother of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, had raised them to the highest power and dignity, because they were commended above others for their knowledge of the Scriptures, their integrity of life and their sanctimony. For they diligently expounded the Scriptures (from which most think they took their name), they referred all things to the providence of God, or rather to the Stoic fate, they asserted the free will of man, they were regular in fasts, prayers and alms, and they did not shrink from public affairs, in which they generally held the highest offices. Their chief and most pernicious error, however, was that, elated by the merits of their works and by confidence in their own righteousness, they did not rightly esteem the grace of God, and so, while they tried to establish their own righteousness, they rejected the righteousness of God. Next to them came the Sadducees, men too much inclined to worldly policy, or indeed plain Epicureans, who, although they wished not to be alien to religion and therefore admitted the books of Moses, nevertheless denied the chief foundations of faith and religion: the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies. Yet, that the commonwealth and peace among men might stand, they taught that justice must be cultivated, not from any hope of a future reward, but for justice's own sake. Therefore there were constant quarrels between these and the Pharisees, yet they were later able to agree in attacking Christ, as will be said in its place. To these three there was added the Essenes, who, while they rightly detested the impious opinions of the Sadducees, and saw among the Pharisees more hypocrisy than true and solid piety, withdrew from both and followed a new way of life, utterly austere, laborious, frugal and harmless. For devoted to agriculture, they sought nothing beyond a very modest sustenance; they thought it wrong to own slaves; they held all goods in common; likewise they abstained from public sacrifices, lest they be polluted by the contagion of others or share in the crimes of others. They were much like the Anabaptists, whom partly the persuasion of their own holiness and partly an immoderate license of the common people led into a similar error. Yet they were very few in number, and they had no authority, since their opinions did not tend to the overthrow of the commonwealth, and they condemned private property along with marriage. But the Pharisees and Sadducees had advanced to such a point that few could be found who were not followers of one or the other. Nevertheless, each had its leaders and forerunners, who excelled the rest in authority. It is said that many of these came to John's baptism, and it was to them that he gave the address which Luke describes in the present passage. Its parts are four, which we shall examine in order.

units.la: Prima hypocrisim & simulatū pietatis aut resipiscentiæ studium arguit, quo se venditabant, & verbis omnino gravibus vtitur: Progenies viperarum (inquit) quis præmonstrauit vobis, vt fugeretis à futura ira? Progeniem viperarum eos dicit, vt totum illorum ordinem comprehendat, & hunc iam inde ab ipsa origine & progenitoribus ipsorum corruptum esse ostendat. Perinde ergo hoc est, ac si malorum coruorum (quod proverbio dicitur) mala ova, aut malorum parentum pessimos filios dixisset: Imò quia viperarum meminit, non obscurè diaboli filios esse innuit, quem scripturæ verem serpentem vocant. Per iram verò venturam excidium vrbis & gentis repudium intelligit, cuius illi præcipui erant authores, et quod ipsis imminere nō poterat ignorare. Nam vt infinita alia prophetarum vaticinia taceamus, Malachias, cùm de Christi in carnem aduentu deq; eius anteam bulone, Ioanne Baptista, verba faceret, inter alia illu seueri iudicis instar fore dixerat, qui ordinem sacerdotalem reformaturus & infidos omnes pro meritis sit punituros. Ecce venit (ait) Dominus exercituum. Quis diem aduentus eius sustinebit? aut quis, cùm apparuerit, consistet? Est enim veluti ignis excoquens, & vt Borit siue saponaria aut radicula fullonum. Et sedebit excoquens & repurgans argentum, & filios Leui emundabit, &c. Et paulò post ipse Dominus ait: Et appropinquabo vobis ad iudicium, eroq; testis festinus cōtra præstigiatores, contra adulteros et falso iurantes, &c. Hæc igitur & multa alia huius generis, cùm non nesciret Ioannes, & insuper per spiritum sanctum de futura populi totius calamitate admoneretur, hanc illis ob oculos statuit, & contumaciam exprobrat, quam externo resipiscentiæ simulatæ fuco tegere conabantur. Itaque verborum sensus est: Mirum equidem videri poterat, vos huc venire, & quam ab omnibus requiro resipiscentiam profiteri. Sed vrget vos scelerum conscientia, & inuiti licet sentitis imminere iam publicum illud & à prophetis olim denuntiatum excidium, cuius vos præcipui estis authores, qui & populum Dei in partes scidistis, & Legis diuinæ doctrinam corrupistis, & cultum omnem prophanastis. Ideo ne officio deesse videamini adestis, & pœnitentiæ seu resipiscentiæ studium simulatis. Itáne verò im pudentes estis, ô infelix viperæ antiquæ progenies, vt qui populum hucusque seduxistis, nunc ipsum Deum fuco vestro falli posse putetis, vt propter hunc iram suam restinguat, & iamiá imminens vobis exitium auertat? Multū certè fallimini, et vosipsos miserè perditis, dum hac ratione vobis consuli posse putatis. Nec enim externis lauris capitur, qui in spiritu & veritate coli vult: neque fuco aut splendore fallitur, qui corda & renes scrutari solet, et quem ne cogitationes quidem hominum latere possunt. Aliaigitur via vobis ingrediendum erit, & longè alijs studijs opus est, si iram Dei & paratas vobis pœnas velitis effugere, &c.
units.tr: The first point exposes their hypocrisy and the pretended zeal for repentance by which they displayed themselves, and he uses very severe words: "You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?" He calls them a brood of vipers to take in the whole of their order and to show that it has been corrupted from its very origin and from its forefathers. It is as if he had said they were the bad eggs of evil crows (as the proverb goes), or the worst sons of wicked parents. Indeed, by mentioning vipers he plainly hints that they are sons of the devil, whom the Scriptures call the old serpent. By the wrath to come he means the destruction of the city and the rejection of the nation, of which they were the chief authors, and which they could not have failed to see was hanging over them. To pass over the countless other prophecies, Malachi, speaking of Christ's coming in the flesh and of his forerunner John the Baptist, had said among other things that he would be like a stern judge, who would reform the priestly order and punish all the faithless according to their deserts: "Behold, the Lord of hosts comes. Who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fuller's soap. He will sit refining and purifying the silver, and he will cleanse the sons of Levi," and so on. And a little later the Lord himself says: "I will draw near to you for judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, against adulterers and against those who swear falsely," and so on. Since John did not ignore these and many other things of this kind, and since he was moreover warned by the Holy Spirit of the coming calamity of the whole people, he set these before their eyes and rebuked their stubbornness, which they tried to cover with the outward varnish of a feigned repentance. So the sense of his words is this: "It might well seem strange that you come here and profess the repentance that I require of everyone. But the consciousness of your crimes presses upon you, and although you are unwilling, you feel that the public destruction, long ago announced by the prophets, is now hanging over you, and you are its chief authors. You have divided the people of God, you have corrupted the doctrine of the divine law, and you have profaned all worship. So, lest you seem to be wanting in duty, you come here and pretend a zeal for penitence or repentance. Are you really so shameless, O unhappy offspring of the ancient viper, that you who have led the people astray up to now think that God himself can be deceived by your pretence, so that for your sake he will quench his wrath and turn away the destruction now hanging over you? You are gravely mistaken, and you ruin yourselves miserably while you think that you can be helped in this way. For he who wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth is not caught by external display, nor is he deceived by a mask or show, he who is accustomed to search the heart and the reins and whom even the thoughts of men cannot escape. Therefore you must take another path, and you need quite different pursuits, if you wish to escape the wrath of God and the punishments prepared for you," and so on.

units.la: Hæc omnia, & quæcunq, huius generis in hac sententiam dici possunt, Ioannes paucis hisce verbis comprehendit. Vbi obseruatu dignum est, quòd tam duriter eos tractat, penes quos præcipua erat in rebus sacris authoritas, & qui supremam sanctitatis existimationem sustinebant. Non ma ledices (inquit Lex) principi populi tui. Cur ergo Ioannes istos viperarum progeniem vocat, qui & propria dignitate pollebant, & ab Hierosolymitano Senatu & toto Sacerdotum ordine ad ipsum missi venerant, sicuti in Euangelio Ioannis scribitur? Annon nimius est, & conuitiator dici merè tur? Nequaquam. Imò officium facit, & vt ita fieret opus erat. Nam primò ita in suorum operum fiducia hypocritæ obstupescunt, vt nisi durius tractentur, nunquâ de se dici intelligant. Deinde cùm proditorio animo venirent, & sub respiscentiæ prætextu insidias ipsi struerent (quod proprium & germanum diaboli opus est) omnino sic tractari merebantur. Adhæc cur illis parceretur, qui cùm malorum omnium essent authores, effræni tamè licentia perrumpere conabantur? Requirebat certè hoc publica totius populi salus, vt illorum artes & corruptissimi mores omnibus innotescerent, quò facilius cauerì possent, & vt reliqui omnes seriò Dei timore perculsi curarent, ne simili hypocrisi ille porrò offenderetur. Minimè ergo conuitiator dici debet Ioannes, cùm suo erga Deum & populum, imò erga hos ipsos officio fortiter defunctus sit. Et quod illi licuit, hoc ipsum omnibus verbi administris licet, vt liberius accusent personatos antistites, quicunque horum similes non solùm ipsi officium suum negligunt, verùm etiam alijs peccandi authores sunt. Fecerunt hoc olim prophetæ, quorum fidem & constantiam spiritus sanctus hoc potissimum nomine commendat. Idem Christum quoque fecisse constat, qui cùm apud Matthæum Scribis & Pharisæis maiorum scelera & indignas prophetarum cædes exprobrauisset, tandem ijsdem omnino verbis infert: Serpentes, progenies viperarum, quomodo fugere possitis à iudicio gehennæ? Et apostolos eadem dicendi libertate spiritus armauit, vt ijsdem in faciem obiecerint quæcunq; aduersus Christum & eius doctrinam designarent. Docent ista quid hodie nobis faciendum sit, quibus cum Papa et eius clero negotium est, qui suis articulis ecclesiam totumque orbem Christianum similiter in partes sciderunt, et hisce Iudæorum Scribis & Pharisæis multo sunt deteriores. Hi enim etsi correptionem non reciperent ex animo, simulabat tamen respiscentiæ studium, neque vim faciebant Ioanni, cùm ab eo tam duriter tractarentur. At nostri illi palàm aduersus Christum insurgunt, & omnia hostiliter faciunt, vt non tam serpentes & viperæ, quàm lupi & leones dici debeant, qui seipsos iam pridem ad ecclesiæ totius exitium devouerunt. Attollant ergo contra illos vocem suam ministri, artes eorum arguant, increpent, accusent, & Dei iudicium illis intonent, vt etsi incurabiles ipsi maneant, alij tamen comminationibus hisce terrifici, eò diligentius sibi ab illorum doctrina & exemplo caveant.
units.tr: John sums up all these things, and whatever of this kind can be said to this effect, in these few words. Here it is worth noting how harshly he treats those who held the chief authority in sacred matters and enjoyed the highest reputation for holiness. "You shall not revile the ruler of your people," says the Law. Why, then, does John call a brood of vipers those who were eminent in their own dignity, and who had come to him sent by the Jerusalem senate and the whole order of priests, as is written in the Gospel of John? Is he not excessive, and would he not rightly be called a reviler? By no means. He is doing his duty, and it had to be done in this way. For first, hypocrites are so stupefied by their confidence in their own works that unless they are handled more sharply they never understand that the words are said about them. Next, since they came with a treacherous mind and under the pretext of repentance laid snares for him (which is the proper and genuine work of the devil), they fully deserved to be treated in this way. Moreover, why should they be spared, when they were the authors of all evils and tried to break out with unbridled licence? Surely the public safety of the whole people required that their tricks and most corrupt morals be made known to all, so that they could more easily be guarded against, and so that all the rest, struck with a serious fear of God, might take care not to be offended again by such hypocrisy. John, therefore, ought by no means to be called a reviler, since he discharged his duty bravely towards God and the people, indeed towards these very men themselves. And what was permitted to him is permitted to all the ministers of the Word, so that they may more freely accuse the masked bishops, whoever are like them, who not only neglect their own office but are also authors of sin for others. The prophets did this long ago, and the Holy Spirit especially commends their faith and constancy for this very reason. It is well known that Christ also did the same, who, when in Matthew he had rebuked the Scribes and Pharisees for the crimes of their forefathers and the unworthy murders of the prophets, at last concludes with exactly these words: "Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of hell?" And he armed the apostles with the same freedom of speech, so that they flung in the faces of these men whatever they had planned against Christ and his doctrine. These things teach what we must do today, since we have to deal with the Pope and his clergy, who by their articles have likewise torn the Church and the whole Christian world into parties, and are far worse than these Jewish Scribes and Pharisees. For although these men did not receive the correction from the heart, they nevertheless pretended a zeal for repentance, and they did not resist John, though he treated them so harshly. But those men of ours openly rise up against Christ and do everything in a hostile manner, so that they ought to be called not so much serpents and vipers as wolves and lions, who long ago devoted themselves to the destruction of the whole Church. Let the ministers, therefore, raise their voice against them, expose their arts, rebuke, accuse them, and thunder the judgment of God upon them, so that, even if they themselves remain incurable, others, terrified by these threats, may take greater care to guard themselves against their doctrine and example.

units.la: Cæterùm increpationi doctrinam subijcit Ioannes, quæ altera huius concionis pars est, quà vera effugij viam tradit, dicens: Ferte igitur fructus, qui respiscentiam deceant. Opponit hoc moribus eorum, qui pietatem omnem (vt diximus) in externis consistere arbitrabantur: si nimirum ieiunarent, sacra obirent, eleemosynas cum ostentatione facerent, aut preculas demurmurarent in publico. Nam his studijs illos in primis addictos fuisse, Christus non vno loco testatur. Ostendit ergo longè aliud ab ipsis requiri, nimirum interiorem totius hominis innouationem, quæ sese dignis fructibus in tota vitæ consuetudine exerat. Est autem hæc doctrina totius scripturæ, circa quam omnes prophetas, adhæc ipsum Christum & apostolos in primis laborauisse constat. Etenim cùm peccando à Deo recedamus, quæ omnium malorum unica causa est, saluti nostræ è contra non aliter consuli poterit, quàm si ad Deum reuersi cum eo reconciliemur. Ideo pœnitentiam rectè definiunt plerique, esse conuersionem ad Deum, quæ non aliter quàm animo fieri potest vera fide instructo. Vnde constat, vehementer falli eos, qui pœnitentiam actuari vel ad Diuos conuertuntur, vel ad cerimonias & frigida quædam superstitionum exercitia, quibus neque Deus coli potest, neque homo melior redditur. Discant ergo illi, respiscentiam in eo consistere, vt primùm quidem se peccatores & modis omnibus corruptos esse sentiant, idque apud Deum priuatim atque publicè fateantur: deinde verò ad thronum gratiæ confugiant per fidem in Iesum Christum, qui nobis à patre iustitia & satisfactio datus est, quiqué suos ex verbi semine per spiritus virtutem regenerat, vt totis animis innotentur. Qui ita respiscunt, ij respiscentiam hanc fructibus dignis testari solent. Inter quos primus est seria & assidua Dei inuocatio, quam proprium verae fidei exercitium esse scriptura docet. Sequitur hanc mortificatio carnis & sanctitatis aut innocentiæ studium, quibus non possunt non studere, quicunque in Dei conspectum venire cupiunt, & eius gratia sibi opus esse sentiunt. Coniuncta his est dilectio proximi, quæ beneficentiam parit, & ab omni maleficio abstrahit. Et quia haec omnia ex vera conversione ad Deum oriuntur, fieri nequit, quin in his omnibus Dei gloriam quaerant, quicunque vere & ex animo resipiscunt. Haec igitur resipiscentia illa est, quam in praesenti Ioannes praecipit, & quae nobis hodie in primis necessaria est, cum irae Dei indicia passim in oculos nostros incurrant. At plerique hominum vel fucatam poenitentiam agunt, qualem in Pharisaeis Ioannes hic accusat, vel momentaneam, quae ut primum periculi metus evanuit, in maiorem licentiam erumpit: qualis fuit, quam apud Hoseam Deus in Israelitis reprehendit. Quid ergo poenas diuturniores miramur, quando nec hus quidem contumacia nostra domari aut corrigi potest?
units.tr: Moreover, John adds to the rebuke the teaching, which is the second part of this sermon, in which he shows the true way of escape, saying: "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." He sets this against the conduct of those who, as we have said, thought that all piety consisted in outward things: that is, if they fasted, performed sacred duties, gave alms with ostentation, or muttered prayers in public. For Christ testifies in more than one place that they were especially devoted to these practices. He shows, therefore, that something quite different is required of them, namely the inward renewal of the whole man, which displays itself in worthy fruits throughout the whole course of life. This doctrine, moreover, is the substance of all Scripture, and it is well known that the prophets, and Christ himself and the apostles especially, laboured over it. For since we turn away from God by sinning, which is the sole cause of all evils, on the other hand our salvation can be secured only if we turn back to God and are reconciled to him. Therefore most people rightly define repentance as conversion to God, which cannot take place except in a mind furnished with true faith. From this it is clear how greatly they are mistaken who think that repentance is carried out either by turning to the saints or to ceremonies and certain cold exercises of superstition, by which neither God can be worshipped nor man made better. Let them learn, then, that repentance consists in this: first, that they feel themselves to be sinners and corrupted in every way, and that they confess this before God both privately and publicly; then that they flee to the throne of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, who has been given to us by the Father as righteousness and satisfaction, and who regenerates his own from the seed of the Word by the power of the Spirit, so that they may be renewed with their whole souls. Those who repent in this way are accustomed to bear witness to their repentance by worthy fruits. Among these the first is earnest and constant calling upon God, which Scripture teaches is the proper exercise of true faith. Following this come the mortification of the flesh and zeal for holiness or innocence, which all must pursue who wish to come into God's sight and feel that they need his grace. Joined to these is love of neighbour, which produces beneficence and turns us away from every wrong. And since all these things arise from true conversion to God, it cannot be that all who repent truly and from the heart do not seek God's glory in all of them. This, then, is that repentance which John now commands, and which is especially necessary for us today, since the signs of God's wrath meet our eyes everywhere. But most people either perform a feigned repentance, such as John here accuses in the Pharisees, or a momentary one, which, as soon as the fear of danger has vanished, breaks out into greater licence; such as that which God rebukes in the Israelites through Hosea. Why, then, do we wonder at longer punishments, when not even these have been able to tame or correct our stubbornness?

units.la: Porro nō ignorabat Ioannes quidistos maxime remorabatur, quō minus resipiscerent: nimirum generis fiducia, quōd se Abrahami filios esse gloriarentur, ad quos foedus salutis proprie pertineret. Fuit enim hic communis Iudaeorum error, qui eō usque apud plerosque progrediebatur, ut Deum ipsis ita obstrictum putarent, ut illis reiectis aut perditis neque Dei veritate neque ecclesiam consistere posse arbitrarentur. Oriebatur ille ex perperam intellectu Dei promissionibus, & quod nescirent qui nam apud Deum germani filij Abrahami censeantur. Eō autem magis ista fiducia Scribae & Pharisaei inflabantur, quōd ecclesiae titulum ipsi ad se transtulissent, & proinde se salvos fore sibi persuaderent, etiamsi totum reliquum vulgus execrabile esset, sicuti Ioannis septimo cap. loquuntur. Hanc ergo securitatem graviter Baptista reprehendit (quae tertia huius concionis pars est) & sic ait: Et ne coeperitis dicere apud vosipsos, Patrem habemus Abrahamum, &c. Ita vero in animos eorum penetrat & confidentem cordis cogitationem eruit. Ea enim est hypocritarum confidentia, ut non solum apud homines disertis verbis sese venditent, verum etiam intra animos suos in ipsius Dei conspectu superbiant, & hunc sibi debitorem facere conentur. Sed procul (inquit) e cordibus vestris stulta haec fiducia eliminetur: imo ne in mentem quidem vobis veniat, vos Abrahami filios esse, cum iampridem ab eo degeneraveritis, quod Deus ille non ignorat, qui nullo fuco externo fallitur. Ita fere ipse Christus verba ista exponit, apud Ioannem octavo cap. illis dicens: Si filij Abrahami essetis, opera Abrahami faceretis: Nunc autem quaeritis me interficere, hominem qui veritatem vobis locutus sum, quam audivi a Deo: hoc Abraham non fecit. Vos facitis opera patris vestri, &c. Ne autem in praesenti oggannirent, Ergo ne nulli posthac erunt liberi Abrahamo? Ubi ergo promissionis divinae fides, quae Abrahami semen stellas caeli & arenam maris multitudine superaturam esse testatur? per Antypophoram Ioannes illos praevenit, dicens: Dico enim vobis, posse Deo etiam ex lapidibus istis excitare filios Abrahamo. Quasi dicat: Minime apud vos astricta est Dei promissio, neque periclitabitur eius veritas, etiamsi vos ut digni estis male pereatis. Qui enim olim ex sterili Sara et effacto Abrahami corpore novam prolem educere potuit, quae in multitudinem innumerabilem excrevit, idem etiam nunc si opus sit, vel ex lapidibus istis Abrahamo excitabit filios germanos, qui promissionum omnium haeredes sint. Quod autem dicit Ioannes, id tam in Iudaeis quam gentibus verissime impletum esse constat. Inter illos enim reiectis Pharisaeis propriae sanctitatis fiducia & ecclesiae titulo turgentibus, ex vulgo vocati & veri filij Abrahami facti sunt, qui paulo ante vix abiectissimorum lapidum loco habebantur. Inter gentes vero, qui prius idola lignea & lapidea colentes horum similes erant (ut in Psalmo dicitur) ij per fidem emolliti, imo in vivos lapides mutati sunt, ex quibus super fundamentum Christum ecclesia aedificata in immensum creuit. Debet autem ex istorum exemplo generalis doctrina peti, inanē & inutilem esse in aeternae salutis negotio fiduciam omnē, quae vel in generis praerogativa, vel in maiorum aut quorumcunque aliorum virtute sive iustitia collocatur. Nam ut in Euangelio Ioan. scribitur, filij Dei non ex carne, neque ex hominis voluntate nascuntur. Imo quoad carnis generationem, omnes in peccato concipimur & nascimur, & ut salvi fiamus, regeneratione opus est, quae nobis in uno Christo obtingit. Qui enim hunc recipiunt, iis dignitas ista conceditur, ut filij Dei sint, renati nimirum ex aeterni & immortalis verbi semine. Haec ergo unica & vera generis nobilitas est, quam neque vitae genus ullum, modo per se honestum sit, neque egestas, neque morbus, neque mundi huius infamia, nulla denique alia calamitas impedit. Quoad vero aliorum iustitiam, nihil illa ad nos: quin potius maiorum exemplo damnantur, quicunque ab illis turpiter degenerant. Solius Christi haec gloria est, quod suam iustitiam nobis communicat & eos ab omni damnatione eximit, qui ipsi per fidem inseruntur. Ita subinde ad hunc redit tota salutis nostrae ratio, quam nunquam assequentur, quicunque ab illo alieni sunt. Debet autem hoc ipsum ad eos etiam extendi, qui quoad huius seculi felicitatem maiorum nobilitate & virtute gloriantur, & propter hanc in pretio haberi volunt, cùm ipsi vitijs obruti sint, neque digni qui tantorum virorum posteri censeantur.
units.tr: Yet John did not fail to see what chiefly held these people back from repentance: namely, their confidence in their descent, because they boasted that they were sons of Abraham, to whom the covenant of salvation properly belonged. This was a common error among the Jews, and among many it went so far that they thought God was so bound to them that, if they were rejected or destroyed, neither God's truth nor the Church could continue to exist. It arose from a wrong understanding of God's promises, and from not knowing who are regarded before God as the true sons of Abraham. The Scribes and Pharisees were puffed up with this confidence all the more because they had transferred the title of the Church to themselves and so persuaded themselves that they would be saved, even if all the rest of the common people were accursed, as is said in the seventh chapter of John. The Baptist therefore sharply rebukes this complacency (which is the third part of this sermon) and says: "And do not begin to say among yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father,' etc." He penetrates their minds in this way and draws out the confident thought of their heart. For such is the confidence of hypocrites that they not only boast of themselves in plain words before other people, but also within their own minds they take pride in the very sight of God, and try to make him their debtor. "But," he says, "let this foolish confidence be cast far out of your hearts. Indeed, let it not even come into your minds that you are the sons of Abraham, since you have long since degenerated from him; God, who is not deceived by any outward disguise, does not fail to know this." Christ himself explains these words in much the same way, in John chapter eight, saying to them: "If you were the children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God; Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father," etc. Lest they should now murmur, "Then will there be no children of Abraham from now on?", where is the faith in the divine promise, which testifies that Abraham's seed will surpass the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea in multitude? John forestalls them by way of an anticipated objection, saying: "For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham." As if he were saying: "The promise of God is by no means bound to you, and its truth will not be endangered even if you perish, as you deserve. For he who long ago was able to bring forth a new offspring from barren Sarah and from the dead body of Abraham, which grew into an innumerable multitude, is able even now, if there is need, to raise up from these stones true children for Abraham, who will be heirs of all the promises." What John says has been most truly fulfilled among both the Jews and the Gentiles, as is plain. For among the Jews, when the Pharisees, who were puffed up with confidence in their own holiness and with the title of the Church, were rejected, true children of Abraham were called from the common people and made sons, people who shortly before had scarcely been regarded as the most despised stones. Among the Gentiles, those who formerly worshipped wooden and stone idols and were like them (as the Psalm says) were softened by faith, and indeed were changed into living stones, out of which the Church is built upon the foundation of Christ and has grown immensely. From the example of these people a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that all confidence which is placed either in the prerogative of birth, or in the virtue or righteousness of ancestors or of anyone else, is empty and useless in the business of eternal salvation. For, as is written in the Gospel of John, the children of God are born not of flesh, nor of the will of man. Indeed, as regards natural generation, we are all conceived and born in sin, and for our salvation we need regeneration, which comes to us in Christ alone. For those who receive him are granted this dignity, that they should be sons of God, namely reborn from the seed of the eternal and immortal Word. This, then, is the one and true nobility of birth, which is hindered neither by any manner of life that is honourable in itself, nor by poverty, nor by sickness, nor by the disgrace of this world, nor finally by any other calamity. As for the righteousness of others, it has nothing to do with us; rather, by the example of their ancestors, those who shamefully degenerate from them are condemned. This glory belongs to Christ alone, that he communicates his righteousness to us and frees from all condemnation those who are grafted into him through faith. And so the whole reckoning of our salvation returns again and again to him, and those who are alienated from him will never attain it. This must also be extended to those who boast of the nobility and virtue of their ancestors, in regard to the happiness of this age, and want to be held in esteem on account of it, when they themselves are overwhelmed with vices and are not worthy to be counted the descendants of such great men.

units.la: Sed ad Ioannem redeamus, qui cùm sciret verbus nihil profici apud hypocritas, postrema parte grauem poenae iam imminentis comminationem subijcit. Iam verò et securis (inquit) ad radicem arborum posita est. Omnis ergo arbor non ferens fructū bonum exciditur, & in ignem abijcitur. Argumentum ab agricultura sumitur eiusmodi: Quemadmodum agricolae arbores inutiles & steriles excindere solent, ne terram frustra occupent: ita Deus homines, qui nullum respiscentiae verae fructum edunt, perdere & ab ecclesiae suae consortio eijcere consueuit. At vos arbores estis steriles, imò ad fructus pessimos & Deo exosos nimium fecundae. Ergo excidemini, ne locum in ecclesia amplius occupetis. Ita verò haec proponit Ioannes, ut singula verba emphasim habeant. Nam primò securim dicit, non virgam aut baculum, quibus leviores poenae denotari solent. Deinde posita est, inquit, non ponetur: ut ijs occurrat, qui ex dilatione poenarum sibi perpetuam impunitatem pollicentur. Tertiò non ad ramos aut truncum arboris, sed ad radicem ait securim positam esse, ut excidium extremum et irreparabile exprimat. Tandem in ignem abijciendos dicit, quo aeternae damnationis supplicium significatur. Perinde ergo hoc est, ac si dixisset: Saepe quidem maiores vestros & vos puniuit Deus, quando Iudicum tempore diversis gentibus vexandos praebuit, quando item Assyrios & Babylonios illis induxit. Multa etiam post reditum ex Babylone acciderunt, quibus illorum contumaciam castigauit. Quin vosipsi multa passi estis hucusque, quando Hircani & Aristobuli fratrum ambitio bella civilia excitaurt, quorum hic finis fuit, ut Romanorum armis subacti nunc sub alienis dominis seruitutem feratis grauissimam. Sed leuia sunt ista omnia, si cum ijs, quae mox passuri estis, conferantur. Hactenus enim ramos solos flagellauit Deus, & interdum aliquos decussit. At nunc de summa rerum agetur, & securim id est, iudicium atrocissimum in vos stringet, quo non solùm respublica vestra destruatur, sed vos simul omnes amisso populi Dei & ecclesiae titulo in totum orbem terrarum dispergamini, & post hanc vitam omnibus modis miseram et calamitosam aeternas gehennae flammas subeatis. Et haec quidem non multò post euenerunt. Nam cùm post indignam filij Dei mortem aduersus apostolos quoque & Euangelij doctrinam hostiliter insurgerent, & insuper aduersus Romanos praesides seditiose tumultuarentur, bellum exortum est, quo vrbs cum templo perijt, infelices autem populi reliquiae in omnes gentes dispersae sunt, and illis in hunc vsque diem iustae irae & vindictae indicia videre licet: & cùm a Christo simul & ecclesiae eius societate auulsi sint, non aliud eos manet post huius vitae curriculum, quàm ut in ignem aeternum abijciantur, sicuti de palmitibus a vite resectis Christus loquitur.
units.tr: But let us return to John, who, since he knew that words accomplish nothing with hypocrites, subjoins at the end a grave threat of the punishment now about to fall. "Now indeed," he says, "the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire." The argument is drawn from farming, in this way: just as farmers are accustomed to cut down useless and barren trees, lest they occupy the ground to no purpose, so God is accustomed to destroy men who produce no true fruit of repentance and to cast them out from the fellowship of his Church. But you are barren trees, indeed far too fruitful in the worst fruits, which are hateful to God. Therefore you will be cut down, lest you occupy any longer a place in the Church. John presents this in such a way that each word carries emphasis. First, he speaks of an axe, not a rod or a staff, by which lighter punishments are usually signified. Next, it is said to be "laid" and "will not be laid," to meet those who promise themselves perpetual impunity from the delay of punishments. Thirdly, he says the axe is laid not to the branches or the trunk of the tree, but to the root, to express final and irreparable destruction. Finally, he says they are to be cast into the fire, by which the punishment of eternal damnation is signified. The meaning is therefore the same as if he had said: "Indeed, God has often punished your forefathers and you as well: when in the time of the Judges he delivered them to be harassed by various nations, and likewise when he brought the Assyrians and Babylonians upon them. Many things also happened after the return from Babylon, by which he chastised their stubbornness. Indeed you yourselves have suffered many things until now, when the ambition of the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus stirred up civil wars, the end of which was that, subdued by the arms of the Romans, you now endure a most grievous slavery under foreign masters. But all these things are slight if they are compared with those things which you are about to suffer. For hitherto God has only lashed the branches, and at times struck some of them off. But now the matter will be decided, and he will strike at you with the axe, that is, the most dreadful judgment, by which not only your commonwealth will be destroyed, but you yourselves, having lost the title of the people of God and of the Church, will be scattered throughout the whole world, and after this life, wretched and calamitous in every way, you will undergo the eternal flames of hell." And indeed these things came to pass not long after. For when, after the unworthy death of the Son of God, they raged in hostility against the apostles also and against the doctrine of the Gospel, and moreover rose up in sedition against the Roman governors, war broke out, in which the city perished together with the temple, and the unhappy remnant of the people was scattered among all nations; and to this day one may see the signs of God's just wrath and vengeance upon them. And since they have been torn away both from Christ and from fellowship with his Church, nothing else awaits them after the course of this life than to be cast into eternal fire, just as Christ speaks of branches cut off from the vine.

units.la: In his autem nos meminisse oportet, Iudaeorum exemplo admonitionem generalem cötineri, quae omnium seculorum institutioni seruiat. Quoties enim Deus gratiae suae thesauros in Christo aperit per Euangelij praedicationem, tunc simul iudicij quoque sui rigorem profert aduersus contumaces gratiae oblatae contemptores. Etenim meretur horum ingratitudo & impietas, ut grauius puniantur, qui non contenti peccauisse, insuper aduersus Dei bonitatem et salutis doctrinam sese violenter attollunt. Tunc autem duo fere fieri consueuerunt. Primum, excinduntur a radice illa sancta, ne porrò Abrahami filij & ecclesiae membra sint. Quia ferre non poteest, ut qui nomen suum impie polluunt atque prophanant, locum in ecclesia occupent cum publica nominis Christiani contumelia. Deinde ijdem in ignem quoque abijciuntur, quia non alius eorum vsus est, qui a Christo alieni facti sunt, quàm ut aeternum ardeant, & iusti iudicis seueritatem sentiant, qui clementiam eius agnoscere noluerunt. Sunt haec omnium seculorum exemplis confirmata, quae euidenter docent, Deum quoties per verbum suum homines ad respiscentiam vocat, simul securim ad arborum radices ponere, neque procul ab excidio abesse eos, qui gratiae praedicatione contumaciter reijciunt. Sic ante diluuium, sic in Sodomis, sic in Aegypto olim factum fuisse scimus. Et nimis tristia sunt, quae in Orientalibus & Graecis ecclesijs extant exempla, quas omnes funditus extirpatas esse videmus, & dirae Mahumeticorum tyrannidi iam subesse eas gentes, inter quas olim Apostolorum voces sonuerunt, & clarissima ecclesiae lumina fulserunt. Et quid nos sperare debeamus, ex infelicibus praeludijs facilè intelligunt, qui non cum pietate rationem quoque & sensum omnem amiserunt. Ardet certè ignis diuinæ vindictæ passim, & securim suam extenso brachio librat Deus, neque diutius differet pœnæ iampridem meritæ executionem, nisi fructus feramus nostra professione dignos. Singuli ergo sibi dictum meminerint, quod Iudæis dixit Ioannes, & depositâ studiorum suorum malitia ad Deum totis animis conuertantur per fidem in Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In this, moreover, we ought to remember that the Jews' example contains a general warning that serves the instruction of all ages. For whenever God opens the treasures of his grace in Christ through the preaching of the gospel, he at the same time displays the severity of his judgement against those who scorn the grace offered. Indeed, the ingratitude and impiety of these people deserve to be punished more severely, since, not content with having sinned, they violently rise up against God's goodness and the doctrine of salvation. Two things usually happen then. First, they are cut off from that holy root, so that they are no longer children of Abraham or members of the Church. For it cannot bear that those who impiously defile and profane their name should occupy a place in the Church to the public disgrace of the Christian name. Second, they are also cast into the fire, because those who have been made strangers to Christ have no other fate than to burn for ever and to feel the severity of the just judge, since they refused to acknowledge his mercy. These things are confirmed by the examples of all ages, which clearly teach that whenever God calls men to repentance through his word, he at the same time lays the axe to the roots of the trees, and that those who stubbornly reject the preaching of grace are not far from destruction. So we know it was done before the flood, so in Sodom, so long ago in Egypt. And the examples that remain in the Eastern and Greek churches are all too sad. We see that all of them have been utterly uprooted, and that those nations, among which the voices of the Apostles once resounded and the most brilliant lights of the Church once shone, now lie under the dreadful tyranny of the Mohammedans. And what we ought to hope for, those who have lost not only piety but also all reason and sense can easily understand from these unhappy foretastes. Surely the fire of divine vengeance blazes everywhere, and God brandishes his axe with outstretched arm, and he will not delay for long the carrying out of the punishment long since deserved, unless we bear fruit worthy of our profession. Let each one therefore remember the saying that John spoke to the Jews, and, having laid aside the malice of their studies, let them turn to God with their whole souls through faith in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIX.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXIX.

units.la: Tunc interrogauit eum turba, dicens: Quid igitur faciemus? Respondens autem dixit eis: Qui habet duas tunicas, impertiat non habenti: & qui habet escas, similiter faciat.
units.tr: Then the crowd asked him, saying: "What then shall we do?" And he answered and said to them: "Whoever has two coats, let him share with the one who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise."

units.la: REgnum Dei non in nuda rerum cœlestium cognitione, neque etiam in externa aut quantumuis magnifica fidei in Iesum Christum confessione consistit, sed in eo potissimum, ut huic per fidem insiti vitam nouam & verè Christianam viuamus, & ut singuli suam vocationem sequantur, & pro huius ratione officium faciant. Rectè igitur Ioannes Baptista primo quidem generali doctrina omnes homines excitat, ut per veram resipiscentiam ad Christum excipiendum præparentur: at mox idem ille singulosferè omnis loci & ordinis homines docet, quid vnumquemque in sua functione aut vitæ genere facere deceat. A pharisæis autem & Sadducæis exorsus, penes quos summa erat apud omnes authoritas, grauiter in illis accusauit simulatum sanctimoniæ & resipiscentiæ studium, simul que generis Abrahami fiduciam eripuit, monens, ut ex animo resipiscant, seq; resipuisse dignis fructibus testentur, siquidem capitibus suis imminentem Dei iram effugere velint. Et erant isti durius tractandi, eò quòd multis scandalo essent, & sua doctrina simul atque exemplo infelicem populum in erroribus retinerent. Sequitur secunda concio, qua vulgus hominum instituit, paucis verbis rem maximi momenti comprehendens, quò magis nos animum intendere oportet, ut sub hac breuitate latentem doctrinam rectè intelligamus.
units.tr: The kingdom of God does not consist in a bare knowledge of heavenly things, nor even in an outward confession of faith in Jesus Christ, however splendid that confession may be. It consists chiefly in this: that we who have been grafted into Christ through faith live a new and truly Christian life, that each person follows his own calling, and that he performs his duty according to its demands. John the Baptist therefore rightly, first of all, stirred up all people with a general teaching, so that they might be prepared through true repentance to receive Christ. Soon afterwards, however, he taught almost every person of every place and rank what each ought to do in his own office or way of life. He began with the Pharisees and Sadducees, who held the highest authority among all people. He severely accused them of a feigned zeal for holiness and repentance, and at the same time he stripped them of their confidence in being descendants of Abraham. He warned them to repent from the heart, and to show by worthy fruits that they had repented, if they wished to escape the wrath of God hanging over their heads. These men had to be handled more harshly, because they were a stumbling block to many, and because by their teaching and their example they kept the unhappy people in error. Next follows the second sermon, in which he instructed the common people. In a few words he set out a matter of the greatest importance, and so we ought all the more to attend closely, so that we may rightly understand the teaching hidden beneath this brevity.

units.la: Commodè autem occasio præmittitur, quæ de his rebus concionandi Baptistæ data fuit. Interrogauit enim eum turba, dicens: Quid igitur faciemus? Audierant enim, quàm duriter eos excepisset, qui omnium sanctissimi & optimi videbantur: & quòd secuturis iam posita esset ad radicem arboris, ideoq; toti Iudæorum genti exitium horribile immineret. Et ista quidem Pharisæos & Legisperitos non mouerunt, qui propriæ iustitiæ fiducia inflati, consilium Dei aspernati sunt, ut Christus postea cap. septimo testabitur: maior tamen fuit hominum vulgarium, imò publicanorum & mitium religio vel pietas, qui intra animos suos de publica omnium ordinum corruptione deq; suis viris diligentius cogitare cœperunt, & tam horum quàm pœnæ ad fores excubantis consideratione per culpi consilium sibi dari petunt, quid faciant, & qui nam proprij illi resipiscentiæ fructus sint, quibus exitium illud declinare aut subterfugere possint. Est hoc exemplum perquàm memorabile, quo primum docemur, Dei verbum nunquam absq; omni fructu prædicari. Nam vt apud Isaiam dicitur, pluuiæ aut imbris instar est, qui ersi in scopulis & locis natura sterilibus nihil proficiat, inuenit tamen agros & prata aut hortos, qui si cœlestibus vndis rigentur, fructus vberrimos ferunt. Itaetsi magna & tantùm non vniuersalis sit mundi totius impietas, & plerique doctrinam vel securè contemnant, vel etiam hostiliter aspernentur & reiciant, habet tamen vbiq; locorum suos electos Deus, qui vt gemmæ pretiosæ inter mundi huius lutosas plaudes dispersi, Verbo eius mouentur, seque ipsos huius doctrinæ & institutioni accommodant. Debet hoc verbi administris animos addere, ne omni profectus spe abiecta sua statione temere deserant, si quos initiò præfractiores esse vident. In primis autem hic obseruatu dignum est, quòd ijs auditis, quæ in Pharisæos & Sadducæos dicebantur, ipsi quid sibi faciendum sit quærunt. Solet hoc fieri apud electos, penes quos non simulatum est discendi & resipiscendi studium. Sunt enim frugi filiorum instar, qui si patrem iratum videant, toti commouentur, deq; ira eius placanda cogitant, etiam si ipsi sibi nullius grauioris scelerisi conscij sint. Et vt impij vndiq; occasiones arripiunt, quibus ad maiorè peccandi licentiam abutantur: ita pijs omnia ad resipiscentiam seruiunt, & mox animis percelluntur, si quando Deum sibi aut aliis irasci audiunt.
units.tr: The occasion for John's preaching on these matters is set out fittingly beforehand. The crowd asked him, saying, "What then shall we do?" For they had heard how harshly he had dealt with those who seemed the most holy and upright of all, and that the axe had already been laid to the root of the tree, so that a dreadful destruction hung over the whole Jewish nation. These words did not move the Pharisees and the lawyers, who, puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, rejected the counsel of God, as Christ later testifies in the seventh chapter. Yet the religion and piety of the common people, and even of the tax collectors and the gentler sort, was greater. They began to think more carefully within their own hearts about the general corruption of all orders of society and about their own men, and, considering both this and the punishment standing ready at the gates, they asked for counsel: what they should do, and what the proper fruits of repentance were, by which they might avert or escape that ruin. This is a most memorable example, from which we are first taught that the word of God is never preached without some fruit. For, as is said in Isaiah, it is like the rain, which, falling on rocks and naturally barren places, accomplishes nothing, yet finds fields and meadows or gardens, and when these are watered by heavenly showers, they bear the richest fruit. So although the impiety of the world is great and almost universal, and although most people either carelessly despise the teaching or even hostilely scorn and reject it, God nevertheless has his elect in every place. Like precious gems scattered amid the muddy mire of this world, they are moved by his Word and adapt themselves to this teaching and instruction. This ought to encourage the ministers of the Word, so that they do not rashly abandon their post and lose all hope of progress because they see some who are at first more stubborn. Above all, it is worth noting here that, having heard what was said against the Pharisees and Sadducees, they ask what they themselves should do. This usually happens among the elect, in whom there is no feigned zeal for learning and repenting. For they are like good sons, who, if they see their father angry, are wholly moved and think about how to appease his anger, even though they are not conscious of any serious wrongdoing. And just as the wicked seize every opportunity to abuse them for greater licence in sinning, so all things serve the godly for repentance, and they are at once struck with fear whenever they hear that God or others are angry with them.

units.la: Occasio huius concionis
units.tr: The occasion of this sermon.

units.la: Isa. 55.
units.tr: Isa. 55.

units.la: Admonent autem suo exemplo, quales nos in audiendo Verbo Dei esse conveniat. Primò, quaecunque dicuntur, nobis dici putemus. Etsi enim non ijsdem sceleribus omnes obnoxij simus, omnes tamen natura vitiosi & corrupti sumus, neque ullum tam immane scelus est, quod non in unumquenque cadere possit, si suam manum aut gratiam nobis Deus subducat. Auditis autem correptionibus & communationibus verbi Dei, singuli in seipsos descendant, & latentem in carne sua vitiositatem excutiant, sicque mox sentient ea quoque, ad se omnino pertinere, à quibus ipsi alienissimi videbantur. Sequeturex eo sancta illa animorum consternatio et salutifer terror, qui nos de salutis ratione solicitos reddit, et consilium quaerere cogit, quod secuti imminentia mala effugiamus. Hic autem anxiè cavendum est, ne nostrae rationis figmenta sequamur, sed Dei voluntatem inuestigemus, quae non aliunde, quam ex verbo eius discitur, cuius minus antea territi fuimus. Hac via olim Niniuitae ingressi denuntiatum suae urbi & regno excidium declinaverunt. Hoc ipsum primi Apostolorum auditores Hierosolymae fecerunt, quando Petri graui comminatione audita, totis animis compuncti postularunt sibi salutis consilium dari. Et qui hos imitantur, ij terram illam bonam afferunt, in qua Verbi semen germinat et fructum fert copiosissimum. At quam paucos istorum similes hodie invenias? Praedicatur quidem Dei Verbum, accusantur publica scelera, denuntiatur Dei ira incurabilibus & poenitere nescijs, neque desunt qui ista audiant: sed qui ex illis emendentur, paucos admodum esse videre. Plerique enim exultant, si alios acriter corripi audiunt, & quae dicuntur, nihil ad se pertinere putant: imò quasi audita cantilena aliqua (ut apud Ezechielem ait Dominus) domum redeunt. Alij verò, qui de se dici sentiunt, mox rabie accensi aduersus Verbu & eius ministros iram & odium concipiunt, & ut canes in se proiectos lapides mordicus inuadunt, ita ipsi sacras conciones calumniantur & omni conuitio rum genere laniant. Quò fit, ut maximus eorum numerus sit, qui cùm scelera in publico regnent, & in singulis mundi partibus Dei irati signa manifestissima conspiciantur, eos tamen doctores quaerant, qui blandis sermonibus, & mellitis diuinae gratiae promissis aures omniū demulceant. Multi etiam in ipsum Dei spiritum sibi ius & imperium vendicant, dum Verbi ministros suo officio liberius fungentibus dicendi leges praescribere audent. Inueniunt isti omnes fere sui similes praecones, qui ut pinguiora stipendia obtineant & in pretio habeantur, illorum libidini sese accommodant, et sua illa igna uia primo quidem scelerum licentiam augent, deinde fidis Christi ministrus suam authoritatem minuunt, tandem verò tam sibi ipsis quàm sectatoribus suis exitium accersunt, &c.
units.tr: Their example also teaches us how we ought to be when we hear the Word of God. First, let us think that whatever is said is said to us. For although we are not all liable to the same crimes, we are all naturally vicious and corrupt, and there is no crime so monstrous that it could not fall upon any one of us, if God were to withdraw his hand or his grace from us. When we hear the rebukes and threats of the Word of God, let each of us descend into himself and search out the viciousness hidden in his flesh. Thus we will soon feel that those things also pertain entirely to us, from which we seemed most far removed. From this follows that holy dismay of soul and saving terror, which makes us anxious about the way of salvation and compels us to seek counsel, so that by following it we may escape the evils that threaten. Here, however, we must be most careful not to follow the inventions of our own reason, but to investigate the will of God, which is learned from nowhere else than from his Word, the word by which we were previously less moved to fear. By this way the Ninevites once entered and turned aside the destruction announced to their city and kingdom. The first hearers of the Apostles at Jerusalem did the same, when, having heard Peter's severe warning, they were pierced to the heart with their whole soul and asked that counsel for salvation be given them. Those who imitate them bring forth that good ground in which the seed of the Word sprouts and bears the most abundant fruit. But how few like them can you find today? The Word of God is indeed preached, public crimes are denounced, God's wrath is announced to the incurable and to those who know not how to repent, and there are no lack of those who hear these things. Yet we see very few of those who are amended by them. For most rejoice if they hear others sharply rebuked, and they think that what is said has nothing to do with them; indeed, like someone who hears a song, they go home again (as the Lord says in Ezekiel). Others, however, who feel that these things are said of them, are soon inflamed with rage against the Word and its ministers, and they conceive anger and hatred. Like dogs that bite at stones thrown at them, they slander the sacred sermons and tear them apart with every kind of abuse. The result is that the greatest number of people are those who, while wickedness reigns in public and the signs of God's anger are most plainly seen in every part of the world, nevertheless seek out teachers who soothe the ears of everyone with smooth words and honeyed promises of divine grace. Many even claim for themselves a right and authority over the Spirit of God itself, while they dare to prescribe rules of speaking to the ministers of the Word who discharge their office more freely. Almost all such people find heralds like themselves, who, in order to obtain fatter stipends and to be held in esteem, accommodate themselves to their lust. And so they first increase the licence of sins by flattering these people, then they diminish the authority of the faithful ministers of Christ, and at last they bring ruin upon themselves as well as upon their followers, etc.

units.la: Porrò tempus est, ut ad Ioannis concionem accedamus, cuius argumentum est, quòd misericordiam & beneficentiâ suadet, & ut his fructibus se vere & ex animo respiciisse testentur. De his autem potissimum admonet, non quòd haec potiora aut praestantiora sint fide in Deum & vero eius cultu, qui in spiritu & veritate consistit: sed ut hypocritis occurrat, qui si quando intra animos suos convicti sunt, ad frigidas ceremonias cõfugere solent, & de cultu externo interrogare, quasi ira Dei per illum placari possit. Sic apud Micheam olim quaerebant: Quanam re occurram Domino? Incurvabor ne coram Deo excelso? Num occurrā ei cum holocaustis, vitulis anniculis? Num complacitum est Deo in mille arietibus, aut decies mille torrentibus olei? Num dabo primogenitum meum pro hostia peccati mei, aut fructum ventris mei pro peccato animae meae? Et apud reliquos prophetas frequens est templi, ieiuniorum, sabbatorum, circuncisionis & similium ceremoniarum mentio, ex quibus sibi hypocritae Dei gratiam & impunitatem pollicebantur. Nequae dubium est plerosque istorum, cùm legalia sacra adhuc in usu essent, de his potius, quàm de veris solidae pietatis exercitijs cogitasse. Quod ergo prophetae solent, dum hypocritas ad secundae tabulae praecepta reuocant, & examen vitae eorum diligentius instituunt: hoc ipsum in praesenti Ioannes etiam facit, & ea praesupponens quae ad fidem et Dei cultum proprie spectant, atque omnium consensu praestantissima sunt, docet fidem & pietatem erga Deum non inanibus aut frigidis ceremonijs, sed mutuae charitatis & beneficentiae officijs esse declarandā. Et solent haec ipsa scripturae omnes passim praecipere, & notum est illud Iacobi Apostoli: Religio pura & immaculata apud Deum & Patrem haec est, inuisere orphanos & viduas in afflictione sua, & immaculatum seipsum seruare à mundo. Vbi orphanorum & viduarum nominibus omnes eos comprehendit, qui nostro auxilio siue beneficentia opus habent: altero autem membro vitae innocentiam & non fucatum sanctimoniae studium requirit. Et cum Apostolo Micheas conuenit, qui hypocritis de ratione placandi Dei (ut ante dictum est) interrogantibus respondet. Indet: Indicauit tibi ô homo quid bonum sit: & quid à te requirit Dominus, nisi facere iudicium, diligere beneficentiam, & humiliari vt ambules cum Deo tuo? Nec sine causa fieri putabimus, quòd charitatem & beneficentiam potissimum Deus praecipit. Hac enim coniunctionis nostrae, quae nobis in Christo Iesu per fidem intercedit, & ex qua salus nostra omnis dependet, testera est omnium certissima, ipso Christo teste, qui dicit: Ex hoc cognoscent omnes quòd discipuli mei sitis, si charitatem habueritis alij in alios. Deinde vt Paulus ait, per charitatem mutuam Lex impletur, eo quòd vniuersa se cundae tabulae praecepta sub illa vna comprehendantur. Quibus adde, quòd qui ad huius regulam se se examinant, ij mox vident quantum adhuc ipsis deest, qui se ad metà perfectionis Christianae iam pridem peruenisse putabant. Quae causa est, quòd Christus iuuenem legalis iustitiae fiducia turgentem omnia sua diuendere & in pauperes distribuere iussit: quem hoc mandato accepto Euangelista tristem omnino discessisse scribunt, quòd sentiret, quàm parum hucusque in verae pietatis studio profecisset. Recte ergo hoc ipsum Ioannes quoque in praesenti obseruat apud eos, qui cum toti ex Lege & eius operibus penderent: illius tamen verum sensum non tenebant, & se omni officio defunctos putabant, si in externis sacris frequentes essent.
units.tr: Now it is time to come to John's sermon, whose subject is that he urges mercy and beneficence, and that people should show by these fruits that they have truly and from the heart repented. He admonishes them chiefly about these things, not because they are more important or excellent than faith in God and the true worship of him, which consists in spirit and truth. Rather, he does so to meet the hypocrites, who, when they are convicted in their own hearts, are accustomed to flee to cold ceremonies and to ask about outward worship, as though the wrath of God could be appeased by it. Thus of old in Micah they asked: "With what shall I come before the Lord? Shall I bow myself before the high God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousand rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" And throughout the other prophets there is frequent mention of the temple, of fasts, of sabbaths, of circumcision, and of similar ceremonies, from which the hypocrites promised themselves God's favour and impunity. Nor is there any doubt that most of them, while the legal sacred rites were still in use, thought about these rather than about the true exercises of solid piety. Therefore, what the prophets are accustomed to do, when they call hypocrites back to the precepts of the second table and examine their lives more carefully, this same thing John also does here. Presupposing those things which properly concern faith and the worship of God, and which are by universal agreement the most excellent, he teaches that faith and piety toward God are to be declared not by empty or cold ceremonies, but by the duties of mutual love and beneficence. And all the Scriptures commonly enjoin these very things, and that saying of the Apostle James is well known: "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world." Here, under the names of orphans and widows, he includes all those who need our help or kindness, and in the second part he requires innocence of life and a sincere zeal for holiness, not feigned. And Micah agrees with the Apostle, who, when the hypocrites ask about the way of appeasing God (as was said above), replies: "He has shown you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: only to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God." Nor shall we think it is without cause that God especially commands charity and beneficence. For this is the most certain testimony of that fellowship which we have with Christ Jesus through faith, and on which all our salvation depends, Christ himself bearing witness, who says: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Then, as Paul says, the law is fulfilled by mutual love, because all the precepts of the second table are comprehended under that one. To these add that those who examine themselves by this rule soon see how much they still lack, though they thought they had long since reached the goal of Christian perfection. This is why Christ ordered the young man, swollen with confidence in legal righteousness, to sell all his goods and distribute them to the poor; and the Evangelist writes that he went away altogether sad after receiving this command, because he perceived how little he had so far advanced in the pursuit of true piety. Rightly, then, John also observes this in the present passage, among those who depended wholly on the Law and its works, yet did not hold its true meaning, and thought they had discharged every duty if they were frequent in the outward sacred rites.

units.la: Porrò vt circa opes huius seculi plurimùm vbique peccatur, ita vix aliud argumentum occurrit, de quo citius laboriosius & periculosius sit, quàm de diuitijs & earum vsu, aut diuitum conditio ne. Quaecunque enim hic apud eos dicuntur, qui vera pietate nondum instructi sunt, ea illi semper pro affectuum suorum libidine in sensum alienum detorquere consueuerunt. Diuitcs enim quando diuitiarum possessionem & legitimum earum vsum defendi audiunt, mox confidentiores facti, se illarum dominos esse arbitrantur, et securi nimis omnes alios inhumaniter negligunt, adhaec opibus tuntur ad luxum & libidinem abutuntur. Rursus pauperes, quando diuites ad beneficentiam excitantur, illico hos sibi debitores faciunt, imò in alienas opes sibi ius sumunt & imperium, & vt Minoes & Rhadamanti quidam omnes eos mira confidentia damnant, qui non tantù largiuntur, quantum ipsi postulant. Sunt item qui cum opum administrationem periculi plenam esse videant, salutis iactu ram se factuaros metuunt, nisi omnibus in vniuersum renuntient. Quibus deinde scrupulos plures & molestiores inijciunt fanatici quidam, qui sub religionis praetextu vel communionem rerum omnium Platonicam inducere studeant, & ideo ius proprietatis nimium arroganter damnant: vel voluntariam paupertatem profesi ex alieno viuunt & ditissimi omnium fiunt, adhaec immunitate quadam ab omnibus publicis oneribus fruuntur: vt non inepte in illos dixeris, quod Asaph de impiorum prosperitate pronuntiat: Non sunt illis nexus ad mortem, quin pingues sunt & praevalidi: In labore hominum non sunt, & cum hominibus non flagellantur. Quibus merito adnumeraueris ἀπὸ τῆς illos, de quibus Paulus ad Thessalonicenses disserit, qui quasi falsus omnis in mendicitate consistat, egestatem ipsi sibi accersunt, & omni legum cum politicarum tum ecclesiasticarum disciplina excusata otiosi atque inertes oberrant. Quorum errorum atque vitiorum omnium praecipua causa est, quòd plerique de diuitijs & paupertate perperam iudicant. Meretur ergo haec res diligentem consideratio nem, quam hoc ordine prosequemur, vt primùm de rerum aut bonorum huius seculi proprietate, deinde de eorundem possessione & legitimo vsu dicamus, vbi simul tota beneficentiae Christianae ratio consideranda veniet, vnà cum ijs quae hic à Ioanne dicuntur. Postremò vt in omnibus hus vtrinque peccetur, docebimus.
units.tr: Just as people sin in almost every way with regard to the wealth of this world, so there is hardly any other subject on which it is more difficult and more dangerous to speak than riches, their use, and the condition of the rich. For whatever is said here to those who are not yet instructed in true piety, they always twist to a sense foreign to the text, according to the desires of their own passions. When the rich hear that the possession of wealth and its lawful use are defended, they soon become overconfident, think themselves its masters, and, feeling secure, carelessly and inhumanly neglect everyone else; moreover, they revel in their resources and abuse them for luxury and lust. Conversely, when the rich are urged to beneficence, the poor at once make them their debtors. Indeed, they claim for themselves a right and authority over the wealth of others, and, like Minos and Rhadamanthus, they condemn with remarkable boldness everyone who does not give as much as they demand. There are also those who, seeing that the administration of goods is full of danger, fear that they will shipwreck their salvation unless they renounce all possessions. Certain fanatics then raise further and more troublesome scruples: under the pretext of religion, some seek to introduce a Platonic community of all goods, and so arrogantly condemn the right of property; others, professing voluntary poverty, live at the expense of others and become the richest of all, while enjoying an exemption from all public burdens. One may fairly say of them what Asaph says of the prosperity of the wicked: "There are no bands in their death, but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men, neither are they plagued like other men." Among these we should rightly count those of whom Paul writes to the Thessalonians, who, as if poverty were a pretext for idleness, bring want upon themselves and, freed from all discipline both civil and ecclesiastical, wander about idle and lazy. The chief cause of all these errors and vices is that most people judge wrongly about riches and poverty. This matter therefore deserves careful consideration, which we will pursue in this order: first we will speak of the property of the goods of this world, then of their possession and lawful use, where the whole rationale of Christian beneficence will also have to be considered, together with what John says here. Finally, we will show how people sin in both respects.

units.la: Quoad primum, ante omnia tenere oportet, proprietatem diuitiarum, quantumuis hae magnae & amplae sint, non pugnare cum verbo Dei, nec aliquem propter opes damnari debere. Nam has ex Dei benedictione obtingere, scriptura docet. Benedictio Domini (inquit Solomon) diuites facit. Quod reipsa probari ostendit sapiens ille Sirachides. Nam est (inquit) qui laboret, moliatur, et satagat, qui tamen egeat multò magis. Est rursum, qui tardus & opus indigus viribusq; destitutus sit, & abundè pauper, quem Dominus oculo fauente respicit, & attollit eum ab humili forte sua, caputq; ipsius conquassatu erigit, vt multis spectantibus sit miraculo. Quod cum quotidiana experientia probetur, ampliori demonstratione nequaquam opus habet. Hoc solum addemus, opes diuina benedictione non ijs solis distribui, quorum felicitas (vt ferè tenuioris fortuna hominess sentiunt) huius vitae finibus continentur: verumetiam pijs & electis Dei cultoribus, quibus aeternae regni coelorum diuitiae in Christo recondita sunt. Notum est enim illud Dauidis: Beatus vir, qui timet Dominum, & praeceptis eius delectatur: Copia rerum & diuitiae erunt in domo eius, & iustitia eius stabit in aeternum. Et exempla sunt in Abrahamo & reliquis patribus, in Iosepho item Arim athaeo, Lazaro Bethanieńsi & sororibus eius, multisque alijs, quorum fides & pietas in nouo Testamento commendatur, cum opulentissimi fuerint. Deinde rerum proprietas ad ciuiles leges & politicas ordinationes pertinet, quas Christus minimè aboleuit, & quas retinendas esse docent apostoli, quando vnicuiq; quod suum est, reddere iubent. Quid? annon Deus furari prohibet, & idem in prophetis & Lege vsuras, fraudes & omnis generis rapinas accusat & damnat? Atqui nullus furto locus esset, si nemini quid proprium possidere liceret, neq; aliquis esset legum earum vsus, quae de reddenda operarij mercede, de mensuris ite& ponderibus, de reddendo deposito, de non transferendis terminis & infinitis eiusmodi rebus habentur. Esse ergo diuinis legibus contrarium quod illi petunt, qui communitate bonorum omnium inducere conantur: & ijdem sublata omni oeconomia simul & maxima legum politicarum parte confusionem nobis darent, quae turbas & seditiones continuas gigneret. Adhaec circa id laborant, quod effectu est impossibile. Nam vt iam iam aequalis omnium agrorum, domorum, bonorum deniq; mobilium & immobilium distributio fieret, eadem vix ad vnius horae spatium durare posset; cum multorum ea sit in profundendo prodigalitas, tanta item multorum in suis seruandis negligentia, vt nullis legibus coerceri aut emendari queat. Vanissimum ergo commentum est, quicquid fanatici illi aduersus legitimam bonorum possessionem nugantur. Obijciunt quidem nobis primitiuae Ecclesiae exemplum, in qua omnia credentes communia habuisse, nec quenquam aliquid suum dixisse Lucas scribit. Sed neq; ex illo vnquam euincent quod volunt. Nam vt locos illos secundùm literam accipias, nullum illic dogma generale traditur, neq; forma constituitur, quae vbique terrarum recipi & omnibus seculis retineri debeat: sed quid tunc factu fuerit narratur, cum vt ita fieret in magna egentium turba res ipsa postulaother, ne qui propter fidem Christianam excommunicabantur, vel fame perirent, vel propter egestatem ad Iudaicas superstitiones reuerterentur. Vt autem alibi idem observatur, Apostolos nusquam mandauisse legimus. Veruntamen si propius rem consideremus, nihil minus quam Platonica aut Anabaptistica omnium bonorum communio credentibus tunc quoq; in mentem venit. Nam ibidem distributionis quoq; fit mentio, cuius ratio fuit, prout quisq; opus habebat, non quod quisque quantum ipsi lubebat acceperit. Deinde domuum quoque meminit Lucas, in quibus ad sacros coetus conuenerunt. Ergo multi suas domus retinuerunt, inter quos Maria Ioannis Marci mater nominatim censetur. Adhaec si Petri verba consideres, quibus Ananiam & Sapphiram corripuit, in vniuscunq; arbitrio positum erat, vel omnia sua in publicum ecclesiae aerarium conferre, & ex eo deinde cum reliquis pauperibus suum dimensum recipere, vel aliquam partem ex spontanea liberalitate ecclesiae pauperibus decidere, reliqua autem in suum vsum sibi seruare. Neq; quod aliquid illi seruassent, morte subita multantur, sed quod se omnia sua ad ecclesiam contulisse simulauerunt, & ex eius aerario posthac viuere constituissent, cum ex parte quam sibi seruarant viuere possent. Ita vero & Spiritui sancto mentiebantur, & sacrilegium committebant ea retinendo, quae pro prij oris testimonio ecclesiae consecrauerant. Deniq; nulla illic fuit coactio, sed communia illis erant omnia, quoad voluntatem & charitatis affectu (qua ratione amici omnia communia habere dicuntur) non quòd alicui ius esset manum pro suo arbitrio in res alienas inijcere. Ideo diserte ait Lucas: Nemo aliquid eorum, quae possidebat (en possidendi verbum) suum esse dicebat. Ergo possidebant quidem sua, non autem ea sibi solis vendicabant, sed in hoc erant, vt ex suis fratrum egentium necessitati subueniretur. Et vt locum istum absoluamus, non alium huius sua oeconomiae finem ecclesia primitiua sibi propositum habuit, quam vt veterem Legem reduceret, quae mendicos esse prohibet, & quae partim sacerdotum auaritia, partim populi Iudaici inhumanitas abrogauerat. Possumus his addere Christi authoritate, qui etsi discipulos aliquos occultos habuerit, qui diuitijs praediti fuerunt, nihil tamen huius ab illis requisiuit: quod ipsum Apostoli quoq; in Cornelio Centurione, Sergio Paulo, Philemone & horum similibus obseruarunt. Et haec quidem sufficere possunt vere pijs: si quibus autem contendere adhuc libet, hoc illis per nos licet, vt qui rationibus nullis cedunt, animos seditiosos & a pietate alienos proprio iudicio prodant.
units.tr: As for the first point, we must first of all hold that the ownership of riches, however great and abundant they may be, is not contrary to the Word of God, and that no one should be condemned on account of wealth.
