For Scripture teaches that these come by the blessing of God. "The blessing of the Lord," says Solomon, "makes rich." The wise son of Sirach shows this to be true in fact: "There is one who labours, toils and hurries, yet is all the more in want. There is another who is slow and in need of help and destitute of strength, and yet utterly poor, whom the Lord regards with a favourable eye and lifts up from his lowly state, and raises his head, so that many are amazed at him." Since this is proved by daily experience, it certainly needs no further demonstration. We will add only this: divine blessing is not distributed only to those whose happiness, as most people of humble fortune feel, is confined within the limits of this life, but also to the pious and chosen worshippers of God, to whom the eternal riches of the kingdom of heaven are laid up in Christ. For that saying of David is well known: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord and delights greatly in his commandments. Wealth and riches shall be in his house, and his righteousness endures for ever." There are also examples in Abraham and the other fathers, in Joseph of Arimathea, in Lazarus of Bethany and his sisters, and in many others, whose faith and piety are commended in the New Testament, although they were very wealthy. Next, the ownership of property belongs to civil laws and political ordinances, which Christ did not at all abolish, and which the apostles teach us to retain, when they command that to everyone be rendered what is his. What then? Does not God forbid theft, and in the prophets and the Law condemn and denounce usury, fraud and every kind of robbery? Yet there would be no place for theft if it were lawful for no one to possess anything as his own; nor would there be any use for those laws which deal with paying a labourer's wage, with measures and weights, with returning a deposit, with not moving boundary stones, and with countless matters of this kind. Therefore, what those men seek who try to introduce a community of all goods is contrary to the divine laws; and, by abolishing all household management and the greater part of the political laws at once, they would bring upon us a confusion that would breed constant tumults and sedition. Moreover, they labour over what is in fact impossible. For even if an equal distribution of all fields, houses, and goods, both movable and immovable, were made at once, it could scarcely last the span of a single hour, since many people are so prodigal in spending, and many so careless in keeping what is theirs, that no laws can restrain or correct them. Therefore, whatever those fanatics babble against the lawful possession of goods is a most empty fiction. They do indeed object to us the example of the primitive Church, in which, as Luke writes, all believers had all things in common, and no one called anything his own. But from this they will never prove what they want. For even if you take those passages according to the letter, no general doctrine is taught there, nor is a form established that should be received everywhere on earth and retained in every age. Rather, what was then done is related, when, because of the great crowd of needy people, the situation itself demanded that it be so, so that those who were excommunicated for the Christian faith should not either perish of hunger or, through poverty, return to Jewish superstitions. As for the fact that the same thing is observed elsewhere, we read that the apostles nowhere commanded it. Yet if we consider the matter more closely, the believers at that time were thinking of nothing less than a Platonic or Anabaptist community of all goods. For the same passage also mentions distribution, the principle of which was that each received according to his need, not that each took as much as he pleased. Then Luke also mentions houses in which they gathered for the holy assemblies. Therefore many kept their own houses, among whom Mary, the mother of John Mark, is specifically named. Furthermore, if you consider Peter's words, with which he rebuked Ananias and Sapphira, it was left to each person's choice either to bring all his goods into the common treasury of the Church and then receive from it his portion along with the other poor, or to give some part of his own free generosity to the poor of the Church and keep the rest for his own use. Nor were they punished with sudden death because they had kept something back, but because they pretended that they had brought all their goods to the Church and had resolved to live from its treasury thereafter, when they could have lived from the part they had kept for themselves. Thus they were lying to the Holy Spirit and committing sacrilege by keeping back what they had consecrated to the Church by their own word. In short, there was no compulsion there; rather, all things were common to them in will and in the affection of charity (which is the sense in which friends are said to have all things in common), and not because anyone had the right to lay hands on the goods of others at his own pleasure. Therefore Luke says plainly: "No one said that any of the things that he possessed (note the word for possessing) was his own." So they indeed possessed their goods, but did not claim them for themselves alone; they were concerned that the need of their needy brothers should be relieved from their resources. And to finish this point: the primitive Church had no other purpose in this arrangement than to restore the old Law, which forbids there to be beggars, and which the greed of the priests and the inhumanity of the Jewish people had in part abrogated. To these we may add the authority of Christ, who, although he had some secret disciples who were endowed with riches, nevertheless required nothing of them. The apostles observed the same in Cornelius the centurion, Sergius Paulus, Philemon and others like them. These arguments may suffice for those who are truly pious. But if any still wish to dispute, we allow them to do so, since they yield to no reasons, and they will betray their own seditious minds, which are alien to piety, by their own judgment.

units.la: Caeterum alteri huius tractationis caput videamus de opum possessione & legitimo earundem vsu. Vbi ante omnia cauere oportet, ne per dolum & impostouras, aut per vim vel alijs modis illicitis diteditescere velimus, & eius causa charitatis aut iustitiae leges violemus. Nam qui hoc agunt, ij quae non sua sunt coaceruant, & Dei maledictionem incurrunt, quā prophetae talibus passim minantur. Vae ei (inquit Habakuk) qui adauget non sua (quo vsq; tandem?) & qui aggravat super se densum lutum. Et apud Micheam clamat Dominus: Audite virgam & eum qui decernit. Annon adhuc ignis in domo impij, thesaurus (inquam) iniquus, & Epha exiguum quidem, sed iniquitatis plenum? Num iustificabo cum bilance iniqua, & cum sacculo, in quo sunt lapides fraudulenti? Quia eius divites impleuerunt rapina, & habitatores eius loquuntur mendacium, lingua eorum dolosa est in ore eorum. Quin & ego infirmabo te caedendo, & te disperdam propter peccata tua. Tu comedes, & non saturaberis, &c. Et huius generis multa passim in prophetis occurrunt, quibus recensendis non opus est insistere, cum res ipsa loquatur, fere infelicem esse eorum finem, qui opes per fas nefas congerunt, & eiusmodi diuitias raro ad tertium vsque haeredem peruenire. Deinde non minus videndum est, ne diuitijs ex Dei benedictione affluentibus cor apponamus, et in illis collocatam habeamus fiduciam, quae soli Deo debetur. Nam qui hoc faciunt, ij idololatriae crimen incurrunt (vt Paulus ait) et Deum sibi faciunt Mammona siue Plutum, tandemq; Deo vero graues poenas exoluunt. Adhaec cauere oportet, ne inter homines opum fiducia elati, impunitatem captemus: quod vitiū diuitibus nimis vulgare est, dum disciplinam omnem excutiunt, et crabronum instar leges omnes perrumpunt. Peccant in eo graviter in ipsum Deum, quem eo sanctius colere debebant, quo maiorem ex illo benedictionem sentiunt. Vsus vero opum sit, vt necessitati seruiant, quantum natura exigit: quae vt paucis contenta est, ita luxum & intemperantiam odit. Horum consideratio αὐταρκείᾳ, id est, forte sua contentos reddit, quae & charitatis & omnium virtutum ciuilium nutrix est fidissima. Imo ad quemuis fortunae euentum intrepidos & constantes facit. Cur enim in periculis & opum amissione desperent, qui se non multis opus habere, omnia autem sua ex Dei benedictione & prouidentia pendere sciunt? Potuit olim Biam Prieneum, cum patria eius ab hostibus diriperetur, animosum & inuictum facere, quod humanae sapientiae visum alijs hominibus praestantiorem haberet, & ideo dicebat, Omnia mea mecum porto: Quanto maior ergo debet esse Christianorum hominum fiducia, qui Christo insiti sunt, in quo aeternos gratia Dei & salutis thesauros obtinuerunt, quos nulla vis hostilis eripere, neque ipsi daemones intercipere possunt?
units.tr: Next, let us look at the second chapter of this subject: the possession of wealth and its lawful use. Above all we must take care not to grow rich by deceit and trickery, by violence, or by other unlawful means, thereby breaking the laws of love or justice. Those who do this heap up what is not theirs, and they incur the curse of God, which the prophets constantly threaten against such people. "Woe to him," says Habakkuk, "who increases what is not his (how long?) and who loads himself with thick clay." In Micah the Lord cries out: "Hear the rod, and him who appointed it. Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, an unjust treasure, and a short measure that is small indeed but full of iniquity? Shall I justify the wicked with unjust scales and with a bag of deceitful weights? For their rich men are filled with robbery, their inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. Indeed I will make you sick by striking you and will destroy you because of your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied, etc." Many passages of this kind occur throughout the prophets. There is no need to list them here, since the matter speaks for itself: the end of those who pile up wealth by fair means or foul is nearly always unhappy, and such riches seldom pass even to the third heir. Next, we must be no less careful not to set our heart on wealth that flows to us from God's blessing, and not to place in it the trust that is owed to God alone. For those who do this fall into the sin of idolatry, as Paul says, and make Mammon or Plutus their god, and in the end they pay heavy penalties to the true God. Besides this, we must take care that, proud of our trust in wealth among men, we do not seek impunity. This vice is all too common among the rich, who shake off every discipline and, like hornets, break through all laws. In this they sin grievously against God himself, whom they ought to honour all the more holily the greater the blessing they feel from him. The use of wealth, however, should serve necessity, as far as nature requires. Nature, which is content with little, hates luxury and intemperance. Consideration of this makes people content with their own lot, which is [self-sufficiency, αὐταρκείᾳ], that is, contentment with what is one's own. This is the most faithful nurse of love and of all civic virtues. Indeed, it makes people fearless and steadfast in the face of any turn of fortune. For why should those despair in dangers or in the loss of wealth who know that they need few things, and that all they have depends on God's blessing and providence? Bias of Priene, when his country was being plundered by enemies, could make himself courageous and unconquerable, since human wisdom regarded him as more outstanding than other men; and so he used to say, "I carry all my possessions with me." How much greater, then, ought the confidence of Christians to be, who are engrafted into Christ, in whom they have obtained the eternal treasures of God's grace and salvation, which no hostile force can snatch away, and which not even the demons themselves can intercept?

units.la: In primis autem in vsu opum meminisse oportet, eas non nobis solis datas esse, sed nos earum quasi oeconomos & dispensatores esse a Deo constitutos, vt per nos aliorum etiam necessitati seruiant. Itaq; beneficentiam colere & liberaliter alijs egentibus subuenire debent, qui prae alijs abundant. Id in praesenti symbolicis locutionibus (quales apud veteres infrequenti vsu fuerunt) Ioannes docet, cum ait: Qui habet duas tunicas, impertiat non habenti, & qui habet escas, similiter faciat. Ponit ergo species duas, victum & amictum, & sub his omnem huius mundi substantiam comprehendit, non aliud interim iubens, quam quod alibi praecipit Deus, vt nudum vestiamus, panem frangamus esurienti & pro viribus subleuemus eorum necessitatem, quos opis indigos esse videmus. Et conuenit hoc cū natura legibus, inter quas praecipua & aliarum omnium compendium est: Omnia quae volueritis vt faciant vobis homines, ita & vos facite ipsis. At quis obsecro hominum est, qui si famelicus, nudus, exul & peregrinus oberret, aut ex morbo decumbat, aut quacunq; alia fortuna aduersa prematur, non cupiat se ab alijs pasci, vestiri, colligi, curari & iuuari vel defendi? Imo si nos ab iis deseri videamus, quibus iuuandi facultas est, illorum inhumanitatem accusare & supplicio dignam putare solemus. Aequum ergo fuerit, vt eadem lege singuli se alijs quoq; hominibus obstrictos esse cogitent, & ad iuuandum parati sint, vbicunq; sese occasio & facultas offert. Hoc (inquam) vult Ioannes, cui nihil minus in mente venit, quam fanaticus illis cauillandi occasionem dare, qui nefas esse clamant, duas tunicas possidere, aut aliquid habere, quo non in praesenti statim vtaris. Nam si ea Dei mens esset, idem Christus quoq; docuisset, idem passim iussissent apostoli. Itaq; optimus Ioannis interpres est Paulus, qui Timotheo suo sic scribit: Ijs qui diuites sunt in hoc saeculo denuntia, ne efferantur animo, neq; spem ponant in diuitijs incertis, sed in Deo viuo, qui praebet nobis omnia copiose ad fruendum: vt benefaciant, vt diuites sint operibus bonis, faciles ad impertiendum, facilis communicatus. Idē in posteriori ad Corinthios beneficicentiā certis quoq; Legibus comprehendit, sic dices: Quisquis sicut praeoptat corde, id est vltro apud se constituit, ita conferat, nō ex tristitia aut necessitate: nam hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Etenim si prius adsit promptus animus, is acceptus est pro eo quod habet aliquis, non pro eo quod non habet. Non enim ut alijs relaxatio fit, vobis autem angustia: sed pari conditione, ve-stra abundantia illorum defectum farciat, et ut illorum abundantia vestrum defectum suppleat, ut fiat æquabilitas. Ex quibus verbis tria colligi possunt. Primum, ut quisq; largiatur secundum sui animi propositum. Nemo igitur hic alij legem præscribere debet, quid aut quantum quisque largiri debeat, aut etiam quibus. Nec enim aliquis aliorum fortunas facile omnes perspectas habet; & ut omnino noris, quantum quis possit, idem tamen suis fortasse ad alios vsus opus habet, neq; semper tenetur, ut tibi aut alijs suarum rerum rationem reddat. Quod vnum satis aperte docet, non rigidius secundum literam accipi debere, quod in præsenti de duabus tunicis dicitur. Et ut aliquis maximè egeat, sit tamen sæpe, ut is cuius opem ille implorat, alios habeat sibi propiori vinculo obstrictos, quibus id præstare cogitur, quod alter ille perit. Itaq; nimis temerarij sunt, qui sibi in aliorum fortunas simul & conscientias ius sumunt, dum cuiq; quid & quantum largiri debeat præscribunt. Altera lex esto, ut ex animo benefacias. Nam ut Deus bilarem datorem requirit, ita misericordiæ in scripturis viscera vel σπλάγχνα, id est, naturales affectiones tribuuntur, quas qui intra se se sentiunt, ij nihil perin-de optant, quam ut egentem iuuare possint. Idem etiam non sua quærunt, dum alijs succurrunt, ita deniq; proximo opem ferunt, ut sinistra ipsorum nesciat, quid faciat dextera, id est, ut beneficentiæ quam exercent, nullus affectus sinister concurrat. Tertia lex est, ut modum teneamus in largiendo, ne dum nostra in alios profundimus temere, ipsi ad egestatem redacti posteaqu̇ aliorum opem consu-gere, & quæ pauperioribus debebantur, intercipere cogamur. Et apparet in eo plus quam paterna Dei bonitas, qui cum prosuo iure omnia à nobis exigere possit, paucis tamen contentus est, et nostris nos rebus cōsulere patitur, ne alios iuuando nobisipsis molestia accersamus. Quò minus excusari potest eorum duritiei, qui nulla egentium miseria tanguntur, & proinde quosuis siccis oculis negligunt. At quia caro nostra hic tardior est, proderit rationes considerauisse, quæ nòs ad benefaciendum excitare possint. Prima in ipso opus vsu occurrit, qui quoad nos nullus esse potest (de legitimo & laudabili siue honesto loquor) quàm ut nostræ necessitati seruiant, quoad victu & amictum, sub quibus hospitium quoq; aut domicilium comprehenditur. At in his natura paucis contenta est, & commodius multo viuunt qui in istis modum seruant, quàm qui cupiditatibus carnis suæ indulgent. Vbi verò ad vitæ finem accessimus, nulla ad nos ex diuitijs quantiscunq; vtilitas redit, neq; aliquis dies vel hora redimi potest, quæ vitæ curriculo iam elapso adijciatur. Et quæ reliqua manent, ea relinquimus ignaris, quibus nam illa cedant. Nā vt nudi ex vtero matris egressi sumus, ita nudi in antiquā matris, terræ nimirum, viscera redimus. Quæ ergo stultitia est, aliorum necessitati ea negare, quibus tu non veteris? Adde his alterum argumentum ex opum natura aut conditione petitum, quas fluxas & instabiles esse constat. Qui ergo scis, num te inuito dilapsuræ sint, aut hostibus præda futuræ, quas tu egentibus & Christi nomine opem petentibus negas? Tertio cogitemus, non sine Dei prouidentia fieri, quòd alij opibus superfluis abundant, alijs verò necessaria quoque desunt. At quæ huius con-silij ratio alia apud Deum inueniri poterit, quàm quòd charitati mutuæ & beneficentiæ occasio-nem dare voluit, quæ locum non haberent, si eadem omnium hominum esse conditio? Itaq; qui plu-ra possident, se Dei œconomos esse meminerint, in œconomo autem vel dispensatore hoc in primis re-quiri, ut fidelis sit, neque sibi soli vsurpet, quod in aliorum vsus accepit. Quartò communem homi-num sortem nobis ob oculos ponamus, quæ est, quòd nihil humani à quoquam alienum est, & quòd nobis eadem calamitas accidere potest, qua ij nunc premuntur, qui à nobis opem flagitat. Est hic sti-mulus ad mouendam misericordiam vehementissimus, quo qui non mouentur, ij se ab omni humani-tatis sensu alienos & ἀσπόργος plane esse ostendunt, quos Paulus inter nouissimi seculi pestes nume-rat. Postremò proderit cogitare, quòd ex pauperibus plura & maiora commoda sperare possumus, quàm illi ex nobis percipiant. Nam ut nihil dicamus de officijs, quæ illi nobis præstant, dum agros colunt, artificia manuaria exercent, & alia infinita faciunt, sine quibus vita hæc consistere non po-test: si in eos incidamus, qui nihil huius nobis præstare possunt, hi tamen ipsi preces habent, quas pro nobis fundant, & pro iisdem fidem suam nobis obstrinxit Christus, qui eos sibi substituit, & in nouis-simo illo die sibi factum putabit, quod vni illorum per nos factum fuerit. Et ideo infra cap.16.dicet: Facite vobis amicos ex mammone iniquo, ut cum defecerit, vos recipiat in æterna tabernacula. Hac & Hæc & alia infinita huius generis si crebrò animis nostris versemus, & ijsdè coniungamus promissiones Dei, quibus in hac etiam vita retributionem liberalissimam pollicetur illis, qui in suo nomine egentibus benefaciunt, mox nos efficacissimè ad faciendum officium excitari sentimus.
units.tr: Above all, when we use our wealth we should remember that it has not been given to us alone. God has appointed us as its stewards and managers, so that through us it may also serve the needs of others. Those who have more than others should therefore cultivate kindness and generously help those in want. John teaches this in the present passage in figurative language (of the kind that was rarely used by the ancients) when he says: "He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise." He names two kinds of goods, food and clothing, and by these he includes the whole substance of this world. In saying this he commands nothing other than what God commands elsewhere: that we clothe the naked, break bread for the hungry, and, as far as we are able, relieve the need of those whom we see to be in want. This agrees with the law of nature, whose chief principle, and the summary of all the others, is: "Whatever you want others to do to you, do so to them." But who, I ask, is there who, if he wandered hungry, naked, an exile and a stranger, or lay sick, or was oppressed by some other misfortune, would not wish to be fed, clothed, sheltered, cared for and helped or defended by others? Indeed, if we see that those who have the means to help us desert us, we are accustomed to accuse their inhumanity and to think them worthy of punishment. It is therefore fair that, under the same law, each one should consider himself bound to other people too, and be ready to help wherever the occasion and the means present themselves. This (I say) is what John means, and he had no thought at all of giving occasion for mockery to those fanatics who cry out that it is wicked to possess two coats, or to have anything that you do not use at once. For if this were God's intention, Christ himself would have taught it, and the apostles would have commanded it everywhere. Thus Paul, who wrote to his Timothy in this way, is the best interpreter of John: "Charge those who are rich in this world not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to give, willing to share." In the second letter to the Corinthians he also sets out beneficence under certain rules, saying: "Let each one give as he has purposed in his heart, that is, as he has decided within himself of his own accord; not out of sadness or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver. For if the willing mind is present, it is acceptable according to what a man has, not according to what he does not have. For it is not that others should be relieved and you burdened, but by equal measure your abundance should supply their lack, and their abundance should supply your lack, so that there may be equality." From these words three things can be gathered. First, that each person should give according to the purpose of his own mind. No one should therefore prescribe a law here to another as to what, or how much, or even to whom each should give. For no one easily has a full view of the fortunes of others; and although you may know well how much a person is able to give, he may perhaps need the same things for other uses, and he is not always bound to render an account of his affairs to you or to others. This one thing teaches quite plainly that what is said here about the two coats should not be taken too rigidly according to the letter. And although a man may be in great need, it often happens that the one whose help he implores has other people bound to him by a closer tie, to whom he is compelled to provide what the other man is lacking. Those therefore are too rash who claim for themselves a right over the fortunes and consciences of others, while prescribing to each what and how much he must give. The second rule is this: that you do good from the heart. For just as God requires a cheerful giver, so in the Scriptures the bowels of mercy, or splanchna [σπλάγχνα], that is, natural affections, are ascribed to people, and those who feel these within themselves desire nothing more than to be able to help the needy. Likewise, they do not seek their own things while they help others; and so they bring aid to their neighbour in such a way that their left hand does not know what their right hand is doing, that is, no sinister affection mingles with the kindness they practise. The third rule is that we keep moderation in giving, lest, having rashly poured out our own goods upon others, we ourselves be reduced to poverty and afterwards be forced to seek the help of others, and to take away what was owed to the poorer. And in this it appears that God's goodness is more than fatherly: though he could by his own right demand everything from us, he is nevertheless content with little, and allows us to provide for our own affairs, so that by helping others we do not bring trouble upon ourselves. All the less can the hardness of those be excused who are moved by no misery of the needy, and therefore neglect anyone with dry eyes. But because our flesh is slow here, it will be useful to consider the reasons that can stir us to do good. The first arises from the very use of wealth, which, as far as we are concerned (I speak of its lawful and praiseworthy or honourable use), can be only this: to serve our necessities, as regards food and clothing, under which shelter or a home is also included. But in these matters nature is content with few things, and those who keep to moderation in them live far more comfortably than those who indulge the desires of their flesh. Yet when we come to the end of life, no advantage from riches, however great, returns to us, nor can any day or hour be bought back and added to the course of a life already run. And what remains we leave to we know not whom, who will inherit them. For as we came naked out of our mother's womb, so we return naked into the bosom of our old mother, the earth. What folly, then, is it to deny to the necessity of others those things which you will not need? Add to this a second argument, drawn from the nature and condition of riches, which are known to be fleeting and unstable. Who knows, then, whether, against your will, they may slip away, or become the prey of enemies, those riches which you refuse to needy people who ask for help in the name of Christ? Third, let us consider that it is not without the providence of God that some abound with superfluous wealth while others lack even necessities. But what other reason for this plan can be found with God, than that he wished to give an occasion for mutual love and beneficence, which would have no place if the condition of all men were the same? Therefore let those who possess more remember that they are the stewards of God, and that in a steward or manager the first requirement is that he be faithful, and that he not claim for himself alone what he has received for the use of others. Fourth, let us set before our eyes the common lot of mankind, which is that nothing human is foreign to anyone, and that the same calamity which now oppresses those who seek help from us may befall us. This is a most powerful spur to stirring up mercy; those who are not moved by it show themselves quite alien to all human feeling and astorgoi [ἀστόργοι], without natural affection, whom Paul counts among the plagues of the last age. Lastly, it will be useful to reflect that from the poor we can hope for more and greater benefits than they receive from us. For, to say nothing of the services they render us while they cultivate the fields, practise manual crafts, and do countless other things without which this life cannot stand, if we fall among those who can offer us nothing of this kind, they nevertheless have prayers which they pour out for us, and Christ, who has set them in his place, has pledged his own faith on their behalf, and on that last day he will count as done to himself whatever is done for one of them through us. And therefore, below in chapter 16, he will say: "Make friends for yourselves by means of the unrighteous mammon, so that when it fails, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings." If we often turn these and countless other considerations of this kind over in our minds, and join to them the promises of God, by which he promises the most generous reward even in this life to those who do good to the needy in his name, we will soon feel ourselves most powerfully stirred to perform our duty.

units.la: At si ista ad nostri seculi mores transferamus, undiq; peccata occurrent, ut non temere Christus divitias spinis similes esse dixerit: non quòd ex Dei benedictione aliquid noxiù aut perniciosum pro veniat, sed quòd ea sit nostri ingenij infelicitas, ut non vno modo nobis noxiù faciamus, quod per se bonum & utile est. Peccatur autem plurimùm, imò omnium in hac causa errorum fons est, quòd plerique hominis beatitatem in divitiarum abundantia sitam esse existimant. Itaq; ut illarum acervos congerant, fallunt, furantur, rapiunt, peierant, ius & leges venales habent, fœnerantur, dissidia & bella movent, denique nullum flagitium tam immane & atrox est, quod non sibi licere putent, si spes lucri affulserit. Tales ergo & sibi ipsis maledictionem accersunt, ut supra diximus, et rempub. labefactant, & plerunq; publicorum motuum authores sunt. Nec minus opibus iam acquisitis in possidendo peccatur, dum vel fiduciam omnem in illis collocant divites, vel propter illas impunitatem sibi vendicant, qua disciplinam omnē evertunt, & pauperum capitibus insolenter nimis insultāt, atq; eorundem sudore summa cum iniquitate abutuntur, neq; unquam de charitate aut beneficentia cogitant. Itaq; in ipsos dicuntur quæ Dominus Iacobus cum gravissima comminatione talibus denuntiat: Agite nunc divites, flete ululantes super miserijs vestris, quæ superuenient. Diuitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, vestes vestræ tineis obnoxiæ factæ sunt; aurum & argentum vestrum ærugine vitiatum est, & ærugo eorum testabitur contra vos, & exedet carnes vestras veluti ignis. Thesaurum congestistis vltimis diebus. Ecce merces operariorum qui messuerunt regiones vestras, à vobis incercepta, clamat, & clamores eorum qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt, &c. Quòd si vero tales opum suarum iacturâ faciant, mox noua illis offertur peccandi occasio. Nam impatientia doloris superati vitulant, aduersus Deum fremunt, & omnipse abiecti tam seipsos quàm eos devouent, quos illis mali huius authores esse arbitrantur. Et in his quidè fere peccat diuites. Quòd si pauperes inspicias, ij quoq; non omnino extra culpam sunt. Plerique enim eorum charitatis Lege ad solos diuites pertinere putant, & quasi ipsi nemini quicquâ debeant, sed ad accipiendū modò nati sint, otiosi & inertes oberrant, ab omnibus flagitant, accepta turpiter consumunt, & ut ipsi exleges sunt atq; absq; omni disciplina vitā degunt, ita liberos quoq; suos in otio & mendacitate educant, deniq; neq; priuatim neq; publicè alicui vtiles, sed omnibus molesti, adhæc publica quædam nota aut labes sunt ecclesiæ, propter quam fides Christiana malè audit & proscinditur apud eos, qui illius veritatè ignorant. Cogitent ergo omnes, Ioannem ista publicè toti populo dixisse, in quo erant omnis loci et ordinis homines, & proinde legem hanc beneficentiæ Christianæ ad omnes pertinere. Itaq; huius prima pars est, ne cui oneri simus, nisi itanos cogat extrema necessitas. Curent ergo singuli, ut honesto aliquo labore seipsos & suos alant, quoadeius fieri potest. Et hoc suarū partium esse pauperes meminerint. Altera huius legis pars sit, ut omnibus pro virili benefaciamus, & ita testemur nos Dei patris filios esse, ad quos regni cælorū hæreditas pertineat, quam nobis suo merito acquisiuit Dominus & seruator noster Iesus Christus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But if we apply these things to the morals of our own age, sins meet us on every side, so that it was not without reason that Christ said riches are like thorns. This is not because anything harmful or pernicious comes from God's blessing, but because of the unhappiness of our nature, which turns what is good and useful in itself into something harmful for us in many ways. Sin is committed most of all in this matter, indeed every error here springs from one source: most people think that human happiness consists in an abundance of riches. So, in order to heap up their piles of wealth, they deceive, steal, plunder, swear falsely, treat law and justice as things for sale, lend at interest, stir up quarrels and wars; in short, there is no crime so monstrous and savage that they do not think it allowed to them, if the hope of gain has shone upon them. Such people bring curses upon themselves, as we said above, overthrow the commonwealth, and are very often the authors of public disturbances. Nor is sin committed less in the possession of wealth once acquired, when the rich either place all their trust in it, or on account of it claim impunity for themselves, which overturns all discipline, insolently trample upon the heads of the poor, and abuse their sweat with the greatest injustice, never thinking of love or beneficence. Therefore, the words that the Lord James addresses to such people with a most grave threat apply to them: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have become moth-eaten; your gold and silver is corroded, and their rust will bear witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have heaped up treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, kept back by you, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth," etc. But if such people suffer the loss of their possessions, a new occasion of sin is at once offered to them: overcome by impatience at their grief, they rage against God, and, cast down in every way, they curse both themselves and those whom they think to be the authors of their misfortune. And in these matters the rich generally sin. But if you look at the poor, they too are not altogether free from blame. For most of them think that the law of charity pertains only to the rich, and, as though they owe nothing to anyone, but were born only to receive, they wander about idle and lazy, beg from everyone, shamefully squander what they receive, and, just as they are lawless themselves and live without any discipline, so they bring up their children too in idleness and lying; finally, they are useful neither privately nor publicly to anyone, but a burden to all, and moreover they are a certain public stain and disgrace to the Church, on account of which the Christian faith is ill spoken of and torn apart among those who are ignorant of its truth. Let all therefore consider that John said these things publicly to the whole people, among whom were men of every place and rank, and that therefore this law of Christian beneficence pertains to all. So the first part of it is that we should not be a burden to anyone, unless extreme necessity compels us to it. Let each therefore take care to support himself and his own by some honest labour, as far as this can be done. And let the poor remember that this is their own part. The other part of this law is that we should do good to all according to our ability, and so bear witness that we are the sons of God the Father, to whom the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven belongs, which our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ has acquired for us by his merit, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXX.

units.la: Venerunt autem & publicani vt baptizarentur, & dixerunt ei: Magister quid faciemus? Ipse verò dixit eis: Nihil amplius quàm quod constitutum est vobis, exigite.
units.tr: Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and said to him, "Teacher, what shall we do?" And he said to them, "Collect no more than what has been appointed to you."

units.la: Quemadmodum arbor bona non potest non fructus bonos ferre: ita qui ex verbi Dei semine renati Christi vera fide apprehendunt & ex animo respipiscunt, ij fide hanc et respipiscentia esse suis aut fructibus dignis testantur. Recte ergo Ioannes fidei in Christum Iesum & verae respipiscentiae doctor, non obiter modò & in genere doctrinā istam proponit, verumetiam omnis loci & ordinis hominibus eam accommodat. Et ab omnibus quidem simul charitatis & beneficentiæ officia requirit, sed quòd his continentur quæcunq; de iustitia & innocentia vitæ dici possunt. Sequitur nunc noua cōcio, vel potius nouae concionis argumentum, qua publicanos instituit, & qua multa continentur, quae & magistratus & eos qui publica munera administrant, deinde singulos etiam priuatim in ijs instituere possunt, quae ad opum acquisitionem pertinent.
units.tr: Just as a good tree cannot but bear good fruit, so those who have been born again from the seed of God's Word and grasp Christ with true faith, and who truly repent, testify by their works and fruits that their faith and repentance are genuine. Rightly, then, John, the teacher of faith in Christ Jesus and of true repentance, does not set out this doctrine only in passing and in general terms, but applies it to men of every station and rank. From all alike he requires the duties of love and beneficence, and also whatever can be said about justice and innocence of life. Now comes a new sermon, or rather the subject of a new sermon, in which John instructs the tax collectors. It contains much that can also instruct the magistrates and those who administer public offices, and then each private person too, in matters that concern the acquisition of wealth.

units.la: Priusquam vero Ioannem audiamus, de publicanis dicendum erit, vt eorum quae dicuntur, sensus & vsus rectius intelligantur. Dicuntur autem publicani, teste Vlpiano, qui publico fruuntur, vnde etiam nomen acceperunt. Ad eos tamen proprie hic titulus pertinet, qui vectigalia & alios reipub. aut principum reditus exigendos certo pretio redimunt. Solebat enim Romani in prouincijs vectigalia locare certis hominibus, qui quotannis mandatam ipsis pecuniae summam ad aerarium deferebat: ideoque magna eorum erat dignitas & authoritas, vt de illis Cicero non veritus sit dicere: Flos equitum Romanorum, ornamentum ciuitatis, firmamentum reipub. publicanorum ordine continetur. Neque id temere dictum est, cum neruos reipub. in aerario potissimum consistere certum sit, quod vectigalibus maxime dicatur. At longe alia de illis erat Iudaeorum opinio. Quia enim ipsi Romanum Imperium indigne ferebant, & ad veterem libertatem totis animis aspirabant, non poterant non eos odisse, qui priuati commodi studio suam Romanis operam locabant, & aduersus fratres siue gentiles suos alienae tyrannidis erant ministri: eoque acerbius erat odium illud, quod seruitutem illam in religionis patriae contumeliam redundare putarent. Accedebat praeterea, publicanorum auaritia & crudelitas, quae non contenti ea exegisse, quae ex more debebantur, nouas quotidie rationes excogitabant, quibus vectigalia magis aggrauabantur, quo plus lucri ad ipsos rediret: sicuti infra Zachaei confessio testabitur. Itaque fiebat, vt omnibus exosi & infames essent publicani, & simul cum his male audirent qui earum ipsorum amici aut fautores erant. Quae causa fuit, quod Christum per conuitium publicanorum socium & patronum dicerent. Sunt haec propter aliam quoque causam nobis diligentius consideranda. Docemur enim Iudaeorum exemplo, quid fere omnibus euenire, qui libertatis dono nesciunt vti, & proinde hoc amisso aliorum libidini subijciuntur. Fuerant illi multis seculis electum illud Dei peculium, & prae alijs gentibus libertate vti fuerant, qua nihil inter terrena bona praestantius, nihil item homini ingenuo magis exoptandum est. At ijdem (vt alibi quoque audiuimus) nunc eorum duro & auaro imperio premuntur, quos propter idololatriam & superstitiones nefarias merito abominabantur, & quos ipsi etiam Deo inuisos esse sciebant. Deinde vectigalia exteris soluunt, & insuper tributis & censibus extraordinarijs praeter morem grauantur. Et ne quid iniuriae desit, accedunt ex propria ipsorum gente publicani & officiales, quorum artibus magis spoliantur, quia illis eo erant intolerabiliores, quod plus nocere possent quam alieni, qui singulorum conditione & fortunas non tam probe cognitas habebant. Quae autem istorum omnium causa fuit? Non alia nimirum, quam inobedientia & ingratitudo erga Deum, & quod priuatis affectibus abrepti ciuilia bella mouerunt, de quibus in sequenti Sermone amplius dicetur. Neque in his finem habuit infelicis populi calamitas. Sed cum non ad Deum conuerterentur, sed nouis indies seditionibus libertatem amissam recuperare vellent, Romanorum arma aduersus se prouocarunt, & in illos exemplum factum est, cuius simile in nullis historijs extat. Debent ista non oscitanter expendere ij omnes, quibus hodie datum est libertate frui, ne quando ea amissa similes poenas Deo iusto vindici exoluant.
units.tr: Before we hear John, we must say something about the tax collectors, so that the meaning and use of what is said may be understood more correctly. The tax collectors, according to Ulpian, are called "publicani" because they make use of public revenue, and from this they also took their name. Yet this title properly applies to those who, for a fixed price, contracted to collect the taxes and other revenues of the state or of the rulers. For the Romans were accustomed to let out the taxes in the provinces to certain men, who each year brought to the treasury the sum of money entrusted to them. Hence their dignity and authority were great, so that Cicero did not hesitate to say of them: "The flower of the Roman knights, the ornament of the state, the pillar of the commonwealth, is contained in the order of the tax collectors." Nor was this said rashly, since it is certain that the sinews of the commonwealth rest chiefly in the treasury, which is mainly fed by taxes. But the opinion of the Jews about them was quite different. For since they bore the Roman empire with indignation, and aspired with all their hearts to their old liberty, they could not but hate those who, for the sake of private gain, hired out their services to the Romans, and who were ministers of foreign tyranny against their brothers, that is, their own people. That hatred was all the more bitter because they thought that servitude of this kind was a disgrace to their country's religion. In addition there was the avarice and cruelty of the tax collectors, who, not content to exact what was owed by custom, devised new methods every day by which the taxes were made heavier, so that more profit would come back to themselves, as Zacchaeus's confession will show below. And so it came about that the tax collectors were hated and infamous to everyone, and at the same time those who were their friends or supporters also got a bad name. This was the reason why they called Christ, by way of insult, a friend and patron of tax collectors. For another reason too, these matters must be considered more carefully by us. We are taught by the example of the Jews what generally happens to all who do not know how to use the gift of liberty, and who, having lost it, are therefore made subject to the lust of others. For many centuries they had been that chosen possession of God, and they had enjoyed a liberty above other nations, a thing than which nothing is more excellent among earthly goods, and nothing is more to be desired by a free man. Yet these same people (as we have heard elsewhere) are now oppressed by the harsh and greedy rule of those whom they rightly abhorred on account of idolatry and wicked superstitions, and whom they knew to be hateful to God as well. Then they pay tribute to foreigners, and in addition are burdened beyond custom with extraordinary tributes and levies. And that no injury may be lacking, tax collectors and officials from their own nation are added, by whose devices they are plundered all the more, because these were more intolerable to them than strangers would have been, since they could do more harm, knowing the circumstances and fortunes of each individual rather closely. What, then, was the cause of all this? Surely none other than disobedience and ingratitude toward God, and that, carried away by private passions, they stirred up civil wars, of which more will be said in the following sermon. Nor did the misery of this unhappy people end here. But since they did not turn to God, and instead wished day by day to recover by new seditions the liberty they had lost, they provoked the arms of the Romans against themselves, and an example was made of them such as is found in no histories. All of us to whom it is now given to enjoy liberty ought to weigh these things carefully, lest at some time, having lost it, we pay similar penalties to the just vengeance of God.

units.la: His praemissis ad loci huius tractationem accedamus, vbi primum publicanorum quaestio occurrit, qui perinde vt prius alij ex populo, Ioannem interrogant: Magister, quid faciemus? Ergo ipsi etiam animis suis perculsi, intelligunt sibi non minus quam alijs repigiscentia opus esse: neque dubium est eos doctrina de beneficentia vehementer fuisse commotos. Quia enim audiebant hoc ab omnibus requiri, vt ex suis facultatibus in quosuis benefici sint, facile intellexerunt, se minime extra culpam esse, qui hucusque gentiles suos artibus proditorijs circumuenissent, & Romanae tyrannidis iugu, per se plus satis graue & intolerabile, sua auaritia & crudelitate magis aggrauassent. Et enim quaestionem hanc non curiosam, neque in Ioannis contemptum per ludibrium propositam fuisse (vt saepe illusores impij de multis interrogare consueuerunt) ex Christi verbis patet, qui illos audita Ioannis doctrina Deum iustificauisse & baptizatos fuisse ait. Et apud Matthaeum Pharisaeus idem dicit: Amen dico vobis, quod publicani & meretrices praeeunt vobis in regnum Dei. Venit enim ad vos Ioannes via iustitiae, & non credidistis ei: publicani vero & meretrices crediderunt ei, &c. Obseruemus nos in horum exemplo paternam Dei bonitatem, qui (vt apud Ezechielem ait) non vult mortem pec-
units.tr: With these things set out, let us come to the treatment of this passage, where first the question of the tax collectors arises. Like the others from the people before them, they ask John: "Teacher, what shall we do?" Thus they too, struck in their minds, understand that they need repentance no less than others, and there is no doubt that they were powerfully moved by the teaching on beneficence. For when they heard that this was required of everyone, that they should be beneficent to whomever they could from their own resources, they readily understood that they were far from blameless, since until now they had cheated their fellow countrymen by treacherous arts, and had made the yoke of Roman tyranny, already heavy and intolerable enough in itself, heavier still by their own avarice and cruelty. That this question was not a curious one, nor put forward to mock and despise John (as impious scoffers have often been accustomed to question many people), is clear from the words of Christ, who says that they, having heard John's teaching, justified God and were baptized. And in Matthew the Pharisee says the same thing: "Truly I say to you, that tax collectors and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but tax collectors and harlots believed him," and so on. Let us observe in the example of these men the fatherly goodness of God, who (as he says through Ezekiel) does not want the death of the sin-

units.la: Luc. 7. Matth. 21. tem peccatoris, neq; ad se venientes peccatores aspernatur aut fastidit, sed benignè suscipit, ut salui fiant. Venerunt isti, non aliqua iustitiæ propriæ fiducia inflati, sed quòd se peccatis obnoxios esse sentirent, & Dei iram declinare cuperent; ideo animos eorum illuminat Dei Spiritus, ut in æternæ salutis negotio progressus faciant non pœnitendos. Hinc ergo consolatione petant quicunq; peccatorum suorum multitudine & gravitate intra conscientiam suam tentantur: neq; publicanos hosce aliquo privilegio singulari vsos putent, cum generales promissiones passim occurrant, quibus eandem gratiam omnibus pollicetur Deus, qui ad ipsum conuerruntur [?]. Simul verò officij hoc omnes admonet, ut ipsi quoque audita pœnitentiæ doctrina de se agi cogitent, & de illis diligenter atque serio inquirant, quæ ipsis agenda sunt: Ut enim gratiam suam nobis offert Deus liberalissimè, ita graviter eorum improbitatem & socordiam vlciscitur, qui illius prædicationem negligunt.
units.tr: Luke 7; Matt. 21. ner, nor does he reject or disdain sinners who come to him, but receives them kindly that they may be saved. These men came not puffed up by any confidence in their own righteousness, but because they felt themselves bound by sins and wished to avert the wrath of God; therefore the Spirit of God enlightens their minds, so that they make progress in the business of eternal salvation, progress that need not be regretted. Hence let whoever is troubled in conscience by the multitude and weight of his sins take consolation here; and let them not think that these tax collectors enjoyed some singular privilege, since general promises occur everywhere by which God offers the same grace to all who turn to him. At the same time this passage admonishes everyone of their duty, so that, having heard the doctrine of repentance, they also think that it concerns themselves, and inquire carefully and seriously about what they must do. For just as God offers his grace to us most generously, so he severely punishes the wickedness and sloth of those who neglect his preaching.

units.la: Porrò Ioannem audiamus illis ad hunc modum concionantem: Nihil amplius quàm quod con- stitutum est vobis, exigite. Breuis concio, sed quæ plurima ad rempub. et priuatorum hominum vitam pertinentia comprehendit. Quia verò in verbis obscuritas nulla est, res ipsas excutiemus.
units.tr: Let us next hear John preaching in this manner: "Collect no more than what has been appointed to you." A brief sermon, yet one that comprehends very much that pertains to the commonwealth and to the life of private persons. But since there is no obscurity in the words, we shall examine the matters themselves.

units.la: In his primum est, quòd paucis hisce verbis & communè populi Iudaici de suo statu, in quo tunc erat, opinionem, & quæ tunc regnabat, pharisaicam doctrinam aperte atq; libere condemnat. Nam vt ante diximus, Iudæis indignum videbatur, populum Deo sacrum impuris et prophanis gentibus seruire, censum qui olim Deo debebatur ijsdem persoluere, vectigalibus item & tributis quotidie onerus grauari, & ideo non solùm modo, verumetiam totum publicanorum ordinem, quasi Deo inimicum & publicam patriæ pestem, abominabantur. Erant in eadem sententia Pharisæi quoque qui simul sanctitatem omnem in externis ritibus & sacrificijs, in primis autem in suarum traditionum & pharisaismi obseruatione cõsistere putabant. Et si hos interrogauissent publicani, procul dubio nõ aliud responsuri erant, quàm trita illa: Afferte sacrificia in templum, quibus admissa scelera expietis, pecunias deponite in gazophylacium & corbonam, relictis item telonijs & vectigalibus nouum vitæ genus sequimini, multiplicate certas preculas, ieiunate bis aut ter in sabbato, lauamini quotidie, decimate mentham & anethum, & infinita alia huius generis, quæ ab illis anxiè obseruata fuisse constat. At longè aliter Ioannes concionatur. Nihil amplius (inquit) quàm quod constitutum est vobis, exigite. Ergo licuit illis per Ioannem publicanis manere, ad telonium sedere et vectigalia colligere, nec tamen dubium est, quin eos ad pœnitentiam hæc ipsa dicendo hortatus sit. Itaq; damnat vulgi opinionem seditiosam, qua plerique decepti immunitatem quærebat, & quod Romani in illam gentem obtinebant imperium doctrina sua cõfirmat: simulq; monet, scelera nõ externis ceremonijs, ieiunijs, preculis, sed solius Christi sanguine expiari, ab ipsis autem exigi iustitiam, ne quem sui cõmodi causa præter ius & æquum grauent aut prædentur. Hinc ergo generalis doctrina colligi debet, li- cere magistratui vectigalia, tributa, census & quæ alia sunt huius generis à subditis exigere, neque etiam peccare eos, qui in his colligendis illi seruiunt. Quia enim principes publicū munus sustinent, quo pax publica conseruatur, patria communis defenditur, ius cuique dicitur, & ijdem vias publicas, muros, fontes & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi instaurant atq; seruant, quibus omnes promiscuè fruuntur: æquum planè iustumq; est, ut publicè ab omnibus conferantur sumptus, qui in istas res sunt faciendi. Neq; sumptus soli conferri debent, sed cùm operarius dignus sit mercede sua, tantum exigere licet, quantum illis alendis & ad tuendam magistratus authoritatem sufficit. Iubet hoc communis sensus & naturæ Lex, quam omnium animis insculpsit Deus, & qua fit, ut mos iste iam inde à rerum origine apud omnes gentes receptus fuerit, quotquot aliqua reipub. forma sunt vsæ. Quòd si quis obijciat, ista non alia quàm humana authoritate & consuetudine niti, nos negamus humanam traditionem censeri debere, quod cum Lege naturæ conuenit. Huius enim opus cordibus inscriptum esse dicit Apostolus, & proinde ad Deum authorem referri debet, qui solus in corda hominum ius habet, ut ea illuminet, moueat, inclinet & regat. Deinde sanctissimos reges adducimus, quorum fides & pietas in scripturis commendatur, qui tamen suo illo iure in subditos vsi sunt absq; omni spiritus sancti reprehensione. His postremò Christi authoritatem addimus, qui morem istum exemplo simul suo & doctrina probauit. Nam sub censu natum fuisse supra audiuimus, & idem pro seipso & Petro censum persoluit, nimirum vt ijs occurreret, qui sub libertatis Christianæ prætextu immunitatem ab oneribus politicis vsanantur, aut (quod papisticus ille clerus solet) ecclesiastica dignitate ad hoc abuntur. Idem à Iudæorum præsulibus de hac re interrogatus, Reddite (inquit) quæ Cæsaris sunt Cæsari, et quæ Dei sunt Deo. Quem postea Paulus Apostolus secutus, de magistratus authoritate multis disserit, et hanc diuinitus institutam esse probat, cui omnes obedire debeant: inter officia autem subditorum vectigalia & quæ huius generis sunt comprehendit. Propter hoc enim (inquit) et vectigalia soluitis; siquidem ministri Dei sunt in hoc ipsum incumbentes. Reddite igitur omnibus quod debetis: cui tributum debetur, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem; cui honorem, honorem. Debendi verbo vtitur, et tributa atq; vectigalia cum timore & honore coniungit, quæ nos superioribus non ex dispensatione aliqua, sed diuino iure debere nemo negauerit, nisi qui à communi sensu fuerit alienus. Minimè ergo audiri merentur Anabaptistæ furiosi et fanatici homines, quibus non satis est ecclesiæ ordinem turbauisse, nisi rempub. quoq; inuadant, magistratus omnes ex suo solio detrahant, potestatem tenebrarum eos dicant, confusionem rerum omnium inducant, adeoq; cælum terræ misceant. Sunt hi non solum reipub. & magistratuum hostes, verumetiam pestes humani generis, cum ea è medio tollant, sine quibus societas humana consistere non potest. Confutantur hi non ijs modo, quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, sed præsenti etiam Ioannis exemplo, qui non ipsum publicanorum ordinem damnauit, neq; ab eo illos discedere iussit, sed quales in suo officio obeundo esse debeant docuit. Quòd si ergo illis licuit operam suam in colligendis vectigalibus Tiberio Imperatori præstare, neq; hoc obstitit quò minus salui fierent nimium profectò morosi sunt, qui Christianos principes et eorum ministros hodie isto nomine damnant.
units.tr: First, in these few words he openly and freely condemns the common opinion of the Jewish people about their condition at that time, and the Pharisaic teaching that then prevailed. As we said before, the Jews thought it unworthy that a people holy to God should serve impure and profane nations, should pay to them the tribute once owed to God, and should be daily burdened with customs duties and taxes. For this reason they abhorred not only the tax collectors but the whole order of publicans, as enemies of God and a public plague of the country. The Pharisees shared this view. They thought that all holiness consisted in external rites and sacrifices, and above all in the observance of their own traditions and Pharisaism. If the publicans had asked these men what to do, they would doubtless have answered with the familiar formulas: bring sacrifices into the temple by which you may atone for your sins; deposit your money in the treasury and the corban; leave off the toll-booths and taxes and follow a new way of life; multiply your set prayers; fast twice or three times on the Sabbath; wash daily; tithe mint and dill; and countless other things of this kind, which are known to have been observed by them with anxious care. But John preaches quite differently. "Demand nothing more," he says, "than what has been appointed for you." So it was lawful for these publicans, through John, to remain in their posts, to sit at the toll-booth and collect the taxes; and yet there is no doubt that by saying this he was exhorting them to repentance. Thus he condemns the seditious opinion of the common people, by which most were deceived, who sought exemption, and by his teaching he confirms that the Romans held rule over that nation. At the same time he warns that sins are not expiated by external ceremonies, fasts or prayers, but by the blood of Christ alone, and that justice is required of them, so that they should not burden or plunder anyone beyond right and fairness for their own advantage. From this, then, a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that the magistrate may lawfully exact from his subjects customs duties, taxes, levies and other things of this kind, and that those who serve him in collecting them do not sin. For since the princes bear the public office by which public peace is preserved, the common fatherland is defended, justice is administered to each, and they likewise maintain and keep in repair the public roads, walls, springs and other such things which all use in common, it is plainly fair and just that the expenses needed for these things should be contributed publicly by all. Nor should the expenses fall only on some, but since the workman is worthy of his wage, it is lawful to demand only as much as is sufficient to support the rulers and to maintain the authority of the magistrate. Common sense and the law of nature command this, the law which God has engraved on the minds of all, and because of which this custom has been received among all nations from the very beginning of things, as many as have used some form of commonwealth. But if anyone objects that these things rest on nothing but human authority and custom, we deny that what agrees with the law of nature ought to be counted a human tradition. For the Apostle says that this work is written on hearts, and therefore it must be referred to God the author, who alone has the right over the hearts of men, to enlighten, move, incline and rule them. Next we adduce the most holy kings, whose faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures, who nevertheless used this right over their subjects without any rebuke from the Holy Spirit. Lastly we add the authority of Christ, who approved this custom both by his example and by his teaching. For we heard above that he was born under the census, and he himself paid the census for himself and for Peter, doubtless to meet those who, under the pretext of Christian liberty, claim exemption from political burdens, or (as that Papist clergy is wont to do) abuse ecclesiastical dignity for this purpose. When the leaders of the Jews asked him about this matter, he said: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Afterwards the Apostle Paul followed him, and discourses at length on the authority of the magistrate, and proves that it was instituted by God, and that all must obey it; among the duties of subjects he includes taxes and things of this kind. "For this reason," he says, "you also pay tributes, for they are ministers of God, attending continually to this very thing. Render therefore to all what you owe: tribute to whom tribute is due, customs to whom customs, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour." He uses the word "owe," and joins tributes and customs with fear and honour; and no one would deny that we owe these to the rulers above not by some arrangement but by divine right, unless he were a stranger to common sense. Therefore the furious and fanatical Anabaptists do not deserve to be heard at all. It is not enough for them to have thrown the order of the Church into confusion; they also attack the commonwealth, drag all magistrates down from their thrones, call them the power of darkness, bring about confusion of all things, and so mix heaven with earth. They are not only enemies of the commonwealth and the magistrates, but also plagues of the human race, since they remove from the midst those things without which human society cannot exist. They are refuted not only by what has been said so far, but also by the present example of John, who did not condemn the order of publicans itself, nor bid them withdraw from it, but taught how they ought to conduct themselves in their office. But if it was lawful for them to render their service in collecting the taxes to the Emperor Tiberius, and this did not stand in the way of their being saved, then surely they are far too fastidious who today condemn Christian princes and their ministers under that name.

units.la: Cæterum quod Ioannes publicanis dicit, latius extendi debet, quando omnium est nihil amplius, quàm ipsis debeatur, à quoquâ exigere. Primùm ergo hoc sibi dictum meminerint principes viri et qui cunq; magistratu gerunt, ne suæ fidei creditum populum exactionibus immodicis aggrauent. Nam vt modò diximus, debetur illis tributa, census & vectigalia omnis generis. At quia ipsi vicissim populo debent defensionem & curam paternam, istorum omnium exactiones non pro suo arbitrio auge re, sed pro ratione fortunarum populi instituere, & publicis quoq; impensis, quoad fieri potest, parcere debent, ne plebem prorsus exhauriant. Vt enim reipub. nerui in ærario magna ex parte siti sunt, ita qui in hoc conferuntur redditus durabiles esse non possunt, nisi iusti & moderati sint. Prudenter ergo olim Traianus ærarium lieni conferebat, quia vt hoc crescente reliqua membra cotabescunt: ita cum immodicis exactionibus ærarium augetur, fieri non potest, quin attenuentur subditorum fortunæ & tandem cum his respub. tota deficiat. Quodipsum Tiberius quoq;, quo regnante Ioannes & Christus docuerunt, obseruauit. Nam suadentibus nonnullis, vt prouincias tributis maioribus oneraret, respondit: Boni pastoris est tondere gregem, non deglubere. Potuerunt ista videre prophani principes, qui non aliam quàm naturæ legem secuti sunt. Quin ergo erubescitis Christiani reges & principes, qui hodie miseros agricolas, cives, opifices, adhæc viduas & pupillos deglubitis, & horum labo ribus partas pecunias vel in ædificia insana, vel in turpe aleam, vel in conuiuia luxuriosa, vel infa stuosum aulæ & gynæcei apparatum, vel in venationes & canes, vel etiâ in scurras & lenones in sumitis: adhæc bella mouetis nō necessaria, quibus quicquid infelix populus reliquum habet, id quoq; totum partim ab hostibus partim à socijs diripitur & vastatur? Nefas olim putabat Dauid aquâ bibere, quam cum manifesto vitæ periculo viri fortes adipsum detulerant. At vobis leuiculum videtur ipsum sanguinem subditorum exigere, & miseros tantùmnon fame enecare, vt vestræ libidini & luxuriæ satis sit. Debent quidem ista patienter ferre Christiani homines, at non patienter illa ferret Deus, qui subditorum sanguine de manibus vestris requiret, & insolentiam vestram dignis pænis coercebit. Discite ergo ijs animum attendere, quæ ad reipub. conseruationem faciunt. Meminer ritis item, vos populi pastores & patres à Deo esse constitutos, & vobis etiam dictum cogitate, ne quid amplius quàm vobis constitutum est exigatis. Nec est quod vobis ex eo aliquid decessurum esse verearimini. Magnum enim vectigal est parsimonia, & si ex aulis vestris profligetis luxum et intemperantiam, mox sentietis & ærarium augeri & populi fortunas florere, sicque ad omnem euentum eritis instructissimi. Accedat huic curæ alia quoque, ne officia publica vel pretio vendantur, vel hominibus auaris aut prodigis committantur. Nam vt Alexander Seuerus Imperator dicebat, necesse est vendat qui emit. Alteris verò illis nihil sufficit, & qui tales ad rempub. admittunt, ijsdem socios se faciunt, & populum illis propinant exugendum, quos sua authoritate coercere coercere debebant. De Thebanis tradunt historiæ, neminem apud illos ad rempub. administrationem admissum fuisse, qui non prius per annos decem à mercatura abstinuisset. Putabant enim difficile esse, vt homines lucro & luxui dediti & assueti in altiori dignitatis gradu mores mutarent.
units.tr: Moreover, what John says to the publicans ought to be extended more widely, since it is the duty of all to demand from anyone nothing more than what is owed to them. Let princes first, then, and all who bear magistracy, remember that this has been said to them as well: they must not burden the people entrusted to their faith with excessive exactions. For, as we have just said, taxes, levies and customs duties of every kind are owed to them. But since they in turn owe the people defence and a fatherly care, they must not increase all these exactions at their own pleasure, but fix them according to the means of the people, and they must also spare public expenses as far as possible, lest they utterly drain the common folk. For just as the sinews of the commonwealth lie for the most part in the treasury, so the revenues gathered in this way cannot be lasting unless they are just and moderate. Wisely, then, Trajan once compared the treasury to the spleen, because as this grows the other members waste away; so when the treasury is swollen with immoderate exactions, it cannot but be that the fortunes of the subjects are weakened and in the end the whole commonwealth fails along with them. Tiberius too, under whose reign John and Christ taught, observed this. For when some urged him to burden the provinces with heavier tributes, he replied: "It is the mark of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it." Profane princes, who followed nothing but the law of nature, were able to see these things. Why, then, are you not ashamed, Christian kings and princes, who today flay the wretched farmers, citizens, craftsmen, and moreover widows and orphans, and who spend the money gained by their labours either on mad buildings, or on shameful gambling, or on luxurious banquets, or on the expensive display of court and women's quarters, or on hunting and hounds, or even on buffoons and pimps; and who moreover wage unnecessary wars, by which whatever remains to the unhappy people is plundered and laid waste, partly by enemies and partly by allies? David thought it wrong to drink the water which brave men had brought to him at the manifest risk of their lives. But to you it seems a trifle to extract the very blood of your subjects and almost to starve the wretched to death, so that it may suffice for your lust and luxury. Christian men ought indeed to bear these things patiently, but God will not bear them patiently; he will require the blood of the subjects at your hands and will punish your insolence with fitting penalties. Learn, then, to give your attention to those things which serve the preservation of the commonwealth. Remember also that you have been appointed by God as shepherds and fathers of the people, and take to heart the saying addressed to you as well: that you should demand nothing more than what has been appointed for you. Nor have you cause to fear that anything will be lost to you from this. For thrift is a great revenue, and if you banish luxury and intemperance from your courts, you will soon see both the treasury increased and the fortunes of the people flourishing, and so you will be most fully equipped for every event. To this care let another be added: that public offices should neither be sold for money nor entrusted to greedy or prodigal men. For, as the Emperor Alexander Severus used to say, the buyer must necessarily sell. Those others, however, are never satisfied, and those who admit such men to the commonwealth make them partners and offer the people to them to be drained, whom they ought to restrain by their own authority. Histories tell of the Thebans that no one was admitted among them to the administration of the commonwealth who had not first abstained from trade for ten years. For they thought it hard for men devoted to gain and luxury, and accustomed to them, to change their manners once they had risen to a higher rank of dignity.

units.la: At non satis erit principes viros officium fecisse, nisi quotquot sub illis officia publica obeunt, Baptistæ præceptum ad se pertinere cogitent, nec à quoquam quid amplius extorqueant, quàm ipsis iure debetur. Quin studeant potius sua facilitate onera populi tolerabiliora reddere, & principibus eius generis consilia suggerant. Ita enim & his fidi erunt, & populum ingenti beneficio sibi demerebuntur, & ad reipub. incolumitatem plurimum adiumenti conferent. E contra si nimij sint, & vel sibi ipsis plus æquo vendicent, vel principibus authores sint, vt populus nouis tributis atque exactionibus grauetur, seipsos quidem grauissimo scelere polluunt, & alienæ libidinis ministri fiunt, simul vero non sibi ipsis solùm, verumetiam principibus suis inuidiam atque odium conflant, & saepe seditionum grauissimarum semina iaciunt. Exemplum huius rei euidens in Roboami historia sacræ literæ proponunt. Cùm enim is populo, tributorum alleuationem postulanti, ex iuniorum & coætaneorum suorum consilio durius respondisset, omnium animos abs se alienauit, & mox regni scisma secutum est, quod tandem genti vniuersæ exitium attulit. Similiter Lacedæmonij olim, postquam à maiorum frugalitate degeneres per suos præfectos & officiales imperia in subditos auarius exercuerunt, tam sibi ipsis quàm toti Græciæ odia & bella concitarunt exitialia. Ideo apud Romanos non minus prudenter quàm grauiter obseruata fuit Lex repetundarum, quam primò L. Piso cognomento Frugi tulit, postea autem Iulius Cæsar instaurauit: qua cauebatur, ne quis in prouinciam missus cum potestate pecuniam vllam à prouincialibus aliisue acciperet, præter quàm à personis sanguine sibi coniunctis: item vt vrbani magistratus ab omni sorde abstinerent: qua etiam plectebantur, qui ob rem iudicandam aut non iudicandam, ob denuntiandum vel non denuntiandum testimonium pecuniam accepissent. Et vt Cicero in Verrinis docet, Lex ista in primis sociorum causa lata fuit, ne videlicet proconsulum aut præsidum auaritia & iniquitate grauarentur: cuius legis authoritatem minus valuisse suo tempore vir prudentissimus non sine causa queritur, quò eadem opera rempub. vehementer labefactata esse videret. Quòd si nostri temporis mores inspiciamus, hæc fere omnium malorum in repub. causa est, quod qui rebus administrandis præsunt, immodica habendi cupiditate accensi opes vndiq; corradunt, & authoritate publica ad suum commodum abutuntur. Ergo omnium illorum auribus intonari debebat Ioannis nostri vox: Nihil amplius, quàm quod constitutum est vobis, exigite.
units.tr: Yet it will not be enough for princes to do their duty unless all who hold public offices under them also take to heart the precept of the Baptist, and do not extort from anyone more than is due to them by right. Rather, they should strive to make the burdens of the people more bearable by their own fairness, and offer such counsel to princes of this kind. In this way they will be faithful to the princes, will win great goodwill from the people, and will contribute much help to the safety of the commonwealth. On the other hand, if they are greedy, and either claim more for themselves than is fair or urge the princes to burden the people with new taxes and levies, they defile themselves with a most grievous crime and become the servants of another's lust. At the same time they stir up hatred and odium not only against themselves but also against their princes, and often sow the seeds of most serious seditions. Holy Scripture sets before us a clear example of this in the history of Rehoboam. When he answered the people, who asked for a reduction of their taxes, more harshly on the advice of his young companions of the same age, he alienated the minds of all from himself. Soon afterwards came the division of the kingdom, which at last brought ruin upon the whole nation. Likewise the Lacedaemonians once, after they had fallen away from the frugality of their ancestors, exercised their dominion over subjects more greedily through their governors and officials, and so stirred up deadly hatreds and wars both for themselves and for all Greece. Therefore among the Romans the law on extortion was observed no less wisely than seriously. It was first passed by Lucius Piso, surnamed Frugi, and afterwards renewed by Julius Caesar. By it, care was taken that no one sent into a province with authority should accept any money from the provincials or others, except from persons related to him by blood. Likewise, urban magistrates were to abstain from every kind of filthy gain. Those also were punished who had accepted money for judging or not judging, or for giving or not giving evidence. As Cicero teaches in the Verrine orations, this law was passed chiefly for the sake of the allies, lest the proconsuls or governors should be burdened by greed and injustice. That this law had less force in his own time, a most prudent man complains, and not without reason, since he saw that the commonwealth was at the same time greatly weakened. But if we look at the morals of our own age, this is almost always the cause of every evil in the commonwealth: those who preside over public affairs, inflamed by an immoderate desire to have, gather wealth from every side and abuse public authority for their own advantage. Therefore the voice of our John ought to have rung in the ears of all those men: "Demand nothing more than what has been appointed for you."

units.la: At eadem non minus ad homines priuatos pertinet, quibus præclara occasio de rebus suis rectius cogitandi hic proponitur. Peccant enim in hanc legem mercatores, dum pretium iniquum petunt, aut etiam ponderibus & mensuris iniustis vtuntur, vel merces ipsas malitiosè corrumpunt. Peccant etiam opifices, dum opera sua maioris indicant: mercenarij item qui in operè segnes & ignaui, mercedem tamen plenam sibi numerari postulant. Peccant praeterea qui mutuum dando charitatem & beneficentiam simulant, interim vero suis intenti plus recipiunt quàm ipsis debeatur. In qua re nostro seculo tam ingeniosa & subdola est auaritia, vt nemo artibus & impostoris, quibus passim peccatur, enumerandis sufficiat. Alij enim debitores in ipsa forte defraudant, dum non tantum illis numerant, quantum illi reddere coguntur. Alij etsi tantum dedisse videantur, dolosè tamen vel nummos maioris æstimant, quàm exponi possint, vel pecunijs fruges, pecora, aut alia infinita admiscent, quorum pretium iniquissimum indicant: multi debita, de quibus iampridem tantùmnon desperauerunt, egentibus obtrudunt, & quæ isti nunquam possunt integra recipere. Sunt qui census nimios postulant, & (vt Amos loquitur) onus frumenti miseris imponunt, & ita eos miserabiliter opprimunt, quos sua ope subleuare videri volunt. Debent his propolæ adnumerari, & qui monopolia exercent, quorum omnium hoc studium est, vt fruges & alias omnis generis merces in suam potestatem redigant, neque eas prius diuendant, quàm illarum pretium ad summum vsque excreuisse viderint. Et hi quidem omnes se rebus suis quàm optimè consulere arbitrantur, seq; excusatos putant, quòd non alia ratione ditescere possint. At idem Dei iudicio fures sunt, & illius iram incurrunt, imò plerunque publicorum malorum sunt authores: sicuti non obscurè per Amos prophetam Dominus docet. Audite (inquit) istud vos, qui absorbetis pauperes, & inopes è terra exterminatis, dicentes: Post mensem venum exponemus annonam, & exacta hebdomade aperiemus frumentum, epha diminuemus, siclum autem maiorem faciemus, & bilancem dolo se depravabimus, vt comparemus tenues argento, & inopem pro pari calceamentorum, deinde & quisquilias cum frumento distrahemus. Quid vero hic aliud dicit propheta quàm quod hodie passim fieri videmus? Sed audi simul pœnam, quam moribus istis Deus denuntiat: Iurauit Dominus per excellentiam Iacobi si vn-quam obliuioni tradam omnia opera eorum. Annon super hoc terra contremiscat? Et lugebit omnis, qui in ea habitat. Quin vniuersa vt fluuius incumescet, &c. Ergo non tam incolas quàm terram ipsam per eiusmodi homines grauari Deus docet, & constat ex historijs, apud omnes gentes ferè publicorum motuum & seditionum causas præbuisse homines auaros & vsurarios, qui suis commodis cum aliorum incommodo consulere solent. Apud Romanos certè hinc occasionem tumultuandi non se-mel sumpserunt, qui vel nouas tabulas fieri, vel legem agrariam instaurari postulabant. Vidimus multa huius generis etiam nostro seculo, & non obscura indicia sunt, quæ docent graviora pericula breui vbiq; terrarum exoritura esse, nisi auaritiæ & rapacitati multorum frænum iniiciatur. Quapro-pter in istorum consideratione frequentes sint omnis ordinis & loci homines, & singuli sibijpsis appli-cent Ioannis regulam, quam publicanis præscribit, ne quid præterquàm quod ipsis ex iure debetur, exigant. Inscribatur (inquam) ea omnibus ædium parietibus, officinis omnibus, legatur in curia, in foro, in omnium deniq; auribus atq; animis perpetuo resonet. Nec est, quòd quisquâ ex eo inopiam aut egestatem metuat. Sunt enim Deo curæ res hominum, & qui huius benedictionem expectant ea in præsenti seculo fruentur, & simul æternæ vitæ hæredes fient per fidem in Iesum Christum: cui debe-tur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But the same applies no less to private persons, for whom a splendid opportunity of thinking more rightly about their own affairs is set before them here. Merchants sin against this law when they ask an unfair price, or use unjust weights and measures, or wickedly adulterate their wares. Craftsmen also sin when they overvalue their work. Likewise hired workers sin when they are idle and lazy at their task, yet demand their full wages to be counted out to them. Furthermore, those sin who, in lending, feign charity and kindness while in fact, intent on their own gain, they receive more than is owed to them. In this matter, in our century, avarice is so ingenious and crafty that no one is equal to listing the tricks and frauds by which people everywhere sin. Some debtors defraud in the very counting, for they do not count out as much as the creditors are forced to repay. Others, though they seem to have given as much, deceitfully either value the coins above what they can be spent for, or mix in with the money crops, livestock, or countless other things, whose price they set at the highest possible rate. Many thrust upon the needy debts of which they had long almost despaired, and which those men can never recover in full. There are those who demand excessive rents, and (as Amos says) lay a burden of grain upon the wretched, and so miserably oppress those whom they wish to seem to relieve by their help. Forestallers should be counted among these, as should monopolists, all of whose aim is to bring grain and every kind of goods into their own power, and not to sell them until they see the price has risen to the highest point. All these men think they are looking after their own affairs as well as possible, and they suppose themselves excused because they cannot grow rich in any other way.
