Yet in the judgment of God they are thieves, and incur his wrath; indeed, they are for the most part the authors of public calamities, as the Lord teaches not obscurely through the prophet Amos. "Hear this" (he says), "you who swallow up the poor and bring the needy to an end in the land, saying: After the month we will sell our corn, and when the week is over we will open the grain; we will diminish the ephah, make the shekel greater, and falsify the balances by deceit, so that we may buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes, and sell even the refuse with the wheat." What else does the prophet say here than what we see happening everywhere today? But hear also the punishment which God threatens for such manners: "The Lord has sworn by the excellency of Jacob that if I ever forget any of their works. Shall not the land tremble for this? And everyone who dwells in it shall mourn. Indeed, all of it shall swell up like a river, etc." Therefore God teaches that it is not so much the inhabitants as the land itself that is burdened by men of this kind. And it is established from histories that among almost all nations greedy and usurious men, who are accustomed to look after their own convenience at the expense of others, have provided the causes of public disturbances and seditions. Among the Romans, certainly, those who demanded either new account books or the restoration of an agrarian law often took from this an occasion for riot. We have seen many things of this kind in our own age too, and there are clear signs teaching that graver dangers will soon arise everywhere on earth unless a bridle is put upon the avarice and rapacity of many. Therefore let men of every rank and place often consider these things, and let each apply to himself the rule of John, which he prescribed to the tax collectors: that they should demand nothing beyond what is owed to them by right. Let it be written (I say) on the walls of every house and every workshop; let it be read in the senate-house, in the marketplace, and finally let it resound perpetually in the ears and minds of all. Nor is there any reason for anyone to fear poverty or want from this. For the affairs of men are a care to God, and those who look for his blessing will enjoy it in the present age, and at the same time will become heirs of eternal life through faith in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXI.

units.la: Interrogauerunt autem eum etiam milites, dicentes: Et nos quid fa-ciemus? Et ait eis: Neminem concutite, neq; calumniemini: & contenti estote stipendijs vestris.
units.tr: The soldiers also asked him, saying: "What shall we do?" And he said to them: "Do violence to no one, and do not accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages."

units.la: IOannis Baptistæ officiū fuit, populum per pœnitentiæ prædicationem ad Christū dignè excipien-dum præparare. Idergo sic facit, vt nō solum generalem doctrinam siue admonitionem proponat, sed singulos ferè omnis loci & ordinis homines instituit, sicq; suo exemplo docet, quæ ratio docendi in pœnitentiæ articulo tenerí debeat: ea nimirum, vt singuli de se agi sentiant, simulq; intelligant, quid ipsis vitandum quidve faciendum sit. Et hactenus quidem illū Pharisæis, deinde promiscuo vulgo, & nuper publicanis concionantem audiuimus: ex quibus concionibus generalis doctrina peti potest, eos demum vere pœnitentiam agere, qui procul reiecto omni fuco aut hypocrisi, ad Deum ex animo conuertuntur per fidem in Iesum Christum, seq; vere conuersos esse charitatis & beneficentiæ stu-dio, iustitia item in omnibus vitæ suæ actionibus testantur. Sequitur nouæ cōcionis argumentū, qua milites instituit: vbi rursus paucis verbis multa comprehenduntur scitu & obseruatu dignißima.
units.tr: It was the office of John the Baptist to prepare the people, through the preaching of repentance, to receive Christ worthily. He therefore does not only set out a general teaching or exhortation, but addresses almost every individual of each place and rank. In this way he shows by his own example how the method of teaching should be kept in the matter of repentance: namely, that each person should feel that the matter concerns himself, and at the same time understand what he must avoid and what he must do. So far we have heard him preaching to the Pharisees, then to the common crowd, and lately to the tax collectors. From these sermons a general teaching may be drawn: those truly repent who, having cast off all pretence and hypocrisy, turn to God from the heart through faith in Jesus Christ, and who show that they are truly converted by their zeal for love and kindness, and likewise by righteousness in all the actions of their lives. Now follows the subject of a new sermon, in which he instructs the soldiers. In a few words many things most worthy of being known and observed are again comprehended.

units.la: Ante omnia autem videndum erit, qui nam & quales fuerint milites illi, de quibus hic agitur. Sunt enim, qui ista de mercenarijs militibus, quales hodie passim inueniuntur, exponentes, ei homi-num generi ex Euangelij doctrina patrocinium quærunt, quo nullum et reipub. pernitiosius & à Chri-stiana fide atq; religione magis alienū est. Atqui militibus ordinarijs concionatur Ioannes, qui sub magistratu legitimo ad Imperij Romani & pacis publicæ defensione arma gerebant, & quorū tunc magnus numerus per Syriam totam & Iudæa dispositus erat, sicuti ex historijs apparet. Cùm enim inter duos fratres, Hircanū & Aristobulū, de regno & sacerdotio lis exorta in bellū ciuile exarsis-set, vtriq; ad externa auxilia concursum est. Et Hircanus quidē à fratre eiectus, primùm ex An-tipatri Idumæi consilio ad Aretam Arabiæ regem confugit, qui etiam collectis copijs illum in rea-gnum reducere conatus est. Aristobulus autem Scaurum Romanum imperatorem muneribus attra-xit, vt ipsius defensionem susciperet: quæres Aretam terruit, vt dimisso exercitu in Arabiam ad sua rediret. Nō multò post, cùm Pompeius Magnus à debellato Tigrane Damascū venisset, hunc quoque Aristobulus magnis muneribus in partes suas pertrahere satagit. Adest & Hircanus, ipse etiam Romanorum auxilia implorat. Aristobulus, quòd pactis non staret, Pompeium commo-uit, vt vrbem irrumperet, & templo simul per vim & non sine horribili Iudæorum strage occupato in Sanctum sanctorum ingrederetur, & ea spectaret, quæ nemini præterquàm summo Pontifici videre licebat. Et Hircano quidem Pontificatum concessit, sed corona vti prohibuit. Itaq; sceptrū tunc à Iudæis ablatum fuit, & regnum sibi in illos vendicarunt Romani. Aristobulus autem à Pompeio Romam missus est ad triumphum, vbi ex carceribus elapsus & in Iudæam reuersus nouos tu multus excitauit: sed mox iterum captus à Gabinio & Romā missus atq; illic veneno occisus est. At huius filius Antigonus aduersus Hircanum patruum Parthos excitat, qui vrbem occuparunt & diripuerunt, Hircano autem capto aures abscinderunt, ne vnquam ad Sacerdotiū redire posset. Antigonum verò illi substituunt. Hunc cum vix tribus annis regnasset, obsidione premunt Sofius & Herodes, & tandem captum Antiochiam transmittunt ad Antonium, qui eum trucidari curauit. Iudæae autem regnum ex Romanorum beneficio Herodi cessit, vt alibi diximus. Quia verò Parthi prioris victoriæ fiducia & prædæ spe accensi, non cessabant in Syriam crebras incursiones facere, Romani per totam illam prouinciam præsidia disposuerunt, vt & barbaros coercerent, & se ditionibus assuetam Iudæorum gentem in officio continerent, vtq; ad omnem euentum paratas haberent legiones in illis locis, vbi ab hostium incursionibus & prouinciarum defectione plurimum periculi imminebat. Et hi milites illi atq; Centuriones sunt, quorum frequens fit mentio apud Euangelistas, & quibus Ioannes in præsenti concionatur. Nihil ergo ista ad nostri seculi Cares faciunt, qui neq; legitimo magistratui militant, neq; pacem publicam tuentur, sed bellorum faces circumferunt, & maximorum malorum præcipui sunt authores, vt postea demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Before all else we must consider who and what kind of soldiers these were of whom he speaks here. For there are some who, expounding this passage about mercenary soldiers, such as are found everywhere today, seek from the doctrine of the Gospel a patronage for that class of men, although no class is more harmful to the commonwealth and more alien to the Christian faith and religion. But John preaches to ordinary soldiers, who bore arms under lawful magistracy for the defence of the Roman Empire and of public peace, and of whom a large number was then stationed throughout all Syria and Judea, as appears from the histories. For when a dispute over the kingdom and the priesthood had arisen between two brothers, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, and had flared into civil war, each of them had recourse to foreign help. Hyrcanus, driven out by his brother, first fled, on the advice of Antipater the Idumaean, to Aretas, king of Arabia, who, having gathered forces, tried to restore him to his kingdom. Aristobulus, however, won over the Roman commander Scaurus with gifts, so that he would take up his defence; and this frightened Aretas, so that he dismissed his army and returned home to Arabia. Not long afterwards, when Pompey the Great came to Damascus after defeating Tigranes, Aristobulus strove to draw him too to his side with great gifts. Hyrcanus was also present, and he too implored the help of the Romans. Aristobulus, since he did not keep his agreements, moved Pompey to break into the city; and, the temple having been seized by force and not without a dreadful slaughter of the Jews, Pompey entered the Holy of Holies and looked upon those things which it was lawful for no one to see except the High Priest. He granted the pontificate to Hyrcanus, but forbade him to use the crown. Thus the sceptre was then taken from the Jews, and the Romans claimed the kingdom over them for themselves. Aristobulus was sent by Pompey to Rome for a triumph; there, escaping from prison and returning to Judea, he stirred up new tumults; but he was soon captured again by Gabinius, sent to Rome, and killed there by poison. His son Antigonus, however, roused the Parthians against his uncle Hyrcanus, who seized and plundered the city, and when Hyrcanus was taken they cut off his ears, so that he could never again return to the priesthood. They then set up Antigonus in his place. When he had reigned scarcely three years, Sosius and Herod besieged him, and at last sent him, captured, to Antony at Antioch, who saw to it that he was put to death. The kingdom of Judea then passed to Herod by the favour of the Romans, as we have said elsewhere. But because the Parthians, inflamed by confidence in their earlier victory and by hope of plunder, did not cease to make frequent raids into Syria, the Romans stationed garrisons throughout that whole province, both to restrain the barbarians and to keep the Jewish nation, accustomed to rule, in obedience, and to have legions ready for any event in those places where the greatest danger threatened from enemy incursions and the defection of the provinces. These are the soldiers and centurions, whose frequent mention is made in the Evangelists, and to whom John is preaching now. So these things have nothing in common with the mercenaries of our own age, who serve no lawful magistrate and do not guard public peace, but carry about the torches of war and are the chief authors of the greatest evils, as we shall show afterwards.

units.la: Nunc autem non omnino alienum ab instituto nostro visum est, si in horum narratione diligentiores essemus. Docemur enim hoc exemplo, quorsum exire soleant ciuiles discordiæ & bella intestina. Graue equidem est his in partes scindi cives, qui eiusdem corporis membra dici merentur, & qui coniunctis studijs communē patriam tueri debebant. Et constat nulla bella maiori cum animorum contentione & crudelius geri, quàm quæ inter fratres & cives exoriuntur. Acutius enim feriunt & vulnerant animos iniuriæ, quæ ab ijs inferuntur, quos nobis nihil non debere putamus propter summam, quæ nobis cum illis est, coniunctionem. Et vt Aristoteles scribit, qui immensum aut immodicè amant, ijdem immodicè oderunt. Accedit autem aliud multò grauius, quòd odij & iræ vehementia abrepti vtrinq; ad externa auxilia confugiunt, & sæpe hostes patriæ veteres adducunt, quorum armis & ipsi vtrinq; opprimuntur, & communis patria discerpitur. Fit ergo, vt qui cives & fratres ferre noluerunt, postea exteros tyrannos & horum satellites, omnis nequitiæ ministros, ferre cogantur. Et impletur tunc illud Christi: Omne regnum in se diuisum, destruitur. Euenit hoc ambitiosis hisce fratribus, Hircano & Aristobulo, totiq; Iudæorum genti, quæ illorum ambitione sese in partes scindi passa est. Illi enim hominibus prophanis supplices factî sunt, & vterq; cum extrema ignominia vitam infelicem finiuit: Iudæi verò simul omnes immanißimorum militū libidini subiecti, & in seruitutem miserrimam redacti fuerunt. Idem olim sub Regibus maiores ipsorum passi fuerant, quando hi quidē Syros, illi verò Assyrios contra fratres suos in belli societatem pertrahendo vtrisque populis occasionem dedere eos perdendi, quos maximè perditos volebant. Et in Romana historia hic semper bellorum ciuilium exitus fuit, vt à maioribus deuictæ gentes sub Romanis ducibus aduersus Romam pugnarent, & ea occasione clades olim acceptas vlciscerentur. Imò illa viam strauerunt Tiberijs, Claudijs, Caligulis, Neronibus, Domitianis, & infinitis alijs tyrannis, quorū pleriq; ex barbaris gentibus oriundi veteris Romæ maiestatē vilißimus mancipijs & libertis suis conculcandam prostituerunt. Simile exemplū non sine orbis Christiani summo periculo in Græcia ante annos trecentos æditum est, quando de Orientis Imperio inter Cantacuzenum & Ioannem Palæologum contentio exorta est, & in auxilium euocati sunt Turcæ, qui ab eo tempore ad occupandam Græciam animum adiecerunt, & ea non multò post potiti sunt, & ex eo magnam Europæ partem occuparunt. Quid verò in Hungaria nostro tempore acciderit, notius est, quàm vt multa commemoratione opus habeat. Vtinā verò tanti periculi consideratione principes excitati dissidijs funestis finem imponerent, & de communi potius hoste propulsando, quàm de religione opprimenda & stabilienda Pontificum tyrannide consultarent. Quod cùm optare facilius sit quàm impetrare, periculum est, ne cum Germania quicquid adhuc Christiani nominis superest, Turcarum potentiæ subijciatur, & (quod olim Lactantius fore prædixit) imperium in Orientem reuertatur, & rursus seruiat Occidens. Debent ergo in horum meditatione diligenter versari, quicunque communem patriam & fortunas suas salvas volunt, vt concordiæ studeant, qua nihil in humanis salutarius & magis necessarium est. Regula autem concordiæ sit, quam Christus præscribit, vt nimirum in ipso vnum simus, & Deum quidem vna fide & vno ore colamus, inter nos autem mutuæ charitati & beneficentiæ studeamus, sicq; nos germanos filios patris cœlestis esse testemur.
units.tr: Now, however, it has seemed not entirely foreign to our purpose that we should be more careful in the telling of this history. For this example teaches us where civil discords and internal wars are wont to lead. It is indeed grievous that citizens should be torn into parties, who deserve to be called members of the same body, and who ought to guard their common country with united efforts. And it is clear that no wars are waged with greater bitterness of spirit and more cruelly than those which arise between brothers and fellow citizens. For injuries inflicted by those whom we think we owe everything, because of the very close bond we have with them, strike and wound the mind more sharply. And as Aristotle writes, those who love immoderately also hate immoderately. Moreover, there is another and much graver consequence: carried away by the violence of hatred and anger, each side flees to foreign help, and often brings in the ancient enemies of the fatherland, by whose arms both sides are themselves overpowered, and the common country is torn apart. So it comes about that those who would not bear with fellow citizens and brothers are afterwards compelled to bear with foreign tyrants and their satellites, the servants of every wickedness. Then that saying of Christ is fulfilled: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation." This befell those ambitious brothers, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, and the whole Jewish nation, which by their ambition allowed itself to be split into parties. For they became suppliants to profane men, and both ended their unhappy lives with extreme disgrace; and the Jews, all together, were subjected to the lust of most savage soldiers and reduced to most wretched slavery. The same thing had happened long before under their kings, when their forefathers, one by drawing the Syrians and the other the Assyrians into a war alliance against their own brothers, gave both peoples the occasion of destroying those whom they most wished to ruin. And in Roman history this has always been the outcome of civil wars: nations conquered by their elders fought against Rome under Roman leaders, and took the opportunity to avenge the defeats they had once suffered. Indeed, such wars paved the way for the Tiberiuses, Claudiuses, Caligulas, Neros, Domitians, and countless other tyrants, most of whom, sprung from barbarian peoples, gave over the majesty of old Rome to be trampled by their most vile slaves and freedmen. A similar example, not without the greatest danger to the whole Christian world, took place in Greece three hundred years ago, when a dispute over the Eastern Empire arose between Cantacuzenus and John Palaeologus, and the Turks were summoned to help. From that time they set their minds on occupying Greece, and not long afterwards they gained possession of it, and from it they have seized a large part of Europe. What has happened in Hungary in our own time is too well known to need much recounting. Would that princes, roused by the consideration of such great danger, would put an end to their deadly quarrels, and would deliberate about repelling the common enemy rather than about oppressing and establishing religion by the tyranny of the Popes. But since this is easier to wish than to obtain, there is a danger that, together with Germany, whatever remains of the Christian name will be made subject to the power of the Turks, and that (as Lactantius long ago foretold) the empire will return to the East, and the West will serve again. Therefore all who wish to keep their common fatherland and their fortunes safe ought diligently to dwell upon these things in their meditation, so that they may pursue concord, than which nothing is more healthful or more necessary among men. Let the rule of concord be that which Christ prescribes: namely, that we should be one in him, and should worship God with one faith and one mouth, and among ourselves should strive for mutual love and kindness, and so bear witness that we are the true brothers of our heavenly Father.

units.la: Porro quoad nostros bosce milites, satis apparet, illos etiam Ioannis doctrina non leuiter commotos fuisse. Cum enim audirent, pœnitentia omnino opus esse, & simul intelligerent, inter huius operæ siue fructus beneficentiam non postremum locum obtinere: procul dubio vehementer illos terruit vitæ anteactæ recordatio, cum iam illis ob oculos versarentur rapinæ, incendia, cædes vrbium excidia, agrorum vastationes, oppressio innocentum, calumniæ & infinita alia, quæ in bello fieri consueuerunt. Itaq; serio pietatis sensu perculsi, quid ipsos facere conueniat quærunt. Vbi apparet, quantum possit verbum Domini, si in animos semel admittatur. Erant milites isti ex varijs gentibus collecti, & quæ Iudæis dicebantur, talia videri poterant, quæ nihil ad ipsos pertinerent. Neque periculo carebat, a religione deficere, quæ Romani Imperij auctoritate & longo vsu confirmabatur. Verum tamen quia Dei verbum non sciranter audiunt, mox propriæ conscientiæ testimonio conuicti sententiunt, sibi quoq; necessarium esse, vt mores mutent, & voluntati diuinæ sese accommodent, siquidem imminentes sibi pœnas subterfugere velint. Habet istos effectus etiam hodie verbum istud, & hospleriq; sentiunt, qui ad illud cedunt. In eo autem fere erratur, quod multi surgentem in ipsis Dei timorem restinguere & reluctante etiam conscientia omnem de pœnitentia agenda cogitationem procul ex animis suis eijcere conantur. At quia isti suo vitio perennt, eò magis nos annuti decet, ne carnis cupiditatibus indulgeamus, & potius quid iustum & salutare sit quam quid carni doleat consideremus. Ex hoc enim studio pulcherrimi illi fructus enascuntur, quos in Centurione illo spiritus sanctus suo loco prædicabit, cuius fidem toti Israelitarum genti Christus commendat, & quales in Cornelio & multis alijs conspiciuntur.
units.tr: As for these soldiers of ours, it is clear enough that they too were not lightly moved by John's teaching. When they heard that repentance was altogether necessary, and at the same time understood that beneficence holds no small place among the fruits of this work, the recollection of their past life no doubt terrified them greatly, as there rose before their eyes the plunder, fires, murders, destruction of cities, devastation of fields, oppression of the innocent, false accusations and countless other things that are wont to happen in war. Struck therefore with a serious sense of piety, they ask what it becomes them to do. Here it appears how much the word of the Lord can do, once it is admitted into minds. These soldiers were gathered from various nations, and what was said to the Jews could seem to be something that did not pertain to them. Nor was there no danger of falling away from a religion confirmed by the authority of the Roman Empire and long custom. Yet because they did not hear the word of God in vain, soon convicted by the testimony of their own conscience they judge that it is necessary for them too to change their ways and conform themselves to the divine will, if indeed they wish to escape the punishments hanging over them. This word has these effects even today, and those who yield to it feel them. People commonly err in this: many try to quench the fear of God rising within them and, even while conscience resists, to cast far from their minds every thought of repentance. But since those men perish through their own fault, all the more should we be admonished not to indulge the desires of the flesh, and rather to consider what is just and salutary than what pleases the flesh. For from this zeal those most beautiful fruits spring forth, which the Holy Spirit will set forth in its proper place in that centurion, whose faith Christ commends to the whole nation of the Israelites, and such as are seen in Cornelius and many others.

units.la: Admonemur præterea hoc exemplo, religionis & resipiscentiæ studium omne genus hominum decere, neq; quenquam sibi hic debere immunitatem vendicare, cuiuscunq; sit loci aut ordinis. Vt enim omnes a Deo conditi sumus, ita hoc quoque ad diuersas functiones nos vocat, eiusq; fauore & protectione omnibus opus est, qui suam vocationem cum laude siue aliquo cum fructu sequi volunt. Et huius in primis meminisse debent milites, eò quod in nullo alio vitæ genere plura & grauiora pericula tam animabus quam corporibus imminent. Nam qui bella gerunt, ij vitam quodammodo in manibus suis gestant, deq; illa omni momento periclitantur, dum modo repentinus hostium aduentus castris terrorem incutit, modo si hostem inuestigant & ad pugnandum lacessunt, modo horribiles bombardarum tonantium globi ante & retro cadunt, modo eminus alij telis, alij cominus hastis aut gladijs conficiuntur: multos etiam ruentium murorum ruinæ opprimunt, multos equitatus vndiq; circumfusus proterit. Deniq; mille necis species & plurima mortis imago occursat passim & letalia vulnera miscet. Neq; in minori periculo æterna animarum salus tunc constituta est, quando vel causa belli iniusta vno reatu omnes implicat, vel in iusto etiam bello multa in miseros agricolas, imbelles fœminas, viduas, pueros aut senes iniuste & crudeliter fiunt: vel in ipsa vindicta cupiditate aut odij irâq; ardore plerique occiduntur, & ita in suis peccatis pereunt. Aduerusus quæ pericula omnia remedium aut scutum tutissimum est pietas & non sucatu religionis studium, quod & belli consilia regit, & carnis affectus moderatur, ne nos extra iusti & æquilimites abripiant. Non temere ergo olim per Mosen institutum fuit, vt sacerdotes in ipsa acie populum hortarentur, & iam pugnaturus Dei promissiones atq; præcepta in mentem reducerent. Et hunc morem nos Heluetij ama toribus nostris, pijssimis & fortissimis viris, accepimus, vt quoties pro patria & libertate bellum geritur, ecclesiæ ministri in castris conciones frequentes habeant, & in acie constitutos Dei verbo confirment. Quid autem de sacerdotibus aut verbi ministris dicere opus est, quando constat fortissimos veteris testamenti heroas, Ioabum, Dauidem, Iosaphatum, Ezechiam, Iudam Machabæum tunc quàm maximè de Deo & eius cultu apud exercitus suos disseruisse, quando hostem in conspectu habe-
units.tr: We are further admonished by this example that zeal for religion and repentance befits every kind of person, and that no one should claim exemption from it, whatever his place or rank. For as we have all been created by God, so he also calls us to diverse callings, and everyone who wishes to follow his calling with praise or with some profit needs his favour and protection. Soldiers above all ought to remember this, because in no other kind of life do more and graver dangers threaten both souls and bodies. For those who wage war carry life, as it were, in their hands, and are in peril of it every moment: now the sudden arrival of the enemy strikes terror into the camp, now when they search out the enemy and provoke him to battle, now the dreadful balls of thundering cannon fall before and behind them, now some are struck down from afar by missiles, others at close quarters by spears or swords. Many are crushed by the collapse of falling walls, many are trampled by cavalry surrounding them on every side. In short, a thousand kinds of death and countless images of mortality meet one everywhere and mingle deadly wounds. Nor is the eternal salvation of souls then in any less danger, when either an unjust cause of war binds all in one guilt, or even in a just war many wrongs are done unjustly and cruelly to wretched farmers, defenceless women, widows, children or old men; or when in the very lust for vengeance, or in the heat of hatred and anger, many are slain and so perish in their sins. Against all these dangers the surest remedy or shield is piety, and not any careless zeal for religion; this piety both governs the counsels of war and moderates the affections of the flesh, lest they carry us away beyond the limits of what is just and fair. It was not without reason, therefore, that Moses of old ordained that the priests should exhort the people in the very battle line, and remind them, as they were about to fight, of God's promises and commands. We Swiss have received this custom from our forefathers, most pious and brave men: whenever war is waged for country and liberty, the ministers of the Church hold frequent sermons in the camps and strengthen those stationed in battle with the Word of God. But why should I speak of priests or ministers of the Word, when it is established that the bravest heroes of the Old Testament, Joab, David, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Judas Maccabeus, spoke most of all about God and his worship among their armies, when they had the enemy in view,

units.la: Deut. 20. Ku habebant? Quòd ipsum Christiani etiam Imperatores, Constantinus, Theodosius & alij horum similes obseruarunt. Quibus merito accenseri debent Iuliani milites, qui exauctorari potius vel etiā omnino occidi maluerunt, quam fidem abnegare, aut Dei cultum aliqua superstitione polluere. Item his vetustiores, qui sub M. Aurelio Antonino contra Quados & Marcomannos bellum gerente pro tibus publicis pluuias impetrarunt. Minimè ergo audiri debent, qui religionem nihil ad milites pertinere arbitrantur, horū autem propria officia esse aiunt deierare, execrari, potare, aleæ vacare, vio lare matronas, constuprare virgines, pugnas cum commilitionibus temerarias mouere, adhæc vestitu, incessu, vultu & voce non aliud quàm minas & ab omni humanitatis sensu alienam barbariem atq; crudelitatem referre. Marius olim, cùm in bello quædam Romanis legibus contraria fecisset, & de hoc admoneretur, respondebat, se inter armorum strepitum leges non posse audire. At hæc non hominis Christiani, imò neq; boni ciuis, multò minus egregij imperatoris vox fuit, cuius est propatria & legibus patrijs pugnare: sed sanguinarij latronis, qui victorijs de hoste partis contra patriā abusus est, & priuata ambitione superatus rempub. totam in extremum discrimen adduxit. Vtinā vero non eadem hodie sententia esset præcipuorum belli ducum, qui nō leges solùm ciuiles negligunt, sed etiā verbi Dei fulmina atq; tonitrua surdis auribus praetereunt. Et hi sunt, quos vt Encelados & Herculesnouos Turcarum armis opponimus, sed quam infelici euentu, res ipsa loquitur: neq; aliter fieri potest, quando illi ipsi sceleribus suis & effræni licentia præcipui malorum omnium authores sunt, quibus immundum ingratum & contumacem Deus vlcisci tur.
units.tr: Deut. 20. What did they have? That very practice the Christian emperors also observed, Constantine, Theodosius and others like them. Among these the soldiers of Julian rightly deserve to be counted, who chose rather to be discharged or even wholly put to death than to deny their faith or pollute the worship of God with any superstition. Likewise, older than these, were those who under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, while he waged war against the Quadi and Marcomanni, obtained rain for the public needs. Therefore those who think religion has nothing to do with soldiers must by no means be heard; they say that it is the proper business of soldiers to swear, curse, drink, gamble, violate matrons, debauch virgins, start rash brawls with their comrades, and moreover to show by dress, gait, countenance and voice nothing but threats and a barbarity and cruelty alien to every sense of humanity. Marius once, when in war he had done certain things contrary to Roman laws, and was admonished of this, replied that amid the clash of arms he could not hear the laws. But this was not the voice of a Christian man, nor even of a good citizen, much less of an excellent commander, whose duty it is to fight for his country and its ancestral laws; it was the voice of a bloodthirsty robber, who abused his victories over the enemy against his own country, and, overcome by private ambition, brought the whole commonwealth to the utmost peril. Would that the opinion of the chief leaders of war today were not the same, who not only neglect civil laws but also pass over the thunderbolts and thunder of God's Word with deaf ears. And these are the men whom we set against the Turks as new Enceladuses and Hercules, but with what unhappy outcome the thing itself speaks; nor can it be otherwise, since they themselves are the chief authors of all evils through their crimes and unbridled licence, by which God punishes an unclean, ungrateful and stubborn people.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt Ioannem militibus concionantem audiamus. Neminem concutite (inquit) neque calumniemini: & contenti estote stipendijs vestris. Vbi ante omnia obseruabimus, quòd illos non iubet abiectis armis à militia discedere, sed vt in sua illa vocatione se gerere debeant, admonet. Itaque non obscurè totam reipub. administrationem, & qui huic coniunctus est armorum vsum approbat. Si enim hic per se illicitus & impius esset, haud dubiè hoc vitæ genus simpliciter damnauisset, qui ad docendum poenitentiam & singulos Christo præparandum missus erat. Liberè autem ista docet, cùm non ignoraret Deum olim per Mosem de bello leges tulisse, vt paulò ante diximus. Scimus hoc nonnullis absurdum videri, qui Christum dicentem audiunt: Ne resistatis malo, sed si quis te ceciderit in dextram maxillam, obuerte illi & alteram. Item, diligite inimicos vestros. Sed non oportet Christi verba in sensum alienum detorquere. Cùm enim ista diceret, populo concionabatur, & proinde quid singulos facere conueniat docuit: vt nimirum iniurias patienter ferant, & à priuata vindicta abstineant, quæ vt charitati Christianæ inimica est: ita turbas concitat & seditiones parit nunquam finiendas. Quid verò hoc ad magistratum, quem Paulus in hunc finem gladio armatum esse docet, vt homines noxios puniat, probos & bonos tueatur? At si vnum & alterum furem siue latronem occidere licet, imò vt id faciat in mandatis habet magistratus, num integras legiones eorum impunè grassari patietur, qui subditorum fortunas diripiunt, agros populantur, villas incendunt, innoxios trucidant, matronas, virgines & immaturas puellas libidine nefaria polluunt, adhæc reipub. vna cum religione euersam & extinctam volunt? Vel num vnius hominis fortunas aduersus paucorum vim iniustam principes gladio tueri debent, & nefas erit hostilem exercitum repellere, à quo commune toti genti periculum imminet? Cur ergo impios defensores Dei armis coercere iussit, si exteris permissum est, vt fidem & religionem simul omnem extirpent? Quòd si his resistere nefas est, iam Abrahamum patrem credentium, Mosem item, Iosuam, Gedeonem, Iephtaem, Samsonem, Dauidem & optimos quosque Dei cultores damnabimus, quos Apostolus ad Hebræos scribit per fidem regna expugnauisse, robustos in bello factos esse, et ex terorum hostium exercitus in fugam vertisse. At si hoc illi per fidem fecerunt, eam nimirum fidem, quæ in nouo testamento docetur, cur eos hodie Christianos esse negabimus, qui bella necessaria suscipiunt, & remp. cum sacris aduersus prophanos hostes defendunt? Liber hic commemorare, quæ D. Augustinus ad Marcel. epist. 5. in hunc locum commentatus est: Si Christiana disciplina omnia bella culparet, hoc potius militibus consilium salutis petentibus in Euangelio diceretur, vt abijcerent arma, seq; militiæ omnino subtraherent. Dictum est autem eis: Neminē concusseritis, nulli calumniam feceritis, sufficiat vobis stipendium vestrum: Quib. proprium stipendium sufficere debere præcepit, militare vtiq; nō probibit. Proinde qui doctrinā Christi aduersam dicūt esse reip. aut exercitū tale, quales doctrina Christi esse milites iussit: dent tales prouinciales, tales maritos, tales coniunges, tales parentes, tales filios, tales dominos, tales seruos, tales reges, tales iudices, tales deniq; debitorum redditores & exactores ipsius fisci, quales esse praecepit doctrina Christiana, & audeant eam dicere aduersam esse reipub. imo vero dubitent eam confiteri magnam, si ei obtemperetur, salutem esse reipub. Haec (inquam) & multa huius generis Augustinus scripsit, quem a sanguinis studio alienissimum, pacis vero studiosissimum fuisse constat.
units.tr: But it is time that we hear John preaching to the soldiers: "Do violence to no one, nor accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages." Here we shall first of all observe that he does not bid them lay down their arms and leave military service, but admonishes them to conduct themselves in their calling. Thus he does not obscurely approve the whole administration of the commonwealth and the use of arms that belongs to it. For if this way of life were in itself unlawful and impious, he would undoubtedly have condemned it outright, he who was sent to teach repentance and to prepare individuals for Christ. But he teaches these things freely, since he was not unaware that God had long before, through Moses, enacted laws concerning war, as we said a little earlier. We know that this seems absurd to some, who hear Christ saying: "Do not resist evil, but if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also," and likewise, "Love your enemies." But the words of Christ must not be twisted into an alien sense. For when he spoke these things he was preaching to the people, and so taught what each individual ought to do: namely, that they should bear injuries patiently and abstain from private vengeance, which, being hostile to Christian charity, stirs up quarrels and produces seditions that are never ended. But what has this to do with the magistrate, whom Paul teaches to be armed with the sword for this purpose, to punish evildoers and to protect the upright and good? If it is lawful to kill one or another thief or robber, and indeed the magistrate has it in his commission to do so, will he allow whole legions of those men to rage with impunity, who plunder the fortunes of his subjects, lay waste their fields, burn their villas, slaughter the harmless, defile matrons, virgins and immature girls with unspeakable lust, and moreover wish both the commonwealth and religion overthrown and extinguished? Or ought rulers to protect with the sword the property of one man against the unjust violence of a few, and will it be wrong to repel a hostile army from which danger threatens the whole nation in common? Why then did God command that impious despisers be restrained by arms, if it is permitted to outsiders to root out faith and religion altogether? But if it is wrong to resist these, we shall condemn Abraham, the father of believers, and Moses likewise, and Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, David and all the best worshippers of God, of whom the Apostle writes to the Hebrews that through faith they conquered kingdoms, became mighty in war, and turned to flight the armies of foreign enemies. But if they did this through faith, that faith surely which is taught in the New Testament, why shall we deny today that they are Christians who undertake necessary wars and defend the commonwealth with the sword against profane enemies? It is worth recalling what blessed Augustine, commenting on this passage in his letter to Marcellinus, says: "If Christian discipline condemned all wars, then in the Gospel this advice would be given to soldiers seeking salvation, that they should cast away their arms and withdraw altogether from military service. But they were told: 'Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages.' He who ordered them to be content with their wages certainly did not forbid them to serve as soldiers. Therefore those who say that the teaching of Christ is hostile to the commonwealth or to the army, let them produce such provincials, such husbands, such wives, such parents, such children, such masters, such servants, such kings, such judges, and finally such collectors and exactors of debts for the very treasury, as the Christian doctrine commands; and let them dare to call it hostile to the commonwealth, or rather hesitate to acknowledge that, if it were obeyed, it would be the great salvation of the commonwealth." These things, I say, and many of this kind, Augustine wrote; a man known to have been most alien to the love of bloodshed and most devoted to peace.

units.la: Interim etiam atq; etiam cauendum est Christianis principibus, ne praecipiti aliquo affectu abrepti, aut etiam inconsulto terras suas defendendi studio decepti, bella non necessaria moueant. Solet enim fere infelix & tristis horum exitus esse, sicuti exempla innumera docent, inter quae memorabile in primis est Iosiae, optimi & pijssimi principis, qui dum populo suo consultum voluit, & ad arma temere concurrit, miserabiliter caesus est, et suo interitu iam imminens totius gentis excidium accelerauit. Meminerint ergo principes, bellum ex eorum remediorum genere esse, quae non sine toti us corporis & vitae periculo, cum nulla alia salutis spes superest, adhibentur: quales sunt resectiones membrorum, vstiones aut erosiones in membris vitalibus, potiones violentae, & alia quae ipsi naturae quodammodo bellum mouent, & in quibus aut hanc succumbere, aut morbum cedere oportet. Vt ergo periti medici illis non nisi in summa necessitate, & quidem inuiti vtuntur: ita bella quoq; nun quam suscipi debent, nisi cum absq; manifesto reipub. totius & salutis publicae periculo non possunt in terminis. Itaque inter belli causas prima censeri debet religio, quando hanc exteri, quibus nullum in nos ius est, violenter corrumpere, & totum populum ad fidei verae abnegationem atque ad illicitos cultus cogere conantur. Si enim Deus in lege iubet vrbem, quae nostrae ditionis est, excindere, si Deos alienos colat, & in impietate contumaciter perseueret: multo iustius & magis necessarium fuerit, ijs resistere, qui nobis Deos alienos & nefarias superstitiones obtrudere volunt, & salutiferam verbi diuini doctrinam humanarum traditionum toxico inficere. Qui illud licere negant, ij neq; gloriam Dei diligunt, neq; propriae salutis studio tenentur: imo naturae legem ignorant, quae nos omnia nostra Deo debere docet, & per quam olim Athenienses illuminati, ciues suos iuramento publico obstringebant, vt pro Dijs suis & sacris & soli cum alijs pugnarent. Deinde belli causa iusta & necessaria est, quando exteri nullis iniurijs prouocati alienos fines inuadunt, praedantur, rapiunt, ferro & igne omnia miscere volunt, neq; vllas pacis conditiones recipiunt. Si enim hic esset magistratus, populi sui ignauus, aut etiam perfidus defertor dici meretur. Et qui tunc legitimo magistratui militant, ij & patriae quod debent officium praestant, & principibus suis vere fideles sunt. Praeterea non raro fit, vt ex pacto ijs opem ferre oporteat, qui aut nobis confoederati, aut in praesidijs dispositi de summa rerum periclitantur. Tales enim sine scelere deseri non possunt, & inexcusabilis est eorum principum ignauia, qui eos ab hostibus opprimi patiuntur, qui in eiusmodi necessitate communis patriae salutem sui capitis periculo defendere satagunt. Sunt & aliae causae bellorum, quae pro loci & temporis ratione se offerunt, sed hae praecipuae sunt, ad quas aliae omnes possunt referri: in quibus considerandum magna circumspectione opus est, ne nobis caecus aliquis affectus imponat in re, quae cum publica salutis periculo coniuncta est. Sed facile error omnis cauebitur, si sola necessitas & publica salus spectetur, finis vero consiliorum sit pax & innocentia defensio.
units.tr: Christian princes must also be warned again and again not to be swept along by some headlong passion, or deceived by a zeal to defend their lands when it is unconsidered, and so stir up wars that are not necessary. The outcome of such wars is usually unhappy and sad, as countless examples show, and foremost among them is that of Josiah, an excellent and most godly prince. Wishing to provide for his people, he rashly rushed into arms, was miserably slain, and by his own death hastened the destruction of the whole nation, which was already at hand. Let princes therefore remember that war belongs to the class of remedies that are applied only at the risk of the whole body and of life itself, when no other hope of safety remains. Such are the amputation of limbs, cauterising or cutting into vital organs, violent purgatives, and other things that stir up a kind of war against nature itself, and in which one must either yield to them or be cured of the disease. As skilled physicians use these only in the greatest necessity, and even then unwillingly, so wars too must never be undertaken unless the matter cannot be settled without manifest danger to the whole commonwealth and the public safety. Therefore, among the causes of war, religion ought to be counted first, when foreigners, who have no right over us, try to corrupt it by force and to compel the whole people to renounce the true faith and adopt unlawful worship. For if God in the law commanded the destruction of a city that lies within our jurisdiction, should it worship other gods and persist stubbornly in impiety, then it will be far more just and far more necessary to resist those who wish to force upon us foreign gods and impious superstitions, and to poison the saving doctrine of the divine Word with human traditions. Those who deny that this is lawful neither love the glory of God nor are concerned for their own salvation. Indeed, they are ignorant of the law of nature, which teaches that we owe all that we have to God, and by which the Athenians of old, being enlightened, bound their citizens by public oath to fight together with others for their gods, their sacred rites, and their soil. Next, a war is just and necessary when foreigners, provoked by no injuries, invade our borders, plunder, seize, and wish to throw everything into confusion with fire and sword, and accept no conditions of peace. If a magistrate were idle in the face of such things, or a treacherous deserter of his people, he would deserve to be called that. And those who then serve the lawful magistrate both perform the duty they owe to their country and are truly faithful to their rulers. Moreover, it often happens that, by treaty, one must bring aid to those who are allied with us, or who are stationed in garrisons and are in danger of their lives. Such men cannot be abandoned without wickedness, and the cowardice of those princes is inexcusable who allow them to be overwhelmed by enemies, when in such necessity they strive to defend the common safety of the country at the peril of their own heads. There are also other causes of war, which present themselves according to circumstances of place and time, but these are the chief ones, and all the rest may be referred to them. In these matters great caution is needed, lest some blind passion impose on us in a matter that is bound up with danger to the public safety. But every error will easily be avoided if only necessity and the public good are looked to, and if the aim of our counsels is peace and the defence of innocence.

units.la: At non minor cura adhiberi debet, cum iam ad arma ventum est, ne tunc quoque clementiae erga hostes, aut officij sui erga subditos principes obliuiscantur. In Lege iubet Deus, vt qui vrbem oppugnare instituerunt, prius ei pacis conditiones offerant, & amice respondentes humanius tractent, atque tributo & obedientiae officijs contenti, vitae ipsorum atque reliquis fortunis parcant. Debet hoc passim & semper obseruari. Quia enim bello nihil inhumanius, nihil item periculosius & nocentius est, nulla etiam in medio armorum strepitu pacis honestae & tolerabilis occasio negligi debet. Curandum quoque, ne qui iusta arma susceperunt, omni humanitatis sensu abiecto, vel in innoxios crudeliter grassentur, quos non propria malitia, sed principum suorum libido in periculum istud adduxit: vel etiam suos absque causa periculis gravioribus obijciant (vt fere solent, qui rem temere praeliorum fortunae committunt) aut insano furore suos ad locorum munitissimorum expugnationem cum certo vitae discrimine cogant. Deus certe olim graviter monuit, ne dum vrbes obsidentur, quis arbores excindat, quæ fructus ferunt esui aptos. Quis ergo nō scelus dixerit esse immanissimum agricolas innoxios occidere, segetes vastare, in sexum muliebre, in infantes aut senes decrepitos sœuire? Istis flagitijs olim Babylonios Dei iram sibi conflauisse prophetæ testantur, cùm à Deo mandatum bellum contra Iudæos truculentius gererent. Est ergo multa laude dignissima Aureliani Imperatoris clementia, qui vicario suo eiusmodi mandata dedit: Si vis tribunus esse, imò si vis viuere, manus militum contine, nemo pullum alienum rapiat, quem nemo contingat, quam nullus auferat. Et in veteri historia Indorum mores commendantur, qui militiæ tempore agricolas intactos relinquebant, ne quid mali paterentur homines innocentes, & qui suo labore reliquis omnibus victum parant. At qui suos homines temere periculis obijciunt, ij fere capitibus eorum ludere videntur, & in magistratus officium grauiter peccant, cuius est populi sui sanguinem pretiosum ducere. Et merito laudatur Scipio Africanus, qui cum hoste nunquam confligendum esse dicebat, nisi aut occasio aut necessitas cogeret. Videbat enim multo rei militaris vsu edoctus, nunquam tam feliciter pugnari, quin aliqui occumbant, quorum vita reipublicæ & patriæ vtilis esse poterat. Quod ipsum Antoninus Pius quoque obseruauit, qui neminî vnquam bellum intulit, sed infe-rentes repressit, nunquam non illud Scipionis dictum in ore habens, se malle vnum ciuem seruare, quàm mille hostes occidere. Iudicabunt isti olim Christianos principes, qui vt ad bella non necessaria temere ruunt: ita in hostium agros immanissimè sæuiunt, & suos quoque homines vix pecudum loco habent, neq; solùm hostibus eos trucidandos propinant, sed fame etiam enecant, dum stipendia illis maligne soluunt, ipsi interea luxui dediti & circa omne libidinis genus occupati. Quæ vitia tunc demum corrigentur, si principes Deum timeant, & veram pietatem cum patria communis amore coniungant.
units.tr: Yet no less care must be taken, once it has come to arms, that princes do not then also forget clemency towards enemies and their duty towards subjects. In the law God commands that those who have set out to attack a city should first offer it terms of peace, and that, if it answers in a friendly way, they should treat it humanely, and, being content with tribute and the duties of obedience, spare the lives and remaining property of its people. This ought to be observed everywhere and always. For since nothing is more inhuman in war, and nothing is more dangerous and harmful, no opportunity for an honourable and tolerable peace should be neglected, even in the midst of the clash of arms. Care must also be taken that those who have taken up just arms do not, having cast off all sense of humanity, rage cruelly against the innocent, who were brought into that danger not by their own malice but by the lust of their princes. Nor should they expose their own men to graver dangers without cause (as those usually do who rashly commit matters to the chance of battle), or in mad fury force them to storm the strongest places at the certain risk of their lives. God indeed long ago warned sharply that, while cities are besieged, no one should cut down trees that bear fruit fit for food. Who, then, would not call it a most monstrous crime to kill innocent farmers, to lay waste the crops, and to rage against women, infants, or decrepit old men? The prophets testify that the Babylonians brought God's anger upon themselves by these outrages, when they waged the war against the Jews, which God had commanded, too savagely. Therefore the clemency of the emperor Aurelian is most worthy of great praise, for he gave his deputy orders of this kind: "If you wish to be a tribune, indeed if you wish to live, restrain your soldiers' hands; let no one seize another's chicken, let no one touch another's ..., let no one take anything away." And in the ancient history of the Indians their customs are commended, for in time of war they left the farmers untouched, so that innocent men, who by their labour provide sustenance for everyone else, should suffer no harm. But those who rashly expose their own men to dangers seem to make sport of their lives, and grievously sin against the duty of the magistrate, whose task it is to hold the blood of his people precious. And Scipio Africanus is rightly praised, who said that one should never engage an enemy unless either opportunity or necessity compelled it. For, taught by long experience of military affairs, he saw that a battle is never won so happily that some do not fall, whose lives might have been useful to the commonwealth and the fatherland. Antoninus Pius also observed the same, who never made war on anyone, but repressed those who attacked, always having on his lips that saying of Scipio, that he preferred to save one citizen rather than kill a thousand enemies. Those future judges will condemn Christian princes who, as they rush rashly into unnecessary wars, so savagely rage over the enemy's fields, and who hardly count their own men as more than cattle, not only handing them over to be slaughtered by enemies, but also letting them die of hunger, paying their wages grudgingly, while they themselves are given over to luxury and occupied with every kind of lust. These vices will at last be corrected only if princes fear God and join true piety with love of the common fatherland.

units.la: Quia verò à militibus quoque gregarijs plurimum tunc peccabatur, & etiam hodie passim peccatur, præcepit tribus illorum petulantiam Ioannes coercet, quorum summa est, ne sub legitimæ militiæ prætextu populum opprimant, aut latronum more in eos grassentur, quos defendere debebant. Præstat tamen singula videre. Primum est, Neminem concutite. Prohibetur hoc vis iniusta, quam plerunq; in cives & agricolas peccant milites præsidiarij, dum ex amicorum etiam aut sociorum agris prædas agunt, hospites suos immaniter tractant, eorundem vxores, filias & ancillas constuprant, nullum denique iniuriæ genus prætermittunt. Pugnat hoc cum fine belli legitimi, qui est vt omnia ad populi & pacis publicæ defensionem dirigantur. Et quis obsecro fructus ex bello sperari debet, si ea faciunt socij, quæ ex hostibus timentur? Quòd si historias euoluamus, inuenire licebit multos, qui ad hostes defectionem fecerunt, & patriam dulcissimam inuiti prodiderunt, vt militum præsidiariorum improbitate liberarentur. Et vtinam non hodie etiam extarent exempla multorum, qui seipsos & terras suas Turcis dedere maluerunt, quàm Christianos milites defensores admittere, quorum libidinem & auaritiam prius experti fuerant. Quòd si hodie Aureliani Lex valeret, quam paulò ante adduximus, bella felicius gererentur.
units.tr: Because, moreover, much wrong was done then, and is still done everywhere today, by common soldiers too, John restrained the insolence of these men with three precepts, the sum of which is that they must not oppress the people under the pretext of lawful military service, or rage against those whom they ought to defend, in the manner of robbers. Still, it is well to look at each one separately. The first is: "Do violence to no one." This forbids the unjust force that garrison soldiers commonly use against citizens and farmers, when they carry off booty even from the fields of their friends or allies, treat their hosts monstrously, violate their wives, daughters and maidservants, and in short leave no kind of injury undone. This is at odds with the aim of a lawful war, which is that everything be directed to the defence of the people and of public peace. And what fruit, I ask, can be hoped for from a war if our allies do the very things that are feared from enemies? If we run through the histories, we shall find many who went over to the enemy and reluctantly betrayed their dearest fatherland, so that they might be freed from the wickedness of garrison soldiers. And would that there were not even today examples of many who preferred to surrender themselves and their lands to the Turks rather than admit Christian soldiers as defenders, whose lust and greed they had first experienced. And if the law of Aurelian, which we cited a little while ago, were in force today, wars would be waged more successfully.

units.la: Alterum mandatum Ioannis est: Neminem calumniemini. Calumniæ vocabulo apertas quoque accusationes & quæcunque sub iuris prætextu aduersus innocentes instituuntur, compre-hendit. Erat autem hoc frequens admodum apud Romanos milites, vt calumnijs eos circumuenirent, qui vel libidini ipsorum resistebant liberius, vel ex quibus lucrum sperare poterant. Solebant enim Romani eos proscribere, qui de ipsorum imperio minus honorificè loquebantur, aut alias ob causas suspecti erant. Proscripti verò aut occidebantur, aut deportabantur in exilium, eorundem autem bona militibus in prædam dabantur, aut saltem maior illorum pars accusatoribus cedebat. Exempla huius iniquitatis multa in historijs occurrunt: & credibile est plus licuisse militibus apud Iudæos, gentem multis nominibus inuisam. Hodie certè huius generis multa fiunt inter eos, qui ab exteris principibus deuicti militum præsidia in vrbes & domus suas recipere cogun-tur. At omnibus istis Ioannes concionatur, vt meminerint hæc non fine scelere fieri. Etenim cùm calumnia nihil turpius sit in quouis hominum genere, ea demum in milite turpissima est, qui ex fortibus factis laudem quærere debet, & cuius est (vt poeta inquit) parcere subiectis & debellare superbos.
units.tr: The second command of John is: Do not accuse anyone falsely. By the word "false accusation" he means not only open accusations but also any cases brought against innocent people under a pretext of law. It was very common among the Roman soldiers to entrap by false accusations those who resisted their lust more freely, or those from whom they hoped to gain. The Romans used to proscribe those who spoke rather disrespectfully of their rule, or who were suspected for other reasons. The proscribed were either put to death or sent into exile, and their goods were given to the soldiers as plunder, or at least most of their property went to the accusers. Many examples of this injustice occur in histories, and it is credible that the soldiers had even more power among the Jews, a nation hated for many reasons. Today certainly many things of this kind happen among those who, conquered by foreign princes, are compelled to receive garrisons of soldiers into their cities and homes. But John preaches to all of them that they should remember these things are not done without wickedness. For although calumny is shameful in every kind of person, it is most shameful in a soldier, who ought to seek praise from brave deeds, and whose task is (as the poet says) to spare the defeated and to subdue the proud.

units.la: Quia verò omnis iniustitiæ & crudelitatis præcipua causa est auaritia & intemperantia, apud milites in primis, quorum petulantia et libido facit, ut vix quicquam illis sufficiat, tertio mandata remedium vitiis hisce prioribus adhibet, quando eos iubet stipendijs suis contentos viuere. In Graeco obsonij vox habetur, quae significat quicquid praeter panem & vinum apponitur. Solet autem pro militari stipendio usurpari, eo quod antiquitus non pecunia solum, sed victus militibus daretur, quem morem maiores nostri obseruarunt, & adhuc Helueticorum respub. obseruat, quando pro patria bellum geritur: ut nimirum milites in tribus & contubernia distributi in commune viuant & ex publico alantur. Apparet ex eo quantum apud veteres fuerit frugalitatis studium, quando milites commeatum suum secum ferebant, & omnia soli necessitati seruiebant. Est autem illa in bello maxime necessaria: quia sine hac nullum stipendium tam liberale est, quod militibus sufficere queat: quae causa est, quod vel cum hostibus proditoria consilia conferunt, vel amicos & socios depredantur; & plerunque fit ut ebrij vincantur, qui prius vinci non poterant. Recte igitur olim Agesilaus, cum per Thasiorum agrum cum copijs iter faceret, cibos delicatiores, quos illi offerebant, inter manci pia distribuere iussit, dicens, eos qui probitati fortitudinique studerent, non decere huiusmodi ganeis & gulae irritamentis delectari. Et Pescennius Niger militibus vinum petentibus respondebat: Nilum habetis, & vinum quaeritis? At quae nostri temporis corruptio est, respondet hoc vix vlli militès admitterent, cum eo res deuenerit, ut in castris quoque legibus sumptuarijs opus sit, quibus militum luxus in vestitu & victu coerceatur. At si ijdem meminissent, furtum esse, quicquid praeter stipendium ordinarium ab alijs extorquetur, procul dubio frugaliores essent, & Deum sibi magis propitium haberent. At quod militibus dicitur, non minus omnium aliorum institutioni seruit, ut nimirum sua sorte contenti viuant, & toti ex Dei benedictione pendeant: quem uberrimum quaestum esse, alibi ex Paulo Apostolo monuimus. Sed frustra (ut Cato Senior dicebat) verba fiunt, ventri non habenti aures. Ut vero aliquando dicendi finem faciamus, si quae hucusque dicta sunt, cum militibus ijs conferamus, qui hodie pretio conducti castra quaeuis sequuntur, illorum institutum hic non probari, sed totum damnari & euerti patebit. Nam pleriq; illorum non legitimo magistratui, sed exteris principibus militant: imo fere contra suorum principum edicta in militiam mercenariam excurrunt. Deinde vocationem, quam a Deo habent, turpiter deserunt, & relictis artificijs manuarijs aut agricultura, hoc vitae genus sequuntur, quo vix vllum hodie sceleratius excogitari potest. Finem vero non alium sibi propositum habent, quam ut sit quod ipsorum libidini sufficiat, & ut male parta peius dilapident. Quae causa est, ut absq; omni discrimine pro hostibus habeant omnes, ex quibus praeda sperari potest. Sunt hi nocentissimi homines, & fere regnus atque gentibus suum exitium accelerant. Perseguitur enim illos maledictio Dei, qui iampridem execratione & exitio dignos pronuntiauit eos, qui pro pretio fundunt sanguinem innoxium. Et ex historijs constat, nulli regno aut genti impune cessisse belligerendi libidinem. Sed meretur hoc quoq; flagellum incurabilis seculi nostri impietas: quod tunc demum a nobis auferetur, si Ioannis consilium secuti respipiscamus, & a peccatis in viam iustitiae & salutis redeamus per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Since greed and intemperance are the chief cause of all injustice and cruelty, the third command, addressed especially to soldiers, whose wantonness and lust make it so that nothing is enough for them, applies a remedy to these earlier vices, when it bids them live content with their pay. In Greek the word is opsonion [ὀψώνιον], which signifies whatever is served besides bread and wine. It is customarily used for military pay, because in antiquity soldiers were given not only money but also provisions, a custom our ancestors observed and the Helvetic commonwealth still observes when war is waged for the fatherland: namely, that the soldiers, distributed into companies and messes, live in common and are fed from public funds. From this it appears how great was the zeal for frugality among the ancients, when soldiers carried their own supplies with them and submitted everything to bare necessity. This is especially necessary in war, because without it no pay, however generous, can suffice for soldiers. This is the reason why they either plot treachery with the enemy or plunder their friends and allies; and it often happens that men who could not be conquered before are overcome when they are drunk. Rightly, then, Agesilaus once, when he was marching with his forces through the territory of the Thasians, ordered the more delicate foods that they offered to be distributed among the common soldiers, saying that those who strive for uprightness and courage ought not to take delight in such enticements of gluttony and the belly. And Pescennius Niger, when soldiers asked him for wine, replied: "You have the Nile, and you ask for wine?" But what corruption there is in our own time! It is hardly to be thought that any soldiers would tolerate such an answer, since things have reached the point where even in camps sumptuary laws are needed, by which the luxury of soldiers in dress and food is restrained. But if they remembered that whatever is extorted from others beyond the ordinary pay is theft, they would undoubtedly be more frugal and would have God more favorable to them. And what is said to soldiers serves no less the instruction of all others: namely, that they live content with their lot and depend wholly on God's blessing. We have shown elsewhere from the Apostle Paul that this is the most abundant gain. But words are spent in vain (as Cato the Elder used to say), for they are spoken to a belly that has no ears. Yet, to bring our discourse at last to an end: if we compare what has been said so far with those soldiers who today, hired for pay, follow any camp whatever, it will be clear that their practice is not approved here but wholly condemned and overturned. For most of them serve not a lawful magistrate but foreign princes; indeed they rush into mercenary service almost against the edicts of their own princes. Then they shamefully desert the calling they have from God, and, abandoning manual crafts or agriculture, they follow a way of life than which scarcely anything more wicked can be devised today. Moreover, they have no other aim before them than that there be something to satisfy their lust, and that they may squander ill-gotten gains even more badly. This is why they regard without any distinction as enemies all from whom plunder can be hoped for. These are the most harmful of men, and they almost always hasten the ruin of kingdoms and nations. For the curse of God pursues them, who long ago pronounced accursed and worthy of destruction those who for pay shed innocent blood. And from histories it is clear that no kingdom or nation has ever escaped unpunished for the lust of waging war. But our incurable age, in its impiety, also deserves this scourge; and it will be removed from us only if we follow John's counsel, repent, and return from sins to the way of righteousness and salvation, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honor, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXII.

units.la: Expectante autem populo & cogitantibus omnibus in cordibus suis de Ioanne, num ipse esset Christus ille: respondit Ioannes, dicens omnibus: Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua; sed venit qui validior me est, cuius non sum dignus qui soluam corrigiam calceorum. Ipse vos baptizabit spiritu sancto & igne. Cuius ventilabrum in manu ipsius, & perpurgabit aream suam, & coget triticum in horreum suum, paleam autem exuret igne inextinguibili.
units.tr: As the people waited, and all were pondering in their hearts whether John himself might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying: "I indeed baptize you with water; but there comes one mightier than I, the thong of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly purge his floor and gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire."

units.la: Quoniam Dominus noster Iesus Christus vniuersalis omnis generis hominum seruator atque redemptor est, talem quoq; illius anteambulonem esse oportuit, qui omnis loci & ordinis homines ad illum excipiendum excitaret, & singulos sui officij admoneret. Hoc qua fide & diligentia Ioannes præstiterit, hucusq; Lucas prolixè exposuit. Ifiis nunc commodè subijcitur, vt illius doctrina homines affecti fuerint, tam boni scilicet quàm mali. Et in præsenti quidem de illo agitur, qui præclarè, imò nimis magnificè de illo senserunt, quorum errori ille nouam de Christo concionem opponit, qua omnem ecclesiastici ministerij & humanæ salutis rationem comprehendit. Illis autem posted Herodes opponitur, typus reproborum, qui ad Verbi prædicationem deteriores fiunt.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ is the Saviour and Redeemer of all people of every kind, it was fitting that he should have such a forerunner, one who would rouse people of every place and rank to receive him and remind each of his duty. Luke has set out at length how faithfully and diligently John did this. Now it is fitting to add how people were affected by his teaching, both the good and the bad. At present the passage concerns those who thought very highly, indeed excessively highly, of him, and against their error John sets a new sermon about Christ, which embraces the whole of the ministry of the Church and the way of human salvation. Opposed to these people, later on, is Herod, a type of the reprobate, who become worse when the Word is preached.

units.la: Quoad priores illos, Lucas eos expectauisse, & in cordibus suis cogitauisse ait, num ipse esset{ } Christus ille, id est, promissus ille Rex & Sacerdos, quem venturum omnes sperabant, vt populum plus satis afflictum vindicaret. Expectandi verbo desiderium & admirationem exprimit, quæ apud omnes exorta fuit, cùm & doctrinæ genus nouum audirent, eoq; intra animos suos non leuiter affice rentur, & in vita atq; moribus Ioannis sanctimoniam viderent non pharisaicam aut fucatam, sed in qua præsens Spiritus sancti virtus elucebat. Inde verò illis occasio data fuit cogitandi, nū Ioannes promissus ille Seruator sit. Non autem apud rude vulgus solum hæc suspicio enata fuit, sed Sacerdotum quoq; & Seniorum, qui Hierosolymis erant, animos perculit, qui ideo aliquos ex Pharisæorum ordine ad illum emiserunt, qui num ipse Christus ille esset percontarentur, aut qua authoritate docendi & baptizandi munus sibi vsurparet. Quo loco inter multa alia hoc quoq; obiter est obseruandum, totum illud negotium, cuius minister & executor fuit Christus, non nouum & prisci temporibus inauditum esse, sed illum magno omnium desiderio expectatum venisse. Nam vt alibi diximus, extabant de illo promissiones patribus datæ, & eas prophetæ suis vaticinijs prolixè interpretati fuerant, neque alius sermo apud totum populum frequentior erat, quàm qui de illo ferebatur. Antistitum verò & scribarum illius temporis partim socordia partim malitia fiebat, vt pauci veram Messiæ cognitionem tenerent, sed plerique neglectis bonis æternis atq; cœlestibus, nihil in illo præter temporariam felicitatem quærerent. Quod ipsum hodie etiam accidere videmus, quando Christum quidem omnes in ore habent, & ab illo Christiani denominari volunt, pauci verò inueniuntur, qui illius meritum atque huius virtutem agnoscant, & plerique procul relicta fide in Christum circa frigidas & inanes superstitiones occupantur. Et hoc quoq; personatis episcopis atq; bullatis Doctoribus debemus, qui vt suo honori & quæstui consulant, infelicem populum in errore detinent. Vt vt verò ista habeant, faciunt ista ad afferendam fidei et doctrinæ Christianæ dignitatem atq; certitudinem: & vt olim eò minus excusationis habuerunt Iudæi, quòd quem diu expectarant, improbè reiecerunt: ita hodie nullam veniam meretur eorum ignorantia, qui Euangelio Iesu Christi credere dedignantur, quem vnum subinde in ore habent.
units.tr: As for those first people, Luke says that they were waiting and pondering in their hearts whether he himself was that Christ, that is, the promised King and Priest whom everyone hoped would come to deliver a people already sorely afflicted. By the word "waiting" he expresses the longing and wonder that arose among them all: they heard a new kind of teaching, which stirred their minds not lightly, and they saw in John's life and conduct a holiness that was not Pharisaic or feigned, but one in which the present power of the Holy Spirit shone forth. This gave them occasion to wonder whether John was the promised Saviour. Nor did this suspicion arise only among the common people; it also troubled the minds of the chief priests and elders at Jerusalem, who therefore sent some from the order of the Pharisees to ask him whether he was the Christ himself, or by what authority he took upon himself the office of teaching and baptizing. At this point, among many other things, we should also observe in passing that the whole business of which Christ was the minister and executor was not new, nor unheard of in earlier times, but that he came when he had been longed for by everyone. For, as we have said elsewhere, promises concerning him had been given to the fathers, and the prophets had expounded them at length in their prophecies, and no other subject was more frequent among the whole people than what was said about him. But because of the indolence and the malice of the high priests and scribes of that time, few held a true knowledge of the Messiah; most, neglecting the good things that are eternal and heavenly, sought in him nothing but temporal happiness. We see this happening even today: everyone has Christ on his lips and wants to be called a Christian, yet few are found who acknowledge his merit and his power, and most, having abandoned faith in Christ, busy themselves with cold and empty superstitions. We owe this too to the mitred bishops and the bonneted doctors, who, to look after their own honour and profit, keep the unhappy people in error. However they may explain these things, they serve to establish the dignity and the certainty of the Christian faith and doctrine. And just as the Jews had less excuse, because they shamefully rejected the one they had long awaited, so today the ignorance of those deserves no pardon who disdain to believe the Gospel of Jesus Christ, whom they keep constantly on their lips.

units.la: In primis autem obseruari hic debet, quid ijs fere accidere soleat, qui in aliquo publico munere versantur. Idem nimirum, quod ijs, qui in publico ædificant. Vt enim hi spectatores habent innumeros, quorum tot sunt sententiæ quot capita, & nemo fere tam vilis & abiectus est, qui non in illos sibi Ædilitiam potestatem sumat: ita multorum iudicijs expositi sunt omnes, qui ecclesiæ ædificium curant, & eò illa iniquiora sunt, quò minus ea intelligunt homines, quæ ad regnum Dei & æternæ salutis negotium pertinent. Exempla huius generis in prophetis passim occurrunt, & de Apostolis quoq; varia & diuersa iudicia fuisse constat. Quo minus ministros ecclesiarum hodie offendi decet, quando ipsum Christum mundi temeritatem in hoc expertum esse scimus, vt supra in Simeonis Cantico multis est dictum. Idem verò ad se transferant qui rempublicam regunt & in aliquo magistratu constituti sunt. Nam etsi illorum sit de alijs iudicium facere, & ipsis populus obedire debeat, nunquam tamen effugient, quò minus de ipsis alij iudicent, & interdum bene facta finistrè interpretentur. Et peccant quidem sua temeritate, qui in hoc sibi nimium indulgent, possunt tamen ex illa non pœnitendum fructum decerpere principes, si ea rectè vtantur. Primò enim si huius suæ conditionis probè memores sint, minus peccabunt. Nam vt nævus in facie latere non potest: ita quicquid præter officium faciunt qui in altiori aliquo gradu sunt collocati, id mox omnibus innotescit, & aut maleuolorum conuitijs laniatur, aut in exemplum trahitur ab ijs, qui ad malum iam ante plus satis proclives sunt. Itaq; qui istud non obseruant, ij vel magistratus authoritatem turpiter produnt, vel alienis quoque peccatis se grauant, quæ alij ipsorum exemplo deteriores facti designant. Deinde si vulgi de se iudicia principes diligentius obseruent, de multis admonebuntur, quæ ipsi prius ignorabant, & quæ nemo purpuratorum illis dicere audet: ita vero sæpe præclaram occasionem inueniunt, vel bene agendi, vel corrigendi, quod male factum fuerat. Quod ipsum priuatis quoq; homini-bus accidit, si quid de ipsis dicatur non omnino negligant.
units.tr: But first, we must observe here what usually happens to those who hold some public office. It is the same as happens to those who build in public. For just as such builders have countless spectators, each with his own opinion, and there is scarcely anyone so mean and worthless that he does not claim for himself the right of an aedile to judge them, so all who take charge of the building of the Church are exposed to the judgments of many, and these judgments are the more unfair the less people understand the matters that pertain to the kingdom of God and the business of eternal salvation. Examples of this kind occur everywhere among the prophets, and it is plain that there were various and differing judgments about the apostles too. All the less should ministers of the Churches be offended today, since we know that Christ himself experienced the recklessness of the world in this matter, as was said at length above in the Canticle of Simeon. Let those who govern the commonwealth and hold some magistracy apply the same to themselves. For although it is their business to judge others, and the people must obey them, they will never escape others judging them, and sometimes interpreting their good deeds in an unfavourable light. Those who indulge themselves too much in this are at fault through their own rashness; yet rulers can still gather some useful fruit from it, if they use it rightly. First, if they are duly mindful of their condition, they will sin less. For just as a mole on the face cannot be hidden, so whatever those placed in some higher rank do beyond their duty soon becomes known to everyone, and is either torn to pieces by the abuse of the ill-disposed, or is taken as an example by those who are already more than inclined to evil. Therefore, those who do not observe this either shamefully betray the authority of the magistracy, or burden themselves with the sins of others, whom their example has made worse. Next, if rulers observe more carefully what the common people judge of them, they will be warned about many things they previously did not know, and which none of the courtiers dares to tell them; and so they often find a splendid opportunity either to act well or to correct what had been done amiss. This also happens to private persons, if they do not altogether neglect what is said about them.

units.la: At ne in hac re impatientia superemur, vulgi ingenium nouisse oportet, quod ut totum affecti-bus rapitur, sic nihil illo inconstantius & mutabilius est. Aut enim nimium extollit, & ad Deos usque euehit homines mortales, in quibus illustrior virtus relucet: aut maligne nimis odit & con-culcat eos, à quibus se laesum arbitratur. Nunc quidem Messiae honorem Ioanni spontè deferunt: at mox eius causam simul omnes deserunt, quando ab Herode in carcerem detruditur, & in me-retricis incestae gratiam indigna morte multatur. Idem Christus quoque expertus est, quem modò regem suum creare volunt, & promissum illum Seruatorem esse publicè fatentur: modò ad Pilati tribunal ad mortis supplicium deposcunt, & eidem Barrabam, hominem seditiosum & re-centi caede infamem, anteponunt. Quoad apostolos verò, multa eius generis exempla Actorum liber nobis exhibet. Quod ipsum in republica etiam fieri consueuit. Nam illic subito fauore vulgi ad caelum usque extolluntur, qui beneficium aliquod publicum dederunt: ijdem verò mox dete-cti ab omnibus laniantur, si vel infelicius rem gerant, vel non omnium votis aut libidini satisfa-ciant. Sensit hoc Dauid, quem primum Sauli praeferunt propter caesum Goliam, at non multò post, eundem à Saule iniquissima regni affectati suspicione grauari & in exilium eiji patiuntur. Et rursum extincto Saule ad illum certatim confluunt, & ecce (inquit) nos sumus os tuum & caro tua, &c. Alibi quoque de illo acriter contendunt cum tribu Iuda, quae propter cognationem si-bi Dauidem proprium vendicabat: at cùm post Solomonis obitum filius eius Roboam iuuenili confidentia inflatus ad ipsorum postulationem durius aliquanto respondisset, mox omnium vete-rum beneficiorum obliti clamant: Quae pars nobis in Dauide? Non est hereditas in filio Isai: ad tentoria tua o Israel, prouide domui tuae Dauid. Similia multa in prophanis historijs extant. Athe-thenienses certè Alcibiadem ob bellum in Sicilia male gestum in exilium egere, eundè verò reuoca-tum, cum Lacedaemonios terra mariqué vicisset, non humanis solum verumetiam diuinis honori-bus dignum iudicarunt: at mox cum eodem duce bellum in Asia gererent, & ipse praedandi studio intentus cladem accepisset, rursus illum exilio multarunt. Idem Phocionem ignominiose dam-natum neque funere neque sepulchro dignati sunt: sed paulò post statuam illi posuerunt, & in-uentas eius reliquias publicis sumptibus sepulturae mandarunt. Quid verò de Romanorum plerif-què dicemus, qui modò triumphantes vrbem ingressi, modò ex eadem profugere & latebras quaere-re coacti sunt? Et Imperatores eorundem nunc adoratos, nunc à militibus discerptos, & tandem rursus in Deorum numerum relatos fuisse legimus. Sed dies me deficeret, si quaecunque extant huius generis exempla recensere velim.
