Debent autem illa obseruari ab ijs, qui in ecclesia & republica praesunt, ne mundi iudicijs moueamur, sed suae conditionis memores suam stationem constan-ter teneant, ut Deo probari possint.
units.tr: But so that we may not be overcome by impatience in this matter, we ought to know the nature of the common people, which is wholly swept along by its passions, and nothing is more inconstant and changeable than it. For either it extols mortal men in whom a more outstanding virtue shines, lifting them up even to the gods, or it hates and tramples on, to excess, those by whom it thinks itself wronged. Now indeed they freely confer the honour of the Messiah upon John; but soon they all desert his cause together, when he is thrust into prison by Herod, and is put to an unworthy death for the sake of an incestuous harlot. Christ too experienced the same: the people now want to make him their king, and publicly confess that he is the promised Saviour; now they demand his death before Pilate's tribunal, and prefer to him Barabbas, a seditious man infamous for a recent murder. As for the apostles, the Book of Acts presents us with many examples of this kind. The same thing is also customary in the commonwealth. For there those who have given some public benefit are suddenly raised to heaven by the favour of the crowd; yet the same men, soon exposed, are torn to pieces by everyone if they manage affairs with less success, or do not satisfy the wishes or the desires of all. David experienced this: they first preferred him to Saul because of the slaying of Goliath; but not long afterwards they suffered him to be burdened by Saul with the most unjust suspicion of aiming at the kingdom, and to be cast into exile. And again, when Saul was dead, they flocked to him eagerly, saying: "Behold, we are your bone and your flesh," etc. Elsewhere too they contended fiercely about him with the tribe of Judah, which claimed David as its own because of kinship; but when after Solomon's death his son Rehoboam, puffed up with youthful confidence, answered their request somewhat harshly, they at once, forgetting all the old benefits, cried out: "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel; now see to your own house, David." Many similar things are found in profane histories. The Athenians indeed banished Alcibiades because of the badly conducted war in Sicily; but when he was recalled and had conquered the Lacedaemonians by land and sea, they judged him worthy of divine as well as human honours; yet soon, when they were waging war in Asia under the same general, and he, intent on plunder, had suffered a defeat, they again punished him with exile. They also condemned Phocion, and then refused him a funeral and a tomb; but a little later they set up a statue of him, and at public expense they gave his bones, once found, a burial. And what shall we say of the greater part of the Romans, who were at one time entering the city in triumph, and at another compelled to flee from it and seek hiding places? We read that their emperors were now adored, now torn apart by the soldiers, and finally again enrolled among the gods. But the day would fail me if I wished to recount all the examples of this kind that exist. These things ought to be observed by those who preside in the Church and the commonwealth, so that they may not be moved by the judgments of the world, but, mindful of their condition, may hold their station constantly, so that they can be approved by God.

units.la: Sed Ioannem concionantem audiamus, qui ut falso conceptam de se vulgi opinionem declinet, praeclarum de Christo fert testimonium, & omnes abs se adhunc vnum remittit. Summa & vsus concionis totius est, neminem neque in signis externis neque in horum administris haerere debere, sed ad Christum ascendere, vnicum salutis authorem, & qui quod signis adumbratur, reipsa fruen-dum exhibet ijs, qui per fidem ad ipsum accedunt. Partes duae sunt.
units.tr: But let us hear John preaching, who, to set aside the opinion the crowd had formed of him, bears a remarkable witness to Christ and sends all men away from himself to him alone. The sum and purpose of the whole sermon is that no one should cling either to external signs or to their ministers, but should rise to Christ, the one author of salvation, who gives in reality what the signs foreshadow to those who come to him by faith. There are two parts.

units.la: Prima inter se & Christum distinguit, vel potius seipsum & hunc confert, ut ex ea collatio-ne appareat, quàm alte supra ipsum Christus emineat, & quàm errent, qui ipsum salutis authorem putent. Ego quidem (inquit) aqua baptizo, id est, externi modo signi administer sum, nec quic-quam praeterea amplius conferre, aut in hominum animis operari possum: Id enim humanas vires longè superat. Venit ergo me multò validior, qui virtute, potentia & authoritate in tantum me ex-cellit, ut si quis me ex propria dignitate aestimet, ne abiectissimo quidem officio, quod illi debetur, possim sufficere. Nam non dignus ero, qui vel calceos eius portem, vel solearum vincula soluam. Ad hunc ergo contendite, hunc patribus promissum vindicem esse credite, et salui eritis. Is enim vos baptizabit spiritu sancto et igne, id est, ipsum spiritu sancto vobis conferet, qui animas peccatorum sordibus pollutas abluit, homines regenerat, & ea in animis eorum operatur, quae ad consequendam salutem salutem necessaria sunt. Quamuis autem haec omnia unus spiritus perficiat, & ideo apud Marcum huius solius mentio fiat, ignem tamen ei coniungit: partim, quod illum sub specie ignis dandum fore ex peculiari revelatione sciebat: partim ut illius virtutem & effectus commendet. Solet enim spiritus sanctus homines excoquere, perinde ut ignis aurum & argentum excoquit. Idem animos quoque rerum caelestium desiderio accendit, adhaec agiles & industrios reddit ad ea exequenda, quae non nisi a Deo iniunguntur. Et haec quidem Ioannes in praesenti dicere voluit, non autem (ut quidam sentiunt) inter suum & Christi baptismum discernere, quasi hic a suo sit alius. Nam quoad externum baptismum, non alium administrauit Ioannes, quam quo hodie ecclesia utitur. Quod si qui negare velint, ii simul apostolos vere baptizatos fuisse negent oportet, una cum omnibus iis qui per baptismum Christo nomen dederunt, priusquam ille baptizandi munus illis mandaret. Constat enim Christum ipsum in docendo quidem assiduum fuisse, baptizauisse autem neminem. Per Ioannem ergo apostoli baptizati sunt, & vere quidem, nisi nos illis quoad baptismum praeferre libeat. Quid autem de Apostolis dicere attinet, quando Christum non alio quam Ioannis baptismo tinctum fuisse scimus? Ut vero ille per Circuncisionem ecclesiae veteris testamenti associari voluit: ita ut in novi quoque populi album adscriberetur opus erat, ut illum utriusque testamenti seruatorem esse constaret. At quomodo eum ad nos pertinere, nosque eius coheredes esse sciemus, si ipse alio baptismo tinctus est, quam quo nos in externam ecclesiae societatem adoptamur? Aut quam rationem adducere poterimus, propter quam ille baptizari debuerit, si non eundem nobiscum baptismum suscepit? Ergo ut diximus, Ioannes non duos & inter se diversos baptismos facit, quoad externum ecclesiae ritum, sed primo inter suam et Christi personam distinguit, deinde externam baptismi actionem a spirituali baptismo discernit, & huius authorem facit unum Christum, ut huic soli omnis laus & gloria salutis nostrae transcribatur, sibi ipsi vero nihil praeter externum ministerium reseruat, cuius effectus omnis ex spiritus virtute dependet. Neque ideo scripturae locis contradicit, in quibus verbi praecones regenerare, oculos aperire, seruare, peccata remittere dicuntur. Tunc enim cum externo ministerio ipse Dei filius coniungitur, qui hominibus coadiutoribus seu cooperarijs uti dignatur, & abs se institutum ministerium eiusmodi titulis exornat, ut huic libentius sese auditores accommodent. Debet hinc generalis doctrina peti, ut de ecclesiae ministerio & Sacramentis iudicandum sit, ne vel ministri sibijpsis nimium tribuant, vel ijsdem seruiliter addicti sint homines, aut etiam eos improbe contemnant. Poterant haec copiosius tractari, sed quia & de hoc & de multis aliis, quae in hisce Ioannis verbis obseruanda sunt, in Marco nostro diximus, ista modo sufficiant. Hoc unum in praesenti addimus, Ioannem ita soli Christo vindicare humanae salutis gloriam, ut ab eius societate omnes homines excludat. Si enim qui sanctissimus est inter eos, qui ex mulieribus nati sunt, eo usque infra illum subsidit, ut ne soluendis quidem corrigijs eius sufficiat, quid de aliis dicemus, qui nec ad Ioannis dignitatem accedunt? Sufficit hoc ad confutandam Romanorum Pontificum insolentiam, qui se Christi vicarios dicere audent. Si enim tales sunt, ea possint praestare oportet, quae ad Christi officium pertinent: qualia sunt, largiri spiritum sanctum regenerare, a peccatis abluere, Deo reconciliare, ecclesiae passim adesse, sin gulis eius membris vitae spiritum distribuere, aduersus omnes hostes tam visibiles quam invisibiles tueri, & quae alia sunt huius generis. Atqui superant ista vires humanas, neque ea quisquam sibi ipsi tribuere potest, nihil simul affectata diuinitatis crimen incurrat. Itaque procul relictis arrogantibus illis Salmoneis, nos uno Christo contenti simus, qui (ut de illo Isaias praedixit) principatum suum ipse suis humeris sustinet, & ecclesiae suae semper praesens adest, ideoque vicarijs minime opus habet, verbi autem ministros dedit, quorum est per Euangelij praedicationem & legitimum Sacramentorum usum ecclesiam colligere, & ad ipsum unum omnes adducere. Caeterum quia maior auditorum Ioannis pars ex hypocritis & poenitere nescijs constabat, alteram quoque concionis suae partem subijcit, qua iustum & graue iudicium omnibus denuntiat, qui inani pietatis specie gloriantur, cum a serio eius studio alieni sint. Cuius ventilabrum (inquit) in manu eius, id est, qui ventilabrum iam manu tenet, & perpurgabit aream suam: & coget triticum in horreum suum, paleam autem exuret igne inextinguibili. Parabola vtitur ex re rustica, quae praesenti negotio probe convenit. Quia enim Dei filius hominum salute tantopere delectatur, ut hanc suum cibum esse dicat, merito credentes panibus aut tritico puriori conferuntur. Et hoc fortissimus ille Martyr Ignatius respexisse videtur, qui cum Romam ad bestias duceretur dicebat: Frumentum Christi sum, & dentibus bestiarum molor, ut mundus panis Dei inveniar. Itaq; per aream Christi Ioannes ecclesiam intelligit, cuius titulus & nomen tunc penes Iudaeos erat, & haec dicendo corruptissimae eius statum perstringit, qui reformatione & purgatione seueriori opus habeat, quem admodum nuper ex Malachia docuimus, qui hoc ipsum alio simili a fullonibus desumpto docet. Recte autem ecclesia, quae in terris est, area confertur. Ut enim in hanc manipuli toti una cum stramine & paleis congregantur, quorum omnium simul collectorum ingens aceruus est: Ita ad aeternam ecclesiae societatem multi conueniunt, tam pij nimirum & vere credentes, quam fucati fidei professores, & hi quoque simul omnes innumeram multitudinem conficiunt, ut interdum ecclesia prae aliis sectis excellere & florere videatur. Quemadmodum vero post triturationem ventilabro aut vanno vtitur agricola, quo triticum a paleis discernit: ita cum Euangelij purior praedicatio infertur, mox vere pij ab hypocritis & sceleratis secernuntur, dum illi quidem Christum ex animo recipiunt, hi vero lucis & disciplinae impatientia exagitati manifestam faciunt secessionem ab ecclesia, quae tunc ad exiguum numerum redigitur, ut vix grex pusillus appareat, quae prius frequenti plurimorum concursu strepebat. Et hac quidem ventilatione Christum v furum esse Ioannes Iudaeis denuntiat, ut intelligant frustra eos ecclesiae titulo superbire, qui praeter inanem pietatis fucum nihil in Dei conspectum afferunt. Ut vero id factum sit, euangelica historia docet. Nam Christo praedicante, horribilis multorum impietas patuit, & vix palearum nomine digni fuerunt, qui paulo ante sanctissimi videbantur, & in ecclesia externa primatum obtinebant. Idem postea apostolorum quoque temporibus accidit, & hodie hoc ipsum pati fieri videmus. Idem enim, qui olim, Euangelij in hominum animis effectus est, neque aliter fieri potest, cum in ecclesiam promiscue boni & mali coeant, sicuti Christus alibi per sagenae piscatoriae & agri similitudines docet. Est hoc diligenter obseruandum, ne quod Anabaptistae solent, confusione aut commixtione illa externa ecclesiae offendamur, neque etiam terreamur si multos ab illa resilire videamus. Ex nobis enim exeunt, quia non sunt ex nobis, neque palearum leuitas quicquam officit tritico, quod illarum reiectione potius purgatur, ut praestantius sit & illustrius. Interim meminerint hypocritae impossibile esse, ut Christi oculos diu lateant, aut iudicium eius subterfugiant. Videt enim ille intimos cordium recessus, & iusto iudicio ita illos excaecat & rapit, ut proprio indicio seipsos turpiter prodant, qui prius toti ecclesiae sua hypocrisi imposuerunt.
units.tr: In the first part he distinguishes himself from Christ, or rather compares himself with him, so that from this comparison it may appear how far Christ rises above him, and how far those are mistaken who think John is the author of salvation. "I, indeed," he says, "baptize with water, that is, I am only the minister of an external sign, and I can contribute nothing further or work in men's souls, for that far exceeds human powers. There comes after me one far mightier than I, who in virtue, power and authority so surpasses me that if anyone judges me by my own dignity, I could not even suffice for the most menial service owed to him. For I am not worthy to carry his sandals or to loose the thongs of his shoes. Therefore, turn to him, believe that he is the deliverer promised to the fathers, and you will be saved. For he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire, that is, he will himself confer the Holy Spirit upon you, who cleanses souls polluted with the filth of sins, regenerates men, and works in their minds whatever is necessary for obtaining salvation. Although one Spirit accomplishes all these things, and therefore in Mark mention is made of him alone, nevertheless he joins fire to him: partly because he knew from a special revelation that the Spirit would be given under the appearance of fire, and partly to commend his power and effects. For the Holy Spirit is accustomed to refine men, just as fire refines gold and silver. The same Spirit also kindles hearts with a longing for heavenly things, and makes them nimble and diligent to carry out those tasks that are enjoined only by God." And this is what John wished to say at present; he did not, as some think, mean to distinguish between his own baptism and Christ's, as if the one were different from the other. For as far as external baptism goes, John administered no other than the one the Church uses today. If anyone wishes to deny this, he must at the same time deny that the apostles were truly baptized, together with all those who gave their names to Christ through baptism before he commissioned them to baptize. For it is established that Christ himself was constant in teaching, but baptized no one. Therefore the apostles were baptized through John, and truly so, unless we prefer to set ourselves above them in respect of baptism. But why need we speak of the apostles, when we know that Christ himself was baptized with no other baptism than John's? Indeed, just as John wished to join him to the church of the Old Testament through circumcision, so it was necessary that he be enrolled in the register of the new people too, so that it might be clear that he is the Saviour of both covenants. But how shall we know that he belongs to us and that we are his co-heirs, if he himself was baptized with a different baptism from that by which we are adopted into the external fellowship of the Church? Or what reason could we give for which he ought to have been baptized, if he did not receive the same baptism as we do? Therefore, as we have said, John does not make two baptisms differing from each other as regards the external rite of the Church; rather, he first distinguishes between his own person and Christ's, and then separates the external action of baptism from the spiritual baptism, and makes Christ alone its author, so that all praise and glory of our salvation is ascribed to him alone, while he reserves for himself nothing but the external ministry, whose whole effect depends on the power of the Spirit. Nor does he for this reason contradict those passages of Scripture in which the preachers of the Word are said to regenerate, open eyes, save, and forgive sins. For then the Son of God himself is joined with the external ministry, and he deigns to use men as helpers or co-workers, and adorns the ministry instituted by himself with such titles, so that hearers may more willingly submit themselves to it. From this a general doctrine ought to be drawn, that we must judge concerning the ministry of the Church and the sacraments, lest either ministers attribute too much to themselves, or men become slavishly attached to them, or even contemptuously despise them. These matters could be treated more fully, but since we have discussed both this and many other things to be observed in these words of John in our exposition of Mark, let what has been said suffice. We add only this at present: John so claims for Christ alone the glory of human salvation that he excludes all men from fellowship with him. For if he who is the most holy among those born of women so stoops beneath him that he is not even sufficient to loose his thongs, what shall we say of others, who do not approach John's dignity? This is enough to refute the arrogance of the Roman Pontiffs, who dare to call themselves Christ's vicars. For if they are such, they ought to be able to perform those things that belong to the office of Christ: such as bestowing the Holy Spirit, regenerating, washing away sins, reconciling to God, being present everywhere in the Church, distributing the spirit of life to each of its members, defending it against all enemies, visible and invisible, and other things of this kind. But these things surpass human powers, nor can anyone claim them for himself without at the same time incurring the crime of affected divinity. Therefore, let us put aside those arrogant Salmoneans and be content with Christ alone, who (as Isaiah foretold of him) bears his government upon his own shoulders, and is always present with his Church, and therefore has no need of vicars; but he has given ministers of the Word, whose task is to gather the Church through the preaching of the Gospel and the lawful use of the sacraments, and to bring all to himself alone. But because the greater part of John's hearers consisted of hypocrites who did not know how to repent, he adds the other part of his sermon, in which he announces a just and severe judgment against all who boast of an empty show of piety while being estranged from its earnest pursuit. "Whose winnowing fork (he says) is in his hand, that is, he who now holds the winnowing fork in his hand, will thoroughly clean his threshing floor, and will gather the wheat into his barn, but will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire." He uses a parable from rural life, which fits the present matter well. For since the Son of God so delights in men's salvation that he calls it his food, believers are rightly compared to bread or to the purest wheat. And the most valiant martyr Ignatius seems to have had this in mind, who, when he was being led to Rome to the beasts, said: "I am the wheat of Christ, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread of God." So by the threshing floor of Christ John means the Church, whose title and name at that time belonged to the Jews; and by saying this he censures its state, which had become very corrupt and needed a more severe reformation and purging, as we taught recently from Malachi, who teaches the same thing by another similar image taken from fullers. Rightly, too, the Church that is on earth is compared to a threshing floor. For as the sheaves are gathered together on it along with the straw and chaff, and all of these collected together make a huge heap, so to the eternal fellowship of the Church many come together, truly pious and sincere believers no doubt, but also professors of a feigned faith; and all of these together make up an innumerable multitude, so that at times the Church seems to excel and flourish above other sects. But just as, after threshing, the farmer uses a winnowing fan or sieve to separate the wheat from the chaff, so when the purer preaching of the Gospel is brought in, straightway the truly pious are separated from hypocrites and wicked men: the former receive Christ from the heart, while the latter, vexed by impatience with the light and with discipline, make a manifest secession from the Church, which is then reduced to a small number, so that it scarcely appears a little flock, though before it resounded with the crowded gathering of many. By this winnowing John announces to the Jews that Christ is the one who will separate, so that they may understand that they vainly pride themselves on the title of the Church, if they bring nothing into God's sight beyond an empty mask of piety. How this came to pass, the gospel history shows. For when Christ preached, the dreadful impiety of many was revealed, and those who shortly before seemed most holy and held the first place in the external Church were scarcely worthy of the name of chaff. The same happened afterwards in the times of the apostles too, and today we see this very thing happening. For the same effect that the Gospel produced in men's minds long ago still occurs, nor can it be otherwise, since good and bad alike come together indiscriminately into the Church, as Christ teaches elsewhere by the similitudes of the fishing net and the field. This must be carefully observed, so that we are not offended by that external confusion and mixture in the Church, as the Anabaptists are wont to be, nor frightened if we see many leap back from it. "They went out from us, because they were not of us"; nor does the lightness of the chaff harm the wheat, which is rather purged by their rejection, so that it may be more excellent and more illustrious. Meanwhile let the hypocrites remember that it is impossible for their hypocrisy to remain hidden from Christ's eyes long, or to escape his judgment. For he sees the innermost recesses of hearts, and by a just judgment so blinds and carries them away that they shamefully betray themselves by their own evidence, having previously deceived the whole Church with their hypocrisy.

units.la: Quia vero multus leuiculum videtur ab ecclesia eijci, imo multorum ea est improbitas, ut sponte ab illa discedendi occasionem quaerant, de futuro etiam piorum praemio & impiorum supplicio illos Ioannes admonet. Coget (inquit) triticum in horreum suum, paleam autem exuret igne inextinguibili. Horrei nomine beatae immortalitatis locum nobis Christi merito in coelis paratum intelligit, in quem olim colligentur pij, ut aeternum cum illo viuant, secundum promissionem: Volo ut vbi ego sum, illic etiam sit minister meus. Item: Volo pater, vbi ego sum, etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Continetur istis promissionibus tota hominis felicitas. Nam in hoc seculo agentibus nihil iucundius et beatius accidere potest, quam ut ecclesiae Dei cives sint. Beati enim (inquit Dauid) qui in domo tua habitant, perpetuo te laudabunt. Potior est dies in atrijs tuis, quam mille alij: malo defidere ad limen domus Dei, quam habitare in tentoriis impiorum. Completur autem felicitas ista, quando animae corporis vinculo solutae ad coelestes sedes migrant, corpora autem in spe requiescunt, ipsa quoq; restituenda olim in magno illo die, quando Christus ad iudicandum veniet. Et haec quidem pijs & vere credentibus euentura esse Ioannes pollicetur. Quid vero impijs et hypocritis, qui palearum nomine designantur? Exuret eos (inquit) igne inextinguibili. Per ignem hunc aeternos inferorum cruciatus intelligit, qui quales futuri sint, verbis exprimere non possumus. Non igitur opus est disputare de igne illo, materialis ne sit, aut minus. Horribile certe sit oportet supplicium illud, cuius sensus mediocris in hac carne agentes frequenter ad desperationem adigit, & ut sibi ipsis manum inferant eos cogit, qui nihil hac vita praesenti charius habent. Et quia corpora resurgent, non dubium nobis esse debet, quin ad haec quoque cruciatus ille redundaturus sit. Postulat enim hoc iniustitia Dei, ut qui in corpore peccarunt, in corpore etiam recipiant digna factis suis praemia. Sunt hæc dira admodum & horrorem incutiunt merito ijs, qui in eorum consideratione non ofcitan-ter versantur. Sed ea plerorumq; est stupiditas, ut ista vel non credant, vel nunquam cogitent. Di-scant ergo verbi administri ad Ioannis exemplum ita prædicare Christum, ut omnes hunc non ser-vatorem modo, sed iustum et severum impietatis vindicem esse intelligant. Ideo magna libertate ad Dei tribunal citent eos, quos præfractiores esse vident. Meminerint item singuli, non sufficere ad sa-lutem, si in externa ecclesiæ societate censeantur, nisi triticum sint purum & bonum, quo Dominus delectari possit. Cogitent præterea fore aliquando finem huius mundi, & tunc omnes homines ad Christi tribunal sistendos esse, ut irrevocabilem vel salutis vel damnationis æternæ sententiam audiant. Non proderit tunc ecclesiæ oculos fefellisse, aut inter homines sanctimoniæ existimatione su-stinuisse. Aperientur enim tunc libri, & tam Christi iudicis quam totius mundi oculis patebit, quales aliquando fuerimus. Nihil etiam præsidij erit in opibus, honoribus & vniuerso mundi fastu: quia vno igne prius omnia illa ardebunt, & ipsa etiam elementa liquefient. Horum igitur meditatione excitati pietatem veram colamus, ut nobis lætus illucescat dies ille, & in beata regni cœlestis horrea colligamur per Christum Iesum, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Since, however, many people think it a trifling matter to be cast out of the Church, and indeed so great is the wickedness of many that they seek an occasion to withdraw from it of their own accord, John also warns them about the future reward of the godly and the punishment of the wicked. "He will gather," he says, "the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire." By the name of the barn he understands the place of blessed immortality prepared in heaven for us by the merit of Christ, into which the godly will one day be gathered to live with him eternally, according to the promise: "Where I am, there my servant also will be." Likewise: "Father, where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me." The whole happiness of man is contained in these promises. For nothing more joyful or blessed can befall those who live in this age than to be citizens of the Church of God. For, as David says, "Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ever. A day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere; I would rather stand at the threshold of the house of God than dwell in the tents of the wicked." This happiness is completed when souls, released from the bond of the body, pass to the heavenly seats, while the bodies rest in hope, to be restored themselves in that great day when Christ comes to judge. John promises that these things will come to pass for the godly and for those who truly believe. But what of the wicked and hypocrites, who are designated by the name of chaff? "He will burn them," he says, "with unquenchable fire." By this fire he understands the eternal torments of the lower world, which we cannot express in words as to what they will be like. There is therefore no need to dispute whether that fire is material or not. That punishment must surely be dreadful, since even a moderate sense of it, while we live in this flesh, often drives people to despair and compels those who hold nothing dearer than this present life to lay hands on themselves. And since the bodies will rise again, there ought to be no doubt in our minds that this torment will extend to them as well. For the justice of God demands that those who have sinned in the body should also receive in the body rewards worthy of their deeds. These things are very dreadful and rightly strike horror into those who do not dwell on them carelessly. But most people are so stupid that they either do not believe them or never think about them. Let the ministers of the Word therefore learn to preach Christ after John's example, so that everyone understands him to be not only Saviour but also the just and severe avenger of impiety. Let them, therefore, with great boldness summon before God's tribunal those whom they see to be more stubborn. Let each one also remember that it is not enough for salvation to be counted in the external fellowship of the Church, unless they are pure and good wheat, in which the Lord can take delight. Let them further consider that there will one day be an end to this world, and then all people must stand before the tribunal of Christ to hear the irrevocable sentence of eternal salvation or damnation. It will then be of no benefit to have deceived the eyes of the Church, or to have maintained among men the reputation of holiness. For the books will then be opened, and it will be plain to the eyes of Christ the Judge, and to those of the whole world, what we once were. Nor will there be any protection in wealth, honours and all the pomp of the world, since all those things will first burn with a single fire, and the elements themselves will melt. Therefore, stirred up by meditation on these things, let us cultivate true piety, so that that joyful day may dawn upon us, and we may be gathered into the blessed barns of the heavenly kingdom through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXIII.

units.la: Multa igitur etiam alia exhortans euangelizabat populo. Herodes autem tetrarcha, cum argueretur ab eo de Herodiade, uxore Philippi fratris sui, degq; omnibus sceleribus, quæ ipse fecerat, adiecit & hoc super omnia, quod inclusit Ioannem in carcere.
units.tr: So with many other exhortations he preached the good news to the people. But Herod the tetrarch, when he was rebuked by him concerning Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, and concerning all the wicked deeds which he had done, added this also above all, that he shut up John in prison.

units.la: QVoniam Ioannes primus noui testamenti minister fuit, in eodem exemplu proponi oportuit, in quo tota ministerij ecclesiastici ratio adumbraretur, & quod omnes imitentur, qui Euangelium prædicant. Non temere igitur Euangelistæ tanta diligentia describunt quid ille docuerit, & qualem se gesserit in hoc suo ministerio. Et dixit hucusque multa Lucas, quæ nos de illo atque doctrina eius iudicare docent. Quia tamen omnium, quæ ille dixit & fecit finis esset Christus, cui populum præparare & adducere debuit, & ad quem ille omnes auditores suos remisit: ijs contentus, quæ ad confirmandam testimonij eius de Christo fidem sufficiebant, ad res ipsius Christi describendas festinat. Ideo in præsenti summatim comprehendit, quæ de eius doctrina simul & exitu vitæ dicenda restabant. Summa omnium est, Ioannem fidelem verbi Dei præconem & Christi anteambulonem fuisse, qui nullam occasionem prætermiserit, quin omnes maxima qua potuit industria fit exhortatus ad capessendam salutem, quæ tunc in foribus erat, neq; vllius hominis authoritate siue potentia se passus sit ab officio revocari, quodq; suam doctrinam atque ministerium tandem proprio sanguine sanciuerit. Hæc etsi paucis verbis Euangelista complectatur, multa tamen hic latent diligenti consideratione dignissima, & ideo de singulis ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Since John was the first minister of the New Testament, it was fitting that he be set forth as an example in which the whole plan of the ecclesiastical ministry is shadowed forth, and which all who preach the Gospel should imitate. It is therefore not without reason that the Evangelists describe with such care what he taught and how he conducted himself in his ministry. Luke has so far related many things which teach us to judge of him and of his doctrine. Yet since the end of all that he said and did was Christ, for whom he was to prepare and lead the people, and to whom he sent all his hearers away, Luke, being content with those things which were sufficient to confirm faith in John's testimony about Christ, hastens on to describe the things concerning Christ himself. Therefore in the present passage he briefly sums up what remained to be said about John's doctrine and the outcome of his life. The sum of all is this: John was a faithful herald of God's Word and forerunner of Christ, who let no opportunity pass without exhorting all people, with the greatest diligence he could, to seize the salvation which was then at the door; who allowed himself to be called back from his office by no man's authority or power; and who at last sealed his doctrine and ministry with his own blood. Although the Evangelist sums these up in few words, many things lie hidden here that are well worth careful consideration, and so we shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Principio de Ioannis doctrina sic dicit: Multa igitur etiam alia exhortans euangelizabat populo, &c. In quibus verbis primùm occurrit, quid docuerit. Multa nimirum alia præter ea, quæ hucusque audiuimus. Quod non sic accipi debet, quasi nonnulla ab his diuersa tradiderit, aut quod non sufficiant ad salutis cognitionem ea, quæ Euangelistæ literis mandarunt. Hoc sophismate, aut cauillo potius vtuntur nonnulli, qui suas aut patrum suorum traditiones tueri satagunt, ut eandem illis, quæ scripturis sacris debetur, authoritatem vendicent. Sed facile est illos confutare. Quia enim Spiritus sancti ministri & amanuenses (ut sic loquar) fuerunt Prophetæ & Apostoli, inexcusabilis blasphemia fuerit, si eos aliquid prætermisisse dicamus eorum, quæ nobis ad salutem consequendam cognitu aut obseruatu necessaria sunt. Et si ea propius examinemus, quæ Ioannem de Christo, de pœnitentia & singulorum hominum officijs differentem audiuimus, non obscure apparebit, illis omnem salutis doctrinam contineri. Adhæc Euangelizandi verbo vtitur Lucas, ut ostendat Ioannem non aliud, quàm Euangelium prædicauisse, cuius summa & partes singulæ in Apostolorum prædicatione & scriptis tam perfectè & perspicuè continentur, vt anathema censeri mereatur quicunq; aliud quid prædicarit, etiamsi Angelus de cœlo fuerit. Non igitur de doctrinæ Ioannis argumento, sed concionum eius numero aut frequentia loquitur Lucas, & sensus est, eum non has solùm conciones habuisse, sed plures alias quoque, quarum idem fuit argumentum, quòd nimirum ad pœnitentiam quosuis est hortatus, & simul de Christo testimonium tulit, vt ex hoc consolationem & certam salutis fiduciam conciperent, qui serio pœnitentiæ sensu tangebantur. Ioannes certè Euangelista quatuor testimonia eius ex ordine recenset, quibus suam authoritatem Christo constantissimè asseruit aduersus pharisæos et falsas de seipso vulgi opiniones. Inter quæ præclarum omnino est, quo dicit: Is est de quo dicebam, Qui post me venit, prælatus est mihi, quia prior me erat. Et ex plenitudine ipsius omnes sumpsimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Nam Lex per Mosem data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Item: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. In primis tamen memorabile est, quòd discipulos Christum stultè æmulantes graviter corripit, & eosdem ad Christum remittit dicens: Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi, qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi: hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est. Illum oportet crescere, me verò minui. Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit in manum eius. Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam, &c. Vt verò de Iesu Christo pluribus & sæpe disseruit, prout occasio data est: sic non dubium est, quin privatim singulos ad pœnitentiam quoque exhortatus sit, & publicè hoc vnum egerit, vt quam plurimos ad Christum perduceret. At si eadem semper Ioannis doctrina fuit, nimium audaces sunt, qui hodie novas traditiones ecclesiæ obtrudunt, quibus Christi meritum obscuratur, & rerum imperiti à veritatis via adineptas & frigidas superstitiones abducuntur.
units.tr: First, he speaks thus of John's teaching: "So with many other exhortations he preached the good news to the people," and so on. In these words what he taught first comes to notice: indeed many other things besides those we have heard so far. This should not be taken as if John delivered some things different from these, or as if what the Evangelists committed to writing were not sufficient for knowledge of salvation. Some people use this sophism, or rather quibble, who strive to defend their own traditions or those of their fathers, so as to claim for them the same authority that is owed to the holy Scriptures. But it is easy to refute them. For since the prophets and apostles were the ministers and, so to speak, the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, it would be an inexcusable blasphemy to say that they omitted anything of those things which are necessary for us to know or observe in order to obtain salvation. And if we examine more closely what we have heard John speaking about Christ, about repentance, and about the duties of individual men, it will plainly appear that all the doctrine of salvation is contained in these. Moreover, Luke uses the verb "to evangelize" to show that John preached nothing other than the Gospel, whose sum and individual parts are so perfectly and clearly contained in the preaching and writings of the Apostles that whoever preaches anything else deserves to be accounted accursed, even if he be an angel from heaven. Luke therefore speaks not of the subject matter of John's teaching but of the number or frequency of his sermons, and the sense is that he gave not only these sermons but many others too, on the same subject: namely, that he urged people to repentance of every kind, and at the same time bore witness concerning Christ, so that those who were seriously touched by a sense of repentance might conceive from this consolation and a sure confidence of salvation. The Evangelist John indeed recounts in order four testimonies of John the Baptist, by which he most steadfastly asserted his authority for Christ against the Pharisees and the false opinions of the crowd about himself. Among these there is one truly remarkable, where he says: "This is he of whom I spoke: he who comes after me has been preferred before me, because he was before me. And of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace. For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Likewise: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." Yet first of all it is memorable that he sharply rebukes the disciples who foolishly rivalled Christ, and sends them back to Christ, saying: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. This my joy therefore is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life," and so on. But that he spoke at length and often of Jesus Christ, as occasion was given, is not doubtful; so also there is no doubt that he exhorted individuals privately to repentance too, and publicly did this one thing, that he might lead as many as possible to Christ. But if John's teaching was always the same, then they are too bold who nowadays thrust new traditions upon the Church, by which the merit of Christ is obscured, and the ignorant are led away from the way of truth into idle and cold superstitions.

units.la: Secundo modum quoque indicat Lucas, quem inter docendum Ioannes secutus est. Multa alia (inquit) exhortans euangelizabat. Sic ergo pœnitentiam & fidem in Christum tradidit, vt simul obedientiam ab omnibus exigeret, et hanc præstitu necessariam esse doceret. Finis autem & scopus omnium fuit, vt de salute in Christo exhibita omnes certi redderentur, inq; eius possessione venirent. Apparet autem in eius exemplo, quæ vera sit prædicandi ratio. Sunt qui sufficere dicant, si scripturæ loci verbotim recitentur, & omnem eius interpretationem superuacaneam esse putant. Quasi verò his auditis, mox omnes intelligant quid facto opus sit. Attamen vt hoc illis demus, non tamen in eo finis ministerij consistit, vt intelligant modo auditores, quid olim dictum factumúe sit, sed vt ista omnia ad se pertinere norint, & vitam omnem secundum divinæ voluntatis regulam instituant. Ideo pro locorum & temporum ratione verbum Dei secari debet, & singulorum institutioni applicari quæcunque illo traduntur. Admonet de hoc Paulus, qui cum in epistola ad Titum summam doctrinæ Christianæ breviter & perspicuè complexus esset, tandem infert: Hæc loquere, & exhortare, & argue cum summa authoritate vel imperio, idest, ita age, vt te Christi Iesu legatum esse omnes intelligant, neque causam habeant contemnendi tuam doctrinam. Et in posteriori ad Timoth. idem sic scribit: Obtestor ego coram Deo & Domino Iesu Christo, qui iudicaturus est viuos & mortuos in illustri illo suo aduentu & regno suo: Prædica sermonem, insta tempestiuè, intempestiuè, argue, obiurga, exhortare cum omni lenitate & doctrina. Neque hoc temeremonet Apostolus. Quia enim scriptura sacra vtilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem & ad institutionem, ita illam tractari oportet in ecclesia, vt imperiti doceantur, hypocritæ & erronei spiritus arguantur, scelerati corrigantur, omnes denique in salutis æternæ studio proficiant. Ita in hoc munere olim prophetæ versati sunt, vt in eorum sermonibus est videre. Secutus est eandem docendi rationem Christus, & post hunc Apostoli quoque. Ab ea igitur quicunque hodie discedunt, ij vel canes muti sunt, vel seductores, & proinde pijs omnibus merito suspecti esse debent.
units.tr: Second, Luke also indicates the method which John followed in teaching. "Exhorting many others," he says, "he preached the good news." So he set forth repentance and faith in Christ, while at the same time requiring obedience from all and teaching that this obedience must be rendered. The end and aim of all was that everyone should be made certain of the salvation offered in Christ and come into possession of it. Now the true method of preaching appears from his example. There are those who say it is enough if passages of Scripture are recited word for word, and they think any interpretation of them superfluous, as if, once these are heard, everyone would straightway understand what needs to be done. Yet even granting them this, the end of the ministry does not consist in the hearers merely understanding what was said or done long ago, but in their knowing that all these things pertain to themselves, and in ordering their whole life according to the rule of the divine will. Therefore the Word of God must be cut up according to the circumstances of places and times, and whatever is delivered in it applied to the instruction of individuals. Paul gives a warning about this, who, having briefly and clearly summed up the sum of Christian doctrine in his Epistle to Titus, finally concludes: "Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority or command," that is, act so that everyone understands that you are an envoy of Christ Jesus and that they have no cause for despising your teaching. And in the later letter to Timothy he writes thus: "I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the living and the dead at his glorious coming and in his kingdom: preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season, rebuke, reprove, exhort with all patience and teaching." Nor does the Apostle admonish this rashly. For since Holy Scripture is profitable for teaching, for rebuke, for correction and for instruction, it must be handled in the Church in such a way that the unlearned are taught, hypocrites and those of erroneous spirit are rebuked, the wicked are corrected, and in short all make progress in the pursuit of eternal salvation. Thus the prophets were occupied in this office of old, as can be seen in their sermons. Christ followed the same method of teaching, and after him the Apostles too. Therefore whoever today departs from this method is either a dumb dog or a seducer, and for that reason ought rightly to be suspect to all the godly.

units.la: Tertiò, quibus Ioannes prædicarit, indicatur. Toti nimirum populo, Quo nomine omnis loci & ordinis homines comprehenduntur, quibus singulis doctrinam suam accommodauit, vt conciones eius, quas nuper audiuimus, testantur. In illis enim non rude vulgus solùm docuit, sed publicanos & milites, quos Romani Imperij authoritas commendabat, officij admonuit: imò Scribas & Sacerdotes maxima cum seueritate corripuit. In præsenti Herodis etiam Regis fit mentio, quem propter Herodiadem, Philippi fratris uxorem, & alia scelera arguisse dicitur. Fuit is Antipas dictus, multis atque gravissimis flagitiis infamis. Intemperantiae equidem & libidini addictissimus fuisse, hoc unum abunde probat, quod inter ipsum & Herodiadem accidit. Fuerat haec uxor Philippi, quem Iturae & Trachonitidis tetrarcham supra dixit Lucas, & quae modo rati & mansuetissimi ingenij virum fuisse Iosephus tradit. Ad hunc cum fratre Herodes Romam proficiscens ex itinere diuertisset, Herodiadis amore captus cum ea pactus est, & postea ex Roma reversus a fratre abductam uxoris loco habuit, dimissa uxore priori, Aretae Arabum Regis filia. In quo facto scelera multa & in primis horrenda concurrunt. Primo enim ius hospitij violavit, quod gentibus olim sacrosanctum fuit, adeo ut Iouem Ξένιον, id est, hospitij praesidem & vindicem crederent. Deinde perfidiam istam atrociorem reddit cognationis vinculum: quando non in hospitem modo, sed in fratrem germanum, eumque virum optimum & mansuetissimum peccat. Accedit coniugij prophanatio & adulterium duplex, quo utrinque peccatum fuit, cum & illa maritum legitimum deserat, & hic uxori propriae datam fidem turpiter violet. Superat autem haec omnia incestus, quo fratris uxorem ille polluit, haec aut mariti sui fratri miscetur: quod diuinis legibus prohiberi non ignorabat. Per Mosem enim ille sic loquitur. Verenda uxoris fratris tui ne retegas: ignominia enim est fratri tuo. Item, Si quis acceperit uxorem fratris sui, abominanda res est, turpitudinem fratris sui retexit, orbi erunt. Auget praeterea scelus hoc matifestus numinis contemptus, qui in eo apparet, quod nec Archelai fratris exemplo movetur, qui cum Alexandri fratris iampridem defuncti uxorem, Glaphiram nomine, duxisset, non multo post regno excidit, & exilio multatus est, et illa quoque diris insomnijs agitata vitae exitu tristem atque infelicem habuit. Fuit ergo deplorate nequitiae homo Herodes iste, quem neque pudor, neque publicae honestatis respectus, neque Legis diuinae authoritas, neque publicus omnium consensus, neque retens adhuc diuini iudicij exemplum in officio continere potuit, ut anni prijs incestis abstineret, si modo nuptiae dici merentur, in quibus nihil praeter inanis coniugij titulus nefariae libidini praetexitur. Qualis autem vita eius vniuersa fuerit, qui item aulae totius mores, ex epulo illo cordatus quisque aestimare potest, quod in natalitio die Satrapis & tribunis suis exhibuit. At non potuerunt haec fieri, quin simul infelicem populum tributis & exactionibus premeret, & praefectus suis occasionem daret multa pro libidine & auaritia eorum licenter nimis designandi. Haec igitur & quaecunque huius generis erant, Ioannes accusavit, & quidem liberrime, ut ex eo apparet, quod Regi in faciem dicebat (sicuti Matthaeus & Marcus annotarunt:) Non licet tibi habere uxorem fratris tui. Quae verba etsi pauca sint, & nihil durum in se contineant, intolerabile tamen & nulla venia dignum videtur Regibus, si quis dicat, illis non licere quod faciunt. Omnium enim animis insidet, quod impura illa nouerca Antonino Bassiano dicebat: Si libet, licet. Et quod parasiti finxerunt: Augustus & Augusta non tenentur legibus. Eo autem durior & periculosior erat Ioannis conditio, quod haec dicendo, non obscure incestum Regi exprobrabat, & simul Herodiadem accusabat, cuius iram prouocare cum aperto discrimine erat coniunctum. Est ergo hoc ingens magnae fidei & constantiae argumentum, quo suum ministerium Ioannes ornauit. Et admonentur hoc loco Reges & principes, ut meminerint, se quoque verbo Dei subiectos esse, & proinde non decere ipsos, ut sua potentia vel authoritate aduersus illud abutantur. Quia enim honorem & potestatem omnem a Deo acceperunt, aequum est, ut vicissim hunc suum Dominum agnoscant, hunc reuereantur, & verbo sive praeceptis eius obtemperent. Neque aliter illis suus honor constabit, nisi Deo debitum obsequium praestent. Huius enim vox est: Honorantes me honorabo, at qui me contemnunt, contemnentur. Et principum exemplis malis vniuersam magistratus authoritatem prostitui & contemptissimam red dinotius est, quam ut multa demonstratione opus habeat. Verissime enim Claudianus cecinit:
units.tr: Thirdly, the people to whom John preached are indicated: namely, the whole people. This name takes in men of every place and rank, and he adapted his teaching to each of them, as his sermons, which we heard recently, bear witness. For in them he not only taught the common crowd but also admonished the tax collectors and soldiers, who were under the authority of the Roman empire, about their duties. Indeed, he rebuked the scribes and priests with the greatest severity. In the present passage mention is made of King Herod as well, whom John is said to have accused of his crimes, above all of his taking Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, and of other wrongs. This Herod was called Antipas, and he was notorious for many grave and shameful offences. That he was utterly given over to intemperance and lust is proved abundantly by one fact alone, what happened between him and Herodias. This woman had been the wife of Philip, whom Luke has just called tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis, and whom Josephus reports to have been a man of a quiet and most gentle disposition. Herod, on his way to Rome with his brother, turned aside to visit him; captivated by love for Herodias, he made a pact with her, and afterwards, on returning from Rome, he took his brother's wife away and held her in the place of a wife, having put away his earlier wife, the daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabs. In this deed many crimes, and especially horrible ones, come together. First, he violated the right of hospitality, which was once held sacred among the nations, so much so that they believed Jupiter Xenios [Ξένιον], that is, the guardian and avenger of hospitality, presided over it. Next, the bond of kinship makes this treachery more atrocious, since he sins not only against a host but against his own full brother, and a most excellent and gentle man at that. Added to this is the profaning of marriage and a double adultery, by which sin was committed on both sides, since she deserted her lawful husband and he shamefully broke the faith he had pledged to his own wife. But above all this stands the incest, by which he defiled his brother's wife, and she, having been his brother's wife, was joined to him; he did not fail to know that the divine laws forbid this. For through Moses God speaks thus: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; for it is your brother's shame" (Levit. 18.). Likewise: "If a man takes his brother's wife, it is an abominable thing; he has uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless" (Levit. 20.). Moreover, this crime is aggravated by a manifest contempt of God, which appears in the fact that he was not moved by the example of Archelaus, his brother, who, after taking as his wife Glaphyra, the widow of Alexander, another brother who had died long before, was not long afterwards thrown from his kingdom and punished with exile; and she too, troubled by dreadful nightmares, ended her life in sorrow and misery. Herod was therefore a man of desperate wickedness, whom neither shame, nor regard for public decency, nor the authority of the divine Law, nor the universal consensus of all people, nor the example of divine judgment still before his eyes, could restrain from his duty, so that he would abstain from such incest, if indeed they deserve the name of marriage, in which nothing but the empty title of marriage is put forward as a cover for unspeakable lust. What his whole life was like, and likewise the morals of his entire court, any sensible person can judge from that banquet which he gave to his satraps and tribunes on his birthday. But these things could not happen without his at the same time crushing the unhappy people with taxes and exactions, and giving his officials the opportunity to plunder, at their own wanton will and greed, in very free fashion. John therefore accused these things and all things of this kind, and indeed most freely, as is clear from the fact that he said to the king to his face (as Matthew and Mark have noted): "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife." Although these words are few and contain nothing harsh in themselves, it seems intolerable and deserving of no pardon for kings that someone should say they are not permitted to do what they do. For that saying of the impure stepmother to Antoninus Bassianus lodges in everyone's mind: "If it pleases, it is lawful." And the saying that the flatterers invented: "The Augustus and the Augusta are not bound by the laws." Yet John's position was all the harder and more perilous, because in saying this he openly reproached the king with incest, and at the same time accused Herodias, whose anger to provoke was attended by an open danger. This is therefore a great proof of strong faith and constancy, with which John adorned his ministry. And here kings and princes are admonished to remember that they too are subject to the word of God, and therefore it is not fitting for them to abuse their power or authority against it. For since they have received all honour and power from God, it is fair that in turn they acknowledge him as their Lord, revere him, and obey his word and precepts. Nor will their honour stand otherwise, unless they render due obedience to God. For this is his voice: "Those who honour me I will honour, but those who despise me shall be despised" (1 Sam. 2.). And it is more evident than it needs much demonstration that the authority of the whole magistracy is prostituted and made most contemptible by the bad examples of princes. For Claudian sang most truly:

units.la: Componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum: nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta valent, quam vita regentis.
units.tr: The world is shaped by the example of its king: nor can edicts bend human minds as much as the life of the ruler does.

units.la: Recte ergo olim Deus praecepit Regibus, ut Legis librum perpetuo penes se habeant, in illo legant, & ex eo consilia petant, quibus in repub. administranda utantur. Idem etiam Ieremiae mandauit, ut non vulgo soli, sed sacerdotibus, principibus item & regibus concionaretur. Mirum ergo est, hodie Christianos aliquos principes sibi ipsis immunitate quandam vendicare, cum olim qui inter gentes... tes prudentia & virtute excelluerunt, principes viros institutione cumprimis opus habere intellexe rint. Plato eas demum respub. felices fore dicebat, in quibus aut philosophi regnarent, aut reges philosopharentur. Et Alexander ille Magnus Homeri Iliadem circumgestare & eandem dormiturus vna cum pugione puluinari supponere consueuerat, vt inde virtutis praecepta & exempla hauriret. Quanto magis ergo Christianos decet Dei verbum audire, eo admoneri, doceri, corrigi denique & increpari, si quid praeter officium fecerunt? At fatemur hoc (inquiunt nonnulli) sed intollerabile & seditiosum nobis videtur, si ecclesiarum ministri principes publice reprehendant & accusent. Exeo enim occasionem arripiunt, qui iam ante ad res nouas nimium proclives sunt, vt rempub. turbent & motus excitent periculosos. Quibus responderi poterat publico remedio in morbus publicis & apertis opus esse, & per ipsos fieri posse ne palam arguantur, si nemini in publico mali exempli authores sint. Sed praeterea dicimus, Deum, qui magistratus authoritatem sacrosanctam esse voluit, ministerij quoq; ecclesiastici authorem esse, & ratum perpetuo esse eius mandatum, quo praecepit, vt qui verbi eius administri sunt scelera publica accusent, arguant, corripiant, & ijsdem iram suam denuntient, vt quamuis qui illa designarunt incurabiles manent, alij tamen terreantur, & e medio tollatur offendiculum, quo plures ad peccandum poterant prouocari. Vt ergo cessantibus in officio suo ecclesiarum ministris principes suam authoritatem interponere, & illos ad faciendum officium cogere debent (quod olim sanctissimos Reges & Imperatores fecisse constat) ita si quid praeter officium principes cum publico scandalo designant, ministrorum est illos vel admonere, vel etiam grauius & liberius accusare, prout facti aut sceleris commissi ratio postulat. Neque ideo vel seditiosus vel in magistratum iniurius censeri debet minister, si hoc facit. Non enim seditionis author est, qui publica scelera ex officio corripit, sed qui praeter officium quiduis pro sua libidine facit, & suae petulentiae prauo exemplo legum authoritatem violat, disciplinam publicam euertit, iura & iudicia dissipat, & pro pastore lupum, pro rege tyrannum agit. Ita olim per Eliam prophetam nos spiritus sanctus admonuit.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, God once commanded kings to keep the book of the Law always by them, to read in it, and to seek from it the counsels which they should use in governing the commonwealth. He likewise charged Jeremiah to preach not only to the common people but also to priests, princes and kings. It is strange, then, that some Christian princes today claim for themselves a certain immunity from instruction, when once those among the nations who excelled in wisdom and virtue understood that princes above all need training. Plato said that those commonwealths would at last be happy in which either philosophers ruled or kings philosophized. And Alexander the Great used to carry Homer's Iliad about with him and, when he was about to sleep, place it under his pillow along with his dagger, so that he might draw from it precepts and examples of virtue. How much more, then, does it befit Christians to hear the word of God, to be admonished by it, taught, corrected, and finally rebuked, if they have done anything beyond their duty? But some say: "We admit this, yet it seems to us intolerable and seditious if the ministers of the churches publicly rebuke and accuse princes. For from this they seize an occasion, those who are already too inclined to new things, to disturb the commonwealth and stir up dangerous commotions." To these one could reply that public diseases and open ones require a public remedy, and that it can come about through the princes themselves that they are not rebuked openly, if they are not themselves the authors of a bad example in public. But we add that God, who willed the authority of the magistrate to be sacred, is also the author of the ecclesiastical ministry, and that his command is binding for ever, by which he ordered that those who are the ministers of his Word should accuse, reprove and rebuke public crimes, and declare his wrath against them, so that, although those who committed them remain incurable, others may be frightened, and the stumbling block be removed from the midst, by which many more might have been provoked to sin. Therefore, just as princes ought to interpose their authority and compel the ministers of the churches to do their duty if they are failing in it (as is known to have been done by the most holy kings and emperors of old), so, if princes commit anything beyond their duty to public scandal, it is the task of the ministers either to admonish them or even to accuse them more severely and more freely, as the nature of the deed or crime committed requires. Nor should a minister be judged either seditious or injurious to the magistrate for doing this. For he is not the author of sedition who rebukes public crimes as his office requires; rather it is he who does whatever he likes beyond his office, and by his wanton example violates the authority of the laws, overturns public discipline, scatters rights and judgments, and makes a wolf out of a shepherd and a tyrant out of a king. So once the Holy Spirit admonished us through the prophet Elijah.

units.la: Cum enim illi Achab dixisset: Annon tu ille es, qui conturbat Israelem? Respondit ille: Ego non turbo Israelem, sed tu & domus patris tui, cum deseruKeritis praecepta Domini, &c. Et saepe alias prophetae testantur, terram sub illis moueri & contremiscere, qui praeter ius & fas opes ex aliorum sanguine colligunt, pauperes opprimunt, per libidines vagas grassantur, & omne iugum disciplinae reiiciunt. Et quod illi dicunt, id omnium seculorum exemplis probari potest. Constat enim potentissimae gna & florentissimas respub. principum libidine dissipatas, aut saltem periculose mutatas esse, quae prius prophetarum & seruorum Dei industria atque labore constituta fuerant. Quoad vero magistratus authoritate, ea diuini verbi admonitionibus atq; correptionibus non labefactatur, sed confirmatur potius, si illas patienter ferat qui populi oculos atq; animos aliquo malo exemplo offenderunt. Ita enim colligunt, illos non deuota animi malitia, sed ex cognata homini infirmitate peccauisse, & veniam mereri, cum culpam agnoscant, & eam emendare velint. Imo si verum fateri libeat, non alium honorem maiorem aut officium magis necessarium principibus praestare possunt Verbi ministri, quam si illos a peccatis in viam salutis reuocat, & pijs correptionibus tam ipsos quam respub. eorum fidei creditas ab interitu reducunt. Vt enim nimium officiosus fuerit, qui vt capillis parcat alicuius, eum in aquis periclitante otiosus spectat, & perire finit: Ita non honore viros principes afficit, sed illis extremae contumeliae & perditionis author est, qui ad illorum scelera conniuet, & in exitij praecipitio constitutos negligit, ne quid dicat, quod eorum maiestati & dignitati minus conueniat. Hoc ergo recte expenderunt prophetae, inter quos Samuel a Petro primus quodammodo numeratur. Ille vero etsi Saulem regem tenerrime amaret, & propter ipsum sese grauissime affligeret, eundem tamen publice arguere & accusare non est veritus, cum is publice peccauisset. Idem de alijs possumus dicere, quorum exempla ex ordine recitare longum foret.
units.tr: When Ahab had said to him, "Are you the one who troubles Israel?", he answered, "I do not trouble Israel, but you and your father's house, since you have forsaken the commandments of the Lord, etc." The prophets often testify that the land is shaken and trembles under those who gather wealth from the blood of others beyond right and law, oppress the poor, rage through wanton lusts, and cast off every yoke of discipline. What they say can be proved by the examples of all ages. It is established that the most powerful kingdoms and most flourishing commonwealths, which had earlier been set up through the diligence and labour of the prophets and servants of God, have been dissipated by the lust of princes, or at least dangerously changed. As for the authority of the magistrate, it is not weakened by the admonitions and corrections of the divine word but rather strengthened, if those who have offended the eyes and minds of the people by some bad example bear such correction patiently. For thus it is concluded that they sinned not from a devoted malice of mind but from the weakness common to man, and that they deserve pardon when they acknowledge their fault and wish to amend it. Indeed, if we may speak the truth, the ministers of the Word can render princes no greater honour or more necessary service than when they recall them from sin to the way of salvation and, by godly corrections, bring back from ruin both them and the commonwealth entrusted to their faith. Just as he would be too dutiful who, to spare someone's hair, idly watches him perishing in the water and lets him drown, so he does not honour princes but is the author of their extreme disgrace and ruin who winks at their crimes and neglects them when they stand on the brink of destruction, lest he say anything less fitting to their majesty and dignity. The prophets rightly judged this, and among them Samuel is in a way numbered first by Peter. Yet although he loved King Saul most tenderly and grieved greatly on his account, he did not hesitate to rebuke and accuse him publicly, since Saul had sinned publicly. The same can be said of others, whose examples it would be long to recite in order.

units.la: Quod vero de principibus dicitur, hoc ipsum in omnium aliorum apertis flagitijs atque scelerib[us] obseruari debet: vt qui peccando alicuius publici scandali authores fuerunt, liberè a Verbi ministris accusentur & sui admoneantur officij. Neque hic eorum rationes audiri debent, qui id facto opus esse negant, eò quòd plerique contumaciores sint, quàm vt correptionibus curari possint: multi etiam ex ijs peiores et proteruiores fiant. Nam quod ante diximus, vt hoc maximè verum sit, scan dalo tamen occuri debet, & publica adhiberi correptio, ne qui exemplum prauum sequantur. Et quia constat eos, qui natura ad malum proclives sunt, ferè ab exemplis argumenta petere, quibus vitia sua excusent, hîc omnino necesse est, vt quod proverbio dicitur, ministri ecclesiarum scapham scapham & ficum ficum dicant: ne vel canes muti sint, vel ex eorum numero, qui apud Ezechielem puluinaria confuere dicuntur, quibus scelerati & poenitere nescij suauiter indormiant. Vt ergo Herodi diserte edixit Ioannes: Non licet tibi fratris vxorem habere. Ita omnibus, qui aduersus Dei leges peccant aperte inculcandum est, hoc ipsos praeter officium facere, & poenas daturos esse Deo, nisi in tempore resipiscant. Quod si qui non faciunt, vt mundi huius gratiam demereantur, ij Dei serui non sunt, & de illorum manibus olim requiretur sanguis omnium, qui per ipsorum incuriam aut negligentiam pereunt.
units.tr: What is said of princes must also be observed in the open vices and crimes of all others: those who by sinning have been authors of some public scandal should be freely accused by the ministers of the Word and reminded of their duty. Nor should the reasons of those be heard who deny that this is needful, on the ground that most are too stubborn to be cured by correction, and many even become worse and more shameless through it. For although, as we said before, this is most true, scandal must nevertheless be met and public correction applied, lest others follow the bad example. And since it is established that those who are naturally prone to evil usually seek from examples arguments to excuse their vices, here it is altogether necessary that the ministers of the churches, as the proverb says, call a spade a spade and a fig a fig. Otherwise they are dumb dogs, or of the number of those who, in Ezekiel, are said to sew cushions on which the wicked, who know not how to repent, sleep sweetly. So John plainly told Herod: "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife." In the same way, it must be plainly impressed on all who sin against God's laws that in doing so they act beyond their duty and will have to give account to God unless they repent in time. But if some do not do this, in order to win the favour of this world, they are not servants of God, and from their hands will one day be required the blood of all who perish through their carelessness or negligence.

units.la: Porrò audiamus quid Herodes fecerit, vt simul discamus quam gratiam infelix mundus fidis monitoribus referat. Adiecit & hoc (inquit Lucas) super omnia, quòd inclusit Ioannem in carcere. Paucis verbis multa & immanissima scelera comprehendit. Nam vt Marcus scribit, initiò Ioannem in pretio habuit, nimirum propter eximiam virtutem, & quae doctrinae eius coniuncta erat, authoritatem. At vbi ipsum quoque liberius corripit Ioannes, & illud vlcus tangit, quod ipse in primis intactum volebat, non contentus ijs, quae antea designarat, insuper sanctissimo viro manus iniicit, et in carcere conclusum detinet, ne in publico docere pergat. Et quamuis hoc dignissimè faciat, sceleri tamen tam manifesto boni principis officium praetexit. Nam vt Iosephus scribit, metuens ne qui defectione facta rempub. turbarent, ad pacem conseruandam hoc factu necessarium esse censuit, ne rebus turbatis seram & inutilem poenitentiam ageret. Ideo non in carcere modò virum innocentissimum conclusit, sed eundem paulò post in gratiam scorti impudentissimi non minus iniustè quàm crudeliter occidit, sicuti in Marco prolixè diximus.
units.tr: Let us next hear what Herod did, so that we may learn at the same time what thanks the unhappy world returns to faithful monitors. "He added this too," Luke says, "above all things: that he shut John up in prison." In a few words he comprises many monstrous crimes. For, as Mark writes, at first he held John in esteem, no doubt on account of his outstanding virtue and the authority joined to his teaching. But when John rebuked him more freely and touched that sore which Herod especially wished to be left untouched, Herod, not content with what he had already done, laid hands on the most holy man, kept him shut up in prison, and so prevented him from continuing to teach in public. Although this was most worthily done, he cloaked his manifest crime with the pretence of a good prince's duty. For, as Josephus writes, fearing that some who had made a revolt might disturb the commonwealth, he judged this necessary for keeping the peace, lest he should make a late and useless repentance once affairs were in turmoil. Therefore he not only shut up that most innocent man in prison, but a little later, to gratify a most shameless harlot, put him to death no less unjustly than cruelly, as we have set out at length in Mark.

units.la: Nunc primò principum mores nobis inspiciendi veniunt, vt discamus, quàm imprudentes sint, qui cùm priuatim viuere & libertate frui possint, sese illis mancipant. Simulant illi interdum iustitiae & veritatis studium, vt eò maiorem apud omnes authoritatem consequantur. Et ideo frequenter spectatae virtutis & sapientiae viros ad se accersunt, cum ijs familiariter colloquuntur, eosdem mensae & consiliis adhibent. Sed eo praetextu non aliud quàm suae libidinis patrocinium quaerunt, & vt aliena virtute suam nequitiam tegant. Patet hoc ex eo, quòd quàm diu illi ipsi adulantur & eorum mores excusant, tantisper eos in honore & pretio habent. Quàm primùm verò se liberius corripi, vel etiam obliquè perstringi sentiunt, mox summa se iniuria affectos esse clamant, & in rabiem conuersi eos crudeliter laniant, à quorum consilijs toti pendere videbantur. Fecit hoc Herodes, quem ideo Christus non temere vulpem dixit, vt suo loco audiemus. Simile quid de Ioa Rege Iudaeorum legitur: qui cùm Iehoiada sacerdotem propter eximia in ipsum beneficia non posset non in pretio habere, tandem eius filium Zachariam, quòd liberius ab eo corriperetur, lapidibus obruendum curauit. Et huius generis exempla in historijs prophanis quoq; multa occurrunt. Sic Callisthenē philosophum olim ad se Alexander Macedo euocauit, vt verae philosophiae fuco sibi maiorem authoritatem pararet: at vbi is Aristotelis praeceptoris immemor (qui ipsum cum Rege aut rarissimè aut iucundissimè loqui iusserat) fastum Persicum liberius in illo accusat, & inuitum ad mores Macedonicos reducere studet, in carcerem ab illo coniicitur, vbi morbo pediculari perijt. Similis ferè Senecae fortuna apud Neronem fuit. Et Antonini Bassiani similem crudelitatem expertus est Papinianus iurisconsultus, quòd indignam Gaetae caedem excusare iussus respondisset: Non tam facile est parricidia excusare, quàm facere. Et vtinam hodie non etiam similia exempla extarent. Sunt ergo infelices & miseri, qui aulicae vitae seruitutem tanto periculo redimunt. At qui in aulis Verbi admi- nistros agunt, & ad munus istud legitimè vocati sunt, eos exemplis hisce nequaquam terreri decet: quin imitentur illi Ioannis constantiā atq; libertatem, se verò ipsos & vitā suam Deo committant. Caeterum inter priuatos homines Herodis ingenium referunt, qui vt Euangelicae veritatis fautores habeantur, eius praecones laudant & venerantur, vitam verò viuunt ab Euangelij professione alienissimam. Dissimulant isti virus animi sui, quoad ipsis licet quod libet. Quam primum verò se corripi sentiunt, in apertos hostes degenerant, & quasi iniuriam summam passi sint, quidus sibi aduersus ministros licere arbitrantur.
units.tr: Now at last we come to examine the morals of princes, so that we may learn how imprudent they are who, though they could live privately and enjoy liberty, make themselves slaves to princes. Princes sometimes feign a zeal for justice and truth, in order to gain greater authority with all. And so they often summon to themselves men of proven virtue and wisdom, converse with them familiarly, and admit them to their table and councils. But under that pretext they seek nothing other than a patron for their lust, and a way to cover their wickedness with another's virtue. This is evident from the fact that as long as those very men flatter them and excuse their morals, so long do princes hold them in honour and esteem. But as soon as they feel themselves rebuked more freely, or even obliquely touched, they at once cry out that they have suffered the greatest injury, and, turning to rage, they cruelly tear to pieces those on whose counsels they seemed wholly to depend. Herod did this, and for that reason Christ rightly called him a fox, as we shall hear in its place. Something similar is read of Joash, King of Judah, who, since he could not but hold the priest Jehoiada in esteem for his outstanding benefits to him, at last had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned to death, because Zechariah rebuked him more freely. Many examples of this kind also occur in profane histories. So Alexander the Macedonian once summoned the philosopher Callisthenes to himself, so as to gain greater authority by the cloak of true philosophy. But when Callisthenes, forgetful of his teacher Aristotle (who had told him to speak with the king rarely or most agreeably), more freely accused Alexander's Persian pride and tried to bring him back unwillingly to Macedonian ways, he was thrown into prison and died there of a lice disease. Seneca's fate under Nero was much the same. Papinian the jurist experienced a similar cruelty from Antoninus Bassianus, because when ordered to excuse the unworthy slaying of Geta he answered, "It is not so easy to excuse parricide as to commit it." Would that similar examples did not exist today as well. Those, then, are unhappy and wretched who buy the slavery of court life at such great danger. But those who serve as ministers of the Word in courts, and are lawfully called to that office, ought in no way to be frightened by these examples. Rather let them imitate John's constancy and freedom, and commit themselves and their life to God. Meanwhile, among private men there are those who resemble Herod's temper: that they may be held as supporters of evangelical truth, they praise and venerate its heralds, yet live a life most alien from the profession of the gospel. These men conceal the poison of their mind as long as they are allowed to do as they please. But as soon as they feel themselves rebuked, they degenerate into open enemies, and, as if they had suffered the greatest injury, they think they may act thus against the ministers.

units.la: Obserua deinde locutionē, Adiecit & hoc super omnia, &c. Ea enim docet spiritus sanctus, hunc lophon. demum omnis nequitiae & impietatis colophonem esse, si qui non contenti peccasi ipse insuper admonitionibus exacerbati aduersus fidos monitores hostiliter insurgant. Vt enim morbus deploratus est qui medicina aut remedijs exacerbatur, & deterior fit: ita nihil de illorum emendatione sperare nobis licet, qui Dei verbo ad maiorem impietatem accenduntur, quo debebant ad poenitentiam excitari. Inter alia autem vitia vehementissimus est libidinis affectus, cuius proprium fere est, vt quemadmodum canes & sues impatienti coitus appetitu in rabiem aguntur, ita quicunque illi indulgent, si mul cum pudore rationem quoque amittunt, neque impudenter modo multa designant, sed quae facere aut facere instituerunt, crudeliter & non sine sanguine defendunt, si ab aliquo fortius coercean-tur. Exempla huius mali in Paride Troiano, in Sexto Tarquinij regis filio, in Dauide domi, optimo alioqui & piissimo Rege, habemus, quem effrenis libido non solum beneficiorum Dei immemorem, sed insuper sanguinarium carnificem fecit, vt fortissimi viri Vriae sanguine innoxio se pollueret. Et permittit ista fieri Deus iusto iudicio, vt qui prioris scelelis gravitate agnoscere nolunt, ex ijs, quae inde oriuntur, magno suo malo intelligant, quam graue violati pudoris & vinculi coniugalis culpa sit. Prodest ergo Christianos homines in eiusmodi exemplorum consideratione frequenter versari, quo magis excitentur ad restinguendos libidinis affectus, priusquam illa indomitum ardeat.
units.tr: Notice then the phrase, "He added this also above all, etc." For the Holy Spirit teaches that this is the final crowning point (colophon) of all wickedness and impiety, when a man, not content with sinning, is further provoked by admonitions and rises up in hostility against faithful admonishers. For just as a disease is past cure when it is aggravated by medicines and remedies and grows worse, so we may hope for nothing toward the amendment of those who are inflamed to greater impiety by the Word of God, when they ought to have been stirred to repentance. Among the other vices, the most violent is the passion of lust, and it is almost characteristic of it that, as dogs and swine are driven to frenzy by an impatient desire for mating, so whoever gives way to it, while he loses shame, loses reason as well. Such men not only defend their wicked designs shamelessly, but, if they are restrained by someone stronger, they defend what they have done or have set out to do cruelly and not without bloodshed. We have examples of this evil in Paris of Troy, in Sextus, son of King Tarquin, and in David at home, otherwise the best and most pious of kings, whom unbridled lust made not only forgetful of God's benefits but also a bloody butcher, so that he polluted himself with the blood of the innocent and most brave Uriah. And God permits these things to happen by a just judgment, so that those who will not recognise from the gravity of the earlier sin how serious is the guilt of violated chastity and the marriage bond may learn it to their great cost from the consequences that spring from it. It is therefore profitable for Christians to dwell often on the consideration of such examples, so that they may be the more roused to quench the passions of lust before they blaze up unbridled.

units.la: Admoneret praeterea nos locus iste de administrorum Verbi sorte, quam in hoc mundo sustinent. Non potest quis ferre lucem, qua eius opera mala arguuntur. Hinc ergo fit, quod illius ministris iratescitur, eosdem odit, & in eorum interitu omnem suam felicitatem constistere putant.
