Senserunt hanc mundi rabiem omnes prophetae & apostoli, imo ipse Dei filius, qui ne beneficijs quidem quotidianis & miraculosis illam restinguere potuit. Non debent tamen ista eos terrere, qui hoc saxum bodie voluunt: quin potius Ioannis constantiam imitentur, nec illorum furori cedant, quos certum est nihil contra nos posse, nisi id ipsis permittat Deus, qui illorum opera interdum in exercendo suorum patientia vtitur. Videtur quidem ille aliquando suos negligere, sed revera discurrunt eius oculi super omnem terram, in primis autem eos ceu fidus aliquis agonothetes spectat, qui in ecclesiae suae palaestra siue ministerio desudant. Viribus ergo & intrepida animi fiducia eos instruit, & filij sui in cruce collegas reddit, vt cum eodem olim glorificentur. Vt deniq; ille olim per crucem triumphauit, sic etiam ministri eius per crucem vincunt, quando doctrina suam proprio sanguine obsignant, & ipsis in coelo regnantibus impij & sanguinarij hostes contemptae veritatis graues poenas exoluunt. Sed & in terris fama ministrorum Christi asseritur, vt posteris innocentia eorum tandem innotescat, qui cum in vinis essent, publica infamia notati & ignominiosis supplicijs extincti fuerunt. Est enim (vt diu nus ille Psalmes canit) pretiosa in oculis Domini mors sanctorum eius. Patet hoc evidenter nimis in Ioanne nostro. Quid enim eius morte felicius? quid memoria eius de celebrius? Vt enim mortis cau-sa honestissima & sanctissima fuit, sic illius beneficio exemptus curis & laboribus ea non vidit, quae ei quouis supplicij genere acerbiora fuissent: indignam nimirum Iesu Christi mortem, gentis suae incu-rabilem & indies in peius prombuente maliciam, graues patriae motus, seditiones & miserabile vr-bis excidium. Et vt in coelis vita beata eius mens fruitur, ita corpus in spe resurrectionis quiescit, nominis autem fama totum orbem terrarum percurrit & implet. Quod si huic Herodem opponas, quid hoc infelicius, miserius, calamitosius inuenies? Cum Areta socero congressus cladem infandam accipit. Soluuntur mox omnium ora & linguae, quia vnum Ioannem audire noluit, vno omnium ore damnatur, qui cladem illam (vt Iosephus scribit) Ioannis indignae morti acceptam tulerunt. Inde ex Herodiadis consilio Romam profectus ampliandi regni causa, clam ab illius fratre Agrippa apud Caium Caesarem accusatur per literas, vt qui cum Artabano Parthorum rege consilia aduersus Romanos conferat, & ideo cum incesta coniuge Lugdunum exulatum mittitur, qui ex Ioannis praedicatione seditionem & populi defectionem timuerat. Et haec quidem leuia videri possunt, si cum per petua nominis infamia, quam ad posteros transmisit, & cum aeternis cruciatibus conferantur, quos apud inferos cum omnibus illis sustinet, qui (vt propheta loquitur) terrorem suum posuerunt in terra viuentium. Quis ergo tam vecors & stupidus est, qui his diligenter consideratis non malit Ioannem, quam Herodem agere? Similia videbimus, si prophetas & apostolos cum suis hostibus conferamus. Excitent nos ista, vt virtuti & pietati operam demus, atque a Deo creditam stationem constanter teneamus. Ita enim nullum mortis genus nobis miserum accidere poterit, sed vbi vitae huius curricurriculum emensi fuerimus, fama quidem in terris apud pios gloriosa manebit, animae autem in coelis viuent, tandemq; corporibus quoq; restitutis æternum regnabimus, cum Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage also warns us about the lot that the ministers of the Word endure in this world. No one can bear the light by which his evil works are exposed. Hence it follows that they grow angry at the ministers of the Word, hate them, and think that all their happiness consists in their destruction. All the prophets and apostles felt this rage of the world, and indeed the Son of God himself, who could not quench it even by his daily and miraculous benefits. Yet these things should not terrify those who today roll this stone: rather, they should imitate the constancy of John and not yield to the fury of those who, as is certain, can do nothing against us unless God permits it, and who sometimes uses their works to exercise the patience of his own people. He does indeed seem at times to neglect his people, but in truth his eyes range over the whole earth, and above all he watches those who toil in the arena of his Church, that is, in the ministry, like a faithful president of the games. Therefore he equips them with strength and an fearless confidence of spirit, and makes them fellow-sufferers with his Son on the cross, so that they may one day be glorified with him. Just as he once triumphed through the cross, so his ministers conquer through the cross, when they seal their teaching with their own blood, and while they reign in heaven, the impious and bloodthirsty enemies of the despised truth pay heavy penalties on earth. Yet even on earth the good name of Christ's ministers is vindicated, so that at last their innocence becomes known to posterity, those who, though they were in chains, were branded with public infamy and put to death with shameful punishments. For (as that divine Psalm sings) the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord. This is shown quite clearly in our John. For what was more fortunate than his death? What is more widely celebrated than his memory? Just as the cause of his death was most honourable and most holy, so by the benefit of it he was spared the cares and labours, and did not see those things which would have been more bitter to him than any kind of punishment: namely, the unworthy death of Jesus Christ, the incurable malice of his nation growing worse by the day, grave disturbances in the homeland, seditions, and the wretched destruction of the city. And just as his soul enjoys a blessed life in heaven, so his body rests in the hope of resurrection, while the fame of his name runs through and fills the whole world. But if you set Herod against him, what will you find more unhappy, more wretched, more calamitous than this? When he joined battle with his father-in-law Aretas, he suffered an unspeakable defeat. Soon the mouths and tongues of all men were loosed, since he had refused to hear John alone; with one voice of all, he was condemned, and they (as Josephus writes) took that defeat as the due reward for the unworthy death of John. Then, on the advice of Herodias, he set out for Rome to enlarge his kingdom, but was secretly accused by letter before Gaius Caesar by his brother Agrippa, as one who was planning with Artabanus, king of the Parthians, schemes against the Romans; and therefore he was sent into exile at Lyons with his incestuous wife, he who had feared sedition and the revolt of the people arising from John's preaching. And these things may seem trivial if they are compared with the perpetual infamy of his name, which he has handed down to posterity, and with the eternal torments which he suffers in hell with all those who (as the prophet says) have set their terror in the land of the living. Who then is so senseless and stupid that, having carefully considered these things, he would not prefer to act like John rather than like Herod? We shall see similar things if we compare the prophets and apostles with their enemies. Let these things stir us to devote ourselves to virtue and piety, and to hold constantly the station entrusted to us by God. For thus no kind of death can befall us as a misfortune; but when we have run the course of this life, our fame will remain glorious on earth among the godly, our souls will live in heaven, and at last, with our bodies also restored, we shall reign forever with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIV.

units.la: Factum est autem cum baptizaretur omnis populus, & Iesus baptizatus esset & precaretur, vt apertum sit coelum, ac descenderit spiritus sanctus corporea specie tanquam columba, supra eum, & vox de coelo exiterit, dicens: Tu es filius ille meus dilectus, in te mihi bene complacitum est.
units.tr: Now it came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also was baptized and was praying, that the heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven, saying: "You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased."

units.la: SCriptura sacra tam veteris quàm noui Testamenti promissum humani generis vindicem atq; redemptorem CHRISTI, id est, VNCTI nomine appellare consueuerunt, vt hunc nobis à Deo Regem & Sacerdotem datum esse doceant. Est autem hic antiquissimus mos, vt qui in Reges aut Sacerdotes electi sunt, publica & solenni ceremonia in suo munere confirmentur, vt à populo pro talibus agno scantur, et simul omnes excitentur ad præstandum quod illis debetur officium. Hoc ipsum ergo in Dei filio ex Maria in carne genito fieri oportuit, & quidem vt fieret necesse fuit, cum in vili & contempta assumpti ab illo hominis specie nihil appareret, quod vel regiam maiestatem vel sacerdotalem dignitatem præse ferret. Quapropter Lucas, cum absoluta Ioannis Baptistæ historia ad res Christi describendas transitum facere instituisset, ab eo facit narrandi initium, vt quæ aut qualis eius inauguratio fuerit intelligamus, eoq; maior apud nos sit eius doctrinæ & omnium quæ fecit authoritas. Duo autem in illam inciderunt: Baptismus nimirum, quem ab Ioanne accepit, & Patris Dei testimonium, quo toti mundo commendatus est. Elucet itaq; in ista etiam actione multiplex et infinita Dei bonitas, qui passim nostro ingenio atq; moribus sese accommodat, quo efficacius excitemur ad amplectendam salutem, quam nobis in filio suo proponit. Cæterum de vtroq; ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: The Holy Scriptures, both of the Old and of the New Testament, are accustomed to call the promised deliverer and redeemer of mankind by the name of Christ, that is, the Anointed One, so that they may teach us that he was given to us by God as King and Priest. This is an ancient custom: those who are chosen as kings or priests are confirmed in their office by a public and solemn ceremony, so that they may be recognized by the people as such, and at the same time everyone may be stirred to render the service that is owed to them. It was therefore fitting that this same thing should happen to the Son of God, born of Mary in the flesh; and indeed it was necessary that it should happen, since in the lowly and despised form of man that he had taken on, nothing appeared that displayed either royal majesty or priestly dignity. For this reason Luke, when he had finished the history of John the Baptist and had decided to pass on to the describing of Christ's deeds, begins his narrative at this point, so that we may understand what his inauguration was and what kind it was, and so that the authority of his teaching and of all that he did may be greater for us. Two things fell into this event: namely the baptism that he received from John, and the testimony of God the Father, by which he was commended to the whole world. Therefore in this action too there shines forth the manifold and infinite goodness of God, who everywhere adapts himself to our understanding and our habits, so that we may be more effectively stirred to embrace the salvation that he sets before us in his Son. But of each of these we shall speak in order.

units.la: Quoad Baptismum Christi, causa primum quærenda est, propter quam ille baptizari voluit. Nam si eum, qualis in se est, consideremus, minimè opus eius fuit, vt baptismi aqua tingeretur. Est enim Baptismus (vt alibi à nobis dictum est) actio sacra, qua in externam Ecclesiæ societatem ad optamur, & qua Deus regenerationis & remissionis peccatorum beneficium nobis obsignat, nosque nostræ conditionis simul & officij admonet, vt nimirum innatæ pollutionis memores, in ea cauenda vigilemus, & tanto pretio abluti innocentiam atq; puritatem nostram sedulò tueamur. Quid verò horum opus fuit Christo, qui vt æternus Dei filius est, ita absq; omni hæreditariæ & originalis vitiositatis labe homo factus, neq; peccatorum ablutione, neq; eorundem gratuita remissione, multoq; minus regeneratione opus habuit? Quin ipse ecclesiæ suæ fundamentum & caput est, ex quo vita salusq; in singula eius membra deriuatur. Sciuit equidè hoc Ioannes, & ideo ad baptismum suum accedentem (vt in Matthæo legitur) abs se remittit, dicens: Mihi, vt abs te baptizer, opus est, & tu venis ad me? Quibus verbis rectè quidem diuinam Christi potentiam & dignitatem prædicat, suam verò infirmitatem fatetur, simul tamen peccat zelo præposteo et imprudenti, vt omnes solent, qui carnis rationem in consilium adhibent, quando de rebus diuinis agitur. Sedibidem ipse Christus sui instituti causam non obscurè indicat. Omitte nunc (inquit) sic enim decet nos implere omnem iustitiam, id est, præstare & perficere omnia, quæ nobis ex officio agenda incumbunt. Vt ergo propter nos in mundum venit & homo factus est Dei filius, ita propter nos quoq; baptizari voluit, vt omnibus ijs defungeretur, ad quæ ipsum Pater æterno suo decreto destinauerat. Huc verò in primis pertinebat, vt baptismum quoq; suscieperet. Primùm enim eo testari oportuit, ipsum veram carnem assumpsisse, & hominem verum, imò fratrem nostrum factum esse, & proinde ad nos petinere omnium eorum fructum, quæ fecit aut passus est. Deinde eodem nobiscum fœdere illum comprehendi, & ijsdem conditionibus obstringi necesse fuit, quibus nos in baptismo obstringimur, vt obedientiæ, quæ nobis præstitu impossibilis erat, ipse præstaret, & suo merito nos à damnatione eximeret. Quo nomine eum circuncisum quoq; fuisse, suo loco diximus. Adhæc nostrum baptismum sanctificauit, vt constaret, nos cum baptizamur, in eius mortem quodammodo intingi, & cum ipso sepeliri, ut in eodem ad vitae novitatem resurgamus. Quae omnia ut nos ad officium faciendum vehementer excitant, sic in omni tentatione mirifice cosolantur & invictos reddunt. Cur enim villis malis aut diaboli insultibus succumbat, qui se Christi membrum esse novit, qui serpentis caput contriuit, & cui omnis potestas data est in caelo & in terra? Addit his hanc quoque, causam D. Augustinus, quod ipsum exemplo esse decuerit futurus filijs Dei, qui per baptismum filios Dei fieri docebat: & qui credentibus Spiritum sanctum a Deo dari promittebat, debuit illud in semetipso visibiliter demonstrare, quo coperto credentes invisibiliter se posse Spiritum sanctum habere sperarent. Postremo Sacramentorum usum & totum ecclesiae ministerium suo exemplo nobis commendauit, ut discamus canendum nobis esse, ne illa tontemnendo aut negligendo alicui graviori scandali simus authores. Seruit ergo Christi exemplum iis confutandis, qui publicos ecclesiae coetus, conciones sacras, preces publicas & Sacramentorum usum negligunt. Nituntur hi rationibus, quarum alias male detorquent, alias ex suo cerebro confictas proferunt, ut inani perfuasione seipsos fallant. Nam externa illa nihil ad salutem prodesse aiunt, nisi spiritus divini virtute efficacia fiant. Quia vero hic ipsdem minime alligatus est, eorum usum inutilem & superuacaneum esse colligunt. Adhaec fidei in Christum perfuasione atque titulo turgidi per sectionem se iam attigisse putant, & proinde se elementis hisce (sic enim illi loquuntur) nequaquam opus habere vociferantur. Sed possunt ista facile refutari. Quoad primum enim, ipsi quoque fatemur, externa illa exercitia sine vivifica spiritus virtute nihil posse in animis hominum, neque ad salutem aeternam aliquid conferre. Non tamen inde sequitur, illa contemni aut negligi debere. Quia enim ea Deus instituit, ut per ea in animis nostris agat, & nos eorundem usu fidem nostram exerceamus atque publice testemur, negligi non possunt, quin simul nos audaces nimium & prophanos Dei & institutorum eius contemptores esse prodamus. Imo Deum tentant, quicunque sine verbi doctrina, sine ordinario Sacramentorum usu & precibus in fide proficere & salutem consequi volunt. Confert quidem Paulus ecclesiae ministerium agricolationi, ut omnem profectum ad Deum authorem referri debere doceat. At nos ex eodem simili colligimus, quod ut merito inopia & fame pereunt, qui agricultura damnant, quam a Deo institutam esse scimus, ita iusto iudicio a salute excluduntur, qui ad eam non illa via contendunt, qua suos Deus deducere consueuit. Neque ideo Spiritus sancti virtutem ad externam verbi praedicationem aut ad Sacramentorum usum astringimus (spirat enim ille ubi cunque vult) nos autem ad ordinem a Deo institutum alligatos esse dicimus, quoad ille suam ergo nos voluntatem atque gratiam non aliquo modo extraordinario declarat. Ista vero simul ad alterius quoque argumenti confutationem possunt sufficere. Quia fides obedientiae studium & supremi numinis reuerentiam parit, falso nobis suam perfectionem iactant, qui Dei instituta contemnunt, vel pro superuacaneis negligunt. Et exempla sunt plurima, quibus illorum confidentia arguitur. Erat in fide institutus a Philippo Candacis reginae Eunuchus, & ex animo ijs credebat, quae de Christo docebantur; idem tamen visa aqua baptizari voluit, & Philippum de eo non sine magni desiderij significatione compellat. Imo cum illius mentem Deus occulta spiritus virtute illuminare posset, ut Isaiae prophetias intelligeret, Philippum tamen excitat, ut per hunc in fide instituatur. Sic Paulus, cum iam manus dedisset Christo, ad Ananiam tamen remittitur, qui ipsum plenius edoctum baptizaret. Et Cornelio centurioni angelum quidem mittit Deus, sed non ut ab illo fidem discat, sed ut per eum admonitus Petrum accersat, qui & Euangelium ipsi praedicet, & baptismum administret. Denique cum Apostolos suos Christus in totum orbem ad praedicandum & baptizandum emisit, & in ijsdem fancuerit ecclesiae ministerium, nunquam pro credentibus aut perfectis in fide agnoscipoterunt, quicunque verbi praedicationem externam & Sacramentorum usum contemnunt. Et ut omnia alia argumenta omittamus, unius Christi exemplum illis confutandis sufficit.
units.tr: As regards the baptism of Christ, the first question to be asked is the reason why he wished to be baptized. For if we consider him as he is in himself, there was by no means any need for him to be washed with the water of baptism. Baptism is (as we have said elsewhere) a sacred action by which we are admitted into the external fellowship of the Church, by which God seals to us the benefit of regeneration and the forgiveness of sins, and by which we are at the same time reminded of our condition and our duty: namely, that, mindful of our inborn uncleanness, we should be watchful in guarding against it, and, having been washed at so great a price, we should diligently preserve our innocence and purity. But what of these things was needful for Christ, who, as the eternal Son of God, was made man free from every stain of hereditary and original sinfulness, and so had no need of washing away of sins, nor of their free forgiveness, and much less of regeneration? Indeed he is the foundation and head of his own Church, from whom life and salvation flow into each of its members. John certainly knew this, and therefore, when Christ came to his baptism, he held him back (as we read in Matthew), saying: "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" In these words he rightly proclaims the divine power and dignity of Christ, and confesses his own weakness; yet at the same time he errs through a preposterous and unwise zeal, as all do who take the counsel of flesh and blood when divine matters are at issue. But Christ himself there clearly indicates the reason for his institution: "Let it be so now," he says, "for thus it becomes us to fulfil all righteousness," that is, to perform and accomplish all those things that are laid upon us as our duty to do. Therefore, just as he came into the world for our sake and the Son of God was made man, so too he wished to be baptized for our sake, so that he might discharge all those things to which the Father had appointed him by his eternal decree. Now among these it belonged chiefly to him that he should also receive baptism. For first it was fitting that by this he should bear witness that he had assumed true flesh, and had become a true man, indeed our brother, and that therefore the fruit of all that he did or suffered belongs to us. Next, it was necessary that he should be included in the same covenant with us and bound by the same conditions by which we are bound in baptism, so that he himself might render the obedience that was impossible for us to render, and by his merit deliver us from condemnation. For this reason we have said in its place that he was also circumcised. Moreover, he sanctified our baptism, so that it might be established that when we are baptized we are in some measure dipped into his death and buried with him, so that in the same way we may rise again to newness of life. All these things both powerfully stir us up to perform our duty and wonderfully console us in every temptation and make us invincible. For why should he who knows himself to be a member of Christ, who has crushed the serpent's head, and to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, yield to evil things or to the assaults of the devil? To these reasons Saint Augustine adds this also: that it was fitting for him to be an example to those who were to be the sons of God, since he taught that through baptism men are made the sons of God; and since he promised that the Holy Spirit would be given by God to those who believe, he ought to demonstrate this visibly in himself, so that, the thing having been shown, believers might hope that they could have the Holy Spirit invisibly. Lastly, by his own example he commended to us the use of the sacraments and the whole ministry of the Church, so that we may learn that we must take care not to become the authors of some more serious scandal by despising or neglecting them. Christ's example therefore serves to refute those who neglect the public assemblies of the Church, the holy sermons, the public prayers and the use of the sacraments. These men rely on arguments, some of which they twist badly, and others of which they bring forward, invented out of their own brains, so that they deceive themselves with an empty persuasion. For they say that those external things profit nothing for salvation unless they are made effective by the power of the divine Spirit. And since the Spirit is not bound to these, they conclude that their use is useless and superfluous. Moreover, puffed up with the persuasion and title of faith in Christ, they think that they have already attained to perfection through regeneration, and therefore they loudly declare that they have no need of these elements (for so they speak). But these claims can easily be refuted. For as to the first, we ourselves also admit that those external exercises can accomplish nothing in the minds of men without the life-giving power of the Spirit, nor contribute anything to eternal salvation. Yet it does not follow from this that they ought to be despised or neglected. For since God has instituted them, so that through them he may work in our minds, and so that by their use we may exercise our faith and bear public witness to it, they cannot be neglected without at the same time showing ourselves to be too bold and profane contemners of God and of his institutions. Indeed, those who wish to make progress in faith and to obtain salvation without the teaching of the Word, without the ordinary use of the sacraments and without prayers, tempt God. Paul indeed compares the ministry of the Church to agriculture, to teach that all progress must be referred to God as its author. But from the same comparison we conclude this: just as those who despise agriculture, which we know was instituted by God, rightly perish through want and hunger, so by a just judgement those are excluded from salvation who strive towards it by a way other than that by which God is accustomed to lead his own. Nor do we therefore bind the power of the Holy Spirit to the external preaching of the Word or to the use of the sacraments (for he breathes where he wills); but we say that we are bound to the order instituted by God, unless he declares his will and grace to us in some extraordinary way. These things may at the same time suffice for the refutation of another argument as well. For since faith brings forth obedience and reverence for the supreme Deity, those men falsely boast of their perfection who despise God's institutions or neglect them as superfluous. And there are very many examples by which their confidence is shown to be unfounded. The eunuch of Candace, the queen, was instructed in the faith by Philip, and he sincerely believed the things that were taught about Christ; yet he nevertheless wished to be baptized when water was seen, and he addresses Philip about it with no small expression of desire. Indeed, although God could have enlightened his mind by the hidden power of the Spirit so that he understood the prophecies of Isaiah, he nevertheless stirred up Philip so that through him he might be instructed in the faith. Thus Paul, although he had already submitted himself to Christ, was nevertheless sent back to Ananias, who was to baptize him after instructing him more fully. And God indeed sent an angel to the centurion Cornelius, but not so that he might learn the faith from him; rather, that, being admonished through him, he might summon Peter, who would both preach the gospel to him and administer baptism. Finally, when Christ sent out his apostles into the whole world to preach and to baptize, and had established in them the ministry of the Church, those who despise the external preaching of the Word and the use of the sacraments can never be acknowledged as believers or as men perfected in faith. And, to omit all other arguments, the example of Christ alone is sufficient to refute them.

units.la: Porro videamus etiam ubi & cum quibus ille baptizatus sit. Cum baptizaretur (inquit Lucas) omnis populus, tunc Iesus quoque accessit & baptizatus est. Ergo in publico, & in Iordane (ut reliqui omnes) est baptizatus, & quidem cum toto populo, ex quo promiscue omnis loci & ordinis homines ad Ioannem veniebant, ut baptismi lauacro tingerentur. At quales nam plerique isti erant? Peccatores, sceleribus & flagitijs infames, incurabiles & poenitere nescij, et qui optimi erat, ij simulato poenitentiae fuco sese palliabat, sicuti de Pharisaeis nuper audiuimus. Eodem tamen cum illis baptismo tingi voluit in carne manifestatus Dei filius, & eodem initiatos fuisse constat Apostolos quoq;, & quotquot illo tempore mundo exhibitum Seruatorem fide vera amplexi sunt. Arguitur hic illorum arrogantia, qui propter vitae genus aut conditionem excellentiore nolunt ijsdem cum ecclesia Sacramentis vti, & quando vel infantes eorum baptizantur, vel ipsi Cœnae mysticae communicare volunt, vasis pretiosioribus vtuntur, vt splendore suo in ijs etiā ostentent, quae Deus omnibus ex æquo communia esse vult. Præstat ergo in ecclesia singulis vnū habere baptisterium, in quo omnes tingantur; vnā quoq; esse mensam Domini, et eadem vasa, ex quibus omnes, cuiuscunq; sint loci aut ordinis, corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi Sacramentū percipiant. Quam primum enim hoc negligitur, mox in æqualitas quaedam in ecclesia enascitur, & scismatis causa fit, quod Christianae societatis & communionis vinculum esse debebat. Et hoc illud est, quod Paulus in Cor. reprehendit, qui Cœnam Dominii in priuatas epulas conuerterant. Confutantur praeterea Christi exemplo, qui hodie ab ecclesijs secessionem faciunt, & neq; Dei verbum audiunt, neq; Sacramentis ijsdem vti volunt cum illis, quos peccatis pollutos esse, & in illis abstq; poenitentia pergere vident, aut potius se videre putant. Rationē suae sententiae hanc afferunt, quod qui cum talibus ad eandem ecclesiā colliguntur, vnū cum illis corpus fiant, & proinde eorundem sceleribus communicent, eandem cum illis olim damnationem subituri. Fuit haec olim Donatistarum sententia, qui ideo baptismum habebant peculiare, et (vt Augustinus scribit) altare contra altare erigebant, & grauissimi pernitiosissimiq; scismatis in ecclesia erant authores. Et hodie eorum furores Anabaptistae sequuntur, qui fictitij periculi metu multos territant, & ab ecclesiae societate abducunt. Fallūtur autē in eo, quod per Sacramenta nos in vnum & idem corpus colligi aut coalescere, & proinde in ijsdem scelerū & vitae communione fieri arbitrantur. Atqui corporis ecclesiastici vinculum est fides in vnum Christum, quam spiritus sua virtute in nobis gignit. Sacramenta vero vnitatis illius externa tesserae & exercitia sunt, quibus tam boni quam mali vti possunt; illi quidē cum fructu eximio, eo quod spiritui locū dent; hi vero non solum inutiliter, verumetiā cum salutis propria iactura, cum impia hypocrisi spiritui sancto mentiantur, & sacrosancta Dei instituta impio atq; prophano abusu polluant. Minime ergo eorum hypocrisi aut perfidiae pij communicant, qui Dei verbū cum fide audiunt, & Christi Sacramentis digne vtuntur. Nec enim fieri potest, vt in ecclesia vnum & idem corpus fiant cum illis, qui ad ecclesiā non pertinent, neq; eius membra sunt, cum nihil habeant cum credentibus communē praeter externam fidei professionem. Et nisi hoc demus, simul omnes veteris testamenti patres damnabimus, qui ad vnū templum et ad eadem sacra cum illis conuenerunt, quorū plerique, aut hypocritae aut palam flagitiosi erant, sicuti prophetarū sermones testantur. Imò Christum damnare oportebit, qui vt eodem baptismo cum ijs tinctus est, quos vitijs teterrimis pollutos esse non ignorabat, ita Iudam quoq; proditorē ad Cœnam suā admisit, cuius perfidia & impietatem probè habebat perspectam. Sed vt ipsi non obfuit, quod baptismum cum impijs & hypocritis accepit: ita neq; apostolis caeteris tunc nocuit, quod ad eandem cum illis mensam Iudas accumberet. Etsi enim (vt D. Augustini verbus vtar) mensa vtrisque vna esset, non tamen vtrisque ad vnum valuit, quia ipsi non erant vnum. Et non vnum fuisse dicit Iudam & alios discipulos, etiam si de vna eademq; mensa omnes simul comederint. Quia enim neq; Iudas fidem habuit, neque ipsi per fidia in Christum vsi sunt, nulla inter illos animorū coniunctio, et multo minus scelerum communio esse potuit. Rectè ergo Augustinus hanc nobis regulā præscribit: Memento Sacramentis Dei nihil obesse mores malorum hominum, quo illa vel omnino non sint, vel minus sancta sint: sed ipsis malis hominibus, vt hæc habeant ad testimonium damnationis, non ad adiutorium sanitatis. Nam eadem pascua sub vno pastore & oues & hirci pascuntur, donec vt debita recipiant, segregentur, &c.
units.tr: Let us also see where and with whom he was baptized. When all the people were being baptized (says Luke), Jesus too came and was baptized. So he was baptized in public, in the Jordan, like all the others, and indeed together with the whole people, since men of every place and rank came to John indiscriminately to be washed in the bath of baptism. But what sort of people were most of them? Sinners, notorious for crimes and shameful deeds, incurable and unwilling to repent. Even the best of them covered themselves with a pretence of repentance, as we heard a little while ago about the Pharisees. Yet the Son of God, made manifest in the flesh, willed to be dipped in the same baptism with them, and it is clear that the Apostles too, and all who at that time embraced the Saviour shown to the world with true faith, were initiated with the same baptism. Here the arrogance is rebuked of those who, on account of their way of life or higher rank, refuse to use the same sacraments as the Church. When their infants are baptized, or when they themselves wish to take part in the mystical Supper, they use more costly vessels, so that by their splendour they display themselves even in those things which God wills to be common to all alike. It is better, therefore, that in the Church each congregation have one baptistery in which all are dipped, and also one table of the Lord and the same vessels, from which all, of whatever place or rank, receive the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ. For as soon as this is neglected, a certain inequality straightway springs up in the Church and becomes a cause of schism, when it ought to have been the bond of Christian fellowship and communion. This is what Paul rebukes in 1 Cor., those who had turned the Lord's Supper into private feasts. Moreover, they are refuted by Christ's example: those who today secede from the churches, and neither hear the Word of God nor wish to use the same sacraments with those whom they see, or rather think they see, to be polluted with sins and to persist in them without repentance. They give this reason for their view: those who are gathered with such people into the same church become one body with them, and therefore share in their sins and will undergo the same condemnation with them. This was formerly the opinion of the Donatists, who for that reason kept a separate baptism and (as Augustine writes) set altar against altar, and were the authors of the most grievous and most pernicious schism in the Church. Today the Anabaptists follow their frenzies. They terrify many with the fear of an imaginary danger and draw them away from fellowship with the Church. They are mistaken in this, that they think we are made one body, or grow together, through the sacraments, and therefore become sharers in the same sins and way of life. Yet the bond of the ecclesiastical body is faith in the one Christ, which the Spirit by his power begets in us. The sacraments of that unity, however, are external tokens and exercises, which both good and bad may use: the good with remarkable fruit, because they give room to the Spirit; the bad not only without profit but also to their own loss of salvation, lying to the Holy Spirit with impious hypocrisy and polluting God's most holy institutions with an impious and profane abuse. Therefore the godly by no means share in the hypocrisy or faithlessness of those who hear God's Word with faith and use Christ's sacraments worthily. For it cannot happen that they become one and the same body in the Church with those who do not belong to the Church and are not its members, since they have nothing in common with believers except an outward profession of faith. And unless we grant this, we shall condemn together all the fathers of the Old Testament, who met in the one temple and at the same sacred rites with those men, most of whom were either hypocrites or openly wicked, as the sayings of the prophets testify. Indeed we shall have to condemn Christ, who was baptized with the same baptism as those whom he knew to be polluted with the most foul vices, and likewise admitted to his Supper Judas the traitor, whose treachery and impiety he knew well. But just as his receiving baptism with the impious and hypocrites did him no harm, so neither did it harm the other Apostles that Judas reclined at the same table with them. For although (to use the words of St Augustine) the table was one for both, it did not avail both alike, because they were not one. He says that Judas and the other disciples were not one, even though they all ate from one and the same table. For since Judas had no faith, and the others did not show faithfulness toward Christ, there could be no union of minds among them, and much less any communion in sins. Rightly, therefore, Augustine prescribes this rule for us: Remember that the morals of evil men do no harm to God's sacraments, so that they are either wholly not sacraments or less holy; rather, they are for the evil men themselves, to have as a testimony of their damnation, not as an aid to health. For both sheep and goats feed in the same pasture under one shepherd, until they are separated to receive what is their due, etc.

units.la: Reliquū est, vt quid fecerit Christus videamus, cum baptizaretur. Lucas precatū esse ait, Matthaeus aut eundem confestim ex aqua ascendisse scribit. Et illum quidē frequenter orauisse legimus, cum quia hominem verū assumpserat, quem consolatione & spiritus virtute opus habuisse, passionis historia abunde docet: tum quia Sacerdos est, qui & pro nobis assiduē apud patrem intercedit, & exemplo nobis esse voluit, vt ipsi quoq; in precibus frequentes & assidui simus. Esţ ergo quod hic fecit nobis nō oscitanter considerandū. Qui enim Sacramentorū omnium author, adhæc materia & finis est, suo exemplo docuit, quid nos facere conueniat, quādo illis participamus. Meminerimus ergo ante omnia religione & pia animi deuotione opus esse, vt in rem præsente intenti, pijs precibus Dei gratiam imploremus, vt is nobis fructuosa & efficacia ad salutem faciat symbola illa, quæ nisi spiritus virtus accedat, mortua et inutilia sunt. Et erat hoc maximè obseruandum quando baptismus administratur, & per hunc in ecclesiæ societatem adoptantur, qui ex Christianis parentibus nati sunt, aut iampridem relictis superstitionibus Christo nomen dant. Vt vero Christus peractis ijs, quæ ad baptismi ceremoniâ pertinebant, illico ex aqua ascendit: ita nos quoq; non in signis aut actione externa hæc rere, sed per fidei contemplationem animos ad Deum extollere debemus, vt quæ signis adumbrantur percipiamus. Recte ergo olim ministri in Cœnæ dominicæ administratione populum monebant, Sursum corda: illo vicissim respondente, Habemus ad Dominum. At hodie in vtramq; partem plurimum peccatur. Alij enim solis signis addicti, ea pro rebus accipiunt, quam miserrimam animæ seruitutem Augustinus dixit. Et hinc fit, quòd neglecto vero Sacramentorum vsu, de signis et actione externa contentiones scandali plenas & nunquam finiendas instituunt, quibus & ecclesiæ vnitas scinditur, & in multorum animis superstitio confirmatur. Alij vero scurrili impietate circa religionem ludunt, & sacra mysteria non maiori reuerentia tractant, quàm si ad ludum aliquem Scenicum accederent. Fiunt huius generis multa in baptismi actione, siue susceptores, qui in rei testimonium adhibentur, spectes, siue factum & apparatum quo multi in templis sese ostentant: siue conuiuiorum luxum, quæ nonnulli eo prætextu instituunt. Debebat hos mouere Corinthiacæ ecclesiæ exemplum, quam lue multatam fuisse Paulus scribit, quòd Domini Cœnam in epulum prophanum commutassent. At nos cum non vno modo peccemus, tamen quasi omnia optime constituta sint, & Dei nos castigantis manum admiramur, deque nimia eius seueritate conquerimur.
units.tr: It remains to see what Christ did when he was baptized. Luke says he prayed, while Matthew writes that he came up out of the water straightway. Indeed we read that he prayed often: both because he had assumed true man, who needed consolation and the strength of the Spirit, as the history of the passion abundantly teaches; and because he is the priest who constantly intercedes for us with the Father, and he willed to be an example to us, so that we too should be frequent and persistent in prayer. What he did here is therefore not to be considered carelessly. For he who is the author of all the sacraments, and their matter and end, taught by his example what it becomes us to do when we partake of them. Let us therefore remember above all that there must be religious reverence and devout piety of mind, so that, attentive to the matter at hand, we implore God's grace with godly prayers, that he may make those tokens fruitful and effective for our salvation. Without the power of the Spirit they are dead and useless. This ought especially to be observed when baptism is administered and, through it, those who were born of Christian parents, or who have long since abandoned superstitions and take the name of Christ, are adopted into the fellowship of the Church. But just as Christ, when the things pertaining to the ceremony of baptism were done, straightway came up out of the water, so we too should not rest these things in signs or external action. Rather, we ought to raise our minds to God through contemplation of faith, so that we may receive what is shadowed forth by the signs. Rightly, therefore, the ministers of old, in administering the Lord's Supper, admonished the people, "Lift up your hearts," and in turn the people answered, "We have them lifted up to the Lord." But today there is much sin on both sides. For some, devoted only to signs, take them for the things themselves, a most wretched bondage of the soul, as Augustine called it. Hence it comes that, neglecting the true use of the sacraments, they stir up contentions about signs and external action, full of scandal and never to be ended, by which both the unity of the Church is torn apart and superstition is confirmed in the minds of many. Others, with scurrilous impiety, play with religion and handle the sacred mysteries with no more reverence than if they were going to some stage play. Many things of this kind happen in the action of baptism: whether sponsors, who are brought in as witnesses, are gazed at, or the display and pageantry by which many show themselves off in the churches, or the luxury of feasts which some arrange under that pretext. The example of the Corinthian church should have moved them, which Paul writes was smitten with plague because they had turned the Lord's Supper into a profane feast. Although we sin in more ways than one, yet, as if everything were arranged in the best possible way, we marvel at the hand of God chastising us and complain of his excessive severity.

units.la: Cæterum tempus est, vt ad alteram huius historiæ partem transeamus, quæ diuinum et cœleste testimonium continet, quo Christum commendari oportuit, ne quis de eius merito & authoritate dubitaret. Est autem memorabilis valde eius modestia atq; patientia, qui etsi vitæ conditione egenam et laboriosam sustineret, hucusq; tamen expectauit, neq; ad obeundum munus suum prorupit, donec publico patris testimonio est commendatus. Fecerunt hoc olim Prophetæ quoq; & post illos Apostoli: qui omnes suo exemplo præcipitem illorum confidentiam arguunt, qui non missi currunt, & vel lucri vel honoris causa seipsos ecclesijs obtrudunt. At hic inciderunt, quæ diligentius considerari merentur.
units.tr: It is now time to move on to the second part of this history, which contains the divine and heavenly testimony by which Christ had to be commended, so that no one would doubt his worth and authority. His modesty and patience are truly remarkable. Although he endured a poor and laborious way of life, he waited until the Father's public testimony commended him, and did not burst forth to take up his office. The prophets did the same, and after them the apostles. By their example they all refute the rash confidence of those who run without being sent and thrust themselves upon the churches for gain or for honour. Several things here deserve closer consideration.

units.la: Primum cœli aperti sunt, et id Ioanne vidisse Marcus narrat. Itaq; de re visibili & verè gesta hic agitur, & de cœlis sermo est, qui supra nos sunt, quibus apertis aut scissis ea vidit Ioannes, quæ orbibus astrorum & cælo illo elementali altiora sunt. Neque opus est quærere, qui hoc fieri potuerit, cum oculorum acies tam procul non penetret. Quia enim hic singulare quid fecit Deus, idem etiam procul dubio visum Ioanis (vt Stephani postea) acutiori lumine donauit, vt præsenti negotio sufficere posset. Non temere autem istud omne factum est. Primo enim suam præsentiam Deus hoc signo testari voluit, & omnes homines docere, negotium hoc Christi diuinum & cœleste esse, & proinde nihil in illo terrenum siue temporarium quæri debere. Deinde indicatur iam adesse tempus illud præfinitum, quo cœlos referare nobis velit Deus, quos primi parentis lapsus & ex hoc propagatum in omnes posteros peccatu nobis clauserat. Quod autem in præsenti obscurius adumbratur, posthæc in morte & resurrectione Christi eiusq; in cœlos ascensione reuera impletum & præstitum fuit, quando ille expiatis mundi peccatis et deuicta morte corpus suum in cœlos subuexit, et ita viam sanctorum nobis aperuit, vt eodem nobis etiam nunc aditus pateat. Et hoc illud est, quod vltima Cœna discipulis dixit: In domo patris mei habitationes multæ sunt, sin minus, dixissem vobis. Vado vobis paraturus locum. Et cum abiero, et parauero vobis locu, rursus veniam & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi sum ego, et vos sitis. Thoma autem de via interrogante, amplius respondet: Ego sum via et veritas & vita. Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Quæ verba cum hac cœli apertione, quasi demonstratio ne oculari confirmentur, minimè nos de eorum veritate dubitare decet, simulq; in Christo nobis quæ renda est regni cœlorum possessio.
units.tr: First, the heavens were opened, and Mark reports that John saw this. So this is a visible event, truly done, and the passage speaks of heavens above us, which John saw opened or torn apart, and which lie higher than the spheres of the stars and that elemental heaven. There is no need to ask how this could happen, since the sharpness of the eye does not reach so far. Because God was doing something singular here, he undoubtedly gave John a sharper light of vision, as he later did for Stephen, so that it would be enough for the present matter. Nor did all this happen by chance. First, God wished to attest his presence by this sign and to teach all people that this work of Christ is divine and heavenly, and that therefore nothing earthly or temporary should be sought in it. Second, it is shown that the time now at hand has come, the time appointed when God wished to open the heavens to us, which the fall of our first parent, and the sin propagated from it to all his descendants, had closed to us. What is here shadowed more obscurely was afterwards truly fulfilled and accomplished in the death and resurrection of Christ and in his ascension into the heavens, when, having expiated the sins of the world and overcome death, he lifted his body into heaven and so opened the way for the saints, so that access stands open to us even now. This is what he said to his disciples at the last supper: "In my Father's house there are many dwellings; if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be also." When Thomas asked about the way, he answered more fully: "I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me." Since these words are confirmed by this opening of the heavens, as if by an ocular demonstration, we ought in no way to doubt their truth, and at the same time we should recognise that the possession of the kingdom of heaven is to be obtained for us in Christ.

units.la: Deinde descendit super eum Spiritus sanctus corporea specie tanquâ columba. Factum hoc primo propter Ioannem, quem isto signo in Christi agnitione confirmari oportuit, cum iampridem illi dictum esset: Super quem videris spiritum descendentem ac manentem super eum, hic est qui baptizat Spiritu sancto. Adhæc astantes quoq; admoneri & excitari oportuit, vt de Christo aliquid hominis maius conciperent, et facilius fidem adhiberent ijs, quæ de illo dicebantur. Sed & nos admonemur, Iesum hunc promissum illum regem & vindicem esse, quem oleo laetitiae prae omnibus consortibus suis vngendum fore olim Spiritus sanctus praedixerat. Psal. 45. Item propter ipsum Christi hoc contigit, vt etsi ab vtero matris spiritu praeditus fuisset, nunc tamen noua et plena virtute opus habebat, cum dfunctione, cui ipsum Pater destinauerat, accedere deberet. At quaerat aliquis, cur in columbae specie nunc apparuerit spiritus, qui alibi per aerem, alibi per ignem suam praesentiam testatus est? Cui nos respondemus, hanc speciem praesenti negotio conuenientissimam fuisse. Respondet enim factu hoc veteri typo, qui in diluuij historia praecesserit. Cum enim aquis per totum orbem terrarum diffusis & summa quoq; montium cacumina operientibus, Noa post longa moram salutis periculum facturus columbam secundo emisisset, redijt illa sub vesperam oliuae ramu rostro ferens: quo indicio ille intelligebat, deferbuisse iam Dei iram, et aquis subsidentibus nouam pacem terris diuinitus promitti. At quia haec maioris mysterij figura fuit, recte nunc in columbae specie Spiritus sanctus super Christum descendit, vt omnibus constet, hunc esse pacis veræ & perpetuae authorem, qui Dei iram solus placarit, & sub lata maledictione salutem certam humano generi attulerit. Docuit item columbae species, Christum non terribili diuinae iustitiae & iudicij gladio armatum, sed spiritu mansuetudinis instructum adesse, qui non stricto iure in hominum delicta animaduertere, sed illis ignoscere et medicam manum admouere paratus sit. Debebant ergo in hoc spectaculo mentis oculos attentius defigere, qui hodie Christum sibi durum & inexorabilem fingunt, apud quem matre Virgine aduocata opus fit, quae prolixis precibus, & beneficiorum commemoratione iram eius leniat, adeoq; per viscera et vbera materna illum ob testetur. At longe aliter in Euangelio se nobis ille praebet, quando omnes, qui laborant & onerati sunt, ad se vocat, & ijsdem, si ad se veniant, animarum pacem & refocillationem pollicetur. Praeterea officij nostri admonemur, vt nimirum qui in Christo seruari cupimus, eundem cum illo spiritu ducem sequamur, & moribus verè columbinis viuamus. Pertinet huc primo Christi praeceptum, Estote simplices vt columba. Vbi non stolidi & fatui esse iubemur, sed innocui & adolo malo alieni, id quod totius vitae puritatem atque innocentiam comprehendit. Deinde mansuetudo requiritur, vt ad seren das iniurias potius quam ad vindictae cupiditatem parati simus. Accedat his fides, quae pia & probae sponsae instar vnum Christum amemus, colamus & eidem obtemperemus. His indicijs patebit, nos Christi spiritu donatos, & proinde ipsius membra esse: & ita alas illas verè columbinas nobis parabimus, quas Dauid sibi dari optabat, quibus ex huius mundi horribili deserto & vndique ruentium turbinum procellis ad beatae immortalitatis sedes euadere poterimus. Psal. 55.
units.tr: Then the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove. This happened first for the sake of John, who had to be confirmed in recognising Christ by this sign, since it had been said to him long before: "The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." Moreover, those standing by also had to be reminded and stirred to conceive something greater of Christ than of a man, and to give more ready faith to what was said about him. We too are reminded that this Jesus is that promised king and deliverer, whom the Holy Spirit had long before foretold would be anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. (Ps. 45.) Likewise, it happened for Christ's own sake: although he had been endowed with the Spirit from his mother's womb, he now needed a new and full power, since he was to undertake the office for which the Father had appointed him. But someone may ask why the Spirit appeared now in the form of a dove, when elsewhere he made his presence known in air and in fire. To this we answer that this form was most fitting for the present matter. For it corresponds to an ancient type that preceded in the story of the flood. When the waters had spread over the whole earth and covered the highest mountain peaks, Noah, about to test the danger to his salvation after a long delay, sent out a dove a second time, and it returned towards evening carrying an olive branch in its beak. By this sign he understood that God's anger had now subsided, and that with the waters going down a new peace was divinely promised to the earth. But since this was a figure of a greater mystery, it was rightly the Holy Spirit who now descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, so that all might know that he is the author of true and lasting peace, who alone appeased God's anger and, with the curse lifted, brought certain salvation to the human race. The form of the dove also taught that Christ is present not armed with the terrible sword of divine justice, but furnished with the spirit of gentleness, who is not ready to punish the sins of men by the strict law, but to forgive them and apply a healing hand. Therefore those who today imagine Christ as hard and implacable should have fixed the eyes of their minds more attentively on this spectacle. For them, one must call on the Virgin Mother, who by long prayers and by recounting her benefits softens his anger, and so entreats him through her maternal bowels and breasts. But in the Gospel he presents himself to us quite differently, when he calls to himself all who labour and are burdened, and promises them, if they come to him, peace of soul and refreshment. Furthermore, we are reminded of our duty: those of us who desire to be saved in Christ should follow the same Spirit as our leader and live with truly dovelike manners. Here belongs first Christ's precept, "Be innocent as doves." We are bidden not to be foolish and senseless, but harmless and free from guile, which comprises the whole purity and innocence of life. Next, gentleness is required, so that we are ready to bear injuries rather than to desire revenge. Let faith be added, so that, like a pious and faithful bride, we love, worship and obey Christ alone. By these signs it will be clear that we, endowed with the Spirit of Christ, are his members, and so we shall prepare for ourselves those truly dovelike wings which David wished to be given him, with which we may escape from the horrible wilderness of this world and from the storms of whirlwinds rushing on every side, to the seats of blessed immortality. (Ps. 55.)

units.la: Sequitur vox Patris coelestis, quae singularem consideratione meretur, eo quod nulla vnquam de coelo laetior & iucundior audita est, & quae sola conscientiae terrores ex lege in nobis nascentes dissipare & animas ad desperationem proclives exhilarare potest. Qui enim antea minis terrificis ful minabat, & (vt Paulus ait) iram suam coelitus reuelabat, vt eius argumenta in singulis mundi partibus extarent, nunc de coelo filium suum in carne conspicatus clamat: Tu es filius ille meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacitum est. Quod autem hic ipse pater è coelo pronuntiat, hoc ipsum olim per prophetas ijsdem omnino verbis dixerat. Nam per Dauidem in Psal. 2. de Christo ait: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Et de eode apud Isaiam cap. 24. sic concionatur: Ecce seruus meus, quo nitar, electus meus, quo placatur anima mea. Vbi non temere factum putabimus, quod non alijs verbis nunc coelitus vtitur, quam quae olim seruis suis per spiritum suggesserat. Ex eo enim apparet, non aliud esse noui testamenti spiritum, qui hic super Christum descendit, quam qui olim per Prophetas locutus fuit. Et simul asseritur hoc argumento scripturae sacrae authoritas, vt constet illius libris Dei verbum contineri, neq; aliunde petenda esse doctrinam, quae in ecclesia praedicetur. Nam cum ipse Deus scriptu rae verbis de coelo concionatus sit, & filius Dei in carne manifestatus ex eadem concionum suarum argumenta desumpserit, imo ex mortuis rediuiuus suae mortis & resurrectionis rationem discipulis ex Mosis & prophetarum libris reddiderit, nimium audaces et plus aequo confidentes erunt, qui ex suo cerebro fingunt, aut ex aliorum commentis petunt quod ecclesiae obtrudant. Et sufficiant ista consu tandis omnibus illis, qui ad diuitis epulonis exemplum doctores è coelo aut ex inferis sibi dari vellent, quibus certò possent credere. Digni sunt illi, qui incertis hominum traditionibus in errorum Labyrinthos abducantur. Sed praestat singulas huius oratuli voces excutere.
units.tr: Next comes the voice of the heavenly Father, which deserves particular consideration, because no more joyful or pleasant voice was ever heard from heaven, and it alone can dispel the terrors of conscience that arise in us from the law and cheer souls prone to despair. For he who before thundered with terrifying threats, and (as Paul says) revealed his wrath from heaven, so that the evidence of it stood out in every part of the world, now, having looked down from heaven upon his Son made flesh, cries out: "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Moreover, what the Father himself here pronounces from heaven, he had long before spoken through the prophets in almost the same words. For through David in Psalm 2 he says of Christ: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you." And concerning the same one in Isaiah chapter 42 he preaches thus: "Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights." Here we shall not think it accidental that he now uses from heaven words other than those which he had earlier suggested to his servants through the Spirit. For from this it appears that the Spirit of the New Testament who here descended upon Christ is no other than he who formerly spoke through the prophets. And at the same time, by this argument, the authority of Holy Scripture is asserted, so that it is clear that the word of God is contained in its books, and that the doctrine to be preached in the church is not to be sought from anywhere else. For since God himself spoke from heaven in the words of Scripture, and the Son of God, manifested in the flesh, drew the grounds of his own discourses from the same, and indeed, rising from the dead, gave his disciples the reason for his death and resurrection from the books of Moses and the prophets, those will be too bold and overconfident who invent from their own brain, or seek from the fancies of others, what they thrust upon the church. And let these considerations suffice for all those who, after the example of the rich man in the parable, would wish teachers to be given them from heaven or from the dead, whom they could surely believe. They deserve to be led into the labyrinths of error by the uncertain traditions of men. But it is better to examine the individual words of this little oration.

units.la: Primò, Tu es (inquit) filius ille meus. Tu es εἰχλινῶς ait, vt constet de quo nam sermo sit: de eo nimirum, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus erat, & super quem tunc spiritus specie visibili descenderat, quia ab Ioanne baptizabatur. Hunc filium suum dicit Deus, non autem eo sensu, quo nos propter adoptionem gratuitam filij Dei dicimur: sed quòd ab æterno ex patre genitus, et proinde verus et naturalis (ut sic dicam) filius, et patri coæternus atq; coessentialis est. Ideo hunc Pater apud Zachariam coæqualem suum dicit, & passim prophetæ nomen Iehouæ illi tribuit, quo ipsa Dei essentia denotatur. Ipse etiā de hoc nos non obscurè admonet, quādo ait: Ego & pater vnum sumus: Qui me videt, patrem videt: Glorifica me pater apud teipsum ea gloria, quā habui apud te, priusquā hic mundus exisset. Habemus igitur hoc loco evidens adorandæ Trinitatis mysterium, non verbis solum sed reipsa expressum, ut sensibus perc-ipi potuerit. Astat enim in carne manifestatus æternus Dei filius. Descendit super huc visibili specie spiritus sanctus. E cælo autem patris vox auditur, qui filium suum agnoscit atq; fatetur. Et quod hic factum est, hoc ipsum in nostro etiam baptismo nobis ob oculos ponitur, quando qui vnius Dei cultores sumus, ex Christi tamen mandato baptizamur in nomine Patris, Filij, et Spiritus sancti. At nisi tres istæ personæ vnus sunt Deus, sacrilega audacia fuerit illas simul omnes in eodem gradu collocare.
units.tr: First, he says, "You are that son of mine." The Greek, σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱός μου [σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱός μου], makes clear who is meant: namely the one who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, and on whom the Spirit then descended in visible form, when he was being baptized by John. God calls this man his Son, but not in the sense in which we are called sons of God through free adoption. He is the Son in the sense that he was begotten of the Father from eternity, and so is a true and natural (so to speak) Son, co-eternal and co-essential with the Father. For this reason the Father, in Zechariah, calls him his fellow, and the prophets everywhere ascribe to him the name Jehovah, by which the very essence of God is denoted. He himself also warns us of this plainly when he says: "I and the Father are one"; "He who sees me sees the Father"; "Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before this world existed." We have here, therefore, in this passage the evident mystery of the adorable Trinity, expressed not only in words but in fact, so that it could be perceived by the senses. For the eternal Son of God stands there, manifested in the flesh. The Holy Spirit descends upon him in visible form. And from heaven the voice of the Father is heard, acknowledging and confessing his Son. What happened here is also set before our eyes in our own baptism, when we, who worship the one God, are nevertheless baptized by Christ's command in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But unless these three persons are one God, it would be sacrilegious audacity to place them all together on the same level.

units.la: Secundò dilectum dicit, quod superfluum videri poterat. Quis enim non diligat filium ex se natum, qui nullum vnquam contumaciæ specimen dedit? Sed opus erat hoc addi, partim ut scandalo medeatur, quod ex vili et ignobili illa assumpti hominis specie oritur: partim, ut intelligamus illum etsi homo factus sit, esse tamen filium illum dilectum, per quem dilectio illa Dei ad nos quoq; redundet, ita ut propter eum nos etiam nunc filiorum loco habeamur. Et hæc præcipua causa est, quòd de Christo in carne manifestato & iam homine facto id pronuntiari oportuit, ut discamus naturam humanam et quæ huic connexæ sunt miseriæ & infirmitates, non obstare, quo minus ipsi quoq; Dei filij simus, siquidem Christo per fidem insiti, corporis ipsius membra efficiamur. Facit ergo hoc ad asserendam salutis nostræ certitudinem, simulq; nostri officij nos admonet, ut Deum hunc totis animis redamemus, qui filio proprio non pepercit, sed eum pro nobis in mortem tradidit.
units.tr: Secondly, he calls him "beloved," which might seem superfluous. For who would not love a son born of himself, who has never given any sign of disobedience? But it was necessary to add this, partly to remedy the scandal that arises from the lowly and humble form of the man he assumed, and partly so that we may understand that, although he was made man, he is nonetheless that beloved Son through whom God's love also overflows to us, so that for his sake we too are now reckoned in the place of children. This is the chief reason why it was fitting to pronounce this of Christ, now manifested in the flesh and already made man: so that we may learn that human nature, and the miseries and infirmities joined to it, do not stand in the way of our also being sons of God, since, grafted into Christ through faith, we become members of his body. This therefore serves to establish the certainty of our salvation, and at the same time reminds us of our duty, that we should love in return with all our heart this God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up to death for us.

units.la: Et ad huius confirmationem facit adiectum membrum, In quo mihi bene complacitum est. Eo enim publicè testatur, se porro non habere, cuius causa nos damnet aut iratus perdat, qui huic filio suo dilecto insiti sumus. Itaq; oraculi huius diuini hic sensus est: Hactenus quidem mihi cum infelici hominum genere convenire non potuit, imo non potui non illis simul omnibus irasci & iram meam è cælo revelare, quādo cunctos defecisse, omnes pariter corruptos esse, et ne vnum quidem reliquum vidi, qui quod bonum est faceret. At quia nunc inter illos filium istum meum consp-icor, mihi coæternum & vnicum dilectum, qui ex meo decreto carne mortale assumere et homo verus nasci voluit, quiq; in assumpta carne divinam sanctitatem retinet et omnibus numeris perfectam obedientiam mihi præstat, iam nunc inter me & homines pax fancita est, iam illis placatus sum, iam gratia dignos iudico omnes, qui hunc meum dilectum filium fide vera & constanti amplexi fuerint. Etsi enim peccatores sint, hic tamen eorum peccata expiat, hic illis iustitia, satisfactio, redemptio et sanctificatio abs me datus est, et proinde in illo salutem certam inuenient. Hæc & alia huius generis breui ista sententia Deus concludit. Itaq; filium suum quasi digito nobis monstrat: ut hunc sciamus Mediatorem esse vnicum, qui nos cum illo in gratiam redux-erit, adeoq; in quo Deus (ut Paulus ait) reconciliarit sibi omnia, pacificatis per sanguinem crucis eius, tum quæ in terra tum quæ in cælis sunt. Quæ causa est, quòd alibi pax nostra & primogenitus omnis creaturæ dicitur. Etsi enim Angelos, qui nō peccarunt, Deo reconciliari minime opus fuerit, quia tamen Christus eam gloriam nobis meruit, in cuius reuelatione (ut ad Rom. scribitur) vniuersa hæc orbis creati machina vindicabitur ex seruitute corruptionis, nō immerito illius beneficium ad Angelos quoq; extendi dicimus, quos ex hominum salute et reconciliatione cū Deo gaudiū et lætitia singulare concipere idē ille testatur. Sunt hæc plena dulcissimæ consolationis, & ut in omni tentatione nobis sufficere possunt, ita omne nostræ salutis gloria vni Christo in solidum transcribunt, de cuius certitudine non possumus dubitare, cum tam luculento & irrefragabili Patris cæleslis testimonio cōfirmetur. Quicunq; ergo salutē extra Christū quærunt, & alios sibi apud Deū Mediatores fingunt, ij et salutis nostræ certitudine labefactant, et Deū ipsum (ut Ioānes scribit) mendacij argunt, cuius testimonio tā impudenter obloquuntur. Itaq; totis animis ista recōdamus ô fratres, & cum tanto precio & labore nos Deo reconciliari oportuerit, caueamus pro virili, ne illū deuota & impia peccandi licentia rursus adiram prouocemus. Amplectamur autem cōstanti fide Mediatorem nostrū Iesum Christum, ut huius beneficio in filios Dei adoptati, ipsius cohæredes simus, et cum eodē bonis cœlestibus æternum fruamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: To confirm this, the added clause, "in whom I am well pleased," also serves. By it he testifies publicly that he no longer has any cause to condemn us or to destroy us in anger, we who have been grafted into this beloved Son of his. Thus the sense of this divine oracle is this: "Hitherto I could not agree with the unhappy human race; indeed, I could not but be angry with them all and reveal my wrath from heaven, since I saw that all had fallen away, all had been corrupted together, and that not even one remained who did what is good. But now, because I behold among them this Son of mine, co-eternal with me and my only beloved, who by my decree willed to take on mortal flesh and be born a true man, who in the flesh he assumed retains divine holiness and renders to me perfect obedience in every respect, now peace has been established between me and men; now I am reconciled to them; now I judge all worthy of grace who have embraced this my beloved Son with true and steadfast faith. For although they are sinners, he nevertheless expiates their sins; in him, justification, satisfaction, redemption and sanctification have been given to them by me, and therefore they will find certain salvation in him." God concludes these and other things of this kind in this brief sentence. So he points out his Son to us, as it were with his finger, so that we may know that he is the only Mediator, who has led us back with himself into favour, and in whom God (as Paul says) has reconciled all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross, both things on earth and things in heaven. This is why elsewhere he is called our peace and the firstborn of every creature. For although the angels who did not sin had no need at all to be reconciled to God, yet because Christ merited this glory for us, in whose revelation (as it is written in Romans) this whole machinery of the created world will be set free from the bondage of corruption, we rightly say that his benefit extends also to the angels, whom the same apostle testifies conceive singular joy and gladness from the salvation and reconciliation of men with God. These things are full of the sweetest consolation, and as they can suffice for us in every temptation, so they ascribe the whole glory of our salvation entirely to Christ alone, whose certainty we cannot doubt, since it is confirmed by such a clear and unanswerable testimony of the heavenly Father. Therefore, whoever seeks salvation outside Christ, and imagines other mediators for themselves with God, both undermine the certainty of our salvation and accuse God himself (as John writes) of lying, since they so shamelessly contradict his testimony. Therefore, brothers, let us store these things up with all our heart, and since we had to be reconciled to God at such a price and with such labour, let us take care, as far as we can, not to provoke him to anger again by a devoted and impious license to sin. Let us rather embrace with steadfast faith our Mediator Jesus Christ, so that by his benefit we, adopted as sons of God, may be his co-heirs and enjoy eternally with him the heavenly goods. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: Quoad ætatem sic ait: Ipse autem Iesus incipiebat esse quasi annorum triginta. Fuit ergo ætas eius iam matura satis, & vulgi etiam iudicio rebus agendis idonea. Quod in primis obseruari debet in ijs, qui vel ad rem p. accedunt, vel ecclesiæ ministerium suscipiunt: ne propter ætatem contemnantur, & vnà secum ipsum quoq; munus, cui destinati sunt, in contemptum adducant. Non tamen negamus, quasdam in iuuenili adhuc ætate res magnas gessisse, neq; ad certum annorum numerum astrictam esse spiritus diuini virtutem, quo minus in pueris quoque se exerat: sed in præsenti, non quid Deus possit, sed quid nos obseruare conuenit, docemus, nisi nos exemplo Christi ... Quod autem ex Christi exemplo Anabaptistæ colligunt, neminem, priusquam ad virilem ætatem peruenerit, baptizandum esse, turpem infscitiam & rerum sacrarum ignorantiam produnt, qua fit, vt illius exemplum violenter ad vsum alienum detorqueant, neq; videnit, quam ingens inter illum & nos discrimen sit. Nam quoad Christum, poterat is baptismum omnino negligere, cum illo nequaquam opus habaret, vt in proximo sermone diximus. At alia longè est nostra conditio, quos ipsius Christi mandatu premit & vrget, vt et ipsi publicè nomen demus, quamprimum fui cognitione nos illuminare dignatur: & eidem nostros quoq; infantes consecremus, ad quos regnum cælorum pertinere ille testatur. Quia ante alia ratio, qua infantes Christo adducantur, inueniri nõ potest, quàm vt per baptismum in corporis fui, id est, ecclesiæ societatem adoptentur, illa omnino nobis vtendu erit, nisi & in illum ingrati esse, & ex nobis natos salutifera et necessaria in primis ipsius communione, quan tum in nobis est, spoliare velimus. Deinde cum hactenus nõn in vsu fuisset baptismus, Chriftu priuf- quam hic institutus effet, baptizari impossibile fuit. Quia enim euangelij Sacramentu est baptismus quo nouus ille Dei populus initiari debuit, non conueniebat illu cuiquam dari, priufquà Euangelii prædicari cœpisset. Recte ergo in hunc vfq; diem baptismum suum distulit Dominus, qui Circuncifio nem, quæ in vsu erat, ne vnam quidem horam differre voluit, quò minus octauo die à sua natiuitate circumcideretur. Accedit his, quòd tunc demũ adfuit tempus illud præfinitum, quo promissus ille hu- mani generis vindex sese manifestare debuit, & ea aggredi, quorũ causa in mundũ venerat. Tunc enim agebatur quartus annus septuagesimæ hebdomadis, in qua Chriftũ fœdus cõfirmaturũ et lega les victimas abrogaturum esse Daniel olim prædixerat, & nos alibi prolixius demonstrauimus. Fa ciunt ergo Anabaptistæ idẽ, quod qui in aquis periclitantur. Vt enim hi quiduis obuia arripiût, et in terdũ ea etiã, quæ ipsis noxia sunt: ita illi, vt sua deliria tueantur, omnia temere adducũt, quæcunq; ipsis aliqua ex parte patrocinari videntur, quæ plerunq; eiusmodi sunt, vt fi propius inspiciatur, con tra ipsos quam maximè faciant. Ex quorũ numero hoc etiam Christi exemplum censeri debet. Quia enim is suo baptismo nouũ testamentum inchoauit, in quo veteres ritus aboleri oportuit, et nouos in ftitui, vtiq; simul nobis quoq; eam libertatẽ fecit, vt quicunq; noui testamenti membra sunt, eiusdem sacris initientur, quemadmodum olim licebat veteribus sacris vti ijs omnibus, qui non ob aliquâ sin gularẽ causam prohibebantur. Quapropter cũ baptismus in locum Circuncifionis fucceffierit, quã ad infantes quoq; pertinuisse constat, plus quàm stupidi & pertinaces sunt, qui illos baptizandos esse negant. Itaq; relictis hominibus illis nõ minus pertinacibus quàm rixosis, & ad turbandas ecclesias natis, illud potius fpeftemus, quod suo exemplo Christus nos docuit: Nimirum non festinandum esse in rebus arduis, sed expectandam vocatione Dei, qui vt sua tempora singulis constituit, ita quos vo cat, donis quoq; necessarijs instruit, vt vocationi suæ sufficere possint, quæ nõ possunt sperare, qui non vocati currunt. Si quis ergo vocetur iuuenis adhuc (quod Ieremiæ & quibusdam alijs accidisse sci- mus) ut fe Deo morigerum et obedientem præbeat. Quòd fi alicuius vocatione Deus in senectam vf que differt, is moram hanc patienter ferat, neq; conetur Dei consilium præcipiti affectu abreptus præ uertere, ne magno suo malo aliquid tentet viribus suis maius, & cui ferendo humeri non sufficiant. Obseruandum hoc non solùm in ecclesiæ ministerio, verumetiam in repub, ne caca ambitione decepti leges publicas turbemus, & multorũ malorum authores fimus, quæ legitimo & recepto ordine fubla to exoriri solent. Commendatur ab historicis, et meritò quidem Spartani cuiufdam dictum, qui cũm generis nobilitate & morum sanctitate præstaret, in magistratus autem petitione victus effet à com petitoribus, maximæ sibi lætitiæ esse prædicauit, quòd patria sua aliquot fe meliores viros haberet. Potuit ille repulsam tam patienter ferre, quòd publicum totius patriæ iudicium priuatæ suæ petitio ni anteferret. Quantò magis ergo Christianos homines in eiusmodi casibus patientes esse decet, qui omnia nostra diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio gubernari sciunt, cui reluctari nefas & impium est? Sed debemus hoc etiam malum nostrorum temporum iniquitati, qua fit, vt qui rebus agendis minimè idonei sunt, ad quæuis tamen munera cùm ecclesiastica tum politica aspirant, & magna iniuria fe affici arbitrantur, fi quis viros meliores & magis exercitatos illis præferat. Sed transeamus ad alteram huius loci partem, qua Iesu Christi genealogiam ad Adamum vsq; Lucas contexit. Vbi ante omnia obseruari debet, non pugnare hoc cum Spiritus sancti præcepto, qui per Paulum monet, ne genealogijs operam demus, et has cum quæstionibus inutilibus atq; noxijs con iungit. Ibi enim de superstitiosis & ambitiosis agitur, quas omnibus ferè seculis apud omnes populos in vsu fuisse constat: Iudæi quidem in suis contexendis superstitiosissimi fuerunt: non sanè vt Dei bonitatem & prouidentiam agnoscerent, qui gentem ipsorum inter ferocissimos hostes in exilijs & transmigrationibus periculosissimis mirificè seruauerat: sed vt generis fiducia non solum alijs gentibus sese praeferrent insolentius, verum etiam aduersus Deum insurgerent, & superstitiosa inanium titulorum confidentia ebrij illum sibi facerent debitorem. Dictum de hoc nuper, quando Ioannis doctrinam ideo aspernati sunt, quòd poenitentia sibi non opus esse putarent, quia filij essent Abrahami. Quin ipsi Christo eos ad amplectendam Dei gratiam hortanti in faciem dicere ausi sunt: Semen Ab rahami sumus, neq; cuiquam seruiuimus vnquam: quomodo tu dicis nos vindicandos esse, aut vindice opus habere? Erat etiam inter gentes multa in hac re superstitio, vt Theogoniae testatur, quibus parum Deorum suorum generationem exponebant, partim Heroum genus ad Deos referebant, & ex his illos procreatos esse fabulabantur. Fuit hoc horribile diaboli artificium, qui non contentus terras stupris & adulteriis polluisse, coelos quoq; & Deos, quos miseri homines colebant, illis flagitijs infames fecit. Et credibile est Apostolus adhuc viuentibus errorem illum pullulare coepisse, quo postea haeretici quidam decepti Aeones suos & nescio quos principes coelites gradibus suis distinctos finxerunt, vt vi dere est apud Irenaeum & Epiphanium. Eiusmodi ergo genealogias omnes Apostolus ex spiritus sug gestione prohibet, quia ambitionis fomenta sunt, & superstitiones pariunt non tam ridiculas quàm nefarias & cum manifesta impietate coniunctas. Et hodie nō immeritò damnantur, qui inani generis fiducia elati, sese ob solam natiuitatē omnibus aliis praeferunt: quorum aliqui eò dementiae processerunt, vt suae familiae originē ex ipsa Noae arca deducere conati sint; ridiculi plane homines, qui sibi solis ausi fuerunt vendicare, quod omnis loci atq; ordinis hominibus commune est. Quia enim diluuij tempore in sola arca Noae humani generis seminarium Deus seruauit, ex illa nō Reges modò & principes, verumetiā agricolas, opifices, bubulcos, nautas & quosuis alios prodijsse constat. Ita vero sei psos vlcisci atur oportet, qui prae alijs eminere volunt. At longè alia est genealogiae Iesu Christi ratio, quam in praesenti Lucas et in sui scripti euangelici initio Matthaeus contexit. Ea enim demonstrat, Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, esse Christum, id est, promissum illum Regem & Sacerdotē, qui ex Abrahami & Dauidis semine nasci debuit. Deinde scandalo medetur, quod ex vili & ignobili Iosephi & Mariae specie emanabat, quos ex regia stirpe genus ducere vix credibile videri poterat. Eusebius certè ex Egesippo narrat, Domitianū quorundā delatione & calumniis exacerbatum, constituisse aliquando vniuersam Dauidis posteritatem delere, quòd ex illa regnū nouum oriturum suspicaretur: sed eundem mox à coeptis abstinuisse, cùm eos, qui adhuc reliqui erant, homines obscuros & pauperes esse comperisset, qui manuum labore victitarent. Quod ergo sanguinarium tyrannum mouit, ne quid regium in pauperculis agnosceret, hoc ipsum multis alijs suspicionem mouere potuisset, ne Dauidis filiū crederent esse Iesum hunc, cuius mater desponsata fuerat Iosepho, obscuri oppidi incolae, & qui manuario opificio sibi & familiae victū quaerebat. Quamobrem vile, imò nec cessarium erat genealogiam eius diligenter conscribi, ne vel malignis fidei hostibus calumniandi occasio daretur, vel infirmiores scandalum haberent, quo in fide Christi impedirentur.
units.tr: Concerning his age, he says: "Now Jesus himself was about thirty years old" (Luke 3:23). His age was therefore already mature enough, and in the judgment of the common people fit for affairs. This should be noted first of all by those who enter public office or take up the ministry of the Church, so that they are not despised on account of their age and do not bring into contempt the office for which they were destined. Yet we do not deny that some have accomplished great things in their youth, nor that the power of the Holy Spirit is bound to a fixed number of years, so that it cannot also work in children. But at present we are teaching not what God can do but what we ought to observe, and we urge that we follow the example of Christ. As for the Anabaptists' inference from Christ's example, that no one should be baptized before he has reached adult age, they betray a shameful ignorance and lack of understanding of sacred things. By this they twist his example violently to a use not its own, and they do not see how great a difference there is between him and us. For as regards Christ, he could altogether neglect baptism, since he had no need of it, as we said in the sermon before. But our condition is quite different. Christ's own command presses and urges us to give our name publicly as soon as he deigns to enlighten us with the knowledge of himself, and also to consecrate our infants to him, for he testifies that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.
