Since no other way can be found by which infants may be brought to Christ, except that they be adopted through baptism into the fellowship of his body, which is the Church, we must altogether use that means, unless we wish to be ungrateful to him and, as far as in us lies, to deprive our own offspring of his saving and necessary communion. Further, since baptism had not been in use until Christ was instituted here, it was impossible for him to be baptized before then. For baptism is the sacrament of the gospel, by which that new people of God ought to be initiated, and it was not fitting that it be given to anyone before the gospel had begun to be preached. Therefore the Lord rightly deferred his own baptism until this day, though he was unwilling to delay even one hour the circumcision that was then in use, so that he was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth. Add to this that the appointed time had only then arrived, when the promised deliverer of mankind was to make himself known and undertake the things for which he had come into the world. For then the fourth year of the seventieth week was running, in which Daniel had long ago foretold that Christ would confirm the covenant and abolish the legal sacrifices, as we have demonstrated more fully elsewhere. So the Anabaptists do what those who are in danger in the waters do. As these seize whatever comes to hand, and sometimes even things that are harmful to them, so they, to defend their delusions, rashly bring forward everything that seems in any way to support them, though these things are for the most part of such a kind that, if they are looked at more closely, they tell most strongly against them. This example of Christ ought to be counted among them. For since he began the new covenant by his baptism, in which the old rites had to be abolished and new ones instituted, he at the same time granted us this liberty: that all who are members of the new covenant should be initiated into its sacred rites, just as formerly the ancient sacred rites were open to all who were not excluded for some particular reason. Therefore, since baptism has succeeded to the place of circumcision, which is agreed to have pertained also to infants, those who deny that infants are to be baptized are more than stupid and obstinate. So, leaving aside those men, who are no less obstinate than quarrelsome and born to disturb the churches, let us rather consider what Christ taught us by his example: namely, that one must not hasten into difficult undertakings, but wait for the calling of God, who, as he appoints to each his times, so also furnishes those whom he calls with the gifts necessary for them to meet their calling, gifts which those who run without being called cannot hope for. If, then, someone is called while still young (as we know happened to Jeremiah and certain others), he should show himself compliant and obedient to God. But if God defers the calling of someone until old age, let that person bear this delay patiently, and let him not, carried away by rash feeling, try to anticipate God's counsel, lest to his great harm he attempt something beyond his strength, and for which his shoulders are not sufficient to bear the load. This must be observed not only in the ministry of the Church but also in the commonwealth, so that, deceived by blind ambition, we do not disturb the public laws and become the authors of many evils, which are wont to arise when an established and accepted order is overthrown. Historians commend, and rightly, the saying of a certain Spartan who, though he excelled in nobility of birth and holiness of character, was defeated by his rivals in seeking a magistracy, and declared that it was a matter of great joy to him that his country had several men better than himself. He could bear the rejection so patiently because he placed the public judgment of his whole country above his private petition. How much more, then, ought Christians to be patient in such cases, who know that all our affairs are governed by the counsel of divine providence, against which to resist is wicked and impious? But we ought also to attribute this evil of our times to its iniquity, by which it comes about that those who are least fit for public business aspire to every office, ecclesiastical as well as civil, and think they are greatly wronged if anyone prefers better and more practised men to them. But let us pass to the other part of this passage, in which Luke has woven the genealogy of Jesus Christ back to Adam. Here, first of all, it must be noted that this does not conflict with the precept of the Holy Spirit, who, through Paul, warns us not to give heed to genealogies, and joins them with useless and harmful questions (1 Tim. 1:4; Titus 3:9). For there he is dealing with superstitious and ambitious genealogies, which are known to have been in use among all peoples in almost every age. The Jews indeed were most superstitious in drawing up their own: not, certainly, so that they might acknowledge the goodness and providence of God, who had marvellously preserved their nation amid the fiercest enemies, in exiles and most perilous transmigrations, but so that, through confidence in their stock, they might not only set themselves more insolently above other nations, but even rise up against God, and, drunk with superstitious trust in empty titles, make him their debtor. We have spoken of this recently, when they despised John's teaching because they thought they had no need of repentance, since they were children of Abraham. Indeed, when Christ exhorted them to embrace the grace of God, they even dared to say to his face: "We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say that we shall be set free, or that we need a deliverer?" Among the Gentiles, too, there was much superstition in this matter, as the Theogony attests, in which they set forth the generation of their gods in some detail, partly referred the race of heroes to the gods, and fabled that they were begotten by them. This was a horrible artifice of the devil, who, not content to have polluted the earth with debauchery and adultery, also made heaven and the gods whom wretched men worshipped infamous by these crimes. And it is credible that this error had already begun to sprout while the Apostle was still living, the error by which later certain heretics, deceived, invented their Aeons and I know not what heavenly princes distinguished by their ranks, as may be seen in Irenaeus and Epiphanius. The Apostle therefore, by the prompting of his Spirit, forbids all such genealogies, because they are fuel for ambition and give rise to superstitions that are not so much ridiculous as impious and joined with manifest godlessness. And today those are rightly condemned who, puffed up by empty confidence in their stock, set themselves above all others on the ground of birth alone. Some of them have gone so far in madness that they have tried to derive the origin of their family from Noah's very ark. Men who are plainly ridiculous, who have dared to claim for themselves alone what is common to people of every place and rank. For since God preserved in the ark of Noah alone the seed of the human race at the time of the flood, it is agreed that from it came forth not only kings and princes but also farmers, craftsmen, oxherds, sailors, and all sorts of others. Thus those who wish to stand out above others ought to be humbled in this way. But the reason for the genealogy of Jesus Christ is quite different, which Luke now sets down, and Matthew at the beginning of his gospel. For it shows that this Jesus, who was born a man of the virgin Mary, is the Christ, that is, the promised King and Priest, who had to be born of the seed of Abraham and David. Then it remedies a stumbling block, arising from the lowly and obscure appearance of Joseph and Mary, whom it could scarcely seem credible to trace their descent from a royal stock. Eusebius indeed relates on the authority of Hegesippus that Domitian, provoked by the accusations and slanders of certain men, once decided to destroy the whole posterity of David, because he suspected that a new kingdom would arise from it. But he soon desisted from his undertaking, when he found that those who were still left were obscure and poor men, who got their living by the labour of their hands. What moved that bloodthirsty tyrant so as not to recognise anything royal in these poor folk might well have stirred suspicion in many others, lest they believe that this Jesus, whose mother had been betrothed to Joseph, an inhabitant of an obscure town and one who earned a living for himself and his household by manual craft, was a son of David. Therefore it was of little use, indeed it was not even necessary, to write out his genealogy carefully, lest either malicious enemies of the faith be given an opportunity to slander, or the weaker be scandalised and hindered in their faith in Christ.

units.la: Atqui ex genealogia ista calumnias graues olim struxerunt nonnulli, qui fidem Christianā ludibrio exponere conati sunt. Alijs enim ridiculū visum est, Iosephi genus recenseri, cùm Christus absq; eius cogressu ex virgine intemerata natus credatur. Alij Matthaeū cum Luca dissentire clamarunt cùm hic quidem Iosephi patre Heli, ille verò Iacobū fuisse scribat. Inde enim colligunt, duos Iosepho patres tribui, quod cum naturae legibus pugnet. At prioribus iam pridem responsum est, legem fuisse, qua puellae in alias tribus abnubere prohibebātur. Quia verò Iosephum ex tribu Iuda oriundū fuisse constat, non dubium est, ad eandem tribum Mariā quoq; pertinuisse: cùm ea vtriusq; pietas fuerit, vt eos in lege Dei peccare voluisse nō fit verisimile: & ideo Iosephi genus recensuisse sufficiebat. Quod si quis obijciat, nō inde necessario sequi, Mariam ex Dauidis stirpe prognatam fuisse, quando satis erat ex eadem tribu natam esse, tribus autem familijs plurimis constabant? huic nos respondemus, Apostolorū temporibus haec omnibus cōpertissima fuisse, quae causa fuit, vt in his recensendis minus curiosi fuerint. Cuius rei argumentum in Matthaeo apparet, qui vt lectorū memoriae cōsuleret tres Tessaradecades facit, & vt haec constarent, in secunda Reges Iuda quinq; omittit, primò nimirū tres continuos, Ochoziam, Ioam & Amaziam, deinde verò Ioachan & Iehoiakim, qui Iechoniā proximē praecesserunt. Neq; tamen à quoquam accusatus est falsi, quòd haec omnibus notissima essent. Posteris demū temporibus exorti sunt Porphyrius & Iulianus, scurrae nequissimi, qui haec & alia multa vellicarunt, quorum vestigijs insistunt, qui hodie ista odiosius exagitant, aut sua sophistica in dubium vocant. Damnantur isti omnes veterū Iudaorū silentio, qui etsi Christianae fidei infensissimi hostes & simul scriptorum apostolicorum Aristarchi aut censores acerrimi fuerint, genealogias tamen has intactas reliquerunt: nimirum, quod eas cum veritate & tribuum archiuis conuenire viderent. Ad alterum quoq; facilis est responsio, si dicamus Heli & Iacobum fratres fuisse, quorum hoc abque liberis mortuo, ille ex relicta coniuge semen ei excitauit, Iosephum sicuti in lege Deus mandauerat. Itaq; tam Heli quàm Iacobus Iosephi pater fuit, hic quidem legalis, quia ex lege ad ipsum Iosephus pertinebat: ille verò naturalis, quod ex ipso verè esset genitus. Scio alios Heli patrem Mariæ, & eundem cum Ioachimo facere, cuius filius dicatur Iosephus, eò quod gener eius fuerit. Sed hoc est genealogias non contexere, sed confundere, & cum Lucæ verbis pugnat, qui diserte Iosephum filium ipsius Heli fuisse scribit. Quòd si cui libet Iosephi patrem binomine facere, vt vnus idemq; sit, quem Lucas Heli, Matthæus Iacobum nominat, hoc ei per me licet. Prior tamen solutio mihi minus cota, & illius seculi moribus, quando legis disciplina adhuc vigebat, conuenientior esse videtur.
units.tr: Yet from this genealogy some men long ago built up serious calumnies, trying to make the Christian faith a laughingstock. For some found it ridiculous that the lineage of Joseph should be recounted, since Christ is believed to have been born of the undefiled virgin without any intercourse with him. Others cried out that Matthew disagrees with Luke, since the one writes that Heli was Joseph's father and the other that it was Jacob. From this they infer that two fathers are assigned to Joseph, which conflicts with the laws of nature. But it was answered long ago that there was a law forbidding girls to marry into other tribes. Since it is established that Joseph was descended from the tribe of Judah, there is no doubt that Mary also belonged to the same tribe, for their piety was such that it is not likely they wished to sin against the law of God; and so it was enough to recount Joseph's lineage. But if someone objects that it does not necessarily follow that Mary was born of the stock of David, since it was enough to be born of the same tribe, and the tribes consisted of very many families, we reply: in the times of the apostles these things were all very well known, and this is why they were less careful in recounting them. Evidence of this appears in Matthew, who, to help the memory of his readers, makes three series of fourteen, and so that these might hold together, he omits five kings from the second series of the kings of Judah: first, namely, three consecutive ones, Ochoziah, Joash and Amaziah, and then Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim, who immediately preceded Jeconiah. Yet he was never accused of falsehood by anyone, because these things were most widely known to all. Later in time there arose Porphyry and Julian, most wicked buffoons, who attacked these and many other things, and those who today criticise these matters more bitterly, or call them into doubt with their sophistries, follow in their footsteps. All of these are condemned by the silence of the ancient Jews, who, although they were the most hostile enemies of the Christian faith and at the same time the sharpest critics or censors of the apostolic writings, like Aristarchus, nonetheless left these genealogies untouched, clearly because they saw that they agreed with the truth and with the archives of the tribes. The other point also has an easy answer, if we say that Heli and Jacob were brothers, and that when the one died without children, the other raised up seed for him from his widow, namely Joseph, as God had commanded in the law. Thus both Heli and Jacob were Joseph's father: the one legal, because by law Joseph belonged to him; the other natural, because Joseph was truly begotten by him. I know that others make Heli the father of Mary, and the same man as Joachim, and say that Joseph is called his son because he was his son-in-law. But this is not to weave the genealogies together but to confuse them, and it clashes with the words of Luke, who plainly writes that Joseph was the son of Heli himself. But if anyone wishes to make Joseph's father a double name, so that one and the same man is called Heli by Luke and Jacob by Matthew, I, for my part, allow this. Nevertheless, the first solution seems to me less strained and more in keeping with the customs of that age, when the discipline of the law was still in force.

units.la: Nunc obseruemus ante omnia spiritus sancti diligentiam, quain seruanda linea Iesu Christi vt ipsus est. Vt enim Iudaeorum gentem, ex qua ille præfinito tempore nasci debuit, Circumcisione & Leuiticis sacris à reliquis gentibus distinctam esse voluit: ita iam inde ab ipsa rerum origine lineam certam duxit eius generis aut familiæ, ex qua prodire debebat, & eandem literis consignauit, vt posteris constaret certius, quis nam pro Messia & humani generis vindice agnosci deberet. Et primo quidem, cùm huius promissione Adam accepisset, inter eius filios Seth nominatur, ex quo linea illa ducitur vsque ad Noam, quem ex diluuij aquis Deus beneficio singulari seruauit. Deinde cùm huic filij tres essent, ne incerta fieret Christi propago, eius promissio ad Semum restringitur, & ab hoc rursus certo ordine ad Abrahamum vsque deriuatur. In huius familia Isaacum quasi digito monstrat Deus, dicens: In Isaaco nominabitur tibi semen. Rursus cùm hic in Esaum primogenitum suum nimis esset intentus, admirabili diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio fit, vt inuitus & ignarus rerum benedictionem in Iacobum transferat, ex cuius posteritate Christus nasci debebat. Inter Iacobi autem filios duodecim Iudas designatur, benedictæ illius lineæ pater, & cùm ex hoc descendens tribus postea in plures familias diuisa esset, Messiæ promissionem ad Iesseam seu Dauidicam familiam retulit, & in hac non sine manifesto prouidentiæ suæ consilio perpetuam regum atque principum successionem inter horribiles & varios vtriusq; regni, Iudaici & Israelitici motus, & diuturna totius gentis exilia atque dispersiones conseruauit. Inter quæ cumprimis memorabile est, quod post Ochoziæ mortem accidit. Cùm enim is propter impietatem & illicitam cum domo Achabi coniunctionem sine liberis extinctus esset, & eius mater Athalia, ne regnum in aliam familiam transferretur, vniuersum genus regium e medio tollere decreuisset, admirabili Ioiadæ Sacerdotis industria Ioas, infans adhuc, seruatus est, qui ex Nathano Dauidis filio descenderat, & in eius posteritate promissi illius seminis linea maneret. Quæ causa est, quòd Lucas naturalem ordinem secutus Christi lineam non per Solomonem, sed per Nathanum deducit, ad cuius familiam extincta vniuersa Solomonis posteritate regnum vna cum promissionibus Dauidi datis translatum fuit. Neque ideo à Christi genere Solomo excluditur, in quo promissio illa, quæ 2. Samue. 7. capite extat, fundata fuit. Quia enim Ioas illius posteris propter generis propinquitatem & consanguinitatem coniunctissimus fuit, et vt hæres legitimus in regno succesßit, non immeritò in historia sacra Ochoziæ filius dicitur. Ab illo autem rursus Christi genealogiam certo ordine ad Salathielem eiusq; filium Zorobabelem euangelistæ deducunt, in quibus Lucas & Matthæus pulchrè conueniunt. Vbinon imprudenter quidam obseruarunt, eundem esse Salathielis patrem, quem Matthæus Iechoniam, Lucas autem Neri, id est, lucernâ dicit. Nam vt apud Ieremiam habetur, fuit Iechonias ille instar anuli signatorij, per quem promissionem Dauidi factam Deus seruare voluit, & ideo Euilmerodachi animum mouit, vt illum libertate donatum in regiâ dignitatem eueheret, & in summo pretio haberet, & sic in eo rursus accenderetur lucerna illa Dauidicæ domus, quæ in excidio vrbis & totius gentis exilio iam prorsus extincta esse videbatur. A Zorobabele autem ad Christum vsque gradus viginti Lucas numerat, cùm apud Matthæum non plures quàm vndecim habeantur. Sed in illis conciliandis non multa cura opus est. Iam antè enim demonstrauimus, Matthæum, qui lineam legalem contexuit, sibi consultò aliquid permisisse, vt genealogiam omnem in tres Tessaradecades posset distribuere: quod non similiter Lucæ licuit, cuius institutum fuit, Christi genus ordine naturali ad primum vsque parentem deducere. Et quod nuper diximus, sufficiat nobis Iudaeorum veterum testimonium, qui cum rationem texendarum genealogiarum rectius quam nos hodie perspectam haberent, suo tamen silentio utriusque Euangelistae narrationem probauerunt. Nos itaque finem & scopum, qui utriq; propositus fuit, obseruemus: ut nimirum Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria virgine hominem verū assumpsit, credamus esse Christum, benedictum scilicet illud semen Abrahami & Dauidis filium, in quo sancti patres omnem suae salutis fiduciam habuerunt collocatam.
units.tr: Let us observe above all the diligence of the Holy Spirit in preserving the line of Jesus Christ as it truly is. For just as he willed that the Jewish nation, from which he was to be born at the appointed time, should be distinguished from the other nations by circumcision and the Levitical rites, so from the very beginning of things he drew a certain line of that race or family from which he was to come, and he set it down in writing, so that it would be more certain to posterity who ought to be acknowledged as the Messiah and deliverer of the human race. And first, when Adam had received the promise of him, Seth is named among his sons, from whom that line is traced down to Noah, whom God preserved from the waters of the flood by a singular kindness. Then, when Noah had three sons, lest the descent of Christ become uncertain, the promise was restricted to Shem, and from him it was again traced in a certain order down to Abraham. In the family of Abraham God points out Isaac, as it were with his finger, saying: "In Isaac shall your seed be named." Again, when Isaac was too absorbed in Esau his firstborn, by the wonderful counsel of divine providence it came about that, unwilling and unaware of the matter, he transferred the blessing to Jacob, from whose posterity Christ was to be born. Among the twelve sons of Jacob, Judah is designated as the father of that blessed line, and when the tribe descended from him was afterwards divided into many families, he referred the promise of the Messiah to the family of Jesse, or the Davidic family, and in this family, not without a manifest purpose of his providence, he preserved a perpetual succession of kings and princes amid the terrible and varied upheavals of both kingdoms, the Jewish and the Israelite, and the long exiles and dispersions of the whole nation. Among these, one thing especially is memorable, which happened after the death of Ahaziah. For when he had died without children, because of his impiety and his unlawful alliance with the house of Ahab, and his mother Athaliah had resolved to wipe out the entire royal stock, so that the kingdom should not pass into another family, Joash, still an infant, was saved by the remarkable diligence of the priest Jehoiada; he was descended from Nathan, son of David, and in his posterity the line of that promised seed remained. This is why Luke, following the natural order, traces Christ's line not through Solomon but through Nathan, to whose family the kingdom, along with the promises given to David, was transferred when the whole posterity of Solomon had been extinguished. Yet Solomon is not for this reason excluded from the race of Christ, in whom that promise which stands in the seventh chapter of 2 Samuel was founded. For since Joash was most closely joined to Solomon's posterity by family proximity and kinship, and succeeded to the kingdom as its lawful heir, he is not without reason called the son of Ahaziah in the sacred history. From him again the evangelists trace Christ's genealogy in a sure order down to Shealtiel and his son Zerubbabel, in which Luke and Matthew agree beautifully. Here some have rightly observed that the father of Shealtiel is the same person whom Matthew calls Jeconiah and Luke calls Neri, that is, "lamp." For, as is found in Jeremiah, that Jeconiah was like a signet ring, by which God wished to preserve the promise made to David; and therefore he moved the heart of Evil-merodach to set him free and raise him to royal dignity and hold him in the highest honour, and so the lamp of the Davidic house, which seemed utterly extinguished in the destruction of the city and the exile of the whole nation, was lit again in him. But from Zerubbabel to Christ Luke counts twenty generations, whereas in Matthew there are not more than eleven. Yet little care is needed in reconciling these. For we have already shown earlier that Matthew, who wove together the legal line, deliberately allowed himself some liberty so that he could distribute the whole genealogy into three series of fourteen; this liberty was not similarly permitted to Luke, whose plan it was to trace Christ's descent in natural order back to the first parent. And as we said recently, let the testimony of the ancient Jews suffice for us, who, although they understood the method of composing genealogies more correctly than we do today, nonetheless by their silence approved the account of each evangelist. Let us therefore observe the aim and purpose set before both: namely, that we believe this Jesus, who took true manhood from the virgin Mary, to be Christ, that blessed seed of Abraham and son of David, in whom the holy fathers placed all their confidence of salvation.

units.la: Quòd verò Matthaeus Christi genealogiam non ultra Abrahamum deducit, Lucas autem ad Adamum, imò ad huius creatorem Deum usque ascendit, non absque certa ratione factum putabimus. Hic enim dum Adami meminit, qui communis omnium hominum parens est, non obscurè docet, Christum uniuersalem omnium gentium redemptorem esse, eiusq; meritum ad primum usque patrem nostrum extendi: quo nomine alibi agnus ille dicitur, qui immolatus fit iam inde ab ipsa mundi origine. Matthaeus autem in Abrahamo subsistit, imò Christum initio statim simpliciter filium Abrahami & Dauidis nominat (Liber generationis, inquit, Iesu Christi, filij Dauidis, filij Abrahami) ut ostendat redemptorem illum uniuersalem, qui Adamo promissus est, non alibi quàm in Abrahami semine & Dauidis domo quaeri debere. Ut ergo Lucas consolationem uniuersale omnis loci & ordinis hominibus adhibet: ita uicissim cauet Matthaeus, ne in quaerenda salutis ratione post nostrae rationis figmenta vagemur, neque eorum sequamur, non minus pernitiosam quàm erroneam sententiam, qui unamquamq; gentem in sua religione, sibi à maioribus quasi per manus tradita, seruari posse contendunt.
units.tr: That Matthew does not trace Christ's genealogy beyond Abraham, while Luke goes back to Adam, and even to God, the creator of Adam, we will think was not done without a sound reason. By mentioning Adam, the common parent of all men, Luke clearly teaches that Christ is the redeemer of all nations, and that his merit reaches back to our first father. For this reason elsewhere the lamb is said to have been slain from the very beginning of the world. Matthew, on the other hand, stops at Abraham. Indeed, at the very start he simply calls Christ the son of Abraham and David ("The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham"), to show that the universal redeemer promised to Adam is to be sought nowhere but in the seed of Abraham and the house of David. So while Luke offers consolation to people of every place and rank, Matthew in turn guards against our wandering after the inventions of our own reason in seeking salvation. He warns us against following those who maintain, no less pernicious than false, that every nation can be kept in its own religion, handed down to it as if by the hands of its ancestors.

units.la: Deinde ad Deum totius humani generis Creatorem genealogiae huius principium refert. Lucas, ut eorum dubitationi medeatur, quibus impossibile videtur, Christum ex casta virgine absque viri congressu hominem natum esse. Cur enim hoc impossibile dicemus, quando constat, Adamum solius Dei virtute ex terra olim conditum fuisse, quae similiter nullo semine fecundata omne genus frugum una cum arboribus & plantis reliquis initio procreauit. Obseruauit hoc olim sanctissimus Christi Martyr, Irenaeus, cuius haec verba leguntur libro 3. capite 31. Quemadmodum protoplastes ille Adam de rudi terra & adhuc virgine (nondum enim pluerat Deus, & homo nondum coluerat terram) habuit substantiam, & Dei manu formatus est, id est, verbo Dei (Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt: Et sumpsit Dominus limum de terra, & formauit hominem) ita Adam in se recapitulans verbum hoc existens ex Maria, quae adhuc erat virgo, rectè accipiebat Adami generationem, &c. Est & alia ratio, propter quam ad Deum usque Lucas ascendit, ut nimirum offendat, omnes veteris Testamenti patres, quotquot in Christum venturum crediderunt, eius merito Dei filios factos esse, adeoque ipsum Adamum, per quem peccatum & mors introierunt, in Christo promissò habuisse spiritum adoptionis, ut filius Dei factus sit ex gratia, qui seipsum irae filium fecerat. Sunt autem prae terea haec nobis adhuc duo consideranda.
units.tr: Next, Luke traces the beginning of this genealogy back to God, the Creator of the whole human race. He does this to meet the doubt of those who find it impossible that Christ was born of a chaste virgin without a man's intercourse. For why should we call this impossible, when it is established that Adam was once formed from the earth by the power of God alone, and that the earth, likewise unfertilised by any seed, produced at the beginning every kind of grain together with trees and other plants? This was noticed long ago by Irenaeus, the most holy martyr of Christ, whose words are read in book 3, chapter 31: "Just as that first-formed Adam received his substance from raw earth, still virgin (for God had not yet sent rain, and man had not yet tilled the soil), and was formed by the hand of God, that is, by the Word of God (for all things were made through him, and the Lord took clay from the earth and formed man), so Adam, recapitulated in himself through this Word, who was born of Mary while she was still a virgin, rightly received his generation," and so on. There is also another reason why Luke ascends to God: namely, to show that all the fathers of the Old Testament, as many as believed that Christ would come, were made sons of God through his merit, and that Adam himself, through whom sin and death entered, had the spirit of adoption promised in Christ, so that he who had made himself a son of wrath became a son of God by grace. Moreover, there are two further things for us to consider here.

units.la: Primum est generis Christi nobilitas, quoad carnem. Numerantur hic primi generis humani progenitores, & ita generis eius vetustas asseritur, quae hodie omnis nobilitatis fundamentum esse putatur. Sequuntur hos Patriarchae populi Dei siue ecclesiae, Abraham Isaac & Iacob, quos Deus sibi foedere coniunctos esse & sociorum loco habere voluit. Inde ad Dauidem usque venitur, cuius familia omnes, quotquot unquam in orbe terrarum fuerunt, longe superat, siue antiquitatem aut longi temporis successionem spectes, siue Regum, qui ex illa progeniti sunt, numerum, potentiam, victorias, opes & reliqua huius seculi ornamenta consideres. Taceo nunc prophetas & innumeros alios, qui hic non recensentur, quos virtute & meritis illustrissimos fuisse constat. Superat tamen haec omnia, quòd aeternus Dei filius cum familia ista uniri, & ex ea humanam naturam in eiusdem personae unitatem assumere voluit. Est huius considerationis multiplex usus. Primo de Dei bonitate nos admonet, qui tantam dignitatem nobiscum communicare dignatus est. Quia enim per fidem Christo inferimur, & in eodem spiritu adoptionis donamur, filij Dei & Christi coheredes sunt, quotquot in hunc credunt. De quo cùm saepe alias dictum sit, nunc prolixiori demonstratione non est opus. Nunc potius (quod secundum hic occurrit) tantae dignitatis memores, gradum nostrum tueri satagamus, ne huius seculi impuris voluptatibus immersi, nosipsos spoliemus caelestium bonorum haereditate, quae nobis in Christo parata est. Tertiò honestè sentire
units.tr: The first is the nobility of Christ's race according to the flesh. The first progenitors of the human race are counted here, and thus the antiquity of his lineage is asserted, which today is thought to be the foundation of all nobility. These are followed by the patriarchs of the people or Church of God, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom God wished to be joined to himself by covenant and to hold as companions. From there we come down to David, whose family far surpasses all those that have ever existed in the world, whether you look at its antiquity or its long succession, or consider the number, power, victories, wealth and other ornaments of this age of the kings descended from it. I pass over now the prophets and the countless others who are not listed here, who are known to have been most illustrious in virtue and merit. Yet all of this is surpassed by the fact that the eternal Son of God wished to be united with this family and to take from it human nature into the unity of his own person. This consideration has several uses. First, it reminds us of the goodness of God, who has deigned to share with us such great dignity. For since we are brought to Christ through faith and receive the same spirit of adoption, all who believe in him are sons of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Since this has often been said elsewhere, there is no need for a longer demonstration now. Rather, let us, mindful of such great dignity, take care to keep our standing (which is the second point that comes to mind), so that we do not, immersed in the impure pleasures of this world, rob ourselves of the inheritance of heavenly goods prepared for us in Christ. Thirdly, let us learn to think honourably

units.la: Vide Rom. 8. homil. discamus de proximis, qui eundem nobiscum Christum profitentur. Nam qualescunque sint, quoad huius seculi conditionem, filij tamen Dei, & proinde nostri fratres atque coheredes sunt. Non ergo illos, sed nosipsos ignominia afficimus, si eos habeamus contumeliose: imo in ipsum Christum iniuria omnis redundat. Quis autem tu es o superbe, qui eum contemnis & tua amicitia indignum iudicas, pro quo Christus mori dignatus est, ut filium Dei & fratrem suum efficeret? Quarto admonet nos ista consideratio, ne huius seculi felicitati aut splendori fidamus. Quid enim firmum aut stabile fore sperabimus, quando regia illa & tot victoriis nobilitata Davidis familia, ex qua Dei filius hominem assumere voluit, eo usque prius deiecta, & hodie in vniuersum extincta est, ut nulla veteris splendoris vestigia appareant? Aut cur maiorum virtutibus & stemmate efferris, ipse ignauus & inglorius? Et ut multos numeres ex tuis progenitoribus, qui virtute & egregijs factis illustres fuerunt, si tamen altius ascendas, fortasse illud Satyricum tibi dici poterit: Maiorum primus quisquis fuit ille tuorum, Aut pastor fuit, aut illud quod dicere noló.
units.tr: See the homily on Romans 8. Let us learn to think well of our neighbours, who profess the same Christ as we do. For whatever their condition in this world, they are nevertheless sons of God, and therefore our brothers and fellow heirs. So if we treat them with contempt, we do not disgrace them but ourselves; indeed, every insult done to them rebounds upon Christ himself. Who are you, proud man, who despise him and judge him unworthy of your friendship, for whom Christ deigned to die, so that he might make him a son of God and your brother? Fourthly, this consideration warns us not to trust in the happiness or splendour of this world. For what firmness or stability can we hope for, when that royal house of David, ennobled by so many victories, from which the Son of God wished to take human nature, has been cast down so far and today is wholly extinct, so that no trace of its former splendour appears? Or why do you boast of your ancestors' virtues and pedigree, while you yourself are lazy and inglorious? And even if you count many of your forebears who were famous for virtue and noble deeds, if you climb higher still, perhaps that line of Satire may be said to you: "Whoever was the first of your ancestors, he was a shepherd, or else something I would rather not say."

units.la: Praeterea multam consolationem affert diligenter considerata generis nostri, vel potius regeneratio nus nostrae in Christo factae nobilitas. Quia enim Dei filij & Christi fratres sumus, nunquam nos negliget ille, qui nos ex gratia in tantam dignitatem euexit. Solent nobiles huius seculi generis sui splendorem in illis etiam cognatis suis tueri, quos alioquin oderunt. Quanto magis Deus illorum honorem atque salutem tuebitur, qui ipsum patris nomine invocant? Idem etiam facile omnes eos nobis cōtilia bit, qui germani ipsius filij sunt, ut nobis bene velint, et sua nobis officia praestent. Nos modo studeamus in omni periculorum genere inuicta fidei constantia uti, ut ex ea constet, nos veros Dei filios esse, & generosiori spiritu moveri. Turpe & indignum videtur, si qui avos & atavos generosos name rant, in periculis muliebri pusillanimitate succumbunt. At turpius multo fuerit, eos ignobili metu facere, qui se ex Dei semine natos esse gloriantur. Haec igitur nobis in mente veniant, quando vel pro fide Christi aliquid audendum est, vel morbis lethalibus grauamur, aut quacunque alia calamitate exercemur, & mox nos mirifica consolatione confirmari sentiemus.
units.tr: Moreover, a great consolation comes from carefully considering our race, or rather the nobility of our regeneration made in Christ. For since we are sons of God and brothers of Christ, he who has raised us by grace to such dignity will never neglect us. Nobles of this world are accustomed to uphold the splendour of their family even in those relatives whom otherwise they hate. How much more will God protect the honour and salvation of those who call upon him by the name of Father? In the same way, all who are true brothers of his Son will easily be moved to wish us well and to render us their services. Let us only strive to use unconquered constancy of faith in every kind of danger, so that it may be evident that we are true sons of God and are moved by a nobler spirit. It seems shameful and unworthy that those who boast of noble grandfathers and great-grandfathers should give way in dangers with womanish timidity. Much more shameful would it be for those who glory in being born of God's seed to act with base fear. Let these thoughts come to mind whenever something must be dared for the sake of Christ's faith, or we are weighed down by deadly diseases, or troubled by some other calamity, and we will soon feel ourselves strengthened by a wonderful consolation.

units.la: Restat alterum, quod hoc loco nobis considerandum esse diximus: Quod nimirum in Christi genealogia tam boni quam mali numerantur, imo peccatores maximi, & quidam tantis flagitijs infames, ut indigni possint censeri, qui inter viros bonos nomen habeant. Nam ut a Iuda exordiamur, constat hunc & scelerus fratrum in Iosephum admisisse consciu fuisse, & filium Phares ex incesto concubitu cum Thamare nuru sua genuisse. Inter reges Iuda Achas & Manasses censentur, impij & aperti puriores doctrinae & diuini cultus hostes: quorum vestigia secuti sunt filij Iosiae, Ioachas, Ioachim, Iechonias, & Zedechias. Ex mulieribus praeter Thamarem Matthaeus Betsabam adulterio infamem nominat, & Rhutam, pietate quidem eximiam, sed Moabitidem, & a populi Dei societate prius alienam. De Rahaba autem quid dicere attinet, quae & Chananaea fuit, & corpore turpem quaestum fecit, priusquam Salmon eam sibi uxorem duceret? Poterat hoc facile cauere Deus, ne qui in istum catalogum venirent: sed ita omnibus testatum fieri oportuit, Christum Iesum non asperari peccatores, sed (ut Paulus ait) propter hos potissimum in mundum venisse, ut eius merito salui fierent, qui propter sua scelera damnari merebantur. Docet hoc ipse in Euangelio, & idem adsevocat omnes, qui laborant & onerati sunt. Soletur hoc nos in conscientia tentationibus, quando infer rum terrores, & iudicij diuini rigorem nobis Satan obijcit, ut ad desperationem adducat. Admonet simul hoc quoq, neminem vel suorum maiorum splendore insolentius gloriari, vel alijs suos progenitores exprobrare debere. In omnibus enim familijs tam bonos quam malos esse inuenire.
units.tr: There remains the other point which we said must be considered in this place: namely, that in Christ's genealogy both good and bad are counted, indeed the greatest sinners, and some so infamous for their crimes that they might be judged unworthy to have a name among good men. To begin with Judah: it is established that he was an accomplice in his brothers' plot against Joseph, and that he begot Perez by an incestuous union with Tamar, his daughter-in-law. Among the kings of Judah, Ahaz and Manasseh are counted, impious and open enemies of purer doctrine and of divine worship; and the sons of Josiah followed their footsteps: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah. Among the women, besides Tamar, Matthew names Bathsheba, infamous for adultery, and Ruth, indeed outstanding in piety, but a Moabite and earlier alien to the people of God. As for Rahab, what need is there to say that she was a Canaanite and made a living by her body before Salmon took her as his wife? God could easily have guarded against such people coming into this list; but it was necessary that it be shown to all that Christ Jesus does not shrink from sinners, but (as Paul says) came into the world chiefly for these, so that those who deserved to be condemned for their sins might be saved by his merit. The Gospel itself teaches this, and it calls to itself all who labour and are burdened. This consoles us in the temptations of conscience, when Satan sets before us the terrors of hell and the rigour of divine judgement in order to drive us to despair. This also warns us that no one should boast too arrogantly of the splendour of his own ancestors, nor reproach others for theirs. For in every family you will find both good and bad.

units.la: Nobilitas autem vera est, si Dei filij simus: tales vero erimus, si Christum Iesum vera fide complexi, in eodem vitam viuamus vere Christianam.
units.tr: True nobility, however, is ours if we are sons of God; and we shall be such if, embracing Christ Jesus with true faith, we live in him a truly Christian life.

units.la: Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: IEsus autem plenus spiritu sancto reuersus est à Iordane, & actus est à spiritu sancto in deserto, fuitq; diebus quadraginta tentante eum diabolo : & nihil comedit per illos dies, sed ijs exactis, postea esurijt.
units.tr: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, being tempted by the devil for forty days. And he ate nothing in those days, but when they were ended, afterwards he was hungry.

units.la: EXposuit in proximo Capite Lucas Ioannis Baptiste conciones, quibus omnis loci & ordinis homines ad poenitentiam & fidem in Iesum Christum hortatus est, quem etiam in signi testimonio publice commendauit. Addidit hic publicam Christi inaugurationem, quae cum ille baptizaretur facta esset, & eiusdem genealogiam per Dauidis & Abrahami prosapiam usque ad primum humani generis parentem, Adamum: diligenter contexuit. Quorum omnium hic finis & scopus est, ut intelligamus & credamus, Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria virgine homo verus est, esse Christum, id est, promissum mundi seruatorem & magnum illum prophetam, qui verba vitae aeternae habeat, & quem audire atq; fide constanti omnes amplecti debeant, quicunque seruari volunt. Sequitur nunc ipsius Christi historia, qui accepto baptismo & publico patris testimonio confirmatus, mox ea agere coepit, quae ad hominum redemptionem pertinebant. Inter quae primus locus tribuitur tentationibus, in quibus certamen cum communi hoste nostro, diabolo suscepit, quem pugna graui & memorabili vicit, et quantumuis pertinacem a se repulit. Oportuit autem ab hic initium fieri, quando constat perditionem nostram a tentatione coepisse, in qua primi parentes nimium infeliciter cum veteri serpente congressi & ab eo victi, peccatum atque mortem in universam posteritatem propagauerunt. Quia ergo illorum lapsus nos terrere poterat & omnem victoriae spem nobis adimere, necesse fuit, ut Christus sua victoria nobis ad deuincendum hostem illum vires nouas acquireret, & spe bona impletos ad pugnam istam alacres atque intrepidos faceret. At quia de hoc postea suo loco commodius dicetur, nunc ex ordine de ijs agemus, quae ad praesentis loci tractationem faciunt.
units.tr: In the preceding chapter Luke set out the sermons of John the Baptist, by which he exhorted men of every place and rank to repentance and to faith in Jesus Christ, whom he also publicly commended as the one signified by his testimony. Here Luke adds Christ's public inauguration, which took place when he was baptized, and he carefully sets out his genealogy through the line of David and Abraham back to Adam, the first parent of the human race. The purpose and aim of all of this is that we should understand and believe that this Jesus, who is a true man born of the Virgin Mary, is the Christ, that is, the promised Saviour of the world and that great prophet who has the words of eternal life, and whom all who wish to be saved ought to hear and embrace with steadfast faith. Now follows the history of Christ himself, who, having received baptism and been confirmed by the public testimony of the Father, at once began to do those things which pertained to the redemption of men. Among these, the first place is given to the temptations, in which he took up the contest with our common enemy, the devil, and overcame him in a severe and memorable struggle, and repelled him however stubborn he was. But it was fitting that the story should begin here, since it is established that our ruin began with temptation, when our first parents, too unhappily engaged with the old serpent and conquered by him, passed on sin and death to all their posterity. Because their fall could terrify us and take away all hope of victory, it was necessary that Christ, by his own victory, should acquire for us new strength to overcome that enemy, and should make us, filled with good hope, eager and fearless for that struggle. But since this will be more fittingly discussed in its own place, we will now, in order, treat those matters which bear on the present passage.

units.la: Exordiemur autem a tentandi verbo, ut rem ipsam, de qua in praesenti agitur, rectius intelligamus. Tentare idem proprie est, quod experiri aut periculum facere de aliquo, ut quis aut qualis sit intelligas. Vsus verbi huius de re qualibet est: quando autem de homine usurpatur, tam in bonam quam in malam partem accipi solet. In bonam partem Deus homines tentare dicitur, quando fidem nostram nosq; totos explorat, non quod ipsum aliquid lateat, sed ut nos nobisipsis cognoscendos praebeat, aut in nobis exempla fidei & reliquarum virtutum aliis proponat, quorum contemplatione ad imitationem excitentur. Fit hoc, quando vel pericula grauiora nobis ob oculos ponit, vel nouas rerum agendarum occasiones obijcit, aut aliqua praecipit, quae carni dura & a ratione aliena videntur. Sic Abrahami fidem tentauit Dominus, quando illum e terra sua discedere & exilium sponte suum subire iussit, quando iussis suis parentè fame, vxoris raptu, domesticis dissidijs, bellicis turbis, & in primis diuturna promissi seminis dilatione exercuit: & in primis, quando illi mandauit, ut Isaacum, filium in extrema senecta sibi natum, & in quo promissiones omnes datae erant, manibus proprijs immolaret. Fuerunt haec omnia non solum dura, sed absurda, iniqua & impia videri poterant; sed in illis fides Abrahami eluxit, quam etsi Deus non ignoraret, istis tamen medijs illam exercere, & toti mundo in exemplum proponere voluit. Idem de reliquis patribus dicere possumus, adeoque de omnibus aduersis, quibus nostram fidem tentari sentimus. Dicitur etiam tentare Deus, quando pseudoprophetae surgunt, qui falsa dogmata & illicitos cultus tradunt, doctrinam verò suam non solum verborum phaleris & argutis disputationibus, verumetiam signis & miraculis confirmant. Ea enim ratione periculum de nobis facit Deus, num tanta sit verbi sui apud nos authoritas, ut illud omnibus aliis rebus anteponamus, quae mundo & communi rationi aut sensui nostro magnifica atque eximia putantur. Et elucet in his omnibus Dei bonitas, qui ne fides nostra torpore & otio corrupta langueat, eam his quasi cotibus a cuere & nos de nostra infirmitate admonere solet, quam ipsi prius ignorabamus, ut nimirum ea cognita ad preces & ardentius verae pietatis studium excitemur. Et hoc illud saluberrimum tentandi genus est, de quo Iacobus ait: Beatus vir, qui tolerat tentationem: quoniam cum probatus erit, accipiet coronam vitae. Quo Paulus quoque respiciens, pios in afflictionibus gloriari dicebat, eo quod afflictio patientiae exercendae materia praebeat, patientia vero Dei bonitatem novis indies exemplis experiatur, unde spes nascitur & augetur, quae nos minime fallit. Rursus in malam partem sumitur Tentatio, quando diabolus quacunque occasione vel ex nobis vel aliunde sumpta, nos ad peccandum solicitat, ut a Deo & salutis via abductos aeternae damnationi manciper. Sic Euam tentavit ut veriti pomi desiderium in illa excitaret. Sic quotidie nos tentat, quando fastum mundi & infinitas scelerum illecebras nobis obicit. Sic cruce & afflictionibus tentat, ut nos qui natura pacis & felicitatis temporariae appetentes sumus, a fide & pietate abstrahat, ut vel Deum omnino abnegemus, vel adversus illum murmuremus, quando non omnia nobis pro animi nostri arbitrio succedunt. Et permittit ista Deus iusto iudicio, sive electos & vere pios, sive reprobos & impios spectes. Nam pios ad hunc etiam modum tentari prodest, ut suae fidei specimen edant, aut (ut ante diximus) propriae infirmitatis sensu territi in posterum diligentiores excubias agant. Impios autem iusto iudicio excaecat & tradit in sensum reprobum, ut diaboli praestigiis & propriae cupiditatis fascino decepti mensuram impietatis impleant, & quod iam pridem meruerunt, excidium accelerent. Et huc Antichristi signa & efficaces illi errores referri debet, quibus novissimo tempore multos irretiendos esse Christus & apostoli praedixerunt. Ubi tamen observabimus, Satanam ex nobis ipsis plerunque occasionem captare, & in nobis praecipuam culpam haerere, quando illius tentationibus victi praeter officium aliquid facimus. Quae ratio est, quod Iacobus scribit: Unusquisque tentatur, dum a propria cupiditate abstrahitur & illectatur.
units.tr: We shall begin with the word "to tempt", so that we may understand more correctly the matter itself which is under discussion here. To tempt properly means the same as to try or make trial of someone, so that you may learn who or what he is. The use of the word applies to anything, but when it is used of a man it is customarily taken in a good or a bad sense. In a good sense God is said to tempt men when he examines our faith and our whole selves, not because anything is hidden from him, but so that he may make us known to ourselves, or set before others in us examples of faith and of the other virtues, by contemplating which they may be stirred to imitate them. This happens when he either places before our eyes more serious dangers, or presents new occasions for acting, or commands things which seem hard to the flesh and foreign to reason. Thus the Lord tested the faith of Abraham when he ordered him to leave his land and voluntarily undergo exile; when he exercised him by the famine that his parents suffered, the abduction of his wife, domestic quarrels, wars and turmoil, and above all by the long delay in the promised seed; and above all when he commanded him to sacrifice with his own hands Isaac, the son born to him in extreme old age, and in whom all the promises had been given. All these things could seem not only harsh but absurd, unjust and impious; yet in them the faith of Abraham shone forth, which God, though he was not ignorant of it, nevertheless wished to exercise by these means and to set before the whole world as an example. We may say the same of the other fathers, and indeed of all the adversities by which we feel our faith to be tested. God is also said to tempt when false prophets arise, who hand down false doctrines and unlawful forms of worship, and who confirm their teaching not only with the embellishments of words and subtle disputations, but also with signs and miracles. For by this means God makes trial of us, whether the authority of his Word among us is so great that we set it above all other things, which are thought by the world and by common reason or our senses to be splendid and outstanding. And in all these things the goodness of God shines forth, who, so that our faith may not languish corrupted by sloth and idleness, is accustomed to sharpen it, as it were, on these whetstones, and to remind us of our weakness, which we ourselves had previously not known, so that, once this is recognized, we may be stirred to prayer and to a more ardent zeal for true piety. And this is that most wholesome kind of temptation of which James says: "Blessed is the man who endures temptation; for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life." Looking to this too, Paul said that the godly glory in afflictions, because affliction provides material for exercising patience, and patience daily experiences the goodness of God in new examples, whence hope is born and grows, which does not in the least disappoint us. On the other hand, temptation is taken in a bad sense when the devil, on whatever occasion, whether taken from ourselves or from elsewhere, incites us to sin, so as to lead us away from God and the way of salvation and to hand us over to eternal damnation. Thus he tempted Eve, so as to arouse in her the desire for the forbidden fruit. Thus he tempts us every day, when he sets before us the pride of the world and the endless allurements of sins. Thus he tempts by the cross and afflictions, so as to draw us, who by nature seek peace and temporal happiness, away from faith and piety, so that we either utterly deny God or murmur against him when everything does not turn out for us according to the desire of our minds. And God permits these things by a just judgment, whether you look at the elect and truly pious, or at the reprobate and impious. For it is profitable for the godly to be tempted in this way too, so that they may show a proof of their faith, or (as we said before) so that, terrified by the sense of their own weakness, they may keep more diligent watch in future. But the impious, by a just judgment, he blinds and delivers over to a reprobate mind, so that, deceived by the devil's illusions and the enchantment of their own lust, they may fill up the measure of their impiety and hasten the destruction which they have long deserved. And to this the signs of Antichrist and his powerful errors ought to be referred, by which Christ and the apostles foretold that many would be ensnared in the last times. Here, however, we shall observe that Satan for the most part seizes his opportunity from ourselves, and that the chief blame clings to us when, overcome by his temptations, we do something contrary to our duty. This is the reason why James writes: "Each one is tempted, when he is drawn away and enticed by his own lust."

units.la: His praemissis ad praesentem Iesu Christi historiam accedamus, in quo nihil horum locum habebet. Neque enim illius fidem aut constantiam explorari, aut ipsum suae imperfectionis (quae nulla omnino in ipso erat) admoneri oportuit. Multo minus dignus fuit, qui Satanae ludibrium fieret, & aliquid gravioris mali pateretur. In nobis ergo & redemptionis nostrae negotio causae quaerendae sunt, cur Christus, qui propter nos in mundum venerat, tentationum huiusmodi palaestram ingressus sit. Neq; hic aliquis obiiciat, tentari non potuisse Christum, cum ab omni prava cupiditate alienus nullam se tentandi occasionem diabolo dederit. Quia enim Adamum, cum adhuc bonus & perfectus esset, tentavit Satan, nequaquam insolens aut absurdum videri debet, si quid huius passus est Dei filius, qui ut nos a lapsu reficitaret, homo factus fuerat. Et quamvis nulla in illo naturae vitiositas fuerit, sponte tam nostras infirmitates in se recepit, & nobis (uno peccato excepto) per omnia similis factus est, ut tentationibus subjici posset. Nam ut hoc fieret, multas ob causas necesse fuit. Ut enim initio diximus, quia ad destruenda diaboli opera Dei filius in mundum venerat, ab eo ordiri debuit, quo diabolus sibi in miseros mortales regnum vendicarat. Atqui tentatione primos parentes victos, & diaboli mancipia cum omni posteritate factos fuisse constat. Itaque eundem hunc hostem nostrum communem ab Adamo secundo in tentationum pugna vinci & quasi sub iugum mitti oportuit. Deinde opus fuit nos admoneri, quam infestus nobis sit Satan, quidq; nobis sperandum sit, quoad illius insidiis patemus. Agnoscunt hoc pauci homines, & illum nobis & commodis nostris omnino consultum velle putant, quando ea suadet, quae carni eiusque cupiditatibus pravis arridente. At cum constet, illum aeterno Dei filio non aliam ob causam negotium fecisse, quam quod ut nostrae salutis ergo in mundum venerat, negari non potest, illum salutis humanae hostem acerrimum esse, & proinde nobis debere suspecta esse, quaecunque ille suadet aut consulit. Tertio cum magna sit nostra infirmitas, consolationibus nos instrui & armari oportuit, quae hic nobis multae & efficacissimae occurrunt. Quia enim Christum nostras infirmitates in se recepisse, & perinde ut nos tentatus fuisse videmus, certo hinc colligi potest, eum nobis per omnia similem factum esse, & proinde Pontificem esse fidelem, qui nostris miseriis afficiatur, & causam nostram serio agat. Quod in tota hac historia Paulus ad Hebraeos scribens diligenter observavit. Docemur item, tentationes non esse Dei irati argumentum, cum ipsum filium suum subjici voluerit, & quidem tunc, quando paulo ante hunc filium lium suum dilectum esse testatus fuerat. Scimus quidem aduersa omnia ex peccato originem duxisse, & si in sua natura aestimentur, inter illius poenas censeri debere. Sed sanctificauit illa omnia suo merito Dei filius, vt iam fidei exercitia sint, & proinde nemo propter illa desperare debet, vt se Deo minus acceptum putet. Adhaec, quia in carne assumpta diabolum vicit Christus, non obscure testatur, illum porrò ab homine vinci posse. Ita enim illius vires atriuit Dei filius, & eiusdem chirographum, quo aduersus nos litigabat, aboleuit, vt causam suam obtinere non posset. Quare etsi adhuc insaniat, & ferociam indomitam praese ferat, conteret tamen illum sub credentium pedibus Christus, & facile illum vincunt, qui fidei clypeo tela eius excipiunt. Postremò exemplum nobis praebere voluit Dei filius, vt ex ipso discamus, qua arte et quibus armis quadrulator ille vincendus sit. De quo cùm in sequenti Sermone plura dicenda veniant, nunc ista obiter attigisse sufficiat. Nunc autem probe a nobis obseruari debet Dei bonitas, qui filium suum vnigenitum, & magno suo merito dilectissimum, eò vsq; demitti & humiliari voluit, vt non modò per infandum crucis supplicium nos redimeret, sed exemplum quoq; praeberet, quod nos quouis casu de rebus agendis admonere, & simul consolationibus certis confirmare posset. Indignum videtur Regum filijs, si ad singulare certamen a mi lite gregario aut nulla generis nobilitate illustri prouocentur. At Dei filius maiorem nostrae salutis quàm propriae dignitatis rationem habendam esse putauit, quando pro nobis duello aduersus eum homtem dimicauit, quo nullus foedior, infelicior & infamis magis fingi potest.
units.tr: Having set out these points, let us turn to the present history of Jesus Christ, in which none of these considerations applies. For it was not necessary that his faith or constancy be tested, nor that he be reminded of his own imperfection, which in him was entirely absent. Much less was he worthy to become Satan's plaything and to suffer some more serious harm. The causes of this must therefore be sought in us and in the business of our redemption, namely why Christ, who had come into the world for our sake, entered the arena of such temptations. Nor should anyone object here that Christ could not be tempted, since, being free from every wicked desire, he gave the devil no occasion to tempt him. For Satan tempted Adam while he was still good and perfect, and so it ought not to seem strange or absurd if the Son of God underwent something of this kind, he who had become man in order to restore us from our fall. And although there was no corruption of nature in him, he willingly took upon himself our infirmities and was made like us in all things, sin excepted, so that he could be subjected to temptations. For this to happen, there were many reasons. As we said at the outset, the Son of God came into the world to destroy the works of the devil, and so he had to begin at the point where the devil had claimed for himself a kingdom over wretched mortals. Now it is certain that our first parents were overcome by temptation and made the slaves of the devil, together with all their posterity. It was therefore fitting that this same common enemy of ours be conquered by the second Adam in a battle of temptation, and, as it were, brought under the yoke. Next, it was necessary that we be warned how hostile Satan is to us, and what we may expect so long as we lie open to his snares. Few people recognise this, and they think he wishes us and our interests well whenever he urges those things that please the flesh and its wicked desires. But since it is clear that he had no other reason for opposing the eternal Son of God than that the Son had come into the world for our salvation, it cannot be denied that he is the bitterest enemy of human salvation, and that therefore whatever he urges or advises ought to be suspect to us. Thirdly, since our weakness is great, we needed to be instructed and armed with consolations, and these present themselves here in abundance and great power. For since we see that Christ took our infirmities upon himself and was tempted just as we are, it can certainly be concluded from this that he was made like us in all things, and therefore that he is a faithful High Priest, who is moved by our miseries and pleads our cause earnestly. Paul, writing to the Hebrews, carefully observed this throughout this whole history. We are also taught that temptations are not a sign of God's anger, since he willed his own Son to be subjected to them, and indeed at the very time when, shortly before, he had testified that this Son was his beloved Son. We certainly know that all adversities arose from sin and, if they are judged by their own nature, ought to be counted among its punishments. But the Son of God has sanctified all these things by his merit, so that they are now exercises of faith, and therefore no one should despair on account of them, as if he thought himself less acceptable to God. Moreover, since Christ overcame the devil in the flesh he had assumed, he clearly bears witness that the devil can in turn be overcome by a man. For the Son of God thus wore down his strength and abolished the bond with which he had pressed his case against us, so that he could not maintain his claim. Therefore, although he still rages and displays his untamed fierceness, Christ will nevertheless crush him under the feet of believers, and those easily conquer him who catch his darts on the shield of faith. Lastly, the Son of God wished to give us an example, so that from him we might learn by what skill and with what weapons that charlatan is to be conquered. Since more is to be said about this in the following sermon, it is enough for now to have touched on these things in passing. But now we must carefully observe the goodness of God, who willed that his only-begotten Son, most dear to him for his great merit, should be brought down and humbled to such an extent that he redeemed us not only through the unspeakable punishment of the cross, but also gave us an example that could remind us in every circumstance of what we must do, and at the same time confirm us with sure consolations. It seems unworthy of the sons of kings to be challenged to single combat by a common soldier or by someone of no illustrious noble birth. But the Son of God thought that he should have regard for our salvation rather than for his own dignity, when he fought a duel on our behalf against that enemy, than whom no more foul, unhappy and infamous foe can be imagined.

units.la: Porrò tempus & locum certaminis huius videamus, de quibus Euangelistae diligenter disserunt. Lucas enim historiam hanc cum ijs, quae in baptismo Christi accederunt connectens, vt nihil intermedium accidisse ostendat, sic scribit: Iesus autem plenus Spiritu sancto reuersus est a Iordane, & actus est a spiritu in desertum. Marcus autem: Et continuò spiritus illum expellit in desertum, &c. A cuius verbis Matthaeus nihil dissentit. Quàm primùm ergo ab Ioanne baptizatus & coelesti patris testimonio inauguratus fuit Christus, mox omni mora abrupta spiritum ducem secutus est, vt in deserto tentationum pugnam aduersus diabolum sustineret, & nostrae redemptionis initium faceret. Est hoc memorabile exemplum obedientiae, quam patri in sequenda sua vocatione Christus praestitit. Alius quidam vel domum reuersus cum suis de re tanti momenti consultauisset; alius penes se omnia expendens, saltem expectandum putasset, donec constaret, quid de Ioanne facturi essent Iudaeorum Seniores & Rex Herodes: alij de voce illa caelitus delata quaestionem mouissent. Scimus enim quàm ingeniosa sit caro in excogitandis rationibus, quibus sese excusat, ne Deo obediat in ijs, quae cum aliquo labore & periculo coniuncta sunt. Et fere ipsi nobis pericula fingimus, vt plus ponderis habeat nostra excusatio. Quid, quòd pietatis praetextu multi ad tuendam inobedientiam suam abutuntur, & multa de officio suo, quod parentibus, coniugibus, liberis, aut etiam communi patriae debeant, differunt. Sed omnes istorum rationes Christus suo exemplo confutat. Impium enim est vel alios homines vel propriam prudentiam atque rationem in consilium adhibere, quando suam voluntatem nobis Deus diserte exposuit. Inobedientiae autem apertae indicium est de euentu rei disputare, priusquam quod facere Deus iussit executus fueris. Neque pius dici potest, qui parentes, liberos, coniugem, patriam aut quicquid praeterea nominare licet, Dei mandatis antepo-nit. Ita enim illis debemus pietatis officia, vt interim suum ius Deo apud nos integrum maneat. Nihil ergo inquam procrastinatores illi proficiunt: quia quò plures rationes secum ineunt, eò plures remoras obijcit Satan, quibus in Dei cultu & obedientia impediantur, & (vt Poeta ait) qui non est hodie, cras minus aptus erit. Ideo quod in praesenti Christus fecit, hoc ipsum omnibus praecipit, quando quidam patrem prius sepelire volenti dicit: Sine, vt mortui sepeliant mortuos suos, tu autem me sequere. Item: Qui manu ad aratrum admota respicit a tergo, non est aptus regno Dei. Lucae capite nono.
units.tr: Next let us look at the time and place of this conflict, about which the Evangelists speak carefully. For Luke, connecting this history with what happened at the baptism of Christ, so that it might be shown that nothing intervened, writes thus: "And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness" [Luke 4:1]. Mark says: "And immediately the Spirit drives him out into the wilderness," etc. Matthew does not differ from these words. Therefore, as soon as Christ had been baptised by John and inaugurated by the testimony of the heavenly Father, without any delay he followed the Spirit as his leader, so that in the wilderness he might sustain the battle of temptation against the devil and make a beginning of our redemption. This is a memorable example of the obedience which Christ rendered to the Father in following his calling. Another man, having returned home, would have consulted with his family about a matter of such importance; another, weighing everything by himself, would at least have thought he must wait until it was known what the elders of the Jews and King Herod would do about John; others would have raised a question about that voice delivered from heaven. For we know how ingenious the flesh is in devising reasons by which it excuses itself from obeying God in things that are attended by some labour and danger. And we often invent dangers ourselves, so that our excuse may carry more weight. What of the fact that many, under the pretext of piety, abuse it to defend their disobedience, and put off many duties that they owe to parents, spouses, children, or even to the common fatherland? But Christ refutes all these excuses by his example. For it is wicked to take counsel from other men or from our own prudence and reason, when God has plainly set forth his will to us. Moreover, it is a clear sign of open disobedience to dispute about the outcome of a matter before you have carried out what God has commanded. Nor can he be called pious who puts parents, children, spouse, fatherland, or anything else one may name before the commands of God. For we owe them the duties of piety in such a way that, meanwhile, God's right over us remains whole. Therefore, I say, those procrastinators gain nothing, for the more reasons they devise, the more delays Satan throws in the way, by which they are hindered in the worship and obedience of God; and, as the poet says, "he who is not fit today will be less fit tomorrow" [Horace, Epistles 1.2.40]. Therefore what Christ did in the present case he commands to all, when to a certain man who wished first to bury his father he says: "Let the dead bury their dead; but you, follow me" [Luke 9:60]. Likewise: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" [Luke 9:62]. Luke, chapter nine.

units.la: Adumbratur praeterea Christi exemplo, quae omnium membrorum eius sors sit, id est, omnium, qui ipsi in baptismo nomen dant, & Dei vocationem serio sequuntur. Illico hi in desertum extrudatur, id est, desertum esse sentiunt mundum hunc, qui carni deditus paradisus videtur. Nam vt deserta inculta & sterilia sunt, adhaec sentibus & veneribus horrent: ita mundus hic nulla Dei cognitione excultus ad bonum faciendum prorsus sterilis & ineptus est, scatet autem vitiorum & scelerum sentibus, quae bonis omnibus scandalo sunt, & simul dolorem ferunt maximum. Rursus
units.tr: Moreover, the example of Christ foreshadows the lot of all his members, that is, of all who give their name to him in baptism and earnestly follow God's calling. Immediately they are driven into the wilderness, that is, they feel that this world, which seems a paradise to those given over to the flesh, is a desert. Just as deserts are uncultivated, barren, and bristling with thorns and brambles, so this world, untilled by any knowledge of God, is utterly barren and unfit for doing good. It teems with the thorns of vices and crimes, which are a stumbling block to all good people and at the same time bring them the greatest grief. Again

units.la: Christus mox a baptismo tentationibus obicitur.
units.tr: Christ is soon exposed to temptations after his baptism.

units.la: Communis omnium credentium conditio. deserti itinera incerta & perplexa sunt: sic mundus hic infinitis superstitionum & omnis generis errorum Labyrinthis intricatur, ut vix quicquam difficilius sit, quam inter illos salutis viam recta tenere. Item ut deserta loca cum propter feras tum propter praedones & latrones periculorum plena sunt: ita vbiq; in mundo hoc pericula nobis occurrunt ex ijs, qui immanissimas belluas & crudelissimos grassatores sua truculentia & plus quam sanguinario quosvis perdendi studio vincunt. Illic enim grassatur vetus ille homicida diabolus, qui rugientis leonis instar oberrat, quaerens quem devoret. Inter homines autem, tanquam in Circaeo stabulo, omnis generis bestiae cernuntur. Illic libi dinosi suum & porcorum instar grunniunt, iracundi vrsorum similes vncant, obtrectatores canes latrant, voraces lupi vlulant, rapidi lynces orcant, tigrides indomitae rancant, fraudulentae vulpes ganniunt, mordaces pardi cauriunt, calcitrosi asini et onagri rudunt, serpentes venenosi sibilant: deniq; haec omnia cum publico omnium exitio faciunt, qui procul reiecto omni humanitatis & pietatis sensu in feras degenerauerunt; neq; tantum periculi nobis imminet a bellus, quantum ab ijs, qui eiusdem nobiscum naturae consortes sunt: ut non temere veteres dixerint, hominem homini lupum esse. Accedunt tamen his graviora animae pericula ex lupis & vulpibus personatis, qui sub religionis praetexu miseros seducunt, & non contenti fortunas illorum rapuisse, e rundem corporibus quoque turpiter illudunt, & simul animas ad sempiternum exitium demergunt. Cumque isti omnes se mutuo facile ferant, vnanimi tamen consensu & furore aduersus Christi cultores insurgunt, quos luce veritatis illuminatos diuersam ab ipsis viuendi rationem sequi vident. Nihil ergo sibi ipsis illi policeri debent, quam perpetuas pugnas & assidua certamina, quicunque in Christo pie viuere voluerint. Magna ergo eorum est infelicitas, qui mundo hoc delectantur, inexcusabilis vero multorum perfidia, qui cum Christo nomen dederint, cum mundo tamen colludunt, & cum hoc in omnem licentiam effunduntur.
units.tr: This is the common condition of all believers. The paths of the wilderness are uncertain and perplexing, and in the same way this world is entangled in the endless labyrinths of superstitions and errors of every kind, so that there is scarcely anything more difficult than to keep to the right path of salvation amid them. Likewise, just as deserts are full of dangers, both from wild beasts and from robbers and bandits, so everywhere in this world dangers confront us from those who surpass the most savage beasts and the cruelest brigands in their ferocity and in a desire to destroy that is more than bloodthirsty. For there the old murderer, the devil, prowls, roaring like a lion and going about seeking whom he may devour. Among men, moreover, as in Circe's stable, every kind of beast is to be seen. There the lustful bleat like goats and grunt like pigs; the angry, like bears, growl; the backbiters bark like dogs; the greedy wolves howl; the rapacious lynxes screech; the untamed tigers roar; the crafty foxes yelp; the biting leopards snarl; the kicking asses and wild asses bray; the poisonous serpents hiss. In short, they do all these things to the common ruin of all, having cast off every sense of humanity and piety and degenerated into beasts. And the danger that threatens us from our fellow men is no less than that from the wild animals, since they share the same nature with us; so the ancients rightly said that man is a wolf to man. Yet there are graver dangers to the soul added to these, from wolves and foxes in sheep's clothing, who under the pretext of religion lead wretched people astray, and not content with having plundered their fortunes, shamefully abuse their bodies as well and at the same time drag their souls down to everlasting destruction. And although all these people readily bear with one another, they nevertheless rise up with united consent and fury against the worshippers of Christ, whom they see, enlightened by the light of truth, following a way of life different from their own. Therefore, whoever wishes to live godly in Christ should promise himself nothing but perpetual battles and constant conflicts. Great, then, is the unhappiness of those who take delight in this world; but inexcusable is the faithlessness of many who, though they have given their name to Christ, nevertheless play along with the world and let themselves be poured out into every licence along with it.

units.la: Audiamus nunc quo duce Iesus in desertum exiuerit. Lucas a spiritu actum fuisse scribit. Marcus autem expellendi, vel potius eijciendi verbo vtitur: non vt Christum praeter animi voluntatem inuitum aut reluctantem eiectum esse offendet, sed vt efficace spiritus motum exprimat, qui ipsi author fuit, vt relicta priori conditione, qua priuatus & plebei instar vixerat hucusq; nunc nouum vitae genus suscipere, & impositam sibi a patre functionem obiret. Et de Dei spiritu hoc intelligi debere, ex eo constat, quod spiritu sancto plenus eo exiisse dicitur. Semper quidem illi spiritus sanctus affuit, attamen pro assumpti hominis natura nouis incrementis indies sese in illo declarauerat antea, vt non obscure Lucas docuit, quando eum spiritu roboratum & sapientia impletum fuisse scripsit, vt maiores quotidie progressus faceret. Vt nunc, cum tempus illud instaurandae humanae salutis instaret, vniuersa spiritus plenitudo in illum effusa est, vt eadem ex illo in nos etiam redundaret, atq; in eius cum doctrina tum operibus aliquid homine maius posset agnosci. At nobis hinc generalis doctrina petenda est, tentationes non temere aut fortuito incidere, sed has quoq; certo diuinae prouidentiae consilio dispensari & regi. Oberrat quidem instar leonis rugientis satan, & perditos capit: at idem nihil in nos iuris habet, nisi quantum ei permittit Deus, cuius nutu omnia gubernantur. Exemplis pluribus hoc doceri poterat, inter quae cum primis memorabile est, quod in Iobi historia habetur. Est hoc plenum consolationis, si cogitemus Deum ipsum esse agnothetam nostrum, qui & in arenam hanc nos deducit, & pugnantes spectat, imo viribus quoque & armis instruit, vt certaminibus huiusmodi sufficere possimus. Quia enim fidelis est, suos non supra vires tentari finit, & vna cum tentatione euentum felicem largitur. Et vt alibi ait Apostolus, spiritus Dei nostras infirmitates subleuat, vt ea quoque vincere possimus, quae hominis vires longe superant. Nemo igitur vel metu succumbat, vel desperatione absorbeatur, quando tentationes vndique surgere videt. Interim vero curent singuli, ne propria temeritate aut confidentia tentationibus sese obiiciant. Quia enim infirmiores sumus, quam vt nostris viribus vel Satanam repellere, vel carnem in officio continere possimus, stultum fuerit pericula non necessaria sibi ipsi accersere: & exempla sunt, quae docent parum feliciter cedere nobis, si quid huius temere aggrediamur. Debebant de hoc diligenter cogitare, qui vel lucri vel gloriae causa, vel etiam turpi ventris studio sese impiorum aut superstitiosorum hominum consortijs immiscent, aut etiam eorum seruitijs sese mancipant, quos Christi & euangelicae veritatis hostes esse non ignorant. Pollicentur illi sibi ipsis multa de suis viribus, & se in fidei vera professione constantissimos fore confidunt. Sed quando de religione & fide interrogantur paulo durius ab illis, quorum authoritate & favore ipsis maximè opus est, tunc idem fere eis, quod Petro ad Caiaphae prunas sese calefacienti, accidit, ut aut turpi dissimulatione fidei confessionem obscurent, aut Christum eiusq; euangelium palàm abnegent. Nec enim spiritus sancti virtute confirmantur, qui eo neglecto sui spiritus temerarias suggestiones sequuntur, & huius seculi commoda æternæ salutis per Christum nobis acquisitæ beneficio præferunt. Idem illis, quoad mores & reliquam vitæ consuetudinem, accidere solet, qui ebriosorum, scortatorum, aleatorum, commerciis se immiscent, aut militiæ mercenariæ se mancipant. Etsi enim in animum inducant, se nil præter officium facturos esse, passim tamen & singulis momentis male agendi occasiones Satan objicit, & facilè vincuntur crebris tentationum assultibus, qui se inuictos fore putabant. Ergo procul relicta Babylone, in ecclesiæ Christi gremio maneant singuli, superstitionum occasiones vitent, improborum consortia caveant, & in vnius Dei voluntatem intenti, huius spiritum sequantur. Laborent item in tollendis publicis scandalis magistratus, quò minus qui infirmiores sunt exemplis malis aut scelerum illecebris tententur. Quod si verò Deus ipse nos in palæstram tentationum deducit, & necessariò cum illis agendum est, qui nos ad illicita solicitant, tunc intrepido animo pugnam capessamus, neq; deerit nobis spiritus sanctus, qui nos omni tentatione superiores reddet.
units.tr: Let us now hear under what leader Jesus went out into the wilderness. Luke writes that he was driven by the Spirit. Mark, however, uses the word "cast out," or rather "thrust out," not to show that Christ was driven out against his will or reluctantly, but to express the powerful impulse of the Spirit, who was its author, so that, having left his former condition, in which he had lived until now as a private person and like a commoner, he might take up a new way of life and undertake the office laid upon him by the Father.
