And that this must be understood of the Spirit of God is clear from the fact that he is said to have gone out full of the Holy Spirit. Indeed the Holy Spirit was always with him, yet in keeping with the nature of the man he had assumed, the Spirit had already been revealed in him with new increases day by day, as Luke clearly taught when he wrote that Jesus was strengthened in spirit and filled with wisdom, so that he made greater progress every day. So now, when the time of restoring human salvation was at hand, the full measure of the Spirit was poured out upon him, so that it might overflow from him to us as well, and so that in his teaching as well as his works something more than human might be recognised. But from this we must draw a general doctrine: temptations do not fall upon us rashly or by chance, but are also dispensed and governed by the certain counsel of divine providence. Satan indeed prowls like a roaring lion and seizes those who are lost; yet he has no right over us except as far as God permits, by whose nod all things are governed. This could be taught by many examples, among which the most memorable is what we have in the history of Job. It is full of comfort if we consider that God himself is our champion, who both leads us into this arena and watches us fight, and indeed equips us with strength and weapons so that we may be able to endure such contests. For since he is faithful, he does not allow his people to be tempted beyond their strength, and along with the temptation he grants a happy outcome. And as the Apostle says elsewhere, the Spirit of God lifts up our weaknesses so that we may be able to overcome even those things that far exceed human strength. Therefore let no one give way through fear, or be swallowed up by despair, when he sees temptations rising on every side. Meanwhile, however, let each take care not to throw himself into temptations through his own rashness or overconfidence. For since we are too weak to repel Satan or to keep the flesh in check by our own powers, it would be foolish to bring upon ourselves dangers that are not necessary; and there are examples which teach that it turns out badly for us when we rashly undertake such things. Those should think carefully about this who, for the sake of gain or glory, or even from a shameful desire for their belly, mingle with the company of impious or superstitious men, or even put themselves in bondage to those whom they know to be enemies of Christ and of the gospel truth. They promise themselves much from their own strength, and they trust that they will be most steadfast in the true profession of faith. But when they are questioned somewhat sharply about religion and faith by those whose authority and favour they most need, then it happens to them much as it happened to Peter warming himself at Caiaphas' fire: either they obscure their confession of faith by shameful dissimulation, or they openly deny Christ and his gospel. For they are not strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, since, having neglected him, they follow the rash suggestions of their own spirit and prefer the advantages of this age to the benefit of eternal salvation acquired for us through Christ. The same usually happens to them with regard to morals and the rest of their way of life, who mix themselves in the company of drunkards, whoremongers, and gamblers, or who bind themselves to mercenary soldiering. For although they make up their minds that they will do nothing beyond their duty, yet Satan throws in their way occasions for wrongdoing everywhere and at every moment, and those who thought themselves invincible are easily overcome by the frequent assaults of temptation. Therefore, let each one leave Babylon far behind, remain in the bosom of the Church of Christ, avoid occasions of superstition, beware of the company of the wicked, and, intent on the will of the one God alone, follow his Spirit. Let the magistrates also labour to remove public scandals, so that those who are weaker may not be tempted by bad examples or the allurements of sin. But if God himself leads us into the wrestling-ground of temptations, and we must of necessity deal with those who solicit us to unlawful things, then let us take up the fight with a fearless mind, and the Holy Spirit will not fail us, who will make us superior to every temptation.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, de quo sic scribit Lucas: Fuitque diebus quadraginta tentante eum diabolo, & nihil comedit per illos dies, sed ijs exactis, postea esurijt. Vnde colligitur, non solùm tres illos cum diabolo congressus eum sustinuisse, de quibus postea dicetur, sed totos quadraginta dies in pugnis & tentationibus assiduus transegisse. Interea autem toto illo tempore nihil comedit, quo exemplo Papistici doctores ad stabiliendum quadragesimale ieiunium abutuntur, vt etiam Mosis & Eliæ, de quibus simile quid sacra historia tradit. Sed facilè conuinci possunt, si rem ipsam propius in spiciamus. Primò enim non modò nihil comedit Christus, sed ne esurijt quidem. Nam exactis demum quadraginta diebus illum esuriuisse Lucas scribit. Non ergo ieiunij aut abstinentiæ seu temperantiæ exemplum hic proponitur, sed miraculum describitur, quo Deus filium suum commendare, & publicè testari voluit, Iesum hunc eum esse, de quo Moses & prophetæ omnes olim vaticinati sunt. Deinde ad ipsum confirmandum hoc maximè seruiuit, & facilius ei fuit postea diffidentiæ telum, quo eum Satan tentauit, eludere, cum proprio exemplo edoctus esset, hominem non solo pane viuere, sed quovis verbo, quod exit ab ore Dei. Adhæc non quotannis hoc fecit Christus, sed semel tantùm, quod ipsum de Mose etiam & Elia dici potest. Inepte ergo in exemplum trahitur, quod neque illi ipsi iterauerunt, & quod nemo veterum vnquam imitari conatus est. Confidentiæ autem nimiæ fuerit, tentare quod vires nostras longè superat: & cùm reliqua Christi miracula quenquam ad hoc adigere, quod non magis ab homine præstari possit, quàm si illum quinque panibus quinque hominum millia pascere, aut mortuos excitare iubeas? Accedit præterea superstitio cum impietate coniuncta, quando salutis meritum in suis illis ieiunijs constituunt, & Deum illis coli tradunt, frustra illo apud Zachariam clamante: Quando ieiunatis, vobis ieiunatis; & quando editis, vobis editis. Procul ergo facessant histriones illi, qui Christum & quaecunque is fecit, sibijpsis ludum faciunt, & sub illius nomine imperitis rerum impudenter insultant. Interim non negamus, sobrietate & vero ieiunio cumprimis opus esse, quando fidem nostram grauius tentari, aut nos ad libidinem & alia vitia solicitari sentimus. Solet enim caro spiritui resistere, & quò indulgetius illa tractatur, eò magis ferocit, & spiritum languentiorem reddit. Ideo intemperantiam & ebrietatem scripturæ passim damnant, & pios in precibus & ieiunijs frequentes esse iubent. Hæc autem neque certis diebus astringi, neque in ciborum discrimine constitui debent: sed quando sic opus est, ea carni nos subducere debemus, quaecunque eam vel ferociorem, vel in pietatis officijs segniorem reddere possunt. Et vtinam hodie tam facile nobis esset, temperantiam & verè Christiana ieunia omnibus persuadere, quàm facile est superstitiones damnare, vt his reliquis omnes ad libertatem Christianam aspirent, qua plerique ad licentiam abutuntur.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, of whom Luke writes thus: "And he was for forty days being tempted by the devil, and he ate nothing during those days; but when they were ended, afterwards he was hungry." Hence it is gathered that he endured not only those three encounters with the devil, of which he will be spoken of later, but spent the whole forty days in constant struggles and temptations. Yet meanwhile during that whole time he ate nothing; and the Papist teachers abuse this example to establish the Lenten fast, as they do also the examples of Moses and Elijah, of whom sacred history relates something similar. But they can be easily refuted if we look more closely at the matter itself. For, first, Christ not only ate nothing, but was not even hungry; for Luke writes that he was hungry only after the forty days were finished. Therefore no example of fasting, abstinence, or temperance is set forth here, but a miracle is described, by which God wished to commend his Son and publicly testify that this Jesus is the one of whom Moses and all the prophets long ago prophesied. Next, this served greatly to confirm this, and it was easier for him afterwards to parry the dart of distrust with which Satan tempted him, since he had been taught by his own example that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Moreover, Christ did not do this every year, but only once, which can also be said of Moses and Elijah. It is foolish, therefore, to draw into an example what neither they themselves repeated, and what no one of the ancients ever tried to imitate. And would it not be excessive confidence to attempt what far exceeds our strength? And since the rest of Christ's miracles do not compel anyone to do what a man can no more accomplish than he could feed five thousand men with five loaves, or raise the dead when ordered to? Besides, superstition joined with impiety is added when they place the merit of salvation in those fasts of theirs, and teach that God is worshipped by them, though in vain Zechariah cries out: "When you fasted and mourned, did you fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves?" Let those mockers therefore depart, who make a game of Christ and of whatever he did, and who shamelessly mock the ignorant in his name. Meanwhile we do not deny that sobriety and true fasting are especially needful when we feel our faith is more severely tested, or when we are stirred up to lust and other vices. For the flesh is wont to resist the spirit, and the more indulgently it is treated, the more it grows wild and makes the spirit more sluggish. Therefore the Scriptures everywhere condemn intemperance and drunkenness, and bid the pious be frequent in prayers and fasts. Yet these ought not to be bound to fixed days, nor made to depend on distinctions of foods; but when there is need, we ought to withdraw from the flesh whatever may make it wilder or make it more sluggish in the duties of piety. And would that it were as easy today to persuade everyone of temperance and truly Christian fasting as it is easy to condemn superstitions, so that all might aspire to the other things of Christian liberty, which most people abuse into licence.

units.la: Quod autem Christus exactis quadraginta diebus esuriuisse dicitur, verae humanitatis argumentum est, cuius infirmitas naturalis mox se se exeruit, quamprimùm in ea reprimenda virtus divina cessauit. Ita alibi sitiuisse & ex itinere fatigatus fuisse dicitur. Sunt haec in eum finem obser-uanda, vt eius meritum ad nos pertinere discamus, & vt in fide confirmati intelligamus, nos neque miseros neque à Dei gratia alienos esse, etiamsi fame, siti & aliarum rerum inopia nos Deus exerceat. Suscinuit haec omnia propter nos Dei filius Iesus Christus, in quo certa nobis esse debet salutis fiducia, vt in illo tentationes omnes vincere, & olim cum eodem in coelis triumphare possimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: That Christ is said to have been hungry after forty days had passed is evidence of true humanity: his natural weakness showed itself at once, as soon as the divine power ceased to restrain it. So too he is said elsewhere to have thirsted and to have been weary from the journey. These things are to be noted to this end: that we may learn his merit belongs to us, and that, being confirmed in faith, we may understand that we are neither wretched nor cut off from the grace of God, even if God exercises us with hunger, thirst and lack of other things. The Son of God, Jesus Christ, bore all these things for our sake, and in him we ought to have a sure confidence of salvation, so that we may overcome all temptations in him and one day triumph with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVII.

units.la: Tunc dixit ei diabolus: Si filius es Dei, dic isti lapidi, vt fiat panis. Et respondit ei Iesus dicens: Scriptum est, non pane solo viuet homo, sed omni verbo Dei.
units.tr: Then the devil said to him: "If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." And Jesus answered him, saying: "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.'"

units.la: INter Dei opera nullum excellentius & admirabilius inuenitur, quàm quòd filium suum vnigenitum hominem verum nasci voluit, vt in vna eademque persona duae diuersissimae naturae, diuina & humana, indissolubili vinculo sociarentur. Quia autem hoc carnis rationi impossibile videtur, creditu vero necessarium est, veram Christi humanitatem multis argumentis testatissimam fieri oportuit. Ex ea enim apparet, illum fratrem nostrum esse, eiusque meritum ad nos proprie pertinere. At inter argumenta illa facile primum est, quod tentationum certamen subijt. Nam quaecunque de actionibus corporis dicuntur, nonnullis imaginaria videri poterant, & scimus olim aliquos fuisse, qui & corpus Christi phantasticum, & omnes eius actiones imaginarias fuisse dicerent. In tentationibus autem eius manifeste apparet, illum nobis (excepto vno peccato) per omnia simile factum fuisse, neque ei quicquam deesse eorum, quae humanae naturae propria sunt. Quamobrem non temere factum est, quod haec historiae de Christo partem Euangelistae tanta diligentia describunt. Lucas certe illum totis diebus quadraginta in tentationum palaestra defudasse scribit, & vt nobis certius constet, quibus arietibus illum Satan oppugnauerit, nunc tres congressus ex ordine narrat, ex quibus & hostis nostri communis artes agnoscere, & simul discere licebit, quibus armis ille repelli & vinci possit.
units.tr: Among the works of God none is found more excellent and wonderful than that he willed his only-begotten Son to be born a true man, so that in one and the same person two most diverse natures, divine and human, might be joined by an indissoluble bond. But since this seems impossible to human reason, yet must be believed, the true humanity of Christ had to be attested by many arguments. For from it appears that he is our brother, and that his merit belongs properly to us. Yet among those arguments the first is easily that he underwent the struggle of temptation. For whatever is said about the actions of his body could seem to some to be imaginary, and we know that there were once some who said that Christ's body was a phantom and all his actions imaginary. But in his temptations it plainly appears that he was made like us in all things (apart from one sin), and that nothing belonging to human nature was lacking in him. Therefore it was not by chance that the Evangelists describe this part of Christ's history with such great care. Luke certainly writes that he sweated in the wrestling-ground of temptation for forty whole days; and so that we may be more certain with what battering-rams Satan assailed him, he now narrates three encounters in order, from which it will be possible both to recognise the arts of our common enemy and at the same time to learn with what weapons he can be repelled and conquered.

units.la: Primus autem producitur hic diabolus, quem Matthaeus tentatorem vocat, eò quòd is olim primos parentes tentauit, & hodie etiam omnium tentationum proprius author est, quibus ad peccandum solicitamur. Et huius nominis nos assiduè meminisse conuenit, vt vigilantiores simus aduersus eius insidias, quibus nos circumuenire & à statione nostra deijcere satagit. Quam enim securitatem nobis polliceri possumus, quibus cum eo res est, qui aduersus dilectum & aeternum Dei filium in arenam descendere ausus fuit? Quòd si quaeras, qua ratione in illo tentando vsus sit, & visibiline forma ei apparuerit atq; voce clara sit locutus, vel occultis & internis suggestionibus mentem eius solicitarit? nihil certi responderi potest. Vtrumq; enim ab illo fieri solet. Non dubium verò mihi est, improbum illum omnes suas artes protulisse eoq; terribiliorem sese praebuisse, quò fortiorem aduersarium sibi oppositum esse sciebat. Sed audiamus quibus verbis eum compellarit. Si filius es Dei (inquit) dic isti lapidi, vt fiat panis. Vbi ante omnia tempus & occasionem expendere oportet, quam Satan obseruauit. Dictum autem est nuper Christum totis diebus quadraginta ab omni cibo abstinuisse, & ijs euolutis esuriuisse. Quo loco famem vehementè denotari puto, & quae illum pro assumptae carnis infirmitate quàm grauissimè afflixerit. Mox ergo adest tentator ille, & qui hactenus nihil se profecisse videbat, nunc occasionè sibi oblatam arbitratur, qua Christū debellare & prosternere possit. Patet in hoc indefessum illius studium nocendi, astutia item eiusdem, qua occasiones ex nobis captare nouit, quando nos vel in aduersis impatientiores esse, vel iam ante desiderium aliquod illicitum animo concepisse videt. In Christo quidem, qui ab omni naturae vitiositate alienus erat, nihil huius inuenire potuit, fame autè vidit, cuius homines impatientissimos esse sciebat, et quòd ea vrgete multi nihil nō sibi licere arbitrantur, quo nomine veteres illa malesuada dixerunt. Itaq; ista occasione sibi minimè negligenda esse putauit. Et hoc eius vetus stratagema est, quo Euam matre nostra expugnauit. Cum enim sola per paradisum vagaretur, & arboris vetitae aspectu gauderet, deq; Dei praecepto (vt ex eius verbis facile colligitur) iam penes se dubitare inceperet, illico adest ille, colloquij occasionem captat, de mandato Dei quasi ignarus omnium quaerit, re audita periculum extenuat, imo aliquid periculi subesse negat, adhaec magnificis promissis & ipsius divinitatis spe animum Euae ac cendit, vtque magis eam moveat, Deum illi fingit invidum & consortis impatientem, qui ne homines ad divinam gloriam vnquam pertingant, arboris illius vsum interdixerit. Et quamuis impudenter nimis haec omnia fingat, occasionem tamen ista dicendi ex Eua arripuit, quae illius dictis eo citius cessit, quod ea cum desiderio vetiti fructus conuenire audiebat. Simile quid Dauidi accidisse legimus. Cum enim otio deditus domi desideret, & in Vriae vxorem incautius lauante oculos intentius defixisset, confestim animum quoque eius aggreditur, carnis cupiditate incendit, mulieris potiundae spem facit, & simul rationes suggerit, quibus negotium hoc possit confici. Propria ergo culpa Davides diaboli insidijs et telis patuit, qui illi grauissimorum scelerum postea fuit author. Et hodie idem omnibus accidit, qui cum natura ad libidinem proclives sint, alienas formas diligentius spectant, & inde conceptas cupidinis flammas non ocyus restinguunt. Patiuntur idem qui ad diuitias animum adiecerunt. Nam hic quoque optatissima occasione oblata Satan habendi desiderium magis accendit, & nouas indies monstrat rationes, quibus per fas & nefas ditescant. Eadem illorum ratio est, qui in cruce & afflictionibus aliquod impatientiae specimen praebent, & de Dei iustitia aut fide quiritari incipiunt. Nam apud illos quoque abs que mora instat quadruplator ille, & omnis generis rationes profert, quibus Dei gratiam atque veritatem in dubium vocet, & illos eo adducat, vt vel impie aduersus illum murmurent, vel turpi abnegatione salutem propriam prodant. Et hoc illud est, quod Iacobus Apostolus vnumquemque a propria concupiscentia tentari scribit. Multa ergo cura & vigilanti studio opus est, ne quam occasionem hosti tam improbo demus, & ideo oculos ab illicitis auertere, aures ad colloquia prava obturare, a cogitationibus iniustis animum revocare, cupiditatum principia restinguere, peccati blanditias procul arcere, carnis querulae murmurationibus obsistere, denique ab omni specie mali abstinere debemus, ne nos perdendi occasionem Satan in nobis ipsis inueniat.
units.tr: The first to be brought forward is this devil, whom Matthew calls the tempter, because he once tempted our first parents, and today too is the proper author of all the temptations by which we are urged to sin. We ought constantly to remember this name, so that we may be more watchful against his snares, by which he strives to circumvent us and drive us from our post. For what security can we promise ourselves, when we have to do with one who dared to enter the arena against the beloved and eternal Son of God? But if you ask in what manner he went about tempting him, whether he appeared to him in visible form and spoke with a clear voice, or whether he troubled his mind by hidden and inward suggestions, nothing certain can be answered. For he is wont to do both. Yet I have no doubt that the wicked one brought forth all his arts and showed himself the more terrible, the stronger he knew the adversary set against him to be. But let us hear with what words he addressed him. "If you are the Son of God," he says, "tell this stone to become bread." Here, before all else, one must weigh the time and the occasion which Satan observed. It was said a little while ago that Christ had abstained from all food for forty whole days, and when they had passed he hungered. In this place I think hunger is strongly marked, and how very grievously it afflicted him on account of the weakness of the flesh he had assumed. Straightway, therefore, that tempter is at hand, and he who until now seemed to have achieved nothing now judges that an opportunity has been offered him by which he can overthrow and prostrate Christ. In this appears his tireless zeal for harming, and likewise his cunning, by which he knows how to seize occasions from us, when he sees us to be more impatient in adversity, or already to have conceived some unlawful desire in our minds. In Christ, indeed, who was free from all vitiousness of nature, he could find nothing of this; but he saw hunger, of which he knew men to be most impatient, and that under its pressure many think they may do anything; for which reason the ancients called hunger an evil persuader. So he thought this occasion by no means to be neglected. This is his old stratagem, by which he overcame our mother Eve. For when she was wandering alone through paradise, and rejoicing in the sight of the forbidden tree, and had already begun to doubt within herself about God's command (as is easily gathered from her words), straightway he is there. He seizes the opportunity of conversation, asks about God's command as if ignorant of everything, and, having heard it, lessens the danger, or rather denies that any danger lies there. Besides, with magnificent promises and the hope of divinity he kindles Eve's mind, and so that he may move her the more, he feigns God to be envious and jealous of his partner, who has forbidden the use of that tree lest men should ever attain to divine glory. And although he feigns all these things too impudently, he nevertheless seized from Eve the occasion of speaking, and she yielded to his words the more quickly because she heard that they agreed with her desire for the forbidden fruit. We read that something similar happened to David. For when he, given over to idleness at home, lingered, and had fixed his eyes too intently on the wife of Uriah as she bathed, at once Satan attacks his mind as well, inflames him with lust of the flesh, holds out the hope of possessing the woman, and at the same time suggests the means by which the business can be accomplished. Therefore David, through his own fault, lay open to the snares and darts of the devil, who afterwards was the author to him of the gravest crimes. And today the same befalls all who, being naturally prone to lust, gaze more closely at other people's forms, and do not quickly quench the flames of desire thus kindled. Those who have set their minds on riches suffer the same. For here too, when a most welcome occasion has been offered, Satan kindles the desire of having more, and daily shows new reasons by which they may grow rich by right or wrong. The same is the case with those who, in the cross and afflictions, show some sign of impatience and begin to complain about God's justice or faithfulness. For that informer is also at hand among them without delay, and brings forward every kind of reason by which he may call God's grace and truth into doubt, and lead them either to murmur impiously against him or to betray their own salvation by shameful denial. And this is what the Apostle James writes, that each one is tempted by his own concupiscence. Therefore much care and vigilant zeal are needed, lest we give so wicked an enemy any occasion. So we ought to turn our eyes away from unlawful things, stop our ears against wicked conversations, call the mind back from unjust thoughts, quench the beginnings of desires, keep far away the flatteries of sin, resist the complaining murmurs of the flesh, and finally abstain from every appearance of evil, lest Satan find in us the occasion of our destruction.

units.la: Sed praestat ipsa diaboli verba propius inspicere, vt quis illi in Christo tentando finis propositus fuerit intelligamus. Si filius es Dei (inquit) dic isti lapidi, vt fiat panis. Quae verba primo intuitu nihil impium aut a Christi vocatione alienum sonare videntur, sed potius hoc exigere, vt non inglorius & obscurus in deserto lateat, sed potius insigni aliquo miraculo se Dei filium esse declaret, vt omnium animi ad ipsum excipiendum excitentur. Sed longe aliud vult versutus ille, qui (vt Paulus scribit) in angelum lucis se transfigurare nouit. Nam quod totius salutis humanae caput est, ipsam nimirum fidem Christi euertere conatur, ex qua omnis ea obedientia manauit, qua nos a peccato noxa & damnatione liberati sumus, quam primi parentis inobedientia inuexit. Et si rem omnem probe excutias, videbis hanc diaboli postulationem directe Patris caelestis testimonio opponi, quo hic Iesum istum filium suum dilectum esse pronuntiauerat, propter quem cum toto hominum genere in gratiam redierit. Perinde enim est, ac si diceret: Tu quidem re maximi momenti aggrederis, humani nimirum generis redemptionem, ea scilicet fiducia fretus, quod dilectus ille sis Dei filius, quem Pater aeterno suo decreto ad hoc negotium destinauit. Neque inficior, me quoque audiuisse vocem illam, quae ad te nuper delata est cum ab Ioanne baptizareris. Sed num huic credere tutum sit nondum video, quando constat mirificis praestigijs hominum sensus & animos ludificari. Et in eo, quod tu conaris, non verbis, sed factis opus erit, quae te filium illum Dei esse testentur, qui miseris opem ferre & perditos seruare possis. At quae haec est tua conditio, nihil huius prae te ferre videris. Si enim humani generis vindex & redemptor es, cur inter feras potius quam inter homines vitam degis? Si mundi seruator videri cupis, cur in loco inculto & inhabitato tam diu moraris? Si deniq; vitae aeternae author & gratiae diuinae mediator es, qui animas iustitia atq; vitam esurientes pascis & recreas, cur tu nunc inedia ringeris? Scilicet haec fieri permitteret Deus, si te filij loco haberet? Scilicet tu animas mortalium saturare poteris, qui ne corpus quidem proprium a dira fame potes defendere? Quin ergo ad miracula aedenda accingeris, vt & ipse melius habeas, & quam plurimos ad te trahas? Nec est quod quaeras, quid facto opus sit. E re praesenti consilium petito, & quod extrema necessitas iubet facito. Fame te cruciari sentis, quam nisi ocyus tibi eximas, pereas oportet. At cibus in promptu nullus est, neq; hunc aliunde petendi occasio datur. Quid ergo agendum superest? En lapis hic, quem si panem feceris, procul dubio te panem illum vitae esse omnes intelligent. Neque in hoc consiciendo multa cogitatione aut labore opus est. Nam si Dei filius es, & quidem dilectus ille, in cuius gratiam caeli scissi sunt, et spiritus sanctus revera visibili specie descendit, ipsa rerum natura tibi cedat oportet. At quod potes, id omnino velle debes, quando & tua gloria & communis hominum salus, ut hoc facias, postulat. Haec & omnia alia, quae in hanc sententiam dici poterant, pauca haec dicta verba continent. Quid autem his effectum voluit? Hoc nimirum, ut Christus patris oraculum in dubium vocet, & tandem diffidentia superatus vel mox deserat stationem suam, vel miraculo non necessario divinitatem suam tunc probet, quando extreme humiliari & senostris infirmitatibus obnoxium esse demonstrare debebat. Hi enim proprij diffidentiae fructus sunt, quod aut subito stationem nostram deserimus, aut praecipiti desiderio abrepti ordinem a Deo praefixum abrumpere aut anteuertere conamur, ut glorificari velimus priusquam cruce & afflictionibus, ut par est, probati sumus. Quod autem in praesenti Satan Christo obiecit, hoc ipsum postea quoque in cruce pendenti per Sacerdotes et scribas, per milites, per plebeios homines exprobravit, cum illi palam dicerent: Tu ille qui dissoluis templum et in triduo aedificas, serva temetipsum. Si filius Dei es, descende a cruce. Alios seruauit, seipsum seruare non potest. Si rex Israel est, descendat nunc a cruce, & credemus ei. Confidit in Deo, liberet eum nunc, si vult eum, &c. Quibus omnibus hoc unum quaerebat diabolus, ut inter acutissimos ignominiosissimosque dolores diffisus Patris erga se voluntate per miraculum ex cruce descenderet, & ita quodiam in procinctu erat humanae redemptionis opus abrumpere cui illum Pater destinarat.
units.tr: But it is worth looking more closely at the devil's own words, so that we understand what end he set himself in tempting Christ. "If you are the Son of God," he says, "tell this stone to become bread." At first sight these words seem to contain nothing impious or foreign to Christ's calling. They seem rather to demand that he not lie hidden and unknown in the desert, but declare himself the Son of God by some striking miracle, so that everyone's minds would be stirred to receive him. But that crafty one, who (as Paul writes) knows how to disguise himself as an angel of light, means something quite different. For he sets out to overthrow the very faith of Christ, which is the head of all human salvation, and from which came all that obedience by which we have been freed from the guilt and condemnation of sin, which the disobedience of our first parent brought in. If you examine the whole matter carefully, you will see that this challenge of the devil is directly set against the testimony of the heavenly Father, by which he declared this Jesus to be his beloved Son, through whom he had been reconciled with the whole human race. The devil's meaning is as if he said: "You are indeed undertaking a matter of the greatest weight, the redemption of the human race, relying on the confidence that you are that beloved Son of God whom the Father destined for this work by his eternal decree. I do not deny that I too heard that voice which was announced to you recently, when you were baptized by John. But I do not yet see whether it is safe to believe it, since it is well known that men's senses and minds are deceived by wonderful juggling. And in what you attempt, there will need to be not words but deeds, which will bear witness that you are that Son of God who can bring help to the wretched and save the lost. But what is your condition? You seem to show none of this. For if you are the avenger and redeemer of the human race, why do you live among beasts rather than among men? If you wish to be seen as the saviour of the world, why do you linger so long in a wild and uninhabited place? If finally you are the author of eternal life and the divine mediator of grace, who feed and refresh with righteousness and life souls that hunger, why are you now worn out by hunger? Would God allow these things to happen if he regarded you as his Son? Surely you can satisfy the souls of mortals, when you cannot even protect your own body from dreadful hunger? Why not then get ready to perform miracles, so that you may both do better yourself and draw very many to yourself? Nor need you ask what must be done. Seek counsel from the present situation, and do what extreme necessity commands. You feel that you are tormented by hunger, which unless you quickly relieve, you must perish. But there is no food at hand, nor is any opportunity given to seek it elsewhere. What then remains to be done? Here is this stone, which, if you make it bread, everyone will undoubtedly understand you to be that bread of life. Nor is much thought or labour needed to accomplish this. For if you are the Son of God, and indeed that beloved one in whose favour the heavens were torn open and the Holy Spirit truly descended in visible form, then nature itself must yield to you. And what you are able to do, you must surely be willing to do, since both your glory and the common salvation of men require you to do it. These few words contain this and all the other things that could be said to this effect. But what did he want to achieve by them? Surely this: that Christ should call the Father's oracle into doubt, and, overcome by distrust, either at once abandon his post, or prove his divinity by an unnecessary miracle at the very time when he ought to show that he was brought low and subject to our weaknesses. For this is the proper fruit of distrust: either we abandon our post at once, or, carried away by headlong desire, we try to break off or anticipate the order fixed by God, wanting to be glorified before we have been tested, as is right, by the cross and afflictions. What Satan then threw at Christ, he afterwards also hurled at him as he hung on the cross, through the priests and scribes, through the soldiers, through the common people, when they openly said: "You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants him, etc." In all these words the devil sought only this: that, amid the most acute and shameful sufferings, distrustful of the Father's will towards him, he should come down from the cross by a miracle, and so break off the work of human redemption which the Father had appointed him to accomplish, and which was now about to be completed.

units.la: Et haec illa tela sunt diaboli, quibus sanctos quoque Dei cultores oppugnat. David certe sibi hoc ipsum ab aduersarijs suis non semel obiectum fuisse queritur, quod a Deo derelictus scelerum poenas exoluleret, & frustra in eius opem atque promissiones respiceret, cuius ira ipsi subinde ob oculos versaretur. Eodem telo etiam hodie contra nos publice & priuatim vtitur. Sentiunt hoc qui morbis diuturnioribus excruciantur. Tunc enim suggerit Satan: Quid in Dominosperas & eius auxilio fidis, quem tui oblitum, aut etiam tibi inimicum esse vides? Quam multi enim interea ex morbis grauioribus seruati sunt, te nequicquam in Deo sperante? Quin ipse tibi consulis, & quae multos alios seruarunt remedia adhibes? Quorsum vero illa tendunt? Ut & Dei fiducia abiecta & relictis medijs naturalibus ad illicita conuertamur: ad exorcismos nimirum, magicos susurros, amuleta & quaecunque alia huius generis homines vel superstitiosi vel etiam palam impij excogitare solent. Idem fit in rerum penuria & fame. Tunc enim Satana suggerente cogitationes ista exoriuntur: Tu ne ex filiorum Dei numero te esse credis, qui Christo iubente clamant, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie? Quis enim pater filium famelicum negligit? Aut quis tam durus & crudelis est, ut panem petentibus liberis paruulis lapides apponat, aut etiam immerentes virgis caedat? At te non solum negligit Deus, sed nouis quotidie calamitatibus exercet, dum quae tibi praesto sunt eripit, dum laboribus tuis debitum fructum negat, & ne minima quidem fui fauoris indicia praebet. Quin ergo aut vitam laqueo abrumpis, ut semel omne miseriam effugias, aut ad artes conuerteris, quae multis alijs profuerunt? Frustra hodie iustitia & vitae integritas colitur: rapinis, furtis, impostturis, dolis, vi aperta & indomita audacia opus est, si quis rebus suis consultum velit, &c. In primis autem ingeniosus est Satan, si quando propter religionem & puriorem de Christo doctrinam periclitamur, & vel in exilium pulsi incertis vagamur sedibus, vel adinopiam extremam redacti cum nostris eurimus, vel omnium ludibrio expositi omne infamiae genus sustinemus, aut carceribus inclusi mortem & dirissima quaeque supplicia expectamus. Tunc enim mirifice rhetoricatur ille. Haec ne (inquit) est fides illa, quae Dei filios facit, quae iustos reddit, quae Dei fauorem conciliat, quae omnia vincit, quae montes loco mouet, quae denique sola felices & beatos facit? Egregij profecto filij Dei sunt, quos suo nomine periclitantes ille negligit. Praeclara sane iniustitia est, quam nemo sapiens & in aliquo dignitatis gradu constitutus agnoscit, & cuius cultores pro haereticis, scismaticis, seditiosis & publicorum malorum omnium authoribus habentur. Egregius autem Dei fauor est, exultare, egere, algere & infamem esse. O victores & triumphatores gloriosos, qui patrijs bonis cedere, cum inopia conflictari & omnium ludibria perpetuo sustinere coguntur. Si montes transferre possunt qui vere credunt, quia ex humeris vestris crucem eijcitis, regum edicta abrogatis, & vestram illam ecclesiam ex periculorum tantorum metu liberatis? Id vero cum nemo vestrum possit, aut tot illa fides vestra falsa est, aut ipsi non vere creditis, & proinde nequicquam vobis Dei favorem & omnia laeta pollicemini. Audiuntur haec & infinita alia huius generis passim hodie, & plura adhuc sibi licere putant infelicia diaboli organa, quorum linguis ille abutitur, si quando tota regna & respub. florentissimae propter Christi doctrinam periculis gravioribus exercentur. Tunc enim voces illae plus quam diabolicae sonant: Iamne sentitis, vestri illius Euangelij fructum? Iamne quid Christus ille vester possit experimini? Agite nunc fidei vestrae vires ostendite, nunc ex fide illa vobis victum, auxilium, defensionem quaerite, & c. Sed tunc pijs in mentem veniat, quod eadem olim Christo exprobrauit Satan, & quod olim similia multa audiuerunt sanctissimi homines, ideoq; istis non offendamur, quasi noua sint & insolita. At non circa haec solum calumniatoris istius diaboli sophistica versatur. Sed in ipsas hominum conscientias altius penetrare solet, quando Legis diuinae difficultatem et illius minas nobis ob oculos ponit, cumq; illis nostras vires confert, quae prorsus nullae sunt. Nam ex eo etiam colligit, nequaquam pro filijs suis Deum eos agnoscere, quos conditionibus praestitu impossibilibus obstrinxerit, & inuiolabili legis suae decreto iampridem ad mortem damnarit. Est haec tentatio omnium grauissima, quia & pro pria conscientiae testimonio & expresso Legis pronuntiato confirmatur. Multi ergo ea superati fiduciam omnem diuinae bonitatis abijciunt, & sibi ipsi mortem consciscunt, ut intolerabiles inferorum terrores effugiant, qui illis ipsa morte graviores sunt. At non ideo nos animum despondere oportet. Voluit enim tentationis huius ariete Christus quoq; concuti, ut in hac etiam parte vires diaboli frangeret, & nobis hanc vincendi viam monstraret, adeoq; armis ad hanc pugnam necessarijs instrueret.
units.tr: These are the darts of the devil, with which he also assails the holy worshippers of God. David certainly complains that this very charge was levelled at him more than once by his enemies, that he was forsaken by God and was paying the penalty for his crimes, and that he looked in vain for God's help and promises, whose anger was constantly before his eyes. Even today he uses the same dart against us, both publicly and privately. Those who are tormented by long illnesses feel this. For then Satan suggests: "Why do you hope in the Lord and trust in his help, when you see that he has forgotten you, or even that he is hostile to you? How many have meanwhile been saved from more serious diseases, while you hope in God in vain? Why do you not look to yourself, and use the remedies that have saved many others?" And where do such thoughts lead? To abandoning trust in God, and, with natural means set aside, turning to unlawful things: to exorcisms, magical whisperings, amulets, and whatever else of this kind superstitious or openly impious men are accustomed to devise. The same happens in want and hunger. For then, at Satan's suggestion, these thoughts arise: "Do you really believe you are among the number of the sons of God, who, at Christ's command, cry out, 'Give us this day our daily bread'? For what father neglects a hungry son? Or who is so hard and cruel that he would set stones before little children asking for bread, or beat even the innocent with rods? But God not only neglects you, he daily afflicts you with new calamities, while he takes away what is at hand, while he denies the due fruit of your labours, and gives not the least sign of his favour. Why then do you not either cut short your life with a noose, so that you may escape misery once and for all, or turn to those arts which have helped many others? In vain is righteousness and integrity of life cultivated today: if anyone wishes to look after his affairs, he needs robbery, theft, fraud, deceit, open violence and unbridled boldness, etc." Satan is especially clever when we are endangered for religion and for the purer doctrine concerning Christ, and either driven into exile we wander without fixed homes, or reduced to utter poverty we are reduced with our families, or exposed to the mockery of all we endure every kind of disgrace, or shut up in prisons we await death and the most dreadful torments. For then he speaks with wonderful eloquence: "Is this that faith which makes the sons of God, which makes men righteous, which wins God's favour, which overcomes all things, which moves mountains, and which alone makes men happy and blessed? Truly they are splendid sons of God, whom he neglects while they are in danger for his name! What a remarkable injustice, which no wise man and no one placed in any rank of dignity would acknowledge, and whose adherents are held to be heretics, schismatics, seditious men and the authors of all public evils! Splendid indeed is God's favour: to be exiled, to be in want, to be cold and to be infamous! O glorious victors and triumphers, who are compelled to yield their patrimony, to struggle with poverty, and to endure the mockery of all without end! If those who truly believe can move mountains, why, since you throw the cross off your shoulders, do you not repeal the edicts of kings and free your church from fear of such great dangers? But since none of you can do this, either your faith is false, or you do not truly believe, and therefore you promise yourselves God's favour and all joyful things in vain." Such words, and countless others of this kind, are heard everywhere today, and the unhappy instruments of the devil, whose tongues he abuses, think they may still do more, whenever whole kingdoms and flourishing commonwealths are exposed to graver dangers for the sake of Christ's doctrine. For then those voices sound more than devilish: "Do you now feel the fruit of that gospel of yours? Do you now experience what that Christ of yours can do? Come now, show the strength of your faith, now seek from that faith your food, help and defence, etc." But let the godly then call to mind that Satan threw the same reproach at Christ, and that the most holy men have long heard many similar things, and so let us not be offended by these as if they were new and unusual. But the sophistry of this slanderous devil is not concerned with these things alone. He is accustomed to penetrate more deeply into men's consciences, when he sets before us the difficulty of the divine Law and its threats, and compares them with our strength, which is wholly nothing. For from this he also infers that God does not acknowledge as his sons those whom he has bound by conditions impossible to fulfil, and long ago condemned to death by the inviolable decree of his law. This temptation is the most grievous of all, because it is confirmed both by the testimony of one's own conscience and by the express pronouncement of the Law. Many, therefore, overcome by it, cast away all confidence in divine goodness and bring death upon themselves, so that they may escape the intolerable terrors of hell, which are worse to them than death itself. But we ought not on that account to lose heart. For Christ also willed to be shaken by the battering-ram of this temptation, so that he might break the devil's strength in this part too, and show us the way of conquering it, and so equip us with the arms necessary for this fight.

units.la: Itaq; illum diabolo respondentem audiamus. Scriptum est (inquit) non pane solo viuet homo, sed omni Verbo Dei. Poterat infinitis argumentis exprobrationem illam confutare, & aliqua diuinitatis suae declaratione improbu terrere, ut quam ocyssime e medio abiret. Sed ijs armis voluit uti, quibus nos quoq; pugnare possumus, ut simul spem faciat, posse diabolum ab homine vinci, modo ido neis armis instructus ad pugnam istam accedat. Describit ea Paulus prolixe ad Ephes. cap. 6. vbi balthaei veritatis, thoracis iustitiae, galeae salutis, scuti fidei, atq; gladij spiritus meminit. Est is Verbum Dei, quo vno reliqua omnia comprehenduntur. In hoc enim Veritas aeterna inuenitur, in eodem iustitia Christi nobis offertur, quae nos thoracis instar munit & ad Dei tribunal defendit; hoc nobis Christum ipsum tradit, qui & galea salutis & caput nostrum est, ex quo vitae spiritus in nos omnes deriuatur: idem hoc verbum illud fidei est, & fidem tradit, qua quicunque praediti sunt, ij ad omnia diaboli tela excipienda & restinguenda satis instructi sunt. In primis autem gladij loco est credentibus Dei verbum, quia non solum in fide eiusq; officijs nos instruit, verum etiam ad Satanam profligandum facit, qui non alia re magis quam illo terretur. Quia enim regnum eius vniuersum ex mendacijs constat & ijsdem quasi fulcru nititur, argumenta quoq; eius, quibus nos ad diffidentiam atq; inobedientiam solicitat, mere sophistica & salsissima sunt, intolerabilis illi est Veritatis lux, quae radijs suis illius nebulas atq; fucos penetrat, & piorum omnium ludibrio ipsum exponit, qui paulo ante nescio quid magnificum proferre & de nobis triumphaturus esse videbatur. At cum Dei Verbum nominamus, non de incerto quodam & interno loquimur, quale sibi fingunt, qui nescio quas reuelationes & inspirationes priuatas somniant: sed de eo, quod in scripturis continetur, quas Paulus a Deo inspiratas & ad docendum, arguendum, corrigendum & perficiendu hominem Dei idoneas & sufficientes esse testatur. Ex his enim ipse Dei filius gladium illum depromit, quo in toto hoc certamine diabolum deuicit. Vbi tamen nemo putauerit, exemplum hoc superstitiosis et magicarum artium sectatoribus patrocinari, qui nuda verborum scripturae recitatione quiduis confici posse arbitrantur, & proinde ex illis exorcismos fingunt, quibus malignos spiritus fugari, morbos pelli & infinita alia mala arceri fingunt. Est hic abusus verbi Dei impijssimus, ab ipso diabolo machinatus, qui se exorcismis eiusmodi terreri & in ordinem cogi simulat, ut ea persuasione homines decepti in nuda verborum demurmuratione acquiescant, & ita fidem atq; obedientiam neglegant, quae Dei verbo debentur, & quae solae illud nobis efficax & salutare reddunt. Cū fide ergo gladius ille spiritualis aduersus diabolū stringi debet, & nimirum fide, quae homine totum Deo mancipat pat,et ita eum diaboli insidijs subducit,qui frustra eos oppugnat,qui toti ab vno Deo dependent. Et ita Dei verbo ex scripturis Christum vsum esse,totus historiæ huius contextus abunde docet. Commendatur autem nobis illius exemplo sacræ scripturæ studium, in cuius lectione & meditatione nos assiduos esse necesse est, vt in promptu nobis sint arma, quibus diaboli suggestiones eludamus. Etenim qui scripturas contemnunt,ij & in licentiam effrænem effunduntur, & si qua grauior tentatio oritur,mox victi succumbunt,cum penes se nihil inveniant,quo fidem suam confirmare,diaboli paralogismos deprehendere,& illius suggestionibus resistere possint. Sunt ergo hominum pernitiosissimi,imo humani generis hostes publici censeri merentur,quicunq; scripturæ sacræ libros ex hominum manibus excutiunt, & ne illi in linguis vulgaribus legantur prohibent. Quid enim hi aliud agunt, quàm quod vnicè confectum vult Satan, vt nimirum nudos & inermes opprimat? Eadem enim opera miseris arma eripiunt,quibus contra hostem communem pugnent,adeoque claudunt (quantum in ipsis est) instructissimum illud Spiritus sancti armamentarium, quod Deus omnis loci & ordinis hominibus patere vult, vt inde arma telaque habeant, quibus sese aduersus Diaboli assultus tueantur.
units.tr: So let us hear him answering the devil. "It is written," he says, "man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." He could have refuted that taunt with countless arguments, and by some display of his divinity he could have terrified the devil into leaving as quickly as possible. But he chose the weapons with which we too can fight, so that he might give us hope that the devil can be overcome by a man, provided that the man comes to this battle equipped with the right arms. Paul describes these at length in Ephesians chapter 6, where he mentions the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit. The Word of God comprises all of these in one. In it the eternal truth is found, and in the same Word the righteousness of Christ is offered to us. It guards us like a breastplate and defends us before the judgment seat of God. It hands over to us Christ himself, who is both our helmet of salvation and our head, from whom the breath of life flows into all of us. This same Word is the word of faith, and it delivers the faith by which those who possess it are sufficiently equipped to receive and quench all the darts of the devil. But the sword in particular is the Word of God for believers, because it not only instructs them in faith and its duties, but also puts Satan to flight, for he is terrified by nothing more than by this. His whole kingdom rests on lies and is propped up by them, so his arguments, by which he urges us to distrust and disobedience, are purely sophistical and utterly foolish. The light of truth is unbearable to him. Its rays penetrate his mists and shams and expose him to the mockery of all the godly, though a little before he seemed about to utter something grand and to triumph over us. But when we speak of the Word of God, we do not mean some uncertain inner thing of the kind that those dream of who imagine private revelations and inspirations, whatever they may be. We mean what is contained in the Scriptures, which Paul testifies were inspired by God and are fit and sufficient for teaching, reproving, correcting and equipping the man of God. It is from these Scriptures that the Son of God himself draws that sword with which he conquered the devil in the whole of this conflict. Yet no one should think that this example lends any support to the superstitious and to the practitioners of magic arts, who believe that anything can be accomplished by the bare recitation of the words of Scripture, and who therefore devise exorcisms from them, by which they imagine evil spirits can be driven out, diseases expelled and countless other evils warded off. This is the most impious abuse of the Word of God, devised by the devil himself, who pretends to be frightened by such exorcisms and to be brought into order by them, so that men, deceived by this persuasion, rest content with the mere mumbling of the words and so neglect the faith and obedience that are owed to the Word of God, and which alone make it effective and salutary for us. The spiritual sword must therefore be drawn against the devil with faith, and indeed with that faith which wholly commits a man to God, and so withdraws him from the snares of the devil, who fights in vain against those who depend entirely on the one God. The whole context of this history amply teaches that Christ in this way used the Word of God from the Scriptures. We are also commended, by his example, to a zeal for Holy Scripture, in whose reading and meditation we must be diligent, so that the weapons with which we may repel the devil's suggestions are ready to hand. Those who despise the Scriptures give themselves over to unbridled licence, and if some heavier temptation arises they soon succumb, since they find nothing within themselves by which they can confirm their faith, detect the devil's fallacies and resist his suggestions. Therefore those who snatch the books of holy Scripture from men's hands and forbid them to be read in the vulgar tongues are the most pernicious of men, and deserve to be counted public enemies of the human race. For what else do they accomplish but what Satan alone desires, namely to crush men who are naked and unarmed? By the same act they take from the wretched the weapons with which they might fight against the common enemy, and so they close (as far as in them lies) that most well-stocked armoury of the Holy Spirit, which God wishes to be open to men of every place and rank, so that they may have from it the arms and weapons with which to defend themselves against the assaults of the devil.

units.la: Porrò ipsum scripturæ locum inspiciamus,quem in præsenti Christus adducit. Extat in Deut. 8.cap. vbi Moses ad fidem constantem & piam præceptorum Dei obseruationem Israelitas exhortans,inter alia sic dicit: Recorderis totius itineris, per quod duxit te Dominus Deus tuus his quadraginta annis per desertum, vt affligeret te, & tentaret te, vt sciret deniq; quid esset in corde tuo, num scilicet seruares præcepta eius,an minus. Afflixit itaq; te, & passus est te fame laborare,aluitq; te Manna, quod neq; tu neque patres tui nouerunt: vt scilicet ostenderet tibi,quòd non solo pane viuit homo, sed omni eo quod exit ab ore Domini homo viuet,&c. Hebraica autem phrasi exitus oris Domini dicitur quod ipse decernit & iubet. Sic apud Danielem exitus verbi significat decretum de instauranda vrbe Ierosolyma,quod anno septimo Artaxerxis Longimani factum fuit. Panis autem nomine omnis hominis victus & recepta hunc parandi ratio intelligitur. Itaque verborum Mosis sensus est: Deus vos totis annis quadraginta nouo atq; prius inaudito modo aluit, & cùm in ijs locis ageretis, in quibus neq; sementem neq; messem facere poteratis,simulq; impossibile esset aliunde annonam aduehere,quæ tantæ multitudini sufficeret,ille cœli fenestras vobis aperuit, & panem angelorum dedit, vt victum nullo vel pretio vel labore partum habueritis. In quo non præsens modò beneficium obseruare,sed simul Dei omnipotentiam agnoscere debetis,qui vt ut res in posterum quoq; cedant, vos alere et seruare poterit, etiamsi ipsa natura rerum in vestram pernitiem coniurauisse videatur, &c. Recte ergo & proprie sententiam hanc diabolo hic opponit Christus, & simul exemplum illud vetus in mente reuocat, vt de Patris potentia & bonitate nouam fiduciam animo concipiat. Perinde enim hoc est,ac si dixisset: Etsi fame crucier, & in præsenti nihil esui aptum occurrat, ideoq; ea rerum facies esse videatur, vt aut fame mihi pereundum,aut cibus miraculose parandus sit: nunquam tamen me vt id nunc faciam persuadebis,quando me humanis infirmitatibus subijcere,non autem diuinæ maiestatis argumentum miraculo minimè necessario declarare debeo. Et vt id faciam minimè opus est,quando veteribus exemplis & diserto Dei verbo edoctus sum, hominem non solito modo victu sustentari, sed adillum seruandum quoduis Dei decretum sufficere. Neq; vnquam putauero,illum passurum vt fame peream,cùm longè aliud eius de me statutum sit: vt nimirum gratiæ eius Mediator sim, & humani generis salutem meo merito instaurem. Sic ergo Dei verbo pugnauit Christus, quòd nimirum hoc constanti fide apprehensum aduersus hostem vibrauit, ne diffidentiæ telum in ipso hærere posset.
units.tr: Let us next look at the very passage of Scripture that Christ cites here. It is found in Deuteronomy chapter 8, where Moses, exhorting the Israelites to a steadfast and pious faith and to the observance of God's commandments, says among other things: "You shall remember the whole way by which the Lord your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, to humble you and to test you, that he might know at last what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not. So he humbled you and let you suffer hunger, and he fed you with manna, which neither you nor your fathers knew, to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord," and so on. Now in Hebrew idiom the going forth of the mouth of the Lord means what he himself decrees and commands. So in Daniel the going forth of the word means the decree to restore the city of Jerusalem, which was made in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus. The name of bread, moreover, stands for all of a man's sustenance and the accepted way of procuring it. The sense of Moses' words is therefore this: God nourished you for forty years in a new and hitherto unheard-of manner. When you were in places where you could neither sow nor reap, and when it was impossible to bring in from elsewhere grain sufficient for so great a multitude, he opened the windows of heaven for you and gave you the bread of angels, so that you had food obtained neither by any price nor by any labour. In this you ought to observe not only the present blessing, but at the same time to acknowledge the omnipotence of God, who will be able to feed and preserve you in time to come, however things turn out, even if nature itself seems to have conspired for your destruction, and so on. Christ therefore rightly and properly sets this sentence against the devil, and at the same time recalls that old example to mind, so that he may conceive new confidence in the power and goodness of the Father. It is as if he had said: "Even if I am tormented by hunger, and nothing fit to eat presents itself at the moment, so that the state of affairs seems to be that I must either perish of hunger or have food miraculously provided, you will never persuade me to do this now, since I ought not to subject myself to human weakness, nor to demonstrate by a miracle, which is by no means necessary, a proof of the divine majesty. And there is no need for me to do this, since I have been taught by ancient examples and by the plain word of God that a man is sustained not in the usual way, but that any decree of God is sufficient for his preservation. Nor shall I ever think that he will allow me to perish of hunger, since his purpose for me is quite different: namely that I should be the Mediator of his grace and restore the salvation of the human race by my merit." So Christ fought with the Word of God, for he seized it with a steadfast faith and hurled it against the enemy, so that the dart of distrust could not lodge in him.

units.la: Nobis autem idem huius dicti vsus esse debet, in quo si nos probè exercuerimus,vnum hoc aduersus omnem diffidentiæ tentationem nobis sufficere poterit. Quoties ergo solicitam de victu parando curam Satà inijcit, & ea nos ad opes parandas excitat,imò ditescendi rationes iniquas & illicitas suggerit,tunc nobis in mentem veniat,non solo pane hominem viuere,neq;(vt alibi Christus ait) in opu abundantia vitæ nostræ consistere,sed hanc omnem à Dei prouidentia pendere. De eius autem cura paterna minimè nos dubitare conuenit,quando promissiones & exempla passim habentur,quæ fidem nostram confirmare possunt. Et vt multa alia omittamus,sufficere nobis debet Christi dictum: Quærite ante omnia regnum Dei et iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia vobis adijcientur. Nam ibidem nos ad aues & coruorum pullos, ad flores item temere in agro nascentes reuocat, ut inde colligamus, nunquam passurum Deum, ut homo fame pereat, qui suam vocationem secutus fuerit. Et si communem hominum vitam inspiciamus, fere omnium commodissimè & beatissimè viuunt, qui paruo contenti intra suæ vocationis limites sese continent: cum alij curis inutilibus & assiduo labore, adhæc rixis & iurgijs circa opum aceruos tumultuentur. Idem in morbis cogitemus, quando remedia fallunt, & ad magicas præstigias nos remittit Satan. Verè enim tunc quoq; respondere illi possumus: Non solis istis medijs conseruatur aut recuperatur hominis valetudo, sed omni eo, per quod nos seruare Deo placuerit. Similiter cum pro fide Christi exulandum est, certò nobis persuasum sit, patriam nostram non vni terrarum angulo alligatam esse, sed nos vbicunq; simus, sub Dei patris protectione agere, qui nos cum ipsi visum fueris, in cœlestis patriæ sedes recipiat. Deniq; in omni periculo, cum solita & ordinaria auxilia nos deficiunt, recordemur, non posse exhauriri diuinæ sapientiæ & scientiæ thesauros, & proinde non defutura esse media Deo, quibus nos adiuuet. Quòd si Legis mi nas & propriæ conscientiæ testimonium aduersus nos Satan producit, in promptu nobis sit responsio: Non sola suorum operum iustitia iustificatur & viuit homo, sed ea, quam suo decreto Deus stabilivit. At quænam illa est? Christus Iesus, qui nobis ab illo factus est iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Habet ergo locus hic vberrimam & multiplicem consolationem, quæ ad omnes casus accommodari potest, ne vnquam diffidentia victi fidem in vnum Deum abnegemus, aut aliquid faciamus, quod ab eius professione sit alienum. In primis autem nos in pugna ista animare & confirmare debet Iesu Christi exemplum, qui vt nobis vicit, ita suis vires & arma suppeditat, quibus illi quoq; vincant, ut vna secum viuant & regnent. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: For us the use of this saying ought to be the same. If we have exercised ourselves in it properly, this one thing will be enough for us against every temptation to distrust. Whenever Satan puts anxious care for getting our food into our minds, and stirs us up to acquire wealth, or even suggests unfair and unlawful ways of growing rich, then let this come to mind: man does not live by bread alone, nor (as Christ says elsewhere) does our life consist in the abundance of possessions, but all of it depends on the providence of God. We ought not to doubt his fatherly care, since there are everywhere promises and examples that can confirm our faith. And to pass over many other things, the saying of Christ ought to be enough for us: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. For in the same place he calls us to the birds and the ravens' young, and likewise to the flowers that grow carelessly in the field, so that we may gather from them that God will never allow a man who has followed his calling to perish of hunger. And if we look at the common life of men, almost all of those who live most comfortably and happily are those who, content with little, keep themselves within the bounds of their calling, while others are thrown into turmoil by useless cares, constant labour, and quarrels and wrangling over heaps of wealth. Let us think the same in sickness, when remedies fail and Satan sends us back to magical trickery. For then too we can truly answer him: health is not preserved or recovered by these means alone, but by everything through which it has pleased God to preserve us. Similarly, when we must go into exile for the faith of Christ, we should be sure that our homeland is not bound to one corner of the earth, but that wherever we are we live under the protection of God the Father, who will receive us into the seats of the heavenly fatherland when it seems good to him. Finally, in every danger, when the usual and ordinary helps fail us, let us remember that the treasures of divine wisdom and knowledge cannot be exhausted, and therefore God will not lack means by which to help us. But if Satan brings forward against us the threats of the Law and the testimony of our own conscience, let our answer be ready: man is not justified and does not live by the righteousness of his own works alone, but by that which God has established by his decree. And what is that? Christ Jesus, who has been made by God our righteousness, sanctification and redemption. This passage therefore holds a most abundant and manifold consolation, which can be applied to every circumstance, so that we may never, overcome by distrust, deny our faith in the one God, or do anything that is foreign to its profession. Above all, in this struggle the example of Jesus Christ should encourage and strengthen us: as he conquered for us, so he also supplies his own with strength and weapons, so that they too may conquer, and live and reign with him for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVIII.

units.la: Et cum subduxisset eum diabolus in montem sublimem, ostendit ei omnia regna terræ puncto temporis. Et ait ei diabolus: Tibi dabo potestatem hanc vniuersam, & gloriam istorum (nā mihi tradita est, & cuicunq; voluero do eam:) itaq; si tu adoraueris me, erunt tua omnia. Respondens autem Iesus dixit ei: Abscede à me Satana. Scriptum est enim: Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & ei soli seruies.
units.tr: And the devil, taking him up into an exceedingly high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the earth in a moment of time. And the devil said to him: To you I will give all this power and the glory of these (for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whomever I will); therefore, if you will worship me, all of it shall be yours. But Jesus answered him: Get behind me, Satan. For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone.

units.la: Quoniam Dei filius in mundum venit & homo factus est, ut peccatores saluos faceret, ab eo illum redemptionem nostram inchoare oportuit, vnde perditionis nostræ initium factum fuerat. Cœpit hæc àtentatione, qua diabolus sub serpentis specie primos parentes circumuenit & seduxit, ut in Dei præceptum peccarent, & peccando morti subijcerentur. Rectè ergo Christus mox à baptismo in desertum, quasi in palæstram tentationum se recepit, & illic cum hoste nostro communi congressus est: partim quidem, ut eum deuinceret, qui hucusque nimium contra nos potuerat; partim verò, ut nobis quoque vires sufficeret, quibus illum vincamus, simulque consolatione certa & firma instrueret, quando videmus illum nobis per omnia, solo peccato excepto, similem factum esse, & proinde nostris infirmitatibus condolere posse, neque passurum, ut illis succumbamus. Vidimus nuper primum in hac pugna congressum, in quo diffidentiæ telis pugnantem Satanam Christus profligaut, adducto Dei verbo, quo Moses nobis illius omnipotentiam simul atque paternam pro nobis curam commendat. At non propterea ex arena ille discedit, sed mox aliis armis atque alia via Christum aggreditur: quod nobis in tota hac historia probè observandum est, ne si quando nobis primus conatus succedit, nos otio & securitati dedamus. Vt enim in militia sæpe post partam victoriam subitò cladem accipiunt, qui hostes deuictos insolentius contemnunt, & poculis somnoque indulgent: ita non raro fit, ut dum minimè arbitrantur diabolo prædâ fiant, qui sibi ipsis omnia tuta pollicentur. Semper ergo nobis in mentem veniat, quòd Petrus diabolum instar leonis rugientis obambulare scribit, & indesinenter quærere quem deuoret. Si enim tanta eius est audacia, ut æternum Dei filium denuo aggredi non sit veritus, quam obsecro securitatem nobis polliceri possumus, qui & proprijs cupiditatibus abrepti ad malum feriimur, & ipsi occasiones praebemus hosti illi, quibus pugnam aduersus nos instaurct? Admonet de hoc nos Christus, quando spiritum immundum in hoc cumprimis esse ait, vt domum, vnde semel eiectus est, iterum occupare possit. Semper ergo nos in excubijs stare, semper armis spiritualibus munitos esse, semper gladiû spiritus ore simul & manibus vibrare conuenit, ne Christi merito partam victoriam nostra socordia amittamus. Sed praestat secundi huius congressus historia & singulas eius partes propius inspicere.
units.tr: Since the Son of God came into the world and was made man so that he might save sinners, it was fitting that he should begin our redemption at the point where our ruin had begun. It began with that temptation by which the devil, under the form of a serpent, deceived and seduced our first parents, so that they sinned against God's command and by sinning became subject to death. Rightly, therefore, Christ withdrew into the desert immediately after his baptism, as into a wrestling-ground of temptations, and there he met our common enemy in combat. He did so partly to overcome the one who had prevailed so far too much against us, and partly to give us strength to overcome him in turn, and at the same time to instruct us with a sure and firm consolation: for we see that he has become like us in all things, sin excepted, and therefore can sympathise with our weaknesses and will not allow us to succumb to them. We have lately seen the first encounter in this battle, in which Christ routed Satan fighting with the darts of distrust, by bringing forward the word of God, by which Moses commends to us both his almighty power and his fatherly care for us. Yet Satan does not for that reason leave the field, but at once attacks Christ with other weapons and by another route. This we must observe carefully throughout this whole story, so that if our first attempt sometimes succeeds, we do not give ourselves over to idleness and carelessness. For just as in war men who despise a defeated enemy too boldly often suddenly suffer disaster after a victory has been won, and indulge in drinking and sleep, so it often happens that those who promise themselves everything is safe become prey to the devil when they least suppose it. Let us therefore always keep in mind that Peter writes that the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking without ceasing whom he may devour. For if his boldness is so great that he has not been afraid to attack again the eternal Son of God, what security, I beg you, can we promise ourselves, who are both carried off by our own desires and strike ourselves into evil, and who ourselves give that enemy opportunities for renewing the battle against us? Christ warns us of this when he says that an unclean spirit, especially in this way, returns to occupy the house from which it was once cast out. Therefore we must always stand on guard, always be armed with spiritual weapons, and always brandish the sword of the Spirit with both mouth and hands, lest by our carelessness we lose the victory that Christ's merit has won. But it is better to look more closely at the history of this second encounter and at its individual parts.

units.la: Rursus autem primus pugnam capessit Satan, de quo Lucas sic scribit: Cum subduxisset Iesum diabolus in montem sublimem, ostendit ei omnia regna terrae puncto temporis, et dixit ei: Tibi dabo potestatem hanc vniuersam, & gloriam illorum (nam mihi tradita est) & cuicunque voluero, do eam: itaque si tu adoraueris me, erunt tua omnia. Quae verba satis testantur, diabolum Christi mentem ambitione & dominandi libidine tentauisse, ideoque omnia suggessisse, quae ambitionem & fastum huius mundi comitari solent. Fuit quidem Christi animus a cupiditate ista (vt ab alijs quoq; vitijs) alienissimus, neq; aliquis putare debet, illum cogitationibus eiusmodi, qui etsi nihil aliud accedat, per se peccati nomine censentur, vel momento indulsisse. Externus tamen sensibus ista obiecit Satan, & ita Christum, quem verum hominem, non truncum aut stipitem factum sciebat, gloriae & potentiae huius seculi blanditijs capere & prosternere studet. Nec temere nunc isto ariete illum oppugnat. Est enim superbiae & ambitionis vis maxima in hominum cordibus: & vt hac deuictus Adam Satanae succubuit (quo nomine superbia peccati principium dicitur) ita omnes gloriae & honorum naturam appetentes sumus, quae plerunq; (nisi efficaci spiritus freno retineamur) maximorum scelerum causa est. Hac certe extimulatus Cain fratrem Abelum occidit, ne hic sibi orbis dominium praeriperet. Hac accensi Iacobi filij omnes fratrem Iosephum vendere non sunt veriti. Eadem prius Esaum moverat, vt Iacobum germanum & vterinum fratrem necare in animum induceret. Ista cupiditate inflammatus Saul Dauidem, optime de se & regno toto meritum persecutus est, & innoxio sacerdotum Domini sanguine se polluit. Ambitione nefaria excitatus Abfolon patre iam senem eijcit, inceflu nefario domum patriam inquinat, & populum vniuersum in periculum praesens adducit. Et si exteras historias inspiciamus, nullum vnquam regnum fuit, quod non aliquo ipsius furiae assultu oppugnatum & concussum fuerit. Hinc parricidia & indignae fratrum caedes enascuntur, quales de Cambyse, Romulo, Bassiano Caracalla historiae commemorant. Hinc perfidia & impia peierandi libido, quae ita olim apud multos regnauit, & etiam hodie regnat, vt fere omnium principum animis insculpta videri possit Iulij Caesaris sententia: Si ius violandum est, regnandi causa violandum est. Et illud Lysandri, pueros astragalis, viros iureiurando falli debere. Haec vnica bellorum ciuilium semper fax fuit, sicut Syllae & Marij, Iulij & Pompei, Antonij & Augusti, multorumq; aliorum exempla testantur, qui tam sibi ipsis quam communi patriae immodico gloriae priuatae studio exitium accersiuerunt. Eadem olim in ecclesia dissensiones et haereses excitauit, quae plus mali dederunt, quae omnes crudelissimorum tyrannorum machinationes, qui illam ferro & flammis excindere conati sunt. Et tanta huius mali vis est, vt fere generosiores hominum animos in primis tentet, & ijs etiam sese insinuare potest, qui prae alijs sapientiam veram sequi & rerum huius mundi contemptores esse videntur. Quod in philosophis Cicero diligenter obseruauit, qui illis ipsis libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribebant, nomina sua praefigere consueuerant, vt ex eo gloriam vanarentur, quo alios ab eius studio & cupiditate abstrahere conabantur. Fuit ergo haec admodum grauis tentatio, eoque acutius Christi animum ferire potuisset (fiquidè possibile fuisset eum Satanae telis succumbere) quod nihil aliud hic pollicitus est, quam quod illi iure optimo debebatur. Huic enim olim dictum fuerat: Postula a me, daboq; gentes vt sint hereditas tua: & terminos terrae vt sint possessio tua. Itaq; plausibi liuris & aequi praetextu tentatio haec velata fuit, cum nihil obstare videretur, quo minus regnum sibi a patre promissum & destinatum Christus abs[q;] mora arriperet. Sed astu mirifico hoc quaerit improbissimus Tentator, vt partim ante tempus illud iuadat, & quod prius agendum erat intactum relinquat: partim vt ex diaboli manu accipiat, quod non nisi a Patre accipi poterat, neq; aliunde ex pe&tari aut sperari debebat. Et hoc illud est, quo etiam hodie multis Satan imponit, vt in ijs peccent grauissime, quae per se illicita non sunt, dum ad ea illicitè medijs contendunt.
units.tr: Again, Satan begins the fight, and of this Luke writes thus: When the devil had taken Jesus up into an exceedingly high mountain, he showed him all the kingdoms of the earth in a moment of time, and said to him: To you I will give all this power and the glory of them (for it has been delivered to me), and I give it to whomever I will; therefore, if you will worship me, all of it shall be yours. These words sufficiently show that the devil tempted Christ's mind with ambition and the lust for ruling, and therefore set before him everything that usually accompanies the ambition and pomp of this world. Christ's mind was indeed most remote from that desire, as from other vices, and no one should think that he indulged for even a moment in thoughts of that kind, which, even if nothing else followed, are reckoned sins in themselves. Yet Satan presented these things to his outward senses, and so he sought to catch and overthrow Christ, whom he knew to be a true man and not a block or a stump, by the enticements of the glory and power of this age. Nor does he attack him with this battering-ram without reason. For there is the greatest force of pride and ambition in men's hearts, and just as Adam was conquered by this and yielded to Satan (for which reason pride is called the beginning of sin), so we all desire the nature of glory and honours, which, unless we are restrained by the effective bridle of the Spirit, is most often the cause of the greatest crimes. Cain, certainly, was spurred on by this when he killed his brother Abel, lest this one snatch from him dominion of the world. Inflamed by this, all the sons of Jacob were not afraid to sell their brother Joseph. The same passion had earlier moved Esau to resolve to kill his brother Jacob, his own full brother from the same mother. Saul, driven by this desire, persecuted David, who deserved very well of him and of the whole kingdom, and polluted himself with the innocent blood of the priests of the Lord. Absalom, roused by nefarious ambition, drove out his father, already an old man, defiled the family home by his unlawful incest, and brought the whole people into immediate danger. And if we look at foreign histories, there has never been a kingdom that has not been assailed and shaken by some assault of this same fury. Hence come parricides and the unworthy slaughter of brothers, such as the histories record concerning Cambyses, Romulus, and Bassianus Caracalla. Hence come treachery and the impious lust for perjury, which has reigned so long among many, and still reigns today, so that the saying of Julius Caesar may seem almost engraved on the hearts of nearly all princes: if law must be broken, it must be broken for the sake of ruling. And that saying of Lysander's too: boys should be deceived with dice, men with oaths. This has always been the one torch of civil wars, as the examples of Sulla and Marius, Julius and Pompey, Antony and Augustus, and many others testify, who brought ruin both on themselves and on their common country through an immoderate pursuit of private glory. The same passion once stirred up dissensions and heresies in the Church, which have done more harm than all the schemes of the most cruel tyrants who tried to destroy it with sword and fire. And so great is the force of this evil that it tends to attack the most noble minds of men first, and it can insinuate itself even into those who seem, above others, to follow true wisdom and to despise the things of this world. Cicero carefully observed this in the philosophers, who were accustomed to put their own names on the very books they wrote on despising glory, so that they hunted for glory by the very means by which they tried to draw others away from its pursuit and desire. This was therefore a very grave temptation, and it could have struck Christ's mind all the more sharply (if indeed it had been possible for him to yield to the darts of Satan), because the devil promised him nothing other than what was rightly owed to him. For it had once been said to him: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. So this temptation was veiled under the pretext of a plausible and fair right, since nothing seemed to stand in the way of Christ at once seizing the kingdom promised and appointed for him by the Father. But this most wicked Tempter seeks by a marvellous cunning to bring it about that, partly, he urges him to act before the appointed time and leaves undone what ought to have been done first; and partly, that he receives from the devil's hand what could be received only from the Father, and was not to be sought or hoped for from any other source.
