And this is that by which Satan still today deceives many, so that they sin most gravely in things that are not unlawful in themselves, while they unlawfully strive for them by unlawful means.

units.la: Caeterum videamus, qua arte hic vsus sit hostis noster, dum per Christi latus vniuersum genus mortalium letaliter vulnerare cœpit. Primò subduxit eum in altum vel sublimem montem, & pun-cto temporis omnia regna terræ oculis eius subijcit. Quod ego non nuda modò imaginatione factum fuisse existimo. Ista enim simplici narratione, vt rem vere gestam, Euangelistæ exponunt, & tam diligens loci atque temporis notatio id omnino innuere videtur. Quàmuis ergo imaginatio vehe-mens accesserit, simul tamen externos etiam sensus, oculos in primis, splendor ille regnorum per-strinxit, vt eum magis moueret, quem verum hominem factum esse sciebat. Neque hic opus est quærere, quomodo omnia terræ regna vno quasi momento conspici, & oculorum acies per totum or-bem extendi potuerit. Scimus enim quàm efficaces sint diaboli illusiones, qui etiam hodie res procul absentes, imò ante multa secula gestas, in crystallis & alijs magicis instrumentis spectandas pro-ponere solet. Et quia propter nos tentari voluit Christus, eò vsque demisit se, vt eius quoque sensibus Satan interea abuteretur. Est autem hic antiquus hostis nostri mos, quòd cùm animum rebus præsentibus maximè moueri intelligat, ipsos sensus excitet ad eorum contemplationem, per quæ nos seducere conatur. Sic Eua olim fructum vetitum spectauisse dicitur, nimirum ex serpentis sugge-stione, vt eius aspectu, forma & fragrantia ad illius esum vehementius alliceretur. Ita libidinosos ad formas alienas spectandum mouet, & infinitas libidinis illecebras obijcit, quibus abrepti nefa-riæ cupiditati indulgeant. Quod Dauidem expertum fuisse sacra historia testatur, quando Bethsa-bam lauantem conspicatus & eius illicito amore correptus est. Ita auaris opes & spem prædæ fre-quenter proponit, vt æstuantem in illorum animis habendi cupiditatem magis incendat. Ita odio et vindictæ studio flagrantibus eos in conspectu adducit, quos perditos volunt, vt rabiem maiorem illis moueat. Ambitiosos autem plerunq; præsentis gloriæ & splendoris publici conspectu & aulico stre-pitu perstringit, vt de sua gloria augenda attentius cogitent. Et huic tentationi in primis obnoxij sunt, qui in altiori aliquo dignitatis gradu constituti, parasitorum adulatorijs dictis & inanium ti-tulorum ineptissimis repetitionibus inebriantur, & propter potentiam atque authoritatem, quà su-pra alios omnes eminent, sibi nihil non licere putant. Hinc inconsulti regum conatus, quibus & pro-pria regna & exteros populos horribiliter turbant. Hinc diuitum insolentia, qua leges et iura publi-ca euertunt. Hinc episcoporum licentia olim exorta est, qua sibi etiam hodie in ecclesia tyrannidem vendicant. Quò magis adiuigilare opus est omnes eos, qui potentia & authoritate sublimes sunt, ne dum mundi gloriam & delitias otiosi spectant, ambitione superentur, seq; diabolo circumuenien-dos propinent.
units.tr: Let us consider, then, by what craft our enemy went to work when he began to wound the whole human race mortally through the side of Christ. First he took him up into a high, lofty mountain, and in an instant he set all the kingdoms of the earth before his eyes. I do not think this happened merely in imagination. The evangelists relate it as a real event, and such a careful note of place and time seems to indicate exactly that. So although imagination was certainly at work, the splendour of those kingdoms also struck his outward senses, above all his eyes, so as to move more strongly the one whom he knew to have become a true man. Nor do we need to ask here how all the kingdoms of the earth could be seen as if in one moment, and how the sight could be extended across the whole world. We know how effective the devil's illusions are, since even today he is accustomed to present distant things, indeed things done many centuries ago, to be viewed in crystal balls and other magical instruments. And because Christ willed to be tempted on our behalf, he so lowered himself that Satan could in the meantime make use of his senses as well. It is, moreover, the old custom of our enemy that, when he perceives that the mind is most stirred by present things, he excites the senses themselves to contemplate those things by which he tries to seduce us. Thus Eve, it is said, looked upon the forbidden fruit, of course at the serpent's suggestion, so that by its appearance, form and fragrance she might be drawn more strongly to eat it. So he moves the lustful to gaze upon the forms of others, and sets before them countless enticements of lust, by which they are carried away and indulge in wicked desire. Sacred history testifies that David experienced this, when he saw Bathsheba bathing and was seized by illicit love for her. So he often sets before the greedy wealth and the hope of plunder, so as to kindle still more the burning desire of possessing in their minds. So he brings before the eyes of those who burn with hatred and the zeal for revenge the very people they want to destroy, so as to stir up greater fury in them. But the ambitious he usually strikes with the sight of present glory, public splendour and courtly bustle, so that they think more carefully about increasing their own glory. Those most exposed to this temptation are those who, placed in some higher rank of dignity, are intoxicated by the flattering words of parasites and by the most silly repetition of empty titles, and who, on account of the power and authority by which they stand out above all others, think that nothing is forbidden to them. From this come the reckless undertakings of kings, by which they terribly disturb both their own kingdoms and foreign peoples. From this comes the insolence of the rich, by which they overturn laws and public rights. From this came the licence of bishops, which arose long ago and by which even today they claim tyranny for themselves in the Church. All the more, then, must we keep watch over all those who are exalted by power and authority, lest, while they idly gaze upon the glory and delights of the world, they be overcome by ambition and, being deceived, hand themselves over to the devil.

units.la: Non enim contentus est improbus ille oculos spectaculo otioso pauisse, sed quoque verbis ma-gnificis Christum aggreditur. Tibi dabo (inquit) potestatem hanc vniuersam, & gloriam istorum regnorum: nam mihi tradita est, & cuicunq; voluero, do eam, &c. Iam ergo totius orbis dominium Christo pollicetur, & vt pondus promissioni addat, sibi in omnia regna legitimam potestatem esse ait, vt ea pro suo arbitrio & nutu dispensare & transferre possit. At hoc dicendo, non minus tur-piter quàm splendide impudens ardelio mentitur. Constat enim ex scripturis, Deum terræ cœlique dominum esse, qui vt illa gentibus distribuit, & singulas eius partes certis terminis conclusit, ita ipse etiam regna vel seruare, vel transferre, aut etiam euertere solet. Neq; potestate hanc vlli creaturæ vnquam tradidit, præter quam filio suo vnigenito Iesu Christo, vt supra ex Psalmo annotaui-mus; & hoc ipse testatur, quando postq; deuitam mortem dixit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra, &c. Diabolo autem adeò nihil iuris est in res creatas, vt ne porcos quidem pro sua libidine inuadere & perdere potuerit (vt Euangelica historia docet) nisi hoc à Christo supplicitèr impetrauisset. Quod ipsum vniuersa Iobi historia luculentissimè demonstrat. Dicitur quidem prin-ceps huius mundi, sed iniusta vsurpatione titulum hunc obtinuit, cuius illi causam dedit hominis inobedientia, qui sibi delatum à Deo honorem peccando amisit, & diaboli mancipium factus fuit. Non tamen ita homines illius libidini & imperio permisit Deus, vt ipse rerum huius mundi gu-bernacula deseruerit, quin potius is est, qui vt cœlis & terris imperat, ita diabolum quoque frenô suo coercet, ne pro suo arbitrio vel in homines, vel in alias creaturas grassetur. Interim multa ei per mittit interdum, partim vt suorum fidem exploret & spectabiliorem reddat, vt in Iobo, Paulo & similibus videmus: partim vt efficaci illusione, prout digni sunt, impij demententur, & vbi suæ im-pietatis mensuram compleuerunt, pœnas dudum meritas exoluant. Et hinc est, quòd venefici & magisfepe mira quædam & stupenda faciunt, quos impia & sacrilega persuasione eò vsq; Satan inebriat, vt sibi in cœlestes quoq; orbes ius esse arbitrentur, vt nimirum Lunam cœlo deducant, Solis radios extinguant, pluuias & grandines euocent, fulmina & tonitrua moueant, adeoq; elementa omnia perturbent. Sed sunt hæc inanes diaboli præstigiæ, quibus nemo moueri debet; quando non minori sacrilegio sibi istorum potestatem vendicant, quàm quo in præsenti regnorum omnium ius sibi transcribit.
units.tr: For that wicked one was not content merely to feed their eyes with an idle spectacle, but he also attacks Christ with magnificent words. "I will give you," he says, "all this power, and the glory of these kingdoms; for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whomever I will, etc." Now he promises Christ dominion over the whole world, and to add weight to the promise he says that he has lawful power over all kingdoms, so that he can dispense and transfer them at his own pleasure and nod. But in saying this, this shameless busybody lies no less basely than splendidly. For it is plain from the Scriptures that God is the Lord of heaven and earth, who distributes the earth among the nations and confines each of its parts within fixed boundaries, and who likewise is accustomed to preserve, transfer, or even overthrow kingdoms. Nor has he ever given this power to any creature, except to his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, as we noted above from the Psalm; and he himself testifies to this when, after escaping death, he said: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth, etc." But the devil has so little right over created things that he could not even attack and destroy swine at his own pleasure (as the gospel history teaches), unless he had obtained this by entreaty from Christ. The whole history of Job demonstrates this most clearly. It is true that he is called the prince of this world, but he obtained this title by unjust usurpation, the cause of which was given to him by the disobedience of man, who, by sinning, lost the honour delivered to him by God and became a slave of the devil. Yet God did not so hand over men to his lust and command that he himself abandoned the reins of the affairs of this world; rather, it is he who rules heaven and earth, and so he also restrains the devil with his bridle, so that he does not rage at will either against men or against other creatures. Meanwhile God sometimes allows him many things, partly to test the faith of his people and make it more conspicuous, as we see in Job, Paul and similar men; partly so that the wicked, by an effective delusion, as they deserve, may be driven mad, and when they have filled the measure of their impiety, may pay the penalties long since earned. And hence it is that sorcerers and magicians often do certain marvellous and astonishing things, whom Satan so intoxicates with impious and sacrilegious persuasion that they think they have right even over the heavenly spheres, namely that they can draw down the moon from heaven, extinguish the rays of the sun, summon rains and hailstorms, stir up lightnings and thunders, and so disturb all the elements. But these are the empty tricks of the devil, by which no one should be moved; since they claim power over these things with no less sacrilege than that by which he assigns to himself the right over all the kingdoms of the present world.

units.la: Sed conditionem audiamus, sub qua tantum imperium Christo pollicetur. Si tu (inquit) adoraueris me, erunt tua omnia. Adorandi verbo omnia comprehenduntur, quæ ad cultum faciunt, neque hic tam de corporis gestu agitur, quâ de eo, vt Christus relicta Patris vocatione, diabolum audiat, huic obtemperet, credat, seruiat, adeoq; eius beneficio regnum orbis terrarum accipiat, quod ipsi scripturæ promittebant. Vt enim Dei cultus in fide & obedientia potissimum consistit, & qui ista habent, externus quoque ritibus ex Dei verbo institutis animi religionem testantur: ita qui posthabito Dei verbo diaboli promissis fidem habent, eius consiliis & suggestionibus obtemperant, & per illicita media ad honores, opes & reliqua vitæ huius atq; felicitatis præsidia contendunt, ij diabolum ad orare & colere merito dicuntur. Et qui ita affecti sunt, ijdem cultibus quoq; superstitiosis occupantur, simulachra adorant, & ea in religione faciunt, quæ diabolo summam voluptatem afferunt. Itaq; hoc vnum Satan in præsenti effectum cupit, vt Christus à Patris vocatione discedat, & alia, quàm debebat, via ad regni cœlestis possessionem aspiret. Sciebat enim illum per crucem in gloriam patris ingressurum & simul de mundo & omni aduersaria potestate triumphaturum esse. Nam de illo Isaias olim vaticinatus fuerat: Domino placuit ipsum infirmando atterere, vt vbi posuerit animam suam hostiam peccati, videat semen, proroget dies, & voluntas Domini prospere cedat in manu eius. Et Dauid: De torrente in via bibet, & ideo caput extollet. His ergo, ad quæ illum sese præpara re videbat suam sophisticam Satat opponit, quasi diceret: Scio quid de te olim Deus per prophetas promiserit, nec dubito te certa regni promissi fiducia niti. Sed næ stultus nimis es, qui hac via te eò venturum putas, & per ambages assequi conaris non minus laboriosas quàm periculi plenas, ad quod breui & expedito compendio peruenire poteras, si salutaria monentem audire velles. Etenim multorum seculorum experientia constat, nunquam eos ad altiora emergere, sed miserrimos esse mortalium, qui de vocatione nescio qua nimiùm soliciti, omna ad Dei voluntatem & præceptorum suorum regulam instituunt, neque aliquid audent, quod vel latum vnguem ab ea dissentire videtur. Quin ergo tu me audis, qui viam tibi monstrabo planam, breuem, facilem, qua finem tibi propositum attingas. Hæc est, si relicta hac tua vocatione, quam tuipse tibi fingis, me adores, mihi seruias, atque meis monitis obtemperes. Quid autem hac conditione æquius, facilius, honestius? Non aliena, sed quod tibi iure debetur, regnum inuades. Quis de hoc queri, aut istud tibi vitio vertere poterit? Quid, quò minus illud efficias, obstabit? En coram in conspectu sunt regna orbis huius omnia. En ego, qui horum princeps dicor, tibi illa resigno meumq; in ea ius tibi renuntio. Tu igitur iure nunc vtitor, quod & te magis decebit, & tuis erit vtilius multò, quàm si & teipsum & tuos omnes periculis non necessarijs obijcias, &c. Hæc verborum istorum sententia est. Quòd si quæras, seriò ne ista locutus sit Satan, ego eum seriò locutum esse minimè dubitauero. Nam etsi ipsius non erat dare quod pollicebatur, procul dubiò tamen maluisset Christum terrenum Regem & orbis totius dominum, multo auro gemmisq; ornatum & armis fulgentem conspicere, quam in cruce exaltatum, cuius virtute se & regnum suum destructum iri sciebat.
units.tr: But let us hear the condition under which he promises Christ so great a dominion. "If you," he says, "will worship me, all will be yours." By the word worship, all that pertains to worship is comprehended; and here it is not so much a matter of bodily gesture as of this: that Christ, abandoning the calling of the Father, should listen to the devil, obey him, believe him, serve him, and so receive by his favour the kingdom of the world, which the Scriptures themselves promised to him. For just as the worship of God consists chiefly in faith and obedience, and those who have these things also bear witness, by outward rites instituted in God's Word, to the inward devotion of the mind, so those who, setting aside God's Word, put faith in the promises of the devil, obey his counsels and suggestions, and strive by unlawful means for honours, riches and the other supports of this life and of happiness, are rightly said to pray to and worship the devil. And those who are so disposed are also occupied with superstitious rites, they adore images, and they do in religion those things that give the devil the greatest pleasure. So Satan desired this one thing in the present case: that Christ should depart from the calling of the Father, and aspire to the possession of the heavenly kingdom by a way other than he ought. For he knew that Christ would enter into glory by the cross, and at the same time triumph over the world and every hostile power. For Isaiah had long before prophesied concerning him: "It pleased the Lord to crush him by weakness, so that when he has made his soul a sacrifice for sin, he may see his seed, prolong his days, and the will of the Lord may prosper in his hand." And David: "He shall drink of the brook in the way, and therefore shall he lift up his head." Therefore Satan sets his sophistry against those things for which he saw Christ preparing himself, as if he were saying: "I know what God long ago promised about you through the prophets, and I do not doubt that you rest on the sure hope of the promised kingdom. But you are truly foolish, who think you will reach it by this way, and who try to attain it by circuitous paths no less laborious than full of danger, when you could have arrived at it by a short and easy shortcut, if you were willing to hear one who gives you wholesome advice. For the experience of many centuries establishes that those who are overly anxious about some calling they know not what, and arrange everything by the will of God and the rule of his precepts, never rise to higher things, but are the most wretched of mortals, and dare nothing that seems even a hair's breadth to differ from it. Why then do you not hear me, who will show you a way that is level, short and easy, by which you may attain the end you have proposed? It is this: if, abandoning this calling of yours, which you yourself invent for yourself, you worship me, serve me, and obey my admonitions. What could be more just, easier, or more honourable than this condition? You will invade a kingdom not foreign to you, but one owed to you by right. Who will be able to complain about this, or to find fault with you for it? What will stand in the way, so that you do not accomplish it? Behold, the kingdoms of this whole world are here before your eyes. Behold, I, who am called their prince, resign them to you, and renounce my right in them in your favour. Therefore, use now the right that will suit you better and be far more useful to your people, than if you were to expose both yourself and all your people to unnecessary dangers, etc." This is the sense of those words. But if you ask whether Satan spoke these things in earnest, I shall have no doubt that he spoke in earnest. For although it was not his to give what he promised, he would undoubtedly have preferred to see Christ as an earthly king and lord of the whole world, adorned with much gold and jewels and shining in arms, rather than lifted up on the cross, by whose power he knew both himself and his kingdom would be destroyed.

units.la: Quod autem in Christo conatus est, hoc ipsum hodie etiam non vno modo tentare solet, vt nimirum persuadeat, felicitatem omnem in honorum, gloriæ & bonorum huius seculi abundantia consistere, & ita viam cœlestis regni præcludat, quam nobis Christus per crucem aperuit, & quam Paulus æterno Dei decreto sic definitam esse docet, vt primò imagini filij eius conformes efficiamur, quoad crucem & afflictiones, deinde eiusdem coheredes & gloriæ immortalis cum illo consortes simus. Hac ratione episcopos circumuenit Satan, & suis consilijs obsequentes terrarum dominos & ipsis regibus superiores fecit, neque hanc dignitatem illis inuidet, modo ecclesiæ curam negligant, & miserum gregem errorum laqueis atq; scelerum illecebris in exitium abripi patiantur. Eodem stratagemate principes viros & Reges aggreditur, quos partim ad arma excitat, vt vicina regna inuadant, uadant, immerentes populos crudeliter opprimant, caedium, rapinarum, stuprorum, incendiorum & immanissimorum flagitiorum authores sint, & haec agendo illi cultum longe gratissimum exhibeant: partim sub religionis praetextu excaecat, dum per Pontifices ijsdem prope verbis eos solicitat, quibus hic ad Christum vsus est, vt sese superstitionum & idololatriae patronos praebeant, & in dique surgentem Christi doctrinam ferro & igne excindere conentur. Annon enim hodie Pontifi- cum verba sunt: Nostra sunt regna orbis terrarum omnia, nos illa conferendi & transferendi potestatem liberam & absolutam a Christo, cuius vicarij sumus, accepimus? Itaque qui nos adorant, qui ad pedes nostros deosculandos prosternuntur, qui Romanae sedis authoritatem & primatum se defensuros esse iurant, illos in regnis suis confirmabimus, & nostra dignabimur benedictione. Si qui secus fecerint, eos excommunicationis fulmine percussos a sacrorum communione excludemus, & eorundem subditos a fidei ipsis datae vinculo liberabimus, ne illis porro obtemperent. Haec iam seculis aliquot audita esse historici fide digni testantur, & fulmina illa non semel potentissimi Reges & fortissimi Imperatores experti sunt, qui ijsdem vel inuiti succubuerunt olim, cum superstitionum tenebrae omnium mentes adhuc occuparent. Et vtinam non hodie etiam inueniretur, qui vt personatos illos Christi vicarios sibi propitios habeant, ad pedum eorum osculla cernui procumbunt, manifestos abusus tuentur, & in suae fidei creditum populum crudelissime saeviunt. Quid vero apud nobiles & antiquo stemmate claros idem ille impostor iactat? Annon per eosdem interpretes, Nostrae sunt (inquit) Abbatiae omnes, nostri sunt episcopatus, nostra cathedralium ecclesiarum collegia, nos item quoad terrenam iurisdictionem longe latè imperamus? Atqui vestra erunt ista omnia, si nos adorare & Papatum fulcire pergatis. Ex vestris enim filijs alij Abbates, alij Episcopi, alij Canonici creabuntur, vobis praefecturas & quae alia sunt eius generis officia mandabimus, vt generis et familiae veterem splendorem tueri, et ad maiorem dignitatem ascendere possitis. Quae promissa, cum non omnino vana sint, multos movent, vt praeter propriae conscientiae testimonium eos adorent, quos mendaciorum magistros & selecta diaboli organa esse nouerunt. Vt vero omnes hominum ordines simul complectamur, annon apud omnes hoc vnum agit Satan, vt (quod olim Malachiae temporibus quidam dicebant) illorum animis persuadeat: Frustra nimirum seruiri Deo, felices autem & beatos esse, qui sese mundi studijs accommodant, id est, Veneri, Bacho, Marti, Mercurio sacra faciunt, dum libidini, gulae, caedibus, dolis atque impostoris gaudent? Hinc certe communis illa Erinnys regnum obtinuit, qua fit, vt nemo sua sorte contentus vivat, sed ad altiora omnes aspirent, & quod salua pietate obtinere non possunt, cum manifesta Christi ab negatione consequantur. Et hic mons ille sublimis est, in quem quotidie multos subducit Satan: haec eius est iactantia, qua sese adhuc hodie ostentat: hae illius promissiones sunt plus quam aureae, quibus multorum oculos perstringit, vt (quod dictu horrendum est) ad pedes eius denoluti ipsum turpiter adorent.
units.tr: Satan tries the same thing against Christ today, and he does not do it in only one way: he persuades people that all happiness lies in the abundance of honours, glory and the goods of this world, and so he blocks the way to the heavenly kingdom that Christ opened for us through the cross. Paul teaches that by God's eternal decree this way is fixed so that we are first made conformable to the image of his Son in the cross and afflictions, and then become his co-heirs and sharers with him in immortal glory. By this method Satan has gained bishops, and he makes those who follow his counsels lords of the earth, greater than kings themselves. He does not begrudge them this dignity, provided they neglect the care of the Church and allow the wretched flock to be dragged to ruin in the snares of error and the allurements of sin. By the same stratagem he attacks princes and kings. Some he stirs to arms, to invade neighbouring kingdoms, to oppress cruelly innocent peoples, and to be the authors of slaughter, plunder, rape, arson and the most monstrous crimes, and by doing these things they offer him the worship most pleasing of all. Others he blinds under the pretext of religion, while through the Popes he urges them with almost the same words that Satan used with Christ, to make themselves patrons of superstition and idolatry, and to try to cut down with sword and fire the doctrine of Christ rising up everywhere. For are not these the words of the Popes today: All the kingdoms of the earth are ours, and we have received from Christ, whose vicars we are, the free and absolute power to confer and transfer them? Therefore those who worship us, who prostrate themselves to kiss our feet, who swear that they will defend the authority and primacy of the Roman see, we will confirm in their kingdoms and deign to bless with our benediction. If any act otherwise, we will strike them with the thunderbolt of excommunication, exclude them from communion with the sacred things, and free their subjects from the bond of the faith given to them, so that they no longer obey them. Trustworthy historians testify that these things were heard many centuries ago, and that the most powerful kings and the bravest emperors have more than once felt those thunderbolts, and that they sometimes succumbed to them, even against their will, when the darkness of superstition still held all minds. And would that today too there were not found men who, in order to have those masked vicars of Christ favourable to them, bow down to kiss their feet, defend manifest abuses, and rage most cruelly against the people entrusted to their faith. What does that same impostor boast among the nobles and those famous for ancient lineage? Does he not say, through the same interpreters: All the abbeys are ours, the bishoprics are ours, the colleges of the cathedral churches are ours, and we also rule far and wide in earthly jurisdiction? Yet all these things will be yours, if you continue to worship us and to uphold the Papacy. For from your sons some will be made abbots, some bishops, some canons; we will entrust to you prefectures and other offices of that kind, so that you may preserve the old splendour of your race and family and rise to greater dignity. These promises, since they are not altogether empty, move many people to worship, against the testimony of their own conscience, those whom they know to be teachers of lies and chosen instruments of the devil. And to embrace all orders of men together: does Satan not everywhere pursue this one aim, to persuade their minds (as some used to say in the time of Malachi) that it is vain to serve God, and that those are happy and blessed who accommodate themselves to worldly pursuits, that is, who sacrifice to Venus, Bacchus, Mars and Mercury, while they delight in lust, gluttony, slaughter, fraud and imposture? From this surely that common Fury has obtained her kingdom, so that no one lives content with his lot, but all aspire to higher things, and what they cannot obtain without losing godliness, they obtain by manifest denial of Christ. And that is the lofty mountain to which Satan daily leads many; this is his boasting, by which he still shows himself off today; these are his promises, more than golden, by which he dazzles the eyes of many, so that (a horrible thing to say) they fall down at his feet and shamefully worship him.

units.la: Praestat ergo Christum videre & audire, vt quibus armis haec tela eludere & hostem vincere possimus, nobis constet. Abscede a me (inquit) Satana. Scriptum est enim, Adorabis Dominium Deum tuum, & ei soli seruies. Habet responsio ista partes duas. Prima cum indignatione diabolum reijcit, vt quem porro audire nefas sit. Antea quidem mitius responderat, quia sufficiebat certum & euidens fidei in Deum argumentum contra diffidentiae telum produxisse. At quia nunc manifesta impietas iubetur, nullum modestiae locum amplius reliquum esse videt, & ideo qui natura mitissimus est, in vocem istam iustae indignationis plenam erumpit. Idem videmus factum ab eo fuisse, si quando ei cum illis res fuit, qui cum manifesta nominis diuini prophanatione infelicem populum seducebant, & veritatis doctrinam extinguere conabantur. Quem animum in Apostolis quoque fuisse constat, si quando honorem Dei vel in seipsos, vel in alios translatum esse viderunt: vt in Pauli & Barnabae exemplo apud Lystrenses edito est videre. Quibus exemplis docemur patientia minime tunc vtendum esse, quando Dei cultus in periculum venit, & ad impiam Dei abnegationem solicitamur. Feruet enim zelo diuinae gloriae fides, & vt in proprijs iniurijs ferendis patientissimos facit, ita impatientissimos reddit eorum, quae gloriae Dei aliquid derogant, aut nos impediunt, quo minus nostrum officium illi praestemus. Minime ergo audiri debent lepidi illi, qui in vtrumque latus claudicare didicerunt, & vt proximum quodque periculum declinent, ea quoque sub Christianae patientiæ prætextu admittunt, quæ cum manifesta veræ fidei atque cultus diuini abnegatione sunt coniuncta.
units.tr: It is therefore better to see and hear Christ, so that we may know with what weapons we can parry these darts and conquer the enemy. Get away from me, Satan, he says. For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him only. This answer has two parts. The first rejects the devil with indignation, as one whom it is wrong to listen to any longer. Earlier, indeed, he had answered more gently, because it was enough to bring forward the sure and evident proof of faith in God against the weapon of distrust. But now, since a manifest impiety is being commanded, he sees that there is no longer any room for moderation, and so he, who is by nature most gentle, bursts out into a word full of just indignation. We see that he did the same whenever he had to deal with those who, with a manifest profaning of the divine name, led an unhappy people astray and tried to extinguish the doctrine of truth. It is certain that the apostles too felt this way whenever they saw the honour of God transferred to themselves or to others, as can be seen in the example of Paul and Barnabas at Lystra. From these examples we are taught that patience must by no means be used when the worship of God is in danger and we are urged toward the impious denial of God. For faith glows with zeal for the divine glory, and just as it makes us most patient in bearing our own injuries, so it makes us most impatient of anything that detracts from the glory of God or hinders us from performing our duty to him. Therefore those charming men must by no means be listened to, who have learned to limp to both sides, and who, to avoid every nearby danger, admit under the pretext of Christian patience even those things that are joined with a manifest abandonment of true faith and of the worship of God.

units.la: Altera parte ad diaboli tentationem respondet, & rursus huic Dei verbum ex scripturis desumptum opponit. Ita vero docet, non credendum esse diaboli promissionibus, vt neque eiusdem minis pios terreri conuenit. Nam etsi magnifice suas opes iactet, & vires quoque terribiliter ostentet, revera tamen (vt Christus ipse monuit) mendax & mendacij pater est. Itaque eos, qui ipsum audiunt, splendidis promissis demulcere & spe multa implere solet, sed quæ infelices tunc miserè fallit, quando res ipsa serio agitur. Exemplum huius perfidiæ cumprimis miserabile in primis parentibus edidit, quibus cum diuinitatis spem amplissimam fecisset, eosdem in extremas ignominias & miseriæ angustias coniecit, in quibus posteri omnes adhuc luctantur. Sic Caino orbis totius dominium pollicitus, eidem author fuit, vt à facie Domini eiceretur: & quamuis vrbe extructa cum posteritate sua florere & regnare videretur, ea tamen diluuij aquis in vniuersum tandem deleta est, superstite filiorum Dei progenie, quam per Noam ille beneficio arcæ conseruauit. Quo vero Saulem suis suggestionibus adduxerit, & infinitos alios, qui regnum quærentes fortunæ ludibrium facti sunt, longum esset commemorare. Atqui eandem comminationum eius rationem esse, contraria his piorum exempla docent, quos mirificis turbis & periculis sæpe terruit, ex quibus tamen feliciter, & magna cum gloria eluctati sunt: quales fuerunt Ioseph, Moses, Dauid, Ezechias, Daniel & innumeri alij, quos breuitatis causa omittimus. Itaque contemptis mendacissimi huius Thrasonis promissionibus simul atque minis, nos vnum Deum audiamus, qui vt ipsa est veritas, ita Verbum eius æternum & immutabile manet, etiamsi cæli corruant & terræ fundamenta loco moueantur.
units.tr: In the second part he answers the devil's temptation, and again opposes to him a word of God taken from Scripture. He teaches that the promises of the devil are not to be believed, and that it is not fitting for the godly to be terrified by his threats either. For although he boasts magnificently of his wealth, and displays his power in a fearsome way, in truth (as Christ himself warned) he is a liar and the father of lies. Therefore he is accustomed to soothe those who listen to him with splendid promises and to fill them with many hopes, but he wretchedly deceives the unhappy when the matter is seriously at stake. He gave a most miserable example of this treachery especially in our first parents: after he had held out to them the widest hope of becoming like God, he cast them into the utmost disgrace and the straits of misery, in which all their posterity still struggle. So too, after promising Cain dominion over the whole world, he was the author of his being cast out from the face of the Lord; and although, with his posterity, he seemed to flourish and reign once a city had been built, that city was at last utterly destroyed by the waters of the flood, though the race of the sons of God survived, which Noah preserved by the benefit of the ark. It would be a long task to recount how he led Saul by his suggestions, and countless others who, seeking a kingdom, became the sport of fortune. But that his method of threatening is the same, the examples of the godly, which show the opposite, teach us. He has often terrified them with wonderful disturbances and dangers, yet from these they escaped happily and with great glory: such as Joseph, Moses, David, Hezekiah, Daniel and innumerable others, whom we omit for the sake of brevity. Therefore, having despised the promises and threats of this most lying braggart Thraso, let us listen to the one God, who, as he is truth itself, so his Word remains eternal and unchangeable, even if the heavens fall and the foundations of the earth are moved from their place.

units.la: At quoad scripturæ locum, quo Christus vtitur, extat in Deuteron. quinto Cap. vbi Moses veræ pietatis officia ex ordine recensens, inter alia ait: Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & ei seruies. Timendi autem verbum in adorandi Christus conuertit, vt præsenti instituto locus hic melius conueniat. Neque ideo scripturas vel corrumpit, vel violenter detorquet, sed potius illustrat & exponit. Ita enim coniuncta sunt adoratio & timor dei, vt neutrum sine altero possit consistere. Qui enim Deum vere timet, eundem cultu debito prosequetur, cuius cum pars præcipua sit adoratio, eam negligere non poterit. Rursus illum ex animo non adorabit, qui non serio & ingenuo eius timore afficitur. De suo autem addit Christus particulam SOLI: & hoc etiam merito. Quia enim Deus vnus est & idem zelotes atque honoris sui vindex acerrimus est, neque adorationem neque quencunq; alium cultum recipiet, nisi qui ei soli impenditur. Cæterum comprehendunt duo ista omnes diuini cultus & religionis partes. Ad adorationem enim siue inuocationem interna omnia vnà cum precibus & gratiarum actione referri possunt. Altero membro vniuersa alia pietatis exercitia continentur. Summa autem & finis huius præcepti est, apud vnum Deum quarenda esse, quæcunque ad hominis incolumitatem atque salutem faciunt, & proinde illum quoq; solum adorari & inuocari debere, adhæc nulli creaturæ quantumuis nobili & præstanti tribuenda esse, quæ Deus ad suum cultum instituit. Rationes huius sententiæ alibi produximus, neque eas hic repetere opus est, quando vnius Christi authoritas Christianis hominibus omnium argumentorum loco esse debet. Sufficit ergo locus hic confutandis omnibus, qui Diuorum inuocatione & cultum stabilire satagunt. Quærunt quidem illi effugium, quo se expediant, hic nimirum de diaboli adoratione agi, quam nemo sanæ mentis probare possit, & Mosem cum ista scriberet, ad gentium Deos respexisse, quos alibi scriptura dæmones dicit, & proinde locum hunc malitiosè nimis contra Diuos cælites proferri, qui & olim fidei Dei cultores fuerint, & nunc in cælis cum Christo viuant & regnent. Audimus quidem ista, neq; inficiamur Christo cum malo dæmone, Mosi autem cum gentium Dijs negotium fuisse: at simul dicimus præcepto hoc, ipso Christo interprete, cultum & adorationem omnem ita vni Deo vendicari, vt omnes aliæ res creatæ, tã bonæ quàm malæ excludantur. Nam ab vniuersali ad particulare argumentatur: Nemo præter vnum Deum adorari debet, ergo diabolum adorare nefas est. Quoad ergo antecedens ratum manet, eodem argumento omnium aliorum inuocatio prohibetur. Ideo Augustinus inter angelos bonos & malos discernere docebat, quod hi quidem Dei cultu vel sibi ipsis vendicarent, vel in alios transferre iuberent, illi vero homines in vnius Dei cultu atq; inuocatione retinerent. Sufficiant hæc nobis ne dum nimis religiosi esse volumus, animas nostras turpi fornicatione polluamus, & in illos ipsos iniurij simus, qui Dei cultum & invocationem proprio sanguine olim asseruerunt. Opponamus autem hoc dictum diabolo, quoties nos per avaritiam, ambitionem, superbiam, aut quascunque alias cupiditates ad defectionem solicitat. Adoremus autem & colamus unum Deum in spiritu & veritate per Iesum Christum, Mediatorem Dei & hominum unicum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: As for the passage of Scripture that Christ uses, it is found in Deuteronomy, chapter 5, where Moses, listing in order the duties of true piety, says among other things: "You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him." Christ changes the word "fear" to "worship," so that this place fits the present purpose better. He does not thereby corrupt the Scriptures or twist them by force; rather he clarifies and expounds them. For worship and the fear of God are so bound together that neither can stand without the other. He who truly fears God will also serve him with due worship, and since worship is its chief part, he cannot neglect it. Again, no one will worship God from the heart who is not seriously and sincerely moved by his fear. Christ, moreover, adds the particle "only" to the text of his own accord, and rightly so. For since God is one, and is a jealous God and the most zealous avenger of his own honour, he will accept neither worship nor any other service except that which is offered to him alone. Indeed these two words comprise all the parts of divine worship and religion. All inner acts, together with prayers and thanksgiving, can be referred to worship or invocation. The second part contains all the other exercises of piety. The sum and purpose of this precept is that whatever contributes to a person's safety and salvation is to be sought from the one God alone; accordingly he alone is to be worshipped and invoked, and nothing that God has appointed for his own worship is to be given to any creature, however noble and excellent. We have set out the reasons for this view elsewhere, and there is no need to repeat them here, since the authority of Christ alone ought to be, for Christians, in place of all arguments. This passage is therefore sufficient to refute all who labour to establish the invocation and worship of the saints. They do seek a way out for themselves: here, they say, it is plainly a matter of worshipping the devil, which no sane person could approve; and when Moses wrote these words he had in view the gods of the nations, whom Scripture elsewhere calls demons; so this passage is maliciously brought forward against the heavenly saints, who were once worshippers of God's faith and now live and reign with Christ in heaven. We hear these claims, and we do not deny that Christ had to do with the evil demon, and Moses with the gods of the nations. But at the same time we say that, with Christ himself as interpreter, this precept claims all worship and adoration for the one God so completely that every other created thing, whether good or evil, is excluded. For he argues from the universal to the particular: no one ought to be worshipped except the one God; therefore it is wrong to worship the devil. So long as the antecedent stands, by the same argument the invocation of all others is forbidden. For this reason Augustine taught that good and evil angels are to be distinguished in this way: the evil ones either claim worship for themselves or order it to be transferred to others, whereas the good ones keep people in the worship and invocation of the one God. Let these things suffice for us; let us not, while wishing to be too scrupulous, pollute our souls with shameful fornication, and let us not be unjust to those very men who once defended the worship and invocation of God with their own blood. Let us oppose this saying to the devil whenever he tempts us to desertion through avarice, ambition, pride, or any other desires. But let us worship and serve the one God in spirit and in truth, through Jesus Christ, the one Mediator between God and men: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIX.

units.la: Tunc duxit eum Hierosolymam, & eum statuit supra pinnas templi, & dixit ei: Si Filius Dei es, iace teipsum hinc deorsum. Scriptum est enim: Angelis suis mandabit de te, ut custodiant te: & ut in manibus tollant te, ne quando offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum. Respondens autem Iesus dixit ei: Dictum est, Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Et finita omni tentatione, diabolus abscessit ab eo ad tempus.
units.tr: Then the devil took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here. For it is written: 'He shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone.'" Jesus answered him: "It has been said, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God.'" And when every temptation was finished, the devil departed from him for a time.

units.la: Multa quidem & grauia pericula miseros mortales in vitae huius curriculo exercent, at omnium grauissimum est, quod (ut Paulus scribit) nobis non solum adversus carnem & sanguinem luctla est, sed adversus imperia & potestates & dominos tenebrarum seculi huius, id est, adversus malos spiritus, qui mundi imperium sibi vendicat, & qui omnes homines aeterno exitio, cui ipsi iam olim destinati sunt, demergere conantur. Quorum astutia ut profunda nimis est & ineffabilis, ita indefesso studio saluti nostrae insidias struunt, & quamuis saepissime repellantur, pugnam tamen subinde instaurant. Opus ergo adversus illos armis idoneis & invicta fidei constantia, ne eorum telis prostrati salutis nostrae iacturam faciamus. Praecipua tamen victoriae spes nobis in Christo Iesu esse debet, qui ut nostri causa in mundum venit & propter nos egestatem, infamiam & dirum mortis supplicium sustinuit: ita propter nos tentationibus quoque Satanicis sefesubiecit, cum ut hostem illum vinceret, qui hucusque invictus videri poterat, tum ut suo exemplo nos eundem vincere doceret. Utilissimum ergo fuerit omnes historiae huius partes diligenter inspexisse, ut primo quidem hostis istius pugnam subinde instaurantis improbitas nos ad vigilantiam excitet: deinde vero Christi constantia fidem nostram confirmet, nosque ad omnem euentum intrepidos reddat. Restat autem tertius huius certaminis congressus, quem eodem, quo priores, ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: Many grave dangers trouble wretched mortals in the course of this life, but the most serious of all is what Paul writes: that our struggle is not only against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, the powers, and the world-rulers of this darkness, that is, against evil spirits, who claim dominion over the world and try to plunge all people into the eternal ruin for which they themselves were long ago destined. Their cunning is so deep and unspeakable that they lay snares for our salvation with tireless zeal, and although they are very often repelled, they renew the fight again and again. We must therefore oppose them with suitable weapons and an unconquerable constancy of faith, so that we do not, struck down by their missiles, suffer the loss of our salvation. Yet our chief hope of victory must rest in Christ Jesus, who for our sake came into the world and endured poverty, disgrace, and the dreadful punishment of death. In the same way, for our sake, he submitted himself to Satanic temptations, both so that he might conquer that enemy who might have seemed until then invincible, and so that by his own example he might teach us to conquer him too. It will therefore be most useful to examine carefully all the parts of this story: first, so that the wickedness of this enemy, who renews the fight from time to time, may rouse us to watchfulness; and then so that Christ's constancy may strengthen our faith and make us fearless in every outcome. There remains the third encounter of this conflict, which we shall examine in the same order as the earlier ones.

units.la: Nam rursus prior ad pugnam redit Satan, & diversa plane via Christum aggreditur. Qui enim prius eum neque diffidentiae telo sternere, neque ambitione & regnandi cupiditate ab officio, quod Deo omnes debemus, abstrahere potuit, iam prioribus contraria arma profert, & inani confidentia eum inebriari studet, ut ea elatus extra suae vocationis fines egrediatur, & sibi ipsi exitium ante tempus accersat. Id vero facit ex ipsius responsionibus occasione sumpta: Quia enim videbat Christum de Patris erga se voluntate nihil dubitare, & proinde cultus quoque, qui illi debetur, studiosissimum esse: mox eum Hierosolymam deductum supra templi pinnas statuit, & hisce verbis eum solicitat. Agedum si tam certo tibi constat, te Dei filium esse, cur hactenus in obscuro Galilaeae oppido latuisti? cur circa artificium sordidum & ignobile fuisti occupatus? cur a baptismo in desertum abiisti, ubi nulla declarandae tuae maiestatis & divinae potentiae occasio tibi data fuit? Quin nunc tandem in loco totius orbis celeberrimo qui sis publice testaris, & ad hoc tibi oblata occasione actutum uteris? En in templi fastigio constiisti, & in te omnium oculi coniecti sunt. Quin ergo animoso saltu te e sublimi in terram deiicis, ut omnes intelligant, te Dei filium illum dilectum esse, si in tam alto & praecipiti casu incolumis seruaris? Nec est quod periculum aliquod timeas, quando scis, quid de te olim David vaticinatus sit: fore nimirum, ut Deus Angelis suis mandata det, ut te custodiant, imo manibus tollant & gestent, ne pedes ad lapidem aliquem offendas. Si ergo tanta apud te est scripturarum authoritas, ut earum dictis constanter insistendum esse putes, decet certe vt huic quoq; promissioni fidem habeas, & illa fretus tuae diuinitatis specimen ædas. Nam si id detrectes, non modò illius existimatio tibi periclitabitur, sed & fides tua in dubium veniet, quam hactenus tanta cum fiducia professus es, & c. Hæc verborum istorum sententia atq; summa est. Quid autem his quærit Satan? Hoc nimirum quod ante diximus, vt temeraria & ambitiosa magis quam sancta fiducia propriæ dignitatis & diuinæ protectionis inflatus, seipsum absq; Dei vocatione in periculum non necessarium coniiciat, & paternæ erga se voluntatis Dei experimentum capiet, vbi minimè opus erat, & quod sine manifesta impietate nō poterat fieri. Sed vtile fuerit singula, quæ hīc fecit & dixit Satan, diligentius excutere.
units.tr: For again Satan returns first to the fight, and approaches Christ by a quite different route. Since he could neither strike him down with the weapon of distrust, nor draw him away by ambition and lust for power from the duty that we all owe to God, he now brings out weapons opposite to the earlier ones, and strives to puff him up with empty confidence, so that, lifted up by it, he would go beyond the limits of his calling and bring destruction upon himself before the appointed time. He does this by seizing an occasion from Christ's own answers. For since he saw that Christ had no doubt about the Father's will toward him, and therefore that he was most eager in the worship that is due to him, he soon led him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and urged him with these words: "Come now, if it is so certain to you that you are the Son of God, why have you hitherto lain hidden in an obscure town of Galilee? Why have you been occupied with a sordid and humble trade? Why after your baptism did you go off into the desert, where you were given no opportunity to declare your majesty and divine power? Indeed, now at last, in the most famous place in the whole world, why not publicly bear witness to who you are, and make use at once of the opportunity offered to you? See, you have stood on the summit of the temple, and the eyes of all are fixed upon you. Why then do you not leap boldly from this height down to the earth, so that everyone may understand that you are that beloved Son of God, if you are kept safe after so high and so dangerous a fall? Nor have you any reason to fear peril, since you know what David once prophesied about you: namely, that God would give his angels charge to guard you, indeed would lift you in their hands and bear you, so that you would not strike your foot against any stone. If, then, the authority of the Scriptures is so great with you that you think you must stand firmly by their words, it is surely fitting that you also trust this promise, and relying on it, display a proof of your divinity. For if you refuse, not only will your reputation be endangered, but your faith too, which you have hitherto professed with such confidence, will be called into doubt, and so on." This is the sense and summary of those words. But what does Satan seek by them? Surely just what we said before: that, puffed up by a rash and ambitious confidence rather than a holy trust in his own dignity and divine protection, he should cast himself into unnecessary danger without God's calling, and should test the Father's will toward him where there was no need, and where it could not be done without plain impiety. But it will be useful to examine more carefully each thing that Satan did and said here.

units.la: Primò duxit Christum Hierosolymam, quam Matthæus ciuitatem sanctam dicit. Etsi enim illic dominarentur impij magistratus & Sacerdotes, ambitione atque odio doctrinæ purioris infames, in ea tamen Deus cultus sui sedem constituerat, & reliquæ adhuc erant piorum reliquiæ, ex quibus ecclesiam oportebat instaurari. Et hæc ratio est, propter quam ecclesiæ etiam hodie sanctæ dicuntur, quàmuis multi in eis hypocritæ, multi etiam palàm flagitiosi inueniantur: quod si Anabaptistæ obseruaret aliquanto attentius, minus temerarij essent in damnandis ecclesijs, quæ aliqua labe aut vitio laborant. Cæterum Hierosolymæ nō Prætorium, non Antoniam aut quemuis alium locum ædit iorem ad certamen hoc sibi delegit Diabolus, sed ipsum templum Domini, & in huius sastigio summo Christum statuit. Ita verò omnem suspicionem procul remouere conatus est. Quis enim in templo, & quidem eo, de quo promissiones Dei præstantissimæ extabat, sibi à diaboli insidijs aut periculo impietatis timeret? Sed vt omni tempore in armis esset ille, ita nullus locus nos ab eius insidijs tutos reddit. Et quod in Christo conatus est, hoc ipsum multi quotidie sentiunt. Sic eos maximè oppugnat, qui in ecclesiæ sastigio constituti, propter eximiam dignitatem animis suis efferuntur: & non raro fit, vt dum illi æquò confidentiores sibi ipsis immunitatem vendicant, sequè propter muneris ecclesiastici dignitatem extra omne erroris aut grauioris lapsus periculum constitutos putant, semetipsos non sine publico totius ecclesiæ malo præcipites dent. Sic in Apocalypsi stellæ de cælo cecidisse dicuntur, Episcopi nimirum, quos sua confidentia decepit, vt relictā rerum cœlestium cura huius seculi honores & imperia ambire coeperint, quæ ipsis turpissimæ ruinæ causa fuit. Et vtinam non hodie multi horum similes essent, quos suæ conditionis fiducia eò vsque extollit, vt non solùm in propria vita & moribus, verumetiam in doctrina & cultu Dei quibus sibi permittant, leges figant & refigant, adeoque pro libidine sua omnia faciant. Sed & priuatos homines hic maximè aggreditur diabolus, vt inter media sacra vanis cogitationibus indulgeant, vestium luxu & oculorum lasciuia atque gestibus incompositis ecclesiam offendant. Multos autem Euangelij fiducia inani excæcat, vt propter huius professionem sibi nihil non impunè licere putent. Et hi omnes, dum supra communem hominum sortem in gradum aliquem ecclesiæ Dei se euectos esse sibi persuadent, non procul à lapsu absunt, qui illis tanto grauior accidit, quò altius efferuntur.
units.tr: First, he led Christ to Jerusalem, which Matthew calls the holy city. For although wicked magistrates and priests, notorious for ambition and hatred of purer doctrine, ruled there, God had nevertheless established the seat of his worship in that city, and there still remained some remnants of the godly, from whom the Church had to be restored. This is the reason why churches are even today called holy, although many hypocrites, and many openly wicked people, are found among them. If the Anabaptists observed this a little more carefully, they would be less rash in condemning churches that suffer from some stain or fault. Yet the devil did not choose for this contest the Praetorium, the Antonia, or any other more prominent place, but the very temple of the Lord, and he set Christ on its highest summit. Thus he tried to remove every suspicion. For who in the temple, and indeed in that temple of which God had given the most excellent promises, would fear the devil's snares or danger of impiety? But just as he is always armed, so no place makes us safe from his snares. And what he attempted against Christ, many feel every day. He most of all attacks those who are placed on the summit of the Church, and who are puffed up in their minds by their outstanding dignity. And it often happens that, while they claim immunity for themselves with excessive confidence, and think that because of the dignity of their ecclesiastical office they are placed beyond all danger of error or of graver fall, they hurl themselves headlong, not without public harm to the whole Church. So in the Apocalypse stars are said to have fallen from heaven: namely bishops, whom their own confidence deceived, so that, abandoning the care of heavenly things, they began to seek the honours and dominions of this world, which brought them the most shameful ruin. And would that today there were not many like them, whom confidence in their own position lifts up so far that they not only set and unset laws for their own life and conduct, but also for doctrine and for the worship of God, as they please, and do everything at their own whim. But the devil also attacks private persons here above all, so that in the midst of sacred things they indulge in vain thoughts, and offend the Church by luxury in clothing, wanton eyes, and unseemly gestures. Many, moreover, the empty confidence of the gospel blinds, so that they think it is permitted to them with impunity to do anything at all because of their profession of it. And all of these, while they persuade themselves that they have been raised above the common lot of humanity to some rank in the Church of God, are not far from a fall, which comes to them all the more grievously the higher they have been lifted up.

units.la: Quid verò iubet aut suadet Christo diabolus? Si Filius Dei es (inquit) iace te hinc deorsum. Repetit quod in primo congressu dixerat, Si Filius Dei es: & est repetitio hæc admodum vehemens & acuta. Nam & cœlestem vocem in dubium vocat, & fiduciam Patris cœlestis exprobrat, idque in eum finem, vt temerario ausu abreptus confidentia peccet, vt supra dictum est. Latet ergo sub his admirabile diaboli artificium, qui ita hanc tentationem temperauit, vt aut diffidentia aut confidentia necessariò peccaturus videretur Christus. Si enim quod iubetur facere detrectet, iā Dei Patris oraculo & veteribus promissis diffidere dicetur. Sin verò obtemperet, Deum tentabit, & simul confidens nimium sibi ipsi exitiū afferet. Vtrinq; autem cōcurrit gloriæ studium, quā nullo iure negligere posse videbatur, cum simul & patris gloria & humani generis salus in periculū venirēt. At dum gloriam Christi prouehere videtur, illi infamiam et interitum struit. Quo loco Satanæ ingenium à diuino diuersum, & huic prorsus contrarium apparet. Dei enim proprium est suos humiliare & deprimere, vt mox cum gloria vera & immortali exaltentur: vt in multorum exemplis est videre, quæ alibi commemorauimus. Et contra diabolus in altum euehi, aut saltè nos in summo gloriæ fastigio constitutos esse nobis persuadere conatur, vt postea præcipites det et sempiterno exitio demergat. Quod sapientissimus ille mortalium Solomon olim obseruauit, cùm diceret: Ante contritionē est superbia, & ruinam præcedit spiritus elatio. Et ideo mox infert: Melior est humilitas spiritus cum abiectis, quàm dividere spolia cum superbis. Exempla quibus ista confirmentur, passim occurrunt. Hoc enim primos parentes suo malo & communi totius posteritatis ruina expertes fuisse scimus. Passi sunt idem, qui post diluvium turrim Babel ædificaturi mox admirabili & ridicula linguarum diuisione impediti sunt. De Senacheribo autem Assyriorum tyranno quid dicere attinet? Qui enim Orientem totum vastarat, gentium fines sustulerat, & de ipsis Diis abs se deiectis gloriabatur, repente amisso exercitu profugus domi suæ à proprijs filijs iugulatur, & publicum confidentiæ exemplum factus est, quod Ægyptij statua publica posteritati commendarunt, cum in scriptione: Qui me intuetur, pius esto. Idem de Balthazare & Nabuchodonosore, Babyloniorum regibus, dici poterat. Quid de Sylla dicemus, qui cùm seipsum Felicem, Filium verò Faustum diceret, mox è summo honoris & potentiæ gradu deiectus fœdo morbo periit, nominis verò memoriam bonis omnibus detestabilem reliquit? At quid exemplis veteribus opus est, quando multa huius generis priuatim & publicè accidunt? Nobis autem horum omnium vsus sit, vt arrogantes illas animi persuasiones, quas Satan suggerit, in tempore restinguamus, ne dum ijs ad tempus cum aliqua voluptatula indulgemus, nobis graviorùm ruinæ causa sint.
units.tr: But what does the devil urge or suggest to Christ? "If you are the Son of God," he says, "throw yourself down from here." He repeats what he had said at the first encounter, "If you are the Son of God." This repetition is very forceful and sharp. For he calls the heavenly voice into doubt and taunts Christ with his heavenly Father's trust, aiming to make him sin through rash presumption, as was said above. Hidden under these words lies the devil's remarkable craft. He so framed this temptation that Christ seemed bound to sin either by distrust or by presumption. If Christ refused to do what he was told, he would be said to distrust both the Father's oracle and the old promises. But if he complied, he would be tempting God, and at the same time, by reckless confidence, would bring ruin upon himself. In either case the desire for glory comes into play, which Christ seemed to have no right to neglect, since both the Father's glory and the salvation of mankind were at stake. Yet while he seems to advance the glory of Christ, he is preparing his disgrace and destruction. Here the devil's character appears as different from God's and altogether opposed to it. For it is God's proper work to humble and cast down his own, so that they may afterwards be exalted with true and immortal glory, as may be seen in many examples which we have mentioned elsewhere. The devil, on the other hand, tries to lift men up on high, or at least to persuade us that we stand at the very summit of glory, so that afterwards he may throw us headlong and plunge us into everlasting destruction. The wisest of mortals, Solomon, long ago observed this when he said: "Before destruction pride goes, and before a fall a haughty spirit." And so he immediately adds: "Better is a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide spoils with the proud." Examples confirming these things occur everywhere. We know that our first parents were not spared, to their own harm and the common ruin of all their posterity. The same happened to those who after the flood set out to build the tower of Babel and were soon checked by the marvellous and ridiculous division of tongues. What need is there to speak of Sennacherib, the tyrant of the Assyrians? He had laid waste the whole East, abolished the boundaries of nations, and boasted of the gods themselves that he had cast down; yet, having suddenly lost his army, he fled home and was slain by his own sons, and became a public example of overconfidence. The Egyptians commended this to posterity in a public statue with the inscription: "Whoever looks upon me, let him be pious." The same could be said of Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar, kings of the Babylonians. What shall we say of Sulla, who called himself "Felix" and his son "Faustus," and yet was soon cast down from the highest rung of honour and power, died of a foul disease, and left a name detestable to all good men? But why need we old examples, when many things of this kind happen privately and publicly every day? Let us use all these instances so that we may quench in time those arrogant persuasions which Satan suggests, lest, while we indulge them for a while with some small pleasure, they become the cause of our far greater ruin.

units.la: In primis autem in hoc congressu consideratione peculiarem meretur, quòd scripturæ testimonio Satan vti voluit, nimirum vt scripturis pugnantem Christum armis suis spoliaret. Vbi num audaciam eius, vel audacem impudentiam magis admirere incertum est. Quid enim astutum magis fingi potest, quàm scripturis, quæ fidei & pietatis doctrinam continent, ad persuadendam impietatem abuti posse? Quid verò audacius, impudentius & proterius, quàm eum gladium in manus sumere, quem vnicè odit, & cuius fulgorem ne eminus quidem ferre potest? Quantam autem confidentiam dicemus, quòd scripturis aduersus eum pugnat, cuius spiritum illas dictauisse non poterat ignorare? Sed audiamus quàm confidenter & artificiosè eas adducat. Scriptum est (ait) Angelis suis mandabit de te, vt custodiant te, & quòd in manibus tollent te, ne quando offendas ad lapidem pedum tuum. Extat locus ille Psal.91. quem nonnulli à Davide compositum esse putant, cùm Deus populum Israeliticum immani peste puniret, quæ intra triduum septuaginta millia virorum absumpsit. Et non male cum horum sententia conuenit, quod in illo de peste in tenebris grassante & luce meridiana scribitur. Commendat autem illic spiritus sanctus diuinæ prouidentiæ protectionem, quà pij & credentes in quouis periculo tuti & incolumes seruantur, & inter alia dicit: Non accedet tibi malum, neq; plaga tabernaculo tuo appropinquabit. Nam angelis suis de te mandabit, vt in omnibus viis tuis te custodiant. Manibus te gestabunt, ne ad lapidem pes tuus impingat, &c. Vere ergo in scripturis sacris habetur quod Satan dicit: sed quod illic rectè & piè dicitur, improbus ille impostor ad sensum alienum & impiû detorquet. Illic enim Spiritus sanctus de ijs loquitur, qui Dei vocationem sequuntur, & in vijs suis, id est, à Deo sibi præscriptis ambulant. Diabolus autem promissionem illam ad omnes simpliciter extendit, & quidem ad eos quoque, qui vel impia confidentia, vel quauis alia temeraria cupiditate abrepti in pericula non necessaria sese conjiciunt. Et ideo plus quam sacrilega temeritate particulam illam (In omnibus vijs tuis) omittit. Nec enim via Christi aut Patris vocatio erat, vt è pinna templi se præcipitem daret, aut alijs miraculis, periculosis quidem ad nihil autem vtilibus (vt agyrtæ & circulatores solent) diuinæ suæ gloriæ & virtutis argumentum præberet. Est ergo hoc exemplum probè nobis obseruandum, ne mentione scripturarum oculos nobis perstringi patiamur, sed potius probemus omnia, ne vel ipsius diaboli vel organorum eius fallacijs nos subducendos præbeamus.
units.tr: Above all, in this encounter, something deserves special consideration: Satan wished to use the testimony of Scripture, clearly so that he might strip Christ, who was fighting with Scripture, of his own weapons. It is uncertain whether we should marvel more at his audacity or at his shameless boldness. For what can be contrived more craftily than to abuse the Scriptures, which contain the doctrine of faith and piety, to persuade men to impiety? And what is more daring, shameless and insolent than to take in hand that sword which he hates above all and whose flash he cannot bear even from afar? And how great a presumption shall we call it that he fights against Scripture with Scripture, when he could not be ignorant that its Spirit dictated it? But let us hear how confidently and artfully he brings these words forward. "It is written," he says, "He shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest at any time you dash your foot against a stone." That passage is in Psalm 91, which some think was composed by David when God was punishing the people of Israel with a terrible plague, which within three days carried off seventy thousand men. And what is written there, about the pestilence that stalks in darkness and at midday, agrees well enough with this view. There the Holy Spirit commends the protection of divine providence, by which the godly and believing are kept safe and unharmed in any danger, and among other things it says: "No evil shall befall you, nor shall any plague come near your tent. For he shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. They shall bear you in their hands, lest your foot dash against a stone," and so on. Truly, then, what Satan says is found in the holy Scriptures, but that wicked impostor twists what is rightly and piously said there to a foreign and impious sense. For the Holy Spirit there speaks of those who follow God's calling and walk in their ways, that is, in the ways prescribed to them by God. But the devil extends that promise simply to all, and indeed even to those who, carried away by impious confidence or by some other rash desire, cast themselves into dangers that are not necessary. And therefore, with more than sacrilegious rashness, he leaves out the phrase "in all your ways." For it was not the way of Christ, nor a calling from the Father, to throw himself headlong from the pinnacle of the temple, or to give a proof of his divine glory and power by other miracles that are perilous indeed but useless, as charlatans and mountebanks are wont to do. This example, then, we must observe well, so that we do not allow our eyes to be dazzled by the mention of Scripture, but rather that we test all things, lest we give ourselves over to the deceits of the devil himself or of his instruments.

units.la: Quod enim hic fecit hostis ille noster, hoc ipsum frequenter apud nos efficere conatur, & quidem bifariam. Principio in ijs, quæ ad animam & salutis æternæ negotium faciunt. Solet hic nonnullos in supremum fidei fastium euehere, id est, ea persuasione inebriare, vt se ea assecutos putent, quæ in toto illo negotio excellentissima & omni captu humano sublimiora sunt: & tunc vel occultis suggestionibus, vel etiam per Sophistas artibus fallendi probè instructos, ita eos compellat: Si fide in Iesum Christum verè iustificatus & iam filius Dei factus es, imò si æterno Dei decreto electus & ad vitæ æternæ hæreditatem prædestinatus es in Christo, quid opus est teipsum assiduo vitæ nouæ fluxio, carnis mortificatione, tuiipsius abnegatione, & solicita præceptorum Dei obseruatione fatigare, adhæc mundi odia prouocare, & vitam ipsam tibi amaram reddere? Etenim scriptum est{C}: Non est volentis neq; currentis, sed miserantis Dei. Item vocatio et dona Dei eiusmodi sunt, ut eorum hunc pænitere nō possit. Et Domino exercituum aliquid cōstituente, quis illud faciat irritum? Vel num Christi vocem ignoras? Ego sum pastor bonus, qui pono animam pro ouibus, & nemo pe{C}tēs{C}otues rapere de manu mea, &c. Hæc et alia huius generis infinita hodie passim audiuntur. Quis autem horum omnium scopus diabolo propositus est? Hic nimirum, ut negligeto salutis studio nos securitati dedamus, & vel superstitiones communes sectemur, vel effræni licentia cum infelici mundo in omne scelus ruamus. Quid enim aliud faciant, qui hisce fallacijs decepti, ab inani & imaginaria Dei electione sic dependent, ut Verbi Dei studium, vitæ nouitatem, preces & quæcunq; sunt alia virtutis pietatis exercitia pro superuacaneis ducant? At non in his solum diaboli improbitas nobis negotium facit, sed in iis etiam, quæ ad corpus spectant, iisdem armis atq; artibus nos adoritur. Hic enim sub prætextu prouidentiæ imponit multis, ut pro fidelibus confidentes, aut potius securi & impij dominorum institutorum contemptores fiant. Profert ergo scripturas, quibus Deus dicitur aues cœli & pullos coruorum pascere, flores agri vestire, & quod idem necessaria omnia largiturus sit ijs, qui regnum suum & eius iustitiam quærero satagunt. Et hic quidem ita rhetoricatur, ut illum ista seriò agere, & omnino hoc velle iurares, ut homines abiecto omni rerum terrenarum studio, solum Deum suspiciant, & ab huius prouidentia toti pendeant. Sed longè alia ei mens est. Nam œconomiam euertere & ab ipso Deo nobis mandatum rei domesticæ studium abolere conatur, ut hoc neglecto homines ad extremam egestatem redacti, vel impiè aduersus Deum murmurent, vel ad iniustas artes & media illicita conuersi per fas & nefas ditescere studeant. Ita frequenter in morbis naturalia remedia in odium adducit, & vitam nostram Deo curæ fore persuadet, qui herbarum aut radicum præsidijs minimè opus habeat. Sed quorsum ista quoque tenduut? Num ut spe bona impleat, & Deum vitæ mortiuq; authorem vnicum esse nobis persuadeat? Nequaquam: sed ut cæca confidentia ebrij morbos nobis propria incuria incurabiles reddamus, quæ deinde nobis vel belluini eiulatus contra Deum, vel etiam superstitionum causa fit, ut apud Magos et veneficos, vel etiam apud Diuos cœlites, vel potius apud eorum statuas quæramus salutem, quam initio licitis et à Deo ordinatis remedijs tueri noluimus. Solet hoc ipsum in bellicis quoq; periculis interdum fieri, ut confidentia lo co constantis & intrepidæ fidei nobis instillet, & ea occasione deinceps ad ea cogat, quæ vel cum manifesta impietate, vel cum præsenti exitio coniuncta sunt. Deniq; nullum vitæ genus, & nulla in humanis actio est, quæ non hisce diaboli consilijs atque suggestionibus turbetur, quæ eo periculosiores sunt, quòd plausibili pietatis & fidei veræ prætextu pallientur. Quo magis nos admigilare necesse est, ne nos incautos & securos opprimat.
units.tr: Our enemy does the same thing that he did here, and he tries to do it among us often, in two ways. First, in matters that concern the soul and the business of eternal salvation. He often lifts some people to the highest rung of faith, that is, he intoxicates them with the belief that they have already attained what is most excellent in the whole matter and higher than any human grasp. Then, either by secret whisperings or through Sophists well trained in the arts of deception, he addresses them in this way: "If you are truly justified by faith in Jesus Christ, and have already become a son of God, indeed if you have been chosen by God's eternal decree and predestined in Christ to the inheritance of eternal life, why do you need to wear yourself out with constant renewal of life, mortification of the flesh, self-denial and anxious observance of God's commandments? Why provoke the hatred of the world and make your own life bitter for yourself? For it is written: 'It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy' (Rom. 9.16). Likewise, the calling and gifts of God are of such a kind that he cannot repent of them. And when the Lord of hosts has decreed something, who will make it void? Or do you not know the voice of Christ? 'I am the good shepherd, who lays down my life for the sheep, and no one will snatch them out of my hand,' and so on." Today such arguments, and countless others of this kind, are heard everywhere. But what is the aim the devil has set before all of these? Surely this: that, neglecting zeal for salvation, we should give ourselves over to complacency, and either follow common superstitions or rush headlong into every crime with unrestrained licence, along with an unhappy world. For what else will those do who, deceived by these fallacies and dependent on an empty and imaginary election of God, regard the study of the Word of God, the newness of life, prayers, and all other exercises of virtue and piety as superfluous? But the wickedness of the devil does not trouble us only in these matters. He also attacks us with the same weapons and arts in those things that concern the body. For under the pretext of providence he persuades many to become confident, as though they were faithful, or rather secure and impious despisers of the ordinances of their masters. So he brings forward Scriptures in which God is said to feed the birds of the heaven and the young ravens, to clothe the flowers of the field, and that he will likewise give all necessary things to those who seek earnestly his kingdom and his righteousness. And he argues in such a way that you would swear he was in earnest and wanted precisely this: that men, casting off all concern for earthly things, should look only to God and depend wholly on his providence. But his mind is quite different. For he tries to overturn household management and to abolish, by God's own command, the care of domestic affairs, so that, with this neglected, men reduced to extreme poverty either murmur impiously against God, or turn to unjust arts and unlawful means and strive to grow rich by right or wrong. So too in illnesses he often brings natural remedies into hatred and persuades us that our life is a concern for God, who has no need of the help of herbs or roots. But to what end do these things also tend? Is it so that he may fulfil a good hope and persuade us that God alone is the author of life and death? By no means. Rather, it is so that, drunk with a blind confidence, we may make illnesses incurable through our own carelessness; and then, from this, either bellowing like beasts against God, or, for the sake of superstition, we seek salvation from magicians and sorcerers, or even from the saints in heaven, or rather from their statues, which at the beginning we were unwilling to protect by remedies that are lawful and ordained by God. The same thing sometimes happens in dangers of war too: confidence, in place of a steady and fearless faith, is instilled in us, and on that occasion he then drives us towards those things that are joined either with manifest impiety or with present ruin. In short, there is no way of life and no human action that is not disturbed by these counsels and suggestions of the devil, which are all the more dangerous because they are covered with the plausible pretext of piety and true faith. So much the more, then, we must be watchful, lest he overwhelm us while we are heedless and secure.

units.la: Sufficiet hic nobis vnius Christi exemplum, si hoc non ofcitanter consideremus. In quo ante omnia obseruabis, illū rursus scripturarum gladio vsum fuisse. Ergo non propterea has abijciendas putauit, quòd Satan illis turpiter & impiè abusus esset. Vnde apparet, non probari illi eos, qui sacros libros plebeis hominibus, adeoq; toti populo Christiano ex manibus excutiunt, eò quòd illis abstantur hæretici & impostores, quorum fraudes non omnes possint obseruare. Cur verò non eosdem à cibis simul omnibus abstinere iubent, ne veneficis sese occidendos præbeat? Atqui ut vitam cibo sustentemus necesse est, aiunt. Quasi verò minus necesse sit animā verbo Dei pasci & regi, ne inter tot æternæ salutis pericula misere succumbat? Quin potius nos cogitare conuenit, Deū diabolo & organis eius inter alia hoc quoq; non sine iusta & graui causa permittere, ut scripturas sacras detorqueant, & ex vitæ fontibus morte cum sibi ipsis tum multis alijs propinent. Id verò facit, non ut ipsorū libidine & audacia sua indulgentia foveat, sed ut nos ad serium verbi sui studium excitet, ut dolos ommes obseruare, verum scripturæ sacræ vsum tenere, et locorū singulorū collatione diligentimaiores quotidie in vera pietate progressus facere studeamus. Hac certè vna Christus in præsenti fallaciam Satanæ detegit, & eum nō minus ineptum quàm impudentem asinū esse ostendit, qui mirificus in scripturis examinandis artifex videri volebat. Et sanè hac omnes fallacias deprehendendi atq; confutandi compendiosissimam rationem esse constat, si diuersi scripturæ loci inter se diligentius conferantur, & secundum fidei analogiam explicentur. Quod si hodie passim obseruaretur, minus esset contentionum, & facilis esset sententiarum, quibus ecclesia scinditur, conciliatio.
units.tr: One example, that of Christ alone, will suffice for us here, if we consider it attentively. In it, above all, you will observe that he again used the sword of Scripture. He therefore did not think the Scriptures should be cast aside because Satan had shamefully and impiously abused them. Hence it appears that those are not to be approved who snatch the holy books out of the hands of ordinary people, and indeed of the whole Christian people, on the ground that heretics and impostors abuse them and not everyone can detect their frauds. Why do they not also bid people abstain from all food, lest they expose themselves to being killed by poisoners? "Yet," they say, "we must sustain life with food." As if it were less necessary for the soul to be fed and ruled by the Word of God, lest amid so many dangers to eternal salvation it wretchedly succumb! Rather, we ought to consider that God, not without just and weighty cause, permits the devil and his instruments, among other things, also to twist the holy Scriptures and to hand out death from the springs of life, both to themselves and to many others. He does this not to indulge and foster their lust and audacity, but to rouse us to earnest study of his Word, so that we may observe all their tricks, keep the true use of holy Scripture, and by diligently comparing individual passages strive to make greater progress daily in true godliness. By this one thing Christ in the present case exposes Satan's deceit and shows him to be an ass no less foolish than shameless, who wished to seem a marvellous craftsman in examining the Scriptures. And indeed it is clear that this is the most compendious method of detecting and refuting all deceits: if different passages of Scripture are more carefully compared with one another and explained according to the analogy of faith. If this were everywhere observed today, there would be less contention, and the reconciliation of the opinions by which the Church is torn would be easy.

units.la: Videamus ergo, ut ex scripturis Christus diabolo respónderit: Dictum est (inquit) Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum.
