Quo responso diuinae sapientiae spectacle edit, quando vna sententia duo, quae maximi momenti erant, conficit. Primò fucum abstergit aduersario, & quid hic moliatur aut quaerat, docet. Deinde illud factu nefas esse ostendit. Itaque responsionis huius sensus est: Tu quidem meae gloriae & existimationis studiosissimus videri vis, quasi hoc quaeras, ut diuinae maiestatis experimentum aliquod publicum praebeam, quo quàm plurimis innotescat, quid de me debeant sentire: Et ut quod vis mihi persuadeas, Scripturae sacrae oraculum adducis. Atqui de huius fide ego nequaquam dubito, & quod prius dixi, me Patris decreto firmiter niti in iis, quae meae sunt vocationis, etiamsi ipsa rerum natura mihi aduersa videatur, id ipsum nunc quoq; sentio. Quòd autem tuam postulationem non recipiam, neq; me hinc deorsum praecipitem mittam, in causa est, quòd aliud Dei dictum tuae suggestioni prorsus contrarium esse video. Nam iubes tu, ut praeter necessitatem praesens vitae periculum subeam. At ego Mosem ex Spiritus sancti suggestione clamantem audio: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Quare etsi de diuina protectione certus sim, simul tamen minimè admittendum puto, ut eius temeraria fiducia ad tentandum Deum abutar, &c. Hic (iquam) verborum Domini sensus mihi esse videtur.
units.tr: Let us see, then, how Christ answered the devil from Scripture: "It is written (he says), You shall not tempt the Lord your God." In this answer he displays a sample of divine wisdom, since with one sentence he accomplishes two things of the greatest importance. First, he wipes away the devil's pretence and teaches what he is plotting and seeking. Second, he shows that the deed itself is wicked. The sense of the answer, then, is this: "You indeed want to seem most zealous for my glory and reputation, as if you sought that I should give some public proof of my divine majesty, by which as many people as possible might learn what they ought to think of me; and to persuade me of what you want, you bring forward the oracle of Holy Scripture. But I have no doubt of its truth, and what I said before, that I rest firmly on the Father's decree in those things that belong to my calling, even if nature itself seems opposed to me, I still feel the same now. But I will not accept your demand, nor cast myself headlong down from here, because I see that another saying of God is wholly contrary to your suggestion. For you bid me undergo present danger to life without necessity. But I hear Moses, moved by the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, crying out: You shall not tempt the Lord your God. Therefore, although I am certain of divine protection, I nonetheless think it by no means to be allowed that I should abuse that protection by a rash confidence to tempt God," and so on. This, I say, seems to me to be the sense of the Lord's words.

units.la: Extat autem locus iste apud Mosem Deuteron. sexto cap. vbi exemplo adiecto declaratur quid eo praecepto Deus prohibeat. Ait enim: Ne tentetis Dominum Deum vestrum, sicut tentastis in Massa. Respicit autem ad historiam, quae Exod. 17. ad hunc modum describitur: Castrametati sunt filij Israel in Raphidim, vbi non erat aqua, ut biberet populus. Et expostulauit populus cum Mose, & dixerunt: Date nobis aquam, ut bibamus. Est ne Dominus in medio nostri, annon? Id vero factum Moses exponens, respondit illis: Cur mecum expostulatis? cur tentatis Dominum? &c. Et locum illum ab euentu Massa & Meriba, id est tentationem & contentionem vocauit. Ergo Deum tentauisse dicuntur Israelitae, quando non contenti signis & beneficijs, quibus suum fauorem ille iampridem abunde declarauerat, nouum illius experimentum quaerunt, adeoque illum in dubium vocant, vel etiam omnino negant, nisi modo insolito aquas ipsis profundat. Simili audacia eos peccauisse in Psal. 78. scribitur, vbi exhibito aquarum beneficio sic subijcit propheta: Adhuc tamen peccauerunt ei, & exacerbauerunt Altissimum in solitudine. Et tentauerunt Deum in corde suo, cùm postularent cibum animabus suis, & contra Deum locuti sunt, dicentes: Num potest Deus mensam instruere in deserto? En petram percussit, & effluxerunt aquae, & fluuij inundarunt. Num vero & panem dare poterit? Num parare carnes poterit populo? Ex quibus iterum colligitur, Deum tentari, si qui non contenti verbo eius, ipsi insuper modum, locum, tempus & res agendas praescribunt, ut eius bonitatem, sapientiam, iustitiam, potentiam nouis modis experiantur. Et hoc modo Israelitas in historijs modò commemoratis Deum tentauisse constat. Similis fuit ciuium Bethuliae tentatio, qui Dei auxilium ad dierum quinque spatium restrinxerant, quibus euolutis vrbem hostibus tradituri essent, nisi coelitus iuuarentur. Quorum temeritatem Iudith accusans dicit: Qui tandem estis vos, qui Deum hodie tentandum putaueritis, Dei partes inter homines occupetis? Non est iste sermo, qui misericordiam impetret, sed iram potius excitabit, &c. Et est hoc tentandi Deum genus admodum vulgare, si quando res prorsus desperatae sunt, ut publicè in re militari, priuatim in morbis, egestate aliisque aduersis siue periculis est videre. Tentatur item Deus, quando contemptis ordinarijs medijs siue praesidijs homines petunt, ut ille nouo & insolito modo ipsis opem ferat. Faciunt hoc, qui electione et praedestinatione gratuita abutuntur, ut vocationem, quae per verbum Dei fit, Sacramentorum vsum, admonitiones, hortationes, consolationes, preces cum publicas tum priuatas & omnia alia pietatis exercitia negligant. Quid enim hi aliud faciunt, quàm quòd Deo nouam regni sui rationem praescribunt? Imo dum praedestinationem plenis buccis iactant, eandem ipsa negant, quando salutis media contemnunt ut superuacanea, quae sub aeterna praedestinatione Dei contineri scripturae docent. Nam quos praescuit (inquit Paulus) eos & praedestinauit, ut conformes sint imagini filij eius, ut ipse sit primogenitus inter multos fratres. Quos autem praedestinauit, eos & vocauit, (nimirum foris quidem per Euangelij praedicationem, intus autem illuminatione et tactu Spiritus sancti.) Quos vero vocauit, eos & iustificauit (nimirum per fidem, qua Christum amplexi sunt.) Et quos iustificauit, eosdem glorificauit. Qui ordo satis docet nimium audaces Phaetontes & Icaras, imò nefarios diuinæ bonitatis tentatores esse, qui absq; intermedijs gradibus ab electione ad ipsam vsque glorificationem transilire conantur. In quorum albo etiam censeri merentur, qui signa, quibus fidem nostram Deus olim confirmauit, aut etiam hodie confirmat, pro inutilibus ducunt, & ipsi noua postulant à Deo, vt hunc suæ libidini subijciat. Quod olim Iudæos fecisse legimus, quando signū è cælo petebant, &c. In externis verò & temporalibus Deum similiter tentant, qui agriculturam, rei domesticæ administrationem, politicas leges, naturalem medicinam, studium literarium contemnunt, & tamen sibi ea pollicentur à Deo, quæ ís per hæc quasi media dare consueuit. Est præterea tertium tentandi genus, quando nos absque legitima vocatione Dei periculis non necessarijs obijcimus, vt quam Deo curæ simus expiamur. Et sub hoc referri debet, quo Christum Satan aggressus est. Nec enim vlla Patris vocatione vrgebatur, vt diuinitatem suam præcipiti saltu ex templi pinnis probaret: neq; vt id faceret necesse erat, cùm non deessent scalæ aut gradus, per quos ex alto descenderet. Est autem hoc quoq; tentationis genus admodum frequens. Nam in hoc peccant, qui non vocante Deo, imò plerunque illo prohibente, fidem suam apertis periculis subijciunt, quando Episcoporum, Abbatum aut principum seruitijs sese mancipant, quos & fidei hostes esse & huius confessionem liberam odisse norunt. Magis temerarij sunt, qui insuper sacris illicitis communicant, & in ipsa fidei abnegatione salutem certam sibi pollicentur. Similes horum etiam sunt, qui relicto Christianæ libertatis beneficio, iugum ceremoniarum inutilium humeris suis accersunt, & conscientias tam suas quàm aliorum inutiliter, imò pernitiose grassant. A quibus Deum tentari, Petrus in Actu diserte monet. Peccant hic etiam, qui vel fœdera cum impijs iungendo, vel connubijs imparibus sese implicando fidem suam in periculum adducunt. Deum item tentant, qui castitatem vouendo, thori legitimi vsum damnant, & ita sibijpsis stuprorum, adulteriorum, incestuum & nefandissimæ libidinis materiam atq; fomenta accersunt. Quibus adnumerari possunt, quotquot devoto animo in omne scelus ruunt, & se Dei bonitate niti, deq; salute sua optimè sperare clamant, etiamsi nihil non faciant eius voluntati contrarium. Adijciantur his omnibus agyrtæ, sunambuli, & qui veteres Retiariorum atq; Mirmillonum ludos reducere satagunt. Vides ergo peccatum hoc tentandi Deum latissimè patere, & omnibus hisce speciebus occinendum esse, quod Christus ex Mose aduersus Satanam adduxit, Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum.
units.tr: This passage is found in Moses, Deut. chapter 6, where by an added example it is declared what God forbids by that precept. For he says: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God, as you tempted him at Massah." He refers to the story which is described in Exod. 17 in this way: "The children of Israel encamped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. And the people quarrelled with Moses and said: 'Give us water that we may drink.' Is the Lord among us or not?" And when Moses explained this deed, he answered them: "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you tempt the Lord?" and so on. He called that place, from the outcome, Massah and Meribah, that is, temptation and strife. Therefore the Israelites are said to have tempted God when, not content with the signs and benefits by which he had long since abundantly declared his favour toward them, they sought a new trial of him, and so called him into doubt, or even denied him altogether, unless he poured out water for them in some unusual way. The Psalm 78 records that they sinned with similar audacity, where, after the benefit of water had been shown, the prophet adds: "Yet they sinned still against him, and provoked the Most High in the wilderness. And they tempted God in their heart, when they asked food for their souls, and spoke against God, saying: 'Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, and waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed. Can he also give bread? Can he prepare flesh for his people?'" From these words it is again gathered that God is tempted when people, not content with his word, prescribe to him in addition the manner, place, time and things to be done, so that they may test his goodness, wisdom, justice and power in new ways. And in this way it is plain that the Israelites tempted God in the histories just mentioned. A similar temptation was that of the citizens of Bethulia, who had restricted God's help to a space of five days, after which they were to surrender the city to the enemy unless they were aided from heaven. Judith, accusing their rashness, says: "Who then are you, who have thought that God is to be tempted today, and have taken upon yourselves the place of God among men? This is not a word that will obtain mercy, but rather will stir up wrath," and so on. This kind of tempting God is quite common, when things are utterly desperate, as may be seen publicly in matters of war, and privately in sicknesses, want and other adversities or dangers. God is likewise tempted when, having scorned the ordinary means or safeguards, people ask that he help them in some new and unusual way. Those do this who abuse gratuitous election and predestination, so that they neglect the calling that comes through the Word of God, the use of the sacraments, admonitions, exhortations, consolations, prayers both public and private, and all other exercises of godliness. For what else do these men do than prescribe to God a new plan for his kingdom? Indeed, while they boast of predestination with full cheeks, they deny it itself, when they despise the means of salvation as superfluous, which the Scriptures teach are contained under the eternal predestination of God. For, as Paul says: "Those whom he foreknew he also predestined, that they should be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. And those whom he predestined, these he also called (namely outwardly indeed through the preaching of the gospel, but inwardly through the enlightening and touch of the Holy Spirit). And those whom he called, these he also justified (namely through faith, by which they embraced Christ). And whom he justified, these he also glorified." This order sufficiently teaches that they are over-bold Phaethons and Icaruses, indeed impious tempters of divine goodness, who try to leap from election to glorification itself without intermediate steps. Among their number also deserve to be counted those who regard as useless the signs by which God once confirmed our faith, or still confirms it today, and themselves demand new ones from God, that he may subject himself to their lust. This we read that the Jews once did, when they sought a sign from heaven, and so on. In external and temporal matters, too, they tempt God who despise agriculture, the management of household affairs, civil laws, natural medicine and the study of letters, and yet promise themselves from God those things which he is accustomed to give through these as it were means. There is, moreover, a third kind of tempting, when, without lawful calling from God, we expose ourselves to unnecessary dangers in order to test whether we are cared for by God. To this class should be referred the temptation with which Satan assailed Christ. For he was not urged by any calling of the Father to prove his divinity by a headlong leap from the pinnacle of the temple, nor was it necessary for him to do so, since there were ladders or steps by which he might come down from on high. This kind of temptation is also very frequent. For those sin in this way who, without God calling, or rather often with God forbidding, expose their faith to open dangers when they hand themselves over to the service of bishops, abbots or princes, whom they know to be enemies of the faith and to hate the free confession of it. More rash still are those who, in addition, take part in unlawful sacred rites, and promise themselves certain salvation in the very denial of the faith. Like these are also those who, having abandoned the benefit of Christian liberty, bring upon their own shoulders the yoke of useless ceremonies, and in vain, or rather perniciously, trouble their own consciences as well as those of others. Peter plainly warns in Acts that God is tempted by these things. Those also sin who, by joining alliances with the impious or entangling themselves in unequal marriages, bring their faith into danger. Likewise they tempt God who, by vowing chastity, condemn the use of lawful marriage, and so provide for themselves the material and fuel of debauchery, adultery, incest and most abominable lust. To these may be added all who rush into every crime with a devoted spirit, and cry out that they rely on God's goodness and hope well for their salvation, even though they do nothing that is not contrary to his will. Add to all these the jugglers, tightrope-walkers, and those who strive to revive the old games of the retiarii and the murmillones. You see, then, that this sin of tempting God extends very widely, and that what Christ adduced from Moses against Satan, You shall not tempt the Lord your God, must be sounded against all these kinds.

units.la: Conclusurus eram locum hunc, sed condonabitis mihi fratres dilecti, si ijs prius respondero, qui ex præcepto hoc suæ ignauiæ & diffidentiæ patrocinium quærunt. Sunt enim, qui vt primum iubentur, quod cum aliquo periculo coniunctum est, mox clamant: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Quo fit, vt nihil vnquam laude dignum faciant, & fidei atque charitatis Christianæ officia tunc maximè negligant, quando pulcherrima sese in his exercendi occasio offertur. Auditur enim vox ista ex multis, qui vt fidei professionem faciant, euocantur ad inquisitorum aut iudicum tribunalia. Vtuntur eadem ignaui ciues, si quid pro patria & publica salute audendum est. Illam in ore habent, qui dum lues in vrbibus grassatur, monentur, vt vicinis, amicis, cognatis, conciuibus præstō sint, & laborantibus necessaria vitæ subsidia subministrent. Adeò ingeniosus est Satan, vt sub plau sibili pietatis prætextu fidem abnegare, patriam prodere & in proximos quosque extremam impietatem exercere doceat. Sed vna responsio omnibus illis sufficit, Non tentari scilicet Deum, quando eius vocatione excitati præsens periculum adimus, adeoq; in mortis fauces nosmetipsos ingerimus. Est enim hoc obedientiæ officium, quam Deo negare non possumus, qui vitæ & necis nostræ ius habet atque imperium. Atq; generalia Dei præcepta sunt, vt fidem in Christum publicè & intrepidè fateamur, vt à sacris superstitiosis abstineamus, vt patriæ & ciuibus in periculo constitutis succurramus, vt ægrotos visamus & omni prosequamur officiorum genere, vt denique pestem & quaecunque alia Dei flagella sunt, non turpi fuga, sed assiduo pœnitentiæ studio, precibus, charitate mutua & dilectione euadere conemur. Istis ergo quicunq; sese accómodant, iij non Deum tentare dicuntur, sed officium facere. Quòd si autem interea succumbunt, næ illi beati sunt, quibus in Dei vocatione, vt serus frugi & fidus, occumbere datum est.
units.tr: I was about to conclude this passage, but, beloved brethren, you will forgive me if I first answer those who seek in this precept a cover for their own laziness and distrust. For there are some who, as soon as they are told to do something that carries some danger, at once cry out: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." The result is that they never do anything worthy of praise, and most of all they neglect the duties of faith and Christian love at the very moment when the finest opportunity to exercise them is offered. That voice is heard from many who, when they are summoned to the tribunals of inquisitors or judges to make a profession of faith, use it. Lazy citizens use the same words if something must be risked for the fatherland and the public safety. They have it on their lips when plague is raging in the cities and they are urged to stand by their neighbours, friends, relatives and fellow citizens, and to supply the necessities of life to those who are suffering. So crafty is Satan that under the pretext of a specious piety he teaches men to deny the faith, betray their country, and commit the utmost impiety against all their neighbours. But one answer suffices for all these cases: namely, that God is not tempted when, roused by his call, we face a present danger and thereby thrust ourselves into the jaws of death. For this is the duty of obedience, which we cannot refuse to God, who holds the right and power over our life and death. And the commands of God are general: that we confess faith in Christ publicly and fearlessly, that we abstain from superstitious rites, that we help our country and citizens who are in danger, that we visit the sick and attend them with every kind of service, and finally that we strive to escape the plague and whatever other scourges of God there are, not by shameful flight but by constant zeal for repentance, by prayers, and by mutual charity and love. Those, therefore, who adapt themselves to these duties are said not to tempt God but to do their duty. But if, meanwhile, they succumb, truly they are blessed, to whom it has been granted to die in the calling of God, like a ripe and faithful servant.

units.la: Reliqua est historiæ totius conclusio, quàm his verbis Lucas absoluit: Et finita omni tentatione, diabolus abscessit ab eo ad tempus. Ergo non antea quies data fuit Christo, quâ toto hoc certamine probè defunctus est. Quo exemplo admonemur, ne ipsi nobis ferias indicamus, priusquam quod nobis à Deo mandatum est fideliter executi fuerimus. At quamuis tunc abscesserit Satan, non tamen pax certa facta fuit, sed ad tempus induciae fuerunt, quibus ad graviora, quae mox secuta sunt, certamina Christus praepararetur. Nam etsi vehementes & acres fuerint pugnae, quas in praesenti sustinuit, leviores tamen velitationes videri possunt, si cum illis conferantur, quae per Sacerdotes, Scribas, Pharisaeos, Sadducaeos, Pilatum, Iudam & horum complices adversus illum excitavit. Nos itaque meminerimus, vitam nostram militiam esse perpetuam, & nimium socordes aut negligentes esse, qui dum huius vitae palaestra durat, sibi ipsis plenam victoriam atque triumphos pollicentur, quibus in coelo demum frui dabitur. Interim consolationis plenum est, quod Matthaeus & Marcus Angelos Christo ministrasse scribunt. Est is angelorum princeps & dominus, & quia nos bonorum suorum consortes esse vult, nobis quoque Angelos ministros & custodes destinavit: non quidem, quales Satan persuadere voluit, quorum impia fiducia adversus Deum insurgamus, eumque impie tentemus: sed ut divinae protectionis tamen fidelis praesidii spe cerca freti, in omni tentationis genere intrepidi, stationem nostram constanter teneamus, & tandem finito certamine omni, aeternae & beatae immortalitatis corona donemur in Christo Iesu, Domino nostro, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The remainder is the conclusion of the whole story, which Luke finishes with these words: "And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him for a time." Therefore rest was not given to Christ before he had faithfully carried through this whole contest. By this example we are admonished not to grant ourselves holidays before we have faithfully carried out what God has commanded us. Yet although Satan then departed, peace was not made certain; there were only truces for a time, in which Christ was being prepared for the harsher struggles that soon followed. For although the battles he endured at present were fierce and sharp, they may seem lighter skirmishes if they are compared with those which he stirred up against him through the priests, scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, Pilate, Judas and their accomplices. Let us therefore remember that our life is a perpetual warfare, and that they are too careless and negligent who, while the arena of this life lasts, promise themselves complete victory and triumphs, which will be granted them only in heaven. Meanwhile it is full of consolation that Matthew and Mark write that angels ministered to Christ. He is the prince and lord of the angels, and because he wishes us to be partakers of his goods, he has also appointed angels as our ministers and guardians: not indeed such as Satan wished to persuade us of, on whose impious confidence we rise up against God and impiously tempt him, but so that, relying on the hope of the faithful protection of divine care, we may stand fearless in every kind of temptation, constantly hold our post, and at last, when the whole contest is finished, be crowned with the crown of eternal and blessed immortality in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XL.
units.tr: HOMILY XL.

units.la: Et reuersus est Iesus cum virtute spiritus in Galilaeam, & fama de eo exijt in totam circumiacentem regionem. Et ipse docebat in Synagogis eorum, omnibus eum glorificantibus.
units.tr: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report of him went out into all the surrounding region. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. (Luke 4:14–15)

units.la: NArrauit hucusque Lucas, vt Dominus noster & seruator, Iesus Christus, ad munus seu officium, cui illum Pater aeterno decreto destinauerat, publice ordinatus atque praeparatus sit. Praecipuum in tota illa historia fuit tentationis certamen, quod diebus circiter quadraginta aduersus diabolum sustinuit. Visus eius nobis hic est, vt Christum hostis nostri communis victorem, adhaec pontificem nostrum fidelem esse credamus, qui nostras infirmitates in se receperit, & proinde pia nostrae miseriae commiseratione tangatur. Qui denique hostem illum ita nobis vicerit, vt nobis quoque illum vincendi vires hodie donet. Admonuit praeterea nos hoc exemplo Spiritus sanctus, neminem publicis officijs obeundis idoneum esse, nisi qui diaboli suggestionibus resistere didicit, & iam non ob securam sanctae illius victoriae trophaea statuit. Quid enim in ecclesia, quid in repub. proficiet, qui ipse tyranni omnium crudelissimi & impurissimi est mancipium? Aut num ad destruendam diaboli tyrannidem & erigendum regnum Dei aliquid momenti conferet, qui totus quantus est illius libidine rapitur, & ad quemuis pravi affectus affulgum turpiter succumbit? Prudenter quidem & graviter a veteribus dictum est, Nemo bene imperat, nisi qui servire didicit. At multo verius & iustio ri de causa nos dicere possumus, neminem vel in repub. vel in ecclesia alijs hominibus feliciter praesse, quam qui excusso diaboli iugo, eum iampridem subegit, & ab hoc accensas in nobis carnis cupiditates coercere novit. At quia de his alibi commodius dicetur, pergamus nunc cum Luca in coepta Iesu Christi historia, vt videamus, quomodo commissum sibi munus, ille in publico obire coeperit. Quo loco, quia rem maximi momenti Euangelista paucis verbis comprehendit, singulae circunstantiae dili gentiorem considerationem merentur.
units.tr: Luke has related so far how our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, was publicly ordained and prepared for the office or function to which the Father had destined him by eternal decree. The chief matter in that whole history was the contest with temptation, which he endured against the devil for about forty days. Its purpose for us here is that we may believe Christ to be the victor over our common enemy and also our faithful high priest, who took our infirmities upon himself and is therefore moved by pious compassion for our misery; who, in short, so conquered that enemy for us that he grants us today the strength to conquer him too. The Holy Spirit also warns us by this example that no one is fit to discharge public offices unless he has learned to resist the suggestions of the devil and no longer sets up trophies of a secure victory over him as if already won. For what will he accomplish in the Church or in the commonwealth who is himself the slave of the most cruel and most impure of tyrants? Or will he contribute anything of weight to destroying the devil's tyranny and raising up the kingdom of God, who is wholly carried away by that devil's lust and shamefully yields to every glow of wicked passion? The ancients said prudently and gravely, "No one rules well unless he has learned to serve." But for a far truer and juster reason we may say that no one rules happily over other men, whether in the commonwealth or in the Church, unless he has shaken off the yoke of the devil, by which he was long subdued, and knows how to restrain the fleshly desires the devil has kindled in us. But since these things will be said more fittingly elsewhere, let us now go on with Luke into the beginning of the history of Jesus Christ, to see how he began to discharge in public the task committed to him. Here, since the evangelist comprehends a matter of the greatest importance in few words, each single circumstance deserves a more diligent consideration.

units.la: Principio author totius negotij indicatur, Spiritus sanctus. Nam cum virtute spiritus in Galilaeam reuersus esse dicitur Christus, ne quis eum ex priuato carnis affectu aliquid fecisse putet. Virtutem vero spiritus dicit Lucas ipsum spiritum, qui visibili specie in eum descendit & super eum mansit (vt Ioan. 1. Capite scribitur) nunc vero suam praesentiam operibus miraculosis efficaciter & publice declarauit, quibus ad excitandos hominum animos opus erat, vt maior apud omnes esset doctrinae authoritas. Itaque vno verbo nostrer hic comprehendit, quod Matthaeus fusius describit: sic dicens: Circumiuit totam Galilaeam Iesus, docens in Synagogis ipsorum ac praedicans Euangelium regni: & sanans quemuis morbum, & quemuis languorem in populo. Tunc peruenit fama eius in totam Syriam, & obtulerunt ei omnes male affectos, varijs morbis ac vexationibus detentos, & daemoniacos, & lunaticos, & paraliticos, sanauitq; eos. Faciunt haec ad commendandum totum Christi ministerium, & hoc non humanum, sed diuinum & coeleste fuisse demonstrant. Et est hoc obseruandum diligenter, cum vt de Euangelij doctrina honorificentius iudicemus, tum vt certior nobis sit salutis fiducia, quae per illam nobis offertur. Cur enim de earum promissionum veritate quis dubitet, quas aeternus Dei filius nobis fecit, & quidem ipso spiritu impulsore & authore, quo illum quoad assumptam quoque hominis naturam prae omnibus alijs hominibus abundauisse constat? At simul suo exemplo Christus admonet, neminem nisi spiritus donis instructum ad docendi munus accedere debere. Quia enim animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei, & ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus, nihil vnquam in hoc munere proficient, qui spiritu destituti solius carnis ratione ducuntur. Adhaec authoritate singulari opus est, quam non pij modo, verum etiam impij agnoscere cogantur, & quam ijdem vel inuiti formident. Alioqui furioso impetu mox aduersus ministros insurgunt, & bi illorum conatibus territi stationem suam turpiter deserunt, & ita ministerij sacri dignitatem produnt. Ideo olim prophetas peculiari spiritus virtute purgatos & confirmatos fuisse legimus, vt tanti muneris laboribus sufficere & impios aduersariorum conatus vincere possent: sicut in Isaia, Ieremia & Ezechielis historijs est videre. Et Apostolos non ante ad praedicandum exire voluit Christus, quam illos spiritus virtute ex alto armauisset. Qua illi deinde instructi non apud electos modo in honore & precio fuerunt, verumetiam reprobis terrorem incusse-re, quando Christi in ipsis loquentis experimentum (vt Pauli verbis vtar) agnoscere coacti sunt. Hoc rarior est Spiritus sancti virtus, quia pauci vocationem legitimam expectant, & non tam gloriae Dei studio, quam ventris causa ad ecclesiae ministerium aspirant: multi autem quibus vocatio legitima obtigit, suae dignitatis parum memores, eam foede nimis prostituunt, quando non docendi diligentia, non morum grauitate, non seria scelerum correptione, sed ignaua dissimulatione & tantum non proditoria indulgentia apud infelicem mundum fauorem & authoritatem sibi ipsis conciliare studeant.
units.tr: First, the author of the whole undertaking is indicated: the Holy Spirit. For Christ is said to have returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, lest anyone think he acted from private fleshly feeling. Luke calls the power of the Spirit the Spirit himself, who descended upon him in visible form and remained upon him (as is written in the first chapter of John), but who now openly and effectively declared his presence by miraculous works, which were needed to rouse men's minds, so that the authority of his teaching might be greater in the eyes of all. Thus Luke comprehends in one word what Matthew describes more fully, saying: "Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. Then his fame spread into all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, held by various diseases and torments, the demon-possessed, the lunatics and the paralytics, and he healed them" (Matt. 4.23–24). These things serve to commend the whole ministry of Christ, and show that it was not human but divine and heavenly. This should be noted carefully, both so that we may judge the doctrine of the gospel more honourably and so that our confidence of salvation, which is offered to us through it, may be more certain. For who could doubt the truth of the promises which the eternal Son of God made to us, and indeed under the impulse and authority of the Spirit, of whom it is established that, even as to the human nature he assumed, he abounded beyond all other men? At the same time, by his own example, Christ warns that no one should come to the office of teaching unless he is furnished with the gifts of the Spirit. For "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2.14), and we are of ourselves not even fit to think, so those who are destitute of the Spirit and are led only by the reason of the flesh will never make progress in this office. Moreover, a singular authority is needed, which not only the godly but even the ungodly are compelled to acknowledge, and which they fear even against their will. Otherwise they soon rise against the ministers with furious assault, and the ministers, terrified by their attempts, shamefully desert their post and so betray the dignity of the sacred ministry. Therefore we read that the prophets of old were purified and strengthened by a special virtue of the Spirit, so that they could endure the labours of so great a task and overcome the impious attempts of their adversaries, as may be seen in the histories of Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel. And Christ did not want the apostles to go forth to preach until he had armed them with the power of the Spirit from on high. Having been so equipped, they were afterwards not only held in honour and esteem by the elect, but also struck terror into the reprobate, when these were compelled to recognise in them the proof of Christ speaking (to use Paul's words). This power of the Holy Spirit is rarer now, because few await a lawful calling, and they aspire to the ministry of the Church not so much out of zeal for God's glory as for the sake of their belly. And many to whom a lawful calling has come, forgetful of their dignity, prostitute it most foully, when they strive to win favour and authority for themselves among the unhappy world not by diligence in teaching, not by gravity of life, not by earnest rebuke of sins, but by idle dissimulation and an indulgence that is almost treacherous.

units.la: Deinde quid Christus primum omnium fecerit, Euangelista tradit. Ipse docebat (inquit) in Synagogis ipsorum. Matthaeus doctrinae genus exprimens, illum Euangelium regni praedicauisse scribit. Hoc vt primum fecit in carne manifestatus Dei filius, ita in eodem illum postea frequentissimum fuisse constat. Imo hoc quasi vnicum eius fuit negotium, cui se totum addixit ad eum vsque diem, quo mortis supplicium pro nobis subiuit. Nam etsi miracula simul multa & stupenda fecerit, eadem tamen ad doctrinam referri debent, quando in eum modo finem illa facta esse scimus, vt doctrinae sigilla essent, & eam nobis confirmarent. Commendatur bis verbi Dei aut Euangelij ministerium, quo nullum in orbe terrarum antiquius, nullum, quoad primum eius authorem & postea secutos ministros, celebrius & praestantius habetur. Nam si primum illius authorem quaeras, quem alium praeter vnum Deum inuenies, qui ipse primis parentibus nostris primus in paradiso conciona tus est de femine mulieris, quo caput serpentis conculcari, & cuius merito humanum genus ab interitu vindicari oporteat? Eundem postea quoq; patribus non vno modo eandem doctrinam reuelauisse scimus. Et cum iam illi placeret ministerium verbi sui certis hominibus committere, in eo occupatos ille habuit omnes eos, qui propter pietate singularem & eximias animi dotes prae alijs hominibus commendantur. Nam ipse Deo teste, propheta, id est, voluntatis & verbi diuini interpres atq; praeco fuit Abraham. Tales item fuerunt Isaac, Iacobus & Ioseph. Adide munus Moses quoq; Imperator omnium quotquot fuerunt & futuri sunt, gloriosissimus, destinatus fuit, qui maiorem laudem retulit ex Legis diuinae promulgatione per ipsum facta, quam ex redemptionis Aegyptiacae beneficio & victorijs, quibus ferocissimas gentes domuit. Nam nisi illa accessisset, inutilis, imo exitialis fuisset externa illa populi liberatio, qui ne sic quidem per omnia contineri potuit, quo minus libertate sua ad proprium exitium abuteretur. Idem de Dauide victoriosissimo & Solomone sapientissimo atq; gloriosissimo Rege dicere possumus, quos non puduit Verbi Dei doctrinam partim sui seculi hominibus coram viua voce, partim posteris scripto commendare, adeo vt in hodiernum vsq; diem Ecclesiastarum fidelissimorum officio fungantur. Quod si ad eos accessenimus, qui in veteri testamento Prophetarum nomine compellari solent, illorum chorum ex omnis loci & ordinis hominibus conbus constare videbis. Nam ex regio semine Isaias & Daniel progeniti fuerunt sacerdotem habuit patrem Ieremias, Elisetus & Amos ad agricolas & pastores suae gentis originem referunt. De aliis etsi nihil certi haberetur, ex eo ipso tamen colligere possumus, ex variis hominum ordinibus ad munus hoc vocatos fuisse, ne in officio suo cessantibus sacerdotibus ordinariis, Deus alicui ordini astrictius esse videretur. Ita denique idem ille testari voluit, omnes homines verbo suo subiectos esse debere, neque vllum ordinem habere causam iustam, ob quam eos muneris huius pudeat, cum iam olim ex omnibus aliqui ad illud destinati fuerint. Idem de Apostolis & horum successoribus dici poterat, si res ista aliquod dubium habere videretur. Isti certe praedicandi munus tanti fecerunt, ut erarij ecclesiastici & pauperum curam, munus per se sanctissimum, aliis committendam putarent, ne per illam in docendi officio impedirentur. Quid autem de illa dico, quando fere Sacramentorum ad ministrationem in alios reiecerunt, ut ipsi liberius & maiori cum fructu Euangelium praedicare possent? Paulus certe se quam paucissimos baptizauisse scribit, & causam sui facti affert, quod non ad baptizandum, sed ad euangelizandum missus fuerit. Vnde tamen nemo colligat, Sacramenta aut omnino omitti, aut negligentius tractari debere: sed quando haec cum Dei verbo conferebant, facile illis fuit videre, quanto hoc illis praestantius sit, & Christi exemplo ducebantur, qui cum in docendo frequens & assiduus fuerit, neminem tamen vnquam baptizauisse legitur. Nec temere ista tam in ipso quam Apostolis sic obseruata fuisse patebit, si Verbi divini vsum, & quam hic nobis necessarius sit consideremus. Constat enim nos ex ipsis natalibus peccatores, caecos item & divinorum omnium ignaros, adhuc ad bonum vel quaerendum vel apprehendendum ineptos esse, & perinde alie nos etiam a Deo & coelestium bonorum haereditate. At per verbum suum non solum voluntatem suam nobis Deus manifestat, verumetiam in filio suo iustitiam & satisfactionem pro peccatis offert, mentes illuminat, viribus novis instruit, denique se totum nobis communicat: quo nomine verbum hoc lucerna pedum nostrorum, lumen semitarum nostrarum, vitae regula, veritas, vita salusq; & dicitur. Quae omnia Paulus vno verbo comprehendens, illud Sermonem reconciliationis cum Deo vocat, ex qua reconciliatione tota hominis felicitas dependet. Et haec non absq; causa prolixius tractamus. Nam vt verbi ministerium commendant, ita improbos eius contemptores damnant, qui hoc vnu agunt, vt partim scurrilibus dictis & atrocibus conuitijs vulgo exosum reddant, partim Theologiae candidatos ab eo abstepreant. Placent illi fere sibi in sua nequitia, sed magno haec illis olim constabit, quando ipsa vita se privatos sentient, cuius verbum nunc improbe aspernantur. Et quid olim passi sint, qui simili impietate peccarunt, historiae docent, neq; nostri seculi exempla desunt, quae iis fidem faciunt, at plerisq; oculi desunt, quibus Dei iudicia & proprijs ipsorum ceruicibus imminentes poenas obseruent.
units.tr: Next, the Evangelist records what Christ did first of all. "He taught," he says, "in their synagogues." Matthew, describing the kind of teaching, writes that Christ preached the gospel of the kingdom. As soon as the Son of God was made manifest in the flesh he did this first, and it is clear that he did it most often afterwards. Indeed, this was, as it were, his one business, to which he devoted himself wholly until the day when he underwent the punishment of death for us. For although he also performed many wonderful miracles, these must still be referred to his teaching, since we know that they were done for this end only, to serve as seals of his doctrine and to confirm it for us. The ministry of God's Word, or of the gospel, is commended twice over. No ministry in the world is older, and none, from its first author and the ministers who followed him, is held in higher honour or greater excellence. For if you ask who was its first author, whom will you find besides the one God, who himself first preached in Paradise to our first parents about the seed of the woman, by whom the serpent's head was to be crushed and by whose merit the human race ought to be rescued from destruction? We know that he afterwards revealed the same doctrine to the fathers in more than one way. And when it pleased him to entrust the ministry of his Word to certain men, he employed in it all those who were commended above other men for singular piety and outstanding gifts of mind. For Abraham, as God himself bears witness, was a prophet, that is, an interpreter and herald of the will and Word of God. Isaac, Jacob and Joseph were likewise such men. Add that Moses, the most glorious commander of all who have been or will be, was also appointed to this office; he gained greater praise from the promulgation of the divine Law made through him than from the benefit of the Egyptian redemption and the victories by which he subdued the fiercest nations. For unless the Law had been added, that outward deliverance of the people would have been useless, indeed deadly, since even so the people could not be restrained from abusing their liberty to their own destruction. The same we may say of David, the most victorious king, and of Solomon, the wisest and most glorious king, who were not ashamed to commend the doctrine of the Word of God, partly to the men of their own age by the living voice, partly to posterity in writing, so that to this very day they fulfil the office of most faithful ministers of the Church. If we come to those who are usually called prophets in the Old Testament, you will see that their company was made up of men of every place and rank. For Isaiah and Daniel were born of the royal line; Jeremiah had a priest for his father; Elisha and Amos traced their origin to the farmers and shepherds of their nation. Of the others, although nothing certain is known, we may still gather from this very fact that they were called to this office from various ranks of men, so that God should not seem to be bound more strictly to any one order, when the ordinary priests were failing in their duty. Thus at last he wished to show that all men ought to be subject to his Word, and that no order has a just reason to be ashamed of this office, since from of old some had been appointed to it from all ranks. The same could be said of the apostles and their successors, if the matter seemed to admit any doubt. Those men certainly valued the office of preaching so highly that they thought the care of the church treasury and of the poor, a task holy in itself, should be committed to others, lest they be hindered by it in the duty of teaching. But why do I speak of that, when they almost passed the administration of the sacraments on to others, so that they themselves might preach the gospel more freely and with greater fruit? Paul certainly writes that he baptized very few, and gives as the reason for his action that he was sent not to baptize but to preach the gospel. Yet from this no one should conclude that the sacraments are to be omitted altogether or treated more carelessly. Rather, when they compared these with the Word of God, they could easily see how much more excellent the Word is, and they were led by the example of Christ, who, although he was frequent and diligent in teaching, is nowhere read to have baptized anyone. Nor will it be doubtful that these things were so observed both by him and by the apostles, if we consider the use of the divine Word and how necessary it is for us. For it is established that we are sinners from our very birth, blind too and ignorant of all divine things, still unfit either to seek or to lay hold of what is good, and in the same way estranged from God and from the inheritance of heavenly goods. But through his Word God not only makes his will known to us, but in his Son also offers righteousness and satisfaction for sins, enlightens our minds, equips us with new strength, and at last communicates himself wholly to us. For this reason the Word is called the lamp to our feet, the light of our paths, the rule of life, truth, life and salvation. Paul, comprehending all these things in one word, calls it the word of reconciliation with God, on which the whole happiness of man depends. We treat these matters at greater length not without cause. For just as they commend the ministry of the Word, so they condemn its wicked despisers, who work to make it hateful to the common people by means of buffoonish speech and savage abuse, and who try to draw candidates of theology away from it. Such men take pleasure in their own wickedness, but one day this will cost them dearly, when they feel themselves deprived of life itself, whose Word they now shamelessly spurn. What those suffered who sinned by similar impiety in former times, the histories teach; nor are there lacking examples from our own age to confirm this. But most people lack eyes to observe the judgments of God and the punishments hanging over their own necks.

units.la: Confutantur item Christi exemplo, qui neglecta doctrina circa solos externos ritus & inanes ceremonias occupantur, quasi in illis vniuersus Dei cultus atque salutis ratio consistant. At qui olim per prophetas ea reijciebat Dominus, quae secundum Legis suae praescriptum fiebant, & Apostoli circa baptismum minus occupati fuerunt, ne quid praedicationi decederet. Et in veteri Ecclesia non quotidianus fuit Eucharistiae vsus: nimirum, ne Sacramenta Verbo pretiosiora aut magis necessaria esse putarentur. Qua ergo ratione suam sive audaciam sive superstitionem excusabunt, qui dies noctesque in suffitibus faciendis, in aspersionibus, in suffigendis ceres, in lectionibus & psalmodijs peregrina lingua decantatis transfigunt, & sexcentis alijs, quae nulla Dei authoritate confirmantur, Verbum autem Dei ita negligunt, vt totus fere annus absque concionibus sacris transeat? Imo si quae omnino habenda sunt, eas aut de Sanctis non tam superstitiosas quam ridiculas instituunt, aut quos sibi interpretandos sumunt scripturae locos, ineptissimis glossis corrumpunt, & ad sensum prorsus alienum detorquent. Fiunt haec omnia hodie in Papatu, & itafiunt, vt si ista fululeris, maxima regni illius pars, quasi fulcris suis destituta, sponte collabatur. Erant ergo haec obseruanda hodie ijs, qui Ecclesiae reformatores haberi volunt. Frustra enim circa alia occupabantur, nisi verbi Dei vsum frequentiorem restituant, & eius doctrinam ad populi instiurionem atque consolationem accommodent. Ne tamen sub doctrinae praetextu nobisipsis aut alijs imponamus, meminisse oportet, ne in praedicatione quia quidem nuda Dei cultum consistere: sed in ea prædicatione, qua regnum eius prædicatur, & ad fidei obedientiam homines adducuntur. Dicitur ea Euangelium regni Dei, quia ad eum scopum tendit, vt in nobis quidem, quoad hic viuimus, regnet Deus, nos autem vicissim eius virtute carne & mun do atq; principe eius superiores factos, olim cum illo in cælis æternum viuamus atque regnemus. Sed tempus est, vt in Lucæ verbis progrediamur.
units.tr: Likewise, the example of Christ refutes those who, neglecting doctrine, busy themselves only with external rites and empty ceremonies, as if the whole worship of God and the way of salvation consisted in these. Yet the Lord rejected through the prophets those things that were done according to the prescription of his Law, and the apostles were less concerned with baptism, lest anything be taken from preaching. Also, in the early Church the Eucharist was not used daily, doubtless so that the sacraments would not be thought more precious or more necessary than the Word. By what reasoning, then, will they excuse their audacity or superstition, who spend day and night in burning incense, in sprinklings, in fixing up wax candles, in readings and psalm-singing in a foreign tongue, and in six hundred other things that are confirmed by no authority of God; yet they neglect the Word of God so much that almost the whole year passes without sacred sermons? Indeed, if they do institute those things that must be had at all, they make them about the saints in a way that is not so much superstitious as ridiculous, or they corrupt the passages of Scripture they take upon themselves to interpret with the most absurd glosses, and twist them to a sense wholly foreign to them. All these things are done today in Papacy, and they are done in such a way that if you knocked away these props, the greatest part of that kingdom would fall of its own accord, as if deprived of its supports. Therefore these matters ought to be observed today by those who wish to be considered reformers of the Church. For they labour in vain over other things unless they restore the more frequent use of God's Word and adapt its teaching to the instruction and comfort of the people. Yet, lest under the pretext of doctrine we deceive ourselves or others, we must remember that the worship of God does not consist in bare preaching of any kind, but in that preaching by which the kingdom of God is proclaimed and men are brought to obedience of faith. It is called the gospel of the kingdom of God because it aims at this goal: that God may reign in us, so long as we live here, and that we, in turn, made superior by his power to the flesh, the world and its prince, may afterwards live and reign eternally with him in heaven. But it is time to proceed with the words of Luke.

units.la: Sequitur autem vbi nam locorum Christus prædicauerit? Nimirum in eorum Synagogis. Qua rum cum frequens fiat apud Euangelistas mentio, quædam de illis erunt dicenda. Templum Iudæi omnes vnicum habuerunt, cuius locum Hierosolymis Deus constituerat. Erat hoc instar parochiæ, ad quam tota gens colligebatur, ne in sectas scinderentur, sed omnes in fide promissi Seruatoris coa lescerent, qui præfinito tempore Hierosolymis pro peccato totius mundi immolari debebat, & qui to illo cultu Leuitico repræsentabatur. Ideo tribus festis folennibus, in Pafchate nimirum, Pentecoste & Tabernaculorum folennitate illuc conueniebant, vt fidei & cultus vnitatem profiterentur, neq; alibi quam illic licebat sacra facere. At ne interea religionis exercitium prorsus negligeretur, & Legis diuinæ cognitio apud vulgus omnino intercideret, per omnes tribus in vrbibus & castellis alijsq; locis frequentioribus certa domus cœtibus sacris destinatæ erant, quas Synagogas dicebant, eò quòd illuc populus diebus Sabbati conuenire ad audiendum Legem & ad preces publicas. Quæ etiam causa fuit, quòd Leuitæ non certam aliquam terræ partem tenerent, sed in tribus omnes dis- persi effent, vt omnibus instituendis sufficerent. Iniftis Synagogis Christus docuit frequenter, ne quid præter ordinem a Deo institutum faceret, & in populo sicut ma excitaret, neue doctrinam suam suspectam redderet, si in locis obscurioribus vulgaretur. Et hoc illum in primis spectauisse, ipsius ad Caiaphan verba testantur. Cum enim ab hoc de doctrina sua & discipulis interrogaretur, respondebat: Ego aperte locutus sum mundo, ego semper docui in synagoga & in templo, quo vndique Iudæi conueniunt, & in occulto locutus sum nihil, &c.
units.tr: Next comes the question of where Christ preached. Of course it was in their synagogues. Since the Evangelists mention these often, something must be said about them. All the Jews had one temple, whose site God had fixed at Jerusalem. This served as a kind of parish to which the whole nation gathered, so that they would not split into sects but would all unite in faith in the promised Saviour, who was to be sacrificed at Jerusalem for the sin of the whole world at the appointed time, and who was represented by that Levitical worship. For this reason they assembled there three times a year, at the feasts of the Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, to profess the unity of their faith and worship, and it was not lawful to offer sacrifice anywhere else. Yet so that the exercise of religion would not be entirely neglected in the meantime, and knowledge of the divine Law would not wholly die out among the common people, in every tribe, in towns, villages and other more populous places, certain houses were set aside for sacred assemblies. These they called synagogues, because the people gathered there on the days of the Sabbath to hear the Law and for public prayers. This was also the reason why the Levites did not hold any particular portion of the land, but were scattered throughout all the tribes, so that they would be sufficient for teaching everyone. Christ often taught in these synagogues, so that he would not do anything beyond the order instituted by God, nor stir up the people, nor make his teaching suspect by having it spread in obscure places. That this was his chief concern is shown by his words to Caiaphas. When he was questioned by him about his teaching and disciples, he answered: "I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where the Jews gather from every side, and I have said nothing in secret," and so on.

units.la: Simul autem publicos ecclesiæ cœtus suo exemplo Christus commendat, & non solum impios & prophanos sacrorum omnium contemptores damnat, verumetiam sceleratam eorum hypocrisim argu it, qui communia templa nolunt ingredi, & a cœtibus ecclesiæ in vniuersum abstinent, ne aliorum vitijs & peccatis polluantur. Sunt inter hos nostro sæculo facile principes Anabaptistæ, qui cum propria vitia & suæ sectæ hominum flagitia pulchre dissimulare & excusare norint, in alienis notandis plus quam Lynces sunt & serpentes Epidaudrij, vt poetæ verbis vtar. Quam primum ergo aliquos ex nostris vident manifestioribus vitijs pollutos, tunc fe iustissimam ab ecclesiis nostris discedendi causam inuenisse putant: imò vt a nobis separationem faciant necessarium esse aiunt, ne alium scelerib. communicent. Atqui in ecclesia non scelerum, sed sacrorum & rerum cœlestium communio est, quæ quia in fide & spiritu consistit, ad eos solos pertinet, qui per fidem vera Christi membra facti sunt. At cum fide destituantur omnes impij, & quotquot deuoto ad impietatem animo in peccatis suis incurabiles pergunt, possunt quidem illi in externam ecclesiæ societatem sese insinuare, membra autem ecclesiæ non esse possunt, cum non eodem spiritu animentur & regantur. Quod ergo pollutionis aut communionis periculum pijs, qui non eiusdem corporis cum illis membra sunt? Aut quo iure falsa fidei professio, quam isti homines faciunt, pijs fraudi erit, qui ab omni dolo alieni fidem in Christum sancte coluntVerbum Dei reuerenter audiunt, et Sacramentis ecclesiæ secundum Christi institutum religiose vtuntur? Sed sufficit illis hominibus confutandis vnu hoc Christi exemplum, si quæ tunc fuerit inter Iudæos rerum conditio probe expendamus. Vbi circa doctrinam humanæ traditiones occurrent, quibus legis sensum obscuratum & tantum non sepultum fuisse constat. In exterr no autem cultu non solum superstitiosa sacrorum fiducia dominabatur, sed in turpem quaestum tota religio degenerauerat. Quanta autem tunc apud omnes ordines morum corruptio, & quam effrenus scelerum licentia fuerit, nemo ignorat, qui eius sæculi historias vel obiter inspexit. Neque inter vulgares modo & plebeios ista fiebant, sed ab illis maxime peccabatur, qui in ecclesia & repub. præalijs authoritate & dignitate eminebant. Non tamen idcirco a templo & Synagogis eorum Christus abstinet: sed quia penes populum illum adhuc erat ecclesiæ titulus (quia templum cum sacris illis diuina authoritate nitebatur) & Synagogas ipse Deus instituerat, & saltem aliqui adhuc reli qui erant, qui aut tunc illis rectè vtebantur, aut ad frugem meliorem reduci poterant, Christus maioris partis partûs improbitatem & hypocrisim non tanti facienda putat, vt cum publico scandalo sanctissima Dei instituta simul euerti, coetus omnes aboleri, & scisma non necessarium inuehi debeat. Neq; ipse aut alij pij in coetibus illis ex aliorum consortio aliquid contagij contraxerunt. Quod ipsum in Apostolis & Iuda proditore & infinitis aliis exemplis obseruari debet. Sunt ergo nostri illi nimis delicatuli, quos aliorum peccata sic offendunt, vt propter aliquos malos totas ecclesias damnare non verentur. Et est hic mirificus Satanae astus, qui sub pietatis et religionis praetextu hominibus ita imponit, vt dum alieni sceleris contagium fugiunt, seipsos scelere omnium immanissimo polluant et Ecclesiae vnitate scindant, qua Deus vnice delectatur. Caueant ergo sibi ab ab eorum impostura pij, & primo quidem meminerint praecipuum religionis verae exercitium circa coetus sacros versari, in quibus Dei verbum praedicatur, preces publicae fiunt & Sacramenta Christi dispensantur. Illis ergo seruandis studeant, neque aliquam scismatis aut secessionis causam praebeant, quicunque Dei cultores esse volunt. Deinde cogitent ad coetus istos locis certis opus esse, qui sacri esse debent, id est, alieni ab omni vsu prophano, vni autem Deo & cultui eius consecrati. Proculergo eijciantur, quaecunq; mentes hominum a Deo auocare solent, neq; alicui liceat locos istos negotijs prophanis polluere. Peccatur hodie inter Christianos in vtramque partem. Alij enim templa Duorum cultui consecrant, & eadem simulachris, altaribus, lampadibus, cereis, velis alijsq; superstitionum vanissimarum instrumentis sic farciunt, vt in illis gentilitiae idololatriae formam potius quam veteris Christianismi vestigia inuenias. Alij vero dum superstitiosi haberi nolunt, impij & prophani fiunt sacrorum omnium contemptores, simulq; templa in contemptum extremum adducunt, dum in illis quaeuis negotia tractant, imo pueris quoq; suos in illis ludos permittunt. Fiunt haec non sine publico scandalo, & animos ab omni religione alienos arguunt.
units.tr: At the same time, by his own example, Christ commends the public assemblies of the Church. He not only condemns the impious and profane despisers of all sacred things, but also exposes the wicked hypocrisy of those who refuse to enter the common temples and abstain altogether from the assemblies of the Church, lest they be polluted by the vices and sins of others. Among these in our own age the Anabaptists are easily the leaders. Although they know well how to overlook and excuse their own vices and the crimes of the people of their sect, they are sharper than lynxes in noting the faults of others, and are "Epidaurian serpents," to use the poet's words. As soon as they see some of ours stained by more obvious vices, they think they have found a most just reason for leaving our churches. Indeed, they say it is necessary to separate from us so that they do not share in our wickedness. Yet the communion of the Church is not a communion of sins but of holy things and heavenly realities. Since this communion rests on faith and the Spirit, it belongs only to those who have become true members of Christ through faith. But all the impious lack faith, and all who persist in their sins, incurable and devoted to impiety, can indeed insinuate themselves into the outward fellowship of the Church, but they cannot be members of the Church, since they are not animated and governed by the same Spirit. What danger of pollution or communion, then, is there for the godly, who are not members of the same body as these people? Or by what right will the false profession of faith made by these men be a deception to the godly, who are free from all guile, who devoutly worship faith in Christ, reverently hear the Word of God, and religiously use the Sacraments of the Church according to Christ's institution? But to refute these men, it is enough for us to weigh carefully this one example of Christ, and the condition of things among the Jews at that time. There, in matters of doctrine, human traditions abounded, by which it is clear that the sense of the Law was obscured and all but buried. In the external worship, not only did superstitious trust in sacred rites hold sway, but the whole religion had degenerated into shameful profit-making. As for how great the corruption of morals was then among all ranks, and how unbridled the licence of crime, no one who has glanced even briefly at the histories of that age can be ignorant. These things were done not only among the common and plebeian people, but the greatest sins were committed by those who stood out in the Church and the state, in authority and dignity. Yet Christ did not on this account abstain from their temple and synagogues. The reason was that the title of the Church still belonged to that people (since the temple, with its sacred rites, rested on divine authority, and God himself had instituted the synagogues), and because at least some who remained could either use these things rightly at that time or could be brought back to a better way of life. Christ did not think the wickedness and hypocrisy of the greater part was of such weight that the most holy institutions of God should be overturned together with public scandal, all assemblies abolished, and an unnecessary schism introduced. Nor did he or other godly men catch any contagion from fellowship with others in those assemblies. This same thing must be observed in the case of the Apostles, of Judas the traitor, and in countless other examples. Therefore those fastidious people of ours are far too squeamish, offended by the sins of others to such an extent that they do not hesitate to condemn whole churches on account of some wicked men. Here is the marvellous craft of Satan, who, under the pretext of piety and religion, so deceives people that, while they flee the contagion of another's crime, they pollute themselves with the most monstrous crime of all and tear apart the unity of the Church, in which God alone takes delight. Let the godly therefore beware of their imposture. And first let them remember that the chief exercise of true religion lies in the sacred assemblies, in which the Word of God is preached, public prayers are made, and the Sacraments of Christ are dispensed. Let them strive to preserve these, and let whoever wishes to be worshippers of God give no cause for schism or secession. Next, let them consider that for these assemblies certain places are needed, which ought to be sacred, that is, free from all profane use and consecrated to the one God and his worship. Therefore let whatever usually draws men's minds away from God be cast far out, and let no one be allowed to defile these places with worldly business. Today among Christians there is fault on both sides. Some consecrate temples to the worship of demons, and so crowd them with images, altars, lamps, candles, veils and other instruments of most vain superstitions, that in them you find the form of pagan idolatry rather than the traces of the ancient Christianity. Others, while unwilling to be thought superstitious, become impious and profane despisers of all sacred things, and at the same time bring the temples into the utmost contempt, since they conduct all kinds of business in them, and even allow their children to play games there. These things are done not without public scandal, and they reveal minds that are alien to all religion.

units.la: Caeterum vt locis certis opus est, in quibus religio exerceatur, ita eidem tempus quoque certum destinari debet, quo homines relictis aliis rebus omnibus se totos Deo & cultui eius dedicent. Quia enim natura ad ea, quae carni seruiunt, procliuiores sumus, difficile fuerit animum inter huius seculi negotia in rerum coelestium meditatione subuehere. Ideo in ipsa rerum origine Deus septimum diem sibi consecrauit, & perpetua lege postea sanciuit, vt eum homines cum religioso & sancto otio transfigant, abstineant autem ab omni labore profano & non necessario, quo Dei cultus impediri possit. Obseruauit igitur in hac etiam parte Patris sui statuta Christus diligentissime (vt in ijs, quae proximo sermone sequuntur, diserte dicetur) & simul suo exemplo dierum sacrorum obseruationem commendauit. Exigit hanc a nobis iustitiae lex. Quia enim vniuersum nostrae vitae tempus, imo nostra omnia Deo debemus, nimium iniusti & iniqui erimus, si cum sex nostri aeui partes nobis integras ille relinquat, nos septimam quoque quae illi debetur, ipsi negemus. Deinde necessitas ipsa iubet, ne diei huius religionem negligamus. Nam vt corporis vires quiete & otio instaurari oportet: ita animo quoque sua quies concedenda est, vt curis & laboribus huius vitae vacuus, in Domino recreetur. Neque hoc nobis molestum aut rei domesticae noxium videri debet. Facilis enim tantilli temporis iactura est, si cum multiplici fructu, qui inde ad nos redundat, conferatur. Imo exsculari potius debemus Dei paternam prouidentiam, qui quietis & otij, quo corpus carere nullo modo potest, hunc finem & vsum inuenit, vt tunc maxime ea agamus, quae ad tuendam salutem aeternam faciunt. Hinc tam graues minae aduersus Sabbati violatores apud prophetas audiuntur. Hinc mortis supplicium ijsdem in lege destinatum fuit. Et cum in huius executione Sacerdotes & reges cessarent, Deus peccatum illud vna cum multis alijs totius vrbis & gentis excidio, atque septuaginta annorum exilio in Babylone expiari voluit. Quod ita obseruauit Nehemias, vt inter alia, quae post reditum in patriam correctione diligentiori opus habebant, Sabbatum non postremo loco habuerit. Ex hoc igitur vno de nostri seculi moribus iudicium facere possemus, si quid hic fiat attentius ispicere liberet. Quod enim totius anni tempus dabis, magis a Dei cultu alienum, quam quod huic totum consecratum esse debebat? Plerique certe dies Dominicus in ignauo otio, fluoso & ad libidinem compositio corporis ornatu, in poculis & comessationibus, in choris & ludis lasciuioribus, in stupris, adulteriis, iurgijs, rixis, execrationibus aliisq; huius generis flagitijs transfigunt, quae insana & pudoris expers ebrietas parit. Qui vero his honestiores videntur, ij rationes negotiorum suorum eo tempore inspiciunt, debita exigunt, consilia vsuraria ineunt, aut etiam seipsos atq; familiam omnem aliquo labore manuario fatigant. Fit ergo vt qui Deo sacer esse debebat dies, fere totus Baccho, Veneri, Marti, Mercurio, imo potius ipsi diabolo consecretur. Qui autem nondum omnem pietatis sensum exuerunt, ij se omni officio defunctos putant, si matutino tempore cocionem sacram audiant, reliquum vero diei tempus studijs vanissimis tribuant. Et haec quidem ita fiunt palam, vt nemo negare possit: & adhuc Dei iram vndique sese exerentem admiramur?
units.tr: Moreover, just as fixed places are needed in which religion is exercised, so too a fixed time ought to be set apart for it, when people, leaving aside all other affairs, may devote themselves wholly to God and his worship. For since we are by nature more inclined to those things that serve the flesh, it would be difficult to lift the mind up to the meditation of heavenly things amid the business of this world. Therefore, at the very origin of things, God consecrated the seventh day to himself, and afterwards sanctioned it by a perpetual law, that people should spend it in religious and holy leisure, and abstain from all profane and unnecessary labour by which the worship of God might be hindered. Christ, therefore, observed most diligently in this respect also the statutes of his Father (as will be explained clearly in what follows in the next sermon), and at the same time by his example commended the observance of sacred days. The law of justice requires this of us. For since we owe to God the whole time of our life, indeed everything we have, we shall be exceedingly unjust and unfair if, when he leaves us six parts of our age entire, we deny him the seventh, which is owed to him. Then necessity itself commands that we not neglect the observance of this day. For just as the strength of the body must be restored by rest and leisure, so the mind too must be granted its own repose, so that, freed from the cares and labours of this life, it may be refreshed in the Lord. Nor ought this to seem burdensome to us or harmful to our domestic affairs. For the loss of so small a time is easily borne if it is weighed against the manifold fruit that flows back to us from it. Indeed, we ought rather to admire the fatherly providence of God, who has found in rest and leisure, which the body can by no means do without, this purpose and use, that we may then especially do those things that contribute to securing eternal salvation. Hence such grave threats against the violators of the Sabbath are heard in the prophets. Hence capital punishment was appointed for the same offence in the Law. And when priests and kings ceased to carry out this punishment, God wished that sin to be expiated along with many others by the destruction of the whole city and nation, and by the seventy years of exile in Babylon. Nehemiah so observed this that, among the other things which needed more careful correction after the return to the homeland, he did not place the Sabbath in the last rank. From this one thing alone we could judge the morals of our age, if it pleased us to look at closely what is done here. For what portion of the whole year will you give that is more alien to the worship of God than the day which ought to have been wholly consecrated to it? Indeed, most people spend the Lord's Day in idle leisure, in loose and wanton display of the body, in drinking-bouts and revels, in dances and more lascivious games, in debauchery, adultery, quarrels, brawls, curses and other crimes of this kind, which mad and shameless drunkenness brings forth. Those who seem more respectable spend that time reviewing their business affairs, collecting debts, devising usurious schemes, or even wearing out themselves and their whole household with some manual labour. And so it comes about that the day which ought to have been sacred to God is almost entirely dedicated to Bacchus, Venus, Mars, Mercury, or rather to the devil himself. Those who have not yet cast off all sense of piety think they have discharged every duty if they hear the sacred sermon in the morning, and give the rest of the day to the emptiest pursuits. And these things are done so openly that no one can deny them. And do we still wonder that the anger of God is displayed on every side?

units.la: Porro quis doctrinae Christi effectus fuerit, Lucas indicat, quando omnes eum glorificatuisse, id est, commendauisse & eximijs praeconijs extulisse scribit. Id vero Marcus pluribus verbis enun tians ait: Stupebant super doctrina eius: Erat enim docens eos tanquam authoritate praeditus, & non sicut Scribae. Mox ergo noua & prius nunquam visa maiestas atque virtus in illius praedica- tione refulsit, quam intra animos suos sentiebant, qui illos nondum indurarant, neq; malitioso con- tradicendi studio abripiebantur. Estque semper coiuncta Verbo Dei virtus illa, quam & pij & im- pij intra semetipsos sentiunt: illi quidem, vt tandem illuminati & emolliti Deum vocantem sequan tur: hi vero, vt intra semetipsos conuicti, propriae conscientiae testimonio damnentur. Debet hoc Ver bi administris animum facere, ne profectus ipsem omnem abijciant, & in munere suo remissiores fi- ant. At quia quae hic dicenda erant, in Marci expositione diximus, nolumus in praesenti prolixiores esse. Agnoscamus autem in breui Lucae narratiuncula immensam Dei bonitatem, qui filium suum, Iesum Christum, nobis doctorem & prophetam dedit, simulque eius in nobis instituendis industriam exosculemur. Finis vero omnium nobis hic esto, vt eius vocem secuti omnes huius vitae pericula euadamus, & olim caelestis regni haereditate fruamur cum ipso, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke shows what effect the teaching of Christ had, when he writes that all glorified him, that is, commended him and extolled him with remarkable praise. Mark, expressing this in more words, says: "They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." Immediately, therefore, a new majesty and power, never seen before, shone forth in his preaching, which those felt within their minds who had not yet been hardened and were not carried away by a malicious spirit of contradiction. That power is always joined to the Word of God, and both the godly and the ungodly feel it within themselves: the godly, that once enlightened and softened they may follow God calling them; the ungodly, that being convicted within themselves they may be condemned by the testimony of their own conscience. This ought to make the ministers of the Word careful not to cast away the progress itself, and not to grow more lax in their office. But because what had to be said here we have said in our exposition of Mark, we do not wish to be longer at present. Let us acknowledge, however, in this brief little narrative of Luke, the immense goodness of God, who gave his Son, Jesus Christ, to us as teacher and prophet, and at the same time let us embrace his diligence in instructing us. And may the goal of all of us be this: that, following his voice, we may escape the dangers of this life, and at length enjoy the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLI.

units.la: Et venit Nazarethum, vbi fuerat nutritus, & intrauit vt consueue- rat, die Sabbati in Synagogam, & surrexit vt legeret. Tunc datus est ei liber Isaiae prophetae, cumq; explicuisset librum, inuenit locum, in quo scriptum erat, Spiritus Domini super me, propterea quod vnxit me: vt euangelizem pauperibus misit me: vt sanem contritos corde, vt praedicem captiuis dimissionem, & caecis visus recuperationem, & vt con- fractos emittam in libertatem: vt praedicem annum Domini acceptum. Et complicatum librum cum reddidisset ministro, sedit: & omnium in Synagoga oculi erant intenti in eum. Coepit autem eis dicere: Hodie impleta est haec scriptura in auribus vestris.
units.tr: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as was his custom, and stood up to read. And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Isaiah. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him. And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

units.la: SIcuti Deus filium suum Iesum Christum humani generis Seruatorem dedit: ita eundem salutis etiam & vitae doctorem vniuersalem & irrefragabilem esse voluit. Recte ergo ille munus suum a verbi praedicatione orditur, in qua toto eo tempore, quo in terris vixit, diligentissimus fuit, adeo vt nullam vnquam praedicandi occasionem inutiliter elabi passus sit. Quin, vt nuper audiuimus, & Synagogas studiose ingressus est, & dies Sabbati obseruauit, vt quam plurimos sibi lucre face- ret. Quod vt eius fidem & studium magnifice commendat: ita de verbi ministerio nos iudicare do- cet, ne tanquam inutile aut superuacaneum contemnamus, in quo Dei filium tam assiduum & fre- quentem fuisse constat. Sequitur modo, quid Nazarethi egerit, vbi educatus fuit, & quae ipsi propter Mariam matrem & Iosephum nutritium suum patriae instar erat. Quae historia eo dili- gentiori consideratione digna est, quod integram Christi concionem, vel potius integrae concionis argumentum continet, quo docemur, vt in ecclesia conciones sacrae institui debeant: quis item sit Christus, quid nobis conferat, & qui nam bonorum caelestium, quae ille nobis meruit, participes possint fieri.
units.tr: Just as God gave his Son Jesus Christ as the Saviour of the human race, so he also willed that the same Son should be the universal and infallible teacher of salvation and life. Rightly, then, he began his office with the preaching of the Word, in which he was most diligent during the whole time he lived on earth, so much so that he never allowed any opportunity for preaching to slip away unused. Indeed, as we heard a little while ago, he eagerly entered the synagogues and observed the Sabbath days, so that he might win as many as possible for himself. This both magnificently commends his faith and zeal, and teaches us to judge rightly of the ministry of the Word, so that we do not despise it as useless or superfluous, since it is clear that the Son of God was so constant and frequent in it. Next we consider what he did at Nazareth, where he was brought up, and what his home country was to him, on account of Mary his mother and Joseph his foster father. This story deserves all the closer consideration because it contains the whole of Christ's sermon, or rather the whole subject of a sermon, by which we are taught how sacred sermons ought to be delivered in the church; likewise who Christ is, what he confers on us, and who may become partakers of the heavenly goods which he has merited for us.

units.la: Priusquam vero ad ipsam concionem accedamus, non ofcitanter obseruari debet, Christum inter primos, quibus praedicauit, suos quoque Nazarethanos censuisse, etsi non ignoraret, illos publica quadam infamia notari (vt ex Nathanielis verbis apud Ioannem apparet) & prophano rerum caelestium contemptu laborare. Commendat nobis hoc exemplo pietatem in patriam, & vt gratos nos iis praebeamus, qui in nos aliquod beneficium contulerunt. Enimuero patriae amorem nobis naturae lex commendat, vt nimirum eam terram prae aliis diligamus, quae maioribus nostris diuturnum hospitium praebuit, quae nos nascentes prima excepit, quae infantiam & pueritiam nostram pertulit, & in qua nobis a pueris multa iucunda, multa etiam aduersa acciderunt. Ideo inter gentes etiam patriae studiosissimi fuerunt, quotquot a virtute & sapientia commendantur, quorum plerique non solum labores & curas omnis generis sustinuerunt, verumetiam vitam propriam dederunt, vt patriae periclitanti succurrerent. Et noti sunt poetae versus: Nescio qua natale solum dulcedine captos Attrahit, immemores nec finit esse sui. Alij vero nos post Deum primam gratiam patriae debere dixerunt. Constat denique eas modo respubli. felices fuisse, in quibus pietas in patriam floruit: perijsse autem infeliciter omnes eas, quarum ciues priuatum commodum publicae saluti anteposuerunt. Et vtinam exemplis peregrinis opus esset ad hoc demonstrandum: sed quae nostri seculi est infelicitas, vix aliqua gens inuenitur, quae non magno aliquo malo istud sentiat. Nam vt quae ad rempub. spectant omittamus, quam aliam superstitionum, dissidiorum, seditionum et bellorum ci uilium quae sub religionis praetextu excitantur, causam esse dicemus, quam quod plerique vt ventri & honoribus suis consulant, cum Pontificibus potius coniurare malunt, quam patriae salutem tueri, & exterae tyrannidis iugum ab illius ceruicibus remouere? Et in hoc maxime peccant, qui sibi in ecclesia Christi primatum vendicant, & apostolorum successores dici volunt: qui tunc demum se officium facere putant, si principes suos vna cum dulcissima patria Antichristi pedibus subijciant. Longe aliter Christus, qui Nazaretho suo Euangelij lucem attulit, vt ea illuminati libertate & salute vera fruerentur.
