Et huius exemplum secutus Paulus, etsi gentium Apostolum se esse sciret, suis tamen gentilibus Iudaeis se in primis debitorem esse fatebatur, & pro illis anathema fieri cupiebat, vt ipsi in Christo salui fierent. His praemissis ad loci praesentis tractationem accedamus, quo Christi concio apud Nazarethanos habita describitur.
units.tr: Before we come to the sermon itself, we must carefully note that Christ, among the first to whom he preached, reckoned his own Nazarenes as well, although he was not unaware that they were marked by a certain public infamy (as appears from the words of Nathanael in John) and were afflicted with a profane contempt for heavenly things. By this example he commends to us love of country, and that we should show ourselves grateful to those who have conferred some benefit upon us. Indeed, the law of nature commends to us love of our country, namely that we should cherish above others that land which gave our forefathers a lasting home, which first received us at birth, which bore our infancy and boyhood, and in which many pleasant and many also unpleasant things have happened to us from boyhood. For this reason, among the nations too, all who are commended for virtue and wisdom have been most devoted to their country; most of them not only endured labours and anxieties of every kind, but even gave their own lives to come to the aid of their country in peril. And the verses of the poet are well known: "I know not what sweetness draws us captive to our native soil, and does not let us forget ourselves." Others have said that after God we owe our first grace to our country. Finally, it is established that those commonwealths were happy in which love of country flourished, and that all those perished unhappily whose citizens placed private advantage before the public safety. Would that foreign examples were needed to demonstrate this! But such is the unhappiness of our age that hardly any nation is found which does not feel this through some great evil. For, to leave aside matters that concern the commonwealth, what shall we say is the cause of so many superstitions, dissensions, seditions and civil wars stirred up under the pretext of religion, other than that many prefer to conspire with the Papists rather than to guard the safety of their country and throw off the yoke of foreign tyranny from its neck, so that they may look after their bellies and their honours? And they sin most grievously in this who claim for themselves the primacy in the church of Christ and wish to be called successors of the apostles, and who think they have done their duty only when they have placed their princes, together with their most beloved country, beneath the feet of Antichrist. Far otherwise did Christ act, who brought the light of the gospel to his Nazareth, so that they might enjoy true liberty and salvation by that light. And Paul, following this example, although he knew he was the apostle of the Gentiles, nevertheless confessed that he was above all a debtor to his own countrymen, the Jews, and wished to become accursed for their sake, so that they might be saved in Christ. With these things premised, let us come to the treatment of the present passage, in which the sermon of Christ delivered among the Nazarenes is described.

units.la: Principio modum & ritum narrat Euangelista, quem Christus inter docendum tenuit. In quo primum est, quod die Sabbati pro more in Synagogam & publicum coetum ingressus est. Vbi rursus videmus, illum vbique, quoad eius fieri potuit, receptum morem aut ordinem seruauisse, ne quid turbulentius facere videretur. Quod in primis obseruandum est in publico aliquo munere versantibus. Nam vt omnis mutatio reipubl. pernitiosa est, sic quae in ecclesia fiunt receptorum ritMATIONES, fere religionem omnem cum doctrina suspectam reddunt, & grauissimorum scismatum causa sunt. Nemo igitur temere mutare conetur, quod salua pietate tolerari poterit. Alia eorum ratio est, quae Dei gloriam laedunt, & cum fidei abnegatione atque manifesto salutis discrimine coiuncta sunt. Deinde cum iam opportunum esset, surrexit Christus, vt legeret. Surrexit autem in locum aeditiorem, qui lectioni & scripturarum interpretationi destinatus erat. Illic consisti datus est liber Isaiae prophetae, quem fortasse tunc Synagoga eius loci prae manibus habebat. Certe non temere hoc factum fuit, sive occultam Dei prouidentiam spectes, sive veteris ecclesiae morem, qui (vt in D. Ambrosio habetur) inter Christianos quoque in vsu fuit, vt tam veteris quam noui testamenti libros ex ordine in publicis lectionibus recitarent. Ideoque libri quoque publici erant, & in opulentioribus ecclesijs bibliothecae instructiores habebantur, quae toti coetui seruirent. Librum sibi oblatum Christus explicat, quaerit locum quem ecclesiae interpretetur, inuentum alta voce recitat, & tandem cum librum denuo complicuisset, ministro eum reddit, ipse vero loci, quem recitauerat, interpretationem aggreditur, quem sic tractat, vt singulas eius partes ad populi totius institutionem atque consolationem accommodet, dum iam exhibitum esse, imo se esse docet promissum populi redemptorem, quem venturum patres expectarint, &c.
units.tr: At the outset the evangelist relates the manner and ritual which Christ observed in teaching. Here the first thing is that on the Sabbath day he entered the synagogue and public assembly as was customary. Here again we see that he kept, so far as he could, the custom or order that was accepted everywhere, so that he might not seem to do anything disorderly. This must be especially observed by those engaged in some public office. For just as every change in the commonwealth is pernicious, so changes in the received rites of the church render nearly all religion together with its doctrine suspect, and are the cause of the most serious schisms. Let no one therefore rashly attempt to change what can be tolerated without harm to piety. It is otherwise with those things which injure the glory of God and are joined with the denial of the faith and a manifest danger to salvation. Next, when the time was now fitting, Christ stood up to read. He stood up, moreover, in the more elevated place, which was set apart for reading and for the interpretation of the Scriptures. There was handed to him the book of the prophet Isaiah, which the synagogue of that place perhaps then had at hand. Certainly this was not done by chance, whether you regard the hidden providence of God or the custom of the ancient church, which (as is found in Ambrose) was also in use among Christians, that they should read the books of both the Old and the New Testament in order in the public lessons. Therefore the books too were public, and in the wealthier churches libraries were kept better furnished, to serve the whole congregation. Christ unrolls the book that was offered to him, seeks the passage which he would expound to the church, reads it aloud when found, and at last, when he had closed the book again, gives it back to the minister; then he himself undertakes the interpretation of the passage which he had read, and treats it in such a way that he applies each of its parts to the instruction and consolation of the whole people, declaring that the Redeemer of the people, whom the fathers awaited as one to come, has now been shown, nay, that he himself is that promised Redeemer, and so on.

units.la: Apparet autem in hoc exemplo, quis vetustissimus & optimus docendi mos sit, qui etiam hodie in ecclesia retineri debeat. Nam quod in praesenti Christus fecit, hoc alias quoque factum fuisse legimus. De legis certe promulgatione post reditum ex Babylone per Esdram & sacerdotes facta in libro Nehemiae capite octavo sic scribitur: Stetit Esdras scriba super turriculam ligneam, quam in hunc vsum fecerant, stetitque penes eum Mathanias, Sema, Anaia, Vrias, Hilkias & Maasias. ad dextram eius: ad leuâ verò eius Pedaia, Mifael, Malkia, Hafum, Hasbaddana, Zacharias, & Mesullam. Et aperuit Esdras scriba librum in conspectu totius populi (eminebat enim supra omnem populum) cumque illum aperuisset, stetit vniuersus populus, & laudauit Esdras Dominum Deum magnum, responditque cunctus populus, Amen Amen: sublatisque manibus suis, inclinatoque vertice et facie ad terram adorarunt Dominum. Porrò Iesua, Bani, Serebia, Iamin, Accab, Sabethai, Hodia, Maasia, Kelita, Azaria, Iosabad, Hanan, Pelaia & Leuitae docebant populum in Lege, & populus erat in statione sua. Et legerunt in libro, in Lege Dei luculenter, explicantes sensum, et erudientes inter legendum, &c. Conueniunt his maxima ex parte, quae in libro Actorum capite 13. & in priori ad Corinthios cap.14. habentur. Quo loco Anabaptistae abutuntur, vt euincant vnicuique licere, vt quod sentit, publicè in ecclesia proponat. Atqui disertè illic Paulus de ordinarijs scripturae interpretibus, aut etiam ijs, qui interpretandi dono praediti erant, loquitur, & inter alia ait: Quòd si quis non sit interpres, taceat in ecclesia. Quia autem tunc coetus per aliquot horas extrahebantur, & saepe ad vesperam vsque, ideo plures erant interpretes, qui decenti ordine sibi succedebant, cùm vnus tot horis non posset sufficere. Et honoris ergo peregrinis quoque locus dabatur, si qui authoritate graues & ad docendum idonei adessent, vt in Actis loco supra citato esse videre. Nihil ergo ista seruiunt Anabaptistis, qui ambitioso furore perciti hoc vnum quaerunt, vt omnem in ecclesia ordinem euertant, & ipsi dominentur. Et cùm pro coetuum sacrorum, qui hodie habentur, ratione, vnus verbi administer sufficiat, neq; in tanta sententiarum varietate tutum sit quosuis, nisi prius probè examinatos, admittere, ne rudis populus magis distrahatur: minimè opus fuerit morem illum veterem postliminio reuocare, modò in ecclesijs singulis obseruetur, quod in praesenti Christus fecit. Sit ergo in quauis ecclesia locus certus, quem ij soli conscendant, quibus docendi populi munus commissum est. Hunc antiquitus cathedram sacram dixerunt, eò quòd sedentes docerent: & inde cathedrales ecclesiae dicebantur, in quibus conciones fiebant, eoq; distinguebantur ab Oratorijs, quae solis precibus erant destinata. In cathedram ascendat cum singulari reuerentia minister, & se ad rem sanctissimam & maximè necessariam tractandam accedere meminerit. Et debetur sane verbo Dei reuerentia summa, cùm in eo ipse Deus nobis loquatur. Ideo Christus surrexit ad legendum, et Paulus monet, vt aperto capite suum munus obeant, qui scripturas interpretantur. Deinde è loco sacro nihil recitetur, quàm quod in aliquo certo scripturae sacrae libro verbotim contineatur. Quia enim Ecclesia domus Dei est, non alia quàm huius vox in illa audiri debet. At haec eon in philosophorum libris, neq; in Sybillae antro, aut Delphico oraculo, sed in solis scripturis sacris habetur, quas ideo Paulus θεοπνεύστους, id est, à Deo inspiratas dicit, et quae reuera os illud Domini sunt, ex quo Ezechiel propheta conciones suas depromere iubetur. Et quò minus suspecta res esset, vetus ille mos ia olim obtinuit, vt ex libris ipsius ecclesiae proprijs loci recitaretur, quod ipsum Christus quoq; obseruauit, etiamsi ipse libro minimè opus haberet. Est ergo iure reprehendenda eorum ambitio, qui vt alijs doctiores apparēat, aut numine quodam nouo afflati putentur, absq; libro in cathedram ascendunt, & saepe vix nominato authore locum aliquem memoriter recitant, quem populo interpretentur. Peccant isti in scripturae sacrae & verbi Dei maiestatem, cui plurimum derogant, dum suae existimationi consultū volunt. Quid verò de Rapsodis dicemus, qui per scripturas temere vagantur, et ferè absq; delectu modò hunc modò illum locum recitant, vt populus quantùmuis diligens quid ex illis auditurus sit prorsus ignoret, donec illi loqui coeperint? Pugnat hoc cum vetustissimo ecclesiae more, quae integros libros ex ordine audire solita fuit, neque multùm ad populi aedificationem conferunt, qui inter docendum certi nihil sibi propositum habent. Superat tamen omnes abusus eorum impietas, qui nullum verbo Dei in ecclesia locum relinquunt, nisi quòd lectiones aliquas lingua peregrina recitant, populo autem hominum traditiones & legendas sanctorum (vt ipsi loquuntur) obtrudunt, ex quibus praeter impias & imanes superstitiones nihil discì possit. Regnat ista audacia hodie in Papatu, vt negari non possit, foedior esse inter Christianos ecclesiae faciem, quàm olim inter Iudaeos sub Pontificibus Anna & Caiapha fuerit. Nam etsi patrum traditiones tunc dominarentur, suus tamen scripturis locus adhuc reliquus erat in Synagogis, & (vt Iacobus in Actis ait) Moses per singula sabbata publicè legebatur. At hodie nostri illi non contenti suas traditiones obtrusisse, scripturas simul omnes ex populi manibus excutiunt, imò illas impiè accusant, dum ex ijs errores & hæresum seminaria hauriri clamant, populum verò infelicem ad simulachra remittunt, quæ illi libros laicorum vocant. Produnt illi se- sefatis hoc vno indicio, & proinde indigni sunt, quorum authoritate moueamur. Discant autem in ecclesijs suis scripturas seruare & audire, quicunque sibi bene esse volunt. At non satis erit illas recitauisse, sed easdem interpretari & rebus præsentibus applicare opportet, ut & publicè ecclesiæ totius ædificationi & singulorum institutioni seruiant. Id Paulus rectam verbi secationem vo-cat, & eam ministerio in primis necessariam esse docet. Nam si præter nudam recitationem nihil addatur, multa rudiores & imperiti non intelligent, plerique verò quæcunque dicuntur, nihil ad se pertinere putabunt, & ita non plus proficient ecclesiarum ministri, quàm si quis carnes quidem pin-guissimas in mensam afferat, sed crudas adhuc & proinde esui inutiles. Ideò apud Nehemiam scri-bitur, sacerdotes non modò recitauisse ex libro legis præcepta Domini, verumetiam inter legendum sensum explicuisse & populum erudiuisse, ut singuli scirent, quid ipsis facto opus esset. Quem morem prophetas quoque obseruauisse ipsorum sermones satis testantur. Et idem in præsenti Christus fecit, & sæpe aliàs, ut suo loco audiemus. Quod cùm iam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus in Ecclesia veteri obseruatum fuerit, nimis ridiculi sunt, qui nudam scripturarum recitationem suf-ficere putant.
units.tr: This example shows what the oldest and best method of teaching is, and one that should still be kept in the Church today. For what Christ does here, we read that others did as well. The promulgation of the Law after the return from Babylon, made through Ezra and the priests, is described in the eighth chapter of Nehemiah: "Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for this purpose; and beside him stood Mattaniah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah on his right hand; and on his left hand stood Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah and Meshullam. And Ezra the scribe opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he was above all the people), and when he opened it, all the people stood up. And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, Amen, Amen, lifting up their hands; and they bowed their heads and worshipped the LORD with their faces to the ground. Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah and the Levites caused the people to understand the Law, and the people stood in their place. So they read in the book, in the Law of God, clearly, giving the sense and causing them to understand the reading." This agrees for the most part with what is found in Acts chapter 13 and in the first letter to the Corinthians chapter 14. The Anabaptists abuse this passage to prove that anyone may publicly propose in the Church whatever he thinks. Yet Paul there speaks plainly of the ordinary interpreters of Scripture, or of those who had the gift of interpreting, and among other things he says: "But if anyone is not an interpreter, let him keep silent in the church." Since the assemblies then sometimes lasted for several hours, and often until evening, there were several interpreters who succeeded one another in good order, since one man could not suffice for so many hours. And out of respect, a place was also given to strangers, if any were present who were weighty in authority and fit to teach, as can be seen in Acts in the passage cited above. Therefore these things help the Anabaptists nothing; they, stirred by an ambitious frenzy, seek only this, to overturn all order in the Church and to rule over it themselves. And since, for the form of the sacred assemblies held today, one minister of the Word is enough, and since in such a variety of opinions it is not safe to admit just anyone unless he has first been carefully examined, lest the untrained people be more divided, there would be no need at all to recall that old custom by right of return, provided that in each church what Christ does here is observed. Let there therefore be in every church a fixed place which only those ascend to whom the duty of teaching the people has been entrusted. Of old they called this the sacred chair, because those who taught sat in it; and from this the churches in which sermons were given were called cathedral churches, and they were thereby distinguished from oratories, which were set aside for prayers alone. The minister should ascend the pulpit with particular reverence, and remember that he is approaching the handling of a most holy and most necessary matter. Indeed the highest reverence is owed to the Word of God, since God himself speaks to us in it. For this reason Christ stood up to read, and Paul warns that those who interpret the Scriptures should discharge their office with head uncovered. Next, nothing should be recited from the holy place except what is contained word for word in some fixed book of Holy Scripture. For since the Church is the house of God, only the voice of its Owner ought to be heard in it. But this voice is not found in the books of the philosophers, nor in the cave of the Sibyl, nor in the Delphic oracle, but in the Holy Scriptures alone; these Paul calls "God-breathed" [θεοπνεύστους], that is, inspired by God, and these are truly the mouth of the Lord, from which the prophet Ezekiel was commanded to draw forth his sermons. And so that the matter might be less open to suspicion, that ancient custom long prevailed that passages were read from the church's own books, which Christ also observed, even though he himself had no need of a book. Therefore the ambition of those is rightly to be censured who, in order to appear more learned than others, or to be thought inspired by some new divine power, ascend the pulpit without a book, and often, scarcely naming the author, recite from memory some passage which they then expound to the people. Such men sin against the majesty of Scripture and the Word of God, which they greatly diminish while they wish to look after their own reputation. What shall we say of the rhapsodists, who wander rashly through the Scriptures and recite now this passage, now that, almost without any selection, so that the people, however attentive, know nothing at all of what they are going to hear from them until they begin to speak? This conflicts with the most ancient custom of the Church, which was accustomed to hear whole books in order, and such men contribute little to the edification of the people, since they have no definite aim in view while teaching. Yet their impiety surpasses all their abuses, for they leave no place for the Word of God in the Church, except that they recite some lessons in a foreign tongue, and foist upon the people the traditions of men and the legends of the saints (as they themselves call them), from which nothing can be learned except impious and monstrous superstitions. This audacity reigns today in the Papacy, so that it cannot be denied that the face of the Church among Christians is more foul than it once was among the Jews under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. For although the traditions of the Fathers then held sway, still the Scriptures had their own place in the synagogues, and (as James says in Acts) "Moses was read publicly on every sabbath." But today those men, not content with having imposed their traditions, tear all the Scriptures out of the hands of the people; indeed they impiously accuse them, crying that errors and seedbeds of heresies are drawn from them, and they send the unhappy people back to images, which they call the books of the laity. By this one sign they reveal themselves, and therefore they are unworthy that we should be moved by their authority. Let all who wish to be well, however, learn in their churches to keep and to hear the Scriptures. Yet it will not be enough to have recited them; they must also be interpreted and applied to present circumstances, so that they serve both the edification of the whole Church in public and the instruction of each individual. Paul calls this "rightly dividing the word of truth," and teaches that it is especially necessary for the ministry. For if nothing is added beyond the bare recitation, many of the less skilled and unlearned will not understand, and most will think that whatever is said has nothing to do with them; and so the ministers of the churches will profit no more than if someone brought very fat meats to the table, but still raw, and therefore useless for eating. Hence it is written in Nehemiah that the priests not only read out the precepts of the Lord from the book of the Law, but also, while reading, explained the sense and instructed the people, so that each might know what needed to be done. The prophets too are sufficiently shown by their sermons to have observed this custom, and Christ did the same in the present passage, and often elsewhere, as we shall hear in its place. Since this has been observed in the Church from the times of the Apostles onward, those are utterly ridiculous who think that the bare recitation of the Scriptures is enough.

units.la: Sed tempus est, ut ipsum Christum concionantem audiamus. Argumentum concionis ex Isaiæ cap.61. sumitur, quo loco de populi restitutione & ecclesiæ instauratione agit Propheta, quam Messias facturus sit: & ut res sit euidentior magisque moueantur auditorum animi, ipsum Mes-siam loquentem inducit: Spiritus Domni super me, propterea quod unxit me, &c. Christus verò cùm locum illum recitauisset, eundem sibi accommodans subdit: Hodie impleta est hæc scriptura in auribus vestris. Quæ verba breue vaticinij istius interpretatione comprehendunt, quà ab illo dili-gentius & fusius tractatam fuisse non est dubium. Nam perinde hoc est ac si dixisset: Iam exhibitus vobis est Vnctus ille Domini, Rex verus & Sacerdos æternus ecclesiæ, & hunc ipsi iam coràm cer-nitis & auditis. Ego enim nunc lætum salutis nuntium pauperibus prædico. Ego contritos corde sa-no; ego captiuis liberationem & cæcis visus recuperationem annuntio; ego confractos & afflictos di-mitto liberos; ego deniq; Iubileum illum diu expectatum proclamo, qui omnibus certam salutem fe-ret, & ad patriæ cœlestis possessionem aditum faciet. Non ergo alius Messias vobis expectandus erit, sed quam ego vobis prædico, saltem gratis animis & fide constanti apprehendite, &c. Cæterùm quia locus hic plenam Christi descriptionem continet, proderit singulas eius partes excutere, vt quæ hic dicuntur ad nostram quoq; institutionem accommodemus.
units.tr: But it is time that we hear Christ himself preaching. The subject of the sermon is taken from Isaiah chapter 61, where the prophet treats of the restoration of the people and the renewal of the Church, which the Messiah is to accomplish; and so that the matter may be clearer and the minds of the hearers more deeply moved, he introduces the Messiah himself speaking: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me," and so on. When Christ had recited that passage, applying it to himself, he added: "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears." These words sum up the interpretation of that prophecy, which he undoubtedly treated more carefully and at greater length. For it amounts to saying: The Anointed One of the Lord, the true King and eternal Priest of the Church, has now been presented to you, and you now see and hear him here in person. For I now proclaim the joyful news of salvation to the poor. I heal the broken-hearted; I announce liberty to captives and recovery of sight to the blind; I set free the crushed and afflicted; and finally I proclaim that long-awaited Jubilee, which will bring certain salvation to all and will open the way to possession of the heavenly homeland. Therefore no other Messiah is to be expected by you, but the one whom I announce to you; at least receive him with grateful hearts and with steadfast faith, and so on. Moreover, since this passage contains a full description of Christ, it will be useful to examine its individual parts, so that we may apply what is said here to our own instruction as well.

units.la: Primùm à sua vocatione vel Missione orditur, ne quis ipsum putet negotium priuatum aut à Dei voluntate alienû agere. Dicit ergo: Spiritus Domini super me. Quasi diceret: Non cæco carnis affectu rapior, neq; priuato consilio feror, sed spiritum Domini mearum actionum omnium ducem atq; rectorem habeo. Id verò probat, cùm addit: Propterea quòd unxit me. Vnctionis enim nomine esse-ctum spiritus sancti intelligit, quo præclara illa spiritus dona omnia comprehenduntur, quæ in illo e-luxerunt, et quæ alibi Isaias pluribus verbis enumerans ait: Requiescet super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, spiritus consilij & fortitudinis, spiritus scientiæ & timoris Domi-ni, & sagacem illum reddet in timore, &c. Etenim non ad mensuram datus est spiritus sanctus Christo, sed vnctus est oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus suis, & ita in illum plenitudo spiritus effusa est, vt ex eo in nos omnes redundet, qui ipsi per fidem inferimur. Quomodo igitur cæco carnis affectu feratur, aut priuatum terrenum negotium agat, qui nobis omnibus spiritum sanctum communicat? Facit autem hoc non parum ad nostræ salutis certitudinem, Qua enim Deus ipse Christum nobis salutis Mediatorem dedit, & eundem donis necessarijs instruxit, minimè dubia esse potest salus, quam in illo speramus. Simul autem obseruemus in Christo veterem & communem morem Dei, qui quos re- bus magnis & arduis destinat, eos donis quoq; & facultatibus necessarijs armat, vt credito sibi mu-neri sufficere possint. Exempla huius rei habemus in Mose, Iosua, Gedeone, Iephtae, Samsone, Da-uide, Prophetis, Apostolis, & qui hos secuti sunt, veteris ecclesiæ doctoribus. Debent ista eos solari, qui legitimè vocantur ad ecclesiâ vel rempub. regendam. Nam vbi de vocatione Dei nobis constat, non opus est spectare quid nos possimus, sed quid Deus velit videndum est, qui officium suum probè facientibus nunquam deerit. Interim tam Christi quàm apostolorū exemplis arguitur eorum ambitio, qui successionis & vocationis solius titulis superbi, sibi in ecclesia dominiū vendicant, & se spirituales illos esse dicunt, quibus necessariò debeant obedire, quicunq; seruari volunt. Sed non satis est ô Patres, dicere: Spiritus domini super nos est: nisi etiam verè positis dicere: Propterea quod vnxerit nos. At si efficaciter vos vnxit suo spiritu Dominus, quæ sunt in vobis spiritus effectus? Vbi enim spiritus illæ sapientiæ & intelligentiæ? Quibus indicijs sese exerit spiritus consilij & fortitudinis? Quo argumento vos spiritu scientiæ & timoris Dei agitari probatis? Huius certè effecta sunt nostri ipsius abnegatio, carnis mortificatio, regeneratio, sanctificatio, vitæ nouitas. Hæc quia in vobis nulla sunt, desinite vobisipsis blanditias facere, & sacrosanctam Christi Iesu sponsam, ecclesiam, mendacibus titulis lacerare, &c.
units.tr: First he begins with his calling or mission, so that no one thinks he is carrying on a private business or one foreign to the will of God. He says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." It is as if he said: I am not carried away by a blind affection of the flesh, nor driven by a private purpose, but I have the Spirit of the Lord as the guide and ruler of all my actions. He proves this when he adds: "because he has anointed me." By the name of anointing he means the effect of the Holy Spirit, which comprehends all those excellent gifts of the Spirit that shone forth in him, and which Isaiah elsewhere lists at greater length, saying: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord, and he shall make him quick of understanding in the fear of the Lord," and so on. For the Holy Spirit was not given to Christ by measure, but he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and so the fullness of the Spirit was poured out upon him that it overflows from him to all of us who are brought into him by faith. How, then, can he be carried by a blind affection of the flesh, or carry on a private and earthly business, when he imparts the Holy Spirit to all of us? This contributes not a little to the certainty of our salvation. For since God himself has given Christ to us as the Mediator of salvation and has furnished him with the necessary gifts, the salvation we hope for in him can by no means be doubtful. At the same time we should observe in Christ the old and common manner of God, who arms with the gifts and abilities needed those whom he appoints to great and difficult tasks, so that they may be equal to the office entrusted to them. We have examples of this in Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, David, the Prophets, the Apostles, and those who followed them, the teachers of the early Church. These things ought to comfort those who are lawfully called to govern the Church or the commonwealth. For where we are assured of God's calling, we need not look at what we are able to do, but must see what God wills, who never fails those who faithfully perform their duty. Meanwhile, by the examples of Christ and the apostles the ambition of those is refuted who, proud of the mere titles of succession and calling, claim lordship over the Church and say that they are those spiritual men whom everyone who wishes to be saved must necessarily obey. But it is not enough, O Fathers, to say: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon us," unless you also truly can say: "because he has anointed us." But if the Lord has effectively anointed you with his Spirit, what are the effects of the Spirit in you? For where are those spirits of wisdom and understanding? By what signs does the spirit of counsel and strength show itself? By what argument do you prove that you are moved by the spirit of knowledge and the fear of God? Certainly the effects of this Spirit are self-denial, mortification of the flesh, regeneration, sanctification, and newness of life. Since these are none in you, cease to flatter yourselves and to tear the most holy bride of Christ Jesus, the Church, with lying titles, and so on.

units.la: Deinde Missionis & Vnctionis suæ finem exponit. Nam minimè otiosa in nobis esse vult dona sua Deus, sed vt illis negotiemur præcipit, sicuti in talentorum parabola Christus docet. Dicit ergo: Vt euangelizem pauperibus misit me, vt sanem contritos corde, vt prædicent captiuis dimissionem, & cæcis visus recuperationem, & vt confractos emittam in libertatem, vt prædicem annum Domini acceptum. Continetur his verbis vniuersa salutis nostræ cognitio. Nam primùm exprimitur, quæ totius mundi facies fuerit ante Christi in carnem aduentum, & quæ omnium hominum conditio sit, priusquam ille nobis innotescit. Pauperes sumus quoad nostram originem, & omni bono vacui, quibus in singula tempora & momenta opus est exclamare, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Quid enim ex seipsis habeant, quibus ne sperare quidem licet pro suo arbitrio, & qui ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sunt? Sumus item contriti & vulnerati cordibus nostris, eo quod propriæ conscientiæ testimonio conuincimur, quæ nobis omnia infesta, & ipsam vitam quoque amaram reddit. Adhæc in errorum & peccatorum laqueis Satan captiuos detinet, eoque exitialior est ea captiuitas, quod neque carceris huius tam tetri fœtorem, neque letales vinculorum istorum nodos sentimus, sed his vt re omnium beatissima delectamur. Accedit his malis cæcitas & salutis ignorantia, quæ & ipsa eò grauior est, quod nobis egregie sapere videmur, & noctuarum instar tenebras amamus. Adde his, quod confracti sumus membris omnibus, vt quamuis oculos nobis aperiat Deus, & ex carcere isto tenebroso exeundi copiam faciat, inde tamen exire non possumus, nisi idem ille nos viribus nouis iaffauret & fulciat. Denique vt de semetipso Paulus loquitur, toti carnales, & sub peccatum venundati sumus, neque in nobis aliqua spes superest recuperandi, quam in primis parentibus amissimus, patriæ æternæ possessionem. Et de his frequenter nos admonent scripturæ, quia nisi ista in nobis verè agnoscamus, & nostræ miseriæ sensu seriò afficiamur, nunquam ad Christū Iesum festinabimus. Exemplo nobis sunt pharisæi, quos suæ corruptionis ignorantia & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia Christi hostes fecit. Et hodie non alij salutis doctrinam maiori odio oppugnant, quàm qui se sibijpsis sufficere putant. Ideo Christus medicum se esse ait, qui ad curandum ægrotos venerit, & eos ad se imitat, qui oneribus peccatorum depressi laborant, deque proprijs viribus desperant, quos in præsenti pauperes, & alibi pauperes spiritu dicit.
units.tr: Next he sets out the end of his mission and anointing. For God does not want his gifts to lie idle in us, but commands us to trade with them, as Christ teaches in the parable of the talents. So he says: "He has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind, and to set at liberty those who are bruised, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." In these words the whole knowledge of our salvation is contained. For first it is expressed what the whole face of the world was before Christ came in the flesh, and what the condition of all men is before he becomes known to us. We are poor as to our origin and empty of all good, and at every time and moment we must cry out: "Give us this day our daily bread." For what do those have of their own who cannot even hope at their own discretion, and who are not fit even to think? We are also broken and wounded in our hearts, since we are convicted by the testimony of our own conscience, which makes everything hostile to us and even life itself bitter. Besides, Satan holds us captive in the snares of errors and sins, and that captivity is the more deadly because we feel neither the stench of this so foul prison nor the lethal knots of these chains, but rather take delight in them as if they were the happiest of things. To these evils is added blindness and ignorance of salvation, which is itself the heavier because we seem to ourselves to be wise, and like owls we love darkness. Add to these that we are broken in all our limbs, so that although God opens our eyes and gives us the opportunity to leave that dark prison, we cannot get out of it unless the same God strengthens and supports us with new powers. Finally, as Paul speaks of himself, we are wholly carnal and sold under sin, and no hope of recovery remains in us, the possession of the eternal fatherland which we lost in our first parents. And the Scriptures often warn us of these things, because unless we truly acknowledge these things in ourselves and are seriously affected by a sense of our misery, we will never hasten to Christ Jesus. The Pharisees are an example to us, whom ignorance of their own corruption and confidence in their own righteousness made enemies of Christ. And today no one opposes the doctrine of salvation with greater hatred than those who think they are sufficient for themselves. Therefore Christ says that he is a physician who has come to heal the sick, and he calls to himself those who labour oppressed by the burdens of sins and despair of their own strength, whom he calls here "poor," and elsewhere "poor in spirit."

units.la: Quid verò is nobis confert? Est hoc alterum huius partis caput obseruatu dignissimum. Initio autem omnia simul complectens, se ad euangelizandum pauperibus missum esse ait. Ergo lætò gratiæ Dei & reparatæ salutis nuntio mundum infelicem Christus exhilarat. Es rectè ei euangelizandi munus tribuitur, cum magnus ille Propheta sit, quem venturum esse olim Moses prædixit, & qui postea se ideo exiuisse fatebitur. Nam vt olim in propria persona docendi munere functus est, ita hodie adhuc vnus ille euangelicæ prædicationis verus author est, cum ipse dona spiritus sui inter homines distribuat, & ecclesiæ suæ doctores, pastores, euangelistas, prophetas excitet, quorum labore & industria illa ædificetur. At non modò euangelizat Christus, verumetiam sanat contritos corde, & quod verbo pollicetur, reipsa præstat: in quo ministros omnes superat, qui ex hominibus constituuntur. Sanat autem contritos & vulneratos intra conscientias suas, dum merito suo peccata expiat, & de gratia Dei certos reddit eos, qui prius iram Dei intra animos suos pertimescebant. Idem captiuis lætam dimissionem denuntiat, ne porrò sub fathana errorum & peccatorum laqueis detineantur. Et quia ipse lux est totius mundi, quæ suo in carnem aduenum.
units.tr: But what does he bring us? This is the second point of this part most worthy of notice. At the beginning, embracing everything at once, he says that he has been sent to preach the gospel to the poor. Therefore Christ cheers the unhappy world with the joyful news of the grace of God and of restored salvation. And rightly is the office of preaching the gospel assigned to him, since he is that great Prophet whom Moses foretold would come, and who later will confess that he has therefore come forth. For just as he once discharged the office of teaching in his own person, so today too he alone is the true author of the evangelical preaching, since he himself distributes the gifts of his Spirit among men and raises up teachers, ministers, evangelists, and prophets for his Church, by whose labour and diligence it is built up. But Christ not only preaches the gospel, but also heals the broken-hearted, and does in fact what he promises in words; in this he surpasses all the ministers who are appointed from among men. He heals the broken and wounded within their consciences, while by his merit he expiates sins and makes certain of the grace of God those who before trembled within their souls at the wrath of God. He likewise proclaims joyful release to the captives, so that they are no longer held under Satan in the snares of errors and sins. And because he himself is the light of the whole world, which by his coming in the flesh

units.la: aduenum aduentu omnem hominem illuminat, uisus quoque recuperationem ijs per Euangelium offert, qui prius & ipsi caecutiebant, & sub tenebrarum potestate infelices detinebantur. Sequitur ex eo, quod ijdem uiribus nouis instaurati in libertatem ex infelici Satanae seruitio & captiuitate exeunt, et Deo seruiunt in libertate spiritus. Adumbrauit hoc olim euidenter, quando paralytico dicebat: Surge, tolle grabbatum tuum, & ambula. Quo audito ille mox firmatis neruis & membrorum compagibus in pedes erectus incedebat. Christus denique est, qui nobis praedicat annum Domini acceptum, id est, qui ea solus praestat, quae olim anni Iubilaei publico & solenni gaudio adumbrabantur. Nam Leuit. capite 25. sic dicit Moses: Numerabis tibi septem sabbata annorum, id est, annos septies septem, eruntq; tibi septem sabbata annorum quadraginta nouem anni. Et circummittes clangorem buccinae in mense septimo, in decimo die mensis, qui dies est expiationum, circummittetis (inquam) cornu per uniuersam terram: & consecrabitis annum illum, annum uidelicet quinquagesimum, & proclamabitis libertatem in terra omnibus habitatoribus eius: Iubileus enim erit hic annus vobis, & redibit quisque ad possessionem suam, & quisque ad cognationem suam reuertetur. Dicebatur ergo annus Iubilaeus a iubilo vel clangore tubae, qui sub eius ineuntis initium per omnes terrae fines laetissimus audiebatur. Tria autem erant, quae annum hunc acceptum & iucundissimum faciebant. Primum libertas, quae seruis obtingebat. Alterum debitorum remissio, aut quod nomina exigere non liceret. Tertium, quod singuli ad pristinam hereditatem & bona vendita reuertebantur. Nec enim agros aut domus perpetuo contractu alijs vendere licebat, sed eorum modo vsum fructum vsq; ad annum Iubilaeum. Et habebant quidem haec vsum ciuilem quoque in repub. Israelitica, & ad familiarum atque tribuum conseruationem faciebant, simulque obstabant auarorum artibus & rapacitati, qui cum aliorum damno aedes aedibus & agris agros coniungere satagunt. Eadem vero Christi typum habebant, qui per Euangelij tubam tempus illud acceptum & annum beneplaciti aut gratiae diuinae indixit, quo credentibus libertas filiorum Dei conceditur, ne posthac Legis iugo admortem premantur: quo item peccatorum remissio plena obtingit & gratuita: quo denique nobis reditus patet in paradisum, id est, in caelestis patriae haereditatem, quam primi parentes nobis abstulerant. Arripuerunt hinc superstitiosissimi figmenti occasionem Romani Pontifices, qui Iubilaeos annos in nouum testamentum reduxerunt, quibus plenam peccatorum remissionem & praesentem felicitatem pollicentur omnibus qui Romam veniunt, & per portam, cui patefaciendae Papa primum iictum malleo aureo infert, ingrediuntur. Sunt haec ecclesiae Christi ludibria non minus impia quam pudenda & inepta. Nam ad Legis ritus iampridem abolitos reuocant homines Christianos, virum sus contra Apostoli praeceptum dies & tempora observent, qui ab uno Christo debebant pendere. De inde sibijpsis & malleo suo excantato vendicant, quod solius Christi est. Adhaec meritum huius non eiusdem virtutis & efficaciae semper esse fingunt, quasi certis temporibus nouas vires coneipiat. Denique ludos sibi fabricant ex toto humanae redemptionis negotio. Sed magno illis constabit haec fabula, nisi serio resipiscant. Nos vero eiusmodi commentis omnibus opponamus, quod in praesenti Christus dixit: Hodie impleta est scriptura haec in auribus vestris. Et quoties Euangelium praedicatur, tunc nos laetum illum & salutiferum iubilum audire meminerimus, qui nobis in IesuChristo peccatorum remissionem, libertatem & regni caelestis legitimam possessionem denuntiat. Excipiet iubilum hunc olim vox archangeli & tubae Dei clangor, ad quem in nouissimo die mortui resurgent, & quando ipse Christus suis dicet: Venite benedicti patris mei, & possidete regnum, quod vobis praeparatum est ab origine mundi. Tunc tota haec mundi machina (vt Paulus monet) in reuelatione filiorum Dei a corruptione & seruitute, sub qua nunc gemit & parturit, liberabitur, & erit sabbatum ex sabbato, &c. Vide Isa. 66.
units.tr: The coming of the Son into the flesh enlightens every man by his coming. He also offers, through the Gospel, the recovery of sight to those who were once blind themselves and were held wretched under the power of darkness. It follows that these same people, restored with new strength, go out into liberty from the wretched servitude and captivity of Satan, and serve God in freedom of spirit. Long ago he plainly foreshadowed this when he said to the paralytic: "Rise, take up your bed, and walk." At these words the man immediately rose, his sinews and the joints of his limbs made firm, and walked on his feet. Christ, finally, is the one who proclaims to us the acceptable year of the Lord; that is, he alone bestows those things which the year of Jubilee once foreshadowed with its public and solemn joy. For Moses speaks thus in Leviticus chapter 25: "You shall number seven sabbaths of years for yourselves, that is, seven times seven years, so that the seven sabbaths of years make forty-nine years for you. Then you shall cause the trumpet to sound abroad in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, which is the day of atonement; you shall sound the horn (I say) through all your land, and you shall consecrate that year, namely the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty in the land to all its inhabitants. For this year shall be a jubilee for you, and each of you shall return to his own possession, and each shall return to his own family." The year was therefore called the year of Jubilee from the shout or the sound of the trumpet, which was heard most joyfully throughout all the borders of the land at its beginning. Three things made that year acceptable and most welcome: (1) the liberty granted to slaves; (2) the remission of debts, or the fact that it was not lawful to exact debts; (3) the return of each man to his former inheritance and to the goods that had been sold. For fields and houses could not be sold to others by a permanent contract, but only their use and fruits until the year of Jubilee. These things also had a civil use in the Israelite commonwealth, and they served to preserve families and tribes, and at the same time they stood in the way of the arts and rapacity of the greedy, who with the loss of others strive to join house to house and field to field. Yet these same things were a type of Christ, who through the trumpet of the Gospel proclaims that acceptable time and the year of God's good pleasure or grace, in which freedom of the sons of God is granted to believers, so that they are no longer pressed to death under the yoke of the Law; in which also full and free remission of sins is obtained; and in which, finally, the way back to paradise is open to us, that is, to the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland, which our first parents had taken from us. From this the most superstitious Roman Pontiffs seized the occasion for their invented fable: they brought the Jubilee years back into the New Testament, promising full remission of sins and present happiness to all who come to Rome and enter through the door, which the Pope strikes first with a golden hammer to open it. These are mockeries of the Church of Christ, no less impious than shameful and foolish. For they recall Christian men to the rites of the Law, long since abolished, and they observe days and times, though against the command of the Apostle, which ought to depend on Christ alone. Then they claim for themselves, and for their hammer which has been consecrated, what belongs to Christ alone. Moreover, they pretend that the merit of this year is not always of the same virtue and efficacy, as though it conceived new powers at fixed times. Finally, they make a game for themselves out of the whole business of human redemption. But this fable will cost them dearly, unless they seriously repent. Let us, however, oppose all such inventions with what Christ said in the present time: "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears." And whenever the Gospel is preached, let us remember that we hear that joyful and saving jubilee, which announces to us in Jesus Christ the remission of sins, liberty, and the lawful possession of the heavenly kingdom. That jubilee will one day be followed by the voice of the archangel and the sound of God's trumpet, at which the dead will rise on the last day, and when Christ himself will say to his people: "Come, blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Then this whole machine of the world (as Paul warns) will be set free in the revealing of the sons of God from the corruption and servitude under which it now groans and travails; and there will be sabbath after sabbath, etc. See Isaiah 66.

units.la: At simul ista officij admonent eos, qui tanta bona ex Christo Iesu percipiunt. Decet hos in primis gratitudo, & vt tanto pretio redemptam libertatem constanti fide tueantur. Curent ergo, ne se porro Satanae telis exponant, neq; eius laqueis sese irretiri patiantur: ne quod mala frugis homines solent, denuo in nassam foeneratoris illius improbissimi, diaboli, se pertrahi sinant. Deinque cum illis iam in Christo vera lux fulgeat, vt filij lucis in luce ambulent, vitamque omnem instituant ad Dei gloriam, &c.
units.tr: At the same time, these things admonish those who receive such great blessings from Christ Jesus about their duty. Gratitude first befits them, and that they should guard with constant faith the liberty purchased at so great a price. Let them take care, then, that they no longer expose themselves to the darts of Satan, nor allow themselves to be entangled in his snares, lest, as wretched men usually do with bad grain, they again let themselves be dragged into the net of that most wicked usurer, the devil. And since the true light now shines for them in Christ, let them walk as children of the light in the light, and order their whole life to the glory of God, etc.

units.la: Reliquum est in huius loci expositione quod de auditoribus dicitur, omnium qui in Synagoga erant, oculos in Christum intentos fuisse. Ergo non dubium est, quin illorum animos Deus motuerit, ut rei insolitae admiratione abrepti aliquandiu concionantem audirent, quem postea contempserunt & occisum voluerunt. Ita hodie Dei virtute fit, ut interdum praeter omnem expectationem nobis aures praebeant, qui Euangelium plus quam hostiliter oderunt. Quod autem isti stupore quodam capti fecerunt, nos pio & sancto studio discendi accensos facere convenit. Audiamus ergo attentis animis loquentem nobis in Euangelio Dei filium, Iesum Christum, ut eius beneficio redempti cum illo viviamus & regnemus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: What remains in the exposition of this passage is what is said of the hearers: that the eyes of all who were in the synagogue were fixed on Christ. There is therefore no doubt that God moved their minds, so that, carried away by the wonder of an unusual thing, they listened for a while to the preacher, whom afterwards they despised and wanted to kill. So today it happens by God's power that sometimes they lend us their ears beyond all expectation, those who hate the Gospel more than hostilely. But what those men did, seized by a kind of amazement, we ought to do, kindled by a devout and holy zeal for learning. Let us therefore listen with attentive minds to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, speaking to us in the Gospel, so that by his benefit, redeemed, we may live and reign with him. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLII.

units.la: Et omnes testimonium ei dabant, & mirabantur super sermonibus gratiae, qui procedebat ex ore ipsius, dicebantque: Nonne iste est filius Iosephi? Et dixit ad eos: Omnino dicetis mihi hoc proverbium: Medice, cura teipsum. Quaecunque audiuimus facta fuisse in Capernaum, fac etiam hic in patria tua. Dixit autem: Amen dico vobis, Nemo propheta acceptus est in patria sua.
units.tr: And they all bore witness to him and marvelled at the gracious words that came out of his mouth, and they said, "Is not this Joseph's son?" And he said to them, "Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' Whatever we have heard was done at Capernaum, do here also in your own country." And he said, "Truly, I say to you, no prophet is welcome in his own country."

units.la: Qvamuis Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, communis & universalis omnium hominum atque nationum seruator sit, non temere tamen salutem & eius praedicationem Galilaeis suis, & inter hos Nazarethanis primis offerre voluit. Ita enim gratiam bonam iis rependit, qui ipsi huc vsque hospitium praebuerant, & inter quos a pueris erat educatus: simulque suo exemplo pietatem in patriam commendat, cuius optimi quique omnibus seculis studiosissimi fuerunt. Docuit autem ex Isaia Propheta, quis nam ipse sit, & paucis comprehendit, quaecunque ad veram aeternae salutis cognitionem faciunt. Nam eo vaticinio aperte traditur, Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria Virgine homo factus est, esse Christum, id est, vnctum illum Dei, Regem & Sacerdotem ecclesiae, qui salutem non solum annuntiat atque pollicetur, verumetiam reipsa confert omnibus, qui ipsum fide vera apprehenderunt. Sequitur nunc, ut Nazarethani doctrinam hanc acceperint, & quid cum ingratis & incredulis Dominus egerit.
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ is the common and universal Saviour of all men and nations, he chose not to offer salvation and his preaching carelessly, but first to his own Galileans, and among them to the men of Nazareth. For in this way he repaid with kindness those who had until now given him lodging, and among whom he had been brought up from boyhood; and at the same time by his example he commended piety towards one's country, which the best men in every age have most diligently practised. He also taught, from the prophet Isaiah, who he himself is, and in a few words summed up all that bears on the true knowledge of eternal salvation. For in that prophecy it is plainly set forth that this Jesus, who was made man of the Virgin Mary, is the Christ, that is, the anointed one of God, the King and Priest of the Church, who not only announces and promises salvation but in fact bestows it on all who have laid hold of him by true faith. It follows now to consider how the men of Nazareth received this teaching, and what the Lord did with the ungrateful and unbelieving.

units.la: Quod Nazarethanos, nuper de illis dixit Euangelista, quod omnium oculi in Christum docentem intenti fuerint: Nam mirum & insolens erat, hominem idiotam & a pueris artificio manu ario occupatum, publice docendi munus sibi sumere. Et ita illos detinuit occulta Dei virtus, ne illum exibilarent, sed taciti et attenti audirent docentem, donec concionem absoluisset. Nunc maiora sequuntur, quibus in Verbo elucens Dei virtus magis commendatur. Sic enim scribit Lucas: Omnes testimonium ei dabant, et mirabantur super sermonibus gratiae, qui procedebant ex ore ipsius. Exprimit hic admirabilem Verbi Dei vim atque gratiam, qua in hominum animis operatur. Nec enim aures modo eorum ferijt sonus dictorum Christi, sed in ipsos animos Verbum penetrauit, & hos ita coepit, ut non possent non assentiri iis, quae ab ipso dicebantur. Itaque cum dixisset, Hodie impleta est scriptura haec in auribus vestris: mox hoc eius dictum suo testimonio palam confirmant, & testantur Iesum hunc esse eum, qui contritos corde sanet, qui captiuis dimissionem, caecis visus reuperationem praedicet, qui item confractos emitat in libertatem, & Iubilaeum verum nuntiet, in quo nobis cum libertate filiorum Dei & plenaria peccatorum omnium remissione, olim amissa patriae caelestis possessio restituitur. Poterat hoc mirum & stupendum videri, Nazarethanos ex vna concione Christi tantum profecisse. Sed meminisse oportet, hanc spiritus Dei virtutem fuisse, quae animos eorum mouit, ut quae dicebantur cum signis atque miraculis conferrent, quorum fama iampridem apud illos diuulgata fuerat. Quia ergo nihil audiunt, quod non reipsa confirmetur, coguntur vel inuiti veritatis testimonium ei deferre, etiamsi animos haberent prophanos & a verae pietatis studio alienissimos, sicuti in sequentibus patebit. Accedit huc, quod sermones gratiae, id est, gratia pleni illos in admirationem rapiebant. Nec enim ex vulgarium doctorum numero fuit Christus, quos inanis eloquentiae fucus & verborum splendor rudis & stupidi vulgi auribus admirabiles reddit: sed (vt olim de illo prædixerant prophetæ) gratia in labijs eius diffusa erat, & quæcunque eius ore pro cedebant, insolita dulcedine simul atque grauitate commendabantur. Ideo alibi docuisse dicitur, non vt scribæ, sed vt is, cuius dictis authoritas diuina coniuncta erat, quæ in ipsos auditorum animos altius penetrabat. Et hanc gratiam Nazarethani quoque senserunt: qui iam videri poterant veræ fidei principia habere, & ad salutem quam proximè accessisse. Sed mox spiritus bonam suggestionem excutiunt, & ipsi sibi scandalum ponunt, quo impediuntur, ne maiores in fide progressus faciant. Clamant enim, Nonne iste est filius Iosephi? Et vt Marcus annotauit, infinita alia in eius contemptum congerunt. Vnde (inquiunt) huic ista? & quæ est hæc sapientia, quæ data est ei? Nonne est iste faber ille, qui filius est Mariæ, frater Iacobi & Iosæ & Iudæ & Simonis? Nonne & sorores eius hic sunt apud nos? Ita vero non contenti illius personam traduxisse, aliunde etiam corrardunt, quæ ipsum contemptum & abiectum reddant. Et cum in doctrina nihil reprehensione dignum inueniant, imò Spiritus sancti & diuinæ gratiæ vim ipsi intra animos suos sentiant, personæ eius contumeliose inuadunt. Quid? cum Dei gratia se eo luculentius exereret, quo contemptior erat Christi persona, ipsi nimis maliti ose exeo calumniandi occasionem arripiunt. Et quid obsecro illud est, quod canto conceptu & odio dignum iudicant? Num vita inhonestè à pueris transacta? Num mores iuuenili leuitate infames? Num familiæ vetera maleficia? Num nutritij Iosephi aliquod flagitium? Num suspecta Mariæ matris pudicitia? Num fratrum & sororum, id est, cognatorum, quos Hebræi fratres & sorores dicere consueuerunt, improbitas? Nequaquam. Sed generis obscuri tatem, quæ tunc erat, & manuarium artificium, & cognatorum omnium conditionem pauperculam illi exprobrant. Quàm vero iniquum hoc fuit, propter externa hæc Verbum Dei contemnere, & pro priæ conscientiæ testimonio reluctari, cum constet, illius veritatem non ab hominum arbitrio pendere, sed propria authoritate niti? Neq; etiam ignorabant, plerosque ex veterum prophetarum numero natales obscuros habuisse. Atque hoc illud scandalum est, quod etiam hodie Iudæi magno studio fouent, quando Iesu nostri paupertatem, labores, persecutiones & indignum crucis supplicium mirificè amplificant, & insuper horrendis conuicijs tam ipsum quàm eius sectatores suos hominibus inuisos & exosos reddunt. Sed & ipsa miracula in præsenti extenuant, vt ex Christi responso patebit, quanto plura & maiora ex vulgi rumoribus & fama audierant, quàm nunc coràm viderent. Ita fit, vt ex concione Christi omnium luculentissima grauissimaq; nullum omnino fructum retulerint, imò potius testimonium suæ damnationis audierint, quod per se salutare & viuificum erat.
units.tr: The evangelist recently said of the men of Nazareth that the eyes of all were fixed on Christ as he taught. For it was remarkable and unusual that a man untrained, and occupied from boyhood with a manual craft, should take upon himself the public office of teaching. And the hidden power of God so restrained them that they did not hiss him down, but listened in silence and attention while he taught, until he had finished his sermon. Now greater things follow, by which the power of God shining forth in the Word is more clearly commended. For Luke writes thus: "All bore witness to him and marvelled at the gracious words that came out of his mouth." Here he expresses the wonderful force and grace of the Word of God, by which it works in men's minds. For the sound of Christ's words did not merely strike their ears, but the Word penetrated into their very minds and began to so move them that they could not but assent to what was said by him. Therefore, when he had said, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing," they at once confirmed this saying of his by their own testimony, and bore witness that this Jesus is he who heals the broken in heart, who proclaims release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, who also sets the oppressed free, and announces the true Jubilee, in which, together with the liberty of the sons of God and the full remission of all sins, the heavenly inheritance lost long ago is restored to us. It might seem remarkable and astonishing that the men of Nazareth profited so much from a single sermon of Christ. But we must remember that it was the power of the Spirit of God that moved their minds, so that they compared what was said with the signs and miracles whose fame had long before been spread among them. Therefore, since they hear nothing that is not confirmed by the facts, they are compelled, even against their will, to bear witness to the truth of him, even though their minds were profane and most alien to the zeal for true godliness, as will appear in what follows. Moreover, the gracious words, that is, words full of grace, carried them away into admiration. For Christ was not one of the number of common teachers, whom the empty varnish of eloquence and a showy display of words make admirable to the ears of a rude and foolish crowd; but (as the prophets had foretold of him long ago) grace was poured out on his lips, and whatever came from his mouth was commended by an unusual sweetness and at the same time by gravity. Hence he is said elsewhere to have taught not as the scribes, but as one whose words were joined with divine authority, which penetrated more deeply into the minds of his hearers. The men of Nazareth also felt this grace: they could already seem to have the beginnings of true faith and to have come very near to salvation. But soon they cast off the good prompting of the Spirit, and set a stumbling-block before themselves, by which they are hindered from making greater progress in faith. For they cry out, "Is not this Joseph's son?" And, as Mark noted, they heap up countless other things to his contempt. "Whence has this man these things?" they say, "and what wisdom is this that has been given to him? Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" Yet they are not content with thus disparaging his person; they also search out other things from elsewhere that might make him despised and abject. And although they find nothing blameworthy in his teaching, indeed feel within their own minds the power of the Holy Spirit and of divine grace, they attack his person with insults. What then? When the grace of God shone forth all the more brightly, the more despised was the person of Christ, they, in their extreme malice, seize the opportunity to slander him. And what, I beg you, is that which they judge so worthy of such great outrage and hatred? Was it a life spent dishonourably from boyhood? Was it morals infamous for youthful levity? Was it some old crime of his family? Was it some disgrace of Joseph his foster father? Was it the chastity of his mother Mary, which they suspected? Was it the wickedness of his brothers and sisters, that is, of his kinsfolk, whom the Hebrews were accustomed to call brothers and sisters? By no means. Rather, they reproach him with the obscurity of his birth, which was then the case, with his manual craft, and with the very humble condition of all his kinsfolk. How unjust it was to despise the Word of God on account of these external things, and to resist the witness of one's own conscience, since it is plain that its truth does not depend on the judgement of men, but rests on its own authority! Nor were they ignorant that many of the old prophets had obscure birth. And this is the stumbling-block that even today the Jews foster with great zeal, when they magnify with remarkable exaggeration the poverty, labours, persecutions and unworthy death on the cross of our Jesus, and moreover make him and his followers hateful and odious to men by horrible reproaches. And even the miracles they now belittle, as will be clear from Christ's answer, since they had heard from the rumours and reports of the crowd far more numerous and greater things than they now saw with their own eyes. So it comes about that from the sermon of Christ, most splendid and weighty as it was, they gained no fruit at all; rather, they heard a testimony of their own condemnation, which was in itself saving and life-giving.

units.la: Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quæ sit Verbi Dei conditio, & quibus causis eius profectus inter homines impediatur. Eloquia Dei (inquit Dauid) eloquia munda, adeoque argentum sunt excoctum in catino terreo septies defecatum. Et eòdem pertinet, quod idem in Legis diuinæ commendationem dicit: Lex Domini integra est, conuertens animam, testimonium Domini verum, imperitis sapientiam suppeditans. Decreta Domini recta sunt, cor exhilarant: præceptum Domini repurgatum, illuminans oculos. Timorem Domini mundum parit, constat sibi perpetuò: iudicia Domini vera simul & iusta. Magis expetibilia sunt quàm aurum præstantissimum, & dulciora fauis melle stillantibus. Et hæc quidem non temere Dauidi excidisse pijo- nes experiuntur, qui illud dignè audiunt. Adde tamen his, quod propria virtute & efficacia armatum corda auditorum penetrat. Quod Apostolus in epistola ad Hebræos obseruans, de illo sic scripsit: Viuus est sermo Dei & efficax, & penetrantior quouis gladio ancipiti: ac pertingit vsque ad diuisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumque & medullarum, & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis. Et hoc quoque verissimè dici constat, quando sæpe fit, vt singuli qui contiones sacras audiunt, de se foliis agi, & ministrum corda ipsorum inspexisse, iamque omnium oculos in se connersos esse putent. Sic Dauidis animum hoc gladio Nathan penetrauit, & ipsas medullas cupiditatum atque cogitationum scrutatus, sceleris confessionem & serium pœnitentiæ studium ei extorsit, qui securus nimium iam ad interitum inclinabat. Et hinc fit, vt impij quoque & oscitantes Verbi Dei vim sæpe agnoscere, virtutem eius admirari & eidem testimonium ferre cogantur. Exempla huius passim occurrunt. Noluit Deo meliora monenti obedire Cainus, cùm fraterni odij flammas iam animo concepisset. At cùm patrato iam parricidio Deus de fratre illum interrogat, & improbè respondenti sceleris atrocitatem vnà cum pœna ob oculos statuit, mox ille intra animŭ suum quasi fulmine iƈtus clamat. Maior est iniquitas mea, quàm vt remittatur: & infeliciter tremit atq; trepidat, qui paulò ante ipsi Deo lite mouere videbatur. Simile quid in Achabo cernitur. Is enim cùm ad occupandā Nabothi crudeliter et iniuste occisi vineam descenderet, Eliam sibi occurrentem minaciter admodum compellat: Deprehendi stime hostis meus? At idē ille non multò post, audita verbi Dei sententia, instar agni mitescit, vt cilicium induat, cinerem capiti inspergat, & ita sceleris suum publicè fateatur. Ieremiam quoq; concionantē diu contempserunt Iudæi, sed rebus iam deploratis & perditis ab eode Rex primo, deinde qui ex populo reliqui erant, consilium petierunt: ex quo satis apparet, Dei verbum antea quoq; in eorum animos altius penetrauisse, quàm ipsi fateri vellent. Ezechieli quoq; ipse Dominus de Iudæis dicit: Veniunt ad te quemadmodum populus venire solet, sedentq; coram te populus meus, & audiunt sermones tuos, quos tamen non faciunt, &c. At ijdem ne venirent quidem ad Prophetæ conciones, nisi intra animos suos se occultiori aliqua vi trahi sensissent, quæ illas auditu dignas esse monebat, etiam si obedire nollent. Et quod Nazarethi nunc accidit Christo docente, hoc ipsum Hierosolymæ factum fuisse Ioannes scribit: quando qui ad illum capiendum emissi erant, ad heros suos reuersi, eius doctrinæ testimonium tulerunt, dicentes: Nunquam ita locutus est homo. Accidunt huius generis multa hodie, & non raro fit, vt qui hostili & insidioso animo ad conciones sacras venerunt, nō modò nihil audiant, quod reprehendere possint, verumetiam sibi omnia egregiè placuisse testentur.
units.tr: This is a memorable example, by which we are taught what the condition of the Word of God is, and by what causes its progress among men is hindered. "The sayings of the Lord," says David, "are pure words, indeed silver refined in an earthen furnace, purified seven times." And to the same point he says in praise of the divine Law: "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ever; the judgements of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. They are more to be desired than much fine gold, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." And that David did not say these things at random, the godly find who hear them worthily. Add to this that the Word, armed with its own virtue and efficacy, penetrates the hearts of its hearers. The Apostle, observing this in his Epistle to the Hebrews, wrote thus of it: "The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and it pierces even to the dividing of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart." And this too is known to be most truly said, since it often happens that each one who hears sacred sermons thinks that the matter is about himself alone, and that the minister has looked into his heart, and that the eyes of all are now turned upon him. Thus Nathan pierced David's mind with this sword, and searching the very marrow of his desires and thoughts, he wrung from him a confession of his crime and a serious zeal for repentance, when he was already too secure and inclining towards ruin. And hence it happens that the wicked and the careless are often also compelled to acknowledge the force of the Word of God, to admire its power, and to bear witness to it. Examples of this occur everywhere. Cain refused to obey God when he warned him of better things, although he had already conceived in his mind the flames of hatred towards his brother. But when, the murder now committed, God asks him about his brother, and he answers wickedly, God sets before his eyes the atrociousness of his crime together with its punishment; at once he, as if struck by a thunderbolt, cries out within himself: "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven," and wretchedly he trembles and quakes, who a little before seemed to be bringing a lawsuit against God himself. Something similar is seen in Ahab. For when he was going down to seize the vineyard of Naboth, who had been cruelly and unjustly put to death, he addressed Elijah, who met him, very threateningly: "Have you found me, O my enemy?" Yet the same man, not long afterwards, having heard the sentence of the Word of God, grows meek as a lamb, so that he puts on sackcloth, sprinkles ashes on his head, and so publicly confesses his crime. The Jews long despised Jeremiah preaching, but when matters were now desperate and lost, the king first, and then those of the people who were left, sought counsel from him; from which it is quite clear that the Word of God had earlier also penetrated their minds more deeply than they themselves would admit. The Lord himself also says of the Jews to Ezekiel: "They come to you as my people usually come, and sit before you, and hear your words, but they do not do them," and so on. And yet they would not even come to the prophet's sermons, unless they had felt within their minds some more hidden force drawing them, which advised that those words were worth hearing, even though they were unwilling to obey. And what has now happened at Nazareth while Christ was teaching, John writes that the same happened at Jerusalem: when those who had been sent out to seize him returned to their masters, they bore witness to his teaching, saying, "No man ever spoke like this." Many things of this kind happen today, and it is not rare that those who came to sacred sermons with a hostile and treacherous mind not only hear nothing that they can find fault with, but even testify that everything has pleased them exceedingly.

units.la: Quæ ergo causa est (inquis) quòd apud istos homines Verbum non fructum fert dignum? Et cur non ipsi in Veritatis cognitione, quantum satis est, proficiunt? Annon satis efficax est Verbum illis permouendis & trahendis, vt Christo manus dent? Est sanè, sed hominum improbitate hæc siunt, qui ipsi sibi obstacula quærunt, perinde ac si ægrotus consultò ingerat in stomachum, quæ pharmaci à medico dati virtutem remorentur. Solent illi vt in omnibus aliis, ita etiam circa Dei Verbum, non nisi terrena quærere, & ideo in externa modò rerum specie hærent. Ergo quàm primùm non inuenire quod quærunt, aut externa illa votis suis minus respondent, mox calumniandi occasiones vænantur. Et quia pudet doctrinam ipsam aggredi, & hanc nullis argumentis euerti posse norunt, ipsos doctores vel in odium, vel in contemptū adducere satagunt. Ita olim Prophetas aggressi sunt impij hostes. Et quod Christo apud Nazarethanos suos accidit, hoc ipsum vbique gentium passi sunt eius Apostoli. Et hodie in struendis eiusmodi calumniis mirè ingeniosi sunt aduersarij nostri, qui nihil non in deteriorem partem rapere consueuerunt, vt verbi administrus odium aut ignominiam conflent. Nam si quis iuuenis sit, puerum aiunt: qui neque vsu rerum valeat, neque graui prudentia res suas moderetur, sed iuuenili impetu omnia dicat & faciat. Sin senectam grauem iam attigerit, delirum esse clamitant, qui senili morositate nihil eorum ferre possit in alijs, quibus ipse per ætatem non amplius sufficiat. Ita si tenuioris fortunæ & ex obscuris parentibus sit doctor, indignū putant, tot viros nobiles, diuites, optimè de repub. meritos, adeoq; populum totum ab vnius erroris ore pendere, cui nihil sit quod amittat, etiamsi rempub. vniuersam in extremum adducat discrimen. At si contra ex nobiliori familia verbi præco prodijt, & opibus paternis abundat, mox illum generis & opum fiducia efferri dicunt, & indignum esse cui fides habeatur, cùm nihil in ipso sit, quod apostolicâ tenuitatem referat. Idem fit si doctus aut indoctus concionetur. Hunc enim asinum ineptum, illum versutum Sophistam esse calumniantur. Eadem peregrini & ciuis nati ratio. Hunc enim propter familiaritatē & omnibus notos natales contemnunt, illum verò propter gentē aut nescio quas gentis iniurias odio prosequuntur. Fiunt ista & multa huius generis hodie passim: sed neminē mouēant iniqua hæc mundi infelicis iudicia. Subijt ea ipse Dei filius, non autem illis territi sunt Apostoli, quò minus Christum Domini & eum agnoscerent, qui solus verba vitæ æternæ habet. Accedamus ergo ad audiendum verbum, non curiositate aut alicuius boni temporarij desiderio, sed cognoscendæ veritatis studio accensi. Quàm primùm verò in animos nostros verbum penetrat, tunc nō pigeat ei testi monium perhibere, & pro Veritatis verbo agnoscere: ne dum propriæ conscientiæ testimonium im-probè testinguimus, tandem in ipsum Spiritum sanctum peccemus, qui illud in nobis excitanit. Neq; nos externa rerum species vel detinere vel absterrere debet: sed qualis qualis sit minister ecclesiæ, nos Dei gratiam admirari & celebrare cōuenit, qui per verbum suum nobiscum per omnis generis homi nes colloqui dignatur, per illud ipsum inscrutabilem aliàs cordis nostri malitiam arguit, adhæc nos monet, hortatur, ducit, consolatur, & suae voluntatis conscios reddit. Est hoc inter Dei beneficia post exhibitum nobis Filium facile primum. Nam ex eo (ut ipse Christus ait) constat, illum nos amicorum loco habere, qui olim cum ipso in coelis regnaturi sint. Qui hoc beneficium vere agnoscunt, & animo honesto atq; discendi cupido ad audiendum Verbum accedunt, ij procul efficacem intra semet ipsos Spiritus sancti virtutem sentient, & fructus ferent Christiana professione dignos, ut suo loco pluribus dicetur.
units.tr: "But what is the reason," you ask, "that among these people the Word does not bear worthy fruit? And why do they not make progress in the knowledge of the truth, as far as is enough? Is the Word not powerful enough to move and draw them, so that they give their hands to Christ?" It certainly is powerful, but these things happen through the wickedness of men, who put obstacles in their own way, just as a sick man who deliberately swallows things that counteract the power of the medicine the doctor has given him. Like everything else, they seek only earthly things in the Word of God too, and so they cling only to its outward appearance. Therefore, as soon as they fail to find what they seek, or the outward things do not match their wishes, they immediately hunt for occasions to slander. And because they are ashamed to attack the doctrine itself, and know it cannot be overturned by any arguments, they strive to bring the teachers themselves into hatred or contempt. So the wicked enemies once attacked the prophets. And what happened to Christ among his own people at Nazareth, his apostles suffered everywhere among the nations. And today our opponents are remarkably ingenious in devising such slanders; they are accustomed to twist everything to the worse, so as to stir up hatred or disgrace against the minister of the Word. For if he is young, they call him a boy, who has neither the experience of affairs nor the wisdom to govern his own business with gravity, but says and does everything with youthful impetuosity. But if he has already reached a grave old age, they cry out that he is a dotard, who in his senile crankiness cannot tolerate in others the things for which he himself is no longer fit because of his age. So too, if the teacher is of humble means and of obscure parents, they think it outrageous that so many noble and wealthy men, who have deserved well of the commonwealth, and indeed the whole people, should hang on the mouth of one man of no account, who has nothing to lose, even if he brings the whole commonwealth to the brink of ruin. But if, on the contrary, the herald of the Word comes from a more noble family and abounds in his father's wealth, they immediately say that he is puffed up with confidence in his birth and riches, and is unworthy to be believed, since there is nothing in him that resembles the poverty of the apostles. The same happens whether the preacher is learned or unlearned: they slander the one as a foolish donkey and the other as a crafty sophist. The same reasoning applies to a foreigner and to one born a citizen. They despise the native because of his familiarity and his birth, which everyone knows, but they pursue the foreigner with hatred on account of his nation, or some injuries of the nation I know not what. These things, and many of this kind, happen everywhere today; but these unjust judgments of an unhappy world move no one. The Son of God himself underwent them, nor were the apostles frightened by them from acknowledging Christ the Lord, who alone has the words of eternal life. Let us therefore come to hear the Word, not out of curiosity or a desire for some temporal good, but kindled by a zeal for knowing the truth. But as soon as the Word penetrates into our minds, let us not be slow to bear witness to it and acknowledge it as the word of truth; lest, while we shamefully stifle the testimony of our own conscience, we at last sin against the Holy Spirit himself, who has stirred it up within us. Nor should the outward appearance of things either hold us back or frighten us away; but whatever sort of minister of the Church he may be, we ought to admire and celebrate the grace of God, who deigns through his Word to speak with us, men of every kind, and through that same Word reproves the malice of our heart, which is otherwise unsearchable, and besides admonishes, exhorts, leads, and comforts us, and makes us conscious of his will. This is, after the Son given to us, easily the first of God's benefits. For from it (as Christ himself says) it follows that he counts us in the place of friends, we who are one day to reign with him in heaven. Those who truly acknowledge this benefit, and come to hear the Word with an honest mind and a desire to learn, will feel within themselves the far more effective power of the Holy Spirit, and will bear fruits worthy of the Christian profession, as will be said at greater length in its place.

units.la: Nunc quid Christus fecerit videamus.
