Vbi ante omnia observandum venit, quod non ad omnia respondet, quae illi exprobrabant, sed ea dicit, quae, si animum attendere voluissent, & ipsos potes rant meliores facere, & scandalum removere, quod multis aliis hic obijciebatur. Etenim facile ipsi fuisset negare se Iosephi filium esse. Sed ex eo homines prophani novam concertandi occasionem arripuissent, & ita scandalum quoque gravius fuisset exortum. Itaque hoc omisso, ad ea, quae adhuc in illorum animis latebant, responsionem dirigit, & occultiores cordium cogitationes protrahit & arguit, quibus maxime impediebantur, quo minus ipsi crederent. Debebat hoc in quavis contentione observari, & ita facilius multo & citius componerentur lites, quae vel privatim vel publice exurgunt. At quia plerique privatae gloriae studio accensi, minutissima quaeque odiosius exagitant, fit fere, ut ob unum verbulum temere elapsum excitata contentio lites pariat nunquam finiendas. In quo utinam non prae aliis peccarent, qui sal terrae esse debebant, & ecclesiarum concordia nihil antiquius ducere. Audiamus ergo Christum, ut eius exemplo discamus quid facto opus sit. Responsionis eius partes sunt duae. Prima, ut diximus, in animos illorum penetrat, dicens: Omnino dicetis mihi hoc proverbium, Medice cura teipsum. Quaecunq; audivimus facta fuisse in Capernaum, fac etiam hic in patria tua. Ex quibus verbis apparet, Nazarethanos honestum & plausibilem suae incredulitatis atq; contumaciae praetextum quaesivisse. Sentiebant enim, Christum optimo iure ab ipsis contemni & reiici, qui hucusq; homines exteros suae patriae & propriis cognatis anteposuisset; & Capernaum quidem, civitatem alioqui satis celebrem, signis & miraculis infinitis nobilitavisset: nihil autem horum faceret inter cives suos, quibus meliore gratia deberet, imo gentiles atq; cognatos suos plusquam satis miseros & infelices esse pateretur. Hanc vero excusationem suam, ut plausibilior esset, proverbiali sententia vestiebant: Medice cura teipsum. Quasi dicerent: Ut iure contemnitur medicus, qui sibi ipsi & suis non potest mederi: ita nemo non iniquitatis accusare poterit, si te non agnoscamus salutis authorem, qui & ipse miser es, & eos nimium secure negligis, qui propter arctioris cognationis vinculum tibi coniunctissimi esse debebant. Ista vero sive inter se musitarent, sive intra animos suos cogitarent, non obscure eius concionem suggillabant, & ipsum vanae atq; mendacis iactantiae insimulabant. Na perinde hoc erat, ac si dixissent: Si tu Vnctus ille Domini es, qui pauperes laeto salutis nuntio beas, qui curis omnibus mederis, qui captivis dimissionem, caecis & ignorantibus visus recuperationem nuntias, qui denique libertatis diu expectatae author es, & omnibus ad amissas maiorum possessiones aditum paras: quin a teipso & propriis cognatis tantae rei initium facis? Cur non tuis auitam Davidis hereditatem, et tuae familiae promissum regnum restituris? Egregius scilicet Messias, qui foris & miraculis & signis apud ignotos te venditas, & alijs aureos montes pollicendo teipsum & tuos negligis. Fuit ergo cum exectabili euangelicae praedicationis contemptu coniuncta Nazarethanorum incredulitas. Et hac causa fuisse scribunt Matthaeus & Marcus, quod non multa signa inter illos facere potuerit Christus.
units.tr: Now let us see what Christ did. Here, above all, it must be observed that he does not answer everything that they threw in his face, but says what, if they had been willing to attend to it, could have made them better and removed the stumbling block that was being put before many others here as well. For it would have been easy for him to deny that he was the son of Joseph. But from that, profane men would have seized a new occasion for wrangling, and so the scandal would have arisen even more seriously. Therefore, leaving this aside, he directs his reply to what was still hidden in their minds, and draws out and exposes the more secret thoughts of their hearts, which were chiefly hindering them from believing. This ought to be observed in any dispute, and so quarrels, whether private or public, would be settled much more easily and quickly. But because most people, kindled by a zeal for private glory, harshly pursue even the smallest matters, it usually happens that a contention started over a single careless word gives rise to quarrels that are never ended. Would that in this they did not sin more than others, those who ought to be the salt of the earth and to hold nothing more important than the harmony of the churches! Let us therefore listen to Christ, that by his example we may learn what needs to be done. His reply has two parts. The first, as we said, penetrates into their minds, saying: "Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself. Whatever we have heard was done in Capernaum, do also here in your own country.'" From these words it appears that the Nazarenes were seeking a respectable and plausible pretext for their unbelief and obstinacy. For they felt that Christ was rightly despised and rejected by them, since he had hitherto preferred foreigners to his own country and his own kin; and he had indeed made Capernaum, a city otherwise quite famous, renowned by countless signs and miracles, while he did nothing of the kind among his fellow citizens, to whom he ought to have been more favourably disposed, but allowed his kinsfolk, who were more than wretched and unhappy, to be left in their misery. They clothed this excuse of theirs in a proverbial saying, so that it might seem more plausible: "Physician, heal yourself." As if they were saying: just as a physician is rightly despised who cannot heal himself and his own people, so no one could fail to accuse you of injustice if we do not acknowledge you as the author of salvation, when you yourself are wretched and so carelessly neglect those who, by the bond of closer kinship, ought to have been most closely joined to you. But whether they muttered these things to one another or thought them within their own minds, they plainly disparaged his preaching and accused him of empty and false boasting. For it was just as if they had said: "If you are that Anointed One of the Lord who brings good cheer to the poor with the joyful news of salvation, who heals all cares, who proclaims release to the captives and sight to the blind and the ignorant, who in short is the author of the liberty so long awaited and prepares for all of us access to the lost possessions of our forefathers, why do you not begin such a great work with yourself and your own kinsfolk? Why do you not restore to your own people the ancestral inheritance of David and the kingdom promised to your family? A fine Messiah indeed, who advertises yourself among strangers by miracles and signs, but neglect yourself and your own, while promising golden mountains to others!" So the unbelief of the Nazarenes was joined with an execrable contempt for the evangelical preaching. And for this reason Matthew and Mark write that Christ could not do many signs among them.

units.la: Nam etsi gratia & potentia Dei nostrae fidei minime alligata sit (Quid enim, inquit Paulus, quod aliqui fuerunt increduli? num eorum incredulitas Dei fidem facit irritam? Absit: ita tamen res ordinavit ille, ut ijs se praesentem & propitium praebeat, qui certa & indubitata fide promissiones eius apprehendunt. Quarum complementum cum in solo Christo habeatur, fieri nequit, ut beneficiorum eius consortes fiant, qui huic non credunt. Quod unusquisque hodie observemus, non mirabimur, pauciores esse qui Dei opem hodie sentiunt, cum paucissimi sint, qui Dei promissis fide habeant, aut Christum suum vindicem & servatorem ex animo agnoscant, si quid gravioris periculi immineat. Docent autem ista, quanti verbum suum faciat Deus, quando eius contemptum sic punit, ut quam prius sponte obtulit gratiam, mox e medio auferat. Debebant hoc diligentius expendere qui de solo verbo externo agi putat, & ideo non multum movetur, si quis illud a nobis auferendum dicat. Imo non desunt, qui se tunc demum beatos fore arbitrantur, si nemo ut qui docendo, monendo, hortando, increpando ipsis molestiam exhibeat. At quia per Verbum suum gratiam Deus nobis offert, hoc sublato illam quoq; vnà cum beneficijs omnibus aufert quibus antea fruebamur. Exemplo nobis sint Iudæi, qui & olim cessante prophetia miserè dissipati, & postea in vniuersum excisi sunt, postquam Euangelij prædicationem ab illis Deus abstulit. Et quod illi passi sunt, hoc ipsum ecclesijs Orientalibus, Asiaticis & Græcis accidisse constat, quorum exemplum vtinam hodie nos emendaremus, & c.
units.tr: Although the grace and power of God are by no means bound to our faith (For what, says Paul, if some did not believe? Will their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid), yet God has so ordered things that he shows himself present and gracious to those who apprehend his promises with a certain and undoubting faith. Since the fulfilment of those promises is found in Christ alone, it cannot happen that those who do not believe in him become partakers of his benefits. If each of us observes this today, we shall not be surprised that fewer people feel God's help today, since very few have faith in God's promises or acknowledge from the heart Christ as their defender and saviour, should any more serious danger threaten. These things teach how highly God values his Word, when he punishes its contempt by taking away at once the grace he had previously offered freely. Those who think that only the external word is at stake ought to weigh this more carefully, and so they are not much moved when someone says that it should be taken away from us. Indeed, there are not lacking those who think they will only be happy if no one causes them trouble by teaching, admonishing, exhorting or rebuking. But because God offers us grace through his Word, when that Word is removed he also takes away the grace, together with all the benefits we previously enjoyed. Let the Jews be an example to us, who, when prophecy ceased, were miserably scattered, and afterwards were utterly cut off, once God had taken from them the preaching of the Gospel. And it is clear that what they suffered also happened to the churches of the East, of Asia and of Greece, whose example we would that we today might amend, etc.

units.la: Cæterùm, ne quis Nazarethanorum incredulitate atq; contumacia offendaretur, tanquam reno ua & insolita, argumento ab antea factu vtitur, quo veterem & auitam Iudaicæ gentis impietatem atq; rebellionem perstringit, sic inquiens: Amen dico vobis, Nemo propheta acceptus est in patria sua. Apud Marcum vero hoc ita enuntiat: Non est propheta inhonoratus nisi in patria sua, & inter cognatos suos, & in domo sua. Videtur autem hæc quoq; proverbialis sententia esse, quæ inter Iudæos vulgo tria fuerit. Fuit enim Iudæa prophetarum patria, & Iudæis prophetiæ donum quasi proprium Deus dederat, vt non vno loco testatur. At constat illos nusquam contemptius habitos fuisse, quàm inter Iudæos. Nam vt postea audiemus, Eliæ & Elisæi maior fuit apud exteros authoritas, quàm apud Israelitas, ex quibus illi prodierant. Ionas vero apud Niniuitas vna concione plus profecit, quàm prophetæ simul omnes quotidianis & assiduis admonitionibus apud Iudæos proficere potuerint. Sic ad Nabuchodonozoris aures Ieremiæ fama peruenit, et apud Babilonios in precio fuit, qui apud cives suos non modò contemnebatur, sed proditoris loco habebatur. Deniq; ea rabie & contumacia aduersus Dei seruos Iudæi vsi sunt, vt infra Christus dicat, Prophetam non alibi quàm Hierosolymis mori posse. Inde proverbiũ hoc exortũ fuisse videtur, cuius in præsenti Christus meminit, vt scandalo medeatur, quod aliqui infirmiores ex Nazarethanorũ incredulitate captare poterant.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone be offended by the unbelief and obstinacy of the Nazarenes as something strange and unusual, he uses an argument from what has happened before, by which he strikes at the ancient and inherited impiety and rebelliousness of the Jewish nation, saying: "Verily I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country." In Mark he puts it thus: "A prophet is not without honour except in his own country, and among his kinsfolk, and in his own house." This saying also seems to be a proverb, which was commonly current among the Jews. For Judea was the homeland of the prophets, and God had given the gift of prophecy to the Jews as if it were their own, as he testifies in more than one place. But it is certain that the prophets were nowhere held in more contempt than among the Jews. For, as we shall hear later, the authority of Elijah and Elisha was greater among foreigners than among the Israelites from whom they sprang. Jonah, indeed, accomplished more among the Ninevites in a single sermon than all the prophets together could accomplish among the Jews by their daily and constant admonitions. So the fame of Jeremiah reached the ears of Nebuchadnezzar, and he was held in esteem among the Babylonians, while among his own citizens he was not only despised but regarded as a traitor. Finally, the Jews used such rage and obstinacy against the servants of God that Christ later says a prophet cannot die anywhere but at Jerusalem. From this the proverb seems to have arisen, which Christ here recalls in order to remedy the stumbling-block that some weaker people could take from the unbelief of the Nazarenes.

units.la: At nos meminerimus, perpetuum hoc esse, vt qui Verbum Dei summa fide prædicant, apud nullos minori in precio sint, quàm apud cives suos, inter quos nati sunt & educati. Et possunt huius malicæ causæ aliquot adduci ex communi hominum sensu atq; experientia. Nam primò vulgare hoc est, vt non facilè magnificentius de illis sentiamus, quos à pueris nouimus, & quos pueros vidimus multa ineptius, multa etiam præter decorum & officium facientes. Et debebant huius omnes iam inde à pueris meminisse, vt iuuentutem vitijs polluerent, quorum olim ipsos pudere posset, & quæ in publico aliquo munere versantibus authoritatem omnem labefactent. Deinde multùm hîc poterit æmulatio, qua fit, vt iniquum videatur eos nobis præesse, quos nobiscum educatos esse scimus, & qui fortasse quoad natales & maiorum conditionem nobis minimè sunt conferendi. Accedit hïs commune vitium, quòd ferè peregrina admirari, domestica fastidire solemus. Fit hoc in vestitu, victu, moribus. Imò patriam plerique fastidiunt, vt peregrinis lautitijs fruantur. Et inueniuntur, qui magistratui extero subesse malint, quàm domi nostræ natis principibus. Quæ leuitas vt multorum aliorum scelerum causa est, ita Verbi quoq; Dei contemptum parit, quo huius ira maximè prouocatur. Adde, quòd cum natura disciplinæ impatientiores simus, solemus ferè in monitoribus vitia, si quibus laborant, & quæcunq; alia ipsis contemptum parere possunt, diligentius multò obseruare, quâ dona Dei quibus ornati sunt. Deniq; nihil non nobis in eos licere putamus, quibus aliquando familiariter consueuimus. Nam vt prouerbio dicitur, familiaritas parit contemptum. At est hæc immanis & nulla venia digna hominum peruersitas atque ingratitudo, qui Deum & eius dona impudentius contemnunt, quo familiariorem ille se nobis præbet. Faciunt ergo plerique quod malæ frugis & deploratæ indolis filij, qui patris indulgentia ad suam nequitiam abutuntur. Debent autem in horum consideratione diligenter versari ministri ecclesiarum, vt patienter ferre discant fortem, quæ ipsis cum sanctissimis Dei seruis communis est. Arment ergo se e inuicta animi constantia, & se Dei seruos esse meminerint, qui remunerator suorum est fidelissimus. Alij vero omnes veteribus exemplis admoniti, infelicis vulgi iudicia suspecta habeant, & procul relicta hominum quorumuis authoritate, Dei verbum magni faciant, vt in eo loquentem Iesum Christum apprehendant, in hoc vitam atque salutem æternam consequantur. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us remember that this is a perpetual pattern: those who preach the Word of God with the greatest faith are held in no higher regard by anyone than by their own fellow citizens, among whom they were born and brought up. Several causes of this malice can be drawn from common human feeling and experience. First, it is commonly the case that we do not think highly of those whom we have known from boyhood, and whom we saw as boys doing many foolish things, many even contrary to propriety and duty. All of them, from boyhood on, ought to remember that they polluted their youth with vices of which they could be ashamed, and which undermine all authority in those who hold some public office. Next, rivalry plays a large part here, so that it seems unfair that those should be set over us whom we know to have been brought up alongside us, and who perhaps, as regards birth and the condition of their ancestors, are by no means to be compared with us. To this is added a common fault: we are accustomed to admire what is foreign and to despise what is our own. This happens in clothing, food and manners. Indeed, most people despise their homeland so that they may enjoy foreign luxuries. And there are those who would rather be subject to a foreign magistrate than to princes born in our own land. This levity, as it is the cause of many other crimes, so also produces contempt for the Word of God, by which God's anger is especially provoked. Add that, since we are by nature more impatient of discipline, we usually observe far more carefully, in those who admonish us, any faults they may have, and anything else that can produce contempt for them, than the gifts of God with which they are adorned. Finally, we think we may do anything at all to those with whom we have once been on familiar terms. For, as the proverb says, familiarity breeds contempt. But this perversity and ingratitude of men is monstrous and unworthy of any pardon, since they despise God and his gifts all the more shamelessly the more familiar he shows himself to us. So most people act like the sons of a bad and hopeless character who abuse their father's indulgence for their own wickedness. The ministers of the churches ought to dwell diligently on these considerations, so that they learn to bear patiently the lot that they share with the most holy servants of God. Let them arm themselves with unconquered constancy of mind, and remember that they are servants of God, who is the most faithful rewarder of his own. All others, admonished by these ancient examples, should regard the judgements of the unhappy crowd with suspicion and, setting aside the authority of any men whatever, should hold the Word of God in high esteem, so that in it they may apprehend Jesus Christ speaking, and in him obtain life and eternal salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIII.

units.la: Sed in veritate dico vobis, multæ viduæ erant diebus Eliæ in Israel, quando clausum fuit cœlum ad annos tres & sex menses, adeo vt fuerit fames magna per totam regionem. Sed ad nullam illarum missus est Elias, nisi Sareptam Sidoniæ, ad mulierem viduam. Et multi leprosi erant in Israel sub Elisæo propheta, sed nemo eorum purgatus est nisi Naamã Syrus. Tum repleti sunt omnes excandescentia in Synagoga, hæc audientes. Et cum surrexissent, eiecerunt eum extra vrbem, & duxerunt eum vsq; ad supercilium montis, super quem vrbs eorum erat ædificata, vt præcipitarent eum. Ipse vero transiens per medium eorum, profectus est.
units.tr: But in truth I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut up for three years and six months, so that there was a great famine over all the land. Yet Elijah was sent to none of them, but only to Zarephath in Sidon, to a widow woman. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, yet none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian. Then all in the synagogue were filled with wrath as they heard these things. They rose up, drove him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built, so that they might throw him down. But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.

units.la: Multa quidem cum fide & magna diligentia Dominus noster Iesus Christus ciuibus suis Nazarethanis, inter quos educatus fuerat, æternæ vitæ doctrinam prædicauit, et quò minus de ea dubitarent, ex Isaia prophetarum celeberrimo diserte docuit, quis nam ipse sit, & quanta bona in ipso Deus Pater toti mortalium generi offerat. At pauci admodum & tantumnon nulli fuerunt, qui doctrinæ eius crediderint, & oblatam in ipso salutem, qua decet fide & animi gratitudine amplexi sint. Causa tam stupidæ incredulitatis fuit, quod in externam solum Christi speciem intenti, nullam bonorum cœlestium, quæ offerebat, rationem habuerunt. Offendit ergo eos familiæ eius egestas, artificium manuarium quod a pueris exercuerat, & quod qui multis miraculose opem ferebat, suos omnes miseros & egenos esse patiebatur. Denique quod omnes solent qui carnis studijs addicti sunt, miracula potius videre, quam conciones eius audire voluissent. Itaque graviter admodum cum illis agit Dominus, & postquam offendit quibus remoris potissimum detineantur, mox scandalo mederi studet, quod aliqui infirmiores ex eorum incredulitate capere poterant. Offendit enim hanc non nouam esse, sed iam olim eam fuisse prophetarum sortem, vt nusquam contemptiores fuerint, quàm in Iudæa, quæ non immerito illorum patria dici poterat. Id vero in præsenti duobus exemplis confirmat, & ijsdem simul se excusat, qui exteros ciuibus & domesticis suis hucusque præstulerit: deinde quid tandem ipsis propter incredulitatem & ingratitudinem suam euenturum sit, monet: Vt nimirum Deus regnum suum & vniuersum salutis promissæ beneficium ad gentes transferat. Quæ vt generalem doctrinam & ad nos quoq; pertinentem continent: ita simul consolantur nos, ne spem regni Dei abijciamus, si hoc ab illis reijci & concultari videmus, qui illud in primis amplecti debebant. Nam nihil potest ex eo decedere Deo aut communi salutis negotio. Habet enim vbi, loco rum suos electos Deus, & vbicunq; ipsi lubet, ecclesia suæ domicilium inuenit.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, with great faith and diligence, preached the doctrine of eternal life to his fellow citizens of Nazareth, among whom he had been brought up, and, so that they might not doubt it, he taught them plainly from Isaiah, the most celebrated of the prophets, who he himself is and how many good things God the Father offers in him to the whole human race. Yet there were very few, and almost none, who believed his teaching and embraced the salvation offered in him with the faith and thankfulness that befit it. The cause of such stupid unbelief was that they fixed their attention only on Christ's outward appearance and took no account of the heavenly goods he offered. His family's poverty offended them, and the manual craft which he had practised from boyhood, and the fact that he, who miraculously brought help to many, allowed all his own people to be wretched and needy. Finally, as all do who are given over to the pursuits of the flesh, they wished to see his miracles rather than hear his sermons. So the Lord deals very severely with them, and, having pointed out what chiefly held them back, he at once sets about curing the stumbling-block which some of the weaker ones could take from their unbelief. For he shows that this is not a new thing, but that it has been the lot of the prophets from of old, that nowhere were they more despised than in Judea, which could not without reason be called their homeland. He confirms this now by two examples, and at the same time excuses himself for having preferred foreigners to his fellow citizens and household until now. Then he warns them what will finally befall them on account of their unbelief and ingratitude: namely, that God will transfer his kingdom and the whole benefit of the promised salvation to the Gentiles. These words contain a general teaching which also pertains to us, and at the same time they comfort us, so that we do not cast away hope in the kingdom of God if we see it rejected and trampled by those who ought above all to embrace it. For nothing can be taken away from God or from the common business of salvation. God has places where he can have his elect, and the Church finds her dwelling wherever he pleases.

units.la: Primum exemplum, quod Christus adducit, de Elia propheta est, & in primo lib. Reg. cap. 17. describitur. Erat illo tempore sub Achabo Rege Israelitarum statvs longè corruptissimus. Cum enim antea vitulos aureos modo colluissent, quos Ieroboã regni sui confirmandi causa instituerat, Achab ducta in vxorem Iezabele Regis Sidoniorum filia, Baalis quoq; cultum inuexit, cui templum in Samaria ædificauit, aras et lucos hinc inde posuit, & populum totum peregrinis superstitionibus miserime seduxit. Comitata sunt idololatriam (vt fieri solet) omnis generis scelera, inter quæ præcipua erant, quòd veri Dei altaria diruebant, Verbum Dei odio habebant, & prophetas eius hostiliter persequebantur. Fiebat ergo, vt maior populi pars in scelerus societatem veniret, & ij quoq; qui optimi erant (exceptis paucis millibus eorum, quos sibi Deus ex peculiari gratia ab omni idololatriæ labe alienos seruauerat) in vtrumq; latus clandicarent, cum & Baalim colerent, & Deo vero gloriaren tur, qui patres eorum ex Ægypto eduxerat. Cum ergo docendo & monendo nihil proficerent Prophetæ, & disciplina seueriori opus esset, Elias publice siccitatem trium annorum & sex mensium minatur. Viuit (inquit) Dominus Deus Israelis, coram quo ministro, si fuerit hisce annis ros aut pluuia, nisi iuxta os meum. Et mox euentum suum habuit comminatio illa. Itaq; cum per regionem vniuersam dira fames inualesceret, & (vt modò diximus) aliquot millia eorum reliqui essent, qui genua sua Baali nunquam inflexerant, nemo tamen ex illis est inuentus, qui Eliam ad se recipiat, & veritatis doctrinæ aduersus regem patrocinetur. Quapropter necesse erat vt seruo suo alia ratione Deus prospiceret:
units.tr: The first example that Christ brings forward is of the prophet Elijah, and it is described in the first book of Kings, chapter 17. At that time, under King Ahab of the Israelites, the state was most corrupt. For although previously they had worshipped the golden calves which Jeroboam had set up to confirm his kingdom, Ahab, having taken as his wife Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, introduced also the worship of Baal, built a temple to him in Samaria, set up altars and groves on every side, and most wretchedly led the whole people astray into foreign superstitions. Idolatry (as usually happens) was accompanied by every kind of wickedness, chief among which was that they overthrew the altars of the true God, hated the Word of God, and hostilely persecuted his prophets. So it came about that the greater part of the people entered into this wicked fellowship, and even those who were best (except for a few thousand whom God, by his special grace, had preserved free from every stain of idolatry) halted between both sides, both worshipping Baal and boasting of the true God who had led their fathers out of Egypt. Therefore, since the prophets accomplished nothing by teaching and admonishing, and a stricter discipline was needed, Elijah publicly threatened a drought of three years and six months. "As the Lord God of Israel lives," he said, "before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years, except at my word." And soon that threat had its outcome. So when a dreadful famine grew strong throughout the whole region, and (as we have just said) there remained some thousands of them who had never bent their knees to Baal, yet no one was found among them who would receive Elijah and defend the doctrine of the truth against the king. Therefore God had to provide for his servant by another means.

units.la: Cap. IIII. Iubet ergo vt primum in torrente Christ se occultet, vbi illum pascit coruorum ministerio, qui quotidie sub auroram & vesperam panem & carnem adipsum deferebant. At cū præ siccitate & æstu aqua torrentis deficeret, Sareptam (quod Sidoniorum oppidum erat) illū abire iubet, ad mulierem viduam, quæ ipsum hospitio suscepturafit. Erat mandatum hoc nouum & insolens, & vix credibile videbatur, prophetam apud exteram gentem domicilium inuenturum esse, què domestici & ciues eius omnes negligebant. Attamen paret iubenti Domino, & praeter expectationem inter Sareptanos fidei constantis exemplum inuenit, quale nullum in Israele extabat. Nam cùm ad ciuitatis portam venisset, in mulierem ligna colligentem incidit, à qua paululum aquæ petijt, qua sitim ex longo itinere contractam leuaret. Illa autem abeunte, panis quoque buccellam sibi afferri postulauit. Ad quam postulationem cùm illa respondisset: Viuit Dominus Deus tuus, si est mihi panis coctus, solum pugillum farinæ habeo in cado, & parum olei in lecytho, & en colligo ligna duo, vt ingrediar, & apparem illum mihi & filio meo, comedamusque ipsum, & deinde moriamur. Dixit ei Elias: Ne timeas, vade & fac secundum verbum tuum: veruntamen fac mihi primum inde paruum subcinericium panem, & affer ad me, tibi autem & filio pares postea. Quoniam sic dicit Dominus Deus Israelis, Farina cadi non deficiet, & oleum lecythi non minuetur vsque ad eum diem, quo Dominus pluuiam dederit super faciem terræ. Credidit promissioni huic mulier, & prophetæ mandato paruit, sicque promissionis fructum percepit, vt multis interea in Israele & vicinis locis partim fame pereuntibus, partim miserè laborantibus, ipsa vnà cum filio & Elia hospite suo victum sufficientem haberet. Itaque merces prophetæ ad exteros transfertur, qui illi hospitium dabant. At quod illi beneficium contulit Deus, hoc ipsum Israelitis quoque simul omnibus conferre potuisset, imo voluisset conferre, nisi illi sua incredulitate atque contumacia prophetam tanti boni authorem & æternæ salutis nuntium à se repulisset. Digni ergo erant, à quibus propheta discederet, & secum bona Dei simul omnia ad exteras gentes transferret. Conueniebat autem historia hæc per omnia temporibus Christi, & quæ tunc erat Iudæorum conditioni, & ideo rectè illam in præsenti contra Nazarethanos suos adducit. Peccarant enim iam multis annis aduersus Deum, qui iampridem doctrinam verbi ab illis abstulerat, & humanarum traditionum magistris permiserat seducendos. Iam ergo passim regnabat sanioris doctrinæ inopia & fames illa, quam per Amos prophetam Deus olim minatus erat: eoque pernitiosius laborabant, quod malum hoc non sentirent Iudæi, & se probè saturos putarent. Quamuis autem indignissimi essent, quos respiceret Deus, vicit tamen iustitiæ rigorem bonitas, & primò quidem Ioannem misit, qui salutis iam adfores appropinquantis spem faceret: illum verò mox Christus secutus est, qui non pugillum farinæ, non parum olei, sed inexhaustos gratiæ Dei thesauros secum attulit, neque aliud ab ipsis postulauit, quàm vt primò ipsius de siderium, quo illorum salutem esuriebat, saturarent, inde verò ipsi bonis cœlestibus affatim expleren tur. Nunquam tamè hoc ab illis impetrare potuit, vt se Patris verbo obsequentes præberent. Quid ergo fieri debebat aliud, quàm vt illis relictis Euangelium suum & quæcunque in hoc nobis prædicantur bona, ad alios transferret? Et quia hic præ aliis Nazarethani peccabant, digni quoque erant, qui præ aliis punirentur: neque à quoquam accusari merebatur Christus, etiamsi (vt olim Elias fecerat) illis contemptis & reiectis ad alios transfiret. Quia verò historia hæc cognitu iucundissima est, & alia quoque continet, quæ ad huius causæ illustrationem faciunt, proderit illa ex ordine considerare.
units.tr: Chap. 4. He therefore bids him first hide himself in the brook Cherith, where he feeds him by the ministry of ravens, which every day, in the morning and the evening, brought him bread and flesh. But when, because of the drought and heat, the water of the brook failed, he bids him go to Zarephath (which was a town of the Sidonians), to a widow woman who would receive him as a guest. This command was new and strange, and it seemed hardly credible that a prophet would find a dwelling among a foreign nation, while his own household and fellow citizens neglected him. Nevertheless he obeys the Lord's bidding, and beyond expectation he finds among the people of Zarephath an example of steadfast faith such as there was none in Israel. For when he came to the gate of the town, he met a woman gathering sticks, and asked her for a little water to relieve the thirst he had contracted on his long journey. As she was going away, he also asked that a morsel of bread be brought to him. When she answered this request, "As the Lord your God lives, I have no baked bread, only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a jug; and see, I am gathering two sticks so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and then die." Elijah said to her, "Do not fear; go and do as you have said. Yet make for me first a small cake baked in the ashes, and bring it to me, and afterwards prepare for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: the meal in the jar shall not fail, and the oil in the jug shall not be diminished, until the day that the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth." The woman believed this promise and obeyed the prophet's command, and so she received the fruit of the promise: while in the meantime many in Israel and in the neighbouring places were partly perishing of hunger and partly suffering wretchedly, she herself, together with her son and Elijah, her guest, had sufficient food. Thus the prophet's reward was transferred to foreigners, who gave him lodging. But what God bestowed on that woman he could have bestowed on all the Israelites together, nay, would have bestowed, had they not by their unbelief and obstinacy rejected from themselves the prophet, the author of so great a good and the messenger of eternal salvation. They were therefore worthy that the prophet should depart from them and carry all God's good things with him to the foreign nations. Moreover, this history fits in every respect the times of Christ and the condition of the Jews at that time, and therefore he rightly brings it forward now against his Nazarenes. For they had already been sinning against God for many years; God had long since taken the teaching of the word from them and allowed them to be led astray by teachers of human traditions. Now therefore a lack of sounder doctrine and that famine, which God had once threatened through the prophet Amos, reigned everywhere, and they suffered the more harmfully because the Jews did not feel this evil and thought they were thoroughly well fed. Yet, although they were most unworthy for God to look upon, goodness overcame the rigour of justice, and first he sent John, who was to give hope that salvation was now close at hand; and soon Christ followed him, who brought with him not a handful of meal or a little oil, but the inexhaustible treasures of the grace of God, and asked nothing else from them than that they should first satisfy the longing with which they hungered for their salvation, and then be filled to the full with heavenly goods. Yet he could never obtain from them that they would yield themselves obedient to the Father's word. What else, then, ought to have happened, than that, leaving them, he should carry his gospel and all the good things proclaimed to us in it over to others? And since the Nazarenes sinned here more than others, they were also worthy to be punished more than others; and Christ deserved to be blamed by no one, even if (as Elijah once did) he passed over to others when they were despised and rejected. But since this history is most pleasant to know, and also contains other things which serve to illustrate this cause, it will be profitable to consider them in order.

units.la: Primum in his occurrit, quòd non raro grauissimis calamitatibus totas gentes Deus implicat, & Verbi sui lucem ab illis etiam populis aufert, in quibus aliqui non omnino mali sunt, imò in quibus sunt, qui cultum verum studiosè retinent. Factum hoc fuit Eliæ temporibus: Etsi enim impietas & tyrannis longè lateq; dominarentur, seruarat tamen sibi Deus (vt ante diximus) septem millia virorū, qui genua sua ante Baalis statuas nò incuruauerat. Et hodie videmus multos veri cultus amantissimos esse, qui tamè et ipsi communè cum alijs pœnam subire videntur, quando Verbum suum Deus è medio tollit. Mirantur hoc multi, & in Deo æquiorem iustitiæ atque iudicij sui moderationem requirunt. Quibus simpliciter respondeti poterat: Ehò qui nam vos estis, quibus factorum suorum rationem Deus reddat? Aut quis nam ille est, qui se gratia dignum esse gloriari possit? Annon liberum est Deo pro sua bona voluntate Verbi sui lucem dispensare? Attamen vt infirmitati quorundam consulamus, iudicij sui rationem in hoc exemplo monstrari posse dicimus. Erant quidem plurimi in Israele, quibus impietas & tyrannis displicebant, qui item se ab omni idololatria puros & immaculatos seruabant. At quotus quisq; erat, qui impijs edictis & publicis superstitionibus se palàm opponeret? qui Eliae causam suscipéret? qui verum Dei cultum propugnaret? Ita certè omnes latebant, ut Elias se solum putaret reliquum esse. Carebant igitur zelo Domini, quo pios ardere decet, & ideo digni erant, qui iustas ignauiae suae poenas sentirent. Solet hocferè vbique fieri, neque culpam suam diffitentur, quos serius diuinae gloriae sensus afficit. Nemini ergo iniuriam facit Deus. Nam etsi eadem omnium poena esse videtur, magnum tamen inter pios & impios discrimen est: quia hi quidem supplicium sua impietate dignum patiuntur, quo ferè malè pereunt: illi verò disciplina & castigatione hac meliores fiunt, & excitantur, ut maiori cum zelo & industria Domini negotium agant.
units.tr: The first lesson here is that God sometimes visits whole nations with the most severe calamities and takes away the light of his Word even from peoples among whom some are not wholly wicked, indeed among whom there are some who earnestly hold to the true worship. This happened in Elijah's time. Although impiety and tyranny held sway far and wide, God had kept for himself (as we said before) seven thousand men who had not bent their knees before the image of Baal. Today too we see many who love the true worship most dearly, and yet they seem to undergo the same punishment as others when God removes his Word from the midst. Many people wonder at this and demand a fairer measure of justice and judgment from God. To such people one could simply reply: "Who are you, to whom God should give an account of his deeds? Or who is he who can boast that he deserves grace? Is it not lawful for God, by his good pleasure, to dispense the light of his Word?" Yet, to help the weakness of some, we say that the reason for his judgment can be shown in this example. There were indeed very many in Israel who disliked impiety and tyranny, and who likewise kept themselves pure and undefiled from all idolatry. But how few were there who openly opposed the impious edicts and public superstitions? Who took up Elijah's cause? Who defended the true worship of God? So utterly were all of them in hiding that Elijah thought he alone was left. They therefore lacked that zeal for the Lord which becomes the godly to burn with, and so they deserved to feel the just penalty of their cowardice. This commonly happens everywhere, and those whom a late sense of God's glory strikes do not deny their own fault. God therefore does no wrong to anyone. For although the punishment seems the same for all, there is nevertheless a great difference between the godly and the wicked: the latter suffer a punishment fitting their impiety, by which they generally perish miserably, but the former are made better and stirred up by this discipline and chastisement, so that they may carry on the Lord's work with greater zeal and diligence.

units.la: Deinde admonemur exemplo hoc, calamitates eiusmodi neque Dei verbo, neque ecclesiae eius quicquam detrahere. Illud enim aeternum est, & perpetuò ratum manet: Ecclesiae verò suae vbique terrarum sedem aliquam inuenit Deus, vbi vel apertius cultum suum exerceat, vel obscurius latéat, & tamen fructum ferat non poenitendum. Et in hac re in primis admirabilia sunt opera Domini. Nam vt huius exempli vestigijs insistamus, quis coruos nutritios Eliae fore credidisset, quem Israelitae simul omnes negligebant? Quis eidem in Sidoniorum terra hospitium polliceri ausus fuisset, vnde Baalis cultum nefarium impia Iezabel in Israelis regnum aduexerat? Sareptae tamen hospitium tutum & liberale Elias inuenit, & ibidem non sine publica Israelitarum ignominia ecclesiolam habet Deus rara fide & miraculis celebrem. Vidimus huius generis multa hodie, quando in illis terris praeter omnem expectationem ecclesiae emerserunt, ex quibus paulò ante acerrimi euangelicae lucis hostes prodierant. Sunt ergo stulti nimis, qui vel Deum suis locis & vrbibus alligatum putant, vel de ecclesia in vniuersum omni actum esse vociferantur, si vna aut altera gens dignas suae incredulitatis & contumaciae poenas exoluat.
units.tr: Next, this example warns us that calamities of this kind take nothing away from the Word of God or from his Church. For that Word is eternal and remains firm forever, while God always finds for his Church some seat somewhere on earth, where he either exercises his worship more openly or lies hidden more obscurely, and yet bears fruit that is not to be regretted. And in this matter the works of the Lord are especially wonderful. For, to follow the footsteps of this example, who would have believed that ravens would feed Elijah, when all the Israelites together neglected him? Who would have dared to promise him lodging in the land of the Sidonians, from where impious Jezebel had brought the wicked worship of Baal into the kingdom of Israel? Yet Elijah found a safe and generous lodging at Zarephath, and there God has a small church, famous for its rare faith and its miracles, not without public shame to the Israelites. We have seen many things of this kind today, when in those lands, beyond all expectation, churches have arisen, out of which, shortly before, the bitterest enemies of the gospel light had come forth. They are therefore very foolish who either think God is bound to certain places and cities, or who cry out that the Church has altogether perished if one or another nation pays the just penalty of its unbelief and obstinacy.

units.la: Docet praeterea locus hic, quid facere oporteat temporibus difficillimis, ne ipsi quoque salutis iacturam faciamus. Potest hoc vno verbo expediri: Vt nimirum viduam Sareptanam imitemur. Quia enim hanc prae omnibus alijs Deus elegit, ad quam Elias diuerteret, non dubium est in ea fide vera & absoluta exemplum proponi. Quid ergo illa fecit? Primò prophetae verbis credidit. Hinc nos quoque exordiamur necesse est. Nisi enim Dei verba apud nos fidem inueniant, nunquam aliquid faciemus, quod Deo probari possit. Deinde fidem suam non inanibus verbis, sed ipsa, id est, obedientia testatur: & quidem in re maxima, quae cum ratione & communi sensu pugnare videbatur, & à qua illam rationes infinitae poterant abstërrere. Cùm enim tantillum modò farinae & olei haberet, quod in vnicum prandiolum sibi & filio suo vix sufficere posset, Elias autem sibi priori ex illo panem coqui mandaret, mox absque omni tergiuersatione obtemperat. Quantam verò hanc eius fidem fuisse putas, quae illam vt in tanta famis necessitate & in praesenti vitae periculo hoc faceret, monuit? Etenim si communes hominum mores examines, paucos inuenire licet, qui in summa rerum abundantia aliquid hominibus notis & bene de se meritis decidant, si quid periculi imminere videtur. Neque tamen in eo pedem sistit, sed Dei promissione freta Eliam hospitio excipit, & longo tempore domi suae sustentat, quod ipsum quoq; periculo non carebat. Erat enim Achabo regi exosus valde, qui illum Israelis turbatorem dicere solebat. Achabo autem vel socer vel affinis proximus erat. Sidoniorum rex, ad cuius imperium Sarepta pertinebat. Sunt haec praeclara fidei argumenta, quibus hodie studere nos conuenit. Obediamus Dei verbo, & huic subijciamus carnis nostrae sensus & rationes omnes. Obediamus autem, non modò cùm tutum est, sed tunc quoque, quando res cum periculo grauissimo coniuncta esse videtur. Audendum est enim aliquid pro veritate et salute publica: ne ex eorum numero videamur esse, quos Christi & Euangelij eius pudet coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero. Et haec ferè praecipua sunt, quibus fidem suam declarauerint olim, quotquot eius nomine commendantur. Quorum vestigijs si insistamus, procul dubio Christum retinebimus, & eiusdem beneficijs laeti fruemur.
units.tr: This passage also teaches what we ought to do in the most difficult times, so that we ourselves do not suffer the loss of salvation. This can be explained in one word: namely, that we should imitate the widow of Zarephath. For since God chose her above all others as the one with whom Elijah should lodge, there is no doubt that she is set before us as an example of true and complete faith. What then did she do? First, she believed the prophet's words. We too must necessarily begin here. For unless the words of God find faith among us, we will never do anything that can please God. Second, she bore witness to her faith not by empty words but by deeds, that is, by obedience, and indeed in a matter of the greatest importance, which seemed to clash with reason and common sense, and from which countless reasons could have turned her aside. For when she had only a little meal and oil, barely enough for one small meal for herself and her son, and Elijah bade her first make him bread from it, she immediately obeyed without any evasion. And how great do you think her faith was, which moved her to do this in such great need of food and in present danger to her life? For if you examine the common customs of men, you will find few who, in the greatest abundance, would give up anything to men they know and who have deserved well of them, if any danger seems to threaten. Yet she did not stop there; relying on God's promise, she received Elijah into her house and sustained him there for a long time, which likewise was not free from danger. For he was greatly hateful to King Ahab, who used to call him the troubler of Israel. Now the king of the Sidonians, under whose rule Zarephath lay, was the father-in-law or at least the nearest relative of Ahab. These are illustrious proofs of faith, which it becomes us to strive after today. Let us obey God's Word, and let us subject to it all the feelings and reasons of our flesh. And let us obey not only when it is safe, but also when the matter seems bound up with the gravest danger. For we must dare something for the truth and the public good, lest we seem to belong to the number of those who are ashamed of Christ and his gospel before this crooked and adulterous world. And these are almost the chief things by which all who are commended in his name have in former times shown their faith. If we follow in their footsteps, we will without doubt keep hold of Christ, and happily enjoy his benefits.

units.la: Alterum exemplum de Elisaeo propheta & Naamano Syro est. Incidit ea historia in tempora Ioram, qui Achabi filius fuit, & extat in secundo libro Regum Cap.5. Erat tunc idem ferè in Israele rerum status, qui sub Achabo fuerat, nisi quòd Baalis cultum ex parte Ioram sustulerat. Docebat tunc posteà Eliæ raptum in cœlos Elisæus, & doctrinam suam miraculis multis & magnis confirmabat, & per eundem victoriam contra Moabitas insignem Deus dederat. Erant hæc quidem in omnium ore, neque negari poterat Dei virtus, quæ in illo sese exerebat. At non ita isti moue-bantur Israelitarum animi, ut doctrinæ illius serió crederent, & eum salutis præconem atque ministrum agnoscerent. Accidit autem, ut Naamanus, qui apud Syriæ regem Magister equitum erat, vir bello & rebus gestis eximius, lepra autem infectus, puellæ Israeliticæ & apud vxorem eius seruientis narratione de Elisæo permotus, sibi ad eum proficiscendum esse putaret. Itaque impe-ratis à Rege suo literis commendatitijs, magno cum apparatu equorum & curruum, neque sine honorarijs muneribus, eò profectus est. Venientem Elisæus primò non in conspectum admisit, mandauit autem per nuntium, ut septies in Iordane tingeretur, & ex eo purgationem leprae pollicitus est. Tulit hoc Syrus indignissimè, & ut hoc hominum genus solet, in verba faustus & indignatio-nis plena erupit, En, cogitabam (inquit) apud me, Omnino exibit, & stans invocabit nomen Domini Dei sui, admouebitque manum suam ad locum, & curabit lepram: Annon præstant Abana & Parpar fluuij Damasci omnibus aquis Israelis? Annon si lauero in eis, mundus ero? At per famulos admonitus prophetæ mandato paruit, & à lepra mundatus est, sicque homo exterus & pe-regrinus beneficium ab Elisæo ingens accipit, quod nulli leprosorum, quorum apud Israelitas infi-nitus erat numerus, contigit. At si caussam quæras, ea in promptu est: quòd nimirum nemo Israe-litarum in tanta existimatione habuit Elisæum, ut eius ope sibi vtendum putaret. Non ergo eius malignitate hoc factum est, sed Israelitarum incredulitate, in qua sic obstupuerant, ut omnium oculis & sensibus se ingerentem Dei virtutem non obseruarent, neque accusari meretur Elisæus, qui quod Israelitæ omnes aspernabantur beneficium, ad Naamanum exterum transtulit. Seruit autem exemplum hoc mirificè Christi instituto, & Nazarethanos egregiè confutat, qui indignius fere-bant, quòd ille plura alibi quàm apud ipsos miracula ædidisset. Nam laborabant ipsi simul om-nes lepra peccati, non purgabantur autem Christi beneficio, non quòd is salutem ipsis inuideret, sed quòd hanc illis liberaliter offerentem contemnerent. Propria ergo culpa peribant, & optimo iure Christus saluificam suam virtutem ad alios transferebat. Interim non obscurè ille innuit, quid Iudæis simul omnibus fit eventurum: quòd nimirum regnum suum Deus ab ipsis ad gentes transla-turus sit, ipsos autem reiecturus, eò quòd in auita contumacia pergant, & nullis neque signis neque admonitionibus moueantur, quæ multis alijs mouendis sufficiant. Nam si Naamanum spectemus, eius facilitate Israelitas simul omnes damnari videbis. Non contempsit vt puellulæ captiuæ, extera & ex hostili gente oriundæ narrationem de Elisæo. At hunc coràm docentem & miracula ædentem Israelitæ aspernabantur. Venit ille longo itinere, magno cum apparatu & impensis maximis. Hi, quem domi suæ habebant, fastidiunt. Etsi ille initiò indignationem aliquam animo conciperet, mox tamen famulos meliora monentes audit, & prophetæ obtemperat. At Israelitæ prophetarum sermonibus semel offensi perpetua odia & inimicitias nunquam finiendas animo concipiebant. Et quod olim patres fecerant, hoc ipsum Christi & Apostolorum temporibus Iudæos fere omnes fe-cisse constat. Cùm enim Apostolis, hominibus peregrinis gentes crederent, & Christum ma-gno studio amplecterentur, Iudæi gentiles suos contemnebant, & immani odio accensi vbique lo-corum turbas excitabant, quibus Euangelium opprimerent. Magno igitur suo merito puniti & à regni Dei societate exclusi sunt. At hic meminisse oportet, in illis exemplum proponi, quo omnium locorum & temporum homines docentur, quid expectent, si similí contumacia & incredulitate Chri-sti doctrinam reijciant. Sibi ergo ista applicent, qui illum hodie in Euangelio loquentem audiunt, ne aliquando frustra quærant eum, quem prius improbè contempserunt. Obseruari idè hoc debet in alijs omnibus Dei beneficijs, ne dum vel ea contemnimus, vel ijsdem abutimur, non illa modò amitta-mus, verumetiam pœnis dignis multemur.
units.tr: The second example is that of the prophet Elisha and the Syrian Naaman. That story falls in the time of Jehoram, who was the son of Ahab, and it is found in the second book of Kings, chapter 5. The state of affairs in Israel was then much the same as under Ahab, except that Jehoram had in part removed the worship of Baal. Elisha, who after Elijah's ascension into heaven was teaching, confirmed his doctrine by many great miracles, and through him God had given a remarkable victory against the Moabites. These things were indeed on everyone's lips, and the power of God which showed itself in him could not be denied. But the minds of the Israelites were not so moved as to believe his teaching earnestly and acknowledge him as the herald and minister of salvation. It happened, however, that Naaman, who was commander of the horsemen at the court of the king of Syria, a man outstanding in war and in his deeds, but afflicted with leprosy, was moved by the account of an Israelite girl who served his wife, and thought he should go to Elisha. So, with letters of recommendation obtained from his king, with a great retinue of horses and chariots, and not without gifts of honour, he set out there. Elisha did not admit him to his presence when he came, but sent word through a messenger that he should wash seven times in the Jordan, and promised him from this the cleansing of his leprosy. The Syrian took this very badly, and, as this sort of men usually do, he burst out into angry and indignant words: "Look," he said, "I thought to myself, he will surely come out, and standing will call upon the name of the Lord his God, and will move his hand over the place and cure the leprosy. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Would I not be clean if I washed in them?" But, admonished by his servants, he obeyed the prophet's command, and was cleansed of leprosy, and so this foreigner and stranger received a great benefit from Elisha, which had come to none of the lepers, who were countless among the Israelites. If you ask the reason, it is ready to hand: namely, that none of the Israelites held Elisha in such high esteem that they thought they should make use of his help. This was therefore not done through his ill will, but through the unbelief of the Israelites, in which they had grown so dull that they did not notice the power of God, which thrust itself upon the eyes and senses of all; and Elisha does not deserve to be accused for transferring to the foreigner Naaman a benefit which all the Israelites scorned. This example also serves wonderfully the purpose of Christ, and thoroughly refutes the Nazarenes, who took it badly that he had performed more miracles elsewhere than among them. For they were all together afflicted with the leprosy of sin, yet they were not cleansed by Christ's benefit, not because he begrudged them salvation, but because they despised him when he offered it to them freely. They therefore perished by their own fault, and with the best right Christ transferred his life-giving power to others. Meanwhile he indicates quite clearly what is going to happen to all the Jews together: namely, that God will transfer his kingdom from them to the nations, and will reject them, because they persist in their ancestral obstinacy and are moved by no signs or admonitions, although these would be enough to move many others. For if we consider Naaman, you will see that by his readiness all the Israelites together are condemned. He did not scorn the account of Elisha given by a captive little girl, a foreigner born of a hostile nation. But the Israelites scorned him when he taught in their presence and worked miracles. He came by a long journey, with a great retinue and very great expense. They looked down on the one they had at home. And although at first he conceived some indignation in his mind, soon afterwards he listened to his servants who gave better advice, and obeyed the prophet. But the Israelites, once offended by the words of the prophets, used to conceive in their minds perpetual hatreds and enmities that were never to end. And what the fathers had done long before, it is plain that almost all the Jews did in the times of Christ and the Apostles. For when the nations believed the Apostles, who were foreign men, and embraced Christ with great eagerness, the Jews despised their own countrymen, and, inflamed with monstrous hatred, stirred up uproars everywhere in the places, by which they might crush the gospel. Therefore they were punished, and rightly so, and were excluded from fellowship in the kingdom of God. But here we must remember that this example is set before us so that people of every place and time may learn what they should expect, if they reject the teaching of Christ with the same stubbornness and unbelief. Let those who hear him speaking today in the gospel apply these things to themselves, lest at some time they seek in vain him whom before they wickedly despised. This ought to be observed in all the other benefits of God as well: lest, while we either despise them or abuse them, we not only lose them, but are also punished with due penalties.

units.la: Sed audiamus, quomodo Christi verba sine admonitionem Nazarethani acceperint. Re-pleti sunt omnes (inquit Lucas) excandescentia in Synagoga, hæc audientes. Sentiunt ergo se perstringi, & in suam contumeliam ista dicta esse, atque ideo non leuiter irascuntur, sed furore ac-censi in rabiem aguntur. Non desunt ergo aures impijs, quibus Dei verbum audiant. Non etiam ratio et intellectus illis deest, sed de se agi vident, & quid ipsis facto opus sit intelligunt. Deest autem voluntas bona, & quia toti affectibus pessimis reguntur, iniuriam sibi fieri putant intolerabilem, si quid dicatur, quod eorum desiderijs repugnat. Apparet autem ex eo, quanta Verbi Dei vis sit, quando eorum quoq; animos tam efficaciter penetrat, qui hoc unum agunt, ut illud scurrili & impio contemptu eludant. Ergo quamuis de illo contemptissimè loquantur, & se illud nullius facere simulent, longè aliter tamen intra animos suos sentiunt, ubi acerrimis stimulis punguntur, qui omnia illis infesta & acerba reddunt. Non autem excandescunt modò Nazarethani, sed postquam dimisso coetu surrexerunt, ex urbe Christum eijciunt, ut indignum, qui porro pro cive & alumno agnosci debeat. Imò ut patriæ pestem ad supercilium montis, super quo oppidum illud extructum erat, rapiunt, ut ex eo praecipitem dent, & infami morte perdant. Habet enim suos progressus impietas, & qui Verbo Dei obstrepere audent, mox maiori sumpta audacia aduersus seruos quoq; Dei hostiliter insurgunt, neq; ut vi aperta & iniusta abstinent. Quò magis nos anniti decet, ut affectuum initijs resistamus, & ut mansuetudinis spiritu furores istos impiorum vincamus. Pulchrè autem, ceu in tabula, hic nobis adumbratur, vel depingitur potius, ministrorum Dei conditio, quam in hoc mundo sustinent. Si Euangelium simpliciter praedicant, fere ridentur. Stultitia enim videtur carnis rationi, in homine crucifixo salutis fiduciam collocare, carnem cum suis affectibus abnegare, mundo & huius amicitiæ longum valere dicere, deniq; propter cœlestia & æterna bona relinquere ea, quæ nobis ad manum sunt, & in quibus tota hominis felicitas consistere putatur. Non multum ergo doctrina hæc afficiuntur, qui toti mundo & carniediti sunt. Quòd si autem ministri longius progressi, scelera quoq; accusent, ingratis & rebellibus Dei iram denuntient, & vel inuitos ad illius tribunal pertrahant: tunc in furorem & rabiem aguntur, qui prius Verbum obiter contemnere videbantur. Hinc ergo atroces impiorum irae, saeuæ comminationes, cruenta edicta, & publici etiam motus exoriri solent: & plerunq; fit, ut qui patriæ pestes sunt, eos è ciuitatibus eijciant, qui patriæ salutem vnicè quærunt, & pro ea dies noctesq; excubias agunt. Exultant ergo frequenter fideles Christi ministri, regnantibus interea impunè adulteris, raptoribus, vsurarijs, homicidis, sacrilegis et impijssimis quibusq;, quorum sceleribus Dei ira quotidie prouocatur. At non offendant ista pios, quando hæc olim Christo apud eos acciderunt, qui illum præ alijs magni facere debebant. Soletur autem eos, quòd patriam & ciuitatem permanentem atq; stabilem in cœlis habent, in quam nihil iuris habent tyranni, qui & ipsi olim in tenebras exteriores eijcientur, viuentibus & regnantibus cum Christo pijs omnibus, quosil liin terris persecuti sunt.
units.tr: But let us hear how the Nazarenes received Christ's words, without any admonition. "All of them," says Luke, "were filled with anger in the synagogue as they heard these things." They felt themselves stung and took the words as an insult to themselves, and so they did not grow angry lightly but were roused to fury and driven into rage. Wicked men are not without ears to hear God's Word. Nor do they lack reason and understanding; they see that the matter concerns them and understand what they need to do. What they lack is a good will. Since they are wholly governed by the worst passions, they think it an intolerable injury to be told anything that runs against their desires. Yet this shows how powerful the Word of God is, since it penetrates even the minds of those whose only aim is to mock it with scornful and impious contempt. Although they speak of it with the greatest disdain and pretend that it means nothing to them, they feel something quite different inside, where they are pricked by sharp goads that make everything hostile and bitter to them. Nor do the Nazarenes merely rage. When the assembly is dismissed and they rise, they cast Christ out of the city, as one unworthy to be acknowledged any longer as a citizen and fellow townsman. Indeed, they drag him as if he were a plague on the fatherland to the brow of the hill on which the town was built, to hurl him headlong from it and destroy him by a shameful death. Impiety makes its progress in this way: those who dare to clamour against the Word of God soon, growing bolder, turn their hostility against the servants of God as well, and they do not refrain from open and unjust violence. So much more ought we to strive to resist the first stirrings of the passions and, in the spirit of gentleness, to overcome these furies of the wicked. Here, as on a painted panel, or rather as in a picture, is set before us the condition of God's ministers in this world. If they preach the Gospel plainly, they are almost laughed at. For it seems foolish to the reason of the flesh to place our hope of salvation in a crucified man, to deny the flesh with its passions, to bid farewell to the world and its friendship, and finally to leave behind for heavenly and eternal goods what lies to hand and in which a man's whole happiness is thought to consist. Therefore those who are wholly given over to the world and the flesh are little moved by this teaching. But if the ministers go further, accuse even crimes, announce God's wrath to the ungrateful and rebellious, and drag them, even unwilling, before his judgment seat, then those who seemed merely to despise the Word in passing are driven into fury and rage. Hence the savage rages of the wicked, cruel threats, bloody edicts, and even public uprisings usually arise. And it often happens that those who are the plague of their country cast out those who seek the country's welfare alone and keep watch for it day and night. So Christ's ministers often rejoice when adulterers, robbers, usurers, murderers, sacrilegious men and the most impious of all reign with impunity in the meantime, by whose crimes God's wrath is provoked every day. Yet such things should not offend the godly, since these same things once happened to Christ among those who ought to have held him in the highest regard above others. They are comforted too by the fact that they have a fatherland and a city that is lasting and stable in heaven, over which tyrants have no right. These tyrants will themselves one day be cast into outer darkness, while all the godly live and reign with Christ, and those whom they have persecuted on earth.

units.la: Cæterùm præstat videre, quid inter furentis populi conatus de Christo factum sit, quod hic Lucas narrat: Ipse transiens per medium eorum profectus est. Indicant hæc, illum non sine miraculo seruatum fuisse, cuius tamen modus non exprimitur. Cùm enim illum urbe eiecerint, cùm ad montis præcipitium duxerint, eum utiq; manibus suis tenebant, neq; aliqua in humanis spes salutis reliqua erat. Elapsus tamen est ex manibus eorum, neq; (vt de Proteo & Vertumno suo poetæ fabulantur) in aliam formam mutatus euasit, sed per medium illorum transiens profectus est quò voleBat. Diuinæ ergo virtutis hoc opus fuit, quæ eum seruauit, ne quid pateretur priusquam hora eius venisset. Sunt exempla eiusmodi probè obseruanda, ut illum postea voluntariè mortuum esse intelligamus, ut sua obedientia patris iram placaret, et iustitiam veram nobis mereretur. Admonent præterea hæc, nihil periculi metuendum esse ijs, qui in Dei vocatione ambulant. Quia enim sub Dei providentia sumus, qui et passerculos curat, & pilos capitis nostri numeratos habet, nihil nobis neq; nocere poterunt, donec fatalis illa hora (quam Christus duodecimam vocat) aduenerit, nosq; ad cursus nostri metam appropinquauerimus. Nam quod de Christo dicitur, hoc ipsum Apostolis quoq; non semel accidit, ut ex carceribus & hostium manibus mirificè seruarentur præter omnium expectationem. Ista nos confirment, ut Verbum Dei sanctè colamus, & Christum Iesum vera fide amplexi officium faciamus, neque dubitemus eum nobis affuturum esse, ut euitato mundi huius infelicis præcipitio, ad ipsum in cœlestis patriæ sedes colligamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth seeing what was done to Christ amid the attempts of the raging people, as Luke relates here: "But he, passing through the midst of them, went on his way." These words show that he was preserved without a miracle, though the manner is not expressed. For when they had thrown him out of the city and led him to the brink of the hill, they surely had him in their hands, and no human hope of rescue remained. Yet he slipped from their hands, and he did not escape by being changed into another form, as the poets fable of their Proteus and Vertumnus, but passed through the midst of them and went on his way whither he willed. This was therefore the work of divine power, which kept him safe so that he would suffer nothing before his hour had come. Such examples are to be carefully observed, so that we may understand that he afterwards died willingly, to appease the Father's wrath by his obedience and to merit for us true righteousness. These things also warn us that those who walk in their calling from God need fear no danger. For since we are under God's providence, who cares even for the sparrows and has the hairs of our heads numbered, nothing can harm us until that fated hour, which Christ calls the twelfth, has come and we have drawn near to the goal of our course. For what is said of Christ also happened more than once to the apostles, who were marvellously preserved from prisons and from the hands of enemies beyond all expectation. Let these things strengthen us, so that we may honour God's Word reverently, embrace Christ Jesus with true faith and do our duty, and not doubt that he will be present with us, so that, having escaped the headlong fall of this unhappy world, we may be gathered to him in the seats of our heavenly fatherland. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Et descendit in Capernaum vrbem Galilææ, ibiq; docebat eos Sabbatis. Et perculebantur super doctrina eius: erat enim sermo ipsius cum authoritate. Erat autem in Synagoga quidam habens spiritum dæmoniacum impurum, qui exclamauit voce magna, dicens, Ah, quid nobis tecum Iesu Nazarene? Venisti vt perdas nos? Noui te quis sis, nimirum Sanctus ille Dei. Et obiurgauit eum Iesus dicens: Obmutesce, & exi ab eo. Tunc dæmonium, abiecto illo in medium, exijt ab eo, nihilq; ei nocuit. Et obortus est pauor in omnibus, & colloquebantur inter se, dicentes: Quid hoc rei est? Quia cum authoritate & potestate imperat immundis spiritibus, & exeunt. Et peruenit rumor de eo in omnem locum circumiacentis regionis.
units.tr: And he came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the Sabbaths. And they were astonished at his doctrine, for his word was with authority. Now in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean devil spirit, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying: "Ah, what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, that holy one of God." And Jesus rebuked him, saying: "Be silent, and come out of him." Then the demon, throwing the man into the midst, came out of him and did him no harm. And amazement seized them all, and they talked among themselves, saying: "What is this matter? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out." And the report of him went out into every place of the surrounding region.

units.la: Ioannes Apostolus & Euangelista de filio Dei in carne manifestato differēs, illum in sua venisse, & à suis autem non receptum fuisse scribit. Quod etsi de tota Iudæorum gente verisimè dicatur, praealijs tamen se ingratos & crudeles præbuerunt Nazarethani, inter quos ille educatus fuerat. His enim non factis fuit doctrina eius contempsisse, sed insuper cum ab eo liberius admonerentur, in rabie acti, illum vrbe eiecerunt, & de rupe præcipitem dare conati sunt. Describuntur hæc in eum finem, vt primo non offendamur, si quid huius etiam hodie Euangelij eius ministris accidit; deinde vt exemplo illius discamus, quid tunc nobis facto sit opus. Et huc magna ex parte pertinent, quæ modo recitauimus. Narrat enim Lucas, quid fecerit Christus, vbi à Nazarethanis digressus est, & quanto cum successu euangelium, quod illi non minus ignominiose quam hostiliter retulerant, alibi prædicarit.
units.tr: The Apostle and Evangelist John, speaking of the Son of God manifested in the flesh, writes that he came to his own, and that his own did not receive him. Although this may truly be said of the whole nation of the Jews, the Nazarenes showed themselves especially ungrateful and cruel towards him, among whom he had been brought up. For they did not merely despise his teaching when it was set before them, but when he admonished them more freely, they were driven into rage, cast him out of the city, and tried to hurl him headlong from the cliff. These things are recorded for this end: first, that we should not be offended if something of this kind happens even today to the ministers of his Gospel; and second, that by his example we may learn what we ought to do then. And what we have just recited pertains largely to this. For Luke tells what Christ did when he withdrew from the Nazarenes, and with how much success he preached the Gospel elsewhere, which they had rejected no less shamefully than hostilely.

units.la: Et primo quidem, quò se receperit, indicatur. Descendit (inquit) in Capernaum, vrbem Galilææ, ibiq; docebat eos Sabbatis. Est hoc memorabile bonitatis et mansuetudinis diuinæ exemplum. Nam digni erant Nazarethani, qui graues pœnas darent. Si enim (vt Christus alibi monet) Sodomæ & Gomorrhæis grauius punientur in die iudicij, quotquot homines euangelij prædones reijciunt: quo nō supplicio digni erunt, qui ipsum Dei Filium cum verbo suo extinguere conantur? Et extant passim exempla horrenda in eos edita, qui Dei seruos aut legatos violare ausi sunt. Facile etiam erat Christo de illis pœnas sumere. Qui enim totam cohortem, quæ ad ipsum capiendum missa fuerat, vno verbulo prosternere potuit, hic quoq; ingratam & crudelem vrbem abs q; labore & negotio funditus euertere, aut eius ciues quocunq; supplicij genere punire potuisset. At non ad perdendum, sed ad seruandum venerat: neq; tunc vindicta dies erat; sed acceptum illud tempus, quo Deus peccatores in gratiam recipere, & promissam salutem mundo offerre decreuerat. Ideo vindictam Deo patri permittens, ipse in officio pergit, & relictis hominibus indignissimis, alios quærit, quos maiori cum fructu doceat. Est hoc exemplum multa obseruatione dignissimum. Eo enim omnes admonentur, minimè deserendam esse vocationem, cui nos Deus destinauit, propter nonnullorum ingratitudinem: neq; spectandum semper, quid mereantur ij, quibus cum nobis res est, sed quid nos facere conueniat.
units.tr: And first, the place to which he withdrew is indicated: "He came down," it says, "to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the Sabbaths." This is a memorable example of divine goodness and gentleness. For the Nazarenes deserved to suffer severe punishment. For if (as Christ warns elsewhere) it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for all who reject the preachers of the Gospel, what punishment will they deserve who try to extinguish with their word the very Son of God? Horrible examples have been published everywhere against those who have dared to violate God's servants or messengers. It would also have been easy for Christ to take vengeance on them. For he who could overthrow with a single word the whole band sent to seize him could have destroyed utterly, without labour or trouble, that ungrateful and cruel city, or could have punished its citizens by whatever kind of punishment he chose. But he had not come to destroy but to save; nor was it then the day of vengeance, but the accepted time, in which God had decided to receive sinners into favour and to offer the promised salvation to the world. Therefore, leaving vengeance to God the Father, he himself goes on with his task, and, leaving the most unworthy men, seeks others whom he may teach with greater fruit. This example is most worthy of careful notice. For by it all are reminded that the calling to which God has appointed us must by no means be abandoned because of the ingratitude of some; nor should we always consider what those deserve with whom we have to do, but what it is fitting for us to do.

units.la: Pertinet doctrina hæc ad omnis loci et ordinis homines. Nam qui rempub. administrat, si in suo munere fideles & diligentes sint, mox non ingratos modò, verumetiam rebelles & seditiosos aduersus se sentient eos, pro quorum salute ipsi dies & noctes excubant. Accidit hoc olim Mosi, quem non semel conuitijs grauissimis prosciderunt Israelitæ, imò lapidibus obruere conati sunt, in quorum gratiam ipse aulam Ægyptiacam & honores amplissimos reliquerat. Quid Dauidi euenerit post mille bellorum discrimina & labores pro publica salute infinitos, ex historia sacra & Psalmis eius notius est, quàm vt multa commemoratione opus habeat. Fuit eadem Ezechiæ et Iosiæ sors, quorum vterq; parùm fidos habuit eos, quorum consilijs maximè vtebatur, & hi deinde populum infelicem ad rebellionem excitabat. In exteris verò historijs exempla huius generis multa occurrunt, vt vere dici possit, apud omnes fere gentes nullos indignius & iniquius tractatos fuisse omnibus seculis, quàm eos, quorum maxima in rempub. merita extiterunt. Et quid hodie optimi quiq; patiantur, non sine maximo animi dolore omnes boni vident. At non debent hæc viros prudentes mouere, vt propterea rempub. deserere, et populi ad interitum ruentis improbitati indulgere velint. Vt enim non probabitur nauclerus, qui
units.tr: This teaching applies to men of every place and rank. For whoever administers the commonwealth, if he is faithful and diligent in his office, will soon find that those for whose safety he watches day and night are not only ungrateful but also rebellious and seditious against him. This happened once to Moses, whom the Israelites more than once assailed with the most grievous reproaches, and even tried to stone, though he had left the Egyptian court and its very great honours for their sake. What befell David, after a thousand dangers of war and endless labours for the public safety, is better known from sacred history and his Psalms than it needs much recounting. Ezekiah and Josiah had the same fate: each had little trust in those whose counsel he used most, and these men then stirred up the unhappy people to rebellion. In foreign histories many examples of this kind occur, so that it can truly be said that among almost all nations, in every age, none have been treated more unworthily and unjustly than those whose greatest services were rendered to the commonwealth. And what the best men suffer today, all good people see with the greatest grief. But these things ought not to move wise men to desert the commonwealth and to indulge the wickedness of a people rushing to ruin. For just as no one would approve of a pilot who,

units.la: rus, quis rius, qui propter vectores aliquos immodestius se gerentes a gubernaculo discedit, nauim̃ q̃ tota pe rire sinit: Ita neq; sibi ipsis neq; communi patriæ fidelis fuerit, qui populi improbitate & ingratitudine se superari sinit, vt remp. exitio proximam deferat. Tunc potius consilio vtendum est, & remis ma xime incumbendum, vt si omnino naufragium facere oportet, saltem aliquos illi seruent, & suâ fidem apud omnes liberent. Cogitent hoc ipsum sibi etiam dici verbi præcones & ecclesiarum ministri. Referunt hi quoq; pessimâ gratiam ab ijs, quorum saluti vnicè cupiunt consultum; & de hoc non semel illos Christus admonuit. Sed non ideo ab ecclesiæ ministerio discedere, sed potius cum mundi ingratitudine luctari conuenit, vt nos Deo simul & illis fidos præbeamus, qui nobis maximè aduersantur. Fecerunt hoc incredibili constantia prophetæ, quorum aliqui annis amplius quinquaginta sæpius hoc voluerunt in ingratissima Iudæorum gente, ex qua nihil præter conuicia, iniurias et cædes indignas sperare poterant. Inter quos laudem peculiarem meretur Ieremias, qui post captam vrbem cum pauperum reliquijs manere maluit, quàm in Babylone promissis sibi honoribus frui. Imò cum ijdem obstinata contumacia in Ægyptum descenderent, illis se committem præbuit, ne infelices doctrina verbi omnino destituerentur. Et Christi exemplum Apostoli magno studio secuti sunt, qui nullis iniurijs vinci potuerunt, vt à Christo creditam stationem desererent. Certe vt vnum Paulum videamus, quid ille non passus est ab Iudæis, quos vbiq; terrarum hostes infestissimos reperit? Idem tamen nihilominus semper in illorum Synagogas diuertit, & quàmuis gentibus in primis Apostolus destinatus esset, illis tamen primùm vbiq; Christum prædicauit, si qua ratione ex infelici illo gentis totius naufragio aliquas reliquias (vt Prophetæ olim prædixerant) saluas faceret. Eodem zelo & studio omnes ardere conuenit, qui in ecclesiæ ministerio versantur. Cur enim mundi ingratitudine abstterreantur, qui non mundo, sed Deo seruiunt? Vel cur ipsi officium deserendo eos imitentur, quorum contumaciam & ingratitudinem detestantur? De his vtinam diligentius cogitarent, qui hodie ecclesias totas deserunt, in quibus aliquos morum disciplinæ audacius resistere, & alia multa præter decorum fieri vident. At si idem olim Christus et Apostoli fecissent, quas obsecro illi nobis dedissent ecclesias? Alia tamen eorum ratio est, qui doctrinæ veritatis sese hostiliter opponunt, & verbi præcones violenter eijciunt: de quibus suo loco & tempore dicemus.
units.tr: because of certain passengers behaving too wantonly, leaves the helm and lets the ship go down entirely, so neither is he faithful to himself nor to his common country who allows himself to be overcome by the wickedness and ingratitude of the people, so that he hands the commonwealth over to near destruction. Rather, in such a case, counsel must be used and the oars pulled with the greatest effort, so that, if shipwreck must in any case occur, at least some are saved and he frees himself from blame in the eyes of all. Let the preachers of the Word and the ministers of the Church consider that this same thing is said to them as well. They too often receive the worst return from those whose salvation they desire above all, and Christ warned them of this more than once.
