But they ought not on that account to withdraw from the ministry of the Church; rather they should struggle against the ingratitude of the world, so that we may prove ourselves faithful both to God and to those who oppose us most. The prophets did this with incredible constancy; some of them, for more than fifty years, persisted in this course among the most ungrateful Jewish nation, from which they could hope for nothing but reproaches, injuries and unworthy slaughter. Among them Jeremiah deserves special praise, who after the city was taken preferred to remain with the remnant of the poor rather than enjoy the honours promised him in Babylon. Indeed, when the same people, in stubborn obstinacy, went down into Egypt, he offered himself to them so that they would not be utterly deprived of the teaching of the Word. The Apostles also followed Christ's example with great zeal; no injuries could overcome them so that they abandoned the post entrusted to them by Christ. Indeed, to look at Paul alone, what did he not suffer from the Jews, whom he found to be his most bitter enemies everywhere on earth? Yet nonetheless he always turned aside into their synagogues, and although the Apostle was chiefly appointed to the Gentiles, he nevertheless first preached Christ to them everywhere, if by any means he might save some remnants from that unhappy shipwreck of the whole nation (as the prophets had foretold long before). All who serve in the ministry of the Church ought to burn with this same zeal and eagerness. For why should those be frightened by the ingratitude of the world who serve not the world but God? Or why should they, by deserting their office, imitate those whose obstinacy and ingratitude they detest? I wish those who today abandon whole churches, in which they see some men resisting the discipline of morals too boldly and many other things done contrary to propriety, would think more carefully about these matters. But if Christ and the Apostles had done the same thing in former times, what churches, I ask, would they have given us? The case is different, however, for those who set themselves hostilely against the doctrine of truth and violently cast out the preachers of the Word; of these we will speak in their proper place and time.

units.la: Nunc duo nobis consideranda veniunt, quæ ad huius loci nostri tractationem pertinent. Primum est locus, quo Christus diuertit, vt doceret. Fuit is ciuitas Capernaum, quam non procul ab ostio Iordanis lacum Tiberiadis ingredientis sitam, & proinde ob loci commoditatem hominum frequentia & negotiorum commercijs celeberrima fuisse constat. Delegerat eam sibi iam antea Christus & tam illi familiarem sese præbuit, vt à Matthæo ciuitas Domini dicatur. Fecit hoc ille certo consilio: primum quidem, vt doctrinæ & miraculorum eius fama citius & latius vulgaretur ad finitima loca: deinde verò, vt vrbi multis vitijs laboranti medicinam in tempore afferret. Scimus enim in vrbibus frequentioribus ferè mores corruptissimos esse, dum & peregrini eò confluentes quotidie nouum quid atq; insolens important, & diuitiæ luxui & libidini materiam vberrimam ministrant. Est hoc ingens bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui homines saluos fieri cupit, & ideo salutis doctrinâ longè lateq; propagari curat. Ex eadem enim causa factum est, quòd Hierosolymam quoq; Christus frequentauit, & plerunq; festis celebrioribus interfuit, vt plures per ipsum instituerentur. Obseruatu idem postea quoq;, quando Apostolos in vrbes totius orbis celeberrimas deduxit, & in illis ecclesias constituit, ex quibus Euangelij doctrina in viciniam totam disseminaretur: quales fuerunt Antiochia, Ephesus, Corinthus, Athenæ, & rerum domina Roma, vbi ecclesiam longè clarissimam fuisse Paulus testatur. Et hodie passim illustriores vrbes et populi, qui nostro seculo Euangelij doctrinæ primum hospitium præbuerunt. Nam est quidem hæc non vulgaris dignitas, sed quia eadem non ex hominum meritis, sed Dei gratia dependet, durabilis esse non potest, nisi hanc gratiam animis agnoscamus.
units.tr: Two things now come before us for consideration, which pertain to the treatment of this passage. The first is the place to which Christ turned aside in order to teach. This was the city of Capernaum, which lies not far from the mouth of the Jordan where it enters the Lake of Tiberias, and therefore, because of the convenience of its position, is well known to have been very busy with crowds of people and the trade of commerce. Christ had already chosen it for himself, and showed himself so familiar with it that by Matthew it is called "his own city." He did this for a definite purpose: first, so that the fame of his teaching and miracles might spread more quickly and widely to the neighbouring places; and then, so that he might bring timely medicine to a city suffering from many vices. For we know that in the more crowded cities morals are generally most corrupt, since strangers flocking there every day bring in something new and unusual, and wealth supplies abundant material for luxury and lust. This is a great proof of the goodness of God, who wishes men to be saved and therefore takes care that the teaching of salvation be spread far and wide. For for the same reason it came about that Christ also frequented Jerusalem and was often present at the more celebrated feasts, so that more people might be instructed through him. The same thing may be observed later as well, when he led the Apostles into the most famous cities of the whole world and established churches in them, from which the doctrine of the Gospel might be spread throughout the whole neighbourhood; such were Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth, Athens, and Rome, the mistress of the world, where Paul testifies that the church was by far the most illustrious. And today too there are everywhere the more notable cities and peoples which in our age have first offered a welcome to the doctrine of the Gospel. For this dignity is indeed not a common one, but because it depends not on the merits of men but on the grace of God, it cannot be lasting unless we acknowledge this grace in our hearts.

units.la: Matth. 11.
units.tr: Matth. 11.

units.la: Alterum, quod hic obseruemus, felix ille successus est, quo inter docendum Christus est vsus: Per- cellebantur (inquit) super doctrina eius. Ergo non obiter modo admirati sunt eius eximiā in docen- do facultatem, verumetiam totis animis perculsi sunt, eo quod in eius concionibus aliquid humano captu maius & sublimius sentirent. Estq; hæc rerum vicissitudo admirabilis, quod eum cum reueren- tia magna admirantur & suscipiunt Capernaitæ, diuitijs & multo rerum vsu celebres, quem Na- zarethani mortalium in tota Galilæa contemptissimi tam indignis modis reiecerant. Ita nunquam suis deest Deus, si quam hic illis imposuit, functionem bona fide obeant: neq; ei difficile est; illic etiam successum dare felicissimum, vbi minime speres. Sic olim apud Niniuitas multo cum fructu Ionas prædicauit, qui apud Israelitas, vt & reliqui prophetæ, contemptissimus fuerat. Et apud Babylonios maximum verbi Dei effectum fuisse scimus, qui paulo ante templum cum toto Dei cultu euerterant. Et in nouo Testamento inter Samaritanos & gentes ostium Euangelij Deus aperuit Apostolis, cum à Iudæis improbe reiecerentur. Debent exempla ista pios confirmare, ne de Ecclesia & Euan- gelio actum putent, si eos hostili in illud animo esse videant, qui præ alijs crediturii videbantur. Nec enim vlli loco aut genti alligatus est spiritus Domini, & vt pluuia nunquam omni effectu caret, quamuis ea rupes & loca innumera emolliri non possint: ita non deerunt, qui Euangelium cum fru- ctu audiant, etiamsi multorum impietas incurabilis maneat.
units.tr: The second thing we notice here is the happy success that Christ had while teaching: they were astonished (it says) at his teaching. So they did not merely marvel in passing at his remarkable ability in teaching, but were struck with their whole minds, because in his sermons they perceived something greater and more sublime than human understanding could grasp. And this reversal of fortunes is remarkable: the Capernaites, famous for their wealth and their wide experience of affairs, receive him with great reverence and admiration, while the Nazarenes, the most despised of mortals in all Galilee, had rejected him in so unworthy a manner. Thus God is never wanting to his people, if they faithfully perform the function he has laid upon them here; nor is it difficult for him to give the most happy success even where you least expect it. So long ago Jonah preached among the Ninevites with great fruit, though among the Israelites he had been most despised, as had the other prophets. And we know that the Word of God had its greatest effect among the Babylonians, who had shortly before overthrown the temple together with the whole worship of God. And in the New Testament God opened the door of the Gospel to the Apostles among the Samaritans and the Gentiles, when they were wickedly rejected by the Jews. These examples ought to strengthen the godly, so that they do not think the Church and the Gospel are finished if they see those who seemed most likely to believe bearing a hostile mind towards it. For the Spirit of the Lord is bound to no place or nation; and just as the rain never lacks effect, although countless rocks and places cannot be softened by it, so there will not be lacking those who hear the Gospel with fruit, even though the unbelief of many remains incurable.

units.la: Porrò causa indicatur, quæ Capernaitas mouit, vt Christi doctrinam tanti fecerint. Erat enim (inquit Lucas) sermo ipsius cum authoritate. Quem locum Marcus collatione clarius illustrat, di- cens: Docebat enim tanquam authoritate præditus, & non vt Scribæ. Authoritatis nomine vis quæ- dam & maiestas singularis notatur, quæ Christi doctrinam auditoribus commendabat, vt eam à scribarum concionibus multùm differre viderent. Etenim non aliud quàm Dei verbum Christus do- cebat, vt verissimè posset dicere: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed eius qui misit me: Scribæ autem hu- manas traditiones vrgebant, quarum obseruatio in externo fuco consistebat, & ipsis erat quæstuosa. Christus non de sua, sed patris gloria solicitus, hoc vnum agebat, vt veram huius cognitionem atq; cultu apud omnes propagaret: At Scribæ, vilissimæ ambitionis mancipia, in hoc erant, vt sibi apud rude vulgus authoritatem pararent, & eam faste quodam externo & falsa sanctitatis specie vana bantur. Christum salutis humanæ studium ardens vrgebat, vt nulli occasioni deesset, qua aliquos seu- uari posse videbat: Scribæ vero populum ouium instar absq; pastore palantium facile negligebant, modo ipsorum existimationi & quæstui nihil decederet. Christus inter docendum animos hominum penetrabat, & in ijs spiritus virtute efficaciter operabatur: Sed scribæ solas auditorum aures sua- rum traditionum commemoratione demulcebant. Præterea suam doctrinam Christus non miraculis modo, verumetiam totius vitæ exemplo confirmabat, adeo vt in illo viuum veritatis et sanctitatis exemplar eluceret. E contra Scribæ titulis inanibus turgidi, sua auaritia, ambitione, intemperan- tia & omni alio vitiorum genere optimos quosq; offendebant. Itaq; non difficile erat inter hos & il- lum discernere, & in Christo relucentem spiritus virtutem obseruare.
units.tr: Next, the cause is indicated that moved the people of Capernaum to esteem Christ's teaching so highly. For (Luke says) "his word was with authority." Mark illustrates this passage more clearly when he compares it, saying: "For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." The word authority signals a certain power and singular majesty, which commended Christ's teaching to his hearers, so that they saw it differed greatly from the sermons of the scribes. Indeed Christ taught nothing other than the word of God, so that he could truly say: "My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me." The scribes, however, pressed human traditions, whose observance consisted in outward show and was profitable to themselves. Christ, anxious not for his own glory but for the Father's, did this one thing: he spread among all the true knowledge and worship of God. The scribes, slaves of the basest ambition, were intent on winning authority for themselves among the uneducated crowd, and they boasted of it with a certain outward pomp and the false appearance of holiness. Christ was driven by an ardent zeal for human salvation, so that he left no opportunity unused by which he saw that some might be saved. The scribes, on the other hand, readily neglected the people, who wandered like sheep without a shepherd, provided nothing was lost to their own reputation and gain. Christ, while teaching, penetrated men's hearts and worked effectively in them by the power of the Spirit; but the scribes only soothed their hearers' ears by recounting their traditions. Moreover, Christ confirmed his doctrine not only by miracles but also by the example of his whole life, so that a living pattern of truth and holiness shone forth in him. By contrast, the scribes, puffed up with empty titles, offended all the best people by their avarice, ambition, intemperance and every other kind of vice. So it was not difficult to distinguish between them and him, and to observe in Christ the shining power of the Spirit.

units.la: Admonent ista verbi ministros, quæ optima ratio sit parandi & seruandi authoritatem, qua illis omnino opus est, siquidē cum aliquo fructu creditum sibi munus obire velint. Et audiuntur pas- sim querelæ de collapsa ministrorū authoritate, & de totius ordinis ecclesiastici contemptu. At quid aliud fiat, quando paucissimos est videre, qui officium serio faciant, plerique autem hominum poten- tum fauorem & auram popularem gloriæ Dei atq; auditorum saluti longè præferunt? Fit ergo, vt verbi Dei minus recte secetur, doctrina tota langueat, & simul æmulatione & contentionibus aper- tis scindantur, qui coniunctis viribus mundi & huius principe oppugnare debebant. Itaq; iure con- temnuntur, qui de sua functione tam turpiter sentiunt, & seipsos studijs mundi huius vanissimis pro- phanant. Quod de verbi ministris dicimus, hoc ipsum ad eos quoq; pertinet, qui magistratu gerūt. Nam horum quoq; authoritas tunc demum salua erit, si Deum sui muneris authore esse intelligant, huius gloriam prouehant, leges bonas tueantur, & procul relicto priuati commodi studio publica po- puli totius salutem vnicè quærant, deniq; omnia sua secundum Dei voluntatem instituant, quà hic in lege sua manifestauit. Idem parentes quoq; ad liberorum institutionem, obseruare conuenit. Nisi ipsi de artibus authoritate sua, qua eos natura donauit, tueantur, nihil vnquam laude dignū efficient.
units.tr: These things admonish the ministers of the Word what the best way is of acquiring and keeping the authority they absolutely need, if they wish to discharge the office entrusted to them with any fruit. And everywhere complaints are heard about the collapse of the ministers' authority and the contempt for the whole ecclesiastical order. But what else should one expect, when we see very few who carry out their duty seriously, while most put the favour of the powerful and popular applause far above the glory of God and the salvation of their hearers? The result is that the word of God is handled less correctly, all teaching grows feeble, and those who ought to be attacking the world and its prince with united strength tear themselves apart by open rivalry and quarrels. Therefore they rightly be despised who think so basely of their function and profane themselves by the most worthless pursuits of this world. What we say of the ministers of the Word applies equally to those who hold magistracy. For their authority too will be safe only if they understand that God is the author of their office, if they advance his glory, if they protect good laws, and if, putting aside the pursuit of private advantage, they seek solely the public safety of the whole people, and finally order all their affairs according to the will of God, which he has made known in his law. The same holds for parents in the upbringing of their children. Unless they guard by their own authority the skills that nature has given them, they will never achieve anything worthy of praise.

units.la: Sed ad Christū redeamus, qui cum Capernaitas æquiores suæ doctrinæ æstimatores esse videret, eam miraculis quoq; pluribus confirmat. Inter quæ primum fuit hominis dæmoniaci liberatio. Præmisit hanc aliis miraculis, ut publicè testaretur, se promissum illud mulieris semè esse, cuius officium sit serpentis veteris caput conterere & homines infelices ex eius tyrannide vindicare. Versatur in huius cognitione tota salutis nostræ ratio. Et quia miser iste communis omnium nostrum typus est, & non alia ratione nos redimi oportet, quàm qua hunc liberatum fuisse Evangelistæ narrant, non tam mere in historiæ huius descriptione illi tam diligentes sunt. Continet enim illa ceu in tabula depictum hostis nostri Satanæ ingenium, & quæ nostra sit sub huius tyrannide conditio. Deinde divinam Christi potentiam & per hunc nobis exhibitum redemptionis nostræ beneficium adumbrat. Docet præterea, quid eos facere deceat, qui salutificam Christi virtutem experti sunt. Timent huius miraculi ipsi factores, & in Christo virtutem humana maiorem agnoscunt, remq; omnem ad alios divulgant. At quia de his omnibus in Marco nostro prolixè & ex ordine diximus, minimè opus est superuacanea eorundem repetitione Lectores obtundere. Nostrum fuerit immensam Dei bonitatem agnoscere, quam in Christo Iesu nobis exhibuit. Hunc autem fide vera amplectamur, & per hunc præstiti beneficii memores libertatem nostram constanter tueamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who, seeing that the people of Capernaum were fairer judges of his doctrine, confirmed it also with many miracles. Among these the first was the deliverance of a demoniac. He placed this before the other miracles so that he might openly bear witness that he is the promised seed of the woman, whose task is to crush the head of the old serpent and to rescue unhappy men from his tyranny. The whole reckoning of our salvation turns on the knowledge of this. And because this wretched man is a common type of all of us, and we ought to be redeemed in no other way than that by which the Evangelists tell that he was freed, they are not merely careful in describing this history. For it contains, as if painted on a tablet, the nature of our enemy Satan and what our condition is under his tyranny. Then it sets forth the divine power of Christ and the benefit of our redemption exhibited to us through him. It also teaches what those ought to do who have experienced the saving power of Christ. The very doers of this miracle are afraid, and they acknowledge in Christ a power greater than human, and they spread the matter abroad to others. But since we have spoken about all these things at length and in order in our homily on Mark, there is no need to weary the readers with the needless repetition of the same. Let it be our part to acknowledge the immense goodness of God, which he has shown us in Jesus Christ. Let us embrace him with true faith, and, mindful of the benefit bestowed through him, let us constantly guard our liberty. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLV.
units.tr: HOMILY XLV.

units.la: Cum surrexisset autem Iesus è Synagoga, introiuit domum Simonis, socrus autem Simonis detinebatur febri magna, & rogauerunt eum pro illa. Et ille astans super illam, obiurgauit febrim, & febris eam dimisit: Illa verò cum illico surrexisset, ministrauit eis. Occidente autem Sole, omnes qui habebant ægrotantes morbis variis, ducebat eos ad ipsum: Ille verò vnicuique ipsorum impositis manibus, sanauit eos. Exibant autem etiam dæmonia ex multis, clamantia & dicentia, Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei. Sed ipse obiurgans, non sinebat ea loqui, quod scirent ipsum esse Christum. Orto autem die egressus profectus est in desertum locum: & turba quærebat eum, venerunt{que} usque ad ipsum, & retinebant ipsum ne ab ipsis discederet. Ille verò dixit eis: Certè etiam aliis urbibus oportet me euangelizare regnum Dei; nam ad hoc missus sum. Et prædicabat in Synagogis Galilææ.
units.tr: When Jesus had risen up and left the synagogue, he entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was held by a great fever, and they asked him on her behalf. He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and the fever left her. She immediately rose and served them. When the sun was setting, all who had sick people suffering from various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on each one and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, "You are the Christ, the Son of God." But he rebuked them and would not let them speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. At daybreak he went out and departed to a desert place. The crowd sought him, came to him and tried to keep him from leaving them. But he said to them, "I must preach the kingdom of God in other cities also, for I was sent for this purpose." And he preached in the synagogues of Galilee.

units.la: Via Iesus Christus æternum Dei verbum esset, doctrinam eius neq; hominum authoritate, neq; miraculis aut signis confirmari necesse fuit. Idem tamen propter nos illi signa omnis generis coniunxit, partim quidem, ut tardiores excitaret, & in fide confirmaret: partim ut impijs & prophanis sui nominis contemptoribus omne excusationis prætextum eriperet. Et hæc etiam causa est, quòd non ut Magi præstigiatores solent, miracula ad nudam atq; inanem ostentationem composita ædidit: sed eiusmodi, quibus & in præsenti magna utilitas coniuncta erat, & quæ illius virtute atq; fine sui in carne aduentus euidentissimè depingunt. Vidimus hoc nuper in liberatione hominis dæmoniaci, quem impurus spiritus miserè exagitauit. Ea enim docuit Christus se promissum illum vindicè esse, qui ut diaboli opera destrueret in mundum venerit, nosq; in libertate filiorum Dei vindicaret. Huic in præsenti alia Lucas subiicit, inter quæ proximū à priori locum merito habet, quo Petri socrus ardentissima febri liberata est. Hac enim innata nobis naturæ vitiositas notatur, quæ ex primò parente in nos propagata, hominem totum desiderijs noxijs inflammat, & ad omne boni opus tardos atq; imbecilles reddit. Parit eadem ex se omnis generis peccata actualia (ut vocant) quorum typus in variis illis morbis habetur, quorum hic mentionem facit Euangelista. Ita verò offendit, Christum humani generis vindicè esse perfectissimū, in quo salutem omnibus numeris absoluta consequamur. Nam ut hostē nostrum commune debellauit, regnumq; eius destruxit: ita naturæ etiā corruptæ medetur, et quæcunq; ex hac protuberant peccata, suæ mortis merito plenè expiat. Neq; in iuuandō difficilè se præbet, sed salutifero suæ incarnationis attactu omnes eos dignatur, quicunq; ad ipsum contendunt, ut in eo salutem inueniant. Diximus de his aliquanto fusius in Marci expositione, at quia
units.tr: Although Jesus Christ was the eternal Word of God, his teaching did not need to be confirmed by human authority, or by miracles and signs. Yet for our sake he nevertheless joined signs of every kind to it: partly to rouse the slower sort and strengthen them in faith, and partly to take from the impious and profane despisers of his name every pretext for excuse. This is also why he did not perform miracles in the manner of the Magi and charlatans, which are contrived for bare and empty display. Rather, they were of such a kind that great benefit was joined to them in the present, and they most clearly portray his power and the purpose of his coming in the flesh. We saw this lately in the liberation of the demoniac man whom an unclean spirit cruelly tormented. For by it Christ showed that he is the promised deliverer who came into the world to destroy the works of the devil and to vindicate us in the liberty of the sons of God. Luke next adds other things to this, among which the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, who was freed from a burning fever, rightly has the place next to the previous one. For this signifies the inborn corruption of our nature, which, propagated in us from our first parent, inflames the whole man with harmful desires and makes him sluggish and feeble for every good work. The same corruption begets from itself every kind of actual sin (as they are called), whose type is found in those various diseases which the Evangelist here mentions. Thus it is clear that Christ is the most perfect deliverer of the human race, in whom we obtain salvation complete in every respect. For just as he has overcome our common enemy and destroyed his kingdom, so he also heals corrupted nature, and fully expiates by the merit of his death whatever sins spring from it. Nor is he hard to help, but by the saving touch of his incarnation he deigns to receive all who come to him, that they may find salvation in him. We have spoken of these things somewhat more fully in the exposition of Mark, but because

units.la: Marcus Hom. 13. & 14. singulis circunstantijs multa insunt, de quibus nos sæpius admoneri prodest, non grave nobis debet videri, si hic quoq; summa rerum capita perstringamus.
units.tr: Many things are contained in the individual circumstances in Mark's Homilies 13 and 14, about which it is profitable for us to be reminded often. It ought not to seem burdensome to us if here too we touch on the main heads of the matter.

units.la: Primum a loco exorsus rei gestæ occasionem Lucas narrat, dicens: Cum surrexisset autem Iesus e Synagoga, introiuit domum Simonis, socrus autem Simonis detinebatur febri magna, & rogauerunt eum pro illa. Descripta fuit prius Simonis & Andreæ fratris vocatio, & hi omnibus relictis Christum secuti esse dicti sunt. Nunc & domus Simeonis mentio fit, in quam cum Christo, vt propriam, diuertit, & socrus, quæ ipsum vxoratum quoque fuisse ostendit. Obseruari hæc debent, vt quomodo Apostoli omnia sua reliquerint, intelligamus: nëue audiamus vel Monachos hypocritas, vel errones Anabaptistas, qui temere relictis coniugibus & liberis, sub religionis prætextu vagantur, & ex alieno viuunt. Nihil enim huius Apostoli fecerunt, qui & reculis suis pie vsi sunt, & familiæ suæ curam gesserunt, quoad hoc facere licuit per functionem illam Euangelicam, cui illos Christus destinauerat. Imò cum ab ascensione Domini in orbem terrarum ipsos dispergi oporteret vt Euangelium passim prædicarent, tunc quoque vxores suas secum circunduxerunt, neque sub religionis aut ministerij Apostolici prætextu violandum siue abrumpendum esse putarunt sacrosanctum illud coniugij vinculum, de quo Christum pronunciauisse sciebant: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne dirimat. Teste m horum habemus Paulum, qui in priori ad Corinth. hoc illos non solum fecisse, sed iure fecisse docet, ac sibi idem licere probat. Sufficit ergo exemplum istud confutandis tam fanaticis illis cum Reipub. tum rei domesticæ turbatoribus, quàm superstitiosis, vel potius impuris cælibatus defensoribus, qui dum Ecclesiarum ministris coniugio interdixerunt, fortandi licentiam inuexerunt, quæ vt mores publicos corrupit, ita Christianam religionem Iudæus & Turcis suspectam fecit, & ludibrio expos uit.
units.tr: First, beginning from the place, Luke relates the occasion of the event, saying: "When Jesus had risen up and left the synagogue, he entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was held by a great fever, and they asked him on her behalf." Earlier the calling of Simon and his brother Andrew was described, and these two are said to have followed Christ after leaving everything. Now mention is made of Simon's house, into which Christ went as into his own, and of the mother-in-law, which shows that he was also married. These things should be noted so that we understand how the apostles left all that they had; and so that we do not listen to either hypocritical monks or the errant Anabaptists, who rashly abandon their wives and children and wander about under the pretext of religion, living at others' expense. For these apostles did nothing of the kind: they made proper use of their own property and looked after their families, as far as this was lawful within that evangelical office to which Christ had appointed them. Indeed, after the Lord's ascension, when they had to be scattered throughout the world to preach the gospel everywhere, they still took their wives about with them, and they did not think that the sacred bond of marriage, which they knew Christ had pronounced, "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder," should be violated or broken under the pretext of religion or the apostolic ministry. We have Paul as witness to this, who in his first letter to the Corinthians teaches that they not only did this but did so rightly, and proves that he himself has the same liberty. This example is therefore sufficient to refute those fanatics who disturb both the commonwealth and domestic affairs, and also the superstitious, or rather impure, defenders of celibacy. By forbidding marriage to the ministers of the churches, they introduced licence to fornicate, which has corrupted public morals and, in the same way, made the Christian religion suspect to Jews and Turks and exposed it to mockery.

units.la: Exhibetur præterea hic familiæ piæ & verè Christianæ exemplum. Non amplas fuisse Petri fortunas satis constat. Idem tamen Christum secum domum deducit, neque eius comitatu abstinere tur, quem is numerosum habebat. Neque ideo reliqui domestici murmurant. Est hoc euidens pietatis testimonium, & quòd sua omnia Christo eiusque membris impartire ipsis non graue fuerit. Charitatis autem est, quòd fratres duo, & fortassis vterque vxorati, simul habitant: quod item socrum Petri febricitantem non solùm curant & officijs debitis iuuant, verumetiam saluam cupiunt, proq; eius salute apud Christum intercedunt: cum fere passim socrus inuisæ aut contemptæ esse soleant. Tales esse decet hominum Christianorum familias. Prima illis cura sit religionis, vbi hoc maximè videndum, vt Christum hospitem, imò præsidem & herum habeat, quando hic vnicus benedictionis diuinæ mediator est, sine qua domus feliciter gubernari nequeunt. Deinde charitati ac concordiæ studeant, qua nihil vtilius, nihil magis necessarium est ad vitæ tranquillitatem & rei domesticæ conseruationem. Possunt enim modicus facultatibus honestè viuere qui simul cohabitant fratres, qui si hæreditate diuisa distrahantur, omnes fere egeni ac inopes fiunt. Scribit Plutarchus in vita Pauli Æmilij, ex nobili Tuberonum familia sedecim viros cum coniugibus et liberis suis in ijsdem ædibus, & quidem modicus habitauisse: quod adeò non molestum & aut ignominiosum fuit visum illius seculi hominibus, vt in illam domum Æmilius bis Consul & triumphalis filiam suam nuptui dederit. At quæ nostri seculi infelicitas est, vix patri cum filijs iam adultis, nedum fratribus eorumque vxoribus conuenire potest. Et huic malo veterum familiarum dissipationes & egestatem debemus. Debent præterea in honore & pretio haberi parentes, soceri, socrus aut quicunque ætate, prudentia & rerum vsu reliquis præstant. Hos enim peculiari præcepto commendat Deus, cui longæuitatis promissionem adiecit. Et prophanos atq; barbaros planè animos produnt, qui singulare illud senectæ donu non agnoscunt in suis & colunt, ad quod omnes naturali vitæ desiderio aspiramus. Prophanus certè Poeta inter corruptissimi seculi, quod diluuium proximè præcesserit argumenta, hoc quoq; commemorat: Filius ante diem patrios inquirit in annos. Quod vitium hodie tam vulgare est, vt multi se eo infeliciores esse putent, quòd parentes vita longiori fruuntur.
units.tr: Here too is set forth an example of a pious family, truly Christian. It is well established that Peter's means were not great. Yet he brings Christ home with him and does not refrain from receiving his company, which was large. Nor do the other members of the household complain on that account. This is clear evidence of piety, and that it was no burden to them to share all their goods with Christ and his members. It is an act of charity that two brothers, and perhaps both of them married, live together; likewise that they not only care for Peter's feverish mother-in-law and help her with the due services, but also wish her to be well and intercede with Christ for her health, since mothers-in-law are generally thought to be disliked or despised almost everywhere. Such should be the households of Christian men. Their first concern should be religion, and there they must above all see to it that they have Christ as guest, indeed as protector and master, since he alone is the mediator of divine blessing, without whom households cannot be governed happily. Next, they should strive for charity and concord, than which nothing is more useful or more necessary for the tranquillity of life and the preservation of domestic affairs. For brothers who live together can live honourably on modest means, whereas if they are separated by dividing an inheritance, nearly all of them become needy and destitute. Plutarch writes in the Life of Aemilius Paullus that sixteen men of the noble family of the Tuberones lived with their wives and children in the same house, and a modest house at that; and this seemed so little troublesome or disgraceful to the men of that age that Aemilius, twice consul and triumphant, gave his daughter in marriage from that house. But such is the unhappiness of our age that a father can hardly live with his sons once they are grown, let alone with his brothers and their wives. And to this evil we owe the break-up and poverty of old families. Moreover, parents, fathers-in-law, mothers-in-law, and whoever surpasses others in age, prudence and experience, should be held in honour and esteem. For God commends these by a special precept, and he added to it the promise of long life. And those souls are plainly profane and barbarous who do not acknowledge that singular gift of old age in their own elders and honour it, the gift to which we all aspire from the natural desire for life. Certainly a profane poet, among the arguments of a most corrupt age, which immediately preceded the flood, also records this: "A son asks about his father's years before their time." This vice is so common today that many think themselves unhappier for the reason that their parents enjoy a longer life.

units.la: Admonet præterea huius familiæ exemplū, quod apud solum Christum tam corporum quàm animarum salutem quæri debere. Est quidem medicina vsus magnus, & hunc nobis à Deo datum esse, ex herbarum & similium rerum viribus colligere licet. His autem ita nos vti deeet, vt in omnium istorum authorem respiciamus, & hæc nihil profutura credamus, nisi ille istis benedixerit. Obseruanit Obseruauit hoc Dauid, cuius fidem Psalmi in grauissimis morbis compositi testantur. A cuius exemplo cum Asa Rex deflexisset, Spiritus sancti iudicio reprehenditur. Quòd si vero naturalibus remedijs fidere nefas est, quanto grauior eorum culpa fuerit, qui in Diuis coelitibus spem collocant, & hos morborum praesides fingunt, vel potius tortores, qui vel irritati eos nobis immittant, vel placati rursus propellant? Et tanta est in hac re superstitiosorum hominum caecitas, vt quidam ex hoc ipso exemplo erroris occasionem arripuerint: qui ex socru Petri Petronellam finxerunt, quae febricitantibus medeatur. Taceo nunc reliquos Diuos, de quibus multa magis ridicula atque superstitiosa traduntur.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of this household shows that both bodily and spiritual health are to be sought from Christ alone. Medicine is certainly of great use, and from the powers of herbs and similar things we may gather that God has given it to us. But we ought to use these things in such a way that we look to the author of them all, and believe that they will profit nothing unless he blesses them. David observed this, and the Psalms he composed in the most serious illnesses bear witness to his faith. When King Asa turned away from this example, he was rebuked by the judgment of the Holy Spirit. But if it is wrong to trust in natural remedies, how much graver is the fault of those who place their hope in the saints in heaven and imagine them to be presiding over diseases, or rather as tormentors, who, when provoked, send them upon us, and when appeased, drive them away again? Such is the blindness of superstitious people in this matter that some have seized on this very example as an occasion for error, and from Peter's mother-in-law have made up a Petronella who cures people with fever. I say nothing now of the other saints, of whom many more ridiculous and superstitious stories are told.

units.la: Sequitur ipsum miraculum, in quo diuina & salutifica Christi virtus elucet, qui simul suae etiam bonitatis specimen praebuit. Nec enim multis aut prolixis precibus opus fuit apud eum, qui pietate & fide hominum mouetur. Et hunc suae pietatis fructum vberrimum isti reportarunt, quòd absque mora ipsorum votis ille annuit. Nam astans supra febricitantem, & eius manu prehensa (vt Marcus scribit) febrim obiurgauit, quae mox ab ea recessit. Solet hoc ipsum erga omnes facere, qui ipsum ex fide inuocant. Astat enim miseris nobis, vt qui ideo in mundum venit, vt peccatores seruaret. Nec manum modò prehendit, sed totos nos complectitur, cum humanam naturam in eius dem personae societatem assumpserit, & ita nos suo attactu dignatus est. Idem vicissim a nobis quoque apprehendi gaudet, cum non alia re magis quàm hominum salute delectetur. Habet autem coniunctam cum bonitate quiduis perficiendi potestatem. Vt enim hic febrim increpat, & solo verbo abigit: ita alibi ventis imperauisse, daemones corripuisse, & alios morbos infinitos profligauisse legitur. Ex istis ergo exemplis consolationem petamus in omni tentationum genere. In primis autem ad nos pertinere putemus, quod de Petri socru restituta dicitur: Eam nimirum illico surrexisse, & ministrauisse illis. Nam etsi hoc ad miraculi veritatem afferendam faciat, hoc tamen exemplo simul officij nostri admonemur: quod est, vt Christi beneficio restituti surgamus ex sordibus peccatorum ad vitae nouitatem, & nos totos ipsius consecremus seruitio. Quod vtinam tam facile nobis persuaderi posset, quàm proclives sumus ad petendam opem atque liberationem, si quando nos graviora discrimina circunstant.
units.tr: There follows the miracle itself, in which the divine and saving power of Christ shines forth, and which at the same time displayed a sample of his goodness. For he had no need of many or lengthy prayers, since he is moved by the piety and faith of men. And these people reaped a most abundant fruit of their piety, because he assented to their prayers without delay. For standing over the feverish woman and taking her by the hand (as Mark writes), he rebuked the fever, and it straightway left her. He does the same for all who call upon him in faith. For he stands by us in our misery, since he came into the world to save sinners. He does not merely take us by the hand, but embraces us altogether, since he has taken human nature into fellowship with his own person, and so has deigned to touch us. Again, he rejoices to be laid hold of by us in turn, since nothing delights him more than the salvation of men. Moreover, he joins to his goodness the power to accomplish whatever he wills. For just as here he rebukes the fever and drives it away with a single word, so elsewhere we read that he commanded the winds, rebuked demons, and drove away countless other diseases. From these examples, then, let us seek consolation in every kind of temptation. Above all, let us think that what is said of Peter's mother-in-law, once restored, applies to us: that she immediately rose and ministered to them. For although this serves to establish the truth of the miracle, by this example we are at the same time reminded of our duty, which is that, restored by the benefit of Christ, we should rise from the filth of sin to newness of life, and wholly consecrate ourselves to his service. Would that this could be as easily persuaded in us as we are quick to seek help and deliverance whenever greater dangers surround us!

units.la: Subijcit hus nouam narrationem Lucas, quae huius miraculi fructum, qui ad plures alios redundauit, continet, & simul Christi diuinam virtutem magis illustrat. Nam occidente iam Sole, omnes qui habebant aegrotantes morbis varijs, ducebant eos ad ipsum. Est quidem in illis laude dignum, quòd in priuata domo aeditum signum non contemnunt, sed ex eo spem maiorem de illo concipiunt. Id tamen excusari non potest, quòd suos modò, qui corporibus laborabant, adducunt, nemo autem petit, vt idem animorum vitijs medeatur, quibus omnes plus quàm onerati & depressi erant. Duplex enim hic error est. Nam & minus bonum quaerunt neglecto praestantiori, & de aliorum salute soliciti propriam negligunt. Est vtrumque admodum vulgare hodie. Plures enim inuenias, qui in Euangelio opes, dignitates & libertatem huius seculi quaerant, quàm quos aeternae salutis desiderium teneat. Etsi qui reperiuntur, qui Christum animarum medicum agnoscunt, ij tamen alios quidem illo opus habere fatentur, & vt ad eum festinent ipsis authores sunt: de seipsis vero nunquam cogitant: sed quasi nihil ipsis deest, illius doctrinam, admonitiones, correptiones securi negligunt.
units.tr: Luke then adds a new narrative, which contains the fruit of this miracle, which overflowed to many others, and at the same time sets forth more clearly the divine power of Christ. For when the sun was now setting, all who had sick people suffering from various diseases brought them to him. Indeed, there is something praiseworthy in them, that they do not despise the sign given in a private house, but conceive from it a greater hope concerning him. Yet this cannot be excused, that they bring only those who were suffering in their bodies, while no one asks that he heal the vices of the soul, by which all were more than burdened and oppressed. For here is a twofold error. They seek the lesser good while neglecting the greater, and in caring for the salvation of others they neglect their own. Both are very common today. For you will find more who seek in the gospel wealth, honours and the freedom of this age, than those who are held by a desire for eternal salvation. Yet there are some who acknowledge Christ as the physician of souls, and yet they confess that others have need of him, and they urge others to hasten to him; but they never think of themselves. Rather, as if nothing were lacking to them, they carelessly neglect his teaching, admonitions and corrections.

units.la: At hic nouum suae mansuetudinis atque facilitatis exemplum Christus edit. Nam etsi multa essent, quae causari & praetexere possent, adeò tamen non negat opem miseris, vt potius vnicuique eorum manus imponat, eosque sanet. Etenim manuum impositione, qua minime opus erat, testari voluit, quàm non fastidiat eos, qui ad ipsum veniunt. Negant hanc eius bonitatem, aut saltem in dubium vocant, qui hodie durum ac difficilem fingunt, apud quem aliis intercessoribus sit opus. At nos ex hus, quae hoc loco & alibi dicuntur, consolationem petamus, & simul discamus ipsum imitari, ac non fastidire eos, qui nostra ope indigent, neque (quod homines carnales solent) vndique corradere rationes, quarum praetextu nos negligamus, qui nobis propter communionem, quae inter fideles in Christo est, commendatissimi esse debebant. Singuli potius in semetipsos descendant, & videbunt ipsis & gratia Dei & aliorum auxilijs non minus opus esse, quàm illis, quos nunc superbè ac insolenter nimis fastidiunt.
units.tr: But here Christ displays a new example of his gentleness and readiness. For although there were many things that could be alleged and used as pretexts, he nonetheless does not deny help to the wretched; rather, he lays his hand on each of them and heals them. Indeed, by the laying on of hands, which was in no way necessary, he wished to show how far he is from disdaining those who come to him. Those who today imagine him to be hard and difficult, so that one needs other intercessors with him, deny this goodness of his, or at least call it into doubt. But from what is said in this place and elsewhere, let us seek consolation, and at the same time learn to imitate him, and not to disdain those who need our help, nor (as carnal men are wont to do) to gather from every side reasons under the pretext of which we neglect those who ought to be most commended to us, because of the fellowship that the faithful have in Christ. Rather, let each one descend into himself, and he will see that he has no less need of the grace of God and the help of others than those whom he now disdains so proudly and insolently.

units.la: Christus febricitanti medeatur.
units.tr: Christ heals the feverish woman.

units.la: Porrò quid hic Christus fecerit, videamus, quae praecipua huius loci pars est. Primùm omnis generis morbos miraculosè curauit, & daemones quoque ex multis inuitos atque reluctantes, vel etiam blanditiis ipsum demulcere volentes, eiecit. Est ergo reuera promissus ille seruator, qui infirmitates nostras ferre & languores omnes curare, denique serpentis veteris caput conculcare & conterere debuit. Nam quod hic in corporibus male affectis fecit, hoc ipsum ad animas quoque debet referri, quas vna cum corporibus à peccatorum noxa & inferorum cruciatibus liberauit, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Est autem hoc loco peculiari obseruatione digna actio, quae cum daemonibus ipsi intercesserit. Clamabant illi: Tu es Christus ille filius Dei. Sed noluit vt hoc dicerent, & cum graui increpatione silentium illis imposuit. Nam blanditiis istis inducias quaerebant, quibus regnum suum aliqua ex parte stabilirent: Noluit ergo illis quicquam dare, ne vel commercium aliquod cum ipsis habere videretur, quod doctrinam suam suspectam faceret: & simul nos quoque docet, vt qui ipsi nomen dedimus, diabolo in vniuersum renuntiemus. Est enim inter hunc & nos perpetua sancta inimicitia, quando serpenti Deus dixit: Ponam inimicitias inter te & ipsam mulierem, inter semen tuum & semen illius. Et qui in Christi nomen baptizantur, ij in Christi castra transeunt, vt huius auspicijs contra communem hostem diabolum militent. Est ergo inexcusabilis illorum curiositas, qui Exorcistas & illicitis vaticinandi artibus deditos consulunt. Nam Christi gloriae derogant, quem Prophetam illum Magnum esse Moses docet, qui solus consuli & audiri debeat. Et dum à mendace & homicida veritatem atque opem requirunt, merito falluntur atque pereunt. Vide tristia Saulis & Ochoziae exempla, quibus ista impietas exitium peperit. 1. Sam. 28. 2. Regum. 1.
units.tr: Next, let us see what Christ did here, which is the principal part of this passage. First, he miraculously cured diseases of every kind, and he also cast out demons from many who were unwilling and resisting, or even wishing to win him over by flattery. He is therefore truly that promised Saviour who was to bear our infirmities, cure all our languors, and at last tread down and crush the head of the old serpent. For what he did here in bodies that were ill, the same must also be referred to souls, which together with bodies he has freed from the harm of sin and the torments of the lower world, as we have shown elsewhere. But in this place the action deserves particular notice, in which he interposed himself with the demons. They cried out: "You are that Christ, the Son of God." But he would not have them say this, and with a severe rebuke he imposed silence upon them. For they sought by these flatteries a truce, by which they might in some measure establish their kingdom. He therefore chose to give them nothing, lest he seem to have any dealings with them, which would make his teaching suspect; and at the same time he teaches us also that we, who have given our name to him, should renounce the devil altogether. For there is a perpetual and holy enmity between him and us, since God said to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed." And those who are baptized into the name of Christ pass over into the camp of Christ, so that under his leadership they may fight against the common enemy, the devil. Therefore the curiosity of those is inexcusable who consult exorcists and men given over to forbidden arts of divination. For they detract from the glory of Christ, whom Moses teaches to be that great Prophet, the only one who ought to be consulted and heard. And while they seek the truth and help from a liar and murderer, they are rightly deceived and perish. Consider the sad examples of Saul and Ahaziah, whose impiety brought them to ruin. 1 Sam. 28. 2 Kings 1.

units.la: Secundò sub diluculum exit in locum desertum: quod eum orandi causa fecisse, Marcus scribit. Orauit autem frequenter, non quod ipsi precibus opus esset, sed vt nostrum ageret Mediatorem, & suo exemplo nos ad orandum excitaret. Quod in eum finem obseruari debet, ne alios nobis intercessores apud Deum quaeramus. Cur enim de eius fide dubitemus, qui non requisitus tam frequens & diligens fuit in precibus, quas pro nobis funderet? Confirmet nos potius haec eius industria, vt nos meriti eius fiducia armati nostras preces per eius nomen Deo Patri indesinenter offeramus.
units.tr: Secondly, at dawn he went out into a desert place, which Mark writes that he did for the sake of prayer. He prayed often, however, not because he had any need of prayers, but so that he might act as our Mediator and by his example rouse us to pray. This must be observed to this end, that we do not seek other intercessors for ourselves with God. For why should we doubt his faithfulness, when he, though not asked, was so frequent and diligent in the prayers he poured out for us? Rather, let his diligence strengthen us, so that, armed with confidence in his merit, we may without ceasing offer our prayers to God the Father through his name.

units.la: Additur his postremum, quod cùm turba eum quaesiuisset, & inuentum retinere vellet, respondit: Certè etiam aliis vrbibus oportet me Euangelizare Regnum Dei: nam ad hoc missus sum. Commendatur his verbis Dei Patris bonitas, qui miseris mortalibus Filium suum doctorem dare dignatus est. Is non modo facilem se omnibus praebuit, verumetiam vt plures seruaret, non diutius in illis locis substitit, in quibus iam quies aliqua parta esse videbatur, sed ad alios diuertit, & vitae aeternae doctrinam longè lateque diuulgat. Et quod olim fecit, cùm carne vestitus in terris ageret, hoc ipsum hodie quoque facit, dum Spiritus sui virtute indies excitat ministros, quorum opera Euangelium praedicatur. In praesenti autem magnae modestiae argumentum est, quòd non insolenter ab istis discedit, sed abitus sui rationem reddit, Dei nimirum Patris sui missionem allegans. Longè ergo alienus est à personati sui Vicarij moribus, de quo in iure Canonico scribitur: Papa dicitur habere caelestè arbitrium, & ideo potest sententiam, quae nulla est, aliquam facere: Quia in his quae vult, est pro ratione voluntas: Nec est qui dicat ei, Cura ita facis? Imò si cum illius modestia & laboribus Pontifices conferas, mox videbis nihil his cum illo simile aut commune esse. Itaque nos reliquis ignauis illis sponsis Penelopes, istos imitemur, qui Iesum Christum apud se fluduerunt retinere: & cùm vs se nobis liberalissimè offerat, in ipso constantes simus, in quo vno omnis salus habetur, & cui vni soliquè debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, this is added: when the crowd had sought him and wanted to keep him once he was found, he answered: "I must also preach the Kingdom of God to the other cities, for I was sent for this purpose." In these words the goodness of God the Father is commended, who has deigned to give his Son as teacher to wretched mortals. He not only showed himself easy of access to all, but also, so that he might save more, did not stay longer in those places where some peace seemed already to have been won; he turned aside to others and spreads the teaching of eternal life far and wide. And what he did once, when he lived on earth clothed in flesh, he does today as well, while by the power of his Spirit he daily raises up ministers through whose work the Gospel is preached. Moreover, in the present case it is a sign of great modesty that he does not leave them insolently, but gives the reason for his departure, namely alleging the mission of God his Father. He is therefore far removed from the manners of that counterfeit vicar of his, of whom it is written in the Canon Law: "The Pope is said to have a heavenly judgment, and therefore he can make a sentence, which is no sentence, into some sentence, because in those things which he wills, his will stands in place of reason; nor is there anyone who says to him, 'Why do you act so?'" Indeed, if you compare the Pontiffs with his modesty and labours, you will soon see that there is nothing similar or common between them and him. Therefore let us, unlike those other idle suitors of Penelope, imitate those who wished to keep Jesus Christ with them; and since he offers himself to us most generously, let us be steadfast in him, in whom alone all salvation is found, and to whom alone is due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVI.

units.la: FActum est autem cum turba immineret ei, vt audiret Verbum Dei, ipse stabat iuxta stagnum Genezareth: vidit que duo nauigia, quae ad stagnum erant: piscatores autem cum ex iis descendissent, abluebant retia. Ingressus autem in vnum illorum nauigiorum, quod erat Simonis, rogauit eum, vt a terra produceret paululum: cumque consedisset, docebat turbam ex nauigio. Vt cessauit autem loqui, dixit ad Simonem: Prouehito in altum, & demittite retia vestra ad capturam. Tum respondens Simon ait ei: Magister, cum per totam noctem nos fatigauerimus, nihil cepimus, tamen ad verbum tuum demittam rete. Et cum hoc fecissent, concluserunt piscium multitudinem magnam: dirumpebatur autem rete eorum. Et innuerunt sociis, qui erant in altero nauigio, vt venirent & ipsis opitularentur. Venerunt igitur, & impleuerunt ambas naues: ita vt mergerentur.
units.tr: It came to pass that, while the crowd pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he stood by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats lying at the water's edge, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. He got into one of the boats, which belonged to Simon, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowd from the boat. When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: "Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch." Simon answered him: "Master, we toiled all night and caught nothing; nevertheless, at your word I will let down the net." When they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, and their net began to break. So they signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came, and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.

units.la: HOMO per peccatum non modo a beatitudine & gloria, ad quam initio conditus erat, excidit, sed vilissimum quoque peccati mancipium factus, rationis siue intellectus lucem atque vsum amisit, vt iam non percipiat ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei, neque viam salutis consequendae intelligat. Ideo non eo modo redemptore opus erat, qui peccatum expiaret, & nos vendicaret in libertatem filiorum Dei: verum etiam doctore & magistro, qui aeternae salutis doctrinam traderet, & mentes ipsas hominum voluntatis diuinae rerumque coelestium cognitione illustraret. Vtrumque Iesus Christus fidelissime praestitit, qui ideo vindex noster & Propheta dicitur, quem omnes audire debeant. Itaque minus dubitaremus, miracula multa & minime vulgaria edidit, quae euidenter docent, ipsum esse benedictum illud semen, quod diaboli regnum destruit, peccati & mortis vires frangit, iustitiam sempiternam reducit, & salutem omnibus numeris perfectam miseris mortalibus confert. Coniunxit autem miraculis doctrinam, in qua tam assiduus fuit, vt nihil fere quentius fecerit, & se ad euangelizandum a patre missum esse, nuper publice testatus sit. Id vero nunc amplius confirmat. Describitur enim prima huius Cap. parte noua Concio, quam in confertissima hominum turba habuit: cui deinde subiicitur vocatio aliquot discipulorum, Simonis Petri nimirum & Andreae, Ioannis item & Iacobi, quos sibi discipulos domesticos fecit, vt eorum opera atque ministerio postea in Euangelio per totum orbem propagando vteretur. Est autem historia haec fecundissima, & multa continet quae fidei instituendae & confirmandae seruiunt: qua causa est, quod eam Lucas prolixe & diligenter admodum describit.
units.tr: Through sin, man not only fell from the blessedness and glory for which he was originally created, but, having become the most abject slave of sin, he also lost the light and use of reason or understanding. Now he no longer perceives the things of the Spirit of God, nor does he understand the way to obtain salvation. Therefore he needed a redeemer of a different kind, not only one who would expiate sin and claim us into the liberty of the sons of God, but also a teacher and master who would deliver the doctrine of eternal salvation and illuminate men's minds with knowledge of the divine will and of heavenly things. Jesus Christ performed both most faithfully, and for this reason he is called our vindicator and Prophet, whom all ought to hear. So that we might have fewer doubts, he worked many miracles, and not at all ordinary ones, which clearly teach that he is that blessed seed who destroys the kingdom of the devil, breaks the power of sin and death, restores everlasting righteousness, and bestows salvation, perfect in every respect, on wretched mortals. He joined his teaching to the miracles, and was so constant in it that he hardly did anything more often, and he has recently declared publicly that he was sent by the Father to preach the gospel. Now this is confirmed still further. For the first part of this chapter describes a new sermon which he delivered to a very dense crowd of people. Then follows the calling of some disciples, namely Simon Peter and Andrew, and also John and James, whom he made his household disciples, so that he might later use their work and ministry in spreading the gospel throughout the world. This history is very fruitful and contains much that serves to establish and confirm faith, which is why Luke describes it at such length and with such care.

units.la: Principio summam historiae praemittit, & Christum rursus publice contionatum fuisse scribit. Locus indicatur ad lacum Genezareth, qui alio nomine apud Euangelistas mare Tiberiadis aut Galileae dicitur. Et quia mox secuta est Simonis Petri & Andreae vocatio, constat non procul a Bethsaida hoc factum fuisse, quam Petri & Andreae patriam fuisse Ioannes docet. Occasionem vero docendi dedit populus, qui ad illum cateruatim confluebat, & circumquaque ei imminebat, vt Dei verbum audiret. Exprimitur his verbis ardens audiendi Christi desiderium, cuius causa procul dubio fuit, quod salutis doctrina diu fuerant destituti. Fuit enim vltimus prophetarum veteris testamenti Malachias, qui annis circiter quadringentis & quinquaginta fili Dei in carnem aduentum praecessit: A quo tempore nemo fuit, cuius nomen & memoria extet, qui Dei Verbum serio & qua decet fide praedicarit, vsque ad Ioannem Baptistam, quem primum noui testamenti ministrum fuisse alibi diximus. Erat quidem ingens sacerdotum numerus, & scribae infiniti erant, qui Legis diuinae scientiam profitebantur: sed ij simul omnes auaritia & ambitione excaecati sacra omnia vanalia fecerant, Legis doctrinam humanis traditionibus corruperant, & circa frigidas modo
units.tr: At the outset he gives a summary of the story and writes that Christ again preached publicly. The place is indicated as the lake of Gennesaret, which is called by other names in the Evangelists, the Sea of Tiberias or of Galilee. And since the calling of Simon Peter and Andrew followed soon after, it is clear that this took place not far from Bethsaida, which John tells us was the homeland of Peter and Andrew. The occasion for teaching was given by the people, who flocked to him in crowds and pressed around him so that they might hear the word of God. These words express the ardent desire to hear Christ, the cause of which was without doubt that they had long been deprived of the doctrine of salvation. For Malachi was the last of the prophets of the Old Testament, and he went before the coming of the Son of God in the flesh by about four hundred and fifty years. From that time on, until John the Baptist, whom we have said elsewhere was the first minister of the New Testament, there was no one whose name and memory survive who preached the word of God earnestly and with the faith it deserves. There was indeed a great number of priests, and countless scribes who professed knowledge of the divine Law; but all of them, blinded together by greed and ambition, had made all sacred things a matter of trade, had corrupted the teaching of the Law with human traditions, and, occupied with cold ceremonies, taught things that could by no means appease consciences afflicted and weighed down by the burden of sins.

units.la: Ioan. 1. ceremonias occupati ea docebant, quae afflictas & peccatorum pondere grauatas conscientias nequa-quam placare poterant. Itaque (vt in Euangelio scribitur) infelix populus omnium instat eberra-bat, quae pastore fido & inducstrio destituuntur. At Christus, vt nuper dictum est, Dei verbum praedicabat, idq; cum singulari authoritate, & non aures solas inani verborum dulcedine demulcebat, sed vivifica spiritus virtute ipsos animos auditorum penetrabat, vt aliosquidem serio poenitentiae studio accenderet, alios autem certa remissionis peccatorum atque aeternae salutis spe recrearet. Neque in eo lucrum aut honorem priuatum quaerebat, sed in vnam auditorum salutem toto animo erat intentus. Hinc nouum illud studium populi enatum est, vt & proprio animi motu & mutuis exhortationibus excitati vndique ad illum concurrerent, & cum importunitate quadam eiimmi-nerent, vt diu optata veritatis doctrina reficerentur. Fuit ergo tunc temporis inter Iudaeos eadem rerum conditio, quae hodie inter eos est, quibus vncti & rasi Papisticarum superstitionum anti-stites dominantur. Habent enim illi quoque Monachos & sacrificos infinitos, qui doctorum uten-silium superbiunt, & quos maximis impensis alere coguntur. At plerique illorum nunquam docent, & vt ignauum suum silentium tueantur, imagines & simulachra dicunt libros laicorum esse, ex quibus populus suum officium discere, & quorum contemplatione ad hoc praestandum excitari de-beat. Sunt illi reuera pastores illi, quos Zacharias idola vocat, cum praeter mutam pastorum for-mam siue persona nihil habeant. Alij vero aut Patrum & Conciliorum traditionibus toti va-cant, & ad earum obseruationem omnes adigunt, aut e suggestu narrationes de Sanctis recitant, quarum pleraeque fabulosae sunt, & plenae superstitiosum, quibus conscientiae hominum mirifice qui-dem lactantur, ad certam vero salutis fiduciam nunquam perueniunt. Sitiunt ergo & esuriunt in-felices illi, & in omnem salutis occasionem intenti sunt. Quo fit, vt si qui illis Euangelium prae-dicent, mox turmatim omnes confluant, & zelo abrepti multa quoque faciant satis importune, & saepe priuata authoritate ad reformationem ecclesiae faciendam manum admoliantur. Fiunt tunc multa tumultuarie, dum animi feruent, ex quibus aduersarij occasionem calumniandi arripiunt, et principes interdum vulgi feruore irritati ad arma ruunt, & crudeliter in quosuis saeuiendo ipsi quo-que modum excedunt. Sed cur non rem ipsam prius expendunt, & maiori supplicio dignos esse vi-derent falsos antistites, qui in manifesta ecclesiae totius corruptione nullum remedium hactenus adhibuerunt, sed potius vndique surgentem veritatis lucem nouis quotidie nebulis atque tene-bris obscurare conantur? Et quid mirum est, si panem verbi Dei oblatum auidius & (vt ita dicam) immodestius arripiunt, quos eius audiendi fames iam pridem in rabiem quandam ad-duxit?
units.tr: Therefore (as is written in the Gospel) the unhappy people wandered like sheep, as the sheep that are deprived of a faithful and diligent shepherd. But Christ, as was said just now, preached the word of God, and did so with singular authority. He did not merely soothe the ears with the empty sweetness of words, but penetrated the minds of his hearers by the life-giving power of the Spirit, so that he kindled some to a serious zeal for repentance and refreshed others with the sure hope of forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation. Nor did he seek gain or private honour from this, but was wholly intent on the salvation of his hearers. Hence arose that new eagerness of the people, so that, stirred both by their own inner impulse and by mutual exhortations, they ran to him from every side, and with a certain importunity pressed in on him, so that they might be refreshed by the long-desired doctrine of the truth. So at that time among the Jews the situation was the same as it is today among those over whom the anointed and shaven prelates of Papist superstitions hold sway. For they too have countless monks and priests, who take pride in the trappings of teachers, and whom they are forced to support at great expense. But most of them never teach, and to defend their idle silence they say that images and statues are the books of the laity, from which the people ought to learn their duty and be stirred to perform it by contemplating them. Those are truly the shepherds whom Zechariah calls idols, since apart from the dumb form or outward appearance of shepherds they have nothing. Others again are wholly given over to the traditions of the Fathers and the Councils, and compel everyone to observe them, or from the pulpit recite stories about the saints, most of which are fabulous and full of superstition. These wonderfully delight the consciences of men, but they never bring them to a sure confidence of salvation. Those unhappy people therefore thirst and hunger, and are intent on every chance of salvation. The result is that if anyone preaches the Gospel to them, at once they all flock together in crowds, and carried away by zeal they do many things rather intemperately, and often, on their own private authority, they set their hands to reforming the Church. Many things are then done tumultuously while their minds are aflame, and adversaries seize on these as an occasion for slander; and princes, sometimes roused by the fervour of the common people, rush to arms and, raging cruelly against whomever they like, themselves also exceed due measure. But why do they not first weigh the matter itself, and see that the false prelates, who have hitherto applied no remedy to the manifest corruption of the whole Church, but rather try to darken with new clouds and shadows the light of truth rising on every side every day, deserve greater punishment? And what wonder is it if those whom a hunger for hearing the word of God has long since driven into a kind of frenzy seize the bread of God's word when it is offered more eagerly and (so to speak) more immoderately?

units.la: Caeterum vt ut ista habeant, admonemur populi istius exemplo, circa Dei verbum studio ar-denti opus esse. Vt enim in omnibus aliis negotijs nihil proficitur, nisi diligentia & feria fedu-litas accedat: ita hac in Dei verbo audiendo in primis opus est, eo quod caro ab illo natura ab-horret, quod suis studijs aduersum & inimicum esse sentit. Hic ergo nunquam non cogitare de-bemus, salutem nostram sine verbo hoc consistere non posse. Nam vt scriptura omnis testa-tur, natura peccatores & filij irae sumus. At Dei verbum semen illud regenerationis est, ex quo in Dei filios regeneramur. Per idem hoc fides datur, quae sola Christum apprehendit, & nos bo-norum omnium, quorum hic nobis Mediator est, participes reddit. Notum enim est illud Pau-li: Fides ex auditu est, auditus vero per verbum Dei. Idem cum salutis doctrina vitae quoque regulam nobis exhibet, quam qui sequuntur, ij & Deo placent, & in hoc etiam seculo felices at-que beati sunt. Ex illo etiam consolationis argumenta petuntur, quae nobis aduersa omnia mi-tigant, & vitam hanc, quae aerumnarum & malorum plena est, iucundam atque suauem red-dunt. Denique per verbum suum Deus nobis seipsum & suae gratiae atque bonitatis thesauros o-mnes offert, ideoq; de omnibus, qui eius beneficijs fruuntur, dici potest, quod in Psalmo de quibus-dam dicitur: Misit verbum suum, & sanauit eos. Quae omnia Paulus probe considerans dicebat: Non me pudet Euangelij Iesu Christi, siquidem potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Et quicunque ista non ofcitanter expendunt, cumque his sui ingenij atque totius humanae naturae infe-licitatem conferunt, nisi plus quam ferrei aut plumbei sint, nouo quodam amore & studio verbi au-diendi se accendi sentient.
units.tr: However these things stand, we are reminded by the example of that people that we need an ardent zeal for the word of God. For just as in all other undertakings nothing is achieved unless diligence and constant application are present, so above all in hearing the word of God there is need of this, because the flesh by nature shrinks from it and feels that it is opposed and hostile to its pursuits. Therefore here we must always reflect that our salvation cannot stand without this word. For, as all Scripture testifies, by nature we are sinners and children of wrath. But the word of God is that seed of regeneration by which we are born again as sons of God. Through the same word faith is given, which alone apprehends Christ and makes us partakers of all the good things of which he is our Mediator. For that saying of Paul is well known: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God" (Rom. 10). The same word, along with the doctrine of salvation, also sets before us the rule of life, which those who follow it both please God and are happy and blessed even in this world. From it too are drawn the arguments of consolation, which soften all adversities for us and make this life, which is full of troubles and evils, pleasant and sweet. Finally, through his word God offers himself to us and all the treasures of his grace and goodness, so that of all who enjoy his benefits one may say what is said in a Psalm of certain people: "He sent his word and healed them" (Ps. 107). Paul, weighing all these things carefully, said: "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." And whoever weighs these things not carelessly, and compares them with his own intellect's frailty and the wretchedness of all human nature, will feel himself kindled with a new love and eagerness for hearing the word, unless they are harder than iron or lead.

units.la: Admonet nos istorum consideratio, quae causa sit, quòd hodie docendo & praedicando minus proficitur. Refriguit apud plerosque vetus ille zelus, quo sub initiu instaurati Euangelij omniu animi ardebant. Et quia otio & pace abundant, quantus ille thesaurus sit non cogitant: itaque nescien tibus fere ipsis satietas Verbi obrepit, dum se sine hoc saluos fieri posse arbitrantur. Etsi ergo quotidie omnes invitet Christus, multi tamen non veniunt, neque putant sibi doctrina & institutione opus esse. Alij vero ne omnino a religione alieni dicantur, pro more diebus dominicis ad sacros coetus conueniunt, & Dei populum simulantes Verbum audiunt, & quàmuis interdum dicentis facundiam admirentur, interdum cum gemitu & suspirijs quaedam excipiant, multa aperte probent, eadem tamen nihil ad se facere existimant, & ideo non plus inde fructus referunt, quàm si fictam aliquam narrationem aut cantilenam de rebus nouis aut peregrinis, nihil autem ad se pertinentibus audiuissent. Sunt hic peiores multi, qui vt censores & iudices veniunt, & in Dei verbum sibi ius sumunt. Hi vt primùm audiunt quod moribus & studijs ipsorum aduersatur, mox iras animo concipiunt, dira quaeque Verbi administris minantur, & ijsdem dicendi leges praescribunt. Quid vero apud tales proficiat Christus, quantumuis per suos ministros sedulò doceat, moneat, hortetur, increpet? Ista ergo emendari oportet, & serio salutis studio accendi, si quem Deus nobis offert aeternae salutis fructum, ex Verbo ipsius referre cupimus.
units.tr: Consideration of these matters reminds us why so little progress is made today in teaching and preaching. That old zeal, with which everyone's heart burned at the beginning of the restored Gospel, has cooled among most people. Because they abound in leisure and peace, they do not reflect on how great a treasure this is. And so, almost without their noticing, satiety with the Word creeps over them, while they suppose that they can be saved without it. Therefore, although Christ invites everyone every day, many do not come, and they do not think they need teaching and instruction. Others, so that they will not be thought wholly alien to religion, gather on the Lord's day for the holy assemblies as usual. Pretending to be God's people, they hear the Word, and although at times they admire the eloquence of the speaker, and at times receive certain things with groans and sighs, and clearly approve many points, they nevertheless think these things have nothing to do with them. So they carry away no more fruit than if they had heard some invented story or song about new or foreign matters that did not concern them at all. There are also many worse than these, who come as censors and judges and claim for themselves a right over the Word of God. As soon as they hear something that runs counter to their morals and pursuits, they immediately conceive anger in their minds, threaten the ministers of the Word with dreadful things, and prescribe to them the rules of how they must speak. But what can Christ accomplish among such people, however diligently he teaches, admonishes, exhorts and rebukes through his ministers? These attitudes therefore must be corrected, and we must be fired with a serious zeal for salvation, if we wish to gain from his Word the fruit of eternal salvation that God offers us.

units.la: Videamus autem quid fecerit Christus, cùm ipsi populus undique immineret, vt in littore consistendi vix locum habere posset. Vidit adesse duas naviculas piscatorias, ex quibus piscatores ad retia abluenda descenderant. Ingreditur ergo in alteram earum, quae Simonis Petri erat, & eo vocato iubet vt paululum prouehat a littore, & ita ex naui ad populum circumstantem conciona-tur. Et quàmuis importunos illos & immodestos alia ratione compescere potuisset, hominum tamen moribus sese accommodare, & diuinam virtutem ad tempus dissimulare voluit, vt suae bonitatis & facilitatis luculentius specimen ederet. Interim suo exemplo docet, nullam negligendam esse occasionem prouehendi regni Dei, & cùm rei necessitas iubet, quemuis locum doctrinae & religioni ferre posse. Nam extant huius generis exempla alia multa, in quibus illum saepe in locis desertis, in agris, in priuatis aedibus docuisse legimus. Fecerunt idem Apostoli, qui initio quidem in templo praedicare, et coetus sacros in porticu Solomonis cogere soliti fuerunt: at vbi id per Sacerdotes et Senio res non amplius illis licuit, tunc in domibus fidelium, quae commodiores erant reliquis, doctrinae & religionis exercitia instituerunt: imò cùm ex vrbe eiecti ad exteras gentes se reciperent, passim praedicarunt, vbicunque populum confluere & docendi occasionem sibi offerri videbant. Sic Caesareae in Cornelij Centurionis domo concionem sacram Petrus habuit, Paulus vero ad portas Lystrensium, Philippi extra vrbem prope fluuium, Athenis in vico Martio docuit: neque propter locum minor fuit Verbi Dei effectus. Quod autem de loco dicitur, hoc ipsum de tempore sentire debemus, quod sine militer necessitati seruire debet, ne eius gratia oblatam rei bene gerendae occasionem negligamus. Ideo veteres Christiani vt locis occultioribus, ita fere nocturno aut antelucano tempore conuenire solebant, cùm interdiu tuto conuenire non possent. Sunt haec propter eos obseruanda, qui inde calumniandi occasionem hodie arripiunt. Faciebant idem olim Christiani nominis hostes, qui horrenda scelera & nefanda in coetibus illis designari dicebant. Sed vt veteres sua innocentia defendebat apud Dei tribunal: ita nostros ipsa necessitas excusat, et potius accusari merentur, qui sua tyrannide pios cogunt ad occulta fidei suae exercitia confugere, impunè interim per omne genus libidinis grassantibus ijs, qui omnem religionem iampridem abnegarunt. Non tamen illis patrocinamur, qui occultos coetus agunt, cùm in illis locis viuant, vbi libera Verbi praedicatio permittitur, & Sacramentorum vsus secundùm Christi institutionem exercetur. Nam vt Paulus ait, debet omnia in ecclesia decenter & cum ordine fieri. Minimè ergo a templis publicis discedendum est, neq; clancularijs coetibus, vbi nulla vrget necessitas, locus dari debet, ne vel schismata excitentur, vel occasio detur aduersarijs, qua totum religionis negotiu suspectum reddant. Rectè ergo & prudenter Christus passim qui dem docuit, idem tamen Synagogas et templum ipsum non subterfugit, sed coram ipsis sacerdotibus & scribis doctrinam suam proposuit, nequid monstri alere videretur. Quid autem in praesenti docuerit non opus est inquirere. Quia enim sibijpsi semper constat, non dubium est, quin veram salutis rationem tradiderit, quam aliae eius conciones comprehendunt, quae ab Euangelistis descripte sunt.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what Christ did when the crowd pressed upon him from every side, so that he could scarcely find room to stand on the shore. He saw two small fishing boats nearby, from which the fishermen had gone down to wash their nets. So he got into the one that belonged to Simon Peter, and, calling him, asked him to put out a little from the shore, and so he preached to the surrounding crowd from the boat. And although he could have restrained those troublesome and unruly people by another means, he chose for the time being to accommodate himself to human ways and to conceal his divine power, so that he might give a more striking display of his goodness and affability. Meanwhile, by his own example he teaches that no opportunity for advancing the kingdom of God is to be neglected, and that, when the need of the matter demands, any place can serve for teaching and religion. For there are many other examples of this kind, in which we read that he often taught in deserted places, in fields, and in private houses. The Apostles did the same. At first they were accustomed to preach in the temple and to gather holy assemblies in Solomon's porch; but when the priests and elders no longer allowed them to do this, they then set up exercises of teaching and religion in the houses of the faithful, which were more convenient than the rest. Indeed, when they were driven out of the city and withdrew to foreign nations, they preached everywhere, wherever they saw that a crowd was gathering and an opportunity for teaching was offered to them. Thus Peter held a holy sermon at Caesarea in the house of Cornelius the centurion; Paul taught at the gates of Lystra, at Philippi outside the city near a river, and at Athens in the Areopagus [Mars' Hill]; nor was the effect of the Word of God any less because of the place. But what is said of place we ought to think of time as well: it ought to serve necessity without any hindrance, so that we do not neglect an opportunity of doing a good work that is offered, for the sake of time. Therefore the early Christians used to gather in more hidden places, and generally at night or before dawn, since they could not gather safely in the daytime.
