These things are to be observed on account of those who today seize on them as an occasion for slander. The enemies of the Christian name did the same in the past, claiming that horrible crimes and unspeakable deeds were being planned in those assemblies. But just as the ancients were defended by their innocence before the tribunal of God, so our people are excused by the very necessity they face; and rather, those deserve to be accused who by their tyranny compel the godly to take refuge in secret exercises of their faith, while those who have long since renounced all religion rage unpunished in every kind of lust. Yet we do not defend those who hold secret assemblies where free preaching of the Word is permitted and the use of the sacraments is administered according to Christ's institution. For, as Paul says, all things must be done decently and in order in the Church. Therefore one must by no means depart from public churches, and no place should be given to clandestine assemblies where no pressing necessity exists, lest either schisms be stirred up or an occasion be given to adversaries by which they make the whole cause of religion suspect. Rightly and wisely, then, Christ taught in various places, yet he did not shun the synagogues and the temple itself, but set out his teaching before the very priests and scribes, lest he seem to nourish something monstrous. But there is no need to inquire what he taught on this occasion. Since he is always consistent with himself, there is no doubt that he delivered the true way of salvation, which his other sermons, recorded by the Evangelists, contain.

units.la: Cap. V.
units.tr: Chapter V.

units.la: Nunc conditionem minist̄erij ecclesiastici & eorum, qui in hoc constituti sunt, videamus, quæ in Christi exemplo egregiè adumbratur. Non licet Christo in littore pedem figere, sed cathedram sibi constituit in navicula, quæ à littore subducta inter fluctus & ventos agitabatur. Tutior autem est auditorum statio, qui in terra stantes Verbum salutis ex ore eius audiunt. Indicat typus hic laboriosam & plenam periculi esse eorum functionem, qui Dei Verbum prædicant. Est enim mundus hic maris instar, & ut hoc quiescere non potest, cum & naturali motu æstuet & ventis diversis agitatum turbetur: ita impijs quoque, ex quibus mundus hic maxima ex parte constat, pax nulla est, quando etiam ipsi proprijs affectibus turbantur, & simul aliunde oblatis occasionibus novas quotidie adversus pios tumultuandi occasiones inveniunt. Quia tamen Christo omnis potestas data est in cælo & in terra, in illo sibi quoque locum reperit, ubi Evangelij sui cathedram collocet, et ferè ijs in locis ubi minimè speres. Quod si fiat, tutius ferè circa prædicationis initiû agunt, qui illud audiunt, at contra Evangelij prænones mox fluctus & ventorum diversissimorum turbines insurgunt. Odit enim mundus Veritatis lucem, et confessim novos furores concipit. Insidiosis disputationibus & vafanis clamoribus pugnant impostores, qui populi ignorantia & superstitione antehac ad suum quæstum abusi sunt. Iuvant hos summi Pontifices, qui ut Æoli quidam novos quotidie ventos excitant, & ipsos principes quoq; excommunicationis fulminibus perterrefaciunt, ne in terris suis Christi doctrinæ locum dent. Itaq; alij quidem ex principum numero propria malitia excitati, alij Pontificum improbitate & minis coacti, e dicta faciunt & vim parant, ut Christum finibus suis expellant. Tunc verò plerunque persecutionis initium fit à doctoribus, quia his ejectis aut oppressis à populo nihil periculi reliquum esse videtur. Est hoc probatu omnium seculorum exemplis, & multa quotidie fiunt, quæ ijs abunde fidem faciunt. Accidit tunc ferè, ut quàmuis de publica omnium salute agatur, & propter hanc ministri in periculo constituti sint, iniquissimos tamen suorum laborum censores habeant illos ipsos, quorum saluti consultum cupiunt. Imò qui ex vulgo paulò ante sibi ipsis omnia læta pollicebantur, & Evangelium totis animis videbantur completi, mox nova rabie accensi, doctores suos immodestiæ, importunitatis, imprudentiæ, temeritatis, seditionum deniq; accusant, et eorum capitibus atq; sanguine pacem redimere conantur. At non debent ista aliquem offendere, quàdo constat, eandem Christi Iesu sortem fuisse, qui ingratissimos expertus est eos, quorum salutem doctrina & miraculis assiduè prouehebat. Pergant igitur Verbi administri, & se Dei servos esse meminerint, qui ipsis digna suæ fidei præmia retribuet. Auditores verò Dei beneficium agnoscant, et doctores suos ob Dei verbum periclitantes, si non alio officio possunt, saltem pijs votis adiuvent, & quo possunt studio se illis gratos præbeant.
units.tr: Let us now consider the condition of the ecclesiastical ministry and of those who are appointed to it, which is excellently foreshadowed in Christ's example. Christ did not set his foot on the shore, but established his chair for himself in a little boat, which had been drawn up from the shore and was tossed among the waves and winds. The station of the hearers is safer, since they stand on land and hear the word of salvation from his mouth. This type indicates that the office of those who preach God's Word is laborious and full of danger. For this world is like the sea, which cannot be still: it both surges with its own natural motion and is stirred into turmoil by contrary winds. So the wicked, of whom this world for the most part consists, have no peace, since they are themselves troubled by their own passions, and at the same time they find, from whatever occasions are offered from elsewhere, new grounds for stirring up tumult against the godly every day. Yet because all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, he finds a place for himself there too, where he sets up the chair of his Gospel, and often in places where you would least expect it. When this happens, those who hear it are generally safer at the beginning of the preaching, but on the other hand the heralds of the Gospel soon face waves and whirlwinds of the most varied winds. For the world hates the light of truth, and at once conceives fresh rages. Impostors, who in the past have abused the ignorance and superstition of the people for their own gain, fight with crafty disputations and with cunning outcries. The supreme Pontiffs help them: like certain Aeolus, they stir up new winds every day, and they terrify even princes with the thunderbolts of excommunication, so that they will not give the doctrine of Christ a place in their lands. Thus some of the princes, roused by their own malice, and others, compelled by the wickedness and threats of the Pontiffs, do as they are told and prepare force to drive Christ out of their borders. Then, indeed, the persecution often begins with the teachers, because once they have been expelled or crushed, the people seem to have no danger left. This is proved by the examples of all ages, and many things happen every day that amply confirm it. It then usually happens that, although the public salvation of all is at stake, and the ministers are placed in danger on its account, they nonetheless have as their harshest judges those very people whose salvation they desire to secure. Indeed, those from the common people who a little before promised themselves every happy outcome, and who seemed to be filled with the Gospel with their whole hearts, are soon inflamed with new madness, and accuse their teachers of arrogance, importunity, imprudence, rashness, and finally of sedition, and try to buy back peace with their heads and blood. But these things ought not to trouble anyone, since it is clear that Jesus Christ himself had the same lot, for he found the most ungrateful those whose salvation he was advancing by his teaching and his miracles. Let the ministers of the Word therefore carry on, and remember that they are servants of God, who will repay them with the rewards their faith deserves. And let the hearers acknowledge God's benefit, and if they cannot help their teachers, who are in peril for the sake of God's Word, by any other service, at least let them help them with pious prayers, and show themselves grateful to them with all the zeal they can.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius historiæ partem, qua Simonis Petri & Andreæ, Ioannis itè et Iacobi vocatio describitur. Sunt enim in eius narratione breviores Matthæus et Marcus. Lucas autem miraculum quoq; præmittit, quo illos Christus excitavit, ut ad ipsum sequendum alacriores essent. Est autem huius miraculi præterea usus multiplex. Primus est, quem cum omnibus alijs communem habet, quòd nimirum suam doctrinam Christus illo confirmare voluit. Deinde præsenti negotio illud accommodavit, ut discipulos, quos iam vocaturus erat, typo hoc sui officij admoneret, adeoq; omnem sui ministerij rationem ob oculos poneret. Præterea consolationem communem habet, quæ pollicetur nihil defuturum ijs, qui Christum recipiunt & ab hoc mandatam sibi vocationem sedulò sequuntur. Et de hoc quidem in præsenti dicemus, de ijs proximo sermone dicturi, quæ ad Apostolatum & ministerium Verbi pertinent.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the other part of this history, in which the calling of Simon Peter and Andrew, and of John and James, is described. For Matthew and Mark give briefer accounts of it. Luke, however, first sets out the miracle by which Christ roused them, so that they would be more eager to follow him. This miracle has, moreover, several uses. The first is one it shares with all the others: namely, that Christ wished to confirm his teaching by it. Next, he adapted it to the present business, so that by this type he might remind the disciples, whom he was about to call, of their office, and so set before them the whole plan of their ministry. Besides this, it carries a general consolation, promising that nothing will be lacking to those who receive Christ and diligently follow the calling entrusted to them by him. We will speak of this now, and of those things that pertain to the apostleship and the ministry of the Word we will speak in the next sermon.

units.la: Primò cùm dicendi finem fecisset, iubet Petro, ut longius in altum prouecti retia demittant ad piscium capturam. Ita verò tam illum quàm socios admonet, ne otium ignavi aut inanem nominis splendorem sibi polliceantur, sed labores sibi propositos esse semper cogitent. Quod etsi in Verbi ministerio in primis locum habet, simul tamen ad omnes pertinet, qui Evangelium professi Christo & ecclesiæ eius nomen dederunt. Non enim suis otij & inertiæ author est Christus, sed hoc potius vult, ut singuli honesto aliquo labore sibi & suis victum parent, ne & alijs graves atque molesti sint, & sibijpsis multorum scelerum occasionem præbeant. Constat enim omnium seculorum exemplis, otio nihil nocentius & bonis moribus magis inimicum esse. Quia enim hominis ingenium natura inquietum est, & semper aliquid vel meditatur vel agit, fieri non potest, quin in malas meditationes & noxia studia deflectat, si nullo honesto labore aut actione bona occupetur. Quod M. Cato olim prudenter obseruauit, cuius dictum celebratur: Nihil agendo homines male agere discunt. Et idem idcirco monebat, non minus otij quàm negotij rationem extare debere. Hæc cùm olim ethnici viderint, quos humanæ sapientiæ studium & quotidianus rerum vsus reliquis prudentiores fecit, quanto magis homines Christiani ista obseruare debent, ne sub religionis prætextu otientur, & cum publica ecclesiarum infamia ex alieno viuant? Est eorum hodie ingesnumerus, qui egestatem sibi quastum vberrimum faciunt, & cùm corporis atq; ingenij viribus valeant, nihil tamen operis honesti faciunt, sed incertis sedibus vagando à quibusdam obuijs pecunias, vestes aut cibos per Christi nomen extorquent. Sunt hi magni charitatis Christianæ & misericordiæ prædones, & nunquam non Christi dicta in ore habent, quibus pauperes nobis commendauit. At debebant simul meminisse, charitatis hanc quoq; legem esse, ne cui temere graues & molesti simus, & Christum manuaria artificia omnemq; laborem honestum sua doctrina simul & exemplo commenda uisse. Quid, quòd in ecclesia minimè merentur censeri, qui omni ordine politico & œconomico turbato otiosi vagantur? Paulus certè, quem pauperum studiosissimum fuisse constat ἀπράκτως, id est, inor dinatos illos coercere iubet, & hanc inter homines Christianos legem perpetuam esse vult, ne ex publico aut alieno edat qui non vult laborare. Vide 1. Thess. 5. Item 2. Thess. 3. cap.
units.tr: First, when he had finished speaking, he tells Peter to put out farther into the deep and let down the nets for a catch of fish. In this way he admonishes both Peter and his companions not to promise themselves idle leisure or empty glory of name, but always to bear in mind that labours are set before them. Although this applies first of all to the ministry of the Word, it nonetheless pertains to all who have professed the Gospel and given their name to Christ and his Church. For Christ is not the author of idleness and sloth for his people; rather he wishes that each one should provide for himself and his family by some honest labour, so that they are not burdensome and troublesome to others, and do not give themselves occasions of many sins. For the examples of all ages show that nothing is more harmful than idleness, and nothing more hostile to good morals. Since human nature is restless by disposition and always either plans or does something, it cannot but be that a man turns to wicked schemes and harmful pursuits if he is occupied with no honest work or good activity. Marcus Cato once wisely observed this, and his saying is famous: "By doing nothing, men learn to do evil." And for this reason he also advised that there ought to be no less an account of leisure than of business. If the heathen, who were made wiser than the rest by the study of human wisdom and by daily experience of affairs, once saw this, how much more ought Christians to observe it, lest under the pretext of religion they should live in idleness and, to the public disgrace of the churches, live at the expense of others? Today there is an immense number of those who make their poverty a most abundant source of gain, and although they are strong in body and mind, they nevertheless do no honest work, but wander about with no settled dwelling and extort money, clothes or food from whomever they meet, in the name of Christ. These are great robbers of Christian charity and mercy, and they always have the sayings of Christ on their lips, by which he commended the poor to us. But they ought at the same time to remember that this too is the law of charity, not to be rashly burdensome and troublesome to anyone, and that Christ, by his teaching and also by his example, commended manual crafts and every honest labour. What of those who, having thrown the whole political and domestic order into confusion, wander about idle? They certainly do not deserve to be counted in the Church. Paul, who is known to have been most zealous for the poor, bids such disorderly people [ἀτάκτως] be restrained, and wills this to be a perpetual law among Christian men, that whoever will not work shall not eat at public or others' expense. See 1 Thess. 5. Likewise 2 Thess. 3. chapter.

units.la: Petrus, etsi totam noctem inani labore sese fatigassent, audito tamen Christi mandato ait: Magister, cùm per totam noctem nos fatigauerimus, nihil cœpimus: tamen ad verbum tuum, id est, tuo iussu demittam rete. Vnde apparet, eum ex Christi concionibus & miraculis fidei principia concepisse, vt iam de illo magnificè sentiret, & doctorem non vulgarem esse agnosceret. Est quoq; hoc nō contemnendum fidei verè exemplum, cuius proprium est homines Deo obedientes reddere. Itaq; Petrum imitari debent, quicunq; fidei nomine & titulo gloriantur. Id verò ij demùm facient, qui sensus & intellectum omnem Dei verbo subijciunt: Quod vt fiat, in primis obseruandum est, ne vel ad nostros vel aliorum conatus respiciamus, quibus minus feliciter successit quod iubentur facere. Solet enim successus eos fallere, qui sine Deo aliquid tentant. At si ijdem Dei verbo sese accommodent & eius promissis credant, tutum & facile esse videbunt, quod prius cum periculo coniunctum & impossibile esse videbatur. Petrus certè in præsenti, dum Christi mandato obtemperat, piscium tantam multitudinem concludit, vt huic atrahendæ non sufficiant, qui cum ipso in nauierant, quà item rete grauatū ex parte scinditur, & quæ vtrumq; nauigiū impleuit & pondere suo tantum non demersit. Ex hoc igitur exemplo consolatione petant omnis loci & ordinis homines, vt officiū suum sedulò et fide constanti obeant, neq; ijs moueantur, quæ caro & mundus obijcit. Etenim vt à Verbi administris exordiamur, multa occurrunt, quæ ipsos ab officio suo absterrent: qualia sunt ætas, inscitia, infantia, & quod tam multi eruditione, eloquentia & pietate graues hucusq; cum mundi contumacia nequicquā luctati sunt. Sed aduersus hæc omnia cum Petro dicat ecclesiæ minister: Etsi hactenus non multum profecerint, qui hoc saxū voluerunt, & ego de meipso nihil mihi polliceri possim: quia tamen tu me ad Verbi tui ministerium vocauisti ô Deus, & quia tu iubes, vt rete illud Euangelicum in mare istud turbulentissimum demittam, vt doceam, moneā, horter, increpem, consoler: agedum tuo iussu & numine fretus faciam quod iubes, & tibi rei totius euentum permittam. Sic (inquam) rationem secum ineant Verbi prædicones, & proculdubio plus proficient quàm sperare possint. Idem faciant qui magistratum gerunt, & qui rempub. administrant. Habent enim hi quoq; desertum Dei verbum, qui suas Leges tueri, ius dicere, honestatem publicam propagare & scelera excindere iubet. Cui si obtemperauerint, non deerit successus, etiamsi multa obstare videantur. Similiter ad se hoc dictum transferant priuatim, qui vel agriculturæ vacant, vel artificia manuaria exercent, & hoc vnū spectent, vt retia sua ad Verbum Domini demittant, cuius benedictionem liberalem illico sentient. Atqui vtinam hunc fructum ex huius historiæ cognitione omnes referrent, vt de istis serio cogitarent. Sed in hoc publicè et priuatim peccatur, quod pleriq; lucem Euangelicam fugiunt, & inter humanæ rationis tenebras piscantur, non autem secundum Dei Verbum retia sua demittunt, id est, non in hoc intenti sunt, vt sua studia atq; actiones ad diuinæ voluntatis regulam dirigant.
units.tr: Peter, although they had wearied themselves all night in vain labour, nevertheless, when he heard Christ's command, said: "Master, though we have toiled all night, we have taken nothing; nevertheless, at your word, that is, at your command, I will let down the net." From this it appears that from Christ's sermons and miracles he had received the beginnings of faith, so that he now thought highly of him and recognised him as no ordinary teacher. This is also a truly notable example of faith, whose proper work is to make men obedient to God. Therefore all who glory in the name and title of faith ought to imitate Peter. And they will do so only if they submit all their feeling and understanding to God's Word. To bring this about, we must first take care not to look to our own efforts or to those of others, which have had less success in doing what they are commanded. For success tends to deceive those who attempt anything without God. But if they accommodate themselves to God's Word and believe his promises, they will see that what before seemed dangerous and impossible is safe and easy. Peter, at least in the present case, while obeying Christ's command, enclosed such a multitude of fish that those who were with him in the boat were not enough to haul it in; also the net, weighed down, was partly torn, and the catch filled both boats and nearly sank them with its weight. Let men of every place and rank therefore take consolation from this example, so that they may carry out their duty diligently and with constant faith, and not be moved by the objections that the flesh and the world raise. For, to begin with the ministers of the Word, many things present themselves that frighten them away from their office: such as their age, their lack of skill, their youth, and the fact that so many men weighty in learning, eloquence and piety have hitherto struggled in vain against the obstinacy of the world. But against all these things the minister of the Church, with Peter, should say: "Although those who wished to take this rock have not made much progress until now, and although I can promise nothing for myself, yet because you, O God, have called me to the ministry of your Word, and because you bid me let down that Gospel net into this most turbulent sea, so that I may teach, admonish, exhort and console, come now, relying on your command and power, I will do what you bid, and I will entrust the outcome of the whole matter to you." Thus, I say, let preachers of the Word reckon with themselves, and without doubt they will make more progress than they can hope for. Let those who hold magistracy and administer the commonwealth do the same. For these too have the Word of God set before them, which bids them uphold their laws, pronounce justice, advance public honesty and cut out crimes. If they obey it, success will not fail them, even though many things seem to stand in the way. Likewise let those who are devoted to agriculture or practise manual crafts, and who look to this one thing alone, apply this saying privately to themselves: that they let down their nets at the Lord's Word, and they will at once feel its generous blessing. Indeed, would that all men drew this fruit from the knowledge of this history, so that they would think seriously about these things. But the fault, both public and private, is that most people shun the Gospel light and fish among the darkness of human reason, and do not let down their nets according to God's Word, that is, they are not intent on directing their studies and actions by the rule of the divine will.

units.la: Postremò ipse Christus nobis spectandus venit, qui Petro ob præstitū sibi officium gratiam retribuit tanta liberalitate, quantā ille non ausus fuisset sperare. Docet autem suo exemplo, vt ipsi quoq; mentem gratitudo commendatur. gratos nos præbeamus illis, à quibus beneficium accepimus. Admonet de hoc natura lex, quæ in brutis quoque animantibus beneficij accepti sensum atque memoriam extare voluit. Quare rectissimè olim à Cicerone dictum fuit: Nihil est tam inhumanum, tam immane, tam ferum, quàm committere vt beneficio, non dicam indignus, sed vitius esse videare. Ostendit præterea Christus hoc facto, se maris, adeoq; totius machinæ mundi huius Dominum esse, qui & gratiam suis referre, & eosdem vbiq; alere possit. Extant huius generis infinita exempla. Idem enim ille est, qui Israelitis in deserto cotur nices adduxit, manna depluit, aquarum perennes fontes in petris aperuit: quiitem discipulis suis sic prospexit, vt nihil illis vnquam defuerit, etsi sine pecunijs & commeatu ab ipso emitterentur. Imò idem ille in animos hominum ius habet, & quosuis excitare potest, vt se seruis ipsius beneficos præbeant. Nimium ergo imprudentes & fatui sunt, qui dum huic seruiunt, sibi ab inopia & hominum insidijs metuunt. Nos potius agnoscamus eius virtutem, quæ in Euangelio se exerit, et secundum hoc instituamus nostra omnia, vt eius fauore & gratia tuti felices & beati viuamus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, Christ himself comes before us to be considered, who repaid Peter for the office he had performed with such generosity as Peter would not have dared to hope for. By his own example he also teaches that gratitude is commended to us. Let us show ourselves thankful to those from whom we have received a benefit. Nature's law advises us of this, since it willed that even in brute animals there should be a sense and memory of a benefit received. Therefore Cicero rightly said long ago: "Nothing is so inhuman, so monstrous, so savage, as to be seen to be ungrateful for a benefit—I will not say unworthy of one, but unwilling to return it." Christ also shows by this deed that he is Lord of the sea, and indeed of the whole machinery of this world, since he is able both to repay his followers with favour and to feed them everywhere. Examples of this kind are endless. For he is the same one who brought quails to the Israelites in the desert, rained down manna, and opened perpetual fountains of water from the rocks; and he so provided for his disciples that nothing ever failed them, even though they were sent out by him without money or provisions. Indeed, that same one has power over the minds of men and can stir up whomever he wishes to show themselves beneficent to his servants. Therefore those are very foolish and senseless who, while they serve him, fear for themselves from poverty and the plots of men. Rather let us acknowledge his power, which shows itself in the Gospel, and let us order all our affairs accordingly, so that under his favour and grace we may live safe, happy and blessed. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVII.

units.la: Cum autem hoc vidisset Simon Petrus, accidit ad genua Iesu, dicēs: Discede à me: nā homo peccator sum, Domine. Pauor enim occupa-rat eum, & omnes qui cum eo erant, super captura piscium, quā com-prehenderant. Similiter autem & Iacobum & Ioannem, filios Zebe-dæi, qui erant socij Simonis. Et ait ad Simonem Iesus: Ne metue, ab hoc tempore homines viuos capies. Illi autem cum subduxissent in terram nauigia, relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum.
units.tr: When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus' knees, saying, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." For terror had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish that they had taken, and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners of Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, "Do not fear; from now on you will catch men alive." When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

units.la: Omnes quidem gratiæ suæ & æternæ salutis thesauros Deus nobis in filio suo vnigenito mira & incredibili liberalitate offert, nosq; ad eum amplexandum magnificis promissionibus excitat atq; hortatur: at plerique hominum vili & obscura eius specie offensi, eum seruatorem & redemptorem suum agnoscere dedignantur. Sciebat ille hoc fore, & ideo ne quis iustam offensionis causam haberet, doctrinæ suæ miracula omnis generis coniunxit, quibus se & à Deo missum & virtute diuina instructum, imò Deum verum esse abunde docuit; & miracula illa confiato sic temperauit, vt neminem terrerent diuinæ virtutis splendore, sed potius iucundo & salutari bonitatis eius gustu omnes ad ipsum recipiendum inuitarent. Huius generis est, quod nuper in mirifica piscium captura æditum vidimus. Eo enim ostendit Christus se maris & omnium, quæ in mari sunt, Dominum esse: quod verè diuinitatis argumentum est euidentissimum. Quis enim hominum pisces sine lege natantes ex imis gurgitibus euocare & temere vagantes in vnum cògere potest præter Deum, qui illos creat & regit? Deinde docet nihil defore ijs, qui ipsi credunt atq; obediunt, ideoq; plurimum fecit miraculum hoc ad confirmandam quatuor discipulorum fidem, quos ad Apostolicum ministerium vocare voluit, ne relicta piscatione, ex qua hucusque vixerant, sibi fame perennndum putarent. Accedit etiam his tertium, quod eodem tota prædicationis euangelicæ aut ecclesiastici ministerij ratio adumbratur, de quo in præsenti, quod Dominus dederit, dicemus.
units.tr: God offers us all the treasures of his grace and eternal salvation in his only-begotten Son, with a wonderful and incredible generosity, and he stirs us up and urges us to embrace him with magnificent promises. Yet most people, offended by his lowly and obscure appearance, disdain to acknowledge him as their Saviour and Redeemer. Christ knew this would happen, and so, lest anyone have a just cause for offence, he joined to his teaching miracles of every kind, by which he amply showed that he was both sent by God and endowed with divine power, indeed that he was the true God. And he so tempered these miracles that they did not terrify anyone with the splendour of divine power, but rather invited all to receive him by the pleasant and healthful taste of his goodness. Of this kind is what we have lately seen in the wonderful catch of fish. For by it Christ showed that he is Lord of the sea and of all that is in the sea, which is a most evident proof of his divinity. For who but God, who creates and rules them, can draw up from the deep waters fish that swim without any law, and gather into one place those that wander at random? Next, he teaches that nothing will be lacking to those who believe in him and obey him; and so this miracle served greatly to confirm the faith of the four disciples, whom he wished to call to the apostolic ministry, so that they would not think they would starve for good by giving up the fishing by which they had lived until then. To these is added a third point: in this miracle the whole plan of the evangelical preaching or of the ecclesiastical ministry is foreshadowed, about which we shall speak in the present matter, as the Lord grants.

units.la: Prius tamen videre oportet, vt miraculo hoc Petrus & socij eius affecti fuerint, de quo sic scribit Lucas: Cum hoc vidisset Simon Petrus, accidit ad genua Iesu, dicens: Discede à me, nam homo peccator sum. Et mox huius dicti causa indicatur: Pauor enim occuparat ipsum, & omnes qui cum eo erant, super captura piscium, quam comprehenderant. Similiter autem & Iacobum & Ioannem, filios Zebedæi, qui erant socij Simonis. Primò ad genua Iesu concidisse dicitur, qui antiquitus supplicantium mos fuit. Quid verò petit? Discede à me, inquit. Et quare? Nā homo peccator sum. Mira sanè postulatio, & mirabilior multò postulationis istius causa. Quid enim magis absurdum atque noxium magis peti poterat, quàm vt Christus à nobis discedat, sine quo salus nostra consistare nullo modo potest? Et hoc quidem petunt, qui vel Deum & sacra omnia oderunt, vel propriæ iustitiæ fiducia elati, nullo alio seruatore sibi opus esse putant. At nimis ineptum & imprudens dens fuerit, hominem peccatorem velle, vt à se Christus discedat, qui solus peccata expiat, & nos cum Deo patre in gratiam reducit. Eò magis ergo nos Christi præsentiam expetere debemus, & nos peccatorum cupla grauatos esse sentiamus. Sed minus mirabimur Petrum, si causam huius diffidentiæ & animum illius propius inspiciamus. Nec enim diffidentiæ aut desperationis hæc vox est, multoque minus animi à Christo alieni indicium, sed potius eius, qui Christi maiestatem & accepti beneficij magnitudinem rectè æstimabat. Cùm enim antehac (vt ex Ioannis Capite primo colligere possumus) Christum doctoris loco habuisset, nunc in tanto miraculo diuinam quoque eius potentiam agnoscit, & cùm hac suam indignitatem conferens, seque mortalem & peccatorem esse cogitans, non potest non tanta illius familiaritate terreri, eò quòd simul in mentem veniebat, Christum abs se minus honorificè tractatum esse. Exempla similia in aliis quoque occurrunt, quorum pietas & fides in scripturis commendantur. Dauid certè cùm à Deo promissionem de Messia ex posteris suis nascituro accepisset, tantæ bonitatis & beneficentiæ consideratione abreptus dicebat: Quis sum ego Domine Deus, & quæ domus mea, quòd me tantopere euehis? Et nota est Centurionis vox, qui Christo domum eius subituro dixit: Domine non sum idoneus vt sub tectum meum intres, &c. Et sunt hæc quidem singularis pietatis argumenta, sed quæ simul de nostra miseria & infirmitate testantur, qua fit, vt qui Dei præsentia in primis opus habent, ea tamen terrentur, neque illam ferre possunt, nisi is in tempore nobis consolationem adhibeat. Est ergo plus quàm belluinus illorum stupor, qui cùm huius generis exempla passim occurrant, tamen adeò non humiliantur in Dei conspectu, vt potius propriæ iustitiæ fiducia turgidi eum tantumnon sibi debitorem facere audeant.
units.tr: Yet first we must see how Peter and his companions were affected by this miracle, of which Luke writes thus: "When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.'" And straightaway the reason for this saying is given: "For terror had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish that they had taken." Likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners of Simon. He is said first to have fallen at Jesus' knees, which was from ancient times the custom of suppliants. But what does he ask? "Depart from me," he says. And why? "For I am a sinful man." A strange request, and far stranger the cause of this request. For what could be more absurd or more harmful to ask than that Christ depart from us, without whom our salvation can in no way stand? And indeed those ask this who either hate God and all sacred things, or, puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, think they have no need of any other Saviour. But it is far too foolish and imprudent for a sinful man to wish that Christ depart from him, who alone expiates sins and restores us to favour with God the Father. Therefore all the more we ought to seek the presence of Christ, and feel ourselves weighed down by the burden of our sins. But we shall marvel less at Peter if we look more closely at the cause of this fear and at his state of mind. For this word is not a sign of distrust or despair, much less of a mind alienated from Christ, but rather of one who rightly estimated the majesty of Christ and the greatness of the benefit received. For since before this (as we can gather from the first chapter of John) he had regarded Christ as a teacher, now in so great a miracle he recognises also his divine power; and comparing with this his own unworthiness, and thinking of himself as mortal and a sinner, he cannot but be terrified by such close familiarity with him, because at the same time it came to mind that he had treated Christ with too little honour. Similar examples occur also in others, whose piety and faith are commended in the Scriptures. David certainly, when he had received from God the promise of the Messiah to be born from his descendants, carried away by consideration of so great a goodness and beneficence, said: "Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you raise me up so highly?" And the word of the centurion is well known, who said to Christ about to enter his house: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof," etc. These are indeed signs of singular piety, but they also bear witness to our misery and weakness; hence it comes about that those who especially need the presence of God are nonetheless terrified by it, and cannot bear it unless he, in due time, brings them consolation. Therefore that stupor of those men is more than brutish, who, although examples of this kind occur everywhere, are nonetheless so far from being humbled in the sight of God that, swollen with confidence in their own righteousness, they dare to make him, as it were, their debtor.

units.la: Admonemur autè insuper hoc exemplo, vt Dei beneficia à nobis considerari debeat, vt verum atq; proprium salutis fructum ex illis percipiamus. Proderit primò diligenter inter se conferre Dei maiestatem siue excellentiam atque nostram conditionem. Ibi mox tanta elucebit inæqualitas, vt nulla inter nos & illum communio intercedere possit, nisi ille sese ad nos demittere dignetur. Est enim ille æterna sapientia: nos quanti quanti sumus, stultitia sumus, neque percipere possumus quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Ille Veritas est: nos mendaces sumus, & ex mendacijs siue seriis siue ludicris summam voluptatem capimus. Ille vis est omnia penetrans & sese per omnia diffundens: nos infirmi, miseri & imbecilli sumus, siue animum siue corpus nostrum consideres. Ille iustitia est, nos in peccato concepti & nati nihil quàm peecare possumus. Ille summum bonum est, quod & sibiipsi sufficit, & omnibus creaturis sum ESSE largitur: nos ita omnium indigni sumus, vt vix vllum animal inuenias, quod pluribus subsidijs opus habeat. Accedit huic comparationi altera consideratio, qua multiplicem Dei beneficentiam nobis ob oculos ponamus, in qua exponenda facilius fuerit dicendi initium quàm finem inuenire. Nam vt ad generis nostri primam originem accedamus, quæ vnquam bonitas admirabilior fuit, quàm quòd hominem ex luto creauit Deus, vt esset cui benefaceret? In singulis autem eiusdem bonitatis indicia elucent, quando in vtero delitescentes mirificè seruat, tuetur, alit, & tandem quasi ex sepulchro extractos in lucem producit. Ad hæc in nobis pascendis & seruandis omnes mundi partes occupatas habet. Nobis enim cœli pluuiam, nives, rorem destillant: nobis vndique circumfusus aër monetur, vt & nos & reliqua omnia propter nos foueat atque vegetet: nobis perennes fluuiorum aut aquarum fontes fluunt, nobis terra omnis generis fruges producit: nobis perpetuo calore ignis vbique operatur: nobis equi, boues, asini, & reliqua animalia omnia laborant: ad nostrum denique obsequium aues, pisces, feræ omnes veniunt, vt in corruptissima hominis natura atque infelici conditione adhuc pristinæ aut veteris dignitatis vestigia agnoscas. Taceo nunc herbarum, gemmarum et plurium aliarum rerum vires, quibus eas instruxit Deus, vt valetudini tuendæ seruire possint. Sunt hæc tanta tamen multa diuinæ beneficentiæ argumenta, vt nullum tempus, imò nulla hominum exercitatissimorum facundia illis enumerandis possit sufficere, Maiora tamen sunt, quæ ad æternæ salutis negotium pertinent. Nam qui nullius indigus est, nobis miseris & plus quam miseris, imò perditis, fœdere coniungi dignatus est: & vt nos ipsi sociorum atque amicorum loco esse constaret, voluntatem suam & quæcunq; nobis cognitu necessaria sunt regni sui mysteria manifestauit, eaq; omnia literis mandari voluit, ne ab incertis reuelationibus pendentes impostorum fallacijs atque insidijs pateremus.
units.tr: We are admonished moreover by this example that we ought to consider the benefits of God, so that we may receive from them the true and proper fruit of salvation. It will first be useful to compare carefully with one another the majesty or excellence of God and our condition. There will at once shine forth such great inequality that no communion can exist between us and him, unless he deigns to stoop down to us. For he is eternal wisdom; we, however great we are, are foolishness, and cannot perceive the things of the Spirit of God. He is Truth; we are liars, and from lies, whether serious or playful, we derive our greatest pleasure. He is a power penetrating all things and diffusing itself through all things; we are weak, wretched and feeble, whether you consider our soul or our body. He is righteousness; we, conceived and born in sin, can do nothing but sin. He is the supreme good, who both suffices for himself and bestows being on all creatures; we are so unworthy of everything that you can hardly find any animal that needs more help. To this comparison is added another consideration, by which we set before our eyes the manifold beneficence of God, in describing which it will be easier to find a beginning of speech than an end. For, to come to the first origin of our race, what goodness was ever more admirable than that God formed man out of clay, that there might be someone to whom he could do good? In the individual parts, too, the signs of this same goodness shine forth, when, while we lie hidden in the womb, he wondrously preserves, protects and nourishes us, and at last brings us forth into the light as if drawn from a tomb. Besides, in feeding and preserving us he has all parts of the world at work. For the rain, snow and dew of heaven drip down for us; the air that surrounds us on every side is commanded to cherish and quicken both us and all other things for our sake; for us the perennial streams of rivers and the springs of waters flow; for us the earth produces every kind of fruit; for us the fire works everywhere with its perpetual heat; for us horses, oxen, asses and all other animals labour; finally, for our service birds, fish and all wild beasts come, so that in the most corrupt nature of man and his unhappy condition you may still recognise traces of his former or original dignity. I say nothing now of the powers of herbs, gems and many other things, with which God has furnished them, so that they may serve to preserve our health. These are such great and many proofs of divine beneficence that no time, indeed no eloquence of the most practised men, could suffice to enumerate them. Greater still, however, are those things that pertain to the business of eternal salvation. For he who needs nothing deigned to join himself to us by a covenant, who are wretched and more than wretched, indeed lost; and that it might be established that we are in the place of companions and friends, he made known his will and the mysteries of his kingdom that are necessary for us to know, and he willed that all these things be committed to writing, lest, depending on uncertain revelations, we be exposed to the deceits and snares of impostors.

units.la: {x} 4 Neq; in his subsistit Dei beneficentia, sed quasi nihil in nos vnquam contulisset, filium quoque vnigenitum dedit, cùm nobis eo ad reparandam salutem opus esse videret. Venit is non in humilem modò & abiectam Petri piscatoris naviculam, sed in mundum hunc venit, in vallem lachrimarum venit, imò in carnem miseram & mortalem venit, vt nobis vnitus naturam nostram Deo reconciliaret. Et cùm in carne ageret, non solùm docendo & factis miraculosis se nobis familiarissimum praebuit, verumetiam facinorosis accenseri, & cum his infame crucis dirae supplicium subire dignatus est, vt nos ab omni scelerum nexu exolueret. Neque abiecit semel susceptum infelicis carnis pondus, cùm ea ad peragendam generis nostri redemptionē vsus esset, sed in corruptibilitate & immortalitate donatam in caelos subuexit, vt illic pignoris loco esset, quod nos de regni caelestis possessione olim obtinenda certos atq; securos faceret. Quodq; olim in terris agens fecit, hoc ipsum quotidie facere satagit, quando nobis praesens adest, & seipsum atq; salutem aeternam nobis per euangelium offert, adeoq; expansis brachijs & clara voce omnes ad se inuitat, qui laborant & onerati sunt. Adde his quàm patienter mores nostros ferat, quàm clementer nostrum delictis ignoscat, quanta indulgentia nostras querelas & indignissima murmura audiat, & nullum in illo patris indulgentissimi officium desiderabis. Qui ista intra animos suos probè secum expendunt, ij non poterunt non exclamare: Exi à nobis Domine, nam homines peccatores & tantis beneficijs indigni sumus. Ecquid est homo mortalis, vt memoriam eius habeas? & filius hominis, vt eum inuisas? Sedò infelicem & deploratam nostri seculi ingratitudinem, qua plerique & temporalia & spiritualia Dei beneficia contemnunt, vel etiam ijsdem turpiter ad omnem nequitiam abutuntur. Causa tanti malies, quòd etsi ex illis fructum multiplice percipiant, nunquam tamen expendunt vnde ea habeant, nisi quando praeter expectationem in aliquam calamitatem proiecti se miseros et infelices esse sentiunt. At ne tunc quidem pristinam Dei bonitatem & suam ingratitudinem agnoscunt, sed indignissimè secum agi clamant, & quasi quae illis propria sint Deus eripuerit, eum tantum mnò in ius vocare audent, deq; iniusto illius rigore conqueri, quando supplices ad eius genua procidere deq; illo sibi reconciliando cogitare debebant. Sunt praeterea alij, qui ne iudiciorum quidem Dei exemplis mouentur, & ea secuti contemnunt: aut si quando hunc sibi iratum esse sentiunt, tunc vel ferociter nimis aduersus illum insurgunt, vel desperabundi eius faciem oderunt atq; fugiunt. Et haec cùm hodie passim fiant, adhuc tamen nos miseros atq; infelices esse miramur?
units.tr: 4 Nor does God's kindness stop there. As if he had never given us anything, he also gave his only-begotten Son, since he saw that we needed him to restore our salvation. He came not merely into the humble and despised little boat of Peter the fisherman, but into this world, into the vale of tears, indeed into miserable and mortal flesh, so that, united with us, he might reconcile our nature to God. And while he lived in the flesh, he not only presented himself to us as most familiar through his teaching and miraculous deeds, but also deigned to be counted among criminals and to undergo with them the infamous punishment of the dreadful cross, so that he might free us from every bond of sin. Nor did he cast off the burden of frail flesh once he had taken it up, though he used it to accomplish the redemption of our race. He carried it up into the heavens, given incorruptibility and immortality, so that there it might serve as a pledge, making us certain and secure about the future possession of the heavenly kingdom. What he did once while living on earth, he now strives to do every day, when he is present with us and offers himself and eternal salvation to us through the gospel. With outstretched arms and a clear voice he invites all who labour and are burdened. Add to this how patiently he bears our ways, how mercifully he pardons our sins, how great his indulgence in hearing our complaints and most unworthy murmurings; you will find no office of a most indulgent Father lacking in him. Those who weigh these things carefully within their minds cannot but cry out: "Depart from us, Lord, for we are sinful men and unworthy of such great benefits. What is man, that you should remember him, or the son of man, that you should visit him?" But look at the wretched and hopeless ingratitude of our age, by which most people despise both the temporal and the spiritual benefits of God, or even shamefully abuse them for every kind of wickedness. The cause of so great an evil is that, although they receive manifold fruit from these benefits, they never consider where they come from, unless, cast unexpectedly into some calamity, they feel themselves wretched and unhappy. Yet not even then do they acknowledge God's former goodness and their own ingratitude. Instead they cry out that they are treated most unworthily, and, as if God had snatched away what was rightly theirs, they dare to summon him to court and complain of his unjust severity, when they ought to fall as suppliants at his knees and think about being reconciled to him. There are others who are not moved even by the examples of God's judgments; despising them, they go their own way. Or if at any time they feel that he is angry with them, then either they rise up against him too fiercely, or in despair they hate his face and flee from it. And since these things are done everywhere today, do we still wonder that we are wretched and unhappy?

units.la: Porrò ad Christum veniamus, qui pia & sancta infirmitate laborantibus mox succurrit: & ita eos consolatur, vt simul miraculum hoc & historiam omnem praesenti instituto accommodet. Nam ad Simonem, qui plus aliis trepidabant, conuersus ait: Ne metue, ab hoc tempore homines viuos capies. Quibus verbis hoc dicere videtur: Terret te tanti miraculi consideratio, & meae virtutis sensu consternatus trepidas: sed non in eum finem illud edidi, vt timeas, sed vt spem bonam animo concipias, & ad functionem, cui te destinaui, fortiter accedas. Nunc enim multò maius opus te vocat. Qui enim hucusq; piscibus capiendis intentus fuisti, vt te tuamque familiam aleres, ab hoc tempore homines capies, & quidem viuos, vt illis vita & salutu aeterna administer fis, &c. Quàmuis autem in praesentarium vni Petro loquatur, haec tamen ad eius quoque socios pertinuisse ex Matthaei & Marci narratione constat, qui eandem historiam succinctius descripserunt. Continetur autem his tot ministerij ecclesiastici ratio, de qua aliquid dicemus.
units.tr: Let us now come to Christ, who soon comes to the aid of those who labour under a holy and pious weakness, and so comforts them that he fits this miracle and the whole story to the present purpose. For turning to Simon, who was more alarmed than the others, he says: "Do not be afraid; from now on you will catch men alive." By these words he seems to say: "The consideration of so great a miracle terrifies you, and, dismayed by the sense of my power, you tremble. But I did not perform it so that you should be afraid, but so that you should conceive good hope in your mind and approach boldly the task for which I have destined you. For now a much greater work calls you. You who until now have been intent on catching fish to feed yourself and your family, from now on will catch men, and indeed alive, so that you may minister to them life and eternal salvation," and so on. Although he speaks for the moment to Peter alone, it is clear from the accounts of Matthew and Mark, who described the same history more briefly, that these words pertained also to his companions. This passage contains the whole rationale of the ecclesiastical ministry, about which we shall say something.

units.la: Primùm hic consideranda venit mundi & in hoc agentium hominum conditio. Illum per mare adumbrari, nuper diximus. In eo itaq; homines vitam degunt, instar piscium. Nam vt bi nullis legibus parent, sed temere vagantur, & alij alios deuorant atq; perdunt: ita nisi maior aliqua vis homines coërceat, ipsi quoque excusso legum iugo incerti dubijsq; affectibus ducuntur, & sibiipsis multum interitum struunt. Est hoc notius, quàm vt multa demonstratione opus sit. Magna autem in hoc elucet Dei bonitas, qui talium rationem habet, deq; illis colligendis & ab exitio vindicandis cogitat. Debet huius consideratio nos excitare, ne in carnis & affectuum licentia felicitatem nostram sitam esse putemus, sed Deo nos in ordinem redigendos praebeamus.
units.tr: First, the condition of the world and of the people acting in it must be considered here. We said recently that the world is foreshadowed by the sea. In it, then, men live their lives like fishes. For just as fishes obey no laws but wander at random, and one devours and destroys another, so unless some greater force restrains men, they too, having shaken off the yoke of laws, are driven uncertainly and by doubtful passions, and they prepare great ruin for themselves. This is too well known to need much demonstration. Yet in this shines forth the great goodness of God, who takes account of such people and thinks about gathering them in and rescuing them from destruction. This consideration ought to stir us, lest we think our happiness lies in the licence of the flesh and the passions, but rather we should present ourselves to be brought back into order by God.

units.la: Qua autem ratione suos ex huius mundi pelago Deus colligit? Per Euangelij praedicationem. Nam quos praesciuit (inquit Apostolus) eosdem & praedestinauit: quos verò praedestinauit, eos & vocauit. Vocationis vero externa medium siue instrumentum est Euangelium, quod non obscurè Christus stus innuit, Apostolis dicens: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ, &c. Et idem hoc apud Matthæum sagenæ confert, qua piscatores in numero fiori piscium captura vti con sueuerunt. His vero prædicationem, non angelis, sed hominibus certis commendat Dominus, quos ex communi mortalium sorte delectos ad hoc munus destinauit. Et est hic probè obseruandum, quod in Matthæo dicit: Ego vos faciam piscatores hominum. Quia enim nos non capimus quæ sunt spi ritus Dei, & ne ad cogitandū quidem idonei sumus, nemo hic quicquam proficiet, nisi à Deo vocatus & missus fuerit. Ideò Paulus ad Ephesios scribit, Christum dona spiritus distribuere, & doctores, pastores, prophetas, Apostolos dare, qui Ecclesiam colligant atq; ædificent. Et alibi, Quomodo (in- quit) prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Et huc quoq; pertinet, quòd qui prius tota nocte nihil cœperant, nunc tantam prædam trahunt, quando ex Christi mandato retia laxauerunt. Etenim in tenebris nequicquam piscantur, qui nõ expectata Domini vocatione priuato affectu docendi prouinciam su- scipiunt. Discant ergo legitimam vocationē expectare, qui ad ecclesiæ ministerium aspirant, ne dum banc præuertunt, & sibi ipsis onus imponant, cui ferendo nõ possint sufficere, & simul ecclesijs dam- num dent. Qui vero ministros vocandi ius habent, eos quærant quorum eruditio, pietas & docendi dexteritas iam ante satis perspecta sit. Nam etsi hic rudes & illiteratos piscatores vocarit Domi- nus, non tamen hoc in exemplum trahi debet, vt hodie ab Anabaptistis fieri solet. Licuit enim Chri- sto qualescunq; vocare, quia nouas mentes formare & subito spiritus donis suos instruere poterat: quod illum in Apostolis fecisse constat. At longè alia est eorum conditio, qui vt eligendo & vocando falli possunt: ita errore ipsi corrigere non possunt, cùm in hominum mentes nihil iuris habeant. Ad- monet de hoc Paulus quando episcopum eligere iubet ἐπίσκοπον, id est, qui ad docendū sit idoneus.
units.tr: By what means does God gather his own out of the sea of this world? Through the preaching of the gospel. "Those whom he foreknew," says the Apostle, "he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called." The outward means or instrument of calling is the gospel, which Christ clearly indicated when he said to the Apostles: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature," and so on. He likewise compares it, in Matthew, to a net, which fishermen are accustomed to use for catching a great number of fish. The Lord entrusts this preaching not to angels but to certain men, whom he chose from the common lot of mortals and appointed for this office. And here it must be carefully observed what he says in Matthew: "I will make you fishers of men." For since we do not grasp the things of the Spirit of God, and are not even fit to think of them, no one will accomplish anything here unless he has been called and sent by God. Therefore Paul writes to the Ephesians that Christ distributes the gifts of the Spirit, and gives teachers, pastors, prophets and Apostles, who gather and build up the Church. And elsewhere: "How," he says, "shall they preach unless they are sent?" This also pertains here: those who had caught nothing all night now draw in such a great catch, because at Christ's command they let down the nets. For those who take up the office of teaching without waiting for the Lord's calling, moved by private desire, fish in vain in the dark. Let those who aspire to the ministry of the Church therefore learn to wait for a lawful calling, lest by anticipating it they impose on themselves a burden they cannot bear, and at the same time cause loss to the churches. Those who have the right to call ministers should seek out men whose learning, piety and skill in teaching have already been sufficiently tested. For although the Lord here called rude and unlettered fishermen, this must not be drawn into an example, as the Anabaptists are wont to do today. Christ was free to call whatever sort of men, because he could form new minds and suddenly furnish them with the gifts of the Spirit, as is clear he did in the Apostles. But the condition of those who can be deceived in choosing and calling, and who cannot in turn correct the error themselves, since they have no right over men's minds, is quite different. Paul warns about this when he orders that a bishop [ἐπίσκοπον] be chosen, that is, one fit for teaching.

units.la: Cæterum doctoris officium quoq; parabola hæc & ipsius Christi verba pulchrè adumbrant. Pi-scator in alto progressus rete iacit, & quicquid hoc completitur trahit, neq; de separandis inutilibus cogitat, donec vel in nauim adductos videt pisces, vel in littus redijt: Ita ministrorū est in mundum exire, Verbū publicè omnibus prædicare, & ad ecclesiæ Christi societatē trahere omnes qui accedunt & se trahi patiuntur, neq; circa initia statim nimia curiositate inquirere, qui nam illa digni aut indigni sint. Nam vt ferè prædam omnē quasi è manibus amittunt, qui inter piscandū separationem faciunt, & vt triticū cum zizanijs euellunt, qui priusquā segetes adoleuerint illa tollere conantur: ita importuni quidam priusquam ecclesias constituant, intempestiuis excommunicationibus plerosq; abster rent, ne ad rete illud euangelicū accedant: quæ causa est, vt interdū magna segetis spes in ipsa herba extinguatur. Meminerint ergo omnes, se ad colligendum potius quàm ad dissipandum destinatos esse, neq; temerè in alienas conscientias sibi ius & imperium vendicent. Deinde viuos capere debent homines, & vt ijdem Christo viuant curare. Quis enim piscatorē probauerit, qui adhuc reti inclusos pisces occidit? Ita nunquam poterunt viuifici Verbi administri censeri, qui docendo homi-nibus mortem accersunt. Faciunt autem hoc, qui aut nimio rigore ad desperationem adducunt, aut indulgentia nimia authores sunt, vt in vitijs atq; sceleribus computrescant, qui Christo viuere de-bebant. Hic ergo simul officij admonentur, qui ex credentium numero haberi volunt. Horum est, vt & se capi patiantur per Euangelium, & capti viuant. Nõ enim Christi pisces sunt, qui adhuc in mundo vagantur, & huius desiderijs vacant: neq; illi gratus cibus sunt, qui non se illi hostiam viuen tem sistunt, vt per ipsos Deus glorificetur. Ideò passim Apostoli monent, vt quotidie peccato moria mur, resurgamus autem ad vitam nouam. Sitit & esurit Christus salutem nostram. Huius ergo de-siderium satiare debent pia fidei obedientia, quicunq; ecclesiæ ipsius membra esse cupiunt.
units.tr: The parable and Christ's own words also beautifully picture the office of the teacher. The fisherman goes out into the deep, casts his net, and draws in whatever it encloses, and he does not think of separating out the useless ones until he sees the fish brought into the boat or returns to shore. So it is the task of ministers to go out into the world, to preach the Word publicly to all, and to draw into the fellowship of Christ's Church all who come and allow themselves to be drawn, not inquiring at the outset, with excessive curiosity, who are worthy or unworthy. For just as those who make a separation while fishing almost lose the whole catch from their hands, and as those who try to pull up the tares with the wheat before the crop has grown lose the harvest, so certain rash men, before they have established churches, by ill-timed excommunications keep most people away, so that they do not come to that gospel net. This is why sometimes a great hope of the harvest is quenched in the very blade. Let everyone therefore remember that they are appointed to gather rather than to scatter, and not rashly claim for themselves right and rule over other people's consciences. Next, they must catch men alive, and take care that these same men live for Christ. For who would approve a fisherman who kills the fish still enclosed in the net? So those who bring death to men by their teaching can never be counted ministers of the life-giving Word. Yet those do this who either by excessive severity drive men to despair, or by excessive indulgence cause those who ought to live for Christ to rot away in vices and wickedness. Here, then, those who wish to be counted among believers are at the same time reminded of their duty. It is theirs both to allow themselves to be caught by the gospel and, having been caught, to live. For those who still wander in the world and give themselves to its desires are not Christ's fish, nor is he pleased with those who do not present themselves to him as living sacrifices, so that God may be glorified through them. Therefore the Apostles everywhere warn us that we must die daily to sin and rise again to new life. Christ thirsts and hungers for our salvation. Therefore whoever desires to be a member of his Church ought to satisfy this longing with pious and faithful obedience.

units.la: Cæterum dum officium magno cum successu faciunt pij euangelicæ doctrinæ prædones, duo ferè incommoda incidere solent, quæ & ipsis in miraculi huius historia Christus adumbrari voluit. Primò rete scissum fuisse audiuimus: quo indicatur, semper fore aliquos, qui simplici Veritati doctrinæ contradicant, & ecclesiæ vnitatem scindant. Nam vt Paulus ait, oportet sectas esse, vt manifesti fiant qui probati sunt. Et harum fere authores sunt, qui aut veteris superstitionis fermentum cum Euangelio miscent (quod olim fecerunt, qui cùm ex Pharisæis Christiani facti essent, Legis iugum credentibus imponere ausi sunt) aut ambitionis æstro exagitati præ alijs spere volunt, & vt emineant nouorum dogmatum authores fiunt. Ita Arium olim impiam doctrinam inuexisse, et pestilentissimū scisma excitauisse historici tradunt, quòd Alexandrinæ ecclesiæ episcopatum non potuissent obtinere: quod ipsum multis aliis accidisse constat. Atq; vtinam non idem hodie etiam fieret ab iis, qui ne quid ignorauisse aut in aliquo errauisse videantur, praecipua Papistica superstitionis fulcra, Christum impanatum & simulachrorum vsum in templis, pertinacissimè defendunt, & maximum negotium faciunt iis, qui in reducenda primitiuae Ecclesiae puritate laborant. Alterum incommodum fuit, nauiculae nimio pondere depressae submersio. Accidit, & hoc frequenter, vt Ecclesiae maximo oneri sint & eam tantum non deprimant, qui non alio quàm carnis studio ad illam accedunt. Ex horum numero sunt, qui aut commodum priuatum quaerunt, aut sub Euangelicae libertatis praetextu peccandi licentiam venantur. Tales Apostolorum numero fuere Ananias, Simon Magus & ἀταξτοι illi, id est, inordinati & exleges, de quibus in Epistolis Paulinis frequens fit mentio. Hodie etiam maximus eorum numerus est, qui non alia de causa Euangelium profitentur, quàm vt ex ecclesia & coenobiorum bonis ditescant, & excusso omnis disciplinae iugo licenter viuant. Sunt hi grauissima Ecclesiae onera, & labes sunt publicae, quibus tota Euangelij doctrina infamis redditur. Attamen non terreant horum exempla pios. Vt enim in praesenti in littus educuntur pisces illi, quàmuis & rete fundatur, & nauicula tantum non submersa fatisfcat: ita nihil obstabit, quo minus electos suos in beatae immortalitatis littus ex furentis mundi oceano Christus educat, vt cum ipso viuant & regnent.
units.tr: But while the pious preachers of the evangelical doctrine carry out their office with great success, two inconveniences usually befall them, which Christ wished to foreshadow even in the history of this miracle. First, we heard that the net was torn: by this is indicated that there will always be some who oppose the simple truth of the doctrine and split the unity of the Church. For, as Paul says, there must be sects, so that those who are approved may be made manifest. The authors of these are for the most part those who either mix the leaven of the old superstition with the Gospel (as those did who, having been Pharisees and become Christians, dared to impose the yoke of the Law on believers), or, driven by the goad of ambition, wish to stand out above others and become authors of new dogmas so that they may be prominent. Thus historians record that Arius of old introduced an impious doctrine and stirred up a most pestilential schism, because he could not obtain the bishopric of the Church of Alexandria; and it is well established that this has happened to many others too. And would that the same did not happen today with those who, lest they seem to have been ignorant of anything or to have erred in any point, most obstinately defend the chief props of Papist superstition, the impanation of Christ and the use of images in the temples, and make the greatest trouble for those who labour to restore the purity of the primitive Church. The second inconvenience was the sinking of the little boat, weighed down by too great a load. This also happens frequently: those who approach the Church for no other reason than fleshly interest become a very great burden to it and all but sink it. Among their number are those who seek private advantage, or who hunt for a licence to sin under the pretext of evangelical liberty. Of this sort among the Apostles' company were Ananias, Simon Magus, and those ἀταξτοι, that is, the disorderly and lawless, of whom frequent mention is made in the Pauline Epistles. Even today the number of such people is very large: they profess the Gospel for no other reason than to grow rich from the goods of the Church and of the monasteries, and, having shaken off the yoke of all discipline, to live licentiously. These are the heaviest burdens of the Church and the blots of the public, by which the whole doctrine of the Gospel is brought into disrepute. Yet let not these examples terrify the godly. For just as, in the present miracle, those fish are drawn to shore, although the net is torn and the little boat is all but sunk, so nothing will hinder Christ from leading his elect out of the ocean of this raging world to the shore of blessed immortality, that they may live and reign with him.

units.la: Redeamus nunc ad Petrum & socios eius, qui cum nauigia in terram subduxissent, relictis omnibus Christum secuti sunt. Atqui multa erant, quae illos ab instituto revocare poterant, sicuti in Marco nostro annotauimus. Sed maior est diuinae vocationis atque fidei vis, quàm vt vllis remoris impediri possit. Nam vt supra diximus, quos praedestinauit Deus, eosdem efficaciter vocare solet, vt intra animos suos illuminati Verbo eius credant & spiritus sancti tractum studiose sequantur. Et huc pertinet illud Christi: Oues meae vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur eam. Etenim qui diuinae bonitatis gustu fide non ficta percipiunt, iis nihil antiquius est, quàm cum Deo coniungi, & ideo non possunt non Christum sequi & amplecti, quem nobis gratia diuina mediatorem datum esse audiunt. Similis obedientiae exemplum in Abrahamo Moses proponit, qui Deo vocante solum natale cum domo patria & agnatus omnibus reliquit, etiamsi nesciret vbi nam terrarum ipsi sedes nouas parauisset Deus. Quod ipsum à Matthaeo quoq; factitatum fuisse, non multò post audiemus.
units.tr: Let us now return to Peter and his companions, who, when they had drawn their boats to land, left everything and followed Christ. Yet there were many things which could have called them back from their purpose, as we noted in our treatment of Mark. But the power of the divine calling and of faith is greater than that it can be hindered by any obstacles. For, as we said above, those whom God has predestined he is accustomed to call effectually, so that, enlightened within their souls by his Word, they believe and eagerly follow the pull of the Holy Spirit. To this belongs that saying of Christ: My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me. For those who perceive the taste of divine goodness with unfeigned faith have nothing more precious than to be joined to God, and therefore they cannot but follow and embrace Christ, whom they hear has been given to us by divine grace as Mediator. Moses sets before us a similar example of obedience in Abraham, who, at God's calling, left his native land, his father's house and all his kindred, even though he did not know where on earth God had prepared a new dwelling for him. We shall hear shortly that Matthew did the same thing.

units.la: Attamen minimè superuacaneum fuerit videre, quomodo Apostoli omnia sua reliquerint. Abutuntur enim horum exemplo multi, qui & ipsos perperam imitantur, & promisicuè ab omnibus, vt idem faciant, exigunt. At si Euangelistas audiamus, ita in praesenti sua reliquerunt, vt ijsdem quam diu licebat, adhuc vsi sint. Nam in domum suam postea Petrus iterum diuertit, & nauim atq; retia habuit, quibus ad piscandum adhuc vsus est, cum Christus ex mortuis resurrexisset: quod Ioannes diligenter narrat. Interea verò, quia illos ad functionē altiorem Christus destinauerat, necesse fuit, vt sibi eos familiariores faceret, & vt comites ipsius indiuulsi essent, quod à vulgo credentium minime requisiuit, quibus domi suae subsistere & rebus suis vacare licuit, vt in Iosephi, Nicodemi, Simonis & Lazari, ciuium Bethanien sium, & multorum aliorum exemplis est videre. Tandem cùm tempus illud venisset, quo Euangelium in toto orbe pedicari oportuit, tunc procul relictis omnibus commissum sibi munus summo studio obiuerunt. Praepositeri ergo & inepti nimis (& ne quid grauius dicam) Apostolorum imitatores sunt, qui cùm nulla Dei vocatione vrgeantur, relictis vxoribus, liberis & rebus domesticis omnibus, incerti oberrant, & cùm nemini vtiles sint, ex alieno tamen viuunt. Idem de Monachis dici potest, nisi quòd hi Christo et Apostolis simul turpissimè illudunt, quando paupertatem professi voluntariam in omni rerum abundantia securi & otiosi delitiantur. Itaq; in sanctorum gestis non omnia in exemplum trahi debent, ne dum praeter vocationem nostram illos imitamur, impij simus nostrae stationis desertores. Verbi quidem administris ista necessitas incumbit, vt posthabitis aliis rebus omnibus, se totos functioni suae dedicent, ad quam vocati sunt. Reliquis sufficit, si suae etiam vocationi intenti, in ea officium sedulo faciant, simulq; parati sint, si ita ferat necessitas, omnia sua relinquere & extrema quaeuis pati pro Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet it will by no means be superfluous to see how the Apostles left all their possessions. Many abuse their example, both imitating them wrongly and demanding indiscriminately of all that they do the same. But if we listen to the Evangelists, they left their possessions in such a way that they continued to use them for as long as it was permitted. For Peter afterwards went back to his own house again, and he had a boat and nets, with which he still went fishing after Christ had risen from the dead, as John carefully relates. Meanwhile, since Christ had destined them for a higher function, it was necessary that he make them more intimate with himself, and that they be his inseparable companions, which he did not require of the common crowd of believers, who were allowed to remain at home and attend to their own affairs, as can be seen in the examples of Joseph, Nicodemus, Simon, Lazarus, citizens of Bethany, and many others. At last, when the time came when the Gospel had to be spread through the whole world, then they, having left everything far behind, performed with the greatest zeal the task committed to them. Therefore those who, though pressed by no calling from God, leave wives, children and all domestic affairs, and wander about uncertain, and though useful to no one, nevertheless live at others' expense, are imitators of the Apostles that are most preposterous and foolish (and not to say anything more severe). The same can be said of the monks, except that these shamefully mock Christ and the Apostles at the same time, when, having professed voluntary poverty, they revel in carefree idleness amid every abundance of goods. Therefore not everything in the deeds of the saints ought to be drawn into example, lest, while we imitate them beyond our calling, we become impious deserters of our station. Indeed, this necessity lies upon the ministers of the Word, that, setting aside all other things, they dedicate themselves wholly to the function to which they have been called. For the rest it is enough, if they too, intent upon their own calling, faithfully perform the duty in it, and at the same time are ready, should necessity so require, to leave all their possessions and to endure any extremity for Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVIII.

units.la: Et factum est cum esset in quadam vrbe, tum ecce adfuit quidā plenus lepra, ac viso Iesu procidens in faciem rogauit eum, dicens: Domine, si velis, potes me mundare. Iesus autem extensa manu tetigit eum, dicens, Volo, mundator. Et statim lepra abiit ab eo. Ipse vero praecepit ei, vt nulli hoc diceret, sed vade (inquit) ostende teipsum Sacerdoti, & offer pro mundatione tui, prout praecepit Moses, in testimonium illis. Dimanabat autem eo magis rumor de illo, & conueniebat turba multa, vt audirent, & per eum sanarentur à morbis suis. Ipse vero secedens erat in desertis, & precabatur.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when he was in a certain city, behold, a man full of leprosy saw Jesus, fell on his face, and besought him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." And Jesus put forth his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately the leprosy departed from him. He charged him to tell no one, but said, "Go and show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a testimony to them." But the report of him spread abroad all the more, and great crowds came together to hear and to be healed of their infirmities. But he withdrew into the wilderness and prayed.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus filium suum vnigenitum humani generis seruatorem esse voluit, & in eo omnia dedit, quae ad nos seruandos necessaria sunt: ita eundem priusquam incarnaretur pluribus scripturae veteris testimonijs, postea autem cum iam carnem assumpsisset, infinitis & stupendis miraculis commendauit. Id vero non ipsius Christi causa factum est, qui testimonijs alienis minimè opus habet, sed propter nos, quorum ea est peruersitas, vt in externa solùm intenti, eius contempta et ignobili specie facilè offendamur, nisi subinde sub hac latentis diuinae virtutis argumenta in oculos nostros incurrant. Debent ergo quae de eius miraculis Euangelistae scribunt, non vt prophanae aliquae narrationes legi, sed penitius excuti & inspici, vt ea in illis probè obseruemus, quae nos in illius pleniorem cognitionem inducere, & simul nostri officij admonere possunt. Et hic iste etiam miraculi, quod modo recitauimus, nobis vsus esse debet, eò quòd ceu in speculo contemplanda proponit, quaecunque nobis in toto humanae salutis negotio cognitu & obseruatu necessaria sunt. Primò enim in leprosi persona infelix & deplorata nostrae naturae corruptio adumbratur, qua fit, vt à Dei conspectu & Ecclesiae eius societate exclusi vagemur, neque vlla humana arte aut virtute restitui possimus. Deinde eiusdem exemplo docet spiritus sanctus, quid nos facere deceat, si purgari & seruari velimus: nimirum, vt agnitione peccatorum & infelicis nostrae conditionis territi, ad Christum confugiamus, & certa fiducia eum esse credamus, qui nobis salutem afferre possit, neque de eiusdem voluntate desperemus. Qua in re potior est nostra quàm huius leprosi conditio: quia ex Euangelio certiores reddimur, illum nihil perinde cupere, quàm vt nos purgari patiamur. Quod ipsum in praesenti etiam historia apparet. Tertiò enim Christus se medicum animae & corporis esse declarat, & ita quidem, vt suam in nobis iuuandis facilitatem, imò ardens & ad quaevis obeunda paratum nostrae salutis studium euidentissimè testetur. Quartò, mundatum à lepra ad Sacerdotes ablegat, qui ex Dei instituto lepræ inspectores erant. Itaq; politico ordini sese accommodat Dominus, simulq; eo facto non tam leprosum illum sui officij admonet, quàm nos omnes docet, perfectè nos ab ipso purgari, ita vt in ipsius Dei iudicio subsistere possimus, & illic pro iustis atque sanctis habeamur, si ipsi per fidem inferamur. Subijcitur his posteremò miraculi effectus siue fructus, qui ex eo ad plures alios redundauit: & quid porrò Christus fecerit. Quia verò de tota huius miraculi historia & primis quatuor eius capitibus in Marco nostro abunde dictum est, nunc illis relictis, quae de postremo dicenda sunt, videbimus.
units.tr: Just as God willed his only-begotten Son to be the Saviour of mankind, and gave in him everything necessary for our salvation, so he commended the same Son, before his incarnation, by many testimonies of the Scripture of the Old Testament, and afterwards, when he had now taken on flesh, by countless and wonderful miracles. This was not done for Christ's own sake, for he has no need of the testimony of others, but for our sake, whose perversity is such that, being intent only on outward things, we are easily offended by his despised and humble appearance, unless from time to time signs of his hidden divine power fall under our eyes. Therefore, what the evangelists write about his miracles ought not to be read as some profane narratives, but examined and inspected more deeply, so that we may carefully observe in them those things which can lead us into a fuller knowledge of him and at the same time remind us of our duty. And this miracle which we have just recited ought to be of use to us here too, since it sets before us, as if in a mirror, everything that is necessary for us to know and observe in the whole business of human salvation. First, in the person of the leper is portrayed the unhappy and desperate corruption of our nature, by which we wander, shut out from the sight of God and the fellowship of his Church, and cannot be restored by any human art or virtue. Next, by the example of the leper the Holy Spirit teaches what it becomes us to do if we wish to be cleansed and saved: namely, that, struck with fear by the knowledge of our sins and of our wretched condition, we flee to Christ, and believe with firm trust that he is the one who can bring us salvation, and do not despair of his willingness. In this matter our condition is better than that of this leper, because we are made more certain by the Gospel that he desires nothing so much as that we should allow ourselves to be cleansed. This very thing appears in the present story too. Third, Christ declares himself to be the physician of soul and body, and does so in such a way that he most clearly bears witness to his readiness to help us, and indeed to his ardent zeal for our salvation, ready to undertake anything. Fourth, he sends the man made clean from leprosy to the priests, who, by God's appointment, were inspectors of leprosy. Thus the Lord accommodates himself to the political order, and at the same time, by this act, he admonishes the leper of his duty less than he teaches all of us that we are perfectly cleansed by him, so that we can stand before the very judgment of God and be counted there as righteous and holy, if we are engrafted into him by faith. Finally, there follows the effect or fruit of the miracle, which flowed from it to many others, and what Christ further did. Since the whole history of this miracle and its first four chapters have already been discussed at length in our Mark, we will now leave those and consider what remains to be said about the last part.

units.la: Primam eius partem his verbis Lucas comprehendit: Dimanabat autem eò magis rumor de illo, & conueniebat turba multa, vt audirent, & per eum sanarentur à morbis suis. Rumorem de illo longè lateque vulgatum fuisse scribit. At huius causam Marcus exprimit, quòd nimirum leprosus, vbi se mundatum vidit, acceptum ab eo beneficium passim praedicarit. Fuit hoc animi pij & grati argumentum, non tamen omni culpa vacat, si id contra Christi praeceptum fecit, priusquam se Sacerdoti ostendisset. Et solet hoc pijs frequenter accidere, vt bono & pio zelo abrepti non leuiter peccent, si suis affectibus & propriae rationis consilio indulgeant. Neque sufficit ad illos excusandos zelus diuini cultus, eò quòd nunquam ritè colitur Deus, nisi quando illius mandatis obedimus. Eius enim vox est: Obedire praestat sacrificijs, & auscultare praestantius est adipe arietum. Quò magis nos carnis nostra cogitationes atque placita suspecta habere conuenit, ne sub plausibili pietatis praetextu seducamur. Quia tamen Deus pro sua bonitate & sapientia suorum errori-bus bene vti novit, hic quoque leprosi illius lapsu siue error fructum non poenitendum habuit. Eo enim factum est, vt tantus ad Christum concursus populi fieret, vt prae turba non posset civitatem ingredi. Causa vero tam ferventis studij duplex affertur. Prima, quod docentem audire voluerunt. Et haec ad vere pios referri debet, qui (vt Christus apud Ioannem ait) pastoris sui vocem illico agnoscunt, & nihil antiquius habent verbo Dei, quo certam & praesentem medicinam animae contineri norunt.
