Et huius studium nos quoque trahere debet, vt reliquis rebus omnibus ad Christum in Euangelio nobis loquentem festinemus. Altera fuit, quod a morbis suis sanari cupierunt, cum eius virtute leprosos quoque purgari audiuissent. Fuerunt hi procul dubio carnales, quos vitae praesentis studium traxit, & quorum semper maximus numerus esse solet inter eos, qui se Christi discipulos esse profitentur. Sic alibi millia aliquot sectatorum habuit, cum illos epulo gratuito exciperet, & non vno loco legimus, miraculo aliquo singulari totum populum ad illum quaerendum sive sequendum excitatum fuisse. Et haec quidem hodie etiam praecipua causa est, quod seculo hoc quantumuis corruptissimo plures inueniuntur, qui Christo nomen dant. Habet enim vbique gentium Deus electos suos, qui serio salutis aeternae studio tanguntur, & proinde Euangelium, vt par est, audiunt. His autem infinita eorum turba accedit, quos alicuius commodi temporalis spes trahit, & qui morbis teterrimis laborant, quibus in Euangelio medicinam quaerunt. Alios enim insatiabilis habendi cupiditas accendit, alios disciplinae impatientia & quiduis designandi impunitas mouent, multos vindictae studium excitat aut alius quispiam affectus, cui remedium in Christi doctrina & fidei verae professione inueniri posse sperant: non quidem quod ipsos tanto malo liberet, sed quod materiam praebeat, qua insana eorum cupiditas satietur. At qui ita affecti sunt, ij ad tempus quidem manent, quoad aliqua spes eos laetat: quam primum vero Christum & Euangelium eius studijs suis inimicum esse sentiunt, se deceptos esse queruntur, & turpissimam ab illo faciunt secessionem. Vt ergo talibus nos nequaquam fidere debemus, ita cauendum est diligenter, ne eiusmodi affectibus apud nos locus detur, & ne fidei atque Euangelij praetextu ad nequitiam nostram abutamur.
units.tr: Luke comprehends the first part of this in these words: "But the report of him spread abroad all the more, and great crowds came together to hear and to be healed of their infirmities." He writes that the report of him was spread far and wide. Mark, however, expresses its cause: namely, that the leper, when he saw himself cleansed, published everywhere the kindness he had received from him. This was a sign of a devout and grateful mind, yet it was not free from fault, if he did this against Christ's command, before he had shown himself to the priest. And it often happens to the godly that, carried away by a good and pious zeal, they sin not lightly if they indulge their own feelings and the counsel of their own reason. Nor does zeal for divine worship suffice to excuse them, since God is never rightly worshipped except when we obey his commands. For his voice is: "To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." So much the more it becomes us to regard the thoughts and inclinations of our flesh with suspicion, lest we be led astray under the plausible pretext of piety. Yet because God, in his goodness and wisdom, knows how to make good use of the errors of his people, here too the fall or error of that leper produced a fruit not to be regretted. For it came about that such a great crowd of people gathered to Christ that, because of the throng, he could not enter the city. Now two causes are given for so fervent an eagerness. The first is that they wished to hear the teacher. This ought to be ascribed to those who are truly godly, who (as Christ says in John) at once recognise the voice of their shepherd, and hold nothing more precious than the Word of God, in which they know that a sure and present remedy for the soul is contained. This eagerness ought to draw us too, so that we hasten to Christ speaking to us in the Gospel above all other things. The second was that they desired to be healed of their diseases, having heard that lepers too were cleansed by his power. These were doubtless carnal people, whom the concern for the present life drew, and such people always make up the largest number among those who profess themselves disciples of Christ. Thus elsewhere he had several thousand followers, when he received them with a free feast; and we read in more than one place that the whole people were stirred up by some singular miracle to seek and follow him. And this is even today the chief cause why, in this most corrupt age, many are found who give their name to Christ. For God has his chosen ones everywhere in the world, who are moved by a earnest concern for eternal salvation, and therefore hear the Gospel as they ought. To these is added an endless crowd of those whom the hope of some temporal advantage draws, and who suffer from the most loathsome diseases, for which they seek a remedy in the Gospel. For some are fired by an insatiable desire for possessions, others are moved by impatience with discipline and the impunity to do whatever they please, many are stirred by a passion for revenge or some other affection, hoping to find a remedy for it in the doctrine of Christ and the profession of the true faith: not indeed because it will free them from so great an evil, but because it provides material by which their mad desires may be satisfied. But those who are so disposed remain only for a time, as long as some hope cheers them; yet as soon as they perceive that Christ and his Gospel are hostile to their pursuits, they complain that they have been deceived and make a most shameful withdrawal from him. Therefore, just as we must by no means trust such people, so we must take diligent care that no place is given among us to such affections, and that we do not abuse the pretext of faith and the Gospel for our wickedness.

units.la: Quid vero Christus? quae altera huius postremi loci pars est. Eum secessisse scribit Lucas in deserta loca, & illic precatum esse. Secessionis huius causae variae adduci possent. Primo enim vt id faceret opus erat, ne eorum errorem foveret, qui in ipso non alia, quam quae carnis sunt, quaerebant. Deinde inanis gloriae studium cauet, & nos simul suo exemplo modestiam docet, ne nostri honoris causa ambitiosius vtamur Dei donis, quae nobis in finem longe alium ab illo data sunt. Adhaec quieti honestae se dedit, vt hac recreatus ad labores alacrius redeat. Et in omnibus istis admodum memorabile est, quod precibus interea vacauit. Nam his illum minime opus habuisse constat: quia vero propter nos hominem assumpserat, propter nos quoque omnia, quae hominis sunt, subire voluit. Et quia simul Sacerdotis personam suscepérat, pro nobis eum intercedere opertuit apud patrem. Quod vt ardentius faceret, in praesenti grauis & necessaria causa eum mouit. Nam paulo ante discipulos quatuor elegerat, quos ad functionem apostolicam destinaret. Videbat praeterea infelicem populi Iudaici conditionem, qui pastoribus destitutus per traditionum humanarum atua oberrabat. Videbat item praepositorum multorum studium, qui carnalibus & temporarijs solis intenti, salutem aeternam negligebant. Neq; ignorabat, sibi labores grauissimos & periculosissima certamina propositae esse, in quibus praesenti spiritus auxilio opus erat ei, qui cum homine vero nostras quoq; infirmitates assumpserat. Itaq; ad preces conuersus, his & communem omnium salutem adiuuat, & semetipsum recreat atque confirmat. Habet autem hoc Christi factum dulcissimam consolationem, quae nos in omni tentationis genere confirmat, quando videmus illi salutem nostram adeo cordi esse, vt non doctrina solum diligenti & crebris miraculis, verumetiam assiduis precibus eam iuuare voluerit. Nam hinc simul apparet, eum etiam nunc ad patris dexteram fidei intercessoris officio fungi, sicuti scriptura testantur.
units.tr: But what did Christ do? This is the other part of this last section. Luke writes that he withdrew into the desert places and prayed there. Various causes of this withdrawal could be adduced. First, it was necessary for him to do this so that he would not foster the error of those who sought in him nothing but what belongs to the flesh. Next, he guards against the desire for vainglory, and at the same time teaches us modesty by his example, lest for the sake of our own honour we use the gifts of God more ambitiously, gifts which have been given to us for an end quite different from that. Besides, he gave himself to honest rest, so that, refreshed by it, he might return more cheerfully to his labours. And in all these things it is very memorable that in the meantime he gave himself to prayer. For it is clear that he had no need of these; but since he had taken on manhood for our sake, he willed for our sake to undergo also all that belongs to man. And since at the same time he had assumed the office of priest, it was fitting that he should intercede for us with the Father. And to make him do this more ardently, a grave and pressing cause moved him at the present time. For a little before he had chosen four disciples, whom he was to appoint to the apostolic office. Moreover, he saw the unhappy condition of the Jewish people, who, lacking shepherds, wandered astray through the ceremonies of human traditions. He saw likewise the zeal of many leaders, who, intent only on carnal and temporal things, neglected eternal salvation. Nor was he ignorant that the most grievous labours and most dangerous conflicts lay before him, in which he had need of the present help of the Spirit, he who, being true man, had also taken on our weaknesses. Therefore, turning to prayer, he both helped the common salvation of all by this means, and refreshed and strengthened himself. Moreover, this deed of Christ holds a most sweet consolation, which strengthens us in every kind of temptation, when we see that our salvation was so dear to him that he willed to help it not only by diligent teaching and frequent miracles, but also by constant prayers. For from this it appears at the same time that he even now performs the office of intercessor of faith at the right hand of the Father, as the Scriptures testify.

units.la: Deinde obseruatu dignissimum est, quod recreationem non ex mundi studijs aut ignauo somno, sed ex precibus petit: itanimirum docens, quid nos facere conueniat, quando nos aut labore nimio fatigatos esse, aut nouis & indies grauioribus periculis vrgeri sentimus. Tunc (inquam) ex precibus
units.tr: Next, it is most worthy of notice that he seeks refreshment not from worldly pursuits or idle sleep, but from prayer. He is clearly teaching us what we ought to do when we feel worn out by excessive labour, or pressed by new and daily more serious dangers. Then (I say) let us seek refreshment from prayer,

units.la: petamus refocillationem, quibus pio homini nihil iucundius, dulcius & efficacius obtingere potest. Si enim te maxima laboris aut doloris parte leuatum putas, si homini amico & beneuolo animi curas exponere & eius consilio frui licet: quanto magis recreantur, quibus cum Deo colloqui datur, qui precibus nostris aures faciles praebet, qui easdem spiritus sui suggestione regit & adiuuat, & qui se eas exaudire vel iampridem pollicitus est? Sed o infelices, qui cum sibi consolatione opus esse vident, eam in iis rebus quaerunt, quae voluptatem aut omnino nullam aut momentaneam, vel etiam cum turpitudine coniunctam habent, & proinde nobis tandem labores atque dolores acutiores pariunt. Quod vnum si recte omnes expenderent, maiores in vera pietate progressus facerent, & Deo magis propitio vterentur.
units.tr: let us seek refreshment, which can bring a godly man nothing more pleasant, sweeter or more effective. For if you think yourself relieved of a great part of your labour or grief when you may lay your cares before a friendly and kindly man and enjoy his counsel, how much more are those refreshed to whom it is given to converse with God, who gives ready ears to our prayers, who governs and helps them by the prompting of his Spirit, and who has already promised that he will hear them? But, O unhappy people, when they see that they need consolation, they seek it in those things which give either no pleasure at all, or only momentary pleasure, or pleasure joined with baseness, and so in the end produce for us sharper labours and griefs. If everyone would weigh this one thing rightly, they would make greater progress in true piety and would find God more favourable.

units.la: Postremo omnes verbi sui ministros suo exemplo Christus admonet, vt in salute communi omnium prouidenda seduli quidem sint & industrij, at simul caueant, ne nimia cum omnibus familiaritas ipsis contemptum pariat. Accidit hoc frequenter iis, qui vt in minori pretio sint, & plurimos sibi amicos faciant, promiscue omnium commercijs se immiscent, omnibus arridٍent, & nunquam non in publico conspiciuntur. Nam etsi sua facilitate multos sibi concilient, plurimum tamen labefactatur simul doctrinae authoritas, & plerique ex eo sibi impunitatem pollicentur, quod doctores suos tam familiares habeant. Proderit ergo, vt vbi suo officio functi sunt, secessum quaerant, & domi suae vel lectioni sacrae incumbant, vel precibus se recreent atque confirment, vt cum vsus postulat, ad opus maiori feruore & quasi nouis viribus aucti redire possint. Quod vt verbi ministri facere debent, ita omnium est, Iesum Christum salutis suae authorem vnicum agnoscere, huic vni fidere, & exemplum, quo nobis ille praeiuit imitari. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, by his own example Christ admonishes all ministers of his word that, while they should be earnest and diligent in providing for the common salvation of all, they should at the same time take care that excessive familiarity with everyone does not bring them contempt. This often happens to those who, wishing to be held in lower esteem and to make many friends, mingle indiscriminately in everyone's affairs, smile on everyone, and are always seen in public. For although by their affability they win over many, at the same time the authority of their doctrine is greatly weakened, and many promise themselves impunity because they have their teachers so familiar. It will therefore be useful, once they have discharged their duty, to seek seclusion and to devote themselves at home either to sacred reading or to refresh and strengthen themselves by prayer, so that when need requires, they may return to the work with greater zeal and as if with new strength. As the ministers of the word ought to do this, so it is for everyone to acknowledge Jesus Christ as the sole author of their salvation, to trust in him alone, and to imitate the example he has gone before us in. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIX
units.tr: HOMILY XLIX

units.la: Et factum est quodam die, cum ipse doceret, essentque Pharisaei sedentes ac Legis doctores, qui venerant ex omnibus vicis Galilaeae & Iudaeae, & ex Hierosolyma, atque potentia Domini adesset ad sanandum illos: Tunc ecce adfuerunt quidam ferentes in lecto hominem, qui erat paralyticus, & studebant eum inferre & ponere in ipsius conspectu. Et cum non invenissent qua parte eum inferrent propter turbam, ascenderunt supra domum, & per tegulas demiserunt eum cum lectulo in medium, ante Iesum. Qui vt vidit eorum fidem dixit: Homo, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua.
units.tr: And it happened on a certain day, as he was teaching, that there were Pharisees and doctors of the Law sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judaea and from Jerusalem, and the power of the Lord was present to heal them. Then behold, some men brought on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they sought to bring him in and set him before him. And when they could not find a way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and let him down through the tiles with his bed into the middle, before Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: "Man, your sins are forgiven you."

units.la: Quoniam Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, nobis a Deo patre redemptor & seruator datus est, idem se talem esse passim testatur. Nam aeternae salutis doctrinam omnibus bona fide tradit, neque vno loco subsistit, sed terram omnem circuit, vt plures in veritatis agnitionem adducat. Addit doctrinae miracula non ad ostentationem instituta, qualia impostorum fere esse solent, sed vera & salutaria, quibus quam plurimos iuuat. In omnibus autem iis non tam mansuetudini quam modestiae studet diligenter, vt omnibus constet, ipsum non aliud quam hominum salutem quaerere. Debet istorum consideratio nos ad eum amandum excitare, vt & salutis fiduciam omnem in illo vno collocemus, et eidem indiuulse adhaereamus. Idem ergo nobis historiam, quam modo tractabimus, vsus esto, qua tam verbis quam reipsa docetur, Christum verum humani generis seruatorem esse, qui & animas peccatorum nexibus liberet, & patri reconciliatos ex omnibus aduersis & periculis seruet, quibus in vitae huius curriculo exercemur.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ has been given to us by God the Father as redeemer and saviour, he bears witness to being such everywhere. For he delivers the teaching of eternal salvation to all in good faith, and he does not remain in one place but goes through the whole land, so that he may bring more people to the knowledge of the truth. He adds miracles to his teaching, not instituted for display, as impostors are usually wont to do, but true and salutary, by which he helps very many. In all these things, moreover, he takes care not so much to be gentle as to be modest, so that it is plain to all that he seeks nothing but the salvation of men. The consideration of these things ought to stir us to love him, so that we may place all our confidence of salvation in him alone and cling to him without division. Therefore, use this story, which we shall now treat, as it teaches by words as well as by deeds that Christ is the true saviour of the human race, who both frees the souls of sinners from their bonds and keeps those reconciled to the Father safe from all the adversities and dangers with which we are exercised in the course of this life.

units.la: Occasionem totius facti vna cum loci & temporis circumstantijs Matthaeus & Marcus diligentius narrant, qui illum post dies aliquot, quos in deserti secessu transegerat, in suam ciuitatem Capernaum scilicet, rediisse scribunt. Non autem in vrbem modo, verumetiam ad docendi munus redijt, cui se in primis destinatum esse sciebat. Itaque fama eius excitati vicini vndique confluunt, imo ex remotioribus quoque Galilaeae & Iudaeae locis, adeoque ex ipsa Hierosolymorum vrbe multi ad-
units.tr: Matthew and Mark relate more carefully the occasion of the whole event, together with the circumstances of place and time. They write that after some days, which he had spent in the solitude of the desert, he returned to his own city, Capernaum to be precise. And he came back not only to the city but also to the office of teaching, for which he knew he had been chiefly appointed. So, stirred by his fame, neighbours flocked together from every side, indeed also from the more distant places of Galilee and Judaea, and from the city of Jerusalem itself many came

units.la: Vide Marc. 2. Homil. 16. fuerunt, inter quos pharisæi quoque & Scribæ vel Legis doctores dominantur. Ne ergo populi expectationem frustretur, aut suo officio desit, vitæ æternæ verbum illis prædicat, & simul doctrinam signis confirmat. Nam Domini potentiam siue virtutem ei adfuisse Lucas scribit, vt ægrotos aut morbis affectos sanaret. Quæ causa fuit, vt paralyticum illum, de quo postea dicetur, ad illum afferrent. Ita eò, vnde prius digressus fuerat non sine fœnore Christus redijt, quod illi perpetuum esse in Marco diximus.
units.tr: (See Mark 2; Homily 16) and among them Pharisees and scribes, or doctors of the Law, were prominent. Therefore, lest he disappoint the people's expectation or fail in his duty, he preaches to them the word of eternal life, and at the same time confirms the teaching by signs. For Luke writes that the power or virtue of the Lord was present with him, so that he might heal the sick or those afflicted with diseases. This was the reason why they brought to him that paralytic, of whom we shall speak afterwards. Thus Christ returned, not without interest, to the place from which he had previously departed, which we said in Mark was a perpetual gain for him.

units.la: In præsenti autem obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd ad docendum redijt, & quòd tunc sese exeruit viuifica Dei virtus, quæ multis ad ipsum confluentibus salutem attulit. Eo enim admonemur, in Christo maximam doctrinæ eius rationem debere haberi. Nam vt eius causa se in mundum venisse alibi fatetur, ita per hanc nobis vitam & salutem offert, cuius reuera participes fiunt, qui illam fide apprehendunt. Imò vt Deus initio orbem terrarum & vniuersam huius mundi machinam verbo suo creauit: ita per verbum quoque eain nobis agit, quæ ad nostram salutem faciunt. Admonet de hoc diuinus ille & regius Psalmes, cùm ait: Misit verbum suum, & sanauit eos. Est ergo turpis & pernitiosus eorum error, qui cùm Christi sectatores videri velint, neglecta tamen eius doctrina, circa alia occupantur, & huius sæculi bona in illo quærunt, qui vt nobis cælestium bonorum author esset à Patre exiuit & homo factus est.
units.tr: In the present passage, however, it is most worthy of notice that he returned to teaching, and that then the life-giving power of God showed itself, which brought salvation to many who flocked to him. For we are reminded by this that in Christ the greatest regard must be had to his doctrine. For just as he declares elsewhere that he came into the world for this purpose, so through it he offers us life and salvation, of which those become truly partakers who grasp it by faith. Indeed, just as God in the beginning created the earth and the whole structure of this world by his word, so also through the word he works in us those things which pertain to our salvation. The divine and royal Psalm reminds us of this when it says: "He sent his word and healed them." Therefore, the error of those is base and pernicious who, while wishing to seem followers of Christ, neglect his teaching, occupy themselves with other things, and seek in him the goods of this age, when he came forth from the Father and was made man so that he might be the author of heavenly goods for us.

units.la: Obseruabis præterea, quòd etsi Pharisæos & Legis doctores in cætu illo assidentes videret Christus, nihilominus tamen docere perrexit. Atqui totum illum ordinem, ex iuratis fui nominis & doctrinæ suæ hostibus constare sciebat, vt iam de illis nihil dicamus, qui Hierosolyma aduenerant, nimirum vt eum insidiose obseruarent & accusandi ipsum occasiones venarentur. Sed non potuit istorum omnium præsentia illum terrere, vt ipsum verbi patris sui puderet, vel vt eos re infecta dimitteret, qui discendi studio aduenerant. Est exemplum hoc probe obseruandum omnibus ecclesiarum ministris, ne vnquam eos veritatis pudeat, & ne eorum præsentia aut minis se terreri patiantur, quos publica authoritate armatos & verbi Dei hostes esse nouerũt. Paulus olim dicebat: Non me pudet Euangelij Christi, potentia siquidem Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Et idem non vul gò solum prædicabat, sed coram pharisæis, sacerdotibus, tribunis, præsidibus Romanis, imò coram regibus Christi causam fortissimè, ex vinculis quoque verba faciens, tuebatur. Adhæc etsi Iudæorum improbitatem atq; cutumaciam sæpe expertus esset, et plerosq; iam reiectos et reprobatos à Deo esse sciret, nõ destitit tamen subinde illis prædicare, vt vel aliquos ex vniuersali illo & communi gentis illius exitio eriperet. Est ergo detestabilis illorum ignauia, qui dum res in tuto sunt, apud indoctam plebem audacter et non sine magnificis protestationibus Euangelium prædicant, mox autem vel obmutescunt, vel turpiter tergiuersantur, si in aliquos incidant, quos iniquos huius causæ iudices esse sciunt. Similiter zelo inconsulto & præposteró peccant, quibus nefas esse putatur in ijs cœtibus docere, quibus improbi aliqui & incurabiles intermixti sunt. Atqui Christus docere perrexit, etsi Pharisæi & Legis doctores & Sacerdotum Hierosolymitanorum emissarij præsentes adessent, quorum animos optimè perspectos habebat. Quin ergo huius exemplum imitentur, quod Apostoli postea non sine laude & fructu imitati sunt. Quæ enim iniquitas est, propter improbos aliquos æternæ salutis doctrina eos fraudare, qui animo minimè malo præditi sunt, & non fucato salutis atq; veritatis studio ducuntur? Deus, qui impietatis vindex & vltor est acerrimus, iudicia sua sic temperare solet, ne aliorum cotumacia aut ingratitudo electis suis fraudi sit: cur ergo qui illius præcones haberi volunt, aliquorum improbitate se adduci patiuntur, vt eos quoque deserant, de quibus spes adhuc bona est, & in quibus non obscura fidei & electionis indicia apparent? Et hæc quidem de historia tetius occasione dicta sufficiat. Sequitur nunc miraculum in paralytico editum, cuius singulas circunstantias ex ordine inspexisse proderit.
units.tr: Further, you will observe that although Christ saw Pharisees and doctors of the Law sitting in that assembly, he nevertheless went on teaching. Yet he knew that that whole company consisted of sworn enemies of his name and teaching, not to mention those who had come from Jerusalem, plainly to watch him craftily and to seek occasions for accusing him. But the presence of all these could not terrify him, so that he would be ashamed of the word of his Father, or so that he would dismiss empty-handed those who had come with a zeal to learn. This example is to be well observed by all ministers of the churches: that they never be ashamed of the truth, and that they not allow themselves to be terrified by the presence or threats of those whom they know to be armed with public authority and enemies of the Word of God. Paul once said: "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." And he not only preached this in public, but before the Pharisees, priests, tribunes, and Roman governors, indeed before kings, he defended the cause of Christ most boldly, speaking even from his chains. Moreover, although he had often experienced the wickedness and obstinacy of the Jews, and knew that most of them had already been cast off and reprobated by God, he did not cease from time to time to preach to them, so that he might snatch some of them from that universal and common destruction of that nation. Therefore, the cowardice of those is detestable who, while matters are safe, preach the Gospel boldly and not without magnificent protestations to an untaught common people, but soon afterwards either fall silent or shamefully shuffle away if they fall in with some who they know are unfair judges of this cause. Likewise, they sin through an ill-considered and preposterous zeal who think it wrong to teach in those assemblies in which some wicked and incurable persons are mixed. Yet Christ went on teaching, although the Pharisees and doctors of the Law and the agents of the priests of Jerusalem were present, whose minds he saw very clearly. Why then do they not imitate this example, which the apostles afterwards imitated not without praise and fruit? For what injustice is it, on account of some wicked men, to defraud of the doctrine of eternal salvation those who are endowed with no evil intent and are led by a sincere zeal for salvation and truth? God, who is the most fierce avenger and punisher of impiety, is accustomed so to temper his judgements that the obstinacy or ingratitude of others may not be a hindrance to his elect. Why then do those who wish to be considered his heralds allow themselves to be led by the wickedness of some to desert even those in whom good hope still remains, and in whom no obscure signs of faith and election appear? Let this suffice for what is to be said about the occasion of the story. Now follows the miracle wrought on the paralytic, whose individual circumstances it will be useful to examine in order.

units.la: Primus autem hic paralyticus ipse spectetur, qui in nobis nostræ naturæ corruptionem & quæ ex hac dependet infelicem humani generis conditionem adumbrat. Est enim paralysis neruorum resolutio, quæ ex frigido & crasso humore neruos plus æquo humectante & laxante enata, sensum fere & motum omnem membris aufert. Itaque qui hoc morbo laborant, viuunt quidem & homines sunt, at nullum vitæ aut veri hominis officium præstant. Atqui ea est omnium nostrum, quoad agnatam nobis naturam, conditio. Quia enim in peccato concipimur & nascimur, fit ut ita in nos totos illud redundet, ut etsi vita corporis fruamur, & propter animam immortalem corpori coniunctam homines dicamur & simus, nihil tamen eorum praestemus, quae veri hominis & ad Dei imaginem conditi officia sunt. Rationis enim lux crassissimis cupiditatum prauarum nebulis atq; humoribus obscurata, non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Iisdem voluntas quoq; corrupta non nisi ad malum fertur. Et quamuis suam voluntatem nobis Deus reuelet, vires tamen nobis nulla sunt, quibus quod bonum esse didicimus, faciamus. Describit hanc miseriam nostram, in propria persona Paulus admodum diligenter ad Romanos septimo Cap. & idem alibi nos ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneos esse ait: quod ab illo verissime dictum esse fatebuntur, quotquot seipsos et naturam suam omnem diligentius inspexerint. Ut ergo paralytici nullam sibi ipsis opem ferre possunt, sed toti ab aliorum auxilijs pendent: ita quo nosipsos nuuemus in nobis nihil esse, sed à Dei gratia pendeamus oportet, qui solus laboranti naturae mederi, & ad bonum faciendum ineptos atq; impotentes nouis viribus instruere potest. Agnoscant ergo hanc suam miseriam, quicunq; seruari cupiunt, neinani & falsa suarum virium atque operum fiducia elati, semetipsos Dei gratia spolient, quae sola nobis per Christum medetur, ut suo loco audiemus.
units.tr: Let us first look at this paralytic himself, who in us portrays the corruption of our nature and the unhappy condition of the human race that depends upon it. For paralysis is a loosening of the nerves, which, arising from a cold and thick humour that moistens and relaxes the nerves more than is right, removes almost all feeling and movement from the limbs. Thus those who suffer from this disease live indeed and are men, but perform no office of life or of a true man. Yet this is the condition of all of us, as far as our inborn nature is concerned. For since we are conceived and born in sin, it so overflows into us entirely that, although we enjoy bodily life and, on account of the immortal soul joined to the body, we are called and are men, we nevertheless perform none of those duties which belong to a true man and one created in the image of God. For the light of reason, obscured by the thickest clouds and humours of depraved desires, does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God. In the same way, the corrupted will is carried only toward evil. And although God reveals his will to us, we have no strength by which we may do what we have learned to be good. Paul describes this our misery very carefully in his own person in the seventh chapter of Romans, and elsewhere he says that we are not even fit of ourselves to think; and those who examine themselves and their whole nature more carefully will confess that this was said most truly by him. Therefore, just as paralytics can bring no help to themselves but depend entirely on the help of others, so we must recognise that we are nothing in ourselves and depend on the grace of God, who alone can heal our labouring nature and equip us, who are unfit and powerless to do good, with new strength. Therefore, let all who desire to be saved acknowledge this their misery, and, not lifted up by a vain and false confidence in their own powers and works, let them strip themselves of the grace of God, which alone heals us through Christ, as we shall hear in its place.

units.la: Nunc eos videamus, qui miserum hunc ad Christum attulerunt, in quibus fidem cum charitate non fucata coniunctam fuisse, ex multis eorum factis apparet. Nisi enim eum, qui humana arte amplius curari non poterat, à Christo curari posse credidissent, nunquam eum ad hunc voluissent afferre. Itaque etsi nondum plenam Christi cognitionem habeant, eum tamen diuina virtute instrui esse credunt, & procul dubio Messiam esse cogitant, quem caecis, surdis, mutis & claudis salutem allaturum esse olim Isaias praedixerat. Deinde fidei non languidae argumentum est, quod cum prae turba hominum, qui ad domus ostium confluxerant, via nulla pateret, qua in Christi conspectum venire possent, tecto confecto paralyticum per tegulas retectas demittunt. Adeo ingeniosa est fides, ut illic quoque rerum gerendarum rationem inueniat, vbi humanus intellectus nihil huius videre potest. Adhaec laborum tolerantes & in quouis periculo animosos & fortes reddit, sicuti in multorum exemplis est videre, quos verae fidei nomine Scriptura commendat. At nunquam ista fecissent illi, nisi amore paralytici huius accensi, ipsius saluti ex animo voluissent consultum. Est ergo hoc quoque fidei ardentis & viuae indicium, quam per charitatem agere Paulus testatur. Sunt haec probe obseruanda ijs, qui fidei nomine se esse venditant, ne sibijpsis inani persuasione imponant, dum ab ijs alieni sunt, quae propria sunt verae fidei effecta. In primis vero adeos spectat huius exempli consideratio diligens, quibus cum inualidis & aegrotantibus res est: ne horum vel morositate, vel feditate se adduci patiantur, quo minus in illis fouendis & curandis seduli sint & industrij. Commendat illos passim Deus, & notum est illud Dauidis: Beatus qui prudenter agit cum aegrotante, in die mala eripiet eum Dominus. Dominus custodiet eum, valetudinem restituet ei, &c. Et Christus in se collata olim putabit, quae in tales conferuntur officia. Pudeat ergo suae inhumanitatis eos, qui suos morbis debilitatos morose nimis fastidiunt, vel contagij metu turpiter deserunt. Excusant hi se multis argumentis, sed quae eiusmodi fere sunt, ut illos fide etiam vacuos esse appareat, quando morbos fingunt, qui abrupto diuinae prouidentiae freno temere grassentur. Ut vero isti paralyticum Christo adduxerint, ut corporis valetudini eius beneficio restitueretur: ita nobis curandum est, ut qui animi morbis laborant, peccatis nimirum, Christo coniuncti, in eo paenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum assequantur. Quod etsi omnibus dicatur, maxime tamen ad vetbi administros pertinet, qui nisi in vno Christo animarum medicinam monstrent, indigni sunt qui aliquem in ecclesia locum obtineant.
units.tr: Let us now consider those who brought this sick man to Christ. That their faith was joined with a sincere love appears from many of their actions. For unless they had believed that Christ could heal the man whom human skill could no longer cure, they would never have wanted to bring him to Him. So although they do not yet have full knowledge of Christ, they believe that He is taught by divine power, and without doubt they think of Him as the Messiah, who Isaiah had long before foretold would bring salvation to the blind, the deaf, the dumb and the lame. Next, the sick man's bearers showed a faith that was not weak. When the crowd of people gathered at the door left no way open by which they could come into Christ's presence, they broke open the roof and lowered the paralytic through the stripped tiles. Faith is so ingenious that it finds a way of acting even where human understanding can see nothing of the kind. Moreover, it makes people endure labours and become brave and strong in every danger, as can be seen in the examples of many whom Scripture commends for the sake of true faith. But they would never have done these things unless they had been fired with love for this paralytic and had wished, from their hearts, to care for his salvation. This too, then, is a sign of a burning and living faith, which Paul testifies works through love. Those who boast of being believers must observe these things carefully, lest they deceive themselves with an empty persuasion while they are estranged from the things that are the proper effects of true faith. Above all, a careful consideration of this example concerns those who have to deal with the infirm and the sick: let them not be drawn away, either by the peevishness or by the foulness of such people, from being diligent and zealous in cherishing and curing them. God commends such people everywhere, and that saying of David is well known: "Blessed is he who acts wisely toward the sick; in the day of evil the Lord will deliver him. The Lord will keep him and restore his health," and so on. And Christ will count as done to Himself whatever services are rendered to such people. Let those be ashamed of their inhumanity who fastidiously and excessively scorn their sickly relatives, or shamefully desert them out of fear of contagion. They make excuses for themselves with many arguments, but these are mostly of such a kind that it appears they are empty of faith too, since they invent diseases which run wild recklessly once the bridle of divine providence is cast off. But just as these men brought the paralytic to Christ so that his bodily health might be restored by His benefit, so we must take care that those who labour under diseases of the soul, namely sins, be joined to Christ and obtain repentance and forgiveness of sins in Him. And although this is said to all, it pertains most of all to the ministers of the Word, who, unless they show the remedy for souls in Christ alone, are unworthy to hold any place in the Church.

units.la: Seruit his confutandis exemplum eius, quod in praesenti proponitur. Elucet enim in eo singularis mansuetudo atque bonitas, quod etsi ipsi sua importunitate tectum effringerent, paralyticum ex funibus in lecto suspensum demitterent, quod absque strepitu fieri non poterat: non tamen indignatur, quod sermonem ipsius, quem procul dubio de rebus grauissimis habebat, interturbarent, & simul domum alienam non sine periculo conscenderent. Quin amicè hominem compellans, se factum hoc omne probare ostendit. Ita vero reipsa probat quod apud Ioannem dicit: Eum, qui venit ad me, non eijcio foras. Est ergo ridiculus nimis & vanus eorum praetextus, qui religione & pio metu se abstrerent aiunt, ne ad Christum accedant: & proinde sibi apud illum intercessoribus Diuis opus
units.tr: The example set before us now serves to refute these people. For in it shines out a singular gentleness and goodness: although they themselves, by their importunity, were breaking through the roof and lowering the paralytic on ropes while he lay on his bed, which could not be done without noise, He is not offended that they disturbed His discourse, which He was undoubtedly holding on the most weighty matters, and that they climbed into another man's house not without danger. Rather, He addresses the man kindly and shows that He approves of all that was done. Thus in fact He proves what He says in John: "Him who comes to me I will not cast out." Therefore the pretext of those who, under the guise of religion and pious fear, say they hold back lest they come to Christ, and who for that reason think they need saints as intercessors with Him, is exceedingly ridiculous and vain. For it is not piety but impiety to imagine Him cruel, hard, difficult or peevish, when He offers Himself to us of His own accord and has never rejected any of those who asked help from Him. But more will be said about this elsewhere.

units.la: Fides eorum, qui paralytici Christo adduxerunt.
units.tr: The faith of those who brought the paralytic to Christ.

units.la: Christi facilitas erga infirmos.
units.tr: Christ's readiness toward the sick.

units.la: Psal. 41. esse putant. Non enim haec pietas, sed impietas est, crudelem, durum, difficilem aut morosum eum fingere, qui & sponte se nobis offert, & neminem unquam reiecit eorum, qui ab ipso auxilium postulaverunt. Sed de hoc plura alibi dicentur.
units.tr: Psal. 41. they think to be. For it is not piety but impiety to imagine Him cruel, hard, difficult or peevish, when He offers Himself to us of His own accord and has never rejected any of those who asked help from Him. But more will be said about this elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc quid Christum moverit videamus, ut se iis tam facilem praeberet. Ut vidit eorum fidem, dixit: Homo, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Ergo non opus eorum respexit, sed fidem, quae operis istius causa erat, et quam nisi isti habuissent, opus hoc laudem nullam merebatur. Nam quod non ex fide fit (inquit Apostolus) peccatum est. At hic neminem moveat, quod eorum fidem Christus respexisse dicitur, qui paralyticum ad ipsum adduxerunt, cum alibi iustum sua fide viuere, scriptura doceat. Nam paralyticum quoque Christo credidisse ex eo apparet, quod ea secum fieri passus est, quae sine labore & periculo fieri non poterant. Deinde agebatur hic de corporis valetudine, non aeterna totius hominis salute. At in externis nos aliorum fide & pietate plurimum adiuuari certum est, eo quod foedus & promissiones suas Deus ad credentium posteros quoque extendit, & propter illos frequenter omnibus iis benefacit, quibus cum illi viuunt. Sic Labanum opibus auctum fuisse legimus, cum Iacobi opera & ministerio uteretur. Et Iosephi pietatem primum Putiphari heroi eius, deinde toti Aegypto profuisse constat. Debet hoc in eum finem observari, ut magnifaciamus piorum consuetudinem atque commercia. Ut enim impii plerunque suis conuiuioribus malum dant: ita ex pijs multa ad omnes, qui illis conuersantur, utilitas redit, & non raro fit, ut ea occasione veram & aeternam salutem inveniant, qui initio non nisi carnalia & temporaria bona quaerebant: quod hic etiam accidisse totius historiae exitus docebit.
units.tr: Now let us see what moved Christ to show Himself so ready toward them. When He saw their faith, He said: "Man, your sins are forgiven you." So He regarded not their work but the faith which was the cause of that work, and unless they had had this faith, the work would have deserved no praise. For "whatever is not of faith (says the Apostle) is sin." But let no one be troubled by the fact that Christ is said to have regarded the faith of those who brought the paralytic to Him, since Scripture teaches elsewhere that the righteous lives by his own faith. For that the paralytic too believed in Christ appears from the fact that he allowed things to be done to him which could not be done without labour and danger. Next, the matter here concerned bodily health, not the eternal salvation of the whole man. But it is certain that in external matters we are greatly helped by the faith and piety of others, since God extends His covenant and promises also to the posterity of believers, and for their sake often does good to all those who live with them. Thus we read that Laban was enriched with wealth while he used the labour and service of Jacob, and it is established that the piety of Joseph first benefited his master Potiphar, and then the whole of Egypt. This should be noted to the end that we may value the company and dealings of the godly. For just as the wicked generally bring harm to their companions, so from the godly much advantage flows to all who associate with them, and it often happens that on this occasion those who at first sought only carnal and temporal goods find true and eternal salvation. The outcome of the whole story will show that this happened here too.

units.la: Nam ad paralyticum conuersus Dominus (ut apud Matthaeum habetur) illi dixit: Confide fili, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Ergo de corporis valetudine solicito peccatorum remissionem offert, ex qua totius hominis salus dependat. Neque hoc cuiquam absurdum videri debet. Nam veri medici, imo Messiae officio fungitur, dum morbi causam tollit, peccata nimirum, ex quibus omnia ea originem ducunt, quae miseros mortales in terris hisce infestant. Et quia fortasse miserrille non tam corporis dolore quam admissorum scelerum conscientia cruciabatur, tempestiua admodum & necessaria fuit consolatio haec, qua & filium vocat, & gratuitam remissionem illi promittit, qui se a Dei conspectu exclusum esse metuebat, neque aliquid in se boni inueniebat, quo eum sibi demereri posset. Obseruent ergo hunc Christi ordinem, quicunque cum morbis aut alio aduersorum genere conflictantur, ne frustra sese fatigent, dum de illis remouendis cogitant, neglecta interim peccatorum remissione, sine qua nihil nobis fauxtum felix, obtingere potest. Et haec breuius nunc perstringimus, quia de iisdem alibi dictum est, & nusquam non de his dicendi occasio sese offert. Agnoscamus nunc Dei bonitatem, qui filium suum Iesum Christum, nobis medicum & seruatorem dedit, & in hoc quaeramus quacunque, nobis ad salutem consequendam necessaria sunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: For when the Lord turned to the paralytic (as is recorded in Matthew), He said to him: "Take courage, son, your sins are forgiven you." So, although the man was anxious about his bodily health, He offers him forgiveness of sins, on which the salvation of the whole man depends. Nor should this seem absurd to anyone. For He performs the office of a true physician, indeed of the Messiah, when He removes the cause of the disease, namely sins, from which all those things arise that plague wretched mortals on this earth. And perhaps because this man was tormented less by the pain of his body than by the consciousness of his wicked deeds, this consolation was most timely and necessary: by it He calls him son and promises him free forgiveness, since he feared he was shut out from the sight of God and found in himself nothing good by which he could earn His favour. Let all those who struggle with sicknesses or other kinds of adversity observe this order of Christ, so that they do not weary themselves in vain while they think about removing these, neglecting in the meantime the forgiveness of sins, without which nothing happy can come to us. And we touch on these things briefly now, because they have been spoken of elsewhere, and the occasion for speaking of them presents itself everywhere. Let us now acknowledge the goodness of God, who gave us His Son Jesus Christ as physician and saviour, and let us seek in Him whatever is necessary to us for obtaining salvation. To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA L.
units.tr: HOMILY L.

units.la: Tunc coeperunt ratiocinari Scribae & Pharisaei, dicentes: Quis est iste qui loquitur blasphemias? Quis potest remittere peccata, nisi solus Deus? Iesus autem cum nosset eorum ratiocinationes, respondens dixit eis: Quid ratiocinamini in cordibus vestris? Vtrum est facilius dicere, Remissa sunt tibi peccata: an dicere, Surge & ambula? Vt autem sciatis Filiu hominis habere potestatem in terra remittendi peccata (ait paralytico) Tibi dico, surge, & sublato lectulo tuo proficiscere domum tuam. Is autem cum illico surrexisset in conspectu eorum, sublato eo in quo iacuerat, abiit domum suam glorificans Deum. Et stupor coepit omnes, & glorificabant Deum, & repleti sunt timore, dicentes: Certe vidimus inopinata hodie.
units.tr: Then the scribes and Pharisees began to reason, saying: "Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" But Jesus, knowing their reasonings, answered and said to them: "Why do you reason in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins" (he said to the paralytic), "I say to you, rise, take up your bed, and go home." And at once he rose in their sight, took up the bed on which he had lain, and went home glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with fear, saying, "We have seen unexpected things today."

units.la: Multa quidem Iesu Christi miracula Euangelistae describunt, at inter ea non facile aliud inuenies, quod huic praeferi mereatur, quod de paralytico restituto Lucas in praesenti narrat. Ita enim hoc ædidit, vt facto & verbis disertis testetur, se promissum illum humani generis Seruatorem esse, quem patres olim expectarunt. Et huc in primis facit, quòd cum paralysi mederi vellet, à peccatorum remissione exorsus est. Atqui ex peccato morbos, famem, sitim & omnia alia aduersorum genera vnà cum morte originem duxisse, notius est, quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Cùm ergo illa Christus remittat, simulq; ex his enatum morbum vno verbo curet, dubium non est, quin semen illud benedictum sit, quod serpentis caput conterere, regnum diaboli abolere, & miseros nos ex eius potestate eripere debuit. At ne quis de eius erga nos voluntate dubitaret, nuper præclarum mansuetudinis & bonitatis specimen dedit, quando nimium importunos non modò non corripuit aut reiecit, sed misero & gementi peccatorum remissionem pollicitus est. In præsenti verò non minus evidenter docet, sibi hanc potestatem à Patre datam esse, & id primò quidem verbis ostendit, deinde verò reipsa confirmat.
units.tr: Many miracles of Jesus Christ are described by the evangelists, yet among them you will not easily find another that deserves to be preferred to this one, the restoring of the paralytic which Luke relates here. For he published it in such a way that by the deed and by plain words he bears witness that he is that promised Saviour of the human race whom the fathers of old looked for. And this bears most directly on the point: that when he wished to heal the paralysis, he began with the remission of sins. Now, that diseases, famine, thirst and all other kinds of misfortune, together with death, took their origin from sin, is too well known to need proof. Since Christ therefore remits sins, and at the same time cures with a single word the disease that springs from them, there is no doubt that he is that blessed seed which was to crush the serpent's head, destroy the kingdom of the devil, and rescue us wretched people from his power. But lest anyone should doubt his will towards us, he lately gave a notable example of gentleness and goodness, when he not only did not rebuke or reject those who were too importunate, but promised forgiveness of sins to the wretched and groaning man. In the present passage he teaches no less clearly that this power has been given to him by the Father, and he shows this first by words, and then confirms it in fact.

units.la: Rursus autem ab occasione totius disceptationis Lucas orditur, quam Scribæ & Pharisæi præbuerunt. Hi enim audita consolatione, qua Christus paralytico peccatorum remissionem denunciabat, non quidem illi palàm & in faciem contradicunt, sed tamen intra animos suos rationes & argumenta colligunt, quibus eum summæ impietatis & arrogantiæ sacrilegæ accusent. Quis est iste (inquiunt) qui loquitur blasphemias? Et rationis loco subijciunt: Quis potest remittere peccata, nisi solus Deus? Est hoc argumentum per se firmissimum, si ita colligas: Quisquis sibi vendicat, quæ solius Dei sunt, is blasphemus est & sacrilegus: At solius Dei est peccata remittere. Ergo impius est & sacrilegus, qui hanc potestatem sibi vsurpat. Falluntur autem turpiter isti, quando argumentum hoc aduersus Christum torquent, & non vno modo suam malitiam produnt. Primò enim non opus erat ita ratiocinari, cùm nihil adhuc de sua potestate Christus dixisset. Nam consolatione solùm adduxerat, quales multæ apud prophetas habentur, quibus Dei gratia peccatoribus adhunc conuersis denuntiant. Deinde si omnino dixisset Christus: Ego tibi peccata tua remitto: non tamen iudicio tam præcipiti damnandus erat, cùm iam non pauca ædidisset diuinæ virtutis argumenta, & prophetæ non vno loco inter Messiæ beneficia peccatorum remissionem numerent. Ipse vulneratus est (inquit Isaias) propter transgressiones nostras: multa pacis nostræ super eum, & liuore eius nos sanati sumus. Item: Scientia sua multos iustificabit iustus seruus meus, quorum iniquitates ipse baiulabit. Ieremias autem de Messia inter alia dicit: Et hoc nomen eius, quo vocabunt eum, IEHOVA iustitia nostra. Quibus verbis diserte & diuinitatem veram & potestatem remittendi peccata illi tribuit. Apud Zachariam verò sic ait de Christi aduentu Dominus: In die illa fons aperietur domui Dauidis & habitatoribus Ierusalem pro peccato & menstrua immunditie, &c. Vbi duobus vocabulis tam actualia peccata (vt loquuntur) quàm innatam nobis naturæ vitiositatem comprehendit, & vtriusque mali expiationem seu ablutionem in Christo pollicetur. Taceo infinita huius generis testimonia, quæ cùm Scribæ & Legis doctores nunc ignorarent, nimis aperte animi odio & cæco liuore plenos produnt, quando tam audacter ad Christum damnandum prosiliunt. Imò extrema impudentiæ argumentum est, quando hoc nomine illum damnant, cùm ipsi suis operibus, quæ maiori ex parte secundùm hominum traditiones fiebant, meritum salutis & peccatorum remissionem tribuerent. Sed si quid hic coniecturis tribui debet, non alia re illos magis offensos fuisse crediderim, quàm quòd Christum gratis polliceri audirent id, ex quo ipsi quæstum vberrimum habebant. Et hæc illa Helena est, pro qua nostri etiam sæculi Pharisæi pugnant, quod metuunt, ne admissa Christi iustitia totius ipsorum quæstus euertatur, quem ex operum meritis, conductitijs preculus, peregrinationibus, votis & igne purgatorio faciunt. Atqui vtinam nostri illi tam ingenui essent, quàm Iudæorum Pharisæi fuere, qui etsi propriam iustitiam stabilire conarentur, hoc tamen verè salutis principium palàm confessi sunt, Neminem præter solum Deum peccata remittere posse. At nostri hodie hæreticos esse clamant omnes eos, qui ita sentiunt, & doctrinam istam ferro & igne persequuntur: adhæc potestatem illam sibi impudenter vendicat, eò quòd vncti & rasi characterem bestiæ acceperint. Ioram Israelis rex, etsi in alijs satis impius esset, intolerabilem tamen blasphemiam esse putauit, quòd Syriæ rex ab eo petijsse, vt Naamanum à lepra purgaret. Nam scissis vestibus suis clamabat: Egone Deus sum, vt occidam & vitæ restituam? At istorum audacia atq; arrogantia eò usque procedit, vt quod mains est sibi transcribant, & in hominum animabus purgandis
units.tr: Again, Luke begins from the occasion of the whole dispute, which the scribes and Pharisees gave. For they, having heard the comfort with which Christ announced the forgiveness of sins to the paralytic, do not indeed contradict him openly and to his face, but within their minds they gather reasons and arguments by which to accuse him of the highest impiety and sacrilegious arrogance. "Who is this," they say, "who speaks blasphemies?" And in place of a reason they add: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" This is in itself a most firm argument, if you draw the conclusion thus: whoever claims for himself what belongs to God alone is a blasphemer and sacrilegious; but forgiving sins belongs to God alone; therefore whoever usurps this power is impious and sacrilegious. But these men are shamefully mistaken when they turn this argument against Christ, and they reveal their malice in more than one way. First, there was no need to reason thus, since Christ had not yet said anything about his own power. For he had only offered consolation, of the sort found in many places in the prophets, by which the grace of God is announced to sinners who are now converted. Next, even if Christ had plainly said, "I forgive you your sins," he still ought not to have been condemned by such a headlong judgment, since he had already shown not a few proofs of divine power, and the prophets in more than one place count the forgiveness of sins among the benefits of the Messiah. "He was wounded," says Isaiah, "for our transgressions; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed." Likewise: "By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities." Jeremiah too says of the Messiah, among other things: "And this is his name by which they shall call him: JEHOVAH our righteousness." In these words he plainly ascribes to him both true divinity and the power of forgiving sins. Again, in Zechariah the Lord speaks thus of the coming of Christ: "In that day a fountain shall be opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness," and so on. Here in two words he comprehends both actual sins, as they are called, and the innate corruption of our nature, and promises in Christ the cleansing or washing away of both evils. I say nothing of the countless testimonies of this kind, which the scribes and doctors of the Law, now ignorant of them, betray all too clearly as full of hatred and blind envy, when they so boldly rush forward to condemn Christ. Indeed it is an extreme argument of shamelessness that they condemn him under this name, when they themselves attributed merit for salvation and the forgiveness of sins to their own works, which for the most part were done according to human traditions. But if anything here should be inferred by conjecture, I would believe they were offended by nothing more than by hearing Christ promise freely that from which they themselves had a most abundant gain. And this is that Helen for whom the Pharisees of our own age also fight, since they fear that, if the righteousness of Christ is admitted, the whole of their profit will be overturned, which they make out of the merits of works, paid masses, pilgrimages, vows and purgatorial fire. Yet would that our men were as ingenuous as the Pharisees of the Jews were, who, although they tried to establish their own righteousness, nevertheless openly confessed this true principle of salvation: that no one but God alone can forgive sins. But our men today cry out that all who think thus are heretics, and they pursue that doctrine with sword and fire. Besides this, they shamelessly claim for themselves that power, because they have received the mark of the beast, having been anointed and shaven. Joram, king of Israel, although in other respects he was quite impious, nevertheless thought it an intolerable blasphemy that the king of Syria had asked him to cleanse Naaman of leprosy. For tearing his clothes he cried out: "Am I God, to kill and to restore to life?" But the audacity and arrogance of these men go so far that they claim for themselves what is worse, and boast that they can cleanse and free human souls, which Joram saw was impossible for a man to do in curing the body.

units.la: Pharisæi Christum blasphemiæ accusant.
units.tr: The Pharisees accuse Christ of blasphemy.

units.la: Isa.53.
units.tr: Isa. 53.

units.la: Ier.23.
units.tr: Jer. 23.

units.la: Zach.13. aut liberandis seid posse iactent, quod in corpore curando Ioram impossibile homini esse videbat.
units.tr: Zech. 13. or to free souls, which they boast can be done, when, in curing the body, Joram saw it was impossible for a man.

units.la: Porrò Christum audiamus, qui & istorum calumniam graviter confutat, & suam authoritatem constanter asserit. Nam primò reipsa docet, se Deum esse, & proinde non debere blasphemum censeri, etiamsi remissionem peccatorum penes se esse dicat. Id vero probat, dum quod illi intra animos suos voluebant videt & arguit. Quid (inquit) ratiocinamini in cordibus vestris? Atqui cordium arcana atque cogitationes novisse solius Dei est, ut non uno loco scriptura docent, & res ipsa loquitur. Etsi enim magnum sit in multis inquirendis humani ingenij acumen, nemini tamen vnquam datum fuit in aliorum corda penetrare, nisi singularis spiritus sancti revelatio accesserit. At Christum nihil unquam latuit, & idem absens quoque vidit quae alibi fiebant, ut multa eius exempla docent. Verus ergo Deus sit oportet. Ut autem hoc ad nostram consolationem & vitae totius institutionem accommodari debeat, in Marci expositione & multis aliis locis diximus. In praesenti aliud argumentum subijcit Christus, quo stupidos illos excitat, ut rem rectius expendant. Utrum (inquit) est facilius? dicere, Remissa sunt tibi peccata tua; an dicere, Surge & ambula? Quorum verborum hic sensus est: Eiusdem virtutis est peccata remittere & morbis solo verbo absque omni naturalis medicinae praesidio mederi. At alterum hoc me posse non negabitis, nisi cum ratione pudore quoque omnem abiecistis. Cur ergo blasphemus dicor, si & alterum illud mihi vendicem? Sed agedum, quia liuor & animi malitia vos non patitur ea in mentem revocare, quae hucusque feci, in hoc etiam sanando quid possim declarabo, ut constet me etsi filius hominis factus sim, & mortali carne vestitus in terris agam, habere tamen potestatem remittendi peccata. Et mox ad paralyticum conversus, eum surgere, lectulum in humeros attollere, & domum abire iubet. Nec mora, exilit ille, & magna cum omnium admiratione facit quod iussus fuerat. Invidi autem illi, etsi affectum impium non exuant, obmutescunt tamen, neque habent quod contradicant.
units.tr: Next let us hear Christ, who both sharply refutes their calumny and steadily asserts his own authority. For first he shows by the deed that he is God, and therefore should not be counted a blasphemer, even though he says that the forgiveness of sins is in his power. He proves this when he sees and exposes what they were turning over in their minds. "Why," he says, "do you reason in your hearts?" Now the secrets and thoughts of hearts belong to God alone to know, as Scripture teaches in more than one place, and the matter itself speaks so. For although the sharpness of human wit is great in searching out many things, yet no one has ever been granted to penetrate the hearts of others, unless a singular revelation of the Holy Spirit has come to him. But nothing was ever hidden from Christ, and he saw even absent things that were being done elsewhere, as many of his examples show. He must therefore be true God. How this ought to be applied to our consolation and to the whole ordering of life, we have said in our exposition of Mark and in many other places. In the present passage Christ adds another argument, by which he rouses those dullards to weigh the matter more rightly. "Which," he says, "is easier: to say, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'?" The sense of these words is this: it takes the same power to forgive sins as to heal diseases by a single word, without any help of natural medicine. But you will not deny that I can do the second, unless you have cast off all reason and shame as well. Why, then, am I called a blasphemer, if I claim for myself that other power also? But come, since envy and the malice of your minds do not allow you to call to mind what I have done so far, I will show what I can do in this healing too, so that it may be plain that, although I have been made the Son of Man and clothed in mortal flesh and live on earth, I nevertheless have the power to forgive sins. And straightway, turning to the paralytic, he bids him rise, lift his bed on his shoulders, and go home. At once the man leaps up, and, to the great astonishment of all, does what he was ordered. Those envious men, however, although they do not cast off their impious feeling, are struck dumb, and have nothing to say in reply.

units.la: At nos inter alia hoc quoque in Christi verbis observabimus, confutari hís Exorcistas & qui verbis conceptis morbos pelli aut alia confici aiunt, quae vires humanas superant. Quia enim divinae virtutis est solo verbo res conficere, revera blasphemi & sacrilegi sunt, qui verborum recitationi & suffurris suis illud tribuunt. Neque audiendi sunt, qui illis hoc nomine patrocinantur, quod frequenter effectus cum verbis & exorcismis eiusmodi coniunctus fit, & multi per eos interdum iuvenitur. Sunt enim haec mali daemonis praestigiae, quibus Deus iusto iudicio eos deludi patitur, qui non ab ipso uno pendent, & qui a verbi sui veritate declinant. Et extat in tales horribile exemplum in filios Scenae olim editum, qui Ephesi Paulum in eijciendis daemonijs imitari voluerunt, eo nimirum errore decepti, quod verbis vim illam inesse putarent. Pie ergo olim sanctum est, ne qui tales audiant, & ut ab ecclesia excludantur, quicunque artibus istis vacaverint. Et extant in iure Pontificio canones non pauci, quibus ista damnantur. Vide causam 26. quaest. 5.
units.tr: But among other things we will also observe in Christ's words that exorcists are refuted here, and those who claim that diseases are driven out, or other things that exceed human powers are accomplished, by spoken formulas. Since it belongs to divine power alone to accomplish things by a word alone, those who attribute this to the recitation of words and their fumigations are truly blasphemers and sacrilegious. Nor should we listen to those who defend them on the ground that an effect often follows when such words and exorcisms are used, and that many are sometimes found helped through them. These are the illusions of the evil demon, by which God, in just judgment, allows to be deluded those who do not depend on him alone and who turn aside from the truth of his Word. There is a dreadful example of this in the sons of Sceva, who once wanted to imitate Paul in casting out demons at Ephesus, deceived by the error that power lay in the words themselves. It has therefore long been piously decided that such people should not be heard, and that whoever has devoted himself to these arts should be excluded from the Church. Indeed, there are not a few canons in the Papist law by which these practices are condemned. See Causa 26, Quaestio 5.

units.la: Continet praeterea locus iste omnia, quae ad peccatorum remissionem pertinent, ex qua salus nostra omnis dependet. Author huius indicatur unus & solus Deus. Causam ipsam remissionis vocabulum innuit, & hanc in Dei gratia sive misericordia gratuita nobis offendit. Mediator vero illius est Christus aeternus Dei filius, qui ideo hominem assumpsit, ut nos patri reconciliaret. Remittit autem Deus peccata plene, ut simul a poena omni liberet, Et remissionem hanc per Euangelium nobis offert, quod qui cum fide audiunt, ij & illam & cum hac salutem atque vitam aeternam apprehendunt. At quia de his omnibus in Marco prolixe egimus, eadem hoc loco repetere superuacaneum foret, & ideo capita modo praecipua annotamus. Vnum tamen hoc in praesenti addere liber, ad remissionis peccatorum doctrinam pertinere, quod paralyticus mox ad Christi mandatum lectulo sublato domum abit, & Deum glorificat. Admonet hoc officij eos, qui per Christum a peccatis liberati sunt: ut nimirum huic sese morigeros praebeant, ex peccatorum caeno surgant, & reliquis prioris vitae studijs ad Dei domum contendant, ut ecclesiae eius membra efficiantur: vitam denique omnem & actiones huius vniuersas ita instituant, ut in illis Deus glorificetur. Et hoc illud est, quod Paulus monet, ut nos Deo sistamus hostiam viventem. Est autem haec pars probe tenenda, ne vel gratuita remissionis doctrina ad carnis licentiam abutamur, vel eorum calumnijs offendamur, qui Euangelium hoc nomine infamant, quod sceleribus fenestram aperiat, in hominum animis securitatem & socordiam pariat, adeoq; bonis operibus inimicum sit. Restat miraculi effectus, quem his verbis Euangelista comprehendit. Et stupor cepit omnes, & glorificabant Deum, & repleti sunt timore, dicentes. Certè vidimus inopinata hodie. Ergo non paralytico solùm salutem attulit Christus, neque aduersariorum modò ora obturauit, verumetiam ad omnes spectatores fructus redijt non vulgaris. Nam primum rei insolitæ euentus attonitos reddit, & stuporem parit, qui aliquantulum dubios & animi incertos fecit. At non belluinum fuisse stuporem hunc, ex eo apparet, quòd mox Deum glorificarunt: quod fieri non poterat, nisi animos rursus collegissent. Agnoscunt ergo Deum tanti miraculi authorem, adeoque in Christo virtutem diuinam prædicant. Comitatur tamen hæc timor pius, cuius causæ non leues fuerunt, quòd & propria soccordia illis in mentem venit, qua Christum hucusque neglexerant, & quòd eundem à Sacerdotibus & scribis nunc quoque ignominiosius tractatum fuisse viderent. Et hinc fit, quòd Christo palàm virtutis diuinæ testimonium ferunt, quando se inopinata & quæ nunquam auditu fuissent sperare, vidisse fatentur. Est hoc veræ fidei non leue argumentum, quòd non verentur aduersarios Christi quantumuis potentia & authoritate præstantes, quò minus de illo honorificè sentiant et loquantur. Rursus ergo elusit aduersariorum conatus & consilia Christus: quando hic gloriam eius illi prouexerunt, & illustriorem reddiderunt, dum blasphemiæ notam ipsi inurere student. Quem fere exitum esse consiliorum omnium, quæ hostes Christi concipiunt, non uno loco diximus. At scribuntur hæc nobis in exemplum, & vt istos imitemur multa nos mouere debent. Nam vt salutificam suam virtutem per Euangelium nobis Christus offert, & passim edit iudiciorum exempla in hostes suos. Pergit tamen infelix mundus, & pleriq; sua contumacia exitium sibi accersunt. Itaque sancto eius timore excitati surgamus ex peccati luto, coniungamur autem ecclesiæ eius, & illius beneficium prædicemus. Cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage contains everything that pertains to the forgiveness of sins, on which all our salvation depends. The author is named as one and only God. The word "remission" itself points to the cause, and shows that this cause is in the grace or free mercy of God toward us. Its mediator is Christ, the eternal Son of God, who assumed humanity so that he might reconcile us to the Father. God forgives sins fully, so that he frees us at the same time from all punishment, and he offers this remission to us through the Gospel; those who hear it with faith lay hold of both the remission and, with it, salvation and eternal life. But since we have treated all these matters at length on Mark, it would be superfluous to repeat the same things here, and so we note only the main headings. I will add just one thing for now, which pertains to the doctrine of the forgiveness of sins: that the paralytic, at Christ's command, immediately takes up his bed, goes home, and glorifies God. This admonishes those who have been freed from their sins through Christ of their duty: namely, that they should show themselves obedient to this command, rise out of the mire of sin, and, leaving their former pursuits, press on to the house of God so that they may become members of his Church; and finally, that they should so order their whole life and all their actions that God is glorified in them. This is what Paul also urges, that we present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice. This part, moreover, must be firmly held, lest we either abuse the doctrine of free remission as a license for the flesh, or be offended by the slanders of those who defame the Gospel on this ground, that it opens a window for crimes, produces security and sloth in men's minds, and is therefore hostile to good works. There remains the effect of the miracle, which the Evangelist sums up in these words: "And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying: We have seen unexpected things today." Clearly Christ brought salvation not only to the paralytic, and not only stopped the mouths of his adversaries, but also brought an unusual fruit to all the onlookers. For first, the event of an unaccustomed matter struck them with astonishment and produced amazement, which made them somewhat doubtful and uncertain in mind. But that this amazement was not brutish is evident from the fact that they soon glorified God, which could not have happened unless they had gathered their minds again. So they acknowledge God as the author of so great a miracle, and so proclaim the divine power in Christ. Yet this amazement is accompanied by a godly fear, whose causes were not slight: both because the thought of their own negligence came to them, by which they had hitherto neglected Christ, and because they saw that he was now treated even more shamefully by the priests and scribes. And hence it comes about that they openly bear witness to Christ's divine power when they confess that they have seen unexpected things that they had never thought to hear of. This is no small proof of true faith, that they do not fear, however powerful and influential Christ's adversaries may be, to think and speak honourably of him. Thus Christ again mocked the attempts and plans of his adversaries: for these men, while striving to fix the stain of blasphemy on him, have only raised his glory and made it more illustrious. We have said in more than one place that this is nearly the outcome of all the plans that Christ's enemies devise. But these things are written to us as an example, and many things ought to move us to imitate them. For just as Christ offers us his saving power through the Gospel, so he also everywhere displays examples of his judgments against his enemies. Yet the unhappy world goes on, and most men, by their obstinacy, bring destruction upon themselves. Therefore, roused by his holy fear, let us rise out of the mire of sin, let us join his Church, and proclaim his benefit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LI.
units.tr: HOMILY LI.

units.la: Et post hæc exiuit, & conspexit publicanum nomine Leui, sedentem ad telonium, & dixit ei: Sequere me. Et ille relictis omnibus surrexit, & secutus est eum. Et fecit ei Leui epulum magnum domi suæ, eratq; turba multa publicanorum & aliorum, qui cum ipsis accumbebant.
units.tr: "And after these things he went out, and saw a publican named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom, and he said to him: Follow me. And he, leaving everything, rose up and followed him. And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a great crowd of publicans and others who were reclining with them."

units.la: Lvcas Euangelista hunc suæ historiæ finem atq; scopum sibi constituit, vt Iesum Christum, qui ex Maria Virgine homo natus est, verum & æternum Dei filium, rerumq; omnium Dominum, & proinde promissum humani generis seruatorem esse demonstret. Id verò non verbis nudis aut humani ingenij rationibus, sed reipsa probat, dum opera eius miraculosa diligenter exponit. Inter hæc cumprimis memorabile est, quod nuper in paralytico editum fuisse audiuimus. Hunc enim non fortuito, sed propter peccata quædam singularia in morbum incidisse, & ideo non solùm corpore verum etiam animo grauiter excruciatum fuisse, ex Christi verbis apparet. Illi ergo peccatorum remissionem gratuitam pollicetur, simulq; eum à morbo & huius causa, peccato nimirum liberat, atq; eo facto se redemptorem & salutis veræ authorem esse testatur. At ne quis ipsius potentia & maiestate territus, eum ad peccatores insigniores & qui vitijs non vulgaribus grauati sunt, pertinere dubitaret, aut ijsdem gratiam quidem aliquam conferri, non autem in aliquo pretio eos apud Deum esse arbitraretur, commodè historiam, quam modò recitauimus, subijcit Lucas, qua publicanum auaritiæ & iniustitiæ infamem ex ipsa officina (vt sic dicam) iniquitatis euocauit, & eundem in Apostolorum suorum gregem assumpsit. Est igitur historia hæc digna, in cuius consideratione non ofcitanter versentur, quicunq; se peccatorum conscientia grauari sentiunt.
units.tr: Luke the Evangelist set this as the aim and purpose of his history: to show that Jesus Christ, who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, is the true and eternal Son of God and Lord of all things, and therefore the promised Saviour of mankind. He proves this not by bare words or human reasoning, but by the facts themselves, when he carefully sets out his miracles. Among these, the one we heard of recently, performed on the paralytic, is especially worth remembering. From Christ's words it is clear that this man had fallen into his illness not by chance, but on account of certain particular sins, and so he was grievously tormented not only in body but also in mind. Christ therefore promises him the free forgiveness of sins, and at the same time frees him from his illness and its cause, which is sin, and by this deed he testifies that he is the Redeemer and the author of true salvation. But lest anyone, terrified by his power and majesty, should doubt that he applies to the more notorious sinners, those burdened with vices that are not ordinary, or should think that some grace is indeed offered to them but that they are of no worth in God's sight, Luke rightly adds the story we have just recited. In it he called out of the very workshop (so to speak) of iniquity a publican infamous for greed and injustice, and took him into the company of his Apostles. This story is therefore worth considering by all who feel that their consciences are weighed down by sin, and they should not dwell on it half-heartedly.

units.la: Hi vt consolationem efficaciorem habeant, ipsum Leui (qui alio nomine Matthæus dictus fuit) diligentius inspicere debent. Sedit vt ad telonium, & proinde ex publicanorum ordine fuit, de quibus Cap. tertio prolixè est dictum. Ex quæstu autem hoc ditissimum factum fuisse, & inter publicanos gradum aliquem eminentiorem tenuisse, ex conuiuio apparet, ad quod tam multi confluxerunt. Multa igitur fecerit oportet præter ius & æquum, priusquam dives fieret, & ad eum dignitatis gradum peruenire t sub Romanis præsidibus, qui omnia ad suum quæstum instituebant. Hunc tamen adrelonium sedentem & præsenti lucro intentum Christus vocat, & vt vocationi obtemperet trahit: Ita nimirum docens, se fortem illum Heroem esse, qui diaboli domum invadere & eius vasa diripere debuit. Quod enim hic fecit, sæpe alias factum est, quando & meretrices relicto turpi quæstu pudicitiæ & pietatis studium sequi coegit, & plures alios publicanos ad se pertraxit, imo ex pharisæorum ordine Nicodemum sibi discipulum fecit, & inter milites sanguinarios invenit, qui fidem in ipsum publicè profiterentur.
units.tr: So that they may have a more effective consolation, they ought to look more carefully at Levi himself, who was also called Matthew. He sat at the receipt of custom, and so he was of the order of publicans, about whom we spoke at length in the third chapter. That he had become very rich from this trade, and held a rather prominent rank among the publicans, is clear from the banquet to which so many gathered. He must therefore have done many things beyond what was right and fair before he became rich and reached that rank under the Roman governors, who arranged everything for their own profit. Yet Christ calls this man, sitting at the receipt of custom and intent on present gain, and draws him to obey the call. In doing so he teaches, no doubt, that he is that strong hero who had to invade the house of the devil and plunder his goods. What he did here he often did elsewhere: he drew harlots away from their shameful gain to pursue chastity and piety, he drew many other publicans to himself, and indeed from the order of the Pharisees he made Nicodemus his disciple, and among bloodthirsty soldiers he found men who openly professed faith in him.

units.la: Ac hic non sine singulari consilio factum est, quod Matthæus non solùm à quæstu avaro & iniquo avocatur, sed ex publicano Apostolus fit, qui & viva voce Euangelium Iesu Christi prædicauit, & idem hoc inter primos scriptis mandavit. Causæ huius consilij certæ sunt. Prima, vt omnis pagati Euangelij gloria Deo cederet, & huius authoritatem non ab hominibus pendere, sed æterno diuinæ prouidentiæ decreto niti constaret. Nam si humana ratione audire libeat, non facilè fidem meruissent, qui vel vitæ genus inhonestum prius secuti fuerant, vel propter egestatem contemnebantur. Quia tamen idem orbis totius domitores facti sunt, & gentes prope omnes ad Christi obedientiam adduxerunt, quis non videat, hoc Dei opus fuisse, qui vt sic fieret, ab æterno constituerat? Docent idem multorum aliorum exempla, qui vel ex philosophorum scholis, vel militum castris egressi, postea præclaram ecclesiæ Christi operam nauauerunt.
