Debent ista obseruari, ne quem offendat vilis & contemptibilis administrorum Verbi conditio, aut etiam vita anteacta: quin potius in ipsum Verbum intenti eos imitemur, qui relictis studijs deterioribus sese totos Christo & ecclesiæ eius consecrarunt. Altera causa est, quod proderat gratiam Dei, quæ per Euangelium offertur, in ipsius præconibus commendari, vt facilius eius promissis crederent, qui prooter scelera graviora intra conscientias suas fluctuant. Huc ergo referri debet, quòd Matthæus ex publicano Euangelista, Petrus ex abnegatore Christi fidelissimus eiusdem præco, Paulus ex crudeli carnifice & lupo sanguinario vigilantissimus ecclesiarum pastor, reliqui item omnes ex ambitiosis & contentiosis regni terreni amatoribus regni cælestis præcones & fidei atq; humilitatis Christianæ doctores facti sunt. Quid, An non latronem eo honore Christus dignatus est, vt de ipsius innocentia publicum testimonium ferret, & ex cruce, seu cathedra aut suggestu sacro ipsum prædicaret & invocaret, qui & Concilij generalis & Pilati præsidis authoritate publica damnatus fuerat? Adde his Centurionem & milites, qui cum Christo non minori cum fœuitia quàm scurrilitate illusissent, paulò post totis animis conuersi, illum & iustum & Dei filium esse testati sunt. Excitent nos ista, vt Euangelio credamus, & tot exemplis in eo relucentem Dei gratiam fide constanti amplectamur.
units.tr: And it was not without a special purpose that Matthew was not only called away from avaricious and unjust gain, but was made an Apostle from a publican, one who both preached the Gospel of Jesus Christ by the living voice and committed it to writing among the first. There are certain reasons for this purpose. The first is that all the glory of the Gospel preached should go to God, and that it should be plain that its authority does not depend on men but rests on the eternal decree of divine providence. For if one wished to judge by human reasoning, those who had previously followed a dishonourable way of life, or were despised on account of their poverty, would hardly have deserved to be believed. Yet the same men became conquerors of the whole world and brought almost all nations to obedience to Christ. Who does not see that this was the work of God, who had determined from eternity that it should happen so? The examples of many others teach the same, who, coming out either from the schools of philosophers or from the camps of soldiers, afterwards rendered distinguished service to the Church of Christ. These things ought to be noted, so that the lowly and despised condition of the ministers of the Word, or even their former life, may not offend anyone. Rather, let us attend to the Word itself and imitate those who, having left their worse pursuits, consecrated themselves wholly to Christ and his Church. The second reason is that the grace of God offered through the Gospel would be commended by the very heralds of it, so that those who wavered in their consciences because of graver sins might more easily believe its promises. To this belongs the fact that Matthew, from a publican, became an Evangelist; that Peter, from a denier of Christ, became his most faithful herald; that Paul, from a cruel executioner and bloodthirsty wolf, became the most watchful pastor of the churches; and that the rest likewise, from men ambitious and contentious for an earthly kingdom, became heralds of the heavenly kingdom and teachers of Christian faith and humility. What? Did Christ not honour the robber with this distinction, to bear public witness to his innocence, and to proclaim and invoke him from the cross, or from the sacred chair or pulpit, though he had been condemned by the public authority of a general council and of Pilate the governor? Add to these the centurion and the soldiers, who had mocked Christ with no less cruelty than buffoonery, and who, a little later, turned with their whole hearts and testified that he was both just and the Son of God. Let these things stir us to believe the Gospel, and to embrace with steadfast faith the grace of God shining forth in it through so many examples.

units.la: Habet præterea exemplum hoc typum vocationis nostræ, quæ (si rem omnem probè expendamus) nobis cum Matthæo planè eadem est. Vt enim hunc in officina auaritiæ sedentem ex mera gratia vocat Christus, dum præteriturus & aliud facturus videbatur: ita nos quoque in fabrica scelerum occupatos et nihil minus quàm de salute nostra cogitantes, absque omni operum nostrorum respectu Deus vocat, & plerunq; tunc vocat, quando nos negligere & nostri curam omnem iampridem deposuisse videri potest. Sic Iudaicam gentem inter prætereundum vidisse, & omnibus modis corruptam atq; fœdatam adoptauisse, apud Ezechielem dicitur. Fatebuntur idem de seipsis quicunq; in semetipsos altius descenderint, & diligentius examinarint suos mores atq; studia, quibus priusquam ad Christi cognitionem venirent, occupati fuerunt. Neq; hic mihi quis eos obijciat, qui salutem anxiè quærere videntur, dum ceremoniarum operosissimarum exercitio & operum splendidissimorum studio indefinenti cælos scandere conantur. Hi enim omnes eò longius à salutis via recedunt, quò ardentius eam inquirunt; & (vt de Iudæis Paulus loquitur) quia Dei iustitiam ignorant, et pro priam stabilire atq; fulcire satagunt, diuinæ non subijciuntur, quam ille nobis in Christo offert, & quæ sola nos apud Dei tribunal tueri potest. Eò maior ergo & abundantior est bonitatis Dei thesaurus, quando ad aliquos illorum quoq; redundat, qui apertum bellum quodam modo cum illius gratia gerunt, & gigantum instar congestis undiq; suorum operum montibus in cælos euadere, & hos tanquam non expugnare studeant.
units.tr: Moreover, this example is a type of our calling, which (if we weigh the whole matter carefully) is entirely the same for us as it was for Matthew. For just as Christ called him from his sitting in the workshop of greed, out of pure grace, while seeming to pass by and to be about to do something else, so God calls us also, when we are busy in the forge of sins and thinking nothing of our salvation, without any regard to our works. And he often calls us just when it may seem that we have neglected ourselves and long ago cast off all care for ourselves. Thus, according to Ezekiel, God saw the Jewish nation as he passed by, and when it was corrupted and defiled in every way, he adopted it. Those who descend more deeply into themselves, and examine more carefully their own ways and pursuits, in which they were occupied before they came to the knowledge of Christ, will confess the same about themselves. Nor should anyone here object to me those who seem to seek salvation anxiously, while they strive without ceasing to climb to heaven by the most laborious exercise of ceremonies and the eager pursuit of splendid works. For all these move the further away from the way of salvation the more eagerly they seek it. And (as Paul speaks of the Jews) because they are ignorant of the righteousness of God, and busy themselves to establish and prop up their own, they do not submit to the divine righteousness which he offers us in Christ, and which alone can defend us before the tribunal of God. Therefore the treasure of God's goodness is so much greater and more abundant, when it overflows also to some of those who wage open war, as it were, against his grace, and who, like giants, strive to escape to heaven on mountains of their own works piled up on every side, and to storm it, as if they were not to be overcome.

units.la: Sed ad Matthæum nostrum redeamus, qui mox relictis omnibus surrexit & Christum vocantem secutus est. Est hoc præclarum obedientiæ fidei exemplum, quod eò illustrius erit, si cogites, quàm multa enim retinere potuerint. Nam vt de quæstu longè pberrimo nihil dicamus, quem nondum subdum subductis rationibus relinquere stultum simul & iniquum videbatur, saltem quaerere poterat, quo nam iturus esset Christus? Unde viuat? Ubi suis prospiciat? quae ipsius sub eo futura sit conditio? Metuendum item erat vulgi iudicium, aequalium & sociorum inimicitia, praesidum indignatio, domesticorum fremitus & murmur, atque infinita alia, quae si quid huius faciendum esset, ratio nostra nobis suggerit. Sed nihil huius admittit fides, quae moram omnem abrumpere & Christum sequi iubet. Nam ut Paulus ait, captiuum ducit intellectum omnem, & Dei verbo rationes omnes subiicit, sicuti multorum similium exempla testantur. Ex his autem apparet, cur hodie plerique Deo tam difficulter obediant. Ideo nimirum, quia fides rara est, neque Deo putamus credendum esse, nisi rem ipsam cum promissis eius coniunctam & praesentem adesse videamus. Quae causa est, quod carnis rationes atque consilia audimus, quae in Dei praeceptis non quid huic debeamus spectat, sed potius difficultatem & pericula quaerit, & cupit inuenire rationes, quibus inobedientiam suam excuset. At longe aliud fidei ingenium est, quae quia ex Deo tota dependet, & huic placere cupit, omnia nobis non modo possibilia, verumetiam levia & iucunda reddit, dum Dei amore inflammant, quo fit, ut nihil nobis suauius sit, quam huic gratum officium praestare.
units.tr: But let us return to our Matthew, who, leaving everything at once, rose up and followed Christ calling him. This is an excellent example of obedient faith, and it will shine the more clearly if you consider how many things he might have held back. For, to say nothing of the very profitable business he had not yet reckoned up and which it seemed foolish and unjust to leave, he could at least have asked where Christ was going. Where would he live? Where would he provide for his own? What would his condition be under him? He also had to fear the judgement of the crowd, the enmity of his equals and associates, the indignation of the governors, the grumbling and murmuring of his household, and countless other things, which our reason suggests to us if anything of this kind is to be done. But faith admits none of this, which bids us break off all delay and follow Christ. For, as Paul says, it leads every understanding captive and subjects all reasonings to the word of God, as the examples of many similar men bear witness. From this it appears why so many people today obey God so reluctantly. Surely this is because faith is rare, and we think God is not to be believed unless we see the thing itself, joined to his promises, actually present. This is the reason we listen to the reasons and counsels of the flesh, which, when faced with God's commands, do not look at what we owe him, but seek out difficulty and danger, and try to find reasons by which to excuse their disobedience. But the nature of faith is quite different. Since it depends wholly on God and desires to please him, it makes everything not only possible for us but even light and pleasant, while it inflames us with the love of God, so that nothing is sweeter to us than to render this grateful service to him.

units.la: Est etiam hic obseruatu dignissima virtus diuinae vocationis apud electos. Difficile quidem est carni Christum sequi, & augent difficultatem hanc vehementer diuitiae, quibus Matthaeum ab undauisse initio diximus. Nec temere a Christo dictum est, facilius esse ut camelus per foramen acus transeat, quam ut diuites in regnum Dei ingrediantur. At vincunt difficultatem omnem electi, quia pastoris sui vocem norunt, & per aures in animos transmissam sequuntur. Debet hoc obseruari, ne de nostra aut aliorum salute facile desperemus, aut etiam temere damnemus eos, quos adhuc remoris difficilioribus, ceu pedicis quibusdam detineri cernimus. Qui enim verbi sui virtute ex tenebris lucem euocare, & vniuersam hanc mundi machinam ex nihilo producere potuit, idem ille viam facile inuenit, qua suos, quando tempus est, ex tenebrarum potestate in lucem educat, & ex nolentibus volentes efficiat, qui abiectis omnibus impedimentis ipsum sequantur.
units.tr: There is also a most worthy virtue of divine calling to be observed among the elect. It is indeed difficult to follow Christ in the flesh, and the riches by which, as we said at the beginning, Matthew was overflowed greatly add to this difficulty. Nor did Christ speak carelessly when He said that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for the rich to enter the kingdom of God. Yet the elect overcome every difficulty, because they know the voice of their shepherd and, once it has passed through their ears into their minds, they follow it. This should be observed, so that we do not readily despair of our own salvation or of that of others, nor rashly condemn those whom we see still held back by heavier hindrances, as though by certain snares. For He who could call light out of darkness by the power of His Word, and bring this whole machine of the world into being out of nothing, is the same One who easily finds the way by which, when the time comes, He leads His own out of the power of darkness into the light, and makes the unwilling willing, so that, with every hindrance cast aside, they follow Him.

units.la: At non modo vocantem Christum relicto telonio Matthaeus sequitur, sed eundem domum suam deducit, & conuiuio excipit honorario, ad quod multi publicani & peccatores (id est, qui etsi non eiusdem ordinis essent, flagitiis tamen & vitiis infignioribus infames erant) confluxerunt. Quia enim publicani (ut alias diximus) Iudaeis exosi erant, neque ad honestiorum consortia admittebantur, facile in suam societatem recipiebant eos, qui propter vitae genus inhonestum aut mores minus laudatos excludebantur ab iis, qui reliquis honestiores volebant videri. Proderit autem conuiuium illud cum suis conuiuis propius inspexisse. Nam in genere quidem hoc exemplo hospitalitas nobis commendatur, & arguuntur rigidi illi Catones, qui dum honestatem & virtutis studium prae aliis simulant, omnia fere humanitatis officia damnare solent, quasi nefas sit aliquem conuiuio lautiori excipere, & aliquas impensas facere extraordinarias. Confutantur illi multorum sanctorum exemplis, & in primis Christi, quem eiusmodi epulas non semel sua praesentia ornauisse legimus. Interim minime probamus luxum & intemperantiam, quibus hodie passim peccatur, sed humanitatem docemus, qui facile omni culpa vacabit, si omnia ex charitate syncera fiant secundum fidei regulam, quae a Dei verbo nos discedere non sinet. Quoad vero Matthaeum gratitudinis officium ille praestat Christo, & quid nos eidem debeamus docet pro eo beneficio, quo infelices ex diaboli seruitio in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit. Excipiamus illum totis animis, & nos ipsos ei sistamus viuentem hostiam, qua nullum epulum lautius & iucundius illi parari poterit. Deinde in membra eius benefici simus, quo loco nobis esse debent, quicunque ipsum vera fide amplexi sunt. Neque istos solum diligamus, sed regnum illius quam latissime propagemus ad eos quoque, qui ab eius cognitione adhuc alieni sunt. Et huc referri debet, quod Matthaeus alios quoque complures ad epulum istud admittit, ut nimirum salutis socios habeat, quos paulo ante scelerum socios habuerat. Iubet hoc gloria Dei, cuius nos studiosissimos esse decet, & hoc ipsum charitatis lex praecipit: quam minime seruant, quicunque aliorum salutem securi negligunt. Quales autem censeri debent, qui quos Christo adducere debebant, effreni morum licentia & vitae exemplo corruptissimo offendunt? Est hoc nimis vulgare hodie, neque dubium alicui esse debet, Deum hoc potissimum nomine nobis irasci, quod exigua gloria ipsius cura tangimur. Est præterea obseruatu dignissima publicanorum facilitas, qui Matthæum accedere dignantur, quem ab ordine ipsorum defecisse videbant. Solent enim fere qui vitijs affuenerunt vehementer offendi, si qui deserta ipsorum societate ad vitæ genus honestius transeunt. Imò quia isti Christum quoque non oderunt neque fastidiunt, qui Matthæum ab illis abstraxerat, non obscure testantur, se etiam veritatis & salutis studio teneri. Quia enim ea erat ipsorum conditio, vt peccata sua neque negare neque dissimulare possent, facilius excitari potuerunt ad recipiendam pœnitentiæ & salutis æternæ doctrinam, quam Pharisæi propriæ iustitiæ fiducia turgentes fastidiebant. Quòd verò istorum mensæ adesse Christus Dominus, consolationem dulcissimam affert afflictis conscientijs. Eo enim testari voluit, quòd ad se conuersos vere in gratiam recipiat, & amicorum loco habeat. Minimè ergo audiri debent, qui noua quotidie satisfactionum atque expiationum genera fingunt, quibus infirmorum animos territant. Nos potius vocantem nos Deum audiamus, & relicto mundi & principis eius infelici seruitio Christum Iesum sequamur, qui vt in huius vitæ studio laborantibus adesse, ita hoc emensos ad se colligit, vt in domo patris sui eadem cum illo mensa fruantur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But Matthew did not merely follow Christ calling him away from the tax booth; he also brought Him to his house and received Him at a splendid feast, to which many tax collectors and sinners (that is, those who, though not of the same rank, were nonetheless notorious for their disgraceful and conspicuous vices) flocked. For since the tax collectors (as we have said elsewhere) were hateful to the Jews and were not admitted to the company of the more respectable, Matthew readily received into his fellowship those who were shut out by an unseemly way of life or by less commendable conduct, by those who wished to appear more honourable than the rest. It will, however, be profitable to look more closely at that feast and at its guests. For in general this example recommends hospitality to us, and it condemns those stern Catos who, while they pretend to honesty and zeal for virtue above others, are accustomed to condemn almost all the duties of humanity, as though it were wrong to entertain someone at a rather lavish table and to incur some extraordinary expense. They are refuted by the examples of many saints, and above all of Christ, whom we read to have graced such banquets with His presence more than once. Meanwhile we by no means approve of the extravagance and intemperance by which people everywhere sin today, but we teach humanity, which will easily be free from blame if all things are done from sincere charity according to the rule of faith, which will not allow us to depart from the Word of God. As for Matthew, he performs a duty of gratitude to Christ, and he teaches what we owe Him for the benefit by which He rescued the unhappy from the bondage of the devil into the liberty of the sons of God. Let us receive Him with our whole souls, and present ourselves to Him as a living sacrifice, than which no feast more splendid and pleasing can be prepared for Him. Then let us be members of His benefit, in the place which all who have embraced Him in true faith ought to have. Nor should we love these alone, but spread His kingdom as widely as possible, also to those who are still strangers to its knowledge. To this also belongs the fact that Matthew admits many others to that feast, that is, so that he may have as companions of salvation those whom shortly before he had as companions of sins. The glory of God, which we ought most zealously to seek, commands this, and the law of charity itself prescribes this very thing; those who carelessly neglect the salvation of others keep it very little. But what must they be judged to be who offend by unrestrained licence of morals and by a most corrupt example of life those whom they ought to bring to Christ? This is far too common today, and there ought to be no doubt for anyone that God is angry with us chiefly on this account, that we are moved by too little care for His glory. Moreover, the readiness of the tax collectors is worth most careful notice, since they deign to approach Matthew, whom they saw had withdrawn from their order. For those who have grown accustomed to vices are usually greatly offended if any of them leave their company behind and pass over to a more honourable way of life. Indeed, because these men did not hate or scorn Christ, who had drawn Matthew away from them, they clearly bear witness that they too are moved by a zeal for truth and salvation. For since their condition was such that they could neither deny nor conceal their sins, they could more easily be stirred to receive the teaching of repentance and eternal salvation, which the Pharisees, puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, despised. But that Christ the Lord is present at their table brings the sweetest comfort to afflicted consciences. For by this He wished to testify that He receives truly into favour those who turn to Him, and holds them in the place of friends. Therefore those should by no means be heard who daily devise new kinds of satisfactions and expiations, with which they terrify the minds of the weak. Rather let us hear God calling us, and, leaving behind the unhappy service of the world and its prince, let us follow Jesus Christ, who, as He is present with those who labour in the pursuit of this life, so gathers to Himself those who have come through it, that they may enjoy the same table with Him in the house of His Father. To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LII.
units.tr: Homily 52.

units.la: Qui autem ex eis erant Scribæ & Pharisæi, murmurabant aduersus discipulos eius, dicentes: Quare cum publicanis & peccatoribus editis & bibitis? Et respondens Iesus dixit eis: Non opus est iis qui sani sunt, medico, sed iis qui male affecti sunt. Non veni vt vocarem iustos, sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam.
units.tr: Now the scribes and Pharisees who were among them grumbled against his disciples, saying, "Why do you eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" But Jesus answered and said to them: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."

units.la: Multis quidem & magnificè gratiam Dei nobis scripturæ commendant: sed quia immani scelerum pondere oppressis & iustam Dei iram intra animos suos vere sentientibus nulla verba sufficiunt, exempla plurima proponunt eorum, qui ex peccati seruitio erepti, non solùm cum Deo in gratiam redierunt, sed præclara quoq; misericordiæ & gloriæ vasa facti sunt. Est inter illa non postremum, quod in Matthæi conuersione Euangelista proponunt, qui & peccatorum suorum remissionem gratuitam inuenit, & ex publicano infami Iesu Christi discipulus, & gratia in hoc nobis exhibita præco factus est. Continet ea historia dulcissimam consolationem simul & doctrinam necessariam de eorum officio, qui Dei bonitatem sentiunt. At quia non omnium ea est industria, vt quæ cognitu necessaria sunt obseruent, ipse Christus exempli huius vsum modò exponit, & idem omnium hominum institutioni atq; consolationi accommodat.
units.tr: Scripture commends the grace of God to us in many places and in splendid terms. But since no words are enough for those who are crushed under the weight of their sins and who truly feel God's just anger in their hearts, it sets before us many examples of people who, snatched from the bondage of sin, not only returned into favour with God but also became notable vessels of mercy and glory. Among these is no small example, the one the Evangelist sets forth in the conversion of Matthew. Matthew found the free forgiveness of his sins, and from an infamous publican he became a disciple of Jesus Christ and a herald of the grace shown to us in him. That story contains both the sweetest consolation and the necessary teaching about the duty of those who feel God's goodness. But since not everyone takes the trouble to notice what is necessary to know, Christ himself now sets out the use of this example, and applies it to the instruction and comfort of all people.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi præbuerunt Scribæ & Pharisæi, qui aderant. Cùm enim Christum in Matthæi domum diuertere, & illic cum turba publicanorum & dissolutioris vitæ hominum discumbere, eademque cum illis mensa vti viderent, aduersus eius discipulos murmurant, & non tam Christum quàm illos accusant. Quare (aiunt) cum publicanis & peccatoribus editis & bibitis? Ita verò & Christum licentiæ magistrum fingunt, & discipulos stultitiæ insimulant, qui temere hunc sibi doctorem eligerint, relictis melioribus. Quasi dicerent: Egregius sanè magister, & dignus, quem relicta religione patria settlemini, qui vos publicanis et sceleratis aggregat, quorum consortio ipse delectatur. Si hoc quærebatis, licebat vobis sine illo talibus esse, neq; opus erat scisma facere, quod simul religionem turbaret & populum totum in partes distraheret, &c. Fuit hæc non leuis tentatio iis, qui adhuc infirmiores & rerum imperiti erant: & eò grauius eos essensos fuisse non est dubium, quod ista Scribæ & Pharisæi exprobrabant, ex quibus illi rerum diuinarum cognitionem profitebantur, bi vero præ aliis iustitiæ & sanctitatis existimationem præcipuam sustinebant. Et mirum videri poterat, istos passim Christo aduersatos esse, nisi Scribas circa patrum traditiones & inutiles genealogias potius quàm circa Legis & prophetarum lectionem occupatos, Pharisæos autem superbia iustitiæ fucatæ fiducia ebrios fuisse sciremus: quæ causa fuit, vt non possent non odisse Christum, qui vtrique ordini laruam detrahebat, vt minor iam esset eorum apud plerosq; authoritas. Est hoc probè obseruandum, ne offendamur, quando hodie etiam Euangelio Iesu Christi se pra alijs hostiliter opponunt, qui vulgò sapientissimi, doctissimi & sanctissimi putantur. Nunquam enim humanae sapientiae cum diuina conuenit, & diuinae iustitiae splendorem non ferre possunt hypocritae, qui sese ina ni fuco venditant. Nam vt noctuae in tenebris aliquem oculorum vsum habent, in Sole autem caecutiunt: ita illi dum superstitionum & humanarum traditionum tenebrae mentes hominum occupant, oculatissimi videntur, at exorto Christo, aeterno iustitiae Sole, caecissimi fiunt, & plus quàm ridiculos sese praebent pijs, dum in luce meridiana ipsi sibi tenebras effundunt. Dolet id illis, qui religionem omnem quaestu metiuntur, & de sua potius quàm Dei gloria solliciti sunt: ideoque omnem lapidem mouent, vt lucem veritatis extinguant, quod cum non pafsint, calumniis saltem illam apud imperitos suspectam & inuisam reddunt.
units.tr: The Scribes and Pharisees who were present gave occasion for this discussion. When they saw Christ turn aside into Matthew's house, and recline there with a crowd of publicans and people of loose life, and share the same table with them, they grumbled against his disciples, and accused them rather than Christ. "Why," they say, "do you eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" In this way they make Christ out to be a teacher of licence, and charge the disciples with folly, for choosing this man as their teacher when better men were available. It is as if they said: "A fine teacher indeed, and worthy of you to abandon your ancestral religion for him, who associates you with publicans and wicked men, in whose company he himself takes pleasure! If this is what you were seeking, you could have lived among such people without him, and there was no need to create a schism which would at once disturb religion and split the whole people into factions, and so on." This was no slight temptation for those who were still weak and inexperienced in these matters, and there is no doubt they were the more distressed because the Scribes and Pharisees, from whom they professed knowledge of divine things, were the ones making these reproaches, while the Pharisees above others held the reputation of justice and holiness. It might seem strange that these men were everywhere opposed to Christ, if we did not know that the Scribes were occupied with the traditions of the fathers and with useless genealogies rather than with reading the Law and the prophets, and that the Pharisees were intoxicated with pride and with confidence in a pretended righteousness. This was the reason they could not help hating Christ, who stripped both groups of their mask, so that their authority with most people was already diminished. We must observe this carefully, so that we are not offended when even today those who are commonly thought the wisest, most learned and most holy set themselves hostilely against the gospel of Jesus Christ. For human wisdom never agrees with divine wisdom, and hypocrites, who peddle themselves under a false colouring, cannot bear the brightness of divine righteousness. Just as owls have some use of their eyes in darkness but are blinded in the sun, so these men, while the shadows of superstitions and human traditions occupy people's minds, appear most keen-sighted; but when Christ, the eternal Sun of righteousness, has risen, they become most blind and make themselves more than ridiculous to the godly, since in broad daylight they spread darkness around themselves. This grieves those who measure all religion by profit, and who care more for their own glory than for God's. Therefore they move every stone to extinguish the light of truth, and when they cannot suffer it, they at least make it suspected and hated among the unlearned by slander.

units.la: In primis autem proderit in Scribis & Pharisaeis istis artes obseruasse, quibus veritatis hostes vti consueuerunt. Primò non ipsum Christum adoriuntur, quem ad respondendum instructum esse sciebant, sed discipulos minus adhuc exercitatos, et quos suae authoritatis splendore nonnihil terreri posse sperabant. Itaque rei militaris peritos duces imitantur, qui vrbes illic loci oppugnant, vbi munitas esse vident: quod vetus Satanae stratagema esse, ex primorum parentum historia & infinitis aliis exemplis apparet. Et Christi factum sic accusant, vt culpam in ipsos quoque discipulos redundare ostendant, qui ipsum imitentur. Faciunt idem hodie aliqui quidam, qui apud populum rudiorem & opifices, vel etiam apud mulierculas, multa in administrorum Verbi Dei contumeliam dicunt, & quaestiones mouent, quibus homines imperitos intricari posse putant, atque inde ipsis insidiandi occasiones venantur. Deinde vitio vertunt quod per se non malum erat, & facile poterat excusari, cùm in peccatorum gratiam nihil vnquam fecisset Christus reprehensione dignum. Adde his, quòd dum illi sine causa accusant, interim securi negligunt turpissimos errores & immania flagitia, quae illis Christus non semel exprobrauerat. Est boc proprium calumniatoribus, quod alienis delictis sua tegere satagunt, & vt hoc possint, multa fingunt, multa ità in peiorem partem interpretantur: & hoc inprimis hypocritae faciunt, qui aduersus Veritatis doctrinam iampridem coniurauerunt. Quò magis nos aduigilare decet, ne illorum calumniis & mendacijs nos seduci patiamur. Est enim haec fors ministrorum Euangelij, vt calumnias omnino effugere non possint, eò quod nun quam non in illis inuenit infelix mundus, de quo quiritetur. Asserit tamen suorum famam & honorem Dominus, quod in praesenti quoq; factum fuisse audiemus.
units.tr: Above all, it will be useful to notice in these Scribes and Pharisees the tricks that enemies of the truth are accustomed to use. First, they do not attack Christ himself, whom they knew to be prepared to answer, but his disciples, who were still less practised and whom they hoped could be somewhat frightened by the splendour of their own authority. So they imitate skilled military commanders, who assault those cities they see to be fortified. This is an old stratagem of Satan, as appears from the history of our first parents and from countless other examples. They also accuse Christ's action in such a way as to show that the blame falls on the disciples too, since they imitate him. Some people do the same today: among the cruder people and artisans, or even among silly women, they say many things to the shame of the ministers of God's Word, and raise questions by which they think unlearned people can be entangled, and from these they seek opportunities to lay traps for them. Next, they find fault with what was not evil in itself and could easily have been excused, since Christ had never done anything worthy of reproach in favouring sinners. Add to this that while they accuse them without cause, they carelessly overlook their own most shameful errors and monstrous crimes, which Christ had more than once rebuked them for. It is characteristic of slanderers that they labour to hide their own faults by the faults of others, and to do this they invent much and interpret much in the worst sense. Hypocrites especially do this, having long ago conspired against the doctrine of truth. So much the more we ought to be on guard, lest we allow ourselves to be led astray by their slanders and lies. For this is the lot of the ministers of the gospel, that they cannot altogether escape slander, since the unhappy world never fails to find grounds for complaint against them. Nevertheless the Lord defends the reputation and honour of his own, as we shall hear was done in the present case too.

units.la: Audita enim aduersariorum calumnia Christus, mox causam suscipit, & ita factum suum, tuetur, vt illorum errorem simul perstringat, qui duplex erat. Nam & officium ipsius ignorabant, & sacos confutat, (vt paulò ante diximus) suorum delictorum securi alios nimis insolenter fastidiebant. Constat autem tota responsio sententijs grauissimis, quas inspexisse proderit ex ordine.
units.tr: For when Christ heard the adversaries' slander, he at once took up the cause and defended his action in such a way that he also struck at their error, which was twofold. For they were ignorant of his office, and, secure in their own sins, they too arrogantly despised others. The whole answer consists of the weightiest sayings, and it will be useful to examine them in order.

units.la: Prima proueerbialis est, & simili constat omnibus noto & adrem praesentem commodissimo. Non opus est ijs (inquit) qui sani sunt, medico: sed ijs, qui male affecti sunt. Argumentum ita formari poterit: Medici est eos visere & curare, qui eius consilio & arte in primis opus habent, aegrotos nimirum & morbis affectos: Atqui ego animarum medicus veni, vt peccatis laborantibus salutarem medicinam adhibeam: Ergo peccatores non (vt vos soletis) fastidire, sed amicè cum illis versari & ad meliorem frugem reducere debeo. Huic argumento apud Matthaeum grauem ignorantiae exprobrationem subijcit: dicens: Quin potius ite & discite quid sit, Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. Extat locus iste apud Hoseam sexto cap. vbi Deus Israelitas hoc nomine accusat, quòd poenitentiam theatricam & momentaneam solùm agerent, & circa externos sacrorum ritus occupati beneficentiae officia & quae ad ipsius cognitionem faciunt negligerent. Erat ergo non leuis istorum culpa, qui cùm scripturarum cognitionem proficerentur, ad eundem tamen cum patribus lapidem offendebant. Neque dubium est, quin vehementer illis doluerit haec exprobratio, cùm soli sapere & sanctissimi videri vellent. Sed eò grauius arguendi sunt tales, vt intelligant sibi cum Deo rem esse, qui externis laruis minimè fallitur.
units.tr: The first is a proverb, and rests on a similarity known to all and most fitting to the present case: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do." The argument may be framed thus: it is the physician's task to visit and cure those who especially need his counsel and skill, namely the sick and those affected by diseases. But I have come as a physician of souls, to apply a saving remedy to those labouring under sin. Therefore I ought not (as you are accustomed to do) to despise sinners, but to live with them in friendship and to bring them back to better conduct. To this argument, in Matthew, he adds a severe rebuke of their ignorance, saying: "But go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." This passage is found in Hosea chapter 6, where God accuses the Israelites of this very thing, that they performed a theatrical and momentary repentance only, and, busy with the external rites of worship, neglected the duties of kindness and those things which serve the knowledge of him. So the fault of these men was no small one: although they professed knowledge of the Scriptures, they stumbled over the same stone as their fathers. And there is no doubt that this rebuke pained them greatly, since they wished to seem alone wise and most holy. But such people must be reproved all the more severely, so that they understand they have to do with God, who is not deceived by external masks.

units.la: Obseruatu autem dignissimum est, quòd peccatores infirmis aut aegrotantibus similes facit Christus. Ita enim & infelicem eorum conditionem exprimit, & eosdem simul officij admonet, vt ni mirum periculi sui memores sibijpsis nequaquam blandiantur, sed de medicina serio cogitent, & sese runtur.
units.tr: It is worth noting especially that Christ makes sinners like the weak or the sick. In this way he both expresses their unhappy condition and at the same time reminds them of their duty: that, mindful of their danger, they should not flatter themselves, but think seriously about the remedy and submit to it.

units.la: Artes hostium veritatis.
units.tr: The arts of the enemies of the truth.

units.la: Christus Pharisaeos confutat.
units.tr: Christ refutes the Pharisees.

units.la: Ab officio aut fine.
units.tr: From the duty or the end.

units.la: Peccatores ea grotis conse- runtur. offerentem medicum admittant. Est doctrina hæc admodum necessaria, eò quòd pauci intelligunt, quàm exitialis sit peccatorum seruitus, & plerique sibi blanditias fingunt, ne morbos suos agnoscere & fateri cogantur. Quæ causa est, quòd in peius quotidie proficiunt, & tandem in peccatis suis moriuntur. Excitet ergo nos tanti periculi consideratio, & moueat simul medici nostri facilitas atque indulgentia. Est is Christus Iesus, qui cùm ipse in assumpta carne infirmitates nostras senserit, facile nobis condolere potest, neque aliud in votis habet, quàm vt miseros & iam pereuntes ab interitu auocet. Itaque bis peccant, qui non contenti delictis prioribus, insuper illum quoque manum saluificam sibi admonentem reiiciunt. Errant in eo non solùm scelerati illi, qui se totos ad omnem impietatem deuouerunt, verumetiam multi non mali, qui dum Christum ex suo ingenio æstimant, ad ipsum accedere verentur, & proinde alios sibi Mediatores atque Seruatores quærunt. At cùm ipse, vt peccatores saluos faceret, in terras hasce descenderit, præposterè religiosi sunt, qui sibi ab illo timent, & ex medico indulgentissimo iudicem, vel potius carnificem crudelem fingunt. Seruit etiam Christi exemplum ijs confutandis, qui peccatores fastidiunt, & plus quàm censoria severitate omnes in sacrorum & ecclesiæ communione excludunt, quos aliqua insigniori labe affectos esse vident. Clamant illi indignissimum esse, vt ad ecclesiæ, sponsæ Christi immaculatæ, societatem admittantur, quorum vitia manifesta sunt omnibus: impium item & prophanum Sacramentorum ecclesiæ abusum esse aiunt, si eodem baptismo electi & reprobi tingantur, & ad eandem Christi membram boni cum malis accedant. Sed vtinam illi omnes de colligendo potius quam de excludendo & dissipando soliciti essent, & seipsos penitius inspicerent. Viderent enim procul dubio, se eodem cum Pharisæis & Scribis errore teneri, dum & seipsos falsæ iustitiæ fiducia fallunt, & Christi officium ignorant, imò hunc in nobis accusant, dum illud in nobis reprehendunt, quod ipsum olim fecisse constat: quando eodem cum publicanis & hypocritis baptismo ipse tinctus est, promiscuè omnes ad Verbum audiendum admisit, Iudam proditorem mensæ suæ adhibuit, denique inter latrones medius pendere & peccatum fieri voluit, vt nos in ipso iustitia Dei efficeremur. Interim legitimam ecclesiæ disciplinam non damnamus, sed ne huius prætextu & inconsulta temeritate ecclesiæ dissipentur, admonemus.
units.tr: Sinners should admit the physician who offers himself to the sick. This teaching is very necessary, because few understand how deadly the slavery of sin is, and most flatter themselves so that they are not compelled to recognise and confess their diseases. This is why they make daily progress for the worse and at last die in their sins. Let the consideration of so great a danger therefore stir us, and let the readiness and kindness of our physician move us at the same time. He is Christ Jesus, who, having himself felt our infirmities in the flesh he assumed, can easily sympathise with us, and he has no other desire than to call the wretched and those already perishing away from destruction. Therefore those sin twice who, not content with their earlier offences, also reject that saving hand which admonishes them. Not only those wicked men who have devoted themselves wholly to every impiety are in error, but also many who are not evil, who, while they judge Christ by their own disposition, shrink from approaching him and therefore seek other mediators and saviours for themselves. But since he descended to these lands in order to save sinners, they are absurdly scrupulous who fear him, and who imagine from a most kindly physician a judge, or rather a cruel executioner. The example of Christ also serves to refute those who despise sinners and, with more than censorial severity, exclude from the communion of the sacraments and the Church all whom they see stained with some more notable blemish. They cry out that it is most unworthy that those be admitted to the fellowship of the Church, the immaculate bride of Christ, whose vices are plain to all; they also say that it is an impious and profane abuse of the sacraments if the elect and the reprobate are baptised with the same baptism, and if good and bad alike come to the same member of Christ. But I wish that all of them were anxious about gathering rather than about excluding and scattering, and that they looked more searchingly into themselves. For they would doubtless see that they are held by the same error as the Pharisees and Scribes, while they deceive themselves with confidence in a false righteousness and ignore the office of Christ; indeed they accuse him in us, while they find fault in us with that very thing which he is known to have done once: when he himself was baptised with the same baptism as the tax collectors and hypocrites, admitted all indiscriminately to hear the Word, admitted Judas the traitor to his table, and finally hung between thieves and was willing to be made sin, so that in him we might be made the righteousness of God. Meanwhile we do not condemn lawful church discipline, but we admonish that under its pretext and by rash inconsideration the churches are not scattered.

units.la: Sed alteram Christi sententiam videamus, qua priorem ipse interpretatur, dicens: Non veni vt vocarem iustos, sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Iustos vocat eos, qui propria iustitiæ fiducia efferuntur, seque pro iustis venditant: & aduersarios suos perstringens simul rationem reddit, cur cum publicanis & peccatoribus potius, quàm cum ipsis commercium habeat. Et est ratio hæc gravis admodum, eò quòd à fine aduentus Christi in carnem sumitur, qui non alius constituì potest, quàm vt miseri & iam periturì peccatores ad Deum conuersi seruentur. Est igitur sententia hæc plena consolationis, & sola sufficere potest aduersus consciencie terrores, quibus nos exagitat Satan, dum persuadere conatur, nos propter scelera nostra Deo itá inuisos esse, vt ne pœnitentiam nostram ille admittere possit aut velit. At tunc maior apud nos esse debet fides Christi, cui Paulus subscribens dixit: Fidus est hic sermo, & modus omnibus dignus quem amplectamur, quòd Christus Iesus venit in mundum, vt peccatores seruaret. Neque hic aliquem terreat scelerum multitudo siue atrocitas, quando nos ab ipso Christo inuitari scimus, qui (vt ipse ait) neminem ad se venientem eiicit, nec vnquam aliquem eorum aspernatus est, qui serio pœnitentiæ studio accensi per ipsum Deo patri reconciliari cupiuerunt.
units.tr: But let us look at the other saying of Christ, by which he himself interprets the first, saying: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Matt. 9.13). He calls the righteous those who are puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness and pass themselves off as just; and while he strikes at his adversaries, he at the same time gives the reason why he has fellowship with tax collectors and sinners rather than with them. And this reason is very weighty, because it is taken from the purpose of Christ's coming in the flesh, which can be understood to be nothing other than that wretched sinners, who are about to perish, should be turned to God and saved. This saying is therefore full of consolation, and alone can suffice against the terrors of conscience with which Satan torments us, when he tries to persuade us that we are so hateful to God on account of our crimes that he cannot or will not accept our repentance. But then faith in Christ ought to be greater with us, to which Paul added his assent when he said: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" (1 Tim. 1.15). Nor let the multitude or the atrocity of our crimes terrify anyone here, since we know that we are invited by Christ himself, who (as he says) casts out no one who comes to him, and has never spurned any of those who, kindled by a serious zeal for repentance, have desired to be reconciled to God the Father through him.

units.la: Continet præterea hæc sententia vniuersam doctrinam de salute nostra, & ideo hoc etiam nomine dignissima est, cuius singulas voces diligentius consideremus. Primò enim peccatores nominantur, quibus seruandis Christus venerit. Atqui peccatores quidem sunt omnes homines, non autem omnes seruantur, quia de illis solis sermo est, qui se peccatores esse agnoscunt, & medicum admittunt, vt modò diximus. Voluit tamen absque omni discrimine sic loqui Christus, vt omnes simul comprehenderet, qui suæ vitiositatis & ex ea manantium scelerum sensu oppressi gratia Dei sibi opus esse intelligunt, & salutem in ipso quærunt. Non est enim respectus personarum apud Deum, & in Christo non est Iudæus neq; Græcus, non liber neque seruus, non mas aut fœmina. Errant itaq; ipsi, qui sibi noua discrimina fingunt, & Dei promissiones, quas hic ad omnes credentes extendit, pro sui cerebri figmento ad pauciores restringunt. Deinde author atq; mediator salutis nostræ vnus Christus monstratur, quem solum nobis pater aeterno decreto praedestinavit, ut nostra iustitia, satisfactio, sanctificatio et redemptio fieret. De quo apostolicum illud testimonium extat: Non est in quoquam alio salus: neque enim est aliud nomen sub caelo datum inter homines, in quo nos oporteat salvos fieri. Atqui ipse in Evangelio clamat: Ego sum Via, & Veritas, & vita: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per me. Tertio modum & rationem, qua ad salutem venitur, Christus exprimit, quando peccatores abs se vocari ait. Eo enim & gratiam Dei nobis commendat, & quid nobis in hac apprehendenda facto opus sit, docet. Loquitur enim de vocatione efficaci, cui tractus Spiritus sancti (de quo alibi dixit) coniunctus est. Atqui gratuitum hoc est Dei beneficium, quod qui a nobis invocari debebat, prior nos vocat, et sua vocatione excitat, ut nobis salute opus esse sentiamus, deque illa serio cogitemus. Exemplum huius gratiae in primo parente aedidit, qui fugientem & se nequicquam occultantem, nisi Deus vocasset, in fuga illa totus periturus erat. Et quod tunc accidit, in nobis ipsis etiam experimur, quos fere securos & salutis propriae negligentes per Evangelij praedicationem & Spiritus sui suggestionem vocat atque movet, ut ad ipsum conversi salutis consilium admittamus. At tunc demum salutaris erit vocatio illa, si nos vocantem sequamur, & eius praebeamus regendos. Fide ergo opus est, quae sola Verbum digne audit, & eius semen animis nostris inserit, ut ex eo renati debitum Deo praestemus obsequium. Ideo fide servari & iustificari dicimur. Et poterant ista multis explicari, nisi consulto breuitati studeremus, cum de his non semel prolixe sit dictum. Postremo finem quoque vocationis nostrae, quoad huius vitae curriculum, Christus nobis indicat, poenitentiam vel resipiscentiam: nimirum ut iis occurrat, qui gratiae Dei & merito ipsius ad peccandi licentiam abutuntur. Fuit horum ingens numerus semper, & hodie tales passim regnant, qui etiam causa sunt, ut Evangelium apud multos male audiat. Atqui longe alius eius finis est. Ideo enim ante mundi creationem in Christo elegit Deus, & ideo nos per Evangelium vocat, ut ipsius efficiamur peculium, & adipsum conversi inculpatam & sanctam vitam viuamus, atque eius virtutes praedicemus, qui nos euocauit ex tenebris in admirabilem lucem suam. Est ergo inexcusabilis eorum ingratitudo atque contumacia, qui cum Christo & salute eius merito acquisita glorientur, ea tamen faciunt, quibus innumeri alij offenduntur, ne ad Christum & ecclesiam eius accedant. Sentient illi procul dubio, poenas quas scandalorum authoribus ille iam olim constituit. At quia de poenitentia alibi diximus, inde petantur, quae ad pleniorem huius loci interpretationem faciunt. Nunc vsum horum omnium consideremus o fratres. Agnoscamus nos miseros & propter peccata exitio dignos esse. At simul incomparabilem quoque Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui cum nulla alia salutis ratio restaret, filium suum vnigenitum misit, ut non medicum modo fidum ageret, sed seipsum pro nobis in mortem traderet. Vocat hic nos per Evangelium, ut relictis prioribus studijs ad Deum conuertamur, & conuersis sui regni consortium pollicetur. Audiamus ergo vocantem & sequamur, ut huius vitae studium emensi, cum illo in caelis viuamus: Cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this saying contains the whole doctrine of our salvation, and therefore it is most worthy on this account too, that we consider its individual words more carefully. First, sinners are named, for whose salvation Christ came. Yet all men are sinners, but not all are saved, because the discourse concerns only those who acknowledge that they are sinners and admit the physician, as we have just said. Nevertheless Christ wished to speak in such a way, without any distinction, that he might embrace all together who, oppressed by the sense of their wickedness and of the crimes flowing from it, understand that they need the grace of God and seek salvation in him. For there is no respect of persons with God, and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither bond nor free, neither male nor female. Those therefore err who invent new distinctions for themselves, and who restrict the promises of God, which here extend to all believers, to a few, as a figment of their own brain. Next, Christ alone is shown to be the author and mediator of our salvation, whom the Father alone predestined by his eternal decree, so that he might be made our righteousness, satisfaction, sanctification and redemption. Concerning him stands that apostolic testimony: "Neither is there salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Acts 4.12). And yet he himself cries out in the Gospel: "I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life; no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14.6). Third, Christ expresses the manner and the means by which one comes to salvation, when he says that he calls sinners. For by this he both commends to us the grace of God and teaches what must be done on our part in laying hold of it. For he speaks of an effectual calling, to which the drawing of the Holy Spirit (of which he spoke elsewhere) is joined. Now this is the gratuitous benefit of God: he who ought to be called upon by us calls us first, and by his calling stirs us up, so that we feel that we need salvation and think seriously about it. We have an example of this grace in our first parent, who, fleeing and vainly hiding himself, would have perished totally in that flight unless God had called him. And what happened then we also experience in ourselves: he calls and moves us, who are for the most part secure and negligent of our own salvation, through the preaching of the Gospel and the suggestion of his Spirit, so that, converted to him, we may accept the counsel of salvation. But that calling will be saving only if we follow the one who calls and offer ourselves to be guided by him. Faith is therefore needed, which alone hears the Word worthily and implants its seed in our minds, so that, reborn from it, we may render due obedience to God. Therefore we are said to be saved and justified by faith. These matters could be explained at greater length, had we not deliberately aimed at brevity, since they have been discussed at length more than once. Finally, Christ also indicates to us the end of our calling, as far as the course of this life is concerned: repentance or conversion; namely, that he may meet those who abuse the grace of God and his merit as a licence to sin. The number of these has always been great, and today such people reign everywhere, and they are also the cause why the Gospel is badly spoken of by many. But its end is quite different. For God chose us in Christ before the creation of the world, and therefore calls us through the Gospel, so that we may become his own people, and, converted to him, may live a blameless and holy life, and proclaim his virtues, who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. Therefore inexcusable is the ingratitude and obstinacy of those who glory in Christ and in the salvation acquired by his merit, and yet do those things by which countless others are offended, so that they do not come to Christ and his Church. Those will doubtless feel the punishments which he long ago appointed for the authors of scandals. But since we have spoken of repentance elsewhere, let those who seek a fuller interpretation of this passage look there. Now let us consider the use of all these things, brothers. Let us acknowledge that we are wretched and worthy of destruction on account of our sins. But at the same time let us also acknowledge the incomparable goodness of God, who, when no other means of salvation remained, sent his only-begotten Son, so that he would not only act as a faithful physician, but would hand himself over to death for us. He calls us here through the Gospel, so that, having left our former pursuits, we may turn to God, and to those who have turned he promises fellowship in his kingdom. Let us therefore hear him calling and follow him, so that, having finished the pursuit of this life, we may live with him in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIIII.

units.la: Ipsi autem dixerunt ei: Quare discipuli Ioannis ieiunant crebro, & deprecationes facunt, similiter & discipuli Pharisaeorum, tui vero edunt & bibunt? Ipse autem dixit eis: Num potestis facere, ut filij thalami, quo tempore cum ipsis est sponsus, ieiunent? Aderunt autem dies, cum tolletur ab eis sponsus, tunc ieiunabunt illis diebus.
units.tr: They said to him, "Why do John's disciples fast often and make prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?" And he said to them, "Can you make the sons of the bridechamber fast while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days."

units.la: Multa quidem sapientiae & omnipotentiae diuinae argumenta sunt, at inter ea fere primatum tenet, quod Christi regnum aduersariorum conatibus & consilijs adeo non potest euerti aut obscurari, ut potius per illa prouehatur atque illustretur. Quod ipsum in Veritatis etiam doctrina accidere solet, quam dum hypocritae oppugnant, sua sophistica eam illustriorem reddunt, suam vero produnt inscitiam cum impietate coniunctam. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, in historia Christi multa occurrunt, inter quae admodum memorabile est, quod in ea actione habetur, quae illi postea vocatum: Matthæum cum Pharisæis intercessit. Cùm enim inter publicanos accubuisset, ex eo illi ipsum accusandi occasionem arripiunt, vt offendant licentiæ & nequitiæ patronum esse, qui cum illis familiarius viuat, qui & sceleribus infames erant, & cum publico patriæ incommodo Romanæ tyrannidis se præbebant ministros. Ad istam verò calumniam ita Christus respondit, vt perspicuè ea explicarit, quæ ad ipsius & salutis communis cognitionem pertinent, & quorum consideratio nobis in omni tentationis genere consolationem certam & efficacem afferre potest. Cæterum non quiescit animus impiorum, & ideo nullæ rationes ipsis sufficere possunt, vt veritati se subijciant. Itaque novus congressus sequitur, quo illi Christum adoriuntur, cuius exitus non minus felix est. Nam non solùm suam atque discipulorum innocentiam tuetur Dominus, verumetiam aduersariorum incurabilem malitiam eiusque fontes arguit, & simul tractationi huic doctrinam interserit de ieiunijs, quæ vniuersam disciplinæ Christianæ rationem cum multis alijs, quæ cognitu necessaria sunt comprehendit.
units.tr: There are indeed many proofs of God's wisdom and omnipotence, but among them the chief place belongs to this: that the kingdom of Christ cannot be overturned or obscured by the efforts and plans of its adversaries, but is rather advanced and made more illustrious by them. This commonly happens also with the teaching of the truth: when hypocrites attack it with their sophistries, they make it more illustrious, and they reveal their own ignorance, joined with impiety. Many examples proving this occur in the history of Christ, and among them the following is very memorable: the dispute with the Pharisees that took place at the banquet of Matthew, after he was called. For when Christ had reclined among the tax collectors, the Pharisees seized on this as an occasion to accuse him, and tried to make him out to be a patron of licentiousness and wickedness, since he lived so familiarly with men who were infamous for their crimes and who, to the public harm of their country, served as agents of Roman tyranny. Christ answered this slander in such a way that he clearly explained what pertains to the knowledge of his own person and of our common salvation, and the consideration of which can bring us a sure and effective consolation in every kind of temptation. But the minds of the wicked are not at rest, and therefore no reasons are sufficient to make them submit to the truth. So a new encounter follows, in which they assail Christ, and its outcome is no less favourable. For the Lord not only defends his own innocence and that of his disciples, but also exposes the incurable malice of his adversaries and its sources; and at the same time he introduces into this discussion a teaching about fasting, which takes in the whole system of Christian discipline, together with many other things that need to be known.

units.la: Porrò videamus ante omnia, qui nam Christi aduersarij fuerint. Lucas cæptam narrationem persequens eosdem facit, qui prius cum illo litigarant, Scribas nimirum atque Pharisæos: Marcus autem bis coniungit Ioannis quoque discipulos, quos illi in partes suas pertraxerunt, ne soli hostes Christi viderentur. Imò Ioannis discipulos ita illi suborarunt, vt ipsi quæstionem hanc nouam Christo proposuerint, & huius certaminis fuerint instauratores, vt apud Matthæum est videre. Fuit hoc illis non difficile factu, eò quòd inter Pharisæos & Ioannis discipulos quo ad ieiunia & vniuersam victus rationem magna similitudo esset, Christus verò diuersam rationem sequendo vtrosque simul damnare videretur. Et Ioannis discipulos adhuc rudiores, adhæc Christi æmulatores fuisse, ex alijs locis apparet. Itaque se à Pharisæis in societatem trahi patiuntur, immemores planè sui præceptoris, qui illos à Christo pendere insferat. Admonemur hoc exemplo, quæ sit hostium veritatis astutia, quando eos quoque aduersus Christum armare possunt, qui huic coniunctissimi esse debebant. Erat Ioannes Christi minister & amicus, in hoc vnum incumbens, vt quàm plurimos illi adduceret. At qui ipsi nomen dederant, Pharisæorum dolis se circumueniri sinunt, vt suam his operam præstent aduersus Christum, quem Ioannes supra omnes eminere cupiebat. Equidem cum Pharisæis coniurant, qui Ioannem non minus quàm Christum oderant. Tanta est æmulationis vis, quæ tunc in apertas inimicitias erumpit, quando aliqua sententiarum & externorum rituum diuersitas aut saltem diuersitatis species siue suspicio accedit. Tantum certè hoc potuit apud istos, vt in sola externa intenti, Ioannis de Christo testimonia prosus neglexerint, & impijssimis hostibus se coniunxerint, qui illum cum tota veritatis doctrina extinctum volebant. Videtur hoc multis admirabile, sed vtinam non etiam hodie huius generis exempla extarent, quæ vt vetera minus miremur, monent. Reuelata est nostris temporibus singulari Dei beneficio Veritatis lux, quæ sub Papisticarum superstitionum caligine aliquot seculis obscura latuerat. In eius cognitione alij alijs plus profecerunt, & multi Papatu simul omni abiecto ecclesias suas ab omni fermento humanarum traditionum repurgarunt: alijs interea imagines, sacrorum externorum ritus, & crassam atque superstitiosam de corporali Christi in Cænæ vsu præsentia atque manducatione opinionem mordicus retinentibus. Peperit ista dissimilitudo contentiones grauissimas inter eos, qui primi Veritatis evangelicæ instauratores fuerunt, & hi in partes scissi sunt, qui vnum Christum professi in eandem fidem totis animis coalescere debebant. Hinc factum, vt multi æmulatione cæca & contentionis impetu abrepti, apertis Euangelij hostibus aures præbeant, Pontificum & Regum edicta probent, quibus illi superstitionum cuersores & germanos Iesu Christi discipulos proscribunt: quid, quod multi carnificibus impijs tantum non enses & faces in manus tradunt, quibus eos crudeliter occidant, qui cum ipsis insanire nolunt? Scio hoc durum dictu & auditu intolerabile multis videri. Sed quid aliud faciunt, qui dissensionibus eiusmodi in eadem vrbe exortis, suas vires cum Papistis coniungunt, vt fratres in nonnullis dissentientes opprimant? Turpe illis videtur à recepta & per multos annos defensa sententia discedere. Sed vtinam cogitarent, quanto turpius sit Veritatem oppugnare, in fratrum vicera sæuire, & hostium Christi rabiem augere atque iuuare. Inuulerunt sibi ipsis perpetuam infamiæ notam Ioannis discipuli, qui cum Pharisæis conspirauerunt, vt sui magistri authoritatem tuerentur. Accidet idem omnibus, qui hodie cum pharisaicarum superstitionum pronum propugnatoribus coniurant, ne quando errauisse aut in pugna succubuisse videantur. Vos autem utrinque hortor o fratres, ut communis periculi memores charitatem inter vos foveatis mutuam, neque contentionum materiam ex iis petatis, quae Christus Christianae societatis symbola esse voluit. Turpis & infelix nimium est victoria, quae cum publico ecclesiae scandalo coniuncta est, & in qua apertis Christi hostibus laniandi propinantur, pro quibus ipsi mortem opperiri debebamus. Neque diu fruentur victoriae suae fructu, qui dum fratres opprimunt, suas copias minuunt atque infirmiores reddunt. Et quia insatiabilis est hostium Veritatis rabies, non quiescunt una parte oppressa, donec alteram quoque opprimant, cuius opera prius insidiose abusi sunt. Fit etiam plerunque (quod Paulus monuit) ut qui se invicem mordent atque devorant, alij ab alijs consumantur. Sint ergo suspectae nobis eiusmodi hominum amicitiae, qui Christi ecclesiam aperte oppugnant; & quo minus illi apud nos possint, omnem inter nos dissensionis speciem diligenter vitemus: ita tamen, ne suam cuiquam eripiamus libertatem in iis, quae per se media & indifferentia sunt.
units.tr: Next let us see first of all who the adversaries of Christ were. Luke, following the narrative he had begun, names the same men who had earlier contended with him, namely the scribes and the Pharisees. Mark, however, couples with them also the disciples of John, whom the Pharisees had drawn over to their side, so that Christ should not seem to have only enemies. Indeed, they so suborned the disciples of John that these men put this new question to Christ and became the renewers of this contest, as can be seen in Matthew. This was not difficult for them to do, because between the Pharisees and the disciples of John there was a great similarity as regards fasting and the whole manner of living, whereas Christ, by following a different way of life, seemed to condemn both alike. And that the disciples of John were still rather crude, and moreover rivals of Christ, appears from other passages. So they allow themselves to be drawn into alliance with the Pharisees, quite forgetful of their own teacher, who had taught them to depend upon Christ. We are warned by this example of the cunning of the enemies of the truth, since they can arm against Christ even those who ought to have been most closely joined to him. John was a minister and friend of Christ, devoting himself to this one thing, that he might bring as many as possible to him. But those who had given their names to John allow themselves to be deceived by the tricks of the Pharisees, so as to lend their efforts against Christ, whom John desired above all to be exalted. Indeed, they conspire with the Pharisees, who hated John no less than they hated Christ. So great is the power of rivalry, which then breaks out into open enmity when some difference of opinions or outward rites, or at least the appearance or suspicion of a difference, arises. Certainly this had such power among them that, intent only on outward things, they utterly neglected John's testimony concerning Christ, and joined themselves to the most impious enemies, who wished to extinguish him together with the whole doctrine of the truth. This may seem wonderful to many, but I wish that examples of this kind did not also exist today; and they serve as a warning, so that we may wonder the less at the old ones. In our own times, by a singular benefit of God, the light of the truth has been revealed, which for several centuries had lain hidden under the darkness of Papist superstitions. Some have made more progress in knowing it than others, and many, having at the same time cast off the Papacy altogether, have purged their churches from every leaven of human traditions; while others still cling stubbornly to images, outward sacred rites, and the gross and superstitious opinion of a bodily presence and manducation of Christ in the use of the Lord's Supper. This difference has produced most serious contentions among those who were the first renewers of the gospel truth, and they have been split into parties, though they professed the one Christ and ought to have united with all their hearts in the same faith. Hence it has come about that many, carried away by blind rivalry and the impulse of strife, lend their ears to the open enemies of the gospel, approve the edicts of pontiffs and kings by which these men proscribe the overthrowers of superstitions and the true disciples of Jesus Christ; and what is more, many hand over to impious executioners torches and swords, by which they may cruelly kill those who will not share their madness. I know that this seems hard to say and intolerable to hear for many. But what else do they do, who, when such dissensions have arisen in the same city, join their strength with the Papists in order to crush brethren who differ from them in some points? They think it shameful to depart from an opinion that has been received and defended for many years. But I wish they would consider how much more shameful it is to attack the truth, to rage against the bowels of their brethren, and to increase and assist the fury of Christ's enemies. The disciples of John, who conspired with the Pharisees in order to defend the authority of their master, brought upon themselves a lasting mark of infamy. The same will happen to all who today conspire with the defenders of Pharisaic superstitions, lest they should ever seem to have erred or to have given way in the battle. But I exhort you, brethren, on both sides, to remember the common danger, to cherish mutual charity among yourselves, and not to seek the material of contention from those things which Christ wished to be the badges of Christian fellowship. Victory is too base and unhappy when it is joined with public scandal to the church, and when slaughter is offered to the open enemies of Christ, for whom we ought rather to be awaiting death ourselves. Nor will they long enjoy the fruit of their victory, who, while they oppress brethren, diminish their own forces and make them weaker. And because the rage of the enemies of the truth is insatiable, they do not rest, once one part is crushed, until they crush the other as well, whose services they had earlier abused by stealth. It also often happens (as Paul warned) that those who bite and devour one another are consumed by one another. Let us therefore regard with suspicion the friendships of those men who openly attack the church of Christ; and, that they may have less power among us, let us carefully avoid every appearance of dissension among ourselves, yet in such a way that we do not take from anyone his freedom in those things which are in themselves means and indifferent.

units.la: At ne longius aequo excurramus, quaestionem videre oportet, qua Christum illi aggressi sunt: Quare (inquiunt) discipuli Ioannis ieiunant crebro & deprecationes faciunt, similiter & discipuli Pharisaeorum, tui vero edunt & bibunt? De ieiunijs ergo quaerunt, quibus antiquitus preces coniungebantur, ut ex Christi verbis patet, qui a discipulis de spiritu immundo, quem ipsi non potuerant eijcere, interrogatus respondit: Hoc genus nulla re potest exire, nisi oratione & ieiunio. At hic de illis agitur, quae ipsi secundum patrum traditiones observabant. Olim etenim unum modo ieiunium Deus instituerat, quod in festum expiationum incidebat, & publice ab omnibus agebatur. At posteri (ut in Prophetarum sermonibus apparet) variis de causis plura commenti sunt, quae & ipsa certis diebus observari solebant. Nam apud Zachariam mentio fit ieiunij, quod mense quinto & septimo fiebat ab iis, qui in Babylone degebant: eo quod in mense quinto urbs cum templa excusta ipsi vero in Babylonem translati essent: septimo autem mense Godolias occubuisset, quae nouae dispersionis occasio fuerat. Et pium erat tantae cladis memoriam fovere, quo magis ad poenitentiam & preces excitarentur. Et ab Hestera atque Mardochaeo dies Purim institutos fuisse legimus, in quorum initio ieiunijs & precibus vacabant, postea autem laeti epulabantur, ut & periculi publici, quod toti Iudaeorum genti Haman struxerat, memoriam servarent, & Deo pro liberationis beneficio dignas gratias agerent. Cuius generis multa posteris quoque temporibus instituta fuisse credibile est. Sed non sufficerunt ista iis, qui alijs sanctiores & religiosiores haberi voluerunt: ideo ipsi frequentius ieiunabant, & quidem bis in hebdomade (ut infra Capite decimo octavo in pharisaeorum exemplo Christus docebit) idque non sine publica ostentatione, ut idem apud Matthaeum Capite sexto innuit. Etsi vero Ioannes superstitiosam ieiuniorum eiusmodi observationem minime probaret, eos tamen imitari videbantur, cum ita viveret, ut tota eius vita ieiunium perpetuum videri posset: neque dubium mihi est, multos ex eius discipulis a Pharisaeorum moribus non procul abfuisse, cum in Ioannis doctrinam minus intenti essent, neque in eam rationem respicerent, quae ipsum monebat, ut ex Dei instituto vitae genus sequerentur. At Christus vitae rationem liberiorem sequebatur, neque discipulos suos ad ieiunia certa siue stata obstringebat, eo quod sui officij esset, abolito cultu Leuitico & umbratili religionis exercitio, hominum mentes ad cultum spiritualem assuefacere. Hinc ergo disputandi occasionem arripiunt, & ut Christum magis inuisum reddant, ut qui ventris & gulae studio diuersam ab ipsis & Ioannis moribus viuendi rationem sequatur, non sine stomacho dicunt: Quare discipuli Ioannis ieiunant crebro, & deprecationes faciunt, similiter & discipuli Pharisaeorum, tui vero edunt & bibunt? Et quamuis in ipso Christo nihil reprehendere possint, quod intemperantiae suspicionem iustam praebeat, hoc tamen illi exprobrant, quod discipulis per ipsum liceat edere & bibere, dum alij ieiunijs & precibus vacant. Ita vero crimen, quod prius illi intentarunt, probare volunt, quod dissolutorum hominum socius & licentiae magister sit. Et maius erat iste criminis pondus, quod ieiunia illa (ut ante diximus) patrum auctoritate & publico optimorum quorumque exemplo niterentur, inter quos Ioannes totius populi iudicio eminebat.
units.tr: But, lest we run on further than is fitting, we must look at the question with which they attacked Christ: "Why," they say, "do John's disciples fast often and make prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?" They therefore ask about fasts, to which prayers were anciently joined, as is clear from the words of Christ, who, when asked by his disciples about the unclean spirit which they had not been able to cast out, answered: "This kind cannot come out by any means, except by prayer and fasting." But here the question concerns those fasts which they observed according to the traditions of the fathers. For God had originally instituted only one fast, which fell on the feast of Atonement, and was observed publicly by all. But later generations (as appears from the sayings of the prophets), for various reasons, devised more, which were also customarily observed on fixed days. For in Zechariah there is mention of a fast which those who dwelt in Babylon kept in the fifth and seventh months: in the fifth month because the city and the temple had been burned, and they themselves had been carried away to Babylon; and in the seventh month because Gedaliah had been killed, which had been the occasion of the new dispersion. And it was a pious thing to keep alive the memory of so great a calamity, so that men might be the more stirred up to repentance and prayer. We read also that the day of Purim was instituted by Esther and Mordecai, on which at the beginning they devoted themselves to fasting and prayers, but afterwards they feasted joyfully, so that they might both keep in memory the public danger which Haman had prepared for the whole Jewish nation, and render due thanks to God for the benefit of their deliverance. It is credible that many institutions of this kind were also made in later times. But these were not enough for those who wished to be thought more holy and more religious than others. Therefore they fasted more often, indeed twice a week (as Christ will teach in chapter eighteen by the example of the Pharisees), and that not without public ostentation, as the same passage in Matthew, chapter six, hints. And although John did not at all approve of such superstitious observance of fasts, nevertheless his disciples seemed to imitate them, since he lived in such a way that his whole life could seem to be a perpetual fast; and I have no doubt that many of his disciples were not far from the manners of the Pharisees, since they were less intent upon John's teaching and did not regard that rule which admonished them to follow a way of life according to God's institution. But Christ followed a freer manner of life, and did not bind his disciples to fixed or stated fasts, because it was his office, with the Levitical worship abolished and the shadowy exercise of religion set aside, to accustom men's minds to spiritual worship. Hence therefore they seize on an occasion for disputing, and, in order to make Christ more hateful, since he, out of concern for his belly and gullet, followed a manner of living different from theirs and from that of John, they say with ill humour: "Why do John's disciples fast often and make prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?" And although they could find nothing in Christ himself to reprove that might give just cause for suspicion of intemperance, they nevertheless charge him with this, that by him his disciples are permitted to eat and drink while others are occupied with fasting and prayers. And thus they wish to prove the charge which they had earlier brought against him, that he is a companion of dissolute men and a teacher of licentiousness. And this charge had greater weight, because those fasts (as we said before) rested upon the authority of the fathers and the public example of the best men, among whom John stood out in the judgment of the whole people.

units.la: Est autem obseruatu dignissimum, quod Christo exprobrant id, quod discipuli faciebant. Eo enim odium suum produnt, eorum similes, qui si quos oderunt, eorum domesticos & liberos insidiose
units.tr: It is worth noting, however, that they reproach Christ for what the disciples were doing. In this they reveal their hatred, and resemble those who, when they hate someone, lie in wait for his household and children.

units.la: Discipulorum factum exprobratur Christo obseruant, ut aliquam inueniant calumniandi occasionem. Fit hoc ipsum frequenter hodie, ut in Euangelij contumeliam rapiantur, quae ab ijs praeter officium fiunt, qui illius doctrinam profitentur. Et tanta est odij contra veritatem vis, ut nullum vitium tam leue sit, quod impij non possint amplificando capitale facere. Hic certe summum flagitium esse ducunt, quod discipuli Christi edant et bibant alijs ieiunantibus: quasi vero ne edamus et bibamus Deus alicubi prohibuerit. Quo magis nos armiti decet, ne vel licentia immoderata, vel inconsulto libertatis Christianae abusu aduersarijs ansam demus aliquid dicendi, quod fidei doctrinam infirmis et rerum imperitis suspectam aut inuisam facere possit.
units.tr: They watch what the disciples do so that they may find in Christ a ground for slander. This happens often today too: things done by those who profess Christ's teaching, and done beyond their duty, are seized upon to bring disgrace on the Gospel. Hatred of the truth is so strong that no fault is so slight that the ungodly cannot magnify it into a capital crime. Here they certainly count it a great outrage that Christ's disciples eat and drink while others fast, as if God had forbidden us to eat and drink anywhere. All the more reason for us to be on our guard, lest by immoderate liberty or careless abuse of Christian freedom we give our adversaries occasion to say something that can make the doctrine of the faith suspect or hateful to the weak and the inexperienced.

units.la: Est praeterea in hoc exemplo obseruandum, quo nomine fere accusetur Christi doctrina: Eo nimirum, quod patres et ab his traditam cultus rationem damnet, quodque salutis rationem tradat facilem nimis, quae carnis securitatem et licentiam peccandi pariat. Sunt haec crimina minime contemnenda. Hoc enim detestantur quicunque honesti et boni studiosiores sunt, illud vero vnum sufficit ad quorumuis odia excitanda, eo quod patrum authoritas apud omnes sacrosancta est, et illos damnare plerisque non modo durum, sed impium quoque et quouis supplicio dignum videtur. Nemo tamen quando haec audit, ijs tanquam nouis et inauditis antea offendatur. Scimus enim de his olim prophetas et apostolos accusatos fuisse: imo sufficere nobis debet, quod ista Christo obiecerunt humanarum traditionum atque superstitionum propugnatores. In utroque autem magnam nobis iniuriam faciunt aduersarij. Nec enim statim impius est, qui patrum instituta violat aut transgreditur. Clamat equidem propheta: In via patrum vestrorum ne ambulaueritis. Et apud Ieremiam Iudaeos propter illicitos cultus, quos a patribus suis didicerant, Deus corripit. Nam in duplici differentia sunt patres. Alij veteres illi sunt, quorum fidem Spiritus sanctus in scripturis probat, quia a Deo traditas leges sancte obseruarunt.
