Alij intermedij sunt, qui relictis priorum vestigijs sua commenta secuti superstitiones inuexerunt, et verum Dei cultum corruperunt. Vt ergo a priorum patrum exemplo deflectere summum scelus est, ita posteriores hos sequi non possumus, nisi cum ipsis perire libeat. Nec enim vlla vel patrum vel quorumcunq; aliorum hominum authoritate excusabimur si ea faciamus, quae a Deo prohibita esse scimus. Et in religione, non quid homines probent, sed quid Deus iubeat, videndum est. Quo ad alterum crimen, notior est quae hoc continetur calumnia, quam vt multa confutatione opus habeat. Qua enim ratione licentiam peccandi inuebit Christi doctrina, cuius hic finis et scopus est, vt ex verbi semine renati nos totos per fidei obedientiam Deo submittamus, vt hic in nobis et operibus nostris glorificetur? Et portento simile videtur, quod hodie nos et doctrinam Euangelicam hoc nomine tam odiose accusant, qui disciplinam morum oderunt, et ideo lucem illius extinctam volunt, ne per eam arguantur, et vitae genus, cui nimis diu assueuerunt, mutare cogantur.
units.tr: Moreover, in this example we should observe under what heading Christ's teaching is usually accused: namely, that it condemns the traditions of the fathers and the manner of worship handed down by them, and that it teaches a way of salvation too easy, which produces security of the flesh and licence to sin. These charges are not to be despised. For all who are upright and more earnest in goodness detest them, and the first charge alone is enough to stir up the hatred of anyone, because the authority of the fathers is held sacrosanct by all, and to condemn them seems to most people not only harsh but also impious and deserving of any punishment. Yet no one should take offence at these things as if they were new and previously unheard of. For we know that the prophets and apostles were accused of them in former times; indeed it should be enough for us that the defenders of human traditions and superstitions threw these things at Christ. In both respects our adversaries do us great wrong. For a man is not at once ungodly if he violates or transgresses the institutions of the fathers. The prophet indeed cries out: "Do not walk in the way of your fathers." And in Jeremiah, God rebukes the Jews for the unlawful forms of worship which they had learned from their fathers. For the fathers are of two kinds. Some are those ancient ones whose faith the Holy Spirit approves in the Scriptures, because they faithfully observed the laws given by God. Others are the intermediate ones, who, abandoning the footprints of the former, followed their own inventions, introduced superstitions, and corrupted the true worship of God. Therefore, just as it is the greatest wickedness to turn aside from the example of the earlier fathers, so we cannot follow these later ones unless we are willing to perish with them. For we shall not be excused by the authority of any fathers or of any other men if we do what we know God has forbidden. And in religion, we must look not to what men approve but to what God commands. As to the second charge, the calumny contained in it is too well known to need a long refutation. For by what reasoning would the doctrine of Christ introduce licence to sin, when its purpose and goal is this: that we, born again from the seed of the Word, should submit ourselves wholly to God through obedience of faith, so that he may be glorified in us and in our works? And it seems a portent that today they accuse both us and the Gospel teaching so bitterly of this charge, those who hate the discipline of morals, and therefore want its light extinguished, lest they be convicted by it, and be compelled to change the way of life to which they have grown accustomed for so long.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad Christi responsionem, quae duabus partibus constat. Prima discipulos defendit, altera rationem ostendit, qua aduersarij impediantur, quo minus veritati locu dent. In priori, quam modo recitauimus, argumento vtitur a temporis circumstantia desumpto dicens: Num poteritis facere, vt filij thalami, quo tempore cum ipsis est sponsus, ieiunent, &c? Filios thalami dicit Hebraica phrasi eos, qui in nuptijs agunt, ad quas legitime inuitati sunt. Est ergo argumentum eiusmodi: Qui nuptijs intersunt, ij nulla ratione ad ieiunandum cogi debent, quoad nuptiae durant et sponsus illis praesens adest: At mei discipuli me, qui sponsus ille animarum olim a Deo promissus sum, praesentem habent, et iam tempus illud est, quo nuptiae caelestes agi incipiunt, in quibus illis locus praecipuus debetur: Ergo absurdum foret, illos ad ieunia et austeriorem vitae rationem adigere. Itaque finite illos hac libertate frui, neque eis fortem meliorem inuidete, quando haec non perpetua illis erit. Nec enim procul abest tempus, quando me e terris sublato omnis generis molestias atque aduersa sustinebunt, et tunc illis ieiunandi causa nunquam non suppeditabitur. Petitur argumentum hoc partim ex communi hominum vsu, partim ex scripturis propheticis, quae passim nostram cum Deo coniunctionem, cuius nobis author sive Mediator Christus est, coniugij, et nuptiarum parabolis adumbrant. Voluit autem eadem hic vti Dominus, vt discipulorum Ioannis stupiditatem arguat, qui cum ex magistro suo iampridem audiuissent, Christum esse sponsum, cui omnes coniungi oporteat, adhuc tamen illum aemulabantur. Eadem vero opera omnes
units.tr: Let us now come to Christ's answer, which has two parts. The first defends the disciples; the second shows the reason by which the adversaries are hindered from giving place to the truth. In the first part, which we have just recited, he uses an argument drawn from the circumstance of time, saying: "Can you make the sons of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?" In the Hebrew idiom, "sons of the bridechamber" means those who take part in a wedding to which they have been lawfully invited. The argument, then, is of this kind: those who are present at a wedding ought not to be compelled to fast in any way, as long as the wedding lasts and the bridegroom is present with them. But my disciples have me, who am that bridegroom of souls promised long ago by God, present with them, and now is the time when the heavenly wedding begins to be celebrated, in which they are owed a principal place. Therefore it would be absurd to drive them to fasting and a more austere manner of life. Let them, then, enjoy this liberty, and do not begrudge them their joy, since it will not be perpetual for them. For the time is not far off when, I being taken from the earth, they will endure every kind of trouble and adversity, and then there will never be lack of cause for them to fast. This argument is drawn partly from the common usage of men and partly from the prophetic Scriptures, which in many places picture our communion with God, of which Christ is the author or Mediator, by the images of marriage and wedding. The Lord was willing to use the same argument here so as to rebuke the stupidity of John's disciples, who, though they had long since heard from their master that Christ is the bridegroom to whom all must be joined, were still jealous of him. And by the same act he rebukes all

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. omnes quoque arguit, qui pijs lætiorem fortunam inuident, neque aliquos Christianorum loco habendos esse arbitrantur, quibus datur in otio & pace degere. Est hoc hominum genus frequens hodie, quos sub plausibili pietatis prætextu cæca ambitio exagitat. Ignorant illi bonitatem Dei, qui suos interdum indulgentius tractat, donec viribus auctì ad maiora onera ferenda possint sufficere. At tunc meminerimus non perpetuam esse pacem, quæ in hoc mundo agentibus obtingit, & ideo tunc quoque nos ad crucem præparemus, ne hac ex improuiso obruti turpiter deficiamus. Poterit nos hic plurimum iuuare diligens parabolæ istius consideratio, si nos Christi sponsam esse, & hanc coniugij legem esse cogitemus, ut qui huius vinculo constricti sunt, omnem fortunam inter se communem habeant. At quia huius parabolæ mysterium alibi exposuimus, plura hoc loco addere non est opus. Similiter de ieiunio in Marco & propheta non semel abunde dictum est, unde petant Lectores, quæ in hunc locum dici poterant. Illud tamen propter superstitiosos veteratis admiratores monemus, nunquam in primitiua Ecclesia certas de statu ieiunij leges fuisse, & sua libertate singulas Ecclesias tunc quoque vsas esse, cum res ad superstitionem inclinare iam inciperent. Recte ergo Dius Augustinus, Ego (inquit) euangelicis & apostolicis literis totoque instrumento, quod appellatur testamentum nouum, animo id reuoluens, video præceptum esse ieiunium: Quibus autem diebus non oporteat ieiunare, & quibus oporteat, præcepto Domini vel Apostolorum non inuenio definitum. Quæ verba abunde testantur, humanas traditiones esse, quæ posteris temporibus de ieiuniorum obseruatione factæ sunt: quarum quàm parua esse debeat apud pios authoritas nemo ignorat, qui Scripturæ sacræ libros vel à primo limine salutauit. Nostrum fuerit, Dei bonitatem agnoscere, qui nos sibi in filio suo desponsare dignatus est, & nos illi præbere sponsam absque ruga & macula, hocque vnum agere, ne nostra vel intemperantia vel immunditia sponsum hunc à nobis alienemus, à quo omnis nostra vita salusque dependet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: {y} Ioan. 3. all also who begrudge the pious their happier lot, and think that those should not be counted Christians to whom it is granted to live in leisure and peace. This kind of people is common today; blind ambition, under the plausible pretext of piety, drives them on. They do not know the goodness of God, who sometimes deals more indulgently with his own until, strengthened in their powers, they are able to bear greater burdens. Then let us remember that the peace which falls to those who live in this world is not perpetual, and therefore let us then also prepare ourselves for the cross, so that, overwhelmed by it unexpectedly, we may not shamefully give way. Careful consideration of this parable will greatly help us here, if we think that we are the bride of Christ, and that this is the law of marriage: that those who are bound together by its tie should have all their fortune in common. But because we have set out the mystery of this parable elsewhere, there is no need to add more here. Likewise, concerning fasting, both in Mark and in the prophet, it has been said more than once and at sufficient length; let readers seek there what could be said on this passage. Yet we warn, on account of the superstitious admirers of antiquity, that in the primitive Church there were never fixed laws about the observance of fasts, and that even then, when matters had already begun to lean towards superstition, individual Churches used their own liberty. Rightly therefore Augustine says: "I (he says), turning it over in my mind in the evangelical and apostolic letters and in the whole instrument which is called the New Testament, see that fasting is commanded; but on what days it is not fitting to fast, and on what days it is fitting, I do not find defined by a precept of the Lord or the Apostles." These words abundantly testify that the human traditions which were later made concerning the observance of fasts are of no authority; and how small their authority ought to be among the pious, no one is ignorant who has greeted the books of Holy Scripture even from the threshold. Let it be our part to acknowledge the goodness of God, who has deigned to betroth us to himself in his Son, and to present us to him as a bride without spot or wrinkle, and to take care of this one thing: that we do not, by our intemperance or our uncleanness, estrange this bridegroom from us, on whom all our life and salvation depend. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIIII.

units.la: Dicebat autem eis etiam parabolam: Nemo panniculum noui vestimenti immittit in vestimentum vetus: alioqui & illud nouum findit vetus, & veteri non conuenit panniculus ex nouo. Et nemo infijcit vinum nouum in vtres veteres: alioqui disrumpet vinum nouū vtres & ipsum effundetur, & vtres peribunt. Sed vinum nouum in vtres recentes infundendum est, & vtraque conseruantur. Et nemo qui biberit vetus, statim vult nouum, dicit enim: Vetus melius est.
units.tr: He also told them a parable: "No one puts a piece from a new garment on an old garment; otherwise the new garment is torn, and the piece from the new does not match the old. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine will burst the skins, and the wine will be spilled and the skins will be ruined. But new wine must be poured into fresh skins, and both are preserved. And no one who has drunk old wine immediately wants new, for he says, 'The old is better.'"

units.la: Christus Iesus, Dominus & Seruator noster, ad quæstionem de ieiunijs ita nuper respondit, vt paucis omnia complexus sit, quæ de horum vsu vero & necessario dici possunt, & quæ cum veterum prophetarum doctrina probe conueniebant. Miretur ergo quis non immeritò, qui factum sit, quòd Pharisæi & qui cum his coniurauerant, nihilo meliores facti in sua contumacia perseuerauerint. Itaq; huius mali causas nunc ostendit, quam alteram suæ responsionis partem esse nuper dixi mus. Est hic locus multa consideratione dignus. Primò enim singulos homines docet, quid maximè cauere debeant, si Euangelium cum aliquo fructu audire velint. Deinde scandalo medetur, quod multi sibi ipsi obijciunt, quando eos incurabili peruicacia aduersus Veritatis doctrinam pugnare vident, qui & in authoritate summa constituti sunt, & vulgo optimi & sapientissimi mortalium esse putantur. Vtitur autem pro suo more similibus ex vsu quotidiano & re domestica petitis, vt facilius quod dicitur omnes intelligant, & vt nunquam non occurrat de his cogitandi occasio. Quàmuis vero trium similitudinis idem sensus & scopus sit, præstat tamen singulas seorsim inspicere, vt magis faciant ad nostram institutionem.
units.tr: Christ Jesus, our Lord and Saviour, lately answered the question about fasting in such a way that in a few words he embraced everything that can truly and necessarily be said about their use, and which agreed well with the teaching of the ancient prophets. So anyone may justly wonder how it came about that the Pharisees and those who conspired with them became no better, but persisted in their obstinacy. Therefore he now shows the causes of this evil, which I said lately was the second part of his answer. This passage deserves much careful thought. First, he teaches individual people what they must above all guard against if they wish to hear the Gospel with any profit. Second, he heals a scandal that many raise against themselves when they see people of the highest authority, and whom the common crowd thinks the best and wisest of mortals, fighting against the doctrine of truth with incurable stubbornness. He uses, as is his custom, comparisons drawn from everyday life and household matters, so that all may more easily understand what is said, and so that there is never a lack of occasion to think about these things. Although the three comparisons have the same meaning and aim, it is nonetheless better to look at each one separately, so that they may serve our instruction more fully.

units.la: Primum his verbis proponitur: Nemo panniculum noui vestimenti immittit in vestimentum vetus: alioqui & illud nouum findit vetus, & veteri non conuenit panniculus ex nouo. Per vetus vestimentum veterem & longo vsu stabilitam humanarum traditionum atque superstitionum assuetudinem intelligit, vel potius ipsos Pharisæos atq; horum sectatores, quorum animi in illis iam pridem consenuerant, vt nihil admittere possent, quod à veteri consuetudine dissentiret. Ex altera parte panniculum nouum dicit doctrinam Euangelij, quæ non circa ceremonias & superstitiosa corporis exercitia occupatur, sed ipsas hominum mentes reformat, & ad altiorem veræ pietatis contemplationem atque visum euehit. Ita verò loquitur, vt ipsorum sensui & captui se accommodet. Nam si rem ipsam rectè æstimemus, Euangelij doctrina non noua, sed omnium, quæ vnquam in orbe exiterunt, prima & proinde vetustissima est. Nam æterno Dei decreto nititur, qui & filium suum vt noster redemptor esset prædestinauit, & nos in illo elegit priusquam mundus iste conderetur. Primus autem eius author simul atque præco est Deus, qui cum parentes primos ex Paradiso eijcere vellet, peccati conscientia & iræ suæ sensu consternatos ista promissione consolatus est: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Ita verò filium suum promisit, qui absque viri congressu ex Virgine homo factus diaboli regnum euertit, & miseros nos ex illius tyrannide vindicauit. Est deinde omnibus seculis subinde repetita & instaurata hæc promissio, & eiusdem interpretes fuerunt Moses & prophetæ, qui vno ore omnes populum monuerunt, vt relicta ceremoniarum fiducia salutem in promisso illo semine quærerent. At Sacerdotum & Scribarum partim incuria partim malitia factum erat, vt plerique circa ritus externos & traditionum obseruationem occupati nescirent, quæ sanctissimorum patrum fides fuisset, & simul Messiæ aut promissi vindicis (quàmuis hunc nunquam non in ore haberent) vera cognitione destituerentur. Ita fiebat, vt noua putaretur doctrina, quæ iam inde à prima rerum origine durauerat, vetustatis autem nomine commendaretur superstitio, quæ ineptissimorum hominum traditionibus non ita pridem inuectis nitebatur. Est hæc veritatis sors, quam hodie etiam experimur, quando in omnium ore versantur veteris & nouæ doctrinæ seu religionis nomina: vulgò autem nouitatis insimulatur Euangelium, vetus autem & antiqua religio dicitur Papatus, cuius authores & concinnatores aliquot demum post Apostolorum tempora seculis exorti sunt, neque eodem simul tempore omnes vixerunt. Quæ causa est, quòd plerique ad Euangelij prædicationem non secus quàm si Troglodytas aut Garamantes loquentes audirent, obstupescunt, multi verò illam sub invidioso novitatis prætextu hostiliter persequuntur. Debemus nos quoque malum hoc personatis præsulibus, qui religionem sibi quæstum fecere, & vulgi ignorantiam fouent, ne quando è gradu suo deiciantur. Quò magis omnes animi decet, vt Veritatem ex ipsis sacræ scripturæ fontibus hauriant, & inde discant, quid in toto religionis negotio vetus aut nouum dici mereatur. Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, quorum hic sensus est: Non miror ego vos à mea doctrina tantopere abhorrere, vt nullis rationibus aut signis vestra obstinatia expugnari possit. Vt enim vestis attrita & lacera frustra assuitur panniculus nouus, eò quòd neque hic illi conuenit, neque ista hunc ferre potest, & proinde scissura maior efficitur: ita cùm vos traditionibus & superstitionibus assueueritis, & hæ vobis vestis loco sint, qua vos ornari, defendi & seruari putatis, neque ab illis auelli vnquam vos patiamini, nequicquam ego vobis æternum patris consilium prædico, quod vobis nouum & prius inauditum est. Nam vt mea doctrina cum vestris superstitionibus non potest conuenire: ita si eam obtrudere vobis velim & vtrasque simul miscere, nihil aliud profecero, quàm vt superstitionum vestrarum lacera atque fœda confusio magis appareat, neque vos ex mea doctrina fructum aliquem habeatis. Et quia Ioannis discipulorum ea est stupiditas, vt ipsi quoque vos potius sequi quàm magistri sui admonitionibus parere malint, non aliud de illis etiam iudicare possumus. Nisi ergo vtrique centones illos veteres exuatis, nunquam in cognoscenda patris cœlestis Veritate profectum aliquem facere poteritis. Hæc (inquam) Dominus paucis hisce verbis completitur. In quibus obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd traditiones & quæ ex his instituuntur superstitiones vesti veteri & attritæ seu lacerae confert. Nam vt hæc non tegit corpus, & multò minus ornat vel calefacit, ita quæ in humanis traditionibus & cultibus superstitiosis quæritur iustitia, minimè tegere potest peccata, quibus iam pridem Deum offendimus. Typum huius rei in Adamo habemus, qui vt nuditatem suam tegeret, ficus folia contexuit, sed nequicquam, adeò vt Deo ipsum vrgente suam turpitudinem ipse fateri cogeretur. Quod ipsum omnibus accidit, qui suis figmentis peccata sua vel expiare vel occultare volunt. Quidenim hæc facerent, quando Isaias iustitiam, quam pij ex præceptis Dei sectantur, centonũ sordidorum
units.tr: The first is set forth in these words: "No one puts a piece from a new garment on an old garment; otherwise the new garment is torn, and the piece from the new does not match the old." By the old garment he means the old custom of human traditions and superstitions, long established by use; or rather, he means the Pharisees themselves and their followers, whose minds had long since grown old in these things, so that they could admit nothing that differed from their old custom. By the new piece he means the doctrine of the Gospel, which is not occupied with ceremonies and superstitious exercises of the body, but reforms the minds of men themselves and lifts them up to a higher contemplation and vision of true godliness. He speaks in this way so that he adapts himself to their understanding and grasp. For if we judge the matter rightly, the doctrine of the Gospel is not new, but is the first and therefore the most ancient of all that have ever existed in the world. For it rests on the eternal decree of God, who both predestined his Son to be our Redeemer and chose us in him before the world was founded. Its first author and herald at once is God, who, when he wished to drive our first parents out of Paradise, consoled them, dismayed by the consciousness of sin and the sense of his wrath, with this promise: "The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent." In this way he promised his Son, who, made man of a Virgin without intercourse with a man, overthrew the kingdom of the devil and delivered us wretched people from his tyranny. Then this promise has been repeated and renewed in every age, and Moses and the prophets were its interpreters, who with one voice all warned the people that, having abandoned confidence in ceremonies, they should seek salvation in that promised seed. But it came about, partly through the negligence and partly through the malice of the priests and scribes, that most people, occupied with external rites and the observance of traditions, did not know what the faith of the most holy fathers had been, and at the same time were without true knowledge of the Messiah or the promised deliverer, although they always had his name on their lips. And so it happened that the doctrine which had endured from the very beginning of things was thought to be new, while superstition, which rested on the traditions of the most foolish men introduced not long before, was commended under the name of antiquity. This is the lot of the truth, which we experience even today, when the names of old and new doctrine or religion are on everyone's lips: the Gospel is commonly accused of novelty, while the old and ancient religion is said to be Papism, whose authors and compilers arose only some centuries after the time of the Apostles, and not all lived at the same time. This is why many, on hearing the preaching of the Gospel, are amazed, as if they were hearing Troglodytes or Garamantes speak, and many persecute it with hostility under the hateful pretext of novelty. We too ought to attribute this evil to the bishops who have made religion a source of gain and foster the ignorance of the common people, lest at some point they be cast down from their rank. All the more should every mind be eager to draw the truth from the very springs of Holy Scripture, and learn from there what in the whole business of religion deserves to be called old or new. But let us return to the words of Christ, whose meaning is this: "I do not wonder that you so greatly shrink from my doctrine that your obstinacy cannot be overcome by any reasons or signs. For just as a new patch sewn on a worn and torn garment is in vain, because the one does not fit the other and the other cannot bear it, and so the tear becomes greater, so, since you have grown accustomed to traditions and superstitions, and these serve you as the garment in which you think you are adorned, defended and kept safe, and you will never allow yourselves to be torn from them, I preach to you in vain the eternal counsel of the Father, which is new to you and never heard before. For just as my doctrine cannot agree with your superstitions, so if I wished to force it upon you and mix both together, I would accomplish nothing except to make the torn and foul confusion of your superstitions more apparent, and you would gain no benefit from my doctrine. And since the disciples of John are so dull that they too prefer to follow you rather than to obey the admonitions of their own master, we can judge nothing else about them. Unless therefore you both strip off those old patches, you will never be able to make any progress in knowing the truth of the heavenly Father." These things, I say, the Lord completes in these few words. In which it is most worthy of notice that traditions, and the superstitions instituted from them, are compared to an old and worn or torn garment. For just as this does not cover the body, and much less adorns or warms it, so the righteousness that is sought in human traditions and superstitious worship can by no means cover the sins by which we have long since offended God. We have a type of this matter in Adam, who, to cover his nakedness, sewed together fig leaves, but in vain, so that, with God pressing him, he was forced to confess his own shame. This happens to all who wish either to atone for or to hide their sins with their own inventions. For why would they do this, when Isaiah says that the righteousness which the godly pursue from the precepts of God is like filthy rags?

units.la: Superstitiones sunt lacera vestis. didorum instar esse dicit? Quid vero ad ornatum illa ipsa conferrent, quae ne tegere quidem possunt? Ut vero animos Dei amore accendant & salutis securos reddant, multo minus sperandum est. Constat enim eos, qui superstitionibus dediti sunt, vera Dei cognitione destituti, & proinde hunc neque amare possunt, neque salutem sibi ipsis certam polliceri. Quare etsi in superstitionum exercitio fervent, feruor tamen ille ex conscientiae aestuantis inquietudine nascitur, qua fit, ut aut eadem sacra subinde repetant, aut nova instituant, dum ex iis quae antea fecerunt nullam consolationem sentiunt. Solus Christus suam nobis iustitiam communicans veste illa nuptiali nos induit, qua ornati coram Deo comparere possumus, & quae simul animum nouo indies & feruentiori Dei amore accendit, ut salutis quidem securi simus, simul tamen maiores subinde in vera pietate progressus faciamus.
units.tr: Superstitions are a torn garment. Or like filthy rags? But what would those very things contribute to adornment, when they cannot even cover? Still less can it be hoped that they will kindle the minds of men with the love of God or make them secure of salvation. For it is clear that those who are given over to superstitions, being without true knowledge of God, can therefore neither love him nor promise themselves certain salvation. Therefore, although they burn with zeal in the practice of superstitions, that zeal arises from the restlessness of a seething conscience, with the result that they either repeat the same rites again and again, or institute new ones, since from what they did before they feel no consolation. Christ alone, communicating his own righteousness to us, clothes us with that wedding garment, in which, adorned, we can appear before God, and which at the same time kindles the mind with a new and more fervent love of God every day, so that we are indeed secure of salvation, and yet at the same time make ever greater progress in true godliness.

units.la: Admonet nos praeterea hic locus: frustra eos laborare, qui hodie Papatum cum Euangelio conciliare student. Si enim Christum & Euangelium eius non potuerunt admittere Pharisaei, quos liberi arbitrii, suarum item virium & propriae iustitiae fiducia inflabat, non minus ad illum recipiendum inepti erunt qui Papatum mordicus retinent, in quo praeter Pharisaicum fermentum infiniti alij abusus & foedissimi errores conspiciuntur: quales sunt idololatria, sacra pro defunctis, Dei uorum invocatio & alia huius generis, quorum tanta est absurditas, ut nihil huius prisci illis Pharisaeis ne in mentem quidem venerit. Si qui ergo ista cum Euangelij doctrina & verae fidei professione coniungere satagunt, ij nihil aliud efficiunt, quam quod confusionem inducunt, quae ex superstitionis tandem palam impios facit, & omnem religionis sensum in animis hominum restinguit. Quid enim de religione & tota salutis ratione praeclarum sentire possunt homines rudes & illiterati, quando ab iis, qui prae aliis sapere putantur, dogmata diversa & palam inter se pugnantia misceri vident? Fatemur quidem pare & concordia nihil in ecclesia utilius & magis necessarium esse, sed inter ea concordiam constitui posse negamus, quae contradictoria sunt, & simul consistere non possunt. Quod ergo in alia causa Paulus dixit: quae communio lucis cum tenebris? hic in primis observari debet, ne concordiae praetextu decepti a Christi regula discedamus, qui suos unum esse cupit in ipso, & cuius vox est: Qui non colligit mecum, dispergit. Minime ergo audiri debent compositores aut conciliatores illi, qui hodie passim exoriuntur, & qui ut apud omnes bonam gratiam ineant, omnes quotquot sunt superstitiones facile cum fidei Christianae doctrina conciliari posse dicunt, & dum hanc illis accommodant, scissuram & deformitatem in ecclesia maiorem faciunt, & Christum ipsum multis inutilem reddunt. Quia enim hic solus audiri & solus pro sponso agnosci vult, nequaquam eos pro bare possit, qui simul aliis quoque occupati meriti eius virtutem euacuant.
units.tr: This passage also warns us that those who today try to reconcile the Papacy with the Gospel are labouring in vain. If the Pharisees, puffed up with confidence in free will, their own strength and their own righteousness, could not accept Christ and his Gospel, then those who cling stubbornly to the Papacy will be no more fit to receive him. Besides the Pharisaic leaven, the Papacy displays countless other abuses and most foul errors: idolatry, masses for the dead, the invocation of the dead, and others of this kind, whose absurdity is so great that nothing like them ever entered the minds of those Pharisees. Those who strive to join such things to the teaching of the Gospel and the profession of true faith achieve nothing but confusion. This confusion ends by making men openly impious under the name of superstition, and it extinguishes every sense of religion in the minds of people. For what can simple and unlettered folk think of religion and the whole plan of salvation when they see that those who are thought to be wiser than others mix together doctrines that are different and openly contradict one another? We grant that peace and concord are the most useful and necessary things in the Church, but we deny that a concord can be established between things that are contradictory and cannot stand together. So when Paul said in another context, "What fellowship has light with darkness?" (2 Cor. 6.14), we must take care above all that, deceived by the pretext of concord, we do not depart from the rule of Christ, who wants his people to be one in him, and whose word is: "He who does not gather with me scatters" (Matt. 12.30). Therefore we must by no means listen to those compromisers and conciliators who spring up everywhere today. In order to win everyone's goodwill, they say that all the superstitions there are can easily be reconciled with the doctrine of the Christian faith. In accommodating the faith to them, they make the rent and the deformity in the Church greater and make Christ himself useless to many. For since he alone wishes to be heard and alone to be acknowledged as Bridegroom, he cannot in any way approve of those who, at the same time, busy themselves with others and thereby empty his merit of its power.

units.la: Restat alterum simile, quod de re vinaria est, & quo iacturam, quae ex ineptis illis conciliationibus oritur, evidentius exprimit. Nemo (inquit) infundit vinum nouum in vtres veteres: alioqui disrumpet vinum nouum vtres, & ipsum effundetur, & vtres peribunt, &c. Loquitur pro illorum temporum aut locorum ratione, vbi vinum in vtres ex pellibus aut corio factos condebatur. Nec male vino nouo Euangelium adumbratur. Nam vt illud feruere solet, & vix illis vasis contineri potest: ita Euangelij doctrina spiritus virtute accensa efficaciter agit in hominum animis, & hunc sibi finem atque scopum habet propositum, vt hominem totum immutet, & se in eius actionibus vniuersis proferat. Hinc vehementes illi motus, qui sub euangelicae praedicationis initium fere oriri solent, dum & singuli subito mutantur & simul publicam reformationem inuehere studeant. Illos autem prophani homines seditiosos dicunt, sed vtinam rem diligentius expenderent principes, ne dum armis Christo in suorum animis feruenti se opponunt audacius, seipsos simul & suae curae commissum populum perderent: quod hodie non vno loco factum vidimus. Vt vero mustifuerorem non ferunt vtres veteres aut dolia pertusa & vetustate iam corrupta: ita qui animos veteri superstitione corruptos & incertis opinionibus diffluentes habent, ij Euangelium ferre non possunt, neque huic cum illis (vt antea monuimus) conuenire possunt, eo quod Euangelij doctrinae inimicum est, quicquid praeter Christum in salutis negotio creditur aut praedicatur. Hinc ergo duplex iactura nascitur. Primo vtres disrumpuntur, id est, homines ipsi pereunt. Quia enim superstitionibus, quibus affuerunt, renuntiare nolunt, Euangelium vero illos omnino aduersari vident, tunc aut indignatione accensi illud reijciunt & hostes fiunt manifesti: aut religionem inter res medias & indifferentes habere incipunt, & ita paulatim ad Epicureifmum declinant, & Deum sibi fingunt, qui religionum diuersitate nequaquam offendatur, adeoque res mortalium non multum curet. Itaque eò tandem delabuntur, vt religione omnino nulla teneantur, aut eam quaestu metian tur, & sub eius praetextu res suas agant, quod olim Ieroboamum, primum Israelitarum regem, fe- cisse legimus. At quodcunque ex istis fiat, certus hominis interitus sequitur. Deinde altera tactura est, quod vinum effunditur, id est, Euangelium ipsum apud tales diffluit, & non solum ipsis inu- tile fit, verumetiam propter ipsos omnium ludibrio exponitur. Exempla huius generis hodie passim extant, sed qui illa obseruent, & ijs bene vtantur, paucissimos esse videre. Addit autem Christus alterum simile ex priori desumptum, quod ipsius instituto optime conuenit, & quo Pharisaeos pro- prius ferit dicens: Et nemo qui biberit vetus, statim vult nouum, dicit enim: Vetus melius est. Qua si diceret: Idem vobis, quoad meam doctrinam, quod ijs accidit, qui vino veteri & leniori assueue- runt. Vt enim illi nouum vinum, etsi generosius sit, minus ferunt, eo quod fortius est & feruen- tius: ita vos, qui patrum traditionibus & superstitionibus, operosis quidem in speciem, sed ad quae- stum & ambitionem compositis, assueuistis, non potestis meam doctrinam admittere, eo quod ipsos animos penetrat, & totius hominis innouationem exigit. Exuendus ergo erit vetus ille animus & renuntiandum inueterata consuetudini, si in vera pietate proficere velitis.
units.tr: There remains a second comparison, taken from wine, which more clearly expresses the loss that arises from those foolish compromises. "No one," he says, "pours new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be spilled, and the skins will perish," etc. (Luke 5.37). He speaks in accordance with the custom of those times and places, when wine was stored in skins or leather bottles. And the Gospel is not badly pictured by new wine. For just as new wine tends to ferment and can scarcely be held in such vessels, so the doctrine of the Gospel, kindled by the power of the Spirit, works effectively in the hearts of men, and it has this aim and purpose set before it: to change the whole man and to show itself in all his actions. Hence those violent movements, which usually arise at the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, when individuals are suddenly changed and at the same time strive to bring about a public reformation. Profane men call these men seditious, but I wish that princes would weigh the matter more carefully, lest, while they oppose Christ too boldly with arms, in those who burn with his Spirit, they destroy both themselves and the people committed to their care. We have seen this done in more than one place today. Just as old wineskins or cracked casks, already corrupted by age, cannot bear new wine that ferments, so those whose minds are corrupted by old superstition and dissolving in uncertain opinions cannot bear the Gospel. Nor can they agree with it (as we said before), because whatever is believed or preached in the matter of salvation apart from Christ is hostile to the doctrine of the Gospel. From this, then, a twofold loss arises. First, the skins burst, that is, the men themselves perish. For since they are unwilling to renounce the superstitions in which they have been brought up, and since they see that the Gospel is wholly opposed to them, then either, kindled with indignation, they reject it and become open enemies, or they begin to regard religion as one of the indifferent matters and so gradually decline into Epicureanism, and they fashion for themselves a God who is not offended by the diversity of religions and who therefore does not greatly care about human affairs. Thus they finally fall to such a point that they are held by no religion at all, or they measure religion by profit and under its pretext pursue their own affairs, as we read that Jeroboam, the first king of the Israelites, once did. But whichever of these happens, certain destruction of the man follows. Second, there is the loss that the wine is spilled, that is, the Gospel itself runs out among such people, and it becomes not only useless to them but is also exposed to the mockery of all. Examples of this kind are found everywhere today, but few, I see, observe them and make good use of them. Christ also adds another comparison, drawn from the earlier one, which fits his purpose very well and strikes the Pharisees more directly, saying: "And no one who has drunk old wine immediately wants new, for he says: The old is better" (Luke 5.39). It is as if he said: "What happens to those who have grown accustomed to old and milder wine happens to you with regard to my doctrine. For just as they bear new wine poorly, though it is finer, because it is stronger and more fermenting, so you, who have been accustomed to the traditions of the fathers and to superstitions, which are elaborate in appearance but devised for gain and ambition, cannot admit my doctrine, because it penetrates the very minds and demands the renewal of the whole man." That old mind must therefore be put off and the long-standing custom renounced, if you wish to make progress in true godliness.

units.la: Haec autem ita Pharisaeis dicuntur, vt nostrorum quoque temporum institutioni seruiant. Docet enim istorum consideratio, quae tanta corruptionis & impietatis causa sit, quae hodie passim grassatur, & quae remedia ad eam profligandam aut coercendam adhiberi debeant. Etenim non te- mere quidam mirantur, quod in manifesta & omnium oculis sese ingerente Euangelij luce pauci emendentur, plerique autem incurabili peruicacia in impietate pergant. Poterat his respondeti, hos esse nouissimorum temporum mores, quos tales fore olim Christus praedixit. Idem vero hic nobis huius mali causam veram & propriam indicat, quod nimirum plerique eorum, qui Euangelij fcla- tores videri volunt, pannum hunc nouum centonibus attritis assuere, & vinum nouum in vtres ve- teres condere satagunt. Alij enim quia se Euangelij cursum impedire non posse vident, ad artes conuersi conciliationes priorus doctrinae & Papisticae instituunt, & Euangelium quidem audiunt, sed ea conditione, ne errores & superstitiones arguantur. Manet ergo in hominum animis fermen- tum vetus, & dum duabus sellis sedent, paulatim ab omni religione deficiunt, denique omni veste religionis spoliati se prorsus nudos & turpes cum publica infamia praebent. Alij vero, qui iam ante religionem omnem contemnunt, ne aperti hostes Dei videantur, Euangelio quidem locum dant, eidem tamen leges praescribunt, ne in alicuius mores aliquid liberius dicatur, ne scelera publice accu- sentur, neue leges conscribantur nouae, quibus morum licentia frenetur. Ita vero non audacia modo plus quam Cyclopica peccatur, sed manifestus quoq; verbi Dei contemptus accedit, quem hic inul- tum vel impunitum non potest dimittere. Fit ergo vt iusto Dei iudicio traditi in reprobum sensum, quotidie in peius proficiant, vt tandem impleta suae impietatis mensura dignas poenas exoluant, Et illa quidem verissime dici fatebuntur, quicunque huius temporis mores propius inspexerint. Quas enim Ecclesias hodie dabimus, in quibus non aliqui superstitionum centones retineantur, aut effraenis licentia regnet?
units.tr: These things are said to the Pharisees, but they also serve the instruction of our own times. For consideration of them teaches what a great cause of corruption and impiety there is, which rages everywhere today, and what remedies ought to be applied to crush or restrain it. Indeed, some people are not without reason amazed that, while the light of the Gospel shows itself plainly and before the eyes of all, few are amended and most persist in impiety with incurable obstinacy. One could answer them that these are the morals of the last times, which Christ foretold would be such. But here he also points out to us the true and proper cause of this evil: namely, that most of those who wish to be seen as promoters of the Gospel try to sew this new cloth onto worn-out patches and to pour new wine into old wineskins. For others, seeing that they cannot hinder the course of the Gospel, turn to tricks and set up compromises between the former doctrine and Papistry. They listen to the Gospel, but on condition that their errors and superstitions are not refuted. So the old leaven remains in men's minds, and while they sit on two stools, they gradually fall away from all religion, and at last, stripped of every garment of religion, they show themselves utterly naked and shameful, with public infamy. Others, who already despise all religion, so as not to appear open enemies of God, give room to the Gospel, yet prescribe laws for it: nothing is to be said too freely about anyone's morals, crimes are not to be publicly accused, and no new laws are to be drawn up by which the licence of morals might be curbed. In this way they sin not only with a audacity more than Cyclopean, but there is also added a manifest contempt for the Word of God, which here cannot let it go unpunished or unavenged. So it comes about that, given over by the just judgment of God to a reprobate mind, they make progress for the worse every day, until at last, when the measure of their impiety is filled up, they pay the penalties they deserve. Those who have looked more closely at the morals of this time will confess that these things are most truly said. For what churches shall we point to today in which some patchwork of superstitions is not retained, or in which unbridled licence does not reign?

units.la: Quod si huius mali remedium quaeras, hoc quoque praefens iste locus nobis monstrat. Quia enim neque pannus nouus veteri & attritae vesti conuenit, neque vinum nouum in vtres veteres con- di potest, vt toti innouemur opus erit. Et hic quod priuatim singuli agant inuenient omnis loci & ordinis homines. Exuant primo centones superstitionum, & abs se procul reiiciant, quicquid cum Dei verbo pugnare vident. Deinde curent, vt totis quoque animis innouentur, seque ad capiendum vinum illud Euangelij salutiferum praeparent. Proderit hic quoque plurimum, si a pueris rectè & pie omnes instituantur. Nam si tenelli animi erroribus & superstitionibus assuescant, difficile postea fuerit, eos adducere, vt veritati locum dent. Et quantum possit institutio puerilis, in primi mundi hominibus sacra historia docet, qui simul omnes Nephilim, id est, defectores & prophani omnis religionis contemptores facti sunt, cum ex imparibus coniugijs nati a parentibus in diuersas partes distraherentur. Vehementer ergo peccant, qui liberos suos in ijs locis educari & instrui curant, in quibus falsa doctrina dominatur, & vbi neque praedicationi veritatis, neque confessioni puriorus puriori fidei locus est. Illic ergo veste illa veteri induuntur, qua vix unquam postea exui possunt, & cui Euangelij pannus conuenire non potest: animos item eiusmodi concipiunt, quibus nullo cum fructu vinum illud infunditur, quod vnum tam homines quàm Deum vere exhilarat. At non sufficit priuatim singulos monuisse, nisi publicè officium faciant ij, quos in gradum eminentiorem Deus evexit. Itaque verbi administris & ecclesiarum pastoribus in primis aduigilandum est, ne doctrinæ suæ aliquid admisceant, quod humanas traditiones aut superstitionem redoleat. Non fert enim mixturam aliquam Euangelij vinum, ideoque hoc purum merum infundere debent, quicunque auditores suos saluos volunt. At qui magistratum gerunt, & publica authoritate Ecclesiarum atque religionis reformationem instituunt, illi etiam atque etiam curent, vt simul omnia è medio tollantur, quæ ab hominibus præter Dei verbum inuenta sunt: neque eos audiant, quibus sufficere videtur, si idola vel simulachra ex animis hominum remoueantur, & externa illa puriori religioni nihil officere aiunt, si animi probè sint instituti. Ridiculi plane homines, qui religionem fingunt, cuius nulla indicia foris appareant, aut quæ cultum externum habeat ab animi sententia & fidei confessione prorsus dissentientem. Quin potius Deum audiunt per prophetam omnibus dicentem, vt fornicationes, id est, superstitiones & idololatriam à facie simul & veribus remoueant. Quia enim nos sibi totos ille vendicat, non poterunt veri ipsius cultores dici, qui quod in animo se sentire aiunt, non etiam cultus externi exercitio profitentur. Hæc vos cogitare velim principes Christiani, qui cùm Euangelicæ doctrinæ propugnatores haberi vultis, publica tamen authoritate simulachra, altaria, vestes superstitiosas & infinitas alias papisticæ superstitionis sordes defenditis. Annon hæc ex excelsorum numero censeri possunt, propter quæ relista & defensa accausantur Reges, qui in repurgando Dei cultu alioqui operam non omnino pœnitendam nauauerunt? Vtimini ergo semel oblata occasione, & causam piè susceptam magno animo agite, Josiam & Ezechiam imitati, qui ne minimas quidem superstitionum quisquilias relinquendas esse putarunt. Videbant enim optimi & piissimi principes, quàm facile ad illicitos cultus relabantur, qui aliquam occasionem sibi dari vident: neque suo exemplo, ceu præiudicio quodam, successores suos grauari volebant, quod ferè fieri solet, si quid intactum ab illis relinquatur, quorum authoritas merito apud omnes in pretio est. Studeant ergo omnes pro sui ordinis aut loci ratione, vt sublatis omnibus errorum atque abusuum reliquijs, sola Euangelij vox in omnium auribus resonet, vt vnus Iesus Christus in omnium animis regnet atque triumphet: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But if you seek a remedy for this evil, this same passage also shows it to us. For since neither a new patch suits an old and worn garment, nor new wine can be poured into old wineskins, we must be renewed entirely. Here people of every place and rank will find what each may do privately. First, let them strip off the patches of superstition and cast far from them whatever they see to be at odds with the Word of God. Then let them take care to be renewed in their whole hearts, and prepare themselves to receive that saving wine of the Gospel. It will also greatly help if all are rightly and piously instructed from boyhood. For if tender minds grow accustomed to errors and superstitions, it will afterwards be hard to bring them to give place to the truth. And how much childhood teaching can achieve, sacred history teaches in the case of the first men of the world, who all became Nephilim, that is, deserters and despisers of all true religion, because they were born of unequal marriages and were drawn apart by their parents in different directions. They therefore sin grievously who take care to have their children reared and taught in those places where false doctrine holds sway, and where there is room neither for the preaching of the truth nor for the confession of the purer faith. There they are clothed in that old garment, from which they can scarcely ever afterwards be stripped, and to which the patch of the Gospel cannot be fitted; they also form such minds that the wine which alone truly gladdens both men and God is poured into them to no profit. But it is not enough to admonish individuals privately, unless those whom God has raised to a higher rank also perform their duty publicly. Therefore, above all, the ministers of the Word and the pastors of the churches must take care not to mix into their teaching anything that smells of human traditions or superstition. The wine of the Gospel does not bear any admixture, so those who want their hearers saved ought to pour out this pure, unmixed wine. But those who bear the magistracy, and by public authority carry out the reformation of the Churches and of religion, let them take most careful heed that everything which men have invented beyond the Word of God be removed altogether; and let them not listen to those who think it enough if idols or images are taken out of men's minds, and who say that those outward things do no harm to a purer religion if the minds of men are rightly taught. Truly ridiculous are those men who invent a religion with no outward signs visible, or one that has an external worship utterly at odds with the opinion of the heart and the confession of faith. Rather, let them hear God speaking through the prophet to all: that they remove the whoredoms, that is, the superstitions and idolatry, both from his face and from his teeth. For since he claims us wholly for himself, those cannot be called true worshippers of him who say they feel one thing in their mind but do not also profess it by the practice of outward worship. I would have you consider these things, Christian princes, who wish to be counted as defenders of the Evangelical doctrine, and yet by public authority you defend images, altars, superstitious vestments and the countless other filths of Papistical superstition. Can these not be counted among the high places, on account of which the kings are accused of having left them standing and defended them, although in other respects they laboured in no small measure to cleanse the worship of God? Use therefore the occasion once offered, and carry out your pious undertaking with great courage, imitating Josiah and Hezekiah, who thought that not even the smallest rubbish of superstitions should be left behind. For those excellent and most pious princes saw how easily men fall back into unlawful worship when they see any opportunity given them; nor did they wish their successors to be burdened by their example as by some precedent, which usually happens if anything is left untouched by those whose authority rightly holds great weight with all. Let all, therefore, according to the place and rank of each, strive that, with every remnant of errors and abuses removed, the voice of the Gospel alone may resound in everyone's ears, and that Jesus Christ alone may reign and triumph in everyone's hearts; to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HOMILIA LV.
units.tr: HOMILY LV.

units.la: FActum est autem, vt Sabbato secundo primo pertransiret per fata, & vellebat discipuli eius spicas edebant, & confricantes manibus. Quidam verò Pharisæorum dixerunt eis: Cur facitis quod non licet facere Sabbatis? Tunc respondens Iesus dixit eis: ne hoc quidem legistis quod fecit Dauid cum esuriret ipse & qui cum eo erant? Quomodo intrauit in domum Dei, & panes propositionis sumpserit, ederitq;, ac dederit etiam iis qui secum erant: quos panes non licet edere nisi solis Sacerdotibus? Et dicebat eis: Filius hominis, Dominus est etiam Sabbati.
units.tr: It happened that on the second Sabbath after the first, he passed through the grainfields, and his disciples plucked the ears of corn and rubbed them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said to them: Why do you do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbaths? Then Jesus answered and said to them: Have you not even read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him? How he went into the house of God, took the loaves of the presentation, ate them, and gave them also to those who were with him, though it is not lawful to eat those loaves except for the priests alone? And he said to them: The Son of Man is also Lord of the Sabbath.

units.la: MVLTA quidem sunt, quæ vt veram religionem atque Dei cultum corrumpunt, ita hominem à recta salutis via reuocant: at inter ea duo ferè sunt omnium nocentissima, hu-manarum videlicet traditionum doctrina, & ceremoniarum ab ipso etiam Deo præceptarum superstitiosa fiducia. Quia enim nostris figmentis natura delectamur, & externis vt plurimùm addiĉti sumus, perquam difficile est animum ab ijs abducere, quæ multorum authoritate probantur, & longo temporis vsu confirmata sunt. Quòd si ijsdem diuina authoritas accedat, iam optimi quoque omnem salutis fiduciam in illis solis collocant, reliĉtis ijs, quæ sola Deo vere accepta sunt & nos salvos faciunt. Est ergo in vtroque confutando Christus admodum diligens. Et hac Ġenus quidem aduersus traditiones hominum grauiter disputauit, cùm de ieiunijs inter ipsum & Scribas contentio exorta esset, atque docuit eos nunquam proficere posse in vera pietate, qui veteres pannos & animos diuturniori superstitionum vsu induratos nondum deposuerunt. Nunc ad alterum accedit, & eos confutat, qui in superstitiosa Sabbati obseruatione Dei cultum atque hominis salutem consistere putabant, docens, illud non ita præceptum esse à Deo, vt non potior eorum habenda sit ratio, sine quibus homo saluus esse non potest: sicque isto exemplo admoner, in omnium ceremoniarum obseruatione non literæ superstitiosius inhærendum, sed animos altius euehendos esse, vt illarum finem atque scopum probè obseruemus, qui si negligatur, illa prorsus inutiles, vel etiam pernitiosæ fiunt.
units.tr: There are many things which corrupt true religion and the worship of God, and so call a man back from the right path of salvation; but among them two are almost the most harmful of all: the doctrine of human traditions, and the superstitious trust placed in ceremonies even when God himself has commanded them. For since we delight in our own inventions by nature, and are for the most part given over to outward things, it is very hard to draw the mind away from those things which are approved by the authority of many and confirmed by long use. If divine authority is added to these, even the best people place all their confidence of salvation in those alone, and leave aside those things which are truly acceptable to God alone and which save us. So in refuting both, Christ is most careful. And indeed he disputed sharply against the traditions of men when a dispute arose between him and the scribes about fasting, and he taught that those can never make progress in true godliness who have not yet put off the old rags and minds hardened by long practice of superstitions. Now he comes to the second point and refutes those who thought that the worship of God and the salvation of man consisted in the superstitious observance of the Sabbath, teaching that it was not so commanded by God that the regard due to those things without which a man cannot be saved should be set aside. And so by this example he warns that in the observance of all ceremonies we must not cling to the letter too superstitiously, but lift our minds higher, so that we rightly observe their end and aim; if this is neglected, those ceremonies become utterly useless, or even harmful.

units.la: Præmittitur autem tractationis huius occasio, quæ ex discipulorum facto enata fuit. Cùm enim Dominus Sabbato secundoprimo, id est, primo sabbato festi hebdomadum, quo frugum primitiæ offerri solebant, (Solent enim Iudæi festa omnia Sabbati nomine dignari, & ea ratione primum, id est, præcipuum omnium Sabbatorum est dies Paschæ, secundum dies Pentecostes: sicque Sabbatum secundoprimum erit primus dies secundi festi annui, quem Græci à die\um à Paschate numero Pentecosten dixerunt) per sata transiret, discipuli fame coacti inter eundum spicas vellere & ex his grana manibus exterere atque edere cœperunt. Licebat hoc per legem, in qua Moses humanitatis & beneficentiæ officia secundùm iustitiæ regulam exigere & præstare docens, inter alia sic scribit: Cùm veneris in vineam proximi tui, vuas comede pro animi tui desiderio, quantum satis est, sed non colliges in vas tuum. Etsi pertransieris per segetem proximi tui, spicas quidem manu tua decerpas licet, sed in segetem proximi tui falcem ne miseris. Non ergo in charitatis & iustitiæ leges peccant discipuli, neque eo nomine à Pharisæis accusantur, sed quod distud die Sabbati fiat illi reprehendunt, vt postea audiemus.
units.tr: The occasion for this discussion is given first, arising from the disciples' action. For when the Lord passed through the fields on the second-first Sabbath, that is, the first Sabbath of the weeks' festival, on which the firstfruits of the harvest used to be offered (for the Jews are accustomed to honour all festivals with the name of Sabbath, and so the first, that is, the chief, of all the Sabbaths is the day of the Passover, and the second is the day of Pentecost; thus the second-first Sabbath will be the first day of the second annual festival, which the Greeks called Pentecost from counting fifty days from the Passover), the disciples, compelled by hunger, began as they went along to pluck ears of grain and to rub out the grains with their hands and eat them. This was allowed by the law, in which Moses, teaching that the duties of kindness and beneficence must be required and performed according to the rule of justice, writes among other things as follows: When you come into the vineyard of your neighbour, you may eat grapes to your heart's desire, as many as are enough, but you shall not gather any into your vessel. If you pass through your neighbour's standing corn, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbour's corn. The disciples therefore do not sin against the laws of charity and justice, nor are they accused by the Pharisees on that account; rather they object to the fact that it is done on the day of the Sabbath, as we shall hear afterwards.

units.la: Nunc autem Christi disciplina consideranda venit, qua discipulos ad maiora certamina præparauit, & horum patientia, qui cùm domi suæ commodius & minori cum inuidia viuere possent, illum tamen constanter secuti sunt, neque (quod carni & mundo deditì solent) ab eo refilierunt, qui ipsos cum paupertate & inedia conflictari patiebatur. Est hoc ingens fidei & pietatis argumentum, quam postea in grauioribus periculis in finem vsque retinuerunt. Docemur autem hoc exemplo, vt ipsi quoq; dum res magis pacata & tutæ sunt, nos ad crucis certamina præparemus, ne his offensi salutis iacturam faciamus, si quando præter omnem expectationem ad illa abripimur. Vt enim qui in paternis ædibus indulgentius educantur, externis nunquam obediunt, neque ferunt patienter disciplinam, qua fidi præceptores ad virtutem eos instituunt: ita qui sibi ipsis nimium indulgent, & circa carnis atque voluptatum desideria occupati omnem molestiam suterfugiunt, ij fere turpissimos sese dant, quando aliquid egregium pro Christo & publica salute est faciendum. Proderit autem in hac re, si huius vitæ conditionem probè consideremus, & quæ hic nobis ferenda sunt, cum promissa æterna & beata immortalitatis præmijs conferamus: si denique in Christi exemplum intenti simus, & cogitemus hunc nihil à nobis exigere, quod non ipse prior nostri causa fecerit. Sed friget in hac parte studium nostrum, quæ causa est, quòd pace atque otio nostro turpiter abutimur ad Christiani nominis infamiam, in periculis autem succumbimus cum infami Iesu Christi & salutis propriæ abnegatione.
units.tr: But now the discipline of Christ must be considered, by which he prepared his disciples for greater struggles, and the patience of these men, who, although they could have lived more comfortably at home and with less hatred, nevertheless followed him constantly, and did not (as those given over to the flesh and the world are wont to do) fall away from him who allowed them to struggle with poverty and hunger. This is a great proof of faith and godliness, which they afterwards kept to the end amid more serious dangers. We are taught by this example that, even while things are calmer and safer for us, we too should prepare ourselves for the struggles of the cross, lest, offended by them, we suffer loss of salvation if at any time we are dragged into them beyond all expectation. For just as those who are brought up too indulgently in their father's house never obey outsiders, nor patiently bear the discipline by which faithful teachers train them to virtue, so those who indulge themselves too much, and, occupied with the desires of the flesh and of pleasures, avoid every hardship, generally show themselves most shameful when something excellent must be done for Christ and for the public good. It will be useful in this matter if we consider carefully the condition of this life, and compare what must be borne here with the promised eternal and blessed rewards of immortality; and finally if we keep our eyes fixed on the example of Christ, and reflect that he requires nothing of us which he did not first do for our sake. But our zeal grows cold in this respect, and the cause of this is that we shamefully abuse our peace and leisure to the disgrace of the Christian name, while in dangers we give way, with the shameful denial of Jesus Christ and of our own salvation.

units.la: Porrò sequitur, vt ex discipulorum facto nouam calumniandi & cum Christo altercandi occasionem Pharisæi arripuerint. Et in præsenti quidem cum stomacho discipulos aggrediuntur & clamant: Cur facitis quod non licet facere Sabbato? At eo non contenti, cùm discipuli nihil responderent, aut etiam respondere non possent, adipsum Christum conuersi (vt Matthæus scribit) huic illorum factum exprobrant, dicentes: Ecce discipuli tui faciunt, quod non licet facere Sabbato. Istis verò omnibus partim pertinax tuenda superstitionis studium notatur, partim malitiosum illorum hominum ingenium exprimitur, qui quicquid ab alijs fit, in Christi contumeliam rapiunt, & violatæ religionis eum accusare non verentur, in quo viuû & perfectum omnis pietatis & veræ sanctimoniæ exemplum elucebat. Neque dubium est illos eò maiori atque confidentiori animo ad hoc certamen descendisse, quòd scirent Sabbatum ab ipso Deo institutum & eius obseruationem seuerissimis legibus mandatam esse. Iam ergo se inuenisse putant, quod ille nunquam negare posset, & proinde sibi certam de illo victoriam pollicentur. Apud vulgus autem imperitum summam religionis & pietatis existimationem hoc nomine captant, quòd in asserendo Sabbato tam oculati aut rigidi censores sunt.
units.tr: Next, the Pharisees seized on the disciples' action as a new occasion for slandering and quarrelling with Christ. For the present they attack the disciples with bitterness and cry: Why do you do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? But not content with this, since the disciples made no answer, or could not answer, they turn to Christ himself (as Matthew writes) and reproach him with their action, saying: Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath. In all these words, on the one hand, a stubborn zeal for defending superstition is shown, and on the other hand the malicious character of those men is expressed, who snatch at whatever is done by others to Christ's reproach, and do not hesitate to accuse of violating religion him in whom the living and perfect example of all godliness and true holiness shone forth. Nor is there any doubt that they entered this contest with greater and more confident spirit, because they knew that the Sabbath had been instituted by God himself and that its observance was enjoined by the most severe laws. Now therefore they think they have found what he could never deny, and so they promise themselves certain victory over him. Among the unlearned crowd, meanwhile, they win the highest esteem for religion and piety by this very pretence, because they are such watchful or strict censors in defending the Sabbath.

units.la: Est autem diligenti obseruatione dignum, quòd Pharisæi tanto studio Christum sequuntur, adeoque indiuulsi comites ceu pedisequi sunt eius, quem cane & angue peius oderant. Fecerunt ergo hoc non veritatis cognoscendæ studio, sed vt calumniandi occasionem inuenirent. Et horum similes sunt hodie, qui piorum atque fidelium societatem colunt, cœtus sacros frequentant, & interdum Sacramentis Ecclesiæ communicant, interim verò hoc vnum agunt, vt veritatis doctrinam vel omnino extinguant, vel saltem apud imperitum vulgus exosam atque suspectam reddant. Apparet in eo, quòd vt Pharisæi discipulorum delicta & errores ipsi Christo exprobrant: ita isti quicquid in Ecclesia perperam & male fit, hoc Euangelij doctrinæ & huius præconibus acceptum ferre consueuerunt, etiamsi non ignorent ea contra horum voluntatem fieri, & cum Euangelij legibus aperte pugnare. Et non immeritò miretur aliquis istorum hominum patientiam, qui cùm verbum Dei totis animis detestentur, & ab omni religione alienissimi sint, tam multum tamen laboris & molestiæ devorare possunt in ijs audiendis atque videndis, quæ ipsis ex animo dolent. Sed hoc illud est, quod infra Dominus dicet, filios huius seculi prudentiores magisque industrios esse quàm filios lucis. Et tanta odij aduersus veritatem concepti vis est, vt qui illo ardent, nihil non ferre & facere possint, ex quo aliquam illius extinguendæ occasionem sperare possunt. Exempla huius generis in nostri seculi Pharisæis & horum sectatoribus, quos pontificiæ culinæ nidor trahit, passim occurrunt. Solent hi interdum & conciones sacras audire, & piorum manus prehensare, verbi administris omne officium deferre, nunquam non adesse vbi quid de religione agitur, & cum animos vere hostiles gerant, amicitiam tamen simulare possunt, vt facilius quod volunt assequantur. Debent ista nos excitare, vt & insidias hostium veritatis diligenter caueamus, & eò ardentius sectemur innocentiæ & sanctitatis studium, ne illi facilè inueniant quod calumniari possint. Imò interdum à nostro iure nos discedere decet, ne habeant quod suis sophismatis in Euangelij contumeliam trahant. Admonet de hoc Paulus grauiter, quando de semetipso dicit: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia ædificant. Nemo quod suum est quærat, sed quisque quod alterius est. Item, Estote sine offendiculo & Iudæis, & Græcis, & Ecclesiæ Dei, sicut & ego per omnia omnibus placeo, non querens meam ipsius vtilitatem, sed multorum, vt seruentur. 1. Corinthiorum 10. Rursus meminerimus non minori studio nobis opus esse in tuenda veritate, quàm hostes in ea oppugnanda vtuntur. Turpe enim fuerit nos in optimæ & sanctissimæ causæ defensione ab ijs vinci, qui vt Dei hostes sunt, ita causam sustinent non iniustam solùm & iniquam, sed cum manifesta impietate & publico omnium exitio coniunctam.
units.tr: It is worth careful notice that the Pharisees follow Christ with such eagerness, and are such inseparable companions, like servants at his heels, of him whom they hated worse than dog or snake. They did this therefore not from zeal for knowing the truth, but in order to find an occasion for slander. And like them today are those who cultivate fellowship with the pious and faithful, frequent sacred assemblies, and sometimes take part in the sacraments of the Church, but meanwhile do this one thing, to extinguish the doctrine of the truth altogether, or at least to make it hateful and suspect among the unlearned crowd. It appears in this, that just as the Pharisees reproach Christ himself with the faults and errors of his disciples, so these men are accustomed to lay to the account of the doctrine of the gospel and its heralds whatever is done amiss and badly in the Church, even though they are not ignorant that such things are done against the wishes of the gospel's ministers and clearly conflict with the laws of the gospel. And one may well wonder at the patience of these men, who, though they detest the word of God with their whole souls and are most alien to all religion, can nevertheless endure so much toil and discomfort in hearing and seeing those things which grieve them from the heart. But this is what the Lord will say below, that the sons of this age are wiser and more diligent than the sons of light. And so great is the force of hatred conceived against the truth, that those who burn with it can endure and do anything from which they hope for some opportunity of extinguishing it. Examples of this kind are found everywhere among the Pharisees of our age and their followers, whom the smell of the Papists' kitchen draws. These men sometimes hear sacred sermons, shake hands with the pious, offer every courtesy to the ministers of the Word, are always present wherever religion is discussed, and though they bear truly hostile hearts, they can feign friendship so that they may more easily achieve what they wish. These things ought to rouse us both to guard carefully against the snares of the enemies of the truth, and to pursue more eagerly the zeal for innocence and holiness, lest they easily find something they can slander. Indeed, at times it is fitting that we give up some of our rights, so that they have nothing to twist into a sophism to the reproach of the gospel. Paul admonishes us seriously on this, when he says of himself: All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify. Let no one seek his own, but each the good of another. Likewise: Be without offence to both Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God, just as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, that they may be saved. 1 Corinthians 10. Again let us remember that we need no less zeal in defending the truth than our enemies use in attacking it. For it would be shameful for us to be conquered in defence of the best and holiest cause by those who, as enemies of God, uphold a cause that is not only unjust and iniquitous but joined with manifest impiety and the public ruin of all.

units.la: Deinde hypocritarum mores hic ceu in tabella depicti proponuntur. Primò in alijs minima observant Pharisæi, at quæ ipsi grauissima atrocissimaq; designabant securi negligunt. Putant enim capitale scelus esse Sabbato spicas manibus conterere, vt habeas quo fames eximatur: cùm ipsi interim quouis die domus viduarum et orphanorum devorarent sub falso religionis prætextu, et insuper miserorum animas falsa doctrina occiderent. Quid verò hoc aliud est, quàm in proximi oculo festucam videre, in tuo autem trabem non animaduertere? Adhæc in Christi discipulis maligne notant, quod commodè & piè poterat excusari: in suis verò sectatoribus non reprehendunt ea, quæ nullam veniam merebantur. Venalia erant sacra, & religio omnis in quæstum abierat: cum Romanis præsidibus colludebant Sacerdotes in manifestam populi perniciem: vagabantur passim meretrices, quas Deus ex Israele eijciendas mandarat: famelici hinc inde oberrabant pauperes, & contra Dei leges oftiatim & ad templi fores victum mendicabant, cùm interea ex ecclesiæ bonis ditarentur nequissimi impostores: & infinita alia huius generis fiebant vulgò ab ijs, qui Pharisæorum studiosissimi habebantur. At nemine horum illi accusant, neminem reprehendunt, imò ne interrogant quidem paulò seuerius, cur hæc aut illa faciant, aut ab alijs fieri patiantur: quin potius hos omnes pro catholicis & orthodoxis habent: at solus Christus cum suis haereseos & violati cultus divini crimine grauatur, quod ad famem pellendam spicas digitis contriuissent. Quid vero aliud faciunt hodie Monachi, qui in nobis legitimum coniugij vsum, Christianam quidus edendi libertatem, neglectas ferias à Pontificibus superstitiose institutas, votorum monasticorum refcissionem & sexcenta alia magnis clamoribus accusant, & propterea dignos iudicant, qui ferro & igne excindamur: at ijdem suos sectatores in cælos vsque euehunt atq; in Deorum numerum referunt, etiamsi eos ventri, gulae & Veneri seruire, adhaec rapinis, furtis, bellis non necessarijs, incendijs & sanguine omnia foedare atq; infesta facere videant? Quid quod ipsi fere illis talium scelerum sunt authores? Est ergo idem vtrorumq; spiritus, nosq; eo minus offendi decet istorum clamoribus, quando eorum omnino similes sunt, qui olim aeterno Dei filio in faciem resistiterunt.
units.tr: Next, the morals of the hypocrites are set out here, as if painted on a tablet. First, the Pharisees observed the smallest things in others, yet carelessly neglected the gravest and most atrocious matters that they themselves were guilty of. They thought it a capital crime to rub ears of grain in the hands on the Sabbath, so that you might have something to relieve your hunger, while meanwhile every day they devoured the houses of widows and orphans under the false pretext of religion, and besides, by false teaching they destroyed the souls of wretched people. What else is this than to see the speck in your neighbour's eye and not notice the beam in your own? Moreover, they maliciously noted in Christ's disciples what could have been excused decently and piously, but in their own followers they did not blame things that deserved no pardon. Sacred things were for sale, and all religion had turned into profit. The priests colluded with the Roman governors to the manifest ruin of the people. Prostitutes, whom God had commanded to be cast out of Israel, wandered everywhere. Hungry poor people roamed about on all sides and, contrary to God's laws, begged for food from door to door and at the gates of the temple, while meanwhile the most wicked impostors grew rich from the goods of the Church. Countless other things of this kind were commonly done by those who were regarded as the most zealous of the Pharisees. Yet they accuse none of these men, they reprove none of them, they do not even question them with any great severity as to why they do this or that, or allow others to do it. Rather, they hold all of these men to be Catholic and orthodox. Only Christ is burdened with the charge of heresy and violation of divine worship, because he and his disciples rubbed ears of grain in their fingers to drive off hunger. And what else do the monks do today, who accuse us of the lawful use of marriage, of Christian freedom in eating, of the holidays superstitiously instituted by the Pontiffs being neglected, of the annulment of monastic vows, and of six hundred other things, with great outcry, and therefore judge us worthy to be cut off by sword and fire? Yet they lift their own followers up to heaven and count them among the gods, even when they see them serving their belly, gluttony and lust, and moreover defiling and making hostile everything with plunder, theft, unnecessary wars, arson and blood. What is more, they themselves are almost the authors of such crimes. The spirit of both is therefore the same, and we ought the less to be offended by their clamours, since they are wholly like those who once resisted the eternal Son of God to his face.

units.la: Sed reliquis monstris hisce infelicibus Christum audiamus, qui vt discipulis suis aduersus Pharisaeos patrocinatur, ita horum impudentem arrogantiam fortiter confutat, & simul docet, quid de externis ritibus simul omnibus sentire debeamus, si quis casus similis incidat. Et esset plenum consolationis, quod pauperes & obscuros non destituit suo patrocinio Dominus, sed illis aduersus eos etiam adesset, quorum summa erat apud Iudaeorum gentem authoritas. Debet hoc nobis in mentem venire, si quando cum ijs res nobis esset, quibus vix sufficere videmur. Nam etsi non adsit nobis corporis sui praesentia Dominus, spiritus tamen virtute in suis agit, qui fidi aduocati instar consolatio-nis argumenta simul & consilia sana suggerit, quibus hostium quantumuis astutissimorum artes eludamus. Caeterum breuitati studet Lucas in recitando Christi responso, quapropter illud ex Matthaeo & Marco ita supplieri poterit: Ne hoc quidem legistis quod fecit Dauid, cum esuriret ipse & qui cum eo erant? Quomodo introierit in domum Dei, & panes Propositionis sumpserit, ederitque, ac dederit etiam ijs qui secum erant, quos panes non licet edere nisi solis Sacerdotibus? Aut non legistis in lege, quod Sabbatis Sacerdotes in templo Sabbatum prophanant, & sine crimine sunt? Dico autem vobis templo maiorem hic esse. Quod si noscetis quid sit, Misericordiam volo & non sacrificium, non condemnassetis insontes. Sabbatum propter hominem factum est, non homo propter Sabbatum. Nam Dominus est etiam Sabbati Filius hominis. Est haec grauis admodum confutatio, & quinq; argumentis constat, quae ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ, who, as he defends his disciples against the Pharisees, so also firmly refutes the shameless arrogance of these men, and at the same time teaches what we ought to think about external rites, all of them together, should a similar case arise. And it would be full of consolation that the Lord did not abandon the poor and obscure with his protection, but was present to help them even against those whose authority among the Jewish nation was highest. This should come to mind for us whenever we have to deal with those whom we scarcely seem able to withstand. For although the Lord's bodily presence is not with us, yet he acts among his people by the power of his Spirit, who, like a faithful advocate, suggests to us arguments of consolation and sound counsels, by which we may elude the arts of enemies, however cunning they may be. Moreover, Luke aims at brevity in recounting Christ's reply, so that it can be supplied from Matthew and Mark as follows: "Have you not even read what David did, when he was hungry, he and those who were with him? How he went into the house of God and took the bread of the Presence, and ate it, and also gave it to those who were with him, which it is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone? Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are without blame? But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here. But if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the innocent. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. For the Son of Man is also Lord of the Sabbath." This is a very weighty refutation, and it consists of five arguments, which we shall see in order.

units.la: Primum ab exemplo Dauidis sumitur, qui panes propositionis, quorum esus solis sacerdotibus concessus erat, olim comedit. Extat historia in primo Samuelis cap.21.
