De panibus autem illis Moses Leuit.24. disserit. Fiebant hi ex similia aut farina purissima, duodecim numero, & diebus sabbati singulis noui imponebantur mensae aureae cum phialis thure plenis. Erant autem typus Christi, qui verus ille panis vitae est, quique è caelo ad nos missus carnem purissimam & omnis peccati expertem ex castissima virgine assumpsit. Debet is semper proflare in ecclesia, vtq; eius cognitio per Verbi administros Iubinde instauretur necesse est, vt & certa nobis esse possit salutis fiducia, & vt preces nostrae (quae per thus adumbrantur) Deo gratae sint. Solis autem sacerdotibus licecat illos edere, non quod ijsoli Christo frui possint, qui sacris externis initiati sunt: sed quod non alij illo vescuntur ad vitam aeternam, nisi quos ille Deo patri Sacerdotes fecit: in quo numero censentur, quot quot illum fide non fucata apprehendunt. Hi enim seipsos Deo viuentem hostiam sistunt, & quosq; cunque possunt eidem adducere student. Commode ergo Dauidis exemplum allegat Dominus, & quidem non sine exprobratione ignorantiae aut malitiae, qua Pharisaei moti discipulorum factum calumniabantur: Ne hoc quidem legistis (inquit) quod fecit Dauid, &c? Quasi diceret: Mirum est vos in meis ea etiam calumniari, quae infinitis exemplis scripturae sacrae excusari poterant. At non multis hic opus est, quando vnum Dauidus factum discipulos meos omni culpa liberat. Quod si nunquam legistis indigni estis, qui vobis censuram in alios sumatis. At si legistis, & nihilominus hoc facitis, satis constat vos malitiose agere, & veritatis luce potius quā Sabbati violatione (quae hic nulla admissa est) offendi. Etenim constat panes propositionis non minus interdictos fuisse laicis, quam nequis Sabbatum aliquo seruili opere prophanet: Attamen Dauid, cum Saulis insidias fugiens fame laboraret, neque alius cibus ad manum esset, illos comedit & ex ijsdem suis quoque comitibus distribuit: Quae ergo nequitia est in praesenti discipulos meos accusare, quos eadem necessitatis ratio excusat? Vel nū vos Abiathare sacerdote religiosiores estis, quid de sola prophanatione, quae per immunditiam committitur, solicitus, de reliquo facile & pie dispensauit? Ia vero Dauidis exemplo ad confutandam Pharisaeorum hypocrisim vtitur, vt simul eodem discipulorum fidem confirmet, ne inopia & fame offendantur, quando constat eandem olim illorum fortem fuisse, qui Dauidem, Christi typum, secuti sunt.
units.tr: The first is taken from the example of David, who once ate the bread of the Presence, the eating of which had been permitted to the priests alone. The story is found in 1 Samuel 21. Moses discusses that bread in Leviticus 24. These loaves were made of fine flour, twelve in number, and on each Sabbath new ones were placed on the golden table with vessels full of incense. They were a type of Christ, who is that true bread of life, and who, sent to us from heaven, took on a most pure flesh, free of all sin, from a most chaste virgin. He ought always to be proclaimed in the Church, and his knowledge must be renewed from time to time through the ministers of the Word, so that the confidence of salvation may be certain for us, and so that our prayers (which are foreshadowed by the incense) may be acceptable to God. Only the priests, however, were permitted to eat those loaves, not because only those who have been initiated into the external sacraments can enjoy Christ, but because no others feed on him unto eternal life except those whom he has made priests to God the Father. Those who lay hold of him with unfeigned faith are counted in this number. For they present themselves to God as a living sacrifice, and they strive to bring as many as they can to him. The Lord therefore fittingly cites the example of David, and indeed not without rebuking the ignorance or malice by which the Pharisees, moved by the disciples' deed, were slandering it: "Have you not even read," he says, "what David did, etc.?" As if he were saying: "It is strange that you should slander in my disciples even those things which could be excused by countless examples of Holy Scripture. But there is no need for many examples here, since the one deed of David frees my disciples from all blame. But if you have never read it, you are unworthy to take upon yourselves the censure of others. But if you have read it and nevertheless do this, it is quite clear that you act maliciously, and that you are offended by the light of truth rather than by a violation of the Sabbath, which is not committed here at all." For it is certain that the bread of the Presence was no less forbidden to laymen than it is forbidden for anyone to profane the Sabbath by any servile work. Yet David, when fleeing the snares of Saul and suffering from hunger, and when no other food was at hand, ate those loaves and also distributed them among his own companions. What wickedness, then, is there in accusing my disciples now, whom the same reason of necessity excuses? Or, if you are more scrupulous than the priest Abiathar, who was anxious only about the profanation committed through uncleanness, did he not dispense the rest easily and piously? Indeed, he uses the example of David to refute the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, and at the same time to confirm the faith of his disciples, so that they may not be offended by poverty and hunger, since it is clear that the same lot once fell to those who followed David, the type of Christ.

units.la: Interim de duobus obseruatu dignissimis hoc loco nos Christus admonet. Primum, quod externa omnia charitati cedere debeant, quae vt vitae totius, ita ceremoniarum omnium tutissima regula & fidissima moderatrix est. Quia enim hae omnes in eum finem institutae sunt, vt homini ad salutem adminicula sint, nimis iniqui sunt, qui illas rigidius vrgent, vt ad perdendum potius quam seruandum faciant. Vidit hoc Moses, qui in circumcisione similiter dispensauit. Nam etsi lex infantes octauo a partu die circumcidere iuberet, ille tamen in deserto neminem circuncidit, cum & loci iniquitas & profectiones subitae obstarent, quo minus cura ea adhiberi posset, quae in medendo ei vulneri necessaria erat. Pie ergo in illud tempus usque res delata est, quo terram promissam ingressi sunt. Obseruemus hoc aduersus eos, qui salutem sacramentis ita astringunt, vt & paruulos omnes, qui morte praeuenti absque baptismo decedunt, & eos qui Coenae Dominicae communicare non possunt, temere damnent & ab omni salutis spe deiiciant. Sunt hi non in homines solos iniurij, sed Deum ipsum crudelitatis insimulant, qui sacris abs se institutis in eas angustias nos adducat, vt nobis necessario pereundum sit. Alterum quod Dauidem non regia dignitas neque prophetici spiritus excellentia, sed sola necessitas excusat: sed & ipse Abiathar non pontificia authoritate circa panes propositionis dispensauit, sed charitatis rationem habuit, quae iubet vt famelicis pro virili succurramus. Arguit hoc eorum temeritatem, qui illustribus personis omnia licere putant: quasi vero Deus aliquem exlegem fecerit: qui item profuo commodo in sacris omnibus dispensant, vt vel quae stum faciant maiorem, vel magnatum amicitiam sibi demereantur, &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile, Christ here admonishes us about two things most worthy of notice. The first is that all external things ought to yield to charity, which is the safest rule and most faithful guide of all of life, and likewise of all ceremonies. For since all of these have been instituted with this end in view, that they may be aids to man for salvation, those are far too unjust who press them more rigidly, so that they act to destroy rather than to save. Moses saw this, who likewise dispensed in the matter of circumcision. For although the law commanded that infants be circumcised on the eighth day after birth, yet he circumcised no one in the desert, since both the unsuitability of the place and sudden departures stood in the way, so that the care necessary for healing that wound could not be applied. Therefore the matter was piously deferred until that time when they entered the promised land. Let us observe this against those who bind salvation so tightly to the sacraments that they rashly condemn all infants who die prematurely without baptism, and those who cannot communicate at the Lord's Supper, and cast them down from all hope of salvation. These men do wrong not only to human beings, but they also accuse God himself of cruelty, as though he, by the sacraments instituted by himself, were bringing us into such straits that we must necessarily perish. The second thing is that David is excused not by his royal dignity nor by the excellence of the prophetic Spirit, but by necessity alone. And Abiathar himself did not dispense the bread of the Presence by pontifical authority, but took account of the rule of charity, which bids us succour the hungry as far as we can. This refutes the rashness of those who think that everything is permitted to illustrious persons, as though God had made anyone exempt from the law. Likewise, those who dispense all sacred matters for their own advantage, either to make a greater profit or to win for themselves the friendship of the great, and so on.

units.la: At ne Dauidis exemplum Pharisaei eluderent, secundum argumentum ab exemplo Sacerdotum petit Christus, qui in ipso templo Sabbatum prophanare videri poterant, quando sacra operantur, vbi & ligna secare, & pecudes iugulatas in frusta discindere, ignem accendere, vasa sacra & seipsos abluere opus est. Attamen haec omnia sine crimine faciunt, quia templi religione & cultus diuini ratione excusantur. Quanto minus ergo (inquit Christus) damnari debent mei discipuli, qui vt me sequantur & mihi seruiant, famem sustinent, & eam inter eundum spicarum contritione sedant? Est ergo argumentum hoc a comparatis: quia quanto Christus maior est templo & omni cultu externo, tanto minor erat discipulorum, quam Sacerdotum, culpa. Docet autem Christus Sabbati praecepto non prohiberi ea, quae ad Dei cultum faciunt. Quia enim illud cultus ergo institutum est, si ultum fuerit eius praetextu ea intermittere, quibus Deus maxime colitur. Atqui cultus ille non in externis solum ceremonijs consistit, sed (vt Iacobus ait) religio pura & immaculata apud Deum & Patrem haec est, inuisere orphanos & viduas in afflictione sua, & immaculatum seipsum seruare a mundo. At si sabbati religio charitati & vero cultui Dei cedere debet, stulta nimis est eorum superstitio, qui ne hominum traditiones violent, omnia quae tam Deo quam hominibus debentur pietatis officia secure negligunt. Damnantur igitur hoc Christi dicto omnes, qui in Monachorum regulis & frigidissimarum ceremoniarum observatione cultum Dei & salutis meritum consistere putant.
units.tr: But so that the Pharisees could not evade David's example, Christ draws a second argument from the example of the priests, who in the temple itself seemed to profane the Sabbath when they performed the sacred duties. There they had to cut wood, cut up slaughtered animals into pieces, kindle fire, and wash the sacred vessels and themselves. Yet they do all this without blame, because they are excused by the sanctity of the temple and the requirements of divine worship. "How much less, then," Christ says, "ought my disciples to be condemned, who suffer hunger while following me and serving me, and who relieve it by rubbing ears of corn as they go?" This argument therefore proceeds by comparison: the greater Christ is than the temple and all outward worship, the less the fault of his disciples is than that of the priests. Christ teaches that the commandment of the Sabbath does not forbid those things that are done for the worship of God. For the Sabbath was instituted for the sake of worship, so it would be wrong to use its pretext to omit those things by which God is chiefly honoured. Yet that worship does not consist only in outward ceremonies. As James says, "pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world." If the religion of the Sabbath must give way to charity and true worship of God, then the superstition of those is utterly foolish who, lest they break the traditions of men, carelessly neglect all the duties of piety owed both to God and to men. By this saying of Christ, therefore, all are condemned who think that the worship of God and the merit of salvation consist in the rules of monks and in the observance of very cold ceremonies.

units.la: Sequitur tertium argumentum a pronuntiatis, quod & ipsum cum ignorantiae exprobratione adducit. Quod si nosset is quid sit, Misericordiam volo, et non sacrificium, non condemnasseris in-son-tes. Extat locus hic apud Hosaeam Cap.6. Accusat illic Deus fucatum religionis studium, quo Iudaei simul & Israelitae scelera sua expiari putabant. Consistebat illud partim in simulata & momentanea paenitentia, quam nubeculae in summo aestu exorienti & mox euanescenti atque rori matutino confert: partim in sacrificiorum frequentia & crebra iteratione, quibus illos in primis confisos fuisse, ex aliorum quoque prophetarum sermonibus constat. Sed huic fiduciae Deus istud dictum opponit, ex quo in praesenti Christus argumentum ducit, quod per comparationem amplificatur. Si enim sacrificia, quae externi cultus pars praecipua fuerunt, sine misericordia Deo non probantur, imo si haec illis longe praestat, nimium iniqui sunt & iniusti, qui propter sabbatum aliquos fame perire volunt. Quartum argumentum ex fine sabbati petitur, & communi sensu confirmatur, quo omnes norunt causam finalem destinatis omnibus esse praestantiorem, & haec vel mutanda vel etiam omnino negligenda esse, si a scopo, ad quem destinata primo sunt, abludant. Atqui sabbatum (inquit) propter hominem factum est, non homo propter sabbatum. Unde sequitur huius otium non ita superstitiose coli debere, quin aliquo opere interrumpi possit, si hominis salus in periculum veniat. Et est in his omnibus probe observanda plus quam paterna Dei bonitas, qui ea etiam, quae ut suo cultui serviant instituit, nobis subiecta esse vult. Quid quod totus cultus nobis potius quam Deo seruit? Nec enim Deus nostris sacris indiget, & ad illum nulla redit utilitas, sive feriemur, sive laboremus, sive baptizemur, sive ad coenam mysticam accedamus, sive etiam verbum eius audiamus, aut in periculis opem ipsius imploremus. Nam etsi nihil horum fiat, nihil tamen eius honori, maiestati aut potentiae decedit. Nobis autem illa profuxt, & propter nos ab illo instituta sunt, ut hisce exercitiis in eius cognitione atque fide confirmati aeternum serviemur. Est ergo immanis eorum ingratitudo atque impietas, qui ista vel negligunt, vel etiam scurriliter insectantur. Sunt hi digni, qui tandem in reprobum sensum traditi tam corpore quam anima male pereant.
units.tr: Next follows a third argument, drawn from what Christ said, which he also introduces with a rebuke for ignorance: "But if you had known what this means, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, you would not have condemned the innocent." This passage is found in Hosea, chapter 6. There God accuses the feigned zeal for religion by which the Jews and the Israelites alike believed their sins could be atoned for. It consisted partly in a pretended and momentary repentance, which God compares to a little cloud rising in the heat of the day and soon vanishing, or to morning dew; and partly in the great number and constant repetition of sacrifices, in which they trusted above all, as the words of the other prophets also make plain. But God sets against this confidence the saying from which Christ now draws his argument, which is amplified by comparison. For if sacrifices, which were the chief part of outward worship, are not approved by God without mercy, and indeed if mercy far surpasses them, then those are much too unjust and unrighteous who wish people to perish with hunger on account of the Sabbath. The fourth argument is taken from the purpose of the Sabbath, and is confirmed by common sense, by which everyone knows that the final cause of all things is more excellent than the means, and that the means must be changed, or even wholly neglected, if they depart from the goal for which they were first appointed. Yet the Sabbath, Christ says, was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath. From this it follows that its rest ought not to be observed so superstitiously that it cannot be interrupted by some work, if a man's safety is in danger. In all these things we must carefully observe God's goodness, which is more than fatherly. He wills that even those things which he instituted to serve his worship be subject to us. Indeed, all worship serves us rather than God. For God has no need of our sacred rites, and no advantage comes to him whether we rest or labour, whether we are baptized, or come to the mystical supper, or hear his Word, or implore his help in dangers. For even if none of these things is done, nothing is taken from his honour, majesty or power. But these things profit us, and were instituted by him for our sake, so that by these exercises, being strengthened in the knowledge and faith of him, we may serve him for ever. Therefore the ingratitude and impiety of those is monstrous who either neglect these things or even mock them in buffoonery. They deserve to be given over at last to a reprobate mind, and to perish miserably in both body and soul.

units.la: Restat quintum argumentum, quod priorum omnium confirmationem habet: Nam Dominus est etiam sabbati Filius hominis. Loquitur autem de se ipso Christus, & ne temerarius videatur, qui in sabbati praecepto dispensare velit, sibi hoc ius esse docet, ut cum omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra habeat, sabbati quoque Dominus sit, & proinde homines soluere possit a superiori illa, quae prius tenebantur, legis disciplina. Etenim constat Dei filium ideo in mundum venisse & hominis filium factum esse, ut legis maledictionem aboleret, & iugum illud a nostris ceruicibus tolleret, quod (ut Petrus ait) neque nos neque patres unquam ferre potuerunt. Est ergo hoc inter alia non vulgare Christi beneficium, quod eam libertatem nobis contulit, ut omnibus, quae in mundo sunt, tanquam nostris, uti possimus, quatenus nostrae salutis ratio postulat. Ideo Paulus illum nobis sanctificationem factum esse ait, quod non solum nos Deo patri consecrat, verumetiam omnium creatorum usum nobis liberum & sanctum fecit, ut illis salva conscientia uti possimus. Puris enim, id est, per ipsius spiritum purificatis, pura & sancta sunt omnia. Quo etiam referri debet, quod idem Apostolus Corinthiis, nimis quorundam ministrorum admiratoribus, scribebat: Omnia vestra sunt; sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive praesentia, sive futura: Omnia (inquam) vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei, &c. Nostrum vero est Dei bonitatem agnoscere, neque eorum calumniis offendi, qui etiam hodie libertatem hanc nobis invid… curemus modo, ne ea ad carnis licentiam abutamur, sed omnia nostra dirigamus ad Dei gloriam, & tandem in Christo Iesu beatae immortalitatis consortes simus: Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains a fifth argument, which has the confirmation of all the previous ones: "For the Son of man is Lord also of the Sabbath." Christ speaks here of himself, and so that no one may think it rash for him to dispense with the commandment of the Sabbath, he teaches that this right is his, since he has all power in heaven and on earth, and is therefore also Lord of the Sabbath, and so can free men from that former discipline of the law by which they had been bound. For it is established that the Son of God came into the world for this reason, and became the Son of man, so that he might abolish the curse of the law and take away from our necks that yoke which, as Peter says, neither we nor our fathers were ever able to bear. Therefore among his other benefits, which are not small, this is one: he has granted us such liberty that we may use all things in the world as our own, so far as the reason of our salvation requires. Hence Paul says that he was made sanctification for us, because he not only consecrates us to God the Father, but also makes the use of all created things free and holy for us, so that we may use them with a clear conscience. For to the pure, that is, to those purified by his Spirit, all things are pure and holy. To this also should be referred what the same Apostle wrote to the Corinthians, who were too much admirers of certain ministers: "All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's," and so on. It is for us to acknowledge the goodness of God, and not to be offended by the slanders of those who even today begrudge us this liberty; we need only take care that we do not abuse it for licence of the flesh, but direct all our things to the glory of God, so that at last we may be partakers in Christ Jesus of blessed immortality. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 56.

units.la: Factum est autem etiam alio Sabbato, ut ipse ingrederetur in Synagogam ac doceret: & erat ibi quidem, cuius manus dextera erat arida. Obseruabant vero eum Scribae ac Phatisaei, an Sabbato sanaturus esset illum, ut inuenirent accusationem aduersus eum. At ipse nouerat cogitationes eorum, & dixit homini qui habebat manum aridam: Surge, & sta in medio. Ille vero surgens stetit. Dixit igitur eis Iesus: Interrogabo vos quiddam: Licet ne Sabbatis benefacere, an malefacere? hominem seruare, an perdere? Et cum eos omnes circumspexisset, ait homini: Extende manum tuam. Ille autem ita fecit: & restituta est manus eius sana, sicut altera. Ipsi autem repleti sunt amentia, & colloquebantur inter se, quid nam facerent Iesu.
units.tr: It happened on another Sabbath also that he entered the synagogue and taught. And there was a man there whose right hand was withered. The scribes and Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find an accusation against him. But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man who had the withered hand, "Rise up and stand in the midst." And he arose and stood. Then Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one thing: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do evil? To save life, or to destroy it?" And when he had looked round on them all, he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And he did so, and his hand was restored, as sound as the other. But they were filled with madness, and talked among themselves what they might do to Jesus.

units.la: ETsi Iesum Christum Pharisaei & Scribae multis criminibus grauarint, quibus illum populo inuisum facere & in capitis periculum adducere conati sunt, praecipuè tamen inter illa fere fuit Sabbati prophanatio, quam illi prae aliis multoties exprobratam & publicè obiectam fuisse Euangelistae scribunt. Quod ideo factum fuit, quòd superstitiosam huius diei obseruationem vulgo ita per suaserant, vt impius putaretur & quouis supplicio dignus, qui illo opus aliquod quantumuis exiguum & leuiculum fecisset. Ideò Christus non minori studio hoc agit, vt non solùm se excusct, verùmetiam publico errori medeatur, & populum infelicem rectius instituat. Nuper ergo docuit, Sabbatum propter hominem institutum esse, & proinde neminem, qui in necessitate constitutus sit, salutem suam propter hoc negligere debere. At nunc alia historia subiicitur, qua amplius ostendit, Sabbati religionem non obstare, quò minus in proximum quoque beneficiemus, si ita res postulat: imò hoc proprium Sabbati opus esse, vt proximo laboranti aut periclitanti opem feramus, & quaecunque alia sunt verae pietatis officia obeamus. In qua tractatione obseruari debet, hoc ipsum ad omnia externa debere referri, ne dum his nimium addicti simus, ea negligamus, quae vel nostrae vel aliorum saluti seruiunt.
units.tr: Although the Pharisees and scribes burdened Jesus Christ with many charges, by which they tried to make him hateful to the people and bring him into danger of his life, the chief of these was the profanation of the Sabbath, which the evangelists write was often thrown in his face and publicly laid against him before others. This happened because they had so persuaded the common people of a superstitious observance of this day that anyone who did any work, however small and trivial, on it was thought impious and deserving of any punishment. Therefore Christ takes up this matter with no less care, so that he not only excuses himself but also remedies the public error and instructs the unhappy people more rightly. Recently, then, he taught that the Sabbath was instituted for man, and therefore that no one who is placed in necessity ought to neglect his own safety on that account. But now another story is added, which shows more fully that the religion of the Sabbath does not stand in the way of doing good to our neighbour also, if the situation requires it. Indeed, it is the proper work of the Sabbath to bring help to a neighbour who is in labour or in danger, and to perform whatever other duties of true piety there are. In this discussion we must observe that this very thing must be referred to all external matters, so that, while we are too devoted to them, we do not neglect those things which serve either our own salvation or that of others.

units.la: Praemittitur autem tractationis istius occasio, quam ipse Christus singulari studio quaesiisse videtur. Nam mox sequenti Sabbato iterum Synagogam ingreditur, & eorum quidem, qui prius factum ipsius improbissimè calumniati fuerant. Est hoc magnum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quae nobis etiam inuitis, aut saltem aliud agentibus, pro nostra salute excubat: cuius studij exempla innumera in nobis ipsis quotidie experimur. Hic vero in primis memorabile est, quòd etsi in Synagogis hostes Christi acerrimi regnarent, & sibi ab illis vbique insidias struisciret, non tamen à coetibus illis abhorruit, neque populum sua doctrina ideo fraudandum esse putauit. Soletur hoc nos aduersus impiorum deploratam audaciam atque impietatem, ne hanc nobis apud Deum fraudi fore putemus. Vt enim prudens pater etiamsi filios aliquos propter incurabilem contumaciam abdicet et è domo eijciat, alios tamen, qui officium faciunt, non modo non negligit, sed potius teneriori amoris affectu complectitur, vt quem ex illorum abdicatione dolorem animo concepit, horum consuetudine leniat atque mitiget: ita Deus impios quidem & desperatae rebellionis homines dignis supplicijs mulctat, interea vero suorum rationem habet, & eò uberiori gratia eos dignatur, quos in suo culru constantiores esse cernit. Neminem ergo vel impiorum multitudo offendere, vel Dei eos punientis seueritas terrere debet, quò minus hunc colat & obseruet. Semper enim ratum erit, quod Isaias pronuntiauit: Dicite iusto quod bonum, siquidem fructu studiorum suorum fruetur; Vae impio malo, quoniam secundum opera manuum suarum rependetur ei. Isa.3.
units.tr: Now the occasion of this discussion is introduced, which Christ himself seems to have sought with particular care. For on the very next Sabbath he enters the synagogue again, and among those who had previously most wickedly slandered what he did. This is a great proof of divine goodness, which watches over our salvation even when we are unwilling, or at least busy with other things; we experience countless examples of this care in ourselves every day. But here it is especially worth remembering that, although the bitterest enemies of Christ ruled in the synagogues, and everywhere laid snares for him, he did not shrink from those assemblies, nor did he think that the people ought therefore to be deprived of his teaching. Let this console us against the despairing audacity and impiety of the ungodly, lest we think that it will be a disadvantage to us before God. For just as a prudent father, even if he disowns some sons for their incurable obstinacy and casts them out of the house, does not neglect the others who do their duty, but embraces them with a more tender affection, so that he may soothe and mitigate by their company the grief he has conceived in his mind from the disowning of the others, so God indeed punishes the ungodly, men of hopeless rebellion, with due punishments; meanwhile he takes account of his own, and honours with the richer grace those whom he sees to be more constant in his way. Therefore neither the multitude of the ungodly should offend anyone, nor the severity of God punishing them should frighten anyone from worshipping and observing him. For what Isaiah declared will always stand: "Tell the righteous that it shall be well with him, for he shall eat the fruit of his doings. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for the reward of his hands shall be given him." Isa. 3.

units.la: At non frustra quaerit occasionem Christus, qua & hostes magis quam antea confutat, & populum de vera Sabbati obseruatione instituit. Inuenit enim in Synagoga hominem, cuius dextera manus exaruerat, vt humana ope aut remedio naturali restitui non posset. Ita nobis quoq; si officio fungi velimus, bene agendi occasiones nunquam deerunt. Solet enim eas nobis offerre Deus, & simul aures nobis vellicat, vt quid nobis facto opus sit cogitemus. Est igitur inexcusabilis eorum ignauia, qui se non habere aiunt quod agant. Ita enim suo sese indicio produnt, quòd aut vocationem suam nunquam adhuc rectè intra animum suum expenderint, aut aliorum fortunam minimè curent: quorum hoc à charitate Christi ana alienissimum, illud verò animi plus quàm hebetis et osci tantis est argumentum. Et vt non sit, in quo aliquis tuam operam requirat, semper tamen occurrit de rebus tuis cogitandi occasio, vt iam de precibus, de verbi Dei meditatione, de publica salutis cura nihil dicamus. Vidit hoc Scipio, alienus à Christiana philosophia, qui dicere solebat, nunquam se minus esse otiosum, quàm cum esset otiosus: nimirum quòd otio et vacatione à laboribus ad honestas & reipub. vtiles cogitationes vteretur. Quò & alter ille respexit, qui aiebat, praestat otiosum esse quàm nihil agere. Quae ideo commemoramus, vt Christianos homines suae socordiae atque ignauiae pudeat, qua plerique hodie altùm dormiunt, cùm passim & bene agendi occasiones & pericula occurrant, quae nos excitare possent, nisi cum pietate sensum quoq; communem exuissemus.
units.tr: But Christ does not seek the occasion in vain: by it he refutes his enemies more than before, and instructs the people in the true observance of the Sabbath. For in the synagogue he found a man whose right hand had withered, so that it could not be restored by human help or natural remedy. So also for us, if we wish to perform our duty, opportunities for doing good will never be lacking. For God is accustomed to offer them to us, and at the same time to tug at our ears, so that we may consider what needs to be done by us. Therefore the idleness of those who say that they have nothing to do is inexcusable. For by this they betray themselves: either they have never yet rightly weighed their calling in their own mind, or they care not at all for the fortunes of others. The first is most alien from the charity of Christ, the second is proof of a mind more than dull and drowsy. And even if there is no one from whom your help is sought, there is always an occasion to think about your own affairs; not to mention prayer, meditation on the Word of God, and public care for salvation. Scipio saw this, although he was a stranger to Christian philosophy; he used to say that he was never less idle than when he was idle, namely because in his leisure and freedom from labours he made use of thoughts that were honourable and useful to the commonwealth. To this also that other man alluded, who said that it is better to be idle than to do nothing. We mention these things so that Christian people may be ashamed of their carelessness and sloth, by which very many today sleep soundly, although on every side both opportunities for doing good and dangers present themselves which could rouse us, unless we had also cast off common sense together with piety.

units.la: Sed quia haec alterius loci sunt, nunc Pharisaeos & scribas videamus, qui Christum obserua- uisse dicuntur, num die Sabbati homine curaturus esset. Sciebant enim illum quibusuis obuijs opem ferre, & vel eo ipso eius innocentiae testimonium ferunt, & suam improbitatem produnt: quando ex eo, quod laudem merebatur, ipsum accusandi occasionem insidiosè captant. Neque illum tacitè modò observaruut, sed cùm ille non nihil cunctaretur, ipsi (vt Matthæus scribit) priores quæstionem ea de re moverunt, qua eum in nassam pertraherent. Elucet in eo magna improbitas cum impudenti temeritate coniuncta. Nuper enim in eiusdem argumenti disputatione ab illo vicii non habuerunt quod respondérent, & in multis alijs congressibus eius sapientiam iam pridem experti fuerant. Attamen certamen instaurant, & ideo maiori cum impietate faciunt, quòd eadem opera miseri illius hominis salutem impedire conantur, cuius ipsos miserari, & pro quo apud Christum intercedere decebat. At neque prioris ignominiæ recordatio, neque calamitosi illius miseria moventur, quos avaritiæ & ambitionis affectus ita excæcaverat, vt nihil non sibi adversus eum licere putent, quem quæstui ipsorum & honori obstare sciebant. Sunt huius generis infinita exempla, quorum omnium hic nobis vsus esse debet, vt discamus quanta sit vis avaritiæ & ambitionis, & quàm male sibi ipsis prospiciant, qui illis indulgent. In repub. certè nullam nocentiorem pestem esse, Pharaonis, Saulis, Absolomi, Syllæ, Marij, Iulij, Pompeij & similium exemplis docemur. In ecclesia autem nihil sanum & integrum consistere potest, quàm primùm Sirenes illæ eorum animos excæcant, qui toti populo pietatis & modestiæ magistri esse debebant. Possem hic quoque exempla omnis generis proferre, sed veteribus minimè opus est, quando non sine nostro malo experimur, quàm parum de illis sperari debeat, qui religionis & ecclesiæ prætextu ad quæstum & honorem privatum abutuntur. Solent illi in umbratili modò iustitia hærere, & interea securi eç negligunt, quæ præcipua sunt cultus diuini capita. Quòd si ab aliquo liberius arguantur, & existimationem suam in periculum venire videant, mox in furorem versi nihil non faciunt, quo illam defendi posse confidunt. At simul artibus vtuntur, quibus conatum suum astutè celant, quasi pro Dei gloria pugnent, quando suas res agunt, & doctrinam veritatis cum vniuerso cultu extinguere student.
units.tr: But because these matters belong to another place, let us now look at the Pharisees and scribes, who are said to have watched Christ to see whether he would heal the man on the Sabbath day. For they knew that he brought help to whoever met him, and they bear witness to his innocence by this very fact, and reveal their own wickedness, since they snatch at an occasion of accusing him from what deserved praise. Nor did they merely watch him in silence, but when he hesitated somewhat, they themselves (as Matthew writes) first raised the question about this matter, by which they might draw him into a net. In this there shines great wickedness joined with shameless rashness. For recently, in a dispute about the same matter, they had no answer to give him, and they had long since experienced his wisdom in many other encounters. Yet they renew the contest, and do so with all the greater impiety because at the same time they try to hinder the salvation of that unhappy man, for whom they ought to have pitied him and interceded with Christ. But neither the memory of their earlier disgrace nor the misery of that wretched man moves them; the desires of greed and ambition had so blinded them that they think they may do anything against him whom they knew to stand in the way of their gain and their honour. There are countless examples of this kind, and from all of them we ought to profit here, so that we may learn how great is the power of greed and ambition, and how badly they provide for themselves who indulge them. Certainly we are taught by the examples of Pharaoh, Saul, Absalom, Sulla, Marius, Julius, Pompey and the like that in the commonwealth there is no more harmful plague. In the Church, however, nothing sound and whole can stand, as soon as those Sirens blind the minds of those who ought to have been teachers of piety and modesty to the whole people. I could bring forward examples of every kind here too, but there is no need of old ones, since we experience to our cost, and not without harm, how little should be hoped from those who, under the pretext of religion and the Church, abuse them for gain and private honour. They are accustomed to cling to a justice that is merely for show, and meanwhile they neglect with confidence the chief heads of divine worship. But if someone argues against them rather freely, and they see their reputation coming into danger, straightway, turned to fury, they do whatever they trust will defend it. At the same time they use arts by which they cleverly conceal their attempt, as if they were fighting for the glory of God, when they are pursuing their own affairs and striving to extinguish the doctrine of truth together with all worship.

units.la: Cæterum non latent Christum hostium suorum insidiæ, qui in præsenti quoque istorum cogitationes cognitas habuisse scribitur, quas ita arguit, vt in ipsorum contumeliam redundet, quod illi aduersus eum instituerant, simulq; suam de Sabbato doctrinam amplius illustret atque confirmet. Solet hoc accidere veritatis hostibus, vt dum in cælum expuunt seipsos contaminent, & dum Solis lucem extinguere conantur, in suis illis tenebris, quas ipsi sibi offuderunt, seipsos omnium risui atque ludibrio exponant. Minimè ergo eiusmodi hominum conatibus nos offendi aut terreri decet, sed potius Christum imitari, qui admodum graviter causam suam agit. Nam primò hominem surgere & in medium cœtum prodire, ibique consistere iubet: ita nimirum omnium mentes in diligentem rei huius considerationem excitans. Deinde quæstionem aliam ipsis opponit, dicens: Licet ne Sabbatis benefacere, an malefacere? hominem seruare an perdere? Quibus verbis contraria inter se confert, vt facilius convincere & captos tenere possit, quos anguillæ instar per omnes rimas elabi sciebat. Beneficia enim prohibere inexcusabilis impudentiæ erat, at eadem differre saltem velle non aliud erat, quàm Sabbatum in otium ignauum atque inutile convertere. Et quia satis noverat non tam impudentes esse, qui Sabbato malefaciendum alicui esse dicerent, expositionis loco alterum membrum subijcit, An hominem seruare aut perdere licitum putent? Perdit enim, non modò qui vim alicui facit & malum dat, verùmetiam qui opem laboranti negat, aut illam saltem differt, cùm absque mora eam ferre possit. Intelligunt hoc illi, & proinde intra animos suos conniti tacent, tacendo autem suam produnt malitiam, quando fateri nolunt quod licitum & sanctum esse non ignorabant. Circunfert ergo oculos Dominus, & illis partim irascitur, partim condolet, quòd homines in tanta apud omnes existimatione constitutos & qui legis scientiam profitebantur, tam excæcatos & recordes esse cerneret. Itaque cum iusta ira bonitatis & mansuetudinis suæ temperamentum coniungit, vt offendat quàm facilè sit erga eos, qui cum ipso in gratiam redire ferio cupiunt. Adhæc suo exemplo docet, iram freno coercendam esse etiam tunc, quando eius causas graues & iustas habemus. Nisi enim id fiat, affectus vehementia abrepti ea desiginamus, quorum nos paulò postea pudet atque pænitet. Proderit autem, si moram interponamus, vt interea flamma illa vehementior subsidat & ex ea accensus ardor remittat. Meritò igitur laudatur Architæ Tarentini dictum, qui villico ob agros negligentius cultos iratus dixisse fertur: Meritò de te supplicium sumerem, nisi iratus essem. Cui simile est Platonis ad seruum, qui deliquerat: Age Dijs gratias, nam nisi iratus essem, te concidissem. Habuerunt ergo philosophi quoque animis suis inscriptam Apostoli sententiam, Ira viri non operatur iustitiam, & proinde iustam quoque vltionem putarunt differri debere, donec ardor ille deferbuerit. Nam quae nostrae naturae vitiositas est, in iis etiam affectibus modum excedimus, qui per se bonifunt, nisi eos aut mora aut alia aliqua ratione temperemus. Vbi etiam cumprimis vtile fuerit communem omnibus humanae naturae miseriam in mentem revocare. Eius enim consideratio mox admonebit, non debere nos alicui propter ea impotentius irasci, quae in nos quoque cadere possunt. At quoad Christum, hic quidem eiusmodi rationibus in frananda ira sua minime opus habuit, cum qui ipsa iustitia est, modum excedere non posset, paterni autem favoris argumentum fuit, quod hostium caecitate, quam illis non multo post exitij causam fore sciebat, tantopere afficitur. Et quia incurabiles erant, ad miserum illum conuersus ait: Extende manum tuam, quod cum ille fecisset, mox ea restituta est sana, sicuti altera: & sic ipso facto docet Christus, quod illi verbis fateri noluerunt, licitum videlicet esse Sabbato ea facere, quae proximi salutem adiuuant. Apud Matthaeum tamen hoc ipsum argumento probat, quod ab exemplo communi & quotidiano petit, quod nimirum Sabbato liceat ouem aut bouem in puteum sine fouea delapsum extrahere: Vnde colligit, praepositos religiosos esse, qui hominem perire aut periclitari sinant, propter quem pecora omnia creata sunt, & cuius imperio tota haec mundi machina necessario subijcitur.
units.tr: Yet Christ is not unaware of the plots of his enemies. It is recorded that he knew their thoughts even on this occasion, and he so exposed them that what they had devised against him turned to their own shame, and at the same time his teaching about the Sabbath was made clearer and more firmly established. It usually happens to the enemies of the truth that, while they spit at heaven, they defile themselves, and while they try to extinguish the light of the sun, they expose themselves, in the very darkness they have spread around themselves, to the laughter and mockery of everyone. We ought therefore not to be offended or frightened by the attempts of such men, but rather to imitate Christ, who conducts his case with great seriousness. For first he orders the man to stand up, come forward into the middle of the assembly, and stand there, thereby evidently stirring the minds of all to a careful consideration of the matter. Then he puts another question to them: "Is it lawful to do good on the Sabbath, or to do evil? To save a man's life, or to destroy it?" In these words he sets opposites side by side, so that he might more easily convict them and hold them fast, since he knew they would slip through every crack like eels. For to forbid doing good was a shameless impudence, while to put it off, even merely to wish to put it off, was nothing other than turning the Sabbath into idle and useless leisure. And since he knew well that they were not so shameless as to say that harm should be done to someone on the Sabbath, he adds, by way of explanation, the other clause: "Do they think it lawful to save a man's life, or to destroy it?" For a person destroys not only when he uses violence against someone and inflicts harm, but also when he refuses help to one who is suffering, or at least defers it, when he could bring it at once without delay. They understood this, and therefore they kept silent, holding their peace within their own minds; but by their silence they betrayed their malice, since they were unwilling to confess what they were not unaware was lawful and holy. The Lord therefore looks around at them, and partly is angry, partly grieves, because he saw that men held in such high esteem by all, and who professed knowledge of the law, were so blinded and dull of heart. Thus he joins the tempering of his goodness and gentleness to his just anger, so that he might show how readily he is disposed toward those who desire earnestly to be reconciled with him. Moreover, by his own example he teaches that anger must be restrained by the bridle even when we have serious and just causes for it. For unless this is done, carried away by the vehemence of passion, we act on things for which we are soon ashamed and sorry. It will be helpful, however, to interpose a delay, so that meanwhile that flame may subside more violently and the ardour kindled by it may abate. Rightly, therefore, is the saying of Archytas of Tarentum praised, who, angry with a farmer for fields carelessly tended, is said to have said: "I would rightly exact punishment from you, if I were not angry." Similar is Plato's saying to a slave who had done wrong: "Go and thank the gods, for if I were not angry, I would have cut you down." The philosophers therefore also had inscribed in their minds the saying of the Apostle, "The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God," and so they thought that even just vengeance ought to be deferred until that heat had cooled. For it is a fault of our nature that we exceed the measure even in those affections which are good in themselves, unless we temper them by delay or by some other means. Here it is especially useful to call to mind the misery common to all human nature. For the consideration of this will soon remind us that we ought not to be angry immoderately with anyone for things which may also befall us. But as for Christ, he indeed had no need of such reasons to restrain his anger, since he who is justice itself could not exceed the measure; yet it was a sign of his Father's favour that he was so moved by the blindness of his enemies, which he knew would soon be the cause of their ruin. And because they were incurable, he turned to the unfortunate man and said, "Stretch out your hand." When he had done so, it was at once restored, sound like the other. Thus by the deed itself Christ teaches what they would not confess in words, namely that it is lawful on the Sabbath to do those things which help the salvation of a neighbour. In Matthew, however, he proves this same point by an argument drawn from a common and everyday example: that it is lawful on the Sabbath to pull out a sheep or an ox that has fallen into a pit without a ditch. From this he concludes that those are the ones who are truly religious who allow a man to perish or be endangered, the man for whose sake all animals were created, and to whose command this whole machinery of the world is necessarily subject.

units.la: Quoniam autem inscripturis Sabbati praeceptum vetustissimum est, & tam multa de hoc contentio Christo cum suis aduersarijs intercessit, quaedam de illo nobis fusius dicenda erunt, vt quid nam illud sit intelligamus, in quo item verus eius vsus consistat, quibus denique modis prophanetur. Sabbati vox quietem aut vacationem ab opere significat. Hic autem pro die septimo sumitur, quem Deus quieti huic destinauit, & (vt scripturae loquuntur) sibi sanctum esse voluit. Estque huius obseruatio antiquissima, eo quod in ipsa rerum creatione Dei exemplo instituta, & tandem peculiari praecepto confirmata fuit. Causae eius tres adduci possunt, quibus eiusdem vsus quoque legitimus & verus continetur. Prima politica & oeconomica est, & corporibus seruit, quorum vires laboribus fatigatas & exhaustas refici oportet. Et huc facit, quod in Decalogo seruorum, ancillarum & iumentorum Deus meminit, & alibi dissere monet, vt horum ratio habeatur, ne nimijs & indefinitentibus laboribus succumbant. Nam in Exodo Cap.23.ait: Sex diebus facies opera tua, septimo autem die quiesces, vt quiescat bos tuus, & asinus tuus, & vt respiret filius ancillae tuae, & peregrinus. Et rursus Deuteronom.quinto Capite: Non facies die septimo vllum opus, neque tu, neque filius tuus, neque filia tua, neque seruus tuus, aut ancilla tua, neque bos tuus vel asinus tuus, aut vlla ex iumentis tuis, neq; peregrinus qui est intra portas tuas: vt quiescat seruus tuus & ancilla tua, sicut tu. Et meminerris, quod & tu seruus fueris in terra Aegypti, & eduxerit te Dominus Deus tuus illinc, &c. Secundam causam instituti Sabbati ecclesiasticam dicere possumus, eo quod circa Dei cultum & publica siue externa religionis exercitia versatur. Quia enim inter Iudaeos lex publice doceri, & sacra exerceri debebant, certum diem esse oportuit, quo ad coetus sacros simul omnes conuenirent, & eiusdem legis disciplina sacrorumque eorundem vsu testarentur, se eiusdem Dei cultores, fidei eiusdem professores, & ecclesiae eiusdem membra esse. Nam erit vtile et pium esset ista quotidie fieri, non tamen eadem omnium est conditio, vt id sine rerum suarum iactura facere possint. At si singulis libertas detur tempus deligendi pro suo arbitrio, mox coetus sacros minui, & confusionem in ecclesia oriri videremus. Quia ergo Deus omnia rite & ordine decoro atque honesto fieri vult, tam loca quam tempora certa esse necesse est, quae sacris vsibus destinata sint. Tertia Sabbati causa sublimior & vere spiritualis est, atque ad aeternam hominis salutem propius pertinet. Illo enim typo spiritualis illa quies adumbratur, qua ab operibus carnis & mundi feriari debemus, vt Deus suo verbo & spiritu in nobis operari possit. Et hoc praecipuum est, quod in Sabbati obseruatione passim prophetae vrgent, ne hanc in ignauo otio aut superstitiosa ab omnibus operibus cessatione constitere putarent, sed ita corpore quiescerent, vt animos totos circa diuinae voluntatis meditationem & vitae sanctae officia occupatos haberent, adeoque operum suorum & anteactae vitae recordatione seipsos ad poenitentiam & pietatem exercerent. Ideo Sabbatum sanctificare, idest, totum Deo consecrare debebant, & idem hoc signum esse dicitur, quòd Deus Israelem sanctifi-cet, & sibi in peculium vindicet. Quæ causa est, quòd prophetæ, quoties de Dei cultu prophanato et fœdere violato populum accusant, in primis fere de Sabbatorum prophanatione queruntur. Ipsius ergo præcipuus & proprius Sabbati is est, quem Isaias his verbis comprehendit: Si auerteris pedem tuum Sabbato, quo minus facias tuam voluntatem in die sancto meo, & vocaueris Sabbatum delitias ad sanctificandum Dominum gloriosum, & glorificaueris eum, vt non facias vias tuas, neque inuenias tuam voluntatem ad loquendum sermonem: tunc delectaberis in Domino, & ego vehàm te super excelsa terræ, & faciam te comedere hæreditatem Iacob patris tui. Isa.58.
units.tr: Since the commandment concerning the Sabbath is the most ancient in the Scriptures, and since there was so much contention about it between Christ and his adversaries, some things must be said about it more fully, so that we may understand what it is, in what its true use consists, and finally in what ways it is profaned. The word Sabbath signifies rest or cessation from work. Here it is taken for the seventh day, which God appointed for this rest and (as the Scriptures speak) willed to be holy to himself. Its observance is most ancient, because it was instituted by the example of God in the very creation of things, and at last confirmed by a particular precept. Three causes of it may be given, by which its lawful and true use is also contained. The first is political and domestic, and it serves bodies, whose strength, worn out and exhausted by labours, ought to be restored. To this belongs the fact that in the Decalogue God mentions male servants, female servants and beasts of burden, and elsewhere he admonishes that their interests be taken into account, so that they do not sink under excessive and unending labours. For in Exodus chapter 23 he says: "Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest, so that your ox and your ass may rest, and that the son of your handmaid and the stranger may be refreshed." And again in Deuteronomy chapter 5: "On the seventh day you shall do no work, neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your ass, nor any of your beasts, nor the stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as you do. And remember that you too were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out from there," and so on. The second cause of the institution of the Sabbath we may call ecclesiastical, because it concerns the worship of God and the public or external exercises of religion. For since among the Jews the law had to be taught publicly and sacred rites performed, it was necessary that there be a fixed day on which all might come together to the holy assemblies, and by the practice of that law and the use of those same sacred rites bear witness that they were worshippers of the same God, professors of the same faith, and members of the same church. For although it would be useful and pious for these things to be done every day, yet not everyone is in a position to do so without loss of his own affairs. But if liberty were given to each to choose a time at his own discretion, we would soon see the holy assemblies diminished and confusion arising in the church. Because God wills that all things be done properly, in fitting order and decency, both places and times must of necessity be fixed and set apart for sacred uses. The third cause of the Sabbath is more lofty and truly spiritual, and pertains more closely to the eternal salvation of man. For by that type is shadowed that spiritual rest, from which we ought to cease from the works of the flesh and of the world, so that God may work in us by his word and Spirit. And this is the chief point which the prophets everywhere press in the observance of the Sabbath: that they should not suppose it to consist in idle leisure or in a superstitious cessation from all works, but that they should rest in body in such a way that their minds are wholly occupied with meditation on the divine will and the duties of a holy life, and by recalling their works and their past life they might exercise themselves in repentance and godliness. Therefore they ought to sanctify the Sabbath, that is, to consecrate it wholly to God; and the same thing is said to be the sign that God sanctifies Israel and claims it for his own possession. This is why the prophets, whenever they accuse the people of profaning the worship of God and violating the covenant, complain above all about the profaning of the Sabbaths. The principal and proper meaning of the Sabbath is therefore the one which Isaiah comprehends in these words: "If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath, so as not to do your own pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight, to sanctify the Lord glorious, and glorify him, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own will, nor speaking your own word: then you shall delight yourself in the Lord, and I will make you ride upon the high places of the earth, and I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father." Isaiah 58.

units.la: Et ista quidem olim de Sabbati obseruatione veteribus mandata fuerunt, quæ si ad nos transferas, non minus illa nobis conuenire patebit. Nam etiam hodie otio & quiete opus est, qua vires defessas recreemus, & animum quoque à curis rei domesticæ reuocemus. Ne verò otium illud alicuius mali occasio fiat & libidinis fomentum sit, totum Deo consecretur necesse est. Requiruntur ergo hic externa pietatis exercitia, vt nimirum in cœtus sacros veniamus, in verbo suo nobis loquentem Dominum audiamus, precibus publicis atque priuatis opem eius imploremus. Sacramentis vtamur cum solenni gratiarum actione, adhæc vitam omnem examinemus, & quod perperam à nobis factum est corrigamus, feriemur denique ab operibus huius seculi, locum autem demus spiritui sancto, vt ea hic in nobis operetur, quæ ad Dei gloriam & tam nostram quàm aliorum salutem faciant. Apparet ergo eius diei religionem non obstare, quò minus proximo in necessitate aliqua constituto opem feramus, aut quocunque alio opere pio & sancto Deum glorificemus. Imò vt hoc fiat, miraculo præsenti Christus docet. Suffinet enim miser iste de quo hic agitur, typum omnium nostrum, qui peccati ex Adamo contractinoxa eò vsq; debilitati sumus, vt dexteras manus aridas habeamus, id est, vt ex nobis ipsis nihil boni possimus, & (vt Paulus ait) ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus. Estque malum hoc immedicabile, neque vlla arte aut remedio humano curari potest. Solus Christus huic medetur, vt alibi quoque diximus, dum peccata expiat, & ex verbo suo renatos nouis viribus instruit, quibus faciamus quæ Deo probantur. Huc autem Sabbato dexteram suam restituit, vt ostendat illo die potissimùm nos ad pietatis officia & opera verè bona accingi debere, de quibus modò diximus. Et hoc Sabbatum illud verè Christianum est, cuius finis & præmium erit æterna quies, qua olim pijfruentur, quando abolita hac mundi machina sabbatum cum sabbato continuabitur, & Deus omnia erit in omnibus. Et debent quidem in istis sese iugiter exercere Christiani homines vt Sabbatum perpetuò agant, & à malis quidem operibus ferientur, Deo autem viuant: attamen quia multis etiam huius vitæ negotijs occupati sumus, quæ vt plurimùm animos à feria cœlestium meditatione abstrahunt, certum diem exercitijs hisce destinatum esse non minus hodie, quàm olim, necesse est.
units.tr: These things indeed were commanded of old to the ancients concerning the observance of the Sabbath, and if you transfer them to ourselves, it will be plain that they apply to us no less. For even today we need rest and quiet, by which we may refresh our worn-out strength and also call our minds back from the cares of domestic affairs. But lest that rest become an occasion for some evil and a fuel for lust, it must be wholly consecrated to God. Therefore outward exercises of piety are required here: namely, that we come to holy assemblies, hear the Lord speaking to us in his Word, and implore his help by public and private prayers. We should partake of the sacraments with solemn thanksgiving; besides this, we should examine our whole life and correct what we have done amiss. Finally, we should refrain from the works of this age and give place to the Holy Spirit, that he may work in us those things which tend to the glory of God and to our own salvation and that of others. It therefore appears that the sanctity of that day does not prevent us from bringing help to a neighbour in some necessity, or from glorifying God by any other good and holy work. Indeed, Christ teaches by a present miracle that this should be done. For that wretched man of whom we are speaking bears the image of all of us, who through the guilt of sin contracted from Adam have been so weakened that we have withered hands; that is, that of ourselves we can do nothing good, and (as Paul says) are not even fit to think. This evil is incurable, and cannot be healed by any human art or remedy. Christ alone heals it, as we have said elsewhere, by expiating sins and by equipping those reborn through his Word with new strength, by which we may do what is pleasing to God. Now on the Sabbath he restored his hand, to show that on that day above all we ought to apply ourselves to the duties of piety and to truly good works, of which we have just spoken. And this is the truly Christian Sabbath, whose end and reward will be eternal rest, which the godly will one day enjoy, when this machine of the world is abolished and the Sabbath will continue with the Sabbath, and God will be all in all. Christian people ought indeed to exercise themselves continually in these things, so as to keep a perpetual Sabbath, and they will be restrained from evil works and live to God. Nevertheless, since we are occupied with many affairs of this life, which for the most part draw our minds away from the heavenly meditation of the holiday, it is no less necessary today than it was of old that a fixed day be set apart for these exercises.

units.la: Quòd si quæras, cur septimum diem potius quàm alium huic rei Deus consecrauerit, & annon Sabbatum quoque, vt & aliæ ceremoniæ in Christi morte abolitæ sint? ego quæstiones eiusmodi superuacaneas esse arbitror. Nam quoad primam, eadem opera quærere poteras, cur in quinque solum digitos manum tibi Deus fecerit? aut cur binos tibi oculos & binas aures dederit? Sufficiat nobis Dei voluntas, quam & proprio exemplo & præcepto diserto commendauit. Et illius agnoscamus bonitatem, qui cùm pluribus ferijs nos grauare, totumq; vitæ nostræ tempus sacris exercitijs vendicare posset, nostrorum tamen negotiorum rationem habuit: septimum autem diem nobis sanctum fecit, vt huius recordatione nos ad sui exempli imitationem magis excitaret. Quoad alteram quæstionem, quod in Sabbato Iudæorum ceremoniale fuit, id per Christum abrogatū esse fateor: at minimè abrogata est quies illa sancta, qua nobis ob causas supra commemoratas opus esse hucusq; demonstrauimus. Ideo Apostoli (vt ex scriptis eorum & patrum veterum traditionibus apparet) ne eccle sia cum Iudæorum superstitionibus aliquid commune haberet, otium illud sacrum in sequentè diem transtulerunt, qui Dominicus dictus est, vel quòd illo Christus à mortuis resuscitatus humani generis redemptionem perfecit, vel vt ipso nomine docerent illum totum Domino consecratum esse debere. At idem non tantum sibi permiserunt, vt ferias vel plures instituerent, vel à Deo præceptam diei septimi obseruatione in decimum aut quemcunq; alium extenderent. Horū igitur exemplo nos instituere conflere conuenit, ne sub libertatis Christianae praetextu in illis ludamus, quae Deus certa cum ratione instituit, & illa tandem in licentiam degeneret, quae ut confusionem gignit, ita animos tandem ab omni religione alienat. Neq; hic mihi quisquam Paulum obijciat, qui Galatas damnat, quòd dies obseruarent, & qui dies festos inter umbras rerum futurarum recenset. Iam ante enim diximus, quid in Sabbato abrogatum sit, & quod eiusdem obseruatio hodie non minus quàm olim necessaria sit, cum ijsdem causis, quibus olim Iudaei, urgeamur. Non ergo piam feriandi rationem Paulus reprehendit, sed superstitionem, qua nonnulli detenti cum Iudaeis in ignauo otio, & non tam superstitiosa quàm ridicula Sabbati obseruatione Dei cultum & salutis meritum collocabant. Et credibile est, plerosq; eorum eo usque progressos fuisse, ut aut Sabbatum Iudaeorum diei Dominico praeferrent, aut utrumque colendo ferias augerent. Ista ergo Apostoli merito accusarunt, ut & in Ecclesia paci publicae consulerent, & omnium mentes ab externis ad fidem Christi atque cultum spirituali revocarent.
units.tr: But if you ask why God consecrated the seventh day rather than another to this purpose, and whether the Sabbath too was not abolished in Christ's death, as other ceremonies were, I think questions of this kind are superfluous. For as to the first, you might as well ask why God made your hand with only five fingers, or why he gave you two eyes and two ears. Let the will of God suffice for us, which he commended both by his own example and by a plain precept. Let us acknowledge his goodness, who, although he could have burdened us with more days of rest and claimed the whole time of our life for holy exercises, nevertheless took account of our affairs, and made the seventh day holy for us, so that by remembering it he might stir us the more to imitate his example. As to the second question: I grant that what was ceremonial in the Sabbath of the Jews has been abrogated by Christ; but that holy rest, which, for the reasons mentioned above, we have hitherto shown to be necessary for us, has by no means been abrogated. Therefore the Apostles (as appears from their writings and the traditions of the ancient Fathers) transferred that sacred rest to the following day, which is called the Lord's Day, so that the Church might have nothing in common with the superstitions of the Jews; either because on that day Christ rose from the dead and accomplished the redemption of mankind, or so that the very name might teach that the whole day ought to be consecrated to the Lord. Yet they did not permit themselves to institute more holidays, or to extend the observance of the seventh day which God had commanded to the tenth or to any other day. It is therefore fitting that we arrange ourselves by their example, lest under the pretext of Christian liberty we trifle with those things which God instituted with a certain reason, and lest that liberty at last degenerate into licence, which, as it begets confusion, so at last estranges minds from all religion. Nor let anyone object to me here Paul, who condemns the Galatians because they observed days, and who counts festivals among the shadows of things to come. For we have already said what was abrogated in the Sabbath, and that its observance is no less necessary today than it was of old, since we are pressed by the same causes by which the Jews were pressed. Paul therefore does not condemn the pious manner of keeping holiday, but the superstition by which some, held fast with the Jews in idle inactivity, placed the worship of God and the merit of salvation in a Sabbath observance that was not so much superstitious as ridiculous. And it is credible that most of them went so far as either to prefer the Sabbath of the Jews to the Lord's Day, or, by honouring both, to multiply holidays. The Apostles therefore rightly accused these practices, both to provide for public peace in the Church and to recall the minds of all from outward things to the faith of Christ and spiritual worship.

units.la: Itaq; in horum consideratione nobis quoque itaque versandum est, ut abusum omnem diei Dominici sedulo caveamus, qui varius est & multiplex. Peccant enim qui illo non contenti, feriras nouas instituunt, & ita primam praecepti Dominici partem transgrediuntur, qua sex diebus laborare iubemur. Vbi grauior eorum culpa est, qui feriras in Diuorum honorem consecrant, quod ut nullo veteris ecclesiae exemplo probari potest, ita diuinis legibus palam repugnat, qua feriae omnes uni Deo sacras esse iubent, ut poteque ad cultum Dei in primis pertineant. Scimus equidem post Apostolorum tempora pio zelo institutas fuisse Martyrum memorias, ut eorum exemplo ad fidei constantiam & virtutis studium omnes excitarentur. At quia hoc nullo Dei praecepto nitebatur, mox superstitiones peperit infinitas, quibus plerique à vera fide & unius Dei cultu ad idololatriam & Diuorum invocationem adducti fuerunt. Praestat ergo eam simplicitatem retinere, quam nobis in verbo suo Deus praescripsit. Nam quae humani ingenij est ad superstitiones propensio, difficile est illi modum praescribere, si semel à via Domini discedamus. Peccant praeterea, qui diei Dominici obseruatio nem in otio inani consistere putant, quasi Dei cultus sit nihil omnino agere. Et hic quoq; prae aliis erant, qui insuper tetus sacros & à Christo nobis tradita religionis exercitia negligunt. Abutuntur item sabbato, qui totum illum diem auaritiae consecrant, & hac impulsi opera faciunt minimè necessaria, quibus seipsos & familiā omnem fatigant: qui item merces uenales habent, qui rationes suas subducunt, aut (quod à Christiana religione & charitate alienissimum est) debitorum exactione eos contristant, quibus diem hunc Deus quietis & recreationis diem esse voluit. Quid verò de ijs alceamus, qui Domino sacrum diem Bacchò, Veneri, Marti dedicant, dum vel ebriosis comessationibus vacant, vel vestitu petulanti lasciuiunt, scortantur, mœchantur, saltant, vel gladiatoria exercent, & circa ludorum tnrpissimorum spectacula occupantur? Fiunt ista omnia hodie, et si verum fateri liceat, nullo tempore plura & atrociora committuntur flagitia, quàm eo quod totū Deo & pietati impendi debebat. Puniuit hoc olim Deus gravissimè, ut Prophetarum sermones docent, & nos hodie eius iram ubiq; sese exerentem miramur? Discant ergo hæc emendare, qui rebus suis consultum volunt. At quia plerique hic negligentiores sunt, ad magistratus hæc cura in primis pertinet, ut (quod olim Nehemias fecit) suam authoritatem in re maximè necessaria interponant. Fecerunt hoc olim Christiani Imperatores, quorum Leges alibi recitauimus, quae si hodie apud omnes valerent, Deo magis propitio uteremur. Et hæc quidem de Sabbatis modò dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Therefore, in considering these matters, we too must take care to guard diligently against every abuse of the Lord's Day, which is varied and manifold. They sin who, not content with that day, institute new holidays, and so transgress the first part of the Lord's precept, by which we are commanded to labour six days. Their fault is graver who consecrate holidays to the honour of saints; this cannot be proved by any example of the ancient Church, and it openly contradicts the divine laws, which command that all holy days be sacred to the one God, and that they especially pertain to the worship of God. We know indeed that after the time of the Apostles memorials of the martyrs were established out of pious zeal, so that all might be stirred by their example to constancy in the faith and zeal for virtue. But because this rested on no precept of God, it soon gave birth to endless superstitions, by which many were led away from the true faith and the worship of the one God to idolatry and the invocation of saints. It is better, therefore, to keep that simplicity which God has prescribed to us in his Word. For the human mind is prone to superstition, and once we have strayed from the way of the Lord, it is hard to set any limit to it. Moreover, they sin who think that the observance of the Lord's Day consists in idle inactivity, as if the worship of God were to do absolutely nothing. Here too there were some who, beyond this, neglect the holy assemblies and the exercises of religion delivered to us by Christ. They also abuse the Sabbath who devote that whole day to greed, and, driven by this, do works that are by no means necessary, by which they weary themselves and all their household; likewise those who have goods for sale, who reckon up their accounts, or (which is most alien to the Christian religion and charity) who distress by the demanding of debts those for whom God wished this day to be a day of rest and refreshment. But what shall we say of those who dedicate the holy day of the Lord to Bacchus, Venus and Mars, while they give themselves to drunken feastings, or wantonly indulge in wanton dress, whoring, adultery, dancing, or engage in gladiatorial shows and are occupied with the most shameful spectacles of the games? All these things are done today, and, if it is permitted to speak the truth, at no time are more and more atrocious crimes committed than on the day which ought to have been wholly given to God and to piety. Did God once punish this most severely, as the sermons of the Prophets teach, and do we today wonder that his wrath shows itself everywhere? Let those who wish to look to their own welfare learn to amend these things. But since many are rather careless here, this care belongs chiefly to the magistrates, that they (as Nehemiah once did) interpose their authority in a matter that is most necessary. Christian emperors once did this, whose laws we have recited elsewhere; if these were in force among all people today, we would enjoy God's favour more. And let it suffice to have said these things about the Sabbaths for now.

units.la: Reliquum est ut videamus, quomodo Christi doctrinam tanto miraculo confirmatam eius aduersarij acceperint, & quid ille porrò fecerit. Illos amentia repletos, & inter se collocutos fuisse Lucas scribit, quidnam facerent Iesu, Marcus addit, Pharisaeos mox egressos cum Herodianis consultauisse, ut eum perderent. Est hoc incurabilis obstinatiae & extremae impietatis exemplum. Quid enim Christus vel dixit vel fecit, quod mortis supplicio dignum sit? Aut num ipse prior huic facto initium dedit? Nonne ipsi priores disputationem hanc exorsi sunt? Quid verò Christus? Amicè & absq; conuitio de causa hac tota disputauit, homini misero beneficium dedit, eum nō sine miraculo curauit, & non solùm Sabbati verum usum illis ostendit, verumetiam se verum Dei filium & promissum humani generis seruatorem esse demonstrauit. Quid ergo hic reprehensione, nedum supplicio dignum est? Num quòd Sabbato hæc fecit? Atqui hoc non humanum, sed diuinum opus est, neq; aliud ille fecit, quam quòd Pater nunquam non agit, quando vniuersam hanc orbis totius machinam in singula momenta seruat, regit atq; tuetur. Cur ergo Sabbati violati reus agatur, qui Deum tam aperte imitatus est? Sed nihil horū videre possunt, qui auaritia & ambitione excæcati iampi dem Dei metum animo excusserant. Et apparet in illis, quo spiritu agantur, qui hodie etiam intra animos suos conuicti, aperta tamen veritati contradicunt: qui item de perdendis fidus monitoribus consultant, quando de emendatione morum & vitæ cogitandum erat. Est horum magnus numerus hodie inter eos etiam, qui Christiani dici volunt. Sed revera Christi hostes sunt, & olim easdem illi pœnas dabunt, quibus iflorum impietatem ille non multò post multauit.
units.tr: It remains for us to see how Christ's adversaries received his teaching, confirmed by so great a miracle, and what he then did. Luke writes that they were filled with madness and conferred among themselves what they should do to Jesus; Mark adds that the Pharisees, going out at once, took counsel with the Herodians how they might destroy him. This is an example of incurable obstinacy and extreme impiety. For what had Christ said or done that deserved the punishment of death? Or did he himself give the first beginning to this deed? Did they not themselves begin this dispute? And what did Christ do? He discussed the whole matter kindly and without insult, he gave a benefit to a wretched man, he healed him not without a miracle, and he showed them not only the true use of the Sabbath but also demonstrated that he is the true Son of God and the promised Saviour of mankind. Why then is he worthy of rebuke, let alone of punishment? Is it because he did this on the Sabbath? But this is not a human work but a divine one, and he did nothing other than what the Father never ceases to do, when he preserves, governs and sustains this whole machinery of the world at every moment. Why then is he charged as a guilty violator of the Sabbath, when he imitated God so plainly? But those who, blinded by greed and ambition, had long since cast off the fear of God cannot see any of these things. And it is apparent in them by what spirit they are driven, those who even today, though convicted within their own minds, nonetheless contradict the manifest truth; and who likewise take counsel about destroying the faithful monitors, when they ought to be thinking about the correction of morals and life. The number of such people today is large, even among those who wish to be called Christians. But in truth they are Christ's enemies, and they will one day pay the same penalties by which he punished their impiety not long afterwards.

units.la: Cæterùm præstat videre quid isti egerint. Primò amentia replentur, quod mirum videri poterat in iis, qui cum Legis scientiam vitæ etiam morum, grauitatem singularem profitebantur. Sed non mirum est amentia repleri eos, qui suis traditionibus infelicem populum diu captiuum tenuerunt, quando per Christum libertatem restitutam & miserus vires datas esse vident, quibus iugum illud excutiant. Hodie certè hoc vnum male habet Monachos & horum patronos, quòd plerisque iam oculos, aures, manus & pedes esse videant, quibus in Christo nobis collatum æternæ salutis beneficium amplectantur. Deinde exeunt, & animo conceptum furorem dissimulant. Inde mox sibi Herodianos iungunt, homines à sua professione alienissimos, & quos cane & angue peius oderant, cumque his sua de Christo occidendo consilia conferunt. Qui ergo reliquis sanctiores haberi volebant, ii Christum quidem verae sanctimoniae magistrum oderunt, cum Herodianis autem aulico fastu, libidine & quouis alio scelere corruptissimis coniurant. Sunt hi impiorum mores, quòd virus animi interdum celare possunt, clam autem omnia tentant, quæ ad veritatis lucem extinguendam facere videntur. Neque hic eos aliquius flagitij aut sodalitij pudet. Quò magis nos vigilare decet, ne eorum insidijs circumuenti ipsam Veritatem nobis cum in periculum adducamus. Et quàmuis inter dum inter se graribus dissidijs scindantur, nemo tamen ex eo sibi meliorem fortem promittat. Faci lè enim conueniunt impij, si quid aduersus Veritatem tentandum est. Interim neminem terreant eorum conatus. Nam vt Marcus scribit, consultantibus illis Christus ad mare secesserit, & ingens populi multitudo ipsum secuta est: quiq; prius aliquot dies vno in loco substiterat, nunc finitimam regionem omnem Euangelij prædicatione illustrat. Ita vincit Dei filius, & inuito mundo atq; personatis præsulibus triumphat, regniq; sui pomaeria sub crucis vexillo prouehit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth seeing what these men did. First, they are filled with madness, which might have seemed strange in those who professed a unique knowledge of the Law, and even a singular gravity of life. But it is not strange that those are filled with madness who for a long time held an unhappy people captive by their own traditions, when they see that through Christ liberty has been restored and strength given to the wretched to throw off that yoke. Certainly today this alone troubles the monks and their patrons, that they see that for most people eyes, ears, hands and feet are now given, by which they may embrace in Christ the benefit of eternal salvation offered to us. Then they go out, and conceal the fury conceived in their minds. Straightway they join the Herodians to themselves, men most alien to their profession, whom they hated worse than dog or snake, and with them they confer their plans for killing Christ. Those who wished to be regarded as holier than the rest hate Christ, the teacher of true holiness, while they conspire with the Herodians, men thoroughly corrupted by courtly pride, lust and every other kind of wickedness. Such is the character of the impious: they can sometimes hide the poison of their minds, but in secret they attempt everything that seems to serve to extinguish the light of truth. Nor are they ashamed of any crime or any fellowship here. So much the more ought we to be watchful, lest, circumvented by their snares, we bring Truth herself into danger along with ourselves. And although they are sometimes split by serious dissensions among themselves, let no one promise himself a better lot from this. For the wicked agree easily when something is to be attempted against the Truth. Meanwhile let their efforts terrify no one. For, as Mark writes, while they were taking counsel Christ withdrew to the sea, and a great multitude of people followed him; and he who had earlier remained for some days in one place now brightens all the neighbouring region with the preaching of the Gospel. Thus the Son of God conquers, and triumphs over an unwilling world and over masked prelates, and extends the boundaries of his kingdom under the banner of the cross. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVII.
units.tr: HOMILY LVII.

units.la: Factum est autem illis diebus, abijt in montem ad precandum, & pernoctauit precans Deum. Et cum dies ortus esset, aduocauit discipulos suos, & cum ex ipsis elegisset duodecim, quos & apostos nominauit (nempe Simonem, quem etiam nominauit Petrum, & Andreā fratrem eius, Iacobum & Ioannem, Philippum & Bartholomæū, Matthæum & Thomam, Iacobum Alphæi, & Simonem qui vocatur Zelotes, Iudam Iacobi, & Iudam Iscariotem, qui etiam fuit proditor) descendit cum eis stetitq; in loco campestri: turbaq; discipulorum eius & multitudo magna plebis ex tota Iudæa & Hierosolyma, & ex maritima regione Tyri & Sydonis, qui venerant vt audirent eum & sanarentur à morbis suis, & qui torquebantur à spiritibus impuris: et sanabantur.
