Et tota turba studebat eum tangere; quia virtus ab eo exibat, & sanabat omnes.
units.tr: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God. And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples, and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles (namely Simon, whom he also named Peter, and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who is called the Zealot, Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, who was also the traitor). He came down with them and stood in a level place, and the company of his disciples and a great multitude of the people, from all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea-coast of Tyre and Sidon, came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases, and those who were vexed with unclean spirits were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him, for there went virtue out of him and healed them all.

units.la: Memoratu dignum & plenum consolationis est Pauli Apostoli dictum, quo Iesum Christum in mundum venisse testatur, vt peccatores saluos faciat. Verè autem hoc docet, non modo ex eo apparere, quòd semetipsum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, verumetiam quòd quàm diu in terra vixit, rù vixit, assidua doctrina & prædicatione quàm plurimos in veritatis cognitionem adducere stu-duit, neq; in eo vllis laboribus pepercit. Quia verò ipse solus ad hoc non sufficiebat, quoad assumptæ humanitatis modulum, & idem peracto nostræ redemptionis negotio terras relicturus erat, ex disci-pulis aliquos ordinauit, quibus ceu symmysti⁠s aut conseruis vteretur, & qui ipso in cælos subuecto Euangelij doctrinam in toto terrarum orbe diuulgarent. De horum itaq; electione in præsenti agi-tur, quam ita describit Lucas, vt ostendat Christum fidelissimi patris instar nihil eorum prætermi-sisse, quæ ad domus aut familiæ suæ incolumitatem faciunt. Docet præterea exemplum hoc quæ ratio sit ministerij ecclesiastici, quanta eiusdem sit authoritas, & quid in ordinandis ministris potissimum obseruari debeat. Vt tamen ista nostræ cùm institutioni tum consolationi magis seruiant, singulas huius loci partes inspiciemus.
units.tr: A saying of the apostle Paul is worth remembering and full of comfort, in which he testifies that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. And this is truly taught not only by the fact that he gave himself up to death for us, but also because, as long as he lived on earth, he strove by constant teaching and preaching to bring as many people as possible to the knowledge of the truth, and in this he spared no labour. But since he alone was not sufficient for this, as far as the measure of the humanity he had taken on was concerned, and since he was about to leave the earth once the business of our redemption was finished, he appointed some of his disciples, whom he might use as fellow-workers and co-servants, and who, once he had been taken up into heaven, would spread the doctrine of the gospel throughout the whole world. It is the choice of these men that is now under discussion, and Luke describes it in such a way as to show that Christ, like a most faithful father, omitted nothing that pertains to the safety of his household or family. This example also teaches what the nature of the ecclesiastical ministry is, how great its authority is, and what ought above all to be observed in ordaining ministers. But so that these things may serve our instruction and our comfort more, we shall examine the individual parts of this passage.

units.la: Primùm author totius negotij proponitur, vnus solusq; Christus. Vnde colligitur Euangelij mi-nisterium non ex hominibus originè duxisse, sed ab ipso Dei filio esse institutum. Qui enim olim pro-phetas (vt Petrus admonet) suo spiritu donauit, vt huius suggestione excitati de ipso vaticinaren-tur, idem nunc quoq; ex discipulorum numero aliquos selegit, vt verbi sui præcones essent, & etiam hodie spiritus sui dona inter homines distribuit, & alios quidem suæ ecclesiæ dat apostolos, alios Eu-angelistas, alios pastores, alios doctores, vt Paulus in epistola ad Ephesios annotauit. Sunt hæc no-bis diligentius obseruanda, vt intelligamus quanta apud nos esse debeat doctrinæ apostolicæ autho-ritas, & quàm graue eorum scelus sit, qui huic contradicunt. Quia enim Apostolos Christus rerum abs se gestarum præcones, imò testes esse voluit, non in illos modò iniurij sunt, quotquot doctrinam eorum falsi insimulant, verumetiam ipsum Christum extrema ignominia afficiunt. At quia de hoc alibi commodius dicetur, nunc quanta illorum ingratitudo sit obseruemus, qui verbi administros, a-deoq; vniuersum ecclesiæ ministerium contemnunt atq; oderunt, eò quòd per hoc peccata ipsorum ar-guuntur. Esse hoc commune huius mundi vitium, vt cùm totus in malo obrutus iaceat & ex scele-ribus summam capiat voluptatem, eadem tamen argui & accusari nolit; & plerique nō alios acerbio-res hostes se habere arbitrantur, quàm qui fidis correptionibus ipsos in viam salutis reducere fata-gunt. At hic cogitandū erat ministerij huius authorem esse Christum, & huius institutum esse vt spi-ritus sanctus per Euangelij ministros mundū arguat de peccato. Ioan.16. Atqui de illo nihil hostile aut saluti nostræ inimicum suspicari possumus, cùm se totum pro nobis impenderit. Deinde quòd nos ergui & corripi omnino necesse est, tam propter quotidiana delicta, quàm propter innatā nobis stu-piditatem, qua fit vt quæ in omnium ore & oculis sunt ipsi in nobis non animaduertamus. Quod⁠⁠y-num qui nō ofcitanter obseruant, ij facilè intelligunt vix aliud euidentius diuini fauoris argumen-tum esse, quàm quòd nos in exitium ruentes non seueritoribus, vt digni eramus, plagis coercet, sed pa-ternis admonitionibus in viam reuocat. Quòd si ex inimicis hanc vtilitatem captare docuerunt phi-losophi, vt ex illis audiamus, quæ in nobis alij dissimulant aut omnino nō obseruant: quanto magis patienter audiri debent quos Deus humani generis amantissimus nobis monitores constituit? Qui-bus adde, quòd obstrependo nihil proficimus, sed (vt filij contumaces) Dei iram magis prouocamus, & pœnas grauiores nobis accersemus: quod omnium seculorum exempla abunde testantur. Horum consideratio olim supremos Reges & victoriosissimos principes mouit, vt Prophetarum correptio-nes patienter ferrent. At hodie qui ex sece vulgi sunt, Dei Verbo obloqui non verentur, quæ præci-pua malorum nostri seculi causa est.
units.tr: First, the author of the whole business is set before us: one and only Christ. From this it is gathered that the ministry of the gospel did not originate from men, but was instituted by the Son of God himself. For he who once gave his Spirit to the prophets (as Peter reminds us), so that, stirred by his prompting, they might prophesy concerning him, now likewise chooses some from the number of his disciples to be heralds of his word; and even today he distributes the gifts of his Spirit among men, and gives to his Church some as apostles, others as evangelists, others as pastors, others as teachers, as Paul noted in his epistle to the Ephesians. These things we must observe more carefully, so that we may understand how great the authority of apostolic doctrine ought to be among us, and how grave the wickedness is of those who contradict it. For since Christ willed the Apostles to be the heralds, indeed the witnesses, of the things he had done, not only do they wrong those Apostles who falsely accuse their doctrine, but they also heap the utmost disgrace upon Christ himself. But since this will be said more fittingly elsewhere, let us now observe how ungrateful those are who despise and hate the ministers of the Word, and so the whole ministry of the Church, because through it their sins are rebuked. It is a common vice of this world that, while it lies wholly buried in evil and takes the greatest pleasure in wicked deeds, it does not want to be reproved or accused for them; and most people think they have no more bitter enemies than those who strive by faithful rebukes to lead them back into the way of salvation. But here we ought to consider that the author of this ministry is Christ, and that its purpose is that the Holy Spirit, through the ministers of the gospel, convicts the world of sin (Ioan.16.). Yet of him we cannot suspect anything hostile or inimical to our salvation, since he gave himself wholly for us. Next, it is entirely necessary that we be admonished and corrected, both on account of our daily offences and on account of the dullness innate in us, by which it happens that we do not notice in ourselves the things that are on everyone's lips and before everyone's eyes. Those who observe this not carelessly easily understand that there is scarcely any clearer proof of divine favour than this: that when we rush headlong into ruin, he restrains us not with the harsher blows we deserved, but calls us back into the way by fatherly admonitions. But if the philosophers taught us to draw this benefit from enemies, that we should hear from them what others conceal in us or do not notice at all, how much more patiently ought we to listen to those whom God, most loving of the human race, has appointed as our monitors? To these add that by clamouring against them we gain nothing; rather, like stubborn children, we provoke God's anger further and bring heavier punishments upon ourselves, as the examples of all ages abundantly testify. The consideration of this once moved the supreme kings and most victorious princes to bear the rebukes of the prophets patiently. But today those who come from the dregs of the common people do not hesitate to speak against the Word of God, and this is the principal cause of the evils of our age.

units.la: Secundò modus indicatur, quem Christus tenuit, & qui instar præparationis fuit ad negotium hoc non minus arduum quàm sanctum. Ascendit in montē, vt ibi precetur, & noctem totam in pre-cibus transfigit. Quo exemplo nobis duo commendat, quæ in ministrorū electione obseruatu in primis necessaria sunt. Primum, vt animos à carnis affectibus & rerum terrenarū cura in altum, id est, in sublimiorem & seriam cælestium contemplationem attollamus, deq; solo regno Dei prouehendo so-liciti simus. Quia enim negotium hoc totum diuinum est, neq; alium finem habet, quàm vt Dei re-gnum inter homines floreat, procul arceri debent quæcunq; nos ab eo reuocare possunt. Itaque in ipso limine (vt aiunt) offendunt, qui terrenis desiderijs immersi hoc vnum agunt, vt aut ijs quoad huius seculi fortunam consulant, quibus bene volunt; aut canes mutos inueniant, qui quidus dissimulent & apertis quoque sceleribus abblandiantur. Peccatum in hoc est omnibus seculis, & hinc olim veteris testamento sacerdotalis & prophetici ordinis dissipatio enata fuit, quòd in ministerio sacro partim quaestum, partim impunitatem peccandi plerique quaesiuerunt. Nam in populo erant, qui blanda & quae studijs ipsorum conuenirent, dici vellent: & bi facile inueniebant infelicia ventris mancipia, quibus non adeò grave erat ijs morem gerere, ex quibus aliquod emolumentum poterant sperare. Herodes certè hoc ad regni sui confirmationem facere putauit, si deleta veterum sacerdotum prosapia, alios ex sece vulgi substitueret, quibus posset dicendi leges praescribere: quo stratagemate prius Ieroboamum quoq; in stabiliendo regno Israelitico vsum fuisse, fortassis audiuerat. Et vtinam non etiam hodie paucim haberentur, qui hoc vnum quaerunt, quando de ministerio sacro agitur. Sed impletur quotidie quod de nouissimorum temporum hominibus Paulus dixit, fore nimirum vt sanam doctrinam non sustineant, & ad fabulas conuersi doctores roaceruent, qui prauis desiderijs prurientes aures ipsis demulceant. Alterum est, vt precibus ad Deum feriis & ardentibus vtantur, quicunque verbi administros deligere & ordinare instituerunt. Postulat hoc ipsa ministerij ratio. Quia enim munus hoc periculi plenum & in primis arduum est, & in eo absq; Dei ope nihil proficitur, hanc petant oportet quicunq; in eligendis doctoribus falli nolunt. Debet eos etiam excitare communis periculi consideratio, quando constat ministros non sibi solis peccare, sed toti simul populo, qui ipsorum fidei creditus est. Nam vt is qui ad clauum sedet, si quid vel negligentia vel malitia peccet: non sibi soli malum dat, sed nauim totam vna cum vectoribus perdit: ita totas ecclesias, aut saltem maiorem partem doctores mali aut negligentes secum in exitium abripiunt. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter Apostoli et qui in primitiua ecclesia rebus praefuerunt. Nam etsi eorum, qui ordinandi erant, virtus atq; fides ipsis satis perspecta esset, voluerunt tamen negotium hoc omne diuino spiritu gubernari, & idee ieiunijs simul & precibus vacarunt, quibus Dei gratiam atq; opem impetrarent. Accessit deinde impositio manuum, quae ipsa quoq; non sine publicis precibus fiebat, vt plus authoritatis ministerio accederet. Quae omnia cum hodie negligantur omnino, aut nimis frigide tractentur, minimè mirum est tam paucos haberi, qui munus istud digne & cum aliquo fructu obeant.
units.tr: Second, the manner is indicated which Christ observed, and which served as a preparation for this business, no less arduous than holy. He went up into the mountain to pray, and spent the whole night in prayers. By this example he commends to us two things that are especially necessary to observe in the choice of ministers. First, that we lift our minds from the affections of the flesh and the cares of earthly things on high, that is, to a higher and more serious contemplation of heavenly things, and that we be anxious only for the advancement of the kingdom of God. For since this whole business is divine, and has no other end than that the kingdom of God may flourish among men, whatever can call us back from it must be kept far away. Therefore those stumble at the very threshold, as they say, who, immersed in earthly desires, do only this: either they seek to provide for the fortune of this age for those whom they favour, or they look for dumb dogs who may conceal things and even flatter open crimes. This sin has existed in every age, and from it of old came the dissolution of the priestly and prophetic order under the Old Testament, because in the sacred ministry many sought partly gain and partly impunity for sinning. For there were in the people those who wished to be told flattering things that suited their inclinations, and such men easily found unhappy slaves of the belly, to whom it was not too hard to humour those from whom they could hope for some profit. Herod certainly thought he would do this for the confirmation of his kingdom, if, the line of the old priests having been destroyed, he substituted others from the dregs of the common people, whom he could prescribe the laws of speaking; perhaps he had heard that Jeroboam too had earlier used this stratagem in establishing the kingdom of Israel. And would that even today there were not a few who seek only this when the sacred ministry is under discussion! But every day what Paul said of the men of the last times is fulfilled: that they will not endure sound doctrine, and, turned aside to fables, will heap up teachers who, itching with depraved desires, tickle their ears. The second thing is that all who undertake to choose and ordain ministers of the Word should use earnest and fervent prayers to God. The very nature of the ministry demands this. For since this office is full of danger and especially arduous, and nothing prospers in it without God's help, all who do not wish to be deceived in choosing teachers ought to seek this help. The consideration of the common danger should also stir them, since ministers do not sin for themselves alone, but at the same time against the whole people, who have been entrusted to their faith. For as the one who sits at the helm, if he errs through negligence or malice, does not bring harm on himself alone but loses the whole ship along with its passengers, so bad or negligent teachers drag whole churches, or at least the greater part of them, with them into ruin. The Apostles and those who presided over affairs in the primitive Church observed this diligently. For although the virtue and faith of those who were to be ordained were sufficiently known to them, they nonetheless wished the whole business to be governed by the divine Spirit, and so they devoted themselves to fasting together with prayers, by which they might obtain God's grace and help. Then followed the laying on of hands, which was itself also done not without public prayers, so that more authority might accrue to the ministry. Since all these things are now either altogether neglected or handled too coldly, it is no wonder at all that so few are found who discharge that office worthily and with some fruit.

units.la: Tertiò, quos elegerit aut quales, videndum est. Docet hoc vno verbo Marcus, quando electos dicit, quos ipse voluit: non eos, qui aut ipsi hoc munus ambiebant, aut hominum authoritate commendabantur. Voluit autè procul dubio eos, quos pater aeterno decreto ad hoc munus destinauerat. Nihil ergo hic aut hominum dignitati aut meritis datum est, sed totum hoc negotium ex Dei gratia dependet, quod ipse Christus apud Ioannem his verbis diserte testatur: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Solet hoc idem etiam hodie fieri. Etsi enim multi sua sponte currant, & priuatis affectibus ducti munus istud capessant, nihil tamen absq; diuinae prouidentiae certo consilio fit, & (vt supra ex Paulo demonstrauimus) Christus is est, qui ecclesiae pastores dat. Caeterum hoc loco carnis rationi absurdum vel etiam iniquum videtur, quòd multis praeteritis, qui fide et pietate praestabant, Iudam elegerit, quem furacem esse, & tandem proditorem fore non poterat ignorare. Etenim cùm natura commodi priuati studio teneamur, nemo facile inter domesticos suos eum asciscit, ex quo malum ali quod ingens sibi imminere nouit. D. Bernhardum certè olim huius consilij siue facti consideratio mouit, vt exclamaret: Domine Iesu, cùm esset electio illa in manu tua, quare elegisti diabolum episcopum? Sed idem mox subijcit: Fratres, sic facit Iesus hodie eligens sibi multos diabolos episcopos. Quia verò aeterna Sapientia est Christus, non dubium est, quin illi certa huius consilij ratio constiterit, & etiamnum hodie illi constet: quod vnum nobis sufficere debet in ijs, quorum ratio in scripturis non dicitur reddita. Veruntamen si quis hic pijs coniecturis locus est, non inepte dicemus, Christū hoc exemplo voluisse scandalo mederi, quod ex corruptis verbi administrorum moribus & ecclesiae confusione, quae ex his fere emanat, exoriturum sciebat. Solent enim ex his calumniandi occasione captare, qui verbi lucem prius oderunt, & huminum vitia doctrinae imputant, vt eam omnibus inuisam atq; suspectam reddant. Et hi fere nunquam nō in ore habent Apostolorum exemplum vt per hoc omnes eos damnent, quos vel latum vngue ab eo discedere vident. Atqui fatemur quoq; nos eos demū vere apostolicos & honore dignos esse, qui Apostolorum vestigijs quoad doctrinam simul & vitae consuetudinem, insistunt: interim vero inter hanc & illam distinguendū esse dicimus, neq; doctrinam propter corruptos doctoris mores damnari debere. Nam si hoc demus, ex hominum virtute & dignitate tota doctrinae authoritas pendebit, & cum Iuda ipsum quoq; euangelii reiici merebitur, cuius illum praesentem. præconem fuisse scimus. Et quia omnibus seculis erunt qui Iudam imitentur, nunquam non in periculum veniet Euangelij veritas, qua labefactata salutis nostræ fundamentū consistere non poterit. Quoad vero Christi discipulos, qui cum Iuda meliores essent, non tamen in Apostolorū chorum adoptati sunt, nullam illis iniuriā fecit Dominus. Nihil enim ex eo saluti eorum decessit, & ijdem nihilominus locum in cælis habent inter beatorum spiritus, quos pater ab æterno elegit. Imò caueri oportuit, ne qui Christi discipuli sunt, simul etiam Apostolos & Euangelij præcones sefore putarent. Quæ persuasio olim Corinthios mouit, vt propter spiritus χαρίσματα tumultuarentur, & ecclesiam totam scinderent, cum omnes in illa eminere vellent. Quos Paulus admonet, eandē esse ecclesiæ ratio nem, quæ Reipub. vel etiam quæ corporis humani est. Vt enim membra omnia vnum corpus constituunt, & ad idem corpus pertinent, etiamsi magna inter illa diuersitas & ingens discrimen sit, siue vsum siue dignitatem spectes & sicuti certæ atq; distinctæ in Repub. functiones sunt, quas si auferas, neq; Reip. ordo, neq; œconomia inter priuatos consistere poterit. Ita in Ecclesia (inquit) aliquos constituit Deus primum quidē Apostolos, secundò Prophetas, tertiò Doctores, &c. Et paulò post infert: Num omnes, Apostoli? num omnes, Prophetæ? num omnes, Doctores? &c. Quasi diceret: Res ipsa loquitur, discrimina hæc functionū à Deo esse introducta. Nam quæ Ecclesia inueniri poterit, in qua omnes sunt Apostoli, aut Doctores, aut verbi interpretes? Neq; enim in externa Verbi prædicatione salus nostra fundata est, sed in fide, qua Christum apprehendimus. Voluit præterea Christus discipulos ad patientiam & prudentiam exercere, quando Iudam illis admisit. Qui enim inter initia suæ functionis collegam tam improbum & infidum senserant, procul dubio postea sibi à sal sis fratribus diligentius cauerunt, & minus offensi sunt, si quando tales viderunt obrepere. Seruit ergo nostræ etiam institutioni hoc Christi factum, ne indignius feramus, si qui nobis coniunguntur, quorum fides nobis non immeritò suspecta, aut etiam satis manifesta est improbitas. Solet hoc in tanta hominum corruptione frequenter fieri, & hanc ferè Christi & seruorum eius sortem esse Dauidis, & Pauli & similium exempla testantur. At nunc magna prudentia simul & inuicta patientia opus est, ne dum ius nostrum rigidius persequimur, toti ecclesiæ aut reipub. malum demus, et publicarum dissensionum simus authores, quarum plerunq; infelix est exitus. Admonentur præterea Iudæ exemplo omnes, qui in gradum aliquem sublimiorem euecti sunt, ne insolentia superbiant, sed curent potius ne cadant, & ita sibi ipsis infamiæ maioris authores sint.
units.tr: Thirdly, we must consider whom he chose, or what sort of men. Mark teaches this in a single word when he says that he called those whom he himself wanted: not those who sought this office for themselves, or who were recommended by the authority of men. He certainly wanted those whom the Father had appointed to this office by his eternal decree. Nothing here, therefore, is granted to human dignity or merit, but the whole matter depends on God's grace, as Christ himself plainly testifies in John in these words: "You did not choose me, but I chose you." The same thing is still done today. For although many run of their own accord and, moved by private desires, take up this office, nothing happens apart from the certain counsel of divine providence, and (as we showed above from Paul) it is Christ who gives the ministers to the Church. Yet at this point it seems absurd to the reasoning of the flesh, or even unjust, that he should have chosen Judas, when many better men, eminent for faith and piety, had been passed over, though he could not have failed to know that Judas was a thief and would in the end be a traitor. Indeed, since by nature we are bound by concern for our private advantage, no one readily admits among his own household a man from whom he knows some great harm is hanging over him. Certainly the consideration of this plan, or deed, once moved St Bernard to exclaim: "Lord Jesus, since that choice was in your hand, why did you choose the devil as bishop?" But he immediately adds: "Brethren, this is what Jesus does today, choosing for himself many devils as bishops." Since Christ is eternal Wisdom, there is no doubt that a certain reason for this counsel was and still is clear to him; and this alone ought to suffice for us in matters whose reason is not stated in the Scriptures. Nevertheless, if there is room here for pious conjecture, we may not unfitly say that by this example Christ wished to remedy a scandal which he knew would arise from the corrupt morals of those who administer the Word and from the confusion in the Church that usually flows from them. For from these things those who hated the light of the Word from the start seize the occasion to calumniate, and they impute men's vices to the doctrine, so as to make it hateful and suspect to all. And such men almost always have on their lips the example of the Apostles, so that they may condemn by it all those whom they see departing in the least degree from it. Yet we too confess that only those are truly apostolic and worthy of honour who follow the footsteps of the Apostles both in doctrine and in the manner of life; meanwhile we say that a distinction must be made between the two, and that doctrine must not be condemned on account of the corrupt morals of the teacher. For if we grant this, the whole authority of doctrine will depend on the virtue and dignity of men, and it will deserve to be rejected together with Judas, even though we know that he was a herald of the gospel while present. And since there will be in every age those who imitate Judas, the truth of the gospel will never cease to be in danger, and once it is shaken the foundation of our salvation cannot stand. As for the disciples of Christ who, though better than Judas, were not adopted into the company of the Apostles, the Lord did them no wrong. For nothing was taken from their salvation by this, and they nonetheless have a place in heaven among the spirits of the blessed, whom the Father chose from eternity. Indeed, it was necessary to guard against the thought that those who are disciples of Christ are at the same time Apostles and heralds of the gospel. This persuasion once moved the Corinthians to riot on account of the gifts of the Spirit (χαρίσματα) and to tear the whole Church apart, since all wanted to stand out in it. Paul admonishes them that the reason of the Church is the same as that of the commonwealth or of the human body. For as all the members make up one body and belong to the same body, even though there is great diversity and wide difference among them, whether you look at their use or their dignity; and as in a commonwealth there are certain and distinct functions, which, if you remove them, neither the order of the state nor the household economy of private persons can stand; so in the Church, he says, "God has appointed some, first Apostles, second Prophets, third Teachers," and so on. And a little later he adds: "Are all Apostles? Are all Prophets? Are all Teachers?" As if he were saying: the thing itself speaks, these distinctions of functions have been introduced by God. For what Church could be found in which all are Apostles, or Teachers, or interpreters of the Word? Our salvation is not founded on the outward preaching of the Word, but on the faith by which we lay hold of Christ. Moreover, Christ wished to exercise the disciples in patience and prudence when he admitted Judas among them. For those who had perceived at the beginning of his ministry such a wicked and faithless colleague would certainly afterwards take more careful heed of such brethren, and would be less offended if they saw such men creeping in. Christ's action therefore also serves our instruction, so that we may not bear it too impatiently if there are joined to us those whose faith we rightly suspect, or whose wickedness is clear enough. In such great corruption of men this often happens, and the examples of David, Paul and others like them testify that this is almost the lot of Christ and his servants. But now great prudence and unconquered patience are needed, lest, while we pursue our right too strictly, we bring harm to the whole Church or commonwealth and become the authors of public dissensions, whose outcome is usually unhappy. Moreover, by the example of Judas all are admonished who have been raised to some higher rank, not to be puffed up with arrogance, but rather to take care that they do not fall, and so become the authors of greater infamy for themselves.

units.la: Quartò finem quoq;, in quem illi delecti sunt, Euangelistæ indicant, vbi quod Lucas vnico Apostolorum nomine comprehendit, Marcus in suas quasi species diducens tria dicit. Primum, hoc voluisse Christum, vt isti duodecim secum essent, indiuulsi nimirum comites, adeoq; discipuli domestici, quos ille priuatim instituaret & factorum suorum omnium testes haberet. Nondum ergo illis docendi munus credidit, cum rerum adhuc ignari & prorsus rudes essent. Alterum, vt suo tempore ab ipso ad prædicandum emitterentur, ex quo Apostolorum, id est, legatorum nomen acceperunt. Initium functionis huius, vel potius eius præludium infra Cap. 9. describitur, quam postea cum plenis mandatis obiuerunt, quando post acceptum spiritum sanctum in totum orbem ad prædicandum digressi sunt. Tertium fuit, vt peculiari spiritus virtute instructi morbus mederentur, & Satanam ex hominibus eijcerent: quod missionis ipsorum testimonium publicum fuit, quale legatis per literas publicæ fidei aut credentiæ (vt vulgò loquuntur) dare consueuit. Continet tria hæc omnes Euangelici ministerij partes, in quibus sedulos esse conuenit omnes eos, qui hoc cum laude & fructu aliquo obire volunt. Necesse enim est, vt cum Christo familiarius versentur, hunc in scripturis loquentem audiant, & spiritui eius intra animos suos locū dent, ficq; ex illo discant, quod suæ fidei credita præ dicent. In prædicando autem non minus fidi quàm industrij sint, ne quid dissimulent ignauo metu superati, neue aliquam docendi occasionem prætermittant. Finis verò hic illis propositus sit, vt mor bis animi medeantur, id est, peccata procul arceant, & Satanam ex possessione inter homines male vsurpata eijciant. Facient hoc magno cum profectu, si eius fraudes & dolos arguant, superstitiones oppugnent, dogmata falsa confutent, scelera corripiant, & quosfuis vel reluctantes ad Dei tribunal citent. In his enim olim prophetas & Apostos diligentissimos fuisse scimus. Poterant hæc latissimè diduci, sed sufficiat cogitandi occasionem præbuisse ijs, qui serio huius muneris studio tenentur. Plura in Marco diximus.
units.tr: Fourthly, the Evangelists also indicate the purpose for which those men were chosen. Where Luke comprehends them under the single name of Apostles, Mark, dividing the matter into what are as it were its parts, names three things. First, that Christ wished these twelve to be with him, that is, unseparated companions, and therefore his household disciples, whom he might instruct privately and have as witnesses of all his deeds. He did not yet entrust to them the office of teaching, since they were still ignorant of things and altogether untrained. Second, that at the proper time they should be sent out by him to preach, from which they received the name of Apostles, that is, legates. The beginning of this function, or rather its prelude, is described below in chapter 9; they afterwards discharged it with full commissions, when, after receiving the Holy Spirit, they went out into the whole world to preach. Third, that, being furnished with a peculiar power of the Spirit, they should heal diseases and cast out Satan from men; this was a public testimony of their mission, such as is usually given to legates by letters of public faith or credence (as people commonly say). These three things contain all the parts of the Evangelical ministry, and in them all who wish to discharge this office with praise and some fruit ought to be diligent. For they must associate with Christ more closely, hear him speaking in the Scriptures, and give his Spirit a place within their minds, and so learn from him what they are to preach as the things entrusted to their faith. And in preaching they must be no less faithful than diligent, so as not to conceal anything out of cowardly fear, nor let slip any opportunity of teaching. Let this end be set before them: that they heal the diseases of the soul, that is, keep sins far away, and drive Satan out of the possession he has wrongly seized among men. They will do this with great profit if they expose his frauds and tricks, attack superstitions, refute false doctrines, rebuke crimes, and summon to God's judgment-seat both those who resist and those who are willing. For we know that the most diligent prophets and Apostles were engaged in these things. These matters could be spread out at great length, but it is enough to have offered an occasion for thought to those who are seriously devoted to the study of this office. We have said more on Mark.

units.la: Finis ministerij apostolici.
units.tr: The end of the apostolic ministry.

units.la: Partes ministerij euangelici.
units.tr: The parts of the evangelical ministry.

units.la: Sequitur quinto loco Apostolorum catalogus, quem à Matthæo quoque & Marco Spiritus sanctus contexi voluit. Primò enim necesse fuit eorum nomina extare, qui ab ipso Christo Veritatis & salutis æternæ doctores nobis dati sunt: quò facilius caveri possint pseudoapostoli, qui suis figmentis atque mendacijs Christi nomen prætexere audent. Cæperunt tales olim exoriri passim, cùm in vivis adhuc essent veri Apostoli, & horum nomine etiam nunc circumferuntur Canones quidam, Apostolorum à spiritu tam alieni, ut merito quis miretur tantam in aliquem mortalium impudentiam cadere potuisse, ut sanctissimis atq; fidelissimis Christi servis commenta eiusmodi non minus ridicula quàm superstitiosa adscribere ausus fuerit. Et hodie adhuc sub apostolici nominis prætextu toti orbi imponunt Romani Pontifices, qui sibi omnem in ecclesia Christi potestatem vendicant, & æternæ salutis leges pro suo arbitrio figunt atque refigunt. Probè ergo nobis Spiritus sanctus consuluit, qui omnibus nota esse voluit verorum Apostolorum nomina, quos Christus orbis terrarum doctores catholicos fecit. Et ut minus possent impostores, illos etiam occulta suggestione movit, ut doctrinam salutis non solùm viva voce traderent, verumetiam scriptis mandarent, quæ in hunc usque diem extant. Frustra igitur sese venditant hodie apostolicorum titulis, qui traditionibus superstitiosis & ceremonijs frigidissimis ecclesiam gravant. Nec enim pro apostolicis haberi possunt, nisi qui istorum vestigijs insistunt, qui hic ab Evangelista recensentur. Quæ verò eorundem doctrina fuerit, ex ipsorum scriptis patet, à quibus quicunque dissentiunt, fidem omnino nullam merentur. Notum est enim illud Pauli: Si ego ipse, vel etiam angelus de cælo evangelizet vobis præter id quod evangelizavimus, anathema sit. Gal. 1.
units.tr: Fifth, the Holy Spirit wished the catalogue of the Apostles to be set down, and he wished Matthew and Mark also to record it. For it was first necessary that the names of those be known who were given to us by Christ himself as teachers of truth and of eternal salvation, so that false apostles, who dare to put forward the name of Christ in support of their fictions and lies, could more easily be guarded against. Such men began to arise here and there in earlier times, while the true Apostles were still alive, and even now certain canons are circulated under their names. These are so alien to the Spirit that one may well wonder how such shamelessness could fall upon any mortal, that he dared to ascribe to the most holy and faithful servants of Christ inventions of this kind, no less ridiculous than superstitious. And even today the Roman Pontiffs impose on the whole world under the pretext of the apostolic name. They claim for themselves all power in the Church of Christ, and they make and remake the laws of eternal salvation at their own pleasure. The Holy Spirit has therefore provided for us well, for he wished the names of the true Apostles, whom Christ made the catholic teachers of the whole world, to be known to everyone. And so that impostors might have less room, he also moved the Apostles by a secret prompting to hand down the doctrine of salvation not only by the living voice but also to commit it to writing, and those writings survive to this day. In vain, then, do those who burden the Church with superstitious traditions and most frigid ceremonies boast today of the titles of apostolic men. For they cannot be regarded as apostolic unless they follow in the footsteps of those who are listed here by the Evangelist. What the teaching of the Apostles was is plain from their own writings, and whoever dissents from them deserves no faith at all. For that saying of Paul is well known: "If I myself, or even an angel from heaven, preach to you anything beside what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." Gal. 1.

units.la: Est præterea observatu dignissimum, quod totus iste catalogus neminem regia dignitate aut aliqua huius seculi authoritate insignem continet, sed homines partim plebeios & illiteratos, partim pauperculos, aut etiam ob vitam anteactam infames, qualem Matthæum fuisse scimus. Causam huius consilij Paulus in priori ad Corinthios Capite primo his verbis exponit: Videtis vocationem nostram fratres, quòd non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: Verùm quæ stulta sunt in mundo elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat sapientes: & quæ infirma sunt in mundo elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat ea quæ sunt robusta: & quæ ignobilia sunt in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, elegit Deus, & ea quæ non sunt, ut ea quæ sunt aboleret. Ut ne gloriaretur vlla caro coram eo. Hocitaque spectavit Deus, ut toti mundo constaret, vniversum humanæ redemptionis negotium, cuius author & mediator nobis est Iesus Christus, non humanum aut terrenum, sed divinum & cælestè esse, quod ut non armis huius seculi, neque humanæ sapientiæ consilijs, sed sola spiritus virtute confectum est: ita nullis etiam hominum machinationibus impediri potest, quò minus suum effectum habeat in omnibus illis, qui Christum fide non fucata apprehendunt. Seruit ergo ista consideratio nostræ cùm institutioni tum consolationi. Admonet enim nos, ne quid nostris viribus aut meritis tribuamus, sed in vnius Dei gratiam recumbamus, qui nos antequam mundus hic crearetur in Christo Iesu elegit, & eundem præfinito tempore hominem nasci voluit, ut ab æterno decretam humani generis redemptionem perageret, nosque per Euangelij prædicationem ex regno tenebrarum in lucem suam admirabilem & ad regni sui cælestis possessionem vocare dignatus est. Docet item, ne quæ huius mundi sunt in Christo quæramus, sed cælestibus solis fimus intenti. Rursus consolationis plenum est, quòd audimus regnum Christi, quo vno omnis salus nostra nititur, non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde mundi vicibus minime subiectum esse. Exeo enim sequitur, frustra aduersus illud mundi principes tumultuari, imò salvum & incolume fore, etiamsi cælum & terra transeant. Licet ergo nobis cum Davide dicere: Deus nobis suffugium & robur est, in aduersitate auxilium præsentissimum. Ideo nihil timebimus, etiamsi loco moveatur terra, & montes nutent in medio maris. Tumultuentur gentes, motus excitent regna, & terra cum fragore dehiscat: Dominus tamen exercituum a nobis stat, arx sublimis est nobis Deus Iacob, &c. Quid enim in terris hisce damni accipere possunt, quorum pater, civitas, patrimonium, vita salus in cœlis est? Sed video me à præsenti loco longius progredi, in quo plura adhuc dici poterant de Apostolorum conditione, deq; nominibus eorum, quæ quibusdam Christus mutavit: sed cùm ea in Marci expositione iampridem tractauerimus, nunc ea repetere nequaquam est opus. Itaq; in ijs pergamus, quæ proximè sequuntur. Nam ne quis Christum Apostolos ideo delegisse putaret, vt ipse in illos reiecta omni cura ec-
units.tr: Moreover, it is most worthy of notice that this whole catalogue contains no one distinguished by royal rank or by any authority of this world. It contains men who are partly of common and unlettered stock, partly poor, or even infamous for their former life, as we know Matthew was. Paul sets out the reason for this plan in the first chapter of his first letter to the Corinthians, in these words: "Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, and God chose what is low and despised in the world, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh should boast before him." Thus God intended that the whole world should understand that the entire business of human redemption, of which Jesus Christ is the author and mediator, is not human or earthly but divine and heavenly. Accomplished not by the arms of this age nor by the counsels of human wisdom but by the power of the Spirit alone, it can likewise be hindered by no human schemes from achieving its effect in all those who lay hold of Christ with a sincere faith. This consideration therefore serves both our instruction and our comfort. It warns us not to attribute anything to our own strength or merits, but to rest in the grace of the one God, who chose us in Christ Jesus before this world was created, who at the appointed time willed his Son to be born as a man, so that he might carry out the redemption of the human race decreed from eternity, and who deigned to call us, through the preaching of the gospel, out of the kingdom of darkness into his wonderful light and into possession of his heavenly kingdom. It also teaches us not to seek the things of this world in Christ, but to be intent on heavenly things alone. Again, it is full of comfort that we hear that the kingdom of Christ, on which alone all our salvation rests, is not of this world, and therefore is by no means subject to the changes of the world. For it follows from this that it is vain for the princes of the world to rage against it; indeed, it will remain safe and unharmed even if heaven and earth pass away. So we may say with David: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth be moved and the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea. Though the nations rage and the kingdoms are moved, and the earth melts, the Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our high fortress." For what loss can they suffer on earth whose Father, city, inheritance, life and salvation are in heaven? But I see that I am going further than the present place allows, where much more could be said about the condition of the Apostles, and about the names which Christ changed for some of them. But since we have already treated these things in the exposition of Mark, there is now no need to repeat them. Let us therefore go on to what immediately follows. For lest anyone think that Christ chose the apostles so that he, having cast every care of the church upon them, might rest in quiet leisure,

units.la: clesiae quietus otiaretur, docet Lucas, vt ad docendi munus redierit. Qui locus eo diligentius considerari debet, quod Romanorum Pontificum audaciam arguit, qui sub Apostolicae successionis praetext tu se vicarios Christi, tanquam absentis, constituunt, omnemq; in ecclesia potestate sibi vendicant. Vt enim hoc illi demus, quod Petri sedem teneant, & legitimo ordine Apostolis successerint; num vero propterea Christi Iesu vicarij sunt, & quidem statuendi ius habent? Vicario opus habet, qui vel omnino absens est, vel officio suo non potest fungi. At Christus corpus quidem e terris in coelos sustulit, Deitate vero sua vbique praesens est, & corporis loco spiritum substituit, qui & ecclesiae toti & singulis credentibus paracleti fidissimi instar est, & promissionem Christi habemus dicentis: Ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi. Apostolis vero docendi munus certa lege commisit, vt nimirum ea tradant quae ab ipso acceperint: non vt ipsi pro suo arbitrio nova dogmata fingant, aut ea obtrudant, quae nullis scripturae testimonijs probari possunt. Ergo nouum in ecclesia magistratum instituerunt Pontifices, qui eo intolerabilior est, quod & Christum e solio deijcere, & honorem, qui ipsi debetur, in se transferre conantur. Itaque non frustra in praesenti Dominus, cum duodecim illos delegisset, quos ad praedicandum emitteret, mox ad officium redit, & maiori quam prius industria Verbum salutis praedicat. Sic enim scribit Lucas: Descendit cum eis, stetitq; in loco campestri, turbaq; discipulorum eius & multitudo magna plebis ex tota Iudaea & Hierosolyma, & ex maritima regione Tyri & Sydonis, qui venerant vt audirent eum, & sanarentur a morbis suis, & qui torquebantur a spiritibus impuris: & sanabantur, &c. Quo loco inter multa alia, quae dicuntur, tria potissimum considerari debent.
units.tr: Luke teaches that he returned to the office of teaching. This passage deserves to be considered the more carefully because it exposes the audacity of the Roman Pontiffs, who, under the pretext of apostolic succession, set themselves up as vicars of Christ, as though he were absent, and claim for themselves all power in the Church. Let us grant them that they hold the seat of Peter and have succeeded the Apostles in legitimate order. Are they then truly vicars of Jesus Christ, and do they indeed have the right to lay down laws? A vicar is needed by one who is either wholly absent or unable to perform his office. But Christ indeed took his body from the earth into heaven, yet by his deity he is present everywhere, and in place of his body he has put his Spirit, who is like a most faithful Paraclete both to the whole Church and to each of the believers. We have Christ's promise saying: "I am with you always, even to the end of the age." To the Apostles, however, he entrusted the office of teaching under a fixed rule, namely that they should pass on what they had received from him, and not that they should invent new doctrines for themselves at their own pleasure, or impose things that cannot be proved by any testimony of Scripture. The Pontiffs have therefore set up a new magistracy in the Church, which is the more intolerable because they strive both to cast Christ down from his throne and to transfer to themselves the honour which is due to him. Hence the Lord, in the present passage, not in vain, after he had chosen those twelve whom he would send out to preach, soon returns to his office and preaches the word of salvation with greater diligence than before. For Luke writes thus: "He came down with them and stood in a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon, who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases, and those who were troubled by unclean spirits; and they were healed." In this passage, among many other things that are said, three points above all should be considered.

units.la: Primum confluit vndiq; populus turmatim, & quidem non solum ex Iudaea & Hierosolyma, verumetiam ex finibus Tyri & Sidonis nonnulli, qui gentilitijs superstitionibus imbuti Deum ve-rum hucusq; ignorauerant. Atqui paulo ante pharisei cum scribis & Sacerdotibus no semel de Christo occidendo consultarunt. Mirum ergo, quod neq; sua authoritate, neq; supplicij metu populum continere possunt, quo minus ex ipsa Hierosolyma, vbi in primis dominabantur, ad illum audiendum concurrant. Quin noua fit accessio ex gentibus, quae vt docet Christum vniuersalem totius generis humani seruatorem esse: ita quid no multo post futurum esset ostendit: Nimirum, vt Iudaeis propter suam contumaciam & ingratitudinem reiectis, in eorum locu gentes succederent, sicuti olim Prophetae praedixerunt. Fuit id graue & horrendum Dei iudicium, quo admonemur, ne quis aliqua dignitatis externae praerogatiua glorietur, aut Deum sibi ita obstrictum putet, vt non possit reijci & ab ecclesiae consortio excludi. Habuerunt enim Iudaei omnia, quae ad ecclesiae externae dignitate faciut, & ex ipsis carnem assumpsit aeternus Dei filius, seq; illis familiarissimu praebuit. At idem postea ab ingratis & rebellibus regnum Dei transtulit ad gentes, & inter has inuenit, qui ipsum vera fide amplexi sunt. Quid ergo tunc factum est, hoc ipsum etiam hodie potest fieri, imo multis ecclesijs iam prodem accidisse scimus, vt repudium passae Christum & salutem amiserint, eo quod Dei beneficium noluerunt agnoscere. At simul hic consolationis plenum est, quod videmus, Christi regno & ecclesiae nihil decedere ex hostium machinationibus, qui illud oppressum et extinctum volunt, sed potius eo magis crescere & propagari, quo magis premitur & oppugnatur. Quia enim Christo omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terra, facile ei fuerit hostium suorum consilia atq; conatus eludere, inq; ipsorum capita effundere, quae aduersus eum machinantur. Et vt David olim docuit, proprium hoc Christo est, vt in medio hostium suorum regnet atq; dominetur. Deinde ecclesia persecutionibus non euerti-tur neq; imminuitur, sed vt frumentum cribratur, & vt aurum igne probatur atque purgatur, imo latius ad eos etiam extenditur, quos nunquam ad illam accessuros esse putauisses. Est ergo non vtile modo, verumetiam necessarium, vt persecutiones interdum excitentur. Vt enim palea frumento permixtae manent, donec ventilabrum agricola expedit, & vt auro scoria fecesq; e terra agnatae adhaerent, quoad non purgatur in igne: ita in ecclesijs semper locum habebunt tam hypocritae quam palam impij, & in singulis credentibus carnis desideria se exerunt, quoad Deus ignem probationis accendit, qui & illos procul eijcit, & ista prorsus exurit, adeoque nos cogit, vt relictis terrenis studijs ad caelestia & aeterna bona aspiremus. Adhaec vt incendium in vna domo ortum latius diffunditur si ventus accedat, qui flammas & tabulas ardentes hinc inde disjicit: ita quae in vna vrbe ardet
units.tr: First, people flock together from every side in crowds, and not only from Judea and Jerusalem, but also some from the territory of Tyre and Sidon, who, steeped in pagan superstitions, had until then been ignorant of the true God. Yet a little before this, the Pharisees with the scribes and priests had more than once taken counsel to kill Christ. It is remarkable, then, that they could not restrain the people, either by their authority or by fear of punishment, from running together to hear him, even from Jerusalem itself, where they chiefly held sway. Indeed, a new accession comes from the Gentiles, which shows that Christ is the universal Saviour of the whole human race, and also indicates what was going to happen not long afterwards: namely, that the Gentiles would succeed in the place of the Jews, who were rejected because of their obstinacy and ingratitude, as the Prophets had foretold long before. That was a grave and dreadful judgment of God, by which we are warned not to glory in any external prerogative of dignity, or to think that God is so bound to us that he cannot be cast off and excluded from fellowship with the Church. For the Jews had all the things that pertain to the outward dignity of the Church, and the eternal Son of God took flesh from them and showed himself most familiar to them. Yet afterwards he transferred the kingdom of God from the ungrateful and rebellious to the Gentiles, and among these he found men who embraced him with true faith. What happened then can happen today as well; indeed, we know that it has already befallen many churches, which, having been cast off, have lost Christ and salvation, because they were unwilling to acknowledge the benefit of God. At the same time, it is full of comfort that we see that nothing is taken from the kingdom of Christ or from the Church by the schemes of enemies, who wish it crushed and extinguished. Rather, it grows and spreads all the more, the more it is pressed and attacked. For since all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, it is easy for him to frustrate the counsels and attempts of his enemies and to turn back upon their own heads the things they plot against him. And as David taught long ago, it is proper to Christ to reign and rule in the midst of his enemies. Next, the Church is not overthrown or diminished by persecutions, but, like wheat, it is sifted, and as gold is tested and purified by fire; indeed, it is extended more widely even to those whom one would never have thought would come to it. Therefore persecutions sometimes being stirred up is not only useful but necessary. For as chaff remains mixed with the grain until the farmer winnows it with the fan, and as dross and dirt grown from the earth cling to gold until it is purified in the fire, so in the churches hypocrites as well as openly wicked men will always have a place, and the desires of the flesh show themselves in each of the believers, until God kindles the fire of testing, which both casts those men far away and utterly burns up those things, and thus compels us to leave earthly pursuits and aspire to heavenly and eternal goods. Moreover, as a fire that has broken out in one house spreads more widely if a wind comes and scatters the flames and burning boards this way and that, so the fire which burns in a single city...

units.la: Psal. 118.
units.tr: Psal. 118.

units.la: Euangelij fax, confestim multas alias corripit, si persecutionum procellis pij dissipentur. Exemplum huius rei prima persecutio præbuit, quæ Saulo authore Hierosolymis excitata occasionem præbuit pijs, ut qui prius illic hærebant, tunc longè lateq; dispersi non solum Iudæam, sed Samariam quoq; et Phæniciam omnem Verbi prædicatione illustrarent. Et possent huius generis multa adduci, nisi quæ nostro seculo plurimis in locis vidimus, nobis in hac re abunde fidem facerent. Visus autem eorum hic nobis esse debet, ne vllis hostium Euangelij consilijs aut conatibus offendamur. Nam etsi interdum multum profecturi videntur, et sanguine innoxio manus polluunt, hoc vnum tamen agunt, quòd regnum Christi eo latius extendunt, quo ardentius & crudelius aduersus illud sæviunt.
units.tr: The torch of the Gospel quickly kindles many others when the godly are scattered by the storms of persecution. The first persecution gave an example of this. Stirred up at Jerusalem under the leadership of Saul, it gave the godly the occasion to be scattered far and wide, so that those who had previously stayed there now illuminated, by the preaching of the Word, not only Judea but also Samaria and all of Phoenicia. Many instances of this kind could be cited, but those we have seen in very many places in our own age are enough to convince us of this matter. Their example should be before us here, so that we are not offended by any plans or attempts of the enemies of the Gospel. For although at times they seem likely to make great progress, and stain their hands with innocent blood, they accomplish this one thing: they extend the kingdom of Christ all the more widely, the more fiercely and cruelly they rage against it.

units.la: Secundo loco causæ nobis considerandæ sunt, quæ populū mouerunt, ut tanto studio ad Christum confluxerint. Duæ indicantur: Vt nimirū eum audirent, & ut sanarentur à morbis suis. Fuit ergo in illis magnum salutis cum corporis tum animæ studium. Nam quò minus ad Christū concurrerent, multa eos absterrere, multa impedire poterant: vtpote labor, sumptus, rei domestici iactura, periculū item multiplex, quod non immeritò timebatur, cum potentissimos quosq; illi inimicos esse non ignorarent. At nihil horum eos remoratur aut terret, quibus salus sua verè cordi est, & qui eam in Christo haberi credunt. Debent autem icтos imitari, quicunq; huius discipuli esse volunt. Nam qui opes, honores, parentes, coniugem, liberos, vitam deniq; propria Christo præferunt, eo digni non sunt. Paulus certè quæcunq; in mundo pretiosa habebat, pro stercoribus & rebus nocentissimis duxit, ut Christum lucrifaceret. Est ergo detestabilis eorū ignauia, qui vbi nihil periculi est, sola itineris longitudine, aut leuissima rei familiaris iactura se detineri patiuntur, quo minus cociones sacras accedant. Regnat hoc vitiū passim hodie, & ex eo apparet, quàm facile Euangelium & Christū contemnāt, qui tamen eius nomē profitentur. Quòd si qui his meliores sunt, ij curare debent, ut in eo, quod bene cœperunt, constanter pergant, ne vbi manu aratro admouerunt, rursus à tergo respiciant, & se ad capessendum regnum Christi parum idoneos esse demonstrent. Peccarunt in eo isti, quando cruce eius offensi sunt, & eum tunc deseruerunt, quem nunc miraculis clarum tanto studio sunt amplexi. Et hoc illud est, quo etiam hodie multi peccant, & salutem amittunt, quā manibus iam tenere videbantur.
units.tr: Second, we must consider the reasons that moved the people to flock to Christ with such eagerness. Two are indicated: namely, that they might hear him, and that they might be healed of their diseases. There was therefore in them a great concern for salvation, both of body and of soul. For many things could have deterred them and hindered them from coming to Christ: toil, expense, loss of property at home, and also the manifold danger, which was not unreasonably feared, since they knew that the most powerful men were their enemies. But none of these things delays or terrifies those for whom their salvation is truly dear, and who believe it is to be found in Christ. Whoever wishes to be his disciple ought to imitate them. For those who put wealth, honours, parents, wife, children, and finally their own life before Christ are not worthy of him. Paul certainly counted all the things in the world that he had held precious as dung and most harmful things, so that he might gain Christ. Therefore the cowardice of those is detestable who, when there is no danger at all, allow themselves to be held back from approaching the holy Supper merely by the length of the journey or the slightest loss of property. This vice reigns everywhere today, and from it one can see how easily they despise the Gospel and Christ, though they profess his name. But if some are better than these, they ought to take care to persevere steadfastly in what they have begun well, lest, having put their hand to the plough, they look back again and show themselves unfit to take up the kingdom of Christ. Those men sinned when they were offended by his cross and then deserted him, whom they now embrace with such eagerness, having been made famous by his miracles. And this is also the sin by which many today sin and lose the salvation which they seemed already to hold in their hands.

units.la: Docemur præterea istorum exemplo, quid in Christo quæri debeat, quod obseruatu in primis necessarium est. Falluntur enim in eo plerique, quòd sub fidei Christianæ prætextu ea quærunt, quæ Christus vel non promisit, vel etiam ab eo prorsus aliena sunt. Nos itaq; istos imitemur, & ante omnia doctrinam Veritatis quæramus, cuius diuulgandæ ergò ille in mundum venit. Est hæc pars illa optima, quam Maria Lazari soror elegit (ut suo loco audiemus) & qua in primis delectantur, qui si de præditi sunt non fucata. Oues meæ (inquit Christus) vocem meā audiunt, & sequuntur eam. Et vt hoc faciamus necesse est, quando neq; regni Dei mysteria proprij ingenij acumine inuestigare possumus, neq; in filios Dei renasci, nisi Verbi semen animis nostris concipiatur. Connexa est doctrinæ salus cum externi tum interni hominis, cuius etiam vnus Christus nobis author est. Quia enim peccata tollit, eadē opera simul omnibus malis medetur, quæ per hæc in mundum irrepserunt. Ideò verba vitæ æternæ illum habere Petrus dixit, & Paulus Euangelij prædicationem ministerium vitæ vocauit. Sunt quidē omnis generis afflictionibus obnoxij pij, sed qui Christo infixi sunt, ijs omnia adiumento sunt ad bonum, vt saluti ipsorum ea seruiant, quæ alijs exitium afferunt. Num quam ergo spe sua fideles frustrantur, falluntur autem (vt diximus) imo potius seipsos fallunt, qui in Christo carnalia & terrena solum quærunt.
units.tr: Besides, we are taught by the example of these men what ought to be sought in Christ, a point especially necessary to observe. For most people go wrong in this, that under the pretext of the Christian faith they seek things which Christ either did not promise, or which are altogether alien to him. Let us therefore imitate these men, and above all seek the doctrine of truth, for the sake of spreading which he came into the world. This is that best part which Mary, the sister of Lazarus, chose (as we shall hear in its place), and in which those delight above all who are truly endowed with it, if they are of sound mind. "My sheep," says Christ, "hear my voice, and follow it." And in order to do this we must, since we can neither investigate the mysteries of the kingdom of God by the keenness of our own wit, nor be born again as children of God, unless the seed of the Word is conceived in our minds. Salvation is bound up with doctrine, both of the outward and of the inward man, and Christ alone is its author for us. For because he takes away sins, by the same act he heals at once all the evils which have crept into the world through them. That is why Peter said that he has the words of eternal life, and Paul called the preaching of the Gospel the ministry of life. Indeed the godly are subject to afflictions of every kind, but to those who are fixed in Christ all things serve for good, so that those things which bring ruin to others serve for their salvation. Therefore the faithful are never disappointed in their hope, but those (as we have said) are deceived, or rather they deceive themselves, who seek in Christ only carnal and earthly things.

units.la: Huc facit quod tertium in huius loci consideratione occurrit. Nam istos à morbus suis sanatos fuisse scribit Lucas, multos item à spiritibus impuris Christus liberauit, vt in Marco annotatur. Addit autem in præsenti plenioris expositionis loco Euangelista: Et tota turba studebat eum tangere: quia virtus ab eo exibat, & sanabat omnes. Quo loco ordine & modum, quo in his sanandis Christus vsus est, propius considerauisse proderit. Primò tangere eum cupiunt, qui morbis detinebantur, & in eo mulieris illius similes sunt, quam ex vestis Christi contactu à sanguinis fluxu conualuisse Matthæus scribit. Est hoc infirmitatis humanæ argumentū, quæ etsi in Christo salute quærat, extrinsecus tamen adminiculis opus habet, & proinde ad ea etiā respicit. Et fert hanc ille patienter, imò seipsum nobis accommodat in doctrina, quā parabolis vestit et sacramētis, quibus sensus quoq; excitatur, vt maiores in fide progressus faciamus. Interim meminerimus, omnibus qui seruari volunt Christi contactu
units.tr: What comes next in our consideration of this passage is to the same purpose. For Luke writes that these people were healed of their diseases, and Christ also freed many from unclean spirits, as is noted in Mark. But in the present passage the Evangelist adds, in a fuller account: "And all the crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all." It will be useful to consider more closely here the order and manner which Christ used in healing them. First, those held by diseases desire to touch him, and in this they resemble that woman who, as Matthew writes, recovered from her flow of blood by touching the garment of Christ. This is a proof of human weakness, which, although it seeks salvation in Christ, still needs outward aids, and therefore looks to these also. And Christ bears this patiently; indeed he accommodates himself to us in his teaching, which he clothes in parables and sacraments, by which the senses too are stirred, so that we may make greater progress in faith. Meanwhile let us remember that all who wish to be saved need contact with Christ,

units.la: Matt. 9. contactu opus esse: non quidem corporeo (quo iam frui non datur) sed spirituali. Hunc in fide consistere ipse docet. Hac enim animi nostri supra coelos euectii illum apprehendunt, ut & ipse in nobis sit, & nos in illo. Eadem nos Christum induere Paulus scribit, & per eandem Christo nos desponsari totius scripturae consensus testatur. Fide ergo vere & salubriter tangitur Christus. Sine fide autem illum tangunt, qui eum vel ore modo profitentur, vel etiam in Sacramentis adumbratum habent, cum animis ab illo prorsus alieni sint. Et hi quamuis eo magnifice glorientur, in salute tamen vera nihil proficiunt. Nam Iudae proditoris, aut eorum falsae similes sunt, de quibus Dominus apud Matt. cap. 7. sub finem disserit. Deinde, ne quis vel vestibus Christi, vel externo contactu salutem acceptam ferret, virtus illa salutifica ab ipso, aut ex ipso exiuisse dicitur. Et hoc idem ipse testatur, quando sanata haemorrhoissa (de qua paulo ante diximus) virtutem ex se exiuisse sensit. Omnis ergo salus in Christo habetur, & ex illo in nos derivatur, neque nobis licet alios medicos aut salutis authores fingere. Olim quidem miraculose multos sanarunt prophetae, quod Apostolos quoque deinceps fecisse scimus: at non ex ipsis manauit virtus illa, quae morbis medebatur, sed invocato Christi nomine ista fecerunt, ut hunc nostrae salutis authorem atq; fontem perennem esse docerent. Nimium ergo inepti sunt, qui miracula per Sanctos coelites olim facta studiose conquirunt, ut hos invocandos esse euincant. Ita enim & suam inscitiam produnt, et illis iniuriam faciunt maximam, quando in eos transferunt Christi gloriam, pro qua illi sanguinem suum profundendum esse putarunt. Omissis ergo superstitionibus & harum magistris, unum Iesum Christum audiamus & sectemur, qui ut Veritatis aeternae doctor est vere catholicus, ita salutis quoq; author, fons & mediator est unicus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Matt. 9. contact: not indeed bodily contact (which is no longer granted to us to enjoy), but spiritual contact. He himself teaches that this consists in faith. For by faith our minds, lifted above the heavens, lay hold of him, so that he is in us and we in him. Paul writes that we put on Christ by the same faith, and the agreement of all Scripture testifies that we are betrothed to Christ by the same faith. Christ is therefore truly and savingly touched by faith. But without faith they touch him who merely profess him with their lips, or who even have him shadowed forth in the sacraments, while their hearts are wholly alien from him. And although these boast greatly in him, they gain nothing in true salvation. For they are like Judas the traitor, or like those false men of whom the Lord speaks near the end of Matthew chapter 7. Next, so that no one should take salvation from the garments of Christ or from outward contact, that saving power is said to have gone out from him, or out of him. He himself bears witness to the same thing, when, after healing the woman with the issue of blood (of whom we spoke a little earlier), he perceived that power had gone out from himself. All salvation is therefore had in Christ and flows from him to us, nor are we permitted to invent other physicians or other authors of salvation. Long ago the prophets indeed healed many miraculously, and we know that the Apostles afterwards did so too; but that power which healed the diseases did not flow out from them, but they did these things by invoking the name of Christ, so as to teach that he is the author of our salvation and its perennial fountain. Therefore they are too foolish who eagerly seek out the miracles wrought long ago through the heavenly saints, in order to prove that these saints are to be invoked. For in this way they betray their own ignorance and do the greatest wrong to those saints, when they transfer to them the glory of Christ, for which those saints thought their blood must be poured out. Setting aside, therefore, superstitions and their teachers, let us hear and follow the one Jesus Christ, who, as the teacher of eternal truth, is truly catholic, and as the author, fountain and mediator of salvation is the only one. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LVIII.

units.la: Ipse vero sublatis oculis suis in discipulos, dicebat: Beati pauperes quia vestrum est regnum Dei. Beati, qui nunc esuritis: quia saturabimini. Beati, qui nunc fletis: quia ridebitis. Beati eritis, cum vos oderint homines, & separauerint vos, & conuitiati fuerint vobis, & nomen vestrum ut malum eiecerint, propter Filium hominis. Gaudete in illo die & exultate. Ecce enim merces vestra multa est in coelis. Nam itidem faciebant prophetis patres eorum.
units.tr: And he, lifting up his eyes on his disciples, said: "Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who now hunger, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you when men hate you, and separate you from them, and revile you, and cast out your name as evil, for the sake of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven. For their fathers did the same to the prophets."

units.la: Paulus Apostolus Iesum Christum nobis a Deo patre non modo iustitiam, sed sapientiam quoq; factum, & in eodem omnes thesauros sapientiae & cognitionis Dei absconditos esse testatur. Vt ergo hic humani generis redemptor est unicus, ita catholicus quoque veritatis aeternae doctor est, quem omnes audire & sequi debent, qui seruari volunt. Et functus est quidem ille doctoris officio fidelissime, quam diu in terris vitam egit: at quia has peracto redemptionis nostrae negotio relicturus, & corpus quod ex Virgine matre assumpsit, in coelestes beatae immortalitatis sedes subuecturus erat, discipulos sibi aliquot delegit, quos familiarius institueret, & deinde eorundem opera in Euangelij doctrina per totum orbem propaganda veteretur. De his nuper dixit Lucas, & eorum nomina recensuit. In praesenti vero integram Christi concionem describit, ut ex ea omnibus constet, quae illa doctrina sit, quam ipsi postea praedicare debuerunt. Et meretur concio illa diligentem considerationem, partim quia summam praeceptorum Christi continet, & proinde ad omnium hominum institutionem plurimum facit: partim quia canonis & Lydij lapidis instar est, ad quem doctrinas omnes probare, & veram a falsis discernere possumus. Partes illius sunt quatuor. Prima de summo hominis bono disserit, et in quo nam felicitas aut beatitudo sita sit, docet. Secunda charitatis Christianae praecepta tradit, ubi priuatam vindictam maxime prohibet. Tertia doctores instituit, docens ut hi admonitiones & reprehensiones cum publicas tum priuatas instituere debeant. Postrema vere pietatis studium graviter commendat, & hanc a falsa sive simulata distinguit.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul testifies that Jesus Christ has been made for us by God the Father not only righteousness but also wisdom, and that in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of God are hidden. Therefore, just as he is the only redeemer of the human race, so he is also the true teacher of eternal truth, whom all who wish to be saved must hear and follow. He faithfully discharged the office of teacher for as long as he lived on earth. But since he was about to leave these things once the work of our redemption was finished, and to carry the body he had taken from the Virgin Mother up to the heavenly seats of blessed immortality, he chose for himself several disciples, whom he might instruct more closely, and through whose work the doctrine of the Gospel might afterwards be spread throughout the whole world. Luke recently spoke of these and recounted their names. In the present passage he describes the whole sermon of Christ, so that from it everyone may learn what that doctrine is which they were afterwards bound to preach. That sermon deserves careful consideration, partly because it contains the sum of Christ's precepts and so contributes greatly to the instruction of all people, and partly because it serves as a rule and a touchstone by which we can test all doctrines and distinguish the true from the false. It has four parts. The first treats of the highest good of man and teaches in what happiness or blessedness consists. The second gives the precepts of Christian love, where it above all forbids private vengeance. The third instructs teachers, teaching that they must give admonitions and rebukes both public and private. The last earnestly commends the zeal of true piety and distinguishes it from false or feigned piety.

units.la: Non temere autem a beatitudine aut felicitate dicendi exordium facit. Constat enim omnes homines huius desiderio naturali teneri, eius vero consequendae viam ignorare, neque hanc invenire faciats posse, quoad sui ingenij aut humanæ rationis acumen sequuntur. Exemplo nobis sunt philosophi, qui omnes de summo hominis bono magna animorum contentione disputauerunt, & in varias sententias scissi sunt, quarum tamen nulla veritatis scopum attigit. Et inter Iudæos non vnam viam in hoc consequendo omnes tenuisse, ex diuersis sectis apparet, quas annis circiter centum et triginta ante Christi in carne aduentum exortas fuisse alibi diximus. Necesse igitur erat disputationibus illis semel finem imponere, quod nemo commodius et maiori cum authoritate facere poterat, quàm filius Dei, cuius aduentū sancti omnes tot seculis expectarant. Quia autem pleriq; felicitatem in huius seculi bonis consistere arbitrantur, & discipulos ex communi errore, qui tunc inter Iudæos regnabat, regnum terrenum somniare Christus sciebat, errori huic ab initio statim occurrit, & aduersus omnes hominum prophanorum sententias docet, beatitatem veram non in terrenis bonis inueniri, sed in cœlestium bonorum possessione consistere, huius autem seculi afflictionibus aut miserijs adeo non tur bari, vt potius per has nobis ad illam accessus pateat. Vnde colligit, nō miseros aut infelices esse, qui cum paupertate conflictantur, qui esuriunt, plorant, mundi odia, cŏuitia, probra & persecutiones sustinent; sed potius beatos censeri debere, quòd pulcherrima virtutis exercenda materia ipsis proposita sit, laborum autem & afflictionum præmium immarcessibile in cœlis habeant, quo olim æternum fruentur. Et quia hoc carni persuadere admodum difficile est, & eorum quoq;, quæ tam didicimus, facile obliviscimur, sententijs breuibus quidem sed grauissimis & primo intuitu paradoxis, rem omnem comprehendit. Sunt hæ quatuor numero, quibus totidem contrarias opponit, quæ mundi stulti-tiam cofutant apertius, qui in ijs beatitatem quærit, quæ potius extremæ infelicitatis materia præ-bent. Quàmuis autem (vt ex Matthæo patet) doctrina generalis hic proponatur, & magnæ hominum multitudini Christus ex sublimiori loco concionatus sit, in præsenti tamen sermonem ad discipu-los conuertit, qui propter difficillimam apostolatus functionem, cui destinati erat, præ alijs institutio-ne & consolatione diligentiori opus habebant. Audiamus ergo de ijs cocionantem Christum, quæ no-bis ad beatitatem viam sternunt. Primum. Beati (inquit) pauperes, quia vestrum est regnum Dei. Opponitur sententia hæc dire stè huius mundi iudicio, qui vnanimi consensu eos demum beatos & felices dicit, qui diuitijs abundant, & ideo illos in honore & pretio habet, & ijsdem quiduis audendi impunitatem concedit. Estq; error hic omnium perniciosissimus. Ex eo enim insanum illud ditescendi studium enascitur, quod vt curis et laboribus immodicis corpus fatigat, ita animam quoq; vitijs atrocissimis grauat. Nam vt Paulus ait, qui ditescere volunt, ij incidunt in tentationem & laqueum & cupiditates multas ame-tes & damnosas, quæ demergunt homines in exitium et interitum. E contra nihil egestate infelicius & intolerabilius esse vulgò putatur, & ideo vt hanc effugiant pleriq; nihil nō sibi licere arbitrantur. At omnibus istis hoc dictum Christus opponit, ita nimirum admonens, vt apertis animi oculis rem ipsam propius inspiciamus, ne nobis communis ille vulgi errori imponat. At hic ante omnia diligenter videndum erit, de quibus sermo sit. Paupertas enim, si per se consideretur, res media est, vt & diuitiæ: imò constat quibusdam paupertatem ex Dei maledi-ctione incumbere, vt eis exitij causam afferat: & vt inter electos Dei cultores aliquos fuisse scimus diuitijs illustres: ita ex pauperum numero multi impatientia superati ea designant, quæ ipsis à Dei veri cognitione & timore alienissimos esse declarant. Apertius ergo Matthæus Christi mentem expressit, qui pauperes spiritu nominat. At spiritus vocabulo hominis mentem siue animum deno-tari hoc loco, non est dubium. Sunt ergo pauperes spiritu primùm ij, qui contemptis omnibus, quo-rum fiducia plerique ingentes spiritus animo concipiunt, in vno Deo sperant, & in hoc sibi bona omnia reposita esse neuerunt. Deinde, qui aduersis & ærumnis fracti, ad diuinæ misericordiæ thronum recurrunt, seque supplices illius voluntati submittunt. Denique pauperes spiritu di-cuntur, qui neque in semetipsis neque in toto hoc mundo aliquid habent, cuius fiducia vel aduersus Deum vel homines superbiant. His opponuntur, qui suarum virium & propria dignitatis fiducia inflati, nihil non sibi promittunt, & si quid ipsis præter animi sententiam accidit, mox ad-uersus Deum fremunt, & ab hoc sibi iniuriam fieri arbitrantur. Damnant hos passim sacræ literæ, alteres vero illos in præsenti Christus felices atque beatos pronuntiat, & ab his doctri-nam hanc orditur, quia hoc obedientiæ fidei principium est, qua in primis delectatur Deus & quæ in quouis aduersorum genere patientes facit. Qui enim eò vsq; profecerunt, vt suos spiritus domare norint, ij tam de huius sæculi rebus quàm de seipsis rectè iudicant. Et illas quidem vanas atq; corruptibiles esse, seipsos verò peccatores & quouis supplicio dignos esse intelligunt. Itaq; non efferuntur præsentium bonorũ fiducia, sed ita illis vt student, ne abutantur: neq; indignius ferunt, si illa Deus eripiat, sed cum Iobo Dei nomen prædicant, & huius iudicia iusta, sanĉta & salutaria esse fatentur. Est ergo hæc spiritus paupertas certissima animi pax, adeoq; portius tutissimus aduersus omnes turbines, quibus mundus hic agitatur: ideoq; si nihil aliud accedat, præ alijs beati sunt, quibus illa frui datum est.
units.tr: He does not begin his discourse on blessedness or happiness without reason. For it is agreed that all people are held by a natural desire for it, but that they do not know the way to attain it, and cannot find it, so long as they follow only the keenness of their own wit or human reason. The philosophers are examples for us: they all disputed about the highest good of man with great contention of minds, and were torn into various opinions, none of which, however, reached the goal of truth. And that among the Jews not all followed one way of attaining it is clear from the different sects, which, as we have said elsewhere, arose about a hundred and thirty years before the coming of Christ in the flesh. It was therefore necessary to put an end once and for all to those disputes, and no one could do this more fittingly and with greater authority than the Son of God, whose coming all the saints had awaited for so many ages. But since most people think happiness consists in the goods of this age, and since Christ knew that the disciples, from the common error which then reigned among the Jews, were dreaming of an earthly kingdom, he met this error at once from the beginning, and against all the opinions of profane men he teaches that true blessedness is not found in earthly goods but consists in the possession of heavenly goods; and that it is not disturbed by the afflictions or miseries of this age, but rather that through these the way to it is opened to us. Hence he concludes that those are not wretched or unhappy who struggle with poverty, who hunger, weep, and endure the hatred, reproaches, insults and persecutions of the world; but rather that they ought to be counted blessed, because the most beautiful matter for exercising virtue is set before them, and because they have in heaven an unfading reward for their labours and afflictions, which they will one day enjoy for ever.
