And because this is very difficult to persuade the flesh, and because we also easily forget even what we have learned well, he sums up the whole matter in sayings that are brief but most weighty, and at first sight seem paradoxical. There are four of them, and against each he sets a contrary one, which more plainly refutes the folly of the world, which seeks blessedness in those things that rather provide the matter of extreme unhappiness. Although, as is clear from Matthew, this doctrine is set forth in general, and Christ preached from a higher place to a great multitude, nevertheless here he turns his speech to the disciples, who, because of the very difficult office of apostleship for which they were destined, needed more careful instruction and consolation than others. Let us then hear Christ preaching about those things which pave the way for us to blessedness. First: "Blessed," he says, "are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." This saying is directly opposed to the judgment of this world, which with one accord calls those people blessed and happy who abound in riches, and therefore honours and esteems them, and grants them impunity to dare whatever they like. And this error is the most pernicious of all. For from it arises that mad eagerness to grow rich, which, as it wearies the body with immoderate cares and labours, so it also burdens the soul with the most atrocious vices. For, as Paul says, those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge men into destruction and perdition. On the contrary, it is commonly thought that nothing is more unhappy and intolerable than want, and so, in order to escape it, most people think they may do anything at all. But Christ sets this saying against all of these, plainly admonishing us, so that with the eyes of our mind open we may look more closely at the thing itself, and not let that common error of the crowd deceive us. Here, however, we must first of all look carefully at what is being discussed. For poverty, considered in itself, is a neutral thing, just as riches are; indeed, it is agreed that for some poverty comes from the curse of God, to bring them to ruin; and just as we know that some of the chosen worshippers of God were illustrious for their riches, so from the number of the poor many, overcome by impatience, show by their conduct how far removed they are from the knowledge and fear of the true God. Matthew therefore expressed Christ's meaning more plainly when he called them poor in spirit. There is no doubt that by the word spirit is here meant the mind or soul of man. Those, then, are poor in spirit, first, who, having despised all those things in whose confidence most people conceive great pride of soul, hope in the one God alone, and know that all good things are laid up for them in him. Then, those who, broken by adversities and troubles, flee to the throne of divine mercy, and submit themselves as suppliants to his will. Finally, those are said to be poor in spirit who have nothing in themselves or in this whole world in whose confidence they might boast either against God or against men. Opposed to these are those who, puffed up with confidence in their own strength and proper dignity, promise themselves everything, and if anything happens to them against their own judgment, at once they rage against God and think that an injury is being done to them by him. Holy Scripture everywhere condemns these people; but Christ now pronounces the others happy and blessed, and from them he begins this teaching, because this is the principle of obedient faith, in which God above all takes delight, and which makes people patient in every kind of adversity. For those who have advanced so far as to know how to tame their spirits judge rightly both of the affairs of this age and of themselves. They understand that the former are vain and perishable, and that they themselves are sinners and deserving of any punishment. Therefore they are not puffed up with confidence in present goods, but use them as they ought, so as not to abuse them; nor do they bear it with less equanimity if God takes them away, but with Job they bless the name of God and confess that his judgments are just, holy and salutary. This poverty of spirit is therefore the surest peace of mind, and indeed the safest harbour against all the storms with which this world is troubled; and so, even if nothing else is added, those to whom it has been granted to enjoy it are blessed beyond others.

units.la: Cæterum amplius quid illis Christus pollicetur? Vestrum (inquit) est regnum Dei. Comprehendit hoc omnem felicitatem hominis tam præsentis quàm futuri seculi. Qui enim Dei regno fruuntur, & hunc in se regnantem habent, ijs nihil in hoc mundo deesse, nihil item nocere potest. Est enim Deus reuera fons bonorum omnium, adhæc suorum vindex & tutor, qui pericula omnia vel repellit, vel in medijs periculorum fluctibus mirificè seruat. Superat autem hæc omnia, quòd illos spiritu suo regit, ne quid vel in secundis vel aduersis præter officium faciant. Vbi verò huius vitæ finem illi attigerunt, tunc ad regni illius cœlestis & æterni professionem transeunt, & Christi cohæredes fiunt, cui seruierunt. Et est hic obseruatu dignißimum, quòd etsi huius vitæ commoda Christus prolixè polliceri potuisset, solius tamen regni Dei meminit. Vult enim suos non in præsentis seculi bonis hærere, quæ caduca & instabilia sunt, sed in sola cœlestia et æterna respicere, vt horum spe confirmati omnem huius vitæ fortunam patienter ferant.
units.tr: Moreover, what more does Christ promise them? "Yours," he says, "is the kingdom of God." This comprehends all the happiness of man, both in the present age and in the age to come. For those who enjoy the kingdom of God, and have it reigning within them, lack nothing in this world, and nothing can harm them. God is truly the fountain of all good things, and moreover the avenger and guardian of his own, who either drives off all dangers or wonderfully preserves them amid the waves of peril. But this surpasses all: he rules them by his Spirit, so that they do nothing contrary to duty, whether in prosperity or in adversity. When they have reached the end of this life, they then pass over to the profession of that heavenly and eternal kingdom, and become co-heirs of Christ, whom they served. And it is most worthy of notice that, although Christ could have promised abundantly the blessings of this life, he mentions only the kingdom of God. For he wills that his people not cling to the goods of the present age, which are frail and unstable, but look only to things heavenly and eternal, so that, strengthened by the hope of these, they may bear patiently every lot of this life.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Christi sermone, qui secundo loco dicit: Beati qui nunc esuritis, quia saturabimini. Est hoc plus quiddam, quàm quod initiò dixerat. Sunt enim aliqui pauperes quidem, sed qui suriunt, non esuriunt, tenui autem & frugali victu contenti, vitam quietam & tranquillam agunt. Et hos gentium quoq; sapientes beatos dixerunt, quòd felicius viuant ijs, qui circa opes immodicas tumultuantur, aut etiam reipub. negotijs non minus periculosis quàm grauibus sunt occupati. Ex horum numero Solon Aglarum beatum esse putauit, quòd fines patrij agelli nunquam excessisset. At si eò vsq; paupertatis onus excrescat, vt samem & suriem pati necesse sit, id demum omnibus miserrimum videtur. Nec temere samem malesuadam dixerunt veteres, cùm viderent huius impatientia multos ad ea perpetranda adduci, de quibus antea ne cogitarant quidem. Et huc sapiens ille respexit, qui ne vel opibus magnis ditaretur, vel ad inopiam extremam adigeretur, Deum orabat, nè videlicet opum fiducia elatus Dei timorem excuteret, aut egestate intolerabili victus furaretur, vel Dei nomen abnegaret. Porrò hic quoq; vulgi sententiam Christus corrigit, & docet nihil obstare, quò minus beati & felices sint etiam ij, qui omnibus necessarijs destituti extrema inopia laborant. Et apud Matthæum eos nominat, qui iustitiam seruiunt & sitiunt. Quod dictum bifariam exponi potest. Primùm de ijs, quos hostium tyrannis & iniuriæ acceptæ ita exagitant, vt nihil peræque esuriant atq; sitiant, quàm vt iudices ipsis dentur iusti, à quibus causa ipsorum cognoscatur. In horum numero sunt ij, quibus sua bona vel erepta sunt, vel per vim detinentur, vt illis non possint vti, quæ ipsis iure debebantur. Solet hoc frequenter pijs accidere dum in hoc mundo peregrinantur, vt non modò improborum vim ferant, sed insuper iudices quoque sibi infensos & tribunalia omnia clausa esse videant. Habentur enim pro turbulentis, seditiosis & rixosis, quibus nihil satisfaciat, sicq; iniquus præiudicijs circumuenti ius suum obtinere non possunt. Passi sunt hoc Israelitæ sub Pharaonis tyrannide, qui illis libertatem à maioribus suis concessam, præter omne meritum eripuit, operibus & laboribus gratuitis eosdem miserè exercuit, et operum exactores non minus crudeles quàm iniquos illis imposuit. Dauidem quoq; Saulis iniusta vis coegit, vt ad Dei tribunal prouocaret, cùm nemo inter homines esset, qui causam suam audire vellet, vel audire auderet. Et prophetis hoc ipsum frequenter accidisse constat. Quæ verò Christianorum conditio olim sub Imperatoribus fuerit, ecclesiasticæ historiæ abunde docent. Iulianus certè illos, si de bonis ereptis aut iniurijs sibi factis quererentur, cum ludibrijs excipiebat, indignè illos facere dicens, qui iure agere vellent, & non potius secundùm præceptoris sui Christi præceptum tunicam quoq; ijs dare, qui pallium abstulissent, & maxillam alteram obuertere, si quando essent percussi. Neque in melius mutata est piorum sors, & hodie quidui licet cuiuis in eos dicere, qui Christi nomen professi aliorum superstitiones atque tyrannidem. nidem damnant: & ea est multis in locis impiorum violentia, vt pijs tutius sit atrocissimas iniu-rias silendo concoquere, quàm ius suum persequendo sese periculis grauioribus obijcere. Taceo nunc eos, qui à parentibus exhæredantur, & quorum hæreditates intercipiuntur ab alijs, hanc vnam ob causam, quòd fidem Christo datam fallere nolunt. Esuriunt hi omnes iustitiam, neq; alia fames grauior & intolerabilior est, quàm si ius suum obtinere non possint, qui se causam bonam tueri norunt, interim vero ipsis esurientibus, impijssimos nebulones in iis bonis voluptuari & libidinari videns, quæ ipsis iure debebantur. At Christus hos omnes beatos pronuntiat, et causam sui dicti affert, Quia saturabuntur: ita fore docens, vt tandem votorum compotes fiant, & ius suum obtineant. Est enim Deus afflictorum vindex & patronus fidelissimus, neq; eorum preces negligit. Testatur hoc ipse in Lege, quando monet, ne quis peregrinos affligat, aut viduis atq; pupillis vim faciat. Clamabunt enim ad me (inquit) & ego exaudiam, & excandescet furor meus, et interficiam vos gladio, &c. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, passim occurrunt. Nam Deo vindice olim Israelitæ liberati sunt, & debitam sibi mercedem ab Ægyptijs receperūt. Eundem iudicem iustum Dauid sensit, quando Saul extinctio ipse in regni fastigium euectus est. Et hodie frequenter fieri videmus, vt vel sua recipiant, vel alia ratione ditentur, qui diu inediam passi sunt. Quòd si nonnulli pauperes & egeni moriuntur, adeoq; cum publica ignominia vitam hanc finiunt, nihilominus tamen ij quoq; saturantur. Nam vere beata eorum mors est, quæ quam diu exoptarunt, laborum suorum finem & vitæ æternæ possessionem ipsis affert: simul vero Deus apud posteros innocentiam eorum asseris & famæ consulit, vt sancti & pij dicantur, qui facinorosorum instar habiti fuerunt. Fruuntur hac gloria hodie prophetæ & Apostoli apud eos quoq;, qui de ipsorum doctrina & fide adhuc parum honorificè sentiunt. Olim vero in totius mundi conspectu saturabuntur, quando Dei filius in nubibus cœli ad iudicandum veniet, & ipsi quidem coram oppressoribus suis (vt in libro Sapientiæ scribitur) in gloria comparebunt, & dulcem illam Christi vocem audient, quaeos ad sui regni consortium vocabit, alteri vero illi cum diabolo ad æternas inferorum pœnas remittentur. Hæc vt pios Christi cultores ad patientiam armare, sic impios tyrannos terrere debet, ne vim illis faciant, qui vindicem habent eum, ad cuius tribunal procul dubio sistentur, vt digna suis factis præmia in proprijs corporibus recipiant. Vide Matth.25.2. Corinth.5.
units.tr: But let us go on to Christ's words, which in the second place say: "Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be satisfied." This is something more than what he had said at first. For there are some who are poor indeed, but who do not hunger; content with a thin and frugal diet, they live a quiet and tranquil life. Even the wise men of the nations have called these blessed, because they live more happily than those who are caught up in immoderate wealth, or who are occupied with public affairs no less dangerous than burdensome. Of this number, Solon thought Aglaus blessed, because he had never gone beyond the bounds of his ancestral field. But if the burden of poverty grows to such a point that one must suffer hunger and famine, this seems to all the most wretched of conditions. Nor did the ancients rightly call hunger an evil counsellor, since they saw that its impatience drove many to commit deeds they had not even thought of before. To this the wise man looked, who prayed God that he be neither enriched with great wealth nor driven to extreme want; lest, lifted up by confidence in riches, he cast off the fear of God, or, driven by intolerable need of food, should steal, or deny the name of God. Here too Christ corrects the opinion of the crowd, and teaches that nothing stands in the way of those also who, destitute of all necessities and labouring under extreme want, are blessed and happy. And in Matthew he names those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. This saying can be explained in two ways. First, of those whom the tyranny of enemies and the wrongs they have received so harass that they hunger and thirst for nothing more than for just judges to be given to them, by whom their cause may be heard. In this number are those whose goods have either been snatched away or are held by force, so that they cannot use what was rightly theirs. This often happens to the godly while they wander in this world, so that they not only bear the violence of the wicked but also see judges hostile to them and all tribunals closed. For they are considered troublesome, seditious and quarrelsome, and nothing satisfies such people; thus, circumvented by prejudices, they cannot obtain their right. The Israelites suffered this under the tyranny of Pharaoh, who, without any merit on their part, snatched away the liberty their forefathers had granted them, cruelly wore them down with unpaid works and labours, and set over them taskmasters no less cruel than unjust. The unjust violence of Saul also compelled David to appeal to God's tribunal, when there was no one among men who would, or dared, hear his cause. And it is clear that the prophets frequently suffered the same. What the condition of Christians was under the emperors of old, ecclesiastical history teaches abundantly. Julian, at any rate, met with mockery those who complained of goods seized or wrongs done to them, saying that they acted unworthily who wished to go to law, and did not rather, following their teacher Christ's precept, give the tunic also to those who had taken the cloak, and turn the other cheek when struck. Nor has the lot of the godly changed for the better; today anyone may say what he likes against those who, professing the name of Christ, condemn the superstitions and tyranny of others. In many places the violence of the impious is such that it is safer for the godly to swallow most atrocious injuries in silence than, by pursuing their right, to expose themselves to graver dangers. I pass over now those who are disinherited by their parents, and whose inheritances are seized by others, for this one reason alone: that they will not break the faith given to Christ. All of these hunger for righteousness. No hunger is more grievous or more intolerable than when one who knows how to defend a good cause cannot obtain his right, and, while he himself hungers, sees the most impious scoundrels reveling and wallowing in those goods which were rightly due to him. But Christ pronounces all of these blessed, and gives the reason for his saying: "For they shall be satisfied," teaching that it will come about, so that at last they become masters of their desires and obtain their right. For God is the faithful avenger and most sure patron of the afflicted, nor does he neglect their prayers. He himself testifies this in the Law, when he warns that no one should afflict strangers or do violence to widows and orphans: "For they will cry to me," he says, "and I will hear them, and my anger will burn, and I will slay you with the sword," etc. Examples proving this occur everywhere. For under God as avenger the Israelites were once freed, and received from the Egyptians the wages due to them. The same just judge David experienced, when Saul was put to death and David himself was raised to the summit of the kingdom. And today we often see that those who have long suffered want either recover what is theirs or are enriched in some other way. But if some poor and needy die, and so end this life with public disgrace, nevertheless they too are satisfied. For truly blessed is their death, which brings them the end of their labours, which they have long desired, and the possession of eternal life; and at the same time God, among posterity, vindicates their innocence and provides for their reputation, so that those who were held as criminals are called holy and godly. The prophets and apostles enjoy this glory today even among those who still think rather poorly of their doctrine and faith. But in time to come they will be satisfied in the sight of the whole world, when the Son of God comes in the clouds of heaven to judge; they themselves will appear in glory before their oppressors (as is written in the Book of Wisdom), and will hear that sweet voice of Christ calling them to share his kingdom, while those others will be sent with the devil to the eternal punishments of hell. This saying ought to arm the godly worshippers of Christ to patience, and to terrify impious tyrants, lest they do violence to those who have as their avenger him before whose tribunal they will without doubt be set, to receive in their own bodies rewards worthy of their deeds. See Matth.25.2. Corinth.5.

units.la: Potest deinde hæc Christi sententia altiori aut allegorico sensu de iis exponi, qui veram iustitiam esuriunt, in hoc vnum scilicet totis animis intenti, vt & ipsi pro iustis Deo probentur, & vt iustitia publice apud omnes regnet. Est hoc votum commune electorum omnium, quibus acutissime dolet, quòd se peccatores esse & legem peccati in membris suis vigere sentiunt, qua præter hominis interioris voluntatem ad ea abripiuntur, quæ Deo improbari & damnatione digna esse norunt. Clamant ergo cum Paulo Apostolo: O nos infelices, quis nos liberabit à corpore mortis? Non minus autem ijsdem dolet, si plerosque deuoto animo in omne scelus ruere, pios autem contra ius & leges publicas affligi, spoliari & opprimi videant. Exemplum huius doloris in Lotho Petrus proponit, quem inter Sodomæos molestissima hominum libidinosissimorum & nefariorum conuersatione fatigatum fuisse scribit, cùm animam suam iustam quotidie iniquis illorum factis videndo & audiendo excruciaret. Quod ipsum hodie multis in hac mundi quotidie in peius vergentis senesta accidit. Qui omnes sancta fame accensi ingemiscunt, & cum Ioanne orant: Veni Domine Iesu. Et cum prophetis: Quousque Domine clamo, & non exaudis? vociferor ad te ob violentiam, & non seruas? Cur ostendis mihi iniquitatem, & facis vt aspiciam molestiam? &c. Atsaturantur hi quoq; omnes suo tempore. Quoad ipsos enim, iustitiam veram in Christo Iesu per fidem inueniunt. Adhæc erit aliquando, neq; procul abest, infelicis huius mundi finis, in quo Christus persus abolita diaboli tyrannide, sempiternæ iustitiæ regnum suscitabit, in quo nulla vis & nulla iniquitas dominabitur.
units.tr: This saying of Christ can further be explained in a higher or allegorical sense, of those who hunger for true righteousness, intent with their whole souls on this one thing: that they themselves may be approved by God as righteous, and that righteousness may reign publicly among all. This is the common desire of all the elect, who grieve most keenly that they feel themselves to be sinners, and that the law of sin flourishes in their members, by which, against the will of the inner man, they are dragged to those things which they know are displeasing to God and worthy of condemnation. So they cry out with the apostle Paul: "O wretched men that we are! Who will deliver us from the body of this death?" Yet they grieve no less when they see many rushing headlong into every crime with devoted minds, while the godly are afflicted, despoiled and oppressed against right and public laws. Peter sets forth an example of this grief in Lot, whom he writes was worn down among the Sodomites by the most troublesome company of the most lustful and wicked men, while he tormented his righteous soul daily by seeing and hearing their unlawful deeds. The same thing happens today to many in this old age of the world, which daily tends for the worse. All of these, kindled with holy hunger, groan and pray with John: "Come, Lord Jesus." And with the prophets: "How long, Lord, shall I cry, and you not hear? I cry out to you about violence, and you do not save? Why do you show me iniquity, and make me look upon trouble?" etc. But all these too are satisfied in their time. For as far as they are concerned, they find true righteousness in Christ Jesus through faith. Moreover, there will be an end to this unhappy world, and it is not far off, in which Christ, having utterly abolished the tyranny of the devil, will raise up the kingdom of everlasting righteousness, in which no violence and no iniquity will hold sway.

units.la: Tertiò, Beati (inquit) qui nunc fletis, quia ridebitis. Facit hoc quoq; ad eorum, quæ præcesserunt amplificationem & confirmationem. Sunt enim quidam eo ingenio præditi, vt quamuis fortunam negligant, & tantum non exuto omni humanitatis sensu nullis casibus moveantur: quos vulgus beatos dicit, quia nihil sentiunt, aut etiam sentire nolunt. Sed non magis illi beati sunt quàm trunci & lapides, imò eò miseriores sunt, quòd cum sensu rationem quoque exuerunt. At longè aliter affecti sunt pij, qui procul relicta indolentia illa Stoica, tam proprijs quam alienis malis commouen-tur, & ita quidem, vt in lachrymas quoq; erumpant, neq; dissimulare possunt, quem animo concepe-runt, dolorem. Hos autem propterea miseros & infelices esse Christus negat, quin potius beatos pro-nuntiat. Et opponitur haec etiam sententia directè vulgi iudicio. Plerique enim beatos dicunt, quibus datum est in tripudijs, ludis, comessationibus & gaudio vitam transfigere, & qui securè omnia neglí-gunt, quibus alij vel priuatim vel publicè premuntur. Hinc supina illa securitas & Cyclopicus in-diciorum Dei contemptus, quem in sui seculi hominibus prophetae passim accusant, & quem nouissi-mis temporibus regnaturum Christus praedixit. At idem hic eos potius felices esse dit, qui vitam in pijs lachrymis transigunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, "Blessed are those who now weep, for they shall laugh" (he says). This also serves to amplify and confirm what has gone before. For there are some men so constituted that, though they disregard their fortune and have all feeling of humanity stripped away, they are moved by no misfortunes. The crowd calls these people blessed, because they feel nothing, or even refuse to feel. But they are no more blessed than stumps and stones; indeed they are more wretched, since with feeling they have also lost reason. The godly, however, are affected quite differently. Far from that Stoic insensibility, they are moved by their own troubles and by those of others, so much so that they break out into tears and cannot hide the grief they have conceived in their hearts. Christ, however, denies that these are wretched and unhappy; rather he pronounces them blessed. This saying is also directly opposed to the judgement of the crowd. For most people call blessed those who are allowed to spend their lives in revelry, games, feasting and joy, and who carelessly ignore everything by which others are oppressed, privately or publicly. Hence that supine complacency and Cyclopean contempt of God's judgements, which the prophets everywhere lay to the charge of the men of their own age, and which Christ foretold would reign in the last times. Here, however, he says rather that those are happy who spend their lives in godly tears.

units.la: Vbi ante omnia videre oportet, de quibus Dominus loquitur. Atqui discipulis suis illum lo-qui, verborum contextus docet, sub quibus pios siue credentes omnes comprehendi non est dubium, quando eadem omnium illorum sors est. Flere autem illos dicit, quia hoc fere illis proprium est, cum nouae indies lachrymarum causae illis occurrant. Est enim vita haec, si nihil aliud accedat, vallis lachrymarum (vt Dauid us verbo vtar) in quam ex vtero matris cum fletu & eiulatu ingre-dimur, & quem tunc incipimus fletum perpetua quasi serie continuamus. Quo Iacobus respiciens, vitam suam peregrinationem vocat, cuius dies quidem non admodum multi, sed acerbi & labo-riosi sint. Sed non tam propter communem omnium sortem plorant pij, quàm quod innatam sibi na-turae suae vitiositatem quotidie sentiunt, & ex hac enascentibus peccatis sese indies grauari cer-nunt. Nec enim possunt non vehementer dolere, quando Dei iram simul animo concipiunt, quam se peccatis suis meruisse non possunt negare. Et hae sunt sanctae illae lachrymae, quibus Dauid olim lectum suum rigabat, & quibus peccatrix illa (de qua Capite septimo dicetur) pedes Domini abluit. Hic pius ille dolor est, qui Paulum exclamare coegit: Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit ab hoc corpore mortis? Accedit huic dolori alius grauior, quòd simul mundum totum incurabili malitia in proprium interitum ruere vident. Quia enim & gloriam Dei prouectam volunt, & omnium ho-minum saluti consultum cupiunt, non possunt eam infelicis mundi conditionem siccis oculis intueri, qua plerique & Dei gloriam conculcant, & sibijpsis exitium accersunt. Sic Lothum semetipsum ex cruciauisse Petrus scribit (vt paulo ante diximus) cum inter Sodomaeos ageret. Sic Mosi conti-nuum luctum peperit Israelitarum contumacia. Sic Saulem à Deo reprobatum flebat Samuel: & Paulo Iudaicae gentis perditio sic doluit, vt pro illis anathema fieri optaret. Quae satis docent, quàm alieni sint à spiritu Christi, qui alijs scandalorum authores sunt, & ita pios in nouas quotidie lachrymas conjiciunt. His adde nefarios impiorum conatus, qui pios vna cum religione omnino extinctos volunt, vt mox sequetur. Et hic quidem inter persecutiones vberrimus lachrymarum fons sese aperit: qui tunc maximè augetur, quando pij à sociis se deseri vident, de quorum fide & auxilio sibi optima quaeque pollicebantur. Solet enim fere fieri, vt dum quisque sibi consulit, alios in periculis turpiter deferat: vt iam nihil de illis dicamus, qui vel proditorio animo cum hostibus colludunt, vel saltem horum artibus sese circumueniri patiuntur, vt suam illis operam praestent. Fiunt haec hodie passim, & qui ista non ofcitanter secum expendunt, non possunt non toti in pias lachry-mas soluti, quia has perpetuas & quasi indiuulsas comites habent, plerique eos miseros & infelices esse arbitrantur.
units.tr: Here, above all, we must see who it is of whom the Lord speaks. That he is speaking to his disciples the context of the words shows, and there is no doubt that all the godly or believers are included under them, since their lot is the same. He says that they weep, because this is almost their own characteristic, since new causes of tears meet them every day. For this life, if nothing else were added, is a vale of tears (to use David's word), into which we enter from our mother's womb with weeping and wailing, and the weeping we then begin we continue in an unbroken series. Looking to this, James calls his life a pilgrimage, whose days are not very many, but bitter and full of toil. Yet the godly weep not so much because of the common lot of all, as because they feel daily the sinfulness of their nature that is in them, and see themselves weighed down day by day by the sins that spring from it. Indeed they cannot but grieve deeply, when at the same time they conceive God's wrath, which they cannot deny they have deserved by their sins. These are those holy tears with which David once watered his bed, and with which that sinful woman (of whom it will be said in chapter seven) washed the feet of the Lord. This is the godly grief that forced Paul to cry out: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" To this grief is added another, heavier, because they see the whole world rushing to its own destruction through incurable wickedness. For since they desire God's glory to advance and wish the salvation of all men to be consulted, they cannot look on the wretched condition of the world with dry eyes, in which many trample underfoot the glory of God and bring destruction on themselves. So Peter writes that Lot tormented himself daily while he lived among the Sodomites (as we said a little earlier). So the stubbornness of the Israelites brought Moses continual mourning. So Samuel wept for Saul, who had been rejected by God; and the ruin of the Jewish nation so grieved Paul that he wished to be made an anathema for them. These things sufficiently show how far removed from the spirit of Christ are those who are authors of scandals to others and so cast the godly into fresh tears every day. To these add the wicked attempts of the impious, who wish the godly to be utterly destroyed together with their religion, as will shortly follow. And here indeed, amid persecutions, a most abundant fount of tears opens up; it is increased above all when the godly see themselves deserted by their companions, on whose faith and help they had promised themselves every good. For it usually happens that while each looks to his own interests, he shamefully deserts others in danger; and we say nothing now of those who either collude with the enemy in treachery, or at least allow themselves to be cajoled by their arts, so as to render them service. These things happen everywhere today, and those who weigh them carefully cannot but dissolve wholly into godly tears; since they have these as constant and, as it were, inseparable companions, many think them wretched and unhappy.

units.la: At Christus (vt modò diximus) eos beatos pronuntiat, & causam dicti sui affert: Quia ride-bitis. Apud Matthaeum consolationem pollicetur, ducem nimirum & vere efficacem, quae dolorem omnem mitiget, simulque animum gaudio sancto atque solido exhilaret. Est ea duplex: Pimò dum hic viuunt, consolationem accipiunt ex diuinae bonitatis argumentis, quae sese non vno modo exe-rit. Nam sese Deo curae esse norunt, & hunc sibi in Christo reconciliatum esse firmiter credunt. Quo-ad verò mundi contumaciam, hanc neque Dei gloriae officere, neque suam salutem ea impediri in-telligunt. Inter afflictiones autem ad Deum clamant, & preces suas ab eo exaudiri, & lachrymas (vt Dauid ait) in Dei lagenulam colligi atque in eius rationarium ascribi sentiunt: adhuc in-ter media pericula auxilio Dei praesenti subleuantur, & inde spem indies maiorem animo conci-piunt. Et huc Paulus respiciens dicebat, pios in afflictionibus quoque gloriari, eò quòd afflictio pa-tientiam efficiat, patientia verò experientiam, experientia autem spem, quae nos fallì aut pudefieri non sinat, cum Dei dilectione tentatur, qua nos in Christo Iesu complexus est. Deinde maior & efficacior consolatio accedit, quam ex futurae vitae gustu pij percipiunt. Mors enim vltima linea rerum huius seculi, vt vitae huic mortali, sic etiam malis quae hunc comitantur, omnibus finem imponit, & illam caelestis vitae hereditas sequitur, in quam recte transeunt, quicunque in fide Christi decedunt. Itaque etsi multa patiantur Christi cultores, quae ipsis gemitus & lachrymas cient, ijdem tamen fide promissionum Dei confirmati intra animos suos gaudio incredibili perfunduntur, quod se crucis Christi socios esse sentiant, simulque mundi infelicis consilia atque spes inanes rident, tandem vero in Christi regnum succedunt, vbi lachrimae omnes abstergentur, suspiria cessant, dolor omnis euanescit, dum in Dei conspectu ipsis bonorum omnium saturitas offertur. Seminant ergo isti omnes cum lachrymis (vt Psalmi verbis vtar) sed metunt cum iubilo, & c. Psal.126.
units.tr: But Christ (as we have just said) pronounces them blessed, and gives the reason for his saying: "for you shall laugh." In Matthew he promises consolation, namely a guide that is truly effective, which softens every grief and at the same time cheers the mind with holy and solid joy. It is twofold. First, while they live here, they receive consolation from the proofs of divine goodness, which show themselves in more ways than one. For they know that they are cared for by God, and they firmly believe that in Christ they have been reconciled to him. As for the world's obstinacy, they understand that it neither harms the glory of God nor hinders their salvation. Amid afflictions they cry out to God, and they feel that their prayers are heard by him, and that their tears (as David says) are gathered into God's little bottle and written into his account book. Still, amid dangers, they are sustained by the present help of God, and from this they conceive greater hope day by day. Looking to this, Paul used to say that the godly also glory in afflictions, because affliction works patience, patience experience, and experience hope, which does not let us be deceived or put to shame, since the love of God, with which he has embraced us in Christ Jesus, is poured out in our hearts. Then a greater and more effective consolation is added, which the godly receive from a foretaste of the life to come. For death, the last boundary of the things of this age, puts an end both to this mortal life and to the evils that accompany it, and the inheritance of heavenly life follows, into which all who die in the faith of Christ pass over. Therefore, although Christ's worshippers suffer many things which draw from them groans and tears, yet, confirmed by faith in God's promises, they are filled within their hearts with incredible joy, because they feel themselves to be partners in the cross of Christ, and at the same time they laugh at the designs and empty hopes of the unhappy world. At length they enter into the kingdom of Christ, where all tears are wiped away, sighs cease, and every grief vanishes, while in the sight of God the fullness of all good things is offered to them. So all these who sow with tears (to use the words of the Psalm) reap with rejoicing, etc. Psalm 126.

units.la: Porro propius ad discipulorum consolationem Christus accedit, & diserte eos de ijs, quae passuri erant, admonet, vt scandalo medeatur, quod ex cruce & persecutionibus enasciturum esse sciebat. Estque huius loci doctrina observatu & meditatu in primis necessaria, eo quod pios sine cruce viuere vix possibile est; & (vt Paulus ait) quotquot volunt pie viuere in Iesu Christo, persecutionem patientur. Poterat hoc mirum videri, & reuera pij ad omnes in honore & precio esse debebant, cum neminem laedant, omnibus autem pro virili benefaciant, atque propter ipsos Deus respub. & omnem mundi huius machinam conseruet. Sed ea est filiorum saeculi huius improbitas, vt nullos alios perinde extinctos cupiat. Causam ipse Christus Ioan. tertio Cap. indicat, quod veritatis lucem mundus oderit, neque ferre possit, vt opera sua mala arguantur. Quia ergo quid discipulis eventurum esset non ignorabat, de his ex professo agit his verbis: Beati eritis cum vos oderint homines, & separauerint vos, & vobis conuitiati fuerint, & nomen vestrum vt malum eiecerint propter Filium hominis: Gaudete in illo die, & c. Quibus verbis discipulos quidem confirmare & praeparare voluit ad certamina, ne periculis improuisis offensi succumberent: at quia simul generalem doctrinam proponit, singulas partes ex ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ comes closer to the consolation of the disciples and plainly warns them of what they were about to suffer, so that he might remedy the scandal which he knew would arise from the cross and persecutions. And the teaching of this passage is especially necessary to observe and meditate upon, since godly people can scarcely live without the cross; and (as Paul says) all who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. This might seem strange, and indeed the godly ought to be held in honour and esteem by all, since they harm no one, but do good to all as far as they can, and for their sake God preserves the commonwealth and the whole machinery of this world. But such is the wickedness of the children of this age that they desire no others to be destroyed so thoroughly. Christ himself indicates the cause in John chapter three, namely that the world hates the light of truth and cannot bear that its evil works be exposed. Therefore, since he knew what would befall the disciples, he deals with it expressly in these words: "Blessed are you when men hate you, and separate you, and revile you, and cast out your name as evil, for the sake of the Son of man: rejoice in that day," etc. By these words he wished to strengthen the disciples and prepare them for the conflicts, lest, taken unawares by dangers, they should give way and be overcome. But since at the same time he sets forth a general teaching, let us look at its individual parts in order.

units.la: Prima, quae piorum in hoc mundo sors sit, docet, & quod vno verbo dici poterat, in suas quasi species distinguit. Et primo quidem hominibus exosos fore ait, quod viro bono admodum grave est. Vt enim pij quosuis amant & omnibus benefaciunt, ita ab alijs etiam amari volunt. Non possunt ergo non dolere, si se alijs inuisos & exosos esse sentiant: in primis vero intolerabile videtur, si ij te oderint, de quibus te optime meritum esse nouisti. At solet hoc pijs Christi cultoribus apudeos etiam accidere, qui nondum omnino mali sunt, & a vi adhuc abstinent. Nam plerique, qui Euangelicae doctrinae fautores videri volunt, ab eorum tamen commercijs abstinent, quos eius zelo ardere sentiunt, & hos morosiores esse aiunt, dum non omnia probant, quibus huius seculi filij delectantur. Superat tamen eorum numerus, qui eo vsq; progrediuntur, vt in illorum morte felicitatem suam omnem continere arbitrentur. Secundo separationis meminit aut exclusionis a Synagoga, quam hodie Excommunicationem dicunt. Erat haec non ignominiosa modo, verumetiam et domestica aduersa et damno sa, eo quod excommunicatus cum nemine contrahere, aut vllis commercijs se immiscere liceret. At qui hanc a Pharisaeis publica authoritate aduersus Christi discipulos decretam fuisse, Ioannes Euangelista Cap.9. & 12. diserte scribit. Et hodie hoc fulmine in primus Pontifices pugnant, quo iam seculis aliquot potentissimos Reges debellarunt, quando non contenti ipsos ab ecclesiae societate excludere, insuper populum eis subiectum fidei aut iurisiurandi dati religione liberatum aduersus ipsos ad arma excitauerunt. Neq; dubium est, maiorum exemplis multos hodie absterreri, ne quod verum esse sciunt profiteantur, neue in suis terris ecclesiarum reformatione instituant. Tertio conuitijs & probris obruendos ait, quibus generosiores animi magis quam armis aut telis ferreis vulnerantur. At his vbiq; diffamatos fuisse Apostolos, Actorum liber testatur. Inter Iudaeos enim accusabantur, & Mosi contradicerent, legis praecepta violarct, templum cum sacris euersum vellent, adeoq; pro publicis hostibus habebatur. Inter gentes vero passim illae seditiosorum voces sonabant. Qui orbe terrarum turbant, venerunt etiam ad nos. Et creuit cum temporis progressu conuitiandi libido eo vsq; vt nullum tam immane & detestabile facinus sit, cuius non insimulati fuerint Christiani. Nam in caetibus suis infantes martare, asini caput adorare, promiscua libidine vti, humanis carnibus vesci, adhaec pacem publicam turbare, cum Romani Imperij hostibus coniurare, disciplinam omne abolere, & suis sceleribus iram Deorum rum aduersus totum mundum pronocare dicebantur. Itaque siue æstus nimius agros adureret, siue aquarum inundationibus fruges perirent, seu grandine vineta vastarentur, siue pestis per vrbes regnaret, aut infelicius aduersus hostes pugnaretur: mox Christiani ad leones, & rogos, ad triremes, in metalla & ad quæuis alia supplicia abripiendi dicebantur, vt suo sanguine Deorum iram placarent. Et quod illis olim accidit, hoc ipsum hodie passim fieri videmus: Imò cùm cuiuis improbo aduersus Christianæ fidei professores quidus fingere liceat, ipsis ad obiecta sibi crimina respondere & innocentiam suam tueri non licet. Sed addit his aliud Christus, quo extrema & æterna infamia significatur. Nam eijcient nomen vestrum (inquit) tanquam malum, id est, dignos iudicabunt, quorum nomen quoq; cum vita prorsus extinguatur. Et hoc quoq; olim factum esse, & hodie adhuc fieri notum est, quàm vt multa demonstratione opus habeat. Huc enim pertinet, quòd fidelium domus apud quosdam solo æquantur, quòd ipsorum familijs totiq; posteritati infamiæ publicæ nota inuritur, quòd item bella suscipiuntur funesta, & vrbes totæ funditus excinduntur, quæ Christi doctrinæ hospitium præbuerunt. At voluit nos de his omnibus admonere Dominus, ne ijs tanquam nouis & inauditis offendamur, simulq; cogitemus, nos propterea non miseros, sed veré beatos esse. Hoc enim ille simul affirmat & sui dicti rationes mox subijciet.
units.tr: The first thing he teaches is what the lot of the godly in this world is, and he divides into what might be called its parts what could have been said in one word. He first says they will be hated by men, which is very hard for a good man to bear. For the godly love everyone and do good to all, and so they also want to be loved by others. They cannot help grieving if they feel that they are hated and disliked by others, and it seems especially intolerable if those who hate you are people to whom you know you have done the greatest service. This commonly happens to the pious worshippers of Christ even among the Jews, who are not yet altogether wicked and still refrain from violence. For many who wish to be seen as supporters of the Gospel nevertheless keep away from the company of those whom they perceive to be burning with zeal for it, and they say these people are too peevish, since they do not approve of everything that the sons of this age delight in. Yet the number of those who go so far as to think all their happiness lies in the death of such people is still greater. Second, he mentions separation or exclusion from the synagogue, which today is called excommunication. This was not only disgraceful but also harmful to domestic life, since an excommunicated person was not permitted to deal with anyone or to take part in any transactions. That this was decreed against the disciples of Christ by public authority of the Pharisees, John the Evangelist writes plainly in chapters 9 and 12. And today the popes fight with this same thunderbolt, with which for several centuries they have overthrown the most powerful kings, when, not content merely to exclude them from the fellowship of the Church, they have also stirred up against them the people subject to them, freed from the bond of faith and of the oath they had sworn. Nor is there any doubt that many today are deterred by the examples of their elders from professing what they know to be true, or from setting up the reformation of the Church in their own lands. Third, he says they will be overwhelmed with insults and reproaches, by which generous spirits are wounded more than by arms or iron weapons. That the apostles were everywhere defamed in this way the Book of Acts bears witness. For among the Jews they were accused of opposing Moses, violating the precepts of the law, and wanting to overthrow the temple and its rites, and so they were regarded as public enemies. Among the Gentiles, too, those cries of seditious men were heard everywhere: "They who have turned the world upside down have come to us also." And with the passing of time the lust for insulting grew to such a point that there is no crime so monstrous and detestable that Christians were not accused of it. For they were said to slaughter infants at their assemblies, to worship the head of an ass, to indulge in promiscuous lust, to feed on human flesh, moreover to disturb the public peace, to conspire with the enemies of the Roman Empire, to abolish all discipline, and by their wickedness to provoke the anger of the gods against the whole world. Thus, whether excessive heat scorched the fields, or floods ruined the crops, or hail laid waste the vineyards, or plague reigned in the cities, or a war against the enemy went badly, the Christians were at once said to be dragged off to the lions and the pyres, to the galleys, to the mines, and to whatever other punishments, so that with their blood they might appease the anger of the gods. And what happened to them then we see happening everywhere today. Indeed, while any wicked person may feign whatever he likes against the professors of the Christian faith, they themselves are not permitted to answer the charges laid against them or to defend their innocence. But Christ adds something else to these, by which extreme and eternal infamy is signified. "They will cast out your name," he says, "as evil," that is, they will judge that the name of those people is worthy to be utterly extinguished along with their life. That this too has happened in the past, and still happens today, is known well enough to need no lengthy demonstration. To this belong the facts that the houses of the faithful are in some places levelled to the ground, that the mark of public infamy is branded upon their families and their whole posterity, and likewise that deadly wars are waged and whole cities utterly destroyed which gave hospitality to the doctrine of Christ. But the Lord wished to warn us of all these things, so that we would not be offended by them as new and unheard of, and at the same time that we would consider that we are for this reason not wretched but truly blessed. For he affirms this at the same time, and he will presently add the reasons for his saying.

units.la: Interim obseruare nos oportet causam, ob quam mundus hic nos odit, separat, conuitijs proscindit, et nominis nostri memoriam excindere studet. Propter filium hominis, inquit, id est, propter me, qui etsi æternus sim Dei filius, hominem tamen assumpsi, vt humani generis vindex sim, miseris autem illis non alius quàm nudus homo videor. Beati ergo eritis (inquam) si ista vobis acciderint propter me: Nimirum quòd mei discipuli & serui sitis, quòd in me speretis, quòd me vnicum humanæ salutis authorè profiteamini, & regnum meum propagare studeatis. Et sanè hæc est causa odiorum & persecutionum omnium, quibus pij exercentur. Nolunt enim superstitiones suas damnari idololatræ, & ideo Christi doctrinam oderunt, quòd per hanc omnes alios cultus excludi, & omnes alias salutis consequendæ rationes reijci audiunt. Et hi cnon ij soli hodie peccant, qui à Christo prosus alieni sunt, verumetiam multi, qui religionem Christianam profitentur, non autem vni Christo fidunt, sed eius merito infinita alia admiscent, quæ non alia quàm humanarum traditionum authoritate nituntur. In hoc certè omnium contentionum cardo vertitur, quæ nobis cum Papistis intercedunt. Nos enim cum Apostolis dicimus, extra Christum Iesum non esse aliud nomen sub cælo hominibus datum, in quo nos seruari oporteat. Illi verò præter Christum Diuos cœlites, operum merita, Romanas indulgentias, purgatorium ignem, Monachorum fraternitates et sexcenta alia nobis obtrudere satagunt. Quæ cum nos admittere non possimus, eò quòd Christi gloria in periculû veniat, propter hunc illi nos oderunt atque persequuntur. Est hæc magna crucis nostræ gloria, cuius consideratio nos confirmare debet, ne vllis aduersariorum iudicijs aut conatibus offendamur. Nam etsi nihil aliud accederet, vnum hoc nostræ beatitudinis testimonium est irrefragabile: quando constat cum Christo in cœlis victuros & regnaturos esse eos, qui cum illo & propter illum moriuntur & huius mundi aduersa ferunt. Debet autem hoc propter eos etiam obseruari, qui se beatos & felices putant propter odia atq; persecutiones, quas non propter Christi nomen, sed propter superstitiones nefarias & impia dogmata sustinent. Gloriabantur olim hoc nomine Donatistæ, contra quos Augustinus dicebat, non pœnam, sed causam martyres facere, neq; martyrum mortem eos habere posse, qui non vitam degunt Christianorum. Quod ipsum hodie Anabaptistæ dici debet, qui crucis Christi gloriam in se transferunt, cùm extra Christi fidem vagentur, & eius ecclesiam impiè discindant. Fateamur quidem in Dei conspectu beatos esse etiam eos, qui scelerum pœnas exoluunt, si pœnitentia non sucata ad Christum conuertantur: quod latronè qui cum illo crucifixus est, fecisse scimus. At hic de illis sermo est, qui propter solum Christum mundi odijs atq; insidijs exercentur: in quorum catalogo nequaquam censeri merentur, qui suas superstitiones & impia dogmata mordicus defendunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile we ought to observe the cause on account of which this world hates us, separates us, tears us with insults, and seeks to root out the memory of our name. "On account of the Son of Man," he says, that is, on account of me, who, although I am the eternal Son of God, have nevertheless taken on man, so that I might be the avenger of the human race, yet to those wretched men I seem to be no more than a bare man. "You will be blessed," I say, "if these things befall you on my account." Namely, because you are my disciples and servants, because you hope in me, because you profess me as the sole author of human salvation, and because you strive to extend my kingdom. And certainly this is the cause of all the hatreds and persecutions with which the godly are tried. For idolaters do not wish their superstitions to be condemned, and therefore they hate the doctrine of Christ, because they hear that through it all other forms of worship are shut out and all other ways of obtaining salvation are rejected. And it is not only those who are utterly alien to Christ who sin in this way today, but also many who profess the Christian religion, yet do not trust in Christ alone, but mingle with his merit countless other things which rest on nothing but the authority of human traditions. Certainly the hinge of all the controversies that lie between us and the Papists turns on this point. For we, with the apostles, say that there is no other name under heaven given to men in which we must be saved, outside Christ Jesus. But they, besides Christ, strive to thrust upon us the heavenly saints, the merits of works, Roman indulgences, the fire of purgatory, the fraternities of monks, and six hundred other things. Since we cannot admit these, because the glory of Christ would thereby be put in danger, for this reason they hate and persecute us. This is the great glory of our cross, and the consideration of it ought to strengthen us, so that we are not offended by any judgments or attempts of our adversaries. For even if nothing else were added, this one testimony of our blessedness is irrefutable: since it is certain that those who die with Christ and for him, and bear the adversities of this world, will live and reign with Christ in heaven. But this must also be observed on behalf of those who think themselves blessed and happy because of the hatreds and persecutions which they suffer, not for the name of Christ, but on account of wicked superstitions and impious dogmas. The Donatists once gloried in this name, against whom Augustine said that it is not the punishment but the cause that makes martyrs, and that those who do not live the life of Christians cannot have the death of martyrs. The same ought to be said today of the Anabaptists, who claim for themselves the glory of the cross of Christ, although they wander outside the faith of Christ and impiously tear apart his Church. Let us indeed admit that in the sight of God those also are blessed who pay the penalties of their crimes, if they turn to Christ in unfeigned repentance, as we know the thief who was crucified with him did. But here the discussion concerns those who are harassed by the hatreds and snares of the world solely on account of Christ, and those who stubbornly defend their superstitions and impious dogmas do not deserve to be counted in that number at all.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt consolationem audiamus, quam propter nomen suum periclitatibus dulcissimam Christus adhibet. Gaudete (inquit) et exultate in illo die. Quasi diceret: Adeò nõ succumbere, aut dolore vosmetipsos conficere debetis, vt potius vobis gaudendû atq; exultandû sit, si quid huius contingat. Id verò duabus rationibus solidissimis confirmat. Prima, Ecce merces vestra multa est in cælis. Demonstratiua particula ad promissionis certitudinem facit, & præmiû quasi præsens ob-
units.tr: But it is time that we hear the consolation which Christ, most sweet to those in peril on account of his name, offers. "Rejoice," he says, "and exult in that day." It is as if he were saying: you ought not to give way or wear yourselves down with grief; rather, you ought to rejoice and exult if anything of this kind befalls you. He confirms this by two very solid reasons. The first: "Behold, your reward is great in heaven." The demonstrative particle adds to the certainty of the promise, and the reward is set before them as if already present, ob-

units.la: Epist. 61. ad Dulcitium.
units.tr: Letter 61, to Dulcitius.

units.la: Causæ persecutionum.
units.tr: The causes of persecutions.

units.la: Consolatio eorum qui persecutionem sustinent. oculos statuit. Hoc autem non definit, vt auari solent, sed multum & vberrimũ fore pollicetur. Ete nim vt Apostolus ait, quae in hoc tempore perpertimur, minime paria sunt futurae gloriae, quae olim revelabitur: & vt Isaias clamat, neq; visu, neq; auditu, imo ne cogitatione quidem comprehendi possunt, quae Deus ijs parauit, qui ipsum diligunt. In caelis vero gloriam hanc nobis monstrat, vt futuram expectemus, & eandem sciamus per mortem non amitti, sed potius inueniri atq; obtineri. In caelis enim patria nostra est, & illic nobis locum parauit Christus, quem non aliter quàm in fide eius merendo ingrediemur. Mercedis autem vocabulo vtitur, non vt meritis nostris aliquid deberi testetur, sed vt doceat compensationem fore laborum & afflictionum, quas hic sustinemus. Et patres imitatur, qui cum filijs nihil debeant, praemij tamen promissione eos ad obedientiae studium pelliciunt. Nam si proprie loqui libeat, gratuitum est quicquid nobis Deus promittit aut largitur, neq; vllus apud eum merito locus est, cum imperfecta, mutila & centonum instar polluta sint quaecunq; à nobis fiunt. Alteram rationem ab exemplo sumit, dicens: Nam itidem faciebant prophetae patres eorum. Quasi dicat: Non primi estis qui hoc saxum voluerit, sed eadem olim prophetarum sors fuit, quorum fama hodie in terris celeberrima est, animae autem in caelis viuunt & regnant. Ad hos ergo nos quoq; colligendos fore pollicetur. Quod vt pij nunquam non cogitare debent, ita horum persecutores meminerint, quorum ipsi aliquando socij futuri sint, nisi ab inceptis desistant: eorum nimirum, qui olim puerunt terrorem suum in terra viuentium (vt Ezechiel dicit) nunc autem apud inferos torquentur, vbi est fletus & stridor dentium. Constat autem ex his omnibus, non miseros, sed beatos nos esse, si propter Christi nomen pauperatem, famem, luctum, odia, contumeliae & persecutiones feramus. Nemine ergo ista offendant. Nam vt amicitia huius mundi est inimicitia cum Deo, ita pro amicis hic eos habet, quos mundus inimicorum loco iudicat. Iudex autem omnis carnis est Iesus Christus, qui (vt in caeci nati historia docemur) ad se colligit, quos impij antistites excludunt. Idem quoq; in medijs periculis suos tuetur, et olim promissa fidei ipsorum praemia retribuet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Consolation for those who endure persecution. He sets it before their eyes. He does not, however, leave it vague, as misers are wont to do, but promises that it will be abundant and very great. For as the Apostle says, the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that shall hereafter be revealed; and as Isaiah cries out, the things that God has prepared for those who love him cannot be grasped by sight, or by hearing, nor even by thought. He shows us this glory in the heavens, so that we may await it as something to come, and know that it is not lost through death but rather found and obtained. For our fatherland is in heaven, and Christ has prepared a place for us there, which we shall enter only by deserving it through his faith. He uses the word "reward," not to testify that anything is owed to our merits, but to teach that our labours and afflictions, which we endure here, will be recompensed. And he imitates fathers, who, though they owe their sons nothing, nonetheless entice them to eagerness in obedience by the promise of a reward. For, to speak properly, whatever God promises or bestows upon us is a gift of grace, and there is no place for merit before him, since whatever is done by us is imperfect, maimed, and, like a patchwork, defiled. He takes a second argument from example, saying: "For so did their fathers the prophets." It is as if he said: You are not the first to be struck by this blow; the same lot fell upon the prophets long ago, whose fame is most celebrated on earth today, while their souls live and reign in heaven. He therefore promises that we too shall be gathered to them. The godly ought always to think of this; so let the persecutors of these people remember whose companions they themselves will be, unless they desist from their undertakings: namely, of those who once set their terror in the land of the living (as Ezekiel says), but who now are tormented among the dead, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. It is clear from all these things that we are not wretched but blessed, if for the name of Christ we bear poverty, hunger, mourning, hatred, reproaches, and persecutions. Let no one, therefore, be offended by these things. For just as friendship with this world is enmity with God, so he counts as friends here those whom the world judges to be enemies. Moreover, the judge of all flesh is Jesus Christ, who (as we are taught in the story of the man born blind) gathers to himself those whom the wicked prelates shut out. He also protects his own in the midst of dangers, and will one day repay them the rewards of the faith that he promised. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIX.
units.tr: Homily 59.

units.la: Veruntamen vae vobis diuitibus: nam reportatis consolationem vestram. Vae vobis qui impleti estis: nam esuritis. Vae vobis qui ridetis nunc: nam lugebitis & flebitis. Vae vobis cum bene vobis dixerint omnes homines: nam itidem faciebant pseudoprophetis patres eorum.
units.tr: But woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers did the same to the false prophets.

units.la: Quoniam omnes homines sibi bene esse volunt, & naturali quodam summi boni atq; beatitudinis desiderio tenentur, necesse est norint, in quo nam haec consistat, quibus idem studijs eadem impediatur. Nisi enim hic probe instituti sint, carnis affectibus & mundi iudicio facile excaecabuntur, vt mala pro bonis apprehendant, bona pro malis auersentur. Et hoc illud argumentum est, in cuius tractatione omnes huius saeculi sapientes turpissime falsi sunt, sicuti philosophorum de summo hominis bono disputationes testantur. Non temere igitur Christus ab hoc eam concionem orditur, quam discipulos suos & cum his nos simul omnes de ijs docere instituit, quae ad salutem cognitu necessaria sunt. Ita vero rè tractat, vt erroneis & falsis mundi iudicijs diligenter occurrat. Primo enim beatos pronunciauit eos, quos mundus mortalium miserrimos iudicat, pauperes nimirum, & eos qui esuriem patiuntur, qui item lugent, & propter ipsum persecutionem, odia, contumelia & omnis generis aduersa sustinent. Hi enim omnes in medijs afflictionibus vindicem & tutorem habent Deum, tandem vero in caelis retributionem accipient beatae immortalitatis. Caeterum vt causa haec magis per spicua fit, Christus diuersas à prioribus sententias opponit, quibus infelices et maledictos pronuntiat eos, quos mundus profelicissimos habere consueuit. Estq; huius oppositionis aut comparationis magnus vsus. Nam & impios terret, ne in sua fortuna confidentiores sint, & fideles excitat, ne huius saeculi blanditijs sese irretiri patiantur: monet praeterea, ne quem prosperitas impiorum offendat. Nos ergo singula ex ordine videamus.
units.tr: Since all men wish to be well, and are held by a natural desire for the highest good and happiness, it is necessary that they know in what this consists, and what hinders it through the same pursuits. For unless men are properly instructed here, they will easily be blinded by the desires of the flesh and the judgment of the world, so that they grasp evils in place of goods and turn away from goods as if they were evils. This is the very subject in which all the wise men of this age have been most shamefully mistaken, as the disputations of the philosophers about the highest good of man bear witness. It is not without reason, then, that Christ begins with this sermon, which he set out to teach his disciples, and with them all of us, about those things that are necessary to know for salvation. He handles the matter in such a way that he diligently meets the erroneous and false judgments of the world. For first he pronounced blessed those whom the world judges the most wretched of mortals: namely the poor, and those who suffer hunger, who likewise mourn, and who for his sake endure persecution, hatred, insult and every kind of adversity. For all of these, in the midst of their afflictions, have God as their defender and protector, and at last will receive in heaven the reward of blessed immortality. But so that this point may be made more clear, Christ sets against the earlier sayings others that are different, and pronounces unhappy and accursed those whom the world is accustomed to regard as most fortunate. And this contrast or comparison has great use. For it both frightens the wicked, lest they be too confident in their fortune, and rouses the faithful, lest they allow themselves to be caught in the enticements of this age; it also warns that no one should be offended by the prosperity of the wicked. Let us therefore look at each point in order.

units.la: Principio in diuites maledictionem stringit, clamans. Veruntamen vae vobis diuitibus: nam reportatis consolationem vestram. Opponitur haec sententia directe mundi iudicio, qui solet fere divites beatos æstimare, eò quòd illi in honore et pretio sunt, quòd vitam in deliciis & omni voluptatum genere transigunt, & quòd ijsdem quod libet licet. At Christus væ illis imprecatur, quæ vox multas ledetiones & diras omnes, & cum his omnem tam futuræ quàm præsentis vitæ infelicitatem in se complectitur. Estq; eò terribilior ista imprecatio, quòd eo authore denuntiatur, cui pater omne iudicium dedit, cuius item sententiæ omnes ratæ sunt, & à cuius tribunali nulla provocatio conceditur.
units.tr: First, he launches a curse against the rich, crying out: "But woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation." This saying runs directly counter to the judgment of the world, which is accustomed to count the rich as blessed, because they are held in honour and esteem, because they pass their lives in luxury and every kind of pleasure, and because they may do whatever they like. But Christ calls down woe upon them, a word which embraces many misfortunes and all dire calamities, and with them every unhappiness of both future and present life. And this curse is all the more terrible because it is pronounced by him to whom the Father has given all judgment, whose sentences are all firm, and from whose tribunal no appeal is allowed.

units.la: At hic ante omnia probè videndum est, de quibus hic agitur. Nam vt nuper diximus, divitiæ & paupertas res mediæ sunt, & vt multi ex pauperum numero impiè viuunt, ita diuites inuenire est, qui Deum piè colunt & quibusuis benefaciunt. Et vt innumeros alios omittamus, opulentissimum fuisse constat credentium patrem Abrahamum. At cum adeò non perdiderunt opes illæ, vt æterna beatitudinis sedem Christus Abrahami sinum vocitet. Et memorabile est, quod in eo D. Augustinus obseruauit, sic dicens: Vt noueris quia non diuitiæ puniuntur, habebat Abraham multum auri, argenti, pecorum, familiæ. Diues erat, & in eius sinum Lazarus pauper sublatus est. In sinu diuitis pauper. At potius ambo Deo diuites, ambo cupiditate pauperes. Et idem non pecuniâ in diuite, sed auaritiam condemnari affirmat. Non ergo simpliciter ad omnes, qui diuitiis instructi sunt, Christi sententia extendi debet, ne in sanctis Dei cultoribus huius quoq; benedictionem damnemus, ex qua diuitiæ veræ & iustæ hominibus obtingunt. De illis enim loquitur Dominus, qui primùm in diuitijs spem & fiduciam suam collocant, & (vt alibi dicit) has suû thesaurum esse ducunt, cui cor totum consecrauerunt. Hi enim opes per fas nefasq; corradunt, easdem sibi solis seruant, & his amissis omnem simul salutis & vitæ spem turpiter abijciunt. Quo nomine Paulus talibus idololatriæ crimen impingit: & quidem merito, cùm pecuniarum aceruos sibi Deum faciant, & ijsdem quoad externa quoq; officia non minus quàm suis idolis idololatriæ seruiant. Ex horum numero iuuenis ille diues erat, qui omnia vendere et Christum sequi iussus, tristis abijt, eò quòd opes multas haberet, vel potius ab illis haberetur. Ite alter ille, qui cùm ex agris suis prouentus solito maiores collegisset, ijs perin- de additus hæsit, ac si in posterum extra omnem fortunam esset constitutus & ideo securus iudiciû Dei dicebat: Anima, habes multa bona reposita in annos multos, requiesce, comede, bibe, oblectare. Deinde eos etiam intelligit Christus, qui diuitijs suis ad luxum & fastum abutuntur, neq; meminerunt, se à Deo dispensatores esse constitutos, & proinde pauperum rationem in primis habendam esse, quos ille nobis commendatissimos esse vult. Describit horum ingenium & mores Dominus in epulonis diuitis personã, quem quotidie molliter vestiri et splendidè epulari solitum fuisse ait, pauperes verò ita neglexisse, vt Lazaro, egenti simul & vlceribus obsito micas de mensa sua cadentes denegarit. Est illorum magnus numerus hodie, qui omnes in charitatis legem immanissimè peccant. Nam non modò quam pauperibus debent opem crudeliter negant, sed ijsdem (quantum in ipsis est) impatientiæ et murmuris aduersus Deû authores sunt, dum suo luxu et paupertatis fastu onus illis in tolerabilius reddunt. Adde his tertio loco filios Belial, qui opum fiducia iugum excutiunt, & propter has sibi impunitatem arroganter vendicant. Regnat hoc quoq; hominum genus passim, & bi fe re sunt, qui crabronum instar telas legum publicarum (vt Anacharsis olim dicebat) perrumpunt, disciplinam ecclesiasticam eruerunt, & non minus impiè quàm superbè ad licentiam peccandi eo abuntur, quo se Deo præ cæteris hominibus obstrictos esse sentire debebant. Typum istorum in Doego Idumæo Dauid proponit, quem his verbis describit: En virum, qui non posuit Deum robur suum, sed in multitudine diuitiarum suarum spem posuit, & roborauit se prauitatibus. Quid enim aliud faciunt, qui in opum abundantia quiduis audendi licentiam venantur, seq; terribiles ijs præbent, quibus sua liberalitate debebant succurrere?
units.tr: Here, however, above all we must see clearly of whom he is speaking. For, as we said recently, riches and poverty are indifferent things, and just as many of the poor live wickedly, so one may find rich people who worship God piously and do good to anyone. And, to pass over countless others, it is well established that Abraham, the father of believers, was exceedingly wealthy. Yet his wealth did not so destroy him that Christ calls the bosom of Abraham the seat of eternal blessedness. And what St Augustine observed on this point is worth remembering; he says: "So that you may know that it is not riches that are punished, Abraham had much gold, silver, cattle and household. He was rich, and Lazarus the poor man was carried into his bosom. The poor man in the bosom of the rich man. Rather, both were rich before God, both poor in covetousness." And he likewise asserts that it is not money in the rich man that is condemned, but avarice. Therefore Christ's saying ought not to be extended simply to all who are furnished with riches, lest we condemn among the holy worshippers of God also this blessing, by which true and just riches come to men. For the Lord speaks of those who first place their hope and trust in riches, and (as he says elsewhere) count these their treasure, to which they have wholly consecrated their heart. These men gather wealth by right or wrong, keep it for themselves alone, and when they lose it they shamefully cast away every hope of salvation and life at once. For this reason Paul charges such men with the crime of idolatry; and rightly so, since they make heaps of money their god, and serve these, in outward duties also, no less than they would serve their idols in idolatry. Of their number was that rich young man, who, when bidden to sell everything and follow Christ, went away sad, because he had great possessions, or rather was possessed by them. Similar to him was the other man, who, having gathered a harvest from his fields larger than usual, clung to these as if he were set beyond all chance for the future, and therefore, secure in God's judgment, said: "Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry." Then Christ also has in view those who abuse their riches for luxury and pride, and do not remember that they have been set up by God as stewards, and that therefore the account of the poor must above all be taken into consideration, since he wishes them to be most commended to us. The Lord describes the disposition and manners of such men in the person of the rich feaster, who, he says, was accustomed to dress softly and feast splendidly every day, but so neglected the poor that he refused Lazarus, needy and at once covered with sores, the crumbs falling from his table. There is today a great number of such men, who all sin most cruelly against the law of charity. For they not only cruelly deny the help they owe to the poor, but they are also (so far as lies in them) the authors of impatience and murmuring against God, while by their luxury and the pride of their wealth they make the burden of the poor heavier. To these add, in the third place, the sons of Belial, who shake off the yoke on the strength of their riches, and arrogantly claim impunity for themselves on account of them. This kind of men also reigns everywhere, and there are those who, like hornets, break through the webs of public laws (as Anacharsis once said), who overthrow church discipline, and who no less impiously than proudly abuse to a licence for sinning that very obligation which they ought to feel they owe to God above other men. David sets forth a type of these men in Doeg the Edomite, whom he describes in these words: "Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in wickedness." For what else do those do who, in abundance of wealth, hunt for licence to dare anything, and make themselves terrible to those whom by their generosity they ought to have helped?

units.la: Subiftis speciebus omnes comprehendi posse puto, quibus in præsenti Christus maledictionem & væ illud horrendum denuntiat. Et cum tam grauis sententiæ causas plurimas ex eorum cor- ruptissimis moribus adducere posset, vnam protulisse contentus est, quæ ad eripiendam opum fiduciam & ad perterrendos securos illos atq; superbos plurimùm facit. Nam reportatis (inquit) consolationem vestram, id est, iam habetis omne id, quod ex vestris opibus sperare potestis, neque vlla alia felicitatis spes vobis est reliqua. At quàm vanum, inane & miserum fit hoc omne, quo nunc tantopere delectamini, mox magno vestro malo sentietis. Vere autem hoc illus Christum interminari, res ipsa docebit, si hos omnes iterum ex ordine considerauerimus. Primi enim illi fiducia opum delectantur, & vt ex earum concessione voluptatem capiunt, sic non alia illis consolatio maior obtingit, quàm cùm domus magnificè structas incolunt, agros & latifundia sua obambulant, frugum acervos numerant, rationes suas penes se euoluunt, & rerū securi nummos contemplantur in arca. Alteri verò fastu gaudent, & quia apud omnes in pretio sunt atq; titulis ambitiosis exornantur, se ab hominum sorte exemptos & semideos esse putant, ideoq; nihil periculi sibi porrò metuendum esse censent. Quòd si luxus accedat, & immunitas à malis, quorum vita hominum in hoc seculo plena est, iam quasi portum felicitatis ingressi sint, spei simul & fortunæ longum valere renuntiant, & securè voluptuantur. At postremi illi, quia in impunitate & indomita quiduis audendi licentia omnem felicitatem consistere putant, ipsi quoq; consolationem suam omnem recipiunt, dum illa fruuntur. Quid autem fit? Aut opes, quarum possessio fluxa & incerta est, præter omnem expectationem subitò diffluunt, & tunc omnis illorum consolatio, fastus, luxus, immunitas simul intermoritur & corruit: aut si opes maneant, ipsis tamen ex hac vita discedendum est, ignaris cui nam ea cedant, quæ propria vita chariora habuerunt, sicuti in fatuì illius diuitis parabola Christus admonet. Itaque omnis illorum consolatio atque felicitas opum instabili possessione aut vitæ huius spatio brevissimo terminatur: & vt talibus opum amissio luctum intolerabilem parit, ita ex improuiso obrepens mors desperationis causa est. Adeò enim nihil præsidij tunc in diuitijs suis repositum habent, vt potius in illis testimonium luculentum esse videant suæ auaritiæ, rapacitatis, crudelitatis, superbiæ & immanissimorum aliorum scelerum, quibus Dei iram aduersus se prouocauerunt. Sequitur tandem æternus cruciatus, quando cum epulone illo diuite ad inferos descendunt, vt dignas suorum peccatorum pœnas luant. Verè ergo væ horrendum Christus omnibus istis denuntiat, & paucis verbis comprehendit, quod Iacobus Apostolus, fidelissimus huius loci interpres, ad hunc modum expo suit: Agite nunc diuites, flete, vlulantes super miseriis vestris, quæ superuenient. Diuitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, vestimenta vestra à tineis devorata sunt. Aurum & argentū vestrum ærugine vitiatum est, & erugo eorum testabitur contra vos, & exedet carnes vestras velut ignis. Thesaurum congestistis vltimis diebus. Ecce merces operariorum, qui messuerunt agros vestros, à vobis intercepta, clamat: & clamores eorum qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt. In delitijs vixistis super terram, & luxuriastis: enutriuistis corda vestra, vt in die mactationis, &c. Et huius generis multa in scripturis habentur.
units.tr: I think all the kinds I have described can be included under those in whom Christ now pronounces a curse and that dread woe. And although he could have brought many causes of so grave a sentence from their most corrupt manners, he was content to set forth one only, which tends most of all to tear away the trust in wealth and to terrify those secure and proud men. For he says: "For you have received your consolation"; that is, you already have all that you can hope for from your riches, and no other hope of happiness remains for you. But how empty, void and wretched is all this in which you now delight so greatly, you will soon feel to your great harm. That Christ really threatens this will be shown by the thing itself, if we consider all these men again in order. For the first sort delight in trust in wealth, and take pleasure from its possession; thus no greater consolation comes to them than when they dwell in magnificently built houses, walk about their fields and estates, count their heaps of grain, unroll their accounts before them, and, secure in their property, gaze at the coins in their chest. Others rejoice in pride, and because they are held in esteem by all and adorned with ambitious titles, they think themselves exempt from the lot of men and half-gods, and therefore judge that they need fear no danger further. But if luxury be added, and immunity from those evils with which human life in this age is full, they then, as if they had entered a harbour of happiness, renounce hope and fortune for a long time, and take their pleasure in security. But those last men, because they think all happiness consists in impunity and in an untamed licence to dare anything, receive all their consolation also, while they enjoy it. And what happens? Either their riches, whose possession is slippery and uncertain, suddenly melt away beyond all expectation, and then all their consolation, pride, luxury and immunity together die and collapse; or, if the riches remain, they must nevertheless depart from this life, not knowing to whom those things will fall which they held dearer than their own life, as Christ warns in the parable of the foolish rich man. Thus all their consolation and happiness is ended by the uncertain possession of wealth or by the very short span of this life; and just as the loss of such wealth brings unbearable grief, so death, creeping upon them unexpectedly, is the cause of despair. For they then find so little help laid up in their riches that they see in them rather a clear witness to their avarice, rapacity, cruelty, pride and the most monstrous other crimes, by which they have provoked the wrath of God against themselves. At last comes eternal torment, when they descend with that rich feaster into hell, to pay the penalties due to their sins. Truly, then, Christ pronounces that dread woe upon all these men, and in a few words he comprehends what the Apostle James, the most faithful interpreter of this passage, set forth in this manner: "Go to now, you rich, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are eaten by moths. Your gold and silver are cankered, and their rust will be a witness against you, and will eat your flesh like fire. You have heaped up treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, kept back by you, cry out; and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. You have lived in pleasure upon the earth, and have been luxurious; you have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter, etc." And many passages of this kind are found in the Scriptures.

units.la: Quid ergo facere conuenit diuites, vt iram Domini & maledictionem effugiant?
