Hic alium Apostolum audiamus ô fratres, Paulum scilicet, qui ad Timoth. suum sic scribit: Ijs qui diuites sunt in hoc seculo denuntia, ne efferantur animo, neq; spe ponant in diuitijs incertis, sed in Deo viuo, qui præbet nobis omnia copiosè ad fruendū: vt benefici atq; diuites sint bonis operibus, faciles ad impertiendum, facilis conuiictus: Recondentes sibijpsis fundamentū bonum in posterum, vt apprehendant æternam vitam. Possunt hæc in tria capita redigi, quæ si diuites obseruarint, nihil damni ex diuitijs accipient. Primum est, ne propter eas vel aduersus Deum vel homines superbiant. Neq; temere de hoc primùm admonet, quando constat arrogantiam fere perpetuam & indiuulsam diuitiarum comitem esse. Sed facilè eam abs se propellent homines, si meminerint illarum tractationem periculosissimam esse, vt non immeritò laqueis & spinis conferantur. Alterum est, ne spem ponant in diuitijs, sed in Deo viuo. Conuenit hoc cum Dauidis præcepto: Opes si affluunt, ne cor apponatis. Hanc enim idolatriæ speciem esse, iam ante diximus. Quam vt fortius oppugnet Paulus, diuitias cum Deo confert, & illas quidem incertas & fluxas, hunc verò viuum vocat, & eum esse dicit qui nobis copiosè largiatur, quæ ad vitam hanc sustentandam necessaria sunt. Facit autem ad incertitudinem opum tota vitæ nostræ conditio, quam peregrinationem dicunt sacræ literæ, eò quòd non habemus hic ciuitatem permanentem, & proinde certi quoq; nihil possidere possumus. Quàm ergo stultum fuerit, relicto immortali Deo & liberalissimo omnium bonorum datore, fiduciam in rebus caducis atq; incertis collocare? Tertio beneficentiam præscribit, vt nimirum (quod Christus monuit) meminerint se dispensatores esse, non rerum dominos, & proinde nō negligant pauperes, quos Deus nobis commendatissimos esse iubet. Qui istis studeant, ij fundamentum sibijpsis bonum recondunt. Nam ipsi Deo fœnatur (inquit Solomon) qui largitur pauperi, et vt suo loco Dominus testatur, amicos sibi parabunt, qui ipsos in æterna cœlestis vitæ tabernacula recipiant. At qui hæc negligunt, ijs Dei maledictio incumbit, & exitium opes illis afferent, ex quibus sibi læta omnia pollicentur. Qui ergo de ijs dicemus, qui insuper malis artibus ditescere student, & pauperes ijs quoq; spoliant, quæ ipsis ex aliorum liberalitate aut singulari Dei benedictione obtigerunt?
units.tr: What, then, is fitting for the rich to do, so that they may escape the wrath and curse of the Lord? Let us hear another Apostle here, brethren, namely Paul, who writes thus to his Timothy: "Charge those who are rich in this world not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with all things to enjoy; that they be rich in good works, ready to give, willing to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life." These points can be reduced to three heads, and if the rich observe them, they will suffer no harm from their riches. (1) First, they must not be proud, either against God or against men. Paul does not mention this first without reason, since it is established that arrogance is nearly always and inseparably the companion of riches. But people will easily drive it away from themselves if they remember that handling riches is most dangerous, so that they are not unjustly compared to snares and thorns. (2) The second is that they must not set their hope on riches but on the living God. This agrees with David's precept: "If riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them." For we have already said that this is a kind of idolatry. To attack it more strongly, Paul compares riches with God, calling the one uncertain and fleeting, and the other living, and saying that he is the one who generously bestows what is necessary for sustaining this life. Moreover, the uncertainty of wealth is confirmed by the whole condition of our life, which the sacred writings call a pilgrimage, because we have here no lasting city, and so we can possess nothing with any certainty. How foolish it would be, then, to abandon the immortal God, the most generous giver of all good things, and to place our confidence in perishable and uncertain things! (3) Third, Paul prescribes beneficence, so that people may remember (as Christ taught) that they are stewards, not owners of things, and therefore not neglect the poor, whom God commands us to regard as most entrusted to us. Those who devote themselves to this lay up a good foundation for themselves. For, as Solomon says, "he who gives to the poor lends to God himself," and, as the Lord testifies in his own place, they will make friends for themselves who will receive them into the eternal tabernacles of heavenly life. But those who neglect these things are subject to the curse of God, and their riches, from which they promise themselves every happiness, will bring them ruin. What, then, shall we say of those who, moreover, strive to grow rich by wicked arts, and also plunder the poor of what has come to them from the generosity of others or from the singular blessing of God?

units.la: Sed ad Christum reuertamur, qui dicit: Væ vobis qui impleti estis; nam esurietis. Est hæc quoque sententia carni paradoxa, quæ cum præsentibus modo intenta sit, nihil vnquam ijs deesse posse arbitratur, qui in præsenti abundant. Primum autem eos intelligit, qui hac fiducia freti in præsentium bonorum affluentia aut felicitate, quam nunc fruuntur, aquiescunt, nihil de futuris soliciti. Ridentbi admontiones, correptiones, hortationes, minas, quibus ad virtutis studium excitantur: imò exempla iudiciorum Dei contemnunt, eò quòd non credunt Deum esse, cuius res mortalium curæ sint. Sunt ergo ex eorum numero, qui apud Isaiam dicunt: Pepigimus fœdus cum morte, & cum inferis pactum fecimus, flagellum inundans cum pertransierit; non pertinget ad nos &c. Deinde lurcones & helluones Christus territat, qui (vt apud eundem prophetam dicitur) mane surgunt, vt seden-tur siceram; & conuiuia ad crepusculum, imò in multam noctem vsq; extendunt vino incensi, vt crapulam vix vnquam concoquere possint; & proinde perpetuò saturi & pleni naturalem edendi aut bibendi appetitum nunquam sentiunt. Talem describit epulonem illum Christus, quem quotidie genio indulsisse & splendide epulatum fuisse dicit. Tales idem nouissimorum temporum homines fore vaticinatur, qui vt olim Noæ & Lothi seculis factum fuit, securi edant & bibant. Et regnat vtrunq; hoc hominum genus hodie, & ita quidem, vt portento simile videri possit, in tantis periculis, quæ toti terrarum orbi vndiq; incumbunt, quenquam inueniri posse; qui sibi aliquid tutum pollicea-tur, nedum qui tam multis cum egestate & fame conflictantibus helluari aut comessari velit. Sed ea est noştri seculi infelicitas, vt plerique cum timore Dei rationem quoq; omnem exuerint; neq; proprio-rum malorum sensu tangantur, nedum vt ex alienis dolorem concipiant.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who says: Woe to you who are full, for you will be hungry. This too is a saying paradoxical to the flesh, which, being intent only on the present, thinks that those who abound now can never lack anything. Christ first means those who, relying on this confidence, rest content in the abundance or happiness of present goods that they now enjoy, anxious about nothing in the future. They scorn admonitions, rebukes, exhortations and threats by which they are roused to the pursuit of virtue; indeed they despise the examples of God's judgments, because they do not believe that there is a God whose care extends to human affairs. They are therefore among those who, in Isaiah, say: "We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have made an agreement; when the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not reach us," and so on. Next, Christ alarms the gluttons and drunkards who (as the same prophet says) rise early to pursue strong drink, and prolong their feasts into twilight, indeed far into the night, inflamed with wine, so that they can scarcely ever digest their surfeit; and therefore, always sated and full, they never feel the natural appetite for eating or drinking. Christ describes such a feaster, whom he says indulged his belly every day and feasted splendidly. The same Christ foretells that such people will be found in the last times, who, as happened in the days of Noah and Lot, will eat and drink without a care. And both kinds of men rule today, and so much so that it might seem a portent that, amid such great dangers that press upon the whole world on every side, anyone could be found who promises himself anything safe, let alone one who wishes to feast and carouse while so many are struggling with poverty and famine. But such is the unhappiness of our age that most people, having cast off the fear of God, have also cast off all reason; they are not moved by the feeling of their own evils, much less do they conceive grief from the evils of others.

units.la: Porrò omnibus istis maledicit Christus, et infelicissimos pronuntiat. Causam verò infelicitatis adducit. Quia esurietis: quod ab illo veritissimè dici res ipsa docet. Nam priores illi spe sua frustran-tur, & plerunque quando felicissimi esse videntur, præter omnium expectationem repentinis malis circumuenti, se mortalium miserrimos esse sentiunt. Exemplum huius rei memorabile est in Crœso Lydorum rege, qui cum Solonem dicere audiisset, neminem ante obitum debere beatum dici; risit, quòd se iam beatissimum esse putaret, sed non multò post à Cyro bello victus & rogo impositus ar-denti, Solonem subinde in ore habuit, & dictum eius veri ssimum esse expertus est, quod prius petu-lanter contemperat. Et frequenter istis hominibus fieri solet; vt miserè esuriant non modò prioris vitæ desiderio, verumetiam famæ Verbi Dei accensi, cuius admonitiones prius improbè contempse-runt. Alteri verò reuera esuriunt. Nam fere sua prodigalitate rem familiarem dissipant, aut belli-cis tumultibus aliisq; infortunijs diuinitus immissis irretiti opes in vniuersum omnes amittunt; at-que ad extremam egestatem redigantur. Neque desunt exempla, quæ opulentissimis hominibus in terra fertilissima hoc accidisse docent. Nabuchodonosor Babyloniorum rex potentissimus, qui re-gni & victoriarum fiducia plenus dicere solebat: Annon hæc est Babylon, quam ego feci? mox ra-tionis vsu amisso in syluas & deserta profugit; vbi longo tempore herbis atque radicibus crudis in-felicem vitam sustentauit, quas regijs delitijs assuetum palatum nunquam admisisset; nisi fame plus quàm Saguntina coactus. Idem de Iudæis dicere possumus, qui cum terram lacte & melle fluen-tem incolerent, non semel tamen famis necessitate ad cibos infandos compulsi sunt, & eò adducti, vt matres in propria viscera, in infantes nimirum ex se natos; inaudita prius crudelitate graffaren-tur. Quid in Italia, Insubria, Hungaria aliisq; regionibus fœcundissimis nostra memoria contigerit, vix aliquis est qui ignoret. Et vtinam non hodie orbis fere totus inopia & fame laboraret; quia Deus effrenem comessandi & inebriandi libidinem nequicquam punit. Quod si nihil huius accidat, plerunque tamen morbus eiusmodi excruciantur helluones isti; qui aut guttum omnem eripiunt; aut concoctionem impediunt, aut stomachi cruditate gignunt, vt præter aquam nihil illis sapiat, & ἀoρ ξιᾳ καὶ ἀτροφίᾳ miserè pereant, qui prius gulæ studio inflammati in conquirendis cibis lautioribus terras simul omnes atq; maria fatigare solebant. Quoties ergo molliculos illos & intemperantes hel-luones cholicis passionibus rotari, aut calculi doloribus excruciari, aut fœdis iliacæ eructationibus torqueri, aut intercute tumescere, inter̄q; circumstantia pocula siti inextinguibili torqueri & consu- {ε} mi vides,tunc tibi illud Christi in mentem veniat: Vae vobis qui impleti estis,nam esurietis. Ex eo autem non miseris illis insultandi occasionem arripe, sed eorum exemplo temperantiam discito, ne quid huius tibi quoq; accidat. Scimus equidem morbos istos interdum pijs quoq; immitti. Sed sunt haec occulta Dei iudicia, qui & gloriam suam ea ratione illustrat (vt in caeci nati historia Christus ait) & illis fidei atque patientiae materiam suggerit. Ferant ergo isti patienter quod ita Domino visum est: alteri vero illi iustum eius iudicium agnoscant, peccata sua fateantur, & ea sibi per Christum remitti orent. At qui rebus praesunt, ij exemplis quotidianis excitati leges sumptuarias tueantur, vt gulae indies crescenti frenum injiciant.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ curses all these people and pronounces them most unhappy. He also gives the cause of their unhappiness: for you will be hungry; and the thing itself shows that the Lord spoke this most truly. For those first people are cheated of their hope, and most often, when they seem most fortunate, beset by sudden evils beyond all expectation, they feel themselves the most wretched of mortals. A memorable example of this is Croesus, king of the Lydians, who, when he heard Solon say that no one should be called happy before death, laughed, because he thought himself already most happy; but not long after, defeated by Cyrus in war and placed on a blazing pyre, he kept Solon constantly on his lips, and found by experience that the saying which he had previously scorned so wantonly was most true. And this often happens to such people: they are miserably hungry not only with longing for their former life, but also burning with hunger for the word of God, whose admonitions they had previously contemptuously despised. Others are truly hungry, for they squander their household property almost by their own prodigality, or are caught in wars and other misfortunes sent from God, and lose all their wealth altogether, and are reduced to the utmost poverty. Nor are there lacking examples that teach this has happened to the most opulent men in a most fertile land. Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful king of the Babylonians, who, full of confidence in his kingdom and victories, used to say, "Is not this Babylon which I have built?", soon, having lost the use of reason, fled into the woods and wildernesses, where for a long time he sustained his wretched life on raw herbs and roots, which his palate, accustomed to royal delicacies, would never have admitted, unless he had been forced by a famine more severe than that of Saguntum. We may say the same of the Jews, who, though they dwelt in a land flowing with milk and honey, were nonetheless more than once driven by the necessity of famine to unspeakable foods, and were brought to such a point that mothers raged against their own entrails, namely against the infants born of themselves, with a cruelty unheard of before. What happened in our own memory in Italy, Insubria, Hungary and other most fertile regions, scarcely anyone is ignorant of. And would that today almost the whole world were not labouring under want and famine; for God punishes in vain the unbridled lust for feasting and drunkenness. But even if nothing of this happens, such gluttons are nonetheless often tormented by diseases of that kind: they either lose all appetite, or impede digestion, or produce such crudity in the stomach that nothing tastes to them but water, and they perish wretchedly of [anorexia] and [atrophy], who, once inflamed with the zeal of the belly, used to weary lands and seas alike in searching out more dainty foods. Whenever you see those soft and intemperate gluttons writhing in colic, or racked by pains of the stones, or tormented by foul belchings of the ileum, or swelling with dropsy, and consumed by an unquenchable thirst amid the cups around them, then let that saying of Christ come to your mind: "Woe to you who are full, for you will be hungry." Do not seize on this as an occasion to mock them in their misery, but learn temperance from their example, lest anything of this befall you too. We know indeed that such diseases are sometimes sent upon the pious too. But these are the hidden judgments of God, who in this way both displays his glory (as Christ says in the story of the man born blind) and supplies them with matter for faith and patience. Let those, then, bear patiently what has seemed good to the Lord; let the others acknowledge his just judgment, confess their sins, and pray that they be forgiven them through Christ. And let those who hold office, roused by these daily examples, uphold sumptuary laws, so as to put a bridle on gluttony, which grows daily.

units.la: Sequitur in Christi verbis: Vae vobis qui ridetis nunc, nam lugebitis & flebitis. Opponit hanc sententiam priori, qua beatos dixit eos, qui flent & lugent. Pugnat autem etiam haec cum mundi iudicio, qui de illis optime agi putat, qui omnem luctum procul ex animo expuere norunt, & securi ludunt atque rident. Non debet tamen secundum literam de omnibus intelligi, quibus gaudere & ridere contingit. Frequenter enim sancti gaudent, & nos in Domino gaudere iubet Apostolus: cum{?} gaudium animi cantu pio & exultatione liberiori testari liceat, multo magis ridere licet. Est enim risus actio naturalis, & quidem homini propria, cuius sedem & originem physici circa praecordia constituerunt: nimirum quod eius causa sit animi affectio, quae si per se bona & honesta fuerit, neq; modum excesserit, risus quoq; damnari nequaquam debet: vt nec lachrymae improbantur, quas iustus dolor extorquet, & quae intra fines iustos sese continent. Itaque Vae illud in praesenti Epicuraeis denuntiatur, qui carnis & mundi gaudijs addicti, aliorum doloribus atque periculis nihil moventur, dummodo ipsis bene sit. Et hi sunt qui laeti perpetuo conviviantur, conviviis citharas, nablas, cantus & iubilos adhibent, interea autem neque opus Domini considerant (vt prophetae verbis vtar) neq; ipsis cordi est, quòd Ioseph, id est, vulgus miserum atq; infelix atteritur. Adnumerari his merentur, qui cum male fecerint ridٍent, vt qui ex stupris, rapinis, caedibus et alijs flagitijs voluptatem capiunt, & illorum commemorationem cum risu prosequuntur. Primus tamen inter hos omnes locus debetur illusoribus, qui coelos & inferos rident, & vel taciti in sinu suo, vel etiam publice disertis verbis dicunt: Scilicet hic superis labor est, hac cura quietos solicitat. Quorum magnum numerum fore novissimis temporibus, Christus & Apostoli praedixerunt. Petrus certè vaticinatur, illusores fore, qui cum risu & ludibrijs prosequantur, quaecunq; de mundi consummatione, novissimo Christi adventu & extremo iudicio scriptura sacra tradit. Et hi quidem omnes hodie passim audiuntur, vtq; priores illi omnem humanitatis sensum exuerunt, ita alteri ab omni numinis metu alienissimi sunt.
units.tr: There follows in Christ's words: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep." This sentence is set against the earlier one, in which he called blessed those who weep and mourn. It also runs counter to the judgement of the world, which thinks that those are doing well who know how to cast all grief out of their minds and play and laugh without a care. Yet it should not be understood literally of everyone who happens to rejoice and laugh. For holy people often rejoice, and the Apostle bids us rejoice in the Lord. Since we may express a joyful spirit with devout song and freer exultation, we may laugh much more. For laughter is a natural action, and indeed proper to man, whose seat and origin the natural philosophers placed about the heart. Its cause is a disposition of mind which, if it is good and honourable in itself and does not exceed due measure, ought by no means to be condemned, just as tears are not disapproved when just grief wrings them out and they keep within just limits. Therefore this "Woe" is pronounced here against the Epicureans, who, devoted to the joys of the flesh and the world, are moved by nothing in the sorrows and dangers of others, provided it goes well for themselves. These are the ones who feast merrily without end, who bring harps, psalteries, songs and jubilant music to their banquets, and meanwhile do not consider the work of the Lord (to use the prophet's words), nor do they care that Joseph, that is the wretched and unhappy common people, is being crushed. Those deserve to be counted among them who laugh when they have done wrong, who take pleasure in adulteries, robberies, murders and other crimes, and pursue the recollection of them with laughter. Yet the first place among all these is owed to the mockers, who laugh at heaven and hell and say, either silently in their own hearts or even publicly in plain words: "Surely the gods have no labour; no care disturbs their quiet." Christ and the Apostles foretold that there would be a great number of these in the last times. Peter indeed prophesied that there would be mockers who pursue with laughter and derision whatever Holy Scripture teaches about the consummation of the world, the last coming of Christ and the final judgement. All these are heard everywhere today; and just as those former ones have cast off all human feeling, so these others are wholly estranged from any fear of God.

units.la: At his quoque omnibus tristissima quaeque & extremum exitium Dominus imprecatur. Causam verò subjicit: Nam lugebitis & flebitis. Docet ergo revera miseros esse, qui quid ipsos maneat ignorent, adeoq; in suo exitio gaudeant. Etenim in hoc seculo omnium rerum vicissitudo est. Itaq; istorum fere omnium gaudium luctu finitur, & flere tandem eos oportet, quando ad pauperatem extremam redacti egent, & suam inopiam deplorant, quos aliena non monit: aut morborum doloribus excruciati eiulant, aut infames facti oberrant: quando item talionis lege eos punit Deus, vt suos quoque agros vastari, domus exuri, filios crudeliter occidi, vxores cum filiabus a barbaris militibus constuprari videat. In primis tamen haec Christi comminatio ad impios illos aduentus Christi illusores pertinet. Nam vt Paulus ait, cum dixerint, Pax pax, repentinus illis imminebit interitus, & quamuis inuiti ad Iesu Christi tribunal sistentur, vbi ad inferorum ignes damnabuntur, in quibus sempiternus est fletus & stridor dentium. Exempla, quae his fidem faciant, passim occurrunt, & quotidie fiunt multa, quae docent immodicis impiorum gaudijs atq; exultationibus fere comitem esse luctum cum acerbis lachrymis & infelici cruciatu coniunctum.
units.tr: Yet the Lord pronounces the most dreadful things and final ruin upon all these people too. He gives the reason: "for you will mourn and weep." He thus teaches that they are truly wretched, since they do not know what awaits them, and so they rejoice in their own destruction. For in this age there is a turn of fortune in all things. Accordingly, the joy of almost all of these people ends in grief, and at last they must weep, when they are reduced to utter poverty, lack necessities, and lament their want, they whom the misfortunes of others did not warn; or when they are tormented by the pains of disease and wail, or become infamous and wander about; and when God, by the law of retaliation, punishes them so that they see their fields laid waste, their houses burned, their sons cruelly slain, and their wives and daughters violated by barbarian soldiers. Yet this threat of Christ applies first of all to those impious mockers of the coming of Christ. For, as Paul says, when they shall say "Peace, peace," sudden destruction will hang over them; and although unwilling, they will be brought before the judgement seat of Jesus Christ, where they will be condemned to the fires of hell, in which there is everlasting weeping and gnashing of teeth. Examples that bear this out occur everywhere, and every day many things happen which teach that the immoderate joys and exultations of the impious are almost always accompanied by grief, joined with bitter tears and wretched torment.

units.la: Quid ergo (inquis) nobis est faciendum? Primum apostolici praecepti memores semper gaudeamus in Domino Iesu Christo, qui peccatum omne sustulit, patris iram placavit, & eam gratiam nobis meruit, vt afflictionibus quoque gaudere & gloriari possimus, quando in his nouam indies habemus fidei declarandae materiam, & per easdem nobis in regnum Dei aditum patere scimus. Est hoc gaudium sanctum & solidum, quod neque impuris mundi desiderijs vitiatur, neque crucis & afflictionum acerbitate turbatur. Et hoc ipsum est quod Christus apud Ioannem Cap. 16. plurimis argumentis argumentis commendat. Quoad caetera vero lugeamus, & ploremus. Quod ut fiat, multae & graves causae nos movent: Propriae nimirum naturae vitiositas, quae pios quoq; à via salutis transfersos abripit, & cum Paulo clamare cogit: Miseros nos, quis nos eripiet ex corpore mortis huius? Instabilis item rerum huius seculi conditio, & mortis hora incerta. Adhaec quae in mundo indomitum grassantur, immanis Dei contemptus & effrenis peccandi licentia, ut iam de audaci impiorum Christi hostium ferocia, & piorum oppressione indignissimis q; martyrum Christi supplicijs nihil dicamus. Accedunt his infinita alia, quae etsi ad animam vsq; non pertingant, tamen eusmodi sunt, ut pijs dolorem merito moveant. Quotquot ergo in istorum consideratione non oscitanter versantur, ij pro-cul dubio Christianos Heraclitos agent, & maiorem multo plorandi quàm ridendi occasionem sibi propositam esse videbunt. Itaq; etsi quod ex Christo conceperut gaudium nemo turbare possit, idem tamen hoc pio & sancto luctu temperabitur, quem coelestis & sempiterni gaudij praemium excipiet.
units.tr: "What then (you ask) must we do?" First, mindful always of the apostolic precept, let us rejoice in the Lord Jesus Christ, who took away all sin, appeased the Father's wrath, and merited for us that grace by which we can rejoice and glory even in afflictions, since in them we have each day a new matter for declaring our faith, and we know that through them the way into the kingdom of God lies open to us. This joy is holy and solid, neither corrupted by the impure desires of the world nor disturbed by the bitterness of the cross and of afflictions. And this is the very joy that Christ commends with many arguments in John, chapter 16. As for the rest, however, let us mourn and weep. Many and grave causes move us to do so. There is, of course, the vitiated nature that is ours, which drags even the godly aside from the way of salvation and compels us to cry out with Paul: "Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Likewise there is the unstable condition of the things of this age, and the hour of death, which is uncertain. Besides these, there rage through the world the untamed things: immense contempt of God and unbridled licence to sin; not to mention the bold fierceness of the impious enemies of Christ, the oppression of the godly, and the most unworthy punishments of the martyrs of Christ. Added to these are countless other things which, though they do not reach the soul itself, are nevertheless of such a kind that they rightly move the godly to grief. Therefore all who do not idly busy themselves in considering these things will undoubtedly become Christian Heraclitus, and they will see that a far greater occasion for weeping than for laughter has been set before them. And so, although no one can disturb the joy conceived from Christ, that joy will nevertheless be tempered by this holy and godly grief, which will be followed by the reward of heavenly and everlasting joy.

units.la: Restat postrema ex Christi maledictionibus, quam his verbis enuntiat: Vae vobis cum bene vo-bis dixerint omnes homines: Nam itidem faciebant pseudoprophetis patres eorum. Vbi rursus an-te omnia videndum est, de quibus loquatur. Nam non statim maledictus & Deo invisus est, quc ho-mines laudant. Et ut boni laudem merentur, ita ijdem nominis atq; famae suae rationem in primis habere debent, ne forsitan in ipsis Dei quoq; gloria periclitetur. Exempla sunt sanctissimorum hominum, qui innocentiam suam publice defenderunt, & interdum eò vsq; progressi sunt aduersariorum calumnijs coacti, ut nimij propriae virtutis praecones videri possint: quales fuerunt Dauid, aliqui prophetarum, & in primis Paulus Apostolus. Adhaec multos publicis ecclesiarum testimonijs commendatos atque laudatos esse legimus. Itaq; Dominus hoc loco eorum ambitionem damnat, qui omnibus hominibus placere studeant, & quorumuis praeconia auide venantur. Emphasis ergo & vis huius sententiae est in eo quod dicit, Omnes homines. Ea enim particula impios quoq; & impuros hujus seculi filios comprehendit, quibus quicunq; probari volunt, ij (ut de seipso Paulus loquitur) Christi servi esse non possunt. In summa eos hic perstringit, qui popularis aurae maiorem rationem habent, quàm suae vocationis. Quia enim mundus hic totus in malo iacet, fieri non potest, quin multa praeter officium faciant, quicunque huius favorem atq; praeconium ambiunt. Merito igitur Dei iram atque maledictionem illis denuntiat Christus. Si enim infelix & miser est, qui ut apud seditiosos reipublicae turbatores magnus habeatur, legitimi magistratus iram aduersus se provocat: quanto infeliciores sunt censendi, qui Deum sibi iratum faciunt, ut à mundo laudentur, qui sub suo principe diabolo plus quàm seditiose aduersus creatorem suum tumultuatur?
units.tr: There remains the last of Christ's curses, which he expresses in these words: "Woe to you when all men speak well of you; for their fathers did the same to the false prophets." Here again, before all else, we must see of whom he is speaking. For the one whom men praise is not at once accursed and hated by God. And as good men deserve praise, so they themselves ought above all to take account of their name and reputation, lest perhaps the glory of God too be put in danger through them. There are examples of the most holy men who publicly defended their innocence, and at times went so far, compelled by the slanders of their adversaries, that they could seem to be overly loud heralds of their own virtue: such were David, some of the prophets, and above all the Apostle Paul. Besides, we read that many were commended and praised by the public testimonies of the churches. Therefore the Lord in this place condemns the ambition of those who strive to please all men and eagerly hunt for the praises of anyone at all. The emphasis and force of this sentence therefore lies in what he says: "all men." For that little word includes also the impious and impure sons of this age, and whoever wishes to be approved by them cannot (as Paul says of himself) be a servant of Christ. In short, he here censures those who have more regard for popular favour than for their own calling. For since this whole world lies in evil, it cannot but be that whoever courts its favour and applause will do many things beyond their duty. Rightly, therefore, Christ denounces God's wrath and curse upon them. For if he is wretched and miserable who is held great among seditious disturbers of the commonwealth, he provokes the anger of the lawful magistrate against himself; how much more wretched must they be judged who make God angry with them, so that they may be praised by the world, which under its prince the devil rages even more seditiously against its Creator?

units.la: Quia vero in praesenti Christus cum discipulis agit, quos ad Euangelij ministerium ordinaverat, dicti quoq; sui rationem affert, quae ipsis maximè conveniebat. Nam itidem (inquit) faciebant pseudoprophetis patres eorum. Ei ergo ignominiae hac opponit, quam Apostoli inter Iudaeos potissimum subituri erant, qui ipsos propter Christi praedicationem pro publicis suae gentis hostibus habuerunt, flagellis ceciderunt, et ut alienos ab omni religione à Synagogis excluserunt. Erat ea non leuis neque contemnenda ignominia, eò quòd ecclesiae titulus adhuc penes eum populum esset. Admonet igitur, non debere ipsos illorum iudicio commoveri, eò quòd maior foret ignominia, si ab illis laudarentur. Nam patrum impiorum vestigijs eos insistere ait, qui pseudoprophetas laudarunt, fidos autem Dei seruos odio prosecuti sunt, & omni iniuriarum genere affecerunt. At cum constet pseudoprophetas Deo exosos esse, & proinde mortalium infelicissimos: eadem quoque vestra fors foret, si impijs illis Verbi Dei hostibus probaremini. Possunt ad huius loci confirmationem referri, quae sub Achabo regeimpio inter Heliam & Baalis mystas, Micheam item & pseudoprophetas gestafunt. Similia sunt ijs, quae de Phassure et Hanania, Ieremiae aemulis, scribuntur. Denique ea fuit omnibus seculis populi Iudaici infelicitas, ut cum Deus eum prophetiae dono prae alijs gentibus ornauisset, ipsi veros prophetas exosos, falsos autem & nequissimos impostores in pretio habuerint. Ideo Micheas dicebat: Si vir essem spiritu ambulans & mentiens fallaciter, prophetarem q; tibi pro vino & sicera, tunc propheta essem huic populo gratus. Atqui eadem est etiam hodie mundi huius conditio, & nouissimis temporibus hoc vitium maximè regnaturum esse Paulus praedixit, ut veritatis doctrinam non ferant, eos autem sibi coaceruent, qui aures eorum prurientes fallacibus promissis, & assentatoris sermonibus demulceat. Neminē ergo mundi infelicis iudicia mouere debent. Vt enim nuper bea
units.tr: But because at present Christ is speaking with the disciples whom he had ordained to the ministry of the Gospel, he also gives the reason for his saying, which was especially fitting for them. "For in the same way," he says, "their fathers did to the false prophets." He sets against this the disgrace which the Apostles were chiefly to undergo among the Jews, who on account of their preaching of Christ held them as public enemies of their nation, beat them with rods, and excluded them from the synagogues as aliens to all religion. This was no slight or contemptible disgrace, because the title of Church still belonged to that people. He therefore warns that they should not be moved by their judgement, since it would be a greater disgrace to be praised by them. For he says that they walk in the footsteps of impious fathers who praised false prophets, but pursued the faithful servants of God with hatred and treated them with every kind of injury. But since it is certain that false prophets are hateful to God, and therefore the most unhappy of mortals, the same fate would be yours if you were approved by those impious enemies of the Word of God. To confirm this passage, there may be cited what happened under the impious king Ahab between Elijah and the priests of Baal, and likewise Micaiah and the false prophets. Similar are the things written of Pashhur and Hananiah, the rivals of Jeremiah. Finally, it was the unhappiness of the Jewish people in every age that, although God had adorned them with the gift of prophecy above other nations, they hated the true prophets and held in esteem the false and most wicked impostors. Hence Micah said: "If a man walking in the spirit and lying falsely were to say, I will prophesy to you of wine and strong drink, then he would be the prophet pleasing to this people." And yet the condition of this world is the same even today, and Paul foretold that in the last times this vice would reign most of all, so that people would not endure the doctrine of truth, but would heap up for themselves teachers who tickle their itching ears with deceitful promises and the speech of flatterers. No one, therefore, should be moved by the judgements of the unhappy world. For just as Christ recently pronounced blessed those who are ill spoken of on his account, and promised a great reward for them laid up in heaven, so without doubt they will be unhappy who are praised for lies, and they will pay everlasting penalties to God among the dead,…

units.la: {a} 1. Reg. 18. 22. tos pronuntiauit Christus eos, qui propter ipsum male audiunt, & mercedem illis magnam in cœlis repositam esse promisit: ita procul dubio infelices erunt, qui propter mendacia laudantur, & ijdem apud inferos poenas dabunt sempiternas Deo, cuius nomine in palliandis mendacijs suis abusi sunt. Nunquam enim fallet Deus, qui eos non impune laturos minatus est olim, qui nomen suum indigne usurparint.
units.tr: {a} 1. Reg. 18. 22. Just as Christ pronounced blessed those who are evil spoken of on his account, and promised them a great reward laid up for them in heaven, so without doubt those will be wretched who are praised on account of lies, and they will pay everlasting penalties before God in hell, in whose name they have abused themselves in cloaking their lies. For God, who once threatened that those who wrongly usurp his name would not go unpunished, will never be deceived.

units.la: Debet ergo hinc generalis doctrina peti, quam omnis loci & ordinis homines ad se transferant: ut nimirum studeant Deo probari, non hominibus. Amicitia enim huius mundi (ut Iacobus ait) est & inimicitia adversus Deum. Et notum est illud Apostoli, qui Christianos monet, ne huic seculo configurentur, sed transformentur per innovationem mentis suae, ut probent, quae sit voluntas Dei bona, accepta & perfecta. In primis autem nos moneat, quod nulla hominum authoritate defendi poterimus, si Deo minus fidi simus, & eius iram in nos provocemus. Etsi vero ista ad omnes pertineant, debent tamen praesertim alijs in horum consideratione diligenter versari, qui munus aliquod publicum sustinent, & inter hos maxime, quos Verbi sui administros Deus constituit. Horum est mundum arguere de peccato, de iustitia, & de iudicio. Quod si faciant, mox mundi odium exardescet, qui opera sua prava argui non vult, laxabuntur omnium linguae ad conuitia, acuentur calumniatorum dentes, excogitabuntur nova crimina, iniquis prementur iudicijs, & non de fama solum verumetiam vita periclitabuntur. Terrent haec multos, qui ideo sibi licere putant, ut multa dissimulent, quod cum mundi contumacia se frustra luctari sentiunt. Sed ut res cadat, audendum est aliquid pro gloria Dei, neque alicui licet a Deo sibi creditam stationem deserere. Quod enim Ieremiae dicitur, Quaecunque tibi dixero loqueris, hoc ipsum doctores omnes sibi dictum putare debent. Eadem est eorum, qui magistratum gerunt, conditio. Nam & hi plerunque apud eos pessime audiunt, pro quorum salute ipsi dies noctesque excubant. Sed sufficiat illis, si sibi ipsis bene conscij fidem suam Deo probare possint. Meminerint denique omnes homines, beatitudinem suam non in fluxu opibus, non in rerum omnium abundantia, non in impuris huius seculi gaudijs, neque in mundi applausu consistere: sed in eo potius, ut per fidem veram Deo consecrati omnem fortunam aequo animo feramus, Deo probemur, & in filio eius Iesu Christo renati vitam viuamus nostra professione dignam. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: From this, then, a general doctrine ought to be drawn, which men of every place and rank should apply to themselves: namely, that they should strive to be approved by God, not by men. For the friendship of this world (as James says) is enmity against God. And well known is that saying of the Apostle, who warns Christians not to be conformed to this age, but to be transformed by the renewing of their mind, so that they may prove what is the good, acceptable and perfect will of God. Above all, this should admonish us that we shall be defended by no authority of men if we are less faithful to God and provoke his wrath against us. Although these things pertain to all, nevertheless those who bear some public office should especially be diligent in considering them, and among these above all those whom God has appointed as ministers of his Word. It is their task to convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. If they do so, straightaway the hatred of the world will blaze up: since the world does not wish its wicked works to be reproved, the tongues of all will be loosed to reproaches, the teeth of slanderers will be sharpened, new crimes will be invented, they will be oppressed by unjust judgments, and they will be endangered not only in their reputation but also in their lives. These things frighten many, who therefore think it lawful for them to pass over many things, since they feel that they strive in vain against the obstinacy of the world. But whatever the outcome, something must be dared for the glory of God, nor is anyone permitted to desert the post entrusted to him by God. For what is said to Jeremiah, "Whatever I shall tell you, you shall speak," all teachers ought to regard as said to themselves. The condition of those who bear the magistracy is the same. For these too for the most part are very badly spoken of by those for whose salvation they keep watch day and night. But it is enough for them if, being conscious of themselves, they can prove their faith to God. Finally, let all men remember that their blessedness does not consist in fleeting wealth, in the abundance of all things, in the impure joys of this age, or in the applause of the world, but rather in this: that, consecrated to God through true faith, we bear every lot with an equal mind, are approved before God, and, reborn in his Son Jesus Christ, live a life worthy of our profession. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LX.
units.tr: HOMILY 60.

units.la: Sed vobis dico qui auditis: Diligite inimicos vestros: benefacite iis, qui vos oderunt. Benedicite iis, qui detouent vos: & precamini pro iis, qui infestant vos. Et verberanti te in maxillam praebe & alteram: & ab eo qui tollit tibi pallium, etiam tunicam ne prohibeto. Cuiuis autem petenti abs te dato: & ab eo qui tollit res tuas, ne repetito.
units.tr: "But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who abuse you. To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and from him who takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who asks of you, and from him who takes away your goods, do not demand them back."

units.la: POstquam Dominus noster & aeternae veritatis doctor vere catholicus, Iesus Christus, falsa sapientum huius seculi de summo hominis bono aut beatitudine iudicia confutauit, ut doceret, eam non in terrenis bonis, sed in caelestibus quaeri debere: nunc Legis olim per Mosis ministerium latae interpretationem aggreditur. Et hanc non temere cum iis, quae proxime praecesserunt, connectit. Quia enim Lex de Dei voluntate bona & sancta nos perfecte instruit, simulque nobis paedagogi instar est ad Christum, in quo omnis salus & felicitas continetur, illius sensum probe tenere necesse est, qui beate viuere & aeternum seruari volunt. At legem universam Scribae & Sacerdotes suis expositionibus atque additionibus ita partim corruperant, partim obscurarant, ut vix unus reliquus esset, qui illius finem & usum recte cognitum haberet. Non debuit ergo hanc doctrinae partem praetermittere, qui non minus docendi quam seruandi humani generis causa in mundum venerat. Lucas autem, qui in huius concionis descriptione breuitati studere voluit, omissis iis quae in specialium praeceptorum explicationem ab illo dicta sunt (ut Matth. quinto Cap. est videre) ea modo recitat, quibus dilectionis proximi praeceptum expo suit. Quia enim dilectio (ut Paulus ad Romanos docet) legem totam complectitur, non poterit in eius sensu aberrare, quisquis in proximi dilectione recte instítutus fuerit. Nobis ergo res paulò altius repetenda & consideranda erit.
units.tr: Since our Lord and teacher of eternal truth, Jesus Christ, the truly catholic teacher, has refuted the false judgments of the wise men of this age about the highest good or happiness of man, teaching that it is not to be sought in earthly goods but in heavenly ones, he now takes up the interpretation of the law once given through the ministry of Moses. He does not connect this lightly with what immediately preceded. For since the Law instructs us perfectly about God's good and holy will, and is also like a schoolmaster leading us to Christ, in whom all salvation and happiness is contained, those who wish to live blessedly and be saved forever must hold its meaning rightly. But the scribes and priests had so partly corrupted and partly obscured the whole Law by their expositions and additions that scarcely one remained who rightly understood its purpose and use. Therefore he who came into the world not less to teach the human race than to save it could not pass over this part of doctrine. Luke, however, wishing in his account of this sermon to be brief, omits what was said by Christ in explaining the particular precepts (as can be seen in Matthew chapter five), and recites only those words in which he set out the command to love our neighbour. For, as Paul teaches to the Romans, love embraces the whole law, so whoever has been rightly instructed in love of neighbour cannot go astray in its meaning. We must therefore take up the matter somewhat more deeply and consider it.

units.la: Charitatis legem Deus apud Mosem Leuit. 19. cap. his verbis complexus est: Diliges proximum tuum, vt teipsum. Extenditur illa (vt infra cap. 10. dicetur copiosius) ad omnes homines: & voluit ea lege Dominus partim beneficentiam commendare, quam erga omnes nostrae opis indigos exercere conuenit: partim iniurias simul omnes prohibere, quibus proximus laditur. Ideo praemiserat: Ne odeas in corde tuo fratrem tuum, sed libere reprehendas proximum tuum, ne feras propter eum peccatum. Ne vlciscaris, neq; fis iniuriarum memor ergo filios populi tui, &c. Quid vero scribat? Omissis aut praeteritis ijs, quae modo recitauimus, proximi nomen ad eos solos restringebant, qui se nobis benevolos & amicos praebent, quique propter accepta beneficia aut alias causas priuatas nobis praealijs commendati sunt: & ex eo colligebant, quod ignotos & peregrinos negligere, inimicos autem & qui nobis damnum dedissent odisse liceret. Et ad hunc modum Christus illorum sententiam recitat Matth. 5. dicens: Audistis quòd dictum sit, Diliges proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Atqui posterius illud membrum nusquam in lege sua Deus pronuntiarat, ipsi autem Dei praecepto illud adjuere ausi fuerant, & id falso colligebant. Proximum enim (vt modò diximus) non alium dici putabant quàm qui amicus est, & hunc inimico ita opponebant, vt eadem lege quae amicum diligere iubet, inimicum odisse iubeamur. Ita vnius vocis error diuinae legis mentem prorsus obscurauerat, imò corruperat. Neq; tamen is error ignorantiae erat, cum eodem loco (vt audiuimus) Deus vindictam simul & acceptarum iniuriarum memoriam aperte prohibeat. Erat autem haec Scribarum doctrina multorum errorum atq; malorum causa. Primò enim charitatem omnem quasi abolebat inter homines. Quia enim iniuriarum plena sunt omnia, & natura ad suspiciones nimium propensi atq; proclives sumus, fiebat vt plerique se nullum dilectionis officium ijs debere existimarent, à quibus aut laesi iam erant, aut se laedi posse suspicabantur. Deinde causa quoque erat, vt odijs libertas indulgerent, quae nisi inter principia restinguantur, tandem in apertas inimicitias erumpunt, & omne genus iniuriarum pariunt. Praeterea cum reliquas gentes prophanas ducerent, & ideo inimicorum loco haberent, falsa hac legis interpretatione in earundem odio confirmabantur, & vicissim gentium omnium odia aduersus se quotidie magis provocabant. Hinc concertationes surgebant acerrimae, quae postea religionem quoque turbarunt, & Ecclesia vnitatem miserè sciderunt, cùm se mutuò damnarent, qui sub vno capite Christo in vnum corpus coalescere debebant. Quae omnia cùm Iesum Christum minimè latèrent, diligenter admodum huius praecepti sensum verum asserit, & ostendit in charitate exercenda non spectandum esse quid quisque mereatur, sed quo quisque opus habeat. Nam si meritum spectetur, iam non charitatis officium praestare, sed debitum exoluere dicemur, si quibus benefacimus. At quia ex innato nobis philautia vitio priuatum commodum vbique captamus, mirè etiam ingeniosi sumus in captandis effugijs & excusationibus, ne vel acceptas iniurias condonare, aut nostrae opis indigis subuenire cogamur: Ideo Christus rem hanc sic tractat, vt omnem elabendi & tergiuersandi viam nobis praecludat.
units.tr: God embraced the law of charity in Leviticus 19 in these words: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." This extends (as will be said more fully below in chapter 10) to all men, and by this law the Lord wished partly to commend the beneficence which it is fitting to show to all who are in need of our help, and partly to forbid all injuries by which a neighbour is harmed. Therefore he had prefaced: "Do not hate your brother in your heart, but freely rebuke your neighbour, lest you bear sin because of him. Do not take vengeance, nor be mindful of the injuries of the sons of your people," and so on. But what did the scribes write? Passing over or ignoring what we have just recited, they restricted the name of neighbour to those alone who show themselves kind and friendly to us, and who, on account of benefits received or other private causes, are commended to us above others. From this they concluded that it was permitted to neglect strangers and foreigners, and to hate enemies and those who had done us harm. In this way Christ recites their opinion in Matthew 5, saying: "You have heard that it has been said, You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy." Yet God never pronounced that second part in his law; the scribes had dared to add it to God's precept and falsely inferred it. For they thought that "neighbour" (as we have just said) meant none other than a friend, and they set the enemy over against him in such a way that by the same law which bids us love the friend, we were bidden to hate the enemy. Thus the error of a single word had utterly obscured, indeed corrupted, the mind of the divine law. Nor was this error one of ignorance, since in the same place (as we have heard) God openly forbids both vengeance and the remembrance of received injuries. Now this doctrine of the scribes was the cause of many errors and evils. First, it almost abolished all charity among men. For since all things are full of injuries, and we are by nature too prone and inclined to suspicion, it came about that most people thought they owed no duty of love to those by whom they had already been harmed or whom they suspected could harm them. Secondly, it was also a cause for indulging freedom in hatreds, which, unless they are extinguished at the beginning, at last break out into open enmities and bring forth every kind of injury. Moreover, since they regarded the other nations as profane and therefore held them in the place of enemies, they were confirmed in hatred of them by this false interpretation of the law, and in turn they provoked the hatred of all nations against themselves more and more each day. Hence arose most bitter contentions, which afterwards also disturbed religion and miserably split the unity of the Church, when they condemned one another, though they ought to have grown together into one body under one head, Christ. Since all these things were by no means hidden from Jesus Christ, he very carefully asserts the true sense of this precept, and shows that in exercising charity we are not to look at what each man deserves, but at what each man needs. For if we look at merit, we shall be said not to perform an office of charity but to pay a debt, if we do good to those who deserve it. But because from our innate vice of self-love we everywhere seek private advantage, we are also marvellously ingenious in devising evasions and excuses, so that we are not forced either to pardon received injuries or to help those in need of our aid. Therefore Christ handles the matter in such a way as to cut off from us every way of escape and of shifting the blame.

units.la: Et primò quidem apertè docet salsissimam esse Scribarum interpretationem siue sententiam ad quod proximi vocabulum ad inimicos quoq; extendi debeat. Ait enim: Sed vobis dico qui auditis, Diligite inimicos vestros. Quasi diceret: Tam abest, vt inimicos odisse liceat, vt potius eos amare prosequi debeant, quicunq; me audire & discipuli mei esse voluerint. Emphasim enim habet, quod ait: Sed vobis dico qui auditis: Ita vero in genere summatim comprehendit, quod mox in suas species diductum diligentius explicabit.
units.tr: And first of all he plainly teaches that the scribes' interpretation or opinion, by which the word neighbour is extended only to friends, is most false. For he says: "But I say to you who hear, love your enemies." As if he said: "So far is it from being permitted to hate enemies that, on the contrary, all who wish to hear me and to be my disciples ought to pursue them with love." For the emphasis lies in what he says: "But I say to you who hear." Thus he sums up in general terms what he will afterwards divide into its particular kinds and explain more carefully.

units.la: Nunc vero obseruabimus, non minus quàm Iudaeorum Scribas hodie eos errare, qui quae Christus in praesenti iubet, praecepta esse negant, sed consilia modò esse contendunt, quae ad Christianam perfectionem faciant, ad quam non omnes homines astringantur. Habent isti quoque sui commenti causas, vt ipsi existimant, minimè leues. Quia enim liberi arbitrij vires magnificè extollere solent, vt ex eo operum suorum merita statuant, ea autem quae hic Christus tradit, maiora & graviora esse videntur, quàm quae ab homine praestari possint, hoc effugio elabuntur, quòd ea non praecepto-rum, sed consiliorum loco habenda esse docent: & laudem quidem eximiam eos mereri aiunt, qui his obtemperant, non tamen eiusmodi esse, vt legis transgressores dici mereantur, qui ad perfectionem istam non pertingunt. Minimè enim possunt isti homines eum legis sensum ferre, qui & naturæ ne-stræ vitiositatem arguit, & meriti nostri fiduciam euertit. Ad istud ergo cōmentum recurrunt, quo & gloriæ & quæstui suo consuli posse sperant. Sed facile est illud confutare. Primū enim ea verbo-rum grauitate Christus vtitur, vt satis constet eum pro imperio loqui. Et cur non profuo in nos iu-re mandaret ista, qui vt perfectionis doctor & magister esset, in mundum venerat? Aut num lusis-se eum dicemus, quando tam multis inculcat, quod præstitu non sit necessarium? Deinde in veteri lege hoc ipsum mandari, ante ostendimus. Et eodem facit, quod in Exodo scribitur: Si occurreris bouí inimici tui, aut asino eius erranti, mox reduces eū illi. Si videris asinum eius qui te odit succumben-tem sub onere suo, non cessabis, neq; derelinques eum. Et in Deuteronomio hæc ipsa prolixè repetens Moses, simpliciter fratris nomine vtitur: ita nimirū ostendens, eos etiam nobis fratrum loco esse de-bere, quos hostili in nos animo esse non ignoramus. Nam etsi illi fraternæ dilectionis vinculū abrum-pant, nos tamen illud, quantū in nobis est, sanctum & inuiolatum seruare debemus. Qua ergo fron-te nostri illi liberū & indifferens faciunt, quod in lege adeò diserte mandatur? Adde his rationem qua Christus postea nos ad istorū obseruationem astringit, dicens: Vt sitis filij Altissimi illius, &c. Nisi ergo hūc animū concipiamus, inter Dei filios nō censebimur. Itaq; proculfacessant Sophistæ, qui dū ex Christi præceptis consilia faciunt, tā sibijpsis quā aliorū saluti pessimè cōsulunt. Nos verò le-gis & verborū Christi sensum simplicè teneamus, qui inimicos diligere, et quā verbis profitemur be-neuolentiā reipsa pro virili præstare iubet. Ita vero Dominus paucis cōprehendit, quæcunq; ad hāc causam faciunt. Nā si inimicos diligamus, iā & ab iniurijs omnibus abstinebimus, & Christiana pa-tientia vincemus omnia, quæ carnis sensui intolerabilia esse putātur. Vt tamen nobis melius consulat Christus, & omnem excusationis prætextū eripiat, præceptū hoc generale in species aliquot diauit.
units.tr: Now we shall observe that no less than the scribes of the Jews, those today err who deny that the precepts Christ gives here are commands, and maintain that they are only counsels which make for Christian perfection, to which not all men are bound. These men too have, as they themselves think, no slight reasons for their invention. For since they are accustomed to extol magnificently the powers of free will, so as to establish from this the merits of their works, and since the things that Christ teaches here seem greater and heavier than man can perform, they escape by this evasion, teaching that these things are to be held not as precepts but as counsels; they say that those who obey them indeed deserve exceptional praise, but that those who do not attain to this perfection are not such as deserve to be called transgressors of the law. For these men can by no means bear that meaning of the law which both exposes the corruption of our nature and overturns the confidence of our merit. They therefore have recourse to this contrivance, by which they hope both their glory and their profit can be secured. But it is easy to refute it. For, first, Christ uses such weight of words that it is quite clear he speaks with authority. And why should he not lay these things upon us as a right, since he came into the world to be the teacher and master of perfection? Or shall we say that he was joking, when he so often impresses upon us what is not necessary to perform? Next, we have shown above that this very thing was commanded in the old law. The same is true of what is written in Exodus: "If you meet the ox of your enemy or his ass going astray, you shall at once bring it back to him. If you see the ass of him who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not cease, nor leave him." And Moses, repeating these very things at length in Deuteronomy, simply uses the name of brother, thus clearly showing that those whom we know to be hostile to us ought also to be in the place of brothers to us. For although they break the bond of brotherly love, we ought nevertheless, so far as lies in us, to keep that bond holy and inviolate. By what face, then, do these men make optional and indifferent what is so plainly commanded in the law? Add to this the reason by which Christ afterwards binds us to the observance of these things, saying: "That you may be sons of the Most High," and so on. Unless we conceive this mind, we shall not be counted among the sons of God. Let the Sophists therefore go far away, who, while they make counsels out of Christ's precepts, consult most badly both their own salvation and that of others. But let us hold simply to the sense of the law and of Christ's words, which bids us to love our enemies and to show in deed, as far as we are able, the goodwill we profess in words. And indeed the Lord comprehends in a few words everything that bears on this matter. For if we love our enemies, we shall at once abstain from all injuries, and by Christian patience we shall overcome all things which are thought intolerable to the sense of the flesh. Yet, that Christ may better provide for us, and snatch away every pretext of excuse, he has divided this general precept into several particular kinds.

units.la: Primùm, Benefacite (inquit)ijs, qui vos oderunt. Opponit hoc illis, qui se neminem odisse, sed omnes homines diligere protestantur, at nullū interea dilectionis officium præstant illis, à quibus læsi sunt. Docet ergo nō verbis modò (vt Ioannes inquit) aut intra animos nostros solùm diligendos se-se inimicos, sed in eos etiam nos beneficos esse debere, qui nos odio capitali persequuntur & extinctos volunt. Et huic quidem præcepto obtemperant, quicunq; vera fide & pietate præditi in vnū Deum respiciunt. Quia enim hunc norunt innocentiæ vindicem, & seuerū vltorem esse omnium, qui iustos opprimunt & incurabili contumacia in impietate pergunt, non graue ipsis est illi causam suam com-mittere, & ideo vindictæ cupiditatem facilè restinguunt. Interea verò, quia omniū hominum saluti consultum volunt, hostes suos beneficijs demereri & vincere student. Exemplum huius memorabile in Dauide historia sacra proponit. Qui cùm ipsum Saul non minus iniusto & iniquo quàm implaca-bili odio persequeretur, neq; vllum in legibus et iure publico præsidiū sibi reliquum esse videret, Deo quidem causam suam omnè permisit, & vt innocentiæ suæ patrocinaretur orauit, interea autem ab omni maleficio abstinuit, & non solùm pepercit Sauli, cùm eum occultè et impunè perdere posset, ve-rumetiā eius terras & vrbes aduersus Philistæos fortiter defendit. Imitati sunt eum prophetæ o-mnes, qui diu noctuq; pro eorū salute laborauerunt, quibus se quàm maximè exosos esse sciebant. Id verò ex spiritus Christii impulsu fecere, qui tam exempla istorū quàm doctrinam hanc suam proprio exemplo confirmauit. Docent hæc quo loco haberi mereantur ingrati homines, quibus non satis est hoc Christi præceptum neglexisse, nisi insuper eos etiā odio persequantur & omni iniuriarum genere vexent, qui ipsos amant & beneficijs quotidie nouis accumulant. Est hoc hominū genus hodie pas-sim obuium, & cum horum ingratitudine perpetuò luctandum est ijs qui aut Ecclesiæ aut reipub. si-deliter seruiunt. Sunt illi indigni prorsus, qui homines dicantur, nedum Christiani homines: quando eo etiam sensu destituuntur, quæ natura brutis animalibus indidit, vt suos nutritios atq; benefactores agnoscant & obseruent. Dabunt ergo ingratitudinis suæ graues pœnas. At qui ab illis diuexan-tur, ij præcepti Christi memores amore et beneficentia pugnet, si quo modo illos vincere et demereri, aut saltē aliqua ex parte eorum ferociam mitigare possint. Soletur autem pios, quòd etsi omnia sal-lant quæ in humanis sunt, non fallet tamen Deus, qui beneficiorum est remunerator liberalissimus.
units.tr: First, "Do good," he says, "to those who hate you." This is directed against those who claim that they hate no one and love all people, yet in the meantime show no kindness at all to those by whom they have been wronged. So he teaches that our enemies must be loved not merely in words (as John says) or only in our hearts, but that we must actually be kind to those who persecute us with deadly hatred and wish us destroyed. Those who fear God truly and piously, and look to the one God, obey this precept. Knowing that God is the avenger of innocence and the severe punisher of all who oppress the righteous and persist in impiety with incurable obstinacy, they find it no burden to commit their cause to him, and so they readily put aside the desire for revenge. Meanwhile, since they want the salvation of all people, they strive to win over and overcome their enemies by kindness. Holy history sets before us a memorable example of this in David. Although Saul pursued him with a hatred no less unjust and wicked than implacable, and David saw no remaining protection for himself in the laws or the public right, he committed his cause entirely to God and prayed that he would defend his innocence. Meanwhile he abstained from every wrong, and not only spared Saul when he could have destroyed him secretly and with impunity, but also bravely defended Saul's lands and cities against the Philistines. All the prophets, who laboured day and night for the salvation of those whom they knew hated them most of all, imitated him. They did this from the impulse of the Spirit of Christ, who confirmed this teaching of his by his own example as well as by theirs. These things show what place ungrateful people deserve. For it is not enough for them to neglect this precept of Christ; they also persecute with hatred and harass with every kind of injury those who love them and daily heap new benefits upon them. This kind of people is met everywhere today, and those who faithfully serve the Church or the commonwealth must constantly struggle against their ingratitude. They are utterly unworthy to be called human, let alone Christian, since they lack even that sense which nature has given to brute animals, to recognise and honour those who nourished and benefited them. Therefore they will pay heavy penalties for their ingratitude. But those who are harassed by them should, mindful of Christ's precept, fight with love and kindness, if somehow they can overcome and win them over, or at least soften their fierceness in some measure. Pious people are comforted by the thought that, although everything in human affairs may deceive, God does not deceive, and he is the most generous rewarder of kindnesses.

units.la: Secundò, Benedicite (inquit)ijs, qui denouent vos. Repetit præceptū hoc ijsdē ferè verbis Pau-lus ad Romān. scribens: Benedicite ijs, qui vos insectantur: benedicite (inquam) et ne imprecemini. Et in huius obseruatione Apostolos diligentissimos fuisse, idē in priori ad Cor. sestatur. Nā cōmitijs affectis affecti (ait) bene precamur, &c. Nec temere de eo peculiare praeceptum dedit Dominus. Est enim hoc praesens irae remedium, & quasi frenum quoddam, quo retinemur, ne aliorum diris & imprecationibus accensi aliquid praeter officium faciamus. Ut enim aliorum verbis animus noster commoneretur: ita multo magis nostris accenditur, et totidem fere faces irae nostrae subijcimus, quot contumelias et imprecationes profundimus in eos, a quibus nos laesos putamus. At qui verbis parcunt, & meliore mentem precantur hostibus suis, ij ea ratione iram ebullientem refinguunt, & simul in charitate fraterna paulatim longius progrediuntur. Est ergo gravis illorum culpa, qui execrationibus assueti dira omnia imprecantur ijs, quibus irati sunt. Ita enim irae fomenta addunt, & omnes charitatis leges violant. Accedit plerunque manifesta impietas, quando fere Dei nomine ad exaturandum hunc animi furorem abutuntur, imo Iesu Christi vulnera, mortem, crucem adhibent, et ea hominibus exitialia esse volunt, quae humani generis redemptioni seruiunt. Multi vero ne his quidem contenti, insuper divos caelites invocant ut vel morbis, vel aliis calamitatibus eos perdant, in quos ipsi debacchantur. Quid enim isti aliud faciunt, quam quod Deum patrem indulgentissimum, Christum omnium nostrum seruatorem, Divos item (quorum cultores haberi volunt) carnifices suos fieri volunt, qui ipsorum furoris in feriuntur? Sed ut plurimum suae impietatis poenas dant, et videmus fere miseros & infelices esse prae aliis eos, qui os & linguam suam ad eiusmodi imprecationes assuefecerunt.
units.tr: Second, "Bless those who curse you," he says. Paul repeats this precept in nearly the same words in his letter to the Romans: "Bless those who persecute you; bless them, I say, and do not curse." And in his first letter to the Corinthians he testifies that the apostles were most diligent in keeping it: "Being reviled, we bless," and so on. The Lord did not give this special precept without reason. It is a present remedy for anger, and a kind of bridle by which we are restrained from doing anything beyond our duty when we are inflamed by the curses and imprecations of others. For just as our minds are stirred by the words of others, so they are kindled even more by our own, and we add almost as many firebrands to our anger as the insults and curses we pour out on those by whom we think we have been wronged. But those who spare them with words, and pray for a better mind for their enemies, in this way cool down the boiling anger, and at the same time advance gradually further in brotherly love. Therefore the fault of those is grave who, accustomed to execrations, call down every dreadful curse upon those with whom they are angry. For they add fuel to anger and violate all the laws of love. Usually there is also plain impiety, since they abuse almost the name of God to vent this fury of the mind; indeed, they invoke the wounds, death and cross of Jesus Christ, and wish those things which serve the redemption of the human race to be deadly to men. Many, not even content with this, further invoke the heavenly gods to destroy by diseases or other calamities those against whom they rage. For what else do such people do than make the most indulgent God the Father, Christ the Saviour of us all, and the saints too (whose worshippers they want to be considered) into executioners for their own fury? But for the most part they pay the penalties of their impiety, and we see that those who have accustomed their mouths and tongues to such imprecations are generally more wretched and unhappy than others.

units.la: Sequitur tertia species, qua dilectione hostium declarare debemus. Precamini (inquit) pro ijs, qui infestant vos. Est hoc plus quiddam quam quod modo iussit. Vult enim, ut non obiter modo saniorem mentem precemur ijs, qui nos diris insectantur, sed ut ferias quoque preces ad Deum fundamus pro hostibus, quos videmus contumaciores esse, quam ut beneficijs & facilitate nostra vinci aut emolliri possint. Fecit hoc ipse Christus, qui pro ijs apud Patrem intercessit, a quibus in crucem suffigebatur. Et ne quis hoc illi soli datum putet, aliorum quoque exempla extant, qui idem fecerunt. Israelitas Mosi in deserto multis modis infestos fuisse, et eundem atrocissimis iniurijs affecisse legimus: At quoties de illis poenas summere voluit Dominus, toties pro ipsis se ille interposuit, et suum potius nomen ex libro Dei deleri volebat, quam infelices & ingratum populum perire. Extant etiam Ieremiae preces et querelae acerbae, quas pro illis fudit, qui vitae ipsius insidiabantur. Et Stephanus protomartyr, cum inter lapidum vndiq; ruentium grandine prostratus caderet, clamabat: Domine, ne statuas eis peccatum hoc. Adnumerari his debet Paulus Apostolus, qui pro Iudaeis, hostibus suis grauissimis, assidue orauit, & anathema a Christo fieri optauit, ut ipsi salutem consequerentur. Veteres item Christianos publicas & privatas preces quotidie fecisse constat pro Imperatoribus, quos in ipsorum perniciem coniurauisse non ignorabat. In his ergo nos quoque esse debemus hodie, qui cum indomita mundi contumacia luctamur. Et est hoc maximum dilectionis proximi argumentum: quod facile apparebit, si cogitemus, quanta sit nostra segnities in precibus, quas pro nobis ipsis facere debemus. Quotus enim quisque est, qui nisi extrema necessitate prematur, animum totum precibus et divinae gratiae meditationi addicere possit? Magnaer go eius amoris vim esse oportet, quae ut pro inimicis nostris serio precemur, nos excitat. Imo si verum fateri libeat, nunquam id faciet homo, nisi in Christo renatus, seipsum et carnis cupiditates abnegarit. Huc ergo constanti fide apprehendam oportet, ut quae a nobis ille requirit, charitate praestare possim.
units.tr: There follows a third kind, by which we must show our love for enemies. "Pray," he says, "for those who mistreat you." This is something more than what he commanded just now. For he wants us not merely to wish in passing for a better mind for those who attack us with curses, but also to pour out earnest prayers to God for enemies whom we see to be too stubborn to be overcome or softened by our kindnesses and goodwill. Christ himself did this, interceding with the Father for those by whom he was being fixed to the cross. Lest anyone think this was granted to him alone, other examples also exist of people who did the same. We read that the Israelites were hostile to Moses in the wilderness in many ways and treated him with the most savage injuries; yet whenever the Lord wished to take vengeance on them, Moses interposed himself on their behalf, and preferred that his own name be blotted out of the book of God rather than that the wretched and ungrateful people should perish. There are also the prayers and bitter lamentations of Jeremiah which he poured out for those who plotted against his life. And Stephen, the first martyr, when he fell prostrate under the hail of stones raining from every side, cried out, "Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge." Paul the Apostle should be counted among these, who prayed constantly for the Jews, his most bitter enemies, and wished himself to be made accursed by Christ so that they might attain salvation. It is also well established that the early Christians offered public and private prayers every day for the emperors, though they knew that these were plotting their destruction. We too ought to be among these today, who struggle with the unbridled obstinacy of the world. And this is the greatest proof of love for our neighbour, which will be plain enough if we consider how great our sloth is in the prayers which we ought to make for ourselves. For how few are there who, unless pressed by extreme necessity, can devote their whole mind to prayer and meditation on divine grace? There must therefore be great power in that love which stirs us to pray earnestly for our enemies. Indeed, if we are willing to speak the truth, a man will never do this unless he has been reborn in Christ and has denied himself and the desires of the flesh. Therefore we must grasp this firmly by faith, so that we may be able to show with love what he requires of us.

units.la: Caeterum Christi sententiae obstare videbatur lex talionis, quam Deus Israelitis dederat. Extat ea in libro Exodi cap. 21. ubi de eius poena loquens Moses, qui mulierem praegnantem percusserit, inter alia sic dicit: Quod si noxa fuerit letalis, dabit animam pro anima, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente, manum pro manu, pedem pro pede, adustionem pro adustione, vulnus pro vulnere, liuorem pro liuore. Et Leuit. 24. eandem legem his verbis repetit Dominus: Qui damnum dederit proximo suo, huic fiet quem admodum ipse fecit: Fracturam pro fractura, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente: quicquid deniq; vitii aut detrimenti intulerit cuiquam, hoc idem etiam ipsi inferatur. Et qui percusserit iumentum, reddat ipsum, qui vero hominem percusserit, interficiatur. Pertinent etiam ad huius legis expositionem, quae Deut. 10. de falsis testibus habentur, quos eodem supplicio multari vult Moses quod ipsi falsum dicendo aliis irrogare conati sunt. His autem suam de lege dilectionis sententiam Scribae defendebant, & ita colligebant: Lex talionem permittit aduersus eos, qui aliquem laeserunt: ergo inimicos odisse & paria paribus referre liceat. Fallebantur autem in eo, quod legem talionis, quam iudicibus dederat Deus, ipsi ad omnes extendebant, & cuius privato permissum putabant, ut hostis suum vlcisceretur. Atqui idem Deus priuatis dixerat: Mihi vindicta debetur, ego retribuam. Occurrit itaq; Christus, & ne sub legis praetextu in charitate peccemus, quid singulis priuatim obseruandum sit, docet. Planius autem & apertius apud Matthaeum sic ait. Audistis quod dictum fuerit, Oculum pro oculo, dente pro dente. Ego vero dico vobis, ne resistatis malo: sed si quis ceciderit te in dextram tuam maxillam, obuerte ei & alteram, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the law of retaliation, which God had given to the Israelites, seemed to stand in the way of Christ's saying. It is found in the book of Exodus, chapter 21, where Moses, speaking of the penalty for one who strikes a pregnant woman, says among other things: "But if there is a fatal injury, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise." And in Leviticus 24 the Lord repeats the same law in these words: "Whoever causes injury to his neighbour, it shall be done to him as he has done: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever blemish or harm he has inflicted on anyone, the same shall be inflicted on him. And whoever strikes an animal shall restore it, but whoever strikes a man shall be put to death." What is found in Deuteronomy 19 about false witnesses also bears on the explanation of this law: Moses wants them punished with the same penalty, because by lying they tried to bring it upon others. The scribes, however, defended their own opinion about the law of love with these words, and reasoned thus: "The law permits retaliation against those who have injured someone; therefore it is lawful to hate enemies and to repay like with like." But they were mistaken in this, because they extended to everyone the law of retaliation, which God had given to judges, and they thought it was permitted to a private person to avenge himself on his enemy. Yet the same God had said to private persons: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay." Christ therefore comes to meet this, and, lest we sin against love under the pretext of the law, he teaches what each private person ought to observe. He says this more plainly and openly in Matthew: "You have heard that it was said, 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.' But I say to you, do not resist the evil one; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also," and so on.

units.la: Obseruabis hic ante omnia, Christum cum priuatis hominibus agere, & quid singulos in priuatis iniurijs facere conueniat, docere, non autem de magistratus aut iudicum officio loqui. Detorquent ergo Christi verba Anabaptistae, & a Deo distinctos hominum ordines confundunt: imo audaces nimium id prohibent, quod Deus diserte mandat. Magistratus enim officium est, non solum resistere malo, verumetiam illud extirpare, ut qui boni & probi sunt, suo iure ut et tuto viuere possint. Ideo in lege passim iudicibus dicitur: Excindes malum e medio populi. Et in Psal. 27. de Rege bono inter alia dicit spiritus sanctus: Liberabit pauperem clamantem & afflictum cui non est adiutor. Redimet animas eorum a foenore & violentia, &c. Quod si phanatici illi haec ad vetus testamentum pertinere obijciant, audiant quaeso Paulum in nouo sic scribentem: Non est potestas nisi a Deo, & quae sunt potestates, sunt a Deo ordine distributae. Ite: Magistratus non sunt terrori bonus operibus, sed malis. Vis autem non timere potestatem? quod bonum est facito: & feres laudem ab ipsa. Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum. Quod si feceris quod malum est, time. Non enim temere gladium gestat. Nam Dei minister est: vltor ad iram ei, qui quod malum est fecerit, &c. Sunt haec tam plana & perspicua, ut amplioriresponsione non digni sint, qui Christi praecepto aduersus magistratum abutuntur.
units.tr: Here you will observe above all that Christ is dealing with private persons and teaching what each individual ought to do in private injuries, and is not speaking of the office of magistrates or judges. The Anabaptists therefore twist Christ's words and confuse the orders of men that God has distinguished. Indeed, in their excessive boldness they forbid what God plainly commands. For it is the office of the magistrate not only to resist evil but to root it out, so that those who are good and upright may live securely and enjoy their rights. Hence the law tells judges everywhere: "You shall remove the evil from the midst of the people." And in Psal. 27, the Holy Spirit says of a good king, among other things: "He shall deliver the poor man who cries out, and the afflicted who has no helper. He shall redeem their souls from usury and violence," etc. But if those fanatics object that these things pertain to the Old Testament, let them hear Paul writing thus in the New: "There is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained by God." And again: "Magistrates are not a terror to good works but to evil ones. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God's minister for your good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid. For it does not bear the sword in vain: it is God's minister, an avenger for wrath against him who does evil," etc. These words are so plain and clear that they do not deserve a longer answer from those who abuse Christ's precept against the magistrate.

units.la: Quoad autem priuatos homines, meminerimus duplicem esse modum resistendi malo. Primus, quo vrgente necessitate iniurias legitime propulsamus, non quidem nocendi studio, sed vt vel nosipsos seruemus, vel eos, quorum defensio iure ad nos pertinet. Hic no licitus modo, verumetiam ad charitatem inter homines conseruandam necessarius est. Nam nisi improbis illis legitime resistatur, accenditur piorum facilitate atq; indulgentia furor illorum, & intolerabilis fiet eorundem rabies, qua omnia infesta reddent, neq; alijs modo promiscue nocebunt. sed nimia licentia abrepti seipsos quoq; in exitium abducent.
