Quare vt verbis aut correptionibus, & si his nihil proficiatur, alijs quoq; modis legitimis coerceantur necesse est. Nam si furiosum in mente captu catenis vincere, aut alia ratione continere licet, ne sibi ipsi aut alijs malum det, eadem ratio eos etiam coercere iubet, qui alio prauo affectu impulsi tam sibi ipsis quam alijs nocere volunt. Docent hoc sanctissimorum hominum exempla, quos Dei spiritu ductos fuisse non est dubium. Nam vt a patre credentium Abrahamo exordiamur, annon is malo resistit, quando Reges Orientales insecutus, copias eorum dissipauit, & praedam iniustis armis quaesitam ex manibus eorum eripuit? Nonne Lothus malis Sodomaeorum conatibus sese opposuit, cum hostibus non sine execrando scelere vim facere instituissent? Et vt ad nouí quoque Testamenti historiam veniamus, quis nescit Paulum non semel Legum & Romanae ciuitatis ius implorauisse, cum contra leges caederetur? Imo idem, cum viros quadraginta aduersus vitam suam coniurauisse resciuisset, ad legitimam magistratus defensionem confugit, & armato praesidio se seruari inq; locum tutiorem deduci passus est. Et hoc faciens adeo non violauit charitatis legem, vt potius vera & syncera charitatis officium fecerit, quando & seipsum Ecclesijs seruauit, & illis obstitit ne manus suas sanguine innocenti polluerent. Alter resistendi modus est, quo ex vindictae cupiditate & nocendi studio par pari referre & (vt aiunt) vim vi repellere conamur. De hoc in praesenti Christus loquitur, & ne eo vtamur prohibet. Rationes huius prohibitionis multae & graues sunt. Primo enim vt ipsi hostes vlciscamur non semper necesse est, nos autem ad patientiam exerceri vehementer prodest, vt in ea confirmatiores fiamus, dum plures iniurias ferimus. Deinde vindictae cupiditatem restingui omnino oportet, quia qui illa ardent, ij mentis tranquillitate, qua nihil inter huius vitae bona iucundius est, frui non possunt, & dum odium semel animo conceptum fouent: nouos quotidie sibi labores accersunt, & vitam ipsam sibi amaram reddunt, vt in Caini, Saulis & similium historijs est videre. Adde his, quod vindictae cupiditate impedimur, ne vnquam cum ijs in gratiam redeamus, qui nos quocunq; modo laeserunt. Ita vero charitate in nobis prorsus extinguit, quae propria & germana discipulorum Christi aut filiorum Dei nota est. Quid, quod non sine sacrilegio nobis vendicamus, quod solius Dei est, qui vindictam (vt supra diximus) adse solum pertinere testatur. Vt ergo tot tantisq; malis occurrat Dominus, talionis legem scriba-rum interpretatione corruptam & male detortam corrigit, & ne malo temere aut illegitimè refista-mus monet. Quod autem in genere dixit, mox tribus præceptis Symbolicis illustrat, & in suas quasi species diducit.
units.tr: As for private persons, let us remember that there are two ways of resisting evil. The first is that by which, when urgent necessity requires, we lawfully repel injuries, not with a desire to harm but in order to preserve either ourselves or those whose defence rightly belongs to us. This is not only permitted but is necessary for preserving charity among men. For unless those wicked men are lawfully resisted, the fury of the wicked is kindled by the gentleness and indulgence of the good, and their rage becomes intolerable; it makes everything hostile and does harm not only to others indiscriminately, but, carried away by excessive licence, it also leads themselves to destruction. Therefore they must be restrained by words and rebukes, and if these achieve nothing, by other lawful means. For if it is lawful to bind a madman in chains, or to restrain him by some other means, lest he harm himself or others, the same reason also bids us restrain those who, driven by some other depraved passion, wish to harm both themselves and others. The examples of the holiest men teach this, men who were without doubt led by the Spirit of God. To begin with Abraham, the father of believers: does he not resist evil when he pursues the Eastern kings and scatters their forces, and snatches from their hands the plunder won by unjust arms? Did not Lot oppose himself to the wicked attempts of the Sodomites, when they had set out to do violence to the strangers with an accursed crime? And to come also to the history of the New Testament, who does not know that Paul more than once appealed to the law and the rights of Roman citizenship when he was being beaten contrary to the laws? Indeed, when he learned that forty men had conspired against his life, he took refuge in the lawful defence of the magistrate, and allowed himself to be kept safe by an armed guard and led to a safer place. And in doing this he did not violate the law of charity at all; rather he performed a true and sincere office of charity, both preserving himself for the churches and standing in the way lest they pollute their hands with innocent blood. The second way of resisting is that by which, out of a desire for revenge and a wish to harm, we seek to repay like with like and, as they say, to repel force with force. It is this that Christ speaks of in the present passage, and he forbids us to use it. The reasons for this prohibition are many and weighty. First, it is not always necessary for us to take vengeance on our enemies themselves, whereas it greatly benefits us to be trained to patience, so that we may become more steadfast in it while we bear many injuries. Next, the desire for revenge must altogether be quenched, because those who burn with it cannot enjoy tranquillity of mind, which is the most pleasant of all the goods of this life; and while they cherish a hatred once conceived in the mind, they bring upon themselves new troubles every day and make their very life bitter to themselves, as can be seen in the histories of Cain, Saul and their like. Add to these that, being hindered by the desire for revenge, we never return to favour with those who have injured us in any way. Thus charity is utterly extinguished in us, which is the proper and genuine mark of the disciples of Christ and the sons of God. And what of the fact that we claim for ourselves, not without sacrilege, what belongs to God alone, who testifies that vengeance (as we said above) pertains to himself alone? So, in order to meet with the Lord's remedy so many and so great evils, he corrects the law of retaliation which the scribes had corrupted by false interpretation and wrongly twisted, and he warns us not rashly or unlawfully to resist evil. What he said in general terms he then illustrates by three symbolic precepts, and divides them into their several kinds.

units.la: Primum est: Verberanti in maxillam præbe & alteram. Sub maxillæ percussione, quæ semper ignominiosa fuit, omne genus iniuriarum complectitur, quo aut corpus nostrum violatur, aut famam suis conuitiis hostes lædunt. Sensus autem verborum Christi est, non vt ignaua & stolida vel etiam ridicula indulgentia, improbitatem et proteruiam petulantiam hominum foueamus, sed vt priuatæ vindictæ cupiditati adeò non indulgeamus, vt potius nos ad nouam iniuriam recipiendam præpare mus. Ridiculi ergo sunt, qui præceptum hoc secundùm literam aut τὸ ῥητὸν intelligendum esse contendunt. Nam diuersum docent sanctissimorum hominum exempla, quot ipse spiritus sanctus absoluit, quàmuis longè aliud fecerint. Micheas certè propheta, cùm à Zedechia impostore in maxillam cæderetur, non alteram obuertit, sed improbo illi pœnas imminentes magna cum grauitate denunciauit. Quod ipsum Paulus quoq; fecit, cùm Ananias ipsum pro se verba factură percutere iussisset: Percutiet te (inquit) Deus, paries dealbate: & tu sedes iudicans me secundùm legem, & contra legem iubes me percuti? Sed ipsius Christi, qui suæ legis procul dubio interpres est fidelißimus, exemplum videamus, qui à famulo Caiaphæ percussus, non alteram genam illi præbuit, sed vim iniustam publicè reprehendit. Itaq; quod illi licuit, nobis quoq; licebit, nisi illum peccasse dicamus. At hic nobis ea cautio adhibenda est, vt in ijs quidem, quæ ad nos solos spectant, iniuriarum patientissimi simus: ius autem nostrum constanter tueamur, si quando in nobis veritas & Dei gloria periclitantur. At hodie diuersum pleriq; faciunt, qui in afferenda Dei gloria plus quàm ignaui sunt, & turpem veritatis desertionem Christianæ charitatis & patientiæ titulo palliant, in suis autem iniurijs vindicandis ita ardent, vt cælum terræ potius miscere, quàm cum teruntij vnius iactura iure suo cedere velint.
units.tr: The first is: "To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also." The blow to the cheek, which has always been a mark of disgrace, comprehends every kind of injury by which either our body is violated or our reputation is harmed by the insults of enemies. The meaning of Christ's words, however, is not that we should foster the wickedness and shameless insolence of men by a lazy and foolish, or even ridiculous, indulgence; rather, we should not so indulge the desire for private vengeance that we instead prepare ourselves to receive a new injury. Those therefore are ridiculous who contend that this precept must be understood according to the letter, or according to [τὸ ῥητὸν] the literal sense. For the examples of the holiest men, which the Holy Spirit himself records, teach otherwise, although they acted quite differently. Micaiah the prophet, when he was struck on the cheek by the impostor Zedekiah, did not turn the other cheek, but with great gravity declared the punishments hanging over that wicked man. Paul did the same when Ananias ordered that he be struck on the mouth: "God shall strike you, whitewashed wall," he said; "and do you sit judging me according to the law, and contrary to the law order me to be struck?" But let us look at the example of Christ himself, who is without doubt the most faithful interpreter of his own law: when he was struck by a servant of Caiaphas, he did not offer the other cheek to him, but publicly rebuked the unjust violence. So what was lawful for him will also be lawful for us, unless we say that he sinned. Yet here we must observe this caution: in those matters which concern us alone, we should be most patient under injuries; but when the truth and the glory of God are in peril in us, we should constantly defend our right. Today, however, most people do the opposite. They are more than lazy in asserting the glory of God, and they cover a shameful desertion of the truth with the name of Christian charity and patience; yet in avenging their own injuries they burn so fiercely that they would rather turn heaven upside down than yield their right in the loss of a single small coin.

units.la: Alterum Christi præceptum est: Et ab eo, qui tollit tibi pallium, etiam tunicam ne prohibeto. Id apud Matthæum clarius & significantius exprimitur his verbis: Et qui vult tecum iudicio contendere, ac tunicam tuam capere, dimitte & pallium. Et quisquis angariauerit ad milliare vnum, abi cum eo duo. In priori quidem membro de iniurijs, quæ corpori violenter inferuntur egit: nunc quid cum illis fieri debeat docet, qui sub iuris prætextu nos fortunis nostris exuere aut nostra opera abuti, adeoq; nos sibi seruos facere conantur. Proderat autem de hoc etiam nos peculiariter admonere. Nam vt grauiter peccant qui iuris & legum prætextu aliena invadunt, ita difficile est, vt quis incuendo iure suo modum seruet, & nihil in Christianæ dilectionis leges delinquat. Et frequenter fit, vt tunc quoq; non leuiter peccent viri alioqui non mali, quando causam bonam tuendo affectibus nimium indulgent. Monet ergo Christus, vt potius bonis nostris cedere, & nouam iacturam facere paratisimus, quàm vt propter res temporarias charitatem violemus, nosq; ipsos intricemus molestijs grauioribus. Idem ergo huius admonitionis & præcepti, qui priorus sensus est. Et proinde non simpliciter damnantur iudicia forensia, quasi ijs vti non liceat, sed vt maiorem charitatis quàm fortunarum nostrarum rationem habeamus, præcipit. Debebant hoc obseruare litigatores temerarij, qui aliena inuadunt, & lites odiosissimas ad posteros usque transmittunt. In primis verò, qui fratribus eundem Christum profitentibus lites mouent apud iudices prophanos & fide alienos. Reprehendit hos acriter Paulus in priori ad Corinthios. Et sanè, si singoli cogitent, quid fraternæ charitati debeant, qui labores, quæ molestiæ & impensæ ferendæ sint, quantum condonandum causidicorum insidiosæ rapacitati & iudicũ iniquitati: mox videbunt quantò tutius sit & vtilius Christi præceptum sequi, quàm pelago huic periculosissimo voracißimoq; seipsum atq; fortunas omnes committere. Interim minimè damnandi sunt, qui hæredipetarum dolos, prædonum audaciam, fœneratorum iniquisimas artes, legum atq; iudiciorum præsidio coercent, & seipsos atq; sua aduersus illos tuentur; modò charitatis fraternæ non obliuiscantur, & nihil immodestiùs agant.
units.tr: The second precept of Christ is: "From him who takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either." Matthew expresses this more clearly and more forcefully in these words: "And if anyone wishes to contend with you in judgement and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two." In the first member he dealt with injuries that are violently inflicted on the body; now he teaches what must be done with those who, under the pretext of law, seek to strip us of our property or to use our labour, and so try to make us their slaves. It was useful, however, to admonish us about this in particular as well. For just as those who invade what belongs to others under the pretext of right and law sin gravely, so it is difficult for anyone, in pursuing his own right, to keep due measure and not to offend in some respect against the laws of Christian love. And it often happens that even men who are otherwise not bad sin not lightly then too, when in defending a good cause they indulge their passions too much. Christ therefore warns us that we should rather be most ready to yield our goods and to suffer a new loss, than violate charity for the sake of temporal things and entangle ourselves in more serious troubles. So the meaning of this admonition and precept is the same as the former. He does not therefore simply condemn legal courts, as if it were not lawful to use them, but he commands us to have a greater regard for charity than for our property. Rash litigants who invade the goods of others, and who hand down most hateful lawsuits even to posterity, ought to observe this. Above all, those who bring lawsuits against brothers who profess the same Christ, before profane judges and men alien to the faith, should observe it. Paul sharply rebukes such men in his First Letter to the Corinthians. And indeed, if individuals were to consider what they owe to brotherly charity, what labours, troubles and expenses must be borne, how much must be conceded to the deceitful rapacity of lawyers and the injustice of judges, they would soon see how much safer and more useful it is to follow Christ's precept than to commit themselves and all their goods to this most dangerous and most voracious sea. Yet in the meantime, those who restrain the tricks of heirs-hunters, the audacity of robbers, and the most unjust arts of usurers, by the protection of laws and courts, and who defend themselves and their property against them, are by no means to be condemned, provided they do not forget fraternal charity and do nothing too immoderately.

units.la: Tertiū præceptū est: Cuius peteti abs te dato, et ab eo qui tollit res tuas, ne repetito. Vbi de illis agit, qui absq; iuris prætextu iniqua à nobis petūt, vel etiā per vim nostra auferunt. Et monet ne his quoq; lite temere moueamus, sed potius studeamus iniurias omnes nostra bonitate & indulgētia vin cere, sicuti Paulus ad Rom. admonet. Interim meminerint qui in magistratu sunt, sui officij esse, vt improbos illos coerciant, quàmuis nemo accuset. Publicae enim pacis custodes sunt, quae nisi illud fiat, consistere non poterit. Magistratus ergo etiam non requisitus bonos tueatur, & sycophantas atq; raptores digna severitate coerceat. Graviter ergo peccant, qui iniuriam passos ad charitatis & patientiae Christianae leges remittunt, quod olim Iulianum Apostatam fecisse legimus, &c. In primis autem proderit, si omnes in Iesu Christi exemplum respiciant, qui ut nos à iusto & aequo aberrare non sinet, ita suorum iniurias atque oppressiones iusto iudicio ulcisci consueuit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The third precept is: "Do not demand back from him who takes away your goods what you have given to him who asks of you." Here he speaks of those who, without any pretext of right, demand unjust things from us, or even seize our goods by force. And he warns that we should not rashly stir up lawsuits against these people either, but rather strive to overcome all injuries by our goodness and forbearance, as Paul admonishes in Romans. Meanwhile, let those who hold the magistracy remember that it is their duty to restrain those wicked men, even though no one brings an accusation. For they are the guardians of public peace, which cannot stand unless this is done. Therefore the magistrate should protect the good even when not asked, and check sycophants and robbers with fitting severity. Those therefore sin grievously who, when they have suffered injury, remit it in the name of Christian charity and patience, as we read that Julian the Apostate once did, etc. Above all it will be profitable if all look to the example of Jesus Christ, who, as he does not allow us to stray from what is just and fair, so he is accustomed to avenge the injuries and oppressions of his own by a just judgment. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXI.
units.tr: Homily 61.

units.la: Et prout vultis ut faciant vobis homines, vos etiam facite eis similiter. Nam si diligitis eos qui vos diligunt, quae vobis erit gratia? nam peccatores quoque diligunt eos à quibus diliguntur. Et si benefeceritis iis, qui vobis benefaciunt, quae vobis erit gratia? nam & peccatores etiam idem faciunt. Et si mutuum dederitis iis, à quibus speratis vos recepturos, quae gratia erit vobis? nam & peccatores peccatoribus dant mutuum ut recipiant paria. Itaque diligite inimicos vestros, & benefacite, & mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes: & erit merces vestra multa, ac filii eritis illius Altissimi: nam & ipse benignus est erga ingratos & malos. Estote ergo misericordes, prout & Pater vester misericors est.
units.tr: "And as you would that men should do to you, do you also to them likewise. For if you love them which love you, what thank have you? for sinners also love those that love them. And if you do good to them which do good to you, what thank have you? for sinners also do even the same. And if you lend to them of whom you hope to receive, what thank have you? for sinners also lend to sinners, to receive as much again. But love you your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and you shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be you therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." [Luke 6:31-36]

units.la: Inter vitae Christianae officia nihil praestantius, utilius & magis necessarium est fraterna charitate. Per hanc enim Lex tota impletur, & eadem huius etiam vitae molestias, quae multa & carni nostrae nimium graves sunt, non modo tolerabiles, verumetiam iucundas & suaves reddit. Non temere ergo Iesus Christus illam nobis passim commendat, & in praesenti ita de ea disserit, ut simul omnia diligenter remoueat, quae illam extinguere, vel aliqua ex parte impedire possunt. Primo enim quia in proximi vocabulo, quem lex diligere iubet, plerique hallucinantur, eo omnes comprehendi docet, quos nostrae opis indigos esse videmus & omne personarum discrimen ita tollit, ut inimicos etiam diligere, & iis benefacere iubeat, qui nos iniurijs non vulgaribus affecerunt. Quid ergo non debemus aliis, à quibus nunquam laesi sumus, & qui nos amicorum loco habent, dum nostram opem implorant? Deinde cum talionis lege multi abutantur, & quiduis putent sibi licere in eos, qui in ipsos vel aperta vi, vel etiam sub iuris praetextu deliquerunt: Christus omnem priuatam vindictam sic prohibet, ut doceat Christianos homines ad nouas potius iniurias ferendas, quàm ad veteres ulciscendas paratos esse debere. Quae duo si probè observentur, nullus inter homines iniurijs locus reliquus erit, omnes autem beneficentiae mutuae studio accendentur. Sequuntur tamen adhuc quaedam, quae ad huius doctrinae explicationem ampliorem pertinent. In quibus primò summatim comprehendit quaecunque de charitate & eius officijs dici possunt. Deinde rationibus nonnullis persuadere studet, ne graue putemus quod de diligendis inimicis praecepit. Tandem verò locum istum concludit exemplo Dei patris, quod imitari debent qui eius filij censeri volunt.
units.tr: Among the duties of the Christian life there is nothing more excellent, more useful, or more necessary than brotherly love. For through it the whole Law is fulfilled, and it makes the troubles of this life, which are many and very burdensome to our flesh, not only bearable but even pleasant and sweet. It is therefore no accident that Jesus Christ commends it to us everywhere, and in the present passage discusses it in such a way that he at the same time carefully removes everything that can extinguish it or in some measure hinder it. First, since many go astray over the word "neighbour", whom the Law bids us love, he teaches that all are included whom we see to be in need of our help, and he so removes every distinction of persons that he bids us love even our enemies and do good to those who have wronged us in no ordinary way. Why, then, should we not owe help to those by whom we have never been injured, and who regard us as friends while they implore our aid? Next, since many abuse the law of retaliation and think they may do whatever they like to those who have offended them either by open violence or even under the pretext of law, Christ forbids all private vengeance in such a way as to teach Christians that they ought to be prepared to bear fresh injuries rather than to avenge old ones. If these two things are properly observed, no place will remain among men for injuries, and all will be inflamed with eagerness for mutual kindness. Yet there are still some points that pertain to a fuller explanation of this teaching. In these he first sums up briefly whatever can be said about love and its duties. Then he endeavours to persuade us, by several arguments, not to regard as burdensome what he has commanded about loving enemies. Finally, he concludes the passage with the example of God the Father, which those who wish to be counted his children ought to imitate.

units.la: Summa doctrinae huius est: Prout vultis ut faciant vobis homines, vos etiam facite eis similiter. Comprehendit sententia haec legem & prophetas (ut apud Matthaeum habetur) imò hac ipsissima naturae Lex est, quàm omnium hominum cordibus Deus inscripsit. Quàmuis autem verba clara sint, ut tamen eius sensum rectè intelligamus, ante omnia inquirendum erit, ad quam hominis voluntatem Lex ista extendi debeat. Nam si absque omni exceptione de omni eo exponatur, quod nobis fieri volumus, mox leges publicae abolebuntur, iudicia cessabunt, sceleirum poenae è medio tollentur, & hus sublatis quiduis audendi licentia regnum obtinebit. Vult enim qui in leges ciuiles peccauit, ut ipsi ignoscatur: ergo iudici quoque in neminem animaduertere licebit. Volent auari, ut omnes suis bonis cedant, & horum potestatem ipsis faciant: ergo ipsi quoque sua aliis largiri aut permittere debebunt. Volent qui aere alieno oppressi sunt, nomina sua expungi: idem ergo omnibus praescribetur, ne debitum à quoquam exigant. Denique quod nunc iste volet sibi fieri, hoc ipsum mox alius quispiam ab ipso postulabit, & ita iniquissimarum postulationum, turbarum & inextricabilis extricabilis confusionis nullus erit finis. Non igitur in genere de omnibus quae volumus fieri, sententia haec exponi debet, sed ad eam voluntatem restringi, quae non pugnat cum aequitate & legibus naturae: Atqui natura sic affecti sumus, ut nemo se aliqua iniuria affici velit, ut iniurias privatas sibi condonari omnes cupiant, ut item a suis non negligantur, sed ut quisquis obvius ipsis egentibus aut periclitantibus opem ferat: denique nemo est, qui non velit se amari & apud omnes in honore & pretio esse. Eodem ergo animo & voluntate ipsi quoque erga omnes homines praediti esse debemus. Itaque sententia haec minime tollit iudicia publica, neque fontium poenas abolet: non item rerum proprietati adversatur, ut neque ijs, quae ad legitimam & iustam rei domesticae administrationem pertinent: quin potius corrigit pravas & iniustas hominum voluntates, qui peccandi licentiam inducere student, & ex aliorum incommodis suum commodum quaerunt. Quia enim id tu fieri non vis, ut aliorum libidini tuae res serviant, hoc ipsum ab alijs quoque non debes exigere. Si enim gentium philosophi (ut apud Cyceronem est videre) hanc in amicitia primam legem faciendam esse intellexerunt, ut neque rogemus res turpes, neque faciamus rogati: quanto magis Christiani homines cauere debent, ne Christianae charitatis lege adres iniustas aut inhonestas abutantur?
units.tr: The sum of this teaching is: "As you would that men should do to you, do you also to them likewise." This saying comprises the Law and the Prophets (as it stands in Matthew), indeed it is that very law of nature which God has written in the hearts of all men. However, although the words are clear, in order to understand their meaning correctly we must first inquire to what human will this law ought to be extended. For if it were explained without any exception of everything that we wish done to us, public laws would immediately be abolished, the courts would cease, the punishments of crimes would be removed from the midst, and with these gone, a licence to dare anything would hold sway. For one who has sinned against the civil laws wishes to be pardoned; therefore it would not be lawful for a judge to punish anyone either. Misers would wish all to surrender their goods and hand over their power to them; therefore they too would be obliged to give or to allow their own goods to others. Those who are weighed down by debt would wish their names to be wiped out; therefore the same would be prescribed for all, that no one should demand a debt from anyone. In short, what one man now wishes to be done to himself, another will shortly demand of him, and so there will be no end to the most unjust demands, to disturbances and inextricable confusion. Therefore this saying must not be explained in general terms about everything we wish done, but restricted to that will which does not conflict with equity and the laws of nature. Now we are so constituted by nature that no one wishes to be harmed in any way; all desire that their private injuries be forgiven them; likewise that they should not be neglected by others, but that whoever meets them in need or danger should bring them help; in short, there is no one who does not wish to be loved and to be held in honour and esteem by all. We ought therefore to be disposed in the same spirit and will toward all men. Accordingly, this saying by no means removes public judgments, nor does it abolish the punishment of crimes; nor does it oppose the ownership of property, nor those things which pertain to the lawful and just administration of household affairs. Rather, it corrects the perverse and unjust wills of those men who seek to introduce a licence to sin, and who seek their own advantage from the disadvantage of others. For because you do not wish your goods to serve the lust of others, you ought not to demand this of others either. For if the philosophers of the nations (as may be seen in Cicero) understood that the first law of friendship is this, that we should not ask for base things, nor do what we are asked to do, how much more ought Christians to beware lest they abuse the law of Christian love to unjust or dishonourable ends?

units.la: Porrò redit ad dilectionis praeceptum, & eam partem, qua inimicos diligere iubemur, amplius exponit. Nam quae prius dicta sunt, nunquam sufficiunt ijs, qui carnem in consilium adhibent: Ergo alias adhuc rationes adducit, quibus cunctatores vrgeat, aut effugia quaerentes in officio contineat. Et primò quidem ostendit, nos nisi inimicos diligamus, nihil laude dignum agere, sed ijs adhuc pares esse, quos propter carnis & mundi studia merito detestamur. Id vero multis enuntiat, quò efficacius animos auditorum penetret, atq; eos pudore suffundat, qui sibijpsis mirifice placent atq; blandiuntur, si bene de se meritis aliquam gratiam retulerunt. Sic ergo dicit: Si diligitis eos, qui vos diligunt, quae vobis erit gratia? nã peccatores quoq; diligunt eos, à quibus diliguntur. Etsi benefeceritis ijs, qui vobis benefaciunt, quae vobis erit gratia? nam & peccatores etiam idem faciunt. Et si mutuum dederitis ijs, à quibus speratis vos recepturos, quae gratia erit vobis? nam & peccatores peccatoribus dant mutuum, vt recipiant paria. Peccatores autem dicit, non eos qui ex infirmitate peccant (qua ratione nemo hominum non peccator est: nam in multis labimur omnes, inquit Apostolus) sed eos qui peccati mancipia facti, sese ad omnem licentiam dedouerunt, quos vulgò sceleratos & poenitere nescios dicimus. Quo sensu etiam apud Ioannem Deus peccatores dicitur non audire. Ideo Matthaeus peccatorum loco publicanos nominauit, qui (vt suo loco dictum est) desperata malitia & impietatis homines esse tunc vulgò putabantur. Sensus ergo verborum Christi est, nos si amicos & eos solos diligamus, qui aut iam de nobis bene meriti sunt, aut in posterum nobis gratiam referre possunt, nihilo meliores fore sceleratissimis hominibus, & proinde neq; gratiam apud Deum, neq; inter vere pios & honestos aliquâ laudem mereri. Qui enim ad hunc modum diligunt, ij non proximum, sed seipsos diligunt: & proinde diligendi finem faciunt, vt primum aliorum amorem ergà se refriguisse sentiunt. Idem quoq; non proximo, sed sibijpsis bene faciunt, cum non aliorum sed propria commoda quarant. Quod cum omnes faciant, quos ex primis parentibus innata nobis philautia excaecat, quà obsecro gratiam illi merentur? Est autem magnum huius rationis pondus apud eos, qui suae vocationis & professionis dignitatem recte considerant. Nam sciunt, Christum suos è mundo selegisse, vt eos sibi populum peculiarem faceret, cuius virtus atq; pietas supra omnes alios emineat. Intelligunt ergo se nondum Christiano nomine dignos esse, quando in eodem cum huius saeculi filijs gradu adhuc consistunt. Itaq; nequaquam sufficit, si mundi iudicio iusti & sanctissimi sumus, sed perfectius quid à nobis Christus requirit, & ideo progressu opus est, quoad nos à meta illa Christianae perfectionis abesse sentimus. Arguit hoc eorum stultitiam, qui in aliis quoq; sceleribus sibi blanduntur, & ea exemplis aliorum excusant, qui Christo nondum vere nomen dederunt. Est hoc nimis vulgare hodie, eò quod innatum sit omnibus, vt ad exempla recurrant, quando rationibus iustis destituuntur. Sic ergo fornicationi, adulteriis, ebrietati, chorearum lasciviae, aleae, militiae mercenariae, furis et infinitis aliis sceleribus multi patrocinantur, seq; plus satis excusatos esse putant, quod ea modo designent, quae apud omnes in usu sunt. At hoc dicendo seipsos accusant potius quàm excusant. Ita enim conflat, ipsos nondum è mundo selectos, neq; adhuc Christianos esse, cum ea designant, quae Apostolus inter Christianos ne nominanda quidem esse docet.
units.tr: Again he returns to the command of love, and sets out more fully that part in which we are bidden to love our enemies. For what was said before never suffices for those who take counsel from the flesh: So he now brings forward further reasons, by which he may press the hesitant and keep within their duty those who seek ways of escape. And first he shows that unless we love our enemies we do nothing worthy of praise, but remain on a level with those whom we rightly detest for their devotion to the flesh and the world. He says this in many words so that it may penetrate more effectively the minds of the hearers and bring a blush to those who take great pleasure in themselves and flatter themselves, if they have won some thanks for good deeds done to others. He speaks thus: "If you love those who love you, what thanks will you have? For even sinners love those by whom they are loved. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what thanks will you have? For sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive back, what thanks will you have? For sinners also lend to sinners, that they may receive as much again." By "sinners" he means not those who sin through weakness (for on this ground there is no man who is not a sinner, since we all stumble in many things, as the Apostle says), but those who have become slaves of sin and have given themselves over to every license, whom we commonly call wicked and unable to repent. In this sense also, in John, God is said not to hear sinners. So Matthew named the publicans in place of sinners, who, as was said in its place, were then commonly thought to be men of hopeless wickedness and impiety. The meaning, then, of Christ's words is this: if we love only friends, and only those who have either already deserved well of us or can in future repay us, we shall be no better than the most wicked men, and so we shall merit neither thanks before God nor any praise among those who are truly pious and upright. For those who love in this way do not love their neighbour but themselves; and so they stop loving as soon as they perceive that the affection of others towards them has cooled. Likewise they do good not to their neighbour but to themselves, when they seek not the advantage of others but their own. Since all men do this, whom the self-love innate in us from our first parents blinds, what thanks, I beg you, do they deserve? Moreover, this reasoning carries great weight with those who rightly consider the dignity of their calling and profession. For they know that Christ has chosen his people out of the world, so that he might make them a peculiar people whose virtue and piety should stand out above all others. They understand, therefore, that they are not yet worthy of the Christian name, when they still stand on the same level as the children of this age. Therefore it is by no means enough if we are just and most holy in the judgement of the world; rather Christ requires something more perfect from us, and so we must press on, as long as we feel that we are still far from that goal of Christian perfection. This exposes the folly of those who flatter themselves even in other sins and excuse them by the examples of others who have not yet truly given their name to Christ. This is too common today, because it is innate in all men to have recourse to examples when they lack just reasons. Thus many defend fornication, adultery, drunkenness, the wantonness of dances, dice, mercenary soldiering, theft and countless other crimes, and think themselves more than sufficiently excused because they name only things that are in use among everyone. But in saying this they accuse themselves rather than excuse themselves. For it is thereby plain that they have not yet been chosen out of the world, nor are they yet Christians, when they name those things which the Apostle teaches are not even to be named among Christians.

units.la: Quia vero haec alterius loci sunt, nunc videamus, quo loco haberi debeant, qui ne eos quidem diligere dignantur, à quibus ipsi diliguntur, quiq; ijs pessimam gratiam referunt, à quibus ipsi amplissima beneficia acceperunt, imò quorum beneficentiam quotidie sentiunt. Exuerunt hi communem sensum, & in naturae leges peccant, quae gratitudinem non modò brutis animantibus, verumetiam telluri insseuit. Nam vt animalia suos nutritios agnoscunt, ita terram diligentiori cultura mitescere, & ex sterili tractabiliorem fieri videmus, vt agricolarum laboribus respondeat. Est ergo ingratitudinis vitium ipsius naturae legibus contrarium, & proinde non temere à Cicerone dictum fuit, in ingratitudine nihil non mali inesse. Vidit hoc ipsum vetus Persarum gens, cuius leges hominibus ingratis capitale supplicium decernebant: nimirum quòd illis nihil sceleftius esse crederent. Quid enim maleficij non designabit aliquâ iniuria provocatus, quem beneficia accepta à malefaciendo abstrerere non possunt? At regnat hoc hominum genus hodie passim, & multorum ea est improbitas, vt in eo laudem quarant, si aduersus benefactores suos impie tumultuentur. Faciunt hoc subditi, qui principibus suis obstrepunt, vt legum sanctissimarum iugum excutiant, quibus peccandi licentia coercetur. Ingratitudinis hanc verbi administri sentiunt, quando ab ijs foedissime proscinduntur, pro quorum salute ipsi excubant, & quos pijs admonitionibus ab interitu revocare studient. Quàm immanis vero liberorum erga parentes, & iuvenum prope omnium erga suos praeceptores petulantia ubiq; locorum grassetur, nemo non videt. Eadem est seruorum erga heros impietas, et plerosq; horum lenitate exacerbari constat, ut sibi nihil non licere arbitrentur. Deniq; nihil tam vulgare est quam beneficiorum obliuio, & pro bonis haberi possunt, qui ab iniuria & maleficio abstinent.
units.tr: But since these matters belong to another place, let us now see in what place should be held those who do not deign even to love those by whom they are loved, and who render the worst thanks to those from whom they have received the most ample benefits, indeed whose kindness they feel every day. Such men strip off common sense and sin against the laws of nature, which have engraved gratitude not only on brute animals but also on the earth. For just as animals recognise those who nourish them, so we see the earth become gentler under more diligent cultivation, and from barren becoming more workable, so that it answers the labours of the farmers. Ingratitude, therefore, is a vice contrary to the very laws of nature, and so it was not without reason that Cicero said there is nothing evil that is not present in ingratitude. The ancient nation of the Persians saw this too, whose laws decreed capital punishment for ungrateful men, since they believed that nothing was more criminal. For what wrong will he not commit, provoked by some injury, whom the benefits received cannot restrain from doing evil? Yet this kind of men reigns today everywhere, and many are so wicked that they seek praise in acting impiously against their benefactors. Subjects do this, who rail at their princes so that they may shake off the yoke of the most holy laws by which licence to sin is restrained. The ministers of the Word feel this ingratitude when they are most foully torn apart by those for whose salvation they themselves keep watch, and whom they strive to call back from destruction by pious admonitions. How monstrous, indeed, is the insolence of children towards their parents, and of almost all young men towards their teachers, is seen by everyone, wherever one goes. The same is the impiety of servants towards their masters, and it is plain that most of them are made worse by the gentleness of their masters, so that they think nothing is not allowed them. Finally, nothing is so common as forgetfulness of benefits, and those may be counted good men who merely abstain from injury and wrong.

units.la: At singulari observatione dignum est, quod inter charitatis & beneficentiae opera illud quoque recenset, quo mutuum datur. Est hoc necessarium plane, quando non semper omnibus ad manum est quo opus habent, neq; tantae sunt omnium fortunae, ut sua donare possint quibusfuis. Et constat eos qui mutuum dant, interdum non minus beneficium conferre egenti quam si dono darent. Adhaec charitatis lex minime excludit gratitudinem, quae iubet, ne aliorum beneficentia fraudulenter abutamur, sed bonam gratiam referamus ijs, qui nos sua liberalitate iuuerunt. Vult tamen Christus, ut hic quoque ius nostrum non pertinaciter vrgeamus, neque ijs solis mutuum demus, a quibus nos nostra recepturos esse certa spes est, sed potius spectemus quibus nam alij opus habeant, quam quid nobis debeatur. Quia enim prophani & a fide alieni mutuum dare solent ijs, a quibus sua recipere, & quorum beneficentia ipsi quoque iuuari possunt: nihil praeclari facient, qui cum Christum profiteantur, in hoc gradu pedem sistunt, & non altius ascendunt, ut eam perfectionem assequantur, quam ille a nobis requirit. Quam vero necessaria sit hoc tempore ista admonitio, res ipsa testatur. Ea enim est multorum inhumanitas, ut neijs quidem mutuum dare velint, a quibus sua se recepturos esse, dubitare non possunt. Et est hic auaritiae effectus non postremus, quod ita excaecat hominum mentes, ut quorumuis inopiam atq; miseriam immisericorditer spectare possint, modo interea nummos in arca & ingentes frugum aceruos contemplari liceat, quibus & ipsi non vtuntur, & simul alijs illorum vsum inuident. Regnat ista inhumanitas hodie, & fateor eam illorum perfidia & ingratitudine prouocari atque augeri, qui dum mutuo accipiunt, suos creditores iniquissime fallunt, & in reddendo tam duros & difficiles se praebent, ut in lucro poni possit quicquid ab illis extorseris. Peccant isti graviter, neque ipsorum ingratitudinem Deus inultam sinet; eadem tamen nobis minime causa esse debet, ut conculcata charitatis lege a benefaciendo prorsus abstineamus. Quin potius cum ingrati mundi contumacia nos luctari conuenit, ut nos Dei patris filios esse testemur, quem hominum ingratitudo non impedit, quo minus omnibus benefaciat. Pra alijs autem hic peccant, qui charitatis praetextu ad auaritiam palliandam crudelissime abutuntur, & mutuum quidem dant, sed ea conditione, ut miseros magis grauent, & praedones potius quam benefactores dici mereantur. Ex horum numero sunt, qui pignora recipiunt, quibus miseros illos non sine maximo incommodo carere posse sciunt. Qui item foenus exigunt & vsuras faciunt, quas miseri debitores maiori cum difficultate quam fortem dissoluunt. Sunt illi aspidum instar, quae cum morsu venenum soporiferum instillant, quo paulatim homo extinguitur. Imo volant potius domus, praedia & fortunas debitorum omnes: neque in hos solos iniurij sunt, sed in rempublicam, quae frequenter motibus ciuilibus concutitur, quos eorum impatientia excitat, qui aere alieno ita se grauatos sentiunt, ut nunquam emergere possint. Damnantur vsurariae artes legibus Imperatorum, at hodie in ter Christiani nominis professores passim regnant. Sed cum a sceleratis & prophanis huius seculi filijs, quoad hanc causam, nihil differant, qui absque fraude mutuum dant ijs, quos accepta reditu-ros sciunt, nunquam profecto pro suis eos agnoscet Christus, qui vel neminem prorsus iuuant suis opibus, vel non contenti sua recepisse, insuper debitorum suorum fortunas omnes hiru dinum instar exugunt. Voluptuantur isti vere & superbiunt ex male partis diuitijs: sed latet domi ipsorum ignis (vt Micheas ait) thesaurus nimirum iniquus, & clamant interea ad Dominum per ipsos oppressi pauperes, neq; horum querelas ille negligit, qui vt omnem iniquitatem punit, ita eam maxime odit, quae sub pietatis praetextu exercetur.
units.tr: But it is especially worthy of notice that among the works of charity and beneficence he also reckons that by which a loan is given. This is plainly necessary, since not everyone always has at hand what he needs, nor are the fortunes of all such that they can give their own goods to whoever wishes. And it is clear that those who lend sometimes confer on the needy no less a benefit than if they gave a gift. Moreover, the law of charity by no means excludes gratitude, which bids us not to abuse the kindness of others deceitfully, but to return a good thanks to those who have helped us by their generosity. Yet Christ wills that here too we should not press our right stubbornly, nor lend only to those from whom we are certain to get our own back, but rather look to whom others have need, rather than to what is owed to us. For since profane men, and those alien to faith, are accustomed to lend to those from whom they receive their own back, and by whose kindness they themselves too can be helped, those who profess Christ will do nothing outstanding if they stop at this level and do not climb higher, so as to attain that perfection which he requires of us. How necessary this admonition is at this time, the thing itself bears witness. For such is the inhumanity of many that they are not willing to lend even to those from whom they cannot doubt they will get their own back. And this is no small effect of avarice, that it so blinds men's minds that they can look without pity on the poverty and misery of anyone, provided meanwhile they may gaze upon their coins in the chest and huge heaps of grain, which they themselves do not use, and at the same time begrudge others the use of them. This inhumanity reigns today, and I confess that it is provoked and increased by the treachery and ingratitude of those who, while they borrow, most unjustly cheat their creditors, and show themselves so hard and difficult in repaying that whatever you have wrung from them can be counted as gain. These men sin grievously, and God will not leave their ingratitude unpunished; yet this should by no means be for us a cause to trample the law of charity and utterly abstain from doing good. Rather it is fitting that we should struggle against the obstinacy of the ungrateful world, so that we may bear witness that we are sons of God the Father, whom the ingratitude of men does not prevent from doing good to all. But they sin above others who, under the pretext of charity, most cruelly abuse it to cloak their avarice, and indeed lend, but on such terms that they weigh more heavily upon the wretched, and deserve to be called plunderers rather than benefactors. Of this number are those who take pledges, knowing that those wretched men cannot do without them without the greatest hardship. Likewise those who exact interest and charge usury, which the wretched debtors pay off with greater difficulty than the principal. They are like asps, which drip a soporific poison along with their bite, by which the man is gradually extinguished. Indeed they rather fly upon the houses, estates and fortunes of all debtors; nor are they injurious to these alone, but to the commonwealth as well, which is often shaken by civil disturbances stirred up by the impatience of those who feel themselves so burdened with debt that they can never come up for air. The arts of usury are condemned by the laws of the emperors, yet today they reign everywhere among professors of the Christian name. But since in this matter they differ nothing from the wicked and profane children of this age, those who lend without fraud to those whom they know will repay them will never be acknowledged by Christ as their own; nor will those who either help nobody at all with their resources, or, not content with having received what was theirs, suck dry the entire fortunes of their debtors like leeches. These men truly revel and take pride in riches wrongly gained; but fire (as Micah says) lies hidden in their houses, namely unjust treasure, and meanwhile the poor, oppressed by them, cry out to the Lord, and he does not neglect their complaints, who, as he punishes all iniquity, so he hates most of all that which is practised under the pretext of piety.

units.la: Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, qui quid a nobis fieri debeat, disertis verbis docet: Itaq; diligite inimicos vestros, & benefacite, & mutuum date nihil inde sperantes, &c. Quo loco non aliud quam ficentia praecia gratuitam beneficentiam & charitatem synceram praecipit: vt nimirum abstq; omni priuati commodi respectu benefaciamus etiam ijs, ex quibus nihil nobis sperare licet. Et rursus mutui meminit, quia hoc (vt diximus) inter beneficentiae opera non postremum locum obtinet: simulq; monet, ne nos quorundam perfidia & ingratitudine abstreri patiamur ab hoc officij genere, quo vix aliud inter homi-
units.tr: But let us return to Christ's words, who teaches plainly what we ought to do: "Therefore love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return," etc. In this place he enjoins nothing other than free beneficence and sincere charity, namely that we do good, without any regard to private advantage, even to those from whom we can hope for nothing. And again he mentions lending, because (as we have said) this holds no minor place among the works of beneficence; at the same time he warns us not to let ourselves be drawn away from this kind of duty, than which scarcely anything is more useful and more necessary among men

units.la: Gratuita bene[ficentia] ... pitur.
units.tr: Free beneficence ... pitur.

units.la: De mutuo. nes ad seruandam amicitiam & mutuam beneficentiam vtilius est, & magis necessarium. Itaque quod hic de mutuo dicitur, quidam falso & perperam detorquent ad reditus annuos, qui ex vsufru ctu agrorum aut domuum recipiuntur. Illic enim nō mutuum datur, sed contractus fit legitimus, neq; fænerator dici debet, qui ex agris, ipsius pecunia ex parte emptis, aut saltem seruatis, aliquem fructum percipit. Iniquus autem et iniustus esset, qui ex aliena pecunia agrum aut domum emere, et ex illis solus fructum habere vellet. Fateor quidem in his etiam nonnullos modum excedere, dum onus frumenti (vt Amos loquitur) ab agricolis exigunt, aut miseros censibus grauant maioribus, quàm qui ex agris commode colligi possint. Videant ergo Christiani homines primùm, ne quid in leges publicas peccent, & ne aliis quoq; mali exempli authores sint: deinde valeat in primis Christi lex, vt per hanc legum ciuilium rigorem mitigent. Nec enim Christiano homini fas est, quod per leges ciuiles licet, si id cum alicuius incommodo fit coniunctum. At quia haec tractatio a Christi verbis aliter est, sufficiat nunc obseruauisse, illum hoc loco non aliud iubere, quàm quod infra Cap.14 diligentius exponit dicens: Cùm facis prandium aut cœnam, noli vocare amicos tuos, neq; fratres tuos, neq; cognatos tuos, neq; vicinos diuites: ne quando & ipsi te vicissim vocent, ac retribuatur tibi beneficium. Sed cùm facis epulum, voca pauperes, mancos, claudos, cæcos. Et beatus eris, quia non possunt retribuere tibi: retribuetur autem tibi in resurrectione iustorum. Vbi nemo putauerit, Christum prohibere, ne quid officij præstemus iis, quos cognationis vinculum aut vicinitas nobis propius devinxit, aut qui opulentiores sunt: sed ne sub beneficentiæ prætextu retributionem vberiorem, & priuatum commodum quæramus, prohibet. Interim licet honorarijs conuiuijs amicos cùm peregrinos tum domesticos excipere, licet diuitum amicitiam colere, & ijs obsequium præstare, qui gratiam bonam referre possunt: omne autem illud ex officio Christiana charitatis, non retributionis spe fieri debet. Ita Christiani hominis est mutuum dare egenti, ex quo nihil sperent: at simul eidem licet domus et prædia emere, ex ijsdem fructum percipere, aut etiam eius gratitudine vti, quem sua pecunia adiuuit: curet modo ne charitatis affectus lucri cupiditate turbetur.
units.tr: On lending. For keeping friendship and mutual beneficence, and for that reason it is more useful and more necessary. Yet some people falsely and wrongly twist what is said here about lending into the annual revenues received from the usufruct of fields or houses. For there money is not lent, but a lawful contract is made, and a person should not be called a usurer who draws some fruit from fields bought, at least in part, or kept, with his own money. But it would be unfair and unjust for someone who wished to buy a field or house with another's money and to have the fruit of them for himself alone. I admit indeed that some exceed the proper measure in these matters too, when they exact a burden of grain from the farmers (as Amos puts it), or weigh down the wretched with taxes greater than can fairly be raised from the fields. Let Christians therefore see first that they do not sin against the public laws, and that they are not authors of bad example to others; then let Christ's law above all prevail, so that by it they may moderate the rigour of the civil laws. For it is not right for a Christian to do what the civil laws allow if it is joined with harm to someone else. But since this discussion is different from Christ's words, it is enough for now to have noted that he here commands nothing other than what he explains more carefully below in chapter 14, saying: "When you make a dinner or supper, do not call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your relatives, nor your rich neighbours, lest they also invite you in return and a benefit be repaid to you. But when you make a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; but it will be repaid to you at the resurrection of the just." Here no one should suppose that Christ forbids us to show any kindness to those whom ties of kinship or neighbourhood bind more closely to us, or to those who are wealthier; he forbids us only to seek, under the pretext of beneficence, a fuller repayment and private advantage. Meanwhile it is lawful to receive friends, both foreign and domestic, at honourable feasts, lawful to cultivate the friendship of the rich and to show courtesy to those who can return a good favour; but all of this must be done from the duty of Christian charity, not from hope of repayment. Thus it is the duty of a Christian to lend to a needy person from whom he hopes for nothing; and at the same time it is lawful for him to buy a house and lands, to draw fruit from them, or even to enjoy the gratitude of the one he has helped with his money, provided only that the affection of charity is not disturbed by a desire for gain.

units.la: At quia in his præstandis natura tardiores sumus, stimulos adhibet Christus & rationibus gratissimis nos excitat. Prima est: Erit merces vestra multa. Ad cuius confirmationem facit, quòd alibi pollicetur se in suas rationes ascribere velle, quæ suo nomine in suos conferuntur. Et habet vera pietas promissiones tam præsentis quàm futuri seculi: neq; exempla desunt eorum, quibus beneficia, quæ in homines vel ingratos vel omnium egentes contulerunt, pulchrè fænerata sunt. Debet inter hos censeri Dauid, qui Saulem hostem acerrimum dilexit, & ijs benefecit, ex quibus nihil boni sperare poterat, cùm in suam necem palam coniurauissent. At multa fuit eius merces, quando deinde Saule ipse in regni fastigium euectus est. Et hodie non raró Deum remuneratorem sentiunt, qui homines erga se ingratos experiuntur. Altera ratio est, quòd nos filios Altissimi illius, id est, veri & æterni Dei, cuius gloria supra omnes cœlos exaltata est, fore ait. Cōtinet hæc promissio omnia, quæ ad hominis felicitatem faciunt. Qui enim Dei filius est, idem bonorum eius omnium hæres sit oportet: neq; periculum est, ne filios suos in hoc mundo periclitantes ille deserat, cuius prouidentia ad volucres, feras & homines abs se alienissimos vsq; extenditur. Vt verò minus dubitemus, promissionem argumento ex Dei natura desumpto confirmat, dicens: Nam ipse benignus est erga ingratos & malos. Argumenti vis in eo sita est, quòd pro filijs suis Deus illos agnoscit, qui eius ingenium referunt. At Deus ingratos & indignos suo amore complectitur. Huius ergo similes, imò filij sunt, qui absq; omni personarum respectu quibusuis obuijs benefaciunt. Et hoc illud est, quod gentium philosophi tradiderunt, nos benefaciendo quàm proximè ad Deorum naturam accedere. Est autem hic probè obseruandum, beneficentiam nos non facere Dei filios, sed filiorum Dei signum aut tesseram esse, ex qua illi agnoscuntur. Nam vt filij Dei efficiamur, regeneratione opus est. Hæc autem solis electis contingit ex gratia, qui Iesum Christū fide nō fucata apprehendūt. Frustra ergo ex hisce verbis figmento suo præsidium quærunt, qui operū nostrorum merita propugnant, quasi illis regni cælorum hæreditatem mereamur. Quòd si verò beneficentia nos Dei filios esse declarant, satis apparet non inania consilia esse quæ hic nobis proponuntur, sed præcepta potius, quibus necessariò obedire debeant, quicunq; pro Dei filijs haberi volunt. Nec enim satis est, si tales dicamur, sed quod dicimur factis testari oportet: quando alibi Christus mendaces & homicidas diaboli filios dicit, eò quòd hu-ius opera faciant.
units.tr: But since we are slower by nature in performing these duties, Christ applies spurs and rouses us with most welcome reasons. The first is: "Your reward will be great." To confirm this, it helps that he promises elsewhere that he will credit to his own account what is given in his name. True piety has promises both for the present age and for the age to come, and there is no lack of examples of those whose kindnesses, bestowed on men who were either ungrateful or utterly needy, have been repaid handsomely with interest. David must be counted among these, who loved Saul, his most bitter enemy, and did good to him, though Saul had openly conspired for his death. Yet his reward was great when Saul himself was afterwards raised to the summit of the kingdom. And even today people who experience ingratitude from others often find God to be the rewarder. The second reason is that he says we will be sons of the Most High, that is, of the true and eternal God, whose glory is exalted above all the heavens. This promise contains everything that contributes to human happiness. For whoever is the son of God must also be heir of all his goods; nor is there any danger that he who extends his providence to birds, beasts and men most alien to him should abandon his sons who are in peril in this world. And so that we may doubt less, he confirms the promise by an argument drawn from the nature of God, saying: "For he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil." The force of the argument lies in this: God acknowledges as his sons those who bear his character. But God embraces with his love the ungrateful and the unworthy. Therefore those who are like him, indeed are his sons, are those who do good to whoever meets them, without any regard to persons. And this is what the philosophers of the nations taught, that by doing good we come as near as possible to the nature of the gods. Yet here it must be carefully observed that beneficence does not make us sons of God; rather it is a sign or token of the sons of God, by which they are recognised. For we must be born again before we become sons of God; and this comes only to the elect, by grace, who lay hold of Jesus Christ with unfeigned faith. Those therefore seek a defence in these words for their invention in vain, who champion the merits of our works, as if we could earn the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven by them. But if beneficence declares us to be sons of God, it is plain that the counsels proposed to us here are not empty, but rather precepts which must necessarily be obeyed by all who wish to be regarded as sons of God. For it is not enough to be called such; we must bear witness by our deeds that we are what we are called, since elsewhere Christ calls liars and murderers the sons of the devil, because they do his works.

units.la: Caeterum concludit hanc partem Christus, & ad unius Dei exemplum nos revocans ait: Estote ergo misericordes, pro ut pater vester misericors est. Misericordiam requirit, quae charitatis atq; officiorum omnium erga proximum quasi mater & nutrix est, sicuti infra in Samaritani parabola audiemus. Quia vero huius affectum restinguere conantur, qui carnis ingenium sapiunt, multi quoq; se plus satis profecisse putant, si leuissimum aliquod officium in aliquem conferant, Christus ipsius Dei Patris exemplum nobis misericordiae regulam esse vult. Est ut ipsa charitas, & proinde non opus habet vllis incitamentis, quibus excitetur, ut nobis benefaciat. Deinde nostri non minus miseretur, quàm parens aliquis liberorum suorum. Nouit enim quòd puluis & cinis sumus, & proinde infirmitatibus nostris facile ignoscit. Imò ut apud Isaiam testatur, misericordia eius naturales illas matrum affectiones, quas Graeci σοργὰς dixerunt, longe superat. Adhaec misericordiam non verbis solùm aut inanibus promissis, sed reipsa & factis testatur, ut in toto hoc mundi issius opificio & omnibus ijs est videre, quae quotidie fiunt: ut iam nihil de eo dicamus, quòd filio suo vnigenito non pepercit, sed pro nobis illum tradidit. Et quàmuis interdum nostra contumacia quasi vitius poenas scelerum exigat, in ira tamen sua misericordiae recordatur, & hac illius rigorem temperat. Denique indignissimis quoque benefacit, & (ut in Matthaeo habetur) Solem suum oriri finit super iustos & iniustos, & utrosque pluuijs atque frugum proventu recreat. Et ut Micheae verbis vtar, super scelus transit, iniquitates subigit, & peccata abijcit in abyssum maris. Ista nobis imitanda proponit Christus, ne diligentiori in vitia aliorum inquisitione ipsos negligendi occasionem captemus. Charitatis enim est peccatorum multitudinem tegere, non malignus traducere. Apparet autem hoc loco, quantum humana iustitia à diuina distet, & quòdim- possibile et sit quenquam ad hanc charitatis & misericordiae perfectionem pertingere. Opus ergo est, ut Christum Iesum apprehendamus, qui ut nobis iustitia à Patre factus est, ita suo spiritu nos animare & confirmare potest, ut in ipso possimus omnia. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Christ concludes this part, recalling us to the example of God alone, and says: "Therefore be merciful, as your Father also is merciful." He requires mercy, which is like a mother and nurse of charity and of all duties towards our neighbour, as we shall hear below in the parable of the Samaritan. But because those who savour of the flesh try to quench this affection, many also think they have done more than enough if they confer some very slight service on someone; Christ wills that the example of God the Father himself be our rule of mercy. He is himself charity, and therefore has no need of any incitements by which he might be stirred to do us good. Moreover he has no less pity for us than a parent for his children. For he knows that we are dust and ashes, and therefore he readily pardons our infirmities. Indeed, as he testifies through Isaiah, his mercy far surpasses those natural affections of mothers which the Greeks called [σοργάς]. Furthermore, he testifies to his mercy not by words alone or empty promises, but in very deed and by his works, as can be seen in this whole fabric of the world and in all those things that happen every day; to say nothing more of this, that he did not spare his only-begotten Son, but delivered him up for us. And although at times our obstinacy, like a vice, exacts the punishment of our sins, yet in his anger he remembers mercy, and by it tempers his severity. Finally, he does good even to the most unworthy, and (as is found in Matthew) he lets his sun rise on the just and the unjust, and refreshes both with rain and the abundance of crops. And, to use the words of Micah, he passes over transgression, subdues iniquities, and casts sins into the depths of the sea. Christ sets these things before us to imitate, so that we do not seize the opportunity of neglecting them by a more diligent searching out of the faults of others. For it is the mark of charity to cover a multitude of sins, not to maliciously expose them. And here it appears how far human justice is from divine, and how it is almost impossible for anyone to attain to this perfection of charity and mercy. Therefore we must lay hold of Christ Jesus, who was made righteousness to us by the Father, and who can by his Spirit so animate and strengthen us that we can do all things in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXII.

units.la: Ne iudicate, & non iudicabimini. Ne condemnate, & non condemnabimini. Remittite, & remittetur vobis. Date, & dabitur vobis: mensuram (inquam) bonam, pressam & agitatam & superfluentem dabunt in sinum vestrum. Eadem enim mensura qua metimini, vicissim metientur vobis alij.
units.tr: Judge not, and you shall not be judged. Condemn not, and you shall not be condemned. Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you. Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, will they pour into your bosom. For with the same measure that you measure, others will in turn measure to you.

units.la: MVltis & gravibus argumentis hucusq; vsus est Iesus Christus in commendanda nobis fraterna charitate & beneficentiae studio. Fuit inter haec ordine postremum, ipsius Dei patris exemplum, cuius bonitas atq; misericordia in toto huius mundi opificio & in omnibus eius operibus atque iudicijs elucet. Et huius quidem consideratio apud pios efficacissima est. Vt enim egregiae & bonae indolis filij patriae virtutis commemoratione ita mouentur, ut inexpiabile scelus esse putent, si non illius vestigijs sedulò insistant: sic qui germani filij Dei sunt, nihil antiquius habent, quàm ut huius ingenio se accommodent, & ipsum in moribus, dictis factisq; omnibus referant. At quia nobis, quoad in carne hac vitiosa & mortali viuimus, perpetuò adhaeret philautiae malum, fit, ut nunquam non captemus occasiones eos negligendi, quos nobis Deus commendatissimos esse vult. Quapropter etsi audiamus nos debere inimicos diligere, & illis benefacere, qui gratiam referre vel non possunt, vel etiam nolunt, mox tamen aliud effugium quaeritur: & audiuntur passim eorum voces, qui se inimicis suis optimè velle protestantur, et ad condonandum iniurias sibi factas esse paratos: interim se non posse non eos odisse aiunt, qui cum peccandi licentia Dei contemptum coniunxerunt, & illius iram prouocare nunquam desinunt. Sunt isti (inquiunt) non tam nostri quàm ipsius
units.tr: Jesus Christ has so far used many weighty arguments in commending to us brotherly love and the zeal for doing good. Last among these, he set before us the example of God the Father himself, whose goodness and mercy shine forth in the whole fabric of this world and in all his works and judgments. The consideration of this is most effective among the godly. For just as sons of an excellent and good disposition are moved by the recollection of their father's virtue, so that they think it an unpardonable crime not to follow closely in his footsteps, so those who are true sons of God have nothing more important than to conform themselves to his nature and to reflect him in all their conduct, words and deeds. But because the evil of self-love clings to us constantly, for as long as we live in this flawed and mortal flesh, we are never without occasions for neglecting those whom God wants us to hold most dear. Therefore, although we hear that we ought to love our enemies and do good to those who cannot or will not repay the favour, a way of escape is soon sought. Everywhere one hears the voices of those who profess that they wish their enemies well and are ready to pardon the wrongs done to them; yet, they say, they cannot help hating those who have joined contempt for God with licence to sin and never cease to provoke his wrath. "These people," they say, "are not so much our enemies as enemies of God himself, whose honour our own life ought to make us love. Therefore it is neither godly nor fair to pursue such people with love or to help them with any service."

units.la: Cap. VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: Dei hostes, cuius honorem nos propria vita charitatem habere debemus: & propterea neq; pium neq; æquū est, tales amore prosequi, aut aliquo officio iuuare. Et qui ita sentiunt, fere scripturis vtun- tur, quæ amicitiam mundi huius inimicitiam cum Deo esse docent, & Christi seruos esse negant eos, qui hominibus placere student. Ita vero nimis astutè sub plausibili religionis & pietatis prætexu Christianæ charitatis leges violant: & vt causam suam facilius defendant, in obseruandis & notandis omnium vitiis admodum curiosi & acuti sunt. At ijdem dum sanctissimi videri volunt, non vno scelere sese polluunt. Nam temerarij nimis in quosvis sibi iudicium sumunt, & dum aliorum seuerissimi censores sunt, sibijpsis plus æquo indulgent. Deinde charitatis leges secure violant. Adhæc aliorum quoq; odia prouocant, & ita peccandi materiam ijs præbent, quos suo exemplo in Dei obsequium perctrahere debebant. Concurrunt alia quoque infinita, de quibus suo loco dicetur. Itaq; ne quid eorum omittat Christus, quæ in hac causa nobis cognitu necessaria sunt, in præsenti de his quoq; disserit, & quid in toto isto negotio caueri, quid item fieri debeat, breuiter quidem, sed perspicuè & sufficienter docet.
units.tr: Those who think this way commonly make use of the Scriptures, which teach that friendship with the world is enmity with God, and deny that those who seek to please men are servants of Christ. But in this way, too cleverly, under the plausible pretext of religion and piety, they violate the laws of Christian love; and in order to defend their cause more easily, they are very keen and sharp in observing and noting the faults of everyone. Yet while they wish to seem most holy, they stain themselves with no single crime. For they are too rash in taking judgment upon anyone, and while they are the severest critics of others, they indulge themselves more than is fair. Then they violate the laws of love without a qualm. Moreover, they arouse the hatred of others too, and so give material for sin to those whom by their example they ought to have drawn into the obedience of God. Countless other things also come together, which will be discussed in their place. Therefore, so that Christ may omit nothing of what we need to know in this matter, he discusses these things too in the present passage, and briefly, yet clearly and sufficiently, teaches what must be guarded against in this whole business, and what must likewise be done.

units.la: Et primo quidem, Ne iudicate (inquit) & non iudicabimini: Ne condemnate, & non condemnabimini. Vbi ante omnia cauere oportet, ne Christi verba absq; omni exceptione secundum literā exponentes, in sensum ab illius mente alienum detorqueamus. Constat enim nobis non vno loco præcipi, vt iudicemus. In hoc certè magistratus officium maxima ex parte versatur, cui iudicia sua Deus credidisse dicitur, & passim accusantur apud propheras, qui in iudicando segniores vel etiam iniquiores erant. Quousque tandem iudicabitis inique (ait Asaph) & facies impiorum suscipietis? Iudicate pauperi & pupillo, afflictum & pauperem absoluite, &c. Et Zacharias veræ religionis & pœnitentiæ officia traditurus ijs, qui de ieiunijs superstitiosis quærebant, ab hoc orditur: Iudicate iudicium veritatis, & beneficentiam et misericordiam facite, &c. Et qui ecclesiarum ministri sunt, ij ex Dei verbo de hominum factis iudicare, peccata palàm arguere, & doctrinam ita proponere debent, vt quid corrigi debeat, quidú e probari mereatur omnes intelligant. Ideò sacerdotes olim inter lepram & non lepram iudicabant, & ad eosdem referebantur causæ difficiliores, quas non poterant explicare qui in Legis cognitione minus erant exercitati. Quid quod Ezechieli dicit Dominus? Et tu fili hominis, an non iudicabis ciuitatem sanguinum? Adhæc primati quoq; homines de doctrina & eius ministris iudicare debent, vt quid sequi, quid cauere ipsos deceat, intelligant. Notum est enim illud Pauli: Prophetæ duo aut tres loquantur, & alij dijudicent. Item: Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. Et Ioannes similiter monet, ne cuiuis spiritui credamus, sed vt spiritus probemus num ex Deo sint. Imò vt de proximi moribus iudicium feramus necesse est, siquidem illum corrigere & in viam reducere velimus. Quod cùm inter charitatis officia non postremum sit, non putandi sunt in Christi præceptum peccare, qui istud digna cum libertate & grauitate faciunt.
units.tr: And first of all he says: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged; condemn not, and you shall not be condemned." Here above all we must take care not to interpret Christ's words absolutely according to the letter, without any exception, and so twist them into a sense alien to his mind. For we know that in more than one place we are commanded to judge. Indeed, the greater part of the office of the magistrate consists in this, and to it God is said to have entrusted his judgments; and the prophets constantly accuse those who were slack or even unjust in judging. "How long will you judge unjustly," says Asaph, "and accept the faces of the wicked? Judge the poor and the fatherless, acquit the afflicted and needy," and so on. And Zechariah, about to hand down the duties of true religion and repentance to those who were asking about superstitious fasts, begins with this: "Judge with the judgment of truth, and show kindness and mercy," and so on. And those who are ministers of the churches ought, from the Word of God, to judge men's deeds, to rebuke sins openly, and to set forth doctrine in such a way that everyone understands what needs correcting and what deserves approval. Therefore the priests of old judged between leprosy and non-leprosy, and to them were referred the more difficult cases which those less practised in the knowledge of the Law could not explain. And what of the Lord's words to Ezekiel? "And you, son of man, will you not judge the city of bloods?" Besides, the leading men too ought to judge concerning doctrine and its ministers, so that they may understand what they should follow and what they should avoid. For that saying of Paul is well known: "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge." Likewise: "Test all things; hold fast what is good." And John similarly warns us not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits whether they are from God. Indeed, we must even pass judgment on the conduct of our neighbour, if we wish to correct him and bring him back to the right way. Since this is no small part of the duties of love, those are not to be thought to sin against Christ's command who do it with proper freedom and seriousness.

units.la: Quid ergo in præsenti Christus prohibet? Priuata & temeraria iudicia, quibus proximi vitia maligniùs atq; odiosius notamus, non vt ille melior fiat, sed vt infamis factus odium nostrum aliqua ex parte exaturet. Est hoc malum nobis natura insitum, vt qui in nostris vitiis cæcutire & nabis mirificè blandiri solemus, in alienis obseruandis Lynceo simus oculatiores. Obseruarunt hoc gentium philosophi, & idem in Stoicis Horatius notat his versibus: Cùm tua peruideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum, Quàm aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius?
units.tr: What, then, does Christ forbid in the present passage? Private and rash judgments, by which we note the faults of our neighbour more spitefully and odiously, not so that he may become better, but so that, made infamous, he may in some measure satisfy our hatred. This evil is implanted in us by nature: we who are wont to be blind to our own faults and to flatter ourselves wonderfully, are sharper-eyed than lynxes in observing the faults of others. The philosophers of the nations noted this, and Horace, in his verses on the Stoics, marks the same thing: "When you, bleary-eyed, with your eyes smeared with ointment, see clearly your own evils, why do you see the faults of your friends so sharply, more than an eagle or the serpent of Epidaurus?"

units.la: Æsopus item dicebat, singulos homines binas habere manticas, alteram à pectore, alteram à tergo propendentem: & in anteriorem quidem coniicere quæ ab alijs non rectè fieri vident, sua autem vitia in posteriori occultare, quam tamen nunquam inspiciant. Argutè etiam & verissimè Thales, quid nam difficillimum sit interrogatus, respondit, Seipsum nouisse: Quid verò facillimum? Alios admonere siue arguere. At qui huic malo indulgent, ij fere longius progrediuntur, vt nimirum non contenti iudicauisse, insuper quosuis etiam condemnent, & ita inipsas conscientias hominum sibi ius sumant, & imperium. Ideoq; alterum quoq; membrum Christus adiecit: Ne condemnate, & non condemnabimini, &c.
units.tr: Aesop too used to say that each person carries two wallets, one hanging from the breast and the other from the back; into the front one they throw the faults of others which they see done wrongly, but their own faults they hide in the rear one, which they never look into. Thales, too, shrewdly and most truly, when asked what was most difficult, answered: "To know oneself"; and what was easiest? "To admonish or rebuke others." But those who indulge in this evil generally go further, so that, not content with judging, they even condemn whomsoever they like, and so claim for themselves the right and authority over men's very consciences. Therefore Christ added the other member as well: "Condemn not, and you shall not be condemned," and so on.

units.la: ESt autem præceptum hoc obseruatu dignissimum & in primis necessarium. Nam qui in hoc peccant, ij Dei partes sibi sumunt, dum ex moribus de ipsa hominis conscientia temere pronuntiant, quæ illi soli cognita est, quem scripturæ sacræ corda & renes scrutari testantur. Deinde ijdem leges charitatis aperte violant, cuius proprium est (vt nuper diximus) regere multitudinem peccatorum ne proximo aliqua infamiæ nota inuratur. Imò non alia perniciosior charitatis pestis est, quam in aliorum vitiis traducendis sibi indulgere. Vt enim gloriæ appetentissimi sunt omnes homines, ita non aliam iniuriam intolerabiliorem esse putant, quam si nomen aut famam suam læsi sentiunt. Ex eo igitur irarum flammas concipiunt, ex quibus odia, simultates, ardens priuatæ vindictæ studium & nunquam finiendæ contentiones enascuntur. Neq; inter eos se continet hoc incendium, à quibus cœpit, sed fere familias totas peruadit, & frequenter ceu hereditario iure ad posteros quoq; propagatur. Quo Iacobus Apostolus respexisse videtur, quando linguam ceu infernali igne inflam-matam totum orbem accendere scribit. Accedit huic malo, quod qui in iudicando aut obtrectando sibi indulgere incipiunt, ij dulcedine quadam vitij huius inescati, linguas suas ita ad maledicendum af-fuefaciunt, vt leuissima quaq; occasione oblata Tragœdias horrendas excitent, neq; vllo fræno sese contineri patiantur. Quod ipsum quoque Iacobus obseruauit, eodem in loco sic dicens: Omnis natura & ferarum & volucrum, serpentium & marinorum, domatur & domita est à natura humana, linguam autem nemo hominum domare potest, malum quod coercere non possis: vt quæ plena sit veneno mortifero, &c. Ita verò simul in Christi exemplum peccatur, quod nobis dictorum & factorum omnium regula esse debebat. Is enim peccata nostra in se recepit, eadem suaiustitia tegit & occultat, proq; illis apud patrem intercedit. Eò grauius ergo illi peccant, quòd cùm gloriæ Dei vindices haberi velint, interim filij Dei præcepta simul et exemplum impie conculcant. Adde quòd ijdem sibijpsis egregiè blanduntur, & improba sanctitatis propriæ spe repleti, se extra omnem culpam esse sibi persuadent, quibus à nemine quicquam exprobrari possit. Sed spe sua turpissimè falluntur. Quia enim nemo absque vitio viuit, hoc vnum lucri inde reportant, quod alij plures eorum petulantia & dicacitate accensi ipsos diligentius obseruant. Fit ergo, vt ipsi quoq; ab alijs iudicentur atque condemnentur, & ita talionis lege puniuntur, cuius pars est etiam hæc: Qui quæ vult dicit, quæ non vult audiet. Nam etsi peccent fere, qui aut vindictæ studio, aut alio affectu prauo ipsis detrahunt, in-sto tamen Dei iudicio fit, vt peccatum peccati pœna sit, & qui linguas suas in alijs traducendis nimium laxarunt, sæpe præter omnem expectationem in scelus aliquod prolapsi omnibus fabula fiant, & extrema infamia notentur.
