Et hoc illud est, de quo nos in præsenti Christus admonet. Nihil ergo hæc admonitio & comminatio ad eos pertinet, qui ex officio in aliorum mores & facta inquirunt: ni si quòd illos in primis cauere oportet, ne quæ in alijs reprehendunt, ipsi designent, & ita grauiorùs scandali sint authores.
units.tr: This precept is most worthy of observance and especially necessary. For those who sin in this respect take to themselves the part of God, while they rashly pronounce from men's conduct upon the very conscience of a man, which is known to him alone, whom the Scriptures of God testify to search the hearts and reins. Then, these same people openly violate the laws of love, whose proper task (as we have just said) is to cover the multitude of sins so that no mark of infamy is branded upon a neighbour. Indeed, there is no more destructive plague of love than to indulge oneself in disparaging the faults of others. For as all men are most eager for glory, so they think no injury more intolerable than when they feel that their name or reputation has been harmed. From this they conceive the flames of anger, from which arise hatreds, quarrels, a burning zeal for private vengeance, and contentions that never end. Nor does this fire keep itself within those from whom it began, but it usually spreads through whole families, and often, as if by hereditary right, is passed down to posterity as well. The apostle James seems to have had this in mind when he writes that the tongue, set aflame by hell-fire, sets the whole world on fire. To this evil is added that those who begin to indulge themselves in judging or detracting, being enticed by a certain sweetness of this vice, accustom their tongues to speaking evil so that, on the slightest occasion offered, they stir up dreadful tragedies, and they do not allow themselves to be restrained by any bridle. James also observed this same thing, saying in the same passage: "Every nature of beasts and birds, of serpents and of sea creatures, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature; but no one of men can tame the tongue, an evil that you cannot restrain, full of deadly poison," and so on. Thus, at the same time, sin is committed against the example of Christ, who ought to have been the rule of all our words and deeds. For he took our sins upon himself, covers and hides them with his own righteousness, and intercedes with the Father on their behalf. Therefore those sin the more gravely who, while wishing to be regarded as avengers of God's glory, meanwhile impiously trample underfoot both the precepts and the example of the Son of God. Add that these same people flatter themselves admirably, and, filled with the vain hope of their own holiness, persuade themselves that they are free from all fault, since no one can reproach them with anything. But they are most shamefully deceived in their hope. For since no one lives without fault, they gain only this from it: that many others, inflamed by their impudence and sharp tongues, watch them more carefully. So it comes about that they too are judged and condemned by others, and thus punished by the law of retaliation, of which this too is a part: "He who says what he wishes shall hear what he does not wish." For although those who detract from others, out of a zeal for vengeance or some other wicked motive, usually sin, yet by the righteous judgment of God it happens that sin becomes the punishment of sin, and those who have loosened their tongues too freely in slandering others, often, beyond all expectation, fall into some crime and become the talk of all, and are marked with the utmost infamy. This is precisely what Christ now warns us about. Therefore this warning and threat do not concern those who by their office inquire into the conduct and deeds of others, except that they above all must take care not to commit themselves the very faults they rebuke in others, and so become more grievous authors of scandal.

units.la: Quòd si verò peccant, qui aliorum vitia odiosè & prauo affectu insectantur, quanto grauior eo-rum culpa est, qui quæ bene facta sunt in siniストram partem rapiunt, & de optimè meritis male lo-quuntur? Est hoc genus hominum hodie passim obuium. Tales enim sunt, qui fidos Verbi Dei ad-ministros proscindunt, & eos dissidiorum atque motuum ciuilium authores esse clamant, qui hoc v-num agunt, vt omnes in Christo pacem colant, & Deo propitio vtantur. Adnumerari illis debent, qui magistratus pios conuitijs & dicterijs scurrilibus in odium aut contemptum adducere student, atq; ex eo voluptatem capiunt, si illorum authoritati aliquid decedere videant. Adde his, qui inter amicos & fratres dissidia & simultates seminant, quique (vt de Doego Idumæo Dauid ait) amant verba perditionis, id est, omnia quæ perniciem & exitium alijs afferunt. Sunt hi omnes reuera dia-boli filij, quando cum perdendi studio mendacia coniungunt, quæ duo illi propria esse Christus testa-tur. Et quantum mali dent publicè & priuatim, multi non sine magno dolore experiuntur. Sedò no-stri seculi infelicitatem, quo cuiuis licet temere ea accusare & non sine publico scandalo traducere, quæ dissimulari potius & taceri debebant: & hoc quidem impunè licet per eos, qui interim hoc Chri-sti præceptum rigidissimè vrgent in illis, in quibus iudicio & animaduersione diligenti in primis opus est: nimirum in ijs, quæ ad religionem & fidei atq; æternæ salutis doctrinam faciunt. Hic e-nim vt modesti & humani habeantur, omnes religiones indifferentes faciunt, & si absq; fide in Chri-stum seruari aliquem negemus, mox nobis hæc Christi verba obgannunt: Ne iudicate, & non iudicabimini: Ne condemnate, & non condemnabimini.
units.tr: But if those sin who bitterly and with malicious feeling attack the faults of others, how much graver is the guilt of those who twist what has been done well into a bad sense and speak ill of those who have deserved best? This kind of man is found everywhere today. For these are the people who tear apart the faithful ministers of God's Word and cry that they are the authors of quarrels and civil unrest, when those ministers work only to make everyone cultivate peace in Christ and enjoy God's favour. To these must be added those who strive to bring godly magistrates into hatred or contempt by abusive and scurrilous insults, and take pleasure in it if they see any loss of authority. Add also those who sow discord and enmity among friends and brothers, and who (as David says of Doeg the Edomite) love words of destruction, that is, everything that brings ruin and death to others. All of these are truly children of the devil, since they join lies to the desire to destroy, two things which Christ testifies are proper to him. And many have learned, not without great pain, how much harm such people do in public and in private. Alas for the unhappiness of our age, in which anyone may rashly accuse and, not without public scandal, slander what ought rather to have been overlooked and passed over in silence. And this is allowed with impunity by those who, meanwhile, press this precept of Christ most rigidly against those in whose case careful judgement and correction are above all needed, namely in matters which bear on religion and the teaching of faith and eternal salvation. For in order to be thought moderate and humane, they make all religions indifferent, and if we deny that anyone can be saved without faith in Christ, at once they bark at us these words of Christ: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged; condemn not, and you shall not be condemned."

units.la: Quorsum verò istud? Vt nimirum apud omnes bonam gratiam ineant, dum vnum quenq; in sua religione, vel potius superstitione, seruari posse sentiunt, siue ille Turca siue Iudaeus, siue Christianus sit. At non vident, imò videre nolunt, hac sententia religionem omnem simul aboleri, & illius sensum in hominum mentibus extingui. Si enim Deum eiusmodi fingimus, qui quemuis alium in cultus, qui ipsi debetur, societatem tam facilè admittat: quid obstabit, quò minus eos quoq; seruari dicamus, qui Deum omnino nullum esse credunt, quales olim Epicurei fuerunt, & Nabales illi, quorum Dauid in Psalmis meminit? Sed vt ad illorum argumentum respondeamus, quod ex hoc loco eliciunt, mirum est homines alioqui satis oculatos non videre, quàm turpiter aduersus hoc Christi praeceptum peccent, cuius tam studiosi obseruatores haberi volunt. Si enim iudicare nolunt aliquem ne etiam ipsi iudicentur, cur sibi in ipsum Deum ius sumunt, vt secus quàm ille de toto salutis negotio pronuntient? Annon enim Patris vox est coelitus de Christo in carne manifestato dicentis: Hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum: hunc audite? Annon Filius hic iam in coelos ascensurus ait: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit: Qui verò non crediderit, condemnabitur? At si in quauis religione salus nobis sine Christo obtingere potest, quid opus fuit illum in mundum venire, hominem fieri, mori, resurgere, & assumptam carnem in coelis collocare? Annon stultitiae simul & iniustitiae Pater damnari merebitur, qui aeterno suo decreto rem hanc constituit, quae nobis ad salutem non erat necessaria? Annon cum Christo aeterno Dei filio, ipse quoque Spiritus Sanctus mendacij convincetur, qui per prophetas & Apostolos omnem salutem in vno Iesu Christo nobis monstrauit? Quid verò de sanctissimis Dei seruis dicemus, quibus leue visum fuit vitam et sanguinem profundere, vt Christo inseri & in ipso salutem consequi possent? Et quis non impostores pessimos fuisse dicat Apostolos, qui totius orbis mutationem tanto cum multorum periculo induxerunt, & ad quaeuis supplicia ferenda suos hortati sunt: si abseq; fide in Christum in quauis alia superstitione salus inueniri poterat? Obseruent ergo pij, quanta impietas & quàm multiplex sub istorum plausibili modestia lateat, qui hoc Christi praecepto ad omnium superstitionum defensionem abutuntur. Nemo igitur haec verba extra statum rapiat, quem ille sibi propositum habuit: linguae verò petulantiam ita frenemus, vt interim salua nobis aduersus omnes superstitiones maneat Christi Iesu & fidei in hunc confessio.
units.tr: But to what end is this? Clearly so that they may win the goodwill of all, since they feel that each person can be saved in his own religion, or rather superstition, whether he be a Turk, a Jew or a Christian. But they do not see, indeed they are unwilling to see, that by this opinion every religion is abolished together and the sense of it is extinguished in men's minds. For if we imagine a God who so readily admits to the worship that is due to himself any other kind of worship, what will prevent us from saying that those too are saved who believe there is no God at all, such as the Epicureans of old and that Nabal whom David mentions in the Psalms? But, to answer their argument which they draw from this passage, it is strange that men otherwise quite sharp-sighted do not see how shamefully they sin against this precept of Christ, of which they wish to be thought such zealous observers. For if they refuse to judge anyone, lest they themselves be judged, why do they claim for themselves a right over God himself, so as to pronounce about the whole business of salvation otherwise than he does? Is it not the voice of the Father, speaking from heaven concerning Christ made manifest in the flesh: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him"? Does not this same Son, about to ascend into heaven, say: "He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned"? But if salvation can be obtained for us in any religion without Christ, what need was there for him to come into the world, to become man, to die, to rise again, and to place the flesh he had assumed in heaven? Will not the Father of wisdom and of justice himself deserve to be condemned for stupidity and injustice, if by his eternal decree he established a thing which was not necessary for our salvation? Will not the Holy Spirit himself, together with the eternal Son of God Christ, be convicted of falsehood, since through the prophets and Apostles he has shown us all salvation in the one Jesus Christ? What shall we say of the most holy servants of God, who thought it a small thing to pour out their life and blood, so that they might be grafted into Christ and obtain salvation in him? And who would not say that the Apostles were the worst impostors, who brought about the overthrow of the whole world at such great peril to many, and exhorted their followers to endure any punishment, if salvation could be found in any other superstition apart from faith in Christ? Let the godly observe, then, how great impiety, and how manifold, lies hidden beneath the plausible moderation of these men, who abuse this precept of Christ in defence of every superstition. Let no one, therefore, tear these words out of the context which Christ had in view; and let us so restrain the wantonness of the tongue that the confession of Christ Jesus and of faith in him may remain safe for us against all superstitions.

units.la: Porrò ad Christi verba reuerti, quid hic fieri debeat, videamus. Remittite (inquit) & remittetur vobis: Date, & dabitur vobis, &c. Initio fontem omnis istius mali attingit: qui est, quòd vt amicitiam simulemus, manet tamen altamente reposta acceptarum iniuriarum memoria: qua fit, vt non possimus non aliquo scommate eorum famam aut nomen perstringere, qui nos aliqua in re laeserunt. Et quàmuis id non semper primi faciamus, facile tamen illis consensum praebemus, qui eis maledicere incipiunt. Monet ergo, vt ex animo remittamus aut condonemus iis omnibus, qui aliquam nobis iniuriam aut damnum intulerunt. At hic rursus obseruabis, hoc quoque praeceptum ad priuatos modò homines pertinere, & hoc velle Dominum, ne qui in vlciscendis iniurijs sibi factis sint seueriores. Alia longè est iudicum ratio, & omnium qui in magistratu sunt constituti. Hi enim & propriam authoritatem tueri debent, ne Dei iudicia per ipsorum ignauiam in contemptum veniant, & improborum malitiam punire, adeoque (vt in Lege Deus praecipit) malum è medio populi excindere. Quod nisi faciant, non solum in exequendis Dei iudicijs ofcitantiores sunt (quod per se reprehensionem meretur) sed insuper pios & bonos impijs vexandos propinant, quorum audacia eò magis accenditur, quò frigidiores sunt, qui illam publica authoritate compescere debent.
units.tr: Next, let us turn back to Christ's words and see what ought to be done here. "Forgive," he says, "and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you," and so on. At the start he touches the source of all this evil, which is that, while we pretend friendship, the memory of injuries received remains deeply buried, with the result that we cannot help assailing with some sneer the good name or reputation of those who have harmed us in some matter. And although we do not always begin it ourselves, we readily give our assent to those who begin to speak ill of them. He therefore bids us from the heart to remit or pardon all those who have done us any wrong or injury. But here again you will observe that this precept too pertains only to private persons, and that the Lord does not wish them to be more severe in avenging the injuries done to them. The case of judges, and of all who are set in public office, is very different. For they ought both to maintain their own authority, lest God's judgements come into contempt through their cowardice, and to punish the malice of the wicked and so (as God commands in the Law) to cut out evil from the midst of the people. If they do not do this, they are not only more sluggish in carrying out God's judgements (which of itself deserves reproof), but moreover they expose the godly and good to be harassed by the wicked, and the audacity of the wicked is all the more inflamed the more cold are those who ought to restrain it by public authority.

units.la: Est autem hic obseruatu dignissimum Remittendi verbum. Eo enim per Metaphoram vtitur, & simili à creditoribus desumpto rem illustrat. Solent illi, si humaniores sint, eorum nomina delere, qui non sunt soluendo, idq; remissionem vulgò dicunt. Praecipit ergo gratuitam omnis iniuriae condonationem, & hanc nos facere iubet, etiamsi nulla satisfactio intercedat. Itaque oblivio, seu (vt Graeci loquuntur) ἀμνηστία iniuriarum requiritur: quam minimè praestabimus, nisi prius nosipsos abnegemus, qui natura ad vindictam proclives sumus. At qui iniuriarum ne meminerunt quidem ij, multò minus eas in rationem venire patiuntur, ideoque non modò nullius famam laedunt, sed de illis etiam bene loquuntur, à quibus gravissimè læsi sunt. Exemplum huius indulgentiæ in Christo perfectissimum habemus, qui tam abfuit, vt iniuriarum meminisse vellet, vt ne ad ea quidem conuitia responderit amarulentius, quæ ipsi in faciem dicebantur. Quod vt ipsi quoque faciamus, charitas Christiana iubet, quæ nisi id fiat, considere non potest: neque vnquam pace coibunt, qui inter se dissident, cùm iniuriarum inter homines plena sint omnia. Vidit hoc acerrimi iudicij & spectatæ virtutis vir Thrasybulus, qui cum deletis triginta tyrannis, qui post bellum Peloponnesiacum Athenis iniusta & crudeliaimperia exercuerant, ab exilio in vrbem redijsset, duvnσεias legem sanxit, id est, nullam veterum iniuriarum memoriam extare voluit: quod non alia ratione ciuium animos rursus coalescere posse intelligeret. Fecit idem Romanus Senatus interfecto Iulio Cæsare: sed minori cum fructu fecit, eò quòd ambitiosa Triumuirorum ingenia legibus se coerceri non paterentur. Vt vt tamen res cadat, nunquam omnino fallit Christi promissio, qui dicit, fore vt nobis quoq; remittatur, si in condonandis aliorum delictis faciles simus. Nam etsi multorum ea sit durities & asperitas, vt neq; indulgentia neq; beneficijs vllis vinci possit: non desunt tamen, quos vel ad tempus frangit ista facilitas, vt culpam suam fateantur, & ab inceptis aliquantisper desistant. Exemplum huius rei in Saule, homine contumacissimo, historia sacra proponit: quem Dauidis patientia semel & iterum vicit, vt non sine lachrymis innocentiæ testimonium illi deferret. Quòd si verò de hominibus spes nulla est, æterna tamen salutis ratio, vt illud faciamus, exigit. Nam quæ hic habetur promissio, ad Deum vsq; extenditur, qui (vt in orandi formula Christus docet) non aliis peccata remittet, quàm qui suis quoq; debitoribus delicta & offensas remittere solet. Nisi ergo præcepto huic obtemperemus, nosmetipsos precum præsidio spoliabimus: imò proprij oris iudicio atq; testimonio nosipsos damnabimus, quoties dicimus: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut etiam nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Hoc vtinam attentius considerarent, qui in vindicta præcipuam fortitudinis & virtutis laudem consistere putant.
units.tr: Now the word "forgive" is here worthy of the closest attention. For Christ uses a metaphor and illustrates the matter by a comparison taken from creditors. Such creditors, if they are more humane, are accustomed to strike out the names of those who cannot pay, and this they commonly call remission. Christ therefore enjoins the gratuitous pardoning of every injury, and bids us do this even when no satisfaction is offered. Thus a forgetting, or (as the Greeks say) an oblivion [ἀμνηστία] of injuries is required; and we shall by no means achieve this unless we first deny ourselves, since we are by nature prone to revenge. But those who do not remember injuries at all, much less allow them to come into account, not only do not harm anyone's reputation, but even speak well of those by whom they have been most grievously wronged. We have in Christ the most perfect example of this forbearance, who was so far from wishing to remember injuries that he did not even answer more bitterly those insults which were hurled at his face. Christian charity bids us do the same, and without it there can be no settlement; nor will those who are at odds with one another ever come to peace, since everything among men is full of injuries. The man of most acute judgement and proven virtue, Thrasybulus, saw this: when, after the thirty tyrants who had exercised unjust and cruel rule at Athens after the Peloponnesian War had been destroyed, he returned to the city from exile, he enacted a law of oblivion [ἀμνηστίας], that is, he wished that no memory of past injuries should remain, because he understood that the minds of the citizens could not otherwise be reunited. The Roman Senate did the same after Julius Caesar had been killed, but it did so with less success, because the ambitious natures of the Triumvirs would not allow themselves to be restrained by laws. However the matter turns out, Christ's promise never utterly fails, when he says that it will also be forgiven us, if we are ready to pardon the faults of others. For although some men are so hard and harsh that they can be overcome neither by indulgence nor by any kindness, yet there are not lacking those whom such gentleness breaks, at least for a time, so that they confess their fault and for a while desist from their undertakings. Sacred history offers an example of this in Saul, a most stubborn man, whom David's patience overcame once and again, so that Saul bore witness to David's innocence not without tears. But if there is no hope of men, yet the reason of eternal salvation requires us to do this. For the promise given here extends even to God, who (as Christ teaches in the form of prayer) will not forgive sins to others unless he himself is accustomed to forgive the sins and offences of those who owe him. Unless, therefore, we obey this precept, we shall deprive ourselves of the protection of prayer; nay, by the judgement and testimony of our own mouth we shall condemn ourselves whenever we say: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Would that those who think that the chief praise of courage and virtue lies in revenge would consider this more carefully.

units.la: Cæterùm ex temerarijs iudicijs aliud quoq; malum nascitur. Nam beneficentiæ obstant, & cau sa sunt, vt tenaciores & infacienda eleemosyna maligniores simus, eò quòd indignos putamus qui iuuentur, eos qui à nobis aliquod vitæ subsidium petunt. Itaq; huic etiam vitio occurrens Christus ait: Date, & dabitur vobis: mensuram (inquam) pressam & agitatam & superfluentem dabunt in sinum vestrum. Quasi diceret: Nolim ego vos vestrum iudicium audire, vel affectus carnis vestræ in consilium admittere, quando de proximi necessitate subleuanda agitur. Si ergo occurrant, qui vestra ope indigent & hanc à vobis postulant, tunc meminerinitis, vos nor illorum iudices à Deo constitutos, sed potius facultatem, quas possidetis, dispensatores factos esse, quarum copia siue abundantia illorum inopiam subleuare debeat. Ideo nō quid illi merentur, sed quid vestri sit officij expendite, neq; permittite, vt sinistra manus dextram moderetur: id est, vt sinister aliquis aut prauus affectus officium pietatis interturbet. Nam qualescunq; sint illi, qui à vobis beneficium accipiunt, non tamen vobis gratia illa peribit. Est enim Deus omnis boni remunerator liberalissimus. Date ergo liberaliter, & procul dubio vobis omne hoc rependetur. Quòd si minus grati erga vos sint, qui beneficium accipiunt, alios excitabit Deus, per quos gratiam vobis referat. Et hi mensuram pressam, agitatam & superfluentem dabunt in sinum vestrum, id est, magno vestro commodo vobis liberalissimè retribuent, quicquid sincero fraterna dilectionis affectu in homines ingratissimos contuleritis. Id verò sententia generali confirmat: Eadem enim mensura, qua metimini, vicissim metientur vobis alij. Continet hæc sententia talionis legem, & proinde ex communi sensu & naturæ iure deriuatur, quod est, vt quisq; digna suis factis præmia recipiat.
units.tr: Rash judgements also give rise to another evil. They stand in the way of beneficence and make us more grudging and mean in giving alms, because we think those unworthy of help who ask us for some support for their life. Christ therefore meets this fault too when he says: "Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, they will give into your bosom" (Luke 6:38). It is as if he said: I do not want you to listen to your own judgement, or to let the desires of your flesh into your counsel, when the question is how to relieve a neighbour's need. So if those who lack your help come and ask it of you, remember that you have not been appointed by God as their judges, but rather made stewards of the resources you possess, whose abundance ought to relieve their want. Therefore weigh not what they deserve but what your duty is, and do not allow your left hand to govern your right hand; that is, do not let some sinister or wicked feeling disturb the office of godliness. For whatever sort of people those who receive a kindness from you may be, that grace will not be lost to you. God is the most generous rewarder of all good. Give, then, generously, and without doubt all this will be repaid to you. But if those who receive the benefit are less thankful to you, God will raise up others through whom he will return the favour to you. And these will give into your bosom good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over; that is, to your great advantage they will most generously repay you for whatever you have bestowed on the most ungrateful men out of sincere affection of brotherly love. A general saying confirms this: "For with the same measure that you mete withal, it shall be measured to you again" (Matt. 7:2). This saying contains the law of retaliation, and so it derives from common sense and the law of nature, namely that each person receives rewards corresponding to his deeds.

units.la: Est autem sententiæ huius multiplex vsus, & proinde dignissima est, quæ cum ea, quam nuper audiuimus, in omnibus parietibus, imò omnium cordibus inscribatur. Primò enim ad huius loci caput siue statum extendi potest, ne temerarij nimium simus in iudicandis aliorum moribus: eò quòd qui hic sibi indulgent, in illos pari mensura regeruntur maledicta, quibus ipsorum quoque fama obfuscetur. Deinde ad beneficentiæ studium excitat, ne nobis perire putemus, quod in a iis conferetur. Nam vt Solomon ait, fœneratur Domino, qui largitur pauperi. Nullus autem Thesaurus certior, nulla vsura quæstuosior est, quàm quæ apud Deum, omnis boni fonte redundantissimè deponitur. Et exempla sunt, quæ docent, tunc fere gratiam nobis liberalissimè referri, quando nihil huius sperari amplius potest. Pertinet huc Iacobi exemplum, qui ex officijs in Labanum auunculum collatis amplißimam gratiā retulit, quàmuis is in illum ingratißimus esset & iniustißimus. Adhæc in stitiam nobis commendat, & è contra fraudes, imposturas, rapinas & omnem vim iniustam prohibet. Qui enim iustitiæ student, ij Dei benedictione fruuntur, cuius liberalitas mundi ingratitudinem longè superat. Accipiunt ergo mensuram pressam & redundantem in sinum suum, quam nulla hominum nequitia illis eripiet. Rursus qui per iniustitiam cum aliorum iniuria ditescunt, ij fere talionis lege multantur, vt ipsi quoque aliis præda sint. Notum enim est illud Domini per Isaiam clamantis: Væ qui prædaris, quia tu quoque in prædam daberis. Cui consentiunt quæ Solomon pronunciauit: Qui per iniuriam & violentiam opprimit pauperem, vt ditescat ipse, is dabit diuiti et egebit. Item, qui opes suas fœnore & vsuris auget, congerit eas homini, qui pauperibus benefaciat. Debebant in horum consideratione assidui esse impostores vsurarij, quibus leuiculum videtur quorumuis fortunas inuadere, modò ipsi ditescant. Sed etsi ad tempus superbiant suis opibus, nunquam tamen illæ stabiles sunt, & raro ad tertium vsque hæredem deueniunt. Obseruent hoc ipsum milites mercenarij, qui honestißimum quæstum esse arbitrantur, sanguinem innoxium fundere, prædari, cædibus & incendijs omnia miscere, viduas & pupillos patrijs sedibus eijcere. Fecerunt hæc olim Chananæi, Assyrij, Babylonij, Persæ, Græci, Romani: quorum omnium ea sors fuit tandem, vt similia domi suæ sentirent. Et nostro seculo multa vidimus, quæ his fidem facere poterant, nisi ad omnem malí sensum obstupuissemus. Pertinent in horum catalogum duri & immites, qui aliorum miseriam sic cùm oculis intuentur, dummodo suis desiderijs indulgeant. Tandem enim ipsi quoq; infelices fiunt, ne que inueniunt aliquos, qui ipsorum calamitatibus moueantur. Apostoli enim vox est: Iudicium absq; misericordia erit ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Idem illis dictum esto, qui peregrinos, viduas & orphanos quacunq; ratione opprimunt. Minatur enim illis in lege Dominus, fore, vt & ipsi aliquando patria eiecti incertis sedibus oberrent, & ipsis casis tandem vxores eorum, liberi, viduæ atque orphani fiant. Quid multis? Discant hæc singsuli priuatim & publicè expendere, in vnum verò Deum intenti fraternam charitatem colant in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This saying has many uses, and so it is most worthy to be written on all walls, indeed in the hearts of all, together with the one we heard a little while ago. First, it can be extended to the topic and subject of this passage, so that we are not too rash in judging the conduct of others, since those who indulge themselves in this are repaid in the same measure with slanders against those same people, by which their own reputation is also darkened. Next, it stirs us up to the practice of beneficence, so that we do not think that what is bestowed on the poor is lost to us. For, as Solomon says, "he who gives to the poor lends to the Lord" (Prov. 19:17). Now no treasury is more certain, and no usury more profitable, than that which is deposited most abundantly with God, the fount of all good. And there are examples which teach that the grace shown to us is then usually returned most generously, when nothing more of it can be hoped for. Here belongs the example of Jacob, who, for the kindnesses he had shown to his uncle Laban, received the most ample reward, although Laban was most ungrateful and most unjust towards him. Moreover, it commends righteousness to us, and on the other hand forbids fraud, deceit, robbery and every unjust violence. For those who pursue righteousness enjoy the blessing of God, whose generosity far surpasses the ingratitude of the world. They therefore receive good measure, pressed down and overflowing, into their bosom, which no wickedness of men will snatch away from them. Conversely, those who grow rich by injustice and to the injury of others are generally punished by the law of retaliation, so that they in turn become plunder for others. For the saying of the Lord crying through Isaiah is well known: "Woe to you who plunder, for you too shall be plundered" (Isa. 33:1). Solomon's pronouncement agrees with this: "He who oppresses the poor by wrong and violence, that he himself may grow rich, will give to the rich and will come to want." Likewise, he who increases his wealth by interest and usury is heaping it up for the man who does good to the poor (cf. Prov. 28:8). Those deceivers and usurers should be constant in considering these things, for to them it seems a trifle to seize the fortunes of anyone at all, provided they themselves grow rich. But even if for a time they swell with pride in their riches, those riches are never stable, and rarely pass down even to the third heir. Let mercenary soldiers observe this too, who think it the most honourable gain to shed innocent blood, to plunder, to throw everything into confusion with murders and burnings, and to drive widows and orphans from their ancestral homes. The Canaanites, Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks and Romans did these things once, and the end for all of them was that they at last suffered similar things in their own homelands. And in our own age we have seen many things which could make these matters credible, unless we had become numb to every sense of evil. Among this catalogue belong the hard and cruel, who look upon the misery of others with such indifference, so long as they may indulge their own desires. For in the end they too become wretched, and they find no one who is moved by their calamities. For the voice of the Apostle is: "Judgement will be without mercy for him who has not shown mercy" (James 2:13). Let the same be said to those who in any way oppress strangers, widows and orphans. For the Lord threatens them in the law that they too shall one day be driven from their homeland and wander about without a settled dwelling, and that their own wives, children, widows and orphans shall come to the same condition. What more is there to say? Let each one learn to weigh these things in private and in public, and, intent on the one God, let him cultivate brotherly love in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIII.

units.la: Dicebat autem eis parabolam: Num potest cæcus cæco præsire? non ne ambo in foueam cadent? Non est discipulus supra magistrum suum, sed quisque erit perfectus vt magister suus. Quid autem aspicis festucam, quæ est in oculo fratris tui: trabem autē, quæ est in oculo proprio, non animaduertis? Aut quomodo potes dicere fratri tuo: Frater, sine eijciam festucam, quæ in oculo tuo est, cum ipse trabem, quæ est in oculo tuo, non respicias? Hypocrita, eijce primum trabem illam ex oculo tuo: & tum dispicies, vt eijcias festucam, quæ est in oculo fratris tui. Non est enim arbor bona, quæ fert fructum putrem: neque arbor putris, quæ ferat fructum bonum. Vnaquæque enim arbor ex fructu proprio cognoscitur. Neque enim è spinis colligunt ficus, neque è rubo vindemiant vuuam. Bonus homo ex bono thesauro cordis sui profert bonum: & malus homo ex malo thesauro cordis sui profert malum. Ex abundantia enim cordis loquitur os eius.
units.tr: And he spake a parable unto them: Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch? The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master. And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Or how canst thou say to thy brother, Brother, let me pull out the mote that is in thine eye, when thou thyself beholdest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to pull out the mote that is in thy brother's eye. For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus, de charitate & eius officijs ita hucusque disseruit, vt simul veram Legis diuinæ sententiam tradiderit, docens, per hanc non solum externa opera, sed ipsum hominis animum atque mentem formari, ne quid velimus & optemus, quod in illa prohibetur. Vsus autem huius doctrinæ est, vt nobis inhærentem naturæ nostræ vitiositatem agnoscamus, & ex eo intelligamus, nos promisso illo Seruatore opus habere, qui nostram imperfectionem sarciat, & nos à Legis maledictione absoluat. Caeterùm eras hæc doctrina multis vona & insolens. Nam qui tunc inter Iudaeos primas tenebant Pharisaei, non modo humanis traditionibus infelicem populum grauabant, sed ipsam quoque legis doctrinam falsis interpretationibus iampridem corrupe-rant. Docebant enim illam per nos impleri posse, & inde colligebant, hominem ex legis operibus iu-stificari. Erat haec absurda & nocentissima opinio: Ita enim Christum sibi inutilem reddebant, & dum suam iustitiam stabilire conabantur, eam explodebant, quam nobis Deus in filio suo offert, quaeque sola nos apud eum tribunal tuetur. Ideo Christus admonitionem grauem subijcit, ut a falsa doctrinae praeconibus sibi caueant, perseuerent autem in veritatis doctrina, quam ipse tradidit. Et est dignissimum obseruatu, quod verae & sanae doctrinae istam de vitandis falsis doctoribus admonitionem subiungit. Solet enim hunc ordinem spiritus sanctus in scripturis passim obseruare, & ut ita fiat necesse est. Nam ut frustra viam rectam alicui monstraueris, nisi eundem de auijs, quae saepe tristissima & latissima sunt, admoneas: ita nunquam sufficiet veritatis doctrinam tradidisse, nisi impostores arguantur, & erroneae traditiones confutentur, quas multi veritatis titulo palliare solent, & quae non raro multorum seculorum vsu, & maioris partis hominum exemplo commendantur, & ad quas recipiendas plerique natura proclives sunt. Et tanta in hus arguendis est spiritus diligentia, ut prophetae & apostoli non contenti de illis admonuisse, quae ipsis viuentibus & docentibus disseminabantur, de iis quoq; vaticinati sint, quas nouissimis saeculis exorituras esse praenuidebant. Sunt ergo nimis iniqui, neque satis prouidi, qui hodie iniquius ferunt, si Pontificum traditiones & Monachorum fabulas arguamus. Atqui ut id fiat, res ipsa monet: quando omnia ea palam audiuntur, quae iam olim spiritus praedixit. Sedet enim in templo Dei Antichristus, & diuinos honores sibi vendicat. Sunt passim, qui Christum in desertis & in conclaubus monstrant. Proponuntur publice daemoniorum dogmata, quibus ciborum esus & coniugij vsus prohibentur. Vagantur vbiq; qui verbum Dei corrumpunt, & ex sacrorum nundinatione quaestum faciunt. Et multorum tanta est stoliditas & caecitas, ut in lupsorum fauces & vngues sponte sese ingerant. Quid ergo hic faciant pastores, quibus gregis sui curam Christus commisit? Num lupos in ipso ouili impune grassari, et oues dispergi sinent? Num ipsi otiosi ista audient atq; spectabunt? Num interea blandis sermonibus omnium aures demulcebunt? Qui hoc iubent, ij aut non intelligunt salutis humanae negotium, aut parum fidi sunt Christo, qui ecclesiae suae nihil charius habet & pretiosius. Est ergo locus hic vtilis admodum, & multa consideratione dignissimus, ut excitentur nonnihil, qui hactenus in rema ximi momenti negligentiores fuerunt.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, having so far discoursed on charity and its duties, at the same time delivered the true meaning of the divine Law, teaching that by this Law not only outward works but the very disposition and mind of man is formed, so that we do not wish or desire anything that is forbidden in it. The use of this teaching is that we may recognise the wickedness inherent in our nature, and understand from this that we need that promised Saviour, who may make good our imperfection and absolve us from the curse of the Law. Moreover, this doctrine was already at that time strange and unwelcome to many. For the Pharisees, who then held the first place among the Jews, not only burdened the unhappy people with human traditions, but had long since corrupted the very doctrine of the Law by false interpretations. For they taught that it could be fulfilled by us, and from this they concluded that man is justified by the works of the Law. This was an absurd and most harmful opinion: for in this way they made Christ useless to themselves, and while they tried to establish their own righteousness, they cast aside that which God offers us in his Son, and which alone defends us before his tribunal. Therefore Christ adds a grave warning, that they should beware of the preachers of a false doctrine, and that they should persevere in the doctrine of truth which he himself delivered. And it is most worthy of notice that he joins this warning against false teachers to the teaching of true and sound doctrine. For the Holy Spirit is accustomed to observe this order throughout the Scriptures, and it must be so. For just as it is vain to show someone the right way without also warning him about the byways, which are often very dangerous and wide, so it is never enough to have taught the doctrine of truth unless impostors are refuted and erroneous traditions are confuted, which many are wont to cloak with the name of truth, and which are not seldom commended by the custom of many centuries and by the example of the greater part of mankind, and to which most people are naturally inclined to give way. And the Spirit is so diligent in refuting these that the prophets and apostles, not content to warn against those things which were spread abroad while they themselves were living and teaching, also prophesied concerning those which they foresaw would arise in the last ages. Therefore those are too unjust, and not wise enough, who today take it amiss, and more unjustly, if we refute the traditions of the Papists and the fables of the monks. Yet the thing itself urges us to do this, since all those things are openly heard which the Spirit foretold long ago. For Antichrist sits in the temple of God and claims divine honours for himself. There are everywhere those who show Christ in the deserts and in the closets. The doctrines of demons, by which the eating of foods and the use of marriage are forbidden, are publicly set forth. Those who corrupt the word of God and make gain from the trafficking of sacred things wander everywhere. And so great is the stupidity and blindness of many that they willingly thrust themselves into the jaws and claws of wolves. What then are the ministers to do, to whom Christ has committed the care of his flock? Will they allow wolves to rage with impunity in the very fold, and the sheep to be scattered? Will they themselves listen to and watch these things idly? Will they meanwhile soothe the ears of all with smooth words? Those who demand this either do not understand the business of human salvation, or are little faithful to Christ, who has nothing dearer and more precious than his Church. This place, therefore, is very useful and most worthy of much consideration, so that those who have hitherto been somewhat negligent in a matter of the greatest importance may be roused.

units.la: Sed Christi admonitionem audiamus, cuius propositio aut summa est: Non esse audiendos Pharisaeos aut Scribas, qui diuersum ab ipso doceant. Id argumentis & rationibus probat, ne quid ex affectu loqui videatur. Et debent hoc diligenter cauere doctores, ne imperiose & absque ratione vlla alios damnent, & ita seipsos multis suspectos reddant. Primum argumentum ab illorum persona petit, vtque magis moueat, parabola vtitur, dicens: Num potest caecus caeco praire, aut via dux esse? Caecitatis nomine Legis diuinae & veritatis ignorantiam intelligit, qua Pharisaei laborabant. Quia enim Graeca philosophia imbuti (cuius scholam Iason Hierosolymae aperue rat) liberum arbitrium & proprias hominis vires propugnabant, non poterant verum legis sensum & ipsum videre, qui est, vt per ipsam, ceu paedagogum, ad Christum adducamur, qui nobis a patre satisfactio & iustitia factus est. Itaque vt Paulus ait, ipsi sibi velum imposuerant, quo minus in Mosis faciem intueri & eius mentem intelligere possent. Accidit hoc omnibus, qui circa legis doctrinam absque Christo occupantur. Quia enim lux mundi Christus est, caecutiant oportet & in tenebris ambulent, quotquot illum ignorant. Nam etsi ille se omnium oculis ingerat, illis tamen idem quod lippientibus accidere solet, qui eo minus vident, quo clariori splendore oculos eorum Solferit, & proinde in ipso meridie impingunt. Porro Christi argumentum est eiusmodi: Vt caecus non potest cuiquam viae dux esse, ita legem docere aut in eius vijs ducere alios nunquam poterit, qui ipse verum illius sensum non intelligit: At Scribae & Pharisaei hunc non intelligunt, sed excaecata mente circa sua figmenta oberrant: Ergo illi nemini praire possunt, & proinde nemo illos sequi aut pro veritatis doctoribus agnoscere debet. Admonent nos haec Christi verba, neminem in ecclesia doctoris officio fungi posse, qui non ipse certam veritatis cognitionem habeat. Quid enim alios doceat, qui ipse nihil nouit aut intelligit? At cognicio illa diuinae veritatis diminutus obtingit, quando homo animalis ea non percipit, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Ideo Ieremiae dicebatur: Ecce ego pono verba mea in os tuum. Et Isaiae labia angelus carbone ignito ex altari sumpto purgabat: ita nimirum innuens spiritus ardore & illuminatione opus esse ijs, qui Dei verbum cum aliquo fructu praedicare velint. Quae causa est, quòd Christus discipulos Hierosolymis subsistere, neq; ad docendi munus prodire prius voluit, quam Spiritu sancto coelitus essent donati. At non semper miraculose homines illuminat Deus, sed mediis quoque ordinarijs plerunque utitur. Nam voluntatem suam & salutis aeternae mysteria sacrae scripturae libris comprehendit, ut ex illis discantur, quae populo rudi & indocto praedicari debent. Et scholas in suo populo esse voluit, in quibus, in linguarum & scripturarum cognitione instituantur, qui aliquando ecclesijs docendo serviant. Tales olim filij prophetarum erant Samuelis & Elisaei temporibus, & Paulus Timotheum suum à pueris sacras literas didicisse scribit. Ifius ergo studijs se consecrent, qui ad ecclesiae ministerium aspirant, & in scripturis diligentes sint, ut eas sibi familiarissimas faciant, atque earundem sensum germanum atque verum intelligant. Admonet de hoc Paulus, quando Timotheum lectioni intentum esse iubet. Arguunt ista eorum negligentiam, qui ubi scripturas vix obiter degustarunt, eas postea negligunt, & quasi sufficiat ad ecclesiae gubernacula semel admissum esse, se aut otio ignavo, aut venationi, aut aliis studijs parum honestis & ab ipsorum vocatione alienissimis dedunt. In primis vero eorum arrogantia damnatur, qui homines ineptissimos titulis magnificis exornant, & ijsdem ecclesias committunt, cum neque in sacris literis exercitati sint, neque aliquam regendarum Ecclesiarum rationem reneant. Sunt hi omnes duces caeci, neque aliquid in pietatis et salutis studio proficient, qui illos sibi sequendos proposuerint.
units.tr: But let us hear the admonition of Christ, whose proposition or summary is this: that the Pharisees or Scribes, who teach something different from him, are not to be listened to. He proves this by arguments and reasons, lest he should seem to speak out of feeling. Teachers ought to take great care that they do not condemn others imperiously and without any reason, and so make themselves suspect to many. His first argument is drawn from the persons of those men, and to make it more forceful he uses a parable, saying: Can the blind lead the blind, or be a guide on the way? By blindness he means ignorance of the divine Law and of the truth, under which the Pharisees laboured. For since they were imbued with Greek philosophy (whose school Jason had openly opened at Jerusalem), they defended free will and the man's own powers, and so they could not see the true sense of the Law itself, which is that through it, as a schoolmaster, we are led to Christ, who has been made for us by the Father satisfaction and righteousness. Therefore, as Paul says, they had put a veil upon themselves, so that they could not look into the face of Moses and understand his mind. This happens to all who occupy themselves with the teaching of the Law without Christ. For since Christ is the light of the world, all who are ignorant of him must be blind and walk in darkness. For although he presents himself to the eyes of all, it happens to them as it usually does to those with sore eyes, who see the less, the more brightly the sun shines upon their eyes, and so stumble at high noon itself. Moreover, Christ's argument is of this kind: as a blind man can be a guide to no one on the way, so one who does not himself understand the true sense of the Law can never teach it or lead others in its paths. But the scribes and Pharisees do not understand it, but wander with blinded minds about their own inventions. Therefore they can lead no one, and consequently no one ought to follow them or acknowledge them as teachers of truth. These words of Christ admonish us that no one can perform the office of teacher in the Church who does not himself have a sure knowledge of the truth. For how can he teach others who knows nothing or understands nothing himself? But that knowledge of divine truth is imperfectly given when a natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. Therefore it was said to Jeremiah: Behold, I put my words in your mouth. And an angel purged the lips of Isaiah with a live coal taken from the altar, thus plainly signifying that those who wish to preach the word of God with any fruit need the ardour and illumination of the Spirit. This is why Christ would not allow the disciples to go out to the office of teaching before they had been endowed from heaven with the Holy Spirit, but told them to remain at Jerusalem. Yet God does not always enlighten men miraculously, but for the most part also uses ordinary means. For he has comprehended his will and the mysteries of eternal salvation in the books of Holy Scripture, that from them those things may be learned which ought to be preached to a rude and unlearned people. And he willed that there should be schools among his people, in which those who sometime serve the churches by teaching should be trained in the knowledge of languages and of the Scriptures. Such were the sons of the prophets in the times of Samuel and Elisha, and Paul writes that his Timothy had learned the holy letters from childhood. Let those therefore who aspire to the ministry of the Church devote themselves to these studies, and be diligent in the Scriptures, so as to make them very familiar to themselves and to understand their genuine and true sense. Paul gives this warning when he bids Timothy give himself to reading. These things condemn the negligence of those who, having barely tasted the Scriptures in passing, afterwards neglect them, and, as if it were enough to have been once admitted to the helm of the Church, give themselves over either to idle sloth, or to hunting, or to other pursuits little honourable and wholly foreign to their calling. Above all, the arrogance is condemned of those who adorn the most unfit men with magnificent titles and entrust churches to them, when they are neither practised in the sacred letters nor know any method of governing the Churches. All these are blind guides, and those who have proposed them to themselves to follow make no progress at all in the pursuit of piety and salvation.

units.la: Ne quis tamen eos ineptos modo & inutiles putaret, periculosos quoque esse docet. Nam ait: Nonne ambo in foveam cadent? Evidentius hoc apud Matthaeum enuntiat: Si caecus caeco praebuerit, ambo in foveam cadent. Hic autem interrogatione utitur, ut animos magis penetret, & hoc certò cuenturum esse ostendat. Ergo non soli doctores in periculo constituti sunt, si caeci fuerint, sed una cum illis periclitantur, qui eos sequi volent. Ratio huius sententiae est, quòd nemo ab alterius iudicio pendere, sed omnes Deum in scripturis per filium suum loquentem audire debent, ut de fide sua certi sint. Docet hoc Deus in lege, quando ne illi quidem prophetae credamus admonet, qui doctrinam de alienis Diis colendis, signis aut miraculo aliquo confirmat. Et notum est illud Christi: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, & cognoscunt eas, & sequuntur me: alienum autem nequaquam sequentur, sed fugient ab eo: quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Errant ergo vehementer, qui cuiusvis simpliciter credendum esse aiunt, sed excusatos esse putant, eò quòd culpa omnis in doctoribus haereat. Petexunt illi fere simplicem ignorantiam, quae minime puniri meretur. At si rem ipsam consideremus, in plerisque crassa & voluntaria est ignorantia, ut iam de eo nihil dicamus, quòd ignorantes neminem excusat, qualiscunque sit, eò quòd nos non ignorantes, sed veri cultus gnaros & peritos Deus vult esse. Et ne quid praetexere possemus, voluntatem suam verbo comprehensam in scripturis proposuit, & axiomata quaedam religionis Christianae tradidit, tam certa & perspicua, ut apertis & mulierculis disci & intelligi possint. Continentur ea in Decalogo, Symbolo apostolico, & Oratione Dominica: à quibus quicunque dissentiunt, ij profeductoribus haberi, & modis omnibus vitari debent. Sed & ipsos doctores falsos certis notis insigniuit, ex quibus agnoscantur. Hos enim ex episcoporum grege praediturros, & sedem suam in Dei templo habituros esse Paulus praedixit. Et praecipua illorum dogmata paulo ante commemorauimus. Quae si qui admittunt & sequuntur, ij scientes & volentes sibi falsos doctores deligunt, & proinde digni sunt, qui in eadem cum illis foveam praecipites ruant. Nihil nunc de vita & moribus dico, qui fere eiusmodi sunt, ut non possint non bonis omnibus suspecti esse. Nec, dubium est, plerosq; qui hodie sacrificulos & monachos sectantur, horum fidem adeò suspectam habere, ut pecuniam suam illis minime crederent. Quae ergo lenitas, vel potius insania & impietas est, animam illis credere, & de coelis atq; salutis aeternae ratione loquentes audire, qui sic viuunt, ut satis constet illos nec coelos, nec inferos credere, imo in sinu suo suiter ridere omnia, quae de vita aeterna dicuntur? Sunt ergo inexcusabiles, qui tales sequuntur, nec illis excusandis ullae rationes sufficere possunt, sed ad illos pertinet, quod Christus ait: Qui in forti-bus est, sordescat adhuc. Apoc.22.
units.tr: Lest anyone think these men are merely useless and incompetent, he also teaches that they are dangerous. For he says: "Will not both fall into the pit?" He states this more plainly in Matthew: "If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit." Here he uses a question in order to pierce their minds more deeply and to show that this will certainly happen. So the teachers are not the only ones placed in danger if they are blind. Those who want to follow them are endangered along with them. The reason for this statement is that no one should depend on another's judgment, but all must hear God speaking in Scripture through his Son, so that they may be certain of their own faith. God teaches this in the law, when he warns us not to believe even that prophet who confirms a doctrine about serving other gods by signs or some miracle. There is also the well-known saying of Christ: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; but they will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers." Those therefore greatly err who say that one must simply believe whoever he is, and yet think that people are excused because all the blame rests on the teachers. They commonly plead a simple ignorance, which deserves no punishment at all. But if we consider the matter itself, in most cases the ignorance is gross and voluntary. Let us not even mention that ignorance excuses no one, whatever kind it is, since God wants us not to be ignorant but to be acquainted with and skilled in true worship. And so that we could have no pretext, he has set out his will, comprehended in the Word, in the Scriptures, and has handed down certain axioms of the Christian religion, so certain and so plain that even the simple and women can learn and understand them. They are contained in the Decalogue, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer. Whoever dissents from these must be regarded as a deceiver and avoided by every means. But he has also marked the false teachers themselves with certain signs by which they may be recognised. For Paul foretold that from the flock of the bishops such men would arise and would have their seat in the temple of God. And we mentioned their chief doctrines a little earlier. If anyone admits and follows these, he chooses false teachers for himself knowingly and willingly, and therefore deserves to fall headlong into the same pit with them. I say nothing now about life and morals, which for the most part are of such a kind that they cannot fail to make them suspect to all good people. Nor is it doubtful that most of those who today follow the petty priests and monks hold these men's faith in such suspicion that they would not entrust their money to them. What, then, is it but foolish softness, or rather madness and impiety, to entrust one's soul to those, and to listen to those speaking about heaven and the way of eternal salvation, who live in such a way that it is quite clear they believe neither in heaven nor in hell, but rather laugh sweetly in their hearts at everything said about eternal life? Those who follow such men are therefore inexcusable, and no reasons can suffice to excuse them. To them applies what Christ says: "He who is filthy, let him be filthy still." Rev. 22.

units.la: Ac hic nobis scioli quidam respondant: Esto, caecus sit & errabundus hinc inde vagetur, qui docendi munus in Ecclesia sustinet: At possum ego illum quoad externam professionem, ne scismatis alicuius author videar, pro meo doctore & duce agnoscere, interim vero ipse viam rectam tenebo, neque de salute mea periclitabor. Sed praevenit horum objectionem Christus dicens: Non est discipulus supra magistrum suum, sed quisque erit perfectus, sicut magister suus. Sumit argumentum hoc ex communi sensu. Quasi dicat: Discipuli, si multum proficiant, magistrorum similes fiunt, nec sperare potest, ut quis ex alio discat, quod is ignorat, quem sibi magistrum aut doctorem delegit. Et ruftra ergo tu viam rectam tenere te posse speras, si caeco duce utaris. Vt argumenti in eo consistit, quod cum ex nobis ipsis divina & caelestia non sapiamus, doctrina aut institutione omnino nobis opus est. Nisi ergo haec sana & vera sit, nunquam in veram salutis aeternae cognitionem venire poterimus. Vbi rursus observabis, quam diligenti cura & circumspectione opus sit in deligendis doctoribus aut Ecclesiarum ministris. Nam qui hic committitur error, non in illis solis haeret, sed ad multos alios redundat. Ideo tam prolixe Apostoli ea recensent, quibus praditos & ornatos esse convenit doctrinae antistites, ne fiat quod apud prophetam dicitur: Talis populus, qualis sacerdos. Etenim passim in scripturis populi ignorantia & quae hanc secuta est calamitas, ignavus & male fidus sacerdotibus accepta fertur. Est ergo magna & detestabilis eorum levitas, qui consulto eos verbi administros quaerunt, quos sui similes sperare possint, & quibus pro sua libidine abutantur. Nolunt illi proficere in salutis negotio, quod aut vanum esse putent quicquid de illo traditur, aut quod se iam ante plus satis instructos putant. Simul vero impunitatis spem captant ex pastorum suorum ignorantia & malo exemplo, & se abunde satis excusatos esse arbitrantur, si se pastoribus suis nihilo inferiores esse dicere possint. Illorum enim haec voces sunt: Cur ego in discendo Dei verbo plus laboris & operae insumam, quam noster parochus, qui libros aut nunquam, aut quam rarissime inspicit? Cur a me requiritur, quod ipsi Ecclesiarum antistites non faciunt? Num ego vitae genus sequar sanctius & auctorum magis, quam ii, qui ex religione viuunt? Agnosco opinor eorum verba, qui cum meliores magistros habere nolint, eorundem tamen exemplis suae nequitiae & libidini patrocinantur. Et sunt quidem rationes istorum plausibiles hominum iudicio: sed longe aliter de causa hac tota Deus pronuntiabit, apud cuius tribunal nulla valet criminis translatio, eo quod unusquisque ex suis dictis & factis vel iustificabitur, vel damnabitur.
units.tr: At this point some clever-clever people may answer us: "Granted that he is blind and wanders here and there, the man who holds the office of teaching in the Church: yet I can acknowledge him as my teacher and leader in outward profession, lest I seem to be the author of some schism, while I myself will keep the right way and not be endangered in my own salvation." But Christ anticipated this objection when he said: "A disciple is not above his master, but everyone who is perfected will be like his master." He takes this argument from common sense, as if to say: disciples, if they make great progress, become like their masters; nor can anyone hope to learn from another what that other does not know, the man he has chosen as his master or teacher. And so in vain do you hope that you can keep to the right way if you use a blind guide. The force of the argument lies in this: since we of ourselves do not understand divine and heavenly things, we have absolute need of doctrine and instruction. Unless this instruction is sound and true, we can never come to a true knowledge of eternal salvation. Here again you will observe how much careful diligence and caution is needed in choosing teachers or ministers of the Churches. For the error committed here does not stick only to those men, but spreads to many others. That is why the Apostles so fully list the qualities with which the leaders of doctrine ought to be endowed and adorned, so that what is said in the prophet may not happen: "Such as the priest is, such is the people." Indeed, throughout the Scriptures the ignorance of the people, and the calamity that follows it, is commonly ascribed to the idleness and bad faith of the priests. It is therefore a great and detestable frivolity of those who deliberately seek out ministers of the Word whom they can hope to be like themselves, and whom they may abuse for their own lust. They are unwilling to make progress in the business of salvation, either because they think that whatever is taught about it is empty, or because they think they are already sufficiently instructed. At the same time they catch at a hope of impunity from the ignorance and bad example of their pastors, and they think themselves sufficiently excused if they can say that they are in no way inferior to their pastors. For these are their words: "Why should I spend more labour and effort in learning the Word of God than our parish priest, who never or very rarely looks at books? Why is it required of me what the very leaders of the Churches do not do? Shall I follow a more holy way of life and one more like the authors than those who live by religion?" I suppose I recognise the words of men who, though they do not want better teachers, nevertheless defend their own wickedness and lust by the examples of those same teachers. Their reasons are indeed plausible to human judgment; but God will pronounce quite differently on this whole cause, before whose tribunal no shifting of blame has any force, since each one will either be justified or condemned by his own words and deeds.

units.la: Sed redit Christus ad sui saeculi doctores, Scribas & Pharisaeos, & in eos magna cum gravitate invehitur, quod cum sibi in omnes alios imperium vendicarent, & omnium delicta odiosissime notarent, ipsi interea publicis ijsque gravissimis sceleribus essent infames. Quid autem aspicis (inquit) festucam, quae est in oculo fratris tui, trabem autem, quae est in oculo proprio, non animadvertis? Rursus metaphoris & parabolicis locutionibus vtitur, vt pondus maius orationi accedat. Festucam enim dicit delictum levius & vulgare, trabem vero atrox & immane scelus, quod vulgo omnes vt intolerabile detestantur. Magna autem impudentia illos arguit, quod cum talia multa ipsi committerent, auderent tamen tanta cum severitate & insolentia in aliorum mores sibi censuram sumere. Sensus enim verborum est: Vt merito eorum ridetur impudentia, qui in aliorum oculis aut facie naevos aut maculas leviores notant, in semetipsis autem totius faciei foedam deformitatem non animadvertunt: ita vos nimium ridiculi & impudentes estis, dum in quibusvis aliis leviissima quaeque reprehenditis, non autem obseruatis ea, quae a vobis praeter omne dignitatem & cum publica vestri ordinis infamia designantur. At non temere hoc illos Christus exprobrat. Nam vt ex aliis locis constat, grauissimis vitiis & scelerIbus illi toti scatebant, cum falsa doctrina populum infelicem seducerent, sub religionis praetextu liberis summae in parentes impietatis authores essent, domus viduarum deuorarent, promissi Messiae honorem in se & opera sua transferrent, denique religionem omnem sibi quaestum facerent, & patriam vna secum in exitium abriperent. Quas ob causas illos Christus alibi lupos rapaces, fures item & latrones dicit, hypocritas item, qui foris quidem sanctimoniam simulent, seque venditent sacerdotij & doctrinae titulis, intus autem mendaciorum & rapinarum sint pleni. Adhaec in semetipsis non obseruabant illi, sed quasi nihil in se haberent reprehensione dignum magna cum libertate quosuis corripiebant, & pro leuissimis delictis expiatorias victimas poscebant maximi pretij, aut etiam miseros è Synagogis eiectos ab ecclesiae societate excludebant. Denique, vt exemplo res clarior fiat, Monachis atque sacrificulis isti simillimi fuerunt: qui in Papatu rudi plebeculae ob leuissima delicta plurimum negotij faciunt, & nunquam non excommunicationis fulmen in ore habent, si quis no sese ipsis ad omnia obsequente praebeat: cum ipsi in scripturis & aeterno Dei verbo impie ludant, sacra omnia venalia habeant, thoris alienis insidientur, sanguinarijs consilijs totum orbem terrarum turbent, denique ventris atq; Veneris turpissima sint mancipia. Tales (inquam) scribae illi & Pharisaei erant, & ideo illos Christus festucam in fratrum oculis videre, in proprijs autem oculis trabem non animaduertere ait. Neque eo contentus, graviter admodum addit: Quomodo potes dicere fratri tuo: Frater, sine eijciam festucam, quae in oculo tuo est, cum ipse trabem, quae est in oculo tuo, non respicias? Repetit subinde fratris nomen, vt magis arguat ipsorum iniquitatem, qui ne ijs quidem parcebant, quos non poterant non pro fratribus agnoscere, & quorum rationem diligentissimam debebant habere, ne eos vel intempestiius correptionibus, vel malo exemplo offenderent.
units.tr: But Christ turns back to the teachers of his own age, the Scribes and Pharisees, and attacks them with great seriousness, because while they claimed authority over all others and most harshly marked the faults of everyone, they themselves were notorious for public and most grave crimes. "Why do you look," he says, "at the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam that is in your own eye?" Again he uses metaphorical and parabolic language, so that greater weight may be given to his speech. For he calls a fault a speck, a light and common thing, but a dreadful and monstrous crime a beam, which everyone commonly detests as intolerable. He charges them with great shamelessness, because although they themselves committed many such things, they dared with such severity and insolence to claim for themselves the right to censure the morals of others. For the sense of the words is this: just as men are rightly laughed at for shamelessness when they notice spots or light blemishes in the eyes or face of others, but do not perceive the foul deformity of their own whole face, so you are too ridiculous and shameless when, in any others, you reprove the very smallest faults, but do not observe those things which are marked against you, beyond all dignity and with public infamy to your order. Yet Christ does not rebuke them for this without cause. For, as is clear from other passages, they were utterly steeped in the gravest vices and crimes: while they led the unhappy people astray with false doctrine, they were the authors, under the pretext of religion, of the most extreme impiety toward parents; they devoured the houses of widows; they transferred the honour of the promised Messiah to themselves and their own works; in short, they made a profit out of all religion, and dragged their country down to ruin along with themselves. For these reasons Christ elsewhere calls them ravening wolves, and likewise thieves and robbers, and hypocrites, who outwardly feign holiness and sell themselves under the titles of priesthood and teaching, but inwardly are full of lies and plunder. Moreover, they did not observe these things in themselves; but as if they had nothing in themselves worthy of reproof, they rebuked whoever they pleased with great freedom, and for the very slightest offences they demanded expiatory victims of the greatest price, or even excluded from fellowship with the Church the wretched people cast out of the synagogues. Finally, to make the matter clearer by an example, these men were very like the monks and petty priests, who in the Papacy make a great fuss over the slightest offences among the rude common people, and always have the thunderbolt of excommunication on their lips, if anyone does not offer himself in complete obedience to them; while they themselves play impiously with Scripture and the eternal Word of God, have all sacred things for sale, lie in wait for other men's beds, with bloodthirsty plans throw the whole world into turmoil, and in short are the most shameful slaves of belly and lust. Such (I say) were those Scribes and Pharisees, and therefore Christ says that they saw the speck in their brothers' eyes, but did not notice the beam in their own eyes. Not content with this, he adds very gravely: "How can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,' when you yourself do not regard the beam that is in your own eye?" He repeats the word "brother" again and again, so that he may more strongly charge the wickedness of those men who did not spare even those whom they could not help recognising as brothers, and whose situation they ought to have considered most carefully, lest they offend them either by correcting them at the wrong time or by a bad example.

units.la: Docet autem nos totus iste locus quàm multùm momenti in eo situm sit, vt inculpatos & irreprehensibiles sese praebeant, qui alijs praesunt, & aliorum mores ex officio corrigere debent. Possunt quidem illi verbis instare, & de virtutibus atque vitijs orationes instituere artificiosas: sed nihil aut parum proficient, si ipsi ijsdem vitijs laborant, quae in alijs reprehendunt. Nam vt versus à pueris decantatus monet, Turpe est doctori, si culpa redarguit ipsum. Quod si vero maior licentia peccandi accedat, & ijs sceleribus infames sint ecclesiarum antistites, quae in hominibus plebeis intolerabilia putantur, vnà cum illis tota ministerij ecclesiastici authoritas periclitabitur: & tunc fit, quod de sale infatuato dicit Dominus, qui in sterquilinium proiectus à quibusuis obuijs conculcatur. Exempla huius mala passim hodie occurrunt, quae vtinam ab illis diligentius observarentur, qui de collapsa ministerij authoritate queruntur, cùm ipsi interim ad exemplum filiorum Eli intemperantia & libidine diffluant, & sua nequitia omnium linguas aduersus se provocent. At quod illis dicitur, hoc ad se quoq; pertinere putent, qui in magistratu constituti bonas leges condunt & iudicia publica exercent. Maximum enim robur legibus accedere sentient, si ipsi illis obedierint: at eadem illi co vilescent, si suo exemplo alijs eas violandi occasionem dederint. Eadem est parentum ratio erga liberos, praeceptorum erga discipulos, herorum erga seruos, Christianorum denique omnium. Vult enim nos lucis instar esse Christus, vt exemplo nostro mundi scelera arguamus: & cùm ille nos è mundo selegerit & sibi consecrarit, etiam atque etiam videre nos decet, ne propter nos Dei nomen prophanetur.
units.tr: This whole passage teaches how much depends on those who preside over others and who ought to correct their conduct, presenting themselves as blameless and beyond reproach. They may certainly press their point with words and deliver fine speeches about virtues and vices, but they will achieve little or nothing if they themselves are caught in the same vices they condemn in others. As the verse sung by schoolboys puts it: "It is shameful for a teacher if he is refuted by his own fault." If, however, greater licence in sinning creeps in, and the leaders of the churches are notorious for those crimes that are regarded as intolerable even in common people, the whole authority of the ecclesiastical ministry will be endangered along with them. Then what the Lord says of salt that has lost its savour comes true: it is cast onto the dunghill and trampled underfoot by whoever passes by. Examples of this evil appear everywhere today. I wish that those who complain about the collapse of the ministry's authority would pay closer attention to them, while they themselves, after the example of the sons of Eli, wallow in intemperance and lust, and by their wickedness provoke everyone's tongue against them. What is said to them, let those also consider to apply to themselves who are set in the magistracy, enact good laws and administer public justice. For they will find that the greatest strength is added to laws if they themselves obey them, but that the same laws grow contemptible if they give others an occasion to violate them by their own example. The same holds for parents towards their children, teachers towards their pupils, masters towards their servants, and, in short, for all Christians. For Christ wills us to be like light, so that by our example we may reprove the wickedness of the world; and since he has chosen us out of the world and consecrated us to himself, we ought constantly to take care that the name of God is not profaned because of us.

units.la: Caeterùm ne vitijs patrocinari, & arguendi munus omnino abolere videatur, pergit Dominus, & quid fieri debeat docet. Hypocrita, eijce primùm trabem illam ex oculo tuo, & tum dispicies, vt eijcias festucam, quae est in oculo fratris tui. Hypocritas dicit, non vt conuitietur illis, sed vt fontem huius mali offendat, qui erat, quod propriae iustitiae fuco turgidi, sibi quiduis in omnes alios licere putabant. Et constat, hodie etiam personatos illos doctrinae antistites ex eo audaciam maiorem concipere, quòd magnifico titulorum splendore & habitu insolenti, apud rude vulgus aliquam sanctitatis existimationem sibi parauerunt. At ijsdem cristas non alia ratione facilius depresseris, quàm si laruam hanc detrahas, & omne id hypocriticum esse doceas, quo sese venditant. Et haec causa est, quòd frequenter Pharisaeorum hypocrisim Christus arguit. Porrò praeceptum, quod hic propo nit, duabus partibus constat. Prima, vt à seipsis incipiant monet, qui aliorum peccata arguere & reprehendere volunt. Eijce (inquit) primùm trabem illam ex oculo tuo. Opus ergo hic erit diligentiori suijpsius examine, vt quisq; seipsum probè norit, & quid in se emendationem aut correctionem mereatur, intelligat. Inspiciant ergo legis speculum, & mox infinitae & eximiae trabes occurrent, siue occultas animorum suorum cogitationes, siue dicta & facta sua totamque vitae suae consuetudinem considerent. Deinde vlterius progressi, eos quoq; spectent, quos ipsis Deus praecipuè commendauit, & videant iuxta Graecum versum, Ædibus in proprijs quae recta aut prava gerantur: qui nimirum vxoru mores sint, quae liberorum disciplina, & quid singuli domestici faciant: & dubiù non est, quin hic quoque inuenturi sint, quod corrigi oporteat. Sed plerosque videmus Lamiarum similes esse, quos Plutarchus oculos exemptitios habere scribit, quos domi quidem in loculis reconditos asseruant, foras autem egressurae sumunt, ut quae ab alijs fiunt spectent. At ut domi nostrae & in nostris rebus oculatissimi simus necesse est, ne (ut ante diximus) cum propriae salutis iactura ridiculi fiamus, dum aliorum delicta corriginus, ipsi gravioribus obnoxij. Vbi vero trabes ex nostris oculis eiecimus, tunc (quae altera huius praecepti pars est) de festuca ex fratrum oculis eijcienda cogitemus. Non ergo prohibemur, ne fratrum vitia reprehendamus. Nam qui haec omnino negligunt, aut ignavi dissimulant, ij non charitatis ingenium referunt, sed proximis suis, quantum in ipsis est, exitij sunt authores. At hic dispicere nos iubet, qua ratione festucam ex fratris oculo eximamus. Diligentiam ergo & prudentiam requirit, qua omnino opus est, ne (quod imperiti chirurgi solent) vulnera aut ulcera intempestiuis remedijs irritemus, & incurabilia reddamus. Quare dum aliorum vitia reprehendimus, curandum est, ut dilectionis & coniunctionis fraternae memores amicè cum illis agamus, ne odij aut invidiae possimus insimulari. Nam huius suspicio omnem officij gratiam extinguit & abolet. Deinde finis hic nobis propositus sit, ut proximus aedificetur, & in pietate progressus maiores faciat. In utroque plurimum proderit, si qui nos simus, quidque nobis accidere possit cogitemus, & simul Dei exemplum nobis ob oculos ponamus, qui cum nos perdere possit, neque perdendi causas iustas & graves habeat, sua tamen benignitatis memor, nos corrigere potius & seruare quàm perdere studet. Nolo (inquit) mortem peccatoris, sed ut reuertatur & viuat. Ezechielis decimo octavo.
units.tr: But lest it should seem that he is defending vices and altogether abolishing the duty of reproving, the Lord goes on and teaches what ought to be done: "Hypocrite, first cast out the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the mote that is in your brother's eye." He calls them hypocrites not to revile them, but to strike at the source of this evil, which was that, puffed up with the paint of their own righteousness, they thought they might do whatever they pleased with all others. And it is well known that even today those masked teachers of doctrine conceive greater boldness from this, because by the magnificent splendour of their titles and their unusual dress they have won for themselves some reputation for holiness among the uneducated crowd. But you will more easily cut down their crests in no other way than by tearing off this mask and teaching that everything by which they puff themselves up is hypocrisy. This is why Christ so often rebukes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees. Moreover, the precept he proposes here has two parts. The first is that those who want to reprove and correct the sins of others should begin with themselves: "Cast out first," he says, "the beam from your own eye." There will therefore be need here of a more diligent examination of oneself, so that each person may know himself well and understand what correction or amendment he himself deserves. Let them therefore look into the mirror of the law, and at once countless and enormous beams will appear, whether they consider the hidden thoughts of their minds, or their words and deeds and the whole course of their life. Then, going further, let them look also at those whom God has especially entrusted to them, and see, according to the Greek verse, "what is done rightly or wrongly in one's own house": namely, what the characters of their wives are, what the discipline of their children is, and what each member of the household does. And there is no doubt that they will find here too much that needs correcting. But we see many who are like the Lamiae, whom Plutarch writes have eyes that can be taken out; they keep them stored away at home in their boxes, and take them out when they go abroad, so that they may look at what others do. But it is necessary that we be most keen-sighted at home and in our own affairs, lest (as we said before) while we correct the faults of others we become ridiculous to our own loss, and ourselves liable to graver ones. When we have cast the beams out of our own eyes, then (which is the second part of this precept) let us think of removing the mote from our brothers' eyes. We are therefore not forbidden to reprove our brothers' faults. For those who altogether neglect this, or cowardly connive at it, do not display the nature of charity, but, as far as lies in them, are the authors of ruin to their neighbours. Yet here he bids us examine by what method we may take the mote out of our brother's eye. He therefore requires diligence and prudence, which are altogether necessary, lest (as unskilled surgeons are wont to do) we aggravate wounds or ulcers with ill-timed remedies and make them incurable.
