Therefore, while we reprove the faults of others, we must take care to deal with them in a friendly way, mindful of love and brotherly fellowship, so that we cannot be accused of hatred or envy. For suspicion of this destroys and abolishes all the goodwill of the duty. Then let the end proposed to us be that our neighbour may be built up and make greater progress in godliness. In both respects it will help greatly if we consider what we ourselves are and what may happen to us, and at the same time set before our eyes the example of God, who, though he could destroy us, and has no just and grave causes for destroying us, yet, mindful of his goodness, is more eager to correct and save us than to destroy us. "I do not desire," he says, "the death of the sinner, but that he may turn back and live." Ezekiel 18.

units.la: Porrò redeamus ad Christi verba, qui doctrinam hanc omnem applicat propositioni de vitandis falsis doctoribus: & rationem affert, quòd cum reuera mali sint, nihil boni ex illis sperari possit. Id vero duplici similitudine explicat. Primam a plantis siue arboribus petit, cuius hic sensus est: Vt vnaquaeuis arbor ex suo fructu agnoscitur, sic etiam doctores. Nam non est (inquit) arbor bona, quae ferat fructum putrem: neque arbor putris, quae ferat fructum bonum. Item, Neque ex spinis ficum colligunt, neque e rubo vindemiant uuam. At Pharisaei & Scribae fructus pessimos ferunt: Ergo arbores malae sunt, & plurimum falluntur, qui ex illis bonum quid expectant, aut se saluos fore sperant, si illos sequantur. Quo loco diligenter videre oportet, qui nam fructus illi sint, de quibus loquatur. Nam si hoc simpliciter de vita & moribus exponas, ipsa Veritatis doctrina in multis damnabitur, qui cum pessimè viuant, illam tamen pure & syceriter docent: & simul in Christi praeceptum peccabis, qui Scribis quoque & Pharisaeis obedire iubet, quando in Mosis cathedra sedent, id est, Legis doctrinam proponunt, qualis illa per Mosem tradita est. Propius ergo haec res consideranda debet, & in ipso doctoris vocabulo insistendum erit. Vt enim fructus pyri arboris est pyrum, cerasi cerasum, mali malum, ita doctoris fructus proprie dicetur doctrina. Ideò haec potissimum inspici debet, si quando de illis volumus iudicium facere. Erat autem Scribarum doctrina multis modis corruptissima. Nam ut supra diximus, liberum hominis arbitrium & eius vires, magnificè extollebant, operum suorum merita asserebant, gratiae Dei & Christi merito derogabant: denique authores erant, ut plerique peccata grauissima inanibus & leuiculis ceremonijs expiari posse putarent: quae proxima via est ad effrenem peccandi licentiam. Erant ergo arbores putres, neque bonum aliquod ex illis poterat sperari. Itaq; vides hoc loco, quid de illis iudicari debeat, qui hodie similia tradunt, & Euangelij praedicatione hoc Pharisaico fermento inficiunt. Laudantur hi à multis, maximè si modestiae & mansuetudinis speciem praeferant: sed reuera arbores putres sunt, & proinde ad nihil vtiles, quàm ut excisae & eradicatae in ignem conijciantur, sicuti Christus alibi diserte testatur. Debet praeterea hinc generalis doctrina peti, ut de re quauis ex fructibus eius iudicemus. Est hoc remedium praesentissimum aduersus scelerum blanditias, quibus nos Satan circumuenire studet. Exempli gratia: Ebrietas multis leuicula & vix reprehensione digna videtur. Sed fructus inspice, quos Salomo describit Prouer.23. & quos in veteribus simul ac quotidianis exemplis est videre: & mox patebit, Ebrietatem arborem pessimam esse, & quam inter homines excindi oporteat. Idem dicemus, si scortationis & libidinis fructus intuamur. Vel si quid auaritia pariat speciemus, & quot mala, saepe cum Reipub. totius detrimento inde enata sint. Eadem est omnium aliorum ratio, &c. Et quod de his dicitur, hoc ipsum de fide intelligi debet, ne huius professione nobis ipsis aut alijs imponamus, sed
units.tr: Let us return further to the words of Christ, who applies all this teaching to the proposition about avoiding false teachers, and gives the reason: because they are truly evil, nothing good can be hoped from them. He explains this by a twofold comparison. The first is taken from plants or trees, and its sense is this: as every tree is recognised by its fruit, so too are teachers. For (he says) a good tree does not bear rotten fruit, nor does a rotten tree bear good fruit. Likewise, "they do not gather figs from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble." But the Pharisees and scribes bear the worst fruit. Therefore they are bad trees, and those are greatly mistaken who expect anything good from them, or hope to be saved if they follow them. Here we must carefully see what those fruits are of which he speaks. For if you take this simply of life and morals, the very doctrine of truth will be condemned in many cases, since those who live most wickedly nevertheless teach it purely and sincerely; and at the same time you will be acting against Christ's precept, who bids us obey the scribes and Pharisees also when they sit in Moses' seat, that is, when they set forth the teaching of the law as it was handed down through Moses. The matter must therefore be considered more closely, and we must dwell on the very word "teacher." For just as the fruit of a pear tree is a pear, of a cherry tree a cherry, of an apple tree an apple, so the fruit of a teacher is properly called doctrine. Therefore this ought chiefly to be examined whenever we wish to pass judgement on them. Now the doctrine of the scribes was corrupt in many ways. For, as we said above, they greatly exalted the free will of man and its powers, claimed the merits of their own works, detracted from the grace of God and the merit of Christ; and in short they were the authors of the view that most grievous sins could be expiated by empty and trivial ceremonies, which is the direct road to unbridled licence in sinning. They were therefore rotten trees, and nothing good could be hoped from them. So you see here what ought to be judged about those who today hand down similar things and infect the preaching of the Gospel with this Pharisaic leaven. Such men are praised by many, especially if they show a appearance of modesty and gentleness; but in reality they are rotten trees, and therefore good for nothing except to be cut down and uprooted and thrown into the fire, as Christ plainly testifies elsewhere. Moreover, from this a general rule should be drawn, that we judge any matter by its fruits. This is the most ready remedy against the allurements of sins, with which Satan seeks to ensnare us. For example, drunkenness seems to many a trifling thing, scarcely worthy of rebuke. But look at the fruits that Solomon describes in Proverbs 23, and that can be seen in both ancient and daily examples; and soon it will be plain that drunkenness is a most pernicious tree, which ought to be cut down among men. We shall say the same if we consider the fruit of fornication and lust, or if we look at what avarice brings forth, and how many evils have often sprung from it, to the great detriment of the whole commonwealth. The reasoning is the same for all other things, and so on. And what is said of these things must be understood of faith itself, so that we do not deceive ourselves or others by its profession, but

units.la: E eam operibus (vt Iacobus monet) ceu fructibus dignis testemur. Fructus autem fidei sunt, fiducia in unum Deum, Dei vnius inuocatio, Dei timor, obedientia, Dei cultus ex verbo eius institutus, innocentia & dilectionis studium. Quotquot ergo ab his alieni, vitae fructus longe diuersos & his contrarios ferunt, ij non bonae sed malae arbores sunt, quibus iampridem Christus excidium & ignem aeternum minatus est.
units.tr: We bear witness to this by works, as James admonishes, as worthy fruits. The fruits of faith are: trust in the one God, calling upon the one God, the fear of God, obedience, the worship of God instituted by his Word, innocence, and zeal for love. Therefore, all who are alien to these and bear fruits of life far different from them and contrary to them are not good trees but bad ones, against which Christ long ago threatened destruction and eternal fire.

units.la: Alterum simile ex re domestica petitur, & huius sensus est: Vt vir dives ex thesauro opum suarum res bonas & pretiosas depromit: ita doctor bonus & mysteriorum regni Dei gnarus, ex cordis sui thesauro bona & salutaria dogmata profert, quae ad hominum salutem promouendam faciunt. Rursus vt homo malus & improbus ex suo thesauro mala & noxia proponit: sic doctor falsus & nulla veri Dei cognitione instructus, ex corde noxijs hominum traditionibus imbuto, dogmata propinat falsa, & quae auditoribus exitium ferunt. Atqui constat scribas istos doctrinam eiusmodi spargere. Sunt ergo pessimi patresfamilias & malae fidei promi, quibus tuto credi non potest. Scio nonnullos locum hunc aliter exponere, sed hic sensus argumento praesenti in primis connenire mihi videtur, & ipsius Christi authoritate confirmatur, qui eadem parabola de Scribis loquens vtitur, Matth. 13, sic dicens: Omnis Scriba doctus in regno caelorum, similis est cuipiam patrifamilias, qui effert ex thesauro suo noua & vetera. Quo etiam potest referri, quod alibi de Oeconomo ecclesiastico dicitur, cuius parabolam suo loco tractabimus.
units.tr: The second comparison is taken from household affairs, and its sense is this: as a rich man brings out good and precious things from the treasury of his wealth, so a good teacher, who knows the mysteries of the kingdom of God, brings forth from the treasury of his heart good and wholesome teachings, which serve to advance the salvation of men. Conversely, as a wicked and dishonest man brings out evil and harmful things from his treasure, so a false teacher, who is instructed in no knowledge of the true God, brings forth from a heart steeped in harmful human traditions false teachings, which bring destruction upon their hearers. And it is certain that those scribes spread teaching of this kind. They are therefore the worst heads of households and men of bad faith, to whom one cannot safely trust themselves. I know that some expound this passage differently, but this sense seems to me to fit the present argument best, and it is confirmed by the authority of Christ himself, who, speaking of the scribes, uses the same parable in Matthew 13, saying: "Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old." This can also be related to what is said elsewhere about the ecclesiastical steward, whose parable we shall treat in its place.

units.la: In praesenti admonitionem hanc generali sententia confirmat. Ex abundantia enim cordis loquitur os eius. Quia ergo hypocritarum corda propriae iustitiae fiducia turgent, et humanis traditionibus infecta sunt, quae duo Deus quam maxime odisse solet: fieri nequit vt aliud loquantur, quam quod Deo inimicum, & proinde omnibus ijs noxium est, qui illis obtemperant.
units.tr: In the present passage he confirms this admonition with a general statement: "For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." Since therefore the hearts of hypocrites swell with confidence in their own righteousness and are tainted with human traditions, which two things God is wont above all to hate, it cannot be that they speak anything other than what is hostile to God and therefore harmful to all who obey them.

units.la: At non obstat huius argumenti tractatio, quo minus hinc generale doctrinam eliciamus, cuius in vita totius institutione multiplex vsus est. Vbi primum occurrit, quod cor hominis thesauro continetur. In eo enim (vt Matth. 15. habetur) cogitationes tam bonae quam malae, omnis item generis desideria delitescunt, & idem omnium nostrorum consiliorum atque factorum fons est. Quicunque ergo vitam sanctam viuere volent, a cordis purificatione initium faciant, oportet. At hanc fide perfici, Petrus in Actis constanter docet. Et sufficit hoc ijs confutandis, qui vel inani fuco externarum ceremoniarum Deo seruiri, vel nos ex operibus iustificari sentiunt: cum opera bona facere non possimus, nisi cor prius purificatum sit fide in Christum, qui nos spiritus virtute ex femine verbi sui regenerat.
units.tr: Yet the treatment of this argument does not prevent us from drawing from it a general doctrine, which has manifold use in the whole training of life. The first point that presents itself is that the heart of man is contained in a treasury. For in it (as Matthew 15 has it) lie hidden thoughts both good and evil, and likewise desires of every kind, and it is the one source of all our counsels and actions. Therefore, whoever wishes to live a holy life must begin with the purification of the heart. And Peter in the Acts teaches constantly that this is accomplished by faith. This is enough to refute those who think that God is served by the empty show of external ceremonies, or that we are justified by works, since we cannot do good works unless the heart has first been purified by faith in Christ, who by the power of his Spirit regenerates us from the seed of his Word.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea, quo indicio tam nosipsos quam alios homines probare debeamus. Ex sermone nimirum, qui certissimus animi index est. Neque hic mihi eos aliquis obijciat, qui longe alia quam in animo tegant loquuntur. Nam horum quoque sermo animum fraudulentum & dolosum indicat, vt mendacia mendacem, blasphemiae & execratione impium, sermones spurci obscaeni & libidini deditum arguunt. Eadem est omnium aliorum affectuum ratio, quos facile ex verbis deprehendet, qui haec non osciitanter obseruauerit. In eo autem simul ingens apparet nostri ingenij corruptio. Tam enim notum est omnibus, quod modo diximus, vt gentium quoque philosophi illud nequaquam ignorauerint, qui ideo linguam fraeno coercendam esse monuerunt. Docent hoc ipsum sacrae literae, in quibus admodum memorabile est, quod Dauid dicit: Quisquis vitae cupidus es, & optas videre dies bonos: Serua linguam tuam a malo, et labia tua ne loquantur dolum. Quod ne temere dictum putaremus, Deus linguae situ nos admonere voluit, rem praecipue obseruatu cuprimis necessariam. Nec enim vllum in humano corpore membrum est, quod tot clausulis natura munierit, quot linguae opposita videmus: quae ex pectore surgens per fauces in os extenditur: vbi infra quidem mandibulis, desuper palato ceu fornice quadam, cui cerebrum impositum est, munitur, obiectos autem sibi habet dentium ordines, qui instar muri illam coerceant. Docent ista minime permittendum esse, vt temere vagetur lingua, sed prius animo concipi debere quae loquamur, & simul inter loquendum adhibendam prudentiam, quae tritum illud subinde nobis in mentem reducat, Lingua quo vadis? Adde his exempla innumera eorum, qui vel seipsos, vel patriam dulcissimam, vel amicos, imo totas gentes linguae petulantia in extremum exitium adduxerunt. Ea tamen est nostri ingenij peruersitas, vt plerique hominum nulla istorum omnium ratione habita, omnes honesti & aequi limites transiliant et ex eo non postremam voluptatem capiant, si vel maledicendo, vel mentiendo, vel do, vel turpia & obscaena loquendo animi improbitatem exaturare possunt. Non immerito igitur Apostolus linguam ἀκατάσχετον κακόν, id est, malum dixit, quod nulla ratione se coerceri sinat. Ex eo igitur apparet totius naturae nostrae corruptio, & quo loco simus, nisi aliunde nobis remedium accedat. Ex sermonibus tuis (inquit Christus) iustificaberis, & ex sermonibus tuis condemnaberis. At sermones nostros plerunque vitiosos esse nemo negaverit, nisi qui cum sensu pudorem quoque omnem abstulerit. Damnemur ergo oportet, nisi nobis Christus succurrat, in cuius lingua non est dolus, quia ei iustitiam nobis per fidem communicat. Horum itaque memores, primo quidem suas linguas singuli frenare discant: deinde aliorum sermones, & in primis eorum, qui doctores habentur, observent, neque aliquem audiant, qui nos a Christo Iesu abducere satagit, in quo uno vita & salus inveniturr. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: We are further admonished by what sign we ought to test both ourselves and other men: namely, by speech, which is the most certain index of the mind. Let no one object to me here those who say things quite different from what they hide in their minds. For their speech too reveals a deceitful and crafty mind, just as lies betray a liar, and blasphemies and curses an impious man, and foul, obscene words a man given over to lust. The same is true of all other affections, which will easily be detected from words by anyone who observes these things diligently. In this, moreover, there appears at the same time the great corruption of our nature. For it is so well known to all, as we have just said, that even the philosophers of the Gentiles were by no means ignorant of it, and for this reason they taught that the tongue must be restrained with a bridle. Holy Scripture also teaches this, and in it what David says is very memorable: "Whoever you are who desire life and wish to see good days, keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit." Lest we think this said rashly, God wished to admonish us by the very situation of the tongue, a matter especially necessary to observe. For there is no member in the human body that nature has fortified with as many barriers as we see set against the tongue: it rises from the chest and extends through the throat into the mouth, where below it is protected by the jaws and above by the palate, like a certain vault on which the brain rests, and it has in front of it the rows of teeth, which restrain it like a wall. These things teach that the tongue must not be permitted to wander rashly, but that what we say must first be conceived in the mind, and that prudence must be applied while speaking, which may from time to time bring back to our mind that well-worn saying: "Tongue, where are you going?" Add to these the countless examples of those who by the wantonness of their tongues have brought either themselves, or their dearest fatherland, or friends, or even whole nations to utter ruin. Yet such is the perversity of our nature that most people, taking no account of any of these things, leap over all the bounds of honesty and fairness, and derive no small pleasure from it if by slandering, lying, deceiving, or speaking base and obscene things they can satisfy their wickedness. Not without reason, therefore, the Apostle called the tongue an "unrestrainable evil" [ἀκατάσχετον κακόν], that is, an evil that allows itself to be restrained by no reason. From this, therefore, appears the corruption of our whole nature, and in what state we are, unless a remedy comes to us from elsewhere. "By your words," says Christ, "you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned." But no one will deny that our words are for the most part faulty, unless he has also cast off all shame along with sense. We must therefore be condemned, unless Christ comes to our aid, in whose tongue there is no deceit, because he imparts to us his righteousness through faith. Mindful of these things, let each first learn to bridle his own tongue; then let him observe the speech of others, and especially of those who are held to be teachers, and let him listen to no one who strives to draw us away from Jesus Christ, in whom alone life and salvation are found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIIII.

units.la: Quid autem vocatis me, Domine, Domine: & non facitis quae dico? Quisquis venit ad me, & audit sermones meos, & eos praestat, indicabo vobis cui sit simílis. Similis est homini aedificanti domum, qui fodit & excavavit, posuitque fundamentum super petram. Vbi autem venit inundatio, illisum est flumen domui illi, sed non potuit eam quatere: fundata enim erat super petram. Qui autem audiuit eos, nec praestitit, simílis est homini, qui aedificavit domum suam super terram absque fundamento: cui illisum est flumen: itaque statim cecidit, fuitque ruina domus illius magna.
units.tr: "But why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say? Everyone who comes to me and hears my sayings and acts on them, I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. When the flood came, the river burst against that house, but could not shake it, for it was founded on the rock. But he who heard and did not act is like a man who built his house on the ground without a foundation: against it the river burst, and at once it fell, and the ruin of that house was great."

units.la: EXpositae est hucusque concio filij Dei Iesu Christi saluberrima, qua omnem fidei & salutis nostrae rationem abunde complexus est. Primo enim adversus corrupta & falsa huius mundi iudicia offendit, in quo summum hominis bonum & vera felicitas consistant, & hanc non in terrenis & fluxis huius saeculi bonis, sed in caelestium atque aeternorum spe quaerendam esse docuit. Deinde ad Legis interpretationem accessit, & quia eorum quae ad vitam recte instituendam faciunt, compendium est dilectionis praeceptum, de hoc ita disseruit, ut ostenderit, non solum maleficia prohiberi, aut officia externa praecipi, sed ipsum animum requiri, qui a nocendi studio sive cupiditate alienissimus, adiuuandum vero & benefaciendum promptus & procliuis esse debeat: adeo ut inimicorum quoque saluti consultum esse cupiamus. Quod cum de omnibus praeceptis intelligi debeat, quae similiter hominem totum, quoad animum & corpus, Deo in obsequium vendicant, satis appareret, neminem esse mortalium, qui Legem suis viribus praestare possit, & proinde nobis alia iustitia & satisfactione opus esse, ea nimirum, quam nobis Deus per filium suum in Iesu Christo offert, & quae per solam fidem apprehenditur. At quia hanc praepostera Legis interpretatione & falsae doctrinae traditionibus Pharisaei & Scribae obscurabant, vel potius evertebant, tertio loco de illis cavendis admonitionem grauem & diligentem interposuit, quam nuper audiuimus. Sequitur nunc totius concionis conclusio, qua graviter admodum docet, haec non consilia modo esse (ut Sophistae nostrorum operum atque meritorum assertores nugantur) sed praecepta seria, quibus necessario omnes eos obedire oporteat, qui seruari velint. Continet ergo locus iste doctrinam utilissimam & nostri saeculi hominibus in primis necessariam, atque ideo dignam, in cuius consideratione non ociosanter versemur.
units.tr: Up to this point the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has set out a most wholesome sermon, which has fully embraced the whole account of our faith and salvation. First, he struck against the corrupt and false judgments of this world, about where the chief good and true happiness of man lie, and he taught that this happiness is to be sought not in the earthly and fleeting goods of this age but in the hope of heavenly and eternal things. Next he turned to the interpretation of the Law. Since the precept of love is the summary of what helps to order life rightly, he discoursed on it in such a way as to show that not only are wrongdoings forbidden and outward duties commanded, but that the heart itself is required, which must be utterly remote from any desire or eagerness to harm, and must be ready and inclined to help and to do good, so that we also wish for the welfare of our enemies. Since this must be understood of all the precepts, which likewise claim the whole man, both soul and body, for the obedience of God, it was plain enough that no mortal can fulfil the Law by his own strength, and that we therefore need another righteousness and satisfaction, namely the one which God offers us through his Son Jesus Christ, and which is laid hold of by faith alone. But because the Pharisees and Scribes were obscuring, or rather overturning, this by their perverse interpretation of the Law and by the traditions of false doctrine, he placed in the third part a grave and diligent warning about avoiding them, which we heard recently. Now follows the conclusion of the whole sermon, in which he teaches most seriously that these are not merely counsels (as the sophists, the champions of our works and merits, trifle), but serious precepts, which all who wish to be saved must necessarily obey. This passage therefore contains a most useful doctrine, especially necessary for the people of our age, and so worthy that we should not consider it idly.

units.la: Propositio & summa est: Neminem ipsius seruum aut discipulum, atque salutis in ipso exhibitae cohortem fore, nisi qui praeceptis ipsius obedierit. Et ut maius orationi pondus accedat, interrogationem illam figurat, & ad eos conuersus, qui ipsum magistrum & dominum suum profitebantur, ait: Quid autem vocatis me, Domine, Domine: & non facitis quae dico? Habent ergo haec indignantis speciem, qua non sine stomacho inanem & fucatam fidei professionem reijcit. Hoc ipsum tamen Matthaeus septimo Capite prolixius exponit his verbis: Non quisquis dicit mihi Domine, Domine, introibit in regnum caelorum, sed qui facit quod vult Pater meus, qui in caelis est. Multi dicent mihi in illo die: Domine Domine, nonne per nomen tuum prophetauimus, & per nomen tuum daemonia eiecimus, & per nomen tuum multas virtutes edidimus? Tunc autem profitebor eis: Nunquam noui vos: discedite à me qui facitis iniquitatem. Quod ergo in praesenti ait: Quid vocatis me, Domine Domine, & non facitis quae dico? Hoc apud Matthaeum sic enuntiat: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine Domine, introibit in regnum caelorum: sed qui facit quod vult Pater meus, &c. Unde colligimus, doctrinam Christi eandem esse cum voluntate Patris, adeoq; illum huius esse interpretem. Quod apud Ioannem apertius docet, cùm ait: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed Patris qui me misit. In praesenti autem non obscurè admonet, quando Euangelium in orbe praedicatur, nunquam defuturos esse, qui ad illud animo fucato, & à fide vera alieno accedant, quique intra animos ipsorum latentem impietatem ementita nominis Christiani professione pallient. Et quia huius mali fere praecipui authores sunt falsi antistites, quorum vita atq; mores doctrinae minus respondent, quiq; sua licentia rudes & imperitos seducunt, in Matthaeo aduersus hos in primis orationem dirigit, quam hic in genere adomnes extendit.
units.tr: The proposition and summary is this: no one will be his servant or disciple, or a sharer in the salvation offered in him, unless he obeys his precepts. And so that his words may carry more weight, he gives the question a form and, turning to those who professed him as their teacher and Lord, says: "But why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?" These words therefore have the appearance of indignation, by which he rejects, not without displeasure, an empty and feigned profession of faith. Yet Matthew explains this same point more fully in chapter seven, in these words: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? Then I will declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity." What he here says, "Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?", he expresses in Matthew thus: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father," and so on. From this we gather that the doctrine of Christ is the same as the will of the Father, and that he is therefore its interpreter. John teaches this more plainly when he says: "My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me." Here, however, he warns without obscurity that, wherever the gospel is preached in the world, there will never be lacking those who approach it with a feigned mind and far from true faith, and who, under the pretended profession of the Christian name, cloak the impiety lying hidden in their hearts. And since the chief authors of this evil are generally the false leaders, whose life and morals agree less with their doctrine, and who by their licence lead astray the untaught and unskilled, in Matthew he directs his speech especially against these, though here he extends it generally to all.

units.la: Docet autem hoc loco Dei Filius Christianismum seu religionem Christianam non in externa fidei professione aut qualibuscunq; aliis rebus externis consistere, sed in praeceptorum Dei & voluntatis eius observatione. Nominantur enim apud Matthaeum ex ordine, quaecunq; in ecclesia semper maximi momenti fuerunt. Primum prophetia, id est, ordinaria verbi Dei praedicatio: qua nihil salutarius & magis necessarium, quamq; Paulus cognitioni linguarum & omnibus donis spiritualibus, quorum in ecclesia administratione vsus est, praeferre consueuit. Deinde daemoniorum profligatio siue eiectio, quam proprium Christi opus esse constat, cùm ideo ille in mundum venerit, ut caput veteris serpentis conteret, & opera diaboli destruat. Coniungit his virtutes, quibus tota aedendorum miraculorum facultas comprehenditur. Et ne de iis loqui videatur, quae per magicas artes & media illicita fiunt, diserte eorum meminit, quae in nomine Iesu Christi fiunt. Neque illos falsi arguit, aut quòd mendaci iactantia se ostentent: sed haec omnia illos fecisse concedit. Possunt enim Verbum Dei praedicare, qui fide vera destituuntur, imò multos horum prae aliis facundia & interpretandi facultate instructos esse videmus: quod de suis quoque aemulis Paulus non uno loco fatetur. Ita in Christi nomine daemonia eiecit, & infinita alia miracula fecit Iudas proditor, cuius vestigia posteris temporibus multi alij secuti sunt. Et permittit hoc Christus, ut eò luculentior sit ipsius virtus, quando in iis etiam se exerit, qui nomen ipsius abs fide praetexunt. Quid verò de omnibus illis idem dicit? Nunquam noui vos, id est, nunquam pro meis ego vos habui, neque estis ex electorum meorum numero. Ideo procul à me facessite, qui facitis iniquitatem. Qui enim germani Christi discipuli sunt, ij eiusdem spiritu aguntur, qui illos iniquitatis operarios siue mancipia esse non sinit. Quòd si vero ista non utuntur, quae absque peculiari spiritus operatione non fiunt, quid obsecro de nudis & inanibus ceremonijs dicemus, quae in sola corporis exercitatione consistunt, quam Paulus cum vera pietate conferens, ad nihil utilem esse ait? Potest hoc Prophetarum testimonijs probari, apud quos Deus frequenter circuncisionem, dies festos, coetus & sacrificia, adeoque omnes Leuitici cultus ceremonias, quas ipse in Lege tradiderat, reijcit, eò quòd circa has occupati verae pietatis officia negligerent, & manus sanguine pollutas ad ipsum extenderent. Et ad Christi verba Apostolus respicere videtur, quando in posteriori ad Timotheum ait: Novit Dominus qui sint sui: & discedat ab iniquitate omnis, qui nominat nomen Christi. Ex quibus colligimus voluntatis Dei & praeceptorum eius observationem necessariam esse omnibus, qui Christi discipuli censeri volunt. Nam qui illam negligunt, ij oris proprij professione conuincuntur. Olim Deus per Malachiam Iudaeis ipso patre et domino gloriantibus dicebat: Filius honorat patrem, & serus dominum suum. Si ergo ego pater sum, ubi honor est meus? Si dominus sum vester, ubi metus? Idem ergo ijs dicetur, qui Christo domino & seruatore gloriantur. Si me Dei filium agnoscitis, cur non debito honore me prosequimini? Si me vestrum redemptorem & dominum profitemini, cur non mihi obeditis? Si item Mediator ille sum, qui vos cum patre in gratiam reduxi, cur non huius voluntati obeditis? Et quamuis ista non semper auribus nostris Christus ingerat, cogitemus tamen ad nos pertinere quaecunque olim alijs in hanc sententiam dicta sunt, neque extinguamus Spiritus sancti suggestiones, quibus hic nobis aurem vellicat & officij admonet. Meminerimus item, itẽ, quàm graue olim futurum sit, si hæc nobis exprobrantem Christum audiemus, quando ab eius ore vniuersa corporum & animarum nostrarum salus pendebit.
units.tr: Here the Son of God teaches that Christianity, or the Christian religion, consists not in outward profession of faith or in any other outward things, but in the observance of God's precepts and will. For in Matthew there are named, in order, the things which have always been of greatest importance in the Church. First, prophecy, that is, the ordinary preaching of God's Word, than which nothing is more wholesome or more necessary, and which Paul was accustomed to prefer to the knowledge of tongues and to all the spiritual gifts that he used in the administration of the Church. Next, the casting out or expulsion of demons, which is plainly the proper work of Christ, since he came into the world for this reason, that he might crush the head of the old serpent and destroy the works of the devil. He joins to these the mighty works, by which the whole power of working miracles is comprehended. And lest he seem to speak of those things which are done by magical arts and unlawful means, he expressly mentions those done in the name of Jesus Christ. Nor does he accuse them of falsehood, or of showing off with lying boasting, but he concedes that they did all these things. For those who lack true faith may preach the Word of God; indeed we see that many of them are, above others, endowed with eloquence and the skill of interpreting, which Paul also confesses of his own rivals in more than one place. So Judas the traitor cast out demons in the name of Christ and worked countless other miracles, and many others in later times have followed his footsteps. Christ permits this so that his power may shine out the more clearly, when it is exercised even through those who pretend the name of Christ without faith. But what does he say to all these men? "I never knew you," that is, I never regarded you as mine, nor are you of the number of my elect. "Therefore depart from me, you who work iniquity." For those who are the true disciples of Christ are moved by the same Spirit, who does not allow them to be workers or slaves of iniquity. But if these men do not practise those things which are not done without a special working of the Spirit, what, I beseech you, shall we say of bare and empty ceremonies, which consist in bodily exercise alone, and which Paul, comparing them with true godliness, says are of no use? This can be proved by the testimonies of the Prophets, among whom God often rejects circumcision, festal days, assemblies and sacrifices, and indeed all the ceremonies of Levitical worship which he himself had delivered in the Law, because those who were occupied with these neglected the duties of true godliness and stretched out hands polluted with blood to him. And the Apostle seems to have Christ's words in view when he says in the second letter to Timothy: "The Lord knows those who are his, and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity." From these things we gather that the observance of God's will and precepts is necessary for all who wish to be counted as Christ's disciples. For those who neglect it are convicted by their own profession. Long ago God, through Malachi, said to the Jews, who boasted of their father and lord: "A son honours his father, and a servant his lord. If then I am a father, where is my honour? If I am your Lord, where is my fear?" The same will therefore be said to those who boast in Christ as their Lord and Saviour. If you acknowledge me as the Son of God, why do you not pay me due honour? If you profess me as your Redeemer and Lord, why do you not obey me? If I am also that Mediator who reconciled you with the Father, why do you not obey his will? And although Christ does not always press these things upon our ears, let us nevertheless consider that whatever was said long ago to others to this effect pertains to us too, and let us not quench the promptings of the Holy Spirit, by which he here plucks our ear and admonishes us of our duty. Let us also remember how grievous it will one day be, if we hear Christ reproaching us with these things, when the whole salvation of our bodies and souls will hang upon his mouth.

units.la: Interim scandalo etiam medetur hic locus, quod ex eorum defectione aut consumacia nascitur, qui in ecclesia primatum tenent, & illius columnæ esse videntur. Est hoc obseruatu non minus necessarium quàm vtile. Nam si quid illi praeter officium & à fidei professione alienum faciunt, mox diuersa hominum iudicia audire licet. Alij enim, qui doctrinam de fide in Christum hostiliter oderunt, ex illorum exemplo occasionem arripiunt, qua religionem Christianam proscindunt, & quæ de illa in sacris literis traduntur, dicacitate plus quàm scurrili in dubium vocant. Alij verò non mali, sed tamen rudiores adhuc & rerum imperiti, exemplis eiusmodi offensi, partim ipsi quoq; dubitare incipiunt, partim suæ saluti metuunt, & vix sibi certum quid de sua perseuerantia polliceri possunt, quando eos tam parum sui officij memores esse vident, qui præcipuam doctrinæ & fidei existimationem in Ecclesia sustinent, & quorum opera Deus aliquando in regno suo propagando non infeliciter ẽt vsus. Sed tunc nobis in mentem veniat, Deum etiam malis & improbis bene uti posse, & ministerij efficaciam minimè ab hominum dignitate pendere. Neq; nobis talium lapsus terrorem aut propriæ salutis dubitationem incutere debet: quando ex illo constat, eos nunquam ex electorum Dei numero fuisse, neque Christum illos pro ecclesiæ suæ membris vnquam agnouisse. Nam buius oues de manu eius nemo potest rapere: & si ex nobis illi essent (vt cum Ioanne loquamur) vti, nobiscum manerent, &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile this passage also heals a scandal that arises from the defection or obstinacy of those who hold the leading place in the Church and seem to be its pillars. This is to be observed no less for its necessity than for its usefulness. For if they do anything beyond their office and foreign to the profession of faith, various judgments of men are soon to be heard. Others, who bitterly hate the doctrine of faith in Christ, seize the occasion from their example to tear apart the Christian religion, and with more than buffoonish wit they call into doubt what is handed down about it in the sacred letters. Others, not wicked but still ruder and inexperienced in affairs, offended by examples of this kind, partly begin to doubt themselves and partly fear for their salvation, and can scarcely promise themselves anything certain about their perseverance, when they see that those who maintain the chief esteem of doctrine and faith in the Church are so little mindful of their duty, and through whose labour God has at times not unhappily made use in propagating his kingdom. But let it come to mind then that God can make good use even of evil and wicked men, and that the efficacy of the ministry does not at all depend on the dignity of men. Nor should the fall of such men strike terror into us or cast doubt upon our own salvation, since it is clear from this that they never belonged to the number of God's elect, nor did Christ ever acknowledge them as members of his Church. For no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand; and if they had been of us (to speak with John), they would have remained with us, etc.

units.la: Caterum vt verborum Christi sensum rectius intelligamus, probè tenere oportet, quæ nam illa Patris voluntas sit, quam cum illius doctrina siue mandatis eandem esse supra diximus. Exponit huius summam paucis verbis Ioannes Apostolus, sic scribens: Hoc est præceptum eius, vt credamus nomini filij eius Iesu Christi, & diligamus alij alios, sicut mandauit nobis. Duobus ergo capitibus tota Christi doctrina & Patris voluntas comprehenditur. Primum fides est, qua Christum apprehendimus. Docet hoc ipse, Ioannis sexto cap. quando hoc opus Dei vocat, vt in eum credamus quem ille misit. Et paulò post apertius ait: Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui videt Filium & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Consentit his Ioannes Baptista, qui cæcam discipulorum suorum æmulationem, qua aduersus Christum accensi erant multis corripiens inter alia dicit: Is què misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur: non enim huic admetitur Deus spiritum. Pater diligit Filium, & omnia dedit in manum eius. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam. Qui verò non paret Filio, non videbit vitam: sed ira Dei manet super eum. Neq; ista ex suo cerebro tam grauiter Ioannes pronuntiat. Audiuerat enim Dei Patris vocem, quæ cœlitus intonuerat: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum: hunc audite. Porrò definit veram fidem Apostolus, quando præceptum Dei esse ait, vt credamus nomini filij eius Iesu Christi, id est, si talem esse credamus, qualis nomine suo describitur, & verbo prædicatur. Nomen Filij Dei in carne manifestati est Iesus Christus. Iesus seruatorem significat: & huius nominis rationem reddit Angelus, quòd populum suum seruet à peccatis ipsorum. Christi autem Vnctii vox modum salutis exprimit: Quòd nimirum Rex & Sacerdos corporis & sanguinis sui sacrificio peccata mundi expiarit, & placata Dei ira iustitiam reduxerit sempiternam: quodque hostem nostrum diabolum deuicerit, inferos debellarit, cœlos nobis patefecerit, denique nos asseruerit in filiorum Dei libertatem. Qui illum ita agnoscunt vera & constanti fide, ij nomini eius credere dicuntur. Et cum fide hac totus Dei cultus coniunctus est, tam internus quàm externus. Nam qui sic credunt, ij intra animos suos purificati, Deum in spiritu & veritate adorant, & simul sacra externa omnia secundùm eius voluntatem, quam in Verbo suo manifestauit, instituunt. Etsi ergo Christus hoc loco de solis operibus externis loqui videatur, quæ ad mores & vitæ conuersationem pertinent, nõ excludit tamen fidem: sed hanc in primis exigit, vt quæ voluntatis Patris sui præcipuum caput, vitæ autem Christianæ principium atq; bonorum operum fons est. Hoc quia multi non obseruant, de solis operibus tumultuantur, & dum Christiani veri haberi volunt, Christum gloria sua spoliant. Præ alijs verò hic offendunt Anabaptistæ, qui cum iustificationis doctrinam minimè intelligant, & proinde circa externa sola occupentur, mox ab Ecclesijs discedunt, in quibus non omnia pro suo arbitrio fieri vident, & quasi omnis Ecclesiarum salus in excommunicatione consistat, pro hac vna pugnant: dumque ecclesiam fingunt numeris omnibus absolutissimam, ecclesias quidem omnes scindunt & turbant, ipsi vero nullam constituunt, sed erronum & cerebrosorum hominum conuenticula ecclesiae nomine palliant, & ita fucum faciunt imperitis, qui in fide Christi nondum recte instituti sunt. Probe ergo teneamus, primum voluntatis Dei & doctrinae Christi caput esse fidem, & proinde non abo-peribus, sed ab illa nobis incipiendum esse, si Deo probari velimus. Nam sine fide fieri non potest, ut quis illi placeat, eo quod quicquid sine fide fit, peccatum est. Vide Hebraeorum vndecimo, Romanorum decimoquarto. Alterum caput est diuinae voluntatis, ut alij alios diligamus, sicut mandauit nobis. At dilectionis verae exemplum in semetipso nobis ille proposuit, qui ita dilexit nos, ut pro nobis mori voluerit: & tunc quidem, quando filij irae & inimici eramus. Porro dilectione omnia alia legis praecepta comprehendi, iam ante diximus: & quia eadem proximum (ut Paulus ait) non afficit malo, & vitam omnem prorsus innocuam reddit, consummatio Legis non immerito dicitur. Et haec illa sunt, quae in Euangelio Christus vbique praecipit: neque prolixa locorum recitatione opus est, cum scripturas legentibus passim occurrant. Sufficiat nobis, quod de praecipuo mandatorum Dei a Scriba quodam interrogatus, respondit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua. Illud est primum & magnum mandatum. Secundum autem simile est huic: Diliges proximum tuum, vt teipsum. Qui ergo haec faciunt, ij patris voluntatem faciunt, quam nobis Christus tradidit. At qui ista negligunt, Christiani autem nihilominus dici volunt, ijs in praesenti ille loquitur, & ijsdem falsam nominis sui professionem exprobrat.
units.tr: But that we may understand the meaning of Christ's words more rightly, we must hold firmly what that will of the Father is, which we said above is the same as his teaching or commandments. The Apostle John sets out its sum in a few words, writing thus: "This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he has commanded us" (1 John 3:23). The whole doctrine of Christ and the will of the Father are therefore comprehended under two heads. The first is faith, by which we lay hold of Christ. He teaches this himself in John chapter 6, when he calls this the work of God, that we believe in him whom he has sent. And a little later he says more plainly: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life" (John 6:40). John the Baptist agrees with these words, who, rebuking among other things the blind rivalry of his disciples, by which they were inflamed against Christ, says: "He whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God does not give him the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3:34–36). Nor does John pronounce these things so weightily from his own brain. For he had heard the voice of God the Father, which had thundered from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him" (Matt. 17:5). Moreover, the Apostle defines true faith when he says it is the commandment of God that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, that is, that we believe him to be such as his name describes and his Word proclaims. The name of the Son of God manifested in the flesh is Jesus Christ. Jesus signifies Saviour, and the Angel gives the reason for this name, namely that he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). The word Christ, the Anointed One, expresses the manner of salvation: that as King and Priest he atoned for the sins of the world by the sacrifice of his body and blood, and having appeased the wrath of God restored everlasting righteousness; that he overcame our enemy the devil, vanquished the depths, opened heaven to us, and finally asserted us into the liberty of the sons of God. Those who acknowledge him in this way with a true and steadfast faith are said to believe in his name. And with this faith the whole worship of God is joined, both inward and outward. For those who so believe, being purified within their minds, worship God in spirit and in truth, and at the same time institute all external rites according to his will, which he has made known in his Word. So although Christ here seems to speak only of the external works that pertain to manners and the conduct of life, he does not exclude faith; rather he requires it first of all, as the chief head of his Father's will and the beginning of the Christian life and the fountain of good works. Because many do not observe this, they make an uproar about works alone, and while they wish to be held true Christians, they despoil Christ of his glory. Above others, the Anabaptists stumble here, who, since they do not understand the doctrine of justification, and therefore occupy themselves with external matters alone, soon depart from the Churches in which they see that not everything is done at their own pleasure; and as if the whole safety of the Churches consisted in excommunication, they fight for this one thing alone. And while they imagine a Church most absolute in every respect, they indeed split and disturb all the Churches, yet they themselves constitute none, but cloak the conventicles of erring and crazed men with the name of Church, and so they deceive the inexperienced, who are not yet rightly instructed in the faith of Christ. Let us therefore hold firmly that the first head of God's will and of Christ's doctrine is faith, and that we must therefore begin not from works but from that, if we wish to please God. For without faith it is impossible for anyone to please him, because whatever is done without faith is sin. See Hebrews 11 and Romans 14. The second head of the divine will is that we love one another, as he has commanded us. But he has set before us in himself the example of true love, who so loved us that he was willing to die for us, and that when we were children of wrath and enemies. Moreover, we said before that all the other precepts of the law are comprehended in love; and because love (as Paul says) does no harm to the neighbour and makes the whole of life wholly harmless, it is not unfairly called the fulfilling of the Law (Rom. 13:10). And these are the things Christ everywhere commands in the Gospel; nor is there need of a lengthy recital of passages, since they occur everywhere to those who read the Scriptures. It is enough for us that, when a certain scribe asked him about the chief of God's commandments, he answered: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself" (Matt. 22:37–39). Those therefore who do these things do the will of the Father, which Christ has delivered to us. But those who neglect these things, and yet nonetheless wish to be called Christians, are the ones he now addresses, and he upbraids them with the false profession of his name.

units.la: Porro vt magis excitet nos, rem hanc fusius exponit, & duo facit auditorum Euangelij genera: alterum eorum, qui illud cum fide & serio discendi studio audiunt: alterum eorum, qui (vt apud prophetam dicitur) ore appropinquant, corde autem procul absunt, & proinde nihil in vera pietate proficiunt: simul, quid utrosque maneat docet. Vtitur autem parabola ab aedificantibus sumpta, quae in sacris literis frequens est. Nam & Paulus nos Dei aedificationem esse dicit, & Petrus graviter monet, vt supra Christum, qui vivus ille & pretiosus lapis est, ipsi quoque vivi lapides aedificemur in domum spiritualem & sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias Deo acceptas per Iesum Christum. Videtur autem in praesenti eandem parabolam proponere Christus, vt simul infelicem hominum socordiam arguat, qui cum in extruendis terrenis aedificiis, quae ad huius modo vitae vsum faciunt, tam industrij & providi sint, tamen securi nimis ea negligunt, quae ad sanctum illud & spirituale aedificium pertinent, sine quo aeterna hominis salus consistere non potest. Summa enim & sensus parabolae est: Euangelij professionem inutilem, imo periculosam esse, nisi illius doctrina intra animos nostros radices profundas agat, vt vero salutis fundamento innixi fructus bonos faciamus, & ad omnem euentum in fide fortes & inconcussi stemus.
units.tr: Moreover, to stir us up the more, he expounds this matter at greater length, and makes two kinds of hearers of the Gospel: one of those who hear it with faith and a serious zeal for learning; the other of those who (as is said in the prophet) draw near with their mouths but are far from God in their hearts, and therefore make no progress in true piety. At the same time he teaches what awaits each. He uses a parable taken from builders, which is frequent in the sacred letters. For Paul also says that we are God's building, and Peter earnestly admonishes that we too, as living stones, be built up into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ, resting upon Christ, who is that living and precious stone. Now Christ seems here to set forth the same parable, so that at the same time he may rebuke the unhappy sluggishness of men, who, though they are so diligent and provident in erecting earthly buildings, which serve the use of this present life, are nonetheless too careless in neglecting those things that pertain to that holy and spiritual building, without which the eternal salvation of man cannot stand. For the sum and sense of the parable is this: that the profession of the Gospel is useless, indeed dangerous, unless its doctrine takes deep roots within our minds, so that, resting on the foundation of salvation, we may bring forth good fruits, and stand strong and unshaken in faith whatever the outcome.

units.la: De vere pijs & industrijs auditoribus sic loquitur: Quisquis venit ad me, & audit sermones meos, et eos praestat, indicabo vobis cui sit similis. Similis est homini aedificanti domum, qui fodit & excauauit, posuitque fundamentum super petram. Vbi autem venit inundatio, illisum est flumen domui illi, sed non potuit eam quatere: fundata enim erat supra petram. Quo loco de duobus nos admonet. Primo studia & mores eorum describit, qui Verbum Euangelij recte audiunt. Vbi primum est, quod illos fodere & excauare dicit. Ita vero innuit, illos non obiter modo audire, & eorum quae dicuntur sonum auribus solis capere, sed eadem in ipsos animos demittere: quos simul diligentius scrutentur & expurgent, vt verbo in illis locus sit. Vt enim qui domum nouam extruere instituerunt, ante omnia ipsam aedificij futuri aream praeparant, rudera vetera demoliuntur, cumque his terram quoq; egerunt, & eo vsq; fodiunt, donec solidum quid inueniant, cui aedificium totum tuto inniti possit. Ita cum in nobis multae sint superstitionis veteris vel cognatae nobis malitiae reliquiae, quae nos a Deo abducunt, nunquam poterimus in animis nostris domum illam spiritualem aedificare, quam ille inhabitet, nisi a diligenti & laborioso examine initium fiat, quo ipsos animos nostros & corda scrutemur, & eiectis omnibus verae pietatis impedimentis, verbu imis cordibus reconditum probe asseruemus: vt infra in sementis parabola amplius dicetur. Quod vt fiat, necesse est, vt administri verbi auditores adiuuent, & ipsi in eorum animos altius penetrent arguendo ea, quae illi alias in seipsis vix agnoscunt. agnoscant. Deinde veri illi & germani euangelicæ doctrinæ auditores fundamentum ponunt super petram. Loquitur autem de æternæ salutis fundamento, seipso nimirum, quem Paulus postea funda mentum prophetarum & apostolorum dixit, eo quòd tam hi quàm illi salutem hominum in nullo alio inueniri docuerunt. Apud Isaiam enim sic ait Dominus: Ecce ego fundo in Zione lapidem, lapi- dem probationis, angularem, pretiosum, solidissimum fundamentum: quisquis credit in eum, non pudefiet. Et Petrus Apostolus, cui ex huius petræ confessione nomen impositum fuit, in Hierosolymitano Senatu Isaiæ locum de Christo interpretans, in communi omnium apostolorum persona ait: Hic est lapis ille pro nihilo habitus à vobis ædificantibus, qui factus est caput anguli: neque est in alio quoquam salus. Nec enim aliud nomen est sub cœlo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Et eòdem pertinent, quæ idem Apostolus de hoc unico fidei & salutis nostræ fundamento in prioris epistolæ suæ cap. secundo prolixè disputat. At in Christi verbis obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd germanos doctrinæ suæ auditores magno quidem studio & industria fodere atque excauare dicit, ut omnia veræ pietatis obstacula remoueant, sicq; totos in Dei obsequium consecrent: eosdem verò totius ædificij sui, id est, pietatis & salutis æternæ fundamentum non supra sua opera aut sui ingenij vires, sed supra petram ponere testatur: eam videlicet, quam illum ipsum esse modò demonstrauimus. Vides ergo nihil facere eos, qui vel perfunctorie & quasi aliud agentes verbum audiunt, vel salutis fundamentum aliud extra ipsum quærunt. Nam ut priores illi verbi semen nunquam intra animos suos admittunt, & proinde ex eodem non possunt renasci: ita istiius nili labore seipsos fatigant cùm (ut Paulus ait) nemo possit aliud fundamentum ponere, quàm quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. 1. Cor. 3.
units.tr: Concerning those who are truly pious and diligent hearers, he speaks thus: "Whoever comes to me and hears my sayings and does them, I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation upon the rock. But when the flood came, the river beat against that house, yet could not shake it, for it was founded upon the rock." In this passage he admonishes us on two points. First, he describes the zeal and conduct of those who rightly hear the Word of the Gospel. Here, first of all, is that he says they dig and hollow out. By this he indicates that they do not merely hear in passing, catching only the sound of what is said with their ears, but that they sink these things down into their very souls, examining and cleansing them more carefully so that the Word may find a place in them. Just as those who set out to build a new house first prepare the site of the future building, pull down the old rubble, carry away the earth as well, and dig until they find something solid on which the whole structure can safely rest, so, since many remnants of old superstition, or of the wickedness akin to our nature, are in us and draw us away from God, we can never build that spiritual house in our souls in which he may dwell, unless a diligent and laborious examination is begun, by which we search our minds and hearts, and, once every hindrance to true piety has been removed, firmly establish the Word hidden deep in our hearts, as will be said more fully below in the parable of the sower. For this to happen, it is necessary that the ministers of the Word help the hearers and themselves penetrate deeper into their minds, by reproving what they scarcely recognise in themselves. Then those true and genuine hearers of the evangelical doctrine lay the foundation upon the rock. He speaks, however, of the foundation of eternal salvation, namely Christ himself, whom Paul later called the foundation of the prophets and apostles, because both they and he taught that the salvation of men is found in no other. For the Lord says through Isaiah: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a most solid foundation; whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." And the apostle Peter, to whom the name was given because of his confession of this rock, interpreting Isaiah's passage about Christ before the Jerusalem council, speaks in the name of all the apostles: "This is the stone which was set at nought by you builders, which has become the head of the corner; neither is there salvation in any other. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." The same applies to what the same apostle argues at length about this sole foundation of our faith and salvation in the second chapter of his first epistle. But in the words of Christ the most noteworthy point is that he says his true hearers dig and hollow out with great zeal and industry, so that they remove every obstacle to true piety and so wholly consecrate themselves to the service of God; but he declares that these same hearers lay the foundation of the whole of their building, that is, of piety and eternal salvation, not upon their own works or the powers of their own wit, but upon the rock, namely that which we have just shown to be Christ himself. You see, then, that those accomplish nothing who hear the Word carelessly and as if doing something else, or who seek the foundation of salvation anywhere outside it. For just as the former never admit the seed of the Word into their minds, and therefore cannot be born again through it, so the latter weary themselves to no purpose, since (as Paul says) no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. 1 Cor. 3.

units.la: Alterum, de quo nos in præsenti Dominus admonet, est studij huius & industriæ piorum fructus. Vbi (inquit) venit inundatio, illisum est flumen domui illi, sed non potuit eam quatere, &c. Per inundationem & flumen omnis generis tentationes intelligit, quibus piorum fides oppugnatur quàm primum illi Christo nomen dant. Mox enim falsos doctores Satan excitat, qui ut singulis negotium faciunt, ita ecclesias totas turbant & scindunt. Obstrepit præterea illis mundi exemplum, neque desunt, qui blandis et artificiosis sermonibus illos monent, ne soli sapere velint præ aliis, ne à ciuibus, vicinis, amicis, cognatis remere secessionem faciant. Aries quoq; in oppugnanda fide validissimus est eorum felicitas, qui Christi doctrinæ aduersantur. In primis autem terrificæ sunt persecutionum procellæ, quas ceu ex Æoli antro summa vi excitant, qui ut superstitiones suas, aut quiduis agendi licentiam tueantur, Euangelij lucem extinctam volunt. At nihil horum eos vincere potest, qui ex verbi semine verè renati, certa salutis æternæ fiducia Christo nituntur. Nec enim falsæ doctrinæ tenebris decipi possunt, qui lucem in Christo habent, quæ omnibus tenebris diffugiendis sufficit; neq; mundi exemplo mouentur, qui se ex mundo hoc selectos esse norunt, & quorum sapientia Christus est. Cur verò impiorum felicitas eosdem offendat, quam incertam, momentaneam & tristissimis casibus obnoxiam esse omnes fatentur, qui res huius seculi propius inspiciunt? Durum quidem & difficile est, è solo natali in exilium eijci, incarceres abduci, regum & antistitum odijs infestari, summa iudicum authoritate damnari, vitam crudeli & infami iudicio finire, aut inopem, nudum, famelicum incertis sedibus oberrare. Sed neque ista Christianos homines ex statione sua deijciunt. Sciunt enim nihil ipsis fortuitum accidere. sciunt se sub Dei protectione esse, qui innocentiam ipsorum afferere possit, patriam verò nos in cœlis habere, & olim admirabilem fore rerum vicissitudinem, ut nimirum ipsi cum Christo beati viuant & regnent, miserè interim & nequicquam apud inferos eiulantibus ijs omnibus, qui Christo se opponere & Ecclesiam eius persequi ausi sunt. Horum igitur certa fiducia freti in omnibus aduersis plus quàm victores sunt, neque aliquid est, quod eos separare possit à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Vide Romanorum octauo.
units.tr: The other point on which the Lord now admonishes us concerns the fruit of this zeal and industry of the godly. "When the flood came," he says, "the river beat against that house, but could not shake it," and so on. By the flood and the river he means every kind of temptation by which the faith of the godly is assailed as soon as they give their name to Christ. For Satan soon stirs up false teachers, who attack individuals and also throw whole congregations into turmoil and division. Besides, the example of the world clamours against them, and there are not lacking those who with smooth and crafty words warn them not to want to be wise alone before others, and not to secede rashly from their fellow citizens, neighbours, friends and kinsfolk. The battering ram most powerful against the faith is the prosperity of those who oppose the doctrine of Christ. Above all, the storms of persecution are terrifying, which they stir up with great violence as if from the cave of Aeolus, wishing the light of the Gospel extinguished so that they may defend their superstitions or their freedom to do whatever they please. But none of these can overcome those who, truly born again from the seed of the Word, rest upon Christ with a sure confidence of eternal salvation. For those who have the light in Christ, which is enough to drive away all darkness, cannot be deceived by the shadows of false doctrine; nor are they moved by the example of the world, since they know that they have been chosen out of this world, and their wisdom is Christ. But why should the prosperity of the wicked offend them, since all who look more closely at the affairs of this age admit that it is uncertain, fleeting and liable to the most grievous reverses? It is indeed hard and difficult to be cast out of one's native land into exile, to be led off to prison, to be harassed by the hatred of kings and bishops, to be condemned by the supreme authority of judges, to end one's life by a cruel and infamous sentence, or to wander poor, naked and hungry without any fixed abode. But not even these things cast Christian men from their station. For they know that nothing happens to them by chance; they know that they are under the protection of God, who can vindicate their innocence; and they know that we have our homeland in heaven, and that one day there will be a wonderful reversal of fortunes, so that they themselves will live and reign blessedly with Christ, while all those who dared to oppose Christ and persecute his Church wail wretchedly and in vain in hell. Therefore, relying on the sure confidence of these things, they are more than conquerors in all adversities, and there is nothing that can separate them from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. See Romans 8.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alterum genus auditorum, quod hypocritas & otiosos simulatores habet, qui verbum audiunt quidem, nihil autem eorum præstant, quæ veros Christi cultores decent. Eos similes dicit eorum, qui domum suam absque fundamento ædificant super terram. Nam si in illis radices ageret verbum Domini, & fundamento vero niterentur, præstarent procul dubio ea, quæ cum vera nominis Christiani professione coniuncta sunt. Quid ergo faciunt? Audiunt quidem verbum, sed obiter, & tantum consuetudinis ergo, ne prorsus atheos & ab omni pietate aut religione alie ni videantur. Deinde super terram aedificant, id est, non nisi terrena quaerunt, neque corda sua eo vsque scrutantur, vt carnem & huius studia abnegent, mortificent atque abijciant. Itaq; fidem & huius professionem cum Epicuraeo Dei contemptu & effreni morum licentia coniungi posse existimant. Quid vero fit? Aedificant etiam ipsi, & domum carnis iudicio speciosam extruunt. Nam ieiunijs, preculis, sacrificijs, vestitu superstitioso, gestibus & ceremonijs externis ita se ostentant, vt quantius pretij videri possint. Sed haec omnia (vt propheta ait) instar nubecula matutina & roris sunt, neque diu possunt subsistere. Quia enim mundus hic neque pietatem veram, neque eius professionem ferre potest, mox illos etiam inundatio & tentationum omnis generis fluuij oppugnant. Quod si fiat, nihil apud illos solidum & stabile habetur. Nam quia nulla apud eos est solida Christi cognitio, incerti fluctuant, & quouis doctrinae vento hinc inde agitantur. Exemplum vero mundi huius non possunt non magni facere, cum toti ab huius iudicio pendeant. Eadem est felicitatis & successuum ratio, quibus impios frui vident. Quia enim toti terrenis dediti sunt, religionem omnem ex huius seculi successibus metiuntur. Quod si vis quaedam maior accedat & tyrannorum minae, Pontificum fulmina, suppliciorum tristissimorum exempla audiantur, mox totis animis fracti concidunt. Nec temere dictum putabimus, ruinam istorum magnam fieri. Pudefiunt enim, dum quam proprio ore fecerunt, professionis suae testimonio convincuntur, & eam quoque abnegant, qua vna se palliabant. Deinde salutis spem simul omnem amittunt, cum & Christo careant, & in externis omnibus nihil certi habeant. Itaque desperatione superati peiores fiunt, quam si nunquam credidissent, & (vt Christus ait) fiunt postrema eorum peiora primis: & ideo poenas quoque graviores exoluent, quam ij, qui ab omni fide & eius professione alienissimi fuerunt. Exempla huius mali multa passim occurrunt. Debent illa nos terrere & excitare, vt verbum Dei animis vere pijs au diamus, auditum imo corde reponamus, & ex eo fructum feramus nostra professione dignum. Fundamentum autem salutis nobis repositum sit in vno Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the other kind of hearers, who are hypocrites and idle pretenders, who indeed hear the Word, but perform none of the things that befit true worshippers of Christ. He says they are like those who build their house on the earth without a foundation. For if the Word of the Lord were taking root in them and they rested on a true foundation, they would undoubtedly perform those things which are joined to the genuine profession of the Christian name. What, then, do they do? They hear the word, indeed, but only in passing, and merely out of habit, lest they seem utterly atheistic and alien to all piety or religion. Then they build upon the earth, that is, they seek only earthly things, nor do they search their hearts so far that they deny, mortify and cast away the flesh and its concerns. Hence they think that faith and its profession can be joined with the Epicurean contempt of God and unbridled licence of morals. And what happens? They too build, and they raise up a house of the flesh which seems splendid in their own judgement. For by fasts, prayers, sacrifices, superstitious clothing, gestures and external ceremonies they so display themselves that they may seem of greater worth. But all these things, as the prophet says, are like a morning cloud and dew, and cannot long endure. For since this world can bear neither true piety nor its profession, the flood and the rivers of every kind of temptation soon assault them as well. And if this happens, nothing solid and stable is found in them. For since there is no sound knowledge of Christ in them, they waver uncertainly and are tossed hither and thither by every wind of doctrine. Moreover, they cannot but set great store by the example of this world, since they depend wholly on its judgement. The same reasoning holds for the good fortune and successes which they see the wicked enjoy: since they are wholly given over to earthly things, they measure all religion by the successes of this age. And if some greater force comes upon them, and the threats of tyrants, the thunderbolts of the Pontiffs and the examples of most grievous punishments are heard, they straightway collapse, utterly broken in spirit. Nor shall we think it rashly said that their fall is great. For they are put to shame, while they are convicted by the testimony of their own profession, which they made with their own mouth, and they deny even that by which alone they covered themselves. Then they lose all hope of salvation at once, since they are without Christ and have nothing certain in external things. And so, overcome by despair, they become worse than if they had never believed, and (as Christ says) their last state becomes worse than the first; and therefore they will also pay heavier punishments than those who were most alien from all faith and its profession. Examples of this evil occur everywhere. They ought to terrify us and rouse us, so that we may hear the Word of God with hearts truly pious, receive it not merely heard but deep in the heart, and bear from it fruit worthy of our profession. Let the foundation of our salvation, however, be laid in us in the one Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: HOMILIA LXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXV.

units.la: CVm autem finiuisset omnia verba sua audiente populo, ingressus est Capernaum. Centurionis autem cuiusdam seruus male affectus, moribundus erat, qui erat ipsi pretiosus. Is vero cum audisset de Iesu, misit ad eum Seniores Iudaeorum, rogans eum, vt veniret & seruaret seruum suum. Isti autem cum venissent ad Iesum, precati sunt eum studiose dicentes: Dignus est cui hoc praebeas. Diligit enim gentem nostram, & Synagogam aedificauit nobis.
units.tr: When Jesus had finished all his words in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. A certain centurion's servant, who was dear to him, was sick and near death. When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant. When they came to Jesus, they earnestly pleaded with him, saying, "He is worthy to have this done for him, for he loves our nation and has built us a synagogue."

units.la: INTER praecipua miracula aut signa, quae Dei filius, Iesus Christus, in terris agens edidit, nequaquam postremum censeri debet, quod primo huius cap. parte Lucas describit. Hoc enim non sine gravibus causis & certo consilio mox subiecit nobilissimae illi concioni qua omnia complexus est, quae ad aeternae salutis rationem, & ad fidei atque vitae totius institutionem nobis cognitu necessaria sunt. Ita enim docet, Deum nunquam deesse verbi sui doctrinae aut praedicationi, quo minus aliquem fructum ferat. Vt enim Christum a concione illa Capernaum versus iter facientem ingens populi multitudo (vt Matthaeus scribit) secuta est, quae illi nouas occasiones praebuit, & vt doctrinam suam signis miraculosis confirmaret, & plures alios ad sui cognitionem adduceret. Ita Dei verbum nunquam absque omni fructu praedicatur, sed (vt Isaias ait) pluuia instar semper inuenit aliquos, quorum mentes irriget atque fecundas reddat: & quicunq; in eius ministerio fideles fuerint, ij nouas quotidie occasiones inuenient, quibus adiuti regnum Dei quam latissime pro-
units.tr: Among the outstanding miracles or signs that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, performed while living on earth, this one must not be counted least, although Luke describes it first in this chapter. For not without weighty reasons and a definite purpose he immediately added that most noble sermon, in which he gathered together everything that we need to know for the way of eternal salvation and for the full instruction of faith and life. For thus he teaches that God never fails to give some fruit to his word's teaching or preaching. Just as a great crowd of people (as Matthew writes) followed Christ on his journey from that sermon toward Capernaum, and this gave him new occasions both to confirm his teaching by miraculous signs and to bring many others to knowledge of himself, so the word of God is never preached without some fruit. Like the rain, as Isaiah says, it always finds some people whose minds it waters and makes fruitful. And whoever are faithful in its ministry will find new opportunities every day, by which, helped, they may spread the kingdom of God as widely as possible.

units.la: fime prosimè propagare possint. Deinde Deitatem suam hoc facto Christus asserit, & se promissum illum humani generis seruatorem esse probat, penes quem sit vitæ & mortis imperium, quinque in ipso etiam mortis articulo seruare possit. Præterea homini ethnico & viro militari benefacit, vt partim Iudæ in mentem reuocet prophetarum vaticinia de gentium vocatione, & offendat non defuturos, qui ipsum recipiant, etiamsi illi rebelles & increduli esse pergant: partim vero ciuiles ordines isto exem plo confirmat, & offendit hos non obstare, quo minus aliquis ipsum vera fide amplectatur, & salutis in ipso particeps fiat. Postremò fidei exemplum historia hæc continet, quæ vix vllum illustrius habetur, & quod ipse Christus publico testimonio nobis commendare dignatus est. Et de his quidem singulis suo loco dicetur. In præsenti totius historiæ occasionem cum ijs, quæ in hanc inciderunt, Lucas describit.
units.tr: Next, by this deed Christ asserts his deity and proves that he is that promised Saviour of the human race, in whose power lies the rule over life and death, and who can save even at the very point of death. Moreover, he does a kindness to a Gentile and a soldier, partly to remind the Jews of the prophets' predictions about the calling of the Gentiles, and to show that there would be no lack of those who would receive him, even if the Jews continued in rebellion and unbelief. Partly he confirms the civil orders by this example, and shows that these do not hinder anyone from embracing him with true faith and becoming a partaker of salvation in him. Finally, this history contains an example of faith, which is hardly to be found more illustrious, and which Christ himself deigned to commend to us by public testimony. Each of these points will be discussed in its own place. For the present, Luke describes the occasion of the whole history together with the things that befell it.

units.la: Occasionem miraculo dedit Centurionis cuiusdam famulus aut seruus, qui ex morbo letali iam iam morturus erat. Et quantum ex circumstantijs omnibus colligere licet, Centurio iste præsidio præfuit, quod Capernai erat, & ex eorum militum numero fuit, de quibus capite tertio diximus. Quod ideo monemus, ne huius & aliorum exemplis, quorum mentionem Euangelistæ faciunt, sibijpsis patrocinentur nostri seculi Cares, qui neque legitimo magistratui militant, neque patriam & publicam pacem defendunt, sed à quouis se conduci patiuntur, & absque omni iuris & æqui respectu pro sua libidine in omnes sæuiunt, vt quaslum faciant vberiorem. Contra hos suam sententiam Deus iam olim per Mosem pronuntiauit: Maledictus qui accipit munus, vt percutiat sanguinem innocentem, & omnis populus dicet, Amen. Et de ijsdem exponi debent, quæ apud Isaiam capite trigesimo tertio & passim in prophetarum sermonibus leguntur. Docent præterea omnium gentium historiæ, tales homines fere potentissimis regnis exitium attulisse. Nec enim irrita fieri aut aboleri potest lex illa naturæ: Qua mensura vos metimini, eadem etiam vobis alij metientur.
units.tr: The occasion for the miracle was a servant, or slave, of a certain centurion, who was about to die of a deadly disease. And as far as one can gather from all the circumstances, this centurion commanded the garrison that was at Capernaum, and was one of those soldiers of whom we spoke in the third chapter. We remind of this so that our Carians of this age, who do not serve the lawful magistrate nor defend the fatherland and public peace, but allow themselves to be hired by anyone, and rage against all people without any regard for justice and equity, as their lust dictates, in order to make larger profits, may not defend themselves by the examples of this man and others whom the evangelists mention. God pronounced his sentence against such men long ago through Moses: "Cursed is he who takes a bribe to shed innocent blood. And all the people shall say, Amen." What is read in Isaiah chapter thirty-three, and throughout the sermons of the prophets, must be explained of the same men. Moreover, the histories of all nations teach that such men have nearly always brought ruin upon the most powerful kingdoms. For that law of nature cannot be made void or abolished: "With what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you again."

units.la: Sed reliquis illis nunc obseruemus, quod seruus tanto miraculo occasionem præbuit. Constat enim seruorum conditionem apud veteres miserrimam fuisse. Origo eius fuit ex Chamo, quem ob impietatem in patrem Noam hac pœna Deus multauit, vt eius posteritatem seruituti addiceret. Passus quoque est iugum hoc posteris temporibus magis magisque aggrauari, vt luculentior fieret ipsius ira atque maledictio, quæ omnem impietatem persequitur, & eam quidem in primis, quæ in parentes peccatur. Habebant enim heri in seruos potestatem vitæ & necis, & hi instrumentorum loco abutebantur, vt hodie Turcæ & aliæ gentes barbaræ ijs vti solent, quos aut bello cœperunt, aut ære suo mercati sunt. Eius conditionis hic quoque nosterfuit, quàmuis tollerabilior fuerit eius seruitus, quod in herum incidit, qui eum in pretio habuit, nimirum quod sibi fidelem esse videret. Simul etiam Deus illum peculiari gratia complexus est, quando eum non solum in morbo grauissimo seruauit, verumetiam organum præclarum esse voluit, quo Filij sui gloriam illustraret, non sine eximia piorum omnium consolatione. Impletur ergo in illo dictum illud Christi: Super pauca fidelis fuisti, super multa te constituam. Qui enim in domo Centurionis fideliter seruiuit, etiamnum hodie in domo Dei, Ecclesia, exemplo suo omnibus seruit, qui Deum vere colunt.
