Docet enim, Deum non fastidire aliquem mortalium, quantumuis vilem & abiectum, & beneficium illud salutis, cuius nobis author est Christus, ad omnis loci & ordinis homines pertinere, adeo, vt in illo non sit liber aut seruus, non dives aut pauper, non mas aut fœmina. Ex quo sequitur, debere vnumquemque sortem suam patienter ferre, neque cæco carnis affectu ad altiora aspirare absque certa & legitima Dei vocatione. Qui hoc faciunt, ij plerunque laboribus & periculis grauissimis & minimè necessarijs seipsos implicant. Inueniunt enim omnes in suo munere aut conditione quod agant, vt nouos labores accersere nequaquam sit opus. Recte ergo Paulus monuit, ne quis ad altiora aspiret, sed vt nos humilibus accommodemus, & vt quisque in ea conditione, in qua vocatus est, maneat. Viderunt hoc ipsum olim gentium sapientes, inter quos prouerbio vulgari dicebatur: Spartam nactus es, hanc orna. Quod si omnes facerent, non tot curis atque molestijs multi priuatim grauarentur, & minus turbaretur totus terrarum orbis, qui fere paucorum ambitione sursum deorsum versatur, & tandem non euertitur.
units.tr: But let us now observe the rest, namely that this servant gave occasion for so great a miracle. For it is well known that the condition of servants among the ancients was most wretched. Their origin was from Ham, whom God punished with this penalty for his impiety against his father Noah, by condemning his posterity to slavery. This yoke, too, in later times was made heavier and heavier, so that God's anger and curse, which pursues all impiety, and especially that which is committed against parents, might appear the more conspicuous. For masters had the power of life and death over their slaves, and these were abused as tools, as Turks and other barbarous nations are accustomed to treat those whom they have captured in war or bought with their money. This servant was of that condition too, although his servitude was more bearable because he fell to a master who valued him, namely because he saw that he was faithful to him. At the same time God embraced him with a special grace, when he not only preserved him in a most serious illness, but also willed him to be an outstanding instrument by which the glory of his Son would be displayed, not without an extraordinary consolation for all the godly. Thus that saying of Christ is fulfilled in him: "You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much." For he who served faithfully in the house of the centurion, even today in the house of God, which is the Church, serves all who truly worship God by his example. For it teaches that God does not despise any mortal, however lowly and abject, and that the benefit of salvation, of which Christ is the author, pertains to people of every place and rank, so that in him there is neither free nor slave, neither rich nor poor, neither male nor female. From this it follows that each person ought to bear his lot patiently, and not, from blind fleshly desire, to aspire to higher things without a certain and lawful calling from God. Those who do this usually entangle themselves in very grave labours and dangers, which are by no means necessary. For in their office or condition everyone finds something to do, so that there is no need to seek out new labours. Rightly therefore Paul warned that no one should aspire to higher things, but that we should accommodate ourselves to humble things, and that each should remain in the condition in which he was called. The wise men of the Gentiles saw this too, and among them a common proverb ran: "You have got Sparta; adorn it." If everyone did this, many people would not be burdened privately with so many cares and troubles, and the whole world, which is turned upside down almost by the ambition of a few and at last is not overturned, would be less disturbed.

units.la: Deinde admonemur huius seruuli exemplo, quanti referat cum pijs & fidis Dei cultoribus consuetudinem habere. In alia familia iste fortasis corpore & anima perijsset. At quia hero pio famulatur, totus salvus fit. Meminerint huius, quicunque alijs seruiendo victum quaerunt, ea tamen libertate vtuntur, vt herum ipsi pro suo arbitrio deligant, cui suam operam locent. Solent tales fere lucrum spectare, & illu sese addicere, apud quos salarij maioris spes affulget: multi quoq; vel otium ignauum, vel licentiam quaerunt, & apud eos se melius habituros arbitrantur, qui suos domesticos nulla disciplina seueriori coercent. Sunt autem isti plerunque miserrimi, & dum corpori soli consulunt, saepe infames fiunt, & infelices quoque animas nimia licentia in periculum adducunt. Exempla huius generis in utroque sexu multa occurrunt. Praecipua ergo cura sit, vt heros inueniant honestos, probos & Dei timentes: deinde his fideles esse studeant, neque dubitent de Dei fide, qui promissioni suae, cuius ante meminimus, nunquam deerit. Debent in horum consideratione parentes quoque diligentissime versari, quia & ipsi non raro huius seculi splendore fascinati, liberos suos male perdunt, quando ipsis optime consultum volunt. Alij enim in aulas regum eos detrudunt, vbi aureis compedibus vincti seruitutem seruiunt miserrimam inter illos, quorum consuetudine corrumpuntur, vt vitam omnem inter comessationes ebriosas, scorta, ludiones, scurras cum fastu immani & impio omnis religionis contemptu transfigant, & infelicia sint Satanae mancipia, dum prae alijs liberi videri volunt. Alij vero mercatorijs artibus suos instituì curant, & hoc agunt, vt quaestum faciant negotiando: quod (qui huius nouissimi seculi mores sunt) fieri non potest, nisi impostituris, dolis, mendacijs & vsuris iniquissimis dent operam. At meminisse oportebat, quaestum maximum esse pietatem cum animo sua sorte contento: dignitatem autem nullam posse homini maiorem obtingere, quàm vt Christi seruus sit: qui vt Rex regum est, ita suorum seruitio ad nullas res inhonestas aut noxias abutitur, eosdem neque licentia nimia, neque otio aut ignauia corrumpi sinit: tandem vero suae gloriae & regni sui consortes facit. Eius enim promissio est: Volo, vbi ego sum, ibi etiam sit minister meus. Ioan. 12.
units.tr: Next, we are admonished by the example of this little servant how much it matters to keep company with the godly and faithful worshippers of God. In another household he would perhaps have perished in body and soul. But because he served a pious master, he was saved entirely. Let all those remember this who seek their living by serving others, yet use that freedom so as to choose for themselves whatever master they will hire their labour to. Such people usually look to gain, and attach themselves to those from whom the hope of a larger wage shines forth. Many also seek idle ease or license, and think they will fare better with those who restrain their household by no stricter discipline. Yet such people are usually most wretched, and while they consult only the body, they often become infamous, and by excessive license they also endanger their unhappy souls. Examples of this kind occur in abundance in both sexes. The chief care, therefore, should be that they find masters who are honest, upright and fear God; and then that they strive to be faithful to them, and do not doubt God's faithfulness, who will never fail his promise mentioned earlier. In considering these matters, parents too ought to be most diligent, because they themselves, often dazzled by the splendour of this world, ruin their children when they wish them the best. For some thrust them into royal courts, where, bound in golden fetters, they serve a most wretched servitude among those by whose company they are corrupted, so that they spend their whole lives among drunken revelries, harlots, jesters and buffoons, with immense pride and impious contempt for all religion, and become the unhappy slaves of Satan, while they wish to seem free beyond others. Others take care to train their children in trading arts, and aim to make profit by commerce. This (which are the customs of this latest age) cannot be done without devoting oneself to deceit, frauds, lies and the most unjust usury. But they ought to remember that the greatest gain is piety with a mind content with its lot; and that no greater dignity can fall to a man than to be the servant of Christ. He, as King of kings, does not use the service of his people for any dishonourable or harmful things; nor does he allow them to be corrupted by excessive license, idleness or sloth; and at last he makes them sharers in his glory and his kingdom. For his promise is: "Where I am, there my servant shall be also." John 12.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt Centurionem quoq; videamus, cuius hic seruus fuit. Is cum audisset de Iesu, misit ad eum Seniores Iudaeorum, rogans eum, vt veniret, & seruaret seruum suum. Paucis verbis virtutes viri huius multas & eximias Euangelista comprehendit. Mater atque origo, omnium fuit fides, qua eum praeditum fuisse, non obscure innuit. Audiuit enim de Iesu, eius nimirum doctrina & operibus. Neque obiter & quasi aliud agens audiuit, quae de illo referebantur: sed eadem diligenter consideravit. Hinc spes & fiducia illa enata est, vt seruus suo per hunc subueniri posse crederet, & ideo ad illum legationem honorificam instituerit. At quia de eius fide postea ipse Christus testimonium feret luculentissimum, ista nunc annotauisse sufficiat. Videamus autem ea, quibus fidem suam, quoad externam vitae consuetudinem, declarauit.
units.tr: But it is time that we also look at the centurion, whose servant this was. When he had heard about Jesus, he sent the elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and heal his servant. In a few words the Evangelist sums up this man's many outstanding virtues. The source and foundation of them all was faith, and the Evangelist plainly indicates that he possessed it. For he heard about Jesus, that is, about his teaching and his works. He did not hear what was reported about him in passing, as if he were busy with something else, but he considered it carefully. From this came that hope and confidence that he could get help for his servant through Jesus, and so he sent this honourable embassy to him. Since Christ himself will later bear the clearest witness to his faith, it is enough for now to have noted this. Let us look instead at the things by which he showed his faith in his outward conduct of life.

units.la: Occurrit hic primùm humanitas singularis & dilectio, qua seruum prosecutus est, & ex qua colligi potest, qualis in totam familiam fuerit. Seruum hunc illi pretiosum, id est, charum fuisse, audiuimus. Ergo illum non canis aut iumenti loco habuit, vt tunc vulgus herorum solebat. Et cuius opera hucusque vtiliter vsus erat, eum iam aegrotantem non negligit, multò minus contagij metu, aut sub alio praetextu, domo eijcit, sed amicè & humaniter fouet. Salutem denique eius ita cordi habet, vt praestanrissimos in Iudaeorum gente viros propter ipsum fatigare non erubescat. Est hoc memorabile humanitatis exemplum, quod etsi latissimè exendi possit, in primis tamen heros admonet, quales in seruos suos esse debeant. Cogitandum illis ante omnia, quod etsi propter egestatem alijs seruire cogantur, homines tamen & eiusdem cum ipsis naturae consortes sint. In illis ergo ceu in speculo considerent, quales ipsi futuri fuissent, nisi benedictione sua eos ditasset Dominus, & quales adhuc fieri possint, si suam gratiam ipsis ille subducat. Etenim exempla sunt plurima eorum, qui ex fortuna lautissima subito deiecti ad extremam inopiam deuenerunt. Dionysius ille Siracusanus, potentissimus ditissimusq;, Siciliae rex, regno & diuitijs exutus, Corinthi literas docuit, vt victum sibi pararet. Belisarius item, supremus militiae dux, post praeclaras victorias & imperiu à barbarorum incursionibus sua virtute liberatum, à Iustiniano exoculatus, stipem petijt, & mendicando vitam infelicem sustentauit, qui paulo ante ferocissimis gentibus terrori fuerat. Et in priuatis hominibus huius generis multa quotidie occurrunt, quae docent, quàm incerta & fluxa sit opum quantùmuis maximarum possessio, & quàm facilè depauperentur, quorum thesauros multi inexhaustos esse putarunt. Excitet ergo ista consideratio omnes, ut seruos suos homines esse meminerint, & propriæ fortis memores, illorum laboribus, non inhumaniter abutantur: in primis autem curent, ut sacro illo otio, quod illis in Sabbati lege Deus concessit, frui possint, ut & corpora ipsorum quiete, & anima simul verbi Dei consolatione atque doctrina, recreentur. Inexcusabilis enim crudelitas, imò impietas est, eorum animas perdere, in quorū corpora tibi aliquod ius Deus esse voluit. Quòd si ijsdem aliquid humanitus contingat, ut vel morbis, vel laboribus, aut etiam senio debilitati, nostra vicissim opera opus habeant, hanc illis nullo iure à nobis negari posse cogitemus. Hic enim in primis locum habet illud Dauidis: Beatus, qui cordatè aut prudenter agit cum ægro: in die mala liberabit eum Dominus. Etenim cùm cuiuis ægrotanti opem nostram debeamus, nequaquam à nobis negligi debent, qui nobis prius fidele obsequium præstiterunt. Neque Christianorum nomine digni sunt, qui vel barbara inhumanitate, vel crudeli auaritia abrepti, seruis suis duriter imperant, & eosdē dum valent, laboribus intolerabilibus fatigant, viribus autem exhaustos, aut morbi correptos, vix canum loco habent, aut domo eijciunt, aut turpiter neglectos perire sinunt. Ita certè non raro impatientiæ & desperationis authores sunt ijs, quorum patientiam atque fidem sua humanitate fouere debebant. Quid autem de illis dicemus, qui rapinis & vsurarijs artibus multos ad egestatem extremam redactos seruire cogunt?
units.tr: The first thing that meets us here is the remarkable humanity and affection with which he treated his servant, and from which we can judge what kind of master he was to his whole household. We have heard that this servant was precious to him, that is, dear. So he did not treat him as a dog or a beast of burden, as masters at that time commonly did. And when the man was ill, he did not neglect him, still less cast him out of the house for fear of contagion or on some other pretext, but cared for him kindly and humanely. Indeed, he cared so much for the man's health that he was not ashamed to trouble the most distinguished men among the Jewish people on his account. This is a memorable example of humanity, and although it could be spread much more widely, it especially warns masters what kind of people they ought to be towards their servants. Above all they should consider that although poverty forces some to serve others, they are still human beings and share the same nature as themselves. Let them therefore look at their servants as in a mirror, and consider what they themselves would have become had the Lord not enriched them with his blessing, and what they still might become if he withdrew his grace from them. Indeed there are very many examples of those who, suddenly thrown down from the most splendid fortune, have come to utter poverty. Dionysius of Syracuse, the most powerful and wealthy king of Sicily, stripped of his kingdom and riches, taught letters at Corinth so that he could earn his living. Belisarius likewise, the supreme commander of the army, who after brilliant victories had by his valour freed the empire from the attacks of the barbarians, was blinded by Justinian, and begged for alms, sustaining an unhappy life by begging, though a little before he had been a terror to the most ferocious peoples. And among private persons there happen every day many cases of this kind, which teach how uncertain and fleeting is the possession of even the greatest wealth, and how easily those are impoverished whose treasures many thought were inexhaustible. Let this consideration therefore stir up everyone to remember that their servants are human beings, and, mindful of their own fortune, not to abuse their labours inhumanly. Above all let them take care that they can enjoy that holy rest which God granted them in the law of the Sabbath, so that both their bodies may be refreshed by quiet and their souls at the same time by the comfort and teaching of the word of God. For it is inexcusable cruelty, indeed impiety, to destroy the souls of those over whose bodies God wished you to have some right. But if these servants, being weakened by sickness, labour, or even old age, should happen to need our help in turn, let us consider that this cannot rightfully be denied them by us. For here above all the saying of David applies: Blessed is he who acts wisely or prudently towards the sick; in the day of evil the Lord will deliver him. Since we owe our help to anyone who is ill, those who have first rendered us faithful service must by no means be neglected. Nor are they worthy of the name of Christians who, carried away by barbarous inhumanity or cruel greed, rule their servants harshly, wear them out with intolerable labours while they are able, and, when they are exhausted or struck down by disease, scarcely count them as dogs, cast them out of the house, or let them perish in shameful neglect. In this way they are very often the cause of impatience and despair in those whose patience and faith they ought to cherish by their humanity. But what shall we say of those who, by plunder and usurious arts, force many who have been reduced to extreme poverty to serve them?

units.la: Alterum, quo fidem suam testatus est Centurio noster, religionis studium fuit. Indicia eius non obscura in Seniorum oratione commemorantur: quòd & gentem Iudæorum amauerit, & Synagogam Capernaiticam ædificarit. At nihil erat in ea gente (si carnis iudicium audias) amore dignum, cùm & omnibus modis misera, & propter crebras seditiones Romanis exosa esset. Amauit ergo eam hoc solo nomine, quòd adhuc Dei populus diceretur, & non contemnenda diuinæ bonitatis argumenta in illis elucerent. Apparet hoc in eo, quòd Synagogam illis ædificauit, in qua cœtus sacros pro more agerent, legem Dei & prophetarum libros interpretarentur, & publicas preces facerent. Hunc enim Synagogarum vsum illis fuisse, alibi diximus. Ergo quod Centurio fecit, non solùm magnæ impensæ opus, sed cum inuidia multa, cum odio, cum periculo coniuncta fuit. Erant enim Iudaici cultus apud Romanos publicè inuisi, ut in illius seculi poëtis esse videre, & (ut in Apologetico suo Tertullianus scribit) peregrini ritus & religiones exteræ omnes Senatusconsulto damnatæ erat. Magna ergo Centurionis huius fides fuerit oportet, si locum, quem tenebat, diligentius consideres. Nos autem eius exemplo docemur, quibus exercitijs verè religionis studium testari debeamus. Primùm, amemus Dei populum, Ecclesiam nimirum totam, & singula eius membra. Nec enim temere ab Ioanne dictum est: Qui non diligit fratrem suum, quem videt, quomodo Deum, quem non videt, diligere poterit? Deinde cultum Dei promouebamus, in quo primæ partes doctrinæ verbi debentur. Hæc enim nos de Dei voluntate certos facit, hæc ex verbi semine regenerat, & eadem vitæ totius cursum dirigit. Ideo olim principes viri ad Centurionis huius exemplum Collegia ædificarunt, ijsdem redditus annuos constituerunt, ex quibus à pueris æducarentur, qui postea Ecclesijs docendo seruire possent. At hodie plures inuenire licebit, qui ut luxui suo suffice re possint, quæ ab alijs donata sunt, per fas & nefas rapiant, quàm qui istorum liberalitatem imitentur. Et hæc in præsenti de Centurione hoc dicta sufficiant, de reliquis eius virtutibus suo loco plura dicentur.
units.tr: The second thing by which our centurion attested his faith was his zeal for religion. Clear signs of this are recorded in the speech of the elders: that he loved the Jewish nation and had built them a synagogue at Capernaum. Yet there was nothing in that nation (if you judge by the flesh) worthy of love, since it was wretched in every way and, because of frequent seditions, hated by the Romans. He loved it therefore for this reason alone, that it was still called the people of God, and that in it there shone forth signs of divine goodness not to be despised. This appears in the fact that he built them a synagogue in which they might hold sacred assemblies as was their custom, interpret the law of God and the books of the prophets, and offer public prayers. We have said elsewhere that this was the use of synagogues among them. So what the centurion did was not only a work of great expense, but was attended with much ill will, hatred, and danger. For Jewish worship was publicly hated among the Romans, as can be seen in the poets of that age, and (as Tertullian writes in his Apologeticum) all foreign rites and religions were condemned by a decree of the Senate. Great therefore must have been the faith of this centurion, if you consider carefully the position he held. But we are taught by his example in what exercises we ought to attest a true zeal for religion. First, let us love the people of God, that is, the whole Church, and its individual members. For it was not without reason that John said: He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? Next, let us promote the worship of God, in which the first place is owed to the teaching of the word. For this makes us certain of God's will, this regenerates us from the seed of the word, and this directs the whole course of our life. Therefore in former times leading men, following the example of this centurion, built colleges, and assigned annual revenues to them, from which boys were brought up who could afterwards serve the Churches by teaching. But today one may find many who, so that they may supply their luxury, snatch by right and wrong what has been given by others, but few who imitate their generosity. Let what has been said here about the centurion suffice for now; more will be said about his other virtues in their proper place.

units.la: Nunc Iudæorum Seniores audiamus, qui legationem sibi commissam diligentissimè obeunt. Ad Christum enim veniunt, & non modò beneficium Centurionis nomine petunt, verumetiam dignum esse docent, cui Christus benefaciat. Nam diligit gentem nostram (aiunt) & Synagogam ædificauit nobis. Quo loco admirabile Dei consilium elucet, & quàm facile illi sit Filij sui gloriam illustrare atque regnum eiusdem promouere. Etenim inter huius seculi honores, quibus Reges potentissimi suam gloriam atque maiestatem maximè ostentant, ferè hic primus est, quòd in ipsorum aulas plurimi aliarum gentium atque principum legati confluunt, qui vel auxilia petunt, vel de rebus magnis & arduis cum illis consultant, vel donis & muneribus magnificis eos venerantur. Ideo Dauid Christum sub Regis persona describens, inter alia canit: Reges maris & Cap. VII. Psal.72. insularum munera adferent: Reges Scheba & Saba honoraria adducent. Adorabunt eum omnes reges, omnes gentes seruient ei, &c. Et hoc quidem vaticinium impletum est, quando diuersarum gentium reges & principes ad Christi fidem accesserunt, & tam seipsos quàm regna opesq; suas illi subiecerunt. At maius quidin praesenti fieri videmus. Nam Centurio Romanus (quae illo tempore dignitas erat maxima) legatos mittit, qui illi supplices fiant, neq; tantum virum eius pudet, qui inops, contemptus & plerisque inuisus hinc inde oberrabat, & sedem certam nullibi habebat. Mittit autem non seruulum, aut ex domesticis suis aliquem, sed ex Iudaeorum gente Seniores deligit, qui primum honoris atq; dignitatis locum in ecclesia & repub. tenebant. Et hi ipsi se ad hanc legationem exorari patiuntur, & illius nomine Christo supplicant, quem (vt Euangelica historia passim refertur) cane & angue peius oderant. Quod si causam quaeras, quae illos mouit, non aliam dicere possumus, quàm diuinam Christi virtutem, quae vel inuitos traxit, vt in eius conspectum venirent, & ei supplices fierent. Et apparet hic verissime olim de Christo praedictum fuisse, quod regnaturus sit in medio hostium suorum. Debemus nos ex eo consolationem petere, ne vllis aduersariorum conatibus terreamur, quorum corda sunt in manu Domini.
units.tr: Now let us hear the elders of the Jews, who carry out with the greatest diligence the embassy entrusted to them. For they come to Christ, and not only ask for a favour on behalf of the centurion, but also show that he is worthy that Christ should do him a kindness. For, they say, he loves our nation and has built us a synagogue. Here the wonderful counsel of God shines forth, and how easily it is for him to make the glory of his Son illustrious and to advance his kingdom. For among the honours of this age by which the most powerful kings chiefly display their glory and majesty, this is almost the first: that embassies of many other nations and princes flock to their courts, which either seek help, or consult them about great and difficult matters, or honour them with magnificent gifts and presents. Therefore David, describing Christ under the person of a king, sings among other things: The kings of the sea and of the islands shall bring gifts; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall bring presents. All kings shall adore him, all nations shall serve him, etc. Psalm 72. And this prophecy was indeed fulfilled when the kings and princes of various nations came to the faith of Christ, and subjected themselves as well as their kingdoms and wealth to him. But we see something greater happening in the present case. For a Roman centurion (which at that time was a very high dignity) sends envoys who come to him as suppliants, and he is not ashamed of his man, who was wandering here and there poor, despised, hated by most, and had no fixed dwelling anywhere. Moreover he sends not a little servant or one of his household, but chooses elders from the Jewish nation, who held the first place of honour and dignity in the Church and the commonwealth. And these men allow themselves to be prevailed upon to undertake this embassy, and in his name they make supplication to Christ, whom (as the Gospel history everywhere relates) they hated worse than dog or snake. If you ask what moved them, we can give no other reason than the divine power of Christ, which drew them even against their will, so that they came into his presence and became suppliants to him. And here it appears most truly that it was foretold of Christ long ago that he would reign in the midst of his enemies. From this we ought to take comfort, that we may not be terrified by any attempts of adversaries, whose hearts are in the hand of the Lord.

units.la: Deinde obseruari hic debet Seniorum iflorum peruersitas & plus quàm belluinus stupor. Nam vt Christus homini alienigenae & ethnico opem ferat, supplices orant, interim quam ille ipsis sponte offerebat, gratiam securi negligunt. Alibi quidem suae incredulitatis causas varias adducunt, quibus illam excusent & seipsos tueantur: at vnum hoc factum illis conuincendus sufficit, & prorsus excusabiles facit. Si enim non credunt, gratiae Dei Mediatorem atq; Seruatorem esse Christum, cur Centurionem istum, quem magno suo merito amabant, ad illum recurrere sinunt? cur non ab errore eum reuocant, & admonent, ne ab impostore opem petat? Quòd si credunt, aut aliqua ratione intra animos suos persuasi sunt, illum aliquid posse (id quod hoc facto non obscure fatentur) cur non ipsi quoq; in illo spem collocant? cur non credunt docenti? cur non suae fidei creditum populum ad hunc remittunt? imò cur alibi execrabiles esse dicunt eos, qui relictis hominum traditionibus ipsum seque bantur? Ita saepe suo sese indicio produnt Christi hostes, & simile quid hodie illis accidit, qui Deos colunt & inuocant. Si enim quaeras, cur id faciant, non aliud respondere poterunt, quàm quòd feruentissimi gloriae Christi vindices fuerint, & pro illo cruciatus & tormenta dirissima perpessi sint, vt quàm plurimos ipsi adducerent. At si hoc serio dicut, & illos ideo tantis honoribus dignos iudicant, cur non ipsi quoque illorum vestigiis insistunt? cur non doctrinae illorum obediunt, qui praeter Iesum Christum, & hunc quidem crucifixum, nihil nouerunt?
units.tr: Next, we should note the perversity of these elders and their stupidity, which is more than bestial. They beg that Christ would help a foreigner and a Gentile, yet they carelessly neglect the grace that he was offering them freely. Elsewhere they put forward various causes of their unbelief, by which they try to excuse themselves and defend their position. But this one deed is enough to convict them and makes them wholly inexcusable. If they do not believe that Christ is the Mediator and Saviour of God's grace, why do they allow this centurion, whom they loved for his great merit, to run to him? Why do they not call him back from his error and warn him not to seek help from an impostor? But if they do believe, or have been persuaded in some way in their own minds, that he can do something (which they do not plainly deny by this act), why do they not place their own hope in him? Why do they not believe his teaching? Why do they not send back to him the people entrusted to their faith? Indeed, why do they elsewhere call cursed those who, having abandoned human traditions, followed him and him alone? Thus Christ's enemies often betray themselves by their own testimony, and something similar happens today to those who worship and invoke gods. For if you ask why they do this, they can only answer that they are the most fervent defenders of Christ's glory, and that they have suffered for him the most dreadful torments, so that they might bring as many as possible to him. But if they say this in earnest, and judge that those men are worthy of such honours, why do they not also walk in their footsteps? Why do they not obey the teaching of those who knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified?

units.la: Videmus praeterea in istorum exemplo, qui hypocritarum mores sint. Permittunt vt ad Christi gratiam siue opem Centurio confugiat: at eadem sibi opus esse minimè credunt, sed suarum virium atque meritorum fiducia elati, sed sibi ipsis sufficere putant. Hoc ipsum in nostri quoque seculi iustitiarijs est videre. Facile enim admittunt, aliorum hominum eam esse corruptionem, vt gratia Dei, quam nobis Christus acquisiuit, opus habeant: imò tales fere esse docent, quos Diuorum quoque meritis & intercessione adiuuari oporteat: In seipsis autem nihil huius agnoscunt, sed propriae iustitiae fiducia freti, gratiae praedicationem oderunt, & ipsius Christi meritum hostiliter exibilant. Deinde etsi multae essent in Centurione laude dignissima, ea tamen sola commendant, quae in ipsos contulerat: Diligit (inquiunt) gentem nostram, & Synagogam aedificauit nobis: At hoc dicendo seipsos potius quàm illum commendant, quasi tanta sit ipsorum dignitas, vt quisquis ipsis benefaciat, dignus sit, quem Deus simul & homines suo fauore prosequantur. Quis vero non agnoscat hic Monachorum voces, quibus illi suos fautores laudare consueuerunt? Amat (inquiunt) nostrum ordine familiam nostram omnem mirificè colit, fratres nostros hospitio & mensa dignatur, sacellum & altare nostro templo aedificauit, lucernas perpetuas instituit, redditus nostri collegij annuos auxit, &c. Ista (inquam) illi homines tanti faciunt, vt caelo dignos esse pronuntient eos, qui aliquid huius facere solent. Et hinc superbus ille titulus operum supererogationis enatus est, qui fraternitates & societates peperit superstitionum plenas, & quibus Christi meritum maxima ex parte euacuatur. Discite igitur ex Seniorum istorum sermonibus nostros hypocritas agnoscere, quorum eo maior est impudentia, quòd ne ad Christum quidem suos remittunt, & ad hunc recurrere volentes quocunq; modo impediunt: imò haereticos dicunt omnes eos, qui illum salutis authorem vnicum esse fatentur.
units.tr: Moreover, from the example of these men we can see what hypocrites are like. They allow the centurion to take refuge in Christ's grace or help, but they do not believe that they themselves need the same. Carried away by confidence in their own strength and merits, they think they are sufficient for themselves. The same thing can be seen among the self-righteous of our own age. They readily admit that other men are so corrupt that they need the grace of God which Christ has won for us; indeed, they teach that such people must be helped even by the merits and intercession of the saints. But they recognise nothing of this in themselves. Relying on confidence in their own righteousness, they hate the preaching of grace and hiss at the merit of Christ himself with hostility. Again, even though there were many things in the centurion deserving the highest praise, they commend only what he had done for them: "He loves our nation, and he built us a synagogue." In saying this they commend themselves rather than him, as if their own worth were so great that whoever does them a kindness is worthy to be favoured by God and men alike. And who would not recognise here the voices of the monks, with which they have been accustomed to praise their benefactors? "He loves our order," they say, "he cherishes our whole family wonderfully, he honours our brothers with hospitality and table, he has built a chapel and altar in our church, he has founded perpetual lamps, he has increased the annual income of our college," and so on. I say these men value such things so highly that they declare those who usually do something of this kind worthy of heaven. From this arose that proud title of "works of supererogation," which gave birth to fraternities and societies full of superstitions, and by which the merit of Christ is for the most part emptied out. Learn therefore from the words of these elders to recognise our hypocrites, whose impudence is all the greater because they do not even send their own people back to Christ, and by every means they hinder those who want to run to him. Indeed, they call heretics all those who confess him to be the one author of salvation.

units.la: At priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, ijs respondendum erit, qui hoc exemplo abutuntur ad probandam Diuorum intercessionem, qui iam pridem hac vita defuncti in cœlis agunt. Centurio (inquiunt) cuius fidem Christus tantopere commendauit, apud ipsum aduocatis & intercessoribus vsus est: Ergo nos quoq; intercessoribus apud illum vti debemus. Quibus ego respondere poteram, nimium absurde & inepte eos facere, qui exemplum fidei & religionis petant ex ijs, quos à fide alie-nissimos & apertos Christi hostes fuisse constat. Centurionem quidem laude summa dignissimum esse dicimus, error tamen & plus quam rusticus pudor fuit, quod non ipse in Christi conspectum venit. Seniorum autem hæc arrogantia & impudentia fuit, quæ eos mouit, vt sua authoritate se aliquid effecturos putarent apud eum, quem odio prosequebantur. Sed nolumus hoc modo argumentum aduersariorum eludere, cùm multæ aliæ rationes sint, quibus solui & euerti poterit. Primò enim illorum instituto exemplum hoc minimè conuenit. Nam controuersia omnis inter nos est de defunctis, an scilicet qui iam in beatorum patria agunt, pro nobis in terra viuentibus intercedant: at illi exemplum proferunt eorum, qui adhuc viui pro homine viuente apud Christum in terra adhuc versantem supplices fuerunt. Quis vero nostrum, quò minus alij pro alijs, dum hic viuimus, precentur, vt quam prohibuit? Quin hoc fidei & charitatis opus præcipuum esse dicimus, quæ vt hostium quoque salutem nostris precibus adiuuemus, iubet. Sic olim Abrahamum pro Sodomis intercessisse legimus: & Iobus ex Dei mandato pro amicis orauit, qui multa temere & impudenter in disputatione aduersus illum instituta effutierant. Et huius generis exempla in veteris, testamenti libris passim occurrunt. Ut vero nobis intercessores apud Christum paremus ex defunctorum aut cœlitum numero, id certè nullo scripturæ sacræ testimonio, nullis item sanctorum exemplis probari poterit. Manet (aiunt) charitas, & proinde qui in terris agentes olim omnes amarunt, nunc quoque nos in hac lachrymarum valle laborantes amant, & Deum nobis iratum suis precibus placare studeant. Atqui non negamus, charitatem inter Diuos cœlites locum habere, & illud Christi agnoscimus, qui gaudium in cœlis fore ait coram Angelis super uno peccatore resipiscente. Sed charitatem eiusmodi illis tribuimus, quæ nullo mœroris aut tristitiæ affectu turbetur. Nam si aliter statuere velimus, iam plorabunt etiam Diui, & ex hominum interitu plus doloris sentient nunc, quàm olim cùm in vivis agerent: quod vt beatitudini cœlesti aduersatur, sic etiam cum scripturis pugnat, quæ in cœlis suspiria atq; gemitus cessare, & omnes lachrymas abstergi docent. Et vt huius exempli vestigijs inistamus, vsus est quidem intercessoribus Centurio, sed nihil in horum gratiam fecit Christus, qui (vt sequentia docebunt) beneficium hoc totum fidei dedit, qua Centurionem præditum esse sciebat. Est idem in alijs quoq; exemplis videre. Apud Canam Galilææ, cùm in nuptijs vinum deficeret, de eo Dominum virgo mater admonuit, sed responsum tulit: Quid mihi tecum mulier? Similiter pro Chananæa discipulos intercessisse legimus, sed hi quoq; audiunt: Non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israel. Num vero Christum tam inhumanum erga matrem, aut tam durum atq; difficilem erga discipulos fuisse dicemus? Nequaquam. Sed cauere voluit, ne errori fenestram aperiret, quem circa Diuorum inuocationem oriturum esse sciebat. Ideo Chananæa illa (quod Chrysostomus quoq; annotauit) cùm ipsa accederet, voti compos facta est, non cùm alij pro ea precarentur. Nos itaq; Paulum audiamus dicentem: Vnus Deus, vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus. Apud hunc autem alijs mediatoribus vel aduocatis minimè opus est, cùm ipse omnes qui laborant & onerati sunt, ad se vocet, & neminem ad se venientem reijciat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But before we make an end of speaking, we must answer those who abuse this example to prove the intercession of the saints, who long ago departed this life and now dwell in heaven. "The centurion," they say, "whose faith Christ so greatly commended, used advocates and intercessors with him: therefore we too ought to use intercessors with him." To them I could reply that they act too absurdly and foolishly who seek an example of faith and religion from those who are known to have been most alien to the faith and open enemies of Christ. We say indeed that the centurion is most worthy of the highest praise, yet it was an error, and a shame more than rustic, that he did not come into Christ's presence himself. But it was the arrogance and impudence of the elders that moved them to think that by their own authority they could achieve something with him whom they pursued with hatred. Yet we do not wish to evade our opponents' argument in this way, since there are many other reasons by which it can be refuted and overturned. For, first, this example does not at all suit their argument. For the whole controversy between us is about the dead: whether those who now dwell in the fatherland of the blessed intercede for us who are still living on earth. But they put forward the example of those who, while still alive, made supplication on behalf of a living man before Christ, who was still living on earth. Who among us forbids others to pray for others while we live here? Indeed, we say that this is a chief work of faith and charity, which commands us to help even the salvation of enemies by our prayers. Thus we read that Abraham long ago interceded for Sodom, and that Job prayed at God's command for his friends, who had rashly and impudently said many things against him in the debate. And examples of this kind occur everywhere in the books of the Old Testament. But that we should prepare intercessors with Christ from the number of the dead or of the heavenly ones, this certainly cannot be proved by any testimony of Holy Scripture, nor by any examples of the saints. "Love remains," they say, "and therefore those who once loved all of us while living on earth, now also love us who labour in this valley of tears, and strive to appease God, who is angry with us, by their prayers." But we do not deny that love has a place among the blessed saints in heaven, and we acknowledge that saying of Christ, that there will be joy in heaven before the angels over one sinner who repents. But we ascribe to them a love of such a kind as is not disturbed by any feeling of grief or sadness. For if we wish to think otherwise, then the saints will also weep, and they will now feel more sorrow at the death of men than they did when they were living in the world. This is opposed to heavenly blessedness, and it also conflicts with Scripture, which teaches that sighs and groans cease in heaven and that all tears are wiped away. And to follow the footsteps of this example: the centurion did indeed use intercessors, yet Christ did nothing for their sake; rather, as what follows will show, he gave this whole benefit to the faith with which he knew the centurion was endowed. The same can be seen in other examples too. At Cana of Galilee, when the wine failed at the wedding, the virgin mother admonished the Lord about it, but she received the answer: "Woman, what have I to do with you?" Likewise we read that the disciples interceded for the Canaanite woman, but they too heard: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Shall we say that Christ was so unkind to his mother, or so hard and difficult toward his disciples? By no means. But he wished to take care not to open a window to the error which he knew would arise concerning the invocation of the saints. Therefore that Canaanite woman (as Chrysostom also noted) obtained her desire when she herself came forward, not when others prayed for her. Let us therefore hear Paul saying: "One God, one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." And with him there is by no means any need of other mediators or advocates, since he himself calls to himself all who labour and are burdened, and rejects no one who comes to him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVI.

units.la: Iesus ergo proficiscebatur cum eis, & cum iam non longe abesset domo, misit ad eum Centurio ille amicos, dicens illi: Domine, ne vexare: neque enim sum dignus vt tectum meum subeas. Ideo neque meipsum sum dignum arbitratus, qui venirem ad te: sed dic verbo, & sanabitur puer meus. Etenim ego homo sum sub potestate constitutus; habens sub me milites, & dico huic, Proficiscere, & prosicifcitur:& alteri, Veni, ac venit: & feruo meo, Fac hoc, & facit. Audiitis autem his lesus admiratus est cum, & conuersus dixit turbae, quae ipsum sequebatur: Dico vobis, ne in Israel quidem tantam fidem inueni. Et domum reuersi qui missi fuerant, sanum inuenerunt seruum, qui aegrotus fuerat.
units.tr: Jesus therefore went with them; and when he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. Therefore I did not think myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man set under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it." When Jesus heard these things he marvelled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said: "I tell you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel." And the men who had been sent, returning to the house, found the servant whole who had been sick.

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus apud Ioannem septimo capite ait: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed Patris qui misit me. Causa huius dicti est, quod nihil quam aeternam Dei voluntatem continet, ex qua vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio dependet. Summa huius est, vt primo in ipsum credamus, quem ille nobis redemptorem dedit, & ita salutis per ipsum acquisitae participes efficiamur. Deinde vt illi seruiamus in vitae innocentia, sanctitate & mutua dilectione. Et haec illa doctrina est, quam scriptura passim tradit et inculcat. Quia autem ad haec pro nostri ingenij vitio segnitate tardiores sumus, doctrinam hanc Christus miraculis plurimis confirmauit: inter quae admodum memorabile est, quod hic describitur. Nam re ipsa docet, se promissum illum humani generis vindicem esse, in quo vno salus inueniri possit. Simul autem Centurionis exemplo nos Spiritus sanctus admonet, quales esse debeant, qui in Christo seruari volunt. Et huc pertinent nonnulla, quae nuper audiuimus. Sequuntur reliqua, quibus historia haec absoluitur.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ says in John, chapter seven: "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me." The reason for this saying is that it contains nothing but the eternal will of God, on which the whole order of our salvation depends. Its sum is this: first, that we believe in him whom God has given us as Redeemer, and so become sharers in the salvation acquired through him. Then, that we serve him in innocence of life, holiness, and mutual love. This is the teaching that Scripture hands down and impresses everywhere. But because we are slow to these things through the fault of our nature, Christ confirmed this teaching by very many miracles; among them the one described here is especially memorable. For in fact he shows that he is that promised avenger of the human race, in whom alone salvation can be found. At the same time the Holy Spirit, by the example of the centurion, admonishes us what sort of people those ought to be who wish to be saved in Christ. Some things we heard recently pertain to this too. What follows are the remaining things by which this history is completed.

units.la: Occurrit primum, quod Christus, audita Seniorum legatione, mox iter ingreditur: non quidem eam ob causam, quod absens corpore non posset periclitanti succurrere, sed vt Centurionis fidem, quae paucis adhuc vere cognita erat, in lucem protrahat, idque nobis omnibus in exemplum. Est autem diligenti consideratione dignissima haec illius facilitas, qua & homini ethnico & Senioribus (quorum ordinem ipsi infensissimum fuisse nuper diximus) tam cito morem gerit. Vitur eadem exga omnes, qui ad illius opem recurrunt: Sunt enim vniuersales promissiones: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego requiem vobis praestabo. Item: Quicquid dat mihi Pater, ad me venit: & eum qui venit ad me, non eiciso foras. Confirmantur promissiones istae infinitis exemplis, quae Euangelistae passim commemorant. Venerunt multoties ad Christum mendici, quos proprij gentiles negligebant: at eosdem ille humanissime excepit. Venerunt morbis foedissimis confecti & vlceribus putres, imo leprosi, quos lex ab hominum consuetudine excludebat: quos tamen ille non in conspectum modo admisit, verumetiam contactu dignatus est. Venerunt peccatis & sceleribus infames publicani & meretrices, sed ne hos quidem fastidiuit, quamuis ex eorum consortio ipsum calumniandi occasionem pharisaei arriperent. Venit deniq; ex Pharisaeorum (qui hostes eius acerrimi erant) grege Nicodemus, & quidem noctu venit, quod ipsum adhuc illius puderet: nihilominus tamen amice exceptum a primis fundamentis in fidei & salutis aeternae negotio instituit. Quid autem ista commemoro, quando latronem, qui atrocissimorum scelerum poenas luebat, in extremo mortis articulo ad se conuersum exaudiuit, & eidem respondit, Hodie mecum eris in paradiso? Seruiunt haec exempla ijs confutandis, qui nobis apud illum intercessoribus opus esse aiunt. Faciunt isti homines illi magnam iniuriam, quando immitem & inexorabilem fingunt nunc in coelis, qui propter nos in terras descendere dignatus est, & omnes infirmitates nostras in se recepit, vt fidelem Pontificem esse crederemus, qui nobis condolere posset & compati. Ex his ergo consolationem petamus in omni tentationis genere, ne nos ab illo negligi putemus. Nec enim nostrae indignitatis Christum pudet, & prope adest Dominus (vt in Psalmis habetur) omnibus, qui ipsum inuocant. Quomodo enim ad se venientes & misericordiam eius implorantes fastidiat, qui tota die manus suas extendit adpopulum rebellem & contumacem? Vide Isa.65.
units.tr: First we meet with this: that Christ, on hearing the embassy of the elders, sets out at once on the journey; not indeed for this reason, that being absent in body he could not help the one in danger, but in order to bring out into the light the faith of the centurion, which was as yet known truly to few, and to do so as an example to us all. This readiness of his, by which he so quickly accommodates himself both to a Gentile and to the elders (whose order, as we said recently, was most hostile to him), is most worthy of careful consideration. He treats in the same way all who run to his aid, for the promises are universal: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest." Likewise: "Whatever the Father gives me comes to me, and him who comes to me I will not cast out." These promises are confirmed by the countless examples that the evangelists record everywhere. Beggars, whom their own countrymen neglected, often came to Christ, and he received them most kindly. Men wasted by the most loathsome diseases and rotten with sores, even lepers, whom the law shut out from human society, came to him; yet he not only admitted them to his sight but deigned to touch them. Publicans and harlots, infamous for their sins and crimes, came to him; yet he did not disdain even these, although the Pharisees seized on their company as an occasion to slander him. Finally, Nicodemus came to him from the flock of the Pharisees, who were his bitterest enemies; and he came by night, because he was still ashamed of it; nevertheless, received kindly, he was instructed from the first foundations in the matter of faith and eternal salvation. But why do I recount these things, when he heard the thief, who was paying the penalty of the most atrocious crimes, turning to him at the very point of death, and answered him: "Today you will be with me in paradise"? These examples serve to refute those who say that we need intercessors with him. Those men do him great wrong when they imagine that he is now in heaven harsh and unyielding, who deigned to descend to earth on our account, and took upon himself all our infirmities, so that we might believe him to be a faithful High Priest who could feel with us and sympathise. Let us therefore seek consolation from him in every kind of temptation, and not think that we are neglected by him. For Christ is not ashamed of our unworthiness, and, as it is written in the Psalms, the Lord is near to all who call upon him. For how could he who all day long stretches out his hands to a rebellious and obstinate people disdain those who come to him and implore his mercy? See Isa. 65.

units.la: Porro ad Centurionem redeamus, qui vbi Christum ad se venire, & iam non longe ab eius abesse intellexit, mox amicos ei obuiam mittit, qui eum moneant, ne tantum molestiae ipsius nomine suscipiat. Et rationes subijcit duas. Primam: Quia non sum dignus, vt tectum meum subeas: & ideo neque meipsum sum dignum arbitratus, qui venirem ad te. Alteram, Quia non opus est, vt domum meam ingrediaris, cum rem hanc omnem solo nutu aut vno verbulo possis conficere. Dic (inquit) verbo, id est, manda & praecipe quid fieri velis, & sanabitur ilico puer meus. Quod ne temere elapsum putetur aliquis, proprio exemplo istud confirmat, sic dicens: Etenim ego homo
units.tr: But let us return to the centurion, who, as soon as he understood that Christ was coming to him and was now not far from his house, at once sent friends to meet him, to beg him not to take on so much trouble for his sake. And he adds two reasons. The first: "I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; and therefore I did not think myself worthy to come to you." The second: "There is no need for you to enter my house, since you can accomplish the whole matter by a mere nod or a single word. Say the word" (he says), that is, "command and order what you wish to be done, and my servant will be healed at once." Lest anyone think this was said rashly, he confirms it by his own example, speaking thus: "For I too am a man"

units.la: Matth. 11. Ioan. 6. homo sum sub potestate constitutus, habens sub me milites & dico huic, Proficiscere, & proficiscitur: & alteri, Veni, ac venit: & servo meo, Fac hoc, & facit. Subest his verbis multiplex comparatio, qua ingeniose admodum a minore ad maius argumentatur. Primum, Ego (inquit) homo sum, & quidem nihil quam homo mortalis, & ijs, quae hominibus communia sunt, obnoxius: at tu etsi in carne inter nos versaris, es tamen verus & aeternus Dei Filius. Deinde, ego non sum mei iuris, sed sub potestate constitutus, nimirum Tiberij Caesaris miles: tu vero liber es, imo virtute divina armatus es, & legitimum habes in caelo & in terris imperium. Postremo, ego sub me habeo milites, qui etsi meae conditionis sint, & eidem domino serviant, tamen mihi sunt obedientissimi, & ad meum nutum atque iussum abeunt, veniunt, & quaecunque abs me in mandatis acceperunt, diligentissime exequuntur. Quid ergo non faciant te iubente Angeli tam boni quam mali, morbi, imo mors ipsa? Haec (inquam) omnia, & quaecunque alia in hanc sententiam dici possunt, paucula haec Centurionis verba comprehendunt.
units.tr: Matt. 11. John 6. "...a man set under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it." Underlying these words is a manifold comparison, by which he argues very ingeniously from the lesser to the greater. First: "I am a man" (he says), and indeed nothing but a mortal man, subject to the things that are common to men; but you, although you dwell among us in the flesh, are the true and eternal Son of God. Next: I am not my own master, but set under authority, that is, a soldier of Tiberius Caesar; but you are free, nay, armed with divine power, and have lawful rule in heaven and on earth. Lastly: I have soldiers under me, who, although they are of my condition and serve the same lord, are nevertheless most obedient to me, and go and come at my nod and command, and carry out most diligently whatever they have received from me as orders. What, then, will not the angels, good and bad alike, do at your command, and diseases, nay death itself? All these things (I say), and whatever else can be said to this effect, are comprehended in these few words of the centurion.

units.la: Nos autem priusquam ea tractemus, quae proprie ad huius historiae scopum faciunt, obiter videamus disciplinae militaris exemplum, quam apud Romanos feuerIter admodum observatam fuisse constat. Habebant hi legiones suas ex diversissimis nationibus conscriptas, veruntamen tam severa & arcta apud illos fuit disciplinae ratio, ut Centurionibus quoque nemo militum obloqui aut immorigerum se praebere auderet. Unde colligere licet, quanta apud eosdem legatorum, tribunorum & Imperatorum authoritas fuerit. Etenim exempla eorum non pauca extant, qui gravissimas poenas dederunt, quod contra Imperatoris edictum cum hoste, quamvis feliciter, pugnauissent. Fuit disciplina haec, Romani Imperij amplissimum decus, & (ut Val. Max. qui hoc ipso tempore scripsit, verbis utar) ad stabilimentum imperij, salutari perseverantia ad hoc usque tempus servata fuit. Videbant enim prudentissimi viri, nihil ad rempub. servandam utilius, nihil ad provehendam Imperij authoritatem efficacius & magis necessarium esse, quam obedientiam. Quia si hanc e medio tollas, nihil praeter ordinum omnium confusionem & ἀναρχίαν videbis, quae omnia pessundat ac dissipat. Quod ergo in re militari antiquitus observatum fuit, hoc ipsum ad omnes reipub. partes transferri, & non minus pacis tempore observari debet: ut nimirum suam stationem singuli teneant, & debitam obedientiam ijs praestent, quorum imperio subsunt. Vidit hoc nobilis illa Sabaorum regina, quae cum ad explorandam Solomonis sapientiam longissimo itinere & impensis maximis venisset, in primis servos atque aulicos ministros observauisse legitur, quo ordine nimirum in obeundis suis munibus versterentur, & quae inter illos disciplina servaretur. Ut vero ista locum habeant, ante omnia legibus bonis & sanctis opus est: deinde ut his ipsi principes obtemperent, & sic proprio exemplo legum authoritatem tueantur. Hodie leges quidem fere passim bonas inuenias, at qui his subesse velint, ex magnatibus nonnulli multi reperiuntur. Imo pleriq; authoritate & gloriam suam in immuni tate quadam tyrannica, et petulanti legum atq; disciplinae omnis contemptu consistere putant. Quid ergo ministri publici faciat, quibus legum executio commissa est? Quid ecclesiarum doctores, quam do magnatum exemplo populus seducitur? Hinc ergo fit, ut nemo vel publice vel privatim suam authoritatem obtineat: & huic malo debemus, quod familiae nobilissimae collabuntur, quod orbis Christianus bellis civilibus turbatur, & Turcis diripiendus exponitur.
units.tr: But before we treat those things that properly bear on the aim of this history, let us briefly consider the example of military discipline, which it is well known was very strictly observed among the Romans. They had their legions enrolled from the most diverse nations; yet the system of discipline among them was so severe and strict that no soldier would dare to speak back to a centurion or show himself disobedient. From this one may gather how great the authority of the legates, tribunes and emperors was among them. Indeed, there are not a few examples of men who inflicted the most severe penalties because they had fought against the enemy, even successfully, in defiance of the emperor's edict. This discipline was the most glorious ornament of the Roman Empire, and (to use the words of Valerius Maximus, who wrote in this very period) it was preserved to this time with beneficial steadfastness for the stability of the empire. For the wisest men saw that nothing was more useful for preserving the commonwealth, nothing more effective and more necessary for advancing the authority of the empire, than obedience. For if you remove this from the midst, you will see nothing but the confusion of all orders and anarchy [ἀναρχίαν], which overthrows and scatters everything. What was therefore observed of old in military affairs ought to be transferred to all parts of the commonwealth, and observed no less in time of peace: namely, that each individual should keep his own station and render due obedience to those under whose command they stand. That noble queen of Sheba saw this, who, when she had come on a very long journey and at great expense to test the wisdom of Solomon, is recorded to have observed above all his servants and courtly ministers, in what order they performed their duties and what discipline was kept among them. But for these things to hold, good and holy laws are needed above all; then that the princes themselves obey them, and so by their own example uphold the authority of the laws. Today indeed you will find good laws almost everywhere, but of those who are willing to be subject to them, many are to be found among the great men. Indeed most of them think that their authority and glory consist in a certain tyrannical immunity and in petulant contempt for all law and discipline. What, then, are the public ministers to do, to whom the execution of the laws is entrusted? What are the teachers of the churches to do, when the people are led astray by the example of the great? Hence it comes about that no one maintains his authority either in public or in private; and to this evil we owe it that most noble families collapse, that the Christian world is troubled by civil wars, and is exposed to be plundered by the Turks.

units.la: Sed quod praecipuum huius loci caput est videamus: Nimirum fidem Centurionis nostri, & in hac verae fidei ingenium atque effecta. Primum in hac occurrit, quod (ut nuper dictum est) ad solius Christi opem recurrit, quem a Deo ad homines servandos missum esse credebat. Est hoc fidei caput, ut salutis spem & fiduciam omnem in solo Deo repositam habeamus, idq; per Iesum Christum, quem ille nobis sua gratia Mediatorem constituit. Docet hoc omnis scriptura. Nam si foedus cum Abrahamo factum inspicias, Deum illi dicentem audies: Ego sum Deus Schadai, id est, omnipotens & ad omnia sufficiens, ambula coram me & esto integer: ponamque foedus meum inter me & te, &c. At quia propter peccatum, & quae ex hoc in nos deriuata est, maledictionem, nulla nobis cum Deo communio intercedere potest, eidem Abrahamo semen illud promittitur, in quo gentes omnes benedici oporteat: quem non alium, quam Christum esset, Paulus ad Galatas diserte docet: Non alia ergo Abrahami, quem patrem credentium scriptura vocat, fides fuit, quam quae vno Deo per vnum Iesum Christum nititur. Hanc postea in lege etiam nos Deus docuit. Hanc prophetae omnes uno ore praedicant. Hanc in novo testamento Apostoli nobis tradunt, neque aliam in Symbolo profitemur, quod Apostolicum dicitur. Ergo in ipso limine, quod aiunt, offendunt, qui salutis spem non in uno Deo collocant, & in periculis ad creaturas quascunque recurrunt. Relinquunt hi omnes fontem aquae viventis, & cisternas sibi fodiunt pertusas atque inutiles. Secundo, a solo Dei verbo pendet Centurio, et hoc ad quidvis sufficere credit, Dic (inquit) verbo, et sanabitur puer meus. Est hoc fidei proprium. Quia enim ex verbo Dei illa enascitur, de eiusdem veritate dubitare nullo modo potest. Exemplum huius quoque fiduciae in Abrahamo nobis Paulus monstrat, quem contra spem sub spe credidisse scribit, cum iam sibi centenario ex Sara vetula & ad pariendum inepta (si naturae leges spectemus) filium & posteritatem innumerabilem promitti audiret. Non enim vel suum vel Sarae corpus emortuum respiciebat, sed in unum Deum intentus erat, quem & veracem & omnipotentem esse noverat. Simili fiducia erga omnes armatos esse oportet, qui germani Abrahami filii dici & haberi volunt. Et nulla venia dignus est illorum error, qui vel de Dei praeceptis disputant, vel eiusdem promissiones in dubium vocant: quasi vero ipsi videre possint, quae ille non viderit, qui ipsissima est sapientia. Tertio, etsi Centurio virtutibus maximis ornatus, & fide (ut modo diximus) invicta armatus esset, modestissime tamen de seipso sentit, & toto animo se ad Christi pedes deiicit. Non sum dignus (ait) sub cuius tectum tu ingrediaris, aut in cuius conspectu ego veniam. Et tales quidem nos facit fides. Nam quo propius ad Deum accedimus, & quo familiarius is suae bonitatis atque gratiae thesauros nobis offert, eo clarius videmus qui nos simus, & quam indigni, quos ille tanta pietate complectatur: Exemplo hic nobis rursus fit Abrahamus, qui apud Deum pro Sodomis intercessurus, non suam dignitatem adducit, neque suis meritis gloriatur, sed humili deprecatione vtitur dicens: En obsecro, induxi animum ut loquerer cum Domino meo, qui pulvis sum & cinis. Et David cum se nouis promissionibus a Deo augeri, & Messiam ex sua posteritate nasciturum esse audiret, simili modestia respondet: Quis sum ego Domine Deus, & quae domus mea, quod me tantopere euebis? Quo etiam referri potest, quod passim sanctis se peccatores & Dei beneficiis indignos esse fatentur. Quibus omnibus Petri exemplum addi debet, qui cum ex miraculosa piscium captura Christum secum familiarius agentem agnouisset, mox ad pedes eius prolapsus clamavit: Exi a me, quia homo peccator sum, Domine. Arguitur his exemplis eorum confidentia, qui (ut Pharisaei olim) suorum operum & propriae iustitiae meritu freti, in Dei conspectum impudenter ruunt, & tantum non cum illusionibus ineunt, ut quae ipsis debentur praemia, ab illo reposcant. Neque ideo bona opera a fide excludimus, quando his quoque fidem suam Centurio noster egregie declaravit. Nam ut nuper audiimus, Synagogam aedificavit, & Dei cultum qua potuit diligentia promovit. Populum item dilexit, cui cum praesidio impositus erat, nec dubium est, quin suum erga illos amorem fideli defensione & quotidianis beneficiis testatus sit. Adhaec servulum aegrotantem humanissime tractavit, totusque in hoc fuit, ut eius saluti consuleretur. Habet ergo exemplum hoc vitam verae fidei imaginem, et haec illa opera sunt, quibus hodie fidem suam testari debebant, qui Euangelio gloriantur. At nimium infelices sumus, quando plerique his contraria facimus, & quem ore profitemur, Christum factis negamus: quod cum res ipsa probet, demonstratione alia non est opus.
units.tr: But let us look at the chief point of this passage: the faith of our centurion, and the nature and effects of true faith. First, we notice that, as was said a little while ago, he turns only to Christ's help, believing him to have been sent from God to save men. This is the foundation of faith: that we place all our hope of salvation and all our trust in God alone, and in Jesus Christ, whom he has by his grace appointed as our Mediator. All Scripture teaches this. For if you look at the covenant made with Abraham, you will hear God saying to him: "I am God Almighty, that is, all-sufficient for everything; walk before me and be upright; and I will establish my covenant between me and you," and so on (Gen. 17). But because of sin, and the curse derived from it upon us, no communion with God can exist for us. So the same Abraham is promised that seed in whom all nations ought to be blessed, and Paul plainly teaches the Galatians that this seed is none other than Christ. Therefore the faith of Abraham, whom Scripture calls the father of believers, was no other than that which rests on the one God through the one Jesus Christ. Afterwards God taught us this same faith in the law. All the prophets proclaim it with one voice. The apostles hand it down to us in the New Testament, and we profess no other faith in the creed called the Apostles' Creed. Therefore those who do not place their hope of salvation in the one God, and who in dangers run to any creatures whatever, stumble at the very threshold, as they say. They leave the fountain of living water and dig for themselves broken cisterns that hold no water. Second, the centurion depends solely on the word of God, and believes that this is enough for anything: "Say the word," he says, "and my servant will be healed." This is the proper mark of faith. For since faith springs from the word of God, it can by no means doubt its truth. Paul also shows us an example of this trust in Abraham, of whom he writes that he believed against hope in hope, when he heard that a son and countless posterity were promised him, though he was a hundred years old and his wife Sarah was an aged woman unfit for bearing children (if we consider the laws of nature). For he did not look at his own body or Sarah's dead body, but was fixed on the one God, whom he knew to be both true and almighty. Such trust ought to be shown by all who wish to be and be called the true sons of Abraham. And the error of those is utterly inexcusable who either dispute God's commands or call his promises into doubt, as if they could see what he, who is wisdom itself, did not see. Third, although the centurion was adorned with the greatest virtues and armed with an unconquered faith (as we have just said), he thinks very modestly of himself and casts himself at Christ's feet with his whole heart. "I am not worthy," he says, "that you should enter under my roof, or that I should come into your presence." Faith makes us such as this. For the closer we draw to God, and the more familiarly he offers us the treasures of his goodness and grace, the more clearly we see who we are, and how unworthy we are of being embraced by him with such mercy. Abraham again provides us with an example. When he was about to intercede with God for Sodom, he did not bring forward his own dignity or boast of his merits, but used a humble entreaty, saying: "Behold, I beg you, I have taken it upon myself to speak to the Lord my God, though I am dust and ashes." And David, when he heard from God that he would be enriched with new promises and that the Messiah would be born from his posterity, answered with similar modesty: "Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me so far?" To this may also be referred the frequent confession of sinners among the saints that they are unworthy of God's benefits. To all these examples should be added that of Peter, who, when he recognised from the miraculous catch of fish that Christ was dealing with him very familiarly, straightway fell at his feet and cried: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." These examples expose the confidence of those who, like the Pharisees of old, trusting in the merit of their own works and their own righteousness, rush shamelessly into God's presence, and almost bargain with him, demanding from him the rewards they think they are owed. Nor do we on that account exclude good works from faith, since our centurion has also shown his faith admirably by these. For, as we heard a little while ago, he built a synagogue and promoted the worship of God with all the diligence he could. He also loved the people among whom he had been placed as commander, and there is no doubt that he showed his love for them by faithful protection and daily kindnesses. Besides, he treated his sick servant most humanely and was wholly intent on seeing to his health. This example therefore has the life of true faith as its image, and these are the works by which those who glory in the gospel ought today to attest their faith. But we are far too unhappy, since most of us do the opposite, and by our deeds deny Christ whom we profess with our lips. Since the thing itself proves this, no other demonstration is needed.

units.la: Nunc quid Christus Iesus his auditis fecerit, videamus. Primo fidem hanc admiratus fuisse dicitur. Quod non eo sensu accipi debet, quasi aliquid prius sibi ignotum audierit (ipse enim noverat quaecunque sunt in homine, & non semel cogitationes quoque discipulorum in lucem protraxit) sed pro humanitatis assumptae ratione hoc dicitur, in qua affectiones, quae nobis natura adhaerent, nobiscum communes habet. Et facit haec admiratio ad Centurionis commendationem, cuius fides non potuit non eximia esse, quando eam Dei filius admiratione dignam iudicavit. Deinde ad populum conversus publice illam praedicat, & non sine totius Iudaicae gentis ignominia ait: Nec in Israel quidem tantam fidem inveni. Quod non temere ab eo dictum esse patebit, si Centurionem cum Iudaeis, & cum iis quidem qui optimi inter illos erant, adeoque cum ipsius Christi discipulis conferas. Hi enim omnes communia fidei principia habebant, veteres nimirum promissiones, doctrinam legis, ceremonias typicas & prophetarum vaticinia: quae omnia Iesum Christum vel palam & verbis diserte praedicabant, vel typis & figuris adumbrabant. Denique in omnium ore erat Messias, & adventum eius iam in foribus adesse nemo ignorabat. Ergo portento simile videri poterat, quòd illum sese doctrina & miraculis quotidie declarantem tam pauci agnoscerent. At longè alia fuit Centurionis conditio, qui ex idololatriâ oriundus & in ethnicorum superstitionibus enutritus, nihil horum prius audierat, & qui pro more suorum hominum pro fabulis anilibus ea reputare poterat, quae Iudaei de sua redemptione garriebant. Etenim quis Romanorum credidisset, eam gentem Deo peculiariter cordi esse, quae omnium gentium infelicissima erat, & in qua divini favoris vestigia nulla reliquerant? Magnam ergo fuisse oportet Centurionis fidem, quae per tot obstacula eluctari potuit. Deinde hunc à solo Dei verbo pependisse nuper diximus: at illi nova quotidie signa postulabant, verbum verò & doctrinam eius ridebant. Adhaec qui ex Iudaeis crediderant, ij in corporis praesentia adhuc quaerebant, neque eò usque profecerant, ut illum absentem aliquid posse crederent. Notum est enim Iairi exemplum, qui etsi illum filiae iam moriturae opem ferre posse consideret, urgebat tamen eum, ut festinus veniret, & illi manus imponeret. Sed & nobile illud sororum par, Martha & Maria, etiamsi nihil non pro Christo facturae erant, ei tamen dicunt: Domine, si fuisses hic, frater noster non fuisset mortuus. Loci ergo distantia impeditum putabant, quò minus aegrotanti potuerit opem ferre. Quid verò de discipulis dicemus, qui etsi sexcenties illum de sua morte, resurrectione, ascensione & regno caelesti differentem audiissent, eius tamen difficultia discrutiati fuerunt, ut nihil eorum perciperent, quae ab eo dicebantur? Unde verò hoc? Ex eo nimirum, quòd nondum intelligerent, corporis praesentia minimè opus esse ei, cuius divina virtus per omnia extenditur. Itaque omnes istos longè superauit hic Centurio, qui seruulo suo succurri posse credidit, etiamsi Christus tectum suum non subiret. At hodie, qui Euangelicae veritatis primi propugnatores haberi volunt, haereticos nos dicunt, nisi etiam hodie Christum corpore suo nobis praesentem esse fateamur: imò & Coenam mysticam à nobis evacuari, & Christi omnipotentiam atque maiestatem negare clamant, quòd illum corpore suo in caelesti aeterna & beata immortalitatis loco residere affirmemus, & idem eius corpus manibus contrectari, aut realiter & oraliter (ut illi loquuntur) manducari negemus. Atqui nos historiae Euangelicae narrationi & ipsius Christi verbis insistimus, qui se post hac in mundo fore negauit. Neq; ideo omnipotentiam eius negamus, quando cum Centurione credimus, eius verbum nobis ad omnia sufficere, & illum licet corpore supra omnes caelos euectus sit, suo tamen merito, sua virtute, imò sua carne & sanguine nos alere & feruare ad vitam aeternam: eo nimirum modo, quem sola fides capit, & qui crassa illa & corporea praesentia minimè opus habet. Quòd si verum dicere libeat, aduersarij potius omnipotentiam Christi negant, & eius maiestati derogant, quando nobis Christum infirmiorem hodie fingunt, quàm olim fuerit. Olim enim, cùm mortali carne indutus in terris ageret, procul absens corpore omnia videre, in absentium cordibus operari, & salutem conferre potuit. At si istos audiamus, nunc nihil horum poterit, nisi corpus eius manibus nostris palpetur, ori inferatur, dentibus deniq; atteratur. Sic enim Nicolai Papae verba sonant, quae illorum antesignani omnino retinenda esse contendunt. Sunt haec absurda plane, quare ad alia properemus.
units.tr: Now let us see what Christ Jesus did on hearing these things. First, he is said to have marvelled at this faith. This must not be taken as though he had heard something previously unknown to him (for he knew all that is in man, and more than once brought to light even the thoughts of his disciples), but it is said according to the manner of his assumed humanity, in which he shares with us the affections that cling to our nature. This wonder also serves to commend the centurion, whose faith could not but be outstanding, since the Son of God judged it worthy of admiration. Then, turning to the people, he publicly proclaims it, and says, not without shame to the whole Jewish nation: "I have not found such faith even in Israel." That he did not say this rashly will be clear if you compare the centurion with the Jews, and with those who were the best among them, and indeed with Christ's own disciples. For all of these had the common principles of faith: namely the ancient promises, the doctrine of the law, the typical ceremonies, and the prophecies of the prophets. All these either openly and plainly proclaimed Jesus Christ in words, or shadowed him forth in types and figures. Finally, the Messiah was on everyone's lips, and no one was ignorant that his coming was already at the doors. Therefore it might seem a marvel that so few recognised him, when he daily declared himself by his teaching and miracles. But the centurion's condition was very different. Born of idolatry and reared in the superstitions of the heathen, he had heard none of these things beforehand, and, following the custom of his people, could regard as old wives' tales what the Jews were chattering about their redemption. For who among the Romans would have believed that that nation was especially dear to God, a nation the most unhappy of all nations, and in which they could find no traces of divine favour? Great, then, must have been the centurion's faith, to have struggled through so many obstacles. Next, we have said that he depended solely on the word of God; but the Jews demanded new signs every day and mocked his word and teaching. Moreover, those Jews who had believed still sought him in bodily presence, and had not progressed so far as to believe that he could do anything when absent. For there is the example of Jairus, who, although he considered that Jesus could bring help to his daughter who was about to die, nevertheless urged him to come quickly and lay his hands on her. And the noble pair of sisters, Martha and Mary, although they were ready to do anything for Christ, still say to him: "Lord, if you had been here, our brother would not have died." They thought, therefore, that the distance of place prevented him from bringing help to the sick man. What shall we say of the disciples, who, although they had heard him speaking a thousand times about his death, resurrection, ascension and heavenly kingdom, were so troubled by the difficulty of these matters that they grasped none of the things he said? And whence came this? Surely from this: that they did not yet understand that bodily presence was by no means needed by him, whose divine power extends through all things. Thus this centurion far surpassed all those others, for he believed that his servant could be helped even though Christ did not enter his house. But today those who wish to be counted the foremost champions of evangelical truth call us heretics unless we also confess that Christ is present to us today in his body. Indeed, they cry out that we empty the mystical Supper, and deny the omnipotence and majesty of Christ, because we affirm that he sits in heaven in his body, in the eternal, blessed place of immortality, and because we deny that this same body is handled with the hands, or really and orally (as they put it) eaten. Yet we cling to the account of the gospel history and to Christ's own words, in which he said that he would no longer be in the world. Nor do we deny his omnipotence on that account, since we believe with the centurion that his word is enough for all things, and that, although he has been carried above all the heavens in body, he nourishes and preserves us to eternal life by his merit, by his power, and indeed by his flesh and blood: in that manner, namely, which faith alone grasps, and which has no need of that gross and corporeal presence. But if it is right to speak the truth, it is rather our opponents who deny the omnipotence of Christ and detract from his majesty, when today they make Christ weaker for us than he once was. For once, when he lived on earth clothed in mortal flesh, he could see all things while far away in body, work in the hearts of those who were absent, and bestow salvation. But if we listen to them, now he can do none of these things unless his body is touched by our hands, put into the mouth, and finally ground by the teeth. For such are the words of Pope Nicholas, which their leaders insist must be wholly retained. These things are plainly absurd, so let us hasten on to other matters.

units.la: Nam ut Matthaeus annotauit, Christus huic de Centurionis fide testimonio magnificam propmissionem de gentium vocatione, & comminationem grauem de Iudaici populi repudio interseruit, his verbis comprehensam: Dico autem vobis, quòd multi ab Oriente & Occidente venient, & discumbent cum Abrahamo & Isaaco & Iacobo in regno caelorum: filij autem regni eijcientur in tenebras exteriores, illic erit fletus & stridor dentium.
