Confirmantur hoc Christi testimonio quaecunque de gentium vocatione olim prophetae vaticinati sunt, adeoque gentibus hoc loco ostium aperitur, ut se quoque ad regnum Dei iam accessum habere videant. Diserte autem cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo discubituros dicit, ne nobis vel aliam salutem, vel aliam huius consequenda rationem fingamus, quàm quia olim sancti patres gauisi sunt. Vna enim & eadem est omnium credentium tam veteris quàm noui testamenti Ecclesia, vna & eadem utrisque promissa regni caelestis hereditas, eadem etiam utrisque proposita ratio aut via, qua ad illam perueniant. Oportuit autem prophetarum oracula Iudaeis in mentem reuocare, ut generis sui fiducia superbire desinerent, & Centurionis fidem (quem non immeritò gentium primitias dixerit) imitarentur: deinde scandalo etiam mederi voluit Christus, quod ex Iudaeorum contumacia nascebatur: ut nimirum omnes intelligerent, nunquam defuturos, qui ad ipsius Ecclesiam accedant, & in ipso feruentur, etiamsi ab illu con-
units.tr: For as Matthew notes, Christ, in bearing witness to the Centurion's faith, interwove a magnificent promise about the calling of the Gentiles and a grave threat about the rejection of the Jewish people, expressed in these words: "I say to you that many will come from the east and the west, and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the sons of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." By this testimony of Christ are confirmed whatever the prophets of old foretold about the calling of the Gentiles; and so here a door is opened to the Gentiles, that they may see they now also have access to the kingdom of God. Now he says plainly that they will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that we may not invent for ourselves some other salvation or some other way of obtaining it than that by which the holy fathers of old rejoiced. For there is one and the same Church of all believers, both of the Old and of the New Testament; one and the same heavenly inheritance is promised to both, and the same way, or method, by which they attain it, is set before both. Moreover, it was fitting to recall to the Jews the oracles of the prophets, so that they might cease to be puffed up with confidence in their descent and might imitate the faith of the Centurion (whom one may not unfairly call the firstfruits of the Gentiles). Then Christ also wished to remedy the scandal that arose from the obstinacy of the Jews: so that, of course, everyone might understand that there would never be a lack of those who come to his Church and are nourished in him, even if he is despised by those to whose fathers he was once promised, and who (as is said in the parable of the wedding) were the first invited.

units.la: Gentium vocatio & Iudaeorum repudium. temnatur, quorum patribus olim promissus fuit, & qui (vt in nuptiarum parabola dicitur) primi inuitati fuere.
units.tr: The calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews.

units.la: Caeterum ad Centurionem (ad cuius domum interea accesserat, cum iam ante non procul eum abfuisse Lucas dixerit) conuersus Christus ait: Abi, & vt credidisti, fiat tibi. Nec mora, eo ipso momento seruus conualuit, & sanum inuenerunt qui pro illo rogatum miserant. Ita vero re-ipsa docet, se verum Deum & vitae atque salutis authorem vnicum esse. Salutem vero non vno modo semper omnibus attulit. Alios enim ad se venientes contactu suo seruauit, vt doceret, se per incarnationem nobis seruatorem esse factum. Et huc Paulus spectauisse videtur, cum diceret: Christus Iesus in mundum venit, id est, homo factus est, vt peccatores saluos faceret. Etenim cum nemo hominum adipsum ascendere posset in coelos, eum ad nos descendere necesse fuit, vt nostrae naturae vnitus salutificam suam virtutem in nos transfunderet. Alios autem procul absens curauit, vt seruulum illum, & regij vel aulici filium, de quo Ioannis quarto Capite scribitur: Cananeae item illius filiam, cuius historiam Marcus capite septimo narrat. Quibus exemplis diuinitatem suam apertius declarare, & eorum superstitiones confutare voluit, quos circa corporalem eius praesentiam haesuros esse sciebat, vt paulo ante diximus. Obseruare autem oportet, eum communem & vniuersalem omnis loci & ordinis hominum seruatorem esse, vt minime opus sit vitae genus (siquidem id per se honestum sit) mutare, vt salutis in illo participes efficiamur, sicuti de suis ordinibus & sectis Monachi fabulantur. Nam & milites sua gratia dignatus est, & Iosephum Senatorij ordinis virum in discipulorum numero habuit, & postea per Euangelij praedicationem diuites, pauperes, nobiles, seruos, coniuges, caelibes vocatos fuisse scimus: neq; obscurum est illud Pauli: Quisq; in qua vocatione vocatus fuit, in ea maneat. Hoc potius omnes curent, vt quam ille nobis offert, salutem fide vera & constanti apprehendant. Haec enim sola medium illud est, quo Christum amplecti, & tam ipsius quam bonorum eius participes fieri possumus. Et quia haec in Dei verbum respicit, falli & errare non potest, quin quae illud nobis pollicetur inueniat. Promittitur autem nobis per verbum peccatorum remissio, reconciliatio cum Deo, conscientiae pax, salus denique & vita aeterna. Quicunq; ergo haec dona ipsis Christum meruisse credunt, ij procul dubio ea consequentur. Hinc ergo suum illud dogma Apostoli deriuarunt, Sola fide in Christum nos iustificari & saluos fieri. Eadem est omnium aliorum ratio, quae nobis Dei verbo promittuntur. Dicit Christus: Noli timere pusille grex, nam complacitum est Patri vestro dare vobis regnum. Item: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum. Et rursus: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; in consummationem seculi. His si credamus, fiet nobis secundum fidem nostram, & quamuis totus terrarum orbis fremat, & montes quoq; (vt Psaltes ait) loco moueantur, rata tamen erit promissio illa, neque aliquis obstare poterit, quo minus regnum illud possideamus, quod nobis iam inde ab aeterno destinatum est. Similiter Dei promissio est: In die tribulationis tuae inuoca me, & liberabo te. Credamus ergo his verbis, & inuocemus ex fide Deum, quoties vel egestate premimur, vel morbis excruciamur, vel hostium insidijs circumuenti iam nos periturôs putamus, vel conscientiae terroribus vexamur: & procul dubio nos Deus exaudiet. Ita Christum dicentem audimus: Ne estote soliciti de anima vestra quid edduri sitis, aut quid bibituri: neq; de corpore vestro, qua re sitis induendi. Novit enim Pater vester caelestis, vos indigere his omnibus. Sed quaerite primo regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & ista omnia adijcientur vobis. Isti ergo promissioni fidem habeant, quibus res est angustior, & mox sentient benedictionis diuinae fructus vberrimos. Possent ista fusissime tractari, & exempla passim in scripturis occurrunt, quibus ista confirmantur. Sed sufficiat nunc admonuisse, nihil fortius, nihil magis inuictum, nihil laetius, nihil quaesuos esse fide. Haec enim in periculis imperterritos in media morte inuictos, inter dolorum examina alacres, in omnium rerum inopia diuites & saturos reddit: & de hac veritissime exponitur illud Pauli: Pietas ad omnia vtilis est, vt qua habeat promissiones praesentis & futuri seculi. Nec enim pietas vera esse potest, nisi quam fides in nobis gignit. In horum itaq; meditatione frequentes simus hodie, & salutis nostrae authorem, Iesum Christum, fide constanti amplexemur, vt huic ceu fundamento validissimo impositi ad omnem euentum instructi simus, & olim cum eodem in coelis viuamus atq; regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But Christ, turning to the Centurion (to whose house he had meanwhile come, since Luke had said that he was not far away before), said: "Go, and as you have believed, so let it be done for you." Without delay, at that very moment the servant recovered, and those who had been sent to ask on his behalf found him well. In this way he teaches in fact that he is the true God and the one author of life and salvation. Yet he did not always bring salvation to all in the same way. For some who came to him he saved by his touch, to teach that he had become our Saviour through the incarnation. And Paul seems to have looked to this when he said: "Christ Jesus came into the world," that is, he was made man, "so that he might save sinners." For since no man could ascend to him into heaven, it was necessary that he descend to us, so that, united to our nature, he might transfuse his saving power into us. But others he healed while absent and at a distance: the servant boy, and the son of a royal or courtly official, of whom we read in the fourth chapter of John; likewise the daughter of that Canaanite woman, whose history Mark relates in the seventh chapter. By these examples he wished to declare his divinity more openly, and to refute the superstitions of those whom he knew would cling to his bodily presence, as we said a little earlier. It is necessary, moreover, to observe that he is the common and universal Saviour of every place and order of men, so that there is no need to change one's way of life (provided it is in itself honourable) in order that we may become partakers of salvation in him, as the Monks fable about their own orders and sects. For he has deigned to bless soldiers with his grace, he counted among his disciples Joseph, a man of the senatorial order, and afterwards we know that through the preaching of the Gospel rich, poor, noble, slaves, married and unmarried were called; nor is that saying of Paul obscure: "Let each remain in the calling in which he was called." Rather, let all take care to lay hold, with true and steadfast faith, of the salvation which he offers us. For this alone is the means by which we can embrace Christ and become partakers both of him and of his goods. And because this faith looks to the Word of God, it cannot fail or err, but must find that which it promises us. Now there is promised to us through the Word the remission of sins, reconciliation with God, peace of conscience, and finally salvation and eternal life. Therefore whoever believes that Christ has merited these gifts for them will undoubtedly obtain them. Hence the Apostles derived their doctrine, that we are justified by faith alone in Christ and made safe. The reasoning is the same for all the other things that are promised us in God's Word. Christ says: "Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom." Likewise: "In the world you will have tribulation, but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." And again: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." If we believe these things, it will be done for us according to our faith; and although the whole circle of the earth rage, and the mountains (as the Psalmist says) be moved from their place, that promise will nonetheless stand firm, and no one will be able to prevent us from possessing that kingdom which has been destined for us from eternity. Similarly is the promise of God: "In the day of your trouble, call upon me, and I will deliver you." Let us therefore believe these words, and call upon God in faith whenever we are pressed by want, tormented by diseases, or, surrounded by the snares of enemies, think we are already about to perish, or are troubled by the terrors of conscience; and undoubtedly God will hear us. So we hear Christ saying: "Do not be anxious about your soul, what you shall eat or what you shall drink, nor about your body, what you shall put on. For your heavenly Father knows that you have need of all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." Let those, then, whose circumstances are straitened give faith to this promise, and soon they will feel the most abundant fruits of the divine blessing. These matters could be treated at great length, and examples occur everywhere in the Scriptures which confirm them. But for now it is enough to have admonished that nothing is stronger, nothing more invincible, nothing more joyful, nothing more desirable than faith. For it makes men fearless in dangers, unconquered in the midst of death, cheerful amid the trials of pains, rich and satisfied in the want of all things. And of this very truly is that saying of Paul to be understood: "Godliness is profitable for all things, since it has the promises of the present and of the future life." For true godliness cannot exist unless faith begets it in us. Let us, then, today be frequent in the meditation on these things, and let us embrace with steadfast faith Jesus Christ, the author of our salvation, so that, set upon him as upon a most firm foundation, we may be prepared for every outcome, and one day live and reign with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVII.

units.la: Et factum est die sequenti, proficiscebatur in ciuitatem, quæ vocatur Naim, & proficiscebantur cum eo discipuli eius multi, turbaq; multa. Vt autem appropinquauit portæ ciuitatis, ecce defunctus efferebatur, qui filius vnigenitus erat matri suæ, & ipsi quidem viduæ, turba ciuitatis multa erat cum ea. Et intuitus eam Dominus, misericordia commotus est super ea, & dixit: Ne fleto. Cumq; accessisset tetigit loculum (ij vero qui portabant, substiterunt) & dixit: Adolescens, tibi dico, surge. Tunc resedit qui fuerat mortuus, & coepit loqui: & ille dedit eum matri suæ. Coepit autem omnes timor, & glorificabant Deum, dicentes: Certe Propheta magnus surrexit inter nos, & certe Deus respexit populum suum. Peruenitq; iste de eo sermo in totam Iudæam, & in totam regionem circumiacentem.
units.tr: And it came to pass the day after, that he went into a city called Nain; and many of his disciples went with him, and much people. Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow: and much people of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not. And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother. And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people. And this rumour of him went forth throughout all Judaea, and throughout all the region round about.

units.la: Qvoniam æternus Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, ideo in mundum venit & homo factus est, vt humani generis redemptor atque seruator esset, totus in hoc est, vt tam doctrina quam operibus probet, se nos ex omnibus liberare & afferere posse, quæ nobis noxia & formidulosa sunt. Interea autem facile primas tenet mors, quæ cum per peccatum ingressa, & peccati pœna sit, euidens quoque & certum est iræ Dei argumentum, & proinde hominibus nihil ea terribilius esse consueuit. Sæpe ergo docet Christus se huius victorem atque domitorem esse, neque eam posse hac timeri debere, eo quod ipsius merito deuicta, credentibus ex huius sæculi palestra felix ad æternam vitam & patriam cœlestem transitus facta sit. At quia hoc vix credibile videtur, & rationi humanæ vix quicquam tam absurdum est, quam in morte vitam sperare, promissionem illam & doctrinam suam operibus aliquot miraculosis confirmauit. In quorum numero primum censeri potest, quod in Centurionis Capernaitici seruo editum fuisse nuper audiuimus. Hunc enim morti vicinum, imo iam iam morituram & in extremis agentem ex mortis quasi faucibus, solius Verbi sui virtute eripuit. Cui merito subijci debet, quod infra Capite octauo de Iairi, principis Synagogæ, filia habetur, quæ cum iam expirauisset, per eundem Christum vitæ restituta est. Vtrunque autem superat, quod modo recitauimus. Nam iuuenem, qui ante horas aliquot hac vita defunctus iam ad sepulchrum efferebatur, in maxima populi vndiq; confluentis frequentia in vitam reduxit. Quibus adde maximum omnium, quod Lazarum Bethanien sem, qui & sepultus erat, & quartum iam diem in sepulchro agebat, inde in lucem euocauit. Quæ omnia si simul considerentur, euidentissimè apparebit, Christum & vitæ & mortis dominum esse, neq; ei quicquam obstare posse, quo minus nos ex mortis manibus eripiat, siue iam animam agamus, siue omnino expirauerimus, siue in loculo inclusi efferamur, aut etiam terræ mandati putrescamus, imo in terram & cineres iam redacti simus. Est autem doctrina hæc cognitu valde necessaria, cum fidem nostram efficacissimè confirmet, & sola nobis in mortis articulo laborantibus veram consolationem afferre possit; ideoq; proderit singulas huius historiæ partes propius inspexisse.
units.tr: Since the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, came into the world and was made man, in order that he might be the redeemer and saviour of mankind, his whole aim is to prove, by his teaching as well as by his works, that he can free us from all the things that are hurtful and dreadful to us, and can rescue us from them. Meanwhile, death holds the first place among these: since it entered through sin and is the punishment of sin, it is also a plain and certain sign of the wrath of God, and for that reason nothing is usually more terrible to men. Christ therefore often teaches that he is the conqueror and subduer of death, and that it need not be feared, because by his merit it has been overcome, and for believers the passage out of this world's arena to eternal life and the heavenly fatherland has been made happy. But because this seems scarcely credible, and nothing is so absurd to human reason as to hope for life in death, he confirmed that promise and his teaching by several miraculous works. Among these the first may be counted the one we lately heard was performed on the servant of the Capernaum centurion. For he snatched from the very jaws of death a man who was near to death, indeed about to die at once and at the last gasp, by the power of his Word alone. Rightly to be set alongside this is what is recorded in chapter eight below, about the daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, who, when she had already breathed her last, was restored to life by the same Christ. But what we have just recited surpasses both. For he brought back to life a young man who had died some hours earlier and was already being carried out to the tomb, in the presence of a great crowd of people flocking together from every side. To these add the greatest of all, that he called forth from the tomb Lazarus of Bethany, who had been buried and had already spent four days in the grave. If all these things are considered together, it will be most clearly evident that Christ is the Lord both of life and of death, and that nothing can stand in the way of his rescuing us from the hands of death, whether we are already breathing our last, or have expired altogether, or are carried out shut up in a coffin, or have even been committed to the earth and are rotting, indeed have already been reduced to earth and ashes. Now this teaching is very necessary to know, since it most effectively confirms our faith, and it alone can bring true comfort to us who are struggling at the point of death; therefore it will be profitable to look more closely at the individual parts of this story.

units.la: Orditur autem Euangelista a loci notatione & testibus, qui miraculo huic interfuerunt. Christum enim Naim versus iter fecisse scribit, quæ ciuitas Galilææ fuit, non procul a monte Thabor & Cana, quam aquæ in vinum mutatione nobilitatam a Domino fuisse, Ioannes prodidit. Habuit autem in ea profectione Iesus maximum comitatum ex discipulis, id est, ijs, qui iam ipsi nomen deferant, eumq; magistrum & præceptorem suum agnoscebant. Accessit his ingens multitudo populi, qui ex omnibus locis ad illum diuersas ob causas solebat confluere. Et hi simul omnes iam nonproculà porta ciuitatis aberant, quo loco Iudæi ex veteri more conuentus publicos agere & iudicia exercere solebant. Faciunt ista omnia ad miraculi huius certitudinem, ne quis hic aliquid fingi suspicetur, in primis tamen ipse Christus nobis spectandus est, qui signa sua omnia non sine certa ratione fecit in publico & maxima hominum frequentia: nimirum vt & pluribus innotesceret, & eorundem fructus esset vberior. Ita vero suspicionibus mederi voluit, ne quis eum ex impostorum numero putet, qui cum prestigijs vtantur, consultò angulos & tenebras quærunt, quò facilius apud rudes, & rerum imperitos sua figmenta venditent. Fuerunt tales iam olim, qui (vt Paulus scribit) hoc culte in familias obrepere, & muliercularum superstitiosarum simplicitati insidias struere solebant. Quos hodie ferè fraterculi & monachi imitantur, qui inconsultus & plerunq; inscijs ecclesiarum pastoribus hinc inde sua somnia spargunt, & ementitis miraculis populu circunducunt, quæ nullis certis testibus possunt probari. Neq; multum ab horum moribus absunt Anabaptistæ, qui vt inter suæ farinæ homines audacissimi sunt, & nihil non suis auditoribus pollicentur: ita nihil minus ferre possunt, quàm vt quis eos ad reddendam doctrinæ suæ rationem in lucem protrahat. De quibus omnibus dici potest, quod Ioan.3.cap.dicit Christus: Omnis qui perues: agit, odit lucem, nec venit ad lucem, ne arguantur opera ipsius. Merito igitur pijs omnibus illi suspecti esse debent.
units.tr: The Evangelist begins with the naming of the place and with the witnesses who were present at this miracle. He writes that Christ made his journey to Nain, a city of Galilee, not far from Mount Tabor and Cana, which John reports was made famous by the Lord's changing of water into wine. In that journey Jesus had a great company of disciples, that is, of those who already bore his name and acknowledged him as their master and teacher. A huge crowd of people joined them, who were accustomed to flock to him from all places for various reasons. And all of them were by now not far from the city gate, where the Jews, following their ancient custom, held public assemblies and carried on judicial business. All these things contribute to the certainty of this miracle, lest anyone suspect that something has been invented here. Yet above all Christ himself is to be considered, who performed all his signs not without a definite reason, in public and before a great gathering of people: plainly so that they might become known to many and bear richer fruit. He wished in this way to remove suspicions, lest anyone think him one of those impostors who, when they use tricks, deliberately seek corners and darkness, so that they may more easily peddle their fictions among the simple and the ignorant. Such men existed even in old times, who (as Paul writes) were accustomed to creep craftily into households and to lay snares for the simplicity of silly, superstitious women. Today the little friars and monks largely imitate them: without consultation, and mostly without the knowledge of the ministers of the churches, they scatter their dreams here and there and lead the people about with lying miracles, which cannot be proved by any reliable witnesses. The Anabaptists are not far removed from the ways of these men; since they are the boldest of men of their kind, they promise their hearers everything, yet they can bear nothing less than that anyone should drag them into the light to give an account of their teaching. Of all these men it may be said what Christ says in John chapter 3: "Everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works should be reproved." Rightly, therefore, all the godly ought to regard them with suspicion.

units.la: Sed pergamus in historiæ huius tractatione. Cùm ad portam ciuitatis Christus appropinquasset, pulcherrima ædendi miraculi occasio se obtulit. Ecce enim effertur ad sepulturam quidam defunctus: filius nimirum viduæ cuiusdam, & quidem vnigenitus: quæ causa fuit, vt funus hoc non sine matris luctu acerbissimo & magna ciuium frequentia, qui illam officij causa comitabantur, ducere tur. In hos ergo cum suis Christus incidit: quod Epicureus aliquis fortuitum & ex contingentia nescio quâ factum fuisse diceret. At nos, qui Christum æternam Dei sapientiam esse scimus, qui non præsentia modò, verumetiam quæ præterita & futura sunt cognita habet, illù occulto suæ prouidentiæ consilio profectionem hanc ita instituisse & maturasse credimus, vt occasionem noui miraculi haberet, quo eos etiam ad sui cognitionem excitaret, quibus hucusque incognitus fuerat. Quia enim Deus nos in quærenda salute tardiores esse nouit, ipse pro sua erga nos bonitate nos quærere, & omni occasione diligenter vti consueuit, quâ nobis docendis aut seruandis idoneâ esse videt. Quò magis nos quoq; intentos esse decet, ne quando ipsi nobis defuisse, & illius bonitatem contempsisse videamur. Quid enim tales maneat, multorum exemplis docemur, in primis autem Iudæorum, quos hoc potissimum nomine per prophetas olim Deus accusauit, & de quibus Christus maximè queritur, quòd diem suæ visitationis non agnoscant, & proinde excindendos fore minatur.
units.tr: But let us go on with the treatment of this story. When Christ had come near to the city gate, a most beautiful occasion for performing the miracle presented itself. For behold, a dead man was being carried out for burial: the son, of course, of a certain widow, and indeed her only son. This was the reason why the funeral was led forth not without his mother's most bitter grief and a great crowd of citizens, who accompanied her out of duty. Christ therefore met these people with his followers; an Epicurean might say that this happened by chance and from some contingency or other. But we, who know that Christ is the eternal wisdom of God, who has knowledge not only of present things but also of things past and future, believe that by the hidden counsel of his providence he arranged and hastened this journey in such a way that he would have an occasion for a new miracle, by which he might also rouse to the knowledge of himself those to whom he had hitherto been unknown. For since God knows that we are slow to seek salvation, he, out of his goodness toward us, is accustomed himself to seek us and to make diligent use of every opportunity which he sees fit for teaching or saving us. All the more ought we also to be attentive, lest at some time we seem to have failed him ourselves and to have despised his goodness. For we are taught by the examples of many how such men remain; and especially by the example of the Jews, whom God in times past accused through the prophets chiefly on this ground, and about whom Christ most of all complains, because they do not recognize the day of their visitation, and therefore threatens that they will be cut off.

units.la: Cæterum hoc loco tota funerum ratio nobis consideranda venit, in quibus olim variè erratum fuisse, & hodie etiam passim errari constat. Etsi enim apud gentes olim pleriq; intellexerint defunctorum rationem esse habendam, quos illi sacros esse censebant (vt Plinius & Plutarchus annotarunt) non defuerunt tamen barbari quidam, qui omni humanitatis sensu abiecto, mortuorum corpora partim crudeliter, partim ignominiosè tractarunt. Lothophagi enim illa temere in mare abiiciebant, parum interesse putantes, igne ne aut aqua dissoluerentur. Sabæi defunctos nihil à stercore differre sentiebant, & proinde apud illos regum quoq; corpora in sterquilinium abijci solebant. Apud Troglodytas mos fuit, vt mortui ceruicem pedibus alligarent, & raptim cum risu & iocis efferrent, nullaq; loci ratione habita terræ mandarent, & ad caput cornu caprinum affigerent. Thraces quoque funera cum risu & gaudio publico deduxisse; è contra verò natales suorum lachrymis prosecuti fuisse scribuntur. Quos etsi quidam laudauerint, ego tamen illos summa reprehensione dignos iudico, quia neq; Dei beneficiu, quod in huius vitæ vsu nobis confert, rectè intellexerunt, neq; communem omniū sortem, cuius nos mors admonere debet, obseruarunt. Neq; alia illis huius instituti causa fuit, quàm quòd in præsente modò vitam intenti, quæ curarum atq; laborum plena est, beatæ resurrectionis atq; immortalitatis spem ignorauerunt. Hircanos autem vita functos canibus deuorandos proiecisse, Strabo scribit, quos ideo sepulchrales dicebant. Superarunt hos omnes immanitate Scythæ, qui mortuos inter epulas honoris causa vorare soliti fuerunt. Et hos quidem, vt à communi humanitatis sensu alienos, merito omnes detestantur. Plerisque autem in vsu fuit, vt defunctorum corpora magnificè ornata in rogo sublimiori cum aromatum congerie & rebus pretiosissimis comburerent, inde cineres in vrnam conditos in locum aliquem honorationem collocarent. Apud vulgus tamen sepulturæ mos obtinuit, quòd ea nimio labore & non magnis impensis perficeretur. Plurimùm tamen peccatum fuit superstitione, quæ funeribus sacrificia adhibere, et infinita alia facere docuit, quibus illi defunctorum animas adiuuari credebant, vt citius & facilius ad campos Elysios transirent. Inter Christianos autem, etsi tumulandi mos passim receptus sit, posteris tamen temporibus funera non minus superstitiosè duci coeperunt, quâ olim apud gentes, & ceremoniæ adhibitæ sunt. bitæ sunt, quæ sacrificulis quidem & monachis quæstuosæ fuerunt, salutis verò spem, quam credentibus Christi promissiones faciunt, maxima ex parte labefactarunt. Cuius erroris præcipua causa fuit ignis lustralis aut purgatorij (vt illi loquuntur) commentum, quo animas expiari oportere finxerunt, adiuuari autem sacris illis, quæ pro mortuis facienda esse docebant. Quod vt facilius persuaderent, ossuaria extrui curarunt, in quibus offa è sepulchris eruta in struem compositæ, vt his vt fis ad animas ex purgatorij igne liberandas facilius omnes excitarentur. Itaq; cum temporis progressu creuit superstitio, & huc luxus fastusq; accessit, quo post mortem quoq; vana flemmatum & generis sui ostentatione homines ambitiosi superbire in animum induxerunt. Extruuntur ergo à nonnullis magnificæ monumentorum moles, ornantur hæ peristylijs & insignibus familiarum, suspenduntur arma, & fere armatam sui effigiem illic cum terrore exhibent, quorum corpora iam à vermibus & tineis devorantur. Imò ea nonnullorum est confidentia, vt aromatibus condiri velint, quibus corpora feruentur: ita animirum diuinam sententiam eludere conantes, quæ nos in terram reditu ros statuit. Sunc hæc omnia indigna Christianis hominibus, quos mortis consideratione cumpriimis humiliari, & in funeribus certam salutis per Christum nobis exhibitæ spem publice testari convenit. Videamus igitur in hoc exemplo, quis olim in populo Dei funerum deducendorum mos fuerit, & quid hodie à nobis fieri debeat.
units.tr: Next, we must consider the whole ceremonial of funerals, in which it is clear that people have gone astray in various ways in former times, and still go astray in many places today. Although many among the nations once understood that the dead should be honoured, since they regarded them as sacred (as Pliny and Plutarch observed), there were nonetheless some barbarians who, having cast off all sense of humanity, treated corpses partly with cruelty and partly with contempt. The Lothophagi threw their dead carelessly into the sea, thinking it made little difference whether they were dissolved by fire or by water. The Sabaeans believed the dead differed in no way from dung, and so among them even the bodies of kings were customarily cast onto the dunghill. Among the Troglodytes it was the custom to tie the dead man's neck to his feet, carry him out hastily with laughter and jokes, bury him with no regard for the place, and fix a goat's horn to his head. The Thracians too are written of as having escorted funerals with laughter and public rejoicing, while on the contrary they lamented the birthdays of their own people with tears. Although some have praised these customs, I judge them deserving of the strongest reproof, because they understood neither God's benefit, which he bestows on us in the use of this life, nor the common lot of all, which death ought to remind us of. Nor had they any other reason for this practice than that, being intent only on the present life, which is full of cares and labours, they were ignorant of the hope of a blessed resurrection and of immortality. Strabo writes that the Hyrcanians, when they died, threw their bodies to be devoured by dogs, and for this reason called them "sepulchral." The Scythians surpassed all these in savagery, for they were accustomed to devour their dead at feasts as a mark of honour. These people, as strangers to the common sense of humanity, are rightly detested by all. Most peoples, however, had the custom of burning the bodies of the dead, richly adorned, on a high pyre with a heap of spices and the most precious things, and then of placing the ashes, gathered into an urn, in some honoured place. Among the common people, however, burial prevailed, because it could be carried out with little labour and at small expense. Yet the greatest error was made through superstition, which taught that sacrifices should be added to funerals and countless other rites performed, by which people believed the souls of the dead were helped to pass more quickly and easily to the Elysian Fields. Among Christians, although the custom of burial was generally accepted, in later times funerals likewise began to be conducted with no less superstition than once among the nations, and ceremonies were added, which were indeed profitable to the little priests and monks, but for the most part undermined the hope of salvation which the promises of Christ hold out to believers. The chief cause of this error was the invention of the lustral or purgatorial fire (as they call it), in which they pretended souls must be cleansed, and which they taught could be relieved by those rites that were to be performed for the dead. To persuade people more easily of this, they took care to build charnel-houses, in which bones dug up from graves were piled up, so that by such sights everyone might be more readily stirred to free souls from the fire of purgatory. And so, as superstition grew with the passing of time, luxury and pride were added, and men given to ambition came to think that even after death they might swell with vain pride through the display of their ancestry and family. Therefore some erect magnificent monuments and tombs, which are adorned with colonnades and family crests; weapons are hung up, and an effigy of the deceased, nearly in armour, is displayed there to inspire terror, though their bodies are already being devoured by worms and moths. Indeed some are so bold that they wish their bodies to be embalmed with spices, trying in this way to mock the divine sentence which has decreed that we shall return to the earth. All these things are unworthy of Christians, who ought above all to be humbled by the thought of death, and who ought to bear public witness at funerals to the sure hope of salvation offered us through Christ. Let us therefore see, from this example, what custom once prevailed among the people of God in conducting funerals, and what ought to be done by us today.

units.la: Primò ad portam ciuitatis Christo illi obuiam veniunt, vt defunctum terræ mandarent atq; sepeliant. Hic ergo mos fuit Iudæorum, vt corpora exanima in sepulchra conderent. Est hic mos omnium vetustissimus, vt in Abrahami & aliorum patriarcharum exemplis est videre, & cum Dei sententia conuenit, cuius modò meminimus: Terra es, & in terram conuerteris. Neque hic aliquem moueat, quòd nonnulli sepulchra in petris excìderunt, quale Iosephi Arimathæi fuit, in quo Christi corpus conditum fuisse legimus. Hoc enim fecerunt, vt futuræ resurrectionis spem confirmarent, & publice testarentur fidem suam, qua corpora olim vitæ restituenda fore credebant. Quæ etiam causa fuit, quòd ea condire solebant. Et necesse erat, veterum fidem pluribus adminiculis iuuari, eò quòd illis omnia obscurius promissa & adumbrata erant. At nos illis minimè opus habemus, neq; decet vt ad elementa hæc imbecilliora conuertamur, quibus lux plena & perfecta iampridem in Christo affulsit. Sufficiat ergo nobis simplex sepulcræ ritus, vt in terram corpora deponatur, vnde primi Adami corpus desumptum esse scimus. Nec enim temere sic Deus instituit. Nam nostræ originis simul & conditionis nos ritus iste sepeliendi admonet, quando nos iam à reliqua natura abdicatos (vt Plinij verbis vtar) terræ suo gremio complexa, tum maximè vt mater operit. Quod qui nō ofcitan ter expendunt, ij neq; huius seculi bonis fidunt, neq; aduersus Deum superbiunt. Imò hic ad veram humilitatem acerrimus stimulus est, si sepulchri nos tandem exceptuji foueam nobis sæpe ob oculos ponamus, & cogitemus nos non multò post in terram, quam nunc pedibus calcamus, reuersuros esse. Hæc consideratio Abrahamum mouit, vt quàmuis omni virtutum genere omnes alios excelleret, in Dei tamen conspectu sese extremè humiliauerit: nimirum quòd se puluerem & cinerem esse cogitaret. Quod ipsum de Dauide & aliis sanctis dicere possumus. Deinde ad consolationem notri aduersus mortis terrores plurimùm facit sepulturæ consideratio. Nam sementis instar illa est, & vt semina terræ mandata cum fœnore proueniunt: ita corpora, quæ in terram sepeliuntur, olim glorificata & ab omni corruptione libera resurgent. Admonet de hoc Christus, quando seipsum aduersus mortis horam iam appropinquantem hoc argumento consolatur, sic dicens: Venit tempus, quo glorificetur Filius hominis. Amen amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti lapsum in terram, mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: si verò mortuum fuerit, multum fructum affert. Quibus verbis docemur, non vtile modò, sed necessarium esse, vt corpora nostra in terram resoluantur, & proinde Dei consilium non rectè ab illis expendi, qui alias condendorum aut seruandorum funerum rationes excogitant, aut offa è sepulchris effodiunt, vt ea contra veterus ecclesiæ morem spectanda proponant. Hoc enim perinde est, ac si quis femina priusquam excreuerunt ex sulcis eruat, & inde fructum aliquem speret.
units.tr: First, they come to meet Christ at the city gate, so that they might bury the dead man in the earth and inter him. This was therefore the custom of the Jews, to place lifeless bodies in tombs. This is the oldest custom of all, as can be seen in the examples of Abraham and the other patriarchs, and it agrees with God's sentence which we have just recalled: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Nor should it trouble anyone that some hewed tombs out of rocks, as was the case with the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, in which we read that Christ's body was laid. They did this to strengthen the hope of the future resurrection and to bear public witness to their faith, by which they believed that bodies would one day be restored to life. This was also the reason they used to embalm them. And it was necessary that the faith of the ancients be supported by many aids, because all things were promised to them more obscurely and in shadowy form. But we have no need of those things, nor is it fitting that we should turn back to these weaker elements, since the full and perfect light has long since shone forth in Christ. Let the simple rite of burial suffice us, that bodies be laid down in the earth, from which we know the body of the first Adam was taken. For God did not establish this arbitrarily. This rite of burial reminds us both of our origin and of our condition, since nature, having cut us off from the rest of creation (to use Pliny's words), then embraces us in her bosom and covers us as a mother does. Those who weigh this carefully trust neither in the goods of this age nor are proud against God. Indeed, there is a most piercing spur here to true humility, if we often set before our eyes the pit of the tomb that at last receives us, and consider that we shall soon return to the earth which we now tread under our feet. This consideration moved Abraham, so that although he excelled all others in every kind of virtue, he nevertheless humbled himself greatly in the sight of God, namely because he considered that he was dust and ashes. The same may be said of David and the other saints. Furthermore, the thought of burial greatly serves to console us against the terrors of death. For it is like a sowing, and just as seeds committed to the earth come up with increase, so bodies which are buried in the earth will one day rise glorified and free from all corruption. Christ reminds us of this when, comforting himself with this argument against the hour of death now drawing near, he says: "The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Truly, truly I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." By these words we are taught that it is not only useful but necessary that our bodies be dissolved into the earth, and therefore that God's purpose is not rightly weighed by those who devise other ways of disposing of or preserving the dead, or who dig bones out of tombs, to set them up for veneration contrary to the ancient custom of the Church. For this is just as if someone should dig up seeds from the furrows before they have sprouted, and hope for some fruit from them.

units.la: Deinde extra vrbem illi defunctum, efferunt, ex quo apparet, illius sepulturæ locum non intra mœnia, sed foris fuisse: quod ipsum quoq; ex veteri more cum aliis commune habuerunt. Nam Lazari etiam sepulchrum extra Bethaniam fuisse constat, vt & Iosephi Arimathæi extra Hierosolymam quitus fuerunt. lymam fuit. Et in monumentis, quæ extra vrbem Gergesenorum erant, domicilium suum habuit Dæ moniacus, de quo Marcus Cap. 5. scribit. Quem morem apud gentes quoque alias receptum fuisse, historici tradunt. Persarum enim reges in monte, qui Persepolis arci ab Oriente imminebat, & Re gius dicebatur, sepeliri solebant. Et quàmuis Romæ aliquando sepulchra in vrbe admissa fuerint, illud tamen posteris temporibus sub Cos. Duellio Senatus inhibuit. Et scribit Vlpianus, Adrianum Imperatorem pœnam statuisse aureorum quadraginta in eos, qui in ciuitate sepulchrum fecißent, quam sisco inferri iußit; & eadem pœna etiam magistratus multari voluit, qui id passi forent: quin & locum publicari iußit, & cadauera inde transferri. Quò etiam referri potest, quod Appianus scri bit, inter præcipua, cur legem Agrariam recusarint diuites, fuisse, quòd impium ducerent, monumen ta maiorum ad alienos transferre. At nunquam hoc prætexere poterant, nisi sepulchra illi in agris habuissent. Etsi verò gentibus instituti huius fortassis præcipua causa fuit, vt in vrbibus munditiæ seruaretur, & aer minus inficeretur ex cadauerum putrescentium fœtore, tamen in Dei populo ma ius mysterium obseruatum fuit. Nam funerum deductione extra vrbes publicè testabantur, defun ctos iam è mundo exiuisse, et alterius ciuitatis ciues factos esse: eius nimirum, quam in cœlis habent, quotquot per fidem filij Dei facti sunt. Proderat etiam mos iste ad cauendum superstitionem, ne quæ sacra pro mortuis instituerentur, sed se omni erga illos officio iam defunctos esse scirent, qui illos ho nestè tumulari curauerant. Et morem hunc inter Christianos homines diu seruatum fuisse, multis argumentis probari poterat, & illius vestigia adhuc extant in multis vetustis & celebrioribus op pidis. At postquam crescente superstitione sacra pro defunctis fieri cœperunt, tunc etiam sepulturæ locum templis vicinum esse voluerunt sacrificuli & monachi, vt sacra illa facilius obire, & quæstum maiorem facere possent. Et illis libenter morem gesserunt, qui etiam ipsi superstitione decepti cere moniis illis plus quàm gentilitijs animas iuuari credebant. Constat certè hanc præcipuam supersti tionum causam fuisse, neque vllum vnquam excogitatum esse aucupium quæstuosius, quàm quod ex funeribus & exequijs sacrificuli papistici instituerunt. Nam & locum sepulturæ ex publico priua tum, & sui iuris fecerunt. Eundem postea pretio vendiderunt, Hebrone illo barbaro iniquiores, qui Abrahamo agri sui vsum gratuitum offerebat, vt in eo vxoris corpus sepeliret. Pretium item sepulchri pro loci ratione auxerunt. Nam qui multum numerant, intra vestibulû, aut etiam ipsum templum admitti solent, qui verò minus, iį sub dio compluuntur. Adhæc ex mortuis tributa an nuá colligunt, quando non sufficit ipso sepulturæ die sumptum fecisse, nisi funebria sacra octauo die, tricesimo item, & deinde quotannis repetas. Itaque per illorum auaritiam ne mori quidem & com putrescere gratis licet. Neque illos Superstitionis & nundinationis huius pudet, etiamsi eam nullo venerandæ vetustatis exemplo, multò minus autem Dei verbo probari posse satis norint. Nam et si in Lege sua Deus sacrificia omnis generis instituerit, & eadem in suas species mira diligentia di stinxerit, nullam tamen prorsus sacrorum pro defunctis mentionem fieri scimus: neq; ea inter Chri stianos homines locum habere debent, quando fidem in Christum labefactant, qui eos, qui in se cre dunt, non vllum post mortem iudicium subire, sed recta ad vitam æternam transire docet. Ad mor tuos sane nullam ex iis, quæ superstites faciunt, vtilitatem redire, Cicero intellexit, cuius hæc ver ba in primo Thusc. quæst. leguntur: Mortuorum corpora nihil sentiunt in sepultura: quantum autem consuetudini famæq; dandum sit, id curént viui, sed ita, vt intelligant nihil ad mortuos pertinere. Facilius autem superstitionis huius reliquiæ ex omnium cordibus tollentur, si sepulturæ locus pro cul à templis remoueatur, et passim vetus ille mos reducatur, de quo ante diximus. Etenim nimiùm inepti & ridiculi sunt, qui pro loco sepulturæ contendunt, quando constat omnem terram Domini esse, & olim non terram modò, verumetiam mare & reliquas mundi partes omnes reddituras esse mortuos, qui in illis consumpti sunt. Quin potius, vt bene & pie moriamur, nobis curæ sit: tunc enim quouis loco ossa nostra probè quiescent, & vt prophani poetæ testimonio in superstitiosorum islorum ignominiam vtar:
units.tr: Next, they carried the dead person out of the city, which shows that the place of burial was outside the walls and not within them. They shared this custom with other peoples too, as an old tradition. It is well established that Lazarus's tomb was outside Bethany, and that of Joseph of Arimathea outside Jerusalem. The demoniac described by Mark in chapter 5 also made his home in the tombs outside the city of the Gergesenes. Historians record that this custom was also accepted among other nations. The kings of Persia were buried on the mountain that rose to the east of the citadel of Persepolis, called the Royal Mountain. Although at one time tombs were allowed within Rome, the Senate forbade this in later times, under the consulship of Duellius. Ulpian writes that the Emperor Hadrian set a penalty of forty gold pieces on anyone who built a tomb within the city, which he ordered to be paid into the treasury. He also wanted magistrates who allowed it to be fined the same amount. Indeed, he ordered the site to be confiscated and the bodies to be moved from it. To this may also be referred what Appian writes: among the chief reasons why the rich rejected the agrarian law was that they thought it wicked to transfer the monuments of their ancestors to strangers. They could never have pleaded this unless they had tombs on their estates. Although the chief reason for this custom among the nations was perhaps that the cities might be kept clean and the air less polluted by the stench of rotting corpses, among the people of God a greater mystery was observed. For by carrying the dead out beyond the cities, they publicly bore witness that the departed had now gone out of the world and had become citizens of another city, namely the one they have in heaven, all who have been made children of God through faith. This custom also served to guard against superstition, so that no rites would be established for the dead, and people would know that they had already performed every duty toward those who had seen to it that they were honourably buried. That this custom was long kept among Christians could be proved by many arguments, and traces of it still survive in many old and famous towns. But after superstition grew and rites began to be performed for the dead, the priests and monks wanted the place of burial to lie close to the churches, so that they could perform those rites more easily and make greater profit. And they gladly indulged those who, themselves deceived by superstition, believed that souls were helped more by these ceremonies than by pagan ones. It is certain that this was the chief cause of superstition, and no more profitable racket was ever devised than the one the Popish priests set up from funerals and burial rites. For they took the place of burial out of public use and made it their own private property. Then they sold it again for a price, being more unjust than that barbarian of Hebron who offered Abraham the free use of his field so that he might bury his wife in it. They also raised the price of a grave according to the site. Those who pay a large sum are usually admitted within the porch or even into the church itself, while those who pay less are left to the open air. Besides this, they collect annual dues from the dead, as if it were not enough to have paid the costs on the day of burial unless they repeat the funeral rites on the eighth day, then on the thirtieth, and afterwards every year. So, because of their greed, it is not even permitted to die and rot without payment. Nor are they ashamed of this superstition and trade, though they know well enough that it cannot be supported by any example of venerable antiquity, much less by the word of God. For although God in his Law instituted sacrifices of every kind and distinguished them with wonderful care into their several kinds, we know that no mention at all is made of sacrifices for the dead. Nor ought such things to have any place among Christians, since they undermine faith in Christ, who teaches that those who believe in him do not undergo any judgement after death but pass straight to eternal life. That the living gain no benefit for the dead from what they do for them, Cicero understood, and his words are read in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations: "The bodies of the dead feel nothing in the grave; but how much should be given to custom and reputation, the living must consider, yet in such a way that they understand it has nothing to do with the dead." The remnants of this superstition will be more easily removed from everyone's hearts if the place of burial is moved far from the churches and that old custom, of which we spoke before, is restored everywhere. For those who contend about the place of burial are extremely foolish and ridiculous, since it is established that the whole earth belongs to the Lord, and that one day not only the earth but also the sea and all the other parts of the world will give back the dead who have been consumed in them. Rather, let us take care to die well and piously, for then our bones will rest safely in any place. And, to turn the testimony of a profane poet against the ignominy of those superstitious people:

units.la: — Tabes ne cadavera soluatAn rogus, haud refert: placido natura receptatCunƈta sinu, sinemque sui sibi corpora debent. Item:Libera fortuna mors est, capit omnia tellus, Quae genuit, cælo tegitur qui non habet vrnam.
units.tr: Whether putrefaction or the pyre dissolves the corpse, it makes no difference; nature receives all things in her gentle bosom, and the bodies owe their end to themselves. Likewise: Death is a free fortune; the earth takes all things. He who has no urn is covered by the sky, whatever the earth has produced.

units.la: Interim Christianos homines decet, sepulturæ publicæ locum sacrum putare, neq; permittere vt vllis prophanis vsibus violetur. Etsi enim improborum petulantia defunctis nihil incommodet, eadem tamen frænanda & Christianæ disciplinæ legibus coercenda est, ne eorum fidem ridere & ijs insultare videamur, quorum corpora cum in vius essent, Spiritus sancti templa fuerunt, nunc autem in Christo lopita quiescunt. Veteres certè sepulturæ loca κοιμητήρια, quasi dormitiones dixere, quòd corpora piorum illic quiescant, olim resurrectura sub nouissimum Iesu Christi aduentum, vt & ipsa beatæ immortalitatis præmio ornentur. Etenim, vt rursus ad exteros transeamus, nulla ex gentibus non omnino barbaris tam efferata fuit, quæ non senserit sepulchrorum habendam esse rationem. Apud Athenienses certè tanta eorum cura fuit, vt etiam peremptos bello, si quis dux sepulturæ honore vel per negligentiam fraudasset, capite plecteretur. In Romanis verò legibus, hæc etiam habetur: Vbi corpus demortui hominis condas, locus sacer esto. Et Vlpianus, Sepulchri (inquit) violati actio infamiam irrogat. Imò grauiter multatos olim fuisse legimus, qui bustum violauissent, aut ex sepulchro columnam deiecissent aut fregissent. Quò magis Christianos homines curare decet, vt superstitiones quidem, quæ cum fide nostra pugnant, deuitent, non minus autem caueant, ne publica sepultura prophanis vsibus violentur.
units.tr: Christians ought to regard the public place of burial as sacred, and not allow it to be profaned for any common uses. For although the wantonness of the wicked does no harm to the dead, it must nevertheless be restrained and checked by the laws of Christian discipline, lest we seem to mock their faith and insult those whose bodies, while they were alive, were temples of the Holy Spirit, and which now rest in Christ. Certainly the ancients called the places of burial "cemeteries" [κοιμητήρια], that is, sleeping-places, because the bodies of the pious rest there, to rise again at the last coming of Jesus Christ, and so that they may be adorned with the reward of blessed immortality. For, to turn again to foreign nations, there has been no people, not utterly barbarous and savage, that has not recognised the need to respect tombs. Among the Athenians their care was so great that anyone who, through carelessness or deliberately, denied honourable burial even to men killed in war, was punished by death. In Roman law this also holds: "Where you bury the body of a dead man, let the place be sacred." And Ulpian says: "An action for violating a tomb brings infamy." Indeed, we read that in former times those who violated a grave, or threw down or broke a column from a tomb, were severely punished. All the more, then, should Christians take care to avoid superstitions that fight against our faith, and equally to guard against the public burial place being violated by profane uses.

units.la: Et hucetiam pertinet, quod de funeris deductione hic tertio loco additur: quod nimirum multa ciuitatis turba vidua comitata sit, & hanc defleuisse, Christi ipsam mox consolationis verba testan- tur. Debent ergo funera honestè deduci, vt ita non amorem modò erga defunctos et eorum agnatos, verumetiam fidem atq; spem resurrectionis testemur. Et vt id publicè & cum populi frequentia fiat prodest, vt ad plures redeat fructus, qui ex communis sortis nostræ consideratione nascitur. Quod Solomon obseruauit, sic scribens: Melius est adire domum luctus quàm domum conuiuij: illic enim finis omnium hominum cernitur, & qui superstes viuit id reponit in corde suo. Constat certè vix alia re homines magis abstterreri à peccandi licentia, & ad vitæ innocentiam excitari, quàm si se mortales esse, & vitæ huius finem sibi in singula momenta appropinquare cogitent. Ideo Sirachides ille dicebat: In omnibus factis tuis memento finis extremi, & non vnquam peccabis. At in funeribus cauendum est, ne luctus fit nimius, qualis (vt Paulus ait) eorum esse solet, qui spem resurrectionis & vitæ æternæ prorsus ignorant. Vt enim humanum est eorum mortem lugere, qui de nobis bene meriti sunt, aut quorum vsus in repub. vel ecclesia magnus fuit: ita charitatis officium est, pia compassione eos consolari, ad quos luctus ille propter cognationis vinculum propius pertingit. Et notum est illud Apostoli: Gaudete cum gaudentibus, plorate cum plorantibus. Sunt item exempla sanctissimorum hominum, qui suorum funera pijs lachrymis prosecuti sunt. Fecit hoc in dilecta coniugis Sarae obitu Abrahamus pater credentium. Et Iosephum in Iacobi patris sui mortui faciem ruisse & fleuisse legimus. Stephanum quoq; cum planctu magno extulerunt viri religiosi, quòdipsis doleret, ecclesiam tam præclaro organo orbatam esse. At quid exemplis pluribus opus est, quando solius Christi vnicum sufficit, quem ob Lazari mortem & sororum eius pias lamentationes illachrymauisse, Ioannes testatur? Non ergo vel pij vel fortes aut magnanimes, sed potius inhumani & impij sunt, qui & suorum obitus & aliorum luctum atq; iustum dolorem siccis oculis & absq; omni animorum commotione intueri possunt. Sed vt ante diximus, dolorem nostrum moderari atq; temperari debet fides nostra in Christum, quæ defunctos iam in vitam beatiorem translatos esse, nos autem quoad in huius vitæ palæstra agimus, Deo curæ fore docet. Cauenda item est in funerum deductionibus ambitio: quia vt superbia omni tempore & loco Christianis hominibus indigna, sic detestabilis omnino est, si ei in morte locum demus, quæ (vt poeta ethnicus vidit) æquo pede pulsat pauperum tabernas Regumq; turres, & in qua nobis de communi omnium sorte diligentius erat cogitandum. Et ista quidem de hac re dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: This also applies to what is added here in the third place about the funeral procession: that a great crowd of the city accompanied the widow, and that they wept for her, as Christ's own words of comfort soon bear witness. Funerals ought therefore to be conducted honourably, so that we bear witness not only to our love for the dead and their kinsfolk, but also to our faith and hope in the resurrection. It is useful for this to be done publicly and with a gathering of the people, so that the fruit that comes from the consideration of our common lot may spread to more people. Solomon observed this, writing thus: "It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for there the end of all men is seen, and the one who lives puts it in his heart." It is certain that people are hardly turned more from licence in sinning, and roused to innocence of life, by anything else than by thinking that they are mortal, and that the end of this life draws nearer to them at every moment. Therefore that son of Sirach used to say: "In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin." But at funerals we must take care that grief does not become excessive, such as (as Paul says) is typical of those who are utterly ignorant of the hope of the resurrection and of eternal life. For just as it is human to mourn the death of those who have deserved well of us, or whose service in the commonwealth or the Church was great, so it is a duty of love to comfort, with pious compassion, those whom that grief touches more closely because of the bond of kinship. And the saying of the Apostle is well known: "Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep." There are also examples of the holiest men who followed their dead with pious tears. Abraham, the father of believers, did this at the death of his beloved wife Sarah. We read that Joseph fell on the face of his dead father Jacob and wept. Devout men also carried Stephen out with great lamentation, because they grieved that the Church had been bereaved of so distinguished an instrument. But why need more examples, when the one example of Christ alone is enough, whom John testifies to have wept at the death of Lazarus and at the pious lamentations of his sisters? Therefore those who can look upon the deaths of their own and the grief of others, and their just sorrow, with dry eyes and without any emotion of mind, are not pious or brave or great-souled, but rather inhuman and impious. But, as we said before, our grief must be restrained and tempered by our faith in Christ, which teaches that the dead have already been translated into a more blessed life, while we, as long as we are contending in the arena of this life, are a matter of care to God. Ambition must also be avoided in conducting funerals, for just as pride is unworthy of Christians at all times and places, so it is altogether detestable if we give it a place even in death, which (as the heathen poet saw) strikes with equal foot the huts of the poor and the towers of kings, and about which we ought to have thought more carefully, given our common lot. Let these things suffice on this subject.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad miraculi considerationem, in quo in primis, quid Christus fecerit spectandum est. Primò viduam intuitus, & ex animo illius vicem miseratus est. Hoc enim innuit Graeca vox ἐσπλαγχνίσθη, qua Lucas in præsenti vtitur. Mox verò animi affectu verbis quoq; declarauit, dū illam amicè copellans flere vetat. Tangitur ergo nostris miserijs Christus, et (vt in alijs etiam exemplis videre licet) σοργὰς habet efficacissimas. Quapropter inde consolationes peti debent in omni casu, qui nobis tristior accidit. Nam cum eo, quod hic facit Christus, plane conenit, quod Deus se afflictorum vindicem esse profitetur. Videt ergo nos & nostri cura tangitur, sive cum egestate conflictemur, sive morbis diuturnis contabescamus, sive iniurijs improborum obnoxij simus, aut quocunq; alio infortunio exerceamur. In primis autem hoc observari debet, quoad conscientiæ terrores, ne nobis Deum ἀτοπον fingamus, & proinde de eius bonitate & clementia desperemus. Vt enim se patrem dicit, ita amore plus quam paterno nos prosequitur: & cum nos ab ipso alieni essemus, filium dedit, qui nobis (vno peccato excepto) similis factus per omnia, infirmitatibus ijsdem, quibus nos obnoxij sumus, tentatus est, ut per eum nobis liber & tutus esset ad thronum gratiæ accessus. Quoties ergo intra animos nostros diuini iudicij horror sentitur, toties nobis Christi hominum labores & erumnas miserantis facies in mentem veniat, neq; dubitemus, illum minimè abiecturum esse eos, ad quos seruandos in mundum venire dignatus est.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the consideration of the miracle, in which we must look first of all at what Christ did. First, he looked upon the widow and was moved with pity for her from his heart. For the Greek word ἐσπλαγχνίσθη, which Luke uses here, signifies this [ἐσπλαγχνίσθη]. Then, with kind words, while he addresses her affectionately and bids her not to weep, he also declared the feeling of his mind. Christ is therefore touched by our miseries and (as can be seen also in other examples) has the most effective affections [στοργάς]. Hence consolations ought to be sought in every case that befalls us more sadly. For what Christ does here agrees fully with the fact that God professes himself the avenger of the afflicted. He sees us, and he is moved by our concern, whether we are struggling with poverty, wasting away with lingering diseases, exposed to the wrongs of the wicked, or tried by any other misfortune. Above all, however, this should be observed regarding the terrors of conscience: we must not imagine a God who is absurd [ἄτοπον] towards us, and so despair of his goodness and mercy. For as he calls himself a father, so he cares for us with a love greater than a father's. And when we were estranged from him, he gave his Son, who, made like us in all things except sin, was tempted with the same infirmities to which we are subject, so that through him a free and safe access to the throne of grace might be open to us. Whenever, therefore, the horror of divine judgment is felt in our minds, let the face of Christ, who pities the labours and distresses of men, come to mind, and let us not doubt that he will by no means cast off those whom he deigned to come into the world to save.

units.la: At simul meminerimus, nostri quoq; officij esse, ut aliorum miserijs tangamur. Dum enim naturales illas affectiones in se recipit Christus, easdem suo exemplo nobis commendare voluit: quo Paulus respexisse videtur, quando ἀστοργεῖς inter nouissimorum temporum pestes numerat, à quibus Christiani homines sibi potissimum debeant cauere. Etsi vero omniu nos misereri conueniat, in primis tamen hoc officium viduis debemus, quas pra alijs commiseratione & auxilio dignas esse patebit, si earum conditionem recte consideremus. Quia enim mulieris caput vir est, quid aliud dicetur vidua esse, quam corpus sine capite, id est, rationis & consilij expers, & proinde omnium iniurijs expositum? Nam si senex fuerit, tam sibi ipsi quam suis oneri est: sin iuuencula, mox erunt qui pudicitiæ eius insidientur, & præsens famæ periculum imminet. Si diues, sunt qui eius opibus inhient: sin pauper, ab omnibus deseritur. Si liberos habeat, nouis quotidie curis tentatur: si orba fit, sola suspiriis & dolore consumitur. Merito igitur Deus in Lege & prophetis viduas commendat, & graues poenas ijs statuit, qui illas affligere audent. Nulla viduam (inquit) aut orphanum affligetis: sin vero eos omnino pergatis laedere, indubie ad me clamabunt, & ego certissime eos exaudiam, & excandescet furor meus, atq; interficiam vos gladio, & fient vxores vestræ viduæ, & filij vestri orphani. Et in primitiua ecclesia viduas pijs in primis curæ fuisse, ex Actorum libro & priore ad Timoth. epistola satis constat. Hic ergo officij sui probè meminerint omnes, qui rempub. administrant, tum etiam priuati homines, ne dum suæ cupiditati indulgent, Dei iram aduersus se accendant. Illæ vero ex eo consolationem petant, quod se Deo curæ esse norunt, & eas viduas imitentur, quæ cum vera fide & religione castitatis studium & vitæ innocentiam coniunxerunt: quales olim Iudith, Anna & plures aliæ fuerunt, quas scriptura prædicat.
units.tr: But at the same time let us remember that it is also our duty to be moved by the miseries of others. For when Christ took upon himself those natural affections, he wished by his example to commend them to us. Paul seems to have had this in view when he counts those who are "without natural affection" [ἀστοργεῖς] among the plagues of the last times, against which Christian people especially ought to guard themselves. Although it is fitting that we should pity all, yet we owe this duty especially to widows, who will be shown to deserve compassion and help more than others if we rightly consider their condition. For since the head of the woman is the man, what else is a widow said to be but a body without a head, that is, lacking counsel and judgment, and therefore exposed to the wrongs of all? For if she is old, she is a burden both to herself and to her family; if she is young, there will soon be men who lay snares for her chastity, and the danger to her reputation is at hand. If she is rich, there are those who gape after her wealth; if she is poor, she is deserted by all. If she has children, she is daily troubled by new cares; if she is bereaved, she is consumed by sighs and grief alone. Rightly, therefore, God commends widows in the Law and the prophets, and he appoints heavy penalties for those who dare to afflict them. "You shall afflict no widow or orphan," he says. "But if you go on to harm them in any way, they will undoubtedly cry out to me, and I will most certainly hear them, and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows, and your sons orphans." And that in the primitive Church widows were especially the care of the godly is sufficiently clear from the Book of Acts and from the first epistle to Timothy. Let all who administer the commonwealth therefore be mindful of their duty in this matter, and likewise private persons, lest while they indulge their own greed they kindle the wrath of God against themselves. Let the widows themselves take comfort from this, that they know they are a care to God, and let them imitate those widows who joined a true faith and religion with a zeal for chastity and innocence of life, such as Judith, Anna and many others were of old, whom Scripture commends.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui ad funus accedit, & loculum attingit, quasi manum iniecturus in mortem, ut prædam ante tempus captam ex faucibus illius eruat. Ostendit præterea, sibi neq; mortem, neque feretrum aut sepulchrum horrori esse, quo minus suum in ista omnia imperium exerceat. Deinde mortuum perinde ac si in viuis esset compellans, ait: Adolescens, tibi dico, surge. Nec mora surgit ille vitali spiritu iterum animatus, & astantem populum alloquitur. Inde eum Dominus mætri restituit, quæ eò maius gaudium inde percipit, quò grauiori antea dolore vulnerata fuerat. Idem ergo hic fecit, quod posteà quando Lazarum simili cum authoritate ex monumento prodire iussit, qui & ipse eius dicto mox paruit. Sunt autem hæc certa & indubitata diuinitatis Christi argumenta. Dei enim proprium esse Apostolus docet, ut vocet ea quæ non sunt, ut sint, id est, ut ex nihilo quoq; quod vult producat, & solius Verbi virtute omnia conficiat. At quid hic aliud Christus facit, quando mortuum & exanimem in vitam reuocat, & eundem absq; omni alio adminiculo omnibus facultatibus ad vitam necessarijs instruit? Frustra ergo hæc eius miracula olim eludere conati sunt Porphyrius, Lucianus & alij, qui illa magicis præstigijs similia dixerunt. Nos potius in his cognoscamus Christum eum esse, qui (vt promissiones patribus datæ docent) illum qui mortis habebat imperium, abolere debuit, vt miseros nos mortales primò quidem in vitam spiritualem afferat, inde vero corpora quoq; excitet, vbi nouissimi iudicij dies aduenerit.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who comes to the bier and touches the coffin, as if about to lay hands on death and snatch the prey, taken before its time, out of its jaws. He shows, moreover, that neither death, nor the bier, nor the tomb is a terror to him, so that he cannot exercise his rule over all these things. Then, addressing the dead man as if he were alive, he says: "Young man, I say to you, arise." At once he rises, animated again by the breath of life, and speaks to the people standing by. Then the Lord restores him to his mother, who receives from this a joy all the greater because she had been wounded before by a heavier grief. Therefore he did here what he afterwards did when, with like authority, he bade Lazarus come forth from the tomb, and he too at once obeyed his word. These are, moreover, certain and indubitable proofs of the divinity of Christ. For the Apostle teaches that it is proper to God "to call those things which are not, as though they were", that is, to produce even out of nothing what he wills, and to accomplish all things by the power of the Word alone. But what else does Christ do here, when he recalls to life one dead and lifeless, and, without any other aid, furnishes him with all the faculties necessary for life? Therefore Porphyry, Lucian and others, who said that these miracles were like magical tricks, tried in vain to mock them. Let us rather recognise in them that Christ is he who (as the promises given to the fathers teach) was to abolish him who held the power of death, so that he might first bring us miserable mortals into spiritual life, and then raise up our bodies also, when the day of the last judgment has come.

units.la: Est ergo miraculi huius duplex vsus. Primus, quòd vitæ spiritualis typum nobis exhibet. Vocat enim ad hanc nos quotidie Christus, dum per delicta a mortui iacemus, neq; quicquam eorum facimus aut possumus facere, quæ ad vitam vere Christianam pertinent. Neque uocat modò, sed simul Verbo suo vim addit diuinam, qua animos penetret, atq; nouam in nobis voluntatem nouasq; vires pariat. Et hoc illud est, quod Ioannis quinto Capite ipse his verbis enuntiat: Amen amen dico vobis, quòd veniet tempus, & nunc est, quando mortui audient vocem Filij Dei: & qui audierint, vivent. Ea vero nos officij admonent, ne Christum nos vocantem contemnamus, sed relicto peccatorum luto surgamus ad vitæ nouitatem, nosq; in ipso viuere dictis factisq; palam testemur. Alter vsus est, quòd aduersus mortis terrores solatur, & futuræ resurrectionis spem in nobis confirmat. Vt enim iuuenis iste Domini voce in vitam restituitur, loquitur, ambulat: ita in magno illo die cum tuba Dei & voce Archangeli ille veniet, & qui in monumentis sunt, vocem eius audient, & prodibunt. Quoties ergo de corporum restitutione & resurrectione caro dubitat, & omnis generis obstacula sibi fingit, tunc nos cogitemus, rem hanc omnem non humanis rationibus aut mediis, sed Dei Verbo confici oportere, cuius virtute olim omnia ex nihilo creata sunt. Et quid obsecro obstabit, quò minus Verbo suo omnes homines simul excitet, qui & hunc iuuenem & mox Iairi filiam, postremò Lazarum tam facile excitare potuit? Sufficit vna vox vt omnes in eodem cubiculo dormientes ex pergefiant: & tu Filij Dei vocem minus efficacem putabis erga eos, qui in tota hac mundi machina per mortem sopiti dorminunt? Hæc vt fidem nostram confirmant, & per omnem vitam nos officij admonent: ita aduersus mortis terrores consolationem dulcissimam afferunt. Est quidem natura sic comparatum, vt mortem homo timeat, & ita Deus non sine certa ratione rem constituit. In eo enim quanta sit peccati atrocitas cernitur, & multi cotinentur, ne in tentationibus grauioribus ipsi sibi manum inferant, quando frequenter accidit, vt pij quoque mori potius quàm viuere optent. At non tantus debet esse terror iste, vt mortis effugiendæ causa aliquid à fide alienum & professione nostra indignum faciamus. Non deterret sapientem mors (ait Cicero) quæ propter incertos casus quotidie imminet, & propter breuitatem vitæ nunquam potest longè abesse? Quanto minus ergo homines Christianum terrere debet, qui vitæ dies, imò capillos suos, apud Deum in numerato esse nouit, neq; se moriturum esse, priusquam hora illa præfinita aduenerit? At si simul cogitemus, mortis conditionem merito & virtute Christi mutatam esse, vt iam non peccati pœna sit credentibus, sed transitus ad vitam æternam, nosq; dum hinc migramus, vno momento omnibus huius vitæ miserijs defungi, ad bona autem æterna contendere, quorum hæreditas olim ad corpus quoq; redundatura sit: procul dubio mortis horrorem ita vincemus, vt cupiamus dissolui, quò liberius & propius cum Christo coniungamur. In horum ergo meditatione frequentes nos esse conuenit, & ad huius vitæ felicitatem plurimum nobis accedet, eò quòd tranquillo animo esse non potest, quisquis mortem omnibus horis sibi imminentem metuit.
units.tr: This miracle therefore has a twofold use. The first is that it sets before us a type of spiritual life. For Christ calls us to this every day, while through our sins we lie dead and do nothing, and can do nothing, of those things that pertain to a truly Christian life. And he not only calls, but at the same time adds divine power to his Word, by which he penetrates our minds and creates in us a new will and new strength. This is what he himself declares in the fifth chapter of John in these words: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and they that hear shall live." These words admonish us of our duty, that we should not despise Christ calling us, but, leaving the mire of sins, should rise to newness of life, and bear public witness by our words and deeds that we live in him. The other use is that it comforts us against the terrors of death and confirms in us the hope of the future resurrection. For just as this young man is restored to life by the Lord's voice, speaks, and walks, so on that great day, with the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel, he will come, and those who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth. Therefore whenever the flesh doubts the restoration and resurrection of bodies, and invents for itself all kinds of obstacles, let us then consider that this whole matter must be accomplished not by human reasons or means, but by the Word of God, by whose power all things were once created out of nothing. And what, I beg you, will hinder him from raising all men together by his Word, he who could so easily raise this young man, and soon after the daughter of Jairus, and finally Lazarus? One voice suffices to wake all who are sleeping in the same room; and will you think the voice of the Son of God less effective toward those who lie asleep in death throughout this whole machinery of the world? These things both confirm our faith and admonish us of our duty throughout our whole life, and they also bring the sweetest consolation against the terrors of death. It is indeed the nature of man to fear death, and God has ordained this not without a certain reason. For in it the greatness of the atrocity of sin is seen, and many are restrained from laying hands on themselves in graver temptations, since it often happens that even the godly prefer to die rather than to live. But this terror ought not to be so great that for the sake of escaping death we do anything foreign to the faith and unworthy of our profession. Does not death, which hangs over us every day from uncertain chances, and which because of the brevity of life can never be far away, deter the wise man? (as Cicero says). How much less, then, ought it to terrify a Christian, who knows that the days of his life, indeed the hairs of his head, are counted before God, and that he will not die before that appointed hour has arrived? But if we also consider that the condition of death has been changed by the merit and virtue of Christ, so that it is no longer a punishment of sin for believers, but a passage to eternal life, and that as we depart hence we are freed in a moment from all the miseries of this life and press on to eternal goods, whose inheritance will one day overflow also to the body, then without doubt we shall overcome the horror of death so that we desire to be dissolved, in order to be joined more freely and more closely with Christ. It is fitting, therefore, that we be frequent in meditation on these things, and it will greatly add to the happiness of this life; for no one can have a tranquil mind who fears death, which hangs over him every hour.

units.la: Sequitur miraculi effectus, quem multis Lucas exponit. Primò timor omnes corripuit. Solet hoc fieri, quando Deus suam præsentiam aliquo euidentiori testimonio nobis declarat. At hic pij ab impijs multùm differunt. Hi enim aut belluino stupore oppressi quid faciant nesciunt, aut in rabiem acti aduersus Deum fremunt. Illi vero humiliantur sub potenti manu Dei, & quia in hac paternam bonitatem simul agnoscunt, ei vnicè placere studeant. Ex horum numero isti quoque fuerunt, etiamsi multa adhuc illis defuerint. Additur enim, quòd glorificauerint Deum, & publicè confessi sint, magnum Prophetam surrexisse, & Deum tandem suum populum respexisse. Ergo veteres promissiones in mentem reuocant, & spe bona pleni restitutionem in propinquo adesse sentiunt. Quàmuis interea in eo turpiter errent, quod regnum terrenum somniabant, & in præsentem modò statum intenti animos non poterant in cælum attollere. Tanta tunc erat inter Iudæos doctrinæ confusio, vt licet promissiones omnibus notæ essent, & ea quotidie fierent, quæ patres sperauerant, pauci tamen veritatem ipsam possent intueri. Quo exemplo docemur, quantum mali dent impostores, qui verbi Dei doctrinam humanis figmentis obscurare & inficere audent: & vtinam nō hodie etiam bis similia fierent. Notæ sunt quidem promissiones Euangelij, & in omnium ore versantur fidei Christianæ principia, quæ Symbolo, quod Apostolicum dicunt, continentur. Sed quotus quisq; ista intelligit, aut de eorum sensu serio cogitat? Fit ergo, vt inani professione Christiani nominis pleriq; contenti, ipsum Christum negligant, & circa res inutiles occupentur, quibus Christi meritum obscuratur atq; fides in illum evertitur.
