Postremò rumor de Christo in totam Iudæam & omnem regionem finitimam diuulgatus fuisse dicitur. Est hic fructus agnitionis Christi, quòd confessionem & prædicationem parit. Nec
units.tr: The effect of the miracle follows, which Luke describes in many words. First, fear seized everyone. This usually happens when God declares his presence to us by some more evident testimony. Yet here the godly differ greatly from the ungodly. The ungodly are either overwhelmed by brutish stupor and do not know what to do, or they are driven to rage and rail against God. The godly, however, humble themselves under the mighty hand of God, and because in it they recognise at the same time his fatherly goodness, they earnestly seek to please him alone. Some of these people were among those who feared, although many things were still lacking in them. For it is added that they glorified God and openly confessed that a great Prophet had risen up and that God had at last visited his people. So they call to mind the old promises, and, full of good hope, they perceive that the restoration is near at hand. Yet in the meantime they err shamefully in this, that they dreamed of an earthly kingdom, and, intent on the present state of things, they could not raise their minds to heaven. So great was the confusion of teaching among the Jews at that time that, although the promises were known to all, and the things the fathers had hoped for were happening every day, few were able to see the truth itself. From this example we are taught how much harm impostors do, who dare to obscure and corrupt the doctrine of God's Word with human inventions. Would that similar things were not happening even twice over today! The promises of the Gospel are indeed well known, and the principles of the Christian faith, which are contained in the creed they call the Apostles', are on everyone's lips. But how few understand these things, or seriously consider their meaning? So it happens that most people, content with the empty profession of the Christian name, neglect Christ himself and are occupied with useless matters, by which the merit of Christ is obscured and faith in him is overthrown. Finally, it is said that the report about Christ was spread throughout all Judea and the whole neighbouring region. This is the fruit of the knowledge of Christ: it gives birth to confession and proclamation. For it cannot be that one who has been told and has been made a man does not bear witness to what he has embraced with his whole heart. Therefore David said: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken" [Ps. 116.10]. This argument, however, can be turned around, so that we may say that those who are unwilling to speak, and cannot be brought to make a confession of their faith, never truly believed. Yet at the same time we are taught by their example what we ought to do.

units.la: Effectus miraculi. enim fieri potest, quin dictus & factus homo testetur, quod toto animo amplexus est. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Credidi, & ideo locutus sum. Potest autem argumentum hoc conuerti, vt eos nunquam ad hoc credidisse dicamus, qui loqui nolunt, neq; adduci possunt, vt suae fidei confessionem edant. At si-mul horum exemplo docemur, quid nos facere oporteat. Inuisit enim omnes nos Deus et miseros respexit, quando Filium suum vnigenitum in mundum misit, et hominem fieri voluit. Is propheta ille magnus est, quem per Mosem olim pollicitus fuit. Idem ille nos mortuos per delicta quotidie Verbo suo ad vitae nouitatem excitat. Adhaec morte deuicit, ne nos amplius detinere possit, quo minus ipsi quoq; excussa eius tyrannide olim ad regni cœlorum possessionem resurgamus. Nostrum ergo fuerit, ad Verbi praedicationem contremiscere, vocanti obedire, surgere ex peccatorum sordibus, illum ore & vita confiteri, vt vicissim ille nos pro suis agnoscere possit, cùm in gloria patris veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The effect of the miracle. For God has visited us all and looked upon us in our misery, when he sent his only-begotten Son into the world and willed that he become man. He is that great Prophet whom God once promised through Moses. The same Christ daily raises us, who were dead through sins, by his Word to newness of life. Moreover, he has conquered death, so that it can no longer hold us back, so that we too, once its tyranny has been shaken off, may rise to possess the kingdom of heaven. It is therefore our task to tremble at the preaching of the Word, to obey the one who calls us, to rise out of the filth of sins, and to confess him with our mouth and life, so that in turn he may acknowledge us as his own when he comes in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVIII.

units.la: Et annuntiarunt Ioanni discipuli ipsius de his omnibus, qui conuocatos duos quosdam ex discipulis suis misit ad Iesum dicens: Túne is es qui venturus erat, an alium expectabimus? Cùm ergo venissent ad eum viri illi, dixerunt: Ioannes Baptista misit nos ad te dicens: Túne is es qui venturus erat, an alium expectabimus? Eadem autem hora multos sanauit à morbis & flagellis & spiritibus malis, & cæcis multis visum donauit. Et respondens Iesus dixit eis: Profecti annuntiate Ioanni quae viditis & audistis. Cæci visum recipiunt, claudi ambulant, leprosi purgantur, surdi audiunt, mortui excitantur, pauperibus praedicatur Euangelium: & beatus est, quicunque non fuerit offensus in me.
units.tr: And John's disciples told him all these things. John, calling to himself two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying: "Are you the one who was to come, or are we to look for another?" When the men came to him, they said: "John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying: Are you the one who was to come, or are we to look for another?" At that same hour he healed many of diseases, plagues and evil spirits, and he gave sight to many who were blind. And Jesus answered and said to them: "Go and report to John what you have seen and heard. The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the gospel is preached to the poor. And blessed is whoever is not offended in me."

units.la: Quemadmodum omnis salus in vno & solo Dei Filio, Iesu Christo, habetur: ita vt eam asse quamur, vera & certa Christi cognitione nobis est opus. In eo autem illius erga nos bonitas maximè elucet, quod nihil eorum praetermisit, quae nos in ipsius cognitione instituere & confirmare possunt. Nec enim doctrina solum nobis sese manifestat, sed illam insuper operibus miraculosis illustrat atq; confirmat, quae reipsa talem esse testantur, qualis Verbo praedicatur. Sunt inter opera haec non postremo loco ponenda ea, quae in duobus proximis sermonibus exposuimus. Docent enim illum vitae & mortis dominum esse, qui in ipsa etiam morte seruare, imò ex huius faucibus eripere possit. At quia propter innatam nobis ingenij tarditatem admodum difficile est, de Christi operibus rectè iudicare: commodè hanc historiam Lucas subtexit, qua euidenter & perspicuè docemur, quis illorum omnium finis sit, & quid in illis maximè debeat spectari. Status totius loci aut tractationis huius est, Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, promissum humani generis redemptorem esse, neq; alium posthac esse expectandum. Continet ergo locus hic fundamentum fidei atq; salutis nostrae, & proinde dignus est, in cuius consideratione quam frequentissimè versemur.
units.tr: Just as all salvation is found in the one and only Son of God, Jesus Christ, so that we may obtain it, we need a true and certain knowledge of Christ. In this, God's goodness toward us shines most clearly, in that he has left out nothing that can establish and confirm us in the knowledge of him. Doctrine alone does not reveal him to us; he also illustrates and confirms it with miraculous works, which in fact testify that he is what he is preached to be in the Word. Among these works are not to be placed last those which we explained in the two previous sermons. For they teach that he is Lord of life and death, who can preserve us even in death and snatch us from its jaws. But because, on account of our innate slowness of mind, it is very hard to judge Christ's works rightly, Luke conveniently adds this history, by which we are taught plainly and clearly what the end of all those works is and what in them ought chiefly to be noticed. The aim and subject of this whole passage is that this Jesus, who was born a man of the virgin Mary, is the promised redeemer of mankind, and that no other is to be expected from now on. This passage therefore contains the foundation of faith and of our salvation, and so it deserves to be considered as often as possible.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi fama praebuit, quam de Christo vulgatam fuisse nuper audiuimus. Hanc enim ad Ioannem Baptistam, qui quòd incestas Herodis nuptias reprehendisset iam in carcere agebat, discipuli deferunt, & illi narrant quid de Christo omnium ore praedicetur. Id autem illi fecerunt, non quòd Christo fauerent, & eius virtutem suo praeceptori comendare vellent, sed potius quòd caeca aemulatione accensi, illius gloriam extinctam cuperent. Nam vt Cap. 5. audiuimus, Ioannem Christo praeferre solebat, quòd hic commune viuendi genus sequeretur, ille verò seuerius quoddam ex peculiari Dei mandato sibi delegisset. Imò passim ferebatur, Ioanis discipulos in ieiuniis & precibus frequentes esse, Christi verò cum suis edere & bibere. Et vt in Euangelio secundùm Ioannem Apostolum scribitur, Christum in praeceptorem suum Baptistā nimis iniquum esse querebantur, quòd cum ab eo baptizatus atq; eius testimonio magnificè comendatus esset, nunc discipulos plures attrahendo illum superare niteretur. Quando Ioannes quidè diligenter eos instituit, & quantum interipsum & illum discrimen sit abunde ostendit, non autem tantum profecit, quin in hoc sua errore in hunc vsque diem perseuerarint, & nunc nouas ad ipsum querelas deferant. Sunt ergo isti eorum typus, qui magistrorum
units.tr: The occasion for this discussion was the report, which we recently heard, that had been spread abroad about Christ. For his disciples carry it to John the Baptist, who was already in prison because he had rebuked Herod's incestuous marriage, and they tell him what is being proclaimed about Christ on everyone's lips. They did this not because they favoured Christ and wished to commend his power to their teacher, but rather because, inflamed by blind rivalry, they wanted his glory extinguished. For, as we heard in chapter 5, they used to prefer John to Christ, because Christ followed a common way of life, while John had chosen for himself a stricter manner by a special command of God. Indeed it was commonly reported that John's disciples were constant in fasting and prayer, but Christ's disciples ate and drank with their companions. And as is written in the Gospel of John the Apostle, they complained that Christ was too unfair to their teacher the Baptist, since, though he had been baptized by John and magnificently commended by his testimony, he now tried to outdo him by drawing away more disciples. John indeed instructed them diligently and showed plainly enough what difference there was between himself and Christ, yet he made no such progress that they have not persisted in this error down to this very day, and they now bring fresh complaints against him. These men, then, are a type of those who, carried away by excessive admiration for their teachers, attribute more to them than is fitting; meanwhile, intent on this one thing, that they may look after their teachers' reputation, they carelessly neglect their teaching.

units.la: toan 3. strorum suorum nimia admiratione abrepti, plus quàm par sit illis tribuunt; interim verò in hoc vnum intenti vt ipsorum existimationi consulant, doctrinam eorundem securè negligunt. Fuit hæc omnibus seculis præcipua sectarum & scismatum causa, quibus ecclesiam sæpe grauissimè & periculose concussam fuisse legimus. Et tanta huius mali vis est, vt non solùm doctrina & placitorum diuersitate inter se homines scindantur, sed iij quoq; in partes diuersas abeant, qui eandem à suis præceptoribus doctrinam audiunt. Quod in præsenti factum esse constat. Fuerunt enim animis contun-dissimi Ioannes & Christus, & idem vtrinq; inter docendum scopus fuit propositus; vt nimirum salutis hæredes faceret suos discipulos, quam in semetipso Christus monstrabat, simul Ioanne attestante, & de illo dicente: Ecce Agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Nulla ergo inter præceptores dissensio, nulla doctrinæ diuersitas. Attamen inter discipulos æmulatio est, quæ simultatem et tandem apertam dissensionem peperit. Idem in Corinthiorum ecclesia accidisse legimus. Nam etsi eundem Christum prædicarent Paulus, Cephas & Apollo, & in eiusdem Christi nomen suos auditores baptizarent, præceptorum tamen nimia admiratio inter auditores æmulationem ambitiosam excitauit, qua factum est, vt tantùmnon abiecto Christi nomine, alij quidem Paulini, alij verò Cephaæni, alij Apolloniani dici gauderent. Et olim patrum temporibus multa huius generis facta sunt. Quò minus nos nostri seculi scismatibus offendi decet, quando non sine dolore eiusdem mali vestigia passim cernuntur. Nam qui primi Euangelij doctrinam magno cum successu instaurauerunt, et eandem fidem in Christum concorditer tradiderunt, in vno Cœnæ Dominicæ articulo sententijs scissi, totam ecclesiam in partes diuersas traxere, vnde cõtentiones nimiùm acerbæ et pertinaces exortæ sunt. Et vtinam non plus æquo vtriusq; partis discipuli priuato affectui indulsissent, vel etiam hodie adhuc indulgerent. Facilis tamen erit componendi dissidij ratio, si quid de Christo Iesu, de fide & huius effectis, de vera salutis consequendæ ratione vtriq; vnanimi consensu doceatur, omnes spe stent, & posita æmulatione omni de ecclesiarum pace serio cogitent. Quod si non ab omnibus impetrari potest, adhuc, discant saltem pij hoc facere, neq; ipsi sibi scandalum fabricent, aut ab alijs fabricatum pertinacius foueant.
units.tr: (John 3.) This has been in every age the chief cause of sects and schisms, by which the Church, we read, has often been very gravely and dangerously shaken. The force of this evil is so great that men are divided not only by diversity of doctrine and opinions, but even those who hear the same doctrine from their teachers go off into different parties. This is clearly what has happened in the present case. For John and Christ were of one mind, and the same aim was set before both in teaching: namely, to make their disciples heirs of salvation, which Christ himself displayed, with John bearing witness and saying of him: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. There is therefore no dissension between the teachers and no difference of doctrine. Yet among the disciples there is rivalry, which has at length produced ill will and open dissension. We read that the same happened in the Church of Corinth. For although Paul, Cephas and Apollos all preached the same Christ, and baptized their hearers in the name of the same Christ, excessive admiration for their teachers stirred up an ambitious rivalry among the hearers, so that, almost discarding the name of Christ, some were glad to be called Paulines, others Cephasites, others Apollonians. And in the times of the Fathers many things of this kind happened. How much less does it become us to be offended by the schisms of our own age, since the traces of the same evil are seen everywhere, not without grief! For those who first restored the doctrine of the Gospel with great success, and handed down the same faith in Christ in harmony, split in opinion over the single article of the Lord's Supper, and drew the whole Church into different parties, whence very bitter and stubborn contentions arose. And would that the disciples of both sides had not indulged their private feelings more than was right, or did not indulge them still today! Yet the way of settling the dispute will be easy, if on Jesus Christ, on faith and its effects, and on the true way of obtaining salvation, both sides teach with one accord, all look to the same goal, and, rivalry laid aside, they seriously consider the peace of the churches. But if this cannot be obtained from everyone, let at least the godly learn to do it, and not build a stumbling-block for themselves, or cherish with obstinacy one built by others.

units.la: Sed Ioannem Baptistam videamus, qui vt alias, ita hic quoq; fidum Iesu Christi seruum agit. Quia enim se hucusq; in illis erudiendis minus profecisse videt, duos ex illis (quos credibile est reli-quis superstitiosiores & pertinaciores fuisse) ad ipsum Christum ablegat, qui omnium nomine scisci-tentur. Túne is es, qui venturus erat, an alium expectabimus? Vbi minimè putandus est Ioannes de Christo vel tantillum dubitauisse, vt ipsi institutione ampliori opus fuerit. Quia enim, vt Christi præco & testis esset à Deo missus, & priuatis reuelationibus abunde instructus fuerat, imò qui in vtero matris illi nondum nato testimonium perhibuerat, non potuit ignorare hunc esse promissum illum humani generis vindicem, quem omnes constanti fide amplecti & sequi debeant. Ergo legatione ista (vt modò diximus) discipulorum saluti consulcum voluit, & quia nouerat, se non procul abesse à vitæ fine, in tempore illis remedium adhibet, ne ipso sublato à puriori doctrina omni-no deficiant, & ad pristinas superstitiones relabantur. Nam id fieri facile erat, cùm & Christi gloriæ inuiderent, & (vt ex alijs locis apparet) pharifæos sibi satis haberent propitios ob vitæ mo-rum similitudinem. Fidelem ergo paranymphum agit, quando discipulos suos omnes vni Christo consecratos esse vult, quem sponsum esse sciebat, quem omnes audire debent. Et hoc animo omnes Apostoli præditi fuerunt, vt in Paulo apparet, qui vt neminem abs se denominari voluit, ita hoc vnum effectum studuit, vt auditores suos Christo sisteret virginem puram & nullo superstitionum amore siue consortio contaminatam. Hoc igitur argumento spiritus & doctores omnes probare po-terimus, an ex Deo sint. Quicunque enim simili cum Apostolis et Ioanne studio ad vnum Christum remittunt, & in hoc vno monstrant, quæ ad salutem hominum faciunt, ij fideles Dei serui sunt, quibus tutò credi poterit. At si qui vel sibijpsis discipulos faciunt, vel alios extra Christum salu-tis authores siue mediatores esse docent, ij impurissimorum lenonum similes sunt, qui virginum pu-dicitiam nefarijs artibus & promissis tentant, aut ipsas quoque sponsas corrumpunt, quas suis ma-ritis adducere debebant. Est horum ingens numerus hodie, qui id tam aperte tamque impudenter faciunt, vt mirum sit quenquam adeò vecordem & stupidum inueniri, qui hoc non videat, aut diu-tius in Christi ecclesia ferendos putet.
units.tr: But let us look at John the Baptist, who, as elsewhere, so here too acts as a faithful servant of Jesus Christ. For since he sees that he has so far made little progress in instructing these men, he sends two of them (who were probably more superstitious and obstinate than the rest) to Christ himself, to ask on behalf of all: Are you the one who was to come, or shall we look for another? Here John is by no means to be thought to have doubted Christ even a little, so that he needed further instruction. For, having been sent by God to be Christ's herald and witness, and abundantly furnished with private revelations, indeed having borne witness while still unborn in his mother's womb, he could not have been ignorant that this was the promised avenger of mankind, whom all ought to embrace and follow with steadfast faith. He therefore looked after his disciples' salvation by this embassy, as we have just said, and because he knew that he was not far from the end of his life, he applies a remedy in time, lest, with him removed, they should wholly fall away from purer doctrine and relapse into their former superstitions. This would have been easy to happen, since they both envied Christ's glory and (as appears from other passages) regarded the Pharisees as well disposed to them because of their similar way of life. He therefore acts as a faithful friend of the bridegroom when he wishes all his disciples consecrated to Christ alone, whom he knew to be the bridegroom and whom all ought to hear. All the Apostles were endowed with this same disposition, as appears in Paul, who, wishing no one to be named after himself, strove for this one thing: to present his hearers to Christ as a pure virgin, untainted by any love or fellowship of superstitions. By this test, therefore, we shall be able to judge all spirits and teachers, whether they are of God. For whoever, with the same zeal as the Apostles and John, refers men back to Christ alone, and in him alone shows what contributes to the salvation of men, those are faithful servants of God, whom one may safely trust. But if any make disciples for themselves, or teach that others apart from Christ are authors or mediators of salvation, they are like the most impure pimps, who tempt the chastity of virgins with wicked arts and promises, or even corrupt the brides themselves, whom they ought to lead to their husbands. Today there is a huge number of these, who do it so openly and so shamelessly that it is amazing anyone should be found so mad and stupid as not to see it, or to think they should be tolerated any longer in the Church of Christ.

units.la: Præterea zeli ardentis & indefessi argumentum est, quòd etsi in carcere iam aliquandiu conclusus fuerit Ioannes, et à se vitæ suæ finem non procul abesse intelligat, adhuc tamen officij sui memor est, & Christi gloriam promouere eiq; discipulos adducere studet. Fecit idem Paulus, qui quàm diu licuit, in vinculis quoq; Romæ omnibus ad se venientibus Euangelium prædicauit, & ecclesias scriptis ad eas epistolas ad fidei constantiam & purioris doctrinæ studium hortatus est. Sunt hæc manifesta spiritus Christi indicia, qui cùm ad Oliueti montem diris & acerbis mortis iam vicinæ terroribus angeretur, discipulos tamen itidem innuisit, & dormientes monuit, ne ex improuiso obruerentur: imò cùm iam ab hostibus vinciretur, eorum tamen saluti summa fide consuluit. Arguitur his exemplis eorum ignauia, qui ipsi sibi ferias indicunt, & quàm primùm aliquo labore graviori defuncti se ad noua pericula & nouos labores vocari vident, mox se plus satis sudauisse clamant, & sibi magnam iniuriam fieri putant, si quid ab ipsis præterea exigatur. Atqui in finem vsq; perseuerandum est in functione, ad quam nos Dominus vocauit: & quàm diu nobis vitæ huius vsum Deus concedit, vt ipsi viuamus curandum est: quin ne moriturí quidem illius obliuisci debemus, quò minus pijs admonitionibus nostros confirmemus, vt Deo fideles sint, & cultu eius purū atq; integrū seruent. Fecerunt hoc diligenter patriarchæ, vt in Iacobi historia est videre: & Iosua, fortissimus populi Israelitici dux, hoc sui officij esse putauit, vt sub finem vitæ, in frequenti totius populi concione omnes hortaretur, et in vnius Dei cultu confirmaret. In quo sui antecessoris, Mosis, exemplum secutus est, quem idem fecisse legimus. Posset his Dauid etiam adnumerari, vt iam de Prophetis nihil dicamus, quorum multi ad extremam senectam vsq; in docendi munere constantia incredibili perseuerauerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, a sign of ardent and tireless zeal is that although John has now been shut up in prison for some time, and understands that the end of his life is not far off, he still remembers his office and strives to advance Christ's glory and bring disciples to him. Paul did the same: for as long as he was allowed, even in chains at Rome he preached the gospel to all who came to him, and he exhorted the churches by letters to constancy in faith and zeal for purer doctrine. These are clear indications of Christ's Spirit, who, when in Gethsemane he was distressed by the harsh and bitter terrors of approaching death, nevertheless gave a sign to his disciples and warned them, as they slept, not to be overtaken unawares. Indeed, when he was already being bound by his enemies, he still took the greatest care for their safety with complete faithfulness. By these examples the laziness of those is rebuked who declare holidays for themselves: as soon as they have finished some heavier labour and see themselves called to new dangers and new labours, they at once cry out that they have sweated enough, and think a great injustice is done them if anything further is demanded of them. Yet one must persevere in the office to which the Lord has called us until the end, and as long as God grants us the use of this life we must take care to live for him. Nor ought we, even when about to die, to forget that office, so that by pious admonitions we may strengthen our people to be faithful to God and to keep his worship pure and whole. The patriarchs did this diligently, as can be seen in the history of Jacob. Joshua, the most courageous leader of the Israelite people, thought it part of his office, near the end of his life, in a crowded assembly of the whole people, to exhort them all and confirm them in the worship of the one God. In this he followed the example of his predecessor Moses, who we read did the same. David could also be counted among these, not to mention the prophets, many of whom persevered with incredible constancy in the office of teaching even to extreme old age.

units.la: Sed propius inspicienda est quæstio, cuius formam eiusmodi Ioannes discipulis tradidit: Tu ne is es, qui venturus erat, an alium expectabimus? Sumit hanc ex communi Iudæorum persuasione, quæ omnibus in ore erat. Sciebant enim promissum esse Seruatorem, quem patres omnes spe constanti expectauerant, & ex eo ipsi quoque redemptionem sperabant. Interim nimium oscitantes erant & tardi in ijs obseruandis, quæ à Christo fiebant, & ex quibus non difficile fuisset intelligere, hunc illum esse, quem venturum Moses & Prophetæ promiserant. Erroris causa fuit, quòd alium animo conceperant, quàm scripturæ prædicent, Regem nimirum terrenum, armis & regali pompa atque victorijs insignem. Quia tamen principium hoc promissionum Dei tenebant, Venturum omnino redemptorem, huic illorum expectationi Ioannes quæstionem suam accommodat, simulq; eorum fo cordiam perstringit, qui cùm Messiam & redemptorem certum promissum esse scirent, tamē à Pharisæis pendebant, & quorúmuis delirijs sese decipi atq; seduci patiebantur: eadem verò opera discipulos admonet, vt relictis omnibus superstitiosorum hominum commentis, in vnum illum Messiam intenti sint, & in eo cognoscendo omne studium impendant. Possumus ergo ad hanc quæstionem nos quoq; omnes eos remittere, qui hodie in religionis & salutis causa ambigui hærent, & se nescire quæ runtur quid credant, aut quam viam salutis ingrediantur. Interrogentur illi, num Christiani sint? Fatebuntur id proculdubio. Rursus ergo quæratur: An ergo scitis promissum esse salutis authorem, qui Rex & Sacerdos noster omnia ea perficiat, quæ ad humani generis redemptionem faciunt? Dicent certè, se hoc etiam scire. Quid ergo (dicam ego) incertis & nouis indies opinionibus circumferimini? Cur non relictis omnibus aliorum figmentis, promissum illum Seruatorem quæritis? Imò cùm ipsi nobiscum fateamini, hunc esse Iesum illum, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus, & sub Pilato præside crucifixus, pro nobis mortem diram & infamem subijt, cur non illum auditis, & in illo acquiescitis? Cur non cum Petro Apostolo dicitis? Domine, ad quem ibimus? tu verba vitæ æternæ habes, &c. Est ergo huius quæstionis etiam hodie vsus magnus in conuincendis scepticis illis, qui inter omnis generis superstitiones incerti fluctuant.
units.tr: But the question which John put to the disciples in this form should be examined more closely: "Are you the one who was to come, or shall we look for another?" He takes it from the common belief of the Jews, which was on everyone's lips. For they knew that a Saviour had been promised, whom all the fathers had awaited with steadfast hope, and from him they too hoped for redemption. Meanwhile they were far too sluggish and slow in observing what Christ was doing, from which it would not have been difficult to understand that this is the one whom Moses and the prophets had promised would come. The cause of their error was that they had conceived in their minds a different kind of king from the one the Scriptures describe, namely an earthly king, distinguished by arms, royal pomp and victories. Yet because they held to this principle of God's promises, that a redeemer would certainly come, John adapts his question to this expectation of theirs. At the same time he rebukes the folly of those who, though they knew that the Messiah and redeemer had certainly been promised, nevertheless depended on the Pharisees and allowed themselves to be deceived and led astray by any madness whatever. By the same token he admonishes the disciples that, leaving aside all the inventions of superstitious men, they should be intent upon that one Messiah and devote all their effort to coming to know him. We may therefore refer this question to all those who today hang in doubt in matters of religion and salvation, and do not know what they should believe or what way of salvation they are entering. Let them be asked whether they are Christians. They will undoubtedly confess it. Again let it be asked: "Do you know that the author of salvation has been promised, who as our King and Priest accomplishes all those things which pertain to the redemption of the human race?" They will certainly say they know this too. Why then (I would say) are you carried about by opinions uncertain and new every day? Why, leaving aside all the figments of others, do you not seek that promised Saviour? Indeed, since you yourselves agree with us that this is Jesus, who was born a man of the virgin Mary and was crucified under Pilate the governor, and who underwent a cruel and infamous death for us, why do you not listen to him and rest in him? Why do you not say with the apostle Peter: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life," and so on? This question therefore still has great use today in convicting those sceptics who waver uncertainly amid all kinds of superstitions.

units.la: Et his etiam in primis applicari debet Christi responsio, quæ totius disputationis huius statum pulchrè explicat. Priusquam tamen ad illius tractationem accedamus, obseruari debet, quòd non duriter aut morosius eos reijcit, quos odiosa nominis sui æmulatione vri non ignorabat, & quorum tarditas sola reprehensionem grauem merebatur: sed potius humaniter acceptos amicè instituit. Ita verò præstat, quod alibi pollicetur, se neminem reijcere eorum qui ad se veniunt. Est exemplum hoc plenum consolationis. Si enim eos non aspernatur, qui pessimè erga ipsum affecti in Veritatis tatis tamen cognitione erudiri cupiunt, quanto magis eos admittet atq; feret, qui animo amico veniunt, & cum illo cupiunt reconciliari? Simul autem suo exemplo Verbi administros officij admonet, ne in aliquem nimio rigore vtantur, aut aliquos proterius reijciant. Nam curandum potius est, vt eos etiam colligamus, qui per auia vagantur, quàm vt eos excludamus, qui ad ipsa septa gregis dominici sponte accedunt, & intromitti cupiunt. Et potest fieri, vt qui animo minus sincero venerunt, amica & diligenti institutione emendentur, & non poenitendos in vera pietate progref sus faciant. Polemonem perditae luxuriae adolescentem, vnica Xenocratis oratione de temperantia mutatum esse scribit Valerius, cum ex conuiuio recta veniens per ludibrium ad eius praelectiones ac cessisset: & nos in Christi schola idem fieri posse dubitabimus? Ferantur ergo amicè omnes, qui nondum deplorata malitiae specimina dederunt. Alia vero est incurabilium ratio, qui non contenti sua improbitate, simul alijs quoq; obesse studeant. Hos enim procul arceri necesse est, ne alios quoq; secum in interitum abripiant.
units.tr: Christ's answer, which neatly sets out the whole state of this dispute, ought also to be applied first of all to these people. Before we come to its treatment, it must be noted that he does not reject harshly or peevishly those whom he knew to be inflamed with hostile rivalry against his name, and whose slowness alone deserved a grave rebuke. Rather, he received them kindly and instructed them in a friendly way. And this indeed he does, as he promises elsewhere, that he will cast out none of those who come to him. This example is full of comfort. For if he does not spurn those who are very ill-disposed towards him, yet in the knowledge of the truth wish to be taught, how much more will he admit and bear with those who come in a friendly spirit and wish to be reconciled with him? At the same time, by his own example he admonishes the ministers of the Word of their duty not to use excessive rigour toward anyone, nor to reject some too peremptorily. For we ought rather to take care to gather in even those who wander astray, than to shut out those who of their own accord approach the very fold of the Lord's flock and desire to be admitted. And it may happen that those who came with a less sincere mind are corrected by friendly and diligent instruction, and advance in true piety so that they have no cause for regret. Valerius writes that Polemo, a young man of ruined and dissolute life, was changed by a single speech of Xenocrates on temperance, when, coming straight from a drinking party, he had come to his lectures in mockery. And shall we doubt that the same can happen in the school of Christ? Let all therefore be treated kindly who have not yet given evidence of hopeless wickedness. The case of the incurable is different: they are not content with their own wickedness and at the same time strive to harm others. These must certainly be kept far away, lest they drag others with them to destruction.

units.la: Porrò quoad argumentum aut statum quaestionis, non directè aut simpliciter ad eam Christus respondet. Poterat quidem aperte affirmare quod quaerebant, sed procul dubio nouus scrupulus in il lorum animis hæsisset, qui nondum potuissent videre Messiam esse eum, qui vulgo ab omnibus, in primis autem abijs contemnebatur, qui summam doctrinae & pietatis existimationem sustinebant. Ergo vt non seipsum commendare putetur (quod ambitiosi solent) sed vt res ipsa loquatur, & simul Ioannes maiorem habeat eos amplius instituendi occasionem, ad operum suorum contemplationem illos remittit. Et commodum ea ipsa hora multos à morbis & flagellis curauit, multos item spiritus immundos expulit, adhæc cæcis plurimis visum restituit: sic nimirum gubernante negotium hoc diuina prouidentia, quae temporum momenta et eas quoq; hominum actiones certo consilio moderatur, quas prophani fortuitas & cotingentes esse putant. Quod si omnes semper expenderent, sape praeclaram haberent de salute & officio suo cogitandi occasionem. Christus certè hac occasione diligenter vtitur, & Ioannis discipulis ad hunc modum respondet: Profecti annuntiate Ioanni quae vidistis & audistis: Caeci visum recipiunt, claudi ambulant, leprosi purgantur, surdi audiunt, mortui excitantur, pauperibus praedicatur Euangelium: & beatus est, quicunq; non fuerit offensus in me. Sunt responsionis huius partes duae, & de singulis ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Moreover, as regards the subject matter or the state of the question, Christ does not answer it directly or plainly. He could indeed have affirmed clearly what they were asking, but without doubt a new stumbling-block would have stuck in their minds, since they could not yet see that the Messiah is he who was commonly despised by all, and especially by those who held the highest reputation for teaching and piety. Therefore, so that he should not seem to commend himself (as ambitious men usually do), but so that the thing itself may speak, and so that John may have a greater opportunity of further instructing them, he sends them back to the contemplation of his works. And just at that hour he healed many from diseases and plagues, likewise cast out many unclean spirits, and moreover restored sight to very many blind men. Thus divine providence directs this business, which by a sure counsel governs the moments of time and also those actions of men which the profane think are chance and contingent. If they always weighed this, they would often have a splendid occasion for thinking about their salvation and their duty. Christ certainly makes diligent use of this occasion and answers John's disciples in this manner: "Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the gospel is preached to the poor; and blessed is whoever is not offended in me." There are two parts to this answer, and we shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Prima docet se eum, esse qui venturus erat, & quidem id operibus demonstrat, dum se ea facere ostendit, quae Messiam facturum esse olim Prophetae praedixerant. Alludit autem ad duos Isaiae locos, ex quibus prior extat cap.35. Pollicetur illic Deus, quod salutem plenam & omnibus numeris absolutam afferre velit per Messiam, quem patribus iampridem promiserit, & inter alia sic ait: Fortes estote, ne timeatis, ecce Deus vester cum vindicta & retributione veniet, Deus ipse veniet & seruabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi caecorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur: tunc saliet claudus tanquam cervus, & inhibilabit lingua muti, &c. Quo loco quàmuis de liberatione spirituali potissimum agat Spiritus sanctus, consulto tamen signorum meminit, quibus Messias se mundo manifestaturus, & simul salutem veram ceu in speculo adumbraturus sit. Alter locus cap 61. habetur, & ille ipse est, quem Nazarethi in publica concione Christus ipse exposuit, vt cap. 4. audiuimus. Conuenit per omnia cum priori, nisi quòd de doctrina Christi apertius loquitur, & hunc pauperum atq; afflictorum doctorem fore docet, qui hos læto salutis iam aduentantis, vel potius exhibitae, nuntio exhilaraturus sit. Cùm verò ista omnia Christus palam faceret, iubet vt hoc Ioanni renuntient: quia istud non poterant facere, quin simul proprio ore testarentur, hunc Messiam esse, quem venturum hucusq; expectarint, & proinde nullum alium expectari debere.
units.tr: First, he declares that he is the one who was to come, and he shows this by his works, since he displays himself doing the things which the prophets long ago foretold the Messiah would do. He alludes to two passages of Isaiah, of which the first is in chapter 35. There God promises that he will bring full salvation, complete in every respect, through the Messiah, whom he had long since promised to the fathers; and among other things he says: "Be strong, fear not; behold, your God will come with vengeance and recompense; God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb will sing," and so on. In this place, although the Holy Spirit is chiefly speaking of spiritual deliverance, he nonetheless deliberately mentions the signs by which the Messiah was to make himself known to the world, and at the same time to sketch out, as if in a mirror, the true salvation. The second passage is in chapter 61, and it is the very one which Christ himself expounded in public preaching at Nazareth, as we heard in chapter 4. It agrees in every respect with the first, except that it speaks more openly of the teaching of Christ, and teaches that he would be the teacher of the poor and afflicted, who would gladden them with the news of salvation now drawing near, or rather now given. When Christ made all these things plain, he bids them report this to John, because they could not do these things without at the same time bearing witness with their own mouth that this is the Messiah whom they had hitherto awaited, and that therefore no other ought to be awaited.

units.la: Docet autem locus hic, quis miraculorum Christi finis & vsus sit: Nimirum vt ex his discamus eum esse promissum illum humani generis redemptorem, qui solus animi oculos illuminat, vt ea videant quae sunt spiritus Dei: qui item vires confert, vt in Dei vijs recto pede ambulemus: qui animae lepram, id est, inhærentem nobis naturae vitiositatem, & quae ex hac proueniunt delicta expiat: qui intellectus & mentis aures aperit, vt verbum salutis audire, & ex eo fructum verum capere possimus: qui denique nos in vitam spiritualem asserit, mortis et diaboli regnum euertit, & aeternae salutis nuntio afflictas conscientias consolatur, imò salutis arrhabonem animis nostris inserit, Spiritu sanctum, qui nobis consolator & aduocatus est ad omnia huius vitae discrimina sufficiens. Hæc quidē de illo per Euangelium prædicantur, at quò minus dubitemus, simul operibus miraculosis se talem esse docere voluit. In his ergo nos sublimiora illa & spiritualia bona spectare convenit, non nudis signis inhærere & circa temporalia modò & corporalia bona occupari. Quod ipsum in Apostolorum quoq; signis siue miraculis obseruare conuenit. Quia enim hæc illi non propria, sed Christi Iesu virtute fecerunt, procul dubio doctrinæ ipsorum sigilla sunt, qua illum salutis æternæ Mediatorem vnicum esse testati sunt. Turpiter ergo seipsos fallunt, qui ex signis illis occasione arrepta illos colere & invocare incipiunt, adeoque in illos transferunt honorem, qui vni Christo debetur.
units.tr: This passage also teaches what the end and use of Christ's miracles is, namely that from them we may learn that he is that promised redeemer of the human race, who alone enlightens the eyes of the soul, so that they may see the things that are of the Spirit of God; who likewise bestows strength, so that we may walk on the paths of God with a straight foot; who cleanses the leprosy of the soul, that is, the vitiousness of nature that clings to us, and the sins that arise from it; who opens the ears of the intellect and mind, so that we may hear the word of salvation and draw true fruit from it; who, finally, asserts us into spiritual life, overthrows the kingdom of death and the devil, consoles afflicted consciences with the news of eternal salvation, and indeed plants in our souls the earnest of salvation, the Holy Spirit, who is for us a sufficient comforter and advocate in all the perils of this life. These things are indeed proclaimed of him through the Gospel, but so that we may doubt them the less, he wished to show by miraculous works also that he is such a one. In these things, therefore, we ought to look to those higher and spiritual goods, and not cling to bare signs or be occupied only with temporal and bodily goods. This ought to be observed also in the signs or miracles of the Apostles. For since they did these things not by their own power but by the power of Christ Jesus, they are without doubt seals of their doctrine, in which they testified that he is the only Mediator of eternal salvation. Therefore those men deceive themselves foully who, seizing upon those signs as an occasion, begin to worship and invoke the Apostles, and thereby transfer to them the honour that is due to Christ alone.

units.la: Est præterea hic obseruandum, ad quos nam pertineat Christus & bona, quæ in hoc nobis per Euangelium offeruntur. Pauperes (inquit) euangelizantur, id est, pauperibus annuntiatur læta & faustum gratia Dei partæq; salutis nuntium. Sunt autem pauperes illi, non quotquot quoad fortunæ bona egent & esuriunt, sed qui proprio iudicio pauperes sunt, & suam miseriam in semetipsis sentiunt: & ideo apud Matthæum pauperes spiritu dicuntur, vt Cap. 6. diximus. At quod hic dicit Christus, plurimùm consolatur, & in certam salutis spem omnes eos erigit, qui intra conscientias suas peccatorum mole se grauari sentiunt. Quia enim salutis prædicatio proprie pauperibus destinata est, nequaquam dubitare debent, quin illa ad ipsos quoq; pertineat. Discat modò omnes confidentia cristas deprimere, & in Dei conspectu humiliari, ne sua superbia seipsos Dei gratia & salute indignos faciant. Adhæc scandalo quoq; locus iste medetur, quod tunc obiici solet, quando pauciores ad Christum accedere videmus ex ijs, qui in mundo præclari habentur. Vt enim cibi ijs demum grati sunt, quorum appetitus fame aliqua acuitur, & vt medicum ijsoli animo cupido et morigero admittunt, qui morbi vim intra se sentiunt: ita Euangelium non nisi miseris & afflictis sapit, quos propriæ infirmitatis & miseriæ sensus in mentem & solicitudinem conijcit. Et si in hac causa humani ingenij naturam propius consideremus, adeo non offendemur credentium paucitate, vt potius admiraturi simus aliquos inueniri, qui Euangelio locum dent, quando vix quisquam reperitur, quem non aliquo modo suipsius fiducia inflet. Alij enim fortunæ bonis superbiunt: alij voluptatibus immersi securè omnia ridente, quæ de Dei minis atq; iudicijs dicuntur. Si qui verò vel corpore laborant, vel egeni esuriunt, ij fere in suo illo cruciatu et egestate salutis meritum collocant: qui etsi reuera miseri & pauperes sint, quoad externa omnia, spiritu tamen diuites sunt, id est, spiritus conceperunt grandes & superbos, quibus elati se sibi ipsis sufficere arbitrantur. Meminerimus ergo, nihil dum nos profecisse in salutis negotio, quoad non sentimus nos infelices & miseros esse.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed here to whom Christ and the good things which are offered to us in him through the Gospel pertain. "The poor," he says, "have the gospel preached to them," that is, to the poor is announced the joyful and happy news of the grace of God and of salvation obtained. But those poor are not all who lack and hunger for the goods of fortune, but those who are poor in their own judgement, and feel their misery in themselves; and therefore in Matthew they are called "poor in spirit," as we said in chapter 6. But what Christ says here greatly consoles, and raises to a certain hope of salvation all those who feel that they are weighed down within their consciences by the mass of their sins. For since the preaching of salvation is properly destined for the poor, they ought by no means to doubt that it pertains to them also. Let all learn only to lower their crests of confidence, and to humble themselves in the sight of God, lest by their pride they make themselves unworthy of the grace and salvation of God. Besides, this passage also heals the stumbling-block which is usually raised when we see fewer of those who are held illustrious in the world coming to Christ. For just as foods are pleasant only to those whose appetite is sharpened by some hunger, and just as they admit a physician willingly and compliantly only when they feel the force of the disease within themselves, so the Gospel tastes good only to the wretched and afflicted, whom the sense of their own weakness and misery brings to mind and anxiety. And if we consider more closely the nature of the human mind in this matter, we shall not be offended so much by the small number of believers as rather be amazed that any are found who give room to the Gospel, since scarcely anyone is found whom some confidence in himself does not puff up. For some take pride in the goods of fortune; others, immersed in pleasures, securely laugh at everything that is said about the threats and judgements of God. Those who labour in body, or hunger in poverty and want, for the most part place the merit of salvation in that very torment and destitution of theirs: although they are indeed wretched and poor in all external things, nevertheless they are rich in spirit, that is, they have conceived great and proud spirits, by which, elated, they think themselves sufficient for themselves. Let us remember, therefore, that we have not yet made any progress in the business of salvation, so long as we do not feel that we are unhappy and wretched.

units.la: Altera responsionis Christi pars Anthypopohoram siue Præoccupationem habet, quæ ei scandalo medetur, ad quod ipsos Ioannis discipulos iam tunc offendere sciebat, cum ipsum vili & contemptibili specie inter auditores æquè viles & contemptibiles versari cernerent. Qui enim (vt paulo ante diximus) Regem armis & apparatu magnifico se ostentantem animo conceperant, ijs absurdum videbatur eum pro Messia agnoscere, quo nihil in mundo miserius & contemptius inueniri poterat. Dicit ergo: Beatus est, quicunq; non fuerit offensus in me. Quasi diceret: Scio vobis mirum videri, me tanta præstare posse, qui à plerisq; contemnor, neq; aliquid in mundo proprium possideo, quò vel caput meum reclinem. At non in externa specie vos hærere oportet, sed animos altius in cœlestium bonorum contemplationem attollere, quæ per me pater mundo offert. Multa enim sunt, quæ fidei obstare possunt: sed ij soli beati erunt & felices, qui per omnia scandala eluctantur, & his superiores facti in me vno acquiescunt, qualiscunque mundo stolido & infelici videar.
units.tr: The second part of Christ's answer contains an anthypophora, or prevention of objection, which remedies the stumbling-block by which he knew that the disciples of John were already then being offended, when they saw him living among hearers as lowly and contemptible as himself, in a mean and despised appearance. For those who (as we said a little earlier) had conceived in their minds a king displaying himself with arms and magnificent equipment, it seemed absurd to them to acknowledge him as the Messiah, than whom nothing more wretched and despised could be found in the world. He therefore says: "Blessed is he who is not offended in me." As if he said: I know it seems strange to you that I can accomplish such great things, I who am despised by most, and who possess nothing of my own in the world on which I may even lay my head. But you ought not to cling to the outward appearance, but to lift your minds higher to the contemplation of the heavenly goods which the Father offers to the world through me. For there are many things which can hinder faith; but those alone will be blessed and happy who struggle through all stumbling-blocks, and, having risen above them, rest in me alone, whatever I may seem to the foolish and unhappy world.

units.la: Continent ista generalem admonitionem, cuius nos etiam frequenter meminisse oportet. Nec enim temere Spiritus sanctus Christum petram scandali et lapidem offensionis vocat. Et si enim ille, si ipsum spectes, nihil minus sit, ea tamen est carnis nostræ peruersitas, vt in via plana & luce meridiana offendamus: imò quia natura abhorremus à doctrina Christi, plerique scandala magno studio conquirunt, vt aliquam illius repudiandi occasionem inueniant, & contumaciam suam aliquo plausibili prætextu excusare possint. Et hic breui ingentem materiam caro colligit, ex qua contigeriem scandalorum fabricet. Alios enim offendit vilis & contemptibilis Christi species, quibus nimirum nihil magnificum videtur, quàm quod huius mundi splendore radiat. Sed debebant hi meminisse, regnum eius non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde nihil mundanum aut terrenum in eo quæri debere. Sunt rursus, quos crucis prædicatio offendit, & his stultitia putatur salutis & vitæ spem in eo repositum habere, qui ipse dira & ignominiosa morte occisus est. Quibus dici poterit, proprium hoc Dei esse: quod occidit ut vivificet, deprimit ut exaltet. Alij gratiae doctrina offenduntur, quibus salutis viam aequo faciliorem fingere, & ad Epicureismum atque morum licentiam iter sternere videmur, si homines ex sola gratia per fidem in Iesum Christum iustificari doceamus. Qui si peccati atrocitatem & naturae nostrae vitiositatem expenderent, adhaec cogitarent, quid sit Christo fidere, & quae fidei huius effecta sint, mox sentirent se plus quam stolidos esse, quod in re tam facili & expedita nodos & ambages fingant. Inveniuntur e contra, quos disciplinae Christianae rigor abster ret, & qui iniquè secum agi putant, quòd mundo renuntiare, seipsos abnegare, carnem cum suis desiderijs mortificare, & ab omni specie mali abstinere iubeantur. Sed quae ratio Christum iniquitatis aut nimij rigoris convincet, si sibi totos vult consecratos esse, quos sanguine suo pretio acquisivit? Annon iniqui & perduellionis manifestae rei sunt, qui cum Christi nomen profiteantur, in diaboli tamen castris militant? Alios quoque videas, quos crux, perpetua fidei comes, moratur, ne Christi nomen dent. At nimium delicatuli sunt, qui sibi melius esse volunt, quàm Dei Filio: nimis item stupidi, qui se absque molestia in hoc mundo vivere posse sperant. Multi praeterea dissensiones & partium studia nobis obiiciunt, neque prius ad Christi partes sibi transfeundum esse arbitrantur, donec per omnia consenserint, qui fidem in illum profitentur. Sed cur non observant illi consensum nostrum in iis articulis, ex quibus salus tota dependet? Cur non Apostolici illius dicti meminerunt: Oportet sectas esse inter vos, ut qui probati sunt manifesti fiant? Et cur in seipsos tam iniqui & crudeles sunt, ut propriae salutis curam suspendere & negligere velint propter aliorum dissidia? Accedunt his, qui ex Evangelij doctrina turbas & seditiones oriri clamant, & hanc unam causam sufficere censent, cur cordati & prudentes viri ab eius professione abstineant. At hi si oculos aperirent tumultus Evangelij quidem comites, non autem huius proprios fructus esse viderent: sed hos ab illis extitari, qui ut peccandi licentia diutius frui possint, lucem extinctam volunt. Et cum inter turbas illas omnino periclitandum sit, quamcunque partem sequaris, nimium imprudentes & fatui sunt, qui pro mala potius quàm bona causa sibi laborandum esse putant. Vel annon quovis supplicio dignus est, qui neutralis esse volet, quando de regno Dei & caelesti patria contentio est, cum Solon bonum esse civem negarit, qui in publica seditione neutri parti se se adiungeret? Possent huius generis infinita commemorari, sed iam nunc longius excreuit oratio: & quia de his alibi prolixè dixi- mus, sufficiat nunc monuisse, nobis adversus ista omnia luctandum esse neque aliquid admitti debere, quod nos ab unico salutis authore Iesu Christo abstrahat. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: These words contain a general admonition, of which we too ought often to be mindful. For the Holy Spirit does not rashly call Christ a rock of stumbling and a stone of offence. And although he, if you look at him, is nothing less than this, yet such is the perversity of our flesh that we stumble on a level road and in broad daylight; indeed, because by nature we shrink from the doctrine of Christ, many eagerly seek out stumbling-blocks, so as to find some occasion for rejecting it, and to be able to excuse their obstinacy under some plausible pretext. And here the flesh gathers vast material from which to fashion an endless series of stumbling-blocks. For the mean and contemptible appearance of Christ offends some, to whom nothing seems magnificent unless it shines with the splendour of this world. But these ought to remember that his kingdom is not of this world, and therefore nothing worldly or earthly ought to be sought in it. There are again those whom the preaching of the cross offends, and to them it seems folly to have placed the hope of life and salvation in him who was himself killed by a cruel and shameful death. To these it may be said that this is the peculiar mark of God: that he kills in order to make alive, and humbles in order to exalt. Others are offended by the doctrine of grace, to whom we seem to feign a way of salvation that is too easy, and to pave the road to Epicureanism and licence of morals, if we teach that men are justified by grace alone through faith in Jesus Christ. If they weighed the atrocity of sin and the vitiousness of our nature, and considered besides what it is to trust in Christ and what are the effects of this faith, they would soon perceive that they are more than foolish, in that they invent knots and windings in a matter so easy and so plain. On the contrary, there are some whom the rigour of Christian discipline deters, and who think they are dealt with unjustly because they are commanded to renounce the world, to deny themselves, to mortify the flesh with its desires, and to abstain from every appearance of evil. But what reason will convict Christ of injustice or excessive rigour, if he wishes to have wholly consecrated to himself those whom he has acquired with his own blood as the price? Are not those unjust and manifestly guilty of treason who, while professing the name of Christ, nevertheless fight in the camps of the devil? You may see others whom the cross, the perpetual companion of faith, holds back from giving their name to Christ. But they are too delicate who wish to be better off than the Son of God; too stupid, likewise, who hope that they can live in this world without trouble. Many besides object to us dissensions and party zeal, and think that they must not pass over to the side of Christ until all who profess faith in him have agreed in everything. But why do they not observe our agreement in those articles on which all salvation depends? Why do they not remember that saying of the Apostle: "There must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be made manifest"? And why are they so unjust and cruel to themselves that they wish to suspend and neglect the care of their own salvation on account of the disagreements of others? To these are added those who cry that tumults and seditions arise from the doctrine of the Gospel, and think this one cause sufficient why wise and prudent men should abstain from its profession. But if they opened their eyes, they would see that tumults are indeed companions of the Gospel, but not its proper fruits; rather, they are stirred up by those who wish the light to be extinguished so that they may enjoy a longer licence to sin. And since among those disturbances one must necessarily run some risk whichever side one follows, they are excessively imprudent and foolish who think that they should labour for a bad cause rather than a good one. Or is not he deserving of any punishment who wishes to be neutral when there is a contest over the kingdom of God and the heavenly fatherland, since Solon denied that a man was a good citizen who, in a public sedition, did not join himself to either party? Infinite instances of this kind could be recalled, but my discourse has already grown longer than it should; and since I have discussed these things at length elsewhere, it is enough now to have admonished that we must struggle against all these things, and that nothing should be admitted which draws us away from the one author of salvation, Jesus Christ. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIX.

units.la: Et cum abiissent nuntij Ioannis, coepit de Ioanne dicere ad turbam: Quid existis in desertum ut spectaretis? Arundinem, quae vento agitetur? Sed quid existis ut videretis? Hominem mollibus vestimentis amictum? Ecce qui vestitu honorifico & luxu vtuntur, sunt in domibus regum. Sed quid existis ut videretis? Prophetam? Certè dico vobis, etiam amplius quàm prophetam. Hic est de quo scriptum est: Ecce mitto nuntium meum ante faciem tuam, qui praeparabit viam tuam coram te. Nā dico vobis, inter eos qui gignuntur e mulieribus, nemo est maior Propheta Ioanne Baptista. Sed qui minimus est in regno Dei, maior est eo.
units.tr: And when the messengers of John had departed, he began to speak to the crowd about John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear splendid clothing and live in luxury are in the houses of kings. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Certainly I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one of whom it is written: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. For I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than the prophet John the Baptist. But he who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he."

units.la: Ioannes Baptista à Deo missus fuit, ut de vera luce, Iesu Christo, publicè testaretur, & ad hunc excipiendum omnes excitaret. Quod qua fide & diligentia fecerit, suo loco audiimus. Vt autem in aestimandis Dei seruis varie inter homines peccari solet, iam in Ioanne etiam est factum. Nam qui eius discipuli familiares erant, nimia virtutis & donorum eius admiratione abrepti, illum pro Messia colebant, & Christum invidiose aemulabantur, quòd eum Ioanne indies superiorem fieri viderent. Eos ergo ad Christum ille remisit, qui & verbis & operibus demonstrauit, se unicum humanæ salutis authorem esse, & proinde nullum alium debere expectari. At erant alij ex vulgo, qui cùm prius vinculis & captiuitate Ioannis non parum offensi essent, nunc multò magis quæstione illa offendi poterant, quam ex eius ore discipuli Christo proposuerunt: & credibile est, aliquos ex ea occasione sumpsisse, ut de testimonio, quod ille Christo dederat, & doctrina eius vniuersa dubitarent. Cur enim non dicerent, qui consilij eius rationem nō intelligebant: Quid hæc quæstio sibi vult? Annon nobis iampridem de Christo Ioannes concionatus est, & hunc dixit esse agnum illum Dei, qui peccatum mundi tollat? Qui igne & spiritu baptizet? cuius corrigiam soluere nō sit ipse dignus, & cui vni sponsa adduci debeat? Cur ergo nunc quærit, num hic ille sit qui venturus erat, vel num alius debeat expectari? Si enim prius non temere illa dixit, neque vanus testis fuit, cur de Christo iam quærit? cur quod testatus est, nunc in dubium vocat. At si nunc rerum dubius fuit, cur de illo tam constanter pronuntiauit? Hæc (inquam) multorum tunc cogitationes fuerunt, & fortasse aliqui sermones quoque huiusmodi inter se contulerunt. Itaque cum iis in præsenti agit Dominus, & postquam Ioannis discipuli abierunt, illius authoritatem grauiter asserit, ne quis de testimonij & doctrinæ eius veritate dubitaret. Noluit tamen præsentibus & audientibus eius discipulis hæc dicere, ne hi in nimia Ioannis admiratione confirmarentur, aut cum multorum scandalo nouam de illo disputationem instituerent. Ita vero pia & sanctæ prudentiæ exemplum præbet, qua verbi administros omnes instructos esse conuenit, ut suo loco & tempore dicant atque faciant omnia, ne plures offendant, aut nouis rixis occasionem præbeant, dum quæus absq; omni auditorum respectu tenere dicunt.
units.tr: John the Baptist was sent by God to bear public witness to the true Light, Jesus Christ, and to rouse everyone to receive him. How faithfully and diligently he did this we heard in its proper place. But just as men commonly go wrong in judging God's servants, this happened in the case of John too. For his disciples, who were close to him, carried away by an excessive admiration for his virtue and gifts, honoured him as the Messiah and resented Christ with jealousy, because they saw Christ growing greater than John day by day. So John sent them back to Christ, who by both his words and his works showed that he alone is the author of human salvation and that no other should be expected. But there were others among the common people who, although they had previously been not a little offended by John's imprisonment and captivity, could now be offended all the more by the question his disciples put to Christ on his behalf. It is likely that some took the occasion from it to doubt both the testimony that John had given to Christ and his whole teaching. For why would they not say, those who did not understand the reason for his plan: "What does this question mean? Has John not long since preached about Christ and said that he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, who baptizes with fire and the Spirit, whose sandal strap he is not worthy to loosen, and to whom alone the bride must be brought? Why then does he now ask whether this one is the one who was to come, or whether another must be expected? If he did not speak those things rashly before, and was not a false witness, why does he now ask about Christ? Why does he now call into doubt what he testified? But if he is now uncertain of the facts, why did he pronounce so firmly about him?" These, I say, were the thoughts of many at that time, and perhaps some also discussed such things among themselves. So the Lord deals with them in the present case, and after John's disciples had gone away, he firmly asserts John's authority, so that no one would doubt the truth of his testimony and teaching. Yet he did not wish to say these things while John's disciples were present and listening, lest they should be confirmed in their excessive admiration for John, or should start a new dispute about him to the scandal of many. Indeed, he gives an example of holy and godly prudence, to which all ministers of the Word ought to be trained: that they should say and do everything at the right place and time, so that they do not offend many or give occasion for new quarrels, and do not insist on saying whatever they please without any regard for their hearers.

units.la: Priusquam vero ad verborum Christi tractationem accedamus, probè obseruari debet, quod Ioannem non à generis nobilitate (quam illi ex parentibus magnificam obtigisse cap.1. audiuimus) non à corporis forma, non à principum fauore & amicitijs, non item à fortunæ bonis aliis, sed à virtutibus commendadat: Constantia animi mirum, Fortitudine, Temperantia, Fide deniq; et studio, quo creditum sibi à Deo munus obiuit. Quo exemplo docemur, eam demum veram atq; solidam laudem & gloriam esse, quæ ex virtute manat, non eam quæ à stolidi & leuis vulgi iudicio dependet. Fallunt enim externa omnia, nec temere olim ex Dei mandato clamauit Propheta: Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Et vana est dumtaxat rerum istarum imago, quas mundus tantope re admiratur, ideoq; neq; vera neq; stabilis aut solida esse potest laus sine gloria, quæ illis ceu fundamento nititur. Quod eo magis dices, si cogitaueris quam multi sint, qui illa sibi ipsis uoxia & ignominiosa faciunt, dum carnis desideria atq; cupiditates secuti, illis turpiter abutuntur. Nunquam ergo probari debet eorum sententia, qui in illis laudem & gloriam quærunt, aut ijdem superbiunt, quasi omnem fortunæ euentum longè superarint, quando se bonis huius seculi affluere vident.
units.tr: Before we come to the discussion of Christ's words, we must carefully observe that John is commended not for the nobility of his birth (which we heard in chapter 1 was an honourable one, inherited from his parents), not for his bodily appearance, not for the favour and friendships of princes, nor for any other of fortune's goods, but for his virtues: his wonderful constancy of mind, his fortitude, his temperance, and finally his faith and the zeal with which he discharged the office entrusted to him by God. By this example we are taught that the true and solid praise and glory is that which springs from virtue, not that which depends on the judgment of the foolish and fickle crowd. For all external things deceive, and the prophet rightly cried out long ago by God's command: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the field." The image of those things which the world admires so greatly is empty indeed, and therefore praise without glory, which rests on them as its foundation, cannot be true, stable or solid. This will be even clearer if you consider how many there are who make those things harmful and shameful to themselves, while following the desires and lusts of the flesh and shamefully abusing them. So the opinion of those should never be approved who seek praise and glory in such things, or who become proud as if they had far surpassed every outcome of fortune whenever they see themselves abounding in the goods of this age.

units.la: His præmissis, Christum de Ioanne concionantem audiamus. Laudat illu (vt modò diximus) à virtutibus, quæ in eo eximiæ & præclaræ fuerunt: ex quibus primò constantiam prædicat, & ita quidem, vt illos ipsos testes sistat quibus loquitur. Nam ad populum conuersus ait: Quid existis in desertum vt spectaretis? Arundinem ne, quæ vento agitetur? Ita autem loquendo illis in mentem reuocat ardens illud studium, quo accensi undique ex Galilæa & Iudæa ad Ioannem videndum at que audiendum excurrerant, vt cap. tertio dictum est: & vult vt anteaactorum memores animo repetant, quis Ioannes fuerit, qualem inuenerint, quid item ex eo audiuerint, & proinde non patiantur intercidere eius doctrinæ fructum, quem tanto feruore sint assecuti. Itaque verborum istorum sensus est. Meministis opinor, quantus in vobis ardor fuerit audiendi Ioannis, adeò, vt reliquis rebus vestris omnibus, ad illum excurreretis. Quid verò vos mouit? Num vana quædam & leuis doctrinæ aut virtutis ostentatio? Vel num hominem vos visuros & auditurus putauistis, quin horas mutetur, & arundinis instar quouis vento circumferatur? Non opinor. Quis enim homini leui & inconstanti tantùm tribuat, vt propter eum labores suscipere, sumptus facere, et inuidiam apud plerosque subire velit? Dignum ergo iudicauistis, quem omnes spectarent & audirent, neque vos hæc vestra opinio fefellit. Inueniistis enim hominem inuicta animi constantia armatum, quem neque Pharisæorum præsentia, neque inquisitorum fastus & insidiosæ quæstiones, neque diuersa & iniqua vulgi iudicia, neque Herodis libido & crudelitas, neque vlla alia pericula terrere potuerunt, quò minus docendo pergeret, & doctrinam eandem subinde inculcaret, qua & pænitentiam omnibus præcepit, & de me non minus graviter quàm diserte & ingenuè testatus est. Talem ergo illũ adhuc esse credite, neq; vos offendat quæstio, quam discipuli eius modò moverunt. Neq; enim ille sententiam mutavit, neq; quis ego sim nunc ignorat, sed longè aliam causam subesse cogitate, quæ illum movét, ut hanc ad me legationem mitteret, & c.
units.tr: With these things set down, let us hear Christ preaching about John. As we have just said, he praises him for his virtues, which were outstanding and remarkable in him. Of these he first commends his constancy, and does so by bringing forward as witnesses the very people he is speaking to. For, turning to the crowd, he says: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?" By speaking in this way he recalls to their minds that burning eagerness with which people from all over Galilee and Judea had rushed out to see and hear John, as was said in chapter 3. He wants them to call back to mind what they had done before, who John was, what kind of man they had found him to be, and what they had heard from him, and so not to allow the fruit of his teaching, which they had gained with such fervour, to be lost. So the sense of these words is this: "You remember, I think, how great was your zeal to hear John, so that you ran out to him leaving all your other affairs. But what moved you? Was it some empty display of teaching or virtue? Or did you think you would see and hear a man who changes his mind every hour and is carried about by any wind like a reed? I think not. For who would attribute so much to a light and inconstant man that he would be willing to undertake labours, incur expenses, and bear the hatred of many on his account? So you judged him worthy to be looked at and listened to by all, and your opinion did not deceive you. For you found a man armed with an unconquered constancy of mind, whom neither the presence of the Pharisees, nor the arrogance and insidious questions of the inquisitors, nor the diverse and unjust judgments of the common people, nor Herod's lust and cruelty, nor any other danger could terrify from continuing to teach, and from repeatedly inculcating the same doctrine, by which he commanded repentance to all, and bore witness about me no less seriously than clearly and openly. Therefore believe that he is still such a man, and let not the question which his disciples have just raised offend you. For he has not changed his judgment, and he knows now who I am; but consider that there is a quite different cause underlying the reason which moves him to send this embassy to me, and so on."

units.la: Est autem observatu dignissimum, quod Ioannis commendationem à constantia orditur. Est enim hæc virtutum omnium quasi Colophon aut perfectio seu fulcrum, eò quod illæ vel intermo-riuntur, vel in vitia degenerant, nisi constantia accedat, quæ & illas quotidie auctiores reddit, & nos in officio continet, ne illis relictis post carnis desideria declinemus. Etenim si quibus in iis, quæ bene coeperunt, constantia virtus deest, ij eorum similes sunt, qui in stadio cursuri, strenuè quidem incipiunt, in medio autem cursu subsistunt, aut ignaui considerent. Nam ut hi neq; brauium obtinent, neque aliquam laudem inde referunt: ita isti quoque nihil unquam effectum dant, neque ad beatam illam felicitatis metam perveniunt, quam illi soli attingunt, qui in finem usque perseuerant. Est autem constantia verbi administris quàm maximè necessaria, quos duo hæc firmiter spectare, & tenere oportet. Primum, ut doctrinam eandem constanter prædicent: eam nimirum, quam ex Dei ore, id est scripturæ sacræ libris desumpserunt. Nam qui noua subinde proferunt dogmata, aut quæ prius tradiderunt mox mutant, vel nouis expositionibus detorquent, et cothurnos fingunt, quos in omnem partem interpretari possint, ij sua omnia suspecta reddunt, & multis noxiæ dubitationis aut diffidentiæ authores sunt. Difficile enim est, homines rudes & illiteratos in fide & æternæ salutis doctrina aliquid certum tenere, si eos fluctuare, & vertuni instar subinde mutari videant, quos sibi magistros aut doctores constituerunt. At hic simul videndum est, ut si quis initiò falsus est, eum meliora edoctum non pudeat sententiam mutare, & rectè sentientibus cedere. Nam qui temere conceptas opiniones aut manifestos errores tuentur mordicus, ij non constantiæ laudem merentur, sed pertinaces dici debent: quod vitium à doctore alienissimum esse debere Paulus admo-net, eò quod qui eo laborant, ij fere hæresum & dissidiorum authores sunt, ex quibus publica totius Ecclesiæ dissipatio nascitur. Alterum, ut nullis rationibus se terreri aut adduci patiantur, quo minus sanam doctrinam recte sequentur, & pro temporum atque locorum ratione applicent auditoribus, ut publicæ omnium ædificationi seruire possit. Multa enim verbi administris obijciuntur, ne officium faciant, ut in Prophetis est videre. Sed ut hi constantes fuerunt in iis inculcandis, quibus aduersarios maximè offendi & irritari sciebant, ita etiam hodie fiat oportet. Turpe enim fuerit à mundo eos vinci qui Dei serui sunt, & illius minas pluris facere quàm huius promissiones, quibus suum patrocinium & regni sui consortium omnibus illis pollicetur, qui in verbi sui dispensatione fideles fuerint. At quod ministris dicitur, hoc etiam ij ad se pertinere putent, qui magistratum gerunt. Ingens Dei beneficium est respub. bonis legibus confirmata. In his ergo tuendis constantes sint, qui rempub. administrant, neque eos audiant, qui legibus conqueruntur, & turbas daturi videntur. Nam periculosior est quantulacunque reipub. mutatio, neque ibi pedem sistunt qui leges quascunque abolere volunt, ubi putantur: sed præter opinionem latius vagari solet im-proborum licentia, ubi semel ei habenæ laxatæ fuerint. Et ut torrentes, si vel minima rima pateat, mox aggeres totos perrumpunt, & indomito cursu per campos & agros ruunt, segetes sternunt, arbores radicitus euellunt, & (ut poetæ verbis utar) rapiunt hominumque boumque labores: ita si quibus detur unam aut alteram legem violare, mox & ipsi eo successu audaciores facti alias quoque aggrediuntur, & eorundem exemplo alij prouocati idem tentant, atque crescente indies contumacium numero totius reipub. ruina sequitur. Viderunt hoc sapientissimi quique legislatores, qui leges sacrosanctas esse voluerunt, ne qui eas priuato arbitrio abolere aut mutare audeerent. Laudantur in Romana historia Censores, qui Duronium Senatu monuerunt, quòd Legem de coercendis conuiuiorum sumptibus latam Tribunus plebis abrogauerat. Et exempla multa docent, non semel paucorum constantia rempub. seruatam fuisse, quando in extremum discrimen addu-cta esse videbatur. Debent de hoc etiam frequenter cogitare priuati homines, quibus non minus tam in religione quàm aliis rebus constantia opus est, ne vel ad quemuis ventura noua doctrina sententiam mutent, vel cultus quotidie nouos suscipiant, aut ad nouum vitæ genus temere transeant.
units.tr: It is most worth noting that John's commendation begins with constancy. Constancy is, as it were, the crown or completion and the prop of all the virtues, because the virtues either wither away or degenerate into vices unless constancy is added, which both renews them every day and keeps us in our duty, so that we do not, having abandoned them, turn aside after the desires of the flesh. For if those who have begun well lack the virtue of constancy, they are like men who, running in a race, set off vigorously but halt in the middle of the course or sit idle. For just as these neither win the prize nor gain any praise from it, so those people never accomplish anything and never reach that blessed goal of happiness, which only those attain who persevere to the end. Now constancy is most necessary for the ministers of the Word, who ought to keep two things firmly in view and hold to them. First, that they preach the same doctrine constantly, namely the doctrine they have drawn from the mouth of God, that is, from the books of Holy Scripture. For those who keep bringing forth new dogmas, or who soon change what they have taught before, or twist it by fresh explanations, and devise buskins that they can fit to any shape, make all their teaching suspect and become authors of harmful doubt and distrust for many. For it is hard for simple and unlearned people to hold anything certain in the faith and in the doctrine of eternal salvation if they see those whom they have appointed as their masters wavering and changing like a weathercock. Yet at the same time one must take care that, if someone has been mistaken at the start, he is not ashamed to change his opinion when better taught, and to yield to those who think rightly. For those who obstinately defend rashly conceived opinions or plain errors do not deserve the praise of constancy, but ought rather to be called stubborn; and Paul warns that this fault must be most foreign to a teacher, because those who labour under it are generally the authors of heresies and dissensions, from which the public ruin of the whole Church arises. The second thing is that they must not allow themselves to be terrified or moved by any arguments, so that they fail to follow sound doctrine properly and apply it to their hearers according to the circumstances of time and place, so that it may serve the common edification of all. For many objections are raised against ministers of the Word to stop them from doing their duty, as can be seen in the Prophets. But just as those prophets were steadfast in inculcating those things which they knew most offended and angered their adversaries, so it must be done today as well. For it would be shameful for those who are servants of God to be conquered by the world, and to make more of its threats than of its promises, by which God pledges his protection and a share in his kingdom to all those who have been faithful in dispensing his Word. And what is said to the ministers, those who bear the magistracy should also think applies to them. The republic, confirmed by good laws, is a great blessing of God. Therefore let those who administer the commonwealth be steadfast in defending these laws, and let them not listen to those who complain about the laws and seem ready to stir up disturbances.
