For even the slightest change in a commonwealth is dangerous, and those who wish to abolish any laws whatever do not stop where they think they will; rather, the license of the wicked is wont to spread more widely than expected once the reins have been loosened for it. Just as torrents, if even the smallest crack opens, soon burst through whole embankments and, with unrestrained course, rush over fields and farms, lay low the crops, and tear up trees by the roots, and (to use the poet's words) carry off the labours of men and oxen, so if some are allowed to violate one or another law, soon they themselves, made bolder by that success, attack others too, and others, provoked by their example, attempt the same, and as the number of the obstinate grows daily, the ruin of the whole commonwealth follows. The wisest lawgivers have seen this, who wished their laws to be held sacred, so that no one would dare to abolish or change them by private judgment. In Roman history the Censors are praised, who warned the Senate about Duronius, because a tribune of the plebs had repealed the law restraining the expenses of banquets. And many examples show that more than once the commonwealth has been saved by the constancy of a few, when it seemed brought to the utmost peril. Private persons too ought often to think about this, since they need constancy no less in religion than in other matters, so that they neither change their opinion at every new doctrine that comes along, nor take up new forms of worship every day, nor rashly pass over to a new way of life.

units.la: Notum est enim illud Christi: Nemo, qui vbi manum aratro admouit, a tergo respicit, dignus est regno Dei. Et plerunq; infelices sunt eorum euentus, qui deserta vocatione, quam a Deo habent, rebus alienis & nihil ad se pertinentibus sese immiscent. Recte ergo Paulus monuit: Maneat quisq; in vocatione, qua vocatus est. Potest haec doctrina latissime ad omnes actiones & studia hominum extendi, sed in praesenti sufficiat occasionem dedisse in his diligentius cogitandi.
units.tr: For that saying of Christ is well known: "No one who has put his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." And generally those who abandon the calling they have received from God, and thrust themselves into affairs that are not theirs and have nothing to do with them, have unhappy outcomes. Rightly, then, Paul admonishes: "Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called" (1 Cor. 7). This teaching can be extended very widely to all the actions and pursuits of men, but for the present it will be enough to have given an occasion for thinking more carefully about these things.

units.la: Nunc in Christi verbis progrediamur, qui Ioannem secundo loco a temperantia & fortitudine commendat, & rursus ipsos auditores compellans ait: Quid exiistis vt videretis? Hominem ne mol libus vestimentis amictum? &c. Quasi diceret: Satscio, vos cum tanto ardore & studio ad Ioannem excurreretis, minime quaesiisse hominem molliculum, qui turpiter omnibus obuijs adulareiur, & animum corruptum vestitu molliori & omnis generis delitijs proderet. Nam qui tales sunt, ij non in desertis locis, sed in aulis regum agunt. Illic summa sapientia esse putatur, principi placere, omnibus morem gerere, neque aliquem offendere. Illic generis nobilitatem & splendorem magnifico vestitu ostentant, qui alijs illustriores haberi volunt. Illic enim luxus & intemperantia regnat, quae mores simul omnes corrumpunt. In desertis autem locis nihil huius cerniitur, neque in illis diu subsistunt, quorum animi ad mollitiem & intemperantiam inclinant. Et vos ipsi testari potestis, Ioannem ab eiusmodi moribus alienissimum fuisse. Vidistis enim quis eius victus, quis item vestitus fuerit: frugalis nimirum, & loco conueniens, in quo vitam duxit. Vnde rursus sequitur, illum non in eorum numero habendum esse, qui vt luxui & intemperantiae suae sufficere possint, quorum-uis moribus sese accommodant, & omnibus turpiter nimis atque seruiliter assentiuntur. Quid ergo de me ille pronuntiauit olim, id adhuc firmum ratum est, neq; de doctrinae eius veritate quisquam dubitare debet.
units.tr: Now let us proceed to the words of Christ, who commends John, in the second place, for temperance and fortitude, and again addressing the hearers themselves says: "What did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft raiment?" (Matt. 11). As if he were saying: I know that you ran out to John with such eagerness and zeal not at all to seek a soft, effeminate man, who would shamelessly flatter everyone he met, and who would reveal a corrupt mind by softer clothing and all kinds of pleasures. For such men do not live in deserts but in royal courts. There it is thought the height of wisdom to please the prince, to humour everyone, and to offend no one. There those who want to be thought more illustrious than others display the nobility of their birth and their splendour by magnificent clothing. For luxury and intemperance reign there, and these at the same time corrupt all morals. But in desert places nothing of this is seen, and those whose minds incline to softness and intemperance do not remain there long. And you yourselves can bear witness that John was most alien to such manners. For you saw what his food was, and what his clothing was: plainly frugal, and suited to the place where he lived. From this it follows again that he is not to be counted among those who adapt themselves to any manners whatever so as to satisfy luxury and their own intemperance, and who assent shamefully and servilely to everything. What he once pronounced about me, therefore, still stands firm, and no one ought to doubt the truth of his teaching.

units.la: At hic rursus obseruabis, Ioannem omnibus ijs in exemplum proponi, qui in verbi Dei & ecclesiae ministerio versantur. Decet hos in primis, vt ab adulatorijs artibus & aulica sapientia alienissimi sint, amicos autem habeant ingenuos & fortes, qui non hominibus, sed vni Christo placere studeant. Ad hoc plurimum momenti conferet, si frugalitati & temperantiae assuescant. Nam qui gulae & ventri seruiunt, aut vestitu molliori alijsque rebus ad luxum institutis superbiunt, ij quia multu opus habent, & non semper sumptibus tantis sufficere possunt, non raro coguntur dissimulare quae reprehensione digna esse sciunt, saepe etiam suo suffragio probant, quae intra animos suos damnant, & dum mundo placere volunt, in propriam conscientiam peccant, & neque Deo neque hominibus fideles sunt. Quae mihi causa potissima videtur, ob quam veteres prophetae in victu & vestitu temperantissimi fuerunt. De Elia certe legimus, eum Zona coreacea vsum fuisse; & quam tenuis prophetarum victus fuerit, satis constat ex ijs, quae de Elisaeo & discipulis eius sacra historia perhibet. De Apostolis quid attinet dicere, qui cum prius tenuioris fortunae essent, non dubium est, quin ad Christi exemplum tenuiorem viuendi rationem semper secuti sint? In Apocalypsi ministris, qui nouissimis temporibus de Christo sint testaturi, sacci tribuuntur, vestitus nimirum minime pretiosus, & qui doctrinae de paenitentia propriissime conueniat. Durauit hoc frugalitatis studium in veteri ecclesia, quae ab ornatu quoque templorum sumptuosiori abstinuit: vt quae sciret sacramenta non auro & argento vel gemmis commendari, sed vsu & eorum pietate, qui illis recte vtuntur.
units.tr: But here again you will observe that John is set forth as an example to all who are engaged in the ministry of God's Word and of the Church. Such men above all should be most alien to flattering arts and courtly wisdom, and should have free and brave friends, who strive to please not men but Christ alone. Much will contribute to this if they become accustomed to frugality and temperance. For those who serve their throat and belly, or who pride themselves on softer clothing and other things devised for luxury, since they have many needs and cannot always meet such expenses, are often compelled to dissemble what they know deserves reproof, and often even by their vote they approve what they inwardly condemn; and while they wish to please the world, they sin against their own conscience, and are faithful neither to God nor to men. This seems to me the chief reason why the ancient prophets were most temperate in food and clothing. Indeed we read of Elijah that he used a girdle of leather; and how meagre the food of the prophets was is sufficiently clear from what the sacred history tells of Elisha and his disciples. As for the Apostles, what need is there to speak? Since they were formerly of humble means, there is no doubt that following Christ's example they always adopted a poorer way of life. In the Apocalypse, sackcloth is assigned to the ministers who are to bear witness to Christ in the last times, clearly a garment by no means costly, and one most suited to the doctrine of repentance. This zeal for frugality lasted in the ancient Church, which also abstained from more lavish decoration of the churches, since it knew that the sacraments are commended not by gold, silver or gems, but by the use and piety of those who use them rightly.

units.la: Ita olim D. Ambrosius scribebat: Aurum habet ecclesia, non vt seruet, sed vt eroget, & subueniat in necessitatibus. Item: Aurum sacramenta non quaerunt, neque auro placent, quae auro non emuntur. Quanto magis igitur Sacramentorum administris cauendum est, ne seipsos molliori vestitu ornare instituant: sed vestibus vtantur, quae poenitentiae & Christianae frugalitatis atque modestiae doctores decere possint. Sed posteris temporibus factum est, vt cum imaginum cultu non templorum modo ornatus sumptuosior, verumetiam sacerdotum vestitus scenicus & exquisita mollitie tantum non infamis, inuectus sit. Et ferri poterat luxus ille apud eos, qui crucem Christi iampridem pedibus suis calcauerunt: At dolendum est, hodie inter Euangelij praecones & puriotis doctrinae instauratores passim inueniri eos, qui & papisticum habitum reducere satagunt, & ipsum vestitu mollitie plus quam aulica vtuntur. Excusant se illi principum & regum authoritate, qui haec ita fieri velint: sed maior penes illos debebat esse Christi Iesu authoritas & veteris atque puriotis Ecclesiae exemplum, cuius omnis gloria & ornatus (vt in Psalmo habetur) intus sit. Et cum cùm Ioannis ingenuitatem & in dicendo libertatem Christus ex vestitu probet, satis aperte con- stat, ipsos cùm in hoc tam molliculi sint, non ex eorum numero esse, penes quos fortis & ingenua ve-ritatis prædicatio quæri debeat.
units.tr: Ambrose long ago wrote: "The Church has gold, not to keep it, but to give it out and relieve needs." And again: "Sacraments do not seek gold, nor are they pleased by gold, since they are not bought with gold." How much more, then, must the administrators of the sacraments take care not to adopt softer clothing for themselves, but wear the garments that befit teachers of repentance and of Christian simplicity and modesty. In later times, however, along with the worship of images, a more lavish display came into the temples, and the clothing of the priests became theatrical and, with its exquisite softness, almost disreputable. Such luxury might be tolerated among those who long ago trampled the cross of Christ underfoot. But it is grievous that today, among the heralds of the gospel and the restorers of a purer teaching, there are found everywhere men who both strive to bring back the Papist dress and themselves wear clothing more delicate than that of courtiers. They excuse themselves by the authority of princes and kings who wish these things to be done this way. But the authority of Christ Jesus ought to weigh more with them, and the example of the old and purer Church, whose whole glory and adornment (as the Psalm says) is within. And since Christ, by John's clothing, shows John's uprightness and freedom in speaking, it is quite plain that these men, being so effeminate in this matter, are not of the number among whom the bold and sincere preaching of the truth ought to be sought.

units.la: At debent interea Ioannis exemplum omnes alij priuatim ad se transferre, ne dum vestitu si- bijpsis nimiùm indulgent, eo ipso sese infames faciant, quo maximè superbiunt. Nã quo animo quis- que prædítus sit, vestes ferè indicant: ut non temere molliculi dicantur, qui illis mollioribus vtun-tur: varij & inconstantes, qui nouas quotidie illarum formas fingunt: impudici & obscœni, qui ijsdë inhonestiores corporis partes exprimunt potius quàm tegunt. Sint ergo a Christianis hominibus alie-na prorsus peregrinitatis in vestitu studiû, fastus, luxus & quæcunq; libidinis irritamenta cense-ri possunt. Hæc enim vt viros minimè decent, & virginum atq; matronarum pudicitiam suspectam reddunt: ita rei domesticæ plurimùm incommodant, & multis extremæ egestatis causa sunt. Et tur pe est vestitu eos superbire, qui huius originem ex peccato manauisse norunt, & qui Christo nudo atq; crucifixo gloriantur. Sufficiat ergo vestes habere, quæ corpus honestè tegant, & aduersus cœli iniuriam defendant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, all others ought to take John's example to themselves privately, lest by indulging too much in clothing they make themselves infamous by the very thing in which they take most pride. For clothes generally reveal the disposition of the wearer: so those who wear softer garments are not rashly called effeminate; those who constantly invent new fashions are fickle and inconstant; those who display the more shameful parts of the body rather than covering them are immodest and obscene. Let Christians therefore have nothing to do with a foreign and wholly alien fondness for fashion in dress; pride, extravagance, and whatever can be counted as incitements to lust. For these things do not suit men at all, and they make the chastity of virgins and matrons suspect. In the same way they greatly harm domestic affairs and are the cause of extreme poverty for many. And it is unseemly for those to take pride in clothing who know that its origin flowed from sin, and who glory in Christ naked and crucified. It is enough, then, to have clothes that cover the body decently and protect it against the injuries of the weather.

units.la: Simul autem hoc loco aulicorum mores Christus perstringit, quibus summa sapientia videtur, se ad principis sui nutum accommodare, & consilia omnia ad priuatam vtilitatem instituere. Itaq; omnibus applaudunt, seruiliter adulantur, & nihil in dictis factisq; suis certum habent & solidum; sed vt Luna ad Solis motum nunc crescit, nunc minuitur: ita illi quoque pro principum arbitrio, seu libidine potius, in horas mutantur. Sunt hi non aularum modò, sed principum quoq; pestes nocentis-simæ. Per illos enim stat, quò minus reges saniora consilia audiant, aut admonitiones siue correptio-nes admittant, quæ illos ad reipub. exitium ruentes in officio continere possent. Tanti autem mali præcipua causa est, quòd luxu & delitijs diffluunt: & ideo aureis (vt ille dicebat) compedibus vin-cti turpissimam seruitutem facilè ferunt, modò desiderijs pessimis satisfacere & morum mollitiem tueri possint. Fit ergo vt luxus, intemperantia, libido & voluptatum inhonestissimarum studia nu-squam magis regnent, quàm in principum aulis, vbi omnis generis virtutum exempla florere debe-bant. Est malum hoc nostro seculo nimis vulgare, vt vel hoc vno argumento satis constet, quàm in felix sit mundi iam senescentis & ad finem suum tendentis conditio. Solomon olim clamabat: Væ terræ, cuius rex puer est, & cuius principes manè comessantur. Quàm ergo infelices sunt regiones, in quibus vel lasciuæ fœminæ, vel senes bis puerriminum tenent, qui ab ijs se regi patiuntur, qui continuo comessandi studio, vestitu portentoso, gestu indecoro, incessu deniq; fastuoso aut petulanti animos produnt ab omni honestate alienos? Sabæ regina de Solomonis sapientia & vniuerso regni eius statu, ex aulicorum vestitu et moribus iudicium faciebat. Quid ergo obstat, quò minus hodie ex aulicorum mollitie & petulantia, multorum principum soliditatem agnoscamus: qui cùm ære alie-no tantumnon toti opprimantur, tales tamen ferunt, imò maximis impensis alunt, & tam seipsos, quàm infelices subditos illis expoliandos atq; deglubendos propinant?
units.tr: At the same time, in this passage Christ also rebukes the manners of courtiers, who think it the height of wisdom to accommodate themselves to the nod of their prince and to arrange all their counsels for private advantage. So they applaud everyone, flatter in a servile way, and have nothing certain or solid in their words or deeds; but like the moon, which now waxes and now wanes with the motion of the sun, they change from hour to hour at the will of the princes, or rather at their lust. Such men are the most harmful plague not only of the courts but of the princes themselves. For through them it comes about that kings do not hear wiser counsels, nor admit admonitions or corrections which could keep them in their duty while they rush headlong to the ruin of the commonwealth. The chief cause of so great an evil is that these men are dissolved in luxury and pleasures; and so, bound (as someone used to say) with golden fetters, they bear a most shameful servitude without difficulty, provided they can satisfy their worst desires and maintain their softness of life. Thus it comes about that luxury, intemperance, lust, and the pursuit of the most disgraceful pleasures reign nowhere more than in the courts of princes, where examples of every kind of virtue ought to flourish. This evil is too common in our age, so that from this one argument alone it is plain enough how unhappy is the condition of the world now growing old and tending toward its end. Solomon long ago cried out: "Woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes feast in the morning." How unhappy, then, are those regions in which either wanton women or old men twice childish hold power, and suffer themselves to be ruled by those who, in constant devotion to feasting, in outlandish dress, unbecoming gesture, and finally in proud or wanton bearing, reveal minds alien to all honesty? The queen of Sheba judged Solomon's wisdom and the whole state of his kingdom from the dress and manners of his courtiers. What, then, prevents us today from recognising, from the softness and wantonness of courtiers, the weakness of many princes, who, though they are almost wholly crushed by debt, nevertheless bear such courtiers and indeed feed them at great expense, and offer both themselves and their wretched subjects to be stripped and flayed by them?

units.la: Quia tamen ista non sunt huius loci, rursus Christum audiamus, qui Ioannem ab officio quoq; commendat, & fide, qua in illo obeundo vsus est. Inanis est enim etiam virtutum splendor, nisi in eum finem dirigatur, vt officium faciamus in ijs, quibus nos Deus destinauit. Rursus autem in-terrogando pergens, sic ait: Sed quid existis vt videretis? Prophetam ne? Certè dico vobis etiam amplius quàm prophetam. Ioannem ergo, quoad officium eius & dignitatem supra omnes prophe-tas extollit. Quod ne temere facere putaretur, rationis loco adducit, quòd de illius aduentu & mi-nisterio reliqui prophetæ sint vaticinati. Hic est (inquit) de quo scriptum est: Ecce mitto nun-tium meum ante faciem tuam, qui præparabit viam tuam coram te. Extat locus hic apud Ma-lachiam Capite tertio, & totum Ioannis ministerium comprehendit, de quo cum alibi abundè sit dictum, non opus est in præsenti eadem repetere. Nunc illud modò addemus, veteres quidem prophetas de Christi in carnem aduentu, regni eius instauratione & propagatione, gentium vocatione & tota noui testamenti œconomia olim vaticinatos esse: Ioannem verò hisce omnibus quasi initium dedisse, & primum fuisse noui fœderis atque testamenti ministrum. Deinde illi hæc omnia eminus & obscurius quasi per nebulas aut transennam indicarunt, atque suos auditores in eo spem salutis ac veræ beatitudinis collocare docuerunt, qui post secula & tempora aliquot in carnē venturus erat: at Ioannes cum adhuc in vtero matris delitescens illi nondum in luce edito testimonium ferre coepisset, tandem in carne manifestatum toti populo coràm monstrauit digito, & dixit: Ecce hic est agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Vere ergo Prophetis omnibus maior fuit Ioannes, tantoq; salutarius humano generi fuit eius ministerium, quanto propius iam fuit exhibita salus, quàm olim, cum prophetæ venturam prædicarent.
units.tr: Since these matters, however, do not belong to this place, let us hear Christ again, who commends John also for his office and for the faith with which he discharged it. For even the splendour of virtues is empty unless it is directed to this end, that we perform the duty to which God has appointed us. Continuing his questioning, he says: "But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Certainly I tell you, even more than a prophet." So he exalts John above all the prophets, as regards his office and his dignity. Lest anyone should think he said this rashly, he gives as his reason that the other prophets prophesied about John's coming and ministry. "This is the one," he says, "of whom it is written: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.'" This passage is found in Malachi chapter three, and it comprehends the whole ministry of John; since this has been fully discussed elsewhere, there is no need to repeat the same things here. We will add only this now: the ancient prophets indeed prophesied long ago about the coming of Christ in the flesh, the restoration and spread of his kingdom, the calling of the Gentiles, and the whole economy of the New Testament; but John gave a beginning to all these things, as it were, and was the first minister of the new covenant and testament. The prophets had pointed to all these things from afar and more obscurely, as if through clouds or a lattice, and taught their hearers to place their hope of salvation and true blessedness in him who was to come in the flesh after many ages and times. But John, while still hidden in his mother's womb, began to bear witness to the one not yet brought forth into the light; at last, when he had been manifested in the flesh, he showed him to the whole people with his finger and said: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." Truly, then, John was greater than all the prophets, and his ministry was the more salutary to the human race, as salvation was now nearer to being revealed than when the prophets foretold that it was coming.

units.la: At ne quis Ioannis discipulos imitatus huic vni intentus esset, & interea ipsum negligeret, cuius ille anteambulo & præco fuerat, per Correctionem subijcit: Nam dico vobis, inter eos qui generantur è mulieribus, nemo est maior propheta Ioanne Baptista: Sed qui minimus est in regno Dei, maior est eo. Quibus verbis Ioannem quidem hominibus vniuersis præfert, quorum ministerio Deus olim vsus esset: simul autem suam gloriam & authoritatem constanter asserit, ne quem vilis illa & contempta species offenderet, quam in carne assumpta ostendit. Minimum enim in regno Dei se dicit, partim quia seipsum humiliauit infra omnes angelos & homines, adeò vt seruuli vilissimi personam susceperit (sicuti Paulus ad Philippenses testatur) partim quòd hominum etiam iudicio nemo vnquam contemptior & abiectior in terris visus sit. Nam vt omnia alia omittamus, in passione aut morte illum non solum infra vulgus hominum depressum, sed in facinorosorum numero habitum, imò Barraba latrone inferiorem factum fuisse constat. Quod Isaias in spiritu prænidens de illo scripsit: Non est ei forma neq; decor: videbimus illum: sed non est ei aspectus, vt cupiamus illum. Despectus est & nouissimus virorum, vir (inquam) dolorum, & qui infirmitatem est expertus: erit vt is à quo quis faciem abscanderet, &c. Et ipse in Psalmo dicit: Ego vermis sum, & non vir, opprobrium hominum & contemptus à populo. Ad ista igitur in præsenti respiciens, hoc dicere videtur: Qualemcunque me vulgò homines æstiment, sum tamen ipso Ioanne præstantior, adeoq; is sum, cui omnis gloria debetur, & qui meam gloriam alteri non dabo. Sic ergo Ioannem laudat, vt omnem nostrae redemptionis gloriam sibi integram referuet. Quo loco docemur, ita à nobis quoq; laudari debere sanctos Dei seruos, ne interim in illos transferamus quod Christi est. Faciunt hoc nimis impudenter (ne quid grauius dicam) qui mediatores & aduocatos sibi ex illis faciunt, qui illos in periculis inuocant, qui denique illorum meritis seruari contendunt. At hanc gloriam illi nunquam affectarunt. Sed hunc sui ministerij finem sibi propositum habuerunt, vt omnes homines vni Christo adducerent. Illos ergo honore digno prosequemur, si doctrinae eorum credamus, & fidem imitemur, cuius exemplar illustre fuerunt.
units.tr: But lest anyone, imitating John's disciples, should be intent on John alone and meanwhile neglect him whose forerunner and herald he had been, Christ adds by way of correction: "For I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than the prophet John the Baptist; yet he who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he." By these words he indeed places John above all men through whose ministry God had at any time worked; at the same time he firmly claims his own glory and authority, lest that lowly and despised appearance which he showed in the assumed flesh should give offence to anyone. For he calls himself the least in the kingdom of God, partly because he humbled himself beneath all angels and men, so that he took on the person of a most lowly servant (as Paul testifies to the Philippians), and partly because in the judgement of men no one was ever seen to be more contemptible and abject on earth. For, to omit everything else, it is certain that in his suffering and death he was not only cast down beneath the common people but was counted among malefactors, and indeed was made inferior even to the robber Barabbas. Isaiah, foreseeing this in the Spirit, wrote of him: "He has no form nor comeliness; we shall see him, but he has no appearance that we should desire him. He is despised and the lowest of men, a man (I say) of sorrows, who has experienced infirmity; he will be like one from whom a man hides his face, etc." And he himself says in the Psalm: "I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and despised by the people." Looking at these things, therefore, in the present passage, he seems to say: "Whatever men commonly think of me, I am nevertheless more excellent than John himself; I am the one to whom all glory is due, and I will not give my glory to another." Thus he praises John in such a way as to keep the whole glory of our redemption for himself. In this place we are taught that the holy servants of God ought to be praised by us in such a way that we do not meanwhile transfer to them what belongs to Christ. Those do this most shamelessly (not to say anything harsher) who make mediators and advocates for themselves out of them, who call upon them in dangers, and who finally contend that they are saved by their merits. But those saints never sought this glory. Rather, they set before themselves this as the aim of their ministry: to bring all men to Christ alone. We shall therefore honour them with a worthy honour if we believe their teaching and imitate their faith, of which they were most illustrious examples.

units.la: Interim non ofcitanter hoc loco præterire debemus, quæ Ioannis Baptistæ, viri reuera maximi & præstantissimi inter eos, qui ex mulieribus nati sunt, fors in hoc mundo fuerit. Num enim eius doctrinae aut testimonio omnes crediderunt? Num apud omnes in honore & pretio fuit? Nequaquam. Imò mox deferbuit populi ad illum vndiq; concurrentis studium, interea verò summus pontificibus, scribis, pharisæis & omnibus alijs, qui in alteri dignitatis gradu constituti erant, exosus fuit. Nec multò post Herodes meretricis incestæ blanditiis irritatus illum captum in Macherunte abduxit, vbi post diuturna vincula, in ipso carcere non minus crudeliter quàm iniuste occisus est. Hæc tanti viri in terris fors, & hic eiusdem ex hoc mundo exitus fuit. At hunc cum multis alijs communem sortitus est, qui simili fide & studio infelicis mundi salutem quæsiuerunt. Neminem igitur offendant pericula & aduersa, quibus hodie etiam Christi cultores exercentur, vt ideo illos extra Dei protectionem esse putet. Nouit enim Dominus qui sunt sui, & olim sui regni atque gloriae coheredes faciet eos, qui ipsi crucis & afflictionum socij fuerunt. In præsenti verò Christi in stitutum obseruemus, qui hoc vnum effectum vult, vt populus in Ioannis doctrina constanter perseueret, eiusq; testimonio credat. Quod ipsum non minus ad nos quoq; pertinet. Et elucet in eo magna Dei bonitas, qui Ioannis ministerio vti voluit, ne qui per ignorantiam perirent. Sunt bonitatis eiusdem multa argumenta hodie, quibus nos quoq; excitari conuenit, vt ardenti verae pœnitentiae studio præparemur ad excipiendum Iesum Christum, & in illo salutem consequamur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile we ought not to pass over carelessly at this point what fortune John the Baptist, truly the greatest and most outstanding of those born of women, had in this world. For did all believe his teaching or his testimony? Was he held in honour and esteem by all? By no means. Rather, soon the zeal of the people who had flocked to him from every side cooled, and meanwhile he became hateful to the high priests, the scribes, the Pharisees, and all the others who held a position of some dignity. Not long afterwards Herod, enticed by the flatteries of an incestuous harlot, took him captive and led him off to Machaerus, where, after a long imprisonment, he was put to death in the very prison, no less cruelly than unjustly. Such was the fortune of so great a man on earth, and such was his departure from this world. Yet he shared this lot with many others who sought the salvation of the unhappy world with a like faith and zeal. Let no one, therefore, be offended by the dangers and adversities with which the worshippers of Christ are even today afflicted, as if on that account they were thought to be outside God's protection. For the Lord knows who are his, and one day he will make heirs of his kingdom and glory those who have been partners in the cross and in afflictions. Now let us observe the institution of Christ in the present time, who wills only this one effect: that the people should persevere constantly in the teaching of John and believe his testimony. This pertains no less to us as well. And in this there shines forth the great goodness of God, who chose to use the ministry of John, lest those who perished through ignorance should be lost. There are today many proofs of this same goodness, by which it is fitting that we too be stirred up, so that, with an ardent zeal for true repentance, we may be prepared to receive Jesus Christ and in him obtain salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXX.

units.la: Et his auditis totus populus & publicani iustificauerunt Deum, qui baptizati fuerant baptismo Ioannis, Pharisæi autem & legis interpretes consilium Dei reiecerunt aduersus semetipsos, non baptizati ab eo. Dixit autem Dominus: Cui ergo assimilabo homines nationis istius? & cui sunt similes? Similes sunt pueris sedentibus in foro, & qui alii aliis acclamant, & dicunt: Cecinimus vobis tibiis, & non saltastis: lamentati sumus vobis, & non fleuistis. Venit enim Ioannes Baptista neque edens panem, neque bibens vinum, & dicitis: Ecce homo edax & vinipotor, amicus publicanorum & peccatorum. Et iustificata est sapientia a filiis suis omnibus.
units.tr: And when all the people and the publicans heard this, they justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John. But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not having been baptized by him. The Lord said: "To what then shall I liken the men of this generation? And what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to one another and say: We have piped to you, and you have not danced; we have mourned to you, and you have not wept. For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say: Behold a man gluttonous and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. And wisdom is justified of all her children."

units.la: Dominus & seruator noster Iesus Christus magnificè admodum nuper commendauit Ioannem Baptistam, inquit, ea commendatione fidem & constantiam eius in primis prædicauit, qua in officio sibi credito vsus est, atque eum omnibus Prophetis præstantiorem esse docuit. Finis omnium hic est, vt Ioannis testimonium, quod is de Christo tulit, plus fidei & authoritatis habeat in Ecclesia. Ideo se, quamuis minimus & contemptissimus omnium esse videatur in regno Dei, Ioanne tamen maiorem fuisse excellentiorem esse dixit. Quo loco admonemur, in quem finem & quomodo sancti laudari debeant. Nimirum, vt non ipsis addicti hæreamus, sed vt eorum cum doctrina tum exemplo excitati ad Christum contendamus, in quo illi omnem salutem nobis repositam esse docuerunt. Nam etsi Dei filius seruos suos honore summo dignetur, & eos de spiritus sui donis mirificè ornet, Domini tamen & redemptoris nomen sibi soli seruat, & eam gloriam (sicuti apud Isaiam loquitur) dat nemini. Sequitur commendationis istius effectus, vbi duo hominum genera proponuntur: alterum eorum, quibus Christi concio salutaris fuit: alterum eorum, qui peiores & indurationes facti proprium sibi ipsis exitium accersiuerunt. Quorum exemplis docemur, quid a nobis fieri aut cauere oporteat, & quis exitus eos maneat, qui se Christo salutem nobis offerenti contumacius opponere audent.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ lately commended John the Baptist in very lofty terms, he says. By that commendation he chiefly proclaimed the faith and steadfastness with which John discharged the office entrusted to him, and he taught that John was superior to all the Prophets. The whole purpose of this is that John's testimony, which he gave concerning Christ, may carry more faith and authority in the Church. Therefore he said that, although the least and most despised of all may seem to be in the kingdom of God, he is nonetheless greater than John, or rather more excellent than John. In this passage we are taught for what end and in what manner the saints ought to be praised. Clearly, it is so that we do not cling to them in devotion, but that, stirred by their teaching and their example, we strive towards Christ, in whom they taught that all salvation has been laid up for us. For although the Son of God honours his servants with the highest dignity and adorns them wonderfully with the gifts of his Spirit, nevertheless he keeps the name of Lord and Redeemer to himself alone, and, as he speaks through Isaiah, he gives that glory to no one. There follows the effect of this commendation, where two kinds of men are set forth: the one kind, to whom Christ's preaching brought salvation; the other, who became worse and hardened, and drew upon themselves their own destruction. From their examples we are taught what we ought to do or to beware of, and what end awaits those who dare to set themselves more obstinately against Christ when he offers us salvation.

units.la: Summa loci totius est, vulgus hominum, qui aut propter ruditatem & conditionem abiectiorem contemptibiles, aut etiam peccatis morum, licentia infames erant, Christum amplexos fuisse: Pharisæos autem & legis interpretes, quos propriæ iustitiæ fiducia & doctrinæ aut sapientiæ existimatio inflabat, illum contempsisse. Poterat hoc nobis mirum videri, nisi hanc Euangelij sui fortem esse, Christus iampridem nos admonuisset. Nam apud Ioannem inquit: Ad iudicium ego in hunc mundum veni, vt qui non vident videant, & qui vident, cæci fiant. Et infra decimo cap. hoc nomine Deo Patri gratias agens dicit: Confiteor tibi Pater, Domine cæli & terræ, quod abscondersi hæc à sapientibus & intelligentibus, & revelaris ea infantibus. Et possunt huius rei causæ adduci, quarum aliæ in hominibus, aliæ in Dei æterno consilio sitæ sunt. Inter homines enim ad Christum excipiendum magis idonei sunt, qui cum neq; doctrinæ neq; iustitiæ propriæ splendore se venditare possint, sibi magistro simul & seruatore opus esse sentiunt. Quod cum non intelligant, qui sibi ipsis sapere videntur, & suorum operum iustitia superbè ostentant: ipsum Christum minimè admittunt, ne suam indignitatem fateri, & sub huius potenti manu se humiliare cogantur. Deinde hanc regni sui conditionem esse vult Deus, ne quis hoc ex hominum dignitate & consilio pendere existimet, & vt omnem salutem in ipsius gratia & voluntate confiteri fateantur. Admonet de hoc Paulus, quando in priori ad Corinth. scribit: Postquam in sapientia Dei non cognouit mundus per sapientiam Deum, placuit Deo per stultam prædicationem seruare credentes. Quandoquidem & Iudæi signum petunt, & Græci sapientiam quærunt: nos autem prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis verò stultitiam. Et paulo post huius consilij rationem exponens ait: Videtis vocationem vestram fratres, quod non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: Verum quæ stulta sunt in mundo elegit Deus, vt pudefaciat sapientes: & quæ sunt infirma in mundo elegit Deus, vt pudefaciat ea quae sunt robusta: & quae ignobilia sunt in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, elegit Deus, & ea quae non sunt, vt quae sunt aboleret: Vt ne gloriaretur vlla caro coram eo. Sunt haec diligenter observanda propter eos, qui nobis quidem nostrae partis hominum conditionem miseram & mundi iudicio contemptibilem exprobrant, suae vero factionis splendorem atq; potentiam magnificè extollunt. Quid vero aliud isti faciunt, quàm quòd idem nobis hodie evenire fatentur, quod olim ipsi Christo & eius Apostolis evenit? Neminé ergo illorum tripudia & Thrasonicae gloriationes offendant. Nec enim ex mundo hoc est regnum Christi, & proinde mundi potentia, armis, authoritate, nequaquam stabilitur. Caeterùm accedamus ad huius loci tractationem, & audiamus, quid de utroque auditorum Christi genere Lucas scribit.
units.tr: The sum of the whole passage is this: that the common crowd of people, who were despised either because of their rudeness and lowly condition, or were infamous for the licence of their morals and sins, embraced Christ; but the Pharisees and the lawyers, whom confidence in their own righteousness and the reputation of their learning and wisdom puffed up, scorned him. This might seem strange to us, did not Christ long ago warn us that his gospel is of this kind. For in John he says: "For judgement I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." And later, in the tenth chapter, giving thanks to God the Father for this very thing, he says: "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and the understanding, and revealed them to babes." And the causes of this matter can be adduced, some of which lie in men, others in the eternal counsel of God. For among men, those are better fitted to receive Christ who, since they cannot make a show of learning or of their own righteousness, feel that they need him as both teacher and saviour at once. Those who seem wise to themselves, and proudly display the righteousness of their works, do not recognise this, and so they by no means admit Christ himself, lest they be forced to confess their own unworthiness and humble themselves under his mighty hand. Furthermore, God wills that this should be the condition of his kingdom, so that no one may think it depends on human dignity or counsel, and that they may acknowledge that all salvation lies in his grace and will. Paul admonishes us of this when he writes in the first letter to the Corinthians: "Since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For the Jews ask for a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks." And a little later, explaining the reason for this counsel, he says: "Consider your calling, brothers, that not many of you are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the strong; and the base things of the world, and the things that are despised, God has chosen, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are; so that no flesh should glory before him." These things must be carefully observed on account of those who reproach us, of our party, with our miserable condition and our contemptibility in the judgement of the world, while they magnificently extol the splendour and power of their own faction. What else do they do, indeed, than confess that the very thing which once happened to Christ and his Apostles is now happening to us? Let none of their boastful revelry and Thrasonic bragging trouble us. For the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and therefore it is by no means established by worldly power, arms, or authority. But let us proceed to the treatment of this passage, and hear what Luke writes about both kinds of Christ's hearers.

units.la: Primum vulgus promiscuum & publicanos habet, sub quibus homines idiotas aut illiteratos, adhaec vitiis manifestos infames comprehendi supra diximus. De his duo dicuntur. Primum, quòd iam ante baptismo Ioannis baptizati fuerint. Nam adhuc populi turbam ex tota Iudaea & Galilaea confluxisse scribitur alibi, vt docentem audirent & ab eo baptizarentur. Ergo iam pridem sese Deo addixerant, vt relictis prioribus studijs vitam novam & regni eius civibus dignam viverent. Alterum, quòd audito Christi de Ioanne testimonio Deum iustificarint. Subscripserunt ergo doctrinae Christi, & ita publicè praedicarunt Dei iustitiam & bonitatem, quam nobis ille in filio suo offert. Itaque nunc sese in illis exerit effectus baptismi, quo diu ante tincti fuerant.
units.tr: First, there is the common crowd, mixed together, and the publicans, under whom, as we said above, are comprehended the unlearned and illiterate people, and besides them the infamous and manifest in their vices. Two things are said about these. First, that they had already been baptized with John's baptism before. For it is written elsewhere that a crowd of people had flocked together from all Judaea and Galilee to hear him teaching and to be baptized by him. Therefore they had already long before devoted themselves to God, so that, leaving behind their former pursuits, they might live a new life worthy of the citizens of his kingdom. The second is that, having heard Christ's testimony concerning John, they justified God. They therefore subscribed to the teaching of Christ, and so publicly proclaimed the righteousness and goodness of God, which he offers us in his Son. And so now the effect of the baptism in which they had been immersed long before shows itself in them.

units.la: Docet autem horum exemplo spiritus sanctus, quid nos facere conueniat, quando nobis quoque per Euangelium salus in Christo Iesu offertur. Videndum hic ante omnia, ne media spernamus, quibus erga nos utitur Deus. Sunt haec, verbi doctrina & sacramenta. Illo enim salutis aeternae promissiones nobis proponit & illius rationem omnem exponit, his vero illas obsignat & ipsos etiam sensus ad eas apprehendendas excitat. Verbum ergo diligenter audire, Sacramentis autem religiose uti debemus: neq; hic nobis obstet, quòd non semper initio statim intelligimus, quid haec sibi velint, aut quòd carnis sensui nimis abiecta & inutilia videntur. Ut enim qui in altum ascendere volunt, ab infimis gradibus initium faciant oportet: ita ad sublimiorem fidei gradum & plenam Iesu Christi cognitionem non perue-nient, qui huius rudimenta vel oscitanter negligunt, vel improbè contemnunt. At qui ijsdem piè utuntur, ijs praeparatio sunt non inutilis ad maiora, & suum aliquando fructum ferunt, licet initio vix aliquid profutura nobis esse videantur. Exemplum huius isti satis evidens praebent. Cùm enim baptismo ab Ioanne tingerentur, inanis et inefficax ceremonia haec videri poterat, & credibile est illos ipsos vix maius aliquid animo tunc concepisse. Quia vero ordini à Deo instituto sese accommodant, & quas hic illis offert maioris profectus occasiones non negligunt, praeclarus nunc baptismi illius effectus cernitur. Quod multis etiam hodie obtingere videmus, in quibus prima salutis initia admodum contempta & tenuia aliquando apparebant. Arguunt haec Anabaptistarum errorem, qui infantes aut parvulos baptizari nolunt, eo quòd baptismi mysterium & usum non intelligant, neq; aliquis illius effectus mox appareat. Quasi vero hic admomentum illud temporis alligatus sit, quo infans tingitur, & non potius per omnem vitam sese extendat. Et quid prohibet, quo minus in Sacramentis fiat, quod in verbo fieri ipse Christus fatetur? Hoc enim non semper prima statim hora in auditorum animis fructum facit, sed interdum aliquandiu delitescit, vt extinctum videri possit, suo autem tempore in mentem redit homini, & fructibus minimè praenitendis sese conspicuum praebet. Sed perinde faciunt phanatici illi, ac si quis sementem facere prohibeat, eo quòd spicae maturae & fruges non illico è terra enascantur.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit, however, teaches by the example of these people what we ought to do, since salvation in Christ Jesus is offered to us also through the gospel. Here we must above all take care not to despise the means which God uses towards us. These are the teaching of the Word and the sacraments. For by the one he sets before us the promises of eternal salvation and expounds the whole manner of them, and by the other he seals those promises and stirs up our very senses to lay hold of them. We ought therefore to hear the Word diligently and to use the sacraments devoutly. Nor let it hinder us that we do not at once understand from the beginning what these things mean, or that they seem too low and useless to the sense of the flesh. For just as those who want to climb to a height must begin from the lowest steps, so those who either carelessly neglect or wickedly despise the rudiments of faith will not attain to the higher degree of faith and to full knowledge of Jesus Christ. But those who use them devoutly find them no useless preparation for greater things, and in time they bear their fruit, although at the beginning they may seem scarcely likely to profit us at all. These people give a very clear example of this. For when they were baptized by John, this ceremony might have seemed empty and ineffective, and it is credible that they themselves at that time conceived hardly anything greater in their minds. But because they accommodated themselves to the order instituted by God, and did not neglect the opportunities for greater progress which it offered them, the splendid effect of that baptism is now seen. We see this happening to many even today, in whom the first beginnings of salvation at one time appeared very despised and slight. These things refute the error of the Anabaptists, who will not have infants or little children baptized, because they do not understand the mystery and use of baptism, and because no effect of it appears at once. As if the moment of time at which the infant is baptized were bound to that alone, and it did not rather extend itself through the whole of life! And what prevents that in the sacraments which Christ himself confesses is done in the Word? For the Word does not always bear its fruit in the minds of the hearers at the very first hour, but sometimes lies hidden for a while, so that it may seem extinguished; yet at its proper time it returns to a man's mind and shows itself visibly, with fruits by no means to be despised. But those fanatics act just as if someone forbade sowing because the ripe ears and the crops do not spring up out of the earth at once.

units.la: Deinde Deum iustificare debent ij, quibus Euangelium praedicatur. Requiritur ad hoc, vt nos peccatores esse fateamur, quibus aliena iustitia opus sit. Proximum inde est, vt eam fide firma apprehendamus, quam nobis Deus in filio suo offert. Ita illum iustificabimus, quia illi tribuimus eandem iustitiae, bonitatis, misericordiae & veritatis. Et hic Deo cultus est longè gratissimus, quando illum ex animo talem agnoscimus, qualis revera est, & talem publicè etiam praedicamus. Quod cùm non nisi per fidem fiat, non temere haec tantis praeconijs in scriptura commendatur, quòd nimirum sola nos iustificet & salvos faciat. Ut enim Christum Iesum apprehendit, eiúsque nos inserit, qui iustitia, vita & salus est: ita in se omnia continet, quae ad verum Dei cultum faciunt. Etenim qui Filium nobis à Patre datum esse, & illum miseros nos destructo diaboli regno in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruisse firmiter credit: is profecto Deum veracem esse agnoscit, qui promissionibus olim factis abunde satisfecerit. Idem illius quoq; bonitatem et misericordiam iminensam praedicat, qui ne Filio quidem proprio propter nos parcere voluerit. Iustitiam item Dei agnoscit, cuius ille adeo tenax est, ut peccata nostra Filij potius morte expiare, quam multa & impunita ferre voluerit. Quid vero de illius omnipotentia dicemus, quae & ipsa a nemine tam magnifice praedicatur, ut ab ijs, qui Dei filium in assumpta ex nobis carne misera & mortali tantum potuisse credunt, ut diabolum cum toto suo regno destrueret? Vere ergo Deum iustificant, qui Christo credunt, & ijdem Deo obsequium quoq; praestant fidelissimum: quia fieri non potest, quin se totos illi mancipent, cuius veritatem infallibilem, iustitiam omnibus numeris absolutam, bonitatem inexhaustam, misericordiam plus quam paternam, sapientiam infinitam, & potentiam invictam in Christo agnoscunt. At quia haec omnia humani ingenij captum superat, diuinitus in nobis fides accendatur oportet, ideoq; illam Christus opus Dei vocat, & hic idcirco optimo iure opus illud, cuius ipse in nobis author est, aeternae vitae praemio remunerat. Minime ergo audiri debent, qui ut suorum operum iustitiam stabiliant, de fide contemptim nimis loquuntur, & nos salutis rationem eiusmodi fingere clamant, quae carni habenas laxet, et bonis operibus sit inimica. Quod enim atrocem iniuriam illi tam nobis quam Euangelio Iesu Christi faciant, ex ijs apparet, quae modo diximus. Ipsi vero, dum prae alijs Dei cultores haberi volunt, non uno modo blasphemi fiunt, quando Christum abijciendo simul Dei veritatem, iustitiam, bonitatem, misericordiam et omnia alia negant, quae si ab illo auferas, Deus esse desinet.
units.tr: Next, those to whom the gospel is preached must also justify God. To do this, we must confess that we are sinners who need another's righteousness. The next step is to grasp firmly by faith the righteousness that God offers us in his Son. So we justify him, by ascribing to him the same righteousness, goodness, mercy and truth. This is the most pleasing worship we can give God, when we acknowledge him from the heart as he really is and also proclaim him publicly as such. Since this happens only through faith, Scripture does not commend faith with such great praise without reason, namely because faith alone justifies us and saves us. For whoever lays hold of Christ Jesus and is engrafted into him, who is righteousness, life and salvation, also embraces in himself everything that belongs to the true worship of God. Whoever firmly believes that the Son has been given to us by the Father, and that by destroying the devil's kingdom he has set us wretched people free into the liberty of the children of God, certainly acknowledges God to be true, since he has fully kept the promises made long ago. He also proclaims God's goodness and boundless mercy, since he did not wish to spare even his own Son for our sake. He likewise acknowledges God's justice, which is so strict that he chose to atone for our sins by the death of his Son rather than to bear with many unpunished sins. And what shall we say of his omnipotence, which no one praises as magnificently as those who believe that the Son of God, in the frail and mortal flesh he took from us, was able to destroy the devil together with his whole kingdom? Truly, then, they justify God who believe in Christ, and they also render him the most faithful obedience, because it is impossible that they should not give themselves wholly to him, whose infallible truth, perfectly complete righteousness, inexhaustible goodness, more than fatherly mercy, infinite wisdom and invincible power they recognize in Christ. But since all this surpasses the grasp of human intellect, faith must be kindled in us by God himself. That is why Christ calls it the work of God, and so with good reason he rewards with the prize of eternal life that work whose author he himself is in us. Those who, in order to establish the righteousness of their own works, speak contemptuously about faith, and who cry out that our way of salvation should be framed in such a way as to loosen the reins for the flesh and be hostile to good works, must by no means be listened to. That they do a monstrous wrong both to us and to the gospel of Jesus Christ is clear from what we have just said. But they themselves, while they want to be regarded as worshippers of God above others, become blasphemers in more than one way, since by rejecting Christ they at the same time deny God's truth, righteousness, goodness, mercy and all the other attributes which, if you take them away from him, mean that God ceases to be God.

units.la: Sed ad alterum genus auditorum Christi transeamus, in quo Pharisaeos et legis interpretes sive doctores fuisse, supra diximus: qui duo ordines illo saeculo inter Iudaeos praecipuam doctrinae & iustitiae existimationem sustinebant. Dicuntur hi consilium Dei spreuisse. Quod non tunc demum facere coeperunt, quado Christum de Ioanne concionantem audiuerunt, sed iam pridem cum ipsum Ioannem eiusq; baptismum aspernati fuerant, ut cap.tertio audiuimus. Consilium Dei ergo dicit doctrinam Euangelij, eo quod haec aeternum illud Dei consilium exponit, quo ille nos in Christo Iesu elegit, ut suum peculium efficeremur, & in illo vitae aeternae hereditatem obtineremus. Facit ergo locus hic plurimum ad asserendam Euangelij dignitatem. Nam eius authorem docet esse Deum, qui per illud non rerum nihil ad nos pertinentium narrationes, multo minus fabulas ad aurium oblectationem confictas, sed consilij & decreti sui arcana nobis reuelare dignatus est, ex quo salus nostra omnis dependet. Est hoc magnum diuini amoris argumentum, cuius consideratio nos excitare debet, ne consilio eius improbe reluctemur. Hoc enim in Pharisaeis & legisperitis hoc loco Euangelista reprehendit, quando illos Dei consilium spreuisse dicit. Fuit haec impudens nimium audacia, eoque maiori reprehensione digna, quod nihil audiret, quam quod ex lege & Prophetis iampridem didicisse debebant. Sed propria est hypocritis ista audacia. Quia enim inanis scientiae fiducia eos inflat, omne id scurriliter reijciunt & damnant, quod vel non intelligunt, vel studijs suis aduersum esse sentiunt. Christum ergo & doctrinam de gratuita salute, quae in hoc nobis exhibetur, illi admittere non potuerunt. Vt enim illa mundi huius sapientibus stultitia est, ita intolerabilis omnino illis erat, qui religionem sibijpsis iampridem quaestum fecerant, & huius saeculi gloriam gloriae Dei longe praeferebant, ut non uno loco de illis Christus testatur. Nemo igitur mirari debet, hodie etiam Monachis & sacrificulis sordere Euangelij doctrinam, & ab illis non modo sperni, verum etiam conculcari. Quia fieri non potest, ut patienter eos ferant, qui gratis illud omnibus offerunt, ex quo illi quaestum maximum facere consueuerunt. Sequuntur hos proximo gradu, qui se totos mundo & carnis desiderijs addixere. Nam his quoque non durum modo, sed iniquum & iniustum videtur Dei consilium, qui nos per Euangelium ad vitae nouitatem excitat, & a regni sui hereditate omnes eos excludit, in quibus non certa regenerationis & nouae naturae indicia elucent. Spernunt ergo & scurrili dicacitate omne hanc doctrinam eludunt, imo ex eo sibi laeta omnia pollicentur, si ea liberari possint, ne porro auribus ipsorum obstrepat. Et hi quidem omnes sibi delitias faciunt, quod non Deum reijciant, sed importunos rerum turbatores et Stentores insanos, qui rerum naturas innouare, & totum mundum inaudita ambitione pro suo nutu cogere instituant. Sed reuera ipsius Dei consilium spernunt, & proinde in spiritum sanctum, per prophetas & apostolos loquentem, sunt iniurij. Idem ergo illis quod aegrotis medicorum sana consilia contemnentibus accidet. Vt enim hi sua contumacia fibijpsis mortem accersunt, ita istis quoque obstinata illa temeritas atque proterua exitium afferet.
units.tr: But let us pass to the second kind of hearers of Christ, among whom we said above were the Pharisees and the teachers of the law, or doctors. These two orders enjoyed the highest reputation for doctrine and righteousness among the Jews of that age. They are said to have despised the counsel of God. They did not begin to do this only when they heard Christ preaching about John; rather, they had long since rejected John himself and his baptism, as we heard in chapter three. So by the counsel of God he means the doctrine of the gospel, because this sets forth that eternal counsel of God by which he chose us in Christ Jesus, so that we might be made his own people and obtain in him the inheritance of eternal life. This passage therefore contributes greatly to establishing the dignity of the gospel. For it teaches that God is its author, the one who has deigned to reveal to us, through it, not mere narratives of things that have nothing to do with us, much less fables invented to delight the ears, but the secrets of his counsel and decree, on which our whole salvation depends. This is a great proof of divine love, and the consideration of it ought to stir us not to resist his counsel wickedly. For this is what the evangelist rebukes in the Pharisees and lawyers here, when he says they despised the counsel of God. This was a most shameless audacity, and all the more deserving of rebuke because they ought to have learned long ago from the law and the Prophets what they now heard. But this audacity is peculiar to hypocrites. Since the confidence of empty learning puffs them up, they scornfully reject and condemn everything that they either do not understand or feel to be opposed to their studies. Therefore they could not admit Christ and the doctrine of free salvation offered to us in him. For just as that doctrine is foolishness to the wise of this world, so it was utterly intolerable to those who had long ago turned religion into a source of profit for themselves, and who valued the glory of this age far above the glory of God, as Christ bears witness in more than one place. No one should be surprised, then, that even today the doctrine of the gospel is despised by monks and little priests, and not only spurned by them but trampled underfoot. It cannot be that those who offer this doctrine freely to all should be borne patiently by those from whom they were accustomed to make their greatest gain. In the next rank come those who have given themselves wholly to the world and the desires of the flesh. For to these also the counsel of God seems not only harsh but unfair and unjust, since through the gospel it stirs us up to newness of life and excludes from the inheritance of his kingdom all those in whom no sure signs of regeneration and new nature shine forth. So they scorn this entire doctrine and mock it with scurrilous wit, and indeed they promise themselves every kind of joy if they can be freed from it, so that it no longer rings in their ears. All these men take pleasure in not rejecting God, but in calling him a troublesome disturber of affairs and a madman with a loud voice, who set out to renew the natures of things and to force the whole world, by unheard-of ambition, to obey his nod. But in truth they despise the very counsel of God, and therefore they wrong the Holy Spirit who speaks through the prophets and apostles. So what will happen to them is what happens to sick people who scorn the sound advice of physicians. Just as these bring death upon themselves by their obstinacy, so that stubborn recklessness and perversity will bring ruin on them.

units.la: Sed alterum quoq; de nostris hisce dicitur, quòd ne baptizati quidem sint ab Ioanne. Erum-pit enim in apertum impietas, postquam Dei consilium spernitur, & mox Sacramentorum atque omnis ordinis à Deo instituti contemptum parit. Quia enim omnia suo sensu metiuntur, nihil autem in Sacramentis apparet magnificum, quod carnis expectationi respondeat, idem fere de baptismo omnes illi sentiunt, quod de Iordane olim Naamanus ille Syrus, cum in eo se tingere ab Elifeo iussus esset. En cogitabam (inquit) apud me, omnino exibit, & stans innuocabit nomen Domini Dei sui, admouebit manum suam ad locum, & curabit lepram. Annon præstant Abana & Parpar, flu-uij Damasci, omnibus aquis Israelis? annô si lauero in eis, mundus ero? Ita (inquam) isti quoq; non sine contemptu loquuntur. Magnum quid atq; nouum expectabamus ex Euangelij doctrina, de qua tanta animorum vehementia contenditur. At quid aliud iubemur, quàm vt cœtus sacros ingressi verbum audiamus, vt in Christi nomine aqua baptismi aspergamur, vt certis diebus panis buccella & parum vini cum reliquis eandem fidem profitentibus sumamus? Et quid ista ad animarum salutem facerent? Annon scripturas domi legere, domi etiam lauare & epulum longè splendidius instruere possumus? Sed vtinam, qui ita sentiunt & loquuntur, Naamani seruulos simul imitati vicissim cogitarent. Si quid magnum & arduum iuberet Deus, annon eius mandato parere oporteret? Quæ ergo ingratitudo, imò quæ hæc est impietas, eum contemnere, qui ne cui grauis fit, ineffabilia illa & humani ingenij captum excedentia regni cœlestis mysteria, Sacramentis pauculis & obseruatu facillimis adumbrat atq; obsignat? Sunt hæc nobis probè meditanda, ne ex specie externa de illis iudicemus, quæ non sine certa ratione Deus instituit. Inter quæ primum locum facilè tenent cœtus sacri, in quibus verbum prædicatur, preces publicæ fiunt & Sacramenta administrantur. Est illorum institutio antiquissima, & in lege sua in eum finem Deus festa peculiaria mandauit, vt ad illa ter in anno omnes conuenirent ad audiendam legem, & ad sacra facienda, quæ tunc in vsu erant. In nouo autem testamento ecclesiæ cœtus amplissima promissione Christus ornauit, quòd nimirum & ipse in illis medius adesse velit, & quòd quæ in his fiunt preces, rata sint apud Patrem qui in cœlis est. Quæ causa esset, quòd illos Apostoli summa diligentia instituerunt, & quòd primitiua ecclesia in ijsdem cogendis frequentissima fuit. Imò, si verum fateri libeat, hæc fere omnibus seculis persecutionum initia fuerunt, quòd Christianis hominibus non satis fuit fidem suam intra animos suos fouisse, nisi eandem & publicè profiterentur, et in cœtibus sacris eius exercitia adhiberent, quæ à Christo mandata nobis esse sciebant. At hodie multi illos vnà cum Dei verbo & toto Sacramentorum vsu contemnunt, qui reuera Dei consilium spernunt, vt supra diximus, & hoc vno abunde testantur, se ex Deo non esse, neq; in ouium Christi numero censeri debere, quarum proprium est pastoris vocem audire & gregis societatem integram seruare.
units.tr: But something else is also said of these men of ours, namely that they have not even been baptized by John. For impiety breaks out openly once the counsel of God is despised, and soon it gives birth to contempt for the sacraments and for every order instituted by God. Because they measure everything by their own sense, and because nothing in the sacraments appears splendid enough to answer the expectations of the flesh, almost all of them feel about baptism as Naaman the Syrian once felt about the Jordan, when he was ordered by Elisha to bathe in it. "Behold, I thought," he said, "that he would surely come out and stand and call upon the name of the Lord his God, and wave his hand over the place and cure the leprosy. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? May I not wash in them and be clean?" So these men too speak with no small contempt. "We expected something great and new from the doctrine of the gospel, for which such fervent contention of minds is waged. But what are we commanded to do except enter the sacred assemblies, hear the word, be sprinkled with the water of baptism in the name of Christ, and on certain days take a morsel of bread and a little wine together with the others who profess the same faith? And what could these things do for the salvation of souls? Can we not read the Scriptures at home, and wash at home, and set a far more splendid feast?" But would that those who think and speak this way would in turn imitate the servants of Naaman and reflect. If God had ordered something great and difficult, ought we not to obey his command? What ingratitude, or rather what impiety, is it, then, to despise him who, so that he may be a burden to no one, has set forth and sealed the ineffable mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, which exceed the grasp of human intellect, by a few sacraments that are very easy to observe? We must carefully meditate on these things, so that we do not judge by outward appearance those things which God instituted not without a sure reason. Among these, the sacred assemblies easily hold first place, in which the word is preached, public prayers are offered and the sacraments are administered. Their institution is very ancient, and in his law God commanded special feasts for this very purpose, so that all would gather three times a year to hear the law and to perform the sacred rites then in use. In the New Testament, Christ adorned the assemblies of the Church with the most ample promise: that he himself wishes to be present in the midst of them, and that the prayers offered in them are accepted by the Father who is in heaven. This is why the apostles instituted them with the greatest care, and why the primitive Church was so very diligent in gathering them. Indeed, if we are willing to speak the truth, the beginnings of persecution in almost every age arose from this: it was not enough for Christians to cherish their faith within their own hearts, unless they also professed it publicly and practised in sacred assemblies those exercises which they knew Christ had enjoined upon us. But today many despise those assemblies together with the word of God and the whole use of the sacraments. These men truly despise the counsel of God, as we said above, and they bear sufficient witness to this one thing alone: that they are not of God, and ought not to be counted among the sheep of Christ, whose proper mark is to hear the voice of the shepherd and to keep the flock's fellowship whole.

units.la: Sed obseruent isti, non temere de Scribis & Pharisæis hic dici, quòd Dei consilium præuerint aduersus semetipsos, id est, in proprium exitium. Non ergo ipsi Deo, sed potius nobis fraudi est, verbi sui & sacramentorum contemptus: neque Deum, sed seipsos lædunt, qui quam nobis ille offert gratiam aspernantur. Manet enim in æternum Dei consilium (vt Dauid ait) & eiusdem verbo ex hominum incredulitate sive inobedientia nihil decedit, sibijpsis autem exitij authores sunt, qui illi non obtemperant. Poterat hoc pluribus exemplis illustrari, sufficiat tamen quod publicè in ecclesijs fieri videmus. Etsi enim sæpe corruant & prorsus dissipentur ecclesiæ, quæ prius præ aliis florebant, & quibus pereuntibus nullæ seruari posse videbantur, fit tamen, vt illæ quidem ingratitudinis & inconstantiæ pœnas dent, aliæ tamen præter omnem expectationem salvæ maneant, multæ etiam nouæ apud eos emergant, qui à Christi cognitione prius quàm maximè abhorrebant. Ita verò diuinitatem suam & immensam suam potentiam Christus palàm declarat, eius autem contemptores, dum in cœlum nimis temere expuunt, sibijpsis exitium & ignominiam accersunt sempiternam.
units.tr: But let these men note that it is not said carelessly here about the Scribes and Pharisees that they rejected God's counsel against themselves, that is, to their own destruction. So it is not God who is harmed by contempt of his word and sacraments, but us; and they harm not God but themselves, who spurn the grace he offers us. For the counsel of God remains forever (as David says), and nothing is taken from his word by the unbelief or disobedience of men. Those who do not obey it, however, become the authors of their own ruin. This could be illustrated by many examples, but it is enough that we see it happening openly in the churches. Even though churches which once flourished above others often collapse and are utterly scattered, and though they seemed unable to be preserved when they were perishing, some nevertheless pay the penalty of their ingratitude and inconstancy, while others remain safe beyond all expectation, and many new ones arise among those who before were most averse to knowledge of Christ. In this way Christ openly declares his divinity and his immense power, while those who despise him, by spitting recklessly toward heaven, bring upon themselves everlasting destruction and shame.

units.la: Pertinet huc grauis obiurgatio, qua Christus docet, illos incurabili contumacia aduersus Deum peccare, qui ipsos varijs quidem modis conatus sit in viam reducere, nihil autem hucusq; profecerit. Orationem autem simili siue exemplo figurat à pueris desumpto, vt obiter offendat puerilia esse, quæcunque quacunq; ab hypocritis & propria scientia fiducia inflati fiunt: vt deniq; superbis illis supercilium deprimat, qui cum doctores & Rabbini illuminatissimi haberi vellent, tamen ne ea quidem in semetipsis obseruabant, quae ex pueris in triuijs ludentibus addisci poterant. Cui (inquit) assimilabo homines nationis istius? & cui sunt similes? Interrogatione excitat auditores, & illis (quod hypocritis proprium est) magnam quid expectantibus, infert: Similes sunt pueriuls in foro sedentibus, qui alij alijs acclamant, & dicunt. Cecinimus vobis tibijs, & non saltastis: lamentati sumus vobis, & non fleuistis. Videtur autem tunc inter Iudaeorum pueros in more fuisse, vt praefractus & morosis alij cantilenam eiusmodi occinerent, qua morositatem & contumaciam suam illis exprobrabant. Sensus ergo est, Deo cum ipsis agenti idem omnino accidere, quod melioris indolis pueruli cū proterun & petulanti morositate laborantibus accidere soleat. Vt enim hi sociorum voluntati & insti tuto nunquam se accommodant, sed ipsi omnibus imperare volunt, & nisi hoc illis concedatur, societatem subito abrumpunt, & implacabiles sese praebent: ita ipsos facere ait, quando obduratis animis in sua contumacia pergant, & neq; leniori institutione, neque graviori correptione emolliri possint, vt officium faciant. Id vero non minus euidenter quam graviter reipsa demonstrat. Nam venit (inquit) Ioannes Baptista, qui threnodijs & cantilenis lugubribus vsus esse videtur, quando doctrina seueriore & plena comminationum, adhaec exemplo vitae seueriorus, vos ad poenitentiam et vitae emendationem excitauit, vt ad gratiam Dei, quae praeforibus erat, amplectenda idoneos faceret. Nam neq; panem comedit, neq; vinum bibit, id est, adeo non indulsit genio & carnis cupiditati, vt a communi & concessa omnibus victus ratione abstinuerit, ijs contentus, quae in locis desertis & incultis inueniri poterant, locustis nimirum & melle syluestri. At vos adeo non mouit eius doctrina & exemplum vt potius cum daemonio, id est, spiritu familiari vti dixeritis & magicis praestigijs rudem populum dementare. Successi mox ego, qui carmen laetum & iucundum vobis occinere soleo, dum omnes qui laborant & onerati sunt ad me inuito: dum laborantibus requiem, famelicis panem, sitibundis aquam vitae polliceor. Adhaec vitae genus mitius & ab vsitato more nequaquam alienum mihi propositum: nam vsitatis cibis, vt alij, vescor, potu solito vires recreo, vocatus aliorum mensas accedo, deniq; familiarem & affabilem me omnibus praebeo. At quid vos? Ecce (dicitis) homo edax & vinipotor, amicus publicanorum & peccatorum. Quando igitur neq; disciplina seueriore, neque familiariore & amica institutione corrigi potestis, satis apparet, contumaciam vestram incurabile esse, & vos vestro vitio perire. Itaque iustificata est sapientia a filijs suis omnibus, id est, vos qui filij Dei dici & haberi vultis, & quos olim Moses solos gentem sapientem esse dixit, sapientiam Dei abunde excusatis & omni culpa liberatis (hoc enim sensu Hebraei verbo iustificandi vtuntur) quando vestris hi sce moribus & iudicijs iniquissimis testamini, Deum quidem instar optimi & sapientissimi patris, nihil horum praetermisisse, quae vobis emendandis & seruandis seruire poterant, vos autem indomita perunacia in proprium exitium ruere. Hic verborum Christi sensus est simplicissimus, & illius instituto proprie conuenit. Est ergo exprobratio haec similis illi, qua apud Isaiam sub vineae parabola vtitur, & expositio diligenter studio & labore, quo in illa colenda nequicquam vsus sit, tandem infert: Quid praeterea faciendum erat vineae meae, quod non fecerim ei? Vt enim illic ipsos Iudaeos huius causae iudices constituit: ita hic quoq; non obscure iustorum conscientias appellat, vt proprio testimonio conuicti discant Deo gloriam dare.
units.tr: To this belongs the severe rebuke by which Christ teaches that those who have tried in various ways to lead them back to the way, but have so far achieved nothing, sin against God with an incurable obstinacy. He also gives the matter a figure by a comparison taken from children, so that in passing he may show that whatever the hypocrites do, and whatever is puffed up by their own confidence in knowledge, is childish. Finally, he may humble the haughty pride of those who wished to be regarded as teachers and most enlightened rabbis, yet did not observe in themselves even those things which might have been learned from children playing in the streets. "To what," he says, "shall I liken the men of this generation? And what are they like?" He stirs his hearers with a question, and, as is typical of hypocrites, when they expect something great, he brings in: "They are like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to one another and say: We have piped to you, and you have not danced; we have mourned to you, and you have not wept." It seems that among the Jewish boys it was customary for some to sing a song of this kind to the stubborn and sulky ones, reproaching them for their sullenness and obstinacy. The sense, then, is that the same thing happens when God deals with these people as commonly happens when boys of a better disposition deal with companions who are afflicted with a wanton and petulant sulkiness. For just as these never accommodate themselves to the wishes and rules of their companions, but want to command everyone, and unless this is granted them, they suddenly break off the fellowship and show themselves implacable, so, he says, these people do when, with hardened hearts, they persist in their obstinacy and cannot be softened either by gentler instruction or by sterner correction so as to do their duty. Christ shows this in fact no less clearly than seriously. "For John the Baptist came," he says, who seems to have used lamentations and mournful songs, when with a stricter doctrine full of threats, and with a life of greater severity as an example, he roused you to repentance and amendment of life, so as to make you fit to embrace the grace of God that was at hand. "For he neither eats bread nor drinks wine," that is, he so little indulged his appetite and bodily desire that he abstained from the ordinary and lawful manner of life common to all, being content with those things which could be found in deserted and uncultivated places, namely locusts and wild honey. But you were so little moved by his teaching and example that you said he had a demon, that is, a familiar spirit, and with magical tricks you drove the simple people mad. "Then I came, who am accustomed to sing to you a joyful and pleasant song, calling to me all who labor and are burdened: promising rest to the weary, bread to the hungry, and the water of life to the thirsty." Moreover, my way of life was milder and by no means foreign to common custom: for I eat ordinary food as others do, I refresh my strength with the usual drink, I go to the tables of others when invited, and finally I show myself familiar and courteous to all. "But what do you say?" Behold, you say, "a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" Since, therefore, you can be corrected neither by stricter discipline nor by a more familiar and friendly instruction, it is quite clear that your obstinacy is incurable and that you perish by your own fault. Thus "wisdom is justified by all her children," that is, you who wish to be called and held sons of God, and whom Moses once said were the only wise nation, abundantly clear the wisdom of God and free it from all blame (for the Hebrews use the word "to justify" in this sense), since by your own wicked customs and most unjust judgments you testify that God, like the best and wisest father, has omitted nothing of what could serve for your correction and preservation, while you, with untamed stubbornness, rush headlong to your own destruction. The meaning of Christ's words here is the simplest, and it fits his purpose exactly. This rebuke is therefore like that which he uses in Isaiah under the parable of the vineyard, where, after carefully explaining the diligence and labor with which he had tended it to no purpose, he finally says: "What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done for it?" For just as there he appoints the Jews themselves as judges of this matter, so here too he obscurely calls upon the consciences of the righteous, so that, convicted by their own testimony, they may learn to give glory to God.

units.la: Hic autem obseruanda nobis occurrit Dei bonitas, qui iam inde a primo rerum exordio homines variis rationibus ad serium propriae salutis studium allicere conatus est; & proinde pro ingenio rum diuersitate modos etiam docendi & monendi diuersos adhibuit. Nam cum primae aetatis homi- nibus breuius & succinctius egit, vt promissionibus salutis per Christum instaurandae eos confirmaret, penes quos recens erat conditi mundi & lapsus primorum parentum memoria; quiq; irae ipsius sensu magis afficiebantur. At cum mundus in peius proficeret, & excussò timore Dei in omne scelus petulanter rueret, horrendae generalis diluuij exemplo posteris nouum metum incussit, & legibus quoq; contra caedes atq; vim iniustam latis hominum temeritatem coercere coepit, & eosdem ad ingenium redeuntes supplicio de Sodomaeis sumpto amplius terruit. Tandem Israelitis ex Aegypto eductis legem dedit scriptam & cultus sui formam certam instituit, & tam huius quam doctrinae suae administros dedit Sacerdotes, quorum studio & industria homines in officio continerentur. At his cessantibus in suo munere, Prophetas excitauit ex diuersi loci & ordinis hominibus, ne quis in illis facilè inueniret, cuius causa verbum, quod illi prædicabant, contemni mereretur. Prodierunt ergo ex regijs familijs Isaias & Daniel: ex plebeis Elias, Elizeus, Amos: ex sacerdotibus Ieremias, Zacharias & alij complures: & inter hos quidem omnes, alij iuuenili ardore & alacritate cõmenda biles, alij senio & rerum multarum experientia graues fuerunt.
