Et si sermones eorum inspicias, nunc quidem eos humilius dicendi genus sequi, nunc in altum surgere, modò blandis admonitioni-bus vti, modò tristibus querelis populi infelicis contumaciam deplorare, modò obiurgationibus & minis tantum non tonare audies. Et quod de illis dicimus, hoc ipsum in apostolis esse videre, qui (vt de semetipso Paulus verissimè pronuntiat) omnia factì sunt omnibus, vt quàm plurimos lucri faceret. Nec cessauit hodie hæc Dei industria, sed adhuc passim audiuntur omnis generis doctores, qui æternæ vitæ verbum constanter prædicant, & ipsi quoque pro donorum varietate non vna docendi ratione vtuntur, vt maiori cum fructu auditoribus sese accommodent.
units.tr: Here we are bound to observe the goodness of God, who from the very beginning of things has sought to draw men by various means to earnest concern for their own salvation; and accordingly, in keeping with the diversity of their dispositions, he has also used diverse methods of teaching and admonishing. For with men of the earliest age he dealt more briefly and concisely, to confirm them by promises of salvation to be restored through Christ, among whom the memory of the recent creation of the world and of the fall of our first parents was still fresh, and who were more affected by the sense of his wrath. But when the world advanced for the worse, and, having cast off the fear of God, rushed wantonly into every crime, he struck posterity with a new dread by the terrible example of the universal flood, and he also began to restrain the recklessness of men by laws enacted against murder and unjust violence, and, when they returned to their former disposition, he struck them with greater terror by the punishment inflicted on the Sodomites. At last, when the Israelites had been led out of Egypt, he gave them a written law and established a fixed form of his worship, and he gave priests as ministers of this worship as well as of his doctrine, by whose zeal and diligence men might be kept in their duty. But when these were negligent in their office, he raised up prophets from men of different places and ranks, so that no one could easily find in them a reason why the word they preached deserved to be despised. Thus from royal families came Isaiah and Daniel; from the common people, Elijah, Elisha, and Amos; from the priests, Jeremiah, Zechariah, and several others. Among all these, some were commendable for youthful ardor and eagerness, others weighty for their age and their wide experience of many things. And if you examine their sermons, you will hear that now they follow a humbler style of speaking, now they rise to a loftier height; now they use gentle admonitions, now they lament with sorrowful complaints the obstinacy of an unhappy people, now they thunder with rebukes and threats, as it were. And what we say of them we may see also in the apostles, who (as Paul truly says of himself) became all things to all men, that he might gain as many as possible. Nor has this diligence of God ceased today, but even now teachers of every kind are heard everywhere, who constantly preach the word of eternal life, and who also, according to the variety of their gifts, do not use only one method of teaching, so that they may adapt themselves more fruitfully to their hearers.

units.la: At hic non minor nostri seculi hominum improbitas cernitur, quàm quæ olim inter Iudæos reg-nauit. Quia enim plerique, in immoderata peccandi licentia voluptatem quærunt, nihil illis molesti-us accidere potest, quàm si verbi prædicatione se corripi aut coerceri sentiant. Vt ergo ingeniosa est impietas, ita semper & vbiq; prætextu aliquem, quo verbi contemptum excusent, inueniunt. Et in huius quidem administris multa causantur. Nam si quis adhuc iuuenis sit, rudem & rerum inexpertem, & proinde incautum & plus æquo feruentiorem esse aiunt. Quòd si senem aliquem audiunt, de-lirum & morositate senili intolerabilem esse quiritantur. Similiter si doctus et dicendi facultate in-structus concionetur, versutum & ad fallendum quosuis natum esse dicunt: sin vero indoctus & in-dicendo rudis sit, asinum esse clamant, et proinde indignum qui audiatur. Rursus si honesto loco natus sit doctor, confidentiorem esse putant, non causæ bonitate, sed generis & cognatorum fiducia fretum: quòd si vero plebeius aliquis & obscuro genere natus obtingat, hoc quoq; in doctrinæ contumeliam rapiunt, & illi gentis vitia exprobrant. Idem fiet, si vel in conuiuisu facilis & facetus, vel gra-uis aut seuerus sit. Hunc enim asperum & morosum, illum verò leuem & scurrilem iudicabunt. Ita si cuius aut indigena fuerit, contemptu, sin peregrinus, odio dignus putabitur. Et quod in personis mi-nistrorum fit, hoc ipsum in doctrina et docendi modo fieri consueuit. Nam si graviter accuset & ob-iurget aliquos, seditiosum et turbulentum dicet: sin humaniter et amicè moneat, adulatorem. Quid? annon ex auditoribus quoq; calumniandi occasione multi arripiunt? Nam si vulgus hominum E-uangelio credat, stolidos & rerum nouarum cupidos illud ampleƈti dicunt: at si principes & qui in magistratu sunt illi subscribant, à nouis illis doctoribus seductos & proinde commiseratione potius quàm imitatione dignos esse vociferantur. Alios item ambitione & gloriæ studio, alios rursus auaritia, multos spe licentiæ maioris moueri aiunt, vt doctrinam illã sectentur. Et dum ista prætexunt, se esse extra omnem culpam sibi persuadet, cùm suæ incredulitatis et inobedientiæ causas graues habeant. Sed vehementer isti omnes falluntur: quia hoc vnum inde referunt, quòd Dei sapientiam iu-stificant. seque exitio dignos esse testantur: quando tot tamq; varijs modis se nobis accommodantem Deum reijciunt. Nos ergo huius bonitatem agnoscamus, & eius consilio obtemperemus, qui nos ex gratia elegit in Filio suo Iesu Christo, qui nobis sapientia, iustitia & satisfactio datus est, vt in ipso seruemus & viuamus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But here we see no less wickedness in the people of our own age than there was once among the Jews. For since most people, in their unrestrained licence to sin, seek their pleasure, nothing can be more troublesome to them than to feel themselves rebuked or restrained by the preaching of the Word. So, as impiety is ingenious, it always and everywhere finds some pretext by which to excuse its contempt for the Word. And they find many faults with its ministers. If a minister is still young, they say he is inexperienced and ignorant of affairs, and therefore rash and more fervent than is right. But if they hear an older man, they complain that he is doting and intolerable with senile peevishness. Likewise, if a learned man who is skilled in speaking preaches, they say he was born crafty and to deceive anyone; but if he is unlearned and unskilled in speaking, they cry out that he is an ass and therefore not worth listening to. Again, if a teacher was born to a respectable position, they think he is too confident, relying not on the goodness of his cause but on the confidence of his family and kinsmen; but if he happens to be a commoner of humble birth, they seize on this too to bring teaching into disrepute, and reproach him with the faults of his people. The same happens if he is pleasant and witty in company, or serious and strict. For they will judge the one harsh and peevish, and the other light and buffoonish. So if he is a native, he will be thought worthy of contempt; if a foreigner, worthy of hatred. And what happens in the persons of the ministers is customarily done also in the teaching and in the manner of teaching. For if he rebukes and reproves some people severely, they will call him seditious and turbulent; but if he admonishes them kindly and gently, they will call him a flatterer. What? Do not many also seize on an occasion for slander from among the hearers? For if the common people believe the Gospel, they say that it has been embraced by fools eager for novelties; but if princes and those who hold office subscribe to it, they cry out that they have been seduced by those new teachers and are therefore to be pitied rather than imitated. Likewise, they say that some are moved by ambition and a desire for glory, others again by greed, and many by hope of greater licence, so that they follow that teaching. And while they put forward these pretexts, they persuade themselves that they are free of all blame, although they have serious causes for their unbelief and disobedience. But all these people are gravely deceived: for the only thing they achieve by this is that they justify the wisdom of God and bear witness that they are worthy of destruction, since they reject God, who accommodates himself to us in so many and such varied ways. Let us, then, acknowledge his goodness and obey his counsel, who chose us out of grace in his Son Jesus Christ, who has been given to us as wisdom, righteousness and satisfaction, so that we may be preserved and live in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY 71.

units.la: Rogauit autem eum quidam ex Pharisæis, vt cum ipso vesceretur: itaq; ingressus domum Pharisæi discubuit. Et ecce mulier, quæ erat in vr-be peccatrix, cùm cognouisset eum accubuisse in domo Pharisæi, attulit alabastrum vnguenti, & stans ad pedes eius retro, fiens cœpit lachrymis rigare pedes eius: & capillis capitis sui extergebat & deosculabatur pe-des eius, & vnguento vngebat. Cùm autem id vidisset Pharisæus, qui vo-cauerat eum, dixit apud se: Hic si esset Propheta, nosset quæ & qualis sit hæc mulier quæ tangit ipsum: nam est peccatrix.
units.tr: Now one of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him. So he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman who was a sinner in that city, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, and standing behind at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. But when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: "If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner."

units.la: ETsi Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, salutem & vitam, cuius ipse nobis author atq; mediator est, omnibus hominibus admodum liberaliter offerat, pleriq; tamen tam ipsum quàm doctrinam eius aspernari consueuerunt. Inter hos tamè primatum facile tenent Pharisæi & hypocritæ, qui suorum operum meritis & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia turgent. Tales enim alienam iustitiam aut iustificatore alio se nequaquam opus habere arbitrantur: & ijsdem stultitia magna videtur alienam iustitiam niti velle, & quidem iustitia Christi, qui cum facinorosis damnatus in cruce mortem infamem sustinuit. Non admittunt ergo aeternum illud & salutiferum Dei consilium, qui in uno filio suo nobis iustitiam & salutem perfectam exhibet, & dum propriam iustitiam (ut Paulus ait) constituere volunt, non subijciuntur iustitiæ Dei, quæ sola nos tueri & seruare potest. Exemplum huius rei euidens in ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, vidimus. Cùm enim publicani & plures alij peccatis non vulgaribus infames Christum ampleƒerentur, imò Ioannis doctrina & baptismo iampridem ad pœnitentiæ veræ studium inflammati essent, Pharisæi tamen & Legis interpretes consilium Dei spreuerunt, & tam Ioannem quàm Christum Dominum conuitijs atrocibus insectati sunt. Graviter ergo illos Dominus obiurgat, & idem non temere alibi dicit illis: Amen amen dico vobis, quòd publicani & meretrices præcunt vobis in regnum Dei. Facit ad huius illustrationè historia, quam Lucas in præsenti subijcit. Ea enim primo diluitur eorum calumnia, qui Christum comessatorem & vinipotorem dicebant. Nam docet quomodo & quem finem cum peccatoribus familiarius conuersari soleat, non quidem, ut peccandi licentiam in illis excuseт, sed ut ad pœnitentiam excitet, & ut peccatorum conscientia oppressus conscientijs remedium adhibeat. Ostendit deinde quid plerosq; abstterreat, quò minus ad ipsum accedant & salutis in ipso participes fiant.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, offers salvation and life, of which he himself is the author and mediator, to all men quite generously, yet most people are accustomed to despise both him and his teaching. Among these, the Pharisees and hypocrites easily hold the first place, who swell with confidence in the merits of their works and their own righteousness. For such men think they have no need at all of another's righteousness or of another justifier, and to them it seems great folly to wish to rely on another's righteousness, and indeed on the righteousness of Christ, who, condemned with malefactors, endured an infamous death on the cross. They therefore do not admit that eternal and saving counsel of God, who offers us righteousness and perfect salvation in his one Son; and while they wish to establish their own righteousness (as Paul says), they do not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, which alone can protect and preserve us. We have seen a clear example of this in what came just before. For when tax collectors and many others notorious for grave sins were flocking to Christ, and indeed had already been stirred by the teaching and baptism of John to a zeal for true repentance, the Pharisees and teachers of the Law nevertheless rejected the counsel of God, and assailed both John and the Lord Christ with savage insults. The Lord therefore rebukes them severely, and elsewhere he tells them without hesitation: Amen, amen I say to you, that tax collectors and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God. The story that Luke sets out here serves to illustrate this. For first it refutes the slander of those who called Christ a glutton and a drunkard. For it teaches how and for what purpose he was accustomed to associate more familiarly with sinners, not indeed to excuse in them a license to sin, but to rouse them to repentance, and so that one oppressed by the awareness of sin might apply a remedy to his conscience. It then shows what frightens most people away, so that they do not come to him and become partakers of salvation in him.

units.la: Occasionem totius negotij aut tractationis Pharisæus quidam, Simon nomine, præbuit. Is enim cùm Christum domum suam invitauisset, mulier quædam proflituto pudore et libidine infamis, nunc autem peccatorum conscientia misere pressa, et pœnitentiæ studio ardens, ad illum accedens eius gratiam ambiuit, ut cum Deo reconciliata mortem effugeret. Quod factum ut Pharisæum & reliquos conuiuas offendit, ita Christo de tota hac causa dicendi occasionem præbuit. At nunc primam historiæ partem videbimus.
units.tr: A certain Pharisee, named Simon, provided the occasion for the whole matter and discussion. For when he had invited Christ to his house, a certain woman, infamous for her lost modesty and lust, but now grievously oppressed by the awareness of her sins and burning with zeal for repentance, approached him and sought his grace, so that, reconciled with God, she might escape death. As this deed offended the Pharisee and the other guests, so it gave Christ an opportunity to speak about the whole matter. But now let us look at the first part of the story.

units.la: Primo autem loco Pharisæus se offert, qui etsi non ex aperto & violento Christi hostibus fuit se videatur, malitiosum tamen & astutum hypocritam fuisse apparet, cùm in captandis offensionibus nimium diligens fuerit, ut Christum in contemptum adducere, aut inuidiam illi conflare posset. Egregiè autem hypocritarum ingenium atq; mores exprimit. Nam odium, quo Christum persequebatur dissimulare nouit, quando illum non modò mensæ suæ adhibet, verumetiam officiosè rogat, ut ad se venire dignetur. Quòd si causam quæras, quæ illum mouit, ego hanc præcipuam esse crediderim, ut ea ratione populi fauorem sibi conciliaret, in quo plerosq; de Christo honorificè sentire intelligebat. Dum ergo Christum honorat, priuatum honorem quærit, ne ex eorum numero putetur esse, qui illum propter Veritatis doctrinam & liberiorem Verbi diuini prædicationem extinctum volebant. Est hoc proprium illius, qui sub Euangelij prætextu suum commodum quærunt, quos Christus in semente parabola προσχαίρως, id est, temporarios vocat, eò quòd ad tempus modò de seipsis aliquam pietatis veræ speм præbeant, quæ tamen mox fallit, si quid pro Christo audendum est, aut si illum suis studijs aduersari sentiunt. Est horum non exiguus numerus hodie, qui cùm Euangelium pessimè oderint, tamen & conciones sacras audiunt, & illius præcones in honore habent, & frequenter ad conuiuia honoraria inuitant, ijsdem assentiuntur & suâ opem promittunt; id verò omne non aliam ob causam faciunt, quàm ut apud veros Christi cultores sibi locum parent, ad honores publicos admittantur, & suis rebus consulant. Est igitur insidiosa valde eiusmodi hominum amicitia, eò quòd frequenter ingens aliquod malum dent, si quæ Euangelij opprimendi occasio sese offerat. Et hic in primis impletur illud Christi, qui huius seculi filios in sua generatione prudentiores esse testatur, quàm filios lucis. Quamobrem circumspectione magna opus est, ne illorum artibus circumuenti salutis iaturam faciamus, aut periculorum inextricabilium Labyrinthis implicemur.
units.tr: First of all the Pharisee presents himself, who, although he does not appear to have been among Christ's open and violent enemies, nevertheless is shown to have been a malicious and crafty hypocrite, since he was far too careful in seeking out occasions of offence, so that he could bring Christ into contempt or stir up hatred against him. And he expresses very well the character and manners of hypocrites. For he knows how to conceal the hatred with which he pursued Christ, since he not only admits him to his table but also courteously asks him to deign to come to his house. But if you ask what motive moved him, I would believe the chief one to be this: that by such means he might win the favour of the people, among whom he knew that many thought honourably of Christ. So while he honours Christ, he seeks honour for himself, so that he might not be thought one of those who wanted him put to death because of his teaching of the truth and his freer proclamation of the divine Word. This is characteristic of those who seek their own advantage under the pretext of the Gospel, whom Christ in the parable of the sower calls temporary [προσκαίρως], because for a time only they show some hope of true piety, which soon fails if anything must be dared for Christ, or if they perceive that he stands in the way of their pursuits. Today their number is not small: although they hate the Gospel most bitterly, they nevertheless listen to sacred sermons, hold its heralds in honour, and often invite them to honourable banquets; they agree with them and promise their help. Yet they do all this for no other reason than to secure a place among the true worshippers of Christ, to be admitted to public honours, and to look after their own affairs. Therefore the friendship of such men is very treacherous, because they frequently inflict some great harm whenever an opportunity to suppress the Gospel presents itself. And here in particular is fulfilled that saying of Christ, who testifies that the sons of this age are wiser in their own generation than the sons of light. Wherefore great caution is needed, lest, beguiled by their arts, we suffer the loss of salvation, or become entangled in the inextricable labyrinths of dangers.

units.la: Deinde Christus quoq; non ofcitanter considerandus venit, qui ad Pharisæum diuertit, quàmuis & eum hostili in se animo præditum esse, & hoc ipsum sibi vicio verti sciret, quòd conuiuijs lautio-ribus interesse soleret. Hoc enim ex officio fecit, ut medicus & æternæ salutis doctor, non ut gulæ uertit. seruiat, aut eorum fauorem sibi conciliet, quos incurabili contumacia aduersus Deum pugnare sciebat. Suo igitur exemplo minimè patrocinatur Monachorum & papisticorum praesulum conuiuis, quos solus lautioris culinae nidor, vt canes famelicos allicit, & qui omnibus assentiri iampridem in animum induxerunt, vt gratuitis epulis frui & ex alieno voluptuari possint. Tuentur quidem illi seipsos Christi exemplo, sed verius illis Petri exemplum conuenit. Nam vt hic cum ad eundem ignem cum summi Pontificis famulis sese calefaceret, in zelo Christi frigidior factus eum turpiter abnegauit, cuius causa prius omnia sua reliquerat: ita isti Abbatum & Episcoporum beneficijs & consuetudine frequentiore deuincti, fidem & Christiani hominis officium paulatim dedisc unt, & tandem aperti abnegatores fiunt, ne rusticè nimis ab ijs dissentire videantur, quorum amicitiam sibi quaestuosam esse sentiunt. Vt ergo olim Diogenes dicebat, auream illam libertatem, quae sub Saturno floruit, in pultibus vescendis inueniri, non in regum luxuriosis epulis: ita fidei libertatem facilius seruant, qui contemptis huius saeculi delitijs & Christi hostium fauore, frugalitatis & temperantiae studium sectantur.
units.tr: Next, Christ too must be considered with care, for he went to the Pharisee's house, although he knew that the man was endowed with a hostile mind towards him, and that this very thing would be counted against him, since he was in the habit of attending more sumptuous banquets. For he did this in the discharge of his office, as a physician and teacher of eternal salvation, not to serve gluttony, or to win the favour of those whom he knew to be fighting against God with incurable obstinacy. Therefore he by his example does not in the least defend the banquets of monks and Papist prelates, whom the mere savour of a richer kitchen attracts like hungry dogs, and who have long since resolved to agree with everyone, so that they may enjoy free feasts and take their pleasure at another's expense. Those men indeed shelter themselves under Christ's example, but the example of Peter suits them better. For just as Peter, when he warmed himself at the same fire with the servants of the high priest, grew colder in zeal for Christ and shamefully denied him, though for Christ's sake he had earlier left everything, so these men, bound by the benefits and more frequent company of abbots and bishops, gradually lay aside faith and the duty of a Christian, and at last become open deniers, so that they may not seem too rustic in dissenting from those whose friendship they feel to be profitable to them. Therefore, just as Diogenes once said that the golden liberty which flourished under Saturn was to be found in eating porridge, not in the luxurious feasts of kings, so those who, having despised the pleasures of this age and the favour of Christ's enemies, pursue the zeal for frugality and temperance, more easily preserve the liberty of faith.

units.la: In primis autem hic obseruatu dignissimum est ardens illud Iesu Christi studium, quod in seruandis hominibus adhibuit. Hunc enim cibum suum esse dicit, vt faciat voluntatem patris sui, & opus eius perficiat. Atqui Dei voluntatem Paulus esse testatur, vt omnes homines salui fiant, & in cognitionem Veritatis inducantur. Huic igitur operi sic ille intentus fuit, vt ne eos quidem negligendos esse putarit, quos maligno & hostili in se omnino praeditos, & salute indignissimos esse non ignorabat. Ideo hic Pharisaei domum ingreditur, & insidiosè secum agentibus salutem praedicat. Et alibi neque praesentia neque insidiae hostium illum abterrere possunt, quo minus docendo pergat, & salutificam suam virtutem miraculosis operibus declaret. Hinc ergo consolationem petamus, si quando nos tentationes graviores exercent. Qui enim hostibus & poenitere nescijs tam se amicum & propitium praebuit, nunquam eos fastidire poterit, qui ipsum animo amico & precibus verè pijs inuitaue rint, aut pulsanti aperuerint. Eius enim promissio est: Ecce sto ad ostium, & pulso: Si quis audierit vocem meam & aperuerit ianuam, ingrediar ad illum, & coenabo cum illo, & ipse mecum. Admonet praeterea nos Christi exemplum, minimè deferendam esse vocationem aut munus à Deo nobis iniunctum, etiamsi multos hostiliter erga nos affectos esse, multa etiam in calumniam malignius trahi sentiamus. Christi munus erat docere, oues perditas quaerere, errantes in viâ reducere, lasciuientes coercere, deniq; neminem ad se venientem eijcere foras. Haec ille indefesso studio facere perrexit, neque per eos se auocari passus est, qui & facta eius omnia calumniabantur, et occasiones insidiosè captabant, vt ipsum quàm plurimis inuisum & exosum facerent. Exempla huius studij passim occurrunt euangelicam historiam legentibus. Imitentur hoc omnes homines, in primis autem illi, qui in gradu aliquo sublimiori à Deo constituti sunt, & quorum fidei multorum quoq; aliorum salus commissa est. Etenim qui ecclesijs seruiunt, multos sui ministerij aestimatores iniquos, plerosq; autem ingratos experiuntur, pro quorum salute ipsi dies noctesque excubant: neque calumniatores desunt, qui quae bene aut pie facta sunt, in sensum alienum detorquent. At nihilominus illi pergere debent, neq; hominum ingratissimorum iudicijs moueri, quando haec ipsis fraudi esse non poterunt, modò fidem suam Deo probare possint, qui suorum seruorum vindex atq; renumerator est fidelissimus. Eadem est eorum conditio, qui rempub. administrant. Nam si hi quoq; officiu fecerint, alijs quidem saeui nimium & crudeles, multis iniqui & iniusti videbuntur, & fortassis seditionum authores ipsis periculu flu ent. At non propterea discedendum est à reipub. gubernaculis, sed eo diligentius aduigilare & à Deo commissam functionem obire oportet, ne dum ignauo metu victi succumbunt, tam seipsos quàm infelicem populum in periculum adducant. Debent hoc ipsum priuatim ad se transferre, quicunque Christo nomen dederunt. Quia enim lucem Veritatis mundus odit, multa quoq; in huius sectatores comminisci tur, vt exosos reddat omnibus, quo fit, vt nihil ferè ab illis dici aut fieri possit, quod non impudenter nimis proscindant calumniatores improbi, qui ex eo laudem sibi quaerunt, si Christi cultoribus negotium faciant. Veruntamen hic quoq; constantia opus est, neque ideo intermitti debent verae pietatis exercitia, quibus Deum delectari scimus. In ijs verò, quae vel per se illicita sunt, vel salua fide & pietate vitari possunt, etiam atque etiam videndum est, ne cui infirmo adhuc scandali alicuius authores simus. Vide Rom.14. & 1.Cor.8.10.
units.tr: Especially worthy of notice here is that burning zeal of Jesus Christ which he showed in saving men. For he says that his food is to do the will of his Father and to accomplish his work. Now Paul testifies that it is God's will that all men be saved and brought to the knowledge of the truth. Christ was therefore so intent upon this work that he did not think even those should be neglected whom he knew to be wholly endowed with malice and hostility towards him and most unworthy of salvation. Hence he enters the Pharisee's house and proclaims salvation to men who were dealing with him by stealth. And elsewhere neither the presence nor the snares of enemies could turn him aside from continuing to teach and to display his saving power by miraculous works. Let us therefore draw consolation from this, if ever more grievous temptations trouble us. For he who showed himself so friendly and gracious even to enemies who did not repent will never be able to despise those who have invited him with a friendly mind and truly pious prayers, or have opened to him when he knocked. For his promise is: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me. Moreover, the example of Christ warns us that the calling or office laid upon us by God must by no means be abandoned, even if we perceive that many are hostile towards us, and that many things are twisted by malice into calumny. Christ's office was to teach, to seek the lost sheep, to lead back those who wandered, to restrain the wanton, and finally to cast out no one who came to him. He went on doing these things with tireless zeal, and he did not allow himself to be diverted by those who calumniated all his deeds and lay in wait for opportunities, so that they might make him as hateful and odious as possible to very many. Examples of this zeal occur everywhere to those who read the Gospel history. Let all men imitate this, and above all those who have been set by God in some higher rank, and to whose care the salvation of many others also has been committed. For those who serve the churches find many unjust judges of their ministry, and most of them ungrateful, for whose salvation they themselves keep watch day and night; nor are slanderers lacking who twist whatever has been done well or piously into a foreign sense. Nevertheless they ought to persevere, and not be moved by the judgments of most ungrateful men, since these cannot harm them, provided they can prove their faith to God, who is the most faithful avenger and rewarder of his servants. The condition of those who administer the commonwealth is the same. For if they too do their duty, they will seem excessively harsh and cruel to some, and unjust and unfair to many, and perhaps they will be in danger of being charged as authors of sedition. Yet on that account they must not withdraw from the helm of the commonwealth, but must rather keep watch all the more diligently and discharge the function committed to them by God, lest, overcome by cowardly fear, they give way and bring both themselves and the unhappy people into danger. Whoever has given his name to Christ ought to apply this to himself in private. For since the world hates the light of truth, it also invents many things against the followers of that light, so as to make them odious to all, with the result that scarcely anything can be said or done by them which wicked calumniators do not tear apart with too much impudence, seeking praise for themselves from this, if they can cause trouble for the worshippers of Christ. Nevertheless steadfastness is needed here too, and the exercises of true piety, in which we know God takes delight, ought not on that account to be discontinued. But in those things which are either unlawful in themselves, or can be avoided without loss of faith and piety, we must look again and again to ensure that we are not the authors of some stumbling block to a weak brother. See Rom. 14, and 1 Cor. 8, 10.

units.la: Transfea-
units.tr: Let us pass on

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad mulierem, quae praecipua huius actionis persona est, & quae disputationi, quae mox sequetur, argumentum sive ansam praebuit. De hac sic scribit Lucas: Et ecce mulier, quae erat in urbe peccatrix, cum cognovisset eum accubuisse in domo Pharisaei, detulit alabastrum unguenti, & stans ad pedes eius retro, flens coepit lachrymis rigare pedes eius, & capillis capitis sui extergebat, & deosculabatur pedes eius, & unguento unguebat. Quibus verbis initio mulieris huius conditionem describit. Erat (inquit) peccatrix in urbe. Nam quamvis feria haec conversio ad Christum, illam, quoad Dei iudicium, ab omni culpa liberaverat, apud homines tamen adhuc pessime audiebant, neque alio loco habebatur, quam quo prostituti pudoris feminae habere solent. Quod ideo observari debet, ut illustrior sit Christi bonitas, qui talem in conspectum admittere, & eiusdem in se officia probare, & in gratiam recipere dignatus est. Facit huc demonstrativa particula, ECCE. Ea enim nos ut ad rei novae & considerate dignissimae considerationem Evangelista excitat. Et sane multa admiratione dignum est, mulierem libidine & scortatione infamem, subita peccati cognitio ne perculsam de conversione ad Deum tam serio cogitavisse, ut omni mora abrupta ad Christum con tenderit, & eo intercessore atque mediatore cum illo reconciliari optarit. Non ergo pigeat eam diligentius paulo inspicere.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the woman, who is the chief figure in this action and who gave occasion and material for the discussion that follows. Luke writes of her thus: And behold, a woman who was in the city a sinner, when she knew that he sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment, and standing at his feet behind him, weeping, began to wash his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. In these words he first describes her condition: She was (he says) a sinner in the city. For although her conversion to Christ had now freed her from all guilt in the eyes of God, among men she still had a very bad name, and was held in no higher regard than women of shameless prostitution usually are. This should be noted so that the goodness of Christ may shine more brightly, since he deigned to admit such a woman into his presence, to accept the services she offered him, and to receive her into his favour. The demonstrative particle ECCE belongs here. The Evangelist uses it to rouse us to consider a new matter that is most worthy of thought. Indeed it is very wonderful that a woman infamous for lust and whoring, struck by a sudden knowledge of her sin, should have thought so seriously about turning to God that, breaking off every delay, she hastened to Christ and desired to be reconciled to him through his intercession and mediation. Let us not, then, be unwilling to look into her case a little more carefully.

units.la: Proponitur enim hoc loco poenitentiae exemplum perfectissimum, quod nisi imitemur, salvi esse non possumus. In eo autem primum occurrit peccati cognitio, quam in muliere ista feriam & minime fuit causam fuisse, circumstantiae omnes abunde docent. Nunquam enim adduci potuisset, ut in alienâ domum, & quidem Pharisaei domum, in convivium item honestissimorum hominum, ad haec in Christi conspectu veniret, nisi ex scelerum admissorum cognitione dolorem in animo sensisset incredibile, qui hoc illam facere coegit. Fuit ergo cum peccati cognitione coniuncta cordis contritio & irae divinae sensus, qui ut animum eius mirifice excruciavit, ita eandem movit, ut salutem apud Christum quaereret. Id vero nunquam fecisset, nisi iam in animo eius radices egisset fides, qua illam donatam fuisse, Christus postea dissere testabitur. Accedit huic procul dubio in animo eius Spiritus sanctus, qui ipsi author fuit, ut Christi conciones audiret, & eiusdem miracula diligentius observaret. Audiuerat ergo illum omnes qui laborant & onerati sunt, ad se invitare, et ad se venientibus quietem polliceri; audiuerat medicum esse, qui ad sanandum male affectos in mundum venisset: pastorem item, qui errantes & perditos quaereret, et peccatores vocaret ad poenitentiam; denique clamantem audiuerat: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Item: Amen amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Viderat autem promissiones illas infinitis signis confirmari, in quibus & voluntatem eius ad iuuandum propensissimam, & eiusdem virtutem sive potentiam plane divinam observabat: cum & ne minem quantumuis vilem & indignum abs se reiiceret, & morbis humana arte incurabilibus ipse solo verbo mederetur. Nec dubitaverim ad aures illius iam delatam fuisse famam de paralytici curatione, qua non obscure demonstrauerat, se animi quoque morbis mederi posse, & peccata remittendi potestatem habere. Haec (inquam) fidei in Christum femina fuerunt, quae iam animo concepta Spiritus sanctus vivificavit, ut cum fiducia certa ad illum accederet. Et quia virtutem humana maiore in illo agnoscit, honore etiam dignum iudicat. Ideo alabastrum unguenti pretiosi secum affert, ut eum pro more gentis inungat. At inter haec omnia metus & pudor ex prioris vitae & scelerum conscientia enatus eam impediunt, quo minus recta in illius conspectum se inferat. Itaque a tergo accedens ad pedes recumbentis constitit, & tota in pias lachrymas soluitur, quibus peccata sua deplorat. Mox tamen ubi pudorem & metum fides vicit, pedibus illius adoluitur, quos largo lachrymarum imbre rigat, capillis abstergit, & unguento inungit: hoc nimirum officio indicans, qualem ipsum esse credat, & quid ab eo sperat, cum id verbis non posset expimere.
units.tr: For a most perfect example of repentance is set before us here, which unless we imitate, we cannot be saved. In it, the first thing that appears is the knowledge of sin, which in this woman was clearly the cause of the whole matter, as all the circumstances abundantly show. For she could never have been brought to come into another's house, indeed the house of a Pharisee, to a feast of most honourable men, and so into Christ's presence, unless she had felt from the knowledge of her wickedness an incredible grief in her mind, which compelled her to do this. There was therefore joined with the knowledge of sin contrition of heart and a sense of divine wrath, which, as it wonderfully tormented her mind, so moved her to seek salvation with Christ. But she would never have done this unless faith had already taken root in her mind, by which she was endowed, as Christ will afterwards testify. Without doubt the Holy Spirit also came upon her mind, who was the author of her hearing Christ's sermons and observing his miracles more diligently. She had therefore heard him invite all who labour and are burdened to himself, and promise rest to those who come to him; she had heard that he had come into the world as a physician to heal the sick; likewise as a shepherd who seeks the wandering and lost and calls sinners to repentance; and finally she had heard him crying out: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Also: "Verily, verily I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life." She had seen those promises confirmed by countless signs, in which she observed both his most ready will to help and his plainly divine power: since he rejected no one, however base and unworthy, and healed diseases incurable by human art by a word alone. Nor would I doubt that the report of the healing of the paralytic had already reached her ears, by which he had clearly shown that he could heal the diseases of the mind too and had power to forgive sins. This (I say) was the faith in Christ that the woman had; the Holy Spirit quickened it once conceived in her mind, so that she came to him with sure confidence. And because she recognised a greater power in him, she judges him also worthy of honour. So she brings with her an alabaster flask of precious ointment, to anoint him after the custom of her people. But in all this, fear and shame, sprung from the consciousness of her former life and of her sins, hinder her from presenting herself directly in his sight. So, coming from behind, she stood at the feet of him reclining, and dissolved wholly into pious tears, with which she laments her sins. Soon, however, when faith conquered shame and fear, she falls at his feet, which she waters with a copious shower of tears, wipes with her hair, and anoints with ointment, by this act plainly indicating what she believes him to be and what she hopes from him, since she could not express it in words.

units.la: Habes ergo hic omnes verae & salutaris poenitentiae partes. Haec (ut iam saepe diximus) totius hominis conversio est ad Deum, a quo peccatorum illecebras secuti recessimus. Ubi ante omnia peccatorum cognitione vera opus est. Quia enim natura ad peccandum proclives sumus, & peccatis delectamur, nunquam ipsis relictis ad Deum convertemur, nisi illorum atrocitas probe nobis cognita atque perspecta sit. Ea vero in Legis speculo deprehenditur, si cum praeceptis Dei dicta et facta nostra omnia diligenter conferamus. Et quia lex divinis quoque comminationibus aduersus transgressores fulminat, & iram Dei nobis ob oculos statuit, parit cognitio haec terrores horribiles, qui nobis omnia infesta,
units.tr: You have here, then, all the parts of true and saving repentance. This (as we have often said already) is the conversion of the whole man to God, from whom we have departed following the allurements of sins. Here above all a true knowledge of sin is needed. For since we are by nature prone to sin and delight in sins, we will never turn to God, leaving them behind, unless their atrocity is clearly known and perceived by us. Now this is discovered in the mirror of the Law, if we carefully compare all our words and deeds with the precepts of God. And because the law also thunders against transgressors with divine threats, and sets God's wrath before our eyes, this knowledge produces dreadful terrors, which make everything hostile to us,

units.la: Cap. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: adhoc vitam ipsam iniucundam reddunt. Sensit hoc Dauid, quando in Psalmis clamabat: Transgressiones meas agnosco, peccatum meum semper coram me est. Contremefacta sunt ossa mea, sed & anima mea territa est valde menter. Defatigatus sum in gemitu meo, fluctuare facio tota nocte lectum meum, lachrymis meis grabbatum meum irrigo. Dies noctes ingrauescit super me manus tua, versus est succus meus in siccitates auftiuas. Et huius generis multa in sanctorum exemplis occurrunt, quae ideo obseruare consueuit, ne si quid simile nobis accidit, conscientiae terroribus tota absorbeamur: quin potius agnoscamus in nobis verae poenitentiae initia. Mox autem promissiones & gratiae atque bonitatis eius exempla in mentem revocemus, ut ex his spe veniae concepta in fide confirmemur, sine qua (ut Paulus ait) ad Deum nemo potest accedere. Et nisi fides nos sustentet, peccati cognitio desperationem pariet, sicuti in Caini & Iudae exemplis est videre. Quod ne nobis quoque accidat, facile cauebimus, si in Christo intenti simus, qui nobis gratia Dei mediator, imo iustitia & satisfactio a patre factus est: ut quae nobis desunt, ipse sua perfectione farciat. Adhaec cum promissionibus diuinae gratiae exempla conferamus eorum, qui non vulgaribus delictis grauati cum Deo in gratiam redierunt, & huic meditationi preces coniungamus ardentes, ut & peccatu nostrii propitius sit Deus, & fidem nostram fulciat, spiritu idem sancto nos confirmet, ne de eius bonitate desperemus. Quamuis autem fidem in nobis bene confirmatam sentiamus & de Dei gratia abunde certi simus, non tamen ex eo confidentia spiritus concipere, sed pio metu & pudore humiliari debemus, bonae indolis filios imitati, qui etsi de patris bonitate minime dubitent, eundem tamen reuerentur, & quia suae inobedientiae ipsos pudet, non sine timore ingenuo in eius conspectum veniunt. Est enim fidei coniuncta modestia & humilitas, ut in Petri exemplo vidimus, qui diuinae in Christo virtutis consideratione perculsus, ad pedes eius procidit, clamans: Exi a me Domine, quia homo peccator sum. Et Dauid etiamsi de gratia Dei bonam spem concepisset, tamen in lachrymis (ut modo diximus) assiduus, sibi multitudine miserationum opus esse sentiebat. Vehementer ergo errant, qui suorum operum fiducia elati, perinde in Dei conspectum irrumpunt, ac si ipsi pro suis delictis satisfacere possint. Neque ideo bona opera damnamus, imo his omnino studendum esse dicimus, ut quam verbis profitentur, poenitentiam reipsa testlemur. Quomodo enim ad Deum conuersi esse dicentur, qui adhuc pristinis studijs dediti peccato seruiunt, & carnis cupiditatibus indulgent? Sibi ergo dicta putent, qui veram poenitentiam agere videri volunt, quod ad Romanos Paulus ait: Ne regnet peccatum in mortali corpore vestro, ut obediatis peccato in cupiditatibus corporis. Neque sistite membra vestra arma iniustitiae, sed sistite vos Deo ut ex mortuis viuos, & membra vestra arma iustitiae Deo. Quorum sensus est, ut facultates omnes ad Dei seruitium siue cultum conferamus, quibus aliquando carni atque peccato seruiimus. Excitemus ergo nos quoque odorem bonae fragrantiae Christo, & ita viuamus, ut in nobis ille glorificetur. Et haec vera salutis ratio est, quam scripturae passim docent. De hac enim exponi debet, quod apud prophetam dicit Dominus: Viuo ego, quod nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conuertatur, & viuat. Item, Reuertimini ad me, & ego ad vos reuertar. Hac igitur via nobis etiam hodie ingrediendum erit, si quas tot signis nobis denuntiat Deus, poenas effugere libeat. At in hoc plerique peccant, quod aut nunquam cogitant de vitae & morum suorum emendatione, aut ad creaturas & suorum operum merita conuersi Deum negligunt, aut ludos scenicos instituunt, quos poenitentiae publicae titulo vestiunt, vel etiam poenitentiam agunt momentaneam, et ad pristina studia redeunt, quam primum Dei iram deferbuisse arbitrantur. Sunt hi omnes eorum similes, quos hoc nomine Deus Hosea 6. cap. accusat, &c.
units.tr: They also make life itself unpleasant. David felt this when he cried out in the Psalms: "I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me" (Ps. 51:3). "My bones are shaken, and my soul is also troubled exceedingly" (Ps. 6:2-3). "I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed swim, I drench my couch with my tears" (Ps. 6:6). "Day and night your hand is heavy upon me; my moisture is turned into the drought of summer" (Ps. 32:4). Many examples like these occur in the lives of the saints. We should observe them so that, if anything similar happens to us, we are not swallowed up entirely by the terrors of conscience, but rather recognise in ourselves the beginnings of true repentance. Then we should call to mind God's promises, and his examples of grace and goodness, so that by these we may be strengthened in faith, having conceived hope of pardon, and without faith (as Paul says) no one can approach God. And unless faith sustains us, the knowledge of sin will produce despair, as can be seen in the examples of Cain and Judas. We will easily guard against this happening to us, if we are intent on Christ, who has been made for us by God's grace our Mediator, indeed our righteousness and satisfaction before the Father, so that he may supply by his own perfection what we lack. Moreover, let us set alongside the promises of divine grace the examples of those who, burdened with no ordinary sins, were restored to favour with God, and let us join to this meditation ardent prayers, that God may be merciful to our sins, strengthen our faith, and confirm us by the same Holy Spirit, so that we do not despair of his goodness. Yet although we feel that our faith is well established in us and we are fully certain of God's grace, we ought not therefore to conceive a boastful confidence, but be humbled by a godly fear and shame, imitating good-natured sons who, though they never doubt their father's goodness, nevertheless revere him, and because they are ashamed of their disobedience, they come into his presence not without a noble fear. For humility and modesty are joined to faith, as we saw in the example of Peter, who, struck by the consideration of the divine power in Christ, fell at his feet crying: "Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man" (Luke 5:8). And David, even though he had conceived a good hope of God's grace, nevertheless, constantly in tears (as we just said), felt that he had need of the multitude of God's mercies. Those therefore greatly err who, elated by confidence in their own works, rush into God's presence as if they could make satisfaction for their offences themselves. Nor do we on that account condemn good works; rather we say that they must be pursued altogether, so that we may bear witness by our deeds to the repentance we profess in words. For how can those be said to have turned to God who, still given over to their former pursuits, serve sin and indulge the desires of the flesh? Let those who wish to appear to repent truly take to heart what Paul says to the Romans: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it in its lusts. Neither present your members as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God" (Rom. 6:12-13). Its meaning is that we should devote all our faculties to the service and worship of God, those with which we once served the flesh and sin. Let us therefore also offer ourselves as a sweet-smelling savour of good fragrance to Christ, and live in such a way that he is glorified in us. This is the true way of salvation, which the Scriptures teach everywhere. For it is of this that the Lord's words to the prophet must be understood: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live" (Ezek. 33:11). Likewise: "Return to me, and I will return to you" (Zech. 1:3). Therefore we too must walk in this way today, if we wish to escape the punishments with which God threatens us by so many signs. But in this most people sin: either they never think about amending their life and conduct, or, turned towards creatures and the merits of their own works, they neglect God; or they institute theatrical games, which they dress up under the title of public repentance; or they perform a momentary repentance, and return to their former pursuits as soon as they think God's anger has cooled. All these are like those whom God accuses under this name in Hosea 6, etc.

units.la: Priusquam tamen ab hoc loco digrediamur, in peccatricis exemplo obseruari debet praeterea, quid mulieres in primis deceat. Est sexus iste natura proclivius ad libidinem, & fere quae corpus a stupro intactum custodiunt, ornamentis tamen & cultu delectantur nimio & ad lasciuiam compositio. Nam recto collo faciem fuco depictam ostentant, capillorum crispantium cincinnis fronte exornant, reliquos per humeros sparsis & admodum dorsum versus demissis superbiunt: pectus auro multo ornatum quasi venale exponunt, brachia armillis, digitos gemmis aggrauant, nec contenta corpus totum seriico nimio vestiuisse, & saepe formas vestiu finxisse non satis pudicas, in pedibus quoque superbia & lasciuiae illecebras ostentant. At sunt haec omnia indigna Christianis faeminis, quarum ornatus (ut Petrus scribit) non debet esse externus ille, qui in capillorum nodis, & circumpositio auro, vel palliorum amictu amittu confiltu: sed occultus ille cordis homo, situs in corruptione lenis & quieti spiritus, qui est coram Deo pretiosus. Si quae ergo immodico corporis cultu peccaverunt, peccatrices huius ex animo conversae exemplum imitentur, & meretricium vultus impudici fucum verae poenitentiae lachrymis abluant, pectus ab impuris cogitationibus liberent, brachia & manus superbiae laqueis solutas ad Dei ministerium expediant, corpus totum Christo sistant viventem hostiam, capillos autem, id est ornatum omnem superfluum & quicquid necessitati minus feruit, ad Christi pedes tergendos conferant. Sunt autem Christi pedes (ut Augustinus in historiam Mariae Lazari sororis annotavit) pauperes, quos nobis ille ea conditione commendat, ut in suas rationes se scripturum esse polliceatur officia, quae in illos impendimus. O ergo felices capillos, qui istos extergunt, o vere pretiosos annulos & torques, qui pauperum famem saciant, o purpuram beatam, quae nudos vestit, & inopes morbis contabescentes fouet. Haec vos meditari oportebat o matronae & virgines, quae Christianum nomen profitemini. Nec enim luxum vestrum vel generis nobilitas, vel opum abundantia excusat: quia nobilitas vera est in Christo renatum & filium Dei factum esse, opum vero usus licitus est, ut nostrae necessitati seruiant, & nostra abundantia egentium inopiae succurrat.
units.tr: Before we depart from this passage, however, something should also be observed in the example of the sinful woman about what is especially fitting for women. That sex is by nature more prone to lust, and those who keep their bodies free from unchastity nevertheless often take excessive delight in ornaments and in a dress that is designed for wantonness. For they hold their faces with necks held high, painted with cosmetics; they adorn their foreheads with curls of crimped hair; they take pride in their remaining hair spread over the shoulders and hanging nearly down the back. They display their breasts, decked with much gold, as if for sale; they weigh down their arms with bracelets and their fingers with gems. Not content to clothe the whole body in excessive silk, they often fashion garments into shapes that are not modest enough, and they also display pride and enticements of wantonness in their feet. But all these things are unworthy of Christian women, whose adornment (as Peter writes) ought not to be that outward one, in the knotting of the hair, the wearing of gold around the neck, or the donning of cloaks, but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious before God. If therefore any women have sinned by excessive care of the body, let them, as penitent sinners, imitate the example of this woman: let them wash away with the tears of true repentance the shameless paint of the harlot's face; free their breasts from impure thoughts; release their arms and hands from the snares of pride and devote them to the service of God; present their whole body to Christ as a living sacrifice; and let them give their hair, that is, all superfluous ornament and whatever serves necessity least, to wipe Christ's feet. Now Christ's feet (as Augustine noted in his account of Mary, the sister of Lazarus) are the poor, whom he commends to us on the condition that he promises to count as done to himself the services we render to them. O happy hair, which wipes these feet! O truly precious rings and necklaces, which satisfy the hunger of the poor! O blessed purple, which clothes the naked and cherishes the destitute wasting with disease! These are the things you ought to meditate upon, O matrons and virgins, who profess the Christian name. For neither nobility of birth nor abundance of wealth excuses your extravagance: true nobility lies in having been born again in Christ and made a son of God, while the lawful use of wealth is that it serve our needs, and that our abundance relieve the want of the needy.

units.la: Caeterum Pharisaei Simeonis de hoc facto iudicium audiamus. Prodit is suum ingenium, & indeoccasionem sumit, ut Christo calumniam struat. Caute tamen & astute rem intra animum suum meditatur, priusquam aliquid contra eum pronuntiet, quem ad respondendum satis instructum esse ex anteactis sciebat. Itaq; apud se dicit: Hic, si esset Propheta, nosset quae & qualis sit haec mulier, quae tangit ipsum: nam est peccatrix. Ubi ante omnia observabis, nihil impudicum de Christo illum suspicari, sed prophetiae modo dignitatem illi negare, quam populus ei tribuebat. Unde apparet, eam in Christo innocentiam vitae & modestiam fuisse, ut ne hostes quidem infensissimi in illo iustam ffmistrae aliquius suspicionis causam invenire potuerint. Itaq; talem omnino agnoscit Christum, qui se ab ista muliere tangi minime passurus fuisset, si quae nam & qualis ea sit sciret. Quia autem hoc illum nescire arbitratur, ex eo colligit, ne prophetam quidem esse: quasi vero prophetae omnes omnium facta & mores semper nouerint. Causa erroris huius praecipua est, quod Messiae officium non intellexit, cuius est Mediatorem agere, & miseros peccatores cum Deo in gratiam reducere. Et hoc illud scandalum est, ad quod nostro etiam saeculo Anabaptistae offendunt, quando ecclesias nostras hoc nomine damnant, quod in illis admittantur, qui peccatis & sceleribus infames sunt. Atqui cogitare debebant, Euangelium retis aut verriculi instar esse, quo omnis generis pisces trahuntur, neq; nostre mere nobis de aliorum conscientia iudicium fumere debere. Et ut ad Simonem illum redeamus, si in semetipsum ille defendisset, Christum non ausus fuisset ad mensam suam vocare, sed cum Centurio ne dixisset: Domine non sum dignus, ut sub tectum meum ingrediaris: Imo non minus fuisset admiratus, Christum in suam domum diuertisse, qui muliere hac multo deterior erat, quam quod se ab illa tangi passus erat. Elucet igitur in hoc exemplo, quo ingenio praediti sint hypocritae, qui veritati se opponere semel in animum induxerunt. Sunt hi mortalium oculatissimi in aliorum vitiis notandis, in eorum maxime, quos ab ipsis fecisse nonem fecisse, aut ipsorum studijs aduersos esse norunt. In suis autem vitiis observandis plus quam caeci sunt: imo quamuis illa atrocissima sint, ea tamen mirifice extenuare, & sibi ipsis blanditias facere consueuerunt. At hic praeterea nō ofcitanter obseruari debet, Pharisaeum ex mulieris iatus moribus occasionem arripuisse, quae Christi doctrinam in dubium vocaret. Est hoc admodum frequens hodie. Quia enim tanta est Euangelij doctrinae puritas, ut in illa nemo aliquid inueniat reprehensione dignum, eos oculatissime observant eius hostes, qui illa profitentur, ut aliquam calumniandi causam inueniant. Faciunt hoc (ut Paulo ante dictum est) Anabaptistae, quando in euangelicae doctrinae & fidei nostrae contemptu eos nobis exprobrant, qui in nostris ecclesijs vitam viuunt Christiana professione indignam. Faciunt hoc ipsum Papistae superstitionis fectatores, & ita fit, ut quae ipsi praeter officium facimus, in Christi contumeliam redundent. Erat de hoc nobis saepe cogitandum, & de hoc nos ille admonet, quando nos ciuitatis instar esse dicit, quae in monte sita latere non potest, ex eo autem infert, opera nostra lucere debere, ut per ea pater nostrer glorificetur. Meminerimus ergo hic nō nostram modo causam agi, sed simul in periculum venire Filij Dei Iesu Christi gloriam, cui nos totos consecratos esse convenit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us now hear the judgment of the Pharisee Simon on this deed. He betrays his disposition and seizes the opportunity to contrive a slander against Christ. Yet he deliberates on the matter within himself carefully and cunningly before he pronounces anything against him, whom he knew from past experience to be well able to answer. So he says to himself: "If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner." Here you will observe first of all that he does not suspect anything immodest in Christ, but merely denies him the dignity of a prophet, which the people ascribed to him. From this it appears that in Christ there was such innocence and modesty of life that not even his most bitter enemies could find any just cause for suspicion of impurity. So he recognises Christ as one who would certainly not have allowed himself to be touched by this woman if he had known who and what sort of woman she was. But because he thinks Christ does not know this, he concludes from it that he is not even a prophet, as if all prophets had always known the deeds and characters of everyone. The chief cause of this error is that he did not understand the office of the Messiah, which is to act as Mediator and to reconcile miserable sinners with God. And this is the stumbling-block at which, even in our own age, the Anabaptists take offence, when they condemn our churches on this ground, that those are admitted into them who are notorious for sins and crimes. And yet they ought to consider that the Gospel is like a net or a dragnet, by which fish of every kind are drawn in, and that we ought not to presume to judge the consciences of others. And to return to that Simon: if he had defended himself by his own standard, he would not have dared to invite Christ to his table, nor would he have said with the centurion: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof" (Matt. 8:8). Indeed he would have been no less astonished that Christ had lodged in his house, when he was far worse than this woman, than that he had allowed himself to be touched by her. In this example it is clear with what kind of wit hypocrites are endowed, who have once resolved to set themselves against the truth. They are the most sharp-sighted of men in noting the faults of others, especially of those whom they know to have done them wrong or to be opposed to their pursuits. But in observing their own faults they are more than blind; indeed, although those faults are most atrocious, they are accustomed to diminish them wonderfully and to flatter themselves. But here we should further observe, not carelessly, that the Pharisee seized upon the occasion from the woman's immoral conduct to call Christ's teaching into doubt. This is very common today. For since the purity of the Gospel teaching is so great that no one finds in it anything worthy of reproach, its enemies, who profess it, watch it most keenly so that they may find some cause for slander. The Anabaptists do this (as was said a little earlier), when in contempt of the evangelical doctrine and of our faith they reproach us with those in our churches who live a life unworthy of the Christian profession. The Papists, devotees of superstition, do the very same, and so it comes about that whatever we do beyond our duty redounds to the dishonour of Christ. We should often think about this, and Christ admonishes us of it when he says that we are like a city set on a mountain, which cannot be hidden, and from this he infers that our works ought to shine, so that our Father in heaven may be glorified by them. Let us remember, then, that here not only our own cause is at stake, but at the same time the glory of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom we are bound to be wholly consecrated. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Pharisaeus Christum caeluminatur.
units.tr: The Pharisee slanders Christ.

units.la: Tunc respondens Iesus dixit ei: Simon habeo quiddam quod tibi dicam. At ille ait, Magister, dic. Duo debitores (inquit Iesus) erant cuidam creditori: unus debebat denarios quingentos, alter vero quinquaginta. Cum autem illi non essent soluendo, gratificatus est utrisque. Horum igitur, dic, uter eum plus diliget? Respondens vero Simon dixit: Existimo eum, cui plus gratificatus est. At ille dixit ei: Recte iudicasti.
units.tr: Then Jesus answered and said to him, "Simon, I have something to say to you." "Master," he replied, "say it." Jesus said: "A certain creditor had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When neither could repay, he forgave them both. Tell me, then, which of them will love him more?" Simon answered, "I suppose the one he forgave more." Jesus said to him, "You have judged rightly."

units.la: Lucas Euangelista non temere historiam mulieris peccatricis & Simonis pharisaei summa diligentia & studio describit. Continet enim haec vniuersam redemptionis & salutis nostrae rationem, simulque docet, ad hanc percipiendam magis idoneos esse eos, qui peccatorum debito aut pondere praealijs oppressi sunt, quam illos, qui propter opera in specie bona sibi ipsis, aut etiam alijs hominibus iusti esse videntur. Opponuntur enim inter se mulier libidine infamis & pharisaeus propriae iustitiae fiducia ebrius. Illa peccatorum agnitione territa ad Christum confugit, & suo exemplo docet, quae vera sit poenitentia, & quid nos facere conueniat, si cum Deo in gratiam redire & seruari velimus. Opus hic ante omnia peccatorum agnitione, quae animi contritionem & humiliationem parit, simulque obstat ne nostrarum virium aut meritorum fiducia efferamur. Simul autem per fidem in Iesum Christum ad thronum gratiae confugiamus oportet. Sequetur hinc obedientia, quae nos totos Deo vendicabit, vt is per nos & opera nostra glorificetur. Ab his longe alienissimus est Pharisaeus iste, quem suiipsius fiducia sic dementauit, vt non contentus mulierem iam nimium praecipiti iudicio damnauisse, insuper Christum quoque calumnietur, aut saltem sinistris suspicionibus grauet. Est hoc proprium hypocritis & propriae iustitiae ostentatoribus. Nam vt iusti & sancti putentur, in quosuis obuios sibi censuram sumunt, & vitia omnium obseruant, omnes damnant, & ipsam quoque gratiae praedicationem iniquis calumniis lacessunt, id quod absque Dei patris & Christi Mediatoris contumelia fieri non potest. Caeterum ad horum pleniorem explicationem facit, quae modo sequitur, altera huius historiae pars, quae docetur, quid plerosque hominum abstterreat, quo minus ad Christum accedant. Nimirum quod gratiae Dei in illo nobis exhibitae magnitudinem non agnoscant. Accidit hoc tam Epicureis & apertis omnis religionis contemptoribus, quam illis, qui suae iustitiae meritis confidunt. Nam vt hi gratuita misericordia sibi nequaquam opus esse existimant, ita illi hanc ridentur, eo quod fabulas ipsis vi decur, quicquid scripturae de caelis & inferis, & alterius vitae praemijs aut poenis tradunt. In praesenti tamen Christus aduersus iustitiarios actionem instituit, quae ob singularem grauitatem cum diuina suauitate commixtam, admodum memorabilis & multa consideratione dignissima est.
units.tr: Luke the evangelist does not describe the story of the sinful woman and Simon the Pharisee with such great care and attention by chance. It contains the whole account of our redemption and salvation, and at the same time it teaches that those are better fitted to receive it who are weighed down and oppressed by the burden of sin, than those who seem righteous on account of outwardly good works, either for themselves or in the eyes of other people. For here two people are set against each other: the woman, infamous for her lust, and the Pharisee, drunk with confidence in his own righteousness. The woman, terrified by the knowledge of her sins, flees to Christ, and by her example she teaches what true repentance is and what we ought to do if we wish to be reconciled to God and saved. Here, above all, comes the recognition of sin, which produces contrition and humility of mind, and at the same time keeps us from being puffed up by trust in our own strength or merits. At the same time we must flee to the throne of grace through faith in Jesus Christ. From this follows obedience, which will claim us wholly for God, so that he may be glorified through us and our works. The Pharisee here is very far removed from this. Confidence in himself has so maddened him that, not content with having already condemned the woman with far too hasty a judgment, he also slanders Christ, or at least burdens him with sinister suspicions. This is the mark of hypocrites and of those who display their own righteousness. For in order to be thought righteous and holy, they take upon themselves the role of censors of everyone they meet, they watch the faults of all, they condemn all, and they even assail the very preaching of grace with unjust calumnies, which cannot happen without insult to God the Father and to Christ the Mediator. Moreover, for a fuller explanation of these matters, the other part of this story, which follows, is helpful. It teaches what frightens most people away from coming to Christ: namely, that they do not recognise the greatness of the grace of God shown to us in him. This happens both to the Epicureans and open despisers of all religion, and to those who trust in the merits of their own righteousness. For the latter think that free mercy is not needed by them at all, while the former are mocked because they regard as fables whatever Scripture tells of heaven and hell and of the rewards or punishments of another life. In the present passage, however, Christ takes action against the self-righteous, and this action, because of its singular seriousness mingled with divine sweetness, is most memorable and most worthy of careful consideration.

units.la: Primum occurrit, quod etsi nihil in Christum dixisset Pharisaeus, ille tamen ad occultas animi cogitationes respondet, & haec quasi ex latebris in lucem protractas confutat. At hoc agendo Pharisaeum reipsa erroris conuincit. Nam cogitabat ille: Hic si esset propheta, nosset quae & qualis sit haec mulier, & proinde se ab ea contrectari non pateretur. Ad ista ergo absque mora aut curiosiore inuestigatione Christus respondens, abunde testatur, se mulieris istius mores atque conditionem non ignorare, imo se plus quam prophetam esse, qui & omnia norit, & simul omnibus afflictis possit succurrere. Et est hoc euidens diuinitatis Iesu Christi argumentum. Nam vt alias diximus, constat solius Dei esse, cordium cogitationes & occulta hominum desideria scrutari. At Christum tam haec quam illas nouisse, ex hoc & infinitis alijs exemplis apparet. Deus ergo verus sit oportet. Neque hic mihi aliquas reuelationes somniet, quales olim prophetae habuerunt. Nihil enim huius de Christo traditur, qui vt propria virtute opera fecit humanis viribus maiora, sic etiam ex semetipso omnia nouit, neque aliunde eum aliquid discere opus fuit, in quo omnes scientiae & sapientiae thesauros reconditos esse, & quem nobis a patre sapientiam factum esse. Apostolus scribit. Prodest autem haec omniscientia Christi argumenta obseruare, eo quod dulcissimam consolationem continent, & ad vitam recte pieque instituendam plurimum conferunt. Qui enim mortali carne vestitus suorum labores & bostium occultas cogitationes vidit, is procul dubio nunc quoque in caelesti gloria constitutus nos laborantes spectat, & iusto atque vindice occulo intuetur eorum machinationes qui ecclesiam suam eiusq; membra persequuntur. Quid ergo trepidamus auditis impiorum consilijs? aut cur nobis terrori sunt hominum vires, quas flatu suo facile dissipabit, qui pro suo nutu caelum terramque gubernat? Quid enim illo inscio homines tentare, aut eodem inuito perficere possunt? Certè qui hoc diligentius meditantur, hi ad omnem fortunæ euentum intrepidi & constantes sunt. Ijdem vitam quoque suam & actiones omnes sic instituunt, ne eius oculos offendant, quem olim omnis carnis iudicem venturū esse audiunt. Si enim pudet coram hominibus aliqua authoritate præditis res turpes dissignare, multo magis eos suæ nequitiæ pudebit, qui se in Christi Iesu, iudicis totius terræ conspectu agere cogitant. Et hæc causa est, quòd hoc ferè hominibus persuadere studet Satan, vt cū impio illo Nabale dicant aut sentiant, non esse Deum, qui res hominum inspiciat. Nam est hoc omnis impietatis fundamentum, quod si semel in animo iactum fuerit, mox effectum suum habebunt carnis desideria, quæ nos ad omne scelus proclives abripiunt.
units.tr: First, although the Pharisee had said nothing against Christ, Christ nevertheless answers his hidden thoughts and refutes them, as if they had been dragged out of hiding into the light. By doing so, he really convicts the Pharisee of error. For the Pharisee was thinking: "If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman this is, and so he would not allow himself to be touched by her." Christ, therefore, answers these thoughts at once, without delay or closer inquiry, and abundantly shows that he does not ignore this woman's character and condition, and indeed that he is more than a prophet, since he knows all things and can at the same time help all who are afflicted. This is a clear argument for the divinity of Jesus Christ. For, as we have said elsewhere, it belongs to God alone to search the thoughts of hearts and the hidden desires of men. But that Christ knew both these things and those, appears from this and from countless other examples. Therefore he must be the true God. Nor let anyone here dream up for me some revelations such as the prophets once had. For nothing of this kind is related of Christ, who, by his own power, performed works greater than human strength, and in the same way knew all things from himself, and had no need to learn anything from elsewhere; in him are hidden all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, and he is the one whom the apostle writes was made wisdom for us by the Father. It is useful to observe these arguments for Christ's knowledge of all things, because they contain the sweetest consolation and contribute greatly to leading a life that is upright and godly. For he who, clothed in mortal flesh, saw the labours of his people and the secret thoughts of his enemies, without doubt now also, placed in heavenly glory, watches us as we labour, and with a just and avenging eye looks upon the schemes of those who persecute his Church and its members. Why, then, do we tremble when we hear the counsels of the wicked? Or why are the powers of men a terror to us, when he who governs heaven and earth at his own will will easily scatter them with his breath? For what can men attempt without his knowledge, or accomplish against his will? Surely those who meditate on this more carefully are fearless and steadfast in the face of every turn of fortune. They also order their whole life and all their actions so as not to offend the eyes of him whom they hear will one day come as judge of all flesh. For if men are ashamed to do disgraceful things in the sight of those who hold some authority, how much more ashamed ought those to be of their wickedness who think they are acting in the sight of Jesus Christ, the judge of the whole earth. And this is why Satan takes such pains to persuade people to think or say with that impious Nabal, that there is no God who sees the affairs of men. For this is the foundation of all impiety: once it has been planted in the mind, the desires of the flesh will soon have their effect, and they carry us headlong toward every crime.

units.la: In primis autem hoc loco nobis obseruanda venit Christi mansuetudo, qui hospitem male fidum & ad calumnias nimis procliuem neque relinquit illico, neque (vt merebatur) durius increpat, sed potius humaniter & amicè instituit: imò officij, quod hospites decet, probè memor, honorifica præfa tiunculavtitur, qua docendi copiam sibi fieri petit. Simon (inquit) habeo quiddam quod tibi dicam. Est hæc bonitas illa, quam propheta promisso humani generis redemptori tribuit, sic de illo scribens: Non clamabit, neque efforetur, non faciet audiri in platea vocem suam. Arundinem fractam non conteret, & linum fumigans non extinguet, &c. Visus est bonitate illa etiam priusquam in carnem veniret, cum tota Iudæorum gente, sicuti prophetarum sermones testantur, quos illius spiritu motos fuisse Petrus testatur. Et in Euangelio infinita illius exempla occurrunt, quæ eiusmodi sunt, vt non admiratione solum, sed stupore dignum sit, illum genti ad miraculum vsque contumaci tantum indulgere potuisse. Minus tamen mirabimur, si cogitemus, eum simili facilitate & mansuetudine nobiscum etiam agere, qui non minori proterua admonitiones eius reijcimus & beneficia contemnimus. Ex eo autem apparet, illum nostræ salutis cupidissimum esse: quod vt in tentationibus conscientiæ nos solatur, ita vicissim excitare debet, vt nos illi gratos & obsequentes præbeamus. Quod enim de hominibus olim Mimus dixit, Furor fit læsa diu patientia: hoc ipsum de Deo rectissimè dici potest, qui etsi non cæco furore excandescat, iusto tamen iudicio poenas acrius & seuerius exigit, quando suam mansuetudinem à nobis contemni, & nostram contumaciam incurabilem esse videt. Quod Iudæos olim senisse notius est, quàm vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Interim Iesu Christi exemplum omnes homines imitentur, in primis autem Euangelij præcones, ne proterue nimis aut præcipitantius agendo multos abster reant, quos suis admonitionibus & correptionibus allicere aut lucrifacere debebant. Iubet hoc Paulus in posteriori ad Timotheum sic scribens: Seruum domini non oportet pugnare, sed placidum esse erga omnes, aptum ad docendum, tolerantem malos, cum lenitate erudientem eos, qui contrariè sunt animo affecti, experturum ecquando det eis Deus, vt conuersi agnoscant veritatem. Reliqui verò Simonem hunc sibi imitandum proponant, qui etsi iniquius de Christo iudicaret, & animu eius sinistræ suspiciones iam occupauissent, non tamen reijcit indignius prose dicere volentem, sed aures illi amicè atque patienter præbet. Hæ die multi in eo grauissimè peccant, quòd præiudicijs iniquissimis fascinati ne videre quidem vel audire volunt eos, de quibus suspiciones prauas animo conceperunt, aut quos ab ipsis dissentire norunt. At meminisse oportet, nihil falacius esse suspicione, neq; temere Apostolum dixisse: Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete.
units.tr: In this passage, above all, we must observe the gentleness of Christ, who neither leaves immediately, nor (as he deserved) rebukes more harshly a guest who is untrustworthy and too prone to calumny, but rather instructs him kindly and in a friendly way. Indeed, mindful of the duty that befits a host, he uses a courteous little preface by which he asks that an opportunity to teach be given to him: "Simon," he says, "I have something to say to you." This is that gentleness which the prophet ascribed to the promised Redeemer of mankind, writing thus of him: "He shall not cry out, nor lift up his voice, nor make it heard in the street. A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench" (Isa. 42.). He showed this gentleness even before he came in the flesh, toward the whole Jewish nation, as the words of the prophets bear witness, which Peter testifies were moved by his Spirit. And countless examples of this kind occur in the Gospel, such that it is worthy not only of admiration but of astonishment that he could show such indulgence to a people stubbornly resistant even to miracles. Yet we shall be less surprised if we consider that he deals with us in the same ready and gentle way, though we reject his admonitions with no less insolence and despise his benefits. From this it appears that he is most eager for our salvation; and just as this comforts us in the temptations of conscience, so in turn it ought to stir us up to show ourselves grateful and obedient to him. For what the mime once said of men, "Anger is produced when long-suffering is injured," can be most rightly said of God too. Although he does not blaze up with blind fury, yet by his just judgment he exacts punishment more sharply and severely when he sees that his gentleness is despised by us and our obstinacy is incurable. That the Jews once experienced this is too well known to need proof to many. Meanwhile, let all men imitate the example of Jesus Christ, and above all the heralds of the Gospel, so that by acting too insolently or too hastily they do not drive away those whom they ought to attract by their admonitions and corrections and win for Christ. Paul commands this in his second letter to Timothy, writing thus: "The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient with the wicked, correcting with gentleness those who are opposed, if perhaps God may at some time grant them repentance so that they may come to know the truth" (2 Tim. 2.). Let the rest propose this Simon to themselves for imitation, who, although he judged Christ more unfairly and his mind was already seized by sinister suspicions, nevertheless does not reject him as he wishes to speak more frankly, but kindly and patiently lends him his ear. Nowadays many sin grievously in this, that bound by the most unjust prejudices they do not even wish to see or hear those about whom they have formed wicked suspicions in their minds, or whom they know to dissent from them. But we ought to remember that nothing is more deceptive than suspicion, and that the apostle did not speak rashly when he said: "Test all things; hold fast what is good" (1 Thess. 5.).

units.la: Sed ad Christū redeamus, qui quod dicturus erat, per parabolam exponit, & hanc more Hebræo rum vt rem vere gestam narrat. Vt verò alias omnes, ita istam quoq; ex rebus vulgo notis desumit, iudicium causæ propositæ ipsi Pharisæo permittit, vt magis perspicua sint omnia, & istius impro bitas atq; hypocrisis euidentius arguantur. Scopus totius actionis est, quod primò muliere defendit, quam Simon nimis præcipiti sententia damnauerat, dum adhuc peccatricem & bonorum consuetudine indignam dixit, quam Deus ipse absoluerat: deinde se quoq; excusat, qui per hanc sibi præslita pietatis & dilectionis officia non debuerit respuere: postremò tam Simonis quàm aliorum sui ordinis hominum ingratitudinem perstringit, imò grauiter accusat, qui oblatam sibi à Deo gratiā agno scere & amplecti dedignentur.
