Duo debitores (inquit) erant cuidā creditori: vnus debebat denarios quingentos, alter vero quinquaginta. Cum autem illi non essent soluendo, gratificatus est utrisque. Horum igitur, dic, uter eum plus diliget? Ideo est, uter horum illum plus diligere & dilectionem plus tribuus officijs testari debet? Ad hanc quæstionem Simon ex communi sensu & naturæ legibus reste respondens ait: Existimo eum, cui plus gratificatus est, &c. Per duos debitores Simonem Pharisæum & mulierem istam intelligit, & hanc quidem ei confert, qui denarios 500. debuit; illi vero ei qui solum 50. Eam autem comparationem ex hominum iudicio sic instituit, qui Pharisæos alijs melio res & sanctiores esse putabant, cum in Dei iudicio eò sceleratiores essent, quò magis suæ iustitiæ fidu cia efferebantur. Et Christus cum neutrum ex illis soluendo fuisse ait, utrunque in eodem gradu col locat, & postea (vt suo loco dicetur) hunc mulierem ista peiorem esse docet, quòd non pari gratitudine Dei bonitatem excipiat. Et quia conuiuiis mirum videri poterat, mulierem, quæ libidini et superbiæ atq; luxui assuecuerat, nunc tota in lachrymas soluit, et se ad eius pedes usq; demittere, qui plerisq; con temptus & inuisus erat, huius tam subitæ mutationis animiq; tam officiosi causas indicat; Nimirum quòd tam debiti sui quàm gratiæ sibi factæ magnitudinem agnoscat, & proinde se Deo gratam præ bere cupiat. Ex eo autem colligit, non debere amplius eam pro scelerata & vitiis infami haberi, cui Deus ipse culpam omnem condonarit, quæq; se totam Deo impendere cupiat; simulq; ostendit se quoq; non posse noua grata & accepta habere officia, quæ ex animo vere pio & Dei beneficium digne agno scente proficiscantur. Ita vero (quod iam ante monuimus) seuincit, mulierem hanc qualemcunq; alij iudicent, omnibus Pharisæis præstare, qui Dei bonitate securi contemnant, neq; ullo erga illum gra titudinis officio fungantur. Hic (inquam) parabolæ huius finis, et hoc Christi eam proponentis tu sti tutum est. Quod dum aliqui minus obseruant, totius historiæ sensum & usum verum corruperunt; quasi nimirum mulier ista officijs hisce externis peccatorum remissionem meruerit, cum potius gra tuitæ remissionis sensus atq; agnitio illorum causa fuisse indicetur. Quod ipsum de omnibus alijs dici potest, quorum opera in scripturis commendantur: & ideò non in operibus hærere, sed ad horum son tem ascendere oportet, vt quicquid boni habemus ad solius Dei gratiam referatur. Et debet hinc ge neralis doctrina peti: Ea demum opera Deo grata & accepta esse, quæ ex charitate nõ fucata fiunt, quam fides & misericordia Dei sensus in nobis parit. Hic enim nos totos Deo mancipat, & causa est, vt nostra om̃n a secundum regulam verbi eius instituamus: et vt charitas legis totius impleti est, teste Apostolo: ita peccatum est quicquid non ex fide fit. Cæterum continet parabola hæc vni uersam redemptionis et salutis humanæ rationem, cuius singulas partes propius inspexisse proderit.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who explains by a parable what he was about to say, and tells it in the Hebrew manner as a real event. As with all his others, he takes this one from things commonly known, and he leaves the judgment of the case to the Pharisee himself, so that everything is clearer and his wickedness and hypocrisy are more plainly exposed. The aim of the whole account is first to defend the woman, whom Simon had condemned too hastily when he called her a sinner unworthy of good company, though God himself had absolved her. Next, Christ excuses himself, since he ought not to reject the acts of piety and love she offered him. Last, he rebukes, indeed sharply accuses, the ingratitude of Simon and others of his rank, who disdain to acknowledge and embrace the grace of God offered to them. "There were two debtors," he says, "to a certain creditor: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When they could not pay, he forgave both. Tell me, then, which of them will love him more? That is, which of them ought to show more love and gratitude in his service?" Simon, answering rightly from common sense and the laws of nature, says: "I suppose the one to whom he forgave more," and so on. By the two debtors he means Simon the Pharisee and this woman: he assigns the five hundred denarii to her, and the fifty to Simon. He draws this comparison in the manner of human judgment, since the Pharisees thought themselves better and holier than others, when in God's judgment they were the more wicked, the more they were puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness. And when Christ says that neither could pay, he places both on the same level, and afterwards (as will be said in its place) he teaches that this woman is worse than they, because she does not receive God's goodness with equal gratitude. And since it might seem strange to the guests that a woman who had been given over to lust, pride and luxury should now dissolve completely in tears and throw herself at the feet of one who was despised and hated by most people, he explains the reasons for this sudden change of heart and this devoted behaviour: namely, that she recognises both the greatness of her debt and the greatness of the grace shown to her, and therefore desires to be pleasing to God. From this he concludes that she should no longer be regarded as wicked and infamous for her vices, since God himself has pardoned her every fault, and she desires to devote herself wholly to God. At the same time he shows that he cannot accept new acts of service as pleasing and acceptable unless they come from a truly pious heart that rightly acknowledges God's benefit. And in this way (as we have already noted) he proves that this woman, whatever others may judge of her, surpasses all the Pharisees, who, secure in God's goodness, despise him and render him no service of gratitude. This, I say, is the purpose of this parable, and this is the correct interpretation of Christ's telling of it. While some pay too little attention to this, they have corrupted the true meaning and use of the whole story, as if the woman had merited forgiveness of sins by these outward services, whereas the account indicates that the sense and recognition of free forgiveness was rather the cause of them. The same can be said of all the other works commended in Scripture; therefore we must not rest in the works, but rise to their source, so that whatever good we have is referred to the grace of God alone. And from this a general doctrine should be drawn: those works are at last pleasing and acceptable to God which proceed from unfeigned love, which faith and the sense of God's mercy produce in us. For this love binds us wholly to God, and is the reason why we order all our affairs according to his word; and, as the Apostle testifies, love is the fulfilling of the whole law, so whatever is not done from faith is sin. Moreover, this parable contains the whole plan of human redemption and salvation, and it will be useful to look more closely at its individual parts.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum, quòd Simone Pharisæum & mulierem istam duobus debitoribus confert. Comprehendit sub his totum genus hominum, & ostendit tam eos qui mundi iudicio iusti habentur, quàm illos qui publicis sceleribus & flagitijs infames sunt, in Dei ære, id est, apud Dei tribunal pec-cati atq; mortis reos esse. Nam si ad natales nostros descendamus, eadem omniũ corruptio apparebit: eò quòd in sua imagine, id est, in natura sua corrupta, quam ex prima transgressione contraxerat, Adam omnes suos liberos genuit, & sic (vt Paulus dicebat) peccatũ in mundũ introiuit, et quod de semetipso Dauid olim dixit, hoc omnes dicet, qui verũ fateri voluerint: In iniquitate formatus sum & in peccato conceptit me mater mea. Deinde et si gradus sint peccatorũ, & quoad peccata quæ vocat actualia, alij alijs honestiores & meliores sint, nemo tamẽ hominũ se pror sus iustũ et ab omni pecca-to immunẽ dicere potest. Exerit enim sese in ipsis quoq; infantibus ex primo parente in nos deriuata naturæ vitiositas, et nõ temere à Deo dictũ est, sigmẽta cordis humani praua esse à pueritia sua. Hoc enim verissimũ esse fatebũtur, quicunq; in cunis iacentiũ ingenia, et nõ obscura irę, æmulationis, cõ-tumaciæ et aliorum affectuũ argumẽta diligentius obseruauerint. Crescit autẽ cũ ætate peccati vẽ, & causa est, vt in multis omnes labamur, vt Iacobus Apostolus scribit. Etsi cui datur, vt ab omni maleficio manus & corpus reliquũ abstineat (quod tamen nescio an vlli vnquã datũ sit) æstuat ta-mẽ intra animos nostros peccatorũ desideria, quæ cogitationũ et meditationũ pessimarũ causa sunt, et potiore nostri parte ab ea obedientia abducũt, qua nos totos Deo consecrare debebamus. Itaq; qua-lecunq; simus hominum iudicio, Deo tamen debitores sumus, dum occulta carnis desideria, mentis cogitationes & quæcunque alia sunt eius generis ab illo alienamus. Quid, quòd quæ per se bona & sanctæ sunt opera, à nobis polluuntur, dum in illis ipsis cupiditates noxiæ et cogitationes impuræ cõ-currunt? Quod probè olim Isaias obseruauit, qui pios quoq; et veros cultores Dei exclamare docuit: Sumus Summis nos omnes veluti immundum, & instar vestis centorum abiectissimorum omnes iustitiae nostrae. Et tanta est huius debiti summa, ut ipsi soluendo non simus, cum & nihil possimus ex nobis ipsis, & nova quotidie delicta veteribus accumulemus. Agnouerunt hoc olim sanctissimi quiq; quorum iste fere preces fuisse leguntur. Ratio iniquitatum nostrarum superauit nos: ne ingrediaris cum seruis tuis in iudicium, peccatorum adolescentiae nostrae & scelerum nostrorum ne fis memor: Nam si peccata obseruaueris Domine, quis consistet? Et hoc illud est, quod eadem debitorum parabola Christus apud Matth. cap. 18. fusius exponit. Debent ista diligenter a nobis considerari. Primo enim nos de peccatorum atrocitate admonent, & horum blanditias confutant, quibus plerique capiuntur, ut securi affectibus carnis indulgeant, & in sceleribus suis perseuerent. Atqui peccata debitorum instar sunt, & nos iustitiae Dei obstrictos reddunt, cui nos satisfacere non possumus, nisi quas il la peccatis singulis poenas constituit luamus. Ita vero mortem aeternam sustineamus oportet, quam peccati stipendium esse, scriptura omnis unanimi consensu docet. Vt enim qui in magistratus leges delinquit, in illum ære est, quoad multam non dissoluit: ita mortis rei & inferorum poenis obnoxij manent, quantum in ipsis est, quicunque Dei leges quocunque modo transgrediuntur. Quoties ergo ad peccandum solicitaris, cogita te iam ante plus satis grauatum esse, & homines frugi imitare, qui etsi se ad dissoluendum aes alienum non sufficere sentiunt, cauent tamen ne praeter causam nouis & non necessarijs debitis seipsos onerent. Deinde docet quoq; haec comparatio, vanissimas esse quascunq; homines ex suo cerebro fingunt satisfactiones. Qua enim re diuinae iustitiae satisfaciat homo, qui quantus quantus est, peccatum est, & nouis quotidie delictis Dei oculos offendit? Aut si nos hodie tantum nobis de nostris viribus aut meritis pollicemur, quae ratio olim sanctissimos Dei cultores coegit, ut precarentur, ne cum ipsis ille in iudicium descenderet? Vides ergo gloriosulos illos suarum satisfactionum ostentatores non modo aduersus Dei iustitiam insurgere, sed illos ipsas stolidae & non necessariae subiectionis insimulare, ex quibus verae pietatis exempla capere debebant.
units.tr: Here first we meet the fact that Christ compares Simon the Pharisee and this woman to two debtors. Under these he includes the whole human race, and shows that both those who are considered righteous by the judgment of the world and those who are infamous for public crimes and scandals are, in God's account, that is, before God's tribunal, guilty of sin and of death. For if we go back to our birth, the same corruption of all will appear: because Adam begat all his children in his own image, that is, in his corrupt nature, which he had contracted from the first transgression, and so (as Paul said) sin entered the world; and what David once said of himself, all will say who are willing to speak the truth: "I was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me." Next, even if there are degrees of sins, and some are more honourable and better than others as regards the sins which are called actual, yet no man can say that he is wholly righteous and free from every sin. For the vice of nature, derived to us from the first parent, shows itself even in infants, and it was not said by God without reason that the imaginations of man's heart are evil from his youth. Indeed, all who have carefully observed the dispositions of infants lying in their cradles, and the not obscure signs of anger, rivalry, obstinacy and other passions, will admit that this is most true. But with age the power of sin grows, and this is why we all stumble in many things, as the Apostle James writes. And although, if one is given to abstain from every evil deed with his hands and the rest of his body (though I do not know whether this has ever been granted to anyone), still within our souls the desires of sin boil, which are the cause of the worst thoughts and meditations, and draw the greater part of us away from that obedience by which we ought to have consecrated ourselves wholly to God. So, whatever we may be in men's judgment, we are still debtors to God, as long as we estrange from him our secret desires of the flesh, the thoughts of the mind, and whatever else is of that kind. What of the fact that even works which are good and holy in themselves are polluted by us, when harmful desires and impure thoughts creep into those very works? Isaiah long ago observed this well, and taught even the pious and true worshippers of God to cry out: "We are all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags." And the sum of this debt is so great that we cannot pay it, since we can do nothing of ourselves, and we pile up new offences daily on the old. The holiest men of old, whose prayers are read to have been of this kind, recognised this: "The reckoning of our iniquities has overwhelmed us; do not enter into judgment with your servants; be not mindful of the sins of our youth and of our crimes; for if you mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" And this is what Christ explains more fully in the parable of the debtors in Matthew chapter 18. These things must be carefully considered by us. For first they remind us of the atrocity of sins, and refute the flattery of them by which most people are caught, so that they indulge the desires of the flesh without care and persist in their crimes. Yet sins are like debts, and bind us to the justice of God, which we cannot satisfy unless we pay the penalties which that justice has appointed for each sin. And so we must endure eternal death, which all Scripture with one voice teaches to be the wages of sin. For as one who breaks the laws of the magistrate is held liable until he pays the fine, so all who in any way transgress the laws of God remain, as far as in them lies, subject to the penalties of death and of hell. Therefore, whenever you are tempted to sin, consider that you are already burdened more than enough, and imitate thrifty people, who, though they feel they cannot pay off their debts, take care not to load themselves with new and unnecessary debts beyond what is needed. Further, this comparison also teaches that all the satisfactions which men devise out of their own brains are most vain. For in what way does a man satisfy divine justice, who, however great he is, is a sinner, and daily offends God's eyes with new transgressions? Or if today we promise ourselves so much from our own strength or merits, what reason compelled the holiest worshippers of God of old to pray that he would not enter into judgment with them? You see, then, that those boastful displayers of their own satisfactions not only rise up against the justice of God, but also accuse of foolish and unnecessary submission those very acts from which they ought to have learned examples of true piety.

units.la: Quae ergo ratio est (inquis) per quam a peccatorum debito liberemur? Est hoc alterum huius tractationis caput, quod uno verbo Christus explicat, dicens: Cum illis non essent soluendo, gratifica tus est verisq. Loquitur autem de gratuita Dei misericordia, quam in nobis per Euangelium offert in filio suo, qui nobis ab illo iustitia & satisfactio factus est. Ad eundem modum apud Matth. de seruo, qui soluendo non erat, dicitur: Misertus eius Dominus, dimisit eum, & debitum ei remisit. Er go quoad Deum, omnibus ille gratificatur, & ad delenda nomina se facilem & misericordem praebet. Etenim vniuersales promissiones sunt: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas, idq; propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Item, Ego delebo transgressiones tuas vt densas nebulas, & vt nubem peccata tua: reuertere ad me, quia redemi te. Quod vero no omnes hac gratia fruuntur, eorum contumacia fit, qui promissioni eius non credunt, neq; oblatam sibi peccatorum remissionem quo decet animo excipiunt. Fides etenim sola medium illud est, quod nos Christo insert, & iustitiae atq; satisfactionis, quam in eo nobis Pater offert, participes facit. Fundatur itaque hic praecipuum illud doctrinae Apostolicae caput: Sola fide homines iustificari & saluos fieri. Rursus autem euertuntur omnes satisfactiones aut expiationes peccatorum, quibus homines superstitiosi confidunt. Vbi enim gratis remittuntur debita, aut alterius impensis dissoluuntur, ibi de nostra satisfactione gloriari nequaquam possumus. Et quicunq; hanc statuunt, ij & gratiam Dei nimis impudenter negant, & in filium eius Iesum Christum iniurij sunt, qui solus Patrem nobis propitium reddit. Mirum vero est hodie tam multos pro satisfactionibus suis contendere, quas tamen ipsi negant, quoties nobiscum precantur: Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c.
units.tr: "What, then, is the way (you ask) by which we are freed from the debt of sin?" This is the second main point of this discussion, which Christ explains in a single word, saying: "When they had nothing with which to pay, he graciously forgave both" [Luke 7:42]. He speaks here of God's free mercy, which he offers us through the Gospel in his Son, who has been made for us our righteousness and satisfaction. In the same way, in Matthew, the servant who could not pay is told: "The lord of that servant had compassion on him, let him go, and forgave him the debt" [Matt. 18:27]. So, as far as God is concerned, he shows himself gracious to all, and he presents himself as ready and merciful to blot out names. For the promises are universal: "I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" [Isa. 43:25]. Likewise: "I will blot out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a cloud; return to me, for I have redeemed you" [Isa. 44:22]. That not all enjoy this grace is due to the obstinacy of those who do not believe his promise and do not receive the forgiveness of sins offered to them with the attitude that befits it. For faith alone is the means that joins us to Christ and makes us partakers of the righteousness and satisfaction which the Father offers us in him. Thus the chief point of apostolic teaching is established: that men are justified and saved by faith alone. On the other hand, all the satisfactions or atonements for sins in which superstitious men put their trust are overthrown. For where debts are freely forgiven, or are paid at another's expense, there we can by no means boast of our own satisfaction. Those who maintain it deny the grace of God all too shamelessly, and they wrong his Son Jesus Christ, who alone makes the Father propitious to us. It is indeed strange that today so many contend for their satisfactions, which yet they themselves deny whenever they pray with us: "Forgive us our debts," etc.

units.la: Ergo (inquis) nihil nobis agendum restat, quando sola fides sufficit? Nihil vtiq; praeter fidem requiritur, si de remissionis peccatorum causis interroges. Nā per gratiā nos seruari iam ante euicimus. At hanc Apostolus operum meritis ita opponit, ut duo haec simul subsistere posse neget. Nam si per gratiam (inquit) iam non ex operibus: alioqui gratia non est gratia. Sin ex operibus, iam nō est gratia; alioqui opus iā non est opus. At ex eo minimè sequitur, bona opera non debere fieri, aut nullu eorum vsum esse. Etsi enim qui soluendo non sunt, gratuita remissione opus habent; idem tamē creditorem tam facilem & beneficum diligere & gratitudinem quo possunt officio testari debent. Eadem ratio apud Deum quoq; obseruari debet, de quo etsi nihil mereri possint qui natura peccatores & filij irae
units.tr: "Then (you say) nothing is left for us to do, since faith alone is enough?" Certainly nothing beyond faith is required, if you ask about the causes of the forgiveness of sins. For we have already shown that we are saved by grace. Yet the Apostle sets this grace over against the merits of works in such a way that he denies that the two can stand together. For he says: "If by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if of works, then it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work" [Rom. 11:6]. Yet it by no means follows that good works ought not to be done, or that they have no use. For even those who cannot pay have need of a free remission, yet they ought nonetheless to love such an easy and beneficent creditor, and to show their gratitude by whatever service they can. The same reasoning should be observed before God as well. Although those who are by nature sinners and children of wrath can merit nothing from him, they nevertheless ought to love him and render him every obedience.

units.la: 1 Cor. 1. sunt illum tamen amare, & eidem omne obsequium præstare debent. Ideò Christus Simonem interrogat: Vter horum ex debitoribus creditorem plus diliget? Et rectè respondet Pharisæus, eum existimans, cui plus fit ille gratificatus: Nimirū eum intelligens, qui gratiam sibi factam melius agnoscit. Id verò præ aliis faciunt, quorum peccata tam multa tamq; atrocia et manifesta sunt, ut ea dissimulare non possint. Minimè ergo bonis operibus inimica est doctrina hæc, neq; securos facit homines, sed potius bonorum operum fontes aperit, & nos ad illa sic obstrictos esse docet, ut ea intermittere non possimus, nisi nos mortalium ingratissimos & omni gratia indignos velimus præstare.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1. For this reason Christ asks Simon: "Which of these debtors will love the creditor more?" And the Pharisee answers rightly, thinking of the one to whom more was forgiven; obviously he understood that the one who better recognises the grace shown to him loves more. Those who do this more than others are those whose sins are so many, so grievous, and so manifest that they cannot hide them. Therefore this teaching is by no means hostile to good works, nor does it make men careless; rather, it opens the springs of good works, and teaches that we are so bound to them that we cannot give them up unless we wish to show ourselves the most ungrateful of mortals and unworthy of all grace.

units.la: Cæterum uno verbo comprehendit hic Christus, quid Deo debeant, qui ex fide iustificati sunt: Hoc nimirum, ut illum diligant. Est hic proprius & germanus fidei fructus, quam idcò Paulus per charitatem agere dicit. Nec enim fieri potest, quin Deum ex toto animo redamet, quisquis intelligit quanto amore ille nos complexus sit, ut unigenitum filium suum pro nobis in mortem dederit. Est autem gemina hæc dilectio: quia sic Deum amplectitur, ut simul in proximum redundet, quem is nobis tantopere commendavit. Et quia eius origo in corde aut animo est, quem omnium actionum fontem esse constat, illius effecta per omnem hominis vitam extenduntur, & ideo rectè à Paulo legis totius complementum esse dicitur. Nam qui Deum ex fide vera diligit, is unum hunc observat, colit & audit, neq; aliquid officij detrectat, quo illum delectari nouit. Hinc ergo audiendi Verbi studium accenditur, hinc precandi assiduitas emanat, hinc vitæ innocentia nascitur, hinc misericordia erga calamitosos excitatur, hinc patientia in aduersis, spei inuictum robur, fidei constantia & quicquid præterea Christianorum virtutum est, originem ducunt. Arguit hoc eorum vanitatem, qui cum omnibus istis careant, adhuc tamen fidei titulo superbiunt, & se per fidem iustificatos esse gloriantur. Quos rectè Iacobus compellans ait: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis. Et ijsdem olim Christus dicer: Non noui vos, discedite à me qui operamini iniquitatem, &c. Nos ergo fratres, gratiam nobis in Iesu Christo factâ sic agnoscamus, ut hunc viua fide amplexi in eundem transformemur, nosq; eius spiritu agi testemur dictis & factis nostris omnibus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, in one word Christ here sums up what those owe to God who have been justified by faith: namely, that they love him. This is the proper and genuine fruit of faith, which is why Paul says it works through love. For it cannot but be that whoever understands with how great a love he has embraced us, in giving his only-begotten Son to death for us, loves God again with his whole heart. This love is twofold: it embraces God in such a way that it at once overflows toward the neighbour whom he has so earnestly commended to us. And since its origin is in the heart or mind, which is known to be the fountain of all actions, its effects extend through the whole of human life; and therefore Paul rightly says that it is the fulfilling of the whole law. For whoever loves God from true faith keeps, honours and hears this one God, and shrinks from no duty by which he knows that God is pleased. From this comes eagerness to hear the Word; from this springs constancy in prayer; from this is born innocence of life; from this mercy toward the afflicted is stirred up; from this come patience in adversity, the unconquered strength of hope, constancy of faith, and whatever other virtues belong to Christians. This exposes the vanity of those who, lacking all these things, still take pride in the title of faith and glory that they are justified by faith. James rightly addresses them: "Show me your faith by your works" [James 2:18]. And to these same people Christ once said: "I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity," etc. Therefore, brothers, let us acknowledge the grace done for us in Jesus Christ in such a way that, embracing him with living faith, we are transformed into him, and bear witness in all our words and deeds that we are led by his Spirit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIII.
units.tr: Homily 73.

units.la: Et conuersus ad mulierem dixit Simoni: Vides hanc mulierem? Ingressus sum domum tuam, aquam pedibus meis non dedisti: hæc autem lachrymis rigauit pedes meos, & capillis capitis sui extersit. Osculum mihi non dedisti: hæc autem ex quo intraui, non intermisit deosculari pedes meos. Oleo caput meum non unxisti: hæc autem unguento unxit pedes meos. Cuius rei gratia dico tibi, remissa esse peccata eius multa: nam dilexit multum. Cui autem paululum remittitur, paululum diligit. Dixit autem ad illam: Remissa sunt tibi peccata. Et cœperunt qui simul accumbebant, dicere inter se: Quis est hic, qui etiam peccata remittit? Dixit autem mulieri: Fides tua te seruauit, vade in pace.
units.tr: And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: "Do you see this woman? I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet; but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss; but she, from the time I came in, has not stopped kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, for she has loved much; but the one to whom little is forgiven loves little." And he said to her, "Your sins are forgiven." Then those who were reclining at table with him began to say among themselves, "Who is this who even forgives sins?" And he said to the woman, "Your faith has saved you; go in peace."

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus Simoni Pharisæo, qui propriæ iustitiæ fiducia turgidus et infla tus mulierem peccatricem temere damnauerat, parabolam de duobus debitoribus proposuit, quæ vniuersam nostræ salutis rationem paucis & perspicuè complectitur. Docet enim, omnes homines natura peccatores & ita Deo obnoxios esse, ut huic satisfacere aut eius iudicium sustinere nullo modo possint: iustificari autem gratis per fidem, qua ipsum qui nobis satisfactio a Patre datus est, apprehendunt. Unde colligitur, non aliam esse nostram iustitiam, quam quòd peccata nobis non imputantur, sed Christi merito tegantur, vel etiam delentur, ut olim Prophetæ locuti sunt. Simul verò quæ sint iustificatorum officia, indicatur: nimirum, ut sibi factam à Deo gratiam agnoscant, & animi gratitudinem atq; fidem in Deum dilectionis synceræ officio testentur, quæ summatim omnia comprehendunt, quæ ad præceptorum Dei obseruationem atq; veram obedientiam faciunt. Quod probè tenendum est, ne vitæ & morum licentia ijs calumniandi occasionem demus, qui Euangelij doctrinam hoc nomine suspectam multis faciunt, quòd bonis operibus inimicam esse vociferantur. Sed videamus reliqua, quæ historiam istam absoluunt. Pergis
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ proposed the parable of the two debtors to Simon the Pharisee, who, puffed up and swollen with confidence in his own righteousness, had rashly condemned the sinful woman. In a few words and with great clarity, this parable embraces the whole account of our salvation. For it teaches that all men are by nature sinners and so bound to God that they can in no way satisfy him or bear his judgment; but that they are justified freely through faith, by which they lay hold of him whom the Father has given to us as our satisfaction. From this it follows that our righteousness is nothing other than that our sins are not imputed to us but are covered, or even blotted out, by the merit of Christ, as the Prophets long ago spoke. At the same time, it is shown what the duties of the justified are: namely, that they acknowledge the grace given to them by God, and bear witness to the gratitude of their soul and their faith in God by the duty of sincere love; these things, taken together, comprehend everything that pertains to the observance of God's commandments and to true obedience. This must be firmly held, lest we give occasion for licence in life and manners to those who make the teaching of the Gospel suspect on this very ground, crying out that it is hostile to good works. But let us look at the rest, which completes this story. Continues

units.la: Pergit enim Christus, & parabolam rebus & personis praesentibus, quibus cum agebat, applicat. Priusquam vero ad verborum interpretationem accedamus, exemplum eius observari debet, quod nimirum non contentus rem per parabolam propositam, quae auditoribus attentis, aut non omnino stupidis sufficere poterat, nunc eandem ipse exponit, ut auditorum institutioni magis serviat. Est hoc in docendo in primis necessarium. Ut enim homo animalis suopte ingenio non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei: ita caeco philautiae effectu plerique perstringi solent, ut quae dicuntur, vix putent ad se pertinere. Et hoc illud vitium est, quod in sementis parabola Christus perstringit, de illis loquens, qui semen illud Verbi Dei in viam, id est, in animos securos & patentes excipiunt, & mox per cogitationes carnis & quosdam alios idem sibi eripi patiuntur: eo quod in illo de rebus non multum ad se pertinentibus agi existiment. Quod genus hominum per Ezechielem quoque olim Deus accusavit, quando eos Verbum suum non aliter quam cantilenam aliquam audire ait, cuius effectus aut fructus unā cum sono evanescit. Ideo Christus tam hic quam alibi parabolis explicationes subjicit, & conciones suas omnes ita instituit, ut de se agi non obscure senserint ij, quibus loquebatur. Et hoc illud est, quod Apostolus in doctore requirit, ut Verbum Dei recte scindat: hoc nimirum volens, ut doctrinam prudenter applicando in singulorum animos penetret, & ut singuli id ex illa referre possint, quod ipsis necessarium est. Observarunt id adeo diligenter veteres Prophetae, & quam recte id fecerint, in Nathani & Davidis exemplo apparet. Cum enim hic turpi adulterio seipsum polluisset, & huic homicidium, vel potius parricidium accumulavisset, non sine atroci & manifesta nominis diui ni ignominia, parabolam quidem ei Nathan propositi, quae scelus illud ceu in tabula depictum exhibebatur: sed quia eundem libidinis affectu ita excaecatum cernebat, ut de se agi non sentiret, mox animū eius propius feriens ipsum esse ostendit, qui Dei iram adversus se provocarit, & qui ob imminentem sibi divinam vindictam matura & seria poenitentia opus habeat. Debent eandem in docendo rationem omnes ministri tenere: & salutis quidem rationem sic tradere debent, ut quicunque viam diversam ingrediuntur, se errare sentiant: scelera autem ita arguere & increpare, ut Epicurei quoque percellantur, & eorum securitas siue stupor praedicationis perspicuitate siue vehementia superetur. Consolationes item evangelicas ita adhibeant, ut per illas subleuentur, quicunque conscientia terrores sibi infestos esse, aut aliis molestiis sese premi sentiunt. Est ergo ridiculus & perniciosus illorum error, qui nudam Verbi Dei recitationem sufficere arbitrantur, & proinde indignum ferunt, si doctrina rebus praesentibus & personis accommodetur. Belli profecto & egregij Dei filij, qui Patrem ita loqui volunt, ut ipsis sermonem fieri nemo intelligat. Faciunt autem illi perinde, ac si quis morbo aliquo graviori laborans, medicum accersat, qui de morbo, eius causis & curatione in genere quidem apud ipsum disputet, adhaec pharmaca ipso videnre miscear & emplastra diligenter paret, nolit autem admittere, ut locis affectus illa apponat, aut ipsum ad pharmaca sumenda inuitet, aut cogat. Quid vero isti disputationes quantumuis doctae & elegantes proderunt? quid in abaco dispositā pharmaca & unguenta iuuabunt? Atqui nihilo meliorem fructum ex concionibus Verbi Dei generalibus percipiunt, qui suos errores corrigi & peccata sua argui nolunt. Idem ergo cum mundo contumaci & stupido concionatores faciant, quod cum phreneticis fidi & periti medici: ut nimirum inuitis & multum reluctantibus doctrinam eam ingerant, quam ipsis necessariam esse vident.
units.tr: He goes on, and applies the parable to the persons and things present with whom he was dealing. Before we come to the interpretation of the words, we ought to observe his example: namely, that not content with the matter set forth in the parable, which might have been enough for attentive hearers, or at least for those not entirely dull, he now explains it himself, so that it may serve better to instruct his hearers. This is especially necessary in teaching. For just as the natural man does not, by his own wit, perceive the things of the Spirit of God, so most people are wont to be blinded by a self-love, so that they hardly think what is said applies to themselves. This is the very fault which Christ rebukes in the parable of the sower, speaking of those who receive that seed of the Word of God on the path, that is, into hearts that are careless and open, and soon allow it to be snatched away by the cares of the flesh and by other such things, because they think that the matter being treated does not much concern them. God also long ago accused this kind of people through Ezekiel, when he said that they heard his Word only as some song, whose effect or fruit vanishes along with the sound. Therefore Christ, here as elsewhere, adds explanations to his parables, and arranges all his sermons in such a way that those to whom he spoke could not fail to sense that they were being addressed. This is also what the Apostle requires in a teacher: that he rightly divide the Word of God. Clearly he wishes that by applying the teaching wisely it should penetrate into the minds of each hearer, and that each should be able to take from it what is necessary for himself. The ancient Prophets observed this very diligently, and how rightly they did so appears from the example of Nathan and David. For when David had polluted himself with a shameful adultery, and had added to it a murder, or rather a parricide, to the grievous and manifest dishonour of the divine name, Nathan indeed set before him a parable, in which that crime was exhibited as if painted on a tablet; but because he saw that David was so blinded by the passion of lust that he did not feel that the matter concerned himself, he at once struck closer to his mind and showed him to be the man who had provoked the wrath of God against himself, and who, because of the divine vengeance hanging over him, had need of early and earnest repentance. All ministers ought to keep the same method in teaching: they ought to deliver the doctrine of salvation in such a way that whoever walks along a different path may feel that he is going astray; and they ought to rebuke and reprove sins in such a way that even the Epicureans are struck, and their security or stupor is overcome either by the clarity or by the vehemence of the preaching. Likewise, they should apply the consolations of the Gospel so that those who feel that terrors of conscience are assailing them, or that they are weighed down by other troubles, may be lifted up by them. Therefore the error of those is both ridiculous and harmful who think that the bare recitation of the Word of God is enough, and who consequently take it ill if the teaching is adapted to present circumstances and persons. Indeed, they are foolish and pernicious sons of God, who want the Father to speak in such a way that no one can understand what is said to them. They act just as if a man suffering from some serious sickness were to summon a physician, who discussed the disease, its causes, and its cure in general terms with him, and even diligently prepared medicines and plasters in his sight, but was unwilling to apply them to the places affected, or to invite and compel the patient to take the medicines. What will such disputations, however learned and elegant, profit them? What will medicines and ointments arranged on a shelf help? Yet those who do not wish their errors corrected and their sins reproved receive no better fruit from the general sermons of the Word of God. Therefore preachers, with a stubborn and dull world, do the same as faithful and skilled physicians do with the frenzied: namely, they force upon the unwilling and strongly resisting that teaching which they see to be necessary for them.

units.la: Caeterum quoad parabolae huius interpretationem, hoc agit Dominus, ut ostendat, Simone Pharisaeum maiori reprehensione dignum esse, quam mulierem hanc, quam ille omni consortio aut consuetudine indignam iudicabat. Eadem vero opera seipsum quoque excusat, qui ista dilectionis officia non temere sibi ab illa impendi passus sit. Argumentum, quo Christus utitur, est eiusmodi: Quisquis gratiam Dei magnitudinem, & quam is hominibus offert peccatorum remissionem recte agnoscit, is non potest non me diligere, qui unicus gratiae huius Mediator sum: ideoque amorem hunc officijs externis testatur, quae Deus sibi grata & accepta habet, cum ex fide & charitate non fucata emanent. Atqui mulier ista suum erga me amorem omni officiorum genere declarat, dum pedes meos lachrymis abluit & deosculatur, dum eosdem capillis suis extergit, & unguento pretioso dignos iudicat: Agnoscit ergo sibi facta gratiam, neque ego eius officia aspernari debeo, quorum causa siue origo tam pia & sancta est. Haec (inquit) eorum summa est, quae a Christo in praesenti dicuntur. Ut autem efficacius se riat Pharisaei animum, qui propriae iustitiae fiducia quasi occalluerat: ut gratiae praedicatione non multùm moneri posset. Minorē eleganti comparatione amplificat, qua mulieris istius officiosam munifi centiā cum illius parsimonia, vel sordi tie potius confert. Ego (inquit) ingressus sum domū tuam, aqua pedibus meis non dedisti, hæc autē lachrymis rigauit pedes meos, et capillis capitis sui extersit, &c. Proderit autem singulas huius comparationis partes diligentius excutere. Ego in tuā domum ingressus sum, quem tamen tu neglexisti: ista me in domo aliena quæsiuit, vt dignis officijs profequa retur. Tu ne vulgari quidem aqua meos pedes abluere, & panno siue linteo aliquo reiectitio ablutos tergere dignatus es: at ista lachrymis, quas peccatorū agnitio et pius verę pœnitentiæ dolor extor-sit, illos abluit, & capillis proprijs extersit. Tu osculum, commune amoris & amicitiæ symbolū, ori meo negauisti: ista vero ne à pedibus quidē meis abhorruit, quò minus eos osculis suis, ipsā creberri-mis & iterē repetitis, dignos iudicaret. Tu caput meū oleo vulgari inūgere detrectasti: hæc autē pe-dibus vnguentū pretiosum adhibuit. Vnde verò hæc tua parsimonia, & quæ nā isti tantæ liberali-tatis causa fuit? Hæc nimirum, quòd hæc multū diligit, quia eius peccata multa remissa sunt, &c. Idest, ex scelerum suorum multitudine gratiā sibi factam æstimans, nullū officium tantum esse exi-stimat, quod illi respondere possit: tu verò quia te iustum putas, neq; Dei gratiam agnoscis, neq; mihi aliquo iure te obstrictum esse arbitraris. Ita verò Simonis impudentem confidentiam arguit, qui si-bijpsi de sua pietate & dilectione Dei procul dubio plurimum pollicebatur, cum interim vulgaria quoq; & communia verę pietatis officia secure negligeret. Ex eo autem colligit, eius conditionem multò deteriorem esse, quam mulieris istius, eò quòd ipse nullo adhuc diuinæ misericordiæ sensu tan-gatur, & proinde in reddenda gratia tam frigidum & negligentem sese præbeat.
units.tr: As for the interpretation of this parable, the Lord's purpose is to show that Simon the Pharisee deserves a greater rebuke than this woman, whom he judged unworthy of all company or association. At the same time, he excuses himself, since he did not rashly allow these acts of love to be performed for him by her. The argument Christ uses is of this kind: whoever rightly acknowledges the greatness of God's grace and the forgiveness of sins that he offers to men cannot but love me, who am the only Mediator of this grace; and therefore he testifies this love by outward duties, which God holds pleasing and acceptable when they come from faith and unfeigned charity. But this woman declares her love for me by every kind of duty, while she washes and kisses my feet with tears, wipes them with her hair, and judges me worthy of precious ointment. Therefore she acknowledges the grace done to her, and I ought not to despise her duties, whose cause or origin is so pious and holy. This (he says) is the sum of what Christ says at present. But in order to move more effectively the mind of the Pharisee, which had as it were grown hard through confidence in his own righteousness, so that he could not be much moved by the preaching of grace, he amplifies the point by a more elegant comparison, in which he sets the dutiful generosity of this woman against the other's stinginess, or rather meanness. "I (he says) entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet; but she has wet my feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of her head," and so on. It will be useful to examine each part of this comparison more carefully. "I entered your house, which you nevertheless neglected; she, in another's house, sought me out so that she might pay me worthy duties. You did not deign to wash my feet even with common water, and to dry them with some cloth or rough linen; but she has washed them with tears, which the recognition of sins and the devout sorrow of true repentance have wrung from her, and has wiped them with her own hair. You refused me a kiss, the common token of love and friendship, on my mouth; but she has not shrunk even from my feet, so that she did not judge them worthy of her kisses, and those most frequent and repeated again and again. You refused to anoint my head with common oil; but she has applied precious ointment to my feet." But whence came this stinginess of yours, and what was the cause of such great generosity in her? Surely this: that she loves much, because her many sins have been forgiven. That is, reckoning the grace done to her from the multitude of her sins, she thinks no duty is great enough to answer to it; but you, because you think yourself righteous, neither acknowledge the grace of God nor believe yourself bound to me by any right. In this way he convicts the shameless confidence of Simon, who no doubt promised himself very much of his own piety and love of God, while meanwhile he carelessly neglected even the ordinary and common duties of true piety. From this he infers that Simon's condition is far worse than that of this woman, because he is not yet touched by any sense of divine mercy, and therefore shows himself so cold and careless in returning grace.

units.la: Interim non obscurè apparet in his verbis, cur hæc tam delicata et sumptuosa mulieris istius of-ficia Christus admiserit, quem in cæteris ab omni luxu & delitijs alienissimum fuisse constat. Nimi-rum, quòd & hypocritæ Simonis improbam confidentiam exemplo hoc arguere, & simul eodem ve-ræ pietatis officia nobis commendare voluit. Inter hæc primus locus pœnitentiæ debetur, quam con-uersionem à peccatis ad Deum esse, alibi diximus. Nisi enim hinc exordiamur, inutilis & frustrane-us erit omnis conatus, quem in pietatis negotio adhibemus. At quia pœnitentiā seriam Deus requi-rit, quæ non in theatrica ostentatione consistat, sed cum vera peccatorum agnitione & animi contri-tione coniuncta sit, illam pijs lachrymis testemur oportet. Etenim cum peccati sensus et qui ex eo e-nascitur dolor acerbissimus sit, fieri non potest, quin se totos in luctum conijciant, quicunq; peccata suaviter animo agnoscunt. Hinc Dauidis illæ querelæ manarunt: Transgressiones meas agnosco, & peccatum meum assiduè mihi obuersatur. In te, in te, (inquam) solum peccavi, & malū hoc in oculis tuis admisi. Contremefacta sunt omnia ossa mea, et anima mea turbata est vehementer. Defatig-atus sum in gemitu meo, fluctuare facio tota nocte lectum meum, lachrymis meis grabbatum meum li-quefacio. Nihil integrum est in carne mea propter indignationem tuam, non est pax ossibus meis propter peccatum meum, &c. Sed et Petrum Apostolum amare aut acerbè fleuisse legimus, cum gal-li cantu & efficaci Christi ipsum respicientis virtute excitatus sceleris sui atrocitatem sentiret. At quia dolor iste inutilis, imò noxius erit, nisi ad Deum conuertamur, secundo loco certam veniæ spem animo concipere debemus: quæ ex illius promissionibus facile hauriri poterit, si in illas toto ani-mo intenti de eius veritate simul & omnipotentia seriò cogitemus. Promissiones eiusmodi passim in scripturis obuias, & inter has in primis memorabiles sunt: Viuo ego (dicit Dominus) nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur & viuat. Item: Si peccata vestra fuerint vt coccus, niue albiora red-dentur: si rubeant instar purpuræ, vt nativa lana erunt. Et rursus: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui de-leo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Est etiam con-solationis dulcissimæ plenum, quod Mich. dicit: Quis Deus sicut tu? qui tollis iniquitatem, & super scelus transis reliquijs hæreditatis tuæ? Non retinet iram suam perpetuò, quoniam delectatur bon-itate. Reuertetur & nostri miserebitur, subiget iniquitates nostras, & deijciet in abyssum maris o-mnia peccata eorum. Quibus omnino addi debet Euangelicæ illæ Christi Iesu voces: Non veni ad vo-candu iustos, sed peccatores ad pœnitentiā. Oportet prædicari in nomine meo pœnitentiā et remissio-nē peccatorū, Item, Quisquis crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Cū hīs si eorū exempla con-feramus, qui ex atrocissimis sceleribus ad Dei conuersi remissionē gratuitam inuenerunt, mox nos quoq; mirificè confirmari sentiemus, vt procul abiecta desperatione ad thronum gratiæ recurramus. At hic
units.tr: Meanwhile, these words make it plain enough why Christ admitted this woman's so refined and costly services, since he is known to have been most averse to all luxury and self-indulgence. Namely, he wished both to expose the shameless confidence of the hypocrite Simon by this example and, at the same time, to commend to us the duties of true piety. Among these, the first place belongs to repentance, which we have said elsewhere is conversion from sins to God. For unless we begin here, every effort we make in the business of piety will be useless and vain. But since God requires a serious repentance, one that does not consist in theatrical display but is joined with a true acknowledgment of sin and contrition of heart, we ought to bear witness to it with pious tears. For since the sense of sin, and the most bitter grief that arises from it, cannot but drive those who truly acknowledge their sins to mourning, David's laments flowed from this: "I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only (I say), have I sinned, and done this evil in your sight. All my bones are shaken, and my soul is greatly troubled. I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed swim, I melt my couch with my tears. There is nothing sound in my flesh because of your indignation, there is no peace in my bones because of my sin," etc. We also read that the apostle Peter wept bitterly, when, roused by the crowing of the cock and by the effective power of Christ looking upon him, he felt the enormity of his crime. But since this grief is useless, indeed harmful, unless we turn to God, in the second place we must conceive in our minds a certain hope of pardon. This can easily be drawn from his promises, if we, intent on them with our whole mind, seriously consider both their truth and God's omnipotence. Promises of this kind lie everywhere in the Scriptures, and among them the following are especially memorable: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live." Likewise: "If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; if they are red like purple, they shall be like natural wool." And again: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins." What Micah says is also full of the sweetest consolation: "Who is a God like you, who takes away iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in goodness. He will turn again and have mercy on us; he will subdue our iniquities, and cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." To all of these must be added those evangelical words of Christ Jesus: "I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance"; "repentance and remission of sins must be preached in my name"; likewise, "whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." If with these we compare the examples of those who, from the most atrocious crimes, turned to God and found free remission, we shall at once feel ourselves wonderfully strengthened too, so that, casting off despair, we may run back to the throne of grace. units.la: Matth.9. Luc.24. Marc.16. At hîc etiam atque etiam videndum erit (quod tertium huius tractationis caput est) ne impudenti proteruia in Dei conspectum ruamus. Etsi enim hic nos blandissimis promissis inuitet, nos tamen nostri ipsius pudere debet, vt totis animis contriti cum filio prodigo clamemus: Pater, peccaui, in coelum & in te, neque sum dignus, vt dicar filius tuus. Quem affectum ista quoque peccatrix prodit, quando de Christi bonitate quidem optime sperat, à tergo tamen astans cum lachrymis ad pedes ipsius advoluitur. Postremò vnguentis quoque nostris Christum honorare & eius pedes inungere, & eosdem capillis nostris tergere debemus. Fiet hoc, si nos totos illi consecremus in viuam hostiam, vt propter nos glorificetur nomen eius: simul autem in pauperes eius liberaliter conferamus ea, quae nobis aut super flua sunt, aut prius voluptatum atque superbiae irritamenta fuerunt. Haec ferè sunt pietatis Christianae officia, quibus reuera delectatur Deus, & quibus cum praesentis tum futurae vitae promissiones datas esse Paulus affirmat 1. Tim.4.
units.tr: Matth. 9. Luc. 24. Marc. 16. Here too, again and again, we must see (which is the third head of this discussion) that we do not rush shamelessly and insolently into God's presence. For although he invites us here with the gentlest promises, we ought nonetheless to be ashamed of ourselves, so that, wholly contrite in heart, we may cry out with the prodigal son: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am not worthy to be called your son." This disposition the sinful woman also reveals, when, while she hopes most well of Christ's goodness, she stands behind him and, weeping, throws herself at his feet. Finally, we too ought to honour Christ with our ointments, to anoint his feet, and to wipe them with our hair. This will happen if we consecrate ourselves wholly to him as a living sacrifice, so that his name may be glorified through us; and at the same time we liberally bestow on his poor whatever is superfluous to us, or has been an incitement to pleasure and pride. These are nearly the duties of Christian piety, in which God truly delights, and by which Paul affirms that promises of both the present and the future life have been given (1 Tim. 4).

units.la: Admonet praeterea nos locus iste, quomodo de operibus tam nostris quàm aliorum iudicare debeamus. Fuerunt enim Pharisaeorum opera, quo ad externam speciem, splendidissima. Manus & corpus totum frequenter abluebant, & nefas illis videbatur à foro redeuntes accumbere, priusquam quis probè lotus esset. Simili cura & studio in vasis quoque purgandis versabantur. Ieiunabant item crebrò, eleemosynas multas faciebat publicè, decimas, & quae alia sunt huius generis bona fide, sed debant; adhaec vestitus, incessus & totius corporis gestus ad pietatem & animi devotionem declarandam erant compositi. Et si hunc Simonem spectes, prae aliis illius ordinis hominibus hoc quoque habuit, quòd Christum domi suae excipit; eundem mensa sua dignantur, & quàmuis non satis aequo in illum sit animo, nihil tamen aduersus eum hostile molitur. Verumtamen omnium istorum operibus praefertur id, quod mulier peccatrix fecit. Quòd si causam quaeras, non alia reddi potest, quàm quòd fide praedita fuit, qua Pharisaei omnes destituebantur. Fidei etenim luce excitata in peccatorum suorum cognitionem venit, Dei gratiam humiliter imploravit, seipsam & omnia sua Christi pedibus subiecit, & tota in hoc fuit, vt vitam omnem illi consecraret, quàm prius in turpissimis voluptatibus transegerat. Extant huius generis multa exempla apud Prophetas, qui diuertis verbis eos damnant, qui circa templum & sacra externa occupatissimi erant, è contra verò illos commendant, qui vnum Deum inuocant, iudicium & iustitiam faciunt, benefici sunt, & humiliter cum Deo suo ambulant. Quapropter de operibus hominum nequaquam iudicari debet secundùm externum splendorem. Nam vt Paulus ait, quicquid sine fide fit, peccatum est, neque cum operibus nostris in Dei conspectu comparere possumus, nisi illum nobis propitium reddat Christus Iesus, in quo solo illi complacitum est. At fidei ingenium est, in solius Dei verbum respicere, hoc omnium actionum regulam putare, & salutis fiduciam in vno Christo habere collocatam. Vnde sequitur bona opera non esse, neque Deo placere posse, quae non secundùm Dei verbum fiunt, & in quibus salutis meritum homines superstitiosi quaerunt. Habes ergo hic quod ijs respondeas, qui nos bonorum operum inimicos esse vociferantur, eò quòd nolimus circa ea occupari, quae ipsi ex humanarum traditionum praescripto faciunt. At prius illis probandum erat, ista in bonorum operum censum debere referri. Idque factu impossibile est, cùm hominum traditiones iampridem Deus proprio ore damnarit, & se illis nequaquam coli testetur. Imò ne tergiuersari videamur, liberè & rotundo ore dicimus, patres familias, & horum vxores, agricolas item, operarios mechanicos, magistratus item & quicunque horum similes suam vocationem fideliter obeunt, labores & curas huic coniunctas patienter ferunt, neminem defraudant, & vitam viuunt innocuam, plus bonorum operum habere, quàm omnes vel farificulos vel monachos aut eremitas, quos nescio quae vitae morum asperitas commendat. Quid enim illi simul omnes faciunt, quod diuinis legibus commendetur, aut aliorum hominum commodis siue necessitati seruiat? Enimuerò ex fidei fontibus illorum opera manare nemo dixerit, cùm Dei verbo destituantur, in quod vnum fides incumbit. Est ergo illorum hominum eò turpior confidentia, quòd ab ijs longè superantur apud Dei tribunal, quos ipsi vix conspectu suo aut familiari coloquio dignos iudicant.
units.tr: This passage also teaches us how we ought to judge the works both of ourselves and of others. For the works of the Pharisees were most splendid in outward appearance. They frequently washed their hands and their whole body, and it seemed wrong to them to recline at table on returning from the marketplace before someone had been properly washed. They were similarly careful and zealous in cleansing vessels. They also fasted often, gave generous alms in public, paid tithes, and did other things of this kind in good faith, though they were owed. Besides, their clothing, gait and the whole bearing of their bodies were arranged to display piety and devotion of mind. And if you look at this Simon, he had this too beyond other men of that order: he received Christ into his house, deigned to have him at his table, and although he was not very well disposed towards him, he plotted nothing hostile against him. Nevertheless, what the sinful woman did is preferred to all these works. If you ask the reason, none can be given other than that she was endowed with faith, which all the Pharisees lacked. For, roused by the light of faith, she came to knowledge of her sins, humbly implored God's grace, submitted herself and all she had at Christ's feet, and was wholly intent on consecrating to him the whole life she had previously spent in the most shameful pleasures. Many examples of this kind are found among the Prophets, who condemn in various words those who were most occupied with the temple and external sacred rites, and on the other hand commend those who call upon the one God, do judgment and justice, are beneficent, and walk humbly with their God. Therefore the works of men must in no way be judged by their external splendour. For, as Paul says, whatever is done without faith is sin, nor can we appear with our works in God's sight unless Christ Jesus makes him favourable to us, in whom alone he is well pleased. But it is the nature of faith to look to the word of God alone, to hold this as the rule of all actions, and to place the confidence of salvation in Christ alone. Hence it follows that those works are not good, nor can they please God, which are not done according to the word of God, and in which superstitious men seek the merit of salvation. Here, then, you have what to answer to those who loudly cry that we are enemies of good works because we do not busy ourselves with those things which they perform by the prescription of human traditions. But first they would have to prove that such things ought to be reckoned among good works. And that is impossible, since God long ago condemned human traditions with his own mouth and testifies that he is in no way worshipped by them. Indeed, so that we may not seem to evade the question, we say frankly and plainly that heads of families and their wives, likewise farmers, craftsmen, magistrates, and whoever like these faithfully discharge their calling, patiently bear the labours and cares joined to it, defraud no one, and live an innocent life, have more good works than all the priests, monks, or hermits whom I know not what harshness of life commends. For what do all those men together do that is commended by divine laws, or serves the advantage or necessity of other men? Indeed, no one could say that their works flow from the springs of faith, since they lack the word of God, on which faith alone relies. Therefore the confidence of those men is all the more shameful, in that they are far surpassed before God's judgment-seat by those whom they themselves scarcely judge worthy of their sight or of familiar conversation.

units.la: Porrò ad Christum redeamus, qui ad mulierem conuersus ait illi: Remissa sunt tibi peccata. Poterat hoc superuacaneum videri, cùm hoc ipsum iam ante non semel in debitorum parabola & eius expositione dixisset. Sed fidem mulieris amplius confirmari oportuit, quam non leuiter tentatam fuisse verisimile esset, cum eos sibi aduersarios & infestos esse videret, qui præ alijs iustitiæ & sanctitatis opinione eminebant. Neq; debet aliqua doctrina siue consolatio superuacua videri, quan do singulis horis plurima occurrunt, quæ nos à via salutis transuersos abripiunt, aut fidem nostram aliqua ex parte labefactant. Nos potius Dei bonitatem obseruare & exosculari debemus, qui in tempore nobis adesse, nosq; fidus admonitionibus et consolationibus in officio retinere consueuit. Sed accidit in præsenti alia etiam causa. Nam nouas cogitationes siue calumnias occultas Pharisæo rum in lucem protrahere voluit, ut ea occasione fontes remissionis peccatorum apertius indicaret. Etenim his auditis offenduntur conuiuæ, et inter se dicunt: Quis est hic, qui etiam peccata remittit? Offensionis aut scandali causa est, quod Messiæ officium non intelligunt, quem diuinæ gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum Mediatorem nobis fore, olim Prophetæ prædixerant, ut supra in paralytici historia demonstrauimus. Et hic ille lapis est, ad quem etiam hodie iustitiarij hypocritæ impin gunt: quibus hoc proprium est, quod & miseris peccatoribus remissionem gratuitam inuident, & eandem in Christo monstrari indignissime ferunt, eo quod utrumque gloriæ ipsorum officit, & opera rum iustitiam euertit, quæ illi quam maxime superbiunt. Auget vero errorem hunc, quod seipsos & peccata sua non agnoscunt. Nam si inhærentem sibi propriæ naturæ vitiositatem & quæ ex hac quotidie promanant peccata propius intuerentur, sibipsis eodem remedio opus esse viderent, quod in alijs indignius ferunt.
units.tr: Let us return, then, to Christ, who turned to the woman and said to her: "Your sins are forgiven." This might seem superfluous, since he had already said the same thing more than once before, in the parable of the debtors and its explanation. But the woman's faith needed to be strengthened further, since it was likely to have been sorely tested, seeing that those who were especially esteemed for their reputation for righteousness and holiness were hostile and opposed to her. Nor should any teaching or consolation seem superfluous, since every hour brings many things that turn us aside from the way of salvation or weaken our faith in some measure. We should rather observe and embrace the goodness of God, who is wont to be present with us in time of need and to keep us in our duty by faithful admonitions and consolations. But in the present case there was also another reason. For Christ wished to bring into the light the new thoughts, or hidden slanders, of the Pharisees, so that on that occasion he might point out more plainly the sources of the forgiveness of sins. For when the guests heard this, they were offended and said to one another: "Who is this, who even forgives sins?" The cause of their offence and scandal was that they did not understand the office of the Messiah, whom the prophets had long before foretold would be the Mediator for us of divine grace and the forgiveness of sins, as we showed above in the history of the paralytic. And this is the stone against which the self-righteous hypocrites still stumble today. It is characteristic of them that they grudge gratuitous forgiveness to wretched sinners, and bear it most unworthily when the same is shown in Christ, because both things detract from their own glory and overturn the righteousness of works in which they take such great pride. Moreover, this error is increased by the fact that they do not recognise themselves or their own sins. For if they looked more closely at the inborn corruption of their own nature and the sins that daily spring from it, they would see that they need the same remedy for themselves, which they resent so indignantly in others.

units.la: At qualescunque isti sint, in eo laudem merentur, quod sola Messiæ ignorantia, quæ tunc omnibus communis erat, peccant; interim vero hoc fidei & religionis veræ principiū constanter retinent, quo docemur, peccatorum remissionem in solius Dei potestate esse, & apud hunc solum quæri debere. At hodie impurissimi homines sacrilega audacia in ipsius Dei ditionem (ut sic loquar) manum inferunt, & quod huius solius est sibi & coniuratis suis vendicant: neque eo contenti, insuper miseros & rerum imperitos cogunt, ut peccata singula ipsis in aurem confiteantur, & eorundem remissionem ab ipsis prece & pretio redimant. Sunt hi Iudæorum pharisæis deteriores, & mirum est Christianum orbem illorum tyrannidem tam diu ferre potuisse, cuius prætextu innumeros principes prodito rie circumuentos esse omniū prope gentium historiæ testantur, ut iam de tentata sæpius matro narum pudicitia, & interceptis hæreditatibus alienis nihil dicamus. Abutuntur illi ad suæ audaciæ defensionem Christi verbis, quibus is claues regni cælorum discipulis credidit. At sub clauibus istis non aliud, quàm Euangelij prædicationem & legitimum ecclesiæ ministerium intelligi debere res ipsa clamitat: per quod verè credentibus peccatorum remissio, incredulis autem & pœnitere ne scijs æternæ damnationis sententia denunciatur: quod utrumq; in cælis ratum est, non quia sic vnctii & rasi pronunciant, sed quia sic Dei filius ex æterno patris decreto constituit, dicens: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Quisquis crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, ser uabitur. Qui vero non crediderit, damnabitur. Sed plura de his alibi.
units.tr: However these men may be, they deserve praise in this, that they sin only through ignorance of the Messiah, which was then common to all; yet meanwhile they steadfastly hold to this principle of the true faith and religion, by which we are taught that the forgiveness of sins lies in the power of God alone and ought to be sought from him alone. But today the most impure men, with sacrilegious audacity, lay hands upon the very dominion of God (if I may so speak), and claim for themselves and their accomplices what belongs to him alone; and not content with this, they also compel poor and inexperienced people to confess their individual sins into their ears, and to buy back the remission of them from them by prayers and payment. These men are worse than the Pharisees of the Jews, and it is a wonder that the Christian world has been able to endure their tyranny so long, under whose pretext, as the histories of almost all nations bear witness, countless princes have been betrayed and beset, not to mention for now the chastity of matrons often attempted and the inheritances of others seized. They abuse the words of Christ, by which he entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to his disciples, to defend their audacity. But the thing itself cries out that under these keys nothing else is to be understood than the preaching of the Gospel and the lawful ministry of the Church: through which forgiveness of sins is truly announced to believers, but to unbelievers and the impenitent the sentence of eternal damnation. And that both of these are ratified in heaven is not because they are pronounced thus by men anointed and shaven, but because the Son of God has so established from the eternal decree of the Father, saying: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptised shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned." But more on these matters elsewhere.

units.la: Pergamus nunc in Christi actione, qui nihil moratus hypocritarum & hominum superstitiosissimorum iudicia, mulierem nova consolatione confirmat, et idem fontes salutis euidentius demon strat. Fides tua (inquit) te seruauit, vade in pace. Quasi dicat: Non est, quod criticorum iustorum sententiam formides, aut propter illos de salute tua quicquam dubites. Quia enim Dei promissionibus credidisti, & peccatorum tuorum remissionem apud me, qui huius Mediator à Patre constitutus sum, quæ suisti, hæc tua fides tibi salutem attulit certam & indubitatam, quæ iustorum iniquis & te merarijs iudicijs neque euerti neque eripi poterit. Tu igitur in hac tua fide acquiescito, & læta atq; salutis securâ abiresq, tuas agito. Est hæc totius actionis conclusio, quæ diligenti consideratione & assidua meditatione dignissima est. Primum enim eos confutat, qui ex ijs, quæ præcesserunt, ansam arripiunt, ut suæ iustitiæ meritum statuant. Ex his enim verbis satis apparet, peccatorum remissionem mulieri isti ex sola fide obtigisse, cuius effecta siue fructus fuere, quæ prius commemorauimus, pietatis & dilectionis officia. Neque hæc Christo placuissent, nisi ex fide facta fuissent. Firmiter ergo & constanter teneamus axioma illud doctrinæ apostolicæ, Sola fide in Christum nos iustificari et seruari. Hæc enim sola Christum apprehendit, qui nobis à Deo Patre iustitia, satisfactio, sanctificatio & redemptio facta est. Non possumus ergo iustitiæ & salutis fiduciam in quacunq; alia re collocare, quin Dei filium suo honore spoliemus, & hunc aut in creaturas aut nostra opera transferamus. ramus. At quia fides Dei donum est, & ad Christum nemo venit, nisi eum Pater traxerit, salu- sem quoq; gratuitæ Dei misericordiæ beneficium esse constat.
units.tr: Let us now proceed to the action of Christ, who, not delaying over the judgements of hypocrites and the most superstitious men, confirms the woman with new consolation, and shows more clearly the same sources of salvation. "Your faith," he says, "has saved you; go in peace." As if he were saying: "There is no reason for you to fear the verdict of the self-styled righteous, or to doubt your salvation on their account. For since you have believed the promises of God, and the forgiveness of your sins which you have sought is with me, who have been appointed by the Father as the Mediator of this, your faith has brought you a salvation that is certain and undoubted, which cannot be overturned or taken away by the unrighteous judgements of the just, or by your own rash judgements. Therefore rest in this your faith, and go away glad and secure in your salvation." This is the conclusion of the whole action, and it is most worthy of careful consideration and constant meditation. For first it refutes those who from what has gone before seize upon an occasion to set up the merit of their own righteousness. For from these words it sufficiently appears that forgiveness of sins came to this woman from faith alone, and its effects or fruits were those duties of piety and love which we mentioned before. Nor would these have pleased Christ unless they had been done from faith. Let us therefore hold firmly and constantly to that axiom of apostolic doctrine: we are justified and saved by faith alone in Christ. For this alone apprehends Christ, who has been made to us by God the Father righteousness, satisfaction, sanctification and redemption. We cannot therefore place our confidence of righteousness and salvation in any other thing without robbing the Son of God of his honour and transferring it to creatures or to our own works. But since faith is the gift of God, and no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him, it is evident that salvation too is a benefit of the free mercy of God.

units.la: Secundo fructum veræ fidei hoc dicto nobis Christus indicat. Est is pax & tranquillitas conscientiæ, quæ ex eo nascitur, quòd Deum nobis propitium iam esse scimus, qui prius propter peccata nobis infensus erat. Quò Paulus respiciens dicebat: Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem etiam fide habuimus aditum in gratiam hanc, per quam stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Superat pax ista (vt idem Apostolus monet) omnem intellectum mundi, eò quòd in medijs afflictionibus inconcussa manet, & tunc maximè suam virtutem exerit, quando nulla in humanis spes nobis est reliqua. Est ergo in comparabilis verè credentium thesaurus, quem rectè æstimabimus, si eos nobis ob oculos ponamus, qui desperationis æstro exagitati horribiles conscientiæ terrores adeoq; inferorum diros cruciatus sentiunt. Procul ergo vt publici salutis humanæ hostes arceri debent, qui pacem iflam ex imperitorum animis auferunt, quando hominem salutis suæ certum fieri posse negant, & proinde de salute & gratia perpetuò dubitandum esse docent. Adhæc falsi arguuntur hoc loco absolutiones Pontificiæ, quas sacrificuli & Monachi super illorum capita demurmurant, qui ad ipsorum genua prouoluti peccata sua illis confitentur. Hæ enim non pacem aut tranquillitatem animorum gignunt, sed quia his ad sa-tisfactiones miseri remittuntur, novos labores, curas & molestias, adhæc perpetuam conscientiæ fluctuantis carnificinam exhibent. Et qui his nituntur, in illis perpetuò impleri solet quod Christus Samaritidi dicebat. Quisquis biberit ex aqua ista, quem ipse haurit suis viribus & industria, sitiet iterum, &c. Nos ergo ad verum & unicum gratiæ fontem contendamus, quem in filio suo nobis Deus aperuit: neque hypocritarum iudicijs moueamur, quos cæca superstitio in rabiem agit, vt nos eo nomine damnent, quòd vno Christo contenti sumus. Vt enim ridiculus & irritus eorum labor est, qui solem puluere iniecto extinguere aut obscurare conantur: ita nihil proficient Sophistæ, dum lucem illam vitæ æternæ ex credentium animis eripere volunt, aut diuinæ gratiæ effectum impedire. Nobis ergo singulis priuatim dici putemus, quod mulieri huic dicitur, ideoq; firmi & intrepidi stemus, & precemur Deum patrem, vt nos in credendo omni gaudio & pace impleat, vt spe inuita abundemus per virtutem Spiritus sancti, & olim cum Christo Iesu in cælis viuamus atque regnemus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Second, Christ indicates to us by this saying the fruit of true faith. It is peace and tranquillity of conscience, which arises from our knowing that God is now propitious to us, who before was hostile to us on account of our sins. Paul, looking to this, said: "Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained by faith access into this grace in which we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." That peace surpasses (as the same Apostle warns) all understanding of the world, because it remains unshaken in the midst of afflictions, and then especially exerts its power when no human hope is left to us. There is therefore an incomparable treasure of those who truly believe, which we shall rightly value if we set before our eyes those who, goaded by the sting of despair, feel the dreadful terrors of conscience and the dire torments of hell. Far away, therefore, must be kept those enemies of the public salvation of mankind, who take that peace from the minds of the unlearned, when they deny that a man can be made certain of his salvation, and accordingly teach that concerning salvation and grace one must doubt continually. Moreover, the Papal absolutions are here convicted as false, which the priests and monks mutter over the heads of those who, prostrate at their knees, confess their sins to them. For these do not produce peace or tranquillity of souls; rather, since wretched men are sent away by them to satisfactions, they bring new labours, cares and troubles, and besides a perpetual torment of a conscience tossed about. And those who rely on them are commonly fulfilled in that which Christ said to the Samaritan woman: "Whoever drinks of this water, which he draws with his own strength and industry, will thirst again," and so on. Let us therefore hasten to the true and only fountain of grace, which God has opened to us in his Son; and let us not be moved by the judgements of hypocrites, whom blind superstition drives to madness, so that they condemn us on this account, that we are content with Christ alone. For as ridiculous and vain is the labour of those who try to extinguish or obscure the sun by throwing dust upon it, so the Sophists accomplish nothing while they want to snatch that light of eternal life from the minds of believers, or to hinder the effect of divine grace. Let us then each think privately that what is said to this woman is said to us, and therefore let us stand firm and fearless, and pray God the Father that he may fill us in believing with all joy and peace, so that we may abound in unshaken hope through the power of the Holy Spirit, and at length live and reign with Christ Jesus in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.
