units.la: ET factum est deinceps, ipse iter faciebat per singulas urbes & vicos, prædicans & euangelizans regnum Dei: & duodecim illi erant cum eo, simulq; quædam mulieres, quas sanauerat à spiritibus malis & morbis: Maria, quæ vocabatur Magdalene, ex qua septem dæmonia exierant: & Ioanna vxor Chuzæ procuratoris Herodis, & Susanna, & aliæ multæ, quæ ministrabant ei ex facultatibus suis.
units.tr: And it came to pass afterward, that he went throughout every city and village, preaching and showing the glad tidings of the kingdom of God, and the twelve were with him, and certain women which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, and Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.

units.la: VONIAM vniuersa humanæ salutis ratio in vno Dei filio, Iesu Christo, continetur, nihil nobis tam vtile & necessarium est, quàm vt vera eius cognitione illuminati ipsum fide firma & constanti complectamur. Et hæc causa est, quod et ipse passim sese omnibus tam publicè quam priuatim menifestauit, & quæcunq; ad eius cognitionem faciunt ab Euangelistis tanta diligentia describuntur. Pertinet huc locus iste, quem modo recitauimus, cum ijs, quæ proximè sequuntur. Narrat enim Lucas primò quàm sedulus in docendo fuerit, vt quam plurimos ad salutis & vitæ æternæ hereditatem pertraheret. Deinde quod doctrinæ aut prædicationis argumentum fuerit: Tertiò quos habuerit comites, & quales esse conueniat, qui salutis per illum partæ heredes fieri cupiunt. Sed proderit singula, quæ dicuntur, inspicere.
units.tr: Since the whole plan of human salvation is contained in the one Son of God, Jesus Christ, nothing is more useful or necessary for us than that, enlightened by true knowledge of him, we embrace him with a firm and steadfast faith. This is why he revealed himself everywhere, both publicly and privately, and why the Evangelists describe with such care everything that serves the knowledge of him. This passage we have just recited belongs with what immediately follows it. For Luke first relates how diligent Christ was in teaching, so that he might draw as many as possible to the inheritance of salvation and eternal life. Second, he sets out the subject of his teaching and preaching. Third, he names his companions, and says what sort of people ought to be those who desire to become heirs of the salvation won through him. But it will be useful to look at each of the things said.

units.la: Principio illius in docendo industriam paucis verbis, sed admodum perspicuis comprehendit, sic dicens: Et factum est deinceps, ipse iter faciebat per singulas urbes & vicos, praedicans & Euangelizans regnum Dei. Quo loco nobis in genere observanda venit paterna Dei bonitas, qui nos salutem non modo quaerere iubet, sed eandem non quaerentibus ipse offert, & cunctantes atque securos ad illam amplectendam hortatur. Exemplum huius studij in primaeva rerum origine praebuit, quando Adamum scelerum admissi conscientia trepidum atque fugitivum quaesivit, & paternis planè vocibus ex fruga retractu salutis per semen mulieris instaurandae promissione consolatus est. Eiusdem bonitatis fuit postea, quod Abrahamum ex terra idololatrica eque medio idololatrarum contubernio evocavit, ut cum eo foedus salutis instauraret, quod in diluvio totum inter cidisset & abolitum esse videbatur: quod item eius posteros Aegyptiorum superstitionibus excaecatos, & nihil minus quam puriorem Dei cultum quaerentes per Mosen miraculose eduxit, & legem dedit, quae per foedum voluntatis ipsius compendium una cum veri cultus ratione & promissi redemptoris typum pulcherrimis continet. Quod si ulterius progredi libeat, dies nos prius deficeret, quae omnia gratiae & bonitatis illius exempla exponeremus, quae docent, quoties illos in proprium exitium ruentes retraxerit, quoties tenebrarum caligine immersi lucem veritatis accenderit, quoties iterum poenas diutissime diiudicaverit, ut non indignis modo, verum etiam improbe reluctantibus poenitentiae agendae tempus atque occasionem praeberet. Queritur de hoc ille non uno loco per prophetas, quod nequicquam manus porrexerit, & tota die manus expanderit apud populum rebellem & contumacem: at non ita quaeritur, ut ipsius bonitatem horum contumacia vincere potuerit, quo minus eorum salutem provehere atque iuvare studeret. Imo quasi nihil adhuc fecisset, tandem Filium unigenitum misit, qui nostram carnem indutus, omne id fecit, quod durissimis quibusque emolliendis sufficere poterat, nisi illorum impietas quasi callo obducto incurabilis facta fuisset. Et ut priora repetamus, quoties obsecro ingratos, pertinaces & hostili in se animo praditos expertus est eos, pro quorum salute ipse excubabat? Addo, quod ubique in Synagogis Scribae & Pharisaei occurrebant, qui iam centies conati erant suis insidijs & artibus plus quam proditoris circumuentum perdere. Pergit tamen ille, & adhuc per singulas urbes & vicos Euangelium praedicat, ne quos defraudet, de quibus spes aliqua adhuc reliqua erat. Experti sunt hanc Dei bonitatem, & filij eius in seruando humano genere indefessam industriam alij quoque omnes. Nam ut Isaias ait, omnes tanquam oves erravimus, & cum nemo esset (ut apud Ezechielem clamat Dominus) qui perditos quaereret, verus ille David prodijt, qui per montes & valles diffusos collegit, & multos quasi humeris impositos ad gregem portavit, ne diabolo, Leoni illi rugienti, praeda fierent. Et quod olim fecit Dei filius, cum in carne manifestatus vitam in terris ageret, hoc ipsum hodie quoque facit, quando Euangelij doctrinam in toto terrarum orbe quasi circumfert, & ad vitae aeternae hereditatem omnes homines invitat. Horum consideratio ut nos officij erga Deum admonet, ita perversum nostrae carnis ingenium arguit. Nostrarum enim partium erat tantam Dei gratiam digne aestimare, & oblatam nobis salutem gratis animis amplexi. At constat nihil hodie tam contemptum, tam inusitatum & exosum esse, quam verbi divini ministerium, per quod suam gratiam & salutem nobis offert Dominus. Olim quidem, cum superstitionum tenebrae omnium animos excaecavissent, & Romani Pontifices immani crudelitate & ambitione insaturabili in omnium corpora atque animas sibi imperium vendicarent, nulla familia tam diues & illustris, nulla tam obscura & egena erat, quae non aliquos ex suis ecclesiae ministerio consecrarent, & plerique fraudatis haeredibus legitimis opes suas sacrificulorum & monachorum collegijs legabant, ne de religione minus honorifice sentire, aut animarum salutem negligere viderentur. At hodie maior hominum pars hanc summam ignominiam esse ducit, si quae familiae verbi ministros ex se progenitos habeant. Cuius mali causa est, quod pro hominibus turbulentis, seditiosis & publicorum malorum authoribus vulgo habentur, quotquot in Christi praedicatione operam fidelem nauant. Passim ergo Achabicae illae voces audiuntur: Tu ne ille es, qui turbas Israel? Et ut olim Amasiae sacerdoti concionem Amos prophetae tales videbantur, quas ne ipsa quidem terra posset sustinere: ita hodie nihil molestius, nihil intolerabilius, nihil publicae paci tam inimicum putatur, quam libera & ingenua verbi Dei praedicatio, per quam homines ex errorum tenebris & a mortis praecipitio in lucem & vitae aeternae viam revocantur. Neque filij Dei exemplum multos monet, quo minus ex eo sibi
units.tr: At the start, Luke sums up in a few words, but very clearly, Christ's diligence in teaching, saying: "And it came to pass afterward, that he went throughout every city and village, preaching and evangelizing the kingdom of God." Here we must observe, in general, the fatherly goodness of God, who not only bids us seek salvation but himself offers it to those who do not seek it, and urges the hesitant and the secure to embrace it. He gave an example of this concern at the very origin of things, when he sought out Adam, trembling and fleeing in the consciousness of his sin, and consoled him with the plainly paternal promise, out of the ruin of the fall, of restoring salvation through the seed of the woman. Of the same goodness it was that he afterwards called Abraham out of an idolatrous land and from the midst of the company of idolaters, so as to renew with him the covenant of salvation, which seemed to have been wholly destroyed and abolished in the flood. Likewise, he miraculously led out through Moses the descendants of Abraham, blinded by the superstitions of the Egyptians and seeking nothing less than a purer worship of God, and he gave them the law, which contains in most beautiful fashion, in the covenant of his will, a summary together with the true manner of worship and the type of the promised Redeemer. If we were to go further, the day would fail us before we could set out all the examples of that grace and goodness, which teach how often he drew back those rushing headlong to their own destruction, how often he kindled the light of truth in those immersed in the darkness of shadows, and how often, though he had long since judged them worthy of punishment, he nevertheless gave time and opportunity for repentance, not only to the unworthy but also to those who stubbornly resisted. He complains of this through the prophets in more than one place, that he had stretched out his hands in vain, and had spread them out all day to a rebellious and obstinate people. Yet he does not so complain as to let their obstinacy overcome his goodness, so that he ceased to strive and help toward their salvation. Indeed, as though he had done nothing yet, at last he sent his only-begotten Son, who, clothed in our flesh, did all that could soften even the hardest hearts, had not their impiety, like a callus grown over, made them incurable. And, to return to what went before: how often, I beg you, has he found those who were ungrateful, stubborn, and endowed with a hostile mind toward him, for whose salvation he himself kept watch? I add that everywhere in the synagogues the scribes and Pharisees were present, who had already a hundred times tried with their snares and arts to destroy him, more treacherously than a betrayer would. Yet he goes on, and still preaches the Gospel through every city and village, so as not to defraud those for whom some hope still remained. All others also have experienced this goodness of God and the tireless diligence of his Son in preserving the human race. For, as Isaiah says, "we have all gone astray like sheep," and since there was no one (as the Lord cries out in Ezekiel) who sought the lost, that true David came forth, who gathered those scattered over mountains and valleys, and carried many on his shoulders to the flock, so that they would not become prey to the devil, that roaring lion. What the Son of God did once, when he was made manifest in the flesh and lived on earth, he does today also, when he carries the doctrine of the Gospel, as it were, through the whole circuit of the earth, and invites all men to the inheritance of eternal life. The consideration of these things reminds us of our duty toward God, and at the same time exposes the perverse disposition of our flesh. For it was our part to value worthily so great a grace of God, and to embrace with grateful minds the salvation offered to us freely. But it is certain that today nothing is so despised, so unfamiliar, and so hateful as the ministry of the divine Word, through which the Lord offers us his grace and salvation. Once, indeed, when the darkness of superstition had blinded all minds, and the Roman Pontiffs, with monstrous cruelty and insatiable ambition, claimed dominion over the bodies and souls of all, no family was so rich and illustrious, none so obscure and needy, that did not dedicate some of its members to the ministry of the Church, and many, cheating their lawful heirs, bequeathed their wealth to colleges of priests and monks, lest they seem to think meanly of religion or to neglect the salvation of souls. But today the greater part of men counts it the greatest disgrace if their families have produced ministers of the Word. The cause of this evil is that everyone who labours faithfully in the preaching of Christ is commonly regarded as a troublemaker, a seditious man, and an author of public evils. So everywhere those Ahab-like words are heard: "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" And just as once the prophet Amos seemed to Amaziah the priest to speak words that the very land could not bear, so today nothing is thought more troublesome, more intolerable, or more hostile to public peace than the free and sincere preaching of the Word of God, through which men are called back from the darkness of error and from the precipice of death into the light and the way of eternal life. Nor does the example of the Son of God move many to refrain from seeking for themselves, in his case, the chief praise, namely that they dare, together with the ministers of the Word, to despise and trample underfoot the Gospel itself with scurrilous insolence.

units.la: Isa 53. Ezec 34. [illegible, ~6 letters]hi laudem præcipuam quærant, quòd cum verbi administris ipsum Euangelium scurrili proteruia contemnere & conculcare audeant. Porrò non aliam isti homines laudem inde referunt, quàm quòd palàm testantur, se nequaquam ex filiorum Dei numero esse, & proinde indignos se esse, qui ad cœlestis patriæ hereditatem admittantur. Notum est enim illud Christi: Qui ex Deo natus est, is verba mea audit. Item, Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur eam. Quem verò suæ impietatis finem isti homines sperare debeant, Iudæorum exemplo docemur: quos vna cum vrbe & templo horribiliter perijsse, & hodie adhuc in exemplum diuinæ vltionis in toto orbe incertis sedibus & omnibus inuisos vagari constat, quòd diem visitationis suæ agnoscere noluerunt. Vide Christi comminationes Luc.19. Matth.23.24. & c.
units.tr: Isa 53. Ezec 34. [illegible]hi laudem præcipuam quærant... Moreover, these men gain no other praise from this than that they openly bear witness that they are by no means among the number of the children of God, and that therefore they are unworthy to be admitted to the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland. For that saying of Christ is well known: "He who is born of God hears my words." Likewise: "My sheep hear my voice, and follow it." And what end such men ought to expect for their impiety we are taught by the example of the Jews, who, together with the city and the temple, have terribly perished, and who even today, as is well known, wander as an example of divine vengeance over the whole world, without fixed abode and hated by all, because they would not recognise the day of their visitation. See Christ's threats, Luke 19, Matthew 23, 24, etc.

units.la: Præterea suo exemplo Christus omnes homines sui officij admonet, quod est, vt singuli suam functionem, ad quam diuinitus vocati sunt, pari studio & diligentia obeant. Nam fuit hæc (vt alibi monuimus) vocatio & peculiaris functio filij Dei in carne manifestati, vt magnum illum Prophetam ageret, quæ venturum esse Moses prædixerat, & pauperibus Euangelium, captiuis dimissionem prædicaret. In ea ergo obeunda assiduus & indefessus est, & neque laborum molestia, neque populi ingratitudine, neque Sacerdotum & magnatum contumacia, non item periculis vllis, quæ vndiq; imminebant, se abstterreri patitur, quò minus stationem suam teneat, & omnē docendi occasionē studiosissimè vanetur. Debent exemplū hoc imitari omnes, quibus ecclesiæ ministerium Deus credidit. Est quidē functio eorum laboris & periculi plena: quia cum mundo illis res est, qui vt pessimis studijs delectatur, ita plus quàm hostili animo ijs se opponit, qui illū retrahere & ad obsequium Deo præstandum hortari studēt. Omnibus ergo, qui in illo munere versantur, idem accidit, quod Ieremiæ dicebat Dominus: Pugnabūt aduersus te: sed ijdē sibi quoq; dici putent: Ne paueas à conspectu eorū, ego enim tecū sum vt te liberē, dicit Dominus. Prædicet ergo sermone, insistet tempestiuè et intempestiuè, arguat, obiurgent, exhortentur cū omni lenitate & doctrina: Neq; eos audiant, qui sufficere arbitrantur, si semel & iterum doceant quid singulis facto sit opus, nec enim æquum esse, vt nos inutili labore fatigemus, aut periculis obijciamus propter eos, in quibus corrigendis nihil proficias, cùm admonitiones omnes vnà cum monitoribus fidis odio prosequantur. Nam ideo instare iubet ministros Paulus, quòd ex spiritus reuelatione sciret fore tempus, quo saniorem doctrinam mundus hic tolerare nollet: id quod hodie passim fieri videmus. Sed nunc (vt nuper diximus) cū contumacia mūdi nos luctari oportet, vt licet nemo emendetur, nostras tamē animas ipsi liberemus, vt olim Ezechieli Dominus dicebat.
units.tr: Moreover, by his own example Christ reminds all men of their duty: that each person should carry out his own office, to which he has been called by God, with equal zeal and diligence. For this was (as we have noted elsewhere) the calling and particular office of the Son of God made manifest in the flesh, that he should act as that great Prophet whom Moses had foretold would come, and preach the Gospel to the poor and release to the captives. In discharging this office he was constant and untiring. Neither the toil, nor the ingratitude of the people, nor the stubbornness of the priests and great men, nor any of the dangers that threatened on every side, could frighten him away from keeping his post and seeking every opportunity of teaching with the utmost eagerness. All to whom God has entrusted the ministry of the Church ought to imitate this example. The function is indeed full of labour and danger, because they have to deal with a world which, delighting in the worst pursuits, opposes with more than hostile feeling those who strive to draw it back and urge it to render obedience to God. Therefore, what the Lord said to Jeremiah happens to all who engage in that office: "They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you; for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord" (Jer. 1). Let them therefore preach the word, press on in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke and exhort with all gentleness and teaching. Nor should they listen to those who think it enough if they teach once or twice what each person must do; for it is not right that we should wear ourselves out with fruitless labour, or expose ourselves to dangers, on account of those whom we cannot correct at all, since they hate every warning together with the faithful warners. For Paul bids ministers to press on because, by revelation of the Spirit, he knew that a time would come when the world would refuse to tolerate sounder doctrine, which we see happening everywhere today. But now (as we said lately) we must struggle against the obstinacy of the world, so that, although no one is amended, we may at least free our own souls, as the Lord once said to Ezekiel.

units.la: At quod de verbi administris dicitur, hoc ipsum ad se pertinere arbitretur, qui repub. administrat. Quàm laboriosa enim & periculosa horum quoq; functio sit, multorū exempla testantur, qui non ingratos modò & inobedientes, sed rebelles & seditiosos, imò hostes apertos senserunt eos, pro quorū salute ipsi dies noctesq; excubabant. Accedit huic malo effrenis populi libido, qui in morū licentia felicitate omnem cōsistere putat, faeneratorum itē & vsurariorū artes, quibus deprehendendis, nedum coercendis, vix vlla industria potest sufficere. Taceo nūc quotidianos labores & molestias, omitto iniqua multorū de bonis legibus iudicia, quæ multos olim mouerūt, vt à reipub. gubernaculis procul abscederent, & in otio honesto potius viuere, quàm curis & negotijs publicis se nequicquā fatigare mallent. At longè alia debet esse hominū Christianorum sententia, quos ad repub. Deus vocauit.
units.tr: But what is said of the ministers of the Word, let those who administer the commonwealth take to apply to themselves. For how laborious and dangerous the office of these men too is, the examples of many testify, who have found those for whose salvation they watched day and night not merely ungrateful and disobedient, but rebellious and seditious, indeed open enemies. To this evil is added the unbridled desire of the people, who think that happiness consists in licence of morals, and also the arts of usurers and moneylenders, which can scarcely be detected, let alone restrained, by any diligence. I say nothing now of the daily labours and troubles, and I pass over the unfair judgements of many about good laws, which once moved many to withdraw far from the helm of the commonwealth and prefer to live in honourable leisure rather than vainly weary themselves with public cares and business. But the opinion of Christian men, whom God has called to the commonwealth, ought to be quite different.

units.la: Meminerint illi, neminē sibi soli natū esse, et nos plurimū debere communi patriæ, cuius salus vt omnibus cōmendatissima esse debet, ita negligi non potest, quin Dei gloriæ aliquid decedat, cuius nisi studiosissimi simus nunquā salui erimus. Pergat ergo magistratus in tuēdis bonis legibus, in puniendis improbis, in Dei cultu prouehendo, & in primis curent, vt vrbes suas Christo cōsecrent, & ecclesiæ hospitiū præbeant, quā in terris isti peregrinari, vel potius exulare cōstat. Hæc si illis cordi fuerint, sentiet se plus proficere, quàm quis sperare audeat. Solet enim suo spiritu Deus priorū conatus iuuare, & in periculis eos tueri, qui pro ipsius gloria & salute publica aliquid audent: sicuti in Dauidis, Ezechiæ, Constantini, Theodosij & similium exemplis est videre. Transferant ad se quoq; istam doctrinam parentes, quos liberorum æducatio solicitos habet: præceptores item publici & priuati, qui in iuuentute instituenda laborant. Cogitent se Deo laborare, & proinde cura & studio indefesso opus esse, ne eos sua negligentia perdant, quos reipub. & ecclesiæ spem esse, non immeritò dixeris.
units.tr: Let them remember that no one is born for himself alone, and that we owe very much to our common country, whose safety, as it ought to be most commended to all, so cannot be neglected without some loss to the glory of God, and unless we are most zealous for it we shall never be safe. Let the magistrate therefore continue in defending good laws, in punishing the wicked, in advancing the worship of God, and above all let them take care to consecrate their cities to Christ and to offer hospitality to the Church, which is known to be a stranger and rather an exile on earth. If these things are dear to them, they will feel that they accomplish more than anyone dares to hope. For God is wont to aid the efforts of those before them by his Spirit, and to protect in dangers those who venture something for his glory and the public good, as may be seen in the examples of David, Hezekiah, Constantine, Theodosius and the like. Let parents also, whom the upbringing of their children makes anxious, apply this teaching to themselves; likewise public and private teachers, who labour in instructing youth. Let them consider that they labour for God, and therefore that they need care and tireless zeal, lest by their negligence they lose those whom one may not unfairly call the hope of the commonwealth and the Church.

units.la: Porrò priusquam à Christi exemplo discedamus, quæ nam eius doctrina, aut quod huius argumenti. mentum fuerit, videre oportet. Comprehendit hoc uno verbo Lucas, quando eum regnum Dei praedicauisse & euangelizauisse scribit. Dicitur autem regnum Dei in scripturis universum humanae salutis negotium, eo quod huius finis & scopus sit, ut quoad in terris vivimus, suo verbo & spiritu in nobis Deus regnet, nos a mundo & huius principe, carni deniq; nostra & ipsa morte tandem superiores facti, cum illo in coelis vivamus atq; regnemus. Et hoc illud est, quod in Apocalypsi de Christo dicitur, eum nos Patri suo sacerdotes & reges fecisse. Extant de hoc regno Dei infinitae promissiones & veterum prophetarum vaticinia. Huc enim referri debent, quaecunq; sub regni parabolis de humani generis redemptione, de ecclesia ite & eius felici propagatione atq; statu beatissimo passim dicuntur. Hoc igitur regnum praesoribus iam adesse Christus docuit, & ad illud gratis animis excipiendum omnes hortatus est. Recte autem euangelizandi verbo Lucas utitur. Nec enim aliud nuntium humano generi laetius & iucundius potest afferri, quam cum docetur, Dei filiu deuicto diabolo nos in libertate vindicauisse, & regni sui cohaeredes fecisse eos, qui prius infelicia Satanae mancipia erat, & morte aeterna merebatur. Quanta aute huius doctrinae authoritas apud nos esse debeat, hoc uno argumento abunde docemur, quod ut eius promissionem Deus primus in paradiso vulgauit, ita nunc Filius Dei illius minister atq; praeco fieri dignatus est. Sunt autem hic nobis duo observanda.
units.tr: Furthermore, before we depart from the example of Christ, we ought to see what his teaching was, or what was the subject of it. Luke comprehends this in one word, when he writes that he preached and evangelised the kingdom of God. Now in the Scriptures the kingdom of God is said to be the whole business of human salvation, because its end and aim is that, as long as we live on earth, God should reign in us by his word and Spirit, and that, having at last become superior to the world and its prince, to our flesh and even to death itself, we should live and reign with him in heaven. This is what is said in the Apocalypse of Christ, that he has made us priests and kings to his Father. There are infinite promises about this kingdom of God and prophecies of the ancient prophets. For to this must be referred all those things which, under the parables of the kingdom, are said everywhere about the redemption of mankind, about the Church, its happy propagation and most blessed state. Christ taught that this kingdom was already present to those who were before him, and he exhorted all to receive it with willing minds. Luke uses the word "evangelise" rightly. For no more joyful and pleasing news can be brought to the human race than when it is taught that the Son of God, having conquered the devil, has freed us into liberty and made heirs of his kingdom those who were before slaves of Satan, unhappy and deserving eternal death. How great the authority of this doctrine ought to be among us we are taught abundantly by this one argument: that just as God first published its promise in paradise, so now the Son of God has deigned to become its minister and herald. There are two things here for us to observe.

units.la: Primum, Euangelio regnū Dei contineri: illud nimirum, quod inter orandū requirimus, ex Christi praescripto dicetes: Adueniat regnū tuū. Ex eo enim sequitur, a nobis obedientia requiri, neq; nos illam Deo negare posse, nisi manifestam rebellionē meditari, vel etiā cum illo ludere velimus, dum vita & moribus regni illius leges atq; disciplinā reijcimus, quod nobis aduenire postulamus. Observauit hoc diligenter Paulus Apostolus, quādo euangelicae doctrinae & praedicationis fine esse scripsit, obedientia fidei, qua intellectu & sensum omne vna cum carnis desiderijs Dei verbo subijcere debeamus: adhaec illius administros armis instructos esse ait, quae non carnalia, sed divina virtute animata & efficacia sint ad deprimendam omne sublimitate, quae aduersus Dei cognitione extollitur: & ut captiuam ducant omnem cogitatione ad obediendū Christo. Arguunt haec illorū impudentia, qui cum fidem in Christū Iesum profiteantur, & Euangelij studiū simulent, interim tamen diabolo seruiunt, & hunc in ipsis regnare patiuntur, cuius caput Christus contriuit, ut nos ex eius tyrannide asserteret. Pugnant hi cum fine Euangelij & totius Christianismi, adeoq; eorum similes sunt, qui postquam imperatori militia nomen dederunt, cū hostibus tamen colludunt, & in eorū castris desident.
units.tr: First, that the kingdom of God is contained in the Gospel: that, namely, which we ask for in prayer, saying, according to Christ's precept: "Thy kingdom come." For from this it follows that obedience is required of us, and that we cannot deny it to God unless we are plotting manifest rebellion, or even wish to trifle with him, while we reject in life and manners the laws and discipline of that kingdom, which we demand should come to us. The Apostle Paul carefully observed this, when he wrote that the end of evangelical doctrine and preaching is the obedience of faith, by which we ought to subject every understanding and feeling, together with the desires of the flesh, to the word of God. Besides this, he says that the ministers of it are armed with weapons which are not carnal but mighty through divine power, and are effective for pulling down every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and for leading every thought captive to the obedience of Christ. These things expose the impudence of those who, while they profess faith in Jesus Christ and pretend zeal for the Gospel, nevertheless serve the devil and suffer him to reign in them, whose head Christ has crushed, that he might rescue us from his tyranny. Such people are at odds with the aim of the Gospel and of the whole of Christianity, and they are like those who, after they have given their name to the emperor's army, nevertheless collude with the enemy and sit idle in their camps.

units.la: Alterum, quod regnum hoc Dei, non armis huius mundi, sed verbi praedicatione propagatur. Poterat quidem Christus vel angelorum legionibus ad nutum suum uti, vel Romanos rerum tunc dominos subito mutare, ut ipsi armis sumptis tam Iudaeos quam gentes reliquas ad amplectendam religionem Christianam cogerent: Sed ipse vrbes & vicos circuire, Euangelium praedicare, & in eodem praedicando Apostolorum opera sine ministerio postea uti voluit, ut hominum mentes veritatis doctrina illuminata sua sponte ad Dei regnum concederent, impij vero intra animos suos iugulati locum ipsi dare cogerentur. Et hoc illud est, de quo Isaias vaticinatus fuerat, dicens: Terram percutiet virga oris sui, & spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium. Et Dauid eidem populum spontaneum tribuit, qui nimirum spiritus virtute ex verbi aeterni semine renatus voluntarium ipsi obsequium praestet. Docent ista regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde armis mundi neque prouehi, neque defirui posse. Vult quidem Deus reges suae Ecclesiae nutritios esse, & ut ijdem Christum exosculentur Dauidi iubet: at huius decreti causa est, non quod Regum authoritate sine armis ipsi opus sit, sed quod politicum magistratum abs se institutum honoretanto Deus dignatur, & eundem sui officij admonet, ne concessam sibi potestatem in proprium exitium conuertat. Nobis vero dulcissimam consolationem paris, quod regnum Christi, cuius cives sumus, mundi huius viciibus minime subiectum esse audimus, & proinde non timenda esse eorum arma, qui ad eius extirpationem coniurant. Docet praeterea de Euangelij praedicatione in primis solicitos esse debere eos, qui regnum Christi propagatum & defensum volunt. Scholastici aperiant pij principes, verbi administros tueantur, coetus sacros defendant, impostores & seditiosos authoritate publica coerceant. Ita Ecclesiae nutritij erunt, & Christo officium praestabunt longe gratissimum. E contra patet hic, quo loco habendi sint, qui Iulianum apostatam imitati, schólas claudunt & dissipant, verbi ministris stipendia subducunt, coetus publicos Ecclesiae prohibent, falsis doctoribus & superstitionum magistris patrocinantur, omnia deniq; faciunt, quibus Euangelij cursus impeditur. Sunt hi hostes regni Dei, & procul dubio olim sceptro Christi ferreo coercebuntur, sicuti Dauid illis minatur.
units.tr: Second, this kingdom of God is spread not by the weapons of this world but by the preaching of the Word. Christ could indeed have used the legions of angels at his command, or suddenly changed the Romans, who then ruled, so that they, taking up arms, would compel both the Jews and the other nations to embrace the Christian religion. But he chose to go about towns and villages himself, to preach the Gospel, and in that preaching to use the work of the apostles afterwards, without any ministry of force, so that minds enlightened by the teaching of truth would of their own accord yield to the kingdom of God, while the impious, slain in their own minds, would be compelled to give it place. This is what Isaiah prophesied when he said: "He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked." David likewise promised him a willing people, who, reborn by the power of the Spirit from the seed of the eternal Word, would render him voluntary obedience. These things teach that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and therefore cannot be advanced or destroyed by the weapons of the world. God indeed wills that kings be nursing fathers of his Church, and he bids them kiss the Son, as David says; but the reason for this command is not that the Church needs the authority of kings with the aid of arms, but that God deigns to honour the civil magistrate he has instituted, and reminds that magistrate of its duty, lest it turn the power entrusted to it to its own destruction. For us this is a most sweet consolation: we hear that the kingdom of Christ, whose citizens we are, is in no way subject to the changes of this world, and therefore we need not fear the arms of those who conspire for its extirpation. Moreover, this teaches that those who want the kingdom of Christ propagated and defended must above all be concerned for the preaching of the Gospel. Let godly princes open schools, protect the ministers of the Word, defend sacred assemblies, and restrain impostors and seditious men by public authority. So they will be nursing fathers of the Church and will render Christ a service most pleasing to him. On the other hand, it is clear here what place must be assigned to those who, imitating Julian the Apostate, close and break up the schools, withhold stipends from the ministers of the Word, forbid public assemblies of the Church, shelter false teachers and masters of superstitions, and, in short, do everything by which the course of the Gospel is hindered. These are enemies of the kingdom of God, and without doubt they will one day be restrained by the iron sceptre of Christ, as David threatens them.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua Christi comitatus describitur, non magnifico apparatu terribilis, neque huius mundi splendore illustris; sed vilis admodum & contemptus, qualem fore olim Prophetæ prædixerant. De Christo enim Isaias scribit: Non clamabit, neq; efferetur, non audiri faciet in platea vocem suam. Et notum est illud Zachariæ: Exulta filia Zion, iubila filia Ierusalem, en Rex tuus venit tibi iustus & seruator, pauper siue mitis, &c. Quæ verissimè olim prædicta esse, in eius comitatu apparet. Primum in eo locum obtinent duodecim Apostoli, quos (vt cap.sexto audiuimus) in eum finem sibi domesticos discipulos fecerat, vt eorum ministerio tandem vteretur ad Euangelium in toto orbe diuulgandum. Erant autem illi omnes obscuro loco nati, adhæc homines illiterati, qui vel manuarijs opificijs victum sibi parauerant antea, vel ex publicanorum ordine erant vocati, quos omnibus inuisos & quasi publica infamia notatos fuisse, supra dixi mus. Cur vero tales Christus elegerit, alibi ex priori ad Corinth. docuimus, & proinde non opus est eadem repetere. Nunc cum duodecim discipulis mulieres aliquot numerantur, quas per illum à spiritibus malis & morbis sanatas fuisse scribitur: & ex his quidem aliquæ ob vitam anteactam, vt go infames fuerunt, qualem Mariam fuisse scimus, quæ ad aliarum eiusdem nominis differentiam à loco natali Magdalene dicitur: aliquæ autem opibus simul & conditione illustres, vt pote Ioanna vxor Chuza, qui Herodis Regis procurator fuit, & Susanna quædam, quam huius sociam & fortasse eiusdem conditionis fuisse, verisimile est. Accesserunt his multæ aliæ, de quibus omnibus dicitur, quòd non modò secutæ aut comitatæ sint Christum, sed quod eidem ex suis facultatibus victum & impensas submin istrauerint.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the other part of this passage, in which the company of Christ is described: not terrible with a magnificent display, nor illustrious with the splendour of this world, but very humble and despised, as the prophets had foretold it would be. For Isaiah writes of Christ: "He shall not cry out, nor lift up his voice, nor make his voice heard in the street." And that saying of Zechariah is well known: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you, just and a saviour, lowly or meek," etc. That these things were most truly foretold long ago appears in his company. First, among those who hold the first place are the twelve apostles, whom (as we heard in the sixth chapter) he had made his household disciples for this purpose, that he might at last use their ministry to spread the Gospel throughout the whole world. Now all of them were born in obscure places, and moreover were unlettered men, who had earlier won their living by manual trades, or had been called from the order of tax collectors, who, as I have said above, were all hated and marked with public infamy. But why Christ chose such men I have shown elsewhere from the earlier letter to the Corinthians, and therefore there is no need to repeat it here. Next, along with the twelve disciples, several women are numbered, whom Scripture says he healed of evil spirits and diseases. Some of them, on account of their former life, were infamous, as we know Mary was, who is called Magdalene, from her birthplace, to distinguish her from others of the same name. Others were illustrious in wealth as well as in rank, such as Joanna, the wife of Chuza, who was the steward of King Herod, and a certain Susanna, who is likely to have been her companion and perhaps of the same rank. Many others joined them, of whom it is said that they not only followed and accompanied Christ, but also ministered to him from their own means, providing food and expenses.

units.la: Quo loco ipse Christus primum considerandus venit, qui tales in suum comitatum, vel contubernium potius admisit, quarum consuetudo & familiaritas ipsi parum honorifica erat multorum iudicio. Sed ita testari voluit, se non fastidire peccatores, neq; nobis fraudi fore vitam anteactam & quapridem designauimus scelera, sed totis animis ad ipsum conuersi, ipsius discipuli fieri cupiamus. Etenim stupendum bonitatis exemplum est, quòd Magdalene, quæ paulò ante à septem immundis spiritibus obsessa vilissimum Satanæ mancipium fuerat, inter suos familiares locum tribuit. Quod vt consolationem dulcissimam affert ijs qui peccatorum suorum conscientia grauantur: ita eorū audaciam atq; hypocrisim arguit, qui peccatores simul omnes ita fastidiunt, vt ecclesias quoque totas nimium præcipiti iudicio damnent, in quibus aliquos cōspicantur, qui vitijs qualibuscunq; notati sunt. Et vt maiorem sanctitatis existimationem sibi concilient, excommunicationem subinde in ore habent, & modò hos modò illos excludendos esse clamitat. Atqui de colligendis potius fratribus quàm dissipandis nos solicitos esse oportet, & infirmos nõ statim rescindere, sed cum omni lenitate assumere iubet Apostolus. Clamant illi, ecclesiā oportere esse absq; ruga & macula. Agnosco Apostoli verba: sed respondeo Christum minimè eiusmodi ecclesiam inuenisse, sed talem fecisse sui sanguinis lauacro eam, quæ rugis & maculis, imò morbis fœdissimis, tota erat obsita. Quam cùm ille nō horruerit, quò minus eam suo contactu, imò suo sanguine dignatus sit, cur ipsi tam delicatuli aut morosi sunt, vt mox sectione aut vstione opus esse putent, vbi remedia leniora adhuc locum habere poterant? Deinde non hoc vult Apostolus, vt nos ad eam perfectionem vnquam, quoad in carne viuimus, peruenire posse doceat: quomodo enim sine ruga & macula dicentur, qui legem peccati adhucin membris suis circumferunt, & qui quotidie ex Christi mandato precantur, Remitte nobis debita nostra? sed vt Christi beneficium & meritū commendet, quo is peccata nostra tam probè tegit (vt Dauidis verbo vtar) vt coram Dei iudicio pro iustis & sanctis habeamur, etiamsi multa nobis adhuc labes & peccata inhæreant, & in multis frequenter erremus. Nos quidem assiduè anniti decet, vt ad perfectionem maiorem pertingamus, at non temerarij esse debemus in ijs damnandis, qui cum Christo coniungi cupiunt, & quos hic tam benignè & amicè complectitur. Et hic quidē singularem consideration meretur, quo bonitatis suæ exemplū Dei Filius in mulieres potissimum ædere voluit. Eo enim publicè testatur, se huius quoq; sexus seruatorem esse: quod multas ob causas peculiari demonstratione doceri oportebat. Per mulierem enim peccatum & mors in mundum introierant, &
units.tr: Here Christ himself must first be considered, who admitted into his company, or rather into his household, women whose association and familiarity was thought by many to be little honourable to him. But in this way he wished to bear witness that he does not disdain sinners, and that a past life, and the sins I have already described, will not hinder us, provided we turn wholeheartedly to him and desire to become his disciples. Indeed it is a stupendous example of goodness that Magdalene, who shortly before had been possessed by seven unclean spirits and was the most wretched slave of Satan, was given a place among his intimate companions. As this brings the sweetest consolation to those who are weighed down by the consciousness of their sins, so it exposes the audacity and hypocrisy of those who so despise all sinners that they condemn even whole churches with too hasty a judgment, in which they see some who are marked with any kind of vice. And in order to win for themselves a greater reputation for holiness, they constantly have excommunication on their lips and cry out that this person or that must be excluded. Yet the apostle bids us be concerned to gather in the brethren rather than to scatter them, and not to cast off the weak at once, but to receive them with all gentleness. They cry out that the Church ought to be without spot or wrinkle. I acknowledge the apostle's words; but I answer that Christ did not find such a Church, but by the washing of his own blood he made it such, when it was covered all over with wrinkles and spots, indeed with most foul diseases. Since he did not shrink from it, so as not to deign to touch it, and indeed to shed his blood for it, why are they so dainty and fastidious that they think at once that cutting or burning is needed, where milder remedies could still have place? Further, the apostle does not mean that we can ever attain such perfection, as long as we live in the flesh; for how could those be called without spot or wrinkle who still carry the law of sin in their members, and who daily pray, at Christ's command, "Forgive us our debts"? Rather, he commends the benefit and merit of Christ, by which he so thoroughly covers our sins (to use David's word) that we are counted just and holy before the judgment of God, even though many stains and sins still cling to us, and we often err in many things. We indeed ought constantly to strive to reach greater perfection, but we must not be rash in condemning those who desire to be joined to Christ, and whom he here embraces so kindly and friendly. And this deserves particular consideration: that the Son of God chose especially to display the example of his goodness towards women. For by this he bears public witness that he is also the saviour of this sex, which needed to be taught by a special demonstration for many reasons. For through a woman sin and death had entered the world.

units.la: K Heuam non modò priorem peccauisse, verumetiam viro peccati causam fuisse sacra historia docet. Ideo sexum hunc grauioribus quoq; poenis & molestijs pluribus Deus multauit. Ne ergo inter has tentationibus superatæ de gratia Dei desperarent, & promisse salutis authorem, Iesum Christum, nihil ad se pertinere arbitrarentur, hic ex muliere homo nasci voluit, & mulieres in suo comitatu habuit, iisdem Euangelium prædicauit, & in illarum morbus curandis miracula ædidit non vulgaria: imò (vt alibi annotauimus) resurrectionem suam, quæ nostræ salutis complementum est, mulieribus in primis voluit innotescere. Hinc ergo consolationem petant in omni tentationum genere, neq; desperent de salutis suæ certitudine, quam Dei filius tot argumentis confirmauit.
units.tr: For sacred history teaches that Eve not only sinned first, but was also the cause of sin for her husband. Therefore God laid heavier punishments and many troubles upon this sex. Lest therefore women, overcome by these temptations, should despair of the grace of God, and think that Jesus Christ, the author of the promised salvation, had nothing to do with them, he wished to be born of a woman, and had women in his company, preached the Gospel to them, and worked remarkable miracles in healing their diseases. Indeed (as I have noted elsewhere) he wished his resurrection, which is the completion of our salvation, to be made known first of all to women. Let them therefore draw consolation from this in every kind of temptation, and not despair of the certainty of their salvation, which the Son of God has confirmed by so many proofs.

units.la: Deinde præclarum fidei et gratitudinis exemplum mulieres istæ præbêt. Senserant Christi gratiam, qui beneficia omnis generis, tam spiritualia quàm corporalia in eas contulerat. Ergo gratiam, quam possunt, illi referunt, & ita se ei totas consecrant, vt neq; honoris & exististimationis suæ, neque opum, neq; etiam propriæ vitæ aliquam rationem habeant, dummodo suo ergà illum officio defungantur. Etenim turpe videbatur Christum & discipulos eius incertis sedibus oberrantes sequi: neque dubium est malevolos ex eo calumniandi occasionem auidè arripuisse. Ioannæ idem illud periculosum fuit, quæ maritum habuit, quem heri sui Herodis simillimum fuisse verisimile est: quod ipsum de Susanna quoque & multis aliis possumus sentire. Accedit hus rei domesticæ cura, quæ sola eas ab instituto revocare poterat. Sed nihil huius curant, quæ vero Christi amore ardent, & gloriæ eius prouehendæ zelum iam animo suo conceperunt. Neque illum sequuntur modò, vt aut verbi eius auditione aures pascant, aut miraculorum spectatione curiositati (quæ huic sexui familiaris est) suæ satisfaciant: sed vt illi adsint, suis eum officijs subleuent, & ex facultatibus suis tam ipsum quàm discipulos eius alant. Iam ergo illud Apostoli intra animos suos sentiunt, æquissimum esse, vt corporalia ex nobis beneficia metant, qui spiritualia seminauerunt. Suo igitur exemplo nostri seculi ingratitudinem istæ arguunt, quando plerique etsi ex Euangelio Christi beneficia quotidie infinita percipiunt, nihil tamen pro illo audent, neque alicuius inuidiam siue odium illius causa subire volunt: & tam abest, vt aliquid in egentia Christi membra & Euangelij ministros conferant, vt potius maiorum liberalitate ditatas ecclesias ipsi spolient, & collegiorum redditus insatiabili rapacitate vel sibi ipsis vendicent, vel in vsus alienos conuertant. Sunt hæc indigna nomine Christiano, neque inultam sinet Deus ingratitudinem istam, quæ cultum suum vehementer impedit, & hostibus calumniandi materiam præbet.
units.tr: Next, these women set before us a notable example of faith and gratitude. They had felt the grace of Christ, who had bestowed on them benefits of every kind, spiritual as well as bodily. So they repay that grace as best they can and devote themselves wholly to him, taking no account of their honour and reputation, nor of their wealth, nor even of their own lives, provided they discharge their duty towards him. For it seemed shameful to follow Christ and his disciples as they wandered without a fixed abode, and there is no doubt that malicious people eagerly seized on this as an occasion for slander. The same danger attended Joanna, who had a husband, most likely very like her master Herod; and we may think the same of Susanna and of many others. Added to this was the care of household affairs, which alone could have called them away from their purpose. But they care for none of this, because they burn with the love of Christ and have already conceived in their minds a zeal to advance his glory. Nor do they follow him merely so that they may feed their ears on hearing his word, or satisfy their curiosity (which is familiar to this sex) by watching his miracles. They follow him so that they may be present, relieve him with their services, and support both him and his disciples from their own means. Now they feel in their hearts that saying of the Apostle, that it is most just that we reap bodily benefits from those to whom we have sown spiritual ones. By their example, then, these women rebuke the ingratitude of our age, when most people, although they receive countless benefits daily from the Gospel of Christ, dare nothing for him and are unwilling to incur any hatred or ill will on his account. So far are they from contributing anything to the needy members of Christ and the ministers of the Gospel that they rather despoil the churches enriched by the generosity of their forebears, and with insatiable rapacity either claim the revenues of the colleges for themselves or turn them to other uses. These things are unworthy of the Christian name, and God will not leave this ingratitude unpunished, since it greatly hinders his worship and gives enemies material for slander.

units.la: Continet præterea locus iste eximium diuinæ prouidentiæ exemplum, quo nos in rerum omnium angustia atque inopia solemur. Captus erat propter liberiore verbi prædicationem Ioannes Baptista: at nihilominus per totam Galilæam Christus cum suo comitatu tutus peregrinatur. Huius item gratia res suas omnes discipuli reliquerant, & ipsum sequuti erant, qui non habebat quò caput suum reclinaret. At diuinitus excitantur ex eo hominum genere, de quo quàm minimum sperari poterat, qui illos cum suo præceptore alant. Neque ad breue modò tempus subsidium istud durauit, sed quàm diu in Christi seruitio fuerunt, nihil illis vnquam defuit (sicuti in vltima cœna ipsimet testantur) etiamsi ab illo absq; pecunia & commeatu mitterentur. Debent hoc exemplo sese consolari omnes, qui in Dei vocatione ambulant. Meminerint se sub illius prouidentia agere, qui & vitæ dies & capitis nostri capillos in numerato habet. Cogitent præterea, illi varias esse rationes, quibus suos serua re & alere potest. Olim sanè Israeliticam gentem prope innumerabilem per annos quadraginta sterili Arabiæ deserto, absque semente & messe mirifice & liberalissimè aluit. In Prophetis autem multa huius generis exempla occurrunt, quos modò per tyrannorum seruos aulicos (quales Abdias & Abdemelech fuerunt) modò coruorum ministerio aliisq; inusitatis rationibus seruauit. Sunt ergo nimium stulti, qui in præsentem modò rerum angustiam oculos defigunt, & non potius animum ad Deum attollunt, qui cum florum in agro nascentium & auium tam accuratam rationem habeat, eos negligere non potest, quos ipse rebus grauioribus & magis arduis destinauit.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage contains an outstanding example of divine providence, by which we are comforted in every strait and want. John the Baptist had been taken prisoner for preaching the Word more freely, yet Christ, with his company, travels safely through all Galilee. Likewise the disciples had left all their possessions for his sake and followed him, though he had nowhere to lay his head. Yet God raised up support for them from a class of people from whom very little could have been expected, and they fed them together with their teacher. Nor did this help last only a short time. As long as they were in Christ's service nothing was ever lacking to them (as they themselves testify at the Last Supper), even though he sent them out without money or provisions. All who walk in God's calling ought to take comfort from this example. Let them remember that they act under the providence of him who holds the days of our life and the hairs of our head in reckoning. Let them further consider that he has various means by which he can preserve and feed his people. Long ago he marvellously and most generously fed the Israelite nation, almost countless in number, for forty years in the barren desert of Arabia, without seed or harvest. In the Prophets many examples of this kind occur, whom he preserved sometimes through the servants of tyrants at court (such as Obadiah and Ebed-melech were), and sometimes by the ministry of ravens and other unusual means. They are therefore far too foolish who fix their eyes only on the present straits of affairs and do not rather lift their minds up to God. Since he takes such careful account of the flowers growing in the field and of the birds, he cannot neglect those whom he has destined for weightier and more arduous tasks.

units.la: Postremò ordinaria ministrorum ecclesiæ stipendia Christus suo exemplo confirmat. Qui enim axioma illud ex lege naturæ desumptum, Dignus est operarius mercede sua, alibi ad Apostolos transfert, idem nunc ipse eorum liberalitate se & suos ali atq; sustentari patitur, quibus salutis æternæ verbum prædicabat. Atqui facile illi fuisset vel absq; omni cibo suos in vita conseruare, vel per miraculum illis cœlitus aut aliunde prospicere. Sed ea ratione vti voluit, quam olim Leuitis in lege præscripse-rat, & quæ in omnibus aliis vitæ generibus obseruatur (sicuti Paulus agricolarum, pastorum & militum exemplis demonstrat) ne quis à ministris verbi peculiare quid & sublimius exigeret, & vt singpuli gratitudinis & beneficentiæ exercendæ occasionem atque materiam haberent. Neminem ergo hominum inuidorum calumniæ moueant, qui cum non alia ratione Euangelij doctrinam vulgo inuisam & suspectam facere possint, ministrorum stipendia odiose exagitant: quasi vero quicquam illis dari possit, quod æternæ vitæ thesauros suo precio superet. Discant potius singull Dei bonitatem agnoscere, qui nos verbi sui luce dignatur: hanc vero animis piis & gratis excipiant, neq; pigeat in eius ministros ea conferre, quæ infelix mundus in turpissimos vsus & fœda diaboli mancipia profundere consueuit. Indiuulsis autem animis Iesu Christo adhæreamus, qui & hic nihil nobis defieri patietur, & olim æterne vitæ coheredes faciet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Christ by his own example confirms the ordinary stipends of the ministers of the Church. For he who elsewhere transfers to the Apostles that axiom drawn from the law of nature, that the labourer is worthy of his hire, now himself allows himself and his followers to be fed and sustained by the liberality of those to whom he preached the word of eternal salvation. And yet it would have been easy for him to keep his people alive even without food, or to provide for them by miracle from heaven or from elsewhere. But he chose to use that method which he had long before prescribed in the law for the Levites, and which is observed in all other walks of life (as Paul shows by the examples of farmers, shepherds and soldiers). This was so that no one would demand anything peculiar or more exalted from the ministers of the Word, and so that each individual would have occasion and matter for exercising gratitude and beneficence. Let no one be moved by the slander of envious men, who, since they cannot otherwise make the doctrine of the Gospel hateful and suspect to the common people, bitterly harass the stipends of the ministers. As if anything could be given to them that outweighs the treasures of eternal life! Rather, let each learn to acknowledge the goodness of God, who has deigned to enlighten us with the light of his word. Let them receive this with pious and thankful minds, and not begrudge contributing to his ministers those things which the unhappy world is accustomed to squander on the most shameful uses and on the foul slaves of the devil. Let us cleave to Jesus Christ with undivided hearts, who will suffer nothing to be lacking to us here and will one day make us co-heirs of eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXV.

units.la: Cùm autem multa turba conueniret, & qui in singulis vrbibus erant proficiscerentur ad eum, dixit per parabolā: Exiit quidam seminator ad seminandum semen suum: & in seminando aliud cecidit in viam, & con culcatum est, & volucres cœli deuorarūt illud. Et aliud cecidit super pe tram, & enatum exaruit, quia nō habebat humorem. Et aliud cecidit in ter spinas, & simul enatæ spinæ suffocarunt illud. Et aliud cecidit in ter-ram bonam, & cùm enatum esset dedit fructum centuplum. Hæc di-cens clamabat: Qui habet aures ad audiendum, audiat. Interrogabant autem eum discipuli eius, dicentes, quæ esset ista parabola? Ipse vero di-xit eis: Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni Dei: reliquis autem per pa-rabolas loquor, vt videntes non videant, & audientes non intelligant.
units.tr: When a great crowd came together, and those who were in each town came out to him, he spoke by a parable: "A sower went out to sow his seed, and as he sowed, some fell by the road and was trodden underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. Other seed fell on rock, and when it grew up, it withered away because it had no moisture. Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. Other seed fell into good ground, and when it grew up, it yielded a hundredfold." As he said these things, he cried out: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." His disciples asked him what this parable meant. And he said to them: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest I speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand."

units.la: EXposuit Lucas ardentissimum Iesu Christi in propagando regno Dei & seruandis hominibus studium: vt nimirum comitantibus ipsum discipulis suis & aliquot mulieribus, quæ tam ipsum quàm discipulos eius suis facultatibus aluerūt, Euangelium per singula oppida atq; vicos prædicarit. Quo loco & Dei bonitate didicimus, qua is saluti nostræ consultum cupit, & mulierū istarū exemplo didicimus, nostri etiam officij esse, vt singulí pro sua conditione Christum adiuuent, & regnum Dei pro viribus promoueant. Nam vt olim ad tabernaculi constructionem alij aurū, alij argentum, alij gemmas, alij sericum, alij pelles caprinas conferebant, omniū vero munera Deo grata & accepta erant: ita singulí habebunt, quo Euangelij prædicationem & huius ministros adiuuet, siquidē vero pietatis zelo ardeant, & singulorū officia Deus digno aliquo præmio remunerabitur. Christi enim promissio est, quòd mercede sua minimè amissurus sit, qui vel poculum aquæ frigidæ vni suorum dederit eo no-mine, quòd ipsius discipulū esse audit. Sequitur in præsenti, vt populus Christi exceperit, & nō minori studio ad eū audiendū vndiq; cōuenerit, quæ ite eius fuerit doctrina, qua ad se veniētes instruxit.
units.tr: Luke sets out the very earnest zeal of Jesus Christ in spreading the kingdom of God and saving men: namely, that accompanied by his disciples and some women, who supported him and his disciples from their own means, he preached the gospel through every town and village. Here we learn from the goodness of God, by which he seeks our salvation, and from the example of these women we learn that it is also our duty, each according to his station, to help Christ and to advance the kingdom of God as far as our strength allows. For just as in former times, for the building of the tabernacle, some gave gold, some silver, some gems, some silk, some goatskins, and yet the gifts of all were pleasing and acceptable to God, so each person will have something by which he may help the preaching of the gospel and its ministers, provided he burns with zeal for godliness, and God will reward the duties of each with some worthy recompense. For it is Christ's promise that he who gives even a cup of cold water to one of his followers, on the ground that he is a disciple, will by no means lose his reward. What follows in the present passage is that the people received Christ, and gathered to hear him from every side with no less eagerness; let us see what his teaching was, with which he instructed those who came to him.

units.la: De populo summatim & in genere hoc dicitur, quòd frequens ad illum confluxerit, quodá; qui in vrbibus singulis habitabant, profecti sint, vt eu audirent. Id vero tanto cū importunitate & violen-tia fecerunt, vt ne cibi quidem capiendi otium haberet (sicuti in Marco annotatur) & tandē ex lit-tore in nauim conscendere, & hac nonnihil in altum subductā, inde populum in littore astantem do-cere coactus fuerit. Et hic concursus concioni, quam mox audiemus, occasionem præbuit. Nunc pri-usquam ad illius explicationem accedamus, duo obseruanda veniunt, quorum alterum ad populum, alterum ad ipsum Christum pertinet. In populo mundi huius ingenij apparet, qui rebus nouis mox capitur, diuersis autē studijs intentus mox frigescit, vt se sua spe falli sentit. Quod istis accidisse, se-quens historia docebit. Etenim cùm Christus nō omnium votis satisfaceret, adhæc præpostera illorū studia non obscurè accusaret, mox ad sua dilapsi sunt. Sunt autem eiusmodi exempla in eū finem di-ligenter obseruanda, vt neq; fidamus mundo temere, neq; eiusdē leuitate & inconstantia offendamur. Nec enim aliter possunt facere, qui natura mendaces et sui amantes sunt. Mutantur horum mores & instituta in singulas horas, neq; aliquid apud se certum aut stabile possunt constituere. At fibijpsi semper constat Deus, & ideo falli non possunt quicunq; in illius verbum respexerint. In Christo autem nouum bonitatis exemplum proponitur. Etsi enim istorum mores & animos inconstantes non ignorarent, non tamen propterea suo officio deesset, sed eadem qua prius industria atq; studio in illis instituendis vtitur, et doctrinam morbo ipsorum, quo potissimum laborabant, prudenter accommodat, vt suo loco videbimus. Prodest autem in horum consideratione frequenter versari, vt ea fidem nostram in tentationum lucta vacillantem confirmemus. Qui enim tam benignè eos excepit & instituit, quorum maximam partem minus honorificè de ipso sentire & ab ipso prorsus aliena quaerere sciebat, nunquam certè eos fastidire aut abijcere poterit, qui serio verae pietatis atq; salutis suae studio ad illum accedunt. Minimè ergo formidemus doctoris & seruatoris tam fidi & humani congressum. Simul autem memini nobis in exemplum proponi illius facilitatem, vt nimirum eam imitemur, ne in fratres nostros ipsi duriores simus, quam ille erga nos fuit, quos optimo iure abijcere poterat, si nostris moribus & factis digna praemia reddere voluisset.
units.tr: Concerning the people, this is said in general and in brief: that a great crowd flocked to him, and that people who lived in each town set out to hear him. They did so with such insistence and force that he had no leisure even to take food (as is noted in Mark), and at last he was compelled to climb from the shore into a boat, and to draw it out a little way into the water, and from there to teach the people standing on the shore. This crowd gave occasion to the sermon which we shall hear shortly. Now, before we come to its explanation, two things are to be observed, one of which concerns the people, the other Christ himself. In the people of this world there appears a nature that is quickly captured by new things, but, being intent on various pursuits, soon grows cold when it perceives that its hope has been disappointed. The history that follows will show that this happened to these people. For when Christ did not satisfy all their wishes, and besides, plainly rebuked their perverse eagerness, they soon slipped away to their own homes. Such examples, however, must be carefully observed to this end: that we should neither trust the world rashly, nor be offended by its fickleness and inconstancy. For those who are by nature liars and lovers of themselves can do nothing else. Their manners and purposes change from hour to hour, and they cannot settle on anything certain or stable in themselves. But God is always consistent with himself, and therefore all who look to his word cannot be deceived. In Christ, however, a new example of goodness is set before us. For although he did not fail to know their inconstant minds and hearts, he did not on that account neglect his duty, but he uses the same diligence and zeal as before in instructing them, and wisely adapts his teaching to the disease of which they were chiefly sick, as we shall see in its place. It is also useful to dwell often on the consideration of these people, so that we may strengthen our faith, which wavers in the struggle of temptations. For he who received and taught so kindly those of whom most knew less honourably of him and sought things utterly alien to him, will certainly never be able to despise or cast away those who come to him in earnest, with a zeal for true godliness and their own salvation. Let us therefore not in the least fear the meeting with so faithful and humane a teacher and Saviour. At the same time, let us remember that his gentleness is set before us as an example, so that we may imitate it, and not be harsher toward our brothers than he was toward us, whom he could most justly have cast away, had he wished to repay us according to our manners and deeds.

units.la: Nunc ad concionem eius accedamus, quam ex naui ad populum habuit. Constat eam meris parabolis, vt apud Matthaeum & Marcum est videre, qui plures ex ordine ab eo adductas descripserunt. Lucas vnius modò meminit de seminatore, quae auditoribus, quos tunc habuit, egregiè seruit, & scilicet dalo, quod ex illis enasci solet probè medetur. Vt enim olim mirum videri potuit, quòd ipso Dei filio tanta cum industria docente et doctrinam suam signis miraculosis confirmante, tam pauci crediderunt: ita hodie multi vehementer offenduntur, quando verbi tam exiguum fructum apud eos vident, qui se Euangelicos esse profitentur. Fit enim, vt multi aut verbum Dei esse dubitent quod praedicatur, aut ecclesiam omnino extinctam & deletam esse arbitrentur, & proinde incerti fiant, cui nā cætui sese debeant coniungere. Hisce ergo scandalis remedium ista parabola Christus adhibet, qua & verbi Dei vim atq; naturam, & ecclesiae hoc in seculo conditionem graphicè adumbrata proponit. Primo enim docet ecclesiam Dei illic esse, vbi verbum legitimè praedicatur, etiamsi non omnes credant & obediant. Vt enim agricola prudens nō nisi agro semina committit, nea minimè dubitandum est Dei agrum illic esse, vbi verbi sui semen ille spargit, neq; nos moueat, si sentibus & spinis totum fere obsitum aut etiam lapidibus tectum videamus. Deinde ostendit verbum hoc per se fructiferum esse, non autem apud omnes fructum dignum edere, eò quòd plerique animos parum idoneos afferant. Unde colligit, culpam omnem in auditoribus haerere, neq; propter hos de verbi veritate aut virtute esse dubitandum. At hoc dicendo, simul auditores, quos tunc habebat, acriter pungit, qui magno quidem studio & diligenti attentione docentem audiebant, plerique autem pessimis affectibus occupati instar terrae sterilis & incultae erant, in qua frustra sementem agricola fecerit. Quod si verò tales censentur Christi iudicio, qui per longa itinera non sine periculo et luculento rerum suarum dispendio ad illum conuenerunt, & in quibus mira arsit eius audiendi auiditas, quantò nos hodie infeliciores sumus, qui iam pridem nauseam verbi Dei animo concepimus, qui ad fores nostras concionante Christum audire detrectamus, & quos piorum magistratuum editis cogi oportet, vt ad cætus sacros veniant, cociones audiant, vt vel aliqua ex parte professioni Christianae sese accomodent, ne alijs mali exempli auctores sint? Nostrae ergo institutioni parabola ista plurimum feruit. Nam & studium verbi in nobis accendet eius consideratio, et docebit quae vitia cauenda sint ijs, qui illud non sine fructu audire volunt. Adhaec ministris ecclesiae consolationem dulcissimam hic adhibet Christus, ne sui ministerij fructu desperent, aut de illo temere deferendo cogitent, si non tantum proficiunt, quantum ipsi cupiebant. Vt enim agricola semè per agrum spargit, etiamsi aliud ab auibus mox denoratu iri, aliud inter spinas, aliud in locus petricosis periturū, multa etiam fortassis per grandines & tempestatum procellas vastanda fore, non omnino nescit: Ita verbi administros in suo officio constanter pergere couenit, ne per eos abslerreri, quos ad omnē doctrinam iam pridem obriguisse & incurabiles factos esse constat. Meminerint potius inter vepres & saxa terrae bona aliquam portiunculam inueniri posse, in quā verbi semen fructum suum proferat. Qui enim olim apud Israelitas, cùm ager non modò inultus sed potius desertum horribile videri possent, septem millia suorum electorum habuit, in quibus instituendis prophetae non frustra laborauerunt; idem ille omnibus seculis & vbiq; locorum aliquos habet, qui verbum ipsius digne audiunt, & ex eo meliores fiunt. At quia de his postea dicetur, quando ipse Christus parabolam iflam exponet, nunc ad alia transeamus, quae hic nobis sunt observanda.
units.tr: Now let us come to his sermon, which he delivered to the people from the boat. It consisted purely of parables, as may be seen in Matthew and Mark, who wrote down several that he related in order. Luke mentions only the parable of the sower, which served his hearers at that time admirably, and which also cures well the offence that usually arises from them. For just as it once might seem strange that so few believed, when the Son of God himself taught with such diligence and confirmed his doctrine by miraculous signs, so today many are greatly offended when they see so little fruit of the word among those who profess themselves evangelical. For it happens that many either doubt that the word of God is what is preached, or think that the Church has been wholly extinguished and destroyed, and therefore become uncertain with which assembly they ought to join themselves. Against these stumbling-blocks Christ applies this parable as a remedy, in which he sets forth, in a vivid picture, both the power and nature of God's word and the condition of the Church in this age. For first he teaches that the Church of God is where the word is lawfully preached, even if not all believe and obey. For just as a wise farmer sows seed only in a field, so there is no doubt that the field of God is where he scatters the seed of his word, and we should not be disturbed if we see it almost wholly overgrown with brambles and thorns, or even covered with stones. Next he shows that this word is in itself fruitful, but does not yield worthy fruit among all, because most bring unsuitable minds. From this he concludes that all the fault lies in the hearers, and that on account of them we ought not to doubt the truth or power of the word. Yet in saying this he also sharply pricks the hearers he then had, who indeed listened to the teacher with great eagerness and close attention, but most of whom, occupied with the worst affections, were like barren and untilled ground, in which a farmer's sowing is in vain. But if such people are judged by Christ, who came to him over long journeys, not without danger and manifest loss of their own goods, and in whom there burned a wonderful eagerness to hear him, how much more unhappy are we today, who long ago conceived a loathing for the word of God, who refuse to hear Christ preaching at our very doors, and whom pious magistrates must compel by edicts to come to the sacred assemblies and hear sermons, so that at least in some measure they may conform themselves to the Christian profession and not become authors of bad example to others? This parable therefore greatly profits our instruction. For its consideration will both kindle in us a zeal for the word, and teach what vices must be avoided by those who wish to hear it without loss. Moreover, Christ here offers the most sweet consolation to the ministers of the Church, so that they may not despair of the fruit of their ministry, or think rashly of abandoning it, if they do not advance as much as they desired. For just as a farmer, though he knows that some seed will be devoured by birds, some will perish among thorns, and some on rocky places, and that much may perhaps be destroyed by hail and storms, yet scatters seed over the field, so it is fitting that the servants of the word persevere constantly in their office, lest they be frightened off by those who are known to have long since grown numb to all teaching and to have become incurable. Rather let them remember that among the brambles and stones a small portion of good ground can be found, in which the seed of the word may bring forth its fruit. For the God who once among the Israelites, when the field seemed not only untilled but a dreadful wilderness, had seven thousand chosen ones, for whose instruction the prophets did not labour in vain, has the same God in all ages and in every place some who hear his word worthily and become better by it. But since these things will be spoken of later, when Christ himself expounds this parable, let us now pass on to the other matters which we must observe here.

units.la: Primum hic occurrit, quod in frequentissima auditorum turba non de cultu Dei externo & cere monijs disserit, sed de verbo Dei, vt huius virtutem omnes intelligant, seq; ad hoc digne audiendum praeparent. Ita vero non obscure admonet, verbum Dei omnibus externis ceremonijs praestare, & verum Dei cultum in illius studio potius quam in externis sacris consistere. Viderunt hoc olim quoque sancti homines, cum adhuc in vsu essent Leuitica ceremonia. Dauid certe vera legis Dei cognitione sibi obtingere in primis optat, neque aliud magis precatur, quam vt in illius semitis ambulet. Idem beatum pronuntiat non eum, qui sacra sacris accumulat & victimas caedit infinitas, sed eum, qui in lege Domini dies & noctes pia meditatione trasigit. Neq; temere ita senserunt pijssimi Dei cultores. Videbant enim omnem externum cultum in corporali exercitatione consistere, quae nihil aut parum vtilitatis habet. At Dei verbum ipsas hominum mentes Deo vendicat in fidei obedientiam, qui illi cultus est longe gratissimus. Externa ita sacra, si verbu ab illis auferas, oculos modo pascunt, & animum ad breue temporis momentum leuicula devotione detinent, quae fere superstitionem parit: at verbum Dei efficacissimum illud & salutiferum regenerationis semen est, ex quo per spiritus vir tutem omnes eos renasci oportet, qui regni coelestis haereditatem adire volent. Deniq; Dei verbum vitae regula, lucerna pedum nostrorum, diuinae voluntatis testimonium, doctrina simplicium, infirmorum consolatio, & iamiam pereuntium praesentissima medicina est. Recte ergo Christus in praesenti de illius natura atq; effectis, deque auditorum eius officio, disserit, apud eos, quorum saluti consultum volebat: & idem in docendo quidem assiduus fuit, circa ceremonias vero parcissimus, adeo, vt ne baptismum quidem ipse admidistrauerit, sicut Ioannes testatur. Sunt ergo inepti nimis, qui hodie ecclesia nouis quotidie ceremonijs onerat, et ijs quidem, quas vel ex antiquata per Christi Mosis lege postlimi nio reducunt, vel quae nudis atq; friuolis hominum superstitiosorum traditionibus niituntur. Istis debemus veri Dei ignorantiam & immanem omnis numinis contemptum cum effreni morum licentia, quae hodie passim regnum obtinent. Quid enim sub illis magistris infelix populus proficiat, qui totos dies in frigidissimis ceremonijs & cantionibus peregrinis consumunt, vix toto anno vnam aut alteram horam feriae verbi Dei praedicationi tribuunt? Eo vsq; certe multorum inscitia progressa est, vt no alias scripturas sacras esse putent, quam fragmenta illa Euangelica, quae in Postillis (quas vocant) extant. Et quia illorum quoq; interpretatio aut omnino nulla est, aut inepta & frigida est, quae neq; locis neq; personis praesentibus accommodatur, fructus ex illis nullus enasci potest. Sed recens indies verbi Dei ignorantia apud alios quidem superstitiones parit infinitas, alios autem in Epicurum vel Cyclopicum potius omnis religionis contemptum adducit. Quicunq; ergo ecclesias reformare, & religionem Christianam a sordibus repugare, aq; veri Dei cultum puriorem reducere voluerint eos de verbi Dei praedicatione instaurânda cumprimis solicitos esse oportet, quae sola hominum mentes erroribus liberabit, & eosdem Deo gratos atq; acceptos faciet.
units.tr: First, the point here is that in a very large crowd of hearers he speaks not about external worship and ceremonies but about the word of God, so that all may grasp its power and prepare themselves to hear it worthily. In this way he clearly warns that the word of God surpasses all external ceremonies, and that true worship of God consists in the study of that word rather than in external rites. The holy men of old also saw this, while the Levitical ceremonies were still in use. David, for his part, above all desires to attain a true knowledge of God's law, and asks for nothing more than to walk in its paths. He pronounces blessed not the man who heaps up sacred rites and slaughters countless victims, but the man who spends day and night in pious meditation on the law of the Lord. Nor did the most godly worshippers of God think this without reason. For they saw that all external worship consists in bodily exercise, which has little or no profit. But the word of God claims the minds of men for God in the obedience of faith, and this is by far the most welcome worship to him. External sacred rites, if you take the word away from them, only feed the eyes and hold the mind for a brief moment with a slight devotion, which almost gives birth to superstition. The word of God, however, is that most effective and saving seed of regeneration, from which all must be born again by the power of the Spirit who wish to enter the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Finally, the word of God is the rule of life, the lamp to our feet, the testimony of the divine will, the teaching of the simple, the consolation of the weak, and the most ready medicine for those who are already perishing. Rightly, then, Christ in this passage discourses about the nature and effects of the word, and about the duty of its hearers, to those whose salvation he wished to secure. He was indeed constant in teaching, but very sparing with ceremonies, so much so that he did not even administer baptism himself, as John testifies. So they are far too foolish who today burden the Church with new ceremonies every day, and indeed with those which they either bring back by a kind of postliminy from the law of Moses, which was abrogated by Christ, or which rest on the bare and frivolous traditions of superstitious men. To these men we owe the ignorance of the true God and the monstrous contempt of all divinity, together with the unbridled licence of morals, which now hold sway almost everywhere. For what can the unhappy people gain under such teachers, who spend whole days on cold ceremonies and foreign chants, and scarcely give one or two hours in the whole year to the preaching of God's word? Certainly the ignorance of many has gone so far that they think there are no holy Scriptures except those fragments of the Gospels which are found in the Postils (as they call them). And since the interpretation of these too is either entirely lacking or silly and dull, not suited to the places or the people present, no fruit can come from them. But this ever-fresh ignorance of God's word breeds endless superstitions in some, while it leads others to the Epicurean, or rather Cyclopean, contempt of all religion.
