Therefore whoever wishes to reform the churches, to purge the Christian religion of its filth, and to restore the purer worship of the true God, must above all be concerned to restore the preaching of God's word, which alone will free men's minds from errors and make them pleasing and acceptable to God.

units.la: Sed vt ad Christi redeamus, hoc quoq; in eius exemplo obseruari debet, quo re maximi momenti parabola ex vulgo aut re rustica desumpta illustrat. Quod in scripturis tam veteris quam noui testamenti admodum frequens esse sciunt, quicunq; illas vel a primo limine salutauerunt. Quod si causam quaeras, ex ijs, quae postea Christus dicet, duplex adduci poterit. Altera ad reprobos pertinet, cum quibus obscurius agi oportet, vt iusto Dei iudicio magis excaecati, tandem dignas suae impietatis paenas luat. Altera in electis est, qui etsi aenigmata ista non semper primo intuitu intelligant, mox tamen illuminantur, & res per terrenas adumbrata regni Dei mysteria melius intelligunt, deq; ijsdem cogitandi occasiones passim obuias habet, quibus ad diligentiorem illorum consideratione excitantur. Simul autem ista nos admonent, causam salutis nostrae & vniuersum religionis Christianae negotium per se planum & facile traditum esse. Nam etsi coelestia humanis excellentiora sint, tamen per res terrenas, adeo per eas, quae in vulgari & quotidiano vsu sunt, adumbrari possunt. Quo etiam pertinet, quod ista Deus pueris quoq; & mulieribus, opificibus & rusticis, omnis deniq; loci & ordinis hominibus tradi voluit. Minime ergo audiendi sunt, qui mysteria quaedam Eleusina in scripturis cotineri fingunt, quae nemo nisi vnctus & rasus intelligat, & inde colligunt, a librorum sacrorum lectione procul arcen dos esse omnes alios homines, ne erroribus quotidie nouis inuoluantur. Male ergo (si horum iudicium
units.tr: But to return to Christ: this too must be observed in his example, that he illustrates matters of the greatest importance by a parable drawn from common life or from rural affairs. Anyone who has greeted the Scriptures, even from the threshold, knows that this is very frequent in both the Old and New Testaments. If you ask the reason, a twofold one can be drawn from what Christ will say afterwards. One concerns the reprobate, with whom matters must be handled more obscurely, so that, blinded all the more by God's just judgment, they may at last pay the penalty due to their impiety. The other concerns the elect, who, although they do not always understand these riddles at first sight, are soon enlightened, and understand better the mysteries of the kingdom of God, which are shadowed forth by earthly things; and they have everywhere at hand occasions for thinking about these things, by which they are stirred to a more diligent consideration of them. At the same time these things remind us that the cause of our salvation and the whole matter of the Christian religion is plain in itself and easily taught. For although heavenly things are more excellent than human ones, yet they can be shadowed forth through earthly things, indeed through those which are in common and daily use. To this also belongs the fact that God wished these things to be taught to children and women, craftsmen and peasants, in short to men of every place and rank. Therefore those are by no means to be listened to who pretend that certain Eleusinian mysteries are contained in the Scriptures, which no one understands unless he is anointed and shaven, and who conclude from this that all other men must be kept far from reading the sacred books, lest they be daily entangled in new errors. Wrongly, therefore (if their judgment

units.la: Cap. VIII.
units.tr: Chapter VIII.

units.la: audiamus) humano generi Deus consuluit, et imprudes nimium dici poterit spiritus sanctus, qui ita loqui vult, ut à nemine intelligatur. Reprobis quidem omnia obscura & cæca sunt, quorum mentes Deus huius seculi (ut Paulus ait) obtenebrauit, & qui ipsi in mediam lucem tenebras inferunt. At alia est electorum ratio, in quorum gratiam balbutire etiam dignatur spiritus sanctus, ut rectius illum intelligant: adhæc fidelissimi præceptoris instar sese ad captum nostrum demittit, & in exemplis vulgaribus ea demonstrat, quæ nudis verbis proposita minus intelligeremus.
units.tr: let us hear them), God would seem to have dealt badly with the human race, and the Holy Spirit could rightly be called foolish, if he wished to speak in such a way that no one understood him. Indeed, all things are obscure and blind to the reprobate, whose minds, as Paul says, the god of this age has blinded, and who themselves bring darkness into the midst of light. But the case of the elect is different: for their sake the Holy Spirit condescends even to stammer, so that they may understand him more accurately. Moreover, like the most faithful teacher, he lowers himself to our capacity and sets forth in common examples what we would understand less well if it were put in bare words.

units.la: Arguitur præterea hic illorum error, qui simulachra vel imagines in templa inferunt, ut libri laicorum sint, quorum contemplatione de multis ad salutem pertinentibus admoneantur, qui scripturas legere non possunt. Peccant isti in Dei præceptum, quo imagines simul omnes ad cultum propositæ prohibetur. Nam nō postrema cultus species est, quod illis parem cū scripturis dignitatem tribuunt, quod per illas nos doceri volunt, quod ijsdem Deum et quæ ad hunc spectant exprimi posse affirmant: neq; prophetam audiunt, qui horrendum illud væ omnibus denuntiat, qui ex simulachris (quæ mendacij magistros vocat) volunt discere. Deinde ijdem stulto et inutili labore sese fatigant. Quid enim opus est ex mutis simulachris discere eos, qui scripturæ libros habent, & qui Deum in his loquentē quotidie audire possunt? Quæ ite væsania est administrorum verbi loco, quos in ecclesia sua Christus ordinauit, imagines mutas substituere? Offendant illi primùm, quis ipsis tantâ authoritate dederit, vel tantum iuris in ecclesiâ concesserit, ut ordinem in illa ab ipso Deo institutum mutare audeant? In templis certè Dei verbum sonare & Sacramenta exerceri debent, quæ si cum verbi doctrina proponantur, omnes hominis sensus ad beneficiorū Dei contemplationem ita excitant, fidemq; promissionum eius tam certo nobis obsignant, ut simulachris præterea alijs minimè sit opus. Adde his, quòd nihil in tota rerū natura est, quod non ipse spiritus sanctus in eū vsū destinarit, ut nos de regni Dei mysterijs & nostro officio admoneat. Ideo enim parabolas eiusmodi ex rebus vulgo vsitatissimis petit, ut quoties hæ in conspectū veniunt, toties de illis cogitandi occasio occurrat, quæ ijs adumbrantur. Quod ut rectius intelligat, quos vetus et diuturnus error aliquato obstinatiores fecit, exempla paucula addu cemus, quibus facilè ostendetur, quàm inutilis sit sumptus ille & labor, qui imaginibus fingendis impenditur. Per viam publicam ambulas, Annon succurrere debet illud Christi: Ego sum via veritas & vita: Nemo venit ad patrē nisi per me? Quid ergo necesse est in triuijs et capitis crucifixi imaginem proflare, quando ipsa via tibi Christum adumbrat? Per ostiū in ædes proprias siue alienas ingrederis. Quòd si hic quoq; in mente veniat Christi vox, Ego sum ostiū, per me si quis introierit, seruabitur, et ingredietur, & pascua inueniet, nō opus erit alia imagine, quæ tibi Christū repræsentet.
units.tr: Here too the error of those is refuted who bring images or pictures into churches, so that they may be books for the laity, by whose contemplation those who cannot read Scripture may be reminded of many things pertinent to salvation. These men sin against the command of God, by which all images set up for worship are forbidden. For it is not the least form of worship that they give such images equal dignity with Scripture, that they want us to be taught by them, and that they affirm God and the things that pertain to him can be expressed by them. Nor do they listen to the prophet, who pronounces that dreadful woe on all who wish to learn from images, which he calls teachers of lies. Furthermore, these same men wear themselves out with a foolish and useless labour. For why is there any need to learn from dumb images those who have the books of Scripture, and who can hear God speaking in them every day? What madness is it to substitute dumb images for the ministers of the Word, whom Christ has ordained in his Church? Let them first answer who gave them such authority, or granted them so much right in the Church, that they dare to change the order instituted in it by God himself. In churches, certainly, the Word of God ought to sound and the sacraments ought to be administered; and when these are set forth together with the teaching of the Word, they so stir up all the senses of man to contemplate the benefits of God, and so certainly seal to us the faith of his promises, that there is no need at all for other images. Add to this that there is nothing in the whole nature of things which the Holy Spirit himself has not appointed for this use, namely, to remind us of the mysteries of the kingdom of God and of our duty. For that is why he takes such parables from the most commonplace things, so that whenever these come into view, an occasion for thinking about the things they foreshadow may present itself. To understand this more accurately, let us add a few examples, by which it will be easily shown how useless is that expense and labour which is spent on fashioning images, especially for those whom long-standing error has made somewhat more obstinate. You walk along a public road: does not that saying of Christ come to mind, "I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6)? Why then is it necessary to set up in the crossroads a picture of the crucified Christ, when the road itself foreshadows Christ for you? You enter through a door into your own house or another's. But if here too the voice of Christ comes to mind, "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and find pasture" (John 10:9), there will be no need for another image to represent Christ to you.

units.la: Ita si sponsum cū sponsa sua ad templū deduci et nuptias legitimè celebrari videas, anno viuâ occurrit Christi & ecclesiæ imago, quæ arctissimum nostræ cum illo coniunctionis vinculum, eius erga nos amore, & quæ vicissim nos ei debemus officia, quasi in tabula depicta exhibet? Et vt præsenti paro bolæ insistamus, quando sementem fieri, aut segetes adolescere, vel in herba præfocari vides, mox tibi tota verbi Dei natura consideranda venit, et plus inde discès, quàm si simulachra simul omnia inspexeris. Eadem est ratio panis in mensa appositi, vini itē et vitis vel vineæ, fontium, piscationis, rei pastoritiæ, arborum, ouium, Solis & lucis, rerum deniq; omnium, quæ in vsu habetur. Nimium ergo simplices et rudes sunt, qui præterea imagines desiderant, inexcusabilis autem eorum est cōtumacia, qui cùm in scripturis probè versati sint, & ista non ignorent, adhuc tamen imaginum vsum in templis defendunt, & suo exemplo infelicis vulgi superstitionem confirmant. Sed plura de his alibi.
units.tr: Likewise, if you see the bridegroom led with his bride to the temple and the wedding lawfully celebrated, does not a living image of Christ and the Church meet you, which, as in a painted picture, sets before us the closest bond of our union with him, his love towards us, and the duties we owe him in return? And, to keep to the present parable: when you see seed being sown, or the crops growing up, or being choked in the blade, straightway the whole nature of the word of God comes to your mind, and you will learn more from this than if you had looked at all the images together. The same is true of the bread set on the table, and of wine, and of the vine or vineyard, of springs, of fishing, of pastoral affairs, of trees, of sheep, of the sun and light, and finally of all things that are in use. Therefore those are too simple and rude who still desire images besides these; but inexcusable is the obstinacy of those who, though well versed in the Scriptures and not ignorant of these things, nevertheless still defend the use of images in churches, and by their example confirm the superstition of the unhappy common people. But more on this elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc ad Christi discipulos transeamus, qui etiam ipsi parabolam istam non intellexerūt. Ea enim humani ingenij est hebetudo, ut quàmuis perspicuè proponantur quæ ad regnum Dei spectant, ea tamē nō percipiamus, eò quòd mens alijs affectibus fere occupata circa res huius seculi vagatur. Quod discipulis quoq; regni terreni expectatione detentis nō semel accidisse cōstat. Quò minus mirari nos decet, quòd non viderint quorsum seminis parabola spectarit, aut quid ea dominus docere voluerit. At laudem non vulgarem merentur, quòd suâ ignorantiâ non dissimulant rustico pudore: sed quia sibi persuasum habent, Christū non nisi de rebus arduis & cognitu necessarijs concionari, inter rogando potius infeitiâ suam profiteri, quàm aliquid ignorare malūt eorum, quæ sine salutis iactura ignorari nō possunt. Modestiæ autem argumentum est, quòd non in publico quærunt, neq; concionem Christi importuno clamore interrūpunt, sed (vt Matthæus et Marcus annotauerunt) priuatim cū eo agunt, cùm se domum iam recepissent. Imitemur nos illorum exemplum, & ferio proficiendi studio accensi nihil eorum omittamus, quae nos ad pleniorem cognitionem Christi & æternæ salutis possunt adducere. Quàm enim hoc Christo placeat, in præsenti videmus. Nam nō reijcit interrogantes, neq; suam ignorantiam illis contumeliosè exprobrat, sed amicè respondet: Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni Dei, reliquis autem per parabolas loquor, ut videntes non videant, & audientes non intelligant. Ita verò duo facit auditorum genera, & per comparationem Dei beneficium, quo discipuli frue bantur, amplificat, & simul iudicium Dei omnium oculis exponit, qui Iudæorum contumaciam imitantur. Primum genus discipulos Christi & cum his electos simul omnes comprehendit. His datum esse ait, ut mysteria regni Dei norint. Audiunt enim ut omnes placidæ vocem pastoris sui, & ea delectantur, ideoq; eandem sequuntur: Alterum genus reprobæ mentis homines habet, qui cùm Christi & veritatis odio toti ardeant, nihil videre vel intelligere volunt, imò oculos ipsi claudunt & aures obturant, ne ingerentem sese verbi divini lucem admittere cogantur. Id verò Isaiæ verbis enuntiat quæ alij Euangelistæ fuius recitant: ut partim causæ excæcationis iustæ plenius intelligantur, partim conster malum hoc non nouum esse, sed auitum siue hæreditarium, quo olim maiores quoq; illorum sibijpsis exitiû accerfuerint. At quia de hoc loco non semel alibi diximus, nunc sufficiat annotauisse, quantum scelus sit verbi divini contemptus & crassa illa ignorantia, qua multi etiam hodie sibiipsis tenebras offundunt. Ut enim inter Dei beneficia præcipuum est, quòd miseros nos verbi sui luce dignatur, & per illud nobis Filium suum & in hoc salutem omnem offert: ita non potest alia ingratitudo atrocior esse & impudentior, quàm si qui verbum illud audire dedignentur, & mendacia veritati, tenebras lucifcientes atq; volentes anteponant. Ita certè illa offenditur Deus, ut quasi ingenium & naturam suam mutarit, verbum suum aut omnino auferat, aut obscurius reddat, ut quod per se salutiferum & odor vivificus est ad vitam, istis hominibus toxici instar mortem atq; exitium afferat. Fieri ergo non potest, quin contemptus ille verbi omnes huius mundi partes hominibus infestas reddat, & extremæ perditionis causa sit. Et hoc nō obscurè docet Deus, quando in eo loco, quem in præsenti Christus adducit, Prophetæ interroganti, quam diu cæcitas illa duratura sit, respondet: Donec vastate fuerint vrbes, ut nemo sit qui inhabitet & in domibus nullus sit homo, tellusq; redigatur in solitudinem. Longissimè autem ablegabit homines Dominus, eritq; desolatio multa in terra. Quibus omnino consentiunt, quæ Iudæis, & Hierosolymæ Christus alibi minatur, eò quòd diem visitationis suæ non agnoscant. Horum itaq; consideratio nos excitet, ut cogitemus nos institutione opus habere, & proinde agnoscamus Dei bonitatem, qui illam per verbum nobis adhibet. Ampletamur autem totis animis Dei verbum, ut ex eo renati, germani Dei filij & Iesu Christi fratres atq; coheredes efficiamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now let us turn to the disciples of Christ, who themselves also did not understand this parable. For such is the dullness of the human mind that, however clearly the things pertaining to the kingdom of God are set forth, we do not perceive them, because our mind, occupied almost entirely with other affections, wanders among the things of this age. It is clear that this happened more than once even to the disciples, who were held by the expectation of an earthly kingdom. So much the less ought we to wonder that they did not see to what end the parable of the seed pointed, or what the Lord wished to teach by it. Yet they deserve no small praise, because they do not dissemble their ignorance out of rustic shame; rather, since they were persuaded that Christ preached only about lofty matters and those necessary to know, they preferred to confess their ignorance by asking questions, rather than to remain ignorant of things which cannot be left unknown without loss of salvation. Moreover, it is a sign of modesty that they do not ask in public, nor interrupt Christ's sermon with unseasonable clamour, but (as Matthew and Mark have noted) speak with him in private, once they had withdrawn home. Let us imitate their example, and, kindled with a zeal for advancing, let us omit nothing that can lead us to a fuller knowledge of Christ and eternal salvation. How pleasing this is to Christ we see in the present passage. For he does not reject those who ask, nor does he reproach them contemptuously for their ignorance, but answers kindly: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest I speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand" (Matt. 13:11, 13). In this way he makes two kinds of hearers, and by comparison he magnifies the benefit of God which the disciples enjoyed, and at the same time sets before the eyes of all the judgment of God upon those who imitate the obstinacy of the Jews. The first kind comprehends the disciples of Christ and, together with them, all the elect. To these, he says, it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God. For they listen, like sheep, to the voice of their shepherd, and delight in it, and therefore follow it. The second kind comprises men of reprobate mind, who, since they burn wholly with hatred of Christ and of the truth, wish to see or understand nothing; indeed they close their own eyes and stop their ears, lest they be compelled to admit the light of the divine Word which presses in upon them. This he declares in the words of Isaiah, which the other evangelists also recite: partly so that the cause of this just blindness may be understood more fully, and partly so that it may be established that this evil is not new, but ancestral or hereditary, by which their forefathers once brought ruin upon themselves. But since we have spoken of this passage more than once elsewhere, it is enough now to have noted how great a crime is contempt of the divine Word, and that gross ignorance by which many even today bring darkness upon themselves. For as among God's benefits the chief one is that he deigns to enlighten us wretched men with the light of his Word, and through it offers us his Son and in him all salvation, so no ingratitude can be more atrocious and more shameless than when men disdain to hear that Word, and prefer lies to the truth and darkness to light. God is certainly so offended by this that, as if he had changed his nature and disposition, he either takes away his Word altogether or makes it more obscure, so that what in itself is saving and a life-giving fragrance unto life becomes, for these men, like poison, bringing death and destruction. It is not possible, therefore, that this contempt of the Word should not make every part of this world hostile to men, and be the cause of utter perdition. And God teaches this plainly, when, in the passage which Christ now cites, he answers the prophet asking how long that blindness would last: "Until the cities are laid waste, so that there is no one to dwell in them, and there is no man in the houses, and the land is brought to desolation. The Lord will remove men far away, and there will be great desolation in the earth" (Isa. 6:11-12). Entirely in agreement with this are the threats which Christ elsewhere makes against the Jews and Jerusalem, because they did not recognise the day of their visitation. Let the consideration of these things therefore stir us up to think that we have need of instruction, and so let us acknowledge the goodness of God, who offers it to us through his Word. Let us embrace the Word of God with our whole souls, that, being born again through it, we may become true sons of God and brothers and co-heirs of Jesus Christ; to whom be blessing, honour, glory, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 76.

units.la: Est autem hæc parabola: Semen est verbum Dei. Qui autem in viam, ij sunt qui audiunt: deinde venit diabolus, & tollit sermonem è corde eorum, ne, cum crediderint, seruentur.
units.tr: The parable is this: "The seed is the word of God. Those by the way side are they that hear; then cometh the devil, and taketh away the word out of their hearts, lest they should believe and be saved."

units.la: Omnis tam noui quàm veteris testamenti scriptura, non aliud nobis perinde ut Dei verbû commendat. Hoc enim vitæ lucernam, morû atq; actionum omnium regulam, panē & potum animæ, semen regenerationis, deniq; saluificam Dei potentiā dicere consueuit, & simul omnes homines ad huius studium & crebram meditationem excitat. At ea est hominum corruptio, ut multi illud omnino reijciant, & hostiliter oppugnent, pleriq; verò, qui huius studiosi videri volūt, id absq; omni profectu audiāt. Est hæc multorû et nocentissimorû scandalorum causa. Alij enim de verbo, quod prædicatur, dubitare incipiunt, an scelicet Dei verbû sit, cuius fructum adeò rarum aut fere nullum conspicantur. Alij, quorum audacia longius progreditur, id aperte negant, & auditorû vitia eam vnā ob causam odiosè exagitant, ut suam Dei verbo authoritatē detrahere possint. Faciunt hoc mira impudentia. Anabaptistæ, qui hoc potissimū argumento rudes et rerū non satis peritos circumueniunt, ut eos ab ecclesijs abstrahant. Multi quoq; dum verbi prædicatione tam parum profici vident, verbū fingūt, nō scriptū, quod per revelationes peculiares nobis innotescat: ita verò illusionibus Satanæ fenestram aperiunt. Accedit his, quòd non raro verbi administros suæ industriæ & laborum tædere incipit, vt de deferenda vocatione sua cogitent, ne absq; fructu cum incurabili impiorum contu-macia amplius luctari cogantur. Exempla huius impatientiæ in præstantissimis prophetis, Elia & Ieremia, extant: Nam ille quidē è terra profugere instituit, & cum Deo expostulat, quòd alijs prophetis omnibus è medio sublatis, ipse solus hoc saxum voluere cogatur: hic verò exclamat: Væ mihi ô mater mea, quòd me peperisti virū litigatorem, & virū controuersiæ vniuersæ terrę, &c. Et Isaias non vno loco de eorū paucitate queritur, qui verbo per ipsum prædicato credebant. At omnibus istis Christus suo exemplo medetur. Etsi enim ex sua doctrina fructum ferè nullum enasci videret apud Iudæos, qui instar terræ inculte & sterilis semen verbi nequaquam in animos demittebat, pergit tamen docendo, neq; aliquam concionandi occasionem negligit. Deinde cùm ex infirmioribus multos offendi sciret, parabolam istam proponit, quà & verbi Dei naturam & hominum mores atq; ingenia euidentissimè depingit. Docet enim illud per se viuū & efficax esse, hominum autē vitio fieri, quòd non apud omnes, qui hoc audiunt, dignum fructum ædat. Quæ admonitio, cùm admodum necessaria sit, ipse eam ita petentibus discipulis diligentius interpretatur, & singulis auditorum generibus applicat. Quo loco, priusquam ad Christi verba accedamus, duo nobis consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: All of Scripture, both the New Testament and the Old, commends nothing to us so much as the Word of God. It is accustomed to call this the lamp of life, the rule of all morals and actions, the bread and drink of the soul, the seed of regeneration, and finally the saving power of God, and at the same time it stirs all people to study it and to meditate on it often. Yet such is human corruption that many people utterly reject it and attack it with hostility, while most of those who want to seem devoted to it hear it without any profit. This is the cause of many very harmful scandals. Some begin to doubt the word that is preached, whether it is indeed the Word of God, since they see its fruit so rare or almost nonexistent. Others, whose boldness goes further, flatly deny it, and bitterly censure the faults of the hearers for this one reason alone, so that they can detract from the authority of the Word of God. They do this with remarkable shamelessness. The Anabaptists especially use this argument to deceive the simple and those not well versed in affairs, so that they may draw them away from the churches. Many also, when they see so little progress from the preaching of the Word, make up a word that is not written, which is made known to us through private revelations; and in this way they open a window to the illusions of Satan. Added to this is that the ministers of the Word often begin to be weary of their own diligence and labours, so that they think of abandoning their calling, lest they be forced to struggle any longer, to no profit, against the incurable obstinacy of the wicked. Examples of this impatience are found in the most outstanding prophets, Elijah and Jeremiah. For the one resolved to flee from the land and complained to God that, with all the other prophets removed from the midst, he alone was forced to roll this stone; the other cries out: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me a man of strife and a man of contention to all the earth," and so on. And Isaiah, in more than one place, complains of the small number of those who believed the word preached through him. But Christ heals all these by his own example. For although he saw that almost no fruit would spring from his teaching among the Jews, who, like uncultivated and barren land, by no means let the seed of the Word sink into their minds, he nevertheless went on teaching and did not neglect any opportunity for preaching. Then, knowing that he offended many of the weaker sort, he put forward this parable, in which he most vividly portrays both the nature of the Word of God and the morals and dispositions of people. For he teaches that the Word is living and effective in itself, but that it comes about through human fault that it does not bear worthy fruit among all who hear it. Since this admonition is very necessary, he explains it more carefully to the disciples when they ask for it, and applies it to each kind of hearer. At this point, before we come to the words of Christ, two things come before us for consideration.

units.la: Primum, quomodo prædicari debeat verbum Dei, de quo etsi non semel sit dictum, sæpius tamen dicendum est propter eos, qui cùm ipsum verbum palàm damnare aut ex ecclesia eijcere non audeant, ad artes conuersi, verum illius vsum impedire conantur. Aiunt enim sufficere, si obiter recitetur, in dignißimè autem eos ferunt, qui verum eius sensum diligenti scripturarum collatione eruunt, atque ex eodem doctrinas, admonitiones, hortationes, increpationes & cõsolationes eliciunt, quas auditoribus accommodant, prout rerum & temporum ratio postulare videtur. At perinde homines illi faciunt, ac si quis pannum quidem multū proferri velit, nolit autem ex eo vestes scindi, quæ corporibus hominum seruiant, aut etiam vestes iam factas induere prohibeat. Quam autem stupidi sint plerique in iis obseruandis, quæ ad ipsos maximè pertinēt, quotidianis exemplis docemur, & in semetipsis sin-guli sentient, modò oculos aperire velint. Et confutantur alteri illi doctrinæ iudices siue Censores ipsius Christi exemplo, qui etsi occulta spiritus virtute discipulorum mentes illuminare posset, vt pa-rabolam intelligerent & suæ institutioni accommodarent, ordinariam tamen rationem sequi volu-it, & quod illis obscurius erat, clariori interpretatione illustrauit. Fecit idem olim Deus, quando le-gem, quam decem præceptis comprehensam promulgauerat, multis exposuit, & pro delictorum omnium generis casuum ratione in plures species diduxit, vt omnis loci hominibus vitæ totius regula esset, & iudices ex eadem iudiciorum suorum formulas petere possent. Neq; eo contentus, insuper le-gis interpretes dedit Prophetas, qui populum de eius vsu quotidie admonerent. Secuti sunt hæc ex-empla Apostoli quoq;, quorum omnium vestigijs eos insistere decet, qui docendi munus in ecclesia su-stinent. Nimium autem arrogantes sunt, qui nouam docendi rationem ecclesijs obtrudere, & vete-rem tot exemplis & omnium sæculorum vsu comprobatam abolere conantur.
units.tr: First, how the Word of God ought to be preached. Although this has been said more than once, it must be said again and again on account of those who, not daring to condemn the Word itself openly or cast it out of the church, turn to tricks and try to hinder its use. For they say it is enough if it is recited in passing, but they bear with ill grace those who draw out its true sense by careful comparison of the Scriptures, and from it derive doctrines, admonitions, exhortations, rebukes and consolations, which they apply to the hearers as the nature of things and of the times seems to require. But those men act just as if someone wanted a great deal of cloth to be brought forth, yet did not want clothes that serve people's bodies to be cut from it, or forbade anyone to put on clothes already made. How stupid most people are in observing those things that pertain most to themselves, we are taught by daily examples, and each will feel it in himself, if only he is willing to open his eyes. And those other judges or censors of doctrine are refuted by the example of Christ himself, who, although by the hidden power of the Spirit he could have enlightened the minds of the disciples so that they understood the parable and applied it to their instruction, nevertheless chose to follow the ordinary method, and what was rather obscure to them he illustrated by a clearer explanation. God did the same once, when he expounded at length the law which he had promulgated, comprehended in the ten commandments, and divided it into many species according to the circumstances of every kind of offence, so that there might be for people in every place a rule of their whole life, and judges might draw from it the forms of their judgments. And not content with this, he also gave the prophets as interpreters of the law, who would admonish the people daily about its use. The apostles also followed these examples, and all those who undertake the office of teaching in the church ought to follow in their footsteps. But they are too arrogant who try to thrust a new method of teaching upon the churches and to abolish the old one, which has been approved by so many examples and by the practice of all ages.

units.la: Secundò admonet nos locus iste, vnde verbi Dei interpretatio peti debeat, quæq; huius sit regula, quæ falli aut aberrare non sinat. Vendicat, sibi authoritatē interpretandi Scripturas Romanus Pontifex, neq; ad hoc munus aliquem admittit, qui nõ ipsius charactere fuerit insignitus. Sed quā turpiter in verbo Dei iam multis seculis hallucinati sint Pontifices, notius est quā vt demonstrari oportet. Nos ergo Apostolorū exemplū obseruemus, quos Christū interrogauisse nuper audiuimus, qui nūc parabolæ, cuius ipse author fuerat, interpretem quoq; agit fidelißimum. Itaq; ex eiusdem ore nos quoq; verum verbi Dei sensum requirere debemus. Docuit hoc olim Deus per oraculi typū, quando ad Propitiatorij venientibus responsa dabat, & ideo Dominus inter Cherubim habitas dicebatur. Quò etiam referri debet, quod in casus difficilioribus ad Summū Sacerdotem recurrebat, vt legem ex eius ore (vt Malachias ait) audirent. Nam sacerdotes illos Christi personā siue typū sustinuisse scimus. Quod si obijcias, Christū iam pridem in cœlos abijsse, neq; coram interrogari à nobis posse, & ideo necesse esse, vt aliquis illius vices in terris obeat. Respondemus, ab illo quidem Euangelij præco-nes esse institutos, non autem tanta eos authoritate instruxisse, vt ipsius tanquam absentis vicarij sint, aut pro oraculo habeatur quicquid illi dixerint, sed aliam rationem monstrauisse, qua cum ipso in colloquium venire, & ipsum de patris voluntate interrogare possimus. Scripturas enim dedit, in quibus ipse loquitur, & vt illas scrutemur monuit. Si quis ergo locus occurrit dubius aut ob-scurum scurus, scripturarum collatione nos vti decet, & (vt Paulus docuit) ad fidei analogiā omnes locos exigere, quam qui sequuntur, falli non possunt. Sunt enim certa fidei Christianæ capita, quæ Symbo lo (quod Apostolicum vocant) continentur. Et hanc Apostolicā traditionem & fidei verę regulam esse, vetustissimi & Apostolorū temporibus proximi scriptores, Irenæus & Tertullianus, testatur. Illis ergo insistamus, & pernitiosè errare non poterimus. Nam etsi non semper germanū & propriū loci controversi sensum attingamus, nihil tamen statuemus, quod nos ab vnius Dei cultu & vera salu tis ratione abducat. Adeundē quoq; Canonem, ceu Lydiū lapidem, probare poterimus aliorum interpretationes, neq; latere nos poterit fucus, si quē nobis aliqui facere conantur. Poterat res ista exemplis illustrari, sed quia passim illa occurrunt, & quædū alibi adduximus, eadē aut similia nunc repetere superuacaneum foret. His præmissis ergo, Christum suæ parabolæ optimum interpretem audiamus.
units.tr: Second, this passage reminds us from where the interpretation of the Word of God ought to be sought, and what the rule of it is, which does not allow it to be mistaken or to go astray. The Roman Pontiff claims for himself the authority to interpret the Scriptures, and admits to this office no one who has not been marked with his own character. But how shamefully the Pontiffs have gone astray in the Word of God for many centuries is better known than needs to be demonstrated. Let us therefore observe the example of the apostles, who, as we have just heard, questioned Christ, who now is himself the most faithful interpreter of the parable of which he was the author. Therefore we too ought to seek the true sense of the Word of God from his own mouth. God taught this of old through the type of the oracle, when he gave answers to those who came to the mercy seat, and for this reason he was said to dwell between the cherubim. To this also must be referred the fact that in more difficult cases they had recourse to the high priest, so that they might hear the law from his mouth, as Malachi says. For we know that those priests bore the person or type of Christ. But if you object that Christ has long since departed into the heavens, and cannot be questioned by us face to face, and that therefore it is necessary that someone should take his place on earth, we answer: he indeed appointed heralds of the gospel, but did not equip them with such authority that they should be his representatives as though he were absent, or that whatever they said should be held as an oracle. Rather, he showed us another way by which we can come into conversation with him and question him about the Father's will. For he gave us the Scriptures, in which he himself speaks, and he admonished us to search them. If therefore any passage occurs that is doubtful or obscure, it becomes us to use a comparison of the Scriptures and (as Paul taught) to bring all passages into conformity with the analogy of faith, which those who follow cannot go astray. For there are certain heads of the Christian faith, which are contained in the creed that they call Apostolic. And the most ancient writers, Irenaeus and Tertullian, who lived closest to the times of the apostles, bear witness that this Apostolic tradition is the true rule of faith. Let us therefore keep to these, and we shall not be able to err grievously. For although we may not always attain the genuine and proper sense of a disputed passage, we shall nevertheless decide nothing that draws us away from the worship of the one God and from the true way of salvation. We shall also be able, by testing them against the canon, as the Lydian stone, to prove the interpretations of others, and no deceit, if anyone tries to practise it upon us, will escape us. This matter could be illustrated with examples, but since they occur everywhere, and since we have already adduced some elsewhere, it would be superfluous to repeat the same or similar ones now. With these things set forth, let us then hear Christ, the best interpreter of his own parable.

units.la: Primo quia per omnes parabolæ partes seminis vox repetitur, quid ea significetur, docet. Semen (inquit) est verbum Dei, id est, per semen hic ipsum Dei verbū figuratur & intelligitur. Vtitur autem verbo substantiuo Est, non vt doceat, semen illud naturale, quod terræ mandatur, reuera & ef sentialiter ipsissimum Dei verbum esse: sed vt ostendat, hoc per illud verè adumbrari, & verbū hoc suo modo semen esse: dū in regenerandis hominibus hoc ipsum agit, quod reliqua semina in frugibus producendis agere solent. Itaq; nō superuacaneum est verbum illud substantiuum Est, neq; illo ludit Christus, etiamsi eo Tropicè vtatur. Quod propter eos annotamus, qui in locutionibus sacramentalibus hodie hac vna particula nobis negotium faciunt, quasi nobis in ipsum Christū ius & imperium vendicemus, eò quòd non secundum literam, sensu nimum crasso accipimus, quod ille de pane mysti-co pronuntiauit. Imò sunt qui nos in Cœnæ verbis particulā illam prorsus abijcere aiunt, vt qui nihil in tota illa actione, quam inanem & otiosam significationē agnoscamus. Faciunt illi nobis atrocem iniuriam. Agnoscimus enim Christi vocem, qui ita loqui debuit, vt non tam quid panis ille significet doceret, sed insuper testaretur quoq; se panē illum vitæ esse verum, qui fide manducatus nos pascat ad vitam æternam. At quia de his alibi commodius dicetur, nunc quàm probè seminis typus Dei verbo conueniat videamus. Vbi tamen semper memoria tenendum est, Christū de eo verbo loqui, quod per ministros ecclesiæ prædicatur. Nam mox eorum, qui hoc audiunt, mentione facit. Pro cul ergo faciessant, qui nobis verbum quoddam Dei non scriptum obtrudere conantur, & eo figmento religionem & salutis rationem omnem prorsus dubiam & incertam reddunt. Rectè autem & verè verbum istud semen dicitur. Nam vt semen res vilis & exigua videtur; ita Dei verbum homi- num iudicio contemptissimum est, imò quæ hoc continentur dogmata, huius seculi sapientibus vel stolida & stulta hominum superstitiosorum commenta, vel etiam scandali plena esse putantur. Vt verò semini vis generandi inest, quæ omnem humani ingenij captum superat, & quā frustra in a-lijs rebus humana industria & arte factis requiras (quis enim, nisi experientia edoctus, viso grano aliquo, ex eo vel spicam culmo procero nitentem, vel olus latis foliis sese extendens, vel etiam arbo-rem alto vertice & ramis hinc inde diffusis superbam atq; fructibus graue enasci putaret?) Ita Dei verbum virtute occulta & nobis inscrutabili hominum mentes mutat, voluntatem nouā generat, actiones sanctas & honestas gignit, & non singulos modo homines innouat, sed totius regnū & orbi terrarum vniuerso nouam faciem inducit. Ea denique agit inter homines, quæ nullis prudentissimo rum virorum consilijs, nulla ingeniosissimorum hominum arte, nulla regum potentia perfici, vel eti am quò minus fiant, impediri possunt. Et huc referri debet parabola de grano sinapis, qua hanc verbi sui vim atq; naturā Christus apud Matthæū describit. Deinde vt semen fructū non feret, quoad in horreis asseruatur, neq; etā si vt gemus fieri solet, auro includatur, vel manibus aut sinu gestetur, sed terræ sulcis mandetur oportet: ita etsi Dei verbū in libris descriptum habeas, auro, argento, sericō & gemmis exornes, in manibus & ore circumferas, nullus tamen ex eo fructus nascetur, qui nos Deo cōmendet, & salutem nostram adiuuet, nisi intra animi penetralia reconditum operandi locum inueniat. Vidi ego in celeberrimo verbis Imperialis cœnobio codicē multo auro & gemmis pretiosissimū, in quo quatuor Euangelistarū historia in membranā tenuissimam descripta erat, & qui non nisi honoris gratia viris illustribus ostendebatur. At quis inde fructus, cùm in ea vrbe superstitiones re-gnarent, & nulla esset Christi cognitio? Satius certè fuisset vel ex sordidissimo libello Dei verbum prædicari, vt homines docerentur de ijs, quæ ad veri Dei cultum & salutem æternam faciunt. Præterea, ut non aliam ob catsam semina sulcis comtiuntur, quàm ut fructum edant: ita nō alius praedicationis verbi finis constitui debet, quàm ut inter homines fructificet, dum ex hoc renati innouantur & Deo viuunt, qui prius per delicta mortui erant. Hic ergo scopus verbi administris propositus sit, non ut eruditione & eloquentiam suam ostentent, aut populi fauore sibi concilient, siue aures inanis vocis oblectatione demulceant. Et haec causa est, ob quam Spiritus sanctus non doceri modò vult homines, verùmetiam admonitionibus & hortationibus, imò increpationibus & minis quoque vrgeri, vt officium faciant. Et quemadmodum semente facta de terra indicare licet, fecunda ne sit & fructibus ferendis idonea, an sterilis & maledictioni obnoxia: ita vbi Dei verbum inter homines praedicatur, mox hominum ingenia & mentes reuelantur. Nam qui ex electorum & ouium Christi numero sunt, ij pastoris sui vocem agnoscunt, & hanc secuti innouantur: reprobi verò, quia sese vrgeri sentiunt, maiori contumacia sese Deo opponunt, & quotidie in peius proficiunt. Et vt ad eundem ignem cera quidè mollescit, lutum verò durius & intractabilius redditur: ita eiusdem verbi praedicatione pij mouentur, vt relictis studijs prioribus voluntarium Deo obsequium praestent, impij verò praefractio res facti magis aduersus illum proterunt. Non ergo verbum accusari meretur, si quid huius accidat, sed hominum vitiositas agnosci debet, eoque magis annitendum est, vt illi Deus remedium adhibeat. Vt enim nullus ex semente fructus nascetur, nisi caelestis benedictio accedat, & ipse Deus incrementum det: ita neq; verbi praedicatio apud homines frugifera erit, nisi illorum mentes Deus aperiat, sicut de Lydia purpuraria scribitur. Quod vt ad preces nos excitare debet: ita monet quoq; ne quid ad ministrorum verbi industriae tribuamus, sed omnem nostri profectus gloriam vni Deo transcribamus, qui animos nostros spiritus virtute trahere & illuminare dignatus est.
units.tr: First, because the word "seed" is repeated through every part of the parable, he teaches what it signifies. "The seed," he says, "is the word of God." That is, the seed here figures and represents the word of God itself. He uses the substantive verb "is," not to teach that the natural seed committed to the earth really and essentially is the very word of God, but to show that the word is truly prefigured by it, and that the word is seed in its own way, since in regenerating people it does what other seeds usually do in producing crops. So the verb "is" is not superfluous, and Christ is not playing with words, even though he uses the figure. We note this on account of those who today make trouble for us over this one particle in the sacramental words. They suppose that we claim a right and power over Christ himself, because we do not take in the crude sense, according to the letter, what he said about the mystical bread. Some even say that we throw this particle away altogether in the words of the Supper, as if we recognised nothing in the whole action beyond an empty and idle sign. They do us a monstrous wrong. For we acknowledge the voice of Christ, who had to speak so that he would not merely teach what that bread signifies, but would also testify that he himself is the true bread of life, which, eaten by faith, feeds us to eternal life. But since these matters will be discussed more fittingly elsewhere, let us now see how well the figure of the seed fits the word of God. Yet we must always keep in mind that Christ is speaking of that word which is preached through the ministers of the Church, for soon he mentions those who hear it. Far away, then, be those who try to force upon us some unwritten word of God, and by that invention make religion and the whole way of salvation utterly doubtful and uncertain. The word is rightly and truly called seed. For just as seed seems a cheap and small thing, so the word of God is most despised in human judgement. The doctrines it contains are thought by the wise of this age to be either the foolish and silly inventions of superstitious people, or even full of offence. But just as seed has a power of generating which surpasses all the grasp of human intellect, and which you would seek in vain from human industry and art in other things (for who, unless taught by experience, seeing some grain, would think that from it there might spring a spike standing up on a tall stalk, or a herb spreading its broad leaves, or even a tree proud with a high crown and branches spreading on every side, heavy with fruit?), so the word of God by hidden power, which is beyond our understanding, changes human minds, generates a new will, begets holy and honourable actions, and renews not only single people but also a whole kingdom, and brings a new face to the whole world. Finally, it accomplishes among people what no counsels of the wisest men, no skill of the most gifted, no power of kings can bring about, or prevent from being done. To this belongs the parable of the grain of mustard seed, in which Christ, in Matthew, describes this power and nature of his word. Again, just as seed does not bear fruit so long as it is kept in barns, nor even if, as is often done with gems, it is enclosed in gold, or carried in the hand or in the bosom, but must be committed to the furrows of the earth, so even if you have the word of God written in books, adorned with gold, silver, silk and gems, and carry it about in your hands and on your lips, no fruit will spring from it that commends us to God and helps our salvation, unless it finds a place of working hidden in the inner recesses of the mind. I once saw, in a very famous imperial monastery, a codex most precious with much gold and gems, in which the history of the four Evangelists was written on very thin parchment, and which was shown only as a mark of honour to distinguished men. But what fruit came from it, when superstitions reigned in that city and there was no knowledge of Christ? It would certainly have been better to preach the word of God even from a most shabby little book, so that people might be taught about the things that pertain to the true worship of God and eternal salvation. Furthermore, just as seeds are committed to the furrows for no other reason than to bear fruit, so no other end of the preaching of the word should be set than that it bear fruit among people, while those who have been born again through it are renewed and live to God, though before they were dead through their sins. Let this aim, then, be set before the ministers of the word: not that they display their learning and eloquence, or win the favour of the people, or charm the ears with the pleasure of an empty voice. And this is why the Holy Spirit wishes not only that people be taught, but that they be urged on to do their duty with admonitions and exhortations, and even with rebukes and threats. And just as, after sowing, one can judge from the ground whether it is fertile and fit to bear fruit, or barren and liable to curse, so when the word of God is preached among people, straightway the dispositions and minds of people are revealed. For those who belong to the number of the elect and the sheep of Christ recognise the voice of their shepherd and, following it, are renewed. But the reprobate, because they feel themselves pressed, oppose themselves to God with greater stubbornness, and every day advance for the worse. And just as wax softens at the same fire that makes clay harder and less workable, so by the preaching of the same word the godly are moved to give voluntary obedience to God, leaving their former pursuits, while the wicked, hardened in their deeds, become more reckless against him. Therefore the word does not deserve to be blamed if anything of this kind happens; rather, the viciousness of people must be acknowledged, and all the more effort must be made that God apply a remedy to it. For just as no fruit springs from seed unless heavenly blessing comes, and God himself gives the increase, so the preaching of the word among people will not be fruitful unless God opens their minds, as is written of Lydia the seller of purple. This ought to stir us to prayer; it also warns us not to attribute anything to the diligence of the ministers of the word, but to ascribe all the glory of our progress to God alone, who has deigned to draw and enlighten our minds by the power of his Spirit.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Christi expositione, qui de verbi auditoribus diligenter admodum disserit. Vbi animadvertes, nihil hoc loco de apertis & iuratis verbi hostibus agi, sed ijs, qui in externo ecclesiae coetu censentur, & attentione atq; obedientiae studium egregie simulant. At si inter hos maior fere eorum pars est, apud quos Verbi fructus euanescit, quid obsecro de alteris illis iudicabimus, qui aperto furore aduersus Deum insurgunt? At dum inter auditores suos ita distinguit Dominus, duplicem eorum ecclesiam facit, Hypocriticam nimirum & Christianam verè. In illa ponit tria hominum genera qui omnes verbum abiicit, fructu audiunt, & in his simul causas indicat, quibus singuli impediuntur, ne ex illo fructum aliquem referant. Primum genus eos habet, qui semen illud diuinum non admittunt in animos, sed nuda & otiosa audicione contenti nihil praeterea de suo officio cogitant. Alterum eorum est, qui admittunt quidem verbum, sed non ita, vt radices in ipsis agere et fructu ferre possit. Tertij sunt, qui etsi in ipsis radices agat verbum, hoc tamen intra se praefocari patiuntur, ne vnquam seges illa adolescat. Et haec quidem a nobis ita considerari debent, vt vitia, quae hic perstringuntur, cauere, alteros verò illos imitari discamus, quos in vera ecclesia Christus numerat.
units.tr: But let us go on in the exposition of Christ, who speaks very carefully about the hearers of the word. Here we should notice that nothing is said at this point about the open and sworn enemies of the word, but about those who are counted in the outward assembly of the Church and cleverly feign attentiveness and zeal for obedience. But if among these is the greater part of those in whom the fruit of the word vanishes, what, I beg you, shall we judge about those others who rise up against God in open rage? By thus distinguishing among his hearers, the Lord makes their Church twofold: the hypocritical, namely, and the truly Christian. In the former he places three kinds of people, who all hear the word and bear no fruit, and in these he also indicates the causes by which each is hindered from bearing any fruit from it. The first kind includes those who do not admit that divine seed into their minds, but, content with bare and idle hearing, think of nothing further about their duty. The second are those who indeed admit the word, but not in such a way that it can strike roots in them and bear fruit. The third are those who, although the word does take root in them, nevertheless allow it to be choked within them, so that the crop never grows up. These things should be considered by us in such a way that we learn to beware of the vices that are here censured, and to imitate those others whom Christ counts in the true Church.

units.la: Videamus ergo primum illud genus eorum, qui semen verbi in viam excipere dicuntur. Sunt hi qui audiunt quidem, sed (vt modò diximus) non in animos vsq; demittunt verbum, vt id penes se recondant & diligenti meditatione foueant, vt aliquando fructum suum ferat. Hi viae publicae comparantur, vel terrae quae instar viae tritissimae indurata nequicquam feritur, cùm in summam modo superficiem semina excipiat. Sunt ergo tales, qui animos habent nimium patentes, quiq; dum quibusdam cogitationibus & opinionibus locum dant, nihil in toto fidei & religionis negotio certi habere possunt, & proinde intra animos suos aut Deum omnino negant, aut religionem pro indifferenti habent, quae certis legibus astringi neque possit neque debeat. Idem ergo isti in religione faciunt, quod olim in philosophia gentilium Pyrrhonij, qui nihil unquam certi constituebant, sed in aliorum modo sententijs oppugnandis versabantur: quos idcirco Graeci Scepticos dixere, quod semper ampliori consideratione opus esse dicerent. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, quibus nemo vnquam satisfaciat. Hi tamen ne pro impijs & ab omni religione alienis habeantur, ad conciones quidem sacras accedunt, sed non eo animo, vt Dei verbum esse credant, quod illis praedicatur, cui omnem hominis intellectum atque sensum subijci oporteat. Audiunt ergo & aliquid facturi videntur, sed mox aut priores opiniones in mentem reuocant, aut nouas admittunt, & dum in illis aliquam veri similitudinem sibi fingunt, de eo dubitare incipiunt, quod ex Dei verbo iam didicisse videbantur. Qui verò inter hos optimi sunt, hi ex verbo Dei Lesbiam regulam fingunt, quam omnium nimm sententijs atq; opinionibus accomodant, & ea ingenij volubilitate vti norunt, vt cum omnem religione iampridem animo eiecerint, omnes tamen probare videantur. Habentur ergo isti in pretio apud plerosq; & supremam modestiæ & prudentiæ laudem referunt. Sed revera animos habent quaus via publica patentiores, quibus nouæ in singulas horas suggestiones occurrunt, neq; vnquam prosi-cient, nisi mentem mutauerint.
units.tr: Let us look first at that kind of people who are said to receive the seed of the Word on the path. These are the ones who do hear, but (as we have just said) do not let the Word sink down into their minds, so as to keep it within themselves, cherish it by diligent meditation, and so let it bear its fruit in time. They are compared to the public road, or to ground hardened like a well-trodden path, which is sown in vain, since it takes the seed only on its very surface. These people, then, have minds too open; while they give room to various thoughts and opinions, they can have nothing certain in the whole business of faith and religion, and therefore in their minds they either deny God altogether, or regard religion as a matter of indifference, which can be bound by no fixed laws and ought not to be. These men, then, do in religion what the Pyrrhonists once did in the philosophy of the Gentiles: they never laid down anything as certain, but busied themselves only with attacking the opinions of others. For this reason the Greeks called them Sceptics, because they said that a fuller consideration was always needed. There is a great number of such people today, whom no one can ever satisfy. Yet, so that they are not thought impious and alien to all religion, they do come to the holy sermons, but not with the mind to believe that what is preached to them is the Word of God, to which every human understanding and feeling ought to be subjected. So they listen, and seem about to act, but soon either call back their former opinions into mind or admit new ones, and while they invent for themselves some semblance of truth in these, they begin to doubt what they seemed to have already learned from the Word of God. But the best among these people make of the Word of God a Lesbian rule, which they adapt to the opinions and views of everyone, and they know how to use such a pliant cleverness that, though they have long since cast out all religion from their minds, they still seem to approve of all. These men are therefore held in high esteem by most, and win the highest praise for modesty and prudence. But in truth they have minds more open than a public road, where new suggestions meet them every hour, and they never make progress unless they change their minds.

units.la: De hoc igitur nos graviter Christus admonet. Venit (inquit) diabolus, & tollit sermonem è cor de eorum, ne cum crediderint, seruentur. Quo loco multa consideratione dignissimum est, quod isti cum diabolo rem esse ait. Putant quidem illi leuiculum esse quod agunt, & se ab hominibus solis dis-sentire, quos vel superstitio manus, vel cæca sapientiæ propria persuasio hinc inde impellat, aut in sen-tentia semel animo concepta pertinaciores faciat. Sed totū hoc diaboli opus est. Quia enim is perdi-tos vult homines, & instar famelici atq; rugientis leonis oberrans semper quærit quos deuoret, ferre non potest, vt vitæ semen, per quod ab interitu liberamur, in animis nostris radices agat. Itaq; dum illud audiunt isti, mox ille obrepit, & (vt Christus ait) aues suas immittit, quæ verbum hoc ex animis eorum auferant, vel ita conculcent, vt germinare nullo modo possit. Et hic quidem primus locus debe-tur prauis affectibus & iam ante cœceptis opinionibus, à quibus recedere multis nefas & ignominio-sum esse videtur. At his admissis, mox omnis verbi fructus impeditur, & paulatim diffluunt quæ nō male intellecta putabantur. Excitat præterea nouas cogitationes Satan, quas probabilitatis specie vestit, vt in verbi doctrina nihil certi haberi persuadeat. Et in primis nocentissima avis est Securi-tas, qua multi decepti, nihil ad se pertinere putant, quæ Dei verbo traduntur. Est hæc Harpyiæ in-star, quia dū virgineo & amico vultu sese insinuat, mox fœdissima ventris proluuie & unguibus rapacissimis semen illud partim horribiliter fœdat, partim discerpit & aufert, ex quo nos renasci et ad vitam æternam pasci oportebat. Accedunt his illusores, qui mirifica & plus quam scurrili dicacitate in dubium vocant omnia, quæ Dei verbo traduntur, & Deum nobis fingunt, qui mortalia non curet, sed sola animorum nostrorum intentione contentus, nihil præterea requirat. Est & aliud auium his omnibus turpius & nocentius, eorum scilicet, qui & animarum immortalitatem, & corporum resurrectionem aperte negant, & ea ratione ipsissima religionis fundamenta in hominum animis conuellunt. Non possunt ergo Dei verbo credere, quicunq; illis locum dant, & proinde absq; fructu audiunt, neq; salutem assequuntur. Vt enim hæc nobis per verbum offertur, ita eius percipiendæ nulla alia est ratio, quam fides, quæ apud tales nulla esse potest.
units.tr: Christ warns us seriously about this. "The devil comes," he says, "and takes away the word from their hearts, lest they believe and be saved." Here it is most worthy of careful consideration that he says these people have to do with the devil. They think what they are doing is a trifle, and that they differ only from other men, whom superstition or the blind self-persuasion of their own wisdom drives this way and that, or whom a view once conceived in the mind makes more obstinate. But all this is the devil's work. For since he wants men lost, and like a hungry, roaring lion wanders about always seeking whom he may devour, he cannot bear that the seed of life, through which we are freed from destruction, should take root in our minds. So while these people are hearing it, he at once creeps in and, as Christ says, sends his birds, which carry this word away from their minds, or trample it so that it cannot sprout in any way. And this first place is indeed given to depraved affections and opinions already held before, from which to withdraw many think is wrong and shameful. But once these are admitted, straightway all fruit of the word is hindered, and little by little those things slip away which were thought to be rightly understood. Satan also stirs up new thoughts, which he clothes with a semblance of probability, so as to persuade that nothing certain is to be held in the teaching of the Word. And above all the most harmful bird is Security, by which many are deceived into thinking that what is handed down in the Word of God does not concern them. She is like a Harpy, for while she insinuates herself with a maidenly and friendly face, straightway with the most foul discharge of her belly and with most rapacious claws she partly befouls that seed in a dreadful way, and partly tears it apart and carries it off, though by it we ought to have been born again and nourished to eternal life. To these are added the mockers, who with wonderful and more than buffoon-like wit call into doubt all that is delivered in the Word of God, and invent for us a God who does not care for mortal things, but, content only with the attention of our minds, requires nothing else. There is also another bird more shameful and more harmful than all these, namely those who openly deny both the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, and by this means overthrow in men's minds the very foundations of religion. Those who give place to such men therefore cannot believe the Word of God, and so they hear without fruit and do not obtain salvation. For as this is offered to us through the Word, so there is no other way of receiving it than faith, and among such people faith cannot exist.

units.la: Proderit ergo tanti mali remedium nouisse, quod mox apparebit, si rem omnem diligentius ex-pendamus. Cogitemus ergo nos in Dei conspectum venire, quoties ad audiendum verbum cætus sa-cros ingredimur; venire autem non iudices aut censores, sed discipulos, qui doctrinæ institutione & consolatione opus habeant. Proderit hoc ad excutiendam securitatem & domandam ferociam, qui-bus vitijs plerique impediti, vel non attendunt ijs quæ dicuntur, vel eadem superbè contemnunt: vt ni-hil ad se pertinentia. Et hoc est, quod Iacobus his verbis docet: Abiecta omni sordicie & excremen-to malitiæ cum lenitate aut mansuetudine admittite insitum sermonem, id est, eum qui Ministro-rum opera inseritur. Vt enim in artibus discendis nihil proficiunt ferocis ingenijs iuuenes, qui præ-ceptores contemnunt, & se iam plus satis dicicisse sibi persuaserunt: ita neque ex verbi diuini doc-trina aliquem fructum referent, nisi qui procul abiecta confidentia animi, se ipsos Spiritus Sancti magisterio regendos præbent. At quia plerique de verbo minus honorifice sentiunt, quòd in solam Ministri personam respiciant, proderit animum altius attollere & cogitare, illos Dei nomine loqui & Iesu Christi legatos agere, qui de illis dixit: Qui vos audit, me audit: qui verò me audit, eum au-dit qui misit me. In eo autem Ministri auditores iuuare debent, vt nimirum eo spiritus ardore & gravitate sermonem prædicent, vt aperta Christi per ipsos loquentis experimenta præbeant, sicut Paulus Corinthijs nimium petulanter ipsum contemnentibus dicebat. Deinde meminerimus, vix alibi nobis Satanam magis insidiari, quàm hic vbi maximè salus nostra agitur. Exemplo nobis sint dæmoniaci, in quibus immundi spiritus tunc sæuissimos sese præbuerunt, & modò horrendis clamoribus, modò ementitis blanditijs suum in miseros imperium retinere conati sunt, quando Christum præsentem adesse viderunt. Diaboli igitur suggestionem esse ne dubites, quicquid tibi in mentem venit, quo vel ab audiendo verbo revocaris, vel vt eius Veritatem in dubium trahas, moneris. Itaq; vigilare, & simul precibus apud Deum instare oportet, ne is nos suggestionibus prauis succum bere sinat, vtq; nos à malo liberet. Accedat his tertia cura, vt tibi ipsi applices quæcunq; dicuntur, ne que putes in concionibus sacris de rebus superuacaneis aut nihil ad te pertinentibus agi. Vbi necessefuerit, vt innatam vitiositatem & quæ ex ea nascuntur vitia semper ob oculos habeas. Ex eo enim intelliges, nihil aduersus sceleratissimos quosq; & flagitia deterrima tam grauiter dici, quo non tu quoq; opus habeas ad frenanda carnis desideria, quibus optimi quiq; abripiuntur præter omnē expectationem, si vel modicum illis indulserint. Debent ad hoc nos excitare multorum exempla, quæ partim in scripturis habentur, partim quotidie in oculos incurrunt. Imò exemplis non multis opus est, quando quæ in nobis ipsis quotidie experimur, stimuli acerrimi loco nobis esse poterunt. In horum consideratione (inquam) si non officanter versemur, primo huic vitio facilè medebimur, proculitem pellemus à nobis infelix illud diaboli anitium, quo pulso verbum ita audiemus, vt ex eius semine in filios Dei renati cælestis regni hæredes efficiamur per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The remedy for so great an evil will therefore be of use, which will soon appear if we weigh the whole matter more carefully. Let us then consider that we come into the sight of God whenever we enter the holy assembly to hear the Word; and we come not as judges or censors, but as disciples, who need instruction and comfort in doctrine. This will help to shake off security and tame the pride by which most people are hindered, who either pay no attention to what is said or proudly despise the same things as having nothing to do with them. And this is what James teaches in these words: "Putting aside all filthiness and overflow of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls." For just as young men of wild temperament make no progress in learning the arts, when they despise their teachers and have persuaded themselves that they have already learned enough, so neither will they gain any fruit from the teaching of the divine Word, unless they cast far away the confidence of their own mind and submit themselves to be governed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit. But because most people think less honourably of the Word, looking only at the person of the minister, it will be useful to raise the mind higher and to think that those men speak in the name of God and act as ambassadors of Jesus Christ, of whom he said: "He who hears you hears me, and he who hears me hears him who sent me." In this the hearers of the minister ought to help, namely by preaching the word with such fervour and seriousness of spirit that they show the open proofs of Christ speaking through them, just as Paul said to the Corinthians, who contemned him too insolently. Next let us remember that Satan lies in wait for us almost nowhere more than here, where our salvation is chiefly at stake. Let the demoniacs be examples to us: in them the unclean spirits showed themselves most savage, and now with horrible cries, now with feigned flatteries, they tried to keep their dominion over the wretched men, when they saw Christ present. Do not doubt, then, that whatever comes into your mind by which you are called back from hearing the Word, or by which you are urged to call its truth into question, is the suggestion of the devil. Therefore we must watch, and at the same time press on with prayers before God, that he may not allow us to succumb to wicked suggestions, and that he may deliver us from evil. To these let there be added a third care: apply to yourself whatever is said, and do not think that in holy sermons things superfluous or nothing to do with you are being treated. Where it is necessary, keep always before your eyes your innate vitiousness and the vices which arise from it. For from this you will understand that nothing is said so severely against the most wicked and the most vile crimes but that you too have need of it, to bridle the desires of the flesh, by which the best of men are carried away beyond all expectation if they have indulged them even a little. The examples of many should rouse us to this, some of which are in the Scriptures and some of which daily meet our eyes. Indeed, there is no great need of many examples, since what we daily experience in ourselves can serve us as the sharpest goads. If, I say, we are not idle in the consideration of these things, we shall easily cure this first fault, and drive far from us that unhappy nest of the devil; and with it cast out, we shall so hear the word that from its seed, reborn as sons of God, we shall be made heirs of the heavenly kingdom through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 77.

units.la: Qui vero supra petram, ij sunt, qui cum audierint, cum gaudio excipiunt sermonem, sed isti radicem non habent, qui ad tempus credunt, & tempore tentationis abscedunt. Quod autem in spinas cecidit, ij sunt, qui audierunt, sed profecti à sollicitudinibus & diuitiis ac voluptatibus vitæ suffocantur, nec fructum proferūt. Quod autem in bonam terram cecidit, ij sunt qui in corde honesto & bono auditū sermonem retinent, & fructum adferunt per patientiam.
units.tr: But those on the rock are the ones who, when they have heard, receive the word with joy, yet they have no root. They believe for a while, and in the time of temptation they fall away. What fell among the thorns are those who have heard, but who, being carried away by cares, riches and the pleasures of life, are choked and bear no fruit. What fell on good ground are those who, with an honest and good heart, hold fast the word they have heard, and bring forth fruit with patience.

units.la: NOn absq; grauibus causis Dominus et Seruator noster Iesus Christus tam diligenter de vitijs disserit, quibus verbi Dei profectus in nobis impeditur. Ita enim quid ijs cauendum sit docet, qui illud cum fructu audire volunt, & simul scandalis medetur, quæ enasci solent, quando pauci ex verbi prædicatione meliores, multi vero etiam deteriores, aut saltem in pietate languidiores fiunt. Est ergo doctrina hæc admodum necessaria, & ideo vt magis perspicua fiat, parabola vestitur, cuius interpretationem ipse Christus subijciens, verbi auditores (vt nuper diximus) in duas quasi ecclesias distinguit. Prima hypocritas habet, qui etsi verbi studium initio simulent, vel etiam à pietate non omnino sint alieni, multis tamen aliis vitijs obnoxij sese detineri patiuntur, quo minus proficiant. Sunt inter hos tria hominum genera, inter quæ primum locum tenent, qui etsi verbū audiunt, id tamen non admittunt in animos, sed duri nimium & paculi diabolicis suggestionibus locū dant, quæ semen hoc quàm primum feritur, rursus ex animis ipsorū auferunt. Et de his quidē in proximo sermone egimus. Sequuntur alia duo genera eorum qui Verbum admittunt quidem, vt fructum facturi videantur, mox tamen impedimentis aliunde oblatis reuocantur, ne fructus iste ad maturitatem perueniat. His omnibus deinde electorum seu verè piorum ecclesia opponitur, qui vt par est, ad Verbum accedunt, & ex eo renati pietatem dignis fructibus testantur.
units.tr: The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ did not discuss so carefully the vices by which the progress of the Word of God is hindered in us without serious reasons. For he teaches what must be guarded against by those who wish to hear it with fruit, and at the same time he remedies the offences that usually arise when, from the preaching of the Word, few become better, many indeed become worse, or at least grow more lukewarm in piety. This teaching is therefore very necessary, and so that it may be clearer it is clothed in a parable. Christ himself gives its interpretation and divides the hearers of the Word, as we said recently, into two kinds of church. The first contains hypocrites, who, although at the start they pretend zeal for the Word, or are not altogether strangers to piety, nevertheless allow themselves to be held back by many other vices, so that they do not make progress. Among these there are three kinds of people. The first place belongs to those who hear the word but do not admit it into their minds. Being too hard and too shallow, they give room to diabolical suggestions, which snatch the seed from their minds as soon as it is sown. We have already spoken of these in the previous sermon. Then follow two other kinds of those who indeed receive the Word, as if they were going to bear fruit, but soon they are called back by hindrances offered from elsewhere, so that this fruit does not reach maturity. Over against all these is set the church of the elect, or of those who are truly pious, who approach the Word as they ought, and being born again through it, witness to their piety by worthy fruits.

units.la: Porro secundum genus eorum, qui verbum inutiliter audiunt, eos habet, qui semen illud excipiunt in loca petricosa, vbi radices viuas agere non poterit, & proinde ne adolescere quidem, vt aliquando fructum edat. Differunt hi à primis in eo, quod illi nullam fructus spem vnquam de se præbent, cum verbum in ore solum & cordis superficie (vt sic loquar) gestent, vbi mox difluit atq; euanescit: isti verò illud in animos vsq; admittunt, eo delectantur, ideo magnificè laudant, & magna alacritate rem agentes bonis omnibus de se spem maximam faciunt: tandem verò, si quæ grauior tentatio incidit, non constant in ipsis, sed turpiter deficiunt, quando per seuerantia in primis opus erat. Recte ergo per loca precios eos intelliges, qui animos habent natura vehementiores, & proinde mox promptè quicquid bonum, verum & salutare esse apparet, non autem adhuc subacti sunt vera Dei cognitione, neque ceruicem suam adhuc emollierunt, vt Christi iugum suscipere & ferre possint. Isti cum natura minimè mali sint, ad Euangelij prædicationem alacri mente accedunt, & magnam ex ea voluptatem capiunt, quando gratuita Dei misericordia & peccatorum remissio miseris mortalibus annunciatur, quando item superstitiones accusantur, impostores arguuntur, et omnes vocantur ad capessendum libertatis per Christum acquisitae beneficium. Sequuntur ergo doctrinam istam, eandem omnibus commendant, eius praecones laudibus in coelum usque euehunt, denique Euangelij patronos & vindices sese praebent acerrimos. At quae tanti feruoris atque alacritatis causa est? Hac nimirum, quod praesentibus modo & temporariis bonis intenti, carnalia fere cogitant; & sub libertatis praetextu fere nō aliud quàm ieiuniorum & disciplinae omnis relaxationem, sub gratiae Dei promissione peccandi licentiam & impunitatem, adhaec opes, honores, multorum amicitias, pacem huius seculi & omnia alia animo concipiunt, quae carni magnifica & iucunda videntur. Et hos quidem ad tempus credere dicit Christus, fidei nomine ornans primum illum assensum, quem Euangelio praebent, qui tamen durabilis non est, sed cum tempore mutatur, ut postea audiemus; ideoq; apud Matthaeum & Marcum πρόσκαιρος vocat, partim quod tempori seruiunt (ut proverbio dicitur) proper priuata commoda; partim quod mox deficiunt, si quid accidat, quod ipsis durius & cum periculo aliquo coniunctum esse videtur. Tales olim fuerunt, qui Christum miraculis & signis florentem magnis agminibus secuti sunt, & eidem regni honorem sponte detulerunt, cum ipsius vera cognitione destituerentur. Tales Samaritani Sichemitae fuere, quos vnius mulierculae testimonium excitavit, ut ad Christum exirent, & eum in urbem reciperent. Ad horum album Galatae etiam pertinent, qui Paulum ut Dei angelum excepere, & eundem oculis proprijs chariorem habuerunt, mox autem publicum lieuitatis & inconstantiae exemplum facti sunt. Et horum ingens numerus est hodie, quorum leuitas & defectio cum multos offendat, semper meminisse oportet, Christum nos de illis admonuisse, & nunquam praedicari Euangelium, quin aliquos ex hoc genere auditores habeat.
units.tr: Next, the second kind of those who hear the word to no profit are those who receive that seed on rocky places, where it cannot put down living roots, and so cannot even grow up to bear fruit at any time. These differ from the first in this: the first never give any hope of fruit in themselves, since they hold the word only on the tongue and on the surface of the heart, so to speak, where it soon melts away and vanishes. But the second admit it right into their minds, take delight in it, therefore praise it greatly, and with great eagerness they give high hopes of themselves in every good matter. But at last, if some heavier temptation arises, they do not stand firm, but shamefully give way, when perseverance was needed above all. Rightly, then, you will understand by the rocky places those who have naturally more vehement minds, and therefore quickly and readily embrace whatever appears good, true and salutary, but who are not yet subdued by the true knowledge of God, and have not yet softened their neck so that they can take up and bear the yoke of Christ. Since these are by nature not at all bad, they come to the preaching of the gospel with a ready mind, and take great pleasure in it, when the free mercy of God and the forgiveness of sins are announced to wretched mortals, when superstitions are likewise condemned, impostors are exposed, and all are called to seize the benefit of liberty acquired through Christ. Therefore they follow this teaching, commend it to all, raise its heralds to heaven with praise, and finally show themselves the most fierce defenders and champions of the gospel. But what is the cause of such zeal and eagerness? Clearly this: being intent only on present and temporary goods, they think mostly of carnal things. And under the pretext of liberty they conceive in their minds almost nothing but the relaxation of fasts and of all discipline; under the promise of God's grace, a licence and impunity for sinning; besides these, riches, honours, the friendships of many, the peace of this age, and all other things that seem splendid and pleasant to the flesh. Of these people Christ says that they believe for a while, adorning with the name of faith that first assent which they give to the gospel. Yet it is not lasting, but changes with time, as we shall hear afterwards. Therefore in Matthew and Mark he calls them [πρόσκαιρος], partly because they serve the time (as the proverb says) for private advantages, and partly because they soon fail if anything happens which seems harsher to them and attended with some danger. Such were those who once followed Christ in great crowds, flourishing in miracles and signs, and of their own accord offered him the honour of the kingdom, though they lacked the true knowledge of him. Such were the Samaritans of Sychar, whom the testimony of a single little woman roused to go out to Christ and receive him into their city. To this class also belong the Galatians, who received Paul as an angel of God and held him dearer than their own eyes, but soon became a public example of levity and inconstancy. And the number of such people is huge today. Since their levity and defection offend many, we must always remember that Christ warned us about them, and that the gospel is never preached without having some hearers of this kind.

units.la: Proderit autem diligentius videre, quid isti patiantur. In parabola femine in loca petricosa cecidisse, & enatu exaruisse dixit, nimirum exorte aestu (ut apud Matth. loquitur) eo quod non haberet humorem, quae terra plantis per radices in ipsa actas submini strare solet. Id in praesenti breuiter & uno quasi verbo exponens, eos tempore tentationis abscedere, id est, a fide deficere, vel potius ea abnegare, & ecclesiae societatem relinquere dicit. Per aestum ergo tentationes graviores intelligit, quibus succumbunt, qui fidei radices veras non habent, neque viua & solida Christi cognitione illustrati sunt. Sunt autem tentationes in duplici differentia. Aliae enim ex cruce & afflictionibus enascuntur, quas per petuas Euangelij comites esse, tam saepe diximus.
