Et recte has per ignis aestum adumbrat Christus, quia his fides nostra perinde ut aurum igne probatur atque illustrior redditur. Afflictiones enim patientia pariunt, patientia experientiam, haec vero spem, quae nos fallit & pudefieri non finit. Quid, quod ignis iste carnis scoriam excoquit, innatas cupiditates restinguit, cogitationes noxias procul arcet, securos antea animos excitat, ut maiori fidei ardore in Deum respiciant, & relictis mundi studijs illi se totos consecrent? Et hic quidem crucis atque afflictionum effectus est in electis, qui Dei verbum ita audiunt, ut vera Iesu Christi cognitio in animis eorum vivas radices agat. At longe aliae sunt hypocritarum & hominum carnalium conditio, qui non serio pietatis sensu afficiuntur. Hi enim quia vt religionem omnino nullam habent, sed simulant tantum, aut illa quaestu & utilitate metiuntur, aestu illo crucis offendi solent, & cum solidi auri in illis nihil sit, scoria illa, quae inani fulgore ad tempus splenduit, omnis in fumum euanescit. Vel ut praesentis parabolae vestigijs insistamus, ut seges in loco petris obsito enata, nimio Solis ardore aduritur, eo quod humore nullo vegetetur, qui ad fructus perducendos necessarius est: ita isti aduersis & periculis superati nullo fidei constantis fructum edunt, cum solida Christi cognitione careant, quae solana aduersus mundi & huius principem inuitos reddit. Neque mirum est hoc istis accidere, quando electi etiam saepe succumbunt ad tempus, ut fidem aut dissimulent turpiter, aut etiam aperte negent (ut in Petro est videre) qui tamen mox in viam redeunt, eo quod semen illud Verbi, cum vere in animis eorum radices egerit, totum emori non possit. Est deinde aliud tentationum genus, quod intra nos ex innato carnis ingenio & eius vitiositate oritur. Haec enim cupiditates omnis generis accedit, quibus homines carnales abrepti, se totos peccato mancipant. Et ex his quidem multi (ut supra diximus) Euangelij doctrinam cum gaudio excipiunt, eo quod hanc licentiae morum patrocinari, opum, honorum & voluptatum materiam submini strare arbitrantur. At ijdem vbi carnis mortificationem, sui ipsius abnegationem, vitae nouitatem & innocentiam praecipi, scelera argui & accusari, seq; seuerius corripi & vrgeri sentiunt, ut vita sua professione digna
units.tr: It will be useful to look more carefully at what these people suffer. In the parable he said that the seed fell on rocky places and, once sprouted, dried up, namely when the heat arose (as Matthew puts it) because it had no moisture, which the earth usually supplies to the plants through the roots sent down into it. Explaining this briefly in the present passage, as if in a single word, he says that they withdraw in the time of temptation, that is, they fall away from faith, or rather deny it, and leave the fellowship of the church. By the heat, then, he means the heavier temptations to which those succumb who do not have true roots of faith, and who have not been enlightened by a living and solid knowledge of Christ. Temptations, however, are of two kinds. For some arise from the cross and afflictions, which, as we have said so often, are the perpetual companions of the gospel. Christ rightly represents these by the heat of fire, because by them our faith is tested, just as gold is tested by fire, and is made more brilliant. For affliction produces patience, patience produces experience, and experience produces hope, which does not disappoint us nor allow us to be put to shame. And what of the fact that this fire burns away the dross of the flesh, quenches innate desires, drives away harmful thoughts, rouses minds that were previously secure, so that they look toward God with a greater ardour of faith, and, leaving the pursuits of the world, devote themselves wholly to him? This is indeed the effect of the cross and of afflictions in the elect, who hear the word of God in such a way that the true knowledge of Jesus Christ strikes living roots in their minds. But the condition of hypocrites and carnal men is far different, since they are not affected by any earnest sense of piety. For since they have no religion at all, but only pretend to have one, or measure it by gain and advantage, they are usually offended by that heat of the cross; and since there is nothing of solid gold in them, that dross which shone for a time with an empty glitter vanishes altogether into smoke. Or, to follow the trail of the present parable: as a crop sprouting on a place covered with stones is scorched by the excessive heat of the sun, because it is not nourished by the moisture necessary for bringing fruit to maturity, so these people, overcome by adversities and dangers, bear no fruit of constant faith, since they lack that solid knowledge of Christ which alone makes us unconquered against the world and its prince. Nor is it strange that this happens to them, since even the elect often succumb for a time, so that they either shamefully conceal their faith, or even openly deny it (as may be seen in Peter), yet they soon return to the right path, because that seed of the Word, once it has truly struck roots in their minds, cannot die altogether. Then there is another kind of temptation, which arises within us from the innate nature of the flesh and its corruption. For this includes desires of every kind, by which carnal men, carried away, surrender themselves wholly to sin. Of these, indeed, many (as we said above) receive the doctrine of the gospel with joy, because they think it will serve as a defence for licence of morals and as material for riches, honours and pleasures. But when these same people perceive that mortification of the flesh, self-denial, newness of life and innocence are being enjoined, that their crimes are being exposed and condemned, and that they are being more severely rebuked and pressed, so that they might live a life worthy of their profession...

units.la: L viuant, tunc prøinnata nobis malitia illos nouis quasi flammis accendi videmus, & maiori quàm antea furore in omnem licentiam profundi. Nam vt Poeta olim dixit, Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusq; negata. Itaq; illi eò plus sibi licere putant, quòd Euangelio aures præbuerint, quòd multis alijs hoc admittendi fuerint authores, quòd propter eius ministros multorum odia incurrerint: ideoque indignè secum agi dicunt, quòd ob rem tantillam publicè accusentur, aut ipsis negetur quod multis alijs liceat, qui aperte aduersus veritatem coniurauerunt. Fit ergo, vt aut disciplinæ impatientia superati manifestam faciant ab ecclesia secessionem, aut Euangelij prætexu ad peccandi licentiam abutantur, & paulatim intermoriente in animis ipsorum Verbi semine, nihil præter inanem professionem nominis Christiani retineant, quæ illis tandem in iustæ damnationis testimonium seruiat. Est ergo malum hoc nocentissimum, quod per terram petricosam adumbratur, & ex his apparet, non sufficere, vt Verbum leuiter in animos admittatur, nisi penitus reconditum radices agat.
units.tr: When they live as the Gospel teaches, we see them, as if kindled by new flames from the malice innate in us, plunge into every licence with greater fury than before. For as the Poet once said: "We always strive for what is forbidden, and we desire what is denied." So they think they may do all the more because they have lent their ears to the Gospel, because they have been the authors of it for many others, and because on account of its ministers they have incurred the hatred of many. They say they are treated unworthily, because they are publicly accused for so small a matter, or because what is allowed to many others who have openly conspired against the truth is denied to them. It therefore happens that either, overcome by impatience with discipline, they openly secede from the Church, or they abuse the Gospel as a pretext for licence in sinning, and, as the seed of the Word gradually dies out in their minds, they keep nothing but the empty profession of the Christian name, which in the end serves as testimony to their just condemnation. This evil is therefore most harmful, and it is shadowed forth by the stony ground. From this it appears that it is not enough for the Word to be received lightly into the mind, unless it has been hidden deep down and takes root.

units.la: Sed proderit remedium tenere, quo malū istud arceri poterit. Ostendet hoc Christus cap.14. vbi per parabolas ex re militari et ab ædificantibus desumptas monet, vt seipsos diligenter explorent, quicunq; ipsi nomen dare voluerint. Præparatione ergo diligenti et virium nostrarum probatione opus est, ne temere concepta animi alacritas, & quâ de fide nostra præbemus, spes subitò evanescant. Ad hanc præparationem duo in primis necessaria sunt. Alterū est vera Christi cognitio: vt nimirum intelligamus, quis ille sit, quid in eo nobis Pater dederit, et quæ regni eius in terris sit conditio. Hæc qui ignorant, ij tantum non Iudaico errore decepti, Regē & regnū terrenum somniant, et terrena commoda in illo quærunt, ideoq; non possunt non offendi, quando spe sua frustrantur. Semper ergo ob oculos versetur, Dei Filium nobis æternæ salutis authorē datū esse, et regnū eius non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde non præsentis vitæ commoda, sed cœlestia & æterna bona in illo quæri debere. Horū autem spē, dum hic viuimus, crucis amaritudine condiri, vt procul abiecto rerum huius seculi studio ad sola cœlestia aspiremus. Ista consideratio nos excitabit, vt ad crucē ferendam nos præparemus: quod qui faciunt, illa non possunt offendi, vt nec miles classico & prælij instantis periculo consternatur, qui iam pridè se armis idoneis instruxit. Alterū est, vt de Verbo Dei rectè iudicemus, & in quem finem prædicetur, intelligamus. Atqui illud in scripturis salè dici scimus, nimirū quòd vitā omnem condi-at, & à carnalium desideriorū putredine conseruet: Lucernam ite, quia via præceptorū Dei nobis mostrat, et peccata, quæ vel ipsi ignoramus, vel maligne dissimulamus, arguit: Gladium deniq;, eò quòd animos penetrat, et mactatis cupiditatibus belluinis, nos Deo viuentem hostia sistit. Quæ cum verbi propria sint, quid mirum, si mordeat, arguat, vulneret, & quacunq; alia ratione carni molestia exhibeat? Quis enim vero rationis vsu præditus, creaturis alijs indignatur, si naturali motu ad id feratur, ad quod illas naturæ opifex destinauit? Quæ ergo temeritas vel insania potius est, indignius ferre eius Verbi effecta, cuius virtute tota hæc mundi machina regitur? Certè, qui duo iam rectè intra animos suos expendūt, ij tanquam arnū aliquod excolentur, vt semen illud Verbi admittant, et fructus ferant sua vocatione dignos. Debet autem his coniungi modestiæ et humilitatis studium, ne primo succcessu confidentiores facti, postea fatiscant, vbi grauior aliqua moles incumbit.
units.tr: But it will be useful to hold to the remedy by which this evil can be kept off. Christ shows it in chapter 14, where, through parables drawn from warfare and from builders, he advises that whoever wishes to give his name to him should carefully test himself. Careful preparation and a testing of our own strength are therefore needed, so that the eagerness of mind conceived rashly, and the hope which we show concerning our faith, do not suddenly vanish. Two things are chiefly necessary for this preparation. The first is a true knowledge of Christ: namely, that we understand who he is, what the Father has given us in him, and what the condition of his kingdom on earth is. Those who are ignorant of these things, and who, deceived by a Jewish error, dream of a king and an earthly kingdom, and seek earthly advantages in him, cannot help being offended when their hope is disappointed. Let it therefore always be before our eyes that the Son of God has been given to us as the author of eternal salvation, that his kingdom is not of this world, and that accordingly we ought to seek in him not the advantages of the present life but heavenly and eternal goods. While we live here, our hope of these things should be seasoned with the bitterness of the cross, so that, having cast far away the pursuit of the things of this age, we may aspire to heavenly things alone. This consideration will rouse us to prepare ourselves to bear the cross; those who do so cannot be offended, just as a soldier who has long since equipped himself with suitable arms is not dismayed by the trumpet call and the danger of the battle now at hand. The second thing is that we judge rightly concerning the Word of God, and understand to what end it is preached. Now we know that it is said in the Scriptures, quite rightly, that it orders the whole of life and preserves it from the rot of carnal desires; that it is a lamp, since it shows us the way of God's commands, and it reproves the sins which we either do not know or wickedly pass over; and finally that it is a sword, because it penetrates the minds and, having slain the bestial lusts, presents us to God as a living sacrifice. Since these are the proper works of the Word, why wonder if it bites, reproves, wounds, and in whatever other way causes trouble to the flesh? For who, endowed with the use of reason, is angry with other creatures if they are carried by natural motion to that for which the Maker of nature has destined them? What rashness, or rather madness, is it, then, to bear with ill temper the effects of that Word by whose power this whole machine of the world is governed? Surely those who already weigh these two things rightly within their minds are being cultivated, as it were, like a well-tilled field, so that they may receive that seed of the Word and bear fruit worthy of their calling. But with these must be joined a zeal for moderation and humility, so that, having become overconfident from early success, they do not later faint when some heavier burden presses upon them.

units.la: Sequitur tertiū genus eorum, quibus Verbum abfq; fructu prædicatur. Hos terræ spinis horridæ confert Christus, per spinas aut solicitudines et curas huius seculi, diuitias item & voluptates vitæ præsentis intelligi debere ipse docet: et tribus hisce speciebus omnes cupiditates illicitas coprehēdit, quæ ferium Verbi Dei studium in nobis reflinguunt, & eiusdem fructum impediunt, quò minus succrescere et ad maturitatem perduci possit. Rectè autē hæc omnia spinis comparantur. Quid enim cu-ris & solicitudinibus huius seculi spinosius? quid acutius? quid magis dolorificum? Certè, qui his locum dant, ij nec quiescere possunt vnquam, neq; somni beneficio fruuntur, neq; ex cibo et potu voluptatem aliquam capiunt, deniq; ijdem vitam ipsam sibi amaram reddunt. Neq; corpus solum macerant, sed animum quoq; excarnificant, & coripsum crudeliter exedunt. Exempla huius mali multa in illis occurrunt, quos gloriæ cupiditas in curas exitiales adduxit. Hac enim extimulatus Saul ipsum et regnum totum in persequendo Dauide fatigauit. Hæc Themistoclem insomnes noctesducere coegit, quòd Miltiadis triumphos subinde animo volueret. Eadem Alexandrum accendit, vt orbis vnius imperio non contentus, nescio quid insolentius animo conciperet. Quod autem istis accidit, hoc ipsum omnibus euenire solet, qui quibuscunq; alijs affectibus inflammati, curis inde enatis indulgent. Et quia curarum materia vbiq; occurrit, non habent illi quò se vertant, sed quodcunq; vitæ genus sequantur, nouis curis se pungi & vulnerari sentiunt. Eadem est diuitiarum conditio, quas spinarum acutissimarum fasciculum verissimè dixeris. Vt enim has neq; contrectare; neq; dissoluere aut loco mouere potes, quin punüuram aliquam sentias: ita siue diuitias acquirere, siue quaesitas vti, siue easdem relinquere aut amittere velis, semper occurret, quo animum tuum non leuiter laedi senties. Imò inter spinas tutius multò consederis, quàm ij, qui opum studio superati, se totos Mammonae seruitio consecrarunt. De voluptatibus verò quid attinet dicere, quando haec nō tam spinae sunt, quàm scorpiones, qui letali aculeo incautos vulnerant? Et vt Solomon voluptatem, quae ex ebriosorum conuiuijs capitur, aspidis morsui conferti: sic idem eam, quae in illicito mulierum amore quaeritur, prunis ardentibus & sagittis animam vulnerantibus similem esse dicit. Fieri ergo non potest, vt Verbum vitae apud eos fructum edat, qui spinis & aculeis letiferis locum dant. Vt enim spinae celerius multò enascentes segetem in ipsa herba deprimunt: ita cum curis & cupiditatibus eiusmodi noua quotidie ex mundo & innata nobis vitiositate alimenta accedant, breui tantis viribus augentur, vt ipsum Dei verbum superent, & omnem eius fructum in nobis impediant.
units.tr: There follows the third kind of those to whom the Word is preached without fruit. Christ compares them to the ground bristling with thorns. He himself teaches that by the thorns are to be understood the cares and anxieties of this age, and likewise riches and pleasures of the present life; and by these three kinds he comprehends all unlawful desires which hinder earnest study of the Word of God in us, and prevent its fruit from growing and being brought to maturity. These things are rightly compared to thorns. For what is more thorny than the cares and anxieties of this age? What is sharper? What causes more pain? Surely those who give them room can never rest, nor enjoy the benefit of sleep, nor take any pleasure from food and drink; finally, they make life itself bitter for themselves. They not only wear out the body, but also torment the mind, and devour it cruelly. Many examples of this evil occur among those whom the desire for glory has led into deadly cares. Saul, driven by this, wearied himself and the whole kingdom in persecuting David. This made Themistocles pass sleepless nights, because he kept turning over in his mind the triumphs of Miltiades. The same thing inflamed Alexander, so that, not content with the rule of one world, he conceived I know not what more insolent thing in his mind. Now what happened to these men usually happens to all who, inflamed by other passions, indulge in the cares that spring from them. And because the matter of cares meets us everywhere, such people have nowhere to turn; whatever way of life they follow, they feel themselves pricked and wounded by new cares. The condition of riches is the same: you could rightly call them a bundle of the sharpest thorns. For just as you cannot handle them, nor loosen them, nor move them from their place, without feeling some sting, so whether you wish to acquire riches, or to use those you have gained, or to leave or lose them, you will always find that they wound your mind not lightly. Indeed, you will settle among thorns far more safely than those who, overcome by the pursuit of wealth, have wholly consecrated themselves to the service of Mammon. And as for pleasures, what need is there to say more, since these are less thorns than scorpions, which wound the unwary with a deadly sting? And just as Solomon compares the pleasure drawn from the banquets of drunkards to the bite of an asp, so he says that the pleasure sought in the unlawful love of women is like burning coals and arrows that wound the soul. It is therefore impossible for the Word of life to bear fruit among those who give room to thorns and deadly stings. For just as thorns, springing up much more quickly, crush the crop in the very blade, so when, every day, new nourishment for such cares and desires comes from the world and from the vice innate in us, in a short time they grow to such strength that they overcome the very Word of God and hinder all its fruit in us.

units.la: Quid ergo fieri debet (inquis) vt huic malo remedium inueniatur? Num abiectis simul curis omnibus in vtramque aurem suauiter dormiendum, neque aliquis admittendus, qui alicuius rei tristioris mentionem faciat? Aut num opes omnes in mare aut profluentem abijciemus, quod Crates Thebanus olim fecisse dicitur, quòd putaret diuitias & virtutes simul haberi non posse? Vel num omneid fugiemus, quod oblectare nos possit? Aut Monachos ne imitabimur, quibus religio est pecuniam manibus contrectare, & qui paupertatem vouent voluntariam? Nihil huius sacrae litera praecipiunt. Quin potius curas aliquas sanctas & necessarias esse docent, quales sunt, quas in reipub. administratione boni magistratus, in ecclesia gubernatione fidi pastores, in familia seruan-da & liberis probe educandis pij parentes, in curandis negotijs frugi famuli sustinent. Et diuitias ex Dei benedictione interdum sanctissimus hominibus obtingere, multosque opibus abundauisse scimus, quorum pietatem spiritus sanctus magnificè praedicat. Sunt & voluptates aliquae honestae & licitae, quibus vitae huius labores atque molestias miseris mortalibus Deus mitigare consueuit. Neq; multùm profeceris, etiamsi reliquis istis omnibus vitam solitariam procul omni hominum con-sortio exclusus vixeris. Ager etenim ille, quem Verbi semine conseri oportet, cor est. Ex hoc igitur spinas euelli necesse est. Quod tunc fiet, si nimias illas et mordaces curas sustuleris, quae animum totum studijs huius seculi mancipant, & proinde obstant, quò minus ijs attendamus, quae ex Dei Verbo didicimus: sitem cogitationes vanas ex animo eijcias, quae auaritiae, libidini & fastus volu-ptatibus alimenta ministrant. Hic autem magno studio & cura inde fessa opus est, quia spinae istae & multae sunt, & imis cordibus infixae haerent, perq; omnia vitae huius studia sese longe lateq; extendunt, adhuc euulsae liceat, vel potius fractae, repullulant, eò quòd vix vnquam radicitus extirpantur. Plurimùm tamen proficies, si tria haec adhibeas: Prouidentiae diuinae fiduciam, Diuitiarum huius seculi & Vitae totius consideratiouem diligentem. Cur enim curis seipsum excruciet, qui omnia nostra ex aeterno Prouidentiae Dei decreto pendere credit? Cur sibi aut suis metuat hominum, qui se Patri caelesti curae esse intelligit? Aut num immodico opum studio sese accendi patietur, qui quàm vanae, fugaces, & ad vitam seruandam inutiles illae sint, recte perspexerit? Num item voluptatum aculeos admittet, qui has quidem momentaneas, dolorem verò, qui ex illis enascitur, perpetuum esse cogitat? Haec qui secum non ofcitanter expendunt, & hisce meditationibus assiduum Verbi studium & preces indesinentes coniungunt, ij mox sentient spinas istas magna ex parte intra animos suos minui. Verbum enim Dei gladius ille est acutissimus, qui corda & medullas penetrans ea excindit, quae saluti nostrae officiunt: precibus autem pijs & ex fide non fucata manantibus sanctus ille & salutifer ignis spiritus diuini elicitur, qui illa insuper adurit & conficit, ne vnquam nouas radices agere & Verbi fructum impedire possint.
units.tr: What, then, (you ask) ought to be done so that a remedy may be found for this evil? Should we, casting off all cares together, sleep sweetly with both ears, and admit no one who mentions anything rather sad? Or shall we throw all our wealth into the sea or into a flowing river, as Crates of Thebes is said to have done once, because he thought riches and virtues could not be had together? Or shall we flee everything that could delight us? Or shall we not imitate the monks, who think it a sin to handle money with their hands and who vow voluntary poverty? Sacred Scripture prescribes none of this. Rather, it teaches that there are some holy and necessary cares, such as those which good magistrates bear in the administration of the commonwealth, faithful ministers in the government of the Church, pious parents in keeping the household and bringing up their children well, and thrifty servants in managing affairs. And we know that sometimes riches fall to very holy men by the blessing of God, and that many have abounded in wealth, whose piety the Holy Spirit magnificently praises. There are also some honest and lawful pleasures, with which God is accustomed to lighten the labours and troubles of this life for wretched mortals. Nor would you gain much even if, leaving aside all those things, you lived a solitary life, shut off far from all human company. For the field in which the seed of the Word must be sown is the heart. Therefore the thorns must be torn out of it. This will be done if you remove those excessive and biting cares which wholly enslave the mind to the pursuits of this age, and which therefore stand in the way so that we do not attend to those things we have learned from the Word of God; and if you cast out of the mind the vain thoughts which supply nourishment to avarice, lust, and the pleasures of pride. Here, however, great zeal and care are needed, because these thorns are many, cling fixed in the innermost hearts, and spread far and wide through all the pursuits of this life; even when they seem to be plucked out, they sprout again, broken, because they are scarcely ever uprooted completely. Yet you will make very good progress if you apply these three things: confidence in divine providence, careful consideration of the riches of this age, and of the whole of life. For why should a man torment himself with cares who believes that all our affairs depend on the eternal decree of God's providence? Why should a man fear for himself or his people, who understands that he is a care to the heavenly Father? Or will he allow himself to be kindled by an immoderate zeal for wealth, who has rightly perceived how empty, fleeting, and useless for preserving life those riches are? Will he likewise admit the stings of pleasures, who considers that these are momentary, but the pain that springs from them is lasting? Those who weigh these things carefully, and who join to these meditations a constant study of the Word and unceasing prayers, will soon feel that those thorns are for the most part diminished within their minds. For the Word of God is that most sharp sword, which penetrating hearts and marrow cuts out what hinders our salvation; and by pious prayers which flow from faith, unfeigned, that holy and saving fire of the divine Spirit is kindled, which burns up and consumes those thorns as well, so that they can never again put forth new roots and hinder the fruit of the Word.

units.la: Porrò eorum ecclesiae, quibus frustra Verbum Dei annuntiatur, veros & germanos auditores opponit, quos bonae & fecundae terrae similes esse ait. Quod in bonâ terrâ cecidit, ij sunt (inquit) qui in corde honesto & bono auditu sermonem retinent, & fructu adferunt per patientiam. Videndum hic ante omnia, qui nam terra illa bona sint. Nam si hominem propius inspiciamus, omnes in peccato concepti & natos esse patebit, vt non immerito Christus dixerit: Nemo bonus est, praeter solum Deum, Boni tamè hic dicuntur, quos Deus in hoc seperauit, vt fructus ferant, quibus ipse coli possit: & los scriptura Electos dicere consueuit. Nemo igitur terra bona dici meretur, nisi quem Deus ex gratia elegit, & spiritus virtute idoneum fecit, vt Verbum admittat, & se huic prabeat obsequentem. Quod in eum finem obseruari debet, ne eorum delirijs nos decipi sinamus, qui nos fructus ex nobisipsis & propria virtute edere putant, & in eo suum meritum quaerunt, in quo Dei gratiam agnoscere debebant. Quia vero vnum modo genus facit eorum, qui Euangelium digne audiunt, cùm priores il los in tria genera distinxerit, non obscure innuit, minorem semper fore priorum numerum, qui fructum aliquem ex Euangelio referunt. Quod apertius alibi docet, his verbis: Multi sunt vocati, pauci electi. Et prodest hoc contra eos obseruare, qui dum ex operibus auditorum de doctrina iudicium faciunt, ipsissimum Dei Verbum in dubium vocare audent, quos hac parabola confutari, supra quoq; diximus.
units.tr: Moreover, he sets over against those churches to which the Word of God is preached in vain true and genuine hearers, whom he calls like good and fertile soil. "What fell on good ground," he says, "are those who hold the word they have heard in an honest and good heart, and bring forth fruit with patience." Here we must first consider above all who those good soils are. For if we look more closely at man, it will be plain that all are conceived and born in sin, so that Christ rightly said: "No one is good except God alone." Yet those are called good here whom God has set apart for this purpose, that they may bear fruit by which he himself may be honoured; and Scripture is accustomed to call them the Elect. No one therefore deserves to be called good soil unless he is one whom God has chosen out of grace and made fit, by the power of the Spirit, to receive the Word and to yield himself obedient to it. This must be observed to this end: that we not let ourselves be deceived by the follies of those who think they produce fruit from themselves and by their own virtue, and who seek their merit in that in which they ought to recognise the grace of God. But because he makes only one kind of those who hear the Gospel worthily, although he has divided the former into three kinds, he obscurely hints that the number of those who bring forth any fruit from the Gospel will always be smaller than the number of the former. He teaches this more plainly elsewhere, in these words: "Many are called, few are chosen." It is useful to note this against those who, while they judge doctrine by the works of hearers, dare to call the very Word of God into doubt; we have said above that this parable refutes them as well.

units.la: Caeterum quid isti faciant, audiamus. Tria de illis dicit. Primum, quod etiam ipsi Verbum audiant. Ergo non offenduntur aliorum vitijs (vt hodie Anabaptistae solent) neq; quas iam ante animis inscriptas habent, notitijs communibus tantum tribunt, vt se institutione externa nequaquam opus habere putent: neq; Verbum aliquod non scriptum fingunt, sed potius Dei bonitatem agnoscunt, qui nobiscum loqui dignatur, & quia sic ab illo institutum esse sciunt, vt per Verbi praedicationem fides et aeternae salutis cognitio hominibus obtingat, illi sese obsequentes accommodant. Et huc illud Christi pertinet, Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, et sequuntur eam. Unde colligimus, ex electorum numero minime censendos esse eos, qui Verbum audire dedignantur. Deinde Verbum auditum animo quoq; concipiunt & retinent. Ergo non locum dant infelici illi malarum cogitationum & impiorum illusorum auditio, quod semen auferre & devorare solet, neque persecutionum et cupiditatum carnalium astu illud aduri patiuntur, neq; spinas succrescere sinunt (de quibus modo diximus) quae illud suffocent. Sed quod audiere diligenti meditatione repetunt atq; ruminant, vt in vero eius sensu atq; fide magis confirmentur. Et hoc illud est, quod in Berœensibus Lucas commendat, quos Paulum attentis animis audiuisse, et domi scripturas diligenter scrutatos esse scribit, num ita haberet ea, quae ex illo audierat. Quod vt fiat, omnino necesse est. Ita enim in usum nostrum applicatur doctrina, quae alioqui nihil ad nos pertinere putabimus. Ideo David beatum pronuntiat, qui in Lege Domini dies & noctes meditatur. Sequitur ex his tertium, quod fructum adferunt per patientiam. Fructum dicit ea, quae Deus Verbo suo praecipit, & quae à nobis secundum eius praescriptum fiunt. Possumus illa omnia sub fide & operibus fidei comprehendere, quae omnia vitae innocentia, charitate & obedientia continentur. At fructum hunc per patientiam addi docet, vt ostendat hanc rem non levis momenti, sed magni laboris opus esse. Ut enim semen no primo statim die prouenit, & vbi germinauit varijs tempestatum vicibus exercetur, atq; modo pluuijs tantum no obruitur, modo rore rigatur, mox pruinis aduritur, diu etiam sub nimibus altissimis quasi sepultum delitescit, adhuc ventorum diuersissimorum turbinibus atq; procellis agitatur: ita qui Verbi semen animo coeperunt, & aliquam de seipsis spem fructus praebent, illis multa occurrunt, quae fructum hunc impeditura videntur, et de quibus iam ante est dictum. At qui bona terra sunt, & animos habent serio verae pietatis studio ardentes, ij per omnia obstacula superiores fiunt, vt per infinitas hyemes in aeterna vita horrea ad Christum colligantur. Frustra ergo Euangelij nomine superbiunt, qui fructus omnino nullos ferunt, ex quibus fidem eorum agnoscere possu. Ubi tamen minimè probamus eorum seueritatem, qui praecipiti iudicio omnes damnant, in quibus nulla adhuc fidei fructificantis indicia apparent. Vrgendi quidem sunt illi, vt officium faciant: interim vero memi nerimus, fructum in multis tardius enasci, quos non ideo reijcit Deus, sed ad se conuersos benignè recipit. Iubet etiam charitatis lex, vt bene speremus de omnibus, qui Verbo Dei locum dant, licet non semper illi mores eorum respondeant. Debet hoc ipsum in diuersitate etiam fructuum obseruari, quam Christus apud Matthaeum & Marcum euidentius exprimit, quando alios quidem centuplum, alios sexagecuplum, alios trigecuplum proferre ait. Ut enim in feminibus aliud alio fœcundius est: ita inter homines alij alijs maiores in Verbo Dei progressu faciunt. Ut vero agricola segetem totam colligit, neq; spicas tenuiores contemptim abijcit: ita Deus oes, qui pro gratia sibi concessa fructu quantulumcunq; edut, sua bonitate copletti, & (vt in talentorum parabola Christus pollicetur) dona sua in illis augere solet, qui in parvo fideles fuerint. Prodest hoc obseruasse, ne vel eos contemnamus, qui nobis inferiores sunt, vel animum despondeamus, si nos à supremo perfectionis gradu longius adhuc videamus abesse. Asquia
units.tr: Let us hear, however, what these people do. He says three things about them. First, that they too hear the Word. Therefore they are not offended by the faults of others (as the Anabaptists are wont to be today), nor do they give credit merely to common notions already inscribed on their minds, so that they think they have no need of external instruction; nor do they invent some unwritten word, but rather acknowledge the goodness of God, who deigns to speak with us. Knowing that he has so ordained that faith and knowledge of eternal salvation come to men through the preaching of the Word, they submit and accommodate themselves to him. To this belongs Christ's saying: "My sheep hear my voice, and follow it." From this we gather that those who disdain to hear the Word are by no means to be counted among the elect. Second, they also receive the heard Word into their mind and retain it. Therefore they give no place to that unhappy thing, the hearing of evil thoughts and ungodly delusions, which is wont to snatch away and devour the seed; nor do they allow it to be scorched by the craft of persecutions and carnal desires, nor do they let thorns grow up (of which we have just spoken) to choke it. But what they have heard they repeat and chew over with diligent meditation, so that they may be more firmly confirmed in its true sense and faith. This is what Luke commends in the Bereans, who, he writes, heard Paul with attentive minds and, searching the Scriptures diligently at home, checked whether what they had heard was so. For this to happen is entirely necessary, for thus doctrine is applied to our use, which otherwise we would think has nothing to do with us. Therefore David pronounces blessed the one who meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night. Third follows from these: they bring forth fruit with patience. By fruit he means those things which God commands in his Word, and which are done by us according to his prescription. All of these we can comprise under faith and the works of faith, which are contained in innocence of life, charity and obedience. But he teaches that this fruit is added with patience, to show that this is no matter of slight importance but a work of great labour. For just as seed does not come up on the first day, and once it has sprouted is exercised by the changing weather, now not overwhelmed only by rains, now watered by dew, soon scorched by frosts, and lies hidden for a long time as if buried under clods, still tossed by the whirlwinds and storms of very contrary winds: so those who have received the seed of the Word in their minds and give some hope of fruit from themselves encounter many things which seem likely to hinder this fruit, of which we have already spoken. But those who are good soil, and have minds burning with a serious zeal for true piety, these rise above all obstacles, so that through countless winters they are gathered to Christ into the barns of eternal life. Vainly, then, do they boast in the name of the Gospel who bear no fruit at all by which their faith may be recognised. Yet we by no means approve the severity of those who with rash judgement condemn all in whom no signs of fruit-bearing faith yet appear. Such people are indeed to be urged to do their duty; meanwhile let us remember that fruit is slower to sprout in many, whom God does not therefore reject, but kindly receives when they turn to him. The law of charity also bids us hope well of all who give place to the Word of God, although their manners do not always correspond. The same must be observed in the diversity of fruits, which Christ expresses more clearly in Matthew and Mark, when he says that some bring forth a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold. For as among seeds one is more fruitful than another, so among men some make greater progress than others in the course of the Word of God. But as the farmer gathers in the whole crop and does not contemptuously throw away the thinner ears, so God, who fills with his goodness all who yield whatever fruit, however small, according to the grace given them, is wont (as Christ promises in the parable of the talents) to increase his gifts in those who have been faithful in little. It is useful to note this, so that we neither despise those who are inferior to us, nor lose heart if we see ourselves still far from the highest step of perfection. And yet

units.la: At quia neque terra bona erimus, neque fructus feremus aliquos ex nobis ipsis, Deo Patre indesinenter oremus necesse est, ut animos nostros muret, trahat, & ad omne bonum idoneos reddat in Filio suo dilecto, Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But since we shall be neither good soil nor bear any fruit from ourselves, we must unceasingly pray to God the Father that he may move, draw and make our hearts fit for every good thing, in his beloved Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXVIII.

units.la: Caeterum nemo, ubi lucernam accendit, eam operit vase, aut subter lectum ponit: sed candelabro imponit, ut qui ingrediuntur videant lumen. Non est enim quicquam occultum, quod non fit futurum manifestum, nec abscònditum, quod non fit cognoscendum, & venturum in apertum. Videte ergo quomodo audiatis. Quisquis enim habet, dabitur ei, & quicunque non habet, etiam quod videtur habere, tolletur ab eo;
units.tr: Nobody, when he lights a lamp, covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, but sets it on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light. For there is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest, nor anything secret that will not be known and come to light. Take care, then, how you hear. For whoever has, to him more will be given, and whoever does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away from him.

units.la: Magnum quidem & incomparabile bonitatis divinae argumentum est, quod miseris & indignis mortalibus Verbum suum manifestare dignatur, ut ex eo renati fructus dignos ferant, & tandem regni caelestis haereditatem adeant. At non minus nostrae vitiositatis indicium est, quod Verbum hoc plerique contemnunt, inter eos autem, qui illud audiunt, pauci reperiuntur, in quibus fructus ferat. Ideo nuper Christus eleganti parabola omnium oculis expositum, quaecunque nobis in hac causa cognitu necessaria sunt. Docuit enim quae Verbi Dei natura sit, in quem finem praedicetur, quae vitia sive obstacula fructum eius impediant, quales denique nos esse oporteat, si illud digne & utiliter audire velimus. Huic doctrinae nunc commode sententias aliquos proverbiales subjicit, quibus Verbi studium commendat. Simul & docet, qua ratione illud in ecclesia proponi debeat & tractari. Seruit ergo locus hic Ministrorum institutioni in primis, simul tamen alios quoque homines officij admonet, ne illud propter liberiorem Verbi praedicationem succenseant.
units.tr: Great indeed and matchless is the proof of God's goodness that he deigns to make his Word known to wretched and unworthy mortals, so that those who are reborn by it may bear worthy fruit and at last attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Yet it is no less a sign of our wickedness that most people despise this Word, and that among those who hear it, few are found in whom it bears fruit. Therefore Christ lately set before everyone's eyes, in an elegant parable, all that we need to know in this matter. For he taught what the nature of the Word of God is, to what end it is preached, what vices or obstacles hinder its fruit, and finally what we ought to be if we wish to hear it worthily and profitably. To this teaching he now fittingly adds some proverbial sayings by which he commends eagerness for the Word. At the same time he shows how it ought to be set forth and handled in the Church. This passage therefore serves chiefly to instruct ministers, but it also reminds other people of their duty, that they should not take offence at the freer preaching of the Word.

units.la: Primo veram docendi rationem breui sententia comprehendit: Nemo, ubi lucernam accendit, eam operit vase, aut super lectum ponit: sed candelabro imponit, ut qui ingrediuntur videant lumen. Lucernam dicit Verbum Dei, qua Metaphora Dauidem quoque in Psalmis vti scimus. Prius autem sic dicitur, sive illud quale in ipso est, sive eius effecta consideres. Ut enim lux sua natura purissima & a sordibus alienissima est: ita Dei Verbum purum, sanctum, mundum & argento septies excocto (ut Dauid inquit) purgatum est. Lucernam vero in eo superat, quod impuritatem, quae in nobis est, tollit, & ex immundis mundos facit eos, qui illud vera fide apprehendunt. Docet hoc Christus, quando discipulis dicit: Iam vos mundi estis propter Verbum meum quod locutus sum vobis. Praeterea ut lux aerem illuminans facit, ut visui pateat, quae prius tenebris tecta latebant: ita Dei Verbo illuminantur omnia, ut ea etiam a nobis cognosci possint, quae per se captum humani ingenii longe superant. Adhaec Dei Verbi lux illa est, quae hominis ex illo renati actiones omnes dirigit, ut totus bonis operibus illustris fit, qui prius sub tenebrarum potestate constitutus in errores & exitium ruebat. Deniq; ut lux pleno fulgore caelum & aerem irradians serenitatem inducit: ita Dei Verbum mentes peccatorum conscientia obnubilatae illuminantur, ut erroribus procul pulsis nova luce gaudeant, dum divinae bonitatis vultum sibi in Christo oriri vident. Recte ergo lucernae comparatur huius doctrina. Veruntamen amplius quid hac Metaphora Christus docere instituit: nimirum ut ostendat quomodo in Verbi huius tractatione versari debeamus.
units.tr: First, in a brief saying he sums up the true method of teaching: "Nobody, when he lights a lamp, covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, but sets it on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light." By the lamp he means the Word of God, a metaphor which we know David also uses in the Psalms. Now this is said both with regard to what the Word is in itself and with regard to its effects. For just as light is by its nature most pure and most remote from filth, so the Word of God is pure, holy, clean, and purged, as David says, "like silver refined seven times." But the lamp surpasses in this, that it removes the impurity that is in us and makes clean from unclean those who receive it with true faith. Christ teaches this when he says to his disciples, "Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you." Further, just as light illuminates the air and makes visible what was previously hidden in darkness, so by the Word of God all things are illumined, so that even those things which far exceed the grasp of human understanding may be known by us. Moreover, the Word of God is that light which directs all the actions of the man reborn by it, so that he who before was under the power of darkness and rushing headlong into errors and destruction is wholly made bright by good works. Finally, just as light with its full brightness irradiates heaven and air and brings in clear weather, so the minds of sinners, darkened by a guilty conscience, are illumined by the Word of God, so that with errors driven far away they rejoice in the new light, while they see the face of divine goodness rising for them in Christ. Rightly, then, this teaching is compared to a lamp. But Christ wished to teach something more by this metaphor, namely to show how we ought to conduct ourselves in handling this Word.

units.la: Quo loco primum occurrit, quod ut lucerna accendi oportet, siquidem illius aliquis usus esse debet: ita Dei Verbi inter homines praedicatione & interpretatione idonea illustretur necesse est, eo quod nisi id fiat, plerique sensum eius non intelligent, aut false illud non putabunt ad se pertinere. In interpretatione aut duo observanda veniunt, quorum alterum caveri, alterum fieri convenit. Ad prius pertinet, ne lucernam hanc sub vase aut modio (ut alibi Christus loquitur) vel sub lecto occultemus. Sub modium cogunt Dei Verbi, qui humanae rationis examen adhibent, & illud carnis sensu metiuntur, dum nihil credendum aut recipiendum putant, quod non humanis rationibus probari possit. Faciunt hoc, qui vel philosophiam cum illo miscent, vel civili sapientia in eo tradendo utuntur, quorum illi quidem longissime a Veritatis scopo aberrant, & sub praetextu Verbi Dei tam in huius, quam in ipsius hominis cognitione falluntur: hi vero ex eo Lesbiam regulam fingunt, & dum nimium politici sunt, Verbu sibi prorsus inutile reddunt. Subter lectu vero lucernã istam recondunt ignaui & mala fidei doctores, qui ex Euangelio doctrinæ quoddam genus molliculum & blandulum eliciunt, quo eos etiam sibi demereri student, qui vitã à Christi professione alienißimam viuere consueuerunt. Itaq; omissa scrum redargutione, omissis itẽ increpationibus, hortationibus & iudicij diuini comminatione, ea modo loquuntur, quæ sceleratissimis & pœnitere nescijs probari possunt. Ex horum numero fuere, qui olim puluillos (vt Propheta ait) inter concionandum impijs substernebant, quibus innixi suauiter dormirent, qui potius comminationum tonitruis excitari debuerant. Et vtinam non magnus horum numerus hodie etiam haberetur, in principum aulis maximè & vrbibus opulentioribus, vbi propter luxum & effrenem omnium scelerum licentiam liberiori accusatione opus erat.
units.tr: Here first occurs the point that, as a lamp must be lit if it is to be of any use, so the Word of God must be made to shine among people by fitting preaching and interpretation. For unless this is done, most people will not understand its meaning, or they will wrongly think it does not concern them. In interpretation two things must be observed, of which one must be avoided and the other done. The first concerns our not hiding this lamp under a vessel or a bushel (as Christ speaks elsewhere) or under a bed. People hide the Word of God under a bushel when they subject it to the examination of human reason and measure it by the sense of the flesh, thinking that nothing should be believed or accepted unless it can be proved by human arguments. Those do this who either mix philosophy with it or use civil wisdom in delivering it. The former indeed wander very far from the goal of truth and are deceived, under the pretext of the Word of God, both in knowledge of it and in knowledge of man himself. The latter make of it a Lesbian rule, and, while they are too political, they render the Word wholly useless to themselves. Under a bed, however, lazy teachers of bad faith hide this lamp, who from the Gospel draw out a soft and flattering kind of doctrine, by which they strive to win the favour even of those who are accustomed to live in a way most alien to the profession of Christ. So, leaving out the rebuke of sin, leaving out likewise reproofs, exhortations and the threat of divine judgement, they say only those things which can be approved by the most wicked and by those who know not how to repent. Of this number were those who once, as the Prophet says, placed cushions under the ungodly while preaching, so that they might rest sweetly leaning upon them, when they ought rather to have been roused by the thunder of threats. And would that this great number were not found today too, especially in the courts of princes and in the richer cities, where because of luxury and the unbridled licence of every kind of wickedness, a freer accusation is needed.

units.la: Porrò quid fieri velit, videamus, quod alterũ huius tractationis caput esse diximus: Candelabro (inquit) lucerna imponitur, vt omnes qui ingrediuntur videant. Candelabro publicũ ecclesiæ ministerium significari, ex Tabernaculi Leuitici historia patet. In eo enim candelabrum totum aureum prostabat, quodin septẽ hastilia siue brachia diuisum totidẽ lampades sustinebat, in quibus igne sacrum sacerdotes magna diligentia asseruabat, vt & Tabernaculũ illuminaretur, & ex eo accedere tur sacrificia atq; thymiamata, in quibus offerendis igne alieno vti capitale erat, vt filiorũ Aaronis exemplo Deus docuit. Nec enim possunt illi placere cultus, qui nõ secundùm Verbi sui præscriptũ instituuntur. Vult ergo in ecclesia ministerium hoc perpetuò seruari, quàdo sine hoc ecclesia cõsistere nõ potest. Vt enim hæc ex Verbo nascitur, quod vnicũ regenerationis semẽ est: ita per illud regatur quæ que oportet. Est ergo hic ecclesiæ thesaurus pretiosissimus, quẽ inter beneficia Dei ferè Scripturæ sacræ primo loco numerat. Itaq; huius admonitionis sensus est, Dei Verbũ in ecclesia publicè annunciari, et instar lucernæ ita proponi debere, vt omnium oculi et mentes eo illuminetur, et singulì intelligat, quid ipsis facto opus sit. Quod vt Apostolis et horũ successoribus in primis dicitur, ne quid in alicuius gratia dissimulet, aut fidei dogmata ambiguis interpretationibus inuoluat et obscurèt: ita eorũ audacia arguit et cõsutat, qui illis dicendi leges præscribũt, et plus quàm Cyclopica insolentia in Verbum Dei sibi ius & imperiũ vendicat, vt hæc quidè dici, illa verò taceri velint, quæ studijs suis minus conuenire sentiunt. Tales olim erant Prophetarũ temporibus, qui videntibus dicebant, Ne videatis: et contemplantibus, Ne contemplemini nobis plana, loquimini nobis blanda, contemplamini illusiones, recedite à via, declinate à semita, quiescere facite à facie nostra Sanctũ Israelis. Itẽ alibi Prophetas stillare prohibent, ita nimirum Verbi prædicatione stillicidio molesto & intolerabili comparantes. Patrum verò vestigia secuti sunt Sacerdotes et Pharisæi, qui Apostolis cũ graui comminatione edixerunt, ne in nomine Iesu docerent. Et hodie passim audiuntur, quibus intolerabile & nulla venia dignum flagitium videtur, si Verbi administri errores, superstitiones, illicitos cultus & corruptos hominũ mores liberius arguant. Ex eo enim seditiones oriri, hominum mentes exacerbari, odia & simultates excitari, & multorum famam atq; honorem in suspicionem adduci clamant. Itaq; doctrinæ formulam nouam illi nobis fingunt, qua simpliciter doceatur quid credi & fieri debeat, non autem alicuius vitæ & moribus Verbum applicetur. Et hoc ferè à nobis exigunt, quorum summa est in Repub. authoritas & formidabilis potentia. Sed non debent aliquem istorum rationes aut minæ mouere, quò minus Christo obtemperet, qui verbi lucernam accendere & candelabro imponere, idest, ita prædicare iubet, vt singulì intelligant de se agi, & ex eo discant quidin ipsis emendatione opus habeat. Et vt olim Prophetæ & Apostoli inuicta animi constantia perexerunt, eò quòd scirent Deo potius quàm hominibus esse obediendum: ita non minori fortitudine cum insolentium istorum dominatorum ecclesiæ audacia luctari debent omnes, qui in ecclesiæ ministerio constituti suam operam Christo probari, et ex laboribus suis aliquem fructum enasci cupiunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us see what is to be done, which we said is the second head of this treatment: "the lamp," he says, "is placed on a lampstand, so that all who come in may see." That the lampstand signifies the public ministry of the Church is clear from the history of the Levitical tabernacle. For in it stood the whole golden candelabrum, which, divided into seven branches or arms, held as many lamps, and the priests with great care kept fire in them, both so that the tabernacle might be illuminated and so that sacrifices and incense might be offered from it. It was a capital crime to use strange fire in offering these, as God taught by the example of the sons of Aaron. For those worships cannot please him which are not instituted according to the prescription of his Word. He therefore wills that this ministry be preserved perpetually in the Church, since without it the Church cannot exist. For just as the Church is born from the Word, which is the only seed of regeneration, so by the same Word it must be ruled in all things that are fitting. This ministry is therefore the most precious treasure of the Church, which Scripture almost always counts first among the blessings of God. Thus the sense of this admonition is that the Word of God should be publicly proclaimed in the Church, and set forth like a lamp in such a way that the eyes and minds of all are illumined by it, and each one understands what needs to be done by him. What is said first to the Apostles and their successors is that they should not conceal anything for the sake of anyone's favour, nor wrap and obscure the doctrines of faith in ambiguous interpretations. In the same way, it exposes and refutes the audacity of those who prescribe laws to them about what they may say, and who, with more than Cyclopean insolence, claim for themselves right and rule over the Word of God, so that they want some things said and others kept silent, namely those which they feel are less agreeable to their pursuits. Such people existed in the times of the prophets of old, who said to those who saw, "Do not see," and to those who contemplated, "Do not contemplate for us what is right; speak to us smooth things; contemplate illusions; turn aside from the way, turn out of the path; cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us." Likewise elsewhere the prophets are forbidden to drip, that is, to compare preaching of the Word to a troublesome and intolerable dripping. Indeed the priests and Pharisees followed the footsteps of the fathers, who with grave threats ordered the Apostles not to teach in the name of Jesus. And today there are people everywhere who think it an intolerable and unpardonable outrage if the ministers of the Word argue more freely against the errors, superstitions, unlawful worships and corrupt morals of men. They cry out that from this seditions arise, minds are exasperated, hatreds and quarrels are stirred up, and the reputation and honour of many are brought under suspicion. So they devise for us a new formula of teaching, by which only what must be believed and done is simply taught, and the Word is not applied to anyone's life and morals. And this they chiefly demand of us, those whose authority in the commonwealth is supreme and whose power is formidable. But none of these men's arguments or threats ought to move anyone so as to make him disobey Christ, who bids us kindle the lamp of the Word and set it on the lampstand, that is, to preach in such a way that each one understands that he himself is being addressed, and learns from it what needs correcting in himself. And just as the prophets and Apostles of old carried on with invincible steadfastness of spirit, because they knew that God must be obeyed rather than men, so all who are placed in the ministry of the Church, and who desire that their labour be approved by Christ and that some fruit spring from their toils, ought to struggle with no less fortitude against the audacity of these insolent lords of the Church.

units.la: At hoc moneti Christo aliquis obijceret: Si Verbũ Dei publicè prædicari, & doctrina hæc ea per spicuitate tradi debet, vt omnium institutioni seruiat, cur tu eam parabolis inuolus? cur nõ diserte quod res est eloqueris? cur item obscuro Iudæa & Galilæa angulo quasi inclusus ignobili plebeculæ eam proponis, & non potius toti orbi diuulgas? Istas obiectiones ille præoccupans ait: Nonèst quicquam occultum, quod non sit futurum manifestum: nec absconditum, quod non sit cognoscendum, & venturum in apertum. Subest autem verbis istis argumentum à tempore desumptum, & sensus est: Nunc quidem pro temporis huius ratione obscurius paulò prædico, & intra Iudææ fines doctrinæ huius buius cursum contineo : sed mox aliud tempus aderit, quo omnia euidentius toti mundo proponen-tur : neq; aliquid est in toto salutis humanae negotio tam obscurum aut abstrusum, quod non omnium oculis tunc coram exponi oporteat. Neminem ergo vestrum moueat haec, quam nunc sequor, docendi ratio: quin potius vbi tempus illud elluxerit, vos alacri mente in totum orbem digressi Euangelium omnibus praedicate, & quod nunc vobis in tenebris dico, vos in aperta luce dicite, quod audit in aurem auditis, clara voce in tectis annunciate. Ita vero paucis verbis multa Christus comprehendit. Primo enim seipsum omni suspicione liberat, ne quis ipsum obscurius loqui arbitretur, quod alicui mortalium salutis & veritatis cognitionem inuideat. Hic vero Dei Patris bonitatem nobis commendat, qui vt omnibus seculis promissiones salutis dedit, quae sufficere poterant, itanoui-mis temporibus, quae tenebris densioribus inuoluenda sciebat, lucem abundantiorem destinauit, vt (quod olim per Isaiam promiserat) omnis terra scientia Domini repleatur. Deinde Apostolus excitat, vt intrepido animo munus suum capessant, & in toto orbe terrarum libere Euangelium praedicent. Adhaec spem illis victoriae certam facit, quando pollicetur fore, vt doctrina haec omnibus innotescat, nequicquam aduersus eam luctantibus ijs, qui superstitionum atque errorum tenebras lucí aeternae veritatis praeferunt. Et ista quidem suum habuere eucntum, quando illi intra breue paucorum annorum curriculum omnes gentes luce illa illustrauerunt: & tantum fuit hoc Euangelij tonitru, vt non solum Iudaeorum Synagogas, verumetiam omnes philosophorum scholas, curias & fora omnia, principum item aulas, & ipsam Romam rerum dominam penetrauerit. Voluit de his Apostolos Christus admonere, quo alacriores essent in suo munere. Quia vero ista adhuc hodie fieri vidimus, & promissio nobis quoque facta est, fore, vt ante nouissimum iudicij diem Euangelium in toto orbe praedicetur, nos quoque ex eo spem laetam concipere & nos strenuos Christi milites praebere conuenit. Furit quidem infelix mundus Antichristo duce, qui ipsum quoque Acheronta mouere satagit, vt & aeternae salutis doctrinam in tenebris detineat, & suas fraudes celet, quibus iam seculis aliquot terrarum orbem decepit, diripuit, & in seruitutem miserrimam adduxit, & quibus detectis regnum suum subito ruiturum sentit: Nunquam tamen efficiet, vt aut Dei verbum tenebris obruatur, aut suae artes perpetuo lateant. Nam vt Euangelium in toto orbe diuulgari necesse est, ita istius quoq; meretricis dolos detegi, & ipsas vestium fimbrias supra caput attolli oportet, vt eius turpitudinem omnes gentes videant.
units.tr: But someone might object to Christ on this point: If the Word of God is to be preached publicly, and this doctrine is to be taught so clearly that it serves the instruction of all, why do you wrap it in parables? Why do you not speak plainly, saying what the matter actually is? Why do you present it to the common people of an obscure corner of Judaea and Galilee, as if you were shut away there, instead of spreading it abroad to the whole world? Anticipating these objections, he says: "There is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest, nor anything concealed that will not be known and come into the open." The words rest on an argument from time, and the sense is this: For now, given the circumstances of the time, I teach somewhat more obscurely and confine the course of this doctrine within the borders of Judaea. But soon another time will come, when all things will be set forth more openly to the whole world. Nothing in the whole business of human salvation is so obscure or abstruse that it will not then have to be laid open before everyone's eyes. Therefore let none of you be troubled by the method of teaching I now follow. Rather, when that time has dawned, go out into the whole world with a cheerful mind and preach the Gospel to all. What I now tell you in darkness, say in the open light; what you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim with a loud voice from the housetops. Christ thus comprehends much in few words. First, he frees himself from all suspicion, lest anyone think he speaks more obscurely because he begrudges any mortal the knowledge of salvation and truth. Here he commends to us the goodness of God the Father, who, as he gave promises of salvation in all ages, which were sufficient, so for these latest times, which he knew would be wrapped in thicker darkness, he appointed a fuller light, so that (as he had promised long before through Isaiah) the whole earth may be filled with the knowledge of the Lord. Next, the Apostle stirs them up to take up their task with a fearless spirit and to preach the Gospel freely throughout the whole world. Besides this, he gives them a sure hope of victory, when he promises that this doctrine will become known to all, though those who prefer the darkness of superstitions and errors to the light of eternal truth struggle against it in vain. And indeed these things have had their outcome: within the short course of a few years they enlightened all nations with that light. So great was the thunder of this Gospel that it penetrated not only the synagogues of the Jews, but also all the schools of the philosophers, the courts, and all the markets, the halls of princes, and Rome itself, the mistress of the world. Christ wished to forewarn the Apostles of these things, so that they might be the more eager in their office. And since we have seen these things still happening today, and since the promise has been made to us also, that before the last day of judgment the Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world, it is fitting that we too conceive a joyful hope from this and show ourselves vigorous soldiers of Christ. The unhappy world indeed rages under Antichrist as its leader, who labours even to stir up Acheron itself, so as to keep the doctrine of eternal salvation hidden in darkness and to conceal his frauds, by which for some centuries now he has deceived, plundered and brought the whole earth into most wretched servitude, and which, once detected, he feels will bring his kingdom suddenly crashing down. Yet he will never bring it about that either the Word of God is overwhelmed by darkness or that his arts remain hidden for ever. For just as the Gospel must be spread throughout the whole world, so also the tricks of that harlot must be uncovered and her skirts lifted above her head, so that all nations may see her shame.

units.la: Sed in Christi verbis pergamus, qui locum istum grani admonitione concludit, qua ad seriu audiendi verbi studium omnes excitat, sic dicens: Videte ergo quomodo audiatis: Quisquis enim habet, dabitur ei: et quicunque non habet, etiam quod videtur habere, tolletur ab eo. Quasi dicat: Non leviter in his versari oportet. Nec enim res superuacanea hic agitur, sed in primis seria, & ex qua omnis hominum salus dependet. Videte ergo, quid vobis dicatur, & qua vobis offerit salutem Deus animis gratis excipite, et quid is a nobis vicissim requirat, diligenter expedite, ne vnquam vestro officio desitis. Quisquis enim habet, id est, quisquis collata sibi gratia Dei agnoscit, eaque retinere studet, et donis sibi datis ad illustrandum illius regnum sedulo vtitur, illi plura addentur. Solet enim Pater mensae facere, quod prudentes rei domesticae administratores, qui plura & maiora negotia ijs feruis credunt, quos prae aliis in suo officio industrios atq; fidos esse sentiunt. At si quis non habet, id est, non agnoscit gratiae dona, et quasi nihil vnquam a Deo acceperit, secus rerum omnia negligit, quae ad salutem consequenda necessaria sunt, illi id quoque eripietur, quod habere videbatur. Tales enim, cum prius ingenij dotibus instructi esse, & iudicio atq; prudentia non parum valere putarentur, mox ista quoq; euanescere sentiunt, & tandem belluinae stupore correpti nihil porro videre aut intelligere possunt. Meretur hoc ingratitudo illorum, quam Deus inultam non sinit. Exempla huius rei multa extant, & in primis horrendum est, quod in Iudaeorum gente Deus edidit. Habuerunt illi amplissima gratiae diuinae dona, promissiones, legis doctrinam, prophetiam, vt non immerito Moses hanc sclam gentem sapientem dixerit. At quia haec pro nihilo aestimarunt, neque donis istis vsi sunt, vt par erat, ad illustrandam & propagandam Dei gloriam, ita illis spoliati sunt, vt nulla hodie in orbe terrarum gens sit, quae illi conferri mereatur, siue scripturarum ignorantiam, siue superstitiones anilas, siue barbaram artium omnium insitiam, siue belluinum omnium disciplinarum contemptum consideres. Et quod illi passi sunt, hoc multis ex gentibus ecclesijs accidisse scimus, quae hodie dura Turcarum tyrannide oppressae gemunt, eo quod syncerorem Euangelij doctrina contempserunt, & licenter nimis ad philosophicas rationes ea traxerunt, quae sola fide cognosci & apprehendi possunt. Docent haec, quae causa sit, cur multis hodie verbum Dei nequicquam praedicetur. Quod nimirum non vident quid aut quomodo audiant, id est, non agnoscunt beneficium Dei, quod is infelici mundo per Euangelij praedicationem in Christo offert, neque adsepertinere putant quae dicuntur. Audiunt ergo, ut ij quos ad Ezechielis conciones non maiori studio quam ad cantiones aliquas convenire, olim Deus querebatur. Et hi quidem optimi videri possunt, si cum illis conferantur, qui verbum hoc sciurriliter ridente, vel etiam in maiorem rabiem conversi aperte contumelijs proscindunt. Quare iusto iudicio hanc ingratitudinem mundi Deus vlcisciur, ut in luce meridiana pleriq; caecutiant, & in salutis negotio plus quam pueri sint, qui in alijs mira sollertia & ingenij acumine omnes excellunt. Fit deniq;, ut qui iam multum profecisse videbantur, subito in errores elapsi omnem veritatis cognitionem amittant. Debet ergo omnium animis probe recondita ista admonitio, ut meminerint, Euangelij doctrinam absque certo salutis periculo contemni non posse. Eam ergo patienter ferant, Dei paternam bonitatem agnoscant, huius voluntati se per fidei obedientiam submittant, seq; totos Filio eius Iesu Christo consecrent, in quo vno vita & salus inveniatur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us go on with the words of Christ, who concludes this passage with a weighty admonition, by which he stirs all to a serious attention to the hearing of the Word, saying: "Take heed therefore how you hear; for whoever has, to him will more be given, and whoever does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken from him." It is as if he said: You ought not to take these things lightly. For the matter here is not some idle trifle, but things of the greatest seriousness, on which the whole salvation of men depends. Take heed, therefore, to what is said to you, and receive gladly the salvation that God offers you; and carefully work out what he in turn requires of us, so that you never fall short of your duty. "Whoever has," that is, whoever acknowledges the grace of God bestowed upon him, and takes care to keep it, and diligently uses the gifts given him to advance his kingdom, to him more will be added. For the Father of the household does as prudent stewards of domestic affairs do, who entrust more and greater business to those servants whom they perceive to be the more diligent and faithful in their office than the rest. But "whoever does not have," that is, does not acknowledge the gifts of grace, and as though he had never received anything from God, neglects all those things that are necessary for attaining salvation, from him will be taken away even what he seemed to have. For such people, though they were once thought to be furnished with gifts of mind and to excel not a little in judgment and prudence, soon feel even these fading away, and at last, seized by bestial stupidity, they can no longer see or understand anything. Their ingratitude deserves this, and God does not let it go unpunished. There are many examples of this, and especially the dreadful one that God displayed among the nation of the Jews. They had the most ample gifts of divine grace: the promises, the teaching of the law, the prophecy, so that Moses rightly called them a wise nation. But because they esteemed these things as nothing, and did not use these gifts, as they ought, to illustrate and spread the glory of God, so they were stripped of them, such that today there is no nation on the face of the earth that deserves to be compared with them, whether you consider their ignorance of the Scriptures, their old-wives' superstitions, their barbarous ignorance of all the arts, or their bestial contempt of all learning. And we know that what they suffered has happened to many churches among the nations, which today groan under the harsh tyranny of the Turks, because they despised the purer doctrine of the Gospel and too freely drew into philosophical reasoning those things which can be known and grasped by faith alone. These things teach us what the reason is why the Word of God is preached in vain to many today. They do not see what they hear, or how they hear it; that is, they do not acknowledge the benefit of God which he offers to the unhappy world in Christ through the preaching of the Gospel, nor do they think that what is said pertains to them. So they listen as those whom God once complained did not come to Ezekiel's sermons with any greater eagerness than to some songs. And these people might seem the best, if they are compared with those who mock this word with buffoonery, or who, turned into even greater fury, openly tear it apart with insults. Therefore, by a just judgment, God punishes this ingratitude of the world, so that many grow blind in broad daylight, and in the business of salvation are more like children than those who excel all others in wonderful skill and sharpness of wit. Finally it comes about that those who seemed to have made great progress suddenly slip into errors and lose all knowledge of the truth. Therefore this warning ought to be deeply stored in the minds of all, so that they remember that the doctrine of the Gospel cannot be despised without certain danger to salvation. Let them therefore bear it patiently, acknowledge the fatherly goodness of God, submit themselves to his will by the obedience of faith, and devote themselves wholly to his Son Jesus Christ, in whom alone life and salvation are found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXIX.

units.la: Venerunt autem ad eum mater & fratres eius, & non poterant eum conuenire propter turbam: & annuntiatum est ei dicentibus nonnullis: Mater tua & fratres tui stant foris, cupientes te videre. Ipse vero respondens dixit eis: Mater mea & fratres mei sunt, qui sermonem Dei audiunt & eum praestant.
units.tr: And his mother and brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. He was told, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wanting to see you." But he answered them, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and put it into practice."

units.la: Quemadmodum vnus solus, Deus bonus est, idemque bonorum omnium thesarum in seipso habeat: ita bona haec nobis fruenda offert per verbum suum, & eodem illa consequendi viam atque rationem nobis commonstrat. Nihil ergo homini utilius, nihil salutarius, nihil magis necessarium est, quam ut verbum Dei sedulo audiat, & ad huius doctrinam seipsum atque actiones suas omnes componat. Nam qui in hoc aberrarint, ij salutis suae iacturam faciunt. Quae causa est, quod nuper Christus de verbi Dei natura & effectus copiose desseruit, simulq; ad huius studium omnes homines graviter hortatus est. Commodè autem illi tractationi huius loci historiam subijcit, qua docemur, quanto apud Deum in honore & pretio sint, qui verbum eius, ut par est, audiunt & huic se se morigeros atq; obsequentes praebent.
units.tr: Just as God alone is good and holds all the treasures of goodness in himself, so through his word he offers us these goods to enjoy, and he shows us the way and method of attaining them. Nothing is therefore more useful, more saving, or more necessary for a man than to hear the word of God diligently and to shape his teaching and all his actions by it. Those who go astray in this lose their salvation. This is why Christ recently spoke at length about the nature and effects of the word of God, and urgently exhorted everyone to study it. He fittingly adds to that discussion the history of this passage, by which we are taught how highly esteemed before God are those who hear his word as they ought and show themselves compliant and obedient to it.

units.la: Orditur autem narrationem hanc Lucas ab ijs, qui Christo de hac re differendi occasionem praebuerunt. Fuerunt ij mater & fratres eius, quo nomine ex Hebraeorum more consobrinos & propiori cognitionis gradu coniunctos significari, iam saepe diximus. Veniunt isti illo in domo quadam docente, & cum prae auditorum frequentia ingredi non possent, mittunt aliquem (ut Marcus annotavit) qui ipsum foras euocaret. Vbi non immerito quis miretur, cur non illi quoque eum assidue comitati & secuti sint, interea eius auditores primi consederint? Atqui Mariam Virginem eius obseruantissimam fuisse satis constat; de eiusdem vero fratribus siue cognatis Ioannes scribit, quod non crediderint in eum, et quod eius omnia aperte calumniati sint. Comitantur tamen nunc illi Maria, vel quod hoc officium illi negare non possunt, vel quod nunc demum eius ipsos non amplius pudet, quando eum apud populum in summo pretio esse vident. Ideo satis pro imperio illum foras euocant, ut melius pateat omnibus, ipsos propter cognationem ius aliquod in illum obtinere. Est hoc magnum corruptae aut vitiosae naturae in nobis argumentum, quando ad credendum tardissimi sunt, qui prae alijs Christum agnoscere & amplecti debuissent, cum iam inde a tenera aetate spiritum & indolem humana maiorem multis argumentis declarasset, quae illi non poterant ignorare, qui ipsi coniunctus. Sed ut ex familiaritate fere contemptus nascitur, sic illa invidiam quoque & odium parit, ut indignius feramus eos nobis praeferri, qui nobis ex sanguinis propinquitate aut alias ob causas arctius coniuncti sunt. Exempla huius generis multa passim occurrunt, & in tota Iudaeorum gente impletum fuisse conflat, quod de istis dicitur. Nam etsi ex Iudaeis Christus secundum carnem natus esset, & eandem generis sui originem Apostoli quoq; haberent, nulli tamen tam Christi quam Apostolorum acriores hostes fuere, quam illi ipsi, ad quos ille propter promissiones patribus factas in primis pertinebat. Eadem quoq; Christo teste, omnium piorum atq; credentium fors est, ut domesticos suos fere hostes sentiant, qui illos calumnijs & criminibus falsis insectatur. Queritur de hoc Dauid no vno loco, ut iam de multis aliis nihil dicamus, qui eandem fortunam passi sunt. At cum hoc ipsum Dei filio accideret, in quo nihil contemptu aut odio dignum inueniri potuit, nequaquam nos offendi decet, qui saepe in causa bona affectibus prauis abrepti ea facimus, quae reprehensionem merentur.
units.tr: Luke begins this narrative with those who gave Christ the occasion to speak on this matter. They were his mother and brothers, a term which, as we have often said, in the Hebrew manner signifies cousins and relatives joined by a closer degree of kinship. They came to a certain house where he was teaching, and since they could not get in because of the crowd of hearers, they sent someone (as Mark noted) to call him outside. Here one may reasonably wonder why they had not also accompanied and followed him constantly, while his hearers were the first to sit down. Yet it is quite certain that Mary the Virgin was his most devoted follower; but of his brothers or cousins John writes that they did not believe in him and openly slandered all his doings. Nevertheless, they now accompany Mary, either because they could not refuse this duty to her, or because they are no longer ashamed of him now that they see him held in highest esteem by the people. So they summon him outside with an air of authority, so that it may be more plainly seen by all that they, because of their kinship, have some right over him. This is a great sign of a corrupt or depraved nature in us, when those who ought to have recognised and embraced Christ before others are the slowest to believe, although from his tender age he had shown a spirit and character greater than human by many proofs, which those close to him could not fail to know. But just as contempt is often born of familiarity, so it also gives birth to envy and hatred, so that we resent more bitterly being preferred over us by those who are more closely joined to us by blood or other ties. Examples of this kind occur everywhere, and it is plain that what is said of these people was fulfilled in the whole Jewish nation. For although Christ was born of the Jews according to the flesh, and the apostles too had the same origin of their race, yet none were more bitter enemies of Christ and the apostles than those very people to whom he especially belonged because of the promises made to the fathers. Likewise, as Christ himself testified, it is the lot of all the godly and believing to find their own household almost their enemies, who harass them with slanders and false accusations. David complains of this in more than one place, not to mention many others who suffered the same fate. But since this happened to the Son of God himself, in whom nothing worthy of contempt or hatred could be found, we ought by no means to be offended when we, who are often carried away by wrong passions in a good cause, do things that deserve reproof.

units.la: Audiamus nunc Christi responsum, in quo recitando Lucas breuitati studuit, nimirum quod hoc a Matthaeo & Marco plenius expositum esse sciret, qui sic eum respondisse scribunt: Quae est mater mea, & fratres mei? Et mox cum circumspexisset in circuitu circum se discipulos sedentes, protensa in illos manu dixit: Ecce mater mea, & fratres mei. Mater enim mea & fratres mei sunt, qui sermonem Dei audiunt, & cum praestant. Sunt ergo responsionis huius partes duae. Prima durius reijcit nuntium hoc, quo foras euocabatur. Quae (inquit) est mater mea, & fratres mei? Quae verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi aut matrem abnegarit, aut fratrum atq; cognatorum ipsum puduerit: sed quod ipsum sibi a Patre caelesti commissum munus obeuntem importunius reuocarent, reprehendit, seq; nihil hic illis debere ostendit. Idem ergo hic dicit, quod supra, quando a virgine matre reprehensus, quod in urbe manifestet et in templo doceret, respondit: Quid est quod quaerebatis me? an nesciebatis, quod in iis quae patris mei sunt, oporteat me esse? Nemo igitur hinc impietatis occasionem arripiat, ut parentes, aut eos, quibus obstrictus est, deserat, & debitum illis officium neget: quod hodie Monachi & Anabaptistae non minus impudenter quam inhumaniter faciunt.
