Constat enim in aliis Christum matris obseruantissimum fuisse, & ut ipsum patris putatitij non puduit, quo minus cum illo ac temfabrilem exerceret: ita matre ne moriturus quidem neglexit, sed sui erga eam officij probe memor, illam Ioanni dilecto discipulo commendauit. Desinant ergo crudeles illi pietatis praetextu & Christi exemplo ad impietatis suae defensionem abuti. Sunt enim ipsi ex ἀσορῳον numero, quos nonnullis temporibus exorituros esse Paulus praedixit, & quos idem infidelibus deteriores esse pronuntiat, quando innatas nobis affectiones extinguunt, & eos etiam crudeliter negligunt, quos naturae lex nobis commendat, & quos alieni a fide maximi facere consueuerunt.
units.tr: Let us now hear Christ's answer. In recounting it Luke aimed at brevity, no doubt because he knew that Matthew and Mark had set it out more fully; they write that he answered thus: "Who is my mother and my brothers?" And soon afterwards, when he had looked round at the disciples sitting about him, he stretched out his hand towards them and said, "Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever hears the word of God and does it, he is my mother and my brother." So there are two parts to this answer. First, he rejects the message by which he was summoned outside, rather sharply: "Who," he says, "is my mother and my brothers?" These words should not be taken to mean that he disowned his mother, or that he was ashamed of his brothers and kinsfolk; rather, he rebukes them for recalling him too importunately while he was discharging the office committed to him by the heavenly Father, and he shows that he owes them nothing in this matter. So he says here what he said above, when the Virgin his mother rebuked him for revealing himself in the city and teaching in the temple, and he answered: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?" Let no one therefore seize on this as an occasion for impiety, to desert parents or those to whom he is bound, and to deny them the duty they are owed; this the Monks and Anabaptists do today no less shamelessly than inhumanly. For it is plain that Christ was most dutiful to his mother in other respects, and that he was not ashamed to work as a carpenter alongside his supposed father; likewise, even when about to die, he did not neglect his mother, but, mindful of his duty to her, he commended her to John, his beloved disciple. Let those cruel men therefore cease to abuse the pretext of piety and the example of Christ to defend their impiety. For they are of the number of the "without natural affection" [ἄστοργοι], whom Paul predicted would arise in later times, and whom he declares to be worse than unbelievers, since they extinguish the affections implanted in us and cruelly neglect those whom the law of nature commends to us, and whom even those alienated from the faith are wont to hold in highest regard.

units.la: Nemo igitur exemplum hoc filij Dei extra praesentis argumenti fines longius extendere debet. Hoc enim solum docere vult, eos qui in Dei vocatione versantur, omnibus alijs rebus relictis huic uni vacare debere, adeo, ut (si opus sit) ἐργάτας quoq; id est, affectiones naturales exuant, neq; aliquem mortalium tanti faciant, ut in eius gratiam ab officio suo discedant. Qui enim (ut D. Ambrosius scribit) alijs dicebat: Qui non reliquerit patrem suum & matrem suam, non est me dignus: seipsum primus eidem sententiae subiecit, ut suo exemplo nobis praeiret. Sibi ergo haec dici meminerint, qui cunq; in ecclesiae ministerio agunt. Debet illi parentibus suis omnia pietatis officia. At si ijdem ipsos in verbi praedicatione impedire, aut ab officio suo prorsus retrahere instituant, indignos tunc putent, quos parentum loco habeat. Obseruarunt hoc olim Prophetae & Apostoli. Elizeus cerete cum ab Elia vocaretur, & vocatione hanc ex Deo esse intelligeret, mox parentibus valedixit, & relictis boum iugis & aratro, illum secutus est. Quod ipsum Christo vocante Petrum & Andream, Ioannem & Iacobum fecisse scimus. Ijdem sui quoque muneris esse sciant, qui Rempub. administrant. Quia enim bis patriae communis & populi totius salus credita est, minime decet, ut propter parentes aut cognatos suos, qui minima eius populi pars sunt, publicam salutem negligant. Laudatur in historijs Romanus ille Consul, qui patrem ad se venientem ex equo descendere iussit, ne maiorem priuatae pietatis quam publicae authoritatis rationem habere videretur. Quanto magis ergo hoc tunc obseruari debet, quando publica salus in periculum venit? At quod de publicis personis dicitur, non minus ad singulos priuatim pertinet: ut nimirum quam a Deo habent vocationem omnibus rebus praeferant. Vocamur autem omnes ad Christum, ut procul relictis superstitionibus & mundi huius studijs, illi soli nos consecremus, & per hunc nos Patri caelesti sistamus viuentem hostiam. Tueamur ergo vocationem nostram, neq; aliquid tanti a nobis fiat, ut eius gratia fidem Christo datam violemus. Debent autem haec alij quoq; expendere, quibus cum nobis res est: ne videlicet indignius ferant, si ipsis
units.tr: No one, therefore, should extend this example of the Son of God beyond the limits of the present subject. For he wishes only to teach that those who are engaged in God's calling should, with all other things set aside, devote themselves to this alone, so much so that (if need be) they should also become eunuchs [εὐνοῦχοι], that is, strip off natural affections, and value no mortal so highly that for his sake they depart from their duty. For Ambrose writes that he who said to others, "He who does not leave his father and mother is not worthy of me," first submitted himself to the same sentence, so that he might go before us by his example. Let all who serve in the ministry of the Church therefore remember that these words are said to them. They owe their parents every duty of piety. But if their parents set out to hinder them in preaching the word, or to drag them away from their office altogether, let them then think them unworthy to be regarded as parents. The prophets and apostles observed this in former times. Elisha indeed, when he was called by Elijah, and understood that this calling was from God, at once bade his parents farewell, and, leaving his yoke of oxen and his plough, followed him. We know that Peter and Andrew, John and James did the same when Christ called them. Let those too who administer the commonwealth know that this is part of their duty. For since the common safety of the fatherland and of the whole people has been entrusted to them, it is by no means fitting that they should neglect the public welfare for the sake of their parents or kinsfolk, who are the smallest part of that people. In histories the Roman consul is praised who ordered his father, coming to him, to dismount from his horse, so that he might not seem to give more weight to private piety than to public authority. How much more, then, ought this to be observed when the public safety is in danger? But what is said of public persons applies no less to each individual in private: namely, that they should set the calling they have from God above all things. Now we are all called to Christ, so that, with superstitions and the pursuits of this world left far behind, we may dedicate ourselves to him alone, and through him present ourselves to the heavenly Father as a living sacrifice. Let us therefore guard our calling, and let nothing be valued so highly by us that for its sake we violate the faith pledged to Christ. Those who have dealings with us should also weigh these things, lest they bear it more indignantly if we deny them obedience in those matters which cannot be done without sacrificing obedience and the piety we owe to God. For who are you, O man, that the divine majesty should yield to your will?

units.la: Val. Max. lib. 2. cap. 1. obsequium negemus in iis, quae salua obedientia & pietate, quam Deo debemus, fieri non possunt. Tu enim quis es o homo, cuius voluntati diuina maiestas cedere debeat? Improbantur filij, qui ut sodalium petulantiae morem gerant, parentum iussa negligunt: & tu ab aliquo mortalium requiris, ut propter te Dei mandatum transgrediatur?
units.tr: Val. Max. lib. 2. cap. 1. Let us refuse obedience in those things which cannot be done while keeping the obedience and piety we owe to God. For who are you, O man, that the divine majesty should yield to your will? Sons are rightly condemned who, to please their companions' wantonness, neglect their parents' commands. And will you ask any mortal to transgress God's command for your sake?

units.la: Seruit praeterea locus hic iis confutandis, qui ut Mariae Virgini & diuis caelitibus rem gratam (ut ipsi sentiunt) faciant, relicto Christo illos sibi aduocatos & Mediatores faciunt, illos inuocant, & eisdem sacra faciunt. Possumus nos quoque illis dicere: Et quae est Mariae? & qui iunt Diui caelites, ut propter illos fidem in Iesum Christum abnegare, & qui huic uni debetur, honorem in illos transferre debeamus? Maria quidem electum illud organum est, quo Deus ex singulari gratia uti dignatus est, ut ex ea Filius eius aeternus hominis filius fieret, & illam saluo atque illaeso virginitatis flore Dei Filium ex Spiritu Sancto concepisse atque postea peperisse credimus & fatemur. Eandem vero pro nobis intercedere, periclitantibus adesse, & proinde inuocari & diuinus honoribus coli debere negamus: quia nihil huius docent sacrae literae, neque exempla habemus veteris & primitiuae Ecclesiae quibus id defendi possit. Apostolorum enim omnium doctrina atque sententia fuit: Non esse aliud nomen sub caelo hominibus datum, in quo nos seruari oporteat, praeter unum Iesum Christum. Item, Vnus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus. Et rursus: Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud Deum, Iesum Christum. Neque legimus, quenquam ex sanctis illis Martyribus, quos primitiua Ecclesia per annos amplius quingentos dedit, vel Mariae virginis, vel Diuorum intercessione confisum esse & illos inuocasse: fuerunt quidem Apostoli & qui post eos Euangelij doctrinam in orbe terrarum diuulgarunt, fideles Christi serui, quorum opera ille in regno suo propagando feliciter usus est: at ijdem adeo nihil sibi tribui voluerunt, sicuti Ioannis & Petri, Pauli item & Barnabae exempla testantur. Qui ergo illud hodie faciunt, ij & Christum & Diuos atroci iniuria afficiunt, quando illi quidem suum honorem eripiunt, horum autem nominibus abutuntur in stabiliendis superstitionibus, qui ut Christo suum honorem vendicarent, sanguinem proprium fuderunt.
units.tr: This passage also serves to refute those who, in order to do what they think is a pleasing service to the Virgin Mary and the heavenly saints, set them up in place of Christ as their advocates and mediators, invoke them, and offer them sacred rites. We may say to them: What is Mary to us, and what are the heavenly saints, that for their sake we should deny faith in Jesus Christ, and transfer to them the honour that is due to him alone? Mary was indeed the chosen instrument which God in his singular grace deigned to use, so that from her his eternal Son might become the Son of man. We believe and confess that she conceived the Son of God by the Holy Spirit and afterwards bore him, her virginity still whole and unharmed. But we deny that she intercedes for us, stands by those in peril, and therefore that she should be invoked and honoured with divine worship. For the holy Scriptures teach nothing of this, nor do we have examples from the old and primitive Church by which it could be defended. For the teaching and judgement of all the apostles was: there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved, except Jesus Christ alone. Likewise: there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. And again: if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ. Nor do we read that any of those holy martyrs whom the primitive Church produced over more than five hundred years trusted in the intercession of the Virgin Mary or of the saints, or invoked them. The apostles were indeed, and so were those who after them spread the teaching of the gospel throughout the world, faithful servants of Christ, through whose work he prospered the propagation of his kingdom. Yet they wanted nothing of this kind to be attributed to themselves, as the examples of John and Peter, and likewise of Paul and Barnabas, bear witness. Therefore those who do this today do a grievous wrong both to Christ and to the saints. They snatch away his honour from him, while they abuse the names of the saints to establish superstitions, though these saints shed their own blood to vindicate Christ's honour.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad alteram responsionis Christi partem, quam mira cum grauitate enunciat. Prius enim discipulos in circuitu sedentes circumspiciens, quasi magnum quid animo iam volueret (ut reuera faciebat) inde manu in illos protensa ait: Ecce mater mea & fratres mei. Et mox dicti sui rationem adducit: addens: Mater enim mea, & fratres mei sunt, qui sermone Dei audiunt, & eum praestant. Est autem tota huius sententiae ratio in Christi officio fundata. Ne enim aliqui superstitiosiores felicitatem in carnali cognatione, quae pauculis istis cum Christo intercedebat, consistere putarent, diserte docet, hanc ad aeternam salutem nihil nobis conferre, neque se paucorum modo Seruatorem esse, sed omnium, qui verbum Dei audiunt, & audito obediunt. Non ergo Virginem matrem contumeliosius prius negauit, neque cognatos superbo contemptu fastidiuit, sed ex erroris occasione, quae oblata erat, doctrinam generalem infert et omnibus necessariam, qui cum ipso coniungi & filij Dei fieri cupiunt. Et quod Ambrosius annotauit, non obscure Iudaeis repudium denuntiauit, quos carnis & generis praerogatiua in primis superbiuisse, & in hac salutis fiduciam habuisse scimus. Ostendit ergo, quod illis reiectis, qui ex patribus sanctissimis oriundi erant, & ex quibus ipse homo natus fuerat, eos in filiorum Dei locum succedere oporteat, qui ipsi per fidem recte coalescunt.
units.tr: But let us pass to the second part of Christ's answer, which he states with remarkable gravity. For first, looking around at the disciples sitting in a circle, as if he were now about to say something great (as indeed he was), he stretched out his hand towards them and said: Behold my mother and my brethren. And straightaway he gives the reason for his saying, adding: For whoever hears the word of God and does it, these are my mother and my brethren. The whole reasoning of this statement is grounded in Christ's office. Lest some who were too superstitious should think that happiness lay in the fleshly kinship that linked a few people with Christ, he teaches plainly that this kinship contributes nothing to our eternal salvation, and that he is the Saviour not only of a few but of all who hear the word of God and obey it once heard. So he did not disown his virgin mother in a contemptuous way, nor did he disdainfully scorn his kinsmen. Rather, taking the occasion offered by their error, he sets forth a general teaching necessary for all who desire to be joined to him and to become sons of God. And what Ambrose has noted, he plainly renounced the Jews, whom we know were especially puffed up by the privilege of flesh and descent and placed their confidence of salvation in it. He shows, then, that when these people are rejected, although they sprang from the most holy fathers and Christ himself was born from them, those who are truly united to him through faith must take their place as sons of God.

units.la: At hic nobis ante omnia probe obseruandum est, quod nam illud verbum Dei sit, de quo Christus loquitur. Sunt enim, qui (ut alibi diximus) verbum nescio quod internum & non scriptum somniantes, sese vanissimorum hominum illusionibus seducendos praebent. At quod hic de verbo dicit, hoc apud Matthaeum & Marcum voluntati Dei patris caelestis tribuit: Qui fecerit (inquit) voluntatem patris mei, qui est in caelis, hic meus frater, & soror, & mater est. De nullo igitur verbo locus iste intelligi debet, quam quo suam voluntatem nobis Deus reuelauit. Id autem scripturis conuineri, nemo negare poterit, nisi qui ipsam Dei voluntatem in dubium vocare velit. Et ut uno verbo rem expediamus, Sermo ille Dei non aliud est, quam Euangelium, quo Christus praedicatur, & in hoc nobis iustitia, sanctificatio, redemptio & salus offertur. Huius argumentum & summam prima promissio continet de semine mulieris, per quod serpentis caput conteri & Adamum cum sua posteritate ex diaboli servitio & morte asseri oporteat. Ad huius expositionem pleniorem & confirmationem faciunt Lex & Prophetae, quibus deinde lux clarior & perfectior accessit, quando Dei Filius in carne manifestatus, ipse aeternum hoc Patris consilium praedicavit, & idem ipsius iussu Apostoli in toto terrarum orbe divulgaverunt. Ideo apud Ioannem ille ait, Amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam. En de suo sermone Christus loquitur, quem non alium quam Euangelium esse, ex ijs apparet, quae Apostolus in mandatis dedit, dicens: Ite in orbem universum & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae, & doce- te omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos servare omnia, quae mandavi vobis. At idem alibi testatur, doctrinam suam non esse suam, sed Patris, qui ipsum misit. Ergo Euangelij doctrina salutifera illud Dei verbum continet, de quo hic sermo est, hoc ipsum vero Dei quoque voluntatem nobis indicat, quam qui faciunt, in Dei Filios renati vitae aeternae haereditatem obtinebunt. Docet hoc Christus Ioannis sexto sic dicens: Haec est voluntas Dei, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. Et haec quidem diligentius tractanda fuerunt propter rudes & rerum imperitos, ne phanaticorum somniis decepti, Verbum Dei & eius voluntatem extra scripturas quaerant, & errorum laqueis intricentur.
units.tr: Here we must first of all carefully observe what that word of God is of which Christ speaks. For there are some (as we have said elsewhere) who dream of I know not what inward and unwritten word, and so allow themselves to be led astray by the delusions of the most empty men. But what he says here about the word, he attributes in Matthew and Mark to the will of God the heavenly Father: Whoever (he says) does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister and mother. Therefore this passage must be understood of no word except that by which God has revealed his will to us. That this is proved by the Scriptures no one can deny, unless he wishes to call into doubt the very will of God. And to settle the matter in one word: that word of God is nothing other than the gospel, by which Christ is preached, and in which righteousness, sanctification, redemption and salvation are offered to us. The argument and sum of this is contained in the first promise, concerning the seed of the woman, by which the head of the serpent must be crushed and Adam, with his posterity, must be rescued from the slavery and death of the devil. The Law and the Prophets serve to expound and confirm this more fully, and afterwards a clearer and more perfect light was added when the Son of God, manifested in the flesh, himself preached this eternal counsel of the Father, and the apostles, at his command, spread it throughout the whole world. Therefore in John he says: Truly I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. Here Christ speaks of his own word, which is evidently nothing other than the gospel, as appears from the commission the apostles were given: Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature, and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you. Yet he elsewhere testifies that his teaching is not his own but that of the Father who sent him. Therefore the saving teaching of the gospel contains that word of God of which he speaks here, and this same word also shows us the will of God, which those who do it, being born again as sons of God, will obtain as the inheritance of eternal life. Christ teaches this in John chapter six, saying: This is the will of God who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. These matters had to be treated more carefully on account of the untrained and ignorant, lest, deceived by the dreams of fanatics, they seek the word of God and his will outside the Scriptures, and become entangled in the snares of error.

units.la: Deinde tenere oportet, ut in verbo hoc versari debeamus. Loquitur autem de illis Christus, qui sermonem Dei audiunt, & eum praestant. Primum ut illum audiamus necesse est, eo quod nisi id fiat, nulla nobis illius cognitio poterit obtingere. Quomodo credent ei (inquit Paulus) de quo non audierunt? Et nota est Patris vox de Filio coelitus delata, Ipsum audite. In ipso igitur limine offendunt, qui Euangelium ne audire quidem volunt, sive illud hostili animo, sive confidenti praesumptione faciant. At ne quis in otiosa verbi auditione, vel etiam lectione salutem consistere putet, alterum addit, ut quod audivimus factis praestemus. Non enim in sermone aut locutione (ut Paulus ait) est regnum Dei, sed in virtute spiritus. Et alibi Christus eos quoq; abs se reijcit, qui verbi ministri quidem fuerunt, non autem fecerunt voluntatem Patris sui, qui in coelis est. Praestant autem sermonem Dei, qui (ut paulo ante ex Ioannis sexto annotavimus) Filium eius Iesum Christum recte agnoscunt, & in illo uno omnem suae salutis spem atq; fiduciam collocant. Est enim hoc praecipuum divinae voluntatis caput, ex quo omnia alia deriuantur. Fides enim haec ita nos Christo insérit, ut eius spiritu animati illum vita & moribus referamus, eandemq; charitatem in nobis gignit, qua legem totam impleri Apostolus testatur.
units.tr: Next we must hold fast so that we may abide in this word. Christ speaks of those who hear the word of God and do it. First, it is necessary that we hear it, since unless this happens, no knowledge of it can come to us. How will they believe him, says Paul, of whom they have not heard? And the voice of the Father from heaven concerning the Son is well known: Hear him. Those, then, stumble at the very threshold who do not wish even to hear the gospel, whether they do so from hostile feeling or from confident presumption. But lest anyone think that salvation consists in idle hearing or even reading of the word, Christ adds another requirement: that we carry out in deeds what we have heard. For, as Paul says, the kingdom of God is not in speech or talk, but in power of the Spirit. And elsewhere Christ casts off those too who were indeed ministers of the word but did not do the will of his Father who is in heaven. Those, however, carry out the word of God who (as we noted a little earlier from John chapter six) rightly acknowledge his Son Jesus Christ and place all their hope and confidence of salvation in him alone. For this is the chief point of the divine will, from which all other things derive. This faith so engrafts us into Christ that, animated by his Spirit, we express him in our life and conduct, and it begets in us that same love by which the Apostle testifies the whole law is fulfilled.

units.la: Ex hoc igitur praeclarus ille & admirabilis verbi Dei effectus sequitur, quem in praesenti nobis Christus commendat, quando eos, qui illud audiunt & praestant, suos fratres, sorores, imo matrem quoque esse ait. Quia enim (ut Ioannis primo scribitur) filij Dei fiunt, qui Christum Iesum apprehendunt fide, ijdem huius etiam fratres & sorores sint necesse est. Sed & mater Christi esse dicuntur: Quia verbum illud intra animi & cordis sinus concipiunt, ex quo Christus cum in ipsis tum in alijs generatur, quos ipsi Deo adducunt. Quem verbi effectum Paulus obseruans, Galatis dicebat: Filioli mei, quos iterum pariurio, donec formetur Christus in vobis. En Christum in illis formari, adeoque novum nasci cupit, & hunc sui ministerij finem sibi propositum habet. Minime ergo eorum similis fuit, qui hodie vnctionis & tonsionis Pontificia authoritate acceptae fiducia freti, quaeque verborum susurris Christum ex crustula panis formare satagunt. Nec enim ut ex pane, aut in pane, sed ut in hominibus Christus formetur necesse est. Quod cum fiat quando verbum audimus & praestamus, magna huius dignitas sit oportet. Quid? quod ipsius etiam Christi spon sa efficimur, quam is sanguine suo ablutam & mundatam, sibi aeterni foederis vinculo plus quam adamantino copulavit, ut & regni sui & bonorum coelestium consortem habeat? Magna igitur & detestabilis eorum ingratitudo est, qui cum tam expeditam rationem sibi propositam videant, qua Filij Dei, fratres, sorores, mater denique & sponsa fieri possunt, eam tamen securi negligunt, & mundo potius placere studient. Impietas autem plus quam diabolica eorum est, qui tantam Dei bonitatem hostiliter infestantur: neq; eo contenti sunt, quod ipsi fratres & sorores Christi fieri nolunt, verumetiam alijs ferro & igne se opponunt, ne ad dignitatem illam peruenire possint.
units.tr: From this, then, follows that remarkable and admirable effect of the Word of God, which Christ commends to us in the present passage, when he says that those who hear it and put it into practice are his brothers, sisters, and even his mother. For since (as is written in the first chapter of John) those who lay hold of Jesus Christ by faith become children of God, they must also be his brothers and sisters. But they are also said to be the mother of Christ: because they conceive that word within the bosom of their mind and heart, from which Christ is begotten both in themselves and in others, whom they bring to God. Paul, observing this effect of the Word, said to the Galatians: "My little children, for whom I labour again in birth until Christ be formed in you." Behold, he desires that Christ be formed in them, and so be born anew, and he has this as the aim of his ministry. He was therefore by no means like those who today, trusting in the anointing and tonsuring received by Papal authority, and who by whispered words labour to form Christ out of a little crust of bread. For Christ must be formed not in bread or from bread, but in men. Since this takes place when we hear and practise the word, its dignity must indeed be great. What more? Are we not also made the spouse of Christ himself, whom he, having washed and cleansed her with his own blood, has joined to himself by the bond of an eternal covenant, stronger than adamant, so that she may have a share in his kingdom and in the heavenly goods? Great, therefore, and detestable is the ingratitude of those who, though they see so easy a way set before them by which they may become sons of God, brothers, sisters, mother and finally bride, nevertheless carelessly neglect it, and strive rather to please the world. Their impiety, moreover, is more than devilish, who wage hostile war against so great a goodness of God: and they are not content merely to refuse to become brothers and sisters of Christ, but they even oppose others with sword and fire, lest they be able to attain that dignity.

units.la: Cap. VIII.
units.tr: Chapter 8.

units.la: Commendatur nobis praeterea Christianorum hominum dignitas, qui a nobis maximi fieri debent. Si enim praeclarum mundo videtur, ex illustri viro natum esse, & auitus stemmatum nobilissimorum ornamentis gloriari posse, quanto maior eorum gloria censeri debet, quos pro germanis filijs Deus agnoscit, eo quod Filij sui unigeniti fratres per fidem facti sint? Heroes suos Poetae hoc potissimum nomine commendant, quod ex Diis genitos & a Ioue enutritos esse fabulantur. At ijdem dum hoc faciunt, Deos quidem suos libidine & stupris infames faciunt, illis autem legitimi thori natales negant. Et quibus gradibus fere hodie ad nobilitatis fastigium plerique ascendant, non opus est dicere, quando tota illa gloria in diuitijs consistit, quas vel lenocinio, vel vsura & fraudibus, vel etiam caedibus & rapinis parari scimus. Neminem ergo inanis mundi splendor aut caeca hominum vanissimorum iudicia fallant: quin his contemptis toti in hoc simus, vt ex verbo Dei renati, Christi fratres efficiamur, quae vt vera nobilitas est, sic salutem quoque aeternam sibi coniunctam habet. Debet praeterea locus iste nos ad charitatis & beneficentiae studium excitare. Si enim non facile negliguntur principum & magnatum filij, eo quod nihil non ex illis sibi pollicentur, qui eos in aliquo periculo aut rerum angustia laborantes iuuant: multo minus negligi debent, qui per fidem in Christum Dei filij facti sunt. Vt enim hos pro suis fratribus agnoscit aeternus Dei Filius, ita olim in magno illo die tanquam sibi facta officia remunerabitur, quaecunque illis facta fuerint. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Next, the dignity of Christians is commended to us, and they ought to be held in the highest esteem by us. For if it seems a splendid thing to the world to be born of an illustrious man and to be able to boast of the ornaments of most noble ancestry, how much greater should their glory be judged to be, whom God acknowledges as his own true sons, because they have become brothers of his only-begotten Son through faith? Poets commend their heroes chiefly on this ground, that they are fabled to have been born of the gods and nurtured by Jupiter. Yet in doing this they make their gods infamous through lust and debauchery, and deny that those heroes were born of lawful wedlock. And there is no need to say by what steps most people today climb to the summit of nobility, since all that glory consists in riches, which we know are acquired by pandering, by usury and fraud, and even by murders and robberies. Let no one, therefore, be deceived by the empty splendour of the world or by the blind judgements of the most foolish men; rather, let us all, having despised these things, aim at being born again of the Word of God and becoming brothers of Christ. This is true nobility, and it has eternal salvation joined to it. Moreover, this passage ought to stir us up to a zeal for love and beneficence. For if the sons of princes and great men are not readily neglected, because men expect everything from them, how much less should those be neglected who through faith in Christ have become sons of God, when they are helped in some danger or distress? For just as the eternal Son of God acknowledges these as his brothers, so on that great day he will reward, as if done to himself, whatever kindness has been shown to them. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY 80.

units.la: Factum est autem quodam die, ipse ingressus est in naviigium, ac discipuli eius, & dixit eis, Transeamus in vlteriorem ripam stagni. Et profecti sunt. Navigantibus autem eis sopitus est, & descendit turbo venti in stagnum, & complebantur, ac periclitabantur. Accedentes autem expergefecerunt eum, dicentes: Magister, magister, perimus. Ipse vero experrectus obiurgauit ventum ac fluctuationem aquae, & cessauerunt, factaque est tranquillitas. Dixit autem eis: Vbi est fides vestra? Timentes autem mirati sunt, dicentes ad alios: Quis nam iste est, vt ventis quoque & aquae imperet, & auscultent ei?
units.tr: It happened on a certain day that he himself got into a boat, with his disciples, and he said to them, "Let us cross over to the far side of the lake." And they set out. But as they sailed he fell asleep, and a violent squall of wind came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. They came and woke him, saying, "Master, master, we are perishing!" He, awakened, rebuked the wind and the rough water, and they ceased, and there was a calm. Then he said to them, "Where is your faith?" But they were afraid and marvelled, saying to one another, "Who then is this, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?"

units.la: Quoniam salus nostra omnis in eo potissimum consistit, vt Dei verbum digne audiamus, & quae in hoc nobis offeruntur, fide constanti apprehendamus, Christus Iesus illius studium itanobis commendat, vt simul vitijs omnibus diligenter medeatur, quae aut nos ab illo revocare, aut eius fructum impedire possunt. Primum inter illa locum habent prauì affectus, qui animum totum a Deo & verbo eius alienant, eoque vehementiores sunt, si diaboli suggestionibus, mundi exemplo atque illecebris accendantur. Istos autem corrigere & ijsdem sua fomenta subtrahere docuit, per sementis parabolam. Deinde admonitionem subiecit grauem, qua docuit vt verbum hoc tractari debeat, & quod hoc nemo impune contemnat aut negligat. Quia vero plurimum hic nocent mundi iudicia, qui eos fere contumelijs & infamia obruit, qui serio verbi studio tenentur, ijsdem consolationem adhibuit, qua supremam gloriam illis pollicetur, dum nos sibi fratrum, sororum & matris loco fore docet. Nunc ad illud accedit, quo caro nostra quam maxime abster- reretur, persecutiones nimirum, quas omnibus illis paratas esse Apostolus monet, qui in ipso volunt pie viuere. Et cum alibi nos doctrina instruat, & promissionibus amplissimis confirmet, nunc insigni miraculo demonstrat, se illis nunquam defuturum esse, qui propter ipsum periclitantur, neque sibi vires deesse, quibus eos liberet, & omnibus tentationibus superiores faciat. Continet praeterea locus iste vtilem doctrinam de fidei imbecillitate, quae in sanctis quoque interdum inuenitur, de aduersorum & persecutionum causis, & quid nos in illis facere conuenit: Quam quia nobis Dei Filius, quasi in tabella depictam propositi, eo nos diligentiores esse oportet in eius consideratione, vt quoties opus est, nobis ob oculos & in animo versetur.
units.tr: Since our whole salvation depends chiefly on this, that we hear God's word worthily and grasp with steadfast faith what is offered to us in it, Christ Jesus recommends this zeal to us so that at the same time he carefully heals all the faults that can either call us back from him or hinder the fruit of his word. Among these, first place is held by wicked affections, which estrange the whole mind from God and from his word, and which are all the more violent if they are kindled by the suggestions of the devil, the example of the world and its allurements. He taught us to correct these and to take away their fuel, by the parable of the sower. Next he added a grievous warning, by which he taught how this word ought to be handled, and that no one can despise or neglect it with impunity. But because the judgements of the world do great harm here, which overwhelm with insults and disgrace those who are seriously devoted to the study of the word, he applied to them a consolation, promising them the highest glory, while he teaches that we shall be his brothers, sisters and mother. Now there is added that which would most of all terrify our flesh, namely the persecutions which the Apostle warns are prepared for all who want to live godly in him. And although elsewhere his teaching instructs us and his very ample promises strengthen us, here by a remarkable miracle he shows that he will never fail those who are in danger on his account, and that he lacks no power to deliver them and make them superior to all temptations. Moreover this passage contains useful teaching about the weakness of faith, which is sometimes found even in the saints, about the causes of adversities and persecutions, and about what we ought to do in them. Since the Son of God has set these before us as if painted on a tablet, we ought to be all the more diligent in considering them, so that, as often as need is, they may be before our eyes and in our minds.

units.la: Occasionem totius negotij ipse Christus praebuit, qui stagnum traijcere volens, discipulos iubet, vt in ea ut in eo suam operam præstent. Narrat hoc diligenter Marcus, qui ea ipsa navi eos traiecisse scribit, ex qua ad populum in littore stantem ille concionatus fuerat. Unde apparet, historiam, quam proximè audivimus à Luca non observato ordine temporis, sed propter argumenti similitudinem interpositam fuisse, ut Verbum Dei magis commendaretur. In præsenti autem observari diligenter debet Christus, qui etsi non ignoraret, quid esset futurum, tamen institut, & discipulos soluere iubet, adeoque sciens & consulto illos periculo maximo obijcit, in quo perituros se putauerunt. Istud vero tunc fecit, quando de Verbo Dei & eius effectis concionem luculentam & dulcissimam consolationis plenam habuerat. Ita vero re ipsa docere voluit, ne sub Euangelij prætextu otium & voluptates quæramus, sed meminerimus laborès & omnis generis pericula eos manere, qui ipsi nomen derunt, & crucem Verbi sui comitem esse indiuulsam, ad quam ferendam discipulos suos præparari oporteat. Admonet de hoc nos sæpius differtis verbis, & nunquam non debet in auribus nostris sonare vox illa: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Coniungamus huic exempla, quæ in veriusq; Testamenti libris plurima habentur, & facile intelligemus, nihil nouum aut insolens nobis accidere, si nos quoq; laboribus & periculis nouis quotidie exerceamur. Soletur autem nos in hisce certaminibus, quod nihil insscio aut inuito Christo nobis accidit. Pendent enim omnia nostra à Dei prouidentia, qui cum aulibus & reliquis animantibus prospiciat, procul dubio ecclesiam suam non fortuitis & incertis cæca fortunæ vicibus fluctuare finit, sed certo & prudenti consilio eam regit atque gubernat. Quoties ergo periculis undiq; immi nentibus premimur, & in extremo rerum discrimine sumus constituti, tunc cogitemus hoc non absq; Dei consilio fieri, qui fidem nostram hac ratione exercet, nostræ infirmitatis nos admonet, patientiæ materiam præbet, & postremò suam in nobis liberandis atq; defendendis potentiam eò illustriorem reddit, quò grauius & periculosius nos tentari finit. Neq; de euentu nos multum solicitos esse conuenit. Nam fieri non potest, quin is felicissimus ijs obtingat, qui Christo iubente se & res suas periculis committunt. Nam ut Apostolus ait, fidelis est Deus, qui non finit nos tentari supra id quod possumus, sed præstat cum tentatione etiam euasionem, ut possimus sufferre. Quòd si autem dura & aduersa multa sentiunt, qui Christum vocantem aut iubentem sequuntur, quid de illis speramus, qui cæcas carnis cupiditates secuti se mundi huius pelago committunt, & manifestis periculis obijciunt, ut diuitias consequantur, honoribus publicis ornentur, vel etiam ut libidini suæ & voluptatibus illicitis indulgeant? Videntur quidem illi interdum felicissimi mortalium, & trahit illos fortunæ blandientis insidiosus fauor, ut contemptis admonitionibus sibi omnia læta polliceantur, & scientes atq; volentes Satanæ laqueis seipsos obijciant. Accidit ergo illis tandem quod Syrachides ille dixit: Qui amat periculum, peribit in eo.
units.tr: Christ himself gave the occasion for the whole matter, for wishing to cross the lake he bids the disciples to do their work in it and on it. Mark relates this carefully, writing that they crossed in the very boat from which he had preached to the people standing on the shore. Hence it appears that the story we have just heard from Luke was inserted, not in the order of time, but because of the similarity of the subject, so that the Word of God might be more commended. In the present passage, however, Christ must be observed carefully: although he did not fail to know what would happen, nevertheless he lay down and bids them loose the boat, and so, knowingly and deliberately, he exposes them to the greatest danger, in which they thought they would perish. He did this just after he had given a splendid sermon about the Word of God and its effects, full of sweet consolation. He wished in fact to teach by this that we should not seek leisure and pleasures under the pretext of the gospel, but remember that labours and dangers of every kind await those who bear his name, and that the cross is the inseparable companion of his Word, for which his disciples must be prepared to bear it. He admonishes us of this more often in other words, and that voice should never cease to sound in our ears: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Let us add to this the examples which are very many in the books of both Testaments, and we shall easily understand that nothing new or strange happens to us if we too are daily exercised by new labours and dangers. Moreover in these conflicts we are comforted by the fact that nothing happens to us without the knowledge or against the will of Christ. For all our affairs depend on the providence of God, who watches over the birds and the other living creatures, and who undoubtedly does not allow his Church to be tossed about by the blind and uncertain turns of fortune, but governs and steers it by a certain and wise counsel. Therefore, whenever we are pressed by dangers threatening on every side, and are placed in the extreme peril of affairs, let us then think that this does not happen without the counsel of God, who exercises our faith in this way, reminds us of our weakness, provides matter for patience, and finally makes his power in delivering and defending us all the more illustrious, the more heavily and dangerously he allows us to be tested. Nor is it fitting that we be very anxious about the outcome. For it cannot be that it should not turn out most happily for those who commit themselves and their possessions to dangers at Christ's bidding. For, as the Apostle says, "God is faithful, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able, but with the temptation also provides the way of escape, that we may be able to bear it." But if those who follow Christ when he calls or commands suffer many hard and adverse things, what are we to hope for those who, following blind fleshly desires, commit themselves to the sea of this world and expose themselves to manifest dangers, in order to obtain riches, be adorned with public honours, or even to indulge their lust and unlawful pleasures? Indeed they sometimes seem the most fortunate of mortals, and the treacherous favour of a flattering fortune draws them on, so that, scorning warnings, they promise themselves all happy things, and knowingly and willingly throw themselves into the snares of Satan. Therefore what that son of Sirach said finally happens to them: "He who loves danger will perish in it."

units.la: Porrò videamus quid in præsenti passi sint, qui iubente Christo nauigarunt. Descendit turbo Tempestatis venti in flagnū, & complebantur, ac periclitabantur. Paucis verbis tempestatem grauissimā & periculi plenam describit, quam Marcus euidentius expressit, sic dicens: Et oritur procella venti magna, & fluctus irruebant in nauim, ita ut illa iam impleretur. Et erat ipse in pupi super ceruical dormiens. Ventus ergo vehemens exortus est, nec vulgaris, sed turbo, qui quauis obuia vertit & rotat, & ex quo pericula nauigantibus maxima enasci solent. Hic certè fluctus in altum elevati in nauim irruerunt, quæ tantùmnon aquis obruta naufragio proxima fuit. Et auget periculi metum, quòd interea Christus dormit, in quo vno salutis spes reliqua erat. Habent ista euidentem ecclesiæ typum, quæ dum in terris hisce versatur, nauiculæ per mare nauigantis similima est. Vt enim fiæ. hæc aliquando per aquas placidas & tranquillas aura secunda fertur, repente autem surgentibus ventu & vndu intumescentibus periclitatur: ita ecclesia interdum in mundo pace & otio fruitur, & magnis incrementis Christi regnum augetur, sed raro diuturna est tranquillitas illa, quin ex improuiso turbæ oriuntur, quæ extremum excidium minantur. Et fit hoc, quam primùm Christus dormit, id est, ut primùm ille quasi depositā Ecclesiæ cura, eam mundi arbitrio permittere videtur. Tunc enim Satan, ut suum regnum stabiliat, vel hypocritas Sophistas excitat, vel tyrannos armat, vel simultates & contentiones intestinas accendit, & vndique imminentibus periculis ipsos ministros inter se committit, qui remigum inflar tunc in primis vnanimi studio & coniunctis viri bus remis incumbere debebans. Et dum hæc fiunt, sæpe Christus quasi altum dormiens dissimulat.
units.tr: Furthermore let us see what those suffered in the present case who sailed at Christ's bidding. "A violent squall of wind came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger." In a few words he describes a very grievous tempest full of danger, which Mark has expressed more clearly, saying: "And a great storm of wind arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so that it was already filling. And he himself was in the stern, asleep on a cushion." A violent wind therefore arose, and not an ordinary one, but a whirlwind, which turns and spins whatever stands in its way, and from which the greatest dangers are wont to arise for those who sail. Surely the waves, lifted high, beat into the boat, which was all but overwhelmed by the water and close to shipwreck. And the fear of danger is increased by the fact that meanwhile Christ is asleep, in whom alone was the remaining hope of safety. These things carry a clear image of the Church, which, while it dwells in this earth, is very like a little ship sailing across the sea. For just as this ship is sometimes carried over calm and quiet waters by a favourable breeze, but suddenly, when winds rise and waves swell, is put in peril, so the Church sometimes enjoys peace and leisure in the world, and the kingdom of Christ is increased by great growth; but that tranquillity is rarely lasting, but unexpectedly disturbances arise which threaten utter destruction. And this happens as soon as Christ sleeps, that is, as soon as he seems to have, as it were, laid down the care of the Church and to allow it to be at the mercy of the world. For then Satan, in order to establish his kingdom, either stirs up hypocritical sophists, or arms tyrants, or kindles internal quarrels and contentions, and on all sides, with dangers threatening, sets the very ministers against one another, who, like rowers, ought then above all to bend to the oars with united zeal and joined strength. And while these things are happening, Christ, as if sleeping deeply, often pays no heed.

units.la: {M} omnia, ut & fidem suorum tentet (ut supra diximus) & eorum socordiam castiget, qui nimium sC- curi ante salutem propriam neglexerunt. Fuit hæc ecclesiæ conditio iam inde à prima rerum origi- ne. Quàm sæva enim & atrox procella eam quassauit ô fratres, quando Abelus, qui eius propaganda ipes unica erat, ab impio fratre trucidatus est? Nonne tunc naufragium iam fecisse videri poterat? Quibus verò procellis & fluctibus iactata est, cùm omnem terram longè lateq; operientibus diluuij aquis, illa intra arcæ parietes quasi in media morte pependit? Quàm varijs vero & periculosis casibus iactati sunt patriarchæ, Abraham, Isaac et Iacob, qui soli ferè cum suis domesticis ecclesiæ nomen sustinebant? Quid autem de filijs Israel sub Mose in deserto agentibus dicemus? Quæ ma- tu tempestas, qui ventorum turbines, qui fluctus, quæ Syrtes, qui scopuli certius naufragium minari possunt, quàm quod tunc timeri potuit totius ecclesiæ excidium, quando illam & externi hostes oppugnarunt, & domesticæ seditiones perpetuò exercuerunt? Nec multò melior fors eam excepit, cùm sedes olim patribus promissas iam tenerent, sicuti in Iosuæ et Regum libris est videre. Quòd si ad primitiuæ ecclesiæ historiam accedamus, ibi cum Iudæus ipsos Romanos Imperatores, cum philosophis proconsules & omnis propè ordinis atq; loci homines in ecclesiæ exitium conspirauisse, & nonnas quotidie tempestates excitatas fuisse videbis, quibus illa obrueretur. Et durat hæc fors in istum usq; diem, neq; mutatio aliqua in melius sperari potest, cùm & mundus hic ingenium suum non mutet, & Christiani quoq; homines sua negligentia & ingratitudine disciplinam eiusmodi mereantur. Neminem ergo motus isti offendere debent, quasi novum quid & insolens nobis hodie accidat: quin potius quid nos facere deceat quæramus, id quod suo exemplo discipuli docebunt.
units.tr: All these things happen both to test the faith of his people (as we said above) and to chastise the carelessness of those who, too secure, neglected their own salvation. This has been the condition of the Church from the very beginning of the world. For how fierce and savage a storm shook it, brothers, when Abel, who was the only hope of propagating it, was murdered by his impious brother? Could it not then seem that it had already been wrecked? And with what waves and tempests was it tossed, when the waters of the flood covered the whole earth far and wide, and it hung within the walls of the ark as if in the midst of death? How variously and dangerously were the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob tossed, who almost alone with their households bore the name of the Church? What shall we say of the sons of Israel under Moses in the desert? What storm, what whirlwinds, what waves, what Syrtes, what rocks could threaten shipwreck more surely than the destruction of the whole Church, which could then be feared, when both external enemies assailed it and domestic sedition constantly harassed it? Nor did it fare much better when they held the seats promised long before to the fathers, as can be seen in the books of Joshua and Kings. But if we come to the history of the primitive Church, there you will see the Jews, the Roman emperors themselves, proconsuls with philosophers, and almost every rank and place of men conspiring for its ruin, and daily storms raised up by which it might be overwhelmed. This lot lasts even to this day, nor can any change for the better be hoped for, since this world does not change its nature, and Christians too, by their negligence and ingratitude, deserve discipline of this kind. Therefore let these disturbances offend no one, as if something new and unusual were happening to us today; rather let us seek what it becomes us to do, which the disciples will teach by their example.

units.la: De illis enim sic loquuntur Euangelistæ, ut illos vehementer timuisse constet. Nam ad Christum recurrunt, eum non sine querulis verbis & exprobratione plenis expergefaciunt. Magister, magister (inquiunt) perimus. Imò (ut Marcus annotauit) clamant: Magister, non est tibi cura quod perimus? Etsi ergo timor per se vitiosus non sit, & sanctos Dei cultores sæpe timuisse, neq; idcò reprehensos fuisse legamus, peccant tamen illi, quòd metu superati modum excedunt, & non tam certa animi fiducia, quàm consternatione ad Christum confugiunt, neq; reuerenter eius opem implorant, sed illum potius accusant, ut qui præter suum officium immerentes negligat. Vitij huius causa est, quòd toti in carnis præsentiam defixi, illum non aliter suis adesse et opem ferre putant, quàm si præsentiam suam corporali & inter homines usitato more ostendat. Nam si illum rectè agnouissent, facilè credidissent somnum hunc ad corpus solum pertinere, ex eo autem nihil decedere Deitati, quæ (ut ipse Ioannes quinto cap. ait) semper operatur et efficaciter agit ea, quæ ad nostram salutem faciunt. Solet hæc fidei infirmitas, sæpe in sanctos cadere, & hæc eas querelas parit, quæ in Psalmis passim occurrunt. Quòusq; mei obliuisceris Domine? Quòusq; clamo, & non exaudis? Exurge Domine, & iudica, &c. Et ijs cogitationibus nostram quoq; fidem tentari sentimus, quando aut egestate & fame graviori, aut morbis diuturnioribus, aut persecutione & exilio exercemur. Sed non ideo nos desperare conuenit, quando illis sanctissimos quosq; tentatos olim fuisse constat. Interim neq; delitias hic nobis facere debemus, sed toti in hoc simus, ut fidei fundamentum in nobis saluum maneat, & ut animos fluctuantes mox confirmemus, apud illum opem quærendo, quem caro dormire aut nostri curam depositus suspicatur.
units.tr: For the Evangelists speak of them in such a way that it is clear they feared greatly. They run to Christ and rouse him with complaining words full of reproach. Master, master, they say, we perish. Indeed (as Mark noted) they cry: Master, do you not care that we perish? Although fear in itself is not sinful, and we read that holy worshippers of God often feared and were not on that account rebuked, yet these men sin in that, overcome by fear, they exceed due measure. They flee to Christ not with a firm confidence of mind but in consternation, and do not reverently implore his help; rather they accuse him, as one who undeservedly neglects them beyond his duty. The cause of this fault is that, fixed wholly on his bodily presence, they think he is present to them and brings help only if he shows his presence in bodily form and in the usual manner among men. For had they rightly known him, they would easily have believed that this sleep pertains only to the body, and that nothing is taken from the Deity, which (as John himself says in chapter five) always works and efficaciously effects those things which pertain to our salvation. This weakness of faith often falls upon the saints, and it gives birth to those complaints which occur everywhere in the Psalms. How long will you forget me, O Lord? How long shall I cry, and you not hear? Arise, O Lord, and judge, etc. We feel our faith too being tested by such thoughts when we are exercised either by greater want and hunger, or by longer diseases, or by persecution and exile. But we ought not therefore to despair, since it is certain that all the most holy were tried in the same way. Meanwhile we must not indulge ourselves here, but be wholly intent that the foundation of faith remain safe in us, and that we soon confirm our wavering minds by seeking help from him whom the flesh suspects to be sleeping or to have laid aside care of us.

units.la: Itaq; discipulos hosce imitemur, qui etsi infirmitate fidei peccent, ad Christum tamen confugiunt, & eo testantur, quòd neq; de potentia eius diuina, neq; propensa erga ipsos voluntate omnino desperauerunt. Est hoc ante omnia factu necessarium, ut nimirum ad Christum nos recipiamus, qui verus atq; fidelis suæ nauiculæ gubernator est, & in omnes ventos atq; procellas imperium habet, quibus illa Satan obruere conatur. Iubet hoc ille singulos priuatim, cùm dicit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, et ego vobis requie præstabo. Publica aut promissio est: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed forti animo estote, ego vici mundum. Ite: Ecce mihi data est omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra, et ego vobiscum usq; in consummationem seculi. In ipso igitur limine (quod dici solet) offendunt, qui in quibuscunq; periculis alio, quàm ad Christum recurrunt, qui ut nobis Patre propitium reddidit, ita solus ad nos seruandos sufficit. Ad hunc autem nō aliter, quàm pœnitentia vera et seria conuertemur. Quomodo enim cum eo illis coeniet, qui in superstitionibus & peccatis defixi manent? Pœnitentia autem cum erroru & delictorum cognitione fidem coniunctam habere, alibi diximus. Et hæc preces parit, quibus omnino opus esse, cùm Deus inuocari velit, & in ijsdem constantia, adeoq; importunitas sanctæ requiritur, eò quòd ille opem aliquando diutius differt, quò magis fidem nostram exerceat, vt infra in viduæ & imqui iudicis parabola audiemus. Hæc (inquam) nobis in discipulorum exemplo spiritus sanctus commendat. At hodie in omnibus ferè peccatur. Furit quidem infelix mundus, & inter hu ius machinationes ecclesia fluctuat, & interdum peritura videtur. At hic pleriq; ad principum faede ra, ad exterorum auxilia et præsidia armorum recurrunt, quasi istis Christo opus sit. Pœnitentiæ au tem ratio nulla habetur, imò inter eos etiam scelera sceleribus accumulantur, & superstitiones quo tidie crescunt, qui Christianissimi haberi volunt. Preces item aut omnino nullas, aut frigidas admo dum fundimus: vt iam nihil de illis dicatur, qui nihil præter vlulatum belluinum in Dei cospectum afferunt. Ista ergo emendare oportebit, si nobis consultum esse velimus.
units.tr: Let us therefore imitate these disciples, who, although they sin through weakness of faith, nevertheless flee to Christ, and by this they testify that they had not wholly despaired either of his divine power or of his well-disposed will toward them. This above all must be done: we must betake ourselves to Christ, who is the true and faithful pilot of his little boat, and who has command over all the winds and storms by which Satan tries to overwhelm it. He bids this each one privately when he says: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest. His promise is public: In the world you will have affliction, but be of good courage, I have overcome the world. Go: Behold, all power is given to me in heaven and on earth, and I am with you even to the end of the age. They stumble, then, at the very threshold (as the saying goes) who in whatever dangers run anywhere other than to Christ, who, as he has made the Father propitious to us, so alone suffices to save us. We shall turn to him only by true and earnest repentance. For how can fellowship with him belong to those who remain fixed in superstitions and sins? We have said elsewhere that repentance has faith joined with knowledge of errors and offences. And this begets prayers, which are altogether necessary, since God wishes to be invoked; and in them steadfastness and holy importunity are required, because he sometimes delays his help longer in order the more to exercise our faith, as we shall hear below in the parable of the widow and the unjust judge. These things, I say, the Holy Spirit commends to us in the example of the disciples. But today people sin in almost everything. The unhappy world indeed rages, and amid its machinations the Church wavers and sometimes seems about to perish. Yet here most people run to the protection of princes and to the help and defences of foreign arms, as if they had need of these rather than of Christ. No account is taken of repentance; indeed among those who want to be called most Christian, crimes are heaped upon crimes, and superstitions grow daily. Likewise our prayers are either altogether absent or are poured forth very coldly; not to mention those who bring before the sight of God nothing but bestial howling. These things, then, it will be necessary to amend, if we wish to have regard for our own good.

units.la: Excitet hic nos Christi facilitas, qui etsi importunius agant discipuli, absq; mora tamen opem fert periclitantibus. Et primò quidem mox expergiscitur, vt offendat, se minimè surdum esse, neque suorum preces negligere. Deinde ventum et aquæ fluctuationem increpat, & mox tranquillitas ma gna fit. Vbi nemini absurdum videri debet, quòd muta elementa verbo compellat. Ita enim docet, se eum esse, cuius virtute illa in principio creata sint, & proinde suo imperio ea quoq; parere, quæ nul lius alterius leges admittunt. Est hoc euidens veræ Deitatis in illo argumentum, quod si qui nega re velint, idem Patris quoq; diuinam virtutem negent, quā Prophetæ passim his argumentis asse rūt, quòd ventos creet, maris fluctus coerceat, tempestatibus imperet, elementis deniq; omnibus pro suo arbitrio vtatur. Seruit autem exemplum hoc consolationi nostræ in aduersis & afflictionibus. Qui enim hic ventis et fluctibus cum authoritate præcipit, idem alibi morbos etiam increpat, adeoq; in ipsam mortem ius habet. Et in Psalmis reges in ira sua corripere, & ijsdem arma vel intra ma nus confringere, vel etiam ex manibus extorquere dicitur. Et quod hic factum est, vt tranquillitas subita tempestate sæuissimam excipiat, hoc ipsum sæpe fieri videmus, vt tyrannus vndiq; aduersus ecclesiam surgentibus, & rebus in extremū discrimen adductis, vnius & alterius improuisa mors, aut præter expectationem omnem accepta clades, toti terrarum orbi pacem optatam afferat. Sunt hæc nobis diligenter obseruāda, ne de Dei ope dubitemus, aut fidem nostram labefactari patiamur, si mundus hic cum suo principe aduersus nos insaniat. Addit tamen tertium Christus, quòd discipu los increpat, dicens: Vbi est fides vestra? Et apud Marcum, Quid timidi estis adeò? Qui fit, quod nō habeatis fiduciam? Sic ergo nobis opem fert ille, vt interim minimè patrocinetur vitiis nostris, multò minus aduletur ijs, qui reprehensione digni sunt. Et sanè feriam reprehensionem merentur, quicunq; Christo præsente timent & trepidant. Si Deus pro nobis (inquit Paulus) quis contra nos? Atqui hunc pro nobis stare & in Christo nobis propitium factum esse scimus, qui idem se nobiscum futurum pollicetur, neq; passurum, vt aliquis oues ex manibus ipsius eripiat. Istis ergo promissioni- bus & minis Dei nostri potentia freti, pericula omnia intrepidi subeamus, & pro nostræ vocatio- nis ratione nostrum illi præstemus obsequium.
units.tr: Let the readiness of Christ stir us here: although the disciples act too importunately, he nevertheless brings help to those in peril without delay. First, he immediately wakes, to show that he is by no means deaf and does not neglect the prayers of his own. Then he rebukes the wind and the tossing of the water, and at once there is great calm. No one should think it absurd that he addresses the dumb elements with a word. For he teaches that he is the one by whose power they were created in the beginning, and therefore by his command they obey even those things which admit no other laws. This is clear evidence in him of true Deity; if anyone wished to deny it, he would also deny the divine power of the Father, which the Prophets everywhere assert by these arguments: that he creates the winds, restrains the waves of the sea, commands the tempests, and finally uses all the elements at his will. This example, moreover, serves our consolation in adversities and afflictions. For he who here commands the winds and waves with authority elsewhere also rebukes diseases, and so has right even over death itself. In the Psalms he is said to rebuke kings in his wrath, and to break their weapons in their hands or even to wrest them from their hands. And what happened here, that a sudden calm follows the fiercest tempest, we often see happen too: when a tyrant rises on every side against the Church and affairs are brought to the utmost peril, the unforeseen death of one or another, or a defeat received beyond all expectation, brings the longed-for peace to the whole world. These things must be carefully observed, lest we doubt God's help, or allow our faith to be shaken if this world rages against us with its prince. Yet Christ adds a third thing, rebuking the disciples and saying: Where is your faith? And in Mark: Why are you so fearful? How is it that you have no confidence? So he brings help to us in such a way that he by no means defends our faults in the meantime, much less flatters those who deserve reproof. And indeed those deserve a severe reproof who fear and tremble when Christ is present. If God is for us (says Paul), who is against us? Yet we know that he stands for us and has been made propitious to us in Christ, who promises that he will be with us and will not suffer anyone to snatch his sheep out of his hands. Relying therefore on these promises and on the power of our God, let us undergo all dangers fearlessly, and render him our obedience according to the measure of our calling.

units.la: Sequitur miraculi effectus, quem his verbis Lucas comprehendit: Timentes autè mirati sunt, dicentes alij ad alios: Quis nam iste est, vt ventis quoq; & aquæ imperet, & auscultent ei? Primò timuisse dicuntur. Nec enim diuinæ potentiæ sensum caro nostra absque terrore & metu ferre po- test, vt multa sanctorum exempla testantur. Quid ergo de impijs fiet, quando Deum sibi irasci & fulmina in se vibrare sentient? Deinde non succumbunt isti ignauo metu, sed mox linguas & ora in Christi laudes soluunt, & non obscurum ei diuinæ virtutis testimonium perhibent. Est hoc proprium fidei officium, vt quemadmodum nos in periculis Deum inuocare docet, ita eidem pro liberatio- ne gratias agere iubeat, neq; verba modò nobis suggerit, quibus id faciamus, sed nos totos Deo vin- dicat, vt hunc vita & factis nostris omnibus prædicemus. In primis autem obseruari debent insi- gniora Dei beneficia, vt quando ea fiunt, quæ nulla hominum virtute & consilio perfici poterant, illius manum præsentem agnoscamus, & nomen eius prædicemus in Christo Iesu Do- mino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æter- num, Amen.
units.tr: There follows the effect of the miracle, which Luke sums up in these words: "And they being afraid wondered, saying one to another, Who is this, that he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him?" First, they are said to have been afraid. For our flesh cannot bear a sense of divine power without terror and fear, as many examples of the saints bear witness. What then will become of the ungodly, when they feel God angry with them and hurling thunderbolts against them? Next, these men do not give way to cowardly fear, but at once loosen their tongues and voices in praise of Christ, and they bear no obscure testimony to the divine power. It is the proper office of faith that, just as it teaches us to call upon God in dangers, so it bids us give thanks to him for deliverance; and it not only supplies us with words by which we may do this, but claims us wholly for God, so that we proclaim him by our whole life and all our deeds. Above all, the more remarkable benefits of God ought to be observed: when things are done which no human strength or counsel could bring about, we should acknowledge his present hand and proclaim his name in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXI.

units.la: Et nauigarunt in regionem Gadarenorum, quæ est in ripa oppositá Galilææ. Ipli autem egresso in terram occurrit ex vrbe vir quidam, qui habebat dæmonia à temporibus multis, & vestimento non induebatur, neque in vlla domo manebat, sed in monumentis. Is ergo cùm vidisset Iesum & exclamasset, procidit ante illum, & voce magna dixit: Quid mihi tecum Iesu Fili Dei altissimi? rogo te ne me torqueas. Præcipiebat enim spiritui impuro, vt exiret ab eo homine: nam à multo tempore corripuerat eum. Itaque vinctus ille catenis & pedicis, custodiebatur; sed disruptis vinculis agitabatur à dæmone in deserta. Interrogauit autem eum Iesus, dicens: Quod tibi nomen est? Ipse verò dixit, Legio. Nam dæmonia multa ingressa erant in eum. Et rogabant eum, ne imperaret ipsis vt abirent in abyssum.
units.tr: And they sailed to the country of the Gadarenes, which lies on the shore opposite Galilee. When he had come out onto the land, there met him out of the city a certain man who had demons for a long time. He wore no clothes and lived not in any house but among the tombs. When he saw Jesus, he cried out, fell down before him, and said with a loud voice: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the most high God? I beg you, do not torment me." For Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man, since it had seized him for a long time. He was bound with chains and fetters and kept under guard, but he broke his bonds and was driven by the demon into the desert. Jesus asked him, saying: "What is your name?" He said, "Legion," for many demons had entered into him. And they begged him not to order them to depart into the abyss.

units.la: Vt serium & diligens Dei Verbi studium Iesus Christus nobis vnicè commendauit in iis, quæ hucusque expósita sunt: ita omnibus illis grauiter occurrit, quæ huius fructum impedire solent; qualia sunt innatæ nobis carnis cupiditates, sinistra mundi huius iudicia, & persecutionum pericula, quibus exercentur, quicunque Verbum audiunt, & hoc vt rerum agendarum regulam obseruant. At inter omnes salutis nostræ remoras primatum facilè obtinet Satan, qui non modò extrinsecus nos oppugnat, sed ipsis animis sese insinuans, vel socordes & propriæ salutis negligentes reddit, vel in furorem nos agit, quo in proprium exitium horribiliter ruimus. Commodè ergo noui miraculi historiam subtexit Lucas, quo docetur quantæ in perdendis hominibus diaboli vires sint, simul autem demonstratur Iesum Christum esse promissum illud semē, cuius virtute hostis ille noster deuictus sit, & qui vel vno verbo nos aduersus illius tyrannidem tueri, nosque in libertatem asserere possit. Arguitur item hominum ingratitudo, qui cùm toti carnis & mundi studijs immersi sint, tanto Christi beneficio carere potius malunt, quàm illud vel minima suarum rerum iactura redimere. Est ergo historia hæc admodum memorabilis & digna, quæ à nobis diligentissimè consideretur.
units.tr: Jesus Christ has especially commended to us, in the things set out so far, a serious and diligent study of the Word of God. So he also confronts firmly all those things that are wont to hinder its fruit: the innate desires of the flesh, the perverse judgements of this world, and the dangers of persecution, by which all who hear the Word and keep it as the rule of their conduct are exercised. But among all the hindrances to our salvation, Satan easily holds first place. He not only assails us from without, but, insinuating himself into our minds, he either makes us lazy and careless of our own salvation or drives us into a frenzy by which we rush headlong to our own destruction. Luke therefore fittingly adds the story of this new miracle, by which it is taught how great the power of the devil is in destroying men. At the same time it is shown that Jesus Christ is that promised Seed, by whose power that enemy of ours has been overcome, and who can with a single word defend us against his tyranny and assert us into liberty. The ingratitude of men is also rebuked: although they are wholly immersed in the pursuits of the flesh and the world, they would rather go without so great a benefit of Christ than redeem it at the smallest loss of their possessions. This history is therefore very memorable and worthy to be considered by us most diligently.

units.la: Prima pars locum rei gestæ & dæmoniaci, in quo miraculum hoc editum est, describionem continet. Nam transmisso stagno aut lacu venerunt in regionem Gadarenorum, quam ex aduerso Galilææ sitam fuisse dicitur, sic dictam à Gadara ciuitate, à qua nō multum distat Gergesa, quæ eidem tractui Gergesenorum nomen imposuit, quos in huius historiæ narratione Matthæus nominat. Illi vix dum in terram ex naui egresso occurrit ex vrbe, id est, ea via, qua ex vrbe ad lacum ibatur, dæmoniacus quidam, cuius occursum discipulis formidabilem fuisse ex eius descriptione constat. Nouum ergo periculum illis obijcitur, qui iam primùm à naufragio seruati fuerant. Est hæc piorum sors, vt nunquam omnibus aduersis simul defungi possint, sed unde minimè speręnt, noua sibi certamina excitari videant. Exempla huius rei cumprimis memorabilia in Abrahamo, Isaaco, Iacobo, Dauide, Paulo Apostolo habemus, in quorum meditatione nos frequentes esse conuenit, quo minus offendamur iis, quæ nobis quotidie accidunt. Cùm enim cuiusuis hominis vita laborum plena sit, quid mirum fuerit eos grauioribus et crebrioribus molestijs exerceri, quos Dei Filius ex mundo seligit, vt inter huius seculi filios pro exulibus & peregrinis haberi possint? Curemus modò nos vt horum memores semper in statione simus, ne incautos hostis ex improuiso opprimat.
units.tr: The first part contains a description of the place where the event happened and of the demoniac in whom this miracle was performed. For, having crossed the lake or sea, they came into the country of the Gadarenes, which is said to lie opposite Galilee, so named from the city of Gadara, not far from which is Gergesa, which gave its name to the district of the Gergesenes, whom Matthew names in his account of this history. As soon as Jesus had come out of the ship onto the land, there met him from the city, that is, on the road by which people went from the city to the lake, a certain demoniac, whose appearance, as his description shows, was terrifying to the disciples. A new danger therefore confronts those who had just been saved from shipwreck. This is the lot of the godly: they can never get through all adversities at once, but see new struggles stirred up for them where they least expect them. We have especially memorable examples of this in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David and the apostle Paul. It is fitting for us to meditate on these often, so that we may be less offended by those things which befall us every day. For since the life of every man is full of labours, what wonder is it if those whom the Son of God chooses out of the world, so that among the children of this age they may be regarded as exiles and strangers, are exercised by heavier and more frequent troubles? Let us only take care to be always mindful of these things in our post, lest the enemy overwhelm us unawares, when we are off our guard.

units.la: Debet hîc nos excitare, quòd non eaguas diaboli vires esse videmus, & quòd horrenda in hominibus agit, nisi Deus suo imperio atq; potentia illum coerceat. Quales enim faciat, quos semel occupauit, in miseri istius exemplo apparet. Nudus enim discurrit, & neque pudore contemnitur, neque ca li iniuria mouetur, quò minus vestes dilaniet atq; abijciat. Furore item immani abreptus manicas & pedicas abrumpit, neque vllis vinculis contineri potest. Adhæc non seipsum modò, sed simul quosuis alios infestat, vt nemo ipsi tutò occurrere aut cohabitare possit. Postremò ciuitatem & domum fugiens, in loca ab hominum consuetudine remotiora sese recipit, et in mortuorum sepulchris sibi domicilium quærit. Et ista quidem hodie etiam fieri videmus in istis, quorum corpora & naturales facultates mali spiritus occuparunt: ut nimirum vestibus abiectis absque pudore quiduis faciant, viribus item plus quàm humanis catenas disrumpant, effractis repagulis e carceribus elabantur, hinc inde discurrant, & fere locis tetris & foedis delectentur. Sunt isti multa commiseratione digni: at magis deploranda est eorum fors, quorum animos diabolus obsedit, ut se totos ipsius seruitio mancipent. Solent enim illi abster so pudore in omne scelus ruere. Itaque procul abiiciunt innocentiae vestem, qua olim Adamum Deus ornaucrat, & quam nobis Christus suo merito instaurauit. Idem disciplinae omnis cum Politicae tum Ecclesiasticae iugum excutiunt, legum vincula ceu aranearum telas perrumpunt, & in eo laudem quaerunt, quod ea audent facere, à quibus alij pudore aut metu abterrentur. Neque sibi ipsis solùm, sed insuper multis alijs molesti sunt, dum aliorum fortunis damnum inferunt, modo famam aliorum in periculum adducunt, modo pudicitiae insidias struunt, modò in corpora quoque & vitam eorum grassantur, quos vel oderunt, vel quibus temere irascuntur. Et quod omnia illa superat, domum & ciuitatem Dei fingunt, in qua vna tanto malo remedium & certum salutis asylum inuenire poterant: eorum autem consuetudine delectantur, qui iampridem per delicta mortui corpora sua sepulchrorum instar fecerunt, in quibus infelices etiam animae tantùmnon computrescunt & scelerum foetore enecantur. Exempla istorum passim hodie occurrunt, quae his fidem faciunt: quò magis nos admigilare decet, ne locum demus Satanae, sed ei resistamus fortes in fide, tueamur autem libertatem nostram, quam sui sanguinis pretio nobis Christus acquisiuit.
units.tr: Here we ought to be stirred up by the fact that we see the power of the devil is not small, and that he does terrible things to men unless God restrains him by his command and power. For what sort of men he makes of those whom he has once possessed appears in the example of this wretched man. He runs about naked, and is neither restrained by shame nor moved by the injury of the cold, so that he does not tear and cast off his clothes. Likewise, carried away by monstrous frenzy, he breaks his manacles and fetters, and cannot be held by any chains. Moreover, he attacks not only himself but also all others, so that no one can safely come near him or live with him. Finally, fleeing the city and his home, he retreats to places more remote from human society, and seeks a dwelling for himself among the tombs of the dead. Indeed we see these things done even today in those whose bodies and natural faculties evil spirits have seized: they cast off their clothes and do anything without shame; with more than human strength they break their chains; they escape from prisons, the bars being burst open, run hither and thither, and for the most part delight in foul and filthy places. Such people are worthy of much pity. But more to be lamented is the lot of those whose minds the devil has besieged, so that they surrender themselves wholly to his service. For they are accustomed, having cast off all shame, to rush into every crime. Therefore they cast far away the garment of innocence, with which God once clothed Adam, and which Christ by his merit has restored to us. They likewise throw off the yoke of all discipline, both civil and ecclesiastical; they break the bonds of the laws like cobwebs; and they seek praise in daring to do those things from which others are deterred by shame or fear. They are troublesome not only to themselves but to many others as well: sometimes they inflict loss on others' fortunes, sometimes they endanger others' reputations, sometimes they lay snares for chastity, sometimes they rage against the bodies and lives of those whom they either hate or angrily assail without cause. And what surpasses all these things, they despise the house and city of God, in which alone they might have found a remedy for such great evil and a sure refuge of salvation. Instead they delight in the company of those who, long since dead through their sins, have made their bodies like sepulchres, in which the unhappy souls themselves almost rot and are suffocated by the stench of their crimes. Examples of these people occur everywhere today, and they bear witness to these things. All the more, then, ought we to be on our guard, lest we give place to Satan, but rather resist him, strong in faith, and defend our liberty, which Christ has won for us at the price of his own blood.

units.la: At quia de his & aliis hoc loco obseruatu dignis in Marco nostro diximus, nunc alteram historiae huius partem inspiciamus, quae narratur, quid miser iste, vel potius in ipso diabolus fecerit, vbi Christum conspicatus est. Primò, ut Iesum àlonge videt, accurrit, & ad pedes eius prolapsus, exclamat. Quod illum praeter suam voluntatem fecisse, non est dubium. Ita vero suam impotentiam turpiter prodit, qui superbo principis huius mundi titulo superbit, & eius imperium Christo alibi pollicebatur, si ipsum adoraret. Et est hic plenum consolatione, quòd ipse Satan miserum hunc quem perditum volebat, ad Christum medicum & seruatorem humani generis adducit. Verissimè ergo ille dixit: Oues meas nemo poterit rapere ex manu mea. Quid enim homines faciant, quando diabolus velinuitus illi in seruandis hominibus operam praestare cogitur?
units.tr: But since we have spoken of these and other matters worthy of observation in this passage in our commentary on Mark, let us now look at the other part of this history, which tells what this wretched man, or rather the devil in him, did when he caught sight of Christ. First, when he sees Jesus from afar, he runs up, falls at his feet, and cries out. There is no doubt that he did this against his own will. Thus he shamefully betrays his own powerlessness, he who, proud of the haughty title of prince of this world, boasted that Christ would have his kingdom if he would worship him. And here it is full of comfort that Satan himself brings this wretched man, whom he wished to destroy, to Christ, the physician and saviour of the human race.
