Most truly, then, did he say: "No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hand." For what can men do, when the devil himself is forced against his will to lend a hand in saving men?

units.la: Deinde vbi se à Christo vrgeri sentit, palàm fatetur, nihil sibi cum illo esse negotij. Quod verum quidem est, si vtriusque mores & studia consideres. Christus enim Veritas, ipse mendax & mendacij pater est. Christus iustitia & sanctitas, adhaec nobis etiam iustitiae author, atque mediator ipse vero iniustitiae, impuritatis & scelerum magister est. Christus vt peccatores seruaret in mundum venit, at Satan totus in hoc incumbit, vt occidat & ad inferos praecipitet. Reuera ergo nulla inter hunc & illum est communio, & proinde si hoc sensu verba diaboli accipiantur, verissima sunt. At si rem propius consideres, illum hoc dicendo egregiè mentiri & sui defensionem plane Sophisticam struere videbis. Nec enim ideò aderat Christus, vt cum illo societatem inire, aut eum in suas partes trahere vellet, sed opera eius destrueret & ipsum è regni male vsurpati possessione deijcere debebat. Hic ille iniustè & iniquè secum agi clamat, eò quòd nihil ei cum Christo sit negotij. Sed eho mendacissime Sophista & impudentissime quadruplator, quo ore tibi nihil rei cum Christo esse dicis, cùm humanam naturam omnem, cuius ipse particeps est, perditam velis? cùm gentes omnes ipsi iure haereditario promissas iam multis seculis sub dira tenebrarum potestate premas? cùm humani generis redemptionem impedire coneris, quam ille ex aeterno patris decreto facere debuit? cùm Veritatis doctrinam, cuius ipse praeco est, mendaciorum nebulis obscurare subinde tentes? cùm denique iustitiam & vitam indefesso studio oppugnes, quae per ipsum reduci & instaurari oportebat? Iam ergo te mendacem esse vides, & hoc vno tam mendaci dicto meruisse, vt ad imatartara detrusus regnum Christo cedas, cui illud debetur. Haec ideò diligentius annotamus ô fratres, vt diaboli astutias agnoscere discamus, qui tunc quoque sibi nobiscum nihil negotij esse fingit, quando totis viribus in nostram perniciem incumbit. Annon enim multis hodie persuadet, nullum hominibus cum ipso cōmercium intercedere, etiamsi sceleribus seruiant, superstitionibus sese consecrent, ariolos, magos, veneficos consulant, & etiam ipsi artes illicitas sectentur? Annon fidis Christi ministris superstitiones manifestas & idololatriam accusantibus per Pontifices & Episcopos oggannit, nihil sibi cum illis esse negotij? Quibus nos respondere possumus: Cur ergo ecclesiam humanarum traditionum iugo premitis? cur Juam sponsam Christo eripitis? cur ab illo hominum mentes alienatis? cur denique eius regnum, cuius nos ministri sumus, occupare & in eo tyrannidem exercere conamini? Ita semper sui similis est Satan: et qui huius seruitio sese addixerunt, perinde faciunt, quando Christi Verbo vrgentur, vt ij qui legitimis haeredibus litem mouent, qui ipsos ex possessione malis artibus occupata exturbare conantur. Neminem ergo clamores isti mouere debent. Discant autem Christiani homines ex ipsius diaboli ore argumentum arripere, quo suam aduersus illum libertatem tueantur. Cum enim ipse fateatur, nihil sibi cum Christo negotij esse, cur huic obsequium praestent, qui Christo per baptismum consecrati & corporis eius membra sunt? Fugite ergo ô Christiani infelix diaboli commercium, abijcite proculiugum eius, cauete blanditias & insidias eius, qui se Christi hostem esse iampridem testatus est. Sed vtinam ista omnes expenderent, & non passim inuenirentur, qui cum Christi nomen profiteantur, cum diabolo tamen plenis buccis gloriari audent, nihil rei ipsis cum Christo esse. Quid enim aliud faciunt, qui Euangelij doctrinam, admonitiones, hortationes, correptiones nihil ad se pertinere clamant? qui sacros coetus oderunt, quibus ille medius interest? qui sacramentorum vsum fastidiunt, quibus ille sua beneficia nobis obsignat? Atqui horum maximus hodie est numerus, qui tamen Christiani dici & haberi volunt: quorum eo maior est impudentia & impietas, quod & verbis & factis professionem suam conculcant.
units.tr: Then, when he feels himself pressed by Christ, he openly confesses that he has no business with him. This is indeed true, if you consider the character and the aims of each of them. For Christ is Truth, while he is a liar and the father of lies. Christ is righteousness and holiness, and moreover the author of our righteousness, and the mediator himself; but he is the source of unrighteousness, impurity and wickedness. Christ came into the world to save sinners, but Satan devotes himself wholly to this: to kill and to hurl down to hell. Truly, then, there is no fellowship between this one and that, and therefore, if the devil's words are taken in this sense, they are most true. But if you consider the matter more closely, you will see that in saying this he lies outrageously and constructs a plainly sophistical defence. Christ was not present in order to enter into partnership with him or to draw him to his side, but to destroy his works and to throw him down from the kingdom he had seized unjustly. Here he cries out that he is being treated unjustly and wrongfully, because he has no business with Christ. But come now, most lying sophist and most shameless quadruplator, with what face do you say you have nothing to do with Christ, when you wish the whole of human nature, of which he is a partaker, to be lost? When you have for many ages held under your dreadful power all the nations promised to him by inheritance? When you try to hinder the redemption of mankind, which he was bound to effect by the eternal decree of the Father? When you repeatedly attempt to darken the doctrine of Truth, whose herald he is, with clouds of lies? When, in a word, you attack with tireless zeal the righteousness and life which were to be restored and established through him? Now you see that you are a liar, and by this one lying word you have earned being thrust down to the depths of hell and yielding the kingdom to Christ, to whom it is due. We note these things more carefully, brothers, so that we may learn to recognise the devil's cunning: he pretends that he has no business with us even then, when he is bent with all his strength on our destruction. Does he not persuade many today that no intercourse exists between men and himself, even though they serve their wickedness, devote themselves to superstitions, consult soothsayers, magicians and poisoners, and themselves pursue unlawful arts? Does he not snarl, through the Popes and Bishops, at the faithful ministers of Christ who accuse them of manifest superstitions and idolatry, saying that he has no business with them? To which we can reply: why then do you oppress the Church with the yoke of human traditions? Why do you snatch its bride from Christ? Why do you estrange men's minds from him? Why, in short, do you try to seize his kingdom, whose ministers we are, and to exercise tyranny over it? Satan is always like himself: and those who have devoted themselves to his service do the same when they are pressed by the Word of Christ, as those who bring a lawsuit against the lawful heirs and try to drive them out of their possession, which they have seized by evil arts. Let no one, therefore, be moved by those outcries. Christians should rather learn to take from the devil's own mouth an argument by which to defend their liberty against him. For since he himself admits that he has nothing to do with Christ, why do those render obedience to him who have been consecrated to Christ through baptism and are members of his body? Flee then, O Christians, the unhappy fellowship of the devil; cast far from you his yoke; beware the flatteries and snares of him who has long since declared himself an enemy of Christ. But would that all would weigh these things, and that men were not everywhere found who, while they profess the name of Christ, dare nonetheless to boast with full cheeks to the devil that they have nothing to do with Christ. For what else do those do who cry out that the doctrine of the Gospel, its admonitions, exhortations and rebukes, do not concern them? Who hate the holy assemblies in which he himself is present in the midst? Who despise the use of the sacraments, by which he seals his benefits to us? Yet the number of these is today very great, and they nonetheless wish to be and to be called Christians; and their impudence and impiety are the greater because they trample underfoot their profession both in words and in deeds.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad huius maligni spiritus verba, qui Christum, ne ipsum torqueat precatur, imo (vt Marcus annotauit) per Deum adiurat. Iam ergo ex Christi praesentia tormentum sensserat, & quemadmodum reo intolerabilis est iudicis conspectus, ita Christum ferre non potuit Satan, cum per illum se regno suo deijciendum & aeternis tenebrarum catenis constringendum esse sciret. Apud Matthaeum vero tantum non de vi conqueritur, quando se ante tempus torqueri dicit. Atqui iam aderat tempus illud praefinitum, quo Dei Filius ex muliere natus, serpentis caput conterere, & miseros mortales seruare debuit. Sed nullius calumniae pudere potest patrem mendaciorum: & inter alia hoc quoq; illi proprium est, vt quando sibi cedendum esse vider, inducias sibi dari petat, & moras nectat quant ulascunq;, nouam nimirum occasionem captaturus, qua regnum suum stabilire possit. Fit hoc publice & priuatim. Sicubi enim vel ecclesiae vel reipup. reformatio instituitur, mirum est quam multa ex eius suggestione comminisci possint, qui superstitiones & morum licentiam retinere cupiunt. Plerunq; autem, quando illos non potest non pudere errorum atq; scelerum, temporis incommoditatem, pericula imminentia, aduersariorum conatus & infinita alia causantur, quorum omnino rationem haberi volunt, ne quid imprudentius & infelicius tentetur. Si qui vero prima tim vrgentur, vt relictis vitae anteactae studijs ad Deum conuertantur & vitam viuant Christiana professione dignam: mox hi quoq; ad easdem artes conuersi, multa sibi prius agenda restare, neq; istam aetatem mores seueriores ferre posse dicunt. Vtrinque vero omnis mora pernitiosa est, interea enim feruor ille bonus, qui ex parte conceptus erat, deferuescit, nouas autem vires colligit Satan, quibus nos in seruitute detineat. Vt ergo in re militari boni imperatores nullum tempus importunum, et nullam occasionem minus idoneam esse iudicant, qua hostem, priusquam copias maiores contrahat, opprimi posse vident: Ita nobis quoque omne tempus & omnis aetas oportuna videri debet, vt procul profligato Satana, nos in libertatem filiorum Dei vindicemus. Quod si quibus, Christus ante tempus venire, & reformationem atq; poenitentiam intempestiue a nobis requirere videtur, ij eius spiritus ingenium referunt, quem hic de Christo conqueri audimus.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of this malignant spirit, who begs Christ not to torment him, or rather (as Mark noted) adjures him by God. Now, then, Satan had felt torment from Christ's presence, and just as the sight of a judge is intolerable to a guilty man, so Satan could not bear Christ, since he knew that through him he was to be cast down from his kingdom and bound with the eternal chains of darkness. In Matthew, however, he complains almost of force, when he says that he is being tormented before the time. Yet that appointed time had already come, when the Son of God, born of a woman, was to crush the serpent's head and save miserable mortals. But the father of lies can be ashamed of no calumny; and among other things this too is peculiar to him: when he sees that he must yield, he seeks a respite for himself and weaves delays of whatever kind, plainly waiting to seize some new occasion by which he may establish his kingdom. This happens both publicly and privately. For wherever a reformation of the Church or of the commonwealth is undertaken, it is remarkable how many excuses can be devised at his suggestion by those who wish to keep their superstitions and their licence in morals. Usually, when they cannot but be ashamed of their errors and wickednesses, they plead the inconvenience of the times, the impending dangers, the attempts of adversaries and countless other causes, and they want these weighed carefully, lest anything be attempted too rashly and unhappily. If some are pressed too sharply, so that, having abandoned the pursuits of their former life, they turn to God and live a life worthy of the Christian profession, soon these too, turned back to the same arts, say that much must still be done first, and that this age cannot bear stricter morals. But on either side every delay is pernicious, for meanwhile that good fervour which had been partly conceived cools, and Satan gathers new strength by which he may keep us in servitude. Therefore, just as in warfare good generals judge no time inopportune and no occasion less suitable, since they see that an enemy may be crushed before he gathers greater forces, so for us too every time and every age ought to seem opportune, so that, with Satan utterly routed, we may claim ourselves for the liberty of the sons of God. But if there are some to whom Christ seems to come before the time, and to demand reformation and repentance from us unseasonably, they reproduce the character of that spirit whom we hear complaining here about Christ.

units.la: Quid autem iste? Num querelus hisce locum dat, et hosti inducias concedit? Minime, sed occulta virtute sic ei inflat, vt nulla hominis istius porro obtinendi spem sibi superesse videat, sed oret, ne adhuc in abyssum, id est, aeterni cruciatus loca detrudatur. Priusquam tamen eum reijciat, de nomine quaerit, vt & hominis istius vel potius humani generis totius miseria, & redemptionis per ipsum facta beneficium melius innotescat. Fatetur enim nomen suum Satan, & Legionem se nuncupari dicit. Et nominis huius ratio redditur, quod non vnum daemonium, sed multa adeo, ingens daemoniorum exercitus istum occupasset. Erat enim Legionis nomen tunc Iudaeis notissimum, eo quod Romani eo vterentur, qui tunc temporis exercitus suos per totam Syriam dispositos habebant. Et continebat legio militum duodecim millia atq; quingentos. Neq; dubium est, voluisse diabolum, & si se ruituru videret, adhuc suas vires ostentare, ut si non Christo, saltem eius discipulis terrorem incuteret: Sed ita suam potius vanitatem prodit, ut nemini piorum posthac formidabilis esse debeat. Si enim tanta daemoniorum multitudo ne vnicum quidem hominem in sua potestate detinere potuit, nimium ridiculi sunt, qui ab istis ardelionibus sibi adhuc metuunt. Interim discamus hic iudicare, quàm periculosa sit nostra conditio, si Christi praesidio destituamur. Tunc enim toti patemus diabolo insidijs, & non vsus Satan, sed infiniti daemonum exercitus nos infestant. Simul autem agnoscamus Filij Dei beneficium, qui nos ex infelici hoc seruitio vindicauit, ut in illo ipsi quoq; victores simus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But what did he do? Did he give place to these complaints, and grant a truce to the enemy? By no means; rather, by a hidden power he so drives him back that he sees no hope of retaining this man left to him, and begs that he not be thrust down into the abyss, that is, into the places of eternal torment. Yet before he casts him out, he asks his name, so that both the misery of this man, or rather of the whole human race, and the benefit of redemption made through him may be better known. Satan confesses his name, and says that he is called Legion. And a reason is given for this name: it was not one demon but a huge army of many demons that had taken possession of him. For the name Legion was then very well known to the Jews, because the Romans used it, and at that time they had their armies stationed throughout all Syria. A legion contained twelve thousand five hundred soldiers. And there is no doubt that the devil, although he saw that he was going to be overthrown, wished still to display his strength, so that, if not to Christ, at least he might strike terror into his disciples. But he betrays rather his own vanity, so that he ought henceforth to be formidable to none of the godly. For if so great a multitude of demons could not keep even a single man in their power, those are excessively ridiculous who still fear these busybodies. Meanwhile let us learn here to judge how perilous our condition is if we are deprived of Christ's protection. For then we lie wholly open to the devil's snares, and it is not one Satan but whole infinite armies of demons that assail us. At the same time let us acknowledge the benefit of the Son of God, who has delivered us from this unhappy servitude, so that in him we too may be victors; to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXI.

units.la: Erat autem ibi grex porcorum multorum pascentium in monte, et rogabant eu daemonia, ut permitteret ipsis in illos ingredi. Et permisit eis. Egressa autem daemonia ex eo homine, ingressa sunt in porcos, & grex ruit per praecipitium in stagnum, & suffocatus est. Cum autem pastores vidissent quod factu fuerat, fugerunt; & profecti annuntiarunt in urbem & in agros. Exierunt igitur ut viderent quod factum erat, venerunt ad Iesum, & inuenerunt hominem illu, a quo daemonia exierant, vestitu sanae mentis, sedentem ad pedes Iesu: & timuerunt. Annuntiauerunt autem ipsis etiam qui viderant, quomodo liberatus fuisset qui fuerat daemoniacus. Et rogauit eu tota multitudo circumiacentis regionis Gadarenorum ut discederet ab ipsis, quia magno timore tenebantur: ipse autem ingressus nauigium reuersus est. Rogauit autem eum vir ille, a quo daemonia exierant, ut esset cum eo: sed dimisit eu Iesus, dicens: Reuertere domum tuam, & narra quanta tibi praestiterit Deus. Abiit igitur praedicas per totam urbem, quanta ipsi praestitisset Iesus.
units.tr: Now there was a herd of many swine feeding on the mountain, and the devils begged him to let them enter into the swine. And he gave them leave. Then the devils came out of the man and entered into the swine, and the herd rushed violently down a steep place into the lake and were drowned. When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and went away and reported it in the town and in the countryside. So the people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the devils had gone out sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. Those who had seen it also told them how the man who had been possessed had been healed. Then the whole multitude of the surrounding region of the Gadarenes asked him to depart from them, because they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. The man from whom the devils had gone out begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, "Return to your home and tell how much God has done for you." So he went away and proclaimed throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

units.la: Inter ea, quae Dei filius in carne manifestatus fecit, praecipuum est, quod diaboli, communem hu-mani generis hostem deuicit, & miseros mortales ex illius tyrannide asseruit. De hoc enim prima promissio olim data fuit, & de eodem ille frequenter apud discipulos disseruit, ut quid de ipso sperari atq; sentiri debeat, intelligerent. Etsi verò victoriam plenam in cruce demum obtinuerit, quado expiatis mundi peccatis, morte simul atq; inferos exarmauit, priusquam tamen id fieret, saepe cum illo conflictus est, eumq; ex nonnullis singulari beneficio eiecit: partim quidem, ut se redemptorem illum pro missum esse publice testaretur, partim verò, ut nobis cum hoste illo pugnantibus spem victoriae certam faceret, & simul doceret, quibus artibus & armis a nobis deuinci possit. Et hic praecipuus historiae scopus est. Deteguntur enim hic diaboli ingenium, vires & artes, quibus regnum suum stabilire conatur, & contra autem docetur quanta sit Christi potentia, qui reluctantem & multum tergiuersantem uno verbo expellit. Nuper autem miserabile hominis daemoniaci conditione vidimus, & quid ad primum Christi occursum Satan fecerit. Sequuntur nunc reliqua, quae ad hanc historiam pertinent.
units.tr: Among the deeds that the Son of God performed when he was made manifest in the flesh, the most outstanding is that he overcame the devil, the common enemy of the human race, and delivered wretched mortals from his tyranny. For this first promise was given long ago, and of this he often spoke to his disciples, so that they might understand what ought to be hoped for and thought of him. Although he did not win full victory until the cross, when, having expiated the sins of the world, he disarmed death together with hell, nevertheless before that he often engaged in conflict with the devil and cast him out of some people by a singular benefit. He did this partly so that he might publicly testify that he had been sent as Redeemer, and partly so that he might give us a sure hope of victory while we fight with that enemy, and at the same time teach us by what arts and weapons he can be overcome by us. And this is the chief purpose of the history. For here the nature, powers and arts by which the devil tries to establish his kingdom are laid bare, and on the other hand we are taught how great the power of Christ is, who drives out with one word the one who resists and struggles so much. Lately we saw the wretched condition of the demoniac, and what Satan did at Christ's first approach. Now follow the remaining things that pertain to this history.

units.la: Pergit enim Lucas, & narrat ut ex misero hoc legionem daemoniorum Christus eiecerit. Rogarant illa nuper, ne adhuc in abyssum mitterentur, nunc alteram petitionem subijciunt, ut nimirum ingregem porcorum illis transire liceat, qui non procul inde ad montem pascebantur. Fatentur ergo diaboli, se iam pridem damnatos & exitio devotos esse, adhuc tamen in terris versari cupiunt, ut plus mali dent hominibus, quos secum perditos volunt. Elucet in hoc ingenium diaboli, quo ad nocendum subinde procliuis fertur, & tunc quoque damnum dare cupit, quando se victum esse sentit. Exempla huius rei alibi adduximus, & huc in primis pertinet, quod sub Christi aduentum & deinceps totum orbem terrarum bellis ciuilibus & horrendis motibus turbauit, ne inultus ex possessione diu male occupata discederet. Referunt eius ingenium, qui etsi verbo Dei se victos esse sentiunt, nihilominus tamen aliquid moliuntur aduersus illius doctrinam, & illis insidias struunt, quibus bonam gratiam referre debebant. Similes horum sunt, qui scelerum conuiĉti, illa tunc alijs affricare conantur, quando pœnas iam sibi à Deo paratas esse vident.
units.tr: For Luke goes on and tells how Christ cast out of this wretched man a legion of devils. They had lately begged not to be sent into the abyss, and now they make a second request, namely that they be allowed to pass into the herd of swine that were feeding on the mountain not far off. So the devils confess that they have long since been condemned and doomed to destruction, and yet they still desire to remain on earth, so that they may do more harm to the men whom they want to take with them to ruin. In this we see the nature of the devil, who is always prone to do harm, and who wishes to inflict loss even when he feels that he has been defeated. We have given examples of this elsewhere, and especially relevant is the fact that at and after Christ's coming he has disturbed the whole world with civil wars and dreadful upheavals, so that he might not leave the possession he had held so long without causing harm. They show his nature, for although they feel that they have been defeated by the word of God, they nevertheless attempt something against his teaching and lay snares for those to whom they ought to have shown gratitude. Like them are those who, convicted of their crimes, then try to implicate others when they see that punishment is already prepared for them by God.

units.la: In primis tamen obseruari hic debet astutia diaboli, qui tunc quoque regnum Christi labefaĉta re studet, quando ei locum dare videtur. Cur enim in porcos inuadere cupit? Num quòd istos oderit? Nequaquam. Sed vt Christum Gadarenis inuisum reddat, & hos tanta rerum suarum iaĉtura aduersus illum in rabiem accendat. Scit enim homines naturali rei domestica studio teneri, & fortunarum suarum dispendia impatientius ferre. Ideo in Iobi quoq; facultates non minus crudeliter quàm inique olim grassatus est, vt ille harum amissione exacerbatus contra Deum murmuraret, & hunc conuiciis indignus proscinderet. Debemus hoc diligenter expendere, vt quoties nos ad egestatem redigit, vel etiam morbis grauissimis infestari sentimus, simul cogitemus, non tam fortunas & corpus nostrum, quàm animam à diabolo peti, cuius saluti ille per nostram impatientiam insidias struit: quas facile effugiemus, si in Dei prouidentiam intenti omnia nostra in illius arbitrio & potestate sita esse firmiter credamus.
units.tr: Yet above all the cunning of the devil must be noticed here, for he strives to undermine the kingdom of Christ even when he seems to yield it a place. Why does he desire to rush into the swine? Is it because he hates them? By no means. Rather, he wants to make Christ hateful to the Gadarenes and to inflame them with rage against him because of such great loss of their property. For he knows that people are held by a natural attachment to their household goods and bear the losses of their fortunes more impatiently. So too in the case of Job he once raged against his wealth no less cruelly than unjustly, so that Job, exasperated by the loss of these things, might murmur against God and tear him apart with insults. We ought to consider this carefully, so that whenever he reduces us to poverty, or we feel ourselves afflicted with very grave diseases, we may at the same time reflect that it is not so much our fortunes and our bodies that are sought by the devil as our soul, for whose salvation he lays snares through our impatience. We will easily escape these snares if, intent upon the providence of God, we firmly believe that all our affairs lie in his will and power.

units.la: At dum maximè fremit Satan, & in omnes formas sese vertit, vt Christo incommodet, suam impotentiam magis prodit, qua victus seipsum mendacij arguit. Qui enim paulò ante clamauerat. Quid mihi tecum negotij est? nunc supplex petit ne in abyssum detrudatur, & vt in porcos sibi mi grare liceat. Quàm autem ista inter se conueniunt? Si enim nullius iniuriæ in Christum sibi conscius est, cur pœnam deprecatur? Si verò nihil cum Christo habet negotij, cur ad eius pedes supplex proci dit? cur non illo inconsulto aut etiam inuito, quò vult migrat? Quid, quòd qui ingentes copias modò iaĉtauerat, & quasi pugnaturus Legiones totas in ore habuit, nunc tam seruiliter eius nutui se permittit, quo nihil in orbe vilius & contemptius tunc esse putabatur? Adde hïs, quòd qui simplicium animos plerunq; horribiliter terret, & se aduersus nos nihil non posse gloriatur, hîc ne in porcos quidem ius habet, animal non minus fœdum quàm contemptum & ignobile. Et hic ille est, qui olim Altissimo similis fieri voluit, & qui suis serus cœlos pollicetur, cùm ipse sibi non in hara, sed in ipsis porcis domicilium deligat. Extant huius vanitatis et impotentia multa alia exempla, quæ nos diligenter obseruare decet, ne vel eius promissis fide habeamus, vel minus terreamur. Vt enim natura mendax & mēdacij pater est, ita nihil in nos poterit, nisi quod Deus permittit, qui (vt alibi monuimus) nos supra vires tentari non sinet.
units.tr: But while Satan rages most fiercely and turns himself into every shape in order to harass Christ, he rather reveals his impotence, and being conquered he convicts himself of falsehood. For he who a little before had cried out, "What have I to do with you?" now begs as a suppliant that he not be thrust into the abyss, and that he be allowed to pass into the swine. How do these things agree with one another? If he is conscious of no wrong done to Christ, why does he plead for punishment? And if he has no business with Christ, why does he fall suppliant at his feet? Why does he not go wherever he wishes without consulting him or even against his will? What of the fact that he who had just boasted of his vast forces, and who as if about to fight had whole legions on his lips, now submits himself so slavishly to his nod, a thing which at that time was thought to be the most worthless and contemptible in the world? Add to this that he who often terrifies the minds of simple people with horror, and boasts that he can do nothing against us, has no right even over swine, an animal no less foul than despised and ignoble. And this is he who once wished to become like the Most High, and who promises his followers the heavens, while he himself chooses for his dwelling not a sty but the swine themselves. There are many other examples of this vanity and impotence, which we ought to observe carefully, lest we either put faith in his promises or be frightened by him less than we should. For just as he is by nature a liar and the father of lies, so he can do nothing against us except what God permits, who, as we have elsewhere pointed out, will not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength.

units.la: Sed Christum videamus, qui dæmonijs in porcos inuadendi potestatem facit: nec mora, illorum rabie hi agitati in stagnũ præcipites ruunt, & illic grex totus perit, qui porcus circiter bis mille conflabat, vt Marcus annotauit. Quo argumento apparet diabolos spiritus esse, qui sua essentia constent, & proinde vehementer eos falli, qui per illos non aliud quàm prauos affectus intelligunt, qui ex peccato originali in nobis enascuntur. Quod si demus, simile quid de bonis spiritus siue angelis fateri oportebit, quòd nimirum sancti & boni animorum motus sint, quos Deus in nobis excitet. Ita verò Sadducæorum errorem instaurabimus. Vel vt huius historiæ vestigijs insistamus, dicant illi quem locum in porcis habere potuerint auaritia, odium, ambitio & similes prauì affectus, quos illi dæmonia esse dicunt? Poterat hoc minutius videri, aliquid tamen dicendum fuit propter phanaticos quosdam, qui & veteres errores reuocant, & noua quotidie opinionum portenta fingunt, quibus fidei & doctrinæ Christianæ virtutem conuellunt & labefaĉtant.
units.tr: But let us look at Christ, who gives the devils power to rush into the swine. Without delay, the swine, driven by their madness, rush headlong into the lake, and there the whole herd perishes, which, as Mark noted, numbered about two thousand. From this argument it is clear that the devils are spirits who consist in their own substance, and therefore those are greatly mistaken who understand by them nothing but the evil affections that arise in us from original sin. But if we were to grant this, we would have to confess something similar about the good spirits or angels, namely that they are holy and good movements of the mind which God stirs up in us. Thus we would revive the error of the Sadducees. Or, to follow the traces of this history, let them say what place greed, hatred, ambition and similar evil affections could have had in the swine, which they say are the devils. This might seem too minute a point, yet something had to be said on account of certain fanatics who both revive old errors and daily invent new monstrosities of opinions, by which they undermine and shake the strength of the Christian faith and doctrine.

units.la: Quòd si quæras, annon iniustus fuerit Christus, qui impuris spiritibus in eo morem gessit, quod sine multorũ damno fieri non poterat? Ego quæstionem hanc superuacuam, & curiosam potiùs quàm necessariam esse respondeo. Quia enim ille æternus Dei Filius est, cui omnë potestatem in cælo & in terra pater dedit, cuius itẽ est terra & plenitudo eius, licet illi de suo statuere, quod ipsi libuerit. Nec ille alicui quicquam iniustè rapit, sed iusto iudicio rursus aufert, quod ex gratia prius dederat. Quòd si hoc alicui non satis facit, dicat ille, num iniquitatis accusari debeat Deus, quando segetes grandine sternit, vites pruina adurit, aquarũ inundatione campos operit, fulmina cœlitus iaculatur, pecora & homines immissa lue occidit? Potuerunt in his gentes olim iusta Dei irati iudicia aguoscere: quæ ergo insania est illi propter porcorum gregem litem mouere? Quin eius iustitiam cum bonitate plus quàm paterna intuemur, qui etsi Gadareni (quorum ingratitudo quæuis supplicia merebatur) damnũ acceperunt: ijsdé tamen beneficiũ multo maius cõtulit, quando & homine, qui omnibus porcis & pecoribus longè præstat, saluti restituit, & ipsis simul omnibus occasionem dedit, qua in æternæ veritatis cognitionem peruenire & vitæ cœlestis hæredes fieri poterant, nisi tanta bona ingratitu- dine sua reiecissent. Simul autem in hoc exemplo obseruemus, in quos nam Deus diabolo ius & im- perium permittat: In porcos nimirum, qui terrenis modò studijs immersi, dignitate suam, ad quæ con- diti sunt, non agnoscunt, qui ite obscæno grunnitu verbo eius obstrepunt, & cœlestis regni margari- tas impuris pedibus conculcant. In horum numero censeri merentur ebriosi, qui mane surgunt ad po tandum, qui conuiuijs suis clamores & grunnitus impudentes & intemperantiam plane porcinam intermiscent, neq; interea opus Domini considerant. Scortatores item & adulteri, qui libidinis æstu abrepti corpora sua fœdè polluunt, & ex spiritus sancti templis diaboli profribula faciut: Auari quo que quibus lucri bonus odor est ex re qualibet, ut non solùm cum Vespasiano Imperatore ex lotio & alijs excrementis, verumetiam ex sceleribus quibuscunq; & omni stercore fœdioribus quæstum va- nentur. Pertinent eodem blasphemi homines & palàm impij, qui & ipsi terrenis solis immersi, animos & ora nunquâ ad cœlos attollunt, nisi quando aduersus Dei verbu grunniunt, & illius etiâ no mine ad suas deteriores atq; imprecationes impijssimè abutuntur. Quid verò de idololatris dice- mus, qui què Deo debèt cultu simulachris exhibent, quæ scriptura nô vno loco stercora dicit? Isti o- mnes & quicunq; horu similes sunt, quòad non totis animis conuertuntur, à regno Dei exclusi sunt, & proinde Satanæ insidijs patent, imò huius sunt mancipia, qui ipsos quoq; tandè ad exitium præci- pitabit, è quo nunquam emergent. Itaq; nostræ conditionis atq; dignitatis memores, relictis impuræ carnis & mundi infelicis studijs animos nostros ad cœlestium bonorum considerationem erigamus, ad quod, si non alia ratio, ipsa corporis nostri statura nos excitare debet, quam gentilis poëta non o- scitanter obseruans, hominem sanctius animal & mentis capacius altæ dicit, eumq; formatum scri- bit ad effigiem moderantum cuncta Deorum. Quibus mox istos versus subjicit.
units.tr: But if you ask whether Christ was unjust in indulging the unclean spirits, since this could not be done without loss to many, I answer that this question is superfluous and rather curious than necessary. He is the eternal Son of God, to whom the Father has given all authority in heaven and on earth, and whose is the earth and its fullness. He may therefore decide for himself whatever pleases him. He does not seize anything from anyone unjustly, but by just judgment takes back what he had first given out of grace. If anyone is not satisfied with this, let him say whether God should be accused of injustice when he lays low the crops with hail, scorches the vines with frost, covers the fields with floods, hurls lightning from heaven, and kills cattle and men by sending plague. Long ago the nations could recognise in these the just judgments of an angry God. What madness, then, is it to stir up a quarrel with Christ over a herd of swine? Indeed, we see his justice joined with a goodness more than paternal. Although the Gadarenes (whose ingratitude deserved any punishment) suffered loss, he nonetheless gave them a much greater benefit: he restored to health the man who was far more valuable than all the swine and cattle, and at the same time he gave all of them an opportunity to come to the knowledge of the eternal truth and become heirs of the heavenly life, had they not rejected such great goods through their ingratitude. At the same time, let us note in this example to whom God permits the devil right and power: namely, to swine, that is, to those who are sunk only in earthly pursuits, who do not recognise the dignity for which they were created, who with their foul grunting clamour against his word, and trample the pearls of the heavenly kingdom under unclean feet. Drunkards deserve to be counted among these, who rise early to drink, who mix impudent shouting and grunting and an utterly swinish intemperance into their feasts, and meanwhile do not consider the work of the Lord. Likewise fornicators and adulterers, who, carried away by the heat of lust, defile their bodies foully and turn the temples of the Holy Spirit into the devil's brothels. Also the covetous, for whom gain has a good smell from any source whatever, so that they hunt profit not only from urine and other excrement, as the emperor Vespasian did, but from all kinds of crimes and from every filth more foul than dung. Blasphemers and openly impious men belong to the same company. They too are sunk only in earthly things, and never lift their minds and mouths to heaven, except when they grunt against the word of God and wickedly abuse even his name for their worse curses and imprecations. And what shall we say of idolaters, who give to images the worship due to God, which Scripture in more than one place calls dung? All of these, and whoever are like them, insofar as they are not turned to God with their whole souls, are excluded from the kingdom of God, and therefore lie open to the snares of Satan. Indeed they are the slaves of Satan, who will at last hurl them into destruction, from which they will never rise. Therefore, mindful of our condition and dignity, let us put aside the pursuits of the impure flesh and the unhappy world, and raise our minds to the contemplation of heavenly goods. If no other reason moves us, the very stature of our body ought to rouse us to this. The pagan poet observed it not unthoughtfully, calling man a more sacred animal and one more capable of a lofty mind, and he wrote that man was formed in the likeness of the gods who govern all things. Right after this he adds these verses:

units.la: Pronaque cùm spectent animalia cætera terram,
units.tr: Whereas the other animals look down at the earth,

units.la: Os homini sublime dedit, cælumque tueri
units.tr: he gave man a face raised high, and bade him behold the heavens,

units.la: Iussit, & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus.
units.tr: and lift his upright countenance to the stars.

units.la: Hæc cũ obseruare potuerint, qui nulla veri Dei cognitione illuminati fuerũt, pudeat nos nostræ ignauiæ, qui cùm sciamus Iesum Christum, in quo vita nostra (ut Apostolus ait) recondita est, ad de- xtram Dei Patris in cœlestibus considere, adhuc tamen reliquis supernu circa terrena & carnalia occupamur.
units.tr: If those who were not enlightened by any knowledge of the true God could observe this, we should be ashamed of our sloth, since we know that Jesus Christ, in whom our life is hidden (as the Apostle says), sits at the right hand of God the Father in heaven, and yet we are still occupied with earthly and carnal things, which are beneath us.

units.la: Sequitur effectus miraculi, qui pro hominum diuersitatem multiplex fuit. Et primi producêntur pastores, qui his visis illico fugerunt, & rem omnem, ut gesta erat, in urbe Gadarenorum & toto agro circumiacente diuulgarunt. Vult enim Christus toti mundo innotescere, & proinde opera sua passim prædicari vult. In eo autem ferè hominum obscurorum & vilium ministerio vtitur, ne his seruiliter addicti simus, sed in eorum potius contemplatione versemur, quæ illi annuntiant. Et est hoc omnium eorum munus, quos sui gregis pastores ille constituit, ut quæcunq; ipse propter nos fecit, bona fide prædicent, & omnes ad hunc excipiendum excitent.
units.tr: Then follows the effect of the miracle, which was manifold according to the diversity of men. First the herdsmen come forward, who, as soon as they saw this, fled and spread the whole matter, just as it had happened, in the city of the Gadarenes and throughout the surrounding countryside. For Christ wishes to be made known to the whole world, and therefore he wants his works to be proclaimed everywhere. He uses for this the ministry of mostly obscure and humble men, so that we may not be enslaved to them, but may rather dwell on the things they announce. This is the office of all those whom he appoints as ministers of his flock: to proclaim faithfully whatever he has done for us, and to stir up all to receive him.

units.la: Deinde de Gadarenis dicitur, quòd ad Christum egressi, cum coràm omnia vidissent & audissent, timuerint. Ergo sentiunt diuina virtute hoc omne factum esse, timent autem, eò quòd non respiciunt in Dei bonitatem saluificam, quæ in dæmoniaci liberatione sese ipsis omnibus of- ferebat. Fuit ergo hic timor præposterus, qualem in omnibus oboriri videmus, qui solius Dei iudicijs percelluntur, non autem eorum causas & quæ illa comitatur gratiam atque bonitatem eius considerant. Nihilo igitur isti meliores fiunt, sed in peius proficiunt. Rogant enim Chri- stum, ut ex eorum terra discedat, quasi nimirum ipso digressio, poenas simul omnes effugerint, quas adhuc grauiores imminere timebant. Fuit ergo hic plus quàm belluinus stupor, cum immani in- gratitudine coniuncti, quando tantum Christi beneficium non agnoscunt, qui & hominem nul- la humana arte curabilem seruarat, & itinera ipsis tuta fecerat, adeoque totam illam regionem pe- riculo & metu communi liberarat. Est hoc ingenium eorum, qui seculo huic toti sunt dediti. Quia enim nihil sublime & cœlestè sapiunt, semper timent, ne Christi prædicatio turbas det, & ali- cuius periculi grauioris causa sit. Interim neque peccata sua agnoscunt, propter quæ venit ira Dei, neque iudiciorum Dei finem & visum obseruant, qui est, ut his ad pœnitentiam excitentur. Ad- hæc quia terrena cœlestibus præferunt, ne minimum quidem fortunarum suarum dispendium ferre, & Christo potius æternum volunt carere, quàm de rebus suis periclitari. Regnat hoc hominum genus hodie ybiq; locorum, & in eo fere suam prudentiam pleriq; ostentant, quod Christi prædicones, vel silere iubent ad tempus, vel etiam finibus suis emigrare, vt proximum quodq; periculum declinent. Quibus tamen peiores sunt, qui cum pace bona fruantur, Christi tamen doctrina liberari cupiunt, quia hanc moribus suis corruptissimis aduersam esse sentiunt: & hi non raro in tantam rabiem exarde-scunt, vt vim quoq; huius ministri inferant. Atqui vi minimè opus erat. Vt enim à Gadarenis mox abiit Christus, ita sponte ab omnibus discedit, qui horum ingratitudinem imitantur. Non autem ideo illi feliciores aut magis in tuto sunt: imò fere grauioribus malis obruuntur. Quia enim benedictionem omnem cuius ipse vnicus Mediator est, secum aufert, mox irati Dei indicia sese exerunt, & fere fit, vt non propter leuiculas folium, verumetiam turpes ob causas extremum discrimen subeant, qui pro Dei gloria & propria salute periclitari noluerunt.
units.tr: Next it is said of the Gadarenes that, when they went out to Christ and had seen and heard everything there, they were afraid. So they perceive that all this was done by divine power, but they fear, because they do not look to the saving goodness of God, which was offered to all of them in the liberation of the demoniac. Therefore this fear was misplaced, such as we see arising in all who are struck with dread only by the judgments of God, and do not consider their causes and the grace and goodness that accompany them. Hence these men become no better, but advance to something worse. For they ask Christ to depart from their country, as though by his departure they would escape all the punishments which they feared would fall on them still more heavily. This, then, was a stupor more than bestial, joined with monstrous ingratitude, since they did not acknowledge so great a benefit from Christ, who had saved a man whom no human art could cure, had made the roads safe for them, and had thus freed that whole region from common danger and fear. This is the temper of those who are wholly given over to this age. Because they savour nothing lofty and heavenly, they are always afraid that the preaching of Christ will cause disturbances and be the cause of some greater danger. Meanwhile they recognise neither their sins, on account of which the wrath of God has come, nor the purpose and aim of God's judgments, which is that they be stirred to repentance. Moreover, because they prefer earthly things to heavenly, they cannot bear even the smallest loss of their fortunes, and would rather lose Christ eternally than risk their possessions. This kind of men holds sway today in every place, and in this most of them display their prudence: they order the preachers of Christ either to keep silent for a time or even to depart from their borders, so as to avoid each nearer danger. Yet worse than these are those who enjoy good peace, and nonetheless desire to be rid of the teaching of Christ, because they feel that it is opposed to their most corrupt morals. These often blaze up into such a rage that they even use violence against the ministers of this teaching. And yet there was no need for violence at all. For just as Christ soon departed from the Gadarenes, so he willingly withdraws from all who imitate their ingratitude. Nor are they on that account more fortunate or safer; rather they are for the most part overwhelmed by greater evils. For since he, who is the only Mediator of every blessing, takes it away with him, at once the signs of God's anger show themselves, and it often happens that those who were unwilling to risk anything for the glory of God and their own salvation undergo extreme peril for trivial, even shameful, causes.

units.la: Est ergo maiori laude dignus dæmoniacus ille, cuius exemplum nobis imitandum Spiritus sanctus proponit. Sedet is ad pedes Iesu, quod discipulorum esse, ex Pauli verbis patet, qui se ad pedes Gamalielis instítutum fuisse dicit. Deinde sumptis vestibus simul pudorem quoque ingenuum induit, quem diaboli furiæ prius illi abstulerant. Ad hæc mentem saniorem verbis & moribus testatur. Postremò Christi discipulus & comes indiuulsus esse, & relicto patrio solo & ingratis gentilibus cum illo abire cupit. Quod etsi ille non permitteret, non tamen repulsa illa offenditur, sed acceptum ab illo beneficium vbique prædicat. Vnde verò hæc omnia? Exeo nimirum, quòd in Christo non modò diuinæ virtutis formidabilem potentiam, sed eiusdem saluificam quoque beneficentiam obseruauit. Et sunt hæc eorum officia, quos ex diaboli tyrannide Christus asseruit: vt nimirum illum induant, eidem sese per fidei obedientiam submittant, mentis sanitatem vita & moribus probent, illi adhæreant totis animis, & bonitatis eius orædicatione alios quoque illi adducant. Vnde apparet, eos nondum rectè agnoscere gratiam Dei sibi in Christo factam, in quorum vita nihil huius cerneri potest.
units.tr: The demoniac is therefore more worthy of great praise, and the Holy Spirit sets his example before us for imitation. He sits at the feet of Jesus, which is the mark of a disciple, as is clear from Paul's words, where he says that he was taught at the feet of Gamaliel. Then, having put on his clothes, he also regains his natural modesty, which the furies of the devil had earlier taken from him. Besides this, he shows a saner mind by his words and conduct. Finally, he wants to be an inseparable companion of Christ and to go away with him, leaving his native soil and the ungrateful Gentiles. Even though Christ does not allow it, he is not offended by the refusal, but everywhere proclaims the benefit he has received from him. But whence all this? Clearly because he has observed in Christ not only the formidable power of divine might but also his saving kindness. And these are the duties of those whom Christ has rescued from the tyranny of the devil: namely, to put on Christ, to submit themselves to him through the obedience of faith, to prove the soundness of their minds by their life and conduct, to cleave to him with their whole souls, and by proclaiming his goodness to bring others to him as well. From this it appears that those in whose life none of this can be seen do not yet rightly acknowledge the grace of God toward them in Christ.

units.la: Porrò non vult Dominus, vt secum ille ex locis ijs discedat. Nec enim necesse erat ad salutem, vt in Apostolorum gregem assumeretur, aut relicta domo & re domestica ipsum hic inde docentem comitaretur. Et constat plures quoq; alios Christi discipulos fuisse, qui & rem domesticam tuerunt, & quam prius habebant vocationem sedulè secuti sunt: quales fuerunt Lazarus Bethaniensis cum sororibus suis, Nicodemus, Zachæus, Iosephus Arimathæus, & plures alij. Quod obseruari debet propter phanaticos illos, qui ab omnibus requirunt, vt Apostolorum exemplum imitentur: neque cogitant, vocationem eos habuisse peculiarem, ad quam obeundam necesse fuit, vt diuersum ab alijs vitæ genus sequerentur. Interim hic singulare bonitatis suæ specimen Christus edit, qui apud ingratam & quouis supplicio dignam Gadarenorum gentem hunc suæ gratiæ præconem manere voluit, vt eius exemplo simul & prædicatione aliqui saltem ad salutis propriæ studium accenderentur. Ita solet cum nostra contumacia luctari diuina bonitas, cuius exempla plurima passim in scripturis extant. Nos verò quod præcipuum huius historiæ caput est, memoriter repetamus. Fuit enim omnium nostrum eadem, quæ miseri istius dæmoniaci, conditio. Seruauit autem nos, & in filiorum Dei libertatem traxit Iesus Christus. Huic ergo gratias dignas agamus, & illum induti nos atque omnia nostra ei consecremus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord does not wish him to depart from those places with him. For it was not necessary for salvation that he be taken into the company of the Apostles, or that, leaving home and property, he should accompany Christ as he taught here and there. And it is evident that there were also many other disciples of Christ who both looked after their domestic affairs and diligently followed the calling they had before: such as Lazarus of Bethany with his sisters, Nicodemus, Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea, and many others. This ought to be noted on account of those fanatics who require of everyone that they imitate the example of the Apostles, and do not consider that the Apostles had a particular calling, which required them to follow a way of life different from others. Meanwhile, here Christ displays a singular specimen of his goodness, who, among the ungrateful people of the Gadarenes, deserving any punishment whatever, wished this herald of his grace to remain, so that by his example and preaching at least some might be kindled to care for their own salvation. Thus divine goodness is accustomed to struggle with our obstinacy, and very many examples of this are found everywhere in the Scriptures. But let us repeat from memory what is the chief point of this history. For the condition of all of us was the same as that of this wretched demoniac. Jesus Christ, however, has preserved us and drawn us into the liberty of the sons of God. Let us therefore give thanks worthy of him, and, having put him on, consecrate ourselves and all that is ours to him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIII.
units.tr: Homily 83.

units.la: Factum est autem cum reuertisset Iesus, excepit eum turba: nam omnes expectabant eum. Et ecce venit quidam, cui nomen Iairus, qui erat præfectus Synagogæ, cumq; accidisset ad pedes Iesu, rogabat eū, vt ingrederetur domum ipsius: Quia erat ei vnigenita filia, quasi annorum duodecim, eaq; moriebatur. Inter eundum verò turba coarctabat eum. Et mulier, quæ erat in fluxione sanguinis ab annis duodecim, & in medicos impenderat totum victum, nec ab vllo potuerat curari, cum accessit fec set à tergo, tetigit fimbriam vestis ipsius, & illico substitit fluxio sanguinis eius. Tunc ait Iesus: Quis est qui me tetigit? Negantibus autem omnibus dixit Petrus, & qui cum eo erant: Magister, turba te constringit & opprimit, & dicis, Quis est qui me tetigit? Iesus autem ait: Tetigit me aliquis: nam ego cognovi virtutem à me exiisse. Cum autem mulier illa videret, se non latuisse, tremens venit & accidit ei ad pedes, & declarauit ei in conspectu totius populi, quam ob causam tetigisset eum, & ut sanata fuisset illico. Ipse vero dixit ei: Confide filia, fides tua te seruauit: Vade cum pace.
units.tr: It came to pass, when Jesus had returned, that the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And behold, there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell at Jesus' feet and begged him to come into his house, because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, who was dying. As he went, the crowd pressed in on him. And a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years, and had spent her whole living on physicians, and could not be healed by anyone, came up behind him and touched the hem of his garment, and at once her bleeding stopped. Then Jesus said, "Who touched me?" When all denied it, Peter and those with him said, "Master, the crowd is crushing and pressing you, and you ask, 'Who touched me?'" But Jesus said, "Someone has touched me, for I know that power has gone out of me." When the woman saw that she could not go unnoticed, she came trembling and fell at his feet, and in the sight of all the people she declared why she had touched him, and how she had been healed at once. And he said to her, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has saved you. Go in peace."

units.la: Iesus Christus, Dominus & Seruator noster, cum Nicodemo colloquens, inter alia grauiter pronuntiat: Haec est condemnatio, quod lux venit in mundum, sed dilexerunt homines potius tenebras quàm lucem. Exemplum huius ingratitudinis memorabile admodum nuper in Gadarenis vidimus. Venit ad hos Christus, & in vnius daemoniaci liberatione docuit, quis nam ipse sit, & quanta bona secum afferat. At illi leuiculla porcorum iactura offensi eum fastidiunt, & ut ab ipsis alio transmigret precantur. Et huius generis multa fecerunt Iudaei, & aliquando ne à vi quidem abstinuerunt: quae omnia in eum finem considerari debent, ut eò illustrior nobis sit Christi bonitas, qui quà si cum illorum contumacia certamen suscepisset, eò plura in illos beneficia confert, quò illi sunt praefractiores, neq; horum ingratitudinem incurabilem ijs fraudi esse finit, qui ipsum cum fide quaerunt, & se ab ipso cupiunt iuuari. Apparet hoc in sequenti narratione, quae ad finem Cap. vsque extenditur. Continet haec duo miracula, quibus euidentissime demonstratur, ipsum mortis & peccati victorem esse, & proinde Seruatorem verum, in quo vero vita & salus omnis inueniatur.
units.tr: Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, speaking with Nicodemus, pronounces this weighty judgment among other things: "This is the condemnation, that the light has come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light." We recently saw a most memorable example of this ingratitude among the Gadarenes. Christ came to them, and by freeing one demoniac he taught them who he is and what great good he brings with him. But they, offended by the trifling loss of their pigs, reject him and beg him to move on from their district. The Jews did many things of this kind, and at times did not even hold back from violence. All of these things should be considered with this end in view: that Christ's goodness may shine more brightly for us. The more he met their obstinacy, the more benefits he bestowed on them, and the more stubborn they became. Nor does he allow their incurable ingratitude to harm those who seek him in faith and wish to be helped by him. This appears in the following narrative, which extends to the end of the chapter. It contains two miracles, by which it is most clearly shown that he is the conqueror of death and sin, and therefore the true Saviour, in whom alone true life and all salvation are found.

units.la: Praemittit autem Lucas huius loci initio alterius miraculi parasceuen seu praeparationem, quae tria habet. Primùm, quod ex Gadarenorum terra reuersus magno cum applausu & gratulatione populi, qui ipsum auidè expectarat, exceptus fit. Vbi discimus, Christum ab ingratis quidem repelli, eidem tamen non deesse ad quos se recipiat, & quos salute dignetur. Ergo neque regni eius potentia, neque eiusdem benignitas, hominum contumacia aut ingratitudine superatur. Debet hoc nos consolari, ne de eius regno & gratia inter huius mundi motus desperemus: simul autem imitari debemus facilitatem Christi, neque à benefaciendo abstinere, etiamsi beneficia nostra contemni, aut à quibusdam pessimam gratiam nobis referri videmus. Secundò ponitur descriptio personae, in qua miraculum fuit editum. Erat haec Iairi praefecti Synagogae filia duodennis & vnigenita, quae morbo letali correpta iam in extremus agebat. Huius pater, cùm iam reipsa procul dubio experiretur, nullum amplius locum humanis remedijs reliquum esse, ad Christum venit, & hunc ut secum domum eat precatur ad opem ferendam filiae. Adeò magnus afflictionum vis est in electis, ut non tam manuducant quàm cogant ad verum salutis authorem eos confugere, qui dum res secundae sunt, de illo vix obiter cogitant. Et sanè est hoc praeclarum bonitatis diuinae argumentum, quòd ex eo hominum genere, qui Christo infestissimi erant, iflum adducit, ut salutis in eo per fidem participes fiat. De nullo igitur homine nos temere desperare debemus. Habet enim Deus vbique suos, & quorum vult miseretur, neque etiam vel locus vel vitae genus & conditio obstare possunt, quò minus suo tempore efficaciter trahat eos, quos aeterno suo decreto ad salutem praedestinauit. Est & consolatio haec eò efficacior, quòd illum fidei nostrae infirmitate non offendi, sed potius huic sub uentre videmus, ut viribus subinde nouis augeatur. Nam credidit quidem Iairus, sed non tanta eius fides fuit, quantam in Centurione supra vidimus. Etenim corporali praesentia Christi opus esse putat, quod magnum infirmitatis & imperfectionis argumentum est. Non tamen eum ille fastidit, sed absque mora (quod tertium huius Praeparationis caput est) cum illo iter ingreditur, & neque fidei imbecillitatem, neque communem populi ingratitudinem aut inconstantiam, neque impios primatum conatus illi exprobrat, qui ipsum extinctum volebant. Est ergo reuera salutis nostrae cupidissimus, & magnam ei iniuriam faciunt, qui durum & immitem hodie fingunt, apud quem alijs intercessoribus opus sit.
units.tr: At the beginning of this passage Luke sets out a preparation for the second miracle, which has three parts. First, when Jesus returns from the land of the Gadarenes, he is received with great applause and rejoicing by the people, who had eagerly awaited him. Here we learn that Christ is indeed rejected by the ungrateful, yet there are never lacking those to whom he turns and whom he deigns to save. Thus neither the power of his kingdom nor his kindness is overcome by the obstinacy or ingratitude of men. This ought to comfort us, so that we do not despair of his kingdom and grace amid the upheavals of this world. At the same time we should imitate Christ's readiness, and not refrain from doing good even when we see our benefits despised, or when some repay us with the worst thanks. Second, a description of the person on whom the miracle was performed is given. She was the twelve-year-old only daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, and she was seized by a deadly illness and was now at the point of death. Her father, having already undoubtedly experienced that no place was left for human remedies, comes to Christ and begs him to go home with him to bring help to his daughter. So great is the force of afflictions in the elect that they compel, rather than merely lead, those who in prosperity hardly think of him at all to flee to the true author of salvation. Indeed, it is a remarkable proof of divine goodness that he brings to faith in himself, so that they may share in salvation through faith, a man from the very class of people who were most hostile to Christ. Therefore we ought never rashly to despair of anyone. God has his own everywhere, and whom he wills he has mercy on. Neither place, nor manner of life, nor condition can stand in the way, so that at his appointed time he does not effectually draw those whom he has predestined to salvation by his eternal decree. This consolation is all the more effective because we see that he is not offended by the weakness of our faith, but rather stoops to it, so that it may be strengthened with fresh powers from time to time. For Jairus did believe, but his faith was not as great as we saw earlier in the centurion. He thinks that the bodily presence of Christ is needed, which is a strong sign of weakness and imperfection. Yet Christ does not scorn him. Without delay (this is the third part of this preparation) Jairus sets out with him on the journey. He does not reproach him for the weakness of his faith, nor for the common ingratitude and fickleness of the people, nor for the wicked attempts of the leaders who wanted to put him to death. Jairus is therefore truly most eager for our salvation, and they do great wrong to Christ who imagine him today as hard and unkind, so that one needs other intercessors to approach him.

units.la: His praemissis, alterum miraculum Lucas interserit, quo mulierem fluxu menstrui sanguinis incurabili laborantem, & medicorum inscitia atque avaritia ad extremam quoque pauperta-tem redactam Christus curavit. Vbi nemo temere factum putaverit, quod interea dum ad Iairi domum contendit, hoc fecit Dominus. Ita enim & Iairi fidem inter spem & metum fluctuantem confirmari oportuit, & simul totum populum admoneri, Christum etiam primates quaerere incipiant, tamen eorum curam abiecturum esse, qui propter inopiam & vitae genus multis aliis contemptibiles sunt. Praecipuus autem miraculi huius usus est, qui aliorum quoque, ut discamus quam nam sit Christus: verus nimirum Servator, qui ipsum peccatum, ex quo mors enata est, tollat, & non modo ab externis aut actualibus (ut vocant) delictis liberet, sed inhaerentem nobis naturae vitiositatem atque immunditiem eluat, quam menstruorum fluxu adumbrari alibi annotavimus. Facit ergo miraculum hoc ad explicationem promissionis, quae apud Zachariam habetur: In die illa aperietur fons domui David & habitatoribus Ierusalem, ad eluendum peccatum & menstruam immunditiem. Cui Baptista consentiens clamabat de Christo: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Peccatum enim mundi simpliciter dicit, ut omnem id comprehendat, quod sub peccati censum venit. Ideo Ioannes Apostolus id significantius exprimens ait: Sanguis Filii Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato. Est igitur miraculum hoc unum ex praecipuis, cuius usus & fructus ut nobis clarius pateat, primo mulierem ipsam & eius conditionem videre oportet: deinde quae eius fides fuerit, & ut salutem in Christo quaesiverit. Tertio Christum audiemus de eius fide & salute pronunciantem.
units.tr: With these things set down, Luke inserts the second miracle, in which the Lord healed a woman suffering from an incurable flow of menstrual blood, who, through the ignorance and greed of physicians, had been reduced even to extreme poverty. Here no one should think it was done by chance that the Lord did this while he was hurrying to Jairus's house. For it was fitting that the faith of Jairus, wavering between hope and fear, should be strengthened, and at the same time that the whole people should be reminded that Christ, though he begins to be sought by the leading men, will nonetheless not abandon the care of those who are despised by many because of their poverty and manner of life. The chief use of this miracle, however, is that we may learn who Christ is: the true Saviour, who takes away sin itself, from which death has sprung, and frees us not only from external or actual (as they are called) offences, but also washes away the uncleanness and corruption of nature that cleaves to us, which we have noted elsewhere is foreshadowed by the flow of menstrual blood. Thus this miracle serves to explain the promise found in Zechariah: "In that day a fountain shall be opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to wash away sin and menstrual uncleanness." In agreement with this, the Baptist cried out concerning Christ: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." For he speaks simply of "the sin of the world," so that he may embrace everything that falls under the notion of sin. Therefore the Apostle John, expressing it more forcefully, says: "The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin." This miracle is therefore one of the chief ones, and so that its use and fruit may be made clearer to us, we must first look at the woman herself and her condition; then at her faith, and how she sought salvation in Christ; and third, we shall hear Christ pronouncing on her faith and salvation.

units.la: Quoad mulierem, eo morbo laborat, quo sexum illum Deus ceu peculiari flagello castigare & humiliare solet. Faciebat autem ad huius gravitatem olim, quod secundum legem immundae censebantur, quaecunque illo laborabant, adeo ut illis ad sacra accedere non liceret. Nec dubium est pias foeminas, si quid huius patiebantur, non vulgarem dolorem sensisse ex peccatorum suorum recordatione, quae simul Euae matris delictum in mentem ipsis revocabat. Si quae ergo praeter morem naturae illo diutius detinebantur, non parum fidem suam tentari sentiebant, eo quod Deum sibi praealijs inferiorem esse putarent. Itaque miserabilis admodum istius conditio fuit, cum morbus multorum annorum spatio incurabilis factus esset, & illi iam inopia accederet, quae est omnibus gravis fit, ijs tamen intolerabilis esse solet, qui morbis gravioribus affliguntur, & ob virium imbecillitatem ad victum sibi parandum non sunt idonei. Solet autem hoc fere omnibus accidere, qui de morborum causis non recte iudicant, & quam in Deo debebant repositam habere, spem in medicos transferunt. At quia in Christi miraculis non tam de corporum quam animarum salute agitur, observemus, in ista muliere typum nobis proponi, quo omnium nostrum conditio adumbratur, qui ut in peccato concipimur & nascimur: ita huius labe infecti, ad omne bonum inepti, adhaec Dei iudicio immundi sumus, & quoad nos ab Ecclesia & aeternae salutis societate exclusi. Estque malum hoc eo nocentius, quod plerique huius rei non agnoscunt, neque se miseros & infelices esse sentiunt. At si qui hoc intelligunt, ij fere ad humana praesidia confugiunt, parum fidei simul & ineptissimum medicum sibi cunandos praebent. Fiebat hoc frequenter Christi temporibus, quando Scribae & Sacerdotes animarum medicinam profitebantur, nihil autem infelici populo conferebant, quam quod pecuniis etiam emunctis peccatores, quoad corpus & animam miserrimi fiebant, & maiori iudicio peccatorum mole intra animas suas & conscientiam gravabantur. Accidit hoc ipsum hodie multis, qui dum animarum medicinam apud sacrificos & monachos quaerunt, multa quidem patiuntur (ut Marcus de muliere ista annotavit) & impensas magnas faciunt, nihilo autem meliores fiunt, neque scelerum conscientia liberantur, quae ipsos indesinenter infestat. Et tanta est medicorum istorum perfidia, ut quamvis in sectas diversas scissi sint, tamen quasi coniuratione facta sibi invicem mutuas operas tradunt, neque contenti sunt eos spoliavisse, quibus cum ipsis res est, nisi ipsas quoque haereditates intercipiant, & posteros quoque illorum ad inopiam redigant. Senserunt iam saeculis aliquot istorum artes plus quam veneficas infelix mundus, adhuc tamen ea est multorum dementia, ut eas sequantur, & profitentur illis tanquam profecto & artis dimicent. Digni sunt ergo, qui tam corpore quam animam misere pereant.
units.tr: As for the woman, she suffers from that disease with which God is wont to chastise and humble that sex, as with a special scourge. Under the old law, whatever was affected by this complaint was considered unclean, so that it was not lawful for such women to approach the sacred things. Nor is there any doubt that pious women, if they suffered anything of this kind, felt no ordinary grief from remembering their sins, which at the same time brought to mind the transgression of Eve, their mother. If any were detained longer than the usual course of nature allowed, they felt that their faith was not a little tested, because they thought that God regarded them as inferior to others. Therefore the condition of this poor woman was most wretched: the disease had become incurable over many years, and now poverty was added to it. Poverty is grievous to all, but it is usually intolerable to those who are afflicted with more serious illnesses and, because of their feebleness, are not fit to earn a living. This usually happens to all who do not rightly judge the causes of diseases, and who transfer to physicians the hope that they ought to have placed in God. But since in the miracles of Christ the concern is not so much with the health of the body as with that of the soul, let us observe that in this woman a type is set before us, which shadows the condition of all of us. As we are conceived and born in sin, so, stained by its defilement, we are unfit for every good; moreover, in God's judgment we are unclean, and so far as we are concerned, excluded from the Church and from the fellowship of eternal salvation. This evil is the more harmful because most people do not recognize it, nor do they feel that they are wretched and unhappy. But if some do understand it, they mostly flee to human aids, and at the same time they show little faith and offer themselves to the most useless of physicians to be treated. This happened frequently in Christ's time, when the scribes and priests professed to heal the soul, yet conferred nothing on the unhappy people except that, even when they had been fleeced of their money, sinners became most wretched in body and soul, and were weighed down by a greater load of sins within their souls and conscience. This happens today to many who, while they seek the healing of their souls from priests and monks, indeed suffer much (as Mark noted of this woman) and make great expenses, yet are none the better for it, nor are they freed from the sense of guilt that constantly troubles them. And so great is the treachery of these physicians that, although they are split into different sects, they nevertheless, as if by a conspiracy, hand over their services to one another. They are not content to have plundered those with whom they have to deal, unless they also seize the inheritances and reduce their descendants to poverty as well. For some centuries now the unhappy world has felt their arts, which are worse than witchcraft; yet such is the madness of many that they follow them and, as if these were true and genuine arts, they profess them. They are worthy, therefore, to perish wretchedly both in body and in soul.

units.la: Videamus ergo nos, quæ istius mulieris fides fuerit, quidue fecerit, vt eius exemplū imitemur, quod ipse Dei Filius non tam verbis quàm reipsa comprobauit. Primò vbi in medicis operâ & impensam perijsse videt, de Christo autē multa audierat, ad hunc contendit, & se quoq; eius ope curari posse sperat, quæ multis hucusq; salutaris fuerat. Multum ergo illi profuit medicorum siue inscitia siue improbitas. Nam si horum arte fuisset curata, corpore quidem melius habuisset, anima verò in superstitione & erroribus demersa mansisset. Ita frequenter veræ salutis causam nobis affert, quod noxium & diuinæ iræ argumentum esse videbatur. Est autem hic primus ad salutem gradus, vt nos per omnia miseros esse, & humanis viribus aut meritis nihil profici intelligamus. Nam si tunc diuinæ gratiæ per Christum nobis factæ prædicatio accedat, mox nova spes animum nostrum excitabit, vt certa fiducia concepta ad Christum contendamus, qui vnicus animarum medicus atq; seruator est. Ideo Euangelij prædicationem ab hoc articulo Christus inchoandam esse docet, quando de Spiritu sancto, quem Apostoli accipere debebant, ait: Ille arguet mundum de peccato, &c. Et debent redargutionem istam patienter ferre ij, quibus salus sua cordi est, vt maiori desiderio Christi accendantur, & reliquis inutilibus atq; noxijs remedijs, quam ille nobis offert, salutem totam animis amplexentur. Est ergo perniciosa admodum illorum peruersitas, qui aut peccati noxam in semetipsis agnoscere nolunt, aut quàmuis illam sentiant, adhuc tamen Christo relicto circa externas & ab hominibus superstitiosis confictas peccatorum expiationes occupantur.
units.tr: Let us therefore consider what this woman's faith was and what she did, so that we may imitate her example, which the Son of God himself confirmed not so much in words as in deeds. First, when she saw that she had spent her effort and money on physicians, but had heard much about Christ, she turned to him and hoped that she too could be cured by his help, which had hitherto brought salvation to many. So the ignorance or the dishonesty of the physicians greatly benefited her. For if she had been cured by their skill, she would indeed have had a better body, but her soul would have remained sunk in superstition and error. Thus God often brings us the cause of true salvation by means of what seemed to be a harmful sign of his anger. Now this is the first step to salvation: that we understand we are wretched in every way, and that nothing is gained by human strength or merits. For if the proclamation of the divine grace made to us through Christ then comes to us, a new hope will soon stir our minds, so that, with firm trust conceived, we strive towards Christ, who alone is the physician and saviour of souls. Therefore Christ teaches that the preaching of the gospel must begin from this point, when he speaks of the Holy Spirit, whom the apostles were to receive: "He will convict the world of sin," and so on. Those for whom their own salvation is dear ought to bear this rebuke patiently, so that they may be kindled with a greater desire for Christ, and embrace their whole salvation with their hearts, rather than the other useless and harmful remedies that he offers us. Therefore the perversity of those is very pernicious, who either refuse to recognise the harm of sin in themselves, or, although they feel it, still, leaving Christ behind, busy themselves with external expiations of sins devised by superstitious men.

units.la: Deinde à tergo accedit, & fimbriam vestimenti eius tangit. Nam (vt Marcus annotauit) dicebat: Si vel vestimenta eius tetigero, seruabor. Paucis verbis eximiam mulieris fidem Euangelistæ describunt. De Christi enim virtute tantam fiduciâ animo concepit, vt solius pallij tactu se cum rari posse sperret. De voluntate quoq; eius nō omnino dubitat, etiamsi propriæ immunditiei conscientia timidiusculam fecerit. Sciebat enim eas, quæ fluxu sanguinis patiebantur, in Lege pro immundis censeri, & ab hominum commercijs siue consuetudine excludi. Recte ergo trepidat nonnihil, & laudem meretur pudor iste, quem Legis cognitio pariebat. Vincit tamen hunc fides, vt quàmuis nō audit adhuc in conspectum venire, bene tamen speret de illius bonitate, quæ leprosos quoq; ab illo tactos atq; curatos fuisse audierat, & proinde audet eius vestes à tergo contingere. Et est hoc fidei ingenium, vt cum carnis prudentia luctetur, & de Dei quidè gratia nihil non nobis promittat, simul tamen modestos & verecundos faciat, sicuti supra in peccatrice historia vidimus. Constat igitur vel hoc vno argumento à fide alienissimos esse, qui pharisaica suæ dignitatis & meritorum fiducia turgidi in conspectum Dei irrumpunt, vt non tam eius gratiam implorent, quàm ab eo debitam sibi mercedem exigant. Quòd verò mulier ista fimbriam vestimentorum Christi tangere cupiuit, minimè eorum superstitioni patrocinatur, qui illius tunicam adhuc hodie haberi eiusq; aspectum siue contactum salutificum esse fingunt. Neq; eo contenti, Diuorum quoq; reliquias infinitas non minus ridiculè quàm impiè ostentant, & apud illas salutem tam corporis quàm animæ quærere docent. Nihil enim vana superstitione hic factum esse, paulò ante audiuimus, & non in veste Christi bæsit mulier ista, sed in Christi salutificam virtutem respexit. Quin ipse, quasi errorem illum confutare voluerit, mox testabitur, virtutem illam ex se egressam esse, & ita omnem huius miraculi gloriam sibi soli vendicat. Omissis ergo superstitiosorum hominum commentis, mulieré hanc in eo imitemur, vt ipsi quoque eam Christi vestem tangamus, qua indutus in terris olim vixit, & quam secum in gloriam cælestem euexit. Est hæc humana natura, quam ex Virgine matre assumpsit, & quæ sola fide tangi potest, eò quòd per hanc illi vnimur, vt ipse in nobis sit, & nos in illo. Quotquot ergo crediderint, Dei Filium propter nos hominem factum esse, & ea fecisse, quæ ad humani generis redemptionem facta necessaria erant, nunc autem è cælis salutem nobis conferre certam, ij & tangunt illum verè, & ex tactu illo vitam sibi obtingere sentient.
units.tr: Then she comes from behind and touches the hem of his garment. For (as Mark noted) she was saying: "If I touch even his garments, I shall be saved." In few words the Evangelists describe the woman's remarkable faith. For she conceived such confidence in Christ's power that she hoped to be made whole by the mere touch of his cloak. Nor does she altogether doubt his willingness, although the consciousness of her own uncleanness made her rather timid. For she knew that women who suffered a flow of blood were counted unclean under the Law and excluded from the company and customs of men. So she trembles a little, rightly, and that modesty, which knowledge of the Law produced, deserves praise. Yet faith overcomes it, so that, although she does not yet dare to come into his sight, she still hopes well of his goodness, having heard that lepers too had been touched and cured by him, and therefore she dares to touch his garments from behind. Such is the nature of faith: it struggles against the prudence of the flesh, and though it promises itself nothing short of God's grace, it at the same time makes us humble and modest, as we saw above in the history of the sinful woman. It is therefore clear, from this one argument alone, how far removed from faith those are who, swollen with the Pharisaical confidence in their own dignity and merits, burst into God's presence, not so much to implore his grace as to demand from him the reward they think they are owed. But that this woman wished to touch the hem of Christ's garments in no way supports the superstition of those who pretend that his tunic is still kept today and that its sight or touch is saving. Nor are they content with this: they display countless relics of the saints, no less ridiculously than impiously, and teach people to seek salvation of body and soul from them. For we heard a little earlier that nothing was done here by vain superstition, and that this woman did not fix her attention on Christ's garment but looked to the saving power of Christ. Indeed, as if he wished to refute that error, Christ will soon bear witness that power went out from himself, and so he claims for himself alone all the glory of this miracle. Setting aside, then, the inventions of superstitious men, let us imitate this woman in this: that we too touch that garment of Christ, in which he once lived clothed on earth, and which he carried with him into heavenly glory.
