This garment is human nature, which he took from the Virgin mother, and which can be touched by faith alone, because through it we are united to him, so that he is in us and we in him. Therefore all who believe that the Son of God became man for our sake, and did those things which were necessary for the redemption of the human race, and now bestows on us from heaven a sure salvation, these truly touch him, and they will feel that life is obtained for them by that touch.

units.la: Facit huc postrema huius historiæ pars, qua narratur, vt Christus fidem mulieris in lucem pro traxerit, & quam obtinuerat salutem sua promissione confirmarit. Quærit illico, Quis est qui me tetigit? Mirabilis quæstio, & quæ discipulis quoq; absurda atq; superuacanea visa est, cum eû hinc inde à turba premi & coartari viderent. Sed nō tangebant illi Christum, quatenus salubriter tangi potest, vt nec Iudas eū manducauit, cùm bucellam ex ipsius manu sumptam comedisset. Nam vt sola fide eius corpus manducatur & sanguis bibitur ad vitam: sic sola fide tangitur, vt nobis salutifer fiat. Et huius nouum spectime mulier praebet. Etsi enim novo timore perculsa tremeret, non tamen de illius bonitate desperat, sed ad pedes eius supplex procidens rem omnem coram toto populo ex ordine narrat. Fuit ergo hic pius timor, quem & partae salutis cognitio & Christi maiestas illi extorsit, & idem confessionem parit: quae nisi accedat, fides in nobis nulla est. Nam si confessus fuerus ore tuo Dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo (inquit Paulus) quod Deus illum excitavit a mortuis, servaberis. Sunt autem confessionis fidei partes duae: altera, qua nostram indignitatem & peccata fatemur: altera, qua Dei gratiam & salutis gratuitae beneficium nobis in Christo exhibitum praedicamus. Quae duo quicunque vere agnoscunt & fatentur, ij & Deo grati sunt ex animo, & vitam omnem ad illius nutum componunt.
units.tr: The final part of this story bears on this point, in which it is told how Christ drew the woman's faith into the light and by his promise confirmed the salvation she had obtained. Immediately he asks: "Who is it that touched me?" It is a remarkable question, and it seemed absurd and pointless even to the disciples, since they saw him being pressed and crowded on every side by the crowd. But they did not touch Christ in the way in which he can be touched to salvation, just as Judas did not eat him, although he had eaten the morsel taken from his hand. For just as his body is eaten and his blood drunk unto life by faith alone, so he is touched by faith alone, so that he may become saving for us. This woman offers a new example of it. For although she trembled, struck by a fresh fear, she did not despair of his goodness, but falling down suppliant at his feet, she recounted the whole matter in order before the whole people. So this was a godly fear, which both the knowledge of the salvation obtained and the majesty of Christ wrung from her, and the same fear produces confession; and where confession is absent, there is no faith in us. For Paul says: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved." There are two parts to the confession of faith: the one, by which we acknowledge and confess our unworthiness and our sins; the other, by which we proclaim God's grace and the benefit of free salvation offered to us in Christ. Whoever truly acknowledges and confesses these two things is pleasing to God from the heart, and orders his whole life according to his will.

units.la: Porro totius historiae fructum ipse Christus exponit, mulieri dicens: Confide fili, fides tua te servavit, Vade cum pace. Primo consolatur trepidantem, & praesenti animo esse iubet: ut quo efficacior fit consolatio, filiam dicit. Verissime ergo a Ioanne dictum est, Dei filios fieri eos, qui Christum fide apprehendunt. Neminem ergo vel indignitas propria, vel fidei infirmitas terreat, sed accedamus ad Christum, qui nos pro filijs Dei & pro fratribus suis agnoscet, neque fui iudicij rigore in nos utetur. Deinde salutis causam indicat, fide. Exiuerat quidem ex ipso virtus illa salutifica, sed nihil haec profuisset mulieri, nisi eam fides illius apprehendisset. Quoad ergo nos, fides medium illud est, quod nos Christi simul & bonorum eius omnium participes reddit: & ideo nos sola fide iustificari & servari Apostoli docent. Quam doctrinam ipse Christus in praesenti confirmat. Nam non contentus dixisse, Fides tua te servavit, postremo addit: Vade cum pace. Loquitur autem de pace animarum, quam iustificati ex fide (ut Paulus ait) habemus apud Deum. Ita vero salutis certam facit, ne in posterum ullis tentationum fluctibus se superari patiatur. At quia in huius exemplo eam, quae omnibus communis est, salutis rationem Spiritus sanctus adumbrat, nobis haec dici putemus, & proinde salutis nostrae certi ambulemus in pace illa, qua nobis suae mortis merito acquisivit Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ himself sets out the fruit of the whole story, saying to the woman: "Take heart, daughter; your faith has saved you. Go in peace." First he comforts the trembling woman and bids her be of good courage; and so that the comfort may be more effective, he calls her daughter. Therefore it was said most truly by John that those who lay hold of Christ by faith become sons of God. Let no one, then, be frightened either by his own unworthiness or by the weakness of his faith, but let us come to Christ, who will acknowledge us as his sons and as his brothers, and will not use the severity of his judgement against us. Then he indicates the cause of salvation: faith. That saving power had indeed gone out from him, but it would have profited this woman nothing unless faith had laid hold of it. So far as we are concerned, faith is the means that makes us partakers both of Christ and of all his good things; and therefore the Apostles teach that we are justified and saved by faith alone. Christ himself confirms this doctrine in the present passage. For not content with saying, "Your faith has saved you," he finally adds: "Go in peace." He speaks of the peace of souls, which we who are justified by faith have before God (as Paul says). In this way he makes her certain of her salvation, so that from now on she will not allow herself to be overcome by any waves of temptation. And since in this example the Holy Spirit sketches out the way of salvation that is common to all, let us take these words as addressed to us, and so let us walk, certain of our salvation, in that peace which Jesus Christ has won for us by the merit of his death, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 84.

units.la: Adhuc eo loquente, venit quidam a praefecto Synagogae, dicens ei: Mortua est filia tua, ne vexa magistrum. Iesus autem hoc audito respondit ei: Ne metue, crede solummodo, & servabitur. Ingressus vero domum, non permisit ingredi quenquam, nisi Petrum & Iacobum & Ioannem, & patrem ac matrem puellae. Flebant autem omnes & plangebant eam. Ipse vero dixit: Ne flete, non est mortua, sed dormit. Et deridebant eum quod scirent esse mortuam. Ipse vero eiectis foras omnibus, & prehensa manu eius clamavit, dicens: Puella, surge. Et reversus est spiritus eius, ac surrexit illico: & ipse praecepit ut ei daretur cibus. Et obstupuerunt parentes eius, ipse vero praecepit eis, ut nulli dicerent quod factum fuerat.
units.tr: While he was still speaking, someone came from the ruler of the synagogue and said to him: "Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Master." But Jesus, hearing this, answered him: "Do not be afraid; only believe, and she will be saved." When he came into the house, he allowed no one to enter except Peter and James and John, and the girl's father and mother. Everyone was weeping and wailing for her. But he said: "Do not weep; she is not dead, but sleeping." And they laughed at him, because they knew she was dead. But he put them all outside, took her by the hand and called out, saying: "Girl, arise." And her spirit returned, and she rose at once; and he ordered that she be given food. Her parents were astonished, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

units.la: Miraculorum Domini nostri Iesu Christi hic finis & scopus est, ut discamus ipsum esse humani generis servatorem, & salutis eius merito partae per fidem in ipsum participes fiamus. Elucet autem in hoc admirabilis Dei bonitas, qui Filium suum non solum promissionibus amplissimis & evidentibus veterum prophetarum oraculis, sed operibus quoque miraculosis commendari voluit, ut & melius ipse agnoscatur, & nos ad illum amplectendum efficacius excitemur. Debet hic iterum quoque miraculi usus nobis esse, quod in praesenti narratur: in quo multa concurrunt, quae Christi cum bonitatem vere paternam tum divinam potentiam nobis commendant. Agitur enim hic de puella, non morbo aliquo graviori detenta, sed mortua, quam ex mortis faucibus in vitam restituisse oportuit: qui conatus humanae rationi non modo impossibilis, sed ridiculus quoque videtur. Et si huius patrem Iairum spectes, qui tantum beneficium postulavit, non pauca occurrent, quae illo indignum fuisse docebunt. Nam quoad conditionem, Synagogae praefectus sive antistes fuit, quem hominum ordinem Christo infensissimum fuisse constat. Et quamvis Christi opem imploret, fide tamen dubia, aut saltem infirma admodum praeditus fuit. Adfe tamen venientem, & cum infirmitate illa fidei luctantem non reijcit ille, sed mira facilitate se ei accommodans, illum domũ versus sequitur, consolationibus pijs subleuat, & inter eundum fidem illius nouo miraculo (vt nuper audiuimus) confirmat, & tandem filiam modò defunctam vitæ restituens, se vitæ simul & mortis Dominum esse testatur, qui in ipsa etiam morte seruare, & ex inferis quoq; suos reducere possit. Debet igitur historia hæc sic à nobis considerari, vt cogitemus in ea generalem doctrinam siue consolationem proponi, quæ nobis semper ob oculos versetur, quando tentationes graviores surgunt. Et huc in primis seruiet huius loci diligens consideratio.
units.tr: This is the end and purpose of the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ: that we learn that he is the Saviour of the human race, and that through faith in him we become partakers of the salvation he has merited. In this the wonderful goodness of God shines forth, for he willed that his Son be commended not only by the most ample and clear promises in the oracles of the ancient prophets, but also by miraculous works, so that he might be recognised the better and we might be roused more effectively to embrace him. The use of the miracle now related ought to be useful to us again, for in it many things come together which commend to us both the truly fatherly goodness and the divine power of Christ. For here the matter concerns a girl held not by some grave illness but dead, whom he had to restore to life from the jaws of death; an effort which seems not only impossible to human reason but even ridiculous. And if you look at her father Jairus, who asked for so great a benefit, many things will come to mind which will show that he was unworthy of it. As to his rank, he was the ruler or head of the synagogue, a class of men known to have been most hostile to Christ. And although he implores Christ's help, he had a faith that was doubtful, or at least very weak. Yet when he came to him, struggling with that weakness of faith, Christ did not reject him; rather, adapting himself to him with remarkable gentleness, he follows him homewards, lifts him up with pious consolations, and along the way confirms his faith by a new miracle (as we heard recently). Finally, by restoring to life the daughter who had just died, he testifies that he is the Lord of both life and death, who can save even in death itself and lead his own back from the dead. This story must therefore be considered by us in such a way that we think a general teaching or consolation is set out in it, one that should always be before our eyes whenever heavier temptations arise. And a careful consideration of this passage will serve especially for this purpose.

units.la: Vbi primùm occurrit noua & grauissima tentatio, qua Iairi fides rursus oppugnata fuit, cùm iam spem aliquam ex præcedenti miraculo concepisse videretur. Etenim iam ante illam vacillauisse audiuimus, et ideo Christum festinanter domum suam deducere cupiebat. Intercesserat tamen alia mora, quæ illi haud dubiè molestissima fuit, quando omnis mora longissima nobis videtur, quæ nostri animi desideria vel minimum differt. Interea moritur filia, & veniunt nuntij, qui non modò mortem eius nuntiant, sed insuper omnem spem restitutionis illi negant, quando monent, ne porrò Christum fatiget, qui prius opem laturus esse videbatur. Est autem hæc sors sanctorum, vt nouis in singula momenta tentationibus exerceantur, neq; illis inducias longas permittit Satan, qui ex nostra perditione maximam voluptatem capere consueuit. Et quamuis non ignoret, electorum fidem omnino euerti non posse, iucundum tamen illi est, si eos aliqua ex parte terreri & labascere videat. Permittit autem id Deus, partim vt nos exerceat, & ad opem eius implorandam accendat; partim vt in nostra infirmitate ipsius virtus & gratia magis illustretur. Et huc referri debent exempla sanctissimorum hominum, quæ in scripturis occurrunt, & qualia quotidie in illis cernimus, qui Dei vocationem sequuntur, & eius voluntati se accommodant. Si quid ergo huius sentimus, minimè nos desperare decet, neq; aliud facere aut dicere, quod cum nostra professione minus conueniat.
units.tr: Here we meet a new and most grievous temptation, by which Jairus' faith was again assailed, when he seemed already to have conceived some hope from the preceding miracle. For we have heard that he had wavered even before, and therefore he was eager to lead Christ quickly to his home. Yet another delay intervened, which was no doubt most troublesome to him, since every delay seems very long to us when it postpones, even a little, the desires of our mind. Meanwhile the daughter dies, and messengers come who not only announce her death but also deny all hope of her restoration, when they advise him not to trouble Christ any further, who had seemed about to bring help. Now this is the lot of the saints: they are exercised by new temptations at every moment, and Satan, who usually takes the greatest pleasure in our ruin, does not grant them long truces. And although he does not fail to know that the faith of the elect cannot be utterly overthrown, it is nonetheless pleasing to him if he sees them terrified and wavering in some respect. God permits this partly to exercise us and to kindle us to implore his help, and partly so that in our weakness his power and grace may be the more clearly displayed. To this must be referred the examples of the most holy men which occur in the Scriptures, and such as we daily see in those who follow God's calling and submit themselves to his will. If we therefore feel anything of this kind, we ought by no means to despair, nor to do or say anything that is less in keeping with our profession.

units.la: Et hîc mihi non parua laude dignus esse videtur Iairus, cuius animum etsi nuntium hoc de filiæ obitu haud dubiè grauissimè vulnerarit, non tamen in muliebrem eiulatum effunditur, neq; gestibus indecoris doloris impatientiam prodit, multò minus Christum ob momm factam accusat, aut mulieri, quæ moræ causa fuerat, conuiciatur: vt ferè solent, qui nullo veræ pietatis sensu tanguntur: sed intra animum suum dolorem premit, & (vt mox dicetur) Christo se ipsi instituendum præbet. Debent hoc in primis facere Christiani homines, ne ab iis vincantur, qui etsi futuræ resurrectionis spem nullam habuerunt, suorum tamen obitus tulere patienter. De Romano quodam legitur, quòd cùm filij mortem resciuisset, præsenti animo responderit: Equidem sciebam me mortalem genuisse. Dauid autem cùm in filij morbo letali se ieiuniis & precibus asiduis afflixisset, vbi mortuum esse audiuit, mox corpus abluit & vnxit atque mutata veste adorauit Dominum, inde cibum sumpsit, & tam subitæ atque insolitæ mutationis causam quærentibus seruis, dixit: Viuente adhuc puero ieiunauì ac fleui, sic cogitans, Quis scit si misereatur mei Deus, vt puer superstes maneat? nunc autem cùm sit mortuus, quid ieiunarem? num potero eum reuocare vltra? ego vado ad eum, ipse non redibit ad me. Quanto autem sapientior fuit Dauid Solone, qui cùm inter Græciæ sapientes primo loco numeretur, in filij morte eum se præbuit, vt nihil à quoquam stultius dici potuerit. Cùm enim à quodam moneretur, vt luctui parceret, quia nihil proficeret, respondit: At propter hoc lachrymor, quia nihil proficio. O stultum & delirum hominem, qui quasi nouum quid & insolens filio accidisset, plorauit, & lachrymis inutilibus indulgendum esse putauit, cùm de vera consolatione potius cogitare deberet. Atqui illum imitantur hodie multi ex Christiani nominis professoribus, qui suorum funera immodico fletu prosequuntur, & animi dolorem studiose fouent, atque iniuram sibi fieri arbitrantur, si qui ipsis consolationē adhibeant. Prudentius multò Lycij olim fastitarunt, qui in funeribus vestem muliebrem sumebant, vt cultus aut habitus deformitate commoti maturius mœrorem deponerent.
units.tr: Here Jairus seems worthy of no small praise. Although this news of his daughter's death undoubtedly wounded him most grievously, he did not pour himself out in womanish wailing, nor betray impatience in his grief by unseemly gestures, much less accuse Christ of the delay or revile the woman who had caused the delay, as those usually do who are moved by no sense of true piety. Instead he holds his sorrow down within his soul and (as will be said shortly) offers himself to be taught by Christ. Christian people ought especially to do this, lest they be surpassed by those who, although they had no hope of a future resurrection, nevertheless bore the deaths of their own with patience. It is read of a certain Roman that, when he learned of his son's death, he answered with presence of mind: "Indeed, I knew that I had begotten a mortal." And David, when he had afflicted himself with fasting and constant prayer during his son's deadly illness, as soon as he heard that the boy was dead, at once washed and anointed himself, changed his garments, worshipped the Lord, and then took food. When the servants asked the cause of so sudden and unusual a change, he said: "While the child was still alive I fasted and wept, thinking, Who knows whether God will have mercy on me so that the child may remain alive? But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him; he will not return to me." How much wiser David was than Solon, who, although he is counted first among the wise men of Greece, showed himself in his son's death in such a way that nothing more foolish could have been said by anyone. For when someone advised him to spare his grief, since it accomplished nothing, he replied: "But that is exactly why I weep, because I accomplish nothing." O foolish and deranged man, who wept as if something new and strange had happened to his son, and thought that one should indulge in useless tears, when he ought rather to have been thinking of true consolation! Yet many today among those who profess the Christian name imitate him: they follow their dead with immoderate weeping, cherish their sorrow with care, and think themselves wronged if anyone offers them consolation. The Lycians of old were far more prudent, who at funerals put on women's clothing, so that, moved by the ugliness of their dress, they might lay aside their mourning the sooner.

units.la: Quia tamen nos non saxeos natura creauit, & naturale est dilectissimorum hominum obitu commoueri, Christus Iairo mox consolationem adhibet, qua & se eorum curam habere docet, qui in luctu aut mœrore iusto versantur, & nos simul omnes officij admonet, vt secundum apostoli præceptum condoleamus dolentibus, & eorum mœrorem pijs consolationibus subleuemus. Quæ autem consolatio illa est, qua Iairum dolore consternatum & in fide titubantē Christus confirmat? Ne metuë
units.tr: Yet since nature did not make us of stone, and it is natural to be moved by the death of those we love most, Christ at once offers consolation to Jairus. By this he shows that he takes care of those who are in mourning or in genuine grief, and at the same time reminds all of us of our duty: according to the apostle's precept, we should grieve with those who grieve and relieve their sorrow with pious consolations. But what is that consolation by which Christ strengthens Jairus, overcome with grief and wavering in faith? "Do not be afraid"

units.la: 2.Sam.12. (inquit) crede solùmodo, et seruabitur. Sùt haec verba diligenter nobis consideranda. Primò metuere prohibet, & causam addit, quòd filia saluam & viuâ acceptura sit. Atqui vere mortua fuisse, omnes circumstantiæ docent. Ergo neq; vita neq; mors nos separare potest ab ea salute, cuius nobis author est Christus. Nàm si viuamus, Domino viuimus: sin verò moriamur, Domino morimur. Et qui Iesum excitauit à mortuis, is viuificabit etiam mortalia corpora nostra per inhabitantem eius spiritum in nobis. Est haec omnium efficacissima consolatio, quà in funeribus in primis vtendum esse, Paulus in priori ad Thes. docet. Nam quod Christus in præsenti de Iairi filia loquitur, hoc alibi de omnibus nobis pronunciat, quòd à morte in vitam transeamus, olim corporibus quoq; resuscitandi, cùm ipse venerit ad iudicandu viuos & mortuos. At docet simul, quid nos facere oporteat, vt tanto bono fruamur. Crede solummodo, inquit. Solam ergo fidem requirit, vt ostendat in ipso neq; virtute neq; seruandi voluntatem defore, modò illam Iairus admittat. Et sanè nō aliud medium est, quo salutifica, quæ se in Christo nobis offert, Dei virtutem apprehendamus, præter vnam fidem, quæ cor nostra spe certa dilatat & supra cælos evehit, vt diuinæ bonitatis thesauros pleno sinu recipiant. Est hîc probè obseruandū, quòd in re omnium difficillima, & quæ non vires modò humanas, sed omnem quoq; humani ingenij captū excedebat, tam diserte solius fidei Christus meminit. Nimium ergo proterui & impudentes sunt, qui nos hodie ridēt, quòd sola fide homine iustificari et seruari docemus: quasi verò impossibile sit Deo, quod nobis impossibile videtur. Quin Christum audiant alibi dicentem, Omnia possibilia sunt credenti. Quapropter minimè timendum est nobis, ne credendo modū excedamus, vbi de voluntate Dei nobis ex Verbo eius constat. Vt enim bonitas Dei inexhausta & æterna, sic eiusdem potentia inuicta est. In fide ergo promissionum illius consolationē queramus, si quando duriora certamina nobis incumbunt. Qui enim Iairo dixit: Ne metuas, crede solummodo, & seruabitur filia tua: idē nobis quoq; omnibus dicit: Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. Ego sum resurrectio et vita: qui credit in me, etiam si mortuus fuerit, viuet. Item: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed bono animo estote, ego vici mundū. Et rursus: Ne timeas pusille grex, nā complacitum est Patri vestro dare vobis regnum. Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem seculi, &c.
units.tr: (he says) "only believe, and she will be saved." These words must be carefully considered by us. First, he forbids fear and gives the reason: the daughter will receive salvation and be alive. Yet all the circumstances show that she was truly dead. Therefore neither life nor death can separate us from that salvation of which Christ is the author. For if we live, we live to the Lord; and if we die, we die to the Lord. And he who raised Jesus from the dead will also quicken our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us. This is the most effective of all consolations, and it is above all to be used at funerals, as Paul teaches in his first letter to the Thessalonians. For what Christ says now about Jairus' daughter, he declares elsewhere about all of us: that we pass from death to life, and that at some time we shall also be raised in body, when he comes to judge the living and the dead. At the same time he teaches what we must do to enjoy so great a good: "Only believe," he says. He therefore requires only faith, to show that in him there will be neither lack of power nor lack of will to save, provided Jairus admits it. Indeed there is no other means by which we may lay hold of the saving power of God that offers itself to us in Christ, apart from faith alone, which enlarges our hearts with a sure hope and lifts them above the heavens, so that they may receive the treasures of divine goodness with full hands. Here it must be carefully observed that in a matter most difficult of all, one which exceeded not only human strength but every grasp of human understanding, Christ so plainly mentions faith alone. Therefore those are too insolent and shameless who laugh at us today because we teach that man is justified and saved by faith alone, as if what seems impossible to us were impossible to God. Let them rather hear Christ saying elsewhere: "All things are possible to him who believes." Wherefore we need by no means fear that we go beyond measure in believing, when we know from his Word what the will of God is. For as the goodness of God is inexhaustible and eternal, so his power is unconquered. Therefore let us seek consolation in faith in his promises, if at any time harder conflicts press upon us. For he who said to Jairus, "Do not be afraid, only believe, and your daughter will be saved," says the same to all of us: "He who believes in me has eternal life." "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he dies, will live." Again: "In the world you will have tribulation, but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." And again: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," and so on.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad miraculi descriptionem, quam hoc ordine Lucas proponit. Primò de testibus agit, quos Christus adhibuit. Seclusit is vniuersam populi multitudinem, quæ ipsum hucusq; secuta fuerat, in qua pleriq; indigni erant, qui ad tantæ rei spectaculum admitterentur; & exigebat hoc ipsum tempora ratio, cùm hora illa glorificationis nondum adesset. Neq; etiam miraculo aliquid decebat, cùm postea viuam et saluam viderent eam, de cuius morte certum nuntium ad patrem detulerant. Et aliàs quoq; Christum cauisse scimus, ne quid ad ostentationē faceret. Ideo ex discipulis quoq; domesticis tres solos deligit, qui ad rei testimonium sufficere poterant: & illis contingit puellæ parentes, ad quos res maximè pertinebat. Docet autem locus iste, inter germanos Christi discipulos non omnes in eodem dignitatis gradu esse constitutos, sed pro donorum diuersitate alios aliis negotijs destinari. Quæ omnia cùm ipse Deus dispensset, cuius iudicia iusta sunt, nullus inter eos æmulationi locus esse debet, neq; decet, vt quis absq; certa Dei vocatione rebus grauioribus se immiscear. Quod vt in ecclesia, sic in repub. quoq; obseruari debet, alioqui æmulatio cæca simultates & rerum omnium confusionem pariet.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the description of the miracle, which Luke sets out in this order. First he deals with the witnesses whom Christ took. He shut out the whole crowd of people who had followed him up to that point, many of whom were unworthy to be admitted to the sight of so great a thing. The reason of the occasion also demanded this, since that hour of glorification had not yet come. Nor was it fitting for the miracle to be seen by those who had earlier brought word of her death to her father, and who would afterwards see her alive and well. We know that Christ also took care in other cases not to make any show of his works. So he chose from among his own disciples only three, who were sufficient to bear witness to the event, and he admitted the girl's parents, whom the matter chiefly concerned. This passage teaches that among Christ's own disciples not all were set in the same rank of dignity, but that, according to the diversity of their gifts, some were assigned to some tasks and others to others. Since God himself arranged all these things, whose judgments are just, there should be no room for rivalry among them, and it is not fitting for anyone to thrust himself into weightier affairs without a sure calling from God. This should be observed in the Church, and in the commonwealth too. Otherwise blind rivalry will bring forth factions and the confusion of all things.

units.la: Porrò domum ingressus familiam omnem in luctu esse vidit, & (vt Matthæus annotauit) tibicines quoq; inuenit, quos in funeribus olim apud gentes adhibitos fuisse scimus. Est ergo hoc quoq; argumentum corruptæ apud Iudæos religionis, quando contra Dei legem funera gentilitio more duxerunt, cùm vel ipsa mortis mentio eos fidei in Deum & sui erga hunc officij admonere deberet. Idem hodie de Pontificiæ religionis sectatoribus dicere possumus, qui cū Christiani dici & haberi velint, in ipso tamen mortis articulo atq; funeribus ea faciunt, quæ satis docent, ipsos ex Iudaismo et gentilismo vnum veluti chaos superstitionum ineptissimarum conflauisse. At quia de his alibi diximus, nunc eadem repetere non est opus. Obseruemus autem, totum hunc funeris apparatum, qui iam in procinctu fuit, ad miraculi certitudinem et virtutis Christi amplificationem facere. Nam nisi vere mortuam esse sciuissent, nequaquam locus datus esset ijs, qui funus deducere debebant, neq; etiam familia tota in luctu fuisset occupata. Ita Christus pro æterna sua sapientia ijs etiam ad gloriam Dei & nostræ fidei confirmationem bene abutitur, quæ à nobis ineptè, imò impiè aut superstitiosè fiunt. Ne tan
units.tr: Furthermore, when he entered the house he saw the whole household in mourning, and (as Matthew noted) he also found flute-players, whom we know were once employed at funerals among the Gentiles. This too is evidence of the religion of the Jews being corrupted, since they conducted funerals in the manner of the Gentiles, contrary to God's law, when even the very mention of death ought to have reminded them of their faith in God and of their duty towards him. We can say the same today of the followers of the Papist religion, who, though they wish to be called and held Christians, nevertheless at the very point of death and at funerals do those things which sufficiently show that they have mixed together from Judaism and paganism a kind of chaos of most foolish superstitions. But since we have spoken of these matters elsewhere, there is no need to repeat the same things now. Let us observe, however, that this whole funeral display, which was already under way, served to make the miracle certain and to magnify the power of Christ. For unless they had known that she was truly dead, the bearers who were to carry out the funeral would never have been given room, nor would the whole household have been occupied in mourning. Thus Christ, in his eternal wisdom, makes good use even of those things which we do foolishly, or rather impiously or superstitiously, for the glory of God and the confirmation of our faith. Yet lest

units.la: Funeris apparatus ad miraculi certitudinem facit.
units.tr: The display of the funeral serves to make the miracle certain.

units.la: Ne tamen morem hunc probare videatur, tibicines quoq; domo eijcit, domesticis vero consolationem adhibet. Ne flete (inquit) non est mortua, sed dormit. Non autem luctum aut lachrymas simpliciter prohibet, quas nisi modum excedant in funeribus concessas esse supra diximus: sed nunc luctu aut lachrymis minime opus esse docet, eo quod filia no mortua sit, sed dormiat. Quod etsi Christus pro ratione resuscitationis, quae mox secuta erat, dixerit: potest tamen ex ea generali consolatio & doctrina peti, qua nos aduersus mortis terrores confirmemus. Revera enim mors omnibus est, & qui illa soluti hinc migrant, ij non pereunt aut moriuntur, sed obdormiunt. Ut enim post diurnos labores corpora nostra somni beneficio recreantur, & post horas aliquot expergefacta ad opus redeunt: ita post emensum huius vitae curriculum, quod laborum & curarum plenum est, animae nostrae ad beata immortalitatis sedes colliguntur, corpora vero requiescunt a laboribus suis, ut olim cum magnus ille dies Domini illuxerit, ad vitae caelestis & aeterni gaudij possessionem resurgant. Vbi rursum sapientum huius seculi stultitia arguitur, qui morte totum hominem aboleri arbitrantur & proinde consolationè certam ac solidam habere non possunt. Celebres prae aliis sunt ex horum numero Gymnosophistae, quibus cum Alexander Macedo quaestionem propositisset: Vtrum plures sunt vivi an mortui? responderunt, Vivi, eo quod mortui no amplius extent. At si non extant amplius, certe perierint oportet, & cum ijsdem perijt spes omnis, quam in vivis fouerunt. Quam vero misera est haec sapientia, quae cum breui & laborum pleno huius vitae curriculo finitur? Nos ergo Christum audiamus, qui mortuos dormire ait, & alibi Deum Abrahami & Isaaci & Iacobi Deum esse testatur, eo quod illi, etsi quoad corpus obierint, animabus tamen viuant, & olim corporibus quoq; sint resurrecturi.
units.tr: Yet lest he seem to approve this custom, he also drives the flute-players out of the house, and gives comfort to the household. "Do not weep," he says, "she is not dead, but sleeps." He does not simply forbid mourning or tears, which, as we said above, are allowed at funerals so long as they do not exceed due measure. But he now teaches that there is no need for mourning or tears, because the girl is not dead but asleep. Although Christ said this with regard to the resurrection that was about to follow, a general comfort and teaching may nonetheless be drawn from it, by which we may strengthen ourselves against the terrors of death. For death indeed comes to all, and those who depart hence released from it do not perish or die, but fall asleep. For just as after the day's labours our bodies are refreshed by the benefit of sleep, and after some hours are awakened and return to work, so after the course of this life, which is full of toil and cares, our souls are gathered to the blessed seats of immortality, while our bodies rest from their labours, to rise again when that great day of the Lord dawns, to possess the heavenly life and eternal joy. Here again the folly of the wise men of this age is refuted, who think that the whole man is destroyed by death, and therefore cannot have a sure and solid consolation. Among these, the Gymnosophists are especially famous. When Alexander the Macedonian asked them the question, "Which are more numerous, the living or the dead?", they answered, "The living, because the dead no longer exist." But if they no longer exist, they must certainly have perished, and with them has perished every hope that they had cherished for the living. How miserable indeed is that wisdom which ends with the brief and toil-filled course of this life! Let us, then, listen to Christ, who says that the dead sleep, and who elsewhere declares himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, because they, though as to the body they have died, nevertheless live in their souls, and one day are to rise again in their bodies also.

units.la: Sed ridet Christi doctrinam mundus hic, & in primis quidem ij, qui sub religionis praetextu ex funeribus lucrum capiunt, qui in praesenti per tibicines iStos adumbrantur. In quorum numero primatum facile habent sacrificuli & Monachi, qui dum alij mortuos suos lugent, ipsi suaviter cantillant & concinuantur: nunquam profecto hoc cum tanto mundi totius ludibrio facturi, si vel caelos vel inferos esse crederent, aut de resurrectione mortuorum spem quantulamcunque animo suo foue-rent. At magno illis constabit ludus iste. Vt enim in praesenti illos simul omnes eiecit Dominus, ita olim quoq; se a regni caelorum consortio excludi sentient, quando alij cum Christo viuent & regnabunt, qui illius promissis crediderunt. In praesenti autem reipsa istorum risus atq; ludibria Christus confutat. Nam prehensa manu puellae, alta voce clamat: Puella, surge. Nec remora redit illi s eius spiritus, & surgit illa, ut qui ex somno expergefiunt. Iubet autem illi cibum dari Christus, ut omnem dubitationem ex parentum animis eximat, quos interea miserè cruciatos fuisse non est dubium. Ne ergo spectrum aliquod se videre putarent, eodem argumento nunc ipsi miraculo fidem fecit, quo postea sui quoque corporis resurrectionem asseruit. Et quamvis occulta diuinitatis virtute istud omne factum sit, vocem tamen altius extollit, ut offendat se verbum illud Dei esse, cuius vir tute olim omnis haec mundi machina ex nihilo producta sit: & ad quam olim resurrecturi sint omnes, qui ante nouissimum suum aduentum morientur. Est ergo Christus vita & mortis dominus, neq; alicui mirum aut impossibile videri debet, quod illius virtute olim mortuos excitandos esse docemus, quando cum in mortali carne ageret, eius vocem vivifica sua virtute ad mortuos usque penetrauisse constat. Vt vero haec nostrae resurrectionis spem confirmant: ita totum nostrae redemptionis negotium euidentissimè adumbrant, cuius idem Christus nobis vnicus author est, vt in Marco nostro diximus.
units.tr: But this world mocks the doctrine of Christ, and especially those who make gain from funerals under the pretext of religion, who are foreshadowed at present by these flute-players. Among their number the priests and monks easily hold the first place. While others mourn their dead, they themselves sing and chant sweetly. They would never do this to the mockery of the whole world if they believed that there were either heaven or hell, or if they cherished in their minds any hope, however slight, of the resurrection of the dead. But this game will cost them dearly. For just as the Lord has now cast them all out together, so one day they will feel themselves shut out from fellowship in the kingdom of heaven, when others live and reign with Christ, those who believed his promises. Yet in the present case Christ in fact refutes their laughter and mockery. For taking the girl by the hand, he calls out with a loud voice, "Girl, arise." Nor does her spirit return to her in any delay, and she rises as those do who wake from sleep. Christ orders that food be given to her, so that he may remove all doubt from the minds of the parents, who without doubt had been tormented in the meantime. Lest they should think they were seeing some phantom, he gave assurance of the miracle by the same argument by which he afterwards asserted the resurrection of his own body. And although all this was done by the hidden power of the divinity, he nevertheless raises his voice, so that it may be shown that the word is that of God, by whose power this whole machine of the world was once produced out of nothing, and to which all who die before his last coming are one day to rise. Christ, then, is the lord of life and death, and it ought not seem strange or impossible to anyone that we teach that the dead are to be raised one day by his power, since it is evident that when he was in mortal flesh his voice, by its life-giving power, reached even to the dead. But just as these things confirm our hope of resurrection, so they very clearly foreshadow the whole business of our redemption, of which the same Christ is our only author, as we said in our commentary on Mark.

units.la: Caeterum rei nouitate perculsi parentes puellae stupent, quod illis ex carnis infirmitate accidit. Et pium est, ut singularia Dei opera cum timore obseruemus. Prohibet autem Christus, ne cui dicant quod factum fuerat. Quod praeceptum mihi temporarium fuisse videtur. Noluit enim ille sua miracula perpetuo silentio sepeliri. Proderat autem istis, ut rem tanti momenti diligentius secum ex penderent, & in fide vera confirmarentur, priusquam illam temere apud quosvis diuulgarent. Et si-mul cauendum erat, ne miraculo in filia vnigenita & dilectissima adito insolentius superbirent. Ad haec non tam a sacerdotibus periculum erat, qui eius operibus irritabantur, quam a populo, cuius infinita multitudo confluxerat, ne quid in Christo honorando tentaret, quod cum seditioso rerum nouandarum studio coniunctum esse videretur. Quid enim non facturi erant hoc miraculo cognito, qui
units.tr: Moreover, the parents of the girl were astonished and struck dumb by the strangeness of the event, as is natural for human weakness of the flesh. And it is right that we should observe the singular works of God with fear. Christ, however, forbids them to tell anyone what had happened. This command seems to me to have been temporary. For he did not wish his miracles to be buried in perpetual silence. But it was useful for these people that they should weigh such a matter of great importance more carefully among themselves, and be confirmed in true faith, before they rashly spread it abroad to whomever they met. At the same time they had to be careful not to become too proudly insolent because of a miracle wrought upon their only and most beloved daughter. Moreover, the danger came not so much from the priests, who were provoked by his works, as from the people, whose vast crowd had gathered, lest they attempt something in honouring Christ that might seem joined with a seditious desire for revolution. For what would they not have done, once this miracle became known, who

units.la: Christus ridetur. alibi illum regem facere voluerunt, cum ipsos epulo gratuito excepisset? Ita vero docet, nobis quoque in iis, quae facimus, ... rem gloriae Dei & salutis publicae quam priuati honoris rationem esse habendam. Quam enim verig officiant, qui se praecipui carnis affectu abripi patiuntur, exempla cum veteri tum quotidiana abunde docent. Iterum semper nobis ob oculos versetur miraculi istius sepius, ut Christum Iesum credamus vitae verae nobis authorem esse, & proinde huic nos totos consecremus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Christ is mocked. Did they not elsewhere want to make him king, when he had received them with a free feast? Thus indeed he teaches that we too, in what we do, ... must have regard for the glory of God and the public welfare rather than for private honour. For how truly those harm themselves who allow themselves to be swept away by a particular affection of the flesh, both ancient and daily examples abundantly teach. Let this miracle be set before our eyes again and again, so that we believe Christ Jesus to be the author of true life for us, and therefore devote ourselves wholly to him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXV.

units.la: Convocatis autem duodecim discipulis, dedit eis vim ac potestatem in omnia daemonia, & sanandi morbos. Misitque eos ut praedicarent regnum Dei, & sanarent aegrotos. Et dixit eis: Nihil sumite ad iter, neque virgas, neque peram, neque panem, neque pecuniam, neque binas tunicas habete. Et in quamcunque domum intraveritis, illic manete, & illinc exite. Et quicunque non receperint vos, exeuntes ex urbe illa, etiam pulverem a pedibus vestris excutite in testimonium adversus eos. Exeuntes igitur obibant singulos vicos, evangelizantes & sanantes ubique.
units.tr: Then Jesus called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. And he said to them: Take nothing for the journey, neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money, and do not have two tunics. Whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there. And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town, shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them. So they set out and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

units.la: Vidimus hucusque multa & praeclara opera Iesu Christi, quibus abunde demonstratum est eum ideo in mundum venisse, ut miseros nos ex peccati laqueo, & diaboli potestate redimeret. At ne quis existimaret, hoc eius beneficium ad paucos modo pertinere, nunc discipulos emittit, qui ipsum passim per totam Iudaeam praedicent, & homines excitent ad excipiendam eam salutem, cuius ipse nobis author atque mediator est. Quo loco ante omnia observari debet ipsius fides & industria, qua instar optimi pastoris nihil eorum omisit, quibus dispersae illae gentis Iudaicae oves iterum colligi atque servari poterant. Cuius industriae insigne argumentum est, quod neque populi istius ingratitudine & contumacia se ab instituto abstterreri passus est, neque discipulis charissimis pepercit, quo minus hos quoque laboribus fatigaret in iis vocandis, quorum ingratitudinem iam tot argumentis perspectam habebat. Admonent nos ista salutis nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtingere, quando ipsi quoque non alia ratione ad illa vocamur: & proinde nostri officii esse, ut eam totis animis amplectamur, & vicissim nos quoque totos Christo mancipemus per obedientiam fidei. Porro etsi legatio ista, quae hic describitur, specialis fuerit, ut quae paucorum dierum spatio confici debebat, & certus Iudaeae finibus circumscribebatur, quos adhuc exire nefas erat, multa tamen hic continentur, quae nos de omnibus iis admonere possunt, quae ad ministerium verbi Dei & ecclesiae pertinent.
units.tr: We have so far seen many great and remarkable works of Jesus Christ, by which it has been amply shown that he came into the world to redeem us, wretched as we are, from the snare of sin and the power of the devil. But lest anyone should think that this benefit of his pertains only to a few, he now sends out disciples who are to preach him throughout all Judea and to rouse people to accept that salvation of which he himself is for us the author and mediator. Here, above all, we must notice his faith and diligence, by which, like an excellent shepherd, he omitted nothing that could gather and preserve those scattered sheep of the Jewish nation. A remarkable proof of this diligence is that he was not deterred from his purpose by the ingratitude and obstinacy of that people, nor did he spare his dearest disciples, so that he did not also wear them out with labours in calling those whose ingratitude he already knew so well from so many proofs. These things remind us that this salvation comes to us from the free mercy of God, since we ourselves are called to it in no other way. It is therefore our duty to embrace it with our whole soul, and in turn to surrender ourselves wholly to Christ through the obedience of faith. Moreover, although this commission described here was special, since it had to be carried out within a few days and was confined within the borders of Judea, which it was then unlawful to leave, yet much is contained here that can admonish us about all the things that pertain to the ministry of the Word of God and of the Church.

units.la: Occurrit inter haec primum, quod ex toto discipulorum & credentium grege, quem tunc habebat Christus, certos & delectos homines misit, quos prius peculiari vocatione ad praedicandi munus designarat: Nimirum duodecim illos, de quibus in Cap. 6. est dictum. Eo autem facto docet, non statim ad docendum idoneos esse omnes eos, qui in Christi cognitione atque fide instituti sunt. Haec enim omnibus necessaria est, qui servari volunt, neque vel postremum locum in ecclesia illis concedi debet, qui a fide sunt alieni. Ad docendi vero munus aliae insuper dotes requiruntur, quae non omnibus Christianis communes sunt: amplior nimirum & profundior mysteriorum salutis cognitio, dicendi facultas & singularis animi constantia atque fortitudo. Quibus praeterea vocationem legitimam accedere oportet, ne quis ex eorum numero sit, de quibus per Ieremiam queritur Dominus: Currebant, & non miseram eos. Seruit hoc confutandis Anabaptistarum furoribus, qui temere ad docendum prorumpunt, & Pauli loco, qui in priori ad Corinth. cap. 14. habetur, abutuntur, ut cuius in ecclesia loquendi potestatem faciant. Ergo plus illi hodie rusticis cerdonibus permissum volunt, quam prophetis & apostolis olim licuerit, quos non sine certa vocatione ad docendum prodisse constat. Sed & oscitanter nimis Pauli verba inspiciunt, qui ibidem monet, ut omnia decenter & cum ordine fiant, ut qui interpretationis dono non sunt instructi.
units.tr: Among these things, the first that occurs is that from the whole band of disciples and believers that Christ then had, he sent out certain and chosen men, whom he had earlier designated for the office of preaching by a special calling: namely those twelve of whom it was said in chapter 6. By this act he teaches that not all those who have been instructed in the knowledge and faith of Christ are at once fit to teach. For that faith is necessary for all who wish to be saved, and not even the lowest place in the Church should be granted to those who are estranged from the faith. But for the office of teaching, other gifts are required besides, which are not common to all Christians: namely a fuller and deeper knowledge of the mysteries of salvation, the ability to speak, and a singular steadiness and courage of mind. Moreover, a lawful calling must be added to these, so that no one is among those of whom the Lord complains through Jeremiah: "They ran, and I did not send them." This serves to refute the frenzies of the Anabaptists, who rashly rush forward to teach and abuse the passage of Paul in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 14, as if it gave everyone the power to speak in the Church. So they wish to permit today to common cobblers more than was ever permitted to the prophets and apostles, who, as is clear, did not come forward to teach without a definite calling. But they also read Paul's words too carelessly, for he warns in the same place that everything should be done decently and in order, and that those who lack the gift of interpretation should keep silent.

units.la: Secundo in quem finem Apostolos suos Christus miserit, indicatur: Nimirum, ut praedicarent regnum Dei. Solet ita dici Euangelium, vel potius vniuersum nostrae redemptionis negotium, quod illo praedicatur. Ratio istius nominis certa est, quod per Euangelium modus aut via traditur, qua ad regnum Dei peruenitur, & totius praedicationis finis est, ut in nobis regnet Deus, quoad in carne hac mortali viuimus, huius autem vinculo soluti in caelestis regni possessione admittamur. Et non temere Christus Euangelium hoc titulo ornare consueuit. Eo enim auditores illius admonentur, ne quid in ipso terrenum & caducum quaerant, sed in ea soli intenti sint, quae ad vitam aeternam spectant. Est autem hoc praeclarum doctrinae Euangelicae praeconium, quod regnum Dei nobis praedicat, & proinde bona illa caelestia & aeterna nobis offert, quae non solum omnes huius seculi thesauros, verumetiam omnem humani ingenij captum longe superant. Nam quae oculus non vidit, neq; auris audiuit, nec in mentem homini venerunt, ea praeparauit Deus iis, qui ipsum diligunt. Quae causa est, quod Christus Euangelium alibi thesauro & margaritae confert, cuius gratia debeamus omnia nostra diuendere. Vnde sequitur inexcusabilem & quouis supplicio dignam esse eorum ingratitudinem, qui quam illis Deus gratis offert, regni sui promissionem aspernantur. Admonet praeterea hic locus, quis ecclesiae ministris inter docendum finis aut scopus propositus esse debeat: Is nimirum, ut regnum Dei inter homines propagetur. Nam si conditionem, in qua ex Adamo nati sumus, spectes, regnum in nos habuit Satan, qui (ut Paulus monet) dira tenebrarum potestate premebat omnes, quos per peccatum in seruitutem redegerat. Sed ideo in mundum venit Dei Filius, ut diaboli opera destrueret, & Dei regnum inter homines instauraret. Huius praecones ergo cum sint quotquot Euangelium praedicant, idem hoc vnum agere debent, ut ad illud omnes homines adducant. Id autem fieri impossibile est, nisi ea demoliantur, quae ad opprimendum regnum Dei Satan excitare aut erigere solet. Ideo armis spiritualibus ministros suos Christus instruxit, quae (ut Paulus ait) in Deo valida sunt ad subuersionem munitionum, & ad demoliendam omnem sublimitatem, quae aduersus cognitionem Dei extollitur. Oppugnent ergo fortiter falsam doctrinam, superstitiones, nefarios cultus, scelera & peccandi licentiam: neque contenti sint ea aggredi, quae foris apparent, sed in ipsos hominum animos penetrent, ut illic latentem impietatem eruant. Ita olim Dei regnum prophetae praedicarunt, quorum vestigiis postea Ioannes Bap. & Apostoli omnes instiuerunt: nimirum Christi spiritu ducti, qui ipse quoque eandem docendi rationem ingressus est. Docent ista, quo loco habendi sint ministri, qui ad superstitiones conniuent, & aperte quoque sceleribus blanduntur: quorum magnus vbique est numerus hodie, inter eos maxime, qui sub Euangelij praetextu nihil praeter carnem & mundum quaerunt. At quanta quamque execrabilis eorum audacia est, qui fidis Christi praeconibus dicendi leges praescribere audent, & minaciter nimis prohibent, ne aduersus ea conciones suas instituant, quibus diaboli potestas maxime nititur, & regnum Dei impeditur?
units.tr: Second, the purpose for which Christ sent out his apostles is indicated: namely, that they should preach the kingdom of God. The gospel is commonly so named, or rather the whole business of our redemption, which is proclaimed in it. The reason for this name is clear: through the gospel is handed down the manner or way by which one comes to the kingdom of God, and the whole aim of preaching is that God may reign in us for as long as we live in this mortal flesh, and that, released from this bond, we may be admitted to possession of the heavenly kingdom. Nor did Christ rashly adorn the gospel with this title. For by it his hearers are reminded not to seek anything earthly and transitory in it, but to be intent only on those things that look to eternal life. This is indeed the splendid proclamation of the gospel doctrine, that it preaches to us the kingdom of God, and so offers us those heavenly and eternal goods which far surpass not only all the treasures of this age but also the whole grasp of human understanding. For "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him." This is why Christ elsewhere compares the gospel to a treasure and a pearl, for the sake of which we ought to sell all that we have. Hence it follows that the ingratitude of those who spurn the promise of his kingdom, which God freely offers them, is inexcusable and deserving of any punishment. This passage further admonishes what aim or goal ought to be set before the ministers of the Church in their teaching: namely, that the kingdom of God may be spread among men. For if you look at the condition in which we were born from Adam, Satan had the kingdom over us, who (as Paul warns) oppressed all those whom he had reduced to slavery through sin with the dire power of darkness. But for this reason the Son of God came into the world, to destroy the works of the devil and to restore the kingdom of God among men. Since all who preach the gospel are its heralds, they ought to pursue this one aim, that they bring all men to it. But this cannot happen unless those things are torn down which Satan is accustomed to raise up or set in place to oppress the kingdom of God. Therefore Christ equipped his ministers with spiritual weapons, which (as Paul says) are mighty through God for the overthrow of strongholds, and for the demolition of every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God. Let them therefore boldly attack false doctrine, superstitions, impious worship, crimes, and the license of sinning; and let them not be content to assail what appears outwardly, but let them penetrate into the very minds of men, so as to bring to light the impiety lurking there. So once the prophets preached the kingdom of God, and afterwards John the Baptist and all the apostles followed in their footsteps, being led by the Spirit of Christ, who himself also entered upon the same manner of teaching. These things teach us where those ministers should be placed who connive at superstitions and also openly flatter crimes; and of such there is everywhere today a great number, especially among those who under the pretext of the gospel seek nothing but the flesh and the world. But how great and how detestable is the audacity of those who dare to prescribe rules of speech to the faithful heralds of Christ, and who threaten too sternly to forbid them to direct their sermons against those things on which the power of the devil chiefly rests and by which the kingdom of God is hindered?

units.la: Sed ad tertium huius loci caput accedamus, quo missionis istius modus describitur. Ad hunc pertinet, quod Marcus binos missos fuisse scribit. Ita vero Christus infirmitati eorum consulere voluit, quos nondum perfectè institutos esse sciebat. Et est hic Dei mos, quod laborum atque periculorum socios dare solet iis, quorum opera in rebus arduis vult vti. Sic olim Moisi Aaronem fratrem collegam dedit, & virtifq; postea septuaginta seniores adiunxit, qui illos subleuarent. Et huius generis exempla passim occurrunt. Neminem ergo terreat negotiorum difficultas, ad quae à Domino vocatur. Poterit enim is facile excitare aliquos, qui nos iuuent, vel etiam nos ipsos suo spiritu armare, ut ad ea sufficiamus, quibus paulò ante eramus impares.
units.tr: But let us come to the third point of this passage, in which the manner of this sending is described. To this belongs the fact that Mark writes that they were sent out two by two. Christ wished in this way to provide for the weakness of those whom he knew were not yet fully trained. It is also God's custom to give companions in labours and dangers to those whose work he wishes to use in difficult matters. Thus once he gave Aaron his brother as colleague to Moses, and afterwards added seventy elders to both of them, to lighten their burden. Examples of this kind occur everywhere. Let no one, therefore, be frightened by the difficulty of the business to which he is called by the Lord. For he can easily raise up some to help us, or even arm us himself with his Spirit, so that we are sufficient for those tasks for which we were just before unequal.

units.la: Deinde quia Apostoli doctrinam praedicare debebant, quae illius seculi hominibus noua & insolens erat, fidem illis Christus per signa & miracula conciliat. Nam dedit eis vim & potestatem in omnia daemonia, & sanandi morbos. Fuerunt haec instar literarum testimonialium, quas vulgo Credentias vocant. Obseruabis autem potuisse Christum miraculis multo splendidioribus illos instruere: ut nimirum naturas & substantias rerum mutarent, ostentis & prodigijs insolitis quosuis terrarent: qualia olim Moses & Aaron in Aegypto fecerunt. Sed quia ad seruandum genus humanum venerat, & ut Patris gloriam proueberet, non ut inani ostentatione virtutis suae gloriam siue auram popularem venaretur, eiusmodi signa Apostolos instruere voluit, quae negotio quod agebatur, quàm optimè coueniebant. Ita enim omnes admonebantur, iam exhibitū esse femen illud mulierū, quod serpentis caput conculcare debeat, & corruptæ hominum naturam mederi, atque miseros ex morte in vitam restituere. Et hic miraculorum proprius vsus est, vt Christo & doctri-næ eius testimonium ferant, non vt in ea defixi, superstitionum materiam ex illis colligamus. Fa-ciunt hoc inepti quidam, qui dum per aliquos quid præter naturam in curandis hominum morbis aut dæmonibus profligandis factū audiunt, mox illos inuocatione & cultu diuino dignos esse iudicant. Ita vero miraculorum vsum peruertunt, & ex salutaribus noxia, ex veris falsa faciunt. Nec enim vera miracula sunt, nisi quæ veritatis doctrinam suo testimonio confirmant, & ad vnum Christum deducunt. Quæ causa est, quod posteris temporibus miracula cessarunt, cum Euangelij doctrina iam satis confirmata esset, vt alibi prolixius est dictum.
units.tr: Next, since the Apostles were to preach a doctrine that was new and strange to the people of that age, Christ won them over to the faith by signs and miracles. For he gave them power and authority over all demons and to heal diseases. These served as letters of recommendation, which are commonly called credentials. You will observe, however, that Christ could have equipped them with far more splendid miracles, to change the natures and substances of things and to terrify anyone with unusual portents and prodigies, as Moses and Aaron once did in Egypt. But because he had come to save the human race, and to advance the glory of the Father, and did not seek glory or popular applause through an empty display of his power, he chose to equip the Apostles with signs that suited well the business at hand. For by these everyone was reminded that the seed of the woman had now appeared, who was to crush the serpent's head, to heal the corrupted nature of man, and to restore wretched people from death to life. This is the proper use of miracles: to bear witness to Christ and his doctrine, not for us to fix our gaze on them and gather from them material for superstitions. Foolish people do this: when they hear that someone has done something beyond nature in curing human diseases or driving out demons, they at once judge such persons worthy of invocation and divine worship. In this way they pervert the use of miracles, and make wholesome things harmful and true things false. For those are not true miracles unless they confirm the teaching of truth by their testimony and lead people to Christ alone. This is why miracles ceased in later times, once the doctrine of the Gospel had been sufficiently confirmed, as I have said more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Quarto loco Christus Apostolos de commeatu & toto legationis ipsius appamatu admonet, in quibus Regum legati plurimum laborare solent, vt & legationes tutius obire possint, & simul principum suorum magnificentiam atque vires ostentent. Quid autem Christus, Rex regum, cui omnis potestas in cælo & in terra data est? Nil sumite (inquit) ad iter, neque virgas, neque peram, neque panem, neque pecuniam, neque binas tunicas habete. Vbi animo repetere oportet, hic non de Apostolatu perpetuo agi, cuius hora nondum aduenerat, sed de legatione paucorum dierum, quæ vt iuuum vsum tunc habebat peculiarem, ita tyrocinium quoddam erat, quo ad labores maiores præparabantur. Ergo præcepta ista partim symbolica sunt, partim ad professionem, quam tunc suscepturi erant restringi debent, in qua festinatione & celeritate erat opus. Etenim symbolicum esse, quod de virga dicitur, ex eo apparet, quòd quam hic prohibet, in Marco permittit. Vbi nemo vel Christum sibi ipsi contradixisse, vel Euangelistas in recitandis illius præceptis negligentiores & minus circunspectos fuisse putauerit: Nam si virgæ aut baculi vsum duplicem spectemus, facile hunc nodum secabimus. Prior est, quod corpori sustentando & gressibus dirigendis seruit, & quoad hunc pauperta-tem quoq; symbolum est, eò quod ditiores fere iumentis vehi & suas professiones maiori cum apparatu atque commoditate perficere solent. Quò Iacob patriarcha respiciens, vt Dei liberalitatem atque fidem commendaret, dicebat: Cum baculo meo transfiui Iordanem istum, & nunc creui in duas turmas. Alter vsus est, quod ad defensionem gestatur, & proinde cuspidibus sæpe armantur baculi isti siue scipiones, imò interdum gladios occultant. Priori sensu virgam apud Marcum permittit discipulis Christus, posteriori autem probibet in præsenti, vt nimirum admoneat, non debere ipsos de defensione ne solicitos esse, sed se totos Dei prouidentiæ committere, qui omnem iniuriam ab illis facile sit propulsurus. Altera illa de pera, pane, pecunia & binis tunicis ad festinationem pertinent, ne ds commeatu, victu & vestitu sibi parando soliciti cunctentur, sed abrupta omni mora ad iter se accingant & quod in mandatis acceperant, sedulò exequatur. Et sane, nisi hoc sensu accipiantur hæc præcepta, iam ipse Christus peccauisse dicetur, & qui loculos habuit, & commeatum frequenter per discipulos gestari passus est, vt ex quinque & septem panum miraculo appa-ret, & ex so, quod illos aliquando anxios fuisse legimus, quod obliti fuissent panes secum deferre, & c. Similiter Paulus penulā ha-buit, quam Troade reliquam voluit per Timotheum vnà cum libris atq; membranis ad se deferri. Maxime ergo audiri debent phanatici, qui præcepta ista perpetua & vniuersalia esse contendunt, ad quæ omnes ecclesiarum ministri astringi debeant. Quod perinde est, ac si quis inter cursorem, cui per equos dispositos iter quàm celerrimè conficiendum est, & regium dispensatorem discrimen nullum esse velit, quoad habitum & reliquum apparatum.
units.tr: In the fourth place, Christ instructs the apostles about their provisions and their whole equipment for the embassy. In this matter the ambassadors of kings commonly take great pains, both so that they may carry out their missions more safely and so that they may display the magnificence and power of their princes. But what did Christ, the King of kings, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, command? "Take nothing for the journey," he says, "neither staves, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money, nor have two tunics." Here we must bear in mind that this is not about a perpetual apostleship, whose hour had not yet come, but about an embassy of a few days. That embassy had its own particular use at the time, and it was a kind of apprenticeship for the greater labours for which they were being prepared. So these precepts are partly symbolic and partly must be restricted to the particular undertaking they were about to take up, which required haste and speed. That the saying about the staff is symbolic is clear from the fact that what he forbids here he permits in Mark. No one should suppose that Christ contradicted himself, or that the evangelists were careless or less exact in reporting his precepts. For if we consider the twofold use of a staff or stick, we shall easily cut this knot. The first use is that it serves to support the body and steady the steps, and in this respect too it is a symbol of poverty, since the wealthier usually travel on beasts of burden and carry out their business with more equipment and comfort. Looking to this, the patriarch Jacob, to commend God's generosity and faithfulness, said: "With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two companies." The other use is for defence, and for this reason such staves or sticks are often tipped with points, and indeed sometimes conceal swords. In the first sense Christ allows the disciples a staff in Mark; in the second sense he forbids it here, namely to admonish them that they ought not to be anxious about defence, but should commit themselves wholly to the providence of God, who will easily ward off every injury from them. The other points, about the bag, bread, money and two tunics, pertain to haste, so that they should not hesitate, anxious about procuring provisions, food and clothing for themselves, but with every delay cut short should gird themselves for the journey and diligently carry out what they had received in command. And indeed, unless these precepts are understood in this sense, Christ himself would be said to have sinned, since he had a money-box and allowed provisions to be carried often by the disciples, as appears from the miracle of the five and seven loaves, and from the fact that we read that they were at one time anxious because they had forgotten to take bread with them, and so on. Likewise Paul had a cloak, which he wished to have brought to him at Troas, along with books and parchments, through Timothy. Therefore the fanatics should be heard least of all, who insist that these precepts are perpetual and universal, and that all ministers of the churches must be bound by them. This is just as if someone were to wish there to be no difference, in dress and the rest of their equipment, between a courier, who has to complete his journey as quickly as possible by means of relay horses, and a royal steward.

units.la: Interim diligenti consideratione dignum est, quod non maiori cum splendore Apostolos suos Christus emisit. In ista enim tenuitate splendidius elucet illius maiestas & virtus planè diuina. Etsi enim inopes emittat, & quidem in medios lupos (vt Matth. 10. dicit) eosdem tamen seruauit, vt neque periculum vitæ vllum subierint, neque fame aut rerum necessariarum penuria laborarint, sicuti in vltima Cœna ipsimet fatentur. Debet ex eo generalis doctrina peti, ne solicitudine & curâ nimijs grauemur, si quid ex Dei vocatione aut mandato faciendum est. Nouit enim ille, quibus potissimum nobis opus sit, & quia fidelissimus est suorum pater, nunquam eos negliget, qui in eius seruitio diligentes fuerint. Extant huius generis exempla in multis aliis, vt pote Abrahamo, Isaaco, Iacobo, Israelitis in deserto agentibus, Elia: & hodie multa fiunt, quæ possunt fidem facere promissionis, qua
units.tr: Meanwhile it is worth careful consideration that Christ sent out his apostles with no great splendour. For in this poverty the majesty and truly divine power of Christ shine more brightly. For although he sends them out destitute, and indeed into the midst of wolves (as Matthew 10 says), he nevertheless preserved them, so that they suffered neither any danger to life, nor laboured under hunger or the lack of necessities, as they themselves confess at the Last Supper. From this a general doctrine may be drawn: we should not be weighed down by excessive anxiety and care, if anything must be done in accordance with God's calling or command. For he knows what we most need, and since he is the most faithful father of his people, he will never neglect those who are diligent in his service. Examples of this kind exist in many others, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the Israelites wandering in the wilderness, and Elijah; and today many things happen which can establish the faith of the promise

units.la: Apostolorum commeatus. fioni, qua Christus pollicetur, nihil ijs defuturum esse, qui regnum Dei & eius iustitiam ante omnia quaesierint. Et notum est illud Dauidis: Iuuenis fui & nunc senui, neque vidi iustum derelictum, neque posteros eius mendicantes panem. Admonet praeterea nos locus ille, in Christo Iesu & tota fidei Christianae negotio non debere externum splendorem quaeri. Nec enim de mundo hoc est regnum Christi, neque huius mundi praesidijs aut commendatione opus habet. Itaque ipsius exemplo confirmantur Pontifices, qui cum eius se vicarios profiteantur, luxu tamen & saltu reges potentissimos superant: adhaec armatis undique turmis stipantur, vt nimirum in his praesidium habeant, qui armis spiritualibus omnino destituuntur. Denique singuli discunt, Christianorum hominum esse, ne in externo splendore gloriam sibi quaerant. Quid enim stultius est, quam ijs rebus superbire, quae mementanea sunt, & tunc fere dilabuntur, quando illis maxime opus est? Quid autem indignius servo Christi, quam relicto humilitatis exemplo, quo ille nobis praeluit, immodico fastu mundum imitari, e quo nos ille selegit? Ioan. 15.
units.tr: by which Christ promises that nothing will be lacking to those who seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. And that saying of David is well known: "I have been young and now am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread." Moreover, that passage admonishes us that in Christ Jesus and in the whole business of the Christian faith we ought not to seek external splendour. For the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, nor does it need the protection or recommendation of this world. Thus the pontiffs are confirmed in his example: although they profess themselves his vicars, they nonetheless surpass the most powerful kings in luxury and display; and besides, they are surrounded on every side by armed troops, clearly so that they may have in these a defence, although they are altogether destitute of spiritual arms. Finally, each individual learns that it is not the mark of Christians to seek glory for themselves in external splendour. For what is more foolish than to pride oneself on things that are fleeting, and which for the most part slip away just when they are most needed? And what is more unworthy of a servant of Christ than, having abandoned the example of humility by which he went before us, to imitate the world in immoderate pride, from which he has chosen us? (John 15.)

units.la: Quinto, quomodo se in vrbibus & vicis gerant docet. In quamcunque domum intraueritis, illic manete, & illinc exite. Paucis hic dicit, quod infra cap. decimo pluribus explicat. Sensus est: non mutanda esse hospitia, sed in eo esse manendum, quod sibi primum delegerint, donec ex vrbe aut vico discedant. Seruit autem hoc quoq; festinationi, qua illos vti debuisse, iam non semel diximus. Haec enim non sinebat vt in hospitijs quaerendis aut mutandis delicatuli essent, neq; etiam permittebat, vt quem sibi delegissent, hospitem diutius grauarent. Interim omnes verbi ministros prudentia & modestiae admonet: Ne videlicet temere cum quouis commercium ineant, sed hominum animos atq; mores (quoad eius fieri potest) explorent, neue se rebus ad suam functionem nihil pertinentibus immisceant. Illud enim multis nominibus periculosum & cum scandalo coniunctum est: hoc vero vt omnibus alijs, ita peregrinis maxime odium atque inuidiam conciliat. Quis enim virum bonum aut honesti amantem putet eum, qui improborum consuetudine delectatur? Aut quis patienter ferat eum, qui negotia aliena curiosius scrutatur, & relictis proprijs negotijs ea agit, quae nihil ad ipsum pertinent?
units.tr: Fifthly, he teaches how they are to conduct themselves in towns and villages: "Into whatever house you enter, remain there, and from there depart." Here he speaks briefly, which he explains more fully below in chapter 10. The sense is that they should not change their lodgings, but should remain in the one they first chose, until they leave the town or village. This too serves the haste by which, as we have already said more than once, they ought to have been driven. For this did not allow them to be fastidious in seeking or changing lodgings, nor did it permit them to burden for longer the host they had chosen. Meanwhile he admonishes all ministers of the Word to prudence and modesty: namely, that they should not rashly enter into association with just anyone, but should examine (as far as it can be done) the minds and morals of men, and should not involve themselves in matters that have nothing to do with their office. For the one is dangerous in many respects and attended with scandal; the other, as with all others, so especially with strangers, wins hatred and ill will. For who would think a man good or a lover of honesty who delights in the company of the wicked? Or who would patiently endure one who scrutinises the affairs of others too curiously, and, neglecting his own business, busies himself with things that have nothing to do with him?

units.la: At quia non ignorabat Dominus, plerosq; hominum doctrinam Euangelij reiecturos esse, sexto loco admonet, quid cum illis agant, qui illam contemnunt, & ipsos quoque praecones recipere dedignantur. Quicunque (inquit) non receperint vos, exeuntes ex vrbe illa, etiam puluerem a pedibus vestris excutite in testimonium aduersus eos. Primo exire iubet. Ergo verbum Dei non obtrudi debet inuitis, ne forte margaritas porcis, et sanctum canibus proijciamus. At hic multo iudicio opus est verbi administris, ne sibi semper permissum putent, quod tunc Apostoli facere debuerunt, quibus omnino festinandum erat, vt intra paucos dies Iudaeam totam percurrerent. Non poterant illi disputationes longas instituere, aut multis agere cum illis, quos contumaciores esse videbant. Alia est pastorum ratio, quibus Ecclesiae vnius cura commissa est. Hos enim docendo, monendo, hortando, increpando instare iubet Paulus: imo percipit, vt malos quoque tolerent, & cum multa lenitate eos erudiant, qui contrarie sunt affecti. Deinde pulverem a pedibus eos excutere iubet in testimonium aduersus illos. Videtur hoc tunc vulgo in vsu fuisse, vt pulverem aduersus eos excuterent, quos extremo odio aut abominatione dignos esse iudicabant. Eo enim ritu signi ficabatur, eorum consuetudinem tam esse noxiam & detestabilem, vt ne pulverem quidem boni cum illis commune habere debeant. Seruebat hoc probe praesenti negotio: quia qui Dei verbum reijciunt, ij indigni sunt quos terra ferat, & ijdem (vt in Psal. 1. Spiritus sanctus admonet) instar puluueris a vento exagitati disijcientur. Poterat hoc infinitis exemplis probari, sed eorum commemoratione nequaquam opus est, quando conflat, omnibus saeculis infelicissimos fuisse, quotquot Deum in verbo suo loquentem audire noluerunt.
units.tr: But because the Lord did not fail to see that most men would reject the doctrine of the Gospel, he gives a sixth instruction, telling them what to do with those who despise it and refuse even to receive the heralds themselves. "Whoever (he says) do not receive you, when you go out of that city, shake off even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them." He first bids them go out. Therefore the Word of God should not be forced on the unwilling, lest perhaps we cast pearls before swine and what is holy before dogs. Yet here the ministers of the Word need great discernment, lest they think they are always permitted what the Apostles were then obliged to do, since they had to hurry so that within a few days they would traverse all of Judea. Those men could not enter into long disputations or deal at length with those whom they saw to be more stubborn. The method of pastors is different, to whom the care of a single Church has been committed. For Paul bids these men to press on with teaching, admonishing, exhorting and rebuking; indeed he instructs them to bear even the wicked and to instruct with great gentleness those who are disposed otherwise. Next he bids them shake the dust from their feet as a testimony against those people. It seems that at that time it was the custom to shake dust against those whom they judged worthy of extreme hatred or abomination. For by that rite it was signified that their conduct was so harmful and detestable that good people ought not to share even the dust with them. This served the present matter well, because those who reject the Word of God are unworthy of the earth that bears them, and such men (as the Holy Spirit warns in Psalm 1) will be scattered like dust driven by the wind. This could be proved by countless examples, but there is no need to recall them, since it is clear that in every age those have been most unhappy who would not hear God speaking in his Word.

units.la: Est autem obseruanda probe locutio, quod puluerem excutere iubet in testimonium aduersus eos. Ea enim a ministris zelus requiritur, quo accensi se verbi contemptoribus opponant. Est hic necessarius admodum, partim propter ipsos ministros, ne aduersariorum minis terreantur: partim propter auditores, vt qui adhuc curabiles sunt, animo perculsi Deo cedant, incurabiles autem aliquando damnationis iustae testimonium intra semetipsos inueniant. Et est hoc euidens iustitiae diuinae argumentum, quod neminem nisi testibus idoneis conuictum punit. At nemo hinc impunitatem sperem concipere debet. Nam etsi multorum ea sit astutia, vt hominum oculos fallere possint,
units.tr: Moreover, the expression must be carefully noted, that he bids them shake off dust as a testimony against them. For by this zeal is required of ministers, by which, kindled, they should set themselves against the despisers of the Word.
