This is very necessary, partly on account of the ministers themselves, lest they be terrified by the threats of adversaries; partly on account of the hearers, so that those who are still curable may be struck in mind and yield to God, while the incurable may at some time find within themselves the testimony of their just condemnation. And this is a plain proof of divine justice, that it punishes no one unless he has been convicted by fitting witnesses. Yet no one should conceive hope of impunity from this. For although many are so crafty that they can deceive human eyes,

units.la: Puluueris excussio. Deum tamen nemo latere potest, & eidem facillimum est sceleris & inobedientiæ convincere omnes, qui peccant. Si enim pulvis ex ministrorum pedibus excussus sufficit in testimonium adversus eos, qui verbum audire dedignantur, quantum pondus habebunt ipsæ conciones, & assidui labores ministrorum? quid item non poterunt hic tot libri, tot prodigia, tot iudiciorum Dei exempla, quibus pœnitere nescios Deus quotidie excitat? Quòd si obijcias, Atqui non curant hæc omnia impij, ideoq; testimonia eiusmodi facile eludent: Respondeo, Illis etiam invitis conscientiam obrepere, quæ illos sceleris accusat, & in mentem revocat omnia, quæ aliquando audierunt atque viderunt. Quaigitur ratione iudicis sententiam subterfugient, quos propria mens accusat, & qui propriæ conscientiæ testimonio convincuntur? Est autem eadem aliorum quoq; scelerum ratio, quod gentium philosophi quoq; intellexerunt. Et hinc planius ille nascetur, quem impij olim facient, quando Christum in nubibus cœli iudicem venire conspicabuntur. Quid enim aliud faciant, qui intra animos suos sentiunt adesse iam tempus, quo iampridem meritas scelerum pœnas exoluant?
units.tr: The shaking off of dust. Yet no one can be hidden from God, and it is very easy for him to convict of wickedness and disobedience all who sin. For if the dust shaken from the ministers' feet suffices as testimony against those who disdain to hear the Word, how much weight will the sermons themselves and the constant labours of the ministers carry? And what will so many books, so many prodigies, so many examples of God's judgments not be able to do here, by which God daily stirs up those who know not how to repent? But if you object, "Yet the wicked do not heed all these things, and so they will easily evade such testimonies," I answer: even against their will, conscience creeps upon them, which accuses them of wickedness and recalls to mind everything they have at some time heard and seen. By what reasoning, then, will those escape the judge's sentence whom their own mind accuses, and who are convicted by the testimony of their own conscience? The same account holds for other crimes as well, as the philosophers of the nations also understood. And from this will arise more plainly that terror which the wicked will feel when they see Christ coming as judge in the clouds of heaven. For what else will they do, who feel within their souls that the time has now come when they must pay the long-deserved penalties for their sins?

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, qua narratur, vt Christi mandatum Apostoli obierint. Illos autem eximisse scribit Lucas, & obiisse singulos vitos, euangelizantes & sanantes vbique. Paruerunt igitur Christo, quamuis multa essent, quæ ipsos absterrere poterant. Nota enim erat sacerdotum improbitas, magnatum crudelis furor, & populi totius inconstantia. Iniquum quoque poterat videri ex tam magno auditorum cætu, duodecim solos tantis laboribus atque periculis obijcere, imò binos tantùm mittere, vt ita quasi diuisa in multas turmas acie hostes aggrederentur. Sed nihil huius in quæstionem vocant, vt qui iampridem didicerant Deo esse obediendum in ijs etiam, quæ ratione carnis iniqua, vel etiam stulta & impossibilia esse videntur. Neque successus defuit pio infi tuto. Nam vt suo loco audiemus, nihil incommodi passi redeunt, & læti exponunt Domino quid fecerint. Excitet nos istorum omnium consideratio, vt magni faciamus Euangelij doctrinam, qua regnum Dei nobis offertur, & illam constanti fide amplexi, totos nos consecremus Domino & Seruatori nostro Iesu Christo, qui in huius vita stadio currentes tuebitur, & hoc emensos in regni sui cœlestis & beatitudinis æternæ societatem transferet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potes stas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, which tells how the Apostles carried out Christ's command. Luke writes that they set out and went through the villages one by one, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere. They therefore obeyed Christ, although there were many things that could have terrified them. For the wickedness of the priests was well known, the cruel rage of the great men, and the inconstancy of the whole people. It could also seem unfair that the twelve alone should be thrown against such great labours and dangers from so large a gathering of hearers, indeed that they should be sent only two by two, so that they might attack the enemy as if the battle line were divided into many squadrons. But they called none of this into question, since they had long learned that God is to be obeyed even in those things which seem unreasonable to the flesh, or even foolish and impossible. Nor was success lacking to the pious obedience. For, as we shall hear in its place, they returned having suffered no harm, and joyfully reported to the Lord what they had done. May the consideration of all these things stir us to value highly the doctrine of the Gospel, by which the kingdom of God is offered to us, and, embracing it with steadfast faith, to dedicate ourselves wholly to the Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ, who will protect us as we run the course of this life, and, having brought us through it, will transfer us into the fellowship of his heavenly kingdom and of eternal blessedness. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 86.

units.la: Audiuit autem Herodes Tetrarcha omnia quæ fiebant ab eo, & hæsitabat: propterea quod dicebatur à quibusdam, Ioannem excitatũ esse à mortuis: quibusdam vero, Eliam apparuisse: ab alijs autem, Propheta quempiam ex antiquis resurrexisse. Et ait Herodes: Ioannem ego decollaui, quis est autem iste, de quo ego talia audio? Et studebat eum videre. Reuersi autem Apostoli narrauerunt ei quæcunque fecerant. Et ipse assumptis illis, secessit priuatim in locum desertum vrbis, quæ vocatur Bethsaida. Quod cum cognouisset turba, secuta est eum: ipse autem excepit eos, & loquebatur eis de regno Dei, & eos quibus sanatione opus erat, sanabat.
units.tr: Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead; by some that Elias had appeared; and by others that one of the old prophets had risen again. And Herod said: "John I have beheaded, but who is this, of whom I hear such things?" And he sought to see him. And the apostles, when they returned, told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew privately into a desert place of the city called Bethsaida. But when the multitudes knew it, they followed him, and he received them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and healed those who had need of healing.

units.la: Icuti Dominus noster Iesus Christus æterni Patris consilio prædestinatus est, vt humani generis redemptor, adeoq; Rex & Sacerdos æternus fieret: ita benevolentiam suam & propensum nos scruandi studium multis argumentis declarauit. Inter quæ non postremum est, quod non ipse modo passim docuit, sed vt doctrina salutis latius diuulgaretur, discipulos quoque suos ad prædicandum emisit, vt per hos ad ipsum recipiendum omnes excitarentur. Ibidem vero simul suæ sapientiæ & potentiæ diuinæ specimen dedit, quando illos ita instruxit, vt nemini quidem molesti essent, neque tamen ipsis aliquid deesset, quàndiu in hoc suo munere versati sunt. Admonentur illorum exemplo omnes homines, vt demandatam sibi à Deo functionem sedulò & fideliter obeant, neque de externis huius vitæ præsidijs multum solliciti sint. Fieri enim non potest, vt suos seruos negligat Deus, cuius providentia ad ferus & volucres, imò ad flores in agris nascentes extenditur. Subijcit his præsentem hunc tem hunc locum Euangelista, qui ad huius doctrinae confirmationem non parum seruit, & tria continet, quae consideratu dignissima sunt. Primo diuersa vulgi Iudaeorum iudicia de Christo narrantur, inter quae prae aliis memorabile est Herodis iudicium, qui animum admissi sceleris conscientia aestuantem pulchre prodidit. Deinde, vt Apostoli ex legatione sua redierint docet, & vt ad se reuersos Christus exceperit. Additur his nouum bonitatis Christi exemplum, quae populum undique ad se confluentem excepit, quae nouo miraculo occasionem dedit.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ was predestined by the counsel of the eternal Father to be the Redeemer of mankind, and so to become the eternal King and Priest, so he has declared his goodwill and his eagerness to save us by many proofs. Among these is not the least that he not only taught here and there himself, but also sent out his disciples to preach, so that the teaching of salvation might be spread more widely and all might be stirred through them to receive him. Yet at the same time he gave a sample of his wisdom and divine power, when he so instructed them that they were a burden to no one, and yet lacked nothing while they were engaged in this their office. By their example all men are admonished to discharge faithfully and diligently the office laid upon them by God, and not to be greatly anxious about the outward supports of this life. For God cannot neglect his servants, since his providence extends to wild beasts and birds, indeed to the flowers that grow in the fields. The evangelist adds to these things the present passage, which serves no little to confirm this teaching, and it contains three things that are most worthy of consideration. First, the various opinions of the Jewish crowd about Christ are related, among which Herod's judgment is especially memorable, since he revealed well the mind seething with the consciousness of his crime. Next, he teaches that the apostles returned from their mission, and that Christ received them when they came back to him. To these is added a new example of Christ's goodness, who welcomed the people flocking to him from every side, and this gave occasion for a new miracle.

units.la: Primum his verbis exponit: Audiuit Herodes Tetrarcha omnia, quae fiebant ab eo, & haesitabat: propterea quod dicebatur a quibusdam, Ioannem excitatu esse a mortuis: a quibusdam vero Elias apparuisse: ab aliis aut, Prophetam quempiam ex antiquis resurrexisse. Et ait Herodes: Ioanne ego decollaui, quis est autem iste, de quo ego talia audio? Quibus verbis non obscure innuitur, Christum non obscurum aliquem erronem fuisse, qui paucis modo & nullius precij hominibus notus fuerit. Tanta enim fuit nominis eius celebritas, vt in aulam luxu & libidine diffluentem, & adipsius tyranni aures vsq; penetrauerit. Nulla ergo excusatio reliqua est Iudaeis, qui illum & doctrinam eius contempserunt: quando vel solus hic locus abunde docet, eos non ignorantia, sed malitia peccasse. Interim non obseruatu solum, verum etiam admiratione dignum est, quod cum tam variae & multae de Christo sententiae vulgo ferantur, nemo inuentus fuit hucusque, qui verum attigerit, vt promissum illum humani generis vindicem aut seruatorem esse diceret. Atqui temporis illius conditio illos de hoc admonere poterat, vt iam nihil de miraculis eius dicamus, aut de iis quae circa natiuitatem illius accidisse supra audiuimus. Accedit huic errori alius maior & tantumnon pernitiosior. Nam etsi Prophetam aliquem esse sentiant ex eorum numero, quorum sepulchra (vt alibi illis Christus exprobrat) magnifice colebant, non tamen illius doctrinae fidem adhibent, neque qua decet diligentia in eius miracula intenti sunt. Ita vero solent huius seculi filij. Etsi enim tantus veritatis atq; virtutis diuinae splendor sit, vt eum dissimulare aut negare non possint, eide tamen non cedunt, eo quod suis studijs illam repugnare sentiunt. Nos autem istorum exemplo admonemur, religionis causam minime hominum iudicijs subijci debere. Vt enim hi in diuinis nihil sapiunt ex semetipsis: ita affecti bus quoque prauis distrahuntur, qui illos lucem oculis sese ingerentem cernere non sinunt. Itaq; tutissimum est, Deum in scripturis loquentem audire, qui ipsa est veritas.
units.tr: He first sets this out in these words: "Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead; by others that Elijah had appeared; by others that one of the old prophets had risen again. And Herod said: 'John I have beheaded, but who is this, of whom I hear such things?'" By these words it is plainly hinted that Christ was not some obscure wanderer, known only to a few people of no account. For the fame of his name was so great that it penetrated even the court, flowing with luxury and lust, and reached the very ears of the tyrant himself. So no excuse remains for the Jews, who despised him and his teaching, since this one passage alone teaches abundantly that they sinned not through ignorance but through malice. Meanwhile, it is worthy not only of notice but of wonder that, although so many and varied opinions about Christ are current among the people, no one has been found until now who has touched the truth and said that he is that promised deliverer and Saviour of mankind. Yet the circumstances of that time could have warned them about this, not to mention his miracles, or the things that we have heard above happened around his birth. To this error another is added, greater and hardly less harmful. For although they think he is some prophet of their number, whose tombs (as Christ reproaches them elsewhere) they honoured with great display, they do not give faith to his teaching, nor are they attentive to his miracles with the diligence that is fitting. Yet this is the way the children of this age usually are. For although the splendour of divine truth and power is so great that they cannot ignore or deny it, they nevertheless do not yield to it, because they feel that it opposes their pursuits. But we are admonished by the example of these people that the cause of religion must in no way be subjected to human judgments. For just as these men are not wise in divine things from their own resources, so they are also pulled about by wicked affections, which do not allow them to see the light thrust before their eyes. Therefore it is the safest course to hear God speaking in the Scriptures, for he is truth itself.

units.la: Sed ad Herodem veniamus, qui haesitauisse dicitur, quod nonnullos audiret, qui Ioannem ex mortuis resuscitatum esse putarent. Erat enim tunc vulgaris inter Iudaeos error de animarum transmigratione in alia corpora. Et mirum est, illum inter eos locum inuenisse, quorum pleriq; de animarum immortalitate dubitabant. Sed facile fert Satan quemuis errorem, modo a veritatis doctrina nos abducat: imo hoc illi praecipuum studium est, vt nouis quotidie erroribus implicemur, vt magis incertos reddat, & facilius in tenebris nos detineat. At haesitatio illa timoris argumentum est, quem animo concepit Herodes, eo quod Ioannem resuscitatum putaret. Et si verba eius examines, illum quidem timorem hunc dissimulare voluisse videbis, non autem id potuisse, quo minus animum miserè anxium atq; fluctuantem proderet. Nam quasi de Ioanne abs se occiso glorietur, inquit: Ioannem ego decollaui: At mox admirabundus & trepidus subijcit: Quis est autem iste, de quo ego talia audio? Ergo intra animum suum sentiebat virtutem maiorem in Christo relucere, & vel Ioannem ipso nunc maiorem resurrexisse, vel Christum illo longe esse potentiorem. Quo exemplo docemur, impios veritatis hostes nunquam assequi quod volunt, neque metu & curis liberari, etiamsi e medio sublatos videant, quos maxime oderunt. Manet enim alta mente reposita scelerum conscientia, quae infelices excruciat, & quando minime putant, nouos verbi sui praecones excitat Deus, qui aut pari aut etiam maiori spiritus ardore atq; vehementia illos accusant, & intra animos suos sceleris admissi conuincunt. Sic olim Eliae Elisaeus successit, qui Achabi domum atq; posteritate fortius quam ille terruit, imo illam funditus euertit. Neminem ergo tyrannorum successus & laboriosa, quae sub his habetur, piorum conditio offendat. Illi enim sub purpura & vultus laeti simulatione animos assiduis curis concabescentes tegunt: hi autem tandem ad Christum colliguntur, successores autem fere relinquunt, qui causam ipsorum afferunt, & proinde hac vita defuncti de hostibus suis gloriose triumphat.
units.tr: But let us come to Herod, who is said to have been perplexed because he heard some men who thought that John had been raised from the dead. For at that time there was a common error among the Jews about the transmigration of souls into other bodies. And it is strange that it found a place among those of whom many doubted the immortality of souls. But Satan easily tolerates any error, provided it leads us away from the doctrine of truth; indeed this is his chief aim, that we should be entangled daily in new errors, so that he may make us more uncertain and keep us more easily in darkness. But that perplexity was a sign of the fear which Herod conceived in his mind, because he thought that John had been raised. And if you examine his words, you will see that he wanted to hide this fear, but could not prevent it from revealing a mind wretchedly anxious and wavering. For as if he were boasting of having killed John, he says: "John I have beheaded." But soon, amazed and trembling, he adds: "But who is this, of whom I hear such things?" So within his own mind he felt that a greater power shone forth in Christ, and that either John himself had risen greater, or that Christ was far more powerful than John. By this example we are taught that the impious enemies of the truth never attain what they desire, nor are they freed from fear and anxieties, even when they see those whom they most hated removed from the midst. For the consciousness of sins remains deeply hidden in the mind, tormenting the wretched, and when they least expect it God raises up new preachers of his word, who accuse them with a spirit equal or even greater in ardour and vehemence, and convict them within their own souls of the crime they have committed. So once Elisha succeeded Elijah, who terrified the house and posterity of Ahab more strongly than Elijah had, indeed overthrew it utterly. Therefore let no one be offended by the success of tyrants, or by the laborious condition of the godly that exists under them. For the tyrants hide their minds, consumed by constant cares, under purple and the pretence of a cheerful face. But the godly are at last gathered to Christ, and they leave behind successors who take up their cause, and so, having departed from this life, they triumph gloriously over their enemies.

units.la: Caeterum obseruari simul debet curiosa Herodis audacia, vel potius audax atq; impia curiositas. Etsi enim a propria conscientia se morderi & pungi sentiat, & ad Christi mentionem trepidet, videre Christum. eum tamen videre cupit, aut saltem se hoc cupere simulat, ut fortis & intrepidus videatur. Similes huius sunt hodie multi, qui Euangelij audiendi & cognoscendi studium & animi fortitudinem iniuriam prae se ferunt, cum intra se toti trepident, & veritati crudeles insidias struant. At tunc nos Christum imitari conuenit. Is nihil facit in Herodis gratiam, ut neque postea, quando a Pilato ad illum transmissus fuit. Sciebat enim impium & fraudulentum nebulonem esse (quae causa est, quod vulpem infra vocabit) & proinde indignum, quem suo vel conspectu vel colloquio dignaretur. Cuius utinam meminissent, qui hodie principibus nimium seruiliter morem gerunt, ut illorum amicitia atque fauore frui possint. Falluntur hi plerunque, & dum sibi consulere volunt, tam seipsos quam veritatis causam turpiter produnt atque perdunt. Semper ergo in auribus nostris sonet Regij illius Prophetae vox: Ne fidatis principibus, neque filijs hominum, in quibus non est salus.
units.tr: Moreover, we should also notice the curious boldness of Herod, or rather his bold and impious curiosity. For although he feels himself bitten and pierced by his own conscience, and trembles at the mention of Christ, he nevertheless desires to see Christ, or at least pretends that he desires it, so that he may appear brave and fearless. Many today are like him, who show off a zeal for hearing and knowing the gospel and a courage of spirit that is false, while within themselves they tremble completely and lay cruel snares for the truth. But we ought to imitate Christ in this. He does nothing to win Herod's favour, nor later, when he was sent to him by Pilate. For he knew that Herod was an impious and deceitful scoundrel (which is why later he calls him a fox), and therefore unworthy to be honoured with either his sight or his conversation. Would that those who today serve princes too obsequiously, so that they may enjoy their friendship and favour, would remember this. They are often deceived, and while they wish to look out for themselves, they shamefully betray and destroy both themselves and the cause of truth. Therefore let the voice of that royal prophet always sound in our ears: "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation."

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alterum huius loci caput, quo Apostoli ad Christum redijsse dicuntur, & quid hic cum illis egerit narratur. Et illi quidem ei omnia narrarunt, quaecunque fecerant. At quia nullius querimoniae hic mentio fit, satis apparet, legationem hanc illis feliciter cessisse: ita nimirum ipsos seruantes Christo, cui seruiebant. Est, quod inter eius miracula non postremum, quod cum ipsum odissent principes atque Sacerdotes populi Iudaici, & ijdem discipulis quoque propter ipsum infensissimi essent, illis tamen totam terram tuto obire et Euangelium praedicare licuit. Soletur nos exemplum hoc, ne nos ignauo metu absterreri patiamur, si quid ex Dei mandato faciendum est. Ut enim nos viribus instruere, & ad quaeuis idoneos facere potest: ita non difficile eidem fuerit hostium manus continere, & frenum illis iniicere, qui aduersus seruos ipsius insurgunt. Simul autem officij sui admonentur omnes verbi ministri, ut omnem sui ministerij laudem atque gloriam ad Christum referant, & ita res suas instituant, ut huic rationem reddere possint, atque eius iudicio probentur. At quia de hoc alibi non semel diximus, paucula haec modo sufficiant.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the second part of this passage, in which the apostles are said to have returned to Christ, and we are told what passed between them and him. "And they told him all that they had done." Since no complaint is mentioned here, it is clear enough that this mission turned out well for them, because they were serving Christ, whom they served. Among his miracles this is not the least: although the rulers and chief priests of the Jewish people hated him, and these same men were fiercely hostile to his disciples on his account, the apostles were still allowed to travel through the whole land safely and preach the Gospel. This example should comfort us and keep us from letting cowardly fear frighten us away from whatever must be done by God's command. For as he is able to strengthen us and make us fit for any task, so it will not be hard for him to restrain the hands of enemies and to put a bridle on those who rise against his servants. At the same time, all ministers of the Word are reminded of their duty: they should refer all the praise and glory of their ministry to Christ, and order their affairs so that they can give him an account and be approved at his judgment. But since we have said more than once elsewhere what belongs here, these few words will suffice for now.

units.la: Nunc Christum videamus, qui assumptis discipulis secessit primatim in locum desertum urbis Bethsaidae. Causa secessionis huius duplex fuit. Prima, ut Herodis furorem declinaret, & hanc non obscure Matthaeus indicat, qui illum audita Ioannis morte, nauicula in desertum abiisse scribit. Vnde colligimus hanc Apostolorum missionem eo ipso tempore non factam fuisse, quando Ioanne Herodes e medio sustulit. Terruit haud dubie exemplum istud multorum animos, qui Dei verbum sus-piciebant. Ne ergo hoc cum Ioanne extinctum putarent, nouis praeconibus opus fuit, quorum praedicatione confirmarentur. Et credibile est, discipulos Christi licet felicissime ipsis cessisset ea legatio, aliquid tamen humani passos & tanti viri morte perculsos fuisse, cum hoc quasi praeludio admonerentur, quid ipsis aliquando euenturum esset. Ut ergo tyranno saeuitia nouae occasionem dare noluit Dominus, ita simul discipulorum infirmitati consuluit, ut trepidos & consternatos nouis consolationibus recrearet. Apparet autem in Christi facto, quae nam Herodis mens fuerit; & quo consilio illum videre studuerint: nimirum ut per insidias intercepium una cum discipulis occideret. Nec enim mitiores fiunt impij ex conscientia terroribus, sed potius nouos furores animo concipiunt, & desperatione in rabiem aguntur, ut ipsi etiam Deo bellum inferre conentur. Sed ut non potuit Christum falere crudelis illa vulpes: ita neque hodie vllis impiorum consilijs fallitur. Videt enim ex alto, quid illi machinentur, imo qui dintra animos suos statuant, & ideo haec omnia facile eludit. Docet autem suo exemplo licere nobis, ut impiorum furori cedamus, quando id salua gloria Dei & vocatione nostra fieri potest. Nam quod hic facit, id alibi quoque eum fecisse legimus, quoties ante horam ipsi a Patre constitutam hostes eum perdere voluerunt. Et discipulis dicit: Si vos persecuti fuerint in vna ciuitate, fugite in aliam. Veruntamen hic diligenti cautione opus est, ne dum nobis ipsis consulimus, stationem deseramus, in qua a Deo sumus constituti. Itaque si in eas redigamur angustias, ut aut moriendum sit nobis, aut aliquid faciendum praeter officium, tunc vel mori satius fuerit, quam admittere, quae Dei gloria labefactetur.
units.tr: Now let us look at Christ, who, taking the disciples with him, withdrew privately into a desert place near the city of Bethsaida. This withdrawal had a twofold cause. The first was to avoid the fury of Herod. Matthew clearly indicates this, writing that when he heard of John's death he departed by boat into a desert place. From this we gather that the mission of the apostles was not undertaken at the very time when Herod removed John from the scene. Doubtless that example terrified the minds of many who welcomed the word of God. So that they should not think it had been extinguished along with John, new heralds were needed, by whose preaching they might be strengthened. And it is credible that, although that mission turned out most happily for the disciples, they nonetheless suffered some human weakness and were struck down by the death of so great a man. They were being warned, as by a kind of prelude, of what would one day happen to themselves. Therefore, just as the Lord was unwilling to give the tyrant an occasion for fresh cruelty, so at the same time he provided for the weakness of the disciples, to restore them with new consolations when they were frightened and dismayed. Moreover, the conduct of Christ reveals what Herod's intention was and with what purpose they sought to see him: namely, to seize him by treachery and kill him along with the disciples. For the wicked do not become milder through the terrors of conscience; rather they conceive new rages in their minds, and driven by despair into madness, they try even to wage war against God himself. But just as that cruel fox could not deceive Christ, so today he is not deceived by any plans of the wicked. For he sees from on high what they are plotting, indeed what they decide within their own hearts, and so he easily frustrates all of it. By his own example he teaches us that we may yield to the fury of the wicked when this can be done without harm to the glory of God and to our calling. For what he does here we read that he did elsewhere too, whenever enemies sought to destroy him before the hour appointed for him by the Father. And he tells the disciples: "When they persecute you in one city, flee into another" [Matth. 10.23]. Yet here careful caution is needed, lest in looking after ourselves we abandon the post in which God has placed us. Therefore, if we are driven into such straits that either we must die or do something beyond our duty, then it would be better to die than to permit anything by which the glory of God is overthrown.

units.la: Praeter alia autem regni tyrannici & Reipub. male constitutae exemplum locus iste nobis exhibet. Nam Herodis saeuitiam eo vsque progressam fuisse videmus, ut viri boni & Dei amantes tutius in deserto locis inter feras, quam in vrbibus eius imperio subditis agerent: nihil autem interea periculi erat hominibus impuris, incestis, ebriosis, iniustis, sanguinarijs, qui in media eius aula domi nabantur. Similis olim sub Achabo & Iezabele fuit rerum facies, & eius generis exempla multa Imperatorum Romanorum historiae nobis exhibent, qui fidem Christianam persecuti sunt. Etenim non hodie quoque multi ita regnarent, ut ebriosis quidem & adulteris, imò grassatoribus & praedonibus liceat omne genus flagitiis in medijs urbibus designare, pijs autem non liceat in priva ta aliqua domo coetum sacrum agere, in quo Dei verbum audiant, & Sacramenta à Christo instituta communicent. At quid de urbibus aut domibus privatis dico, quando ne in sylvis quidem & inter ferarum lustra tuto degunt, qui puriorem Christi doctrinam profitentur? At non diuturna fuit Herodis potentia, qui non multo post cum incesta & sanguinaria Herodiade terra exutus & in exilium relegatus est, in quo vitae turpiter transactae finem infelice impositum. Et suas etiam poenas dederunt alij tyranni, qui eius vestigia secuti sunt. Debent exempla eiusmodi diligenter observare omnes qui magistratum gerunt: ut in primis quidem Christo Regi gloriae portas suas aperiant, & ecclesiae eius penes se locum dent: deinde verò civium suorum corpora, honorem, famam & fortunas sedulò tueantur. Nam illud quidem religio, hoc autem iustitia requirit, quibus duabus quasi columnis atque fulcris Respub. nititur.
units.tr: Apart from other lessons, this passage sets before us an example of a tyrannical kingdom and a badly ordered commonwealth. For we see that Herod's cruelty had gone so far that good men who love God were safer living in the desert among the wild beasts than in the cities subject to his rule. Meanwhile there was no danger for impure, incestuous, drunken, unjust and bloodthirsty men, who lived at home in the very midst of his court. Similar was the state of affairs under Ahab and Jezebel, and the histories of the Roman emperors who persecuted the Christian faith offer us many examples of this kind. Indeed, do not many rulers today also govern in such a way that drunkards and adulterers, and even robbers and plunderers, are permitted to commit every kind of crime in the middle of the cities, while the godly are not permitted to hold a sacred assembly in some private house, where they may hear the word of God and partake of the sacraments instituted by Christ? But why do I speak of cities or private houses, when those who profess the purer doctrine of Christ do not even live safely in the woods and among the dens of wild beasts? Yet the power of Herod did not last long: not long afterwards he was stripped of his land, along with his incestuous and bloodthirsty Herodias, and was banished into exile, where an unhappy end was put to a life shamefully spent. Other tyrants who followed in his footsteps have also paid their penalties. All who bear the magistracy ought carefully to observe examples of this kind. First, they should open their gates to Christ the King of glory, and give his Church a place among them. Then, too, they should diligently protect the bodies, honour, reputation and fortunes of their citizens. For religion requires the first, and justice the second; these are the two pillars and supports on which a commonwealth rests.

units.la: Altera secessionis Christi causa est, quòd discipulos ex itinere & praedicandi labore fessos recrea re voluit. Et hanc Marcus indicat, qui eum dixisse scribit: Venite vos soli in desertum locum, & requiescite pusillum. Et ibidem causam quoq; assignat dicens: Erant enim multi, qui veniebant & abibant, ut ne cibum quidem capere vacaret. Elucet in eo admirabilis Christi Iesu bonitas, qui non requisitus discipulus otium & quietem permittit, ut vires multo labore exhaustas rursus colligant. Nouit enim infirmitatem nostram, & proinde supra vires nos gravari non finit. Huius nos meminisse decet, si quando morbis aut quibuscunque aliis aduersis gravamur. Est haec Christi palaestra, in qua suos ille exercet, & ut ille Agonothetes est oculatissimus, qui nos certantes spectat, ita laborantibus aut novas vires suggerit, aut praeter omnem expectationem certamini finem imponit. Interim illius exemplum ipsi quoq; imitemur, ne in eos duriores & iniquiores simus, in quos nobis ius est & imperium. Nec enim frustra Sabbatum Deus instituit, in cuius praecepto diligentissima sit mentio servorum, ancillarum, peregrinorum, imò iumentorum quoque. Unde colligimus cum sacrilegio coniunctam esse eorum inhumanitatem, qui à Deo concessam quietem suis inuident aut praeripiunt. At hic non minus videre oportet, ut cum Christo secessum petamus, ne otium illud prophanum fiat, & vitijs occasionem praebeat. Peccatur hodie in utramq; partem, dum alij quidem avaritiae fascinati seipsos & suos laboribus immodicis fatigant, alij verò Sabbati quietem ad voluptates & carnis libidinem abutuntur, ut nunquam magis diabolo serviant, quàm quando toti Deo addicti esse debebant.
units.tr: The second cause of Christ's withdrawal is that he wished to refresh the disciples, who were weary from their journey and the labour of preaching. Mark indicates this, who writes that he said: "Come apart into a desert place by yourselves, and rest a little." And in the same place he also gives the reason, saying: "For there were many who came and went, so that they had no leisure even to eat" [Mark 6.31]. In this the wonderful goodness of Jesus Christ shines forth: though the disciples have not asked for it, he grants them leisure and rest, so that they may regain strength exhausted by great labour. For he knows our weakness, and therefore does not allow us to be burdened beyond our strength. We ought to remember this whenever we are weighed down by sickness or by any other adversity. This is Christ's wrestling-school, in which he trains his people; and just as he is the most watchful president of the games [ἀγωνοθέτης] who looks on at us as we contend, so he either supplies new strength to those who labour, or beyond all expectation puts an end to the contest. Meanwhile, let us also imitate his example, so that we are not harsher and more unjust towards those over whom we have right and authority. For God did not institute the Sabbath in vain, and in its command there is a most careful mention of male servants, female servants, strangers, and even beasts of burden. From this we gather that the inhumanity of those who begrudge or snatch away from their dependants the rest granted by God is joined with sacrilege. Yet here we must also take care that, when we seek withdrawal with Christ, that leisure does not become profane and offer an occasion to vices. Today people sin in both directions: some, bewitched by greed, wear out themselves and their households with excessive labours, while others misuse the rest of the Sabbath for pleasures and the lusts of the flesh, so that they never serve the devil more than when they ought to be wholly devoted to God.

units.la: Sequitur tertium huius loci caput, in quo Christi facilitas atq; bonitas nouo exemplo commendatur. Cùm enim populus intellexisset, eum in desertum secessisse, mox pedestri itinere (ut Marcus scribit) ex multis urbibus magno concursu facto illum sequuntur, & tanta quidem festinatione, ut ipsum praeuenerint. Fuit zelus hic per se bonus & sanctus, in eo autem reprehensione digni sunt, quòd plerique ea modò quaerunt, quae carni serviebant, non ut coelesti doctrina ad vitam aeternam instituantur. Est horum magnus numerus hodie: qui & ipsi circa initium feruent, ut nihil non facturi videantur, at mox frigescunt, si Christum votis ipsorum minus respondere sentiant. Qui ut seipsos salute aeterna spoliant, ita aliis quoque mali exempli authores sunt, & saepe ecclesias totas miserè dissipant. At qualescunque isti fuerint, suo tamen exemplo nostri seculi mores damnant. Nam cùm Christum non nisi temporalium beneficiorum authorem esse putent, nihilominus tanto feruore eum sequuntur, & dignum censent, cuius causa urbes atque domus suas relinquant. At hodie, qui illum aeternae salutis authorem esse profitentur, vix adduci possunt, ut semel aut iterum in septimana ipsum in Euangelio suo loquentem audiant.
units.tr: There follows the third point of this passage, in which the readiness and goodness of Christ are commended by a new example. For when the people understood that he had withdrawn into the desert, they quickly followed him on foot (as Mark writes) from many cities, gathering in great numbers, and with such haste that they arrived before him. This zeal was good and holy in itself, but they deserve blame in that most of them seek only those things which serve the flesh, not that they may be instructed in heavenly doctrine for eternal life. Today there is a large number of such people: at first they burn with zeal, as if they would undertake anything, but soon they grow cold if they perceive that Christ does not answer their wishes. As they rob themselves of eternal salvation, so they are also authors of bad example to others, and often miserably scatter whole churches. Yet whatever such people are like, by their own example they condemn the morals of our age. For although they think Christ is the author only of temporal benefits, nonetheless they follow him with such fervour and count him worthy that for his sake they leave their cities and homes. But today, those who profess that he is the author of eternal salvation can scarcely be brought to hear him speaking in his Gospel once or twice a week.

units.la: Quid verò in praesenti cum illis agit? Sunt in hoc describendo Euangelistae admodum diligentes, ut eius benignitatem omnibus perspectam faciant. Primò enim Marcus eum ad populum profectum dixit, ut (quod hic annotatur) eos exciperet. Ita ergo quietem quaesiuit, ut minimè negligeret eos, à quibus se quaeri videbat. Et ut eos aliquo labore levet, sponte illis obuiam progreditur. O miram facilitatem, & incredibilem inferendis aliorum moribus patientiam. Hodie, qui se eius vicarios profitentur, vix Reges & Imperatores intra suos parietes, ad pedum suorum osculā admittunt, nedum ut ad opificum, agricolarum, mendicorum turbam ipsi progrediantur. Deinde totius
units.tr: What, then, does he do at present with them? The Evangelists are very careful in describing this, so that his kindness may be seen by all. First, Mark says that he went out to the people, so that (as is noted here) he might receive them. He thus sought rest in such a way that he did not in the least neglect those by whom he saw himself being sought. And to spare them some trouble, he goes out to meet them of his own accord. O wonderful affability, and incredible patience in bearing with the manners of others! Today, those who profess themselves his vicars scarcely admit kings and emperors within their own walls to kiss their feet, let alone go out themselves to the crowd of workers, farmers and beggars. Then, of the whole

units.la: O misericordia mouetur super eos (quod etiam Marcus annotauit) eò quòd ouium instar vagarentur, quæ pastorem non habent. Erant quidem infiniti, qui pastores illorum dici atque haberi volebant, Sacerdotes nimirum & Scribæ, sed hi omnes non aliud agebant, quàm quod Ezechiel de suis seculi pastoribus dicit: Pascebant enim seipsos, dum in hoc erant, vt ex populi fortunis ditescerent, nihil interim de doctrina & cultu Dei soliciti. Et cùm ipsi in diuersos ordines scissi essent, fieri non poterat, quin populus quoque sub illis in sectas scinderetur. Hinc ergo dissipatio illa, quam Christus sine acerba animi commotione intueri non potuit, eò quòd cum miserorum exitio coniunctam esse sciret. Nec enim seruari possunt, nisi qui in ipso vnum sunt, & ecclesiæ vnitatem sedulò tuentur. At si eorum miseria commouetur ille, qui dissipati hinc inde oberrant, quis non eundem vehementer illis irasci putet, qui dissipationum eiusmodi authores sunt? Hinc ergo graues illæ increpationes & comminationes, quibus aduersus Pharisæos & scribas fulminauit, quos modò lupos, modò fures & latrones dicit, & horrendum illud væ intonando eosdem exitio devouet. Neque dubium nobis esse debet, illum etiam hodie suorum miseria moueri, & non minus illis irasci, qui ecclesiam eius falsa doctrina & vanissimis superstitionibus dilacerant. Ne autem hæc Christi bonitas in otiosa & inani commiseratione acquieuisse putaretur, addit Lucas: Et loquebatur eis de regno Dei, & eos quibus sanatione opus erat, sanabat. Plus ergo inueniunt isti quàm quærebant. Qui enim carnalibus intenti erant, ijs Dei regnum prædicatur, de quo iam sæpe diximus. Interim non desunt miracula, quibus & morbis eorum medetur, & (qui proprius miraculorum vsus est) doctrinam suam confirmat, ne de eius veritate dubitent. Magna autem apud nos esse debet Euangelij authoritas, quando huius prædicationi maximè vacauit Dei Filius, & ad eius commendationem opera eius miraculosa in primis seruiunt. Agnoscamus ergo beneficium hoc ingens, quo inter postrema mundi huius ad suum finem tendentes certamina, nos Deus dignatur, & audiamus in Euangelio loquentem, vt ex pecca ti laqueis redempti vitæ æternæ hæredes simus cum Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Oh, he was moved with compassion for them (as Mark also notes), because they wandered like sheep that have no shepherd. There were indeed countless men who wanted to be called and held their shepherds, namely priests and scribes, but all of them did nothing other than what Ezekiel says of the shepherds of his own age: "They fed themselves," for while they were in this state, they grew rich from the fortunes of the people, meanwhile caring nothing for the teaching and worship of God. And since they themselves were split into different factions, it could not but be that the people under them were also split into sects. Hence that scattering, which Christ could not look upon without a bitter stirring of his spirit, because he knew it was bound up with the ruin of the wretched. For they cannot be saved unless they are one in him and zealously keep the unity of the Church. But if he is moved by the misery of those who wander scattered here and there, who would not think that he is vehemently angry with those who are the authors of such scatterings? Hence those grave rebukes and threats, with which he thundered against the Pharisees and scribes, whom he calls now wolves, now thieves and robbers, and with that dreadful "Woe!" he devotes them to destruction. Nor ought we to doubt that he is moved today by the misery of his people, and is no less angry with those who tear his Church apart with false doctrine and most vain superstitions. Lest anyone think that this goodness of Christ rested in an idle and empty pity, Luke adds: "And he spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed healing." So those men found more than they were seeking. For to those who were intent on carnal things, the kingdom of God is preached, of which we have often spoken already. Meanwhile there is no lack of miracles, by which he both heals their diseases and (which is the proper use of miracles) confirms his teaching, so that they might not doubt its truth. Great, moreover, ought the authority of the Gospel to be among us, since the Son of God devoted himself most of all to its preaching, and his miraculous works serve chiefly to commend it. Let us therefore acknowledge this great benefit, by which God deigns to regard us amid the last struggles of this world, as it hastens to its end, and let us hear him speaking in the Gospel, so that, redeemed from the snares of sin, we may be heirs of eternal life with Jesus Christ, our Lord: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 87.

units.la: Dies autem cœperat inclinare, & accedentes duodecim dixerunt ei: Dimitte turbam, vt abeuntes in circumiacentes vicos & agros, illuc diuertant, & inueniant cibaria: nam hic in loco deserto sumus. Ipse verò dixit eis: Date ipsis vos quo vescantur. Ipsi autem dixerunt: Non sunt nobis plus quàm quinque panes & duo pisces, nisi nos profecti emamus toti huic populo escas. Aderant enim quasi viri quinquies mille. Ait autem discipulis suis: Facite vt discumbant per singulos quosque dis-cubitus quinquagenì. Ipsi igitur ita fecerunt, & discubuerunt omnes. Ipse verò acceptis quinque illis panibus & duobus piscibus, suspiciens in cœlum, benedixit eis, & fregit, dedítq; discipulis vt apponerent turbæ. Comederunt igitur omnes illi, & saturati sunt. Et sublatū est quod superfuit illis fragmentorum, cophini duodecim.
units.tr: And the day began to wear away; and the twelve came and said to him, "Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place." But he said to them, "Give ye them to eat." And they said, "We have no more than five loaves and two fishes, except we should go and buy meat for all this people." For they were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, "Make them sit down by fifties in a company." And they did so, and made them all sit down. Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and brake, and gave to the disciples to set before the multitude. And they did eat, and were all filled. And there was taken up of fragments that remained to them twelve baskets.

units.la: Quemadmodum Dominus noster Iesus Christus sua doctrina se omnium, qui ad ipsum venirent, seruatorē esse testatur: ita miracula quoq; eiusmodi addidit, quæ nō obiter modo hanc eius doctrinam confirmant, sed nobis quoq; priuatim talem fore docent. Inter ea non postremum cen seri debet, quod modò recitauimus. Hoc enim se panem illum vitæ esse declarat, qui solus nos ad vitam cælestem & æternā alit, simulq; promissionibus suis fidem facit, vt intelligamus ijs, qui ipsum sequuntur, nihil defuturum eorum, quæ ad corporis aut animæ salutem faciunt. Vt ergo hic nobis Dei prouidentia commendatur, quæ omnes homines pascit & seruat: ita ministerij quoq; ecclesiastici typus proponitur, per quod seipsum Christus nobis propinat, vt in ipso salute æterna habeamus. Non temere ergo factum putabimus, quòd huius miraculi historiam Spiritus Sanctus ab omnibus omnibus Euangelistis describi voluit: quorum diligentia nos excitare debet, ut in eius consideratione attentis animis versemur.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ testifies by his teaching that he is the Saviour of all who come to him, so he also added miracles of this kind, which not only confirm this teaching of his in passing, but also teach us, each one privately, that he will be such for us. Among these, what we have just recited should not be counted least. For in it he declares himself to be that bread of life which alone nourishes us to heavenly and eternal life, and at the same time by his promises makes us trust, so that we understand that nothing will be lacking to those who follow him of the things that serve the salvation of body or soul. Just as God's providence is here commended to us, which feeds and preserves all men, so also a type of the ecclesiastical ministry is set before us, through which Christ himself gives himself to us to drink, so that we may have eternal salvation in him. We shall not think it done rashly, then, that the Holy Spirit wished the history of this miracle to be described by all the Evangelists, whose diligence ought to stir us up to dwell with attentive minds on its consideration.

units.la: Primùm occasio totius facti narratur, quam temporis circumstantia prabuit. Iam enim dies inclinare coeperat, ut satis constaret populum, nisi absque mora dimitteretur, in proximos vicos aut urbes peruenire no posse. De eo igitur Christum discipuli admonent, qui mox sese ad opus accingit, ut illis prospiciat, qui iam aliunde cibum non poterant habere. Quo loco singulae personae non oscitanter inspici debent. In populo enim magni zeli atque studij argumentum est, quòd qui ex remotissimis locis conuenerant, eò usque cum Christo manent, & tantam ex eius doctrina voluptatem capiunt, ut nec dies ad occasum inclinans eos de reditu admoneat. Atqui non dubium est, multis hoc valde incommodum fuisse, quos rei domesticae cura reuocare poterat. Sed facile omne taedium ferunt, quos pretiosissimae illius margaritae cupiditas semel accendit, & qui Euangelij dulcedinem iam intra animos suos gustare incipiunt. Nobis autem isti nostram socordiam & ingratitudinem exprobrant, quibus graue est Christum domi nostrae concionantem audire, & qui omnem moram molestè ferimus, quae audiendo verbo tribuitur.
units.tr: First, the occasion of the whole deed is related, which the circumstance of the time provided. For the day had already begun to decline, so that it was plain that the people could not reach the nearby villages or towns unless they were dismissed without delay. The disciples therefore remind Christ of this, and he at once sets himself to the work, so that he might provide for those who could not otherwise get food. At this point each person should be looked at closely and not carelessly. For in the people it is a proof of great zeal and eagerness that those who had gathered from the most distant places stay on with Christ to such an extent, and take such pleasure in his teaching, that the sun sinking towards its setting does not remind them of going home. Yet there is no doubt that for many this was very inconvenient, since the care of domestic affairs could have called them back. But those whom the desire for that most precious pearl has once kindled, and who are beginning to taste the sweetness of the gospel within their souls, bear every weariness easily. Such people, however, reproach us for our sloth and ingratitude, we for whom it is a burden to hear Christ preaching in our own homes, and who take ill any delay that is given to the hearing of the Word.

units.la: At non minor zelus in Christo apparet, qui cùm quietis capiendae gratia eò secum discipulis suis conciliasset, tam diu tamq; patienter illos fert, qui ad ipsum confluxerant, neque eos instituere dedignatur, quos commodi alicuius temporalis spes potius quàm regni Dei studium trahebat. Hinc ergo consolationem petant, qui metuunt, ne ipsos Christus fastidiat, & proinde in precibus frigidiores sunt. Atqui delectatur ille importunitate nostra, & hunc cibum suum esse dicit, ut ex patris sui mandato quàm plurimos feruet. Exemplum autem eius sibi imitandum proponant omnes ecclesiarum ministri, neque eos alicuius laborus aut molestia pigeat, quae in docendo populo publicè aut priuatim devoranda est. Meminerint se hoc officium non tam auditoribus suis, quàm ipsi Christo praestare, qui ecclesiam propria vita & sanguine chariorem habet. Quòd si qui hic negligentiores sunt, nec illi non satis digne gratiam sibi factam aestimant, & olim socordia sua poenas dignas exoluent. At non sine certo consilio miraculum hoc ad vesperam usque distulit Dominus. Ita enim populi fidem atque patientia probari oportebat, ut omnibus constaret, quales esse debeant, qui beneficentia eius frui cupiunt. Simul etiam fidem nostram hoc exemplo confirmat, ne statim desperemus, si quan do nos in angustias extremas venire patiatur. Nam ut nihil praesidij in humanis reliquum sit, semper tamen illi ad manum erit ratio, qua rebus afflictissimis salutem afferat. Nos autem eò usque exerceri utile est, ut salutem nobis ab illo uno obtingere sentiamus, & ea accepta cum gratiarum actione bene & salubriter utamur.
units.tr: But no less zeal appears in Christ, who, though he had brought his disciples apart with him in order to take rest, bears so long and so patiently with those who had flocked to him, and does not disdain to teach those whom the hope of some temporal advantage rather than zeal for the kingdom of God drew on. Let those therefore who fear that Christ may loathe them, and so are rather cold in their prayers, take comfort from this. Indeed he is pleased by our importunity, and he says that this is his food, that he should be busy with as many as possible in obedience to his Father's command. Let all the ministers of the churches set this example before themselves, and let no toil or trouble that must be endured in teaching the people, publicly or privately, weigh them down. Let them remember that they render this office not so much to their hearers as to Christ himself, who holds the Church dearer than his own life and blood. But if any among them are rather negligent here, and do not esteem sufficiently worthily the grace shown to them, they will one day pay the penalty their sloth deserves. But the Lord did not postpone this miracle until evening without a sure purpose. For it was needful that the faith and patience of the people be tested, so that it might be plain to all what sort of people ought to be, who wish to enjoy his bounty. At the same time he confirms our faith by this example, so that we do not despair at once if at some time he allows us to come into the greatest straits. For though no help remains to us from human means, reason will always be at hand to him, by which he may bring salvation to the most afflicted things. It is useful for us, however, to be exercised to this extent: that we perceive salvation comes to us from him alone, and that, having received it, we use it well and profitably, with thanksgiving.

units.la: Porrò de discipulis quoq; aliquid dicendum est, qui Christum de populo dimittendo admonent, & ad hoc argumenta à loco & tempore desumpta proferunt. Poterat hoc charitatis officiū videri, neq; ego negauerim illos populi miseros fuisse, quem tanto cum incommodo huiusq; apud Christum haesisse cernebant. At non caruit vitio ista misericordia. Inexcusabilis enim arrogantia est, quòd populum sibi magis quàm Christo cordi esse, & hunc monitore opus habere putant: imò quòd tantum sibi ipsis tribunnt, ut non vocati aut requisiti suum illi consilium proponant. Deinde Christum negligentiae insimulant, aut etiam superbiae, quasi nulla loci aut temporis ratione habita, populi simplicis patientia abutatur. Praeterea promissionum eius immemores fuisse apparet, eius maximè, quae ut nihil illis defuturum esse pollicetur, qui ante omnia regnum Dei & eius iustitiam quaesierint. Et cur non seipsos considerant, quos ille non sine miraculo hucusq; seruarat, & non ita pridem liberaliter aluerat, cùm eos absq; omni commeatu ad praedicandum ablegauisset? At hi sapientiae humanae fructus sunt, si eius fiducia freti sine Deo sapere instituimus. Hinc enim errores & peccata omnis generis emanant, & multorum exempla extant, quibus propria sapientia exitium attulit: inter quos vel vnus Saul infelici suo exitu nos terrere poterat.
units.tr: Further, something must also be said about the disciples, who admonish Christ to dismiss the people, and bring forward arguments drawn from place and time. This might seem to be an act of charity, and I would not deny that they pitied the wretched people whom they saw clinging to Christ with such inconvenience. But this pity was not free of fault. For it is an inexcusable arrogance that they think the people are dearer to themselves than to Christ, and that he needs a reminder; indeed, that they attribute so much to themselves that, though neither called nor asked, they put forward their own counsel to him. Next, they charge Christ with negligence, or even with pride, as if, taking no account of place or time, he were abusing the patience of simple people. Besides, it is plain that they had forgotten his promises, above all that one by which he pledged that nothing would be lacking to those who first seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness. And why do they not consider themselves, whom he had kept safe until now not without a miracle, and whom not long before he had generously fed, when he had sent them out to preach with no provision for the journey? But these are the fruits of human wisdom, if we, trusting in our own wisdom, undertake to be wise without God. For from this errors and sins of every kind flow forth, and there are many examples in which their own wisdom brought ruin to people; among them Saul alone, by his unhappy end, could terrify us.

units.la: Caeterùm Christus, ut & discipulorum errorem corrigat, & populo esurienti succurrat, ad miraculum accingitur, & simul illos ad diligentiorem eius consideratione praeparat. Iubet enim, ut ipsi tantae multitudini cibum depromant. At hoc factu impossibile esse sciebat: iubet tamen, primùm ut eorum temeritatem arguat: Quasi diceret: Si vobis populus magus quàm mihi cordi est, agite, ipsi illis insternite mensam, ut videam quid vos tanti consultores possitis: deinde ut miraculi veritas sibile.
units.tr: Moreover Christ, both to correct the error of the disciples and to succour the hungry people, sets about the miracle, and at the same time prepares them for a more careful consideration of it. For he bids them set out food for so great a crowd. But he knew that this was impossible to do: yet he bids them, first, so that he may confute their rashness, as if he were saying: "If the people are more important to you than to me, come on, you set the table for them yourselves, so that I may see what great counsellors you can be; then, so that the truth of the miracle may become more certain and clearer to them."

units.la: Occasio miraculi. ipsis certius & luculentius innotescat. Quò etiā facit, quòd apud Marcum illos abire & videre iu-bet, quot panes habeant. Etenim nisi id fecissent, existimare poterant, aliunde allatos fuisse panes & cibaria, quibus illi paulò post saturati sunt. Ergo ad fidem illorum confirmandam facit mandatum hoc quo rem iubebat, quam ipsi praestare non poterant. Quo exemplo confutantur, qui arbitrij nostri libertatem & humanae naturae vires ex praeceptis in lege datis astruere conantur, & nos Deum sin-gere clamat, qui cum hominibus ludat, ea iubendo quae ipsis praestitu impossibilia sint. An ergo cum discipulis suis lusit Christus, quando vt tot millibus hominum convivium parent iussit? Imò vt ita faceret opus erat, vt oscitantes illos & confidentes ad rei, quae tunc agebatur, consideration dili-gentiorem excitaret. At non minus nobis opus est, vt qui natura confidentiores sumus, ad legem remittamur, vt huius pondere superati discamus ad gratuitam Dei misericordiam confugere, & Christum amplecti, qui nobis ab illo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est. Conu-ntur praeterea hoc exemplo, qui miracula nobis obtrudere solent, quae nemo hominum vnquam vi-dit, & quorum ne mentione quidem aliquam Christus fecit: qui (vt Euangelica historia testatur) miracula sua omnibus nota & ab omni fraudis suspicione alienissima esse voluit.
units.tr: The occasion of the miracle. Mark also adds that he bids them go and see how many loaves they have. For if they had not done this, they could have thought the loaves and food, by which they were soon satisfied, had been brought from somewhere else. So this command, by which he orders them to do what they could not do themselves, serves to confirm their faith. By this example are refuted those who try to establish the freedom of our will and the powers of human nature from the precepts given in the law, and who cry out that God is a pretender who mocks men by commanding what is impossible for them to perform. Did Christ then make sport of his disciples when he ordered them to prepare a feast for so many thousands of people? Indeed, in order to act thus he needed to rouse those drowsy and self-confident men to a more careful consideration of the matter then in hand. Yet we too need, since by nature we are rather self-confident, to be sent back to the law, so that, overcome by its weight, we may learn to flee to God's free mercy and to embrace Christ, who has been made for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Moreover, by this example are refuted also those who are accustomed to thrust upon us miracles which no man has ever seen, and of which Christ made no mention at all; for he (as the evangelical history bears witness) wished his miracles to be known to all and wholly free from any suspicion of fraud.

units.la: Sed ad rem ipsam accedamus, quam ita peragit ille, vt in singulis eius partibus divina ipsius potentia se se proferat. Primum enim discipulis praecipit, vt populum hunc discumbere iubeant, & ita quidem, vt per singulos discubitus quinquageni collocentur. Faciebat hoc quoq; ad miraculi cer-titudinem, quia facilius tota haec multitudo numerari poterat, & confusio caveba-tur, quae alioquin negotium hoc omne facile turbauisset, ipsi autem se mutuo spectare poterant epulantes. Memorabile autem obedientiae Christianae exemplum discipuli praebent. Nam etsi ridiculum videretur, tamen multo populum ad discumbendum innitare, cum sibi nihil praeter quinque panes & duos pisces ad manum esse ferent, Christo tamen hoc ita iubenti simpliciter obediunt. Imitemur nos, vt quàm-uis absurdum videatur carnis iudicio quod Deus iubet, neque nobis de rei euentu aliquid certò con-stet, nostrum tamen illi officium praestemus. Nostrum enim obsequium Deus postulat, non autem consilio nostro vtitur, quod in diuinis omnino nullum est. Deinde acceptis quinque panibus & duobus piscibus in caelum suspicit, & illis benedicit. Fuit hic illi mos perpetuus, vt nunquam sine gratiarum actione cibum sumeret: in praesenti tamen rei magnitudo gestus quoque peculiares requirebat, quibus astantes ad magis seriam contemplationem excitarentur. In caelum ergo suspicit, vt nihil hic humanum animo concipiant, sed caelesti & divina virtute hoc omne perficiendum fore cogitent. Etenim necesse omnino erat ad caelum remittere discipulos, quos ob populi multitudinem & commeatus tenuitatem non parum dubitauisse verba eorum testantur. Neque aliud nobis praesentius remedium esse potest in quavis rerum angustia, quàm si terrenis nimium intentos animos in caelum attollamus, & illic nos Patrem habere cogitemus, cuius bonitas immensa, misericordia inexhausta, & potentia inuicta sit. Ista enim consideratio facile o-nes carnis rationes retundit, quibus illa fidem nostram oppugnat. Ideo David in Psalmis canit: Leuo oculos meos ad montes vnde veniat meum auxilium. Auxilium meum venit à conditore caeli & terrae. Et in Oratione Dominica exordimur: Pater noster, qui es in caelis. Benedicit prae-terea panibus & piscibus istis Dominus, partim vt cibos ex Dei benedictione dari doceat, partim vt gratiarum actione commendet, quae sola illos nobis salutares reddit. Suo igitur exemplo eos dam-nat, qui vt bonorum omnium authorem Deum non agnoscunt, ita porcorum instar ad mensas acce-dunt, & neq; petunt sibi à Deo victum dari, neque pro illo iam acceptogratias agunt. Est hac in-gratitudo detestabilis, cùm tam multa argumenta sint, quae terram à nobis nequiquam coli docent, nisi Dei benedictione fœcundetur. Quod qui non agnoscunt, ij & sensum communem exuerunt, & illum donū fere in suum exitium abiuntur. Addit autem hu tertium Christus. Panes enim frangit, vt commodius in populum distribui possint, & fractos discipulis tradit, qui eos discumbentibus apponut. Interim occulta Dei virtute in tra illorum manus ta panes quàm pisces multiplicantur, vt ex illis omnes edant & saturentur. Vbi rursus rei gestae veritas asseritur, & omnis praestigij suspicio remouetur. Quis enim praestigij locum esse potuit, quando panes ad illu discipuli detulerunt, ipse illis videntibus eos fregit, ijdem reddidit, & eorundem ministerio in illis distribuendis vsus est? Et vt demus hic aliquid doli fuisse, apud populum tamen hic minimè habuisse locū, quando omnes illi comederunt & saturati sunt. Quod nisi verè factum fuisset, nunquam ad Christum redijssent, quod illos cras tino die fecisse Ioannes scribit. Adde hus reliquias fragmentorum, quae panes illos quinque ad minimum duodecuplo superauerunt, cùm ex illis cophini duodecim impleti fuerint. At quia nobis cum Christianis hominibus res est, omissis istis, miraculi huius vsum inspiciamus, qui praeter id, quod Christi diuinitate asserit, & eum omnium creatorem esse docet, de tribus adhuc cognitu necessarijs nos admonet.
units.tr: But let us come to the matter itself, which he carries out in such a way that his divine power shows itself in every one of its parts. First he orders the disciples to have the people recline, and to arrange them in groups of fifty at each couch. He did this also to make the miracle certain, since the whole crowd could be counted more easily, and confusion was avoided, which would otherwise have thrown the whole business into disorder, while the diners themselves could see one another. The disciples give a remarkable example of Christian obedience. For although it would have seemed ridiculous to make so great a crowd recline when they had nothing at hand but five loaves and two fish, they simply obeyed Christ when he gave this command. Let us imitate them: however absurd what God commands may seem to human judgement, and however little we may be certain of the outcome, let us still render him our duty. For God demands our obedience; he does not take counsel from us, which in divine matters is never fitting. Then, taking the five loaves and two fish, he looked up to heaven and blessed them. It was his constant custom never to take food without giving thanks; yet in the present case the greatness of the matter required a particular gesture, by which those standing by might be roused to a more serious contemplation. He looked up to heaven so that they might conceive nothing merely human here, but might think that all this would be accomplished by heavenly and divine power. Indeed it was altogether necessary to send the disciples back to heaven, since their words show that they had not a little doubted, because of the size of the crowd and the scarcity of provisions. Nor can we have any more present remedy in any distress of affairs than to lift our minds, too intent on earthly things, up to heaven, and to think there that we have a Father whose goodness is immense, whose mercy is inexhaustible, and whose power is invincible. For this consideration easily beats back all the arguments of the flesh by which it assails our faith. Therefore David sings in the Psalms: "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help comes. My help comes from the Maker of heaven and earth." And in the Lord's Prayer we begin: "Our Father, who art in heaven." Moreover, the Lord blessed these loaves and fish, partly to teach that food is given by God's blessing, and partly to commend it by thanksgiving, which alone makes them wholesome for us. By his own example, therefore, he condemns those who do not acknowledge God as the author of all good things, and who come to their tables like swine, neither asking God to give them their sustenance nor giving thanks for it once received. This ingratitude is detestable, since there are so many arguments teaching that the earth is tilled to no purpose unless it is made fruitful by God's blessing. Those who do not recognise this have cast off common sense, and as far as they can they throw away that gift to their own destruction. Christ adds a third thing. He breaks the loaves so that they can be distributed more conveniently among the people, and he hands the broken pieces to the disciples, who set them before those reclining. Meanwhile, by the hidden power of God, the loaves and fish are multiplied in their hands, so that all eat and are satisfied. Here again the truth of the deed is asserted and every suspicion of trickery removed. For where could there be room for trickery, when the disciples brought the loaves to him, he broke them in their sight, gave them back, and used their ministry in distributing them? And even if we grant that there was some deceit here, it could have had no place with the people, since they all ate and were satisfied. Had it not really happened, they would never have come back to Christ, which John writes that they did the next day. Add the remains of the fragments, which exceeded those five loaves at least twelvefold, since twelve baskets were filled with them. But since our business is with Christian people, let us set those things aside and look at the use of this miracle, which, besides asserting the divinity of Christ and teaching that he is the Creator of all, admonishes us of three things that must still be known.

units.la: Primò promissionem suam obsignat atque confirmat Christus, qua dixit: quaerite ante omnia regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia vobis adijcientur. Vt enim non requisitus à quoquam sponte isiorum misertus est, qui ipsum per longa itinera & multo cum labore secuti fuerant, & eos non modò aluit in praesenti, verum etiam domibus eorum benedixit, ne quid damni interea paterentur: Ita nihil vnquam defieri patietur ijs, qui in ipsum credunt, & doctrinae eius obtemperant. Exempla quibus hoc magis probatur, passim in scripturis plurima occurrunt, & huc illud Dauidis pertinet: Iuuenis fui, & nunc senui, nec vidi iustum derelictum, aut posteros eius mendicantes panem. Veruntamen hic meminisse oportet, non semper rerum abundantia aut lautitias pijs obtingere. Non enim quid caro expetat, sed quid toti homini ad salutem aeternam prosit, Deus spectare solet. Quantum ergo nobis satis est largitur, & plerunque, humi discumbentes panibus hordeaceis pascit, id est, ita nos alit & seruat, vt interim carnem natura lasciuientem crucis disciplina in ordinem redigat. Et hoc non ofcitanter obseruari debet, vt primò quidem procul relicta victus & rerum huius seculi foli citudine in Christo sestando constantes simus: deinde verò non regnum terrenum, non otium, non delicias, sed ea in illo quaeramus, quae ad Dei regnum pertinent, neque offendamur crucis amaritudine, qua vitam hanc condiri omnino necesse est.
units.tr: First, Christ confirms and seals his promise, in which he said: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all the rest will be added to you." For he took pity, of his own accord and without being asked by anyone, on those who had followed him over long journeys and with great labour; and he not only fed them for the moment but also blessed their homes, so that they should suffer no loss in the meantime. So he will never allow anything to be lacking to those who believe in him and obey his teaching. Examples proving this more fully occur everywhere in the Scriptures, and to this belongs the saying of David: "I have been young and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging for bread." Yet here we must remember that abundance of things and luxuries do not always fall to the godly. For God usually regards not what the flesh desires, but what profits the whole man for eternal salvation. Therefore he bestows on us what is enough for us, and often feeds us, reclining on the ground, with barley loaves; that is, he so nourishes and preserves us that, meanwhile, the discipline of the cross brings the flesh, wanton by nature, back into order. And this must not be observed carelessly: first, that having put aside the anxious care of food and the affairs of this age, we should be steadfast in resting on Christ; and then that we should seek in him not an earthly kingdom, nor leisure, nor pleasures, but those things which pertain to the kingdom of God, and that we should not be offended by the bitterness of the cross, with which this life must necessarily be seasoned.

units.la: Deinde se panem illum vitae esse docet Christus, qui vt vitam in semetipso habet, ita eam omnibus communicat, qui ipsum fide vera & constanti apprehendunt. Quod igitur veteribus per Manna adumbratum fuit, hoc istos miraculo praesenti docuit, in o etiam hodie nos eius consideratione excitat, vt non alibi quaeramus panem illum viuificum, qui solus ad vitam aeternam alere & seruare potest. Et huc referri debet tota illa concio, quam huius signi occasione apud Ioannem cap.6. habuit. Vbi plurimum proderit, si nosipsos intueamur paulo diligentius. Ibi enim occurret innata nobis vitiositas, quae nos per omnia miseros esse docet, & ita fame bonorum caelestium accendet, quam qui sentiunt, ij demum ad Christum amplectendum verè idonei & instructi sunt.
units.tr: Next, Christ teaches that he is the bread of life, who, as he has life in himself, so he communicates it to all who lay hold of him with true and steadfast faith. What was therefore foreshadowed to the ancients through the manna, this he taught those people by the present miracle, and by considering it he also rouses us today, so that we do not seek that life-giving bread elsewhere, since he alone can feed and preserve us to eternal life. And that whole sermon, which he delivered in John chapter 6 on the occasion of this sign, must be referred to this. There it will greatly profit us if we look at ourselves a little more carefully. For there the inborn vileness that stands in us will meet us, which teaches that we are wretched in every way, and so it kindles hunger for heavenly goods; and only those who feel this hunger are at last truly fit and prepared to embrace Christ.

units.la: Postremò ministerij ecclesiastici typum continet historia ista, quem hoc loco subijci vtilissimum fuit, cum paulò ante discipulis illud demandauisset. Nam etsi solus Christi fit animas famelicas pascere, idem tamen ex hominibus sibi adiutores aut cooperarios deligit, quorum ministerio vtitur. Est haec suprema hominis dignitas, in cuius consideratione ita versari debent ecclesiarum ministri, vt non superbiant, neque pro suo arbitrio aliquid in ecclesia instituant aut mutent. Vt enim Apostoli ex Christi mandato omnia fecerunt, & ex eius manibus acceptos panes atque pisces discumbentibus apposuerunt: Ita qui hodie munus illud ecclesiasticum sustinent, ij ante omnia Christum audire, & quod ex eius ore didicerunt ecclesijs praedicare debent. Admonet de hoc ille quando Apostolus dicit: Docere eos seruare, quae ego vobis tradidi. Nimium ergo confidentes & temerarij sunt, qui in Dei domum alienas epulas inferre audent, & humanis traditionibus infelices animas onerant, quas Euangelij doctrina instruere & consolari debebant. Et haec quidem nunc breuiter perstringimus, quia de illis alibi copiosius est dictum. Discant singuli beneficium hoc Dei agnoscere, qui vt olim filium suum pro nobis tradidit, vt panis vitae nobis fieret: ita illum quotidie per Euangelium nobis propinat, & ad illum recipiendum exhortatur. Accedamus ergo ad mensam illam, vt in ipso saturati cum eodem viuamus & regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, this story contains a figure of the ecclesiastical ministry, which was most useful to set forth here, since a little earlier he had committed that task to the disciples. For although Christ alone undertakes to feed hungry souls, he nevertheless chooses from among men helpers or fellow workers, through whose ministry he acts. This is the highest dignity of man, and with this in view the ministers of the churches ought so to conduct themselves that they do not become proud, nor institute or change anything in the Church at their own pleasure. For just as the Apostles did everything at Christ's command, and set before those reclining the loaves and fish they had received from his hands, so those who today bear that ecclesiastical office ought above all to hear Christ, and to preach to the churches what they have learned from his mouth. The Apostle reminds us of this when he says: "Teach them to observe what I have delivered to you." Therefore those are over-confident and rash who dare to bring their own feasts into God's house, and burden unhappy souls with human traditions, when they ought to instruct and comfort them with the doctrine of the Gospel. We touch on these things only briefly now, because they have been spoken of more fully elsewhere. Let each one learn to acknowledge this benefit of God, who, as he once gave his Son for us, so that he might become the bread of life for us, so every day he sets him before us through the Gospel and exhorts us to receive him. Let us therefore come to that table, so that, satisfied in him, we may live and reign with him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVIII.
units.tr: Homily 88.

units.la: Et factum est cum ipse solus precaretur, erant cum eo discipuli, interrogauitque eos dicens: Quem me dicit esse turba? At ipsi respondentes tes dixerunt: Ioannem Baptistam: alij autem Eliam: alij vero Prophetam quempiam ex antiquis resurrexisse. Dixit autem eis: Vos vero quem me esse dicitis? Respondens autem Petrus dixit: Christum illum Dei. Ipse vero interminatus eis praecepit vt nulli hoc dicerent, dicens: Oportet Filium hominis multa pati, & reprobari a Senioribus & principibus Sacerdotum & Scribis, & trucidari, & tertia die excitari.
units.tr: And it came to pass, as he was alone praying, the disciples were with him, and he asked them, saying: Whom do the crowds say that I am? They answered and said: John the Baptist; but others say Elijah; and others say that one of the old prophets has risen again. He said to them: But who do you say that I am? Peter answered and said: The Christ of God. But he sternly charged them and ordered them to tell this to no one, saying: The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and rise again on the third day.

units.la: Q Voniam Deus vitam & salutem omnem in Filio suo vnigenito comprehensam esse voluit, in huius etiā cognitione tota salutis consequendae ratio consistit. Docuit hoc olim Isaias de Christo dicens: Cognitione sui iustificabit multos iustus seruus meus. Et ipse apud Ioannem inquit: Haec est, Pater, vita aeterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Quae causa est, quod eius notitiam Deus iam inde a prima rerum origine patribus manifestauit, & quod ipse postquam homo factus est, non solum doctrina, verumetiam operibus miraculosis publice testatus est, se eum esse, cuius merito humanum genus redimi atq; seruari oporteat. At quamuis simplex & facilis eius sit cognitio, multa tamen Satan obijcit, quibus eam difficilem & obscuram reddat: imo ipsi homines sibi suis commentis nebulas offundunt, quibus impediti illum videre non possunt. Quod ijs etiā accidisse scimus, quos ex toto mortalium genere selectos sibi discipulos domesticos fecerat. Ideo vt saepe alias, ita in praesenti quoque illos diligentissime instituit. Est q; locus hic multa consideratione dignissimus, vt qui omnia plene continet, quae nos in vera & perfecta Iesu Christi cognitione possunt instruere. Primo enim falsas, quae tunc inter Iudaeos ferebantur, multorum de illo sententias proponit. Deinde vera & orthodoxa illius confessio subijcitur, quae Apostolicae doctrinae summam continet.
