Tertio ipse Christus redemptionis nostrae modum omnem explicat, & quid in ipso maxime spectari debeat, docet.
units.tr: Since God willed that all life and salvation should be contained in his only-begotten Son, the whole way of obtaining salvation also rests on the knowledge of him. Isaiah long ago taught this about Christ, saying: "By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many." And John says: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." This is why God made known the knowledge of him from the very beginning of the world to the fathers, and why, after he became man, he testified publicly, not only by his teaching but also by his miraculous works, that he is the one by whose merit the human race ought to be redeemed and saved. Yet although his knowledge is simple and easy, Satan throws many things in the way to make it difficult and obscure; indeed, men themselves cast mists over it with their own inventions, so that, hindered by them, they cannot see him. We know that this happened even to those whom he had chosen from the whole human race and made his household disciples. So, as he often did elsewhere, he instructed them with the greatest care on this occasion too. This passage deserves very careful consideration, since it fully contains everything that can teach us the true and perfect knowledge of Jesus Christ. First, he sets out the false opinions of many people about him, which were then current among the Jews. Second, the true and orthodox confession of him is set before us, which contains the sum of apostolic doctrine. Third, Christ himself explains the whole manner of our redemption and teaches what must chiefly be regarded in him.

units.la: Facit autem ad huius doctrinae commendationem, quod Lucas Christum prius precatu fuisse scribit. Ex eo enim apparet, ipsum nihil hic temere fecisse, sed vt de his ageret, feria sua vocationis meditatione fuisse excitatum. Et quia ipse precibus minime opus habebat, ideoq; pro discipulis suis orare solitus fuit, procul dubio inter precandum imbecillitatis, qua laborabant, recordatus, huic remedium adhibere, & ab omni errore mentes eorum liberare voluit. Ideo fidi & periti medici instar a morbi cognitione orditur, & falsa de se vulgi iudicia arguit. Nam discipulos interrogat, dicens: Quem me esse dicit turba? Vbi nemo putauerit, quaestionis huius causam fuisse vel ignorantiam vel ambitionem. Quomodo enim vulgi sermones & quae publice ferebantur ignoraret, qui ipsas quoque cordium cogitationes nouerat, vt non vno exemplo docuit? Aut cur populari aura delectaretur, qui sponte se ad infimi mortalis sortem demiserat, & qui diserte testatur, se ab homine testimonium non accipere? Hoc ergo potius spectauit, vt quae ex diuersis de ipso hominum sententijs nascebantur, scandala e medio tolleret, vtq; discipulos in vera & certa fide confirmaret, ne incertis opinionibus se quoque abripi paterentur. Ideo non contentus ista quaestione, mox quid ipsi sentiant quaerit, & ita verae fidei confessionem ex illorum ore elicit.
units.tr: Moreover, it serves to commend this teaching that Luke writes that Christ had first been praying. For from this it appears that he did nothing here rashly, but was stirred up by reflection on his calling to deal with these matters. And since he had no need of prayers himself, but was accustomed to pray for his disciples, no doubt while praying he remembered the weakness under which they labored, and wished to apply a remedy to it and free their minds from every error. Therefore, like a faithful and skilled physician, he begins with knowledge of the disease and refutes the false judgments of the common people about himself. For he asks the disciples, saying: Whom do the crowds say that I am? Here no one should think that the cause of this question was either ignorance or ambition. For how could he be ignorant of the talk of the crowd and what was publicly rumored, when he knew even the thoughts of hearts, as he showed on more than one occasion? Or why would he delight in popular applause, when he had of his own accord lowered himself to the lot of the lowliest mortal, and when he plainly declares that he does not receive testimony from man? Rather, his purpose was this: to remove from the midst the scandals that arose from the various opinions of men about him, and to confirm the disciples in the true and certain faith, so that they would not allow themselves to be carried away by uncertain opinions. Therefore, not content with that question, he immediately asks what they themselves think, and so draws out from their mouth the confession of the true faith.

units.la: Est autem obseruatu dignum exemplum Christi, qui aliorum de se iudicia audire vult, neque discipulos haec ipsi exponentes reijcit, quin potius vt ea narrent inuitat. Debent hoc ipsum facere omnes homines, & in primis quidem ij, qui alijs praesunt, vt ita de vitijs suis admoneantur, & quid correctione opus habeat intelligant. Quia enim nosipsos diligimus, paucos esse inuenire, qui nauos suos agnoscant: & cum hoc quoque dissimulent plerunque amici, multi etiam seruiliter nobis adulentur, vt vitia nostra ex alijs discamus necesse est. Viderunt hoc gentium philosophi, qui hanc vtilitatem ex inimicis captare docuerunt, vt eorum conuitijs excitati de illis emendandis cogitemus, quae in nobis reprehensione digna sunt. Neque imprudenter faciunt principes nonnulli, qui interdum mutato habitu cum plebeis hominibus conuersantur, & horum de ipsis sermones obseruant. Ea enim occasione de multis admonentur, quae ex suis aulicis nunquam audirent. Curent modo ijdem, ne indignius ferant liberas quorundam voces, & de suis potius moribus corrigendis, quam alijs puniendis cogitent. Quod autem Apostolos de iis Christus interrogat, co ministros Ecclesiarum omnes admonet, non satis esse, si qualemcunque habeant verae doctrinae cognitionem, sed nem, sed vt falsas & erroneas quoque de religione aliorum sententias norint requiri: nimirum, vt de his suae fidei creditos admonere & errores confutare possint. Est id hodie cumprimis necessarium, quando & veteres haereses multi instaurant, & insuper noua absurdissimarum opinionum portenta pariunt.
units.tr: The example of Christ is worth noting: he wishes to hear the judgments of others about himself, and he does not reject the disciples when they report these things, but rather invites them to tell them. All men ought to do this, and especially those who govern others, so that they may be admonished about their faults and understand what needs correcting. For since we love ourselves, it is hard to find few who recognize their own blemishes; and since friends too often conceal them, and many even flatter us slavishly, we must of necessity learn our faults from others. The philosophers of the nations saw this, and they taught us to draw this benefit even from enemies, so that, roused by their reproaches, we may think about correcting the things in us that deserve blame. Some princes do not act unwisely when, sometimes changing their dress, they mix with common people and observe what these say about them. For on such an occasion they are admonished about many things that they would never hear from their courtiers. Let them only take care not to bear too impatiently the frank words of some men, and to think about correcting their own morals rather than punishing others. As for the fact that Christ asks the apostles about these matters, he thereby admonishes all ministers of the churches that it is not enough for them to have some knowledge of true doctrine, but that they should also know the false and erroneous opinions of others about religion, namely so that they may be able to admonish those entrusted to their faith about these things and refute errors. This is especially necessary today, since many revive the old heresies and, in addition, bring forth new monstrosities of most absurd opinions.

units.la: Sed Apostolos audiamus, qui ad propositam quaestionem liberè & fortiter respondent, nosque suo exemplo docent, ne cui turpiter adulemur. Vt enim animi ignaui argumentum est in aliorum gratiam mentiri: ita inter magnates non alia nocentior est pestis, quam ea apud illos dissimulare, quae ipsos scire in primis oportebat. Quod si ijdem falsis laudibus demententur, tam nullus correctioni locus fit reliquus. Et constat multos principibus exitium attulisse, quod populi querelas & optimorum de se iudicia ignorarunt. Quoad autem Apostolos, non aliud respondent, quam quod supra audiuimus in omnium ore fuisse. Alij (inquiunt) te Ioannem Baptistam esse aiunt, alij autem Eliam: alij vero Prophetam quempiam ex antiquis resurrexisse. Sunc haec sententiae multum inter se diuersae, in hoc tamen conueniunt, quod ex eodem παλιγγενεσίας errore promanant, quem inter Iudaeos tunc vul go obtinuisse supra diximus. Tanta enim est errorum fecunditas, vt vnus aliquis admissus mox infinitos alios pariat, & nihil non sibi ipsis in figmentis suis permittunt, qui semel à vero recesserunt. Ita vero tunc de Christo senserunt melior pars hominum, in quibus aliquae religionis puriorís scintillae adhuc reliquae erant, & ecclesiae mox renascituræ seminarium videri poterant. Ioannem enim aliqui esse putant propter doctrinae similitudinem, & quod eius spiritum ex animae regeneratione nouis viribus aut donis auctum esse suspicantur. Alij autem Eliam dicunt, quod eadem arguendi libertate eum in omnes inuehi viderent, qua olim Elias vsus est. Multi Ieremiam vel quemcunque alium ex veterum prophetarum numero fingunt, quod non vulgaria spiritus dona in illo compararent. Certè omnes illi virtutem singularem in illo agnoscunt. Quam multi autem interea fuerunt, qui de illo pessimè senserunt? Pharisaei enim & Scribae eum modo Samaritanum esse, modò daemonio agitari, modo publicanorum amicum & omnis nequitiae patronum esse dicunt. Plerique autem impostorem & seditionum authorem esse clamant, & hoc nomine eum apud Pilati tribunal accusarunt.
units.tr: But let us hear the apostles, who answer the question put to them freely and boldly, and teach us by their example not to flatter anyone shamefully. For just as lying to win the favor of others is a sign of a cowardly spirit, so among great men there is no more harmful plague than to conceal from them the things they above all ought to know. If they are soothed by false praises, then no room is left for correction. And it is well established that many have brought ruin upon princes because they were ignorant of the complaints of the people and of the judgments of the best men about them. As for the apostles, they answer nothing other than what we heard above was on everyone's lips: "Some say you are John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others that one of the old prophets has risen again." These opinions are very different from one another, yet they agree in this, that they all spring from the same error of rebirth [palingenesias, παλιγγενεσίας], which we said above was then widespread among the Jews. For the fruitfulness of error is so great that, once one error is admitted, it soon gives birth to countless others, and those who have once departed from the truth allow themselves every license in their inventions. Thus the better part of men thought of Christ at that time, in whom some remaining sparks of purer religion still survived, and who could seem to be the seedbed of a church soon to be reborn. For some thought he was John, on account of the likeness of his teaching, and they suspected that his spirit, renewed in the regeneration of the soul, had been enriched with new powers or gifts. Others said he was Elijah, because they saw him inveighing against all with the same freedom of rebuke that Elijah once used. Many imagined he was Jeremiah or some other of the number of the old prophets, because they perceived in him unusual gifts of the Spirit. Certainly all of them recognized a singular power in him. But how many, meanwhile, were there who thought very badly of him? For the Pharisees and scribes said that he was now a Samaritan, now possessed by a demon, now a friend of publicans and a patron of every wickedness. Many, moreover, cried out that he was an impostor and a author of sedition, and on this charge they accused him before the tribunal of Pilate.

units.la: At quod illo tempore factum est, ab ipsa rerum origine omnibus seculis factum fuisse constat: vt nimirum variae de religione hominum sententiae fuerint, ex quibus sectae diuersae enatae sunt. Quia enim homo animalis non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei, externis solis ducitur, & pro suo arbitrio sibi Deum aut salutis rationem fabricat. Vehementer ergo errant, qui hodie dissidiis offenduntur, quae inter doctrinae Euangelicae instauratores exortae in hunc vsque diem glisc unt: neque se Euangelio credituros esse aiunt, donec omnes eos, qui huius professione gloriantur, idem sentire & loqui videant. Quid vero si illi omnes in errore aliquo consentirent, an tunc in illorum partes vellent concedere? Vel num Iudaeos illi excusabunt, qui indomita pertinacia Christum reiecerunt? Non opinor. Atqui hi quoque sententiarum de Christo diuersitatem praetexere poterant. Non igitur quid homines sentiant & loquantur spectare debemus, sed quid Deus dicat, & quid vs nobis in Filio suo polliceatur. Et si consensum quaerimus, cui tutò possimus niti; ad scripturam sacram oculos conuertamus; quae nobis Patriarchas, Mosem, Prophetas, Apostolos & innumeros veri Dei cultores atque amicos proponit, qui omnes vno ore & corde confessi sunt, salutem in vno Messia contineri, qui Adamo promissus olim, tandem praefinito tempore ex virgine homo factus, nos cum Deo Patre in gratiam reduxit. His nos coniungamus & non fallemur. Quoad autem infelicis mundi de religione iudicia, neminem hac offendere aut in fide impedire debent. Nam vt Paulus ait, oportet sectas esse, vt qui probati sunt manifesti fiant: & iusto Dei iudicio fit, vt qui in religione ludunt, dum pro sua libidine sibi dogmata fingunt, errorum Labyrinthis impliciti in diuersas partes scindantur. Adde hiis, quod nouissimis temporibus non doctores modò falsos, sed Christos quoque falsos exorituros esse Dominus praedixit. Non ergo nouum aut insolens est, quod hodie fieri videmus, quin potius si verum fateri libeat, hoc proprium & germanum est Euangelij renascentis indicium, quod eius progressum dissidijs intestinis Satan conatur impedire. Etenim in aliis religionibus facile sese mutuo ferunt, qui quoad dogmata & ritus differunt; at qui Euangelium profitentur, maiori animorum contentione inter se pugnant, quàm primum dissensionis speciem aliquam incidit. Quam verò eius
units.tr: But what happened in that time has happened in every age since the very beginning of things: there have naturally been various opinions among men about religion, from which different sects have arisen. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, but is led only by externals, and fashions for himself a God or a way of salvation according to his own judgment. Those therefore err greatly who today are offended by the disagreements that have arisen among the restorers of evangelical doctrine and have grown worse down to this day, and who say that they will not believe the Gospel until they see all who boast of professing it think and speak alike. But what if they all agreed in some error? Would they then be willing to side with them? Or will they excuse the Jews, who in unbending obstinacy rejected Christ? I think not. Yet those Jews too could have pleaded the diversity of opinions about Christ. We ought therefore to look not at what men think and say, but at what God says and what he promises us in his Son. And if we seek agreement on which we can safely rely, let us turn our eyes to holy Scripture, which sets before us the patriarchs, Moses, the prophets, the apostles, and countless worshippers and friends of the true God, who all confessed with one mouth and one heart that salvation is contained in the one Messiah, who was promised to Adam long ago, and who, at last, at the appointed time, was made man of a virgin and reconciled us to God the Father. If we join ourselves to these, we shall not be deceived. As for the judgments of the unhappy world about religion, they ought to offend or hinder no one in faith. For, as Paul says, there must be sects, so that those who are approved may be made manifest; and by the just judgment of God it comes about that those who trifle in religion, while they invent doctrines to suit their own lust, become entangled in the labyrinths of error and are torn into different parties. Add to this that in the last times the Lord foretold that not only false teachers but also false Christs would arise. Therefore what we see happening today is not new or strange; indeed, if we are willing to speak the truth, this is the proper and genuine sign of the renewed Gospel, that Satan tries to hinder its progress by internal dissensions. For in other religions, those who differ in doctrine and rites easily tolerate one another; but those who profess the Gospel fight among themselves with greater heat of mind as soon as any appearance of disagreement arises. And what the cause of this is we shall assign

units.la: Matth. 24. rei causam assiguabimus. Eam nimirum,quod alteros illos facile fert Satan, quando simul omnes à veritatis scopo aberrant. Inter hos autem dissidia excitat & fovet, ne coniunctis viribus regnum ipsius oppugnent atq; evertant.
units.tr: Matth. 24. This, namely: Satan easily bears with the others when they all wander together from the mark of the truth; but among these he stirs up and fosters dissensions, so that they may not join their strength to attack and overthrow his kingdom.

units.la: Quapropter ad alteram huius loci partem accedamus, quæ vera & orthodoxæ fidei confessionem continet. Pergit enim Christus & ait: Quem vero vos me esse dicitis? Non vult ergo, vt interrea dubij & rerum incerti pendeant discipuli, dum reliqui in diuersas partes abeunt, deq; ipso inter se altercantur. Neque etiam illi negotium hoc differendum censent, donec vel alteri illi omnes in vnum conueniant aut publica Sacerdotum atq; Seniorum authoritate decernatur, quid omnes sen tire & credere debeant. Sed mox omnium nomine Petrus respondet, dicens: Tu es Christus ille Dei. Apud Matthæum vero alteram quoq; partem addit: Filius Dei viuentis. Prima parte officium eius definit, & quid nobis in illo datum sit, docet. Tu es (inquit) Christus ille Dei. At Christi vox Vnctum significat, quo nomine olim Reges & Sacerdotes denotabantur, eò quod vnctione solenni initiarentur. Ita vero promissum humani generis Seruatorem scripturæ vocant, quod is regis & Sacerdotis instar omnia ea perfecerit, quæ ad nostram redemptionem pertinebant. De quibus cum iam sæpius dictum sit, nolumus eadem hic repetere. Hoc tamen notatu dignum est, quod non absq; Emphasi dicit: Tu es Christus ille Dei. Nam Christos Dei olim dicebant Reges, quos ipse Deus peculiari gratia in eam dignitatem euexerat: & ea appellatione illis Spiritus authoritatem concilia-bat, ne quis eos laedere aut contemptius tractare auderet. Quo Dauid respiciens Saulem vnctum Domini dixit, quoties rationem reddebat, cur illi manum inferre nollet. Docet ergo Petrus Iesum hunc illum ipsum Christum, id est, Regem & Sacerdotem esse, quem Deus Pater æterno suo consilio ad hoc munus destinarit, & de quo iam inde ab æterno dictum sit: Ego constitui Regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum. Item: Tu es Sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchizedech. Altera parte Filium Dei viuentis (id est, veri Dei, qui nihil cum fictitijs gentium Dijs mutuo, eorundem simulachris commune habeat) esse dicit. Atqui non ignorabat, eum ex Maria hominem factum esse, & ipsum se Filium hominis appellare quotidie audiebat. Itaq; in illo aliquid homine maius agnoscit, & eum esse credit, qui ab æterno quidem Dei Filius verus & Patri coessentialis sit, constituto autem tempore hominem propter nos induerit, vt quæ propria sunt redemptoris at que Mediatoris officia pro nobis obire posset. Et hæc quidem fides vera atq; Apostolica est, quam ex Patris cælestis reuelatione Petrus didicit (vt apud Matthæum ipse Christus testatur) & quam Apostoli simul omnes in toto orbe terrarum prædicauerunt. Consentiunt huic summæ, quæ nos hodie in Symbolo quod Apostolicum dicunt, profitemur. Hæc denique catholica, id est, vniuersalis fides dicitur, eò quod omnium locorum atq; temporum credentibus communis sit, qui per illam simul omnes in vnam ecclesiam coalescunt, cuius caput, sponsus, Rex & Sacerdos est æternus ille Dei Filius de quo hic agitur. In hac ergo fide acquiescant, quicunq; seruari volunt, nec eorum iniquis iudiciis moueantur, qui nos hodie hæreseos damnant, quod præter vnum Iesum Christum nolumus alium Regem & Sacerdotem agnoscere.
units.tr: Let us therefore come to the other part of this passage, which contains the confession of the true and orthodox faith. For Christ goes on and says: "But who do you say that I am?" He does not wish the disciples to remain meanwhile doubtful and uncertain of the matter while the rest go off in different directions and quarrel among themselves about him. Nor do they think this matter should be put off until either all the others come together into one view, or it is decided by the public authority of the priests and elders what all ought to think and believe. But straightway Peter answers in the name of all, saying: "You are that Christ of God." In Matthew he adds also the other part: "the Son of the living God." In the first part he defines his office and teaches what has been given us in him. "You are," he says, "that Christ of God." Now the word Christ means "Anointed," the name by which kings and priests were formerly designated, because they were installed with a solemn anointing. Thus the Scriptures call the promised Saviour of mankind by this name, because, like a king and a priest, he has accomplished all those things which pertain to our redemption. Since these things have been said many times already, we do not wish to repeat them here. Yet this is worth noting, that he says it not without emphasis: "You are that Christ of God." For kings were once called "Christs of God," those whom God himself had raised to that dignity by a special grace; and by that title the Spirit gave them authority, so that no one would dare to harm them or treat them with contempt. Looking to this, David said of Saul, "the anointed of the Lord," whenever he gave the reason why he was unwilling to lay hands on him. Peter therefore teaches that this Jesus is that very Christ, that is, the King and Priest whom God the Father has destined for this office by his eternal counsel, and of whom it has been said from eternity: "I have set my King upon my holy hill of Zion." Likewise: "You are a Priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek." In the other part he says that he is the Son of the living God (that is, of the true God, who has nothing in common with the fictitious gods of the nations, nor with their images). Yet he was not ignorant that he had been made man from Mary, and he heard himself daily called the Son of Man. Therefore he recognises in him something greater than man, and believes him to be the one who, being from eternity the true Son of God and co-essential with the Father, at the appointed time put on humanity for our sake, so that he might perform for us the proper offices of Redeemer and Mediator. And this faith is indeed true and apostolic, which Peter learned from the revelation of the heavenly Father (as Christ himself testifies in Matthew), and which all the apostles together preached throughout the whole world. To this sum agree the things we profess today in the creed that they call the Apostles' Creed. Finally, this faith is called catholic, that is, universal, because it is common to believers of every place and time, through which all are joined together into one Church, whose head, bridegroom, King and eternal Priest is that Son of God of whom we are speaking here. Let therefore those who wish to be saved rest in this faith, and let them not be moved by the unjust judgments of those who today condemn us as heretics because we will not acknowledge any other King and Priest besides the one Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Cæterum non sufficit hæc obiter nouisse, & eandem cum Petro fidei confessionem edere; sed borum vsum probè tenere oportet, qui triplex est. Primus, vt in vno hoc Christo omnem spem & fiduciam habeamus collocatam, neq; alibi quæramus ea, quæ nostra salutis sunt. Et huc Petri dictum pertinet, quod Ioan. 6. ca. habetur. Cum enim multi à Christo deficientibus hic discipulos interrogaret. Num & vos abibitis? Respondit ille: Ah Domine, quo ibimus? Tu verba vitæ æternæ habes, &c. Talé ergo Sacerdotem & Regem agnouit Christum, qui solus seruare & vitam conferre possit. Et hoc dictum nos hodie opponamus iis, qui nos ad defectionem à fide aut Euangelio solicitant. Monstrent illi nobis aliū præter Christū, qui pro nobis homo factus & in crucem suffixus est, qui item in scripturis vitam conferre dicatur. Nec est quod salutis rationem mutata dicant. Est enim Christus sacerdos æternus, & regni eius non est finis: & in æternum Dei consilium peccant, quicunq; illum vel asper nantur, vel ipsi debitū honorem aut officium superstitiose in quoscunq; alios transferunt. Alter vsus est, vt fide hanc obedientiā fidelis studio testemur. Debebatur hæc olim Sacerdotibus: Legē (inquit Malachias) ex ore Sacerdotis requirent. Et apud Mosem capitalis pœna iis statuitur, qui summi Pontificis sententia contradicere audent. Debetur etiā obedientia regibus & omnibus qui Remp. administrant, vt prolixè Paulus ad Rom.docet. Quantò magis ergo eam Christo, summo & aeterno Pontifici debemus, de quo Pater coelicus pronunciauit, Hunc audite? Aut cur illa regi regum & aeterno Dei Filio negaremus, de quo Dauid regibus dicit: Prudenter agite ô reges, erudimini iudices terrae. Seruite Domino in timore, & exultate in tremore. Osculamini Filium, ne forte irascatur & pereatis in via, &c. Tertio consolationi seruit haec fidei confessio in tentationibus. Sunt harum duo genera. Primum ex peccatis nascitur, & proprie ad conscientiam spectat. Sentiunt hoc, quibus Satan persuadere conatur, Deum non fore illis propitium, sed in peccatis perituros esse. Hi ad Christum Sacerdotem recurrant, qui vt vna victima totius mundi peccatum expiauit: Ita fidelis pontifex est, & eadem nobiscum infirmitates expertus (excepto tamen peccato) nobis condolere potest. Ad hunc nos Ioannes remittit scribens: Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud Deum, Iesum Christum, iustum: & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, &c. Quin ipse in Euangelio clamat: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego vos refocillabo. Alterum tentationum genus ex cruce externa nascitur, ad quod morbi, egestas, fames, persecutiones, exilia, bella & quaecunque alia sunt huius generis pertinent. His nos Christum regem opponere debemus, cui omnis potestas in coelo & in terris data est. Hic ergo morbis omnibus mederi poterit, quod infinitis exemplis olim te statuus est. Idem suos alit in ipsa rerum inopia, quod Apostoli sine viatico & commeatu ab eo ablegati, experti sunt. Idem nobis in coelo patriam & sedes firmas parauit, quarum possessione nunquam erient qui nobis terram negant. Adhaec cum Dominus exercituum sit, ecclesiam suam & singula eius membra aduersus diabolum & mundum tueri poterit: quod se facturum esse non vno loco promisit, et iam ab ipso rerum exordio in hunc vsque diem fidelissimè praestitit. Huius denique vox est: Ne timeas pusille grex, quoniam Patri placuit tibi dare regnum. In hoc ergo constantes simus, neque vllis tentationum procellis nos à fidei in illum confessione abstrerri patiamur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not enough to know these things in passing and to make the same confession of faith as Peter; we must also hold fast to the use of them, which is threefold. The first is that we place all our hope and trust in this one Christ, and do not seek elsewhere those things which pertain to our salvation. To this belongs the saying of Peter in John 6, where, when many fell away from Christ, he asked the disciples: "Will you also go away?" He answered: "Ah, Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life," and so on. Thus he acknowledged Christ as such a Priest and King, the only one who can save and bestow life. And let us today set this saying against those who urge us to fall away from the faith or the Gospel. Let them show us anyone other than Christ, who was made man for us and was fastened to the cross, who is likewise said in the Scriptures to bestow life. Nor is there any reason for them to say that the way of salvation has been changed. For Christ is an eternal Priest, and of his kingdom there is no end; and they sin against the eternal counsel of God who either disparage him or superstitiously transfer to any others the honour and office due to him alone. The second use is that we bear witness by faithful zeal to this obedience which we owe through faith. This was once owed to priests: "They shall seek the law at the mouth of the priest," says Malachi; and in Moses the death penalty is appointed for those who dare to contradict the sentence of the high priest. Obedience is also owed to kings and to all who administer the commonwealth, as Paul teaches at length in Romans. How much more then ought we to render it to Christ, the highest and eternal High Priest, of whom the heavenly Father pronounced, "Hear him"? Or why should we deny it to the King of kings and the eternal Son of God, of whom David says to kings: "Be wise now, O kings; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish in the way," and so on. The third use of this confession serves for consolation in temptations. There are two kinds of these. The first arises from sins and properly concerns the conscience. Those feel this to whom Satan tries to persuade that God will not be propitious to them, but that they will perish in their sins. These run back to Christ the Priest, who, as the one sacrifice, expiated the sin of the whole world; so he is a faithful high priest, and, having experienced the same infirmities as we (apart from sin), is able to sympathise with us. John sends us back to him when he writes: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins," and so on. Indeed, in the Gospel he himself cries out: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." The other kind of temptation arises from external affliction, to which belong sickness, want, hunger, persecutions, exiles, wars, and whatever else is of this sort. Against these we ought to set Christ as King, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given. He therefore can heal all diseases, as he showed long ago by infinite examples. He feeds his own even in utter poverty, as the apostles, who were sent out by him without provision or supplies, found. He has also prepared for us a homeland and firm dwellings in heaven, the possession of which those can never be deprived of who deny us earth. Moreover, since he is the Lord of hosts, he will be able to defend his Church and each of its members against the devil and the world; and he promised that he would do this in more than one place, and from the very beginning of things down to this day he has most faithfully performed it. Finally, this is his voice: "Fear not, little flock, for it is the Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." Let us therefore be steadfast in this, and let us not allow ourselves to be torn away from our confession of faith in him by any storms of temptation.

units.la: Facit ad horum explicationem tertia huius loci pars, quam priusquam executiamur, obseruari debet, quod Christus non sine graui interminatione discipulis praecipit, ne cui dicerent, quod nunc de ipso confessi fuerant. Poterat hoc mirum videri, cum confessionem illam (vt in Matthaeo scribitur) magnificè commendauerit, & paulo post omnes horteretur, ne fidem in ipsum ignauo & ignobili metu dissimulent. At non mirabimur, si quales tunc fuerint discipuli cogitemus. Nam etsi illum mundi seruatorem esse agnoscerent, magna tamen erat fidei ipsorum infirmitas atq; imperfectio: cum & regnum terrenum in illo somniarent, & redemptionis humanae modum nondum intelligerent, neq; etiam Spiritus sancti donis adhuc satis essent instructi. Ad tempus ergo illos silere voluit, ne seipsos & fidei doctrinam aduersariorum ludibriis exponant, & vt ipsi interea in fide magis confirmentur. Quo loco decemur non statim ad docendum idoneos esse, qui fidem in Christum verè confitentur, sed praeter dona illa peculiaria, quibus verbi administros oportet instructos esse, vocationem quoq; legitimam requiri, de qua nuper plura diximus.
units.tr: This part of the passage, the third, helps to explain these matters, and before we take it up it must be noted that Christ, under a severe threat, forbids the disciples to tell anyone what they had just confessed about him. This might seem strange, since he had praised that confession so highly (as Matthew writes) and shortly afterwards urged them all not to hide their faith in him out of cowardly and base fear. But we will not wonder if we consider what kind of disciples they then were. For although they recognised him as the Saviour of the world, their faith was still very weak and imperfect: they dreamed of an earthly kingdom in him, did not yet understand the manner of human redemption, and were not yet sufficiently equipped with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He therefore wished them to keep silent for the time, so that they would not expose themselves and the doctrine of faith to the mockery of their adversaries, and so that they might be more firmly established in the faith in the meantime. Here we learn that those who truly confess faith in Christ are not at once fit to teach; besides those special gifts with which ministers of the Word ought to be equipped, a lawful calling is also required, about which we have spoken at length recently.

units.la: Quia vero errorem & ignorantiam, qua discipuli tenebantur, non ignorabat Christus remedium adhibet, & longè aliam regni atq; sacerdotij sui conditionem esse docet, quàm ipsi imaginabatur. Oportet (inquit) filium hominis multa pati, & reprobari à Senioribus & principibus Sacerdotum & Scribis, & tertia die excitari. Quibus verbis non modo quid ipsi euenturum sit, docet, sed haec ita fieri oportere testatur: nimirum, quod sic Patri visum sit, cuius consilio non possit nō obtemperare. Quod ipsum post resurrectionem quoq; apertius indicat, quando duobus discipulis Emaunte euntibus, qui eius morte non parum offensi fuerant, ait: O amentes & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus quae locuti sunt Prophetae: Nonne haec oportuit pati Christum, & intrare in gloriam suam? Et paulo post illis omnibus congregatis inquit: Hi sunt sermones quos locutus sum ad vos, cum adhuc esse vobiscum, quod scilicet oporteret impleri omnia, quae scripta sunt in lege Mosis, & Prophetis & Psalmis de me: Ita enim scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere à mortuis tertio die. Quapropter hic quoq; ad Patris decretum discipulos remittit, quasi diceret: Vos quidem me regem illum pro missum esse agnoscitis, & in me vobis regnum in hoc mundo, opibus & victoriis illustre pollicemini in quo nō postrema gloria & felicitatis pars ad vos redeat. At longè alia est regni mei ratio et mul to aliter de hoc toto humanae redemptionis negotio Pater statuit. Tam enim abest, vt regnum in hoc seculo obtineat, quale vos somniatis, vt potius me multa pati, à discipulo prodi, & quod omnium indi gnissimŭ est) ab illis ipsis reprobari & damnari oporteat, qui me præ aliis amplectì, & omnę populum ad me amplectendum excitare debebant. Veruntamę nolim vos, si ista fiant, animo deiici & offendi. Non enim istud modo Pater decreuit, sed vt hostibus meis & ipsa etiā morte superior fa t tertia die resurgam & regnum mihi promissum obtineam. Adista igitur certamina vos præparare, neq; huius seculi honores, opes, voluptates, sed bona cœlestia & æterna in me quærere debetis.
units.tr: Since Christ knew the error and ignorance in which the disciples were held, he applies a remedy and teaches that the condition of his kingdom and priesthood is quite different from what they imagined. "It is necessary," he says, "that the Son of Man suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be raised on the third day." By these words he not only tells them what will happen to him, but testifies that these things must so come about: plainly because it has seemed good to the Father, whose counsel they cannot refuse to obey. He indicates this even more clearly after the resurrection, when he said to the two disciples going to Emmaus, who had been not a little offended by his death: "O foolish men and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?" And shortly afterwards, gathering them all together, he said: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, namely that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me. For so it is written, and so it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again from the dead on the third day." Wherefore here too he sends the disciples back to the Father's decree, as if to say: You indeed acknowledge that I am the king sent, and you promise yourselves a kingdom in me in this world, glorious with riches and victories, in which no small share of glory and happiness would return to you. But the plan of my kingdom is far different, and the Father has determined this whole business of human redemption in quite another way. For he is so far from my obtaining a kingdom in this age, such as you dream of, that rather I must suffer many things, be betrayed by a disciple, and (which is most unworthy of all) be rejected and condemned by those very men who ought to have embraced me above others and stirred up all the people to embrace me. Nevertheless I would not have you, if these things come to pass, be cast down and offended in spirit. For this is not all the Father has decreed, but that I, superior to my enemies and even to death itself, will rise on the third day and obtain the kingdom promised to me. You must therefore prepare yourselves for these struggles, and seek in me not the honours, riches and pleasures of this age, but heavenly and eternal goods.

units.la: In hunc finem potissimum ista dicuntur: at simul his omnem nostræ redemptionis modum aut rationem comprehendit, quæ ferè tota in eius morte & resurrectione consistit. Mors ad sacerdotiū pertinet. In illa enim sese pro peccatis totius mundi victimam Deo patri obtulit, & ijs expiatus iustitia diuina satis fecit, vt quam nos merueramus, pœnā à nobis auerteret. Resurrectio autem ad regni sui complementum facit. Ea enim mortem deuicit, aculeum mortis sustulit & confregit, inferorum portas euertit, denique se vitæ & mortis Dominum esse ostendit. Et debent ista communi inter docendū, vt in morte quidem Christi peccatorum nostrorum expiationem nobis repositam esse intelligamus, ex resurrectione autem consolationem capiamus, quæ & crucis scandalo medeatur, & non aduersus mortis atque inferorum terrores confirmet. Recte igitur Paulus ad Romanos scribit: Si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominū Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus illum excitarit à mortuis, saluus eris. Accedit duobus istis triumphi loco gloriosa ascensio, qua assumptam ex nobis carnem in cœlos euexit ad dexteram Dei, vt hos quoq; nobis aperiret, & locu parareț, vbi nos cum ipso æternum viuamus atq; regnemus. Et hæc sunt, quæ vnanimi consensu Apostoli prædicarunt, quorum doctrina hodie etiam in ecclesijs retineri & absq; omni humanarum traditionum fermento proponi debet. Singuli autem hæc ita considerent, vt procul relictis diuersis multorum de religione & salutis negotio sententijs, vnum Iesum Christum agnoscant, Regem & Sacerdotem suum, qui propter nostra peccata mortuus & propter iustificationem nostram ex mortuis suscitatus, nunc ad dexteram Dei patris pro nobis intercedit. Huic ita fidant, vt simul ipsi quoq; peccatis quotidie moriantur, resurgant autem cum illo ad vitam nouam & cœlestem, quam emensi tandem ad ipsum colligantur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: It is chiefly for this purpose that these things are said; yet at the same time he comprehends in them the whole manner or plan of our redemption, which consists almost entirely in his death and resurrection. The death pertains to the priesthood. For in it he offered himself to God the Father as a victim for the sins of the whole world, and by it, having been made an expiation, he satisfied divine justice, so that he turned away from us the punishment we had deserved. The resurrection, however, brings his kingdom to its completion. For by it he overcame death, took away and broke the sting of death, overthrew the gates of hell, and finally showed himself to be Lord of life and death. These things ought to be taught together, so that we understand that in the death of Christ the expiation of our sins has been laid up for us, and from the resurrection we take comfort, which both heals the scandal of the cross and strengthens us against the terrors of death and hell. Rightly therefore Paul writes to the Romans: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." To these two there is added, as a kind of triumph, the glorious ascension, by which he carried the flesh he had taken from us up into heaven, to the right hand of God, so that he might open these things to us also and prepare a place where we may live and reign with him eternally. These are the things which the Apostles proclaimed with one accord, and their teaching should still today be retained in the churches and set forth free from all the leaven of human traditions. Let each one consider these things in such a way that, putting aside the many diverse opinions of men about religion and the business of salvation, he acknowledges the one Jesus Christ, his King and Priest, who died for our sins and was raised from the dead for our justification, and now intercedes for us at the right hand of God the Father. Let him trust in him so that at the same time he himself dies daily to sins, and rises again with him to a new and heavenly life, into which, having passed through, at last he is gathered to him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXIX.

units.la: Dicebat autem omnibus: Si quis vult me sequi, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie & sequatur me. Quisquis enim voluerit animam suam seruare, perdet eam: quisquis vero perdiderit animā suam mea causa, is seruabit eam. Quid enim prodest cuipiam, si lucretur vniuersum mundū, seipsum autē perdat, siue seipso mulctetur? Quem enim puduerit mei ac meorum sermonū, eius pudebit Filium hominis, quando venerit cum gloria sua & patris, sanctorumq; Angelorum. Dico autem vobis vere, sunt quidam ex ijs, qui hic astant, qui nequaquam gustabunt mortem, vsq; dum viderint regnum Dei.
units.tr: He said to all of them: "If anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me. For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. For what does it profit anyone to gain the whole world and lose or forfeit himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him, when he comes in his own glory, and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God."

units.la: AVdiuimus nuper Petrum Apostolum, qui omnium discipulorum nomine confessus est, Iesum, qui ex Maria Virgine hominem assumpsit, verum & æternum Dei viuentis Filium adhæc Christum illum Dei, id est, Regem & Sacerdotem esse, quem Deus ad seruandos homines destinarit, & patribus prisci promiserit. At quia discipuli redemptionis & salutis humana modum ignorabant, & communi gentis sua errore decepti regnum in Christo terrenum quærebant, docuit ille paucis, quæ tam regni quam sacerdotij sui sit conditio, & salutem nostram omnem in mortis suæ merito & resurrectionis virtute consistere ostendit. His modo nouam doctrinam subjicit, quā docemur, quid eos facere oporteat, qui salutis, quam ipse nobis meruit, participes fieri volunt. Est autem locus iste inter omnes alios maxime memorabilis, quia nullus ad nos fructus redibit ex omnibus ijs, quæ de Christo & vniuerso redemptionis nostræ negotio traduntur, nisi probè tenaamus rationem, qua eius germani discipuli efficimur, ad quos solos regni ipsius promissiones & hereditas pertinent. Occasionem huic dissertationi Petrus præbuit, qui (vt Matthæus & Marcus scribunt) sermone quem Christus de sua morte habuerat, offensus, eum dehortari cœperat, & ideo grauiter ab illo correptus fuit: Dixit enim illi: Abscede à me Satan, quia non sapis quae Dei sunt, sed quae sunt hominum. Quia vero Christus hoc commune omnibus discipulis vitium esse sciebat, quod adhuc praesentis seculi bonis intenti, à cruce & afflictionibus abhorrerēt, necesse erat eos diligentius & plenius instituì ad patientiam, & simul argumentis solidis confirmari.
units.tr: We recently heard the Apostle Peter, who spoke for all the disciples, confess that Jesus, who took on human nature from the Virgin Mary, is the true and eternal Son of the living God, and that this Christ is the King and Priest of God, whom God has appointed to save human beings and promised to the fathers of old. But because the disciples did not understand the manner of human redemption and salvation, and, deceived by the common error of their nation, sought an earthly kingdom in Christ, he taught them briefly what the condition of his kingdom and priesthood is, and showed that all our salvation rests on the merit of his death and the power of his resurrection. Now he adds a new teaching, by which we are taught what those must do who want to share in the salvation he has earned for us. This passage is especially memorable among all others, because none of the things that are handed down about Christ and the whole business of our redemption will bring any fruit to us unless we firmly hold the principle by which we become his true disciples, to whom alone the promises and inheritance of his kingdom belong. Peter gave occasion for this discourse. Offended by the sermon in which Christ spoke of his death (as Matthew and Mark write), he began to dissuade him, and so was sharply rebuked by him: "Get behind me, Satan, for you do not savour the things of God, but the things of men." But since Christ knew that this was a fault common to all the disciples, that they, still intent on the goods of the present age, shrank from the cross and afflictions, it was necessary that they be instructed more carefully and fully in patience, and at the same time be strengthened by solid arguments.

units.la: Priusquam vero ad Christi verba accedamus, inspexisse proderit, quibus ille loquatur, & ad quos doctrina ista pertineat. Lucas haec illum omnibus dixisse scribit. Marcus autem apertius. Cum aduocasset (inquit) turbam cum discipulis suis, dixit eis, &c. Omnibus ergo hic loquitur, & quae dicuntur, ex aequo ad omnes pertinent, qui eius discipuli esse cupiunt. Nem o igitur haec Apostolis solis aut horum in ecclesiae ministerio successoribus, dicta esse existimet. Communis enim haec regula est, quam Christiani omnes, cuiuscunque sint loci & ordinis, tenere debent. Ut enim in Christo non est mas aut foemina, non servus aut liber, non Iudaeus, Graecus, Scytha, barbarus: ita non obstant exterina haec personarum discrimina, quo minus ipsius regulae omnes obedire debeant, qui fidem in illum profitentur. Dictat enim hoc communis sensus, ut qui Christi discipuli censeri volunt, illius legibus viuant. Cum vero is ad unius regulae observatione omnes suos obstringat, simul omnes alias sectas cum suis regulis aut placitis abolet, quibus qui sub illo unum corpus esse debebant, in partes scindun tur. Paulus certe iis solis pacem & misericordiam à Deo pollicetur, qui secundum hanc regulam, quam nobis Christus praescripsit, gressus suos dirigunt. Galat. 6. At continetur ea tribus praeceptis, quae deinceps ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Before we come to the words of Christ, it will be useful to consider to whom he is speaking and to whom this teaching pertains. Luke writes that he said these things to all. Mark is plainer: "When he had called the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them," and so on. So he speaks here to all, and what is said pertains equally to all who wish to be his disciples. Let no one therefore think that these things were spoken to the Apostles alone, or to their successors in the ministry of the Church. For this is a common rule, which all Christians, of whatever place or rank, ought to keep. For as in Christ there is neither male nor female, neither slave nor free, neither Jew, Greek, Scythian nor barbarian, so these external distinctions of persons do not stand in the way of all who profess faith in him being obliged to obey this rule. For common sense dictates that those who wish to be considered Christ's disciples should live by his laws. But since he binds all his people to the observance of one rule, he at the same time abolishes all other sects with their rules or opinions, by which those who ought to be one body under him are split into parts. Paul, certainly, promises peace and mercy from God only to those who direct their steps according to this rule which Christ has prescribed for us (Gal. 6). This rule is contained in three precepts, which we shall see in order.

units.la: Primum est, quo ut nos ipsos abnegemus iubet. Vult ergo ut à seipsis initium faciant, qui germani ipsius discipuli haberi volunt. Ita vero totam hominis naturam damnat: quia nisi haec vitiosa & modis omnibus depravata esset, abnegatione eius minime esset opus. At hanc necessariam omnino esse facile patebit, si qui nam & quales simus consideres. In peccatis nos concipi et nasci scriptura docet. Quae causa est, ut peccati legem in membris nostris inhaerentē gestemus, qua fit, ut figmenta cordis nostri prava sint ab ineunte aetate. Quod nunquam negare poterunt, qui vel infantes paulo attentius inspexerint, & suas cogitationes atq; cupiditates non ofcitanter obseruarunt. Accedit his malis philautia, qua excaecati nobis ipsis placemus, & nostra omnia sic probamus, ut Dei quoq; verbum hoc solo nomine nobis sordeat, quod illud nostris figmentis atq; desiderijs sentimus contrarium esse. Hinc illa in fingendis novis Diis & illicitis eorundem cultibus audacia, hinc superstitionum multitudo, hinc qua nobis ipsis delitias facimus indulgentia, quae plerunque in effraenem peccandi licentiam erumpit. Nisi ergo seipsum abneget homo, nunquam Christi discipulus erit, qui nos ad eu finem contendere iubet, ut per fidei obedientiam nos totos Deo patri consecremus. Cuius rei exempla alibi in Abrahamo, Iobo, Dauide & utriusque Testamenti Martyribus proposuimus. At hic nos ante omnia carnis rationem frenare, & in hoc seculo (ut Paulus monet) stultos fieri oportet, ut in Deo sapientes efficiamur. Quo initio facto, mox ad carnis desideria progrediamur, ut ea quoq; in ordinem redacta nobis obstrepere desinant. At hic luctam grauem nobis propositam esse videbimus, in qua diuino auxilio opus erit, quando ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus. Hic ergo preces exiguntur, in quibus primum locum merito habebit petitio illa orationis Dominicae, qua ut Dei regnum nobis adueniat rogamus. Accedat precibus diligens nostri officij, cui nos destinatos esse scimus, consideratio, quae sola nos continere poterit, ne quid nostra vocatione indignū committamus. Quod si insuper eorum conditionem propius contemplemur, quae in hoc seculo eximia habentur, mox patebit, nihil in illis esse, cuius gratia aliquid fiat diuinis legibus contrarium.
units.tr: The first is that by which he commands us to deny ourselves. He wills, therefore, that those who want to be counted his true disciples begin with themselves. Indeed, this condemns the whole nature of man, for unless it were corrupt and depraved in every way, there would be no need for such self-denial. That this is absolutely necessary will be easily plain if you consider who and what we are. Scripture teaches that we are conceived and born in sin. That is why we bear the law of sin dwelling in our members, and why the thoughts of our heart are evil from our youth. Those who have looked a little more carefully even at infants, and have observed their thoughts and desires attentively, can never deny this. To these evils is added self-love, by which we, blinded, please ourselves, and so approve all our own things that even God's word is made loathsome to us for this alone, that we feel it to be contrary to our inventions and desires. Hence comes that boldness in inventing new gods and unlawful worship of them, hence the multitude of superstitions, hence the indulgence by which we make pleasures for ourselves, which for the most part breaks out into unbridled licence to sin. Unless therefore a man denies himself, he will never be a disciple of Christ, who bids us strive towards this end, that through obedient faith we consecrate ourselves wholly to God the Father. We have set out examples of this elsewhere in Abraham, Job, David, and the martyrs of both Testaments. But here we must above all curb the reasoning of the flesh, and in this age (as Paul warns) we must become foolish, so that we may become wise in God. Once this beginning is made, we should move on at once to the desires of the flesh, so that these too, being brought into order, may cease to clamour against us. Here we shall see a hard struggle set before us, in which we shall need divine help, since of ourselves we are not even fit to think. Here therefore prayers are required, and first place will rightly be given to that petition of the Lord's Prayer by which we ask that the kingdom of God may come to us. Let there be added to prayers a diligent consideration of our office, to which we know we have been appointed, for this alone will be able to restrain us from committing anything unworthy of our calling. And if we further look more closely at the conditions that are held in high esteem in this age, it will soon become plain that there is nothing in them for the sake of which anything contrary to the divine laws is done.

units.la: Alterum regulae Christi praeceptum est: Tollat crucem suam quotidie. Crux nomine genus omne malorum aut afflictionum designari, alibi diximus, quarū cum numerus sit infinitus, ad duas tamen species referri omnes possunt. Prima eas habet, qua omnibus hominibus propter peccatum communes sunt. Postquam enim Adam in legem à Deo acceptam peccauit, maledictionem tam ipsi quam creaturis reliquis meruit. Itaq; tellus non ut olim fronte sua fruges procreat, sed multo cum labore colitur, & ne sic quidem agricolarū votis semper respondet. Impleri enim oportet, quod Adamo dictum fuit: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Et ut cum dolore & lachrymis in lucem hanc prodimus: sic vita totius cursus dolorum, lachrymarum, laborum & curarum plenus est. Quibus omnibus morbi accedunt, qui tam multi sunt, ut stellas citius quàm illos numerauerit.
units.tr: The second precept of Christ's rule is: "Let him take up his cross daily." I have said elsewhere that the word cross designates every kind of evil or affliction, and although their number is infinite, they can all be referred to two kinds. The first is common to all men because of sin. For after Adam sinned against the law received from God, he merited a curse upon himself and upon the rest of creation. So the earth no longer brings forth its fruits of itself as it once did, but is tilled with much labour, and even so does not always answer the prayers of the farmers. For what was said to Adam must be fulfilled: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." And just as we come into this light with pain and tears, so the whole course of life is full of sorrows, tears, labours and cares. To all these are added diseases, which are so many that one would sooner count the stars than count them.

units.la: Et horum quidem omnium materiam intra nos habemus, quae causa est, ut illos neq; declinare, neque depellere possimus, quando libet. Quibus omnibus ita obnoxij sumus, ut nemo se immunem esse exemptum dicere possit: quo Iob we respiciens dicebat: Homo ad laborem natus est, ut auis ad volandum. Etenim quotidianis exemplis discimus opulentissimos quosq; ad extremam egestatem redigi, potentissimos rerum dominos e folijs suis deturbari, ferocissimos subito in ordine cogi, sapientissimos proprijs consilijs, cum laqueis artissimis constringi, aut morbis ex improuiso consumi, qui morbium beatissimi videbantur. Adde his communem omnibus moriendi necessitatem, cuius recordatio ipsam quoque vitam amaram reddit illis, qui futurae & melioris vitae spem ignorant. Altera malorum aut miseriarum huius seculi species ea continet, quae pijs & credentibus propria sunt. Quia enim veritatis lucem edit mundus, non potest non eos quoq; odisse, penes quos illa lucet, & qui hanc sequendo illius mores prauos suo exemplo arguunt. Ex hoc igitur fonte emanant persecutiones, in quibus Christi fideles falsis criminibus grauantur, in carceres abducuntur, fortunis multantur, in exilium relegantur, vel etiam exemplis horrendis & inauditis e medio tolluntur. Obseruauit hac olim Dauid, & ideo multas esse dixit tribulationes iustorum: et de his non vno loco nos Christus admonet.
units.tr: The matter of all these things we have within ourselves, which is why we cannot avoid or drive them away whenever we like. We are so subject to all of them that no one can say he is free and exempt; looking to this, Job said: "Man is born to labour, as the bird is born to fly." Indeed, from daily examples we learn that the most wealthy are reduced to utter poverty, the most powerful lords of things are thrown down from their seats, the most fierce are suddenly brought into order, the wisest are caught in their own counsels as in the tightest snares, or are unexpectedly consumed by diseases, those who seemed the most fortunate in health. Add to these the necessity of dying common to all, the remembrance of which makes even life bitter for those who do not know the hope of a future and better life. The other kind of evil or misery of this age contains those things which are proper to the godly and believers. For since the world hates the light of truth, it cannot but hate also those in whom that light shines, and who, by following it, condemn its depraved manners by their example. From this source therefore spring persecutions, in which the faithful of Christ are burdened with false accusations, led off to prisons, fined in their property, banished into exile, or even removed from the midst of men by horrible and unheard-of deaths. David observed this long ago, and therefore said that the tribulations of the righteous are many; and Christ warns us about these in more than one place.

units.la: Etsi vetera exempla ab ipso mundi exordio repetere libeat, videbis nos cum Poeta dicere posse, Fraterno primi maduerunt sanguine campi. Abelius enim, primus post Adamum veri Dei cultor, ab impio fratre Caino caesus, suo exemplo docuit, quid pij omnes in hisce terris sperare debeant. Neq; melio-rem multo posterorum fortem fuisse, omnium seculorum historijs probari poterat, si opus esset. At quia haec satis nota sunt, hoc potius in praesenti obseruemus, quod afflictiones quae pijs ferenda sunt, Christus crucis nomine dignatur. Eo enim vocabulo nos communionis admonet, quae nobis cum illo intercedit. Vt enim ipse propter nos in cruce dolores infandos & mortem infamem subijt: ita nos propter illum huic mundo exosi sumus, & quae paulo ante recitauimus ferre cogimur, dum fidem in illu sanctam & illibatam custodimus. Quin ea crucis Christi virtus est, ut quae nobis cum prophanis hominibus communia sunt, per illam sanctificentur, vt iam crux dici possint paupertas, labor, morbi, & quaecunque nobis, dum hic viuimus ferenda sunt. Debet hoc diligenter considerari, quia nostra cum institutioni tum consolationi plurimum seruit. Quia enim cum Christo communionem habemus, aequum est, vt ad eius exemplum grauissima quaeque patienter feramus, quibus nos in hac vita Deus exercet. Nam quid durius aut intolerabilius ijs accidere potest, quae Dei Filius iam pridem propter nos sustinuit? Vt enim vitam eius ab initio considerest, quid in illa aliud praeter paupertatem, labores, infamiam, dolores continuos videbis? Etenim qui totius mundi peccata in se receperat, eum omnibus quoque miserijs exerceri oportebat, quibus nos propter peccatum obnoxij erimus. Quod si vero nos suae crucis socios habere dignatur Dei Filius, qui cubitet nos gloria quoque & regni coheredes illi fore? Ipsum certè promisso est: Vos estis qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis. Ego igitur pacisco vobis, prout pactus est mihi pater meus regnum: Vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo. Item: Volo vt vbi sum ego, illic sit etiam minister meus. Et notum est illud Pauli: Si cum eo mortui sumus, eum eo etiam viuemus: si sufferamus, etiam cum eo regnabimus.
units.tr: Even if we wished to go back to ancient examples from the very beginning of the world, you would see that we can say with the poet, "The fields were soaked with a brother's blood." For Abel, the first worshipper of the true God after Adam, was slain by his impious brother Cain, and by his example taught what all the godly ought to expect in this world. That the lot of later generations was far better could be proved from the histories of all ages, if there were need. But since these things are well known, let us rather observe in the present context that Christ deigns to call the afflictions which the godly must bear by the name of cross. For by that word he reminds us of the fellowship which we share with him. Just as he himself endured unspeakable sufferings and a shameful death on the cross for our sake, so we are hated by this world for his sake, and we are compelled to bear the things we have just recited, while we keep the holy and unblemished faith in him. Indeed such is the power of Christ's cross that what we have in common with profane people is sanctified through it, so that poverty, toil, sickness, and whatever must be borne while we live here can now be called crosses. This ought to be considered carefully, because it greatly serves both our instruction and our consolation. For since we have fellowship with Christ, it is fitting that, after his example, we bear patiently the heaviest things with which God exercises us in this life. For what can be harder or more intolerable than those things which the Son of God long ago endured for our sake? If you consider his life from the beginning, what else will you see in it besides poverty, labours, infamy, and continual sorrows? For he who had taken upon himself the sins of the whole world had to be exercised also with all those miseries to which we shall be liable on account of sin. But if the Son of God deigns to have us as companions of his cross, can we doubt that we shall also be fellow heirs of his glory and kingdom? He himself has certainly promised this: "You are those who have continued with me in my temptations. I therefore covenant with you, just as my Father has covenanted the kingdom to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom." Likewise: "Where I am, I want my minister to be there too." And that saying of Paul is well known: "If we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him."

units.la: Caeterum hic plurimum proderit, Christi verba propius & diligentius inspexisse. Tollat (inquit) crucem suam quotidie. Vbi primum obseruabis, quam crucem quisque ferre debeat. Suam nimirum, id est, eam, quam Deus ipsi quasi propriam imposuit. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi aliorum calamitates negligere & siccis oculis praeterire debeamus. Saepe enim rata manet charitatis lex, quae iubet vt ploremus cum plorantibus, & eam inter nos συμπάθειαν seruemus, quae inter eiusdem corporis membra esse consueuit. Hoc ergo praecipit Dominus, vt in ijs ferendis patientes simus, quae Deus imponit, non autem eis praescribamus, quid nobiscum agere debeat: vt denique non velimus cum alijs onera commutare, vel cruces nihil ad nos pertinentes accersere. Quid enim hoc facere opus est, quando nunquam nobis labores & molestiae deerunt, si in Christo (vt Paulus ait) pie velimus viuere? Damnantur ergo hic superstitiosi, qui vel ieiunijs non necessarijs seipsos conficiunt, vel peregrinationes voluntarias, labore & periculi plenas, vel vitam eremiticam deligunt, aut intra monasteriorum muros se vinculis, chuameunijs, cilicijs & alia disciplina corporis seueriori macerant. Pollicentur illi fibijpsis beatitudinem, quod crucem ferant. At nos illos suam crucem ferre negamus, cum nihil huius vnquam ab illis ab illis requisierit Deus, ipsi vero relicta sua vocatione laboribus & molestijs nihil ad se pertinen- tibus seipsos implicent. Multò minus Christi crucem illi ferunt, qui ista nunquam praecepit, neq; vi- ta genera mutauit, quae Deus inter homines obseruari vult. Idem Anabaptistae respondemus, qui se beatos dicunt, quòd persecutionem patiantur. Sed multùm illos fallit ista opinio, cùm ideo patian- tur, quòd coetibus sacris interesse nolunt, quòd ecclesiae vnitatem scindunt, rempub. turbant, & cum ipsis pijs esse liceat, seditiones & scismata non necessaria mouent. Idem ergo illis dici potest, quod D. Augustinus olim Donatistis similì gloriatione turgidis dicebat: Num martyr continuò aman dus est, quia profuperstitione, quam piam religionem putabat, poenas legibus luit? Item: Non ex passione certa est iustitia, sed ex iustitia passio gloriosa est. Et rursus: Prius quid faciant, & po- stea quid patiantur aduertant: ne cùm aduersus facta sua oculos claudunt, & ad poenas oculos suos aperiunt, & hic frustra temporalia patiantur, & in vltimo iudicio Dei etiam pro hoc ipso, quòd fru- stra eos talibus molestijs vt emendaret admonuit, aeterno supplicio puniantur, &c. Quae omnia cum illo Christi conueniunt: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur iustiae causa. At hic minimè eos dam- namus, qui propter delicta aut facinora sua legibus ciuilibus poenas dant, & in his patientes sunt. Nam & hi à Deo impositam crucem ferunt, & si fide certa in Christum respiciant, in eodem seruan- buntur. Et huc latronis exemplum pertinet, cui ille dixit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso.
units.tr: Moreover, it will be of great profit here to look more closely and carefully at Christ's words. "Let him take up his cross daily," he says. Here you will first observe what cross each one ought to bear: namely his own, that is, the one which God has laid upon him as if it were his own. This must not be taken to mean that we should neglect the calamities of others and pass them by with dry eyes. For the law of charity often remains in force, which bids us weep with those who weep, and keep among ourselves that sympathy (συμπάθεια) which is wont to exist between the members of the same body. The Lord therefore commands this: that we be patient in bearing the things God lays upon us, and not prescribe to him what he ought to do with us; and finally that we should not wish to exchange burdens with others, or summon crosses that have nothing to do with us. For why is there any need for this, since troubles and annoyances will never be lacking to us if we wish to live godly in Christ (as Paul says)? Therefore those superstitious persons are condemned here, who either wear themselves out with unnecessary fasts, or choose voluntary pilgrimages full of toil and danger, or choose the eremitic life, or within monastery walls mortify themselves with chains, scourges, hair shirts, and other severer discipline of the body. They promise themselves blessedness because they bear a cross. But we deny that they bear their own cross, since God has never required any of this from them, while they, having abandoned their own calling, entangle themselves in labours and troubles that have nothing to do with them. Much less do they bear Christ's cross who have never been commanded these things and have not changed the kinds of life which God wills to be observed among men. We give the same answer to the Anabaptists, who call themselves blessed because they suffer persecution. But that opinion greatly deceives them, since they suffer because they refuse to attend sacred assemblies, because they split the unity of the Church and disturb the commonwealth, and, when it is permitted to be with the godly themselves, they stir up seditions and unnecessary schisms. The same can therefore be said to them as blessed Augustine once said to the Donatists, who were puffed up with a similar boasting: "Is a martyr to be loved continually, because he pays penalties under the laws for a superstition which he thought was true religion?" Again: "Righteousness does not come from suffering; suffering is glorious because of righteousness." And again: "Let them consider first what they do, and afterwards what they suffer; lest, while they close their eyes to their deeds and open them to punishments, they suffer in vain in this temporal life, and at the last judgment of God are punished with eternal torment even for this very thing, that they were admonished in vain by such troubles to amend themselves, etc." All these things agree with that saying of Christ: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake." But here we by no means condemn those who pay penalties under civil laws for their faults or crimes, and are patient in them. For these too bear the cross laid upon them by God, and if they look upon Christ with sure faith, they will be preserved in it. The example of the thief belongs here too, to whom he said: "Today you will be with me in paradise."

units.la: Deinde, vt crucem nostram ipsi tollamus, iubet Christus, quo verbo obedientiā & patientiam voluntariam requirit. Sunt enim qui crucē ferunt, sed inuiti, & inter ferendū aduersus Deum qui dem fremunt, homines autē, quos sibi malorum authores esse putant, odio prosequuntur. At non pro- bantur hi Deo, qui vt in alijs obsequium voluntarium à nobis requirit, ita hic in primis nos sponta- neos & alacres esse vult. Tales olim Apostoli fuerunt, quos gaudisos fuisse Lucas scribit, quòd dignos iudicaret Deus, qui propter Filium suum caderentur. Iltes ergo imitentur, quotquot hanc eius re- gulam sibi sequendam proposuerunt. In primis autem eius nos meminisse oportet, quod nos crucem nostram QVOTIDIE tollere iubet. Non ergo omni officio defuncti sumus, si semel & iterum aliquam molestiam patienter sustinuimus. Habent enim singuli dies, imò omnia horarum momenta, suos labores, & nouis indies curis pij exercentur: neq; vllū vitae genus est, quod nō assiduis molestijs referti sit, quas mox sentient, qui suo officio probe fungi voluerint. Peccant hic grauiter, qui quam illis Dominus impositit, crucem per media illicita vel subterfugere, vel ab humeris suis excutere eo nantur. Faciunt hoc, qui in persecutionibus Christum & fidem in illū abnegant, sacris alienum communicant, & impiorum amicitias seruiliter captant. Item, qui inopia sua per furta, rapinas, vsu- ras, militiam mercenariam aut quodcunq; aliud scelus consulere volunt. Quibus merito adnumera- neris eos, qui in rei alicuius amissione aut morbi ad ariolos, magos, incantatores & veneficos con- fugiunt. Quomodo enim illi omnes Christo obediunt, qui quam ipsi sponte in humeros suos attollere debebāt, crucem ijs rationibus reijciunt, quibus nemo sine scelere potest vti? Afam regem scriptura reprehendit, quòd ex pedibus laborans medicos potius quàm Dominum consuluisset: & tu impuni- tatem tibi pollicetis, qui ad Satanam, communem humani generis hostem, recurris?
units.tr: Then Christ bids us take up our cross ourselves, a word by which he requires obedience and voluntary patience. For there are those who bear the cross, but unwillingly; and while bearing it they indeed rage against God, and pursue with hatred the men whom they think are the authors of their evils. But those are not approved by God, who, as he requires voluntary obedience from us in other things, so here above all wants us to be willing and eager. The Apostles were such men of old, of whom Luke writes that they rejoiced because God judged them worthy to be beaten for his Son. Let those, therefore, who have proposed this rule of his to follow imitate them. But we ought especially to remember that he bids us take up our cross DAILY. It is not enough, then, to have discharged every duty if we have patiently endured some annoyance once or twice. For individual days, indeed every moment of the hours, have their own labours, and the godly are exercised daily with fresh cares; nor is there any kind of life that is not filled with constant annoyances, which those will soon feel who wish to perform their office properly. They sin grievously here who seek by unlawful means either to escape the cross the Lord has laid upon them or to throw it off their shoulders. Those do this who in persecutions deny Christ and the faith in him, share in alien worship, and slavishly court the friendship of the impious. Likewise those who want to relieve their poverty by theft, robbery, usury, mercenary soldiering, or any other crime. To these must rightly be added those who, in the loss of something or in sickness, flee to diviners, magicians, enchanters and poisoners. For how do all those obey Christ who reject the cross, which they ought willingly to have taken up on their own shoulders, by means which no one can use without crime? Scripture reproves King Asa, because when he was suffering in his feet he consulted physicians rather than the Lord. And do you promise yourself impunity, you who run to Satan, the common enemy of the human race?

units.la: At dura sunt haec carni, quae in otio & desideriorum suorum licentia voluptatem praecipuam consistere arbitratur. Sed multum ex crucis nostrae & afflictionum omnium pendere decedet, si abne gato carnis iudicio rem ipsam rectè expendamus. Vbi primum occurrat, quòd nihil nobis abstq; certo diuinae prouidentiae consilio accidit. Nam vt Deus mundum hunc omne creauit: ita in singulis eius partibus prouidentiae eius virtus elucet, quae certis vicibus omnia regit, & nihil fortuitū esse finit. Num ergo hominem, quem aliorum omnium principem constituit, temere hinc inde rapi aut circum ferri pateretur? Quicquid ergo aduersi incidit, hoc nobis diuinitus immitti cogitemus. At simul me minerimus, Deo summum in nos ius esse & imperium: iniustus ergo aut iniquus dici non potest, eti- opes auferat, corpus morbis debilitet, imò vitam ipsam eripiat. Licet enim illi de suis quod libet fa- tuere, neq; quicquam nobis eripit, quàm quod ex eius manu prius accepimus. Quo ergo iure aduersus illum actionem instituetis? quibus legibus eum conuinces, vt tecum iniquius se egisse fateatur? Quin potius illud obseruare nos decet, quòd suo in nos iure & imperio nō vt tyrannus vtitur, qui ex mise- rorum eiulatu & cruentis spectaculis voluptatē capit: sed patrem agit indulgentissimum, qui cùm nos melius, quàm nos ipsi, norit, totus in hoc est, vt nos virgis eiusmodi vel in officio cōtineat, ne ex-
units.tr: But these things are hard for the flesh, which thinks its chief pleasure lies in idleness and in indulging its desires. Yet much of the burden of our cross and of all afflictions will be lifted if, setting aside the judgment of the flesh, we weigh the matter rightly. First, we should note that nothing happens to us apart from the certain counsel of divine providence. For just as God created this whole world, so the power of his providence shines in each of its parts, governing all things in fixed courses and allowing nothing to be by chance. Would he then allow man, whom he set over all the others as their prince, to be snatched hither and thither at random? Whatever adversity befalls us, let us think that it is sent to us from God. And at the same time let us remember that God has the highest right and dominion over us. He therefore cannot be called unjust or unfair if he takes away our wealth, weakens our body with diseases, or even snatches away life itself. For although he may decide what he pleases concerning what is his own, he takes from us nothing but what we first received from his hand. By what right, then, will you bring an action against him? By what laws will you convict him, so that he confesses he has treated you unfairly? Rather, we ought to observe that in his right and dominion over us he does not act like a tyrant, who takes pleasure in the wailing of the wretched and in bloody spectacles, but acts as the most indulgent father. Since he knows us better than we know ourselves, he is wholly intent on restraining us with such rods, whether to keep us in our duty, lest we stray,

units.la: P orbitemus: vel in via reducat, ne cum mundo infelici & pœnitere nescio pereamus. Et quàmuis ca- stigatione omnino digni simus, nostra tamen infirmitatis memor, nos supra vires tentari non sinit. Novit enim nos ex pulvere & terra cõstare, ideoq; disciplinæ severitate patria clementia temperat. De his olim sancti homines cogitarunt, & ista consideratione cõfirmati adversus omnibus superiores factifuerunt. Adde his crucis fructus multiplicè, quæ alibi expositimus, & faterentur nos potius Deo gratias agere, quàm aduersus eum murmurare debere, si quid nobis præter animi voluntatem accidere finit.
units.tr: or to lead us back onto the way, lest we perish along with the unhappy world, which does not know how to repent. And although we are altogether deserving of chastisement, yet, mindful of our weakness, he does not allow us to be tested beyond our strength. For he knows that we are made of dust and earth, and therefore he tempers the severity of discipline with fatherly mercy. Holy men of old pondered these things, and being strengthened by this consideration they became superior to all adversities. Add to these the manifold fruits of the cross, which we have set out elsewhere; and let them confess that we ought rather to give thanks to God than to murmur against him, if he allows anything to befall us contrary to our will.

units.la: Sed tempus est, ut ad tertium regulæ Christi præceptum transeamus, quo iubet, ut ipsum sequamur. Disputarunt de hoc prolixè admodum Monachi, qui suis figmentis partim futilibus, partim impiis & superstitiosis, viam quanobis eundum est, difficilem & spinosam fecerunt. Nos igitur omissis illis teneamus, ad sequelam hanc duo potissimum requiri. Primum fides est, qua Christũ vnì cum Seruatorem, magistrum & ducem nostrum agnoscimus. De hac ipse concionatur, dicens: Ego sum lux mundi: qui me sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ. Et hoc ipsum elarius explicans alibi, ait: Dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, ut filij lucis sitis. Quò etiam referri debet, quod Ioannes sub initum operis sui euangelici scribit: Hic erat lux illa vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. In mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus est, sed mundus eum non agnouit.
