Ad suos venit, & sui eum non receperunt: Quotquot autem eum acceperunt, iis hanc dignitatem dedit, ut filij Dei fierent, iis nimirum, QVI CREDVNT in nomen eius. Docent ista, fidem præcipuam illud esse, quo Christum sequi, imò asseqqui & apprehendere possumus. Hac olim Abraham illum secutus est, ut & diem eius videret, & salutis in illo particeps fieret. Eadem illa verè secuti sunt Apostoli, multis alijs eum nequicquam corpore sequentibus, qui fide destituebantur. Est hoc probè obseruandum propter eos, qui se Christi sectatores esse putant, si quod vitæ genus aut sterum deligunt, & corpus disciplina asperiori quidem, sed quæ nullo Dei præcepto commendatur, excruciant. At hi non Christum, sed superstitiosorum hominum traditiones, aut proprij capitis figmenta sequuntur, & quò magis in hac via sua festinant, eò longius à Christo recedunt, dum quæ in eius solius merito repositæ esse debebat, æternæ salutis fiduciam in rebus hisce leuiculis collocatam habent. Porrò ex fide, qua Christum verè sequimur, alterum dependet, totius nimirum vitæ conuersatio, quam ad illius exemplum component, quotquot ipsum fide viua apprehenderint. Sciunt enim illum dixisse: Exemplum præbui vobis, ut sicut ego feci, & vos faciatis. Et illud Petri agnoscunt: Christus passus est pro vobis, exemplar, ut sequamini vestigia ipsius. Opus ergo erit omne, quam in hice terris transegit, Christi vitam inspicere, in qua omnis virtutis exemplar perfectissimum elucebit: obedientiæ nimirum, quam Patri præstiit: innocentiæ, quam ne hostes quidem vllis calumnijs aut falsis testibus polluere potuerunt: charitatis, quæ eum pro hostibus orare compulit: patientiæ, quæ aduersus omnes cruciatus, omnia tormenta, omnes exprobrationes & contumelia, fortis & inuicta constitit: fidei denique, ex qua tunc quoq; Deum patrem inuocauit, cùm nullum eius gratiæ argumentum appareret. Poterant hæc fusissimè extendi per omnes hominum ordines & vitæ actiones vniuersas: sed facilè ista sibi applicabunt, qui serio pietatis sensu afficiuntur. Hoc vnum in præsenti omnes obseruent, nihil in tota hac Christi regula contineri, quod nobis merito iniquum, inhonestum, aut difficile & periculosum videri debeat. Quid enim magis æquum & honestum est, quàm vt Christo conformes fiant, qui ab illo denominantur? Aut cur difficile putemus eum sequi, qui vt suo exemplo nobis præiuit: ita sectatoribus suis manu porrigit, & fessos quoq; nouis viribus instaurat? Num ve rò sibi timeat, qui eum duce sequuntur, qui deuicto mundo & principe eius cœlis & terris imperat?
units.tr: But it is time to pass to the third precept of Christ's rule, in which he bids us follow him. The monks have disputed this at great length, and with their inventions, partly frivolous and partly impious and superstitious, they have made the way we must walk difficult and thorny. Setting those aside, let us hold that two things are chiefly required for this following. The first is faith, by which we acknowledge Christ as our Saviour, teacher and leader. He himself preaches on this, saying: "I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." And explaining this more clearly elsewhere he says: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light." To this also should be referred what John writes at the beginning of his Gospel: "That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave this dignity, that they should become children of God, namely to those who BELIEVE in his name." These things teach that faith is the chief means by which we can follow Christ, indeed attain and grasp him. By this faith Abraham once followed him, so that he saw his day and became a partaker of salvation in him. The apostles truly followed him in the same way, while many others followed him in body to no avail, since they lacked faith. This must be carefully observed on account of those who think they are followers of Christ if they choose some manner of life or austerity and torment the body with a harsher discipline which, however, is commended by no command of God. But these men do not follow Christ; they follow the traditions of superstitious men or the figments of their own heads. And the more they hasten along this path of theirs, the farther they recede from Christ, since they have placed their confidence of eternal salvation in these trifles, when it ought to have been reposed in his merit alone. Moreover, from the faith by which we truly follow Christ there depends the second thing, namely the conduct of the whole life, which all who have grasped him by living faith will shape after his example. For they know he said: "I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also should do." And they acknowledge that saying of Peter: "Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps." It will therefore be necessary to look into the whole life Christ spent on earth, in which the most perfect pattern of every virtue shines forth: of obedience, which he rendered to the Father; of innocence, which not even his enemies could stain with any calumnies or false witnesses; of charity, which compelled him to pray for his enemies; of patience, which stood firm and unconquered against all torments, all tortures, all reproaches and insults; and finally of faith, by which he called upon God the Father even when no sign of his favour appeared. These things could be extended at great length through all ranks of men and all the actions of life, but those who are seriously moved by a sense of piety will easily apply them to themselves. Let all observe this one thing in the present matter: that nothing in this whole rule of Christ can rightly seem unfair, dishonourable, or difficult and dangerous. For what is more fair and honourable than that those who are named after Christ should be made conformed to him? Or why should we think it hard to follow him, who has gone before us by his example, and who stretches out his hand to his followers and restores the weary with fresh strength? Indeed, should he fear for himself who follows as leader the one who has conquered the world and its prince, and rules heaven and earth?

units.la: Cæterùm etsi ista vere dicantur, & sibi aures vellicari sentiant, quotquot de his non omnino o- scitanter cogitant, multa tamen sunt, quæ pios quoq; in hoc instituto sanctissimo remorantur. Alios enim innata omnibus vitæ cupiditas detinet: quibus durum videtur illam in periculum adducere. Alij opum amore fascinantur, vt quidam potius quàm de illis periclitari velint. Multos mundi ambitio & ambitio excæcant, vt Christum abnegare & ab hoc præscriptam regulam transgredi satius esse putent, quàm vt mundo exosi & infames fiant. Sunt qui stultos & ridiculos nimiùm eos esse putant, qui propter Christũ & fidei veræ confessionem seipsos & fortunas suas in periculũ addu cunt, cùm dubia & incerta sint, quæ de cœlis & vita æterna dicuntur. Quæ cùm non ignoraret ille, noua & validissima argumenta profert, quibus omnes istorum rationes grauissimè confutat.
units.tr: However, although these things are truly said, and those who do not consider them altogether carelessly feel their ears tingle, there are many things which hold back even the godly in this most holy undertaking. For innate love of life, common to all, keeps some back, since it seems hard to them to bring it into danger. Others are bewitched by love of wealth, so that some would rather not venture anything of theirs. The ambition and covetousness of the world blind many, so that they think it better to deny Christ and transgress the rule prescribed by him than to become hated and infamous to the world. There are those who think foolish and ridiculous in the extreme those who, for Christ and the confession of true faith, put themselves and their fortunes in danger, since what is said about heaven and eternal life is doubtful and uncertain. Since he was not unaware of these things, he brings forward new and very strong arguments by which he most gravely refutes all their reasoning.

units.la: Primùm de ijs loquitur, qui vitæ consulitŭ volunt in hoc seculo, & sic dicit: Quisquis voluerit animam suam seruare, perdet eam: Quisquis verò perdiderit animam suam mea causa, & seruabit eam. Sumitur argumentum hoc à fine aut officio hominis Christiani, & (vt diximus) eorum errori opponitur, qui ne de anima aut vita periclitentur, à regula ipsius deficiunt, vel etiam fidem in illum abnegant. Ostendit enim, nos nõ tam de huius seculi vita, quàm de futura solicitos esse debere, ne dũ nobis nunc consulimus, vitæ æternæ iacturam faciamus. Et est hæc bipertita sententia. Prima pars te ostendit, eos non modò falli spe sua, qui animam turpi defectione nunc seruare volunt, verumetiam sibijpsis animæ exitium accersere. Adhuc enim ipsis incumbit, quæ omnibus communis est, lex moriendi. At dum hora illa fatalis imminet, tunc spe & consolatione omni destitutis subinde hæc Christi sententia obstrepit: Quemcunq; mei puduerit & Euangelij mei, eius me quoq; pudebit, cùm venero in gloria patris mei. Moriuntur ergo, & simul huius vitæ vsum amittunt, & à cœlesti exclusi manent, ad quam nobis nullus accessus patet, nisi in Christo, quê illi abnegarunt. Altera parte felicem & beatam eorum conditionem exponit, qui animâ aut vitam ipsius causa deponunt, adeoq; perdunt. Nam bi (inquit) seruabunt eam. Ratio promissionis huius certa & euidens est: quia animas suas in Dei manus deponunt, qui remunerator est fidelissimus. Colligit ergo has ille ad Filiũ suum, cum quo viuunt & regnant, & olim ad corpora sua reditur sunt, vt vnà cum hu bona illa cœlestia possideant, quæ omnem huius mundi captum superare scriptura testatur. Isa. 64.
units.tr: First he speaks of those who wish to look after their life in this age, and he says: "Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it." This argument is drawn from the end or duty of a Christian, and (as we have said) it is set against the error of those who, lest they be endangered in soul or life, depart from his rule or even deny him. For he shows that we ought to be concerned not so much with the life of this age as with the future, lest while we now provide for ourselves we suffer the loss of eternal life. And this sentence has two parts. The first shows that those are not only deceived in their hope who now wish to save their soul by shameful defection, but also bring upon themselves the ruin of the soul. For the law of dying, common to all, still lies upon them. But when that fatal hour looms, then, stripped of all hope and consolation, this saying of Christ rings in their ears: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my gospel, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father." So they die, and at once lose the use of this life, and remain shut out from heaven, to which there is no open access for us except in Christ, whom they have denied. In the other part he sets out the happy and blessed condition of those who lay down their soul or life for his sake, and so lose it. For these, he says, will save it. The reason for this promise is certain and evident: because they commit their souls into the hands of God, who is the most faithful rewarder. He therefore gathers them to his Son, with whom they live and reign; and in time they will return to their bodies, so that together with them they may possess those heavenly good things which Scripture testifies surpass everything this world can grasp. Isa. 64.

units.la: At quia remoram hic nobis maximam iniciunt opes, quarũ pleriq; natura appetentes sunt, qui se non pœnitendum lucrum fecisse sibi persuadent, si vitæ huius vsum longius extendant, & simul fortunis suis consulant, ne his exuti oberrent: secundo loco iisdem etiam remedium adhibet, dicens: Quid prodest cuipiam, si lucretur vniuersum mundum, seipsum autem perdat, aut seipso mulc-tur? Conuenit argumentum hoc cum communi sensu, quo docemur, hominem inter res huius seculi nihil seipso præstantius aut charius habere. Ex eo autem sequitur, nihil eos lucrari, sed potius irrecuperabilem iacturam facere, qui vt opes seruent, Christum abnegando seipsos æternum perdunt. Vt enim paulò ante diximus, adhuc moriendi necessitate tenentur, & (vt Psaltes ait) ex illis qui niituntur opulentia sua, & in multitudine diuitiarum suarum gloriantur, nemo fratrem suum vlla ratione redimere potest, neq; Deo pretium redemptionis eius persoluere. Imò fieri videmus, vt ferè præter omnem expectationè nouissima vitæ hora nobis obrepat, & mors atra fores pulsat, quæ neq; muneribus, neq; promissis flectitur. At cum vita opū quoq; vsum amittimus, ignari ferè quibus nã illæ cedant: de quo infra Cap. 12. pluribus dicetur. Verissimè ergo dicitur, nihil vtilitatis aut lucri eos referre, qui seipsos perdunt, vt fortunis suis consulant.
units.tr: But because great wealth, which most people are naturally eager for, puts a huge obstacle in our way, they persuade themselves that they have made no loss if they prolong the use of this life, and at the same time look after their fortunes, so that they do not wander about stripped of them. In the second place, he also applies a remedy to these people, saying: "What does it profit anyone if he gains the whole world but loses himself, or is punished in himself?" This argument agrees with common sense, which teaches us that a person values nothing more highly or dearly than himself among the things of this age. It follows from this that those who deny Christ in order to keep their wealth gain nothing but make an irrecoverable loss, since they destroy themselves eternally. As we said a little earlier, they are still held by the necessity of dying, and (as the Psalmist says) of those who trust in their wealth and boast in the multitude of their riches, no one can by any means redeem his brother or pay God a ransom for him. Indeed, we see that the last hour of life often creeps upon us almost beyond all expectation, and dark death knocks at the door, which is moved neither by gifts nor by promises. And when we lose the use of life we also lose the use of wealth, and we hardly know to whom it will pass; this will be discussed at greater length below, in chapter 12. It is therefore most truly said that those who lose themselves in order to look after their fortunes gain nothing of advantage or profit.

units.la: Cæterum graue & durum multis videtur famæ periculum subire, & ex dignitatũ gradu deijci, adeoq; omnium digitis per contumeliam monstrari: quod plerunq; accidere videmus ijs, qui Christo fideles sunt. Olim certè balteo militari multabantur, qui illi nomen dederant. Inter Iudæos autè è Synagoga excludebantur, quæ extrema erat ignominia. Et hodie, vbi vtcunq; feruntur fidei purioris professores, ijsdem tamen nullus ad publicos honores aditus patet, & Regibus atq; principibus suspecti sunt, eò quòd seditiosi dicantur rerum nouatores, qui soli dominari velint. Sunt autè, qui cùm opum & ipsius vitæ iacturam non magni faciant, ignominiam tamen eiusmodi intolerabile putent. Quapropter hls quoq; consultum volens Dominus, ait: Quem puduerit mei ac meorũ sermonum, eius pudebit Filium hominis, quando venerit cum gloria sua & Patris, sanctorum, Angelorum. Quibus verbis non obscurè docet, abnegationem aut dissimulationem fidei cum maximo scelere coniunctam esse: quia fieri non potest, quin nos sui pudeat. At quid grauius, quid homine indignius dici potest? Aut quo non supplicio dignus erit, quê sui creatoris, redemptoris atq; seruatoris pudet? Auget sceleris atrocitatem comparatio, qua apud Marcum sese & mundum hunc opponit, cuius fauorem ambitiosi illi tanti faciunt. In præsenti verò non opus fuit pœnam apertius exprimere, eò quòd nullo nobis grauior & atrocior irrogari potest, quàm si nostri pudeat Christi in magno illo die, quo ad æternos inferorum cruciatus relegabuntur, quos cunq; pro suis agnoscere dedignatus fuerit. Nec tamen se & Verbum suum coniungit, vt ostendat eos quoq; damnari, qui ne in mundo inglorij sint, cœtus sacros & Euangelij prædicationem negligunt, aut hoc proscindi patiuntur, vel eius cognitionem turpiter dissimulant. Horum consideratio olim Martyres tam animosos fecit, vt nihil nõ sibi ferent dum putarent, ne in iflam Christi sententia incurrerent. Et his intentos esse oportebat eos, quos aulz cus fastus & honores publici suo splendore ita perstringunt, vt Christo longu valere renuntient, ne qua ignominia nota aspergantur: neq; vident miseri homines, se maiore ignominia subire non posse, quam ea sit, quâ sibijpsis sponte accersunt, dum fidem in Christum turpiter dissimulant. Excitent illos exempla eorum, qui olim honoribus multati propter fidei confessionem, non multo post ad Imperatoriæ maiestatis fastigium euecti sunt: quod Iouiniano & Valentiniano accidisse constat. Et similia exempla nostro seculo nõ pauca vidimus. Quod etsi nõ omnibus obtingat, non fallet tamen nos Christus, quin quam hic suo nomine sustinemus ignominiam, æterna regni sui cœlestis gloria compensat.
units.tr: Moreover, many people think it a grave and hard thing to run the risk of losing their reputation, to be cast down from the rank of their dignities, and so to be pointed at with the finger of everyone in scorn; and we see this happening most often to those who are faithful to Christ. Formerly, indeed, those who had given their names to him were punished by being deprived of the military belt. Among the Jews they were excluded from the synagogue, which was the extreme of disgrace. And today, wherever professors of a purer faith are to be found, no access to public honours lies open to them, and they are suspected by kings and princes, on the ground that they are called seditious innovators who wish to rule alone. There are some, however, who do not set much store by the loss of their wealth or even of life itself, but who think such disgrace intolerable. Wishing to provide for these people too, the Lord therefore says: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed, when he comes in his own glory and the Father's, and of the holy angels." By these words he teaches clearly that denial or concealment of the faith is joined with the greatest wickedness, because it cannot happen that we are not ashamed of him. But what could be said that is more grievous or more unworthy of a human being? Or what punishment will not be due to one who is ashamed of his creator, redeemer and saviour? The comparison in Mark, in which he sets himself and this world over against each other, and whose favour those ambitious men value so highly, adds to the atrocity of the crime. In the present passage there was no need to express the punishment more openly, since none can be inflicted on us that is heavier or more atrocious than to have Christ ashamed of us on that great day, when those whom he has refused to acknowledge as his own are consigned to the eternal torments of hell. Yet he does not join his word to himself in order to show that those are also condemned who, so as not to be inglorious in the world, neglect the holy assemblies and the preaching of the gospel, or who allow it to be torn apart, or shamefully conceal their knowledge of it. The consideration of these things once made the martyrs so courageous that they endured everything, provided they did not fall under that sentence of Christ. Those whom the pomp of the court and public honours so dazzle with their splendour that they renounce Christ and bid him farewell, lest they be stained with the mark of disgrace, ought to be attentive to these things; and wretched men do not see that they cannot suffer a greater disgrace than that which they bring upon themselves of their own accord when they shamefully conceal their faith in Christ. Let the examples of those stir them up who, once deprived of honours on account of their confession of the faith, were not long afterwards raised to the summit of imperial majesty; it is well established that this happened to Jovian and Valentinian. And we have seen not a few similar examples in our own age. Although this does not befall everyone, Christ will not deceive us: whatever disgrace we bear here for his name, he will compensate with the eternal glory of his heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Sed non omnes multum mouet hæc doctrina, eò quòd vix fide digna iudicant, quæ de fine huius mundi & nouissimo Christi aduentu, deq; piorum præmijs & impiorum supplicijs æternis dicuntur. Neq; ignorabat ille impios illos illusores, quos Petrus venturos prædixit, & qui hodie passim audiuntur. Ne quid ergo discipuli dubitarent, quorum infirmitas ipsi satis perspecta erat, addit: Dico autem vobis vere, sunt quidam ex ijs qui hic astant, qui nequaquam gustabunt mortem, vsque dum viderint regnum Dei. Apud Matthæum ait: Dum viderint Filium hominis venientem in regno suo, id est, talem me viderint, qualis olim venturus sum, quando regnum Dei cum potestate & gloria toti mundo reuelabitur. Et hoc de historia, quam mox subijciet Lucas, dicitur: in qua coram tribus discipulis transformatus, aut potius clarificatus, cœlestis illius gloriæ gustum vel specimen exhibuit, in qua ad iudicium veniet, & quam nos quoque in nostris corporibus olim obtinebimus. Estq; hoc præclarum bonitatis diuinæ argumentum, quod hac etiam ratione nostræ infirmitati consulere, & futuræ gloriæ spem nobis confirmare voluit. Huius ergo fiducia freti, constantes simus in agnita veritate, & procul relictis mundi huius studijs secundum regulam Iesu Christi ambulemus, qui & inter huius seculi discrimina aduersus hostium tam visibilium quàm invisibilium conatus tuebitur, & olim regni atq; gloriæ sua cœlestis consortes faciet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But this teaching does not move many people very much, because they hardly think credible what is said about the end of this world, the last coming of Christ, and the eternal rewards of the pious and punishments of the impious. Nor did he not know of those scoffers whom Peter foretold would come, and who are heard everywhere today. So that his disciples, whose weakness was well known to him, should not doubt anything, he adds: "Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will by no means taste death until they see the kingdom of God." In Matthew he says: "until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom", that is, they will see me as I shall be when I come hereafter, when the kingdom of God will be revealed to the whole world with power and glory. And this is said of the event which Luke will shortly set out, in which, before three disciples, he was transfigured, or rather made bright, and displayed a taste or specimen of that heavenly glory in which he will come to judgement, and which we too shall one day obtain in our bodies. And this is a notable proof of divine goodness, that by this means too he wished to provide for our weakness and to confirm in us the hope of future glory. Relying therefore on this confidence, let us be steadfast in the truth we have acknowledged, and, leaving far behind the pursuits of this world, let us walk according to the rule of Jesus Christ, who will defend us amid the dangers of this age against the attacks of enemies both visible and invisible, and will one day make us sharers of his heavenly kingdom and glory. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XC.
units.tr: HOMILY XC.

units.la: Factum est autem post hæc verba quasi diebus octo, cum assumptis Petro & Ioanne & Iacobo, ascendit in montem vt precaretur. Et facta est inter precandum species vultus eius alia, & vestitus eius albus ac emicans. Et ecce duo viri colloquebantur cum eo, qui erat Moses & Elias. Qui visi cum gloria dicebant ipsius exitum, quo futurum erat vt defungeretur in Hierusalem. Petrus vero & qui cum ipso erant, grauati erant somno: cum autem euigilassent, viderunt gloriam eius, & duos illos viros, qui stabant cum eo. Et factum est, cum illi discederent ab eo dixit Petrus ad Iesum: Magister, bonum est nos hic esse, & faciamus tria tabernacula, vnum tibi, & vnum Mosi, & vnum Eliæ: nescien s quid diceret. Hæc autem ipso dicente, extitit nubes, quę inumbrauit ipsos: timuerunt autem, dum ingrederentur in nubem. Et vox extitit e nube, dicens: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, ipsum audite. Et postquam vox ista extitisset, inuentus est Iesus solus. Ipsi autem siluerunt, & nulli declararunt per id tempus quicquam eorum quæ viderant.
units.tr: Now about eight days after these sayings, he took Peter, John and James with him and went up into a mountain to pray. And as he prayed, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became white and dazzling. And behold, two men talked with him, who were Moses and Elias. They appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter and those who were with him were weighed down with sleep, but when they woke they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as these were leaving him, Peter said to Jesus: "Master, it is good for us to be here, and let us make three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elias," not knowing what he said. While he was saying this, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying: "This is my beloved Son; hear him." And when the voice had ceased, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

units.la: Multis & grauibus argumentis nuper Christus Iesus omnes homines hortatus est, vt ab ipso præscriptam pie & bene viuendi regulam sedulo sequantur, inq; ea constanter perseuerent. Præcipuum fuit, nouissimus eius ad iudicium aduentus, in quo pudefieri & confundi oportebat omnes eos, quos ipsius puduerit coram mundo hoc prauo atq; adultero. At quia mundi finem pleriq; semper negarunt, & ipse sciebat, nouissimus temporibus paucos credituros esse, quod ad iudicium ipse venturus sit, gustum & specimen aliquod regni cœlestis & aduentus sui pollicitus est, quod vt exhiberet, Lucas ijs verbis, quæ modò recitauimus, describit. Estq; historia ista vna ex præcipuis & maxime memomè memorabilibus, quæ in nouo testamento continentur, & vt alibi diximus, vsum habet duplicem. Primò enim hoc gloriæ suæ specimine docet Christus, qualis olim ad iudicium venturus, & quæ tunc in regno suo futura sit omnium fidelium conditio. Deinde demonstrat, se esse promissum illum humani generis Seruatorem, quem vnum omnes sequi, & suum doctorem atq; magistrum agnoscere debeant. Facit autem utrumq; hoc ad remouendum crucis scandalum, à qua discipulos vehementer abhorruisse constat, & qua hodie etiam multi vehementer offendi solent.
units.tr: Christ Jesus has lately urged all people, by many and weighty arguments, to follow diligently the rule of holy and good living that he has prescribed, and to persevere in it constantly. The chief of these arguments was his final coming to judgment, at which all those ashamed of him before this perverse and adulterous world must be put to shame and confounded. But since many have always denied the end of the world, and he knew that in the last times few would believe that he was to come to judgment, he promised a taste and some specimen of his heavenly kingdom and coming. Luke describes this, in the words just recited, to show it. This history is one of the chief and most memorable in the New Testament, and, as we have said elsewhere, it has a twofold use. First, by this specimen of his glory Christ teaches what he will be like when he comes to judgment, and what the condition of all the faithful will be then in his kingdom. Second, he shows that he is that promised Saviour of mankind, whom all should follow alone and acknowledge as their teacher and master. Both serve to remove the scandal of the cross, from which the disciples are known to have shrunk greatly, and by which many even today are still wont to be offended.

units.la: Quia ergo multiplex huius historiæ fructus est, diligenter omnes eius circumstantias Euangelistæ enumerant. Et Lucas quidem à tempore exorsus intra octauum circiter diem à promissione, cuius modo meminimus, hæc facta esse scribit. Ex quo apparet Christi fidem simul & bonitas: qui vt promissis suis minimè deest, ita non diutius æquo illa differt, sed nostræ infirmitatis rationem habet, ne quod damnum nobis mora ipsius afferat. Quod enim hic factum, hoc illum in resurrectione quoq; sua obseruauisse constat, quam nulla hostium vires atq; machinationes impedire potuerunt, quò minus tertio die fieret, sicuti promiserat. Idem de Spiritus sancti missione dicere possumus, quæ tunc facta est, cùm discipuli illo in primis opus habebant. Sunt exempla hæc nobis obseruanda, ne de illis promissionibus dubitemus, quibus nobis periclitantibus suam opem pollicitus est. Nec enim illarum vnquam obliuiscetur: quòd si quando diutius differt, id singulari eius consilio in nostrum bonum fieri cogitemus.
units.tr: Since the fruit of this history is manifold, the evangelists carefully list all its circumstances. Luke, beginning from the time, writes that these things happened within about eight days of the promise we just mentioned. From this appear both the faithfulness and the goodness of Christ. As he is by no means wanting in his promises, so he does not delay them longer than is fitting, but has regard to our weakness, lest his delay cause us any harm. For what was done here, it is plain that he also observed in his resurrection, which no powers or schemes of enemies could prevent from happening on the third day, as he had promised. We may say the same of the sending of the Holy Spirit, which took place when the disciples especially needed it. These examples are to be observed by us, so that we do not doubt those promises by which he pledged his help to us in our dangers. For he never forgets them; and if at any time he delays longer, let us consider that this is done by his singular wisdom for our good.

units.la: Deinde testes indicantur oculati, Petrus, Ioannes & Iacobus. Sufficiebant isti ad testandum de rei veritate. Sunt autem illi ipsi, quos sæpe aliàs rebus grauioribus adhibuit. Unde apparet, inter electos quoq; non paruum discrimen esse, & vt functiones diuersæ sunt, ita dona quoq;, & ideo alij aliis præstare solent. At hic meminisse oportet, neminem ex eo vel insolescendi vel desperandi, multò minus autem invidiæ aut odij occasionem arripere debere. Nam vt Paulus ait, discrimina quidem donorum sunt, sed idem est Spiritus illorum author: & discrimina ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus omnium: & discrimina facultatum sunt, sed idem est Deus, qui eas omnes efficit in quibusdam. Singuli ergo in hoc potius sint, vt suis quidem donis ad Dei gloriam & multorum ædificationem bene vtantur, in aliis verò obseruent gratiam, qua illos Deus idem dignatus est: & ita current, ne dissensiones ex eo oriantur, quod concordiæ vinculum esse debet.
units.tr: Then eyewitnesses are named: Peter, John and James. These were sufficient to testify to the truth of the matter. They are the very ones whom he often employed elsewhere in weightier matters. Hence it appears that even among the chosen there is no small difference: as the offices are diverse, so the gifts are too, and therefore some excel others. Here we must remember that no one should seize on this as an occasion either for arrogance or for despair, much less for envy or hatred. For as Paul says, there are differences of gifts, but the same Spirit is their author; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord of all; and there are differences of workings, but it is the same God who works all of them in everyone. Let each therefore be intent rather on using his own gifts well, for the glory of God and the building up of many, and in others to observe the grace by which God has deigned to honour them. Let them so run that no dissensions arise from this, which ought to be the bond of concord.

units.la: Tertiò locum quoq; denotat, quando in montem cum tribus ipsis ascendisse eum dicit, & quidem vt precaretur. Fuit autem hoc solenne Christo, vt singulare quid facturus montes & locos sublimio res delegerit, & tunc quoq; in precibus fuerit attentior. Atqui vt illi non opus erat locorum religionem obseruare, ita neq; preces ipsi necessariæ fuerunt, cui facile fuit in assumpta carnis infirmitate virtutis diuinæ potentiam atq; maiestatem declarare quoties voluit. Propter nos ergo ista omnia fecit, vt nobis gratiam apud Deum impetraret, & suo exemplo doceret animos à terrenis cogitationibus supra mundum hunc euehere, vt cœlestis illius gloriæ gustu confirmemur, & olim cum ipso glorificemur. Neq; terreat nos, quòd hoc vires nostras superat. In illo enim omnia poterimus, qui vt hic pro tribus ipsis discipulis orauit, ita pro omnibus nobis apud Patrem assiduè intercedit, & nota est eius promissio: Ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi Pater, dedi eis. Item: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo vt vbi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, vt spectent gloriam illam meam, quam dedisti mihi, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, he also notes the place, when he says that he went up into the mountain with those three, and indeed to pray. It was Christ's custom, when about to do something singular, to choose mountains and higher places, and then too he was more attentive in prayer. But just as he had no need to observe the sanctity of places, so prayers were not necessary for him, to whom it was easy, in the assumed weakness of the flesh, to display the power and majesty of divine might whenever he wished. He did all these things therefore for our sake: that he might obtain grace for us before God, and by his example teach us to lift our minds from earthly thoughts above this world, so that we may be strengthened by a taste of that heavenly glory and in time be glorified with him. Let it not terrify us that this exceeds our strength. For in him we shall be able to do all things, who prayed here for those three disciples, and so constantly intercedes with the Father for all of us. His promise is well known: "The glory which you gave me, I have given to them." Again: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory, which you have given me," etc.

units.la: His glorificationis modus subiicitur, quem Matthæus & Marcus primò transformationem dicunt, deinde hanc diligentius exponentes eorum quoq; meminerunt, quæ hic breuiter de vultu & vestitu eius dicuntur. Facta est (inquit Lucas) inter precandum species eius alia, & vestitus eius albus ac emicans sive fulgurans. Matthæus vultum eius instar Solis splenduisse scribit. Marcus vestitum albedinem siue fulgorem duabus similitudinibus seu comparationibus explicat, dicens: Vestimenta eius facta sunt corruscantia, candida valde vt nix, qualia non potest fullo super terram dealbare. Fuit ergo splendor ille maior, quàm huius seculi natura referre possit, adeoq; cælestis & athereus fuit, nihil tamen de corporis veritate & substantia abstulit. Cùm enim faciei mentio fiat, reliqua membra minimè excluduntur, de quibus ipse diserte loquitur, quando post resurrectionem corporis clarificati veritatem oculari & palpabile demonstratione asserit. Et quomodo corporis substantiam euacuaret clarificatio, quæ ne vestitu quidem substantiâ abolevit? Et hæc quidem veteris & orthodoxæ ecclesiæ sententia est, quæ multispatrum testimoniis probari poterat, Sed sufficiat nobis D. Hieronymus, qui aduersus errores Ioannis Hierosolymitani ad Pammachium sic scribit: Sic Dominus noster in monte transfiguratus est in gloria, nō vt manus ac pedes caeteraq; membra perderet, & subito in rotunditate vel Solis vel sphaerae voluteretur: sed eadem membra Solis fulgore refulgentia Apostolorum oculos perstringerent: Vnde & vestimenta eius mutata sunt in candorem, non in aerem, ne forte & vestes eius aspera spiritualia. Et facies (inquit) eius fulgebat sicut Sol. Vbi autem facies nominatur, existimo quod & caetera membra conspecta sint. Haec Hieron. Petri vero ad Christi gloriam, quod Moses & Elias ipsi astant, & cum eo colloquuntur de exitu aut morte, qua ipsum Hierosolymae defungi oportebat. Ita enim docebatur, Iesum hunc esse redemptorem, de quo olim Moses & Prophetae simul omnes testati sint, neq; aliquem eius morte debere offendi, cum de hac quoq; illi prophetarint, ipse vero eam nō inuitus aut à quoquam coactus, sed vltro subierit, vt aeterno Patris decreto obediens sufficientem pro peccatis totius mundi victimam offerret. At quia hoc ad alterum huius historiae vsum pertinet, nunc in illo nolumus immorari.
units.tr: To this is added the mode of glorification, which Matthew and Mark first call a transfiguration. Then, explaining this more carefully, they also mention the things that are briefly said here about his face and clothing. "The appearance of his face was altered while he prayed," says Luke, "and his clothing was white and dazzling, or flashing." Matthew writes that his face shone like the sun. Mark explains the whiteness or brightness of the clothing by two similes or comparisons, saying: "His garments became shining, exceedingly white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can whiten." So that splendour was greater than the nature of this world can express, and so heavenly and ethereal was it, yet it took nothing away from the truth and substance of the body. For when mention is made of the face, the other members are not excluded, of which he himself speaks plainly when, after the resurrection, he proves by sight and touch the reality of his glorified body. And how would glorification empty the body of its substance, when it did not even abolish the substance of the clothing? This is indeed the view of the old and orthodox Church, which could be proved by the testimonies of many Fathers. But let it suffice for us to cite Jerome, who, writing against the errors of John of Jerusalem to Pammachius, says thus: "So our Lord was transfigured on the mountain in glory, not so as to lose his hands and feet and other members, and suddenly roll about in the roundness of the sun or of a sphere; but the same members, shining with the brightness of the sun, dazzled the eyes of the apostles. Hence his garments too were changed into whiteness, not into air, lest perhaps his garments also become rough and spiritual. And his face," he says, "shone like the sun. But where the face is named, I think the other members were also seen." Thus Jerome. As for Peter's words about the glory of Christ, that Moses and Elias stand by him and talk with him about the departure, or death, by which he had to die at Jerusalem: for it was thus being taught that this Jesus is the Redeemer, of whom Moses and all the prophets together bore witness of old, and that no one ought to be offended at his death, since they prophesied of this too; and that he underwent it not unwillingly or compelled by anyone, but of his own accord, so that obedient to the eternal decree of the Father he might offer a sufficient victim for the sins of the whole world. But since this pertains to the other use of this history, we do not wish to linger on it now.

units.la: Videamus ergo quae ad priorem spectant. Vbi firmiter tenendum est, aeternum Dei Filium, qui ex Maria Virgine homo factus est, in resurrectione assumptam carnem glorificatam esse quidem, non autem depositsse eius substantiam, neq; ea quae corporibus humanis ita propria sunt, vt sine ijs consistere non possint. Glorificatione enim noua maiestas conferetur, veritas autem & substantia minime euacuatur. Ideo vt hic faciem & vestitum retinuit: ita alibi iam resuscitatus, pedum, manuum, lateris, denique carnis & ossium meminit. Vitia ergo, quae ex peccato nostris corporibus accesserunt, in clarificatione auferuntur, non aboletur autem corporum veritas. Itaq; in nubibus caeli olim veniet idem ille Iesus, qui ex Maria Virgine natus, in assumpta carne mortem sustinuit, in qua nunc sedet ad dexteram Dei Patris. Veniet autem cum gloria Patris, latus quidem suis, qui in occursum eius per aerem rapientur, vt aeternum cum ipso viuant: terribilis autem impijs, qui iudicem seueritatem ferre cogentur, quem Seruatorem suum agnoscere noluerunt. In quorum consideratione ita nos versari conuenit, vt & consolationem hinc petamus in tentationibus, & simul horum memores innocentiam & sanctitatem nostram tueamur, vt in illo die subsistere possimus ad tribunal illud supremum, ad quod omnes homines sisti oportet.
units.tr: Let us now see what pertains to the former use. Here it must be firmly held that the eternal Son of God, who was made man from the Virgin Mary, has indeed glorified the flesh he assumed in the resurrection, but has not laid aside its substance, nor those things which are so proper to human bodies that they cannot exist without them. For glorification confers a new majesty, but the truth and substance are not at all annulled. Thus he kept his face and garments here; so elsewhere, now raised, he speaks of his feet, hands, side, and finally of his flesh and bones. Therefore the vices which our bodies have contracted from sin are removed in glorification, but the truth of the bodies is not abolished. So in the clouds of heaven that same Jesus, who was born of the Virgin Mary and suffered death in the flesh he assumed, and in which he now sits at the right hand of God the Father, will one day come. He will come with the glory of the Father, bringing joy to his own, who will be caught up into the air to meet him, so that they may live with him forever; but he will be terrible to the impious, who will be compelled to bear the severe judge whom they refused to acknowledge as their Savior. We ought to dwell on these things in such a way that we both seek consolation from them in temptations and, mindful of them at the same time, guard our innocence and holiness, so that on that day we may be able to stand before that supreme tribunal, before which all men must be brought.

units.la: At simul quae olim nostrorum corporum in resurrectione & regno Dei conditio futura sit, hic admonemur. Frustra enim suam gloriam discipulis Christus spectandam exhibuisset, nisi ea in nos quoque redundaret. Primo autem hoc nobis ratum esto, quod vt Christus neque in clarificatione ista, neque in resurrectione, corporis sui veritatem deposuit: ita nobis quoque corpora, in quibus nunc viuimus, restituentur: non autem vitijs, quibus nunc laboramus, obnoxia, sed gloriosa & corpori Christi conformia. Deinde in Christi faciem discipuli isti tres intuentur. Eius ergo conspectu nos quoque fruemur, & in eo bonis omnibus saturabimur, vt nullo amplioris felicitatis desiderio nos ringi necesse sit. Patet hoc in Petri exemplo, qui huius contemplationis dulcedine abreptus, omnium quae in terris habebat, obliuisci tur, & non vt Lothi vxor ad illa respicit, sed potius ijs relictis illic tabernaculum suum defigi vult, vt perpetuo cum Christo viuat. Et huc facit Isaiae testimonium, qui caelestium bonorum praestantiam commendaturus, inter alia dicit: Quae oculus non vidit, neque auris audiuit, neque in cor hominis ascenderunt, &c. Tertio vident illi cum Christo Moysem & Eliam, quos & agnoscunt licet nunquam antea sese visos. Quo docetur, nos cum sanctis omnibus communionem habituros esse. Fruemur ergo omnium eorum consortio, quorum fides atq; virtus in scripturis praedicatur, & quorum memoria nobis hodie iucunda atq; pretiosa est. Et vt olim Adamus, cum nondum peccauisset, Euam ex suis ossibus & carne sua sumptam esse sciebat, quam numquam antea vidisset: ita nos ab omni ignorantia vitio liberati eos omnes agnoscemus, qui eiusdem regni nobiscum haeredes erunt. At cum ignorantia simul alij quoq; affectus vitiosi excludentur. Nullus ergo erit illic gaudij carnalis excessus, nulla libidinis nos titillantis cupiditas, nullus ex nostrorum desiderio dolor: denique Angelorum similes erimus, quos nullius affectus prauus transuersos abripit. Erit ergo haec perfecta felicitas, quando nihil sentiemus, quo illa turbari possit. Ita vero vt nos ad caelestis patriae amorem atq; desiderium accendere debent: ita in nostrorum obitu nos efficacissime consolantur, ne indignius feramus illorum mortem, qui vitam hanc infelice cum aeternitate commutarunt, & quos ipsi quoq; breui sequemur, &c.
units.tr: At the same time we are reminded what the condition of our bodies will one day be in the resurrection and in the kingdom of God. For Christ would have shown his glory to the disciples in vain, if it did not also overflow to us. First, let this be settled for us: just as Christ laid aside neither the truth of his body in this clarification nor in the resurrection, so our bodies, in which we now live, will be restored to us; yet not subject to the vices with which we now struggle, but glorious and conformed to the body of Christ. Next, those three disciples gaze upon the face of Christ. Therefore we too shall enjoy his sight, and be satisfied with all good things in him, so that there will be no need for us to be tormented by any desire for greater happiness. This is evident in the example of Peter, who, carried away by the sweetness of this contemplation, forgets all the things he had on earth, and does not look back like Lot's wife, but rather wishes his tabernacle to be fixed there, leaving those things behind, so that he may live with Christ forever. The testimony of Isaiah agrees with this, who, when he was about to commend the excellence of heavenly goods, says among other things: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither have they entered into the heart of man," etc. Third, those disciples see Moses and Elijah with Christ, and they recognize them, though they had never seen them before. By this it is taught that we shall have communion with all the saints. We shall therefore enjoy the fellowship of all those whose faith and virtue are praised in the Scriptures, and whose memory is pleasant and precious to us today. And just as Adam, when he had not yet sinned, knew that Eve had been taken from his bones and flesh, though he had never seen her before, so we, freed from all the vice of ignorance, will recognize all those who will be heirs of the same kingdom with us. But with ignorance, other vicious affections will also be shut out. There will therefore be no excess of carnal joy there, no lustful desire that tickles us, no grief over the longing for our own people; finally, we shall be like the angels, whom no depraved affection drags aside. This will therefore be perfect happiness, since we shall feel nothing by which it could be disturbed. And just as these things ought to kindle in us love and longing for the heavenly fatherland, so they most effectively console us in the death of our loved ones, so that we do not bear too unworthily the death of those who have exchanged this unhappy life for eternity, and whom we too shall soon follow, etc.

units.la: Priusquam autem hinc discedamus, videndum est, ut hoc coelestis gloriæ gustu discipuli illi tres affecti fuerint. Primum somno grauantur, dum ista fiunt. Quod illis ex metu, quo consternatos fuisse alij scribunt, accidisse apparet. Tandem vbi ad se redierunt, hæc viderunt & audierunt, quæ tunc secti fuerint agebantur. Quo exemplo non infirmitas modò nostra adumbratur, quæ dum in carne viuimus, diuina & cœlestia non percipit, verumetiam ignauia & tarditas arguitur, qua impediti illa vix obser uamus, vt decebat. Tanta autem illa est, vt neq; læti neq; tristibus excuti aut superari possit. Nā quod hic patiuntur discipuli, hoc ipsum postea ijsdem accidit, quando Christus imminente mortis suæ hora extrema carnis assumptæ infirmitatem coram illis testatus, & eos adexcubias & preces hortatus est. Experimur huius generis multa in nobis ipsis, quorum consideratio nos excitare debet, vt & in precibus feruentiores simus, & Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui indignos nos monet & erigit, ne in veterno isto animarum pernitiosissimo male pereamus.
units.tr: Before we depart from here, we must consider how those three disciples were affected by this taste of heavenly glory. First, they are weighed down by sleep while these things happen. It appears that this came from the fear by which, as others write, they had been dismayed. At last, when they came to themselves, they saw and heard those things which were being done while they had been lulled to sleep. By this example not only is our weakness shadowed forth, which, while we live in the flesh, does not perceive divine and heavenly things, but sloth and dullness are also charged against us, by which, hindered, we scarcely observe those things as we ought. This dullness is so great that it can be neither shaken nor overcome either by joyful or by sad things. For what the disciples suffer here, the same men afterwards suffered, when Christ, with the hour of his death at hand, testified before them to the weakness of his assumed flesh, and exhorted them to watchfulness and prayer. We experience many things of this kind in ourselves, and the consideration of them ought to rouse us, so that we may be more fervent in prayer and acknowledge God's goodness, who admonishes and raises us though we are unworthy, lest we perish wretchedly in this most pernicious drowsiness of the soul.

units.la: Porro huic vitio aliud coniungit Petrus feruore & zelo, quo pra aliis fere flagrauit, abreptus. Cum enim Mosem & Eliam iam discessuros videret, veritus ne spectaculum hoc iucundissimum horum abitu turbaretur, exclamat: Magister, bonum est nos hic esse, & faciamus tria tabernacula, tibi vnum, & vnum Mosi, & vnum Eliæ. Vbi laudem quidem meretur tam sancta contemplationis desiderium, reprehensione autem dignissima est stupida hæc ignorantia, qua illum laborauisse Lucas testatur, & quam non vno argumento produ. Primò enim finem huius visionis ignorat, & quamuis Christum de sua morte non semel concionantem, & de eadem cum illo Mosem & Eliam colloquentes iam nunc audiuisset, ipse tamen quasi re omni confecta sibi iam triumphum fingit, & priusquam aliquid passus sit, regnare cupit. Deinde tabernaculum opus esse putat ijs, quos cœlesti gloria coruscare & extra omnem huius seculi fortunam constitutos esse videbat. Quid, quod nullum discrimen facit inter Christum & eius seruos, & dum his vnà cum illo tabernacula facere conatur, in eodem illos gradu cum eo collocat. Est hoc carnis nostræ ingenium, vt ante tempus nobis triumphos paremus, & fere de nostris consilijs plus quam par sit nobis polliceamur. Fit ergo, vt dum bono zelo abrepti in diuinis sapere volumus, plerunque stultitiam extremam testemur. Poterat hoc multis exemplis probari: sed quia in nobis ipsis hoc frequenter experimur, alienum minime opus est. Discamus potius humiliari sub Dei manu, neq; quicquam bonum putare, quam quod ille decreuit.
units.tr: Further, Peter, carried away by the fervor and zeal with which he almost burned more than the others, joins another fault to this one. For when he saw Moses and Elijah about to depart, fearing that this most pleasant spectacle would be disturbed by their going, he exclaims: "Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." Here such a holy desire for contemplation deserves praise, but this stupid ignorance, by which Luke testifies that he was troubled, is most worthy of reproof, and I shall show this by more than one argument. First, he is ignorant of the purpose of this vision; and although he had heard Christ more than once speaking of his death, and Moses and Elijah conversing with him about the same, yet now, as if everything were already accomplished, he imagines a triumph for himself and wants to reign before he has suffered anything. Next, he thinks that tabernacles are needed by those whom he sees glittering with heavenly glory and placed beyond all the fortune of this age. Moreover, he makes no distinction between Christ and his servants, and while he tries to make tabernacles for them together with him, he places them in the same rank as him. It is the nature of our flesh to prepare triumphs for ourselves before the time, and to promise ourselves from our own plans more than is fitting. So it happens that, while we are carried away by good zeal and want to be wise in divine things, we very often show the greatest folly. This could be proved by many examples, but since we experience it frequently in ourselves, there is no need to go elsewhere. Let us rather learn to be humbled under the hand of God, and to think nothing good except what he has decreed.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius historiæ partem, qua alter illius visus aut fructus continetur: qui docet, Iesum hunc esse Christum, id est, promissum mediatorem, per quem vnum nobis Pater placatus fit, & quem solum audire debeant, quotquot seruari volunt. Id vero Pater ipse docet, qui præsentiam suam partim nube (vt olim sapius) partim cœlesti voce testatus est, dicens: Hic est filius ille meus dilectus (apud Matthæum additur, In quo placatus sum) ipsum audite. Quæ verba ex Mose & Prophetis desumpta esse, alibi ostendimus: vt appareat, non alium esse Christum, quàm de quo Moses & Prophetæ concionati sint: & simul asseritur hic consensus inter vetus & nouum Testamentum, qui nos dulcissimæ illius communionis admonet, quæ nobis cum veteribus intercedit: de qua iam ante diximus. Disertè autem ait: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus: vt partim quidem eum sufficere doceat muneri, ad quod destinatus est: partim vt inter ipsum & Mosem atq; Eliam, adeoq; omnes sanctos distinguat, & ostendat gloriam hanc nostram cum Deo reconciliationis huic vni deberi. Et ideo hunc audire iubet. Ita enim eum nobis doctorem atq; Magistrum præficit, vt (quod olim Moses testatus est) salutem & regni sui hæreditatem omnibus neget, qui ipsum audire nolunt.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the other part of this history, which contains the other sight or fruit of it: which teaches that this Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised mediator, through whom alone the Father is reconciled to us, and whom alone all who wish to be saved ought to hear. The Father himself teaches this, who attested his presence partly by a cloud (as he often did of old) and partly by a heavenly voice, saying: "This is my beloved Son" (in Matthew it is added, "in whom I am well pleased"), "hear him." We have shown elsewhere that these words are taken from Moses and the Prophets, so that it appears that Christ is none other than the one of whom Moses and the Prophets preached; and at the same time this agreement between the Old and New Testament is affirmed, which reminds us of that most sweet communion which we have with the ancients, of which we have already spoken. Moreover, he says expressly, "This is that Son of mine, the beloved"; partly so as to teach that he is sufficient for the office to which he has been appointed, and partly so as to distinguish him from Moses and Elijah, and indeed from all the saints, and to show that this glory of ours, of being reconciled to God, is owed to this one alone. And therefore he bids us hear him. For he thus sets him before us as teacher and master, so that (as Moses once testified) he denies salvation and the inheritance of his kingdom to all who are unwilling to hear him.

units.la: Ideo cum Euangelij sui prædicationem Apostolis mandaret, addit: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur: Qui non crediderit, damnabitur. Ad quorum omnium confirmationem facit, quod cum hanc vocem promulgaret Pater, nemo præter solum Iesum adesse visus est. Quando ergo de æternæ salutis negotio agitur, ita vnus & solus Christus eminere debet, vt procul facessere & euanescere debeant sancti omnes cum suis meritis, nisi quatenus illi testimonium dederint. Semper enim rata erit eius sententia, quam per Isaiam protulit: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Continetur ergo hic æternum Dei Patris decretum, cui Moses & Prophetæ consentiunt, & quod nunc in cœtu selectissimorum Dei hominum solenni & inaudita prius ma-
units.tr: Therefore, when he commissioned his Apostles to preach his gospel, he added: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned." To confirm all of these things, it is relevant that when the Father uttered this voice, no one was seen to be present except Jesus alone. When the matter of eternal salvation is under discussion, therefore, Christ alone must stand out so clearly that all the saints, with their merits, must withdraw and vanish far away, except insofar as they have borne witness to him. For his sentence will always stand, which he pronounced through Isaiah: "I am the Lord; that is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." Here, then, is contained the eternal decree of God the Father, with which Moses and the Prophets agree, and which has now been promulgated in the assembly of God's chosen people with a solemn majesty never heard of before.

units.la: iestate promulgatum est. Huic nos fidere decet, neq; superstitiosorum hominum delirijs moueri, qui nobis Patres nescio quos & Concilia obtrudere satagunt. Nam si illi idem cum Deo Patre loquuntur; illú non est opus. Sin verò diuersum tradunt, & ex semetipsis nouas salutis assequenda rationes nobis fabricant, anathema sunt, neque merentur audiri. Poterat de his sermo in immensum extendi, sed breuitati studemus, quia alibi diximus, quæ ad ampliorem istorum explicationem faciunt.
units.tr: It is fitting for us to trust this, and not to be moved by the delusions of superstitious men, who busily try to thrust upon us I know not what Fathers and Councils. For if they speak the same things as God the Father, there is no need of them. But if they teach something different, and from themselves fabricate new ways of obtaining salvation for us, they are accursed and do not deserve to be heard. This discussion could be extended without limit, but we aim at brevity, because we have said elsewhere what serves a fuller explanation of these matters.

units.la: De discipulis additur, quod taciti hæc omnia sibi seruauerint. Quod illos ex Christi mandato fecisse, Marcus diserte docet. Præceperat enim eis grauiter, ne cui narrarent quæ viderant. Cuius mandati duplex ratio assignari potest. Prima, ipsorum ignorantia, quæ adhuc crassissima erat, adeo enim nondum tenebant regni Christi & salutis mysteria, vt quid resurrectio ex mortuis sit, adhuc ignorarent, vt in Marco est videre. Altera, quod ista non meruissent fidem apud aliquos, cum omnes in regni terreni expectationem intenti essent, & pauci in Christo gloriam cælestem agno scerent. Satius ergo fuit ista ad tempus reticere, quam intempestiua atque inepta prædicatione totum humanæ redemptionis negotium ludibrio aduersariorum exponere. Quamuis autem hodie nihil eorum dissimulari debeat, quæ Dei Filius propter nos fecit, idem tamen à verbi sui dispensatoribus adhuc prudentiam requirit, vt in loco & tempore omnia proponant, & tam suæ tenuitatis quam captus auditorum rationem habeant diligentem. At quod præcipuum huius loci caput est, discant omnes, Iesum hunc, qui ex virgine hominem assumpsit, æternum & dilectum illum esse Dei filium, cuius merito nobis Pater placatus est, & qui olim in gloria veniet, vt hostium quidem contumaciam vlciscetur, suis autem æterna regni promissi præmia rependat. Illum ergo audiamus, eidem credamus, & in ipso seruabimur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: It is added concerning the disciples that they kept all these things to themselves in silence. Mark clearly teaches that they did this in accordance with Christ's command, for he had strictly charged them not to tell anyone what they had seen. A twofold reason for this command can be given. The first is their own ignorance, which was still very gross; for they did not yet grasp the mysteries of Christ's kingdom and of salvation so well that they even did not know what the resurrection from the dead was, as can be seen in Mark. The second is that these things would not have earned credence with some people, since all were intent on the expectation of an earthly kingdom, and few recognised in Christ the heavenly glory. It was therefore better to keep these things quiet for the time being than, by untimely and foolish preaching, to expose the whole business of human redemption to the mockery of the adversaries. Yet although nothing of what the Son of God has done for us ought to be concealed today, he still requires of the dispensers of his word prudence, so that they set out everything in its proper place and time, and take careful account both of their own slenderness and of the capacity of their hearers. But the chief point of this passage is this: let all learn that this Jesus, who took man from the virgin, is that eternal and beloved Son of God, by whose merit the Father has been reconciled to us, and who in time will come in glory, to avenge indeed the obstinacy of his enemies, but to repay his own with the eternal rewards of the promised kingdom. Let us therefore hear him, believe him, and in him we shall be saved. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCI.
units.tr: HOMILY XCI.

units.la: Factum est autem sequenti die, cum ipsi descendissent de monte, occurrit ei turba multa. Et ecce quidam è turba exclamauit, dicens: Magister, rogo te respice ad filium meum: nā vnigenitus est mihi. Et ecce spiritus arripit eum, & repente clamat, & discerpit eum cū spuma, & vix discedit ab eo, conterens eum. Et rogaui discipulos tuos, vt ipsum eiicerent, sed non potuerunt. Respondens autem Iesus ait: O natio incredula & peruersa, quousque tandē ero apud vos, & tolerabo vos? Adduc filium tuum huc. Cum autem adhuc accederet, lacerauit eū dæmonium & discerpsit. Obiurgauit autē Iesus spiritum impurum, & sanauit puerum, & reddidit eum patri suo. Percellebantur igitur omnes super magnifica Dei virtute. Omnibus verò mirantibus super omnibus quæ faciebat, dixit discipulis suis: Reponite vos in aures vestras sermones istos. Futurum est enim, vt Filius hominis tradatur in manus hominum. Ipsi verò ignorabant di&tum illud, eratq; ipsis occultum, adeo vt illud non sentirent, & timebant eum interrogare de hoc dicto.
units.tr: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, saying: "Master, I beg you, look upon my son, for he is my only child. And behold, a spirit seizes him, and suddenly he cries out; it convulses him until he foams, and it scarcely leaves him, bruising him. And I asked your disciples to cast it out, but they could not." Jesus answered and said: "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and suffer you? Bring your son here." While he was still coming, the demon threw him down and tore him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. While they all marvelled at everything he did, he said to his disciples: "Let these words sink into your ears, for the Son of man is about to be delivered into the hands of men." But they did not understand this saying; it was hidden from them so that they did not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about it.

units.la: QVemadmodū Deus Filium suum iam inde ab æterno humani generis seruatorē constituit: ita eundem multis & variis testimoniis commendauit, vt facilius agnosceretur, & plures per ipsum salui fierent. Inter illa autem cum primis memorabile est, quod illi nuper reddidit, quando coram tribus discipulis transformatus cælestis gloriæ specimen dedit. Eo enim hunc Filium suum esse testatus est, in quo vno salus omnis habeatur, & quæ omnes audire atq; sequi debeant. Caeterum ne quis hæc putaret nuda verba esse, opera miraculosa accesserunt, quibus testimonia illa cōfirmantur. Quia enim ea fecit, quæ Messiā factuārum esse olim Isaias & alij Prophetæ prædixerunt, satis confiat, eum esse ipsum, de quo illi vaticinati sunt. Et huc referri debet historia, quā modo recitauimus. Nam dum puerum sanitati restituit, quem Satan ab infantia vsq; occuparat, & in quo manifesta ire Dei argumenta elucebant, quis non videat, nos per illū ex diaboli potestate redemptos & Deo reconciliatos esse? Quod vt rectiùs intelligatur, historiā hanc omnē per partes singulas inspiciemus.
units.tr: Just as God appointed his Son the Saviour of the human race from eternity, so he also commended him by many and various testimonies, so that he might be recognised more easily and more people might be saved through him. Among these, the one most worth remembering is what he recently gave, when before three disciples he was transfigured and showed a sample of heavenly glory. For by it he declared that this is his Son, in whom alone all salvation is found, and whom all ought to hear and follow. Moreover, lest anyone think these were bare words, miraculous works were added, by which those testimonies are confirmed. For since he did the things which Isaiah and the other prophets long ago foretold the Messiah would do, it is plain enough that he is the very one of whom they prophesied. To this the story we have just recited should also be referred. For when he restored to health the boy whom Satan had held from infancy, and in whom the clear signs of God's action shone forth, who does not see that we have been redeemed through him from the power of the devil and reconciled to God? So that this may be understood more correctly, we shall examine this whole story part by part.

units.la: Occurrit inter has primum miraculi occasio, quam Marcus diligentius exponit. Interea enim dum Christus cum discipulis tribus in monte versatus esset, quidam ad alios novem filium suum comitiali morbo secundum Lunae vices (ut Matthaeus annotavit) laborantem & malo daemonio agitatum adduxit, petens ut ei mederentur. Illi vero quia in aliis multis res non infeliciter succes-
units.tr: First among these there occurs the occasion of the miracle, which Mark sets out more carefully. For while Christ had been on the mountain with the three disciples, a man brought his son, who was suffering from epilepsy according to the phases of the moon (as Matthew noted) and was troubled by an evil demon, to the other nine, asking that they heal him. But since in many other matters things had turned out well for them, they set about the task, but in vain.

units.la: serat, ad opus sese accingunt, sed nequicquam. Hinc ergo Scribae adversus illos disputandi occasionem arripiunt, hoc nimirum agentes, ut totum Christi Iesu negotium omni populo suspectum reddant. Est enim hoc proprium hostibus Christi, ut ex eorum vitiis, qui ipsum profitentur, calumniandi occasionem arripiant: quo magis nos anniti decet, ne quam illis praebeamus, &c. Et credibile est, discipulos ea re vehementer turbatos fuisse, cum & se vulgi ludibrijs exponi, & simul Christi gloriam in ipsis periclitari viderent. At hic illis altercantibus ille superuenit, cui mox omnes obuiam excurrunt, rem exponunt, & accedunt his patris miseri preces, & ita miraculi edendi occasionem Christus habuit.
units.tr: Hence the scribes seized upon an occasion to dispute with them, plainly intending to make the whole work of Jesus Christ suspect to all the people. For it is characteristic of the enemies of Christ to seize upon an occasion for slander from the faults of those who profess him; the more reason for us to take care that we do not give them any. And it is credible that the disciples were greatly troubled by this, since they saw themselves exposed to the mockery of the crowd and Christ's glory at risk in them. But while they were arguing, he came up, and at once everyone ran to meet him, explained the matter, and the wretched father's pleas were added. And so Christ had an occasion to perform the miracle.

units.la: Quo loco nobis ante omnia discipuli considerandi veniunt, qui cum a pluribus obsessis daemonia prius eiecerint, hoc tamen eijcere non possunt, quo miser ille agitabatur. Quod etsi miraculo secuturo occasionem praebere debuerit, & Christi potentiam illustrare, simul tamen in genere docet, nihil feliciter ab illis perfici, qui sine Christo aliquid tentant, & non solida fide armati sunt. Solus enim ille nobis Deum propitium reddit, & spiritum illum largitur, qui nos ad omnia idoneos atque instructos facit. Huius ergo meminerint, quotquot in ecclesiae ministerio constituti sunt, & cogitent nihil esse eos qui plantant aut rigant, incrementum vero omne dari a Deo per Christum, quem in sua gratia mediatorem constituit. Idem obseruent qui rempub. administrant: quia nisi Dominus ciuitatem custodierit, frustra excubabunt quotquot eam seruare volent. Viderunt hoc optimi reges olim, quibus prima semper fuit religionis cura, ut Christo propitio uterentur. Quod ipsum ad rem domesticam quoque transferri debet, in qua felices esse non possumus, nisi Deum nobis habeamus praesentem in Christo, qui sola fide apprehenditur. Hoc si diligentius paulo omnes expenderent, mox viderent quae potissima infortuniorum nostri seculi causa sit. Sudant multi in Ecclesiae ministerio, laborant alij in Repub. & rem domesticam alij maximo cum labore obeunt. Interim in ecclesia errores dominantur, in Repub. scelerum licentia regnat, priuatim ira Dei sese passim exerit. Mirantur haec multi, sed quod miremur non est, quando conflat plerosque ad ecclesiae & reipub. administrationem sine Christo accedere, & priuatis solum commodis intentos esse, in re domestica autem fere omnes nimia solicitudine angi, & in artibus malis potius quam in Dei benedictione fiduciam collocare. Caeterum hinc digressi ad miraculi historiam accedamus, qua hoc ordine describitur.
units.tr: Here the disciples above all come to our notice: although they had earlier cast out demons from many who were possessed, they could not cast out this one by which that wretched boy was tormented. Although this was to provide an occasion for the miracle that was to follow and to show forth the power of Christ, it nevertheless teaches in general that nothing is accomplished successfully by those who attempt anything without Christ and are not armed with solid faith. For he alone makes God favourable to us, and bestows that Spirit which makes us fit and equipped for everything. Let all who have been appointed to the ministry of the Church therefore remember this, and consider that those who plant or water are nothing, but that all increase is given by God through Christ, whom he has appointed mediator in his grace. Let those who administer the commonwealth observe the same, for unless the Lord keeps the city, those who keep watch over it in vain will be on guard. The best kings of old saw this, for whom the chief concern was always religion, so that they might have Christ favourable to them. This must also be applied to domestic affairs, in which we cannot be happy unless we have God present with us in Christ, who is apprehended by faith alone. If everyone weighed this a little more carefully, they would soon see what is the chief cause of the misfortunes of our age. Many labour in the ministry of the Church, others toil in the commonwealth, and others carry on domestic affairs with the greatest effort. Meanwhile errors reign in the Church, licence for crimes holds sway in the commonwealth, and the wrath of God shows itself everywhere in private life. Many marvel at these things, but there is no cause for wonder, since it is plain that most come to the administration of the Church and commonwealth without Christ, and are intent only on private advantages, while in domestic affairs almost all are troubled by excessive anxiety and place their trust in wicked arts rather than in the blessing of God. But, turning aside from this, let us come to the history of the miracle, which is described in the following order.

units.la: Primum miseri filius pater producitur, qui Christo rogante (ut in Marco habetur) quid rei ageretur tanta cum altercatione, infelicem filij sui conditionem multis exponit, & ut ipsi opem ferat, precatur. Propositio est: Respice filium meum. Ratio: Nam vnigenitus est mihi. Id vero ad monendum affectum faciebat, & hanc curam patris iustam esse docebat. Nam si pium est pro filijs pluribus solicitum esse, quis eum reprehendat, qui vnigeniti salutem peculiari studio quaesiuerit? Facit tamen ad huius confirmationem diligentior descriptio, quam subijcit. Nam ecce spiritus (inquit) eum arripit, & ut miserabiliter clamet cogit, imo discerpit & lacerat miserum atque spumantem, & vix tandem illo grauissimè multato discedit. Apud Marcum spiritus ille mutus ab effectu dicitur, quod ad augendam miseriam plurimum facit, quando de ea ne queri quidem aut opem aliorum verbis idoneis flagitare possumus. Additur ibidem, quod ab infantia vsque eum afflixerit, & saepe in aquam, saepe in ignem abiecerit, nimirum ut totum perderet. Adumbratur tota hac narratione ingenium diaboli, qui ut ab initio homicida fuit, ita perdendi nobis nunquam non intentus est: Quamvis enim non in omnium corpora ad hunc modum grassetur, idem tamen in omnibus fieri videmus, quos in peccati seruitium adduxit. Nam hos quoque pessimarum cupiditatum laqueis irretitos hinc inde rapit & lacerat. Mutos item reddit quoad Deum, ne cum hoc per preces pias colloquentur, at ijdem quoad scelera nimium vocales & clamosi fiunt, dum & monitoribus fidis obstrepunt, & aduersus Deum quoque linguas virulentas laxant. Spumat ergo in illis peccandi libido, & singulis prope momentis in proprium exitium ruunt, & nisi Deus illis sutcurrrat, tandem in suis desiderijs consumuntur atque pereunt. Exempla horum passim in libidinosis & scortatoribus, in auaris, in ebriosis & infinitis aliis occurrunt. At simul in Lunatico paterna Dei prouidentia nobis consideranda venit, qui non tantum Satana permittit, quantum is cupit, sed occultis frenis furorem eius atque nocendi libidinem coercet. Quod in hoc factum fuisse, res ipsa loquitur. Quia enim infantem adhuc corripuit, procul dubio iam pridem eum perdidisset, nisi Dei virtute fuisset impeditus. Tantum ergo hic ei ad tempus permisit, quantum ad illustrandam per ipsum Filij sui Iesu Christi gloriam sufficere sciebat. Simile quid in Iobi historia videmus, vbi etiam certus finibus Satanam Deus circumsepsit, ne longius quam ipse volebat, in illum manus extenderet. Eadem Dei cura nos quoque seruamur, ne vel dormientes vel alioqui rerum securos improbus ille perdat. Hæc vt nobis pietatis studium commendant & Deo gratos esse docent: ita eorum superstitionem atque vanitatem arguunt, qui in diaboli potestate esse putant, vt nos aut fruges veneficarum & sagarum praestigiis perdat, aut quibuscunque alijs incantationibus damnum nobis inferat. Quam parum enim ille posset, in Ægyptiorum Magorum & Baalami exemplis est videre, vt infinita alia omittamus, quæ in externis historijs habentur. Non ergo diabolum aut hominum illi additorum praestigias timere debent Christiani, sed toti à Deo pendere, cuius facile est suos tueri atque seruare.
units.tr: First the father of the wretched son is brought forward, who, when Christ asks (as is found in Mark) what is going on with such a quarrel, sets out to many the unhappy condition of his son, and prays that he would bring help. The proposition is: "Look upon my son." The reason: "for he is my only child." This indeed served to move the affection and taught that this father's concern was just. For if it is godly to be anxious for several sons, who would blame the one who has sought the salvation of an only child with special zeal? The more careful description which he adds, however, serves to confirm this. For, he says, "behold, a spirit seizes him," and compels him to cry out pitifully; indeed it tears and lacerates the wretched foaming boy, and at last scarcely leaves him, grievously mangled. In Mark that spirit is called mute, from its effect, which greatly adds to the misery, since we can neither complain of it nor ask others for help in suitable words. It is added in the same place that it has afflicted him from infancy, and often cast him into water and often into fire, evidently so as to destroy him altogether. This whole narrative sets forth the nature of the devil, who, as he was a murderer from the beginning, so is he never not intent on destroying us. For although he does not rage in this way against the bodies of all, we see that he does the same to all whom he has brought into the slavery of sin. For he also seizes these, entangled in the snares of the worst desires, and tears them to pieces on every side. Likewise he makes them mute as regards God, so that they cannot converse with him by pious prayers, but these same people become too loud and clamorous in wickedness, since they both shout down faithful advisers and loose venomous tongues even against God. Thus the lust of sinning foams in them, and they rush almost every moment to their own ruin, and unless God comes to their aid, they are at last consumed by their desires and perish. Examples of this are found everywhere among the lustful and whoremongers, the greedy, the drunkards and countless others. But at the same time, in the case of the lunatic, we must consider the fatherly providence of God, who does not permit Satan as much as he desires, but restrains his fury and his lust for harm by hidden bridles. That this happened in this case the thing itself makes plain. For since he seized the boy while still an infant, he would without doubt have destroyed him long before, had he not been hindered by the power of God. Therefore he allowed him here only so much for a time as he knew to be sufficient for showing forth through him the glory of his Son Jesus Christ. We see something similar in the history of Job, where God also hemmed Satan in with fixed limits, so that he could not stretch out his hand against him further than God himself wished. By the same care of God we too are kept, lest that wicked one destroy us either while we sleep or while we are otherwise careless. These things both commend to us the zeal of godliness and teach us that God is pleased with it; and in the same way they refute the superstition and vanity of those who think that the devil is in such power that he can destroy our crops by the tricks of witches and sorcerers, or do us harm by any other incantations. How little he could do may be seen from the examples of the Egyptian magicians and of Balaam, not to mention countless other instances which are found in secular histories. Christians ought therefore not to fear the devil or the tricks of men subject to him, but to depend wholly on God, by whom it is easy for his own to be protected and kept.

units.la: Et hic nos solari debet, quod in præsenti nobis Christus exhibet, sua bonitatis atque fidei plus quam paterna spectimen. Nam etsi graues causæ essent, quæ vt ab ingratis & contumacibus discederet, monebant, non tamen opem suam negat, sed potius non sine amoris & doloris paterni significatione illorum incredulitatem deplorat, dicens: O natio incredula & peruersa, quousque tandem ero apud vos, & tolerabo vos? Quæ verba etsi proprie in apertos & contumaces hostes dicantur omnibus tamen & singulis, qui aderant, ex parte conueniunt. Nam si à discipulis exordiamur, eos in fide infirmiores tunc fuisse patet, cum spiritum hunc impurum non potuerint eijcere. Et alibi quoque ὀλιγοπιστίαν aut fidei tenuitatem in illis Christus accusat. Pater autem pueri ipse apud Marcum fatetur, quam procul adhuc à fidei perfectione absit, quando discipulorum errore offensus de Christi potentia non obscure dubitat, dicens: Si quid potes succurre nobis. Et mox, Credo Domine, succurre incredulitati meæ.
