Quod si Scribas consideres, ij cum incredulitate manifestam quoque impietatem & odium Christi coniunxerant: imo iam quasi exuto omni humanitatis sensu, non tam discipulis quam infelici huic insultabant, qui filium suum ad illos adduxerat. In populo autem etsi aliqui essent non omnino mali, tamen ne inter illos quidem inuentus est, qui Christi gloriam publice tueretur. Itaque iam pridem omnes illi meruerant, vt ab eo reijcerentur, & non immerito de illis omnibus conqueritur. Dum vero incredulitatem potissimum in illis accusat, non obscure docet, illa diaboli regnum maximè stabiliri, quod fide in ipsum destruitur & euertitur. Vt enim hac nos Christo insitos cum Deo coniungit: ita incredulitas à Deo abducit, & vel superstitiones gignit in animis hominum, vel prauis cupiditatibus habenas laxat, & in scelerum licentiam erumpit. Vtilissimum ergo fuerit, vt assidua promissionum gratiæ Dei meditatione atque precibus crebrius fidem in Christo foueant, qui misera & crudeli Satanæ tyrannide liberari volunt.
units.tr: This too should comfort us, that Christ now shows us a proof of his goodness and faithfulness that is more than fatherly. Even though there were weighty reasons that might have moved him to withdraw from these ungrateful and stubborn people, he does not refuse his help. Instead, with a signal of fatherly love and sorrow, he laments their unbelief, saying: "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you, and suffer you?" Although these words are properly spoken to open and stubborn enemies, they apply to all who were present, both to each one and to all together. For if we begin with the disciples, it is clear that they were then weaker in faith, since they could not cast out this unclean spirit. Elsewhere too Christ accuses them of little faith [ὀλιγοπιστίαν]. The father of the boy himself confesses in Mark how far he was still from perfect faith, when, offended by the disciples' failure, he openly doubts Christ's power, saying: "If you can do anything, help us." And soon after: "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief." If you consider the scribes, they joined their unbelief with plain impiety and hatred of Christ. Indeed, as if they had cast off all human feeling, they mocked not so much the disciples as this unhappy father, who had brought his son to them. Among the people, although some were not entirely bad, not one was found who publicly defended the glory of Christ. So all of them had long since deserved to be rejected by him, and he complains of them all, and not without reason. But when he accuses them chiefly of unbelief, he clearly teaches that the kingdom of the devil is strengthened most by this, since it is destroyed and overturned by faith in him. For just as faith joins us, grafted into Christ, to God, so unbelief draws us away from God, and either breeds superstitions in men's minds or loosens the reins of their lusts and bursts out into license for crime. It will therefore be most useful for those who want to be freed from the wretched and cruel tyranny of Satan to nourish their faith in Christ more often by constant meditation on the promises of God's grace and by prayer.

units.la: Poterit autem nos vehementer confirmare huius etiam miraculi diligens consideratio. Nam etsi iustissima esset expostulatio, qua aduersus illos vsus est, mox tamen ad patrem pueri conuersus, vt filium suum adducat iubet. Ita ergo de nobis queritur Deus, vt interim nos ad fe inuitet & nobis consulitum velit, quod exemplis infinitis demonstrari poterat. Vt vero Christus sua facilitate iflorum duritiem ad fidem emollire cupit: ita Satan vires omnes exerit, vt male occupatam possessionem in misero illo retineat. Dum enim is ad Christum adducitur, ille nouis furoribus inflammatus puerum lacerat, discerpit, humi denique prosternit, vt inter pulueres horrendum spumans volutetur. Et cum illi fortius insistere Christus, & inuitum exire cogeret, ita eum multat, vt plerique extinctum putarent. Est hoc Satanæ ingenium, vt quo propius Christum accedere videt, eo magis furat. Sentit enim per illum vires suas imminui & regnum totum destrui, imo caput ipsum conculcari, vt primæ promissionis verba docent. Et quamuis sciat Christi regnum impediri non posse, turbas tamen dat, vt huius præcones & salutis appropinquantes ministros vulgo suspectos & flectos & exosos reddat. Ideo postremi quique illius conatus prioribus graviores atque atrociores sunt. Sic in Ægypto olim factum fuisse legimus. Qui enim initio contentus erat Dei populum libertate spoliauisse, vbi tempus liberationis appropinquare vider, noua rabie Pharaonis animum accendit, vt iam non in viros modò, sed in recens natos infantes saeuiret, & iam nascituros crudeles insidias strueret, adhæc laboribus intolerandis populum grauaret. Quo aßtu effecit, vt Mosis atque Aaronis odium conciperent plerique, & eos de liberatione loquentes porro nollent audire. Sicut militer, cum Babylonici exilij initio tolerabilia fuissent sub Nabuchodonosore & Evilmerodacho regibus, sub illius finem Baltazari extrema impietatis & sacrilegi furoris author fuit, quo religionem & veri Dei cultum omnino abolere conatus est, cuius instaurationem prae foribus adesse videbat: multos item decepit tunc Satan novis periculis, quae in Iudaea oriebantur, vt in Babylone potius manere, quam libertatis beneficio frui mallent. Debent huc referri immanissima crudelitatis plus quam belluinae exempla, quae in toto Romano Imperio per annos circiter trecentos edita fuisse constat, cum fides Christiana per totum orbem longe lateque propagaretur, & Satan cesantibus vbique oraculis & euanescente indies idolorum culu, sibi cedendum esse sentiret. Et quod tunc factum fuit, nunc etiam sub huius mundi finem experimur, quando reges & Pontifices adversus surgentem vbique terrarum Euangelij doctrinam excitat, & regna passim omnia bellis civilibus atque externis turbat, vt quamuis Christi doctrinam prorsus abolere non possit, eam tamen plerisque inuisam reddat, & tantorum malorum causam esse persuadeat. Mirantur haec multi, alij vero vehementer offensi, quo se vertant, nesciunt. At quid opus est ijs, ceu nouis & insolitis offendi, quae euentura olim Christus praedixit? Aut cur nos ista diaboli rabies terreat, quae vt regni Christi passim surgentis indicium est, ita illum cum infelici hoc mundo breui periturum esse testatur? Quin ergo fidei constantia armamur? Breuis enim ille diaboli furor est, eoque citius finem suum attinget, quo magis festinat.
units.tr: Careful consideration of this miracle may also greatly strengthen us. For although the complaint with which he addressed them was most just, he nevertheless turned to the boy's father and bade him bring his son. So God complains of us, and yet in the meantime invites us to himself and wishes to provide for us, as could be shown by countless examples. And just as Christ by his kindness seeks to soften their hardness into faith, so Satan exerts all his strength to keep his ill-gotten possession in that wretched boy. For when the boy is brought to Christ, the devil, inflamed with new fury, tears and rends him, and finally throws him to the ground, so that he writhes foaming among the dust in a dreadful way. And when Christ presses more firmly upon him and forces him to come out against his will, he so mangles the boy that many thought him dead. This is Satan's nature: the closer he sees Christ approaching, the more violently he rages. For he feels that his strength is weakened through him and his whole kingdom is being destroyed, and even that his head is being trampled, as the words of the first promise teach. And although he knows that the kingdom of Christ cannot be hindered, he still stirs up disturbances, so that the heralds of this kingdom and the ministers who bring salvation may be made generally suspected, hated and disliked. Therefore each of his last attempts is more grievous and savage than the earlier ones. We read that this happened once in Egypt. For Pharaoh, who at first was content to have despoiled God's people of their liberty, when he saw the time of their deliverance drawing near, was stirred by a new rage, so that he raged not only against men but against newborn infants, and plotted cruel snares against those not yet born, and burdened the people with intolerable labours besides. By this act he brought it about that many conceived hatred against Moses and Aaron, and would no longer listen to them when they spoke of deliverance. Similarly, when the Babylonian exile began, its early years were bearable under the kings Nebuchadnezzar and Evil-merodach, but toward its end Belshazzar became the author of extreme impiety and sacrilegious fury, and tried to abolish religion and the true worship of God altogether, although he saw its restoration standing at the doors. Satan also then deceived many with new dangers that arose in Judea, so that they preferred to remain in Babylon rather than enjoy the benefit of liberty. To this belong the most savage cruelties, more than bestial, which are known to have been committed throughout the Roman Empire for about three hundred years, while the Christian faith was spreading far and wide over the whole world, and Satan, with his oracles everywhere ceasing and the worship of idols daily fading away, felt that he must give way. What happened then we also experience now, toward the end of this world, when kings and Pontiffs stir up opposition everywhere on earth against the rising doctrine of the gospel, and disturb all kingdoms with civil and foreign wars, so that, although he cannot wholly abolish the doctrine of Christ, he makes it hateful to many and persuades them that it is the cause of such great evils. Many marvel at these things, and others, deeply offended, do not know where to turn. But why should we be offended by these things as new and unusual, when Christ foretold long ago that they would happen? Or why should the raging of the devil frighten us, which is a sign of the kingdom of Christ rising everywhere and testifies that he will perish together with this unhappy world before long? Why then do we not arm ourselves with constancy of faith? That madness of the devil is brief, and it will reach its end all the sooner the more it hurries.

units.la: Et hic nos animare debet Christi exemplum, qui etsi breues inducias diabolo concedat, vt & patris pueri fidem magis exploret, & miraculum illustrius faciat, mox tamen hostem aggressus eum non magno cum negotio eiecit. Etenim increpat eum publice, vt se eius hostem esse testetur. Est hoc consolationis plenum. Cur enim diabolum timeamus, cùm cuius hostem se profiteatur Dei Filius, Dominus ille exercituum, cui omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terra? Et quod Marcus annotauit, suis illum titulis compellat, atque spiritum mutum & surdum vocat: ita nimirum docens non dignum esse, quem aliquis in pretio habeat, aut formidet. Nam vtut ferociat & virtus suas ostentet, reuera tamen surdus & mutus est in Christi conspectu, cum ad huius dicta aures obturet, nec habeat, quod illi respondeat. Praeterea cum authoritate illi praecipit, vt à puero exeat, neque vn quam in illum reuertatur. Habet ergo imperium in illum, cui vel inuitus obedire cogitur. Nam etsi puerum (vt ante diximus) iterum lacteret & prosternat, exit tamen, Christus vero sua manu puerum erigit, & patri suo sanum atque incolumem restituit. Docent ista, Iesum hunc promissum illud femen mulieris esse, cuius merito diaboli caput conteri, & humanum genus redimi debuit. Ad hunc ergo ipsi quoq; accedamus, & proculdubio salui erimus.
units.tr: Here the example of Christ should also encourage us. Although he allows the devil a short respite, both to test the father's faith more closely and to make the miracle more striking, he nevertheless soon attacks the enemy and casts him out without great difficulty. For he rebukes him publicly, so as to show that he is his enemy. This is full of comfort. For why should we fear the devil, when the Son of God, the Lord of hosts, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, professes himself his enemy? And what Mark noted, that Christ addresses him by his titles and calls the spirit dumb and deaf, teaches that he is not worthy to be valued or feared by anyone. For however fiercely he rages and displays his strength, he is really deaf and dumb in Christ's sight, since he stops his ears against his words and has nothing to answer him. Moreover, Christ commands him with authority to come out of the boy and never return to him. So he has power over him, to whom the devil is forced to obey even against his will. For although, as we said before, the spirit tears and throws down the boy again, he nevertheless comes out, and Christ raises the boy with his own hand and restores him sound and unharmed to his father. These things show that this Jesus is that promised seed of the woman, by whose merit the head of the devil was to be crushed and the human race redeemed. Let us therefore come to him ourselves too, and without doubt we shall be saved.

units.la: Interim meminisse nos oportet, nobis quoque cum hoc hoste luctandum esse. Est enim inter nos & illem inimicitia perpetua, quam ipse Deus sanciuit, quando serpenti dixit: Ponam inimicitias inter te & mulierem, inter semen denique tuum & semen illius, &c. Et cum satis constet, quam pertinax sit diabolus in seruando aduersus humanum genus odio, vtque rugientis leonis instar obambulans nunquam non quaerat quos deuoret, minime decet, vt nos remissiores simus, & illi inducias demus. Quin potius meminerimus, nos in baptismo in militiam Iesu Christi adscriptos esse, vt sub eius signo aduersus hostem illum bellum perpetuum & (vt Græci loquuntur) ἀσπονδον geramus. Testemur ergo nos illi inimicos esse. Adhæc suis illum depingamus coloribus, vt se à nobis nequaquam ignorari intelligat. Nec enim alia re magis terretur improbus ille, quam si suum ingenium, artes atque mores sentiat nos non latere. Nam vt impostores locum non habent apud eos, qui ipsorum dolos & artes iampridem perspectas habent: Ita neque diabolus quicquam potest, si mendacia sua & fraudes à nobis agnosci sentiat. Mandemus praeterea illi ex Christi authori-
units.tr: Meanwhile we must remember that we too have to struggle with this enemy. For there is a perpetual enmity between us and him, which God himself ordained when he said to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed," and so on. And since it is well established how stubbornly the devil keeps his hatred against the human race, and how, prowling like a roaring lion, he never ceases to seek whom he may devour, it is by no means fitting that we should be careless and grant him a truce. Rather let us remember that in baptism we were enrolled in the army of Jesus Christ, so that under his banner we may wage against that enemy a perpetual war, without truce [ἀσπονδον], as the Greeks say. Let us therefore testify that we are his enemies. Moreover, let us paint him in his own colours, so that he understands that we are by no means ignorant of him. For nothing terrifies that wicked one more than to perceive that we are not unaware of his nature, arts and manners. For just as impostors have no standing with those who have long since seen through their tricks and crafts, so the devil can do nothing if he perceives that his lies and frauds are recognised by us. Furthermore, let us charge him in the authority of Christ...

units.la: Christus diebus facile eiecit.
units.tr: Christ easily casts out the devil.

units.la: Christiani assiduè cum diabolo luctari debent. tate, ut procul a nobis facessat: neq; deerit felix pugna huic euentus. Qui enim olim aduersus Chri-ftum nihil potuit, ut neque in eos aliquid iuris habet, qui Christo per fidem sunt insiti. In ipso enim nos omnia possumus, & ita nos ipse Patri Deo restituit, ut sub eius protectione tuti omnes hostium insidias facile contemnamus.
units.tr: Christians must wrestle constantly with the devil. By the authority of Christ we should command him to depart far from us, and the struggle will not fail to end happily. For the one who could do nothing against Christ has no right over those who have been grafted into Christ by faith. In him we can do all things, and he has so restored us to the Father God that, under his protection, we can easily despise all the snares of our enemies.

units.la: Sequitur quia miraculi effectus apud spectatores fuerit. Percellebantur (inquit) omnes super magnifica Dei virtute. In Christo igitur virtutem humana maiorem agnouerunt, & eius consideratione perculsi sunt, quod eius officium ignorarent: alioqui enim ex eo consolationem habuissent, quod Dei virtus eo vsque sese in illo demisserat, ut nobis seruandis occuparetur. Sed solet Dei potentia impios quoque terrere, quamuis terror ille inutilis sit, cum breui tempore duret, neque ad pietatem veram illos instituat. Non negauerim tamen aliquos ex his meliores fuisse, in quibus suo tempore signum hoc & vniuersa Christi doctrina fructum tulit. In primis autem obseruemus, quam facile sit Christo hostium suorum petulantiam compescere. Paulo ante discipulis eius insultabant Scriba, & sibi plausibilem occasionem obtigisse putabant, qua illum vulgo contemptum facerent. Fuit hoc diabolo spectaculum suauissimum, qui & ipse in hac sua victoria momentanea exultauit. At ecce vno verbo & huius ferociam frangit Dominus, & illos nouo timore perculsos omnium ludibrio exponit, neque possunt iam diuinam in ipso virtutem negare, qui prius impostorem & nullius pretij hominem dixerant. Fit hoc frequenter impijs, ut subito spe sua fructrentur, quando ad plenam victoriam nihil sibi amplius deesse putant. Et hic maxime habet locum illud Solomonis: Ante ruinam exaltatio.
units.tr: Next comes the effect of the miracle on the onlookers: "All were astonished at the magnificent power of God" (Luke 9:43). So in Christ they recognised a power greater than human, and they were struck with awe at it, because they did not know his office. Otherwise they would have drawn comfort from the fact that God's power had so far lowered itself in him that it was busy with our salvation. But the power of God often terrifies the wicked as well, although that terror is useless, since it lasts only a short time and does not lead them to true godliness. Yet I would not deny that some of them became better men, in whom this sign and the whole teaching of Christ in due time bore fruit. Above all, let us observe how easily Christ restrains the insolence of his enemies. A little before, the scribes were mocking his disciples and thought they had gained a welcome opportunity to make him despised by the common people. This was a most pleasant spectacle for the devil, who also exulted in this momentary victory. But see, with a single word the Lord also breaks their boldness, and, struck with a new fear, he exposes them to the mockery of all; and now they cannot deny the divine power in him, though before they had called him an impostor and a man of no worth. This often happens to the wicked: they suddenly lose their hope when they think nothing more is lacking to complete their victory. Here above all applies that saying of Solomon: "Before destruction comes pride" (Prov. 16:18).

units.la: Caeterum ne discipulos quoque laetitia immodica abriperet & securiores faceret, in tempore remedium adhibet Dominus. Nam omnibus in virtutis & operum suorum admiratione occupatis, illis consideratione horum diligentiorem commendat, dicens: Reponite vos in aures vestras sermones istos: Futurum est enim, ut Filius hominis tradatur in manus hominum. Rursus ergo crucis illos admonet, per quam ipsum in Patris gloriam ingredi & regnum sibi promissum obtinere oporteat: & docet: nec in huius miraculi successu acquiescant, sed potius eius consideratione confirmati ad certaminam maiora se parent. Est ergo haec generalis admonitio, quam hodie etiam non auribus solum percipere, sed imis cordibus recondere debemus: ut quoties res secunda nobis sunt, de aduersis & tristibus, quae nos in hoc seculo manent, diligenter cogitemus. Est enim militia vita hominis super terram, & quamuis interdum pax nobis concessa esse videatur, bea tamen breues modo inducie sunt, quibus nos Deus recreat, ut animosiores ad pugnam redeamus. Quoties ergo ecclesiam florere, nouis indies accessionibus crescere, & hostibus superiorem esse videmus, tunc in animum reuocentur, quae de persecutionibus olim a Christo praedicta sunt; neque putemus iam nos portum attigisse. Ita si quando res priuatae nobis salua & optime constituta putantur, tunc quae rerum humanarum vicissitudo, & quam instabilis sit huius seculi conditio cogitemus. Est haec meditatio vtilis admodum, imo necessaria quoque: quia in officio nos continet, ne vel insolentiores facti rebus latis impie abutamur, vel saltem securitate oppressi salutem propriam negligamus.
units.tr: Moreover, lest immoderate joy also carry off the disciples and make them too secure, the Lord applies a remedy in good time. For while all were occupied with admiration of his power and works, he commends to them a more careful consideration of these things, saying: "Let these words sink into your ears, for the Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men" (Luke 9:44). Again, then, he reminds them of the cross, through which he must enter into the Father's glory, and obtain the kingdom promised to him; and he teaches them not to rest in the success of this miracle, but rather, strengthened by the thought of it, to prepare themselves for greater struggles. This, then, is a general admonition, which we today must not only hear with our ears but also store deep in our hearts: that whenever things go well for us, we should carefully think about the adversities and sorrows that await us in this world. For the life of man on earth is a warfare, and although peace may sometimes seem to be granted to us, it is only a brief truce, by which God refreshes us so that we may return to the fight with greater courage. Therefore, whenever we see the Church flourishing, growing daily with new additions, and gaining the upper hand over its enemies, then let us call to mind what Christ foretold long ago about persecutions, and let us not think that we have already reached harbour. Likewise, if at any time our private affairs seem safe and well settled, then let us think about the changeableness of human things and how unstable is the condition of this world. This meditation is very useful, indeed also necessary, because it keeps us in our duty, lest, grown too proud, we impiously abuse our prosperous circumstances, or, at least overcome by complacency, neglect our own salvation.

units.la: Quam certe necessarium fuerit discipulos de his admoneri, ex eorum ignorantia apparet. Dicit enim Lucas: Ipsi vero ignorabant dictum istud, eratq; ipsis occultum, adeo ut illud non sentirent, & timebant eum interrogare de hoc dicto. Paucis verbis vitia multa comprehendit. Primo quid Christus sibi velit non intelligunt. Deinde nō sentiunt quoq; id est, verbis eius non afficiuntur, ut decebat. Quomodo enim in animos eorum penetrarent quod nō intelligebant? Accessit tertiū, quod nec in terrogare audent. Fuit hic pudor nō rusticus modo, sed pernitiosus valde et reprehensione dignus, siue eū metus siue ambitio pepererit. Quid enim opus erat ab eo sibi timere, cuius facilitas ipsis tot iam exte plus erat perspecta? Quod si ideo non quaerunt, ne ignorantes videantur, nā stulta admodū & nocen tissima fuit haec scientiae simulatio, quae ipsos in ignorantia tenebris detinebat. Poterant haec mira et stupenda videri. Sed meminisse oportet, animos ipsorum falsa de regno Christi terreno opinione praeoccupatos fuisse. Nō potuerunt ergo ea videre, quae de eius morte indigna dicebantur: et ut aliorū impia non multū mouentur, quos opū fiducia inebriat: ita crucis mentio nequaquā eos afficere potuit, quorum mentes nihil quàm regni splendorem, victorias & triumphos somniabant. Et quantū possit in dissimulanda ignorantia gloriæ cupiditas, in nobis ipsis non raro experimur. Excitet ergo nos discipulorum exemplum, ut Christum non ex nostro cerebro nobis nouū fingamus, sed talem agnoscamus, qualis in Scriptura prædicatur. Ignorantia autē nostræ, si quam sentimus, ita nos pudeat, ut simul in melius proficere cura sit. Accedamus ergo ad doctorē ipsum indulgentissimum, qui cum nobis à Deo Patre sapientia factus sit, nos in errorum tenebris perire non sinet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: How necessary it was for the disciples to be admonished about these things is clear from their ignorance. For Luke says: "But they did not understand this saying; it was hidden from them, so that they did not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying" (Luke 9:45). In a few words he sets out many faults. First, they did not understand what Christ meant. Next, they did not even perceive it, that is, they were not moved by his words as they ought to have been. For how could what they did not understand penetrate their minds? A third fault is added: they did not dare to ask him. This shame was not merely rustic but very harmful and deserving of rebuke, whether fear or ambition produced it. For what reason was there to be afraid of him, whose kindness they had already observed in so many ways? But if they did not ask because they did not want to seem ignorant, then this pretence of knowledge was very foolish and most hurtful, since it kept them in the darkness of ignorance. These things could seem wonderful and astonishing. But we must remember that their minds had been preoccupied with a false opinion of the earthly kingdom of Christ. Therefore they could not see what was being said about his unworthy death; and just as the wicked are not much moved by the warnings of others when the confidence of their riches intoxicates them, so the mention of the cross could in no way affect those whose minds dreamed of nothing but the splendour of a kingdom, victories and triumphs. And how much the desire for glory can do in disguising ignorance we often experience in ourselves. Let the example of the disciples therefore stir us up, so that we do not fashion for ourselves a new Christ from our own brain, but acknowledge him as he is preached in Scripture. And if we feel any ignorance of our own, let it shame us in such a way that we also take care to make progress for the better. Let us therefore approach that most kindly teacher, who has been made wisdom for us by God the Father, and he will not allow us to perish in the shadows of error. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 93.

units.la: Incidit autem disceptatio inter eos, quis esset eorum maximus. Iesus autem visa cogitatione cordis ipsorum, acceptum puerulum statuit apud se, & dixit eis: Quicunque exceperit puerulum hunc nomine meo, me excipit: & quicunque me exceperit, excipit eum qui me misit. Nam qui minimus est inter vos omnes, is erit magnus.
units.tr: There also arose a dispute among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, perceiving the thought of their heart, took a little child and set him by his side, and said to them: Whoever receives this little child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all, the same shall be great.

units.la: Scripturæ sacræ non solum præclara virtutis & pietatis exempla in Dei servis eximijs proponunt, sed eorundem vitia quoque commemorant, ut in illis quidem Dei gratiam singularem agnoscamus, nobis autem admoneamur, nihil cuiquam hominum superstitiosius esse tribuendum, & ut tanquam virorum exemplis moniti attentius vigilemus. Obseruari hoc ipsum debet in Iesu Christi discipulis, de quibus aliqua prius narrauit Lucas, quæ laudem singularem merentur. Nam ad prædicandum emissi iniunctum sibi munus fideliter obierunt. Deinde fidei confessionem ediderunt, quæ universam salutis humanæ rationem continet. Præterea tres ex eorum cœtu Christus delegit, ut illis gloriæ suæ & regni cœlestis specimen præberet. Itaque ea viderunt & audierunt, quæ olim multi Prophetæ & iusti cupierunt videre & audire. Ne quis ergo de illis sublimius æquo sentiret, & inde superstitionis materiam venaretur, non sine Spiritus sancti consilio nonnulla eorundem vitia subiiciuntur. Inter quæ primum locum habet fidei imbecillitas, qua illos laborasse in præcedenti historia vidimus. Secuta est mox ignorantia cum stupore quodam coniunctia, quæ causa fuit, ut Christum non intellexerint de ijs differentem, sine quibus hominum salus non potest consistere. Sequuntur nunc alia, quæ ex ordine videmus, & in præsenti quidem ambitio & superbia eorum taxatur, quæ Christo occasionem dedit differendi de humilitate, sine qua discipuli eius censeri non possumus.
units.tr: The Holy Scriptures do not only set forth the notable examples of virtue and piety in the outstanding servants of God, but also record their faults. In the one case we are to acknowledge God's singular grace; in the other we are warned that nothing should be attributed to any man beyond what is due, and that, admonished by the examples of men, we should watch more carefully. This must be observed in the case of the disciples of Jesus Christ, of whom Luke has earlier related things that deserve singular praise. For they were sent out to preach and faithfully performed the task enjoined on them. Then they made a confession of faith, which contains the whole account of human salvation. Moreover, Christ chose three of their company, so that he might show them a sample of his glory and of the heavenly kingdom. Thus they saw and heard things which many prophets and righteous men had long desired to see and hear. So that no one should think of them more highly than is right, and so seek from this a material for superstition, some of their faults are set down, not without the counsel of the Holy Spirit. Among these the first place belongs to the weakness of their faith, in which we saw them struggling in the preceding narrative. Soon after followed ignorance, joined with a certain stupor, which was the reason they did not understand Christ when he spoke about those things without which the salvation of men cannot stand. Now there follow other matters, which we see in order; and in the present passage their ambition and pride are rebuked, which gave Christ occasion to speak of humility, without which we cannot be counted his disciples.

units.la: Vitium eorum Lucas hoc verbis describit: Incidit disceptatio inter eos, quis esset eorum maximus. Matthæus & Marcus hoc in profectione Capernaum versus factum aiunt: cum paulo ante Christus illos de cruce imminenti admonuisset. Facit hoc ad amplificationem huius peccati, quod adeo non mouentur ijs, quæ magistro suo euentura esse audierant, ut interea de primatu cogitent. Oriebatur omnis malifuit (ut nuper quoque diximus) falsa, quæ inter Iudæos tunc vulgò ferebatur de regno Christi opinio. Quia enim illud terrenum fore somniabant, simul illos titillare cœpit innata hominibus supra alios eminendi cupiditas. Accendit autem hanc non leuis occasio, quòd Petrum, Ioannem & Iacobum iam semel & iterum negotijs secretioribus adhibuisset: quod ut tribus ipsis spem aliquam primatus obtinendi facere potuit, ita reliquos ad æmulationem extimulauit. Hinc ergo contentio illa exorta est, in qua multiuariam peccarunt. Primò enim superbiæ & ambitioni locum dant, qui Christi doctrina & exemplo quotidie ad humilitatem & modestiam instituebantur. Deinde præcipiti gloriæ studio abrepti triumphos & regnum animo concipiunt, priusquam in certamine illo vicerint, quod tam Christo quàm ipsis propositum esse audierant. Sunt ergo militum perfidorum similes, qui sub boram præli stipendium sibi numerari volunt, & priusquam hostem vicerunt: imò his deteriores, pugnam quoque detrectant. Accedit hıs, quòd qui ad vnum idemque certamen vocabantur, & proinde coniunctis animis atque viribus pugnā debebant capessere, nunc inter se commissi de regno altercantur. Concurrunt hīc æmulatio, inuidia, odium, simultas, quæ tandem in apertum dissidium eruperunt. Ergo ijs vitijs laborant, quæ vt multis regnis exitium attulerunt, ita à regno Dei excludunt omnes, qui in illis absque pœnitentia perseuerant. Atqui hi sunt illi, quos è mundo se elec-
units.tr: Luke describes this fault in these words: a dispute arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. Matthew and Mark say this happened on the journey toward Capernaum, when shortly before Christ had warned them of the cross that was about to come. This adds to the gravity of the sin: they were so unmoved by what they had heard would befall their master that in the meantime they were thinking about primacy. The whole evil arose (as we said recently too) from the false opinion then commonly held among the Jews about the kingdom of Christ. For since they dreamed that it would be an earthly kingdom, the innate desire of men to rise above others began to tickle them. This desire was kindled by no slight occasion: Christ had already taken Peter, John and James aside, once and again, into more private affairs. This, while it could give those three some hope of obtaining primacy, also stirred the rest to rivalry. Hence arose that contention, in which they sinned in many ways. First, they give room to pride and ambition, though they were being daily trained by the teaching and example of Christ in humility and modesty. Then, carried away by a headlong desire for glory, they conceived triumphs and a kingdom in their minds before they had won that struggle which, as they had heard, was set before both Christ and themselves. They are therefore like faithless soldiers who want their pay counted out before the battle line is formed and before they have defeated the enemy; indeed they are worse than these, for they also shrink from the fight. Add to this that men who were called to one and the same contest, and who ought therefore to take up the battle with united minds and strength, now quarrel among themselves about the kingdom. Here rivalry, envy, hatred and enmity meet together, and at last broke out into open discord. They therefore suffer from those vices which, as they have brought ruin to many kingdoms, so exclude from the kingdom of God all who persist in them without repentance. And yet these are the ones whom Christ confesses he has chosen out of the world, and whom he calls clean because of the word he has spoken to them.

units.la: Cur sanctorum vitia narrentur.
units.tr: Why the faults of the saints are recorded.

units.la: Discipuli de primatu contendunt. gisse Christus fatetur, & quos mundos vocat propter sermonem quem ipsis fit locutus. Admonens nos ista vitiositatis nostrae, & docent quàm imprudenter agant, qui suarum virium aut dignitatis sue fiducia elati supra alios eminere volunt. Fuit sanè multa laude dignissima discipulorum virtus, qua Christum hucusq; secuti sunt, & multis alijs deficientibus cum eo inter omnis generis tentationes perseuerarunt. At vnus hic locus abunde docet, miserè perituros fuisse illos omnes, nisi ex singulari gratia fuissent seruati. Docet praeterea exemplum hoc, quàm parum in regno Christi prosi-ciant, qui nondum renati sunt ex verbi semine. Quia enim circa terrena modò occupantur, animos ad caelestium bonorum contemplationem attollere non possunt, & fere non sine publico scandalo, fidei & religionis praetextu abutuntur. Estq; scandalum hoc eò nocentius, quò sublimior est conditio, qui affectibus ipsis indulgent. Pertinet huc quod de stella caelo delapsa in Apocalypsi legitur, cui data est clauis putei abyssi, quo aperto fumus ascendit, qui & Solem obscurauit, & locustas genuit toti orbi terrarum noxias. Constat enim in eo libro per stellas episcopos aut ecclesiarum ministros denotari, qui de caelo cadere dicuntur, quando relictis regni caelorum fluidijs & doctrina caelestiad terrenas aut huius seculi dignitates atq; opes aspirant. De caelo igitur cecidit magna stella, quando Romani episcopi in ecclesia summum ius & imperium sibi vendicarunt, & eadem occasione Reges & principes pedibus suis subiecerunt. Ab eo autem tempore data est illis clauis, non regni caelorum, qua Apostoli & horum successores hucusq; pie & bene vsi fuerant, sed putei abyssi, id est, infernalis malitiae & diabolicae impostura: quo per illos aperto mox falsae doctrinae fumus Soli iustitiae tenebras inuexit, vt extincta maxima ex parte Christi & meriti eius cognitione, plerique in errorum Labyrinthos inextricabiles immersi sint. Ex fumo autem illo locustarum exercitus prodierunt, sacrificulorum nimirum & monachorum agmina, quorum hypocrisi & dolis ecclesiae passim omnes vastatae, simul autem attritis omnium regnorum opibus Pontificum potentia in immensum aucta fuit. Poterant haec prolixè tractari, sed sufficiat occasione dedisse ijs, qui in ecclesia seruiunt, de his diligentius cogitandi, ne diaboli suggestionibus locum dent, qui ipsis etiam Apostolis opum & regni terreni spem facere ausus fuit, vt Christi regnum impediret, quod ipsorum ministerio propagandum fore sciebat.
units.tr: The disciples contend about primacy. They admonish us of our own faults, and teach how imprudently they act who, puffed up by confidence in their own strength or dignity, want to rise above others. There was indeed a virtue in the disciples most worthy of praise, in that they followed Christ until now and, when many others fell away, persevered with him amid all kinds of temptations. But this one passage sufficiently teaches that they would all have perished wretchedly had they not been preserved by singular grace. This example further teaches how little they profit in the kingdom of Christ who have not yet been born again from the seed of the word. For since they are occupied only with earthly things, they cannot lift their minds to the contemplation of heavenly goods; and they abuse faith and religion as a pretext, almost always to public scandal. And this scandal is the more harmful the higher the rank of those who indulge their passions. To this belongs what is read in the Apocalypse about the star fallen from heaven, to which was given the key of the bottomless pit, and when it was opened smoke rose up, which both darkened the sun and bred locusts hurtful to the whole world. For it is clear in that book that by stars are signified bishops or ministers of the churches, who are said to fall from heaven when, having abandoned the teaching of the kingdom of heaven and the heavenly doctrine, they aspire to earthly dignities or the honours and riches of this age. So the great star fell from heaven when the Roman bishops claimed for themselves the highest right and authority in the Church, and on the same occasion subjected kings and princes beneath their feet. From that time the key was given to them, not the key of the kingdom of heaven, which the apostles and their successors had hitherto used piously and well, but the key of the bottomless pit, that is, of infernal malice and diabolical deceit. When it was opened by them, the smoke of false doctrine immediately brought darkness over the Sun of righteousness, so that, with the knowledge of Christ and of his merit extinguished for the most part, many have been plunged into inextricable labyrinths of error. From that smoke came forth an army of locusts, namely the troops of priests and monks, by whose hypocrisy and tricks the churches everywhere have been laid waste; and at the same time, with the wealth of all kingdoms worn away, the power of the Pontiffs was increased beyond measure. These things could be treated at length, but let it suffice to have given occasion to those who serve in the Church to think about them more carefully, lest they give room to the suggestions of the devil, who dared to hold out to the apostles themselves the hope of wealth and earthly kingdom, in order to hinder the kingdom of Christ, which he knew would be propagated by their ministry.

units.la: Porrò Christum videamus, quem occulta discipulorum disceptatio non latuit, cum quid singuli intra animos suos cogitarent, probè sciret. Et quamuis nullum illis verbum fecerit in itinere, Capernai tamen, cum iam diuertisset, quid inter se altercati sint, interrogat. Quod vt euidens est diuinitatis eius argumentum, ita docet, non temere illum nobis alibi comminatu esse, quòd de quouis verbo otioso rationem simus reddituri. Discipulis certè nunquam in mente venit, haec illi nota esse, quae ipsi furtim inter se mussitabant. At nihil horum ei occultum fuit, & vel inuitos atq; pudore suffusos nunc in medium protrahit, quamq; grauiter peccarint, docet. Horum vtinam hodie meminissent, qui effreni licentia quiduis dicunt & faciunt, impunitatem verò sibi ex eo pollicentur, si vitia sua inter homines celare possint. At frustra celatur apud eos, quae Christi oculis expósita sunt, qui cùm ipsi vt sum fuerit, in res abstrusissimas lucem inferre potest, vt omnibus nota fiant, quae optimè occultata videbantur. Et quia arcanam de primatu contentionem hîc arguit, non obscurè admonet, se ijs etiam irasci, qui intra animos suos caeca aemulatione accensi de fratribus opprimendis aut subigendis cogitant. Adhac consolationis plenum est, quòd discipulos tam grauiter corripit. Ex eo etiam apparet, non latere ipsum eorum consilia, qui falsis Apostolicorum titulis superbi in ecclesiam eius tyrannidem affectant. Colluduntque quidem illi inter se, & profundo astu Reges quoq; in suas partes trahunt, vt horum auxilijs male partum imperium tueantur: sed videt horum machinationes Christus, & quod nostro seculo non semel factum vidimus, proditoria eorum consilia praeter omnem expectationem detegit. At quae illorum hominum est pertinacia, non vllis diuinae iustitiae aut prouidentiae exemplis mouentur, & proinde in peius in dies proficiunt, donec dignas suae impietatis poenas exoluent. Quia verò haec alterius loci sunt, quid Christus cum discipulis egerit, videamus.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us look at Christ, who, as he knew well, was not hidden from the secret dispute of the disciples, nor from what each of them thought within his own mind. And although he said nothing to them on the road, yet when they had reached Capernaum he asks what they had argued about among themselves. This is as clear a proof of his divinity as it teaches that he has elsewhere warned us that we shall give account of every idle word. The disciples certainly never imagined that these things, which they were muttering to one another in secret, were known to him. Yet none of these things was hidden from him, and even against their will and covered with shame, he now brings them into the open and shows how gravely they had sinned. Would that those who, with unbridled licence, say and do whatever they please, and promise themselves impunity from this if they can conceal their faults from men, would remember this today! But it is in vain to hide from them what is laid open to the eyes of Christ, who, since he is God, can bring light into the most hidden things so that they become known to all, though they seemed most carefully concealed. And since he here rebukes the secret contention about primacy, he admonishes unmistakably that he is angry also with those who, inflamed within their minds by blind rivalry, plot to oppress or subdue their brothers. Moreover, there is something full of consolation in the fact that he rebukes the disciples so severely. From this it also appears that their counsels are not hidden from him, those who, proud of the false titles of apostles, aspire to tyranny over his Church. They indeed plot among themselves, and with deep cunning they draw kings also to their side, so that by their help they may defend an empire badly gained; but Christ sees their machinations, and, as we have seen happen more than once in our own age, he lays bare their treacherous counsels beyond all expectation. But such is the obstinacy of those men that they are moved by no examples of divine justice or providence, and therefore they advance from bad to worse day by day, until they pay the penalties due to their impiety. But since these things belong to another place, let us see what Christ did with the disciples.

units.la: Sunt in horum descriptione diligentiores duo alij Euangelistae, quae causa mihi videtur, quòd Lucas breuitati studuit. Marcus illum consedisse & duodecim simul ad se vocauisse scribit: vt vel ita ostenderet, se de re graui & ad omnes ex aequo pertinente esse dicturum. Deinde quia ambitionis spiritum animis eorum altius insedisse sciebat, quàm vt facilè eijci posset, chria vtitur, quae periculum. riculum, quod sibi accersant, ob oculos ponit, & simul occasionem aut materiam præbet cogitandi semper de illis, quæ ipsis observatu necessaria erant. Nam puerulum acceptum apud se statuit, & mox eum complexus ait: Amen dico vobis, nisi conuersi fueritis, & efficiamini puerulorum similes, non ingrediemini in regnum cœlorum. Itaq; à contrario argumentum ducit. Quasi diceret: Vos singuli supra alios in regno meo eminere vultis, at nisi humiliemini, nullus in illo vobis erit locus. Etenim humilitas sola medium fiue scala est, quæ homines euehit, vt in regno cœlorum eximios & Deo acceptos faciat. Fuit ergo hoc dictum graue admodum iis, qui nihil in terris regno Christi antiquius habebant: & solum hoc (siquidem Christiani sumus) nobis quoq; sufficere debet ad deprimendos spiritus illos, quibus supra homines omnes, imo supra Deum ipsum frequenter extollimur. Nunquam enim fallet hæc Christi vox, cui plane consentit, illud Petri: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam.
units.tr: Two other Evangelists are more careful in describing this scene, and I think the reason is that Luke aimed at brevity. Mark writes that Jesus sat down and called the twelve to himself, so as to show that he was going to speak about a serious matter that concerned them all equally. Then, because he knew that the spirit of ambition had settled in their minds too deeply to be easily driven out, Luke uses a chreia, which sets before their eyes the danger they were bringing upon themselves, and at the same time gives them an occasion or subject for always thinking about what they needed to know. For he took a little child, set him before himself, and then, embracing him, said: "Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." So he draws his argument from the contrary. It is as if he were saying: You want each of you to stand out above the others in my kingdom, but unless you humble yourselves, there will be no place for you in it. For humility alone is the middle way, or ladder, that raises men up so as to make them outstanding and acceptable to God in the kingdom of heaven. This saying was therefore very weighty for those who held nothing on earth more important than the kingdom of Christ. And this alone ought to be enough for us, since we are Christians, to bring down those spirits by which we are so often lifted above all men, and even above God himself. For this word of Christ never deceives, and Peter's saying plainly agrees with it: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble."

units.la: At quia in pueris ex innata nobis vitiositate multa insunt, quæ non imitatione, sed reprehensione digna sunt, scire oportet, in quibus illos debeamus imitari. Inter hæc primum est, quod à dominandi desiderio ita alieni sunt, vt quid nam sit dominari prorsus ignorent. Vbi nemo mihi obiiciat, in pueris quoq; non obscura superbiæ & ambitionis indicia apparere. Fatemur nos id, imo eos (si suo iure vti velit Deus) dignos esse dicimus, qui è regno Dei excludantur. Sed Christus de eo hic loquitur, quod in illorum ingenio & moribus vulgò apparet, non quod ex natura vitio in illis occultius hæret. Et quamuis (vt modò diximus) superbiæ spiritus iam nunc in illis agat, non tamen adhuc gradus illos honorum agnoscunt, multò minus de illis omnibus superandis solliciti sunt, sed sua sorte contenti viuunt. Deinde disciplinæ subsunt pueri & eam patienter ferunt (de ingenuis & bonæ indolis puerulis loquimur) ita in regno Dei locus non erit aliis, quàm qui legus Dei disciplinam libenter admittunt, & Filium eius reuerenter exosculantur. Adde hīs, quòd facile cum illis pueruli in gratiam redeunt, qui eos offenderunt, quod euidentissimum est animi de seipso humiliter sentientis indicium. Atqui hoc illud est, quod à nobis Scriptura passim requirit, & de quo nos Christus in orationis formula admonet, vt ea conditione nobis debita nostra remitti petamus, qua nos ab aliis acceptas iniurias condonamus. Hæc quicunq; præstant, ij (vt Paulus ait) non sensibus, sed malitia pueri sunt, & in eorum ordine censeri merentur, de quibus in præsenti Christus loquitur. Voluit autem de his admonere discipulos, vt intelligant quantum via ipsos relegere oporteat, qui se in Christi regno iam plus satis profecisse putabant. Prodest autem, vt ipsi quoq; in bono speculo pueruli nos sæpius contemplemur, vt discamus, quantum adhuc absimus à perfectionis meta, ad quam omnes aspirare oportet.
units.tr: But since children, through the vice we are born with, have many faults that deserve correction rather than imitation, we must know in what respects we ought to imitate them. Among these qualities, the first is that they are so far from any desire to rule that they are entirely ignorant of what ruling even means. Here let no one object to me that signs of pride and ambition are also not hidden in children. We admit this; indeed we say that they (if God wished to use his right) deserve to be shut out of the kingdom of God. But Christ is speaking here of what commonly appears in their disposition and manners, not of what clings to them more hiddenly from their corrupt nature. And although (as we have just said) the spirit of pride already works in them, they do not yet recognise those grades of honour, much less are they anxious to surpass them all, but they live content with their lot. Next, children submit to discipline and bear it patiently (we are speaking of well-bred children of good disposition). So in the kingdom of God there will be no place for anyone except those who gladly accept the discipline of God's law and reverently kiss his Son. Add to these that little children readily make up with those who have offended them, which is the most obvious sign of a mind that thinks humbly of itself. Yet this is exactly what Scripture everywhere requires of us, and what Christ in the form of the prayer warns us of, that we should ask for our debts to be forgiven on the same condition on which we forgive the injuries received from others. Whoever does these things, they (as Paul says) are children not in understanding but in malice, and deserve to be counted in the order of those of whom Christ is speaking here. He wished, moreover, to admonish the disciples about these things, so that they might understand how far they must go back who thought they had already made more than enough progress in the kingdom of Christ. It is also useful that we too, as in a good mirror, often contemplate little children, so that we may learn how far we are still from the goal of perfection to which all ought to aspire.

units.la: Cæterùm ne cui turpe aut indecorum videatur à pueruli discere, hos nobis diligenter commendat. Nam vt ante diximus, istum in vlnas accipit, vt sibi charissimum esse testetur. Cur ergo indignum vitæ & morum exemplar esse putes, quod apud Dei Filium in honore & pretio esse cernis? Non potuit olim Diogenem, acerrimum omnium hominum contemptorem, puerulum manus volas aquas haurientem obseruare, & ex illo discere sibi porrò scutella non opus esse. Nimium ergo superbi & delicati sunt, qui exemplum ab ipso Dei Filio propositu fastidire non verentur. At non contentus ille hoc gestu suum erga infantulos animum declarauisse, insuper addit: Quicunq; exceperit puerulum hunc nomine meo, me excipit: & quicunq; me exceperit, excipit eum qui me misit. Quibus verbis, quoad huius loci statum, admonemur amplius, salutis & veritatis doctrinam propter authorem siue administrum vilem aut despectum nequaquam contemni debere. Solet enim Deus tam hominibus quàm rebus in speciem contemptis vti in nobis erudiendis, vt non ab vllius creaturæ sed ipsius solius authoritate pendere discamus. Simul autem eius bonitatem nos obseruare decet, qui ex empla omnis generis proponit, vt vbiq; nobis occurrat occasio de iis cogitandi, quæ nobis cogniru & obseruatu necessaria sunt. Qui ingenui sunt filij, præceptores sibi à parentibus datos omni honore dignos esse agnoscunt, licet eos sibi neq; generis nobilitate neq; fortunis aut opibus pares esse norint. Eadem ergo est germanorum filiorum Dei indoles, quibus non graue est, si se ad flores agri, ad volucres cœli, ad coruorum pullos, deniq; ad oues, sementem, piscaturam, boues, asinos, remitti audiant, vt illinc discant ea, sine quibus salus nostra non potest consistere. At inter nostri seculi calamitates non postrema est, quòd pleriq; vix aliquem esse putant, cuius magisterio se debeant subijcere. Itaq; dum in omnibus iustas & dignas contemptus causas solicitè quaerunt, fere excusso omni disciplina iugo in licentiam effunduntur, ac tandem miserè pereunt.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone think it shameful or unseemly to learn from little children, Christ commends them to us carefully. For, as we said before, he takes the child into his arms, to testify that he is most dear to him. Why then do you think that a pattern of life and conduct is unworthy, when you see that it is held in honour and esteem by the Son of God? Diogenes, once the sharpest despiser of all men, could not refrain from observing a little boy scooping water in his hands, and learning from him that he no longer needed a dish. Therefore those are too proud and fastidious who do not hesitate to scorn an example set before them by the Son of God himself. But Christ, not content to have declared his affection for the little ones by this gesture, adds further: "Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me." By these words, as far as this passage is concerned, we are further admonished that the teaching of salvation and truth must in no way be despised on account of its author or minister being mean or contemptible. For God is accustomed to use both men and things that seem contemptible in our instruction, so that we learn to depend not on the authority of any creature, but on his alone. At the same time we ought to observe his goodness, who sets before us examples of every kind, so that everywhere an occasion may meet us of thinking about those things which we need to know and to observe. Those who are free-born sons acknowledge that the tutors given to them by their parents are worthy of all honour, even though they know that these tutors are not their equals in noble birth, fortune, or wealth. So the children of God, who are his true sons, have the same disposition: it is no burden to them to hear that they are sent to the flowers of the field, to the birds of the air, to the young ravens, finally to the sheep, the sowing, the fishing, the oxen and the asses, so that they may learn from there those things without which our salvation cannot stand. But among the calamities of our age, it is not the least that most people hardly think there is anyone to whose teaching they should submit. And so, while they carefully seek just and worthy reasons for contempt in everyone, they throw off almost every yoke of discipline, rush into licence, and at last perish wretchedly.

units.la: ESt praeterea hoc loco nobis observandum, commendatissimos nobis esse debere pueruios, quos tanto fauore aeternus Dei Filius dignatus est, & quos nobis ex singulari benedictione Dei obtinge re, Scriptura passim docet. Ad hos certè regnū suum proprie pertinere, alibi Christus testatur. Itaq; etiam atque tiranes cauere decet, ne illos vel negligentia nostra, vel prava institutione perdamus, ut aliquando à Deo secessione facta à regni eius haereditate excidant. Est enim scelus hoc cum sacrilegio coniunctum, quia simul è possessione sua spiritus Dei eijciuntur, qui in illorum cordibus sibi domicilium delegit. Fuerunt in ista meditatione diligentissimi olim Patriarchae, quos non alia ob causam soboles procreandae tanto desiderio arsisse constat, quàm quòd cuperent omnibus seculis quàm plurimos extare, à quibus Deus verè coleretur. At hodie qui liberos gignunt plurimi passim reperiuntur, at qui in illis educandis & piè instituendis operam dignam collocent, paucissimos est videre. Sunt ergo plerique agricolarum ignauorum similes, qui sementem quidem magno cum labore faciunt, sege tes autem iam adolescentes infelici lolio & spinis simul succrescentibus suffocari patiuntur. Et ut ijdem in plantandis aut inserendis arboribus assidui sunt, easdē verò frutescere sinunt, & proinde nullum ex insitione fructu percipiunt: Ita parentes fere liberos quidem gignunt, sed eosdem partim sua negligentia, partim prava institutione, & plerunq; pessimo exemplo corrumpunt. At quia in pue ris reipub. spes consistit, publica authoritate tales in ordinem redigi oportebat, quod olim in bene constitutis regnis atq; ciuitatibus inter gentes factum fuisse scimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we must observe here that little children ought to be most commended to us, those whom the eternal Son of God has deigned to honour with such favour, and whom Scripture everywhere teaches that we obtain by the singular blessing of God. Christ elsewhere testifies that his kingdom properly belongs to such as these. Therefore, like tyrants, we ought to take care not to lose them, whether through our negligence or through bad upbringing, so that at some time, by withdrawing from God, they fall from the inheritance of his kingdom. For this crime is joined with sacrilege, because at the same time the Spirit of God, who has chosen for himself a dwelling in their hearts, is cast out of his possession. The holy Patriarchs were most diligent in this meditation; it is well known that they burned with such desire for offspring for no other reason than that they wished there to be as many as possible in every age by whom God would be truly worshipped. But today many who beget children are found everywhere, while very few are to be seen who devote worthy effort to bringing them up and training them in godliness. So most people are like lazy farmers, who indeed sow with great labour, but allow the crops, when they have grown up, to be choked by unhappy darnel and thorns that spring up together with them. And just as these men are busy in planting or grafting trees, yet let them grow wild and so gain no fruit from the grafting, so parents generally beget children, but corrupt them, partly by their negligence, partly by bad training, and most often by the worst example. But since the hope of the commonwealth rests on the children, such people ought to be brought into order by public authority, as we know was done in times past among the nations in well-ordered kingdoms and states.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui actionem hanc graui sententia concludit: Qui minimus est inter vos omnes, is erit magnus. Seruiebat dictum hoc plurimum ambitiosis & superbis coercendus. Nam ita dicere videtur: Video vos pari studio ad hoc aspirare, ut in regno meo emineatis, & vnū quemq; in hoc esse, ut supra alios excellat. Id autem non improbo, modo ea via ingrediamini, qua solā ad fastigium illud peruenitur. Ea autem longè diuersa est ab ea, quam bucusq; tenuistis. Nam tunc demum se alijs sublimiores fore singuli arbitrantur, si alios deprimant & sibi seruos faciant. At plurimum vos ea opinio fallit. Quia qui minimus fuerit inter vos omnes, id est, qui se aliorū omnium seruū fecerit, ut verè magnus & alijs praestantior esse indicabitur. Et consultò vniuersali par ticula, OMNES, vti voluit, ne quis se officio suo defunctum putet, si infra vnum aut alterum sese demiserit. Vult enim, ut quoscunq; alios nobis praestantiores putemus, quo sensu Paulus hoc dictum interpretatur. Nihil ergo te fecisse adhuc putabis, si ijs te inferiorem facias, qui aut generis praerogatiua, aut opibus, aut meritis & beneficijs te excellunt, sed ut eundem animum erga omnes homines induas necesse est. Vbi tamen nemo putet, Christum legitimos & ab ipso Deo constitutos honorum gradus abolere, sine quibus neq; Respublica, neq; Ecclesia ordo, neq; res domestica consistit. Rata igitur perpetuò manent quae subditi magistratibus, auditores doctoribus, liberi parentibus, vxores maritis & serui heris debent officia. Humilitatem verò praecipit Christus, quae in duobus fere consistit. Primum est, ut à Deo imitio facto, nihil nobis ipsis coram illo arrogemus, sed cum Abrahamo fateamur, nos terram siue pulverem esse, neq; aliquid habere boni aut eximij, quod non ab illo acceperimus. Est hic proprius humilitatis atque modestiae fons, ex quo alterum emanat, quòd neminem prae nobis contemnimus aut fastidimus. Si qui enim nobis inferiores sunt, eò plus nos illis debere agnoscimus, cùm nos ideo donis suis Deus locupletarit, ut nostra copia siue abundantia aliorum inopiae subueniat. Est igitur humilitas fidissima charitatis nutrix, & fecundissima omnium officiorum mater, quibus illa inter homines conseruatur. Fuerunt huius studiosissimi, quotquot in scripturis commendantur. Hac insignis fuit Iosephus, quando fratribus perfidis & parricidis omne dilectionis fraternae officium praestitit, neque ideo illis inferior factus est, sed quò magis sese ad illorum seruitium demisit, eò maiori ac sublimiori honore à Deo coronatus est, & quoad homines quoq; supremum inter illos dignitatis gradum obtinuit. Humilitatis item studio ad regij throni fastigium Dauid ascendit, ex quo Saul propter superbiam deturbatus fuerat. At quid hominum exemplis immorari opus est, quando Iesum Christum non alia ratione in regnum Patris ingressum fuisse constat, quàm quòd serui forma assumpta seipsum humiliauit, adeo ut nullius ipsum officij erga homines ingratissimos puduerit? Sunt ergo nimium ridiculi, qui hominum iniquis.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who concludes this discussion with a weighty saying: "Whoever is least among you all, he will be great." This saying was especially needed to restrain the ambitious and proud. For it seems to say: "I see that you all strive with equal zeal to stand out in my kingdom, and that each of you wants to excel above the rest. I do not disapprove of this, provided you take the road by which alone that height is reached. That road, however, is very different from the one you have followed until now. For each of you thinks he will then be higher than others when he has pushed them down and made them his slaves. But that opinion deceives you greatly. For whoever is least among you all, that is, whoever has made himself the slave of all the others, will be shown to be truly great and more outstanding than the rest." He deliberately used the universal word ALL, as he wished, so that no one might think he has done his duty if he has humbled himself only below one or two others. For he wants us to regard as superior to us all those whom Paul interprets this saying to mean. Therefore you will think you have done nothing yet if you make yourself inferior only to those who surpass you in family rank, wealth, merit or benefits; rather, you must put on the same attitude toward all people. Yet let no one think that Christ abolishes the lawful and divinely established degrees of honour, without which neither the commonwealth, nor the order of the Church, nor domestic life can stand. Therefore the duties that subjects owe to magistrates, hearers to teachers, children to parents, wives to husbands and servants to masters remain firm for ever. Christ, however, teaches humility, which consists in two main things. The first is that, beginning with God, we claim nothing for ourselves before him, but with Abraham confess that we are dust and ashes and have no good or excellent thing that we have not received from him. This is the proper source of humility and modesty, from which the second flows: that we despise or scorn no one in comparison with ourselves. For if some are inferior to us, we acknowledge all the more that we owe them, since God has enriched us with his gifts so that our abundance may relieve the want of others. Humility is therefore the most faithful nurse of charity and the most fruitful mother of all the duties by which charity is kept among men. Those most devoted to it are all who are commended in the Scriptures. Joseph was outstanding in this, when he showed every office of brotherly love to his treacherous and murderous brothers, and was not made inferior to them by doing so; rather, the more he lowered himself to their service, the greater and loftier the honour with which God crowned him, and even among men he obtained the highest rank of dignity. Likewise David, by the zeal of humility, rose to the height of the royal throne, from which Saul had been thrown down on account of his pride. But why linger on human examples, when it is plain that Jesus Christ entered the kingdom of the Father by no other way than this: having taken the form of a servant, he humbled himself, so that he was not ashamed to serve even the most ungrateful men in any office? Therefore they are utterly ridiculous who fear the unjust

units.la: Phil. 2. qui iudicijs terrentur, & ne contemptissimi fiant metuunt, si sponte sese ad aliorum obsequia demittant. Nec enim ex hominum iudicio pendet fidelium gloria, sed eius dispensator Deus est, qui ut puerulos sibi commendatissimos habet, & hos omnibus acceptos facit: ita eorum quoq; honori & saluti consulit, qui eos imitantur. At cum ad humilitatis studium omnes astringat Dei Filius, qui regni sui cives aut haeredes fieri volunt, quis non videat, quo loco habendi sint, quotquot sub religione Christiana praetexu sibi in alios dominium vendicant? Et mirum est tam vecordes aut stupidos esse Pontifices, ut non sentiant, vel hoc uno Christi dicto omnem ipsorum potentiam atque dignitatem destrui, quam sub plausibili successionis Apostolicae titulo sibi vendicant. Si enim Apostolorum successores sunt, cur non sibi dictum cogitant, quod illis dixit Dei Filius? Cur adhuc primatum in ecclesia, & in omnes alios Episcopos imperium affectant? Servos quidem servorum se dicunt, at si dominandi libidinem, fastum, opes, pompam & qua ipsos quoq; Reges conculcant insolentiam considerēs, dominos dominorum potius & Reges regum esse dixerunt. Caeterum non soli illi peccant, sed inter eos quoq;, qui Evangelij doctrinam profitentur, non paucos est invenire, qui soli in ecclesia excellere, & ut dictatores quidam ab omnibus audiri volunt: qui mihi cum Pontificibus non tam pro Christi gloria & ecclesiarum libertate, quam pro primatu pugnare videntur. Accenseri istis debent privati homines, qui dum Evangelium profitentur, hoc unum quaerunt, ut primum in repub. locum obtineant, & honoribus atq; opibus augeantur. Et hi quidem plerunq; super bia spiritu fascinati, ex falsis fratribus tandem aperti hostes fiunt, si res non per omnia votis ipsorum respondeat. Discant ergo omnes humilitati studere, & in eo Iesu Christi exemplum imitentur, ut cum eodem in regno Patris sui vivant & regnent. Illi debetur benedictio, honor gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Phil. 2. who are terrified by judgments, and fear becoming most despised if they willingly lower themselves to serve others. For the glory of the faithful does not depend on the judgment of men; its dispenser is God, who, as he holds little children most dear to himself and makes them acceptable to all, so also takes thought for the honour and salvation of those who imitate them. But since the Son of God binds all to the zeal of humility, and those who wish to become citizens or heirs of his kingdom must do so, who does not see in what position must be held all those who, under the pretext of the Christian religion, claim dominion over others? And it is remarkable that the Pontiffs are so mad or stupid as not to perceive that by this one saying of Christ all their power and dignity, which they claim under the plausible title of Apostolic succession, is destroyed. For if they are successors of the Apostles, why do they not consider the words the Son of God spoke to them? Why do they still aspire to primacy in the Church and to dominion over all other bishops? They call themselves servants of servants, but considering their lust for domination, their pride, wealth, pomp, and the insolence with which they trample even kings, they would have done better to call themselves lords of lords and kings of kings. Yet not only those men sin; among those who profess the doctrine of the Gospel one may find not a few who wish to excel alone in the Church and to be heard by all like dictators. They seem to me to fight for primacy rather than for the glory of Christ and the liberty of the churches, not much unlike the Pontiffs. Private men too should be counted among them, who, while professing the Gospel, seek only this: that they may obtain the first place in the commonwealth and be increased with honours and riches. And these men, bewitched for the most part by the spirit of pride, at last become open enemies out of false brothers, if things do not in every respect answer to their wishes. Let all, therefore, learn to be zealous for humility, and in this imitate the example of Jesus Christ, so that they may live and reign with him in the kingdom of his Father. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIII.

units.la: Respondens autem Ioannes, ait, Magister, vidimus quendam sub nomine tuo eiicientem daemonia, & prohibuimus eum, quia te non sequitur nobiscum. Et dixit ei Iesus: Ne prohibete. Qui enim non est adversum nos, pro nobis est.
units.tr: Then John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow with us. And Jesus said to him: Do not forbid him. For he who is not against us is for us.

units.la: PErgit Lucas Evangelista in commemorandis vitiis, quibus discipuli illi selectiores Iesu Christi laborauerunt: id autem non in eum finem facit, ut infames faciat, aut quicquam authoritati eorum deroget, sed ut melius agnita nostrae naturae vitiositate, intelligamus illis ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtigisse quicquid boni & eximij habuerunt, & ut horum exemplis admoniti non securi aut confidentes simus, si quando nos in Christi doctrina aliquos progressus fecisse cernimus, sed potius vigilemus adversus propria carnis cupiditates, quibus Satan in nostram perniciem abutitur, nisi probe frenentur. Idem ergo praesentis etiam historiae nobis usus esto, in qua Ioannis dilectii illius discipuli, factum narratur, in quo simul temeritate, invidia & ambitione peccatum fuit. Quibus error accessit intolerabilis, quod dum suo honori consultum volunt discipuli, quantum in ipsis est, Christi gloriam impediunt atq; obscurant. Nos singula ex ordine considerabimus.
units.tr: Luke the Evangelist goes on to record the faults of those chosen disciples of Jesus Christ. He does this not to disgrace them or to diminish their authority, but so that, having recognised more clearly the sinfulness of our nature, we may understand that whatever good and excellent qualities they had came to them from the free mercy of God. Warned by their examples, we should not be careless or overconfident when we see ourselves making some progress in the doctrine of Christ. Rather, we should watch against the lusts of the flesh, by which Satan works our destruction unless they are curbed properly. So let us make use of this present history too, in which the act of John, that beloved disciple, is related, a sin in which rashness, envy and ambition were all at work together. To these was added an intolerable error: while the disciples wished to protect their own honour, they hindered and obscured, as far as lay in them, the glory of Christ. We will consider the matter point by point in order.

units.la: Occasionem erroris huic quidam praebuit, qui in Christi nomine daemonia eijciebat, quamuis ipsum non sequeretur, neque ex familiarium ipsius numero esset. At quo animo in illum praeditus fuerit, non exprimitur, videtur tamen non maligno aut iniquo fuisse. Interim temeritate eum peccasse non est dubium, quando absque legitima vocatione rem tantam aggressus est. Non cauit tamen successu conatus ille, quod nimirum Deus etiam hac ratione Filij sui gloriam illustrare, & Iudaeorum contumaciam inexcusabilem facere voluerit. Et hoc non obscure Christus docet, quando iis, qui ipsum Beelzebuli praesidio daemonia eijcere calumniabantur, respondit: Si ego per Beelzebul eijcio daemonia, filij vestri per quem eijciunt? propterea ipsi erunt vestri iudices. In istis certè apparet divina Christi virtus, qua per eos etiam efficacissimè egit, qui in fide adhuc impersecti nomen eius vel temeritate vel curiositate inconsulta vsurpabant: Quod minus mirabimur, si illam in rebus inanimatis quoque non semel eluxisse cogitemus, vtpote Petri Apostoli vmbra & Pauli sudarijs, vt in Actis Lucas testatur. Adde his, quae ad Martyrum sepulchra aliquoties facta sunt, & quod ad Iesu Christi monumentum daemones aliquando rugiisse D.Hieronymus scribit. Quibus omnibus testatum fieri voluit Deus, Iesum hunc Filium suum dilectum & promissum Seruatorem esse, qui serpentis caput conculcarit, diabolum regno suo eiecerit, & quod ea fide homines feruentur, in cuius confessione Martyres constantissime obierunt: Et hic proprium miraculorum omnium vsus est.
units.tr: Someone who cast out devils in the name of Christ gave the occasion for this error, although he did not follow Christ and was not among his intimate companions. What his state of mind was is not stated, yet he does not seem to have been malicious or unjust. Still, there is no doubt that he sinned by rashness, since he undertook so great a task without a lawful calling. Nevertheless, his attempt was successful, because God wished in this way to make the glory of his Son shine out and to render the stubbornness of the Jews inexcusable. Christ teaches this plainly when he answers those who slandered him, saying that he cast out devils by the help of Beelzebul: "If I cast out devils by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges." In these cases the divine power of Christ clearly appears, which worked most effectively even through those who, still imperfect in faith, used his name either rashly or through unconsidered curiosity. We shall be less surprised at this if we reflect that it shone forth more than once even in inanimate things, as in the shadow of the Apostle Peter and the handkerchiefs of Paul, as Luke bears witness in Acts. Add to these the things that have often happened at the tombs of the martyrs, and the fact that Jerome writes that the demons once roared at the tomb of Jesus Christ. By all these things God wished it to be shown that this Jesus is his beloved Son and the promised Saviour, who crushed the head of the serpent and cast the devil out of his kingdom, and that by faith in him men are preserved, in confessing whom the martyrs died most steadfastly. This is the proper use of all miracles.

units.la: In quibus tamen non ofcitanter obseruari debet, illa non semper fidei perfectae aut supremae sanctitatis argumenta esse, vt fere homines superstitiosi fibijpsis persuadent. Quia enim non propter eos proprie fiunt, quorum opera in illis aedendis Deus vtitur, sed propter alios, quos in doctrinae administrationem adduci, aut in fide amplius confirmari oportet: non raro fit, vt qui in fide imperfectissimi sunt, signa faciant in primis stupenda, sicut in isto videmus, de quo hic agitur: imo in ipsis Christi discipulis, qui priusquam Spiritum sanctum accepissent, miracula omnis generis fecerunt, cum tamen neque regni Christi cognitionem adhuc veram haberent, neq; in fide satis confirmati essent, & insuper vitijs grauissimis laborarent. At quid de imperfectis dico, quando hypocritae & iniquitatis operarij de miraculis gloriari possunt Christo teste? ita nimirum permittente Deo, qui regnum Filij sui per illos etiam vult propagari. Qua causa est, quod in Actis Petrus & Ioannes populum ob claudi miraculosam restitutionem in ipsis haerentem ad Christum reuocant, dicentes: Viri Israelitae, quid miramini super hoc? aut intentos oculos in nos habetis, quasi nostra virtute aut pietate effecerimus vt hic ambularet? Deus ille Abrahami & Isaaci & Iacobi, Deus patrum nostrorum, glorificauit Filium suum, &c. Annotamus haec diligentius propter superstitiosos, qui dum in sola miracula intenti sunt, fere gloriam, quae Christo debetur, in eius seruos, aut etiam res inanimatas, vtpote illorum vestes, offa aut quaecunque alia transferunt, non sine manifesta nominis Christiani contumelia. Imo non raro fit, vt diabolo sese illudentes praebeant, qui suos seruos miraculis insignes facit: quod ipsum Deus quoque iusto iudicio permittit, vt suorum quidem fidem tentet, contumaces autem & impios efficaci errore excaecatos digno exitio multet. Itaque in miraculis ante omnia doctrinam, quae illis coniungitur, respicere oportet, & pro falsis putare ea, quae nos a Christo & vnius Dei invocatione abducunt.
units.tr: Yet in these matters we must not observe carelessly that miracles are not always signs of perfect faith or of the highest holiness, as superstitious people commonly persuade themselves. For they are not done primarily for those through whose work God uses them, but for others, who must be brought to the ministry of the doctrine or more firmly confirmed in faith. So it often happens that those who are most imperfect in faith perform the most astonishing signs, as we see in the man of whom we are speaking here. Indeed, the disciples of Christ themselves, before they had received the Holy Spirit, worked miracles of every kind, although they did not yet have a true knowledge of the kingdom of Christ, were not yet sufficiently confirmed in faith, and were burdened with very serious vices. But why speak of the imperfect, when hypocrites and workers of iniquity can boast of miracles, with Christ as witness? God allows this, since he wishes the kingdom of his Son to be spread even through such people. This is why, in Acts, Peter and John, when the people were amazed at the miraculous healing of the lame man, call them back to Christ, saying: "Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this? Or why do you look so intently at us, as if by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son," and so on. We note these things more carefully because of superstitious people, who, while intent only on miracles, transfer almost the glory due to Christ to his servants, or even to inanimate things, such as their garments, bones or whatever else, not without manifest insult to the Christian name. Indeed, it often happens that they allow themselves to be deceived by the devil, who also makes his own servants remarkable by miracles. God too permits this by his just judgment, so that he may test the faith of his own people, while blinding the stubborn and impious with a powerful delusion and punishing them with deserved destruction. Therefore, in regard to miracles, we must above all look to the doctrine joined with them, and count as false whatever draws us away from Christ and from the invocation of the one God.

units.la: Sed ad Ioannem & eius socios accedamus, qui iflum prohibuerunt, ne in eijciendis daemonijs Christi nomine vteretur. Facti autem sui non aliam causam adducunt, quam quod aiunt: Quia te non sequitur nobiscum. At hic in vno facto in speciem leviculo, multi & magni errores (vt inimitio dissimum) concurrunt.
