Primo enim temeritas fuit inexcusabilis, quod in re dubia tantum sibi iuris sumunt, vt imperiose nimis prohibeant id, cuius rationem nondum intelligebant. Et sane nulla venia dignus est, qui in diuinis aliquid statuit, cuius non certa ipsi ratio constat. Deinde invidia & ambitione peccant, quando ipsis dolet, Christi nomen ab eo etiam vsurpari, quem sui loci & ordinis non esse videbant. Quid enim aliud illorum verba sonant, quam, Nolumus hunc nobis aquari, qui non te nobiscum sequitur, neq; eandem vitae rationem nobiscum tenet? Sibi igitur hoc priuilegium vendicant, vt saluifica & diuina Christi virtus in ipsis solis elucere debeat. Eadem ergo illos amulatio excaecat, quam in Ioannis Baptistae discipulis regnauisse alibi diximus. Huc accedit ignorantia cum manifesta superstitione coniuncta, quando omnes Christi discipulos ad vnum vitae genus astringere conantur, neq; putant aliquem illius sectatorem debere censeri, qui non idem ex eius demesticus fit, & ipsorum exemplum secutus omnia relinquat. Quod quid aliud erat, quam Christi regnum intra duodecim virorum numerum finibus plus nimium angustis concludere, & ita illius gloriae obstare, cuius studiosissimi videri volebant? Similis hodie Monachorum & Anabaptistarum error est, qui & ipsi salutem hominum & regnum Dei intra suos quasi parietes concludunt, neq; obseruant non aboleri per Christum ordines hominum, quos ipse Deus instituit, & sine quibus (vt nuper diximus) neq; Respublica neq; res domestica consistit: imo quibus sublatis, in ecclesia nihil praeter barbaram confusionem videre licebit. Cur vero ordines illi aboleantur, quando inter verbi administros ministros discrimina non obscura Christus instituit, vt Paulus admonet, dum alios quidem Apostolos fecit, qui nullis certis locis affixi Euangelium hinc inde praedicant: alios autem pastores, qui sua fidei creditum gregem pascunt, neq; aliorum laboribus sese temere immiscent, &c. Videsigitur in discipulorum facto, quam periculosum sit, si suis opinionibus homines indulgeant, & de rebus nondum plene cognitis aut probe perspectis temere pronuntient. Quamvis autem in his errent discipuli, suo tamen exemplo nostri seculi ignauiam & tepiditatem accusant. Indignum illis videtur, vt aliquis Christi nomine honorifice vtatur, qui non apertus & germanus sit eius discipulus. At hodie qui Christiani ssimi videri volunt, aperta scelera ferre possunt, quae cum multorum scandalo & cum manifesta nominis Christiani ignominia passim designantur. Adhaec illorum quoque audaciam auguntur, qui nos a Christi cognitione atque fide alienissimos esse norunt, eos tamen ecclesijs obtrudunt, & harum pastores faciunt, qui propter rerum diuinarum ignorantiam, prophanum religionis contemptum & corruptissimos mores, ne extremo quidem loco in ecclesia digni sunt, & potius ab eius societate procul reijci debebant. Peccant in eo multum hodie principes viri, & qui ministrorum electionem penes se solos esse volunt. Quorum multi cum religionis puritoris & in primis disciplina ecclesiastica hostes sint, homines leues & sui similes deligunt, vt ita dignum habeat patella operculum & quos ipsi pro sua libidine regere possint. Sunt hi Ieroboami & Herodis similes, quos eodem astu vsos fuisse legimus, quando sub religionis praetextu regnum suum stabilire voluerunt. Sed vt isti poenas graues dederunt, ita nostrorum quoq; audaciam Deus inultam non sinet.
units.tr: But let us come to John and his companions, who forbade that man to use the name of Christ in casting out devils. They give no other reason for their act than that he does not follow with us. Yet in this one act, which seems slight, many great errors (as is not unlike) come together. First, their rashness was inexcusable, since in a doubtful matter they claimed for themselves such authority that they forbade, with too much arrogance, something whose reason they did not yet understand. Indeed, anyone who decides something in divine matters without a sure grasp of the reason for it deserves no pardon. Next, they sinned through envy and ambition, since it grieved them that the name of Christ was used by one whom they saw as not belonging to their place and order. For what else do their words mean than: "We do not want this man, who does not follow with us, to be made equal to us, nor does he keep the same way of life as we do"? They thus claim for themselves the privilege that the saving and divine power of Christ should shine only in them. So the same jealousy blinded them that we have said elsewhere reigned among the disciples of John the Baptist. To this is added ignorance joined with manifest superstition, since they try to bind all the disciples of Christ to one way of life, and do not think that anyone should be counted a follower of him who is not one of his household and does not, following their example, forsake everything. What else was this than to shut up the kingdom of Christ within the narrow limits of twelve men, and so to stand in the way of that glory whose most zealous champions they wished to appear? The error of the monks and Anabaptists today is similar. They too shut up the salvation of men and the kingdom of God within their own walls, as it were, and do not observe that the orders of men instituted by God himself are not abolished through Christ, and without which (as we said recently) neither the commonwealth nor the household can stand. Indeed, if these were removed, nothing but barbarous confusion could be seen in the Church. But why should those orders be abolished, when Christ instituted clear distinctions among the ministers of the Word, as Paul reminds us, for he made some apostles, who, fixed in no certain place, preach the gospel here and there, and others ministers, who feed the flock entrusted to their faith and do not rashly intrude into the labours of others, and so on? In the act of the disciples we see, then, how dangerous it is when men indulge their own opinions and pronounce rashly on matters not yet fully known or properly examined. Yet although the disciples err in these things, by their example they condemn the idleness and lukewarmness of our age. It seems to them unworthy that anyone should use the name of Christ honourably who is not an open and genuine disciple of his. Yet today those who wish to be thought the most Christian can endure open crimes, which are openly committed everywhere to the great scandal of many and the manifest shame of the Christian name. Moreover, the boldness of those is increased who, though they know us to be most alien from the knowledge and faith of Christ, nevertheless force them upon the churches and make them ministers of these churches, although, because of their ignorance of divine things, their profane contempt of religion and their most corrupt morals, they are not worthy of even the lowest place in the Church, and ought rather to be driven far from its fellowship. Princes today sin greatly in this, and those who wish the election of ministers to rest with themselves alone. Since many of them are enemies of pure religion and especially of church discipline, they choose light men like themselves, so that the lid may suit the pot, and men whom they can rule as they please. These are like Jeroboam and Herod, whom we read used the same cunning when they wished to establish their kingdom under the pretext of religion. But just as God gave those men severe punishment, so he will not allow the boldness of our own people to go unpunished.

units.la: Nunc Christum audiamus, qui discipulorum factum improbat, & ne quem in posterum probibe ant, idicit. Rationes apud Marcum tres adducit, ex quibus vnam modo, & quae discipulorum affectui medendo optime conueniebat, Lucas recitat. Hi enim pro Christi hostibus habebant omnes, qui ipsum non publice sequerentur: aut saltem indignos iudicabant, qui illius nomen quacunq; ratione vsurparent. Dicit ergo: Qui no est aduersum nos, pro nobis est. Pro suo ergo agnoscit, quem illi alienum putabant. Interim sententia haec nequaquam ijs patrocinatur, qui sufficere putant, si Christum non aperte oppugnent, interim vero turpi & ignaua dissimulatione vtuntur, vbi constantia & ingenua veritatis confessione in primis opus erat. Nec enim talis erat, de quo hic agitur, cum Christi nomine, quod magnatibus exosum esse sciebat, publice vsus fit, & diaboli regnū oppugnarit, Dei vero regnum & Filij eius gloriam illustrauerit. Non igitur huius exemplo sibi delitias faciant ignaui illi tergiuersatores nisi eundem prius imitentur. Similiter neque erronum licentiam Christus hic defendit, qui abs q; legitima vocatione ius docendi in ecclesia sibi vendicant. Aliud enim est docere, aliud miracula edere, neq; duo illa semper coniuncta sunt. Ferebat quidem Paulus eos, qui ex aemulatione non bona & per contentionem Christum praedicabant: idem tamen non probauit eorum temeritatem, sed Dei prouidentiam in eo agnoscere docet, qui per improbos quoq; regnū suum possit dilatare. Et procul dubio illorum petulantiam coercuisset, si qua ratione commoda id potuisset fieri. Sed multa tunc ferri oportuit, quando ecclesia omni magistratuū praesidio destituta inter medios lupos & vulpes agebant. At hodie in seruando ordine & forma legitima doctrina attentiores esse conuenit eos, quibus libertas maior concessa est, ne tantū Dei beneficiū sua ignauia perire & diffluere patiantur, curent tamē vt huius dicti memores non temere damnet eos, qui adhuc imperfectioret sunt. Nam qui illud faciunt, saepe ad defectionē eos cogūt, & apertos hostes faciunt ex ijs, quorum opera ecclesijs non inutilis esse poterat, si moderatius tractarentur. Interim meminerint omnes, sui officij esse vt suam operam ad propagandum & coseruandū Iesu Christi regnū conferant, & quacunq; ratione possunt nomen eius illustrent. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now hear Christ, who disapproves of what the disciples did and forbids them to stop anyone in future. Mark gives three reasons for this, but Luke recites only one, the one that best suited the disciples' feeling and gave them a remedy. For they regarded as enemies of Christ everyone who did not follow him openly, or at least judged them unworthy to use his name in any way at all. So he says: "He who is not against us is for us." He thus acknowledges as one of his own the man whom they thought to be an outsider. Yet this saying by no means supports those who think it enough not to attack Christ openly, while in the meantime using shameful and cowardly concealment where constancy and a frank confession of the truth were above all needed. The man in question here was not of that kind, since he made public use of Christ's name, which he knew was hateful to the great men, and he attacked the kingdom of the devil while setting forth the kingdom of God and the glory of his Son. Let those cowardly shufflers, therefore, not indulge themselves by appealing to his example unless they first imitate him. Likewise, Christ does not here defend the licence of errorists who claim for themselves the right to teach in the Church without lawful calling. For to teach is one thing, to work miracles another, and the two are not always joined. Paul indeed tolerated those who preached Christ out of unworthy rivalry and contention, yet he did not approve their rashness, but teaches that God's providence is to be recognised in this, since he can extend his kingdom even through wicked men. And without doubt Paul would have restrained their boldness, had it been possible to do so with advantage. But in that time many things had to be tolerated, when the Church, deprived of all protection from the magistrates, lived among wolves and foxes. Today, however, it is fitting that those to whom greater liberty has been granted should be more attentive to preserving order and sound doctrine in due form, so that they do not, through their own laziness, allow this great benefit of God to perish and dissolve. Let them take care, nevertheless, mindful of this saying, not to condemn rashly those who are still more imperfect. For those who do so often drive them to defection and make open enemies of men whose work could have been useful to the churches, had they been treated more moderately. In the meantime, let all remember that it is their duty to contribute their labour to the spreading and preserving of the kingdom of Jesus Christ, and by whatever means they can, to make his name illustrious. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIIII.

units.la: Factum est autem cum impleretur tempus, quo sursum recipere-tur, tum ipse obfirmauit faciem suam, vt proficisceretur in Hierusa-lem. Misitque nuntios ante faciem suam, qui profecti ingressi sunt in vicum Samaritanorum, vt pararent ei hospitium. Sed illi non recepe-runt eum, quod habitum praeferret proficiscentis in Hierusalem.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, that he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem, and sent messengers before his face: and they went, and entered into a village of the Samaritans, to make ready for him. But they did not receive him, because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem.

units.la: Cum autem hoc vidissent discipuli eius, Iacobus & Ioannes, dixerunt: Domine, vis dicamus vt ignis descendat è coelo, & consumat eos, vt etiam Elias fecit? Sed conuersus Iesus obiurgauit eos, dicens: Nescitis cuius spiritus vos estis. Filius enim hominis non venit vt perdat animas hominum, sed vt seruet. Abierunt igitur in alium vicum.
units.tr: And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said: Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, even as Elias did? But Jesus turned and rebuked them, saying: You do not know what spirit you are of. For the Son of man came not to destroy men's souls, but to save them. So they went on to another village.

units.la: EXposuit Lucas quatuor insignes errores aut vitia, quibus discipuli Iesu Christi laborauerunt, fidei nimirum imbecillitatem aut imperfectionem, ignorantiam capitum salutis humanae, ambitionem siue regnandi cupiditatem, caecam item aemulationem, qua accensi Christum eiusque virtutem ad se solos pertinere putarunt: alios vero omnes, qui non ipsorum contubernales erant, pro indignis habuerunt, qui Christi nomen vsurparent. His modo subiicitur peccatum crassius, impatientia nimirum cum praecipiti ira & impotenti vindicta cupiditate coniuncta, quae non solum in charitatis leges, verumetiam in Christi officium peccarunt, dum longe alium hunc fingunt, quam nobis à Patre sit datus. At simul multa alia continet haec historia, quae nos de multis cognitu necessarijs possunt admonere. Quare eam Lucas diligenter narrat, vt suo exemplo nos ad considerationem illius attentiorem excitet.
units.tr: Luke sets out four notable errors or faults into which the disciples of Jesus Christ fell: a weakness or imperfection of faith; ignorance of the chief points of human salvation; ambition, or a desire to rule; and also a blind rivalry, by which, inflamed, they thought that Christ and his power belonged to themselves alone, and they regarded all others who were not their companions as unworthy to use the name of Christ. To these is added a grosser sin: impatience, joined with a headlong anger and an ungoverned desire for vengeance, by which they sinned not only against the laws of charity but also against the office of Christ, since they imagined him to be quite other than the one given to us by the Father. At the same time this story contains many other matters which can remind us of many things that must be known. That is why Luke narrates it carefully, so that by his example he may stir us to a more attentive consideration of it.

units.la: Praemittitur totius negotij occasio, quam temporis circumstantia praebuit. Iam enim instabat hora illa fatalis, qua Christum sursum recipi, id est, per mortem ex mundo exire & corpus suum in coelos inferre oportebat. Ideo qui hucusque intra Galilaea fines se continuerat, nunc faciem suam obfirmat, & certo immobili animi proposito profectionem in Hierusalem instituit, vbi se moriturum esse nouerat. At media inter Iudaeam & Galilaeam (vt Ioannes cap. quarto annotauit) iacebat Samaria, & proinde necessario ei per hanc erat transeundum. Huius ergo fines ingressus, praemittit aliquos ex suis, qui ipsi hospitium parent. Vbi nemo putauerit, Christum vel lauritias quaesiuisse, vel (vt huius seculi principes solent) pompa & faustu insolentiori potentiam suam ostentauisse: sed vt ita faceret, necessitas postulabat, cum in profectione illa comitatum haberet satis numerosum. Nam vt in proximo cap. audiemus, praeter duodecim Apostolos, alios discipulos septuaginta habuit, quos ad praedicandum non multo post emisit. His mulieres accesserunt, quarum mentio supra cap. Stephano facta est, & turba populi undique confluentis. Noluit ergo cum tanto comitatu temere & exim prouiso eos obruere, quos erga Iudaeorum gentem non bene affectos esse sciebat. Itaque civilis insti tia & modestia singularis exemplum praebet, quod peregrinus omnibus est imitandum, ne quid imprudentius agant, neue iis quibus cum viuunt temere molestiam aliquam exhibeant: quod olim Patriarchas sanctissimos magna diligentia cauisse legimus. Interim regni sui iam mox instaurandi spem nobis praebet Christus, quando qui nihil habebat proprium, & neq commeatu instructus erat, neq opes aut dignitates cuiquam pollicebatur, tam multos tamen inuenit, qui ipsum sponte sequuntur, & suis impensis eum alunt, vt supra vidimus. At non agnouerunt hoc Dei consilium Samaritani, ad quos ille diuertere voluit, sed veteris odij memoria accensi, non minus inhumaniter quam indigne hospitium negant hominibus absque maleficio transfire volentibus, & ex quibus nihil hostile timeri poterat. Id vero discipulis erroris occasionem dedit, quem postea audiemus. Nunc ea videamus, quae in hiis diligentiori consideratione digna sunt.
units.tr: The occasion of the whole affair is set out first, which the circumstances of the time supplied. For that fatal hour was now at hand, in which Christ had to be received up, that is, to depart from the world by death and bring his body into heaven. So he who had hitherto kept himself within the borders of Galilee now sets his face and, with a fixed and unwavering purpose of mind, begins his journey to Jerusalem, where he knew he would die. But between Judea and Galilee (as John noted in chapter four) lay Samaria, and therefore he had of necessity to pass through it. So on entering its borders, he sends ahead some of his own people to prepare lodging for him. Let no one suppose that Christ sought luxury, or, as the princes of this age are wont to do, displayed his power with pomp and rather insolent show; he did so because necessity required it, since on that journey he had a fairly large company. For, as we shall hear in the next chapter, besides the twelve Apostles he had seventy other disciples, whom he sent out to preach not long afterwards. To these were added the women, whom we mentioned above in connection with Stephen, and a crowd of people flocking together from every side. He therefore chose not to burden with so large a company, rashly and without warning, those whom he knew to be ill-disposed towards the Jewish nation. Thus his civil justice and singular modesty provides an example which a stranger must imitate, so that he does nothing too rashly and does not rashly cause any trouble to those among whom he lives; as we read that the most holy Patriarchs of old took great care to do. Meanwhile Christ gives us hope of soon restoring his kingdom, since he, who had nothing of his own and was equipped with no provisions, promised wealth or honours to no one, nevertheless found so many who freely follow him and feed him at their own expense, as we saw above. But the Samaritans, to whom he wished to turn aside, did not recognise this counsel of God; inflamed by the memory of an old hatred, they refused lodging, no less inhumanly than unworthily, to men who wished to pass through without doing any wrong and from whom nothing hostile could be feared. This gave the disciples an occasion of error, which we shall hear about later. Now let us look at those things which deserve closer consideration here.

units.la: Inter quae primum occurrit, quod de morte Christi iam appropinquante loquens Euangelista, tempus illud praefinitum in progressu & quasi iam implerum fuisse ait, quo illum oportuit sursum recipi. Conuenit hoc cum eo, quod ipse alibi dicit, se postea non fore in mundo, sed hoc relicto ad Patrem abire velle. Quibus verbis procul dubio vsus est, vt & seipsum, quoad assumptam carnis nostrae infirmitatem, aduersus mortis imminentis terrores consolaretur, & simul discipulos confirmaret, quos tunc scandalum ingens passuros esse non ignorabat. Eodem igitur Lucas etiam respexit. Itaque eodem sensu & fine nos quoque locutiones istas considerare & nobisipsis applicare debemus: vt meminerimus mortem nobis professionem esse ex munido hoc in caelestem patriam: horam vero mortis tempus esse aeterno Dei decreto nobis praefixum, quos vos ex infelici ista & miserabili lachrymarum valle in sedes beatae immortalitatis euehi & in beatorum spirituum gregem assumi oporteat, ut illic cum Christo propius coniungamur. Admonet nos de his Dominus, quando eos qui in ipsum credunt, à morte in vitam transfire, aut (ut de Lazaro infra loquetur) in sinum Abrahami deferri ait. Quod Paulus recte expendens, cupiebat dissolui, ut cum Christo ageret. Est ergo haec efficacissima consolatio, quae omnes terrores procul pellit aut mitigat. Stultissimi autem sunt, qui cum ista norint, mortem tamen metuunt: miserrimos vero rectissimè dixeris omnes, qui de his nunquam, aut certè raro & negligenter cogitant, cum se in terris peregrinos esse non possint negare.
units.tr: Among these, the first thing that occurs is that the Evangelist, speaking of the approaching death of Christ, says that the time appointed beforehand had come, or was nearly fulfilled, at which he had to be received up. This agrees with what he says elsewhere, that he would afterwards no longer be in the world, but would leave it and wished to go to the Father. Without doubt he used these words both to comfort himself, as regards the weakness of the flesh he had taken on, against the terrors of impending death, and at the same time to strengthen his disciples, whom he knew would then suffer a great stumbling-block. Luke therefore also had this in view. So we too ought to consider these expressions with the same meaning and purpose and apply them to ourselves, so that we remember that death is for us a passage from this world into the heavenly fatherland, and that the hour of death is a time fixed for us by the eternal decree of God, when we must be lifted up out of this unhappy and miserable valley of tears into the seats of blessed immortality and taken into the company of the blessed spirits, so that there we may be more closely joined with Christ. The Lord admonishes us of these things when he says that those who believe in him pass from death to life, or (as he will speak below about Lazarus) are carried into the bosom of Abraham. Paul, weighing this rightly, desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ. This is therefore a most effective consolation, which drives away or softens all terrors. Those are most foolish who, knowing these things, still fear death; and we may rightly call wretched all who never, or only rarely and carelessly, think of them, since they cannot deny that they are pilgrims on earth.

units.la: Audiamus igitur quid hoc tempore Christus fecerit, quem perfectissimum omnis virtutis exemplum esse scimus. Faciem suam obfirmasse dicitur, ut Hierosolymam proficisceretur. Qua locutione certum firmumq; animi propositu notatur, quo per omnes remoras constanter eluctatus est. Constat enim illum cum carne simul infirmitates quoq; nostras in se transfulisse, & instar hominis veri fuisse tentatum. Inter illas autem non postrema est, quod mortis metu terremur, & per hunc saepe revocamur, quo minus Deo simus obsequentes. Non dubium ergo est, quin in praesenti luctam vehementem sustinuerit, cum quàm multa & quam dira eum manerent, secum expenderet. Postea certè horum meditatione graviter affectus dixit: Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater, conserva me ab hac hora, &c. Taceo nunc quae ad Olivieti montem passus est, & quae discipulos suos minime celavit. Porro ut tunc forti fiducia vicit, ita hic quoq; vicit obedientia, quam se Patri debere sciebat. Ultrò igitur morti obviam iit, ut sua obedientia nostram inobedientiam expiaret. Imitemur autem nos exemplum eius, quotiescunq; nos gravius tentari sentimus. Multa enim nobis pro priacaro, multa mundus & huius princeps Satan obijciunt, quae nos avocant, quo minus debitum Deo obsequium praestemus. Sed tunc faciem obfirmare, & ipsum animum diligenti officij nostri consideratione armare oportet, ut adversus omnia obstacula eluctemur. Quid enim inter res huius seculi tam magnificum, tam iucundum, tam deniq; quaestuosum est, cuius gratia Deo datam fidem fallere debeamus? Cur vero mortis terror nos vincat, cum huius dolores momentanei, inter hos autem vitae spes certa, & hus superatis regni coelorum gaudia sempiterna sint?
units.tr: Let us therefore hear what Christ did at this time, whom we know to be the most perfect example of every virtue. He is said to have set his face so that he might go to Jerusalem. By this expression a certain and firm purpose of mind is indicated, by which he steadfastly struggled through all delays. For it is agreed that he took upon himself our infirmities together with our flesh, and was tempted like a true man. Among these infirmities is not the least that we are terrified by the fear of death, and are often called back by it from being obedient to God. There is therefore no doubt that in the present case he endured a fierce struggle, as he weighed within himself how many and how dire were the things that awaited him. Afterwards, certainly, deeply moved by the thought of them, he said: Now is my soul troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour, etc. I say nothing now of what he suffered on the Mount of Olives, and what he did not hide from his disciples. Moreover, as then he conquered by a brave confidence, so here too he conquered by the obedience which he knew he owed to the Father. Therefore he went of his own accord to meet death, so that by his obedience he might atone for our disobedience. Let us, however, imitate his example whenever we feel ourselves sorely tempted. For many things are thrown in our way by our own flesh, and many by the world and its prince Satan, which call us away from rendering to God the obedience we owe. But then we must set our face, and arm our own mind with a diligent consideration of our duty, so that we may struggle through against all obstacles. For among the things of this age what is so splendid, so pleasant, and in the end so profitable, that for its sake we ought to break faith given to God? And why should the terror of death overcome us, when its pains are momentary, between this life and the sure hope of it, and once they are overcome, the joys of the kingdom of heaven are everlasting?

units.la: Habet praeterea hoc Christi factum ingens amoris, quo nos prosecutus est, argumentum: quando abnegata propriae vitae cura per medios mortis terrores tanta animi constantia perrupit, ut nostram redemptionem maturaret, quae aliter peragi non poterat. Consoletur nos haec eius in nos promptitudo, si quando tentationibus nos Deus exercet. Nec enim fieri potest, ut nunc nos negligat, qui nos propria vita chariores habuit. Rursus vero hoc nos officij admoneat, ut nullum laborem & periculum detrectemus subire proximi causa, si eius salutem hoc ita postulare videamus. Neq; nos offendat, si in sancto cursu pergentibus aliquam remoram Deus iniciat, aut illos ipsos male gratos experiamur, quibus consultum volumus. Nâ hoc ipsum Christo cum hic tum saepe aliàs accidit, cuius vestigijs nos pie ac fortiter resistere decet.
units.tr: Moreover, this deed of Christ is a great proof of his love toward us: setting aside all care for his own life, he broke through the terrors of death with such constancy that he hastened our redemption, which otherwise could not be accomplished. This readiness of his toward us should comfort us whenever God exercises us with temptations. For he cannot now neglect us, since he held us dearer than his own life. Again, this should remind us of our duty not to shrink from any labour or danger for the sake of our neighbour, if we see that his salvation requires it. Nor should it offend us if God places some hindrance in the way of those who are pursuing the holy course, or if we find that those very people for whose good we are concerned prove ungrateful. For this very thing happened to Christ, both here and often at other times, and we ought to follow his footsteps by resisting piously and bravely.

units.la: Sunt autem nobis paulo diligentius considerandi Samaritani, qui Christum intra vicum suum recipere noluerunt. Ibi non dubitauerim illos multa praetexuisse, quibus inhumanitate suam excusarent: vtpote rerum penuriâ, hospitium multitudine, periculum & insidias, quae ista occasione strui poterant, & sexcenta alia. Sed veram causam Lucas exprimit, illos eum recipere noluisse, quod habitum praeferret proficiscentis in Hierusalem. Ergo religionis odio fecerunt, quicquid hic factum est. Erat enim illud inter duas gentes illas acerrimum, & vetustate iam pridem incurabile factum erat. Origo vel initium eius inde fuit, quod terram, quae olim ab Israelitis habitata fuerat, ipsi occuparent, à Salmanazare Assyriorum rege illuc deducti, cum is decem tribus in exilium suae captiui tatem abduxisset. Factum id annis ante natum Christum septingentis triginta & octo. Fuit autem procul dubio ingratum & molestum Iudaeis, qui terram hanc omnem olim patribus promissam ad se solos pertinere putabant. Creuit autem odium istud, quando hi ex Babylone reuersis Samaritani prae aliis restiterunt, ne urbem & templum aedificarent. Accessit religionis dissimilitudo, & quod illi duce Manasse, impio apostata, templum aedificassent in monte Garizim, & quae illi exercebant cultu exemplo patrum priscorum defenderent. Quae causa erat, quod non raro ad Samaritanos deficerent, qui inter Iudaeos seuerius corripiebantur ob violata legis divinae disciplinâ. Ut ergo Iudaei tales odio ex tremo & abominatione dignos iudicabant:ita vicissim Samaritani ipsos detestabantur, & indi- gnos hospitio existimabant eos,qui propter sacra & dies festos ad templũ Hierosolymitanũ ascen- debant. Et tanta fuit vtriusq; gentis in fouendo odio isto pertinacia, vt tandem ad manus ventum fuerit,& seditionibus initium dederit,qua vtrique genti excidium attulerunt. Cum enim quidam ex Galilaea Hierosolymam proficiscentes à Samaritanis occisi essent,Cumanus autem praeses mu- neribus corruptus in cladis huius authores nollet animaduertere,Iudaei suorum caedem vindicaturi arma caeperunt,& ab eo tempore latrotinijs Iudaea infestari coepit. Quod ideo annotamus, quo mi- nus mirerus,quod hic de Samaritanis istis scribitur.
units.tr: We must now consider rather carefully the Samaritans, who were unwilling to receive Christ into their village. Here I do not doubt that they put forward many pretexts to excuse their inhospitality: the scarcity of supplies, the crowd of guests, the danger and the plots that could be laid under cover of such an occasion, and countless others. But Luke states the real cause: they were unwilling to receive him because he had the appearance of one setting out for Jerusalem. So whatever was done here was done out of hatred of religion. For that enmity between the two nations was very bitter, and by long antiquity it had become an incurable thing. Its origin or beginning lay in this: the Samaritans, who had been brought there by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, when he had carried the ten tribes off into exile, occupied the land that had once been inhabited by the Israelites. This happened 738 years before Christ was born. It was no doubt unwelcome and irritating to the Jews, who thought that all this land, once promised to their fathers, belonged to them alone. That hatred grew when these Samaritans, above others, opposed the Jews returning from Babylon, lest they should build the city and the temple. Religious difference was added, and also the fact that under the leadership of Manasseh, an impious apostate, they had built a temple on Mount Gerizim and defended by the example of their ancient fathers the worship they practised. This was another reason why people often defected from the Jews to the Samaritans, who were corrected more severely among the Jews for violating the discipline of the divine law. So just as the Jews judged such people worthy of extreme hatred and abomination, so in turn the Samaritans detested them and considered unworthy of hospitality those who went up to the temple at Jerusalem for the sacred rites and festivals. And so great was the obstinacy of each nation in nursing this hatred that at last it came to blows, and it gave rise to seditions which brought ruin upon both peoples. For when some men from Galilee, journeying to Jerusalem, had been killed by the Samaritans, Cumanus, the governor, bribed with gifts, refused to punish the authors of that slaughter. The Jews, about to avenge the killing of their people, took up arms, and from that time Judea began to be troubled by brigandage. We note this so that you may be less surprised that this is written here about these Samaritans.

units.la: Docemur autem hoc exemplo,nulla esse atrociora odia,nulla item dissidia grauiora ,quàm quae ex religionis differsione nascuntur. Ea enim religionis vis est, vt totum hominem possideat. Sier- go in superstitionem degeneret, ita aduersus contrarie partis sectatores animos accendit,vt illos non solum oderint,sed posito omni humanitatis sensu in rabiem agantur, & se pios putent,quando ferro & igne omnia miscent. Et quamuis qui veri Dei cultores sunt,eos patienter ferant, & omni officiorũ genere sibi eos demereri studeant,ab ipsis tamen inhumaniter reijciuntur. Christus equidem hoc loco à Samaritanorum consuetudine non abhorret,quin potius dum ad eos diuertere cupit,se lo tum ipsis sponte offert:sed ab illis praeter omne meritũ reijcitur. Simile exemplũ in Samaritidea- pud Ioannem extat.Cum enim hanc quoq; Christus adeo non abominaretur,vt etiã potũ sibi ab ea dari peteret,illa tamen proterue nimis odiũ gentis ei exprobrat,vt indignum offendat, cui aliquid officij praestet.Et multa huius generis ab ipsa rerum origine acciderunt. Dissentiunt in religione & Dei cultu primi fratres,Cain & Abel, & ex dissensione Cain odium concepit, quod neque Dei admonitione grauissima,neq; Abeli simplicitate & consuetudine reflingui potuit: Imò dum hic illũ amice fert,neq; hostile aliquid metuit,ab illo praeter expectationem crudelissimè trucidatur. Sic ab Esau coepit simultas , quae publici & implacabilis inter Israelem & Idumaeos dissidij causa fuit. Quod si ad ecclesiae renascentiũ tempora accedamus,neque Iudaeos neq; Ethnicos Christiani hostili- ter persecuti sunt,sed in eo toti fuerunt,vt omnes homines ad eiusdem salutis atq; felicitatis haeredi- tatem pertraherent:at indomita fuit illorũ rabies,qua & Euangelij doctrinam & ecclesiã simul o- nem extinctã voluerunt.Et nostro seculo multa huius generis experimur,& priuata exempla sunt quae his possunt fidem facere,vt de publicis iam nihil dicamus. Ita vero impletur, quod sub initium mundi Deus praedixit,inimicitias inter serpentem & semen mulieris , adeoq; omnem filiorum Dei generationem fore perpetuas.Iflorum autem nos meminisse oportet,non quidem vt ipsi quoq; odij & simultatum semina in animis nostris foueamus,sed vt cauti simus secundum Christi praeceptum,qui monuit,vt nobis caueamus ab hominibus,eos nimirum intelligens,qui nihil quam homines sunt,& de quibus Propheta dixit:Vafrum & inscrutabile est cor hominis,quis cognoscet illud? Interim Christum imitemur,qui etsi quid factuti essent Samaritani non ignoraret,non dissimulat tamen reli- gionem,sed toto corporis habitu simul & vultu ostendit, se cum suis Hierosolymam ad festum illic agendum profecisci. Non ergo turpi & ignaua fidei dissimulatione illorum amicitiam & hospitium redimere voluit. Suo igitur exemplo eos arguit,qui inter exteros quiduis sibi licere arbitrantur, & oraculi instar semper in ore habent dictum illud ineptum & impium: Si fueris Roma, Romano more viuito more. Quasi vero fides certis locis alligata,& aliquis in orbe terrarum angulus sit, in quo cul- tum Dei negligere,impias autem & illicitas superstitiones exercere liceat.
units.tr: We are taught by this example that there are no more savage hatreds, and no more grievous dissensions, than those that arise from differences of religion. For such is the power of religion that it takes possession of the whole man. When it degenerates into superstition, it so inflames minds against adherents of the opposite party that they not only hate them, but, having cast off all sense of humanity, are driven to frenzy and think themselves pious while they throw everything into confusion with sword and fire. And although those who are true worshippers of the true God bear them patiently and strive to win them over by every kind of service, they are nonetheless cast off by them inhumanly. Indeed Christ, in this place, does not shrink from the custom of the Samaritans; rather, while he desires to turn aside to them, he offers himself to them of his own accord, but he is rejected by them, though he has deserved no such thing. A similar example is found among the Samaritans in John. For when Christ did not so much as abhor her that he even asked her for a drink, she nonetheless, with too much insolence, reproaches him with the hatred between the peoples, as though he were unworthy that she should show him any kindness. And many things of this kind have happened from the very beginning of the world. The first brothers, Cain and Abel, differed in religion and the worship of God, and from this disagreement Cain conceived hatred, which could not be restrained either by the most serious admonition of God or by Abel's simplicity and companionship. Indeed, while Abel treated him kindly and feared nothing hostile from him, he was most cruelly slain by him, contrary to all expectation. Thus enmity began with Esau, which was the cause of the public and implacable division between Israel and the Idumaeans. And if we come to the times when the Church was reborn, Christians did not persecute Jews or Gentiles with hostility; rather, they were wholly intent on drawing all men into the inheritance of the same salvation and happiness. But the raging of those people was untameable, by which they wished to extinguish both the doctrine of the gospel and the Church together. And in our own age we experience many things of this kind, and there are private examples that can give credence to these things, not to mention public ones. And so is fulfilled what God foretold at the beginning of the world: that there would be enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman, and so a perpetual enmity between the serpent's offspring and the whole generation of the sons of God. We ought to remember these things, not so that we ourselves foster the seeds of hatred and enmity in our minds, but so that we may be cautious according to Christ's precept, who warned us to beware of men, meaning of course those who are nothing but men, and of whom the prophet said: "The heart of man is deceitful and inscrutable; who can know it?" Meanwhile let us imitate Christ, who, although he did not fail to know what the Samaritans would do, nevertheless does not conceal his religion, but shows by his whole bearing and countenance that he is setting out with his people for Jerusalem to celebrate the festival there. Therefore he did not wish to buy back their friendship and hospitality by a shameful and cowardly concealment of his faith. By his own example he therefore rebukes those who think they may do whatever they like among foreigners, and who always have on their lips, as if it were an oracle, that foolish and impious saying: "If you are at Rome, live as the Romans do." As if faith were tied to certain places, and there were some corner of the earth where it is permitted to neglect the worship of God and to practise impious and unlawful superstitions.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea Samaritanorum exemplo,quales censeri debeant,qui in hospites inhuma- ni sunt,& eos quidem in primis,qui Christum secuti incertis sedibus oberrant. Hi pienn q. ti (Chri- sto eos excludunt,quorũ consuetudo ipsis vtilissima & certa salutis causa esse poterat,& seipsos pro- rum praesidio nudatos periculis obijciunt,in quibus tandem miserè pereunt. Excludunt Christũ Samari- tani,at ipsdem non multò post Simoni Mago locum dederunt,qui totam illa genti horrendis erroris- bus dementauit,& ab illis factũ est belli initium,quo tam ipsos quam Iudaeos Romani deleuerunt. Atrocius exemplũ olim in Sodomaeos editũ fuit,qui cùm & Angelos hospites violare,& Lothũ eo quod peregrinus esset,scurriliter reijcere auderet,ijs ex vrbe digressũ,mox igne & sulphure caelitus demissũ horribiliter sunt exusti. Et vt Aegypto salutem attulit Pharaonis illius prisci humanitas, qua in Iosephũ et ecclesiã Dei apud se peregrinante vsus est:ita posteris et toti genti exitio fuit,quod tandem
units.tr: We are further warned by the example of the Samaritans as to what kind of people should be judged to be inhospitable to strangers, and especially to those who, following Christ, wander without settled homes. Such people shut out Christ, though their own custom might have been a most useful and sure cause of salvation for them; and, stripped of the protection of those who are bound to them, they expose themselves to dangers in which at last they perish miserably. The Samaritans shut out Christ, yet not long afterwards they gave a place to Simon Magus, who drove that whole nation mad with dreadful errors, and from this came the beginning of the war by which the Romans destroyed both them and the Jews. An even more atrocious example was once given in the Sodomites, who dared to violate the angels as guests and to reject Lot scurrilously because he was a stranger; when the angels had departed from the city, they were soon dreadfully burned by fire and brimstone sent down from heaven. And just as the ancient humanity of that Pharaoh of Egypt brought salvation to Egypt, since he used Joseph, and the Church of God, while they were sojourning with him, so it became a ruin to his descendants and to the whole nation, in that at last...

units.la: Iosephus ant. 20. cap. 7. 8. Bell. lud. 2. cap. 11. Corn. Tacit. lib. 12.
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities 20, chapters 7–8; Jewish War 2, chapter 11; Cornelius Tacitus, book 12.

units.la: Ierem. 17.
units.tr: Jer. 17. ## Inhospitality is condemned

units.la: Inhospitalitas damnatur.

Ios. bel. lud. 3. cap. 12. rande opprimere & inhumaniter vexare ausi fuerunt. Semper ergo animus nostris obuersetur Chriſti diſtum : Peregrinus fui, & collegistis me: neq; graue sit eum excipere, qui vt nemini grauis aut onerosus est: ita omnis boni thesauros in seipso reconditos habet, & solus suo merito nobis Patrem conciliat. Et cum hospitalitas per se laude digna sit, & sæpe multis salutem attulerit, non potest non laudatissima & quouis præmio digna esse, qua ipse Dei filius in membris suis excipitur.
units.tr: Josephus, Bell. Jud. 3. cap. 12. ...dared to oppress them and to harass them inhumanely. So let the thought of Christ's saying always be before our minds: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Nor should it be a burden to receive him, who is a burden to no one. He has in himself all the treasures of good things, and by his merit alone he reconciles us to the Father. And since hospitality is praiseworthy in itself and has often brought salvation to many, it cannot fail to be most praiseworthy and worthy of any reward, when the Son of God himself is received in his members.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad Ioannem & Iacobum, qui dum Samaritanorum impietatem quouis suppli cio dignam esse vident, seipsos non possunt continere, quin nimio Christi zelo abrepti illis inhumaniores & crudeliores fiant. Aiunt enim Domine, vis dicamus vt ignis descendat è cœlo, & consumat eos, vt etiam Elias fecit? Fuit hoc animi vehementer commoti argumentum. Monit aut eos rei in dignitas, quod Christum, cuius causa ipsi sua omnia reliquerant, ab illis tam inhumaniter & impie excludi viderent. Interim non dubitauerim, aliquid hic datum fuisse affectui priuato atq; inimicitijs, quibus illæ gentes (vt ante diximus) inter se dissidebant. Iam ergo iustissimam vindictæ causam sibi obtigisse putant, & sese ad eius executionem paratos esse ostendunt, modo Christus annuat, cuius virtutem ad omnia sufficere sciebant. Interim Elia exemplum prætexunt, quem simile quid fecisse in historia Regum scribitur. Fuit ergo hoc illorum votum siue desiderium carnis iudicio plau sibile, sed multiplex sub illo error delitescit. Primo enim zelus hic præposterus est, neq; scientia veri regitur, cum adhuc Christi officium ignorent, de quo toties illis concionatus fuerat. Accedit huic (vt diximus) vindictæ cupiditas, & quod doctrinæ Christi immemores sibi licere putant, vt malum malo referant. Imo non contenti talionis lege, omnes illius loci incolas cū coniugibus & liberis pror sus extinctos cupiunt, qui etsi hospitium ipsi negassent, saluos tamen & incolumes dimiserant. Ad hæc scripturæ authoritate abutuntur, & Eliæ exemplum ad se transferunt, atq; huic pares esse volunt, cum vocationem similem non habeant. Est igitur exemplum hoc admodum memorabile & dignissimum obseruatu. In eo enim apparet, quam cæco impetu ad vindictam ruant, quotquot carnis rationem in consilium admittunt. Solent isti fere Dei cultum & charitatis officia prætexere & ideo sibi quiduis licere putant. At si rem propius iuspiciamus, fere & charitatis leges violant, & religione abutuntur, imo hanc impiorum ludibrio exponunt. Estq; error iste vulgaris nostro seculo, eo quod pleriq; in charitatis lege duntaxat quid ipsis debeatur vident, securi interim eorum quæ ipsi debent alijs. Quo fit, vt mox exitio dignos iudicent omnes eos, qui non omnibus ipsorum postulatis satisfaciunt, cum ipsi sæpe puniri mereantur, quod iniqua petant, & ijs molesti sint, quos suis officijs subleuare debebant. A seipsis ergo singuli initium faciant & charitatis regulam sibi applicent, prius quam alios de eius transgressione accusent.
units.tr: But let us turn to John and James. When they saw the Samaritans' impiety deserving of any punishment, they could not restrain themselves; carried away by excessive zeal for Christ, they became more inhuman and cruel than those they condemned. For they said: "Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah also did?" This was a sign of a mind greatly stirred. Yet the indignity moved them, because they saw Christ, for whose sake they had left all their possessions, so inhumanly and impiously shut out by these people. Still, I do not doubt that something was given here to private feeling and to the enmities by which those peoples (as we said before) were at odds with one another. Now they think that a most just cause of vengeance has fallen to them, and they show themselves ready to carry it out, provided Christ gives his assent, since they knew his power was sufficient for all things. Meanwhile they put forward the example of Elijah, who is written in the history of the Kings to have done something similar. So their wish, or the desire of the flesh, was plausible to human judgment, but many errors lie hidden beneath it. First, this zeal is misplaced, and it is not governed by knowledge of the truth, since they did not yet know Christ's office, although he had so often preached to them about it. To this is added (as we said) a desire for revenge, and the fact that, forgetful of Christ's teaching, they think they may repay evil with evil. Indeed, not content with the law of retaliation, they wish all the inhabitants of that place, with their wives and children, to be utterly destroyed, though those people, even if they had refused them lodging, had sent them away safe and unharmed. Besides, they abuse the authority of Scripture and transfer Elijah's example to themselves, wishing to be equal to him, although they do not have a similar calling. This example is therefore very memorable and most worthy of notice. For it shows how blindly they rush to vengeance, all who admit the reasoning of the flesh into their counsel. Such people usually put forward the worship of God and the duties of love as a pretext, and so think they may do whatever they please. But if we look more closely at the matter, they usually violate the laws of love and abuse religion, and indeed expose it to the mockery of the impious. This error is common in our age, because most people see in the law of love only what is owed to themselves, while being careless of what they themselves owe to others. Hence it comes about that they soon judge worthy of destruction all those who do not satisfy all their demands, although they themselves often deserve to be punished for asking unjust things and for troubling those whom they ought to relieve by their duties. Let each one, then, make a beginning with himself, and apply the rule of love to himself before he accuses others of transgressing it.

units.la: Admonet præterea locus hic, quam facilis in scripturis & sanctorum exemplis lapsus sit, nisi diligenter attendamus, quæ nostra sit vocatio, & quid ad nos proprie pertineat. Sæpe enim affectu suistro fascinati non videmus germanum eius loci sensum aduersus nos facere, quem nostro institu to seruire putamus. Sic in talionis lege olim Iudæi errabant, cum singuli priuatim ad se raperent, quod iudicibus in puniendis iniurijs erat mandatum. Quoad vero exempla aliorum, non statim omnibus licet aut semper, quod semel vni & alteri licuit. Olim quidem vbiq; locorum sacra facere licebat, cum Deus suo cultui locum certum nondum constituisset. At hoc constituto, scelus fuit alibi sacrificare, & quamuis patrum exemplo sese excusarent qui in excelsis sacrificabant, eosde tamen spiritus sanctus aperte damnat. Quod ipsum de Samaritanis dici potest, quos praua & stolida patrum imitatio decepit, vt neglecto templo Hierosolymitano in monte Garizim cultum Dei exercerent, & Iudæos hostiliter odissent. Et vt Eliam videamus, licuit illi sacerdotes Baalis occidere, & igne cœlitus euocato perdere impios milites, qui ipsum & Dei verbum procaciter ridebant: quia vt hoc fieret, occulta spiritus suggestione, quæ illi vocationis peculiaris loco fuit, admonebatur. At nihil huius habebant Ioannes & Iacobus. Peccant ergo, quando illum volunt imitari: & cum illis etiam hodie peccabunt, si qui ex administrorum verbi numero sibi in sacrificulos & Monachos idem licere putauerint. Non ergo sufficit exempla aliorum adduxisse, nisi primo constet illos recte fecisse: deinde nostri etiam officij esse, vt illos imitemur.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage warns how easily one slips in using Scripture and the examples of the saints, unless we attend carefully to what our calling is and what properly pertains to us. For often, bewitched by our own feeling, we do not see that the true sense of the passage works against us, although we think it serves our purpose. Thus the Jews once erred in the law of retaliation, when each took for himself privately what had been committed to the judges for punishing wrongs. As for the examples of others, what was once permitted to one or another is not immediately permitted to all, or always. Indeed, it was once lawful to offer sacrifices in any place, when God had not yet fixed a certain place for his worship. But once that place was fixed, it was a sin to sacrifice elsewhere; and although they excused themselves by the example of the fathers who sacrificed on the high places, the Holy Spirit openly condemns those same practices. The same can be said of the Samaritans, whom a perverse and foolish imitation of the fathers deceived, so that, neglecting the temple at Jerusalem, they worshipped God on Mount Gerizim and bitterly hated the Jews. And to look at Elijah: he was permitted to slay the priests of Baal, and by calling down fire from heaven to destroy the impious soldiers who insolently mocked both him and the word of God. This was because he was prompted to do it by a secret suggestion of the Spirit, which served him in place of a special calling. But John and James had nothing of this. They sin, therefore, when they wish to imitate him; and they will sin with them today too, if any of the ministers of the Word think that they may do the same against the so-called sacrificing priests and monks. It is not enough, then, to bring forward the examples of others, unless it is first established that they acted rightly, and secondly that it is also our duty to imitate them.

units.la: Porro ipsum Christum discipulis respondentem audiamus. Conuersus enim eos obiurgauit, dicens: Nescitis cuius spiritus vos sitis. Filius enim hominis non venit vt perdat animas hominum, sed ut feruet. Duobus argumentis illos erroris conuincit. Primum ab ipsorum persona sumitur, & illo suae conditionis atque officij eos admonet, ad quod sint destinati. Nescius (inquit) cuius spiritus vos sitis. Quasi diceret: Quae haec est vestra petitio? quae item tam praeceps cupiditas, quae vt vos ipsos ignoretis facit? Maligni enim spiritus opus est perdere homines, quod illum in primis parentibus fecisse constat. At vos mei discipuli estis, & proinde mei spiritus ductum debetis sequi, qui mitis & humilis cum sit, iniuriarum patientes facit, & malum bono vincere docet. Quod autem discipulis Christus dicit, ad omnes nos ex aequo pertinet. Nec enim Christi discipuli erimus, nisi eius spiritu simus praediti, vt Paulus monuit. At quis nam & qualis est ille spiritus? Spiritum Dei discit scriptura, spiritum item sanctum, spiritum veritatis, humilitatis, dilectionis, mansuetudinis, &c. De his ergo cogitemus, quoties nos Satan a Deo abstrahere, mendacijs inescare, ad fraudes, dolos, impostituras & iniurias solicitare satagit: quoties item superbiae ventis animos inflari, aut eosdem in uidiae & odij atq; irae flammis accendi sentimus. Meminerimus tunc, nos alterius spiritus discipulos esse, cui omnino parere oporteat, nisi a Christo diuelli & simul aeterna salutis iacturam facere velimus. Huc certe Paulus respexit, quando a scortatione homines Christianos hoc argumento debortatur, quod nefas sit ea corpora tam turpiter prostituì, quae Christi sanguine abluta & spiritus Dei templa facta sint.
units.tr: Next, let us hear Christ himself answering the disciples. For he turned and rebuked them, saying: "You do not know what spirit you are of. For the Son of man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them." He refutes their error by two arguments. The first is taken from their own person, and by it he reminds them of the condition and office to which they were destined. "You do not know," he says, "what spirit you are of." As if he were saying: "What kind of request is this of yours? And what headlong desire is this, which makes you ignorant of yourselves? For it is the work of an evil spirit to destroy men, as is clear from what he did in our first parents. But you are my disciples, and therefore you ought to follow the leading of my Spirit, who, being gentle and humble, makes people patient under injuries and teaches them to overcome evil with good." What Christ says to the disciples applies equally to all of us. For we shall not be Christ's disciples unless we are endowed with his Spirit, as Paul warned. But what, and of what kind, is that Spirit? Scripture calls it the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, of humility, of love, of gentleness, and so on. Let us think of these whenever we feel that Satan is trying to draw us away from God, to ensnare us with lies, and to urge us to fraud, deceit, deception and injury; and likewise whenever we feel our minds puffed up by the winds of pride, or set on fire by the flames of envy, hatred and anger. Then let us remember that we are disciples of another spirit, whom we must by all means obey, unless we wish to be torn away from Christ and at the same time to suffer the loss of eternal salvation. Paul surely had this in view when he dissuades Christian men from fornication by this argument: that it is wrong to prostitute so shamefully those bodies which have been washed in Christ's blood and made temples of the Spirit of God.

units.la: Alterum argumentum a sua persona Dominus petit, dicens: Filius hominis non venit, vt perdat animas hominum, sed vt seruet. Est haec sententia non postrema inter eas, quibus totum Euangelium comprehenditur, & ideo illam saepe Christus repetit. In praesenti autem huius meminit, vt offendat non iam tempus esse, quo hominum scelera puniat, aut sibi factas iniurias vlciscatur. Obseruabis ergo duplicem in scripturis aduentum Christi praedicari. Primus, quo venit vt ex virgine carnem assumeret, & in assumpta carne pro nobis hostia factus, nos a peccatis simul & morte aeterna redimeret. De hoc aduentu olim Isaias dixit: Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit nos. In eo igitur non nisi salutificae suae virtutis exempla edidit, & ijs quoq; se mitem atq; beneficum praebuit, qui apertis iniurijs eius iram prouocabant, & quouis supplicio digni erant. Quae causa fuit, quod nec hic quidem discipulorum voluntati morem gerere: neq; Samaritanos ob ingratitudinem & indignam repulsam perdere debuit. Restat autem alter aduentus, quo in fine huius mundi in nubibus caeli comparebit ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Siflentur tunc ad eius tribunal omnes homines, vt in corporibus suis & animabus suis digna factis suis praemia recipiant: prodest autem, vt in utriusque aduentus meditatione multum & diligenter versemur. Vt enim prioris consideratio nobis in quouis tentatione genere consolationem dulcissimam affert, & de salute nostra certos facit: ita posterior nos in officio continet, & simul scandalo medetur, quod ex impiorum prosperis successibus & scelerum impunitate, qua fere hic fruuntur, nascitur. Cur enim hanc nos impatientius feramus, aut illorum felicitate offendamur, quando scimus, venturum aliquando Christum iudicem, vt dignas de illis poenas sumat, promissa autem vitae aeternae praemia credentibus retribuat?
units.tr: The Lord draws his second argument from his own person, saying: "The Son of man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them." This saying is not the least of those in which the whole Gospel is comprehended, and therefore Christ often repeats it. Here, however, he mentions it to show that this is not the time for punishing men's crimes or avenging injuries done to himself. You will observe, therefore, that Scripture preaches a twofold coming of Christ. The first is that by which he came to take on flesh from a virgin, and, having been made a sacrifice for us in the flesh he assumed, redeemed us from sins and from eternal death at once. Of this coming Isaiah once said: "God himself will come and save us." In it, then, he displayed only examples of his saving power, and he showed himself gentle and beneficent even toward those who provoked his anger by open injuries and deserved any punishment. This is why he ought not to have gratified the wish of the disciples here, nor destroyed the Samaritans on account of their ingratitude and unworthy rejection. The other coming remains, in which at the end of this world he will appear in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead. Then all men will be summoned to his tribunal, so that in their bodies and souls they may receive rewards worthy of their deeds. It is useful, then, to dwell much and diligently on the meditation of both comings. For as the consideration of the first brings us the sweetest comfort in every kind of temptation and makes us sure of our salvation, so the second keeps us in our duty and at the same time heals the scandal that arises from the prosperous successes of the wicked and from the impunity of their crimes, which they commonly enjoy here. For why should we bear this more impatiently, or be offended at their good fortune, when we know that Christ will one day come as judge, to exact from them the punishments they deserve, and to repay believers with the promised rewards of eternal life?

units.la: Habet praeterea non vulgarem consolationem loci huius conclusio, qua dicitur Christum cum suis in alium vicum abiisse. Ergo non defuerunt alij, qui eum cum suo comitatu reciperent, & quos priorum exemplum non monit vt eos imitari vellent. Habet ergo Dominus vbiq; locorum suos, & facile etiam hodie ecclesiae suae in terris exulanti hospitium inuenit. Ipsius enim est terra & plenitudo eius. Idem in sua manu tenet corda omnium hominum, quorum voluntates etiam inclinare potest, vt suis seruis sese beneficos praebeant. Exempla huius generis alibi adduximus, quae modo repetere non est opus. Nos igitur ista confirmemus, vt in fide Christi constantes, eum intrepide sequamur, neq; nos mundi ingratitudo aut inhumanitas terreat. Quod autem in discipulorum exemplo praecipuum est, discamus, etiam in causa optima zelum nostrum suspectum habere, consiliorum vestrorum & actionum omnium hunc nobis finem atque scopum proponamus, vt & Dei gloria per nos proueba-tur, & quam plurimos ad Iesu Christi cognitionem adducamus, vt salutis in illo nobiscum consortes fiant. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This conclusion of the passage also offers a consolation that is not small: it says that Christ went with his disciples into another village. So there were others who received him with his company, and the example of those before them did not move them to want to imitate them. The Lord therefore has his people in every place, and even today he easily finds a welcome for his Church, which is living in exile on earth. For the earth is his, and the fullness of it. He also holds in his hand the hearts of all men, and he can even incline their wills so that they show themselves kind to his servants. We have brought forward examples of this kind elsewhere, and there is no need to repeat them now. Let us therefore confirm these things, so that, constant in the faith of Christ, we may follow him fearlessly, and neither the ingratitude nor the inhumanity of the world terrify us. And what is most important in the example of the disciples, let us learn to regard even our own zeal with suspicion in a cause that is best of all. Let us set before ourselves this aim and goal of all our counsels and actions: that God's glory may be promoted through us, and that we may bring as many as possible to the knowledge of Jesus Christ, so that they may become partakers with us of salvation in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCV.
units.tr: HOMILY XCV.

units.la: Factum est autem proficiscentibus ipsis, quidam in via dixit ei: Sequar te quocunque iueris, Domine. Dixit autem ei Iesus: Vulpes lustra habent, & volucres caeli nidos: Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput inclinet. Ait autem ad alium quendam: Sequere me. Ille vero dixit: Domine, permitte mihi ut prius abeam, ac sepeliam patrem meum. Dixit autem ei Iesus: Sine ut mortui sepeliant mortuos suos: tu vero profectus annuntia regnum Dei. Dixit autem etiam alius: Sequar te Domine, sed permitte mihi prius, ut valedicam iis qui sunt domi meae. Ait autem ei Iesus: Nemo qui manu sua admota aratro, respexerit ad ea quae retro sunt, appositus est ad regnum Dei.
units.tr: As they were going along the road, a certain man said to him, "Lord, I will follow you wherever you go." Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." To another he said, "Follow me." But he said, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." Jesus said to him, "Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God." Another also said, "I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home." Jesus said to him, "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus in Filio suo unigenito Iesu Christo omnia ea hominibus offert, quae aeternae salutis sunt: ita a nobis exigit, ut eum fide vera apprehensum sedulo & constanter sequamur. Nam nisi id fiat, nullus ex eo ad nos fructus redit, & inanis est omnis ipsius professio. Quia autem in hoc plurimum peccatur, & multi tam aliis quam sibi ipsis turpiter & pernitiose imponunt, dum nudam fidei professionem & externu Sacramentorum usum sufficere putant, hoc loco tria exempla Lucas subjicit, quibus docemur, quid in tota hac causa nos facere, quidve cavere oportet. De singulis igitur ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Just as God offers in his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, all those things that belong to eternal salvation, so he requires of us that, having laid hold of him by true faith, we follow him diligently and constantly. For unless this happens, no fruit comes to us from him, and every profession of him is empty. Because many sin greatly in this matter, and many shamefully and destructively deceive both others and themselves, thinking that a bare profession of faith and an outward use of the Sacraments is enough, Luke sets before us in this place three examples, by which we are taught what we must do in this whole matter and what we must beware of. We shall speak of each one in order.

units.la: Primus ex Scribarum numero prodijt (ut Matthaeus annotat) & hypocrita est, qualesplerique illius loci & ordinis fuerunt. Hic dum Christus cum suis in suscepto itinere pergit, ad illum accedit, dicens: Magister, sequar te quocunque iueris. Magnifica sane promissio, si verba spectes. Nam magistrum & Dominum agnoscit, quem alii Scribae & Sacerdotes vix hominis loco habebant. Denique non vocatus neque requisitus sese offert, & quidem ad omnia. Sequar te (inquit) quocunque iueris. Itaque, absque ulla exceptione se paratum offendit ad labores, pericula, casus deniq; omnes. At hoc illum animo subdolo fecisse ex Christi responsione apparet, qui non tam ad verba eius quam animum loquentis respexit. Est ergo Scriba hic eorum typus, qui sub Christi & religionis Christianae praetextu sua quaerunt, & ad huius seculi bona potius quam ad regnum Dei caelestem respiciunt. Hi caeco carnis affectu abrepti, non expectant vocantem Dominum, sed sponte currunt, & inter discipulos primum locum sibi debere putant, cum quid sit Christi discipulum agere, nondum intelligant. Itaque quo magis festinant, eo longius recedunt a via salutis, quae in illo nobis monstratur. Deinde tunc accedunt, quando res omnis in tuto constituta est, & felici successu regnum Christi propagatur: quam primum vero tempestas aliqua oritur, turpiter pedem referunt. Quae omnia in hoc Scriba nostro cernimus. Videt is Christum miraculis illustrem omnium ore praedicari, cum magno comitatu per Galilaeam & Samariam iter facere, amicorum & mulierum illustrium liberalitate alidiscipulos item eius etiamsi nihil possideant, omnibus tamen necessariis abundare, & ubique locorum habere patronos, qui illos excipiant atque humanissime tractent. Quapropter qui in otio enutritus, nihil praeter vulgi applausum & vivendi rationem minime laboriosam quaerebat, Christum sibi quam maxime convenire putavit: sed (ut mox audiemus) accepto responso quale non expectabat, ab instituto resilit. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, quibus nemo temere fidat. Sunt enim revera ἀπόστασιοι, id est, temporarii illi & praecoci fidei homines, quos in sementis parabola Christus sub eorum typo describit, qui semen in loca petricosa excipiunt, ubi neque radices agere, neque aestum vehementiorem sustinere possit, quo fructum excoqui oportet.
units.tr: The first came from the number of the scribes (as Matthew notes), and is a hypocrite, as most of that place and rank were. While Christ is making his journey with his disciples, this man approaches him and says, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go." A splendid promise indeed, if you look only at the words. For he acknowledges as teacher and Lord the one whom other scribes and priests scarcely regarded as a man. Then, uncalled and unasked, he offers himself, and that for everything: "I will follow you," he says, "wherever you go." So, without any exception, he presents himself ready for labours, dangers, and every kind of hardship. But from Christ's reply it appears that he did this with a deceitful mind, for Christ looked not so much at his words as at the heart of the speaker. This scribe, then, is a figure of those who, under the pretext of Christ and of the Christian religion, seek their own ends, and look to the goods of this age rather than to the heavenly kingdom of God. Carried away by a blind fleshly desire, they do not wait for the Lord to call them, but rush forward of their own accord, and think they ought to have the first place among the disciples, though they do not yet understand what it is to be a disciple of Christ. So the more eagerly they hurry, the further they withdraw from the way of salvation shown to us in him. Then they come forward when everything is secure and the kingdom of Christ is spreading with happy success; but as soon as some storm arises, they shamefully turn back. We see all these things in this scribe of ours. He sees Christ, illustrious for his miracles, praised by everyone, travelling with a great company through Galilee and Samaria; he sees that his disciples, though they possess nothing, nevertheless abound in all necessities through the generosity of friends and noble women, and have patrons everywhere who receive them and treat them most kindly. Therefore this man, who had been brought up in idleness and sought nothing but the applause of the crowd and a very undemanding way of life, thought Christ would suit him very well; but, as we shall soon hear, having received an answer he did not expect, he draws back from his undertaking. There is a great number of such people today, and no one trusts them rashly. For they are truly apostates [ἀπόστασιοι], that is, temporary and premature men of faith, whom Christ in the parable of the sower describes under the figure of those who receive the seed on stony ground, where it can neither take root nor endure the fiercer heat by which the fruit must be ripened.

units.la: Et hac causa est, quod hunc quoque Scribam non recipit Dominus in discipulorum gregem, quamvis alibi dicat: Eum qui venit ad me, non eijcio foras. Nam licet corpore venirent, animus tamen non tam ad Christum quam ad opes, honores & felicitatem huius seculi aspirabat. Et nouerat ille, quam ingens scandalum tales dare solent, quando in publico ecclesiae periculo stationem suam turpiter deserunt. Quamvis autem illum durius accipere & acriter corripere posset, occultius tamen arguit eius vanitatem, quae huius instituti causa ipsi fuerat, cum nullum adhuc offendiculum
units.tr: And for this reason the Lord also does not receive this scribe into the flock of his disciples, although elsewhere he says, "Him who comes to me I will not cast out." For although they came in body, their mind was aspiring not so much to Christ as to the wealth, honours, and happiness of this age. And he knew how great a scandal such men are wont to give, when they shamefully desert their post in the public danger of the Church. Although he could have received him more harshly and rebuked him sharply, he nonetheless more quietly exposes the vanity which had been the reason for his taking up this undertaking, since there was as yet no stumbling-block

units.la: Exemplum hypocritae discipuli.
units.tr: Example of the hypocritical disciple.

units.la: Christus nonnullos hypocritas quaerentem. inde ad alios redundauisset. Vulpes (inquit) lustra habent, & volucres cœli, nidos: Filius autem hominis non habet vbi caput inclinet. Quorum verborum hic sensus est: Tu quidem tibi omnia læta polliceris, & tam opum, honorum & otij beatissimi spem maximam animo concepisti, neq; tibi quicquam eorum, quæ ad vitæ huius felicitatem pertinent, defuturum putas, si in discipulorum meorum album adscribaris. Sed vehementer falleris ô bone. Tam enim abest, vt ego his abundem, aut meus ista conferam, vt ipse potius ferïs & volucribus sim pauperior. Qua enim fera tam misera, quæ bestiola tam infelix est, quæ non lustrum habeat, quò se recipere possit? Quæ auis item tam vaga est, quæ nido destituatur? Vulpes certè, animal inuisum merito, foueas habet, in quibus & ipsa latet & suos catulos educat. Eadem auicularū omnium conditio. At ego, qui vt homines seruarem, Filius hominis factus sum, his omnibus miserior, proprij nihil habeo, vbi vel caput quietus aut somni causa inclinem. Itaq; si vel regnum quæris in hoc seculo, vel ad opes & dignitates aspiras, non est quòd me sequaris, qui non huius mundi bona caduca & momentanea meis largiri soleo, sed cœlestium atq; æternorū Mediator sum, &c. Itaq; admonent ista, eos qui Christum sequi volunt, ad labores, egestatem & quæuis incommoda præparatos esse oportere, ne quande hiis offensi succumbat aut deficiant, vbi fortitudine & constantia cumprimus opus est.
units.tr: Christ, seeking some hypocrites, then turned to others. "Foxes," he says, "have holes, and the birds of the air, nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." The sense of these words is this: You promise yourself everything pleasant, and you have conceived in your mind the greatest hope of wealth, honours, and most blessed leisure, and you think nothing of those things that pertain to the happiness of this life will be lacking to you if you are enrolled on the list of my disciples. But you are badly mistaken, my friend. For far from my abounding in these things, or my bestowing them on my followers, I am rather poorer than the wild beasts and birds. For what wild beast is so wretched, what little creature so unhappy, that it does not have a den to which it can retreat? What bird, too, is so wandering that it lacks a nest? The fox, certainly an animal rightly hated, has holes in which it both hides itself and rears its young. The same is the condition of all the little birds. But I, who was made the Son of Man in order to save men, am poorer than all of these: I have nothing of my own, nowhere to rest my head or lean it down to sleep. Therefore, if you seek a kingdom in this age, or aspire to riches and dignities, there is no reason for you to follow me, who am accustomed to bestow not the perishable and momentary goods of this world on my people, but am the Mediator of heavenly and eternal things, and so on. Therefore these words warn that those who wish to follow Christ must prepare themselves for labours, want, and all sorts of inconvenience, lest at some time, offended by these, they give way or fail where courage and constancy are most needed.

units.la: Docet autem simul his verbis Christus, regnū suum non esse de hoc mundo. Nam non vt in terris dominetur homo factus est, sed vt Veritati testimonium ferret, & Patris promissiones ratas faceret. Debuit ergo eius aduentus humilis, & nullo fastu aut splendore terribilis esse. Vt ergo miserè falluntur, qui in illo terrena quærunt: ita non minus turpis illorum error est, qui cum huius discipuli censeri velint, opes & huius seculi splendorem magnificè ostentant. At si non habuit Christus in terris, vbi caput suum inclinaret, vnde ergo eius vicarij regna, prouincias, arces, oppida, terras longè lateq;, patentes acceperunt? Aut vnde Petrus patrimonium illud habuit, quo suos successores potentissimis quoq; Regibus terribiles fecit? Antichristo Daniel propheta tribuit, quòd in sua potesta te habiturus sit thesauros terræ, Apostolis verò suis nihil huius vnquam Christus promisit. Cæterùm quod de illis dicimus, qui falso nomine Christi se vicarios profitentur, hoc iis quoq; dici putemus, qui cùm puriorís doctrinæ sectatores videri velint, tamen ipsi quoq; opibus congerendis addicti sunt, & vt mundo placeant, omnium moribus atq; studijs sese accommodare solent. Et sanè mirum est tantam esse istorum omnium impudentiam, vt inter immensos diuitiarum aceruos, & superbas magnificorum titulorum appellationes, Christi pauperis & egeni nomen iactare audeant.
units.tr: But at the same time, by these words Christ also teaches that his kingdom is not of this world. For he was made man not to rule on earth, but to bear witness to the truth and to make good the promises of the Father. His coming therefore had to be humble and to be terrifying with no pomp or splendour. Just as those who seek earthly things in him are miserably deceived, so no less shameful is the error of those who, while wishing to be counted his disciples, proudly display wealth and the splendour of this age. But if Christ had no place on earth to lay his head, whence then did his vicars receive kingdoms, provinces, citadels, towns, and lands stretching far and wide? Or whence did Peter have that patrimony with which he made his successors terrible even to the most powerful kings? The prophet Daniel attributes to Antichrist that he will have the treasures of the earth in his power, but Christ never promised anything of this sort to his Apostles. Moreover, what we say of those who falsely profess themselves vicars of Christ, let us think this also said of those who, while wishing to seem followers of a purer doctrine, nevertheless are themselves devoted to heaping up riches, and who are accustomed to accommodate themselves to the manners and pursuits of everyone in order to please the world. And indeed it is remarkable that such great shamelessness exists among all of them, that amid immense heaps of riches and proud titles of magnificence they dare to boast of the name of Christ, who was poor and needy.

units.la: Sed præstat causas diligentius inspicere, ob quas Dei Filius pauper nasci & viuere in terris voluit, vt illis cognitis, ipsum quoq; paupertatis eius teneamus, qui fere tria continet. Primò enim illum in hoc mundo pauperem, egenum, adhæc peregrinum fieri oportuit, vt nobis æterni & cœlestis regni diuitias mereretur, & patriam in cœlis pararet. Deinde omnibus, qui nomen eius profitentur, formam præbere voluit, quam in vita sua & omnibus actionibus suis sequantur: quod vt omnes alij obseruare debent, ita maximè ij, quos Verbi sui administros ille constituit. Nec enim decet, vt isti suam conditionem præstantiore aut beatiorem esse cupiant, quàm sui præceptoris & heri fuerit. Postremò paupertatem & inopiam suo exemplo sanctificauit, vt quæ impijs peccati pœna est, credentibus salutare sit ad veram pietatem exercitium, in quo fidei & patientiæ suæ declarandæ materiam habeant. Nemo igitur vel seipsum vel quenquam alium propter inopiam Deo inuisum aut exosum esse putet. Quin exempli huius pauperes meminerint, vt se Christi socios esse cogitent, vt alacriter onus illud, quo huius seculi filijs nullum grauius esse solet. Potuit olim philosophos in rerum omnium angustia hoc vnum confirmare, quòd se non multis opus habere, & naturam paucis contentam esse scirent. Cur ergo impatientes sint Christiani homines, qui in Christo Iesu sibi bonorum omnium thesaurum & (vt prouerbio dicitur) copiæ cornu propositum esse norunt? Sed & diuitum horum meminisse debent, ne quem contemnant, qui cum inopia aut egestate conflictatur. Nam vt Solomon ait, diues & pauper occurrerunt sibi, sed vtriusq; factor aut creator Dominus est: ideo, qui subsannat pauperem, probris afficit factorem eius. Deus quippe est, qui alios diuites, alios pauperes facere consueuit.
