At si ideò non contemni debet egenus, quanto plurus idem à nobis fieri debet, quòd in ipso Christi in hoc mundo viuentis imaginem cernimus, & quòd hunc in suas rationes ascitum esse scimus, quicquid illi fecerimus?
units.tr: But it is better to examine more carefully the causes for which the Son of God chose to be born and to live on earth as a poor man. Once these are known, we shall also hold fast to the poverty itself, which has roughly three purposes. First, it was necessary that he should become poor, needy and, besides, a stranger in this world, so that he might win for us the riches of the eternal and heavenly kingdom and prepare a homeland for us in heaven. Second, he wished to give to all who profess his name a pattern to follow in their life and all their actions. This all others ought to observe, but especially those whom he has appointed as ministers of his Word. For these men should not desire a condition more distinguished or happier than that of their teacher and master. Last, by his own example he sanctified poverty and want, which is a punishment of sin for the wicked but a means of salvation for believers, a training in true godliness, in which they may have the occasion to show their faith and patience. Let no one, therefore, whether himself or anyone else, think that he is hated or despised by God on account of poverty. Rather, let the poor remember this example, so that they may consider themselves companions of Christ and bear cheerfully that burden which weighs more heavily on the children of this age than any other. Once the philosophers could find this one consolation in the straitness of all things: they knew they had need of few things and that nature is content with little. Why then should Christians be impatient, who know that in Christ Jesus is set before them the treasure of all good things and, as the proverb says, the horn of plenty? But they ought also to remember the rich, so that they do not despise anyone who struggles with want or need. For, as Solomon says, the rich man and the poor man meet together, but the Lord is the maker of both; therefore whoever mocks the poor man insults his maker. For it is God who is accustomed to make some rich and others poor. But if the needy man must not be despised for this reason, how much more must he not be despised by us, since in him we see the image of Christ living in this world, and since we know that Christ has taken him into his own reckoning, whatever we do to him?

units.la: Sed alterum videamus, qui à priori longè alius cunctatorem agit. Nam à Christo vocatus, & iussus vt sequeretur, moras nectit & tergiuersatur, interim vero pietatem in parentes praetexit, dicens: Domine, permitte mihi vt prius abeam, & sepeliam patrem meum. Sciebat ergo se hoc debere Christo, vt eius vocationi obediret, sed infirmum adhuc in fide multa retinebant, quae tamen astutè dissimulat, & eo praetextu vtitur, qui vt honestius erat, ita cum pietate coiunctus esse videbatur. Et hunc quoq; ita proponit, vt quod petebat sibi minimè negandum esse, docere velit. Quasi diceret: Sum equidem paratus vt te sequar Domine, sed vnum me remoratur, quod vt per te prius exequi mihi liceat rogo. Est mihi pater iam senio confectus & morti vicinus: quem cum deferere non possim, neq; debeam, permitte quaeso, vt tantisper illi adsim, donec hac vita defuncto officium extremum praestem, & eum honorificè sepeliam. Fuit haec sanè excusatio pia in specie, & digna quae admitteretur. Sed affectu carnis detentum fuisse, ex Christi responsione patebit. Est ergo hic eorum typus, qui quàmuis se diuinitus vocari sentiant, laboribus tamen & periculis sibi propositis terrentur, & cunctandi causas vndiq; conquirunt. Hi cùm non ignorent, Deo vocanti nequaquam esse relucandum, eiusmodi excusationibus sibi opus esse vident, quae pietatis specie & verbi diuini authoritate colorentur. Alius ergo nostrum hunc imitatus, parentes suos commemorat, & quae illis debeantur officia. Quid (inquit) faciam? Cuperem equidem me totum Christo addicere, & reliquis omnibus huic vni seruire: at parentum me miseret, à quibus discedere non possum, nisi & dolorum acerbissimi illis author sim, & simul vitae subsidia subducâ. Atqui vt parentes honoremus, lex Dei praecipit & communis sensus admonet. O felicem Abrahamum, quem è natali solo discedentem pater sequi dignatus est. At mihi parentes longè alij contigerunt, quos & patriae amor & veteris superstitionis studium detinent, vt me sequi nolint. Quod ergo vnum reliquum est, eorum infirmitati indulgeam oportet, donec aut animum mutent, aut peracto vitae suae curriculo hinc euocentur, &c. Sunt rursus, qui pietatem in patriam praetexunt, & sese verbis non minus splendidis excusant. O beatos & felices (aiunt) quibus hoc datum est, vt sub principibus Christianis Deo seruire & verbo eius parere possint. O felices item, quibus licet salua conscientia ex natali solo discedere, & inter exteros libertate Christiana frui. At quae nostra est calamitas, vtrunq; nobis negauit Deus. Nam & principes dedit partim superstitiosos, partim ignauos & meticulosos, qui etsi mutationem aliquam publicè fieri prohibeant, ad multa tamen conniuent, & non raro nos pro pijs intercedentes clementer audiunt. Quid ergo faceremus? Num ex patria digressi, & hanc & infelices ciues omni patrocinio destitutos Monachorum & Inquisitorum tyrannidi permittemus? Annon satius est, vt nos melioribus feruemus temporibus, & ipsi quoq; multa praeter animi sententiam dissimulando, interea eorum concilia turbemus, qui simul omnibus pijs exitiû struunt? His adde tertio loco eos, qui magistratus authoritate suam ignauiam excusant, & ex scripturis testimonia congerunt, quibus probent, illi omnino esse obediendum. Sunt item, qui cauendum sibi aiunt, ne alicuius scandali cuiquam authores sint, neue pacem & concordiam publicam turbent, aut hominibus seditiosis aliquam occasionem suo exemplo praebeant, qua ad res nouas & reipub. turbationem abutantur. Audiuntur huius generis multa hodie, & ingeniosa admodum est caro nostra in fingendis rationibus, quibus ignauiam suam aut etiam manifestam Veritatis & fidei abnegationem excusat.
units.tr: But let us look at the other man, who, being called by Christ and bidden to follow him, acts quite differently as a laggard. He delays and makes excuses, and meanwhile he puts forward a plea of filial duty, saying: "Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father." He knew, then, that he owed this to Christ, that he must obey his calling; but he was still weak in faith and kept many things hidden, which he cunningly concealed, and he used that pretext, which seemed the more honourable and linked to piety. He presents it in such a way that he wishes to show that what he asks ought in no way to be refused him. As if he said: "I am indeed ready to follow you, Lord, but one thing holds me back, and I ask that I may first be allowed to attend to it through you. I have a father, now worn out with age and near to death. Since I can neither nor ought to abandon him, permit me, I pray, to stay with him for a while, until, when he has departed this life, I may perform the last duty and bury him with honour." This was indeed a pious-looking excuse, and one worthy of being accepted. But from Christ's reply it will be clear that he was held back by fleshly affection. This man, then, is a type of those who, although they feel that they are called by God, are nevertheless frightened by the labours and dangers set before them, and on all sides they seek out reasons for delay. Since they do not doubt that they must by no means resist God calling them, they see that they need excuses of this kind, which may be coloured with the appearance of piety and the authority of the divine Word. So one of us, imitating this man, mentions his parents and the duties owed to them. "What," he says, "shall I do? I would gladly devote myself wholly to Christ and serve him alone in all else. But I pity my parents, from whom I cannot depart unless I am the author of the most bitter grief to them and at the same time withdraw the support of their life. And yet the law of God commands us to honour our parents, and common sense admonishes us. O happy Abraham, whom his father deigned to follow when he left his native soil! But my parents have been quite otherwise: the love of their country and their attachment to the old superstition hold them back, so that they are unwilling for me to follow. So what remains is that I must indulge their weakness, until either they change their minds or they are called away from here when the course of their life is finished, and so on." There are again others who put forward the love of country as a pretext and excuse themselves in words no less splendid. "O blessed and happy," they say, "are those to whom it is granted to serve God and obey his Word under Christian princes! Happy too are those who may, with a clear conscience, leave their native soil and enjoy Christian liberty among foreigners. But our misfortune is that God has denied us both. For he has given us princes, some superstitious, some lazy and timid, who, although they forbid any public change, nevertheless wink at many things, and not seldom they listen kindly when we intercede for the godly. What then should we do? Shall we, having departed from our country, leave both it and its unhappy citizens, deprived of all protection, to the tyranny of the monks and inquisitors? Is it not better that we should wait for better times, and meanwhile, by dissembling many things against our own judgement, disturb the councils of those who at the same time plot destruction for all the godly?" To these add, in the third place, those who excuse their cowardice by the authority of the magistrate, and gather from the Scriptures testimonies by which they prove that the magistrate must be obeyed in every case. There are also those who say that they must take care not to become the cause of any scandal to anyone, nor disturb the public peace and concord, nor by their example give to seditious men any occasion which they might turn to revolution and disorder. Many such excuses are heard today, and our flesh is wonderfully ingenious in devising reasons by which it covers its cowardice, or even its plain denial of the truth and of the faith.

units.la: Ceterùm omnibus istis Christus respondet, cunctatori huic dicens: Sine vt mortui sepeliant mortuos suos, tu verò profectus annuntia regnum Dei. Atqui nô potuit illi displicere pius in parentem senio confectum animus, quando constat ipsum, cùm in cruce penderet, inter acerbissimos mortis dolores matris suae rationem habuisse, & eam Ioanni dilecto discipulo commendasse. Neq; etiam extremum quod mortuus praestatur officium improbat, dum eorum corpora honorificè sepeliuntur. Vt enim de hoc Adamum Deus admonuit: ita per Amos prophetam barbaram eorum inhumanitatem grauiter accusat, qui corpora defunctorum violare audent. Sed quia hunc ad Euangelij praedicatio nem destinarat, vult vt omnibus alijs rebus relictis ad hanc accingatur. Et verisimile est eum ex septuaginta illorum numero fuisse, quorum missionem in sequenti Capite Lucas describet. Etenim cum in veteri Testamento grauiter prohibeat Deus, ne sacerdotes funerû deductionib. & luctu, quo alij mortuos prosequuntur, sese polluant, quanto minus ferre debuit Christus, vt de patre sepeliendo solicitus esset, quem ipse vitae aeternae praeconem fecerat? Mortuos enim hic figurata locutione dicit eos, qui neglecto vitæ cœlestis studio circa res huius mundi occupantur, neq; in hoc sunt, ut Deo viuant, & huic debitum obsequium præstent. Horum (inquit) est funera & quæ ad mortuos spectant, curare. Tu ad regnum Dei destinatus es: huius ergo Verbum prædica, quod homines vitæ veræ restituit.
units.tr: Nevertheless, Christ answers all these excuses in the words spoken to this laggard: "Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God." Yet he could not have been displeased by a pious spirit toward an aged father, since it is clear that he himself, when hanging on the cross, amid the most bitter pains of death, took thought for his mother and commended her to the disciple John whom he loved. Nor does he disapprove of the last duty paid to the dead, when their bodies are honourably buried. For just as God admonished Adam about this, so also through the prophet Amos he severely accuses those who dare to violate the bodies of the dead as barbarously inhuman. But because he had destined this man for the preaching of the gospel, he wills that he, leaving all other things aside, should gird himself for this task. And it is likely that he was one of those seventy whose sending out Luke will describe in the following chapter. For since God in the Old Testament strictly forbids the priests to defile themselves with the funeral processions and the mourning with which others follow the dead, how much less should Christ have tolerated that the one whom he had made a herald of eternal life should be anxious about burying his father? For by a figurative manner of speaking he calls "dead" those who, neglecting the pursuit of the heavenly life, are occupied with the affairs of this world and are not intent on living to God and rendering him the obedience owed to him. "The funerals of these men," he says, "and the things that pertain to the dead, let them look after. You are destined for the kingdom of God: therefore preach its Word, which restores men to true life."

units.la: At si hoc Christi dictum propius inspiciamus, videbis eo confutari & destrui non minimam partem sacerdotij illius, quod Romani Pontifices instituerunt. Christus enim non sacerdotes aut sacrificos, sed Euangelij prænones instituit, qui viuentium curam habeant, & ad vitæ Christianæ officia omnes excitent, deniq; ad cœlestis atque æternæ vitæ hereditatem vocent eos, qui prius mortè digni censebantur. At illi sacrificulos ordinarunt, qui fere neglectis viuis, toti circa mortuos occupantur, neque eo contenti sunt, ut in funeribus sacra faciant, sed eadem tricesimo die repetunt; imo annua sacrificia commenti sunt, quæ perpetuo pro defunctorum salute fieri necesse est. Et ne quid præter rationem facere videbantur, ignem lustralem siue purgatorium (ut illi loquuntur) tradiderunt, in quo animæ pro delictis suis inter grauissimos cruciatus satisfaciant, iuuentur autem fratres eiusmodi, ut pœnæ illæ & tolerabiliores & breuiores fiant. Fuit hoc illis aucupium quæstuosissimum, & bi soli Alchymistæ veri dici possunt, qui à multis diu quæsitam artem inuenerunt. Nec enim ex metallo aut alia quacunque materia, sed ex nihilo, id est, ex vanissimis commentis aurum, argentum, palatia, prædia, reditus annuos, thesauros deniq; conflauerunt, quos ne Cræsi quidem diuitiæ æquauerint. Et cum ceremonias suas partim veteris Testamenti authoritate, partim Apostolorum exemplo tueantur, unum hoc illos in utroque falsi arguit. Qua fronte enim Mosis legem citabunt, qui ut sacra pro defunctis prorsus nulla præcepit olim, ita sacerdotes funeribus nequaquam occupari voluit? Quo item exemplo Apostolico se tuebantur, quando Apostolos nihil huius vnquam fecisse, neque etiam docuisse manifestius est, quam ut demonstrari oporteat? Quicquid ergo isti faciunt, non alio quàm prophanarum gentium exemplo nituntur, quas olim in funeribus sacra eiusmodi fecisse legimus.
units.tr: But if we look more closely at this saying of Christ, you will see that it refutes and overturns no small part of that priesthood which the Roman Pontiffs established. Christ did not institute priests or sacrificers, but heralds of the Gospel, who would care for the living, rouse everyone to the duties of the Christian life, and finally call to the inheritance of heavenly and eternal life those who had previously been considered fit only for death. But the Papists ordained little sacrificers who, neglecting the living almost entirely, devote themselves wholly to the dead. Nor are they content to perform sacred rites at funerals; they repeat them on the thirtieth day, and indeed they have invented annual sacrifices, which must be offered continually for the salvation of the departed. And lest they seem to act without reason, they have handed down a cleansing or purgatorial fire (as they call it), in which souls make satisfaction for their sins amid the most severe torments, and these torments are made more bearable and shorter by the help of their brethren. This was a most profitable fowling-trap for them, and these alone may truly be called alchemists, for they have discovered the art that many have sought for so long. For they have not smelted gold, silver, palaces, estates, annual revenues, and finally treasures out of metal or any other material, but out of nothing, that is, out of the emptiest inventions; such wealth as not even the riches of Croesus could match. And although they defend their ceremonies partly by the authority of the Old Testament and partly by the example of the Apostles, this one thing convicts them on both counts of falsehood. With what face will they cite the law of Moses, which once prescribed no sacred rites at all for the dead, and did not at all wish the priests to be occupied with funerals? Likewise, by what Apostolic example do they defend themselves, when it is more obvious than needs demonstrating that the Apostles never did any such thing, nor even taught it? Whatever they do, therefore, they rely on nothing but the example of the heathen nations, whom we read once performed such rites at funerals.

units.la: Sed omissis illis, quod in Christi responso præcipuum est, videamus. Docet enim nos in Dei vocatione ita pergere debere, ut huic omnia postponantur, quæ nos quocunq; prætextu ab illius obedientia avocare possunt. Est quidem multa laude dignissima pietas, qua bona indolis liberi suos parentes, & boni ciues patriam suam prosequuntur. Multa item sibi mutuo debent coniuges, & arctissimum est vinculum illud fidei, quo subditos suos principibus Deus obstrictos esse voluit. At hæc omnia superat fides quam Deo debemus, qui ut Filium suum Iesum Christum audiamus iussit, & quam hic nobis præscripsit, vitæ totius regulam sequamur. Itaque quoties parentum, coniugum, liberorum aut cognatorum amore nos à fide revocari sentimus, semper verborum Christi memineri- mus, dicentis: Qui amat patrem aut matrem supra me, non est me dignus: qui amat filium aut filiam supra me, non est me dignus. Similiter quoties suam authoritatem nobis magistratus obicit, tunc Christi dictum nobis in mentem veniat: Reddite Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris, & Deo quæ sunt Dei: & cum Apostolis respondeamus: Oportet Deo potius obedire quàm hominibus. Ita si amici & mundus nos retrahunt, cogitemus non temere ab Iacobo dictum esse: Amicitia mundi huius est inimicitia cum Deo. Cui Paulus consentiens dicebat: Si hominibus placerem, Dei seruus non essem. Neq; etiam nos moueant, qui præter rationem scandala sibi fingunt, & ijs offenduntur, quæ nos ex officio facimus.
units.tr: But setting those matters aside, let us consider what is chief in Christ's answer. For he teaches us that in following God's calling we must proceed in such a way that everything which could draw us away from obedience to it, under whatever pretext, is put second to it. Indeed, the piety by which good children honour their parents and good citizens their country is most worthy of great praise. Likewise spouses owe much to one another, and that most binding tie of faith, by which God willed that his subjects be bound to their princes, is very strong. Yet the faith we owe to God surpasses all these, for he commanded us to hear his Son Jesus Christ, and to follow the rule of our whole life which he has prescribed to us here. Therefore, whenever we feel ourselves called away from faith by love of parents, spouses, children or kinsfolk, we must always remember the words of Christ, who says: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." Similarly, whenever the magistrate sets his authority against us, let the saying of Christ come to mind: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's"; and with the Apostles let us answer: "We ought to obey God rather than men." So too, if friends and the world draw us back, let us consider that James was not speaking rashly when he said: "Friendship with the world is enmity with God." Paul, agreeing with him, said: "If I still pleased men, I should not be the servant of God." Nor should we be moved by those who invent offences for themselves beyond reason, and take offence at what we do in the discharge of our duty.

units.la: Nam hu quoque Christus respondet, quando discipulis de Pharisaorum offensione quærentibus dixit: Sinite eos, quia cæci duces sunt cæcorum. At quod in genere dicitur de fide in Christum & vero Dei cultu, hoc ipsum singuli ad seipsos reflringere debent, ut quod ipsis peculiariter iniunxit Deus, sedulò exequantur. Ergo procul relictis omnibus alijs curu, verbum constanter prædicent, qui ad eius ministerium sunt vocati. Absque respectu item personarum ius dicant, qui in magistratu constituti sunt, neque vllis rationibus se ab instituto reuocari sinant. Denique discant omnes homines Deo quidem fideles esse in omnibus, quæ ad cultum eius spectant, priuatim verò & publicè suum quoque officium faciant, & quam Deo sibi creditam habent, statim fortiter tueantur.
units.tr: For Christ also answers them here, when, to the disciples asking about the offence taken by the Pharisees, he said: "Let them alone, for they are blind guides of the blind." But what is said generally about faith in Christ and the true worship of God, each man ought to apply to himself, so that he diligently carries out what God has specifically enjoined upon him. Therefore, setting aside all other cares, let those who are called to the ministry of the Word preach the Word steadfastly. Let those who are placed in the magistracy administer justice without respect of persons, and not allow themselves to be called back from their purpose by any considerations. Finally, let all men learn to be faithful to God in all things that concern his worship, and in private and in public to perform their own duty, and to defend bravely at once the trust which they have received from God.

units.la: Porrò priusquam hinc discedamus, obseruanda etiam nobis venit singularis Iesu Christi bonitas simul atq; prouidentia, qua in deligendis seruis atque discipulis utitur. Nam priorem illum, qui se ipsum sponte & alacri animo ad omne obsequium offerebat, reijcit, eò quòd animum eius perfpe&ti haberet, & ecclesiæ suæ nunquam utilem fore sciret. Hunc verò cunctantem & effugia quærentem efficaciter vocat & vrget, ut ad ministerium hoc ocyus accedat. Sunt ergo admirabilia eius iudicia, quorum rationem etsi non semper assequi possimus, non tamen periculum est ne ille fallatur, qui & corda hominum inspicit, & futura non minus quàm quæ ob oculos sunt cognita habet. Consolationem verò magnam habet hæc eius bonitas, qua infirmum adhuc & fluctuantem non contem plsit, sed in suorum gregem adoptare dignatus est. Quod enim hîc fecit, hoc ipsum in alijs etiam discipulis cernitur, quorum vitia & infirmitates admirabili lenitate pertulit, quàmuis sæpe acerbam reprehensionem meruerint. At ne quis hinc ignaviæ suæ patrocinium quærat, probè observabis, ita huius infirmitati ignouisse Christum, ut interim eam non excusarit præpostera indulgentia quin potius (ut modò diximus) illum vrget, ut affectui valedicat, qui ipsum ab officio retrahebat. Itaq; nos quoq; fratres infirmos ferre conuenit, ut interea eos confirmare & ad faciendum officium excitare satagamus.
units.tr: Before we leave this passage, we must also observe the singular goodness and providence of Jesus Christ, which he displays in choosing his servants and disciples. For he rejects the first man, who offered himself willingly and eagerly for every service, because he saw through his mind and knew that he would never be useful to his Church. But he effectively calls and urges the other, who hesitated and sought excuses, to come to this ministry all the sooner. His judgments, therefore, are wonderful; and although we cannot always grasp their reasons, there is no danger that he who looks into the hearts of men, and knows the future no less than what lies before our eyes, will be deceived. Moreover, this goodness of his gives great comfort, in that he did not despise the man who was still weak and wavering, but deigned to adopt him into the flock of his own. For what he did here is seen also in his other disciples, whose faults and weaknesses he bore with wonderful gentleness, although they often deserved sharp rebuke. But lest anyone seek from this a defence of his own sloth, you will observe carefully that Christ so pardoned this man's weakness that he did not, by misplaced indulgence, excuse it; rather (as we have just said) he urges him to bid farewell to the affection which was drawing him back from his duty. Therefore it becomes us also to bear with our weak brethren, yet in such a way that we take care meanwhile to strengthen them and rouse them to perform their duty.

units.la: Sequitur tertius, quem ambidextrum dicere possumus, eò quòd simul & Christi discipulum agere & res priuatas siue terrenas curare vult. Ait enim: Sequar te Domine, sed permitte mihi prius, ut valedicam iis qui sunt domi meæ. Ea verò locutione vniuersam domus & rei domesticæ dispositionem intelligit, in primis verò id, ut cum bona suorum pace aut venia ipsum sequi possit. Ergo discipulum quidem se fore profitetur, sed interim ei tergum obuertit, non obscurè significans, quòd maiorem rei priuatæ quàm Christi rationem habeat. Eorum autem hic typus est, qui duobus dominis simul seruire volunt, & (quod prouerbio dicitur) vna fidelia duos parietes dealbare. Est magnus istorum numerus hodie. Huius enim ordinis sunt, qui ita Euangelio nomen dant, ut interim nolint à mundi amicitia excidere. Tales passim in Regum aulis reperiuntur, qui cum fidei Christianæ mysteria non ignorent, & hanc apud pios aperte fateantur, non prius tamen à suis principibus abire, & conditionem suam relinquere volunt, quàm id cum bona illorum gratia possit fieri. Grauius tamen peccant multi ex principibus, qui Euangelicæ doctrinæ tutores atq; ecclesiæ propugnatores haberi volunt, interim Verbi ministri dicendi leges præscribunt, & Euangelium ita prædicari posse existimant, ut apertis quoq; hostibus, imo Monachis atq; Episcopis probetur. Est horum turpis admodum error, quòd non cum suis modò (ut nostrer hic) verumetiam cum hostibus Christi & ijs qui nihil ad ipsos pertinent, transfigere volunt, ut per illos ipsis liceat Veritatis doctrinam sequi. Pertinent præterea ad hunc ordinem, qui dum se Christianos profitentur, simul sibiipsis & suis, quoad res huius seculi, prospicere cupiunt in omne euentum, ne quam rerum suarum iacturam faciant. Talis olim Iudas fuit, talis Ananias cum sua Sapphira, qui omnes hoc potissimum speccarunt, ut quoad res Christi salua essent, ipsi quoque sub eo commode agerent, illis autem cadentibus, nihil ipsis periculi esset subeundum. Et vtinam non plures istorum similes passim inter eos inuenirentur, qui primi in ecclesijs censeri cupiunt. Horum certè artibus debemus, quòd Christi regnum minus surgit, & plerique tunc languent atque frigent, quando in primis debebant feruere. Debent his adnumerari, qui ea conditione Christum admittunt, ut simul etiam Baccho & Veneri locus sit, id est, ut voluptatibus & libidini indulgeant, & per omne genus scelerum volutentur. Et hi quidem omnes, cùm & boni omnibus molesti sint, infirmis autem scandala ponant nocentissima, tamen optimi & sapientissimi mortalium esse putantur, & digni quos omnes in pretio habeant.
units.tr: Next comes the third man, whom we may call ambidextrous, because he wishes at once to act as a disciple of Christ and to attend to his private or earthly affairs. For he says: "I will follow you, Lord, but first allow me to bid farewell to those who are at my house." By this phrase he means the whole arrangement of his household and domestic affairs, and above all that he may be able to follow Christ with the goodwill or permission of his own people. He therefore professes that he will be a disciple, yet meanwhile he turns his back on Christ, not obscurely indicating that he has greater regard for his private affairs than for Christ. The type of such people is one who wants to serve two masters at once, and (as the proverb says) to whitewash two walls with one bucket. Today the number of such people is great. For they belong to this class who give their names to the Gospel in such a way that they meanwhile do not wish to fall from the friendship of the world. Such men are found everywhere in royal courts; although they are not ignorant of the mysteries of the Christian faith, and openly profess it before the godly, yet they do not wish to leave their princes and abandon their position until this can be done with their princes' goodwill. More grievously, however, many princes sin, who wish to be regarded as guardians of the evangelical doctrine and defenders of the Church, yet meanwhile prescribe laws for the ministers of the Word, and think the Gospel may be preached in such a way that it is approved even by open enemies, indeed by monks and bishops. This is a most shameful error of theirs: they wish to come to terms not only with their own people (as our men do here), but also with the enemies of Christ and with those who have nothing to do with them, so that through them it may be permitted to them to follow the doctrine of truth. Moreover, belonging to this class are those who, while they profess to be Christians, at the same time wish to provide for themselves and their own, as far as worldly affairs go, against every outcome, lest they suffer any loss of their possessions. Such was Judas of old, and such Ananias with his Sapphira; all of these aimed chiefly at this, that so long as the cause of Christ was safe, they themselves might also act comfortably under its shelter, but if it fell, no danger would have to be faced by them. Would that there were not more like these found everywhere among those who desire to be counted first in the Churches. Certainly we owe it to their devices that the kingdom of Christ rises less, and that many are then lukewarm and cold, when they ought above all to be burning with zeal. To these must be added those who admit Christ on the condition that there may also be room for Bacchus and Venus at the same time, that is, who indulge in pleasures and lust, and wallow in every kind of wickedness. And all these, although they are a trouble to all good men and set most harmful stumbling-blocks before the weak, are nevertheless thought to be the best and wisest of mortals, and worthy to be held in high esteem by all.

units.la: Sed Christum Iesum de his omnibus pronuntiantem audiamus: Nemo qui manu sua admota aratro, respexerit ad ea quæ retro sunt, appositus est ad regnum Dei. Quibus verbis aperte docet, ludeos reijcit, sed ut fistum & eius similes nequaquam pro discipulis & regni sui consortibus agnoscere posse. Nam hic quoq; ad animum potius quàm ad verba loquentis respicit. Scimus enim rei domesticæ curam & quæ familiaribus nostris debentur officia, nusquam à Deo prohiberi, sed potius præcipi: & Paulus Ethnicis ac infidelibus deteriores esse ait eos, qui suis non, ut decet prospiciunt. At hîc fide in primis opus est, ut in Dei prouidentiam intenti, nos nimia solicitudine & immodicis curis non patiamur abripi, neq; propter rem domesticam cunctatores aut negligentes simus in ijs, quæ peculiari mandato nobis Deus iniunxit. Animum ergo Christus liberum & fortem atque constantem requivit, qui procul relictis huius seculi curis in via semel capta pergat, & in finem vsque perseveret. Vtitur autem simili ex re rustica desumpto, vt hoc non temere requiri intelligamus. Vt enim iulcos rectos ducere non potest, qui manu quidem stilum tenet, oculos autem ad ea convertit, quae a tergo sunt: ita impossibile est, vt in regno Dei aliquos progressus feliciter faciant, quotquot huius seculi curus impliciti mundum & huius studia respiciunt, quae iam dudum a tergo reliquisse debebant. Vt enim nulla inter Christum & Belialem conuentio est, ita neque inter mundum & Christum: eo quòd ille quidem totus in malo iacet, & terrenis occupatur, hic autem nos ad caelestia & aeterna vocat. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur passim sunt obuia. Huc enim Lothi vxor pertinet, quae etsi ex Sodomis egressa esset, paulò postea tamen in statuam salis mutata est, cum ad ea respiceret, quae iam reliquerat. Israelitis quoque non profuit, quòd ex Aegypto eos Moses eduxerat: quia enim ad ollas carnium & ceptas atque alia, quae illic habuerant, animum adiecerunt, omnes in deserto horrendis exemplis prostrati & extincti sunt. Adde his Demam, quem Paulus hoc nomine taxat, quòd relictis Christi caeltris praesens hoc seculum amplexus sit. Debent hus omnibus opponi Patriarchae, qui per omne genus laborum atque periculorum vocantem Deum constanter secuti sunt, Apostoli item, qui relictis omnibus cum Christo inter grauissimas tentationes perseuerauerunt. Paulus certè cùm inter Iudaeos genere, eruditione & authoritate praestaret, omnia quae in mundo eximia habentur, pro stercoribus & rebus noxiis habuit, vt Christum lucrifacere posset: ita vero coronam iustitiae obtinuit, quam omnibus parauit Deus, qui Filij sui aduentum diligunt, & eius spe confirmati in fide vera perseuerant. Singuli ergo sibi ipsis applicent, quae de tribus istis hucusque dicta sunt, & primò quidem ad omnia incommoda atque aduersa se praeparent: deinde vero homini bus coniunctissimus simul atque omnibus huius seculi curis longum valere renuntient, vt Christi Iesu discipuli sint, in quo vno vita & salus inuenitur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ Jesus pronounce on all of these: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." In these words he plainly teaches that he rejects the Jews, but that Fistus and men like him can by no means be acknowledged as disciples or fellow heirs of his kingdom. Here too he looks to the mind of the one speaking rather than to his words. For we know that care for household affairs and the duties owed to our family are nowhere forbidden by God but rather commanded, and Paul says that those who do not provide for their own are worse than heathens and unbelievers. Yet here faith above all is needed, so that, intent on God's providence, we do not allow ourselves to be swept away by excessive anxiety and immoderate cares, nor be hesitant or negligent, on account of domestic affairs, in those things which God has laid upon us by a special command. Christ therefore requires a mind that is free, brave and steadfast, one that, having left far behind the cares of this age, presses on along the road once taken and perseveres to the end. He uses a comparison taken from rural life, so that we understand this is not demanded without reason. For just as one who holds the stylus in his hand but turns his eyes to what lies behind cannot draw straight furrows, so it is impossible that those who, entangled in the cares of this world, look back at the world and its pursuits, which they ought long since to have left behind, should make any successful progress in the kingdom of God. For just as there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, so there is none between the world and Christ, inasmuch as the one lies wholly in evil and is occupied with earthly things, while the other calls us to heavenly and eternal things. Examples to prove this are everywhere at hand. To this belongs Lot's wife, who, although she had come out of Sodom, was soon turned into a pillar of salt, because she looked back at what she had already left. It did not profit the Israelites either that Moses had led them out of Egypt, for since they turned their minds to the pots of meat and the onions and the other things they had had there, they were all struck down and destroyed in the desert by dreadful examples. Add to these Demas, whom Paul reproaches on this account, that, having abandoned Christ's camp, he embraced the present age. Over against all these must be set the patriarchs, who constantly followed God calling them through every kind of labour and danger, and likewise the apostles, who, having left everything, persevered with Christ amid the most grievous temptations. Paul certainly, although he excelled among the Jews in birth, learning and authority, counted all the things that are esteemed eminent in the world as dung and harmful things, so that he might gain Christ; and so he obtained the crown of righteousness, which God has prepared for all who love the coming of his Son and, strengthened by that hope, persevere in the true faith. Let each one therefore apply to himself what has been said so far about these three things: first, let him prepare himself for all inconveniences and adversities; then, let him renounce even those most closely joined to him by humanity, and at the same time bid a long farewell to all the cares of this age, so that he may be a disciple of Christ Jesus, in whom alone life and salvation are found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XCVI.

units.la: POsthaec designauit Dominus etiam alios septuaginta, misitque eos binos ante faciem suam in omnem vrbem & locum, quò futurum erat vt ipse veniret. Dicebat ergo eis: Messis quidem multa, sed operarij pauci. Rogate ergo Dominum messis, vt extrudat operarios in messem suam.
units.tr: After these things the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. So he said to them: The harvest is indeed great, but the labourers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send out labourers into his harvest.

units.la: VEMADMODVM Dei Filius, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, nostrae redemptionis & salutis causa in mundum venit & homo factus est: Ita actiones suas omnes sic instituit, vt se salutis nostrae studiosissimum esse, nouis subinde indiciis ostenderet. Vidimus hoc bucusque in eius doctrina & miraculis, maxime tamen id elucet in vltima eius profectione Hierosolymam, quam Lucas proximo Capite describere coepit. Primò enim cùm tempus mortis instare sciret, sponte ad eam accingitur, & quidem obstirmata facie, vt omnes affectus diuer sum suadentes excluserit. Deinde Samaritanos, qui inhospitalitate & ingratitudine in ipsum turpissimè peccarant, non modò non perdit, verumetiam discipulos vindictae studio flagrantes graviter reprehendit. Tertiò tribus exemplis docet, vt eos affectos esse oporteat, qui germani eius discipuli esse, & in ipso seruari cupiunt. Exigitur ab his, ne sua quaerant, sed quae Christi sunt: vt item seipsos & omnia sua abnegent, & postquam illi nomen dederunt, constanter cum eo in finem vsque perseuerent. Pertinet eodem prima huius Capitis pars, qua narratur, vt sui cognitione & appropinquantem humani generis redemptionem per plures diuulgari, & ad hanc excipiendam omnes praparare curauerit. In praesenti autem describit Lucas, quàm multos ad hoc designarit, & quò illos miserit. Deinde instituti sui causam Christus ipse exponit, simulque monet, quid fieri debeat, si ea fit conditio rerum, quae illo tempore inter Iudaeos fuit.
units.tr: Just as the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, came into the world and was made man for the sake of our redemption and salvation, so he arranged all his actions in such a way that he showed himself, by fresh signs from time to time, to be most zealous for our salvation. We have seen this so far in his teaching and miracles, but it shines most clearly in his last journey to Jerusalem, which Luke began to describe in the next chapter. For first, when he knew that the time of his death was at hand, he set out for it of his own accord, and indeed with a set face, so that he shut out every feeling that urged the opposite. Then, the Samaritans, who had sinned most shamefully against him by their inhospitality and ingratitude, he not only did not destroy, but he sharply rebuked his disciples, who were burning with a desire for vengeance. Third, he teaches by three examples how those ought to be disposed who wish to be his true disciples and to be kept in him. It is required of them that they seek not their own things but the things of Christ; likewise that they deny themselves and all that is theirs, and, once they have given their name to him, that they persevere constantly with him to the end. To the same purpose belongs the first part of this chapter, in which it is related that he took care that his own person and the redemption of the human race now drawing near should be made known to many, and that all should be prepared to receive it. In the present passage, however, Luke describes how many he appointed for this purpose and where he sent them. Then Christ himself explains the reason for his plan, and at the same time warns what ought to be done if the state of affairs is such as it was among the Jews at that time.

units.la: Primum hūc verbis narratur: Posthæc designauit Dominus etiam alios septuaginta, misitque eos binos ante faciem suam in omnem vrbem & locum, quò futurum erat vt ipse veniret. Nuper qui dem, cum adhuc in Galilæa ageret, duodecim discipulos, qui Apostoli dicuntur, solos eadem de causa emisit, quod bi in regione angustiori & in populo tractabiliori sufficere poterant. Nunc vero quando Iudææ appropinquat, quæ latius patebat, & in qua Sacerdotes cum Scribis & Senioribus in iis quæ ad religionem spectant, dominabantur, summa autem rerum potestas penes homines prophanos, Romanos nimirum præsides erat, populus vero à Sacerdotum & Seniorum fauore pendens, à Christo & eius doctrina magis abhorrebat, plures præmittit sui aduentus & appropinquantis regni Dei praecones. Et quod in duodecim Apostolis factū fuisse Marcus annotauit, vt bini mitterentur, id in præsenti quoque obseruatur. Solet enim Deus nostræ infirmitatis rationem habere, & ijs laborum atq; periculorum socios adiungere, quos rebus arduis & periculosis destinat. Quod si id non initio statim facit, saltem iam opus iniunctum aggressos non negligit, quin sibi unde minime sperabant, auxilium & opem afferri videant. Exempla huius rei alibi adduximus, quæ modò repetere nō est opus. Debet autem hæc Dei fides & bonitas nos excitare, ne quod ille nobis iniungit detrectemus. Habet enim ille in manu sua omnium corda, vt vel amicos & socios excitare possit quoscunq; voluerit, vel hostium animos continere, ne quod volunt & possunt faciant.
units.tr: The first point is related in these words: After these things the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. Recently, indeed, while he was still active in Galilee, he had sent out the twelve disciples, who are called Apostles, alone and for the same reason, because two by two they could suffice in a narrower region and among a more tractable people. But now, as he approaches Judea, which extended more widely, and in which the priests, together with the scribes and elders, held sway in matters that pertain to religion, while the highest power of affairs rested with profane men, namely the Roman governors, and the people, depending on the favour of the priests and elders, shrank all the more from Christ and his teaching, he sends ahead more heralds of his coming and of the approaching kingdom of God. And what Mark noted was done with the twelve Apostles, that they should be sent two by two, is observed in the present case as well. For God is accustomed to take account of our weakness, and to join as companions in labours and dangers those whom he destines for difficult and perilous tasks. And if he does not do this at the very beginning, at least he does not neglect those who have already undertaken the assigned work, so that they see help and aid brought to them from where they least expected. We have already given examples of this elsewhere, and there is no need to repeat them now. But this faithfulness and goodness of God ought to stir us up, so that we do not shrink from what he enjoins upon us. For he holds the hearts of all in his hand, so that he can either rouse up friends and companions whomever he wishes, or restrain the minds of enemies, so that they do not do what they wish and are able to do.

units.la: Quod si quæras, cur septuaginta numero præmittere voluerit, cum vel plures vel pauciores mittere posset? In promptu causa est. Scimus enim omnia, quæ in novo Testamento gesta sunt, ijs respondere debuisse: quæ veteribus (vt Paulus ait) in figura acciderunt. Fuerunt autem in veteri populo duodecim Patriarchæ, ex quibus tribus duodecim propagatæ sunt, & quos tota gens suos progenitores agnouit. Horum igitur loco Christus duodecim Apostolos esse voluit, quos populi Christiani Patriarchas iure dicere possumus, quando per hos Iudæi simul & Gentes eximmortalis æternæque verbi semine in filios Dei regenerati sunt. Vnde Paulus Corinthijs dicebat: Etsi decem millia pædagogorum habueritis in Christo, non tamen multos patres: In Christo enim Iesu per Euangelium ego vos genui. Et ad Galathas idem scribit: Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, vsquequò formetur Christus in vobis. Quoad vero septuaginta hoscè discipulos, eum numerum obseruare voluit Dominus, qui propter multas causas populo Israelitico in summa authoritate & quadam ratione sacer erat. Nam cum septuaginta animabus in Ægyptum Iacobus descenderat, quibus ita benedixit illic Deus, vt propter infinitam multitudinem, quæ ex illo prognata fuit, filij Israel toti Ægypto formidabiles fierent. Deinde cum in deserto Moses de onere tanti populi regendi quæreretur, iussit Dominus, vt ex præfectis tribuum & familiarum viros septuaginta segregaret, inter quos Spiritus dona non sine miraculo distribuit, & eos Mosi adiunxit, vt eum in onere hoc ferendo adiuuarent. Vnde factum videtur, quod populo ex Babylone reuerso, rursus septuaginta duo Senitores constituti sunt, qui vulgò (vt in numeris eiusmodi fieri solet) Septuaginta Seniores συνέδριον & vel corrupto vocabulo Sanhedrim dicebantur, eò quod su premum totius populi Senatum referrent. Hos quia plerique ex Davidis posteritate defiendebant Herodes, vt regnum suum stabiliret, simul omnes interfici, & Senatum illum abolere curauit. Fuit hoc euidens argumentum, ex quo populi totius dissipatio colligi poterat, cum & regnum penes alienigenam esset, & iam sublatus esset Senatus ille, qui solus veteris aut pristinæ dignitatis speciem aliquam præ se ferebat. Opportunè igitur nunc Septuaginta hos sui aduentus praecones per Iudæam Christus emittit, vt vel ipso numero admoneantur, adesse præforibus nouam populi instaurationem, noui nimirum illius populi Dei, sine Ecclesia, quæ inter Iudæos quidem primum nasci & colligi, inde vero per totum orbem terrarum maximum incrementum diffundi & propagari debeat. Hæc eò diligentius recitamus, vt constet in toto Iesu Christi negotio nihil fortuitum fuisse sed plena mysteriorum esse omnia, & proinde in eorum consideratione non obiter aut ofcitanter nobis esse versandum. Qui vero septuaginta isti fuerint, Euangelistæ nusquam docent, & non tutū est ea curiosius inquirere, quæ in scripturis non traduntur. Haud dubiè ex Christi comitatu fuerunt, quem in vltima hac professione numerosissimum ex vtroque sexu habuit, & si quis locus est conuenturus, ad centum illos & viginti pertinent, qui (vt in Actis Lucas scribit) simul congregati fuere cum Matthias in Iudæ proditoris locum surrogaretur: & credibile est, illos postea quoque in prouebendo regno Christi bonam atque fidelem operam nauauisse. Nomina autem eorum Spiritus san-ctus suppressa voluit, vt discamus regnum Dei non ab hominum splendore siue authoritate pende-re, sed illorum quoque opera Deum vti interdum, qui inter homines ne nomen quidem habent. Vide 1.Corinth.1.
units.tr: But if you ask why he wished to send ahead seventy, when he could have sent either more or fewer, the reason is at hand. For we know that all things done in the New Testament ought to correspond to those things which, as Paul says, happened to the people of old in a figure. Now in the old people there were twelve patriarchs, from whom twelve tribes were propagated, and whom the whole nation acknowledged as its forefathers. Therefore, in their place Christ willed to have twelve Apostles, whom we may rightly call the patriarchs of the Christian people, since through them both Jews and Gentiles were born again as sons of God by the immortal and eternal seed of the Word. Hence Paul said to the Corinthians: Although you may have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel. And he writes to the Galatians: My little children, whom I am again in travail with until Christ is formed in you. As for these seventy disciples, the Lord wished to observe that number which, for many reasons, was in the highest authority and in a certain way sacred to the Israelite people. For when Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls, God so blessed them there that, through the infinite multitude that was descended from him, the sons of Israel became formidable to all Egypt. Then, when in the wilderness Moses complained about the burden of ruling so great a people, the Lord ordered him to set apart from the leaders of the tribes and families seventy men, among whom he distributed the gifts of the Spirit, not without a miracle, and joined them to Moses, so that they might help him in bearing this burden. Hence it seems to have come about that, when the people returned from Babylon, again seventy-two elders were appointed, who were commonly called (as usually happens with numbers of this kind) the Seventy Elders, the Sanhedrin [συνέδριον], or by the corrupted word Sanhedrim, because they represented the supreme senate of the whole people. Because most of them were defending the posterity of David, Herod, in order to establish his kingdom, had them all killed at once and took care to abolish that senate. This was a clear sign from which the dispersion of the whole people could be inferred, since both the kingdom was in the hands of a foreigner and that senate, which alone still bore some appearance of the old and former dignity, had already been removed. Therefore, it was fitting that Christ now send these seventy heralds of his coming through Judea, so that by their very number they might be reminded that a new restoration of the people was at the door, namely of that new people of God, without distinction of the Church, which was to be first born and gathered among the Jews, and then spread and propagated with the greatest increase throughout the whole world. We recount these things so carefully so that it may be clear that in the whole business of Jesus Christ nothing was accidental, but that everything is full of mysteries, and therefore that we ought not to dwell on their consideration carelessly or half-heartedly. Who these seventy were, the Evangelists nowhere teach, and it is not safe to inquire too curiously into things that are not handed down in the Scriptures. Doubtless they were from the company of Christ, which in this last appearance he had in very great numbers of both sexes; and if any number is to be aimed at, they belong to that hundred and twenty who (as Luke writes in Acts) were gathered together when Matthias was chosen to take the place of Judas the traitor. And it is credible that they afterwards also laboured well and faithfully in advancing the kingdom of Christ. The Holy Spirit, however, chose to suppress their names, so that we may learn that the kingdom of God does not depend on the splendour or authority of men, but that God sometimes uses the labours of those too who among men have not even a name. See 1 Corinthians 1.

units.la: Admonemur autem Christi exemplo, Ecclesiarum ministros non ad certum numerum astrin-gi, sed pro locorum & temporum atq; negotiorum ratione plures siue pauciores ordinari debere. Olim sane sub Mose Leuitarum circiter viginti duo millia censebantur, qui postea cum Israelitæ terram promissam occupauissent, per omnes tribus distributi sunt, prout vrbium & cuiusque tribus condicio postulabat. Posterū temporibus, cum illi officio minus fungerentur, extraordinarie vocati sunt Prophetæ, qui populum ex Dei verbo erudirent. Christus vero qui supra duodecim modo discipulos emisit, hic septuaginta illi muneri destinat, cum rem ipsam hoc exigere videret. Et Titum ab Apostolo in Creta relictum fuisse scimus, vt oppidatim presbyteros seu Ecclesiæ ministros constitue-ret: non exprimitur autem numerus certus, quam multi nimirum in singulis oppidis constituì debe-ant: sed quia id à Paulo non potuerat definiri, illud omne Titi iudicio relinquit, vt pro locorum & hominum ratione agat. Sunt hæc propter eos obseruanda, qui cum verbum Dei fastidiant, quàm paucissimos huius præconespe esse vellent, et proinde sufficere putant, si singulis parochijs (vt dicunt) & vrbibus vnus aliquis præficiatur, qui verbum prædicet, & Sacramenta distribuat, neq; aliquam multitudinis rationem habent, quæ sæpe tanta est, vt vix decem vni vrbi sufficiant, vel etiam plu-res, maximè si pestis aut alij morbi grassentur. Sed faciunt isti homines perinde, ac si quis pastorem qui centum oues pascit, multis etiam millibus pascendis sufficere clamet. Vt vero hic dum lumpti-bus parcit, gregem totum lupis obijcit: ita isti dum ministrorum numerum minuunt, Ecclesijs fere dissipationis authores sunt, quæ non sine animarum periculo experiuntur; quando minimè opus e-rat, quid sit fidus pastoribus destitui. Sed plura de hoc postea.
units.tr: We are admonished by Christ's example that the ministers of the Churches ought not to be bound to a fixed number, but that, according to the circumstances of places, times and business, more or fewer should be ordained. Indeed, under Moses the Levites were counted at about twenty-two thousand, who afterwards, when the Israelites had occupied the promised land, were distributed among all the tribes, as the condition of the cities and of each tribe demanded. In later times, when those men performed their office less well, prophets were called out of the ordinary course, to instruct the people from the Word of God. Christ, however, who sent out only twelve disciples above, here designates seventy for that task, since he saw that the matter itself required it. We know also that Titus was left by the Apostle in Crete, so that he might appoint elders or ministers of the Church in every town. Yet no definite number is expressed, how many ought to be appointed in each town; but since Paul could not define this, he leaves the whole matter to Titus' judgement, so that he may act according to the circumstances of places and people. These things must be observed on account of those who, when they despise the Word of God, wish that as few as possible of its heralds be present, and therefore think it enough if, in each parish (as they say) and city, one man is set over it, who preaches the Word and distributes the sacraments, and take no account of the size of the congregation, which is often so great that scarcely ten can suffice for one city, or even more, especially if plague or other diseases are raging. But these men act just as if someone, who feeds a hundred sheep, should cry out that he is enough to feed many thousands. Indeed, just as he who spares expense throws the whole flock to the wolves, so these men, while they diminish the number of ministers, are for the most part the authors of the dissipation of the Churches, which experience this to the peril of souls, when it is least of all needful, what it is to be left destitute of faithful shepherds. But more on this later.

units.la: Nunc præterea obseruabimus, quò nam septuaginta iflos Christus miserit? In omnem locum & vrbem (inquit Lucas) quò futurum erat vt ipse veniret. Fuerunt ergo præcursores, qualis Ioan-nes Baptista fuit, qui homines de eius aduentu admonere, & omnium animos ad ipsum digne excipien-dum excitare debuerunt. Quo loco primum admonemur, quam procul ab impostorum & seductorum ingenio siue moribus Christus abfuerit. Solent illi clam & noctu plerunque, noctuarum & vesperti-onum instar, in vrbes ingredi, & (vt Paulus de illis scribit) in familias obrepere, vt mulierculas & homines rudes rerum, imperitos capiant, & per hos ceu cuniculos quosdam sibi ad plures alios aditum parent. Quod hodie Anabaptistas nō minori aflutia quam impudentia facere videmus. At Christus non ipse modo aperte agit, verumetiam præcursores præmittit, qui ipsum venire nuntient. Est enim lux ipsa, quæ latere non potest: alteri vero illi dum lucem fugiunt, se tenebriones vel nebu-lones, & opera ipsorum praua esse testantur. Nec enim vnquam fallet illud Christi: Omnis qui per-uerse agit, odit lucem, nec venit ad lucem, ne arguantur opera eius. Qui autem syncere agit, venit ad lucem, vt manifesta fiant facta ipsius, quod secundum Deum sint facta. Vide Ioan.3.
units.tr: Next we should observe where Christ sent these seventy. "Into every place and city," says Luke, "where he himself was about to come." So there were forerunners, as John the Baptist was, whose task was to warn people of his coming and to stir every mind to receive him worthily. Here we are first reminded how far Christ was from the character and manners of impostors and seducers. Such men usually creep into cities secretly and by night, like owls and bats, and (as Paul writes of them) slip into households, so that they may capture silly women and ignorant, inexperienced men, and through these, as through certain burrows, make their way to many others. We see the Anabaptists doing this today with no less cunning than impudence. But Christ not only acts openly himself; he also sends forerunners ahead to announce that he is coming. For he is light itself, which cannot be hidden, whereas those others, by shunning the light, show that they are shady rogues and scoundrels and that their works are wicked. Nor will that saying of Christ ever fail: "Everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds be exposed. But whoever acts sincerely comes to the light, so that his deeds may be made manifest, because they are done according to God." See John 3.

units.la: Porro præcipuum huius loci caput est, quòd Christus vt prius Ioannē, ita nunc iflos præcursores habet, qui populū ipsi præparet, nec enim prodest ille, nisi digne à nobis excipiatur. Docet hoc omnes parabolæ quibus seipsum in Euangelio depingit. Dicit se panē vitæ esse: at quæ panis vilitas, si in mensa solū propositus sit, non aut edatur, vt per digestionē in alimentū transeat? Dicitur item fons aquæ viuentis: sed nunquam nobis sitim aqua restinguet, nisi eam bibamus. Similiter lucē mundi se ef-se ait: quid vero lux proderit, nisi visus ergana sint integra, quæ illa apprehendat? Medicū quoq; se esse profitetur: sed quomodo eos curabit medicus, qui ipsum admittere & eius consilio vti nolunt? Ea-dem est pastoris ratio, quem se esse testatur: nec enim huius cura alijs prodest quam ouibus quæ voce eius audiunt atq; sequuntur. Ostiū quoq; dicitur: sed quid tibi ostiū profuerit, si per illud in domū no-lis ingredi? Vides igitur neminē in Christo seruari, nisi qui ipsum vere cognitū toto animo amplexus fuerit. Ideo in precatione illa ardentissima dicebat: Hæc est vita æterna Pater, vt cognoscat te so-lum verū Deū, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Parit enim cognitio illa fidem viuam & veram, vel potius ipsissima fides est, quæ ita Christū apprehendit vt nos in illo simus, ipse vero in nobis agat: nosq; suipsius & bonorum suorum omnium participes reddat. At quemadmodum stomachus, quem mali
units.tr: Moreover, the chief point of this passage is that Christ, as he had John before, so now has these forerunners, who prepare the people for him; for he profits nothing unless he is worthily received by us. All the parables by which he depicts himself in the Gospel teach this. He says he is the bread of life, but what use is bread if it is only set on the table and not eaten, so that by digestion it passes into nourishment? He is likewise called the fountain of living water, but water will never quench our thirst unless we drink it. Similarly, he says he is the light of the world, but what good will light do unless the eyes are sound enough to take hold of it? He also professes to be a physician, but how will the physician cure those who refuse to admit him and to follow his advice? The same is true of the shepherd, whom he declares himself to be, for his care profits none but the sheep that hear his voice and follow it. He is also called the door, but what will the door profit you if you are unwilling to enter the house through it? You see, then, that no one is saved in Christ unless he has truly known him and embraced him with his whole soul. Therefore in that most fervent prayer he said: "This is eternal life, Father, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." For that knowledge brings forth a living and true faith, or rather is itself that very faith, which so apprehends Christ that we are in him and he works in us, and makes us partakers of himself and of all his goods. But just as a stomach filled with bad and harmful humours rejects even the most pleasant and wholesome food,

units.la: Ioan.17. mali & noxij humores repleuerunt, cibum quantumuis suauem & salutarē respuit, & proinde purgatione & confortatione opus habet: ita cum nos natura corrupti simus, & mente partim praui cupiditatibus, partim falsis de religione & summo hominis bono opinionibus praeoccupata habeamus, Christum, panē illum vitæ & fontem aquæ viuentis non admittimus, neq; lucem illam æternam lippientes nostri intellectus oculi ferre possunt, & quod malorū summum est, medicū fugimus, pastore de stamur, & sponte relicto ostio regni Dei ambages & auia quærimus. Itaq; multa & diligenti praparatione nobis hic quoq; opus est, quā Deus per verbi prædicationē adhibet. Per hoc enim innatam naturæ vitiositatem arguit, & quæ ex hac emanant peccata accusat. Quæ causa est, vt nobisipsis displicere, iustitiam esurire & sitire, lucem veritatis toto animo desiderare, pastorem ipsi quærere, & ad vitæ æternæ viā siue oftiū anhelare incipiamus. Ideo ministri Dei pasim à pœnitentia prædicant initiū faciunt, quæ sine fiducia diuinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ esse non potest, & proinde hominem excitat, vt à peccatis & infelici Satanæ seruitio ad Deum conuerti & cum illo reconciliari cupiat. Ibi vero sese Christus offert, quem ille inter se & homines mediatorem constituit. Et hæc illa præpa ratio est, de qua olim Isaias & Malachias vaticinati sunt, & cuius primus in nouo Testamento minister fuit Ioannes Baptista: à cuius deniq; doctrina Christus exorsus tandem Apostolis commendauit, quando ait in suo nomine & pœnitentia & remissione peccatorū prædicari oportere. Quamuis autem doctrinam istam Septuaginta illi plenā & exactā tradere non potuerint, fuit tamen hoc non leue incitamentum ad permouendos hominum animos, vt de salute sua diligentius cogitare in ciperent, quando tot homines per regionem & oppida discurrere, omnes eandē doctrinā tradere, & rerum omnium mutationem, ipsius nimirū Dei regnū, annuntiare audiebant. Nam plus quam stupidus, imò ferreus fuerit oportet, cui non pristinæ vitæ miserabilis conditio in mentem venerit, vt simul cogitaret, quomodo ad excipiendum regnum Dei sese deberet præparare. Arguuntur autem hic primum, qui per Euangelium, bona opera probiberi, & peccandi licentiam plantari clamant: deinde qui sub illius prætextu licenter nimis viuunt, & aduersarijs calumniandi occasionem præbent. Faciunt hi quidem magnam iniuriam Christo, qui in mundum venit, vt opera diaboli destruat, inter quæ peccato primus locus debetur. Alteri vero illi scandalorum, quorū authores sunt, graues pœnas dabunt, quando Christum dicentem audient: Non omnis qui dixerit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum meum, sed is, qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cælis est.
units.tr: Ioan.17. and so needs purging and strengthening, so, since we are by nature corrupted, and our minds are partly depraved by lusts and partly preoccupied with false opinions about religion and man's highest good, we do not admit Christ, that bread of life and fountain of living water. Nor can the bleary eyes of our understanding bear that eternal light. And, what is the greatest evil, we flee the physician, we stray from the shepherd, and having willingly left the door of God's kingdom, we seek winding and trackless paths. Therefore we need here also a great and diligent preparation, which God applies through the preaching of the Word. For through this he exposes our innate corruption of nature and accuses the sins that flow from it. This is why we begin to be displeased with ourselves, to hunger and thirst after righteousness, to desire the light of truth with our whole soul, to seek the shepherd, and to long for the way of eternal life or the door. Therefore God's ministers everywhere begin by preaching repentance, which cannot exist without trust in divine grace and mercy, and so stirs a person to desire to turn from sins and from the wretched servitude of Satan to God and be reconciled with him. There Christ offers himself, whom God has appointed mediator between himself and men. This is the preparation of which Isaiah and Malachi prophesied long ago, and whose first minister in the New Testament was John the Baptist. From his teaching Christ at last began, and he commended it to the apostles when he said that repentance and remission of sins must be preached in his name. Although the Seventy could not deliver that doctrine in full and exact form, it was nonetheless no small stimulus to move people's minds, so that they began to think more carefully about their salvation, when they heard so many men running through the region and the towns, all delivering the same doctrine and announcing a change of all things, namely the kingdom of God itself. For a man must be more than stupid, indeed made of iron, if the wretched condition of his former life never came to mind, so that he might consider how he ought to prepare himself to receive the kingdom of God. Here, however, are first rebuked those who cry that good works are forbidden by the Gospel and that a license to sin is planted by it; then those who, under that pretext, live too licentiously and give the adversaries occasion to slander. Indeed, those men do great injury to Christ, who came into the world to destroy the works of the devil, among which sin holds the first place. But those others, the authors of scandals, will pay heavy penalties, when they hear Christ saying: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of my Father, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven."

units.la: Porro sui instituti causam Christus discipulis exponit, ne se temere mitti suspicentur: Messis quidem (inquit) multa, sed operarij pauci. Apud Matthæum eadem habetur sententia, sed alia occasione tam illic profert. Cum enim populum vidisset, qui doctrina & consolatione destitutus, ad hæc misere distractus & dispersus erat instar ouium, quæ pastorem nullum habent, ex animo eorum miserttus, eadem verba quæ hic habentur, pronuntiauit. In præsenti vero & si idem affectus erga populum in illo haud dubie nondum deferbuisset, tamen potius Septuaginta illos discipulos respicit, quos certa spe erigere iniq, commisso ipsis munere confirmare vult, ne se frustra laboraturos aut periclitaturos esse arbitrentur in tanta populi cæcitate, & antistitum eius contumacia. Sensus enim est: Ne formidetis hunc laborem subire, qui fructu suo minime carebit. Et si enim indomita sit sacerdotum & scribarum audacia, & plerique in populo quoque hactenus nullis neque admonitionibus neque miraculis flecti potuerint, vt mihi obedirent: non tamen eadem omnium mens est atq; sententia. Est enim multa messis, id est, plurimi sunt veritatis cupidi, & multi regnum Dei summo animi desiderio expectant. Qui quod hactenus mihi non accesserint, non alia causa est, quam operariorum inopia, qui Dei negotium fideliter egerint. Vos igitur alacri animo opus hoc aggredimini, admonete verbi diuini falcem, ostendite optatam salutem præ foribus adesse, & appropinquare iam regnum illud Dei, quod tam diu anxij & soliciti expectarunt. Hæc si annuntiaueritis, non deerit successus, & passim inuenietis, qui vos vt par est excipient, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ explains to the disciples the reason for his instruction, lest they suppose they are being sent out rashly: "The harvest indeed is great," he says, "but the labourers are few." In Matthew the same saying occurs, but on another occasion and in a different form. For when he had seen the people, who lacked teaching and comfort and were harassed and scattered like sheep without a shepherd, he was moved with pity for them and spoke the words that are found here. Here, however, although his compassion for the people had certainly not yet cooled, he looks rather to the Seventy disciples, whom he wishes to raise with a sure hope and to strengthen with the office entrusted to them, so that they do not think they will labour in vain or be in danger amid such blindness of the people and the obstinacy of their leaders. The sense is: "Do not be afraid to undertake this labour, which will by no means be without fruit. For although the scribes and priests are unbridled in their audacity, and most of the people hitherto could be moved neither by admonitions nor by miracles to obey me, yet the mind and opinion of all is not the same. The harvest is great, that is, there are very many who desire the truth, and many who await the kingdom of God with the highest longing of mind. That they have not yet come to me is due to no other cause than the scarcity of labourers who have faithfully carried out God's business. Therefore undertake this work with an eager spirit, proclaim the sickle of the divine word, show that the longed-for salvation is at hand, and that the kingdom of God, which anxious and troubled people have awaited for so long, is drawing near. If you announce these things, success will not be lacking, and everywhere you will find people who will receive you as is fitting, etc."

units.la: At miretur hic aliquis, qua ratione adductus Dominus operarios paucos esse dicat, qui populū sa lutis cupidum instituant & ad regnum Dei colligant. Atqui ingens erat Leuitarum numerus, quorum multa millia olim fuisse nuper diximus. Erant præterea infinitæ Synagogæ, in quibus Scribæ & Legisperiti docendi munus sibi vsurpabant. Erant ite superiorus ordinis Sacerdotes, qui se clauē scientia habere gloriabatur, & magna cū authoritate Moßis cathedra sibi vendicabat. Accedebat
units.tr: But someone may wonder by what reasoning the Lord says that the workers are few who could instruct a people eager for salvation and gather them into the kingdom of God. Yet the number of Levites was huge; we said recently that there were once many thousands of them. Besides, there were countless synagogues in which the scribes and lawyers claimed for themselves the office of teaching. There were also priests of the higher order, who boasted that they held the key of knowledge and with great authority claimed Moses' seat for themselves.

units.la: Isa. 49. Mal. 9.4. bis omnibus Pharisæi, penes quos tunc erat summa doctrinæ & sanctitatis exis-timatio. Quomodo igitur absq; pastoribus erat populus iste? aut quis in illa messe operarios paucos fuisse dixerit? Sed hic observandum est, Christum nō de infidis mercenarijs, aut ignauis doctoribus loqui, qui nominis & tituli splendore contenti de munere suo vix unquā cogitant: sed de fidis, laboriosis, & industrijs, qui bus Dei gloria & populi salus vere cordi est, quiq; totum in hoc sunt, vt populum in veritatis cognitione instituant, & ipsi adducant, in quo vno vita atq; salus habetur. Tales in Iudaico populo tunc temporis paucissimi, adeoq; nulli erant. Nam vt Euangelica historia docet, ad hypocrisim & osten-tationem omnia sua instituebant: Legis vero doctrinam iam pridem humanis traditionibus corru-perant, templum autem in emporium, & externum cultum omnem in quæstum priuatum commu-tarant. Seipsos ergo illi omnes pascebant, populus autem salutis incertus circa opiniones vanas vagabatur, cum nulla esset veri Messiæ cognitio, imò hac quoque à scribis & sacerdotibus putidi-simis figmentis obscuraretur. Atqui vtinam non idem in orbe Christiano iam olim accidisset, & hodie multis in locis non adhuc fieret. Quis enim nescit populum Christianum in mille sectas & fraternitates distractum, & disperso gregi, qui pastore destituitur, simillimum fuisse, & etiam hodie in nō nullis locis talem cerni? Atqui non desunt, qui pastorum nomine gloriantur. Est summus ille pastorum princeps, Romanus Pontifex, qui se Christi vicarium in terris esse, & de salutis necessitate esse clamat, vt omnis anima ipsi obtemperet. Habet ù adiunctum sibi augustissimū Cardinalium purpuratorum collegium, qui vt Ecclesiæ proceres & columna videri volunt: ita Senatum supremum orbis Christiani referunt. Et ex his plurimi in aulis regum agunt, vt passim rebus prospiciant. Ac cedunt hi Episcopi, quorum infinitus est numerus, & habent hi quoque suos vicarios, suffraganeos & Canonicos, plerunque generis nobilitate illustres, & annuis Ecclesiarum proventibus egregie ditatos. Habent præterea singulæ parochiæ suos parochos aut pastores, quibus ferè adiuncti sunt sui diaconi. Accedunt hu Sacellani, Ostiarij, Euangelistæ, Lectores, Exorcistæ, Acoluti, quorum tanta est multitudo, vt sæpe in vno templo celebriori quadraginta aut quinquaginta conspiciantur, qui omnes pro publica populi salute excubare videri volunt. His si addas Monachorum greges, fraterculorum examina, Lolhardos, moniales, Beguttas, Deum immortalem quot millia inuenies, quorum singulī se pro Ecclesia laborare gloriantur? Quis ergo sine pastoribus esse dixerit Christianum populum? Sed plerique ex eorum numero sunt, quos (vt Paulus prædixit) ij sibiipsis accersiuerunt, qui sānam veritatis doctrinam ferre non possunt, & ideo omisso verbo Dei circa traditiunculas inanes & ceremonias frigidissimas occupantur. Fit ergo vt plerique in populo quid credant, quidue de religione & toto salutis negotio sentiant incerti sint, sed fide quadam implicita contenti vanis somniis circunducantur. Est hæc miserrima populi conditio, qua nulla infelicior excogitari potest. Soletur tamen nos, quando ista videmus, quod Deus tales etiamsi sic tractari mereantur, non omnino negligit, & vt borum miseretur, ita grauiter ijs irascitur, qui infelicis vulgi simplicitate pro libidine ad quæstum abuti solent. Olim certè per Ezechielem de eiusmodi populi sui sorte graviter conquestum fuisse scimus, cum inquit: Errauit grex meus in omnibus montibus, & in omni colle exelso, & in omni superficie terrae dispersus est grex meus, nec est qui quærat aut requirat. Sed ibi dem horribiles pœnas falsis pastoribus minatur, & se oues suas quæsiturum pollicetur, ne cui porrò præda sint, & in Christo, quem populi dispersi misertum fuisse supra diximus, non inanis aut otiosus affectus fuit, sed non multò post infidos illos pastores per Romanorum arma cum templo & vrbe excidit, prius vero per Apostolos oues suas collegit, & (vt in Prophetis promiserat) reliquias exilo incendio seruauit, quæ ecclesia, quæ inde latissimè propagata fuit, initium dederunt. Vinit autem adhuc Christus, & procul dubio etiam hodie suos dispersos & asslictos videt, quos suo tempore expersonatorum pastorum manibus non sine magno ipsorum malo vindicabit, ne Sponsa suæ Ecclesiæ diutius illudant.
units.tr: Add to all these the Pharisees, in whose hands at that time lay the highest reputation for teaching and holiness. How then was this people without pastors? Or who would say there were few workers in that harvest? But here it must be observed that Christ is not speaking of unfaithful hirelings or lazy teachers, who, content with the splendour of name and title, hardly ever think about their office, but of faithful, laborious and diligent men, for whom the glory of God and the salvation of the people truly lie close to the heart, and who devote themselves wholly to instructing the people in knowledge of the truth and bringing them in, in which alone life and salvation are found. Such men were very few among the Jewish people at that time; indeed there were none. For, as the evangelical history teaches, they arranged everything for hypocrisy and display. They had long since corrupted the doctrine of the Law with human traditions, turned the temple into a marketplace, and changed all external worship into private gain. So they all fed themselves, while the people, uncertain of salvation, wandered about after empty opinions, since there was no true knowledge of the Messiah, and even this was obscured by the most foul fictions of scribes and priests. Would that the same had not long ago happened in the Christian world, and that it still did not happen today in many places! For who does not know that the Christian people has been torn into a thousand sects and factions, and that it has been very like a scattered flock lacking a shepherd, and that even today such a state is seen in some places? Yet there are not lacking those who glory in the name of pastors. There is that highest prince of pastors, the Roman Pontiff, who cries out that he is Christ's vicar on earth and that it is necessary for salvation that every soul obey him. He has attached to himself the most august college of purple-clad Cardinals, who wish to be seen as the nobles and pillars of the Church, and so they represent the supreme senate of the Christian world. Many of them live in royal courts, looking after affairs everywhere. Then come the bishops, who are countless, and they too have their vicars, suffragans and canons, often illustrious by noble birth and richly endowed with the annual revenues of the churches. Besides, each parish has its parish priests or pastors, to whom their deacons are almost always attached. Then come the chaplains, doorkeepers, evangelists, readers, exorcists and acolytes, whose number is so great that often forty or fifty can be seen in one busy church, all of whom want to appear to keep watch for the public salvation of the people. If to these you add the flocks of monks, the swarms of friars, Lollards, nuns and Beguines, immortal God, how many thousands will you find, each of whom boasts that he labours for the Church? Who then would say the Christian people is without pastors? But most of that number are those whom (as Paul foretold) they have gathered for themselves, who cannot bear the sound doctrine of truth, and so, neglecting the word of God, are occupied with empty little traditions and very cold ceremonies. Hence it comes about that most in the people are uncertain what they believe, or what they think about religion and the whole business of salvation, but, content with a certain implicit faith, are led about by empty dreams. This is the most wretched condition of the people, and none more unhappy can be imagined. Yet this consoles us when we see such things: God does not altogether neglect those who deserve to be treated thus, and as he pities them, so he is gravely angry with those who are wont to abuse the simplicity of the unhappy crowd for their own greed and gain.
