Indeed we know that long ago through Ezekiel he gravely complained of the fate of such a people of his, when he said: "My flock has wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill; my flock has been scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there is no one who seeks or searches for them." But there he threatens the false shepherds with dreadful punishments, and promises that he himself will seek his sheep, so that they will no longer be prey to anyone. And in Christ, whom we said above had pity on the scattered people, there was no empty or idle feeling; not long afterwards he destroyed those faithless shepherds, together with the temple and city, by the arms of the Romans. But first he gathered his sheep through the Apostles, and (as he had promised through the Prophets) preserved the remnants from the fire of exile, and these gave the beginning to the Church, which afterwards spread very widely. Christ still lives, and without doubt even today he sees his scattered and afflicted ones, whom in his time he will vindicate from the hands of the impostor shepherds, not without great harm to them, so that they may no longer mock his Bride, the Church.

units.la: Sed vt ad Christi verba redeamus, est in his multa obseruatione dignum quòd in corruptissima & multis modis excæcata gente, multam adhuc messem sibi superesse testatur, eos nimirum intelligens, qui salutis cupidi & ad regnum Dei excipiendum idonei sint. Ita s bique gentium suos electos habet misericors Deus, quos vbi tempus est vocat & colligit, ne cum infelici mundo pereant. Exempla huius rei multa extant. In Sodomis enim Lothum fuisse scimus, sidum cultorem Domini, quem
units.tr: But to return to the words of Christ: there is much in this passage worth noting, namely that among a very corrupt nation, blinded in many ways, he testifies that a large harvest still remains for him, meaning of course those who are eager for salvation and fit to receive the kingdom of God. So merciful God has his elect even among the nations, whom he calls and gathers when the time is right, lest they perish with the unhappy world. Many examples of this exist. For we know that there was Lot in Sodom, a faithful worshipper of the Lord, whom

units.la: {y} Tim.4. Ezech.34. Isa.10. & 1. In corruptis gente super sunt multi electi. quem reliquis omnibus pereuntibus mirifice seruauit. Heliae item temporibus, cum ille piorum nemi nem superstitem putaret, septem millia virorum habuit Deus, qui neq; publicae idololatriae contagio polluti fuerunt, neq; in Achabi & Iezabelis crudeles manus inciderunt. Quod si Actorum librum ex cutias, videbis in Cypro Veneri sacra, Corinthi, in omnis libidinis prostibulo, Ephesi inter curiosarum artium cultores, Romae deniq; & in ipsa Caesaris familia, quasi in medio luporum, Christo multum populum fuisse, qui illius beneficio seruatus est. Spirat enim ventus ille salutifer Domini ubicunque voluerit, neq; vllis hominum viribus, aut impiorum nequitia impediri potest. Quod vt nobis dulcissimam consolationem affert, quando omnia in deterius ruere videmus: ita admonet quoq;, vt diuinae bonitatis atq; virtutis memores, de nemine mortalium temere desperemus.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 4. Ezech. 34. Isa. 10. In a corrupt nation many elect remain. He wonderfully preserved him while all the others perished. Likewise in the time of Elijah, when he thought that he alone of the pious was left, God had seven thousand men who were neither polluted by the contagion of public idolatry nor fell into the cruel hands of Ahab and Jezebel. If you look through the book of Acts, you will see that in Cyprus, sacred to Venus, at Corinth in the brothel of every lust, at Ephesus among the practitioners of curious arts, and finally at Rome, even in Caesar's household, as if in the midst of wolves, Christ had many people who were kept safe by his favour. For that saving wind of the Lord blows wherever it wills, nor can it be hindered by any human strength or the wickedness of the impious. This, while it brings us the sweetest consolation when we see all things going from bad to worse, also warns us, mindful of divine goodness and power, not to despair rashly of anyone among mortals.

units.la: Praeterea non temere fieri putemus, quod Ecclesiam aut electos suos segeti ad messem maturae confert. Est parabola haec frequens in Euangelio, in primis tamen huc pertinet, quod Ioannis cap. quarto Christus discipulis dicit, cum Samaritanos ex Sichem ad se aduentantes videret: Nonne vos dicitis, Adhuc quadrimestre spatium superest, & messis aderit? Ecce dico vobis, attollite oculos vestros, & spectate regiones, nam albae iam sunt ad messem, &c. Docet parabola huius consideratio, Ecclesiam sua habere incrementa, neq; semper constare, qui nam vera & germana illius membra sint. Vt enim semen vbi sulcus commissum fuerit, non statim fructum fert, sed aliquandiu sub glebis delituit, tandem germinat, mox autem pruinis autumnalibus aduritur, nimbis quasi sepeliitur, & verno demum tempore herbescit, postea culmum facit & aristas sine spicas, in quibus modo interpluuias, modo inter intensissimos Solis ardores grana ad maturitatem excoquuntur: Ita verbi semen per praedicationem spargitur, & hominum animis concipitur, vix autem postea multos labores & dura crucis certamina deuenitur, vt in regni caelestis horrea colligamur. Prodest autem vt in horum meditatione frequenter versemur, quo minus offendamur, si vel fructus ex verbi praedicatione nullus initio apparet, vel ecclesiam grauibus tentationibus et aduersis exerceri videamus. Erit tandem illorum omnium latissimus finis, & cum minime speratur, fructum feret verbum Domini, quod prorsus intercidisse videbatur.
units.tr: Moreover, let us not think it happens by chance that God brings his Church or his elect to ripeness like a crop for the harvest. This parable is frequent in the Gospel, but what Christ says to his disciples in John chapter four is especially relevant here, when he saw the Samaritans coming to him from Sychar: "Do you not say, There are yet four months, and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest," and so on. Consideration of this parable teaches that the Church has its own growth, and that it is not always clear who its true and genuine members are. For as seed, once committed to the furrow, does not bear fruit at once but lies hidden under the clods for a while, then at last sprouts, is soon scorched by autumn frosts, is as it were buried by storms, and at last in spring turns green, afterwards makes a stalk and ears, in which the grains are ripened sometimes between showers and sometimes amid the most intense heat of the sun: so the seed of the word is scattered by preaching and received in men's minds, but scarcely afterwards do we reach the storehouses of the heavenly kingdom without many labours and hard struggles of the cross. It is useful to dwell often on these thoughts, so that we may be less offended if either no fruit from the preaching of the word appears at first, or we see the Church exercised by grievous temptations and adversities. In the end the broadest outcome of all these will come, and when it is least expected the word of the Lord, which seemed utterly lost, will bear fruit.

units.la: Reliquat postrema huius loci pars, qua docet Christus, quid nos in fidelium doctorum siue administrorum verbi inopia facere deceat. Dicit enim: Rogate ergo Dominum messis, vt extrudat operarios in messem suam. Primo ad Dominum messis nos remittit, qui non alius quam Deus fingi debet. Nam vt Paulus ait, Dei aruum est ecclesia, & vt illic colitur, ita ad eundem tota quoq; messis & fructus omnis pertinet. Deinde illum orare iubet, vt operarios in messem hanc suam extrudat: si dos nimirum, qui ipsius & publicae salutis negotium serio agant, & illi, non sibi ipsis metant atque congregent, Etenim tales dare solius Dei est. Nam vt Apostolus fatetur, nemo nostrum ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneus est. Vt ergo ad tantam functionem idonei simus, ab illo donu necessarijs instruamur oportet. Ideo Isaiae labia ipse purgauisse, & in Ieremiae os verba sua posuisse legitur. Apostolus quoque spiritum sanctum dedit, priusquam permitteret, vt in totum orbem ad praedicandum exirent. Quo Paulus respiciens dicebat: Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Sciebat enim a Deo neminem nisi idoneum mitti, ineptos autem, vel etiam infidos esse omnes, qui sponte currunt. Quod si vero discipuli orare debuerunt, vt Deus operarios in messem suam extrudat, viq; omnium est, vt hanc causam sibi commendatissimam habeant, & quantum in ipsis est, curent vt ecclesijs quoad fidos ministros prospiciatur. Faciant ergo omni studio id quod negotium hoc pro moueri posse vident. Olim quidem Deus ab aratro & pecorum armentis Prophetas vocabat, & Christum homines illiteratos huic muneri destinauisse scimus, quos miraculose & subito instruxit, vt ad illud idonei essent. Sed iam pridem miracula illa cessarunt: reliqua autem nobis sunt scripturae sacrae cum bonarum literarum & artium studijs, in quibus seipse cum invocatione Dei exercere debent, qui se ad ecclesiae ministerium vocari sentiunt. Magistratus ergo fuerit Scholas instituere, & curare vt in illis ingenui adolescentes probe instituantur. Parentes quoque hanc curam ad se pertinere sciant, vt quos ex suis filijs huic functioni idoneos esse vident, Christo & Ecclesiae consecrent. Et qui non aliud possunt, saltem precibus & pijs votis opus hoc sanctissimum adiuuent. Quod cum omni tempore fieri debeat, hodie in primis facto opus est. Quantam enim & quam copiosam messem videmus o fratres, in potentissimis Europae regnis, vbi ad Euangelij libertatem multa hominum millia aspirant, ea autem frui non possunt, quod vel operarij nulli sunt, vel si qui se offerunt, ij Regum edictis, minus & horrendis supplicijs procul ab opere arcentur? Hic nos afflictorum fratrum ex animo miserari, & apud Deum precibus assiduis instare conuenit, ut tandem tyrannidi finem faciat, & propter nomen suum periclitantibus succurrat.
units.tr: The last part of this passage remains, in which Christ teaches what we ought to do when there is a lack of faithful teachers or ministers of the Word. For he says: "Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send out labourers into his harvest." First, he sends us to the Lord of the harvest, who must be understood as none other than God. For, as Paul says, "You are God's field" [1 Cor. 3:9], and just as the field is cultivated there, so the whole harvest and all its fruit belong to the same God. Next, he bids us pray that he would send out labourers into his harvest; that is, that God would give men who earnestly attend to the business of his own glory and the public salvation, and who gather and harvest for him, not for themselves. For to give such men belongs to God alone. As the Apostle confesses, none of us is even sufficient to think anything of himself [2 Cor. 3:5]. So if we are to be fit for so great a task, we must be equipped by him with the necessary gifts. Thus we read that he himself cleansed the lips of Isaiah and put his words into the mouth of Jeremiah. The Apostles too received the Holy Spirit before he allowed them to go out into the whole world to preach. Paul, looking to this, said: "How shall they preach, unless they are sent?" [Rom. 10:15]. For he knew that no one is sent by God except a fit person, and that all who run of their own accord are unskilled, or even faithless. But if the disciples ought to pray that God would send out labourers into his harvest, it is the duty of all to make this cause their most earnest concern, and, as far as lies in them, to see that the churches are provided with faithful ministers. Let them therefore do with every zeal what they see can be done to further this business. Formerly God called prophets from the plough and the herds of cattle, and we know that Christ appointed unlearned men to this office, whom he instructed miraculously and suddenly, so that they were fit for it. But those miracles have long since ceased. In their place we have the Holy Scriptures together with the study of the liberal arts and sciences, and in these those who feel themselves called to the ministry of the Church ought to train themselves, calling upon God. It is therefore the task of the magistrate to establish schools and to see that gifted young men are thoroughly educated in them. Parents too should know that this care belongs to them, so that those of their sons whom they see to be fit for this office they may dedicate to Christ and the Church. And those who can do nothing else may at least help this most holy work by prayers and godly vows. This ought to be done at all times, but today it is especially necessary. For, brothers, how great and how abundant a harvest do we see in the most powerful kingdoms of Europe, where many thousands of people long for the liberty of the Gospel, yet cannot enjoy it, because either there are no labourers, or, if any offer themselves, they are kept far from the work by royal edicts and dreadful punishments? Here it is fitting that we sincerely pity our afflicted brothers and press God with constant prayers, that he may at last put an end to tyranny and come to the aid of those who are in danger for his name's sake.

units.la: Nec temere putemus Christum hic extrudendi aut eijciendi vocabulo vti. Eo enim innuit: non facile fidos operarios inueniri, qui sua sponte ad opus hoc accedant. Nam qui suas vires cum illius difficultate conferunt, ij illud quauis ratione subterfugere conantur. Cuius rei exempla in Mose, Ieremia, Iona & pluribus alijs cernimus. Diuina ergo virtute opus est, qua non modo idonei fiant qui vocantur, verumetiam voluntarij, qui Christo & Ecclesiae eius operam suam praestare cupiant. Porro qui vocantur, ij se non ad otium, sed ad messem vocari, & operarios dici cogitent. Nec enim externis laruis constat Ecclesiae ministerium, sed tales requiruntur, qui aruum Domini sedulo colant, semen verbi prudenter spargant, incommodis segetum diligenter occurrant, maturas congregent, & ita domino arui fructum vberrimum reddant. Idem docent pastorum, vinitorum, oeconomorum & militum parabolae, quibus alibi scriptura vtitur. Nam apud hos quoque nullus otio aut segnitiei locus est: sed studio, labore, industria vtantur oportet, si officium facere velint. Procul ergo ab Ecclesia facessant operarij mali, & personati pastores, qualibus olim Iudaea scatebat, & quales hodie nimis multi passim inueniuntur. Orent autem omnes Deum Patrem, ut Ecclesiae suae multis modis afflictissimae misertus fidos operarios excitet, qui disperses congregent ad Christum Iesum, in quo aeternum seruiunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Nor should we think that Christ uses the word "send out" or "cast out" here without reason. For by it he signals that faithful labourers are not easily found who would come forward to this work of their own accord. For those who weigh their own strength against the difficulty of the task try by every means to shirk it. We see examples of this in Moses, Jeremiah, Jonah and many others. There is need, therefore, of divine power, which makes not only those who are called fit, but also willing, who desire to offer their labour to Christ and his Church. Moreover, those who are called should consider that they are called not to idleness but to the harvest, and that they are called labourers. For the ministry of the Church does not consist in outward masks, but such men are required as will diligently cultivate the Lord's field, wisely sow the seed of the Word, carefully meet the hazards that threaten the crops, gather in the ripe grain, and so render the fruit of the field abundantly to the Lord. The parables of shepherds, vinedressers, stewards and soldiers, which Scripture uses elsewhere, teach the same thing. For among these too there is no place for leisure or sloth; they must use zeal, labour and diligence if they wish to perform their duty. Let evil labourers, then, and masked shepherds, of the kind with which Judea once swarmed and of whom far too many are found everywhere today, depart far from the Church. Let all pray to God the Father that, having mercy on his Church, which is afflicted in many ways, he will raise up faithful labourers who may gather the scattered to Christ Jesus, in whom they serve for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCVII.

units.la: Abite, ecce ego mitto vos vt agnos in medium luporum. Ne portate crumenam, neque peram, neque calceamenta: & neminem in via salutaueritis. In quamcunque domum ingredianimi, primum dicite: Pax huic domui. Quod si fuerit illic quispiam filius pacis, requiescet super eum pax vestra: sin minus ad vos reuertetur.
units.tr: Go your way; behold, I send you forth as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes; and salute no one on the way. Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house. And if there is there any son of peace, your peace shall rest upon him; but if not, it shall return to you.

units.la: Inter Dei opera nullum praestantius habetur, quam quod Filium suum vnigenitum & sibi coaeternum propter nos hominem fieri voluit, & eundem in mortem acerbam & infamem crucis pro nobis tradidit. Nam vt huius consideratio omnem humanae rationis intellectum superat: ita ab eodem vniuersa nostra salus dependet, quae aliter reparari non poterat. Ideo ipse etiam Dei Filius cum iam hora mortis eius instaret, omnia sua sic instituit, vt omnibus notum fieret, in morte sua humani generis redemptionem contineri. Quo cumprimis facit, quod cum ad crucis supplicium Hierosolymam proficisceretur, & Iudaea iam appropinquaret, Septuaginta discipulos praemisit, qui omnia loca & oppida, quo ipse venturus erat, percurrerent, & singulos admonerent, iam adesse tempus illud optatum, quo diaboli regnum destrui, Dei autem regnum instaurari oporteat. Vsus istius legationis & praedicationis fuit, vt ad eius aduentum omnes excitarentur, & ita concionum suarum, quas vltimas habuit, mortis item & resurrectionis plures testes haberet. Quamuis autem praedicatio istorum initio non admodum fructuosa fuisse videatur, suo tamen tempore fructum tulit non poenitendum, quando post eius Ascensionem in coelos plurimi crediderunt, quibus procul dubio tunc in mentem venit, quod prius ex ipso Christo & eius discipulis audiuerant. Ideo ne se in cassum laboraturos putarent, diserte illos monuit, sibi in gente illa quantumuis corruptissima copiosam messem esse, defuisse autem hucusque fidos operarios, qui homines ad se congregarent. Sequitur nunc diligentior instructio quomodo se in itinere, in vrbibus & hospitijs gerere, quidque praedicare debeant.
units.tr: Among God's works none is held more excellent than that he willed his only-begotten Son, who is co-eternal with himself, to become man for our sake, and delivered him up to a bitter and shameful death on the cross for us. For while the contemplation of this surpasses all the understanding of human reason, our whole salvation depends on it, and it could not be restored in any other way. Therefore the Son of God himself, when the hour of his death was at hand, so arranged all his affairs that it would become known to everyone that the redemption of the human race was contained in his death. To this especially pertains the fact that, when he was setting out for Jerusalem to suffer on the cross, and Judaea was already near, he sent ahead the seventy disciples, who were to run through all the places and towns to which he himself was about to come, and to warn each one that the longed-for time had now arrived, when the kingdom of the devil must be destroyed and the kingdom of God restored. The purpose of this embassy and preaching was that all men should be stirred up at his coming, and so that he might have more witnesses to his sermons, which were his last, and likewise to his death and resurrection. Although the preaching of these men may seem not to have been very fruitful at the beginning, it nevertheless bore fruit in its time, and no small fruit, when after his ascension into heaven very many believed; these men, no doubt, then recalled what they had heard earlier from Christ himself and his disciples. So that they would not think they were labouring in vain, he plainly warned them that, even among that most corrupt nation, there was a plentiful harvest, but that until then faithful workers, who would gather men to him, had been lacking. There now follows a more careful instruction on how they are to conduct themselves on the journey, in the cities and in lodgings, and what they ought to preach.

units.la: Initio tamen de periculis imminentibus admonet, ne sibi tuta & laeta omnia pollicendo securiores & confidentiores fierent. Dicitur igitur: Abite, ecce ego mitto vos vt agnos in medium luporum. Agnis confert, quia inermes & omni praesidio destituti erant. Sacerdotes autem & eos, qui tunc temporum in Iudaea potiebantur, lupos dicit, partim propter rabiem, qua contra veritatis ministros ardebant, partim propter potentiam & vires, quibus ad nocendum erant instructi. Nam & praesidum Romanorum authoritate muniti erant, & ab illis maior populi pars pendebat: & plerunq; fieri solet, vt stolida admiratione eos suspiciat & colat rude vulgus, à quibus decipitur & spoliatur. Est autem haec fere sors piorum omnium in hoc mundo, vt tanquam agni inter lupos versentur. Sunt enim passim falsi antistites, qui sub religionis specie inquisitionibus, delationibus, calumniis & omni insidiarum genere ipsis negotium faciunt. Sunt praeterea tyranni, qui horum consilijs sese regi patiuntur, & in illorum gratiam nihil non audent. Hinc ergo persecutiones oriuntur, in quibus pij vincula, carceres, exilia, mortes infames sustinent, & (vt Paulus ex Psalmo annotauit) non alio loco habentur quam oves, quae ad mactationem destinatae sunt. Inter quae pericula adeo vires & praesidia, quibus sese defendant, nulla habet, vt qui prius ipsis amici erant, tales amplius videri nolint, ne propter eos in periculum, aut saltem in suspicionem veniant. Prodest autem de his saepe cogitare, quo minus offendamur, si quid huius accidit. Et ideo Christus nunc septuaginta illos de hac piorum sorte admonet, quàmuis in ista professione nihil aduersum ipsos subituros sciret. Nam in posterum illis prospicere voluit, ne eundem successum perpetuum fore putarent, sed ad quaevis ferenda sese praemunirent.
units.tr: At the outset, however, he warns them of the dangers that threaten, lest, by promising them that all would be safe and happy, he should make them too secure and over-confident. He says therefore: "Go your way; behold, I send you as lambs in the midst of wolves." He compares them to lambs because they were unarmed and destitute of every protection. He calls the priests, and those who then held power in Judaea, wolves, partly because of the rage with which they burned against the ministers of truth, and partly because of the power and strength with which they were equipped to do harm. For they were fortified by the authority of the Roman governors, and the greater part of the people depended on them; and it commonly happens that the untutored crowd looks up to and honours with foolish admiration those by whom it is deceived and despoiled. Indeed, this is generally the lot of all the godly in this world: that they live as lambs among wolves. For everywhere there are false prelates who, under the guise of religion, make trouble for them by inquisitions, denunciations, slanders and every kind of treachery. Moreover, there are tyrants who allow themselves to be ruled by these men's counsels, and for their favour dare anything at all. Hence persecutions arise, in which the godly endure chains, prisons, exile and shameful deaths, and (as Paul noted from the Psalm) they are regarded as nothing other than sheep destined for slaughter. Amid these dangers the godly have no strength or protection with which to defend themselves, so that those who were formerly their friends no longer wish to be seen as such, lest they themselves fall into danger, or at least into suspicion, on account of them. It is useful, however, to think often about these matters, so that we may be less offended if anything of this kind happens. And therefore Christ now warns those seventy about this lot of the godly, although he knew that in this profession they would suffer nothing adverse. For he wished to provide for them in the future, so that they would not think this success would last forever, but would prepare themselves to bear whatever might come.

units.la: Est autem probè obseruandum, quòd etsi pericula praedicat, tamè ire iubet, & quidem vno verbo, ita nimirum omnem cunctandi aut tergiuersandi occasionem praripiens. Similia exempla alibi quoq; habemus. Nam cùm Mosi & Aaroni legationem ad Pharaonem committeret, simul praedicit, se cor Regis induraturum esse, vt eos minimè audiat. Quid verò illi ex eo aliud, quàm tristissima quae poterant sperare? Vult tamen, vt iniunctu sibi munus exequantur, & prius Mosi illum succenseisse legimus, cùm is illud detrectaret. Idem cum Ieremia factum esse scimus, aduersus quem Reges principes, sacerdotes, populu deniq; totu pugnaturos dicit, nihilominus tamen mandat, vt quaecunq; ab ipso in mandatis acceperit, constanter exequatur. Et quod hic septuaginta istius dicitur, hoc ipsum Apostolus quoq; dictum fuisse Matthaeus scribit. Docent haec neminè periculis aut laborum difficultate terreri debere, vt Dei vocationem negligat. Cùm enim omnis vita laborum & periculorum plena sit, quae stultitia fuerit, pro Deo nihil ferre aut facere velle? In primis verò ignauos istos hac arguunt, qui neq; hominum scelera, neq; superstitiones & errores liberius accusant, & id frustra fieri dicunt, cum nemo emendetur. Quasi verò nihil nos facere conueniat, nisi de euentu certi simus, & non potius Dei mandatum debeat respici, cui cum praesenti etiam vita periculo obedire oportet. Sed isti plausibilem praetextum quaerunt, quo timiditatem & huius saeculi studium excusent, cui ita addicti sunt, vt nihil dicendum aut faciendum esse putent, quo potentum iram contra se prouocent. Actum meminerunt interea, quanto gravius sit incidere in manum Dei viuentis, quàm hominum.
units.tr: It must be carefully observed, moreover, that although he foretells dangers, he nevertheless bids them go, and that in a single word, thus of course snatching away every opportunity for hesitation or evasion. We have similar examples elsewhere. For when he committed to Moses and Aaron the embassy to Pharaoh, he at the same time foretold that he would harden the king's heart, so that he would not listen to them at all. What, then, could they hope for from this other than the saddest things possible? Yet he wills that they carry out the task laid upon them; and we read that he was angry with Moses when Moses shrank from it. We know the same happened with Jeremiah, against whom he said that kings, princes, priests and finally the whole people would fight; nevertheless he commands him to carry out steadfastly whatever he received from him in commands. And what is said here of those seventy, Matthew writes was also said by the Apostle. These things teach that no one ought to be frightened by dangers or by the difficulty of labours, so as to neglect God's calling. For since all life is full of labours and dangers, what folly would it be to be unwilling to bear or do anything for God? Above all, these idle men are refuted by this: they do not accuse the crimes, superstitions and errors of men too freely, and they say this is done in vain, since no one is amended. As if it were not fitting for us to do anything unless we were certain of the outcome, and rather the command of God ought not to be regarded, which we must obey even at the risk of present life. But these men seek a plausible pretext with which to excuse their timidity and their devotion to this age, to which they are so attached that they think nothing must be said or done that would provoke the anger of the powerful against them. In the meantime, they would do well to remember how much more serious it is to fall into the hands of the living God than into the hands of men.

units.la: Itaq; ne quid huius pij patiantur, hoc potius memoriter teneant, quòd qui in medium lupo- rum hoste agnos suos emisit, eosdem mirificè defendit & seruauit, vt nihil aduersi ipsis accideret, quemadmodum ex ipsorum ore suo loco audiemus. Quod ipsum multi alij experti sunt, qui in opere Domini fideles & strenui fuerunt. Nam huc rursus Moses & Aaron pertinent, qui etsi illis cum immanissimo tyranno & aperto Dei contemptore res esset, diuinitus tamen seruati sunt, ne vel ille ipsis manum iniceret, vel ab Aegyptiorum gente ob tot tamq; graues plagas acceptas trucidarentur. Idem de Prophetis possumus dicere, quorum aliqui sub crudelissimis regibus & populo centumaci & impio per annos triginta, aliqui quadraginta, quidam quinquaginta & amplius verbum Dei praedicarunt. Senserunt hanc Dei defensionem Apostoli, qui licet Iudaeorum principes simul & Romanos Imperatores hostes haberent, non antea tamen occisi sunt, quàm cursum suum feliciter absoluissent. Inter quos, si vel vnum Paulum diligentius consideremus, non poterimus nō mirari, illum inter tot insidias seruatum fuisse, ex vinculis & carceribus toties euasisse, imò inter lapidum grandines non occubuisse, denique docendi libertate habuisse Romae, cùm illic sub Nerone, omnis libidinis & crudelitatis portento, captiuus ageret. Nec adhuc extincta est haec Dei fides & potentia. Nam hodie huius generis multa videmus fieri, quando & ministri tuto docent inter apertos hostes, & vt bestes atque principes non admodum potentes seruantur contra potentissimos tyrannos, qui nouis quotidie coniurationibus factis aduersus illos extrema quaeque moliuntur. Quid, quod vt olim inter Neronis domesticos suas oues Christus habuit, ita hodie in aulis Regum impiissimorum tuto satis degunt, & saepe in pretio sunt, qui fidem orthodoxam non diffitentur? Fiunt ista non sine miraculo, & proinde nos in istis Dei nostri potentiam considerare, & inde consolationem petere debemus, vt fortes & animosi simus, si quid ex vocatione nostra pro Dei gloria & publica salute audendum est.
units.tr: Therefore, lest they suffer any harm, let the godly hold fast to this in memory: that he who sent his lambs in the midst of wolves also wonderfully defends and preserves them, so that nothing adverse happens to them, as we shall hear from his own mouth in its place. Many others have experienced the same, who were faithful and vigorous in the work of the Lord. To this pertain once more Moses and Aaron, who, although they had to do with the most savage tyrant and an open despiser of God, were nevertheless preserved by divine power, so that neither did he lay hands on them, nor were they slaughtered by the Egyptian people after so many and such grievous plagues. The same we can say of the prophets, some of whom preached the word of God under the cruellest kings and a stiff-necked and impious people for thirty years, some for forty, and some for fifty or more. The Apostles also felt this defence of God; although they had as enemies both the princes of the Jews and the Roman emperors, they were not put to death until they had happily completed their course. Among these, if we consider Paul alone more carefully, we cannot but marvel that, amid so many plots, he was preserved, escaped so often from chains and prisons, and indeed did not perish under the hail of stones; and finally that at Rome, while under Nero, a monster of every lust and cruelty, he was a captive, he nevertheless had freedom to teach. Nor has this faith and power of God been extinguished even now. For today we see many things of this kind: ministers teach safely amid open enemies, and are preserved, like lesser nobles and princes, against the most powerful tyrants, who every day make new conspiracies against them and devise every extremity. What of the fact that, just as Christ had his sheep among Nero's household, so today in the courts of the most impious kings they live quite safely, and often are held in high esteem, those who do not disown the orthodox faith? These things come about not without a miracle; and therefore we ought to consider in them the power of our God, and from them seek consolation, so that we may be brave and courageous whenever something must be attempted for the glory of God and the public good, from our calling.

units.la: Interim quod apud Matthaeum, vbi idem Apostolis dicitur, Christus admonet, omnes sibi diffidentiam degeneret, quae securos & temerarios reddat, sed cum columbina simplicitate serpentina prudentiam coniungant. Vt enim serpentes, quia se omnibus exosos esse sentiunt, hominum conspectum fugiunt, & in suis latebris se continent: ita cum constet nos toti mundo inuisos esse, & impios omnem nos circumueniendi occasionem captare, quoad eius fieri poterit, nobis ab hominibus huius seculi cauteamus, consilia eorum obseruemus, non necessaria cum illis commercia vitemus, ne illi ex nostra negligentia aut nimia facilitate nobis nocendi occasionem arripiant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in Matthew, where the same charge is given to the apostles, Christ warns them not to fall into a distrust that makes men careless and rash, but to join serpent-like prudence with dove-like simplicity. For just as serpents, knowing that they are hated by everyone, shun the sight of men and keep to their hiding places, so, since it is certain that we are hated by the whole world and that the wicked seek every chance to ensnare us, we should, as far as it can be done, be on our guard against the men of this age. We should watch their plans, avoid unnecessary dealings with them, and not give them, through our carelessness or excessive readiness, an opening to harm us.

units.la: Veniamus nunc ad ea, quae discipulis hisce in itinere obseruanda fuerunt, vbi de duobus admonet. Primum de commeatu sine viatico & toto profectionis apparatu est. Ne portate (inquit) crumenam, neque peram, neque calceamenta. Eadem praecipit quae Apostolis proximo capite mandauit, nisi quod hic calceamenta quoq; prohibet, quibus pro more illius regionis non omnes vtebantur. Fuerunt autem (vt tunc diximus) haec praecepta partim temporaria, & huic modo profectioni accommodata, in qua propter festinationem, qua opus erat, expeditissimos esse oportebat: partim sym bolica, quibus plus quiddam significabatur. Elucet autem in hac tenuitate legatorum Christi, ipsius potentia, qui nihilominus illis prospicere potuit, ne quid rerum necessariarum eis deesset: simulq; nos admonemur, ne in illo splendorem quaeramus externum, neq; ipsius prouidentiae diffidamus, etiamsi non statim ad manum esse videamus, quibus nos putamus opus habere.
units.tr: Let us now come to the things these disciples were to observe on their journey, where he gives two instructions. The first concerns provision for the road and the whole outfit for the journey: "Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals." He gives the same command the apostles received in the previous chapter, except that here he also forbids sandals, which were not all worn in that region as a matter of custom. As we said then, these precepts were partly temporary and suited to this kind of journey, in which, because of the haste required, they had to travel as light as possible; and partly symbolic, signifying something more. In this poverty of Christ's envoys, his power shines forth, for he could nonetheless provide for them so that nothing needful was lacking. At the same time we are reminded not to seek outward splendour in him, nor to distrust his providence even when we do not see at hand the things we think we need.

units.la: Alterum est, ne quem in via salutent. Conuenit hoc cum eo, quod Helisaeus famulo suo Giezi praecipit, cum eius opera in resuscitando Sunamitidis filio vti vellet, Accinge (inquit) lumbos tuos, & tolle baculum meum in manum tuam, & vade. Quod si tibi quispiam obuius factus fuerit, ne salutaueris illum: & si quispiam te salutauerit, ne respondeas ei, & pone baculum meum super faciem pueri, &c. Est autem praeceptum hoc Symbolicum, qualia in scripturis multa habentur. Nam neq; Prophetae neque Christi mens est, vt inciuiles & inhumani simus, qui minima quaque officia neglegamus, quibus frequenter inter ignotos amicitia conciliatur. Sed summa festinatione opus esse doceat, adeo vt inter eundum ne salute quidem aliquem impertiantur, neque salutanti respondeant. Scimus enim saepe ex salutatione, colloquijs prolixioribus occasionem dari, quibus impediuntur & detinentur, qui aliquid grauioris negotij exequi debebant. Hanc ergo moram causam Christus illos vult abrumpere.
units.tr: The second instruction is that they should greet no one on the road. This agrees with what Elisha commands his servant Gehazi, when he wished to use his help in raising the son of the Shunammite woman: "Gird up your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go. If anyone meets you, do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him; and lay my staff upon the face of the child," and so on. This command is symbolic, as many such are found in the Scriptures. For it is neither the intention of the prophet nor of Christ that we should be uncivil and inhumane, neglecting the smallest courtesies by which friendship is often won among strangers. Rather, it teaches that there is need of great haste, so that on the way they should not even give a greeting or return one to anyone who greets them. For we know that a greeting often gives occasion for lengthy conversations, by which those who ought to carry out some more serious business are held up and detained. Christ therefore wishes his messengers to break off such a delay.

units.la: Continet autem praeceptum hoc generalem doctrinam, ne quis sub aliquo praetextu, quantumuis in specie pio & honesto ea praetermittat, quae sui sunt officij. Prum est parentes & cognatos amare & in necessitate constitutos succurrere. At hic simul Christum audire debemus dicentem: Qui amauerit parentes, fratres, sorores, vxorem & liberos plus quam me, non est me dignus. Iustum & aequum est obedire magistratibus. Sed hic quoque Christus audiatur, qui Caesari ita reddere iubet quae sunt Caesaris, vt quae Dei sunt huic etiam fideliter praestemus. Quoties ergo magistratus mandat, quae Dei praeceptis contraria sunt, cum Apostolis dicamus: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Similiter ijs, qui in magistratu sunt, pauperes & afflictos in primis a Deo commendatos esse scimus. At quando illi ad audiendum causas consederunt, tunc sibi ab eodem Deo dictum esse meminerint: Ne ornes pauperem in causa sua: vt nimirum personae eius respectu contra aduersarium illius iniquam feras sententiam. Ita inimicos quidem ex Christi praecepto diligere debemus, sed (vt paulo ante monuimus) abstinendum est ab eiusmodi illorum commercijs, quibus & ipsi in malo confirmari, & nos corrumpi, vel etiam in periculum non necessarium incidere possumus. Et huius generis multa sunt, quae diligenter obseruare oportet, ne sub pietatis praetextu nobis ipsis delitias faciendo, aliquid praeter officium faciamus.
units.tr: This precept, moreover, contains a general teaching: no one should, under any pretext, however pious and honourable it may appear, neglect the duties that belong to his office. It is right to love parents and relatives and to help them when they are in need. Yet here we must at the same time hear Christ saying: "He who loves father, brother, sister, wife, or children more than me is not worthy of me." It is just and fair to obey magistrates. But here too let Christ be heard, who bids us render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, so that we also faithfully give to God what is God's. Therefore, whenever a magistrate commands what is contrary to God's precepts, let us say with the apostles: "We must obey God rather than men." Likewise, we know that the poor and afflicted are commended by God above all to those who hold office. But when they sit down to hear causes, let them remember that the same God has said: "Do not favour the poor man in his cause," that is, do not give an unjust sentence against his adversary out of regard for his person. So, by Christ's command, we must indeed love our enemies, but (as we warned a little earlier) we must refrain from such dealings with them, by which they may be confirmed in evil, we may be corrupted, or we may fall into unnecessary danger. There are many things of this kind which must be carefully observed, so that under the pretext of piety we do not, by indulging ourselves, do something beyond our duty.

units.la: Porro pergit Christus, & de hospitijs quoque septuaginta illos admonet dicens: In quamcunq; domum ingrediamini, primum dicite: Pax huic domui, &c. Apud Matthaeum Apostolos in sua legatione instruens, vrbem aliquam ingressos iubet quaerere, quis dignus sit ad quem diuertant, & cui praedicent. At quia multi falsa pietatis specie commendantur, hic certo etiam indicio & argumento explorare docet, num quae domus ad excipiendam doctrinam de regno Dei idonea sit. Vt enim conuersaconuersationis & consuetudinis ratio diligens habenda est ijs, qui ad res magnas destinati sunt, ne propter malorum consortia bonis & honestis suspecti fiant: ita verbum Dei & aeternae salutis mysteria non temere quibusuis proiici debent, vt Christus Matth. septimo admonet. Hinc enim conteptus verbi nascitur, qui tandem in illius authorem, Deum redundat. Et impij illi, quos Christus porcos & canes dicit, non contenti verbum spreuisse, aduersus eius praecones quoque insurgunt, qui tunc nulla graui & iusta de causa in periculum veniunt. Recte ergo Solomon monebat: Qui erudit illusorem, reportat sibi ignominiam: & qui impium corripit, maculam suam. Noli ergo illusorem corripere, ne te oderit, redargue sapientem, & amabit te. Hinc vero aestimare licet, quam praeclarum sit hoc Dei beneficium, quo verbum suum & per hoc voluntatis suae cognitionem nobis revelat, quia non omnibus frui datur. Debet ergo huius consideratio nos ad gratitudinem & obedientiam voluntariam excitare.
units.tr: Christ goes on, and instructs the seventy also about lodgings, saying: "Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house," and so on. In Matthew, when instructing the apostles for their mission, he bids them, on entering a town, to inquire who is worthy to lodge with them and to whom they should preach. But because many people are commended under a false appearance of piety, here he teaches them to test whether a household is suited to receive the teaching of the kingdom of God by a sure sign and proof. For just as the manner of one's company and conduct must be carefully considered by those who are destined for great things, lest by associating with the wicked they become suspect to the good and upright, so the Word of God and the mysteries of eternal salvation must not be thrown rashly before just anyone, as Christ warns in Matthew 7. For from this contempt of the Word arises a contempt that finally reflects upon God, its author. And those impious men, whom Christ calls swine and dogs, not content with having despised the Word, also rise up against its heralds, who then come into danger for no grave or just cause. Rightly, therefore, Solomon warned: "He who corrects a scoffer gets himself dishonour, and he who rebukes the wicked gets himself a stain. Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you." From this one may judge how great a benefit of God it is that he reveals his Word to us, and through it the knowledge of his will, since it is not given to everyone to enjoy. Consideration of this should therefore stir us to gratitude and to willing obedience.

units.la: At quod nam illud indicium est, quo domus aut familias explorare debuerunt? Dicite (inquit) Pax huic domui. Fuit haec Iudaeis ex prisco more vulgaris & vsitata salutandi formula, vt pacem sibi mutuo precarentur, sed qua totam hominis felicitatem siue incolumitatem comprehendunt. At quia hic nihil vulgare Christus praecipit, plus quiddam innuitur. Nam cum eius legati essent, qui nobis verae pacis & reconciliationis cum Deo Patre authores est, hanc pacem illi ab initio statim, quamprimum domum aliquam ingrediebantur, denuntiare debuerunt, ita vt domestici sentire possent, illos nouae salutis praecones esse. Ideo addit Dominus: Quod si fuerit illic quispiam filius pacis, requiescet super eum pax vestra, &c. Filium pacis dicit, qui doctrinam pacis, ipsum videlicet Euangelium non fastidit, & quem Deus elegit, vt ad verae pacis & salutis cognitionem vocetur. Si quis ergo (inquit) talis in aliqua domo fuerit, ille vos admittet, & quod illi verbis precamini, id revera eueniet, vt nimirum pacis illius fructu fruatur. Ratum enim habet Deus quicquid ministri suijpsius nomine illis pollicentur, qui promissionibus eius fidem adhibent. Quod si filius pacis in domo illa nullus, sed omnes increduli & contumaces fuerint, pax vestra (inquit) ad vos reuertetur. Sensus est: Nihil vobis peribit, vos vestro functi estis officio, & illi quidem in sua incredulitate peribunt, pacis autem denuntiatio vobis salua manebit, vt ea apud alios posstius vti, qui ea digne excipiant. Nec enim ab vllorum hominum dignitate pendet regnum Dei, & nihil ei decedit, etiamsi hi aut isti illud non excipiant, &c. Sunt in hus quaedam ordine obseruanda.
units.tr: But what, then, is the sign by which they were to test a house or a family? "Say," he says, "Peace be to this house." This was among the Jews, from ancient custom, a common and usual form of greeting, by which they wished one another peace, a word that comprehends the whole happiness or well-being of a man. But since Christ here commands nothing commonplace, something more is implied. For since his messengers are the authors to us of true peace and reconciliation with God the Father, they ought from the very beginning, as soon as they entered any house, to proclaim this peace, so that the household could perceive that they were heralds of a new salvation. Therefore the Lord adds: "If there is a son of peace there, your peace shall rest upon him," and so on. He calls a son of peace the one who does not scorn the teaching of peace, that is, the Gospel itself, and whom God has chosen to be called to the knowledge of true peace and salvation. "If, then," he says, "such a person is in any house, he will receive you, and what you pray for in words will in fact come to pass, so that he enjoys the fruit of that peace." For God holds valid whatever his ministers promise in his name to those who give faith to his promises. But if there is no son of peace in that house, but all are unbelieving and obstinate, "your peace," he says, "will return to you." The meaning is: nothing will be lost to you, since you have performed your duty; those indeed will perish in their unbelief, but the proclamation of peace will remain safe for you, to be used with others who will receive it worthily. For the kingdom of God does not depend upon the dignity of any men, and nothing is taken from it even if this man or that does not receive it, and so on. There are certain points to be observed in this matter.

units.la: Primum, per Euangelium nobis pacem denuntiari & offerri. Illo enim praedicatur Christus, quem principem pacis Prophetae vocant, non quidem pacis seculi huius, quae incerta & fluxa, adhaec plerunque maiorum turbarum causa est: sed diuina, caelestis, vera & perpetua, quae in medijs etiam afflictionibus durat, & proinde omnem huius mundi intellectum superat. Nam nos cum Deo reconciliat, cum quo nobis prius propter peccata non conueniebat. Hinc pax conscientiae nascitur, quae adeuersa quaeque nobis non leuia modo, verumetiam laeta & iucunda reddit. Fructus vero eius quoad banc vitam, est, quod homines inter se quoq; conciliat, & causa est, vt qui prius vel inimici erant, vel se mutuo non nouerant, per fidem sub Christo Iesu in vnum corpus coalescant. Itaq; tam priuata quam publica hominum salus ex hac pace suam ducit originem. Patet igitur hoc loco causa turbarum & malorum omnium, quibus hoc seculo infelix mundus exercetur. Est hoc, quod plerique princi pem & authorem pacis, Christum super se regnare nolunt: imo Euangelij praecones, per quos pacem nobis offert, seditiosos esse clamant, similes plane seditiosorum, qui non contenti turbas mouisse, insuper Regios legatos pacem & condonationem omnium delictorum offerentes, omni iniuriarum genere, vel etiam mortis supplio afficiunt. Merito igitur Deus pacis turbatores dat, qui bellis, seditionibus & inimicitijs totum orbem terrarum implent: & ita pax vtraque, humana & diuina amittitur. Neq; nouum hoc est, sed exempla in Iudaeis & gentibus praecesserunt, quibus idem olim accidit. Simus ergo filij pacis, & salua nobis erunt omnia.
units.tr: First, through the Gospel peace is announced and offered to us. For by it Christ is preached, whom the prophets call the Prince of peace: not indeed the peace of this age, which is uncertain and fleeting, and moreover is often the cause of greater disturbances, but a divine, heavenly, true and lasting peace, which endures even in the midst of afflictions and therefore surpasses all understanding of this world. For it reconciles us with God, with whom before, on account of our sins, we had no agreement. From this comes the peace of conscience, which makes all adversities not only light but even joyful and pleasant. Its fruit for this life is that it also reconciles people with one another, and it is the cause why those who were before either enemies or did not know one another are joined together into one body under Christ Jesus through faith. Thus both the private and the public welfare of men takes its origin from this peace. It is plain, therefore, from this place what is the cause of all the disturbances and evils with which the unhappy world is troubled in this age. It is this: that most people are unwilling for Christ, the Prince and author of peace, to reign over them; indeed, the heralds of the Gospel, through whom he offers us peace, they cry out to be seditious men, plainly like seditious men who, not content with having stirred up disturbances, also subject the royal envoys, who offer peace and the pardon of all offences, to every kind of injury, and even to the punishment of death. Rightly therefore God sends troublers of the peace, who fill the whole earth with wars, seditions and enmities, and so both kinds of peace, human and divine, are lost. Nor is this new; examples went before among the Jews and the Gentiles, to whom the same thing once happened. Let us therefore be sons of peace, and all things will be safe for us.

units.la: Secundo loco obseruabis, quod propter vnum filium pacis discipulos in domo illa manere, toti familiae regnum Dei praedicare & salutis spem certam facere iubet. Docemur hic, Deum sui foederis gratiam non in vno patrefamilias sistere, sed simul ad liberos & domesticos omnes extendere. Quod cum Abrahamo factum fuisse notius est, quam vt demonstrari oporteat. Sic propter Zachaeum toti domui salutem obtigisse, & illam Abrahami filiam factam fuisse Christus testatur. Similia exempla in Cornelio Centurione, Lydia purpuraria, carceris custode apud Philippenses, & infinitis alijs biblioteca sacra nobis exhibet. Et hæc causa est, quòd Apostoli totas familias abluerunt mora baptizarunt, in quibus vera fidei professione apud adultiores locum habere videbant: Quorum exempla Novatianus arguunt, qui sua morositate multis authores fuere, ut baptismum in horam mortis usque differrent, & ne hoc accepto iterum peccarent decumbentes, in lectis baptizabantur, unde apud veteres Clinici dicti sunt. Imitantur hos magna ex parte nostri Anabaptistæ, homines ad hoc nati, ut & Ecclesias turbent, & imperitorum conscientijs scrupulum injiciant. Simul autem admonet hic locus, quanto in honore habendi sint viri boni & pij. Nam quod hic de domibus & familijs dicitur, alibi totis regnis & civitatibus accidisse constat, ut paucorum, vel etiam unius pietas & cum fide coniunctionis prudentia illis salutem attulerit. Huc pertinet, quod de Iosepho apud Ægyptios agente scribitur. De Iosia item, quo viuente imminens Iudæis exitium Deus differt. E contra paucorum impietas toti populo sæpe exitialis est, nisi digna seueritate & iustis pœnis coerceantur.
units.tr: Secondly, you will observe that because of the one son of peace he bids the disciples remain in that house, preach the kingdom of God to the whole household and give them a sure hope of salvation. Here we are taught that God does not confine the grace of his covenant to the one head of the household, but at the same time extends it to all the children and servants. That this happened with Abraham is better known than needs to be shown. So Christ testifies that because of Zacchaeus salvation came to his whole house, and that he too had become a daughter of Abraham. The sacred library sets before us similar examples in Cornelius the centurion, Lydia the seller of purple, the jailer at Philippi, and in countless others. And this is why the apostles baptized whole households at once, in which they saw a place for a true profession of faith among the adults. Novatian argues against their examples, who by his obstinacy became the authority for many, so that baptism was put off until the hour of death, and, lest they sin again after receiving it, people were baptized while lying in their beds, whence among the ancients they were called Clinics. Our Anabaptists, men born for this purpose, largely imitate these, so that they both disturb the churches and cast a stumbling block into the consciences of the unlearned. At the same time this passage admonishes us how greatly good and godly men are to be held in honour. For what is said here of houses and households is plainly known to have happened elsewhere to whole kingdoms and cities, so that the piety of a few, or even of one, and the prudence joined with faith, has brought them salvation. To this belongs what is written of Joseph dealing among the Egyptians. Likewise of Josiah, during whose life God put off the destruction impending over the Jews. On the other hand, the impiety of a few is often deadly to the whole people, unless it is restrained with due severity and just punishments.

units.la: Postremò adhuc diligentius expendi debet, quod ait: Pax vestra ad vos reuertetur. Offendit officium & laborem ipsis minimè periturum esse, quando habituri sint quod alijs denuntient. Semper enim inueniuntur, qui Christum ab alijs reiectum magno desiderio & fide constanti apprehendunt. Hinc autem generalis doctrina petenda est. Non frustra eos laborare, qui etiam apud indignos & ingratos officio suo fideliter defunguntur. Nam beneficium ad illos redit, & si non aliud proficiunt, saltem apud Deum excusati sunt, qui remunerator est liberalis & fidelis. Et ad ministros quidem pertinet, quod Ezechieli dicitur, ipsum suam animam liberaturum esse fideliter & diserte monendo impios, etiamsi illi non conuertantur. Idem vero ad se transferre debent omnes alij ordines. Magistratus est pietatem veram & vitæ honestate prouehere, bonos tueri, malos dignis modis coercere. At dum officium facit, sæpe obstat populi contumacia & eorum perfidia, quorum ministerio illum vti oportet: quod olim Dauidi, Ezechiæ, Iosiæ & alijs pijssimis principibus accidisse constat. Sed nihilominus pergere & cum omnium improbitate luctari conuenit, neque deerunt, qui fidem ipsorum agnoscant, & Deus promissis præmijs illos minimè fraudabit. Pertinet item ad patresfamilias, quorum officium est, liberos sanctè instituere, petulantiam eorum frenare, domesticos deniq; omnes ad pietatem & honestatē adiuuefacere. Sed licet illi sanctissimi sint, & officium sedulò faciant, tanta tamen nonnunquam est liberorum contumacia, ut neque admonitionibus, neque correptionibus, & ne virgis quidem aut alia disciplina seueriori flecti possit. Non autem ideo cessandum est, ut saltem suam fidem & industriam Deo approbent, qui illos digno bonore olim remunerabitur. Quod si vero negligentes fuerint, iam ipsis imputantur liberorum scelera, & cum his ipsi quoque multa buntur, cuius rei exemplum memorabile in Heli sacerdote habemus. Eandem ratione secum ineant serui & ancillæ, quibus cum heri duris & inhumanis res est. Sint illi fideles, & ad ipsos redibit beneficij gratia, cui digna præmia Deus retribuet. Idem de illis possumus dicere, qui inimicos habent implacabiles & insuperabili vindictæ cupiditate ardentes. Faciant modò ipsi charitatis officium, & apud Deum hæc gratia eis minimè peribit, alteri vero illi pœnas suo odio dignas subibunt. Denique horum consideratio omnes excitet, ut in officio suo non fatigentur: In primis vero, ut Dei beneficium agnoscant, qui ex filijs iræ filios pacis & gratiæ facere dignatur. Ampletamur ergo constanti fide Iesum Christum, qui huius pacis mediator est, & hunc oremus, ut in ea nos seruare, & tandem in æterna pacis regnum transferre dignetur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, what he says must be weighed still more carefully: Your peace will return to you. It shows that the labour and duty will by no means be lost to them, since they will have something to announce to others. For there are always found those who lay hold on Christ, rejected by others, with great desire and constant faith. From this, however, a general doctrine is to be drawn: that those are not labouring in vain who faithfully discharge their office even among the unworthy and ungrateful. For the benefit returns to them, and if they accomplish nothing else, at least they are excused before God, who is a generous and faithful rewarder. And what is said to Ezekiel pertains to ministers: that he will save his own soul by faithfully and plainly warning the wicked, even if they are not converted. Yet all other orders ought to apply the same to themselves. It is the task of the magistrate to advance true piety and honesty of life, to protect the good and to restrain the wicked by fitting means. But while he performs his duty, the stubbornness of the people and their faithlessness, through whose service he must use his office, often stand in the way; as is known to have happened to David, Hezekiah, Josiah and other most godly princes. Nevertheless one must press on and wrestle with the wickedness of all, and there will not be lacking those who acknowledge their faith, and God will by no means defraud them of the promised rewards. Likewise it pertains to heads of households, whose duty it is to bring up their children holily, to restrain their wantonness, and finally to help all the members of the household toward piety and honesty. But although they are most holy and diligently do their duty, yet sometimes the obstinacy of the children is so great that it cannot be bent by admonitions, nor by corrections, nor even by rods or any stricter discipline. Yet one must not for that reason cease, so that at least they may approve their faith and diligence before God, who will one day reward them with the worthy honour. But if indeed they have been negligent, then the crimes of their children are imputed to them, and with these crimes they too will suffer many things; of which matter we have a memorable example in the priest Eli. Servants and maidservants should deal with their masters in the same way, when they have to do with harsh and inhuman masters. Let them be faithful, and the grace of the benefit will return to them, for which God will render worthy rewards. We can say the same of those who have implacable enemies and burn with an insatiable desire for vengeance. Let them only do the work of charity, and this grace will by no means perish for them before God; but those others will undergo punishments worthy of their hatred. Finally, let the consideration of these things stir all of us up, that we not grow weary in our duty; above all, that we acknowledge the benefit of God, who has deigned to make sons of peace and grace out of sons of wrath. Let us therefore embrace Jesus Christ with a steadfast faith, who is the mediator of this peace, and let us pray to him that he will deign to keep us in it, and at last bring us over into the eternal kingdom of peace. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCVIII.

units.la: Manete autem in ea ipsa domo, edentes & bibentes quæ ab ipsis apposita fuerint. Dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Ne transite e domo in domum. Sed in quamcunque vrbem ingressi fueritis, & exceperint vos, edite quæ apponuntur vobis. Et sanate ægrotos, qui in ea fuerint, & dicite eis: Appropinquauit ad vos regnum Dei. In quancunque autè vrbem ingressi fueritis, & non exceperint vos, egressi in plateas eius dicite: Etiā puluerē, qui adhæsit nobis ex urbe vestra, vobis abstergimus: tamen hoc scitote, appropinquasse ad vos regnū Dei. Dico autem vobis, quod Sodomis tolerabilius erit in die illo, quàm urbi illi.
units.tr: "And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they set before you, for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Do not go from house to house. But into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick who are there, and say to them, 'The kingdom of God has come near to you.' But into whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, 'Even the dust of your city that clings to us we wipe off against you; yet know this, that the kingdom of God has come near to you.' I tell you, it will be more tolerable on that day for Sodom than for that city."

units.la: QVoniam hominum salus potissimum in hoc versatur, vt verbum Dei diligenter audiat, & quam is per hoc nobis offert gratiam, vera fide amplectantur, Christus Iesus discipulos suos quos huic prædicationi destinauit, non sine gravibus causis tanta diligentia instituit. Nec enim sim pliciter docet quid faciant, verumetiam officium suum illis commendat, vt intelligant, nihil tam honestum, tam necessarium denique esse, cuius prætextu illud negligere debeant. Huc enim pertinet, quòd non vult de commeatu aut viatico solicitos esse: quòd item prohibet, ne quem inter eundum salutent: præterea quòd diserte docet illos operam suam minimè lucturos esse, etiamsi in indignos & contumaces incidant, qui verbum pacis audire dedignentur. His nunc alia subijcit, quæ ad ipsorum institutionem pertinent.
units.tr: Since the salvation of men depends chiefly on this, that they listen carefully to the Word of God and embrace with true faith the grace which it offers them, Christ Jesus, who appointed his disciples to this preaching, did not train them with such care without serious reasons. For he does not simply teach them what to do, but also commends their office to them, so that they may understand that nothing is so honourable or so necessary that it may serve as a pretext for neglecting it. To this belongs his command that they should not be anxious about provisions or supplies for the journey; likewise his prohibition against greeting anyone on the way; and besides, his plain teaching that they will not lose their labour even if they fall in with unworthy and stubborn people who disdain to hear the word of peace. Now he adds other things which pertain to their instruction.

units.la: Primum inter hæc est, victus parandi ratio, de qua ipsos exprese admoneri opus erat, cùm absque commeatu & absque pecuniis emitterentur. Poterant enim dicere: Quid edemus? aut quis victum nobis suppeditabit, si nudi aut vacui veniamus? Num in obuia quaque manus injiciemus, & inuitis aut infscijs dominis aliena vsurpabimus? Occurrit ergo Christus & dicit: Manete autem in eadem domo, edentes & bibentes quæ ab ipsis appositæ fuerint: Dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Et mox, vt melius inculcet hoc, quod non parui momenti erat, idem repetens addit: sed & in quamcunq; vrbem ingressi fueritis, & exceperint vos, edite quæ apponuntur vobis. Quibus verbis duo docet. Primum, non defuturum victum in hoc officio versantibus. Eos enim qui ipsos excipiunt & filij pacis sunt, libenter sua cum illis communicaturos esse. Neque dubium est, quin hoc faciant, qui Euangelij prædicationem & quæ per hanc nobis offeruntur bona digne æstimant. Simul autem scrupulum illis eximit, ne se peccare putent, si ab auditoribus victum accipiant. Et ideo illis applicat generalem regulam, ex natura legibus peritam: Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Rursus vero operarios dicit, vt omnes verbi administri intelligant, Christum non pigros & otiosos versantes insituisse, sed qui in Ecclesia, quæ arvum & vinea Dei est, operi strenuè incumbant.
units.tr: The first of these is the way to provide food, about which they had to be expressly admonished, since they were being sent out without provisions and without money. For they could have said: What shall we eat? Or who will supply us with food, if we come empty-handed and destitute? Shall we lay hands on whatever we meet, and seize other people's property against the will and wishes of its owners? Christ therefore meets this objection and says: "Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they set before you, for the labourer is worthy of his hire." And at once, to impress this more firmly, which was of no small importance, he repeats it and adds: "But into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat what is set before you." By these words he teaches two things. First, that those who labour in this office will not lack food. For those who receive them are sons of peace, and will gladly share their goods with them. Nor is there any doubt that those who value the preaching of the gospel and the blessings offered through it as they deserve will do this. At the same time he removes from them the scruple that they might think they sinned if they received food from their hearers. And so he applies to them a general rule, drawn from the very laws of nature: "The labourer is worthy of his hire." Moreover, he calls them labourers so that all ministers of the Word may understand that Christ did not appoint idle and lazy people, but those who apply themselves vigorously to work in the Church, which is God's field and vineyard.

units.la: Stabiliuntur igitur hoc loco ipsius Christi authoritate stipendia administrorum verbi Dei. Mercedus enim nomine omnia intelligutur, quæ ad vitæ huius vsum necessaria sunt. Æquitenim est, vt qui omnibus alijs negotijs relictis, soli Ecclesiæ se totum impendit, ab eadem accipiat victum, amictum & alia, sine quibus vivi non potest. Docet hoc Paulus multis in locis. Nam ad Galatas scribit: Communicet qui instituitur in iermone, ei qui se instituit, omnia bona. Et in priore ad Timotheum: Qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore digni sunt (vbi honoris nomine etiam vitæ subsidia & quæuis erga illos officia comprehenduntur) maximè ij qui laborant in iermone & doctrina. In primis autem in priori ad Corinth. nono capite, contra malevolos & iniquos ministerij ecclesiastici æstimatores, hanc causam diligentissimè tractat, multis argumentis adductis, quibus probat, vt ex verbi prædicatione viuant, qui se totos illi consecrarunt. Primò enim similibus vtitur huic negotio mirè congruentibus. Quis (inquit) militat proprijs stipendijs unquam? Quis plantat vineam, & de fructu eius non edit? Aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte eius non edit? Quasi diceret: Qui militiam sequuntur, à suis imperatoribus stipendia accipiunt, quibus viuant. Cur ergo non idem verbi administris concedatur, qui perpetuò pro Ecclesia in armis sunt contra Satanā, peccatum, mundum & alia, quæ humanæ saluti officiunt? Præterea cùm æquissimum sit, vt vinitores ex suis vineis, pastores ex suo grege victum recipiant, annon similiter ex suis laboribus viuere debent, qui vineam Domini excolunt, & eius gregem pascunt? Deinde ne humanis rationibus in cau sa diuina vti videretur, legem Dei eadem docentem allegat: Num secundum hominem hæc dico? Nonne etiam Lex hæc dicit? Nam in Mosis lege scriptum est, Non obligabis os boui trituranti. Num boues curæ sunt Deo? vt nimirum propter hos leges ferre velit? Vel num propter nos hoc omnino dicit? Propter nos enim hoc scriptum est. Et mox alia similia ex natura legibus & communi more desumpta adducens addit: Nam sub spe debet is qui arat, arare, & qui triturat sub spe, spei suæ particeps esse. Quæ similia huc pertinent, quia verbi præcones Ecclesiæ seruiunt, quæ arvum & area Dei est. Tertiò collationem facit bonorum, quæ utrinque dantur & recipiuntur, vt inde colligat, nihil iniquum hic exigi. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminauimus, magnum ne est si nos vestra carnalia messuerimus? Ostendit illos in lucro esse, eò quòd pro bonis temporarijs, quæ doctoribus suis in vitæ subsidiû largiantur, æterna recipiant & cœlestia. Et tandem Veteris & noui Testamenti comparatione factâ, eandem utrinque, quoad ministrorû stipendia, rationem esse docet. An nescitis (inquit) quòd qui sacris operantur, quæ ex sacrario sunt edunt? qui altari assident, cum altari participant? Ita & Dominus constituit iis, qui Euangelium annuntiant, vt ex Euangelio vi uant. Id verò dicit propter ea, quæ hîc & duodecim Apostolis apud Matthæum à Christo dicta esse sciebat. Et hæc quidem fieri debuerunt eo tempore, quo Ecclesiæ hinc inde dispersæ, opes publicas nullas habebant, nisi quæ ab ipsis fidelibus contribuebantur. Hodie multò tolerabilior est ratio, quando principum & maiorum nostrorum liberalitate Ecclesiæ ditatæ, redditus habent annuos, ex quibus & ministros suos alere, & alijs necessitatibus prospicere possunt. At simul hoc multorum ingratitudinem arguit, qui cùm ipsi nihil dent, nec quisquam ab illis aliquid postulet, ea tamen ministris inuident, qua olim à pijs & sanctis viris sunt donata. At non debet horum malignitas illis aliquem scrupulum inijcere, quò minus iure suo, quod illis Christus fecit, vtantur: curent modò, vt in commisso sibi munere seduli sint, neque eos imitentur, qui maximos Ecclesiarum redditus intercipiunt, illis autem nulla prosus in re seruiunt.
units.tr: Therefore the stipends of the ministers of God's Word are established here by the very authority of Christ. For under the name of wages are understood all things necessary for the use of this life. It is only fair that the one who, setting aside all other business, devotes himself wholly to the Church, should receive from it food, clothing and other things without which he cannot live. Paul teaches this in many places. For he writes to the Galatians: "Let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches." And in the first letter to Timothy: "Elders who rule well are worthy of double honour" (where under the name of honour are included the means of livelihood and every kind of service toward them), "especially those who labour in the word and teaching." Above all, in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter nine, against malicious and unjust judges of the ecclesiastical ministry, he treats this cause most carefully, bringing forward many arguments by which he proves that those who have wholly dedicated themselves to the preaching of the Word should live by it. First he uses similes that agree wonderfully with this matter: "Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock and does not eat of its milk?" As if he said: those who follow the military life receive pay from their commanders, by which they live. Why then should the same not be granted to the ministers of the Word, who are always in arms for the Church against Satan, sin, the world and the other things that stand in the way of human salvation? Besides, since it is most just that vinedressers should receive their food from their vineyards and shepherds from their flock, should not those who tend the Lord's vineyard and feed his flock likewise live by their labours? Then, lest he seem to use merely human reasons in a divine cause, he cites the law of God teaching the same thing: "Do I say these things according to man? Does not the law also say them? For it is written in the law of Moses: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain." Is God concerned about oxen, that he should wish to make laws for them? Or does he say this altogether for our sake? For it was written for our sake. And soon after, bringing forward other similar things taken from the laws of nature and common custom, he adds: "For he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes in hope should be a partaker of his hope." These similitudes belong here, because the preachers of the Word serve the Church, which is God's field and threshing floor. Thirdly, he makes a comparison of the goods that are given and received on each side, so as to conclude from it that nothing unfair is demanded here: "If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?" He shows that they are gainers, since in return for temporal goods, which are bestowed on their teachers for the support of life, they receive eternal and heavenly things. And finally, having made a comparison between the Old and New Testaments, he teaches that there is the same principle on both sides regarding the stipends of ministers: "Do you not know that those who serve at the sacred things eat of the things of the temple, and those who attend the altar share in the altar? So also the Lord has commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel." He says this on account of those things which he knew Christ had also said here and to the twelve apostles in Matthew. And indeed these things ought to have been done at that time, when the Churches were scattered here and there and had no public resources, except what was contributed by the faithful themselves. Today the situation is much more tolerable, since the Churches, enriched by the generosity of our princes and magistrates, have annual revenues from which they can both support their ministers and provide for other needs. Yet at the same time this shows the ingratitude of many who, although they give nothing themselves, and although no one asks anything of them, nevertheless begrudge the ministers those things which were formerly given by pious and holy men. But the malice of these people ought not to cast any scruple upon the ministers, so that they should not use their right, which Christ has granted them. Let them only take care to be diligent in the duty committed to them, and not imitate those who seize the largest revenues of the Churches, yet serve them in no way at all.

units.la: Alterum quod hic Christus agit est, quòd modestiæ & temperantiæ discipulos admonet, quando iubet, vt quæ apponuntur edant & bibant, non autè vt ipsi nouas lautitias petant, aut moriosi ea fa stidiant, quibus alij contenti viuunt. Est hoc vitium intolerabile illis, qui spontanea liberalitate homi nibus peregrinis benefacere student: turpissimum autem est in verbi administris, qui alijs conti nentiæ, frugalitatis & temperantiæ magistri esse debent. At simul admonetur hîc omnes Ecclesiarum ministri, vt ipsi quoq; non immodicas opes, non delitias superfluas, non fastum & splendore ex ternum quærant, sed ijs contenti sint, quæ ad huius vitæ necessitatem faciunt, & quæ dare possunt iis, quibus verbum prædicant. Peccatur in hoc vehementer à nonnullis, quibus nihil satis est, quòd vel insatiabili auariria laborant, vel intemperantius viuunt, quàm homines Christianos, nedum verbi Dei administros deceat. Quæ causa est, vt Ecclesijs intolerabiles fiant, & plerunq; pinguiori stipen dio oblato illas deferant non sine scandalo. Sunt hi ex mercenariorum numero, de quibus Christus loan. 10. disserit, & sæpe in canes mutos degenerant, dum ad publica scelera conniuent, & quibusuis seruiliter blandiuntur, à quibus stipendij auctione sperare possunt. At meminerint quæso illi, quàm immane scelus sit diuinum illud ministerium, quo nihil inter homines sanctius & salutarius est, pro pter quæstum aut ventrem hominibus prophanis prostituere.
units.tr: The second thing Christ does here is to admonish his disciples to modesty and temperance, when he bids them eat and drink what is set before them, and not seek new delicacies, nor, like the fastidious, despise those things with which others are content. This is an intolerable fault in those who strive to do good to strangers by voluntary generosity, but it is most shameful in ministers of the Word, who ought to be teachers of self-control, thrift and temperance to others. At the same time, here all ministers of the Churches are admonished that they too should not seek excessive wealth, superfluous luxuries, pride and external splendour, but should be content with what meets the necessities of this life, and with what those to whom they preach the Word can give them. Many sin gravely in this respect, for nothing is enough for them: they suffer either from insatiable greed or live more intemperately than is fitting for Christian men, let alone ministers of God's Word. This is why they become intolerable to the Churches, and often, when a richer stipend has been offered, they desert them, not without scandal. These are among the hirelings of whom Christ speaks in John 10, and they often degenerate into dumb dogs, while they connive at public crimes and fawn slavishly upon whomever they hope may increase their stipend. But I beg those men to remember how monstrous a crime it is to prostitute that divine ministry, than which nothing among men is holier or more salutary, to profane people for the sake of gain or the belly.

units.la: Est præterea omnibus, cuiuscunq; loci aut ordinis sint, diligenter obseruanda sententia hæc, quam ex lege naturæ desumptam esse diximus, operarium su- mercede dignum esse. Nemo igitur mercede sua fraudari debet. Quod vt erga omnes tenere decet, quorû opera & ministerio vtimur, ita maximè erga eos, qui manuû suarum labore in diem viuunt. Extat de hoc lex Dei: Opus mercena rij ne pernoctet apud te vsq; mane. Et Moses peccatum hoc inter clamantia numerat, quæ omnium atrocissima habetur. Nam in Deut. sic scribit: Ne neges aut retineas mercenario pauperi & inopi, siue sit de fratrib. tuis, siue de peregrinis tuis, qui sunt in terra tua atq; intra portas tuas: die suo da bu ei mercedem suam, neq; Sol occidat super eam: quoniam pauper est, & ad illam attollit animum suum: ne contra te ad Dominum clamet, & cedat tibi in peccatum. Et sapiens ille Sirachides grauiter admodum pronuntiat: Quem quis vitu priuat, eum interficit: & qui mercedem subtrahit mercenario, effundit sanguinem. Sed & apud Malachia Christus ipse inter eos, quos ex Ecclesia sua eiecturus fit, illos quoq; numerat, qui mercenarij mercedem supprimunt. Si enim peccant, qui egenti no subueniunt, quàm graue fit oportet illorum scelus, qui illius simul opera & labore gratis abutuntur? Ideo Iacobus Apostolus horribile Dei iudicii iniustis diuitibus denuntians, inter alia inquit: Ecce merces operariorû, qui messuerunt regiones vestras, quæ fraude non reddita est à vobis, clamat: & clamores eorum, qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierūt. Quid verò de illis dicemus, qui aliorû parta laboribus violenter diripiunt, qui hodie multis quæstus vt vberrimus ita honestis simus iudicatur? Sed quia hæc non sunt huius loci, ad ea quæ in Christi verbis sequitur, pergamus.
units.tr: Moreover, the saying I said was drawn from the law of nature, that a worker deserves his wage, must be carefully observed by everyone, whatever their place or rank. No one therefore should be defrauded of his wages. This ought to be kept towards all whose work and service we use, and most of all towards those who live by the labour of their hands from day to day.
