God's law stands on this point: "The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you until the morning." Moses also counts this sin among the crimes that cry out, and it is considered among the most atrocious. For in Deuteronomy he writes thus: "You shall not oppress or withhold the wages of a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the strangers who are in your land and within your gates. You shall give him his wage on the same day, nor shall the sun go down upon it, for he is poor and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to the Lord, and it be sin to you." And that wise son of Sirach pronounces it very gravely: "Whoever deprives another of his living kills him, and whoever withholds the wage of a labourer sheds blood." But also in Malachi, Christ himself counts among those whom he is about to cast out of his Church those who keep back the wages of a hired man. For if those who do not help the needy sin, how grievous must be the crime of those who at once take advantage of a man's work and toil without payment? Therefore the Apostle James, announcing the terrible judgment of God against unjust rich men, says among other things: "Behold, the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, which were kept back by you through fraud, cry out; and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth." But what shall we say of those who violently seize what others have won by their labours, a gain which today is judged by many to be as abundant as it is respectable? But since these matters do not belong to this place, let us proceed to what follows in Christ's words.

units.la: Leuit. 19. Deut. 19. Eccle. 34. Malach. 3. Iacob. 5. Hîc Hic non modo potestatem facit edendi & bibendi apud auditores, simulque temperantiam praecipit; verumetiam prohibet, ne temere mutent hospitia, quae semel subierint. Ne transfite (inquit) e domo in domum. Serviebat quidem etiam hoc festinationi (vt cap. nono diximus) sed simul vagas & curiosas discursiones vetat, quae peregrinos saepe suspectos & invisos reddunt. Vult item ne pluribus molesti sint, aut ex levitate, aut alio affectu pravo sibi alia hospitia quaerant. Id enim fieri non potest sine priorum hospitum contumelia, qui boni suspectus redditur, quasi sua inhumanitate aut sordicie abire coegerit eos quos semel susceperat: deinde animos leves, delicatulos & quibus nihil suffciat, arguit. Quid vero ad hoc Domini praeceptum respondebunt fratres mendicantes, qui vicatim & oftiatim per totas vrbes & pagos discurrunt, saccos suos & canistra omni lautissimorum ferculorum genere farciunt? Volunt hi quidem Apostolorum & discipulorum Christi imitatores videri, cum neque Euangelium praedicent, neque alijs Christi praeceptis instant. At simul hoc praeceptum nos admonet, civilitatis & honestatis publicae rationem habendam esse hominibus Christianis, ne aliquo facto indecentiore Euangelij doctrinam suspectam aut invisam reddant. Docet hoc Paulus quoque, quando iubet, vt alij alios honore praeveniant. Minime ergo audiendi sunt barbari illi, qui tunc demum se evangelicos & vere Christianos esse putant, si absque omni personarum respectu rustice & inciviliter agant omnia: quasi vero religio civilitati morum adversetur, & ex hominibus canes Diogenianos efficiat. Quanto magis autem cavendum, ne apertis scelaribus Euangelij professionem diffamemus?
units.tr: Lev. 19. Deut. 19. Eccl. 34. Mal. 3. Jas. 5. Here he not only grants the hearers permission to eat and drink, and at the same time enjoins moderation, but also forbids them to change lodgings rashly once they have entered them: "Do not go," he says, "from house to house." This too served haste (as I said in the ninth chapter), but at the same time it forbids wandering and nosy rounds, which often make travellers suspect and hated. He also wills that they not be a burden to many, nor seek other lodgings out of fickleness or some other wicked desire. For this cannot happen without insult to the earlier hosts, who become objects of suspicion, as if they had by their inhospitality or meanness driven away those whom they had once received. Then he rebukes fickle, pampered minds, who are never satisfied. But what will the mendicant brothers answer to this command of the Lord, who run from village to village and from door to door through whole towns and countryside, and stuff their sacks and baskets with every kind of most sumptuous delicacy? These men wish to appear imitators of the Apostles and the disciples of Christ, though they neither preach the Gospel nor press the other precepts of Christ. But at the same time this precept reminds us that Christians must have regard for courtesy and public decency, lest by some more unbecoming act they make the doctrine of the Gospel suspect or hated. Paul also teaches this when he commands that they go before one another in showing honour. Therefore those barbarians must by no means be listened to, who think they are evangelical and truly Christian only if they behave rudely and uncivilly in everything, regardless of persons; as if religion were opposed to civility of manners, and made men into Diogenes' dogs. How much more, then, must we take care that we do not bring the profession of the Gospel into disrepute by open crimes?

units.la: Postquam vero Dominus discipulos praeceptis ad victus rationem & mores pertinentibus instruxit, nunc legationis huius statum exponit, & quid suo nomine praedicare debeant, docet hos ver bis: Sanate aegrotos, qui in ea vrbe fuerint, & dicite eis: Appropinquauit ad vos regnum Dei. Duo mandat, sed prius inter haec est, quod hic ordine posterius ponitur, Annuntiatio nimirum regni Dei. Constat enim miracula propter doctrinam & praedicationem fieri, vt eam confirment: & si quando illam praecedunt, id non alia ratione fit, quam vt homines ad doctrinam audiendam excitentur. Sed singula videamus.
units.tr: After the Lord had instructed the disciples with precepts pertaining to the manner of their living and their conduct, he now sets out the nature of this embassy, and teaches them by these words what they ought to proclaim in his name: "Heal the sick who are in that town, and say to them: The kingdom of God has come near to you." He gives two commands, but the first in order is the one placed last here, namely the announcement of the kingdom of God. For it is established that miracles are wrought on account of the teaching and preaching, to confirm it; and if they ever go before it, this is done for no other reason than to rouse people to listen to the teaching. But let us look at the individual points.

units.la: Primo quid praedicare debuerunt? Regnum Dei, quod nimirum hoc iam appropinquauerit. Ita vero nominat totum redemptionis nostrae negotium, quod Euangelicae praedicationis argumentum est. Appropinquauisse autem dicit, quia iam impletum erat praefinitum illud tempus, de quo Prophetae, & inter hos Daniel in primis, fuerant vaticinati. Et dicitur regnum Dei totum hoc negotium Euangelicum, quia rationem ostendit, vt in nobis Deus regnet, & nos olim regni eius caelestis participes efficiamur. Nam vt alias diximus, primum regnum in mundo hoc toto obtinebat Satan per peccatum, & regni eius finis erat totius hominis perditio. At Christus a Patre missus opera eius destruxit, regnum euertit, & nos in libertatem asseruit, denique Deo Patri suo nos Reges & Sacerdotes fecit, vt in Apocalyp. scribitur. Quae cum alibi fusius tractata sint, nunc consulto breviter studemus. Patet autem ex hoc finem Euangelicae praedicationis esse, vt homines intelligant, regnum Dei iam instauratum esse, & proinde se totos huic consecrent per fidei obedientiam. Quod vt fiat, omnibus obstare debent ministri Ecclesiarum, quae homines impedire aut avocare possunt, quo minus Deum in se regnare patiantur. Sunt inter haec praecipua fere, falsa doctrina, superstitio, idololatria, scelerum licentia, securitas nimia, & quae alia sunt huius generis. Haec olim oppugnarunt omni studio Prophetae, & ad haec demolienda noui Testamenti ministros armis spiritualibus a Deo instructos esse scribit Apostolus. Qui ergo hodie obstant, quo minus ista accusentur & confutentur, ij Christi mandato resistunt, quod impune non ferent.
units.tr: First, what were they to preach? The kingdom of God, which has now, of course, come near. He calls by this name the whole business of our redemption, which is the subject of the evangelical preaching. He says it has come near because that appointed time had now been fulfilled, of which the prophets, and Daniel above all of them, had prophesied. And the whole of this evangelical business is called the kingdom of God, because it shows the way by which God reigns in us and we are made in time partakers of his heavenly kingdom. For, as I have said elsewhere, the first kingdom in this whole world was held by Satan through sin, and the end of his kingdom was the destruction of the whole man. But Christ, sent by the Father, destroyed his works, overthrew the kingdom, and asserted us into liberty; finally he made us kings and priests to God his Father, as is written in the Apocalypse. Since these matters have been treated at more length elsewhere, we now deliberately touch on them only briefly. It is plain from this, however, that the aim of evangelical preaching is that men should understand that the kingdom of God has now been restored, and therefore that they should devote themselves wholly to it through obedient faith. So that this may happen, the ministers of the Churches ought to oppose all those things which can hinder or divert men, so that they do not allow God to reign in them. Among these the chief are almost these: false doctrine, superstition, idolatry, licence in sins, excessive complacency, and others of this kind. The prophets of old assailed these with all their zeal, and the Apostle writes that the ministers of the New Testament were equipped by God with spiritual weapons to pull these down. Therefore those who today stand in the way, so that these things are not accused and refuted, resist Christ's command, and they will not go unpunished for it.

units.la: Secundo doctrinae miracula coniungit, non vana & ad ostentationem composita, sed salutaria & quae praedicationi respondeant. Iubet enim sanare aegrotos aut infirmos. At constat morbos vna cum morte ex peccato originem habere, & propter hoc homines Satanae tradi, qui morbis homines affligat. Ideo alibi eos scripturae flagella vocant, & spiritum infirmitatis habere dicuntur, qui morbis gravioribus laborant. Quando igitur Apostoli & Septuaginta isti morbos in solo Christi nomine profligabant, satis testatum fiebat, tempus salutis adesse, quo peccatum expiari et diabolo vires suas frangi oporteat. Et hic verus miraculorum visus est, non quem homines superstitiosi fingunt, qui ex ijs occasione sumunt, vt relicto Christo Divos colant & inuocent, quos aliquando miraculis claruisse audiunt. Et simul arguuntur hic, qui hodie miracula requirunt, quibus minime opus est, cùm veteribus illis Christiana fides & religio abunde confirmata sit. Elucet praeterea hoc loco divina Christi potentia, qui virtute edendi miracula vera & salutaria, quae ipsi propria est, solo nutu & volun-tatis suae declaratione suis servis potestatem largiri, & simul iis ad suam gloriam vti, quae propter pec-catum inualuerunt, & nostrae perditionis praeludia quaedam censeri poterant: qualia sunt morbi, dae-monum vexationes, denique ipsa mors. In his enim & similibus profligandis maximè ostendit sibi om-nem potestatem datam esse in caelo & in terra. Est ergo revera humani generis seruator, ad quem unum confugere, & in omni necessitate ab illo opem & auxilium postulare debemus.
units.tr: Second, he joins to the doctrine miracles, not vain ones composed for display, but saving ones which correspond to the preaching. For he commands them to heal the sick or infirm. But it is established that diseases, together with death, have their origin in sin, and that for this reason men are delivered to Satan, who afflicts men with diseases. Therefore elsewhere Scripture calls them scourges, and those who suffer from more serious diseases are said to have a spirit of infirmity. When therefore the Apostles and those seventy disciples drove out diseases in the name of Christ alone, it was sufficiently attested that the time of salvation was at hand, in which sin ought to be expiated and the power of the devil broken. And this was the true sight of miracles, not the kind that superstitious men invent, who on the occasion of them, leaving Christ, worship and invoke those saints whom they hear once shone with miracles. And at the same time those are rebuked here who today seek miracles, for which there is no need at all, since the Christian faith and religion were abundantly confirmed for those ancient people. Moreover, the divine power of Christ shines forth in this passage: he who by his own proper power of working true and saving miracles, by a mere nod and declaration of his will, grants power to his servants, and at the same time uses them for his own glory against those things which have grown strong because of sin, and which could be regarded as certain foretastes of our destruction: such as diseases, the vexations of demons, and finally death itself. For in driving out these and similar things, he most clearly shows that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him. He is therefore truly the Saviour of mankind, to whom alone we ought to flee, and from whom in every need we ought to ask help and aid.

units.la: Caeterum poterant discipuli isti propter tam laetum nuntium tamen salutaria miracula sibi om-nia laeta polliceri, quod nimirum ipsos omnes obuijs (quod aiunt vlnus excepturi essent, & ipsos in summo pretio & honore habituri. Ne ergo spe vana sese lastantes postea multorum contumacia of-fenderentur, ostendit plures fore, qui ipsos excludant & audire dedignentur, simulque docet quid cum talibus sit agendum. Verba eius haec sunt: In quamcunque autem vrbem ingressi fueritis, & non ex-ceperint vos, egressi in plateas eius, dicite: Etiam puluerem, qui adhaesit nobis ex vrbe vestra, vobis abstergimus: tamen hoc scitote, appropinquauisse ad vos regnum Dei. Primò in publicas vrbis pla-teas exire iubet, vt qui nihil dissimulanter aut meticulosè agere debeant. Deinde puluerem excuti-ant, contra ipsos in testimonium. Hoc enim innuit publica protestatio, qua vti iubentur, cuius sen-sus est: Nos vobis regnū Dei & salutem veram in foribus adesse nuntiamus, & vos ad hanc exci-piendam hortamur. At vos nuntium hoc fastiditis, & nos procul abire cupitis. Atqui non multo negotio opus est. Sponte enim discedimus, & vt vos nostrum discessum optatis, ita nos vicissim vt stram vrbem tanto studio deuitandam esse iudicamus, vt ne puluerem quidè, qui nobis adhasit, no-bisčum efferre libeat. Eum ergo vobis abstergimus, vt hoc etiam soli fruamini. Interim hic ipse ali-quando contra vos testabitur, quod Deus regnum suum vobis obtulerit, vos autem eius praecones reieceritis, & proinde qucuq; supplicio digni sitis. Fuit autem (vt aliàs monuimus) puluerum excussio Chria tunc vsitata inter Iudaeos. Vt enim testium scissione testabantur quam abhorrerent à blas-phemijs, quibus Dei honor violatur: ita puluerū excussione sceleratos denuntiabant, eos homines ef-se execrabiles, & bonis omnibus fugiendos, adeo vt ne puluerī quidem ipsorum communicare debe-ant. Fuit ergo protestatio eiusmodi cū publica ignominia totius vrbis, in qua fiebat, coiuncta & pro-inde sic vti periculosissimum fuit. Et quam indigne hanc ignominiam Iudaei ferre soliti fuerint, ex-emplum eorum docet, qui Corinthi post puluerū abstersionem à Paulo factā, maiori rabie in illum insurrexerunt. Vnde colligimus, quam forti zelo armatos esse conuenit Christi ministros, vt in af-ferenda gloria Dei & veritatis doctrina, neq; hominū respectu vllo, neq; proprio periculo terreān-tur. Hic tamè multa cautione opus esse monuimus, ne qui ordinarij & certi ecclesiarū pastores sunt, sibi idè permissum putent, quod hic discipulus & alibi Apostolus mandatur. Hi enim nō vni loco assi-xi erant, sed Christi testimonium longe lateq; debebant circumferre. Non licebat ergo illis diutiùs cum impijs altercando moras nestere inutiles. Deinde ab illū modò discedendum fuit, quorum de-plorata contumacia & incredulitas iam satis perspecta erat: & ideo rarissimè Apostolos hac seueri-tate vsos esse legimus. Ergo κακοξηλία peccant pastores nonnulli, qui vt primùm non omnes ipsorū monitis obediunt, sibi ius esse arbitrantur discedendi ab Ecclesijs, etiamsi plurimi sint, qui vt ger-manae oues vocem Christi audiunt, & ipsos pro suis pastoribus agnoscunt. Sunt hi dissipationis Ec-clesiarum autores, & olim poenas dabunt Domino, imò plerunq; seipsos in pericula & casus diffi-ciliores conijciunt. Quod si vero omnino discedendum est, vt cum qui oues videbantur in hircos de-generant, vel propter alicuius ministri praesentiam Ecclesia tota periclitatur, quae illo digresso tu-tius agere poterit, tunc hanc quidem ita relinquere oportet, vt inuitos & non sine acerbo animi do-lore abire omnibus constet, simulque quoad eius fieri potest, curare, vt alius fidus & idoneus succe-dat: erga illos vero fiducia & constantia atq; publica protestatione vti conuenit, qua & Dei gloria asseratur, & qui curabiles sunt, aliquando de salute sua cogitandi occasionem habeant, contumacia vero & incurabilium animis stimulus iniiciatur, qui vbi Dei iudicium supra illos venerit, eius in-stitiae intra conscientias ipsorum testimonium ferat. Sed plura de his alibi diximus, quae omnia nunc repetere superuacaneum foret. Porrò ne quis pulueris excussionem vt rem ridiculam contemneret, quando eam ab hominibus exteris & vagis, qui nulla vel priuata vel publica authoritate commendabantur, fieri videbat, gra-uissimam pœnæ comminationem infert, quam ab exemplo amplificat, dicens: Dico autem vobis, quod Sodomis tolerabilius erit in illo die (nouissimi nimirum iudicij, vt in Matthæo ipse interpretatur) quàm vrbi illi. Sodomæorum historia in Genesi describitur, vbi dicuntur homines pessimi & peccatores coram Domino fuisse, adeo vt illorum clamor ad Dominum ascenderit. Peccata autem eorum Ezechiel definit, fastum, abundantiam panis, felicitatem, otium, quod item manu pauperis & egeni non firmauerint, sed his denù abusi sint pro sua libidine, atque abominanda patrauerint coram Domino, horrendum videlicet & Christianis auribus indignum masculæ Veneris scelus intelligens, cuius nimiû turpe specimen noƈte, quæ ipsis vltima fuit, dederunt, cum Lothi domum obsidentes, hospitese ius Angelos ad nefariam hanc libidinem sibi dari postularent. Propter quæ scelera sub ortum Solis nouo & inaudito exemplo per ignem & sulphur cœlitus demissum vnà cum vicinis vrbibus & tota regione exusti sunt, & in locum terræ, quæ instar paradisi prius fuerat, lacus bitumine & sulphure redolens successit, qui (vt prophani quoq; scriptores tradunt) de eius loci hominû sceleribus si-mul & supplicio testaretur. Ideo prophetæ quoties horrenda flagitia populi accusant, & in hæ pœnas nô vulgares minantur, huius exempli meminisse solet, vt Isaias contra Babylonios, quos uratos ecclesiæ dissipatores fore in spiritu prœuidebat: Ieremias contra Idumæos: Sophonias contra Moabitas & Ammonitas, infestissimas populi Dei gentes. Imò ipse quoties contra Iudæorum scelera altius insurgunt, exemplum idem allegant. Sunt autem hæc in eum finem obseruanda, vt discamus interpec-cata nullum contemptu verbi atrocius esse, quod facile patebit, si Sodomæorum scelera consideres, quibus tamen Christus mitius & tolerabilius iudicium, quam verbi sui contemptoribus denuntiat. At quia collationem hanc in Marco nostro fecimus, eandem hic nolumus repetere. Discant nunc omnes, & in primis qui in magistratu sunt, Reip. incolumitatem & pacem in eo consistere, vt verbum pacis admittatur, quod alibi sceptrum Messiæ dicitur. Est ergo hoc incomparabile Dei beneficium, quod cum Sodomæorum scelera hodie regnent, pœnas tamen ille differt, & interim suam gratiam & pacem nobis offerre dignatur. Itaq; quam chara nobis est salus cum priuata tum publica, nuntium pacis admittamus, vt & diras pœnas euitemus, quæ illius contemptoribus parata sunt, & in Christo Iesu salutem veram consequamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet these disciples, because of such joyful news, could promise themselves that all their saving miracles would be joyful, since they supposed that everyone would welcome them with open arms and hold them in the highest esteem and honour. So that they would not be offended later by the obstinacy of many, boasting of a vain hope, he shows that there will be many who shut them out and disdain to hear them, and at the same time he teaches what is to be done with such people. His words are these: "But into whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, 'Even the dust from your city that clings to us we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has drawn near to you.'" First, he orders them to go out into the public streets of the city, so that they should do nothing covertly or timidly. Next, they are to shake off the dust, as a testimony against those people. For this action signifies a public protest, which they are commanded to make, and whose meaning is this: "We announce to you that the kingdom of God and true salvation are at your doors, and we urge you to receive them. But you despise this message and wish us to depart far away. Yet there is no great difficulty in this. We depart of our own accord, and just as you desire our departure, so in turn we judge your city to be shunned with such zeal that we do not even wish to carry away with us the dust that clung to us. Therefore we wipe it off for you, so that you may enjoy this alone. Meanwhile this same dust will at some time bear witness against you, that God offered you his kingdom, but you rejected his heralds, and therefore you are worthy of punishment, whoever you are." Moreover, as we have noted elsewhere, the shaking off of dust was a ceremony then customary among the Jews. For just as by tearing their garments they testified how much they abhorred the blasphemies by which the honour of God is violated, so by shaking off dust they denounced wicked men, declaring that those people were detestable and to be avoided by all good people, to the point that they ought not even share the dust of such men. This protest, then, was joined with public disgrace to the whole city in which it was made, and so it was used in a most dangerous way. And how unworthily the Jews were accustomed to bear this disgrace, the example of those at Corinth teaches, who, after Paul had shaken off the dust, rose up against him with greater rage. From this we gather how bravely armed the ministers of Christ ought to be, so that in asserting the glory of God and the doctrine of truth they may be frightened neither by any regard for men nor by their own danger. Yet here we have noted that great caution is needed, lest those who are the ordinary and settled ministers of churches think that what is commanded to this disciple, and to the Apostle elsewhere, is permitted to them. For these men were not fixed to one place, but were to carry the testimony of Christ far and wide. Therefore it was not permitted to them to waste time uselessly by disputing longer with the ungodly. Moreover, they had to depart only from those whose obstinacy and unbelief was already sufficiently clear; and therefore we read that the Apostles very rarely used this severity. Therefore some ministers sin by misguided zeal [κακοζηλία], who, as soon as not all obey their admonitions, think they have the right to depart from their churches, even though there are very many who, like true sheep, hear the voice of Christ and acknowledge them as their own shepherds. Such men are the authors of the scattering of churches, and they will one day give an account to the Lord; indeed, they very often cast themselves into dangers and more difficult misfortunes. But if indeed departure is altogether necessary, as when those who seemed to be sheep degenerate into goats, or when the whole church is endangered because of the presence of some minister, which church may act more safely once he has gone, then it is proper to leave it in such a way that it is evident to all that he departs unwillingly and not without bitter grief of mind, and at the same time, as far as it can be done, to take care that another faithful and fit man succeeds him. But towards those people one ought to act with confidence and steadfastness and with public protest, by which the glory of God is vindicated, and so that those who can be healed may at some time have an occasion to think about their salvation, while to the obstinate and incurable a goad is applied, so that when the judgment of God comes upon them, their own conscience may bear witness to its justice. But we have said more on these matters elsewhere, and it would be superfluous now to repeat them all. Moreover, lest anyone should scorn the shaking off of dust as a ridiculous thing, since he saw it done by foreign and wandering men who were commended by no authority, private or public, he brings a most grave threat of punishment, which he amplifies by an example, saying: "I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on that day" (namely, the day of the last judgment, as he himself explains in Matthew) "than for that city." The history of the Sodomites is described in Genesis, where the men are said to have been most wicked and sinners before the Lord, so that their cry rose up to the Lord. Ezekiel defines their sins as pride, abundance of bread, prosperity and idleness, and that they did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy, but abused these things for their own lust, and committed abominations before the Lord; by which he means, of course, the horrible crime of male lust, unworthy of Christian ears, whose shameful example they gave in excess on that night, which was their last, when, besieging Lot's house, they demanded that the angels, who were guests, be given to them for this wicked lust. On account of these crimes, at the rising of the sun, with a new and unheard-of example, they were burned from heaven by fire and brimstone sent down, together with the neighbouring cities and the whole region; and in place of the land which had before been like a paradise there succeeded a lake smelling of bitumen and sulphur, which (as even profane writers relate) bears witness at the same time to the crimes of that place's people and to their punishment. Therefore, whenever the prophets accuse the people of horrible shameful deeds and threaten them with punishments of no common kind, they are accustomed to recall this example, as Isaiah did against the Babylonians, whom he foresaw in spirit would be the burning destroyers of the Church; Jeremiah against the Edomites; Zephaniah against the Moabites and Ammonites, nations most hostile to the people of God. Indeed, whenever they rise up more loudly against the sins of the Jews, they bring forward the same example. These things, however, are to be observed for this purpose: that we may learn that among sins there is none more atrocious than contempt of the Word, which will easily be clear if you consider the sins of the Sodomites, to which nevertheless Christ pronounces a milder and more tolerable judgment than against the despisers of his word. But since we made this comparison in our commentary on Mark, we do not wish to repeat it here. Let all now learn, and above all those who hold magistracy, that the safety and peace of the commonwealth consist in this: that the word of peace is admitted, which elsewhere is called the sceptre of the Messiah. Therefore this is an incomparable benefit of God, that although the sins of Sodom reign today, he nevertheless defers the punishments, and in the meantime deigns to offer us his grace and peace. Therefore, since salvation is dear to us both private and public, let us admit the message of peace, so that we may both avoid the dire punishments prepared for its despisers and obtain true salvation in Christ Jesus. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA. XCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 99.

units.la: Væ tibi Chorazin, væ tibi Bethsaida: nam si in Tyro & Sidone ædi-tæ fuissent virtutes, quæ ædițæ sunt apud vos, olim cum sacco & cinere sedentes resipuissent. Veruntamen Tyro & Sidoni tolerabilius erit in iu-dicio, quàm vobis. Et tu Capernaum, quæ usq; ad cœlum sublata es, vsq; ad inferos deprimeris. Qui vos audit, me audit: & qui vos reiicit, me re-iicit: qui verò me reiicit, reiicit eum, qui misit me.
units.tr: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, who are lifted up to heaven, will be brought down to hell. He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; but he who rejects me rejects him who sent me.

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster Iesus Christus discipulos suos in prædicandi munere diligenter insti-tuit, postremò grauissimam tulit in doctrina ipsorum contemptores sententiam. Docet ea nullum peccatum grauius esse, quàm cum Euangelij contemnitur, eò quod in hoc cum multis alijs sceleribus contemptus gratiæ Dei, quam ù nobis per Euangelium in Filio suo offert, concurrit, qui homines omnino inexcusabiles reddit. Deinde admonemur, Rerumpub. salute maximè in hoc consistere, vt doctrina de Christo & per hunc facta humani generis redemptione locû deut, & vt huic sese omnes per fidei obedientiam subijciant. Caeterum ne hæc inania verba videréntur, sententia hanc nunc exemplis vrbium Galilææ confirmat, quibus hucusq; sine fructu prædicarat, & ideo illis horrendum illud Væ denuntiat, quo omnes tam huius quàm futuri seculi pœnæ comprehenduntur. Estq; hæc actio Christi admiratione & consideratione dignißima, eò quod vt diuus deuouet totas ciuitates, qui ideo in mundum venerat, vt nobis benedictionem & salutem afferret. Sed occasionem illi præbuit præsens hæc discipulorum ad Iudææ vrbes ablegatio. Inter hanc enim animo voluens illarum ciuitatum contumaciam & ingratitudinem, in quibus tam diû docendo nihil profecerat, ab ijs discedens nunquàm rediturus, illis ut dignae erant valedicit, ut nimirum loco benedictionis maledictionem relinquat. Est ergo hoc exemplum in primis horrendum, quo docemur, Christum si ab aliquibus per incredulitatem pellitur, simul suam ab illis gratiam & benedictionem auferre, relinquere aut maledictionem, quam aeternum exitium comitatur. Quod utinam cogitarent diligentius, qui disciplinae Christianae cadio, vel odio potius moti, felicitatem summam sibi ex eo pollicentur, si Euangelij praedicatione ab se repellere possint. Simul autem Christus hic suo exemplo confirmat praeceptum de puluerus excussione, & verbi sui administros docet, ut constanti animo contra incurabiles quoque luctentur, neque ab illis discedant absque diserta iudicij divini denuntiatione, quod subituri sint, si tales esse pergant. Sed singulas huius loci partes videamus.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had carefully instructed his disciples in the office of preaching, he at last pronounced the most serious sentence on those who despised their teaching. He teaches that no sin is graver than contempt for the Gospel, because in it, along with many other crimes, there meets contempt for the grace of God, which he offers us through the Gospel in his Son, and which makes people wholly inexcusable. Then we are reminded that the welfare of the commonwealth consists chiefly in this: that the doctrine concerning Christ, and the redemption of the human race accomplished through him, should have its place, and that all should submit themselves to it in obedient faith. But lest these words should seem empty, the sentence now confirms them by the examples of the cities of Galilee, to which he had hitherto preached without fruit, and so he pronounces upon them that dreadful Woe, by which all the punishments of both this age and the age to come are comprehended. This action of Christ is most worthy of wonder and reflection, in that he, who came into the world so that he might bring us blessing and salvation, curses whole cities as the divine one. But the occasion was given by the present sending of the disciples to the cities of Judea. For while he was turning over in his mind the obstinacy and ingratitude of those cities, in which he had taught for so long with no result, and departing from them never to return, he bids them farewell as they deserved, leaving a curse in place of a blessing. This example is therefore most dreadful, and teaches us that if Christ is driven away by some through unbelief, he at the same time takes away from them his grace and blessing, and leaves behind a curse, which is accompanied by eternal destruction. Would that those who, moved by hatred, or rather by a fall from Christian discipline, promise themselves the highest happiness if they can drive the preaching of the Gospel away from themselves, would think about this more carefully! At the same time Christ here confirms by his example the precept about shaking off the dust, and teaches his ministers of the word to struggle with a steadfast mind even against the incurable, and not to depart from them without a clear declaration of the divine judgment which they will undergo if they persist in being such. But let us look at the individual parts of this passage.

units.la: Primò duas urbes coniungit, dicens: Vae tibi Chorazin, vae tibi Bethsaida, &c. Venit ad lacum Tiberiadis, qui & Genezareth dicitur, sita fuit, quem tractu ante alia Iudaeae & Galilaeae loca Christi praedicatione illustratum fuisse, ex Matth. 4. cap. colligitur. Fuit autem Bethsaida Ioannis & Iacobi patria, qui inter Apostolos non postremi fuerunt. Verum tamen urbi, quasi veteris consuetudinis & in ea collatorum beneficiorum oblitus, vae illud dirum imprecatur. Causa huius execrationis est, quod hucusque non respuerint ad ipsius miracula & praedicatione. Et ne quid possint praexere, addit: Nam si in Tyro & Sidone editae fuissent virtutes, quae editae sunt apud vos, olim cum sacco & cinere sedentes, resipuissent. Fuerunt autem Tyrus & Sidon civitates extra Iudaeae fines, in quibus idololatria & superstitiones regnabant, propter situ vero nobilissimae emporijs, adhaec coloniis quoque, quas in omnes prope orbis habitati partes deduxerunt, ut prophani etiam scriptores testantur. Sed ut fieri solet, commercia cum omnibus gentibus divitias immodicas, hae vero luxum, faustum & turpissimam omnis disciplinae morumque corruptela pepererunt. Sape ergo punitae sunt a Domino. Et Tyri quidem per Nabuchodonosorem expugnata Ezechiel meminit, quo tempore Sidone quoque extrema passam fuisse non est dubium. Instaurata tamen ad pristinos mores redierunt, quare rursus manum suam Deus ad percutiendum extendit. Itaque Sidon cum a Persis defectionem fecisset, et Aegyptios cum alijs multis in societate pellexisset, ab Artaxerxe Ocho per proditionem capta est. Quod ubi cives animaduerterunt, incensis domibus vniuersis, simul omnes cum uxoribus & liberis horribiliter perierunt, ne in hostium potestatem venirent. Inde post sedecim annos Alexander Magnus contra Persas bellum gerens Tyrum post longam obsidionem coepit, in cuius expugnatione octo milia civium crudeliter caesa, triginta autem millia in seruitutem vendita sunt. Veruntamen tanta fuit loci & situs commoditas, ut rursus extrui & habitari coeperint, eadem vero commoditas cum dimittis pristinos quoque mores reduxit, quos non ante reliquerunt, quam irreparabili excidio delta sunt. Cum his confert duarum civitatum, Chorazin & Bethsaidae habitatores, ut eorum contumaciam & ingratitudinem magis amplificet, & simul Iudaeos omnes acrius pungat, qui se solos gentem sanctam esse gloriabantur, reliquos autem omnes prae se contemnebant, cum ipsi interim ijsdem, quibus propbana gentes moribus viuerent, immo his multo esset deteriores. Fuit igitur hoc durum & graue auditu, eos qui in Dei peculio censebantur, infra gentes idololatras a cognitione veri Dei alienas & publicis sceleribus infames, deprimi. Non tacet tamen Dominus, quia illi sic merebantur, & iam tempus instabat, ut Iudaeis reiectis gentes in eorum locum adoptarentur. In primis autem virtutum, id est, mirabilium, in quibus diuina Christi virtus elucebat, meminit, ut plus quam stupidam incredulitatem illis exprobret, quae ne signis quidem expugnari potuerit, quibus ij quoque mouentur, qui a religione alienissimi sunt, & quibus milites aliquos in Christi cognitionem excitatos fuisse scimus.
units.tr: First he joins two cities together, saying: Woe to you, Chorazin, woe to you, Bethsaida, etc. He came to the lake of Tiberias, which is also called Gennesaret, and it is gathered from Matthew chapter 4 that this region was illumined by the preaching of Christ before the other places of Judea and Galilee. Bethsaida was the homeland of John and James, who were not the least among the apostles. Yet he calls down that dire woe upon the city, as if he had forgotten its old custom and the benefits conferred upon it there. The cause of this curse is that until now they have not repented at his miracles and preaching. And so that they cannot plead ignorance, he adds: For if the mighty works done in Tyre and Sidon had been done among them, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Tyre and Sidon were cities outside the borders of Judea, in which idolatry and superstitions reigned; but because of their situation they were most noble trading-posts, and besides they had colonies too, which they sent out to almost every part of the inhabited world, as even profane writers testify. But, as usually happens, commerce with all nations produced immoderate riches, and these brought luxury, pomp, and the most shameful corruption of all discipline and morals. Therefore they were often punished by the Lord. Ezekiel recalls that Tyre was indeed taken by Nebuchadnezzar, and there is no doubt that Sidon too suffered extreme things at that time. Yet, restored, they returned to their former ways, and so God again stretched out his hand to strike. Thus when Sidon had revolted from the Persians and had drawn the Egyptians and many others into alliance with it, it was taken by Artaxerxes Ochus through treachery. When the citizens noticed this, they set fire to all their houses, and all perished together, with their wives and children, in dreadful fashion, lest they fall into the power of the enemy. Then, after sixteen years, Alexander the Great, waging war against the Persians, took Tyre after a long siege; in its capture eight thousand citizens were cruelly slain and thirty thousand were sold into slavery. Yet the convenience of the place and its situation was so great that they began again to be rebuilt and inhabited, and the same convenience, once restored, brought back their former morals too, which they had not abandoned before they were destroyed by irreparable ruin. With these Christ compares the inhabitants of the two cities, Chorazin and Bethsaida, so that he may magnify their obstinacy and ingratitude the more, and at the same time sting all the Jews more sharply, who gloried that they alone were the holy people and despised all others in comparison with themselves, while they themselves lived by the same morals as the profane nations, indeed were much worse than them. It was therefore hard and grievous to hear that those who were counted in God's own possession should be cast down below the idolatrous nations, alien from the knowledge of the true God and infamous for public crimes. Yet the Lord does not keep silent, because they so deserved it, and the time was already at hand when the Gentiles were to be adopted in their place, the Jews having been rejected. Above all he mentions the mighty works, that is, the miracles, in which the divine power of Christ shone forth, so that he may reproach them with a more than stupid unbelief, which could not be overcome even by signs, by which even those who are most alien from religion are moved, and by which we know some soldiers were stirred to the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Vbi non est, quod cum curiosis quibusdam & prophanis disputatoribus quaeramus, cur ergo non Tyri potius & Sidonis Christus docuerit, & miraculosa opera fecerit apud eos, quos ad paenitentiam magis pronos esse sciebat? Et annon Deus author fuerit, quod duae ista civitates non fuerint connumerata, quando doctrina salutis eis no communicauit, sed in ignorantia eas perire passus est? Deus enim cum iudicio agit omnia, no quidem semper aperto (ut D. Augustinus ait) semper autem iusto. Deinde semper tenendum est, eandem esse omnium hominum conditionem: quia omnes in peccatis cocipiuntur & nascuntur, & proinde natura peccatores & in ire Dei sunt: Deus autem nemini quicquam debet. Quis enim (inquit Paulus) prior dedit illi, & reddetur ei? Si quem ergo praeterit, & gratia sua indignum iudicat, nullam illi facit iniuriam, cum is nihil praeter meritum patiatur. Si quos aut vocare & adoptare
units.tr: Here there is no need for us to argue with certain curious and profane disputers, asking why Christ did not rather teach and work miracles among Tyre and Sidon, whom he knew to be more inclined to repentance. And was it not God who ordained that these two cities were not counted among those to whom the doctrine of salvation was given, but who allowed them to perish in ignorance? For God acts with judgment in all things, not indeed always openly (as Augustine says), but always justly. Next, we must always hold that the condition of all men is the same: since all are conceived and born in sins, and so by nature are sinners and under the wrath of God, and God owes nothing to anyone. For (as Paul says) who first gave to him, that it should be repaid to him? If therefore he passes over some and judges them unworthy of his grace, he does them no wrong, since they suffer nothing beyond what they deserve. If he deigns to call and adopt some, those men ought to acknowledge his grace and accommodate themselves to his calling. But if they do not, the grace which God offers them in vain will turn to their condemnation. Therefore, he who justly passed over the Tyrians and Sidonians, so that they, paying the due punishments for their crimes, might become an example to the whole world, has no less justly set before those Galileans, whom he knew would be incurable, his Word confirmed by miracles, so that they might be more inexcusable, and might be taught by his example that they would be punished with heavier penalties, since the contempt of his Son and of his Gospel displeases God. We ought to acquiesce in these things, and not to penetrate into God's secret counsel in the ark, and it is fitting to summon that counsel to render an account. But since Christ himself did not wish to investigate God's predestination here, let us consider those things which properly pertain to this place.

units.la: Chorazin & Bethsaida.
units.tr: Chorazin and Bethsaida.

units.la: Tyrus & Sidon.
units.tr: Tyre and Sidon.

units.la: Cur non Tyri aut Sidonis Christus docuerit. & adoptare dignatur, illi illius gratia agnoscere & vocationi eius se accomodare debent. Quod nisi fecerint, in damnatione eis cedet gratia, qua illis Deus frustra offert. Qui ergo iusto iudicio Tyrios & Sidonios praeterijt, ut dignas scelerum poenas exoluentes toti mundo exemplu fierent: idem no minus iuste Galilaeis istis, quos incurabiles fore sciebat, Verbum suum miraculis confirmatum proposuit, ut inexcusabiles magis fierent, & graujoribus poenis multari docerent suo exemplo, quam di spliceat Deo Filij sui & Euangelij eius contemptus. Hos nos acquiescere, non autem in Dei arca na penetrare; & eam ad rationem reddendam vocare conuenit. At quia nec ipse Christus Dei praedestinationem hic excutere voluit, nos quae ad hunc locum proprie pertinent consideremus.
units.tr: Why Christ did not teach at Tyre or Sidon. And deigns to adopt, they ought to acknowledge his grace and accommodate themselves to his calling. But if they do not, the grace which God offers them in vain will turn to their condemnation. Therefore, he who justly passed over the Tyrians and Sidonians, so that they, paying the due punishments for their crimes, might become an example to the whole world, has no less justly set before those Galileans, whom he knew would be incurable, his Word confirmed by miracles, so that they might be more inexcusable, and might be taught by his example that they would be punished with heavier penalties, since the contempt of his Son and of his Gospel displeases God. We ought to acquiesce in these things, and not to penetrate into God's secret counsel, and it is fitting to summon that counsel to render an account. But since Christ himself did not wish to investigate God's predestination here, let us consider those things which properly pertain to this place.

units.la: Inter haec primum occurrit, quid in istis Dominus maxime desideret: Nimirum quod non resipuerint, quando ille praedicabat, & doctrinam miraculis prius nunquam visis neq; auditis confirmabat. Praecipuum ergo, quod in nobis etiam hodie Christus requirit, est poenitentia, qua conuersione a pecca tis ad Deum esse alibi docuimus ex eius verbis per Ieremiam dicentis: Si reuerti velis, ad me reuertere. Venit enim ideo in mundum Dei Filius, ut diaboli opera destruat, inter quae peccatis primus locus debetur. Quoad ergo nos in illis perseueramus & absq; poenitentia pergimus, ut Deo probemur impossibile est, etiam si quoad reliqua praerogatiuis plurimis & publica etiam dignitate commendemur. Exemplo nobis sunt Chorazin & Bethsaida, quibus si reliqua spectes, nihil defuit. Nam praeter ea, quae paulo ante commemorauimus, externa pietatis indicia no pauca habuerunt, ut multis alijs melio res videri possint fuisse. Nam quae multi alij hostiliter oderant & persequebantur, Iesum Christum, ipsa admittebant, audiebant eius doctrinam, tam hanc quam miracula admirabantur, & (ut in Euangelica historia est videre) saepe in publicam eius confessionem multi ex illis erumpebant. Sed quia non seriò ad Deum conuersi sunt, ut quam nobis in Filio suo offert, gratia constanti fide apprehenderent, haec tam dira & horrenda illis Christus denuntiat, et ethnicis facit inferiores atq; infeliciores.
units.tr: Among these things, the first thing that strikes us is what the Lord most desires in them: namely, that they did not repent when he preached and confirmed his teaching with miracles never seen or heard of before. So the chief thing Christ requires of us even today is repentance, which we have shown elsewhere is conversion from sins to God, according to his words through Jeremiah: "If you wish to return, return to me" (Jer. 4). For the Son of God came into the world to destroy the works of the devil, and sins hold first place among those works. Therefore, as long as we persist in them and go on without repentance, it is impossible for us to be approved by God, even if we are commended in other respects by many privileges and even by public dignity. Chorazin and Bethsaida are examples for us. If you look at their other qualities, nothing was lacking to them. For apart from the things we mentioned a little earlier, they had no small outward signs of piety, so that many others might seem to have been in a better state than they were. For they admitted into their homes those whom many others hated and persecuted with hostility, namely Jesus Christ. They listened to his teaching and marvelled at his miracles, and (as can be seen in the Gospel history) many of them often broke out into public confession of him. But because they were not seriously converted to God, so as to lay hold with constant faith on the grace offered to them in his Son, Christ pronounces these dire and dreadful threats against them, and makes them inferior and more wretched even than the heathen.

units.la: Docet igitur suo exemplo Dominus, quis etiam hodie finis sive scopus verbi sui administris propositus esse debeat: Is videlicet, ut populus vere & ex animo a peccatis & superstitionibus conuertatur ad Deum, veram pietate colat, innocentiae & sanctitati studeat. Hoc Prophetas olim in suis concionibus potissimum egisse scimus. Ab eade doctrina Ioannes Bapt. primus noui Testamenti minister, exorsus est, quando Messiae venturo via praeparabat. Inde etiam praedicandi initiu Christus fecit; & Apostolos suos facere iussit. Imitentur ergo haec tantorum seruorum Dei exempla ij quibus docendi munus est creditum. Quod ut faciant, publici mores & quae apud omnes ordines regnant flagitia, eos admonere possunt. Quis enim ta caecus & stupidus est, ut non videat nouissima tempora haec esse in quae incidimus? Fiut enim quaecunq; de illis prophetae olim, & postea Christus & Apostoli praedixerunt. Inflent ergo tuba verbi Dei, peccata arguat sancta dicedi libertate, securos & dormientes excitent, cotumaces accusent & increpet, cunctantes vrgeat, impijs vero & incurabilibus horrendum Dei iudicium & poenas meritas denuntiet. Quod nisi fecerint no aliquis praetextus illos excusabit, quo minus de ipsorum manibus illorum sanguine requirat Dominus, qui ipsorum incuria aut negligentia pereunt. Nihil ergo agunt canes muti, qui in solius gratiae praedicatione intenti poenitentiae doctrinam prorsus negligunt. Neq; probandi sunt, qui principibus & magistratibus seruiliter blandiuntur, & immodicis laudibus eos in caelos vsq; euehūt, eo quod Euangelio & ecclesiae Christi locu dent; inter rim vero eosdē luxu & libidine diffluere patiuntur, ad eorunde iniquissimas exactiones, immodicu fastu, bella no necessaria, rapinas aliaq; teterrima scelera turpiter coniuent. No ita olim Prophetae egerunt, neq; ita olim Apostoli egissent, si principes habuissent, qui Christianu nomen profiterentur. Magnum quidem & praeclarū est, o principes Christiani, quod Christo aduentanti portas aperitis, quod ecclesiae eius afflictae & exulanti hospitiu praebetis, quod eiusde nutritios agitis. Sed plus quiddam a vobis requiritur: nimirum ut ipsi quoq; Filium Dei osculemini, ut eidem seruiatis cu timore, & exultetis cum tremore. De his vos olim regius ille Psaltes admonuit, quibus vera & seria conuersio ad Deum & vita verè Christiana comprehenduntur. Quod autem principibus dicitur, hoc ipsum singuli ciuitates & qui in his agunt populi sibi dictum cogitent. Praeclarum est Euangelium audire, ex eius praescripto reformatione ecclesiae instituere, abusus tollere, & alia facere, quae illo docentur. Sed ad salutem aeterna nihil haec omnia faciunt, nisi poenitentia & vita accedat, quae Euangelicae professioni respondeat. Alioqui Turcis deteriores iudicabimur, qui cum a vera Christi cognitione alieni sint, vitam tamen viuunt honestiorem & sanctiorem, quam multi faciant, qui Christia no nomine & Euangelij doctrina gloriantur.
units.tr: The Lord therefore teaches by his example what end or aim should be set before the ministers of his Word even today. That aim is, namely, that the people be truly and from the heart converted from sins and superstitions to God, that they worship him in true piety and strive after innocence and holiness. We know that the prophets above all pursued this aim in their sermons in former times. John the Baptist, the first minister of the New Testament, began with this same teaching when he prepared the way for the coming Messiah. From this beginning Christ also started to preach, and he commanded his apostles to do likewise. Let those to whom the office of teaching has been entrusted therefore imitate these examples of such great servants of God. In order to do so, the public morals and the disgraceful sins that reign among all ranks can admonish them. For who is so blind and dull that he does not see that these are the last times into which we have fallen? Everything that the prophets once foretold about them, and afterwards Christ and the apostles, is coming to pass. Let them therefore sound the trumpet of God's Word, rebuke sins with holy freedom of speech, rouse the secure and sleeping, accuse and reprove the stubborn, urge on the hesitant, and announce God's dreadful judgment and deserved punishments to the wicked and incurable. Unless they do this, no pretext will excuse them from the charge that the Lord will require their blood from their hands, since those perish through their carelessness or negligence. Mute dogs, then, accomplish nothing, when they are so intent on preaching grace alone that they utterly neglect the teaching of repentance. Nor are they to be commended who fawn slavishly upon princes and magistrates and raise them to heaven with excessive praise, because they give room to the Gospel and to the Church of Christ, while meanwhile they allow those same rulers to waste away in luxury and lust, and shamefully overlook their most unjust exactions, their immoderate pride, unnecessary wars, plunderings and other most foul crimes. The prophets did not act so in former times, nor would the apostles have acted so, had they had princes who professed the Christian name. It is indeed a great and noble thing, O Christian princes, that you open the gates to Christ when he comes, that you offer a home to his afflicted and exiled Church, that you nourish her children. But something more is required of you: namely, that you too kiss the Son of God, that you serve him with fear, and rejoice with trembling. The royal Psalmist once admonished you about these things, in which a true and serious conversion to God and a truly Christian life are comprehended. What is said to princes, moreover, let each city and the peoples living in them consider as said to themselves. It is a fine thing to hear the Gospel, to reform the Church according to its prescriptions, to abolish abuses, and to do the other things that it teaches. But all these things contribute nothing to eternal salvation unless repentance and a life corresponding to the Gospel profession are added. Otherwise we shall be judged worse than the Turks, who, although they are strangers to the true knowledge of Christ, nevertheless live a more honourable and holier life than many who glory in the Christian name and the doctrine of the Gospel.

units.la: Porro audiamus qualem poenitentiam requirat Christus, & in quibus illa consistat. De Tyrijs & Sidonijs loquitur: Olim cum sacco & cinere respuissent. Dicit hoc pro veterum more & consuetudine. Solebant enim antiquitus in graviori aliquo casu & graviorus irae Dei comminationibus siue iudicijs, sacco, id est, veste strictiori & crassiore induti, & caput cinere aut pulvere conspersi luctu & poenitentiam testari. Accedebat bis, imo praecedebat plerunque vestium scissio, ut in Achabi, Niniuitarum & aliorum exemplis esse videre. Erant haec signa animi maxime dolentis & simul delicta confitentis. Ideo sedebant quoque in pulueribus, ut eo etiam gestu humiliatione animi testarentur, sine qua peccatorum agnitio & vera poenitentia non constiit. Et hac quidem apud Orientales in usu erant qui (ut aliás monuimus) affectibus magis abripi solent, & ideo in his exprimendis multa adhibet, quae aliis populis superflua aut ridicula videri possunt. Et si rem ipsam, de qua hic agitur, recte consideremus, nequaquam in externis hisce poenitentia vera consistit: quod non obscure Ioel Propheta docet clamans: Sed & nunc dicit Dominus, Convertimini usque ad me in toto corde vestro, ieiunio, fletu & lamento: et scindite cor vestrum, & non vestimenta vestra, & couertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum. Nobis ergo haec potius spectanda sunt, quae ceremonijs istis veteris significantur. Primum inter illa est vera peccati agnitio, quomodo enim de admissis poenitentiam aget, qui illorum atrocitatem ne agnoscit quidem? At quia nobis ipsis plerunque blandimur, peccatum quoque ipsum miris blanditijs & lenocinijs sese animis nostris insinuat, diligenti nostrijpsius examine opus est, ut ad veram peccati agnitionem veniamus. Illud autem verbo Dei adiuuare oportet, quae causa est, quod & speculum legis suae nobis Deus proposuit, & verbi sui administros instituit, qui inuitis quoque & reluctantibus illud ingerant, & ijsdem scelera sua ostendant. Itaque, in ipso limine (quod dicitur) offendunt, qui peccata sua argui nolunt. Verbum Dei fugiunt & eius praeliones odio persequuntur. Agnitionem peccati proximo loco sequitur dolor & animi contritio, quam Paulus dicit dolorem secundum Deum. Qui enim fiat, ut non totus horreat, sibi ipsi displiceat & toto animo discruciatur, quisquis videt quot modis contra Deum peccarit, & quanta ira eius magnitudo sit, quantumque dolor ad uersus omnes, qui eius leges transgrediuntur? Huc ergo pertinet quod modo ex Ioele de cordis scissione diximus, quae vestium dilaceratione significabatur. Et illa Dauidis: Nihil integrum est in carne mea propter indignationem tuam, non est pax ossibus meis propter peccatum meum. Nam iniquitates meae transcenduat caput meum, ceu graue onus, graviora sunt quam sim ferendo. Defatigatus sum in gemitu meo, fluctuare facio rota nocte lectum meum, lachrymis meis grabbatum meum madefacio, &c. Haec & alia his graviora sentiunt, qui ex vera peccati agnitione intra animos suos coterum: a quorum ingenio alienissimi sunt, qui cum se de admissis delictis poenitere dicant interim in omnem laetitiam & gaudia vix satis honesta, effundi solent. Contritio aut animi confessione peccati parit, quae Deo vel privatim & occulte, vel etiam publice fit, si ita rei necessitas, aut ipsius gloria pulsulet. Quia enim qui vere poenitent, ad Dei misericordiam confugere, & culpa suam iterum Dei deprecari solent: id sine peccatorum confessione fieri non potest. Et nisi haec fiat, neque intra animos nostros pacem habere, neque peccati remissione obtinere possumus. Docet hoc proprio exemplo Dauid, quando sic dicit: Cum tacere, putruerunt offa mea in fremitu meo quotidie. Nam dies noctesque ingrauescebat super me manus tua, versus est succus meus in siccitates aestiuas. At postquam peccatum meum tibi notum feci, & iniquitatem meam non celaui, sed dicerem: Fatebor contra me transgressionem meam Domino, tu remisisti iniquitatem peccati mei. Exigitur autem peccati confessio, quia per hanc coram Deo humiliamur, & cum iustitia eius quoque misericordia praedicamus. Ideo Ioannes Apostolus scribebat: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nosipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & nos purget ab omni iniquitate. Haec igitur vera & salutaris confessio peccatorum est, quae scriptura tradit, non qua homines superstitiosi in sacrificuli aures sua delicta deponunt, ut ab eo absolutionem siue remissionem accipiant, qui ne seipsum quidem a proprijs sceleribus liberare potest. Simul etiam discimus, quam male sua saluti consulant, qui peccata sua dissimulare & tegere conantur, cum potius illa, ceu nocentissima & letalia vlcera, Deo medico fidelissimo, retegere debebat. Veruntamen non sufficiant ista, de quibus hucusq; dictum est, nisi ab ijs quoq; omnibus abstineamus, quibus Dei oculos offendimus, & quæ carnis petulantiam accendere, ideoq; pœnitentiam impedire possunt. Qua ratione enim de fla gitiijs suis pœnitere & vitæ emendationem meditari dicetur, qui illa fouet, & noua veteribus quo-tidie accumulat? Ideo passim Prophetæ clamant, vt à vijs suis reuertantur qui peccarūt, & in Dei vijs atq; præceptis ambulent. Et hæc illa pœnitentia est, quam à nobis Christus per Euangelium requirit, & ob quā prætermissam Galilææ vrbes diris atq; extremo exitio devouet. In his ergo nos hodie esse oportebat, quando passim irati Dei signa apparent, imò plerisq; in locis ira eius & pœnæ scelerum sentiuntur. Sed actiones externæ, quibus plerique hominum occupantur, vtpote comessatio-nes intemperantes, chorea & saltationes lasciuæ, festa ad omne petulantiam & libidinem seruien-tia, immanis & barbarus vestium luxus, vsuræ insatiabiles, & infinita alia huius generis, satis offendunt, illos de peccatis suis & ira Dei vix vnquam adhuc cogitauisse.
units.tr: Let us next hear what kind of repentance Christ requires, and in what it consists. He speaks of the Tyrians and Sidonians: "They would once have repented in sackcloth and ashes." He says this according to the custom and usage of the ancients. For in former times, in some grave calamity or under threats or judgments of God's heavier wrath, people used to put on sackcloth, that is, a coarser and rougher garment, and sprinkle their heads with ashes or dust, to testify their grief and repentance. Tearing of garments was added to this, or more often preceded it, as we see in the examples of Ahab, the Ninevites and others. These were signs of a mind in great sorrow and at the same time confessing its sins. For this reason they also sat in the dust, so that by this gesture too they might testify to the humbling of the soul, without which the recognition of sins and true repentance do not exist. These customs were in use especially among the Easterners, who (as we have noted elsewhere) are usually carried away more by their emotions, and therefore in expressing them use many things that may seem superfluous or ridiculous to other peoples. But if we consider carefully the thing itself, of which we are speaking here, true repentance does not in fact consist in these outward things. The prophet Joel teaches this plainly when he cries: "Yet even now, says the Lord, turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning; and rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God" (Joel 2:12–13). Rather, we should look to those things that were signified by these ancient ceremonies. The first among them is a true recognition of sin. For how will a man repent of his deeds if he does not even recognise how atrocious they are? But because we often flatter ourselves, sin also insinuates itself into our minds with wondrous flattery and enticements. We need a diligent examination of ourselves, so that we may come to a true knowledge of sin. And this we must aid by the Word of God, for which reason God has both set before us the mirror of his law and appointed ministers of his Word, who thrust it upon us even when we are unwilling and resisting, and show us our crimes. Thus, to put it at the very threshold, those stumble who are unwilling to have their sins rebuked. They flee from the Word of God and hate its preachers with enmity. The recognition of sin is followed in the next place by sorrow and contrition of heart, which Paul calls "godly sorrow" (2 Cor. 7:10). For how could it happen that a man, seeing in how many ways he has sinned against God, and how great is the wrath of God's majesty, and how great the grief against all who transgress his laws, does not wholly shudder, displease himself, and feel tortured in his whole soul? To this belongs what we just said from Joel about the rending of the heart, which was signified by the tearing of garments. And there is David's word: "There is nothing sound in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head like a heavy burden; they are too heavy for me to bear. I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed swim, I drench my couch with my tears," and so on (Ps. 38:3–8; 6:6). These and other things harder than these are felt by those who, from a true recognition of sin, grieve within their hearts. Those are utterly strangers to such a disposition who, while they say they repent of the sins they have committed, usually pour themselves out meanwhile into every kind of mirth and pleasure, scarcely decent enough. Contrition, moreover, brings forth the confession of sin, which is made to God either privately and secretly, or even publicly, if the necessity of the matter or the glory of God demands it. For those who truly repent are accustomed to flee to God's mercy and again to beg God to pardon their guilt. This cannot be done without confessing their sins. And unless this is done, we can neither have peace within our hearts nor obtain forgiveness of sins. David teaches this by his own example, when he says: "While I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was dried up as in the heat of summer. But when I acknowledged my sin to you, and did not hide my iniquity, I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the Lord,' and you forgave the guilt of my sin" (Ps. 32:3–5). Moreover, confession of sin is required because through it we are humbled before God, and together with his justice we also proclaim his mercy. Therefore the Apostle John wrote: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:8–9). This, then, is the true and saving confession of sins that Scripture delivers, not that by which superstitious people lay their offences in the ears of a little priest, so that they may receive absolution or remission from him, who cannot even free himself from his own crimes. At the same time we learn how badly they provide for their salvation who try to dissemble and hide their sins, when they ought rather to lay them open, like most harmful and deadly ulcers, to God, the most faithful physician. Yet these things of which we have spoken so far will not suffice unless we also abstain from all those things by which we offend God's eyes and which can inflame the wantonness of the flesh and so hinder repentance. For how can a man be said to repent of his shameful deeds and to plan the amendment of his life, if he cherishes them and daily heaps new sins upon old? Therefore the prophets everywhere cry out that those who have sinned should turn from their ways and walk in the ways and precepts of God. This is the repentance that Christ requires of us through the Gospel, and for the lack of which he devotes the cities of Galilee to dire and utter destruction. In these things, therefore, we ought to be today, when signs of God's anger appear everywhere, and indeed in most places his wrath and the punishments of sins are felt. But the outward actions with which most people are occupied, such as intemperate feasting, lascivious dances and revelries, festivals serving every wantonness and lust, a monstrous and barbarous extravagance in clothing, insatiable usury, and countless other things of this kind, sufficiently show that they have scarcely yet thought about their sins and the wrath of God.

units.la: Non minus ergo nostri seculi hominibus loquitur Christus, quàm Galilæis istis, & contuma-cibus illis atq; pœnitere nescijs Verbi administri hæc intonare debent: Tyro & Sidoni tolerabilius erit in iudicio, quàm vobis. Etenim ipsis idololatris & Dei veri ignorantibus grauius puniutur ij, qui Dei Verbum contemnunt, & ad eius prædicationem non respiscunt. Videtur quidem hoc multis iniquum, qui hoc nomine sibijpsis blandiuntur, quod qualescunq; sint, Verbo tamen Dei locum dent, & in Christi merito salutis fiduciam collocent. Sed audiant illi Christum ipsis respondentem: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Item: Seruus, qui nouit voluntatem domini, nec se comparauit, nec fecit ex voluntate eius, cædetur multis plagis. Meretur præterea grauius iudicium iflorum hominum le-uitas, qua gentes & Turcas longe superant. Hi enim sue religioni serio student, & ne quid huius professione indignum faciant, cauent sedulo: at nostri illi religionem, quam profitentur, corruptissi-mis moribus & quidius agendi licentia prophanant, & apertis eius hostibus illudendam proponunt. Cur ergo non grauius puniantur? Nec est quòd de Christi verbis dubitemus, eò quòd tales fere in hoc seculo felices & beati sunt, & inter sua scelera impunitate perpetua fruuntur. Nam ad nouissi-mum iudicium illos citat Dominus, quando ad eius tribunal omnes homines sistentur, nec quicquā admittetur eorum, quibus in hoc seculo iudicia interuerti & corrumpi solent. Irreuocabilis autem erit, quæ tunc contra impios feretur sententia, neq; vllus pœnarū finis erit, ad quas damnabuntur. Horum consideratio semper ob oculos nobis versetur, & facilius carnis desiderijs resistemus, ar-dentiori autem pietatis zelo accendemur.
units.tr: Christ therefore speaks no less to the people of our own age than to those Galileans, and the ministers of the Word ought to thunder these things against the stubborn and those who refuse to repent: "It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you." For those who despise the Word of God and do not repent at its preaching are punished more severely than the idolaters themselves, who do not know the true God. Many think this unfair, and they flatter themselves with the thought that, whatever they are, they at least give room to the Word of God and place their hope of salvation in the merit of Christ. But let them hear Christ answering them: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Likewise: "That servant who knew his master's will, and did not prepare himself or act according to his will, shall be beaten with many blows." Moreover, the levity of these men deserves a heavier judgment, for in it they far surpass the nations and the Turks. The Turks take their own religion seriously, and they take careful pains not to do anything unworthy of their profession. But our people profane the religion they profess by the most corrupt morals and by license in acting as they please, and they expose it to be mocked by its open enemies. Why, then, should they not be punished more severely? Nor have we any reason to doubt Christ's words because such men are for the most part happy and blessed in this age and enjoy perpetual impunity for their crimes. For the Lord will summon them to the last judgment, when all men will be brought before his tribunal, and none of those will be admitted whose judgments are usually perverted and corrupted in this age. The sentence then pronounced against the wicked will be irrevocable, and there will be no end to the punishments to which they are condemned. Let us keep the consideration of these things always before our eyes, and we will resist the desires of the flesh more easily and be kindled with a more ardent zeal for godliness.

units.la: Porrò ad Capernaum transfit Christus, facta ad illam Apostrophe, vt grauior fit oratio. Et tu Capernaū (inquit) quæ vsq; ad cœlos sublata es, vsq; ad inferos deprimēris. Fuit autē Capernaum ciuitatum Galilææ celeberrima: nam ad ostium Iordanis lacu introeuntis sita, propter loci commo-ditatem totius regionis emporium fuit frequentissimum. Eam Christus sub initium statim prædica-tionis suæ sibi pra alijs delegerat, ceu statione, in quam se reciperet, & illic frequentissimè docebat: nimirum communi bono hominum, vt eius doctrina & miracula citius atq; latius vulgarentur. Ideo apud Matth.ciuitas Domini dicitur, quo non alius titulus nobilior ciuitatibus tribui potest. Mi-racula autē illic tot tamā prætlara ædidit, vt Nazarethanis inuidiam mouerint, vt supra Cap.4. est dictū. Verè ergo de illa dicitur, quòd vsq; ad cœlos sublata fuerit. Sed quid addit Christus? Vsq; ad inferos deprimêris. Quibus verbis partim extremâ ignominiam, partim excidium cum æternis inferorum supplicijs minatur. Apud Matth.causam eandem adducit, quam prius: vt verò incredu-litatem & contumaciam illorum magis amplificet, cum Sodomæis eos confert, & his deteriores fa-cit. Sed in Sodomis (inquit) facta fuissent virtutes, quæ facta sunt in te, mansissent vsq; ad hodiernū diem. Quin etiam dico vobis, terrā Sodomæorum tolerabilius erit in die iudicij, quàm tibi.
units.tr: Next Christ turns to Capernaum and addresses the city directly, an apostrophe, so that his speech may have more weight: "And you, Capernaum," he says, "who have been lifted up to heaven, shall be brought down to hell." Capernaum was the most famous of the cities of Galilee. Lying where the Jordan enters the lake, it was, because of the convenience of its location, the busiest market of the whole region. Christ had chosen it above the others at the very beginning of his preaching, as a base to which he would return, and he taught there most frequently, no doubt for the common good of people, so that his teaching and miracles might spread more quickly and widely. For this reason Matthew calls it "his own city," a title nobler than any that can be given to a city. He performed there so many and such remarkable miracles that they stirred up envy among the Nazarenes, as was said above in chapter 4. Truly, then, it is said of her that she was lifted up to heaven. But what does Christ add? "Shall be brought down to hell." By these words he threatens her both the utmost disgrace and destruction, with the eternal punishments of hell. In Matthew he gives the same reason as before, but to increase their unbelief and obstinacy further, he compares them with the Sodomites and makes them worse than them: "For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Indeed I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you."

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco, quæ summa sit ciuitatum & nationum gloria. Ea nimirum, si Christū pe-nes se habeant, & eius doctrinæ locum dent. Vt enim præcipua principū gloria est, quòd illos Deus sua Ecclesiæ nutritios constituit: ita ciuitatum & populorū non potest maior esse dignitas, quàm si Ecclesiæ hospitiū dent, imò Ecclesiæ pars fiant. Ita enim vere in cœlos euehuntur, & regni illius cæ-lestis ciues fiunt, quod nobis Dei Filius sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit. Potest tamen etiā de huius seculi gloria hoc intelligi. Nam Dei promissio est, Honorantes me honorabo. Nec obstat, quòd mul-
units.tr: Here we are reminded what the highest glory of cities and nations is. It is certainly this: that they hold Christ among themselves and give room to his teaching. For just as the chief glory of princes is that God has appointed them to be nursing fathers of his Church, so the dignity of cities and peoples cannot be greater than when they give a home to the Church, or rather become a part of the Church. For in this way they are truly lifted up to heaven, and become citizens of that heavenly kingdom which the Son of God has won for us at the price of his blood. Yet this may also be understood of the glory of this world. For it is God's promise: "Those who honour me I will honour." Nor does it stand in the way that

units.la: T tis exosi & inuisi sunt, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam sectantur. Asserit enim nihilominus illorum nomen atq; honorem Dominus, & sua ope eis adesse, vt per omnia obstacula eluctari possint. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, in historijs multa extant. Constantinus certe, qui primus Ecclesiae pacem dedit, immortalem gloriam & Magni nomen ex eo consecutus est, & jub eodem Romanū Imperium, quod prius tyrannorum ambitione & crudelitate dilaceratum fuerat, in pristinam digni tatem est restitutum. Idem de Theodosio dicere possumus, quem cum Christi & Ecclesiae negotium serio ageret, Deus in summam dignitatem extulit, & miraculosis ventorum atq; tempestatum turbinibus contra hostes, Eugenium & Arbogastum, iuuit. At quid veteribus exemplis immorari opus est, cum nostro seculo similia viderimus? Dedit renascenti Euangelio ante alias nationes locum Germania. At quis ignorat, quantū gloriae, dignitatis & authoritatis ab eo tempore illi accesserit? Nam vt alia omittamus, bonis literis exculta est, quae prius barbara erat, & eos viros dedit, quorum eruditio exteris quoq; admirationi fuit. Quotquot ergo patriam vere amant, & illius gloriae consultum volunt, in hoc sua studia & consilia conferant, vt Christi regnum inter nos firmum maneat, atq; reliquis scelleribus Christiani nominis professioni omnes respondeant.
units.tr: those who follow the purer doctrine of the gospel are hated and despised by many. For the Lord nevertheless affirms their name and honour, and is present with them by his help, so that they can struggle through all obstacles. Many examples proving this are extant in histories. Constantine, certainly, who first gave peace to the Church, gained from it immortal glory and the name of Great, and at the same time the Roman Empire, which had previously been torn apart by the ambition and cruelty of tyrants, was restored to its former dignity. We can say the same of Theodosius, whom God raised to the highest dignity when he earnestly pursued the cause of Christ and the Church, and whom he helped against his enemies, Eugenius and Arbogastes, with miraculous whirlwinds of winds and storms. But why should we linger over ancient examples, when we have seen similar things in our own age? Germany, before other nations, gave a place to the renewed Gospel. And who does not know how much glory, dignity and authority it has gained since that time? For, to leave other things aside, it has been adorned with good letters, which before were barbarous, and has produced men whose learning was admired even by foreigners. Therefore, all who truly love their country and wish for its glory should direct their studies and counsels to this end: that the kingdom of Christ may remain firm among us, and that all may respond to the profession of the Christian name by abandoning other wickedness.

units.la: Nam docet simul hic locus, quid eas vrbes & populos maneat, qui hanc suam dignitatem non agnoscunt, neq; fructus ferunt Euangelio dignos. Ad inferos vsq; deprimuntur. Quod in Capernaū impletum esse historiae testantur. Nam vt Iosephus scribit, in Galilaea primo coepit bellum, quo deinceps tota Iudaea miserē vastata, & Iudaei partim caesi, partim in totum orbem dispersi sunt. Vbi cordatus quisq; facile intelliget, quàm horrenda passi sint ij, in quos primus militum furor effusus fuit. Quid autē de Hierosolyma dicemus, quae cum ciuitas Dei diu dicta fuisset, propter Christum tamen occisum & Apostolos indigne reiectos excidium passa est? cuius historia vix aliquis absq; lachrymis legerit. Tito certè hosti & à vera religione alieno tantum horrore peperit, vt manibus in caelum expansis apud Deum protestaretur, se tantarum calamitatum authorem non esse, sed infelices illos se inuito sibi exitium accersere. Sic ad coelos vsq; propter doctrinae puritatem & fidei constantiam infinitis martyrijs probata, sublatae olim fuerūt Antiochia, Alexandria, Ephesus, Thessalonica, Constantinopolis & plures aliae in Graecia & Asia ciuitates. At postquam relicta doctrinae simplicitate philosophis, & horum discipulis, haereticis, locu dederunt, impijs contentionibus inter se commissi illorum locorum Christiani, tyrannis persecutoribus praeda sunt, & qui nunc in illis vrbibus habitant, aut barbara sunt Mahumetanae superstitionis maneipia, aut ob Christi qualemcunq; professionem crudeliter oppressi & omnium ludibrio expositi, nihil praeter gemitus & lachrymas reliqui habent, quibus suam miseriam deplorant. Sunt haec tristia exempla, in quae nos ò fratres Germani, assiduè intueri decebat, ne qui gloria & dignitate propter Euangelij doctrinam excellimus, tandem propter inutiles & superuacaneas contentiones & peccandi licentiam ignominia obruamur indelebili, imò ad inferos vsq; deprimamur, aeternis cruciatibus illic multandi.
