units.tr: For this passage also teaches what awaits those cities and peoples who do not acknowledge this dignity of theirs and do not bear fruits worthy of the gospel. They are brought down to hell. The histories bear witness that this was fulfilled in Capernaum. For, as Josephus writes, the war first began in Galilee, by which afterwards all Judea was miserably laid waste, and the Jews were partly slaughtered and partly scattered throughout the whole world. Any thoughtful person will easily understand from this how dreadfully those suffered on whom the first fury of the soldiers was poured out. But what shall we say of Jerusalem, which, though it had long been called the city of God, nevertheless suffered destruction on account of the killing of Christ and the unworthy rejection of the apostles? Hardly anyone can read its history without tears. Titus, certainly an enemy and one alien to the true religion, was struck with such horror that, with his hands stretched out to heaven, he protested before God that he was not the author of such great calamities, but that those unhappy men were bringing ruin upon themselves against his will. So too Antioch, Alexandria, Ephesus, Thessalonica, Constantinople and several other cities in Greece and Asia, which once were lifted up to heaven and proved by countless martyrdoms for the purity of their doctrine and the constancy of their faith, were brought low. But after they abandoned the simplicity of doctrine and gave place to philosophers and their disciples, the heretics, and the Christians of those places, having been drawn into impious contentions among themselves, became the prey of tyrannical persecutors. And those who now live in those cities are either the wretched slaves of Mahometan superstition, or, cruelly oppressed for whatever profession of Christ they still make and exposed to the mockery of all, have nothing left but groans and tears with which to lament their misery. These are sad examples, which it behooves us, brothers Germans, to look upon constantly, lest we who excel in glory and dignity because of the doctrine of the gospel should at last, on account of useless and vain contentions and license to sin, be overwhelmed with indelible ignominy, or rather be brought down to hell, there to be punished with eternal torments.

units.la: Potest autē & debet doctrina haec ad omnia alia Dei dona transferri, ne illis vel ad fastū inanem aut carnis illicita studia abutamur. Nā quo quis magis excellit, eò ignominiosius deijcitur & grauius punitur, si Dei beneficentiam non agnoscat, & eius donis non rectè vtatur. Exempla huius generis habemus in potentissimis Regibus, quorū gloria nubes transcendere visa fuit, sine verò consumeliosissimum sortita est. Quis Regum vnquā victorijs, regnorū amplitudine, potentia, diuitijs & dignitate Nabuchodonosor fuit gloriosior, quem Spiritus sanctus de Monarchijs mundi dissrens caput aureum dicit? At idem cum immani diffidentia & superbia turgidus diceret, Anno est Babylon, quam ego feci, mox ratione exutus in animal brutū degenerauit, & ex fuorū man. ius elapsus, longo tempore inter feras vitā transfegit? In Persica Monarchia Xerxes habetur, qui cum copiarū suarū multitudine fluuios exiccaret, montes perfoderet, maria nauibus cēu ponte sterneret, potentia aut illa ad opprimendam aliarum gentiū libertatē contra ius & fas abuteretur, a parua Graecorum manu profligatus, piscatoriā nauicula praesidio vitā seruare coactus fuit. Pertinent huc quae de Alexand. Magno, diuinitatis affectatore, de Iulio Caesare, gentiū dormitore, & multis aliis historici scribunt, in quibus omnibus illud Solomonis impletū est: Praeit cōminutionem elatus spiritus, & anteit ruinam superbia animi. Neq; desunt nostro tempore exempla, quae hīs possunt fidefacere. Nec minus ad priuatos homines ista doctrina pertinet. Quā multos enim est videre, quos sua eruditione eruditionis & eloquentiae fiducia in extremum exitium adduxit? Quàm multis opes immodicae interitus ignominiosi causa fuerunt, eò quòd illis licenter nimis abusi sint? Quot ite inueniuntur, quos virium corporis confidentia perdidit? Milonem Crotoniatae ferunt à feris immaniter discerptum fuisse, quòd iam senex in trunco arboris distrahendo vires pristinas experiri voluit. Et hodie huius generis exempla quotidie occurrunt. Cogitent ergo singuli, se nihil ex semetipsis, neque etiam aliquid proprij habere: adhaec propter innatam nobis naturae vitiositatem eò lubriciorem esse conditionem nostram, quò altiori gradu sumus constituti. Quòd si non contenti gloria, quam Deus concesserit, ad altiora aspiramus, fit quod Solomon dicebat: Qui exaltat domum suam, quaerit ruinam. Humilientur ergo omnes sub potenti manu Domini, & ab eo acceptis donis ad ipsius gloriam promouendam, & salutem multorum atque proprium vsum cum gratiarum actione vtantur.
units.tr: This doctrine can and should also be applied to all the other gifts of God, so that we do not abuse them for empty pride or for unlawful pursuits of the flesh. For the more someone excels, the more shamefully he is cast down and the more severely he is punished, if he does not acknowledge God's kindness and does not use his gifts rightly. We have examples of this kind in the most powerful kings, whose glory seemed to rise above the clouds, yet who met with a most disgraceful end. Which of the kings was ever more glorious in victories, in the extent of his kingdoms, in power, riches and dignity than Nebuchadnezzar, whom the Holy Spirit, distinguishing the monarchies of the world, calls the golden head? Yet he, swollen with monstrous self-confidence and pride, said, "Is not this great Babylon which I have built?" Soon afterwards he was stripped of his reason, degenerated into a brutish animal, escaped from the hands of his men, and spent a long time among the wild beasts. In the Persian monarchy there is Xerxes, who, with his vast multitude of forces, dried up rivers, dug through mountains, and laid bridges of ships across the seas. He used that power to crush the freedom of other nations, contrary to right and law, but he was routed by a small Greek force and was forced to save his life in a little fishing boat. What historians write about Alexander the Great, a pretender to divinity, about Julius Caesar, the subduer of the nations, and about many others belongs here too, for in all of them that saying of Solomon has been fulfilled: "Before destruction a haughty spirit goes, and before a fall a proud mind." Nor are examples lacking in our own time that can confirm these things. Nor does this teaching pertain less to private persons. For how many are there to be seen whom confidence in their learning and eloquence has brought to utter ruin? How many have had immoderate wealth as the cause of a shameful destruction, because they abused it too freely? How many are found whom confidence in bodily strength has destroyed? They say that Milo of Croton was savagely torn apart by wild beasts, because in his old age he wished to test his former strength by splitting the trunk of a tree. And today examples of this kind meet us every day. Let each one consider that he has nothing from himself, nor anything of his own. Moreover, because of the vice innate in our nature, our condition is the more slippery the higher the rank in which we are placed. But if we are not content with the glory that God has granted and aspire to higher things, what Solomon said comes to pass: "He who exalts his house seeks ruin." Let all therefore be humbled under the mighty hand of the Lord, and let them receive his gifts and use them with thanksgiving, to promote his glory, the salvation of many, and their own proper good.

units.la: Caeterùm ad Christi verba redeamus, qui ad discipulos simul omnes conuersus totâ hanc tractationem graui sententia concludit, dicens: Qui vos audit, me audit: & qui vos reiicit, me reiicit: qui verò me reiicit, reiicit eum qui misit me. Quibus verbis partim causam reddit dirae illius execrationis, qua vrbes ingratas & cotumaces exitio devouerat: partim discipulos consolatur, vt se Dei praesidio tutos fore sciant, qui authoritatem suam non passurus sit in ipsis impunè violari. Fundatur enim haec sententia in iure gentium, quo legatorum contemptus & illa facta iniuria perinde vindicatur, ac si quis Regem aut principem ipsum violauisset, à quo illi missi sunt. Et ex historijs constat, magnâ adeò sacrosanctam apud omnes gentes legatorum authoritatem fuisse cùm pacis tum belli tempore: eorundemque vero violatione saepenumero bella cruenta peperisse, & multis exitij causam praebuisse. Tarentum certè, opulentissimam ciuitatem & omni praesidiorum genere munitissimam, hoc in primis perdidit, quòd Romanorum legatos iniurijs multis ciues eius affecissent, & illorum in hos ferendis patientia eò vsque effent abusi, vt quidam ex illis vrina quoque conspergeretur. Num ergo Deum in sua authoritate vindicanda remissiore fore putabimus, qui se zelotes esse publicè profiteatur? Porrò nobis huius loci duplex vsus est.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Christ, who, turning to all the disciples together, concludes this whole discussion with a weighty sentence, saying: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." By these words he partly gives the reason for that dreadful curse by which he had devoted ungrateful and stubborn cities to destruction, and partly he comforts the disciples, so that they know they will be safe under God's protection, since he will not allow his authority to be violated with impunity in them. For this sentence is grounded in the law of nations, by which contempt for ambassadors and the wrong done to them is avenged just as if someone had violated the king or prince who sent them. And it is clear from histories that the authority of ambassadors was so sacred among all nations, both in time of peace and in time of war, and that their violation has very often brought about bloody wars and been the cause of many disasters. Tarentum, certainly, a very wealthy city and fortified with every kind of defence, was ruined chiefly because its citizens had inflicted many injuries on the Roman ambassadors, and had abused the patience with which the Romans bore them, to the point that some of the ambassadors were even sprinkled with urine. Shall we then think that God will be more lax in vindicating his own authority, he who publicly professes himself a zealot? Moreover, this passage has a twofold use for us.

units.la: Primum, ne Euangelij doctrinâ propter ministros aut praecones eius viles & obscuros contemnamus. Quid enim vnquam in mundo contemptius fuit Apostolis, de quibus ipse Paulus scribit: Puto quòd Deus nos Apostolos postremos designauit, tanquam morti addictos. Nam spectaculum facti sumus mundo, angelis & hominibus. Attamen de illis pronuntiat Dei filius, Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Quid ergo hodie externum splendorem in verbi ministris requirimus? Quin potius Dei bonitatem nos agnoscere decet, qui cùm sciat nos maiestatis ipsius non esse capaces, Ecclesiae ministerium instituit, quo per homines nobis aequales & ὁμοιοπαθεῖς (vt Paulus ait) nos suam voluntatem edocet. Quod quàm necessarium sit, Israelitarum exemplo admonemur, qui cùm ad montem Sinai Deum propria voce concionantem audirent, eius tremenda maiestate perterriti petierunt, vt interpretetur Moses vicem. Quod cùm illis accidisset, qui horrenda prodigia in Aegypto viderant, & ante paucos dies per maris rubri vadum inter imminentes virium pendentium aquarum moles transfuerant, quid objecto nobis euenturum putemus, si suae vocis maiestate erga nos Deus proferat? Memineri mus ergo hunc illi cultum gratissimum esse, si ipsum per obscuros ministros nobis loquentem patienter audiamus, & Verbo eius voluntariū & alacre praestemus obsequium. Ita enim constat, nos non ab hominibus, sed à solius Dei authoritate pendere. Et vt subditi aut ciuis fidelis indicium est, si vilissimo apparitori aut praeconi, cum magistratus mandato ad se venienti fidem habeat atque obtemperet: ita ex eo apparet nos veros regni Dei cives, imò germanos huius filios esse, si Verbum eius audiamus reuerenter, etiamsi hoc nobis per contemptissimum omnium mortalium praedicetur. E contra, qui propter doctorem illud fastidiunt, cùm Dei Verbum esse negare non possint, ij meminerint, contemptum illum (quod hîc diserte docetur) in ipsum Dei Filium & Patrem redundare. Hoc vt nam diligentius expenderent, qui hodie indignius feruntur, si quando ab aequalibus suis, aut hominibus vel peregrinis, vel alioquin contemptis & obscuris liberius corripiuntur.
units.tr: The first is that we should not despise the doctrine of the Gospel on account of its ministers or heralds being base and obscure. For what has ever been more despised in the world than the Apostles, of whom Paul himself writes: "I think that God has displayed us apostles last, as men condemned to death; for we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men." Yet the Son of God pronounces concerning them: "He who hears you hears me," and so on. Why, then, do we look today for outward splendour in the ministers of the Word? Rather, we ought to recognise the goodness of God, who, knowing that we are not capable of his majesty, instituted the ministry of the Church, by which he teaches us his will through men who are equal to us and "of like passions" (as Paul says) [ὁμοιοπαθεῖς]. How necessary this is we are reminded by the example of the Israelites, who, when they heard God speaking in his own voice from Mount Sinai, were terrified by his awful majesty and asked that Moses should interpret in his place. If this happened to those who had seen the dreadful wonders in Egypt, and only a few days before had passed through the sea of Red Sea on dry ground between the overhanging masses of suspended waters, what do we think will happen to us if God were to address us in the majesty of his own voice? Let us remember, then, that this worship is most pleasing to him if we patiently hear him speaking to us through obscure ministers, and render willing and eager obedience to his Word. For thus it is established that we depend not on men, but on the authority of God alone. And just as it is a mark of a faithful subject or citizen if he gives credit to and obeys the most humble officer or herald who comes to him with a command of the magistrate, so it is evident that we are true citizens of the kingdom of God, indeed its genuine children, if we listen reverently to his Word, even when it is proclaimed to us through the most despised of all mortals. On the other hand, those who disdain the teacher for this reason, since they cannot deny that it is the Word of God, should remember that this contempt (as is plainly taught here) redounds upon the Son of God himself and the Father. Would that those who today take offence too readily, if at any time they are rebuked more freely by their equals, or by strangers, or by men otherwise despised and obscure, would weigh this more carefully.

units.la: Alter huius sententiae vsus est, quod salutis nostrae certitudinē & fiduciā confirmat, cuius promissiones in doctrina Apostolorum proponuntur. Poterant enim aliqui hanc in dubium vocare, eò quòd Apostoli nulla vel publica vel priuata authoritate commendantur. Et hodie audiuntur scurriles hominum prophanorum voces, qui per ludibrium quaerunt, quis nam ille Paulus, quis Ioannes, qui Petrus fuerit, quibus necessariò credi oporteat? Sed his omnibus antidotum Christus, aeternum Dei Filius. lius adhibet, quando hos suos praeconeš & legatos constituit, & seipsum in illis loqui testatur. Cum ergo vere poenitentibus & Christum fide syncera apprehendentibus ex Apostolorum scriptis peccatorum remissio & vita aeterna promittitur, hanc Christi vocem esse, & in coelis ratam fore non dubitemus. Rursus, cum iidem incredulis & poenitere nesciis aeternae damnationis sententiam intonant, haec quoq; Filij Dei vox est, quā nulla mundi huius potentia sive authoritas impedire aut retardare poterit. Et hae claves sunt, quas in Apostolis, Evangelij sui administris omnibus Christus tradidit, quarum usus in duabus hisce sententiis consistit: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, habet vitam aeternam: Et, Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: The other use of this sentence is that it confirms the certainty and confidence of our salvation, whose promises are set forth in the teaching of the Apostles. For some could call this into doubt, because the Apostles are commended by no public or private authority. Even today there are heard the scoffing voices of profane men, who ask in mockery who this Paul was, who John, who Peter, whom we must necessarily believe. But Christ, the eternal Son of God, applies an antidote to all these objections, when he appoints these men as his heralds and envoys and testifies that he himself speaks through them. Therefore, when forgiveness of sins and eternal life are promised to those who truly repent and lay hold of Christ with sincere faith, from the writings of the Apostles, we should not doubt that this is the voice of Christ and will be ratified in heaven. Again, when the same Apostles thunder the sentence of eternal damnation against unbelievers and those who do not know how to repent, this too is the voice of the Son of God, which no power or authority of this world can hinder or delay. These are the keys which Christ handed over to the Apostles, the ministers of his Gospel, and to all of them, and their use consists in these two sentences: "He who believes and is baptized will have eternal life," and "He who does not believe will be condemned."

units.la: Ergo hac Christi sententia, ij soli commendantur, qui ab ipso missi eius verbum annuntiant. Nam neq; ipsos Apostolos audire debuisse, si quid à Christi doctrina diversum praedicarent, ex Pauli verbu constat, qui Galatarum levitate corripiens, inter alia scribit: Etiamsi nos aut Angelus è coelo euangelizet vobis, praeter id quod Evangelizavimus vobis, anathema sit. Nihil ergo locum ipse ad eos, qui sui capitis somnia, aut aliorum figmenta atq; traditiones obtrudunt. Vendicat quidem sibi & suis Creaturis hoc dictum Romanus Pontifex. At Christus non alicuius hominis privatam authoritatem stabilire, sed Evangelij sui certitudinem confirmare & suis ministris fidem facere voluit. Si ergo se audiri volunt, si obedientiam absq; omni contradictione ab omnibus iure exigunt, agendum Evangelij doctrinam praedicent, ad unum Christum omnes remittant, sub huius sceptro ipsi quoq; humilientur, & ita omnus inter nos contentio sopita erit, & eò maiori honore dignos iudicabimus, quo in Christi gloria & meriti eius dignitate afferenda feruentiores fuerint. Quoniam vero vocem alienam protulerint, Christi meritum & gratiam Dei conculcarint humanarū virium & meritorum praedicatione, Ecclesiam deniq; infinitis traditionibus onerauerint, desinant sese pro Apostolico venditare apud eos, qui inter pastoris sui vocem & lupi vlulatu iam pridem discernere didicerunt. Quibus vero hoc contigit, ut Deo grati sint, Evangelium qua decet fide & reuentia audiant, & in hoc loquenti Filio Dei, Iesu Christo, sese obedientes praebeant, ut in ipso salutem veram & aeternam consequantur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore, by this sentence of Christ, those alone are commended who announce his word as sent by him. For from the words of Paul it is clear that even the Apostles themselves ought not to have been heard if they preached anything different from the doctrine of Christ. Rebuking the fickleness of the Galatians, he writes among other things: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you something beyond what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." Therefore this passage has no bearing on those who thrust upon others the dreams of their own head, or the inventions and traditions of others. The Roman Pontiff does indeed claim this saying for himself and for his creatures. But Christ wished not to establish the private authority of any man, but to confirm the certainty of his Gospel and to lend credibility to his ministers. If therefore they wish to be heard, if they demand obedience from all without any contradiction, let them preach the doctrine of the Gospel, refer all men to Christ alone, and humble themselves under his sceptre; and thus the contention among us will be laid to rest, and we shall judge them worthy of the greater honour the more fervently they assert the glory of Christ and the dignity of his merit. But since they have put forward another's voice, have trampled underfoot the merit of Christ and the grace of God by preaching human powers and merits, and at last have burdened the Church with endless traditions, let them cease to pass themselves off as apostolic before those who have long since learned to distinguish between the voice of their shepherd and the howling of the wolf. To those to whom it has been granted that they be pleasing to God, let them hear the Gospel with the faith and reverence it deserves, and let them show themselves obedient to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who speaks in this word, so that in him they may obtain true and eternal salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA C.
units.tr: HOMILY C.

units.la: Reuerti sunt autem Septuaginta cum gaudio, dicentes: Domine, etiam daemonia subjiciuntur nobis per nomen tuum. Ipse autem dixit eis: Spectabam Satanam, ut fulgur, de coelo cadentem. Ecce do vobis potestatem calcandi serpentes & scorpiones, & supra omnem vim inimici: & nihil vos laedet. Veruntamen de eo ne gaudete, quod spiritus vobis subjiciantur: gaudete vero potius, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in coelis.
units.tr: And the Seventy returned with joy, saying: "Lord, even the demons are subject to us through your name." He said to them: "I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning. Behold, I give you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice because the spirits are subject to you; rejoice rather because your names are written in heaven."

units.la: Quoniam salus nostra omnis ex morte Filij Dei, Iesu Christi dependet, cuius merito peccata mundi expiatur, nosq; ex eius seruitio & morte aeterna redempti sumus: sic ille mori voluit, ut mors eius minimè occulta, sed omnibus nota esset, ut illius fructus ad plures redundaret. Ideo ex Galilaea comitatu numerosum secum duxit, & iam Iudaeae appropinquans Septuaginta discipulos praemisit, qui regni Dei instaurationem in fortibus adesse nuntiarent. Instruxit hos variis praeceptis, & ea occasione simul Verbi sui contemptoribus graues poenas minatus est, adhuc ingratas aliquot atq; contumaces Galilaeae civitates exitio devouit, quod adipsius doctrinam & miracula nō respuissent. At hic cogitet aliquis: Quod si Dei Filius, cui in animos hominum ius est, docendo nihil profecit, nisi quod omnium fere odia atq; inimicitias in se provocavit, annon inconsultum plane instituum fuit discipulos hosce, homines rudes atq; rerum imperitos, emittere, qui errorum instar hinc inde discurrentes eandem doctrinam praedicarent? Quid enim hi aliud inde referre potuerunt, quam contumelias, verbera deniq; & vulnera apud eos, quibus Christi doctrina nihil molestius, nihil intolerabilius esse videbatur? Pergit ergo in instituta narratione Lucas, & ut illi legatione sua feliciter peracta ad Christum redierint, & quomodo ab eodem excepti & amplius instituti sint describit. Qui locus multa continet, quae & potentiam Christi divinam, & Euangelij eius virtutem commendant, simulq; nos in nostrae salutis negotio erudiunt.
units.tr: Our whole salvation depends on the death of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, by whose merit the sins of the world are atoned for, and we have been redeemed from his servitude and from eternal death. He wished to die in such a way that his death would not be hidden but known to all, so that its fruit might flow to many. For this reason he led a large company with him from Galilee, and, already approaching Judea, he sent the seventy disciples ahead, to announce that the restoration of the kingdom of God was at hand in its strength. He instructed them with various precepts, and on that occasion he also threatened heavy punishments on the despisers of his Word, and doomed to destruction some Galilean cities, still ungrateful and obstinate, because they had not rejected his teaching and miracles. But here someone may think: if the Son of God, who has a right over men's minds, accomplished nothing by teaching except to stir up the hatred and enmity of almost everyone, was it not plainly ill-advised to send out these disciples, rude men inexperienced in affairs, who would run hither and thither like wanderers and preach the same doctrine? For what else could they bring back from this than insults, blows at last and wounds, from those to whom the doctrine of Christ seemed nothing more troublesome, nothing more intolerable? Luke therefore goes on with the narrative, and describes how they returned happily to Christ when their embassy was completed, and how they were received and further instructed by him. This passage contains much that commends both the divine power of Christ and the virtue of his Gospel, and at the same time instructs us in the business of our salvation.

units.la: Primò Septuaginta illi cum gaudio redijsse dicuntur, & Christo Domino narrasse, quòd adeò nihil obstiterit ipsorum legationi & commissio muneri, ut dæmonia quoq; ipsis nomen eius in occantibus cesserint. Fuit autem hoc gaudium maxima ex parte carnis affectu permixtum, ut ex Christi responsione patebit. Interim si felicem hunc eorum successum cum eo, qui tunc erat, Iudææ statu conferas, & cum periculis, de quibus illos Dominus admonuerat, quòd nimirum instar ouium in medio luporum versaturi essent, illustre habebis diuinæ Christi potentiæ argumentum, euidens item eius protectionis aut defensionis exemplum, quam suis pascim pollicetur. Quod autem ipsis accidit, hoc ipsum Apostoli quoq; experti sunt, qui in vltima Cœna à Christo interrogati, nū quid ipsis defuerit, quando absque commeatu & externo præsidio ad docendum emissi fuerunt, sibi quicquam defuisse negant. Sunt hæc exempla obseruatu dignissima, ut ijs nostram fidem confirmemus, si quid ex Dei mandato agendum est.
units.tr: First, the Seventy are said to have returned with joy, and to have told Christ the Lord that their embassy had been so little hindered, and their commission so successful, that even demons yielded to them in his name. This joy, however, was for the most part mingled with fleshly feeling, as will be clear from Christ's reply. Meanwhile, if you compare this happy outcome of theirs with the state of Judea at that time, and with the dangers of which the Lord had warned them, that they would be like sheep in the midst of wolves, you will have a remarkable proof of the divine power of Christ, and likewise a clear example of the protection and defence that he promises to his own. What happened to them, the Apostles also experienced. When Christ asked them at the Last Supper whether anything had been lacking to them when they were sent out to teach without provisions for the journey and without external protection, they deny that anything was lacking. These examples are most worthy of notice, so that by them we may confirm our faith, if anything is to be done at God's command.

units.la: Debet enim hinc generalis doctrina peti, ijs qui in Dei vocatione ambulant, nihil obstare posse, quo minus perficiant quod ille ab ipsis effectum vult. Potest enim Deus solo nutu è medio tollere quacunq; ipsius voluntati resistunt, vt qui Dominus sit exercituum, id est, creaturarum omnium, quæ vel in cœlis, vel in terra, vel in mari sunt, imò spirituum quoque tam malorum quàm bonorum. Deinde idem ille in promissis suis fidelis & verax est, & quamus obstacula nobis obiiciat, id tamē nostro bono facit, ut fidei exercendæ materiam habeamus, interim nos supra quàm ferre possimus tentari non finit, & præter expectationem nostram leuia & iucunda reddit, quæ grauissima atq; no centissima videbantur. Exempla quibus hoc probetur, passim occurrunt, & memorabile in primis est, quod in liberatione Israelitarum ex Ægypto habetur. Promiserat Abrahamo Deus, fore vt ipsius posteri post duram seruitutē, quam in terra non sua seruituri essent, in terram Chanaan reuertērentur, eamq;, possiderent. Huic Dei decreto opponunt sese, quæcunq; tunc in mundo potentissima videbantur: Pharao nimirum Rex, cuius potentia (vt quidam vetustissimorum scriptorum tradiderunt) tunc longè lateq; extendebatur: Magi Ægyptiaci, qui summam sapientiæ existimationem sustinebant: præfecti regij, ipsorum Israelitarum ingratitudo & malitia, quæ Mosem à Deo prædestinatum liberatorem prius solum vertere coegit: & quod hæc omnia superat, cum post multas difficultates iam iter ingressi essent, mare rubrum sese illis obiicit, imminente ipsis à tergo Pharaone cū valido equitatu, vt miseros ad internecionē cæderet. Quis hic non dubitasset de Dei promissione? Quis inermes & non sarcinis modò, verumetiam mulierū & paruulorum turba impeditos, ex illis angustijs euasuros speraui sset? Populus certè, etsi prius stupēda opera Domini in Ægypto viderat, tamen quasi omnium oblitus, contra Mosem & Aaronē murmurare cœpit, & ipse Moses animi anxium ardentes intra se preces ad Deum fudit, quæ clamorū instar apud illū fuerunt. Num verò hæc omnia Dei decretum & promissam populi sui liberationem potuerunt impedire? Nequaquam. Imò mare ipsum scinditur, & vtrinq; instar muri solidi in altum surgit, ventus autem vadū exiccat, & Israelitæ quidem tutò ac pede sicco transeunt, hos autē insequentes Ægyptij cum Rege suo & toto equitatu aquarū fluctibus obruuntur. Ipsa ergo rerum natura Dei promissioni & in hac ambulantibus cedere coacta fuit. Adde huic exemplo alterā populi liberationē ex Babylone, & idē illic quoq; factum videbis. Dei enim promissio erat, illos post septuaginta exilij annos in suam terram reuersuros, & vrbē cum templo rursus ædificaturos esse. Huic promissioni obstabat populi per Babylonici regni prouincias dispersio, quæ tanta fuit, vt vix vnquā in vnū conuenire posse viderentur. Obstabat ipsa Babyloniorum monarchia, qua nihil tunc in orbe terrarū potentius habebatur. Accessit po stremi Regis, Balthazarus, impietas, qui Dei veri contemptum & populi eius odiū multis modis declarabat. Sed ecce præter omnem expectationē capitur Babylon, & Monarchia Orientis ad Cyrū deuoluitur, qui (vt Isaias prædixerat) Dei spiritu excitatus populo redeundi potestatē facit, & additis quoq; muneribus dimittit. Rursus autē in terrā reuersis & ædificare incipientibus opponunt sese vicini, & modo calumnijs apud Persas populū exosum facere, modò vi vrbs ædificatione impedire conantur. Vincit tamen Dei decretum, nec quicquā obstare potest, quò minus vrbs cū templo instauretur, & verus Dei cultus denuò instituatur. Quòd si priuata exempla requiris, Danie babes, qui cū à Deo rex Israelis designatus esset, aduersariū habuit acerrimū, Saulem, qui populū totū contra illum armauit, & eundē in eas angustias adegit, vt terra Israelitica excedere, & apud
units.tr: From this a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that for those who walk in God's calling, nothing can stand in the way of their accomplishing what he wills to be done by them. For God can, by a mere nod, remove from the midst whatever resists his will, since he is the Lord of hosts, that is, of all creatures that are in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, indeed of spirits too, both evil and good. Next, the same God is faithful and true in his promises, and although he sets obstacles before us, he does so for our good, so that we may have matter for exercising faith; meanwhile he does not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear, and beyond our expectation he makes light and pleasant the things that seemed most grievous and most troublesome. Examples proving this occur everywhere, and especially memorable is what is recorded concerning the liberation of the Israelites from Egypt. God had promised Abraham that his descendants, after a harsh servitude which they would serve in a land not their own, would return to the land of Canaan and possess it. Against this decree of God there set themselves whatever seemed most powerful in the world at that time: namely, King Pharaoh, whose power (as some of the most ancient writers have handed down) then extended far and wide; the Egyptian magi, who held the highest reputation for wisdom; the Egyptian officers; and the ingratitude and malice of the Israelites themselves, who forced Moses, predestined by God as their liberator, to turn back at first. And what surpasses all these: when, after many difficulties, they had now entered upon the journey, the Red Sea lay before them, while Pharaoh bore down on them from behind with a strong cavalry, ready to cut the wretched people down to the last man. Who here would not have doubted God's promise? Who would have hoped that unarmed people, hampered not only by baggage but by a crowd of women and little children, would escape from those straits? The people indeed, although they had earlier seen the amazing works of the Lord in Egypt, nevertheless, as if they had forgotten all of them, began to murmur against Moses and Aaron; and Moses himself, anxious in spirit, poured out burning prayers to God within himself, which were like cries to him. Yet did all these things have the power to hinder God's decree and the promised liberation of his people? By no means. Rather, the sea itself is divided, and on both sides rises up like a solid wall; the wind dries up the bed; and the Israelites indeed cross safely and dry-shod, while the Egyptians pursuing them, with their king and his whole cavalry, are overwhelmed by the waves of the waters. Nature itself, then, was compelled to yield to God's promise, and to those who walked in it. Add to this example the second liberation of the people from Babylon, and you will see that the same thing happened there too. For God's promise was that they would return to their own land after seventy years of exile, and would rebuild the city together with the temple. Against this promise stood the dispersion of the people through the provinces of the Babylonian kingdom, so great that they seemed scarcely ever able to come together in one place. The Babylonian monarchy itself stood in the way, for nothing in the world then seemed more powerful. To this was added the impiety of the last king, Belshazzar, who in many ways showed his contempt for the true God and his hatred of God's people. But behold, beyond all expectation Babylon is taken, and the monarchy of the East passes to Cyrus, who (as Isaiah had foretold) stirred up by the Spirit of God gives the people power to return, and dismisses them with added gifts. Again, when they had returned to the land and begun to build, their neighbours set themselves against them, trying now by slanders before the Persians to make the people hated, and now by force to hinder the building of the city. Yet God's decree prevails, and nothing can stand in the way of the city being restored with the temple and the true worship of God being instituted anew. But if you seek private examples, you have David, who, though designated king of Israel by God, had a most bitter adversary, Saul, who armed the whole people against him and drove him into such straits that he was forced to leave the land of Israel and, among

units.la: Isa. 45. exteros hospitio turu quaerere cogeretur. Sed nihil proficit Saul tyrannus, quàm quòd regno in extremū discrimē adductus, ipse propria manu sibi ipsi mortem consciuit. Dauid autē promissio diuinitus regno potitur. Sed dies me deficeret, si omnia huius generis exempla commemorare vellim. Nos potius illa nobis accommodemus, ut ex illo consolatione confirmatione[que] fidei petamus. Dei vocatio est, ut filium suum Iesum Christum fide constanti apprehendamus, et fidē illā intrepidè coram quibusuis confiteamur. Habemus praeterea promissionem Domini, quòd ipse Ecclesia sua semper praesens adesse eamque tueri velit, quodque verbum salutis nunquam ab ea recessurum sit, quò minus praedicetur. Neminē ergo vel Pontificū vel tyrannorū minæ atque conatus terreant, ut fidē hanc abnegare et ab Ecclesia deficere velit. Non fallet enim Christus, qui oves suas nouit et tuetur, et in aeternum non mutabitur decretum Dei, quo ecclesiae conseruatione et perpetuam Euangelij praedicatione nobis promisit. Quòd si quid nobis patiendum est ob fidei verae confessionem, beati sumus, quos Dei Filius crucis suae socios facere dignatur, et ut nos per crucem vincimus, ita vincit etiā causa quam tuemur, et olim nostra quoque memoria Dominus afferet. Possunt etiam priuatim ad sua vocatione haec exempla singuli accommodare. Laboriosa et periculi plena est magistratus functio, periculosior adhuc eorum conditio, qui in ecclesiae ministerio versantur: at cùm banc illi vocationem à Deo habeat, constanter ea obire debet, neque dubitare de illius ope, cui facile fuerit ea è medio remouere, quae prorsus insuperabilia esse videbantur. Sed ad Septuaginta discipulos redeamus, in quibus laude dignum est, quòd etsi gaudium eorum carnis affectu vitiatum sit, nihil tamen suae virtuti aut dignitati tribuunt, sed omnem gloriam in solidum Christo transcribunt, à quo potestatem illam aedendi miracula acceperunt. Non enim arrogantur dicunt: Daemonia quoque nobis subijciuntur: Sed addunt per nomen tuum. Christi ergo virtute haec omnia confecta esse fatentur, sibi ipsis vero nihil quàm ministerium tribuunt, cui ipsos ille destinare dignatus fuerat. Eadem Apostolorum omnium mens fuit et sententia, quibus intolerabile omnino fuit, si qui stulta et superstitiosa miraculorum admiratione decepti, diuinam virtutē ipsis tribuere voluerunt, sicut in Petri et Ioannis, Pauli et Barnabae exemplis est videre, quae Lucas in Actis describit. Turpiter ergo errant, et atrocem Dium iniuriam faciunt, qui propter miracula olim ab ipsis facta eos in morbis aut aliis periculis inuocant, neque vni Christo adhaerent, cuius virtute illi omnia fecerunt. At simul debet hinc quoque generalis doctrina peti, ut si quid à nobis praeclarē factum fuerit siue publicè siue priuatim, illud omne vni Deo tribuamus, qui nos hac gratia dignatus est. Nam ut in Psalmo scribitur, Nisi Dominus aedificet domum, frustra labores et molestia perfecerint, qui eam aedificare conantur: et nisi idem ciuitates et respub. custodierit, nihil quantumuis sedula custodum aut praesidum cura proficiet. Hoc qui non agnoscunt, ij fere confidentia elati, Dei donis insolenter abutuntur, et ita sibi ipsis exitium accerserunt, ut nuper prolixius demonstrauimus. Caeterum quia nouerat Dominus, discipulos non sine carnis affectu exultare, qui ne altius ascendere rent prohibebat, reprimit eos breui oratione, cuius partes sunt tres. Prima effectum verbi Euangelici et ministerij eius indicat, et ita obiter discipulorum affectum corrigit, qui sufficere putabant, quòd ex quibusdam priuatim daemonia ejecissent, non autem cogitabant, quid iflud porro dederet, et quid ipsis porrò effet faciendum. Docet ergo longius progrediendum esse, et hunc esse ministerij Euangelici finem, ut diabolus toto suo regno eiiciatur. Spectabat (inquit) Satanam, ut fulgur, è coelo cadentem. Quorum verborum sensus est: Nō nouū mihi est, quod dicitur, neque vos temere, ut incertus de euentu, emisi ad praedicandum. Iam pridē enim videbam Satanā ad Verbi mei praedicatione instar fulgurīs de coelo cadere. Hoc potius vobis curandum erit, ut indi possessione male occupata ille pellatur, et miseri mortales ex eius tyrannide liberentur. Est hic ipsignus locus, qui Euangelium ab effectu magnificè commendat. Per illud enim Satan è coelo, id est omni sua potestate et gloria deijcitur, quod non alia ratione fieri potest. Quoad sedes coelestes, iam olim deturbatus est, quando in veritate non stetit. Sed videri potuit priorem potestatem, adeoque coelos ipsos, rursus occupauisse, quando in toto orbe terrarum regnum obtinuit per falsam doctrinam, superstitionē, idololatriam, effrenem peccandi licentiam et immanissima scelera, quae vbiq; impunè grassabantur. Immo coelos sibi ipsis nouos fabricauit, quando gentes superstitionibus demetata cultus diuinos Dijs fictitijs exhibuerunt, qui nusquam in rerum natura erant. Ita enim (ut Moses et Paulus testantur) cultus ille omnis ad diabolum redibat, qui sub idolis et Deorum illorum nomine colebatur. batur. Ergo iam non cœlas modò in hominum animis occupauit, sed Deum sese fecit: quo nomine in scripturis princeps mundi & Deus seculi huius dicitur. Vt vero ipse per Christum deuictus esset, qui caput eius contriuit: Ita per Euangelij prædicationem regnum eius inter gentes quoque & toto orbe terrarum esse euersum. Facta enim mirabilis totius mundi mutatio, quando gentes relictis Diis suis & superstitionibus ad Christi fidem transfuerunt, quando cultus illi magnifici passim considerunt, quando oracula cessarunt, in quibus Satan summum sui regni præsidium constitutum habuit. Eò enim rem adduxerat, vt non priuati modò homines in rebus dubijs diuinos & fatidicos consulerent, verumetiam Reges potentissimi nihil inconsulto oraculo facerent, quæ diabolus vel per idola, vel per mulieres malo spiritu abreptas reddebat. Nonne ergo è cœlo suo deiectus esset, & regno suo prorsus exutus? Quod autem olim esse factum, hoc ipsum hodie etiam fieri videmus. Vbi cunque enim Euangelij doctrina admittitur, ibi mox idolorum cultus corruit, superstitiosæ opiniones in hominum animis intermoriuntur, coercetur peccandi libido, cessant denique omnia, per quæ diabolus sibi in nos regnum vendicat. Ex quibus apparet, eos demum in Euangelio rectè profecisse, in quibus Satan non amplius regnat, & qui studijs eius omnibus ex animo renuntiarunt. Qui vero huius imperium adhuc ferunt, aut qui superstitiones, idololatriam, scelerum licentiam & alia Satanici regni fulcra atq; præsidia renocant & instaurant, ij satis offendunt, se neque infelicem illam ty rannidem, qua Satan homines premit, neque redemptionis per Christum facta beneficium vnquam rectè agnouisse, & proinde Euangelium quoq; nunquam vere in animum admisisse. Quæ enim commu-nio lucis cum tenebris? Christo cum Belial? 2. Cor. 6.
units.tr: Isa. 45. ...was compelled to seek shelter among strangers. But Saul the tyrant achieved nothing except that, with his kingdom brought to the brink of ruin, he took his own life with his own hand. David, by contrast, was given the kingdom by God's promise. But the day would fail me if I wished to recount all examples of this kind. Let us rather apply them to ourselves, so that we may draw from them consolation and strengthening of faith. It is God's calling that we should lay hold of his Son Jesus Christ with a steadfast faith, and that we should confess that faith fearlessly before anyone whatever. We also have the Lord's promise that he himself wishes always to be present with his Church and to protect her, and that the word of salvation will never depart from her so that it cannot be preached. Let no threats or attempts of the Papists or of tyrants, then, terrify anyone into wanting to deny this faith and fall away from the Church. For Christ, who knows and guards his sheep, will not deceive; and the decree of God, by which he promised us the preservation of the Church and the perpetual preaching of the Gospel, will not change for ever. But if we must suffer anything for the confession of the true faith, we are blessed, for the Son of God deigns to make us partners of his cross; and as through the cross we conquer, so the cause we defend also conquers, and the Lord will bring it to victory in our own time. Individuals too may apply these examples privately to their own calling. The office of the magistrate is laborious and full of danger, and the condition of those who serve in the ministry of the Church is even more perilous; but since they have this calling from God, they ought to discharge it steadfastly, and not to doubt the help of him for whom it is easy to remove out of the way those things which seemed utterly insuperable. But let us return to the seventy disciples, in whom it is praiseworthy that, although their joy was tainted by a fleshly affection, they nevertheless ascribed nothing to their own power or dignity, but transferred the whole glory entirely to Christ, from whom they had received the power of working miracles. For they do not arrogate anything to themselves; they say: "Even the demons are subject to us," but they add: "through your name." They therefore confess that all these things were accomplished by the power of Christ, and they attribute to themselves nothing but the ministry to which he had deigned to appoint them. This was the mind and judgement of all the Apostles, for whom it was utterly intolerable if anyone, deceived by a foolish and superstitious admiration of miracles, wished to ascribe divine power to them, as can be seen in the examples of Peter and John, Paul and Barnabas, which Luke describes in the Acts. They therefore err shamefully and do a dreadful injury to God who, on account of the miracles once performed by these men, invoke them in diseases or other dangers, and do not cling to Christ alone, by whose power they did all things. But at the same time a general teaching ought to be drawn from this as well: that if anything has been done nobly by us, whether publicly or privately, we should ascribe all of it to God alone, who has deigned to grant us this grace. For, as is written in the Psalm: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who try to build it labour in vain"; and unless he himself keeps the cities and the commonwealth, all the careful watchfulness of guards or commanders will profit nothing. Those who do not acknowledge this, being lifted up with a kind of confidence, abuse the gifts of God insolently, and so bring ruin upon themselves, as we have recently demonstrated at greater length. Moreover, since the Lord knew that the disciples were rejoicing not without a fleshly affection, he restrains them, lest they should rise too high, with a brief reply, which has three parts. The first points to the effect of the Gospel word and of its ministry, and so in passing corrects the affection of the disciples, who thought it enough that they had cast out demons from certain people privately, but did not consider what this would further yield, and what they should further do. He therefore teaches that one must advance further, and that this is the end of the Gospel ministry: that the devil be cast out from his whole kingdom. "I was watching," he says, "Satan falling like lightning from heaven." The sense of these words is: "This is no new thing that is said, nor have I sent you out to preach rashly, uncertain of the outcome. For I have long been seeing Satan falling from heaven like lightning at the preaching of my word. You should rather take care that he be driven out of the possession he has wrongly seized, and that wretched mortals be freed from his tyranny." This is indeed a remarkable passage, which commends the Gospel magnificently by its effect. For through it Satan is cast down from heaven, that is, from all his power and glory, which cannot be brought about in any other way. As regards the heavenly seats, he was long ago thrown down, when he did not stand in the truth. But it could seem that he had again occupied the former power, and indeed the heavens themselves, when he obtained dominion over the whole world through false doctrine, superstition, idolatry, unbridled licence in sinning, and most monstrous crimes, which everywhere ran riot with impunity. Indeed he fashioned new heavens for himself, when the nations, led astray by superstitions, offered divine worship to fictitious gods who nowhere existed in the nature of things. For thus (as Moses and Paul bear witness) all that worship returned to the devil, which was paid under the idols and the names of those gods. Therefore he did not now occupy only the heavens in the minds of men, but made himself God; by which name in the Scriptures he is called the prince of the world and the god of this age. But just as he himself was conquered through Christ, who crushed his head, so through the preaching of the Gospel his kingdom has been overthrown among the nations also and throughout the whole world. For a wonderful change of the whole world has taken place, when the nations, having abandoned their gods and superstitions, passed over to the faith of Christ, when those magnificent cults everywhere ceased, when the oracles fell silent, in which Satan had established the chief bulwark of his kingdom. For he had brought matters to such a pass that not only private persons in doubtful matters consulted divining and prophesying oracles, but even the most powerful kings did nothing without consulting an oracle, which the devil gave either through idols or through women seized by an evil spirit. Was he not therefore cast down from his heaven, and utterly stripped of his kingdom? And what was done of old, we see being done today as well. For wherever the doctrine of the Gospel is admitted, there straightway the worship of idols collapses, superstitious opinions die out in men's minds, the lust of sinning is restrained, and finally all those things cease by which the devil claims dominion over us. From these things it appears that those alone have truly made progress in the Gospel in whom Satan no longer reigns, and who have renounced all his pursuits from the heart. But those who still bear his rule, or who recall and restore superstitions, idolatry, licence in crimes, and the other props and supports of Satan's kingdom, show plainly that they have never rightly acknowledged either that unhappy tyranny by which Satan oppresses men, or the benefit of redemption made through Christ, and therefore have never truly admitted the Gospel into their minds. For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or Christ with Belial? 2 Cor. 6.

units.la: At singularem considerationem in Christi verbis meretur comparatio, qua diaboli ruinam fulguri confert. Potest id bifariam intelligi. Primo enim fulgur subito emicat: ita Satan cum regno suo plerunque subito & præter omnem expectationem corruit, quando hoc maximè confirmatum esse videtur. Factum hoc tempore Apostolorum, quando regnum suum sic stabiliuerat Satan, vt nullis humanis rationibus euerti posset. Quoad Iudæos enim, his per Romanos suo cultu, qui totus in superstitionem degenerauerat, liberè vti licebat. Gentium vero idololatria eorundem Romanorum authoritate defendebatur: & hi (vt Tertullianus scribit) contra Tiberij voluntatem Senatusconsulto Christum damnauerant, ne quis eum pro Deo coleret. Sed ecce duodecim viri obscuri, ex inuisa Iudæorum gente egressi, Euangelium inter omnes gentes prædicant, & per hoc subito concidit regnum illud tenebrarum, quod tantu præsidijs Satan fulciuerat. Quod si ad nostra tempora accedas, idem videbis. Quis enim nescit quanta Pontificum vires fuerint, in quorum verba Reges & Imperatores iurare coguntur, vt reductas ex Iudaismo & gentilismo superstitiones atque sedes illius Romanæ potentiam tueantur? Accesserunt per omnes vrbes dispositæ monachorum, sacrificorum & nobilium Canonicorum præsidia, quorum erat cauere, ne qua mutatio fieret, aut ne quis contra receptas superstitiones vel mutire auderet. At quando Deus humani generis miseritus iussem Euangelij denuo accensam voluit, subito exorti sunt, qui magno zelo, nec minori successu, novum illud Satanæ regnum maxima ex parte euerterunt, & Ecclesiæ reformatio facta esset, quam nemo auus fuisset sperare. Deinde fulgur emicatio terribilis quidem est, & loca omnia penetrat, sed in momento euanescit: Sic quando è regno suo Satan deiicitur, terribiliter furit, & vires suas omnes exerit, vt vel tunc malum aliquod dare possit, cuius furoris exemplum cap. 9. vidimus: sed conatus iste momentaneus & euanidus est, eò quod neque contra Christum neque contra eos aliquid possit, qui huic per fidem sunt insiti. Debet ergo hæc fulguris & diaboli comparatio probè obseruari vt ex ea consolationem petamus, si quando Satan omnia in suam potestatem redegisse videtur, aut contra Euangelij prædicationem omnibus viribus insurgit.
units.tr: But the comparison by which Christ likens the devil's ruin to lightning deserves a particular consideration. It can be understood in two ways. First, lightning flashes suddenly; so Satan with his kingdom usually falls suddenly and beyond all expectation, when it seems most firmly established. This happened in the time of the Apostles, when Satan had so stabilised his kingdom that it could not be overthrown by any human reasoning. For as regards the Jews, they were freely permitted by the Romans to use their worship, which had altogether degenerated into superstition; and the idolatry of the Gentiles was defended by the authority of those same Romans; and these (as Tertullian writes) had condemned Christ by a decree of the Senate, contrary to the wish of Tiberius, so that no one should worship him as God. But behold, twelve obscure men, come out from the hated nation of the Jews, preach the Gospel among all the nations, and through this that kingdom of darkness, which Satan had propped up with such defences, suddenly collapsed. And if you come to our own times, you will see the same thing. For who does not know how great the power of the Popes was, in whose words kings and emperors are compelled to swear, so that they may defend the superstitions brought back from Judaism and paganism and the power of that Roman see? There were added through all the cities the garrisons, so to speak, of monks, priests and noble canons, whose task was to take care that no change should occur, or that anyone should dare to murmur against the superstitions received. But when God, having pity on the human race, willed the Gospel to be kindled anew, there suddenly arose men who with great zeal, and no less success, for the most part overthrew that new kingdom of Satan, and a reformation of the Church was accomplished, which no one at all would have dared to hope for. Next, the flash of lightning is indeed terrible and penetrates all places, but it vanishes in a moment. So when Satan is cast down from his kingdom, he rages terribly and puts forth all his strength, so that he may even then be able to inflict some harm, of which kind of fury we saw an example in chapter 9; but this attempt is momentary and fleeting, because it can do nothing against Christ or against those who have been implanted in him by faith. This comparison of the lightning and the devil ought therefore to be carefully observed, so that we may draw consolation from it whenever Satan seems to have brought everything under his power, or rises up with all his strength against the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Et huc facit secunda oratio-nis Christi pars, qua consolationem discipulis adhibet, qua illos aduentura certamina armat, dicens: Ecce do vobis potestatem calcandi serpentes & scorpiones, & super omne virtus inimici: & nihil vos laedet. Alludit ad verba Psalm. 61. vbi de pio sub diuinæ prouidentiæ alis delitescente, inter alia scribitur: Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis, conculcabis leonem atq; draconem. Hæc autem Christus peculiariter verbi sui administris accommodat, eò quod his magis quam alijs hominibus Satan insidiatur. Hunc serpenti confert propter nocendi cupiditatem, & quod primos parentes sub serpentis specie decepit. Scorpionem quoq; dicit propter singularem astutiam, qua in nobis circumuenientis uitiur. Vt enim scorpiones uestibus & leētis sese ingerunt, & cauda aculeo armatam indesinenter mouent, ne feriendi occasionem ullam negligant, adhæc recto & obli quo istu feriunt: Ita Satan miris blanditijs sese venditare & in ipsos animos insinuare solet, & no cendi cupidissimus omnem occasionem diligenter obseruat, & siue recta siue palam impia suadeat, non nisi hominis interitum quærit. Addit autem Christus, vim omnem inimici, vno verbo omnes illius vires & artes comprehendens, quibus nocere & hominum salutem euertere conatur. Huc ergo pertinent hypocritæ, sophistæ, tyrànni persecutores, impiorum consortia, & quæcunq; alia sunt eius generis. At omnia ista (inquit Dominus) nihil vos lædent. Ita vero eos excitat, vt in commis so munere constanter pergant, & inuicta fidei fortitudine aduersus diabolum & eius membra pu gnent, quando grauiora certamina instabunt. Nec vana fuit hæc promissio. Nam ex historiis con stat, Apostolos & viros Apostolicos per Euangelium diabolo & omnibus eius membris superiores fuisse: & quamuis tandem ab illis crudeliter occisi sint, ne sic tamen eos læserunt: In fide enim vera defuncti nunc in cœlis gaudent, in terris memoria eorum piis omnibus iucunda & sanctæ est, corpo ra vero in spe futuræ resurrectionis quiescunt, in qua & ipsa immortalitatem induent.
units.tr: The second part of Christ's words also bears on this. In it he comforts the disciples and arms them for the struggles ahead, saying: "Behold, I give you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing will harm you." He alludes to Psalm 61, where, among other things, it is written of the godly man who hides under the wings of divine providence: "You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you shall trample the lion and the dragon." Christ applies this especially to the ministers of his Word, because Satan lies in wait for them more than for other men. He compares Satan to a serpent because of his eagerness to harm, and because he deceived our first parents under the form of a serpent. He also calls him a scorpion because of his singular cunning, by which he works his way around us. For as scorpions insinuate themselves into clothes and beds, and constantly move their tail armed with a sting so as not to miss any chance to strike, and strike both straight and sideways, so Satan is accustomed to make himself agreeable with wonderful flatteries and to creep into men's minds. Most eager to harm, he carefully watches for every opportunity, and whether he urges something right or openly impious, he seeks nothing but a man's destruction. By adding "all the power of the enemy," Christ sums up in one word all his strength and arts by which he tries to harm and overthrow men's salvation. To this belong hypocrites, sophists, tyrant persecutors, fellowship with the impious, and whatever else is of that kind. "But all these things," says the Lord, "will not harm you." He thus encourages them to persevere steadfastly in the office entrusted to them, and to fight against the devil and his members with the unconquered courage of faith, when heavier struggles are at hand. Nor was this promise empty. For it is established from histories that the Apostles and apostolic men, through the Gospel, proved superior to the devil and all his members. And although at last they were cruelly killed by them, yet they were not harmed by it: having died in true faith, they now rejoice in heaven; on earth their memory is pleasant and holy to all the pious; and their bodies rest in the hope of the future resurrection, in which they too will put on immortality.

units.la: Interim admonet locus iste omnes Euangelij ministros, quos finis in suo ministerio ipsis propo situs esse debeat. Olim quidem Papa Alexander, eius nominis tertius, aduersus Fridericum Bar barossam Imperatorem verbis istis non sine publica Imperatoriæ Maiestatis contumelia vsus est. Cum enim ille ad pedum eius osculä supplex procumberet, Papa impuro pede illius ceruicem cal cans dixit: Super aspidem & basilicum ambulabis & conculcabis leonem & draconem. At nihil minus Christo in animo fuit, quam Euangelij sui præcones eiusmodi potestate armare, qua legiti mis magistratibus superbè insultent: sed eius voluntas atque mandatum est, vt diabolum conculcent gladio spiritus iugulatum, & regnum eius quod inter homines per superstitiones, idololatriam, falsam doctrinam & scelerum licentiam obtinet, euertere satagant, vt illius seruitio liberati vni Deo viuere & seruire possint. Ad hunc scopum omnes verbi administri collimare debent, neque vl lis Satanæ minis & conatibus deterreri, quo minus officium faciant. Quod si Reges & principes sese illis opponant, nihil tamen seditiose agendum, sed admonendi potius sunt subditi, vt vel obedien tia pia principum animos flectant, vel (si aliter fieri non potest) crucem patienter ferant, & in pa tientia sua animas suas possideant. At quod verbi doctoribus dicitur, hoc ipsum omnes Christiani sibi dictum putent. Nam singulis quoque perpetua cum diabolo pugna est, quam Deus ipse in pri ma rerum origine sanciuit, serpenti dicens: Ponam inimicitias inter te & mulierem, inter semen tuum & semen illius. Cuius inimicitiæ typus in eo habetur, quod & homines natura à serpentibus abhorrent, & hi vicissim hominum conspectum fugiunt quidem, sed tamen quandocunq; possunt no cent. Et Petrus Apostolus ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam pios excitans, hanc causam subjicit: Nam aduersarius vester, diabolus, tanquam leo rugiens obambulat, quærens quem devoret. At ne quis hæc audiens terreretur, mox addit: Cui resistite firmi per fidem. Cur enim diabolus timeant, qui hunc à Christo iam olim deuistum esse sciunt? Cur illius minis terreantur, qui per fidem Christo sunt in siti, petræ inuicta, aduersus quem ne portæ quidem inferorum aliquid possunt? Firmos ergo nos esse conuenit, neque aliquam timoris speciem præbere. Vt primum enim se timeri sentit improbus ille, mox cristas erigit, & sibi plenam victoriam pollicens maiori conatu contra nos insurgit. Multo mi nus ei aliquid indulgere debemus. Vbi enim pedem semel fixit, illico vlterius progreditur, & indul gentia nostra tandem in serpem ignauiam degenerans, illum indies ferociorem & nocentiorem red dit. Est hæc doctrina admodum necessaria hodie, quando cum dolus vires quoque & arma Satan exerit, vt Christi regnum euertat, & nos ab eo auulsos æterno exitio mancipet. Resistamus ergo fortes in fide, neq; dubitemus Dominum à nobis stare, qui (vt Paulus ait) bostem illum sub pedibus nostris conculcabit.
units.tr: Meanwhile this passage reminds all ministers of the Gospel what goal should be set before them in their ministry. Once Pope Alexander III, using these words against the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, did so not without a public insult to the imperial majesty. When the emperor knelt in supplication to kiss his feet, the Pope, trampling his neck with his unclean foot, said: "You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the dragon." Yet Christ had nothing less in mind than to arm the heralds of his Gospel with a power of this kind, by which they might insolently trample on lawful magistrates. His will and command is rather that they trample the devil, slain by the sword of the Spirit, and that they strive to overthrow his kingdom, which holds sway among men through superstitions, idolatry, false doctrine and licence in sin, so that, freed from his service, they may live and serve the one God. To this goal all ministers of the Word ought to aim, and they must not be deterred from doing their duty by any threats or attempts of Satan. But if kings and princes set themselves against them, nothing seditious should be done; rather, subjects should be admonished either to soften the hearts of the princes by pious obedience or, if this cannot be done, to bear the cross patiently and possess their souls in patience. But what is said to the teachers of the Word, let all Christians take as said to themselves as well. For each one has a constant struggle with the devil, which God himself established at the very beginning of creation, saying to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed." A type of this enmity is found in the fact that men by nature shrink from serpents, and these in turn flee from the sight of men, yet whenever they can, they do harm. The Apostle Peter, urging the godly to sobriety and watchfulness, gives this reason: "For your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, walks about, seeking whom he may devour." But lest anyone hearing this be terrified, he immediately adds: "Resist him, steadfast in faith." For why should those fear the devil who know that he has long since been conquered by Christ? Why should they be frightened by the threats of one who, being joined to Christ by faith, are an unconquered rock, against which not even the gates of hell can prevail? We ought therefore to be steadfast and show no sign of fear. For as soon as that wicked one perceives that he is feared, he raises his crest and, promising himself full victory, rises against us with greater effort. Still less should we indulge him at all. For once he has set his foot down, he immediately advances further, and our indulgence, degenerating at last into a serpent's sloth, makes him fiercer and more harmful day by day. This teaching is very necessary today, when Satan, with cunning, also brings out his strength and weapons, to overthrow Christ's kingdom and to deliver us, torn away from him, to eternal ruin. Let us therefore resist boldly in faith, and let us not doubt that the Lord, who (as Paul says) will crush that enemy under our feet, stands with us.

units.la: Tertia parte à carnis affectu, cui immersi adhuc erant illi discipuli, ad altiora eos Christus e uehit, dicens: Veruntamen de eo ne gaudete, quod spiritus vobis subjiciantur: gaudete verò potius, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis. Non prohibet aut damnat simpliciter & absolutè gau dium illud, quo tunc exultabant. Pium enim est gaudere donis Dei, maximè si his nos cum aliquo successu vti videamus. Sed vt diximus, quod in ipsorum gaudio ex carnis ingenio vitiosum erat, id corrigit. Est enim hoc vitium piis etiam commune, quod in externis & temporalibus Dei beneficiis haerentes, maiorum, quae nobis in coelo repositia sunt minus recordamur: cum potius per illa ad horum contemplationem accendi deberemus. Itaque re discipuli in hac daemoniorum electione acquiescerent, aut etiam paulatim aliquam de propria dignitate fiduciam conciperent, ad fontem omnis gratiae & salutis eos remittit. Electionem nimirum gratuitam. Alludit autem ad morem in civitatibus bene constitutis receptum, in quibus civium nomina in libris publicis describta habentur. Quo Moses quoque respexisse videtur, quando Deum rogabat, ut aut populo, qui peccaverat, culpam condonaret, aut suum nomen deleret de libro, quem ipse scripsisset. Et in Apocalypsi mentio fit libri vitae; qui ad regni coelestis & aeternae vitae hereditatem praedestinatos continear.
units.tr: In the third part, Christ lifts those disciples, who were still immersed in the affections of the flesh, to higher things, saying: "Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven." He does not forbid or simply condemn that joy by which they then exulted. For it is godly to rejoice in God's gifts, especially when we see that we use them with some success. But, as we have said, what was faulty in their joy because of the nature of the flesh, he corrects. For this fault is common even to the godly: clinging to the external and temporal benefits of God, they remember less the greater things laid up for us in heaven, whereas through those external things we ought rather to be kindled to the contemplation of these greater things. Therefore, lest the disciples rest in this success over the demons, or even gradually conceive some confidence in their own worth, he sends them back to the fountain of all grace and salvation, namely free election. He alludes to a custom received in well-ordered cities, in which the names of citizens are recorded in public registers. To this Moses also seems to have looked when he asked God either to pardon the people's sin or to blot out his own name from the book that he himself had written. And in the Apocalypse mention is made of the book of life, which contains those predestined to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and eternal life.

units.la: Quod si quaeras, quis aut qualis iste liber sit, non alium monstrare possumus, quam Iesum Christum, in quo nos priusquam mundus hic crearetur, electos esse, Paulus non uno loco docet. Qui igitur in Christo sunt, eorundem nomina in coelis in libro vitae descripta sunt. Eo igitur discipulos ipsos remittens Dominus, hanc ipsis gaudii omnis materiam esse debere docet, quod Deus ipsos ab aeterno elegerit, & quod per Evangelii praedicationem vocati, electionis suae certissimam testeram habeant, fidem, per quam ipsi insiti & cives regni coelorum facti sint. Hoc verum & solidum Christiani hominis gaudium est, quod Apostolus nobis saepius commendat, quando nos semper gaudere iubet in Domino.
units.tr: But if you ask what sort of book this is, or who it is, we can show no other than Jesus Christ, in whom, as Paul teaches in more than one place, we were chosen before this world was created. Therefore those who are in Christ have their names written in heaven in the book of life. Sending the disciples back to this, the Lord teaches that this must be for them the whole matter of joy: that God chose them from eternity, and that, called through the preaching of the Gospel, they have the most certain testimony of their election, namely the faith by which they have been ingrafted and made citizens of the kingdom of heaven. This is the true and solid joy of a Christian, which the Apostle commends to us often, when he bids us always rejoice in the Lord.

units.la: Quod si ea spectemus, quibus homines in hoc mundo gaudent & exultant, omnia illa incerta, fluxa & plerunque per se noxia sunt: quae causa est, quod eorum exultationes fere finem tristem & flebilem sortiuntur. Imo ne miracula quidem solidi & aeterni gaudii causa dici possunt, neque Evangelii ministerii dignitas & felix in illo successus: quando ista apud hypocritas saepe inveniuntur, ut Christus Matthaei septimo capite docet. At quod hic nobis commendatur gaudium, certum & perpetuum est, quod ne afflictionibus quidem gravimis turbari potest. Sciunt enim pii electionem & vocationem Dei stabilem esse, cuius illum periri non possit. Sciunt gratiam & misericordiam Dei, quae electionis causa est prima, inexhausto & perenni fonte in credentes derivari. Sciunt Christum, in quo electi sunt, pastorem bonum & fortem esse, qui oves suas norit, neque eas sibi ex manibus suis eripi patiatur. Quapropter huius seculi laboribus, curis, molestiis, persecutionibus, vinculis, tormentis, supplicijs denique diris & horrendis, adeo non movemur, ut potius non ipsis exultandi materia fit, si se quoad crucem Filio Dei conformes factos videant. Inde enim colligunt, quod Paulus docuit: Si cum eo morimur, cum eodem vivemus: Si tolleramus, cum eo regnabimus. In horum ergo consideratione nos exerceamus o fratres, quando in nobis ipsis, quo gaudeamus nihil est, in mundo autem non nisi tristissima aut scelerum nefandissimorum, aut horribilium mutationum, persecutionum denique & omnis generis calamitatum exempla occurrunt. Exultemus ergo nos in Christo Iesu, in quo nos Pater ab aeterno elegit, & qui verus ille liber vitae est, in quem adscripti, in coelis olim cum ipso vivemus atque regnabimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: If we look at those things in which people in this world rejoice and exult, all of them are uncertain, fleeting, and for the most part harmful in themselves; and this is why their exultations usually end in sadness and tears. Indeed, not even miracles can be called a cause of solid and eternal joy, nor the dignity of the ministry of the Gospel and its happy success in it, since these things are often found among hypocrites, as Christ teaches in Matthew chapter 7. But the joy that is commended to us here is certain and perpetual, and it cannot be disturbed even by the most grievous afflictions. For the godly know that the election and calling of God are stable, and that they cannot perish. They know that the grace and mercy of God, which is the first cause of election, flows out to believers from an inexhaustible and everlasting fountain. They know that Christ, in whom they have been chosen, is a good and strong shepherd, who knows his sheep and does not allow them to be snatched out of his hands. Therefore we are not moved by the labours, cares, troubles, persecutions, chains, torments, and finally the dreadful and horrible punishments of this age; rather, these things become for us a matter of exultation, if we see ourselves made conformable to the Son of God in the cross. For from this they gather what Paul taught: "If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him." Let us therefore exercise ourselves, brothers, in the consideration of these things, since in ourselves there is nothing to rejoice in, and in the world there meet us only the most sorrowful examples either of most unspeakable wickedness, or of dreadful changes, of persecutions, and of every kind of calamity. Let us exult, then, in Christ Jesus, in whom the Father chose us from eternity, and who is that true book of life, in whom we have been enrolled, and with whom we shall one day live and reign in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CI.
units.tr: HOMILY CI.

units.la: Eo ipso momento exultavit Iesus spiritu, & dixit: Confiteor tibi Pater, Domine coeli & terrae, quod haec abscondoris a sapientibus & intelligentibus, & revelaris ea infantibus: etiam Pater, quia ita placuit tibi. Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo: & nemo novit quis sit Filius, nisi Pater, & quis sit Pater, nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius revelare. Tunc conversus ad discipulos seorsim dixit: Beati oculi, qui vident quae vos videtis. Dico enim vobis, multos Prophetas & Reges cupivisse videre, quae vos videtis, nec vidisse, & audire quae auditis, nec audivisse.
units.tr: At that very moment Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and said: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it has pleased you. All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." Then, turning to the disciples in private, he said: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings have desired to see what you see and have not seen it, and to hear what you hear and have not heard it."

units.la: Postquam septuaginta discipuli Domino nostro Iesu Christo felicem suae legationis successum exposuerunt, praeclaram & dulcem consolationem ille subiecit, quae & illos in posterum adversus omnem periculorum metum confirmat, & Euangelij sui ministerium magnificè commendat. Docet enim per hoc Satanam è regno suo deturbari, & simul plenam hunc vincendi potestatem concedit. Quae etsi de verbi administris praecipue dicantur, generalem tamen consolationem continent, quam omnes Christiani sibi priuatim accomodare debent. Omnibus enim perpetua cum diabolo pugna est, cum hic quidem saluti ipsorum nunquam non insidias struat, illi vero ipsum nullo modo admittere aut ferre possint. Quamuis autem ille vires suas terribiliter ostentet, nihil tamen contra eos potest, qui Christo insiti, & boni illius pastoris oues sunt, qui neminem sibi eripi patitur. Hucommodissimè cohaeret locus, quem modò recitauimus, in quo de auditoribus Euangelij primum, deinde de semetipso ita Dominus disserit, ut varia scandala remoueat, quae hic accidere consueuerunt. Postremo eorum felicitatem praedicat, quibus datur ipsum iam exhibitum mundi seruatorem cognoscere.
units.tr: After the seventy disciples had reported to our Lord Jesus Christ the happy outcome of their mission, he added a remarkable and sweet consolation. It strengthens them for the future against every fear of danger, and it greatly commends the ministry of his Gospel. For by this he teaches that Satan is cast down from his kingdom, and at the same time he grants them full power to overcome him. Although these words are chiefly spoken of the ministers of the Word, they contain a general consolation that all Christians ought to apply to themselves privately. For all people are in constant battle with the devil, since he never ceases to lay snares for their salvation, while they can in no way admit him or bear with him. Yet although he displays his powers terribly, he can do nothing against those who are grafted into Christ and are the sheep of that good Shepherd, who suffers no one to be snatched from him. The passage we have just read fits very well here. In it the Lord speaks first of the hearers of the Gospel and then of himself, in such a way as to remove various stumbling blocks that commonly arise on this matter. Finally, he proclaims the blessedness of those to whom it is given to know the Saviour of the world now made manifest.

units.la: Primùm scandalo occurrit, quod ex contempta & vili Ecclesiae specie nascitur, dum ad hanc fere homines mundi iudicio stulti & rerum ignari, adhaec obscuri & ignobiles, per Euangelij praedicationem colliguntur, abhorrentibus interim ab illa ijs, qui summam sapientiae existimationem sustinent, & apud omnes in precio habentur. Et quia multum in eo situm est, ne hic carnis iudicium audiamus magna grauitate & singularis affectus significatione rem ista tractat. Primo enim scribit Lucas. Eo ipso momento exultauit Iesus spiritu. Tempus indicat, quia ex hoc data fuit occasio de his dicendi. Cùm enim discipulos cum gaudio reuersos latum sua functionis succesum exponentes audiisset, & ipse de mirabili Euangelicae praedicationis effectu verba fecisset, simulque animo volueret, qualem & quam insignem Ecclesiam breui esset habituru, ex obscuris quidem & nulla huius seculi sapientia turgentibus, sed omni virtutum genere ornatissimis hominibus collectam, tunc (inquam) exultauit spiritu, id est toto animo gaudijs est, & gaudium hoc haud dubiè non verbis modo, verumetiam gestu & vultu est testatus. Deinde ne gaudium & exultatio ista carnalis esse putaretur, Deo Patri gratias agit, dicens: Confiteor tibi Pater, Domine coeli & terrae, &c. Confitendi verbo vtitur Hebraica phrasi, qua Deo confiteri dicuntur, qui ei veritatis, iustitiae, bonitatis, sapientiae & misericordiae laudem tribuunt atque illius beneficia celebrant. Publicè ergo praedicat bonitatem & veritatem Dei Patris, qui nunc praestare incipiat, quod ab aeterno decreuit. Vocat autem Dominum coeli & terrae, ut eorum audaciam retundat, qui in hac causa curiosis quaestionibus Dei decretum vellicant. Tertiò quid nam illud sit, docet: Quod haec abscondere à sapientibus & intelligentibus, & reuelare ea infantibus. Et quia hoc carni absurdum vel etiam iniquum videtur, rursus ad Dei decretum siue voluntatem nos relegat, addens: Etiam Pater, quia ita placuit tibi.
units.tr: The first stumbling block that meets us arises from the contemptible and humble appearance of the Church, since people who are foolish by the judgment of the world, ignorant of affairs, obscure and of low birth are gathered into the Church, almost all of them, through the preaching of the Gospel, while those who hold the highest reputation for wisdom and are esteemed by all turn away from it. And because much depends on this, lest we listen to the judgment of the flesh, he treats the matter with great seriousness and a notable expression of feeling. First, Luke writes: "At that very moment Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit." He indicates the time, because the occasion for speaking about these things arose from it.
