For when he had heard the disciples return with joy and report the happy outcome of their task, and when he himself had spoken of the wonderful effect of the preaching of the Gospel, and at the same time was thinking what and how distinguished a Church he would soon have, gathered not from the obscure and the proud in no wisdom of this age, but from people most adorned with every kind of virtue, then (I say) he rejoiced in the Spirit. That is, he was glad with his whole soul, and undoubtedly he showed this joy not only in words but also in gesture and expression. Then, lest this rejoicing and exultation be thought to be carnal, he gives thanks to God the Father, saying: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth," and so on. He uses the word "confess" in a Hebrew manner, in which people are said to confess to God when they ascribe to him the praise of truth, righteousness, goodness, wisdom and mercy, and celebrate his benefits. Therefore he publicly proclaims the goodness and truth of God the Father, who now begins to perform what he has decreed from eternity. He calls him Lord of heaven and earth to beat down the boldness of those who in this matter pluck at God's decree with curious questions. Third, he teaches what that thing is: that he hides these things from the wise and understanding and reveals them to infants. And because this seems absurd or even unjust to the flesh, he again refers us to God's decree or will, adding: "Yes, Father, for so it has pleased you."

units.la: Docent autem haec Christi verba, de fide Christiana non iudicandum esse secundum externam Ecclesiae speciem, & eorum in hoc seculo conditionem, qui hanc amplectuntur. Nam si hoc facere libeat, ipse etiam Christus reprobandus erit, in quo nihil praeter inopiam, contemptum, infamiam & omnia ea videre licet quae mundus pro infaustis & pro extrema miseria reputat. Et hic ille lapis est, ad quem Iudaeorum proceres impegisse, ipsorum verba testantur, quando seruis illius doctrinam cum admiratione praedicantibus responderunt: Num & vos seducti estis? Num quis ex principibus credidit in eum, aut ex Pharisaeis? Sed turba ista, quae non nouit legem, execrabilis est. Quo argumento etiam hodie multi in proprium pernitiem veniunt, dum non quid Euangelio tradatur respiciunt, sed quales sint, quoad huius seculi conditionem, qui illud docent & sequuntur. At nos exclusò & reiecto procul carnis & mundi iudicio, hoc potius obseruemus, quod Christus in spiritu exul tat propter paucos illos & contemptos discipulos, qui mundo pro infantibus & stultis habentur. Ergo qualescunque sint fideles, quoad externam speciem, peculium Dei & unicus illa Christi thesaurus sunt, in quo ille sibi mirifice placet, in quo acquiescit, in quo deniq; gaudet & exultat, ut pater in dulcissimus liberis, & ut sponsus in sponsa dilectissima, quam diu adamatam multo labore sibi tande acquisiuit. Nam ut Paulus de semetipso dicit, dilexit nos Christus & semetipsum pro nobis tradidit. Galat.2.
units.tr: These words of Christ teach that we must not judge the Christian faith by the external appearance of the Church, or by the condition in this age of those who embrace it. For if we were to do so, Christ himself would also have to be rejected, in whom nothing can be seen but poverty, contempt, infamy and all those things that the world counts as unlucky and as the utmost misery. And this is the stone against which the leaders of the Jews stumbled, as their own words bear witness, when they answered the servants who preached his teaching with admiration: "Have you also been deceived? Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed." By this same argument many even today come to their own ruin, since they do not look at what is handed down in the Gospel, but at what sort of people, in respect of their condition in this age, teach it and follow it. But we, having set aside and rejected the judgment of the flesh and the world, should rather observe this: that Christ rejoices in the Spirit because of those few and despised disciples, who are regarded by the world as infants and fools. Therefore, whatever the faithful may be in external appearance, they are God's special possession and that unique treasure of Christ, in which he takes wonderful delight, in which he rests, in which at last he rejoices and exults, as a father in his most beloved children, and as a bridegroom in his most dear bride, whom after long loving he has at last won for himself with much labour. For, as Paul says of himself: "Christ loved us and gave himself for us." Gal. 2.

units.la: Neq; hic eos audiamus, qui non tam curiosi & superuacanei quam impijs quaestionibus Dei gratiam exagitant, dum quarunt: Cur vero stultos, infantes, obscuros & omnium iudicio contemptissimos elegit Deus, ut ipsis Filij sui cognitionem & regni sui mysteria reueleit? Cur eos praeteritquorum quorum authoritas & exemplum multos alios attrahere poterat? Quibus uno verbo Paulus respon-det: Tu quis es o homo, qui ex aduerso respondes Deo? Annon habet potestatem figulus luti, ut ex eadem massa fingat aliud quidem vas ad decus, aliud vero ad dedecus. Et quis obsecro est, qui Deum sibi debitorem possit dicere? Quod si nemini quicquam debet, cur ergo eum in iudicium vocamus? cur ab illo eorum quae agit rationem exigimus? Quin potius sufficiat nobis, eum sic velle, qui est Dominus coeli & terrae, & proinde libera potestate regni sui thesauros, prout ipse voluerit, dispensare potest. Tibi licet in domum tuam recipere quos velis, & ab eadem quos volueris excludere. Et tu Deo idem ius in sua domo non concedes? Et quam alia ratione in praesenti Christus affert? Num Patris arcana & decretum curiosius & altius scrutatur? Minime. Sed ait: Etiam Pater, quia ita tibi placuit. Quod si ergo aeternus Dei Filius relictus omnibus aliis disputationibus, in Patris εὐδοκίᾳ, id est, voluntate & decreto acquiescit, quus non temerarium & impium facinus dixerit, nos homunciones, imo vermiculos vnius horae, altiora scrutari & scire velle? Vt tamen humanae curiositati, quae infinita & insatiabilis est, aliquo modo satisfaceret Spiritus sanctus, ratione diuinihuius decreti aliquam nobis per Paulum Apostolum reuelauit, qui in priori ad Corinth. 1. cap. scribit: Videtis vocationem vestram fratres, quod non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: Verum quae stulta sunt in mundo, elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat sapientes: & quae sunt infirma in mundo, elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat ea quae sunt robusta: & quae ignobilia sunt in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, elegit Deus, & ea quae non sunt, ut ea quae sunt aboleret: Vt ne glorietur, vlla caro coram eo. Ergo ad Dei gloriam illustrandam, & carnis superbae confidentiam atque arrogantiam retundendam facit dispensatio haec diuinorum mysteriorum, cuius in praesenti meminit. Quid ergo vltra quaerimus, quando omnium hoc est officium, ut repressa carnis insolentia, & ambitione quae primos parentes perdidit, vires suas omnes ad gloriam Dei illustrandam conferant?
units.tr: Nor should we listen here to those who, not so much out of curiosity and vain speculation as out of impious questioning, harass the grace of God, asking: "Why then did God choose the foolish, the infants, the obscure and those most despised by everyone's judgment, so that he might reveal to them the knowledge of his Son and the mysteries of his kingdom? Why did he pass over those whose authority and example could have drawn many others after them?" Paul answers these questions in one word: "Who are you, O man, who answer back against God? Does the potter not have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?" And who, I ask, is there who can say that God is his debtor? If God owes nothing to anyone, why then do we call him into judgment? Why do we demand from him an account of what he does? Rather, it should be enough for us that he so wills, since he is the Lord of heaven and earth, and therefore by free power can dispense the treasures of his kingdom as he himself wills. You may receive into your house whomever you please, and exclude from it whomever you wish. And will you not grant God the same right in his own house? And what other reason does Christ give at present? Does he search more curiously and deeply into the secrets and decree of the Father? By no means. He says: "Yes, Father, for so it has pleased you." If therefore the eternal Son of God, setting aside all other disputations, rests in the Father's eudokia, that is, his good pleasure and decree [εὐδοκίᾳ], who would not call it a rash and impious deed for us mere mortals, indeed worms of a single hour, to wish to search out and know higher things? Yet, so that the Holy Spirit might in some measure satisfy human curiosity, which is infinite and insatiable, he has revealed to us through the Apostle Paul some account of the reason for this divine decree, who writes in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1: "Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are of noble birth. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and God has chosen the base things of the world and the things that are despised, and things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh may boast before him." Therefore this disposition of divine mysteries, which he mentions at present, serves to make the glory of God shine forth and to beat down the proud confidence and arrogance of the flesh. Why then should we seek further, since it is the duty of all to suppress the insolence of the flesh and the ambition that ruined our first parents, and to devote all their powers to make the glory of God shine forth?

units.la: Nunc Christi exemplum obseruemus, qui credentium accessione gaudet & exultat. Eo admonemur, nobis etiam in hoc exultandum esse, quando fidelium numerus augetur, & regnum Dei latius propagatur: ideoque (quod modo monuimus) huc omnes studia sua conferre debent pro ratione vocationis suae & talentorum, quae a Domino acceperunt. Et huius nos Oratio Dominica admonet, in qua inter alia petimus: Adueniat regnum tuum. Videndum ergo ne studia nostra cum precatione illa pugnent, & in Dei conspectu hypocritae deprehendamur. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter sanctissimi quiquorum hoc praecipuum studium fuit, ut per ipsos alij plures ad verbi Dei cognitionem atq; cultum adducerentur. Hoc nomine ab ipso Domino commendatur Abrahamus pater credentium. Dauid cum regni rebus vtcunque pacificatus de cultu Dei instaurando cogitaret, & arcam Domini in ciuitatem suam deduceret, tanto gaudio perfusus fuit, ut regiae dignitatis tantumnon oblitus, Ephod indueret, & in conspectu totius Israelis cithara ludens saltaret. Et hic prouehendae gloriae Dei zelus tot nobis tam veteris quam Noui Testamenti Martyres dedit, qui sibi moriendum potius putarunt, quam ea facere, quae in veri Dei contumeliam cessura videbant. Alios quoque non alia ex re maiorem dolorem concepisse constat, quam si fideles tolli & cultum Dei imminui vel aboleri cernerent. Elias Propheta mori optabat, quod se solum in Israele relictum putaret ex cultorum Dei numero. Et vt ad Dauidem redeamus, in suo exilio nihil illi molestius fuisse nonnulli Psalmi testantur, quam quod ab externis verae religionis exercitijs excluderetur. In multis vero alijs Psalmus amarae pietatis querelae continentur de Ecclesiae oppressione, de Dei templo vastato, & cultu vero extincto. Quae exempla satis docent, quo loco habendi sint, quibus dolet, sicubi Euangelium propagari & ad huius doctrinam accessionem nouam fieri audiunt. Quanto autem bis peiores sunt, qui cum Christi nomen profiteantur, cursum tamen Euangelij manibus pedibusq; impediunt, & non contenti propria incredulitate, vel impietate potius, alios quoq; in erroribus & tenebris detinere studeant? Est horum ingens numerus hodie, quorum iudicium non dormitat. Nam quantum in ipsis est, gaudium Christi impediunt, & spiritui sancto sese opponunt, qui nihilominus spirabit vbicunq;, ipse voluerit, illi autem sentient aliquando, quid sit in Solem expuere.
units.tr: Now let us observe the example of Christ, who rejoices and exults when believers are added. We are thereby admonished that we too ought to exult when the number of the faithful grows and the kingdom of God spreads more widely. Therefore, as we have just said, all should direct their efforts to this, according to their calling and the talents they have received from the Lord. Our Lord's Prayer also reminds us of this, in which among other things we ask: "Thy kingdom come." We must take care that our efforts do not conflict with that prayer, and that we are not found to be hypocrites in the sight of God. The most holy men observed this diligently; their chief concern was that through them many others might be brought to the knowledge and worship of God's Word. For this reason the Lord himself commends Abraham, the father of believers. When David, having somehow settled the affairs of the kingdom, was thinking about restoring the worship of God, and was bringing the ark of the Lord into his city, he was so filled with joy that, scarcely mindful of his royal dignity, he put on an ephod and danced, playing the harp, in the sight of all Israel. This zeal for advancing the glory of God has given us so many martyrs, both of the Old and of the New Testament, who judged it better to die than to do those things which they saw would turn out to the dishonour of the true God. It is also evident that others conceived no greater grief from any other cause than when they saw the faithful taken away and the worship of God diminished or abolished. The prophet Elijah wished to die, because he thought he was left alone in Israel from among the worshippers of God. And to return to David: several Psalms testify that nothing was more painful to him in his exile than that he was excluded from the outward exercises of true religion. In many other Psalms there are complaints of bitter piety concerning the oppression of the Church, the temple of God laid waste, and true worship extinguished. These examples sufficiently teach in what place they are to be held who grieve when they hear that the Gospel is spreading and that new additions are being made to its doctrine. But how much worse are those who, while professing the name of Christ, nevertheless hinder the course of the Gospel with hands and feet, and, not content with their own unbelief, or rather impiety, strive also to keep others in errors and darkness? Today there is an immense number of these, and their judgement does not sleep. For as far as lies in them, they impede the joy of Christ and set themselves against the Holy Spirit, who nevertheless breathes where he wills; but they will one day feel what it is to spit against the sun.

units.la: Praeterea admonent nos verba haec, qui nam vere idonei sint ad audiendum Verbum Dei & Christum ampletendum. Patrem mysteria haec regni sui abscondisse dicit a sapientibus & intelligentibus, & reuelauisse autem infantibus. Quo loco non vult sapientiam damnare, quae sclij.
units.tr: Furthermore, these words admonish us as to who are truly fit to hear the Word of God and to embrace Christ. The Father, he says, has hidden the mysteries of his kingdom from the wise and understanding, and has revealed them to infants. In this passage he does not wish to condemn that wisdom

units.la: 1.Reg.19. qua præclarum Dei donum, & ad res recte agendas non vtilis modò verumetiam necessaria est, quemadmodum neq; ignorantiam & inscitiam laudat, quæ potius vituperium merentur. Sed primò, vt huius mundi sapientiliis cristas detrahat, rudes autem & ob rerum ignorantiam contemptos soletur, docet, carnis sapientia nihil facere ad fidei cognitionem et ad regnum Dei consequendum, & è contra neminem ignorantia impediri, quò minus à Spiritu sancto illuminari & ad cognitionem veritatis adduci possit. Deinde non simpliciter inscios & ignaros rerum vel stultos, sed infantes nominat, vt inde colligamus, quales nos fieri oporteat, vt ipsum agnoscere & vera fide amplectipos-simus: Infantes nimirum, qui carnis sapientiæ renuntiauerint, seq; ipsos abnegarint, vt se totos Dei verbo per fidei obedientiam subijciant. Idem alibi monet, quando de primatu contendentes infantum similes vult fieri, & nisi tales fiant, in regnum Dei ingressuros esse negat. Nam vt homo animalis non percipit ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei: ita quoad illius ratione & consilio ducimur, ad veram regni Dei & salutis æternæ cognitionem peruenire non dabitur. Ideo noftrisipsius abnegatione alibi Christus requirit, quam Apostolus per veteris hominis aut carnis mortificationem exprimit. Et huc pertinet, quod Petrus in priori epistola, postquam nos ex verbo Dei renatos esse docuit, mox subijcit: Proinde depositâ omni malitia & omni dolo, & simulationibus, & inuidentijs, & omnibus obtrectationibus, vt modò nati infantes lac illud sermonis syncerum expetite, vt per illud adolescatis. Ea vitia deponere iubet, quæ homini propria sunt, adeoque nobiscum nascuntur. Radix omnium malitia est, innata nimirum natura nostra vitiositas. Parit hæc dolos & simulationes, quibus ita addicti sumus, vt paucos inuenias, qui non alij sint, quam foris apparent. Sequitur inuidentia, id est, dolor, qui ex aliorum prosperis successibus nascitur, & nisi initio statim enecetur, obtrectationes parit, calumnias item, contumelias, iniurias omnis generis, & nonnunquam ad verbera & cædes vsq; descendit. At qui abiuris omnibus alieni syncero animo cum omnibus versantur, suas res negligunt, alienas curant, vindictæ cupiditatem facile reflinguunt, denique se totos ad charitatis regulam componunt, ij mundo infantes, stupidi, stulti, fanatici, imò dementes dicuntur. Sed hi illi sunt, quibus cœlestis Pater æterna salutis mysteria reuelat, & quos ad regni sui hæreditatem inuitat. Neminem ergo impiorum calumnias & peruersa mundi iudicia moueant. Suffiiat nobis Christus, in quo thesauri omnis scientiæ & cognitionis reconditi sunt, & qui nobis à Patre sapientia est, facultas, quæ nos à recto tramite deuiare non sinet.
units.tr: 1.Reg.19. which is a remarkable gift of God, and not only useful but necessary for acting rightly; nor does he praise ignorance and lack of learning, which rather deserve reproach. But first, in order to pull down the pride of this world's wise and to console the simple and those despised for their ignorance of things, he teaches that the wisdom of the flesh contributes nothing to knowledge of the faith or to attaining the kingdom of God, and conversely that no one is hindered by ignorance from being illumined by the Holy Spirit and brought to knowledge of the truth. Next, he does not call them simply unlearned, ignorant or foolish, but infants, so that we may gather what sort we ought to become in order to acknowledge him and embrace him with the truest faith: infants indeed, who have renounced the wisdom of the flesh and denied themselves, so as to submit themselves wholly to God's Word in obedience of faith. He gives the same warning elsewhere, when, disputing about primacy, he wishes them to become like infants, and denies that unless they become such they will enter the kingdom of God. For as the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, so, as long as we are guided by his reason and counsel, it will not be granted us to attain to true knowledge of the kingdom of God and eternal salvation. Therefore Christ elsewhere requires self-denial, which the Apostle expresses as the mortification of the old man or of the flesh. To this belongs what Peter says in his first epistle, after teaching that we have been born again through the Word of God: "Therefore, laying aside all malice and all guile and hypocrisy and envy and all evil speaking, as newborn infants desire the sincere milk of the word, that you may grow thereby." He bids them put away those vices which are proper to man and so are born with us. Malice is the root of all, namely our innate natural corruption. This produces guile and hypocrisy, to which we are so addicted that you will find few who are not other than they appear outwardly. Then follows envy, that is, grief arising from the prosperous successes of others, which, unless it is stifled at once at its beginning, gives birth to backbiting, also slander, insults, injuries of every kind, and sometimes descends even to blows and slaughter. But those who, laying aside all these, live sincerely among all people, neglect their own affairs and care for others', easily restrain the desire for revenge, and finally conform themselves wholly to the rule of charity: these the world calls infants, stupid, foolish, fanatics, indeed madmen. But these are the ones to whom the heavenly Father reveals the mysteries of eternal salvation, and whom he invites to the inheritance of his kingdom. Therefore let not the calumnies of the impious nor the perverse judgements of the world move anyone. Christ suffices for us, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, and who is made to us wisdom from the Father, and power, which will not let us stray from the straight path.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua de semetipso agit Dominus, & quod ex eius vili atq; contempta specie nascitur scandalum remouet. Sic enim ait: Omnia mihi tradita sunt à Patre meo: & nemo nouit quis sit Filius, nisi Pater, & c. Quorum verborum sensus hic est: Scio me à plerisque contemni, nec pro eo, qui reuera sum, agnosci: eò quod non magnifico splendore neque pompa regia aut numerosa satellitio, armorum & strepitu, vt huius seculi principes solent, me ostentem. Sed qualiscunque videat, sum tamen vnigenitus ille & dilectus Dei Filius, cui pater omne iudicium & omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra tradidit. Quod vero non omnes me recipiunt, hinc est, quod præter Patrem nemo scit, qui sim, & cui ille hoc reuelare voluerit: quemadmodum è contra nemo Patrem nouit, nisi Filius, & cui is illum reuelare dignatus fuerit. Ita vero docet, hominum ignorantiam & incredulitatem ipsius maiestati nihil derogare, & simul in Spiritus sancti cho-lam eos remittit, qui in veri Dei & salutis propria cognitione proficere cupiunt. Sunt autem hic præterea hæc consideranda.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the other part of this passage, in which the Lord speaks of himself and removes the scandal arising from his mean and despised appearance. For he says: "All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father," and so on. The sense of these words is this: I know that I am despised by many and not acknowledged for what I truly am, because I do not display myself with magnificent splendour, royal pomp, a numerous retinue, arms and noise, as the princes of this age are wont to do. But however I may appear, I am nevertheless that only-begotten and beloved Son of God, to whom the Father has delivered all judgement and all power in heaven and on earth. The reason why not all receive me is that, apart from the Father, no one knows who I am, except those to whom he wills to reveal this; just as, conversely, no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom he deigns to reveal him. He thus teaches that men's ignorance and unbelief detract nothing from his majesty, and at the same time he sends back to the school of the Holy Spirit those who desire to make progress in the proper knowledge of the true God and of salvation. There are also the following things to be considered here.

units.la: Primum est eximia planeque diuina Christi potentia atque maiestas, de qua sic disserit, vt singula verba ad eius illustrationem faciant. Nam primo OMNIA (inquit) mihi tradita sunt. Nihil ergo excipitur, sed penes Christum est imperium cœli & terræ, spirituum bonorum & malorum, regnorum mundi huius, maris, animalium terrestrium, aquatilium, volatilium, populorum omnium, hominum item singulorum, denique omnium, quæcunque ingens hæc mundi machina continet. Est ergo vere is, quem scriptura Dominum exercituum vocare solet. Creatis enim omnibus tanquam copijs aut exercitibus adnutum suum parantis vtitur. Deinde ait: TRADITA sunt mihi. Quod secundum assumptam hominis naturam ab eo dicitur. Non quoad diuinitatem, Patri coæternus & coessentialis, gloria & potestate nunquam caruit, quod ipsemet testatur, quando iam mortem aditurus dicebat: Glorifica me tu Pater apud temetipsum ea gloria, quam habui apud te priusquam mundus esset.
units.tr: The first is the outstanding and plainly divine power and majesty of Christ, about which he speaks in such a way that each word contributes to its illustration. For first he says: ALL (he says) have been delivered to me. Nothing is excepted; rather, rule over heaven and earth, over good and evil spirits, over the kingdoms of this world, over the sea, land animals, water creatures, birds, all peoples, and individual men, in short over everything that this vast machine of the world contains, lies in the hands of Christ. He is therefore truly that one whom Scripture is wont to call the Lord of hosts. For he uses all created things, as it were, as troops or armies that carry out his nod. Then he says: have been DELIVERED to me. This is said by him according to the nature of man which he assumed, not as regards his divinity: co-eternal and co-essential with the Father, he never lacked glory and power, as he himself testifies when, about to go to his death, he said: "Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was."

units.la: Ioan. 17. te priusquam hic mundus existeret. At qui gloriam & potestate ab æterno habuit, quatenus Deus est æternus, huic illa etiam quoad humanitatem data est, quando ex Patris decreto hominem assumpsit. Et ita hoc exponit optimus interpres, Paulus Apostolus, ad Philippenses sic scribens, Ipse se inaniuit forma servi sumpta, similis hominibus factus, & habitu compertus ut homo: Ipse se submisit factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Quapropter etiam Deus ipsum in sumam extulit sublimitatem, ac donavit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen: Ut ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat, cælestium ac terrestrium & subterraneorum, omnisque lingua confiteatur, quòd Dominus sit Iesus Christus ad gloriam Dei Patris. Interim tradendi verbum nos admonet, potestatem hanc Christi legitimam esse, ut quam non ipse sibi temere usurparit, sed legitimè traditam acceperit. A quo nam? Num à Satana, qui in montem altissimum subductio omnia huius mundi regna & eorum gloriam monstrauit aliquando, & ei se illa omnia daturum esse promisit, si ipsum adoraret? Minimè gentium, Sed A PATRE MEO, inquit. Quod potestatem hanc non modò legitimam & ordinariam, sed firmam quoque & stabilem esse innuit. Quis enim Filio eripiat, quod à Patre Deo accepit? Aut quo iure à paterna hæreditate idem ille deiiciatur? Hæc autem nō sine causa diligentius annotamus. Ex isto enim sequitur, omnes homines, cuiuscunque sexus, ætatis, loci aut ordinis sint, Christo obedientiam debere voluntariam, & rebellionis reos esse apud Dei tribunal omnes, qui illum pro suo Rege agnoscere dedignantur. Ideo Dauid in spiritu hanc illius gloriam præuidens dicebat: Sapite ergo ô Reges, erudimini iudices terræ. Seruite Domino in timore, & exultate cum tremore. Osculamini Filium ne irascatur, & pereatis de via. Deinde dulcissimam consolationem habet hæc potestas Christi consideratio. Quia enim ille in omnes ius habet & imperium, nō est quòd timeamus, ne quis nos ei eripiat, aut illo inuito lædat. Nec negligere poterit eos, quos ipse Pater tradidit: imò eosdem vult esse vbi est. Sed & ne mors quidem nobis timenda est, cum huius quoque sit Dominus, & eam in se credentibus ex peccati pœna in lætam profectionem siue transitum ex hac lachrymarum valle in patriam cælestem commutarit.
units.tr: John 17. before this world existed. But he had glory and power from eternity, inasmuch as he is eternal God; this was given to him also in respect of his humanity, when by the Father's decree he assumed a man. The excellent interpreter, Paul the Apostle, explains it so, writing to the Philippians: "He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made like unto men, and found in fashion as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also has highly exalted him and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, things on earth and things under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." Meanwhile the word "delivered" reminds us that this power of Christ is lawful, since he did not seize it rashly for himself but received it lawfully delivered. From whom? From Satan, who once led him up into a very high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of this world and their glory, and promised to give them all to him if he would worship him? By no means: "from my Father," he says. This indicates that the power is not only lawful and ordinary but also firm and stable. For who will snatch from the Son what he received from God the Father? Or by what right could he be cast out of his paternal inheritance? We note these things more carefully for good reason. For it follows that all men, of whatever sex, age, place or rank, owe Christ voluntary obedience, and all who disdain to acknowledge him as their King are guilty of rebellion before God's tribunal. So David, foreseeing in the Spirit this glory of his, said: "Be wise now therefore, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way." Next, the consideration of this power of Christ holds a most sweet consolation. For since he has right and rule over all, there is no reason for us to fear that anyone will snatch us from him or harm us against his will. Nor will he neglect those whom the Father himself has given him; rather, he wills them to be where he is. Neither should death itself be feared by us, since he is Lord of this too, and for those who believe in him has turned it from a punishment for sin into a joyful departure, a passage from this valley of tears to the heavenly fatherland.

units.la: Secundò obseruari hic debet, Iesu Christi veram & salutarem cognitionē hominibus à solo Deo Patre obtingere, quādo us spiritus sancti luce corda nostra illustrare dignatur. Docet hoc alibi quoq; Dominus. Nam apud Ioannē ait: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Et Petro, qui præclaram de ipso confessione ædiderat, dixit: Beatus es Simon Bar Ionæ, quia caro & sanguis nō reuelauit tibi, sed Pater meus cælestis. Et Isaias credentes omnes θεοδιδακτους, id est, à Deo docentes fore vaticinatur. Inde sequitur, eos solos Christum verè nouisse, qui Patrem de illo testantem audiunt. Habentur autem huius testimonia passim in scripturis tam Veteris quàm Noui Testamenti. Huc enim primæ promissiones pertinent, quibus docetur, illum esse semen illud mulieris, quod serpentis caput conculcaturum sit, & in quo omnes gentes benedici oporteat. Huc typi legales faciunt, quibus totum eius sacerdotium & sacrificium, quod pro peccatis mundi offerre debuit, adumbratur. Qua apud Prophetas habentur, longum foret recensere. Sufficiat ergo omnium epitomen audire, quæ in eo testimonio habetur, quod illi ia in carne manifestato cælitus Pater magna cum maiestate dedit, & bis quidem, quò minus dubia esset illius authoritas. Est hoc eiusmodi: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum: hunc audite. Sunt huius testimonij partes duæ, quarum prior Christi personam, altera officium describit. Ad personam pertinet, quòd eum, quem verum hominē esse omnibus constabat, Filium suum vocat: nimirum verum ex se genitum, sibi coæternum & consubstantialem. Id innuit Dilecti vox, quæ de nullo hominum aliter quàm ex gratia pronuntiari potuit, cùm omnes natura filij iræ essent. Et huc facit, quod Christus apud Ioannē Patri dicit: Dilexisti me ante iacta fundamenta mundi. Est ergo Christus in vna eademq; persona Deus verus & homo verus: Deus quidem ab æterno, homo autem factus ex muliere (vt Paulus ait) cùm prasfinitum illud tempus iam aduenisset. In què verò finem? aut quod eius fuit in carne assumpta officium? Vt Patrem nobis placaret, qui prius propter peccata toti generi humano iratus erat. Id quomodo fecerit, & vt hodie adhuc pro nobis intercedat, alibi sæpe est dictum. In hac ergo Christi cognitio consistit, quam nobis per verbum suum Pater propria voce cælitus reuelauit. In illa ergo nō minus turpiter quàm pernitiosè falluntur, qui vel Deum verum & æternum esse negant, vel humanitatem eius in dubium vocant. Errant etiā, qui cum priora hæc fateantur, nō tamē illo vno contenti sunt, sed alios sibi mediatores & intercessores quaerunt, quorū intercessione ipsis Pater reconcilietur, nec quicquam Christo clamante: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Cum ergo Filium nemo norit, nisi Pater, hic autem quis ille sit tam clarè, tā perspicuè, tam & graviter testetur, huius testimonio nos insistere decet, nec quicquam aliud admittere, quod illi vel minima ex parte aduersatur.
units.tr: Secondly, it must be observed here that the true and saving knowledge of Jesus Christ comes to men from God the Father alone, when he deigns to illuminate our hearts with the light of the Holy Spirit. The Lord teaches this elsewhere too. For in John he says: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." And to Peter, who had made the splendid confession about him, he said: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my heavenly Father." And Isaiah prophesies that all believers will be θεοδίδακτοι [theodidaktoi], that is, taught by God. It follows that only those truly know Christ who hear the Father bearing witness about him. Testimonies to this are found everywhere in the Scriptures of both the Old and the New Testament. To this point the first promises belong, in which it is taught that he is that Seed of the woman who shall bruise the serpent's head, and in whom all nations ought to be blessed. To this point the legal types point, by which his whole priesthood and the sacrifice he was to offer for the sins of the world are foreshadowed. It would be too long to recount what is found in the Prophets. It is enough, then, to hear the summary of all of them, which is contained in that testimony the Father gave from heaven with great majesty to him now manifested in the flesh, and indeed twice, so that his authority might be less open to doubt. It is as follows: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." This testimony has two parts, of which the first describes the person of Christ, the second his office. To the person belongs that he calls "Son" the one whom all agreed was a true man: namely, one truly begotten of himself, co-eternal and consubstantial with him. The word "beloved" implies this, for it could not be pronounced of any man otherwise than by grace, since all were by nature children of wrath. To this also agrees what Christ says to the Father in John: "You loved me before the foundation of the world." Christ is therefore, in one and the same person, true God and true man: God indeed from eternity, but man made of a woman (as Paul says) when the appointed time had now come. And to what end? What was his office in the flesh he assumed? To reconcile the Father to us, who previously was angry with the whole human race on account of sin. How he did this, and how even today he intercedes for us, has often been said elsewhere. In this, then, the knowledge of Christ consists, which the Father himself revealed to us from heaven by his own voice through his Word. Therefore those who either deny that he is true and eternal God, or call his humanity into doubt, are deceived no less shamefully than destructively. Those also err who, while admitting these first points, are not content with him alone, but seek other mediators and intercessors, through whose intercession the Father may be reconciled to them, while Christ cries out: "No one comes to the Father except through me." Since, then, no one knows the Son except the Father, and the Father so clearly, so plainly and so weightily testifies who he is, it is fitting for us to rest upon this testimony and to admit nothing else that opposes it in the least degree.

units.la: Tertiò non minus obseruatu dignum est, Patrus quoque cognitionem non habere, nisi hunc nobis Filius reuelarit. Nam vt Paulus ait, habitat ille lucem inaccessam, neque tanta est humani intellectus lux, vt propria facultate ad eum vsque penetrare, vel immensam atque infinitam eius maiestatem & quae alia illi propria sunt, comprehendere possit. At qui talis est, seipsum nobis in Filio manifestauit, qui vt est splendor gloriae & character personae ipsius, ita nobis omnia ea tradidit, quae de illo cognitu necessaria sunt. Ideo Ioannes Euangelista scribit: Deum nemo vidit vnquam, Vnigenitus ille Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis enarrauit. Damnantur igitur hoc loco omnium gentium religiones, quae Christum non nouerunt, aut etiam contumeliosè reiiciunt. Nam absque Dei cognitione religio vera consistere non potest: illud autem non nisi in Filio cognosci, hic tam diserte affirmatur, vt de eo amplius disputare nefas sit. Adhaec Philippo Christus dicebat: Qui me vidit, Patrem vidit. Quae propositio rectissimè conuertitur, vt dicamus: Qui non vidit Filium, nec Patrem quidem vidit. Habuerunt quidem cognitionem aliquam Dei gentes, quam (vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit) ex huius mundi & partium eius contemplatione conceperunt: at quia Christi notitia deficiuti fuerūt, in errores & superstitiones absurdissimas prolapsi sunt. Et Iudaei se solos esse arbitrantur populum illum sapientem, penes quem sit vera Dei cognitio: sed quia Christum fastidiunt, in tenebris oberrant, & Thalmudicus fabulis circunduci sese patiuntur, quibus nihil absurdius, nihil ineptius, nihil putidius & magis impium fingi potest. Eadem est Turcarum conditio, qui vnius Dei creatoris caeli & terrae cultu atque adoratione gloriantur, de Christo ite nonnulla honorifice praedicant, quem Dei verbum, Dei animam & spiritum esse, & nouissimo die venturum fatentur, vt viuos & mortuos iudicet: quia tamen Dei Filium non agnoscunt, adhaec incarnationis mysterium ignorant, crucis & mortis eius meritum negant, vana & inanis est illorum fides & religio, quae ex Mahumeticis traditionibus, partim fluxa & ridiculas, partim impijs & nefandis constat. Quod si Papisticae superstitionis sectatores inspiciamus, hac illis quoq; omnium errorū & superstitionum causa est, quod etsi Christum in ore habeant, vera tamen & solida meriti & officij ipsius cognitione destituuntur. Hinc enim Missae sacrificium, hinc operum nostrorum merita, hinc satisfactiones, hinc sacra pro defunctis, hinc Diuorū intercessio & inuocatio, hinc Romanae indulgentiae, hinc purgatorius ignis, fraternitates, monastica vota, emptitiae preces & sexcenta alia originem duxerunt. Adde his, quod sola fides in Christū iustificat, & vitae aeternae participes facit. Inutilis ergo omnis religio & cultus Dei, qui absque fide instituitur. Ideo apud Ioannem Christus ait: Pater omne iudicium dedit Filio, vt omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem: Qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem, qui misit ipsum. Possent haec copiosissimè tractari, sed nos vsum istorum obseruemus, qui est, vt totos nos Christi cognitioni dedamus, in quo non solùm Dei iustitia, sapientia, omnipotentia & quae alia in illo gentes agnouere, cernuntur, verumetiā inexhausta eiusdem bonitas, infinita misericordia, & in primis aeternum illud eius decretū manifestatur, ex quo tota humani generis redemptio dependet. Quae cognitio sola fidem veram parit, & proinde sola salutaris est.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is no less worthy of observation that we do not have knowledge of the Father unless the Son reveals him to us. For, as Paul says, God dwells in light unapproachable, nor is the light of human understanding so great that by its own faculty it can penetrate to him, or comprehend his immense and infinite majesty and the other attributes proper to him. But he who is such has manifested himself to us in the Son, who, as "the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person," has so handed over to us all those things about him that are necessary to know. Therefore the Evangelist John writes: "No one has seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him." Those religions of all the nations that do not know Christ, or even reject him with contumely, are therefore condemned in this passage. For true religion cannot exist without knowledge of God, and that God is known only in the Son is affirmed here so plainly that it is wrong to dispute further about it. Moreover, Christ said to Philip: "He who has seen me has seen the Father." This statement is most rightly reversed, so that we may say: he who has not seen the Son has not even seen the Father. The nations indeed had some knowledge of God, which (as Paul writes to the Romans) they formed from contemplating this world and its parts; but because they lacked the knowledge of Christ, they fell into errors and most absurd superstitions. And the Jews think that they alone are that wise people in whose keeping is the true knowledge of God; but because they despise Christ, they wander in darkness, and allow themselves to be led about by Talmudic fables, than which nothing more absurd, nothing more foolish, nothing more stinking and more impious can be invented. The condition of the Turks is the same: they boast of worshipping and adoring the one God, creator of heaven and earth, and speak some honourable things about Christ, whom they confess to be the Word of God, the soul and spirit of God, and who will come on the last day to judge the living and the dead; yet because they do not acknowledge him as the Son of God, and moreover are ignorant of the mystery of the incarnation, and deny the merit of his cross and death, their faith and religion is empty and vain, consisting of Mahometan traditions, partly frivolous and ridiculous, partly impious and abominable. And if we look at the followers of Papistical superstition, the cause of all their errors and superstitions is likewise this: that although they have Christ on their lips, they are nevertheless destitute of a true and solid knowledge of his merit and office. For hence came the sacrifice of the Mass, hence the merits of our works, hence satisfactions, hence masses for the dead, hence the intercession and invocation of the saints, hence the Roman indulgences, hence purgatorial fire, fraternities, monastic vows, mercenary prayers, and six hundred other things have taken their origin. Add to these that faith in Christ alone justifies and makes us partakers of eternal life. Therefore every religion and worship of God that is instituted without faith is useless. So John records Christ saying: "The Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him." These matters could be treated at great length, but let us observe the use of them, which is that we should give ourselves wholly to the knowledge of Christ. In him not only are the justice, wisdom and omnipotence of God, and the other attributes the nations have recognised in him, made visible, but also his inexhaustible goodness, infinite mercy, and above all that eternal decree of his, on which the whole redemption of the human race depends. This knowledge alone brings forth true faith, and therefore alone is saving.

units.la: Admonet nos praeterea locus iste, quantus & quàm pretiosus vera cognitionis Dei thesaurus sit. Nam quaecunq; alia in mundo magnifica habentur, ea vel pretio, vel labore & industria acquiri possunt. At Dei cognitio omnem humani ingenij industriam & acumen superat, & non nisi caelitus ex Spiritus reuelatione obtingit. Inde sequitur, non superbiendum esse ijs, qui se ista cognitione illuminatos esse sentiunt. Quid enim habent, quod non acceperint? Itaq; Deo petimus gratias, & memores se thesaurum hunc pretiosissimum in testaceis, imo vitro fragilioribus vasis gestare, salutem suam operentur cum timore & tremore. Discimus item non temere damnandos aut reiiciendos esse eos, qui Dei cognitione adhuc destituti sunt. Potest enim hos quoq; illuminare Deus, cuius electio & vocatio libera est, nec vlli hominum aut personarum respectui alligata. Interim nostrum fuerit docendo & monendo apud omnes instare, precibus item iuuare salutem omnium hominum, si alia ratione id facere non possumus.
units.tr: This passage also reminds us how great and how precious the true treasure of knowledge of God is. For whatever other splendid things are held in the world can be acquired by price, or by labour and industry. But the knowledge of God surpasses all the effort and cleverness of human talent, and it comes to us only from heaven, by the revelation of the Spirit. It follows that those who feel themselves enlightened by this knowledge must not be proud. For what do they have that they have not received? So we ask God for thanks, and, mindful that we carry this most precious treasure in earthen, or rather glass, vessels more fragile still, let us work out our salvation with fear and trembling. We learn too that those who are still without the knowledge of God are not to be rashly condemned or rejected. For God can enlighten these also, since his election and calling are free and bound to no respect of persons or of rank. Meanwhile it is our task to press on with teaching and admonishing all people, and also to help the salvation of all men by prayers, if we cannot do so in any other way.

units.la: 1. Cor. 4. 2. Cor. 3. Philip. 2. Porrò hīs publicè dictīs, Christus ad discipulos conuersus, illos docet; quàm felix & beata sit ipsorum conditio, vt ea ratione ipsos magis animet & confirmet, ne vllis periculis sese ab ipso abducì patiantur. Beati (inquit) oculi, qui vident, quae vos videtis. Habet sermo hic exclamationis speciem, quae ad amplificationem facit. Et mox causam sui dicti reddit: Dico enim vobis, multos Prophetas & Reges cupiuisse videre quae vos videtis, nec vidisse: & audire quae auditis, nec audiuisse. Quae verba non intelligi debent de externo spectaculo, quo Pharisaei quoq; & alij eius hostes ipsum & miracula eius viderunt: sed de contemplatione fidei, qua discipuli ipsum videbant esse Filium Dei, & promissum humani generis redemptorem, in quo implerentur, quaecunq; olim Deus patribus pollicitus fuit. Habuerunt quidem illi promissiones amplissimas & illustria vaticinia de Christo, & quia his crediderunt, per eam fidem seruati sunt. Interim tamen fieri non potuit, quin incredibili desiderio arderent cotàm videndi promissum illum seruatorem, qui maledictionem auferret, benedictionem reduceret, & miseros mortales cum Deo Patre verè & plenè reconciliaret. Hoc de Abrahamo Christus testatur, quem gestiuisse dicit, vt diem suum videret. Et quantum Dauidis desiderium fuerit, ex eo apparet, quòd locum templi (quo promissus ille redemptor figurabatur) tanto studio quaesiuit, vt cum iureiurando diceret: Si tabernaculum domus meae subiero, si conscendero sponsam lecti mei: Si concessero oculis meis somnum, & palpebris meis dormitionem: Donec inueniam locum Domino, & habitaculum forti Iacob, &c. Adde hīs, quod Petrus scribit, Prophetas veteres Christi spiritu ductos, magna diligentia eius afflictiones & inde secuturam gloriam inquisiuisse: Quod nunquam facturi erant, nisi ardentissimo eius videndi desiderio fuissent accensi. Et hoc ilud est, de quo in praesenti Christus loquitur, vt discipulorum beatitudinem amplificet, quibus datum erat ipsum coram videre & docentem audire. Vbi meminisse oportet, illum non minus nobis loqui, qui etiam hodie ipsum in Euangelio videmus & audimus, adeoq; praestita habemus, quae veteres futura sperabant. Excitet nos huius beneficij consideratio, vt Deo gratiasimus, & alia huius nouissimi seculi incommoda patienter feramus: in primis autem constanti fide retineamus Iesum Christum, in quo vno vita & salus habetur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 4. 2 Cor. 3. Phil. 2. Moreover, after these things were said publicly, Christ, turning to his disciples, teaches them how happy and blessed their condition is, so that by this reasoning he may stir them up and strengthen them, lest they allow themselves to be led away from him by any dangers. "Blessed," he says, "are the eyes that see what you see." This saying has the form of an exclamation, which serves to amplify the point. And soon after he gives the reason for his words: "For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." These words ought not to be understood of the outward spectacle, by which the Pharisees and his other enemies also saw him and his miracles; but of the contemplation of faith, by which the disciples saw that he was the Son of God and the promised redeemer of mankind, in whom would be fulfilled whatever God had long ago promised to the fathers. Indeed those men had the most ample promises and the illustrious prophecies about Christ, and because they believed these, they were saved through that faith. Yet it could not but be that they burned with an incredible desire to see the promised Saviour, who would take away the curse, restore the blessing, and fully and truly reconcile wretched mortals with God the Father. Christ bears witness to this of Abraham, of whom he says that he rejoiced that he might see his day. And how great David's desire was appears from the fact that he sought out the place of the temple (by which that promised Redeemer was prefigured) with such eagerness that he swore an oath: "If I enter the tabernacle of my house, if I climb into the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a habitation for the mighty God of Jacob," etc. Add to these what Peter writes: that the ancient prophets, led by the Spirit of Christ, searched with great diligence into his sufferings and the glory that would follow them; which they would never have done unless they had been kindled with the most ardent desire to see him. And this is what Christ is speaking of at present, in order to magnify the blessedness of the disciples, to whom it was given to see him in person and to hear him teaching. Here we must remember that he speaks no less to us, who even today see and hear him in the Gospel, and so we possess the things which the ancients hoped would come. Let the consideration of this benefit stir us to give thanks to God, and to bear patiently the other troubles of this latest age; above all, let us hold fast with constant faith to Jesus Christ, in whom alone life and salvation are found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CII.
units.tr: HOMILY CII.

units.la: Tum ecce, quidam Legis interpres surrexit tentans eum, & dicens: Magister, quid faciendo vitam aeternam possidebo? At ille dixit ei: In Lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis? Ille verò respondens dixit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex totis viribus tuis, & ex tota cogitatione tua: & proximum tuum vt teipsum. Tum ille dixit ei. Rectè respondisti, Hoc fac & viues.
units.tr: Then, behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying: "Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" He said to him: "What is written in the Law? How do you read it?" And he answered and said: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbour as yourself." Then he said to him: "You have answered rightly; do this and you will live."

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster Iesus Christus in iis, quae praecesserūt, de Euangelij sui praedicatione & eiusdem effectu disseruit, inde in ardentem gratiarum actionem erupit, qua Dei Patris iustitiam simul & bonitatem praedicat, qui haec regni sui & aeternae salutis mysteria hominibus mundi iudicio stultis & contemptis reuelare dignatus sit, abscondérit autem à sapientibus & intelligentibus. Vbi didicimus, qui nam digni & idonei Verbi diuini auditores sint: ij nimirum, qui carnis ratione & sapientiae renuntiant, & reliquis huius seculi rebus omnibus, in hoc vnum intenti sunt, vt Deo se subijciant per obedientiam fidei. Putantur hi esse stultissimi mortalium, sed ijdem verae illius & caelestis sapientiae capaces sunt soli, quae homines in via iustitiae & aeternae salutis dirigit. E contra hanc admittere non possunt, qui humanae sapientiae fiducia turgent, quae vel praesentibus intenta res caelestes & aeterna vitae praemia negligit, vel salutem nostris viribus & nostrorum operum meritis acquiri posse docet. Quod vt rectius intelligamus, commodè nunc Lucas eius rei exemplum subijcit, in quodam Legis doctore, qui ea ipsa hora, qua haec à Christo dicta sunt, talem se praebuit, vt in eo ceu in speculo lucidissimo videre liceat, quàm arroganter sese illi opponant, qui sua sapientia nituntur. Quia autem histeria haec doctrinam quoque praeclaram & perfectam de vita re†e pietq; secundum charitatis regulam instituenda continet, digna est, cuius singulae partes diligen tius ex ordine considerentur.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ, in what went before, had spoken of the preaching of his gospel and its effect, he broke out into a fervent thanksgiving, in which he proclaims the justice and goodness of God the Father, who has deigned to reveal these mysteries of his kingdom and of eternal salvation to people who are foolish and despised by the judgement of the world, while hiding them from the wise and the understanding. Here we learn who are the worthy and fit hearers of the divine Word: namely, those who renounce the reasoning of the flesh and worldly wisdom, and who, setting aside all the other concerns of this age, devote themselves to this one thing, that they may submit themselves to God through the obedience of faith. Such people are thought to be the most foolish of mortals, yet they alone are capable of that true and heavenly wisdom which directs men in the way of righteousness and eternal salvation. On the other hand, those who are puffed up with confidence in human wisdom cannot admit it. Such wisdom either, being intent on present things, neglects heavenly things and the eternal rewards of life, or teaches that salvation can be obtained by our own strength and the merits of our works. So that we may understand this more rightly, Luke now conveniently sets before us an example of this matter, in a certain teacher of the Law, who, at the very hour when these things were spoken by Christ, showed himself such that in him, as in a most clear mirror, one may see how arrogantly those who rely on their own wisdom set themselves against him. Moreover, since this narrative also contains a most excellent and perfect teaching on how life is to be rightly and piously ordered according to the rule of charity, it is worthy that its individual parts be considered carefully and in order.

units.la: Principio legis interpres producitur, de quo sic scribit Lucas: Tum ecce quidam Legis inter pres surrexit, tentans eum & dicens: Magister, quid faciendo vitam aeternam possidebo? Emphasim habent duae istae particulae: Tum ecce, vel (vt in Graeco habetur) καὶ ἰδοὺ, & ecce, quod idem est, cum copulativa particula haec praecedentibus connectat, & Doctorem hunc aduersus Christum de tantis mysteriis differentem insurrexisse ostendat. Perinde ergo hoc est ac si diceret: Cum Dominus ista tanto cum affectu pronunciauisset, vt merito terreri debuerint, qui hucusque propria sapientia fiducia inflati fuerant, adeo tamen apud eos nihil profecit, vt ecce praeter omnium expectationem eo ipso momento surgere ausus fuerit quidam legis interpres, qui illum quaestione captiosa aggredere- tur, qua eum irretire & populo inuisum vel contemptum reddere conatus est. Est ergo hoc memo- rabile exemplum, quo admonemur, quantum possit propria iustitia & sapientia perfuasio, quod non bus non mirum videri debeat, si etiam hodie in aperta Euangelij luce, quam vulgus hominum cernit & ampletitur, indies exacerbantur & praefractiores fiunt, qui summam doctrinae & sapientiae exi stimationem sustinent. Est enim hoc carnis ingenium, vt quo magis vrgetur verbo Dei, eo magis contra illud insurgat atq; ferociat. Et cum Christo docente hoc factum sit, quid mirum si idem hodie fiat, quando Euangelium ab hominibus praedicatur, qui & ipsi communibus affectibus obnoxij sunt, & interdum vitijs quoq; manifestis laborant?
units.tr: First, the teacher of the Law is introduced, of whom Luke writes thus: "Then, behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and saying: Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" These two particles, "Then, behold" (or, as it is in the Greek, καὶ ἰδού, "and behold", which is the same), with the copulative particle, connect this with what precedes and show that this teacher rose up against Christ while he was discoursing on such great mysteries. The meaning therefore is this: when the Lord had declared these things with such feeling that those who until then had been puffed up with confidence in their own wisdom ought rightly to have been terrified, nevertheless he achieved so little among them that, contrary to everyone's expectation, at that very moment a certain teacher of the Law dared to rise up, who set upon him with a captious question, by which he tried to ensnare him and make him hateful or contemptible to the people. This is therefore a memorable example, by which we are admonished how much the persuasion of one's own righteousness and wisdom can do. It ought not seem surprising, then, if even today, in the open light of the gospel, which the common people see and embrace, those who hold to the highest esteem of their learning and wisdom grow daily more bitter and more stubborn. For it is the nature of the flesh that the more it is pressed by the Word of God, the more it rises up against it and grows fierce. And since this happened when Christ himself was teaching, why should it be strange if the same thing happens today, when the gospel is preached by men who are themselves subject to common passions, and sometimes also labour under manifest vices?

units.la: Sed audiamus quaestionem huius Legisperiti. Magister (inquit) quid faciendo vitam aeternam possidebo? Pia quaestio in speciem, imo per se necessaria: sed dum ab isto mouetur, communis error coniunctam habet, qui tunc inter Iudaeos regnabat: quod nimirum hominem suis factis & operibus iustificari & salutem aeternam consequi putarent. Erroris causa erat, quod Legis vsum ignorarent, & in sola promissionum legalium verba intenti, interim non obseruabant virium nostrarum imbe- cillitatem, qua impediti ea non possumus praestare, quae Lex a nobis requirit. Quoad vero superbum hunc Doctorem, mouet vt hanc quaestionem duas ob causas. Primo, quod cum ipse totus a Lege, vel potius adulterino & peruerso legis sensu penderet, non potuit non offendi Euangelij doctrina, quae salutem in mera Dei gratia monstrat, & eandem non nisi per fidem in promissum humani generis seruatorem acquiri posse docet. Putat ergo illam cum Mose pugnare, & proinde esse intolerabilem. Deinde communi Legisperitorum & Scribarum morbo laborat: ambitione nimirum, quae illum mo- uet, vt indigne ferat suam & totius ordinis sui authoritatem minui, & populum ipsis relictis ad Christum confluere. Eiusmodi ergo quaestionem proponit, qua putat ex Christi ore responsum elici posse, quod palam Mosis doctrinae aduersetur, & ita sibi apud populum inuidiam & odium concilia turum esse: quod ipsum illos alias saepe tentauisse scimus.
units.tr: But let us hear the question of this lawyer. "Teacher," he says, "what must I do to possess eternal life?" It is a pious question in appearance, indeed necessary in itself. But as it is asked by this man, it carries a common error, which then reigned among the Jews: namely, that they thought a man is justified by his own deeds and works and obtains eternal salvation. The cause of this error was that they were ignorant of the use of the Law, and, intent only on the words of the legal promises, did not observe the weakness of our powers, by which, hindered, we cannot perform what the Law requires of us. As for this proud teacher, he is moved to ask this question for two reasons. First, since he himself depended wholly on the Law, or rather on a corrupt and perverted sense of the law, he could not but be offended by the teaching of the gospel, which shows that salvation lies in the mere grace of God, and teaches that it can be obtained only through faith in the promised Saviour of mankind. He therefore thinks that this teaching contradicts Moses and so is intolerable. Second, he suffers from the common disease of the lawyers and scribes, namely ambition, which moves him to take it ill that his own authority and that of his whole order should be diminished, and that the people, leaving them, should flock to Christ. He therefore puts forward a question of this kind, by which he thinks a response can be drawn from Christ's mouth that openly contradicts the teaching of Moses, and so he will win for himself hatred and odium among the people. We know that they had often tried this before.

units.la: Et debet diligenter obseruari haec hostium veritatis astutia. Simulant pietatis & salutis aeterna studium, cum animos a pietate alienissimos habeant, & non alio quam proprij honoris & commodi studio ducantur. Deinde scripturas allegare audent, quasi illarum studio serio teneantur, in illis autem ea sola obseruant, quae ipsorum erroribus patrocinari videntur. Et vt aranea ex illis floribus venenum haurit, ex quibus dulcia & salubria mella apes colligunt: ita isti ex scripturis venenata & noxia errorum fomenta decerpunt: non quod illa aliquid huius contineant, sed quod ipsi multos complures impie detorquendo sibi ipsis & alijs noxios reddant. Denique cum quaestiones de religione, de cultu Dei, de fide, de aeterna salutis ratione nunquam non in ore habeant, hoc tamen vnum agunt, vt & veritatem obscurent, & huius studiosos in periculum adducant. Est hodie infinitum istorum hominum numerus, quorum artes magna diligentia obseruari debent, ne nobis falsa pietatis specie imponant, aut etiam incautos in nessam trahant, vt vna cum veritatis doctrina periclitemur.
units.tr: And this cunning of the enemies of truth ought to be carefully observed. They pretend a zeal for piety and eternal salvation, when their minds are most alien to piety, and they are led by nothing but the desire for their own honour and advantage. Then they dare to cite the Scriptures, as if they were seriously devoted to them, yet in them they observe only those things which seem to support their errors. And as a spider draws poison from those flowers from which bees gather sweet and wholesome honey, so these men pluck from the Scriptures venomous and harmful fuel for errors. This is not because the Scriptures contain any such thing, but because they, by twisting them impiously, make them harmful to themselves and to others. Finally, though they always have on their lips questions about religion, the worship of God, faith, and the manner of eternal salvation, yet they do this one thing: they both obscure the truth and lead its students into danger. Today the number of such men is infinite, and their arts must be observed with great diligence, lest they deceive us with a false appearance of piety, or even draw the unwary into the net, so that we are endangered along with the doctrine of truth.

units.la: Porro quod malignus iste legis interpres dolo malo hic agit, hoc nos serio facere decet, vt nimirum de vita aeterna & huius consequendae ratione quaeramus, non autem praesenti huic seculo sim- addicti. Nec enim hic ciuitatem habemus permanentem, sed in mundo peregrini sumus, quorum patria in caelis est: quod ipsi inter orandum fatemur, quoties Patre nostrum innocamus, qui in caelis est. Deinde fluxa & caduca sunt, quaecunque in hoc mundo pro eximijs habentur. Quod apud Isaiam magna cum gravitate docet Dominus. Nam Prophetam clamare, id est, clara voce, ceu rem ad omnes pertinentem promulgare iubet id, quod ipsi erat suggesturus. Et illo quaerente, Quid clamabo? subjicit vox Domini: Omnis caro fenum, et omnis gloria eius sicut flos agri. Exaruit fenum, decidit flos, verbum autem Dei nostri manet in aeternum. O praeclaram sententiam, et nunquam satis considerandam, quam mus exemplo quotidiano confirmetur. Nam si ipsum hominem spectes, quem scriptura fere Carnem dicere consuevit, quid illo miserius, corruptibilius et pluribus casibus obnoxium? Vix ret quidem interdum, et tam robore quam forma corporis conspicuus habetur. At idem mox leui se brevi ula ita attenuatur, ut sui plane dissimilis appareat. Taceo morbos infinitos, quorum numerum ne medici quidem hucusque certum constituere potuerunt, et quorum materiam intra corpus nostrum gestamus, quae moventem illam Domino mox per corpus diffunditur, et omnes eius vires debilitat. Taceo casus, qui aliunde accidunt, quibus enumerandis vix dies totus sufficerit. Quid vero de ipsa mortis hora dicemus, quae plerunque cum minime putatur, obrepit, et circa longe alia studia occupatos abripit? Vere igitur homo graminis instar est, quod etsi ad tempus virenti et smaragdino ornatu terram vestiat, mox tamen vel vento calidiore adustum, vel falce defectu exaresci. Quod si gloriam carnis, id est, ea inspiciamus, quae homini praecipuam authoritatem conciliare, et in quibus ipse etiam in primis gloriari et superbire solet, quid hic aliud quam flores agri temere nascentes et subito arescentes videbis? Fluxa et incerta est divitiarum possessio. Incerti et dubij honores, qui plerunque ab aura populari, quovis vento mutabiliore, dependent. Fallax humanae sapientiae existimatio, ut non temere proverbio iactetur, sapientissimos quosque prae aliis turpiter errare, et vitia detegnare no vulgaria. Eadem deniq; est omnium aliorum conditio. Non temere ergo sapientissimus ille mortalium Salomon, cum quaecunque, sub Sole sunt attentissime considerauisset, tandem exclamavit: Vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas. Quid vero hinc colligemus? Hoc nimirum, ne praesentibus bonis nimium simus addicti, sed (ut Paulus monet) mundo hoc se vtamur, ne illo abutamur, perpetuo autem quaeramus futuram illam civitatem, quam nobis in caelo Christus parauit, quod etiam initio monuimus, serio scrutemur veram vitae aeternae consequendae rationem, eamque nobis in verbo Domini monstratam sedulo sequamur. Quam vero beati et felices essent homines si hunc sibi studiorum suorum scopum proponerent? Ita certe curis, laboribus et periculis infinitis liberarentur, quibus se ipsos immergunt, dum circa vana mundi studia occupantur. Nunquam non ergo ipsi nobis hanc quaestionem occinamus: Quid faciendo possidebis vitam aeternam? Etsi enim huius obtinenda ratio simplex sit, nos tamen quotidie et in horas singulas admoneri necesse est, nos non ad terrenam hanc et mortalem, sed caelestem et aeternam vitam creatos esse, et proinde de hac in primis solicitos esse debere.
units.tr: Moreover, what this wicked lawyer does here with evil intent, we ought to do in earnest: namely, to inquire about eternal life and the way of obtaining it, and not to be devoted to the present age. For here we have no abiding city, but we are strangers and pilgrims in the world, whose homeland is in heaven. This we confess ourselves whenever, in prayer, we call upon our Father who is in heaven. Furthermore, whatever is held in esteem in this world is frail and perishable. The Lord teaches this with great seriousness through Isaiah. For he bids the prophet to cry out, that is, to proclaim with a clear voice, as a matter that concerns everyone, that which he was about to say to them. And when he asks, "What shall I cry?", the voice of the Lord replies: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever." O excellent saying, never sufficiently to be considered, and confirmed by daily experience! For if you look at man himself, whom Scripture is accustomed to call flesh, what is more wretched, more corruptible, and more subject to many accidents? He is sometimes seen as vigorous, and remarkable both in strength and bodily form. Yet soon after, with a slight breath, he is so weakened that he appears quite unlike himself. I say nothing of the endless diseases, whose number even physicians have not yet been able to fix with certainty, and whose matter we carry within our bodies, which is soon spread through the body by the moving force and weakens all its powers. I say nothing of the accidents which befall us from outside, which a whole day would hardly suffice to enumerate. But what shall we say of the very hour of death, which for the most part creeps upon us when least expected, and snatches us away while we are busy with quite other pursuits? Truly, then, man is like grass, which, though for a time it clothes the earth with green and emerald ornament, soon withers, either scorched by a hotter wind or cut down by the scythe. And if we look at the glory of the flesh, that is, those things which are wont to win for a man his chief authority, and in which he himself is especially accustomed to glory and be proud, what will you see here but flowers of the field, rashly springing up and suddenly withering? The possession of riches is frail and uncertain. Honours are uncertain and doubtful, depending for the most part on popular favour, which shifts with every wind. The estimation of human wisdom is deceptive, so that it is not for nothing that the proverb says that the most wise fall shamefully into error more than others, and reveal no common vices. Finally, the condition of all other things is the same. It was not for nothing that Solomon, the wisest of mortals, after he had considered most attentively all things that are under the sun, at last cried out: "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity." What then shall we gather from this? Surely this: that we should not be too much devoted to present goods, but (as Paul advises) use this world as not abusing it, and always seek that future city which Christ has prepared for us in heaven. As we said at the beginning, let us earnestly search out the true way of obtaining eternal life, and diligently follow it, as it is shown to us in the Word of the Lord. How blessed and happy would men be if they set this goal for their studies! Certainly they would thus be freed from the countless cares, labours, and dangers into which they plunge themselves while they are occupied with the vain pursuits of the world. Let us therefore never cease to sing this question to ourselves: "What must you do to possess eternal life?" For although the way of obtaining it is simple, we must nevertheless be reminded every day and every hour that we have been created not for this earthly and mortal life, but for the heavenly and eternal life, and that therefore we ought to be especially anxious about this.

units.la: Porro audiamus tandem Christum, qui longe aliter respondet, quam legis interpres sperabat. Arbitrabatur enim hic, eum novam exorsurum esse orationem, in qua de modo vitae aeternae consequendae dissereret, et rationem ostenderet novam, longeque aliam ab ea, quae olim a Deo per Mosem fuerat tradita. Inde vero sibi occasionem oblatam iri sperabat, qua ipsum posset apud populum traducere, apud quem sacrosancta erat Mosis authoritas. At Dominus, qui eius animum perspectum habebat, aliam illi quaestionem opponit, et eo eum adducit, ut proprii oris testimonio convictus tandem non sine ignominia ex temere suscepto certamine discedat, ut suo loco audiemus. Nam ad legem remittit eum, cuius cognitione in primis superbiebat, et diserte offendit, se nihil ab hac diversum docere. Dicit enim: In lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis? Quasi diceret: Mirum est, hanc quaestionem abs te moveri, qui legis interpres et doctor es. Annon enim Deus in illa vitae aeternae consequendae rationem prolixe et diligenter praescripsit? Anno illic traditur, quid a nobis fieri, quidve caveri debeat, si illo propitio uti, et aeternum seruari velimus? Ex te igitur audire velim, quid illa docet, et tuum est mihi et aliis de lege sciscitantibus respondere. Ita vero eum cogit, ut ipse ad quaestionem abs se propositam respondeat, qua Christum voluerat irretire. Quia enim legis interpres erat, et docendi officio fungebatur, non potuit non respondere ad ea, quae de lege interrogabatur.
units.tr: Let us at last hear Christ, who answers quite differently from what the interpreter of the law expected. For this man supposed that he would begin a new discourse, in which he would treat of the way to obtain eternal life and set out a new method, far different from the one God once delivered through Moses. He hoped that this would give him an opportunity to win over the people, among whom the authority of Moses was held sacred. But the Lord, who knew his mind, puts another question to him and brings him to the point where, convicted by his own mouth, he finally leaves the contest he had rashly undertaken, not without disgrace, as we shall hear in its place. For Christ sends him back to the law, the very thing in which he took the most pride, and plainly shows that he teaches nothing different from it. He says: "What is written in the law? How do you read it?" As if to say: "It is strange that you raise this question, you who are an interpreter and teacher of the law. Has not God set out in that law, fully and carefully, the way of obtaining eternal life? Is it not there taught what we must do, and what we must avoid, if we wish to enjoy his favour and be preserved for eternity? I want you to tell me what it teaches, since it is your task to answer me and others who ask about the law." So he compels him to answer the question he himself had proposed, by which he had wanted to ensnare Christ. For since he was an interpreter of the law and performed the office of a teacher, he could not but answer the questions put to him about the law.

units.la: Etsi vero Dominus diuinae sapientiae specimen hic exhibeat, quae huius seculi sapientes in propria astutia capere solet, simul tamen docet, rationem salutis consequendae nusquam quam in lege Dei quaeri debere. Porro legis vocabulo non solum libri Mosis, sed universa scriptura Veteris testamenti comprehenditur. Christus enim Ioannis decimo capite, locum Psalmi adducturus ait: Annon in lege vestra scriptum est, Ego dixi, Dii estis? &c. Et Paulus Isaiam allegans, legis vo- ce vtitur in priori ad Corinthios cap.14. Ac inter vetus & Nouum Testamentum optimè con- uenire, imò in hoc clarius explicari, quae in illo obscurius tradebantur, alibi est demonstratum. Scri- pturas ergo sacras legant & audiant, qui salutis & vitae aeternae serio studio tenentur. In his enim suam voluntatem nobis Deus reuelauit, quae nos in huius vitae curriculo dirigit, & cuius cognitio nos in omni tentationum genere consolatur. Eadem sola vitae aeternae viam nobis monstrat. Ideo a- pud Ioannem Christus Scribis dicebat: Scrutamini scripturas: nam vos putatis vobis in illis vi- tam aeternam habere. Quibus verbis eos non reprehendit, quod scripturas plus aequo tribuant, sed quod harum studio & cognitione gloriarentur, eadem vero non diligentius inuestigarent, vt quae de ipso in illis habentur, testimonia possent deprehendere. Addit enim: Illae de me testantur. Et Paulus Apostolus, sacras literas à Deo inspiratas, & vtiles atq; sufficientes esse docet, ad hoc, vt homo Dei perfectus fiat, & ad omne opus bonum paratus. Est ergo turpis & pernitiosum illorum error, qui quando de religione & aeternae salutis negotio agitur, ad Canones nescio quos Apostoli- cos, ad Patres, ad Concilia & Pontificum decreta confugiunt. Faciunt hi atrocem iniuriam Spi- ritui sancto, quem insimulant, quasi non plenè tradiderit in scripturis, quae ad salutis humana ra- tionem pertinent. Iugulantur autem vnica Dei sententia, per Isaiam dicentis: Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, sive traditiones hominum.
units.tr: Although the Lord here displays a specimen of divine wisdom, which the wise men of this age are accustomed to catch in their own cunning, he at the same time teaches that the way of obtaining salvation is to be sought nowhere but in the law of God. Now the word "law" comprehends not only the books of Moses but the whole of the Scripture of the Old Testament. For Christ, in John chapter 10, when he is about to cite a psalm, says: "Is it not written in your law, I said, You are gods? etc." And Paul, quoting Isaiah, uses the word "law" in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14. And it has been shown elsewhere that the Old and New Testaments agree very well, and indeed that what was taught more obscurely in the one is made clearer in the other. Let those therefore read and hear the sacred Scriptures who are seriously devoted to salvation and eternal life. For in them God has revealed to us his will, which directs us through the course of this life, and the knowledge of which comforts us in every kind of temptation. Scripture alone shows us the way to eternal life. Therefore Christ said to the scribes in John: "Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life." In these words he does not rebuke them for ascribing too much to the Scriptures, but because they boasted of their study and knowledge of them, while not investigating them more diligently so as to discover the testimonies about himself that are found in them. For he adds: "It is they that bear witness of me." And the Apostle Paul teaches that the sacred letters, inspired by God, are useful and sufficient to make the man of God perfect and ready for every good work. It is therefore a shameful and pernicious error of those who, when the matter of religion and eternal salvation is in question, flee to I know not what apostolic canons, to the Fathers, to councils and to the decrees of the pontiffs. Such men do a monstrous injury to the Holy Spirit, whom they accuse of not having fully set forth in the Scriptures what pertains to the way of human salvation. And they are refuted by the single saying of God, spoken through Isaiah: "In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men."

units.la: Sed redeamus ad legis interpretem, qui ad Christi quaestionem respondet, & duos locos coniun- git, quorum alter Deut.6. alter Leuit.19.cap.habetur. Diliges (inquit) Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex totis viribus tuis, & ex tota cogitatione vel mente tua: & proximum tuum vt teipsum. Vbi obseruabis, quòd etsi haec ab hoste veritatis dicantur, vere ta- men dicuntur. Nam & in praesenti sua responsione haec approbat Christus, & apud Matthaum po- stea ab alio magis ingenuo interrogatus, quod nam inter Dei praecepta primum & praecipuum sit, huic ipsis verbis respondet, & addit: Abiiis duobus mandatis tota lex & Prophetae pendent. Habe- mus igitur hoc loco perfectam pie & rectè viuendi regulam duobus membris sive capitibus compre- hensam, Dilectione Dei nimirum & Proximi.
