In quo paterna Dei bonitas elucet, qui nō infinitis praeceptis nos grauare voluit, vt fere solent, qui inter homines sibi magisterium vendicant: nec etiam alia praescribit, quàm quae per charitatem perfici aut praestari possunt, qua nihil iucundius, nihil amabilius, nihil etiam in tota hominum vita & consuetudine vtilius est & magis necessarium, & quae res difficillimas nobis faciles & iucundas reddit. Quod vnum ad confutandam eorum stultitiam & ingratitudinem sufficit, qui relicta viuendi regula à Deo praescripta, perfectius quid in Monachorum regulis & aliorum hominum traditionibus quaerunt, quae vt nihil vera & solidae pietatis continent, ita inani labore miseros fatigant, & eos qui nummatiores sunt expoliant. Sed vtrunq; praeceptum seorsim excutiamus, vt quid nos facere conueniat, melius constet.
units.tr: But let us return to the interpreter of the law, who answers Christ's question and joins two passages, one of which is found in Deut. 6, the other in Lev. 19. "You shall love," he says, "the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your thought or mind; and your neighbour as yourself." Here you will observe that although these words are spoken by an enemy of the truth, they are nonetheless spoken truly. For Christ both approves this answer in his present reply, and later, when he was asked by another, more ingenuous man in Matthew which is the first and greatest of God's commandments, he answers in these very words and adds: "On these two commandments hang the whole law and the Prophets." We have here, therefore, a complete rule for living piously and rightly, comprehended in two parts or heads, namely the love of God and of neighbour. In this the fatherly goodness of God shines forth, who has not wished to burden us with endless precepts, as men who claim authority over others usually do, nor does he prescribe anything other than what can be accomplished or performed through charity, than which nothing is sweeter, nothing more lovable, nothing more useful in the whole life and society of men, nothing more necessary, and which makes the most difficult things easy and pleasant for us. This one point is enough to refute the folly and ingratitude of those who, abandoning the rule of living prescribed by God, seek something more perfect in the rules of monks and the traditions of other men. These, since they contain nothing of true and solid piety, only weary wretched people with empty labour and strip those who are better off. But let us examine each of the two precepts separately, so that it may be clearer what we ought to do.

units.la: Primum est: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Quid sit diligere & dilectio, alibi diximus, & omnibus per se satis notum est: Nunc hoc ante omnia obseruari operaepretium est, quòd sui dilectionem à nobis Deus postulat. Ergo nō externi cultus magnifico splendore delecta- tur, sed animi ipsi per omnia addicti affectum requirit, qui veram numinis reuerentiam & voluntaria obedientia studium in nobis gignit. Et huc faciunt, quae passim apud Prophetas dicuntur con- tra eos, qui circa victimas solas & reliquum cultum externum occupabantur, interim vero fidem in Deum, eiusdem dilectionem, & quae ei debetur, obedientiam fecerint negligebant. Vt autem merito et iure eum diligere debemus, quia noster creator, pater & protector, adhac summum bonum & omnis boni fons est: ita magnum hoc est bonitatis eius argumentum, quòd à nobis diligi vult, & simul se quoq; totum bonaq; sua omnia nobis fruenda offert. Imò vt Ioannes Apostolus docet, ipse prior nos dilexit, & Filium suum aeterno suo decreto nobis seruatorē destinauit. Qui in hoc secuto generis no- bilitate, diuitijs & dignitatibus excellunt, ij hominum ignobilium & pauperū amicitiam sibi ignomi- niosam esse arbitrantur, & fere cognatos quoq; suos & sanguine iunctos fastidiunt, si qui inter hos pauperiores sunt & obscuri. Quanta ergo haec Dei bonitas est, qui à nobis diligi vult, qui non modò omnib. modis miseri, adhaec mortales, verumetiam peccatores & propter peccatum aeterna morte digni sumus? Hinc ergo consolationis argumenta petamus in tentationibus, & nosipsos ad illius amore excitemus. Nam etsi Deus ipse per suum spiritum dilectionem sui in nobis accendat, & (ut Paulus ait) diffundat in cordibus nostris, plurimum tamen nos hic iuuat frequens & diligens beneficiorum eius meditatio, verbi studium, & preces, quibus nos in primis apud illum instare oportet, ut nostri & mundi amore in nobis extincto, animos nostros syncero & sancto sui amore inflammet.
units.tr: The first is: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc." What it is to love, and what love is, we have said elsewhere, and it is sufficiently known to all in itself. Now it is worth observing above all that God demands our love for himself. He is therefore not delighted by the magnificent splendour of outward worship, but requires the affection of a soul wholly devoted to him, which begets in us true reverence for the divinity and a willing zeal for obedience. And to this point are the many passages in the Prophets, spoken against those who were occupied only with sacrifices and the rest of outward worship, while meanwhile they neglected faith in God, love of him, and the obedience that is owed him. And just as we ought rightly and justly to love him, because he is our creator, father and protector, and moreover is the supreme good and the fount of every good, so this is a great proof of his goodness, that he wishes to be loved by us, and at the same time offers himself wholly, with all his goods, to be enjoyed by us. Indeed, as the Apostle John teaches, he himself first loved us, and from his eternal decree appointed his Son to be our Saviour. Those who excel in nobility of birth, riches and dignities among this world's people think it shameful to be friends with men of low birth and poverty, and they often despise even their own kinsmen and blood relations if these are poorer and obscure. How great, then, is this goodness of God, who wishes to be loved by us, when we are not only wretched in every way and mortal, but also sinners and, because of sin, worthy of eternal death? Let us therefore draw from this the grounds of consolation in temptations, and stir ourselves up to love of him. For although God himself, by his Spirit, kindles the love of himself in us, and (as Paul says) pours it out in our hearts, nonetheless frequent and diligent meditation on his benefits, zeal for the Word, and prayers help us greatly here. In these above all we ought to press upon him, that, with our love of ourselves and of the world extinguished in us, he may inflame our minds with his own sincere and holy love.

units.la: Porrò modum quoque dilectionis Dei Moses diligenter exprimit propter eos, qui qualemcunque amorem suffi cere putant, vel etiam solis verbis diligunt. Docet ergo dilectionem solidam & perfectam requiri, quae hominem totum Deo vendicet, & ideo praecipuas, vel potius omnes hominis facultates ex ordine recenset. Primò, Diliges (inquit) Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo. At qui constat cor fontem esse affectuum omnium. Hos ergo simul omnes in Dei dilectionem dirigere, & per hanc ipsius voluntati subijcere oportet. Quod ut fiat, alias etiā ob causas necesse est. Suae enim affectus nostri praui propter innatam nobis naturae vitiositatem, & ideo ad malum feruntur, & nobis omnis generis vitiorum causa sunt. Correctione igitur opus habent, quae non alia est, quam Dei dilectio. Haec enim illos in officio continet, & ut uni Deo seruiat moderatur. Secundò, Ex tota anima Deū diligere debemus. In anima hominis vita consistit. Haec ergo tota Dei dilectionem spirare debet, nec aliquid faciendum est, quod eum à nobis minus diligi testetur. Et hic peccant, qui melio rem vitae suae partem mundi & diaboli seruitio tribuunt, senectam demum Deo consecraturi, cum tamen ignorent, an unquam ad illam peruenturi sint. Tertio, Ex totis viribus nostris Deus diligen dus est. Intelliguntur omnes corporis vires, bona deniq; externa, quae philosophi fortunae esse dixerunt: qualia sunt opes, honores, dignitates & alia huiusmodi. Et ista quidem omnia iure sibi vendicat Deus. Nam & corpus ipse creauit, & eius donum sunt valetudo bona, robur & vires validae, forma, agilitas & quaecunq; alia inter corporis bene constituti dotes numerantur. Eadem est bonorum externorum ratio, quae non (ut prophani philosophi senserunt) à caeco fortunae fauore proueniunt, sed etiam à Deo dantur, quod non uno loco scripturae docent. Quicquid ergo vel corporis viribus, vel dignitate & authoritate possumus, id omne per Dei dilectionem in hunc finem à nobis dirigi debet, ut in nobis ille glorificetur, & debitum ei praestemus obsequium. Additur quarto loco, Ex tota cogitatione vel mente tua. Mentem superiorem illam animi facultatem dixerunt, quae rationem de rebus agendis aut omittendis init, & cogitationibus suis per omnia mirifica celeritate discurrit. At quia haec quoq; in nobis corrupta est, fit, ut cogitationes nostrae praue, & (ut Deus ipse testatur) omnia cordis aut mentis humanae figmenta mala sint. Quod mox deprehendes, si cogitationes tuas diligentius consideraueris. Quid enim haec aliud versant intra animum tuum, quam opes, honores huius saeculi, libidines foedas, vindictae studium & alia huius generis, quae nos à Deo abstrahunt? Et tanta illarum est improbitas, ut etiam circa bonum aliquod opus occupatis obrepant. Nam eleemosynam facientibus succurrit ambitio, precantibus item infinita alia in mentem veniunt, quae ita nos distrahunt, ut raro Orationem Dominicam quis totam recitare possit, quin et i cogitet, quae ipsum coram hominibus dicere aut facere puderet. Huic igitur malo remedium adhibiturus Moses, monet, ut cogitationibus quoque nostris frenum dilectionis Dei iniiciamus, quo à rebus prauis & illicitis abstrahantur, ad ea autem dirigantur, quae ad Dei gloriam faciunt. Quod si vero haec omnia diligentius expendamus, patebit nullum hypocrisi locum esse, si Deo vere seruire velimus, & simul apparebit, quanta sit humani ingenij corruptio, quando nemo est, qui ista praestare possit; etiamsi ea optimo iure à nobis requiri omnes fateantur.
units.tr: Moreover, Moses also carefully spells out the manner of loving God, for the benefit of those who think that any sort of love is enough, or who love God only in words. He therefore teaches that a solid and perfect love is required, one that claims the whole man for God. Accordingly he lists in order the chief faculties of man, or rather all of them. First, he says, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart." Now it is well known that the heart is the source of all the affections. These, then, all together must be directed to the love of God, and through that love made subject to his will. For this to happen there is need of other reasons too. Our affections are corrupt, because of the inborn sinfulness of our nature, so they tend toward evil and are the cause of every kind of vice. They therefore need correction, and this is nothing other than the love of God. For this love keeps them within their duty and governs them so that they serve God alone. Second, "You shall love God with all your soul." Human life consists in the soul. This whole soul, then, ought to breathe the love of God, and nothing should be done that shows God is loved less by us. Those sin here who give the better part of their life to the service of the world and the devil, intending to consecrate only their old age to God, though they do not know whether they will ever reach it. Third, "You shall love God with all your strength." This includes all the powers of the body and, finally, the external goods, which the philosophers called the gifts of fortune: such as wealth, honours, dignities and other things of this kind. God rightly claims all these for himself. For he himself created the body, and health, strength, vigour, beauty, agility, and whatever else is counted among the endowments of a well-made body, are his gifts. The same holds of external goods, which, as the profane philosophers thought, do not come from the blind favour of fortune but are also given by God, as the Scriptures teach in more than one place. Therefore whatever we can do by bodily strength, or by dignity and authority, all of it must be directed by us, through the love of God, to this end: that he may be glorified in us and that we may render him the obedience owed. Fourth, he adds, "with all your thought or mind." They called the mind that higher faculty of the soul which deliberates on what is to be done or left undone, and which runs through its thoughts with wonderful speed in every direction. But because this faculty too is corrupted in us, our thoughts are evil, and (as God himself testifies) every imagination of the human heart or mind is evil. You will soon discover this if you consider your thoughts more carefully. For what else do they occupy your mind with except wealth, the honours of this age, foul lusts, the pursuit of revenge, and other things of this kind, which draw us away from God? So great is their wickedness that they creep in even when we are busy with some good work. For when we give alms, ambition comes to mind; and when we pray, countless other things occur to us, which distract us so much that scarcely anyone can recite the whole Lord's Prayer without thinking of things he would be ashamed to say or do in front of other people. Wishing therefore to apply a remedy to this evil, Moses advises us to put the bridle of the love of God on our thoughts too, so that they may be drawn away from wicked and unlawful things and directed to those things that serve the glory of God. If we weigh all these things more carefully, it will be clear that there is no room for hypocrisy if we truly wish to serve God. At the same time it will appear how great the corruption of the human mind is, since no one is able to perform these things, although everyone admits that they are rightly required of us.

units.la: Alterum praeceptum est: Diliges proximum tuum, ut teipsum. Proximi nomine omnes homines intelliguntur, qui nostra ope & auxilio indigent, ut in Samaritani parabola sequenti Sermone Christus ipse docebit. Requiritur autem proximi dilectio, quia haec in unum corpus nos colligit, beneficentiae mater est, iniurias omnes probibet, & ideo legem totam implere à Paulo dicitur. Sed huius etiam modum Lex exprimit, quando proximum perinde ut nosipsos diligere iubet. Ita vero praecipit, quia natura φίλαυτοι, id est, nostrii ipsorum amantes sumus, & nobisipsis nimium addicti. Quae causa est, quod quam primum de nostris commodis agitur, proximos facile negligimus. Vult ergo Deus, ut alios homines eodem, quo nosipsos loco habeamus, eorunq; commodis non minus quam nostris studeamus. Simul etiam ijs occurrit, qui ut sese excusent, se nescire aiunt, quatenus & quo usq; proximum diligere debeant. Atqui in teipsum desCende, & quomodo teipsum diligas vide. & non multa quaestione porro opus erit. Temetipsum non simulate, nec verbis solis, sed vere & ex animo diligu: adhaec non frigide, sed ardenter. Simili ergo amore alios quoq; homines prosequere, ne quid animo fucato fiat, neque perfunctorie, sed ardenti illos iuuandi studio. Deinde nostrus commodus studemus: fac ergo proximi quoque commoda, qua potes ratione promoueas. Praeterea non defatigamur nos ipsos amando, etiamsi vitia nobis insint multa quae odium merentur. Ita proximi amor perpetuus & constans sit, qui nec officiorum erga illum difficultate, nec etiam vitijs, quibus ille laborat, extinguatur. Est enim hoc veri amoris proprium, quod etsi amicus satisfaciat, abunde, sibijpsi tamen satisfaciat nunquam, quin se plura debere exstimet. Idem quoque (quodex Solomone Petrus annotauit) multitudinem peccatorum operit, & quae in proximo corrigere non potest, pie dissimulat & patienter fert, eiusque honori consultum cupit. Et haec quidem dicta sufficiant nunc de duobus hisce praeceptis, quae qui obseruarint, ijs ad vitam recte & pie instituendam nihil deerit.
units.tr: The second commandment is: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." By the name of neighbour all men are understood who need our help and assistance, as Christ himself will teach in the parable of the Good Samaritan in the following sermon. Love of neighbour is required because it binds us together into one body, is the mother of beneficence, forbids all injuries, and for this reason is said by Paul to fulfil the whole law. But the law also states the manner of this love, when it bids us love our neighbour just as we love ourselves. It commands this because by nature we are self-lovers [φίλαυτοι], that is, lovers of ourselves, and too much given to ourselves. This is why we readily neglect our neighbours as soon as our own advantages are at stake. God therefore wills that we regard other men in the same place as ourselves, and that we care for their advantages no less than our own. At the same time this answers those who, to excuse themselves, say they do not know how far and to what extent they ought to love their neighbour. Yet go down into yourself and see how you love yourself. No long inquiry will be needed. Love yourself not feignedly, nor in words only, but truly and from the heart; and not coldly but ardently. Then love other men with the same love, so that nothing is done with a counterfeit mind, nor perfunctorily, but with an eager zeal to help them. Next, we are concerned for our own advantage; so promote your neighbour's advantage too, by whatever means you can. Moreover, we do not grow weary of loving ourselves, even though many faults are in us that deserve hatred. So let the love of your neighbour be lasting and constant, one that is not quenched either by the difficulty of the duties owed to him or by the faults with which he struggles. For it is a mark of true love that, even if a friend is fully satisfied, it is never satisfied with itself, but always thinks it owes more. The same love (as Peter noted from Solomon) covers a multitude of sins, and what it cannot correct in a neighbour it dutifully overlooks and bears patiently, and it desires to safeguard his honour. Let these things suffice for now concerning these two precepts. Whoever keeps them will lack nothing for living rightly and piously.

units.la: Restat Iesu Christi responsio, qui paucis infert: Recte respondisti, hoc fac, & vives. Quae verba non sic accipi debent, quasi operum nostrorum iustitiam docere voluerit: sed quia Doctor iste pro communi Iudaeorum errore, de operibus quaesiuerat, responsionem suam illius quaestioni accomodat. Simul tamen verissimum est quod dicit. Si enim faceremus ea, quae ex Mose modo audiuimus, vitam consequeremur aeternam. Nam Dei ipsius verba sunt: Custodietis ritus meos, et iudicia mea quae quisquis fecerit, in eis viuet: Ego Dominus. At cum nemo mortalium ista faciat, nec etiam facere possit (quod Paulus ad Romanos multis docet, & ipsi quotidie in nobis experimur) nemo etiam per opera haec Legis vitam poterit consequi. Vult ergo Christus eum, quem suorum operum fiducia niti sciebat, in seipsum descendere, ad praecepta haec vires suas examinare, vt ita propriae conscientiae testimonio conuictus sentiat sibi alia iustitia opus esse. Habet itaque locus hic egregiam doctrinam de vero Legis vsu. Dedit hanc Deus, & vt per se sancta & bona est, ita eandem amplissimis promissionibus commendauit, quas omnes Dominus hic suo testimonio confirmat. Nec tamen ignorauit Deus, neminem esse, qui illi obedire & omnia eius exequi posset. Dedit tamen, non vt nobis cuiquam luderet, multo minus, vt in desperationem nos coniceret: sed vt nobis speculi instar sit, in quo non solum iam commissa peccata, verumetiam inhaerentem naturae nostrae vitiositatem & nostrarum virium imbecillitatem agnoscamus, & his agnitis conscientiae terrore pressi ad thronum gratiae confugiamus: vbi se Christus offert, qui nobis a Deo Patre iustitia & sanctificatio est factus. Itaque quod Lex neminem seruat, non ipsius, sed nostro vitio fit. Illa enim spiritualis est (vt Paulus ait) nos autem carnales sumus, venundati sub peccatum. Recte ergo illa vtamur, non vt in eius operibus salutem quaeramus, sed vt nobis paedagogi loco sit ad Christum, qui peccatum pro nobis factus est, vt nos iustitia Dei per ipsum efficeremur. Interim lucemur cum innata nobis corruptione, & reliquis mundi studijs Deum supra omnia diligamus, eiusque dilectionem amore proximi testemur. Haec enim propria discipulorum Iesu Christi nota est, quos regni sui caelestis ille olim coheredes faciet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the answer of Jesus Christ, who briefly concludes: "You have answered rightly; do this, and you will live." These words should not be taken as if he meant to teach the righteousness of our works. Rather, since this teacher had asked about works, in line with the common error of the Jews, he adapts his answer to that question. Yet what he says is entirely true. For if we did the things we have just heard from Moses, we would obtain eternal life. These are God's own words: "You shall keep my statutes and my judgements, which whoever does shall live in them: I am the Lord." But since no mortal does these things, nor is even able to do them (as Paul shows at length to the Romans, and as we ourselves daily experience in ourselves), no one can obtain life through these works of the law. Christ therefore wills that the man who trusted in his own works should go down into himself and test his strength against these precepts, so that, convicted by the testimony of his own conscience, he may feel that he needs another righteousness. This passage therefore contains an excellent teaching on the true use of the law. God gave it, and as it is holy and good in itself, so he has commended it by the most ample promises, all of which the Lord here confirms by his own testimony. Yet God did not fail to know that no one can obey him and perform all his commands. He gave the law not to mock us in any way, much less to cast us into despair, but to serve us as a mirror, in which we may recognise not only the sins already committed, but also the sinfulness inherent in our nature and the weakness of our powers. Having recognised these, pressed down by the terror of conscience, we should flee to the throne of grace, where Christ offers himself, who has been made by God the Father our righteousness and sanctification. Thus the fact that the law saves no one is not due to the law itself but to our fault. For it is spiritual (as Paul says), but we are carnal, sold under sin. Let us therefore use the law rightly, not to seek salvation in its works, but so that it may serve as a schoolmaster leading us to Christ, who was made sin for us, so that we might be made the righteousness of God through him. Meanwhile, let us struggle against the corruption inborn in us and against the other pursuits of the world, love God above all things, and bear witness to that love through love of our neighbour. For this is the proper mark of the disciples of Jesus Christ, whom he will one day make co-heirs of his heavenly kingdom. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CIII.

units.la: Ille autem volens iustificare seipsum, dixit Iesu: Et quis est meus proximus? Excipiens autem Iesus dixit: Quidam descendebat ab Hierusalem in Iericho, & incidit in latrones, qui spoliato eo & plagis impositis abierunt, semineccm relinquentes. Forte autem Sacerdos quidam descendit per eandem viam, qui viso eo exaduerso praeterijt. Similiter & Leuita cum venisset ad eum locum, & eum vidisset praeterijt, exaduersus. Samaritanus autem quidam iter faciens, venit ad eum, & eo viso, misericordia commotus est. Et accedens obligauit eius vulnera, infundens oleum ac vinum, & ipsum impositu suo iumento duxit in diuersorium, & eius curam egit. Postero autem die abiens, prolatos duos denarios de dit hospiti, & dixit ei: Curam ipsius age: & quodcunque praeterea insumpserit sumpserit, ego cum rediero, reddam tibi. Quis igitur horum trium tibi videtur proximus fuisse illi, qui incidit in latrones? Ille autem dixit: Is qui usus est misericordia erga eum. Ait igitur ei Iesus: Abi, & tu fac similiter.
units.tr: But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: "And who is my neighbour?" Jesus took him up and said: "A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers, who stripped him, inflicted wounds on him, and went away, leaving him half-dead. By chance a certain priest was going down the same road, and when he saw him he passed by on the opposite side. Likewise a Levite, when he came to that place and saw him, passed by on the opposite side. But a certain Samaritan, travelling, came to him, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion. Going up to him, he bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine, and setting him on his own beast he brought him to an inn and looked after him. On the next day he went away, took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: 'Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.' Which of these three, do you think, was the neighbour of the man who fell among the robbers?" He answered: "The one who showed mercy to him." Jesus therefore said to him: "Go, and do likewise."

units.la: QVemadmodum Deus in omnibus operibus suis suae erga nos bonitatis memor est: ita in iis gibus quoq; & praeceptis, quae nobis tradit, in primis nostrae salutis rationem habet. Nonenim alias nobis leges dat, quam quae omnes sub una charitate aut dilectione comprehendi possunt, ex qua (si rem ipsam probe consideremus) plus boni ad nos redit, quam ad eos, quibus illa impenditur. Primo enim nos ad Dei imaginem reformat, qui (ut Ioannes inquit) charitas ipsa est. Dein de totius vitae, quam propter omnis generis calamitates non immerito vallem lachrymarum dixeris, suavissimum est condimentum. Nam offensis omnibus medetur, infirmitatibus proximi ignoscit, vindictae cupiditatem restinguit, patienter omnia suffert, adversa mitigat, & quae difficillima videbantur nobis levia atque iucunda reddit. E contra ubi huius loco invidia, odium, ira, inimicitiae & simultates regnant, ibi homines ipsi sibi omnia acerba & infesta reddunt, ut exemplis infinitis demonstrari poterat, nisi quae quotidie fiunt, his abunde fide facerent. At maxima charitatis pestis est φιλαυτία, id est, amor ille caecus quo nosipsos prosequimur. Is ut multa alia parit, quae fraternae dilectioni prorsus contraria sunt: ita nos excaecare solet, ut de proximis nostris non recte iudicemus, & undiq; captemus occasiones eos negligendi, quos nostro consilio & auxilio subleuare debebamus. Sequitur ergo plenior huius negotij tractatio, qua quis proximus censeri debeat explicatur, & simul charitatis ingenium atq; officia diligentius ex ordine describuntur.
units.tr: Just as God, in all his works, keeps in mind his goodness towards us, so also in the commands and precepts that he gives us he chiefly has regard for our salvation. For he gives us no laws other than those that can all be comprehended under one charity or love, from which (if we consider the matter rightly) more good comes back to us than to those to whom it is bestowed. For first it reshapes us into the image of God, who (as John says) is charity itself. Then it is the sweetest seasoning of the whole of life, which on account of every kind of calamity may not unfairly be called a vale of tears. For it heals all offences, pardons the weaknesses of our neighbour, quenches the desire for revenge, bears all things patiently, softens adversities, and makes light and pleasant what seemed most difficult to us. On the other hand, where envy, hatred, anger, enmities and quarrels reign in its place, there men make everything bitter and hostile to themselves; this could be shown by countless examples, were it not that what happens every day gives ample proof of it. But the greatest plague of charity is self-love [φιλαυτία], that is, that blind love by which we pursue ourselves. Like many other things it produces, which are utterly contrary to brotherly love, so it is wont to blind us, so that we do not judge our neighbours rightly, and on every side we seize opportunities for neglecting those whom we ought to relieve by our counsel and help. There follows, therefore, a fuller treatment of this matter, in which it is explained who ought to be considered a neighbour, and at the same time the nature and duties of charity are described more carefully and in order.

units.la: Occasionem de his differendi, Legisperiti proteruia & insolentia praebuit. Is enim cum Dominum sibi dicentem audiisset, Hoc fac & vives, se iustificare voluit, id est, pro iusto vendicare, ut qui haec omnia iam pridem praestiterit, & proinde vitam aeternam mereatur. Unde apparet eum ex Pharisaeorum numero fuisse, quos in operibus Legis & propria iustitia merito salutis fiduciam collocauisse scimus. Quia autem Dei dilectionem iactare cuius facile est, quando res ex voto & felicirer procedunt, in proximi autem dilectione hypocrisis maxime detegitur, ad artes sese convertit, & in proximi vocabulo effugium quaerit. Nam hanc Legis divinae partem, Scribae Iudaeorum iamdudum interpretationibus & traditionibus suis corruperant. Per proximum enim non alios quam cognatos & sanguine coniunctos, & cum his amicos & bene de nobis meritos intelligi docebant. Et hinc longius progressi concludebant, quod inimicos odio prosequi liceret: quam particulam illos Legi Dei adiicere ausos fuisse, Christus Matth. 5. cap. diserte testatur. Itaq; isto errore hic etiam imbutus, ut se nullum dilectionis proximi officium neglexisse ostendat, superbe & non sine Sarcasmo Christum interrogat: Et quis est meus proximus? Quasi diceret: Aliud quiddam sublimius abs te expectabam, qui tibi in populo doctoris munus hucusq; sumpsisti. Atqui non aliud iubes, quam ut faciam ea quae modo ex Mosi recitasti: Ut nimirum Deum diligam ex toto corde, ex tota anima, ex totis viribus & tota cogitatione mea: & proximum meum, ut meipsum. At ista me baptismo praestitisse, nemo opinor negauerit. Deo uni adhaereo, hunc colo & pro viribus diligo. Quoad proximum, diligo meae gentis homines, & eos omnes, qui mei proximi, id est, propinqui & amici sunt. Quid ergo prohibet, quo minus vitam & salutem aeternam consequar? nisi tu forte alios mihi proximos monstraueris, quos ego nullos novi, cum nos ab omnibus aliis populis Deus ipse segregauerit, &c. Hic quaestionis illius sensus est, sub quo simul latet acerba & amarulenta doctrinae Christi reprehensio: ut quae inutilis & superuacanea sit, cum huiusq; fine illa Legi diuinae satisfacere & vitam aeternam mereri potuerint. Quo argumento etiam hodie aduersarij nostri praedicationem Euangelij contemptae aut inuisam reddere solent apud rudes & rerum imperitos. Quae lex (inquiunt) vetuit maiores nostros saluos fieri, priusquam nouum hoc Euangelium praedicaretur? Annon semper fidem in unum Deum per filium eius Iesum Christum docuerunt ij, quibus praedicandi munus fuit creditum? Annon illi quoq; ad mutuam charitatem, vitae innocentiam & sanctitatem populum hortati sunt? Si ergo nouui isti doctores non alia requirunt, quid rerum innouatione opus est, quae sine turbis & maximis periculis fieri non potest? Sed facile est argumentis eiusmodi respondere, cum illi proprijs operibus arguantur, quae illos à fide in vnum Deum alienissimos esse conuincunt. Quod ipsum in nostro hoc tam superbo Legis interprete cernimus, qui suo exemplo docet quam audax malum sit hypocrisis cum Veritatis odio coniuncta. Nam infinita erant, quae tam ipsum quam totum illud Legisperitorum Scribarum & Sacerdotum collegium contemptae & neglectae, imò conculcatae Legis Dei conuincerent. Si enim Deum diligebant ex toto corde, cur non legibus ab illo latis contenti erant? cur eas suis figmentis & traditionibus obscurabant, corrumpebant, abolebant? cur cultum eius sibi quae situm faciebant tanta impudentia, vt templum Dei ab emporio & vsurariorum officinis nihil differret? Et tamen superbus iste primum illud de Deo diligendo praeceptum securus praeterit, quasi Deo eo non opus sit vllum verbum facere, cum id diligentissimè ab ipsis obseruetur. Idè de proximi dilectione dici potest, quam non minus impudenter negligebant. Oberrabant passim mendici contra Legem Domini, qui ne mendicus esset in Israel, prohibuerat. Qui vero extra Iudaeae fines habitabant Iudaei, adeo contempti erant, vt qui tempore dierum festorum Hierosolymis moriebantur, sepulturae loco carerent, sicuti in passionis Dominicae historia est videre. Et quae obsecro dilectio vera inter eos esse potuit, qui in sectas diuisi erant, & sententiis de religione & toto humanae salutis negotio scindebantur? Nihilominus arrogans iste doctor, quasi extra omnem culpam sit, per ludibrium quaerere audet, & quis nam sit proximus suus, quem diligere & officijs suis iuuare debeat? Quàm magnus autem eiusmodi hominum numerus est hodie? Oberrant & vagantur nunc quoque mendicantium agmina, quos plerique securi negligunt, & ad clamores eorum aures suas obturant. Eduntur alibi plus quam barbarae crudelitatis exempla in omnis sexus & aetatis homines. At his omnibus pauciissimi condolent, plerique autem interea voluptuantur, & toti opibus coaceruandis inhiant. Inter rim extra omnem culpam censeri volunt, & si de proximo iuuando admoneantur, non minori impudentia quam hic Legis interpres, ogganire audent. Et quis est meus ille proximus, cui mea largiri, & cuius commodis ego, reliquis interea meis rebus, seruire debeo? Volunt ergo hi quoque seipsos iustificare, & apud sui similes facile applausum & patronos inuenient: sed apud Deum omnis haec excusatio calua est. Porro omnis mali causa est, quod neque de proximo recte iudicamus, neque vere aestimamus charitatis officia.
units.tr: The Lawyer's arrogance and insolence gave occasion for discussing these things. For when he had heard the Lord say to him, "Do this and you will live," he wished to justify himself, that is, to claim for himself the title of righteous, as one who had already long performed all these things and therefore merited eternal life. Hence it is clear that he was one of the number of the Pharisees, whom we know to have placed their trust in salvation on the merit of the works of the Law and their own righteousness. But since it is easy to boast of the love of God when things go according to our wish and succeed happily, whereas hypocrisy is most fully exposed in love of neighbour, he turned to tricks and sought an escape in the word "neighbour." For the scribes of the Jews had long before corrupted this part of the divine Law with their interpretations and traditions. They taught that by "neighbour" one should understand none but kinsmen and those joined by blood, and with them friends and those who had deserved well of us. And going further from this, they concluded that it was lawful to pursue enemies with hatred; Christ clearly testifies in Matthew 5 that they had dared to add this clause to the Law of God. Therefore this man, imbued with the same error, in order to show that he had neglected no duty of love towards his neighbour, arrogantly and not without sarcasm asks Christ: "And who is my neighbour?" As if he said: "I expected something loftier from you, who have hitherto assumed for yourself the office of teacher among the people. Yet you command nothing other than that I should do what you have just recited from Moses: namely, that I should love God with my whole heart, my whole soul, my whole strength and my whole mind, and my neighbour as myself. But I think no one will deny that I have fulfilled these things from my baptism. I cling to the one God, I worship him and love him to the best of my powers. As for my neighbour, I love the men of my own nation, and all those who are my neighbours, that is, my relatives and friends. What then prevents me from attaining life and eternal salvation? Unless perhaps you will point out to me other neighbours, whom I do not know at all, since God himself has separated us from all other peoples, etc." The sense of that question is this, under which there lies hidden at the same time a bitter and caustic rebuke of Christ's teaching, as if it were useless and superfluous, since with its end they could satisfy the divine Law and merit eternal life. By this same argument our opponents today are wont to make the preaching of the gospel despised or hateful among the simple and the ignorant. "What law," they say, "forbade our forefathers to be saved before this new gospel was preached? Did not those to whom the office of preaching was entrusted always teach faith in the one God through his Son Jesus Christ? Did they not also exhort the people to mutual charity, innocence of life and holiness? If, then, these new teachers require nothing other, why is there need of a change of things, which cannot be made without disturbances and very great dangers?" But it is easy to answer arguments of this kind, since those who use them are refuted by their own works, which prove that they are utterly alien from faith in the one God. We see this very thing in this proud interpreter of the Law, who by his own example teaches how wicked a thing hypocrisy is when joined with hatred of the truth. For there were countless things which would convict both him and the whole college of Lawyers, Scribes and Priests of having despised, neglected, and indeed trampled underfoot the Law of God. For if they loved God with their whole heart, why were they not content with the laws given by him? Why did they obscure, corrupt and abolish them with their own fictions and traditions? Why did they, with such impudence, make his worship a source of gain for themselves, so that the temple of God differed in nothing from a marketplace and the workshops of usurers? And yet this proud man passes over with confidence the first precept about loving God, as if there were no need to say a word about God, since it was most diligently observed by them. The same may be said of love of neighbour, which they neglected no less shamelessly. The beggars wandered everywhere, against the Law of the Lord, which had forbidden there to be a beggar in Israel. And the Jews who lived outside the borders of Judaea were so despised that those who died at Jerusalem during the festival days were denied a place of burial, as may be seen in the account of the Lord's passion. And what true love, I beg you, could there be among those who were divided into sects, and split apart by opinions concerning religion and the whole business of human salvation? Nevertheless, this arrogant teacher, as if he were free from all blame, dares to ask mockingly who then is his neighbour, whom he ought to love and help by his services. And how great a number of such men there is today! Even now the troops of beggars wander and roam about, whom most people carelessly neglect, and they stop their ears against their cries. Examples of cruelty more than barbarous are put forth elsewhere against men of every sex and age. Yet very few grieve for all these, while most in the meantime take their pleasure and gape eagerly after heaping up wealth for themselves. Meanwhile they want to be considered free from all blame, and if they are admonished about helping their neighbour, they dare to snarl with no less impudence than this interpreter of the Law. "And who is that neighbour of mine, to whom I must give my goods, and whose advantage I must serve, while my own affairs are neglected?" So these men too want to justify themselves, and they will easily find applause and defenders among their like; but before God all such excuse is worthless. Moreover, the cause of every evil is that we neither judge our neighbour rightly nor truly value the duties of charity.

units.la: Quapropter Dominus noster Iesus Christus vtriq; errori aut vitio eleganti parabola medetur. Introducitur in ea homo Iudaeus, qui ex sancta Hierosolymorum ciuitate Ierichuntidem iter insti-tuerit. Hunc à latronibus spoliatum & vulneribus male affectum atque seminecem cum vidissent Sacerdos & Leuita, eo neglecto transierunt. At hos secutus Samaritanus quidam, homo peregrinus & ob gentem suam Iudaeis exosus, cum & ipse infelicem illum vidisset, eius misertus omnis humanitatis & dilectionis officium ei praestitit. Quam parabolam vbi multis Christus recitauit, tandem suum illum aduersarium interrogat: Quis horum trium tibi videtur proximus fuisse illi, qui incidit in latrones? Respondet ille: Is qui vsus est misericordia erga eum. Ita vero rei veritate convictum cogit Christus verum fateri contra receptam inter illos de proximo sententiam, & seipsum neglectae charitatis fraternae damnare, quod nunquam facturus erat hypocrita, si Christus rem ipsam simpliciter absque omni inuoluto proposuisset. Tantum enim erat apud Iudaeos omnes gentium ex terarum odium, vt ex his oriundos vix hominum, nedum proximi loco harerent.
units.tr: Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ heals both of these errors, or faults, with an elegant parable. In it a Jewish man is introduced who was travelling from the holy city of Jerusalem down to Jericho. Robbed by thieves, badly wounded and half dead, he was seen by a priest and a Levite, who passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, a foreigner who was hated by the Jews because of his nation, followed them. When he saw the unhappy man, he took pity on him and showed him every kindness and act of love. After Christ had recited this parable to many, he finally questioned his adversary: "Which of these three seems to you to have been the neighbour of the man who fell among the robbers?" He replied, "The one who showed mercy to him." Thus Christ, having convinced him by the truth of the matter, compelled him to confess what was true, contrary to the opinion about the neighbour that was commonly held among them, and to condemn himself for neglecting brotherly love. A hypocrite would never have done this if Christ had simply set out the matter itself without any disguise. For among the Jews the hatred of all the foreign nations was so great that people born of them hardly counted as men, let alone as neighbours.

units.la: Consultò autem hominem Iudaeum & ex Hierosolyma venientem inducit, cui à suae gentis Sacerdote & Leuita neglecto opem tulerit Samaritanus. Ita enim Iudaeorum inhumanitatem perstringit, qui magnificè quidem vnum patrem Abrahamum iactabant, & se vnius Dei cultores, imò peculiũ illud Dei esse gloriabantur, quod vt sibi ex omnibus populis selegisset: interim verò plus quam barbara crudelitate se inuicem negligebant, adeò vt (quod paulò ante etiam diximus) nulla neque cognationis, neque religionis communis, neque etiam Legis Dei ratione habita, pauperes suos paterentur famelicos oberrare, & non ofiatim modò, verumetiam ad templi fores ab introeuntibus & exeuntibus stipem mendicare. Pra aliis autem Sacerdotum & Leuitarum meminit, qui vt aliis sanctiores haberi volebant, ita huius etiam mali praecipui erant authores. Quia enim sacerdotiū venale fecerant, publicas quoq; opes ecclesiae sibi vendicabant, ex quibus pauperes ali debebant. Et vt quaestu maiorem facerent, non ad misericordiam & fraternae dilectionis studium populum hortabantur, sed vt in templo frequentes adessent, sacrificia multa adducerent, & pecunias in corbonâ aut gazophylacium lacium deponerent. Deniq; eò impudentia progressi iam erant, vt quæ liberi in parentum senio confoìforum alimonia debebant conferre, illi ad se deferri iuberet, seq; tam pro parentibus quam ipsis libe-ris sacrificaturos & preces facturos pollicebatur, et ea ratione (quod infra illu Christus exprobrat) devorabant domus viduarum & orphanorum sub longæ precationis prætextu. Quam ergo subuen-tionis pauperum curam fuisse putabimus apud eos, qui parentes senio graues, viduas & orphanos o-mni præsidio destitutos non solùm negligebant, verumetiam depræda-bantur? Docet igitur hac pa-rabola Christus, illos Samaritanis esse deteriores, apud quos Lex naturæ & communis sensus huma-nitatis plus valeat, quàm apud ipsos Lex Dei & magnifica vera religionis professio.
units.tr: Christ deliberately introduced a Jewish man, coming from Jerusalem, whom a priest and a Levite of his own nation neglected, while a Samaritan gave him help. In this way he exposes the inhumanity of the Jews, who boasted loudly that they had the one father Abraham, that they were worshippers of the one God, and even gloried that they were that peculiar people of God whom he had chosen from all the peoples. Yet meanwhile they neglected one another with more than barbarous cruelty. So it was that (as we said a little earlier) they, having no regard for kinship, for common religion, or even for the law of God, allowed their poor to wander about starving, and to beg alms not only in the streets but also at the doors of the temple from those going in and out. He mentions the priests and Levites in particular, because they wished to be regarded as holier than others, and so they were the chief authors of this evil. For, having made the priesthood a matter of trade, they also claimed for themselves the public resources of the Church, from which the poor ought to have been supported. And in order to make more profit, they did not exhort the people to mercy and the pursuit of brotherly love, but urged them to attend the temple in crowds, to bring many sacrifices, and to deposit their money in the corban or the treasury chest. At last they had progressed to such shamelessness that they ordered that what children ought to contribute to the support of their aged parents be brought to them, promising that they would offer sacrifices and prayers both for the parents and for the children themselves. In this way (as Christ rebukes them below) they devoured the houses of widows and orphans under the pretext of long prayers. What care for the relief of the poor, then, can we suppose there was among those who neglected, and even plundered, parents burdened with age, and widows and orphans deprived of all protection? Christ therefore teaches by this parable that these men were worse than the Samaritans, among whom the law of nature and the common feeling of humanity counted for more than the law of God and the noble profession of the true religion did among them.

units.la: At vtinam non idem de nobis dici posset hodie, qui Christiani esse & haberi volumus. Ditatæ sunt olim principum & diuitum hominum liberalitate Ecclesiæ, instituta collegia magnifica & opulenta, in quibus Ecclesiarum ministri alerentur, theologiæ candidati instituerentur, & pauperum necessi-tate subuenire tur. At postquam Episcopi relicta maiorum suorum frugalitate, fastu turgere, & cum principibus luxu & apparatu magnifico certare cœperunt, mox communia Ecclesiæ bona in suam po-testatem redegere, & eos sibi asciuerunt collegas aut socios, qui ijsdem moribus prædicti, quod illi reli-quum fecerunt sibi vendicarunt. Hinc factu, vt ministri pij & docti ab ecclesijs expulsi sint, in col-legia autem nouum hominum genus, cucullatum, ineptum, ambitiosum, vorax & veritati inimicum irrepserit. Simul autem pauperes ad eleemosynas relegati sunt, quas hinc inde colligerent, voluptuan-tibus interim & luxurianti bus ecclesiarum redditibus fucus illis ignauus, qui & ipsi sub religionis prætextu paulatim agros, villas & opes tam nobilium quàm plebeiorum in suam nassam attraxe-runt. Quàmuis autem Euangelij lucem Deus ex singulari gratia nouissimis hisce temporibus resti-tuerit, & multis in locis facta sit Ecclesia & religionis reformatio, hic tamen fere reformationes o-mnes pedem sistunt, vbi de reducendo vetere bonorum Ecclesiæ vsu agitur. Causa huius cessationis est, quòd alibi principes & magistratus, alibi homines priuati illa sibi vendicant, & sub plausibili dispen-satorum ecclesiæ prætextu ditescunt. Horum omnium insatiabili cupiditati debemus miserabile illam mendicantium multitudinem, qui famelici & omnium egeni, multi etiam morbis confecti, adhæc vl-ceribus & tabo diffluentes, magna cum Christiani nominis ignominia oberrant. Queritur de hoc pij & boni multi, & reformationem aliquam fieri postulant. Sed vnica omnium responsio est, rem eò de-uenisse, vt mutatio aliqua fieri non possit, & impossibile esse tantam hominum egentium multitudi-nem alere. Sed vtinam illi primitiuæ Ecclesiæ exemplum inspicerent, in qua priuati homines contri-butione facta res ita instituerunt, vt inter medios persecutionum fluctus egeni ex publico alerentur, neq; aliqua vel fames vel rei domesticæ angustia victum ab alijs emendicare cogeret. Quòd si exem-plum hoc longius petitum videtur, agedum nostri seculi Iudæos inspiciant, qui cum hinc inde disper-si viuant, & plerisq; in locis per publicas leges illis neq; agros possidere, neque artificia manuaria exercere liceat, neminem tamen ex suis mendicare patiuntur, magnum scilicet nefas æstimantes, ho-minem circumcisum & ex sancta Abrahami stirpe oriundum, prophanorum Goijm (vt ipsi lo-quuntur) contemptui & ludibrio exponere. Et nobis qui in pace & otio agimus, qui opibus priuatis & publicis abundamus, qui Ecclesias & Collegia habemus maiorum liberalitate ditata, & ex quo-tum reddititibus quotannis multi ditescunt, impossibile est fidei domesticos alere, neq; nos pudet eos ad fidei hostes nostra inhumanitate extrudere, inter quos non sine Euangelicæ doctrinæ contumelia, multa audire & videre, imò multa facere coguntur, quæ cum fidei nostræ professione pugnant. In nos ergo non minus, quàm in suo seculo Iudæos Christiu hanc parabolam stringere cogitemus, qui quo ad pauperum subuentionem Iudæus & Turcus sumus deteriores. Sed ad ea accedamus, quæ præci-pua sunt huius parabolæ capita, in quibus hæc obseruabis.
units.tr: But would that the same could not be said of us today, who wish to be and to be called Christians! Once the Churches were enriched by the generosity of princes and wealthy men, and magnificent and opulent colleges were founded, in which ministers of the Churches were supported, candidates of theology were trained, and the need of the poor was relieved. But after the bishops, having abandoned the frugality of their ancestors, began to swell with pride and to vie with princes in luxury and magnificent display, they soon drew the common goods of the Church into their own power. They took to themselves colleagues or associates who, endowed with the same manners, claimed for themselves whatever remained. Hence it came about that pious and learned ministers were driven out of the churches, while a new kind of men crept into the colleges: hooded, foolish, ambitious, greedy, and hostile to the truth. At the same time the poor were sent off to alms, which they had to collect here and there, while the idle drones, who themselves little by little drew the fields, farms and wealth of nobles and commoners alike into their net under the pretext of religion, enjoyed and luxuriated in the revenues of the churches. Although God, in his singular grace, has in these latest times restored the light of the gospel, and in many places the Church and the reformation of religion have been achieved, nearly all these reformations come to a halt where the restoration of the ancient use of the Church's goods is concerned. The cause of this stalling is that in some places princes and magistrates, and in others private men, claim those goods for themselves and grow rich under the plausible pretext of being stewards of the Church. To the insatiable greed of all of these we owe that wretched multitude of beggars who wander about with great shame to the Christian name, starving and destitute of everything, many also worn out with diseases, and moreover oozing with ulcers and filth. Many pious and good people complain about this and demand some reformation. But the one answer given by all is that the matter has reached such a point that no change can be made, and that it is impossible to feed so great a multitude of needy people. Would that they would look at the example of the primitive Church, in which private persons, by making a contribution, so arranged things that, in the midst of the waves of persecution, the needy were supported from the common fund, and neither hunger nor any domestic distress forced anyone to beg his food from others. But if this example seems too far removed, let them look at the Jews of our own age: although they live dispersed here and there, and in most places by public law they are not permitted to possess land or to practise manual crafts, yet they allow none of their own to beg. They evidently think it a great wrong to expose a circumcised man, born of the holy stock of Abraham, to the contempt and mockery of the profane Gentiles (goyim, as they call them). And for us, who live in peace and leisure, who abound in private and public wealth, who have churches and colleges enriched by the generosity of our ancestors, and from whose revenues many grow rich every year, it is impossible to feed the domestic members of the faith. Nor are we ashamed to thrust them out by our inhumanity to the enemies of the faith, among whom, to the disgrace of the Evangelical doctrine, they are forced to hear and see many things, indeed to do many things, which are at odds with the profession of our faith. We ought therefore to consider that this parable is aimed at us no less than it was at the Jews of its own age, since in relieving the poor we are worse than the Jew and the Turk. But let us come to the chief points of this parable, in which you will observe the following.

units.la: Primum, quem nam Scripturæ sacræ proximi nomine designent? Vnumquenque nimirum ho-minem, in quem incidimus, cuiuscunq; ille gentis, conditionis aut ordinis fuerit. Quia enim omnes ex vno patre originem ducimus, naturale quoddam & sacrosanctum fraternitatis vinculum intercedit, quo omnes homines inter se constringuntur. Quapropter, vt aliquam proximi loco habeat & eidem præstet charitatis officia, nō multis argumentis homo Christianus vrgeri sese patitur. Sufficit enim ei, quòd hominem & eiusdem secum naturæ socium esse videt eum, qui ipsius ope & consilio indiget. Nō igitur amplioribus inquisitione opus est, maximè si quis in ea necessitate constitutus sit, vt res nullæ cunctationem aut moram admittat. Id parabola hac Dominus diserte docet. Proponitur enim homo Samaritanus, alienigena, & qui se in Iudaeorum gente omnibus exosum esse sciebat. Nam ut in Evangelio secundum Ioannem habetur, tantum erat inter duas iflas gentes odium, ut altera alterius consuetudinem detestaretur, & apud Iudaeos vix aliud convicium contumeliosius putabatur, quam si quem Samaritanum dicerent. Nihilominus tamen noster hic in terra hostili beneficiu maximu confert homini ignoto, a suis gentilibus neglecto, saucio, spoliato, semineci, tali deniq, a quo remunera tionem omnino nullam sperare poterat. Quam vero ob causam? Nimirū, quod Lege naturae admonitus sciret hominis esse, cuius egenti ope ferre, & miseris quibuscunq; subuenire. Et quia hunc Christus omnibus imitandum proponit, non obscure omnes eos damnat, qui odiosa personarum discrimina ideo fingunt, & vndiq; causas corradunt, ut misericordia & charitatis officia indigentibus ali quo praetextu negare possint. Est hoc vitium nimis frequens hodie. Alijs enim natale solum exprobratur, in alijs acceptae ab illis iniuriae in memoriam revocantur, alij propter vitam licentius transactam indigni iudicantur quibus beneficiat. Multus hoc vnum ad humanitatis suae excusationem suf ficere videtur, quod nihil vicissim ab ijs sperare possint, qui nunc beneficium ab ipsis postulant. Qua si vero Deus charitate quaestum esse velit, & non potius nos de dando quam accipiendo beneficio se licitos esse iubeat? At si Christi doctrinam cum Samaritani huius exemplo conferamus, mox patebit vanissimas esse excusationes, quas suij ipsius amans caro fingere consueuit.
units.tr: First, what do the words of Holy Scripture designate by the name of neighbour? Clearly every man whom we encounter, of whatever nation, condition or rank he may be. For since we all trace our origin to one father, a natural and sacred bond of brotherhood lies between us, by which all men are bound to one another. Therefore, so that a Christian may regard someone as a neighbour and show him the duties of love, he should not allow himself to be pressed with many arguments. For it is enough for him to see that the man who needs his help and counsel is a man, and a partner of his own nature. There is no need, then, for more lengthy inquiry, especially if someone is in such need that the matter admits no hesitation or delay. The Lord clearly teaches this in this parable. For he presents a Samaritan, a foreigner, who knew that he was hated by all in the Jewish nation. For, as is found in the Gospel according to John, there was so great a hatred between those two peoples that each shunned the company of the other, and among the Jews hardly any insult was considered more offensive than to call someone a Samaritan. Nevertheless, this man of ours, in hostile territory, confers the greatest benefit on a stranger whom his own countrymen neglected: a man wounded, plundered, half dead, one from whom he could in no way hope for any return. And why did he do so? Surely because, warned by the law of nature, he knew that he was a man, and that he should bring help to a needy man and relieve wretched people of whatever kind. And because Christ sets this man before all as one to be imitated, he clearly condemns all those who invent hateful distinctions between persons and gather reasons from every side so that they may deny works of mercy and love to the needy under some pretext. This fault is all too common today. For some are reproached for their native land, in others the injuries they have received from them are recalled to mind, and others are judged unworthy of benefits because of a life lived too licentiously. It seems to many that this one excuse for their inhumanity is enough: that those who now ask a benefit from them can offer nothing in return. But what if God wishes love to be sought for no gain, and rather commands us to be free to give benefits rather than to receive them? And if we compare the teaching of Christ with the example of this Samaritan, it will soon become clear how very vain are the excuses which our self-loving flesh is accustomed to invent.

units.la: Secundo modus dilectionis exprimitur, & quod eius ingenium sit, quibusue officijs sese declaret. Sum ma est, quòd (ut Ioannes ait) non verbis, sed operibus diligere, id est, dilectionis affectu reipsa et benefcijs declarare debeamus. Id vero in Samaritani exemplo Dominus diligenter exponit, & rem nem ceu in tabula depictam exhibet. Primo vbi miserū huc, nudū, vulneratū & ad mortem vsq; iniquissime multatum vidit, misericordia motus est. In Graeco habetur ἐσπλαγχνίσθη, quod imus aut totius visceribus comotū fuisse significat. Et scilicet Hebraei per visceru comotionē naturales illos motus aut affectiones denotare, quas Graeci σπλάγχνα dicunt: quales sunt parentū erga liberos & borum erga illos, fratrum item & sororum erga se mutuò: quarū exemplum & in meretrici altera apud Salomonē pro filio suo litigante historia sacra proponit. Habet ergo vera dilectio misericordiae affectū qui illā cessare aut frigere nō finit. Huius enim effectus est, quod aliena comouemur miseria, cum mox succurrat, nos quoq; homines esse, & proinde humanū nihil a nobis esse alienū; nec quicquā obstare, quò minus nos ijsde quib. calamitosissimi quiq; miseris exerceamur, praeter Dei gratia, qui nos hucusq; seruarit & tutatus sit. Quod qui cogitat, ij no possunt no toto animo comoueri, si quod singulare exemplū humanae miseriae in aliquo conspicantur. Vnde iā colligimus, eos dilectione omnino vacuos esse, qui nullo alienae miseriae sensu tanguntur. Quod Ioannes Apostolus pulchre docet his verbis: Si quis habuerit substantiam mundi, videat aut fratrem suum egere, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quo modo charitas Dei manet in illo? Et Paulus nos afflictis et captiuis condolere iubet, perinde ac si nos in illorū corpore affligeremur: & idē ἀσῶγας, id est, eos qui à misericordia & comuni humanitatis sensu, deniq; ab affectionibus illis, quas natura nobis insitas esse diximus, alieni sunt, inter nouissimorum temporū pestes numerat, à quibus sibi debeat cauere, qui pietatis verae studio tenentur. 2. Tim. 3.
units.tr: Second, the manner of love is expressed: what its nature is and by which duties it shows itself. The sum is that, as John says, we ought to love not in words but in deeds, that is, we should show love in actual fact and by benefits, from the affection of love. The Lord sets this out carefully in the example of the Samaritan and presents the whole matter as if painted on a tablet. First, when he saw the wretched man lying here, naked, wounded, and most unjustly beaten to the point of death, he was moved with pity. The Greek reads [ἐσπλαγχνίσθη], which means that he was moved in his inward parts, or in all his bowels. The Hebrews, too, by the stirring of the bowels, denote those natural motions or affections which the Greeks call [σπλάγχνα]: such as parents feel toward their children and children toward them, and brothers and sisters toward one another. Sacred history also gives an example of this in the story of the harlot who, before Solomon, contended for her son. True love therefore has an affection of mercy, which does not allow it to cease or grow cold. For its effect is that we are moved by another's misery, since it immediately comes to mind that we too are men, and that nothing human is alien to us. Nothing prevents us from being exposed to the same calamities that the most wretched suffer, except the grace of God, who has kept and protected us until now. Those who consider this cannot but be moved in their whole soul when they behold some remarkable example of human misery. Hence we may already gather that those are wholly without love who are touched by no sense of another's misery. John the Apostle teaches this beautifully in these words: "If anyone has the substance of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" And Paul bids us sympathise with the afflicted and the captives, just as if we ourselves were suffering in their bodies. He also counts among the plagues of the last times the [ἄσπονδοι], that is, those who are estranged from mercy and the common feeling of humanity, and finally from those affections which we said are implanted in us by nature. Those who are devoted to the zeal of true piety ought to beware of such people. 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: Secundo accedit Samaritanus ad iacentem humi & proprio sanguine foedatum, neq; praeterit, sicuti Sacerdos & Leuita paulo ante fecerant. Atqui multa erant, quae eum poterant reuocare. Nā cogitaret: Homo es peregrinus, & per gentem tibi tuam omnibus infestam iter facis, quis veroille sit nescis, nec aliquis Iudaeorum hucusque illius aliquam rationem habuit. Quid ergo tu faceres, qui hic absque manifesto periculo nihil potes agere? Nam aut aliqui superuenient, qui hunc abs te spoliatum & tam misere tractatum esse suspicabuntur, teque comprehensum ad iudices trahent, vbi facile fidem inueniet quisquis aduersus Samaritanum aliquid dixerit, aut qui hunc aggressi sunt, latrones forte non procul absunt, & te quoque circa istius curam occupatum adorientur: & ita istum non seruabis, te autem in periculum conijcies. Quin ergo res tuas agis, & iter instituum persequeris? Hac & multa alia huius generis homini cordato & prudenti, qualem hunc Dominus describit, in mentem venire potuerunt. Sed nihil horum eum mouet, quo minus accedat, & infelicem illum propius inspiciat. Est ergo efficax vera dilectionis affectus, nec in nuda aut otiosa commiseratione acquiescit: qualem in illis videmus, qui afflictis bene precantur, faustia & laeta omnia optant, nihil aute præstant officij, quo subleuentur, aut ex quo aliquâ capiant consolationem. De quibus Iacobus verè scribit: Quòd si frater aut soror nudi fuerint, & egentes quotidiano victu, dicat autem eis aliquis vestrûm, Abite cũ pace, calescite & saturamini: non tamè dederitis eis quæ sunt necessaria corpori, quæ erit vtilitas? &c. Sunt hæc probè obseruanda, ne nosipsis imponamus, dum vltra frigidum & otiosum commiserationis temerè conceptæ affectum non progredimur.
units.tr: Second, the Samaritan goes up to the man lying on the ground and defiled with his own blood, and does not pass him by as the priest and the Levite had done a little before. Yet many things could have called him back. For he might have thought: "You are a stranger, and you are travelling through a people hostile to everyone. You do not know who this man is, and no Jew has taken any notice of him until now. What would you do, who can accomplish nothing here without manifest danger? For either some people will come upon you who will suspect that you have stripped this man and treated him so cruelly, and will drag you, seized, before the judges, where whoever speaks against the Samaritan will easily be believed. Or perhaps the robbers who attacked him are not far off, and will fall upon you too while you are busy with his care; and so you will not save him, and will throw yourself into danger. Why not rather attend to your own affairs and pursue the journey you have begun?" These and many other thoughts of this kind could have come into the mind of a sensible and prudent man, such as the Lord describes this one to be. But none of them moves him from approaching and looking more closely at the unhappy man. True love is therefore effective, and does not rest in bare or idle pity, such as we see in those who wish the afflicted well and pray for all things to go happily and gladly for them, yet offer no help by which they might be relieved or from which they might draw any comfort. James writes truly of such people: "If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is that?" etc. These things must be carefully observed, lest we deceive ourselves by going no further than the cold and idle feeling of pity rashly conceived.

units.la: Tertiò vulnera iflius Samaritanus obligat, infuso prius vino & oleo, quæ sola secum habebat, neq; incommoda erant huic officio. Vino enim vulnerum cruor & sanies eluitur, oleû verò dolorem mitigat. Non igitur accessit modò ad faucium & seminecem, sed quod putauit ad vitâ eius seruandam conducere, & quod in ista rerum angustia potuit, fidelissimè præstitit, & nec fœdè hiantiû vulnerum tabo aut sanie absterretur quò minus officium faciat. Vbi rursus charitatis ingenium exprimitur, quæ vt omne periculum vincit, ita nullum officiû tam vile, tam fastidiosum vel nauseæ plenum est, quod propter proximi salutem obire detrectet. Ideò Christus eius officia vsq; ad pedû ablutione extendit: & hæc causa est, quòd circa ægrotos & diutinis grauibusq; morbis detentos in primis occupatur, quos diuinus ille charitatis ignis accendit. At delicatuli, & qui se sibi solis natos putant, omne asspectum fœdû, omne tetrû odore sibi fugiendum censent, & magno cum fastidio ab ægrotantiû visitatione abstinent. Peccatur in hoc plurimûm ab ijs quoq; qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, si quando Deus lue aut peste peccata nostra punit. Tunc enim hac correptos vel domi tanquâ maleficos concludunt, vel ex proprijs ædibus, imò extra vrbis mœnia eijciunt, & minacibus edictis prohibent, ne quis illos accedat, præter eos, qui huic ministerio destinati sunt. Itaq; frequenter accidit, vt nec coniuges, nec fratres & sorores sibi mutuò officiû charitatis præstare possint, sed tunc abs se inuicè magno cũ dolore diuellantur, quando in primis sibi inuicè adesse debebat, ægroti autem hominibus ignotis & ferè infamibus committantur. Causa tam barbaræ crudelitatis est, quòd contagium quoddam fingunt, & sibijpsis persuadent mox à peste eos etiam corripi, qui ex hac laborantes accedunt. Deinde pietatis prætextu impietatem iflam excusant, & aiunt, non tentari debere Deum, id autem eos facere, qui ades peste infectas ingrediantur: nam id perinde esse, ac si quis sciens volens sese in incendium conijciat. Sed velim istos homines suæ professionis meminisse, & rē diligentius expendere. Quod enim de contagio dicunt, exemplis manifestis confutare potest, et scriptura pestilentiâ sagittas Dei vocat, qui quos vult ferit, neq; incertis ictibus grassatur. Et in Da uidi historia Angelus Domini populum percussisse dicitur, cum intra paucos dies multa millia hominum peste absumerentur. Mirum autem est Christianos homines non videre, quod gentiû poetæ intellexerunt. Homerus certè pestem in Græcorû castrû grassantem describens, non contagiû fingit cæcum, sed Apollinem inducit suis telis illos ferientem. Cæterùm vt demum contagio luem hinc inde serpere, nihil tamen hoc quoq; istorum inhumanitati patrocinabitur. Nam contagiosos quoq; morbos per Dei prouidentiam gubernari fateantur oportet, nisi forte nostram deteriorem esse vel ut quàm passerculorum, quos absq; Patrũ sui voluntate mori Christus negat. Ad alterum argumentum de non tentando Deo, respondemus, illos Dei præcepto abuti. Tentatur enim ille, quando absque eius vocatione & iussu nos periculis non necessarijs obijcimus. Atqui Dei mandatum est, vt ægrotantibus aut ex quocunq; morbo laborantibus (nec enim vllus nominatim excipitur præter lepram, de qua alias ob causas legem peculiarem Deus dedit) omne officium præstemus, & in scripturis commendantur, qui in hoc seduli sunt & diligentes. Dauid certè dicit: Beatus qui prospicit ægroto: in tempore aduerso eripiet eum Dominus. Dominus custodiet eum, valetudine restituet ei, &c. Et idem amicus perfidis atq; impijs hoc tribuit, quòd cùm ipse ex peste decumberet, procul constiterint, nimirum contagium veriti. Quid quod Christus in nouissimo die electis suis dicturus est: Ægrotus fui, & inuisistis me? Ista Christianis hominibus sufficere debent, vt quod Samaritanus iste in miseri illius vulneribus abluendis & obligandis fecit, ipsi erga omnes faciant, qui in morbis qualibuscunque ipsorum officium requirunt. Quartò in iumentû proprium imponit, & ipse pedes incedit. Deducit præterea in diuersorium, & illic eius curam ipse agit, ne quid aliorum negligentia peccetur. Postero autem die, cùm ipsum negotia alió vocarent, hospiti eum diligentissimè comendat, pecuniam eius nomine largitur, & insu per fideiussorē sese sistit pro impensis, quas præterea facturus sit. Docent ista quàm officiosa sit charitas, quâ Paulus omnia sufferre, & omnia sustinere dicit. Quid enim ille non facit, quod pater ali- quis filio vnigenito, aut frater fratri charissimo in eius modi necessitate faceret? Nō labori parcit, dum pedes iter facit, vt faciū hunc suo iumento vehat: neq; hoc sibi inhonestum aut indecorū esse putat, dummodo illius saluti cōsulatur. Sumptus quoq; facit, & in posterū quoq; illi prospicit. Hæc an te omnia propter nos dici meminerimus, cum Samaritanū hunc commune charitatis exemplū Christus proponat. Discamus ergo absq; omni personarū discrimine miseris et afflictis condolere, ijsdem opem ferre, & pro virili omnia præstare, quibus illos opus habere videmus. Sed vah quàm variè & grauiter hodie aduersus hæc omnia peccatur. Iacent vbiq; locorū miseri, spoliati et saucij: nec pri uati modò homines, sed totæ gentes periclitantur, Ecclesiæ florentissimæ vastantur, omicula Christi exulant, multi item viri illustres, infinitæ matronæ & virgines incertis sedibus oberrant. Sed pau cos tangit commiserationis sensus, & plerique ista absq; gemitu spectant: pauciores vero accedunt, vt opem ferant: plerique autem optimè secum agi putant, si ipsi rerum secuti aliorum naufragia ex portu spectare possint. Prætexunt quidè illi multa, quibus sese excusent, sed proprijs exemplis conuincun- tur, cum in alijs rebus neq; labori neq; sumptui parcant, & pericula quoq; interdum subeant grauis- sima. Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui ex aliorum calamitatibus occasionem arripiunt res suas au- gendi? Ex horum numero sunt vsurarij auari, qui suis artibus miseros circumueniunt, & quod ad- huc reliquum habent, eripiunt. Crudeliores hi sunt milites mercenarij, qui dum publicæ Ecclesiarū vastationes fiunt, quasi opem laturi aduolant, interim vero absq; omni discrimine prædantur, neq; aliquod inhumanitatis genus omittunt. Et hic hodie quæstus vberrimus atque honestissimus puta- tur. Sed sentient omnes illi aliquando manū Domini, & suæ crudelitatis pœnas dabunt tunc, quan- do rebus suis optimè consultum arbitrantur. Vide Isa.33.
units.tr: Third, the Samaritan binds up the man's wounds, after first pouring in wine and oil, which were the only things he had with him and were not unsuitable for this service. For wine cleanses the blood and matter of wounds, and oil soothes the pain. So he did not merely come to the half-dead man, but faithfully supplied whatever he thought would help to preserve his life, and whatever he could manage in such a narrow situation. Nor was he deterred from doing his duty by the foul discharge and matter of the gaping wounds. Here again the nature of charity is expressed. Charity overcomes every danger, and no duty is so humble, so distasteful, or so full of nausea that it refuses to undertake it for the sake of a neighbour's salvation. Therefore Christ extends its duties even to the washing of feet. This is also why charity is chiefly occupied with the sick and with those held by long and grievous diseases, which that divine fire of charity kindles. But the delicate, who think they were born for themselves alone, judge every foul sight and every noxious smell to be avoided, and with great disdain they abstain from visiting the sick. This is most often done wrongly even by those who profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel, whenever God punishes our sins with plague or pestilence. For then they shut up those seized by it, either at home as if they were criminals, or they cast them out of their own houses, indeed beyond the city walls, and by threatening edicts forbid anyone to approach them except those appointed to this ministry. And so it often happens that neither spouses nor brothers and sisters can perform the office of charity for one another. They are torn from each other with great grief just when they ought most of all to be present to each other, while the sick are left to strangers and almost infamous people. The cause of such barbarous cruelty is that they invent a certain contagion, and persuade themselves that those who approach the sick will at once be seized by the plague too. Then, under the pretext of piety, they excuse this impiety, saying that God must not be tempted, and that those who enter houses infected with plague do so; for this is just as if someone knowingly and willingly threw himself into a fire. But I would wish these men to remember their profession and to weigh the matter more carefully. For as to what they say about contagion, it can be refuted by plain examples, and Scripture calls pestilence the arrows of God, which strike whom they will and do not rage with random blows. In the history of David it is said that the Angel of the Lord struck the people, when many thousands of men were carried off by plague within a few days. It is remarkable, however, that Christian men do not see what the poets of the Gentiles understood. Homer, describing the plague raging in the camp of the Greeks, does not invent a blind contagion but brings in Apollo striking them with his arrows. But even if the plague does creep from one to another by contagion, this too will not defend the inhumanity of these men. For they must confess that contagious diseases also are governed by the providence of God, unless perhaps our condition is worse than that of sparrows, which Christ says do not die without the will of their Father. To the second argument, about not tempting God, we answer that they abuse God's precept. God is tempted when, without his calling and command, we expose ourselves to unnecessary dangers. But God's command is that we perform every duty to those who are sick or suffering from any disease (for no one is named as an exception except leprosy, for which God gave a special law for other reasons), and Scripture commends those who are diligent and zealous in this. David certainly says: "Blessed is he who considers the sick; in the time of trouble the Lord will deliver him. The Lord will keep him and restore him to health," etc. And the same David ascribes it to the faithless and impious that, when he himself lay sick of the plague, they stood far off, fearing of course the contagion. What of the fact that Christ, on the last day, is about to say to his elect: "I was sick, and you visited me"? These things ought to be enough for Christians, so that they do for all who require their service in whatever diseases what this Samaritan did in washing and binding that wretched man's wounds. Fourth, he sets him on his own beast and goes on foot himself. Moreover he leads him to an inn and there takes care of him himself, lest anything be neglected through others' carelessness. Then on the next day, when his business calls him elsewhere, he most diligently commends the man to the innkeeper, gives money on his behalf, and moreover pledges himself as surety for whatever further expenses may be incurred. These things show how dutiful charity is, the charity by which Paul says all things are endured and all things sustained. For what does he not do which a father would do for an only son, or a brother for a most dear brother in such need? He spares no labour: he goes on foot so that he may carry this man on his own beast, and he does not think this dishonourable or unbecoming for himself, provided the man's safety is secured. He also bears the expense and provides for him afterwards as well. Let us remember that all these things are said on our account, since Christ sets this Samaritan before us as a common example of charity. Let us learn, therefore, without any distinction of persons, to sympathise with the wretched and afflicted, to bring them help, and to do to the best of our ability whatever we see them needing. But alas, how variously and grievously all these things are sinned against today! The miserable, plundered and wounded lie everywhere. Not only private men but whole nations are in peril; most flourishing Churches are laid waste; the little ones of Christ go into exile; many illustrious men, and countless matrons and virgins, wander without settled homes. Yet few are touched by any sense of pity, and most look upon these things without a groan. Still fewer come forward to bring help, and most think they are doing very well if, having escaped the wrecks of others, they can watch them from the harbour. They indeed put forward many excuses to defend themselves, but their own examples refute them, since in other matters they spare neither labour nor expense, and sometimes even undergo very grave dangers. But what shall we say of those who seize the occasion of others' calamities to increase their own wealth? Among these are the greedy usurers, who circumvent the wretched with their tricks and snatch away whatever little they still have. Crueler still are the mercenary soldiers, who, while the public Churches are being laid waste, rush in as though to bring help, but meanwhile plunder without any restraint and omit no kind of inhumanity. And this gain is today thought to be most abundant and most honourable. But all those men will one day feel the hand of the Lord and pay the penalty for their cruelty, when they think they have best looked after their own affairs. See Isa. 33.
