units.la: Allegorias, quas hic aliqui tractarunt, consultò prætermittimus, quia partim impiæ sunt, & ad euacuandam gratiam Dei compositæ: partim ineptæ & à Christi instituto alienæ. Prioris generis est, quòd per infelicem illum feminæcem humanam naturam adumbrari dicunt, quam in Adamo vulneratam Christus medicus restituerit. Atqui Adam serpenti morem gerens, non modò vulnera- tus & debilitatus, sed omnino mortuus est, sicuti fore Deus prædixerat: Quacunq; hora ederis ex arbore illa, morte morieris. Ai isti vt liberum arbitrium tuentur, aliquas vires homini adhuc re- liquas fuisse contendunt, & nos per Christum sublevatos modò, non ex morte in vitam restitutos esse docent. Atqui huius disputationis, quæ Christo cum Legisperito intercessit, scopo & instituto confutantur. Ideo enim hunc ad legem remittit Dominus, vt sibi vires omnino nullas esse sentiat ea agendi, quæ ad vitam consequendam faciunt. Et Paulus nos in offensis & peccatis omnino mor- tuos fuisse testatur, & idem suo exemplo docet, in electis quoque & renatis peccati reliquias super- esse, quæ inuitos arripiat, quo minus legi Dei obtemperent. Ad alterum genus pertinet, quod ali- qui hominem peccatorem designari aiunt, cui Christus vino & oleo, id est, per pœnitentiam & pec- catorum remissionem gratuitam medeatur. Dicitur hoc pie & verè: (Est enim Christus à Patre missus, vt nobis pœnitentiam & peccatorum remissionem largiatur) sed non sunt ista huius loci, & quid opus est in scripturis ludere, easq; in sententiam alienam detorquere, cum passim loci aperti occurrant, quibus Christianæ religionis dogmata confirmari possunt? Itaque nos in Christi institu- tum intenti, teneamus, omnes homines necessario charitatis mutuæ vinculo sibi inuicem obstrictos esse: benefaciamus ergo omnibus, & inimicos quoq; diligamus, vt eo argumento testemur, nos germa- nos discipulos esse Iesu Christi, qui vt verbis hoc docuit, ita exemplo suo nobis præiuit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: We deliberately pass over the allegories which some have treated here, because some of them are impious and devised to nullify the grace of God, and others are silly and foreign to Christ's purpose. Of the first kind is the claim that the unhappy woman signifies human nature, which Christ the physician restored after it was wounded in Adam. But Adam, who obeyed the serpent, was not merely wounded and weakened but utterly dead, just as God had foretold: "On whatever day you eat of that tree, you shall die the death." Yet those men who defend free will contend that some powers remained in man, and teach that we have now been raised up only by Christ, not restored from death to life. But these interpretations are refuted by the aim and purpose of that dispute which Christ had with the lawyer. For the Lord sends him back to the law precisely so that he may feel he has no power at all to do the things that lead to life. And Paul testifies that we were wholly dead in offences and sins, and by his own example teaches that even in the elect and the reborn there remain remnants of sin which seize them against their will, so that they do not obey the law of God. The second kind is that which some say is meant to depict a sinful man, whom Christ heals with wine and oil, that is, through repentance and the free forgiveness of sins. This is said piously and truly (for Christ was sent by the Father to bestow on us repentance and the forgiveness of sins), but these things do not belong to this place, and why should we play with the Scriptures and twist them to a foreign meaning, when plain passages present themselves everywhere by which the doctrines of the Christian religion can be confirmed? Therefore let us, intent on Christ's instruction, hold fast that all men are bound to one another by the necessary bond of mutual love. Let us therefore do good to all, and love even our enemies, so that by this argument we may witness that we are true disciples of Jesus Christ, who taught this by his words and went before us in it by his example. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 104.

units.la: Factum est autem inter eundum, ipse ingressus est in quendam vicum: mulier vero quædam Martha nomine excepit eum in domum suam. Et huic erat soror, quæ vocabatur Maria, quæ etiam assidens ad pedes Iesu, audiebat ipsius sermonē. Martha vero distrahebatur circa frequens ministerium; superueniens igitur ait: Domine, non est tibi curæ, quod soror mea reliquit me vt sola ministrem? Dic ergo ei, vt mihi vicissim opituletur. Respondens autem dixit ei Iesus: Martha Martha, solicita es, & turbaris circa multa: atqui vna re opus est. Maria vero bonam partem elegit, quae non auferetur ab ea.
units.tr: Now as they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. But Martha was distracted with much serving; and she came up and said, "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her therefore to help me." But Jesus answered her, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is needful. Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away from her."

units.la: Multa hucusque toto hoc Cap. dicta sunt de Praedicatione verbi Dei, & de illis, qui ea vel admittunt, vel impie aspernantur. Subiecit his Lucas colloquium seu disputationem Iesu Christi cum arrogante & fastuoso Legis interprete, quae summa verae doctrina & omnium mandatorum Dei continet. Consistit haec in duobus capitibus, Dilectione Dei nimirum, quae fidem in hunc & obedientiam veram comprehendit, & dilectione proximi, ex qua vitae innocentia derivatur. Et de proximi dilectione quidem abunde dictum est in Samaritani parabola, qua Christus docuit, quis proximi loco haberi debeat, & quibus officijs charitate sive dilectione erga illum testari debeamus. Ne quis autem hinc colligeret, salute nostrorum operum meritis deberi, comode subtexitur historia, quam modo recitavimus, quae exemplis pulcherrimis tota hanc doctrinam illustrat. Continet enim hospitalitatis praeclarum exemplum, quo omnia charitatis officia traduntur. Vicissim vero docet, quis nam verus Dei cultus sit, quo huius dilectionem testari debeamus, & ex quo tota nostrae salutis ratio dependet: Nimirum, vt Iesum Christum audiamus, quem ille nobis doctorem ac Seruatorem dedit, &c.
units.tr: Much has been said so far in this whole chapter about the preaching of God's Word, and about those who either receive it or impiously despise it. Luke adds to these an account of a dispute between Jesus Christ and a proud and arrogant interpreter of the Law, which contains the sum of true doctrine and of all God's commandments. It consists of two heads: the love of God, which comprehends faith in him and true obedience, and the love of our neighbour, from which the innocence of life follows. Indeed, the love of neighbour was treated at length in the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which Christ taught who ought to be regarded as our neighbour, and by what duties of charity or love we ought to show our regard for him. Lest anyone should infer from this that salvation is owed to the merits of our works, the history we have just recited is fittingly added, which illustrates this doctrine by most beautiful examples. For it contains a notable example of hospitality, by which all the duties of charity are set forth. In turn it teaches what the true worship of God is, by which we ought to testify to our love of him, and on which the whole reckoning of our salvation depends: namely, that we hear Jesus Christ, whom the Father gave to us as teacher and Saviour, etc.

units.la: Oritur autem ab occasione totius historiae, quae fuit, quod Iesus Christus dum iter aut profectionem suam versus Hierosolymam prosequitur, in vicum quendam diuertit ad Martham & Mariam sorores. Vicum hunc Bethaniam, Mariam vero & Martham Lazari sorores fuisse constat ex Ioannis vndecimo Cap. Singulari autem benevolentia familiam hanc Christus prosecutus est, adeo vt cum Lazarus in morbum letalem incidisset, sorores non aliud illi absenti nuntiari curent, quam Domine, is quem tu amas, aegrotat. Et ipse paulo post discipulis ait: Lazarus amicus noster dormit, & illis etiam reluctantibus ob periculi metum Bethaniam abit, & iam quartum diem in sepulchro agentem a mortuis resuscitat.
units.tr: The occasion of the whole history arises from this: as Jesus Christ was pursuing his journey toward Jerusalem, he turned aside into a certain village to Martha and Mary, the sisters. That this village was Bethany, and that Mary and Martha were sisters of Lazarus, is clear from the eleventh chapter of John. Christ loved this family with singular goodwill, so much so that when Lazarus had fallen into a deadly sickness, the sisters did not arrange for anything to be announced to him while he was absent except, "Lord, he whom you love is sick." And he himself said shortly afterward to the disciples, "Our friend Lazarus sleeps"; and although they were reluctant, for fear of danger, he went away to Bethany, and raised him from the dead when he had already been in the tomb for four days.

units.la: Nunc autem ante omnia Christus obseruandus venit, qui etsi Rex regum sit, & omnia illi tradita sint a Patre suo, tamen in aedes alienas diuertit, non aute more regum huius seculi passim per vrbes & vicos celebriores palatia habet, & ipsum expectantes seruos aulicos, qui eum excipiat. Debuit enim in assumpta humanitate, quoad hic vixit, nihil proprium habere, vt nos aeterni regni caelorum bonis locupletaret. At magnum bonitatis eius argumentum est, quod subinde ad homines priuatos diuertit: quod tunc demum nobis recte patebit, si quis ipse sit expendamus. Est enim semen illud Abrahamo promissum, quod maledictionem omnem ab humano genere auertere, benedictionem vero omnibus gentibus reducere debuit. Est dilectus ille & aeternus Dei Filius, in quo Patri copulacuit, vt nobiscum in gratiam rediret. Est vs, in quo omnes thesauri scientiae & cognitionis reconditi sunt, & qui nobis a Deo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptionis nostrae pretium.
units.tr: But now, before all else, we must observe that Christ came here, who, though he is King of kings and all things have been given to him by his Father, nevertheless turned aside into the houses of others. He does not, after the manner of the kings of this age, keep palaces scattered through the more famous cities and villages, with courtly servants awaiting him to receive him. For in the humanity he assumed, as long as he lived here, he was to have nothing of his own, so that he might enrich us with the goods of the eternal kingdom of heaven. But it is a great proof of his goodness that he turned aside from time to time to private persons; this will become plain to us only if we consider who he is. He is that Seed promised to Abraham, who was to turn away every curse from the human race and bring blessing back to all nations. He is that beloved and eternal Son of God, in whom it pleased the Father to be reconciled, so that he might return to favour with us. He is the one in whom all the treasures of knowledge and understanding are hidden, and who has been made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and the price of our redemption.

units.la: Non potest ergo ad aliquem amicè ac familiariter diuertere, quin secum ferat haec sua bona omnia, & ea cum salute certa ijs conferat, quos amicorum loco habet. Ideo infra Zachaei domui salutem contigisse dicet, cum ad illum diuertisset, & ab eodem fuisset exceptus. Et hoc quidem bodie multi fatentur, sed paratos esse aiunt ad illum excipiendum, si modo ad ipsos venire, vt olim ad Zachaeum, ad Lazarum & sorores eius venire dignatus fuit. Atqui vt ita ad nos diuertat, minime opus est. Nam quod illi in terris agendum erat, dudum peregit, & nobis vtile fuit, vt relicto mundo hoc ad caelestes aeterna beatitudinis sedes ascenderet, & nobis illic locum pararet, atq; nunc apud Patrem pro nobis intercedat. Nihilominus tamen ad nos quotidie diuertit per Verbum suum, in quo seipsum & bona sua omnia nobis offert, & amicè vt illis fruamur inuitat. Hic ergo paratas habeamus, non aedes nostras ex lignis & lapidibus extructas, sed mentes nostras, vt Verbum eius cum fide vera excipiamus, & eidem obtemperemus, vt postea prolixius dicetur. Diuertit ad nos etiam in panperibus, & ijs maximè, qui eius nomine exulant: quos in suum locum substituit, vt in suas rationes sese ascripturum polliceatur, quicquid officij in ipsos fuerit collatum. Si quibus ergo tam charus & gratus foret ipsius Christi aduentus, quam ipsi gloriantur, agedum hic sese ad praestanda dilectionis officia accingant, & ipse Christum excepisse iudicabuntur.
units.tr: He cannot therefore turn aside to anyone in friendship and familiarity without bringing with him all these good things of his, and conferring them, together with certain salvation, upon those whom he counts as friends. Hence he says that salvation came to Zacchaeus' house below, when he had turned aside to it and been received by him. Many today indeed confess this, but they say they are ready to receive him, if only he would come to them as once he deigned to come to Zacchaeus, and to Lazarus and his sisters. Yet there is no need for him to turn aside to us in this way. For what he had to do on earth he has long since accomplished; and it was profitable for us that, leaving this world, he should ascend to the heavenly seats of eternal blessedness, prepare a place for us there, and now intercede for us with the Father. Nevertheless he turns aside to us every day through his Word, in which he offers himself and all his goods to us, and kindly invites us to enjoy them. Let us therefore have ready here, not houses built of wood and stone, but our minds, so that we may receive his Word with true faith and obey it, as will be said more fully afterward. He also turns aside to us in the poor, and especially in those who are exiles for his name; these he has substituted in his own place, promising that he will reckon to his own account whatever service of duty is bestowed upon them. If therefore the coming of Christ himself were as dear and welcome to any as they boast, let them now gird themselves to perform the offices of love here, and they will be judged to have received Christ himself.

units.la: Habent illi hoc loco memorabile hospitalitatis exemplum, quod imitentur. Fuit familia haec dives admodum, & inter Iudaeos magnae existimationis, vt in circumstantiis historiae de Lazaro resuscitato, & in facto Mariae Christum pretiosissimo oleo unguentis esse videre. Et ea tunc erat rerum conditio, vt non solum Christus publice exosus esset, verumetiam cum illo periclitarentur, quotquot ipsius discipuli aut sectatores erant. Pharisaei enim, quorum potentia ipsis quoque primatibus formidolosa erat, publico edicto excommunicatione aut exclusionem e Synagoga in omnes decreverat, qui in illum crederent. At venit nunc Christus Bethaniam cum numerosissimo comitatu, vt latere nullo modo posset, & palam in domum illam diverterit. Concurrunt ergo multa simul; quae Lazarum cum sororibus movere poterant, vt aut excluderet eum, aut amicè aut alio diverteret rogaret: summus nimirum ingens, labor non exiguus, molestia magna, & quod haec omnia superat, excommunicationis periculum. Sed nihil horum illos abstterrere potest, quo minus illum cum suo hospitio excipiant: neque id invitii aut cum murmure faciunt, vt solent in quos laborum & impensarum piget: sed omne veri amoris indicium monstrant, totoque in eo sunt, vt amicè & honorificè ab ipsis tractetur. Tales decet esse Christianos, hospitales videlicet, & ita quidem, vt laeto & alacri vultu peregrinus omne hospitalitatis officium praestent. Ut enim Deus ipse hilarem datorem diligit: ita consolationem maximam hoc peregrinis & exulantibus affert, si se diligi & nemini graves aut molestos esse sentiant. Nec nos hic alicuius laboris aut sumptuum pigere debet. Suo enim exemplo nobis praeiuerunt Abraham, Lothus & alij sanctissimi homines, quos non imitari turpe foret. Et ijdem interdum Angelos suscepepunt, cum homines ad se diverterit putarent. Excitent nos praeterea Dei praecepta, quibus peregrinos nobis diligentissimè commendat, & ne quam illis iniuriam faciamus seuerissimè prohibet. Et si lucri spes nobis cordi est, quis a nobis quaestus uberior potest excogitari, quā si ipsum Dei Filium nobis debitorem faciamus, qui se remuneratorem fore pollicetur, & olim in magno illo die in se collatum esse reputabit, quicquid in suos cultores collatum fuerit?
units.tr: In this place they have a memorable example of hospitality to imitate. This family was very wealthy and of great esteem among the Jews, as can be seen from the circumstances of the history concerning the raised Lazarus, and from the deed of Mary, who anointed Christ with very precious ointment. And at that time the condition of affairs was such that not only was Christ openly hated, but all who were his disciples or followers were also in danger along with him. For the Pharisees, whose power was formidable even to the chief men, had decreed by public edict that excommunication, or exclusion from the synagogue, should fall upon all who believed in him. But now Christ comes to Bethany with a very large company, so that he could in no way remain hidden, and openly turns aside into that house. Many things therefore concur at once which could move Lazarus and his sisters either to shut him out, or to ask him kindly to turn aside elsewhere: namely, a great burden of expense, no small labour, great inconvenience, and, what surpasses all these, the danger of excommunication. Yet none of these things can frighten them from receiving him into their hospitality; nor do they do so unwillingly or with murmuring, as people commonly do when they grudge labours and expenses; but they show every sign of true love, and are wholly intent that he should be treated by them in a friendly and honourable manner. Such ought Christians to be, hospitable indeed, and so that they perform every office of hospitality to a stranger with a cheerful and eager countenance. For as God himself loves a cheerful giver, so this brings the greatest comfort to strangers and exiles, if they feel that they are loved and are a burden or trouble to no one. Nor ought we to grudge any labour or expense here. For Abraham, Lot, and other most holy men went before us in this example, and it would be shameful not to imitate them. And these same men at times received angels, when they supposed they were turning aside to men. Moreover, the precepts of God should stir us up, by which he most diligently commends strangers to us and most strictly forbids us to do them any injury. And if the hope of gain is dear to us, what more abundant profit can be devised by us than to make the Son of God himself our debtor, who promises to be the rewarder, and who on that great day will count as done to himself whatever has been bestowed upon his worshippers?

units.la: Quia vero de hūs saepe dictum est, nunc quid in domo Lazari & sororum eius Dominus fecerit videamus, quam primum eo diverterit. Num turpi otio aut ignauo somno se dedidit? vel num pro imperio familiae imperauit statim, quid fieri velit, & qualis apparatus esse debeat? vel num mox epulari coepit? Nihil horum Lucas narrat, sed eum mox docendi officio functum esse, & Petrus caelestis verbum praedicauisse scribit. Nam vt supra audiuimus, comitatum in profectione illa maximum habuit tam virorum quam mulierum, qui omnes illum vt doctrinam eius audirent, sequebantur. Itaque locum commodum nactus, illos instituit, & eadem opera familiae huic Verbum aeternae salutis denuntiat. Est autem observatu dignissima eius industria atque sedulitas, qua in obeundo munere sibi a Patre commissio visus est. Nam vt de illo Isaias vaticinatus fuerat, adeuant gelizandum pauperibus mitti debuit, & ipse non uno loco fatetur, se ideo venisse, vt regnum Dei passim praedicet. Id igitur tam sedulo ac indefesso studio agit, vt ne tunc quidem cessaret, quando locus & tempus otium sive quietem postulare videbantur. Exempla huius industriae multa alia in Euangelio extant, quae ex ordine recitare non est opus, cum legentibus subinde occurrant. Nos hinc colligamus, illum salutis nostrae fidientissimum esse, adeoque (vt apud Ioannem testatur) hunc cibum suum esse, vt ex Patris voluntate atque mandato quam plurimos ad salutem instituat. Hinc ergo consolatio peti debet in tentationibus, ne facile de salute nostra desperemus, quam fidelissimo huic pastori & medico tantopere cordi esse cernimus. Simul autem bonae indolis discipulos imitati industriae eius consideratione excitemur, vt non minori diligentia illum in verbo suo nobis loquentem audiamus, denique praeparemus nos, vt (quod beatus Ignatius olim de seipso diccebat) panis mundus inveniamur, quo Christus saturari atque delectari possit. Praeterea discant exemplo Christi omnes homines, vt ipsi quoque functiones suas, ad quas diuinitus vocati sunt, pari studio obeant, vt olim Deo de illis rationem possint reddere.
units.tr: Since we have often spoken of these matters, let us now see what the Lord did in the house of Lazarus and his sisters as soon as he had gone there. Did he give himself over to shameful idleness or lazy sleep? Did he at once give orders to the household about what should be done and how the preparations ought to be made? Or did he soon begin to feast? Luke records none of these things. He writes that Christ straightway performed the duty of teaching, and that he preached the heavenly word. For, as we heard above, he had a very large company in that journey, of both men and women, who all followed him to hear his teaching. So, finding a suitable place, he instructed them, and at the same time he announced the Word of eternal salvation to this household. Now his diligence and earnestness, with which he showed himself faithful in the office committed to him by the Father, is most worthy of notice. For as Isaiah prophesied of him, he was to be sent to preach the gospel to the poor, and he himself says in more than one place that he came for this reason, that he might preach the kingdom of God everywhere. He pursued this with such zeal and tireless effort that he did not rest even when place and time seemed to call for leisure or quiet. Many other examples of this diligence are found in the Gospel, which need not be recited in order, since they keep meeting the reader. From this we gather that he is most solicitous for our salvation, and that (as he testifies in John) his food is to instruct as many as possible to salvation, according to the will and command of the Father. Hence comfort ought to be sought in temptations, so that we do not easily despair of our salvation, which we see is so dear to this most faithful shepherd and physician. At the same time, let us, as good disciples, be stirred up by considering his diligence, so that we hear him speaking to us in his word with no less care; and finally let us prepare ourselves, so that we may be found (as the blessed Ignatius once said of himself) pure bread, with which Christ may be satisfied and delighted. Moreover, let all men learn from Christ's example to discharge their own duties, to which they have been called by God, with equal zeal, so that they may one day be able to render an account of them to God.

units.la: Hūs praemissis ad duas hasce sorores accedamus, de quibus potissimum hic agitur. Vnus vtriq; affectus, idem in vtraque Christi amor, idem denique studium, quod videlicet illum honorare, & suam erga hunc voluntatem dignis officijs declarare volunt. Id vero non eadem ratione, neque eodem modo faciunt. Quare singulas seorsim inspexisse proderit, vt plus utilitatis & fructus ex consideratione deratione eorum, quæ fecerunt ad nos redeat. Martha, quæ strenua & laboriosa matrisfamilias typum gerit, tota in hoc est, ut domum adornet, conuiuium instruat, omnibus qui venerant digne prospiciat, denique (vt ipse Christus postea ei dicet) circa multa satagit atque occupatur. Maria autem interea ad pedes Iesu docentis confidet, & illum concionantem audit. Displicet hoc Marthæ, non quod eam laboris pigeat, sed quòd sororis opem iam sibi necessariam putet, & ideo Dominum compellans ait: Domine, non est tibi cura, quòd soror mea reliquit me, ut sola ministrem? dic ergo ei, ut mihi vicissim opituletur, vel ut ipsa quoque manus operi admoueat, & me tam multis occupatam adiuuet. Quid vero ad illa Dominus? Martha Martha (inquit) solicita es, & turbaris vel satagis circa multa: atqui vna re opus est. Maria vero bonam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea. Quibus verbis, etsi Martha reprehendatur, Maria autem defendatur, non tamen ita accipi debet, quasi Marthæ sedulitas per se vituperio digna fuerit, & Christo improbetur. Quin potius eo nomine laude digna est, quòd licet diuitiis abundet, & præ aliis multis inter suæ gentis homines in honore sit & pretio, non dedignatur tamen laborem istum subire, & nihil non facit, quo Christum & hospites reliquos honorari posse existimat. Talem mulierum credentium matrem, Saram Moses describit. Nam cùm Abrahamus hospites domum deduxisset, ipsa proueêta iam ætatis farinam subigit, panes & placentas parat, nullum denique detrectat laborem, ut & marito & hospitibus rem gratam faciat. Talem matremfamilias describit Solomon, quæ lanam & linum quærat, & manibus suis cum voluptate operetur: imò quæ de nocte surgat, ut familiæ suæ cibum, & puellis suis pensa sua distribuat: quæ denique ipsa lumbos suos accingat brachiaque sua ad opus faciendum corroboret. Et Paulus Apostolus Christianas fœminas diligentes rei domesticæ administras esse vult, & quæ liberos fideliter educent: quod verunque absque labore & molestia fieri non potest. Pudeat ergo multas suæ ignauiæ, quæ molles & delicatulæ vel domi desident, rei verò domesticæ curam nihil ad se pertinere putant: vel magno cum fastu otiosæ deambulant, equis molliter gradientibus aut rhedis magnificè ornatis vehuntur. Sunt tales fere familiarum calamitas, dum quæ virorum industria parantur, ipsæ turpi fastu & luxu prodigunt. Non talis Martha hæc, cuius pietas alibi quoque commendatur: & ista etiam sedulitas, quam nunc præstat, laudem suam meruisset, nisi (quod pijs sæpe accidit) vitia alia occurrissent, quæ reprehensione digna fuerunt. Primò enim modum excedit, & Christum apparatu splendidiore atq; lautioribus epulis excipere vult, qui frugalitate potius delectatur. Deinde circa hæc, quæ corpori curando seruiunt occupata, salutarem animæ cibum negligit, quem Christus auditoribus suis depromebat. Tertiò de sorore audacius iudicat, & ignauiæ adscribit, quod pio discendi studio ab ea fiebat, se denique illa meliorem putat propter externa hæc, quæ obibat, officia. Accedit hus immodestia, quòd Christum de rebus graui- bus differentem interpellat. Propter ista reprehensione digna fuit, quæ sua industria laudem summam merebatur, si ea & in tempore vsa essent, & eandem vitijs hisce non polluissent. Est ergo hoc memorabile exemplum, quo admonemur, quàm nobis suspecta esse debeant opera & studia nostra omnia, & quàm diligenti cura opus sit, ne tunc quoque, quando quid boni facimus, caeco carnis zelo abrepti exorbitemus.
units.tr: With these things premised, let us turn to these two sisters, about whom the main discussion here is. Both have the same feeling, the same love of Christ, and finally the same zeal, namely to honour him and to show their goodwill towards him by fitting services. But they do not do this in the same way or by the same method. Therefore it will be useful to examine each one separately, so that more profit and fruit may come back to us from considering what each of them did. Martha, who represents the diligent and laborious mistress of the household, is wholly intent on preparing the house, arranging a feast, and providing well for all who have come; in short (as Christ himself will later say to her) she is anxious and busied about many things. Meanwhile Mary sits at the feet of Jesus as he teaches, and listens to him preaching. This displeases Martha, not because she grudges the labour, but because she thinks she now needs her sister's help; so, addressing the Lord, she says: "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me in turn, or at least to put her hands to the work and assist me, who am burdened with so many tasks." But what does the Lord say to her? "Martha, Martha," he says, "you are anxious and troubled, or busy about many things; yet only one thing is needful. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her." Although by these words Martha is rebuked and Mary is defended, yet this must not be understood as if Martha's diligence were in itself deserving of blame and were disapproved by Christ. Rather, she is worthy of praise for this, that although she is rich and held in honour and esteem among the people of her nation above many others, she does not disdain to undertake this labour, and she leaves nothing undone by which she thinks Christ and the other guests can be honoured. Moses describes Sarah, a mother of believing women, in such a way. For when Abraham had brought the guests into the house, she, already advanced in years, kneaded meal, prepared bread and cakes, and in short refused no labour, so that she might do a pleasing service both to her husband and to the guests. Solomon describes such a mistress of the household, who seeks wool and flax and works with her hands with delight; indeed, who rises by night to distribute food to her household and tasks to her maids; who finally girds her loins and strengthens her arms for the work. The Apostle Paul also wants Christian women to be diligent managers of domestic affairs, and to bring up their children faithfully; yet neither of these can be done without labour and trouble. Let many women, then, be ashamed of their laziness, who, being soft and pampered, sit idle at home and think the care of the household has nothing to do with them, or who walk about in proud idleness, carried in carriages with gently moving horses or magnificently decorated coaches. Such women are almost the ruin of their families: while the husband's industry provides the means, they squander them in shameful pomp and luxury. Martha was not such a woman, and her piety is commended elsewhere too. This diligence which she now shows would have earned her praise, had not other faults, such as often befall the godly, appeared, which deserved rebuke. For first, she went beyond measure and wished to receive Christ with a more splendid preparation and richer feasts, when he took more pleasure in simplicity. Second, in attending to these things that serve the care of the body, she neglected the wholesome food of the soul, which Christ was setting before his hearers. Third, she judged her sister too boldly, and ascribed to idleness what was done by her out of a devout desire to learn; and finally, she thought herself better than her sister because of these outward duties which she performed. To this was added an impatience, in that she interrupted Christ while he was speaking of weighty matters. For these things she was worthy of reproof, though her diligence deserved the highest praise, if it had been used at the right time and had not been tainted by these faults. This, then, is a memorable example, by which we are warned how suspect all our works and endeavours ought to be to us, and with how careful a diligence we must take heed that, even when we do some good, we do not go astray, carried away by the blind zeal of the flesh.

units.la: Habemus ergo in Martha typum omnium eorum, qui Deum externis officijs pro sui animi arbitrio colere instituunt. Occupantur hi circa multa. Templa sumptuosa & cum regum palatijs certantia ædificant, addunt his sacella, quæ in compitis quoque & triuijs extruunt: auro & argento illa exornant: preciosissima quæque ad Dei cultum congerunt, discurrunt, suffitum faciunt, accendunt cerea & lampades, cantant, ludunt organis, noctu excubias agunt, sacra celebrant matutina & antelucana, ieiunijs sese immodicè macerant, induuntur cilicijs, humi dormiunt, nudis pedibus & capite discooperto incedunt, denique sexcenta alia faciunt, quæ ipsis magnifica, pia & Deo accepta esse putantur. E contra pios Dei cultores, qui vno Verbo contenti, non eadem cum ipsis faciunt, ignauiæ accusant, & bonorum operum contemptores atq; hostes esse clamant, & tantùm nō Deum ipsum vnà cum cœlis & inferis aduersus illos ad vindictam prouocat. Sed idem illis dici potest, quod in præsenti Marthæ dicitur: Vos quidem soliciti estis, & vobis ipsis labores atq; molestias facitis dum circa multa tumultuamini: atqui ad salutem consequendam vnica re opus est, quæ à vobis negligitur.
units.tr: In Martha, then, we have a figure of all those who undertake to worship God with outward services according to their own mind. They are occupied with many things. They build sumptuous temples that rival royal palaces; they add chapels, which they erect even at crossroads and junctions; they adorn them with gold and silver; they heap together the most precious things for the worship of God; they run about, burn incense, light wax candles and lamps, sing, play on organs, keep vigil at night, celebrate sacred rites at matins and before dawn; they wear out themselves with immoderate fasts, clothe themselves in hair shirts, sleep on the ground, walk barefoot and bareheaded; and finally they do six hundred other things which they think are splendid, pious, and acceptable to God. On the other hand, the godly worshippers of God, who are content with the one Word and do not do the same things as they do, are accused by them of laziness, and are denounced as despisers and enemies of good works; and God himself, together with heaven and hell, is almost provoked by them to take vengeance on these worshippers. But the same can be said to them as is now said to Martha: "You indeed are anxious, and you make labours and troubles for yourselves while you bustle about many things; yet for obtaining salvation only one thing is needful, and this is what you neglect."

units.la: Nam vt ipse Dominus Samaritidi dicebat, Deus externa hæc nō curat: sed cum spiritus sit, in spiritu & veritate vult coli & adorari. Quin olim, cùm externa sacra adhuc in vsu essent, ea tamen abomi natus esset, quoties ijs solis occupati ea negligebat, quae per illa adumbrabantur. Et cùm in Psal. 50. litem institueret aduersus populum Iudaicum, inter alia dicit: Non reprehendam te sacrificiorum causa, holocausta enim tua sunt iugiter coram me: Nec est vt accipiam de domo tua hircum, nec de caulis tuis hircos. Mea enim sunt omnes ferae sylvarum, pecudes in mille montibus. Noui vniuersas in montibus volucres, penes me sunt omnes animantes agrestes. Si esuriero, non est vt tibi indicem, cùm meus sit orbis & quicquid ille continet, &c. Et huius generis infiniti loci apud Prophetas occurrunt. Quod si olim haec Dei mens fuit, cùm cultus ille Leuiticus adhuc durarèt, nunc eum hodie externis bis delectari putabimus, postquam Christus veteribus umbris sublatis cultum substituit simplicissimum, & nos ad spiritum & veritatem reuocat? Non ergo templa illi extrui poterunt, quibus includatur, cuius thronus coelum, scabellum vero pedum terra est. Non aurum & argentum requirit, quae Antichristi Deo Mazim Daniel tribuit. Non ab nobis odores suaues pofluat, qui thura & aromata omnia creauit. No nostris discursionibus delestatur, qui gratia suam, & Filij sui meritum nobis vbique locorum per Euangelij praedicationem effert. Num vero nostrum cereum opus habebit, qui totum orbem terrarum Solis radijs, & noctis tenebras Luna atq; syderibus illustrat? Num item nostrum cantum & ab nobis excogitatorum organorum harmoniam alicuius faciet vs, cui coelestes chori hymnos ineffabiles concinunt, & qui aniculas voce donauit, quae omne humani ingenij artificium longè superat? Num denique ex nostris vigiliis, ieiunijs, ciliciis aliisq; corporis nostri castigationibus voluptatem aliquam capiet, qui somnum dedit, vt vires diuturnola bore fatigatas recreet, qui cibos creauit & ijsdem cum gratia suaue actione resci iussit, qui deniq; aues, feras & flores agri mirificè vestit? Sunt haec cogitatu & dictu puerilia, & pe ssunt haec sola sufficere ad confutandas superstitiones, pro quibus hodie multi perinde pugnant, ac si tota hominis salus ab illis solis dependeret.
units.tr: For as the Lord himself said to the Samaritan woman, God does not care for these external things: since he is spirit, he wishes to be worshipped and adored in spirit and in truth. Indeed, even when the external sacred rites were still in use, he nonetheless abhorred them whenever men, occupied only with those, neglected the things that were foreshadowed by them. And when in Psalm 50 he brought a charge against the Jewish people, among other things he says: "I will not reprove you for your sacrifices, for your burnt offerings are continually before me. Nor will I take a bullock out of your house, nor goats out of your folds. For all the beasts of the forest are mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the mountains, and all the wild creatures of the field are with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine and all that is in it," etc. And countless passages of this kind occur among the Prophets. But if this was God's mind of old, while that Levitical worship still endured, shall we now suppose that he delights in external things today, after Christ has removed the old shadows and set in their place the most simple worship, and calls us back to spirit and truth? Therefore no temples can be built for him, to enclose him whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth. He does not require gold and silver, which Daniel assigns to the god Mauzim of Antichrist. Sweet odours do not flow from us to him who created all incense and spices. He is not delighted by our running about, he who sets forth his grace and the merit of his Son to us everywhere in the preaching of the Gospel. Will he indeed have need of our wax, he who illumines the whole round of the earth with the rays of the sun, and the darkness of night with the moon and the stars? Will he likewise be moved by our singing and the harmony of organs devised by us, he to whom the heavenly choirs sing ineffable hymns, and who gave voice to the little birds, which far surpasses all the art of human genius? Lastly, will he take any pleasure from our night watches, fasts, hair shirts and other castigations of our body, he who gave sleep so that it might restore strength wearied by the long day, who created food and commanded us to take it with thanksgiving, who finally clothes the birds, the beasts and the flowers of the field with wondrous beauty? These things are childish both to think and to say, and these alone cannot suffice to refute the superstitions for which many today fight just as if the whole salvation of man depended on them alone.

units.la: Quod ergo vnicum illud est, in quo verus Dei cultus & vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio consistit, & quo solo opus esse Christus ait? Id hic nobis ceu digito monstrat in Mariae exemplo, quando hanc dicit bonam partem elegisse, quae ab ea nunquam auferetur. Quid vero illa fecit? Sedit ad pedes Iesu, & audiuit verbum eius. Solebant olim discipuli & auditores ad pedes doctorum suorum sedere, quod humilitatis & voluntariae obedientiae signum erat. Ita Paulus ad pedes Gamalielis in Lege patria institutus fuisse dicitur. In hoc igitur verus Dei cultus & salus hominisConsistit, vt primo nos ad pedes Iesu Christi demittamus, id est, vt contrito animo coram illo humiliemur, & reuerenter afficiamur ad Verbum ipsius. Docet hoc ipse per Isaiam sic loquens: Ad quem respiciam? Ad pauperem & contritum spiritu, & qui ad Verbum meum tremiscit. Deinde alterum accedat oportet, vt verbum hoc fide vera amplestamur. Sunt enim qui & verbum audiant, & eo audito conslerantur (cuius rei exemplum in impio Achabo historia sacra proponit). Sed quia fide destituuntur, non credunt promissionibus Dei, & proinde vel impie contemnunt & rid- ent quae dicuntur, vel conscien- tiae terroribus superati desperant. At fides Dei amorem gignit, promissiorum dulci contemplatione animas exhilarat, vnde ardens obedientiae fluidus nascitur, quae causa est, quòd Verbi studus sese per omnem vitam nostram diffundit. Et hoc vnicum illud est, quod Christus solum necessariu esse dicit, & cuius studium alibi quoque omnibus alijs exercitijs & rebus per se sar. Eisimis praeferiur.
units.tr: What then is that one thing in which the true worship of God and the whole reason of our salvation consist, and which Christ says is alone necessary? Here he points it out to us as with a finger, in the example of Mary, when he says that she has chosen the good part, which shall never be taken away from her. But what did she do? She sat at the feet of Jesus and heard his word. Disciples and hearers used of old to sit at the feet of their teachers, which was a sign of humility and voluntary obedience. So Paul is said to have been trained at the feet of Gamaliel in the law of his fathers. In this, therefore, the true worship of God and the salvation of man consists: that first we cast ourselves at the feet of Jesus Christ, that is, that with a contrite spirit we humble ourselves before him and are reverently disposed towards his Word. He teaches this himself through Isaiah, speaking thus: "To whom shall I look? To the poor and contrite in spirit, and to him who trembles at my word." Next, it is necessary that we also come to embrace this word with true faith. For there are some who hear the word and, having heard it, are terrified (of which the sacred history sets forth an example in the impious Ahab). But because they lack faith, they do not believe God's promises, and accordingly either impiously scorn and laugh at what is said, or, overcome by terrors of conscience, despair. But faith begets love of God, it cheers souls with the sweet contemplation of the promises, and from this a burning fluid of obedience is born, which is the reason why the zeal for the Word spreads itself through our whole life. And this is that one thing which Christ says alone is necessary, and whose study he elsewhere also prefers to all other exercises and things of this kind, even those of great esteem in themselves.

units.la: Nam vt ad Veteris testamenti testimonia veniamus, Dauid non temere pronunciat: Victimas & sacrificium cibarium non amas, aures autem perfodisti mihi: holocaustum & hostiam pro peccato non postulauisti. Tum dixi, Ecce ipse adsum, in pagina libri scriptum est de me: Vt faciam quae tu probas o Deus meus, collibuit, & Lex tua in medio viscerum meorum, &c. Quo loco Verbi Dei studium & quae illi debetur, obedientiam (quam per aurium perforationem, locutione ex Lege petita, intelligit) omnibus sacrificijs disertè praefert. Et in primo Psalmo, beatum pronunciat non cum, qui in externo cultu assiduus sit (quod etiam in hypocritis est videre) sed eum, qui procul relistis improborum & illusorum consortijs, in Lege Domini dies & noctes meditatur. Et huius generis multa in Psalmis, in Verbi diuini commendationem dicuntur. Sed alia quoque Christi testimonia audiamus. Matthaei duodecimo Capite cùm inter docendum à matre & fratribus foras euocaretur, non parùit, sed extensa super discipulos manu sua dixit: Ecce mater mea, & fratres mei. Quisquis enim fecerit voluntatē Patris mei, qui est in cœlis, ille meus frater, & soror, & mater est. Et rursus alibi, cum mulier quædam doctrinæ eius admiratione abrepta exclamaret: Beatus venter qui te portauit, & vbera quæ suxisti: Respondit ille, Imò verò Beati, qui audiunt sermonem Dei, et custodiunt eum. Adde hīs Apostolorum exemplum, qui cum initio bonorum Ecclesia dispensatione suscepissent, vt ex ijs victum pauperibus distribuerent (quod officiū pijssimum & sanctissimum est) postea autem sentirent, se à prædicatione verbi Dei revocari, convocaca ecclesia tota muneri huic renuntiarunt: indignum hoc esse arbitrati, vt relicto docendi officio mensis ministrarent. Et Paulus Apostolus tanti fecit Euangelij prædicationem, vt eam Sacramentu quoq; præstantiorem duxerit. Nam cum in priori ad Corinthios se quam paucissimos baptizauisse dixisset, ratione subijcit: Non enim misit me Christus vt baptizarem, sed vt Euangelizarem. In quo ipsius Domini exemplum secutus fuisse videtur, qui & ipse in docendo quidem assiduus fuit, neminem autem baptizauit. At in ter externa exercitia religionis Ecclesia nihil sanctius & salutarius habet Sacramentis. Cum verò hæc infra Dei verbum longè subsidant, manifestè constat, huius studium Deo cultum esse omniū ac ceptissimum & proinde vehementer falli omnes, qui hoc relicto aut contempto, circa externos ritus occupantur. Ideo in præsenti Christus Mariam ait bonam, adeoq; potiorem & meliorem partem elegisse: & addit: Quæ non auferetur ab ea. Quo membro fructum huius studij exprimit, & hunc perpetuum esse & in æternum manere docet. Quod ipsum apud Ioannē quoq; indicat, quando se discipulos misisse dicit, vt prædicando verbum Dei inter homines fructum ferant, & fructus eorum maneat. Et jane non poterit intercidere aut perire Euangelij fructus apud electos Dei, qui illud cum fide audiunt. Christus enim bonus & fidelis ille pastor est, qui omnes suas nouit, & eas ex manibus suis eripi non sinit. Idem quoq; nos Patri suo cœlesti ita reconciliauit, vt neq; afflictio vlla, neq; angustia, neq; persecutio, neq; fames, neq; nuditas, neq; vllius periculi metus, neq; gladius, neq; mors neq; vita, nos ab eius dilectione separare possint. Latet quidem interdum fructus ille, dum pij quoq; carnis desiderijs oppressi, aut securitate circumuenti, officium suum minus faciunt, & Deus jape illos deseruisse videtur: sed quia semen filiorum Dei intra se habent, suscitat hoc suo tempore spiritus Domini, vt in viam redeant, & tunc Deus etiam fauorem suum denuo erga illos exerit, nec in huius modo vita curricu- lo tos tuetur, sed etiam vbi hoc emensi fuerint, regni sui cœlestis hæredes facit.
units.tr: For, to come to the testimonies of the Old Testament, David does not speak rashly: "Sacrifice and meal offering you did not desire, but you have pierced my ears; burnt offering and sin offering you did not require. Then I said, Behold, I am here; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: to do your will, O my God, I have delighted; and your law is within my heart," etc. In this passage he plainly sets the study of God's Word, and the obedience due to it (which he understands through the piercing of the ears, a figure of speech taken from the Law), above all sacrifices. And in the first Psalm he pronounces blessed not the man who is constant in external worship (which may also be seen in hypocrites), but the man who, keeping far from the company of the wicked and the scornful, meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night. And many things of this kind are said in the Psalms in commendation of the divine Word. But let us also hear other testimonies of Christ. In Matthew chapter twelve, when while teaching he was called outside by his mother and brothers, he did not obey, but stretching out his hand over his disciples he said: "Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother." And again elsewhere, when a certain woman, carried away with admiration for his teaching, cried out: "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked," he answered: "Yes rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." Add to these the example of the Apostles, who, when at the beginning they had undertaken the charge of distributing the goods of the Church, so that from them they might supply food to the poor (which is a most pious and most holy office), afterwards perceived that they were being called away from the preaching of the word of God, and, the whole Church being called together, renounced this office, judging it unworthy that, leaving the office of teaching, they should serve tables. And the Apostle Paul held the preaching of the Gospel in such esteem that he judged it more excellent even than the sacrament. For when in his first letter to the Corinthians he had said that he had baptized very few, he adds the reason: "For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel." In this he seems to have followed the example of the Lord himself, who was indeed constant in teaching, but baptized no one. Yet among the external exercises of religion the Church has nothing holier and more wholesome than the sacraments. But since these fall far below the word of God, it is clearly established that the study of this is the most acceptable worship of God of all, and therefore that all those are greatly mistaken who, neglecting or despising this, occupy themselves with external rites. Therefore in the present passage Christ calls Mary's choice good, and indeed the better and superior part, and adds: "which shall not be taken away from her." By this member he expresses the fruit of this study, and teaches that it is lasting and remains for ever. He indicates the same thing also in John, when he says that he has sent his disciples so that by preaching the word of God among men they may bear fruit, and that their fruit may remain. And indeed the fruit of the Gospel cannot perish or be lost among the elect of God, who hear it with faith. For Christ is that good and faithful shepherd who knows all his own, and does not allow them to be snatched from his hands. He has also so reconciled us to his heavenly Father that neither affliction, nor distress, nor persecution, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor fear of any danger, nor sword, nor death, nor life can separate us from his love. Indeed, that fruit is sometimes hidden, while the godly too are oppressed by the desires of the flesh, or overcome by security, and do their duty less, and God seems at times to have forsaken them; but because they have within them the seed of the children of God, the Spirit of the Lord stirs it up in its own time, so that they return to the way, and then God again extends his favour towards them, and does not keep them safe only through the course of this life, but also, when that has been finished, makes them heirs of his heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Hæc si diligentius expendantur, abunde docent, quam turpiter hac historia abusi sint Monachi-non sine atroci omnium aliorum hominum contumelia. Finxerunt illi duo vitæ genera, quorum alterum Contemplatiuum dixere, quod angelus similes faciat, alterum Actiuum, quod circa huius seculi negotia versetur, & homines à rerum cœlestium contemplatione, & meditatione revocet. Illius exemplum in Maria, huius autem in Martha proponi tradiderunt. Et in Actiuo quidem genere versari dicunt omnes eos, qui vel Reipub administrant, vel agriculturam aut artificia manuaria exercent: quorum omnium conditionem tanquam inutilem, imo vt noxiam damnarunt. Contemplatiuum vero vitæ genus sibi tribuentes, illud in otio monastico constituerunt. At vbi nam hoc præcepit Deus, vt quis euitato hominum consortio se in lustrum aliquod abdat, & sibi soli viuat? Aut quæ ratio est, quæ nos ex Mariæ exemplo tale quid colligere doceat? Nunc quidem cum tam præclara se offerret occasio, ad pedes Christi consedit, vt docentem audiret. Num autem illic hæsit perpetuo? annon postea ad rei domesticæ curam redijt? Certè hoc illam fecisse, satis docet quæ Ioannis vndecimo & duodecimo Cap. scribuntur. Et si vitæ humanæ rationem nobis à Deo præscriptam con-ideremus, nihil minus ille vult, quam vt circa ignauam & otiosam contemplationem occupati, ab alijs negotijs ad vitam sustentandam necessarijs abstineamus. Adamo quidem ille promissionem de semine mulieris dedit, in cuius meditatione frequentem & assiduum esse voluit: simul tamen eidem dixit: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Deinde Dei ordinatio est, vt alij quidē rempub. administrent, alij opifices sint, alij alijs rebus necessarijs vacent: & nullum illi acceptius est officium, quam si singuli suam vocationem sedulò sequantur. Nos itaq; omissis Monachorum ineptijs, quibus suam arrogantiam & impietatem produnt, verum huius historiæ vsum obseruemus, qui est, vt discamus, quomodo à nobis Christus excipi debeat. Primum hic est, vt verbum eius sedulò audiamus. Alterum, vt quod ex illo didicimus, factis testemur, & in primis quidem charitatis officijs inter quæ hospitalitas non postremum locum obtinet. Qui duo hæc coniungunt, ij Filium Dei le-
units.tr: If these things are weighed more carefully, they show plainly how shamefully the monks have abused this story, and not without great insult to all other men. They invented two kinds of life. One they called contemplative, because it makes people like angels; the other they called active, because it is occupied with the affairs of this world and calls people away from the contemplation and meditation of heavenly things. They taught that the example of the first is set forth in Mary, and of the second in Martha. They say that everyone who serves the commonwealth or practises farming or manual crafts belongs to the active kind of life, and they condemned the condition of all these people as useless, indeed even harmful. Claiming the contemplative kind of life for themselves, they placed it in monastic leisure. But where has God ever commanded that someone, shunning human fellowship, should hide himself away in some den and live for himself alone? Or what reasoning teaches us to draw such a conclusion from Mary's example? Indeed, when so splendid an opportunity presented itself, she sat at the feet of Christ to hear him teach. But did she cling to that place forever? Did she not afterwards return to the care of household affairs? That she did so is sufficiently shown by what is written in John chapters 11 and 12. And if we consider the plan of human life prescribed to us by God, he wills nothing less than that we, occupied with idle and lazy contemplation, abstain from the other business necessary for sustaining life. To Adam indeed he gave the promise concerning the woman's seed, on which he wished him to meditate frequently and constantly; at the same time, however, he said to him: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. Then it is God's ordinance that some administer the commonwealth, some be craftsmen, and others attend to other necessary things; and no duty is more acceptable to him than when each diligently follows his own calling. So, leaving aside the monks' absurdities, by which they betray their arrogance and impiety, let us observe the true use of this history, which is that we learn how Christ ought to be received by us. The first is that we listen diligently to his word. The second is that we bear witness by our deeds to what we have learned from it, chiefly in the duties of love, among which hospitality holds no small place. Those who join these two together receive the Son of God

units.la: {X 4} sum Christum digne excipiunt, qui ynà cum Patre ad eos diuertet, & quæ in suis seruis ipsi præ- stantur, officia cumulatissimè remunerabitur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: who receive Christ worthily, that is, those with whom together with the Father he will come to dwell, and he will repay most abundantly the services rendered to his servants. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: HOMILIA. CV.
units.tr: HOMILY 105.

units.la: ET factum est, cum ipse precaretur quodam in loco, vt cessauit, dixit ei quidà ex eius discipulis: Domine doce nos precari, prout & Ioan nes docuit discipulos suos.
units.tr: And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place, that when he had finished, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.

units.la: Cclesia electorum Dei & vere credentium, ex institutione capitis & sponsi sui Iesu Chri- sti, duo præcipua habet externa religionis exercitia, Prædicationem verbi Dei et preces, quibus Sacramenta comprehendi possunt, quæ verbi appendices & promissionum Dei atque salutis in Christo exhibitæ sigilla sunt. Quæ duo cum iam inde ab exordio rerum inter veros Dei cultores omnibus seculis in assiduo vsu fuerint, multum haud dubiè refert, vt eorū vsus in po sterum quoq; retineatur syncerus atq; legitimus. Itaq; Dominus noster Iesus Christus, de vtroq; dili genter & sæpe disserit. Et nuper quidè in proximo capite de Euangelij aut verbi sui prædicatione, de eiusdem ministerio & omnibus ijs prolixè egit, quæ tam doctoribus quam auditoribus cognitu ne cessaria sunt. Nunc vero in prima huius capitis parte non minori diligentia de precatione disseret, docens, vt illa fieri debeat, & quam magnus eius apud Deum effectus sit.
units.tr: The Church of God's elect and truly believing people, by the institution of its head and bridegroom Jesus Christ, has two principal external exercises of religion: the preaching of God's Word and prayers, to which the sacraments may be added, since they are appendages of the Word and seals of God's promises and of salvation in Christ. Since these two have been in constant use among the true worshippers of God in every age from the beginning of the world, it undoubtedly matters much that their pure and lawful use be retained in the future also. Accordingly our Lord Jesus Christ discusses both carefully and often. Recently, in the preceding chapter, he treated at length of the preaching of the Gospel or of his Word, of its ministry, and of all those things that are necessary for teachers and hearers alike to know. Now, in the first part of this chapter, he will discuss prayer with no less diligence, teaching how it ought to be made and how great an effect it has with God.

units.la: Rursus antem Lucas pro suo more ab occasione orditur, quæ Christum mouit, vt hanc tracta- tionem institueret. Fuit hæc, quod ipse in quodam loco, secretiori nimirum & a turbis libero, ar- denter precatus est. Hoc quia illum sæpius facere viderunt discipuli, & simul resciuerant Ioannem Baptistam suis discipulis peculiarem precandi formulam tradidisse, ipsi quoque a suo magistro & præceptore in hoc religionis exercitio institui cupiunt: & proinde vnum e toto suo grege deligunt, qui illum omnium nomine roget, idque Ioannis exemplo adduƈto, vt & ipse certam formulam præ- scribat, qua inter precandum vtantur, & quod petunt facile impetrant. Quo loco tam Ioannis quā ipsius Christi exemplum probè obseruandum est, qui cum illo tempore cum vero Dei cultu legiti- mus quoque precum vsus apud plerosque extinƈtus esset, suos discipulos in hoc peculiariter institue- runt. Imitari illos debent parentes, scholarum præfecti, & omnes alij quibus iuuentutis instituenda cura commissa est. Nec sufficere putent, si verba precationis Dominicæ aut aliarum precum suos recitare doceant, sed in hoc sint, vt sensum probè teneant pueri, simulque norint quanta cum fiducia preces debeant fieri. Nam si hanc partem negligant, de sua fide & diligentia non multum poterunt gloriari. In primis vero hac cura Ecclesiarum ministros tangere debet, vt in catechizandis iunio- ribus diligentes sint, & ita Deo adducant etiam eos, qui à suis parentibus negliguntur. Porro quia Christum non puduit in hoc se discipulorum ruditati accommodare, & idem ad preces nos frequen- ter amplißimis promissionibus propositis hortatur, non abs re fuerit locum hunc diligentius tracta- re, & priusquam ad precandi formulam a Christo traditam accedamus, quaedam excutere, quorum cognitio hic in primis necessaria est. Primo autem videamus, an precibus omnino opus sit. Deinde quid sit precatio, & in quas species diuidatur. Postremò, vt ad preces nosmetipsos præparare, quales deniq; inter precandum esse debeamus.
units.tr: Luke, as is his custom, again begins from the occasion that moved Christ to undertake this discourse. It was this: he was praying fervently in a certain place, a more secluded one, clearly, and free from crowds. Because his disciples had often seen him do this, and had also learned that John the Baptist had given his disciples a particular form of prayer, they desired to be instructed in this exercise of religion by their own master and teacher as well. Accordingly they chose one from their whole company to ask on behalf of all, and they appealed to John's example, so that he too would prescribe a fixed form which they might use in praying, and so that they might easily obtain what they sought. Here the example of both John and Christ himself is to be carefully observed. At that time the lawful use of prayer had been almost extinguished among most people, together with the true worship of God, and they trained their disciples particularly in this. Parents, school heads, and all others to whom the care of instructing youth has been entrusted ought to imitate them. Nor should they think it enough if they teach their children to recite the words of the Lord's Prayer or of other prayers; rather they should take care that the children understand the meaning well and at the same time know with what confidence prayers ought to be made. For if they neglect this part, they will not have much ground for boasting of their faith and diligence. Above all, this concern should touch the ministers of the congregations, that they be diligent in catechizing the younger folk, and so bring to God even those who are neglected by their parents. Furthermore, since Christ was not ashamed to accommodate himself to the dullness of his disciples in this matter, and since he exhorts us to prayer so often, setting before us the most ample promises, it will not be out of place to treat this passage more carefully. Before we come to the form of prayer given by Christ, let us examine certain points whose knowledge is especially necessary here. First, let us see whether prayer is altogether necessary. Second, what prayer is, and into what kinds it is divided. Last, how we ourselves should prepare for prayer, and what sort of people we ought to be while praying.

units.la: Quoad primam quastionem, nemo eam superuacaneam, aut curiosam potius quam vtilem puta- re debet. Nam cum hostis noster Satan omne opus bonum impedire satagat, multis etiā in hoc est, vt nos a precibus auocet, in quibus tutissimum asylum ac præsidium nos habere nouit. Et vt olim Epicureos excitauit, qui Deum omnino nullum esse, aut si quis sit, illum humana non curare dice- bant (quorum sententia religionem omnem vnà cum Dei inuocatione tollebat) ita hodie aliquos est audire, qui sub plausibili diuinæ prouidentiæ & prædestinationis prætextu preces inutiles esse contendunt.
units.tr: As to the first question, no one should regard it as superfluous or as mere curiosity rather than useful. For since our enemy Satan strives to hinder every good work, he is also at great pains in this matter to draw us away from prayer, in which he knows we have the safest refuge and defence. Just as he once stirred up the Epicureans, who said that God did not exist at all, or, if he did, that he did not concern himself with human affairs (a view which abolished all religion together with the invocation of God), so today one may hear some who, under the plausible pretext of divine providence and predestination, contend that prayers are useless.

units.la: Occasio doctrinæ Christi de precibus.
units.tr: The occasion of Christ's teaching about prayer.

units.la: An necesse sit orare. contendunt. Quorum argumenta sunt: Deus omniscius est, & nihil eum potest latere: ergo inanis & irritus labor est, illi nostras curas atq; calamitates exponere, quas iam ante perspectas habet. Item Deum ab aeterno statuit quae rerum omnium initia, qui progressus, quis denique finis & eventus esse debeant, & eius decreta revocari aut impediri impossibile est: ergo preces nostrae irritae & inanes sunt. Nam si ea petimus quae ille fieri decreuit, frustra id facimus, cum ea etiam nobis non postulantibus eventura sint. Sin vero postulamus quae cum eius decretis pugnant, non inutilis modo hic labor est, sed inexcusabilis arrogantia scelus est, tantum nobis tribuere, ut Deum propter nos aeternas decreta mutaturum esse putemus. Est autem hoc singulare diaboli stratagema, qui (ut Paulus ait) sese in angelum lucis transformare potest, & hunc ipsis argumentis preces impedire conatur, quibus nos in primis ad precandum excitari oportebat. Itaq; aduersus Sophisticam hanc firmiter teneamus, preces nobis tam esse necessarias, ut sine ijs neq; Deo seruire, neq; salutem consequi possimus.
units.tr: Whether it is necessary to pray. They contend. Their arguments are these: God is all-knowing, and nothing can be hidden from him; therefore it is an empty and futile labour to lay our cares and calamities before him, which he has already seen. Likewise, God from eternity has decided the beginnings of all things, their progress, and finally their end and outcome, and his decrees cannot be revoked or hindered; therefore our prayers are fruitless and vain. For if we ask for things that he has decreed to happen, we do so in vain, since those things will happen even if we do not ask. But if we ask for things that conflict with his decrees, this is not only a useless labour but also a culpable and inexcusable arrogance, to attribute so much to ourselves as to think that God will change his eternal decrees on our account. Now this is a peculiar stratagem of the devil, who (as Paul says) can transform himself into an angel of light, and he tries by these very arguments to hinder prayer, when we ought especially to be stirred up to pray by them. Therefore let us hold firmly against this sophistry that prayers are so necessary to us that without them we can neither serve God nor obtain salvation.

units.la: Primo enim praeceptum Dei est, ut ipsum invocemus. Qui enim seuere admodum mandat, ut se solum agnoscamus pro Deo & ipsi uni fidamus, idem hoc etiam requirit, ut in periculis quibuscunque ab ipso uno opem flagitemus. Sic enim in Psalmis ait: Sacrifica Deo laudem, & persolue altissimo vota tua. In die afflictionis inuoca me, & cum te liberò, glorificato me. Et Christus nos non solum orare, verumetiam pulsare, & inuicta sanctaq; pertinacia in precibus perseuerare iubet, ut suo loco audiemus. Adhaec promissionibus amplissimus nos excitat, atq; fidem nostram confirmat, ne de Patris caelestis benevolentia dubitemus. Deinde ut precemur, necessitas ipsa cum publica tum priuata monet, vel potius cogit. Quicquid enim boni nobis obtingit, id ab uno Deo datur, qui & summum bonum & omnis boni fons atq; origo est. At ut a nobis rogari vult: sicuti Iacobus docet, & paulo ante annotauimus. Adhaec undiq; nos pericula circumstant, & malis infinitis obnoxij sumus in quibus omnibus Dei auxilio opus est. Accedit hic Satan, qui nunquam non nobis insidias struit, & rugiens leonis instar obambulat quaerens quem deuoret. Excitat hic intra animos nostros saepe tentationes grauissimas, quae cum praesenti salutis periculo coniunctae sunt. Vt ergo in periculis, quae humana ope & consilio euitari aut repelli possunt, ad homines prudentes & potentia instructos confugimus: ita in ijs quae vires humanas superant, ad Deum recurramus necesse est. Et huc pertinent exempla sanctorum hominum utriusq; Testamenti, qui non alia in re quam precibus frequentiores fuerunt. Quid, quod ipse Dei Filius interdum totas noctes in inuocatione Patris sui peregrinauit? Quis vero tam impudens est, qui eum circa rem inutilem occupari voluisse dicere audeat, qui ipsissima est sapientia? Sed & ipse Deus cultores suos per Spiritum suum a precibus protul dubio reuocauisset, si nulla earum esset utilitas.
units.tr: For first, it is God's command that we call upon him. For he who commands most strictly that we acknowledge him alone as God and trust in him alone also requires that we seek help from him alone in whatever dangers. For thus he says in the Psalms: Offer to God praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. And Christ bids us not only to pray but also to knock, and to persevere in prayer with unconquered and holy persistence, as we shall hear in its place. Besides, he stirs us up with the most ample promises, and strengthens our faith, lest we doubt the goodwill of our heavenly Father. Then, necessity itself, both public and private, admonishes us, or rather compels us, to pray. For whatever good comes to us is given by God alone, who is both the supreme good and the fountain and origin of all good. Yet he wishes to be asked by us, as James teaches, and as we noted a little earlier. Moreover, dangers surround us on every side, and we are exposed to infinite evils, in all of which we need God's help. Satan also draws near, who never ceases to lay snares for us, and who, like a roaring lion, walks about seeking whom he may devour. He often stirs up within our souls very grievous temptations, which are joined with present danger to salvation. Therefore, just as in dangers that can be avoided or repelled by human help and counsel we flee to prudent men who are equipped with power, so in those things that exceed human strength we must necessarily have recourse to God. To this belong the examples of holy men of both Testaments, who were more frequent in no other activity than prayer. What of the fact that the Son of God himself sometimes spent whole nights wandering in the invocation of his Father? Who is so shameless as to dare to say that he wished to be occupied with a useless matter, he who is wisdom itself? Moreover, God himself would undoubtedly have withdrawn his worshippers from prayer through his Spirit, if there were no benefit in it.

units.la: Vt vero illu quoque respondeamus, qui diuinae omniscientiae & prouidentiae praetextu contra preces abutuntur, tenendum est, nos nequaquam Deo, tanquam ignoranti, nostras necessitates exponere, neque eo animo precari, ut aeterna sua decreta aboleat aut reuocet: sed curas nostras in Dei sinum deponendo fidem nostram testamur. Inter aeterna vero prouidentiae Dei decreta hoc non potremum esse scimus, quod eorum preces exaudire vult, qui animo contrito & vere resipiscente opem illius inuocant, & cum ipso in gratiam redire cupiunt. Eius enim promissio est: Reuertimini ad me, & ego ad vos reuertar. Et per Ieremiam ait: Momento ut locutus fuero de aliqua gente aut regno, ut euellam, extirpem & perdam, redieritq; ea gens, contra quam locutus eram, a malitia sua iam & me poenitebit mali, quod ei facere cogitaueram. Atqui hoc ipsum de singulis hominibus intelligi debere, apud Ezechielem docet his verbis: Num desidero aut volo mortem peccatoris, dicit Dominus? Annon magis ut conuertat se a viis suis, & viuat? Dei ergo aeternis decretis non poenae solum sceleribus constitutae sunt, verumetiam ijdem ratio continetur, qua illas effugiamus, poenitentia nimirum, a qua diuinae gratiae inuocatio separari nullo modo potest. Exempla quibus hoc probetur, passim occurrunt. Quoties Deus Israelem in deserto perdere statuit? At quoties idem ille Moses precibus placatus, manum iam ad percutiendum extensam retraxit? Quod ipsum temporibus ludicum sapissime factum fuisse scimus. Quo etiam referri debet, quod de Niniuitis ad Ionae praedicationem conuersis, de Ezechia item ex peste laborante legitur. Accedunt his exempla quotidiana, quorum tantus est numerus, ut mirum sit, aliquos inueniri, qui preces tanquam ineffices & inutiles reiicere audeant.
units.tr: To answer also those who abuse the pretext of God's foreknowledge and providence against prayer, we must hold that we by no means set out our needs before God as though he were ignorant, nor do we pray with the intention of abolishing or revoking his eternal decrees. Rather, by laying our cares in God's bosom, we bear witness to our faith. Among the eternal decrees of God's providence we know this is not the least: that he wishes to hear the prayers of those who call upon his help with a contrite heart and a truly repentant mind, and who desire to be reconciled to him. For this is his promise: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you." And through Jeremiah he says: "If at any moment I speak of a nation or kingdom, to uproot, break down and destroy it, and that nation against which I have spoken turns from its evil, I will also repent of the evil which I had intended to do to it." That this very thing must be understood of individual men, he teaches in Ezekiel in these words: "Do I desire or will the death of the sinner, says the Lord? Is it not rather that he turn from his ways and live?" So God's eternal decrees have not only appointed punishments for sins, but also contain the means by which we may escape them, namely repentance, from which the invocation of divine grace can by no means be separated. Examples proving this occur everywhere. How often did God determine to destroy Israel in the wilderness? And how often did that same Moses, appeased by prayer, withdraw his hand already stretched out to strike? We know this was done very often in the time of the judges. To this also belongs what we read of the Ninevites who were converted at Jonah's preaching, and of Hezekiah suffering from the plague. To these are added daily examples, so numerous that it is remarkable that some should be found who dare to reject prayers as ineffective and useless.

units.la: Ezech. 18. Jerem. 18. Ezech. 18. Hîs absolutis, videamus quid sit Oratio, & quibus partibus constet. Oratio est colloquium animi fidelis cum Deo, quo vel nobis ipsis vel aliis bonum quid petimus, aut mala deprecamur, aut item pro acceptis beneficijs gratias agimus. Dicitur autem animi cum Deo colloquium, quia orationum loco minimè habentur nuda verba, quae ore aut labijs proferuntur, nisi ex animo fide prædito & certa spe in Dei auxilium erecto procedant. Partes vero eius sunt, Invocatio, qua aliquid petimus aut deprecamur, & Gratiarum actio. Harum Paulus quoq; meminit ad Philippenses scribens: De nulla re soliciti sitis: sed in omni re per prædicationem & obsecrationem cum gratiarum actione petitiones vestræ innotescant apud Deum. Et ad Colossen. In precibus perdurate, inuigilantes ijs cum gratiarum actione. Quæ verba nos admonent, nos inter precandum gratiarum actionis nunquam oblivisci debere. Nam etsi nondum obtinuerimus ea quæ postulamus, magnum tamen hoc Dei beneficium est, quod nobis cum eo colloqui, & eius opem implorare licet. Ideo Paulus & Silas, cum in carcere Philippensi suas ad Deum preces funderent, simul Deum glorificauisse legimus.
units.tr: Ezech. 18. Jerem. 18. Ezech. 18. Having dealt with these matters, let us see what prayer is and of what parts it consists. Prayer is the conversation of a faithful soul with God, in which we ask for something good, either for ourselves or for others, or plead against evils, or likewise give thanks for benefits received. It is called a conversation of the soul with God because bare words, which are uttered by the mouth or lips, count for nothing as prayers unless they proceed from a soul endowed with faith and raised up with a sure hope in God's help. Its parts are: invocation, by which we ask for or plead against something, and thanksgiving. Paul also mentions these in writing to the Philippians: "Be anxious about nothing, but in everything let your requests be made known to God by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving." And to the Colossians: "Persevere in prayers, watching in them with thanksgiving." These words admonish us that we must never forget thanksgiving while we pray. For even if we have not yet obtained what we ask, it is nonetheless a great benefit from God that we are allowed to converse with him and implore his help. Thus we read that Paul and Silas, when they poured out their prayers to God in the Philippian prison, at the same time glorified God.

units.la: Porro ut rem omnem rectius intelligamus, species quoque Orationis obseruari debent. Est enim alia priuata, alia publica. Priuata dicitur, quam singuli penes se priuatim ad Deum fundunt. De hac Christus Matth. sexto Cap. loquitur: Tu cum precaris, introito in conclave tuum, & clauso ostio tuo precare Patrem tuum, qui est in cælis, &c. Et in hac quidem singulos quotidie assiduos esse conuenit, eò quod nunquam non Dei auxilio & protectione nobis opus est. Hinc illæ sanctorum mos, quos matutino & vespertino tempore, adhæc quoties admensam cibi sumendi causa accesserunt semper precatos fuisse legimus. Quem morem suo exemplo Dei Filius confirmauit. At hic tenendum est, priuatas preces neque loco, neque tempori, neq; ad certum corporis habitum aut situm alligatas esse. Iubet enim Paulus viros quosque in loco manus puras ad Deum attollere. Danidem vero in medijs syluis, in speluncis, noctu item in lecto suo, Ionam in ceti ventre, Danielem inter leones, eius vero socios in fornace accensa, Deum inuocauisse, & ab eo exauditos esse scimus. Vbicunq; ergo locorum, aut quocunq; tempore pij & fideles ad Deum preces fuderint ex vera fide, procul dubio hæ illi gratissimæ & efficaces erunt. Quia enim corpora nostra per Christum in templa Spiritus sancti consecrata sunt, non potest non Deo acceptum esse, quicquid in nostro corpore ex eius mandato & cum fide facimus. Hinc ergo consolationem petant, qui morbi confecti neq; genua flectere, neq; manus in cælum attollere, neq; alijs gestibus decoris inter precandum uti possunt. Quia enim viribus destituuntur, Deus non in gestus aut corporis habitum, sed potius corda eorum respicit, quæ si vere humiliata & contrita fuerint, minimè aspernabitur. Exempla huius generis multa in paralyticis, cæcis & mutis Euangelica historia exhibet.
units.tr: Furthermore, to understand the whole matter more rightly, the kinds of prayer must also be observed. There is one kind of prayer that is private, and another that is public. Private prayer is that which individuals pour out to God in their own homes, alone. Christ speaks of this in Matthew chapter six: "When you pray, enter your room, and with your door shut, pray to your Father who is in heaven," etc. And in this kind of prayer individuals ought to be constant every day, because we never cease to need God's help and protection. Hence the custom of the saints, of whom we read that they always prayed at morning and evening, and also whenever they came to the table to take food. The Son of God confirmed this custom by his own example. Yet here it must be held that private prayers are bound neither to a place, nor to a time, nor to a particular posture or position of the body. For Paul bids men everywhere to lift up pure hands to God. We know that David invoked God in the midst of the woods, in caves, and at night in his bed; Jonah in the belly of the whale; Daniel among the lions; and his companions in the blazing furnace, and that they were heard by him. Therefore, wherever or whenever pious and faithful people pour out prayers from true faith, these will undoubtedly be most pleasing and effective to God. For since our bodies have been consecrated through Christ as temples of the Holy Spirit, whatever we do with our body in faith and by his command cannot but be acceptable to God. Let those take comfort from this who, worn out by sickness, can neither bend their knees, nor lift their hands to heaven, nor use other seemly gestures while praying. For since they are deprived of strength, God does not regard their gestures or bodily posture, but rather their hearts, which, if truly humbled and contrite, he will by no means despise. The Gospel history offers many examples of this kind among paralytics, the blind and the dumb.
