units.la: Publicæ preces sunt, quæ multis credentibus simul in cœtu sacro congregatis fiunt, tam pro tota Ecclesia & Repub. quam priuatim hominibus, qui piorum apud Deum intercessionem expetunt. Fuerunt illæ semper in frequenti usu, & propter has etiam cœtus sacri antiquitus instituti sunt. Et quamuis Ecclesia omni tempore certos dies precibus eiusmodi destinatos habuerit, peculiares tamen cœtus indicere solita fuit, si quando bella, fames, pestis aut aliæ calamitates graviores subito exortæ sunt. Exemplum eius rei apud Ioelem extat, qui iub Ezechia Assyriaci belli tempore prophetauit. Et Christus preces istas singulari promissione commendauit, dicens: Dico vobis, si duo ex vobis consenserint in terra, quodcunq; petierint, fiet eis à Patre meo, qui in cælis est. Vbi enim sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, illic sum in medio eorum. Quapropter pij homines, etsi domi suæ in priuatis precibus frequentes sint, publicas tamen minimè negligunt, quin potius singulari cum voluptate & desiderio ad illas conueniunt. Exemplum huius studij in Dauide habemus, qui cum Saulis tyrannide pulsus incertis sedibus oberraret, de hoc potissimum queritur, quod à sacris cœtibus arceretur. Et Lucas testatur Apostolos sub horam precationis publicæ templi frequentare solitos fuisse. Tertullianus vero vetustissimus scriptor hoc præcipuum veteris Ecclesiæ exercitium fuisse statuit, et inter alia sic scribit: Coimus in cœtum & aggregatione, ut ad Deum quasi manu facta precationibus ambiamus orantes. Hæc vis Deo grata est. Confutantur hi, qui cum Christiani dici & haberi velint, cœtus tamen sacros declinant, & preces publicas contemnunt. Gloriantur quidem illi de priuatis suis precibus, sed nequaquam hoc faciunt, quando Dei ordinem tot promissionibus & exemplis confirmatum negligunt.
units.tr: Public prayers are those which are made by many believers gathered together in a sacred assembly, both for the whole Church and commonwealth, and privately for people who seek the intercession of the godly with God. These have always been in frequent use, and sacred assemblies were established in ancient times for their sake. And although the Church has always had certain days set aside for such prayers, it was nonetheless accustomed to call special assemblies whenever wars, famine, plague or other graver calamities suddenly arose. An example of this is found in Joel, who prophesied in the time of Hezekiah during the Assyrian war. And Christ commended these prayers with a singular promise, saying: "I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them." Therefore pious people, although they are frequent in private prayer in their own homes, by no means neglect public prayer; rather, they gather to it with singular pleasure and desire. We have an example of this zeal in David, who, driven out by the tyranny of Saul and wandering without a settled home, complained especially of this, that he was kept away from the sacred assemblies. And Luke testifies that the apostles were accustomed to frequent the temple at the hour of public prayer. Tertullian, a very ancient writer, held that this was the chief exercise of the early Church, and among other things he writes thus: "We come together into an assembly and gathering, so that, as though with hands made, we may surround God in prayer as we pray. This force is pleasing to God." Those are refuted who, while wishing to be called and considered Christians, nonetheless shun sacred assemblies and despise public prayers. They indeed boast of their private prayers, but by no means do so when they neglect God's order, confirmed by so many promises and examples.

units.la: Quamuis autem precationis effectus neq; loco neq; tempori alligatus sit, publicae tamen preces locum certum & tempus statum seu definitum requirunt, ut ordo seruari queat. Haec ergo templorum origo fuit, quae ab ipso Christo domus precationis, & à veteribus Christianis Oratoria dicta fuerunt. Constat praeterea non Sabbatum solum cultui externo & coetibus sacris destinatum, sed in super quotidie tres horas precationis constitutas fuisse, matutinam scilicet, meridianam & vespertinam, quibus ad templum aut Synagogas conueniebant ij, quibus illud per negotia aut valetudinem licebat, qui vero id non poterant, ij domi precabantur, & ita suas preces cum publicis coniunge bant, ut harum quoq; participes fierent. Exemplum huius moris in Daniele habemus, qui etiam contra Regis edictum tribus ijs horis precari solebat. Et Apostolos eandem seruasse, Actorum liber Cap.3. & decimo nono non obscure testatur. Plinius quoq; secundus, qui Traiano Imperante Asiae Proconsul fuit, ad Imperatorem de Christianorum moribus scribens, illos coetus antelucanos agere testatur (nimirum quod interdiu illis propter persecutiones conuenire non liceret) in quibus precentur, & Deum suum communi voce celebrent. Posteriori vero temporibus haec omnia in superstitione degenerarunt: quando nimirum nouae templorum dedicationes fieri, horae Canonicae obseruari, & gratia Dei atq; precum virtus loco atq; temporibus certis alligari coeperunt. Veruntamen non debet hoc pios abster rere, quo minus verum & legitimum precum publicarum vsum retineant. Tem plus itaq; pie & recte vtantur, ea ab omni prophano vsu impolluta seruent, horas vero publicis precibus destinent, quae populo opportunae & commodae sint, & in his omnem superstitionis occasionem, qua possunt, diligentia, deuitent.
units.tr: Although the effect of prayer is bound neither to place nor to time, public prayers nevertheless require a fixed place and a stated or defined time, so that order can be kept. This was therefore the origin of churches, which were called by Christ himself a house of prayer, and by the early Christians oratories. It is further established that not only the Sabbath was set aside for external worship and sacred assemblies, but also three hours of prayer were appointed each day, namely morning, midday and evening, to which those who could, because of business or health, came to the temple or synagogues; and those who could not, prayed at home, and so joined their prayers with the public ones, so that they too shared in them. We have an example of this custom in Daniel, who even against the king's edict used to pray at those three hours. And the book of Acts, chapters 3 and 19, bears clear witness that the apostles observed the same. Pliny the Younger, who was proconsul of Asia under the emperor Trajan, writing to the emperor about the customs of the Christians, testifies that they held meetings before dawn (evidently because they could not assemble during the day on account of persecutions), in which they prayed and celebrated their God with one voice. But in later times all these things degenerated into superstition, when indeed new dedications of churches began to be made, canonical hours began to be observed, and the grace of God and the power of prayer began to be bound to fixed places and times. Yet this should not deter the godly from retaining the true and lawful use of public prayers. Therefore let them use the temples piously and rightly, keep them free from all profane use, and assign hours for public prayers that are convenient and suitable for the people; and in these matters let them avoid, with all diligence, every occasion of superstition that they can.

units.la: Videretur nunc ordo postulare, ut quis nam inuocari debeat, docebimus: at quia de hoc in sua precationis initio Christus admonebit, nunc porro videbimus, ut precaturi se praeparare, & qualis inter precandum esse debeant; si preces suas Deo acceptas esse velint. Quo loco sex potissimum obseruanda veniunt. Primo procul remoueri & excludi debet propria dignitatis & iustitia, adhaec virium nostrarum fiducia, adeo ut toti coram Deo humiliemur, ut qui nos eius gratia & misericordia opus habere agnoscamus. Nam ut Petrus ait, Deus humilibus gratiam largitur, superbis vero & confidentibus resistit. Atqui nulla superbia arrogantior, nulla arrogantia detestabilior est, quam si tantum sibi ipsi homo tribuat, ut se de Deo, qui summum & aeternum bonum est, aliquid mereri, aut apud eius tribunal se propria iustitia confidere posse sibi persuadeat. Et quia tales contempta Dei misericordia, eius iustitiam contra se prouocant, impossibile est, ut precando quicquam impetrent. Docet hoc ipse Christus in Pharisaei & publicani parabola euidentissime, ut aliis rationibus aut argumentis nequaquam opus sit. Intellexerunt hoc olim quoque sanctissimi quique cultores Dei, qui ideo inter precandum clamare soliti fuerunt: Memor esto miserationum tuarum ô Domine, & bonitatis tuae: quoniam à seculo sunt. Peccatorum adolescentiae meae, ac scelerum meorum ne sis memor: memor autem mei sis secundum benignitatem tuam, propter bonitatem tuam ô Domine. Item: Ne iure vtaris cum seruo tuo, quoniam non iustificabitur coram te vlla caro. Et rursus: Si iniquitates obseruaueris Domine, quis subsistet? Quibus & hoc adde: Miserere mei Domine pro bonitate tua: secundum multitudinem misericordiarum tuarum de le scelera mea. Laua me plurimum ab iniquitate mea, & à peccato meo munda me. Nam transgressiones meas agnosco, & peccatum meum assiduè mihi obuersatur. Et ne quis putet, bas solius Dauidis preces fuisse, cuius atrocia scelera eiusmodi humiliationem merebantur, obseruabis, eos etiam ita precari solitos fuisse, qui nihil atrocis flagitij vnquâ designauerunt. Daniel certè, post multa in populum Dei merita & egregia facta, in precibus suis tam sua quam totius populi atq; omnium ordinum peccata ingenue fatetur. Dicit enim, Nos peccauimus & iniquè egimus, impie egimus & deseruimus deflectendo etiam à praeceptis tuis & iudicijs tuis. Neq; obediuimus serui tui Prophetae, qui tuo nomine locuti sunt ad reges nostros, principes nostros, & patres nostros, & ad totum populū terrae. Tibi quidem iustitia debetur Domine, nobis autem pudor; &c. Et post prolixam peccatorum confessionem tandem subiicit: Adhibe mi Deus aurem tuam, ut audias: & aperi oculos tuos, ut videas nostras solitudines: & vrbis quae tuo nomine vocatur: Non enim in precibus nostris quas effundimus coram te, allegamus nostram iustitiam, sed tuam profusissimam misericordiam. Ecce quanta cum animi contritione se demiserit sanctissimus Propheta, quem ipse Deus vi
units.tr: It might now seem that the order requires me to teach whom we ought to invoke; but since Christ himself will instruct us about this at the beginning of his prayer, we shall consider instead how those who are about to pray ought to prepare themselves, and what they must be like while praying, if they wish their prayers to be acceptable to God. Six points chiefly need to be observed here. First, all confidence in one's own dignity and righteousness, and likewise in one's own strength, must be put far away and banished, so that we humble ourselves completely before God, acknowledging that we have need of his grace and mercy. For, as Peter says, God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud and the self-confident. Yet no pride is more arrogant, and no arrogance more detestable, than for a man to ascribe so much to himself that he persuades himself he can merit anything from God, who is the supreme and eternal good, or can trust in his own righteousness before God's judgment seat. And because such people, despising God's mercy, provoke his justice against themselves, it is impossible for them to obtain anything by praying. Christ himself teaches this most clearly in the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, so there is no need for other reasons or arguments. The most holy worshippers of God have understood this from of old, and so they were accustomed to cry out while praying: "Remember your tender mercies, O Lord, and your goodness, for they have been from of old. Do not remember the sins of my youth and my transgressions; but according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness' sake, O Lord." Likewise: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no flesh shall be justified." And again: "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand?" To these add this: "Have mercy upon me, O Lord, according to your goodness; according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." And lest anyone think that these were only the prayers of David, whose heinous crimes deserved such humiliation, you will observe that others too were accustomed to pray in this way, people who had never committed any atrocious wickedness. Daniel certainly, after many meritorious and outstanding deeds on behalf of the people of God, in his prayers openly confesses his own sins and those of the whole people and of all ranks. For he says: "We have sinned and done wickedly, we have acted impiously and rebelled, even turning aside from your commandments and your judgments. Neither have we obeyed your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, our fathers, and to all the people of the land. To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us shame," and so on. And after a long confession of sins he at last adds: "Incline your ear, my God, that you may hear, and open your eyes, that you may see our desolations and the city which is called by your name. For in our prayers which we pour out before you, we do not plead our own righteousness, but your abundant mercy." See with what contrition of spirit this most holy prophet humbled himself, whom God himself...

units.tr: Matth. 11.

units.la: Praeparatio precantium.
units.tr: The preparation of those who pray.

units.la: 1. Humilitas.
units.tr: 1. Humility.

units.la: Dan 9. rum desideriorum dicere consuevit? Et huc in primis referri debet, quod Christus inter orandum nos omnes dicere iubet, Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c. At quo iure id dicemus, nisi nos Deo debitores esse agnoscamus?
units.tr: Dan. 9. ...of desires, as he used to be called? And chiefly to this must be referred what Christ bids all of us say while praying: "Forgive us our debts," and so on. But by what right shall we say this, unless we acknowledge that we are debtors to God?

units.la: Porro vt innata carni confidentia deprimere, & in Dei conspectu vere humiliari possimus, altius in nos ipsos descendamus oportet, vt non solum opera nostra, verumetiam vires nostras vnacum carnis ingenio diligentium cogitemus. Vbi legis speculo opus est: quod si propius intueamur, mox nos no modo peccatores, sed adeo corruptos esse videbimus, vt ex nobis ipsis no aliud quam peccare possimus. Quia enim Adae Dei imagine, ad quam initio conditus erat peccando corrupit, & peccati seruus factus est, non alios quae peccati seruos in corrupta sua & vitiosa imagine generare potuit. Ideo Dauid dicebat: En in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Atqui ex illo ex legitimo coniugio natum fuisse, cuius thorum Paulus sanctum & impollutum esse dicit. Ergo de vitiosa & peccatrice natura hoc Dauid pronuntiat, in qua vt reliqui omnes Adami posteri nati erat. Quo Deus ipse respiciens, homine nihil nisi carne, & humani cordis figmenta a puerit prava esse pronuntiat. Na etsi no peccemus opere aut facto aliquo, quam primu ex matru vt ro prodimus, vitiosum tamen & peccans ingenium, & (vt Paulus loquitur) lex peccati in membris nostris delitescit, quae cum aetatis progressu iefe exerit, & in opus erumpit, vt primum per vires nostras id fieri potest. Itaq; vt lupi catulus lupus est, quamuis oue adhuc nulla laniarit: sic etiamsi dum infantes sumus, non peccemus opere, natura tamen Adami filii & peccatores sumus, & propter natura nostra vitiositatem irae Dei obnoxij. Quod si quando quid boni facimus, id non ex nobis procedit, sed diuina gratia in nobis agentis opus est. Quare peccatoru quide nos pudere debet, quae proprie ex nobis proueniunt, de bonis autem operibus gloriari neq; possumus neq; debemus, sed potius gratias agere Deo, qui illa per nos perficere dignatus est. Haec qui digne expendunt, ij sola Dei gratia fretti, preces suas humiliter facient, vt neq; vlla suae dignitatis fiducia efferentur. At qui sua natura vitiositatem eiusq; effectus non agnoscunt, ij aut salute suam omnino negligunt, aut in Dei conspectu confidenter veniunt, se & iustitiam suam superbe ostentant, adeoq; Deum sibi ipsis debitorem faciunt: quae causa est, quod nec ipsi neq; preces eorum illi placere possunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that we may subdue the confidence innate in the flesh and truly humble ourselves in the sight of God, we must descend more deeply into ourselves, so that we consider not only our works but also our powers, together with the nature of the flesh, with diligent attention. Here we need the mirror of the law; and if we look more closely, we shall soon see that we are not only sinners but so corrupt that from ourselves we can do nothing but sin. For Adam, who was created in the image of God, corrupted that image by sinning and became a slave of sin, and so he could beget only others who were slaves of sin, in his corrupted and vicious image. Therefore David said: "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me." Yet he was born of a lawful marriage, whose bed Paul calls holy and undefiled. Therefore David is pronouncing this about our vicious and sinful nature, in which, like all the other posterity of Adam, he was born. Looking upon this, God himself declares that man, who is nothing but flesh, has a heart whose thoughts are evil from his youth. For although we do not sin by some deed or action when we first come forth from our mother's womb, nevertheless we have a vicious and sinning disposition, and (as Paul puts it) "the law of sin" lies hidden in our members, which, as age advances, shows itself and breaks out into action as soon as our powers allow. Thus, just as a wolf's cub is a wolf even though it has not yet torn any sheep, so even while we are infants, although we do not sin in deed, we are nevertheless sons of Adam by nature and sinners, and because of the vice of our nature we are liable to the wrath of God. And if at any time we do something good, it does not proceed from ourselves, but is the work of divine grace working in us. Wherefore we ought to be ashamed of the sins that properly arise from us, but we can and ought not to glory in good works, but rather to give thanks to God, who has deigned to accomplish them through us. Those who weigh these things rightly, relying on the grace of God alone, will make their prayers humbly, so that they are not puffed up by any confidence in their own worth. But those who do not recognize their vicious nature and its effects either wholly neglect their salvation, or come before God confidently, proudly displaying themselves and their own righteousness; and so they make God a debtor to themselves. This is why neither they nor their prayers can please him.

units.la: Secundo curandum est, ne (quod apud Isaiam Dominus reprehendit) ore & labijs solu Deo appropinquemus, sed vt ex ipso corde oratio procedat. Quia enim Deus ipsissima veritas est, hypocrisin omne odit, & in spiritu atq; veritate adorari vult. At quae hypocrisis est impudentior, quam si quis se precari simulat, & verbis quidem atq; gestu precantis vtitur, cum interim animum suum circa vanissimas cogitationes & foedas carnis cupiditates vagari patiatur? Aut num Deus hanc precationis loco habebit, a qua melior nostri pars, animus nimirum, procul est alienus? Displicet ti bi proximus tuus, si eum in animo suo aliter erga te affectu esse scias, quam illius verba sonent: Num ergo te probaret Deus, si ore quidem illum invoces, animum vero totum auaritiae, superbiae, invidiae, odio, libidini aliisq; nephariis cogitationibus immersum habeas? Hic ergo omnium grauissimum periculu sese offert, quod precaturus solet accidere, cum infinita sint, quae animi deuotione impediunt. Nam vt innatas nobis cupiditates omnino exuamus, fieri non potest quoad in hac carne viuimus. At illae cogitationes varias pariunt, quae mentem turbare & a precibus auocare solent. Accedit hu Satan, qui & ipse multa suggerit, quibus animi deuotio & pia meditationes diffurbantur. Quo fit, vt rarissime animum nostrum a cogitationibus alienis liberum tantisper possimus seruare, vsque quo Orationem Dominicam absoluamus: & frequenter accidit, vt finita precatione, quidnam precati simus, ipsi ignoremus.
units.tr: Second, we must take care not to draw near to God only with mouth and lips, as the Lord rebukes in Isaiah, but that prayer should proceed from the heart itself. For since God is truth itself, he hates all hypocrisy and wishes to be worshipped in spirit and in truth. But what hypocrisy is more shameless than when someone pretends to pray, uses the words and gestures of one who prays, while meanwhile allowing his mind to wander among the most empty thoughts and foul desires of the flesh? Or will God count as prayer that in which the better part of us, namely the mind, is far away? Your neighbour displeases you if you know that his feeling towards you in his heart is other than his words sound; would God then approve of you, if you invoke him with your mouth while your heart is wholly immersed in greed, pride, envy, hatred, lust and other wicked thoughts? Here, then, the gravest of all dangers presents itself, which commonly befalls one who is about to pray, since there are countless things that hinder the devotion of the mind. For it is impossible, as long as we live in this flesh, to strip ourselves entirely of the desires innate in us. And those desires give birth to various thoughts, which are wont to disturb the mind and draw it away from prayer. Satan is added to these, who also himself suggests many things by which devotion of mind and pious meditations are disturbed. The result is that we can very rarely keep our mind free from alien thoughts for as long as it takes to finish the Lord's Prayer; and it often happens that, once the prayer is over, we ourselves do not know what we have prayed for.

units.la: Magna igitur hic cura & diligentia opus est, vt huic vitio medeamur. Ante omnia autem pro derit, si Dei maiestate probe consideremus, coram qua preces nostras effundimus, simulq; togitemus, quanti referat, vt preces nostrae exaudiantur. Qui causam grauem coram Senatu aut iudicum consessu actuari sunt, ij quid dicant diligenter expendunt, neque interea vanis cogitationibus se distrahi patiuntur. Quanto autem magis hoc in suprema illius maiestatis conspectu obseruari debet, vbi non corpora solum & fortunae nostrae, verumetiam animarum salus periclitatur? Quod si praeterea cogitemus, nos aeterno exitio dignos esse, & abs; Dei misericordia atq; fauore ne momento quidem posse consistere, tunc non difficile fuerit cogitationes prauas cohibere, ne animi deuotionem impediant. Deinde necessarium est, vt carni nostræ omnia ea subducamus, quibus male cupiditates confirmantur: qualia sunt cibus potusq; immodicus, vestium luxus & concessæ etiam voluptates. Vbi singuli sibi ipsis optimè consulere poterunt, si diligentius obseruent, quæ nam illa sint, quibus carnis ipsorum libido atq; petulantia maximè accenditur. Et hoc verum illud ieiunium est, de quo scripturæ loquuntur, & cuius disciplina olim sanctissimi quiq; in carne sua coercenda vsi sunt. Id vero non in superstitioso ciborum discrimine aut delectu consistebat, sed in omnium eorum abstinen tia, quæ animos precantium alió solent avocare. Ideo feré precibus coniungitur, vt hæ illo adiutæ feruentiores fiant. Et huc facit, quod Ioel ad publicas preces populum exhortans, sponsum de thala- mo suo exire iubet: & quòd Paulus coniugibus aliquando secubandi potestatem facit, vt ardentius precentur. Sed & cilicijs olim vtebantur, & cineres aut terram capiti inspergebant, vt carnis petu lantia hoc modo domita precandi feruorem minus impediret. Cauenda tamen in hac superstitione, ne meritum in ijs statuamus, quæ non nisi propter preces debent fieri.
units.tr: There is therefore great care and diligence needed here, if we are to remedy this fault. Above all, it will help if we consider carefully the majesty of God, before whom we pour out our prayers, and at the same time think how much it matters that our prayers be heard. Those who argue a serious case before the Senate or a court of judges weigh carefully what they say, and do not allow themselves to be distracted by idle thoughts meanwhile. How much more ought this to be observed in the sight of that supreme majesty, where not only our bodies and fortunes but the salvation of our souls is at stake? If we further consider that we deserve eternal destruction, and cannot stand even for a moment before the mercy and favour of God, then it will not be hard to restrain wicked thoughts, lest they hinder the devotion of our minds. Next, it is necessary that we withdraw from our flesh all those things by which our desires are wrongly strengthened: such as excessive food and drink, luxury in clothing, and even permitted pleasures. Each person will be able to look to his own good if he observes more carefully which things most inflame the lust and wantonness of his own flesh. This is the true fasting of which the Scriptures speak, and by whose discipline the most holy men of old used to restrain their flesh. It did not consist in a superstitious distinction or choice of foods, but in abstaining from all those things which are wont to draw the minds of those who pray away from prayer. Hence fasting is commonly joined with prayer, so that prayers may be more fervent when aided by it. To this purpose also is what Joel does when, exhorting the people to public prayer, he bids the bridegroom come out of his bedchamber; and what Paul does when at times he gives spouses permission to live apart, so that they may pray more ardently. The ancients also wore sackcloth and sprinkled ashes or dust on their heads, so that the wantonness of the flesh, tamed in this way, might hinder the fervour of prayer less. Yet in this practice we must beware lest we ascribe merit to those things which ought to be done only for the sake of prayer.

units.la: Tertiò necesse est, vt certa & indubitata fide vel fiducia erga Deum precemur, sine qua nihil impetrabimus. Nam precatio non potest vere dici, quæ non cum fide coniuncta fuerit. Notum est enim illud Pauli: Quomodo inuocabunt eum, in quem non crediderunt? Qui homini alicui quan- tumuis eximio nō fidunt, ij ab eodem neq; auxilium neq; consilium expectunt. Adhæc ingrata & in- efficaces sunt omnes petitiones nostræ apud eos, qui nos nihil boni de ipsis sperare sciunt. Ita enim na tura comparatum est, vt eos spem bonam de nobis habere velimus, qui opem nostram flagitant. At- qui hoc ipsum à nobis Deum exigere Scriptura passim testatur, quæ insuper docet, cuiu nullum il- li gratum esse, nisi cum vera fide coniunctus est. Huc primus fœderis cum Abrahamo initi articulus pertinet, quo Deus pollicetur, quòd in ipso omnia habituri simus, quæ ad præsentem hanc & futu- ram vitam nobis necessaria sunt. Idem primum Decalogi præceptum docet, quo prohibemur, ne no bis Deos alienos faciamus, id est, ne spem & fiduciam nostram in alio, quàm in vno vero Deo col- locemus. Itaq; preces & fides abse inuicem diuelli non possunt. Qui enim vni Deo fidunt, ij bunc vnum etiam inuocant. Si qui verò absq; fide ad Deum clamant, horum clamor non precatio est ve- ra, sed aut inanis quæda garrulitas, quæ ex hypocrisi procedit, aut belluinus vlulatus, quæ doloris impatientia extorquet, & proinde Deo placere nō potest. Recte igitur Diuus Iacobus scripsit: Qui precatur, vt postulet cum fide, nihil disceptans: nam qui disceptat, similis est fluctui maris, qui ventis agitatur & iactatur: neq; existimet homo ille, se quicquā acceptuum à Domino. Atqui fides donū Dei est, qui hanc per spiritum suum cordibus nostris inserit, & spe certa confirmat. Opus ergo fue rit, vt assiduè cum Apostolis clamemus: Domine adauge nobis fidem. Item, Succurre incredulitati nostræ. Nec enim fides nostra vnquam tam firma & constans erit, quin caro aliquas dubitationes excitet, aduersus quas nos luctari oportebit
units.tr: Thirdly, it is necessary that we pray with a certain and undoubting faith or trust in God, without which we shall obtain nothing. For that cannot truly be called prayer which is not joined with faith. That saying of Paul is well known: "How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?" Those who do not trust a man, however eminent, do not expect help or counsel from him. Moreover, all our petitions are unwelcome and ineffective with those who know that we hope nothing good from them. For it is so ordered by nature that we wish those who ask our help to have good hope of us. Yet Scripture everywhere testifies that God requires this very thing from us, and teaches moreover that no one is pleasing to him unless he is joined to him by true faith. To this pertains the first article of the covenant made with Abraham, in which God promises that in him we shall have all things necessary for this present and future life. The first precept of the Decalogue teaches the same, forbidding us to make other gods for ourselves, that is, to place our hope and trust in anyone other than the one true God. Thus prayer and faith cannot be torn apart from each other. For those who trust in the one God also call upon him alone. But if some cry out to God without faith, their cry is not true prayer, but either an empty chatter that proceeds from hypocrisy, or a beastly howl that impatience of pain wrings out, and therefore it cannot please God. Rightly then the divine James wrote: "Let him who prays ask in faith, doubting nothing; for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Let that man not think he will receive anything from the Lord." Now faith is the gift of God, who implants it in our hearts through his Spirit and confirms it with sure hope. It will therefore be necessary for us to cry constantly with the Apostles: "Lord, increase our faith." Likewise: "Help our unbelief." For our faith will never be so firm and constant that the flesh will not raise some doubts, against which we shall have to struggle.

units.la: Sunt tamen nonnulla, quorum consideratione fidem nostram vehementer confirmare possumus. Inter quæ præcipuum est vera Dei cognitio & diligens eorum, quæ illi propria sunt consideratio, in qua nihil occurret, quod fidem & spem nostram non plurimùm augeat. Primò enim natura bo- nus, beneficus & liberalis est, adeò vt etiam non requisitus bona sua in omnes creaturas distribuat. Nam vt Dauid in Psalmis canit, pecori quoq; pabulum producit, feras in desertis alit, & ijsdem in summis montibus fontes aperit, coruorum pullis prospicit, aues cœli pascit, & flores in agris temere nascentes mirificè vestit & exornat. Num ergo hominem necessaria abs se petente negligeret, qui brutis & inanimatis nihil petentibus tam benignè prospicit? Atqui humani generis amantissimus esse constat. Hominem enim initiò ex mera gratia condidit, vt esset quem bonorum suorum partici- pem faceret. Propter illum alia omnia creauit, & ea illius subiecit imperio. Neq; aliquod temporis momentum elabitur, quo non sentiamus sui erga nos fauoris specimen aliquod. Superat tamen om- nia hæc, quòd cùm miseris nobis & propter peccatum æterna morte dignis Filio eius redemptore opus esset, hunc quoq; pro nobis in mortem tradidit. Quid ergo ab eo maius aut excellentius petere possumus, quod nos impetraturos esse dubitemus? Paulus certè ex eo nos ita argumentari docet: Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum, qui non etiam cum eo omnia nobis gratificetur? Facit etiam ad fidei nostræ confirmationem æterna & constantissima Dei ve- ritas, quæ non patitur vt promissa fallat. At infinitæ promissiones extant, quibus ad se claman-
units.tr: There are, however, some things by whose consideration we can greatly strengthen our faith. Among these the chief is the true knowledge of God and the diligent consideration of those things which are proper to him, in which nothing will occur that does not greatly increase our faith and hope. First, he is by nature good, beneficent and generous, so that even unasked he distributes his goods to all creatures. For, as David sings in the Psalms, he brings forth pasture for the flock, feeds the wild beasts in the deserts, opens springs for them on the highest mountains, provides for the young ravens, feeds the birds of the heavens, and wonderfully clothes and adorns the flowers that spring up at random in the fields. Would he then neglect a man who asks him for what he needs, when he so kindly provides for beasts and lifeless things that ask nothing? And he is known to be most loving of the human race. For he created man at the beginning out of pure grace, so that there might be someone to whom he could share his goods. For man's sake he created all other things and subjected them to his rule. Nor does any moment of time slip by in which we do not feel some token of his favour toward us. Yet all these things are surpassed by this: that when we were wretched and deserving of eternal death on account of sin, and needed his Son as our redeemer, he delivered him up to death for us too. What greater or more excellent thing, then, can we ask of him, whose granting we might doubt? Paul certainly teaches us to reason from this: "He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?" The eternal and most constant truth of God also contributes to the confirmation of our faith, for it does not allow his promises to deceive. And there are countless promises in which he pledges to hear those who cry out to him

units.la: Y tes exauditurum se esse pollicetur. In Psalmo ait: In die afflictionis tuae invoca me, & liberabo te. Item: Praesto adest Dominus omnibus invocantibus eum, omnibus (inquam) invocantibus eum cum veritate. Facit autem quicquid volunt, qui timent eum, & clamorem eorum exaudit, ac servat eos. Apud Isaiam vero ait: Futurum est, ut prius quam invocent, ego respondeam, & adhuc illis loquentibus ego exaudiam. Quae promissiones in Novo Testamento per Iesum Christum confirmantur, qui nos non modo precari iubet, verumetiam ut precari debeamus docet. Petite (inquit) & dabitur vobis. Postulate, & accipietis: quaerite, & invenietis: pulsate, & aperietur vobis. Adhaec seipsum nobis quasi fideiussorem fidit, dicens: Amen amen dico vobis, quaecunque petieritis a Patre in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Hactenus non petistis quicquam in nomine meo: petite, & accipietis, &c. Ut vero promissiones istae plus fidei apud nos habeant, eorum exempla simul coniungere oportet, qui in precibus suis exauditi res humanas viribus impossibiles confecerunt. Clamant in Aegypto ad Dominum filii Israel, & ille mox audito eorum clamore, Mosem illis vindicem destinat. Precatur ad mare rubrum Moses intra cor suum, & Deus illum clamare dicit, & per medias aquas tutum transitum toti populo praebet. Idem ille precibus suis Amalekitas deuicit. Elias precando caelum clausit, ut per triennium neque ros neque pluvia caderet, & rursus illud precibus aperuit. Ezechias ad Deum clamando vitae suae annos prorogat. In Novo Testamento huius generis exemplaria plurima habentur, praecipue in Actorum libro, qui Apostolos non semel piorum orationibus e carceribus liberatos esse commemorat. Neque hic mihi obiicias: Scio quidem iflos a Deo exauditos olim fuisse, at mihi ideo persuadere non possum, quod me quoque exauditurus sit. Nam si in temetipsum descendas, & animo repetas, quae tibi iam inde a pueritia acciderunt, in finita divinae bonitatis argumenta invenies. Annon enim Deus is est, qui (ut David ait) te ex matris utero eripuit, & in hunc usque diem servavit? Annon fateri cogeris, te illum sapius invocasse, & ab eo fuisse exauditum? Quin ergo ex ante actis colligis, quod in posterum quoque te exaudire & servare velit? Haec omnia si diligentius paulo expendamus, & huic considerationi frequens coniungamus verbi Dei studium, fidem in nobis plurimum augeri atque confirmari sentiemus, quae deinde nostras preces apud Deum acceptas & efficaces reddet.
units.tr: ...crying out to him. In a Psalm he says: "In the day of your affliction call upon me, and I will deliver you." Likewise: "The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all (I say) who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, and will hear their cry and save them." But in Isaiah he says: "It shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear." These promises are confirmed in the New Testament through Jesus Christ, who not only bids us pray but teaches us that we ought to pray. "Ask," he says, "and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you." Moreover, he pledges himself to us as our surety, saying: "Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name: ask, and you will receive, etc." But so that these promises may carry more weight with us, we must join with them the examples of those who, heard in their prayers, accomplished things beyond human strength. The children of Israel cried out to the Lord in Egypt, and he, immediately hearing their cry, appointed Moses as their deliverer. Moses prayed at the Red Sea within his heart, and God told him to cry out, and gave the whole people safe passage through the midst of the waters. The same Moses by his prayers overcame the Amalekites. Elijah by praying shut up heaven, so that for three years neither dew nor rain fell, and by prayer he opened it again. Hezekiah by crying out to God prolonged the years of his life. In the New Testament many examples of this kind are found, especially in the book of Acts, which records that the Apostles were more than once freed from prison by the prayers of the godly. Nor should you object to me here: "I know indeed that those men were heard by God in former times, but I cannot therefore persuade myself that he will hear me too." For if you go down into yourself and recall what has happened to you since boyhood, you will find innumerable proofs of divine goodness. For is not God he who (as David says) snatched you from your mother's womb and has preserved you to this day? Are you not compelled to confess that you have often called upon him and been heard by him? Why then do you not gather from things past that he wishes to hear and save you in the future too? If we weigh all these things a little more carefully, and join to this consideration frequent study of the word of God, we shall feel our faith greatly increased and strengthened in us, which will then make our prayers acceptable and effective before God.

units.la: Quarto vita & mores nostri precibus respondeant oportet. Quia enim Deus in nobis glorificari vult, nunquam eorum preces ratas habebit, qui nomen eius suis sceleribus polluunt atque profanant. Non possunt eorum filiorum clamorem magni facere pij patres, quos sibi dedecori esse sentiunt. Cur ergo nos clamantes audiat Deus, si ore quidem filios eius nos esse profiteamur, reipsa autem nos nominis eius hostes declaremus? Talibus per Prophetam respondet Deus: Filius honorat patrem suum, & servus dominum suum: Si ergo ego pater sum, ubi honor est meus? Si vero dominus sum vester, ubi mei timor? Et memorabilis est Salomonis sententia: Qui aurem suam avertit, quo minus Legem audiat, eius precatio quoque abominanda est. Itaque etsi nos ab omni peccato abstinere impossibile sit, cauendum tamen est impium & devotum peccandi studium, quo hodie multi preces suas Deo abominabiles reddunt, dum ad illum non nisi extrema necessitate pressi confugiunt, interim vero nihil eorum praestant, quae ille a nobis exigit. Quorum preces sacrificio Caini simi les sunt, qui & ipse cultor Dei videri volebat, cum animum haberet invidia & odio aestuantem, atque a timore Dei alienissimum. Et servit illi, quod in Psalmo 50. impio dicit Dominus: Quid tibi vis, quod commemoras caeremonias meas? cur ore tuo foedus meum taceas? Cum odio habeas disciplinam, & verba mea post te abicias. Ut vero in omni vita Deo obedire oportet, ita studendum est, ut omnia nostra dicta & facta cum verbis precum nostrarum conueniant. Uno ore Deum patrem nostrum dicimus: Meminerimus ergo nos omnes fratres atque sorores esse, & proinde nemo alios prae se contemnat, multo minus autem odio prosequatur. Imploramus Dei gratiam atque misericordiam: ergo nos quoque in proximos benefici & misericordes esse debemus. Petimus ut Dei nomen sanctificetur: abstineamus ergo ab omnibus, quae illud prophanant. Precamur ut regnum Dei adveniat, & in nobis instauretur: praeparemus ergo nos, ut in nobis Deus regnare possit. Oramus, ut Dei voluntas in terris perinde ut in caelis fiat: itaque huic nos subiicere, nec quicquam ex nostra carnis arbitrio aduersus illam instituere debemus. Hoc ipsum in omnibus aliis petitionibus observatur, siquidem nos exaudiri volumus. Docent ista quid de illorum precibus iudicari debeat, qui non solum in suis sceleribus pergunt, verumetiam ea inter precandum quasi ostentant in Dei conspectu, & in illius laudem atq; gloriam quaerunt. Faciunt hoc, qui vestium luxum in templum inferunt, & quibus non satis est, quod iam ante peccarunt libidine & petulantia, nisi in coetus quoque sacros eum ornatum inferant, quo quam plurimos offendunt. Taceo nunc eos, qui qua scortando, moechando, vsurarijs item artibus, aut etiam militiam mercenariam sectando pararunt, magno cum fastu coram Deo & Ecclesia eius ostentant. Quibus eos etiam recte adnumerauerit, qui insignia & arma sua in templis suspendunt, & iam defunctti imagines suas armatas in sepulchris conspici volunt. Et quis obsecro istorum preces Deo gratas fore putet? Nam vt de seipso exemplum sumas, quis tibi animus foret, si quis abs te aliquid petiturus cum monili aut torque ab vxore aut filia tua, in libidinus praemium accepto, aut cum filij tui abs se occisi vestte adhuc sanguinolenta compareret? Id vero tibi prorsus intolerabile foret. At quam multos est videre, qui cum se preces facturos simulent, foeda libidinum praemia, & filijs Dei detracta spolia in eius conspectum afferunt? Atqui hi revera peccatores illi sunt, quos a Deo exaudiri Scriptura negat. Et contra eosdem Dominus per Isaiam clamat: Cum expanderitis manus vestras, abscondam oculos meos a vobis: & si multiplicaveritis precationem, non exaudiam: quia manus vestrae plenae sunt sanguinibus. Et alibi Propheta suis mandat, ne ipsi pro talibus intercedant, eo quod impunitos dimittere non possit. In horum igitur meditatione diligentes nos esse conveniat, ne vitae impuritate & morum licentia preces nostras non inutiles modo, verumetiam abominabiles & Deo exosas reddamus.
units.tr: Fourthly, our life and conduct must correspond to our prayers. Since God wishes to be glorified in us, he will never regard the prayers of those who pollute and profane his name by their wickedness. Godly fathers cannot esteem the cry of children whom they feel to be a disgrace to them. Why then should God hear us when we cry out, if with our mouths we profess to be his sons but in fact by our deeds declare ourselves enemies of his name? God answers such people through the Prophet: "A son honours his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am your master, where is my fear?" (Mal. 1.6). And Solomon's saying is memorable: "He who turns away his ear from hearing the Law, his prayer too is an abomination" (Prov. 28.9). So although it is impossible for us to abstain from all sin, we must nevertheless beware of the impious and deliberate eagerness to sin, by which many today make their prayers abominable to God. They flee to him only when pressed by extreme necessity, and meanwhile do none of the things he requires of them. Their prayers are like the sacrifice of Cain, who also wished to seem a worshipper of God, though his mind was burning with envy and hatred and was utterly alien to the fear of God. The Lord's words to the wicked in Psalm 50 fit them: "What do you mean by reciting my statutes, or by taking my covenant on your lips? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you" (Ps. 50.16-17). But just as we must obey God in the whole of life, so we must take care that all our words and deeds agree with the words of our prayers. With one mouth we say "Our Father". Let us remember, then, that we are all brothers and sisters, and therefore no one should despise others in his own esteem, much less pursue them with hatred. We implore God's grace and mercy, so we too ought to be beneficent and merciful to our neighbours. We pray that God's name be hallowed, so let us abstain from everything that profanes it. We ask that God's kingdom come and be restored in us, so let us prepare ourselves so that God may reign in us. We pray that God's will be done on earth as in heaven, so we ought to submit ourselves to it and undertake nothing against it by the judgement of our flesh. The same principle is observed in all the other petitions, since we wish to be heard. These things teach what should be judged about the prayers of those who not only persist in their sins but even display them, as it were, in God's sight while they pray, and seek their own praise and glory through them. Those do this who bring the luxury of their clothing into the temple, and who are not content to have already sinned through lust and wantonness, unless they also carry that finery into the sacred assemblies, where they offend very many. I say nothing now of those who, having acquired wealth by prostitution, adultery, usury, or even by pursuing mercenary soldiering, display it with great pride before God and his Church. Among them are rightly counted those who hang their insignia and arms in churches, and who, when dead, want their armed images to be seen on their tombs. And who, I ask, of these would think their prayers pleasing to God? To take an example from yourself: how would you feel if someone who wanted something from you came with a necklace or bracelet given by your wife or daughter as the reward of lust, or with the clothing of your son, whom he had killed, still bloody? That would be utterly intolerable to you. Yet how many are there to be seen who, while pretending to pray, bring before his eyes the foul rewards of lust and the spoils stripped from the children of God? Yet these are truly the sinners whom Scripture says God does not hear. Against the same people the Lord cries through Isaiah: "When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; and though you multiply prayers, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood" (Isa. 1.15). Elsewhere the Prophet orders his people not to intercede for such people, because God cannot let the unpunished go. Therefore we ought to be diligent in meditating on these things, lest by the impurity of our lives and the licence of our conduct we make our prayers not only useless but abominable and hateful to God.

units.la: Quinto, nihil peti debet, quod Deo indignum aut voluntati eius contrarium sit. Quis enim vir bonus ferat, suam operam ad res turpes & inhonestas a quoquam expeti? Atqui eadem est Dei ratio, & proinde eius naturam atq; ingenium probe observari a nobis necesse est. Humani generis amantissimum esse supra diximus: nihil igitur ab eo petendum, quod alijs hominibus fraudi vel damno esse possit. Beneficus, mitis & misericors est Deus: nihil ergo postulari ab illo debet ex invidia & odio, vel vindictae cupiditate. Purus, sanctus & ex omni parte impollutus est: ergo non rogandus erit, vt nobis ad res turpes & flagitiosas opem suam conferat. Iustus, adeoq; iustitia ipsa est: nihil ergo ab eo iniustum vel iniquum postuletur. Verax & ipsa veritas est: minime ergo orandus erit, vt nostris mendacijs, dolis atq; fraudibus faveat. Idem creator est omnium, cui omnis gloria & honor debetur: nihil igitur postulandum quod ipsius maiestati & gloriae deroget. Deniq; diligenter videndum est, quod Dei ingenium & quae eius voluntas sit, vt nostras postulationes per fidei obedientiam illi subijcere possimus, & ne illi temere praescribamus quid aut quomodo nobis cum agere debeat. Quam primum enim maiorem nostrorum desideriorum quam divinae voluntatis rationem habemus, nos Deus exaudire nequit. Cur enim faceret, quod & gloriae ipsius & nostrae salutis fraudi esset? Ideo Ioannes Apostolus scribit: Haec est fiducia, quam habemus apud eum, quod si quid petierimus secundum voluntatem eius, audit nos. Ergo Dei voluntas nostrarum precationum forma & regula esse debet. Et Iacobus de huius seculi filijs scribens, eos exaudiri negat, quia precum suarum finem habeant prava carnis suae desideria. Petitis (inquit) & non accipitis, eo quod male petatis, vt in voluptatibus vestris insumatis. Eiusmodi sunt preces eorum, qui vt carnis cupiditatibus indulgeant, nihil praeter opes, honores, integram valetudinem, formosam coniugem, pacem huius seculi, & alia huius generis postulant, nulla interea vel gloriae Dei vel propriae salutis ratione habita. Non mirum ergo fuerit tales non exaudiri, sed plerunq; votis suis contraria accipere. Sed plura de hoc in tertia petitione Orationis Dominicae dicentur.
units.tr: Fifthly, nothing should be asked that is unworthy of God or contrary to his will. For what good man would endure having his labour sought for base and dishonourable ends? Yet God's reasoning is the same, and therefore we must carefully observe his nature and character. We have said above that he is most loving toward the human race, so nothing should be asked of him that could harm or cost other men. He is beneficent, gentle and merciful, so nothing should be asked of him out of envy, hatred or a desire for revenge. He is pure, holy and in every respect undefiled, so he is not to be asked to help us in base and shameful deeds. He is just, indeed justice itself, so nothing unjust or iniquitous should be requested of him. He is true, indeed truth itself, so he is in no way to be asked to favour our lies, deceits and frauds. He is the creator of all, to whom all glory and honour is due, so nothing is to be asked that would detract from his majesty and glory. Finally, we must consider diligently what God's nature is and what his will is, so that we may submit our requests to him in obedient faith, and not rashly prescribe to him what he ought to do for us or how. For as soon as we give more regard to our desires than to the divine will, God cannot hear us. Why would he do what would be harmful both to his glory and to our salvation? So the Apostle John writes: "This is the confidence we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us" (1 John 5.14). God's will, then, must be the form and rule of our prayers. And James, writing of the sons of this age, denies that they are heard, because the aim of their prayers is the wicked desires of their flesh: "You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures" (Jas 4.3). Such are the prayers of those who, to indulge the desires of the flesh, ask for nothing but riches, honours, sound health, a beautiful wife, peace in this age, and other things of this kind, with no regard at all either to the glory of God or to their own salvation. It is no wonder that such people are not heard, but rather receive what is contrary to their wishes. More on this will be said under the third petition of the Lord's Prayer.

units.la: Restat quod in hac tractatione sextum & postremum est, vt nimirum in precando constantes & perseverantes simus. Saepius enim accidit, vt quamvis cum humilitate & fide a Domino ea petamus, quae ipsius voluntati conueniunt, opem tamen aut promissum beneficium differat, non quod promissionum suarum sit immemor: sed quod aut fidem nostram probare, aut desideria nostra pia & sancta magis accendere, & dona sua nobis iucundiora & pretiosiora velit reddere. Ibi videndum est, ne superbos & confidentes homines imitemur, qui nisi illico eorum postulationi satis facias, indignationem animi concipiunt, & iniquè secum agi arbitrantur. Quin potius in mentem nobis veniat, Deum omnium nostrum amantem, adhaec summe sapientem & iustum esse, ideoq; nos exaudi-
units.tr: The sixth and last point in this treatment remains: that we be steadfast and persevering in prayer. For it often happens that although we ask the Lord with humility and faith for things that agree with his will, he nevertheless delays his help or the promised benefit. This is not because he has forgotten his promises, but because he wishes either to test our faith, or to kindle our pious and holy desires more strongly, and to make his gifts more welcome and precious to us. Here we must take care not to imitate proud and self-confident people, who, unless their demands are satisfied at once, conceive indignation in their minds and think they are being treated unjustly. Rather, let it come to mind that God loves us all, and is moreover supremely wise and just, and therefore that he will hear us

units.la: {a} Contra sceleratos ostentatores. turum esse opportuno tempore, interea vero fidem nostram assidua invocatione testemur, sicut in Euangelio Christus docet, quando nos non solum petere, sed postulare quoq; adhuc quaerere & pulsare iubet. In primis autem huc pertinet elegans illa viduae & iniqui iudicis parabola, quae apud Lucam habetur. Hac enim isto argumento nos Christus ut docet: Cum ab homine iniquo, impio & inhumano indefinenti interpellatione aliquid impetrari possit, multo potius hoc apud Deum fiet, qui natura beneficus & ad iuuandum propensus est. Nam etsi interdum opem differt, non tamen nos (ut Paulus ait) supra quam ferre possimus tentari finit. Interea nostrum est illum expectare cum fide & silentio, neque tantum nobis ipsis tribuere, ut eius iudicia accusare, vel illi praescribere audeamus. Quin potius Cananaeam illam mulierculam imitemur, quae etsi suas preces initio negligi, deinde discipulos intercessores suos reiici, tandem se quoque non sine totius gentis suae contumelia repelli, & canibus conferri audiret, pia tamen & sancta precandi pertinacia impetrauit quod volebat, & laudem immortalem ipso Christo teste meruit, qui fidem eius magnifice praedicat
units.tr: {a} Against wicked boasters. ...that he will grant it at the opportune time. Meanwhile we bear witness to our faith by constant invocation, as Christ teaches in the Gospel, when he bids us not only to ask but also to demand, to keep seeking and to keep knocking. Chiefly to this purpose belongs that elegant parable of the widow and the unjust judge, which is found in Luke. For by this argument Christ teaches us as follows: if something can be obtained from a wicked, impious and inhuman man by unending entreaty, much more surely will it be done with God, who is by nature beneficent and inclined to help. For although he sometimes delays his aid, he nonetheless does not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear, as Paul says. In the meantime it is our part to wait for him with faith and silence, and not to presume so much on ourselves as to dare to accuse his judgments or to prescribe terms to him. Rather, let us imitate that little Canaanite woman, who, although at first her prayers were ignored, then her disciples, her intercessors, were turned away, and finally she heard herself also repelled, not without insult to her whole nation, and likened to dogs, yet by her pious and holy persistence in praying she obtained what she wanted, and earned immortal praise from Christ himself as witness, who magnificently proclaims her faith.

units.la: Haec omnia si diligentius considerentur, mox patebit, cur hodie multorum preces Deus non exaudiat. Nam qui prae aliis zelo pietatis ardere videntur, ij propria iustitia freti in ipsius Dei conspectu superbiunt. Alij plerunq; absq; animi devotione & fide precantur, quasi sufficiat inani multiloquio Dei aures obtudisse. Nihil vero vulgarius est, quam quod pleriq; vitam viuunt, quae precibus quam minime respondet. Adhaec ea petunt, quae & gloriae Dei & propriae ipsorum saluti officiunt. Quod si vero ipsorum votis non statim annuat Deus, mox fremere & aduersus eum murmurare incipiunt, quasi vero pro ipsorum nutu ille omnia administrare debeat. Haec igitur vitia emendent singuli, & quae hucusq; commemorauimus obseruent: ut nimirum humilientur in conspectu Dei, animus totus illi consecratus, & ex fide vera orent, vitam & mores precibus suis conformes faciant, diuinae voluntati se totos permittant, atq; in precando constanter perseuerent. Ita fiet, ut illos Deus absq; dubio exaudiat propter Filium suum Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: If all these things are considered more carefully, it will soon become clear why God does not hear the prayers of many today. For those who seem to burn with zeal for piety above others, trusting in their own righteousness, become proud in the very sight of God. Others pray, for the most part, without devotion of mind and without faith, as though it were enough to have worn out God's ears with empty wordiness. Nothing, however, is more common than that most people live lives that least of all correspond to their prayers. Moreover, they ask for things that stand in the way both of the glory of God and of their own salvation. But if God does not at once assent to their wishes, they immediately begin to rage and murmur against him, as though he ought to govern all things at their nod. Let each one therefore correct these faults and observe what we have hitherto recalled: namely, that they humble themselves in the sight of God, that their whole mind be consecrated to him, and that they pray from true faith, that they make their life and conduct conform to their prayers, that they commit themselves wholly to the divine will, and that they persevere constantly in prayer. In this way it will come about that God will undoubtedly hear them, for the sake of his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CVI.

units.la: Dixit autem eis Iesus: Cum precamini, dicite: Pater noster, qui es in coelis.
units.tr: And Jesus said to them: When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven.

units.la: Quoniam homo per lapsum peccati a prima sua dignitate excidit, & quoad animi atq; corporis vires totus corruptus est, nihil in nobis ipsis boni habemus, nisi quod supernè (ut Iacobus ait) nobis a Patre aeterno datur. Vult autem is, ut bona eius abs se precibus pijs postulemus. Quam obrem necessarium est, ut certo sciamus quomodo preces a nobis institui ac fieri debeant. Diximus de eo nuper in proximo Sermone. Proximum nunc est, ut certam quoq; precandi formulam tenea-mus, ne nostra carnis placitum secuti ex nobisipsis aliquid fingamus, quod tam preces nostras, quam nosipsos Deo minus acceptos reddat. De hoc in praesenti ita differemus, ut primo doceamus, quidin formula precationum vitari debeat. Deinde verum eius formula vsum indicabimus, quam nobis Dei Filius tradidit. Postremo eiusdem Exordium interpretabimur.
units.tr: Because man, through the fall into sin, has fallen from his original dignity, and is wholly corrupted in the strength of both soul and body, we have nothing good in ourselves, except what is given to us from above by the eternal Father, as James says. He wishes us to ask for his good things from him with devout prayers. It is therefore necessary that we know for certain how our prayers ought to be framed and offered. We spoke of this recently in the previous sermon. The next task is that we also hold to a fixed form of prayer, lest, following the pleasure of our flesh, we invent something of our own which would make both our prayers and ourselves less acceptable to God. On this matter we shall proceed as follows: first we shall teach what must be avoided in the form of prayer; then we shall point out the true use of the form which the Son of God has handed down to us; last, we shall expound its opening words.

units.la: Quoad primum, abunde nos Christus ipse instituit, Matthaei sexto Cap. sic dicens: Precantes ne fitis loquaces ut ethnici: putant enim fore, ut in sua illa loquacitate exaudiantur. Ne igitur ipsis assimilemini. Nouit enim Pater vester quibus sit vobis opus, antequam vos petatis ab eo. Quibus verbis docemur, quoad formulam precandi, in primis loquacem & inanem verborum splendorem esse vitandam. Et ne hoc preceptum leue putemus, duobus argumentis illud Christus confirmat. Alterum ab ethnicorum exemplo sumit, qui cum Deos suos ex seipsis aestiment, eos perinde ut homines verbis multis persuaderi & moveri putant. At communis sensus admonet, Christianos homines ab omnibus ethnicorum atque infidelium ritibus aut ceremoniis abstinere debere. Alterum ab ingenio & natura Dei deducit, dicens: Nouit enim Pater vester, quibus sit vobis opus, antequam petatis ab eo. Quo argumento ethnicum illum errorem validissime confutat, ut qui diuinae naturae natura palàm aduersetur. Irritus & superuacuus labor est, si perito & exercitato medico, qui mor-bi tui vim melius quàm tuipse intelligit, eam multis exponere instituas. Atqui eadem est ratio Dei. Quia enim nos creauit, & insuper omnes creaturas suæ prouidentiæ freno gubernat, nihil illum la-tère potest. Nouit ergo omnes labores nostros, & (vt Dauid ait) fugas nostras omnes numerat, la-chrymas suorũ adse colligit, quin capitis nostri pilos in numerato habet. Quid ergo apud illum pro-lixa eorum quæ patimur, commemoratione est opus? Neq; tamen hic mihi obijcias: Ergo ab omni precatione abstinebo, cùm Deo iam ante nota sint omnia. Etsi enim illi nequaquam necesse sit, vt tuas calamitates ei exponas, tibi tamen vt id facias vtile & necesse est, vt hac ratione in fide tua confirmeris, & consolationem aliquam accipias. Et obseruabis hoc loco, Deum preces propter nos instituisse, non quòd ipse illis opus habeat. Itaq; si quando sanċti suas miserias & pericula inter pre-candum multis exponunt (cuius rei exempla in Psalmis est videre) non ethnico errore id faciunt, neq; in hac verborum prolixitate spem aliquam collocant: sed ita Dei promissiones in mentem re-uocant, vt fides eorum magis accendatur. Qua ratione nos quoq; illos imitari poterimus.
units.tr: As to the first point, Christ himself has sufficiently instructed us in Matthew chapter six, where he says: "When you pray, do not be babblers like the heathen, for they think they will be heard for their much speaking. So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him." By these words we are taught that, as to the form of prayer, wordy and empty display of language is above all to be avoided. And lest we think this precept a light one, Christ confirms it with two arguments. The first he takes from the example of the heathen, who, judging their gods by themselves, think that they are persuaded and moved by many words, just as men are. But common sense warns that Christians ought to abstain from all the rites and ceremonies of the heathen and unbelievers. The second he draws from the nature and character of God, saying: "For your Father knows what you need before you ask him." By this argument he most powerfully refutes that heathen error, since it openly contradicts the nature of the divine nature. It is a vain and superfluous labour to set out the nature of your illness at length to a skilled and experienced physician, who understands the force of your disease better than you yourself do. Yet the reasoning about God is the same. For since he created us, and moreover governs all creatures with the rein of his providence, nothing can escape him. He therefore knows all our labours, and (as David says) counts all our wanderings, gathers our tears into his bottle, and indeed has the hairs of our head numbered. What need is there, then, for a lengthy recital before him of what we suffer? Yet do not object to me here: "Then I will abstain from all prayer, since everything is already known to God." For although it is by no means necessary for you to lay out your calamities before him, it is nonetheless useful and necessary for you to do so, so that you may be strengthened in your faith by this means and receive some consolation. And here you will observe that God instituted prayers on our account, not because he himself has any need of them. Therefore, if at any time the saints, while praying, set out their miseries and dangers at length (examples of which are to be seen in the Psalms), they do not do so from heathen error, nor do they place any hope in this prolixity of words; rather they recall God's promises to mind in such a way that their faith is kindled the more. In this way we too may be able to imitate them.

units.la: Confutantur hoc loco errores duo grauissimi, qui inter Christianos longo tempore nimium fue-runt vulgares. Primus eorum est, qui preces suas globulis traiectio fune connexis (quos Rosaria vocant) Deo adnumerant, quasi cauere velint, ne nimium precentur, aut numerum precum mi-nuant. Hinc factum, vt multi mira lingua volubilitate illas absque omni meditatione diligentiori profuderint. At quid aliud hoc est, quàm error ille, quem Christus in præsenti confutat? Quid, quòd superstitio est manifesta, preces & earum effectum certo numero alligare? Accedit diuini no-minis abusus, quod toties frustra & absque fide repetitur. Taceo, quòd maior precum pars Diuis destinatur, quod cum idololatria coniunctum est. Alter eorum est error, qui lingua peregrina & ipsis ignota precantur. Quàm paucos enim reperies inter monachorum armenta siue greges, qui Psalmos lingua vernacula interpretari possint, quos tamen quotidie demurmurant? Quid ergo de monialibus dicemus, quas idem facere cogunt? Fiunt hæc contra Pauli doctrinam, qui diserte præcipit, vt in cœtibus sacris prophetia, psalmodia & preces lingua vulgari & omnibus nota peragantur, & ne quis imperita multitudinis aures lingua peregrina ostentatione fatiget. Quàm-uis vero hic error omnibus manifestus & inexcusabilis sit, non tamen eius emendatio hucusque à Pontificibus & episcopis potuit impetrari: quod vnum satis ostendit, quàm alieni sint ab omni Christiana Reformationis consilio. Quòd si autem simul obserues, quàm impudenter sub pre-cum & Psalmodiarum eiusmodi prætextu domos viduarum & orphanorum devorent, hæreditates intercipiant, & rerum imperitos suis facultatibus emungant, mox videbis hic ethnicum si-mul & Iudaicum errorem concurrere. Quid mirum ergo, orbem Christianum hodie tam grauiter à Deo puniri, quando ira eius precibus huiusmodi provocatur, quæ nobis ad illam placandam seruire debebant?
units.tr: Here are refuted two most serious errors, which among Christians for a long time have been far too common. The first is of those who count their prayers before God by means of little beads strung together on a thread (which they call rosaries), as though they wished to take care not to pray too much, or to reduce the number of their prayers. Hence it happens that many have poured them out with a marvellous fluency of tongue, without any careful meditation. But what else is this than the very error which Christ refutes here? What of the fact that it is plainly superstition to tie prayers and their effect to a fixed number? Add to this the abuse of the divine name, which is so often repeated in vain and without faith. I say nothing of the fact that the greater part of these prayers is directed to the saints, which is joined with idolatry. The second error is of those who pray in a foreign tongue, one unknown to themselves. For how few will you find among the herds or flocks of monks who could translate the Psalms into the vernacular, yet these they mumble over every day? What then shall we say of the nuns, whom the same practice is forced upon? These things are done against the teaching of Paul, who plainly commands that in sacred assemblies prophecy, psalmody and prayers be carried out in the common tongue, known to all, and that no one weary the untrained ears of the multitude with a show of foreign speech. Although this error is manifest to all and inexcusable, yet its correction has not until now been obtained from the Papists and bishops; this alone shows clearly how far they are from every Christian counsel of Reformation. But if you also observe how shamelessly, under the pretext of such prayers and psalmodies, they devour the houses of widows and orphans, seize inheritances, and drain the wealth of the inexperienced, you will soon see here a heathen and a Jewish error meeting together. What wonder, then, that the Christian world today is so grievously punished by God, when his anger is provoked by prayers of this kind, which ought to have served us in appeasing it?

units.la: Debet præterea hic considerari eximia & paterna Dei bonitas, qui vt ad benefaciendum & iuuandum sponte propensus est: ita à precaturis neque copiam verborum neque artificiosum dicen-di ornatum requirit. Ita vero nostræ infirmitati consulit. Nouit enim non omnibus datum esse, vt artificiose dicant quod sentiunt. Nouit item nos interdum ita turbari curis & miserijs, vt quod animo concepimus effari non possimus. Scit denique verborum prolixitate animi devotionem im-pediri, nosq; dum de verborum ornatu soliciti sumus, rem ipsam de qua agitur negligere. Istis er-go vitijs omnibus remedium adhibet, dum ne inter precandum loquaces simus præcipit. Hinc est, quòd Sanċtissimi Dei cultores in maximis periculis ferè precationculis breuissimis vsi sunt: cuius rei exempla in Iacobo Patriarcha, Mose, Elia, imò in ipso Dei Filio Iesu Christo habemus. Is enim cum aliquando totas nôètes in oratione perdurasset, postea cum mortis hora inslaret, quo propius ea accessit, eò preces breuiores ad Patrem quasi eiaculatas est. Istud nos consoletur, si quan-do morborum cruciatibus & aliis periculis siue tentationibus ita vrgemur, vt nesciamus vnde pre-candi initium sumere, aut quibus verbis preces instituere debeamus. Deus enim non verba, sed cor contritum respicit, & gemitus quoq; nostros exaudit. Quid quòd ipsa pericula & calamitates, qui-bus premimur, pro nobis loquuntur, etiamsi nobis ne verbum quidem proferre liceat? Vt enim pa-
units.tr: Moreover, here we must consider the remarkable and fatherly goodness of God, who is inclined of his own accord to do good and to help; he requires neither abundance of words nor an artful ornament of speech from those who pray. He thus provides for our weakness. For he knows that it is not given to all to express what they feel with skill. He knows too that we are sometimes so disturbed by cares and miseries that we cannot utter what we have conceived in our mind. Lastly, he knows that devotion of the mind is hindered by length of words, and that while we are anxious about the ornament of our words we neglect the very matter in hand. Therefore he applies a remedy for all these faults, when he commands that we not be babblers in praying. Hence it is that the most holy worshippers of God, in the greatest dangers, have used very brief prayers; examples of this are in the patriarch Jacob, in Moses, in Elijah, and indeed in the Son of God, Jesus Christ himself. For when he had once spent whole nights in prayer, afterwards, as the hour of death drew on, the nearer he came to it, the shorter were the prayers he poured out to the Father, as it were in darts. Let this comfort us, if at any time we are so pressed by the torments of disease or other dangers or temptations that we do not know where to begin praying or with what words we ought to frame our prayers. For God regards not words but a contrite heart, and he hears our groans too. Indeed, do not the very dangers and calamities which press upon us speak for us, even though we are not permitted to utter a single word? For as a father who sees his beloved little son in peril in water or in fire is moved by natural affection to bring him help, though the child cannot call out his name, so God, whose love surpasses that of parents, is moved by our dangers, sighs and groans, even when only bare or very few words are added.

units.la: ϒ 3 ter, qui filiolum dilectum in aquis aut incendio periclitari videt, naturali affectu mouetur, vt illi opem ferat, quamuis puellus eius nomen inclamare non possit: ita Deus, cuius amor parentum superat, nostris periculis, suspirijs & gemitibus mouetur, licet verba vel nuda vel paucissima accedant.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Christ warns us what we ought to beware of in the form of prayer, so to the disciples who asked this he prescribed a fixed pattern and form, although from whom we are to follow. Here again the immense goodness of God shines forth. For since he not only commands them to pray, but also teaches them the manner in which this ought to be done, and indeed places in our mouth the very words with which we are to speak with him, he attests by a most certain and infallible argument that he wishes to hear us and to bestow on us whatever is useful and necessary for us.

units.la: Porrò vt nos Christus admonet, quid in formula precandi cauere debeat: ita postulantibus hoc discipulis modum & formam certam praescripsit, quamuis à quo sequamur. Vbi rursus immensa Dei bonitas elucet. Quia enim eos non solum iubet precari, verumetiam qua ratione id fieri debeat docet, adeoque verba ipsa ori nostro inserit, quibus cum ipso collocuturi vtamur, certissimo & infallibili argumento testatur, quòd nos exaudire & quacunque nobis vtilia atque necessaria sunt conferre velit.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Christ warns us what we ought to beware of in the form of prayer, so to the disciples who asked this he prescribed a fixed pattern and form, although from whom we are to follow. Here again the immense goodness of God shines forth. For since he not only commands them to pray, but also teaches them the manner in which this ought to be done, and indeed places in our mouth the very words with which we are to speak with him, he attests by a most certain and infallible argument that he wishes to hear us and to bestow on us whatever is useful and necessary for us.

units.la: Quoad verò formulam Dominicae Orationis, minimè putandum est, Christum concepta quaedam verba tradere voluisse, quibus vt quadam infit, quae Deum largiri cogat quae petimus: quemadmodum Iudaeorum Rabbini de suo Schem Hamphoras, & Magi siue venefici de suis Exorcismis fabulantur, per quos vel ore pronuntiatos vel ex collo suspensos mirifica quaedam confici sibi persuadent. Nihil (inquam) huius nos hic sentire decet. Constat enim olim in veteri Testamento multorum preces Deo acceptas fuisse, qui tamen verbis longe aliis precati sunt. Et Apostolos non semper haec ipsa verba recitauisse, & tamen exauditos fuisse scimus. Itaque quemadmodum Christus in proximo Capite Legem totam & Prophetas in breue compendium redegit, & duobus verbis complexus est: ita breui hac formula comprehendere voluit omnes sanctorum preces, quas iam inde ab origine rerum ex spiritus sancti suggestione ad Deum fuderunt. Quapropter verus & proprius Orationis Dominicae vsus in duobus consistit.
units.tr: As for the form of the Lord's Prayer, we must not think that Christ meant to hand down certain set words which, as if by some charm, would compel God to grant what we ask. That is how the Jewish rabbis fable about their Schem Hamphoras, and how magicians and sorcerers talk about their exorcisms, by which they persuade themselves that marvellous things are accomplished when these words are spoken aloud or hung from the neck. Nothing of this kind (I say) should we think here. For it is certain that in the Old Testament the prayers of many were accepted by God, though they prayed in quite different words. And we know that the apostles did not always recite these very words, and yet were heard. So just as Christ in the preceding chapter reduced the whole Law and the Prophets to a brief summary and embraced them in two words, so in this short formula he wished to comprehend all the prayers of the saints, which from the beginning of things they poured out to God at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the true and proper use of the Lord's Prayer consists in two things.

units.la: Primò docet nos Dei Filius, quibus nobis in hac vita opus sit, & quid à Patre suo caelesti petere debeamus. Est hoc scitu valde necessarium: quia plerunque in eo erramus, quòd (vt filijs Zebedaei Christus dicebat) quid oremus nescimus. Et vt illi in regno eius terreno, quod animo concepepant, primatum sibi supra alios discipulos dari petebant: ita nos fere diuitias huius seculi, honores, bonam corporis valetudinem, pacem mundi huius, otium, voluptates, victoriam de hostibus, & alia huius generis postulamus, quae carni arridٍent & iucunda sunt. Qua si darentur, non minus nobis noxia essent, quàm gladius puerulo aut furioso traditus. Illis enim fere pro carnis libidine abutimur, & proinde tam corpora quàm animas nostras perdimus. Quapropter Dominus caecas carnis cupiditates ijs petitionibus, quas in sua precandi formula proponit, circumscribere & quasi coercere voluit, vt ex illis discamus quae nobis ad salutem sint necessaria. Itaque in omni tentatione in hanc formulam respicere, & num vota nostra huic respondeant videre debemus. Certò enim conflat noxium & pernitiosum esse omne id, quod in ea non continetur. Et hic Orationis istius primus atque præcipuus vsus est.
units.tr: First, the Son of God teaches us what we need in this life and what we ought to ask of our heavenly Father. This is very necessary to know, because we most often err in this, that (as Christ said to the sons of Zebedee) we do not know what we ask. Just as they asked for primacy over the other disciples in his earthly kingdom, which they had imagined, so we commonly ask for riches, honours, good health of body, the peace of this world, leisure, pleasures, victory over enemies, and other things of this kind, which please the flesh and are pleasant. If these were given, they would be no less harmful to us than a sword handed to a small child or a madman. For we mostly misuse them for the lust of the flesh, and so lose both our bodies and our souls. Therefore the Lord wished to limit, and as it were restrain, the blind desires of the flesh by the petitions which he sets forth in his form of prayer, so that from them we may learn what is necessary for our salvation. Thus in every temptation we ought to look back to this form and see whether our wishes correspond to it. For it is certain that everything not contained in it is harmful and pernicious. This is the first and chief use of that prayer.

units.la: Alter in eo consistit, vt sciamus quomodo in quauis tentatione aut periculo preces concipere & facere debeamus. Nec enim semper opus est, vt totum Orationis Dominicae contextum recitemus, sed licet Christiano homini ex singulis petitionibus peculiarem precationem formare, prout praesens necessitas requirit. Hoc ipsum Christus fecit, quando ad montem oliuarum eam modò huius Orationis partem excerpsit, qua illi tunc in primis opus erat, cùm diceret: Non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat. Quod vt rectius intelligatur, exemplis rem omnem declarabimus. Videt quis mundi huius statum corruptissimum, immanem apud omnes ordines Verbi contemptum, horribilem denique nominis diuini prophanationem: Is prima petitione vtatur, & dicat: Ab Pater noster, qui es in caelis, Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Affere quaeso gloriam tuam, neque nomen tuum tam turpiter proscindi & prophanari sinas. Ita Christus hac petitione vsus est.
units.tr: The other use lies in this, that we may know how to frame our prayers and offer them in any temptation or danger.
