For it is not always necessary to recite the whole content of the Lord's Prayer; a Christian may form from its individual petitions a particular prayer, as present need requires. Christ himself did this when at the Mount of Olives he picked out only that part of this prayer which was then especially needed by him, when he said: Not mine, but your will be done. To understand this more rightly, we will illustrate the whole matter with examples. Let someone see the very corrupt state of this world, the monstrous contempt of the Word among all orders, and finally the horrible profanation of the divine name. Let him use the first petition and say: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be your name. Grant, I pray, your glory, and do not allow your name to be so shamefully torn apart and profaned. Thus Christ used this petition.

units.la: Cùm enim mortis suae tristi recordatione turbatus dixisset, Pater, libera me ex hora ista: mox subijcit, Atqui propterea veni in horam hanc: Pater, glorifica nomen tuum. Quasi diceret: Cùm ideo in mundum venerim, vt diro mortis supplicio peccata hominum expiem, age vt id faciam patratus sum: da modo ô Pater, vt hoc omne ad tui nominis gloriam faciat, &c. Rursus sentit aliquis diaboli suggestiones & tentationes graviores sibi incumbere, quam sustinere possit, is secunda petitione pugnet, clamans: Adveniat ô Pater, regnum tuum. Vel, O Pater quousque ad diaboli & mundi me tentantis improbitatem connives? quousque pugnam hanc sustinebo, & ei succumbam? Veni quaeso Domine, adiuva me, & tuum regnum in me instaura. Seruit haec ipsa petitio ijs quoque, qui impiorum successibus & piorum aduersis offenduntur, in quem finem illa Prophetae olim usi sunt. Similiter si quis se in morbis aliisque calamitatibus impatientiorem fieri sentit, is ad tertiam petitionem recurrens cum Christo dicat: Pater, si possibile est, transfer a me calicem istum: veruntamen tua voluntas fiat. Da modo, ut quemadmodum in caelo omnes Angeli & beatorum spiritus tibi obediunt: ita ego quoque tuae voluntati me sponte subijciam, &c. Praeterea si quid corpori vel animae defieri sentimus, ita quarta petitione remedium paratum erit, si dicamus: O Pater, etsi hactenus inobedientes & contumaces fuerimus, tui tamen filij sumus. Da ergo panem quotidianum, & nostrae necessitati succurrito, &c. Quod si intra animum tuum peccatorum pondere premeris, & diabolus propriae conscientiae terroribus ad desperationem te solicitat, tunc quinta petitio locum habet, & dicas: Peccavi equidem ô Pater, & debita mea maiora sunt, quam ut sim soluendo: Sed remitte ô Pater, &c. Et ut semel finiamus locum hunc, cum iam pugna tentationum instat, ultima petitione utamur: Ne inducas nos ô Pater in tentationem, aut si ita tibi placet, saltem vires nobis suffice, ut ferendo simus, & nos ex manibus mali illius, imo omnium malorum authoris libera. Est ergo huius precationis usus maximus & salubérrimus in omni afflictionum genere, & singulae petitiones nouae atque peculiares precationis argumentum siue materiam nobis praebent. Interim non prohibemus quo minus tota Oratio quotidie saepius recitetur: imo ut id fiat necesse est, cum nunquam non ijs opus habeamus, quae in hac postulantur: sed docemus solum, ut singulis petitionibus uti & eas praesenti necessitati accommodare debeamus, si quando ita angimur, ut totam ex ordine recitare non possimus.
units.tr: For when, troubled by the sad thought of his death, he had said, Father, save me from this hour, he soon adds, But for this reason I came to this hour: Father, glorify your name. As if he were saying: Since I have come into the world in order to expiate the sins of men by a dreadful death of punishment, see that I have carried it out; only grant, O Father, that all this may be done to the glory of your name, etc. Again, if someone feels that the suggestions and temptations of the devil are heavier upon him than he can bear, let him fight with the second petition, crying out: Let your kingdom come, O Father. Or: O Father, how long will you look on while I am tempted by the wickedness of the devil and of the world? How long shall I bear this struggle and give way to it? Come, I pray, Lord, help me, and set up your kingdom in me. This same petition serves also those who are offended by the success of the wicked and the adversity of the godly, to which end the Prophets used it of old. Similarly, if anyone feels himself more impatient in sickness and other calamities, let him, returning to the third petition, say with Christ: Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; nevertheless your will be done. Grant only that, as in heaven all the angels and the spirits of the blessed obey you, so I too may submit myself willingly to your will, etc. Moreover, if we feel that something is lacking to body or soul, a remedy is ready in the fourth petition, if we say: O Father, although hitherto we have been disobedient and stubborn, yet we are your children. Give us therefore our daily bread, and come to our necessity, etc. But if you are pressed within your mind by the weight of your sins, and the devil, by the terrors of your own conscience, urges you towards despair, then the fifth petition has its place, and you should say: I have indeed sinned, O Father, and my debts are greater than I can pay; but forgive, O Father, etc. And to finish this passage once and for all: when the struggle with temptations is at hand, let us use the last petition: Lead us not, O Father, into temptation; or, if it so pleases you, at least give us strength to bear it, and free us from the hands of that evil one, indeed of the author of all evils. The use of this prayer is therefore greatest and most wholesome in every kind of affliction, and each single petition provides us with new and particular matter for prayer. Meanwhile we do not forbid the whole prayer to be recited more often each day; indeed it is necessary that this be done, since we never cease to need the things asked for in it. We teach only that we should use the individual petitions and adapt them to the present need, if at any time we are so distressed that we cannot recite the whole in order.

units.la: Hís præmissis ad Exordium accedamus, quod est eiusmodi: PATER NOSTER QVI ES IN COLIS. Hís verbis nos preces exordiri docet Dominus, ut ab initio statim admoneamur, quem invocare, & quam de illo spem atque fiduciam animo concipere debeamus. In eo enim pietatis vera cardo versatur, ut unum & solum verum Deum invocemus, & ideo admonet Christus, ne preces nostras ad alium dirigamus, quam eum, cui haec verba conveniunt, ut nostrum omnium Pater esse, & in caelis regnare dici possit. At cui haec conveniant nemo est, praeter unum Deum, qui solus omnium nostrum Pater & Creator est, & qui idem caelis & omnibus quae subijs sunt imperat. Docent hoc passim Scripturae sacrae, & apud Ieremiam hoc nomine potissimum Iudaeos accusat Deus, quod relicto ipso fonte aquae viuae, cisternas pertusas sibi foderint.
units.tr: With these things premised, let us come to the opening, which is as follows: OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN. With these words the Lord teaches us to begin our prayers, so that from the very start we are reminded whom we ought to invoke, and what hope and confidence we ought to conceive in our minds concerning him. For the true hinge of piety turns on this, that we invoke the one and only true God; and therefore Christ warns us not to direct our prayers to anyone other than him to whom these words belong, so that he may be said to be the Father of us all and to reign in heaven. But no one is this except the one God, who alone is the Father and Creator of us all, and who likewise rules the heavens and all that is under them. The Holy Scriptures teach this everywhere, and in Jeremiah God accuses the Jews chiefly under this name, that, having forsaken the fountain of living water, they have dug for themselves broken cisterns.

units.la: Et si cum exordio singulas quoque petitiones conferamus, nemo praeter unum Deum inuenietur, cui illae conuenire possint. Cui enim ex creaturis omnibus salua pietate dicere possumus: Sanctificetur nomen tuum, Adveniat regnum tuum, Fiat voluntas tua in terra, quemadmodum in caelo, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c.? Etenim omnes pij fatentur, solius Dei nomen apud omnes glorificari debere, huic item soli regnum deberi, quodque omnia secundum illius voluntatem geri debeant, denique quod ipse solus is sit, qui tam corpora quam animas nostras pascit, & peccata remittendi potestatem habeat. Adde hu quod solus Deus eas habet dotes, quibus eum oportet instructum esse, qui invocari vult. Hunc omniscium esse oportet, qui nostras curas & labores melius norit quam ipsi verbis exponere possimus: idem ut omnia vidéat & audiat necesse est, ut vbique praesens, adhaec omnipotens & ad nos feruandum promptus sit. Si cui aliquid horum deest, in cum certa spe & fiducia inuocari non potest. At qui solus Deus corda & renes scrutatur, solus omnia videt & audit, solus omnipraesens & omnipotens, & simul nostri amantissimus atque salutis nostrae cupidissimus est. Solus ergo invocari meretur. Deinde invocatio fidei opus est, adeoque fidei nostrae confessio. Vt ergo uni Deo fidere, ita ipsum vnum & solum invocare debemus. Praeterea invocatio cultus di-
units.tr: And if we compare with the opening each of the individual petitions also, no one will be found besides the one God to whom they can apply. For to which of all creatures can we say, with piety intact: Hallowed be your name; Let your kingdom come; Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven; Give us this day our daily bread; Forgive us our debts, etc.? For all the godly confess that the name of God alone ought to be glorified by all, that the kingdom is owed to him alone, and that all things ought to be done according to his will; finally, that he alone is the one who feeds both our bodies and our souls, and has the power of forgiving sins. Add to this that God alone has those endowments with which he must be furnished who wishes to be invoked. He must be all-knowing, who knows our cares and labours better than we can express them in words; he must see and hear everything; he must be present everywhere, and moreover be almighty and ready to save us. If any of these is lacking, he cannot be invoked with certain hope and confidence. But God alone searches hearts and reins; God alone sees and hears all; God alone is everywhere present and almighty, and at the same time most loving towards us and most eager for our salvation. He alone therefore deserves to be invoked. Next, invocation is an act of faith, and so a confession of our faith. Therefore, just as we trust in the one God, so we ought to invoke him alone. Moreover, invocation is a part of divine worship

units.la: Vnus & solus Deus inuocari debet.
units.tr: Only the one and only God ought to be called upon.

units.la: Iere. 2. mini pars, imò gratissimus Deo cultus est, quem is omnibus ceremonijs externis præfert. Vnde rursus sequitur, preces in vnum illum dirigi debere. Et huc facit, quod olim thymiama, quod supra aureum altare quotidie adolebatur, Deus ita sibi soli vendicabat, vt mortis jupplicium et constitue-ret, qui illo ad alios vsus abuteretur. Atqui illud preces adumbrabat, quæ soli Deo in nomine le-su Christi offerri debent, qui per aureum altare figurabatur. Et ita typum hunc veteres intellexis-se, ex Danidis verbis apparet, dicentis: Sit precatio mea proincenso apud te, et lenatio manuum mearum pro vespertino sacrificio. Psal.141. Possent huius generis argumenta plura adduci vnà cū infinitis tam veteris quam noui Testamenti testimonijs: sed ea consultò prætermittimus breuita-tis causa, quando vnicum hoc Orationis Dominicæ exordium sufficit ad confutandum omnes eos, qui vel Deos alienos, vel Angelos, vel Diuos cœlites inuocant.
units.tr: Jer. 2. Prayer is a part of worship, indeed the most pleasing worship to God, which he prefers to all external ceremonies. From this it follows again that prayers ought to be directed to that one God alone. This also bears on the point that the incense which was burned every day upon the golden altar was reserved by God for himself alone, so that whoever misused it for other purposes was to be punished with death. Now that incense foreshadowed the prayers which must be offered to God alone, in the name of Jesus Christ, who was prefigured by the golden altar. That the ancients understood this type in this way is clear from the words of David, who says: "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice." Psalm 141. Many arguments of this kind could be brought forward, together with countless testimonies from both the Old and the New Testament. But we deliberately pass them over for the sake of brevity, since this one opening of the Lord's Prayer is enough to refute all those who invoke foreign gods, or angels, or the heavenly saints.

units.la: Redeamus ergo ad verba huius proœmij, quæ præterea docent, nos certam de Deo spem atque fiduciam animo concipere debere, quod nos seruare velit simul et possit, cum et Pater noster sit, et tam cœlis quam ijs quæ sub his continentur imperet. Sed præstat singula verba seorsim considerare, vt quæ alia quoq; sub his latent mysteria intelligamus.
units.tr: Let us return, then, to the words of this preface, which further teach us that we ought to conceive in our minds a sure hope and trust in God, that he both wishes and is able to keep us, since he is both our Father and rules over the heavens and over all that is contained under them. But it is better to consider each word separately, so that we may also understand the other mysteries hidden under them.

units.la: Primò Deum iubemur Patrem appellare, quod non sine certa ratione fit, cum multa alia nomi-na illi scripturæ tribuant, quæ hominum iudicio augustiora et magnifica magis videri possunt. Nā index vniuersæ terræ, Rex regum, ignis consumens, Dominus exercituum, Boni omnis fons, adeoq; Bonum summum dicitur. At nullius horum nunc mentionem facit Dominus, vt quæ nobis terro-rem possent parere. Nam si Regem diceremus, non posset non nobis formidabilis esse eius potentia et maiestas, cum nos defectores et rebelles esse non possimus negare. Si iudicem, propria conscien-tia damnationis sententiam nobis occineret: Si boni fontem aut Bonum summum, mox audiremus nullum cum illo commercium aut communionem esse posse nobis, qui natura mali et corrupti sumus. Ideo Patris nomine illum inuocare iubet Christus, quo nullum inter homines iucundius, dulcius atq; amabilius est. Nam etsi simul in mentem veniat nos filios esse inobedientes, Patris tamen nomen nos eius bonitatis et indulgentiæ admonet, qua parentes filios immorigeros prosequuntur, si illos mi-serijs domitos ad se recurrere et ipsorum misericordiam implorare videant.
units.tr: First, we are commanded to call God Father, and this is done for a sound reason, since Scripture gives him many other names which may seem more august and magnificent in human judgment. For he is called the judge of the whole earth, the King of kings, a consuming fire, the Lord of hosts, the fountain of all good, and so the highest good. Yet the Lord makes mention of none of these now, since they could cause us terror. For if we called him King, his power and majesty could not but be frightening to us, since we cannot deny that we are deserters and rebels. If we called him Judge, our own conscience would sing to us the sentence of condemnation. If we called him the fountain of goodness or the highest good, we would at once hear that no fellowship or communion can exist between him and us, who are by nature evil and corrupt. Therefore Christ bids us call upon him by the name of Father, a name than which nothing is more pleasant, sweeter, or more lovable among men. For although the thought may arise at the same time that we are disobedient sons, yet the name of Father reminds us of that goodness and indulgence with which parents treat unruly sons when they see them, subdued by misery, come back to them and implore their mercy.

units.la: At hic probè consyderandum erit, vnde nobis hæc libertas et fiducia obtigerit, vt Deum audeamus Patrem nostrum dicere. Nec enim hoc licere est, cum nulla nobis, quoad nostram naturam, commvnio cum illo intercedat. Imò si nos spectes, propter peccatum filij iræ et damnationis sumus. Vnde ergo hoc, quod Deum Patrem vocamus? Num inde, quod nos creauerit? Atqui hoc cum brutis animantibus commune habemus. Eum ergo respiciamus oportet, qui ius filiorum Dei nobis instaurauit, nos cum illo in gratiam reduxit, et nos eius filios fecit. Is est Iesus Christus vnigenitus et naturalis Dei Filius, quem ex sua essentia siue subsistentia sibi coæternum genuit. Hic in mundum venit, et omnibus qui eum receperunt (vt Ioannis ait) hanc potestatem atque dignitatem dedit, vt filij Dei fierent. Nam nos non solum à peccatis liberauit, verumetiam ex femine verbi sui æterni et immortalis regenuit, et Spiritum adoptionis cordibus nostris inseruit, in quo clama-mus, Abba pater. Itaque primum Orationis Dominicæ vocabulum nos ad Christum remittit, cuius merito nobis Deus rursus Pater, et nos eius filij facti sumus. Seruit hoc nobis primum in-stitutioni, vt preces nostras Deo per solum Iesum Christum offeramus, qui solus aureum illud al-tare est, de quo supra diximus. Quis enim non nimium confidenter nos agere diceret, si Deum Patrem nostrum diceremus, eo interim negletto et spreto, qui illam dignitatem nobis meruit? Deinde officij nostri nos istud vocabulum admonet: Quia enim Deum Patrem dicimus, nostrum fuerit illum amare, et ei obedire, ne filij simus degeneres, quales olim fuere, de quibus per Ma-lachiam conqueritur. Præterea consolatur nos hoc Patris nomen, et fidem nostram confirmat. Quia enim Deus Pater dici vult, procul dubio paterna fide et bonitate nobiscum aget. Est etenim ipsa veritas, nec vanis titulis sese vendicat, sed nominibus, quæ ipse sibi imponit, respon-det. Docet hoc Dauidis verbis: Vt pater miseretur liberorum, ita Dominus miseretur timen-tium eum. Et ipse apud Isaiam testatur, se omnes parentum cóρyὰς vincere ea dilectio-ne et cura, qua nos prosequitur. Nam sic ait: Num obliuiscitur mulier infantis sui, quo minus
units.tr: But here we must carefully consider whence this freedom and confidence has come to us, that we dare to call God our Father. For this is not permitted, since, as regards our nature, no communion with him exists for us. Indeed, if you look at us, because of sin we are children of wrath and of condemnation. Whence, then, comes it that we call God Father? Is it because he created us? But we have this in common with the brute beasts. We must therefore look to him who restored to us the right of the sons of God, reconciled us to himself, and made us his sons. This is Jesus Christ, the only-begotten and natural Son of God, whom he begot from his own essence or substance, co-eternal with himself. He came into the world, and to all who received him (as John says) he gave this power and dignity, that they should become the sons of God. For he not only freed us from sins, but also regenerated us from the seed of his eternal and immortal word, and implanted in our hearts the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father." Thus the first word of the Lord's Prayer refers us to Christ, by whose merit God has again become our Father and we have become his sons. This serves first as an instruction for us, that we offer our prayers to God through Jesus Christ alone, who alone is that golden altar of which we spoke above. For who would not say that we act too boldly if we called God our Father while neglecting and despising him who earned for us that dignity? Next, this word reminds us of our duty. For since we call God our Father, it is our part to love him and obey him, lest we be degenerate sons, such as those of old, about whom he complains through Malachi. Moreover, this name of Father comforts us and strengthens our faith. For since God wishes to be called Father, without doubt he will deal with us in a fatherly faithfulness and goodness. For he is truth itself, and does not claim for himself empty titles, but corresponds to the names which he himself imposes. David teaches this in the words: "As a father has mercy on his children, so the Lord has mercy on those who fear him." And he himself testifies through Isaiah that he surpasses all parents in the love and care with which he embraces us. For thus he says: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb?"

units.la: Ioan.1. 1.Pet.1. Rom.8. Galat.4.
units.tr: John 1. 1 Pet. 1. Rom. 8. Gal. 4.

units.la: Psal.103. Isa.49. minus miseretur filij veri sui? Sed esto, obliuiscantur illæ, ego tamen tui non obliuiscar. Ecce in manibus istis ambabus insculpsi te, &c. Manuum meminit, quibus se nomina nostra incidisse ait, vt ostendat non frigidam apud se esse nostri memoriam, sed quod simul nos protegat atq; tueatur. Et hæc quidem in Patris nomine obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: Ps. 103. Isa. 49. "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? But suppose those forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands," etc. He mentions the hands on which he says he has engraved our names, to show that his memory of us is not cold, but that he at the same time protects and keeps us. These matters are to be observed in the name of Father.

units.la: Alterum vocabulum est, NOSTER, quo consolatio & fiducia, quam modò audiuimus, validissime confirmatur. Nec enim profuerit scire Deum Patrem esse, nisi nostrum Patrem esse nobis certò persuasum sit. Diceret enim aliquis: Scio Deum Patrem esse Angelorum, qui in historia Iobi filij Dei dicuntur, electorum item suorum, qui ei iam inde ab origine mundi in vera fide, & charitate non simulata & sanctitate seruierunt, quales fuere Seth, Henoch, Noa, Abraham, &c. Quid ve rò hoc ad te, qui neq; Angelus, neq; tam sanctus es, vt patribus istis conferri queas. Istis obiectionibus Christus occurrit, quando non solum concedit, verumetiam iubet, vt Deum Patrem NOSTRVM dicamus. Et id quidem libere & iure optimo, vel potius diuino, facere possumus. Quia enim vnigenitus & naturalis Dei Filius nos sibi fratres & sorores fecit, fieri non potest, quin omnes qui illi per fidem insiti sunt, vnà cum eo Dei filij fiant. Est hoc probe obseruandum. In hoc enim salutis nostræ cardo versatur, quam perpetuo Satan oppugnat, dum nobis persuadere conatur, Deū nolle nobis Patrem esse, etsi multorum aliorum Pater sit. At dum hoc obijcit quadruplator iste, tu ad Christum recurrito, qui verus liber vitæ est, in quo Deus suos elegit, antequā mundus hic creatur. Si ergo te Christo insitum esse inueneris per fidem, tunc eius frater vel soror, & proinde filius Dei & hæres, atq; Christi cohæres es, &c.
units.tr: The second word is OUR, by which the consolation and confidence we have just heard is most strongly confirmed. For it would not profit us to know that God is Father, unless it were firmly persuaded to us that he is our Father. For someone might say: "I know that God is the Father of the angels, who in the story of Job are called the sons of God, and of his elect too, who have served him from the beginning of the world in true faith and unfeigned love and holiness, such as Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and others. But what does this matter to you, who are neither an angel nor so holy that you can be compared with those fathers?" Christ meets these objections when he not only permits, but commands us to call God OUR Father. And indeed we can do this freely and by the best right, or rather by divine right. For since the only-begotten and natural Son of God has made us his brothers and sisters, it cannot be that all who are grafted into him through faith do not become sons of God together with him. This must be carefully observed. For the hinge of our salvation turns on this, and Satan constantly attacks it, while he tries to persuade us that God is unwilling to be our Father, even though he is the Father of many others. But when that accuser objects this, you must have recourse to Christ, who is the true book of life, in which God chose his own before this world was created. If therefore you find that you have been grafted into Christ through faith, then you are his brother or sister, and consequently a son of God and an heir, and a fellow heir with Christ, and so on.

units.la: Simul autem Dominus primùs bisce verbis nos communionis admonet, quam in ipso habemus: Quia enim non dicimus, Mi pater: sed Pater noster, non in nostra modo persona loquimur, sed in omnium eorum, qui Patrem hunc nobiscum inuocant. Fatemur denique non nos solos filios Dei esse, verumetiam alios omnes, qui eadem nobiscum precatione vtuntur. Omnes ergo vnum & eundem Patrem in cælis habemus, omnes ex eodem semine & per eundem spiritum renati sumus, omnes eodem adoptionis spiritu ad Deum clamamus, & tandem omnes eandem in cælis hæreditatem possidebimus. Vnde sequitur nos omnes in Christo fratres & sorores esse, cuiuscunq; tandem loci aut ordinis aut ex quacunq; natione simus oriundi. Estque fraternitas hæc multò arctior quam eorum, qui ex iisdem parentibus secundum carnem nati sunt, eò quod communio ista in rebus multò sublimioribus consistit. Itaq; officij nostri fuerit, vt nos mutuò fraterna dilectione prosequamur, & sing● guli inter precandum aliorum quoque salutem sibi commendatam habere debent. In horum consideratione diligentius versari conueniebat eos, qui generis nobilitate, aut opum suarum, vel etiam patriæ suæ fiducia adeo efferuntur, vt alios omnes præ se contemnant, & iniuriam sibi fieri putent, si aliorum quoque salutem quærere, & se inferioribus accomodare, cumq; hos familiariter & amicè conuersari iubeantur. Sed responde hic ô bone, quisquis es. Annon tu quoque, quoad carnis generationem, Adami filius, adhæc peccator, & proinde iræ Dei obnoxius es? Vnde ergo tibi hæc dignitas, quod nunc Dei filius censeris, vt dicere audis, Pater noster quies in cælis? Annon ex gratia hanc accepisti per Iesum Christum? Num vero tibi soli hanc gratiā contulit Deus? Nequaquā. Eius enim participes sunt, quotquot Christo per fidem sunt insiti, siue pauperes sint siue diuites, nobiles aut ignobiles, docti vel indocti, Germani denique, Galli, Itali aut quarumcunq; nationum homines. In Christo enim (vt Palus ait) non est seruus aut liber, non mas aut fœmina, non Iudæus aut Græcus, & eius regnum vsque ad fines orbis terrarum extenditur. Itaque idem ille, quem tu contemnis, non minus Dei Filius est, quam tu fis, & fortassis in Christo generosior & opulentior est te, cum à superbia alienus humilitati, patientiæ & constantiæ fidei ex animo studeat. Quem ergo ex tua superbia fructum alium reportas, quam extremam ignominiam, qua teipsum afficis? Eo enim ignorantiam tuam prodis, quod nimirum nondum precari didiceris, neque iucundissimum hoc plenumq; consolationis Orationis Dominicæ exordium adhuc intelligas. Nam si hoc intelligeres, puderet te alium ex Dei filijs contemnere. An vero illud Solomonis ignoras: Qui pauperem contemnit, illudit factori eius? Qua fronte ergo tu Deum Patrē appellas, cum eius dilectos filios contemnere non verearis? Sunt hæc probè obseruanda, ne inter precandum nos ipsos accusemus apud Deum, vel vetiā condemnemus.
units.tr: At the same time, the Lord first reminds us by these words of the communion we have in him. For since we do not say "My Father," but "Our Father," we speak not only in our own person, but in the person of all those who call upon this Father together with us. We therefore confess that we are not the only sons of God, but that all others too who use the same prayer with us are such. All of us, then, have one and the same Father in the heavens; all of us have been born again from the same seed and through the same Spirit; all of us cry to God with the same spirit of adoption; and finally all of us will possess the same inheritance in heaven. From this it follows that we are all brothers and sisters in Christ, from whatever place, rank, or nation we may have sprung. And this brotherhood is much closer than that of those who are born of the same parents according to the flesh, because this communion consists in far more exalted things. It is therefore our duty to embrace one another with brotherly love, and each of us ought to hold the salvation of others also commended to him while he prays. Those who are so puffed up by nobility of birth, or by their wealth, or even by confidence in their country, that they despise all others in comparison with themselves, and think they are wronged if they must seek the good of others too, and accommodate themselves to their inferiors, and are commanded to associate with them on friendly and familiar terms, should have been more diligently engaged in considering these things. But answer here, my friend, whoever you are. Are you not also, as regards natural generation, a son of Adam, and moreover a sinner, and therefore liable to the wrath of God? Whence, then, do you have this dignity, that you are now reckoned a son of God, so that you hear it said, "Our Father, who art in heaven"? Have you not received this by grace through Jesus Christ? Has God indeed conferred this grace on you alone? By no means. For all who are grafted into Christ through faith are partakers of it, whether they are poor or rich, noble or base, learned or unlearned, German, French, Italian, or men of whatever nation. For in Christ (as Paul says) there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, neither Jew nor Greek, and his kingdom extends to the ends of the earth. Thus that very man whom you despise is no less a Son of God than you are, and perhaps in Christ he is more noble and richer than you, since he is free from pride and earnestly strives from the heart for humility, patience, and constancy of faith. What other fruit, then, do you gain from your pride than extreme disgrace, which you bring upon yourself? For you betray your ignorance by this, that you have not yet learned to pray, nor do you yet understand this most pleasant opening of the Lord's Prayer, which is full of consolation. For if you understood it, you would be ashamed to despise any other of the sons of God. Or do you indeed not know that saying of Solomon: "He who despises the poor insults his Maker"? With what face, then, do you call God Father, when you are not ashamed to despise his beloved sons? These things must be carefully observed, lest in praying we accuse ourselves before God, or rather condemn ourselves.

units.la: Porro quoniam patres nostres carnales in terris habemus, ex Christi iussu addimus: QVI ES IN COELIS. Qua particula parentes terrenos ab eo distinguimus, quem hic innoca-mus: testamur item nos non de aliquo hominum loqui sub Patris vocabulo, sed de eo, qui cœlos inha-bitat, vtpote cœli & terrę dominus. Tribuitur autem cœlum Deo in scripturis non eo sensu, quasi-ut loco certo includatur (notum est enim quod per Ieremiam dicit, Cœlum & terram ego impleo) sed aliæ huius dicti rationes sunt. Primò, vt Regum huius seculi potentia atque maiestas nusquam melius perspicitur quam in palatijs, quæ cum suis aulieis incolunt: Ita Dei maiestas in nullis creaturis tam perspicuè elucet, vt in cœlo, cuius ornatus mirificus est, siue Solem & Lunam, siue reliqua astra, siue nubes & mirabiles orbium cœlestium motus consideres. Deinde cœlitus potissimum suam bonitatem & iram Deus declarat. E cœlo enim pluuiæ descendunt & aliæ influentiæ, quibus terra rigatur & fœcunda redditur. Rursus de cœlo manifestatur ira Dei (vt Paulus ait) per grandines, fulgura, tonitrua, fulmina & tempestates noxias, quæ terræ proventum intercipiunt. Præterea cœlum præsentia Dei euidentissimus typus est. Nam vbicunque locorum simus, cœlum supra nos conspicimus. Ita Deus quoque vbique præsens est, vt Dauid in Psal. 139. multis expli-cat. Et hæc præcipua causa est, propter quam inter precandum cœlestis illius habitationis Dei men-tionem facimus. Per hanc enim admonemur, Deum vbique nobis præsentem adesse, & proinde vbi-que nos exaudire posse. Ideo Solomon in templi dedicatione sæpius repetebat, Deum suorum preces exauditurum de loco habitationis suæ, id est, de cœlo. Quod si omnipræsens est Deus, & nos vbi-que exaudire potest, omnipotens quoque sit oportet: quod etiam hic obseruari debet, cum eodem ar-gumento Dauid Dei omnipotentiam asserat. Cum enim gentium Deos & idola damnare vellet, prius veri Dei maiestatem describit paucis hisce verbis: Deus noster in cœlis est, omnia quæ vult facit. Psal. 115.
units.tr: Since we have earthly fathers of our own, we add at Christ's command: WHO ART IN HEAVEN. By this little phrase we distinguish our earthly parents from him whom we invoke here, and we testify that by the name of Father we do not mean any man, but him who dwells in the heavens, as the Lord of heaven and earth. Scripture ascribes heaven to God not in the sense that he is confined to a certain place (for it is well known that he says through Jeremiah, "I fill heaven and earth"), but there are other reasons for the expression. First, just as the power and majesty of the kings of this age are nowhere seen better than in the palaces they inhabit with their courtiers, so God's majesty shines forth in no creature so clearly as in heaven, whose ornament is wonderful, whether you consider the sun and moon, the other stars, the clouds, or the marvellous motions of the heavenly spheres. Next, God declares his goodness and his wrath especially from heaven. For rains and other influences descend from heaven, by which the earth is watered and made fruitful. Again, God's wrath is revealed from heaven (as Paul says) through hail, lightning, thunder, thunderbolts and harmful storms, which cut off the produce of the earth. Moreover, heaven is a most evident type of God's presence. For wherever we are, we see the heaven above us. So God too is present everywhere, as David explains at length in Psal. 139. And this is the chief reason why, in prayer, we mention that heavenly dwelling of God. For through it we are reminded that God is present with us everywhere, and therefore able to hear us everywhere. Therefore Solomon, at the dedication of the temple, repeatedly said that God would hear the prayers of his people from the place of his habitation, that is, from heaven. But if God is omnipresent and can hear us everywhere, he must also be omnipotent; this too ought to be noted here, since David asserts God's omnipotence by the same argument. For when he wished to condemn the gods and idols of the nations, he first described the majesty of the true God in these few words: "Our God is in the heavens; he does whatever he wills." Psal. 115.

units.la: Itaque in istis verbis altera consolatio habetur, quæ precantium fidem confirmat: Ea est, quod Pater noster, quem inuocamus, in cœlis habitet & omnia possit. Est ergo inter hunc & terrenos pa-rentes ingens discrimen. Hi enim liberis suis libenter quidem succurrunt, sed sæpe accidit, vt il-lis subuenire non possint, & non sine acerbissimo animi dolore illorum interitum speƈtare cogantur. At Deus Pater noster omnipotens est, Dominus (inquam) excrcituum est, cui omnes creaturæ tam cœlestes quam terrestres, Angeli item & diaboli, pij & impij, fera & pecora, ignis & aqua, aer & terra & quæcunque alia possunt nominari, seruire coguntur. Omni igitur tempore & loco nobis potest succurrere. Posset hoc multis demonstrari, sed quia omnipotentia & maiestas eius tam nota & euidens est, vt coram ea dæmones quoque contremiscant, pluribus agere non est opus. Sufficiat nunc hoc precationis nostræ exordium diligenter inspexisse, ne de Dei voluntate & omnipotentia dubitemus, certam verò fiduciam animo concipiamus, nos ab illo accepturos esse, quæcunque no-bis vtilia atque necessaria sunt. Priusquam vero huic Sermoni finem imponamus, duo adhuc consi-deranda veniunt.
units.tr: Therefore in these words there is another consolation, which strengthens the faith of those who pray: that the Father whom we invoke dwells in heaven and is able to do all things. There is therefore a great difference between him and earthly parents. For these indeed gladly help their children, but it often happens that they cannot come to their aid, and they are forced to watch their destruction not without the most bitter grief of mind. But our Father God is omnipotent, the Lord (I say) of hosts, to whom all creatures, heavenly and earthly alike, angels and devils too, the pious and the impious, wild beasts and cattle, fire and water, air and earth, and whatever else can be named, are compelled to serve. Therefore he can help us at all times and in every place. This could be shown by many arguments, but since his omnipotence and majesty are so well known and so evident that even demons tremble before them, there is no need to labour the point further. It is enough for now to have carefully considered this beginning of our prayer, so that we do not doubt God's will and power, but conceive in our hearts a sure confidence that we shall receive from him whatever is useful and necessary for us. Before we bring this sermon to an end, however, two further matters must be considered.

units.la: Primum, non debere Christianos homines mundi & diaboli minùs atque furiosis conatibus ter-reri. Quia enim Patrem in cœlis habemus, qui toti mundo & diabolis omnibus imperat, nihil illi nobis nocere poterunt. Nec enim securus quidam aut somnolentus Deus est, qui res nostras mini-me curet, sed zelotes & Deus vltionum est, qui iniurias suis illatas non patitur inultas. Et apud Zachariam dicit: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Nec desunt exempla, quæ docent, quanta cum fide & zelo suorum causam omnibus seculis defenderit. Inter quæ admodum memo-rabilia sunt, quæ de Abeli indigna cæde grauissimè in Caino punita, de filiorum Israel liberatione ex Ægypto & horrendo Pharaonis interitu, de Dauide & multis alijs narrantur. Et in Lege se viduarum, orphanorum & peregrinorum vindicem profitetur. Idem etiam nos per Filium suum potentissimè asseruit, diaboli tyrannidem seuerissimè vltus est, & eius regnum destruxit. Cur ergo aliquem timeant, qui se Dei filios esse nolunt? Quin cum Dauide & Paulo dicimus: Dominus nobis adiutor, cur ergo timeamus nobis ab homine? Si Deus nobiscum, quis con-tra nos?
units.tr: First, Christians ought not to be terrified by the lesser and furious attempts of the world and the devil. For since we have a Father in heaven, who rules over the whole world and all the devils, they will be able to do us no harm. For God is not some careless or drowsy God who takes no care of our affairs, but a zealous God and a God of vengeance, who does not suffer the injuries done to his people to go unavenged. And in Zechariah he says: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Nor are there lacking examples which teach with what faith and zeal he has defended the cause of his people in all ages. Among these are very memorable the accounts of the grievously punished, unworthy slaughter of Abel by Cain, of the liberation of the children of Israel from Egypt and the dreadful destruction of Pharaoh, and of David and many others. And in the Law he professes himself the avenger of widows, orphans and strangers. He has also asserted our cause most powerfully through his Son: he has severely avenged the tyranny of the devil and destroyed his kingdom. Why then should they fear anyone who refuse to be sons of God? Rather, with David and Paul we say: "The Lord is my helper; why then should I fear what man can do to me?" "If God is with us, who is against us?"

units.la: Alterum est, quæ nostræ vitæ in terris sit conditio. Quia enim Patrem in cœlis habemus, vt que ibidem quoque patria nostra erit atque hæreditas. Non habemus ergo (vt Paulus docet) in terris terrä ciuitatem permanentem, sed vita nostra peregrinationis instar est, qua ad patriam cœlestem tendimus. At si patria & patrimonium nostrum in cœlis est, cur terrenis hisce bonis tantopere sumus addicti, quæ plerunq; citius quam putemus, relinquere cogimur? Vel cur mundum timemus, qui bonis cœlestibus damnum nullum inferre potest? Quin faciat ille ex principis sui instinctu omne quod libuerit, non tamen aliud poterit, quam coniugem, liberos, honores, opes & tandem vitam quoque eripere. In cœlesti vero patrimonium nihil potestatis habet, quin ad huius possessionem nos promouet, dum terrenus spoliat. Hæc & alia multa Orationis Dominicæ exordio continentur, dulcissimæ consolationis plenissimaque in quibus paterna erga nos Dei bonitas atq; fides clarissimè elucet, qui per Filium suum precandi formulam tradidit, cuius initium solum totam nostræ salutis rationem continet, & consolatione instruit efficacissima, qua armati vniuersos mundi atque diaboli assultus sustinere & vincere possumus. Itaq; procul relictis humanæ sapientiæ figmentis, hïs verbis Deum compellemus, qui procul dubio in omni necessitate nos exaudiet propter Filium suum Iesum Christum, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The second matter concerns the condition of our life on earth. For since we have a Father in heaven, our homeland and inheritance will be there too. Therefore we do not have here (as Paul teaches) a lasting city, but our life is like a pilgrimage, by which we press on toward our heavenly homeland. But if our homeland and patrimony are in heaven, why are we so devoted to these earthly goods, which we are often compelled to leave sooner than we think? Or why do we fear the world, which can do no harm to heavenly goods? Indeed, let it do whatever it pleases at the instigation of its prince, it can do no more than snatch away wife, children, honours, wealth and at last life itself. Over the heavenly inheritance it has no power at all; rather, while it despoils us of the earthly, it advances us to possession of that one. These and many other things are contained in the opening of the Lord's Prayer, a most sweet and fullest consolation, in which God's fatherly goodness and faithfulness shine most clearly toward us, since he has handed down through his Son the form of prayer. Its beginning alone contains the whole ground of our salvation, and it furnishes us with a most effective consolation, by which, armed, we can withstand and overcome all the assaults of the world and the devil. Therefore, setting aside the figments of human wisdom, let us address God in these words, who without doubt will hear us in every need, for the sake of his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 107.

units.la: PETITIO I. Sanctificetur nomen tuum.
units.tr: PETITION I. Hallowed be thy name.

units.la: Diuus Iacobus Apostolus scribit: Qui orat, postulet cum fiducia, nihil disceptans. Nam qui disceptat, is similis est fluctui maris, qui ventis agitur & iactatur; neq; existimet homo ille, se quicquā à Deo accepturum esse. Non temere ergo Iesus Christus Orationis, quā discipulis tradidit, eiusmodi Exordiū fecit, quo fides precantium validissimè confirmatur. Docet enim Deũ nos exaudire & quæ nobis salutaria sunt absq; dubio largiri velle, cum Pater noster sit, & hoc nomine à nobis innocari velit: Posse item nobis in omni afflictione succurrere, quia cœlos inhabitet, & omnium quæ in cœlis sunt atq; sub his continentur, plenam potestatem penes se habeat. Caeterum ne inter precandum carnis desiderijs & præpostera prudentia decepti, res inutiles, vel etiam nobis noxias postulemus, Christus sex petitiones nobis præscribit, quibus omne id comprehenditur, quod tam corporum quam animarum saluti feruit. Et quia petitiones illæ latissimè extenduntur, singulas seorsim ex ordine considerabimus, & in præsenti de prima solum dicemus, quæ est: Sanctificetur nomen tuum.
units.tr: The divine apostle James writes: "Let him who prays ask in faith, doubting nothing. For he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the winds; and let that man not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord." Not without reason, then, did Jesus Christ begin the prayer that he gave to his disciples in such a way that the faith of those who pray is most strongly confirmed. For he teaches that God hears us, and that without doubt he wishes to grant what is good for us, since he is our Father and wishes to be called upon by us under that name. He teaches also that God can help us in every affliction, since he dwells in the heavens and holds full power over all things that are in the heavens and that are contained beneath them. But lest, in praying, we be deceived by the desires of the flesh and by misguided prudence, and ask for useless things or even things harmful to us, Christ prescribes six petitions for us, which comprehend everything that serves the welfare of both body and soul. And because these petitions extend very widely, we shall consider each one separately and in order, and at present we shall speak only of the first, which is: Hallowed be thy name.

units.la: Ponitur hæc primo loco, partim quidem quod Dei gloria semper primas tenere & ante omnia quæri vel promoueri debet: partim vero, quod initio statim nos filios Dei professi sumus, & hunc patrem nostrum diximus. Quapropter gloria Dei & nominis ipsius nobis magis quā nos ipsi & omnes nostræ res curæ esse debet, adeo vt illam omni studio & pro virili promouamus, ne nobis ille idem respondeat, quod olim Iudæis: Si Pater vester sum, vbi honor, qui mihi à vobis debetur? Vt vero petitionem hanc rectius intelligamus, & ei noc maiori zelo accomodemus, primò quod nam illud Dei nomen sit, videre oportet: deinde quid per sanctificandi verbum hoc loco intelligi debeat.
units.tr: This petition is placed first, partly because the glory of God ought always to hold the first place and to be sought and promoted before all things; and partly because at the very beginning we have professed ourselves children of God and have called him our Father. Therefore the glory of God and of his name ought to be a greater concern to us than we ourselves and all our affairs, so that we promote it with every effort and to the best of our power, lest he answer us with what he once said to the Jews: "If I am your Father, where is the honour that is due to me from you?" So that we may understand this petition more rightly, and apply ourselves to it with greater zeal, we must see first what that name of God is, and then what is to be understood by the word "sanctify" in this place.

units.la: Nomina propriè rerum notæ sunt, quibus abs se inuicem distinguuntur, vt dignosci possint, & ideo ferè rerum naturam & proprietates exprimunt, ita vt audito nomine mox intelligamus, quid illud sit, de quo sermo habetur. At Deo nomen eiusmodi tribui non potest. Quia enim vnicus est; vt ab vllis aliis distinguatur non est opus. Adhæc cum æternus, immensus & infinitus sit, impossibile fuerit nomen aliquod excogitare, quo ille definiatur. Quod enim Iudæi de suis illo Schem Hamphoras, id est, de illustri & eximio nomine Dei fabulantur, quod in Sanctis Sanctorum descriptum fuerit, & cuius virtute miracula fieri potuerint, non aliud quam diabolicum figmentum est, quod in eum finem excogitarunt Rabbini, vt Christi miraculis fides detrahatur. Et iusto Dei iudicio fit, vt infelices illi, qui verum Dei nomen neq; agnoscere neq; sanctificare volunt, magicis eiusmodi fabulis demententur. Quia enim (vt modò diximus) Deus immensum & infinitum æternumq; bonum est, nè cogitandum quidem fuerit, eum vnico vocabulo describi aut definiri posse.
units.tr: The names of things are properly marks by which they are distinguished from one another, so that they may be recognised, and therefore they generally express the nature and properties of things, so that on hearing the name we immediately understand what it is that is being spoken of. But a name of this kind cannot be given to God. For since he is one and unique, there is no need for him to be distinguished from any others. Moreover, since he is eternal, immense and infinite, it would be impossible to devise any name by which he could be defined. As for what the Jews fable about their so-called Shem Hamphorash, that is, the illustrious and outstanding name of God, which they say was inscribed in the Holy of Holies and by whose power miracles could be performed, it is nothing but a diabolical fiction, which the rabbis devised for the purpose of taking away faith from the miracles of Christ. And by the just judgment of God it comes about that those unhappy men, who wish neither to acknowledge nor to sanctify the true name of God, are driven mad by such magical fables. For since God is (as we have just said) immense, infinite, eternal and good, it should not even be thought that he can be described or defined by a single word.

units.la: Nomen autem Dei in scripturis dicitur omne id, quod de illo prædicatur, & quo eius natura atq; ingenium describitur. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Vt nomen tuum ô Deus, ita & laus tua pertingit vsq; ad fines terræ. Itaq; Abrahamo olim per nomen Schaddai sese manifestauit, vt doceret, se omni suffici-entem & eũ ipsum esse, qui ta corpora quam animas saturare solus possit. Apud Mosem sese Iehoua nominat, quia ex seipso ab æterno existit, adhæc omnibus rebus suum esse largitur, & easdem in illo coseruat. Alibi scribitur, nomen eius esse, Dominus, eò quod omnibus imperat atq; omnia gubernat. Græci θεὸν dixerunt à currendo, quia omnia penetrat, et vbiq; præsens adest. Germani illum (Gott) vocant à bono, eò quod vnicum, summum & æternum bonum sit, vnde hauriamus oportet quicquid vsquam boni habetur. In primis vero huc pertinent tituli illi magnifici, quibus seipsum describit, quando Moses vt se illi sprectandum præberet, petebat. Tunc enim coram eo transiens clamauit: Dominus, Dominus Deus, misericors, beneficus, leni animo, immensæ bonitatis ac veritatis, tenax bonitatis in mille, condonans iniquitatem, transgressionem & peccatum: at impunita minimè peccata dimittens, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filijs ac nepotibus, in tertiam & quartam generationem. Hæc (inquam) & quæcunq; alia scripturæ habent, quibus Dei natura describitur, Nomen eius dici solent. Itaq; per illud hoc loco non aliud quam eius gloriam veramq; eius cognitionem intelligere debemus, quæ ex scripturis rectissime perfectissimè, quantum nunc nobis opus est, addiscitur.
units.tr: In the Scriptures, however, the name of God is taken to mean everything that is predicated of him and by which his nature and character are described. Therefore David said: "As your name, O God, so also your praise reaches to the ends of the earth." Thus he once made himself known to Abraham by the name Shaddai, to teach that he is all-sufficient and that he is the one who alone can satisfy both bodies and souls. To Moses he calls himself Jehovah, because he exists of himself from eternity; moreover, he bestows his being on all things and preserves them in himself. Elsewhere it is written that his name is Lord, because he rules over all things and governs all things. The Greeks called him θεόν [theon] from running, because he penetrates all things and is present everywhere. The Germans call him "Gott" from "good", because he is the one, highest and eternal good, from whom we must draw whatever good is found anywhere. But chiefly to this purpose belong those magnificent titles with which he describes himself, when Moses asked that he might be shown to him. For passing before him, he cried out: "The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin; yet by no means leaving sins unpunished, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation." These things, I say, and whatever else the Scriptures contain by which the nature of God is described, are customarily called his name. Therefore by that name in this place we must understand nothing other than his glory and his true knowledge, which is most rightly and most perfectly learned from the Scriptures, as far as we now need it.

units.la: Sanctificare autem proprie idem est quod rem aliquam Deo consecrare, vt eius solius cultui & honori seruiat. Inde sanctum dicitur, quod ab omni prophano aut communi vsu separatum, & vni Deo consecratum est. Græci ἅγιον dicunt, quæ vox teste Platone in Cratylo, compositá est ex priuatiua particula α & γαῖα quod terram significat: nimirum quod ea demum sancta dici merentur quæ cum rebus terrenis nihil commune habent. In præsenti vero sanctificare idem est, quod pro sancto æstimare, honorare & celebrare. Quo sensu Deus ipse hoc verbo vtitur, per Ezechielem dicens: Et magnificabor & sanctificabor, & notus ero in oculis gentium multarum, & scient quia ego Dominus. Quò etiam potest referri illud Isaiæ: Nudauit Dominus brachium suum sanctum in oculis omnium gentium & videbunt omnes fines terræ salutem Dei nostri. Quoad enim nomen Dei, per se sanctum, adeoq; sanctitas ipsa est, nec, quàm eius sanctitati quicquam potest accedere. Quia vero non ab omnibus agnoscitur, & multi partim ex ignorantia, superstitionibus & idololatria, partim malitia & deuoto ad peccandum animo horrendis blasphemijs, execrationibus, deierationibus, manifestis deniq; & scandali plenis sceleribus Dei nomen quotidie proscindunt, atq; quantum in ipsis est, conculcant, prima hac petitione precamur, vt Deus nominis sui gloriam vindicet, & det vt omnes illud vere agnoscant, honorent, laudent & celebrent.
units.tr: To sanctify, properly speaking, is the same as to consecrate some thing to God, so that it serves the worship and honour of him alone. Hence that is called holy which is set apart from all profane or common use and consecrated to the one God. The Greeks call it ἅγιον [hagion], a word which, as Plato attests in the Cratylus, is compounded of the privative particle α and γαῖα, which signifies earth: clearly because those things deserve at last to be called holy which have nothing in common with earthly things. In the present context, however, to sanctify is the same as to esteem as holy, to honour and to celebrate. In this sense God himself uses the word through Ezekiel, saying: "I will magnify myself and sanctify myself, and I will be known in the eyes of many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord." To this may also be referred that saying of Isaiah: "The Lord has made bare his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God." For the name of God is holy in itself, and therefore it is holiness itself, nor can anything be added to his holiness. But since it is not acknowledged by all, and since many, partly from ignorance, superstitions and idolatry, and partly from malice and a mind devoted to sin, tear the name of God every day with dreadful blasphemies, curses, oaths, and finally with manifest crimes full of scandal, and trample it underfoot as far as they are able, we pray with this first petition that God would vindicate the glory of his name, and grant that all may truly acknowledge, honour, praise and celebrate it.

units.la: At hic sciamus oportet, quæ illa sint, per quæ Dei nomen potissimum sanctificatur. Ex eo enim rectius intelligemus, quid prima hac petitione postuletur. Vbi primus locus debetur verae cognitioni Dei. Nec enim sine hac de illo recte sentire, & multo minus nominis eius gloriam prouehere poterimus. Poterant hic multa dici de singulis virtutibus Dei, quas in eo agnoscere & dignis laudibus prosequi debemus, sed sufficiat nunc de duabus dixisse, ne in immensum excrescat oratio. Prima est eius iustitia, cuius reuelatione contra impios nomen eius maximè glorificatur. Illi enim si quando pro sua libidine verbum Dei & Ecclesiam opprimere ac dissipare possunt, non pios modò ab ipsis oppressos, verumetiam Deum ipsum & vnctum eius diris conuitijs petere, & illi insultare incipiunt, quasi ille populum suum tueri & ex ipsorum manibus eripere non potuerit. Exempla huius impietatis memorabilia extant in Pharaone & Senacheribo Assyriorum tyranno, quorum ille dicere audebat: Quis est Iehoua, cui ego obedire debeam? Hic vero victoriarum successu elatus eo dementiae deuenit, vt non gentes modo, sed Deos quoq; earum abs se deuictos esse putaret, & ex eo certâ quoq; de Deo vero & æterno victoriam sibi polliceretur. Habent duo isti hodie multos successores, qui immani insolentia & borrendis conuitijs verbum Dei vnà cum Christo Iesu & vera fide proscindere & extremis contumelijs afficere non verentur, vt primum se rerum potitos putant. Vt vero olim Deus nominis sui gloriam fortissimè vindicauit, quando Pharaonem maris rubri fluctibus obruit, Senacheribi autem exercitum vnius angeli opera totum deleuit, & ipsum à proprijs filijs in conspectu Dei sui fictitij interfici passus est: Ita omnibus seculis nomen eius sanctificatur, quoties suam iustitiam atque potentiam similibus exemplis aduersus verbi sui hostes exerit, & Ecclesiam suam ex illorum tyrannide liberat. Itaque prima ista petitione precamur, ne Deus nomen suum sanctum propter peccata nostra violari aut prophanari patiatur, sed potius nostri miseretur det, vt ipsi quidem dem emendemur, hostes vero incurabiles & pænitere nescij coerceantur, vt omnes homines nomen suum agnoscere discant, & ipse passim timeatur atq; honoretur. Ad hunc modum olim pios Dei cultores precatos fuisse legimus: Non nobis, nō nobis Domine, sed tuo nomini da gloriam, propter boni tatem & veritate tuam. Cur enim dicant Gentes, Vbi est Deus ipsorū? Item: Effunde iram tuam Domine in Gentes, quæ te non agnoscunt, & in regna quæ nomen tuum non invocant. Adiuua nos ô Deus salutis nostræ, propter gloriā nominis tui, & libera nos, & propitius fis peccatis nostris pro pter nomen tuum. Cur dicerent Gentes, Vbi est Deus eorū? Elucescat inter gentes nobis videntibus, vltio sanguinis seruorū tuorum, qui effusus est, &c. At in eiusmodi precibus diligenter cauendū est, ne ex priuata & viciosa vindicta cupiditate, sed sancto nominis & gloriæ Dei zelo procedat, etc.
units.tr: But here we ought to know what those things are by which the name of God is chiefly sanctified. For from this we shall understand more rightly what is asked for in this first petition. The first place is due to the true knowledge of God. For without this we cannot think rightly of him, and much less can we advance the glory of his name. Much could be said here about the individual virtues of God, which we must acknowledge in him and pursue with fitting praises, but for now let it suffice to have spoken of two, lest the discourse grow to an immense length. The first is his justice, by whose revelation his name is most greatly glorified against the wicked. For when they are able, at their own pleasure, to oppress and scatter the word of God and the Church, they not only harass the pious whom they have oppressed, but even God himself and his anointed with dreadful reproaches, and they begin to insult him, as if he had been unable to defend his people and snatch them from their hands. Memorable examples of this impiety exist in Pharaoh and in Sennacherib, the tyrant of the Assyrians. The former dared to say: "Who is Jehovah, that I should obey him?" The latter, elated by the success of his victories, fell into such madness that he thought not only the nations but also their gods had been conquered by him, and from this he promised himself certain victory over the true and eternal God. Today these two have many successors, who, with monstrous insolence and dreadful reproaches, do not hesitate to tear the word of God, together with Christ Jesus and the true faith, and to subject them to the utmost contempt, as soon as they think they have gained control of affairs. But just as God once vindicated the glory of his name most strongly, when he overwhelmed Pharaoh in the waves of the Red Sea, and destroyed the army of Sennacherib entirely by the work of a single angel, and allowed him to be slain by his own sons in the sight of his false god: so in every age his name is sanctified, as often as he displays his justice and power by similar examples against the enemies of his word, and frees his Church from their tyranny. Therefore with this first petition we pray that God, on account of our sins, not allow his holy name to be violated or profaned, but rather have mercy on us, so that we ourselves may be amended, while his enemies, who are incurable and know not how to repent, may be restrained, and that all men may learn to acknowledge his name, and that he himself may be feared and honoured everywhere. In this way we read that the pious worshippers of God once prayed: "Not to us, not to us, O Lord, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your goodness and your truth. For why should the nations say, Where is their God?" Likewise: "Pour out your wrath, O Lord, upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that do not call upon your name." "Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and be merciful to our sins for your name's sake. Why should the nations say, Where is their God?" "Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants, which has been shed, be made known among the nations before our eyes," and so on. But in prayers of this kind great care must be taken that they do not proceed from private and vicious desire for revenge, but from a holy zeal for the name and glory of God, etc.

units.la: Altera Dei virtus, cuius revelatione & cognitione nomen eius sanctificatur, est immensa atq; inexhausta eius bonitas siue misericordia. Vt primum enim hæc recte agnoscitur, mox ad illum re- damandum homines excitantur, & omnibus ijs studere incipiunt, quibus nominis eius gloria proue hi potest. Extant illius plurima argumenta, nullum autem illustrius est, quàm quod in Filio eius habetur, quem pro nobis in mortem tradidit. Quamobrem in huius etiam beneficij consideratione nos potissimum versari consueuit. Nam si illud recte expendatur, mox omnes errores concidunt, qui circa fidem & Dei cultum enasci solent, vbi Christi cognitione homines deflituuntur. Qui autem hac institutus est, vt procul relictis inutilibus mediis, in quibus aliquando salutem quæsiuit, fiduciam omnem in vnum Deum per Iesum Christum collocat. Idem non vllam ex creaturis, sed vnum Deum invocat: abiectis quoque superstitionibus Deum in spiritu & veritate adorat: non porrò mundum, carnem caeco amore prosequitur, sed Deum supra omnia diligit: in cruce & afflictionibus constanter perseverat, nec per has se à Deo abstrahi patitur: & quemadmodum beneficia ex manu Dei lætus & cum gratiarum actione recipit, ita gaudet & exultat, si se eo honore dignum censeri videat, vt pro Christi nomine affligatur, sicut in Apostolorum exemplis est videre. Quia ergo bos tàm eximios fructus parit cognitio gratiæ Dei, quam nobis fecit in Filio suo Iesu Christo, hic quoq; huius primæ petitionis vsus aut scopus est: vt Deus in Filij sui cognitionem omnes homines inducere, & Euangelij lucem passim accendere dignetur, vt vera fide omnes illustrati ipsi vni seruiant, & eius nomen digni laudibus prosequantur. Precamur item, vt nobis quoq; constantiam in vera fide largiatur, ne mundi fauore aut illecebris, vel minus quoq; superati nominis sui gloriam negligamus, sed in eius confessione constantes, eam (si ita opus sit) sanguine etiam proprio obsignemus.
units.tr: The second attribute of God, through whose revelation and knowledge his name is sanctified, is his immense and inexhaustible goodness, or mercy. For as soon as this is rightly recognised, people are at once stirred to love him in return, and they begin to devote themselves to everything by which the glory of his name can be promoted. There are very many proofs of this, but none is more striking than what we have in his Son, whom he delivered up to death for us. For this reason we are accustomed to dwell chiefly on the consideration of this benefit. If it is rightly weighed, all the errors that usually arise concerning faith and the worship of God at once fall away, wherever people are deprived of the knowledge of Christ. But whoever has been taught this, leaving far behind the useless means by which he once sought salvation, places all his trust in the one God through Jesus Christ. He calls upon no creature but the one God; having cast off superstitions, he worships God in spirit and truth; he does not pursue the world and the flesh with blind love, but loves God above all things; he perseveres steadfastly in the cross and in afflictions, and does not allow himself to be drawn away from God by them; and just as he receives benefits from the hand of God gladly and with thanksgiving, so he rejoices and exults if he sees himself judged worthy of the honour of being afflicted for the name of Christ, as may be seen in the examples of the Apostles. Since, then, the knowledge of the grace of God, which he has shown us in his Son Jesus Christ, bears such excellent fruits, the use or aim of this first petition is also this: that God may deign to lead all people into the knowledge of his Son and to kindle the light of the Gospel everywhere, so that all, enlightened by true faith, may serve him alone and celebrate his name with fitting praises. We also pray that he will grant us constancy in the true faith, so that we do not, through the favour or allurements of the world, or even through being overcome in some small way, neglect the glory of his name, but remain steadfast in its confession and, if need be, seal it even with our own blood.

units.la: Est ergo multiplex huius petitionis vsus, & per omnia extenditur quæ nobis in huius vitæ pa- lastra publicè & priuatim accidunt, ideoq; in omni casu semper primas tenere debet. Exempli gratia, quando totum mundum quoad religionem in diuersas sententias scindi, & inde contentiones grauissimas & terribiles motus enasci videmus, tunc precemur, vt Deus omnibus hominibus vera nominis sui cognitionem reuelare, veritatis lucem in omnium animis accendere, & nos in æternæ salutis semita dirigere dignetur, ne à vero aberremus, sed ea faciamus, quæ nominis ipsius gloriæ promouen de seruiunt. Similiter, si quādo sentimus, nos mundi illecebris capi, vt gloria Dei nobis tam minus cordi sit, tunc necessaria plane est ista petitio, vt Deus sui nominis amorem atq; zelum in animis nostris accendat, ne quid faciamus in nominis sui sancti contumeliam. Adhæc si diuitiis & honoribus supra alios homines excellimus, in primis necesse est vt clamemus: Sanctificetur ô Pater, nomen tuum, & da quæso, vt huius seculi opibus atq; honoribus ita vtamur, ne nomen tuū propter nos male audiat, &c. Quàm enim necessarium sit hoc petere, multorū exempla docent, qui opum deside- rio atq; abusu à Deo abstrahuntur, & gloriæ Dei immemores in eius contumeliā ijs abutuntur, quæ ex illius liberalitate acceperunt. Non minus etiam hac petitione opus est, si quando diuitiis amissis ad egestatem redigimur. Tunc enim carnis ingenium omnis inopiæ impatiens sese prodit, quæ Deo etiam obstrepere audet, quasi iniquius & crudelius nobiscum agat. Itaq; ex animo dicamus: Sanctificetur ô Pater, nomen tuum. Iudicia tua iusta, vera & sancta sunt. Tu quidem diuitiis & honoribus me donaueras. At ego vel non bene vsus sum illis, vel tu quid facturus esse m iā vidisti, et ideo ea eripuisti rursus. Quia verò tua sunt quæcunq; hic orbis terrarum continet, tibi de illis statue relicet pro tuo arbitrio, ego autem quod iure de te querar non habeo. Sit nomen tuum benedictum & sanctificetur in æternum, &c. Ita Iobum fecisse legimus, cùm vno quasi momento ex amplissima fortuna in extremas sordes deijceretur. Eadem est bona valetudinis & morborum ratio. Quando enim recte valemus, facile nostri erga Deum officij obliuiscimur. Quare opus est precatione ista, ut valetudine integra ad diuini nominis gloriam recte utamur. In morbis vero & quae tunc sese prodit carnis impatientia, mox in mentem revocemus, quae nostra vita, qui mores, quae studia fuerint, cum valetudine bona uteremur, & mox patebit, Deum non iniquius nobiscum agere: simul autem oremus, ut Deus suum nomen in nobis sanctificet, & ea gratia dignetur, ut alij ex nobis fidei & patientiae Christianae exemplum capere possint. Eadem ratione hanc Orationis Dominicae partem nobis in omni afflictionum genere applicemus, ut ante omnia diuini nominis gloria nobis cordi sit. Ita fiet, ut omnia nobis adiumento sint in bonum, neque aliquis casus vel latus vel aduersus nos separare possit a dilectione Dei, &c.
units.tr: This petition therefore has many uses, and it extends to everything that happens to us in the course of this life, both publicly and privately, and so in every case it must always hold the first place. For example, when we see the whole world divided into different opinions in matters of religion, and from this serious contentions and terrible disturbances arising, then let us pray that God will deign to reveal to all people the true knowledge of his name, to kindle the light of truth in the minds of all, and to direct us in the path of eternal salvation, so that we do not wander from the truth but do those things that serve to promote the glory of his very name. Likewise, if at any time we feel that we are caught by the allurements of the world, so that the glory of God matters less to us, then this petition is plainly necessary, that God will kindle in our minds his love and zeal for his own name, so that we do nothing to the dishonour of his holy name. Moreover, if we excel others in riches and honours, we must above all cry out: "Hallowed be your name, O Father, and grant, we pray, that we may so use the wealth and honours of this age that your name is not ill spoken of on account of us," and so on. For how necessary it is to ask this is taught by the examples of many who, through desire for wealth and its misuse, are drawn away from God, and, forgetful of God's glory, abuse for his dishonour the things they have received from his generosity. This petition is no less needed when, having lost our riches, we are reduced to poverty. For then the nature of the flesh, impatient of every want, shows itself, and it dares to rail even against God, as though he were dealing with us more unjustly and cruelly. Therefore let us say from the heart: "Hallowed be your name, O Father. Your judgements are just, true and holy. You indeed had bestowed riches and honours upon me. But either I have not used them well, or you saw what I was going to do, and so you have taken them away again. Since everything that the whole world contains is yours, dispose of it as you judge best; I, for my part, have no right to complain against you. May your name be blessed and hallowed for ever, and so on." Thus we read that Job did, when in a moment, as it were, he was cast down from the greatest fortune into the lowest squalor. The same reasoning applies to good health and sickness. For when we are well, we easily forget our duty towards God. Therefore this prayer is needed, so that we may use sound health rightly for the glory of the divine name. But in sickness, when that impatience of the flesh shows itself, let us straightway call to mind what our life, our conduct and our pursuits were while we enjoyed good health; and it will soon be plain that God is not dealing unjustly with us. At the same time let us pray that God will sanctify his name in us, and deign to grant this grace, that others may take from us an example of Christian faith and patience. By the same reasoning let us apply this part of the Lord's Prayer to every kind of affliction, so that above all the glory of the divine name may be dear to us. Thus it will come about that all things work together for our good, and that no circumstance, whether high or low, can separate us from the love of God, and so on.

units.la: At quia nuper dictum est, preces non ore modo fieri, sed ex corde non fucato procedere debere, hic in primis necesse est, ut reipsa quoque ijs studeamus, per quae Dei nomen sanctificari & glorificari possit. Illusores enim Dei sunt, qui ore quidem clamant, Sanctificetur nomen tuum, interim vero toti in sceleribus volutantur, per quae illud profanantur. At ijdem precibus suis seipsos accusant, & ultricem Dei iram aduersus se prouocant. Quia enim filij Dei dicimur, quaecunque a nobis fiunt, mundus in Deu referre solet, adeo ut hic propter nos vel bene vel male audiat. Meminerimus ergo nos precari, ut Deus nos gratia & gloria sua vasa facere dignetur: ideoque vitam omnem in cum finem dirigamus, ut illius nomen in nobis sanctificetur. Quo loco bifariam considerari debet officium nostrum, quod Deo praestare debemus.
units.tr: But since it was said a little while ago that prayers must be made not only with the mouth but must proceed from a sincere heart, here it is especially necessary that we in fact also strive for those things through which the name of God can be sanctified and glorified. For those who cry out with their mouths, "Hallowed be your name," yet meanwhile wallow wholly in wickedness by which that name is profaned, are mockers of God. Indeed, by their prayers they accuse themselves and provoke the avenging wrath of God against themselves. For since we are called the sons of God, whatever we do is usually referred to God by the world, so that on our account he is spoken of well or ill. Let us therefore remember that we pray for God to deign to make us vessels of his grace and glory, and so let us direct our whole life to this end, that his name may be sanctified in us. Here our duty, which we owe to God, must be considered in two ways.

units.la: Primo nos ipsos quoad nostras personas omnibus illis studere oportet, per quae Dei nomen sanctificatur, abstinere autem ab omnibus, quibus illud pollui aut profanari potest. Vbi ante omnia requiritur, ut incredulitatem & diffidentiam abijciamus, quae causa est, ut de Dei veritate dubitemus, & extra hunc alibi opem quaeramus atque auxilium. Renuntiemus quoque oportet omnibus superstitionibus, & in primis idolorum cultui, quibus infideles Dei naturam & essentiam adumbrare conantur. Quae enim Deo iniuria maior fieri potest, quam si hominis mortalis imagini similem, & talem esse iudicamus, qui per simulachra ex ligno, lapide, aere, auro denique & argento fácta exprimi possit? Opus praeterea est, ut ab omni nominis diuini abusu abstineamus, quo plurimum peccant, qui per illud deierant, execrantur, aut etiam veneficia & artes magicas, adhaec sub eius praetextu in contractibus imposituras exercent. Quam enim absurdum fuerit, precari quidem, Sanctificetur nomen tuum, interim vero nomine isto ad deierationes temerarias, execrationes, incantationes & veneficia impie abluti? Caveamus item impatientiam, ne in tentationibus hac superati aliquid faciamus aut dicamus nominis huius professione indignum: quod interdum sub diuini zeli praetextu fieri consueuit, ut in Mosis & Aaronis exemplo est videre: qui populi indignis querelis atque murmure vitii, Deo non ut par erat, honorem tribuerunt, & ideo ne unquam in terram patribus promissam ingrederentur, multati sunt. Neque etiam duo haec inter se conuenire possunt, ut Dei nomen sanctificari postulemus, simul autem de eodem conqueramur, quasi iniuste, inique & crudeliter nobiscum agat. Vitari quoque necesse est in tota vitae conuersatione scandalum omne, ex quo impij verum Dei cultu calumniandi possunt arripere. E contra vero totos nos in eo esse decet, ut vera fide praediti, nomine Dei honorifice utamur, patienter feramus quicquid a Deo nobis imponitur, & vitam viuamus sanctam atque innocentem, in qua carni & mundo mortui, nosipsos Deo sistamus viuentem hostiam: ita deniq; viuamus, ut homines videant opera nostra bona, & glorificent Patrem nostrum, qui in caelis est.
units.tr: First, with regard to our own persons, we ought to strive for all those things through which the name of God is sanctified, and to abstain from all those things by which it can be polluted or profaned. Here above all it is required that we cast off unbelief and distrust, which is the cause of our doubting the truth of God and seeking help and assistance elsewhere, apart from him. We must also renounce all superstitions, and above all the worship of idols, by which unbelievers try to misrepresent the nature and essence of God. For what greater injury can be done to God than when we judge him to be like the image of mortal man, and such that he can be expressed by images made of wood, stone, bronze, gold or silver? It is further necessary that we abstain from every abuse of the divine name, which those sin most who swear by it, curse by it, or even practise poisonings and magical arts, and, under its pretext, deceptions in their dealings. For how absurd it would be to pray, "Hallowed be your name," and yet meanwhile with that same name to be impiously polluted by rash oaths, curses, incantations and poisonings! Let us also guard against impatience, lest, overcome by temptations, we do or say anything unworthy of the profession of this name. This is sometimes done under the pretext of divine zeal, as may be seen in the example of Moses and Aaron, who, when the people murmured with unworthy complaints, did not give God the honour that was due to him, and for this reason were punished so that they should never enter the land promised to their fathers. Nor can these two things agree with each other: to ask that the name of God be sanctified, and at the same time to complain of him as though he were dealing with us unjustly, unfairly and cruelly. Moreover, every stumbling-block must be avoided throughout the whole course of our conduct, from which the wicked may seize the chance to slander the true worship of God. On the contrary, we ought to be wholly bent on this: that, endowed with true faith, we use the name of God honourably, patiently bear whatever God lays upon us, and live a holy and innocent life, in which, dead to the flesh and the world, we present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice; and so, finally, let us live in such a way that people see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven.

units.la: Secundo requiritur, ut non ipsi modo tales simus, verum etiam diuini nominis gloria apud alios, quibus cum nobis aliquid negotij est, promoueamus. Vt enim bonae indolis filio non sufficit, si ipse parentem suum honoret, sed eundem ab alijs quoque honorari & in pretio haberi cupit: ita qui germani & veri filij Dei sunt, ijs non satis est, si ipsi Patrem suum caelestem colant atque venerentur, sed insuper huc omne suum studium intendunt, ut quam plurimi alij Deum hunc agnoscant, nomen eius reuereantur & obseruent. Hinc fit, quod qui vera fide praediti sunt, nihil videre aut ferre possunt, quod gloriae Dei & sancto eius nomini officere sciunt: sed quam primum tale quid conspicantur, tamen non omnes modestiae, patientiae & mansuetudinis obliti, zelum suum proferunt, & si opus fit, etiam cum vitæ periculo nominis diuini gloriam vindicant. Vt enim Deum supra omnia diligunt: ita nihil illis perinde vt eius gloria cordi est. Huc pertinent præclara illa seruorum Dei exempla, qui zelum hunc cum præsenti vitæ periculo declararuerunt. Inter quos non postremus locus Mosi debetur. Is cùm populus Israeliticus contra disertum Dei præceptum idololatriæ peccato se[?]fe polluisset, & immortalis Dei maiestatem (vt Dauid ait) commutasset cum imagine vituli comedentis fœnum: sic ira & zelo exarsit, vt tabulas fœderis Dei digito inscriptas, quibus nihil pretiosius hic orbis vidit, abijeret, idolum frangeret, & in puluerem redigeret, quo in aquas iniecto infelices illos etiam coegit, vt hunc suum tam egregium Deum biberent, quò euidentius pateret, quàm turpiter & nefariè errauissent. Adhæc idololatriæ huius authores interfici iubet, quod sine vitæ periculo fieri non poterat.
