Postquā enim Adam per præcepti à Deo accepti transgressionem peccauit, non à dignitate modò, ad quam conditus erat, excidit, verametiam diuino illo & sublimi intellectus acumine est spoliatus, quo ante lapsum præditus fuit. Quo fit, ut homo animalis non percipiat ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Quia ergo intellectus, ex quo omnia hominis consilia, desideria & voluntas deriuantur, corruptus est, volun-tas quoq; nostra mala & diuinæ contraria fit oportet, ideoque non potest non etiam noxia & saluti nostræ inimica esse. Quî enim fieri potest, ut voluntas ad ea prona fit, quæ tu non intelligis? Rectè ergo Deus hominem nihil quam carnem, & omnia cordis humani figmenta praua esse, olim pronun-tiauit. Nam carnis ratio verbo Dei fidem habere non potest, & proinde Deo quoque non fidimus, ut decebat. Adhæc caro ad peccata procliuis est, his delectatur, & ideo pugnam perpetuam aduer-sus spiritum exercet, qui diuinæ voluntati obtemperare cupit. Quod si vero Deus nobis succurrere velit per afflictiones, quas nostro bono immittit, ut carnis petulantiā coerceat, mox impatientes ad uersorū, iugū Dei excutere conamur. Deniq; siue læta siue tristia accidant, voluntatis ac totius natu-ræ nostræ prauitatē prodimus. Nam illis quidē pro libidine nostra abutimur, in his vero fremimus atq; murmuramus aduersus eū, cuius iusta atq; salutarē manum debebamus agnoscere. Minimè er-go orandum est, ut nostræ voluntati Deus indulgeat. Ita enim precando exitiū nobis accerseremus.
units.tr: Before we examine the meaning of this petition, we must consider more carefully why we are commanded to pray that the will of God the Father be done, and not rather that he would indulge our will and wish it to be ratified. For it seems to conflict with common sense that someone should set aside his own will and submit to another's. But the reason lies close at hand. Because Christ teaches us to ask for what is useful and salutary for us, he could not command us to wish that our will be done, since it is evil, unjust and harmful. This will easily appear if we consider carefully our nature and the disposition of the flesh. For after Adam sinned by transgressing the commandment he had received from God, he fell not only from the dignity for which he had been created, but was also stripped of that divine and lofty keenness of understanding with which he had been endowed before the fall. Hence the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. Since therefore the understanding, from which all human counsels, desires and will derive, is corrupted, our will must also be evil and contrary to the divine, and so it cannot fail to be harmful and hostile to our salvation. For how can the will be inclined toward things that you do not understand? Rightly, then, God once pronounced that man is nothing but flesh, and that all the imaginations of the human heart are evil. For the reasoning of the flesh cannot have faith in the word of God, and therefore we do not trust God as we ought. Moreover, the flesh is prone to sin, takes delight in it, and therefore wages perpetual war against the spirit, which desires to obey the divine will. But if God wishes to help us through the afflictions he sends for our good, to restrain the wantonness of the flesh, we straightway, impatient and resentful, try to shake off the yoke of God. Finally, whether things turn out happily or sadly, we display the wickedness of our will and of our whole nature. For in prosperity we abuse God's gifts to satisfy our lust, and in adversity we rage and murmur against him, whose just and saving hand we ought to acknowledge. Therefore we must by no means pray that God indulge our will, for by such praying we would bring ruin upon ourselves.

units.la: Confutantur ergo hic validissimè, qui homini, quoad fidē & salutis negotiū, proprij arbitrij li-bertatem tribuunt, quasi proprijs viribus bonū eligere, & voluntatem quoq; bonam atq; Deo acce-ptam concipere possimus. Vnde aliud quoq; colligunt, hominē suis operibus salutem mereri posse. At si ita res haberet, tum petitio ista stulta & superuacanea esset. Homo enim bona voluntate ex sei-pso coœpta, sic precari deberet: Mea voluntas fiat, ô Domine. Vel, da mihi hoc ô Pater, ut mea vo-luntas fiat. At diuersum omnino Christus docet: vnde patet nostrā voluntatē prauam & noxiā es-se, & si quid boni aliquando volumus, hoc non nostrum, sed Dei donū est, qui (vt Paulus ait) in no-bis operatur tam velle quam facere, cum ipsi ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, & sine Christo vt ipsemet testatur) nihil facere possimus. Quod si ne voluntatem quidem in nostra potestate habe-mus, qui fieri potest, ut ex nobis opera bona faciamus? Itaq; cum neq; voluntatem neq; opera in no-stra habeamus potestate, quicquid verò boni in nobis est, ex Dei gratia donetur, de nullo vtiq; nostro-rum operum merito coram Deo gloriari poterimus. Mox enim nobis responderetur: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? At quid verbu opus est? Fatemur ipsi hac petitione, solius Dei voluntatem iustam & bonam, nostram vero iniustam & ma-lam esse. Imòaduersus nosipsos, ut hostem acerrimum precamur. Etenim reuera hostem neminē no-bispsis nocentiorem habemus, eò quod innata nobis vitiositas nos à Deo & eius voluntate abducit & ad omnem inobedientiam solicitat. Vide Pauli exemplum Rom.7.cap.
units.tr: Here, then, are most forcefully refuted those who grant to man, in matters of faith and salvation, freedom of choice, as though by his own powers he could choose the good and conceive a good will acceptable to God. From this they also infer that man can merit salvation by his works. But if this were so, this petition would be foolish and superfluous. For a man whose good will had begun from himself would have to pray thus: "My will be done, O Lord," or "Grant me this, O Father, that my will may be done." But Christ teaches quite the opposite, whence it is clear that our will is depraved and harmful, and that if we ever desire anything good, this is not our own but the gift of God, who (as Paul says) works in us both to will and to do, since we are not even fit to think anything of ourselves, and without Christ (as he himself testifies) we can do nothing. But if we do not even have the will in our own power, how can we perform good works from ourselves? Therefore, since we have power neither over the will nor over works, whatever good is in us is bestowed by the grace of God, and we can therefore boast of the merit of none of our works before God. For it would straightway be answered us: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" But why need many words be spent? By this petition we ourselves confess that the will of God alone is just and good, and our will unjust and evil. Indeed we pray against ourselves, as against the bitterest enemy. For truly we have no enemy more harmful to us than ourselves, because the innate vice within us draws us away from God and his will and urges us to every disobedience. See the example of Paul, Rom. 7.

units.la: Vt autem non precari debemus, ut nostra voluntas fiat, quæ praua & noxia est: ita ut Patris cœlestis voluntas fiat, nos Christus precari iubet: nimirum quod hæc iusta, sancta, bona & salutaris sit, licet nos id non semper videamus. Quî enim fieri posset, ut quid mali & iniusti vellet si, qui & summum bonum & ipsissima est iustitia? Aut qua ratione aduersus nos malum aut noxium quid inflituat, qui omnium nostrum Pater est, & amore atq; indulgentia parentes omnes longè superat? Carnis quidem interdum hæ cogitationes sunt, Deum durius nobiscum agere, voluntatem eius nimis rigidam & præcepta intolerabilia esse, neque illum semper in suis iudicijs æqui tatem veram obseruare. At si (vt Asaph monet) in eius sanctuarium penetramus, & ipsius mysteria, quatenus per verbum nobis revelantur, vnà cum sine rerum omnium diligentius consideramus, illico patebit, Dei voluntatem non iustam modò & bonam esse, sed in eo omnem nostram salutem consistere, vt & illa fiat, & eidem nos obediamus. Argumenta, quibus hoc probetur, euidentissima habemus in humani generis lapsu & restitutione. Vnde enim cæpit omnium nostrum miseria atq; calamitas? Vnde prauæ cupiditates, æmulatio, invidia, odium, curæ denique, & solicitudines cum multis alijs, quæ animam turbant & excruciant, initium habuerunt? Vnde morbi tam multi & varij, quibus corpora nostra obnoxia sunt? Vnde maledictio illa, quæ terræ imminet, vt non nisi multo labore culta fructum ferat? Cur tanto cum dolore nascimur? Denique vnde casus illi varij, qui nos exercent, & tandem ipsa mors, quæ nos hinc non sine terrore & acutissimis doloribus abripit? Omnium horum non alia causa est, quàm quod Adam contempta Dei voluntate, suam, quam illi serpens suggesserat, secutus est. Hæc (inquam) causa est, quod & illis omnibus, quæmodò commemorauimus obnoxij sumus, & quod insuper fame, peste, bellis, seditionibus eos quotidie punit Deus, qui suæ voluntati minus obtemperant. E contra, quam causam esse dicemus, quod calamitates istæ & pœnæ non exitium æternum nobis afferunt, sed potius disciplinæ loco sunt, quæ Deus nos patrum optimi instar castigat? quod Deus nobis iterum reconciliatus peccata condonat, & inter huius seculi tempestates tuetur, atque tandem æterna felicitatis hæredes facit? Non a-liam certè præter meritum Filij Dei Iesu Christi, qui ex voluntate & decreto Patris sese humiliauit, & obediens fuit vsque ad mortem, & quidem mortem crucis. Huius obedientia nostram inobedientiam quasi è medio sustulit, Deumq; nobis placauit, vt propter hunc Filium suum nobis iam propitius sit. Cum ergo Adami inobedientia maledictionem, calamitates omnes, mortem denique & exitium induxerit, Christus vero sua obedientia nos redemerit, saluos fecerit & cœlestes regni hæredes, necesse omnino est, vt ex animo precemur, ne nostra, sed Dei Patris volun-tas fiat, & vt hic eam nobis gratiam largiatur, vt huic nos accommodare & obedire possimus. At hic obiter consideranda, vel potius deploranda venit multorum cæcitas, qui cum secundum Dei voluntatem in pace & beatè viuere possent, hoc tamen vnum agunt, vt incurabili contumacia suum illud saluberrimum excutiant, & suam voluntatem prauam atque noxias carnis cupiditates sequi malunt, quibus sibi ipsis omni genere curas, labores, pericula, turbas, & exitium accersunt, sicuti multis exemplis demonstrari poterat. Sed paucis nunc id attingimus, vt maiori ze-lo non precemur modo, vt Dei voluntas fiat, verumetiam reipsa hanc, quantum in nobis est, exequi studeamus.
units.tr: But that we must not pray that our will, which is depraved and harmful, be done, and that Christ bids us pray that the will of the Father in heaven be done, is because that will is just, holy, good and salutary, although we do not always see it. For how could he who is both the highest good and very righteousness will anything evil or unjust? Or by what reasoning would he who is the Father of us all, and who far surpasses all parents in love and indulgence, plan anything evil or harmful against us? Indeed, the flesh at times suggests these thoughts: that God deals too harshly with us, that his will is too rigid and his commandments intolerable, and that in his judgments he does not always keep true equity. But if (as Asaph warns) we enter into his sanctuary, and carefully consider together his mysteries, as far as they are revealed to us through the word, and the end of all things, it will straightway be plain that the will of God is not only just and good, but that in it all our salvation consists, so that it may be done and we may obey it. We have most evident arguments to prove this in the fall and restoration of the human race. For whence did the misery and calamity of all of us begin? Whence did evil desires, rivalry, envy, hatred, and finally cares and anxieties, together with many other things that trouble and torment the soul, take their origin? Whence the many and various diseases to which our bodies are subject? Whence that curse which hangs over the earth, so that it bears fruit only with much labour? Why are we born with such pain? Finally, whence come those various misfortunes that trouble us, and at last death itself, which carries us hence not without terror and most acute pains? The sole cause of all these things is that Adam, despising the will of God, followed his own will, which the serpent had suggested to him. This (I say) is the cause why we are subject to all those evils we have just mentioned, and why God daily punishes with famine, pestilence, wars and seditions those who obey his will less. On the other hand, what shall we say is the cause that these calamities and punishments do not bring us eternal destruction, but rather serve as chastisement, by which God corrects us as the best of fathers does? Why does God, reconciled to us again, pardon sins, protect us amid the storms of this age, and finally make us heirs of eternal happiness? Surely no other cause than the merit of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who by the will and decree of the Father humbled himself, and was obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. His obedience has, as it were, removed our disobedience from the midst, and has reconciled God to us, so that for the sake of this Son he is now gracious to us. Since therefore Adam's disobedience brought the curse, all calamities, and finally death and ruin, while Christ by his obedience has redeemed us, saved us, and made us heirs of the heavenly kingdom, it is altogether necessary that we pray from the heart that not our will but the will of God the Father be done, and that he grant us here such grace that we may conform ourselves to it and obey it. But here we must briefly consider, or rather lament, the blindness of many who, although they could live in peace and happiness according to the will of God, nevertheless strive for this one thing: to cast off that most salutary yoke with incurable obstinacy, and prefer to follow their own depraved will and the harmful lusts of the flesh, by which they bring upon themselves every kind of care, labour, danger, turmoil and ruin, as could be shown by many examples. But we touch on this only briefly here, so that with greater zeal we may not only pray that the will of God be done, but also strive to carry it out in deed, as far as lies in us.

units.la: Porro vt ad hoc præstandum promptiores simus, videndum erit, quæ nam illa Dei voluntas sit, vbi simul intelligemus, quis proprius huius petitionis sensus sit. Bifariam autem voluntas Dei consideratur. Primò voluntas est æterna, infinita & omnipotens, secundum quam omnia gubernat, & agit, sicuti ab æterno decreuit. Et hæc voluntas sit semper, adeò, vt nemo eam impedire possit, & eandem plerunque ignoramus, donec in illius operibus atque iudicijs sese exerit. De ista voluntate per Isaiam ipse loquitur: Ego sum Deus, qui dico, & consilium meum ratum est, & quicquid volo facio. Quò & illud Dauidus referri debet: Deus noster in cœlis est, & fecit quæcunque voluit. Item: Dei consilium manet in æternum. Et rursus Isaias: Domino exercituum aliquid constituente, quis illud faciet irritum? Et de hac quidem voluntate Dei non hic nobis sermo est. Quia enim æterna diuina prouidentia & prædestinationis decreta comprehendit, nunquam non suum habet progressum, neq; opus est, vt de eius executione multum soliciti simus. Hoc solum nostri officij est, ne illam accusemus aut reprehendamus, & ne eius arcana curiosius velimus scrutari.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that we may be more ready to accomplish this, we must consider what that will of God is, and at the same time we shall understand what the proper sense of this petition is. Now the will of God is considered in two ways. First, there is his will which is eternal, infinite and omnipotent, by which he governs and acts upon all things, as he has decreed from eternity. This will always is, so that no one can hinder it, and we are for the most part ignorant of it until it shows itself in his works and judgements. Isaiah speaks of this will: "I am God, who say it, and my counsel is established, and whatever I will I do." To this also should be referred what David says: "Our God is in the heavens, and has done whatever he pleased." Likewise: "The counsel of the Lord stands for ever." And again Isaiah: "When the Lord of hosts has determined something, who will make it void?" Yet it is not of this will of God that we are speaking here. For since it embraces the eternal divine providence and the decrees of predestination, it never fails to take its course, and there is no need for us to be much anxious about its execution. Our only duty in this respect is not to accuse or find fault with it, and not to be too curious in searching out its secrets.

units.la: Deinde voluntas alia Dei reuelata est, quà nos scire oportet, cũ absq; eius cognitione seruari non possimus. Hanc omnium clarissimè nobis reuelauit in Filio suo Iesu Christo, quæ catholicu & irrefra-gabile totius orbis doctore constituit, cœlitus de illo pronuntians: Hùc audite. Ideo Ioannes scribit: Deum nemo vidit vnquam, sed vnigenitus Filius Dei, qui est in sinu Patris, is annunciauit vobis. Et ipse discipulis ait: Omnia quæ audiui à Patre meo, manifestaui vobis. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi ab origine rerum vsq; ad Christi incarnationem nulla prorsus inter homines voluntatis diuinæ cognitio fuerit. Nam etsi ille, vt vera lux mundi, suo aduentu omnia plenius illustrauerit, & Dei Patris voluntatem non solùm clarius tradiderit, verumetiam impleuerit: idem tamen olim quoque veteribus, quantum ipsis ad salutem consequendam necesse fuit, illam manifestauit. Cùm patriarchis enim per visiones & revelationes varias egit. Deinde Legem dedit, quæ voluntatis diuinæ declarationem continet. Tandem per Prophetas locutus est, qui simul omnes (vt Petrus testatur) ipsius spiritu ducti eius afflictiones & inde secuturam gloriam scrutati sunt, & totum humanæ redemptionis negotium populo enarrauerunt. Tandem postquam ipse in terras hasce venit, & aliquandiu docuit, eo non contentus, in Apostolis suis Verbi aut Euangelij sui ministerium instituit, & adhuc Ecclesiæ ministros dat, qui Patris sui voluntatem mundo annuncient. Denique ipse æternum, viuum & omnipotens Dei Verbum est, per quod omnia condita sunt, & cuius virtute omnia conseruantur atque reguntur, quique nos etiam hodie illuminat, vt Patris sui voluntatem intelligamus. Dicuntur ista in eum finem, ne illius cognitionem alibi quæramus, sed in eius solius Verbum intenti, omnes hominum traditiones totis animis abominemur, quibus Satan Dei voluntatem & eius cognitionem in multorum animis obscurat, & sæpe omnino extinguit. Et de ista voluntate Dei, quæ in Christo nobis revelata est, petitio hæc potissimum debet intelligi, cuius hic usus & finis est, vt Deus nos in suæ voluntatis semitis dirigere, & animos nostros inclinare dignetur, vt illa delectentur, & eidem obtemperent. Sed præstat videre, quænam voluntatis istius præcipua sint capita, quibus tota comprehenditur.
units.tr: Secondly, there is another will of God, revealed, which we must know, since we cannot be saved without knowledge of it. He has revealed this most clearly of all to us in his Son Jesus Christ, whom he appointed as the catholic and infallible teacher of the whole world, declaring from heaven concerning him: "Hear him." Therefore John writes: "No one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known to you." And he himself says to his disciples: "All that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." This must not be understood as though from the beginning of the world until the incarnation of Christ there was absolutely no knowledge of the divine will among men. For although he, as the true light of the world, by his coming illuminated all things more fully, and not only delivered the will of God the Father more clearly but also fulfilled it, nevertheless he also in former times made it known to the ancients as far as was necessary for them to obtain salvation. For he dealt with the patriarchs through visions and various revelations. Then he gave the Law, which contains a declaration of the divine will. Finally he spoke through the Prophets, who, all of them led by his Spirit (as Peter testifies), searched out his sufferings and the glory that would follow, and set forth to the people the whole business of human redemption. Finally, after he himself came into these lands and taught for a while, not content with this, he instituted in his Apostles the ministry of his Word or Gospel, and still gives ministers to the Church who announce the will of his Father to the world. Lastly, he himself is the eternal, living and omnipotent Word of God, through whom all things were created, and by whose power all things are preserved and governed, and who still today enlightens us, so that we may understand the will of his Father. These things are said to this end: that we should not seek the knowledge of him elsewhere, but, being intent upon his Word alone, we should utterly abominate with all our hearts all the traditions of men, by which Satan darkens the will of God and its knowledge in the minds of many, and often altogether extinguishes it. And it is especially this will of God, revealed to us in Christ, that this petition ought to be understood to concern, the use and purpose of which is that God would deign to direct us in the paths of his will and to incline our hearts, so that we may delight in it and obey it. But it is well to see what the chief heads of that will are, by which it is wholly comprehended.

units.la: Primùm vult Deus, vt salui fiamus per Filium suum Iesum Christum. In eo enim (vt Paulus docet) nos ab æterno elegit, vt regni sui cœlestis hæredes simus. De hac voluntate Patris Christus ipse sic loquitur: Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui videt Filium, & in eum credit, habeat vitam æternam. Itaq; petitione ista ante omnia postulamus, vt Deus tam nos quàm alios homines fide in Christum illuminare dignetur, ne eius voluntas, quoad hanc partem nostra incrudelitate & contumacia impediatur. Vbi simul docemur, fidem donum Dei gratuitum esse, neque nostra industria aut viribus posse obtineri. Quòd Christus ipse non obscurè supra docuit, dicens: Nemo nouit Filium nisi Pater, & is cui Pater eum vult manifestare. Item: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Nam vt alibi monuimus, totum hoc Christi & humanæ redemptionis mysterium carni non obscurum modò, sed absurdum quoque & inutile videtur. Diuinitus ergo illuminemur oportet, vt petitio ista in nobis rata esse possit. Quòd si vero voluntas Dei est, vt per fidem in Christum seruemur, proprijs precibus seipsos damnant, qui per opera electitia & horum merita iustificationem & salutem obtinere conantur. Pugnant enim illi cum æterno Dei Patris consilio, siue decreto, quo vniuersam humanæ salutis rationem in solius Filij sui merito complexus est.
units.tr: First, God wills that we be saved through his Son Jesus Christ. For in him (as Paul teaches) he chose us from eternity, that we might be heirs of his heavenly kingdom. Christ himself speaks thus of this will of the Father: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life." Therefore by this petition we above all ask that God would deign to enlighten us and other men with faith in Christ, lest his will in this part be hindered by our cruelty and obstinacy. At the same time we are taught that faith is a free gift of God, and cannot be obtained by our own diligence or strength. Christ himself taught this plainly above, saying: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and he to whom the Father wills to reveal him." Likewise: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." For, as we have elsewhere observed, this whole mystery of Christ and of human redemption seems not only obscure to the flesh but also absurd and useless. We must therefore be enlightened from heaven, so that this petition may be fulfilled in us. But if indeed it is God's will that we be saved through faith in Christ, then those who strive to obtain justification and salvation through their own works and the merits of these condemn themselves by their own prayers. For they are at odds with the eternal counsel or decree of God the Father, by which he has embraced the whole plan of human salvation in the merit of his Son alone.

units.la: Secundò Dei voluntas est, vt quotquot per Filium eius redempti, & hunc fide amplexi sunt, se illi gratos & morigeros præbeant, atq; in ipsius præceptis ambulent. Nam qui præcepta eius seruat (inquit Ioannes) is in Deo manet, & Deus manet in ipso. Et Lex naturæ admonet, vt qui per sanguinem Filij Dei redempti sunt, illi se totos addicere & consecrare debeant. Possunt autem præcepta eius paucis comprehendi. Primò enim requirit, vt sicut ipse Deus vnicus est, nos quoque ipsum solum agnoscamus, solum colamus, timeamus & amemus supra omnia, ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & totis viribus nostris. Deinde vult, vt qui per Filium suum purificati & à peccatis abluti sumus, posthac ipsi simus consecrati, innocentiæ & puritati studeamus, neq; corpora nostra, quæ ille Spiritus Sancti templa fecit, peccatorum sordibus denuo prophanemus. Huc illa Pauli pertinent: Hæc est voluntas Dei, nempe sanctificatio vestra, vt abstineatis à fornicatione: & sciat vnusquisque vestrum vas suum possidere cum sanctificatione & honore: non cum morbo cupiditatis, sicut gentes quæ non nouerunt Deum. Idem alibi testatur, Deum nos ab æterno elegisse, vt quoad huius vitæ consuetudinem, inculpati simus & irreprehensibiles. Quò etiam in primis referri debet, quod Christus in vltima Cæna de pedibus itidem abluendis admonet. Vult ergo Deus, ne porrò priores carnis cupiditates sequamur, sed vt membra nostra terrestria mortificemus, veteri Adamo moriamur, & ad vitae nouitatem resurgamus, omne denique id pro virili fugiamus, quo homines pollui ac prophanari possunt. Vult praeterea Deus, vt sicuti ipsum supra omnia diligimus, ita propter ipsum proximos nostros perinde vt nos ipsos diligamus, & dilectionem hanc non ore & verbis modo, sed reipsa & factis declaremus. Hoc nouum illud & singulare praeceptum est, quod nobis Christus tradidit, qui nos multis aliis grauare noluit, cum vno hoc abunde comprehendatur, quicquid ad iustitiam & pacem inter homines conseruandam necessarium est. Itaque tribus hisce praeceptis, dilectionis Dei, sanctitatis, & mutuae charitatis, tota Dei voluntas continetur, cuius in hus vitae curriculo studere debemus. Precamur igitur hoc loco, vt Deus sua gratia nobis adsit, vt ipsum ex animo diligamus, sanctitatem & innocentiam colamus, proximum item eodem, quo nosipsos, amore prosequamur, denique vt vitam omnem secundum voluntatis eius sanctae regulam instituamus, vt ita ipsius voluntas in nobis fiat, carnus autem libido atque petulantia coerceatur, nosque toti sub fidei obedientiam redigamus. Rursus ergo cum suis precibus palam pugnant, qui circa alienos aut plures Deos occupantur, qui mundo potius quam illi seruiunt, qui corpora sua libidinibus vagis & omni intemperantiae genere polluunt, aut inuidiae, odio, priuati commodi studijs contrafas nefasque indulgent.
units.tr: Secondly, the will of God is that all who have been redeemed through his Son, and have embraced him by faith, should show themselves pleasing and obedient to him, and walk in his precepts. For "he who keeps his commandments," says John, "abides in God, and God in him." And the law of nature admonishes that those who have been redeemed by the blood of the Son of God ought to devote and consecrate themselves wholly to him. His precepts, moreover, can be summed up briefly. For first he requires that, as God himself is one, so we too should acknowledge him alone, worship him alone, fear and love him above all, with our whole heart, our whole soul, and all our strength. Then he wills that we who have been purified through his Son and washed from our sins should henceforth be consecrated to him, study innocence and purity, and not again defile our bodies, which he has made temples of the Holy Spirit, with the filth of sins. To this pertain those words of Paul: "This is the will of God, namely your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication; and let each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the lust of concupiscence, like the Gentiles who do not know God." He testifies elsewhere that God chose us from eternity so that we might be blameless and irreproachable in the conduct of this life. To this also should especially be referred what Christ, at the last Supper, teaches concerning the washing of feet. God therefore wills that we no longer follow our former fleshly lusts, but that we mortify our earthly members, die to the old Adam, and rise to the newness of life; and, in short, that we flee with all our strength everything by which men can be defiled and profaned. Furthermore, God wills that, as we love him above all, so for his sake we should love our neighbours as ourselves, and declare this love not only with mouth and words, but in deed and in fact. This is the new and singular commandment which Christ gave us, and he chose not to burden us with many others, since this one alone sufficiently comprehends whatever is necessary for preserving justice and peace among men. Thus in these three precepts, of the love of God, of holiness, and of mutual charity, the whole will of God is contained, which we ought to study throughout the course of this life. Therefore we here pray that God by his grace would be present with us, so that we may love him from the heart, cultivate holiness and innocence, pursue our neighbour likewise with the same love as ourselves, and finally order our whole life according to the holy rule of his will; so that his will may thus be done in us, and the lust and wantonness of the flesh be restrained, and we ourselves be brought wholly under the obedience of faith. Therefore those again openly contend against their own prayers who are occupied with strange or many gods, who serve the world rather than him, who defile their bodies with wandering lusts and every kind of intemperance, or who indulge in envy, hatred, and the pursuit of private advantage to the detriment of right and wrong alike.

units.la: Tertio voluntas Dei est, vt imagini Filij sui Iesu Christi conformes efficiamur, id est, vt sicut ille per crucem & diram mortis supplicium in gloriam suam ingressus est, nos quoque dum hic viuimus, cruci obnoxij simus, vt per hanc carne nostra domita, tandem caelestis Regni possessionem adeamus. Nam vt pater bonus liberos, quos diligit, castigat, ne petulantiores fiant: ita Deus multis ac variis calamitatibus nos tentari finit, ne carnis desideriis vincamur, sed potius illi resistere possimus. Quae causa est, quòd Christus suos discipulos ad crucem ferendam inuitat, & hanc quotidie in humeros attollere iubet, innuens nimirum, hanc nunquam defuturam ijs, qui in ipso pie viuere volunt. Et Paulus sic a Deo constitutum esse ait, vt per multas tribulationes nos in Regnum eius ingredi oporteat. Debet autem hoc de omnibus aduersis intelligi, quae in hoc seculo nobis accidere solent: qualia sunt, egestas, fames, morbi, ignominia, persecutio, carceres, & denique ipsa mors. Quae omnia non sine Dei prouidentia immittuntur, qui capillos quoque nostros in numerato habet. Ista ergo petitione omne id postulamus, quo nobis sub cruce laborantibus opus est: vt nimirum Deus nobis fidem & patientiam largiri velit, ne aduersus ipsum murmuremus, sed eius voluntati nos totos submittamus. Et hic quidem suo exemplo nobis Christus praeiuit, qui cum pro assumpta carnis infirmitate imminentis supplicij atrocitate commoueretur, orauit: Pater, si possibile est, auferàme hunc calicem: veruntamen non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat. Quae verba facile quidem ore & labijs enuntiantur, sed quàm difficulter caro adducatur, vt ea vere & ex animo proferamus, quotidie experimur, si vel morbo aliquo diuturniori tentemur. Nec enim fieri potest, vt quis istud vere precetur, nisi prius seipsum prorsus abnegauerit. Petimus praeterea, vt ea gratia nos Deus dignetur, ne impiorum & hostium eius successibus laetis offendamur. Est hoc vitium admodum vulgare, vt hus vitis, & simul perspecta indigna piorum sorte, Dei iudicia accusemus, vel saltem perplexi de ijs dubitemus. Exempla huius in electis quoque, imo in Prophetis ipsis habemus, vt pote Asapho, Ieremia, Habakuko & multis aliis. At si quid huius accidit, mox in mentem reuocemus, Deum iustum & fidelem, adhaec Deum vltorem & remuneratorem esse, qui & culturibus suis promissa praemia retribuat, & hostes suos pro meritis ipsorum puniat. Haec si digne expendamus, mox ad quauis ferenda parati erimus, & ex animo poterimus dicere: O Pater, etsi tua iudicia carnis rationi absurda videntur, te tamen iustum & bonum esse scimus, qui nostrae saluti consuluit velis. Tu nouisti, cur impijs tantum indulgeas, nos autem cruce & aduersis exerceas. Age, tua voluntas fiat. Da modo ô Pater, vt & te cognoscamus, & patientia armati malis omnibus superiores simus, nec vspiam a tua voluntatis via declinemus.
units.tr: Third, God's will is that we be made conformed to the image of his Son Jesus Christ: that just as he entered into his glory through the cross and the dreadful punishment of death, so we too, while we live here, should be subject to the cross, so that, with our flesh tamed by it, we may at last come into possession of the heavenly kingdom. For just as a good father disciplines the children he loves, lest they become more wayward, so God allows us to be tested by many and various calamities, so that we are not overcome by the desires of the flesh but may be able rather to resist them. This is why Christ invites his disciples to bear the cross and bids them lift it on their shoulders every day, clearly signifying that it will never be lacking to those who wish to live godly lives in him. Paul also says that God has so ordained that we must enter his kingdom through many tribulations. This ought to be understood of all the adversities that usually befall us in this world: such as poverty, hunger, sickness, disgrace, persecution, prisons, and finally death itself. All these are sent not without God's providence, who even has our hairs numbered. In this petition, therefore, we ask for everything we need while labouring under the cross: that is, that God would be pleased to grant us faith and patience, so that we do not murmur against him but submit ourselves wholly to his will. Christ himself went before us in this with his own example: when, moved by the frailty of the flesh he had taken on and by the dreadfulness of the punishment that threatened him, he prayed: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done." These words are easily spoken with the mouth and lips, but how hard it is for the flesh to be brought to speak them truly and from the heart, we learn every day if we are tested by some lingering illness. Indeed, no one can truly pray this unless he has first wholly denied himself. We also ask that God would deign to grant us the grace not to be offended by the prosperous successes of the impious and his enemies. This is a very common fault: when we see the unworthy lot of the godly, we accuse God's judgments, or at least, perplexed, we doubt them. We have examples of this among the elect, indeed among the prophets themselves, such as Asaph, Jeremiah, Habakkuk and many others. But if anything of this kind happens to us, let us at once call to mind that God is just and faithful, and moreover that he is an avenger and rewarder, who will repay the promised rewards to his worshippers and punish his enemies according to their deserts. If we weigh these things rightly, we will at once be ready to bear whatever comes, and will be able to say from the heart: "O Father, although your judgments seem absurd to human reason, we know that you are just and good, who have provided for our salvation. You know why you indulge the wicked so much, but exercise us with the cross and adversities. Come, let your will be done. Only grant, O Father, that we may both know you, and, armed with patience, may rise above all evils, and never turn aside anywhere from the way of your will."

units.la: Est hic praecipuus huius petitionis vsus, vt ea nos aduersus afflictionum atq; huius seculi scam dala consolemur: & proinde tunc maxime proferri debet, quando sub cruce & aduersis laboramus. Cum enim diuitijs abundamus, in honore & pretio sumus, valetudine integra fruimur, & feliciter nobis omnia succedunt, facile est dicere, Tua voluntas fiat, Domine. Nec enim alia Dei voluntas nobis tas nobis ob oculos versatur, quàm quae carni quoq; suavis & iucunda est. At quando diutius mor bis confecti contabescimus, à plerisq; contemnimur, iniurias & persecutiones sustinemus, cruce deniq; perpetua fatigamur, tunc demum sentimus, quàm grave & difficile sit id ex animo dicere. Atqui ut ita precemur, & quidem ex animo sic precemur, omnino necesse est. Itaq; in diligenti divinae voluntatis meditatione nos indesinenter versari convenit, ut sciamus, quàm bona, utilis, salutaris & plena consolationis illa sit, & proinde afflictiones omnes facilius superemus.
units.tr: This is the chief use of this petition: that it comforts us against the afflictions and the troubles of this world, and so it ought to be uttered most of all when we labour under the cross and adversity. For when we abound in riches, are held in honour and esteem, enjoy sound health, and all things go well for us, it is easy to say, "Your will be done, Lord." For the will of God that is before our eyes is then only that which is also sweet and pleasant to the flesh. But when we waste away for a long time, worn out by sickness, are despised by most people, suffer wrongs and persecutions, and are finally wearied by a lasting cross, then at last we feel how hard and difficult it is to say this from the heart. Yet if we are to pray in this way, and indeed to pray from the heart, it is absolutely necessary. Therefore we ought to be constantly engaged in careful meditation on the divine will, so that we may know how good, useful, salutary and full of consolation it is, and so overcome all afflictions more easily.

units.la: Porrò modum quoque exprimere docet Christus, quem in voluntate sua in nobis perficienda Deus observare debeat, ut intelligamus, quousque petitio haec extendatur. Dicimus enim: Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in coelo, etiam in terra. Nec sine causa id adjicitur. Ita enim admonet Dominus, quàm perfectam Deo obedientiam debeamus: talem nimirum, qualē coelestes creaturae illi praestant: inter quas nihil invenitur, quod voluntati divinae repugnet. In coelis etenim sunt Angeli, qui iam inde ab origine rerum in veritate perstiterunt, & (ut Daniel scribit) in conspectu Dei perpetuo apparent, ut huic serviant. Ut ergo Deus homines vult salvos fieri: ita illi quoque hominum salute gaudent, & Christo teste exultant, quoties peccator aliquis conversus resipiscit. Et quia spiritus sunt ministrantes, qui ad electorum ministerium emittuntur, salutem quoque nostram promovent, circa nos castrametantur, nos defendunt, & adversus Ecclesiae hostes iudicia Dei sedulo exequuntur: cuius rei exempla cum privata tum publica Scripturae passim proponunt. Praeterea, ut Deus nomen suum sanctificari & celebrari vult: ita Angeli quoq; hoc ipsum fieri summo studio curant, adeo, ut ipsis intolerabile sit, si quis vel ipsos colere, adorare, aut aliis honoribus divinis prosequi velit. Exemplum habes in eo Angelo, qui Ioanni Apostolo regni Christi mysteria & Ecclesiae fata exposuit. Denique tanta est Angelorum industria & obedientia, ut nihil illis tam incundum sit, quàm Dei voluntatem exequi.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ also teaches us to express the measure which God ought to observe in perfecting his will in us, so that we may understand how far this petition extends. For we say: "Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth." Nor is this added without cause. For the Lord thus reminds us how perfect an obedience we owe to God: namely such as the heavenly creatures render to him, among whom nothing is found that resists the divine will. For in heaven are the angels, who from the beginning of things have stood fast in the truth and (as Daniel writes) appear continually in the sight of God to serve him. Therefore, just as God wills that men be saved, so the angels also rejoice in the salvation of men, and, as Christ bears witness, they exult whenever a sinner is converted and repents. And since they are ministering spirits, who are sent out for the ministry of the elect, they also promote our salvation, encamp around us, defend us, and diligently carry out the judgments of God against the enemies of the Church. Scripture sets forth examples of this everywhere, both private and public. Furthermore, just as God wills his name to be sanctified and celebrated, so the angels also take the greatest care that this very thing be done, so much so that it would be intolerable to them if anyone wished to worship them, adore them, or pay them any other divine honours. You have an example of this in the angel who explained to the apostle John the mysteries of Christ's kingdom and the fates of the Church. In short, the diligence and obedience of the angels is so great that nothing is so pleasant to them as to carry out the will of God.

units.la: In coelis quoque sunt electorum, qui ex hac vita decesserunt, spiritus vel animae: quae cum in Dei conspectu (ut David inquit) satietate gaudiorum fruantur, liberae autem sint ab omnibus humani seculi curis atque laboribus: nulla etiam propria aut peculiari voluntate ducuntur, sed divinae adsentiuntur, huic se accommodant, Deo in omnibus suis operibus atque iudicijs laudem & honorem tribuunt. Nec enim ignorant, hunc aeterna sua providentia res omnes iustè, bene & ad salutem hominum instituisse. Typum huius rei elegantissimum Apocalypsis seu Revelatio Iesu Christi Ioanni facta, in libro septem sigillis obsignato & viginti quatuor Senioribus exhibet. Per librum enim providentia Dei adumbratur, quae omnia quae fieri debent, comprehendit, & ab aeterno ad finem suum destinavit. Librum istum nemo aperire potest praeter Agnum, qui est Dei Filius, Iesus Christus. Nam huic data est omnis potestas in coelo & in terra, ideoq; omnia regit, neque aliquid praeter suam voluntatem fieri patitur. Huic & liber datur, ut illum resignatis sigillis aperiat, viginti quatuor Seniores (qui vniversam beatorum & electorum cum Veteris cum Novi Testamenti Ecclesiam adumbrant) coram throno & Agno procidunt, hunc laudant & celebrant, gaudent denique & exultant, omnia secundum Dei decretum & ex Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi administratione fieri.
units.tr: In heaven there are also the spirits or souls of the elect who have departed from this life. Since (as David says) they enjoy in God's sight the fullness of joys, and are free from all the cares and labours of the human world, they are not led by any will of their own or private desire, but assent to the divine will, accommodate themselves to it, and ascribe praise and honour to God in all his works and judgments. For they do not fail to know that he has ordered all things by his eternal providence justly, well and for the salvation of men. The Apocalypse, or Revelation of Jesus Christ made to John, presents a most elegant type of this in the book sealed with seven seals and in the twenty-four Elders. For the book signifies the providence of God, which comprehends all things that must come to pass and has determined them from eternity to their end. No one can open this book except the Lamb, who is the Son of God, Jesus Christ. For to him all power in heaven and on earth has been given, and therefore he governs all things and allows nothing to happen apart from his own will. To him also the book is given, so that he may open it when the seals are loosed; the twenty-four Elders (who represent the whole Church of the blessed and elect, of the Old and New Testament) fall down before the throne and the Lamb, praise and celebrate him, and finally rejoice and exult that all things are done according to God's decree and by the administration of our Saviour Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Angeli & electorum spiritus in vnius Dei voluntate acquiescunt: ita non minus aliae quoque coelestes creaturae huic obtemperant. Coeli motus perpetuus & certus est, quae lem Deus iam inde ab origine rerum constituit. Similiter Sol, Luna & astra reliqua ordinem sibi praescriptum constanter servant. Ver amoenum atque floridum, sicca & arida Aestas, pomifer Aurumnus & glacialis Hyems, secundum Solis cursum certis vicibus quotannis redeunt. Denique etsi ordo istorum omnium iam annis amplius quinq; milibus & sexcentis duraverit, adhuc tamen stabilis manet, neque ullum horum leges sibi à Deo praescriptas transgreditur. Caelum praeterea prout Deo visum fuerit, pluvias destillat, nives spargit, pruinas congelat, grandines & fulmina emiculatur, frigus item & aestum sive calorem distribuit: ut ne in bus quidem aliquid fortuito aut absque Dei providentia accidat.
units.tr: Just as the angels and the spirits of the elect rest in the will of the one God alone, so the other heavenly creatures likewise obey it no less. The motion of the heavens is perpetual and certain, as God established it from the beginning of things. Likewise the Sun, Moon and the remaining stars constantly keep the order prescribed to them. The pleasant and flowery spring, the dry and parched summer, the fruitful autumn and the icy winter return at fixed seasons each year according to the course of the Sun. Finally, although the order of all these things has now lasted for more than five thousand six hundred years, it still remains stable, and none of them transgresses the laws prescribed to it by God. Moreover, the sky, as it pleases God, distils rains, scatters snows, freezes hoarfrosts, hurls hailstones and lightning bolts, and likewise distributes cold and heat: so that not even in these things does anything happen by chance or apart from God's providence.

units.la: Haec si diligentius considerentur, verus petitionis istius sensus nobis patebit, & à nobis requiri intelligemus obedientiam perfectam, qua nostram voluntatem divinae subjiciamus, adeo, ut nihil optemus, postulemus aut velimus, quàm quod Deum velle, & huic placere novimus. At quo magis
units.tr: If these things are considered more carefully, the true sense of this petition will become clear to us, and we will understand that what is required of us is perfect obedience, by which we subject our own will to the divine will, so that we desire, ask for and wish nothing except what we know God wills and is pleased with.

units.la: Obedientia perfecta requiritur. in horum consideratione versabimur, eò luculentius vitiosum nostrae naturae ingenium deprehende mus, quo non pellicimur modò, verum etiam cogimur & impellimur, ut ea cupiamus & velimus, quae cum Dei voluntate pugnant. Nam etsi in petitione ista terrae mentio fiat, de solis tamen hominibus agitur, qui soli inter terrestres creaturas Deo inobedientes atq; rebelles sunt, reliquis omnibus suam stationem firmiter tenentibus, & officium facientibus, ad quod a Deo destinatae sunt. Terra siquidem culturam patienter admittit, ut tam hominibus quam reliquis animantibus victum suum depromat. Aqua currsum & fluxum suum servat, ut reliqua humectet & recreet. Ignis calore suo omnia perpetuo fovet. Aër motum suum servat, ut per ipsum creaturae etiam reliquae feruentur. Arbores tempore praefinito fructus ferunt. Animalia bruta a Deo data legibus obediunt. Ciconia, hirundo, grus, norunt tempus suum, quo venire & abire debent. Equus, etsi robore & celeritate hominem longe vincat, huic tamen obedit, frenum & calcaria admittit. Idem in bobus cornigeris, in asinis quantumuis natura contumacibus, in superbis camelis, voracibus vrsis, saevis leonibus, aflutis serpentibus, aquilis item altiuolantibus, denique animalibus vniuersis cernimus, quod hominem pro suo domino & principe agnoscunt, & praeter ingenium suum sese subigi atque circurari patiuntur, homini denique (quoniam ita Deo visum est) ad necessarios simul vsus & ad voluptatem seruiunt. Solus homo sui officii immemor, Dei quoq; & Creatoris sui obliuiscitur, voluntatem eius fastidit, suis autem cupiditatibus delectatur, quibus deceptus quotidie peccat, & sibijpsi exitium accersit. Taceo eos, qui Dei voluntatem prorsus ignorant, & eandem ne discere quidem volunt. Merito igitur hanc nostram corruptionem deplorare, & perpetuò ad Deum clamare debemus, ut prauam hanc voluntatem in nobis frangat, nouam verò & sanctam creet, ne in nostra hac contumacia atque rebellione miserabiliter pereamus.
units.tr: Perfect obedience is required. The more closely we examine these matters, the more clearly we perceive the faulty nature of our own disposition, which is not only enticed but actually compelled and driven to desire and will the things that are contrary to God's will. For although the petition mentions the earth, it concerns human beings alone, who are the only earthly creatures that are disobedient and rebellious towards God, while all the rest firmly keep their place and perform the duty for which God appointed them. The earth patiently admits cultivation, so that it yields its produce for humans and the other living things alike. Water keeps its course and flow, to moisten and refresh the rest. Fire constantly warms all things with its heat. The air keeps its motion, so that the other creatures also are sustained by it. Trees bear fruit at the appointed time. The brute animals obey the laws given them by God. The stork, the swallow and the crane know the time when they must come and go. The horse, although it far surpasses man in strength and speed, nevertheless obeys him, and accepts the bridle and spurs. The same is seen in horned oxen, in asses, however stubborn by nature, in proud camels, greedy bears, savage lions, cunning serpents, and likewise in high-flying eagles; in short, we see all animals recognise man as their lord and prince, and suffer themselves to be subdued and controlled, beyond their own nature, and at last serve man, as God has willed, both for necessary uses and for pleasure. Man alone, forgetful of his duty, also forgets God, his Creator; he scorns his will, and delights in his own lusts, by which he is deceived and sins every day, and brings ruin upon himself. I say nothing of those who utterly ignore the will of God and do not even wish to learn it. Rightly, therefore, we ought to lament this corruption of ours and cry out to God continually, that he would break this perverse will in us and create in us a new and holy one, lest in this our obstinacy and rebellion we perish wretchedly.

units.la: Sed priusquam tractationem hanc concludamus, videndum erit, de quibus praeterea nos petitio ista admoneat. Et primò quidem, cum precemur, ut Dei voluntas in terris hisce, perinde ut in caelis fiat, non obscurè fatemur atque testamur, Deum non caeli modò, verum etiam terra Dominum atque gubernatorem esse. Quod propter eos obseruandum est, qui sibijpsis Deum fingunt, qui caelestia sola curet, terras autem & quae in his geruntur prorsus negligat. Quae sententia omnis nequitiae & impietatis fons atque origo est, ut quae omnem timorem Dei in hominum animis restinguit: quod Dauid in Psalmis aliquoties euidenter docet. At quis huius petitionis vsus esset, si Deus nos in terris agentes non curaret? At cum precemur, ut illius voluntas in terris quoque fiat, patet vtique hanc sese in terras quoque & ad homines extendere. Et ideò Dauid alibi rectè ait: Domini est terra & plenitudo eius. Ista autem petitione seipsos damnant, quotquot deuoto ad peccandum animo sibi persuadent, se Deo obedientiam aut obsequium non debere.
units.tr: But before we conclude this discussion, we must consider what else this petition reminds us of. And first, when we pray that God's will may be done on earth as it is in heaven, we plainly confess and testify that God is the Lord and governor not only of heaven but also of the earth. This must be observed on account of those who fashion for themselves a God who cares only for heavenly things and utterly neglects the earth and what happens upon it. This opinion is the source and origin of all wickedness and impiety, since it extinguishes in men's minds all fear of God; David clearly teaches this in the Psalms on several occasions. But what would be the use of this petition if God did not care for us as we live on earth? And since we pray that his will may be done on earth also, it is surely evident that his will extends to the earth and to men. Hence David rightly says elsewhere: "The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof" (Ps. 24.1). Those condemn themselves by this petition, all who, with a mind set on sinning, persuade themselves that they owe no obedience or service to God.

units.la: Admonemur deinde hoc loco, nostri officii esse, ut cognitioni voluntatis diuinae diligenter studeamus, & ut alij quoque plures in ea proficiant, authores simus. Fieri enim nequit, ut voluntati Dei obtemperent, qui eam ignorant. Nisi ergo Deum hypocrisi & simulatis precibus offendere libeat, hic nobis studiorum omnium finis sit, ut Dei voluntas ab omnibus cognoscatur, & eidem omnes obediant. Vbi praecipuè eos sui officij meminisse oportet, quos Deus, ut alijs praesint, constituit: quales sunt omnes, qui rempublicam administrant, Ecclesiarum praefecti & doctores, parentes, paedagogi, & qui in scholis iuuentutem instituunt. Quia enim haec petitio omnibus communis est, aequum sane, imò necessarium fuerit, ut eos, qui nobis ex peculiari Dei instituto crediti sunt, quantum in nobis est, in diuinae voluntatis cognitionem adducamus. Quapropter qui in magistratu sunt, sanam Verbi Dei doctrinam pro viribus promouere, doctores eandem fideliter annuntiare, parentes quoq; suos priuatim instituere, omnes autem simul in hoc incumbere debent, ut singuli vitam suam omnem secundùm Dei voluntatem instituant. Qui enim in eo negligentes fuerint, ijs petitio haec in iustae damnationis testimonium feruit.
units.tr: We are then reminded in this place that it is our duty to study diligently the knowledge of the divine will, and to be the cause of its being advanced in many others as well. For those who do not know God's will cannot possibly obey it. Unless, therefore, we are pleased to offend God by hypocrisy and feigned prayers, let this be the end of all our studies: that the will of God be known by all, and that all obey it. Here especially those ought to remember their duty whom God has set over others: such as all who administer the commonwealth, the rulers and teachers of the churches, parents, tutors, and those who teach youth in schools. For since this petition is common to all, it is surely fair, indeed necessary, that we should, as far as lies in us, bring to the knowledge of the divine will those who have been entrusted to us by a special appointment of God. Therefore those who hold magistracy ought to advance the sound doctrine of God's Word as far as they can; teachers ought to announce it faithfully; parents too ought to instruct their own children privately; and all together ought to labour at this, that each one should order his whole life according to God's will. For those who are negligent in this, this petition serves as a testimony of their just condemnation.

units.la: Quòd si verò hic periclitatur, qui sola negligentia & socordia peccant, quanto infelicior illorum fors erit, qui Dei voluntati sese scientes opponunt, cognitione eius obscurant, homines quò minus Deo obtemperent, abstrahunt, imò contra eius voluntatem & Verbum multa facere violenter cogunt? In horum numero sunt falsi doctores, qui humanis figmentis auditores a fide & vero Dei cultu abducunt. Principes
units.tr: But if those are in danger who sin through mere negligence and sloth, how much more wretched will be the fate of those who knowingly set themselves against the will of God, obscure its knowledge, draw men away from obeying God, and even violently compel them to do many things against God's will and Word? Among their number are the false teachers, who lead their hearers away from faith and the true worship of God by human inventions. Princes

units.la: cipes pes item & magistratus, qui Dei verbū palàm persequuntur, & aduersus omnes eos iniusta & cru-deli tyrannide sauiunt, qui in fidei & religionis negotio, atq; toto vitæ suæ curriculo, Dei voluntatem studiose obseruant. Est tyrannus ista tam vulgaris nostro seculo, vt multi reges & principes omnium hominum pestilentissimos sceleratissimosq; iudicent eos, qui præ aliis Deo obtemperare & obedire sludent. Debent hi parentes quoq; adnumerari, qui liberos suos in superstitionibus instituunt, & à pueritia statim ad idololatriā & aperta scelera assuefaciunt. Omnes deniq; qui proximos suos ad peccandū inuitant, & quocunq; modo illis authores sunt, quò minus diuina voluntatis præcepta sequantur. Væ istis omnibus. Quàm enim graue & horrendum supplicium subire eos necesse & instum est, qui ore quidem dicunt, Fiat ô Pater, voluntas tua, sicut in cælo, etiā in terra: interim verò voluntatem Dei, nobis in Scripturis reuelatam hostiliter persequuntur, studiaq; & consilia sua omnia so dirigunt, ne illa suum progressum possit habere? Hi (inquam) omnes cum seruo illo nequam ex proprio ore iudicabuntur, cum quod ore loquuntur, factis improbis oppugnent.
units.tr: Princes likewise and magistrates, who openly persecute the Word of God and rage with unjust and cruel tyranny against all those who zealously observe God's will in matters of faith and religion and throughout the whole course of their lives. Such tyranny is so common in our age that many kings and princes judge those who strive to obey and obey God more than others to be the most pestilent and wicked of all men. Parents must also be counted among these, who bring up their children in superstitions and from infancy accustom them to idolatry and open crimes. Finally, all who invite their neighbours to sin, and in any way are the cause of their not following the precepts of the divine will. Woe to all of them. For how grievous and dreadful a punishment must they undergo, and how justly, who indeed say with their mouths, "Father, your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth," yet meanwhile hostilely persecute the will of God revealed to us in the Scriptures, and direct all their efforts and plans so that it may not make progress? These, I say, will all be judged by their own mouth, like that wicked servant, since they oppose by wicked deeds what they utter with their lips.

units.la: Postremò nos misera & infelicis conditionis, quā in hoc seculo sustinemus, hæc petitio admonet. Dum enim quotidie petimus, vt Dei voluntas in terra fiat, fatemur simul hanc inter homines minimus hucusque obseruatam esse, & quòd inter eos vitam degamus, qui Deo rebelles, huius voluntati audaciter resistunt. Eadem ergo nostra conditio est, quæ olim Lothi fuit, qui (vt Petrus scribit) in Sodomis agens animam suam iustam indies excruciabat, cum fœdissima illorum scelera subinde videre, & obscœna impiaq; dicta audire cogeretur. Et vt probus fidusq; subditus, non potest non toto animo discruciari, si inter homines seditiosos viuere cogatur, qui à principe suo legitimo iniustam defectionem fecerunt: ita doleat & gemat oportet homo verè Christianus, quoties videt, sibi inter eos viuendum esse, qui non solùm non obtemperant voluntati Dei, verumetiā aduersus hunc Creatorem & Patrem nostrum fidelissimum, impudenter insurgere audent. Iure ergo sluli censentur, quos huius seculi vitæ & mundi consuetudo tantopere delectat, vt interea æternæ & cœlestis patriæ nulla cura tangantur. Hi certè Spiritum filiorum Dei nondum apprehenderunt. Quis enim bona indoles filius eorum consuetudine delectatur, à quibus patrem suum omni conuitiorum genere proscindi audit? Quæ ratio ergo iubet, vt germanus Dei filius censeatur, qui mundū hunc diligit, in quo Deus quotidie diris blasphemijs quasi obruitur, & eius sanĉta voluntas sædissimè conculcatur? Debet nos horum consideratio excitare, vt ad æternā atq; cœlestem patriam aspiremus, in qua secundùm Patris nostri voluntatem omnia fiunt, & vbi nihil videre vel audire cogemur, quoд illic nobis parata gaudia interturbet.
units.tr: Lastly, this petition reminds us of the wretched and unhappy condition which we endure in this world. For while we daily pray that God's will be done on earth, we at the same time confess that it has so far been observed very little among men, and that we live among those who are rebellious against God and boldly resist his will. Our condition is therefore the same as that of Lot of old, who (as Peter writes) dwelling in Sodom vexed his righteous soul day by day, being compelled to see their most foul crimes from time to time and to hear obscene and impious words (2 Pet. 2.7–8). And just as a good and faithful subject cannot but be tormented in his whole mind if he is compelled to live among seditious men who have unjustly revolted from their lawful prince, so a man who is truly Christian ought to grieve and groan whenever he sees that he must live among those who not only do not obey the will of God but also dare to rise up shamelessly against this Creator and our most faithful Father. Rightly, therefore, are they judged foolish whom the life of this age and the customs of the world so delight that they are meanwhile untouched by any care for the eternal and heavenly fatherland. Such people have certainly not yet laid hold of the Spirit of the sons of God. For what well-born son delights in the company of those by whom he hears his father torn to pieces with every kind of reproach? What reason, then, requires that he be counted a true son of God who loves this world, in which God is daily almost overwhelmed with dreadful blasphemies, and his holy will is most shamefully trampled underfoot? This consideration ought to stir us to aspire to the eternal and heavenly fatherland, where all things are done according to the will of our Father, and where we shall be compelled to see and hear nothing that disturbs the joys prepared for us there.

units.la: Hæc in tertiam Orationis Dominicæ petitionem dicta sint, quæ eo maiori diligentia considerari debent, quòd omnis nostra salus ex eo dependet, vt diuinæ voluntati obsequamur. Memineremus ergo, voluntatem nostram prauam esse, & proinde necessarium esse, vt nos diuinæ ex toto cor de subijciamus. Nec enim ad cœlestis vitæ hæreditatem peruenire licebit, nisi secundùm cœlestium spirituum & creaturarum exemplum Deo per omnia obtemperemus. Quia verò caro nostra infirma, tarda, imò etiam contumax est, indesinenter nos precari conuenit, vt Deus animos nostros suæ voluntatis cognitione & amore illuminet, vt huic obediamus, & postquam huius vitæ cursum emensi sumus, in cœlis viuere, & cum sanĉto illo cœlitum choro lætus laudibus celebrare possimus Dominum & redemptorem nostrum Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things have been said on the third petition of the Lord's Prayer, which must be considered with all the more care because our whole salvation depends on it, that we obey the divine will. Let us therefore remember that our own will is depraved, and that it is therefore necessary for us to submit ourselves wholeheartedly to the divine will. For we shall not be able to attain the inheritance of the heavenly life unless we obey God in all things, after the example of the heavenly spirits and creatures. But since our flesh is weak, slow, and indeed even stubborn, we ought to pray without ceasing that God would enlighten our minds with the knowledge and love of his will, so that we may obey it, and that, once we have run the course of this life, we may live in the heavens and, with that holy choir of the heavenly ones, joyfully celebrate with praises the Lord and Redeemer our Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CX.
units.tr: HOMILY CX.

units.la: PETITIO IIII.
units.tr: THE FOURTH PETITION.

units.la: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis in diem.
units.tr: Give us this day our daily bread.

units.la: QVoniam Deus hominem ex mera gratia secundùm suam imaginē initiò condidit, eamq; in nobis peccato corruptam & deletam per Filium suum instaurauit, & nos priori dignitati restituit, nostrum officium atque munus est, Dei tam benigni Patris gloriam ante omnia quærere & pro virili nostra promouere. Huius nos Christus quoque per ordinem orationis suæ admonet. Nam primus tribus petitionibus nos ea postulare docet, quæ ad Deum præcipuè spectant: vt nimirum eius nomen in nobis sanctificetur, vt Regnum eius in mundo propagetur & extendatur indies, & vt quotquot in terris adhuc viuunt, ipsius voluntati obtemperent. Quæ non ita accipi debent, quasi ita ad Deum spectent, vt nihil inde fructus aut boni ad nos redeat. Quin potius in his elucet communio, quam cum Deo habemus, quando tunc nobis & saluti nostræ in primis consulitur, cùm Dei gloria & Regnum augentur, & in eius voluntate nos acquiescimus. Etenim cùm nos ille filiorum loco habeat, nobiscum quoque bona sua communia habere cupit. Hoc autem præcipuè nos ordo iste docet, ne vt sui amantes solent, nostra modò quæramus, sed potius Dei gloriam pra omnibus aliis rebus nobis habeamus commendatam. Sequuntur nunc reliquæ petitiones, quæ peculiariter ad nos pertinent, & plenissimè omnia ea comprehendunt, quæ nobis in hoc seculo viuentibus ad corporis simul & animæ salutem necessaria sunt, quæcunque item nos in tentationum palæstra consolari atque fidem nostram confirmare possunt. Inter eas petitiones prima (aliàs quarta ordine) est, quam modò recitauimus: PANEM NO- STRVM QVOTIDIANVM da nobis in diem. Et hæc quidem inter eas, quæ ad nos spectant, non temere primo loco ponitur. Quia enim in Dei conspectum vt eius filij venimus, iure ab eo panem petimus: & quia eius nomen atq; Regnum illustrare & promouere cupimus, adhæc obedientiam & obsequium omne illi offerimus, æquum est, vt ille nobis de victu & reliquis neces- sarijs prospiciat. Vt verò petitionem hanc rectius intelligamus, singula eius verba diligentius nobis consideranda erunt.
units.tr: Since God in his pure grace first created man in his own image, and has restored that image in us through his Son, after it was corrupted and destroyed by sin, and has returned us to our former dignity, it is our duty and calling above all to seek the glory of God, so kind a Father, and to advance it as far as we are able. Christ also reminds us of this in the order of his prayer. For in the first three petitions he teaches us to ask for those things that concern God chiefly: namely, that his name may be sanctified in us, that his kingdom may be spread and extended in the world day by day, and that all who still live on earth may obey his will. These petitions should not be understood as if they concern God in such a way that no fruit or good comes back to us from them. Rather, the fellowship we have with God shines forth in them, since our own salvation is chiefly served when God's glory and kingdom are increased and we rest in his will. For since he regards us as his children, he wishes to share his goods with us as well. This order teaches us especially that we should not, like those who love only themselves, seek only our own affairs, but rather hold the glory of God committed to us before all other things. Now follow the remaining petitions, which pertain to us in particular and fully comprehend all those things that are necessary for us, living in this world, for the salvation of both body and soul, and likewise all those things that can comfort us in the contest of temptations and confirm our faith. Among these petitions the first (fourth in order) is the one we have just recited: GIVE US THIS DAY OUR DAILY BREAD. This petition is rightly placed first among those that concern us, and not without reason. For since we come before the sight of God as his sons, we rightly ask bread from him; and since we desire to glorify and advance his name and kingdom, and besides offer him all obedience and service, it is fitting that he should provide us with food and the other necessities of life. To understand this petition more correctly, we must consider each of its words more carefully.

units.la: Vbi primo loco PANIS vocabulum occurrit, quem nobis dari petimus. Per hoc Hebræi vniuersum hominis victum & quæcunq; ad eius conseruationem requiruntur intelligunt: quod multis scripturæ locis demonstrari poterat, nisi hoc satis notum esset omnibus, qui illam vel à primo limine salutarunt. Scopus ergo & summa huius petitionis est, vt Deus in hac vita degentibus victum & quæcunq; præter hunc nobis necessaria sunt, ex paterni amoris benignitate largiri digne tur. At cùm homo duabus partibus constet, Anima nimirum & Corpore, duplici etiam cibo opus est, quo totus ali atq; conseruari possit.
units.tr: First, the word BREAD occurs, which we ask to be given to us. By this word the Hebrews understand the whole sustenance of man and everything required for its preservation. This could be shown from many passages of Scripture, were it not already sufficiently known to everyone who has greeted Scripture even from its threshold. The aim and sum of this petition, therefore, is that God would deign, out of the kindness of a Father's love, to bestow upon us who live in this life our food and whatever else is needful besides it. But since man consists of two parts, namely soul and body, he needs a twofold food by which the whole man may be nourished and preserved.

units.la: Anima spiritus est, & ideò eius cibum quoque spiritualem esse oportet. Is proprie est æternum illud & omnipotens Dei verbum, Iesus Christus, qui animas nostras merito suæ mortis, in qua carnem suam dedit pro mundi vita, Verbo denique & Spiritu suo, pascit, confortat atque seruat ad vitam æternam. Ideò apud Ioannem, se panem illum vitæ seu viuum esse ait, qui cœlitus venerit, vt omnis qui edit ex eo, non moriatur, sed vitam æternam habeat. Et Paulus illum escam seu cibum spiritualem vocat, quem Veteris Testamenti patres nobiscum manducarint, idque per fidem nimirum, qua Christum Iesum, qui per Verbum ipsis promittebatur, per Manna autem & Legis ceremonias adumbrabatur, apprehenderunt. Vt enim corpora nostra ad hanc temporariam atque mortalem vitam pane confortantur & aluntur: Ita Christus nos ad æternam vitam suo Verbo & Spiritu, denique meriti aut corporis & sanguinis sui pro nobis traditi & effusi virtute, alit atque confirmat, vt in omni tentationum atque diuersorum genere constanter perseuerare, & nostro erga Deum officio defungi possimus. Quapropter petitione ista primò postulamus, vt cœlestis Pater nobis Filij sui Iesu Christi cognitionem reuelare, fidem in hunc veram largiri velit, vt eius merito frui possimus, atque eiusdem Verbo & Spiritu ducamur atque confirmemur. Quia verò panis iste nobis per Euangelij prædicationem offertur, hanc quoque & omnia alia petitio hæc comprehendit, quæ ad Ecclesiæ ministerium conseruandum necessaria sunt. Simul ergo precamur, vt Deus Ecclesiæ suæ ordinem atque disciplinam conseruet, ministros atque doctores fidos excitet, qui cibum hunc fideliter depromant & rectè secent, vt Paulus loquitur. Huc facit, quòd ipse Christus Ecclesiæ ministros seruos confert, quibus ab heris peregre abeuntibus cura domus committitur, vt familiæ suum dimensum dent in tempore, id est, prout opportunum & necessarium esse viderint. Quò Paulus alludens Euangelij præcones mysteriorum Dei dispensatores esse scribit. Et idem Euangelij prædicationem cibo corporali confert, cùm ait, Ie Corinthios lactes potu aluisse, eò quòd cibum solidiorem nondum ferre possent. Debent hoc observare omnes ij, qui Ecclesiæ ministerium contumeliosius aspernantur, ministros oderunt atque persequuntur, cum interea quotidie panem illum cœlestem & spiritualem sibi dari postulent, quem nobis Deus per illorum ministerium offert. Sunt hi similes puerorum contumacium, qui panem summis clamoribus petunt, eundem vero ex manu famulorum, quorum opera in illis alendis parentes vtuntur, nolunt accipere. At qui ita affecti sunt, pane hoc salubberrimo nunquam frui poterunt, quoad verbum externum contemnere perrexerint. Nec enim Deus in eorum gratiam, qui ipsius instituta spernunt, nouum aut singulare quid instituet, &c.
units.tr: The soul is spirit, and therefore its food must also be spiritual. This is properly that eternal and almighty Word of God, Jesus Christ, who nourishes, strengthens and preserves our souls to eternal life by the merit of his death, in which he gave his flesh for the life of the world, and finally by his Word and Spirit. Accordingly, in John he says that he is the living bread which came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die but have eternal life. And Paul calls him the spiritual food and meat which the fathers of the Old Testament ate with us, and that by faith, by which they laid hold of Christ Jesus, who was promised to them through the Word and foreshadowed by the manna and the ceremonies of the Law. For just as our bodies are strengthened and nourished by bread for this temporal and mortal life, so Christ nourishes and confirms us for eternal life by his Word and Spirit, and finally by the power of his merit and of his body and blood given and poured out for us, so that we may persevere constantly in every kind of temptation and adversity, and discharge our duty toward God. Therefore in this petition we first ask that our heavenly Father would reveal to us the knowledge of his Son Jesus Christ, and be willing to bestow on us true faith in him, so that we may enjoy his merit and be led and strengthened by his Word and Spirit. But since this bread is offered to us through the preaching of the Gospel, this petition also comprehends that and all the other things that are necessary for preserving the ministry of the Church. We therefore pray at the same time that God would preserve the order and discipline of his Church, raise up faithful ministers and teachers who may faithfully dispense this food and rightly divide it, as Paul puts it. To this purpose belongs the fact that Christ himself appoints servants as ministers of the Church, to whom, when their masters go abroad, the care of the household is committed, so that they may give the household its portion in due time, that is, as they see fit and necessary. Alluding to this, Paul writes that the heralds of the Gospel are dispensers of the mysteries of God. And the same Paul compares the preaching of the Gospel to bodily food, when he says that he fed the Corinthians with milk, because they could not yet bear more solid food. All those should take note who scornfully despise the ministry of the Church, hate and persecute its ministers, while every day they ask that this heavenly and spiritual bread be given to them, which God offers us through their ministry. They are like stubborn children who ask for bread with loud cries, but do not want to receive it from the hand of the servants whom their parents use to feed them. Those who are so disposed will never be able to enjoy this most wholesome bread, as long as they persist in despising the external Word. For God will not, for the sake of those who spurn his ordinances, institute anything new or singular, etc.

units.la: Quoad vero alteram hominis partem, corpus scilicet, hoc quoque suo pane opus habet, qui terrenus est, cum illud quoque ex terra originem sumpserit. Hic autem panis vocabulo omne id comprehendimus, quoad corporis sustentationem facit, vtpote omnis generis cibos simul & potum, vestes, domicilium, integram valetudinem, & quæcunque alia nominari possunt. Deinde ea quoque, quibus quæ modo recensuimus, vel acquiri vel retineri & seruari solent. Nam vt cibos habeamus, terræ fœcunditate & tempestatibus commodis opus est. Vt amictus suppetat, feris & pecoribus indigemus, quæ præter quod victui seruiunt, lanam, pelles & corium nobis subministrant. Corporis valetudo bonam aeris constitutionem, aquas salubres, fructus ad maturitatem bene excoctos, & cum his herbas, radices, & alia medicinæ seruientia requirit. Vt verò his omnibus commode fruamur, otium & pax publica necessaria sunt, quæ absque magistratu prudenti, fideli & forti, neque obtineri neque seruari possunt. Ergo precamur, vt hunc quoque Deus dare dignetur, vt reliquis illis omnibus honestè & tutò fruamur. Tot & tanta bona petitio hæc comprehendit, quæ primo intuitu nihil præter panem aut vulgarem victum postulare videtur.
units.tr: As for the other part of man, namely the body, it too needs its bread, which is earthly, since it also took its origin from the earth. By the word bread we understand everything that serves to sustain the body: namely all kinds of food and drink, clothing, dwelling, sound health, and whatever else can be named. Then also those things by which the things just listed are usually acquired, or kept and preserved. For to have food we need the fertility of the earth and favourable weather. To have clothing we need wild animals and cattle, which, besides serving for food, supply us with wool, skins and leather. Bodily health requires a good constitution of the air, wholesome waters, fruits well ripened to maturity, and with these herbs, roots and other things serving medicine. And to enjoy all these things conveniently, peace and public order are necessary, which can be neither obtained nor preserved without a prudent, faithful and strong magistrate. We therefore pray that God would also deign to give this, so that we may enjoy all those other things honourably and safely. This petition comprehends so many and so great goods, although at first glance it seems to ask for nothing beyond bread or ordinary food.

units.la: Porrò qualem panem à Deo petimus? Panem nostrum quotidianum (dicimus) da nobis, &c. Quo loco dua hæc vocabula, NOSTRVM & QVOTIDIANVM, diligentius expendi debent. Primo NOSTRVM dicimus, non quidem quod iure noster sit, sed quod hunc nobis Deus ex gratia destinauit, & quod sine eo vitam sustentare non possumus. Nam si proprie loqui libeat, proprium nihil habemus, neque etiam nobis Deus aliquid debet. At quia ipse ex gratia sic res nostras constituit, vt animæ quidem nostræ per Filium suum Iesum Christum, corpora autem externis rebus alantur & sustententur, panis hic noster esse dicitur eadem ratione, qua Christum quoque nostrum Dominum & nostrum redemptorem dicere solemus: non quod nobis aliquod in illum ius sit, sed quod eo nobis opus est Seruatore, & quod nobis eum Pater destinauit, vt nostra esset sapientia, iustitia, redemptio, &c. 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: Moreover, what kind of bread do we ask from God? We say: Give us OUR daily bread, etc. In this place the two words OUR and DAILY must be weighed more carefully. First, we say OUR, not indeed because it is ours by right, but because God in his grace has appointed it for us, and because we cannot sustain life without it. For if we wish to speak strictly, we have nothing of our own, nor does God owe us anything. But because he in his grace so arranges our affairs that our souls are nourished through his Son Jesus Christ, while our bodies are fed and sustained by external things, this bread is said to be ours for the same reason that we are accustomed to call Christ our Lord and our Redeemer: not because we have any right to him, but because we need him as our Saviour, and because the Father has appointed him for us, so that he might be our wisdom, righteousness, redemption, etc. 1 Cor. 1.
