units.la: Adhæc vno hoc vocabulo nostri officij nos Christus admonet, quod est, vt nostro proprio pane, id est, ijs quæ nobis à Deo dantur, contenti simus, neque quæ aliorum sunt præripiamus. Faciunt hoc, quotquot ex aliorum laboribus viuunt, & aliorum facultates medijs illicitis atque iniustis ad se transferunt. Pugnat hoc cum primo Dei instituto, cum charitate denique fraterna & iustitia publica, sine quibus hominum vita consistere non potest. Nam Dei institutum siue Lex Adamo data hæc est: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Tuum (inquit) non alienum. Et Apostolus ait: Qui furabatur, non amplius furetur: sed potius laboret, operando proprijs manibus quod bonum sit, vt possit impertiri cui opus fuerit. Idem præcipit, vt homines ignaui atque otiosi, qui inordinatè ex aliorum facultatibus viuere in animum induxerunt, ab Ecclesia repellantur. Quare vnica hac voce omnes ij accusantur & conuincuntur, qui suis non contenti, aliorum laboribus parta inuadunt. In quorum numero sunt fæneratores & vsurarij, diuites item auari, qui mercenarijs quoque mercedem debitam detinent, milites item, qui pecunia conducti regiones exteras inuadunt, vt ex rapinis & cædibus ditescant: omnes denique, qui non expectata Dei benedictione, per media illicita ingentes diuitiarum thesauros congerunt. Immi net his omnibus maledictio, quam Propheta eis Dei nomine denuntiat, clamans: Væ ei, qui congerit non sua. Item: Væ tibi qui prædaris, quoniam tu quoque præda fies. Quisquis ergo es, qui talia hucusque designauisti, expende diligentius, quid sibi petitio ista velit, qua dicis: Panem nostrum da nobis o Pater. Quo ore enim tuum panem a Deo postulare audes, qui alienum rapuis? Qua fronte itEm precaris vt tuum panem ille det, cuius benedictionem non expectas? Fatearis ergo oportet, te in Dei conspectu nimis impudentem hypocritam agere, & proinde poenas, quae hypocritis debentur, mereri.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ admonishes us of our duty by this one word, that we should be content with our own bread, that is, with what God gives us, and not snatch away what belongs to others. Those do the opposite who live off the labours of others and transfer other people's goods to themselves by unlawful and unjust means. This is contrary to God's first ordinance, to fraternal love and to public justice, without which human life cannot stand. For the ordinance of God, or the Law given to Adam, is this: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread" (Gen. 3). Your bread, it says, not another's. And the Apostle says: "Let him who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labour, working with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to share with whoever is in need" (Eph. 4). He likewise commands that idle and lazy people, who have resolved to live disorderly on the means of others, be cast out of the Church. Therefore by this one word all those are accused and convicted who, not content with their own, seize what has been acquired by the labours of others. Among their number are the usurers and moneylenders, also the rich misers who withhold the wages due to their hired workers, and soldiers who, hired for money, invade foreign lands to grow rich by plunder and slaughter; in short, all who, without waiting for God's blessing, heap up vast treasures by unlawful means. The curse which the Prophet pronounces against them in God's name threatens all these people, crying: "Woe to him who heaps up what is not his" (Hab. 2). Likewise: "Woe to you who plunder, for you too shall become plunder." Whoever you are, then, who have so far been marked by such things, consider more carefully what this petition means when you say: "Give us our bread, O Father." With what mouth do you dare to ask God for your bread, when you have seized what belongs to another? With what face do you pray that he give your bread, whose blessing you do not wait for? You must therefore confess that before God's eyes you act as an all too shameless hypocrite, and so deserve the punishments that are owed to hypocrites.

units.la: Deinde panem QVOTIDIANVM postulamus: qua voce nostram egestatem atque inopiam fatemur, vt qui quotidie Dei ope & beneficentia opus habeamus. Nam etsi semel tam anima quam corpore saturati sumus, id tamen nobis nequaquam sufficit. Quia enim anima quotidie novis tentationibus exercetur, corpora autem labore & ciborum digestione rursus exhauriuntur, confortatione & pane seu cibo quotidiano opus est. Et ideo addimus, IN DIEM, vel (vt Matthaeus habet) HODIE, & dicimus: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, vel in diem, id est, quotidie. Quod perinde est, ac si diceremus: Tu quidem o Pater heri, pridie, nudius tertius, omnibus denique diebus vitae nostrae nos liberalissime aluisti & seruasti. At quia hodie etiam esurimus atque sitimus, & nobis tua beneficentia quotidie opus est, te rogamus, vt hodie quoque nobis victum tam animae quam corporis largiri digneris, ne vnquam in tuorum praeceptorum obseruatione deficiamus, &c. Et hic quidem videre est, quam egregios Deos nos fecerit Satan, qui Euam ad peccandum sollicitans dicebat: Eo ipso die, quo comederitis ex arbore ista, aperientur oculi vestri, & eritis tanquam Dij, scientes bonum & malum. Quam primum enim parentes nostri eius consilium secuti & Dei mandatum transgressi sunt, in hanc egestatem cum posteritate tota devenerunt, vt quotidie esuriamus, sitiamus, algeamus, aestuemus, aegrotemus, & proinde mendicorum instar Dei misericordiam quotidie cogamur implorare. At vtinam vel semel quotidie istud nobis serio in mentem veniret, vt & nostram miseriam & eius originem agnoscere disceremus. Ita enim in Dei conspectu magis humiliaremur, & maiori cum gratitudine donis eius vteremur, quae nobis tam liberaliter confert.
units.tr: Next we ask for DAILY bread. By this word we confess our poverty and need, since we who are every day in need of God's help and kindness. For although we have once been satisfied in both soul and body, that is by no means enough for us. For the soul is exercised every day by new temptations, and the body is again drained by labour and by the digestion of food, so it needs daily strengthening and bread or food. And so we add FOR THE DAY, or (as Matthew has it) TODAY, and we say: "Give us our daily bread today," or "for the day," that is, every day. This is just as if we were to say: "You indeed, O Father, yesterday, the day before, three days ago, in short all the days of our life, have most generously fed and preserved us. But because today too we hunger and thirst, and we need your kindness every day, we ask you to deign to grant us today also food for both soul and body, so that we may never fail in keeping your precepts, and so on." Here one can see how splendid gods Satan made us, when he tempted Eve to sin, saying: "On the very day you eat of that tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." For as soon as our parents followed his counsel and transgressed God's command, they fell with all their posterity into this poverty, so that we hunger, thirst, freeze, swelter, and fall sick every day, and therefore, like beggars, are forced to implore God's mercy daily. Oh, that this might come into our minds seriously, even once a day, so that we might learn to recognise both our misery and its origin. For thus we would be more humbled before God's eyes, and would use with greater gratitude the gifts which he bestows on us so generously.

units.la: Caeterum in duobus hisce vocabulis adhuc considerandum restat, quod Christus nos praesenti & quotidiana Patris sui beneficentia contentos esse vult, ne anxia sollicitudine opum thesauros superfluos congeramus. Nam vt alibi admonet, suus cuique diei labor coniunctus est, vt nos in crastinum minime sollicitos esse oporteat. Vt enim Dominus panem quotidianum nos postulare docuit, ita quotidie nobis Pater ille caelestis prospiciet. Novit enim quibus nobis opus sit, & impossibile erit, vt qui aues caeli & pullos coruorum a patentibus relictos & desertos alit, floresque agri vestit, nos derelinquat, quos initio secundum suam imaginem condidit, deinde per filium suum redemit, & in filios adoptauit. Ne ergo animi aut carnis nostrae desideria longius extendamus, quam petitionis istius verba sonant: quin potius electorum Dei exempla imitemur, qui olim absque omni sollicitudine Dei beneficentia quotidiana contenti vixerunt. Fecit hoc pater credentium, Abrahamus, qui nisi eo animo praeditus fuisset, nunquam certe relicto solo paterno incertam Dei vocationem esse secutus, cum non deessent rationes plurimae, quibus caro retineri poterat. Eundem animum in eius nepote Iacobo cernimus, qui cum fratris Esau insidias declinare, & in Mesopotamiam profugere cogeretur, nihil a Deo praeter victum & amictum petijt. Neque alia Mosis mens fuit, qui relictis Aegyptij diuitijs, afflictio & infelici Israelitarum populo se coniunxit, quod nunquam facturus erat, nisi fides illum a quotidiana Dei liberalitate pendere docuisset. Poterant hic Prophetarum & Apostolorum exempla connumerari: sed quia satis nota sunt, breuitatis causa ea praeterimus. Hoc saltem obseruatu dignissimum est, quod Deus petitionem istam singulari miraculo confirmauit, quando Israelitas in deserto totus annus quadraginta aluit pane caelitus demisso, & graviter mandauit, ne qui ex illo plus colligerent, quam praesentis diei necessitas postularet. Cum vero quidam carnis curiositate & sollicitudine insatiabili decepti, sibijpsis in posterum quoque prospicere vellent, quicquid illis reliquum mansit, tetra putredine & vermibus exesum periit. Quo exemplo Deus toti hominum generi declarare voluit, quam ipsi displicent, qui eius liberalitati, quam quotidie experimur, diffidunt.
units.tr: Besides, there remains to be considered in these two words that Christ wills us to be content with the present and daily kindness of his Father, so that we do not, through anxious care, heap up superfluous stores of wealth. For, as he admonishes elsewhere, each day has its own labour attached to it, so we ought not to be anxious about tomorrow. For just as the Lord taught us to ask for daily bread, so that heavenly Father will provide for us day by day. For he knows what we need, and it would be impossible for him to abandon us, whom he created at the beginning in his own image, then redeemed through his Son, and adopted as sons, when he feeds the birds of heaven and the young ravens left and forsaken by their parents, and clothes the flowers of the field. Let us not, then, stretch the desires of our soul or our flesh further than the words of this petition sound; rather let us imitate the examples of the elect of God, who in former times lived content with God's daily kindness, without any anxiety. Abraham, the father of believers, did this; had he not been endowed with such a spirit, he would never have followed an uncertain calling of God by leaving his native soil, when there were not lacking many reasons by which the flesh could have been held back. We see the same spirit in his grandson Jacob, who, when he was forced to avoid the snares of his brother Esau and flee into Mesopotamia, asked God for nothing but food and clothing. Nor was Moses' mind any different, who, having left behind the riches of Egypt, joined himself to the afflicted and unhappy people of Israel; he would never have done this unless faith had taught him that he depended on God's daily generosity. The examples of the Prophets and Apostles could be listed here, but because they are well enough known, we pass them over for the sake of brevity. This alone is most worthy of notice: that God confirmed this petition by a singular miracle, when for forty years he fed the Israelites in the desert with bread sent down from heaven, and strictly commanded that no one gather from it more than the necessity of the present day required. But when certain people, deceived by fleshly curiosity and insatiable anxiety, wished to provide for the future as well, whatever was left to them perished, eaten away by foul rot and worms. By this example God wished to declare to the whole human race how much they displease him who distrust his generosity, which we experience every day.

units.la: Damnantur hic duo hominum genera, quae hodie passim regnant. Primum eorum est, qui necessarijs non contenti, plura habere cupiunt, vt aut gulæ, aut superbiæ & ambitioni suæ satis faciant. Ex horum grege sunt, qui nouas lautitias quærunt, & contemptu victu, quem patria tellus ex Dei benedictione profert, peregrinos cibos affectant, & conuiuia ad luxum instituunt. Si miles horum sunt, qui vestitu peregrino, ædificijs item insanis & superbis ambitiosos & Deo ingratos animo ostentant. Qui omnes, vbi quid suis cupiditatibus minus respondere vident, mox adversus Deum linguas soluunt, quasi it malignius ipsis prospiciat. Sunt hi Israelitarum similes, qui etsi (vt modò diximus) non minus miraculose quam liberaliter à Deo cœlitus alerentur, eius tamen fidem atque beneficentiam se non prius agnituros dicebant, donec carnes quoque daret, & epulum lautius ipsis in deserto instrueret. Fuit hæc grauis tentatio Dei, qui illorum cupiditati indulsit quidem, & coturnices dedit, quas epularentur: sed cum caro adhuc esset inter dentes eorum, immissa lue horribili locum illum sepulchris extinctorum infamem fecit. Accidit hoc ipsum frequenter luxuriosis & intemperantibus, vt eorum quidem gulæ satisfaciat Deus, sed huic intentos iusto iudicio perdat, vt lupi dum escam à venatoribus appositam auidius vorant, ab ijsdem intercipi ac trucidari solent. Alterum genus est, qui auaritia incensi quotidianam Dei beneficentiam spernunt, & plura appetunt, non vt insumant, sed vt congerant, & (vt Poeta dicebat) nummos contemplentur in arca. Vitij huius causa est diffidentia, quæ sanè facit, vt quamuis præsentibus vti non audeant, per fas tamen & nefas corradant, quibus in posterum vtantur. Imitantur hi eos Israelitas, qui contra Dei mandatum plus Mannæ collegerunt. Vt vero hi nihil inde retulerunt præter vermes in illo natos, putredinem, quæ nauseam ipsis moueret: ita fere fit, vt qui ex congestu diuitiarum cumulis voluptatem aut senectam tranquillam sperabant, nisi præter dolores, lachrymarum & interdum publicæ infamiæ materiam in illis inueniant. Nam aut liberos habent malæ frugis & sceleratos, qui ipsis adhuc vitam amicas illas opes dilapidant: aut morbis ita conficiuntur, vt illis nullo modo frui possint. Accedunt etiam plerumque vermes conscientiam arrodentes, qui omnia illis infesta reddunt, vt & noctes insomnes agant, & tutissima quæque misere timeant. Quod si nihil horum fiat, fere subita morte tunc auferuntur, quando se bonus suis cum otio & voluptate fruituros sperabant, & cui illa cessura sint, planè nesciunt: quod Christus in illius illius diuitis parabola elegantissimè adumbrat. Vbi eandem omnium eorum fortem esse ait, qui thesauros quidem congerunt, non autem in Deo diuites sunt, vt nimirum huic fidant, & ab eius benedictione pendeant. Sunt illi mortalium stultissimi (licet mundi iudicio prudentissimi censeantur) quia & animas suas negligunt, quarum iactura irrecuperabilis est, & fortis suæ mortalis obliuiscuntur, & præterea spem atque fiduciam omnem in opibus collocant, quibus nihil incertius, instabilius & lubricum magis fingi potest. Imò ijdem hac precatione tantum non cum Deo ludunt, dum egentium instar panem quotidianum petunt, cum ipsi iam immensos thesauros congesserint, quos tam sibi quam posteris suis in multa secula satis futuros sibi persuaserunt. Sed na magno illis hic lusus constabit, quando suum iudicium Deus exeret.
units.tr: Here are condemned two classes of men, who today reign everywhere. The first are those who, not content with what is necessary, desire to have more, so that they may satisfy their gluttony, their pride, and their ambition. Of this crowd are those who seek new delicacies, and, scorning the food which their native soil yields by God's blessing, aspire to foreign dishes, and arrange banquets for luxury. Of the same kind are those who display their ambition and ingratitude toward God by foreign clothing and likewise by mad and proud buildings. All of these, when they see that something falls short of their desires, soon loosen their tongues against God, as if he looked on them with ill will. They are like the Israelites, who, though (as we have just said) they were fed from heaven no less miraculously than generously by God, nevertheless said that they would not acknowledge his faithfulness and kindness until he also gave them meat and provided them a richer feast in the desert. This was a grievous temptation of God, who indeed indulged their desire and gave them quails to feast on; but while the flesh was still between their teeth, he sent a dreadful plague and made that place infamous as a sepulchre of the dead. This very thing often happens to the luxurious and intemperate: God satisfies their gluttony, but by just judgement destroys them while they are intent upon it, just as wolves, while they greedily devour the bait set out by hunters, are usually caught and slaughtered by them. The second kind are those who, burning with avarice, spurn God's daily kindness and seek more, not to spend but to hoard, and (as the poet said) to gaze upon their money in the chest. The cause of this vice is distrust, which indeed causes them, though they do not dare to use what they have now, to scrape together by right and wrong what they may use in the future. These imitate those Israelites who, against God's command, gathered more manna. But just as these got nothing from it except worms born in it and a rottenness that made them sick, so it generally happens that those who hoped for pleasure or a tranquil old age from heaping up piles of riches find in them nothing but sorrows, tears, and sometimes matter for public disgrace. For they have either children of bad character and wicked lives, who squander those riches which were to be their livelihood while they still live, or they are worn down by diseases so that they cannot enjoy them in any way. Moreover, there are usually worms gnawing at the conscience, which make everything hostile to them, so that they spend sleepless nights and miserably fear the safest things. And if none of these things happen, they are often snatched away by a sudden death at the very moment when they hoped to enjoy their goods in leisure and pleasure, and they have no idea to whom those goods will pass; Christ depicts this most elegantly in the parable of that rich man. There he says that the same lot awaits all those who indeed heap up treasures but are not rich in God, that is, who do not trust in him and depend on his blessing. They are the most foolish of mortals (though they are considered most prudent by the judgement of the world), because they neglect their souls, whose loss is irrecoverable, and forget their mortal lot, and moreover place all their hope and confidence in riches, than which nothing can be imagined more uncertain, unstable, and slippery. Indeed, by this prayer they all but mock God, when they ask for daily bread like the needy, although they have already heaped up immense treasures, which they have persuaded themselves will be enough for themselves and their posterity for many ages. But this game will cost them dearly when God shows his judgement.

units.la: Sed vt ad petitionis huius verba redeamus, singularem consideratione particula, NOBIS, meretur. Dicimus enim: Panem nostrum quotidianum da NOBIS hodie. Ad quem modum postremæ hæ petitiones omnes efferuntur, & vt initio Deum communem omnium nostrum Patrem appellamus: ita deinceps dicimus: DANOBIS: Remitte NOBIS debita nostra: NE NOS inducas in tentationem: Libera NOS à malo. Ergo non pro nobis solis priuatim precamur, sed in precibus nostris simul omnes homines comprehendimus, qui eundem Patrem cœlestem nobiscum agnoscunt. Id vero nos communionis Christianæ admonet, quæ nobis mutuò tanquam corporis eiusdem membra in Christo Iesu intercedit. Vt enim corpus vnum ex multis membris sub vno capite coagmentatis conficitur: ita secundum Pauli doctrinam vniuersa fidelium Ecclesia corpus vnum est sub vno capite, Iesu Christo, ex quo omnes eundem vitæ spiritum hauriunt. Et quemadmodum inter membra naturalis συμπάθεια siue compaßio est, & nullum sibi soli operatur & consulit, sed in commune alijs omnibus profui officij ratione prospicit: ita Christiani homines sese mutuò iuuant, & singuli aliorum omnium saluti, quantum in ipsis est, consulunt, & (vt alibi Apostolus monet) plorant cum plorantibus, gaudent cum gaudentibus. Quae causa est, quod preces quoq; inter se communes habent, ut & alibi docuimus.
units.tr: But to return to the words of this petition, the particle "US" deserves special attention. For we say: "Give US this day our daily bread." All the last petitions are framed in the same way. Just as at the beginning we call God the common Father of us all, so afterwards we say: "Give US; forgive US our debts; lead US not into temptation; deliver US from evil." Therefore we do not pray for ourselves alone, privately, but in our prayers we include all people together who acknowledge the same heavenly Father with us. This reminds us of the Christian fellowship which binds us to one another as members of one body in Christ Jesus. For just as one body is made up of many members joined under one head, so according to Paul's teaching the whole Church of believers is one body under one head, Jesus Christ, from whom all draw the same spirit of life. And just as among the members of a natural body there is sympathy [συμπάθεια], or compassion, and no member works or cares for itself alone, but by the duty of its office provides for the common good of all the others, so Christians help one another, and each looks to the salvation of all others as far as he is able. And (as the Apostle warns elsewhere) they weep with those who weep, rejoice with those who rejoice. This is why they also have prayers in common with one another, as we have taught elsewhere.

units.la: Quoad vero petitionem hanc, particula ista nos admonet, panem quotidianum & quaecunque alia sunt Dei dona, sic peti debere, ut quae ab illo accipimus; non solis nobis data putemus, sed in eum finem data esse, ut aliorum quoque necessitati seruiant, & (ut Paulus ait) nostra abundantia aliorum inopiam succurrat. Minime ergo iis seruit haec petitio, qui sua modo quaerunt, aliorum vero necessitatem prorsus negligunt. Ludunt hi quoque cum Deo, cum quod omnium Christianorum nomine postularunt, sibi solis vendicent. Meminerimus ergo, illum neque ex ignorantia, neque vllo affectu prauo dona sua inter homines mensura inaequali distribuere: sed consulto id facit, ut locum habeat inter nos charitas, cum alius alterius ope indiget. Itaque qui diuitijs amplissimis abundant, dispensatores Dei sunt, quorum opera & ministerio illis subuenire vult, qui minus ab ipso acceperunt. Iniqui ergo & perfidi dispensatores sunt, qui panem suo soli fruuntur, & cum pauperi frangere detrectant. Neque eos excusat, quod hominum iudicio legitimi possessores censentur; neque vllis legibus accusari possunt. Nam possessionem quidem & proprietatem opum illius concedit Deus, vsum fructum vero non ad ipsos solos pertinere, sed vlterius ad alios quoque extendi vult. Et quamuis, quoad ius humanum a nemine accusari possint, seipsos tamen accusant cum precantur: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis, &c. Cum enim hoc omnium filiorum Dei nomine dicant, sibi tamen soli vsurpant, quod omnium nomine accipiunt.
units.tr: As for this petition itself, that particle reminds us that we ought to ask for our daily bread and all other gifts of God in such a way that we do not think the things we receive from him are given to us alone. They are given for this purpose: that they serve the need of others also, and (as Paul says) that our abundance may supply the want of others. This petition therefore does not serve those who seek only their own things and utterly neglect the need of others. Such people also mock God, since they claim for themselves alone what they have asked in the name of all Christians. Let us remember, then, that he distributes his gifts among people in unequal measure neither from ignorance nor from any wicked motive, but deliberately, so that charity may have a place among us, since one person needs the help of another. Those who abound in very great riches are therefore God's stewards, and through their work and service he wishes to help those who have received less from him. Those who eat their bread alone and refuse to share it with the poor are unjust and faithless stewards. Nor does it excuse them that in the judgement of men they are counted lawful possessors, or that no laws can accuse them. For God grants possession and ownership of wealth, but he wills that the use and enjoyment of it should not belong to them alone but extend further to others also. And although, so far as human law goes, no one can accuse them, yet they accuse themselves when they pray: "Give us this day our daily bread," and so on. For while they say this in the name of all the children of God, they appropriate to themselves alone what they receive in the name of all.

units.la: Postquam vero singula huius petitionis verba excussimus, restat ut videamus, de quibus nos Christus praeterea admoneat, dum a Patre caelesti iubet omnia petere, quae ad corporis & animae sustentationem necessaria sunt. Et primo quidem nostrae conditionis admonemur, quod ex nobis ipsis nihil istorum habeamus. Si enim ea ex nobis haberemus, aut nostris viribus possemus parare, ea a Deo petere non esset opus. Hinc certe Germani trito proverbio dicunt: Selber haben ist für bartlen gut. Et sane, si hoc probe expendamus, patebit nos (quod supra quoque attigimus) coram Deo omnium miserrimos & egentissimos mendicos esse. Nam quoad animam attinet, huius cibus nobis a solo Deo datur ex mera gratia. Notum est enim illud Christi: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum vnigenitum traderet, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Datus ergo Christus, qui panis ille vitae est, non quod nos digni essemus, aut hunc meruissemus (quis enim tantum de Deo nullius indigo mereri poterat) sed quia nos Deus dilexit. Et quales nos dilexit? Peccatores, rebelles, filios irae. Et vt Filium nobis donauit immerentibus: ita fidem quoque, qua apprehenditur, ut noster cibus fiat, gratuito dono nobis largitur, ut alibi prolixe demonstrauimus. Itaque vt ad vitam aeternam alamur, precibus opus est, quibus ad Dei misericordiam, mendicorum instar, recurramus. At non melior est corporum conditio, quoad huius seculi vitam, cuius victum similiter a Deo flagitare nos oportet. Quis enim nostrum vel vnicum frumenti granum, aut vilissimum oluisculum creare potest, vnde cibum habeat? Quis linum aut canabim propria virtute producet, vt eo vestiatur? Annon solus Deus is est qui vbi manum suam aperuerit, omnium animantium desiderium saturat? Ille foenum pecori producit, & herbam ad vsum hominis, vt proferat panem de terra. Idem ille nos canabi & lino vestit, & in eundem vsum animalium quoque pelles & corium largitur. Nam etsi nostro labore terram coli oporteat, non tamen hoc ideo fit, quod nostra opera in bis producendis Deus indigeat, sed peccati poena est, qua nos exercet: interim (vt Paulus ait) nos neque plantando neque rigando quicquam proficimus, nisi ille incrementum dederit. Etsi idem (vt Ezechiel verbo vtar) baculum panis fregerit, omnis labor noster irritus erit, & inutilis. Ergo vt mendici pauperrimi perpetuo ad Dei ostium stamus, & ab eo panem nostrum quotidianum petimus, quem a nemine alio possumus sperare. Et quoties edimus aut bibimus, illius cenuiae sumus, cum praeter hunc nemo sit, qui nos alere queat. Vtinam vero istud serio expenderemus. Ista enim confiderario & superbiae crista deprimeret, & moneret, ne pauperes & egenos fastidiremus tam insolenter, qui victum suum a nobis flagitant. Nam mox succurreret, eandem nostram fortem esse apud Deum, cuius eleemosynam non minus nos ali oportet, quam eos qui ad nostra domus ostium panem mendicant.
units.tr: Now that we have examined the individual words of this petition, it remains to see what else Christ warns us of, when he bids us ask the heavenly Father for everything necessary to sustain body and soul. And first we are reminded of our condition: that we have none of these things from ourselves. For if we had them from ourselves, or could procure them by our own strength, there would be no need to ask for them from God. Hence the Germans have the familiar proverb: "To have it yourself is good for beards" [Selber haben ist für bartlen gut]. And indeed, if we weigh this carefully, it will be plain that we (as we touched on above) are before God the most wretched and needy beggars. For as far as the soul is concerned, its food is given to us by God alone, out of pure grace. That saying of Christ is well known: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." Christ, who is that bread of life, was given not because we were worthy or had deserved him (for who could earn anything from God, who needs nothing?), but because God loved us. And what sort of people did he love? Sinners, rebels, children of wrath. Just as he gave us his Son when we did not deserve him, so too he freely bestows upon us the faith by which he is received, so that he may become our food, as we have shown at length elsewhere. Therefore, if we are to be nourished to eternal life, we need prayers, by which we have recourse to God's mercy as beggars do. But the condition of our bodies is no better as regards life in this age, and we ought likewise to ask God for their sustenance. For who among us can create even a single grain of wheat, or the humblest herb, from which to get food? Who can produce flax or hemp by his own power, to clothe himself with it? Is it not God alone who, when he opens his hand, satisfies the desire of every living thing? He makes hay grow for the cattle and herbs for the use of man, that he may bring forth bread from the earth. The same God clothes us with hemp and flax, and provides skins and hides of animals for the same use. For although the land must be tilled by our labour, this is not because God needs our work to produce these things; it is a punishment for sin, with which he exercises us. Meanwhile (as Paul says) we accomplish nothing by planting or watering, unless he gives the increase. And if he should break the staff of bread (to use Ezekiel's image), all our labour would be vain and useless. Therefore, like the poorest beggars, we stand constantly at God's door and ask him for our daily bread, which we can hope for from no one else. And whenever we eat or drink, we depend on him, since there is no one besides him who can nourish us. Would that we considered this seriously! For this reflection would cut down the crest of pride and warn us not to despise so insolently the poor and needy who ask us for their food. For it would immediately occur to us that our own lot before God is the same, and that we need to be fed by his alms no less than those who beg bread at the door of our house.

units.la: Deinde paternam Dei bonitatem, qua nos prosequitur, hæc petitio commendat. Quia enim po stulare iubet quæcunque nobis necessaria sunt, non dubium est, quin ea quoque largiri velit. Qua- propter plena consolationis promissio hic continetur, velle nimirum Deum tam corpori quam ani- mæ nostræ liberaliter prospicere, ne quid necessariorum nobis desit. Est hoc obseruatu utilissimum aduersus anxiam carnis solicitudinem, quæ auaritiæ & multorum malorum causa est, dum subin- de metuimus, ne quando victus, & quæ alia nobis sustentandis seruiunt, nos deficiant. Consolatur nos, quoad hunc metum, alibi Christus argumentis validissimis. Dicit enim: Annon anima præ- stantior est alimento, & corpus vestitu præstat? Quasi dicat: Cum quod præstantius est, Deus dederit, animam videlicet & corpus, id quod minus est, non negabit, sed ea quoque largietur, quæ ad vtriusque conseruationem faciunt. Deinde volucres cæli & flores agri contemplari iubet, quos Deus mirifice alit, vestit & conseruat. Vnde colligere debemus, illum multo magis nobis prospe- sturum esse, in quorum gratiam omnia alia creauit. Alibi vero vniuersalem Patrem sui bonitatem nobis ob oculos statuit, qui solem oriri sinit super bonos & malos, pluuias demittit piis ac impijs, & terræ proventus ijs quoque liberaliter impertitur, qui nomen eius ignorant. Qui ergo nos negligeret, qui ipsius filij & cultores sumus? At præter promissiones istas, plurimum nos hæc petitio consola- tur, vt de illius beneficentia non possimus dubitare. Qui enim inter homines aliquem abs se petere iubent necessaria, si viri boni sint, eum petentem minime frustrantur. Atqui Deus Pater per Filium suum nos abs se postulare iubet panem quotidianum. Nunquam ergo eos repellet, qui quod ipse instit faciunt. Simul autem hoc latius extendi debet, vt nosipsos in spe salutis æternæ confirme- mus. Quia enim Deus corpora nostra ad hanc vitam temporariam alit & vestit, multo magis to- tum hominem tam animam quam corpore ad vitæ æternæ possessionem seruabit per Filij sui meritum quem pro nobis tradidit.
units.tr: Next, this petition commends the fatherly goodness of God, with which he cares for us. For since he bids us ask for whatever is necessary to us, there is no doubt that he is also willing to bestow these things. Hence a promise full of consolation is contained here: God is willing to provide generously for our body as well as our soul, so that nothing necessary is lacking to us. This is most useful to observe against anxious worry of the flesh, which is the cause of avarice and of many evils, while from time to time we fear that food and the other things that sustain us may fail us. Christ consoles us about this fear elsewhere with very strong arguments. For he says: "Is not the soul more excellent than food, and the body than clothing?" As if to say: since God has given what is more excellent, namely soul and body, he will not refuse what is less, but will also bestow those things which serve the preservation of both. Then he bids us consider the birds of the air and the flowers of the field, which God wonderfully feeds, clothes and preserves. From this we ought to gather that he will care for us much more, for whose sake he created all other things. Elsewhere he sets before us the universal Father's goodness, who lets the sun rise on the good and the evil, sends rain on the pious and the impious, and liberally bestows the produce of the earth even on those who do not know his name. Would he then neglect us, who are his own sons and worshippers? Besides these promises, this petition greatly consoles us, so that we cannot doubt his beneficence. For when men bid someone ask them for what is necessary, if they are good men they by no means disappoint the one who asks. But God the Father, through his Son, bids us ask him for our daily bread. He will never therefore repel those who do what he himself commands. At the same time this must be extended more widely, so that we may strengthen ourselves in the hope of eternal salvation. For since God nourishes and clothes our bodies for this temporary life, much more will he preserve the whole man, soul as well as body, for the possession of eternal life, through the merit of his Son whom he gave up for us.

units.la: Postrema petitione ista admonemur, vt Dei donis debeamus vti. Quo loco nobis duo obseruan da sunt. Primum, vt gratos nos præbeamus Deo, ex cuius manu necessaria quotidie accipimus. Do cet hoc lex naturæ, quam creaturis omnibus Deus præscripsit. Quod enim animal tam ferox est, quod herum suum à quo alitur, non agnoscat? Nouit bos (vt Dominus per Ifaiam loquitur) posses- sorem suum, & asinus præsepe suum. Equi eos diligunt, à quibus curantur. Canes pro heris suis pu- gnant, & eorundem domus custodiunt. Imo in vrsis, leonibus & alijs ferocissimis bestijs hoc ipsum cernitur, quod suis nutritijs gratæ sunt, & in eorum gratiam multa faciunt, quæ cum illarum ingenio & natura pugnant. Terra quoque, si bene colatur, magna cum pronentuum vsura agricolæ labo- ribus respondet. Quanto magis ergo homines gratos esse conuenit Deo, à quo victum & amictum quotidie accipiunt? Sed quia hic nostri officij frequenter obliuiscimur, proderit petitionem hanc sa- pius in mentem reuocare, quæ vt docet nos nihil ex nobis ipsis habere, ita ad gratitudinem Deo præ- standam hortatur, qui nobis tam benigne prospicit. Excitet nos præterea Christi exemplum, qui nunquam sine gratiarum actione panem fregit, vt ex eo disceremus quid nos facere deceat. Vix er go hominum nomine digni sunt, qui Dei immemores, porcorum instar, ad cibos ruunt, & his sumptis perinde abeunt, ac si nihil ex illius manu accepissent. Alterum est, vt Donis Dei ad ipsius honorem & nostram necessitatem temperanter vtamur. Nam & hoc communis sensus monet, vt donis acceptis sic vtamur, ne qua ignominia ad eum redeat, qui illa dedit. Quod ipsum in primis quoad Deum obseruari debet, ne turpi & luxurioso donorum eius abusu ipsius gloriam & nomen prophanemus. Etsi enim scelus hoc per se graue est, Dei tamen iudicio grauius & atrocius censetur, si cum nominis ipsius ignominia ijs abutamur, quæ ille dedit, vt nobis bono essent. Fit hoc, si illis superbia- mus, luxuriemur, & intemperantius gulæ atque alijs desiderijs indulgeamus. Ita enim fit, vt nostri quoque corporis & animi dotes, memoriam, intellectum, valetudinem, formam & quæ alia sunt hu- ius generis turpiter perdamus. Accedit his quod interea pauperes negliguntur, propter quos nobis Deus tam multa dedit, vt supra diximus. Simul etiam tam Dei quam mortalis nostræ sortis obliti, salutem propriam negligimus, quæ nobis ante omnia cordi esse debebat. Et hoc diuitis illius epulonis peccatum fuit, quem Christus quotidie lautius epulatum esse, & bysso atque purpura se- se induisse dicit, nullam autem rationem habuisse pauperis Lazari, qui ad ostium domus suæ prostratus micùs de mensa cadentibus saturari cupiebat. Quis verò illius fuit finis? Improuisa mor te sublatus, & ad inferorum cruciatus horribiles detrusus ess{C}. Hoc ipsum Sodomæ peccatum fuisse, Ezechiel scribit, quod nimirum felicitate à Deo concessa elati, eiusdem donis luxuriose & intem peranter abusi sunt, neglectis interim egenis, quibus in primis prospicere debuissent. Non teme-re ergo Christus de nouissimorum temporum moribus corruptissimis vaticinans, grauiter monet, ne corda nostra grauemus crapula & ebrietate. Quibus verbis non obscurè docet, vitiis istis non tam corpora quam animas nostras læ-di. Quam pauci vero sunt, prob dolor, qui horum hodie memi-nerint? Inter Ecclesiarum ministros inueniuntur, qui nihil quàm pocula quærunt, belluantur, co-messantur, vt canes illi muti, de quibus Isaias loquitur. Qui rempub. administrant, ebrietati & in-temperantiæ præ aliis dediti sunt, cum aliis exemplum frugalitatis præbere deberent. Vulgus au-tem hominum ijsdem vitiis ita laborat, vt malum hoc iam profsus immedicabile factum esse videa-tur. Hinc pernitiosa illa securitas, quæ plerosq; & suæ sortis & ipsius Dei creatoris immemores fa-cit. Remedium autem vllum non aliud præsentius adhiberi poterat, quàm si in huius petitionis me-ditatione frequentes subinde cogitaremus, nos quæcunq; habemus ex Dei Patris cœlestis manu ac-cipere. Itaque nostræ conditionis memores, simul Dei paternam bonitatem consideremus, qui & ani-mas nostras quotidie verbo suo consolatur atque Filij sui merito pascit, & corporibus quoq; libera-lissimè prospicit. Considerationis autem huius finis fit, vt Deo grati simus, donis eius ad ipsius ho-norem & gloriam vtamur, abusum omnem caueamus, & illa non nobis solis vendicemus, sed pau-peribus quoq; distribuamus quantum nostræ facultates ferre poterunt. Ita certè, nos precantes Pa-ter exaudiet, neq; panem modò quotidianum in hoc seculo viuentibus dabit, sed in cœlis quoque par-ticipes faciet mensæ Filij sui Iesu Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æter-num, Amen.
units.tr: We are reminded by this last petition that we ought to use God's gifts, and two things must be observed here. First, that we show ourselves grateful to God, from whose hand we receive daily what we need. The law of nature, which God has prescribed to all creatures, teaches this. For what animal is so fierce that it does not recognise the master by whom it is fed? As the Lord says through Isaiah, the ox knows its owner and the donkey its manger. Horses love those who tend them, and dogs fight for their masters and guard their houses. Indeed, the same is seen in bears, lions and other most savage beasts: they are grateful to those who have nursed them and, for their sake, do many things contrary to their nature and disposition. Even the land, if it is well tilled, repays the farmer's labour with a great return of produce. How much more, then, ought human beings to be grateful to God, from whom they receive food and clothing every day? But because we often forget this duty, it will be useful to call this petition to mind more often. It teaches us that we have nothing of our own, and it urges us to render thanks to God, who cares for us so kindly. Moreover, the example of Christ should stir us, for he never broke bread without giving thanks, so that we might learn from him what is fitting for us to do. Those who, forgetful of God, rush to their food like swine, and go away after eating as though they had received nothing from his hand, are scarcely worthy of the name of men. The second thing is that we should use God's gifts temperately, for his honour and for our own need. For common sense also warns us to use the gifts we have received in such a way that no disgrace comes back to the one who gave them. This must be observed above all with regard to God, so that by a shameful and luxurious abuse of his gifts we do not profane his glory and name. For although such a sin is serious in itself, it is judged by God to be more grievous and atrocious when we abuse, to the dishonour of his name, the things he has given us for our good. This happens when we become proud over them, indulge in luxury, and give ourselves over to gluttony and other desires without restraint. In this way we also shamefully waste the endowments of our body and mind: memory, understanding, health, beauty, and others of this kind. Added to this is the fact that in the meantime the poor are neglected, for whose sake God has given us so much, as we said above. At the same time, forgetful both of God and of our mortal lot, we neglect our own salvation, which ought above all to be dear to us. This was the sin of that rich man who feasted, as Christ says, more sumptuously every day and clothed himself in fine linen and purple, yet took no account of the poor Lazarus, who lay prostrate at his door and longed to be satisfied with the scraps falling from his table. And what was the end of that man? He was snatched away by an unforeseen death and thrust down into the dreadful torments of hell. Ezekiel writes that this was also the sin of Sodom: lifted up by the happiness granted by God, they abused his gifts in luxury and intemperance, while meanwhile they neglected the needy, whom above all they ought to have cared for. Therefore Christ, prophesying about the very corrupt morals of the last times, does not speak rashly when he warns us gravely not to weigh down our hearts with gluttony and drunkenness. By these words he clearly teaches that such vices harm not only our bodies but our souls. But how few, alas, are there today who remember these things? Among the ministers of the Church are found men who seek nothing but cups, who feast and gorge themselves like those dumb dogs of whom Isaiah speaks. Those who administer the commonwealth are given over to drunkenness and intemperance more than others, although they ought to set an example of sobriety to others. The common people are so afflicted by the same vices that this evil seems now altogether incurable. Hence comes that deadly complacency which makes many forget both their own lot and God the Creator himself. Yet no more immediate remedy could be applied than this: that in meditating upon this petition we should often reflect that we receive whatever we have from the hand of our heavenly Father. So, mindful of our condition, let us at the same time consider the fatherly goodness of God, who daily comforts our souls by his Word and feeds them through the merit of his Son, and who also most generously provides for our bodies. The purpose of this consideration is that we be grateful to God, use his gifts for his honour and glory, guard against every abuse, and not claim them for ourselves alone, but distribute them to the poor as far as our means allow. Surely the Father will hear us when we pray in this way; he will not only give us daily bread while we live in this world, but in heaven he will also make us partakers of the table of his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA. CXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXI.

units.la: PETITIO V. Et remitte nobis debita nostra: etenim ipsi remittimus omnibus, qui nobis debent.
units.tr: PETITION V. And forgive us our debts: for we also forgive all who owe us.

units.la: INter alia, quæ salutem nostram promouent, nö postremū est vera bonitatis & misericordiæ Dei cognitio. Ideo illam quotidie multis beneficijs declarat, vt ea cognita in fide confirmemur, et ad æternæ salutis communionē adducamur. At si beneficia illius omnia probè examinemus, inter præ-cipua numerandū erit, quod per Filium suum Iesum Christū veram precandi rationē nobis tradidit. Nam per se magnū & admiratione dignum est, quod miseris nobis in Dei conspectū venire, & eius opem implorare licet, quamuis illi, nequaquā conferendi simus. Superat tamen hoc, quod nobis potestatem dat postulandi res omnium præstantissimas, ex quibus salus nostra potissimum dependet: vt nimirū nomen eius in nobis sanctificetur: vt suo spiritu in nobis regnet, & tandē regni sui cœlestis participes faciat: vt secundum suam voluntatem nos in huius vitæ curriculo dirigat: denique vt in diem largiatur quæcunque tam corporum quam animarum sustentationi seruiunt. Sunt hæc tanta bona, vt quoad nostræ naturæ corruptionem, illis non indigni modo, sed ne capaces quidem simus, nisi nos Deus ex peculiari gratia suo Spiritu præparet, & illis percipiendis idoneos reddat. Fateamur ergo oportet, Deum Patrem fidelissimum esse, qui omnino nos saluos fieri cupiat.
units.tr: Among the other things that advance our salvation, the true knowledge of God's goodness and mercy is not the least. He therefore declares it every day by many benefits, so that, having come to know it, we may be confirmed in faith and brought into fellowship with eternal salvation. But if we carefully examine all his benefits, among the chief will be that, through his Son Jesus Christ, he has taught us the true manner of prayer. For it is in itself a great thing and worthy of wonder that we, wretched as we are, may come into God's sight and implore his help, although we are in no way comparable to him. Yet this surpasses it: that he gives us the power to ask for the most excellent things, on which our salvation chiefly depends: namely, that his name be sanctified in us; that he reign in us by his Spirit and at last make us partakers of his heavenly kingdom; that he direct us according to his will in the course of this life; and finally that he give us day by day whatever serves the sustenance both of bodies and of souls. These are such great goods that, given the corruption of our nature, we are not only unworthy of them but not even capable of them, unless God, by his special grace, prepares us with his Spirit and makes us fit to receive them. We must therefore confess that God the Father is most faithful, who altogether wishes us to be saved.

units.la: At quando ista ab illo postulamus, feré communis noster hostis Satan nos turbat, & peccatorum admissorum conscientia territus huiusmodi cogitationes suggerit: Quæ hæc temeritas est{o} miser homo, vt tuis precibus in Dei conspectum venire audeat? Quo ore illum audes Patrem dicere, cum tu nunquam filium obedientem te præbueris? Annon pudet precari, vt per te su-um nomen illè gloriosum & celebre reddat, cum tu illud quotidie prophanes & polluas? Quæ item ratio te mouet, vt illū cum regno suo ad te venire postules, qui hucusq; Satanæ locū dedisti, & illum in te regnare passus es? Et cur precaris, vt Dei voluntas in te perficiatur, cum illā oderis et deuoto animo in inobedientia ruas? Deniq; annon impudens hæc est temeritas, quòd à Deo panem quotidianû flagitas, cùm hactenus ita vixeris, vt non Dei filius, sed potius canis dici merearis? An nescis Dominum dixisse, non æquû esse vt panis filiorum canibus proijciatur? His & multis alijs similibus cogitationibus inter precandum turbamur, quas in eum finè diabolus suggerit, vt nos penitus ab invocatione Dei abstrahat, vtpote cuius nullus fructus sperari possit, cum tales simus, quales modò descripsimus. At ne tentationibus istis superemur, Christus quintam petitionè prioribus subijcere docet, qua cogitationibus hisce omnibus occurrere, vel etiam eas præuenire possumus. Nam sic dicere iubet: ET REMITTE NOBIS DEBITA NOSTRA: etenim ipsi remittimus omnibus, qui nobis debent. Vel vt apud Matthæum legitur: Sicut nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Quia ergo petitio hæc grauissimū conscientiæ tentationibus & ignitis Satanæ telis opponitur, necesse fuerit, vt germanum & proprium eius sensum probè teneamus.
units.tr: But when we ask these things of him, our common enemy Satan commonly troubles us and, terrifying us with the consciousness of sins committed, suggests thoughts of this kind: "What temerity is this, miserable man, that you dare to come into God's sight with your prayers? With what mouth do you dare to call him Father, when you have never shown yourself an obedient son? Are you not ashamed to pray that he make his name glorious and famous through you, when you daily profane and pollute it? What reason likewise moves you to ask that he come with his kingdom to you, who until now have given place to Satan and allowed him to reign in you? And why do you pray that God's will be done in you, when you hate it and with a devoted mind rush into disobedience? Finally, is it not shameless temerity that you ask God for daily bread, when you have lived so far that you deserve to be called not a son of God but rather a dog? Do you not know that the Lord said it is not fair that the children's bread be thrown to the dogs?" With these and many other similar thoughts we are troubled while praying, which the devil suggests for this very end, that he may wholly draw us away from invoking God, since no fruit can be hoped for from it, as we are such as we have just described. But that we may not be overcome by these temptations, Christ teaches us to place the fifth petition after the earlier ones, by which we can meet all these thoughts, or even forestall them. For he bids us say: "AND FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS: for we also forgive everyone who owes us." Or, as it is read in Matthew: "As we also forgive our debtors." Since therefore this petition is set against the most grievous temptations of conscience and the fiery darts of Satan, it is necessary that we hold firmly to its genuine and proper sense.

units.la: Ante omnia autem videndum erit, quid debiti nomine intelligi debeat. Quoad enim nostrū officium, Deo multis nominibus obstrictî sumus, & ei debemus timorem, obedientiam & dilectionem non sucatam. At non de eiusmodi debitis hic sermo est. Nec enim filios Dei decet precari, vt ab his nos soluteret, quæ & illius gloriæ & nostra salutî seruiunt. Ergo aliud debiti genus hic considerandum venit, Peccatû videlicet, quod nos Deo debitores reddit, dum quam illi debemus obedientiam non præstamus, & proinde pœnas meremur, quibus eius iustitiæ satisfiat. Quia verò hoc nobis intolerabile foret (nam peccati stipendiû siue pœna est mors, æterna nimirum illa, quæ cum inferorum perpetuis cruciatibus coniuncta est) ista petitione gratiam & misericordiam Dei imploramus, & nos quidem pœna dignos esse fatemur, petimus autem ne pro meritis nos puniat, neq; peccata nobis imputet, sed illa clementer remittat atq; condonet: nosq; filiorum loco habeat. Estq; præcatio hæc necessaria admodum, eò quòd germanis Dei filijs nihil gravius aut intolerabilius est Patris sui ira, nosq; seruari impossibile est, quoad Deus peccata imputat, & nos pro meritis punire instituit.
units.tr: Above all, we must see what is to be understood by the word "debt". For as far as our duty goes, we are bound to God by many titles, and we owe him fear, obedience and sincere love. But the discussion here is not about debts of this kind. For it does not befit the sons of God to pray that he release them from those things which serve both his glory and their salvation. Therefore another kind of debt must be considered here, namely sin, which makes us debtors to God, since we do not render him the obedience we owe, and so we deserve punishments by which his justice is satisfied. But since this would be intolerable for us (for the wage of sin, or its punishment, is death, that eternal death which is joined with the perpetual torments of hell), by this petition we implore God's grace and mercy. We confess indeed that we are worthy of punishment, but we ask that he not punish us according to our deserts, nor impute our sins to us, but kindly remit and pardon them, and hold us in the place of sons. This prayer is exceedingly necessary, because nothing is more grievous or intolerable to the true sons of God than the anger of their Father, and we cannot be saved while God imputes sins and determines to punish us according to our merits.

units.la: Porrò si petitionem hanc propius consideremus, ea totum nostræ salutis negotiū contineri patebit. Primò enim, quia remissionem debitorum nostrorum omnes iubemur postulare, proprio ore nos tefari vult Dominus, nos omnes peccauisse, & Deo debitores esse, egenos & inopes, qui iustitiæ eius satisfacere nō possint, sed gratuita condonatione ac remissione opus habeat. Ideo ergo hic fatemur, quod omnis scriptura passim docet, nos nimirū natura prorsus corruptos & perditos esse, & peccato obnoxios. Quia enim (vt Dauid de semetipso fatetur) in peccato concipimur & nascimur, omnes nostræ cogitationes malæ, adeoq; omnia cordis nostri figmenta à pueris prava sint oportet. Quod in nobis ipsis quotidie experimur. Nec enim tā grati sumus Deo pro acceptis beneficijs, quā nos esse decebat. Donum item eius multiuariam abutimur. Verbū Dei & in hoc nobis revelatā eius voluntatē minus observamus. Deniq; (vt Iacobus ait) in multis labimur omnes. Sentimus adhuc, quòd etsi per Dei Spiritū ex verbi semine renati sumus, in nobis tamen naturæ vitiositas adhuc locū habet, quæ sæpe nos grauissimorū delictorū causa est: quod in multis electis Dei cultoribus cernimus, & de semetipso Paulus fatetur, se in membris suis legē peccati inuenire, quæ ipsum contra spiritus voluntatē pecca to captiuū ducit. Vt verò de hoc scriptura testatur, ita idem nos coram Deo & hominibus fateriū bet Christus, vt peccatorū agnitione humiliati, salutē in vnius Dei gratia & misericordia quæramus.
units.tr: Moreover, if we consider this petition more closely, it will be plain that the whole business of our salvation is contained in it. First, because we are all bidden to ask for the remission of our debts, the Lord wills us to testify with our own mouths that we have all sinned and are debtors to God, poor and needy, unable to satisfy his justice, and in need of his free pardon and remission. Here, therefore, we confess what all Scripture teaches everywhere: that we are by nature wholly corrupt and lost, and subject to sin. For, as David confesses of himself, we are conceived and born in sin, and so all our thoughts are evil, and indeed all the imaginations of our heart must be wicked from childhood. We experience this every day in ourselves. For we are not as grateful to God for the benefits received as we ought to be. We also abuse his gifts in many ways. We observe the word of God, and his will revealed to us in it, too little. Finally (as James says) we all stumble in many things. We still feel that, although we have been born again by the Spirit of God from the seed of the word, the vitiousness of nature still has a place in us, which is often the cause of very grave offences. We see this in many elect worshippers of God, and Paul confesses of himself that he finds in his members the law of sin, which leads him captive to sin against the will of the spirit. And as Scripture testifies of this, so Christ wills that we likewise confess it before God and men, so that, humbled by the acknowledgment of our sins, we may seek salvation in the grace and mercy of the one God alone.

units.la: Simul autē hoc loco de peccato iudicare docemur, quo caro delectatur, & cuius blanditiis nos facile decipi patimur, vt Deū quoq; illud non ita detestari putemus, vt quidā affirmant. Est hic error nocentissimus, quia pœnitentiā impedit. At si cogitemus, peccatū debitum esse, quod nos Deo ita obstrictos reddit, vt abs[q] gratuita remissione neq; eo liberari, neq; salutè consequi possimus: mox intelligemus, nihil apud Deum illo detestabilius, nobis autē in toto salutis negotio nihil eodem nocentius & pernitiosius esse. Magnū scelus admiserit oportet filius, quē pater abdicat & exhæredat. Atqui peccatū causa vnica est, ob quā Pater cœlestis nos abdicare & à regni sui hæreditate excludere solet. Huius nos meminisse oportet, quoties carnis cupiditatibus tentamur, & mundi illecebrosò exemplo ad peccata noua solicitamur. Tunc (inquā) meminerimus, nos iam ante Deo debitores esse, qui eius iustitiæ satisfacere nō possint, & proinde inexcusabile fore temeritatē nostrā, si deuoti ad peccandū animis scelera scelerib.accumulemus, malæ frugis hominū similes, qui indies æs alienū magis augēt.
units.tr: At the same time we are taught here to judge concerning sin, in which the flesh delights and by whose allurements we allow ourselves to be easily deceived, so that we do not think God detests it as strongly as some affirm. This error is most harmful, because it hinders repentance. But if we consider that sin is a debt, which binds us to God so that we can be freed from it and obtain salvation only by gratuitous remission, we will soon understand that nothing is more detestable before God, and nothing more harmful and pernicious to us in the whole business of salvation. A son must have committed a great crime whom a father disinherits and cuts off. Yet sin is the sole cause for which the heavenly Father is wont to disinherit us and exclude us from the inheritance of his kingdom. We ought to remember this whenever we are tempted by the lusts of the flesh and urged to new sins by the alluring example of the world. Then, I say, let us remember that we are already debtors to God, who cannot be satisfied by us; and therefore our temerity would be inexcusable if, with minds devoted to sinning, we heaped crime upon crime, like men of bad character who daily increase their debt.

units.la: Secundò docet etiam petitio hæc, per quem hoc peccatorū debito simul & pœna liberemur. Nec solum Deu est.
units.tr: Secondly, this petition also teaches through whom we are freed both from the debt of sins and from their punishment. And it does not concern only God.

units.la: Bb enim alicuius solutionis aut satisfactionis mentionem facimus, sed gratuitam postulamus remissionem. Unde sequitur hanc apud solum Deum quaeri debere, qui debita haec nobis ex gratia & misericordia mera remittit. Quia enim Deo peccamus (vt Dauid de semetipso fatetur) & peccando illius dominus ...
units.tr: For we are not making mention of any payment or satisfaction; we are asking for a free pardon. It follows that this must be sought from God alone, who remits these debts to us out of pure grace and mercy. For since we sin against God (as David confesses of himself), and by sinning become his debtors, no one except the one God will have the right and power to remit this debt, which we know the Pharisees also understood.

units.la: enim alicuius solutionis aut satisfactionis mentionem facimus, sed gratuitam postulamus remissionem. Unde sequitur hanc apud solum Deum quaeri debere, qui debita haec nobis ex gratia & misericordia mera remittit. Quia enim Deo peccamus (vt Dauid de semetipso fatetur) & peccando illius bitores efficimur, nemini praeter vni Deo ius & potestas erit debitum hoc remittendi, quod Pharisaeos quoque intellexisse scimus. Deinde cum ex nobis ipsis nihil boni habeamus, & proinde iustitiae Dei non possimus satisfacere, vt gratuita remissione nobis subueniatur necesse est. Est haec doctrina totius scripturae testimonio confirmata. Dauid enim docere volens, qua ratione homo apud Deum iustifi-catur, nulliusoperis aut meriti nostri meminit, sed ita ait: Beati, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum peccata tecta sunt. Beatus vir, cui Dominus peccatum non imputat. Apud Isaiam vero Dominus ipse clamat: Ego deleui transgressiones tuas vt densas nebulas, & peccatum tuum vt nubem. Et rursus: Ego ego deleo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non amplius recordabor. Qui loci perspicue docent, peccatorum nostrorum remissionem non in nostrorum operum meritis, sed in solius Dei misericordia gratuita consistere. Id vero Christus ipse elegantissima parabola illustrat, quando regnum Dei simile dicit esse homini opulento, cui ratione cum seruis suis subducenti quidam oblatus est, qui decem millia talentorum debebat. Is cum soluendo non esset, herus eum cum uxore & liberis venundari iussit. Tunc ad heri pedes supplex procidit, eius implorauit misericordiam, & ita gratuitam condonationem impetrauit. Herus ille, de quo Christus loquitur, Deus est, cuius famuli aut serui nos sumus. Ratio, quam nobiscum confert, est vita nostra & dictorum factorumque nostrorum examen. Codex rationum Lex est, quae quid illi debeamus prolixe docet, & ad ea praestanda minus gratiosi obstringit. Ad hanc si vitam & mores nostros Deus examinet, eadem omnium nostrum, quae miseri huius seruuli, est conditio. Nos enim in singula Legis praecepta plus millies peccauisse depre hendimur, & quo diligentius ipsi nos in hoc codice examinamus, eo plura debita reperiemus. Quia autem Deus iustus est, hoc vnum restat, vt tam corpus quam anima ad damnationem sempiternam venundentur, & ita scelerum admissorum poenas exoluamus. Nam etsi seruulus ille solutionem suorum debitorum polliceatur, inanis tamen haec promissio est, vt pote quam terror & metus extorsit, non certa tanti promissi praestandi fiducia. Quis enim seruus vnquam decem millia talentorum dissolueret? Ita neq; nos iustitiae Dei vnquam satisfacere possumus, cuiam ante omnia nostra illi debeamus, et (vt Christus ait) serui inutiles sumus, licet omnia praestemus, quae Lex iubet. Qui ergo nunc sumus prob dolor, cum pleraq; praeceptorum Dei partim iocoridia, partim malitia transgrediamur? Hoc ergo vnum nobis reliquum est, vt supplices ad thronum gratiae prolapsi clamemus: Remitte nobis o Pater, debita nostra. Peccauimus quidem in te grauissime, neq; digni sumus, qui filij tui dicamur. Sed propitius nobis esto Domine, neq; intres in iudicium cum seruis tuis. Ne imputes nobis debita nostra, quibus diffidendi sufficere non possumus. Aufer quaeso cruentam illam syngraphum, quae nos accusat & coniuncit, & tua nos dignare misericordia, &c. Haec & hus similia dicamus atq; ingenue fateamur oportet, cum in nostris operibus aut meritis nihil spei aut fiduciae sit reliquum.
units.tr: For we are not making mention of any payment or satisfaction; we are asking for a free pardon. It follows that this must be sought from God alone, who remits these debts to us out of pure grace and mercy. For since we sin against God (as David confesses of himself), and by sinning become his debtors, no one except the one God will have the right and power to remit this debt, which we know the Pharisees also understood. Next, since we have nothing good of ourselves, and therefore cannot satisfy the justice of God, it is necessary that we be helped by free remission. This doctrine is confirmed by the testimony of all Scripture. For David, wishing to teach how a man is justified before God, makes no mention of any work or merit of ours, but says: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin" (Ps. 32). In Isaiah the Lord himself cries out: "I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sin like a cloud" (Isa. 44). And again: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and for my own sake, and I will no longer remember your sins" (Isa. 43). These passages plainly teach that the forgiveness of our sins rests not on the merits of our works but on the free mercy of God alone. Christ himself illustrates this with a most elegant parable, when he says that the kingdom of God is like a wealthy man who, when he was settling accounts with his servants, was presented with one who owed ten thousand talents. Since he could not pay, the master ordered that he be sold, with his wife and children. Then the servant fell down at his master's feet, implored his mercy, and so obtained a free pardon. That master of whom Christ speaks is God, and we are his household servants. The reckoning he makes with us is our life and the examination of our words and deeds. The ledger of accounts is the Law, which teaches at length what we owe him and binds us, less kindly, to pay it. If God examines our life and conduct by this, the condition of all of us is the same as that of this wretched servant. For we are found to have sinned more than a thousand times against the individual precepts of the Law, and the more carefully we examine ourselves in this ledger, the more debts we will find. And because God is just, only this remains: that both body and soul be sold to everlasting damnation, and so we pay the penalty for the sins we have committed. For although that servant promises to pay his debts, this promise is empty, since it was extorted by terror and fear, not by a sure confidence of being able to fulfil so great a promise. For what servant would ever pay off ten thousand talents? So neither can we ever satisfy the justice of God, to whom we owe everything before all our own deeds; and (as Christ says) we are unprofitable servants, even if we do everything the Law commands. What, then, are we now, alas, when we transgress most of God's precepts, partly through carelessness and partly through malice? This therefore is all that remains to us: that, having fallen as suppliants to the throne of grace, we cry out: "Forgive us, O Father, our debts. We have sinned against you most grievously, nor are we worthy to be called your sons. But be merciful to us, O Lord, and do not enter into judgment with your servants. Do not impute to us our debts, against which we cannot stand. Take away, we pray, that bloody bond which accuses and convicts us, and deign to show us your mercy," and so on. These and similar things we ought to say, and frankly confess, since in our works or merits there is no hope or confidence left.

units.la: Haec autem petentibus dulcissimam consolationem afferet, quod Deus ipse per filium suum nos ita precari iubet. Est enim hoc irrefragabile sua erga nos clementia testimonium, quod nos de peccatorum remissione certos facit. Quod ipsum in parabola, cuius modo meminimus, perspicue docet. Quam primum enim seruulus ille supplex heri misericordiam implorat, hunc propitium sibi inuenit. Neminem ergo peccatorum siue multitudo siue atrocitas ita terreat, vt de salute desperet. Superat enim peccata totius mundi misericordia Dei, & (vt Dauidis verbis vtar) quantum caeli a terra distant, tantum praevalet benignitas eius erga omnes, qui ipsum timent: & quam procul ortus ab occasu distat, tam procul remouit a nobis peccata nostra. Semper ergo cogitemus, quod etsi peccata nostra multa & grauia sint, plus tamen misericordiae inueniri apud Deum, qui in omnibus suis proprietatibus omnipotens est, nec ab aliquo potest superari. Et huc referri debent exempla multorum, quae Spiritus sanctus in scripturis proponit, vt ex illis consolatione capiamus, qualia sunt Dauidis adulterii & homicidae nefarii, Petri abnegatoris, Matthaei publicani, Mariae Magdalenae peccatricis infamis, de qua Cap.7 dictum est, Pauli item crudelissimi aliquando ecclesiae persecutoris, & similium multorum. In quibus obseruandum est, Deum in his no peculiare quid agere voluisse, sed promissiones suae gratiae confirmasse, vt eandem sibi quoq; paratam esse norint, qui ad ipsum conuertuntur, quod Paulus de seipso loquens in priori ad Timotheum disserte docet.
units.tr: Moreover, this most sweet consolation will be brought to those who ask, because God himself, through his Son, bids us pray in this way. For this is an unshakeable testimony of his kindness toward us, which makes us certain of the forgiveness of sins. He teaches this plainly in the parable just mentioned. For as soon as that servant implored the master's mercy as a suppliant, he found him merciful. Therefore let no one be so terrified by the number or the atrocity of his sins that he despairs of salvation. For the mercy of God surpasses the sins of the whole world, and (to use David's words) as far as heaven is from earth, so far does his goodness prevail over all who fear him; and as far as the rising is from the setting, so far has he removed our sins from us. Let us therefore always consider that, although our sins are many and grave, more mercy is found with God, who is omnipotent in all his perfections and cannot be overcome by anyone. To this point should also be referred the examples of many whom the Holy Spirit sets forth in the Scriptures, that we may take consolation from them: such as David's adultery and wicked murder, Peter's denial, Matthew the tax collector, Mary Magdalene the notorious sinner, of whom it was said in chapter 7, likewise Paul, once the most cruel persecutor of the Church, and many others like them. In these cases it must be observed that God did not wish to do anything peculiar in them, but to confirm the promises of his grace, so that those who turn to him may know that the same grace is prepared for them too; which Paul, speaking of himself, clearly teaches in his first letter to Timothy.

units.la: Vt vero salutis nostrae certiores simus, tertio loco medium illud nouisse oportet, per quod & cuius causa nobis Deus debita nostra condonat. Nam etsi benignus atq; misericors, & ad nos seruandos propensus sit, idem tamen iustus etiam est, & proinde eius iustitia satisfactione pro peccatis nostris exigit. Quia item peccato maledictionem imposuit, hanc absq; satisfactione à nobis non poterit remoueri. Hic ergo obseruemus, quoad nos, peccata nobis ex mera & gratuita misericordia remissi, nullo nostrorum operum aut meritorum respectu, quae in nobis prorsus nulla sunt: quoad vero Dei iustitiam, huic quoq; nihil derogatur. Quamuis enim nos illi non possimus satisfacere, alius tamen quidam est, qui illi satisfecit, & debitum nostrum omne dissoluit: Aeternus nimirum Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, qui secundum veteres promissiones praefinito tempore in mundum venit, & homo factus de carne nostra in se transtulit, & illa suae mortis merito in ara Crucis dissoluit. Docet hoc Isaias, qui omnium hominum peccata in illo conuenisse, & ipsi nostrae correctionis multam impositam esse ait, vt eius liuore & sanguine ipsi sanaremur. Et Paulus, Deum nos in Filio suo vitae restituisse scribit, qui chirographum peccati in Cruce suffixum suo sanguine deleuerit. Idem Christum dicit pro nobis peccatum factum esse, vt nos per illum Dei iustitia efficeremur. Cùm enim nobis propter peccatum maledictio illa incumberet, Maledictus omnis, qui nõ omnia seruat, quae scripta sunt in libro Legis huius: Christus Dominus illam alia maledictione in se transslata expiauit, Crucis nimirū supplicio, quod similiter maledictioni obnoxium esse Lex docet. Abunde ergo pro peccatorū nostrorum debitis satisfactum est, cùm mors Filij Dei non minus atrox, quàm peccatum, esse censeatur. Quisquis ergo per fidem Christo inseritur, is meriti quoq; illius particeps fit, vt propter illum peccata eius remittantur, & ipse propter fidem in Christum pro iusto habeatur. Ideo Paulus nos per fidem iustificari docet, eò quòd non alio medio aut instrumento quàm fide, Christū apprehendimus. Hic ergo in iustitia Dei strictissima eiusdem quoq; immensa atq; inexhausta misericordia se exerit. Quamuis enim peccata impunita non sinat, tantus tamen in illo humani generis amor, tanta erga infelices nos commiseratio est, vt Filij sui morte nobis subuenire, & hunc potius inter acerbissimos dolores in cruce pendentem, quàm nos in aeternis inferorum tormentis videre voluerit. Eò igitur certior est remissionis peccatorum nostrorum fiducia, quòd illa non sola Dei misericordia, sed iustitia quoq; eiusdem nititur. Quia enim huic pro nobis satisfecit Christus, quem ipse Pater huic negotio destinauit, non est quòd eam posthac formidemus, cùm potius consolationi nobis esse debeat. Quò Ioannes respiciens dicebat: Si confiteamur peccata nostra, Deus fidelis est & iustus, vt remittat nobis peccata nostra, & nos purget ab omni iniquitate. 1. Ioan. 1.
units.tr: Next, so that we may be more certain of our salvation, we ought, in the third place, to know the means by which, and for whose sake, God pardons our debts. For although he is kind and merciful and inclined to save us, he is nonetheless also just, and therefore his justice requires satisfaction for our sins. And since he has laid a curse upon sin, this curse cannot be removed from us without satisfaction. Here, then, let us observe that, as far as we are concerned, sins are forgiven us out of pure and free mercy, with no regard to any of our works or merits, which in us are altogether nothing; but as far as the justice of God is concerned, nothing is taken away from this either. For although we cannot satisfy him, there is another who has satisfied him and has discharged our whole debt: namely, the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, who, according to the ancient promises, came into the world at the appointed time, was made man, took our flesh upon himself, and by the merit of his death on the altar of the Cross paid it off. Isaiah teaches this, who says that the sins of all men met in him, and that the chastisement for our peace was laid upon him, that we might be healed by his stripes and blood. And Paul writes that God restored us to life in his Son, who blotted out the bond of sin, nailed to the Cross, with his own blood. The same Paul says that Christ was made sin for us, so that through him we might be made the righteousness of God. For since that curse hung over us because of sin, "Cursed is everyone who does not keep all the things written in the book of this Law" (Deut. 27), Christ the Lord expiated it by taking upon himself another curse, namely the punishment of the Cross, which the Law likewise teaches is subject to the same curse. Therefore full satisfaction has been made for the debts of our sins, since the death of the Son of God is judged no less dreadful than sin. Whoever, then, is engrafted into Christ by faith, also becomes a partaker of his merit, so that for his sake his sins are forgiven, and for the sake of his faith in Christ he himself is counted righteous. Therefore Paul teaches that we are justified by faith, because we lay hold of Christ by no other means or instrument than faith. Here, then, in the strictest justice of God, his immense and inexhaustible mercy also shows itself. For although he does not allow sins to go unpunished, yet there is such great love for the human race in him, and such compassion toward us wretched people, that he wished to help us by the death of his Son, and to see him hanging on the cross amid most bitter pains, rather than to see us in the eternal torments of hell. Therefore our confidence in the forgiveness of our sins is all the more certain, because it rests not only on the mercy of God but also on his justice. For since Christ, whom the Father himself appointed to this task, has satisfied that justice on our behalf, there is no reason for us to fear it henceforth, since it ought rather to be a comfort to us. Looking to this, John said: "If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1).

units.la: Ex his colligitur, nos per Christi meritum plenè redemptos, & non à culpa solùm (vt Sophistae Scholastici loquuntur) verumetiā a poena liberatos esse. Quia enim debitorum nostrorū Syngrapha deleta est, nemo illa posthac exigere aut nouam satisfactionem à nobis iure postulare poterit. Consu tantur itaq; hoc loco, qui non quidē diserte negant, Christum peccata nostra in Cruce expiauisse, at peccati poenam non sublatā esse aiunt, sed hanc partim in hoc seculo partim in igne purgatorio exolui oportere. Quae doctrina nõ solùm falsa, sed puerilis quoq; & ridicula est. Perinde enim secundum horum sententiā nobiscū Deus ageret, ac si quis debitori diceret: Decem aureos, quos mihi debes, tibi remitto & in libro rationum mearum delebo, ea tamen conditione, vt quoties mihi in vinea cultura operarijs opus est, tu quoq; illic mercenarium agas, donec summam illam omnem dissolueris. Quis vero debitori illi aliquid remissum esse diceret? Atqui non alium isti homines nobis Deum fingunt. Si enim nos pro peccatis nostris vel in hoc vel futuro seculo satisfacere, & illa nostrū laboribus & cruciatibus expiare oportet, nõ multū de Christi merito & satisfactione gloriari possumus. Imò meritum eius, quoad nos, nullum, neq; aliquis huius petitionis fructus erit, qua remissionē gratuitam postulamus. At diuersum nos omnis scriptura docet, quae & meritum Christi apud Patrem summae dignitatis, & preces ex fide factas apud eundē efficacissimas esse estedit. Sed comento isto opus fuit hominibus auaris, vt quaestum tam ex vivis quàm ex mortuis captarent. Hinc enim exequiae sum ptuosae, tricesimae, sacra anniuersaria, liberalissimae donationes & multa alia origine duxerunt, quibus stulti homines istorū doctrina decepti, animas partim in purgatorio iuuari & recreari, partim ex tormentis illis citius liberari putarunt. Nec tamē hus contenti, suam quoq; operā alijs locarunt, quasi ipsi canendo aut psollendo, ieiunando, Missas faciendo, deniq; suorū operū meritis, in illo igne laborantibus subuenire possent. Et haec quidem opera supererogationis dixerunt, quasi hīs ipsi abundaret, et ea proinde aliis pretio erogare aut diuendere possent. Vbi duplex error, & vterq; impietate plenus habetur. Nam contra totius scripturae authoritatem sibi eam sanctitatem tribuerunt, vt se plus etiam praestare posse dicerent, quàm ipsis ad salutem necesse esset: deinde sibi vendicarunt quod solius Christi & qui suam iustitiam nobis communicat, vt propter eam in Dei conspectu iusti censeamur. Nos igitur huius petitionis verbis admoniti, non dubitemus, Deum Patrem, qui ita precari iussit, nobis propter Filium suum Iesum Christum peccata remittere, & ita quidem, vt eorum ne recordetur quidem amplius (quemadmodum in Prophetis loquitur) nedum vt illa à nobis iam defunctis expiari velit. Conuenit cum hoc per omnia articulus fidei, qui in Symbolo Apostolico habetur. Vt enim precando remissionem gratuitam petimus: ita in Symbolo posteorum confessionem, quae pro nobis Dei Filius fecit & passus est, illam ipsam nos credere profitemur. Quod si ergo eâ credimus, & credendo adsequimur, nulla hic emptione, nulla satisfactione humana, nulla etiâ poenarum redemptione pecuniaria opus erit.
