Docet hoc ipsum Christus quoq;, cuius haec verba Ioan.5.Cap.leguntur: Amen amen dico vobis, qui audit verba mea, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitâ aeternâ; & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit à morte in vitam. Confirmatur hac multis exemplis vtriusq; testamenti. Dauidi certè peccatum suum confitenti, & Dei misericordiâ imploranti, Nathan non nouos ignis lustralis aut purgatorij terrores proposuit, sed dixit: Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum. Ita vero ad Messiam promissum illum remisit, in quem totius mundi peccata transferri debuerunt, vt supra ex Isaia docuimus. Et Christus eos, qui apud ipsum peccata defleuerunt, & eius merito cupierunt seruari, in pace abire iussit, eò quòd fides eos seruaret. At quomodo pacatus conscientijs poterunt abire, si ignis illius terribilis cruciatus adhuc illis timendi fuissent? Et in primis hoc facit, quod latroni in ipso mortis articulo se inuocanti respondit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Hīs (inquam) nos insistere conuenit, ignem vero illum fletitiū, monachus & sacrificijs, papisticae culinae eafaloribus, relinquamus: qui nisi cum Deo & Ecclesia eius ludere desinant, aliquando igne illum inextinguibilem sentient, quem ille suis contemptoribus pasim minatur.
units.tr: From this it follows that we are fully redeemed through the merit of Christ, and freed not only from guilt (as the Scholastic Sophists put it) but also from punishment. For since the record of our debts has been cancelled, no one can demand payment of it from us from now on, or rightfully require any new satisfaction from us. So let those be refuted here who do not openly deny that Christ made expiation for our sins on the Cross, but say that the punishment of sin has not been removed, and that it must be paid off partly in this life and partly in the fire of purgatory. This doctrine is not only false but also childish and ridiculous. For on their view God would deal with us as if someone said to a debtor: "I remit to you the ten gold pieces you owe me and will strike them from my account book, on this condition, however, that whenever I need workers in my vineyard you go there as a hired labourer until you have paid off the whole sum." Who would say that anything had been remitted to that debtor? Yet these men imagine no other God for us. For if we must make satisfaction for our sins, either in this life or in the next, and expiate them by our own labours and torments, then we can boast little of Christ's merit and satisfaction. Indeed, his merit would be nothing for us, and there would be no fruit of this petition by which we ask for free forgiveness. But all Scripture teaches the opposite, showing that the merit of Christ is of the highest worth before the Father, and that prayers made in faith are most effective before him. But this fiction was needed by greedy men, who sought gain from the living as well as from the dead. From it came costly funerals, thirty-day masses, anniversary rites, generous bequests and many other practices, by which foolish people, deceived by these men's teaching, thought that souls were helped and refreshed in purgatory, or were more quickly freed from those torments. Yet not content with this, they also hired out their own efforts to others, as though by singing or chanting, fasting, saying Masses, and finally by the merits of their own works, they could come to the aid of those labouring in that fire. And these works they called works of supererogation, as if they themselves had an abundance of them, and could therefore dispense them to others for a price or sell them. Here we find a twofold error, and both are full of impiety. For, contrary to the authority of all Scripture, they claimed for themselves such holiness that they said they could do more than was necessary for their own salvation; and then they claimed for themselves what belongs to Christ alone, who communicates his righteousness to us, so that for its sake we are counted righteous in the sight of God. Therefore, admonished by the words of this petition, let us not doubt that God the Father, who commanded us to pray thus, forgives us our sins for the sake of his Son Jesus Christ, and forgives them in such a way that he does not even remember them any more (as he speaks through the Prophets), much less that he wishes them to be expiated by us, who are already dead. The article of faith found in the Apostles' Creed agrees with this in every respect. For just as in prayer we ask for free forgiveness, so in the Creed we profess that we believe the confession that the Son of God made and suffered for us. If, then, we believe this, and by believing obtain it, no purchase, no human satisfaction, and no payment of punishment in money will be needed here. Christ himself teaches the same thing, and his words are read in John chapter 5: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, he that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation, but is passed from death unto life." This is confirmed by many examples from both Testaments. To David, surely, when he confessed his sin and implored God's mercy, Nathan did not propose new fires of cleansing or the terrors of purgatory, but said: "The Lord has taken away your sin." Thus he also dismissed him to the promised Messiah, on whom the sins of the whole world were to be laid, as we showed above from Isaiah. And Christ ordered those who had lamented their sins before him, and desired to be saved by his merit, to go away in peace, because faith saved them. But how could they depart with consciences at peace, if they still had to fear the terrible torments of that fire? And above all this is shown by his answer to the thief who called upon him at the very moment of death: "Today you will be with me in paradise." On these things, I say, we ought to rest. As for that fiery and fabulous purgatory, let us leave it to the monks and the Papists' kitchen-stoves, the sacrificers; unless they stop mocking God and his Church, they will one day feel that unquenchable fire with which he constantly threatens his despisers.

units.la: At hic obijciūt nonnulli: Cur ergo Deus hominibus flagitiosis & poenitere nescijs iram suam minatur, & poenas grauissimas, vtpote famem & rerum inopiam, pestem item cum alijs morborum generibus nouis & immedicabilibus, adhaec bellū, terrae vastitatē & infinita alia immittit? Iūe: Cur ergo Dauid postquam peccatū suum confessus est, & à Propheta Nathano remissionis promissione accepit, à filio suo Absalone regno eiectus & omni afflictionum genere multatus est, ita vt inter suos liberos incestos cocubitus & parricidia patrari, & coinuges proprias foedissimè violari, senserit? Quis illum peccatorum poenas exoluisse & pro ijs satisfecisse negabit? Sed facilis est ad hanc obiectionem responsio. Primo enim non de impijs & reprobis huius seculi filijs hîc loquimur, quos Deus propter incurabilem malitiam & deuotū peccandi studium, dum hîc viuunt, punire incipit, vt suae iustitiae specimina toti mundo exhibeat. Quae poena (cùm ipsi non solum incurabiles sint, verumetiā illis conuaciores fiant) ipsis aeternae damnationis quasi praeludium sunt. Sed de filijs Dei nobis sermo est, qui propter peccata sua ab illo vtisitantur aduersis & afflictionibus varijs, nō quidē vt hīs peccata sua expient, sed vt ceu paternis virgis caro ipsorum castigetur, ne & ipsi incurabiles facti in scelera altius demergantur, & cū infelici atq; poenitere nescio mundo male pereant. Ita tota hanc causam Paulus explicat, quando de lue, qua Deus Corinthios propter foedum Caenae Dominicae abusum pūniebat, loquens, inter alia sic dicit: Cum iudicamur, à Domino erudimur, siue castigamur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Quasi diceret: Videtur quidē Deus iudicij sui rigore aduersus suos etiā vti, quando morbos, bella, persecutiones & alia aduersa immittit. Sed longè alia est ratio istorum omniū. Nam quæcunq; sunt huius generis, tanquā paternæ castigationes suscipi debent, quibus nos ad emendationem vitæ & poenitentiā excitat, ne in grauem illud & horribile iudicium incidamus, quo mundū contumace & incurabile punire statuit. Quo sensu Petrus quoq; dicit, iudicium à domo Dei incipere, vt huius filij per hoc emendati exitium mundo paratū effugiant. Et huc referri debent, quacunq; Dauidi post factam peccati confessione acciderūt, & quae nobis quoq; in eiusmodi casibus accidere solent: ne poenas putemus, quibus nos pro peccatis nostris iustitiae Dei satisfacere oporteat. Quoad hoc enim iā ante satis demonstratum est, solum Christum esse, qui suae mortis merito peccata nostra expiauerit, & ita quidem, vt nulla alia satisfactione praeterea fit opus. Quotquot vero à fide alieni extrà hunc esse deprehendentur, ij peccatorum poenas exoluent in horrendo illo & aeterno igne, quem diabolo & eius ministris iam inde ab origine rerum paratum esse Scriptura testatur.
units.tr: But here some object: why then does God threaten his wrath to wicked men who do not know how to repent, and send on them the gravest punishments, such as famine and want of goods, also plague with other kinds of new and incurable diseases, besides war, the devastation of the land, and countless other things? Again: why then did David, after he confessed his sin and received from the prophet Nathan the promise of forgiveness, get driven from his kingdom by his son Absalom and afflicted with every kind of suffering, so that he saw incestuous intercourse and murders carried out among his own children, and his own wives foully violated? Who will deny that he paid the penalties of his sins and made satisfaction for them? But the answer to this objection is easy. For first, we are not speaking here of the impious and reprobate sons of this age, whom God, on account of their incurable wickedness and their eager devotion to sinning, begins to punish while they live, so that he may display to the whole world examples of his justice. Such punishment (since those men are not only incurable but grow worse for it) is for them a kind of foretaste of eternal damnation. But our discussion concerns the sons of God, who for their sins are tried by him with various adversities and afflictions, not so that they may expiate their sins by these, but so that their flesh may be chastised as with a father's rods, lest they too, becoming incurable, sink deeper into wickedness and perish miserably with the unhappy and unrepentant world. Paul explains this whole matter in this way, when, speaking of the plague with which God punished the Corinthians for their shameful abuse of the Lord's Supper, he says among other things: "When we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world." It is as if he said: God indeed seems to use the severity of his judgment against his own people when he sends diseases, wars, persecutions and other adversities. But the reason for all these things is quite different. For whatever is of this kind must be received as fatherly chastisements, by which he stirs us up to amend our lives and to repent, lest we fall into that grievous and dreadful judgment by which he has decided to punish the stubborn and incurable world. In this sense Peter also says that judgment begins at the house of God, so that his children, corrected by this, may escape the destruction prepared for the world. And to this must be referred whatever befell David after his confession of sin, and whatever is wont to befall us too in such cases; we must not think of them as punishments by which we ought to satisfy the justice of God for our sins. For on this point it has already been sufficiently shown that Christ alone is he who by the merit of his death expiated our sins, and in such a way that no other satisfaction is needed besides it. But all who are found to be alien to faith and outside of him will pay the penalties of their sins in that dreadful and eternal fire which Scripture testifies was prepared for the devil and his ministers from the beginning of the world.

units.la: Et haec quidem in quintam huius Orationis petitionem de peccatorum remissione aut condonatione diximus. Continent ista totum nostrae redemptionis negotiū. Audiuimus enim nos in Dei conspectu miseros & omnium egenos debitores esse, quibus non aliter succurri posset, quàm per immensam Dei gratiam atq; misericordiā, quam nobis u in Filio suo Iesu Christo praestitit. Hunc, vt peccata nostra expiaret, in mundum misit, & eundem pro nobis tradidit, vt qui credit in illum, non in peccatis suis pereat, sed illius merito seruetur. Quapropter petitio quoq; ista potissimum illius merito nititur, in quod nos respicere, & eius fiducia precari oportet, ne nos Deus, prout peccatis nostris meruimus, puniat, sed propter Filium suum nobis propitius esse dignetur. Unde colligitur, petitionem hanc illis nequaquam seruire, qui aut propriae iustitiae confidunt, aut peccatorum remissionem extra Christum quaerunt. Nam qui suis nituntur operibus, & hus seruari sibi persuaserunt, ij petitione ista sibi minime opus esse arbitrantur. Illis autem qui peccatorum remissionem non in vno Christo quaerunt, eadem prorsus inutilis est, cùm (vt Petrus ait) praeter illud non aliud nomen sub caelo hominibus datum sit, per quod nos seruari oportéat. Actu 4.
units.tr: And these things we have said concerning the fifth petition of this Prayer, on the forgiveness or remission of sins. They contain the whole business of our redemption. For we have heard that we are wretched debtors, lacking everything, in the sight of God, and that we could be helped in no other way than through the immense grace and mercy of God, which he has shown us in his Son Jesus Christ. To make expiation for our sins, he sent him into the world and handed him over for us, so that whoever believes in him should not perish in his sins but be saved by his merit. Therefore this petition too rests chiefly on his merit. We ought to look to that merit and pray with confidence in it, that God would not punish us as our sins deserve, but would deign to be merciful to us for the sake of his Son. From this it is gathered that this petition in no way serves those who either trust in their own righteousness or seek forgiveness of sins outside Christ. Those who rely on their own works and have persuaded themselves that they will be saved by them think this petition is not needed at all. But for those who do not seek the forgiveness of sins in Christ alone, it is utterly useless, since (as Peter says) there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved. Acts 4.

units.la: Porrò peculiare quid huic petitioni connectit Christus, conditionem scilicet certam, qua debita nostra nobis non alia ratione remitti precamur, quàm qua nos ijs ignoscimus, qui in nos peccauerunt. Dicimus enim: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. In quibus verbis ante omnia obseruari debet, ea non (vt quidam sentiunt) intelligenda esse, quasi meritum quoddam statuatur, & quod nobis peccata ideo remittere teneatur Deus, quia nos alijs condonamus quae in nos deliquerunt. Nam vt prolixè alibi docuimus, nostrorum operum meritum nullum est, cùm neq; ex nobis ipsis boni quid faciamus, neq; perfecta, sed propter inhaerentem naturae vitiositatem polluta quoq; sint ea, quae Spiritus sancti virtute adiuti facimus. Et absurdum foret, nos ad nostri alicuius operis meritum in ea ipsa precatione remitti, quia nos Deo debitores esse fatemur, qui gratuita condonatione opus habeamus. Sed & remissionis vocabulum omnem nostri meriti gloriationem excludit.
units.tr: Next, Christ attaches to this petition something peculiar: namely a definite condition, on which we pray that our debts be forgiven us only in the same way as we forgive those who have sinned against us. For we say: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." In these words, first of all, it must be observed that they are not (as some think) to be understood as if some merit were being established, so that God would be bound to forgive us our sins because we pardon others the offences committed against us. For, as we have taught at length elsewhere, there is no merit in our works. We do nothing good of ourselves, nor do we do anything perfect; even what we do, aided by the power of the Holy Spirit, is polluted by the inherent corruption of our nature. And it would be absurd that we should be pointed, in that very prayer, to some merit of our own, when we confess that we are debtors to God and need his gratuitous pardon. Moreover, the very word "remission" excludes all boasting of our own merit.

units.la: Alius ergo huius appendicis sensus necessario quaerendus erit, qui & fidei nostrae praecipuis capitibus & toti scripturae consentiat. Est autem vs, quod Dominus partim nos nostri erga proximū officij admonere, & ad hoc praestandū graui & necessaria conditione obstringere vult: partim nos de peccatorum nostrorum remissione certos facere argumento irrefragabili, quod in nobis ipsis inuenire possimus. Quae causa est, quòd apud Lucam nostrum verba ista sic leguntur: Etenim ipsi remittimus omnibus, qui nobis debent. Quòd si vero in nosipsos descendamus, patebit appendice hanc nobis in primis necessariam esse. Nam primò natura vindictae cupidi sumus, adeo, vt multi in eo gloriam summam consistere putent, si nullam ipsis factam iniuriam inultam abire sinant. At quia charitas Christiana, quae propria filiorum Dei nota est, locum habere non potest, vbi vindictae cupiditas regnat, & proinde haec nobis exitij causa foret, non temere Christus in ea petitione, quae maxime omnium nobis necessaria est, huius nos admonere voluit, vt quoties precamur, nobis in mentem veniat, vindictae omni prorsus longum valere renuntiandum esse, nisi nosipsos proprijs precibus velimus damnare. Deinde sentimus subinde quàm variis tentationib. nos Satan oppugnet, vt fidem nostram, qua gratuitam peccatorum remissionem speramus, labefactet. Necesse ergo nobis est, vt non solum promissionibus Verbi Dei confirmemur, verumetiā intra animos & conscientias nostras certum aliquod gratiae & misericordiae Dei argumentum habeamus. Argumentum eiusmodi est facilitas & bonitas illa, qua ijs ignoscimus, qui nos dicto aut facto aliquo laeserunt. Cùm enim (vt Paulo ante dictum est) naturali quadam vindictae cupiditate rapiamur, iniurias acceptas nunquam condonabimus, nisi Dei Spiritus naturae nostrae vitiositatem corrigat, vindictae ardorem restinguat, & charitatis ignem in nobis accendat. Vbi ergo hoc factum fuerit, certum est, nos Dei Spiritu agi, & proinde (vt Paulus ait) Dei filios esse. Unde colligere possumus, Deū nobis velle propitium esse, & nostrus delictis ignoscere, cùm Spiritum suum nobis donarit, & huius virtute renatos in filiorum suorum numerum adoptauerit. Itaq; huius appendicis proprius sensus, & vsus in duobus
units.tr: Another sense of this appendix must therefore necessarily be sought, one that agrees both with the chief articles of our faith and with the whole of Scripture. It is this: the Lord wishes partly to remind us of our duty towards our neighbour and to bind us to discharge it by a grave and necessary condition; and partly to make us certain of the remission of our sins by an irrefutable argument which we can find within ourselves. This is why in our Luke these words are read thus: "For we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us." If we descend into ourselves, it will be plain that this appendix is especially necessary for us. For, first, we are by nature eager for vengeance, to such an extent that many think their highest glory consists in letting no injury done to them go unavenged. But since Christian charity, which is the proper mark of the sons of God, cannot find a place where the lust for vengeance reigns, and this would therefore be our ruin, Christ did not rashly wish to remind us of it in that petition which is of all the most necessary to us. So whenever we pray, it may come to mind that we must utterly bid farewell to all vengeance, unless we wish to condemn ourselves by our own prayers. Then, we feel from time to time how variously Satan assails us, so as to weaken our faith, by which we hope for the free remission of sins. It is therefore necessary for us to be confirmed not only by the promises of the Word of God, but also to have within our minds and consciences some certain token of the grace and mercy of God. Such a token is that readiness and goodness by which we forgive those who have harmed us by word or deed. For since (as was said just above) we are carried away by a natural desire for vengeance, we will never pardon the injuries we have received unless the Spirit of God corrects the corruption of our nature, quenches the heat of vengeance and kindles the fire of charity in us. Where this has been done, it is certain that we are moved by the Spirit of God and, as Paul says, are sons of God. From this we can gather that God wishes to be merciful to us and to pardon our sins, since he has given us his Spirit and, having reborn us by its power, has adopted us into the number of his sons. Thus the proper sense and use of this appendix consists in two things:

units.la: Summa huius petitionis.
units.tr: The summary of this petition.

units.la: Conditio huius petitionis.
units.tr: The condition of this petition.

units.la: Causae conditionis huius.
units.tr: The reasons for this condition.

units.la: Rom. 8. hisce consistit, quòd & nostri officij admonemur, & de peccatorū nostrorum remissione certiores efficimur. Quare verba hæc Christianis hominibus non (vt quidam sibi persuadent) terrorem, sed potius consolationem dulcissimam afferunt, &c.
units.tr: Rom. 8. It consists in this: that we are both reminded of our duty and made more certain of the remission of our sins. Wherefore these words bring to Christian people not (as some persuade themselves) terror, but rather the sweetest consolation, etc.

units.la: Elucet hîc rursus immensa & plus quàm paterna Dei bonitas, qui pro dono omnium maximo, quod ab ipso postulari poterat, nō aliud à nobis exigit, quàm quod nobis ad huius etiā vitæ tranquillitatem seruandam vtile ac necessarium est. Quid enim ab illo peti potest præstantius, quàm gratuita delictorum remissio, ex qua salus nostra omnis dependet? Quid verò ille vicissim pro hac a nobis exigit? Num aurum, argentū, vestes aut laboriosa aliqua corporis seruitia? Minimè. Sed vnū hoc, vt sicuti ipse nobis ex gratia ignoscit: ita nos quoq; ijs ignoscamus, qui nos offenderūt. Vbi si rectè expendamus, patebit, ad nos ex eo plus cōmodi redire, quàm ad eos, quibus à nobis ignoscitur. Quoad enim vindictæ cupiditas & quæ ex illa nascuntur inuidia atq; odium in nobis regnant, nobispisis molestias & labores infinitos accersimus, dum intra animos nostros ringimur, noctes insomnes ducimus, ira ardemus, & multa alia facimus, quæ tam corpori quàm animæ officiunt. Nam hîs ipsis preces quoq; nobis inutiles, imò noxias reddimus. Quàm primùm verò extinctis hisce prauis affectibus offensas omnes proximi nostris condonamus, mox omnibus hisce liberamur molestijs, & nobis amicos facimus eos, qui prius vt hostes nobis suspecti, & ideo formidini quoq; erant. Quod si verò postremum hoc nos fallat, & tanta sit aduersariorum nostrorum contumacia, vt nostra facilitate & indulgentia vinci non possit, nobis tamen illa minimè fraudi erit, qui iam & Deum nobis propitium esse scimus, & vera animi pace & tranquillitate fruimur. Hæc diligentius considerata docent, Deum perinde nobiscum agere, ac si princeps aliquis clementissimus subditis, qui aduersus ipsum re bellarunt, non modo ignoscat, verumetiam satu factionis loco non aliud mandet, quàm vt actorum omnium ἀμνησίᾳ aut obliuione sancita, ipsi inter se vitam tranquillam degant, nec quisquā alteri aliquid exprobret. Nos enim quoties peccamus, qui alij quàm Deo rebelles sumus? Hîc ergo, nisi æternùm perire libeat, supplices illius gratiā implorare, & vt nobis ignoscat precari cogimur. Tanta autem bonitatis est ille, vt non solum nobis condonet rebellionem istam, sed omnis pœna loco (siquidem ita loquisas est) hoc vnum exigat, vt ipsi eadem facilitate erga nos mutuò vtamur, & vitam viuamus tranquillam atq; beatam. Quis ergo negabit æquum & necessarium esse, vt illi obtemperemus? Quis non dementes & insanos esse dixerit omnes eos, qui ei obedire dedignantur?
units.tr: Here again shines forth God's immense and more than paternal goodness, who, for the greatest of all gifts, which could have been asked of him, demands from us nothing other than what is useful and necessary for us even for keeping the tranquillity of this life. For what can be asked of him that is more excellent than the free forgiveness of sins, on which all our salvation depends? And what, in turn, does he demand from us in exchange for this? Gold, silver, garments, or some laborious bodily services? By no means. He demands only this: that, just as he himself forgives us out of grace, so we too forgive those who have offended us. If we weigh this rightly, it will be clear that more advantage comes back to us from it than to those to whom we grant forgiveness. For as long as the desire for vengeance and the envy and hatred that arise from it reign in us, we bring upon ourselves endless troubles and labours: we are tormented in our minds, we pass sleepless nights, we burn with anger, and we do many other things that harm body and soul alike. Indeed, by these very things we make our prayers useless to ourselves, or even harmful. But as soon as we have put out these wicked passions and forgive our neighbours all their offences, at once we are freed from all these troubles, and we make friends of those who before were suspected by us as enemies and were therefore also feared. But if this last point should disappoint us, and the obstinacy of our adversaries is so great that it cannot be overcome by our readiness and indulgence, it will nevertheless do us no harm, since we already know that God is merciful to us and we enjoy true peace and tranquillity of mind. These things, considered more carefully, teach that God deals with us just as a most merciful prince deals with subjects who have rebelled against him: he not only pardons them but, instead of making satisfaction, commands nothing more than that, with all deeds sanctioned by amnesty [ἀμνησία] or oblivion, they live a peaceful life among themselves, and no one reproach another with anything. For how often do we sin, and what else are we than rebels against God? Here, then, unless we wish to perish for ever, we are compelled to implore his grace as suppliants and to beg that he forgive us. Yet he is so good that he not only pardons us this rebellion, but, in place of any punishment (if we may so speak), requires only this one thing: that we use the same readiness towards one another, and live a tranquil and blessed life. Who, then, will deny that it is fair and necessary that we obey him? Who would not call mad and insane all those who disdain to obey him?

units.la: Erant hæc diligentius consideranda ijs, qui vindictæ studio & odio ita ardent, vt ne minimam quidem iniuriam, quàm accepere, inultam sinant, cùm ipsi grauissimorum scelerum, quibus Deum offenderunt, condonationem ab eo quotidie flagitent. Imitantur hi malignum illum seruum, qui remissione decem millium talentorum sibi factā, à conseruo suo centum denarios violenter exigere ausus est. Quid verò inde lucri retulit? Vnum hoc, quòd ipsum ad carceres perpetuos herus damnauit. Accidit hoc ipsum omnibus, qui proximo offensas suas condonare nolunt, vt sibi prius factā à Deo gratia priuentur, & iustum eius iudicium contra se prouocent. Maior tamen eorum est iniquitas, qui nullis iniurijs prouocati alijs inuident bona, quæ ipsos à Deo accepisse vident, & ijsdem dolo, fraude, vi aperta nocere student. Quo ore isti Dei misericordiam implorabunt, qui eos perditos volunt, à quibus nunquam læsi sunt? Iubet alibi Dominus, vt qui rem diuinam factur sunt, si recordentur proximum aliquid causæ aut litis contra se habere, relicto ad altare sacrificio suo, prius cum illo reconcilientur, quàm illud Deo offerant. At nostra sacrificia preces sunt. Quanto magis ergo precaturi opus est, vt quam ipsi animo conceperunt inuidiam deponant, si preces suas Deo accepras esse velint? Debet præterea hîs accenseri, qui sub sanctitatis nomine fratribus obtrectant, et vitia eorum occultiora quoq; diuulgant. Eo enim argumento testantur, se charitate destitui, qua (vt ex Solomone Petrus annotauit) multitudine peccatorum tegere potius quàm diffamare solet. At perinde isti faciunt, vt hypocritæ illi, quos Christus in oculo fratris festucam obseruare ait, cùm in proprio oculo trabes maiores non sentiant. Adnumerari deniq; istis omnibus debent, qui se proximo ignoscere aiunt, ea tamen conditione, ne ipsis in conspectum veniat, neq; vllum ab ipsis amici officiū vel beneficium expectet. Est hoc genus hominum hodie vulgare, qui se omni officio defunctos putant, si maleficium non dederint, etiamsi à benefaciendo abstineant. At hi quoq; ex ista petitione nō multum fructum referunt. Cùm enim non aliter quàm cum ea conditione, quam modo andiuimus, ijs ignoscant, qui ipsos læserunt, quid aliud petunt, quam vt ipsos quoque Deus à conspectu suo reijciat & nullo beneficio dignetur? Sed ô miseros, quibus hoc accidit. Qui enim à Deo negliguntur, ij omnibus diaboli insidijs patent, ac non possunt non perire. Quid multis? omnia corda penetrat Dominus huius petitionis appendice, & necessario dilectionis vinculo omnes inter se mutuò obstringit, cum aut hanc colere, aut gratia quam nobis in Filio suo fecit, nos priuari oporteat.
units.tr: These things ought to be considered more carefully by those who burn with such zeal for revenge and hatred that they let not even the smallest injury they have received go unavenged, when they themselves ask God daily for forgiveness of the gravest sins by which they have offended him. They imitate that wicked servant who, after ten thousand talents had been forgiven him, dared to violently demand a hundred denarii from his fellow servant. What did he gain from it? Only this: his master condemned him to perpetual prison. The same thing happens to all who are unwilling to forgive their neighbours their offences: they are deprived of the grace God has granted them and provoke his just judgment against themselves. Yet greater is the iniquity of those who, though provoked by no injuries, begrudge others the goods they see others have received from God, and strive to harm them by deceit, fraud and open violence. With what face will those implore God's mercy who wish those to perish by whom they have never been harmed? The Lord elsewhere commands that those who are about to offer sacrifice, if they remember that their neighbour has some cause or lawsuit against them, should leave their sacrifice at the altar and first be reconciled to him before offering it to God. But our sacrifices are prayers. How much more necessary, then, is it for those about to pray to lay down the hatred they have conceived in their minds, if they wish their prayers to be accepted by God? Moreover, those should be counted among these who, under the name of holiness, disparage their brothers and spread abroad even their more hidden faults. By this they testify that they lack charity, which (as Peter noted from Solomon) is accustomed to cover a multitude of sins rather than publicise them. But these men act just like those hypocrites whom Christ says observe the speck in their brother's eye while not noticing the greater beams in their own. Finally, those should be added to all these who say they forgive their neighbour, but on condition that he not come into their sight and expect no friendly service or benefit from them. This kind of person is common today: they think they have fully discharged their duty if they have done no harm, even if they abstain from doing good. But these too gain little fruit from this petition. Since they forgive those who have injured them only on the condition we have just heard, what else do they seek but that God too should cast them from his sight and deem them worthy of no benefit? But O wretched those to whom this happens! For those who are neglected by God lie open to all the snares of the devil and cannot but perish. Why say more? The Lord penetrates all hearts by this appendix to the petition, and binds all together by the necessary bond of love, since we must either cultivate this or be deprived of the grace he has shown us in his Son.

units.la: Caeterum hic aliquos in fide infirmos esse audire, qui dicunt: Scio quidem me nullius hominis odio flagrare, & mei muneris esse, vt omnibus condonem, qui me iniuria aliqua affecerunt. Verunta men me imbecilliorem esse sentio, quâ vt hoc digne & vt par est præstare possim. Exerit enim se sub inde carnis ingenium improbum, quod me ne quod bene instituì perficiam, impedit. Itaque anxius quid faciam nescio, & metuo, ne erga me quoq; Deus sui iudicij rigore vtatur. Et tantum apud non nullos istæ cogitationes efficiunt, vt vltima hæc petitionis istius verba omittant, ne aduersus propriam salutem precentur. Sed inutile est hoc effugium, quod quærunt. Nam etsi verba ista non pronuntiemus, rata tamen manet Christi sententia apud Matthæum dicentis: Si remiseritis hominibus offensas ipsorum, remittet etiam vobis Pater ille cœlestis. Sin autem non remiseritis hominibus ipsorum offensas, neq; Pater vester remittet vobis offensas vestras. Qui vero in fide se imbeciliores esse sentiunt, non ideo desperare debent, quoad propensam ad ignoscendū voluntatem in semetipsis deprehenderint. In eiusmodi enim casu homo bifariā considerari debet, nimirum quoad Spiritū aut internum hominem, & quoad carnem. Pugnant hi duo inter se perpetuò, sicut Paulus admonet & singuli in semetipsis quotidie experiuntur. Quoad vero pugna hæc durat, bene sperandum est, quia ex ea apparet nos carnis affectui nondum succubuisse. Cur enim de victoria desperet miles, qui se hosti adhuc resistere posse sentit, vt fuga minime sit opus? At hic spiritui opem feramus oportet, quod multis modis potest fieri. Proderit enim, quando carnem vel inuitam cogimus hostibus bene facere. Ita enim quod inuita aliquandiu facit, tandem cum voluptate faciet, vbi eo assueuerit. Opus item, vt in Dei verbo nos sedulò exerceamus, inq; beneficiorum eius consideratione simus frequentes: hæ enim meditationes tam Dei quam proximi dilectionem vehementer accendunt. In primis autem necesse erit precibus ad Deum assiduis, vt suum Spiritum in nobis confirmet, & fidem augeat. Qui istis studeant, ijs suam imbecillitatem Deus non imputat, sed potius gratia ea dignatur, vt quotidie in omni virtute proficiant, & tandem perfecta aduersus carnem victoria potiantur.
units.tr: Here we hear that some are weak in faith, who say: "I know indeed that I burn with hatred of no man, and it is my duty to forgive all who have wronged me in any way. Yet I feel myself too feeble to do this worthily and as it ought to be done. The wicked nature of the flesh now and then asserts itself and prevents me from carrying through what I have begun well. So I am anxious and do not know what to do, and I fear lest God also use the rigour of his judgment against me." These thoughts affect some so strongly that they omit the last words of this petition, lest they pray against their own salvation. But this escape they seek is useless. For even if we do not pronounce those words, the sentence of Christ in Matthew stands fast, saying: "If you forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive men their offences, neither will your Father forgive you your offences." Yet those who feel themselves weaker in faith ought not on that account to despair, as long as they find in themselves a willing disposition to forgive. In such a case a man must be considered in two ways, namely as to the Spirit or the inward man, and as to the flesh. These two contend constantly with one another, as Paul admonishes, and each of us experiences this daily in himself. As long as this struggle lasts we may well hope, because it shows that we have not yet succumbed to the desires of the flesh. For why should a soldier despair of victory who feels he can still resist the enemy, so that there is no need to flee? But here we must bring aid to the spirit, and this can be done in many ways. It will help when we compel the flesh, even against its will, to do good to our enemies. For what it does unwillingly for a while, it will at length do with pleasure once it has grown accustomed to it. It is also necessary that we diligently exercise ourselves in the Word of God and be frequent in considering his benefits; for these meditations greatly kindle both the love of God and the love of neighbour. Above all it will be necessary to pray constantly to God, that he may confirm his Spirit in us and increase our faith. To those who devote themselves to these things God does not impute their weakness; rather, he graciously deigns that they make progress daily in every virtue and at last win complete victory over the flesh.

units.la: Postremò propter fanaticos quosdam obseruemus, petitionem hanc non abolere magistratus officium, nec obstare, quo minus ille sceleratos & flagitiosos dignis pœnis coerceat. Priuatus enim hominibus ista seruiunt, & vindictam priuatam prohibent, ne quid ex huius cupiditate in ijs, quæ ad nos spectant, faciamus. Atqui alia est magistratus conditio, quem Deus instituit, vt ipsius iudicia exerceat, & bonos quidem defendat, malos autem, prout meruerunt, puniat: de quo Paulus in epistola ad Romanos multum disserit. Interim firmiter teneamus, nos omnes natura peccatores esse, peccatorum autem remissionem apud solum Deum per Iesum Christum inueniri. Itaque illius gratiam implorare, & omnem remissionis atque salutis spem in vnius Christi merito collocare debemus, cum omnibus verò hominibus charitatem & pacem colamus, vt germani filij Dei, & regni eius hæredes simus cum Iesu Christo Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, on account of certain fanatics, let us observe that this petition does not abolish the office of the magistrate, nor stand in the way of its punishing criminals and wicked men with due penalties. These words serve private persons and forbid private vengeance, so that we do nothing out of that desire in matters which concern us. But the condition of the magistrate is different: God has instituted him to exercise judgment, to defend the good but to punish the wicked as they deserve, a point on which Paul discourses at length in his epistle to the Romans. Meanwhile let us hold firmly that we are all sinners by nature, and that forgiveness of sins is found only with God through Jesus Christ. Therefore we must implore his grace and place all our hope of forgiveness and salvation in the merit of Christ alone; and with all men we must cultivate charity and peace, that we may be true sons of God and heirs of his kingdom together with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXII.

units.la: PETITIO VI.
units.tr: PETITIO VI.

units.la: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem: sed libera nos à malo.
units.tr: And lead us not into temptation: but deliver us from evil.

units.la: Dominus & redemptor noster Iesus Christus, hactenus nos docuit quinque petitionibus omnia ea à Patre nostro cœlesti postulare, quæ ad promouendam sui nominis & regni gloriam, & communem omnium nostrum tam animæ quam corporis salutem pertinent. At quia homines sumus, & quoad in hac carne viuimus, varijs tentationibus oppugnamur, quibus nos ab inobedientia Dei, & aeternae salutis via Satan abducere conatur, necesse est, ut aduersus illius astutias atq; insidias fraudis & astutiae plenas probe armemur, ut in quouis certaminis genere victoriam obtinere possimus. Huic rei seruit, quae nunc recitata est, sexta & ultima orationis Dominicae petitio, in qua ex Christi mandato dicimus: NE INDVCAS NOS O PATER IN TENTATIONEM: SED LIBERA NOS A MALO. Vbi ante omnia (quod in prioribus quoque petitionibus factum est) verba singula expendere oportebit, ut ex illis verus huius petitionis sensus atque usus nobis pateant.
units.tr: Our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ has so far taught us to ask of our heavenly Father, in five petitions, everything that pertains to the advancement of the glory of his name and kingdom, and to the common salvation of us all, both of soul and of body. But because we are human, and for as long as we live in this flesh we are assailed by various temptations, by which Satan tries to draw us away from obedience to God and from the way of eternal salvation, we must be well armed against his cunning and his snares, which are full of deceit and craftiness, so that we may win the victory in every kind of conflict. The sixth and last petition of the Lord's Prayer, which has just been recited, serves this purpose. In it, at Christ's command, we say: LEAD US NOT, O FATHER, INTO TEMPTATION: BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL. Here, above all (as was also done in the earlier petitions), we must weigh the individual words, so that the true meaning and use of this petition may become clear to us.

units.la: Tentare proprie idem est quod experiri, & ex certis indiciis alicuius rei periculum facere, ut sciamus quae eius sit natura, conditio & usus. Varie autem verbum illud usurpatur. Dicitur enim Deus ab hominibus tentari: quando nimirum non credunt verbo eius, quod ipsum bonum, clementem, amantem humani generis, beneficum & omnipotentem esse docet: sed insuper postulant, ut se talem esse certis aliquibus operibus demonstret, quae ipsi illi praescribunt. Sic Israelitae illius bonitatem simul & omnipotentiam tentauisse dicuntur, quando carnes sibi ab illo dari, & quasi epulum in deserto instrui postulauerunt. Et eodem sensu diabolus Christum tentauit, cum petijt, ut sese ex pinnaculo templi praecipitem daret, & eo argumento disceret, num ipsum Deus Angelorum suorum ministerio inter omnia pericula seruare vellet?
units.tr: To tempt properly means the same as to test, that is, to make trial of something by certain signs, so that we may know its nature, condition and use. The word is used in various ways. God is said to be tempted by men when they do not believe his word, which teaches that he is good, merciful, loving toward the human race, beneficent and almighty, but instead demand that he prove himself to be such by certain works which they themselves prescribe. Thus the Israelites are said to have tempted both his goodness and his almighty power when they demanded that flesh be given them by him and a feast be prepared for them, as it were, in the wilderness. And in the same sense the devil tempted Christ when he asked that he throw himself down headlong from the pinnacle of the temple, and by this means learn whether God would keep him safe through the ministry of his angels amid all dangers.

units.la: Vt autem Deus & res aliae a nobis tentantur: ita vicissim nos quoq; tentamur, ut certius constet, qui simus, quod item nostrum sit ingenium, quae animi affectio, & quid alij sibi ipsis de nobis polliceri debeant. Et hoc quidem non vno modo fieri consueuit. Primo enim homo alios tentare solet, ut intelligat ad quid eorum opera ipsi utilis esse possit, & num quid boni vel mali de vnoquoq; sit sperandum. Deinde ab ipso Deo tentamur, non quidem ea ratione, quasi is qui simus non probe norit, sed quod vel nosipsos in propria infirmitatis et imperfectionis cognitionem inducere vult, ne confidentiores simus: vel fidem nostram & dilectionem, quae ipsum prosequimur, manifestam facere, ut plures alij nostro exemplo erudiantur. Sic Abrahamum olim tentauit, quando iussit, ut filium suum Isaacum, quem vnice diligebat, & in quo promissiones omnes acceperat, immolaret. Nã procul dubio intuitam fidei eius constantiã, & ardentissimam dilectionem, quae erga ipsum flagrabat, Deus non ignorauit: Veruntamen eum toti mundo in exemplum voluit proponere, ex quo omnes discant, quousque fides & dilectio debeat extendi: eo vsque nimirum, ut ei non opes modo, verum etiam ex nobis natos, adeoque proprium sanguinem consecremus, & fidei constantiam tunc quoque retineamus, quando ipse Deus aliqua agere vel etiam mandare videtur, quae ipsius promissionibus aduersentur. Simili modo Iobus quoque ex Dei permissione tentatus est, ut in illo commune fidei, obedientiae & patientiae exemplum omnes homines haberent. At de hoc tentationum genere in praesenti non agitur. Quia enim illa a Deo proueniunt, cuius voluntati nos totos in tertia petitione subijcimus, absurdum foret nunc precari, ne quid huius ille nobiscum instituerat. Deinde non potest non felix esse eiusmodi tentationum finis, cum neque supra vires nos grauari patiatur Deus, & euentum bonum ipse etiam largiatur. Ideo Dauid ab illo explorari & tentari cupiebat. Et Iacobus Apostolus scribit: Pro summo gaudio ducite fratres mei, quoties in tentationes varias incider/ quod probatio fidei vestrae parit patientiam, caeterum patientia opus perfectum habet. Item: Beatus vir, qui tolerat tentationem: quoniam cum probatus erit, accipiet coronam vitae, quam promisit Dominus iis, à quibus diligitur, &c.
units.tr: Just as God and other things are tested by us, so in turn we too are tested, so that it may be more certainly established what we ourselves are, what our disposition is, what state of mind we are in, and what others ought to expect of us. And this does not happen in only one way. First, a man is accustomed to test others, so that he may understand what use their work can be to him, and whether anything good or bad is to be hoped from each of them. Next, we are tested by God himself, not indeed as if he did not know thoroughly what we are, but because he wishes either to bring us to a knowledge of our own weakness and imperfection, so that we may not be overconfident, or to make manifest our faith and the love with which we cleave to him, so that many others may be instructed by our example. Thus he once tested Abraham, when he commanded him to sacrifice his son Isaac, whom he loved alone and in whom he had received all the promises. For without doubt God did not fail to see the steadfastness of his faith and the most ardent love that burned in him; yet he wished to set him before the whole world as an example, from which everyone may learn how far faith and love ought to extend: namely, to the point that we dedicate to God not only our possessions but also the children born of us, and indeed our own blood, and keep the constancy of our faith even when God himself seems to do or even command things that are contrary to his promises. In a similar way Job also was tested by God's permission, so that all men might have in him a common example of faith, obedience and patience. But it is not of this kind of temptation that we are speaking at present. For since these come from God, to whose will we wholly submit ourselves in the third petition, it would be absurd now to pray that he not carry out any such thing with us. Next, the outcome of such temptations cannot but be happy, since God does not suffer us to be burdened beyond our strength, and himself also bestows a good result. Therefore David desired to be examined and tested by him. And the apostle James writes: "Count it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various temptations, since the testing of your faith produces patience; but let patience have its perfect work." Likewise: "Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been approved he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord has promised to those who love him," etc.

units.la: Tentamur praeterea à communi nostro hoste diabolo, quem scriptura proprie Tentatorem vocat, eo quod assidue varia molitur, ut nos à Deo abducat, & per incredulitatem aut peccandi licentiam male perdat, quo nomine illum in petitione ista πονηρόν dicimus, quod non simpliciter malum significat, sed eum qui mente & voluntate ad nocendum proclivis alios quoque corrumpere & perdere studet. Ita Graeci πονηρὸν ὕδωρ dicunt τὸ νοσοποιόν, id est, aquam quae morbos parit. Et conuenit hoc epitheton diabolo proprie. Quia enim iam inde ab initio mendax & homicida fuit, hoc suum ingenium perpetuo retinet. Et cum artifex sit astutissimus, innata nobis natura nostrae vitiositate ad suum institutum abuti nouit. Quam primum enim cupiditates pravae in nobis oriuntur, mox ille quoque ex eo occasione sumpta suggestionibus pessimis nos infestat, & eo nos adigere conatur, ut quod animo concepimus in opus quoque erumpat. De hoc tentationum genere hic potissimum nobis sermo est, quae nobis exitio sunt, nisi probe vigilemus. Precamur autem Patrem coelestem, ne nos diaboli insidijs circumueniri patiatur, sed vt ex huius manu liberet, & in tentationibus suo Spiritu conseruet, ne in peccatorum laqueis pereamus. Quo loco de rebus maximi momenti admonemur, quae diligenter obseruari merentur.
units.tr: Moreover, we are tempted by our common enemy, the devil, whom Scripture properly calls the Tempter, because he constantly devises various schemes to draw us away from God and to destroy us, through unbelief or through license to sin. For this reason we call him in this petition evil [πονηρόν], which does not mean simply bad, but one who, in mind and will, is inclined to harm and eagerly seeks to corrupt and destroy others too. Thus the Greeks call that water bad [πονηρὸν ὕδωρ] which is disease-producing [τὸ νοσοποιόν], that is, water that produces sickness. And this epithet properly belongs to the devil. For since he was a liar and a murderer from the beginning, he keeps this nature perpetually. And since he is a most cunning craftsman, he knows how to turn to his purpose the nature innate in us, with its viciousness. For as soon as wicked desires arise in us, he too seizes the occasion they offer and at once assails us with most wicked suggestions, trying to drive us to this, that what we have conceived in our mind should also break out into deed. It is this kind of temptation that is chiefly our concern here, and it will be our ruin unless we watch carefully. We pray, however, that the heavenly Father not allow us to be surrounded by the snares of the devil, but that he deliver us from his hand and preserve us in temptations by his Spirit, so that we do not perish in the nooses of sin. In this place we are reminded of matters of the greatest importance, which deserve to be carefully observed.

units.la: Primò discimus, imò ipsi fatemur petitione ista, quam periculosa sit in hoc seculo vitae nostrae conditio, cum assiduè nobis orandum sit, vt nos Deus in tentationibus tueatur, & ex hoc statu nostri potestate liberet. Nisi enim hic periculum effet ingens, precatione ista minimè esset opus. Sed vt vedi-mus hostem habemus veterem, versipellem, improbum & inquietum, qui indesinenter leonis rugientis instar oberrans quaerit quem deuoret. Medijs autem hic varijs vtitur, & fere inopinatis, ex quibus vix aliquid periculi timemus. Inter quae caro nostra fere primas tenet, cuius desiderijs nos accendit, vt bis plus quam Deo & propriae saluti tribuamus. Ponit item nobis ob oculos illecebrosum huius mundi exemplu, cuius maximae in nobis permouendis vires sunt, cum alioqui voluptatu, opum, fastus & honorum huius seculi appetentes simus. Accedunt colloquia prava, quae per impios, quibus ceu flabellis vtitur, instituit, vt peccati magnitudinem extenuet. Sed & secundis & aduersis rebus abuti nouit, vt nos in via salutis remoretur. Nam si diuitiae et honores affluant, fere diaboli suggestione decepti efferimur & superbimus, atque Dei immemores illis confidimus, deniq; ijs ad fastum & libidinem abutimur. Quo fit, vt ea nobis idololatriae & grauissimorum scelerum causa sint, quibus cum assidua gratiarum actione ad promouendam Dei gloriam vti debebamus. E contra si paupertate, ignominia aut aliis aduersis premamur, mox aduersus Deum murmuramus, iudicia eius accusamus, quasi nobiscum iniquius agat. Idem in valetudine corporis integra & in morbis, in pace & bello, rerum abundantia & caritate, omnibus deniq; alijs, quae in hoc seculo agentibus accidunt fieri solet. Si quid enim carni iucundum est, eo abutimur. Sin minus impatientes & queruli ad media illicita confugimus, quibus contra Dei voluntatem nobisipsis conamur opem ferre. Paupertatem enim pleriq; per dolos, vsuras, furta & rapinas fugiunt. In morbis ad Deos, ad magos, exorcistas & veneficia recurritur. Bellis surgentibus, in impijs & blasphemis militibus spes omnis collocatur. Deniq; quicquid accidat, nunquam desunt hosti nostro occasiones, quibus nos tentet, & a Deo abstrahat. Itaq; vita nostra militia & pugna perpetua est, in qua eò plus periculi imminet, quod hic non de patria terrena, de corporum libertate, fortunis, vxoribus & liberis agitur: sed de caelesti patria & aeterna tam corporum quam animarum salute. Si enim diaboli suggestionibus succumbamus, iam nobis perijt filiorum Dei stipendium, neq; eius loco aliud sperare possumus, quam quod diabolo & eius angelis est destinatum. Vides ergo quanta sit eorum stultitia, qui huius seculi vita, tam plena periculi & miseriarum, ita delectantur, vt in ea spem ac fiduciam omnem collocent.
units.tr: First, we learn, indeed we ourselves confess in this petition, how perilous the condition of our life is in this world, since we must constantly pray that God protect us in temptations and free us from this state by his power. For unless the danger were great, there would be no need for this prayer at all. But as we see, we have an old enemy, crafty, wicked and restless, who wanders about without ceasing, like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. He uses various means here, and mostly unexpected ones, from which we fear scarcely any danger. Among these our flesh holds almost first place; by its desires he inflames us to give twice as much to them as to God and to our own salvation. He also sets before our eyes the alluring example of this world, which has the greatest power to move us, since we are in any case eager for pleasure, wealth, pride and the honours of this age. To these are added wicked conversations, which he arranges through impious men, whom he uses as it were as fans, so that he may diminish the greatness of sin. But he also knows how to abuse both prosperity and adversity, so that he may hold us back on the way of salvation. For if riches and honours flow in, we are commonly deceived by the devil's suggestion and become puffed up and proud; forgetful of God, we trust in them and finally abuse them for pride and lust. Hence it comes about that these things become for us causes of idolatry and of the gravest crimes, whereas we ought to use them with constant thanksgiving to promote the glory of God. On the other hand, if we are oppressed by poverty, disgrace or other adversities, we straightway murmur against God and accuse his judgments, as if he were dealing with us more unjustly than he should. The same is commonly the case in bodily health and in sickness, in peace and in war, in plenty and in dearth, and in all other things that happen to those living in this world. For if anything is pleasing to the flesh, we abuse it; but if not, we become impatient and querulous and flee to unlawful means, by which we try to help ourselves against the will of God. For most people escape poverty by fraud, usury, theft and robbery. In sickness they resort to the gods, to magicians, exorcists and sorceries. When wars break out, all hope is placed in impious and blasphemous soldiers. In short, whatever happens, our enemy never lacks opportunities by which to tempt us and draw us away from God. And so our life is a continual warfare and battle, in which the danger is all the greater because what is at stake is not an earthly fatherland, the liberty of our bodies, our fortunes, wives and children, but the heavenly fatherland and the eternal salvation of both body and soul. For if we succumb to the devil's suggestions, the wage of the sons of God is already lost to us, and in its place we can hope for nothing other than what has been appointed for the devil and his angels. You see, then, how great is the folly of those who take such delight in the life of this age, so full of danger and misery, that they place all their hope and trust in it.

units.la: Docet praeterea haec petitio, nos infirmiores esse, quam hosti huic nostro resistere possimus. Quis enim tam ignauus & meticulosus fuerit, vt alterius opem quaerulus implores, si ipse ad hostem repelendum satis instructus sit? At Dei Filius nos Patris coelestis opem postulare iubet aduersus diabolum & eius machinationes. Ergo nobis in hac pugna vires desunt, quae ad victoriam parandam possint sufficere. Etenim quid ipsi hic efficiamus, cum praecipue hominis facultates nobis aduersentur, imò arma ac tela sint, quibus Satan nos maximè oppugnat? Quid enim intellectus nostler aliud facit, quam quod nobis in hac pugna impedimento est, cum non in Dei verbum respiciat, sed suis placitis ducatur? Quid vero nostrae cogitationes, quam quod diabolo seruiunt, cum a puero (vt Deus ipse ait) praue sint. Itaq; si in hoc certamine nostro intellectui, nostris consiliis & viribus aliquid tribuamus, mox locum diabolo dabimus nos vincendi. Perinde ac si quis belli imperator hostem ijs militibus debellare instituat, quos non solum inuitos ad pugnam procedere, verumetiam hosti fauere nouit. Recte ergo Christus Patris sui opem flagitare iubet, ne nostris viribus & consiliis innixi nobisipsis exitium accersamus.
units.tr: This petition also teaches that we are too weak to resist this enemy of ours. For who would be so cowardly and fearful as to beg for another's help if he were himself equipped enough to repel the enemy? Yet the Son of God bids us ask the heavenly Father's help against the devil and his schemes. So we lack the strength in this struggle that would be enough to win the victory. Indeed, what could we accomplish here by ourselves, when our very human faculties oppose us, and are in fact the weapons and missiles with which Satan attacks us most fiercely? For what does our intellect do but hinder us in this struggle, since it does not look to God's Word but is led by its own preferences? And what do our thoughts do but serve the devil, since from childhood they are evil (as God himself says)? So if in this contest we attribute anything to our understanding, our counsels and our powers, we will soon give the devil the chance to conquer us. It is like a commander of an army who sets out to defeat an enemy with soldiers who not only go into battle unwillingly but are known to favour the enemy. Rightly, then, Christ bids us seek the help of his Father, lest, relying on our own strength and counsels, we bring ruin upon ourselves.

units.la: Non debet autem hoc nos terrere, sed consolari potius. Quia enim nos alibi auxilium quaerere iubet, simul admonet, victoriam non à nobis, sed ab alio pendere, qui nobis maior sit atque potentior. Est haec efficacissima consolatio. Etenim si vel cogitaremus victoriam hanc nostris viribus obtineri oportere, non possemus non desperare, cum tam infirmos & imbecilles nos esse sentiamus. Sed ex Deo illa pendet, quem nemo viribus superat. Certò igitur nobis sperare licet, quod huius operis adiuti superiores futuri & diabolum repulsuri simus. Et huc in primis faciunt huius petitionis verba, quibus dicimus: Ne inducas nos ô Pater in tentationem. Nam etsi non de salutari illo tentationum genere loquamur, quibus nos Deus explorat & probat, sed de illis, quibus Satan nos perdere conatur: perinde tamen loquimur, ac si Deus harum quoque causa & author sit. Nec enim (ut quidam perperam precantur) dicimus: Ne permittas nos induci in tentationem: Sed, Ne inducas, scilicet tu, vel (ut Graeci vocabuli emphasim exprimamus) Ne inferas nos in tentationem. Deo itaque non otiosam permissionem aut consensum, sed actionem ipsam tribuimus. Quod tamen non eo sensu accipi debet, quasi ille nostrorum peccatorum & exitij author sit: sed ideo sic loquimur, quod tam nos quam omnia nostra illius providentiae subiecta sunt, & per hanc ita gubernantur, ut absque eius voluntate & praedestinatione nihil nobis accidat: & ne ipse quidem diabolus nihil contra nos instituere aut aggredi audeat, nisi id ei Deus permittat, & certo consilio definierit. Dicitur quidem diabolus princeps huius mundi, sed non eo sensu, ut in eius potestate sit pro suo arbitrio quicquam agere, sed ideo quod infelices & incurabiles huius saeculi filij illum pro suo principe & domino agnoscunt, & huic potius cum suo exitio in omni scelerum genere, quam Deo in sanctitate servire malunt. Sed & ipse Satan iactabundus se rerum omnium potentem dicere audet: quàm vero inanis & vana sit haec gloriatio, exemplum Iobi & alia infinita testantur. Et quid in hominem ille possit, qui (ut Euangelica historia docet) ne in porcos quidem vilissimos ius habet? Testatur praeterea Christus, quod discipulos quidem ille cribrare expetierit, se autem suis precibus illi obstitisse, ne quid pro ficeret. Recte ergo petitio ista sic enuntiatur, quasi tentationes à Deo immittantur, cum absque huius permissione nihil contra nos possit Satan. Vbi simul tenere oportet, Deum non securum aut negligentem rerum administratorem esse, qui absque certo consilio quicquam fieri permittat: sed ut omnia illius providentiae subiacent, ita eadem sapienter, & iuste gubernat, ut quem ab aeterno decreuit, finem assequantur.
units.tr: This should not terrify us, however, but rather comfort us. For in bidding us seek help elsewhere, he also reminds us that victory depends not on us but on another who is greater and more powerful than we are. This is a most effective consolation. For if we thought this victory had to be won by our own strength, we could not help despairing, since we feel how frail and feeble we are. But it depends on God, whom no one surpasses in strength. Therefore we may confidently hope that, aided by his work, we shall become superior and drive off the devil. The words of this petition, in which we say, "O Father, do not lead us into temptation," are especially relevant here. For although we are not speaking of that salutary kind of temptation by which God tests and proves us, but of those by which Satan tries to destroy us, we still speak as if God were also the cause and author of these. For we do not say (as some wrongly pray) "Do not allow us to be led into temptation," but "Do not lead us," that is, you yourself do not lead us, or (to bring out the emphasis of the Greek word) "Do not bring us into temptation." So we attribute to God not an idle permission or assent, but the action itself. Yet this must not be understood to mean that he is the author of our sins and our ruin. We speak thus because both we and all our affairs are subject to his providence, and are so governed by it that nothing happens to us without his will and predestination; and not even the devil himself dares to undertake or attack anything against us unless God permits it and has determined it by his certain counsel. The devil is indeed called the prince of this world, but not in the sense that it is in his power to do anything at his own pleasure. Rather, it is because the unhappy and incurable children of this age acknowledge him as their prince and lord, and prefer to serve him in every kind of wickedness to their own ruin, rather than serve God in holiness. Yet Satan himself, boasting, dares to say that he is powerful over all things; but how empty and vain this boast is, the example of Job and countless others bears witness. And what power does he have over a man, if he does not even have the right over the most worthless swine (as the Gospel story teaches)? Christ also testifies that he sought to sift the disciples, but that he himself by his prayers resisted him, so that he could accomplish nothing. Rightly, then, this petition is phrased as if temptations were sent by God, since Satan can do nothing against us without his permission. At the same time we must hold that God is not a careless or negligent manager of affairs who permits anything to happen without a certain plan. Rather, as all things are subject to his providence, so he governs them wisely and justly, that they may reach the end he decreed from eternity.

units.la: Hac ut fideles in omni alio casu consolantur: ita nos in hac petitione vehementer in fide confirmant, quod hic in primis fieri necesse est. Nec enim nobis quicquam gravius accidere potest, quam cum non solum, quoad externa turbamur, aut ad peccandum impellimur, verumetiam intra animos nostros tentamur, ut cogitemus nos à Deo derelictos, & diaboli libidini traditos esse. Est haec omnium gravissima tentatio. At si huius petitionis probè memores cogitemus, nihil nobis absque Dei voluntate accidere, mox spe meliori concepta confirmamur, quando constat, illum non iustum modò & sapientem, verumetiam humani generis amantissimum esse. Hinc enim colligimus, tentationes nobis salutares fore, neque illum pássurum, ut supra vires tentemur. Debent huc sanctorum exempla referri, qui ex gravissimis quoque delictis eximios fructus reportarunt, ut in Davide, Petro ac similibus esse videre. Quare in nulla tentatione, quantumuis gravi & periculosa nos desperare decet. Nam ut Dominus & seruator noster Iesus Christus, à Spiritu in desertum ductus est, ut à Satana tentaretur, & ibidem victoriam gloriosam obtinuit: ita nos quoque non sine Dei consilio tentationibus obijcimur, in quibus proculdubio vincemus. Perpetuò enim ratum eris illud Petri dictum: Nouit Deus suos ex tentatione eripere. Ergo non sine certa fiducia precatione hac uti debemus, quam uobis Christus minimè traditurus erat, nisi sciuisset Patrem caelestem nos clementer esse exauditurum.
units.tr: As this consoles the faithful in every other case, so in this petition it powerfully confirms them in faith, which is especially necessary here. For nothing more grievous can befall us than to be troubled not only in external matters, or driven to sin, but to be tempted inwardly, so that we think we have been abandoned by God and handed over to the devil's lust. This is the most grievous of all temptations. But if, mindful of this petition, we consider that nothing happens to us without the will of God, we are at once strengthened by a better hope, since it is certain that he is not only just and wise but also most loving of the human race. From this we conclude that temptations will be salutary for us, and that he will not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. To this we should refer the examples of the saints, who have gained remarkable fruit even from the gravest sins, as we see in David, Peter and others like them. Therefore we ought never to despair in any temptation, however grave and dangerous. For just as our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by Satan, and there obtained a glorious victory, so we too are exposed to temptations not without the counsel of God, and in them we shall without doubt conquer. For that saying of Peter will remain true for ever: "The Lord knows how to rescue his own from temptation." Therefore we ought to use this prayer with sure confidence, which Christ would certainly not have taught us unless he knew that the heavenly Father would graciously hear us.

units.la: Quod verò in alijs petitionibus monuimus, eas non ore solum enuntiari oportere, sed curandum esse, ut nostra studia & actiones illis respondeant, hoc etiam in ista in primis observari debet. Et sanè magna hic nobis occasio offertur de nostro officio diligentius cogitandi. Quoniam enim constat nobis perpetuam pugnam contra diabolum suscipiendam esse, in qua diuini auxilij inuocatione opus sit, sequitur, nos quoque aduersus hostes illius conatus ita pugnare debere, ne quas illi inducias concedamus, multò minus pacem aut foedus cum illo faciamus vllum. Nam minimè decet, ut qui in baptismo Christo nomen dederunt, cum eius hoste acerrimo pacem aut amicitiam colant. Etenim mundi iudicio turpiter facere dicuntur, qui sociorum quidem opem in bello postulant, interim verò clam cum hoste colludunt, & pacem cum sociorum damno ineunt. Atqui eadem hic ratio est. Bellum etenim hoc Deus ipse in prima rerum origine suscitavit, quando dixit, se inimicitias positurum inter serpentem & Vita nostra petitioni huic respondeat. tem & mulierem & inter utriusque semen. Atqui mulieris semen, de quo illic agitur, proprie quidem est Christus: sed huic subsunt omnes Dei filij, qui illius membra dici solent. Cum ergo pugna indesinens sit inter Christum & diabolum, neque inter ipsos ulla communio aut societas esse possit, aequum non fuerit, ut illius membra quoque sub suo capite & Imperatore aduersus eundem hostem perpetuo dimicent, neque ullam cum eo pacem aut communionem habeant. Cur enim Christi miles in diaboli castris & sub huius signis conspiciatur? Quomodo item Christiani hominis nomine amplius censeri merebitur, qui diaboli societatem colit, cum quo Christo nihil commune esse potest? Hic enim humani generis seruator est: diabolus autem hoc perditum cupit. Christus Patris sui voluntatem nobis manifestauit: at hanc diabolus obscurare & suppremere satagit. Christus veritas & lux est: diabolus autem mendax & tenebrarum princeps. Christus seipsum nostrae redemptionis causam in mortem tradidit: diaboli autem studium est, ut in peccato & morte nos detineat. Christi Spiritus est sanctus, purus & omnis boni author: diaboli spiritus impurus & obscenus, ad scelera & vitae impuritatem impellit. Denique, quo diligentius veritatis studia & ingenium consideramus, eo clarius patebit quam inter se dissimiles & contrarij sint. Officij ergo nostri fuerit aduersus diabolum dimicare, siquidem Christi discipuli & membra esse velimus. Perfidi enim in Christum sunt, quotquot sese diaboli seruitio mancipant: eoque detestabilior est eorum perfidia, si interea Dei opem aduersus eum hostem implorent, cum quo tam pridem foedus & pacem fecerunt.
units.tr: What we have noted in the other petitions, that they must not only be uttered with the mouth but that care must be taken that our zeal and actions correspond to them, must above all be observed in this one as well. And indeed here we are given a great occasion to think more carefully about our duty. For since it is certain that we must wage perpetual war against the devil, in which the invocation of divine help is necessary, it follows that we too must fight against his attempts in such a way that we grant him no truce, and much less make any peace or covenant with him. For it is by no means fitting that those who have given their name to Christ in baptism should cultivate peace or friendship with his bitterest enemy. Indeed, by the judgement of the world, those are said to act shamefully who ask for their allies' help in war, yet meanwhile secretly collude with the enemy and make peace at their allies' expense. Yet the same reasoning applies here. For God himself stirred up this war at the very beginning of things, when he said that he would put enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between her seed and his seed. Now the woman's seed of whom he speaks is properly Christ; but under him are all the sons of God, who are commonly called his members. Since therefore the struggle between Christ and the devil is unceasing, and there can be no communion or fellowship between them, it would not be fair for his members too, under their head and commander, to fight without end against the same enemy, and yet to have any peace or fellowship with him. For why should a soldier of Christ be seen in the devil's camp and under his standards? Likewise, how can he deserve to be counted any longer as a Christian who cultivates fellowship with the devil, with whom Christ can have nothing in common? For Christ is the Saviour of mankind, but the devil desires its destruction. Christ has revealed his Father's will to us, but the devil strives to obscure and suppress it. Christ is truth and light, but the devil is a liar and the prince of darkness. Christ gave himself up to death as the cause of our redemption, but it is the devil's aim to keep us in sin and death. The Spirit of Christ is holy, pure and the author of all good; the spirit of the devil is impure and foul, and drives us to crimes and to impurity of life. In short, the more carefully we consider the nature and character of truth, the more clearly it will appear how unlike and opposed to one another they are. It is therefore our duty to fight against the devil, if we wish to be disciples and members of Christ. For all who surrender themselves to the devil's service are faithless to Christ; and their faithlessness is all the more detestable if, meanwhile, they implore God's help against that enemy with whom they have long ago made a covenant and peace.

units.la: At quoniam nullam ad hostem decincendum stratagema utilius est, quam si armis proprijs exuatur, aut ne illius uti possit impediatur, nobis quoque videndum erit, ut diabolo arma praeripiamus, quibus nos potissimum oppugnat. Sunt haec (ut nuper diximus) caro nostra, intellectus & sapientia humana, cogitationes item nostrae, & mundi huius exemplum cum omnibus ijs, quae in mundo iucunda & suauia habentur. Hic ergo necesse fuerit, ut ista aut in nostram potestatem redigamus, aut aduersus ea sic armemur, ne nobis nocere queant. A nobis ipsis ergo pugnam hanc exordiri oportet, ut nimirum propriam carnem domemus & mortificemus, ne per suas cupiditates nobis dominetur. Deinde intellectum & rationem carnis sub fidei obedientiam cogi necesse est, ne nostris placitis ducamur, sed ab uno verbo Dei pendeamus: imo suspectum nobis esse debet, quicquid nostra ratio nobis suadet aut consulit. Cogitationes autem cordis nostri frenari debent, ne possent desideria vagentur. Adhaec de mundo recte iudicare discamus, quod nimirum (ut Ioannes inquit) totus in malo iaceat, & a Dei regno auulsus diabolo seruiat. Hoc qui intelligunt, eius exemplum abominari potius quam sequi solent. Cogitemus item diligenter, quam incerta & fallacia sint, quaecunque mundus praeclara & pretiosa aestimat, utpote opes, honores, voluptates & quae alia sunt huius generis. Nam qui istorum lubricitatem agnoscunt, non multum diabolo per illa eos sollicitanti tribuent. Adhaec omnes peccandi occasiones vitare conuenit. Quo referri debet concupiscentia oculorum, quibus fere accendimur, ut illicita cupiamus & perpetremus: ut in Dauide apparet, cui diligentior Bethsabae lauantis contemplatio adulterij causa fuit, & ideo postea omnes monuit, ut oculos auertant, ne videant vanitatem. Quod qui studiose faciunt, ij aduersus Satanam multum praesidij sibi acquisiuerunt. Eadem aurium quoque & linguae ratio est, quas custodire oportet, ne colloquia lasciua cum quoquam instituamus, aures vero occludamus ad omnia, quae inhonesta & turpia sunt. Verissimum enim est, quod ex Menandro Paulus annotauit, pravi colloquijs bonos etiam mores corrumpi. Imo quae ipsi turpia & obscena dicimus, animos nostros malis desiderijs accendunt, ex quibus cogitationes foedae, & tandem scelera quoque aperta oriuntur. Nec temere Iacobus linguam igni confert, qui ab inferis succendatur, & animos nostros corrumpat. Et alibi dicit scriptura: Qui videre cupit dies bonos, linguam suam custodiat, &c. In primis autem procul excludendae sunt cantilenae obscenae de stupro, adulterijs & scortandi licentia. Hae enim eo plus nocent, quo magis Musicae lepore & vt commendantur. Similiter vestitus ratio habenda est. Nam si ius ad luxum, saltum & libidinem factus fuerit, tam nobisipsis quam aliis multorum scelerum occasionem praebet. Quae causa est, quod Prophetas & Apostolos non puduit de hoc praecepta dare, & luxum eius publice accusare. Multum quoque conducet, si in cibo & potu temperantes simus, ne per ebrietatem ratione omni extincta, carnis desiderijs habenas laxemus. Sunt enim quotidiana exempla, quae satis docent, quantam scelerum segetem ebrietas pariat.
units.tr: But since no stratagem is more useful for disarming an enemy than stripping him of his own weapons, or preventing him from using them, we too must see to it that we snatch from the devil the weapons with which he chiefly attacks us. As we said a little while ago, these are our flesh, our intellect and human wisdom, our thoughts, and the example of the world together with everything in the world that is held to be pleasant and agreeable. Here, then, we must either bring these under our control or arm ourselves against them so that they cannot harm us. This battle must therefore begin with ourselves: we must tame and mortify our own flesh, so that it does not rule over us through its desires. Next, we must compel our intellect and the reason of the flesh to obey faith, so that we are not led by our own opinions but depend on the one Word of God. Indeed, whatever our reason advises or recommends to us ought to be regarded with suspicion. Our heart's thoughts, too, must be restrained, lest our desires wander freely. Furthermore, we must learn to judge the world rightly, namely that, as John says, it lies wholly in evil and, torn away from the kingdom of God, serves the devil. Those who understand this are accustomed to abhor the world's example rather than follow it. Let us also consider carefully how uncertain and deceptive are all the things the world esteems as splendid and precious, such as riches, honours, pleasures and the like. For those who recognise the slipperiness of these things will not give the devil, who tempts them through such things, much power over them. Besides, we ought to avoid all occasions of sin. To this belongs the lust of the eyes, by which we are commonly inflamed to desire and commit what is unlawful, as appears in David, for whom a more careful gazing upon Bathsheba as she bathed became the cause of adultery; and for this reason he afterwards warned everyone to turn their eyes away, lest they see vanity. Those who do this diligently win much protection for themselves against Satan. The same holds for the ears and the tongue, which we must guard: we must not engage in lewd conversation with anyone, and we must close our ears to everything dishonourable and shameful. For it is most true, as Paul noted from Menander, that good morals are corrupted by evil conversations. Indeed, the things we ourselves call shameful and obscene inflame our minds with evil desires, from which foul thoughts and at last open crimes arise. Nor without reason does James say that the tongue is set on fire by hell and corrupts our minds. And Scripture says elsewhere: "He who desires to see good days, let him keep his tongue," and so on. Above all, obscene songs about debauchery, adultery and licence in fornication must be utterly shut out, for they do the more harm the more they are commended by the charm of music. Likewise, regard must be had to dress. For if it is made to serve luxury, dancing and lust, it offers occasion of many crimes both to ourselves and to others. This is why the Prophets and Apostles were not ashamed to give precepts about it and to accuse publicly its extravagance. It will also greatly help if we are temperate in food and drink, so that, reason being extinguished through drunkenness, we do not loosen the reins on the desires of the flesh. For there are daily examples which teach well enough what a harvest of crimes drunkenness produces.

units.la: Nam vt vulgo dicitur, vino illabente ratio & sapientia expellitur, & tunc (vt Solomon ait) oculi alienas formas spectare incipiunt, tunc cupiditatibus prauis accendimur, tunc lingua sermones inprobos & obscenos effert, tunc rixæ, pugnæ, cædes nascuntur, & infinita alia fiunt à pietate & Christiani hominis officio aliena. Vitetur præterea otium, quod multorum scelerum occasionem præbet.
