Quia enim hominis ingenium est, vt quiescere omnino non possit, nisi bonestis aliquibus studijs atq; actionibus occupetur, ad inhonesta & illicita delabitur. Quæ causa est, quod non scripturæ modo sacræ otium damnant, sed apud gentes quoque in bene constitutis ciuitatibus, otiosis pœnæ olim constitutæ fuerunt. Et hæc præcipua sunt, quæ in hoc tentationum certamine diligenter obseruari debent, ne à diabolo nostris proprijs armis vincamur.
units.tr: For, as is commonly said, when wine slips in, reason and wisdom are driven out; and then, as Solomon says, the eyes begin to look upon strange forms; then we are inflamed by wicked desires; then the tongue utters improper and obscene words; then quarrels, fights and murders arise, and countless other things foreign to godliness and to the duty of a Christian man. Idleness, moreover, must be avoided, since it offers occasion for many crimes. For it is the nature of man that he cannot rest at all unless he is occupied with some honourable studies and activities, and so he slides into what is dishonourable and unlawful. This is why not only Holy Scripture condemns idleness, but also among the nations, in well-ordered states, penalties were once established for idle persons. These are the chief things which must be carefully observed in this struggle with temptations, so that we are not conquered by the devil with our own weapons.

units.la: Caeterum vbi hæc fecerimus, vlterius nos progredi oportet, vt arma quoque paremus, quibus hostem repellere & omnino deuincere possimus. Quæ vero illa sint, paucis & perspicuè Paulus docet ad Ephesios sexto cap. sic scribens: Assumite vniuersam illam armaturam Dei, vt possitis resistere tempore aduerso, & omnibus confectis stare. State igitur lumbos circuncinctos veritate, & induti thorace iustitiæ, calceatis pedibus præparatione Euangelij pacis: assumpto insuper scuto fidei, quo possitis omnia iacula Mali illius ignita extinguere. Galeam item salutis accipite, & gladium Spiritus, hoc est, verbum Dei: Omni prece & supplicatione precantes omni tempore per Spiritum, & illi ipsi rei inuigilantes cum omni perseuerantia & supplicatione, &c. Armaturam Dei nobis Apostolus monstrat, ideo nimirum, quod hostis iste nulla humana & externa vi, sed solius Dei virtute vincitur. Armatura vero illam diligenter per partes describit. Primo enim lumbos circumcingere iubet veritate. Hæc igitur Christianorum hominum balteus militaris, adeoque ordinis æquestris & verae nobilitatis insigne est: & prima ordine collocatur, quia vbi illa locum habet, ibi Satan mendacij pater nihil potest proficere dolo & fraudibus suis, quæ per veritatis lucem facile discutiuntur. Secundo thoracem iustitiæ induere iubet, quo nomine non aliud quam meritum Iesu Christi, qui nostra iustitia est, intelligere debemus. Opus autem thorace isto, quia non alia consolatio efficacior est: si quando admissorum scelerum & innatæ vitiositatis conscientia nos diabolus oppugnat, & nos iam victos esse persuadere conatur, eo quod natura peccatores, & propter peccatum damnationi obnoxij simus. At si Christi meritis fide apprehenderimus, hunc eius ictum facile eludemus, & cum Paulo dicere licebit: Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est, qui iustificat, quis ergo qui condemnet? Tertio vt pedes calceatos habeamus monet Euangelio pacis. Pedes enim affectuum typus sunt, eo quod hæc tota hominis vita, perinde vt corpus pedibus, ducitur & regitur. At illi quia natura praui sunt, coerceantur & in ordinem redigantur oportet. Id vero per Euangelium fit, quo totus homo vnà cum intellectu & affectibus suis fidei obedientia subijcitur, ne secundum carnis suæ desideria, sed secundum Dei verbum ambulet. Et ideo Euangelium pacis dicitur, quod non solum pacem Dei nobis annuntiat & offert, verumetiam in illa nos conseruat, ne rursus filij irae efficiamur. Quarto cum Satan tentationibus acutissimis interdum nos infestet, quæ cogitationes & cupiditates varias & periculosas in nobis accendunt, scutum fidei apprehendere iubet Apostolus, quod ad restinguenda diaboli iacula abunde sufficit. Nam si in Deum vere credimus, desperatio apud nos locum nullum inueniet, vt tandem res huius seculi cadant. Neque etiam de eius præceptis dubitabimus, sed ea pro bonis, iustis & salutaribus agnoscemus, ideoque illa non impudenti & impia temeritate transgrediemur. Quinto galea salutis munitos esse conuenit, quæ non alia quam Christus est, quem alibi caput nostrum scriptura vocat. Ipse enim nobis vitam largitur, huius spiritum singulis membris distribuit, & simul nos aduersus omnes diaboli atque mundi assultus tuetur. Sexto gladium Spiritus nobis Paulus tradit, quo Satan vulnerari & omnino repelli solet. Est ille verbum Dei, quo si quis instructus fuerit, & ipsum in omni tentatione vibrauerit dextere, nullus porro Satanæ locus relinquitur, sed arena cedat oportet. Exemplo nobis fit Christus, qui cum in deserto tentaretur, hoc vnu gladio pugnauit & vicit. Hunc ergo imitemur, & quoties aliquid suggerit Satan, mox quid Deus loquatur & iubeat, quidue nobis promittat videamus, & mox hostis illius machinationes prorsus inanes & inefficaces esse patebit, etiamsi victoriam in manibus habere videatur. Exempli gratia, Suggerit ille, te posthac Deo non curæ fore, sed periturum omnino propter peccata tua. Huic suggestioni verbum Dei opponito, quo docemur, illum velle, vt omnes homines salui fiant, & in veritatis cognitionem veniant. Et quod ipse dixit: Viuo ego, nolo mortem peccato ru, sed vt conuertatur & viuat. Rursus obijcit ille quadruplator, Christum quidem mundi seruato rem esse, sed eius meritum nihil ad te pertinere, qui pluribus & gravioribus peccatis, quàm reliqui homines obnoxius fis. Huic calumnia Christi dictum opponito: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego vos refocillabo. Item: Neminē qui venit ad me, eiciam foras. Quòd si autē hostis ille improbus blanditijs peccatorum te capere conetur, dum ea mirificè extenuat, tunc Decalogi praecepta, legis item promissiones atq; minas in mente revocabis, quae fucum illum mox abstergent, vt peccati atrocitas tota tibi pateat. At cùm nostræ vires in hoc certamine nullæ sint, neq; etiam armis istis prout decet vti sciamus, postremò ad preces & supplicationes nos Paulus remittit, & in his assiduos esse iubet. Quia verò de his iam abunde dictum est, & Christus vltima hac petitione idem nos docet, non opus fuerit plura in praesenti addere.
units.tr: Furthermore, when we have done these things, we must go on further, so that we may also prepare the weapons with which we can repel the enemy and utterly overcome him. Paul teaches briefly and plainly what these weapons are, writing thus to the Ephesians in the sixth chapter: "Take up the whole armour of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all taking the shield of faith, with which you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of that wicked one. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication," and so on. The Apostle shows us the armour of God, certainly because that enemy is conquered by no human or external force, but only by the power of God. He describes that armour carefully part by part. First, he bids us gird our loins with truth. This, then, is the military belt of Christian men, and it is indeed the badge of the equestrian order and of true nobility; and it is placed first in order, because where it has its place, there Satan, the father of lies, can accomplish nothing with his deceit and frauds, which are easily dispelled by the light of truth. Second, he bids us put on the breastplate of righteousness, by which name we must understand nothing other than the merit of Jesus Christ, who is our righteousness. This breastplate is needed because there is no more effective consolation: when the devil attacks us with the consciousness of sins committed and of innate corruption, and tries to persuade us that we are already defeated, because by nature we are sinners and liable to damnation on account of sin. But if we apprehend the merits of Christ by faith, we shall easily evade this blow, and we may say with Paul: "Who shall bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies; who then is he who condemns?" Third, he advises us to have our feet shod with the gospel of peace. For the feet are a type of the affections, because the whole of human life is led and directed by them, just as the body is by the feet. But since these are by nature perverse, they must be restrained and brought into order. This is done through the gospel, by which the whole man, together with his intellect and affections, is subjected to the obedience of faith, so that he walks not according to the desires of his flesh but according to the Word of God. And for this reason it is called the gospel of peace, because it not only announces and offers God's peace to us, but also keeps us in it, lest we become again children of wrath. Fourth, since Satan sometimes assails us with most piercing temptations, which kindle in us various and dangerous thoughts and desires, the Apostle bids us take up the shield of faith, which is more than sufficient for quenching the devil's darts. For if we truly believe in God, despair will find no place among us, so that the things of this age at last fall. Nor shall we doubt his precepts, but we shall acknowledge them as good, just and salutary, and therefore we shall not transgress them with shameless and impious rashness. Fifth, we ought to be protected by the helmet of salvation, which is none other than Christ, whom Scripture elsewhere calls our head. For he bestows life on us, distributes his Spirit to the individual members, and at the same time guards us against all the assaults of the devil and the world. Sixth, Paul hands us the sword of the Spirit, by which Satan is usually wounded and utterly driven off. This is the Word of God; if anyone is armed with it and brandishes it skilfully in every temptation, no place is left for Satan, but he must give ground. Christ is our example, who, when he was tempted in the desert, fought and conquered with this one sword. Let us therefore imitate him: whenever Satan suggests something, let us at once see what God says and commands, or what he promises us, and at once the enemy's devices will plainly appear utterly empty and ineffective, even if he seems to have the victory in his hands. For example, he suggests: "From now on God will have no care for you, but you will certainly perish on account of your sins." Set against this suggestion the Word of God, by which we are taught that he wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and what he himself said: "As I live, I desire not the death of a sinner, but that he be converted and live." Again that slanderer objects: "Christ indeed is the saviour of the world, but his merit does not pertain to you, who are more liable to more and graver sins than other men." Against this calumny set the saying of Christ: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Also: "Him who comes to me I will in no way cast out." But if that wicked enemy tries to catch you with the allurements of sins, while magnifying them wonderfully, then call to mind the precepts of the Decalogue, and the promises and threats of the law, which will soon wipe away that deception, so that the whole atrocity of sin lies open before you. But since our strength in this struggle is nothing, and since we do not know how to use these weapons as is fitting, Paul finally refers us to prayers and supplications, and bids us be constant in them. Since these things have already been sufficiently discussed, and Christ teaches us the same thing in his final petition, there is no need to add more at present.

units.la: Quòd si petitionem hanc ad hunc modum expendamus, & simul nostrū consideremus officium, mox apparebit, quàm varie hic peccemus, dum multa facimus, quae illi omnino aduersantur. Prae alijs tamen hac confutantur duo hominum genera. Primum est eorum, qui absque iusta & graui causa seipsos tentationibus periculosissimus immergunt, vt affectuum libidini satisfaciant, cùm interim precentur, ne Deus ipsos in tentationem inducat. In hoc genere sunt, qui quaestus causa ad eos commigrant, inter quos fidem in Christum profiteri non licet, & à quibus ad fidei abnegationē atq; idololatriam cogüntur. Deinde ij quoque, qui cum certam habeant vocationem, in qua Deo libere & tutò seruire possunt, illa tamen temere deserunt, & non vocante Deo ad aliud vitae genus transfeunt, quod periculi plenum esse nō ignorant, & in quo quotidie varie & graviter admodum tentantur. Quibus illos addito, qui improborū consortijs sese immisçent, à quibus ad intemperantes comesationes, aleam infamem, contemptum verbi Dei, scortationē & alia flagitia solicitantur. Deniq; ad hoc genus pertinent, quotquot ab illis non abstinent, per quae diabolo occasione nos tentandi damus audiuimus, & ita hosti arma ipsi tradunt, quibus in hoc certamine vincantur.
units.tr: If we weigh this petition in this way, and at the same time consider our own duty, it will soon become clear how many ways we sin by doing many things that are wholly opposed to it. Two kinds of people are especially condemned by it. The first are those who, without a just and serious cause, plunge themselves most dangerously into temptations in order to satisfy the lust of their passions, while all the time they pray that God would not lead them into temptation. In this group are those who migrate to places for the sake of profit where it is not permitted to profess faith in Christ, and where they are forced to deny the faith and to practise idolatry. Next are those who, although they have a certain calling in which they can serve God freely and safely, rashly abandon it and, without God calling them, pass over to another way of life, which they know is full of danger and in which they are daily tempted in many and very grievous ways. To these we add those who mix themselves with the company of the wicked, by whom they are enticed to intemperate drinking-parties, to infamous gambling, to contempt of the Word of God, to whoredom and other shameful deeds. Finally, this group includes all who do not abstain from those things by which we, as we have heard, give the devil an occasion to tempt us, and so hand over to the enemy the very weapons by which they will be conquered in this struggle.

units.la: Alterum genus omnes eos comprehendit, qui alijs scandalum dant, siue verbis obscenis, siue ad libidinem prouocandā compositis cantionibus, siue impudicis gestibus, vestitu deniq; & totius vitae suae exemplo. Quid autem vtriq; aliud faciunt, quàm quòd precatione hanc sibijpsis lusum iocum q; faciunt, & cum Deo impudenter ludunt? Nam tam suo quàm aliorum fidelium nomine clamant: Ne inducas nos ô Pater, in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo. Simul autem seipsos periculi q; peccatorum obijciunt, & alijs quoq; authores sunt non solum tentationum, verumetiam maximorū scelerum. Sunt hi petulantium nebulonum similes, qui in aquis periclitantes opem sibi ferri magnū clamoribus contendunt, interim verò sponte sese in profundissimos vortices praecipitant, & alios secū in periculi societatem trahunt. Vt verò hi indigni sunt quibus succurratur: ita illis quoque minimè sperandū est, quòd ipsos Deus sit exauditurus in precibus istis, quae non preces dici merentur, cùm his Deum simul & homines ludibrio habeant. Quapropter quod in alijs petitionibus monuimus, omni studio nobis annitendū est, ne quid hic petulanter aut cum hypocrisi fiat, sed vt in Dei conspectu animi intentio cum ore aut labijs consentiat, & actiones nostræ omnes precibus respondeant.
units.tr: The second kind embraces all those who give offence to others, whether by obscene words, by songs composed to provoke lust, by shameless gestures, or finally by their clothing and the whole example of their life. And what else do both kinds do but make a joke and a game of this prayer for themselves and play shamelessly with God? For they cry out in their own name and in the name of all the faithful: "Do not lead us, O Father, into temptation, but deliver us from evil." Yet at the same time they expose themselves to danger and to sins, and they are the authors for others not only of temptations but of the greatest crimes. They are like wanton scoundrels who, when they are in danger in the water, shout loudly for help to be brought to them, but meanwhile throw themselves headlong into the deepest whirlpools and drag others with them into the same peril. Just as such men do not deserve to be helped, so we must by no means hope that God will hear them in these prayers, which do not deserve to be called prayers, since by them they make a mockery of both God and men. Therefore, as we have advised in the other petitions, we must strive with all our zeal that nothing here be done wantonly or with hypocrisy, but that before God's eyes our intention of mind agree with our mouth and lips, and all our actions correspond to our prayers.

units.la: Reliquat Orationis Dominicae conclusio, quae à Luca omissa, apud Matthaeū talis habetur: Quia tuum est regnum, & potentia, & gloria in secula, Amen. Quae verba huc probè conueniunt, & consolationem habent dulcissimā, quae de multis cognitu & obseruatu necessarijs nos admonet: Primò enim Deus hic celebratur, quod inter precandū semper fieri debet, sicut ipse docet in Psalmo dicens: Tempore afflictionis inuoca me, & liberabo te, tu autem me glorificabis. Veruntamē haec ea modo attributa Dei commemorantur, quae in toto hoc negotio prae alijs cōsideratu vtilia & necessaria sunt. Tribuitur enim illi regnum, in coelo videlicet & in terra, cùm omniū creator sit & Dominus. Id verò nos plurimùm solatur aduersus diaboli potentiam atq; minas, quibus ita sese ostentat, quasi ad ipsum pertineat omniū regnorū huius mundi dominiū. At quod hic dicitur, cum tota Scriptura conuenit, quae passim regnū Deo tribuit. Dauid enim ait: Domini est regnū, & ipse dominatur gentibus. Ite: Dominus in coelo parauit thronū, & regnū eius dominatur in omnibus. Deinde potentiā quoq; illi tribuimus, ne quis regnum eius infirmum esse putet, aut quòd principū huius seculi similis sit, qui inanibus titulis superbi, eorum quoq; regnorum dominos sese iactant, quae nunquā viderunt, & in quibus potestate non habent aliquam. Non ea Patris nostri cœlestis cœditio, qui potentia instructus, adhæc æternus & ubiq; præsens est. Præterea gloriam & maiestatem quoq; ei asscribimus, quo & eius potentiam amplius prædicamus, simulq; testamur, ipsi omne gloriam, honorem & maiestatem deberi, cum ab ipso origine ducat omnis potentia, gloria & quicquid in cœlo & in terra boni est. Postremo fatemur, cum ista habere in secula, id est, in æternum. Vt enim Deus quoad essentiam suam æternus & nulli corruptioni obnoxius est: ita regnum quoque & potentia & maiestas eius, & quæcunq; alia de ipso prædicantur, æterna sunt, neq; unquam vel mutantur vel minuuntur. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Regnum tuum regnum æternum est, & imperium tuum durat in omnia secula. Psal.145.
units.tr: The remaining part of the Lord's Prayer is its conclusion, which Luke omits but which Matthew gives as follows: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen." These words fit well here, and they contain a very sweet consolation, and they remind us of many things that must be known and observed. First, God is praised here, which should always be done in prayer, as he himself teaches in the Psalm, saying: "Call upon me in the time of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Yet these attributes of God are mentioned only in so far as they are especially useful and necessary to consider in this whole business. For a kingdom is ascribed to him, in heaven and on earth, since he is the creator and Lord of all. This consoles us greatly against the power and threats of the devil, by which he displays himself as if the dominion of all the kingdoms of this world belonged to him. And what is said here agrees with all of Scripture, which everywhere ascribes the kingdom to God. For David says: "The kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations." Likewise: "The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom rules over all things." Next, we also ascribe power to him, lest anyone think that his kingdom is weak, or that it is like the kingdoms of the princes of this age, who, proud of empty titles, boast themselves as lords of kingdoms they have never seen and over which they have no power at all. Such is not the condition of our heavenly Father, who is endowed with power and is moreover eternal and present everywhere. Besides, we also ascribe glory and majesty to him, by which we both proclaim his power further and bear witness that all glory, honour and majesty are owed to him, since all power, glory and whatever good there is in heaven and on earth derives its origin from him. Lastly, we confess that he has these things for ever, that is, to eternity. For just as God is eternal in his essence and subject to no corruption, so his kingdom, power and majesty, and whatever else is predicated of him, are eternal, and they are never changed or diminished. Therefore David said: "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations." Psal. 145.

units.la: Plurimum vero ista faciut ad fidei nostrae confirmationem aduersus diaboli insidias atq; machinationes, cuius hoc vnicum studium est, vt Regnum Dei inter nos totum euertat. Quoties ergo de huius stabilitate dubitare incipimus, tunc huius conclusionis memores dicamus: Fatemur quidem o Pater, nos indignos esse, qui Regni tui & tantorum bonorum, quæ abs te petimus, participes efficiamur: at cum tuæ gloriæ rationem habere soleas, illa non negabis, ne quid tuo Regno, tuo nomini & maiestati tuæ decedat, &c. Est autem hoc magnum argumentum dignitatis filiorum Dei, fiduciæ item, qua aduersus mundi furores atq; minas nituntur. Nam ipsi fatentur, & quidē per Iesum Christum ita edocti quod Patrem in cœlis habeant, cui omne regnum, omnis potentia, gloria & maiestas in æternum debeatur: Qui item (vt Solomon & omnis Scriptura testatur) Regū corda in sua manu teneat, Reges constituat & e solijs suis deturbet, regna deniq; pro suo arbitrio mutet & transferat. Cur ergo aliquem timeant Christi cultores? Cur Regum minacibus edictis terreantur, cum ipsi Deo subiecti sint, neq; vires suas longius, quàm ille permiserit, possint extendere?
units.tr: These things contribute very greatly to the confirmation of our faith against the snares and schemes of the devil, whose only aim is to overthrow the Kingdom of God among us entirely. Therefore, whenever we begin to doubt its stability, let us remember this conclusion and say: "We confess indeed, O Father, that we are unworthy to be made partakers of your kingdom and of the great goods which we ask from you; but since you are wont to have regard for your own glory, you will not deny them, lest anything be lost from your kingdom, your name and your majesty," and so on. This is also a great argument for the dignity of the sons of God, and likewise for the confidence with which they stand against the fury and threats of the world. For they confess, and have indeed been taught this through Jesus Christ, that they have a Father in heaven to whom all kingdom, all power, glory and majesty belong for ever; who also (as Solomon and all Scripture bears witness) holds the hearts of kings in his hand, sets up kings and casts them down from their thrones, and finally changes and transfers kingdoms at his own pleasure. Why then should the worshippers of Christ fear anyone? Why should they be terrified by the threatening edicts of kings, since they themselves are subject to God, and cannot extend their power any further than he has permitted?

units.la: Præterea sui quoq; officij principes & magistratus omnes admonentur: ne scilicet authoritatis & potentiae suae fiducia elati superbiant, sed meminerint regnū omne & iudicium (vt Iosaphat olim dicebat) Dei esse: qui illos ad tantum honorē & potentiam euexerit, non vt pro sua libidine agant, sed vt ipsius iudicia enuntient, populum pie & sanctè regant, cultum verū provehant, pacem publicam sedulo tueantur. Meminerint item illum vbiq; præsentem, imo medium inter illos adesse, consilia & sententias eorum audire, & quòd ipsi olim suæ functionis ratione reddituri sint in magno illo die, quo omnia regna huius mundi cessabunt atq; abolebuntur, & Filius Dei Regnū Patri tradet, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Nimiū ergo feroces & barbari, imò impij sunt, qui (vt Pharao o-lim) hunc Dominum & Deum suum non agnoscunt, & sibi ipsis omnem potestatē vendicant, quasi liberum ipsis sit quosvis pro sua libidine tractare. Sentient illi aliquando non sine magno suo malo, quòd qui oculum creauit, & aurem finxit, simul etiam ipse omnia videat & audiat, adhæc Deus vltionum sit, qui tyrannidem & populo suo factas iniurias impunitas abire non sinat.
units.tr: Moreover, all princes and magistrates are also reminded of their own duty: that they should not, lifted up by confidence in their authority and power, become proud, but should remember that every kingdom and judgment is God's (as Jehoshaphat once said). He who has raised them to such honour and power did so not that they might act at their own lust, but that they might pronounce his judgments, rule the people piously and holily, advance the true worship, and diligently guard the public peace. Let them also remember that he is present everywhere, indeed standing in the midst of them, hearing their counsels and opinions, and that they themselves will one day have to give an account of their office on that great day when all the kingdoms of this world will cease and be abolished, and the Son of God will deliver the kingdom to the Father, that God may be all in all. Therefore those are too fierce, barbarous and indeed impious, who, like Pharaoh of old, do not acknowledge this Lord and God, and claim for themselves all power, as if it were free for them to treat whomever they like at their own pleasure. Some day they will feel, not without great harm to themselves, that he who formed the eye and fashioned the ear also sees and hears all things, and that God is the avenger, who does not allow tyranny and the wrongs done to his people to go unpunished.

units.la: Postrema Orationis nostrae pars est particula, Amen. Est hoc vocabulū Hebraicum, quo sui consensum testabantur olim in ijs, quae maximi momenti erant, & ad omnes ex æquo pertinebat, vt apud Mosem est videre. Cum enim ille minas atq; maledictiones Dei populo ex ordine pronuntiaret, hic ad singulas respondere iubebatur, Amen. Idem in libro Nehemiæ habetur, quando Esdras librū legis populo recitauit. Et ex priori ad Corinth. patet, olim hunc ecclesiæ morē fuisse, vt populus tam conciones sacras quàm preces publicas huius particulæ acclamatione confirmaret. Quæ more in Romana ecclesia adhuc D. Hieronymi seculo obseruatū fuisse, in ipso proœmio lib.2.commēt.ad Galat. testatur his verbis: Vbi sic ad similitudinem cœlestis tonitrui Amen reboat, & vacua idolorū templa quatiuntur? Sensus vocis est: Ita fiat, vel, Hoc ratum esto. Vsus autē eius in precibus duplex est. Primo ardens animi nostri desiderium testamur, quo ea impetrare cupimus, quæ postulamus. Deinde fidem nostrā quodammodo confitemur, eam videlicet nos de Dei bonitate ipsem & fiduciā concipere, vt nō dubitemus nos ea accepturos esse, quæ ex eius mandato & iussu petimus. Itaq; hæc etiam particula nos nostri officij admonet, vt nimirū ex toto corde & fide certa atq; constanti precemur. Quomodo enim poterimus sub finem hanc consensus & fidei nostræ significationem adijcere, si animi devotione verba precationis ita profundimus, vt ne ipsi quidē quid dixerimus, possimus meminisse? Et qui ita orant, fiducia certa niti nō possunt, & proinde nullū ex suis precibus fructū percipiunt, cùm sola fides eas Deo gratas & acceptas reddat, vt alibi prolixè dicuimus.
units.tr: The last part of our prayer is the little particle, Amen. It is a Hebrew word, by which people in former times testified their agreement in matters of the greatest importance, matters that concerned everyone alike, as can be seen in Moses. For when he set out in order the threats and curses of God to the people, they were commanded to answer to each one, Amen. The same is found in the book of Nehemiah, when Ezra read the book of the law to the people. And from the first letter to the Corinthians it is clear that it was formerly the custom of the Church for the people to confirm both sacred sermons and public prayers with the acclamation of this particle. That this custom was still observed in the Roman Church in the time of St Jerome, he testifies in the very preface to the second book of his commentary on Galatians, in these words: "Where the Amen thus resounds like a heavenly thunder, and the empty temples of the idols are shaken?" The sense of the word is: "So be it," or "Let this be confirmed." Its use in prayer is twofold. First, we testify to the ardent desire of our mind, by which we long to obtain the things we ask for. Then we in some measure confess our faith, namely that we conceive from God's own goodness such trust and confidence that we do not doubt we shall receive the things we ask for according to his command and bidding. So this particle also reminds us of our duty, that we should pray with our whole heart and with a sure and steadfast faith. For how can we add at the end this sign of our agreement and faith, if we pour out the words of prayer with such devotion of mind that we cannot even remember what we have said? And those who pray in this way cannot rest on sure trust, and so they reap no fruit from their prayers, since faith alone makes them pleasing and acceptable to God, as we have said at length elsewhere.

units.la: Iam ergo expositā est à nobis, prout per gratiam à Deo datam potuimus, precatio tota, quam Dei Filius tradidit. Didicimus autem, vt ea vti debeamus, & de quibus nos singulæ eius partes admonēt. admoneant. Quapropter loco conclusionis simul omnes ex corde & fide firma oremus: O Pater noster, qui in cœlis habitas & Omnipotens es rerum Dominus, ex singulari autem gratia eò vsque te demisisti, vt nostei Pater esse dignerus, quos in Filio tuo vnigenito adoptasti: Da quæso, ne nomen tuum per nos prophanetur, sed vt potius illud nostrum cum dictus tu factus sanctificemus, & inter homines illustrius reddamus. Quod vt fiat, tu cum tuo Regno ad nos venias, vt per hoc diaboli illud infelix regnum destruatur, cogitationes praua ex cordibus nostris auferantur, cupiditates noxiæ refinguantur, nosque toti vt bonæ indolis filij sub tuam obedientiam redigamur. Sentimus quidem hoc carni nostræ acerbum videri, prævalet tamen in nobis tuus Spiritus, quo duce tuæ voluntati nos submittere cupimus. Ne ergo o clementissime Pater nobis fraudi sit caro hæc improba, sed da potius, vt quemadmodum cœlestes spiritus tibi obediunt, ita nos quoq; absque murmure & omni contradictione tua voluntate delectemur, & illi obtemperemus sedulò. Quia verò ad hoc præstandum infirmiores sumus, & insuper corpora quoq; nostra multis indigent, tu quæso animas nostras pasce & confirma merito Filij tui Iesu Christi, qui panis vitæ est, & simul ea quoq; largitor, quibus in hoc seculo opus habemus, ne inopiæ impatientia superati illa alibi quæramus, relicto te, omnis boni fonte atq; authore. Fatemur equidem nos indignos esse, quibus bona tanta largiaris, cum tuam Maiestatem tot peccatis & sceleribus offenderimus: Veruntamen cum Filius tuus vnigenitus pro nobis non solum fideiusserit, verumetiam satisfecerit, in nobis verò quod præterea demus, nihil sit: remitte obsecro nobis debita nostra, & Filij tui meritis nostræ satisfactionis loco suscipe, quo vno fidimus, vt quem tu nostram iustitiam & satisfactionem esse voluisti. Vouemus autem & pollicemur, quòd ipsi quoq; tuæ bonitatis exemplo secuti omnibus iis ignoscere velimus, qui nos offenderint. Scimus enim te ipsissimam charitatem esse, & proinde inter tuos filios æmulationem, invidiam, odium & simulta tes ferre non posse. Quoniam autem homines sumus affectibus variis obnoxij, & à Satana assiduè tentamur, in quo certamine tam caro propria quàm mundus hic suo exemplo nobis plurimum negotij faciunt, tu ô Pater causam nostram suscipe, tu viribus & armis male firmos nos instrue, ne tentationibus villis succumbamus. Non otium ignauum petimus, neq; vt ab omni tentatione immunes simus precamur (scimus enim te res nostræ salutis ergo ita instituisse) sed vt nos constantia & fortitudine dones rogamus. Armato igitur nos cui Filij iustitia, balteo veritatis lumbos & renes nostros constringe, deduc nos in semitis Euangelij pacis, galea salutis capita & animas nostras defendito, da scutum fidei, quo Satanæ tela excipere & reflinguere possimus, & vt gladio spiritus feliciter vtamur nos instrue. Deniq; cùm nos ex diaboli tyrannide redemeris incomparabili sanguinis Filij tui vnigeniti pretio, porrò etiam nos seruato, ne illi iterum præda fiamus. Nam etsi hæc nostra potissimum res agatur, tamen vt hæc fiant tua quoque interest. Tuum est enim omne Regnum, tua est omnis potentia, tua est omnis gloria & maiestas. Cur ergo paterere, vt huic propter nos aliquid decederet? Itaq; exaudi nos ô Pater, & da vt preces nostræ sint Etiam & Amen, propter Filium tuum, Iesum Christum, cui vnà tecum & cum Spiritu Sancto, debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: We have now set out, as far as the grace given by God allowed us, the whole prayer that the Son of God handed down. We have learned how we ought to use it, and what each of its parts admonishes us. Therefore, in place of a conclusion, let us all pray together from the heart and with a firm faith: O Our Father, who dwellest in the heavens and art the Lord of all things, yet by singular grace have so far lowered yourself that you have deigned to be called the Father of us whom you have adopted in your only-begotten Son: grant, we beseech you, that your name may not be profaned by us, but rather that we may sanctify it as it is called yours and make it more glorious among men. To this end, come to us with your Kingdom, so that by it that unhappy kingdom of the devil may be destroyed, wicked thoughts may be taken away from our hearts, harmful desires may be restrained, and we may be brought under your obedience as sons of a good disposition, wholly yours. We indeed feel that this seems bitter to our flesh, yet your Spirit prevails in us, under whose leading we desire to submit ourselves to your will. Therefore, O most merciful Father, let not this wicked flesh be a hindrance to us, but rather grant that, just as the heavenly spirits obey you, so we too may delight in your will without murmuring or any contradiction, and may diligently obey it. But since we are weaker for accomplishing this, and our bodies also need many things, we beseech you to feed and strengthen our souls, for the sake of your Son Jesus Christ, who is the bread of life and at the same time the giver of those things which we need in this world, so that, overcome by impatience at want, we do not seek them elsewhere, having left you, the fountain and author of every good. We confess indeed that we are unworthy to receive such great goods from you, since we have offended your Majesty with so many sins and crimes. Nevertheless, since your only-begotten Son has not only stood surety for us but has also made satisfaction, while in us there is nothing we can give besides, forgive us, we pray, our debts, and by the merits of your Son accept them in place of our satisfaction, in which alone we trust, since you have willed him to be our righteousness and satisfaction. We also vow and promise that, following the example of your goodness, we too wish to forgive all who offend us. For we know that you are love itself, and therefore you cannot bear rivalry, envy, hatred and enmities among your sons. But since we are men, liable to various passions, and are constantly tempted by Satan, in which struggle both our own flesh and this world cause us no small trouble by their example, do you, O Father, take up our cause; do you equip us, weak as we are, with strength and weapons, so that we do not succumb to paltry temptations. We do not seek idle ease, nor do we pray to be exempt from all temptation (for we know you have arranged our salvation in this way), but we ask you to grant us constancy and courage. Therefore, armed with the righteousness of your Son, gird our loins and reins with the belt of truth, lead us in the paths of the gospel of peace, defend our heads and souls with the helmet of salvation, give us the shield of faith, with which we may receive and turn back the darts of Satan, and instruct us to use the sword of the Spirit successfully. Finally, since you have redeemed us from the tyranny of the devil at the incomparable price of the blood of your only-begotten Son, keep us safe from now on, lest we again become his prey. For although this matter concerns us chiefly, yet it is also of your concern that these things be done. For the whole kingdom is yours, all power is yours, all glory and majesty are yours. Why then would you allow anything to be taken away from it for our sake? Therefore hear us, O Father, and grant that our prayers may be Yes and Amen, for the sake of your Son, Jesus Christ, to whom, together with you and the Holy Spirit, belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXIII.

units.la: Dixit etiam eis: Quis vestrùm habebit amicum, & proficiscetur ad eum media nocte, & dicet ei: Amice, da mihi mutuò tres panes: quoniam amicus meus venit de via ad me, & non habeo quod apponam ei: & ille intus respondens dicat: Ne mihi molestiam exhibe: iam ostium clausum est, & pueruli mei mecum sunt in cubili: non possum surgere & dare tibi. Dico vobis, etiamsi non dederit ei surgens, eò quod amicus eius sit, at certè propter importunitatem eius surget, ac dabit ei quotquot sunt ei opus. Et ego dico vobis: Petite, & dabitur vobis: quærite & inuenietis: pulsate & aperietur vobis. Quisquis enim petit, accipit, qui quærit inuenit: & pulsanti aperietur. Ecquis autem ex vobis pater, si filius petierit panem, lapidem ei dabit? aut si piscem, num pro pisce da bit ei serpentem? aut si petierit ouum, num dabit ei scorpium? Si vos igitur cum sitis mali, noftis bona dona dare liberis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum Sanctum iis, qui ab eo petierint?
units.tr: He also said to them: "Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight and say to him, 'Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him'; and he, answering from within, says, 'Do not trouble me; the door is now shut, and my little children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything.' I tell you, even though he will not rise and give him anything because he is his friend, yet surely because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. But which of you fathers, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion? If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?"

units.la: AVdiuimus hucusq; orandi formulam, quam Christus Iesus primò quidem suis discipulis, dein de vero per horum ministerium nobis quoq; tradidit. Comprehendit ea paucis, quaecunque tam corporum quàm animarum salutiferuiunt: & simul nos dignitatis nostrae admonet, quam Dei Filius nobis suae mortis merito restituit: Vt nimirum nobis iam liberum sit in Dei conspectum venire, illum Patrem nostrum dicere, & ab illo haec tanta bona petere, ad quae percipienda, si nostram naturam & conditionem consideres, neq; digni neq; idonei sumus. Quia autem in precibus (vt iam saepe diximus) primum fide certa & constanti, deinde perseuerentia opus est, vtrunque verò iflorum varijs tentationibus oppugnatur, & interdum ita euertitur, vt vel dubitemus de Dei bonitate & auxilio, vel à precibus, tanquam inutilibus & superuacaneis, prorsus abstineamus: non temere Dominus noster Iesus Christus tractationem hanc omnem hisce verbis, quae modò recitauimus conclu dit, quibus praecipuas remoras è medio tollit, quibus inter precandum impedimur. Prima est, quòd interdum cogitamus, Deum pluribus & grauioribus negotijs occupatum esse, quàm vt nostri & rerum nostrarum curam suscipiat. Quae persuasio, si in animis hominum confirmetur, non preces modò impedit, sed simul veram Dei cognitionem, huius timorem, religionem deniq; omnem paulatim extinguit. Altera, quòd nostrae conditionis misera & modis omnibus corruptae consideratione perculsi, nos indignos esse putamus, quos exaudiat Deus, & proinde preces esse inutiles. Vtriq; huic remora Christus in praesenti parabolis elegantissimis occurrit: quibus partim nostram conditionem atq; fortem perspicuè adumbrat, partim Dei ingenium & naturam depingit, & quomodo in erga nos affectus fit, docet. Finis & vsus omnium est, vt posthabitis impedimentis omnibus preces nostras fide constanti & inuicta perseuerantia in Dei conspectum proferamus.
units.tr: We have heard so far the form of prayer which Christ Jesus first handed down to his disciples, and afterwards, through their ministry, to us also. In a few words it comprehends whatever serves for the salvation of both body and soul; and at the same time it reminds us of the dignity which the Son of God has restored to us by the merit of his death: namely, that it is now free for us to come into the presence of God, to call him our Father, and to ask from him such great blessings, which, if you consider our nature and condition, we are neither worthy nor fit to receive. But since in prayer (as we have often said) first a sure and steadfast faith is needed, and then perseverance, and since both of these are assailed by various temptations, and sometimes are so overturned that we either doubt the goodness and help of God or altogether abstain from prayer as useless and superfluous, our Lord Jesus Christ did not without reason conclude this whole discussion with the words we have just recited, by which he removes the main obstacles that hinder us in prayer. The first is that we sometimes think God is so occupied with many and weightier affairs that he cannot take up care of us and our concerns. If this notion takes firm hold of men's minds, it not only hinders prayer but at the same time gradually extinguishes the true knowledge of God, the fear of him, and at last all religion. The second is that, struck by the thought of our wretched condition, corrupted in every way, we think ourselves unworthy that God should hear us, and so prayer is useless. Christ meets both of these obstacles in the present parables, which are most apt: in them he sets forth clearly partly our condition and lot, and partly depicts the character and nature of God, and teaches how he is disposed towards us. The aim and use of them all is that, setting aside every hindrance, we may bring our prayers before God with a steadfast faith and an unconquered perseverance.

units.la: Petit autem Christus parabolas iflas pro suo more ex rebus vulgò notis, vt & melius res intelligatur, & firmius memoriae inhaereat. In prima enim duos amicos siue vicinos inducit, qui ita erga se inuicem affecti sint, vt si alteruter vel media nocte ab altero propter improuisum hospitis aduentum panes petere cogatur, vt eos illi minimè sit negaturus. Imò (inquit) etsi amicitiae non tantam habeat rationem, illius tamen importunitate se moueri pateretur. Ista precibus nostris accommodans, Deum eodem erga nos affectu praeditum esse docet: amicus enim nobis est, & proinde licet aliquando nostri curam abiecisse, aut longè alijs negotijs occupatus esse videatur, exauditurus tamen preces nostras, & ea daturus, quae vel corpori vel animae vtilia & necessaria sunt. Et parabolae exhortationem amplissimam promissionibus confirmatam subijcit, quo minus dubitemus: Petite, & dabitur vobis: quaerite, & inuenietis, &c. Vt autem hinc plus consolationis percipiamus, singulas parabolae circumstantias vnà cum eius explicatione expendemus.
units.tr: Christ uses these parables, as is his custom, drawn from things commonly known, so that the matter may be better understood and more firmly fixed in memory. In the first he introduces two friends or neighbours who are so disposed towards each other that if one of them is compelled at midnight to ask the other for loaves, because a guest has arrived unexpectedly, the other will by no means refuse him. Indeed (he says), even if the friendship did not count for so much, he would still allow himself to be moved by the other's importunity. Applying this to our prayers, he teaches that God is endowed with the same disposition towards us. For he is our friend, and therefore, although he sometimes seems to have cast off care of us, or to be busy with quite other affairs, yet he will hear our prayers and give those things which are useful and necessary both for body and soul. And the parable adds a most ample exhortation, confirmed by promises, so that we may not doubt: "Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find," and so on. Now, so that we may gain more comfort from this, let us weigh each circumstance of the parable together with its explanation.

units.la: Primus amicus, cui ex improuiso hospes media nocte aduenit, quemuis fidele aut Christianum adumbrat, & per eum Christus docere vult, quae nostrum omnium sors sit atque conditio. Vt enim ipsi in terris peregrini & hospites sumus: ita nobis quotidie omnis generis hospites aduenium, à quibus fere ex improuiso obruimur, adeò vt nobis securitatem aliquam nunquà possimus polliceri. Eiusmodi hospites primum sunt afflictiones omnis generis, & in primis morbi, quos nos germani vulgò hospites dicere solemus. Eadem est omnium aduersorum ratio. Ita vel subitò irruens vel sensim obrepens paupertas, hospes est: quod ipsum de bello, peste, rerum caritate & omnibus alijs dici potest. Imò nomen illud mors ipsa meretur, quae plerunq; non multata à nobis ex improuiso adest, vt nos ipsos depascatur. Hospites deinde nominantur prauì affectus & noxiarum cupiditatum illecebrae, quibus nos Satan ad peccata & scelera sollicitat. Ratio nominis est, quòd fere initium aliunde sumunt, deinde verò in corrupta & vitiosa nostra natura locu sive hospitiu quaerunt, vt nos ab ea, quà Deo debemus, obedientia abducant. Hoc fenju Nathan propheta cupiditate, qua Dauid accensus adulterij scelus comisit, hospiti cōfert, cui praeter fas & aequū Vriae vxore epulanda apposuerit. Et sanè multos huius generis hospites nobis Satā submittit, quādo per huius seculi voluptates, per opū & honorum
units.tr: The first friend, to whom a guest arrives unexpectedly at midnight, represents any faithful man or Christian, and through him Christ wants to teach what the lot and condition of us all is. For just as we are pilgrims and guests on earth ourselves, so every day guests of every kind arrive for us, by whom we are almost always overwhelmed unexpectedly, so that we can never promise ourselves any security. The first such guests are afflictions of every kind, and above all diseases, which we Germans commonly call "guests." The reasoning is the same for all adversities. Thus poverty, whether it strikes suddenly or creeps on gradually, is a guest; the same can be said of war, plague, dearth, and all the rest. Indeed the very name fits death itself, which, often unexpected and not invited by us, comes to devour us. Next, evil affections and the allurements of harmful desires are called guests, by which Satan entices us to sins and crimes. The reason for the name is that they generally take their beginning from elsewhere, and then seek a place or lodging in our corrupt and sinful nature, so that they may draw us away from the obedience we owe to God. In this sense the prophet Nathan compared to a guest the lust by which David, inflamed, committed the crime of adultery, setting before him, contrary to right and justice, the wife of Uriah to be feasted upon. And indeed Satan sends us many guests of this kind, when through the pleasures of this world, through the flatteries of wealth and honours, and finally through the injuries and threats of wicked men, he invites us to theft, adultery, or usury, to anger and the desire for revenge.

units.la: Ioan. 3. & honorum blanditias, per iniurias denique & minas improborum hominum nos ad fortandum, mæchandum, vel ad vsuras, ad iram & vindictæ cupiditatem inuitat. Et istæ quidem illecebræ ac peccandi occasiones amici dicuntur, eò quòd mirificè blanditijs sese apud nos insinuant, & fausta omnia pollicentur, cùm reuera nocentissimi hostes sint, vt qui suis blanditijs in peccati laqueos adducunt, & inde ad æternam damnationem & inferos præcipitant.
units.tr: John 3. And these allurements and occasions of sinning are called friends, because they insinuate themselves wonderfully into our favour with their flatteries and promise everything prosperous, when in truth they are most harmful enemies, since by their flatteries they lead us into the snares of sin, and from there hurl us headlong into eternal damnation and hell.

units.la: Quando autem hospites eiusmodi nobis aduenerunt, tunc tribus hisce panibus nobis opus est, de quibus hoc loco Christus loquitur. Primo enim patientia & constantia nos confirmari necesse est, ne vel aduersorum & afflictionum pondere, vel peccatorum aut cupiditatum noxiarum illecebris nos vinci patiamur. Deinde fides requiritur, quæ dum Christum apprehendit, facit vt huius virtute & merito pascamur, & eiusdem Spiritu inter grauissima tentationum certamina tuti conseruemur. Postremò consilio & consolatione nos subleuari oportet, quæ in solo Dei verbo certa & solida inueniri possunt. Hæc nisi nobis adsint, hospites illos declinare aut excludere nō poterimus, quin pro culpa dubio nobis malum dent. Atqui ista domi nostræ nō habemus, cùm natura in aduersis impatientes, in affectus & cupiditatum illecebris infirmi nimis, adhæc increduli & rerum dubij simus. Nulla ergo in nobis consolatio, nullum consilium, nullum deniq; auxilium, quibus nici aut nosipsos iuuare possimus. Docent hoc sapientissimorum atque fortissimorum hominum exempla, qui plerunque sapientia & fortitudine deflituuntur, quando hospites illi improbi ipsis aduenerunt.
units.tr: But when guests of this kind have come to us, then we need those three loaves of which Christ speaks in this place. For first, we must be strengthened by patience and constancy, so that we do not allow ourselves to be overcome either by the weight of adversities and afflictions, or by the enticements of sins and harmful desires. Next, faith is required, which, while it lays hold of Christ, causes us to be fed by his power and merit, and to be kept safe by his Spirit amid the most grievous struggles of temptations. Lastly, we must be relieved by counsel and consolation, which can be found sure and solid only in the Word of God. Unless these are with us, we will not be able to turn aside or shut out those guests, but they will give us evil in return for our guilt. Yet we do not have these things at home, since by nature we are impatient in adversity, too weak against our affections and the allurements of desires, and moreover unbelieving and uncertain in our affairs. Therefore there is in us no consolation, no counsel, and finally no help by which we can either help ourselves or others. The examples of the wisest and bravest men teach this, who for the most part are left destitute of wisdom and courage when those wicked guests have come upon them.

units.la: Necesse ergo est, vt amicum aut vicinum habeamus, à quo ista postulemus: Cùm autem eadem sit omnium hominum fors atq; conditio, nullus illorum hæc præstare poterit, & proinde ad Deum nos conuerti & recurrere oportet. Hic amicus noster dicitur, quia nos diligit, & salutis nostræ appetentissimus est: deniq; fidelissimi amici instar bona sua omnia sic nobiscum communia habet, vt Filium quoq; vnigenitum, cum eo nobis opus esset, pro nobis dederit. Itaq; de eius amicitia & fide nullo modo dubitare possumus. Idem vicinus quoq; noster est. Nam etsi in cælis habitet, imò supra omnes cælos (vt Dauid inquit) folium suum collocarit, demittit tamen se se, vt videat quæcunq; in cælis & in terra sunt: adhæc omnia penetrat & vbiq; præsens est, vt nemo ab ipsius prouidentia & gubernatione sese subtrahere possit. Quapropter vbicunq; locorum fuerimus, recta ad illum confugere, & eius opem atq; auxilium implorare possumus. Et huc eorum exempla referri debent, quos diuersis in locis exaudinit: vt Mosis, filiorum Israel, Dauid, Eliæ, Ionæ, Danielis, & multorum aliorum, quorum alij in altis montibus, alij in vallibus & locis desertis, alij ad maris littora, vel etiam in huius abyssio, alij inter medios leones aut alijs locis incommodissimis Dei opem inuocauerunt, & hunc sibi propinquum aut vicinum esse experti sunt. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Deus mihi adstat à dextris, & Dominus prope adest omnibus, qui ipsum inuocant. Est hæc certa & efficacissima consolatio in omni afflictionum genere. Nam etsi ab hominibus vniuersis, adeoq; à parentibus quoq; nostris (vt idem Dauid ait) deseramur, Deo tamen amico & vicino tanto vti possumus, qui & semper nobis adest, & se à nobis inueniri gaudet, vt suo consilio & auxilio in tentationibus sublevemur.
units.tr: It is therefore necessary that we have a friend or neighbour from whom we may ask these things. But since all men share the same lot and condition, none of them can provide these things, and so we ought to turn and have recourse to God. He is called our friend because he loves us and is most eager for our salvation. Indeed, like the most faithful of friends, he holds all his goods in common with us, so that when we needed it, he gave his only-begotten Son for us. So we can by no means doubt his friendship and faithfulness. He is also our neighbour. For although he dwells in heaven, indeed above all the heavens (as David says), where he has set his throne, yet he lowers himself to see all that is in heaven and on earth. Moreover, he penetrates all things and is present everywhere, so that no one can withdraw from his providence and government. Therefore, wherever we may be, we can flee straight to him and implore his help and aid. To this belong the examples of those whom he heard in various places: Moses, the sons of Israel, David, Elijah, Jonah, Daniel, and many others, some of whom called upon God's help on high mountains, some in valleys and deserted places, some on the seashore or even in the depths of the sea, some among lions or in other most unfavourable places; and they found him to be near at hand and their neighbour. Hence David said: "God stands at my right hand, and the Lord is near to all who call upon him." This is a sure and most effective consolation in every kind of affliction. For even if we are forsaken by all men, and indeed by our own parents (as David also says), we may nevertheless make use of so great a God as friend and neighbour, who is always at hand and rejoices to be found by us, so that we may be relieved in temptations by his counsel and help.

units.la: Cæterum accidit interdum, vt Deus ostium suum nobis occlusisse, & insuper dormire videatur, quando nos cum diuturnis miseriis & afflictionibus subindeconflictari patitur, adeò vt nullum vspiam auxilium, & ne spes quidem alicuius liberationis appareat. Et tunc omnes quoque pueruli Dei dormiunt, id est, omnes creaturæ, quoad nos quiescunt & cessant, quibus alias adiuuari poteramus. Exempla huius rei manifesta habemus in morbis diuturnioribus, quibus ea quoque remedia nequicquam adhibentur, quibus multi alij seruati sunt. Sic multis in egestate agentibus nulla inducтria, nullus labor sufficit, vt ex illa emergant. Similiter in bellis sæpe omnia fallut, ex quibus præsens auxilium sperabatur. Vbi tamen minimè putabimus, Deum vel dormire reuera, vel rerum administrationem interdum ad tempus deponere. Nec enim Baalis aut Deorum gentium simile est, qui vel dormire, vel ad Æthiopum epulas profecisci, vel amoribus indulgere, & interea res hominum negligere à poëtis finguntur: Sed sui semper similis est tam quoad essentiam suam, quàm huius mundi & omnium, quæ in eo geruntur, administrationem: & neque somno opus habet, cùm nunquam defatigetur: neque ex loco in locum alium mouetur, cùm cælum & terram impleat: sed neque obliuio rerum aut negligentia in eum cadere potest, qui ipsissima sapientia est, & cuius oculi per totam terram discurrunt. Sed interdum perinde facit, ac si nostri immemor sit, quando vel propropter delicta nostra: pro vt meruimus, vel quod ita nobis vtile & necessarium sit, nos diutius af-fligi atque tentari sinit, vt nos à somno & veterno carnis excitet, vt in nosipsos descendamus, ossi-cium nostrum attentius consideremus, vitia emendemus, carnem denique cum suis cupiditatibus mortificatam corceamus.
units.tr: Yet it sometimes happens that God seems to have shut his door against us and even to be sleeping, when he allows us to be struggling for a long time with miseries and afflictions, so that no help anywhere and not even any hope of deliverance appears. Then, too, all God's little servants sleep, that is, all creatures are quiet and cease, as far as we are concerned, by which we might otherwise have been helped. We have clear examples of this in lingering diseases, against which those remedies by which many others have been saved are applied in vain. So, for many who are in want, no industry or labour is enough to bring them out of it. Likewise in wars, all things often fail on which present help was hoped for. Yet we must by no means think that God really sleeps, or that he sometimes lays down the government of things for a time. For he is not like Baal or the gods of the nations, who, as the poets feign, sleep, or go off to feast with the Ethiopians, or indulge in love affairs, and meanwhile neglect human affairs. Rather, he is always like himself, both in his essence and in the government of this world and of all that takes place in it. He has no need of sleep, since he is never wearied; nor is he moved from place to place, since he fills heaven and earth. Neither can forgetfulness or negligence of affairs fall upon him, who is wisdom itself, and whose eyes run through the whole earth. Yet sometimes he acts as if he were mindful of us no longer, when, either on account of our sins, as we have deserved, or because it is useful and necessary for us, he allows us to be afflicted and tried for longer, so that he may rouse us from the sleep and lethargy of the flesh, that we may go down into ourselves, consider our duty more carefully, amend our faults, and finally restrain the flesh, mortified together with its lusts.

units.la: Quapropter nō statim spem omnem abijcere debemus, quasi nos Deus prorsus dereliquerit: sed vt de amico eam spem concipimus, vt ne media quidem nocte opem & auxilium petentibus quicquam negaturus sit: ita multò magis de Deo sperandum est, apud eum nos nequaquam repulsam passu-ros esse, quacunque tandem hora ipsum invocemus: & quàmuis aliquandiu opem interdum diffe-rat, opportuno tamen tempore daturum quæcunque nobis ad corporis & animæ salutem necessaria sunt. Quia enim cœlum & terram cum omnibus quæ his continentur, propter nos condidit, nullus alijs negotijs occupari poterit, quæillum nostri immemorem reddant. Quin potius, si ita opus sit, creaturas omnes in nostrum auxilium excitabit, & vniuersam huius mundi gubernationem adeum finem diriget, vt nostræ saluti cùm hic tùm in futuro seculo consulatur. Et huc parabolæ huius pars postrema referri debet, in qua Christus ait: Dico vobis, etiamsi non dederit ei surgens, eò quòd ami-cus eius sit, attamen propter importunitatem eius surget, & dabit ei quotquot sunt ei opus. Quibus verbis docet, rerum nostrarum conditione nunquam tam miseram & calamitosam sore, quin Deũ in nostrum auxilium precibus nostris excitare possimus: simulq́ ex nobis ipsis de Deo nos iudicare docet. Quasi diceret: Videtis in ijs, quæ quotidie accidunt, eos etiam qui sui commodi & ocij amantiores sunt, precibus importunis & indesinentibus expugnari posse, vt relicto otio, aut etiā negotijs necessarijs, amicorum necessitati subueniant: Quæ ergo ratio foret, non meliora multò de Deo sperare, qui neque philautiæ vitio laborat, sed natura mitis & beneficus est, neque vllis negotijs, quo mi-nus nos adiuuet, impeditur? Plura vide Luc.18.Cap.
units.tr: Therefore we must not immediately cast away all hope, as if God had utterly forsaken us; rather we should conceive that hope about him as we do about a friend, who will refuse nothing to those who ask for help and aid even in the middle of the night. Much more, then, must we hope about God, that we shall by no means be repulsed by him, at whatever hour we call upon him; and although he sometimes delays help for a while, he will give at a fitting time whatever is necessary for the salvation of body and soul. For since he created heaven and earth with all that they contain for our sake, no other business can occupy him so as to make him forgetful of us. Indeed, if need be, he will stir up all creatures for our help, and will direct the whole government of this world to that end, that our salvation may be provided for both here and in the age to come. To this the last part of this parable should also be referred, in which Christ says: "I tell you, even though he will not rise and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many things as he needs." By these words he teaches that the condition of our affairs will never be so wretched and calamitous that we cannot stir up God to our help by our prayers; and at the same time he teaches us to judge about God from ourselves. As if he were saying: You see that in those things which happen every day, even those who are more fond of their own ease and leisure can be overcome by importunate and unceasing entreaties, so that they leave their leisure, or even necessary business, and come to the aid of a friend in need. What reason, then, would there be for not hoping far better things of God, who is not afflicted by the vice of self-love, but is gentle and beneficent by nature, and is hindered by no business from helping us? See more in Luke, chapter 18.

units.la: Hus autem in præsenti grauem exhortationẽ subijcit, dicens: Et ego dico vobis: petite, & dabi-tur vobis: quærite, & inuenietis: pulsate, & aperietur vobis. Qua exhortatione præterea admone-mur, vt preces nostras instituere, st quo ordine in ijs procedere debeamus. Primùm petere nos iubet: nimirũ ab eo, qui solus omnis boni fons atq; largitor est, Deo. At quia preces nostræ ob causas, quas modò cõmemorauimus, non semper illico exaudiuntur, & Deus sæpe opem promissam aliquandiu differt, secundo loco, vt quæramus admonet. Quærendi autem verbo diligentiam maiorem requirit, quàm vulgò inter precandum adhiberi soleat. Quo sensu Propheta nos Deum quoq; quærere, id est, eius voluntatẽ & opem summo studio expetere iubent, vt solent qui ardentissimo rei amissæ deside-rio tenentur. Quòd si neq; ita aliquid proficiamus, tunc pulsemus oportet. Quo verbo assiduitatem, adeoq; importunam postulandi perseuerantiam denotat. Singulis autem hisce verbis peculiare pro-missionem coniungit: quam pauló post ad omnes homines extendit, ne quis eam de solis Apostolis intelligat. Addit enim: Quisquis enim petit, accipit: & qui quærit, inuenit, & pulsanti aperietur. Quorum verborum sensus est: Quisquis tandem aut qualiscunq; fit homo, si in angustia & periculo constitutus auxilio & liberatione opus habeat, is alacri & fiducia pleno animo ad Deum Patrem cœlestem recurrat, qui eum minimè repelleт. Natura enim propensus est, vt petenti largiatur, quæ-renti se obuium præbeat, & pulsanti aperiat. Pertinent huc omnes etiam aliæ promissiones, quæ in vtroq; testamento hac de re habentur. Similiter exempla quoq; eorum, quibus illud Deus fideliter præstitit, dum exauditus eorũ precibus periclitantes liberauit. At quia hæc in sermonibus, quæ præ-cesserunt, adduximus, ea hic repetere non opus est. Hoc saltem ex ista parabola firmiter teneamus, longè aliam Dei conditionē esse, quàm multi imaginentur, quasi grauioribus negotijs occupatus sit, quàm vt nostris precibus attendere & res nostras curare possit. Quæ enim ista negotia esse queant, cùm omnes mundi partes, omnes spiritus, omnia animalia propter nos creauerit? Nofler item ami-cus & vicinus est, & nos procul dubio exaudit vocantes, etiamsi interdum vel dormire, vel alijs negotijs distineri videatur. Tunc verò neq; de eius ope desperare, neq; precando defatigari, sed o-mni studio petere, quærere & pulsare debemus, & ita non sine fructu id fieri experiemur.
units.tr: Christ, however, now adds a grave exhortation, saying: "And I say to you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you." By this exhortation we are further admonished how we should order our prayers and how we ought to proceed in them. First he bids us ask, namely of God, who alone is the fountain and giver of every good. But because our prayers are not always heard at once for the reasons we have just mentioned, and God often delays the help he has promised for a while, in the second place he bids us seek. But the word "seek" demands greater diligence than is commonly applied in praying. In this sense the Prophet bids us to seek God also, that is, to desire his will and help with the greatest zeal, as those do who are held by the most ardent longing for a lost thing. But if we do not make progress in this way either, then we ought to knock. By this word he signifies persistence, and indeed the unwearied perseverance of asking. Moreover, he attaches a particular promise to each of these words, which a little later he extends to all men, lest anyone should understand it of the Apostles alone. For he adds: "For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened." The sense of these words is this: whoever at all, or of whatever kind, a man is, if he is in distress and danger and needs help and deliverance, let him run with a cheerful and confident mind to God the heavenly Father, who will by no means repel him. For by nature he is inclined to give to him who asks, to offer himself to him who seeks, and to open to him who knocks. To this belong also all the other promises which are found in both Testaments on this matter; and likewise the examples of those to whom God faithfully fulfilled it, when, heard in answer to their prayers, he delivered them from danger. But since we have brought these forward in the sermons that went before, there is no need to repeat them here. Let us hold this firmly from this parable: God's condition is far different from what many imagine, as if he were so occupied with weightier business that he could not attend to our prayers or look after our affairs. For what business could there be, since he created all parts of the world, all spirits, and all animals for our sake? Our friend and neighbour is also near, and he undoubtedly hears us when we call, even if at times he seems to be sleeping or held back by other business. Then indeed we must not despair of his help, nor grow weary in praying, but ask, seek and knock with all our zeal; and we shall find by experience that this is not done without fruit.

units.la: Cæterum alia adhuc tentatione oppugnamur, quæ vt Deo diffidamus, & de eius bonitate dubitemus, nos movet. Et hæc (vt supra diximus) ex nostræ infirmitatis & vitiositatis consi-deratione nascitur. Quando enim cogitamus, nos natura peccatores, & propter peccatum irã Dei obnoxios esse, mox suggeritur aliud quoq; animis nostris: nos nimirum indignos esse, qui maxima haec & sublimia Dei dona recipiamus, & proinde nullum ex precibus nostris fructum nobis esse sperandum. Huic tentationi alia parabola Christus occurrit, quae & ipsa ex vulgo petitur. Deum enim patri, nos autem pueruli a patre suo cibum petentibus confert: Verba eius haec sunt: Ecquis autem ex vobis pater, si filius petierit panem, lapidem ei dabit? aut si piscem, num pro pisce dabit ei serpentem? aut si petierit ovum, num dabit ei scorpium? Ita vero docet, parentes natura erga suos liberos ita affectos esse, ut illis victum conuenientem & necessarium fideliter subministrent, & quamuis non semper quod illi poscunt largiantur, nihil tamen noxium aut pernitiosum dare soleant. Id vero gravissimus verbis ad causam hanc, de qua agitur, extendit dicens: Si vos igitur cum sitis mali, nostis bona dona dare liberis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum iis, qui ab eo petierint? Vis argumenti huius ex collatione nostrae vitiosae naturae & divinae bonitatis dependet. Cum enim paternus affectus & storgē apud homines sui amantes & natura corruptos tanta virtutis sit, ut quamvis liberi nostri quotidie inobedientia & petulantia puerili peccent, ijs tamen victu ne necessarium non negemus, multo minus autem rebus noxijs aut venenatis perdamus: inde nobis colligendum est, Deum multo magis hac paterna bonitate praeditum esse, qui natura bonus, misericors & ad benefaciendum propensus, adhaec ab omni pravo aut vitiosa affectu prorsus liber est.
units.tr: Moreover, we are assailed by yet another temptation, which moves us to distrust God and to doubt his goodness. This temptation (as we said above) arises from considering our own weakness and sinfulness. For when we reflect that we are by nature sinners and liable to God's wrath on account of sin, there immediately comes to mind another thought: that we are unworthy to receive such great and sublime gifts from God, and therefore that no fruit of our prayers is to be hoped for. Christ meets this temptation with another parable, which is also taken from common life: God is compared to a father, and we to little children who ask their father for food. His words are these: "Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone? Or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?" He teaches that parents are by nature so disposed towards their children that they faithfully provide them with suitable and necessary sustenance, and although they do not always grant what the children ask, they are wont to give nothing harmful or pernicious. Christ extends this, most weightily, to the matter under discussion, saying: "If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" The force of this argument depends on comparing our sinful nature with divine goodness. For since parental affection and storge among men, who are self-loving and corrupted by nature, is of such strength that, although our children daily sin by disobedience and childish petulance, we do not deny them the necessary food, much less do we destroy them with harmful or poisonous things, we must conclude from this that God, who is good by nature, merciful and inclined to do good, and who is moreover wholly free from any wicked or vicious affection, is endowed with a fatherly goodness far greater than this.

units.la: Docet igitur hac parabola Dominus, nos dum precamur, non ad nostram infirmitatem aut indignitatem, sed in paternam Dei clementiam atque bonitatem respicere debere, & ita nostras rationes inire: Nos quidem o Pater natura mali sumus, & tuam iram hucusque multis & gravissimis peccatis provocavimus, ideoque (quantum in nobis est) indigni sumus, quibus tanta bona largiaris. Sed quid facias Pater clementissime? Qualescunque simus, tui sumus filij, quos tu initio ex gratia condidisti, & postea Filij unigeniti sanguine redemptos ex Verbi tui femine per Spiritum Sanctum regenuisti, ut Regni tui coelestis haeredes faceres. Nunquam ergo nobis deseri pateris aut negabis quae ad nostrorum corporum atque animarum sustentationem faciunt. Quis enim pater tam imprudens aut durus est, ut propter puerulorum suorum petulantiam sui officij & paterni amoris prorsus obliuiscatur? Cur ergo tu o Pater, tuum ingenium & naturam exueres, eo quod nos mali atque inobedientes sumus? Tua misericordia extenditur ab ortu ad occasum usque, & tuae bonitatis non est finis, sed durat in seculum, &c.
units.tr: The Lord therefore teaches in this parable that when we pray we ought to look not to our own weakness or unworthiness, but to the fatherly clemency and goodness of God, and so to reckon thus: "We indeed, O Father, are evil by nature, and up to now we have provoked your wrath by many and very grave sins, and therefore we are unworthy (so far as lies in us) to whom you should give such great good things. But what will you do, most merciful Father? Whatever we are, we are your children, whom you first created out of grace, and afterwards, redeemed by the blood of your only-begotten Son, you have regenerated through your Spirit from the seed of your Word, so that you might make us heirs of your heavenly kingdom. Therefore you will never allow us to be forsaken, nor will you deny what serves the sustenance of our bodies and souls. For what father is so unwise or hard that, because of the wantonness of his little children, he completely forgets his duty and paternal love? Why then, O Father, would you lay aside your disposition and nature because we are evil and disobedient? Your mercy extends from the rising to the setting of the sun, and there is no end to your goodness, but it endures for ever," and so on.

units.la: Quod si Deum nobisipsis ad hunc modum imaginemur, & quam modo audiuistis, ratione inea mus, mox animos colligemus fiducia plenos, quos nulla nostra indignitatis consideratio a precibus deterrere poterit. Ut vero ad horum meditationem paratiores simus, prima Orationis Dominicae verba, quibus Deum Patrem nostrum dicimus, saepius consideranda & expendenda nobis erunt. Accedat his frequens beneficiorum eius consideratio, quae nobis quotidie confert. Illi debemus originem nostram, cum ab ipso in matris utero formati & anima rationali atque immortali donati simus. Ille nos pascit & vestit, ut alibi demonstrauimus. Ille nos omnium aliorum, quae ab ipso creata sunt, dominos & principes constituit, adeo ut nobis seruire cogantur. Illius beneficium est, quod terra fructum & alimenta reliqua producit: quod aquae hinc inde derivatae terram irrigat, quod ignis suo calore nos fouet, & in multis alijs nos adiuuat: quod aer nos & reliqua omnia sustentat: quod denique animalia quaedam nostros labores adiuuant, quaedam victum & amictum nobis subministrant. Nec quae ista modo nobis Pater coelestis dedit, verumetiam multa alia, quae non tam necessitati, quam voluptati seruiunt: utpote auer, quae cantu suo nos oblectant, flores, qui colore & odore nos recreant. Quae omnia superat, quod Angelos quoque nobis ministros fecit, ut alibi demonstrauimus. Ineffabile autem & rationi quoque comprehensu impossibile est, quod Filium unigenitum pro nobis tradidit. Haec si attentius considerentur, fateamur oportet, Deum Patrem esse indulgentissimum, qui nos necessaria & utilia petentes negligere non possit. Ut vero minus dubitemus, Christus in praesenti domi omnium excellentissimi meminit, quod a Deo postulari potest: Spiritus sanctus nimirum, qui in se dona omnia comprehendit, quae tam praesenti quam futurae vitae seruiunt. Est enim Spiritus Veritatis, iustitiae, sanctitatis, sapientiae, fortitudinis, consilij, timoris Domini, precationum item, adoptionis, consolationis: author denique omnis boni: adeo ut qui hoc instructus est, illi nihil eorum quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, deesse possit. Quid ergo maius, praestantius, utilius peti a Deo possit. test? Quod si vero quod omnia alia superat largiri vult (sicuti in vltima Cœna prolixius & liberalius adhuc Christus pollicetur) num quæ minoris momenti sunt, illum nobis negaturum esse putabimus?
units.tr: If we picture God to ourselves in this way, and reason according to what you have just heard, we shall straightway gather our hearts full of confidence, which no consideration of our unworthiness will be able to deter from prayer. So that we may be more ready for this meditation, the first words of the Lord's Prayer, in which we call God our Father, will need to be frequently considered and weighed by us. To these let us add a frequent consideration of his benefits, which he bestows upon us every day. We owe him our origin, since we were formed by him in our mother's womb and endowed with a rational and immortal soul. He feeds and clothes us, as we have shown elsewhere. He has appointed us lords and masters over all the other things that have been created by him, so that they are compelled to serve us. It is by his kindness that the earth produces fruit and other foods; that waters, drawn off from here and there, irrigate the land; that fire warms us with its heat and helps us in many other ways; that air sustains us and all other things; and finally that some animals help our labours, while others supply us with food and clothing. Nor has heavenly Father given us only these things, but also many others which serve not so much necessity as pleasure: for example, birds which delight us with their song, and flowers which refresh us with their colour and scent. Above all these things, he has made even the angels our ministers, as we have shown elsewhere. Yet it is beyond words, and even impossible for reason to grasp, that he delivered up his only-begotten Son for us. If these things are considered more attentively, we must confess that God the Father is most indulgent, and cannot neglect us when we ask for things necessary and useful. And so that we may doubt less, Christ in the present passage mentions the most excellent of all the things that can be asked of God: namely the Holy Spirit, who comprehends in himself all the gifts that serve both the present and the future life. For he is the Spirit of truth, of righteousness, of holiness, of wisdom, of strength, of counsel, of the fear of the Lord, also of prayers, of adoption, of consolation; in short, the author of every good, so that whoever has been furnished with him can lack none of those things which are necessary for salvation. What greater, more excellent, or more useful thing could be asked of God? But if he wishes to bestow that which surpasses all other things (as Christ promises more fully and more generously still at the Last Supper), shall we suppose that he will deny us those things which are of less importance?

units.la: At singularem considerationem meretur, quod nos liberis nostris bona & vtilia dona largiri, Christus ait, ita nimirum, vt panem, pisces, ova & aliud cibi genus poscentibus, nequaquam lapides multo minus vero serpentes aut scorpiones, vel aliud quidpiam porrigamus, quo lædi aut perdi possent.
