Et sane non solum à paterni amoris ingenio, verumetiam à communi natura & humanitatis sensu alienum facinus censeretur, si quis liberis pro pane clamantibus lapides proijceret, & eos ede re iuberet. Tale quid Satan cum Christo fecit in deserto esuriente. Crudelius tamen foret, si quis illis serpentes, scorpiones, aut alias venenatas bestias apponeret. Deniq; hoc inter homines ex communi more receptum esse videmus, vt licet quis non largiatur ea, quæ paruuli liberi poscunt, nihil tamen noxij dat, & altera illa ideo negat, quod illis noxia fore, aut saltem non necessaria esse intelligit. At quorsum hæc Christus dicit? Vt ostendat idem erga nos esse Dei ingenium. Quia enim pater noster est, alieno in nos animo esse nen potest. Rursus quia natura bonus, vel potius summum bonum & omnis boni fons est, nihil noxium aut pernitiosum dare solet. Vult enim (vt Apostolus ait) nos salvos fieri. Si quid ergo postulamus, quod saluti nostræ seruit, procul dubio id suo tempore largitur. At si ex innata nobis ignorantia aut prauo aliquo carnis affectu petimus, quod nobis damno aut fraudi esse potest, precibus nostris minime mouetur: imo interdum fidi patris instar virgas exerit, vt im-portunos clamores & carnis stulta desideria coerceat. Quando igitur nos precantes nō exaudit Deus id nos non eius duritie & difficultate fieri cogitemus, sed propter ignorantiam nostram, qua decepti ea postulamus, quæ neq; illum decet dare, neq; nobis accipere vtile esset.
units.tr: But the fact that Christ says that we give good and useful gifts to our children deserves special consideration: that is, when children ask for bread, fish, eggs, or other kinds of food, we should by no means give them stones, much less serpents or scorpions, or anything else by which they could be harmed or destroyed. Indeed, it would be considered a deed alien not only to the nature of paternal love but also to common nature and the feeling of humanity, if anyone threw stones to children crying for bread and bade them eat those. Satan did something like this to Christ in the desert when he was hungry. It would be more cruel still if anyone set serpents, scorpions, or other venomous beasts before them. Finally, we see that it is received among men by common custom that, even if someone does not give what small children ask for, he nevertheless gives nothing harmful, and refuses the other thing because he understands it would be hurtful to them, or at least not necessary. But why does Christ say these things? To show that God's disposition towards us is the same. For because he is our Father, he cannot be minded towards us in an alien way. Again, because he is good by nature, or rather is the supreme good and the fountain of all good, he is wont to give nothing harmful or pernicious. For he wishes (as the Apostle says) that we be saved. If therefore we ask for anything that serves our salvation, he undoubtedly grants it in its own time. But if, out of ignorance innate in us or some depraved affection of the flesh, we ask for what could be a loss or harm to us, he is by no means moved by our prayers: rather, like a faithful father, he sometimes raises the rod to restrain our importunate cries and the foolish desires of the flesh. Therefore, when God does not hear us when we pray, let us not think that this happens because of his hardness and unwillingness, but because of our ignorance, by which, deceived, we ask for things which it would neither become him to give nor be useful for us to receive.

units.la: Iam ergo illis responsum est, qui quærunt, Cur preces nostræ non semper à Deo exaudiantur? Primo enim (vt modo diximus) plerunq; stulta & noxia petimus, & ipsimet (vt de filijs Zebedæi Christus loquitur) quid optemus ignoramus. Tunc ergo sapientissimus ille Pater exaudire nequaquam debet. Et hoc illud est, de quo Iacobus scribit: Concupiscitis, & non habetis: inuidetis & stu-diose affectatis, nec potestis assequi: pugnatis & bellatis, non tamen obtinetis, propterea quod non petitis. Petitis, & non accipitis, eo quod male petatis, vt in voluptates vestras insumatis. Dicuntur hæc omnibus, qui non nisi diuitias, honores huius seculi, corporis valetudinem bonam & alia huius generis petunt, neglectis interim iis, quæ ad Dei gloriam & animarum suarum salutem pertinent. Deinde frequenter fit, vt non ingenui & germani filij Dei, sed degeneres & rebelles simus, propter quos nomen Dei passim male audit: tunc ergo in nobis illud Solomonis impletur: Qui obturat aures suas, vt non audiat Legem, huius precatio quoq; abominabilis est. Exemplum huius rei in Israelitis habemus, quibus per Isaiam dicit Deus: Cum expanderitis manus vestras, auertam oculos meos, quia manus vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt. Adhæc interdum absq; fide precamur, & tunc idem nobis accidit, quod Iudæis, qui sine fide iustificari voluerunt, vt Paulus de illis scribit. Præterea sæpe præ scribimus Deo quid largiri, & quomodo nobiscum agere debeat: cum potius nostri officij sit per obe-dientiam fidei nos ipsius voluntati accomodare atque subijcere. Et hæ præcipuæ causæ sunt, propter quas preces non exaudiuntur. At quia hæ in nobis hærent, non Deum, sed nosipsos accusare debemus, si quid præter votum nobis accidat. Emendemus ergo hæc vitia, & preces nostras secundum formulam nobis à Filio Dei traditam instituamus, nec dubitemus, nos reipsa experturos esse promissionis eius veritatem. Exaudiet enim nos Pater cœlestis, & omnia dabit, quæ nostræ salutis ducunt, propter nomen Iesu Christi Domini nostri, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now, then, an answer has been given to those who ask: Why are our prayers not always heard by God? First, as we have just said, we very often ask for foolish and harmful things, and we ourselves (as Christ says of the sons of Zebedee) do not know what we ought to desire. Therefore that most wise Father ought by no means to grant them. This is what James writes about: "You lust, and have not: you envy and eagerly covet, and cannot obtain: you fight and war, yet you do not obtain, because you do not ask. You ask, and receive not, because you ask amiss, that you may consume it upon your pleasures" (James 4). This is said to all who seek nothing but riches, the honours of this age, good health of body and other things of this kind, while meanwhile neglecting those things which pertain to the glory of God and the salvation of their souls. Next, it often happens that we are not genuine and true sons of God, but degenerate and rebellious, and because of us the name of God is badly spoken of everywhere; then in us that saying of Solomon is fulfilled: "He who turns away his ears from hearing the Law, his prayer also is abominable" (Prov. 28). We have an example of this in the Israelites, to whom God says through Isaiah: "When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you, because your hands are full of blood" (Isa. 1). Moreover, we sometimes pray without faith, and then the same thing happens to us that happened to the Jews, who wanted to be justified without faith, as Paul writes of them. Besides, we often prescribe to God what he should bestow and how he should deal with us, whereas it is rather our duty, through obedience of faith, to accommodate and subject ourselves to his will. These are the chief causes for which prayers are not heard. But since these faults cling to us, it is not God but ourselves whom we ought to accuse if anything happens to us contrary to our wish. Let us therefore amend these faults, and frame our prayers according to the form handed down to us by the Son of God, and let us not doubt that we shall in very deed experience the truth of his promise. For the heavenly Father will hear us and will give all things that tend to our salvation, for the sake of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXIIII.

units.la: Eiecit etiam dæmonium, quod erat mutum. Factum est autem, egresso dæmonio, locutus est mutus: & mirata est turba. Quidam vero ex eis dixerunt: Per principem dæmoniorum eijcit dæmonia. Et alii tentantes, signum è cœlo petebant ab eo. Ipse vero cum sciret cogitationes eorum, dixit eis: Omne regnum diuisum aduersus sese, vastatur: & domus aduersus sese diuisa, cadit. Quod si etiam Satanas aduersus seipsum diuidet, quomodo stabit regnum eius? Nam dicitis, per Beelzebul eicere me daemonia. Quod si ego per Beelzebul eicio daemonia, filii vestri per quem eiciunt? propterea ipsi erunt vestri iudices,
units.tr: "He also cast out a devil that was dumb. And when the devil was gone out, the dumb man spoke, and the multitude wondered. But some of them said, He casteth out devils through Beelzebub the chief of the devils. And others, tempting him, sought of him a sign from heaven. But he, knowing their thoughts, said unto them: Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and a house divided against a house falleth. If Satan also be divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand? For ye say that I cast out devils through Beelzebub. And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges."

units.la: Quemadmodum Dei Filius, vt miseros mortales redimeret & seruaret, in mundum venit & homo factus est: ita ne ignotus negligeretur, suam cum voluntatem tum potentiam plurimis miraculis manifestauit. Hic ergo omnium eorum, quae ab Euangelistis describuntur, finis & visus est, vt illum agnoscamus promissum humani generis seruatorem esse, & eundem fide amplexi salutem aeternam consequamur. Eodem igitur, quod hic narratur debet referri: quod ijs, quae proxime praecesserunt, commodissime subijcitur. Nam discipulos & cum his nos quoque omnes precari docuit, & postrema petitionum est, vt nos Pater caelestis liberet a malo illo & improbo hoste Satana, ne ipsius tentationibus victi succumbamus. Quia vero precatio ista admodum necessaria est, fides autem nostra hic grauissime tentari solet, quando & hostis illius improbam astutiam & nostram infirmitatem expendimus, miraculis nouis discipulorum fidem confirmare voluit, dum reipsa demonstrat, se diaboli victorem esse, & proinde ratas fore preces nostras, cum non aliud petamus quam cuius gratia in mundum ipse a Patre missus sit. Nam vt ex Marci cap. 3. colligere licet, plures, qui a Satana obsessi erant, tunc temporis liberauit. Lucas tamen (quemadmodum & Matthaeus) vnius solum mentionem facit, qui disputationi occasionem dedit, qua miraculorum eius modi vsus indicatur.
units.tr: Just as the Son of God came into the world and became man to redeem and save wretched mortals, so, lest he be neglected as unknown, he revealed his will and his power by very many miracles. This, then, seems to be the end and purpose of all the things that the Evangelists describe: that we should acknowledge him as the promised Saviour of mankind, and, embracing him in faith, obtain eternal salvation. What is related here ought therefore to be referred to the same purpose, and it is most fittingly placed after what immediately precedes. For he taught the disciples, and with them all of us, to pray, and the last of the petitions is that the heavenly Father deliver us from that evil and wicked enemy Satan, lest, overcome by his temptations, we succumb. But since this prayer is very necessary, and our faith is especially tried here, when we weigh both that enemy's wicked cunning and our own weakness, he wished to confirm the disciples' faith by new miracles, showing in fact that he is the conqueror of the devil, and that therefore our prayers will be heard, since we ask for nothing other than that for the sake of which he himself was sent into the world by the Father. For, as may be gathered from Mark 3, he freed several people then who were possessed by Satan. Luke, however (like Matthew), mentions only the one who gave occasion for the dispute, in which a miracle of this kind is shown to have been used.

units.la: Breuis autem est in illius narratione Euangelista, & rei gestae summam solum his verbis expo nit: Eiecit etiam daemonium, quod erat mutum. Matthaeus daemoniacum adipsum adductum fuisse scribit, vt ab eo curaretur. Mutum autem daemonium fuisse Lucas dicit ab effectu, eo quod infelici huic omnem sermonis vsum abstulisset. Matthaeus caecum quoque fuisse testatur. Fuit ergo infelix admodum & misera hominis istius conditio, quem diabolus duabus praestantissimis facultatibus priuauit visu nimirum & sermonis vsu, sine quibus homini nihil iucundum, nihil suaue aut etiam vtile esse potest. Visu enim oblectamur quam maxime, dum Dei opera & pulcherrimam hanc caeli & terrae machinam, adhaec homines charos & amicos intuemur. Idem sensus ad res agendas non vtilis modo, sed necessarius quoque est, & a periculis multis defendit, in quae caeci solent incidere. Quam praeclarus autem sermonis vsus sit, vel ex eo constat, quod multi hunc inter discrimina, quibus a brutis discernimur, numerant. Per hunc certe animi sensum & voluntatem alijs exponimus, eoque miseriores sunt qui hoc destituuntur, si aliae calamitates accedant, quae multorum auxilia requirunt: quale hunc fuisse constat. Cum enim a malo daemone obsessus fuerit, non dubium est, quin ille non solum externos sensus, verumetiam rationem & intellectum eius turbarit, vt neque ea, quae ad huius vitae vsum spectant, poterit cernere. Quae omnia docent, quam ingens fuerit beneficium, quod a Christo accepit.
units.tr: The Evangelist is brief in his account and sums up the event only in these words: "He also cast out a devil that was dumb." Matthew writes that the man was brought to him, a demoniac, to be healed. Luke says the demon was called dumb from its effect, because it had taken from this unhappy man all use of speech. Matthew testifies that he was also blind. The condition of this man, then, was very unhappy and wretched, for the devil had deprived him of two most excellent faculties, namely sight and the use of speech, without which nothing pleasant, nothing sweet or even useful, can be had by a man. For we take the greatest delight in sight, as we look upon God's works and this most beautiful machine of heaven and earth, and also upon dear and friendly people. The same sense is not only useful but necessary for carrying on our affairs, and it guards us from many dangers into which the blind are wont to fall. How excellent the use of speech is may be seen from the fact that many count it among the distinctions by which we are set apart from the brutes. Certainly through it we make our mind and will known to others, and those who lack it are the more miserable if other calamities are added which require the help of many, as was the case with this man, as is clear. For since he was besieged by an evil demon, there is no doubt that it disturbed not only his outward senses but also his reason and understanding, so that he could not perceive even those things which pertain to the conduct of this life. All these things teach how great a benefit he received from Christ.

units.la: At nobis hic consideranda venit diaboli potentia simul & malitiosa improbitas, qua ijs potissimum donis & facultatibus insidiatur, quibus nos minime carere posse videt, vt his extinctis aut ab latus nos facilius perdat. Plurimum vero in hoc potest, si illi id Deus permittat. Nam & foris infestat miseros, & simul cordibus quoque sese insinuat, adeo vt ab eius insidijs nihil tutum esse possit. Exempla huius rei in Euangelio passim extant, & multa huius generis ipsi quotidie in ijs cernimus, quos iusto iudicio Deus illius libidini permittit. Nec tamen in illis modo agere putandus est, quorum corpora affligit, & quos omni intellectu spoliatos ad insaniam redigit. Sed multos alios quoque ille obsidet, qui rationis vsum prae alijs solertissimum habere, & hominum sapientissimi esse videntur. Nam multos horum in ijs quae ad hoc seculum pertinent, egregie sapere videmus, qui tamen in diuinis & in aeterna salutis negotio stulti & amentes sunt, dum neque Dei voluntatem vident atque intelligunt, neque salutis propriae vllam rationem habent, vel hanc quaerunt in rebus non vanis modo & inutilibus, verumetiam noxijs, quibus a Deo & vitae aeternae semitis abstrahuntur. Est hace caecitas omnium miserrima, quia totum hominem perdit, nisi Christi beneficio curetur. Sed & mutos reddit Satan multos, qui inter homines quidem loquacissimi sunt, & de rebus prophanis cum magni fico verborum apparatu possunt dissere, cum interim neq; cum Deo, colloqui, neq; de diuinis rebus verbum vllum facere possint. In horum numero sunt, qui fide vacui verum precandi modum ignorant, & vel nunquam cum Deo colloquuntur, vel grauioribus malis oppressi belluino vlulatu auribus eius obstrepunt. Deinde, qui de ijs, quae ad regnum Dei spectant, interrogati, pisce magis muti sunt, nec modo quod respondeant non habent, verumetiam iflorum cognitionem nihil ad se pertinere aiunt. Est hoc hominum genus hodie frequentissimum, quos omnino mutos esse praestaret, ne aliis sermonibus prophanis & obscenis multorum aures offenderent. Debent hi adnumerari, qui cum non ignorent fidei Christianae mysteria & quae ad Dei gloriam faciunt, ea tamen confiterino lunt, ne in periculum veniant, & in afferenda Dei gloria plus quam muti sint, si quando in hostes Veritatis incidunt, qui de toto religionis negotio pessime loquuntur. Volunt illi cauere ne quem offendant, aut rixis occasionem praebeant. At non vident, se & Deum offendere, & multis scandalo esse, quorum fides ipsorum silentio labefactatur. Peiores sunt, qui contra animi sententiae calumniis aduersariorum offensum praebent, & in horum gratia aliqua dicunt, quae veritati repugnant. Debent istis adnumerari impij illi & furiosi, qui linguas suas in diras imprecationes, deierationes, exerationes & omne blasphemiarum genus laxant, quibus sacrosanctum Dei nomen conspuitur, & conculcatur. Taceo nunc eos, qui ex calumniis, obtrectationibus & conuitijs voluptatem capiunt. Peruertunt isti omnes vsum sermonis, qui in primis ad propagandam Dei gloriam & proximi aedificationem accommodari debebat. Sed meminerint, se interea diabolo gratum officium praestare, qui linguas ipsorum cohibet ignauo metu, quando liberrimas esse oportebat, eadem vero soluit & laxat, vbi silere vtilius erat.
units.tr: But here we must consider the power of the devil and at the same time his malicious wickedness, by which he lies in wait especially for those gifts and faculties which he sees we cannot do without, so that, having extinguished these, or taken them from us on one side, he may destroy us more easily. He can do this to a great extent if God permits it. For he both attacks the wretched from without and at the same time insinuates himself into their hearts, so that nothing can be safe from his snares. Examples of this are found throughout the Gospel, and we ourselves daily see many of this kind in those whom God, by his just judgment, allows to be given over to his lust. Yet he is not to be thought to act only upon those whose bodies he afflicts and whom he drives to madness, stripped of all understanding. He besieges many others too, who seem to have the use of reason most skilful beyond others and to be the wisest of men. For we see many of these who in worldly matters appear to be excellently wise, and yet in divine things and in the business of eternal salvation are foolish and mad. They neither see nor understand God's will, nor have any regard for their own salvation, or they seek it in things that are not only vain and useless but even harmful, by which they are drawn away from God and from the paths of eternal life. This blindness is the most wretched of all, because it destroys the whole man, unless it is healed by Christ's benefit. But Satan also makes many dumb, who among men are indeed most talkative, and can discourse about profane matters with great display of words, while yet they can neither speak with God nor say any word about divine things. Among their number are those who, empty of faith, do not know the true manner of praying, and either never speak with God, or, oppressed by heavier evils, clamour in his ears with bestial howling. Then there are those who, when questioned about the things that pertain to the kingdom of God, are more mute than fish; they not only have nothing to answer, but also say that the knowledge of such things has nothing to do with them. This kind of people is very common today, and it would be better for them to be entirely mute, so that they might not offend the ears of many with their other profane and obscene talk. Those must be counted here who, though they do not ignore the mysteries of the Christian faith and what serves God's glory, nevertheless keep silent about them, lest they come into danger; and when they should be asserting God's glory they are more than mute, if at any time they fall in with enemies of the truth who speak most wickedly of the whole business of religion. They wish to take care not to offend anyone or to give occasion for quarrels. But they do not see that they offend God too, and are a scandal to many, whose faith is weakened by their silence. Worse are those who, against the judgment of their own mind, give offence to the slanders of adversaries and say some things in their favour that are contrary to the truth. To these must be added those impious and furious men who loose their tongues in dreadful imprecations, oaths, curses and every kind of blasphemy, by which the most holy name of God is spat upon and trampled underfoot. I say nothing now of those who take pleasure in calumny, detraction and abuse. All these pervert the use of speech, which ought chiefly to be employed for spreading God's glory and building up our neighbour. But let them remember that meanwhile they perform a welcome service for the devil, who restrains their tongues with cowardly fear when they ought to be most free, and loosens and unleashes them where it would be more useful to keep silent.

units.la: Porro vt ad nostrum hunc redeamus, Christus ab alijs adductum mox a daemonio liberat. Quo loco primum observari debet propensa iuuandi voluntas, cuius singulare specimen hic edidit. Venit misser ipse, non sponte aut quod illu seruare posse existimet, sed ab alijs adductus, qui eius miserebantur. Imo quo duceretur, ne videre quidem potuit. Adhaec non petit ipse opem, nec aliquam suam in Christum fiducia confessionem facit. Et quia in talibus rationis quoq; vsus nullus est, haud dubie quid ageretur ignorabat. Nihilominus tamen eius commiseratione Christus tangitur, & ei clemen ter succurrit. Et hoc illud est, quod alibi diximus, apud Deum non verbis multis opus esse, cum misericordia nostra apud illum sermonis loco sit. Nam vt pater filij periclitantis sponte miseretur, & ne requisitus quidem accurrit, vt auxilium ferat: ita Deus paterno in nos affectu praeditus & semper ad iuuandum paratus est. Nec tamen hoc ita accipi debet, quasi preces non necessariae sint, sed vt cognita hac Dei bonitate spem de illo bonam concipiamus, neq; dubitemus in eius conspectum venire. Deinde ne desperemus, si quando morbis aut alijs calamitatibus eo vsq; deprimimur, vt ne precari quidem possimus. Sufficit enim tunc animum ad Deum eleuasse, & gemitu atq; suspiriis eius opem flagitauisse. Praecipuus vero huius consolationis vsus est in mortis articulo, quando iam extinctus sensibus omnibus & intellectu quoq; sopito, omnium ignari iacemus. Tunc enim maxime nobis adest Dominus, vt mortalis huius ergastuli vinculis solutas animas nostras ad se transferat: & ipse spiritus gemitibus inenarrabilibus pro nobis interpellat, vt Paulus ad Rom. cap. 8. docet.
units.tr: But to return to our passage: Christ, the man having been brought to him by others, at once frees him from the demon. Here we must first observe his readiness to help, of which he has given a singular example. The man came not of his own accord, nor because he thought Christ could save him, but brought by others who pitied him. Indeed he could not even see where he was being led. Moreover, he does not ask for help himself, nor make any confession of trust in Christ. And since in such cases there is no use of reason, he doubtless did not know what was being done. Nevertheless Christ is moved by his pity and kindly comes to his aid. This is what we said elsewhere: that with God many words are not needed, since our compassion stands in his presence in place of speech. For just as a father spontaneously takes pity on a son in danger and runs to bring help, even without being asked, so God, endowed with a fatherly affection toward us, is always ready to help. Yet this must not be taken as if prayers were unnecessary, but so that, recognising this goodness of God, we may conceive good hope of him and not doubt to come into his sight. Next, we should not despair if at any time we are so oppressed by sicknesses or other calamities that we cannot even pray. For it is then enough to have lifted up the mind to God and to have begged his help with groans and sighs. The principal use of this consolation is at the point of death, when we are now deprived of all our senses, our understanding also lulled to sleep, and we lie unaware of everything. For then the Lord is most present to us, to carry our souls, loosed from the chains of this mortal prison, to himself; and the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, as Paul teaches in Rom. 8.

units.la: Porro non minus diuina quoq; Christi virtus & potentia hic elucet, qua damonium hoc tam facile eiecit. Nam breuitas narrationis qua Euangelistae vtuntur, hoc absq; multo labore factum esse innuit. Nec imaginaria fuit hac liberatio, qualia solent esse impostorum & praestigiatorum opera: sed vera & solida, quae effectu quoq; confirmatur. Nam Matthaeus eum qui caecus & mutus fuerat, mox & vidisse & locutum esse scribit. Vere ergo is est Christus, qui diaboli opera destruere, & eius caput atq; vires conculcare debuit. Nos autem ex his potentiae eius exemplis siue testimonijs confirmationem petamus, si quando diaboli furores eo vsq; progrediuntur, vt nulla liberationis & salutis spes videatur reliqua esse. Maior enim est qui in nobis agit, & cuius vnicu verbulum ad domandas hostis illius rabiem sufficit. Simul autem admonemur, quales esse velit Dominus eos, quos liberat. Videt ille mox & loquitur. Ita nos, qui illius virtute & merito ex diaboli tyrannide asserti sumus, videre & loqui conuenit. Vident autem qui in Deum respiciunt, eius praecepta obseruant, & operum atque iudiciorum eius contemplatione delectantur. Idem loquuntur etiam quae pia, honesta sancta sunt, dum & Deo pro accepta salute gratias agunt, & eius beneficentia publice praedicant, vt quam plures
units.tr: Moreover, the divine power and might of Christ shine forth here too, since he cast out this demon so easily. The brevity of the narrative that the Evangelists use suggests that this was done without much effort. Nor was this deliverance imaginary, like the works of impostors and charlatans, but true and solid, and its effect confirms it. For Matthew writes that the man who had been blind and mute immediately both saw and spoke. Truly, then, this is the Christ who had to destroy the works of the devil and trample down his head and power. From these examples of his power, let us seek confirmation for ourselves, whenever the devil's rage advances so far that no hope of deliverance and salvation seems to remain. For he who works in us is greater, and a single word of his is enough to tame the fury of that enemy. At the same time we are reminded what kind of people the Lord wishes those whom he delivers to be. He sees and immediately speaks. So we, who have been rescued from the tyranny of the devil by his power and merit, ought to see and to speak. Those see who look toward God, keep his precepts, and delight in contemplating his works and judgments. They also speak what is pious, honourable and holy, when they give thanks to God for the salvation received and publicly proclaim his kindness, so that many more may be brought to know him.

units.la: Christi facilitas in iuuando.
units.tr: Christ's readiness to help.

units.la: Christi potentia. plures alij in eius cognitione adducantur. Unde rursus apparet, quo loco habendi sint, qui caecorum instar oberrant, Dei opera negligunt, & vel muti sunt in eius beneficijs celebrandis, vel impuris potius sermonibus delectantur.
units.tr: Christ's power. That many others may be brought to know him. Hence it appears again which place should be assigned to those who wander like the blind, neglect God's works, and are either mute in proclaiming his benefits or delight in impure talk instead.

units.la: Sequitur miraculi effectus, qui apud spectatores varius fuit, & varia atq; diuersa de Christo in dicia continet. Primò enim de turba & populi plebeis hominibus dicitur, quod admirati sint ta facilem & subitam hominis miserrimi liberationem. Neque leuis & vana fuit haec admiratio, sed per eam excitati longius progrediuntur, atq; (vt Matthaeus annotauit) quaerunt: Nonne iste est Filius ille Danidis, id est, seruator ille & redemptor, quem ex Danidis stirpe nasciturum esse, olim Prophetae praedixerunt? Erat enim vulgo notum, quod Isaias de miraculosis Messiae operibus vaticinatus fuerat, fore nimirum, vt caeci viderent, claudi exultarent & mutorum linguae soluerentur in iubilum. Cum ergo haec tam manifestè fieri viderent, non possunt suam de Christo opinionem dissimulare. Simile quid apud Ioannem habetur, vbi quidam ex vulgo dicunt: Si Messias venerit, num opera hic maiora faciet, quae iste facit? In hus autem exemplum habemus eius, quod supra Christus dixit, Deum Patrem sui regni mysteria paruulis aut obscuris manifestare: eadem aut abscondere a sapientibus huius saeculi. Et mirum est, homines plebeios in Christo virtutem humana maiorem agnoscere potuisse, quam non obseruarunt, qui tunc summam sapientiae & doctrinae existimationem iustinebant. Sunt autem exempla eiusmodi obseruanda, ne similibus hodie offendamur.
units.tr: There follows the effect of the miracle, which varied among the onlookers and contained varied and diverse judgments about Christ. For first it is said of the crowd and the common people that they were amazed at so easy and sudden a deliverance of the most wretched man. This amazement was not slight or empty, but, roused by it, they go further and ask (as Matthew noted): "Is not this the Son of David," that is, that Saviour and Redeemer whom the prophets long ago foretold would be born from the stock of David? For it was commonly known what Isaiah had prophesied about the miraculous works of the Messiah: that the blind would indeed see, the lame would leap for joy, and the tongues of the dumb would be loosed into song. Since they saw these things happening so plainly, they could not hide their opinion of Christ. A similar thing is found in John, where some of the crowd say: "If the Messiah comes, will he do greater works than this man does?" We have here an example of what Christ said above, that the Father reveals the mysteries of his kingdom to little ones or the unlearned, and hides the same from the wise of this age. It is remarkable that common people were able to recognise in Christ a power greater than human, which those who then held the highest reputation for wisdom and learning failed to notice. Such examples, however, must be observed, so that we are not offended by similar things today.

units.la: Secundi fuerunt ex Pharisaeorum & Scribarum Hierosolymitanorum grege, qui non solum ignorantia & stupiditate, sed malitia in Christum peccauerunt. Nam quod diuinae virtutis opus fuit illi diabolo ascribunt, quasi cum hoc occultam & illicitam conspirationem aut communionem Christus habeat. Dicunt enim: Per principem daemoniorum eijcit daemonia. Ita vero populum accusant quasi in stulta miraculorum eiusmodi admiratione ducatur. Quasi dicerent: Quid ista miramini? Et quae stultitia est, mox pro Messia agnoscere velle aliquem, qui daemonia eijcit? An ignoratis quid possint diaboli praestigiae? quam multa item miraculose faciant, qui cum illo coniurarunt, & artes illicitas sequuntur? Et quid hic aliud fieri putabimus, quam quod per Beelzebul principem daemoniorum iste daemonia eijciat? Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quanta sit diaboli & membrorum eius in oppugnando Regno Christi astutia atq; malignitas. Videntur isti populi de Christo existimationem maiorem concepisse. Factum ipsum quod illum mouebat, negare nimis perfrictae impudentiae fuisset. Neq; etiam illud vel extenuare, vel vt malum & noxium accusare possunt. Quid ergo? In diabolum transferunt, quasi huius virtute & ope Christus talia faciat. Tanta odij aduersus veritatem concepti vis est, vt impij honorem, qui Christo debetur, diabolo potius quam illi tribuere soleant. Tanta item eorum caecitas, vt quae bona & salutaria sunt huic adscribere non dubitent, quem ab initio mendacem & homicidam fuisse constat. Faciunt hoc multi hodie, qui cum mirabiles Euangelij effectus neq; negare neq; diserte reprehendere possint, huius praecones a diabolo agitari dicunt, qui illos tanta dicendi facultate instruat, vt quidvis auditoribus suis persuadere possint. Imò calumnia impudentiori, Christo & Euangelio eius dissidia, quibus infelix mundus turbatur, accepta ferunt, magnificè vero extollunt pacem & concordiam, quae durantibus adhuc superstitionibus floruerit. Sed est haec diaboli sophistica, qua seipsum hominibus commendare, Christum vero atq; Euangelium eius omnibus inuisum reddere studet.
units.tr: The second group came from the flock of the Pharisees and the Scribes of Jerusalem, who sinned against Christ not only through ignorance and stupidity but through malice. For the work of divine power they ascribe to that devil, as if Christ had some secret and unlawful conspiracy or fellowship with him. For they say: "He casts out demons by the prince of demons." They accuse the people in this way, as if they were being led astray by a foolish admiration of such miracles. It is as if they were saying: "Why do you marvel at these things? And what folly is it to wish at once to acknowledge as the Messiah someone who casts out demons? Do you not know what the deceptions of the devil can do, and how many marvels also are wrought by those who have conspired with him and follow unlawful arts? And what else shall we think is happening here, than that this man casts out demons through Beelzebub, the prince of demons?" This is a memorable example, by which we are taught how great is the cunning and malignity of the devil and his members in attacking the kingdom of Christ. These people seem to have formed a higher opinion of Christ. To deny the fact itself which moved them would have been an extreme and brazen impudence. Nor could they lessen it or accuse it of being evil and harmful. What then? They transfer it to the devil, as if Christ did such things by his power and help. So great is the force of hatred conceived against the truth that the wicked are accustomed to give to the devil rather than to him the honour that is due to Christ. Equally great is their blindness, that they do not hesitate to ascribe to him what is good and wholesome, though he is known to have been a liar and a murderer from the beginning. Many do this today: since they can neither deny nor openly rebuke the wonderful effects of the gospel, they say that its heralds are driven by the devil, who endows them with such eloquence that they can persuade their hearers of anything whatever. Indeed, with more shameless slander they lay at the door of Christ and his gospel the discords by which the unhappy world is troubled, but they extol with great praise the peace and concord which flourished while superstitions still prevailed. But this is the sophistry of the devil, by which he seeks to commend himself to men and to make Christ and his gospel hateful to all.

units.la: Porro calumniatoribus Scribis & Pharisaeis tertij accedunt, qui illum tentantes signum petunt e coelo. Tentandi verbo indicat Lucas, quo animo & in quem finem haec fecerint: nimirum vt mira cula, quae hucusq; fecerat, extenuent & aliquo modo suspecta reddant. Nam perinde hoc est, ac si dixissent: Tu quidem te a Deo missum esse, & diuina virtute omnia facere videri vis. Quin ergo coelitus aliquod signum edas, quo id manifeste probes? At hoc postulando impietate suam egregie produnt. Conueniebat Christi doctrina cum ijs, quae olim Moses & Prophetae tradiderant. Miraculis quotidie nouis confirmabatur, in quibus diuina virtus tam aperte elucebat, vt ea vulgus quoq; agnosceret. Neq; aliquid erat, propter quod cuiquam merito suspecta esse deberent. His tamen omnibus contemptus signum aliquod caeleste petunt, quod nimirum vulgus hominum non tam facile percipere posset, ipsi autem in eo calumniando occasionem maiorem haberent: Vnde apparet adeo uullum in istis hominibus Veritatis studium fuisse, vt potius hanc obscurare studuerint, ne eius luce arguerentur. Similes eorum sunt hodie, qui cum Christianos se esse profiteantur, scripturas sacras pro veru agnoscant, doctrinæ tamen non credunt, quæ ex illis depromitur, & eam miraculis & signis ano bis confirmari petunt. Interim ipsi quoq; admiranda iudiciorū Dei exempla non obseruant, quibus Euangelij doctrinam aduersus hostium conatus non sine miraculo hucusq; defendit. Produnt ergo bi quoq; impietatem suā, & fere fit, vt in ipsis Deus signa adat, quibus verbi sui contemptum vlci scitur, vt ipsorum exemplis alij territi emendentur.
units.tr: Moreover, a third group joins the slanderous Scribes and Pharisees, who, tempting him, ask for a sign from heaven. Luke indicates by the word "tempting" with what intention and to what end they did this: namely, to diminish the miracles he had done so far and to make them somehow suspect. For it is just as if they had said: "You want it to be thought that you have been sent by God and that you do all things by divine power. Why then do you not display some sign from heaven by which you clearly prove this?" But by asking this they betray their impiety most clearly. Christ's teaching agreed with what Moses and the prophets had long handed down. It was confirmed daily by new miracles, in which divine power shone so openly that even the common people recognised it. Nor was there anything for which anyone could rightly regard him with suspicion. Yet despite all this, with contempt they ask for some heavenly sign, which of course the common people could not easily perceive, while they themselves would have a greater occasion for calumny in it. From this it appears that these men had so little zeal for the truth that they rather sought to obscure it, lest they be convicted by its light. Like them today are those who, while professing themselves Christians, acknowledge the holy Scriptures as true, yet do not believe the doctrine drawn from them, and ask that it be confirmed by miracles and signs. Meanwhile they themselves also do not observe the admirable examples of God's judgments, by which the teaching of the gospel has been defended to this day against the attempts of its enemies, not without a miracle. So these men too betray their impiety, and it often comes about that God works among them signs by which the contempt of his word is punished, so that others, frightened by their examples, may amend their ways.

units.la: Sed audiamus Christū, qui primo Scribis & Pharisæis respondet, inde ad eos transit, qui signū de cælo petebant. Dicitur aut cogitationes illorū sciuisse. Ergo non voces modo audiuit, verumetiā intellexit, quis animi ipsorū sensus atq; affectus esset, ac in quem sine ista ab illis dicerentur. Est hoc euidens diuinitatis eius vera argumentū. Solius enim Dei est corda & renes scrutari, vt scriptura passim testantur, & rerū vsus satis docet. Nec enim vllus vnquā inuentus est, qui absq; arcana spi ritus reuelatione alterius cogitationes nouerit. Quod gentiū sapientes quoq; intellexisse, ex Momi fabula constat, quem fingunt in humani corporis fabrica hoc reprehendisse, quod fenestra pectori de esset, per quā hominis animos atq; cogitationes, vel arcana consilia inspici possent. At Christus propria virtute vidit hominū arcana, & (vt Ioan. ait) non opus habuit, vt quis ipsi aliquius voluntate exponeret, ideo quod ipse sciret, quid sit in homine. Et huius diuinæ virtutis exempla non pauca adi dit, quæ alibi recensuimus. Sunt aut hæc diligenter obseruanda, vt primo memores in cuius conspe ctu versemur, ab omnibus ijs abstineamus, quibus ille offendi potest: deinde vt consolatione suma mus ex eo, quod Christus, qui nostri amantissimus est, tam subdolos hominū conatus, quām nos in o mnibus periculis & aduersis videt, & haud dubie aderit nobis, ne supra vires nostras tentemur.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ, who first answers the Scribes and Pharisees, and then turns to those who asked for a sign from heaven. It is said that he knew their thoughts. Therefore he not only heard their words but understood what the sense and feelings of their minds were, and against whom these things were said without his knowledge. This is a clear proof of his true divinity. For it belongs to God alone to search hearts and reins, as the Scriptures testify everywhere, and experience sufficiently teaches. For no one has ever been found who could know another's thoughts without a hidden revelation of the Spirit. That even the wise men of the Gentiles understood this is clear from the fable of Momus, whom they feign to have found fault in the making of the human body because there was no window in the breast through which a man's souls, thoughts, or secret counsels could be inspected. But Christ by his own power saw the secrets of men, and (as John says) had no need that anyone should tell him anything about a man, because he himself knew what is in man. He also added many examples of this divine power, which we have reviewed elsewhere. These things, however, must be carefully observed: first, that mindful of the presence in which we stand, we may abstain from all those things by which he can be offended; and second, that we may take great consolation from this, that Christ, who loves us most dearly, sees the crafty attempts of men just as he sees us in all dangers and adversities, and will undoubtedly be present with us, so that we are not tested beyond our strength.

units.la: Caterum grauiter admodum & validissimis argumentis hostium calumniam confutat: nimirū propter eos, qui iam de ipso rectius incipiebant sentire. Est enim talium ratio habenda, etiamsi eos incurabiles esse constet, cum quibus nobis res est. Primum argumentū ex eo sumit, quod multorum seculorum atq; gentium exemplis est confirmatū: Omne regnum dissidens aduersus sese, vastatur: & domus aduersus se dissidens cadit. Quod si etiā Satanas aduersus seipsum dissidet, quomodo sta bit regnum eius? Potest ex his verbis argumentū bifariàm formari. Primò ad hunc modum: Dissi dia intestina tam regnis quam familiis dissipationem & ruinam certam afferunt, & proinde non admittuntur abijs qui vel rempub. vel domesticam saluam volunt. Atqui diabolus sui regni propu gnator acerrimus est, & magna astutia in illo propagando vtitur. Nunquam ergo admittet, ví ipse secum dissideat, & suos spiritus impuros hostiliter eijciat ex illis, quos ex ipsius instinctu & vo luntate occupauerunt. Deinde sic quoq; argumentum formari poterit. Quæcunq; regna intestinis dis sidijs scinduntur, diutius consistere non possunt. At si ego per dæmoniorum principem dæmonia eij cio, iam diabolus secum ipse dissidet. Ergo regni eius ruina in foribus adest, & illud breui totum de struetur. Vnde sequitur regnum Dei iam aduenisse, quod per Messiam instaurandum sore, Prophe ta prædixerunt. Et huic postremæ argumentioni fauent Christi verba, quæ postea ipse in hanc sen tentiam subijciet. Sed vt ut ista accipias, finis & scopus ipsius est, se esse promissum illum humani generis vindicem, qui diaboli regnum destruere, Dei autem instaurare debeat.
units.tr: Moreover, he refutes the enemies' slander very weightily and with the strongest arguments, namely on account of those who were already beginning to think more rightly of him. For such people must be taken into account, even when it is certain that those with whom we have to deal are incurable. First he draws an argument from what has been confirmed by the examples of many centuries and nations: Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a house divided against itself falls. And if Satan is also divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? An argument can be formed from these words in two ways. First, thus: Internal divisions bring certain dissipation and ruin to kingdoms as well as to households, and therefore they are not tolerated by those who wish their commonwealth or household to be safe. But the devil is the fiercest champion of his own kingdom, and he uses great cunning in extending it. He will therefore never allow himself to be divided, or hostilely to expel his unclean spirits from those whom they have seized by his instigation and will. Second, the argument can also be formed thus: Whatever kingdoms are torn apart by internal dissensions cannot endure for long. But if I cast out demons by the prince of demons, then the devil is already divided against himself. Therefore the ruin of his kingdom is at the doors, and it will soon be wholly pulled down. Whence it follows that the kingdom of God has already come, which the prophets foretold would be established through the Messiah. And Christ's words, which he himself afterwards adds to this effect, favour this second argument. But whichever form you take, his aim and purpose is that he is that promised avenger of the human race, who ought to destroy the kingdom of the devil and establish the kingdom of God.

units.la: Nititur autem argumentum hoc generali sententia, quam nemo facilè negauerit, qui aliquem habet rerum vsum. Constat enim omniū, quæ in mundo sunt, incolumitatē ex concordi consensu & mutuo auxilio pendere. Vt enim Deus in sua essentia vnus est, ita inter se vniantur oportet, quæ cunq; in illo consistunt. Tolle ex pulcherrima hac mundi fabrica mirabilem harmoniam, quā sphæra cælestes & elementa inter se alioqui diuersissima conueniunt, mox totam corruere videbis. Imò (vt Propheta verbis vtar) nisi cæli terram exaudiant, & duæ hæ remotissimæ mundi partes consensum inter se habeant, prouentu terræ carebimus. Eadem est corprris humani ratio, in quo humores inter se natura diuersi valetudinem bonam conferuant, si rectè temperentur, vt alius alium adiuuet: ijdē verò si turbentur & dissideant, corpori toti exitium afferunt. Idē igitur in Repub. quoq; fieri solet quod prudenter olim Menenius Agrippa obseruauit, qui populum Romanum aduersus senatum et primates tumultuantem Apologo de corporis humani constitutione ad obedientiam & concordia studium reduxit. Et si bistoriat omnium gentium euoluamus, patebit omnibus seculis paruas & con temptibiles Respublicas concordi & consensu mutuo in immensum creuisse, regna autem maxima potentissimas potentissimaq; intestinis dissidijs esse euersa. Israelis certè regnum seditionibus & ambitione regum sese mutuo ingulantium perijt. In Græciam ciuitatū potentissimarum dissidia Persas adduxerunt, qui illa per annos multos crudelibus bellis infestarunt. Macedonico ite aut Alexandrino regno, regū ambitio & hinc exorta bella finem imposuerunt. Romanam rempub. cum potentissima esset, Marij & Sylla factiones primò labefactarunt, deinde Pompeij & Cæsaris ciuilia bella libertate spolia- runt, postremò totam subiugarunt nouæ inter Antonium & Augustum inimicitiæ, ut in Monar- chiæ formulam redigeretur, quæ causa fuit, ut Imperium tandem ad barbaras gentes deuolueretur, quas Romani prius multo labore & sanguine deuicerant. Sed quid opus est vetera exempla com- memorare, cùm multa huius generis nostro seculo in omnibus prope nationibus fieri viderimus? & vtinam fieri iampridem desijssent. Prudenter ergo olim Scillurus Scytharum Rex iam moriturus filios de concordia admonebat, & ut firmior apud eos esset admonitionis tam necessariæ memoria, typo siue chria elegantì rem quasi oculis spectandam proposuit. Nam tela, quæ pro more gentis ge- stabant, in vnum fasciculum omnia colligari, & inde singulos in fasciculo hoc frangendo vires suas experiri iußit. Quod cum frustra tentauissent, præcepit, ut fasciculo soluto singuli suum telum fran- gerent. Et cùm hoc absque labore esset factum subiecit: Ita vos quoq; ô charissimi filij, animis & vo- luntatibus coniunctos nulla vis hostilis debellabit: at discordes quiuis hostis facile vincet, & regnū totum dissipabit. Potuit ergo Rex barbarus videre, quod hodie Christiani principes minus obser- uant, & ne ij quidem omnes, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur. De re domestica, cuius hic quoq; Christus meminit, non opus est dicere, cùm quotidianis exemplis discamus, quantum ea damni ac- cipiat ex domesticorum dissidijs. Hoc verò non possumus tacere, eandem Ecclesiarū quoq; esse con- ditionem, ut concordia & consensu fidelium seruentur & crescant, dissensionibus autem & conten- tionibus pessum eant. Exempla passim sunt obuia. De primitiua & Apostolica Ecclesia scribitur, quòd credentium omnium cor vnum fuerit, at eandem quotidie miris augmentis creuisse legimus. Posterìs temporibus, vbi episcoporum ambitio dissidia induxit, mox & hæreses exortæ sunt, & hos- tibus occasio data est aduersus Christianos homines ferro & igne grassandi. Quid hodie fiat, pij omnes non sine dolore & lachrimis intuentur. Horum ergo meminerint, quotquot rebus subinde in- peius labentibus vel publicè vel priuatim consultum volunt.
units.tr: This argument rests on a general principle which no one who has any experience of affairs would readily deny. For it is agreed that the safety of all things in the world depends on harmonious agreement and mutual help. Just as God is one in his essence, so all the things that subsist in him ought to be united with one another. Remove from this most beautiful fabric of the world its wonderful harmony, by which the heavenly spheres and the elements, otherwise most diverse, agree with one another, and you will soon see the whole collapse. Indeed (to use the prophet's words) unless the heavens hear the earth, and these two most distant parts of the world have agreement between them, we shall lack the produce of the earth. The same is the case with the human body, in which humours that are by nature diverse preserve good health when they are rightly tempered, so that one aids another; but if they are disturbed and at odds, they bring destruction on the whole body. The same thing commonly happens in the commonwealth, as the wise Menenius Agrippa of old observed, who brought the Roman people, who were rioting against the senate and the nobles, back to obedience and a zeal for concord by his fable about the constitution of the human body. And if we unroll the histories of all nations, it will be plain that in every age small and contemptible commonwealths have grown immensely through concord and mutual consent, while the greatest and most powerful kingdoms have been overthrown by internal dissensions. The kingdom of Israel certainly perished through seditions and the ambition of kings who slaughtered one another. Dissensions among the powerful cities of Greece brought the Persians into Greece, who for many years harassed it with cruel wars. The ambition of kings and the wars arising from it put an end to the Macedonian or Alexandrine kingdom. When the Roman commonwealth was at its most powerful, the factions of Marius and Sulla first weakened it; then the civil wars of Pompey and Caesar stripped it of its liberty; finally the new enmities between Antony and Augustus subdued it wholly, so that it was reduced to the form of a monarchy. This was the reason why the empire at last passed to the barbarian nations, whom the Romans had earlier conquered with much labour and blood. But why do we need to recall ancient examples, when we have seen many things of this kind happen in our own age, in almost all nations? And would that they had ceased long ago. Wisely, then, Scyllurus, king of the Scythians, when he was about to die, admonished his sons concerning concord; and so that the memory of this so necessary admonition might be firmer in them, he set the matter before their eyes, as it were, by means of a striking figure or pithy saying. For he ordered that the arrows, which they carried according to the custom of their people, be gathered together into one bundle, and then that each of them try his strength by breaking the bundle. When they had tried in vain, he ordered that the bundle be untied and each break his own arrow. When this had been done without any trouble, he added: "So you also, dearest sons, united in mind and will, will be conquered by no hostile force; but if you are divided, any enemy will easily overcome you and destroy the whole kingdom." The barbarian king could thus see what Christian princes, and not all of those who profess the doctrine of the gospel, observe less well today. As for domestic affairs, of which Christ also speaks here, there is no need to say much, since we learn daily from examples how much harm they suffer from domestic dissensions. But we cannot pass over in silence that the condition of the churches is the same: they are preserved and grow through the concord and agreement of the faithful, but perish through dissensions and contentions. Examples are everywhere to hand. We read that in the primitive and apostolic Church the heart of all believers was one, and we read that the Church grew daily by wonderful increases. In later times, when the ambition of bishops introduced dissensions, heresies soon arose too, and an occasion was given to enemies to rage against Christian people with sword and fire. All who are godly look on with grief and tears at what is happening today. Let therefore all those remember these things who, when affairs are continually sliding into worse, wish to take counsel for them, whether publicly or privately.

units.la: Alterum argumentum ex eo desumit Christus, quod tunc passim fiebat. Quia enim tunc tempo- ris res apud Iudæos depravatissimæ fuerunt, non pauci inueniebantur, qui cum à Christi vera cogni- tione & fide alienissimi essent, tamen vel quæstus vel ostentationis causa, discipulos eius imitaban- tur, vt ipsi quoque in nomine Christi dæmonia eiicerent. Neq; illis deerat successus, non quòd eorum leuitatem Deus probaret, sed vt hac etiam occasione Filij sui cognitio latius propagaretur. Exem- plum huius rei supra cap. 9. audiuimus, vbi Ioannes quendam prohibitum ab ipsis fuisse dicit, ne in Christi nomine dæmones eiiceret, eò quòd ipsos non sequeretur. Et in Actis filij Sceuæ describun- tur, qui cùm nefarij exorcistæ essent, tamen nomine Iesu ad quæstum faciendum voluerunt abuti. Ex eiusmodi ergo exemplis argumentum Dominus petens ait: Quòd si ego per Beelzebul eijcio dæ- monia, filij vestri per quem eijciunt? Filios eorum dicit eos qui illud faciebant, quia ab ipsis nihilo minus pro bonis & pijs agnoscebantur, cùm in Christi partes non transfirent, neq; ipsorum sacra ne- gligerent: quemadmodum hodie etiam dilecti & germani Ecclesiæ filij, catholici item & orthodoxi dicuntur, qui sub Romanæ Ecclesiæ obedientia manent, Missas audiunt, Pontifices venerantur, & nullam reformationem admittunt, licet interea multa faciant, quæ cum pontificijs canonibus & antiquis decretis minus conueniunt. Est autem argumentum eiusmodi: Cùm filij vestri in meo nomine dæmonia eijciat, quid obsecro opus est, ut ego alieno præsidio vtar, & in illis eijciendis Beel- zebul in auxilium vocem? An meam virtutem in meipso minus quàm in alijs posse arbitramini? Et mirum est me à vobis accusari impia cū Beelzebul coniurationis, cùm alteros illos feratis & pro- betis, qui meo nomine ex affectu priuato abutuntur. Est ergo magna huius argumenti acrimonia, quia non tam seipsum excusat Dominus, quàm illorum iniquitatem & corruptum iudicium repre- hendit. Sunt hi calumniatorū & sycophantarū mores: quòd non de factis ipsis iudicant, sed illa pro personarum respectu probant vel improbant. Non possunt ergo non illorum iudicia iniquissima es- se. Quòd si verò affectus ille in magistratus & publicos iudices incidat, nihil ex illis iusto, aut æquō
units.tr: Christ draws a second argument from what was happening then everywhere. For since at that time affairs among the Jews were most corrupt, there were not a few who, though most alien to a true knowledge and faith in Christ, nevertheless for the sake of gain or display imitated his disciples, so that they too cast out demons in the name of Christ. Nor did they lack success; not that God approved their fickleness, but so that on this occasion too the knowledge of his Son might be spread more widely. We heard an example of this above, in chapter 9, where John says that certain man had been forbidden by them to cast out demons in Christ's name, because he did not follow them. And in Acts the sons of Sceva are described, who, though they were wicked exorcists, nevertheless wanted to abuse the name of Jesus to make gain. Taking his argument from examples of this kind, the Lord says: "But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?" He calls "your sons" those who did this, because they were nonetheless acknowledged by them as good and godly men, since they did not go over to Christ's side, nor neglected their own rites; just as today also those who remain under obedience to the Roman Church, hear Masses, venerate the pontiffs and admit no reformation, are called beloved and true sons of the Church, and catholic and orthodox, although meanwhile they do many things that agree poorly with the papal canons and ancient decrees. The argument is of this kind: "Since your sons cast out demons in my name, what, I ask, is the need for me to use another's protection and call in Beelzebub to help in casting them out? Or do you think that I have less power in myself than in others? And it is remarkable that I am accused by you of impious conspiracy with Beelzebub, when you tolerate and approve those others who abuse my name out of private affection." The argument therefore has great sharpness, because the Lord does not so much excuse himself as rebuke their iniquity and corrupt judgement. Such are the habits of slanderers and sycophants: they do not judge the deeds themselves, but approve or disapprove them according to regard for the persons. Their judgements cannot therefore but be most iniquitous. But if that affection falls upon magistrates and public judges, nothing just or fair can any longer be hoped for from them.

units.la: Actor. 19. amplius sperari poterit. Priuatim autem hominibus in religionis & æternæ salutis negotio plurimum nocet: quia frequenter cum præsenti animarum exitio, veritatis doctrinam & pias admonitiones propter doctoris personam fastidiunt.
units.tr: Acts 19. Nothing more can be hoped for. Yet in private it does great harm to men in the matter of religion and eternal salvation: for very often, to the present ruin of souls, they scorn the doctrine of truth and godly admonitions because of the person of the teacher.

units.la: Caterùm comminationem interserit Christus: Propterea ipsi, scilicet vestri filij, erunt vestri iudices. Quasi diceret: Putatis quidem vobis contra me omnia licere, sed quæ facitis nunquam feretis impunè. Nam etsi neque populus contra vos hisce audeat, neque aliquis magistratus sit, qui in vos animaduertat, tamen vestri illi filij iudices vestri erunt: imò iam nunc illorum exemplo condemnamini, cùm meæ virtutis efficacia tam aperte in ipsis manifestetur, quam vos non vultis agnoscere. Accidit hoc impijs omnibus, vt ferè domesticos iudices habeant, à quibus damnentur, & quia omnem excusationis prætextu ipsis auferant. Huc pertinet, quòd in Sophistarum impiissimorū Scholis, Canonicorum libidinosissimorum collegijs, deniq; in tyrannorum aulis fideles Christi discipuli inueniuntur. Quam ergo ignorantiam illi prætexent, cùm in ipsorum lustra vsq; lux veritatis penetret, quam alij amplectuntur? Horum itaq; memores, discamus positis affectibus prauis vera fide excipere vnicum salutis authorem, Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover Christ adds a warning: "Therefore they themselves, namely your sons, will be your judges." As if he were saying: You indeed think that you may do everything against me, but what you are doing you will never bear with impunity. For although neither the people dare to act against you in these matters, nor is there any magistrate who will punish you, nevertheless those sons of yours will be your judges; indeed even now you are condemned by their example, since the efficacy of my power is made as plain in them as you are unwilling to acknowledge it. This happens to all the wicked, that they generally have judges of their own household by whom they are condemned, and who take away from them every pretext of excuse. To this belongs the fact that faithful disciples of Christ are found in the schools of the most impious Sophists, in the colleges of the most licentious Canons, and finally in the courts of tyrants. What ignorance, then, can they plead, when the light of truth penetrates even into their own dens, which others embrace? Mindful of these things, let us learn, laying aside wicked affections, to receive with true faith the only author of salvation, Jesus Christ: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXV.
units.tr: HOMILY CXV.

units.la: Sin autem digito Dei eiicio dæmonia, nempe peruenit ad vos Regnum Dei. Cum validus quispiam armatus custodit aulam suam, in pace sunt ea quæ habet. Vbi verò alius eo validior inuadens vicerit eum, totam armaturam eius aufert, qua considebat, & spolia eius distribuit. Qui nō est mecum, contra me est, & qui non colligit mecum, spargit.
units.tr: "But if I cast out devils by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God is come upon you. When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace: but when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils. He that is not with me is against me: and he that gathereth not with me scattereth."

units.la: CVm Dominus noster Iesus Christus ex homine cæco & muto dæmonium eiecisset, varia de hoc facto fuerunt hominum iudicia. Præ aliis autem iniquissimè de illo pronunciarunt Pharisæi & Scribæ, qui Hierosolyma aduenerant. Nam illum cum Beelzebul dæmoniorum principe conspirauisse, & huius virtute miracula eiusmodi facere dixerunt. Et hanc calumniā, vt & multas alias ille sufferre ac sustinere voluit, ne hodie offendamur, si vel Euangelium, vel eius præcones horrendis criminibus atque conuitijs audimus grauari. De hoc ipse discipulos apud Matthæum admonet, dicens: Si ipsum patremfamilias Beelzebul dixerunt, quanto magis domesticos eius? Veruntamen quia hic nō tam de illius persona, quàm veritatis doctrina & multorum salute agebatur, qui rectius de ipso iam cœperant sentire, diligentem apologiam vel defensionem suæ innocentiæ instituit: suo exemplo docens, nos ita patientes esse debere in perferendis iniurijs, ne interim veritatis causam negligamus, quæ semper cum gloria Dei & multorum salute coniuncta esse solet. Et nuper quidem duo argumenta præmisit, quorum alterum ex communi sensu, multorum jeculorum exemplis & experientia confirmatum, alterum ab eorum exemplo sumpsit, qui licet eius discipuli domestici non essent, eius tamen nomine immundos spiritus eijciebant.
units.tr: When our Lord Jesus Christ had cast a devil out of a man who was blind and dumb, people judged the deed in various ways. The Pharisees and scribes who had come up from Jerusalem pronounced most unjustly about him beyond all others. For they said that he had conspired with Beelzebub, the prince of the devils, and performed such miracles by that one's power. Christ chose to bear this slander, as he bore many others, so that we should not be surprised today if we hear the Gospel, or its heralds, burdened with dreadful accusations and insults. He warns his disciples of this in Matthew, saying: "If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call those of his household?" But because here the matter concerned not so much his own person as the teaching of the truth and the salvation of many, who had already begun to think more rightly of him, he set out a careful apology, or defence, of his innocence. By his own example he teaches us that we ought to be patient in bearing injuries, yet not neglect the cause of the truth in the meantime, which is always joined with the glory of God and the salvation of many. And he had just now put forward two arguments: one drawn from common sense, confirmed by the examples and experience of many, and the other taken from the example of those who, though they were not his household disciples, nevertheless cast out unclean spirits in his name.

units.la: In præsenti autem conclusionem infert, qua tam huius quàm miraculorum omnium finem infert: Sin digito Dei eijcio dæmonia, nempe peruenit ad vos Regnum Dei. Per digitum Dei Spiritus eius intelligi debet, vt ex Matthæo patet, qui eandem historiam describens Spiritum Dei posuit. Ratio nominis est, quòd suo spiritu Deus omnia regit, administrat & feruat, atque per eundem in electis suis agit siue operatur. Est igitur Metaphorica locutio, quæ Iudæus non potuit ignota esse, cùm Ægyptij Magi in Mosis & Aaronis miraculis virtutem diuinam agnoscentes eadem olim vsi essent. Ia verò Spiritus sancti diuinitas exprimitur, qua Patri & Filio (quem Isaias brachium Dei vocat) coessentialis est. Porrò quoad Christi intentionem, euincere vult iam adueniße Regnum illud Dei, quod olim per Prophetas ille promiserat. Potest enim ex verbis eius argumentum huiusmodi colligi: Regnum Dei in mundo non prius quàm Satan eijciatur, constitui aut instaurari potest: At hunc per me eijci videtis, & quidem diuina atque propria virtute: Ergo iam tempus illud Regni Dei adest, & hoc ad vos peruenit. Breui autem hoc argumento duo agit Christus. Primò se promissum missum illud semè mulierù aut Messiam esse docet, quem Veteris testamenti scriptura ad hoc desti natum esse docebat, vt conculcato serpentis capite, & euersò atq; destructo diaboli regno, Dei Regnū instauraret. Alterum est, quòd Scribarum atq; Pharisæorum ingratitudinem arguit, qui Dei gratiam aspernabantur, & hunc ipsis Regnum suum vltrò offerentem supra se regnare nolebant. Quò in primis peruenienti verbum pertinet. Nam perinde est ac si diceret: Vestrum erat Regnum Dei quærere, & in eo quærendo nullis laboribus & impensis parcere, at quæ vestra est iniquitas & ingratitudo, Deum ipsum ad vos venientem & salutificam suam virtutem aperte in me declarantem, neq; agnoscere, neq; Regnum eius admittere dignamini. Fuit autem hæc graus reprehensio, quam admodum ingratam fuisse non est dubium hominibus ambitiosis, qui Regni Dei cupidissimi videri volebant, & se omnia eius mysteria ad vnguem tenere sibi persuaserant.
units.tr: Now he draws the conclusion, in which he states the purpose both of this and of all his miracles: "If I cast out devils by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God is come upon you." By the finger of God the Spirit of God must be understood, as is clear from Matthew, who, describing the same history, put "Spirit of God." The reason for the name is that God by his Spirit rules, governs and preserves all things, and through the same Spirit acts or works in his elect. It is therefore a metaphorical expression, which the Jews could not have failed to know, since the Egyptian magicians, recognising the divine power in the miracles of Moses and Aaron, had used the same expression long before. Indeed, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is expressed in it, for he is coessential with the Father and the Son (whom Isaiah calls the arm of God). As to Christ's intention, he wishes to prove that that kingdom of God has now arrived, which he had long before promised through the prophets. For from his words an argument of this kind can be drawn: the kingdom of God cannot be established or restored in the world before Satan is cast out; but you see that he is cast out by me, and indeed by divine and proper power; therefore the time of the kingdom of God is now at hand, and it has come to you. By this brief argument Christ accomplishes two things. First, he teaches that he is that promised seed of the woman, or Messiah, whom the Scripture of the Old Testament taught was destined for this purpose: that, with the head of the serpent crushed and the kingdom of the devil overthrown and destroyed, he might restore the kingdom of God. The second is that he rebukes the ingratitude of the scribes and Pharisees, who scorned the grace of God and were unwilling that he, who offered them his kingdom of his own accord, should reign over them. To this belongs especially the word "has come." For it is as if he said: "It was your business to seek the kingdom of God, and in seeking it to spare no labour or expense; yet what great iniquity and ingratitude is yours, that you deign neither to acknowledge God himself coming to you and openly declaring his saving power in me, nor to admit his kingdom." This was a severe rebuke, and there is no doubt it was most unwelcome to ambitious men, who wished to seem most eager for the kingdom of God and had persuaded themselves that they held all its mysteries to the last detail.

units.la: Obseruabis autem per Regnum Dei, non aureum seculum, quale Chiliastæ & horum discipuli fingunt, intelligi: sed humanæ redemptionis beneficium, totumq; illud negotium, cuius Christus Ie-sus administer & mediator fuit. Hoc iam ad Iudæos peruenisse dicit, quod minimè potuisset dicere, si per illud vniuersalis pax totius mundi & felicissima piorum in terris conditio intelligi deberet, cum constet res populi Dei nunquam in peiori statu fuisse, quàm cum ista à Christo dicerentur. Spirituale ergo regnū olim Prophetæ promiserunt, & de hoc Euangelistæ & Apostoli loquuntur, quo humani generis redemptio continetur, & quod in hisce terris inchoatum, in cœlis demum suum habet complementum, vbi fideles omnibus curis & laboribus soluti pace verè beata & æterna fruentur. Interim non temere locutione ista & Regni Dei nomine Spiritus sanctus vtitur. Primò enim sic exprimitur redemptionis nostræ finis, qui est, vt destructo in nobis diaboli regno, Deus in nobis regnet, & nos (quemadmodum Petrus admonet) reuera simus genus illud electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, Dei deniq; peculium, qui & ore & vitæ totius consuetudine atq; moribus virtutes eius prædicemus, qui nos ex tenebris vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem. Vnde sequitur, Regnum Dei nequaquam adhuc locum obtinere apud eos, qui diabolo militant, & hunc in se regnare patiuntur. Atqui tales sunt, qui vel superstitionibus contumaciter inhærent, & saniorem veritatis doctrinam contemnunt, vel peccato assiduè seruiant, atque absq; omni pœnitentia in turpissimis sceleribus perseuerant. Hi certè omnes obsequium longè gratissimum diabolo præstant, & proinde Regno Dei frustra gloriantur, quod nisi ex nobis diaboli impurus & mendax spiritus eiciatur, nosq; eius seruitium totis viribus excutiamus, in nobis locum habere non potest. Præterea consolationi quoq; piorum atq; credentium hæc locutio seruit. Quia enim Christus Regnum Dei instaurauit, & destructo diaboli regno nos suos ciues fecit, nihil vtiq; in nos iuris habet hostis ille improbus, neq; etiam aliquid ijs nocere potest, qui Christo per fidem veram sunt insiti. Quòd enim hic in Euangelio dicit: Venit contra me princeps mundi huius, sed in me non habet quicquam: hoc non tam in suo quàm membrorum suorum omnium nomine loquitur, in quos nihil porrò iuris habet diabolus propter peccatum, cum hoc suo merito Christus expiarit, & nobis à Deo iustitia factus sit. Ideo Paulus dicebat, nullam esse condemnationem ijs, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Imò ipse eos, qui verbum eius audiunt, & audito credunt, ne in iudicium quidem venturos, sed à morte in vitam transituros esse testatur. Quid ergo adhuc timemus mendacissimi illius ardelionis minas, qui iam olim deuictus vires amisit, vt absq; Dei permissione nihil tentare ausit? Num verò benignissimum illum Patrem aliquid illi permissurum putamus contra eos, quos pretioso Filij sanguine redemit? Cur item mortem timemus, quæ credentibus non amplius mors est, sed felix animæ in carnis ergastulo laborantis & gementis liberatio, imò transitus ad cœlestem patriam, quo olim corpora quoque suis animabus restituta transferentur.
units.tr: You will observe, moreover, that by the kingdom of God is understood not a golden age, such as the Chiliasts and their followers imagine, but the benefit of human redemption and the whole undertaking of which Jesus Christ was the minister and mediator. That he says this has already come to the Jews is something he could not have said if by it were to be understood a universal peace of the whole world and the most blessed condition of the godly on earth, since it is certain that the affairs of the people of God were never in a worse state than when these words were spoken by Christ. The prophets therefore promised a spiritual kingdom, and of this the evangelists and apostles speak, in which the redemption of the human race is contained, and which, begun in this earth, has at last its completion in heaven, where the faithful, freed from all cares and labours, enjoy a truly blessed and eternal peace. Meanwhile the Holy Spirit does not use this expression and the name of the kingdom of God without reason. For, first, the end of our redemption is thus expressed: that, the kingdom of the devil being destroyed in us, God may reign in us, and that we (as Peter admonishes) may truly be that chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for God's own possession, who proclaim his virtues both by our mouth and by the whole course and manner of our life, he who has called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. Hence it follows that the kingdom of God does not yet hold a place among those who serve the devil and allow him to reign in them. Yet such are those who either stubbornly cling to superstitions and despise the sounder doctrine of the truth, or constantly serve sin and persist in the most shameful crimes without any repentance. All these certainly render the most welcome obedience to the devil, and therefore they boast in vain of the kingdom of God, since, unless the impure and lying spirit is cast out of us, and we shake off his servitude with all our strength, it cannot have a place in us. Moreover, this expression also serves the consolation of the godly and believers. For since Christ has established the kingdom of God, and by destroying the kingdom of the devil has made us his citizens, that wicked enemy has no right at all over us, nor can he harm in any way those who are truly engrafted into Christ by faith. For when he says in the Gospel, "The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me," he speaks not so much in his own name as in the name of all his members, over whom the devil has no further right on account of sin, since Christ has made expiation by his merit and has been made righteousness to us from God. Therefore Paul said that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Indeed, he testifies that those who hear his word and believe it shall not even come into judgment, but shall pass from death to life. Why then do we still fear the threats of that most lying busybody, who was overcome long ago and has lost his strength, so that he dares to attempt nothing without God's permission? Do we really think that the most kind Father would permit him anything against those whom he has redeemed with the precious blood of his Son? Why, again, do we fear death, which for believers is no longer death, but the happy release of the soul labouring and groaning in the prison of the flesh; indeed a passage to the heavenly fatherland, whither the bodies also, restored to their souls, shall one day be carried?

units.la: Sed poterat aliquis obijcere: Si tu ille es, qui Dei digito dæmonia eijcis & Satanam regno suo pellis, cur ille hactenus in tuta & tranquilla possessione mansit, & cur nunc tam multa ille conatur, quibus tuum institutum impediat? Cur non te viso mox cedit, & Regno Dei dat locum? Huic obiectioni per Præoccupationem Christus respondet, & parabolam proponit, qua & negotium hoc totum, de quo agebatur, illustrat, & simul docet, hoc Satanæ ingenium esse, vt violenter ipsum eijci oporteat. Cum (inquit) validus quispiam armatus custodit aulam suam, in pace sunt ea quæ habet: Vbi verò quis eo validior vicerit eum, totam armaturam eius aufert, qua considebat, & spolia eius
units.tr: But someone might object: If you are the one who casts out demons by the finger of God and drives Satan from his kingdom, why has he remained so long in his safe and quiet possession, and why does he now try so hard to hinder your undertaking? Why does he not withdraw at once when you appear and give place to the kingdom of God? Christ answers this objection by anticipation and proposes a parable, which illustrates the whole matter under discussion and at the same time teaches that this is Satan's nature, that he must be driven out by force. He says: "When a strong man armed keeps his palace, his goods are in peace. But when a stronger than he shall come upon him and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils."

units.la: { } distribuit. Duo rursus Christum agere dicimus. Primo enim quod coepit dicere, plenius exponit, & se diaboli victorem esse demonstrat, & proinde non opus habere, ut ab illo adiuuetur. Et hunc sensum Matthaeus & Marcus exprimunt, qui parabolam hanc paulo aliter narrant, ad hunc scilicet modum: Nam quomodo potest aliquis ingredi domum validi alicuius, & vasa eius diripere, nisi primo vinxerit validum illum? & tunc domum illius diripiet. Quibus verbis tale argumentum continetur: Quisquis potentis & robusti alicuius domum inuadit eam, diripit, illo robustior sit oportet, ut reluctantem quoque vincere possit. Atqui ego domum principis daemoniorum inuado, hunc vinco & constringo, atque inuito etiam eripio illi homines, quibus bucusque vs vasis vsus est: Ergo illo potentior sum, & adeo nihil cum illo habeo commercij, ut potius vs sim, qui eius regnum destruere & totum exarmare debeo. Maior communi omnium sensu probatur, quando omnes naturae res suas saluas volunt, nec aliquis tam ignavus est, qui illas diripi patiatur, si defendere possit. Minorem Christi miracula probabant, quae nunc illis omnia in mentem reuocat, ea autem praecipue, quibus quotidie a daemonijs obsessi per ipsum liberabantur. At simul alterum hic agit, docens nimirum, negotium hoc non absque vi & labore confici, quia Satan aegre loco cedat, & ad defensionem regni sui probe armatus & instructus sit. Et hoc Lucas expressit, cuius verba paulo ante recitauimus. In idem tamen vterque sensus recidit, & paucis verbis Dominus communis nostri hostis ingenium, vna cum toto redemptionis nostrae negotio comprehendit.
units.tr: Here we may say that Christ does two things. First, he explains more fully what he has begun to say, and shows that he is the conqueror of the devil and therefore has no need to be helped by anyone. Matthew and Mark express this same sense, though they relate the parable a little differently, in this way: "For how can someone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house."
