For although the worst of them delights in their pursuits and destruction, this is not enough for it, since it is driven by a constant lust to harm and to destroy as many as possible. As a greedy robber, though he rejoices in plunder already won, cannot rest in it but aims at fresh raids, so the devil has no rest unless a new opportunity offers itself each hour by which he may destroy men. What, then, does he do? Knowing the morals and character of men, who grow fairly careless when their affairs are whole and safe, he thinks of returning to his former dwelling, so as to recover the possession he has lost. Nor does his hope always deceive him. For it often happens that he finds men idle and secure, and moreover given over to the adornment and splendour of this world. For since we are naturally prone to ease, we readily promise ourselves perpetual peace and happiness if God shows himself favourable to us. This assurance, though in itself it is not evil (for the salvation of the elect and of those who truly believe is firm and everlasting), unless it is tempered by a serious zeal for piety, and unless we diligently keep before us the end of our redemption, it makes men confident and secure, and so opens the door to the old and malicious guest, who constantly seizes every chance to harm. Therefore, if he finds such men, still inflamed with the grief of his former expulsion, and in order to provide better for his affairs, he attacks with greater effort. For taking with him other spirits, still more wicked, he returns to the place from which he had gone out; and this is the reason why the condition of such men is worse and more unhappy afterwards than before. Many examples by which this could be proved occur everywhere. For every day we see men who, having been well brought up from boyhood, made great progress in the kingdom of God, afterwards become more careless and puffed up with excessive confidence, by which they also look down on others. But these same men, often beset by fresh snares of Satan, are so possessed by him that they surpass in impiety, contempt of God's Word, licentiousness of morals and lust even those who never tasted that outstanding gift of the grace of the Gospel. And what happens to private persons is wont to happen in whole peoples and churches as well. The Eastern Churches teach this: though they once flourished above others, security and confidence stirred up ambitious contentions among them, which advanced so far that, abandoning the simplicity of the Gospel, they devoted themselves to vain and useless disputations, and each tried to provide for itself by human protections. Seizing this occasion, the devil took back the dwelling he had once held there, and thrust upon them the wretched Mahomet, by whose partly most impious doctrine and partly arms they were subdued and are in a far worse state than when they were once immersed in the superstitions of the nations. The West too has suffered something similar under the Roman pontiffs. And today we have seen examples of some cities which, after the light of the Gospel was crushed and rejected, gave place again to the prince of darkness, and not only fell back into their former superstitions but, at the same time, with the fear of God shaken off and good laws abolished, opened the windows to every kind of wickedness. Truly, then, Christ says that the last condition of such men becomes worse than the first. And Peter writes concerning these same men: "If, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled and overcome, their last state becomes worse than the first. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, having known it, to turn back from the holy doctrine delivered to them." But it has happened to them what is commonly said in a true proverb: "The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the washed sow to the wallowing in mud." Thus God, by just judgment, avenges the contempt of his Word and grace, so that such men, when at length the measure of iniquity is filled, pay the just penalties for themselves. And we see that such men are almost always most unhappy even in this age. For, having often lost also their bodily liberty, they are forced to bear a foreign yoke, and they are the more wretched because, amid the licence of the flesh and of sins, they do not recognise their misery. But these are only the preludes of those things which they will suffer hereafter, when they are relegated with their prince the devil to the eternal torments of the wretched.

units.la: Porro omnia ista in cum finem a Christo dicuntur, vt eorum consideratione simul & tam Iudaeorum quam aliorum exemplis territi, aduersus diaboli insidias vigilemus. Nam etsi in electis spiritus promptus sit & alacer, caro tamen infirma est, & (vt Paulus monet) pretiosissimum hunc Regni Dei & aeternae salutis thesaurum in vasis testaceis gestamus. E contra magna est hostis nostri improbitas, neq; minor in nobis oppugnandis astutia. Quia enim homo vetus ipsius hospitium est, non ignorat qua parte infirmissimi sumus, & quibus artibus potissimum possimus vinci. Multa igitur & diligenti cura opus est, vt omnes illi aditus praecludamus: quod non alia ratione commodius fiet, quam si Christus ei opponatur, qui & olim eum vicit, & petra inuicta est, aduersus quam ne inferorum quidem portae praevalent. Ita ergo haec ad nostri admonitionem dicuntur, vt interim pii & fideles minime terreant. Nam vt vt illorum saluti insidiantur Satan, vt vt ad ipsos opprimendos caelum terrae miscet, nihil tamen aduersus eos poterit, si veritatis lucem semper ob oculos habeant, & omnes mali occasiones pro virili deuitent. Vt vero priuatim haec singuli cogitare debent, ita maxime ad Ecclesiae ministros & reipub. praefectos haec cura pertinet, quorum est videre, vt si quando reformationis occasio ipse offert, nullas superstitionum reliquias relinquant, sed simul omnia tollant, quae cum Euangelio minus conueniunt: & vt ab alijs sublata nō patiantur reduci aut restitui. Commendantur aliqui Reges Iuda, quod Dei cultum a prophanis superstitionibus repurgauerint: sed eosdem Spiritus sanctus propter Excelsa relicta reprehendit: solidam vero laudem Ezechias & Iosias meruerunt, quorum industria & zelo omnia simul sublata sunt, adeo vt ille ne serpenti quidem aeneo pepercerit, cum aliquos ei hucusque sacra fecisse videret. Iflos ergo imitentur, qui publicae salutis consulium volunt: & quod in religione faciunt, hoc ipsum in moribus quoque populi reformandis obseruent, ne aliquid permittant, quod vitijs aliquibus occasionem dare possit. Quod si illorum zelo populi quoque & singulorum priuatim studium accesserit, facile omnis aditus Satanae praeclaudetur, regnum vero suum in nobis Christus Iesus obtinebit, cum quo olim in caelis quoque viuemus atque regnabimus. Illi debetur benedictio, bonor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ speaks all these things to this end: that, terrified both by the consideration of these things and by the examples of the Jews and of others, we may keep watch against the snares of the devil. For although the spirit is ready and eager in the elect, the flesh is nevertheless weak, and (as Paul warns) we carry this most precious treasure of the kingdom of God and of eternal salvation in earthen vessels. On the other hand, the malice of our enemy is great, and his cunning in attacking us is no less. For since the old man is his dwelling, he does not fail to know where we are weakest, and by what arts we can most easily be overcome. Therefore we need much and diligent care, that we may close off all those approaches; and this will be done more conveniently by no other means than by setting Christ against him, who both conquered him of old and is the unconquered rock, against which not even the gates of hell prevail. So these things are said to us by way of admonition, yet in such a way that they do not frighten the pious and faithful. For although Satan lays snares for their salvation, and although he stirs heaven and earth to oppress them, he will nevertheless be able to do nothing against them, if they always keep the light of truth before their eyes and avoid, as far as they can, all occasions of evil. But just as these things ought to be considered by individuals in private, so this care belongs especially to the ministers of the Church and to the rulers of the commonwealth, whose duty it is to see that, if ever an occasion of reformation presents itself, they leave no remnants of superstitions, but at the same time remove everything that agrees less with the Gospel, and do not allow what has been removed by others to be brought back or restored. Some kings of Judah are commended because they purged the worship of God from profane superstitions; yet the Holy Spirit reproves the same kings on account of the high places that were left standing. But Hezekiah and Josiah deserved solid praise, by whose diligence and zeal all such things were removed together; so much so that Hezekiah did not spare even the bronze serpent, when he saw that some had hitherto offered sacrifices to it. Let those therefore imitate them who wish to care for the public welfare; and what they do in religion, let them also observe in reforming the morals of the people, so that they permit nothing that could give occasion to any vices. If the zeal of these rulers is joined by the eagerness of the people also and of individuals in private, the way of Satan will easily be closed off, and Christ Jesus will hold his kingdom in us, with whom we shall also live and reign in the heavens. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXVII.

units.la: Factum est autem cùm hæc diceret, attollens vocem mulier quædam in turba dixít: Beatus venter qui te portauit, & vbera quæ suxisti. Ipse vero dixit: Imò verò beati, qui audiunt Verbum Dei, & illud obseruant.
units.tr: And it came to pass, as he spoke these things, that a certain woman in the crowd lifted up her voice and said to him, "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you." But he said, "Yes, rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it."

units.la: NArrauit hucusq; Lucas, vt Christus Iesus ex homine cæco & muto dæmonium eiecerit, & vt hoc nomine Pharisæi & Scribæ ipsum calumniati sint, quasi cum Beelzebul colluderet & aribus illicitu vteretur. In qua historia, in Iudæis quidem extremæ contumaciæ & impietatis exemplum, in Christo autem diuinæ bonitatis eximium specimen proponitur. Nam etsi indigni essent, quibus cùm amplius versaretur, vt vnum verbum commutaret, tamen adhuc saluti ipsorum consultum cupit. Primò enim calumniam illam diligenter diluit, & ea occasione quis sit docet. Deinde ingratitudinem eorum accusat, & simul poenas graues denunciat, vt si qui forte adhuc curabiles essent, his auditis de emendatione serio cogitarent. Porrò non defuerunt aliqui non mali, qui tamen se omni officio defunctos putabant, si illum sequerentur, verbum vel concionis eius audirent, & miracula quæ plurima edebat admirabundi spectarent. Quare nunc istos etiam officij admonet, & veram salutis consequendæ rationem sic tradit, vt simul superstitionibus occurrat, quibus multi ab illa auocantur.
units.tr: Luke has now related how Christ Jesus cast a demon out of a man who was blind and mute, and how the Pharisees and Scribes slandered him on this account, as if he were colluding with Beelzebul and using the prince of demons. In this story the Jews are set forth as an example of extreme obstinacy and impiety, and Christ as a remarkable specimen of divine goodness. For although they were unworthy, and although he had been among them for so long, he still desires their salvation, so that he may change one word. First he carefully refutes that calumny and, on that occasion, teaches who he is. Then he accuses them of ingratitude and at the same time threatens them with heavy punishments, so that if any of them were perhaps still curable, they might hear these things and think seriously about amending their lives. Moreover, there were some who were not wicked, yet thought they had done their whole duty if they followed him, heard his word or sermon, and gazed in wonder at the many miracles he performed. Therefore he now admonishes these people also of their duty, and so delivers the true way of obtaining salvation that at the same time he meets the superstitions by which many are drawn away from it.

units.la: Occasionem huic doctrinæ dedit mulier quædam, quæ miraculorum & sermonum eius admiratione abrepta se continere non potuit, quin tacentibus aliis omnibus ipsa eum publicè celebraret. Clamat ergo: Beatus venter, qui te portauit, & vbera (scilicet beata) quæ suxisti. Est hæc locutio vulgaris, qua fere vtimur, quando aliquem summis laudibus vehere volumus, prophanis quoq; Scriptoribus vsitata, vt ex illo Poëta dicto apparet: Felices, talem qui te genuere parentes. Inter Iudæos tamè frequentior fuit, qui sciebant felicem & laude digna sobolem inter Dei benedictiones non postremo loco censeri. Opponitur autem hoc mulierculæ obscuræ testimonium Pharisæorum atq; Scribarum impudenti calumniæ, vt hoc exemplo discamus, nunquam defuturos, qui Christo testimonium ferant, & illius gloriam aduersus quosuis hostes libere ac fortiter tueantur. Habet enim Deus suos electos vbiq; locorum, etiam vbi summa impietas regnat, qui interdum ita latent, vt ab ipsis etiam Verbi administris ignorentur (quod Eliæ temporibus accidisse scimus) eosdem tamen ille quando tempus est & ipsa rei necessitas postulat, præter omnem expectationem excitare potest, vt officium faciant, & Veritati palàm, neq; sine fructu, patrocinentur. Quid, quòd hominibus vniuersis tacentibus, lapides potiùs loquentur, quàm Deo suæ gloriæ & bonitatis testes desint, vt Christus olim Sacerdotibus dicebat? Et ipsi cæli (vt Dauid ait) gloriā eius prædicant, vt iam de aliis creaturis nihil dicamus. Consoletur hoc nos aduersus hostium Christi conatus. Hunc illi omnino oppressum et extinctu volunt, ne regnū in ipsos obtineat: & sæpe rem eò deducunt, vt ipsi vicisse videantur: quando nimirum sua authoritate & tyrannide ita omnes terrent, vt vix quisquam mutire audeat. Sed Christo, cui omnem potestatem in cælo & in terra pater tradidit, facile est eorum conatus ludificare, vt omnium risui exponantur, qui se ipsum Deum è cælo deturbare posse sibi persuaserunt. Exempla huius generis historiæ sacræ & ecclesiasticæ multa exhibent. Et constat nouissimis hisce temporibus per annos amplius quingentos, quibus Pontificum auaritia & ambitione Veritatis doctrina ex templis eiecta fuit, & quasi sepulta iacuit, nunquam tamen illius testes defuisse, qui veræ fidei confessionem publicè fecerunt, & eiusdem femina multorum animis inseruerunt, qui deinceps ipsorum vestigia secuti sunt. Seipsos ergo sua impietate & furiosis conatibus infames & Deo exosos facere possunt Christi hostes, at ijdem Veritatis lucem nunquam extinguent, quin scintillæ supersint, quæ ipsos in suis tenebris turpiter exultantes arguant & confundant.
units.tr: The woman gave the occasion for this teaching. Carried away by her admiration for his miracles and words, she could not restrain herself, and while all the others kept silent, she publicly extolled him. So she cries out: "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts (that is, blessed ones) that nursed you." This is a common expression, which we use almost everywhere when we wish to raise someone to the highest praise; it is also used by profane writers, as appears from that saying of the poet: "Happy the parents who begot such a son as you." Among the Jews, however, it was more frequent, since they knew that a happy and praiseworthy offspring was counted not the least among the blessings of God. But this testimony of an obscure little woman is set against the shameless calumny of the Pharisees and Scribes, so that from this example we may learn that there will never be lacking those who bear witness to Christ and defend his glory freely and bravely against any enemies whatever. For God has his elect everywhere, even where the greatest impiety reigns. Sometimes they lie so hidden that they are unknown even to the ministers of the Word themselves (as we know happened in the time of Elijah). Yet when the time comes, and the need of the matter demands it, he can rouse them beyond all expectation, so that they perform their duty and defend the truth openly, and not without fruit. What of the fact that, while all men are silent, stones would rather speak than that witnesses of his glory and goodness should be lacking, as Christ once said to the priests? And the heavens themselves (as David says) declare his glory, not to mention other creatures. This should console us against the attempts of Christ's enemies. They wish him utterly crushed and extinguished, so that his kingdom may not prevail over them. And they often bring things to such a point that they seem to have won, since by their authority and tyranny they terrify everyone so much that hardly anyone dares to murmur. But it is easy for Christ, to whom the Father has given all power in heaven and on earth, to mock their attempts, so that they are exposed to the laughter of all who have persuaded themselves that they can hurl God himself down from heaven. The histories both sacred and ecclesiastical present many examples of this kind. And it is well known that in these latest times, for more than five hundred years, while the avarice and ambition of the Pontiffs drove the doctrine of the truth out of the temples, and it lay as if buried, there have never been lacking witnesses who made public confession of the true faith, and who by their example implanted it in the minds of many who afterwards followed in their footsteps. Christ's enemies may therefore make themselves infamous and hateful to God by their impiety and raging attempts, but they will never extinguish the light of the truth, and sparks will always remain to accuse them and confound them while they shamefully exult in their darkness.

units.la: At hic obseruatu dignissimum est, in tanta hominum turba vnicam mulierculam, eamq; obscuri & ignoti nominis prodire, quæ tacentibus etiam Christi discipulis, eius gloriam asserit, non quidē contra homines sui similes, sed contra Pharisæos, quorum maxima erat authoritas, & contra Scribas Hierosolymitanos, qui in tota illa gente summam doctrinæ & eruditionis existimationem sustinebant. Elucet in eo admirabile Dei consilium, & quod Regnum Christi non sit de hoc mundo, sicuti
units.tr: Yet here it is most worthy of notice that, in so great a crowd, one little woman, of obscure and unknown name, came forward, and while even Christ's disciples kept silent, she asserted his glory. She did so not against men like herself, but against the Pharisees, whose authority was very great, and against the Scribes of Jerusalem, who held the highest reputation for learning and erudition in that whole nation. In this there shines forth the wonderful counsel of God, and the fact that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, as

units.la: E e ipse etiam apud Pilatum testatur. Longè aliter enim solent Reges huius seculi, qui viles & obscuros praecones fastidiunt, grandiloquos autem & multa eruditione celebres scriptores atq; oratores pretio conducunt, qui ipsorum potentiam, victorias, virtutes (quas aut paucissimas, aut omnino nullas habent) scriptis & orationibus ad ostentationem compositis decantent. Vel ipsi sibi in ea re tradunt operas mutuas, ut similes labra lactucas habeant. At Christus, Rex illeregum, ex ore infantium & lactentium laudem recipit, & humilibus atq; obscuris praeconibus delectatur. Neq; mirum nobis videri potest, mulierus huius testimonium ipsi gratum fuisse, si cogitemus, quales Apostolos sibi delegerit, & qualis eius fuerit comitatus, de quo alias diximus. Hinc vero consolationem petere debent, quicunq; ne ob vilem & abiectam suam conditionem, officia eorum Deo minus grata sint metuunt. Nec enim personas ille respicit, sed ut in quavis gente (quemadmodum Petrus Cornelio dicebat) sic etiam in quavis conditione illi acceptus est, quisquis ipsum vere timet, & iustitiam operatur. Vide praeterea quae in hanc sententiam a Paulo dicuntur. Galat. 3. Coloss. 3.
units.tr: he himself also testifies before Pilate. For the kings of this age commonly do quite the opposite: they scorn humble and obscure heralds, and instead hire grandiloquent writers and orators renowned for their great learning, who extol in written and spoken compositions, designed for display, their power and victories and virtues, which they have either very few or none at all. Sometimes they even exchange such services with one another, so that like lips they have lettuces. But Christ, the King of kings, receives praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings, and delights in humble and obscure heralds. Nor can it seem strange to us that the testimony of this woman was pleasing to him, if we consider what kind of Apostles he chose for himself and what kind of company he had, of which we have spoken elsewhere. Rather, all those who fear that their offices may be less pleasing to God because of their lowly and despised condition should take comfort from this. For he does not regard persons; but, as Peter said to Cornelius, in every nation, and so in every condition, whoever truly fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. Consider also what Paul says to this effect: Galatians 3; Colossians 3.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea hoc exemplo, nemine debere ab hominibus pendere in fide & religionis atq; aeterna salutis negotio. Hoc enim non hominum authoritate, sed aeterno Dei consilio nititur, qui hominum authoritate sive suffragijs minimè opus habet. Nam ut ex eius mandato Isaias proclamauit, Omnis caro foenum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri est, & cum hac instar foeni aut floris exarescat & defluat, solum Domini verbum manet in aeternum. Imò Christo teste, Caelum quidem & terra transibunt, ex eius autem verbi nullus apex intercidet. Quid ergo ad divini cultus & aeternae salutis mysteria conferre posset hominum quantumus excellentissimorum authoritas? Quin potius hanc reijcit Deus, & humiles huius mundi eligit, ut omne hominum sapientiam, dignitate, gloria & existimatione pudefaciat. Et exempla multa sunt, quae evidenter docent, quam fallatur pernitiosè, qui in hac causa homines potius quàm Deum respiciunt. In Aegypto Moses populo Dei libertate postulat à Pharaone, neq; aliquem secum habet, qui eius causam probet & adiuuet, praeter vnu Aaronē fratrem. Ex aduersa autem parte sunt Rex Pharao, regni proceres, Magi item, qui tunc mortalium sapientissimi esse iudicabantur. Quis ergo non damnaret Mosis causam, si hominum iudicio res deberet decerni? Sed hunc bona causam iustinuisse, Deus plurimus signis & rei euentu comprobauit. Simile quid postea in deserto accidit, quando tota Ecclesia cum summo Pontifice in aurei vituli cultum consensit, omnibus autem illis rursus Moses cum paucis sese opposuit, vitulum confregit, & tanti seleris authores puniuit. Quid autem de Elia dicemus, qui in publicis totius regni Israelitici comitijs, sive Concilio potius religionis causa indicto, solus veri Dei cultu contra Regem, contra Baalis sacerdotes quadringentos quinquaginta & totum populum asseruit? Sed & Micheas cum pseudoprophetis circiter quadringentis congressus est, neq; eius causa propter horum vel multitudinem vel authoritatem fuit deterior. Idem de Isaia dici potest, qui sub Achas Rege de credentium pauci tate conqueritur, & se cum suis auditoribus portenti instar videri dicit. Neq; melior Ierem. & aliorum Prophetarum fors fuit. Sed exemplo, quod pra manibus habemus, instatur. Damnarunt Christum Pharisaei & Scribae, & quamuis ille sese graviter excusat, silent tamen omnes: Vnica autem muliercula eius innocentia suo testimonio tuetur. Quod si ergo hominum authoritas valere debet, iam Christus daemoniorum socius erit, & religio Christiana tota euersa iacet. Eiusdem generis est, quod Christo publica Concilij authoritate & Romani quoq; Praesidis sententia damnato, etiam inter omnis ordinis hominum impia ludibria in cruce pendenti, vnus latro patronus est, qui de eius innocentia, diuina virtute & saluifico officio ex cruce sua tanquam ex cathedra sacra concionatur, & vere quidem, reliquis omnibus in salutis causa non minus impie quàm turpiter errantibus. Quae exempla omnia eorum stultitiam arguunt, qui hodie in controuersia de religione Concilia requirunt, in quibus res suffragiorum multitudine & hominum authoritate decernatur: & eorum quidem, de quorum tyrannide pijssimi quiq; iam aliquot seculis conquesti sunt, & quorum tanta est cum pertinacia tum impudentia, ut tam in clara Euangelij luce, quae abusus & superstitiones vulgo quoq; manifestauit, ne leuissimum quidem errorem ipsi emendare hucusq; dignati sint: quin eos etiam contumaciter tuentur, quos Dei Verbo palàm aduersos esse, & quibus Christianos simul & exteros offendi non ignorant. Quid ergo ab illis speres? Num ut medici, qui hactenus Ecclesiae morbos tà facile neglexerunt, sibi ipsis nunc eanterius adhibeat? Id certe nunquam faciet. Nū verò interea Christianus orbis in tenebris harebit,
units.tr: We are further admonished by this example that no one ought to depend on men in matters of faith, religion, and eternal salvation. For this rests not on the authority of men but on the eternal counsel of God, who has no need of human authority or votes. For as Isaiah proclaimed at God's command, "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of the field; the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of the Lord endures for ever." Indeed, Christ bears witness that heaven and earth will pass away, but not one jot or tittle of his word will perish. What then could the authority of the most excellent men contribute to the mysteries of divine worship and eternal salvation? Rather God rejects this, and chooses the lowly of this world, so that he may put to shame all the wisdom, dignity, glory, and reputation of men. There are many examples which clearly teach how grievously those are deceived who in this matter look to men rather than to God. In Egypt Moses demanded liberty for the people of God from Pharaoh, and had no one with him to support and assist his cause except his brother Aaron. On the opposing side were King Pharaoh, the nobles of the kingdom, and likewise the Magi, who were then judged the wisest of mortals. Who then would not have condemned the cause of Moses, if the matter had to be decided by human judgment? But God proved by many signs and by the outcome of the event that this man had defended a good cause. Something similar happened later in the desert, when the whole Church, with the high priest, consented to the worship of the golden calf; yet Moses again opposed all those with a few others, broke the calf, and punished the authors of so great a wickedness. And what shall we say of Elijah, who, at the public assembly of the whole kingdom of Israel, or rather at a council convened for the sake of religion, alone defended the worship of the true God against the king, the four hundred and fifty priests of Baal, and the whole people? Micaiah also contended with about four hundred false prophets, and his cause was none the worse for their number or their authority. The same can be said of Isaiah, who under King Ahaz complains of the fewness of believers, and says that he and his hearers seem like a portent. Nor did Jeremiah and the other prophets fare any better. But let us press the example we have before us. The Pharisees and Scribes condemned Christ, and although he defended himself earnestly, all were silent; only one little woman defended his innocence by her testimony. If, then, the authority of men ought to prevail, Christ would already be the companion of demons, and the whole Christian religion would lie overthrown. Of the same kind is this: when Christ had been condemned by the public authority of the Council and also by the sentence of the Roman governor, and while, hanging on the cross, he was the object of impious mockery from men of every rank, one thief was his advocate. From his cross, as if from a sacred pulpit, he preached about Christ's innocence, his divine power, and his saving office, and he did so truly, while all the others were erring in the matter of salvation no less impiously than shamefully. All these examples expose the folly of those who today, in controversies about religion, seek councils in which the matter is decided by the multitude of votes and the authority of men. And they seek this from men whose tyranny the most pious have complained of for some centuries now, and who are so stubborn and so shameless that, in the clear light of the Gospel, which has made abuses and superstitions plain even to the common people, they have hitherto not deigned to correct even the slightest error. Rather, they obstinately defend those things which they well know are openly opposed to the Word of God, and by which they offend both Christians and foreigners. What then can you hope from them? Will they, like physicians who have so far neglected the diseases of the Church so easily, now apply a cautery to themselves? Certainly they will never do so. But meanwhile will the Christian world remain in darkness

units.la: Religio non aestimanda ex homine atq; aeterna salutis negotio. harebit, dum illi resipiscant? Iniquum hoc fuerit ab aliquo exigere. Singuli ergo salutis propriæ curam habeant, & mulieris huius exemplum imitati, fremencibus licet Christi aduersarijs, quam agnouerunt, Veritatem fortiter confiteantur.
units.tr: Religion is not to be judged by the man, and it concerns the eternal business of salvation. Shall they remain in darkness until those men repent? That would be unfair to demand of anyone. Let each individual therefore take care of his own salvation, and, imitating this woman's example, let him boldly confess the truth he has recognised, even though Christ's adversaries rage.

units.la: Porrò respondet mulieris voci Dominus, & inde occasione sumpta docet, in quo nam salus homini & illius consequendæ ratio consistat. Rursus autem veræ humilitatis & modestiæ, quæ cum ardenti nostræ salutis studio coniunctæ fuit, exemplum præbet. Alius enim, quem inanis gloriæ cupiditas titillauisset, aliorum quoq; assensum siue applausum auidè expectassèt, vel hinc occasionem capisset de seipso amplius differendi. At ille seipso quasi neglecto hoc agit, vt communi omnium saluti consulat. Imò verò (inquit) beati, qui audiunt Verbum Dei, & illud obseruant. Habet autem responsum hoc non obscuram reprehensionis speciem, qua quod in huius mulieris præconio vitiosum erat, aut aliis causam erroris præbere poterat, corrigit. Non tamen hoc reprehendit, quòd matrem eius Mariam beatam pronuntiauisset. Verè enim beata & eximiū vas gloriæ & gratiæ Dei fuit, cùm in terris ageret, & nunc in cœlis inter beatorum omnium spiritus viuit, & regni illius æterni gaudijs fruitur, quod nobis Christus suo merito acquisiuit. Reprehensione autem dignum fuit, quòd bona hac mulier admiratione & zelo Christi abrepta, in eius prædicatione id omisit, quod in primis laudem meretur: nimirū quòd ipse Verba vitæ æternæ habet, quòd vnicus inter Deum & homines Mediator, vnicus item salutis humanæ fons atque author est, & quòd ipsum audire & amplecti debent, quicunque seruari cupiunt. Hæc vera & solida Christi gloria est, quam se nemini communicaturum esse apud Isaiam clamat, & quàm Pharisæi cum Scribis obscurare, imò totam extinguere conabantur. Huius ergo quia mentionem nullam faceret mulier ista, & beatitudinem externam, quæ Christo exhibentur, officijs transscribere videbatur (quæ multis grauissimi erroris occasio esse potuisset) merito eius dicta ille corrigit, & vt in ipso salutem consequantur, longè aliud requiri docet. Conuenit ergo locus iste cum ijs, quæ Cap. octauo audiuimus, vbi matrem & fratres suos similiter eos esse dicit, qui Verbum suum audiunt atque custodiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord answers the woman's words and, taking occasion from them, teaches where a person's salvation lies and how it is to be obtained. He also gives an example of true humility and modesty, which goes together with his eager concern for our salvation. Another man, whom a desire for empty glory had tickled, would have eagerly awaited the approval and applause of others, and would have seized this as an occasion to dwell at greater length on himself. But Christ, as if setting himself aside, does this so that he may provide for the common salvation of all. "Rather," he says, "blessed are those who hear the Word of God and keep it." This answer carries no small appearance of rebuke, by which he corrects what was faulty in this woman's praise and what could have given others occasion for error. Yet he does not rebuke her for calling his mother Mary blessed. For she was truly blessed and an outstanding vessel of the glory and grace of God while she lived on earth, and now lives in heaven among the spirits of all the blessed and enjoys the joys of that eternal kingdom, which Christ acquired for us by his merit. What deserved rebuke was that this good woman, carried away by admiration and zeal for Christ, omitted in her praise what most deserves commendation: namely, that he himself has the words of eternal life, that he is the only Mediator between God and men, the only fountain and author of human salvation, and that all who desire to be saved ought to hear and embrace him. This is the true and solid glory of Christ, which he cries out through Isaiah he will share with no one, and which the Pharisees and scribes tried to obscure, or indeed to extinguish altogether. Because this woman made no mention of this, and seemed to transfer to the outward blessedness that is given to Christ by her acts of service, which could have been a cause of very grave error for many, he rightly corrects her words and teaches that something quite different is required for them to obtain salvation in him. So this passage agrees with what we heard in chapter eight, where he says that those who hear and keep his word are likewise his mother and brothers.

units.la: Continetur ergo hic memorabilis & necessaria obseruatu doctrina: Hominis beatitudinem atque salutem adeò non consistere in vllis externis officijs aut operibus, vt ne generatio quidem carnalis aliquid ad hanc conferat. Nam qualiscunque aut ex quibuscunque hæc nobis obtingat, certum est, nos in peccato concipi & nasci, vt albi docuimus. Cælitus ergo regeneremur oportet, quod Christus diserte monet, quando Nicodemum pharisaica propriæ iustitiæ & dignitatis fiducia adhuc turgentem ab ipsis fidei & religionis fundamentis instituere volens, hoc suæ doctrinæ principiū ponit: Amen amen dico tibi, nisi quis natus fuerit denuo, non potest videre regnū Dei. At regeneratio ista neque ex matris vtero fit, neque nostris viribus aut operibus conficitur (quid enim ad eam conferant, qui ad carnis generationē nihil conferre potuerunt?) sed eorum modo est, quibus Christus Iesus fide vera receptus hanc dignitatē contulit, vt filij Dei dicantur. Et semen quidem eius est Verbum Dei, administer autem & author Spiritus Sanctus, cuius virtute illud viuificatum nos renouat. Poterat hoc multis Scripturæ testimonijs demonstrari, sed sufficiat nobis vnius Mariæ Virginis exemplum. Est hæc (vt ante etiam diximus) verè beata & gloriosa, & Elizabeta vocem ex Spiritus suggestione loquetur agnoscimus: Benedicta tu inter mulieres. Beatitudinis verò eius causa hæc non fuit, quòd Dei Filium in carne peperit (nam in progenitorum eius catalogo multos impios & infelices Euangelistæ numerant) quòd eundem suis lactauit vberibus, & reliqua matris fidelissimæ officia exhibuit: sed ex eo potius, quòd Dei verbo credidit, & ex se natum humani generis Seruatorem fide complexa in eo renata est, Fidei enim vox fuit, qua Angelo totum incarnationis Filij Dei mysterium exponenti respondit: Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Et Elizabeta Spiritu sancto plena eidem dixit: Beata quæ credidisti: nam perficientur ea, quæ dicta sunt ei à Domino. Quin ipsa Maria eiusdem Spiritus impulsu sibi ipsi nihil præter vilem & humilem conditionem tribuit, quàm Deus ex gratia respicere dignatus sit, & mox addit: Quia magnificè mecum egit potens ille, cuius sanctum est nomen, & cuius misericordia in omnes ætates parata est timentibus ipsum, &c. At ne quis nos noui dogmatis authores esse putet, Augustini verba ex Tractatu in Ioan. decimo audite: Cùm Dominus in turba admirabilis videretur, faciens signa & prodigia, & ostendens quid lateret in carne, admirata quadam anima dixerunt, Felix venter qui te portauit: Et ille, Imò felices qui audiunt Verbum Dei & custodiunt illud: hoc est dicere: Et mater mea, quam appellatus felicem, inde felix, quia Verbum Dei custodit, non quia in illa Verbum caro factum est, & habitauit in nobis: sed quia custodit ipsum verbum Dei, per quod facta est, & quod in illa caro factum est. Homines non gaudeant prole temporali, exultent si spiritu iunguntur Deo. Hac Aug.
units.tr: Therefore the memorable and necessary doctrine to be observed here is this: a person's blessedness and salvation do not consist in any external duties or works, so much so that even carnal generation contributes nothing to them. For whatever and whatever kind of origin we have, it is certain that we are conceived and born in sin, as we have taught above. We must therefore be regenerated from heaven, as Christ plainly warns when, wishing to instruct Nicodemus from the very foundations of faith and religion, while he was still swollen with Pharisaic confidence in his own righteousness and dignity, he lays down this principle of his teaching: "Amen, amen I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." But this regeneration does not come from the mother's womb, nor is it accomplished by our strength or works (for what can those contribute to it who could contribute nothing to natural generation?). Rather, it comes through those to whom Christ Jesus, received by true faith, has given this dignity, that they should be called sons of God. The seed of this regeneration is the Word of God, and its minister and author is the Holy Spirit, by whose power that Word, made alive, renews us. This could be shown by many testimonies of Scripture, but the example of the Virgin Mary alone is enough for us. She is (as we have also said before) truly blessed and glorious, and we acknowledge that Elizabeth, by the prompting of the Spirit, spoke the words: "Blessed are you among women." But the cause of her blessedness was not that she bore the Son of God in the flesh (for the evangelists count among her ancestors many impious and unhappy men), nor that she nursed him at her breasts and performed the other duties of a most faithful mother. It was rather because she believed the word of God, and embracing in faith the Saviour of the human race born from herself, she was reborn in him. For it was the voice of faith with which she answered the angel, who was setting out the whole mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God: "Let it be to me according to your word." And Elizabeth, full of the Holy Spirit, said to her: "Blessed is she who believed, for those things will be accomplished which were spoken to her by the Lord." Indeed, Mary herself, moved by the same Spirit, attributes nothing to herself but her lowly and humble condition, for which God deigned to regard her out of grace; and she soon adds: "Because he who is mighty, whose name is holy, has done great things with me, and his mercy is prepared for all generations toward those who fear him," and so on. But lest anyone think that we are the authors of a new doctrine, hear the words of Augustine from his Tractate on John, chapter ten: "When the Lord appeared in the crowd as one to be wondered at, doing signs and wonders, and showing what lay hidden in the flesh, a certain soul, struck with admiration, said, 'Happy is the womb that bore you.' And he answered, 'Rather, happy are those who hear the Word of God and keep it.' That is to say: my mother, whom you call happy, is happy for this reason, that she keeps the Word of God, not because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us in her; but because she keeps the Word of God itself, through which she was made, and which was made flesh in her. Let men not rejoice in temporal offspring; let them exult if they are joined to God in spirit." Thus Augustine.

units.la: Confutantur ergo hic praepostert Mariae cultores, qui hoc loco abutuntur, quo vix alius ipsorum errori magis repugnat. Dicunt enim scriptum esse: Beatus venter qui te portauit, & vbera quae suxisti. Addunt hu salutationem Angelicam. Aue Maria, gratia plena, benedicta tu inter mulieres. Item quod Elizabeta adiecit: Benedictus fructus ventris tui. Inde verò concludunt: Ergo Maria inuocari & diuinis honoribus coli debet. Mira sane consequentia. Fatemur equidem Angelum salutatione ista vsum esse, neque negamus quod Elizabeta & mulier ista dixerunt. Sed quod isti ex illis colligunt, id neque scripturarum testimonijs, neque vllis sanctorum exemplis probari posse dicimus. Illae enim vnum Deum inuocandum esse docent, vt alias multis demonstrauimus. Adhaec multis aliis similia vel Angelos vel ipsum Deum dixisse scimus, quos tamen nemo piorum pro Diis coluit & inuocauit. Abrahamo Deus ipse dicit: In femine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. Et hoc ipsum cum Isaaco & Iacobo colloquens repetit. De Dauide etiam testatur: Inueni virum secundum cor meum. Gedeonem Angelus salutat: Sit Dominus tecum heros fortissime. Item: Vade in virtute tua, & tu seruabis Israelem de manu Madianitarum. Quis verò vnquam in veteri Testamento propterea Abrahamum, Dauidem aut Gedeonem inuocauit? Quis in illorum honorem vel templa extruxit, vel aras consecrauit? Nemo vtiq;. Imò ne in quastionem quidem hoc vnquam venit inter pios Dei cultores, quorum fides & pietas in scripturis praedicatur. Est ergo nimis absurda & ridicula istorum hominum argumentatio. Mariam quidem in summo honore & pretio habendam esse fatemur, vt quam Deus Filij sui in carne manifestandi matre esse voluit. Sed inuocandam esse negamus, ne in religionis Christianae principia peccemus, quae honorem ipsum vni Deo tribuunt. Mariam autem vere coles, si exemplum eius imiteris, si quem illa genuit mundi Seruatorem fide constanti amplexa es, & (quod illa ipsit) feceris quacunque ille praeceperit. Ioan. 2.
units.tr: Here then the preposterous worshippers of Mary are refuted, who abuse this passage, which hardly any other passage opposes their error more. For they say that it is written: "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked." They add the angelic greeting: "Hail, Mary, full of grace, blessed are you among women." Likewise, what Elizabeth added: "Blessed is the fruit of your womb." And from this they conclude: "Therefore Mary ought to be invoked and honoured with divine honours." A truly marvellous consequence! We grant indeed that the angel used that greeting, and we do not deny what Elizabeth and this woman said. But what these people draw from those words we say cannot be proved either by the testimonies of Scripture or by any examples of the saints. For those testimonies teach that the one God is to be invoked, as we have shown in many places elsewhere. Moreover, we know that many similar things were said by angels, or even by God himself, to whom nevertheless none of the godly worshipped or invoked as gods. God himself says to Abraham: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," and he repeats this same thing when speaking with Isaac and Jacob. He also testifies of David: "I have found a man after my own heart." The angel greets Gideon: "The Lord be with you, most valiant hero." Likewise: "Go in your strength, and you shall save Israel from the hand of the Midianites." But who in the Old Testament ever invoked Abraham, David or Gideon on that account? Who built temples or consecrated altars in their honour? Surely no one. Indeed, this question has never even arisen among the godly worshippers of God, whose faith and piety are praised in the Scriptures. So the argument of these men is exceedingly absurd and ridiculous. We do grant that Mary is to be held in the highest honour and esteem, since God willed her to be the mother of his Son made manifest in the flesh. But we deny that she is to be invoked, lest we sin against the principles of the Christian religion, which ascribe that honour to the one God alone. Yet you will truly worship Mary if you imitate her example, if you embrace with a steadfast faith the Saviour of the world whom she bore, and (as she herself did) do whatever he commands. John 2.

units.la: Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, qui mox verams salutis consequendae rationem subiecit dicens: Beati, qui audiunt Verbum Dei, & illud obseruant. Sunt verba haec in se clara & perspicua, sed quae bus continentur, diligentem consideratione requirunt. Et primo quidem, cum in ipso vno omnis salus & beatitudo habeatur, & proinde dicere posset: Imò qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam, & tam in hoc quam futuro seculo vere beatus est: aliter hic rem explicat, & ad Verbum Dei nos remittit, non quod diuersum quid doceat ab ijs, quae pasim inculcat, sed vt veram fidei & religionis formam seu regulam praescribat, quam tuto sequamur. Sunt enim (vt de alijs sectis nihil dicamus) qui fide in Christum gloriantur, longe alium vero fingunt, quam verbo Dei tradatur: talem nimirum, apud quem alijs intercessoribus sit opus, qui peccatoribus sese difficiliorem praebeat nunc in cae lis, quam olim in terris agens fuerit, quem Virgo mater per vbera obtestetur, quem quotidie pro pec catis viuorum & mortuorum immolari oporteat: quibus multa alia addunt illo indigna & areli gione Christiana alienissima. Ne quid ergo huiusmodi fingamus, ad Dei Verbum nos relegat. Vbi obseruabis, non aliud intelligi, quam quod in Scripturis sacris continetur. Per has enim nobiscum loquitur Deus, vt nequaquam nouae reuelationes aut inspirationes expectanda sint, quibus quid ille velit edoceamur. Gloriantur illi multi, quibus Ierusalem videtur a solis scripturis pendere: sed ijdem fere suis somnijs decepti, in errores graues & perniciosos incidunt. Nos potius Dei fidem & bonitatem exosculemur, qui certam doctrinae formulam esse voluit, quam sequamur. Ideo per Mosem conscripta sunt quae olim cum patribus egit, qui primas saluris promissiones acceperunt. Idem a Deo acceptam Legem ex eius iussu scriptis mandauit, qua ipsius voluntas plenissime explicatur. Adhaec Prophetae literis comprehenderunt, quae per illos Deus locutus est. Quod ipsum de Apostolis dicere possumus. Et mirum est Scripturae sacrae libros inter tot hostiles insidias, persecutiones, bella & horribiles orbis terrarum motus, in hodiernu vsq; diem seruatos esse, cum interea tot millia librorum interciderint, quos potentissimi Reges seruatos voluerunt. Cur verò idsaltum dicemus? Num vt neglectus Scripturis ipsi nobis nouu doctrina genus fingamus, aut Verbum Dei nouum, vel non scriptum, quaeramus? Minimè gentium. Imò potius, vt certa nobis constaret fidei regula atq; salutis ratio, & ne qua occasio esset, quae nos incertis opinionibus vagari cogeret. Porro non modo ad Verbum Dei remittit Christus, sed ut in eo versari debeamus docet.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Christ, who, straight after, sets out the true way of obtaining salvation, saying: "Blessed are those who hear the Word of God and keep it." These words are clear and plain in themselves, but they require careful consideration of what they contain. And first of all, since all salvation and blessedness is found in him alone, he could have said: "Indeed, whoever believes in me has eternal life, and is truly blessed both in this age and in the age to come." Instead he explains the matter in another way and refers us to the Word of God. This is not because he teaches something different from what he inculcates everywhere, but so that he may prescribe the true form, or rule, of faith and religion, which we may safely follow. For there are some (to say nothing of other sects) who boast of faith in Christ, yet invent a view of him quite different from what is delivered in the Word of God: one, namely, for whom other intercessors are needed, who shows himself more unapproachable now in heaven than when he dwelt on earth, whom the Virgin Mother must implore by her breasts, and who must be sacrificed daily for the sins of the living and the dead. To these they add many other things unworthy of him and most alien to the Christian religion. So that we do not invent anything of this kind, he refers us back to the Word of God. Here you will observe that nothing is meant except what is contained in the holy Scriptures. For through these God speaks with us, so that no new revelations or inspirations are to be expected by which we might be taught what he wills. Many boast that Jerusalem depends on Scripture alone, yet these same people, almost deceived by their own dreams, fall into grave and pernicious errors. Rather let us embrace the faithfulness and goodness of God, who has willed that there be a certain form of doctrine for us to follow. Therefore through Moses were written down the things which God once made covenant about with the fathers, who received the first promises of salvation. Likewise he commanded the Law, received from God, to be put into writing by his order, in which his will is most fully set out. Besides, the Prophets comprehended in writing what God spoke through them. We may say the same of the Apostles. And it is remarkable that the books of Holy Scripture have been preserved to this day amid so many hostile snares, persecutions, wars and dreadful upheavals of the world, while meanwhile many thousands of books have perished, which the most powerful kings wished to have preserved. But why should we say this? Is it that, neglecting the Scriptures, we should invent a new kind of doctrine for ourselves, or seek a new Word of God, unwritten? By no means. Rather, so that a sure rule of faith and a way of salvation might be established for us, and so that there should be no occasion to drive us to wander in uncertain opinions. Moreover, Christ not only refers us back to the Word of God, but also teaches that we ought to be occupied in it.

units.la: Primo ut Verbum audiamus monet. Nam ut Paulus ait, fides ex auditu est. Audiendi autem vocabulo diligens & ferium Verbi studium intelligit, quo etiam lectio & meditatio eorum, quae audivimus & legimus, comprehenditur. Ut enim ipse in sementi, parabola docet, non omnes, qui Verbum auribus percipiunt servantur. Sunt enim qui semen illud in viam, id est, animos pravu affectibus & suggestionibus patentes excipiunt. Sunt qui corda afferunt petricosa, in quibus radices agere non possunt. Sunt qui animos spinis curarum huius saeculi obsitos habent. In quibus omnibus illud fructum aliquem ferre non possunt. Requiritur ergo animus honestus & discendi cupidus, qui quod audivit aut legit, retineat, & diligenti meditatione ruminet, ut veram divinae voluntatis & mysterium salutis cognitionem assequatur. Dum vero Dei Verbum audire iubet, eos omnes confutat, qui humanas traditiones audiunt & sequuntur. Impingunt hi in ipso limine, quando constat, eos nequaquam circa Dei cultum occupari, qui hominum figmentis inhaerent. Simul etiam iis respondetur hic, qui quaeruntur se nescire, quid inter tot tamque graves de religione controversias credere debeant. Atqui uno verbo Christus nos dubitare vetat, quando beatos dicit eos, qui Verbum Dei audiunt. Huius ergo praeceptum sequere, quod te falli aut errare non sinet.
units.tr: First, he bids us hear the Word. For, as Paul says, "faith comes by hearing." By the word "hearing" he understands a diligent and eager study of the Word, which also includes reading and meditating on what we have heard and read. For as he himself teaches in the parable of the sower, not all who receive the Word with their ears are saved. There are some who receive that seed on the path, that is, in minds open to wicked affections and suggestions. There are some who bring hearts full of stones, in which it cannot take root. There are some who have minds choked with the thorns of the cares of this age. In all these cases it cannot bear any fruit. What is required, then, is an honest mind, eager to learn, which retains what it has heard or read and chews it over with diligent meditation, so that it may attain a true knowledge of the divine will and the mystery of salvation. But while he commands us to hear the Word of God, he also refutes all those who hear and follow human traditions. Such men stumble at the very threshold, since it is clear that those who cling to the fictions of men are not occupied with the worship of God at all. At the same time an answer is given here to those who complain that they do not know what they ought to believe amid so many and such serious controversies about religion. Yet Christ forbids us to doubt by a single word, when he calls blessed those who hear the Word of God. Follow therefore his precept, which will not allow you to be deceived or to err.

units.la: At quia nuda auditio Verbi non sufficit, alterum addit, ut illud observemus & custodiamus. Nam ut modo diximus, multa sunt quae Verbum ex animis auferunt, & obstant ne fructum in nobis ferat aliquem. Itaque animo memori & fido commissorum aut depositorum custode opus est. Is verò in nobis non erit, nisi iis quae dicuntur credamus, & ea Dei Verbum esse habeamus persuasum. Hinc deinde mandatorum Dei observatio & obedientia vera nascitur, quam nisi praestemus, Verbum nobisipsis in testimonium audimus, & a salute excidimus. Ideo graviter admodum de hoc Iacobus admonet, sic scribens: Reipsa praestate sermonem, nec sitis auditores solum, fallentes vosmetipsos. Nam si quis audit sermonem, & cum non praestat, similis est viro considerant nativam faciem suam in speculo: Consideravit enim seipsum, & abiit, & statim oblitus est qualis esset. At qui perspexerit in perfectam illam Legem Libertatis, & in ea permanserit, qui non fuerit auditor obliviosus, sed effector operis, beatus erit in opere suo, &c.
units.tr: But because bare hearing of the Word is not enough, he adds the second thing, that we observe and keep it. For, as we have just said, there are many things which snatch the Word from our minds and prevent it from bearing any fruit in us. Therefore we need a mind that is mindful and faithful, a guardian of what has been committed or entrusted to it. Such a guardian will not be in us unless we believe the things that are said and are persuaded that they are the Word of God. Hence the true observance and obedience of God's commandments is born, which, unless we render it, we hear the Word to our own witness and fall away from salvation. Therefore James admonishes us most seriously about this, writing thus: "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone hears the word and does not do it, he is like a man who considers his natural face in a mirror: for he considers himself, and goes away, and straightway forgets what manner of man he was. But whoever has looked into the perfect law of liberty, and has continued in it, not being a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, shall be blessed in his deed, etc."

units.la: Ut vero Verbum Dei recte observemus, quid illo doceatur & mandetur tenere oportet. Possunt ea omnia duobus capitibus comprehendi. Primum est fides in Christum Iesum, sub qua totus Dei cultus tam externus quam internus continetur. De hoc ipse apud Ioannem loquitur his verbis: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem ille misit. Item: Haec est voluntas eius qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam, &c. Et praeceptum nostrum secundum Ioannes Apostolus, inter praecepta Dei similiter hoc primo loco ponit, ut credamus nomini Filii sui Iesu Christi, id est, ut hunc Seruatorem, Regem & Pontificem nostrum summum atque aeternum agnoscamus, qualis suo nomine describitur, & in Scripturis praedicatur, de quo paulo ante diximus. Hic ergo excluduntur omnia, quae illius merito derogant, dum nos salutem alibi, quam in ipso solo quaerere docent. Nam perpetuo ratum erit hoc eius dictum: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Alterum caput est, ut vitam vivamus Christiana professione dignam. Quia enim fides hominem totum Deo vendicat, eundem regenerat quoque, ut tam non ipse vivat, sed Christum in se habeat viventem, ut de semetipso Paulus scribit. Verissime ergo dicimus, eos a fide adhuc alienos esse, qui vitam prophanam viuunt, & sceleribus indulgent. Recte ergo Iacobus ait: Quae utilitas fuerit, fratres mei, si quis fidem habeat, opera autem non habeat? Loquitur enim de nuda & inani fidei professione, quam paulo post fidem mortuam dicit, & addit: Tu fidem habes, id est, fide gloriaris: ostende mihi fidem tuam operibus tuis. Nam ut hominem viuere ex actionibus constat, nec viuere dicetur is, in quo sensus omnes extincti sunt, calor frigvit, nervi & membra obriguerunt, ut nullum vitae indicium sit reliquum: ita fides reipsa & totius vitae studiis sese declarat, & proinde in illis nulla erit, qui non serio promovendae gloriae Dei studio tenentur, in quibus charitas extincta friget, & qui nullum praestant hominis Christiani officium. Sed ne hic quoque cum multis superstitiosis erremus, qui bonorum operum nomine externa quaedam frigidissimarum ceremoniarum exercitia intelligunt, tutissimum erit, ut ipsius exemplum nobis imitandum proponatur.
units.tr: But in order to observe the Word of God rightly, we must hold fast to what it teaches and commands. All these things can be comprehended under two heads. The first is faith in Christ Jesus, under which the whole worship of God, both external and internal, is contained. Of this he speaks himself in John, in these words: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." Likewise: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life," etc. And the Apostle John, in his teaching on the commandments of God, likewise places this first, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, that is, that we should acknowledge him as our Saviour, King and High Priest, eternal, such as he is described by his own name and proclaimed in the Scriptures, concerning whom we spoke a little above. Here, therefore, everything is excluded which detracts from his merit, since he teaches us to seek salvation nowhere but in him alone. For this saying of his will remain forever firm: "I am the Lord; this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." The second head is that we live a life worthy of the Christian profession. For since faith claims the whole man for God, it also regenerates him, so that he no longer lives, but Christ lives in him, as Paul writes of himself. Most truly, then, we say that those who live a profane life and indulge in wickedness are still strangers to faith. Rightly, therefore, James says: "What good is it, my brothers, if someone has faith but does not have works?" For he speaks of a bare and empty profession of faith, which a little later he calls dead faith, and adds: "You have faith, that is, you boast of faith: show me your faith by your works." For just as it is evident that a man lives by his actions, and no one will be said to live in whom all the senses are extinguished, the warmth grown cold, the nerves and limbs stiffened, so that no sign of life remains, so faith too declares itself in deeds and in the pursuits of the whole of life; and therefore there will be no faith in those who are not seriously held by the zeal to promote the glory of God, in whom charity is extinguished and cold, and who perform no duty of a Christian man. But lest here too we err with many superstitious people, who understand by good works certain external exercises of the most frigid ceremonies, it will be safest to set before us his own example to imitate.

units.la: mus. Sic enim ipse monet, quando abs se nos discere iubet, & exemplum se nobis praebuisse dicit. In ipso autem obedientia & humilitas erga Patrem caelestem extrema cernitur, qua se exinaniuit, & forma serui assumpta obediens fuit usque ad mortem, & quidem usque ad mortem crucis, qua nihil atrocius & magis infame fingi poterat. Innocentia studium quoque tantum, ut infensissimis hostibus dicere ausit: Quis vestrum arguet me peccati? Charitatis autem igne ita flagrauit, ut hostibus quoque nunquam cessauerit benefacere, & pro illis etiam preces fuderit, a quibus in crucem suffigebatur. Adhac patientia & fidei constantia tanta armatus fuit, ut inter grauissimas tentationes & immanes mortis appropinquantis dolores Deum inuocarit, & huic animam crediderit. Haec quicunque imitantur, ij Dei verbum obseruant, & proinde vere beati sunt, adeoque Christi cognatu carnalibus praeferuntur, cum & eius germani fratres & veri filij Dei sint. Beati (inquā) sunt, etiamsi innumeris & assiduis calamitatibus exerceantur. Nam inter has de salute sua certi sunt, & huius arrhabonem habent certissimum, Spiritum Sanctum, in quo clamant, Abba Pater. Sorte item sua contenti viuunt, quam non postremam felicitatis partem esse, gentium quoque philosophi intellexerunt. Vbi vero vita sua cursum emensi fuerint, ad Christum colliguntur, cuius promissio est: Volo ut vbi ego sum, etiam sint minister meus. Item: Volo pater, ut vbi sum ego, etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Quia enim huius oues & peculium, imo eius sponsa sunt, nunquam illos abs se diuelli patietur.
units.tr: ...us. For thus he himself admonishes, when he bids us learn from him and says that he has set us an example. In him indeed the utmost obedience and humility toward the heavenly Father is seen, by which he emptied himself, and, taking the form of a servant, became obedient unto death, and indeed unto the death of the cross, than which nothing more atrocious or infamous could be devised. His zeal for innocence was so great that he dared to say to his most hostile enemies: Which of you will convict me of sin? He burned with the fire of love, so that he never ceased to do good even to his enemies, and poured out prayers for those by whom he was nailed to the cross. Moreover, he was armed with such patience and constancy of faith that, amid the most grievous temptations and the savage pains of approaching death, he called upon God and committed his soul to him. Whoever imitates these things keeps the word of God, and therefore is truly blessed, and is preferred to those who are related to Christ according to the flesh, since they are his true brothers and genuine sons of God. They are blessed, I say, even though they are exercised by countless and constant calamities. For amid these they are certain of their salvation, and they have the surest pledge of it, the Holy Spirit, in whom they cry, Abba, Father. Likewise they live content with their lot, which the philosophers of the Gentiles also understood to be no small part of happiness. When they have finished the course of their life, they are gathered to Christ, whose promise is: I will that where I am, there my servant also may be. Again: Father, I desire that where I am, those also whom you have given me may be. For since they are his sheep and his own possession, indeed his bride, he will never suffer them to be torn away from him.

units.la: Traditur ergo breui hac sententia ratio salutis certa, adeoq; pietas illa, quam Paulus cum praesentis tum futuri seculi promissiones habere scribit: Huius autem consideratio diligentior simul nos admonet, quae causa sit calamitatum, quibus hodie totus terrarum orbis affligitur. Disputant de illa multi, & remedia nequicquam quaerunt. Atqui vnica beatitudinis obtinendae ratio est, ut Verbum Dei audiatur & obseruetur. Hanc Lex & Prophetae monstrant, quorum doctrinam Christus in praesenti confirmat. Istam vero paucissimi sequuntur. Multi enim Verbum Dei ne audire quidem dignantur, sed scurriliter contemnunt. Multi insuper illud ferro & igne oppugnant, & in eius sectatores hostiliter saeuiunt. Qui vero audiunt, ij Dei Verbum esse non credunt, & ideo no custodiunt neq; obseruant illud, sicuti in ipsorum moribus apparet. Imo pleriq; eorum sic viuunt, ut propter ipsos illud male audiat. Quod si vero flagella & virgas suas Deus exerat, tunc impatientia superati aduersus illum fremunt & murmurant, adhac non ad ipsum, sed ad media illicita conuertuntur, quibus sibi ipsis opem ferre volunt. Sunt haec nota omnibus. Neminem ergo nostri seculi mala offendant. Quid enim aliud faceret Deus? Discant potius singuli vitia illa emendare, Verbum Dei audire, praecepta eius obseruare, Christum Iesum fide vera ampleti & eius imitari exemplum. Ita & in hoc seculo beati erunt, & hac vita defuncti cum illo aeternum viuent & gaudebunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Thus in this brief saying a sure way of salvation is handed down, and that godliness which Paul writes has the promise of both the present and the future life. A closer consideration of this at the same time reminds us what is the cause of the calamities with which the whole world is today afflicted. Many dispute about it and seek remedies in vain. Yet there is only one way to obtain blessedness: that the word of God be heard and observed. The Law and the Prophets show this, and Christ now confirms their teaching. But very few follow it. For many do not deign even to hear the word of God, but despise it scurrilously. Many moreover assail it with sword and fire, and rage hostilely against its followers. Those who do hear do not believe it to be the word of God, and therefore neither keep nor observe it, as appears from their conduct. Indeed, most of them live in such a way that on their account it is ill spoken of. But when God brandishes his scourges and rods, then, overcome by impatience, they rage and murmur against him, and instead of turning to him they turn to unlawful means by which they wish to bring help to themselves. These things are known to all. Let no one therefore be offended by the evils of our age. For what else would God do? Rather let each one learn to amend those vices, to hear the word of God, to observe his precepts, to embrace Christ Jesus with true faith and to imitate his example. So they will be blessed in this age too, and when they have departed this life they will live and rejoice with him for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 118.

units.la: Cum autem turba congregaretur apud eum, caepit dicere: Natio haec mala est: signum requirit, sed signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum illud Ionae Prophetae. Nam prout fuit Ionas signum Niniuitis: ita erit Filius hominis Nationi isti. Regina Austri surget in iudicio cum viris nationis huius, & condemnabit eos: quod venerit a terminis terrae, ut audiret sapientiam Solomonis: & ecce plus quam Solomon est hoc in loco. Viri Niniuitae resurgent in iudicio cum hac natione, & condemnabunt eam: quod ad praeconium Ionae resipuerint: & ecce plus quam Ionas est hoc in loco.
units.tr: When a crowd was gathering around him, he began to say: "This generation is evil. It seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be to this generation. The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here."

units.la: Exposuit nuper Lucas diuersa hominum de facto Christi, qui daemoniacum curauerat, iudicia: quorum alij pia admiratione capti, aliquid sublimius de illo sentire coeperunt: alij vero, inter quos primi fuere Pharisaei & Scribae Hierosolymitani, ad calumnias conuersi, illu magicus & illicitis artibus deditum esse dixere, ut eius authoritati derogarent, & populo tam doctrinam eius quam quàm miracula suspecta facerent. His tertij accesserunt, qui signum è coelo postularunt, quo probaretur ipsum à Deo magistrum & doctorem datum esse; & divina virtute omnia agere. At hoc pretendo non nisi suffugium quaesiuerunt, quo suam incredulitatem excusarent, ut qui merito non crederent ei, qui terrena modo miracula, nullum autem coelitus aederet. Hactenus autè calumniae Pharisaeorum respondit, & ita quidem, ut reliquos omnibus prae Pharisaeorum & Scribarum metu tacentibus mulierculà quaedam praeclarum illi testimonium dederit. Nunc ergo cum postremus illis agit, qui signum petebant è coelo. Qui locus inter multa alia, quae observatu dignissima sunt, grauem admonitionem, vel comminationem potius continet, qua docemur improbos verbi contemptores, dum signa postulant, eorum loco poenas auferre, quibus illorum impietatem Deus vlcisciturr. Nam alibi idem petentibus Pharisaeis, iratus eos deserit, ut sua gratia indignos esse ostendat. Hic autem diligentius & magno studio rem hanc tractat: nimirum ut eadem opera multis alijs consulat, qui ipsum audiebant,
units.tr: Luke has just described the different judgments people made about Christ's healing of the demoniac. Some, seized by pious wonder, began to think something more exalted of him. Others, and the first of these were the Pharisees and the scribes of Jerusalem, turned to slander and said that he was a magician who practised forbidden arts, so as to undermine his authority and make the people suspicious of both his teaching and his miracles. To these others were added those who demanded a sign from heaven, by which it might be proved that he had been given by God as teacher and master, and that he did all things by divine power. But this pretext was nothing more than an escape, by which they sought to excuse their unbelief, since they would be right not to believe one who performed only earthly miracles and none from heaven. Christ has now answered the slanders of the Pharisees, and he did so in such a way that the rest, who kept silent out of fear of the Pharisees and scribes, were given a remarkable testimony by a certain woman. Now he deals with the last group, those who asked for a sign from heaven. This passage, among many other things worth closest attention, contains a grave warning, or rather a threat, by which we are taught that wicked despisers of the Word, while they ask for signs, bring upon themselves the punishments by which God will avenge their impiety. For elsewhere, when the Pharisees asked the same thing, he left them in anger, to show that they were unworthy of his grace. Here, however, he treats the matter more carefully and with great earnestness, clearly so that at the same time he may help many others who were listening to him.

units.la: Nam occasionem de his maiori cum fructu dicendi ipsum captauisse, Lucas aperte innuit, quan do haec eum dixisse scribit, cum magnus iam concursus populi ad ipsum factus esset; quem partim miraculi in daemoniaco editi fama, partim exorta inter Scribas & illum disputatio excitauerat. Eo autem ostendit Christus, se bona fide & ingenuè cum aduersarijs agere velle, adeò ut testes minime fugiat. Non ergo inuidos calumniatores imitatur, qui aut absentibus obtrectant, aut absque testibus crimina falsa in immerentes congerunt: ita denique agunt, ut semper locus negandi aut elabendi pateat: si quid contra ipsos iure tententur. Non ita Christus egit, sed cum turba vndiq; adipsum congregaretur, coepit dicere: Natio haec mala est, signum requirit, &c. Apud Matthaeum haec prima verba sic enuntiantur: Natio mala & adulterina signum requirit. Nationis aut generationis vocabulo vtitur, ut incredulitatem & contumaciam hanc non nouam, sed veterem & quasi hereditariam esse ostendat. Quo sensu Moses quoque peruersam & detortam generationem vocat in suo Cantico. Quamuis autem indecorum videatur patrum vitia posteris exprobrare, ut tamen id fiat saepe necessitas requirit, praesertim quando incurabilem videmus horum malitiam, & quod patribus glorientur atque superbiant, quod Iudaeis nimium vulgare erat. Tria autem in illis accusat. Primò malos esse dicit. In Graeco vox πονηρος ponitur, qua in Dominica Oratione & in alijs scriptura locis diabolus notari solet. Proprie enim eum significat, qui non simpliciter & sibi ipsi modò malus est, sed alijs quoque sua malitia & improbitate molestiam atque laborem exhibet. Quod diaboli ingenium esse, Scripturae docent, & res ipsa abunde testatur. Recte autem hic titulus Pharisaeis & Scribis conueniebat, qui & ipsi non contenti propria nequitia, insuper populum quoque seducebant, & Christo indesinenter insidiabantur, ut nonam ei molestiam facerent, & salutis communis negotium impedirent, quod ille agebat. Secundo adulterinos vocat, quod perinde est, ac si spurios & illegitimo thoro natos dixisset. Cuius epitheti ratio est, quod cùm Abrahami filij & Israelitae vocari vellent, à sanctis illis patribus iam pridem degenerauissent, & à fide Abrahami essent prorsus alieni. Quo Ioannes quoque Baptista respiciens, progeniem viperarum eos dicit, & ne Abrahamo patre glorientur prohibet. Potest tamen latius quoque huius nominis significatio extendi, ut nimirum adulterina & adultera natio dicantur, quia fidem Deo datam fefellerunt. Scimus enim ex Ezechiele & Hosea Prophetis, hunc illos non modo suum sibi peculiu fecisse, verumetiam despondisse, ut sponsa sua essent, qua cum bona sua communia haberet. At quam tuiter patres eorum post Deos gentium & idola eorum scortati sint, ijdem Prophetae testantur: & quamuis Christi tempore ab idololatria illa crassiori immunes essent, tamen non minori perfidia peccabant, cum legem fide corrumperent, cultum omnem Dei sibi ipsis quaestum facerent, & Filium eius in quo ille nos sibi despondit, non modo contemnerent, verumetiam hostiliter persequerentur. Ergo plus quam adulterina soboles erant, cum in illis ipsis spiritualis illius fornicationis crimen haereret, qua Deus maximè offenditur. Tertio ad rem ipsam accedit Christus, & ideo hanc reprehensionem illos mereri ait, quod signum requirant. Atqui signis confirmari velle, per se impium non est. Fecit hoc olim Gedeon, & quidem importunè satis, cui tamen clementer & patria quasi indulgentia Deus morem gessit. Achazo autem Regi Isaias irascitur, quod iussus signum petere, id facere recusaret. Caeterum longè alia istorum ratio fuit. Nam supra annotauit Lucas, illos tentandi gratia signum è cælo petijsse, vt nimirum contumaciæ suæ prætextum haberent, nisi ipsorum petitioni satisfaceret: rursus autem calumniandi maior esset occasio, si quid huius fieret. Fuit ergo hoc incurabilis malitiæ argumentum, quia ipsorum quoque maiores olim in deserto non semel peccauisse, sacra historia docet. Quid enim opus erat signa noua è cælo postulare, cum quotidie infinita fieri vi derent, quæ non nisi cælesti & diuina virtute perfici poterant? Non ergo (vt diximus) vt in fide confirmentur quærunt, sed vt licentius in sua impietate pergere, & eam apud populum aliquo prætextu excusare possint.
units.tr: For Luke clearly indicates that Christ sought an occasion of speaking about these matters with greater profit, since he writes that he said these things when a large crowd had already gathered around him, stirred partly by the report of the miracle wrought on the demoniac and partly by the dispute that had arisen between him and the scribes. Christ thereby shows that he wishes to deal with his opponents in good faith and openly, so much so that he does not in the least shun witnesses. He therefore does not imitate envious slanderers, who either disparage people in their absence or heap false charges upon the innocent without witnesses. They act in such a way that there is always room to deny or slip away, if anything is rightly brought against them. Christ did not act like this, but when a crowd gathered around him from every side, he began to say: "This generation is evil, it seeks a sign," and so on. In Matthew these first words are expressed thus: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign." He uses the word "nation" or "generation" to show that this unbelief and obstinacy is not new but old and, as it were, hereditary. In this sense Moses too calls them a perverse and distorted generation in his Song. Although it may seem unseemly to reproach posterity with the sins of their fathers, yet necessity often requires that this be done, especially when we see their wickedness is incurable, and when they boast and pride themselves on their fathers, which was all too common among the Jews. Now he accuses them of three things. First, he says they are evil. In Greek the word is "ponēros," which in the Lord's Prayer and in other places of Scripture is commonly used of the devil. For it properly signifies one who is not merely evil in himself, but who also causes trouble and labour to others by his malice and wickedness. Scripture teaches that this is the nature of the devil, and the thing itself bears ample witness to it. This title fitted the Pharisees and scribes rightly, for they, not content with their own wickedness, also led the people astray, lay constantly in wait for Christ so as to cause him every trouble, and hindered the work of common salvation, which he was carrying out. Second, he calls them adulterous, which is the same as if he had called them bastards, born of an unlawful bed. The reason for this epithet is that, although they wished to be called sons of Abraham and Israelites, they had long since degenerated from those holy fathers and were utterly estranged from the faith of Abraham. John the Baptist also had this in view when he called them a brood of vipers and forbade them to boast of Abraham as their father. Yet the meaning of this name can also be extended more broadly, so that the nation is called adulterous and an adulteress, because they broke the faith given to God. For we know from the prophets Ezekiel and Hosea that God not only made them his own peculiar people but also betrothed them, that they might be his bride, with whom he would share his goods. But how wantonly their fathers played the harlot after the gods of the nations and their idols, these same prophets testify. And although in Christ's time they were free from that grosser idolatry, yet they sinned with no less faithlessness, since they corrupted the law by their unbelief, turned the whole worship of God into gain for themselves, and not only despised the Son of God, in whom he had betrothed us to himself, but also persecuted him with hostility. Therefore they were more than an adulterous offspring, since the crime of that spiritual fornication, by which God is most offended, clung to them. Third, Christ comes to the thing itself, and says that they deserve this rebuke because they seek a sign. And yet to wish to be confirmed by signs is not in itself impious. Gideon did this once, and indeed rather importunately, yet God graciously indulged him with a kind of fatherly forbearance. But Isaiah was angry with King Ahaz, because when he was commanded to ask for a sign, he refused to do so. However, the reason for these men was quite different. For Luke noted above that they sought a sign from heaven to test him, so that they might have a pretext for their obstinacy if he did not satisfy their demand; and again, there would be a greater occasion for slander if anything of the kind were done.
