This was therefore a proof of incurable malice, since sacred history teaches that their own forefathers had sinned in the desert more than once. For why was there any need to demand new signs from heaven, when they saw countless things done every day which could be accomplished only by heavenly and divine power? Therefore they seek not, as we have said, to be confirmed in faith, but so that they may continue more freely in their impiety and be able to excuse it before the people by some pretext.

units.la: Imitantur istorum malitiam & adulterinum ingenium, qui hodie in aperta Euangelij luce indies deteriores fiunt, & cum accusantur, per eiusmodi effugia se elabi posse putant, si doctrinamno stram signis confirmari postulent. At si Christiani sunt, agnoscunt utique Christi vocem, quao mnes ad se vocat, & in se vno omnem salutem repositam esse docet. Agnoscunt utique Symboli Apostolici articulos, quibus tota fides Christiana continetur. Neque reijcient à Christo tra ditam precandi formulam, qua vnum Deum Patrem inuocare iubemur, & ab eo solo petere, quæ tă corpori quæm animæ necessaria sunt. At quid ab his diuersum aut alienū docemus? Ostendant quæ si possunt, nos ab istis fidei & religionis Christianæ principijs, vel latu culmu discedere. Quid ergo signis noua est opus ad eam doctrinam confirmandā, cuius veritatem æternus Dei Filius, Apostoli item & sancti Martyres iam olim multis millibus miraculorum demonstrauerunt? Quod si omni no à signis potius quam à Dei verbo pendere volunt, cur non in ea corporis & animi oculos intendunt, quæ quotidie non sine miraculo fiunt? Quis enim miraculum esse neget, Pontificum tyrannidem tot opibus, tot Regum & principum societate, & propria quoque potentia munitam, aliquot item seculorum consuetudine confirmatam, per homines prius obscuros & nulla vel priuata vel pu blica authoritate armatos, subito labefactari, & multis in locis omnino dirui & cuerti potuisse? Quis non admirabilem Dei potentiam agnoscat, qui doctrinam Euangelicæ veritatis iam per annos plus minus quinquaginta aduersus potentissimorum principum conatus, multarum gentium fœdera & conspirationes, inter tot tamque graues totius orbis motus, seditiones, bella item cum extera tum ciuilia conseruauit? Sunt hæc certe maiora multo, quam si daemonia pellerentur, cæci vi sus, surdi auditus, muti linguæ vsus, claudi deambulatio, paralytici & leprosi valetudo integra resti tuerentur. Quod si mortuos resuscitari petunt, cur non eos obseruant, qui mortui per delicta, & in se pulchris scelerum computrescentes, ad Euangelij vocem subito resurgunt, & vitam nouam viuunt in Christo, cuius merito se redemptos esse fatentur? Sed quid hæc dicere necesse est, quando ipsi papisticos errores agnoscunt, & intra proprias conscientias conuicti sunt? Veruntamen adhuc signa petunt, & neq; rationibus, neq; proprij animi iudicio mouentur, vt potentem Dei manum agnoscant qua Euangelium simul & Ecclesiam suā mirificè tuetur. Quid ergo de illis aliud dicas, quam quod de Pharisæis istis Christus pronunciauit? esse nimirum malos & adulterinos, qui à filiorum Dei in genio iam pridem degenerarint, fidem Deo datam fefellerint, & tam huic quam hominibus pijs molestiam exhibeant?
units.tr: Those who today, in the clear light of the gospel, grow worse by the day imitate the malice and adulterous disposition of these men. When they are accused, they think they can slip away by such evasions, if they demand that our doctrine be confirmed by signs. But if they are Christians, they certainly acknowledge the voice of Christ, who calls all to himself and teaches that all salvation is laid up in him alone. They certainly acknowledge the articles of the Apostles' Creed, in which the whole Christian faith is contained. Nor will they reject the form of prayer handed down by Christ, in which we are commanded to call upon one God the Father and to ask of him alone what is necessary both for body and soul. But what do we teach that is different from or foreign to these things? Let them show, if they can, that we have departed from the principles of the Christian faith and religion even by a hair's breadth. Why, then, is there any need of new signs to confirm that doctrine whose truth the eternal Son of God, and likewise the Apostles and holy martyrs, have already long ago demonstrated by many thousands of miracles? But if they want altogether to depend on signs rather than on the Word of God, why do they not fix the eyes of body and mind on those things which happen every day, not without a miracle? For who would deny that it is a miracle that the tyranny of the pontiffs, fortified with so much wealth, with the alliance of so many kings and princes, with their own power as well, and confirmed by the custom of several centuries, could be suddenly shaken and in many places utterly overthrown by men who were at first obscure and armed with no authority, whether private or public? Who does not acknowledge the wonderful power of God, who for about fifty years has preserved the doctrine of evangelical truth against the attempts of the most powerful princes, the alliances and conspiracies of many nations, and amid so many and such grave upheavals of the whole world, seditions and wars, both foreign and civil? These are certainly far greater than if demons were cast out, the blind were made to see, the deaf to hear, the mute to speak, the lame to walk, and the paralysed and leprous were restored to full health. And if they ask that the dead be raised, why do they not observe those who, dead through their transgressions and rotting in their own foul crimes, rise up suddenly at the voice of the gospel and live a new life in Christ, by whose merit they confess that they have been redeemed? But why is it necessary to say these things, when they themselves acknowledge the Papist errors and are convicted within their own consciences? Nevertheless they still ask for signs, and are moved neither by reasons nor by the judgment of their own minds to recognise the mighty hand of God, by which he wonderfully guards both the gospel and his Church. What, then, can you say of them other than what Christ pronounced of those Pharisees: that they are evil and adulterous, who have long since degenerated from the nature of the children of God, who have broken the faith given to God, and who cause trouble both to him and to godly men?

units.la: Neq; hic illis propter magnificos titulos & prærogatiuas, quibus ferè gloriantur, parcendum est. Quomodo enim cū talibus verbi ministri agere debeat, Christus hic proprio exemplo docet. Erat quidē magna illorū authoritas, & Dei peculiū, gens sancta & sacerdotale regnū dicebantur. Quia verò suis illis titulis minus respondebat, Christus nō ad eos, sed quales reuera essent, respicit, et ijs no minibus illos exornat, quæ eorū facta merebatur. Idè ante illius in carne aduentū olim prophetæ sece rūt, qui illos modò Chananæorū posteros, modò Amorrhæos, interdū populū Gomorrhæ dicūt, et me retricibus similes aiunt, quæ perfricta fronte & procul abiecto omni pudore quibusuis obuijs sese pro stituūt. Et quid Baptista fecerit, paulò ante diximus. Nec clementius à Stephano tractantur, quam uis ii sibi iam pereundum esse videret. Ita autem fieri necesse est. Nam nisi hominibus eiusmodi lar ua detrahatur, quase apud vulgus venditant, frustra cum illis egeris: quia nunquam pœnitentia sibi opus esse putabunt, quoad se apud aliquos in pretio esse viderint. Sunt quidem qui modestiæ slu dendum esse dicunt, ne qui adhuc curabiles sunt irritentur & hostes fiant. Idnos non negamus, sed quid contumaces & deplorate spei hostes veritatis mereantur docemus, quales hodie pleriq; sunt, qui Euangelij doctrinam oppugnant, sicuti iam ante demonstrauimus. Sed pergamus in Christi verbis, qui signum quidem pollicetur, non autem quale ipsi petebant, sed quale ipsorum improbitas & contumacia merebatur. Signum (inquit) non dabitur huic generationi, nisi signum Ionae Prophetae. Nam prout fuit Ionas signum Niniuitis: ita erit Filius hominis nationi isti. Quae verba non sic accipi debent, quasi post hunc cum aduersarijs suis congressum nulla porro signa aut miracula fecerit Christus. Nam plurimos a morbis grauissimis liberauit, & quod omnia reliqua superat, Lazarum ex mortuis resuscitauit in vitam. Sed quia haec omnia ab illis contemni sciebat, vnum adhuc superesse dicit, quod & ipsum ipsorum cupiditati minimè satisfacturum sit, optimè autem responsurum eorum moribus, ut ex quo non salutis, sed potius exitij sui, quod dudum meruerint, indicium aut praesagium sint habituri. Exemplo autem Ionae & Niniuitarum rem illustrat, ut olim quoque simile quid factum esse intelligant, & ut simul nouam habeat ipsos corripiendi materiam. Historia satis nota est, quare sensum potius & mentem Christi consideremus. Quemadmodum (inquit) Ionas ex ceti aut balaenae ventre terrae redditus Niniuitis signum loco fuit, quo ad ipsum audiendum & ad poenitentiae studium excitari debuerunt: ita ego quoque tertio die ex mortuis rediuiuus genti huic in signum ero, cuius consideratione omnes excitari & moneri conueniebat, ut me per Apostolos loquentem audirent & resipiscerent. Quibus tam inferri poterat: Quia autem vos Niniuitarum dissimiles poenitentiam minime agetis, sed potius noua rabie accensi contra discipulos meos tumultuabimini, signum hoc resurrectionis meae vobis non ad salutem, sed ad exitium cedet. Ut enim Ionas Niniuen intra quadraginta dies periturum esse minatus est: ita ego à resurrectione mea vobis per annos quadraginta Euangelium praedicari curabo, ut poenitentiam agendi tempus habeatis: quam quia minimè aduri estis, miserè peribitis. Quod illis accidisse, ex historijs certò constat. Cum enim aduersus Christi discipulos, qui huius resurrectionem in suis concionibus potissimum vrgebant, immani odio & crudelitate grassarentur, & non contenti in Iudaea id fecisse, insuper vbique gentium seditiones excitarent, quibus Euangelij doctrina opprimeretur, Deus tandem iusto iudicio Romanorum arma euocauit, qui vrbe cum templo euersa, infelicem gentem in totum orbem disperserunt, ut passim vindictae diuinae exemplum fierent. Quod tamen leuiculum videri poterat prae eo, quod eos omnino repudiatos Deum in reprobum sensum tradidit, & in eorum locum gentes adoptauit, quae prius à repub. Israelis, à foedere Dei & salutis promissionibus exclusae erant. Vt autem in Iudaeos optimè quadrat Ionae & Niniuitarum exemplum: ita Christo etiam probè conuenit, eo quod Crucis siue mortis eius mysterium, atque fructum adumbrat. Cum enim nautae Ionam in mare proijcerent, nihil minus cogitabant, quam quod hoc vllis hominibus salutiferum foret: Ita cum Christum in crucem suffigerent milites, nunquam eis in mentem venit, quod ipse salutem cuiquam mortalium esset daturus. Veruntamen ut Ionas ex maris abysso reuersus Niniuitis poenitentia & salutis author fuit: ita Christus ex mortuis resuscitatus per Apostolos suos gentes omnes à superstitionibus & infelici Satanae seruitio in libertatem filiorum Dei transtulit, & ab imminenti aeternae damnationis supplicio ereptos regni sui heredes fecit.
units.tr: Nor should these men be spared on account of the splendid titles and privileges in which they mostly take pride. Christ shows by his own example how ministers of the Word ought to deal with such people. Their authority was indeed great, and they were called God's special people, a holy nation and a kingdom of priests. Since their conduct did not match those titles, however, Christ does not look at them as they claimed to be but as they really were, and he addresses them with the names that their deeds deserved. For this reason, before Christ's coming in the flesh, the prophets also spoke as they did. They called this people now the offspring of the Canaanites, now the Amorites, at other times the people of Gomorrah, and said they were like harlots, who with brazen brows and every shame cast aside offer themselves to anyone who comes along. What John the Baptist did, we have said a little earlier. Nor does Stephen treat them more gently, although he saw that they were already destined to perish. And it must be so. For unless such men are stripped of the masks under which they peddle themselves before the common people, your efforts with them will be wasted, since they will never think they need repentance as long as they see themselves held in esteem by some. There are indeed those who say that we must pursue moderation, lest those who are still curable be provoked and become enemies. We do not deny this for those people, but we teach what stubborn enemies of the truth, hopeless as they are, deserve, such as most of them are today, those who attack the teaching of the Gospel, as we have already shown. But let us go on with Christ's words, who promises a sign, not indeed of the kind they were asking for, but of the kind that their wickedness and obstinacy deserved. "No sign," he says, "will be given to this generation except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of man will be to this nation." These words should not be taken as though, after this encounter with his adversaries, Christ performed no further signs or miracles. For he freed very many from most grievous diseases, and, what surpasses all the rest, he raised Lazarus from the dead to life. But since he knew that all these things were despised by them, he says that one sign still remains, which would by no means satisfy their desires, but would answer their character perfectly, so that from it they would have, not an indication or foretaste of salvation, but of their own ruin, which they had long deserved. He illustrates the matter by the example of Jonah and the Ninevites, so that they may understand that something similar has happened before, and so that he may at the same time give them a new material for rebuke. The story is well enough known, so let us rather consider the meaning and mind of Christ. "Just as," he says, "Jonah, brought back to land from the belly of the whale or sea monster, was a sign to the Ninevites, by which they ought to have been roused to hear him and to zeal for repentance; so I too, rising from the dead on the third day, will be a sign to this nation, by the consideration of which all ought to have been stirred and warned to hear me speaking through the Apostles and to repent." To them this could also be said: "But because you, unlike the Ninevites, will by no means repent, but rather, kindled with a new rage, will riot against my disciples, this sign of my resurrection will turn out for you not for salvation but for destruction. For just as Jonah threatened that Nineveh would perish within forty days, so I will see to it that from my resurrection the Gospel is preached to you for forty years, so that you may have time to repent. Since you will not be moved by it, you will perish wretchedly." That this happened to them is certainly established from the histories. For when they raged against Christ's disciples, who above all pressed his resurrection in their sermons, with monstrous hatred and cruelty, and not content to have done this in Judaea alone, they stirred up seditions everywhere in the world of the Gentiles, by which the teaching of the Gospel might be crushed, God at last, by his just judgment, summoned the arms of the Romans, who, with the city and temple overthrown, scattered that unhappy nation over the whole world, so that they became everywhere an example of divine vengeance. Yet this might seem a small thing compared with the fact that God, having utterly rejected them, gave them over to a reprobate mind, and in their place adopted the Gentiles, who had previously been excluded from the commonwealth of Israel, from the covenant of God and the promises of salvation. As the example of Jonah and the Ninevites fits the Jews very well, so it also suits Christ admirably, in that it foreshadows the mystery and fruit of his cross or death. For when the sailors threw Jonah into the sea, they had no thought less likely than that this would bring salvation to anyone; so when the soldiers fastened Christ to the cross, it never came into their minds that he would give salvation to any mortal. Yet just as Jonah, returning from the abyss of the sea, became the author of repentance and salvation for the Ninevites, so Christ, raised from the dead, through his Apostles has transferred all the nations from superstitions and the wretched slavery of Satan into the liberty of the sons of God, and, snatching them from the impending punishment of eternal damnation, has made them heirs of his kingdom.

units.la: Habetur autem in his Christi verbis doctrina memorabilis, aduersa nimirum & afflictiones, quae piis Dei cultoribus immittuntur, signorum atq; portentorum instar esse, quibus Deus multum admonet, quid cum impijs & sceleratis actum sit, nisi resipiscant. Et huc referri debet dictum illud Christi, qui de sua morte aiebat: Si hoc fit in viridi ligno, quid fiet in arido? Etenim ut Petrus scribit, solet Deus iudiciorum suorum initium facere à domo sua, partim quidem ne in suis probare videatur ea, quae in alijs punit: partim verò ut suos ad poenitentiam excitet, ne cum mundo incurabili & poenitere nescio aeternum pereant. Inde verò colligere docet Apostolus, quam periculosa impiorum sors sit, cum iusto sua salus tot calamitatibus atq; laboribus constet. Et sanè quod de Iona Propheta & semetipso Christus in praesenti dicit, multorum seculorum exemplis probatum est. Affliguntur in Aegypto grauissimè filij Israelis, qui etsi id suis peccatis meruissent, Dei tamen populus et peculiū erant: At nonne mox grauiora passi sunt Aegyptij, qui post horribiles plagas et primogenitorum caede cum suo rege maris rubri vorticibus absorpti sunt? Ergo quod Israelitis accidit, signum fuit iudicij diuini, quod ipsorum oppressoribus imminebat. Pertinet huc etiam Iosiae Regis sanctissimi miserabilis interitus, qui cum sancto zelo & populi sui amore motus bello non necessario sese implicuisset, in prælio occubuit, & ita signi instar fuit, quo docebatur, quid posteris suis euentu- rum esset, si temerarijs consilijs & exterorum fœderibus iniquis suam impietatem & idololatriam quam Deus punire statuerat, defendere conarentur. Ad eundem modum Babylonica captiuitas, in quam Deus populum suum propter scelera & contumaciam adduci passus est, signum fuit, quo portendebatur, quid de crudeli & sanguinario Babyloniorum imperio futurum esset. Poterant huius generis exempla infinita adduci, sed ijs non multum opus est, cum nostro sæculo non semel videri- mus piorum persecutiones præludia fuisse ingentium calamitatum, quibus regna potentissima op- pressa sunt. Quoties ergo pios Christi cultores exulare, egere, esurire, sedibus insertis vagari & du- rissima quaeque pati videmus, semper in mentem veniat, Deum procul dubio grauius quid de mun- do impio statuisse, quid item nobis sperandum sit, qui in pietatis studio nondum eo usque profecimus, ut quicquam aduersum velimus sustinere. Hæc consideratio & commiseratio nem Christianam pa- riet, & magnum nobis erit ad vitam pie transfigendam incitamentum.
units.tr: Moreover, in these words of Christ there is a memorable teaching: namely, that the adversities and afflictions that are laid upon the godly worshippers of God are like signs and portents, by which God warns us much about what has befallen the wicked and the criminal, unless they repent. To this should also be referred that saying of Christ, who, speaking of his own death, said: "If this is done to the green wood, what will be done to the dry?" For as Peter writes, God is accustomed to begin his judgments at his own house, partly indeed lest he seem to approve in his own people the things he punishes in others, and partly to rouse his own to repentance, lest they perish eternally along with an incurable world that does not know how to repent. The Apostle teaches us to draw from this how perilous the lot of the ungodly is, when the salvation of the righteous costs so many calamities and labours. And indeed what Christ now says about Jonah the prophet and about himself has been proved by examples from many ages. The children of Israel were grievously afflicted in Egypt, and although they had deserved this by their sins, they were nonetheless God's people and his special possession. But did not the Egyptians soon suffer heavier things, who, after the dreadful plagues and the slaughter of the firstborn, were swallowed up with their king in the whirlpools of the Red Sea? Therefore what happened to the Israelites was a sign of the divine judgment that hung over their oppressors. To this also belongs the miserable death of the most holy King Josiah, who, moved by holy zeal and love for his people, entangled himself in a war that was not necessary, fell in battle, and so was like a sign by which it was taught what would befall his posterity if, by rash counsels and unjust alliances with foreigners, they tried to defend their impiety and idolatry, which God had decided to punish. In the same way the Babylonian captivity, into which God allowed his people to be led on account of their crimes and obstinacy, was a sign by which it was foreshadowed what would become of the cruel and bloody empire of the Babylonians. Infinite examples of this kind could be adduced, but there is little need of them, since in our own age we have more than once seen the persecutions of the godly to have been the prelude to great calamities by which most powerful kingdoms have been overthrown. Therefore, as often as we see the pious worshippers of Christ go into exile, lack, hunger, wander with their homes taken away, and suffer the hardest things of all, let there always come to mind that God doubtless has decided something more grievous concerning the impious world, and also what we ourselves may hope for, who in the pursuit of godliness have not yet advanced so far as to be willing to endure anything adverse. This consideration will beget Christian pity and compassion, and it will be a great incentive for us to pass our lives in godliness.

units.la: Cæterum ex Ionæ & Niniuitarum exemplo occasione sumpta, docet non in hoc solum sæculo, verumetiam in futuro puniendos esse: idque probat argumento ex communi sensu desumpto. Vt enim morbis grauioribus remedia quoque vehementiora adhiberi, & membra incurabilia omnino resecari oportet: ita æquum est, vt grauius puniantur, quos ea non mouent, quibus multi alij permo- ti sunt, vt pœnitentiam agerent, & de sua salute diligentius cogitarent. Quanto autem atrociori- bus supplicijs digni sunt, qui cum plures resipiscendi occasiones illis Deus adhibeat, corrigi tamen nolunt, sed prophano contemptu omnes admonitiones & correptiones reijciunt? Atqui tales esse Iudæos duobus exemplis probat. Primum est Regina Austri vel Æthiopiæ, quæ aliàs Regina Sabæ dicitur à Saba regni sede, quæ Meroës insulæ Nili est ciuitas. De illa sic ait: Regina Au- stri surget in iudicio cum viris nationis huius, & condemnabit eos: quod venerit à terminis terræ, vt audiret sapientiam Salomonis: & ecce plus quàm Salomon est hoc in loco. Extat historia in li- bro primo Regum Capite decimo. Habet autem exemplum hoc multiplicem comparationem, qua Iudaicæ gentis contumacia amplificatur, propter quam olim in vniuersali illo iudicio damnandi sunt. Reginam autem Austri furreturam aduersus illos ait, vt eos damnet, non quod illa iudi- candi potestatem habitura sit (hæc enim ad solum Christum pertinet; secundum illud: Pater o- mne iudicium dedit Filio) sed quod illius exemplo tunc conuincendi sint, adeò, vt nullus excusatio- nis prætextus ipsis reliquus maneat. Quod clarius patebit, si comparationis membra inspiciamus. Nam perinde est, ac si dixisset: Illa cum mulier esset, & ad longinquas profectiones minus idonea, tamen hoc fecit: Vos autem qui viri estis tam segnes & vaecordes vos præbetis. Illa gentilitijs su- perstitionibus imbuta tanti fecit sapientiam: vos qui Dei populus & per Circumcisionem in fœde- ris eius societatem assumpti estis, illam tam improbè contemnitis. Illam fama sola excitare potuit: vos autem videtis & auditis, quæ multi iusti & Prophetæ videre & audire cupiuerunt, nec tamen illis mouemini. Illa aduenit longo & periculosio itinere: vos me ad vos venientem reijcitis. Illa sum ptus magnos fecit, & insuper ingentia & pretiosissima dona ad Solomonem attulit: vos me non au- ditis, qui dona maxima ad vos affero, & gratis benefacio omnibus. Quis verò non videat nunc æ- ternam damnationem illos meruisse?
units.tr: Taking occasion from the example of Jonah and the Ninevites, he teaches that men are to be punished not only in this age but also in the age to come, and he proves this from an argument drawn from common sense. For just as more severe diseases need stronger remedies, and limbs past cure must be cut off altogether, so it is only fair that those are punished more severely whom things that moved many others to repent and to think more carefully about their salvation do not move. And how much more terrible are the punishments due to those who, though God offers them many occasions to repent, will not be corrected but reject every admonition and rebuke with profane contempt? That the Jews are such people he proves by two examples. The first is the Queen of the South, or of Ethiopia, who is also called the Queen of Sheba, from the seat of her kingdom Saba, which is the city of Meroë on an island of the Nile. Of her he says: "The Queen of the South shall rise up in judgement with the men of this nation and shall condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, a greater than Solomon is here" (Matt. 12). The story is in the first book of Kings, chapter 10. This example carries a manifold comparison, by which the obstinacy of the Jewish nation is magnified, on account of which they are to be condemned in that general judgement. Now he says that the Queen of the South will rise against them to condemn them, not because she will have the power of judging (for this belongs to Christ alone, according to the words: "The Father has given all judgement to the Son"), but because by her example they will then be convicted, so that no pretext of excuse will remain for them. This will be clearer if we look at the parts of the comparison. For it is just as if he had said: "She, though a woman and less fit for long journeys, nevertheless did this; but you, who are men, show yourselves so sluggish and senseless. She, steeped in pagan superstitions, valued the wisdom so highly; you, who are God's people and have been received into fellowship with his covenant through circumcision, despise it so shamefully. Report alone could move her; you see and hear what many righteous men and prophets desired to see and hear, and yet you are not moved by them. She came by a long and dangerous journey; you reject me as I come to you. She spent great sums and brought great and most precious gifts to Solomon; you do not listen to me, who bring the greatest gifts to you and do good to all freely." Who, indeed, does not see that they now deserve eternal damnation?

units.la: Alterum exemplum Niniuitarum est, quod hus verbis proponit: Viri Niniuitæ resurgent in iudicio cum hac natione, & condemnabunt eam: quod ad prædicationem Ionæ respuerint; & ecce plus quam Ionas est in hoc loco. Subest hus quoque comparatio multiplex, cuius idem, qui prio- ris vsus & finis est. Niniuitæ alieni à populo Dei, & gentilismo immersi sese corrigi passi sunt: Vos qui Legem & veri cultus rationem à Deo accepistis, consumaciter in vestra impieta- te pergitis. Illi vnum Ionam audiuerunt: vos Prophetas innumeros habuistis, quibus Ioannes Ba- ptista & ego succesissimus, qui omnes eandem doctrinam inculcauimus. Illi vno die audierunt im- minentis supplicij comminationem: vobis iam per aliquot sæcula Verbum Dei prædicatum est. Illi cum prædicatione Ionæ nullo inter ipsos signo édito confirmaretur, tamen respuerunt: vos cum signa quotidie noua videatis, tamen & hæc & doctrinam contemnitis. Illos monit hominis peregrini & ex gente inuisa oriundi prædicatio, vos me ex vobis natum fastiditis. Illi dirum & horrendum excidium minantem tulerunt: vos me gratiæ diuinæ & salutis æternæ thesauros osse- rentem
units.tr: The second example is that of the Ninevites, which he sets forth in these words: "The men of Nineveh shall rise up in judgement with this nation and shall condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, a greater than Jonah is here." Here too there is a manifold comparison, with the same purpose and use as the first. The Ninevites, strangers to God's people and immersed in paganism, allowed themselves to be corrected; you, who have received the Law and the right manner of true worship from God, persist obstinately in your impiety. They heard one Jonah; you have had countless prophets, to whom John the Baptist and I have succeeded, and we all have inculcated the same doctrine. They heard the threat of impending punishment on a single day; the Word of God has been preached to you for many centuries now. They rejected the preaching of Jonah, though it was confirmed by no sign performed among them; you see new signs every day, and yet you despise both these and the doctrine. The preaching of a foreign man, born of a hated nation, moved them; you scorn me, who was born among you. They bore with a prophet threatening a dire and dreadful destruction; you judge me, who offer you the treasures of divine grace and eternal salvation, worthy of hatred and death. Finally, they believed a mortal man and a sinner; you do not believe me, who daily show you something greater than man, and whom you cannot convict of any sin. You will therefore have the Ninevites as your judges, who in that great day will convict you by their example and prove that you deserve eternal punishments.

units.la: Iudei in futuro quoque sæculo punientur.
units.tr: The Jews will be punished in the age to come also.

units.la: Regina Sabæ.
units.tr: The Queen of Sheba.

units.la: Niniuitæ. rentem odio & morte dignum iudicatis. Illi deniq; homini mortali & peccatori crediderunt: vos mihi non creditis, qui me homine quid maius habere indies demonstro, & quem nullius peccati potestis arguere. Iudices ergo habebitis Niniuitas, qui in magno illo die suo exemplo vos convincent, & aeternis supplicijs dignos esse probabunt.
units.tr: ...you judge him worthy of hatred and death. Those men, after all, believed a mortal and sinful man, but you do not believe me, who daily show you something greater than man, and whom you cannot convict of any sin. So the Ninevites will be your judges. On that great day they will convict you by their example and prove that you deserve eternal punishments.

units.la: Sunt haec dura admodum, sunt vera tamen, & communi sensu (vt diximus) confirmantur. Debet autem ex illis doctrina seu admonitio generalis peti, quid verbi Dei contemptores maneat, eos (inquam) in primis, qui cum Dei populus & Ecclesiae Christi membra haberi velint, vitam tamen viuunt improbam atque prophanam, neque vllis verbi admonitionibus monentur. Promittunt tales fere sibi ipsis impunitatem & externis titulis atque Sacramentorum vsu sese abunde defendi putant. Sed vana haec spes est, & magno cum ludibrio & aeternae damnationis ignominia olim abijs damnabuntur, qui a veri Dei cognitione alieni honestius vixerunt, & quae ipsi impunita dimittunt scelera, publica authoritate coercuerunt. Potest ergo doctrina haec latissime extendi. Damnabunt Graeci multos Christianorum in nouissimo die: eo quod illi philosophos incertis opinionibus tumultuantes in pretio habuerunt, & de virtute differentes attente audiere: ipsi vero diuini verbi doctrinam certam & sibi ipsi constantem contemnant. Damnabunt quoque multos ex nostris Romani, qui libris Sibyllinis eum honorem detulerunt, vt in rebus dubijs consulendos putarent, etiamsi pleraque in illis obscura & incerta essent: illi vero Scripturas negligant, quae Dei voluntatem continent, & certa atque salutaria consilia suggerunt, quae in secundis & aduersis rebus tuto sequi possumus. Damnabunt gentes suo exemplo Christianos homines, qui virginum stupra, adulteria, vsuras & alia huius generis flagitia nullis poenis coercent, aduersus quae gentium legislatores grauissimas leges tulerunt. Damnabunt nos & Iudaei, qui in tristi & multorum seculorum exilio atque hinc inde dispersi suos pauperes alunt & sustentant: cum nos in pace & otio agentes, fidei domesticos mendicare, & publica inopiae exempla fieri patiamur. Damnabunt ignauos fidei abnegatores Ethnici, qui pro focis & aris mori honestum & gloriosum esse putauerunt. Damnabunt nos maiores nostri, qui in ignorantiae tenebris viuentes sua liberalitate Ecclesias & Collegia ditarunt, quae hodie a plerisque Euangelij luce gloriantibus sacrilega rapacitate spoliantur. Poterant huius generis multa alia addi, sed haec modo sufficiant, quibus insuper admonemur, quis verus historiarum exterarum vsus sit: vt nimirum ex illis quoque virtutis exempla petamus, ne illis inferiores simus, & eorum exemplo condemnemur, qui nullam habuerant verae religionis cognitionem. Quod si nos hactenus peccauisse & illis deteriores fuisse sentimus, nostrum est, vitia emendare, & caelitus iam nobis loquentem Filium Dei Iesum Christum, audire, vt in magno illo die laeta & tranquilla conscientia ad eius tribunal comparere possimus, & cum electus omnibus ad illum in Regni caelestis societatem colligi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: These things are very harsh, yet they are true, and they are confirmed by common sense, as we have said. From them we should draw a general teaching or warning about what awaits the despisers of God's Word, especially those who wish to be counted as God's people and members of Christ's Church, yet live a wicked and profane life and are moved by no admonition of the Word. Such people commonly promise themselves impunity, and think they are amply protected by outward titles and by the use of the sacraments. But this hope is vain. They will be condemned with great mockery and the shame of eternal damnation, those who, though strangers to the knowledge of the true God, lived more honourably and punished by public authority the crimes that these people let go unpunished. So this teaching can be extended very widely. The Greeks will condemn many Christians on the last day, because the Greeks held in high esteem philosophers who tumbled about in uncertain opinions and listened eagerly to those who discussed virtue, while Christians despise the teaching of the divine Word, which is certain and consistent with itself. Many of our own people, the Romans, will also condemn them, who paid such honour to the Sibylline books that they thought them to be consulted in doubtful matters, even though most of those books are obscure and uncertain, while these Christians neglect the Scriptures, which contain God's will and offer certain and saving counsel, which we can safely follow both in prosperity and in adversity. The Gentiles will condemn Christian men by their example, since Christians punish with no penalties the rapes of virgins, adulteries, usury and other crimes of this kind, against which the lawgivers of the nations enacted the most severe laws. The Jews too will condemn us, who, living in a sad exile of many centuries and dispersed here and there, feed and support their own poor, whereas we, living in peace and leisure, allow the members of our faith to beg and become public examples of want. The pagans who thought it honourable and glorious to die for their hearths and altars will condemn the cowardly deniers of the faith. Our forefathers will condemn us, who, living in the darkness of ignorance, enriched the churches and colleges by their generosity, which today are stripped with sacrilegious greed by many who boast of the light of the Gospel. Many other examples of this kind could be added, but these are enough for now. They also remind us what the true use of foreign histories is: namely, that we should draw examples of virtue even from them, so that we are not inferior to them and are not condemned by the example of those who had no knowledge of true religion. But if we feel that we have sinned until now and have been worse than they, it is our task to amend our faults and to hear the Son of God, Jesus Christ, now speaking to us from heaven, so that on that great day we may come before his judgment seat with a joyful and tranquil conscience, and be gathered with all the elect into the fellowship of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXIX.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXIX.

units.la: Nullus vero cum lucernam accenderit, eam in occulto ponit, neque subter modium: sed super candelabrum, vt qui ingrediuntur, splendorem videant. Lucerna corporis est oculus. Cum igitur oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum quoque corpus tuum lucidum erit: sin vero malus fuerit, etiam corpus tuum tenebrosum erit. Consldera ergo num lumen quod in te est, tenebrae sint. Itaque si corpus tuum totum lucidum fuerit, non habens aliquam partem tenebrosam, sic erit lucidum totum, vt cum lucerna, fulgore te illustrat.
units.tr: No one, when he has lit a lamp, puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. The lamp of the body is the eye. So when your eye is sound, your whole body will be bright; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark. Consider therefore whether the light that is in you is darkness. If your whole body is bright, with no dark part in it, then it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp lights you with its radiance.

units.la: In iis, quae proxime praecesserunt, Dominus noster Iesus Christus cum incredulis & contumacibus Verbi sui & miraculorum suorum contemptoribus egit: neque verbis modo nudis incurabilem eorum malitiam corripuit, verumetiam poenas grauissimas comminatus est: Fore nimirum, vt quoniam diuinitus sibi factam gratiam aspernentur, in peius mox proficiant, diabolo suum in ipsis regnum recuperante, vt item horribili excidio pereant, & praeterea in nouissimo die gentium idolo latrarum exemplo ad aeternas inferorum cruciatus damnentur. His commodissimo & quasi naturali ordine locum hunc, quem modo recitauimus subijcit, quo plene & perspicue omnia ea comprehendit, quae ad Dei verbum pertinent. Docet enim quid illud sit, quomodo in Ecclesia tractari, & quus no-bis illius in tota vita nostra vsus esse debeat. Ita vero ista proponit, vt simul nos ad officium faciendum serio exhortetur.
units.tr: In the passage just before this, our Lord Jesus Christ dealt with unbelievers and with those who were obstinate and who despised his Word and his miracles. He rebuked their incurable wickedness not only with plain words but also threatened them with very grievous punishments. Because they scorned the grace granted them from heaven, they would certainly grow worse and soon, with the devil recovering his kingdom in them, would perish in a dreadful destruction; and moreover, on the last day, they would be condemned to eternal torments in hell, as an example to the nations of idolatrous worshippers. Following on from this, and in the most fitting and almost natural order, he adds the passage we have just recited, in which he comprehends fully and clearly all that pertains to the Word of God. For it teaches what that Word is, how it ought to be handled in the Church, and what use of it we ought to make throughout our whole life. He sets these things out in such a way that he at the same time earnestly urges us to carry out our duty.

units.la: Quoad primum similitudine aut Metaphora vtitur, dum Lucernae meminit, per quam non aliud quam Dei verbum debet intelligi. Ita enim olim Dauid Rex & Propheta appellauit, dicens: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Ita vero dicitur partim propter authorem Deum, qui illud nobis per Filium suum iam inde ab origine rerum reuelauit, qui proprie vera illa lux mundi est, quae tenebras in se habet nullas: partim vero propter ipsius verbi naturam atq; effectus. Vt enim in tota rerum natura nihil purius est luce: ita Dei verbum in se purum & ab omni errorum tenebris alienum est: cum e contra omnes aliae doctrinae, quantumuis in speciem splendidae, multa falsa & erronea admixta habeant. Ideo Dauid illud argento septies purgato confert. Deinde vt lux discussis tenebris ea reuelat, quae prius latebant: ita Dei verbum multa manifestat, quae nobis alioqui ignota sunt. Nam & latentem in nobis naturae corruptionem arguit, quam nemo sapientum huius seculi vnquam agnouit, & salutis atque Regni caelorum arcana patefacit, vt ea intelligamus & fide apprehendamus, quae naturalem humani ingenij captum superant. Adhaec vt lucerna greßus atque aliae hominis actiones reguntur: ita Dei verbum rationem simul atque studia consiliaque & facta nostra omnia dirigit, vt ad verum finem pertingant. Denique vt lux cum tenebris animi quoque tristitiam, quae ex illis concipitur, discutere & hominem exhilarare solet: ita Dei verbo hominum conscientiae illuminatae terroribus peccati & aeternae mortis metu liberantur, vt in Christo verè & solidè gaudere possint. Et haec causa est, quod Ioannes Baptista lucerna ardens dicitur, & Apostoli lux mundi appellantur: non quod ipsi hominum mentes illuminare potuerint, sed quod lucis illius verae administri fuerunt, qua nos illustrari oportet. Ista vero nos de mundi conditione admonent. Quia enim Verbum Dei lucerna est, quae suo fulgore nos illuminat & regit, illum in tenebris esse sequitur. Et quemadmodum in exordio rerum tenebrae fuisse scribuntur super faciem abyssi, donec lux a Deo producta est: ita totum mundum tenebrae occupant, & vbi lux illa Verbi deest, ibi ignorantia & errores regnum obtinent. Quarto Paulus gentes, quae verbo Dei ante Christi aduentum caruerunt, sub tenebrarum potestate, imo ipsas tenebras fuisse ait. Facit hoc ad commendationem bonitatis & gratiae Dei, qui infelici & degeneri huic mundo verbi sui lucem accendere, & huius administrum Filium suum constituere dignatus est, ne totus in tenebris periret. Est hoc inter eius beneficia longe praestantissimum: quod facile fatebuntur, quicunque infelicitatem suam & miseriam verè senserunt, qua illis in tenebris & ignorantiae caligine adhuc versantibus conscientias eorum afflixit. Debet ergo huius consideratio nos excitare, vt (quod alibi Christus admonet) in luce illa ambulemus, dum ea suo splendore viam salutis nobis commonstrat.
units.tr: As to the first point, he uses a likeness or metaphor when he mentions the lamp, by which nothing other than the Word of God is to be understood. For in this way King and Prophet David once called it, saying: "Your word is a lamp to my feet." It is so called partly on account of God its author, who from the beginning of things has revealed it to us through his Son, and who is properly that true light of the world which has no darkness in it; and partly on account of the nature and effects of the Word itself. For as nothing in the whole of nature is purer than light, so the Word of God is pure in itself and free from every darkness of error; whereas, on the contrary, all other teachings, however splendid they may look, have many false and erroneous things mixed into them. Therefore David compares it to silver purified seven times. Again, as light, when the shadows are dispelled, reveals what was hidden before, so the Word of God makes manifest many things which would otherwise be unknown to us. For it both exposes the corruption of nature lying hidden within us, which none of the wise men of this age has ever recognised, and opens up the secrets of salvation and of the kingdom of heaven, so that we may understand and grasp by faith those things which exceed the natural capacity of the human mind. Moreover, just as a lamp guides a traveller and the other actions of a man, so the Word of God directs at once his reason, his zeal, his counsels and all his deeds, so that they may attain their true end. Finally, just as light usually dispels with the darkness of the mind also the sadness that arises from it and makes a man cheerful, so by the Word of God the consciences of men, once enlightened, are freed from the terrors of sin and the fear of eternal death, so that they can rejoice truly and firmly in Christ. And this is why John the Baptist is called a burning lamp, and the Apostles are called the light of the world; not because they were able to illuminate men's minds themselves, but because they were ministers of that true light by which we ought to be enlightened. These things, moreover, remind us of the condition of the world. For since the Word of God is a lamp which by its brightness illumines and guides us, it follows that the world is in darkness without it. And just as at the beginning of things darkness is written of as lying over the face of the deep until light was produced by God, so darkness occupies the whole world, and where that light of the Word is lacking, there ignorance and errors hold sway. Fourthly, Paul says that the nations, which lacked the Word of God before the coming of Christ, were under the power of darkness, indeed were themselves darkness. This serves to commend the goodness and grace of God, who has deigned to kindle the light of his Word in this unhappy and degenerate world, and to appoint his Son as its minister, lest the whole world should perish in darkness. This is by far the most outstanding of his benefits among all his gifts, as all those will readily confess who have truly felt their own unhappiness and misery, with which the darkness and the mist of ignorance, in which they still lived, afflicted their consciences. Therefore the consideration of this should stir us up, so that (as Christ elsewhere warns) we may walk in that light, while it shows us by its splendour the way of salvation.

units.la: Et huc in primis pertinet prima huius loci pars, qua Christus docet, vt Dei Verbum in Ecclesijs tractari debeat. Nullus (inquit) cum lucernam accenderit, eam in occulto ponit, neque subter modium: sed super candelabrum, vt qui ingrediuntur, splendorem videant. Apud Marcum, prior huius sententiae pars per interrogationem enuntiatur: Numquid lucerna accenditur, vt subter modium ponatur, aut subter lectum? Qua parte quid in Verbi Dei tractatione caueri debeat, docet: & quia in hoc plurimum momenti situm est, interrogatione vtitur, vt rei absurditatem clarius exprimat, quae accidit, si secus quam fieri oportet tractetur. Absurde & stulte faciunt, qui lucernam accensam vel subter modium vel subter lectum occultant. Quis enim eius sub modio vsus est? Sub lectum vero posita periculum incendij parit, quod vix vlla ratione potest caueri. Ita absurde nimis & periculose eos facere docet, qui Dei Verbum subter modiū aut lectum occultant. At qui nam (inquis) hoc faciunt? Id facile intelligemus, si quid modius & lectus hoc loco & alibi significent, videmus. Modius certa mensura est, qua in aridis distribuendis vulgò vtuntur. Verbum Dei ergo subter modium ponunt, qui illi certos fines & limites praescribunt, dum illud suae rationis modulo metiuntur, quam potius cum suis desideriis & omni intellectu per fidei obedientiam illi subijcere debebant. Peccant in hoc vt plurimum eruditi, quos doctrinae variae cognitio celebres facit. Hi enim dum philosophorum veterum scriptis nimium addicti sunt, ita illorum placita imbibere solent, vt Dei verbum ipsis sapere aut placere non possit, nisi falsis interpretationibus detortum atq; circumscriptum philosophiae prophanae saliuam redoleat. Regnauit hoc hominum genus seculis aliquot in scholis, non sine publico Ecclesiae & religionis Christianae incommodo. Huic enim debemus doctrinam de libero hominis arbitrio & naturalium facultatum effectus, de operum & humanae iustitiae meritis, de igne lustrali seu purgatorio, de exequijs & scriptis pro defunctis, & sexcenta alia, quae partim ex Aristotele & Platone atq; aliorum philosophorum scriptis, partim ex poetarum vanissimorum fabulis desumpta esse, nemo ignorare potest, qui haec vel a primo limine salutauit. His autem finibus sine modio isto Verbum Dei ita incluserunt audacissimi homines, vt neminem ad sacrarum literarum fluidum admiserint, nisi humanae philosophiae placitis probè imbutum. Hinc ergo tenebrae illae secutae sunt, quae Verbi diuini lucem impedierunt, ne suum splendorem diffunderet. Nam etsi ex Postillis suis (vt vocant) alicuius Euangelij aut epistolae locum populo recitarent, eundem tamen aut omnino nulla interpretatione illustrarunt, aut suis figmentis improbè corruperunt, in primis autem cauerunt, ne quis scripturae locos diligentius excutiedo & rebus praesentibus applicando errores detegeret. Et in eum quoq; finem omne fere tempus, quod sacris dabatur, theatrico Missae spectaculo, psalmodijs non intellectus, organorum late resonantiū tinnitibus atq; alijs eiusmodi ceremonijs distribuerunt, vt vix minima portiuncula superesset, qua Euangelij aliquis locus recitari posset. Quia ergo apud Iudaeos olim idè fiebat, & quid nouissimis temporibus futurum esset, Christus praeuidebat, ne quid huius fiat prohibet. At nō minus in hac re à viris politicis & huius seculi sapientibus peccatur. Hi enim quia huius mundi pacē atq; concordiam summum bonū esse existimant, de pace autem Dei & aeterna felicitate non multum soliciti sunt, nihil à Verbi praeconibus dici volunt, quo aliqui hominum offendi possunt. Itaq; dicendi & tacendi leges illis praescribunt, ne scelera arguant, ne poenarū comminationibus aliquem inquietent, ne superstitiones & illicitos cultus damnent, sed vnumquenq; pro sua arbitrio viuere & quam velit religionem sequi patiantur. Regnauit hoc etiam hominum genus Prophetarum tempore, quibus praecipiebant, vt blanda ipsis loquerentur. Et post Christi ascensionem Apostolis mandare audebant Sacerdotes & Seniores Iudaeorum, ne in Christi nomine praedicarent, in primis autè ne aliquam resurrectionis ipsius mentionem facerent. Hodie autem tales multi non inter aduersarios modo apertos, verumetiam inter Euangelicae fidei professores reperiuntur, quos huius temeritatu minimè pudet, imò ex eo sibi summam sapientiae laudem quaerunt, quòd eam docendi rationem se inuenisse arbitrantur, qua Euangelium absq; vllius hominis offensione praedicari possit. Sed ita se homines fluctuissimos esse produnt, qui nec mundi ingenium lucem Verbi odio habentis adhuc cognitum habeant, neq; de Ecclesiae ministerio iudicare possint. Quae causa est, quòd in Dei Verbum, adeoq; ipsum Spiritū sanctum sibi ius sumunt, & quid dici debeat docere instituunt eum, quem in scripturis & ministris suis loquentem audire debebant. Et hi quidem omnes lucernā subter modium ponunt, quod hic grauissimè prohibetur.
units.tr: To this point especially belongs the first part of this passage, in which Christ teaches how the Word of God ought to be handled in the churches. "No one," he says, "when he has lit a lamp, puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light." In Mark, the first part of this saying is put as a question: "Is a lamp lit so that it may be put under a bushel, or under a bed?" In this part he teaches what must be guarded against in the handling of the Word of God; and because much depends on this, he uses a question, so as to express more clearly the absurdity that would follow if it were handled otherwise than it should be. They act absurdly and foolishly who hide a lit lamp either under a bushel or under a bed. For what use is there in putting it under a bushel? And a lamp placed under a bed creates a danger of fire, which can scarcely be guarded against by any means. So he teaches that those act far too absurdly and dangerously who hide the Word of God under a bushel or a bed. "But who," you ask, "do this?" We shall easily understand this if we see what bushel and bed signify here and elsewhere. A bushel is a fixed measure, commonly used for dividing up dry goods. Those, then, put the Word of God under a bushel who prescribe for it definite bounds and limits, measuring it by the measure of their own reason, when they ought rather to subject it to themselves, with their desires and all their understanding, through obedience of faith. Learned men, whom the wide knowledge of various teachings makes famous, most often sin in this way. For while they are too devoted to the writings of the ancient philosophers, they are accustomed to imbibe their opinions so thoroughly that the Word of God cannot seem to them wise or pleasing unless it has been twisted and circumscribed by false interpretations and smells of the saliva of profane philosophy. This kind of men has reigned for some centuries in the schools, not without public harm to the Church and to the Christian religion. For to them we owe the doctrine of the free will of man and the effects of natural powers, of the merits of works and of human righteousness, of the lustral or purgatorial fire, of funeral rites and writings for the dead, and six hundred other things, which no one can be unaware of, who has greeted these matters even from the threshold, are drawn partly from the writings of Aristotle and Plato and other philosophers, and partly from the most empty fables of the poets. But bold men have enclosed the Word of God within these bounds, without that bushel, so that they have admitted no one to the fountain of the sacred letters unless he has been thoroughly steeped in the opinions of human philosophy. Hence came those shadows which hindered the light of the divine Word from spreading its splendour. For although from their so-called Postils they read out to the people some passage of a Gospel or Epistle, yet they either illuminated it by no interpretation at all or wickedly corrupted it with their own fictions; and above all they took care that no one should examine the passages of Scripture more diligently and detect their errors by applying them to present circumstances. And to the same end they distributed almost all the time that was given to sacred things among the theatrical spectacle of the Mass, psalm-singing without understanding, the jangling of loudly resounding organs and other such ceremonies, so that scarcely the smallest portion was left in which any passage of the Gospel could be read. Because this was once done among the Jews, and Christ foresaw what would happen in the latest times, he forbids that anything of this kind be done. Yet no less is sin committed in this matter by men of affairs and the wise men of this age. For since they think that the peace and concord of this world is the highest good, and are not much concerned about the peace of God and eternal happiness, they wish nothing to be said by the heralds of the Word which might offend any men. So they prescribe for them laws about what to speak and what to keep silent: not to denounce crimes, not to disturb anyone with threats of punishment, not to condemn superstitions and unlawful worship, but to allow each man to live as he pleases and to follow whatever religion he wishes. This kind of men also reigned in the time of the Prophets, to whom they gave orders to speak flattering things to them. And after Christ's ascension, the chief priests and elders of the Jews dared to command the Apostles not to preach in the name of Christ, and above all not to make any mention of his resurrection. Today, however, many such men are found not only among open adversaries but also among professors of the evangelical faith; they are not at all ashamed of this rashness, but rather seek for themselves the highest praise of wisdom from it, because they think they have discovered a method of teaching by which the Gospel can be preached without offence to any man. But in this way they show themselves to be most unstable men, who neither know the nature of the world, which still hates the light of the Word, nor are able to judge of the ministry of the Church. This is the reason why they claim for themselves the right over the Word of God, and even over the Holy Spirit himself, and set about teaching what ought to be said, when they ought to have listened to him speaking in the Scriptures and in his ministers. All of these men, then, put the lamp under a bushel, which is here most strictly forbidden.

units.la: Videamus autè eos quoq;, qui illam subter lectum abscondunt. Lectus quieti & somno destinatus est, at eodem multi ad libidinem & illicitas voluptates, aut saltem ad ignauam somnolentiam fouendam abuti solent. Ergo Verbi lucernā sub lectum abscondunt, qui vel ignavia, vel voluptatū studio eam restinguunt. Et hoc proprie ad illius administros pertinet. Ab his enim in hac parte peccatur, quādo vel labores fugiunt, vel odia declinare & suis rebus cōsulere volunt. Vident enim functionem hanc laboris & periculi plenam esse, eò quod mundus hic argui nolit. Vident quid olim Prophetis & Apostolis acciderit, & quid hodie multi patiantur, qui dum Deo fideles sunt, cum fortunis vitaquoq; perdunt. Audiunt praeterea graues impiorū comminationes, & insuper carceres, vincula & mille mortis crudelissimae species sibi iam paratas esse cōspicantur. Itaq; vt & pericula subterfugiant, & otio atq; quieti sua prospiciant, vel omnino tacent, vel sub modestiae & charitatis pretex-tu novum docendi genus comminiscuntur, vt omissa poenitentiae doctrina, solam Dei gratiam & in Christo nobis factam peccatorum remissionem ijs praedicent, qui se peccatores esse nunquam adhuc agnouerunt, & quos propter indomitam contumaciam publice arguere & iudiciorum Dei minus terrere oportebat, vt quamuis ipsi incurabiles maneant, alij tamen eorum exemplo perculsi emendarentur. Et hi canes muti sunt, de quibus Isaias queritur: hi impijs puluillos consuunt atq; substerunt, quibus inter scelera sua indormiant, vt Ezechiel ait: hi deniq; lucernam illam Verbi Dei sub lecto abscondunt, & plerunq; publicarum calamitatum sunt authores. Dum enim fausta & laeta impijs denuntiant, eosdem in sceleribus securos reddunt, quae causa est, vt ipsorum exemplum ad plures alios serpat, & tandem superante & regnante vbiq; malitia, Dei ira exardescat, quae cum populo incurabili ignauos quoq; illos doctores absumit. Exemplis multis hoc probari poterat, sed veteribus minime opus est, cum hodie experiamur, quantum mali dent Ecclesijs, qui vel ditescendi & voluptuandi studio, vel vt dogmata peruersa tueantur, principibus viris turpiter blandiri consueuerunt. Sed hos quoq; suo tempore Deus puniet.
units.tr: Let us now consider those also who hide it under the bed. A bed is intended for rest and sleep, yet many people are accustomed to abuse it for lust and unlawful pleasures, or at least to indulge sluggish drowsiness. So they hide the lamp of the Word under the bed, those who extinguish it either through laziness or through a desire for pleasure. This belongs especially to its ministers. They sin in this respect when they shun labours, or when they wish to avoid hatred and look after their own affairs. For they see that this office is full of toil and danger, because this world does not want to be rebuked. They see what happened long ago to the Prophets and Apostles, and what many suffer today, who, while faithful to God, lose their property and their lives as well. They also hear the grave threats of the wicked, and they see that prisons, chains and a thousand cruel forms of death are already prepared for them. So, in order both to escape dangers and to provide for their ease and quiet, they either keep silent altogether, or under the pretext of modesty and charity they devise a new way of teaching: they omit the doctrine of repentance and preach to those who have never yet recognised themselves as sinners only the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins made ours in Christ. Yet these are people whom, because of their stubborn obstinacy, they ought to rebuke publicly and to terrify with the judgments of God, so that, even if they themselves remain incurable, others may be struck by their example and amended. These are the dumb dogs of whom Isaiah complains. These are the ones who sew and place cushions under the wicked, on which they may sleep among their sins, as Ezekiel says. Finally, these are the ones who hide that lamp of the Word of God under the bed, and they are very often the authors of public calamities. For while they announce happy and joyful things to the wicked, they make them secure in their sins; hence it comes about that their example creeps on to many others, and at last, when wickedness prevails and reigns everywhere, the wrath of God blazes forth, which with the incurable people consumes those idle teachers too. This could be proved by many examples, but there is little need of old ones, since today we see how much harm they do to the Churches, those who, either from a desire to grow rich and live in luxury, or to defend perverse doctrines, are accustomed to flatter powerful men shamefully. But God will punish these too in his own time.

units.la: Quid ergo (inquis) fieri, & quomodo Verbum tractari debet? Christum audi, qui lucernam super candelabrum poni ait, vt omnes qui domum ingrediuntur & negotia illic agunt, splendorem eius videant. Candelabrum in veteris populi templo inter vasa sacra non postremo loco habebatur, & ministerij ecclesiastici typus erat, cum in eo ignis caelo primum demissus assidua Sacerdotum cura ex Dei mandato asseruaretur. Quod mysterium vt obscuraret Satan, inter gentes ignem Vestae Deae excogitauit, quem ad hoc munus delectae virgines nullo cum fructu vouebant, nisi quod superstitiosi homines in idololatria confirmabantur, cum Reipub. & Imperij incolumitatem in huius ignis conseruatione consistere putarent. In Apocalypsi autem Ecclesiae candelabra conferuntur, nimirum, quod lucem Verbi Dei sustineant, & hinc inde diffundant. Sensus ergo Verborum Christi est, Verbi Dei nullo modo occultari, sed ita proponi & annuntiari debere in Ecclesia, vt omnium institutioni & consolationi seruiat: vt deniq; omnis loci & ordinis homines secundum illud actiones, consilia & studia sua possint dirigere, neq; suorum affectuum & cupiditatum caligine decipiantur. Ita vero huius administros officij sui admonet, ne quid celent aut obscurius proponant in alicuius hominis gratiam. Quia enim lucernae instar praelucere debent, ita in suo ministerio versentur oportet, vt singuli suos errores & vitia agnoscere, & ex Verbo Dei horum emendandorum rationem discere possint. Et huc facit, quod Prophetae clamare & instar tubae vocem suam attollere iubentur: quod item Apostolus alibi mandatur, vt super tecta diuulgent & proclament, quae nunc ipsis in aurem dicantur.
units.tr: "What then," you ask, "must be done, and how ought the Word to be handled?" Listen to Christ, who says that the lamp is to be placed upon the candlestick, so that all who enter the house and do business there may see its brightness. In the temple of the old people the candlestick was not regarded as the least of the sacred vessels, and it was a type of the ecclesiastical ministry, since on it the fire first sent down from heaven was kept alive by the constant care of the priests according to God's command. Satan, in order to obscure this mystery, devised among the Gentiles the fire of the goddess Vesta, which chosen virgins vowed to tend to no profit, except that superstitious men were confirmed in idolatry, since they thought the safety of the commonwealth and of the empire consisted in the preservation of that fire. In the Apocalypse, however, the candlesticks are used as figures of the Churches, no doubt because they hold up the light of the Word of God and spread it abroad on every side. The sense, therefore, of Christ's words is that the Word of God must in no way be hidden, but must be set forth and proclaimed in the Church in such a way that it serves the instruction and comfort of all, and that men of every place and rank may then direct their actions, counsels and pursuits by it, and not be deceived by the darkness of their own feelings and desires. He also thus admonishes the ministers of this office not to conceal anything, nor to set it forth more obscurely for the sake of any man's favour. For since they ought to shine before others like a lamp, they must so conduct themselves in their ministry that each person may recognise his own errors and vices, and learn from the Word of God the way of amending them. To this purpose also it relates that the Prophets are commanded to cry aloud and to lift up their voice like a trumpet, and that the Apostle is likewise charged elsewhere to proclaim from the housetops what is now said to them in the ear.

units.la: Docemur praeterea, Dei Verbum ad omnes homines, cuiuscunq; conditionis sint, pertinere, & huic obedientiam debere omnes, qui ex familia Dei vel Ecclesiae eius membra censeri volunt. Vult enim Christus, vt lucernae huius splendorem videant omnes, qui domum ipsius ingrediuntur. Neq; personarum respectus est apud Deum, vt alios quidem legibus coercere velit, alios autem exleges facere, qui pro suo arbitrio vitam suam instituant. Obseruandum hoc erat superbis illis & insolentibus, qui cum Christiano nomine glorientur, tamen immunitate quandam sibi vendicant, & Verbo Dei vitia sua argui atq; se officij admoneri nolunt. Atqui Christus, qui alibi doctorem toti suae familiae praefectum esse docet, idem in praesenti lucerna hanc Verbi sui sic accendi & proponi vult, vt omnibus praeluceat, qui eius domum ingrediuntur. Et olim Ieremiae dicebatur: Ecce ego facio te hodie ciuitatem munitam, columnam ferream & murum aeneum contra omnem terram, contra Reges Iuda, contra principes eius, contra sacerdotes, & contra vniuersum populum terrae. Nihil ergo proficiunt insolentes illi, quam quod se non esse ex Dei familia testantur, quando patris & domus huius sanctae vocem audire nolunt. Non tamen ideo Dei iudicium subterfugient. Nam (vt Paulus ait) qui sine Lege peccauerunt, sine Lege damnabuntur. Deinde eos etiam hic locus confutat, qui laicos a diligentiori Verbi Dei cognitione arcent, & ne hanc aliquando consequantur, non modo ipsi docendi officium intermittunt, verumetiam libros sacros ex illorum manibus excutiunt, & nefas esse clamant, vt hi in linguas vulgaribus legantur. Sed longe aliter Deus in Lege sua instituit, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Et quomodo poterunt lucernam Verbi omnes sequi, si & nemo hoc praedicat, & vt priuatim id legant, prohibentur?
units.tr: We are taught further that the Word of God pertains to all men, whatever their condition, and that all who wish to be counted of the family of God or members of his Church owe obedience to it. For Christ wills that all who enter his house should see the brightness of this lamp. Nor is there respect of persons with God, so that he would wish to restrain some by laws, but to make others lawless, to order their lives as they please. This ought to have been observed by those proud and insolent men who, while they boast of the Christian name, nevertheless claim for themselves a certain immunity, and are unwilling that their vices be rebuked by the Word of God or that they be reminded of their duty. And yet Christ, who elsewhere teaches that a teacher is set over his whole household, in the present passage also wills that his Word be so kindled and set forth as to give light to all who enter his house. And long ago it was said to Jeremiah: "Behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar and a brazen wall against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against the priests and against all the people of the land." Those insolent men therefore achieve nothing except to bear witness that they are not of the family of God, since they refuse to hear the voice of the Father and of this holy house. Yet they will not thereby escape the judgment of God. For (as Paul says) those who have sinned without the Law will perish without the Law. Furthermore, this passage also refutes those who keep the laity away from a more diligent knowledge of the Word of God, and who, so that they may never attain it, not only give up the office of teaching themselves, but also snatch the sacred books from their hands, and cry out that it is wrong for these to be read in the vulgar tongues. But God has ordained far otherwise in his Law, as we have shown elsewhere. And how will all be able to follow the lamp of the Word, if no one preaches it, and they are forbidden to read it privately?

units.la: At quia non satis est Verbum prædicauisse & audiuisse, sed vt omnes vitæ huius actiones illi respondeant, necesse est, grauem admonitionem, quæ simul exhortationis loco est, Christus subiicit. Lucerna corporis (inquit) est oculus. Cùm igitur oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum quoq; corpus tuum lucidum erit: sin verò malus fuerit, etiam corpus tuum tenebrosum erit. Oculi nomine rationem & intelleƨum hominis denotat. Per corpus autem, vitam totam intelligit. Vt enim oculus instar lucernæ toti corpori prælucet, vt membra singula possint officium facere: ita ratio vitam & omnes actiones hominis sua luce dirigere debet, vt recte & legitime instituantur. Vocat autem oculum simplicem, intelleƨum siue rationem synceram & ab affectuum prauorum intemperie liberam: & huic corpus lucidum, id est, vitam sanctam, Christianam & bonis actionibus lucentem tribuit: malum verò oculum dicit rationem corruptam atq; vitiosam, quæ corpus quoq; totum, id est, vitæ totius conuersationem tenebrosam reddit, dum videlicet carnis cupiditatibus abrepti, nunc hìc nunc illic (vt qui in tenebris ambulant) offendimus, & loco operum lucus opera tenebrarũ facimus. Itaq; considera (inquit) num lumen, quod in te est, tenebræ sint. Sensus est: Etiam atq; etiam vide, vt rationem verè illuminatam habeas, ne quæ tibi lucernæ loco esse debebat, tenebras & caliginem tibi offundat. Si enim (vt apud Matthæum habetur) ipsum lumen tenebræ fuerint, ipsæ tenebræ quantæ erunt? Et ne quis seipsum inani professione Verbi Dei fallat, addit: Si corpus tuum totum lucidum fuerit, non habens aliquam partem tenebrosam, sic erit lucidum totum, vt cum lucerna fulgore te illustrat. Id est, si vitâ tuam ita instituerit, vt non nisi lucis opera in te conspician tur, tenebrarum autem operibus nullus apud te locus sit, tunc demum patebit, te cœlesti illa & salutifera Euangelij luce verè illustratum esse. Ex quo iam contrarium colligi potest, eos nondum recté degustaisse Euangelij doctrinam, qui tenebrarum principi seruiunt, & illarum operibus delectantur. Sunt autem in his quædam diligentius consideranda.
units.tr: But since it is not enough to have preached and heard the Word, but all the actions of this life must correspond to it, Christ adds a weighty admonition, which is at the same time in the place of an exhortation. "The lamp of the body," he says, "is the eye. When therefore your eye is single, your whole body also will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body also will be dark." By the name of eye he denotes the reason and understanding of man. By the body, however, he means the whole of life. For as the eye, like a lamp, lights up the whole body so that the single members can perform their functions, so reason ought by its own light to direct the whole life and all the actions of man, so that they may be rightly and lawfully ordered. He calls the eye single, that is, the understanding or reason that is sincere and free from the disorder of wicked affections; and to this he assigns a bright body, that is, a holy and Christian life shining with good actions. But the evil eye he calls reason corrupted and faulty, which also makes the whole body, that is, the conduct of the whole life, dark, while we, carried away by the desires of the flesh, stumble now here, now there (like those who walk in darkness), and in place of works of light we make works of darkness. Therefore, he says, consider whether the light that is in you be darkness. The sense is: look again and again, that you may have reason truly enlightened, lest that which ought to be a lamp to you should pour darkness and mist upon you. For if (as is found in Matthew) the light itself be darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? And lest anyone deceive himself by an empty profession of the Word of God, he adds: If your whole body be light, having no dark part, it will be wholly bright, so as to light you up as a lamp does with its brilliance. That is, if you so order your life that only works of light are seen in you, and there is no place among you for the works of darkness, then at last it will be plain that you are truly illuminated by that heavenly and saving light of the Gospel. From this one can infer the contrary, that those who serve the prince of darkness and take delight in its works have not yet rightly tasted the doctrine of the Gospel. There are, however, certain points in these matters that must be considered more carefully.

units.la: Nimirum, mentem atq; rationem hominis illuminatione cœlesti opus habere. Nam vt aliàs monuimus, Adam in lapsu suo & mandati diuini trangressione non modò à dignitate sua priori excidit, verumetiam perfectam illam intellectus lucem amisit, qua initiò præditus creaturas omnibus nomina imponere, & Euam primo intuitu agnoscere eiusq; originem & vnde desumpta esset, intelligere potuit. Itaq; animalis homo (vt Paulus ait) id est, is qui naturali modò ratione & intellectu ducitur, non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Nimium autem inepti sunt, qui huius loci authoritate abutuntur, vt naturales hominis facultates extollant, & inde arbitrij nostri libertatem atq; meritum nostrorum operum colligant. Dicunt Christum de oculo simplici verba facere, quòd totum corpus lucidum reddat. Fateor, sed prius lucernæ meminit, cuius splendore eorum oculos illuminari oporteat, qui eius in Ecclesiâ ingredi, & germana huius membra esse velint. Nec temere oculi similitudine vtitur. Nam vt is facultatem quidem videndi habeat, eam tamen exerere non potest, nisi lux accedat, qua aër, qui medium visus est, illuminetur: ita etsi homo ratione & intelle&u præditus sit, in diuinis tamen & cœlestibus nihil videt, nihil intelligit, nihil sapit, nisi diuina lux accedat, quæ illa patefaciat, & ipsum quoq; illuminet atq; regat, vt ad illa percipienda idoneus sit. Lucem verò hanc per Verbum suum nobis offert, quo voluntatem suam omnem nobis manifestat, & rationem quoq; regit, ne prauas cupiditates secuta ab illius semitis declinet. Ad huius ergo studium nos Christus adhortatur, & sine illo omnia nobis obscura & tenebricosa esse docet, tam abest, vt hominis facultates extollere, & harũ inani fiducia nos inebriare velit. Si enim intellectus eiusmodi est, vt per se nihil videat & intelligat, quæ obsecro in nobis voluntas bona esse poterit? Hanc enim ex illo generari constat. Neminem ergo suipsius fiducia decipiat, sed meminerint omnes, Deum esse, qui in nobis & velle & facere operatur, ideoq; ad huius gratiam cõfugiant, & mediis, quibus erga nos vtitur, sese obedienter accommodent.
units.tr: Clearly, the mind and reason of man need heavenly illumination. For, as we have noted elsewhere, Adam in his fall and in his transgression of the divine commandment not only lost his former dignity but also lost that perfect light of understanding with which he was endowed at the beginning, by which he could give names to all creatures, recognise Eve at first sight, and understand her origin and from what she had been taken. Therefore the natural man (as Paul says), that is, the one who is led by natural reason and understanding, does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. But those are far too foolish who abuse the authority of this passage to exalt man's natural faculties, and from it infer the freedom of our will and the merit of our works. They say that Christ speaks of the single eye, which makes the whole body bright. I grant it, but first he mentions the lamp, by whose splendour the eyes of those must be illuminated who wish to enter his Church and be true members of it. Nor does he use the likeness of the eye without reason. For although the eye has the faculty of seeing, it cannot exercise it unless light comes, by which the air, the medium of sight, is illuminated. So, although man is endowed with reason and understanding, he sees nothing, understands nothing and savours nothing in divine and heavenly things, unless the divine light comes, which discloses those things and also illuminates and guides him, so that he is fit to perceive them. This light he offers us through his Word, by which he makes all his will known to us and also governs our reason, so that it does not follow depraved desires and stray from his paths. Christ therefore urges us to the pursuit of this light, and teaches that without it all things are obscure and dark to us; so far is he from wishing to exalt man's faculties and to intoxicate us with their empty confidence. For if the understanding is such that by itself it sees and understands nothing, what good will, I ask, can there be in us? For it is agreed that the will is generated from it. Let no one therefore be deceived by confidence in himself, but let all remember that it is God who works in us both to will and to do, and so let them take refuge in his grace and obediently accommodate themselves to the means by which he deals with us.

units.la: Porò totus hic locus Verbum Dei & huius studium nobis commendat. Magnum equidem & præclarum beneficiũ est, quòd sua luce huius mundi tenebras discutit, & simul diaboli regnum labefactat, quod ignorantiæ tenebris maximè stabilitur. Maius autem & excellentius multò, quòd hominis intellectum, qui & tenebris gaudet & cæno fœdissimarum cupiditatũ totus immersus atque obrutus est, illuminat, imò excitat quoq;, vt quasi sublato capite sublimius sapere & ad cœlestium cognitionem aspirare incipiat. Est hoc regenerationis nostræ initium, ex quo mox totius hominis innovatio sequitur, quae in tota vita & actionibus omnibus se exerit, quo fit, ut & Deus in nobis glorificetur, & plures alij nostro exemplo excitati emendentur, & vna nobiscum aeternae salutis participes fiant. Et hic finis est, propter quem Verbum suum nobis Deus revelat. Quapropter grauissimè peccant, qui cum huius doctrina glorientur, vitam viuunt prophanam & impuram. Nec enim suam modo salutem negligunt, sed authores sunt, ut Verbum Dei propter ipsos male audiat, & multi eorum exemplo offensi ab illius doctrina abhorreant. Itaq; duplicem damnationem tales merentur, cum & in Deum eiusq; maiestatem directe peccent, & proximo perditionis causam praebeant. Qui vero lucem hanc odio prosequuntur & prorsus extinctam volunt, eos Ægyptiæ tenebræ manent, ut quamvis inter filios lucis medij versentur, ipsi tamen in tenebris errorum atque affectuum suorum miserè tumultuantur, nec aliquid certum habeant. Exempla huius generis hodie passim videmus in multis, qui cum saeculi huius sapientia alijs fere praestent, in diuinis tamen & ijs, quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt, talpa sunt caeciores. Discant ergo singuli agnoscere Dei beneficium, neque Verbum eius audiant modo aut legant, sed memores quare hoc nobis praedicetur, vitam atque mores suos ad illius regulam examinent, & quae tunc deprehenduntur vitia emendent, ambulent denique in luce illa, quoad ea frui datur, ut olim in Christo Iesu, vera & aeterna luce, aeternum gaudere & exultare possint. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this whole passage commends to us the Word of God and the study of it. It is indeed a great and remarkable benefit that by his light he scatters the darkness of this world and at the same time weakens the kingdom of the devil, which is chiefly upheld by the darkness of ignorance.
