But it is far greater and more excellent that he illuminates the understanding of man, which both delights in darkness and is wholly immersed and buried in the mire of the most foul desires, and indeed also rouses it, so that, as if the head had been lifted, it begins to think more highly and to aspire to the knowledge of heavenly things. This is the beginning of our regeneration, from which soon follows the renewal of the whole man, which shows itself in the whole of life and in all actions, so that God is glorified in us, and many others, stirred up by our example, are amended, and become with us partakers of eternal salvation. And this is the end for which God reveals his Word to us. Therefore those grievously sin who glory in this doctrine yet live a profane and impure life. For they not only neglect their own salvation, but are also the cause that the Word of God is ill spoken of on their account, and many, offended by their example, shrink from its teaching. Thus such people deserve a double condemnation, since they sin directly against God and his majesty and at the same time give cause of ruin to their neighbour. But those who pursue this light with hatred and want it utterly extinguished, the darkness of Egypt remains for them; so that, although they move among the sons of light, they themselves wretchedly stumble about in the darkness of their errors and passions and have nothing certain. Examples of this kind we see everywhere today in many who, though in the wisdom of this age they surpass others almost everywhere, in divine things and those that pertain to eternal salvation are more blind than moles. Let each one therefore learn to acknowledge the benefit of God, and let them not only hear or read his Word, but, mindful of why it is preached to us, examine their life and manners by its rule, and amend whatever faults are then detected, and finally walk in that light for as long as it is granted them to enjoy it, so that, as once in Christ Jesus, the true and eternal light, they may rejoice and exult for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXX.
units.tr: Homily CXX.

units.la: Postquam autem locutus esset, rogauit eum Pharisæus quidam, ut pranderet apud se. Ingressus igitur discubuit. Pharisæus autem cum hoc vidisset, admiratus est eum non prius ablutum fuisse ante prandium. Dixit autem Dominus ei: Vos quidem Pharisæi exteriorem poculi patinæq; partem purgatis: sed quod intra vos est, plenum est rapina & scelere. Dementes, nonne qui fecit quod foris est, etiam id quod intus est fecit? Veruntamen ea quae intus sunt date in eleemosynam: & ecce omnia erunt vobis pura.
units.tr: After he had spoken, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him. So he went in and reclined at table. But when the Pharisee saw this, he marvelled that Jesus had not first washed before the meal. And the Lord said to him: "Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools, did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give for alms those things that are within, and behold, all things will be clean for you." (Luke 11:37-41)

units.la: Quemadmodum homini nihil vel utilius vel necessarium magis est pura & syncera veritatis doctrina: ita nihil exitialius est & pernitiosius quam doctrina falsa, quae externa specie se venditant. Nam ut vera nos Deo adducit: sic falsa ab eodem nos abstrahit, adhaec verum cultum corrumpit, religionis puriorus studium extinguit, & proinde scelerum quoque maximorum quasi mater atque nutrix est. Ideo olim aduersus hanc acerrimè pugnarunt Prophetæ, & Apostoli non contenti eos confutauisse, qui ipsorum temporibus falsa dogmata spargebant, sed illos etiam diligenter posteros praemonuerunt, quos nouissimo saeculo exorituros esse in Spiritu praeuidebant. Sed & Christo perpetua cum Scribis & Sacerdotibus lis fuit propter falsam doctrinam, quia populus ab ipsis seducebatur. Exemplum eius rei in praesenti Lucas commodissimè subijcit. Hactenus enim ille de Verbo Dei aut Euangelio disseruit, docens, lucernam esse, quae homines mentem & rationem illuminari oportet, ne in tenebrarum operibus incertus oberret: sed potius vitae puritate & sanctitatis verae exemplo alijs praeluceat. Hic nunc alia tractatio de doctrina falsa subijcitur, quam mox à priori in domo Pharisæi cuiusdam instituit. Vbi exempli loco quaedam Pharisæorum dogmata graviter exagitat, in quibus illius natura atque effectus cerni possunt, simul autem illorum authoribus poenas graues denuntiat. Quae omnia sic Lucas describit, ut desimilibus facile fit iudicare.
units.tr: Just as nothing is more useful or more necessary for a human being than the pure and sincere teaching of the truth, so nothing is more destructive and more deadly than false teaching, which puts on a show of outward appearance. For as true doctrine leads us to God, so false doctrine draws us away from him; moreover, it corrupts true worship, extinguishes zeal for a purer religion, and so is, as it were, both the mother and the nurse of the greatest crimes. For this reason the prophets fought most fiercely against it of old, and the apostles, not content to refute those who spread false doctrines in their own times, also carefully warned posterity about those whom they foresaw would arise in the last age in the Spirit. But Christ too had a constant quarrel with the scribes and priests over false teaching, because the people were being led astray by them. Luke aptly sets before us an example of this matter at present. Up to this point he has discussed the Word of God, or the gospel, teaching that a lamp is what ought to illuminate people's minds and reason, so that they do not wander uncertainly in the works of darkness, but rather shine before others by the purity of their life and the example of true holiness. Now another discussion about false teaching is introduced here, which he begins shortly after in the house of a certain Pharisee. In it, by way of example, he sharply censures certain doctrines of the Pharisees, in which their nature and effects can be seen, and at the same time he pronounces grave punishments on their authors. Luke describes all these things in such a way that, from the likeness, it is easy to judge the rest.

units.la: Occasionem huic causae Pharisæus praebuit, qui Christum inuitauit, ut apud se pranderet. Hic ergo illi morem gerens, domum eius ingreditur, & non lotus antea discumbit, & hinc disputatio exorta est, quae ipsi de illorum doctrina & moribus dicendi ansam dedit. Priusquam vero ad causae tractationem accedamus, quaedam de Pharisæo & de Christo dicenda erunt. Nam in illo admiratione dignum est, quod hunc domum suam inuitat, & quidem ad conuiuium honorarium, cui plures alios
units.tr: The Pharisee provided the occasion for this matter, for he invited Christ to dine at his home. Christ, then, complying with him, enters his house and reclines at table without having washed beforehand, and from this a dispute arose, which gave him an opening to speak about their teaching and their morals. Before we come to the treatment of the matter, some things must be said about the Pharisee and about Christ. For it is worthy of wonder in the Pharisee that he invites him to his house, and indeed to an honourable banquet, at which several others

units.la: Pharisæus invitat Christum. alios eiusdem ordinis, adhæc Scribas & Legis interpretes interfuisse, suo loco audiemus. Atqui constat, Christo nullos hostes fuisse acriores & magis infensos Pharisæis, quos omnium fere consiliorum aduersus illum præcipuos authores fuisse, Euangelista passim docent. Quia enim externæ iustitiæ speciem sibi venditabant, & salutis spem in suorum operum meritis habebant collocatam, Christum ferre non potuerunt, qui & hypocrisim eorum arguebat, & omnes homines à propria iustitiæ fiducia ad Dei gratiam atque misericordiam reuocabat. Nec est quod miremur, doctrinam hanc, quæ nihil iucundius & suauius homini proponi potest, ita illis displicuisse, cum hodie etiam non alij eius hostes truculentiores sint quàm monachi, & qui horum traditionibus decepti propriæ iustitiæ & meritorum suorum fiducia turgent. Vt enim horum ostentatio ipsis apud vulgus authoritatem conciliat, ita laruam sibi detrahi indignissimè ferunt. Veruntamen Pharisæus ille Dominum honorificè inuitat, imò amicè etiam rogat, ut apud se prandere dignetur. Causæ huius inuitationis variæ adduci possunt. Nam aut bonam gratiam inire vult apud populum, quem Christi studiosum esse sciebat (sciebat enim illud hominum genus nihil aura popolari antiquius habuisse) aut eum blanditiis & gulæ illecebris, vel amicitiæ prætextu atque honorum spe demulceri posse sperat, quem in disputatoriis concertationibus inuictum esse videbat: aut quod verisimilius est, in tanta doctorum turba aliquos inueniri posse arbitratur, qui captiosis quæstionibus irretitum in periculum capitis, vel falsæ in populi odium adducant. Est hoc ergo egregium astutiæ & calliditatis exemplum, qua impij veritatis Euangelicæ hostes aduersus huius professores uti consueuerunt. Vt enim diabolus interdum sese in Angelum lucis transformare & gloriæ Dei studium simulare solet: ita huius ministri sæpe odium veritatis dissimulant, omnia amicitiæ officia huius doctoribus pollicentur, amicè prehensant & salutant, domum deducunt, ita deniq; agunt, ut nemo aliquid hostile suspicari possit. Id vero tunc faciunt, quando (quæ illorum astutia est) tempori seruiendum esse vident. Nisi ergo artes illorum pij diligenter obseruent, facile ipsis securitas obrepit, qua fit, ut multa præter officium faciant, aut dolis eorum circumuenti seipsos & Veritatis causam impiorum ludibrio exponant.
units.tr: The Pharisee invites Christ. others of the same order, and besides them scribes and interpreters of the Law, were present, as we shall hear in its place. Yet it is well established that Christ had no enemies more bitter and more hostile than the Pharisees, who, as the evangelists teach everywhere, were almost the chief authors of nearly all the plots against him. For since they put on a show of outward righteousness and had placed their hope of salvation in the merits of their works, they could not bear Christ, who both exposed their hypocrisy and called all people back from confidence in their own righteousness to the grace and mercy of God. Nor is it surprising that this teaching, which can be set before a human being as nothing more pleasant and sweeter, displeased them so much; for even today none of its enemies are fiercer than the monks, and those who, deceived by their traditions, swell with confidence in their own righteousness and merits. For just as their display wins them authority among the common people, so they bitterly resent having their mask torn off. Nevertheless that Pharisee invites the Lord honourably, and even asks him kindly to deign to dine at his house. Various reasons for this invitation can be offered. Either he wished to win favour with the people, whom he knew to be devoted to Christ (for he knew that this kind of people valued popular applause above everything), or he hoped that Christ could be won over by flattery, the enticements of the table, the pretext of friendship and the hope of honours, since he saw that Christ was unconquered in disputations; or, what is more likely, he thought that among so great a crowd of learned men some could be found who might entangle him in captious questions and bring him into danger of his life, or into hatred with the people as a false teacher. This, then, is a notable example of the cunning and craftiness which the impious enemies of the Gospel truth have customarily used against its professors. For just as the devil sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light and is accustomed to pretend zeal for the glory of God, so the ministers of this devil often conceal their hatred of the truth, promise all the offices of friendship to its teachers, greet them warmly and embrace them, lead them home, and in the end act in such a way that no one can suspect anything hostile. They do this especially when, as is their cunning, they see that they must bow to the times. Unless the godly carefully watch their arts, security easily creeps upon them, with the result that they do many things beyond their duty, or, deceived by their tricks, they expose themselves and the cause of the truth to the mockery of the impious.

units.la: Quid ergo (inquis) faciā? Num amicitiam suam mihi sponte offerentes ego auersabor? num lu- manitatis officia non admittam? Vel num inimicos faciam mea duritie & intractabilitate exijs, qui amici esse cupiunt? Sunt hæc fere quæstiones eorum, qui nimium faciles sunt hodie in admittendis impiorum consortijs. Sed ad illos nos vno verbo respondemus, Christi exemplum esse imitandum, quod nos errare non sinet. Hic morem gerit pharisæo, & ad eum pransurus diuertit, ne alicuius amicitiam subterfugere, aut humanitatis officia superbius fastidire videatur: interea autem sui officij, ad quod à Patre destinatus erat, probè memor, nihil dissimulat in hospitis sui gratiam, neq; ex eorum numero est, qui vt aliena quadra viuere possint, quibusuis seruiliter assentiuntur: quin potius occasionem captat aduersus totum hunc Pharisaeorum, Scribarum atq; Legis interpretum cœtum dispu-tandi, vt tam ipsos quàm populum ab eorum authoritate pendentem superstitione liberet. Nam, quod illos indignè laturos esse sciebat, illico illorum manibus accumbit. Erat enim hæc inter Iudaicas superstitiones non postrema, quòd frequentius lauabantur. Occasionem quidem eius moris siue ritus ex lege Dei habebant, in qua ablutiones aliquæ cum vestium tum corporum præcipiuntur. Qui enim vel cadauer aliquod vel quamcunq; rem immunda tetigerat, immundus censebatur, donec sequndum legem ablutus & expiatus erat. Istis vero Deus veræ puritatis & sanctimoniæ studium populo suo commendabat, simulq; docebat purificatione opus esse, quam in promissi seminis sanguine essent habituri. At quod in aliis ceremonijs posteri fecerunt, hoc ipsum in ista quoq; accidit. Nam neq; in promissum illum seruatorem respexerunt, neq; tijs fuerunt contenti quæ Deus præceperat: sed quasi in externa ablutione vera hominis purificatio atq; salus consisteret, multas alias excogitarunt, quibus absq; magna occasione vtebantur. Etenim vt Marcus annotauit, à foro venientes non edebant, nisi prius loti fuissent. Obseruabant præterea diligenter lotiones crebras poculorum & sextariorum, & æramentorū atq; lectorum, quas à maioribus traditas acceperant. In quem vsum etiam in singulis ferè domibus hydriæ prostabant, sicuti in nuptiarū, quæ in Cana Galilæa factæ sunt, bi-storia apud Ioannem est videre. Eadem ergo superstitio Iudæos tunc temporis tenuit, qua hodie multi laborant, qui aquæ lustralis aspersione se purificari & mundari arbitrantur. Vt ergo huic erroris medeatur Dominus, & de vera hominis purificatione differendi occasionem habeat, illorum manibus accumbit, & illud omittit, quod ciuilitas morum alioqui facere iubet, & quod salua conscientia fieri poterat, nisi illorum errori patrocinari visus fuisset.
units.tr: What then (you say) shall I do? Shall I spurn those who offer me their friendship of their own accord? Shall I not admit the courtesies of humanity? Or shall I make enemies by my harshness and unyielding manner of those who desire to be my friends? These are almost the questions of those who today are too ready to admit the company of the impious. To them we reply in a single word that the example of Christ is to be imitated, and it will not let us go wrong. He complies with the Pharisee and turns aside to dine with him, lest he seem to shun anyone's friendship or to disdain the courtesies of humanity too haughtily; yet meanwhile, being well mindful of the office for which he was sent by the Father, he conceals nothing for the sake of his host, and he is not one of those who, so that they may live at the expense of others, fawn servilely on whomever they please. Rather he seizes the opportunity to dispute against this whole assembly of Pharisees, scribes and interpreters of the Law, so that he may free both them and the people dependent on their authority from superstition. For, knowing that they would take it badly, he at once reclines in their hands. Now among the Jewish superstitions this was not the least, that they washed very frequently. They had indeed the occasion for this custom or rite from the Law of God, in which certain washings of both clothes and bodies are prescribed. For whoever had touched a corpse or any unclean thing was considered unclean until he was washed and cleansed according to the Law. God, however, by these means commended to his people the pursuit of true purity and holiness, and at the same time taught that a purification was needed, which they would have in the blood of the promised seed. But what later generations did in the other ceremonies, this same thing also happened in this one. For they neither looked to that promised Saviour, nor were they content with what God had commanded; but as if true purification and salvation of the human being consisted in outward washing, they devised many other washings, which they used without any great reason. For, as Mark noted, when they came from the market they did not eat unless they had first washed. Moreover, they diligently observed the frequent washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels and couches, which they had received as handed down by their ancestors. For this purpose too, water jars stood ready in almost every house, as can be seen in John's account of the wedding that took place in Cana of Galilee. The same superstition, therefore, held the Jews at that time which still troubles many today, who think they are purified and cleansed by the sprinkling of lustral water. So, in order to remedy this error, and to have an occasion to speak about the true purification of the human being, the Lord reclines in their hands, and omits what otherwise the courtesy of manners requires, and what could have been done with a good conscience, had he not seemed to be lending support to their error.

units.la: Sunt autem in eius exemplo duo non ofcitanter obseruanda. Vnum est, facilitas eius, quae tantum fuit, vt hosti quoq; morem gerere dignatus fit. Vt enim omnes, qui eius ope atq; consilio indigent, ad fe vocat: ita neminem ad fe venientem reijcit. Exempla huius bonitatis multa passim habemus, inter quae admodum memorabilia sunt, quod in muliere peccatrice Cap.7. vidimus, & quod in Nicodemi historia Ioannes describit, quem licet Pharisaeus effet, & fui eum puderet, ideoq; noctu adipsum accederet, amicè tamen in colloquiu admissum à primus rudimentis in toto salutis negotio fidelissime insticuit. Debent autem eiusmodi exempla diligenter obseruari, vt ex illis consolationem petamus in cofcientiae terroribus. Qui enim olim peccatores & filios irae, imo manifestos hostes tam humaniter admisit, qua ratione eos reijceret, quos sui sanguinis merito iam olim Patri reconciliauit, & qui ipsum Seruatorem suum esse agnoscunt, opemq; eius supplices expetunt?
units.tr: There are two things in his example that must be observed carefully. The first is his affability, which was so great that he deigned to indulge even his enemies. As he calls to himself all who need his help and counsel, so he rejects no one who comes to him. We have many examples of this goodness everywhere, among which are quite memorable the case of the sinful woman, which we saw in chapter 7, and what John describes in the story of Nicodemus. Although Nicodemus was a Pharisee and ashamed of it, and therefore came to him by night, he was nevertheless kindly admitted into conversation and most faithfully instructed in the first elements of the whole matter of salvation. Such examples ought to be carefully noted, so that we may seek consolation from them in the terrors of conscience. For if he once admitted with such humanity sinners and children of wrath, indeed manifest enemies, by what reasoning would he reject those whom he has already reconciled to the Father by the merit of his own blood, and who acknowledge him as their Saviour and humbly seek his help?

units.la: Alterum est, de quo iam agere coeperamus: Quatenus nimirum vel conuiuari vel quancunq; aliam consuetudinem per se non inhonestam habere liceat cum iis, quos à vera fide alienos esse scimus: Quatenus videlicet medico cum aegrotis versari liceat. Et ne à Christi exemplo discedamus: Medicus nusquam rectius agit, quàm apud eos, qui ex morbis decumbunt. Haec enim eius vocatio, haec eius area siue palaestra est, in qua suae tam artis quàm fidei specimina edere debet. At quis illi finis est propositus? Num vt ipse sibi ex contagio eundem morbum accersat? vel vt aegroto blandiatur solum, & blanditiis atq; inutilibus, vel etiam noxijs fomentis morbum eius augeat? Minime gentium. Nam ne quid ipse mali patiatur, antidotis sese praemunit, aegrotum vero à morbo liberare studet, & vbi opus est, non vnctionibus modo & potionibus dulcioribus vtitur, sed amariora quoq; pharmaca propinat, & saepe cultros, serras, forcipes et cauteria exerit, vt à carnifice vix quicquam differre videatur. Ad eundem modum Christus fecit, qui se medicum in mundum hunc venisse profitetur. Nam fidei medici instar ad omnes accessit qui eius opem flagitarunt, aut etiam aliis de causis (vt Pharisaeus hic) ipsum vocauerunt. At non eadem medendi ratione apud omnes est vsus. Nam alios quidem, quos peccati agnitio ad desperationis praecipitium deducebat, amicus & blandis gratiae Dei promissionibus reduxit & confirmauit: alios autem qui praefractiores erant, minus terruit: in eos vero, quos omnino incurabiles esse videbat, grauius inuectus est, & laruam exilii mationis quam sustinebant illis detraxit, ne aliis mali exempli authores essent: qua ratione cum Pharisaeus eum egisse postea audiemus, quibus adeo nihil indulsit, vt ne manus quidem more ipsorum abluere dignatus fuerit. Ad hunc modum quoq; cum alienis à fide consuetudinem habere licebit: vt nimirum non noftrū commodum, non lautitias & pontificalia conuiuia, non huius mundi amicitiā, non seculi huius honores aut opes, sed illorum salutem quaeramus. Id vero fiet, si errores ipsorum arguantur, si Veritatis semita ipsis monstretur, & admonitionibus serijs vrgeantur, vt in illa ambulent. Quod si ab illis impetretur, nae bonum opus (vt Iacobus ait) fecerit, qui tanti boni ipsis fuerit author. Vt vero id facilius fiat, studiose admodum cauere oportet, ne vel verbulo vno erroribus ipsorum assentiamur, vel minima ex parte eorundem superstitionibus communicemus. Solent enim isti homines omnia nostra dicta & facta obseruare, & quamus nos propter diuersae ab ipsis fidei & religionis professionem odio prosequantur, tamen vt oraculum quoddam excipiunt quicquid à nobis fit aut dicitur, quod in errorum & superstitionis ipsorum patrocinium rapi posse existimant. Huius ergo memores ab iis etiam abstineamus, quae per se media & indifferentia sunt, & quibus si illi abstinent, salua atq; bona conscientia vti possumus. Nam vt Paulus in priori ad Corinthios admonet, omnia quidem credentibus licent, sed non omnia conducunt, neq; etiam omnia faciunt ad Ecclesiae & fratrum aedificationem. Et potest huc proprie referri tota de carnibus immolatitijs & earum esu disputatio, quam illic prolixe tractat: tum etiam ea, quae de ciborum aliorum delectu atq; discrimine in epistola ad Romanos disserit. Quod si aute à licitis abstinendum est, ne vel superstitiosos vel infirmos in errore confirmemus, quanto magis cauere oportet, ne disertis verbis, aut etiam responsis ambiguis errores eorum probemus, aut in illorum gratiam faciamus, quae prorsus illicita & à fidei Christianae professione aliena sunt? Nec enim (vt Elias dicebat) in vtramq; partem claudicare licet iis, qui veri Dei cultores haberi volunt. Haec si hodie obseruarent & sedulo facerent seruiles isti homines, quos culinæ papisticæ nidor trahit, vt in Monachorum comitatu & deductione conspici, eorundem mensis frequenter accumbere, & ab illis in pretio haberi summum honorem ducant, profectò aut ipsi mox ab incurabilium consuetudine sponte abhorrerent, aut ab illis delicatis patribus excluderentur: quibus nihil durius & iniquius putatur, quam si quis aures eorum audeat mordaci radere vero. Sed longè diuersum fieri videmus: vt nimirum pseudoevangelici illi aperte veritatis hostibus seruiliter blandiantur, omnia dissimulent, imò ne ab ipsorum gratia excidant, nihil non fi- bi faciendum putent: quo fit, vt ipsi quidem quotidie in peius proficiant, illi verò in superstitionibus suis confirmentur. Nihil ergo illis Christi exemplum patrocinatur, cum quo prorsus nihil commune habent.
units.tr: The second is what we had already begun to treat: namely, to what extent it is lawful to share a meal, or any other custom not dishonourable in itself, with those whom we know to be alien from the true faith; that is, whether it is lawful for a physician to associate with the sick. And, not to depart from Christ's example, a physician never acts more rightly than among those who lie ill with disease. For this is his calling, this is his arena or wrestling-ground, in which he ought to display the proofs of his skill as much as of his faith. But what end is set before him? Is it that he should draw the same disease upon himself by contagion? Or that he should merely flatter the patient, and by flatteries and useless or even harmful remedies increase the disease? By no means. For lest he himself suffer any harm, he fortifies himself with antidotes, and he strives to free the patient from the disease. Where need is, he uses not only ointments and gentler draughts but also bitterer medicines, and often he brings out knives, saws, forceps and cautery irons, so that he seems hardly to differ from an executioner. In the same way Christ acted, who professes that he has come into this world as a physician. For like a faithful physician he approached all who asked for his help, or who called him for other reasons (like this Pharisee). But he did not use the same method of healing with all. For some, whom the recognition of sin was leading down to the precipice of despair, he kindly restored and strengthened with the gentle promises of God's grace; others, who were more stubborn, he rebuked less severely; but against those whom he saw to be altogether incurable he spoke more harshly, and he stripped from them the mask of the false security in which they lived, lest they should be authors of bad example to others. In this way, as we shall hear later, he dealt with the Pharisee, to whom he granted so little indulgence that he did not deign to wash his hands in their manner. In this same way it will be lawful for us to have dealings with those alien from the faith: namely, that we seek not our own advantage, not luxuries and pontifical banquets, not friendship with this world, not the honours or riches of this age, but their salvation. This will happen if their errors are refuted, if the path of Truth is shown to them, and if they are urged with serious admonitions to walk in it. And if they are persuaded, indeed (as James says) he will have done a good work who has been the author of so great a good to them. So that this may happen more easily, we must take the most careful precaution that we do not assent to their errors by even a single word, nor share in their superstitions in the least degree. For these men are accustomed to observe all our words and deeds, and although they pursue us with hatred because of our different profession of faith and religion, yet they receive whatever is done or said by us as a kind of oracle, which they think can be seized in defence of their errors and superstition. Mindful of this, we should therefore also abstain from those things which are in themselves indifferent and middling, and from which, if they abstain, we may use with a sound and good conscience. For as Paul warns in the first letter to the Corinthians, all things are lawful for believers, but not all things are expedient, nor do all things build up the Church and the brethren. And the whole discussion about meats offered to idols and the eating of them, which he treats at length there, can properly be referred here; and so too is what he argues in the letter to the Romans about the distinction of other foods. But if we must abstain from lawful things, so as not to confirm the superstitious or the weak in error, how much more must we take care not to approve their errors in express words, or even by ambiguous replies, or to do for their favour things that are altogether unlawful and alien to the profession of the Christian faith? For (as Elijah said) it is not permitted to limp to either side for those who wish to be regarded as worshippers of the true God. If these servile men, whom the smell of the papist kitchen draws, who are seen in the company and escort of the monks, who frequently sit at their tables and think it the highest honour to be held in esteem by them, were to observe these things and diligently do them, they would surely either themselves shrink of their own accord from the custom of the incurable, or be shut out by those dainty fathers, to whom nothing seems harder or more unjust than if anyone dares to scrape their ears with biting truth. But we see something very different happening: namely, these pseudo-evangelicals fawn slavishly upon the open enemies of the truth, dissemble everything, and, lest they fall from their favour, think nothing should be left undone. The result is that they themselves daily advance for the worse, while those others are confirmed in their superstitions. Therefore Christ's example gives no support to them, with whom they have absolutely nothing in common.

units.la: Sed Pharisæum Christi hospitem videamus, quem Lucas admiratum fuisse scribit, quod non sese abluisset ante prandium. Fuit autem admiratio hæc haud dubiè cum indignatione coniuncta, vt eorum qui Matth.15.cap.discipulos Christi eandem ob causam accusarunt. Ita verò occasionem ei præbuit, quam quærebat, vt aduersus superstitiones ipsorum posset differere. Admbrantur autem in huius Pharisæi exemplo omnium hypocritarum mores atque ingenium. Solent illi externam sanctimoniæ speciem, quæ in vanis & inanibus ceremonijs consistit, mirifico & magno studio urge re, cum internam animi puritatem & vitæ innocentiam facile negligant. Tales olim Prophetarum temporibus fuerunt, qui in sacrificijs quidem assidui erant, nunquam verò de mactandis pecuinis affectibus & carnis mortificatione, multò minus autem de fide in promissum humani generis seruatorem cogitabant, qui externo illo cultu adumbrabatur. Sed aliud etiam vitium accedit, quod humanas traditiones violari indignissimè ferunt, cum ipsi diuinas leges absque omni metu transgrediantur, quod postea Christus Pharisæorum factis demonstrabit. Causa omnis mali est, quod suam potius quam Dei gloriam quærunt: imò vix credunt Deum esse, qui ista videat, sed huius nomine turpiter abutuntur, vt & sibijpsis authoritatem concilient, & populum rudem in obedientia contineant. Vtrumque nostro seculo admodum frequens est. Nam si diligentius consideres, in quo nam tota Papistarum sanctimonia, & quidem Monachorum in primis consistat, quid aliud reperies, quam Missas, suffitus, lampades, cerea, vestium nouas & peculiares formas, ciborum delectum, peregrinationes ad longinquas Diuorum imagines, & alia eius generis, quæ exercitatione corporis fere constant, quam Paulus parum utilitatis habere ait, & quæ ipsi propter coniunctam ei mercedem fidelem exitialis est? Vt autem mens sana & pura fit, vt fide in Christum illuminetur, vt vitam vivant verè Christianam, non multum curant, imò vbi alij illis defuncti sunt, sibi nihil præterea agendum esse arbitrantur. Similiter, si ea respicias, propter quæ illi nobis indignantur nosque accusant, rursus Pharisæorum similes videbis. Nec enim nos violata & abiecta legis Dei, aut quod fidem in Iesum Christum abnegauerimus, aut Dei verbum conculcemus accusare possunt, (quin potius quod ista sola apud nos in pretio & honore sint, nobis indignantur) sed hoc indignissimè ferunt, quod abrogato Missæ sacrificio verum Cænæ Dominicæ vsum restituimus, quod imagines & superstitiosum atque superbum templorum ornatum sustulimus, quod ignem purgatorium Dei Verbo extinximus, quod exequias & quæstuosa sacra pro defunctis damnamus, quod Papam cum suis indulgentijs, bullis & anathematismis siue excommunicationibus contemnimus atque ridemus, quod vota monasticæ, dierum obseruationes, ciborum discrimina, ieiunia superstitiosa & alia huius generis infinita improbamus. Hæc (inquam) sunt, propter quæ nobis indignantur, & dignos esse clamant, qui ferro & igne excindamur. At qualia obsecro illa sunt? aut quis ea instituit? Num Deus? num huius serui Propheta? num aliquam horum mentionem fecit vnquam in carne manifestatus Dei Filius, quem vnum nos Pater audire iussit? num quid huius traditerunt Apostoli, quos ille orbis totius doctores constituit? Nunquam profectò hoc illi dicere audebunt, neque si audeant, testimonijs aut rationibus idoneis probare poterunt. Hominum ergo figmenta sunt, & non nisi humanarum traditionum authoritate nituntur, quas iam olim simul omnes Deus damnauit, quando se illis frustra coli dicit. Non est ergo, quod quisquam istorum indignationem metuat, aut temerarias damnationes formidet, aut eorundem calumnijs moueatur. Omnia enim hæc Pharisaicum spiritum redolent, nos autem Verbi Dei authoritas facile excusabit.
units.tr: But let us look at the Pharisee who was Christ's host, whom Luke writes was amazed that Christ had not washed himself before dinner. This amazement was undoubtedly joined with indignation, as in the case of those who accused Christ's disciples for the same reason in Matthew 15. Thus it gave him the opportunity he was seeking, to argue against their superstitions. In the example of this Pharisee the manners and disposition of all hypocrites are mirrored. They are accustomed to press with wonderful and great zeal the external appearance of holiness, which consists in vain and empty ceremonies, while they easily neglect the inner purity of soul and the innocence of life. Such men there were in the times of the prophets, who indeed were constant in sacrifices, but never thought of slaying the lusts of their affections and mortifying the flesh, much less of faith in the promised Saviour of the human race, who was foreshadowed by that external worship. But another vice is added: they bear it most unworthily when human traditions are violated, while they themselves transgress the divine laws without any fear. Christ will later demonstrate this by the deeds of the Pharisees. The cause of every evil is that they seek their own glory rather than God's; indeed they hardly believe that God is one who sees these things, but they shamefully abuse his name, both to win authority for themselves and to keep the ignorant people in obedience. Both are very frequent in our age. For if you consider more carefully in what the whole holiness of the Papists consists, and of the monks above all, what else will you find than Masses, incense, lamps, wax candles, new and peculiar forms of vestments, the selection of foods, pilgrimages to distant images of the saints, and other things of that kind, which consist almost in bodily exercise, which Paul says are of little use, and which, because of the reward joined to them, are deadly to the faithful? But as for making the mind sound and pure, for being enlightened by faith in Christ, for living a truly Christian life, they care little; indeed, when they have done these other things, they think nothing else remains to be done. Similarly, if you look at those things for which they are indignant with us and accuse us, again you will see that they are like the Pharisees. For they cannot accuse us of having violated and cast aside the law of God, or of having denied faith in Jesus Christ, or of trampling underfoot God's word (rather, they are indignant with us precisely because these things alone are held in esteem and honour among us). What they bear most unworthily is that, the sacrifice of the Mass having been abolished, we have restored the true use of the Lord's Supper; that we have removed images and the superstitious and proud adornment of churches; that we have extinguished the purgatorial fire by God's Word; that we condemn funerals and profitable rites for the dead; that we despise and mock the Pope with his indulgences, bulls and anathemas or excommunications; that we disapprove of monastic vows, the observance of days, distinctions of food, superstitious fasts, and other endless things of this kind. These (I say) are the things for which they are indignant with us, and they cry out that we are worthy to be cut down with sword and fire. But what, I ask, are those things? Who instituted them? Did God? Did the prophet of this God? Did the Son of God, manifested in the flesh, whom the Father alone commanded us to hear, ever make any mention of them? Did the Apostles, whom he appointed teachers of the whole world, hand down anything of this kind? They will surely never dare to say so, and even if they dare, they will not be able to prove it by fitting testimonies or arguments. They are therefore human inventions, and rest on no authority except that of human traditions, which God has long ago condemned all together, when he says that he is worshipped in vain by them. There is therefore no reason why anyone should fear their indignation, or dread their rash condemnations, or be moved by their calumnies. For all these things smell of the Pharisaic spirit, but the authority of God's Word will easily excuse us.

units.la: Pharisæorum & hypocritarum mores.
units.tr: The manners of the Pharisees and hypocrites.

units.la: Et hoc in primis faciunt, quae in praesenti Christus aduersus Pharisaeos in sui facti defensionem profert. Primo enim illorum errorem atque hypocrisim arguit, dicens: Vos quidem Pharisaei exte-riorem poculi patinae partem purgatis: sed quod intra vos est, plenum est rapina & scelere. Accu-sat quod puritati & munditiei externae studeant, vt hominibus probentur, nihili autem faciant ani-mi & conscientiae puritatem, quam solam Deus respicit & probat: imo perinde eos facere ait, ac si nihil illis sit cum Deo negotij. Est hic communis hypocritarum morbus, vt paulo ante diximus. Si enim Deum esse crederent, cuius oculi (vt Propheta ait) per omnem terram discurrunt, & qui corda renes, scrutatur, nunquam certe tam impudenter cum illo luderent. Istis autem Christus po-tissimum rapinas & πονηρίαν, id est, malitiosam alios molestandi libidinem exprobrat, quae scele-rum maximorum fecundissima mater est. Fuit hoc durum dictu, & non dubium est, quin plures eo offensi fuerint. Sed vere hoc dicit, & alibi rationem affert validissimam, quod nimirum sub prae-textu longae precationis domus viduarum & pupillorum devorarent, adhaec liberos impietatis in parentes authores essent, quando illos in corbonam ea deponere iubebant, quibus hos senio confectos alere debuissent. Et cur non raptores & praedones, imo sacrilegi dicerentur, qui totum cultum exter-num sibi quaestum, templum autem latronum speluncam fecerant? Quid autem aliud de nostri seculi Pharisaeis, sacrificis & monachis, dici potest? Nonne enim hi quoq; sub externa sanctimonia, pre-cum conductitiarum, Missarum pretio redemptarum, denique operum supererogationis pratextu rapiunt atq; praedantur? Nulla equidem familia est, quae illorum manus effugere potuerit: & con-stat saepe integra patrimonia, fraudatis haeredibus legitimis, per illos intercipi.
units.tr: Christ does this above all in the present passage, where he defends his own action against the Pharisees. First he charges them with their error and hypocrisy, saying: "You Pharisees indeed cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of rapine and wickedness." He accuses them of pursuing outward purity and cleanliness so that they may be approved by men, while they make nothing of purity of mind and conscience, which God alone regards and approves. He even says they act as though they had no dealings with God at all. This is the common disease of hypocrites, as we said a little earlier. For if they believed that God exists, whose eyes (as the Prophet says) run through the whole earth, and who searches the hearts and reins, they would never have trifled so shamelessly with him. Christ rebukes them chiefly for rapine and wickedness [πονηρίαν], that is, the malicious desire to harass others, which is the most fertile mother of the greatest crimes. This was a hard saying, and there is no doubt that many were offended by it. But he speaks the truth, and elsewhere he gives a very forceful reason: under the pretext of long prayers they devoured the houses of widows and orphans; moreover, they were authors of impiety towards parents, since they bade people set aside in the corban those goods with which they ought to have fed their parents, worn out with age. And why should they not be called robbers and plunderers, nay sacrilegious, who had made all external worship a source of gain for themselves and turned the temple into a den of robbers? What else can be said of the Pharisees of our own age, the priests and monks? Do they not also, under outward holiness, plunder and pillage by means of hired prayers, Masses bought back for money, and finally under the pretext of works of supererogation? Indeed there is no family that has been able to escape their hands, and it is constantly reported that whole patrimonies are often intercepted by them, the lawful heirs being defrauded.

units.la: Caeterum errori huic Christus medetur, & quid fieri debeat, docet. Dementes, nonne qui fecit quod foris est, etiam quod intus est fecit? Ad Dei tribunal eos citat, & dementes dicit, qui non meminerint, se a Deo creatos esse, & proinde nihil hunc eorum, quae vel palam vel occulte faciant, latere posse. Simile quid in Psalmo 94. aduersus eos dicit Spiritus sanctus, qui Deum nihil videre et audire putabant. At in praesenti Christus hoc simul suo instituto accommodat. Docet enim, Deum ho-minis corpus & animam creauisse, & ideo non illius solum, verumetiam huius puritati & sanctimo-niae esse studendum, nec tam videndum esse, qui cibi per os ingrediantur, aut num illotis manibus su-mantur, quam quid ex corde exeat. Quod apud Matthaeum diligentius discipulis suis exponit, his verbis: Audite & intelligite: Non quod ingreditur in os polluit hominem: sed quod egreditur ex ore, hoc polluit hominem. Et mox huius dicti rationem reddens addit: Quicquid ingreditur in os, in ventrem cedit: & in latrinam eijcitur. Quae autem proficiscuntur ex ore, ex ipso corde egrediuntur, & illa polluunt hominem. Nam ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malae, caedes, adulteria, fornica-tiones, furta, falsa testimonia, obtrectationes. Haec sunt quae polluunt hominem, illotis autem mani-bus vesci, non polluit hominem. Vult ergo, vt ante omnia animi purificationem quaeramus, qui ac-tionum omnium fons est. Ita enim illae etiam purae & sanctae, ceu riui ex illo fonte emanarunt. Quia autem rapinas & scelere partas opes illis exprobrauerat, alterum quoq; addit: Veruntamen ea quae intus sunt, date in eleemosynam, & ecce omnia erunt vobis pura. Per ea quae intus sunt opes recon-ditas intelligit, & quia haec male acquisitae erant, restitutionem exigit: quae cum a talibus vix, imo ne-vix quidem fieri possit, pauperibus illas erogare iubet, & tunc demum reliqua eorum pura fore do-cet, si scelere parta procul reiecta et sublata fuerint. Inepte ergo hunc locum pro satisfactionibus fuit, quibus nos peccata expiare docent, adducunt. Nec enim hic Christus docere instituit, quae apud Deum sit expiationis aut remissionis peccatorum ratio, sed qua ratione opes purgare possimus, vt earum vsus nobis purus & sanctus sit.
units.tr: Christ, however, cures this error and teaches what ought to be done. "Fools, did not he who made the outside also make the inside?" He summons them to God's tribunal and calls them fools who do not remember that they were created by God, and therefore that nothing they do, whether openly or secretly, can be hidden from him. The Holy Spirit says something similar against those who thought God saw and heard nothing, in Psalm 94. But here Christ applies this to his own purpose at the same time. For he teaches that God created the body and the soul of man, and therefore care must be taken for the purity and holiness not only of the one but also of the other. One should look less to what foods enter through the mouth, or whether they are eaten with unwashed hands, than to what comes out of the heart. He explains this more carefully to his disciples in Matthew, in these words: "Hear and understand: not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man, but that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man." And soon, giving the reason for this saying, he adds: "Whatever goes into the mouth passes into the belly and is cast out into the latrine. But those things which proceed from the mouth come out of the heart itself, and these defile a man. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders. These are what defile a man; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man." He wants us, therefore, to seek above all the purification of the mind, which is the source of all actions. For thus even those actions which are pure and holy flow out like streams from that source. But since he had reproached them with riches gained by rapine and wickedness, he adds the other point as well: "But give as alms those things which are within, and behold, all things will be clean for you." By "those things which are within" he means hidden wealth, and because these were ill-gotten, he demands restitution. Since this can scarcely, indeed hardly ever, be done by such people, he orders them to give those goods to the poor, and then at last he teaches that the rest of their possessions will be clean, once what was gained by wickedness has been thrown far off and removed. So this passage was foolishly brought forward by those who teach the satisfactions by which, they say, we expiate our sins. For Christ did not here undertake to teach what method of expiation or remission of sins there is before God, but by what means we may cleanse our possessions, so that their use may be pure and holy for us.

units.la: Continet autem locus hic praeclaram & in primis necessariam doctrinam de vera purificatione hominis tam interna quam externa. Vt enim Deo probemur, animos nostros purgari necesse est: & haec illa sanctimonia est, sine qua (Paulo teste) Deum nemo videbit. Nam qui spiritus est & veritas, in spiritu & veritate coli vult. At quomodo spiritu & mente sua illum vere colent, qui hanc pessimis cupiditatibus & peccati seruitio subiectam habent? Vt ergo co rda & animi purifi-centur, ante omnia videre oportet. Ad hoc autem nihil proderunt externa corporis exercitia, non ceremoniae illae, non pecuniarum quaelescunque erogationes, aut quaecunque alia huius generis ex-cogitari possunt. Nam etsi illa mundo magnifica videantur, ad animum tamen non pertingunt, proinde huc non possunt purificare. Aliud ergo medium, alia via & ratio quaerenda erit, qua in Dei conspectu purificemur. Est haec sola fides, quae in Euangelio traditur. Hac enim Iesum Christum apprehendimus, cuius sanguis (ut Ioannes inquit) nos emundat ab omni peccato, & qui peccatum id est, hostia pro peccato factus est pro nobis, ut nos per ipsum iustitia Dei efficeremur. Extra hunc nulla purificatio, nulla sanctificatio aut iustificatio inuenitur. Neque nos primi ita docemus, ut aduersarij nostri calumniantur, sed est haec communis Apostolorum omnium doctrina, quam ipsi ex Christi ore didicerunt. Patet hoc ex Actis Concilij vere Apostolici, quod Hierosolymis congregatum fuit aduersus eos, qui gentibus ad fidem conuersis circumcisione & alias legis ceremonias obtrudere conabantur. Illic enim cum multa prius disceptatio fuisset, Petrus tandem exurgens eiusmodi orationem habuit: Viri fratres, vos scitis Deum iam pridem inter nos elegisse me, ut per os meum audirent gentes verbum Euangelij, & crederent. Et Deus, qui nouit corda, dedit eis testimonium, dato ipsis Spiritu sancto, sicut & nobis: nihilque discreuit inter nos & illos, FIDE PURGATIS cordibus illorum. Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum imponendo iugum ceruici discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus? Sed per gratiam Domini IESV CHRISTI CREDIMVS nos seruatum iri, quemadmodum & illi. Quibus omnino consentiunt, quae in Synagoga Antiochena Paulus dixit: Notum sit vobis fratres, annuntiari vobis remissionem peccatorum per Iesum Christum: & ab omnibus, a quibus per Legem Mosis non potuistis absolui, per hunc QVEM VIS QVI CREDAT absolui. Itaque vera hominis purificatio in solo Christo habetur per fidem, sine qua ad Deum appropinquare impossibile est. Quoad vero externum rerum huius seculi vsum, haec quoque nobis purificantur, partim (ut Paulus docet) per gratiarum actionem, partim (quod hic Christus admonet) beneficentia in pauperes. Nam etsi hic de male partis opibus agatur, eas tamen, quae ex Dei benedictione obuenerunt, non alia conditione accipimus, quam ut primo quidem non strae necessitati seruiant, deinde ut nostra abundantia aliorum inopiae succurrat. Vnde sequitur, opes & earum vsum, cibos deniq; & quaecunque ad huius vitae sustentationem faciunt, solius illis polluta est & noxia, qui vel male ea acquisierunt, vel Deum non agnoscunt authorem, & simul pauperes inhumaniter negligunt. At ijs qui per fidem in Iesum Christum purificati sunt, pura sunt omnia: & bi male parta non retinent, ut infra in Zachaei exemplo videbimus, reliqui autem cum gratiarum actione vtuntur, & inopes sibi commendatos habent. Itaque discant omnes, relictis humanorum figmentorum obseruationibus, fide vera ampleCti Dei filium Iesum Christum, qui suo sanguine & spiritu purificatos diriget, ut vitam viuant innocuam, & huius seculi rebus bene vtantur, eosdem vero vbi huius vitae cursum emensi fuerint, in regnum suum caeleste colliget. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage contains an excellent and especially necessary teaching about the true purification of man, both inward and outward. For that we may be approved by God, our minds must be cleansed; and this is that holiness without which, as Paul testifies, no one will see God. For he who is Spirit and truth wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth. But how will they truly worship him with their spirit and mind who have it subjected to the worst desires and to the slavery of sin? Therefore, if hearts and minds are to be purified, one must first look to them. Outward bodily exercises will profit nothing for this, nor those ceremonies, nor any kind of expenditure of money, nor whatever else of this sort can be devised. For although these seem splendid to the world, they do not reach the mind, and so they cannot purify there. Another means, another way and method must therefore be sought, by which we may be purified in the sight of God. This alone is faith, which is delivered in the Gospel. For by it we lay hold of Jesus Christ, whose blood (as John says) cleanses us from all sin, and who, though he knew no sin, was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin, for us, so that through him we might be made the righteousness of God. Outside of him no purification, no sanctification or justification is found. Nor do we teach this first, as our adversaries slander us; it is the common doctrine of all the Apostles, which they learned from the mouth of Christ himself. This is evident from the Acts of the truly Apostolic Council, which was gathered at Jerusalem against those who tried to force circumcision and the other ceremonies of the law upon Gentiles converted to the faith. There, after much debate had taken place, Peter rose up and gave a speech of this kind: "Brethren, you know that God chose me long ago from among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe. And God, who knows the hearts, bore them witness by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, their hearts being PURIFIED BY FAITH. Now therefore why do you tempt God by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also are." What Paul said in the synagogue of Antioch agrees entirely with these words: "Be it known to you, brethren, that the forgiveness of sins is announced to you through Jesus Christ; and from all those things from which you could not be absolved by the Law of Moses, through this one WHOEVER BELIEVES IS ABSOLVED." Therefore the true purification of man is had in Christ alone, through faith, without which it is impossible to draw near to God. As for the outward use of the things of this world, these too are purified for us, partly (as Paul teaches) by thanksgiving, and partly (as Christ here admonishes) by beneficence towards the poor. For although here it is a question of wealth wrongly gotten, yet those things which come to us by God's blessing we receive on no other condition than that, first, they serve our own need, and then that our abundance relieves the want of others. Hence it follows that riches and their use, food finally, and whatever serves the sustenance of this life, are polluted and harmful only to those who either acquired them wickedly, or do not acknowledge God as their author, and at the same time inhumanly neglect the poor. But to those who have been purified through faith in Jesus Christ, all things are pure; and they do not keep what was wrongly gotten, as we shall see below in the example of Zacchaeus, while the rest use their goods with thanksgiving and have the needy commended to them. Let all therefore learn, leaving aside the observances of human inventions, to embrace through true faith the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who, cleansing them by his blood and Spirit, will direct them to live an innocent life and to use the things of this world well, and who, when they have finished the course of this life, will gather them into his heavenly kingdom. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXI.

units.la: Sed vae vobis Pharisaeis, quoniam decimatis mentham & rutham, & quoduis olus, sed praeteritis iudicium & charitatem Dei. Haec autem oportuit facere, & illa non omittere. Vae vobis Pharisaeis, quoniam diligitis primum consessum in conuentibus, & salutationes in foris. Vae vobis Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae, quoniam estis vt monumenta, quae non apparent, & quae nescuint ij, qui super ea ambulant.
units.tr: "But woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and every herb, but pass over judgment and the love of God. These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the chief seats in the synagogues and greetings in the markets. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them."

units.la: DOminus & seruator noster Iesus Christus, in hoc cap. multa dixit de vera doctrina verbi Dei, docens, quae huius sit ratio, quam vtilis item atq; necessaria sit, & quam graues paenae huius temptores maneant. Quoniam vero sub huius praetextu fere ab impostoribus falsa doctrina obtruditur, quae verum Dei cultum corrumpit, & hominum mentes a Deo ad superstitiones auocat, commodissimo ordine nunc de illa quoq; agit, & quid e inter Pharisaeos, qui illo tempore praecipui erant eius professores. Suo autem exemplo docet nequaquam sufficere, si veritatis doctrina pure & simpliciter proponatur, sed falsam quoq; argui oportere, ne simplices & rerum imperiti per ignorantiam seducantur. Exponit autem Pharisaeorum mores atq; studia, ut ex his falsae doctrinae effectus aut fructus cognoscere discamus, & his cognitis illam magis abominemur. Primo loco autem fucata sanctimoniam posuit, quasi se venditabant, quoad ablutiones frequentes & purificationes externas, cum de cordis puritate nihil omnino essent foliciti. Hus in præsenti alia subijcit, nec (vt cœperat) simplici orationis genere vtitur, sed diris imprecationibus agit, partim quod incurabiles esse sciret, & proinde dignos extremis supplicijs: partim vt omnes intelligant hic de re maximi momenti agi, neq; ab ijs se jedu- ci patiantur, quibus leuiculum videtur, etiamsi doctrina, quæ vulgo proponitur, non per omnia cum verbo Dei conueniat.
units.tr: The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, in this chapter, says many things about the true doctrine of the word of God. He teaches what its nature is, how useful and how necessary it is, and what severe punishments await its despisers. Since, however, under the pretext of this doctrine, false teaching is usually imposed by impostors, which corrupts the true worship of God and draws men's minds away from God into superstitions, he now deals with that too, in a most fitting order, and with the Pharisees, who at that time were the chief professors of it. By his own example he teaches that it is by no means enough to set out the doctrine of truth purely and simply; the false must also be refuted, lest the simple and the inexperienced be led astray through ignorance. He sets out the manners and pursuits of the Pharisees so that we may learn from them the effects or fruits of false doctrine, and, having recognised these, may abhor it all the more. First of all he names their feigned sanctity, by which they made a display of themselves in frequent washings and outward purifications, while they took no thought at all for purity of heart. Now in the present passage he adds other woes, and he does not use the simple manner of speaking he had begun with, but utters dreadful imprecations. This is partly because he knew they were incurable and therefore deserving of the extreme penalties, and partly so that everyone may understand that a matter of the greatest importance is being dealt with here, and that they should not allow themselves to be led away by those who regard it as trivial, even though the doctrine commonly put forward does not agree in all things with the word of God.

units.la: Væ vobis Pharisæis (inquit) quoniam decimatis mentham & rutam, & quoduis olus, sed pa- teritis iudicii & charitatem Dei. Obijcit, quod minutissima quæq; anxiè & solicitè obseruent, gra- uiora autem negligant. Est hoc hypocritæ proprium, quod quam minimo labore & sumptu Deum colere cupiunt, ea autem prætermittunt, quæ carni molesta & præstitu difficiliora sunt. At hypocri- sim cum falsa doctrina coniunctam esse, nemo ignorat, quæ in hoc illis assentitur, & ipsa quoq; non nisi externa quædam exigit, quæ per se non magni momenti sunt. Adducit aut exempli loco, quo il- los conuincat, quod circa decimas faciebant, in quibus soluendis diligentissimos fuisse infra in Pha- risæi sua iustitia iactantis parabola patebit. Decimatis (inquit) mentha & rutam, et quoduis olus. Atqui hoc per se non erat reprehensione dignum. Scimus enim à Deo mandatum fuisse, vt filij Israe- lis ex agrorum suorum prouentu decimas ipsi consecrarent, & earundem vsus sanctissimus erat præscriptus. Nam ad cultus diuini conseruationem faciebant, cum ex illis Sacerdotes & Leuitæ alerentur: & quædam illarum pars pauperibus cedebat, quos ita ali volebat Deus, ne inopia & fa- mes illos mendicare, & publica miseria exempla fieri cogeret. Ideo Malachias Propheta sacrilegij eos accusat, qui in decimis fraudem committebant. Num (inquit Dominus) homo Deum spoliabit? Vos autem me spoliastis, & dicitis: In quo te spoliauimus? In decimis & oblationibus. Ideo execra- tione maledicti estis vos tota gens, quod me spoliauistis, &c. Cur ergo (inquis) curiosam & diligente proventuum decimationem Christus ipsis vitio vertit, & propter hanc væ illud horrendum ipsis im- precatur? Non propter hanc quidem id facit, sed quod ea tam Deo quam hominibus fucum facie- bant, & quasi iam omni pietatis officio defuncti essent, ea negligebant, in quibus tam Dei cultus quà vitæ sanctimonia vel innocentia præcipue constituunt, iudicii videlicet & charitatis Dei. Ideo ne quis ex hoc dicto calumniandi occasione arriperet, quasi decimarum solutione damnando Dei le- gem violaret, & populo tumultuandi occasione præberet, per Præoccupationem addit: Hæc autem opor- tuit facere, & illa non omittere. Quod autem ipsis hic exprobratur, id hodie etiam admodum vul- gare est, & in toto Papatu ista hypocrisis regnat. Nam si Monachos inspicias, iulicitos valde vi- debis, ne in vestitu, esu, incessu aliquid faciant ordinis sui legibus siue statutis contrarium. At ple- risq; illorum nulla religio est, rudem populum putidissimis figmentis circunducere, hæreditates alienas intercipere, violare virgines, thoros item alienos polluere, principes aduersus pios Christi cultores inflammare, vt in hos ferro & igne grassentur: deniq; omnes Dei leges securi transgrediuntur, modo sui ordinis exsistimationi & commodis consulant. Imitantur deinde hos, quicunq; ab ipsorum doctri- na pendent. Hus enim durum & inexpiabile scelus videtur, si quis in interdicto die carnes edat, aut ouum degustet, si votum Deo alicui factum non exoluat, si missæ non interfit, si solicitum precularii numerum non quotidie demurmuret, aut quid aliud omittat eorum quæ superstitiosi homines excogitarunt. At ijdem absq; omni numinis metu vsuras iniquissimas exercent, fortantur, mæchantur ebrietate & intemperantia se perdunt, per omnia sacra deierant, bella sectantur mercenaria, in quibus omnia fiunt, quibus Christiani nominis professio turpissime prophanatur. Quid vero hoc a- liud est, quam culicem colare, camelum autem deglutire, vel (quod hic Pharisæus exprobratur) men- thæ & rutæ atq; olerum vilissimorum decimatione velle satisfacere Deo, omissis ijs, quæ is potissi- mum requirit? Sibi ergo dictum putent omnes isti, quod Pharisæus in præsenti dicitur.
units.tr: "Woe unto you, Pharisees," he says, "for you tithe mint and rue and every herb, but pass over judgment and the love of God." He rebukes them because they observed the smallest matters anxiously and carefully, but neglected the weightier ones. This is characteristic of a hypocrite, who wants to worship God with the least possible labour and expense, while he skips over what is burdensome to the flesh and harder to perform. No one doubts that hypocrisy is joined with false doctrine, which agrees with this, and which itself demands only certain external things that are not of great importance in themselves. Christ uses as an example, to convict them, what they did with regard to tithes. In the parable of the Pharisee boasting of his righteousness, which comes later, it will be clear how diligently they paid them. "You tithe mint and rue," he says, "and every herb." Yet in itself this was not worthy of reproof. We know that God commanded the children of Israel to consecrate tithes of the produce of their fields to him, and the most holy use of these was prescribed. For they were given to maintain the worship of God, since priests and Levites were fed from them; and part of them went to the poor, whom God wished to be supported in this way, so that want and hunger would not compel them to beg and become examples of public misery. So the prophet Malachi accuses of sacrilege those who committed fraud in the tithes: "Will a man rob God? Yet you have robbed me, and you say, 'In what have we robbed you?' In tithes and offerings. You are cursed with a curse, you whole nation, because you have robbed me," and so on. Why, then, you may ask, does Christ find fault with their careful and diligent tithing of produce, and pronounce this dreadful woe upon them because of it? He does not do so because of this, but because they used these things to deceive both God and men, and, as if they had already discharged every duty of piety, they neglected those matters in which the worship of God and the holiness, or rather the innocence, of life chiefly consist, namely judgment and the love of God. So that no one might seize on this saying as an occasion for slander, as if by condemning the payment of tithes he were violating God's law and giving the people an occasion for tumult, he adds by way of anticipation: "But these things ought to have been done, and those not left undone." What is reproached in them here is, today, also very common, and in the whole Papacy this hypocrisy reigns. For if you look at the monks, you will see them very scrupulous about their clothing, food and gait, lest they do anything contrary to the rules or statutes of their order. Yet most of them have no religion at all: they lead the uneducated people about with the most foul fictions, seize other people's inheritances, violate virgins, and defile other men's beds; they also inflame princes against the pious worshippers of Christ, so that they may rage against them with sword and fire. Finally, they transgress all the laws of God without a qualm, provided they look after the reputation and advantage of their order. Those who depend on their teaching then imitate them. For it seems to these men a hard and unpardonable crime if someone eats meat on a forbidden day, or tastes an egg, or fails to fulfil a vow made to some god, or does not attend Mass, or does not murmur daily the required number of prayers from the breviary, or omits anything else that superstitious men have devised. Yet these same men, without any fear of the divine power, practise the most unjust usury, commit fornication and adultery, ruin themselves by drunkenness and intemperance, swear by every sacred thing, pursue mercenary wars in which everything is done that most shamefully profanes the profession of the Christian name. What else is this, then, than to strain out a gnat and swallow a camel? Or (what is here reproached in the Pharisee) to wish to satisfy God by tithing mint and rue and the cheapest herbs, while leaving aside those things which he especially requires? Let all these men, therefore, take to themselves what is said here of the Pharisee.

units.la: At simul docet etiam Christus, quæ vera sit legis Dei obseruatio. Sunt in hac quædam grauiora capita siue mandata, quæ apud Matthæum ipse Dominus sic vocat, partim quod in illis Dei cultus & vitæ puritas potissimum consistant, partim quod non nisi à germanis Dei filijs, qui verè renati sunt præstari possint. Ad horum censum totum decalogus pertinet, & quæ hic à Christo nominantur de quibus mox dicemus. Deinde sunt leuiora nonnulla, quæ ab hypocritis quoq; & quibusuis alijs fa- cile possunt perfici, vt decimarum & primitiarum oblationes, sacrificia & (vt uno verbo omnia com- plectar) ceremoniæ seu externi ritus, quotquot in lege præscribuntur. In utroq; mandatorum genere observar
units.tr: At the same time Christ also teaches what the true observance of God's law is. Within it there are certain weightier heads, or commandments, which the Lord himself in Matthew calls by that name, partly because the worship of God and the purity of life chiefly consist in them, and partly because they can be performed only by the true sons of God, who have been truly born again. The whole Decalogue belongs to the number of these, together with what Christ names here and of which we shall speak shortly. Then there are some lighter matters, which can easily be performed even by hypocrites and by anyone at all, such as the offerings of tithes and firstfruits, sacrifices and (to sum up everything in one word) the ceremonies or external rites, however many are prescribed in the law. In both kinds of commandment observ[ance ...]

units.la: Luc. 18.
units.tr: Luk. 18.

units.la: Malach. 3. observari debet regula Christi, quam hic praescribit. Ut nimirum minima quidem haec sedulò praestemus, maiora autem illa & graviora non negligamus. Et in iis quidem, quae minoris videntur esse momenti obedientiae studendum est, quia nihil frustra praecipit Deus, etiamsi nō semper prae eptorum suorum rationem nobis reddat: & quod qui in parvis peccare assuefscunt, ij plerunque ulterius progrediuntur, ut maiora quoque non magni faciant. Exemplum eius rei in Saule habemus, qui a parvis inobedientiae initiis ad incurabilem contumaciam pervenit, quae ipsum tandem ad desperationis praecipitium adduxit. Et haec causa est, quod Deus capitales poenas iis statuit, qui vel circumcisionem neglexissent in suis filijs, vel Paschatis diebus aliquid fermentatum comedissent: quod item Aaronis filios propter alienum ignem ad sacra illatum flammis, coelitus immissis, combusit. Voluit enim exemplâ extare, quae nos perterrefaciant, ne leviculu puremus ab eius praeceptis vel latum unguem deflectere. Caeterum dum in minoribus sumus occupati, diligenter videre nos oportet, ne maiora negligamus: quod ut Pharisaei olim fecere, ita multi hodie faciunt, qui pietatem omnem in externis quibusdam actiunculis consistere putant. Atqui inutilis, adeoque nulla est istorum omnium obedientia. Ut enim non probatur bono patri filius, qui in minimis officijs obeundis sedulus est, ea autem praetermittit, ex quibus familiae totius incolumitas & ipsius patris existimatio atque gloria dependent: ita neque eorum obedientia Deo placebit, qui leviora sedulò praestant, ea autem negligunt, qui bus gloria illius & tam ipsorum quam aliorum hominum salus in primis promovetur.
units.tr: Malach. 3. The rule of Christ, which he prescribes here, ought to be observed: namely, that we should indeed diligently perform these lesser things, and yet not neglect those greater and weightier ones. And in those matters which seem to be of less importance, obedience must be pursued, because God commands nothing in vain, even though he does not always render to us the reason for his precepts; and because those who accustom themselves to sin in small things commonly go further, so that they no longer hold greater things in esteem. We have an example of this in Saul, who from small beginnings of disobedience came to an incurable obstinacy, which at last brought him to the precipice of despair. And this is the reason why God appointed capital punishments for those who had neglected circumcision in their sons, or had eaten anything leavened during the days of the Passover; and likewise why he consumed the sons of Aaron with flames sent from heaven for bringing strange fire into the sacred rites. For he wished examples to stand which might terrify us, lest we should turn aside from his precepts even by a hair's breadth in matters that seem trifling. Yet while we are occupied with the lesser things, we must carefully see to it that we do not neglect the greater; as the Pharisees once did, and as many do today, who think that all piety consists in certain trifling outward acts. But the obedience of all these people is useless and indeed worthless. For just as a good father does not approve of a son who is diligent in the smallest duties but omits those on which the safety of the whole household, and the father's own reputation and glory, depend, so the obedience of those will not please God who diligently perform the lighter things but neglect those by which his glory, and the salvation both of themselves and of other men, is chiefly advanced.

units.la: Ut vero minus peccemus, quae nā graviora illa Legis capita sint, videre oportet. Apud Matth. tria nominantur, Iudicium, Misericordia & fides. In praesenti duo tantum, Iudicium & charitas Dei, quae & fidem & misericordiam complectitur. Iudicij nomine Hebraei fere cuiusque hominis decorā fiu e officium intelligunt, cui pro suae vocationis ratione intentus esse debet. Quod quia in se iustitiam & aequitate vnā cum omnibus, quae alijs hominibus debentur, officijs comprehendit, iudicium facere dicuntur, qui officium faciunt & vnicuique tribuunt, quod suum est. Extenditur ergo primum hoc caput per omnes hominum ordines, & ab hoc ordiri voluit Christus, nō quod quae hominib. debemus, ijs praeferri debeant, quae directè ad Deum pertinent: sed quia in illis facile cernitur, quo animo erga Deū & legem eius simus affecti. Hic ergo singulos videre convenit, quâ personâ ipsis Deus impo-fuerit, & quid alijs debeant. Et ut ab ijs, qui magistratum gerunt, exordiamur, borum est, ut ante omnia Dei gloriā quaerant, & ita se huic gratos praebeant, qui ad tā sublime honoris & dignitatis fastigiū eos euexit. Curet ergo ut huius verbū pure praedicetur, cultus recte instituatur, utq; huius praeceptis populus obtemperet. Quoad vero Reipub. administrationē, Dei iudicia enuntient, non sua placita te mere proferant, ius dicant in iustitia absq; omni persona respectu, ut Dei ingenium referant, cuius vice gerunt. Beneficii item sint in pauperes, cuius vel vetustissimus ille titulus admonere debet, quo Christus illos antiquitus ornatos fuisse testatur. Afflictos vindicent à vi & calumniis: populū à se nore & vsura liberent, & pretiosum ducant sanguine subditorum suorū, ideoq; in iudicijs non praecipites sint, neq; bella moveant nō necessaria. Haec qui praestant, ij in Repub. verè iudicii faciunt. Ut cissim vero populi est, principes suos amare, observare, colere, ijsdem obedire, & si ita opus sit, cū for tunis omnibus sanguine quoq; pro illorū & Reipub. salute deponere: & ita ipsi quoq; iudicium facient. Eadem est ratio inter parentes & liberos. Illorum enim est ex se natos honestè educare, in Dei cognitione & vera pietate instituere, aetatem teneram bonis moribus formare, & ijsdem quoad eius fieri potest prospicere, ut honestè & commode vitā transigere possint. Liberi vero parentes amore & honore prosequi debent, & hunc animum suum obedientia sedula omniq; officiorū genere testlari: in primis autem curare, ne senio confectis aliquid desit. Habent etiā suum iudicium coniuges, quod in eo versatur, ut fide coniugalem vtring; inviolatā feruent, sese mutuū ament, honestati studeant, & omnem fortunam patienter simul ferant. Ita iudicium facient heri, si seruos suos & homines & suos in Christo fratres esse meminerint, & proinde illis non abutantur, vitium item & quod eis praeterea debetur, amicè & liberaliter numerent. Rursus horum officium est, heris obsequi, commodis eorū studere & fideliter praestare, quod illis vel ex pacto, vel ex servitij iure debent. Posset hoc ipsum ad venden tes & ementes, ad opifices, agricolas, milites & ad quosuis alios extendi: sed sufficiat occasione cogitandi dedisse ijs, qui nondū omnē numinis metū abiecerūt: & meminerint omnes, inter praecipua legis capita hoc haberi, ut singuli in sua vocatione officiū faciat. Hoc enim ut nos in Dei obsequio cōtinēt ita etiā plurimū cōsolatur, quod nos in quouis vitae genere ipsi gratū officiū praestare posse scimus.
units.tr: But in order to sin less, we must see which of the Law's weightier heads these are. In Matthew three are named: judgment, mercy and faith. In the present passage he names only two, judgment and the love of God, which also embraces both faith and mercy. Under the name of judgment the Hebrews understand almost the proper duty of each person, to which he must attend according to the nature of his calling. Because this duty includes in itself justice and fairness, along with everything owed to other people, those who perform their duty and render to each what is his are said to do judgment. This first head therefore extends through all the orders of men, and Christ wished to begin with it, not because what we owe to human beings should be preferred to what pertains directly to God, but because in these duties it is easily seen with what attitude we stand towards God and his law. Here, then, we should look at each man: by what person God has placed him, and what he owes to others. To begin with those who bear the magistracy: it is their task, above all, to seek the glory of God, and so to show themselves grateful to him who has raised them to so high a summit of honour and dignity. Let them therefore see that his Word is preached purely, that true worship is established, and that the people obey his precepts. As for the administration of the commonwealth, let them declare the judgments of God and not utter their own whims, and let them dispense justice in righteousness without any respect of persons, so that they reflect the character of God, whose vice-regents they are. Likewise let them be beneficent to the poor, which that most ancient title ought to remind them of, by which Christ testifies that the poor were adorned from of old. Let them defend the afflicted from violence and slander; let them free the people from oppression and usury, and let them count the blood of their subjects precious; therefore let them not be hasty in judgments, nor stir up wars that are not necessary. Those who do these things truly do judgment in the commonwealth. On the other hand, it is the duty of the people to love, observe and honour their princes, to obey them, and, if need be, to lay down for their safety and that of the commonwealth all their fortunes, even their blood; and in this way they too will do judgment. The same reasoning holds between parents and children. For it is the parents' task to bring up honourably those born of them, to instruct them in the knowledge of God and true piety, to form their tender age in good morals, and to provide for them, as far as it can be done, so that they may live honourably and comfortably. Children, for their part, ought to show their parents love and honour, and to attest this disposition by diligent obedience and every kind of duty; and above all to take care that nothing is lacking to them when they are worn out with age. Spouses also have their judgment, which consists in this: that each keeps the marriage bed inviolate in faith, that they love one another, strive for honesty, and bear every fortune patiently together. Masters will do judgment in this way if they remember that their servants are men and their brothers in Christ, and therefore do not abuse them, and that they pay them amicably and generously what is further owed. Again, it is the duty of servants to obey their masters, to be concerned for their interests, and to perform faithfully what they owe them by contract or by the right of service. This could be extended to sellers and buyers, to craftsmen, farmers, soldiers and any others; but let it suffice to have given occasion for reflection to those who have not yet cast off all fear of God. Let all remember that among the chief heads of the Law this is counted: that each one does his duty in his own calling. For this both keeps us in the service of God and also greatly comforts us, because we know that in whatever station of life we are, we can render a pleasing duty to him.

units.la: Secundo loco charitatem Dei ponit Christus, sub qua fidem erga hunc & simul misericordiam comprehendi diximus. Et Deo quidem amorem atque dilectionem deberi, communis sensus docet: quia nos creauit, perditos in Filio suo vnigenito regenuit, in filiorum locum adoptauit, neque his contentus, insuper nobis in singulas horas prospicit, quoad corporis & animae salutem. At qui ista beneficia Dei agnoscunt, ij hunc non vulgari solum amore prosequuntur, verumetiam in eodem omnem spem atque fiduciam collocant, & ab illo vno pendent, vnde obedientia vera, cultus denique Dei purus atq; syncerus nascitur. Neq; abesse potest ab hac Dei dilectione dilectio proximi vel quo rumus aliorum hominum. Quomodo enim hos non amabimus, quos ille nobis tantopere commendat, qui ipsum vnā nobiscum Patris nomine inuocant, qui nostri in Christo fratres atq; coelestis regni coharedes sunt?
