Dilectionis autem huius effectus siue fructus est misericordia, qua fit, vt aliorum miseriis tangamur, & ne requisiti quidem illos nostra ope & consilio iuuemus, quos ijs opus habere cernimus, vt in Samaritani parabola Christus docuit. Ita vero idem ille hoc loco duobus capitibus praecipua legis mandata, imo legem totam comprehendit. Illis ergo singuli studeant, ne hu neglectis circa minutiora quaedam & inutiles ceremonias frustra occupentur, quod hic in Pharisaeis reprehenditur.
units.tr: In the second place Christ puts the love of God, under which, as we have said, faith towards him and mercy are included. That we owe love and affection to God, common sense teaches: because he created us, restored us when we were lost in his only-begotten Son, adopted us into the place of sons, and, not content with this, provides for us every hour, both for the health of body and of soul. Those who acknowledge these benefits of God pursue him not merely with ordinary love, but also place in him all their hope and trust, and depend wholly on him, from whom true obedience and pure and sincere worship of God are born. Nor can love of neighbour, or of the welfare of other men, be absent from this love of God. For how shall we not love those whom he so strongly commends to us, who together with us call upon him by the name of Father, who are our brothers in Christ and co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom? The effect or fruit of this love is mercy, by which we are moved by the miseries of others, and, even without being asked, help with our aid and counsel those whom we see to need them, as Christ taught in the parable of the Samaritan. Thus this same Christ, in this place, comprehends the chief commandments of the Law in two heads, indeed the whole Law. Let each therefore take care not to be occupied in vain with certain minor matters and useless ceremonies while neglecting these, which is what is rebuked in the Pharisees here.

units.la: At si nostri seculi mores diligentius excutiamus, omnis fere loci & ordinis homines ad eundem lapidem offendere videbis. Cum Pharisaei enim peccant Ecclesiarum ministri, qui res leuiores momenti, & quae ipsorum potius comodis quam publicae omnium saluti seruiunt, constanter vrgent & exigunt, nihil interea soliciti de ijs, quibus Dei gloria & populi salus promouetur. Est hoc frequens admodum in Papatu, vbi Missas neglexisse, non confessum esse sacerdoti, non obtulisse pecuniam in altari, votum Diuo nuncupatum non persoluisse, & alia huiusmodi pro capitalibus sceleribus & excommunicatione digna habentur, & in hac magna tum contentione Monachi & Doctores reliqui declamant, qui interim ad aliorum stupra, adulteria, execrationes, vsuras, homicidia quoq; & immanissima quaeq; flagitia conniuent. Neq; ab hac culpa omnino immunes sunt concionatores Euangelici, quorum multi in vulgaribus populi vitijs exagitandis ferunt, in atrocissimis autem magnatum sceleribus canes muti sunt. Peccant hic etiam principes & magistratus, si ijs modo intenti sunt quae ad ipsorum honorem spectant, & lucrum ipsis priuatum, vel etiam publicum ferunt, Dei vero cultum & populi salutem securi negligunt. Peccatur item a priuatis hominibus, vt quando parentes liberis suis solum quoad victum & res huius seculi prospiciunt, non autem curant, vt in Dei cognitione & pietate instituantur, quae praesentis & futuri seculi promissiones habet. Idem fere inter coniuges solet fieri, dum amori quidem coniugali & rei domesticae intenti sunt, pietatis autem officia intermittunt. Quod ipsum de heris quoq; & seruis dici potest, inter quos illi quidem seruos inter dum satis humaniter tractant, nullam autem fidei & religionis ipsorum rationem habent, neq; illis cordi est, vt coetus sacros inuisant, verbum Dei audiant, precibus publicis intersint & Coenae mystica communicent: hi vero ad oculum quidem seruiunt, animis autem ab heris suis sunt alienissimi, adhaec impatienter & cum murmure seruitutis iugum ferunt. Hi omnes dici possunt mentham & anethum siue rutam decimare, ea vero praetermittere, quae grauiora sunt.
units.tr: But if we examine more carefully the manners of our own age, you will see men of almost every place and order stumbling over the same stone. For just as the Pharisees sinned, so do the ministers of the churches, who constantly press and exact matters of lesser moment, which serve their own advantage rather than the common salvation of all, while being unconcerned about those things by which the glory of God and the salvation of the people are advanced. This is very frequent in Papistry, where failing to attend Mass, not confessing to the priest, not offering money at the altar, not paying a vow made to a saint, and other things of this kind are counted as capital crimes and worthy of excommunication; and in this great contention the monks and the other teachers declaim, while meanwhile they connive at the debaucheries, adulteries, curses, usuries, even murders and all the most monstrous crimes of others. Nor are the evangelical preachers wholly free from this fault: many of them rage against the common vices of the people, but against the most atrocious crimes of the great they are dumb dogs. Princes and magistrates also sin here, if they are intent only on those things which regard their own honour, and bring in private gain or even public revenue, but carelessly neglect the worship of God and the safety of the people. Private persons also sin, as when parents provide for their children only as regards food and the things of this age, but take no care that they be instructed in the knowledge and piety of God, which holds the promises of the present and future age. Much the same is usually done between spouses, while they are intent indeed on conjugal love and domestic affairs, but omit the duties of piety. The same can be said of masters and servants: masters sometimes treat their servants quite humanely, yet take no account of their faith and religion, nor do they care that they visit the sacred assemblies, hear the Word of God, take part in public prayers and partake of the mystical Supper. The servants, for their part, serve indeed in appearance, but in their hearts they are most alienated from their masters, and moreover bear the yoke of servitude impatiently and with murmuring. All these may be said to tithe mint and dill or rue, but to pass over the weightier matters.

units.la: Sed in Christi verbis progrediamur, qui tertio loco ambitionem & inanem dignitatis ostentationem Pharisaeis exprobrat, qui etiam falsae doctrinae & antistitum eius proprissimus fructus est. Cur enim hi fucatae sanctimoniae studeant, quam vt magni fiant & ab omnibus in pretio habeantur? Ideo apud Matthaeum hoc illorum vitium diligentius exponens ait: Omnia opera sua faciunt vt spectentur ab hominibus. Quibus verbis discrimen inter hypocritas & vere pios continetur. Hienim studiorum & actionum omnium hunc finem sibi propositum habent, vt & Deo placeant, & alijs bono exemplo sint. Illi vero de Dei gloria parum soliciti, hoc vnum quaerunt, vt coram mundo gloriosi sint. Pij ergo casta & fidelis matronae ingenii atque mores referunt, quae vni marito placere studet, neq; impudicorum amatorum iudicia moratur: hypocritae autem perfidarum vxorum & adulterarum similes sunt, quae neglectis & contemptis maritis suis in aliorum gratiam comuntur atque ornantur. Sed ne Pharisaeis iniuriam Christus facere videatur, speciem vnam atque alteram vanae ostentationis adducit, vt eos conuincat. Dilatant (inquit) phylacteria sua, & producunt fimbrias palliorum suorum. Iusserat Deus, vt praecipua legis suae capita Iudaei in fimbriis vestium descripta gestarent, & postibus ostiorum suorum insculperent, ut ea ratione ad perpetuam suae voluntatis mem ditationem excitarentur. Ut ergo Pharisaei apud vulgus existimationem sibi pararent, quasi prae aliis divinae Legis studiosi essent, phylacteria, id est, memoriales illas fimbrias latissimas facere solebant, ut plures Legis sententias illus possent inscribere, cum interim huius observandae cura nulla illos tangeret. Erat ergo haec inanis ostentatio, quam Dei praeceptum non excusabat, quia & Deum & Legem eius habebant ludibrio. Huic aliam speciem subjicit Dominus, cuius & hic Lucas meminit, qui illum dixisse scribit: Vae vobis Pharisaei, quoniam diligitis primum consessum in conuentibus, & salutationes in foro. Apud Matthaeum formula quoq; salutationum exprimitur, quod Rabbi dici vellent, quae vox excellentis & multiplicis doctrinae hominem significat, & proinde Doctorum titulo respondet, quo hodie in scholis Christianorum superbitur. Non autem simpliciter iustos honorum gradus aut titulos Christus damnat, sed illos reprehendit, quod qui se melioribus debebantur honores, ipsi privata ambitione sibi vendicarent, & in ipsde modum omne excederent. Manet enim firma & rata Lex Dei, qui parentes & eos, qui parentum loco sunt, honorare iubet, & coram cano capite assurgere. Et notum est illud Apostoli, qui monet, ut alij alios honore praeueniant. Quam multos autem hodie est videre, in quos haec Christi verba dici possunt? Inter eos certe, qui primi Ecclesiae totius proceres haberi volunt, nō alium finem aut scopum propositum esse videmus, quam ut ab hominibus spectentur. Ideo enim vestitum sibi peculiarem & plane theatricum excogitarunt, cui cruces varias & alia pietatis insignia addunt. Quam vero ambitiose primos honores ambiant, norunt omnes qui in Regum & principum aulis versantur. Illic enim primae etiam nobilitatis homines Episcopus & Monachus infimo loco natus, & quos neque virtus neq; eruditio commendat, primos accubitos cedere, seq; illis seruiliter submittere coguntur. Taceo Pontificum insolentiam, quos non pudet ad pedum suorum osculā Reges atque Imperatores vocare, Quod si titulos illorum audias, quid aliud quam ambitionem & superbiam plane Luciferianam spirant? Alij enim Pastores vniuersales totius Ecclesiae per orbem dispersae dici volunt, neque eo contenti sunt, nisi Caput etiā Ecclesiae, Vicarij Iesu Christi, Sanctissimi & ipsa Sanctitas dicantur. Alij reuerendissimi & Reuerendi appellantur, & ijdem Beneficorum & ipsius gratia titulos sibi vendicant, qui ex veteri more principibus viri debentur. Inter Monachos autem, qui se mundo mortuos profitentur, Doctorum illuminatissimorum, Seraphicorum, Subtilium, Magistrorum nostrorū nomina sonant. Et vt satis ineptos sese sua ambitione praebeant, sunt quos delectat, si Mallei haereticorum, Candelabra Ecclesiae, Luminaria, imo ipsa Lux mundi dicantur. Vtinam vero extra omnem culpam hic essent nostrum aliquot, quos aurae popularis studium, principum fauor, seruilis scholarium applausus & titulorum insolitorum splendor non minus delectant. Nam vt scholasticos honorum gradus, qui ad diligentiam in iuuenibus excitandam instituti sunt in bonarum artium, Medicinae & Iurisprudentia studio nunquā improbauerim: ita non video qua ratione excusari possint, qui in Theologiae studiū eosdem inferunt, & eos superbi titulis inebriant, qui crucis Christi & humilitatis doctores aliquando fieri debent. Quid autem de illis dicemus, qui postquam in Ecclesiae ministerio multis annis versati sunt, Doctoratus insignibus ornari volunt, vt ad pinguius aliquod munus Ecclesiasticum promoueri, aut sub Superintendentium titulo quaestuosam in alios ministros dominiū obtinere possint? Viderint illi quam procul a Pharisaeorum moribus absint, & annon tota illorum actio Simoniaca dici mereatur? Satis certe testantur, se non adeo magno gloriae Dei studio teneri, quae hodie pacsim periclitatur, cum suam tam anxie quaerant. Interim debet hinc generalis doctrina peti, vt omnes humilitati studeant secundum Christi exemplum, nec in ipsos quoque haec illius tam dira imprecatio cadat, eoq; grauiori lapsu ruant, quo altius sese supra alios extulerunt. Quid enim superbire iuuat, quando in iis quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt, nihil ex nobis ipsis possumus, in exteriorībus autem & huius seculi bonis nihil certum aut stabilire habetur?
units.tr: But let us go on with the words of Christ, who in the third place rebukes the Pharisees for ambition and empty display of dignity, which is also the most characteristic fruit of false doctrine and of its leaders. For why should these men pursue feigned holiness except to become great and be held in esteem by all? So Matthew, explaining this vice of theirs more carefully, says: "They do all their works to be seen by men." In these words the difference between hypocrites and truly godly people is set out. The godly have this one end before them in all their studies and actions: to please God and to be a good example to others. The hypocrites, caring little for the glory of God, seek only this, that they may be admired before the world. The godly therefore resemble a chaste and faithful wife, whose character and manners are such that she strives to please her one husband and does not care for the opinions of shameless lovers. The hypocrites, however, are like faithless and adulterous wives, who neglect and despise their husbands and dress and adorn themselves to win the favour of others. But lest Christ seem to do the Pharisees an injustice, he brings forward one or two examples of their empty show, so as to convict them. "They enlarge their phylacteries," he says, "and make broad the fringes of their garments." God had commanded that the Jews should wear the chief heads of his law written on the fringes of their garments and carve them on the posts of their doors, so that by this means they would be stirred to constant meditation on his will. The Pharisees, however, in order to win esteem among the common people, as if they were more devoted to the law of God than others, used to make their phylacteries, that is, those memorial fringes, very broad, so that they could inscribe more sentences of the Law on them, while at the same time they were not concerned at all to observe it. This was therefore empty display, which the command of God did not excuse, since they made both God and his Law a mockery. The Lord adds another example of this display, which Luke also mentions, writing that he said: "Woe to you, Pharisees, for you love the first seat in the assemblies and greetings in the marketplace." In Matthew the form of greeting is also expressed, that they wished to be called Rabbi, a word which signifies a man of outstanding and wide learning, and so corresponds to the title of Doctor, with which people today in the schools of Christians take pride. Christ does not, however, simply condemn honours or titles of rank, but rebukes the fact that men claimed for themselves by private ambition honours that were due to better men, and exceeded every measure in doing so. For the law of God stands firm and unchanged, which commands us to honour parents and those who take the place of parents, and to rise before the grey head. And the saying of the Apostle is well known, who bids us to go before one another in honour. But how many today may be found to whom these words of Christ may be applied? Among those certainly who wish to be regarded as the leading men of the whole Church, we see no other aim or purpose set before them than that they may be looked upon by men. For they have devised for themselves a special and quite theatrical garb, to which they add various crosses and other badges of piety. And how ambitiously they seek the first honours, all who live in the courts of kings and princes know. There, men of the highest nobility are compelled to give way to the bishop and the monk, born in the lowest rank, and whom neither virtue nor learning commends, and to submit themselves to these men in a servile manner in the places of honour at table. I say nothing of the arrogance of the popes, who are not ashamed to call kings and emperors to kiss their feet. And if you hear their titles, what else do they breathe but an ambition and pride altogether Luciferian? For some wish to be called universal ministers of the whole Church dispersed throughout the world, and are not content with this unless they are also called Head of the Church, Vicars of Jesus Christ, Most Holy, and Holiness itself. Others are styled Most Reverend and Reverend, and these same men claim for themselves the titles of benefices and of grace, which by ancient custom are due to princes. Among the monks, who profess themselves dead to the world, the names of Most Enlightened Doctors, Seraphic, Subtle, and Our Masters resound. And that they may show themselves quite foolish in their ambition, there are some who delight to be called the Hammer of Heretics, Candlesticks of the Church, Lights, and even the Light of the World. Would that some of our own people were free from all blame here, for whom the favour of the crowd, the goodwill of princes, the servile applause of students, and the splendour of unusual titles give no less pleasure. For, while I would never condemn the academic grades instituted to stir up diligence in young men in the study of the liberal arts, medicine, and law, I do not see on what ground they can be excused who introduce the same grades into the study of theology, and intoxicate them with proud titles, when they ought at some time to become teachers of the cross of Christ and of humility. And what shall we say of those who, after they have served many years in the ministry of the Church, wish to be adorned with the badges of a doctorate, so that they may be promoted to some more lucrative church office, or may be able to gain a profitable lordship over other ministers under the title of superintendent? Let them see how far they are from the manners of the Pharisees, and whether their whole conduct does not deserve to be called Simoniacal. They certainly bear witness well enough that they are not held by any great zeal for the glory of God, which today is everywhere in danger, when they seek their own so anxiously. Meanwhile, from this a general teaching should be drawn, that all should strive for humility after the example of Christ, and that this terrible curse of his may not fall upon themselves too, so that they fall with the heavier ruin the higher they have raised themselves above others. For what good is it to be proud, when in those things which pertain to eternal salvation we can do nothing of ourselves, and in outward things and the goods of this age nothing certain or stable can be relied upon?

units.la: Porrò redit ad hypocrisim Pharisaeorum Christus, & quam turpiter ea homines fallant, docet. Vae vobis Scribae (inquit) & Pharisaei hypocritae quoniā estis vt monumenta, quae nō apparent, et quae nesciunt ij, qui super ea ambulant. Apud Matthaeum haec quoque copiosius explicantur his verbis: Vae vobis Scribae & Pharisaei hypocritae quoniam assimiles estis sepulchris dealbatis, quae extra quidem apparent speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum, omniq; immunditia: Ita & vos extra quidem apparetis hominibus iusti, intus autem pleni estis hypocrisi & iniquitate. Coniungit nunc Pharisæos Scribas, vt clarius appareat de doctrina falsa & eius effectu agi. Et verba quidem perspicua sunt, cum ipse Dominus dicit, quid per dealbationem & ornatum sepulchrorum quiditem per ossa mortuorum & reliquas sordes, quæ in illis delitescunt, debeat intelligi. Differunt tamen Euangelistæ in eo, quod alter quidem sepulchrorum, quæ supra terram eriguntur & magnificè ornantur, meminit, alter vero eorum quæ intra humum effodiuntur, et ita rursus obruuntur, vt supra ea ambulare possit, & ita quidem, vt plerique sepulchra abs se calcari nesciant. Sed cum non eodem tempore & loco Christus utrunque dixerit, diuersis similibus vti voluit, vt hypocritis & falsa sanctimonia naturam siue proprietatem melius exprimeret. Ecenim pulchre hoc docetur, quæ illius sit conditio tam quoad Deum quam quoad homines. Speciosa quidem est hominum iudicio, qui præter externam speciem nihil vident: at coram Deo, qui in cordis penetralia vsque penetrat, non minus fœtet quam ossium & sepulchrorum immunditiæ. Mortua enim & nullius pretij sunt omnia opera quæ absque fide fiunt. Et quia Christus solus salutifer ille bonæ fragrantiæ odor est, propter quem Pater se nobis propitium præbet, non possunt non in eius conspectu facere quotquot sine illo Mediatore ad ipsum veniunt. Interim vt super sepulchra multi incedunt, & densos læti graminis cespites mirantur, ignorantes quid pedibus ipsorum subsit, & ideo interdum fractis sub terra mortuorum arcus subsidunt: ita rudes & imperiti rerum falsæ doctrinæ & simulatæ sanctimoniæ fuco decepti, ferè ijs nituntur, & hanc veram salutis viam esse putant, ignari quàm Deo displiceat, & quantum periculi animabus ipsorum hoc prætextu struat: multi etiam magno suo malo experiuntur, quàm turpiter & miserè sua spes ipsos fefellerit. Hæc igitur sic à Christo olim dicta esse meminerimus, vt nobis admonitioni esse debeant. Fugiamus ergo doctores, quotquot Pharisæorum mores & ingenium referunt, neque putemus Deum falso sanctimoniæ externæ prætextu vel demulceri vel falli posse: quin potius in hoc simus, vt cordibus vere purificatis per fidem in Iesum Christum, in eode vita viuamus nostra professione digna. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Again Christ turns to the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and teaches how shamefully men are deceived by it. "Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites," he says, "for you are like graves which do not appear, and those who walk over them do not know it." In Matthew these things are explained more fully in these words: "Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for you are like whitewashed sepulchres, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of all uncleanness. So you too outwardly appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity." Now he joins the Scribes with the Pharisees, so that it may be made clearer that he is speaking of false doctrine and its effect. The words themselves are plain, since the Lord himself says what is to be understood by the whitewashing and adornment of the sepulchres, and by the bones of the dead and the other filth which lies hidden within. The Evangelists differ, however, in this: one mentions the sepulchres that rise above the ground and are handsomely decorated, while the other mentions those that are dug into the earth and then covered over again, so that one can walk over them, and indeed in such a way that many do not know they are trampling on graves. But since Christ did not speak of both at the same time and place, he wished to use different likenesses, so as to express more clearly the nature and property of hypocrites and of false holiness. For this teaches well what their condition is, both in relation to God and in relation to men. It is indeed beautiful in the judgement of men, who see nothing beyond the outward appearance; but before God, who penetrates into the inmost recesses of the heart, it stinks no less than the uncleanness of bones and graves. For all works that are done without faith are dead and of no worth. And since Christ alone is that health-giving odour of good fragrance, on account of whom the Father shows himself favourable to us, all who come to him without this Mediator cannot but be such as to offend in his sight. Meanwhile, as many walk over graves, rejoicing in the thick turf of grass and admiring it, ignorant of what lies beneath their feet, and so sometimes sink through when the vaults of the dead give way beneath them: so the simple and the untaught, deceived by the paint of false doctrine and feigned holiness, lean very largely upon these things, and think this is the true way of salvation, ignorant of how displeasing it is to God and how great a danger it prepares for their souls under this pretext. Many also learn by their great loss how shamefully and wretchedly their hope has deceived them. Let us therefore remember that these things were spoken long ago by Christ, so that they may serve as a warning to us. Let us flee, then, from all teachers who reproduce the manners and temper of the Pharisees, and let us not think that God can be softened or deceived by the pretext of outward and false holiness. Rather, let us be careful that, with hearts truly purified through faith in Jesus Christ, we live in him a life worthy of our profession. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXII.
units.tr: Homily 122.

units.la: Respondens autem quidam ex Legis interpretibus, ait ei: Magister, cum hæc dicis, etiam nos afficis iniuria. Ipse autem dixit: Væ vobis quoque Legis interpretibus, quoniam oneratis homines oneribus difficilibus portatu, sed ipsi vno ex digitis vestris non attingitis onera. Væ vobis, quoniam ædificatis monumenta Prophetarum, patres autem vestri trucidarunt eos. Nempe testimonio vestro comprobatis facta patrum vestrorum: quoniam illi quidem eos trucidarunt, vos autem ædificatis eorum monumenta.
units.tr: Then one of the lawyers answered and said unto him, Master, thou reproachest us also. And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers. Woe unto you! for ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them. Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres.

units.la: QVamvis Dei Filius, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, erga infirmos & miseros peccatores fidelissimi medici instar mitem atque benignum se præbeat, & desperabundos amicè adsuit: idem tamen contra hypocriticos & falsos doctores totus ardet, & in eos acerrime inuebitur, suo nos exemplo docens, quam sæpè & quanto zelo hos oppugnare debeant, quicunque in Ecclesia ministerio versantur. Nam qui tales sunt, ij Veritatem atque lucem Verbi Dei suis traditionibus corrumpunt & obscurant, & vt (apud Ierem. Deus queritur) fritico, quo suum gregem hic pascit, paleas inanes miscent. Deinde verum Dei cultum euertunt, atque syncerum numinis timorem in hominum animis extinguunt. Adhæc suæ iustitiæ fiduciam aduersus Christum efferuntur, & rerum imperitis, vt idem non minus pernitiosè quàm stultè faciant, authores sunt. Ex eo enim sequitur, quòd dum suam stultitiam homines stabilire conantur, à Dei iustitia excidunt, quam vs nobis in Filio suo offert. Sed neque humana, quæ hoc nomine digna sit, assequuntur, cum non nisi fuco inani sese vendiderint, & pro Dei cultoribus vanissimi ostentatores fiant, quod genus hominum ipsi præ alijs omnibus exosum est. Non temere ergo neque cæco odij affectu Dominus tam diris imprecationibus & tanta verborum atrocitate in Pharisæos inuebitur, vt qui nam doctrinæ ipsorum fructus sit, ostendat.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, shows himself mild and kind towards weak and wretched sinners, like a most faithful physician, and gently attends to those in despair, he nonetheless burns with zeal against hypocritical and false teachers and attacks them with the utmost vehemence. By his own example he teaches us how often and how zealously those who serve the ministry in the Church ought to oppose them. For such men corrupt and obscure the truth and the light of God's Word with their own traditions, and, as God complains through Jeremiah, they mix empty chaff with the fodder with which they feed his flock. Then they overturn the true worship of God and extinguish the pure fear of the divine majesty in men's minds. Moreover, they boast of their own righteousness against Christ, and they are the authors of ignorance among the uninformed, which they do no less harmfully than foolishly. For it follows that while men try to establish their own folly, they fall away from the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son. Nor do they attain any human righteousness worthy of the name, since they have sold themselves only for empty show and become the most vain posturers in place of God's worshippers, a kind of men that is itself more hateful than all others. Therefore the Lord does not inveigh against the Pharisees, with such dire curses and such atrocious words, carelessly or out of blind hatred, but to show what fruit their teaching bears.

units.la: Ierem. 23.
units.tr: Jer. 23.

units.la: Quia autem in vltimo quod audiuimus sua correptionis membro, cum Pharifæis scribis coniunxit, mox eius sermonem quidam ex Legis interpretum numero, qui & ipsi ad Scribarum ordinem pertinebant, interrumpit, dicens: Magister, cum hæc dicis, etiam nos afficis iniuria. Non quidem Pharifæorum causam defendandam suscipit, imò altum silentium egit quàm diu de illis solis Christus locutus est: sed nunc nimium putat, & æquo vehementiorem, quando Scribas quoque eodem cum illis reatu inuoluit. Est autem hic communis typus antistitum, qui admonitiones & correptiones Verbi Dei indignius ferunt. Primò iniquum esse putat, suum quoque ordinem reprehendi & taxari. Vnde apparet, Scribas & Legis interpretes prorsus irreprehensibiles videri voluisse. Imitatur hos hodie Papa cum suis Cardinalibus, qui fi in vnum conueniant, Ecclesiæ titulum fibiipfis tribuunt, quàm errare posse negant. Quin eo vsque progressam fuisse scimus Pontificum audaciam, vt ne tunc quidem fe à quoquam mortalium argui aut reprehendi debere in suis decretis ftaturint, fi animas multorum secum ad gehennam abduxerint. Et hi quidem omnes facile patiuntur quosuis alios hominum ordines accusari & durissimè corripi, modò quis ab ipsis abstineat, & ipsorum existimationem intactam relinquat. Quæ causa est, quod cum Iudæos & Turcas suis legibus viue repatiantur, in solos Christi præcones seuerius soleant animaduertere, qui horum prædicatione suam authoritatem atq; dignitatem labefactari sentiunt.
units.tr: But because in the last part of his rebuke, which we have heard, he joined the scribes with the Pharisees, one of the lawyers, who also belonged to the order of the scribes, immediately interrupts his speech, saying: "Master, in saying these things you insult us also." He does not take up the defence of the Pharisees; indeed he kept a deep silence as long as Christ spoke only of them. But now he thinks it too much, and more harsh than is fair, that the scribes too are involved in the same guilt. This is the common response of churchmen who take the admonitions and corrections of God's Word too badly. First, he thinks it unjust that his own order too should be rebuked and censured. From this it is clear that the scribes and lawyers wanted to appear wholly blameless. Today the Pope with his Cardinals imitates them: when they gather together, they claim for themselves the title of the Church, and deny that they can err. Indeed we know that the audacity of the Popes has advanced so far that they have decreed in their decrees that they must not be accused or rebuked by any mortal even if they have led the souls of many with them down to hell. And these men easily tolerate any other orders of men being accused and very harshly reproved, provided that someone spares them and leaves their reputation untouched. This is why, although they tolerate Jews and Turks living under their laws, they are accustomed to punish more severely only the preachers of Christ, who feel that their own authority and dignity are shaken by the preaching of these men.

units.la: Deinde noster hic Legulator iniuriam atque contumeliam esse dicit correctionem, quam illis Christus necessario adhibebat. Est hoc proprium impiis, qui suam authoritatem in iis etiam valere volunt, quæ ad Deum pertinent. Et hoc est, quod Reges atque principes maximè inflammat, quòd atrocem iniuriam fieri sibi persuadent, fi quid aduersus ipsorum statuta aut ab ipsis receptam formam religionis liberius à quoquam dicatur. Sic Ieroboa primus Israelis Rex extenso brachio mox vt lafæ maiestatis reu corripi iubebat Viru Dei, qui aduersus aram & sacra ab ipso instituta prophetauerat. Et Achab Eliam regni turbatorem folebat dicere, quòd ab ipso inuectum Baalis cultum reprehenderet. Posteris temporibus Romani Imperatores suam existimationem grauissimè laedi & totam conculcari putauerunt à Christianis Doctoribus, qui contra ipsorum leges populum ab idolorum cultu ad Christum vocabant. Hodie autem nihil vulgarius est, quàm quòd in principes & reges contumeliosi dicuntur, quicunq; ab ipsis approbatas superstitiones reprehendere audent. Atqui non conuitium facit, neque contumelia aut iniuria quenquam afficit, sed beneficium ingens confert, qui errantes ab errore reuocat, & vt facilius obtemperent, errores eorū liberius arguit. Pestis autem nocentissima est peruersum hoc de fidis doctoribus iudicium: quia & odio maiori animos accendit, & pœnitentia viam præcludit; & proinde causa est, quod qui illo seducuntur, in peccatis suis miserè pereant: quod plerisque istorū, de quibus hic agitur, accidisse constat, sicuti Christus illus præ dixerat. Et huc tendunt, quotquot hodie etiam ministrorum linguas frænare conantur, aut dicendi leges ijdem præscribere audent. Ita enim seipsos Verbo salutis spoliant, & peffimis affectibus imperium permittunt, qui non aliud quàm exitium afferre possunt.
units.tr: Then our lawgiver here calls the correction that Christ necessarily applied to them an insult and an affront. This is characteristic of the impious, who want their authority to prevail even in matters that pertain to God. And this is what chiefly inflames kings and princes: they persuade themselves that a grievous wrong is done to them if anyone speaks too freely against their statutes or against the form of religion they have received. Thus Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, with outstretched arm, immediately ordered the man of God who had prophesied against the altar and the sacred rites he had instituted to be seized as guilty of treason. And Ahab used to call Elijah the troubler of the kingdom because he rebuked the worship of Baal that Ahab had introduced. In later times the Roman emperors thought that their reputation was most gravely injured and utterly trampled by the Christian teachers, who called the people from the worship of idols to Christ contrary to their laws. Today nothing is more common than that those who dare to rebuke superstitions approved by princes and kings are called abusive towards them. Yet he who calls men back from error does not revile, nor does he injure anyone with insult or affront; rather he confers a great benefit, and he argues more freely against their errors so that they may more readily obey. But this perverse judgment about faithful teachers is a most harmful plague: it inflames minds with greater hatred and blocks the way to repentance. Hence it is the cause why those who are led astray by it perish wretchedly in their sins, as is known to have happened to most of those of whom we are speaking here, just as Christ had foretold. To this end also tend all those who today try to bridle the tongues of ministers, or presume to prescribe to them the rules of speaking. For in this way they deprive themselves of the Word of salvation and yield the rule to the worst passions, which can bring nothing but destruction.

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus, qui Legisperito huic respondens diserte affirmat, ea quæ dixerat, non minus ipsis quàm Pharifæis conuenire. Væ vobis quoque (inquit) Legis interpretibus, quoniam oneratis homines, &c. Quasi dicat: Scio equidem vobis indignum videri, si quis vos perstringat & accuset, qui Ecclesiæ lumina, duces cæcorum, eruditores insipientium & magistri infantium haberi vultis: At non minus vestra quàm aliorum causa hic agitur, & vobis in primis leoninam detrahi oportet, qui falsa Legis interpretatione & vestris figmentis atque traditionibus omnis mali in Ecclesia essus authores. Et mox grauissima quædam crimina illis obijcit, propter quæ singula Væ illis imprecatur. Docet autem suo exemplo Dominus, qua libertate & fiducia dicendi Verbi administri in suo munere vti debeant. Sunt hi serui Dei, quos suæ domui præfecit, vt excindant & plantent, diruant & ædificent, vt denique pœnas imminentes scelerantur denuntient, & eosdem ad pœnitentiam exhortentur. Adhæc (vt Paulus scribit) legatio nem Filij Dei obeunt, cuius nomine omnia dicunt & faciunt. Ergo nullius personam respicere, sed suo iure atque priuilegio erga quosuis vti debent, vtut hoc plerisque indignum aut iniquum videatur. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter olim omnes serui Dei, quorum fidem Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis commendat. Nam vt à Mose exordiamur, quàm multa fuerunt, quæ ipsum auocare potes-
units.tr: But let us listen to Christ, who, answering this lawyer, plainly declares that what he had said applies to them no less than to the Pharisees. "Woe unto you also, lawyers," he says, "for you lade men," and so on. As if to say: I know indeed that it seems unworthy to you if anyone calls you to account and accuses you, you who wish to be regarded as the lights of the Church, the guides of the blind, the teachers of the foolish and the masters of infants. But this matter concerns you no less than others, and it is above all you who must be stripped of the lion's skin, you who are the authors of every evil in the Church through your false interpretation of the law and your inventions and traditions. And soon after he brings against them certain most grave crimes, for each of which he pronounces a woe upon them. The Lord teaches by his own example with what freedom and confidence the ministers of the Word ought to exercise their office. They are God's servants, whom he has set over his household, to root out and to plant, to pull down and to build, and finally to denounce the impending punishments for crimes and to exhort the same men to repentance. Moreover, as Paul writes, they perform the embassy of the Son of God, in whose name they say and do all things. Therefore they ought not to regard anyone's person, but to use their right and privilege towards whomever, however unfitting or unjust this may seem to most people. All the servants of God, whose faith the Holy Spirit commends in the Scriptures, have diligently observed this. For to begin with Moses, how many things there were which were able to call him away

units.la: Ier. 1. Ezech. 33. 2. Cor. 5. Rom. 2. rant,ne quid aduersus Pharaonem tentaret. Obstare videbatur pietas, ne se eius voluntati oppone ret,qui ipsius nutritius fuerat, qui ipsum in omni sapientia Ægyptiorum liberaliter institui curarat, & ad honores summos euexerat. Accedebat periculum ob eadem Ægyptij factam, & quòd nimiæ temeritatis facinus censeri poterat, quadraginta annorum exulem eius populi liberatione moliri, quæ Rex oppressum volebat. De quibus & multis alijs Mosem seriò cogitauisse, eius verba indicant, quibus initio munus illud detrectauit. Sed cùm audiret Deum hoc omnino velle, magno & constanti animo rem aggressus est, & Pharaonis contumaciam atque minas facile contempsit, ut Deo obediret. Idem in Prophetis est videre, qui si hominum iudicia spectemus, sæpe grauissimi & iustissimi rationibus moti fuisse videntur, ut in subeundo suo munere tardiores essent. Ionæ certè nō absque causa durum & graue videbatur, hominem Iudæum Niniuitis exitium minitari, qui tunc toti Orienti imperabant. Idem tamen cum periculo edoctus, quàm graue sit Deo sese opponere, aut eius mandatis reluctari, Niniuen professus fortiter suam legationem obijt. Ieremiam verò & suæ ætatis consideratio, & populi contumacia, atque irriti tot tantorumque Prophetarum, qui ipsum præcesserant, labores terrebant, ut sibi à concionandi munere abstinendum esse putaret. At cùm Dei mandato se vrgeri sentiret, paruit & absque omni personarum respectu pœnitere nescijs exi-dium verbis atque templi denuntiauit. Et quàm putas durum fuisse illis omnibus, quando populum illum electum Chananæus & Amorrhæis conferre, principes Sodomæorum principibus similes dicere, & conciones suas directè contra ipsos reges & eos, qui his à consilijs erant, instituere cogebantur? Sed in omnium animis sonuit, quod Amos dicebat: Leo si rugiat, quis non timeret? Dominus Deus locutus est, & quis non prophetaret? Nec minori libertate Noui Testamenti ministros vsque esse videbis, si quæ Ioannes Baptista contra Pharisæos & Sacerdotes declamauit, & quæ idè Herodi in faciem dixit, consideres: quæ item Apostoli Hierosolymis partim in publicis concionibus, partim in Senatu & concilio Antistitum atque Seniorum dixerunt. Quorum omnium exempla cùm Christus tam hîc quàm alibi suo exemplo cõfirmet, illa sibi imitanda proponant, quotquot hoc sceleratissimo seculo Verbum Dei prædicant. Admonet de hoc Paulus, quando Timotheum non modò sermonem prædicare, sed arguere, obiurgare, imò tempestiuè & intempestiuè instare iubet, & sui præcepti hanc rationem affert, quòd futurum sit, ut doctrinâ veritatis non audiant homines, sed doctores sibi accersant, qui aures blandis sermonibus demulceant. Ita verò iis occurrit, qui ideò tacendum esse censent, quòd monendo, hortando, increpando nihil proficere se vident. Atqui eò fortius instare oportet, ut si omnia fallant, suas saltē animas ministri liberent. Nimium verò stulti et infelices sunt, qui id nolunt ferre, quasi Deus in ipsorum gratiam tacere, aut tot seculis vsurpatam docendi rationem mutare debeat. Cur verò Christus tam grauiter in Legis interpretes inuehitur? Oneratis (inquit) homines onere-ribus difficilibus portatu, sed ipsi vno ex digitis vestris non attingitis onera. Duplex crimen illis obijcit. Primùm, quòd qui afflictis conscientijs consulere debebant, oneribus intolerabilibus populum magis grauarent. Id autem partim de Legis doctrina, qualem ipsi tradebant, dicit, est enim illa (vt nuper ex Petri verbis monuimus) iugum importabile, si absque Christo tradatur, ad quæ nobis pædagogi instar esse debet: partim de ipsorum traditionibus, quas Legi addebant, & quibus ea intolerabilior multò reddebatur. His enim crebriores, quàm par erat, purificationes, oblationes & alia multa exigebantur, quæ Sacerdotibus quidem & Scribis quæstuosa, populo autem multas ob causas grauia & portatu difficillima erant. Alterum crimen fuit, quòd ipsi eadem illa onera ne vno quidem digito attingerent. Ergo vita eorum doctrinæ minimè respondebat, cùm ipsi non nisi circa inanes ceremonias & simulatæ sanctimoniæ studium occupararent, ea autem perinde vt Pharisaei negligerent, in quibus verus Dei cultus & hominum salus maximè consistunt. Est autem hoc proprium hypocritis, quòd seueri admodum & rigidi sunt in exigendis pietatis officijs, & nunquam nō excommunicationis, damnationis æternæ & inferorū minas in ore habent, cùm interim sibijpsis nimiū indulgenter blandiantur in grauissimis sceleribus. Causa huius vitij est duplex. Primò austeritate illa nimia, maiorem sanctimoniæ existimationem sibi apud populum rudem parare student. Quis enim non putet totos pietatis zelo ardere, quos tam rigidos obedientiæ erga Deū exactores esse videt, & qui tanto studio aduersus scelera quorumuis publicè declamant? Deinde quia seipsos non nouerunt, manu inani iustitia fiducia turgidi sibi nihil deesse putant, cum interim (qui communis hominum morbus est) in aliorum vitijs notandu oculatissimi sint censores. Hoc igitur in istus quoq; Christus accusat, quòd ἐργοδ ἰωχτῳ illorũ similes, quos Pharao Israelitas prafecerat, multa quidem à populo exigerent, ipsi verò manum operi nullam admouerent.
units.tr: Ier. 1. Ezech. 33. 2. Cor. 5. Rom. 2. could have deterred him from attempting anything against Pharaoh. Piety seemed to stand in the way, since he would be opposing the will of the man who had raised him, had arranged for him to be generously instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and had advanced him to the highest honours. There was also the danger from the Egyptians, who had been wronged by him, and it could be judged a deed of reckless rashness for an exile of forty years to undertake the liberation of a people whom the king wished to keep oppressed. That Moses seriously considered these and many other matters is shown by the words with which he first refused that task. But when he heard that God truly willed it, he undertook the matter with great and steadfast courage, and easily disregarded Pharaoh's obstinacy and threats, so that he might obey God. The same can be seen among the Prophets, who, if we look at human judgments, often seem to have been moved by very grave and very just reasons to be slower in carrying out their office. Certainly it did not seem without cause hard and grievous to Jonah that a Jew should threaten destruction to the Ninevites, who then ruled the whole East. Yet he, having learned through the danger how grave a thing it is to set oneself against God or to resist his commands, boldly professed himself and carried out his embassy to Nineveh. But Jeremiah was terrified by the consideration of his own age, the obstinacy of the people, and the fruitless labours of so many and so great Prophets who had gone before him, so that he thought he ought to abstain from the office of preaching. But when he felt himself urged by the command of God, he obeyed, and without any regard for persons he announced in words and in the temple the coming destruction to those who would not repent. And how hard do you think it was for all of them, when they were compelled to compare that chosen people with the Canaanites and Amorites, to call its princes like the princes of Sodom, and to direct their sermons openly against the kings themselves and those who were their counsellors? But in the minds of all there sounded what Amos said: "If a lion roars, who would not fear? The Lord God has spoken, and who would not prophesy?" Nor will you see the ministers of the New Testament acting with less freedom, if you consider what John the Baptist declaimed against the Pharisees and the priests, and what he said to Herod's face; likewise what the Apostles at Jerusalem spoke, partly in public sermons, partly before the Senate and the council of the chief priests and elders. Since Christ confirms all these examples, both here and elsewhere, by his own example, let all who now preach the Word of God in this most wicked age propose these to themselves for imitation. Paul gives this admonition when he orders Timothy not only to preach the word, but to reprove, rebuke, and even to press on in season and out of season, and he gives as the reason for this command that the time will come when men will not listen to sound doctrine, but will gather for themselves teachers who tickle their ears with pleasing speech. He meets in this way those who think that one should keep silent because they see that they accomplish nothing by admonishing, exhorting, and rebuking. Yet all the more strongly ought they to press on, so that, if everything else fails, the ministers may at least free their own souls. Truly foolish and unhappy are those who will not bear this, as if God ought to be silent for their sake, or change a method of teaching that has been used for so many centuries. But why does Christ inveigh so severely against the interpreters of the Law? "You load men," he says, "with burdens that are hard to bear, but you yourselves do not touch the burdens even with one of your fingers." He brings two charges against them. First, that those who ought to have cared for troubled consciences burdened the people more heavily with intolerable yokes. He says this partly of the teaching of the Law as they delivered it, for that (as we noted lately from the words of Peter) is an unbearable yoke if it is handed on without Christ, to whom it ought to lead us as a schoolmaster does; partly of their traditions, which they added to the Law and by which it was made far more intolerable. For by these were required purifications, oblations, and many other things more frequently than was fitting, which were indeed profitable to the priests and scribes, but for many reasons were burdensome and most difficult to bear for the people. The second charge was that they did not touch those same burdens even with one finger. Therefore their life did not correspond to their teaching, since they occupied themselves only with empty ceremonies and the pursuit of feigned holiness, while they neglected, just as the Pharisees did, those things in which the true worship of God and the salvation of men chiefly consist. Now it is characteristic of hypocrites that they are very severe and rigid in demanding the duties of piety, and always have on their lips threats of excommunication, eternal damnation, and the pains of hell, while meanwhile they indulge themselves far too leniently in the gravest crimes. The cause of this vice is twofold. First, by that excessive austerity they strive to win for themselves a greater reputation for holiness among the uneducated people. For who would not think that those men burn with zeal for piety whom they see to be such rigid exactors of obedience to God, and who so eagerly declaim in public against the crimes of anyone at all? Second, because they do not know themselves, they are puffed up with the empty confidence of their righteousness and think that they lack nothing, while meanwhile (which is the common disease of men) they are the most keen-sighted censors in noting the faults of others. Therefore Christ accuses these men also of this: that, like the taskmasters [ἐργοδιῶκται] whom Pharaoh set over the Israelites, they exacted much from the people but themselves laid no hand to the work.

units.la: Est autem in hisce verbis probè obseruandum, vehementer peccari ab omnibus, qui doctrinam suam faciunt æquo grauiorem atque intolerabilem. Fit hoc non vno modo, in primis tamen, si vitæ quidem præcepta seuerè vrgeantur vnà cum comminationibus, quibus impios horum transgressores Spiritus Sanctus terret, interim verò nulla fiat Iesu Christi mētio, qui transgressiones nostras & iniquitates expiauit, nos cum Patre cœlesti in gratiam reduxit, Spiritu adoptionis nobis dedit, qui & veram in nobis pœnitentiam excitat, & remissionis peccatorum atque salutis Arrhabo est certissimus. Nam si ista omittantur, quid aliud ex Legis doctrina & Euangelicis præceptis enasci potest, quàm horribiles conscientiæ terrores, quibus homo tandem ad desperatinus præcipitium abripitur, nisi illi gratia Dei succurrat? Videt enim miser, se non solum peccauisse, verumetiā eam esse naturæ suæ vitiositatem, vt non possit non peccare, cùm Legę peccati in membris suis circumferat, quæ illum sæpe contra suam voluntatem peccato captiuum abducit. Audit præterea horrendam illam vocem: Maledictus omnis, qui non fecerit omnia verba libri huius, & dicet omnis populus Amen. Nonne hîc exclamare cogetur, Miserum me, quis me liberabit à corpore mortis huius? Et nisi cum Paulo sibijpsi respondere possit, Gratias ago Deo per Iesum Christum, desperationem omnino sequi necesse est. At quomodo illud dicet, qui de Christo nihil vnquam audiuit, qui meritum eius et reconciliationis per ipsum factæ mysterium ignorat, qui deniq; hunc non agnoscit Mediatorem illum esse, qui pro nobis apud Patrem intercedat, sed ad suas satisfactiones remittitur, in quibus nihil certi, nihil solidi & perfecti inuenit, vt illis niti queat? Est ergo hoc doctrinæ genus nocentissimum, eo quòd sub pleusibili pœnitentiæ atq; bonorum operum prætextu à vera salutis via abducit, & æternum Filium Dei suo honore spoliat. At illud in primis vrgent, qui suam infirmitatem & naturæ propriæ corruptionem (vt ante diximus) non agnoscunt. Quare doctoribus non tam vtile quàm necessarium est, vt seipsos frequenter excutiant, & mox videbunt qua moderatione debeant vtiin exigendis Legis diuinæ mandatis, qua verò ratione conscientiis afflictis mederi, & nimijs terroribus prostratas erigere debeant. Deinde ad augendū doctrinæ pondus plurimum facit, si ipsi doctores illa non proprio exemplo commendent, sed potius omnia ips.quæ docent contraria atq; aduersa faciant. Vt enim in re militari militibus nulli labores nimij, nulla pericula iniqua videntur, si Imperatore tadem subire, imò in illis subeundis primum esse cernant: Ita de doctrinæ & præceptorum grauitate non possunt conqueri, qui horum viuum exemplum in doctoribus suis conspicantur. E contrario, vt milites omnis laboris impatientes & periculorum omnium detrestatores reddit, si duces sibi poss principia cauere, se autem solos difficultatibus obiici videant: ita cùm natura à præceptorum Dei obseruatione abhorreamus, mox murmurare, tergiuersandi occasiones quærere, imò ad conuiuia quoq; prorumpere solemus, si illa ne ab ijs quidē obseruentur, qui ea à nobis seuerius exigunt. Hæmunum igitur vitio Dei præcepta intolerabilia fiunt, quæ si rectè proponantur, grauia non sunt, vt dilectus ille discipulus in sua Catholica Epistola docet. 1. Ioan. 3.
units.tr: In these words one must carefully observe that all those sin grievously who make their teaching heavier and more intolerable than is right. This happens in more than one way, but chiefly if the precepts of life are pressed with severity, together with the threats by which the Holy Spirit terrifies the wicked who transgress them, while meanwhile no mention is made of Jesus Christ, who expiated our transgressions and iniquities, restored us to favour with the heavenly Father, gave us the Spirit of adoption, who both stirs up in us true repentance and is the most certain pledge of forgiveness of sins and of salvation. For if these things are left out, what else can be born from the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel precepts than horrible terrors of conscience, by which a man is at last dragged down into the abyss of despair, unless the grace of God comes to his aid? For the wretched man sees that he has not only sinned, but that his nature is so corrupt that he cannot help sinning, since he carries the law of sin in his members, which often leads him away, against his will, captive to sin. Moreover, he hears that dreadful voice: "Cursed is everyone who does not keep all the words of this book; and all the people shall say, Amen." Will he not be forced to cry out here, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?" And unless he can answer himself with Paul, "I thank God through Jesus Christ," it is altogether necessary that despair should follow. But how will he say this who has never heard anything about Christ, who is ignorant of his merit and of the mystery of reconciliation made through him, who finally does not recognise that he is that Mediator who intercedes for us with the Father, but is referred to his own satisfactions, in which he finds nothing certain, nothing solid and perfect, on which he could rest? This kind of teaching is therefore most harmful, because under the plausible pretext of repentance and good works it leads men away from the true way of salvation and strips the eternal Son of God of his honour. But those who do not recognise their own weakness and the corruption of their nature (as we said before) press this above all. Therefore it is not so much useful as necessary for teachers to examine themselves frequently, and then they will soon see with what moderation they ought to use the demands of the divine Law, and in what way they ought to heal afflicted consciences and raise up those cast down by excessive terrors. Next, to increase the weight of their teaching it counts for much if the teachers themselves do not commend it by their own example, but rather do the very opposite of what they teach. For just as in military affairs no labours seem excessive to soldiers, nor any dangers unjust, if they see that the commander himself undertakes them, and indeed is first in undertaking them: so those cannot complain of the severity of the doctrine and the precepts who behold a living example of them in their teachers. On the contrary, just as a leader who takes precautions for himself and leaves the soldiers alone to face difficulties makes them impatient of every labour and contemptuous of every danger, so, since by nature we shrink from keeping God's precepts, we are soon wont to murmur, to seek occasions for evasion, and even to break out into feasting, if the precepts are not observed even by those who exact them from us more strictly. Therefore the precepts of God become intolerable through the fault of men, although if they are rightly set forth they are not grievous, as that beloved disciple teaches in his Catholic Epistle. 1 John 3.

units.la: Porrò si hæc ad nostra tempora transferas, passim ab omnibus peccari videbis, qui docendo & monendo alijs præesse debebant. In Papatu non quidem omittitur Legis diuinæ doctrina, sed ea omnino ratione proponitur, qua apud Iudæos illa Scribæ tractare solebant. Nam omissa Christi prædicatione, hominis vires comendant, operum merita, satisfactiones & infinita alia vrgent, quæ corpus quidem fatigant & oculos exhauriunt, nullam autem conscientiis peccatorum agnitione territuris pacem aut consolationem afferunt. Negant quidem se prædicatione Christi omittere, sed reipsa conuincuntur. Nec enim Christum prædicant omnes, qui nomen eius in ore habent, qui nomē Iesu in concionibus suis cum mirifica vocis ad deuotionis animorum simulatione compositæ modulatione sæpius ingeminant: sed qui causam sui in carnem aduentus, mortis & resurrectionis eius meritum atq; virtutem diligenter exponunt, & qui cum Apostolis docent, nos sola fide in illum iustificari & seruari, eò quòd ipse solus noster apud Patrē Mediator, solus ad thronū gratiæ via & ostiū, solus nobis à Deo sapientia, iustitia, satisfactio, sanctificatio & redeptio sit factus, quòd deniq; præter illum non aliud nomen sub cælo hominibus sit datum, in quo illos seruari oporteat. At si Christum hoc modo prædicant Papistici doctores, quid sibi vult Missæ sacrificium? quid nostrorum operum iustitia atque meritum? quid tot Diui Mediatores? quid satisfactiones & opera supererogationis? quid Pontificum bullæ & indulgentiæ? quid vota Monastica? quid ciborum delectus, peregrinationes ad longinquos Diuos, & sexcenta alia, quæ non alia quàm hominum superstitiosorum authoritate niituntur? Cur item post omnia ista igni Purgatorij lustratione, sumptuosis exequijs, & per petuos pro animarum in igne isto laborantium redemptione sacris opus esse docent? Cur non Christi verbus insistunt, qui credentes in iudicium venire negat, sed recta à morte in vitam transfire ait? Ad de his, quod homines salutis prorsus incertos reddunt, quando aliquè de gratia Dei, dum hic viuit, certum fieri posse negant. Vides ergo illos onera difficilia portatu, imò impossibilia hominum conscientijs imponere, cum & Christum excludant à Legis doctrina, & eandè per se importabilem suis traditionibus magis aggrauent. Quid verò ipsi interea faciunt? Num onus illud suis humeris subeunt, vt suo exemplo id leuius alijs reddant? Nequaquam. Imò securè ex quæstuosis illis sacris delitiantur, in sinu gaudent, & hominum stultitiam penes se rident, adeoque vna omnium vox est, quæ Alexandri VI. Pontificis, bonam esse hanc Christianorum perfuasionem, per quam ipsi regnant atque dominentur. Verè hæc dici, ipsorum vita atque mores testantur. Nam si suis traditionibus ipsi fidem adhiberent, si vel cælum vel inferos aut Purgatorium ignem esse crederent, nunquam tam impudenter scortari, mœchari & grauiora his designare auderent. Sed vtinam in solis istis hæc alteraculpa hæreret, & non inter illos quoque conspticeretur, qui puriore Euangelij doctrinâ prædicans & Christum syncerè docent. Debebant illi vitâ suam ita instituere, vt cum Paulo suis auditoribus dicere possent: Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi sum. Quàm multos autem in illorum ordine inuenies, qui ambitione ebrij in fratres & Symmystas sibi dominium vendicant? qui auaritia accensi per fas & nefas rapiunt atque colligunt? qui inuidia & odio contabescunt? qui contentiones scandali plenas vel de nihilo excitant ipsi, vel ab alijs excitatas fouent? qui vestiu luxu superbiunt, ebrietati, aleæ, venationi sunt dediti? qui denique fidem coniugalem impudenter violant, & fœdissimo adulterij scelere sese polluunt? Et hi illi sunt, propter quos male audit nomen Domini, & qui suis auditoribus doctrinam Euangelij partim intolerabilem, partim suspectam atque contemptam reddunt. Graue ergo illos iudicium manet, & sentient olim quàm horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viuentis, qui tam effrænem atque impiam licentiam impunitatem non dimittet. Quod autem de Euangelij administris dicitur, hoc ipsum ad alios quoque ordines transferri potest. Adeundem enim lapidem multi, qui Reipub. administrant, offendunt, dum Leges per se utiles, salutares atque necessarias suo exemplo graues reddunt, id est, authores sunt populo ad licentiam procliui, vt illas impatientius ferat. Et priuatim in hoc parentes sæpe peccant, qui licentius viuendo liberis causam præbent, vt disciplinam minus libenter admittant. Denique omnium fere admonitionum atque correptionum contemptus hinc nascitur, quòd qui has alijs adhibent, fere ijsdem contraria faciunt.
units.tr: Moreover, if you apply these things to our own times, you will see that everyone who ought to have presided over others by teaching and admonishing sins on every side. Among the Papists the doctrine of the divine Law is not indeed omitted, but it is presented in exactly the way the scribes used to handle it among the Jews. For, with the preaching of Christ set aside, they commend the powers of man and press the merits of works, satisfactions, and countless other things, which wear out the body and exhaust the eyes but bring no peace or comfort to consciences that are frightened by the recognition of their sins. They deny indeed that they neglect the preaching of Christ, but their own deeds refute them. For not everyone who has the name of Christ on his lips preaches Christ, even those who repeat the name of Jesus so often in their sermons, modulating their voices wonderfully to feign devotion of spirit. Rather, those preach Christ who diligently expound the cause of his coming in the flesh and the merit and power of his death and resurrection, and who teach with the Apostles that we are justified and saved by faith alone in him, because he alone is our Mediator with the Father, alone is the way and door to the throne of grace, alone has been made for us wisdom, righteousness, satisfaction, sanctification, and redemption from God, and because there is no other name under heaven given to men in which they must be saved. But if the Papist teachers preached Christ in this way, what would the sacrifice of the Mass mean? What would the righteousness and merit of our works mean? What would so many divine Mediators mean? What would satisfactions and works of supererogation mean? What would the papal bulls and indulgences mean? What would monastic vows mean? What would the selection of foods, pilgrimages to distant saints, and six hundred other things mean, which rest on nothing but the authority of superstitious men? Again, why do they teach that after all these things there is need of sacred rites, through the cleansing of the fire of Purgatory, costly funerals, and perpetual redemption of souls suffering in that fire? Why do they not keep to the words of Christ, who says that those who believe do not come into judgment but pass straight from death into life? Besides, they make men utterly uncertain of salvation, since they deny that anyone can be made certain of God's grace while he lives here. You see, then, that they impose burdens hard to bear, indeed impossible for men's consciences, since they both exclude Christ from the doctrine of the Law and weigh it down further with their own traditions, which are already unbearable in themselves. But what do they themselves do meanwhile? Do they take that burden upon their own shoulders, so as to make it lighter for others by their example? By no means. Rather they revel securely in those profitable rites, rejoice in their bosoms, and laugh at men's folly to their own advantage. And so there is one common saying, that of Pope Alexander VI, that this belief of Christians is a good thing, since through it they rule and lord it over others. That these things are said truly, their own life and morals bear witness. For if they themselves gave credit to their own traditions, if they believed that heaven or hell or the fire of Purgatory really exists, they would never dare to whore so shamelessly, commit adultery, and plan things worse than these. But would that this fault clung only to those men, and were not seen among those too who preach the purer doctrine of the Gospel and teach Christ sincerely! They ought to order their lives so that they could say to their hearers with Paul: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." Yet how many will you find in their order who, drunk with ambition, claim lordship over their brethren and fellow ministers? Who, inflamed with greed, snatch and gather by right and wrong? Who waste away with envy and hatred? Who stir up quarrels full of scandal, either from nothing themselves or nourish those stirred up by others? Who take pride in the luxury of clothing, and are given over to drunkenness, dice, and hunting? Who, in short, shamelessly violate the marriage faith and pollute themselves with the foul crime of adultery? These are the men because of whom the name of the Lord is ill spoken of, and who make the doctrine of the Gospel to their hearers partly intolerable, partly suspect and despised. A heavy judgment therefore awaits them, and they will one day feel how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, who will not let such unbridled and impious license go unpunished. What is said about the ministers of the Gospel can also be applied to the other orders. For many who administer the commonwealth stumble on the same stone, when by their example they make laws, which are in themselves useful, wholesome, and necessary, burdensome: that is, they become the authors of license to the people, who are inclined to it, so that they bear the laws more impatiently. Parents too often sin privately in this way, when by living more licentiously they give their children cause to accept discipline less willingly. Finally, almost all contempt of admonitions and rebukes arises from this, that those who administer them to others often do the opposite themselves.

units.la: Num verò (inquis) excusantur apud Deum, qui ideo doctrinam veritatis aut admonitiones salutares reijciunt? Minimè. Nam de hoc quoque Christus apud Matthæum diligenter admonet, de Scribis & Pharisæis ad populum sic loquens: In cathedra Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi: Omnia ergo, quæ dixerint vobis vt seruetis, seruate & facite: sed secundùm opera eorumne facite: dicunt enim, & non faciunt. In cathedra Mosis sedere dicuntur, qui Legem docent sine traditionibus humanis. Solebat enim hæc diebus Sabbati (vt ex Iacobi Oratione Act. 15. apparet) in Synagogis populo recitari aut prælegi. Itaque verborum Christi sensus est: Quando Legis diuina præcepta illi vobis proponunt, tunc illis obedite, neque illa propter prauum illorum exemplum contemnite. Hoc ipsum ergo nostri seculi homines sibi dictum putent. Prædicat quis Euangelij doctrinam pure & syncerè, huic fidem adhibe & obtempera, etiamsi illum pessimis moribus præditum, aut etiam flagitijs apertis infamem esse videas. Nec enim ab hominibus vllis pendet Verbi diuini authoritas, neque etiam alicuius vitijs minuitur. Et tu si bene docenti obtemperaueris, laudem habebis & præmium coram Deo, improbus autem ille doctor pœnas subibit, quas scandalorum authoribus & Verbi sui prophanatoribus Deus alibi minatur. Eadem est subditorum & Magistratuum siue Principum, liberorum atque parentum ratio, omnium denique qui ab ijs admonentur.
units.tr: But, you will say, are those excused before God who reject the doctrine of truth or wholesome admonitions for this reason? By no means. For Christ also warns carefully about this in Matthew, speaking to the people about the scribes and Pharisees in these words: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do" (Matth. 23.). They are said to sit in Moses' seat who teach the Law without human traditions. For these things were usually recited or read aloud to the people in the synagogues on the Sabbath days (as appears from James's speech in Acts 15.). So the sense of Christ's words is this: when they set before you the divine precepts of the Law, then obey them, and do not despise them because of their bad example. Let the men of our own age therefore take this as said to themselves. If anyone preaches the doctrine of the Gospel purely and sincerely, give him trust and obey him, even if you see him endowed with the worst morals, or infamous for open crimes. For the authority of the divine Word depends on no men, nor is it diminished by anyone's faults. And if you obey a teacher who teaches well, you will have praise and reward before God, but that wicked teacher will undergo the punishments which God threatens elsewhere against authors of scandal and profaners of his Word. The same reasoning applies to subjects and magistrates or princes, to children and parents, and finally to all who are admonished by them.

units.la: Doctorum improbitas, verbi contemptores non excusat. admonentur, qui ipsis inhonestius viuunt. Si enim (vt gentium philosophi docuerunt) ex inimicis hæc vtilitas captanda est, vt ex conuitiis, quæ in nos iaciunt, discamus, quid in nobis emendari debeat, quanto patientius eos ferre conuenit, qui qualescunque sint, nos tamen ex officio admonent?
units.tr: The wickedness of teachers does not excuse those who despise the Word. Those who live more dishonourably than their own admonitions are admonished. For if (as the philosophers of the nations taught) we ought to draw profit from enemies, so that from the reproaches they hurl at us we learn what in us ought to be amended, how much more patiently ought we to bear those who, whatever they are, admonish us as part of their duty?

units.la: Cæterum pergit Dominus, & secundo loco legis interpretibus præposteram Prophetarum ve-terum obseruantiam exprobrat, qua & maioribus suis meliores atq; sanctiores videri volebant, & populi fauore vænabantur, apud quos maxima erat illorum authoritas. Væ (inquit) vobis quoniam ædificatis monumenta Prophetarum, patres autem vestri trucidarunt eos. Apud Matthæum addi-tur, illos de patrum iniquitate conqueri soliti fuisse. Dicebant enim: Si fuissemus temporibus patrum nostrorum, non fuissemus eorum socij in cæde Prophetarum. Quid vero Christus? Ostendit eos maioribus suis longe deteriores, adeoq; mali corui pessimum omnium esse. Nam in Matthæo subijcit: Itaq; te stamini aduersus vosmetipsos: vos esse filios eorum, qui Prophetas occiderunt. Id vero superbæ genera fiduciæ opponit, qua se Abrahami filios esse gloriabantur, & ideo se impunè omnia laturos sibi persuadebant. Atqui latronum filij estis (inquit Christus) & hoc ipsi testamini, dum Prophetarum monumenta magnificè exornatis. Et ne vel hoc nomine sibi placerent, hic addit: Nempe testimonio vestro comprobatis facta patrum vestrorum: quoniam illi quidem eos trucidarunt, vos autem ædificatis eorum monumenta. Videtur autem postremum hoc membrum proverbij loco per Sarcasmum esse dictum, vt idem fit Prophetarum sepulchra extruere, quod illos totos obruere, ne vnquam in sua doctrina resurgant. Nam apud Matthæum sic istud enunciatur: Vos quoq; completis mensuram patrum vestrorum, id est, adeo non estis his meliores, vt potius quod ipsi omiserunt, vos plane effectu detis. Id vero propter se dicit, cuius aduentu cum Prophetæ omnes prædixissent, & in hoc salutem quærere docuissent, ipsi tamen eum hostiliter persequebantur, neq; cessaturi erant, vsq; quo crudeli & infami morte suflulissent. Immo ne tunc quidem cessarunt, sed Apostolos quoq; vbiq; locorum persecuti sunt, & quoad fieri potuit resiterunt, ne Euangelium inter gentes prædicaretur.
units.tr: The Lord goes on, and in the second place reproaches the interpreters of the Law for their perverse observance of the ancient Prophets, by which they wished to seem better and holier than their forefathers, and hunted for the favour of the people, among whom their authority was very great. "Woe to you," he says, "because you build the tombs of the Prophets, but your fathers slew them." In Matthew it is added that they were accustomed to complain of their fathers' wickedness. For they said: "If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the murder of the Prophets." But what does Christ say? He shows that they are far worse than their forefathers, and so the bad sons are the worst of all. For in Matthew he adds: "So you bear witness against yourselves, that you are sons of those who killed the Prophets." He opposes this to the proud kind of confidence by which they gloried that they were sons of Abraham, and so persuaded themselves that they would suffer everything with impunity. Yet, says Christ, you are sons of murderers, and you attest this yourselves while you adorn the tombs of the Prophets magnificently. And lest they should please themselves even on this account, he adds: "Indeed, by your testimony you approve the deeds of your fathers, since they indeed slew them, but you build their tombs." But this last clause seems to be said proverbially and with sarcasm, as if to build the sepulchres of the Prophets were the same as to bury them completely, so that they might never rise again in their teaching. For in Matthew it is stated thus: "You also fill up the measure of your fathers" (Matth. 23.), that is, you are so far from being better than them that you actually do in deed what they left undone. He says this with regard to himself, whose coming all the Prophets had foretold, and had taught that salvation was to be sought in him, yet they persecuted him with hostility, and would not stop until they had removed him by a cruel and infamous death. Indeed, not even then did they stop, but they also persecuted the Apostles everywhere, and as far as they could, they resisted lest the Gospel be preached among the nations.

units.la: Proponitur autem in hisce Iudæorum legisperitis, vel potius in tota Iudæorum gente exemplum præposteri & superstitiosi iudicij de hominibus sanctis & virtute præditis. Prophetas mortuos & à patribus occisos in honore habebant, & eorundem memoriam magnificis monumentorum structuris conseruare studebant: at Christum, qui eandem cum illis doctrinam prædicabat, immo in quem illi omnes respexerant, volebant occisum. Inter gentes quoq; huius generis exempla habentur. Socratis atq; Aristidis mortem Athenienses luxerunt acerbis lachrymis, quos cum in vitus esset, odio capitali per sequebantur. Hodie aut inter Christiani nominis professores multa fiunt similia. Coluntur à multis Apostolorum & Martyrum non sepulchra modò, verumetiam minutissimæ reliquiæ, quarum maxima pars fictitia & adulterina est, & in eorum memoriam templa magnifica extruuntur, dies festi consecrantur, canuntur Missæ & multa alia fiunt, quæ vel superstitiosa sunt, vel vni atq; soli Deo debentur. Idem quoq; qui ista faciunt, nunquam non Diuos in ore habent, & nos horum prophanos contemptores esse aiunt, quando diuinis honoribus colendos esse negamus. At si quis Apostolorum atq; Martyrum fidem profiteatur, aut cum illis doceat, vnum Christum esse nostram iustitiam, satisfactionem pro peccatis, Mediatorem apud Patrem cœlestem, viam vnicam, qua ad salutem venitur, deniq; nihil vel esse vel nominari posse prater illum, quo seruemur: mox hunc hæreticum, blasphemum, schismaticum, verae fidei desertorem, Ecclesiæ hostem, & proinde dignum esse clamant, qui non nisi lento igne aut alio atrociori supplicio occidatur. Vnde vero tanta iudicij peruersitas? Ex eo nimirum, quod illi iam olim mortui nullius vitam & mores reprehendunt, neq; superstitiones & quæstus sacrilegos coràm accusant: at qui hodie ex illorum scriptis docent, ij impijs omnibus molesti sunt: qui tamen vt impietatem suam dissimulent, Diuorum cultores et magnifici veneratores haberi volunt. Sed neminem illorum clamores debent offendere. Nec enim in Diuos contumeliosus est, qui diuinos honores illis negat, quos non solum nunquam affectarunt, verumetiam vt summa impietate detestati sunt (vt Pauli & Barnabæ exemplum in Actis testatur) sed qui ipsorum doctrinam conculcant, & eam, pro qua mortui sunt, fide hæresis accusant. Et quid hos maneat, in iis quæ sequuntur audiemus. Cultores autem & veneratores Diuorum veri erimus, si doctrinæ eorum credamus, exemplū imitemur, & quæ prædicarunt, Iesum Christum fide vera amplexemur, & vnicum esse agnoscamus humani generis Seruatorem: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Here, in these Jewish lawyers, or rather in the whole Jewish nation, we are presented with an example of a perverse and superstitious judgement about holy men endowed with virtue. They honoured the prophets who had died and been killed by their fathers, and took care to preserve their memory with magnificent monuments; yet they wanted Christ, who taught the same doctrine as the prophets, and indeed the one to whom all of them had looked, put to death. Examples of this kind are found among the Gentiles too. The Athenians mourned Socrates and Aristides with bitter tears, though while they were alive they had pursued them with deadly hatred. Today, among those who profess the Christian name, many similar things happen. Not only the tombs of the apostles and martyrs are venerated by many, but even the tiniest relics, most of which are fake and spurious. Magnificent temples are built in their memory, feast days are consecrated, Masses are sung, and many other things are done which are either superstitious or due to the one and only God. Those who do these things always have the saints on their lips, and they say that we are profane despisers of these saints when we deny that they should be worshipped with divine honours. But if anyone professes the faith of the apostles and martyrs, or teaches with them that Christ alone is our righteousness, our satisfaction for sins, our Mediator with the heavenly Father, the only way by which salvation is reached, and finally that nothing else can be or be named besides him by which we are saved, at once they cry out that this man is a heretic, a blasphemer, a schismatic, a deserter of the true faith, an enemy of the Church, and therefore deserves to be put to death by slow fire or some other more atrocious punishment. But whence comes such a perversity of judgement? Clearly from this: those men who died long ago do not rebuke anyone's life or morals, nor do they accuse their superstitions and sacrilegious gains to their faces; but those who today teach from their writings are a nuisance to all the impious. Yet, so that they may conceal their own impiety, these men want to be regarded as worshippers of the saints and magnificent venerators of them. But the outcries of these men ought to offend no one. For he is not insulting to the saints who denies them divine honours, honours which they not only never sought, but which they detested with the utmost abhorrence (as the example of Paul and Barnabas in the Acts bears witness). Rather, it is those who trample underfoot the doctrine of the saints, and accuse of heresy the faith for which they died, who insult them. And what awaits these men we shall hear in what follows. We shall be true worshippers and venerators of the saints if we believe their doctrine, imitate their example, embrace with true faith Jesus Christ, whom they preached, and acknowledge him as the only Saviour of the human race, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Prævaricatio hominum de sanctis iudicis.
units.tr: Perversity of men in judging the saints.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXIII.
