Nec enim Ecclesia ad eos alligata est, qui huius antistites habentur, & magnificis titulis atq; splendore ipse vendicant: sed aliquando floret & vnà cum veris atq; fidis doctoribus quasi triumphat: aliquando autem ad exiguum credentium numerum redacta latet, vt vix illis nota sit, qui docendi munus in ea sustinent. Fit etiam interdum vt maior pars Ecclesiae cum suis doctoribus in nonnullis erret, per sistentibus interea in veritatis doctrina paucioribus, qui postea alteros illos in viam reducunt. Potest hoc exemplis pluribus demonstrari. Ecclesia Dei erant filij Israelis, & huic ad montem Sinai Legem suam Deus propria voce promulgauerat. Legitimus & ordinarius illius antistes erat Aaron. At bi simul omnes errant, nō in leui aliquo articulo, qui ad res huius seculi pertineat, sed in eo, qui ad veram Dei cognitionem & cultum eius spectat, & ex quo hominis salus dependet: dum videlicet Dei simulachrum fieri volunt contra expressum illius mandatum, & illis morem gerit Aaron, adeoq; nefarij cultus ducem atq; magistrum sese praebet. Num autem idcirco nullam tunc amplius in Israele Ecclesiam fuisse dicemus? Hanc certè Moses inuenit. Cùm enim clamaret, Qui Domini est, ad me accedat: mox adipsum congregati sunt omnes filij Leui, quorū tantus fuit zelus in asserenda Dei gloria, vt aduersus fratres quoq; insurrexerint, eosq; trucidarint. Quid item Eliae temporibus accideriit, satis notum est. Eò vsq; tunc regis tyrannus & populi impietas excreuerant, vt Elias ne vnum quidem veri Dei cultorem reliquum factum, sed se solum superstitem esse putaret. Sed quid ei dicit Dominus? Seruaui mihi septem millia virorum, quorū neq; genua incuruata sunt coram Baal, neq; os osculatum est eum. Fuit ergo tunc in Israele Ecclesia, sed occulta, quae non erraui t, etiamsi in erroribus & nefarijs superstitionibus volutarentur, qui prae alijs Ecclesiae & populi Dei nomen sibi vendicabant. Simile quid Israeli seculo sub Rege Achaz accidisse scimus, quando populi maior pars regis & principum exemplum secuta à veri Dei cultu defecit, adeò vt Propheta queratur, se cum paucis discipulis, quos Dominus ipsi dederit, instar portenti esse in gente illa rebelli & contumaci. Quod ipsum de omnibus Prophetis dici potest, quos fere extraordinariè ad docendi munus à Deo vocatos esse scimus, si quando Sacerdotes in suo officio cessarunt, aut regibus idololatris sese seruiliter accommodauerunt. Sed vt ad Christi tempora accedamus, quae vnquam fuit maior corruptio populi Dei, quā quae tunc fuit? In sectas diuersas scissi erant, qui vt vno fœdere Deo erat obstricti, ita vno corde & ore illum colere & laudare debebant. Extinctus erat per Herodem Sacerdotum veterum ordo, & in horum locum successerant homines obscuri, auari, impij & impudentes, quorum artibus sacra omnia in quaestum turpissimum erant conuersa. Ijdem clauè cognitionis Dei, id est, veram legis & verbi Dei doctrinam è medio sustulerant, nec propria impietate contenti, populum quoq; vanissimis traditionibus circunducebat, imò cogebat ad superstitiones. Sed & in populo regnabat prophanus Dei contemptus, ingratitudo erga Dei Filium, & immanis scelerum omnium licentia. Errarunt ergo tunc Sacerdotes, Doctores, legis interpretes, Seniores, populus deniq;, qui simul omnes tunc Ecclesiae nomine censebantur. At habuit nihilominus in illa gente Deus Ecclesiae veras reliquias, Zachariam, Elizabetam, Iosephum, Mariam virginem, Simeonem, Annā prophetissam, cum multis alijs, qui regnum Dei expectabant, cùm veteres prophetias iam impletas esse viderent. Accesserunt hus postea Apostoli cum septuaginta discipulis, de quibus supra audiuimus, mulieres ite aliquot, Nicodemus, Iosephus Arimathæus & plures alij, quorū nomina non exprimuntur. Etsi ergo tunc Ecclesia admodum tenuis esset, & inter publicos antistitū totiusq; populi errores atq; aperta tyrannidem obscura lateret, Ecclesia tamen fuit, quae salutis viam ingressa est, & quam Dei Filius pro sua sponsa agnouit. Quòd si vero historias excutiamus, eandem nouissimorum temporum conditionem esse patebit. Nam etsi Pontifices nō minori impudetia, quàm olim Iudaeorū Sacerdotes doctrinam & veru Dei cultū corruperint, & tyrannidem in Ecclesia exercuerint iniquissimā, quae& Regū authoritate & vulgi consensu fuit confirmata, nunquā tamē defuerunt testes veritatis, qui errores ipsos arguerunt, tyrannidē antistitum accusarunt, & simplice fidei in vnū Deū per Iesum Christum confessionem constanter retinuerunt. Et constat patrū memoria, cùm densissimæ tenebræ omnia tenerent occupauissent, subinde inuētos fuisse, qui rectius sentiebāt, & alijs quidē admirationi fuerūt propter diuersam sententiā de religione, in honore tamē & pretio habiti sunt propter vitæ & morū integritatē. Hi ergo reliquiæ fuerūt verè credentiū, quos ex peculiari gratia sibi Deus seruauit, vt ex illis suo tempore Ecclesiam numerosiore excitaret. Quapropter iniuriam nobis magna aduersarij faciunt, quando clamant, nos Ecclesiam Dei accusare, quasi illa tot seculis erraverit, imo negare illu tempo ribus Ecclesiam fuisse. Nihil enim horum nos vnquam diximus. Hoc autem dicimus & dicere per gemus, Ecclesiam non semper penes eos esse, qui sibi in illam ius & imperium vendicant, neq; nouum esse aut insolens, si isti errent, quando iam olim quoq; claue scientiae abstulerunt, qui alijs ad Regnū Dei ianitores esse debebant. Id autem nos vere dicere de illis, qui hodie islum honorem in se transfe= runt, res ipsa loquitur, & cuius patebit, si illorū mores cū ijs, quae hic à Christo dicūtur, coferamus.
units.tr: called the Church the pillar and ground of the truth. But the answer to these objections is easy. For the Church is not bound to those who are held to be her leaders, and who claim the title and splendour of her for themselves with grand names. Rather, at times she flourishes and, together with true and faithful teachers, as it were triumphs; at other times she is reduced to a small number of believers and lies hidden, so that she is scarcely known even to those who bear the office of teaching within her. It also sometimes happens that the greater part of the Church, together with its teachers, errs in some matters, while meanwhile a few who remain in the doctrine of truth stand firm, and these afterwards lead those others back into the way. This can be shown by many examples. The Church of God was the children of Israel, and God had promulgated his law to them at Mount Sinai with his own voice. Their lawful and ordinary leader was Aaron. Yet they all erred together, not in some slight article that pertains to the affairs of this age, but in that which concerns the true knowledge and worship of God, and on which the salvation of man depends: namely, when they wished to make an image of God contrary to his express command, and Aaron complied with them and so presented himself as the leader and teacher of a wicked worship. Shall we say, then, that there was no longer any Church in Israel at that time? Certainly Moses found one. For when he cried, "Whoever is on the Lord's side, let him come to me," at once all the sons of Levi gathered to him, whose zeal in asserting the glory of God was so great that they rose up even against their brothers and slew them. What happened in the time of Elijah is also well known. By then the tyranny of the king and the impiety of the people had grown so great that Elijah thought that not one worshipper of the true God was left, and that he alone remained. But what does the Lord say to him? "I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, whose knees have not bowed before Baal, nor has their mouth kissed him." There was therefore a Church in Israel at that time, but a hidden one, which did not err, even though those who claimed for themselves the name of the Church and of the people of God above others were wallowing in errors and wicked superstitions. We know that something similar happened in Israel in the age of King Ahaz, when the greater part of the people, following the example of the king and the princes, fell away from the worship of the true God, so that the prophet complains that he, with the few disciples whom the Lord had given him, was like a portent among that rebellious and stubborn nation. The same can be said of all the prophets, who, as we know, were called by God to the office of teaching almost by extraordinary means, whenever the priests ceased to do their duty or servilely accommodated themselves to idolatrous kings. But let us come to the times of Christ. When was there ever a greater corruption of the people of God than that which existed then? They were split into divided sects, though they were bound by one covenant with God and ought with one heart and one mouth to worship and praise him. The old order of the priests had been extinguished by Herod, and in their place had succeeded obscure, greedy, impious and shameless men, by whose arts all sacred things had been turned into the most shameful profit. These men had taken away the key of knowledge of God, that is, the true doctrine of the law and of the word of God, and, not content with their own impiety, they also led the people about with the emptiest traditions and even forced them into superstitions. And in the people reigned a profane contempt of God, ingratitude towards the Son of God, and a monstrous license for every kind of crime. Therefore the priests, teachers, interpreters of the law, elders, and finally the people, who were then all together reckoned under the name of the Church, erred. Yet God nevertheless had true remnants of the Church in that nation: Zacharias, Elizabeth, Joseph, the virgin Mary, Simeon, Anna the prophetess, with many others who looked for the kingdom of God, since they saw the ancient prophecies now fulfilled. After these came the Apostles with the seventy disciples, of whom we have heard above; some women, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, and many others whose names are not given. Although therefore the Church was then very small, and lay hidden amid the public errors of the leaders and of the whole people and their open tyranny, nevertheless it was the Church, which had entered upon the way of salvation and which the Son of God acknowledged as his bride. But if we examine the histories, it will be clear that the condition of recent times is the same. For although the Pontiffs, with no less shamelessness than the priests of the Jews formerly, have corrupted doctrine and the true worship of God, and have exercised a most unjust tyranny in the Church, a tyranny confirmed both by the authority of kings and by the consent of the common people, yet there have never been lacking witnesses of the truth, who have refuted the errors themselves, accused the tyranny of the leaders, and steadfastly retained the simple confession of faith in the one God through Jesus Christ. And it is established by the memory of the Fathers that, when the thickest darkness had occupied and held all things, from time to time there were found men who thought more rightly, and who, though they were objects of wonder to others because of their different opinion about religion, were nevertheless held in honour and esteem because of the integrity of their life and manners. These, then, were the remnants of true believers, whom God by his special grace kept for himself, so that in his own time he might raise up from them a more numerous Church. Therefore our great adversaries do us an injustice when they cry out that we accuse the Church of God, as if it had erred for so many centuries, or even deny that there was a Church in those times. For we have never said any of these things. But this we say, and we shall continue to say with sorrow, that the Church is not always in the hands of those who claim right and rule over it for themselves, and that it is neither new nor unusual, if these men err, since long ago also they took away the key of knowledge, though they ought to have been the gatekeepers of the kingdom of God for others. That we say this truly of those who today transfer that honour to themselves, the thing itself speaks, and it will become plain if we compare their manners with what Christ says here.

units.la: Dedit Christus Iesus suae Ecclesiae & omnibus huius ministris claues, id est, Euangelij minis-terium, quo arcana regni Dei & quacunq; ad hominis salute faciunt, credentibus aperiuntur & cer-to promittuntur, incredulis autem & contumacibus clauduntur siue negantur. Nam quod apud Matth. Petro dicitur: Tibi dabo claues regni coelorum: quicquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatum in coelo: & quicquid solueris in terra, erit solutū in coelo: Hoc ipsum iam à mortuis excitatus discipulis simul omnibus dicit verbis nonnihil mutatis: Accipite Spiritum sanctum: Si quorū remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: si quorū retinueritis, retenta sunt. Vtrumq; vero clarius interpretatur iam coelos confecensurus, quando ait: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturæ: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salus erit: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Et in praesenti de claue cognitionis vel scientiae loquitur. Ex quibus omnibus aperte patet, per claues nō debere absolutam quandam aut priuatā potestatem intelligi, sed doctrinā & praedicatione Euangelij hos denotari, qua ministros suae Ecclesiae Christus donauit, vt quod hi vere credentibus per illa pollicentur, aut impijs aut incurabilibus minantur, Deus ratum habeat: non quia illi verba quaedam concepta pronuntiāt, aut ita fieri volunt, sed quia Christi verbis ipsius Dei voluntate exprimunt, qui aeterno decreto salute omnem in Filio suo vnigenito conclusit, exitio autem & aeternis inferorum cruciatibus eos destinauit, qui hunc recipere dedignātur & in sceleribus absq; omni poenitentia perseuerant. Itaq; si Euangelij doctrinam è medio tollas, simul etiam claues sustulisti, quae sine illa nullae sunt.
units.tr: Christ Jesus gave to his Church and to all her ministers the keys, that is, the ministry of the Gospel, by which the hidden things of the kingdom of God and whatever pertains to man's salvation are opened to believers and surely promised to them, but are shut up or denied to unbelievers and the obstinate. For what is said to Peter in Matthew: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven," this same thing he says to all the disciples together, once they had been raised from the dead, in words somewhat changed: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain those of any, they are retained." Yet he explains both more clearly when he is about to ascend to the heavens, when he says: "Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptised will be saved; he who does not believe will be condemned." And here he speaks of the key of knowledge or understanding. From all these things it is plainly clear that by the keys we ought not to understand some absolute or private power, but that by them is denoted the doctrine and preaching of the Gospel, with which Christ endowed the ministers of his Church, so that what these men promise to true believers through it, or threaten to the wicked and incurable, God may hold as settled. This is not because they pronounce certain words that have been composed, or wish it to be so, but because they express by the words of Christ himself the will of God, who by an eternal decree has shut up all salvation in his only-begotten Son, and has appointed destruction and the eternal torments of hell for those who disdain to receive him and persevere in their sins without any repentance. Therefore, if you take away the doctrine of the Gospel from the midst, you have at the same time taken away the keys, which without it are nothing.

units.la: Quid vero Romani Pontifices iam seculis aliquot fecerunt, & quid adhuc hodie faciunt? Om-nia ea, quae Iudaeorum Scribis & Pharisaeis Christus in praesenti exprobrat. Primo claue scientiae vel cognitionis sustulerunt, vt nulla amplius fuerit in Ecclesia. Nam sublata verbi Dei doctrina, huius interpretationem in sui pectoris scrinio reconditam esse, & non nisi inde peti debere aiunt: ex claubus autem potestatem & dominiū quoddam externum fabricauerunt, quo in animas simul & corpora atq; fortunas hominū vsi sunt. Deinde potestate hanc sibi solis vendicarunt, & tanta quidem impudentia, vt quemadmodum huius seculi principes & nobiles viri suae familiae insignia habent, ita illi duas claues cum triplici corona ostentent, & ita sibi tanquam Christi in terra vicarijs omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra, & in purgatorio igne datam esse testantur, adeo vt se pro suo arbitrio animas in coelum admittere, aut in igne illo lustrali diutius detinere, vel etiam omnino à coelis excludere posse doceant. Neq; hic à quoquam reprehendi volunt, etiamsi animarum turmas atq; cohortes ad inferos deducant. Itaq; potestate sua male vsurpata pessimè vtuntur. Paulus se cum reliquis Apostolis potestatem habere dicebat ad aedificationē, non ad destructionem. At illi de Ecclesiae & hominum singulorū aedificatione in vera fide nihil soliciti, hoc vnum agunt, vt eos destruant & perdant, qui ipsorum decretis obedire nolunt, & de tyrannide eorum conqueruntur, vel etiam de illa abolenda cogitant. Et in eo quidē tanta audacia & temeritate vtuntur, vt in potentissimos Reges & imperatores sub Clauium praetextu suis excommunicationibus fulminent: quae non semel seditionum & horribilium bellorum causa fuit, quibus orbis concussus & periculosae regnorum mutationes factae sunt. Senserunt audaciam hanc Graeci Imperatores, qui per Pontifices Italia pulsi & eiecti sunt. Senserunt & Germani Imperatores plurimi, vtpote Henricus IIII. cum filio Heinrico V. Heinrichus item VII. Friderich: item duo, Primus & secundus, Ludouicus IIII. & sub hoc maiores quoq; nostri in hisce regionibus, quos Pontificia excommunicatio & ex hac enata quorundam tyrannis coegit, vt aeterno foedere sancito libertate suam tuerentur. Quae vero nostris temporibus sub Clauium nomine designarint, lachrymis potius piorum omnium deplorari, quam verbis exponi possunt. Claues ergo, quas Apostolis & Ecclesiae suae Christus dedit, penes illos nullae, sed prorsus sublatae sunt, & proinde eodem cum Scribis istis crimine tenentur.
units.tr: But what have the Roman Pontiffs done for some centuries now, and what do they still do today? All those things which Christ now reproaches in the Scribes and Pharisees of the Jews. First, they took away the key of knowledge or understanding, so that there was no longer any of it left in the Church. For, the doctrine of God's Word having been removed, they say that its interpretation lies hidden in the chest of their own breast, and that it ought to be sought from there alone. Then from the keys they fashioned a certain power and external dominion, by which they have used both souls and bodies and the goods of men. Next, they claimed this power for themselves alone, and with such shamelessness that, just as the princes of this age and noblemen display the insignia of their families, so they display two keys with a triple crown, and thus they testify that all power in heaven and on earth, and in the fire of purgatory, has been given to them as vicars of Christ on earth, so much so that they teach that they can admit souls into heaven at their own pleasure, or detain them longer in that cleansing fire, or even shut them out of heaven altogether. Nor do they wish to be rebuked on this point by anyone, even when they lead troops and companies of souls down to hell. Therefore they use very badly the power they have wrongly seized. Paul said that he and the other Apostles had power for building up, not for destruction. But they, unconcerned about the building up of the Church and of each individual man in true faith, make it their one aim to destroy and ruin those who refuse to obey their decrees, and who complain of their tyranny or even think of abolishing it. And in this they use such boldness and rashness that, under the pretext of the keys, they hurl their excommunications like thunderbolts at the most powerful kings and emperors. This has more than once been the cause of seditions and dreadful wars, by which the world has been shaken and dangerous changes of kingdoms brought about. The Greek emperors, who were driven out and expelled from Italy by the Pontiffs, felt this boldness. Many German emperors also felt it, namely Henry IV with his son Henry V, likewise Henry VII, Frederick, and two others, the first and second, Louis IV; and under him our own forefathers in these regions, whom papal excommunication and the tyranny of certain men arising from it forced to defend their liberty by a covenant sealed for ever. But what they have designated in our own times under the name of the keys can be lamented rather by the tears of all the pious than set forth in words. Therefore the keys which Christ gave to the Apostles and to his Church are not in their possession at all, but have been utterly taken away, and for that reason they are held guilty of the same crime as those Scribes.

units.la: Cap. XI.
units.tr: Chapter 11.

units.la: Quod autem secundò hùs Christus obijcit, hoc quoq; in nostros illis est videre, nimirum quòd licet clauibus regni Dei glorientur, & huius ianitores haberi velint, ipsi tamè foris manent, neq; in illud ingrediuntur. Quod si negare velint, facilè suorum operum testimonio conuincentur. Christi enim vox est: Ego sum ostiū, per me si quis introierit, seruabitur: & ingredietur ac egredietur, & pascua inueniet. Item: Amen amè dico vobis, qui non ingreditur per ostium, sed ascendit aliunde, sur est & latro. Et alibi: Ego sum via, veritas & vita: nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Ex quibus verbis Apostoli docuerunt, salutem in vno Iesu Christo haberi, neq; aliud nomen extare sub cœlo, per quod quisquam seruari possit. At Pontifices illum pro lufu habent, & ostia regni cœlorum infinita fabricarunt, vtpote Diuorum intercessionem, Missæ sacrificium, Indulgentias suas, vota Monastica, Peregrinationes ad varia & diuersa Diuorum simulachra, Fraternitates & sexcenta alia, quæ commemorare longum foret. Deinde his omnibus ad quæstum suum tam impudenter abuntur, vt quiuis cordatus videat, eos istis quoq; nihil tribuere. Quòd si vitam & mores eorum inspicias, aut hypocritas inuenies, qui fucata sanctimoniæ titulo (vt olim Pharifæi) sese palliant, aut paläm flagitiosos, qui ijs etiam sceleribus madent, propter quæ homines à regno Dei excludi scriptura testantur. Possent hæc prolixè demonstrari, sed cùm vbiq; locorum sint oculati testes, qui Romanæ curiæ mores atq; studia coràm viderunt, pluribus argumentis siue exemplis non est opus. Vnum tamen prætermittere non possum: Regnare nimirum illic eos, quibus lusus & iocus est, de corporum resurrectione & animarum immortalitate disputare, & impunè quidem vtramq; multi negant, modò aduersus summi Pontificis potestatem nihil pronuntient. Quomodo ergo in regnum Dei ingrediantur, qui vitam post mortalis huius cursum absolutum nullam superesse credunt?
units.tr: What Christ next charges against them, the same may be seen in our own opponents: namely, that although they boast of the keys of the kingdom of God and wish to be regarded as its doorkeepers, they themselves remain outside and do not enter into it. If they wish to deny this, they will easily be convicted by the testimony of their own works. For the voice of Christ is: "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out, and find pasture." Likewise: "Truly, truly I say to you, he who does not enter by the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber." And elsewhere: "I am the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me." From these words the Apostles taught that salvation is had in the one Jesus Christ, and that there is no other name under heaven by which anyone can be saved. But the Pontiffs treat this as a joke, and have fabricated countless doors of the kingdom of heaven: namely the intercession of the saints, the sacrifice of the Mass, their Indulgences, monastic vows, pilgrimages to various and diverse images of the saints, Fraternities, and six hundred other things, which would be long to recount. Then they abuse all these things so shamelessly for their own profit that anyone with sense can see that they attribute nothing to these things either. But if you examine their life and morals, you will find either hypocrites, who cloak themselves under the false title of holiness (as the Pharisees once did), or openly wicked men, who are steeped in those very crimes on account of which Scripture testifies that people are excluded from the kingdom of God. These things could be demonstrated at length, but since there are eyewitnesses everywhere who have seen with their own eyes the morals and pursuits of the Roman court, there is no need for many arguments or examples. Yet one thing I cannot pass over: there reign there those for whom it is a game and a jest to dispute about the resurrection of bodies and the immortality of souls, and many deny both with impunity, provided they say nothing against the power of the supreme Pontiff. How then do those enter into the kingdom of God who believe that no life remains after the completed course of this mortal life?

units.la: Restat tertium, quod de scribis & legis interpretibus dicitur, eos quoq; ab illis prohiberi, qui in gredi volunt. Idem vero Pontifices cum suis creaturis nimium aperte faciunt. Viam enim, qua ad Christum, qui (vt diximus) vnicū ostium est, venitur, suis traditionibus obstruunt, & ne Euangelium purè prædicetur prohibent, ne qui huius cognitione illuminati, ipsis reliquis in vno Christo acquiescant. Si qui vero nonnihil animosiores de vera salutis ratione interrogant, & quæ ipsos dubios rerumq; incertos faciunt, liberius exponunt, eos aut duris atq; minacibus responsis reijciunt, aut scilicet eludunt, dicentes, accuratiorem istorum cognitionem nequaquam pertinere ad laicos, quorum sit simpliciter credere & in fide Ecclesiæ permanere, reliqua autem ijs relinquere excutienda, qui ad Ecclesiæ gubernacula sedeant. At si quis instet, & vnūquenq; sua fide viuere dicat, iam in furorè conuersi, sincula, gladios & faces exerunt, vt vnius & alterius exemplo alij territi à quæstionibus et disputationibus eiusmodi abstineant. Quòd si vero Respub. aliqua aut princeps Euangelio ostiū apriant, & è medio sublatis abusibus atq; superstitionibus reformatione secundùm Dei verbum instituant, Deū immortale, quas turbas illi excitant? Mittūt legatos à latere, qui istos immane sceleris committere vociferantur, eò quòd propria authoritate rem tentent, quæ ad solum Pontificē & vniuersalis Cōcilij determinatione pertineat: addunt præterea minas, quibus mox excommunicationis fulmina succedunt: indicunt Concilia, in quibus nō alij, quàm qui in ipsorū verba iurarunt, præsident: adhæc citantur quos iā ante hæreseos damnarūt: & si quis comparere, aut Concilij decretis obedire dedignetur, mox aduersus hunc executionē fieri iubent ab ijs, quos cōcilij defensores & propugnatores constituerunt. Hinc ergo seditiones, bella ciuilia & extera, vrbium expugnationes, horribiles rerum motus, cædes, rapinæ, incendia, agrorū vastationes & omnia alia nascuntur, quæ in bellocrū delissimo fieri consueuerūt. Verum me dicere fatebuntur, quicunq; Pontificum historias vel à primo limine salutarunt. Sed quid historijs veteribus, exeplis opus est, quando ista hodie omnia fiunt, ut istorum hominū plus quàm Turcicam crudelitatē non vna solum natio, sed totus ferè orbis Christianus expertus est? Quid verò hoc aliud est, quàm nolle ingredi in Regnū Dei, & eos qui ingredi volunt prohibere? Vt autem ista à Christo olim ideo dicta sunt, vt Iudæi sibi à seduoribus & lupis eiusmodi cauerent: ita nobis quoq; horum omniū hic vsus esse debet, vt ijs qui illos hodie imitantur, procul reliquis, puriorem Euangelij doctrinā sequamur, & grati simus Deo, qui illorū fraudes luce verbi sui detexit, & Ecclesiæ claves regni cælorū atq; verū earundē vsum restituit. Neq; nos terreant istorum hominum minæ & crudeles conatus. Viuit enim & regnat in cælis Christus, Rex regum & dominus dominantium, qui illos videt, & Ecclesiam suam exercere quidem sub cruce sinit, eandem nit, eandem vero euerti & deleri non patitur. Idem quoq; ferreo sceptro tandem in hostibus suis co-ercendis vtetur, qui salutari virga Euangelicæ doctrinæ regi nolunt.
units.tr: There remains the third point, which is said of the scribes and lawyers: that they also forbid those who wish to enter. The Pontiffs, with their creatures, do this all too openly. For they block the way by which one comes to Christ, who (as we have said) is the one door, with their traditions, and they forbid the Gospel to be preached purely, so that those enlightened by its knowledge do not rest in the one Christ alongside the rest. If some who are rather bolder ask about the true manner of salvation, and speak more freely about those matters which make them doubtful and uncertain, they either reject them with harsh and threatening replies, or else mock them, saying that a more exact knowledge of these things does not at all pertain to laymen, whose task is simply to believe and remain in the faith of the Church, while the rest is to be left to those who sit at the helm of the Church to examine. But if anyone presses the point, and says that each man must live by his own faith, they then turn to rage and bring out knives, swords and torches, so that by the example of one or two others, frightened, they may abstain from such questions and disputes. But if some commonwealth or prince opens the door to the Gospel, and, with abuses and superstitions removed, sets about a reformation according to the Word of God, good God, what tumults they stir up! They send legates from their side, who cry out that these men commit an monstrous crime, because they attempt on their own authority a matter that belongs only to the decision of the Pontiff and of a universal Council; they add threats, which are soon followed by the thunderbolts of excommunication; they call Councils, over which none preside except those who have sworn an oath to their words; moreover, they summon those whom they had already condemned as heretics; and if anyone refuses to appear or to obey the decrees of the Council, they at once order execution to be carried out against him by those whom they have appointed as defenders and champions of the Council. Hence arise sedition, civil and foreign wars, the storming of cities, dreadful upheavals of affairs, slaughter, plunder, fires, devastation of fields and all the other things that are wont to happen in the most cruel war. Those will confess that I speak truly who have greeted the histories of the Pontiffs even from the first threshold. But why is there need of ancient histories and examples, when all these things are happening today, so that not only one nation but almost the whole Christian world has experienced the cruelty of these men, more than Turkish? And what is this, indeed, but refusing to enter the kingdom of God and forbidding those who wish to enter? Just as these things were once said by Christ so that the Jews might guard themselves against such seducers and wolves, so too we ought to make use of all these things here: that, keeping far from those who today imitate them, we may follow the purer doctrine of the Gospel, and be grateful to God, who has laid bare their frauds by the light of his Word, and has restored the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the true use of them to the Church. Let not the threats and cruel attempts of these men terrify us. For Christ lives and reigns in heaven, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who sees them, and who indeed allows his Church to be exercised under the cross, yet suffers it not to be overthrown and destroyed. He too will at length use an iron sceptre to restrain his enemies, who are unwilling that he should rule them with the saving rod of Evangelical doctrine.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt videamus, quus tam seriæ correptionis effectus apud Legis interpretes & Pharisæos fuerit, de quo Lucas sic scribit: Cum autem hæc eis diceret, cœperunt Scribæ & Pharisæi vehementer ei imminere, & eum allicere aut provocare ad loquendum de multis, insidiantes ei, & quærentes vænari aliquid ex ipsius ore, vt eum accusarent. Ergo non meliores, sed potius deteriores facti sunt, quod fore Christus non ignorabat, dixit tamen ista (vt initio monuimus) propter simpli-ces, vt hi à lupis istis sibi cauerent. Nos autem horum exemplo admonemur, incurabiles tandem fie-rieos, qui fucatæ sanctimoniæ, gloriæ itè priuatæ & quæstui suo potius quam solidæ pietati & Veri-tati student. Quò enim magis vrgentur, eò magis sæuiunt, & nouis quodammodo viribus collectis aduersus Veritatis doctrinam maiori conatu insurgunt. Diuinæ aut virtutis argumentū est, quod Christus tam diu imprecationibus irritatos continere potuit, ne ad manus venirent, sed verbis & quæstionibus rem agerent. At non modestè & cū ordine aliquo legitimo, vt par erat, id fecerunt: sed multi simul varijs & diuersis quæstionibus eū fatigare conati sunt, quibus haud dubie verba quoq; contumeliosa & iniuriarum plena accesserunt, vt his irritatus aliquid inconsideratius effutiret, ex quo ipsum accusandi ansam haberent. Et tales etiam hodie solent esse Sophistarum Monachorū & omnium eorum disputationes, qui aduersus Euangelij doctrinam coniurarunt. Nam vt liberos cū doctis congressus coram æquis iudicibus studiosè subterfugiunt: ita si quos in suam arenam protra-here possunt, in qua ipsi soli dominantur, tunc gigantum instar victoriæ spe concepta nullum petulan-tiæ & fallaciæ genus omittunt, vt animi perplexos reddant eos, qui veritatis doctrinam tuentur. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, hodie passim habentur. Debent autem ista nos admonere, ne fidei & religionis causam, aut fidos huius propugnatores, temere istorum hominum petulantiæ & corruptis iudicijs commitamus: quod hodie quidā nimis inconsultò faciunt. Quod si vero in illos pij incidunt, ne terreantur: sed fidei & doctrinæ suæ simplicitatem constanter defendant, quæstiones captiosas prudenter declinent, & in Christo Iesu fortes sint, qui nobis os & sapientiā promisit, cui nemo aduersa-riorum possit resistere. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But it is time that we see what the effect of this so serious rebuke was among the lawyers and Pharisees, of which Luke writes thus: "And when he said these things to them, the scribes and Pharisees began to press upon him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him and seeking to catch something from his mouth, that they might accuse him." Therefore they became not better but rather worse, which Christ did not fail to foresee, yet he said these things (as we noted at the beginning) on account of the simple, so that they might guard themselves against those wolves. But we are admonished by their example that those become incurable at last who study false holiness, empty glory and their own gain rather than solid piety and truth. For the more they are pressed, the more they rage, and, as if with new strength gathered, they rise up against the doctrine of truth with greater effort. It is a sign of divine power that Christ was able to restrain those who were so long provoked by his rebukes, so that they did not come to hands but dealt with the matter by words and questions. Yet they did not do this modestly, nor with any lawful order, as was fitting; rather, many at once tried to wear him out with various and diverse questions, to which, without doubt, insulting words full of abuse were also added, so that, provoked by these, he might blurt out something rather rash, from which they might have an occasion to accuse him. And such, even today, are the disputations of the Sophists, the Monks, and all those who have conspired against the doctrine of the Gospel. For just as they carefully avoid meeting free men with learned men before fair judges, so, if they can drag some into their own arena, where they alone rule, then, conceiving hope of victory like giants, they omit no kind of impudence and deceit, so as to render perplexed those who defend the doctrine of truth. Examples by which this is proved are to be found everywhere today. These things ought, however, to warn us not to commit rashly the cause of the faith and religion, or its faithful champions, to the impudence and corrupt judgments of these men, which some today do all too unadvisedly. But if the godly fall in with them, let them not be terrified, but constantly defend the simplicity of their faith and doctrine, prudently avoid captious questions, and be strong in Christ Jesus, who has promised us a mouth and wisdom, against which none of our adversaries can resist. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. ## HOMILY CXXV.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXV.

INterea cum congregata esset multa turba, adeo vt alij alios conculca-rent, cœpit dicere discipulis suis: In primis cauete vobis à fermento Pharisæorum, quod est hypocrisis. Nihil enim opertum est, quod non sit detegendum: neq; occultum, quod non sit cognoscendum. Propterea quæ in tenebris dixistis, in luce audientur: & quod in aurem locuti estis in conclauibus, prædicabitur supra domos.
units.tr: Meanwhile, when a great crowd had gathered, so that they trampled one another, he began to say to his disciples: "First of all, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For nothing is covered that will not be uncovered, nor hidden that will not be known. Therefore whatever you have said in darkness will be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed upon the housetops."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus, in proximo Capite cum Pharisæis & Le-gis interpretibus grauiter expostulauit, qui simulata sanctitatis specie & falsa doctrina populum simplicem & infelicem seducebant, & ideo illis pœnas grauissimas minatus est. Etsi vero hac correptione saluti ipsorum consultum voluerit, illi tamen adeo non emendantur, vt potius in maiorem rabiem accensi, ipsum insidiosis atq; importunis quæstionibus obruere & irretire conati sint. Quo exemplo docemur, quid hodie etiam de omnibus sit sperandum, qui religionem quæ-stu metiuntur, & suæ potius quam Dei gloriæ student. Non possunt tales credere (vt apud Ioannem Christus ait) & proinde in sua impietate incurabiles perseuerant. Quia vero horum exemplum & simplices offendere, & Apostolos terrere poterat, prima huius capitis parte hos in frequenti homi-num turba amicè & fideliter instituit. Et primò quidem monet, ne Pharisæos imitentur, sed ab hy-pocrisi, qua illi peccabant, sibi in primis caueant. Deinde iubet, vt creditam sibi Veritatis doctri-nam constanter & intrepidè prædicent: quo loco multis validissimis argumentis eos aduersus omne metum hostiū & ipsius etiam mortis præmunit & armat. Continet autè locus iste generalem doctrinam, quæ primò ad omnes Verbi Dei administros pertinet, deinde ad Christianos quoq; omnes extendi potest. Ante omnia verò Christi exemplum observari debet, qui cum apud doctrinæ & religionis antistites nihil vel monendo vel corripiendo proficeret, discipulos suos & populum aduersus illos instruit, quò minus illorum fallacijs seduci possint. Non ergo cessare debent in suo munere Evangelij præcones, etiamsi eos incurabiles manere, vel etiam deteriores fieri videant, quorum summa est apud omnes authoritas: sed tunc potius aduersus hos vocem suam attollere, eorum errores & tyrannidem arguere, & quosuis præmonere debent, quo facilius sibi ab illis cauere queant. Quod enim Christus in præsenti fecit, hoc ipsum olim ante ipsum Prophetas & postea Apostolos quoq; fecisse scimus. Sed quoniam de hoc nuper quoq; dictum est, nunc ad huius loci tractationem accedamus.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, in the preceding chapter, sharply rebuked the Pharisees and the interpreters of the Law, who, under a pretended appearance of holiness and with false doctrine, led astray the simple and unhappy people, and therefore threatened them with the most severe punishments. Although he meant this rebuke to serve their salvation, they were so far from being corrected that, rather, inflamed to greater rage, they tried to overwhelm and entangle him with insidious and importunate questions. From this example we are taught what should be expected even today from all those who measure religion by gain and seek their own glory rather than God's. Such people cannot believe (as Christ says in John), and therefore they persist incurable in their impiety. But since the example of these men could offend the simple and terrify the Apostles, in the first part of this chapter he instructs them, in the presence of a large crowd, in a friendly and faithful manner. And first he warns them not to imitate the Pharisees, but above all to beware of hypocrisy, the sin of which those men were guilty. Then he orders them to preach constantly and fearlessly the doctrine of truth entrusted to them; in this passage he fortifies and arms them with very strong arguments against all fear of enemies and even of death itself. This passage contains a general doctrine, which pertains first to all ministers of God's Word, and then can be extended to all Christians as well. Above all, the example of Christ must be observed: when he achieved nothing among the leaders of doctrine and religion, either by admonishing or by rebuking them, he instructs his disciples and the people against them, so that they may less easily be seduced by their deceits. Therefore the heralds of the Gospel must not cease in their office, even if they see that those whose authority is supreme among all remain incurable, or even grow worse. Rather, they ought then to raise their voice against these men, to denounce their errors and tyranny, and to forewarn everyone, so that they may more easily guard themselves against them. For what Christ has done in the present case, we know the Prophets did before him, and the Apostles afterwards. But since this has already been said recently, let us now come to the treatment of this passage.

units.la: Rursus autem pro suo more totius negotij occasionem Lucas præmittit. Fuit hæc ingens populi concursus, in quo myriades hominum confluxisse scribit. Vbi etsi numerus finitus pro infinito ponatur, constat tamen maximam turbam fuisse, cum præ multitudine alij alios conculcauerint. Voluit ergo Dominus dere maximi momenti in frequentissima populi concione differere, ut plures instituerentur. Estq; hic obseruatu dignissimum, quam vana & inania sint magnatum huius seculi consilia aduersus Christum & Verbum eius. Quis enim alius scopus aut finis Pharisæis & Scribis propositus fuit, quàm ut illum accusandi occasionem haberent, & apud omnes in contemptum & odium adducerent? Sed adeò nihil profecerunt, ut potius ista occasione populus ad ipsum audiendum ardenti & maximo studio confluxerit. Quod ipsum sæpe alias factum fuisse apud Euangelistas legimus. Imò, ut Ioannes narrat, cum aliquando seruos suos ad illum capiendum ablegauissent, hi in te plo concionantem attentè audiuerunt, nec solum sine illo reuerti sunt, verumetiam de eius doctrina præclarum tulerunt testimonium. Et in Actorum libro commemoratur, quod quo magis de silentio Apostolis imponendo Sacerdotes & Seniores consultarunt, eò liberius & maiori cum fructu illi de Christo locuti sint. Quid, quod cum Sauli crudelitas Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam dissipauisset, fideles tanquam tabulæ ardentes ex urbis incendio dispersi totam Iudæam & Samariam Euangelij prædicatione accenderunt? Et hoc illud est, quod Dauid dicit, Deum ex alto ridere eorum consilia, qui aduersus ipsum & Vnctum eius conspirant. Cum ergo huius generis exempla non pauca no stro etiam seculo viderimus, debet tam eorum quam veterum consideratio nos confirmare, ne vllis hostium minis aut machinationibus nos è statione deijci patiamur.
units.tr: Again, following his usual practice, Luke first sets out the occasion of the whole matter. This was a huge gathering of people, in which he writes that myriads of men had flocked together. Although a finite number is put for an infinite one, it is plain that the crowd was very great, since in the press they trampled one another. The Lord therefore chose to defer a matter of the greatest importance to a very crowded assembly of the people, so that more might be instructed. And it is most worthy of notice how vain and empty are the counsels of the great men of this age against Christ and his Word. For what other aim or end did the Pharisees and Scribes set before themselves than to find an occasion of accusing him and to bring him into contempt and hatred among everyone? But they achieved so little that, on the contrary, on this very occasion the people flocked together to hear him with ardent and very great eagerness. We read in the Evangelists that this had often happened on other occasions. Indeed, as John relates, when once they had sent their servants to seize him, these men, listening attentively to him as he taught in the temple, not only returned without him but also bore an excellent testimony to his doctrine. And in the book of Acts it is recorded that the more the priests and elders consulted about imposing silence on the Apostles, the more freely and with greater fruit they spoke about Christ. What of the fact that when Saul's cruelty had scattered the Church of Jerusalem, the faithful, like burning torches flung out from a city on fire, set all Judea and Samaria alight by the preaching of the Gospel? This is what David means when he says that God laughs from on high at the counsels of those who conspire against him and his Anointed. Since we have seen not a few examples of this kind in our own age as well, the consideration of these, as of the ancient ones, ought to strengthen us, so that we do not allow ourselves to be thrown from our post by any threats or schemes of enemies.

units.la: Est præterea perquam memorabile & imitatione dignum populi Iudaici exemplum. Sciebant omnes, quàm immani odio Christum proceres cum ecclesiastici tum politici persequerentur, neq; illos latere potuerunt edicta publica de excommunicandis vel è Synagoga eijciendis omnibus, qui ipsum sectarentur: quibus edictis multos ex principum numero territos fuisse scribit Ioannes, ne fidem in illum auderent profiteri. Nihilominus tamen populus ad eum concurrit, & cœtus cogunt frequentissimos, in quibus eum de regno Dei differentem audiunt. Quod cum ij fecerint, qui nondum illi aperte nomen dederant, quanto magis id nos facere conuenit, qui in nomen eius baptizati sumus, & ab illo Christiani denominamur? Meminerimus igitur exemplis huiusmodi nobis cœtus sacros commendari, quibus ad veram pietatem fouendam atq; exercendam nihil vtilius & magis necessarium est. In illis verbum Dei prædicatur, & præsentibus temporibus atq; personis accommodatum altius multò in animos hominum penetrat, quam si illud singuli domi suæ legant. In illis etiam Sacramenta administrantur, quæ vt promissionum & beneficiorum Dei sigilla sunt: ita Christianæ etiam societatis tesseræ sunt & vincula, quibus illa firmius & artius colligatur. Fiunt etiā in cœtibus eiusmodi preces publicæ, quarum maximam vim esse vel vnica Christi promissio docet, qui duos aut tres, quiin suo nomine congregati fuerint, omne id impetraturos esse ait, quod à Patre suo petierint. Ideo cœtus sacros in Lege sua Deus instituit, & in eum finem Leuitas voluit per omnes tribus dispartitos, ut vbiq; essent, qui populum diebus Sabbati collectum ex Verbo suo erudirent. Neq; eo contentus, insuper mandauit, ut quotannis omnes mares ter ad locum tabernaculi siue templi conuenirent, & simul dies festos agerent in veterum beneficiorum eius memoriam. Et constat in festis illis non postremum locum datum fuisse conuocationi aut congregationi sanctæ, ad quam omnes simul conueniebant. Prophetæ etiam, si quando grauiora pericula instabant, populum hortabantur ut cœtus extraordinarios indicerent, in quibus Dei Verbum audiret, & illius iram deprecarentur. Quod si sanctorum exempla inspicias, omnes illos in coetibus sacris frequentandis diligentissimos fuisse vt debit. Dauidi certe sub Saule exulanti nihil molestius fuit, quam quod illos adire non posset, & a sacris publicis excluderetur. In nouo Testamento Christus coetus populi frequentes habuit, & idem eius exemplo Apostoli quoque fecerunt. Inter veteres autem Christianos tantum fuit conueniendi studium, vt persecutionum tempore noctumos potius conuentus magno cum vitae & fortunarum omnium periculo agere voluerint, quam tam necessario pietatis exercitio in vniuersum carere. Quos hodie multi sub tyrannis persecutoribus pie imitantur, qui vt suo exemplo nostram nobis ingratitudinem exprobrant, qui tantum Dei beneficium, quo tuto & cum laude poteramus frui, tam turpiter negligimus: ita olim in magno illo die omnes eos damnabunt, qui coetus sacros deridGent, & eos scurriliter insectantur, qui in illis frequentes & assidui esse consueuerunt. Clamant fere illi: Fides donum Dei est, nec ab aliquo hominum potest dari: Neq; meliores nobis esse videmus eos, qui ad templa frequenter confluunt, vt illic concionantes audiant & precibus publicis intersint. Quis vero negat, fidem a solo Deo dari? aut quis eam a Verbi praeconibus postulat? Tu vero qui prius illud fateris, cur non etiam Paulinum illud obseruas: Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per Verbum Dei? Et illud Christi: Oues meae vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur eam? Quibus manifeste docetur, Deum fidem nobis per Verbi sui praedicationem largiri, & proinde illam nunquam assecuturos esse eos, qui hanc aspernantur. Nec enim aequum est, vt noua & extraordinaria ratione in illis illuminandis Deus vtatur, qui medium illud ordinarium improbe contemnunt, cui sese iam inde ab orbe condito sancti & electi omnes accommodauerunt. Quod autem illi scurriliter quaerunt, in quo ipsis meliores sint ij, qui coetus sacros frequenter adeunt, facilis est responsio. Nam etsi homines sint & affectibus humanis obnoxij, adhuc interdum in vitia quoque aperta prolabantur, eo ipso tamen alteris illis meliores sunt, quod Dei verbum audiunt, eo delectantur, & quidille velit discere studeant. Et vt spes bona est de filio, qui quamuis iuuenilibus desiderijs superatus multa praeter officium facit, patrem tamen monentem audit, & eius correptionem veretur: nihil autem boni sperari potest de eo, qui non contentus peccasse, insuper patris conspectum fugit, admonitiones eius contemnit, correptiones odit, & minas scurrilibus dictis eludit: Ita de Verbi quoque studiosis optime sperare possumus, vt interdum exorbitent, cum de huius oforibus [?] spes salutis omnino sit nulla. In istorum ergo meditatione pij versentur, & a Deo institutis medijs sedulo sese accommodent, neq; improborum istorum cavillis moueantur.
units.tr: Moreover, there is a most memorable example of the Jewish people, worthy of imitation. All knew with what immense hatred the leaders, both ecclesiastical and civil, persecuted Christ, nor could they miss the public edicts ordering the excommunication, or the expulsion from the synagogue, of all who followed him. John writes that by these edicts many of the rulers were so frightened that they did not dare to profess faith in him. Nevertheless the people flocked to him, and they gathered very crowded assemblies, in which they heard him speaking about the kingdom of God. If those who had not yet openly given their name to him did this, how much more fitting is it for us to do so, who have been baptized into his name and are called Christians from him? Let us therefore remember that sacred assemblies are commended to us by examples of this kind, and that nothing is more useful and more necessary for fostering and exercising true piety. In them the Word of God is preached, and, adapted to the present times and persons, it penetrates the minds of men far more deeply than if each read it alone at home. In them the Sacraments are also administered, which, as seals of God's promises and benefits, are also the tokens and bonds of the Christian fellowship, by which it is held together more firmly and closely. Public prayers are also offered in such assemblies, and the very great power of these is taught by the single promise of Christ, who says that two or three gathered in his name will obtain whatever they ask of his Father. Therefore God instituted sacred assemblies in his Law, and to this end he wished the Levites to be distributed among all the tribes, so that they would be everywhere to instruct the people gathered on the Sabbath days from his Word. Not content with this, he further commanded that every year all the males should gather three times at the place of the tabernacle or temple and keep the festivals together in memory of his former benefits. And it is well established that in those festivals no small place was given to the holy convocation or assembly, to which all came together. The Prophets too, whenever graver dangers threatened, exhorted the people to call extraordinary assemblies, in which they might hear God's Word and entreat his wrath. If you look at the examples of the saints, you will find that all of them were most diligent in frequenting sacred assemblies, as they ought to be. Certainly for David, when he was in exile under Saul, nothing was more painful than that he could not approach them and was excluded from the public sacred services. In the New Testament Christ had large gatherings of the people, and the Apostles did the same following his example. Among the early Christians there was such eagerness to meet that in times of persecution they preferred to hold nocturnal assemblies, at great peril to life and all their property, rather than go altogether without so necessary an exercise of piety. Many today under tyrant persecutors piously imitate them, and by their example reproach us for our ingratitude, we who so shamefully neglect so great a benefit of God, which we could enjoy safely and with praise. So in that great day they will condemn all those who mock sacred assemblies, and who scurrilously assail those who have been accustomed to be frequent and diligent in them. Those men almost always cry out: Faith is a gift of God, and cannot be given by any man. Nor do we see that those who flock frequently to the churches, to hear the preachers there and to take part in the public prayers, are any better than we are. But who denies that faith is given by God alone? Or who asks it of the heralds of the Word? But you who confess the first point, why do you not also observe that saying of Paul: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God"? And that of Christ: "My sheep hear my voice, and they follow it"? By these passages it is clearly taught that God bestows faith on us through the preaching of his Word, and therefore that those who despise this will never attain it. For it is not fitting that God should use a new and extraordinary means in enlightening those who wickedly despise the ordinary means, to which all the saints and the elect have accommodated themselves from the foundation of the world. As for what they scurrilously ask, in what way those who frequently attend sacred assemblies are better than they, the answer is easy. For although men are human and subject to human passions, and sometimes slip even into open vices, yet by this very fact they are better than those others: they hear God's Word, delight in it, and are eager to learn what he wills. Just as there is good hope for a son who, though overcome by youthful desires and doing many things contrary to his duty, nevertheless listens to his father admonishing him and fears his rebuke; but nothing good can be hoped for from one who, not content with having sinned, moreover flees his father's sight, despises his admonitions, hates his corrections, and mocks his threats with scurrilous words. So too we may hope well of those who are devoted to the Word, that they sometimes go astray; whereas for those who despise it there is altogether no hope of salvation. Therefore let the godly occupy themselves in meditating on these things, diligently accommodate themselves to the means instituted by God, and not be moved by the quibbles of these wicked men.

units.la: Porro ad Christum veniamus, qui in tam frequenti concione populi discipulos suos instituere in cipit, & initio statim fontem omnis mali in ecclesia obscuraturus ait: In primis cauete vobis a fermento Pharisaeorum, quod est hypocrisis. Per hypocrisim vero magnificam sanctimoniae simul & externi in docendo apparatus ostentatione intelligit, qua Pharisaei sese apud populum venditabant. Nam vt nuper audiuimus, crebro abluebantur, phylacteria & fimbrias vestium dilatabant, stolis longis amicti in publicum prodibant, omnia deniq; faciebant ad ostentationem singularis sanctitatis, vt sibi apud rudes & simplices existimationem & dignitatem maiorem pararent. At quia praecipuus finis erat, quod doctrinae falsae fidem & authoritatem conciliare hoc modo conabantur, hanc quoq; sub isto nomine comprehendit. Vult ergo Christus, vt Apostoli simplicitati & integritati studeant in suo munere, neq; fucum aliquam accersant, quo Euangelij doctrinam commendent. Est enim simplex veritatis oratio, neq; aliunde accersitis coloribus aut ornatu fictitio opus habet. Et qui ista adhibent inter docendum, ij se de propria potius gloria & authoritate, quam de Dei gloria & populi salute solicitos esse produnt. Itaq; hoc Christi dictum omnes eos arguit & confutat, qui insolito vestitu, ambitiosis titulis, incessu & gestibus peculiaribus, pronunciatione theatrica, aut ad lachrymas mulierculis movendas composita sese & suam doctrinam venditare solent. In quibus magni artifices sunt Monachi, qui his potissimum rebus apud simplicem plebeculam sibi authoritatem conciliant. Sed non minus hi peccant quidam Euangelicae doctrinae professores, qui & ipsi titulos superbos multa pecunia redimunt, & vbi hos assecuti sunt, vestitum sibi sumunt a communi aliorum ministrorum habitu diuersum, multa deniq; alia faciunt, quae ambitiosam hypocrisim redolent. At nihil horum vnquam fecerunt Apostoli, qui huius praecepti a Christo accepti memores, modestiae & humilitati studuerunt, in docendo autem fideles, industrij & feruidi fuerunt, & ita doctrinae suae fidem, sibi ipsis vero authoritatem solidam comparárunt.
units.tr: Now let us come to Christ, who, in so crowded an assembly of the people, begins to instruct his disciples, and at once, intending to obscure the source of every evil in the Church, says: "Above all, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy." By hypocrisy, however, he means the display of a magnificent holiness together with an outward show in teaching, by which the Pharisees puffed themselves up before the people. For, as we heard recently, they washed often, enlarged their phylacteries and the tassels of their garments, went out in public clad in long robes, and in short did everything for the display of singular sanctity, so that they might win for themselves greater esteem and dignity among the untutored and simple. But because their chief aim was to win credit and authority for false doctrine in this way, he includes this too under that name. Christ wills therefore that the Apostles aim at simplicity and integrity in their office, and not seek any pretence by which to commend the doctrine of the Gospel. For the speech of truth is simple and has no need of colours brought in from elsewhere or of artificial ornament. And those who employ such things in teaching show that they are concerned rather for their own glory and authority than for the glory of God and the salvation of the people. Therefore this saying of Christ convicts and refutes all those who are wont to puff themselves and their doctrine up by unusual dress, ambitious titles, peculiar gait and gestures, theatrical delivery, or contrivances designed to move little women to tears. Among these the Monks are great artists, who especially by such things win authority for themselves among the simple common folk. But no less do some professors of the Gospel doctrine sin, who also buy proud titles with much money, and when they have obtained these, take to themselves a dress different from the common habit of other ministers, and in short do many other things that smack of ambitious hypocrisy. But the Apostles never did any of these things. Mindful of the precept they had received from Christ, they aimed at modesty and humility, and in teaching they were faithful, diligent and fervent, and in this way won for their doctrine faith, but for themselves solid authority.

units.la: Porro obseruatu digna est Metaphora, qua hypocrisim Christus fermentum dicit. Ea enim huius ingenium, vires & effecta exprimit. Vt enim fermentum massa ita miscetur & vnitur, vt ab ea amplius separari non possit: ita hypocrisis nobis à natura inhaeret, vt quae haereditario iure ex primis parentibus in nos deriuata est. Hos enim post primum lapsum, cum à propria conscientia redarguerentur, ad simulationem sanctitatis & innocentiae confugisse constat. Ex ficuum enim foliis perizomata sibi contexuerunt, quibus nuditatem suam tegerent. Inde verbis quoque satis audacibus vsi sunt, quibus se excusarunt, vt culpam suam non obscure in ipsum Deum transferrent: Quod hodie omnibus hominibus proprium est, vt in pueris & pessimis quibusque cernimus. Illi enim cum vix quicquam adhuc per aetatem sapere videntur, si quid peccarunt, id mirifice tegere & dissimulare solent, conuiciis aut ad nouas artes conuertuntur, & in translatione criminum admodum ingeniosi sunt. Hi vero, etsi illos ad peccandum praeceps libido abripiat, deprehensi tamen & accusati pertinaciter negant, & optimi videri volunt, neque illos alicuius fuci & coloris pudet, modo aliquam suae nequitiae excusationem ex eo sperare possint. Adhaec altas in corrupta hominis natura radices egit hypocrisis, & ideo recte fermento tenacissimo confertur. Deinde vt hoc semel admixtum breui temporis spacio totâ farinae iam conspersae massam penetrat: ita hypocrisis, si ei homo indulgeat, quam celerrime totâ vitâ & mores inficit, vt in omnibus dictis & factis sese exerat. Delectat enim improbissimos quosque simulata virtutis species, cui eo magis student, si se proficere & propter ea in honore & pretio esse videant. Itaque eo vsque tandem progrediuntur, vt quemadmodum hominibus imponunt, ita se Deo quoque fallere posse exist imént. Quae causa est, vt in huius cultu impie ludant, & pietatem magnam simulent, etiamsi animis ab omni religione sint alienissimi. Exempla istorum hominum in Propheta multa describuntur, qui eorum pietatem rori matutino & nubeculae cito transeunti conferunt, eo quod nihil solidum & stabile habeat. Praeterea vt fermentum massam totam inflat & acescere facit: sic hypocrisis superbiae mater homines vana propriae iustitiae fiducia turgidos reddit, vt illa in Dei etiam conspectu gloriari non vereantur. Exemplum huius insolentiae infra in Pharisaeo videbimus, qui bonorum operum suorum catalogum Deo recensuit, quasi cum illo rationem initurus. At nihil inde aliud isti homines referunt, quàm quod seipsos Deo minus acceptos, & omnia sua eidem acida & insipida reddunt. Quia enim hic ipsa Veritas est, mendacium & fucum no potest non odisse. Et cum omnis superbia ei inuisa sit, omnium maxime eam abominatur: qua homines, quos propriae vitiositatis & inde nascentium peccatorum agnitio humiliare & deprimere debebat, apud ipsius tribunal sese pro iustis & sanctis venditant. Haec certe repudij & exitij Iudaeorum causa fuit de quibus hoc Paulus pronunciat, quod suam iustitiam stabiliendo à iustitia Dei exciderint, quam is nobis in Filio suo offert, & quae sola nos ad eius tribunal tueri potest. Et Christus seruo aut aeco nomo domus suae perfido atque dissipatori grauissimum supplicium minaturus, eum differtum iri dicit, vt partem suam habeat cum hypocritis. Haec si diligentius considerentur, sola sufficere possunt ad euertendum totum Papatum & quaecunque in hoc praestantissima habentur. Quid enim in eo praeter vanam inanium titulorum ostentationem & fucatam sanctitatis speciem est videre? Gloriatur vniuersalis Episcopi nomine Romanus Pontifex, qui ne vnius quidem parochiae in vrbe Roma pastorem agit. Idem vt humilitatis nomine se commendet, Seruus seruorum dici vult: interim vero triplici tiara redimitus aliorum humeris sublimis fertur, in Reges & Imperatores imperium sibi vendicat, & ijsdem pedes osculandos obtrudit. Eadem est aliorum Episcoporum conditio, qui nihil minus sunt quam quod dicuntur, cum neque doceant, neque alia obeant munera ecclesiastica, sed immani fastu & pompa cum huius saeculi principibus contendant. Quod si ad sanctissimum in hoc regno Pontificio hominum genus oculos convertas, Monachos nimirum, idem in hu quoque deprehendes. Monachi dicuntur à solitudine: at in mediis vrbibus, in foro, in aulis, in castris deniqué versantur. Vouent paupertatem voluntariam: sed sub huius praetextu omnibus abundant, & securi in otio ex aliorum laboribus viuunt, imo frequenter ad opes & honores amplissimos ascendunt, & principum more dominantur. Vouent obedientiam: at ab omni obedientia, quae secundum leges naturae parentibus & magistratibus debetur, sese eximunt, & immunitatem quandam sibi parauerunt, quae à ciuilibus quoque oneribus liberos reddit. Vouent castitatem nent castitatem: sed qua in cœlibatu solo consistit, cum interim thoros alienos impudentissime pollu-ant, puellarum pudicitiæ insidientur, spurijs suis omnia compleant, & ea quoq; designet, quæ verbis eloqui nefas est. Adhæc vestitu histrionico carnis mortificationem, humilitatem, innocentiam, sanctitatem, zelum gloriæ Dei, charitatis Christianæ ardorem, suijpsius abnegationem, patientiam & omnis virtutis studium profitentur: cæterum nulli magis in carne agunt, nulli insolentius contra Deum & homines efferuntur, nulli turpius viuunt, nulli gloriam Dei & charitatis fraterna officia securius negligunt, nulli deniq; iniurias leuissimas impatientius ferunt. Et huius generis multa recenseri poterant, quæ tam aperta sunt & nota omnibus, vt ea nemo negare possit. Num ergo cultu quem isti homines Deo exhibent, ei probari putabimus?
units.tr: Moreover, the metaphor by which Christ calls hypocrisy leaven is worth noting, for it expresses its nature, powers and effects. Just as leaven is mixed into and united with the dough so that it can no longer be separated from it, so hypocrisy clings to us by nature, having been derived to us by hereditary right from our first parents. For it is established that after the first fall, when they were convicted by their own conscience, they fled to a pretence of holiness and innocence. They sewed for themselves aprons of fig leaves to cover their nakedness. Then too they used rather bold words in excusing themselves, so that they shifted their guilt quite openly onto God himself. This is something common to all men today, as we see in children and in the worst of people. For although children seem scarcely to understand anything yet by reason of their age, if they have done wrong they are wont to conceal and dissemble it wonderfully; when caught they turn to insults or to new tricks, and they are very clever at shifting blame. Those others, though headlong lust carries them off into sin, when caught and accused, obstinately deny it and want to seem most upright, nor are they ashamed of any disguise or colour, provided they can hope for some excuse for their wickedness. Moreover, hypocrisy has struck deep roots in corrupt human nature, and so it is rightly compared to the most tenacious leaven. Next, just as this, once mixed in, in a short space of time penetrates the whole mass of flour already sprinkled with it, so hypocrisy, if a man indulges it, very quickly infects his whole life and manners, so that it shows itself in all his words and deeds. For the most wicked delight in a feigned appearance of virtue, and they strive for this all the more if they see that they are making progress and are on that account held in honour and esteem. Thus they go so far that they think they can deceive God just as they deceive men. This is why they play impiously in his worship and pretend great piety, even though in their hearts they are most alien from all religion. Many examples of such men are described in the Prophet, who compare their piety to the morning dew and to a little cloud that quickly passes away, because it has nothing solid and stable. Furthermore, just as leaven puffs up and sours the whole mass, so hypocrisy, the mother of pride, makes men swollen with vain confidence in their own righteousness, so that they do not fear to boast even in the sight of God. We shall see an example of this arrogance later in the Pharisee, who recounted the catalogue of his good works to God, as if he were about to enter into a reckoning with him. Yet these men gain nothing from it but that they make themselves less acceptable to God and render all their works sour and insipid to him. For since he is Truth itself, he cannot but hate lying and pretence. And since every pride is hateful to him, he abominates it above all: by it men, whom the recognition of their own viciousness and of the sins arising from it ought to have humbled and cast down, sell themselves before his tribunal as just and holy. Certainly this was the cause of the rejection and destruction of the Jews, of whom Paul pronounces that by establishing their own righteousness they fell from the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son, and which alone can keep us safe before his tribunal. And Christ, about to threaten the most grievous punishment on a servant or steward of his house who is faithless and a squanderer, says that he will be cut in pieces so that he may have his portion with the hypocrites. If these things are considered more carefully, they alone can suffice to overthrow the whole Papacy and whatever is held most excellent in it. For what is to be seen in it besides a vain display of empty titles and a painted appearance of holiness? The Roman Pontiff boasts of the name of universal Bishop, though he does not act as pastor even of a single parish in the city of Rome. The same man, to commend himself under the name of humility, wishes to be called the servant of servants; meanwhile, crowned with a triple tiara, he is carried aloft on the shoulders of others, claims dominion over kings and emperors, and thrusts his feet upon them to be kissed. The condition of the other Bishops is the same: they are in no way what they are called, since they neither teach nor perform any other ecclesiastical duties, but vie with the princes of this age in monstrous pride and pomp. And if you turn your eyes to that most holy class of men in this Papal kingdom, namely the Monks, you will find the same thing in them too. Monks are so called from solitude, yet they dwell in the middle of cities, in the market, in courts, and finally in camps. They vow voluntary poverty, but under this pretext they abound in everything, and live securely in leisure from the labours of others; indeed they often rise to very great wealth and honours, and rule in the manner of princes. They vow obedience, but they exempt themselves from all obedience that is owed to parents and magistrates according to the laws of nature, and they have secured for themselves a certain immunity which frees them even from civil burdens. They vow chastity: but it consists in celibacy alone, while meanwhile they most shamelessly defile the beds of others, lie in wait for the chastity of girls, fill everything with their bastards, and also designate those things which it is wrong to speak in words. Moreover, with theatrical dress they profess mortification of the flesh, humility, innocence, holiness, zeal for the glory of God, the ardour of Christian love, self-denial, patience and the pursuit of every virtue; yet no one lives more according to the flesh, no one is more insolently puffed up against God and men, no one lives more shamefully, no one more carelessly neglects the glory of God and the duties of brotherly love, and finally no one bears the slightest injuries more impatiently. Many things of this kind could be listed, which are so open and known to all that no one can deny them. Shall we therefore think that the worship which these men offer to God is pleasing to him?

units.la: Porro quia discipulos in docendi munere sibi ab hoc hypocrisis & vanæ ostentationis fermento cauere iusserat Dominus, & integritati studere, bonaq; fide salutis doctrinam mundo tradere, alias ipse quoq; sui præcepti siue admonitionis rationes affert è communi sensu & experientia quotidiana petitas, vt magis moueat eos, qui carni adhuc addictiores erant. Nihil enim opertum est (inquit) quod non sit detegendum: neq; occultum, quod non sit cognoscendum. Propterea quæ in tenebris dixi vobis, in luce audientur: & quod in aurem locuti estis in conclauibus, prædicabitur supra domos. Sanus est, de ipsorum honore & existimatione hic agi, eò quod omnis simulatio & ostentatio prorsus inutilis fit, cum nihil tam bene tegatur aut occultetur, quin tandem in lucem veniat, vel in hoc vel in futuro seculo. Quasi diceret: Qualescunq; in vestro munere fueritis, id suo tempore omnibus patebit. Itaq; si Pharisæos imitati vos inani fuco ostentetis, doctrinam vero vobis creditam minus syncere proponatis, ad tempus quidem latebitis, sed tandem fraus ista detegetur, & vos impostores fuisse patebit. Rursus, si bona fide agatis, hæc quoq; vestra integritas nota fiet omnibus, etiamsi nunc malevolorum calumnijs obruatur, & multi secus de vobis iudicent. Nec enim celari poterit Euangelium, cuius prædicatio vobis commissa est, sed illud per totum orbem diuulgari oportebit. Itaq; quæ in tenebris & occultius initio dicetis, suo tempore in luce vel publico audientur: & quæ priuatim discipulis in cubiculis interioribus quasi in aurem loquimini, mox supra domorum tecta, quasi publici præconis voce, promulgabuntur. At hæc dicendo non tam a fraude & hypocrisi illos deterret, quam animos illis addit, dum pollicetur, Euangelij doctrinam per omnia obstacula euasuram, vt totum orbem terrarum compleat. Quod factum fuisse, ex historijs apparet, & res ipsa loquitur. Nam etiam si initio obscurior & finibus angustioribus conclusa videretur Apostolorum prædicatio, subito tamen erupit, & ceu tonitru ingens apud omnes populos exaudita, & (vt Paulus annotauit) omni creatu re est annuntiata. Etenim ea veritatis est conditio, vt interdum quidem latet, sed suo tempore victrix erumpat in lucem: quare veteres illam temporis filiam dixerunt.
units.tr: Since the Lord had told his disciples to beware of this leaven of hypocrisy and empty display in their teaching, and to aim at integrity and to deliver the teaching of salvation to the world in good faith, he also offers other reasons for his admonition, drawn from common sense and everyday experience, so that they might move those who were still more devoted to the flesh. For nothing is hidden, he says, that shall not be uncovered; nor secret, that shall not be known. Therefore whatever you have said in darkness shall be heard in the light; and what you have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops. It is clear that the question here is their own honour and reputation, since all pretence and display is wholly useless, because nothing is so well covered or hidden that it will not at last come to light, either in this age or in the age to come. As if he were saying: Whatever you are in your office, that will in its time be open to all. So if you imitate the Pharisees and make a show with empty paint, and set forth the teaching committed to you with less than sincerity, you will indeed lie hidden for a time, but at last that deceit will be exposed, and it will be plain that you were impostors. Again, if you act in good faith, your integrity too will become known to all, even if for now it is overwhelmed by the slanders of ill-wishers and many judge you otherwise. For the Gospel, whose preaching has been committed to you, cannot be concealed, but must be spread abroad through the whole world. So what you say in darkness and more secretly at the beginning will in its time be heard in public in the light; and what you speak privately to the disciples in inner rooms, as if into the ear, will soon be proclaimed from the roofs of the houses, in the voice of a public herald. In saying this, he does not so much deter them from fraud and hypocrisy as encourage their spirits, while he promises that the doctrine of the Gospel will get through every obstacle so as to fill the whole circle of the earth. That this has happened, the histories make clear, and the thing itself speaks. For even if at first the preaching of the Apostles seemed obscure and confined within narrow limits, it suddenly broke out, and was heard among all peoples like a mighty thunder, and (as Paul noted) was proclaimed to every creature. For such is the condition of truth: it sometimes lies hidden, but at its proper time it breaks forth victorious into the light; which is why the ancients called it the daughter of time.

units.la: Est autem huius dicti vsus non vulgaris etiam nobis, si probe expendatur. Primo enim admonet, ne spe latendi aut impunitatis nosmetipsos fallamus, vt licentius peccemus. Nam etsi hominum oculos fallere detur, Dei tamen oculos nunquam effugiemus, qui (vt Propheta ait) per omnem terram discurrunt, & abstrusissima quæq; vident, imo in cordium arcana penetrant. Exempla, quibus id probetur, in omnibus historijs occurrunt. Aduersus Abelum fratrem in agro Cain iniurrexerat, & eum clam, procul remotis arbitris omnibus trucidarat, neq; dubium est, eum rationes quoq; diligenter iniisse, quibus apud parentes facinus illud dissimulari & tegi posse putaret. Sed nihil illum ista omnia iuuant apud Deum, qui fratrem ex eius manu requirit, & se tanti sceleris spectatorem fuisse, & sanguinem iam nunc ad se clamantem audire testatur. Simile huic est, quod Iacobi filijs in Iosephi fratris venditione accidit. Nam etsi hoc suum flagitium apud patrem mirifico astu texissent, vt us a ferus diuerpxtum filium putaret, & res multos tam annos latuisset, tamen publice tandem omnibus magna cum ipsorum ignominia innotuit. Quod ipsum de Dauidis adulterio & indigna Uriæ cæde dicere possumus, quæ Deus per Prophetam arguit, cum ille rem omnem probe contectam putaret. Taceo nunc eos, qui ipsi sæpe scelera sua produnt, in quibus celandis diu magna diligentia sunt vsi, tandem vero vel vno dicto inconsideratius elapso seipsos in periculum adducunt: cuius rei memorabile exemplum in latronibus, qui ibicum Poetam occiderunt, gentium historiæ proponunt. Cum enim iam moriturus grues superuolantes implorasset, vt sua necis testes essent, latrones postea inforo grues videntes inter se dicebant, Ecce Ibici grues. Quæ vox a circumstantibus audita, quàm
units.tr: The use of this saying is also not commonplace for us, if it is weighed carefully. First, it warns us not to deceive ourselves with the hope of hiding or of escaping punishment, so that we may sin more freely. For although it may be possible to deceive men's eyes, we will never escape the eyes of God, who (as the Prophet says) run through the whole earth and see the most hidden things, indeed penetrate the secrets of hearts. Examples proving this occur in all histories. Cain rose up against his brother Abel in the field, and slew him secretly, far from any witnesses, and there is no doubt that he also carefully devised plans by which he thought that crime could be concealed and covered before his parents.
