But all these things availed him nothing before God, who requires the brother at his hand, and testifies that he was a witness of so great a crime, and hears the blood already crying out to him. Similar to this is what happened to the sons of Jacob in the selling of their brother Joseph. For although they had covered their shameful deed before their father with wonderful cunning, so that the wild beast, he thought, had torn his son apart, and the matter had lain hidden for many years, nevertheless it was at last made known publicly to all, to their great disgrace. We can say the same of David's adultery and the unworthy slaughter of Uriah, which God rebuked through the Prophet, when David thought the whole affair was well concealed. I pass over now those who often betray their own crimes, which they had taken great care to hide for a long time, but at last, by a single word let slip too carelessly, bring themselves into danger; a memorable example of this among the histories of the nations is the robbers who killed the poet Ibycus. For when he, about to die, had called on the cranes flying overhead to be witnesses of his death, the robbers afterwards, seeing cranes in the forum, said to one another, "Look, the cranes of Ibycus." When this remark was heard by the bystanders, how

units.la: Hypocrisis odio nus inutilis est.
units.tr: Hypocrisy is hateful and useless.

units.la: Nemo sepe latens dî peccet. Ibi cum amissum dolebant, causa fuit, vt comprehensi scelus faterentur, & meritas pœnas exoluerent. Quam multos item à canibus, ab equis, à corvis proditos fuisse legimus? Quid, quod sæpe con-scientiæ cruciatibus homines scelerati coguntur sua flagitia fateri, quod olim Iudæ proditori acci-dit? Quia autem hæc quotidianis etiam exemplis confirmantur, eò magis nos excitare debent, vt singuli doctrinam hanc ad se transferant, & cogitent nihil tam occulte fieri posse, de quo non ali-quando reddenda sit ratio Deo, qui scelus nullum inultum abire sinit. Itaq; singuli in genere quidem innocentiæ & charitati erga omnes, priuatim vero quoad suam functionem integritati studeant, & quod ipsis Deus mandauit bona fide exequantur. Si quid vero peccauerunt, non ad inanes fucos sed ad Christum conuertantur, qui suo merito & iustitia nostras iniquitates tegit, ne apud Patrũ tri-bunal in rationem veniant.
units.tr: No one who often hides sins against God. When they grieved over what was lost, it was the cause that those caught confessed their crime and paid the punishments they deserved. How many, we read, have also been betrayed by dogs, by horses, by crows? What of the fact that wicked men are often compelled by the torments of conscience to confess their crimes, as once happened to Judas the traitor? And since these things are confirmed also by daily examples, they ought to stir us all the more, so that each one may apply this teaching to himself, and consider that nothing can be done so secretly that some day an account will not have to be rendered to God, who lets no crime go unpunished. Therefore let each one in general strive for innocence and charity towards all, and privately for integrity in his own function, and carry out in good faith what God has commanded him. But if they have sinned at all, let them turn not to empty paint but to Christ, who by his merit and righteousness covers our iniquities, so that they do not come into account before the judgement seat of the Father.

units.la: Deinde consolationem quoq; dulcissimam hoc Christi dictum continet. Vt enim scelera diutius latere non possunt: sic innocentia quoque eorum, qui calumniis & sinistrę suspicionibus grauantur, tandem reuelatur & innotescit. Obseruandum hoc in religionis negotio, vbi fere pro hæreticis & se diuisis habentur, qui vnum Deum colunt, & salutis suæ spem in vnius Christi merito collocatã habent. Sed asserit tandem suorum memoriam Deus, vt qui dum in vita essent, omnium odijs & con-titijs expositi fuerunt, vita hac defuncti in honore sint, & pro veris Dei cultoribus agnoscantur. Exemplo nobis sint Prophetæ, Apostoli & reliqui Martyres, quorum memoria hodie apud eos e-tiam sanctæ & venerabiles esse, qui fidem, quam tradiderunt, odisse & persequi solent. Fit idem in iis, qua ad huius vita vsum spectant, vt qui diu calumniis oppressi fuerunt, tandem liberati suam innocentiam omnibus approbare possint. Sic Joseph impudicæ mulieris falsa accusatione in capitis periculum adductus, postea ad honores summos euectus est. Sic Dauid innocentiam Deus suo tempore contra Saulis calumnias asseruit. Et in prophanis historijs eiusmodi exempla multa extant, neque desunt quotidiana, quæ hanc consolationem confirmare possunt. Vsus autem totius huius loci esto, vt singuli in sua vocatione officium sedulo faciant, neque improborum calumnijs offendan-tur. Sensit has etiam Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui bus superior factus in cœlis nunc viuit & regnat, & suos quoque olim honore & gloria immortali donabit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, glo-ria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Next, this saying of Christ also contains a most sweet consolation. For just as crimes cannot lie hidden for long, so the innocence of those who are burdened with slanders and sinister suspicions is at last revealed and made known. This must be observed in the matter of religion, where those who worship the one God and have their hope of salvation placed in the merit of Christ alone are almost always regarded as heretics and schismatics. But God at last vindicates the memory of his people, so that those who, while they were alive, were exposed to the hatred and quarrels of all, after death are held in honour and acknowledged as true worshippers of God. Let the Prophets, Apostles and the other Martyrs be examples to us, whose memory today is holy and venerable even among those who are accustomed to hate and persecute the faith they handed down. The same happens in matters that pertain to the use of this life: those who have long been oppressed by slanders are at last set free and can prove their innocence to all. So Joseph, brought into peril of his life by the false accusation of an immodest woman, was afterwards raised to the highest honours. So God in his time vindicated David's innocence against the slanders of Saul. And many examples of this kind exist in profane histories, nor are there lacking everyday cases that can confirm this consolation. The use of this whole passage, then, should be that each one faithfully performs his duty in his calling, and is not offended by the slanders of the wicked. Our Lord Jesus Christ also felt these things, who, having been exalted in heaven, now lives and reigns, and will also in time grant his people immortal honour and glory. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVI.
units.tr: Homily 126.

units.la: Dico autem vobis amicis meis, Ne timete vobis ab iis qui trucidant corpus, & postea non habent quod amplius faciant. Præmonstrabo au-tem vobis quem timeatis: Timete eum, qui postquam trucidarit, potesta-tem habet inijciendi in gehennam. Etiam dico vobis, hunc timete. Non ne quinq; passerculi væniunt assarijs duobus, & vnus ex iis non est in obliuione apud Deum? Quin etiam capilli capitis vestri omnes nume-rati sunt. Ne igitur timete. Multis passerculis præstatis.
units.tr: "But I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him. Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God? But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows."

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster Iesus Christus, Pharisæos & Legis interpretes Iudæorum grauiter corrupit, hi vero non solum incurabiles manserunt, sed in rabiem maiorem accensi sunt, ne qui eorum exemplo offenderentur, mox ad discipulos conuersus bos diligenter instituit, & aduersus illo-rum furores armat atq; confirmat. Et principio quidem, quia ad docendi munus destinati erant, ne in eo Pharisaorũ more ostentationi & pompæ studerent, omnis mali fontem obturat, hypocrisim ni-mirum, quæ semper cum inanis gloriæ studio coniuncta est. Dei vero gloriam & hominum salutem facile negligit. Monet ergo vt ipsi bona fide tradant creditam sibi æternæ salutis doctrinam, & in-tegritati studeant. Atqui hoc faciunt, eos infinita pericula & aduersa manent. Nec enim ferre po-test veritatus lucem mundus hic, cum opera eius mala sint. Argui etiam nolunt hypocritæ, qui fe-re in omni hominum ordine dominantur. Inuisa item & exosa est religionis receptæ & diu obserua-te mutatio. Hinc ergo administrorũ Verbi Dei odia nascuntur, quæ insidias occultas, adhæc aper-tas persecutiones pariunt, in quibus ceu ones mastationi destinata (vt Paulus ait) in singulas horas ad crudelissima supplicia rapiuntur. Tunc autem pijs quoq; multum impedimenti affert innata omnibus vitae huius cupiditas & mortis imminentis metus. Et constat interdum optimos quosq; ali quid humanitus pati, ut in fide labascant, & sui officij minus sint memores, sicut in Elia, Iona, Petro & multis alijs esse videre. Itaq; ne quid omittat Dominus, nunc aduersus mortis metum & nimiam huius vitae cupiditatem discipulos instituit, & grauissimis argumentis confirmat. Quae doctrina etiamsi omnibus seculis obseruatu dignissima fuerit, hodie tamen plus quam necessaria est, quan do extremos conatus Satan profert ad regnum suum stabiliendum, & non solus doctoribus, verum etiam principibus Ecclesiae nutritijs & singulis credentibus pericula omnis generis quotidie struuntur, nec iam priuatus supplicijs, sed publicis seditionibus & apertis bellis res agitur, in quibus nationes potentissimae totius Europae inter se committuntur.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had sharply rebuked the Pharisees and the lawyers of the Jews, and they had remained not only incurable but had been inflamed into greater fury, he turned at once to his disciples, lest any of them be offended by the example of those men. He instructs them carefully and arms and strengthens them against the rage of their enemies. And first, since they were appointed to the office of teaching, he forbids them to pursue display and pomp after the manner of the Pharisees. He stops up the source of every evil, namely hypocrisy, which is always joined with a zeal for empty glory, and which easily neglects the glory of God and the salvation of men. He therefore admonishes them to hand on in good faith the doctrine of eternal salvation entrusted to them, and to devote themselves to integrity. Yet when they do this, endless dangers and adversities await them. For this world cannot bear the light of truth, since its works are evil. Hypocrites, who rule over almost every rank of men, also refuse to be reproved. Likewise, a change from a religion long received and observed is hateful and odious. Hence arise the hatreds against the ministers of the Word of God, which bring forth hidden snares and, besides these, open persecutions, in which, as Paul says, they are dragged every hour to the most cruel punishments, like sheep destined for slaughter. Then, too, the innate desire for this life and the fear of impending death bring much hindrance even to the godly. And it is established that sometimes the best men suffer some human weakness, so that they waver in the faith and are less mindful of their office, as we see in Elijah, Jonah, Peter and many others. Therefore, lest the Lord omit anything, he now instructs his disciples against the fear of death and against an excessive love of this life, and confirms them with the weightiest arguments. This teaching, although it deserves to be observed in every age, is today more than necessary, since Satan puts forth his utmost efforts to establish his kingdom. Dangers of every kind are daily prepared not only for teachers, but also for the leaders of the Church, for its nurses, and for each of the faithful. Nor is the matter now confined to private punishments, but it is carried on by public seditions and open wars, in which the most powerful nations of all Europe are set against one another.

units.la: Audiamus ergo nos quoq; attentis animis Christum, & nobis hodie dici putemus, quae olim discipulis eius dicta sunt. Praecipit autem ille initio quid in periculis eiusmodi fieri & obseruari debeat. Et quia hic de re graui & maximi momenti agitur, verbis quoq; gravibus quidem, sed blanda simul & amica summi amoris significatione mixtis utitur. Ait enim: Dico autem vobis amicis meis, Ne timete vobis ab ijs, qui trucidant corpus, & postea non habent quod amplius faciant: Praemonstrabo autem vobis quem timeatis, &c. Amicos suos dicit, ut eos Pharisaeis & Scribis opponat, qui aperti hostes erant, & proinde digni, quos durius tractaret, ut nuper audiuimus. Simul autem doctrinam hanc per se grauem & duram hac blanda compellatione mitigare & emollire vult. Quia enim illos amicorum loco habet, non obscure innuit, se saluti ipsorum consultum velle, & in omnibus periculis suam opem allaturum esse, ne vllis hostium minis aut terriculamentis succumbant.
units.tr: Let us therefore also listen to Christ with attentive minds, and let us think that the words once spoken to his disciples are spoken to us today. He first prescribes what ought to be done and observed in such dangers. And because this concerns a matter of great weight and the highest importance, he uses words that are indeed grave, yet mingled with a gentle and friendly expression of the greatest love. For he says: "But I say unto you, my friends, be not afraid of those who kill the body and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom you shall fear," and so on. He calls them his friends so as to set them against the Pharisees and scribes, who were open enemies and therefore deserved to be treated more harshly, as we heard recently. At the same time he wishes to soften and mollify this teaching, which is in itself grave and hard, by this gentle form of address. For in calling them his friends, he clearly intimates that he cares for their salvation and will bring his help in all dangers, so that they do not yield to any threats or terrors of their enemies.

units.la: Caterum, hoc nomine discipulos suos compellans, simul admonet, doctrinam hanc ad omnes pertinere, qui ipsius amici esse cupiunt. Vnde iam aliud sequitur, persecutiones & aduersa, quibus in hoc seculo pij exercentur, non odij aut irae Dei, sed amoris potius & beneuolentiae argumenta esse, cum Filius eius amicos dicat eos, quos prae alijs hominibus omnis generis pericula atq; calamitates sustinuisse constat. Est autem obseruatu dignissima & consolationis plena haec Christi bonitas, qua sibi ex hominibus amicos accersere dignatur. Inter homines enim ita comparatum est, ut amicitiae & foedera inter aequales difficulter coeant, & potentiorum amicitiae fere infirmioribus insidiosae & periculosae sint. Magna ergo sit oportet & plane incomparabilis ista facilitas, qua aeternus Dei Filius, Patri coessentialis, quiq; nullius indiget, cum hominibus amicitiam inire dignatus est, qui ut omnium indigi, ita natura corrupti & scelerati, & propterea digni sunt, qui a Dei conspectu procul arceantur. Nec est quod Christum hoc loco suos inani titulo fallere putemus. Si enim amicitia (ut gentium philosophi eam recte definierunt) est omnium diuinarum humanarumq; rerum cum beneuolentia & charitate summa consensio, quae ut amici omnia inter se communia habeant, efficit: de Christi amicitia dubitare nullo modo possumus. Nam ut nobiscum coenire posset, in mundum venit, & homo factus simul nostras infirmitates experiri et peccata nostra in se transferre dignatus est: e contra vero nobis manifestauit quaecunq; a Patre suo accepit, quod certissimum veri amoris argumentum esse, ipse apud Ioannem testatur. Adhaec omnia sua bona nobiscum communia habet, & nos mortis sua merito Patri coelesti ideo reconciliauit, ut nos regni sui aeterni coharedes habere posset. Prodest autem in tantae bonitatis Filij Dei consideratione frequenter versari, ut de retinendo eius fauore & colenda cum illo amicitia diligentius cogitemus. Nam si inter homines tanta est amicitiae necessitas, ut Solem e mundo tollere Cicero eos dixerit, qui illam e medio auferunt: quanto magis necesse est, ut Filium Dei amicum habeamus, sine quo neq; Patri coelesti propitio uti possumus, neq; quicquam nobis in hac vita iucundum siue tutum esse potest, cum omnia ijs infesta sint, qui Deum sibi iratum esse sentiunt? At nunquam nobis cum Christo firma coniunctio esse poterit, nisi doctrina, quam hoc loco tradit, probe obseruemus. Itaq; eam ad se trahere debent omnis loci & ordinis homines.
units.tr: Moreover, in addressing his disciples by this name, he also reminds them that this teaching applies to all who wish to be his friends. From this there follows another point: the persecutions and adversities by which the godly are exercised in this age are signs not of God's hatred or anger, but rather of his love and goodwill, since his Son calls them friends, those whom it is plain have endured every kind of danger and calamity more than other men. This goodness of Christ, by which he deigns to draw friends to himself from among men, is most worthy of observation and full of consolation. For among men it is so ordered that friendships and covenants between equals are formed with difficulty, and the friendships of the more powerful are almost always dangerous and treacherous to the weaker. Therefore that facility must be great and altogether incomparable, by which the eternal Son of God, co-essential with the Father and in need of nothing, has deigned to enter into friendship with men, who, being in need of everything and corrupted and wicked by nature, deserve to be shut out far from the sight of God. Nor should we think that Christ here deceives his people with an empty title. For if friendship (as the philosophers of the nations rightly defined it) is a harmony in all divine and human things, joined with goodwill and the highest charity, which makes friends hold all things in common, we can by no means doubt Christ's friendship. For in order to dwell with us he came into the world, and, having become man, he deigned both to experience our weaknesses and to take our sins upon himself. On the other hand, he has made known to us all that he received from his Father, which John himself testifies is a most certain proof of true love. Besides all this, he holds all his goods in common with us, and by the merit of his death he has reconciled us to the heavenly Father, so that he might have us as co-heirs of his eternal kingdom. It is profitable, then, to dwell often on the consideration of the Son of God's great goodness, so that we may think more diligently about retaining his favour and cultivating friendship with him. For if among men friendship is so necessary that Cicero said those who remove it from the midst of life take the sun out of the world, how much more necessary is it that we have the Son of God as our friend, without whom we cannot enjoy the favour of the heavenly Father, nor can anything in this life be pleasant or safe for us, since all things are hostile to those who feel that God is angry with them? Yet our union with Christ can never be firm unless we diligently observe the teaching that he gives in this place. Therefore men of every place and rank ought to draw this teaching to themselves.

units.la: Videamus ergo quae nam illa sit. Ne timete (inquit) vobis ab his, qui trucidant corpus, & postea non habent quod amplius faciant, id est, vos praeterea ladant: Praemonstrabo autem vobis quem timeatis: Timete eum, qui postquam trucidarit, potestate habet injiciendi in gehennam. Et ut hanc doctrinam magis commendet, per repetitionem subijcit: Etiam dico vobis, hunc timete. Prohibet ne homines timeamus, qui corpus occidere possunt. Atqui in scripturis alibi nominantur, qui timeri de beant, & Paulus talibus timorem reddere iubet: quales sunt qui magistratum gerunt, parentes, praeceptores, heri & quicunque nobis sunt superiores. At hic de tyrannis persecutoribus & vniuersis veraे fidei atque doctrinae hostibus sermo est, & hos timere vetamur. Imo generalius quoque accipi debet haec Christi admonitio, ne aliquem mortalium plus timeamus quam Deum, neue in alicuius gratiam fidem in Deum abnegemus, aut ab officio discedamus, cui nos ille destinauit. Etenim fieri non potest, quin verus Dei timor apud nos euanuerit, quam primum vel metu vel gratia hominum ea facimus, quibus Dei ira provocatur. Neque huius amici esse poterunt, qui mundum hunc tanti faciunt. Solet enim hic in omnibus Deo repugnare. Odit & extinctam vult Verbi doctrinam, quam Deus apud omnes homines vult diuulgari: Odit innocentiae studium, quod hic vnice requirit, & sine quo nemo ipsum videbit. Omnia vero charitatis legibus contraria facit, quas nisi obseruemus, Christi discipuli non erimus. Quod si ad religionem & Dei cultum accedamus, huic mundo addicti homines in vanissimis superstitionibus & inutilibus ceremonijs collocant, cum ille spiritu & veritate coli velit. Denique non tam aqua igni repugnat, quam mundus hic Deo aduersatur. Quod Iacobus obseruans, dixit, amicitiam huius mundi inimicitiam esse cum Deo. Quis vero Dei timentem dixerit eum, qui cum eius hostibus amicitiam colere, cum ipso autem inimicitiam apertam suscipere non veretur? Est ergo (vt diximus) multiplex huius admonitionis vsus, & ad omnis losi atque ordinis homines pertinet, qui omnes victoriam aduersus mundi huius cum minas tum illecebras facile obtinebunt, si Deum magis quam homines timere discant. Nam si Verbi praecones cogitent, illi olim rationem sui ministerij reddendam esse, mox pio eius timore pleni, omnibus qui ipsis silentium mandare audent, cum Apostolis respondebunt, Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Similiter qui in magistratu sunt & iudices aliorum constituti, si meminerint Deum in medio ipsorum praesentem adesse, neque audire solum ipsorum sententias, verumetiam corda inspicere, & videre quo animo quoue affectu omnia dicant & faciant, nunquam certe aliquid ex odio cuiusquam aut fauore pronunciabunt. In fidei autem & religionis causa nullum ingenuo & syncero Dei timore fortius est propugnaculum, quo omnes minae & pericula validissime reijciuntur. Nam qui hoc sese munierunt, ij nullis rationibus adduci poterunt, vt Dei Filium negent, quem ille ab omnibus agnoscit atque coli vult. Sentient enim nulla venia dignum scelus esse ab eo defectione facere, qui nos sanguinis sui pretio redemptos sibi in peculium acquisiuit. Cuius rei memorabile exemplum in Polycarpo extat, qui a Proconsule iussus, vt contra religionis Christianae leges per Caesarem fortunam iuraret, & Christo conuitiaretur, respondit: Octoginta & sex annis ei seruio, neque me laesit vnquam: quomodo igitur possum maledicere Regi meo, qui salutem mihi dedit? Sed & in vita & moribus Dei timor, vt verae sapientiae initium, sic fortissimum ad tuendam innocentiam incitamentum est, & idem carnis cupiditates vna cum peccatorum illecebris prorsus reflinguit, ne nos ipsi superari patiamur. Hoc clypeo munitus Ioseph hera impudicae illicitos amores effugit, & periculum in de enatis superior factus est. Eodem Susanna quoque pudicitiam suam aduersus Seniorum libidinem blanditias simul atque minas defendit. Dicebat enim: Melius est mihi, hoc flagitio non admissio, incidere in manus veltras, quam in conspectu Domini delinquere. Quae exempla satis docent a timore Dei alienissimos esse eos, qui hodie in religione impudenter ludunt, aut vitam suam scelerib&s & omni vitiorum genere polluunt,
units.tr: Let us see, then, what that doctrine is. "Do not be afraid," he says, "of those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do," that is, who can do nothing further to harm you. "But I will show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into hell." And to commend this teaching more strongly, he adds by repetition: "Yes, I tell you, fear him." He forbids us to fear men who can kill the body. Yet elsewhere in Scripture some are named who ought to be feared, and Paul bids us give fear to such people: those who hold the magistracy, parents, teachers, masters and all who are set above us. But here the discourse concerns tyrannical persecutors and all enemies of the true faith and doctrine, and we are forbidden to fear these. Indeed this admonition of Christ ought to be understood more generally too: that we should not fear any mortal more than God, nor for the sake of someone's favour deny our faith in God, or depart from the duty to which he has appointed us. For the true fear of God cannot fail to fade away in us as soon as we do, out of fear or to win men's favour, those things by which the wrath of God is provoked. Nor will those be friends of God who make so much of this world. For the world always sets itself against God in everything. It hates the doctrine of the Word and wants it extinguished, though God wills it to be spread among all men. It hates the zeal for innocence, which is the one thing it requires here, and without which no one will see him. Indeed it does everything contrary to the laws of charity, which unless we keep, we will not be disciples of Christ. And when we approach religion and the worship of God, men given over to this world entangle it in the vainest superstitions and useless ceremonies, when he wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth. In short, the world opposes God no less than water opposes fire. James observed this when he said that friendship with this world is enmity with God. Who, indeed, would call him a fearer of God who does not hesitate to cultivate friendship with God's enemies, but openly takes up enmity with him? There is, therefore, as we have said, a manifold use of this admonition, and it pertains to men of every place and rank. All of them will easily win the victory over the threats and the allurements of this world, if they learn to fear God rather than men. For if the heralds of the Word consider that they must one day render an account of their ministry, then, full of godly fear, they will answer with the Apostles to all who dare to order them to be silent: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Similarly, those who hold office and are appointed judges of others, if they remember that God is present in their midst, and that he not only hears their sentences but also inspects their hearts and sees with what mind and affection they say and do everything, will certainly never pronounce anything out of hatred or favour for anyone. In the cause of faith and religion, however, there is no stronger bulwark for a sincere and noble man than the fear of God, by which all threats and dangers are most powerfully repelled. For those who have fortified themselves with this will by no reasoning be brought to deny the Son of God, whom God acknowledges from all and wills to be worshipped. They will feel that it is a crime deserving no pardon to fall away from him who redeemed us at the price of his own blood and acquired us for himself as a peculiar people. A memorable example of this is found in Polycarp, who, ordered by the proconsul to swear by the fortune of Caesar, contrary to the laws of the Christian religion, and to revile Christ, answered: "For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never done me any wrong: how then can I blaspheme my King, who gave me salvation?" But also in life and morals the fear of God, as the beginning of true wisdom, is the strongest incitement to defend innocence, and it likewise completely restrains the lusts of the flesh together with the allurements of sin, so that we do not allow ourselves to be overcome. Armed with this shield, Joseph fled the illicit love of his master's lustful wife and was made superior to the danger that threatened him. By the same means Susanna also defended her chastity against the lust of the elders, against both their flatteries and their threats. For she said: "It is better for me to fall into your hands without committing this crime than to sin in the sight of the Lord." These examples sufficiently teach that those are most alien from the fear of God who today play shamelessly with religion, or defile their lives with crimes and every kind of vice.

units.la: Porro quia vndiq; imminentibus periculis, & inter gladios nudatos rogosq; accensos constitutis difficile est persuadere, vt metu mortis posito fidem in Christum liberè & constanter profitean-tur, admonitioni suae argumenta quoque addit Dominus, quibus suorum fidem labascentem confirmet. Et primum quidem hic ipsis verbis continetur, quibus quid facere quidue cauere debeant, docet, atq; ex communi sensu desumptum est, quo omnes homines admonentur, inter duo pericula leuius esse subeundum, ne gratuiori implicemur. Confert enim inter se tyrannos & Deum, illorum item & huius vires siue potestatem, vitam deniq; hanc fluxam & mortalem cum futura & immortali. Et tyrannis quidem vera fiei persecutoribus tribuit, quod trucidare quidem possint, & vitam hanc alioqui eua niturnam eripere, nihil autem praeterea in nos iuris aut potestatis habeant. Penes Deum vero tam cor-poris quam animae potestatem esse ait, adeo vt corpus occidere vitamq; hanc fluxam eripere, & simul animas in gehenna aeternis cruciatibus torquendas abijcere possit. Ex qua comparatione validissime lidissimè concluditur, Deum potius quàm homines quantacunq; potentia præditos timeri debere. Quid enim illi possunt, si omnia illis permittat Dominus, quod cum æternis inferorum pœnis conseri mereatur? Corpus in carceres abripiunt, & vinculis durissimis constringunt: at interim anima in Christo libertate fruitur, & huius spiritu confirmata exultat. Ducunt deinde ad suppliciū, vbi etsi omnes ingenij sui crudelissimi vires intendant, non nisi horas aliquot corpus excruciare possunt, anima interim cum gaudio suam liberationem expectante, vt ex infelici hoc ergastulo ad beatorum spiritum societatem in cœlis triumphantem euadat. Itaq; beneficium cõferunt tyranni, cum maximè in pios sæviunt. Nam eorum liberationem accelerant, adeoq; eos iuuant, vt vitam hanc fluxam, miseram & mortalem cum immortali commutent. Cur ergo illorum minas & rabiem homo Christianus metuat? Potuit olim Marcum Castricium animare Seneca, vt Cn. Carbonis Consulis minas contemneret. Nam cùm hic illi minitaretur, se multos gladios habere, quibus imperium suum recusantem interficeret, respondit ille: Et ego multos annos habeo: ita nimirum indicans, sibi non posse terribilem esse mortem: quæ exigui temporis iactura sibi iam constet, quo elapso aliquoi moriturus sit. Cui simili plane fuit Cælius, qui cum multa liberius in Cæsarem diceret, amicus ne id faceret monentibus, respondit: Duæ res quæ hominibus amarissimæ videntur, mihi magnam licentiam præbent, Seneca & orbitas. Quod si tantum animi prophanis hominibus & beatæ immortalitatis spem ignorantibus, addere potuit brevitatis vitæ huius præsentis consideratio, quantò fortiores in contemnendis mortis terroribus esse convenit nos, qui animas ad Christum & æterna regni cœlestis gaudia colligi nouimus? Magis autem confirmabimur, si cogitemus, Deum sui cultus desertores & fidei abnegatores æternis inferorum cruciatibus punire. Nam si hos cum ijs conferamus, quæ tyranni & horum ministri nobis inferunt supplicia, nihil in hoc sæculo tam durum, tam triste, tam miserabile esse patebit, quod non patienter ferri debeat, vt futuri sæculi tormenta subterfugiamus. Illic enim vermes illi nunquam intermorientes miserorum tam corpora quàm animas arrodunt: illic ignis ille extinguibilis ardet, quem ætius furoris Domini accendit: illic sempiternus auditur ploratus & stridor dentium. Horum meditatio olim Apostolos & sanctos Martyres confirmauit, vt magno animo omnes minas tyrannorum & iam parata sibi suppliciorum tormenta contemnerent. Et hic rursus nobis exemplo est Polycarpus, cuius paulò ante mentionem fecimus. Nam cùm ei Proconsul ignem minitaretur, respondit: Ignem minaris hunc, qui ad momentum accenditur & ardet, at paulò post extinguitur: quia ignoras futuri iudicij ignem æternum, qui ad perpetuas pœnas præparatus est impiorum. In horum meditatione nos etiam frequenter versari decet, ne huius vitæ incommodis, aut tormentis, quæ impij carnifices nobis adhibent, terreamur: neue homines timeamus, qui in solum corpus rabie sua grassantur, obstare autem non possunt, quò minus animæ statim à morte ad æternas vitæ cœlestis sedes transmigrent, & ipsa quoq; corpora in magno illo die restitutionis omnium resuscitata glorioso Christi corpori conformia fiant, & suis animabus restituta æternùm viuant & gaudeant.
units.tr: Furthermore, since dangers hang over us on every side, and it is hard to persuade men who are placed between drawn swords and blazing pyres to profess faith in Christ freely and steadfastly, with the fear of death set aside, the Lord also adds arguments to his admonition, by which he may strengthen the wavering faith of his people. The first of these is contained in the very words in which he teaches what they ought to do and what to avoid. It is drawn from common sense, by which all men are warned that between two dangers the lesser must be undergone, lest they be entangled in the greater. For he compares tyrants with God, and likewise their power and might with his, and finally this frail and mortal life with the future and immortal one. To the tyrants who persecute the true faith he grants that they can indeed kill and snatch away this life, which in any case is destined to end, but that they have no further right or power over us. But he says that power over both body and soul belongs to God, so that he can both kill the body and snatch away this frail life, and at the same time cast souls to be tormented with eternal punishments in hell. From this comparison it is most powerfully concluded that God, rather than men endowed with whatever power, ought to be feared. For what can they do, if the Lord permits them everything, that is worth setting against the eternal punishments of the lower world? They drag the body off to prisons and bind it with the hardest chains; but meanwhile the soul enjoys freedom in Christ, and, strengthened by his Spirit, exults. Then they lead the body to execution, where, though they exert all the strength of their most cruel ingenuity, they can torment the body for only a few hours, while the soul, with joy, awaits its release, so that it may escape from this unhappy prison to the fellowship of the blessed spirits triumphing in heaven. Thus tyrants confer a benefit, especially when they rage most against the godly. For they hasten their deliverance, and so help them to exchange this frail, wretched and mortal life for an immortal one. Why, then, should a Christian fear their threats and fury? Seneca was once able to encourage Marcus Castritius to scorn the threats of the consul Gnaeus Carbo. For when Carbo threatened him, saying that he had many swords with which to kill him if he refused to obey, he answered: "And I have many years," clearly indicating that death could not be terrible to him, since he already held a brief span of time, after which he was about to die in any case. Caelius was a very similar case: when he said many things rather freely against Caesar, and friends warned him not to do so, he answered: "Two things which seem most bitter to men, Seneca and childlessness, give me great licence." But if the consideration of the brevity of this present life could add so much courage to profane men who did not know the hope of blessed immortality, how much braver we ought to be in despising the terrors of death, we who know that souls are gathered to Christ and to the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom! We will be strengthened still more if we consider that God punishes with eternal torments in the lower world those who desert his worship and deny the faith. For if we compare these with the tortures that tyrants and their ministers inflict upon us, nothing in this age will appear so hard, so sad, so wretched that it ought not to be borne patiently, so that we may escape the torments of the age to come. For there those worms that never cease to die gnaw at the bodies and souls of the wretched alike; there that unquenchable fire burns, which the wrath of the Lord kindled with its own fury; there everlasting weeping and gnashing of teeth is heard. The meditation on these things once confirmed the Apostles and holy Martyrs, so that with great courage they despised all the threats of tyrants and the torments of punishments already prepared for them. And here again Polycarp is an example to us, whom we mentioned a little while ago. For when the proconsul threatened him with fire, he answered: "You threaten me with a fire that is kindled for a moment and burns, but after a little while is extinguished; for you do not know the eternal fire of the future judgement, which is prepared for the everlasting punishment of the impious." We too ought often to dwell on these meditations, so that we are not terrified by the troubles of this life or by the torments that wicked executioners inflict upon us, nor fear men who rage with their fury only against the body, but cannot prevent souls from passing at once after death to the eternal seats of the heavenly life, and the bodies themselves, raised in that great day of the restoration of all things, from being made conformable to the glorious body of Christ, and, restored to their souls, living and rejoicing for ever. Most powerfully it is concluded from this comparison that God, rather than men endowed with whatever power, ought to be feared.

units.la: Est autem hic locus eo etiam nomine memorabilis, quòd præclarum de animarum immortalitate & futura vita testimonium continet. Nam si impij tyranni solum corpus occidere possunt, Deus autem vbi corpus occidit, insuper in gehennā potest conjicere, aliquam hominis partem esse oportet, quæ extincto corpore adhuc superstes manet, & tā supplicij quàm præmij æterni capax sit. Confirmatur hoc multis aliis scripturæ locis & exemplis, quæ nobis diligenter obseruanda sunt propter eos, qui cum corpore animas etiam intermori, & cum huius vitæ curriculo omnia hominis finiri dicunt. Quæ opinio pernitiosissimam securitatem parit, timorem Dei extinguit, & causa est, vt in omni scelerum genere multi sese volutantes, tandem magno suo malo verum esse sentiant, quod nunquam voluerunt credere. Arguit præterea locus iste Pontificum arrogantia, qui & in corpora piorum sæviunt, & animas quoq; eorundem Orco devouent. Atqui negat Christus homines postquam corpus occiderunt, quicquam præterea posse. Est ergo illorum potestas umbratilis, neq; timere sibi debent ab eorum execrationibus pij, quibus Christus benedixit & salutem æternam meruit.
units.tr: This passage is also remarkable for this reason: it contains a clear testimony to the immortality of the soul and the future life. For if wicked tyrants can kill only the body, but God, after he has killed the body, can moreover cast into hell, there must be some part of a man which survives when the body is extinguished, and which is capable of eternal punishment as well as eternal reward. This is confirmed by many other passages and examples of Scripture, which we must carefully observe on account of those who say that the soul too dies with the body, and that with the course of this life everything in man comes to an end. This opinion produces the most pernicious security, extinguishes the fear of God, and is the reason why many, wallowing in every kind of wickedness, at last feel to their great cost that what they never wished to believe is true. Moreover, this passage refutes the arrogance of the Papists, who rage against the bodies of the godly and also consign their souls to Orcus. Yet Christ denies that men, once they have killed the body, can do anything further. Their power, therefore, is a shadowy one, and the godly need not fear their curses, since Christ has blessed them and obtained eternal salvation for them.

units.la: At durum et iniquum aliquibus videri poterat, impios homines in corpora piorum aliquid posse, & hæc crucidandi potestatem habere. Plenius ergo seipsum Christus explicat, & hoc per Concessionem dictum esse ostendit, docens tyrannis ne in corpora quidem nostra quicquam licere, nisi hoc illis
units.tr: But it might seem harsh and unjust to some that wicked men can do anything against the bodies of the godly, and have the power to crucify them. Christ therefore explains himself more fully, and shows that this was said by way of concession, teaching that tyrants are not even permitted anything against our bodies unless this is allowed them

units.la: Animarum immortalitas.
units.tr: The immortality of the soul.

units.la: Tyranni in corpus quidem possunt aliquid. Deus permittat. Id vero probat argumento à Dei prouidentia duêto, qua omnia in hoc seculo re- guntur. Nonne quinq; passerculi (inquit) duobus assarijs vaneunt? & vnus ex ijs non est in ob- liuione apud Deum? Quin etiam capilli capitis vestri omnes numerati sunt, &c. Sensus est, Dei prouidentiam ad omnes creaturas extendi, adeò vt nihil vel extra hominem vel in homine tam vi- le & contemptum requiri queat, quod ille ignoret aut negligat. Et ex eorum quidem numero, qua extra nos sunt, passerculos nominat, quibus nulla inter aues vilior & magis etiam exosa est, vt qui fruges modò consumere nati videntur, & neque tantu delectant, neque in cibum adhibiti sapo- rem gratu habent. Veruntamen hos Deus novit, nec in genere modò, sed ita, vt ne vnius quidem il- lorum obliuiscatur, aut temere perire sinat. Ex ijs vero quæ in homine sunt, capilli allegantur, qui etsi ex corpore emasci soleant, vix tamen inter eius partes & membra numerari merentur, cum excre- menta potius sint ex humoribus superfluis enascentia, & sine illis corpus cōstare possit, adhæc absq; vllo labore resecentur. Sed ne hos quidem à Patre suo negligi Christus dicit, quin eos omnes in nu- merato habeat, vt absq; eius voluntate nullus possit defluere. Ex his autem colligit, multò magis nos Deo curæ esse, nec quicquā nobis absq; eius permissione nocituroc tyrannos, qui fidē verā & huius doctrinam extinctā volunt. Nam mox infert: Ne igitur timete, multis passerculis præstatis. Qui- bus verbis argumentū hoc confirmatur. Qui enim auiculas & omnes alias creaturas tam fideliter protegit & seruat, qua ratione hominē negligeret, propter quem mundi huius totam fabricam cum omnibus quæ illa continentur, creauit? Dignitatis ergo nostræ hic nos admonet, vt huius memo- res eò efficaciorem ex Dei prouidentia consolationem capiamus. Etsi vero dignitas illa omnibus hominibus communis sit, & impijs quoque omnes huius mundi partes seruiant, præcipuè tamen lo- cum habet in electis & credentibus, qui non solum quoad corpus & hanc vitam mortalem à Deo creati, verumetiam in Christo regenerati, & germani filij Dei facti sunt, quos hic æterna etiam vita hæredes esse vult.
units.tr: Tyrants can indeed do something against the body, but only if God permits it. He proves this by an argument drawn from God's providence, by which all things in this world are governed. "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings," he says, "and is not one of them forgotten before God? Indeed, the very hairs of your head are all numbered," and so on. The sense is that God's providence extends to all creatures, so that nothing so cheap and contemptible can be found, either outside man or within man, that he does not know or neglect. Of the things outside us, he names sparrows, which among birds are the cheapest and most despised, seeming born only to eat up grain, giving no pleasure, and having no agreeable taste when used for food. Yet God knows them, and not merely in general, but so that he does not forget even one of them or allow it to perish rashly. Of the things within man, he mentions hair, which, although it grows from the body, scarcely deserves to be counted among its parts and limbs, since it is rather excrement arising from superfluous humours; the body can exist without it, and it can be cut off without any pain. But Christ says that not even these are neglected by his Father; he has them all numbered, so that not one can fall without his will. From this he concludes that we are much more an object of God's care, and that nothing can harm us without his permission, including the tyrants who wish to extinguish true faith and this doctrine. For he adds at once: "Fear not, therefore; you are worth more than many sparrows." By these words the argument is confirmed. For he who protects and preserves the little birds and all other creatures so faithfully, how could he neglect man, for whose sake he created the whole fabric of this world with all that it contains? Here he reminds us of our dignity, so that, remembering it, we may take the greater consolation from God's providence. Although that dignity is common to all men, and all parts of this world serve even the wicked, it holds its chief place in the elect and believers, who have been created by God not only in body and in this mortal life, but have also been regenerated in Christ and made true sons of God, whom he wills to be heirs of eternal life as well.

units.la: Dei prouiden-tia.
units.tr: Divine providence.

units.la: Meretur autem locus hic diligentem consideratiōnem, & dignus est, quem nunquam non in ani mo nostro & recenti memoria feruemus. Nam plurimum facit ad veram Dei cognitionē, quā nos in omni casu officij admonet, & simul in ordine continet, ne exorbitemus. Docet enim Deū non mo dò Creatorem esse cæli & terræ omniumq; eorum quæ his continentur: verumetiā omnia illa certo iudicio & decreto gubernare, singulis item prospicere, vt quoad ipse vult conseruentur. Testantur idem passim sacræ literæ, & Dauid in Psalmis prolixè Dei paternam curam commendat, qui feris quoq; syluestribus & ab omni hominum vsu atq; consuetudine remotis pabulum suum in locis deser- tis procreet, & ijdem in summis etiam montium cacuminibus fontes aperiat, quibus recreentur. In præsenti autē Dominus Patrus sui prouidentiam ad singulos passerculos & capitis pilos extendit, ne quis generalē modò curam Dei fingat: quod multi hodie faciunt, qui etsi eius potentia & sapien- tia mundum hunc regi nō ausint negare, indignum tamen illis videtur, si talem fingamus, qui circa singulas creaturas fit occupatus. Ideo quæ hic Christus dicit, & quæ alia huius generis in Scriptura sacra habentur, per Hyperbolem dicta aiunt, neq; opus esse, vt propterea Deū ad infima hæc & for- dida officia detrudamus. At isti homines dum pro aliis sapere volunt, se omnium sultissimos esse pro- dunt: & dum diuinam maiestatē tueri conantur, eam quam maximè deprimunt & concultant. Ve- lim enim mihi dicant, quid nam per Hyperbolē de Deo dici possit, qui & omnipotens & omniscius & vbiq; præsens est? Certè quicquid illi ab eius cura exemerint, ipsius omnipotentiæ & gubernationi aliquid detrahent. Nec est quod vereantur, ne illū ad sordida eius q; maiestati indigna officia detru damus. Nec enim ea illius, quæ opificum, est conditio, vt cum labore & molestia, aut etiam cum ami mi solicitudine res perficere cogatur: sed nutus eius ad quauis sufficit, quem cæcus ille gentium Ho merus tantæ virtutis esse agnouit, vt simul cælum terramq; concutiat. Imò hoc euidentissimū maie- statis eius argumentū est, quòd oculi eius omnia vident, quod sapientia sua res omnes disponit, quòd in singulis creaturis agit & operatur, quòd singula ad suū finem destinat, & vt eum æquantur di rigit, quòd deniq; illo inscio vel inuito nihil accidit. Procul ergo facessant, qui in Dei Prouidentia nescio quam Contingentiam statuunt, qui proximus ad Epicureismū gradus est. Fatemur quidem nobis multa præter animi voluntatem & institutū accidere, & multa in rerū natura fieri, quæ aliter fieri poterant: at quid hoc ad Deum, qui omnia videt & gubernat, adeò, vt si eius Prouidentia spectes, speĉtes, nihil temere, nihil fortuito fiat? Num illum ex nostro ingenio metiemur, & ne quid de illo dicamus, quod nostrę rationi absurdum videtur, eum à mundi gubernaculis deturbabimus? Sunt hęc indigna Christianis auribus. Nobis ergo persuasum sit, Deum omnipotentem esse, cœlum & terram penetrare, omnia regere, neq; quicquam absq; eius voluntate fieri, quæ nobis quidem (vt D. Augustinus olim dicebat) non equidem semper nota, semper autem iusta est.
units.tr: This passage deserves careful consideration, and is worthy of being always kept in our mind and fresh in our memory. For it contributes greatly to the true knowledge of God, which admonishes us of our duty in every circumstance and at the same time keeps us within bounds, so that we do not go astray. For it teaches that God is not only the Creator of heaven and earth and of all that is contained in them, but also governs all those things by a certain judgment and decree, and likewise watches over each one, so that they are preserved as he wills. The Holy Scriptures testify the same everywhere, and David in the Psalms commends at length God's fatherly care, who provides food for the wild beasts, remote from all human use and custom, in the deserts, and who opens springs on the very tops of the mountains by which they may be refreshed. In the present passage the Lord extends the providence of his Father to each sparrow and each hair of the head, so that no one may imagine a merely general care of God. Many do this today, who, although they do not dare to deny that God's power and wisdom govern this world, nevertheless think it unworthy to imagine a God who is occupied with each single creature. Therefore they say that what Christ says here, and other such things found in Holy Scripture, are said by hyperbole, and that there is no need to thrust God down to these lowly and base offices. But these men, while they wish to be wise on behalf of others, show themselves to be most foolish; and while they try to defend the divine majesty, they most of all belittle and shake it. For I would like them to tell me what could be said by hyperbole about God, who is almighty, all-knowing and everywhere present. Certainly whatever they remove from his care, they take something away from his omnipotence and government. Nor need they fear that we drag him down to base offices unworthy of his majesty. For it is not the condition of that power, which is the condition of a craftsman, to be compelled to bring things to completion with labour and trouble, or even with anxious care of mind; rather his nod suffices for anything, a nod which that blind Homer of the Gentiles recognised as of such power that it shakes heaven and earth together. Indeed, this is the most evident argument of his majesty: that his eyes see all things, that by his wisdom he orders all things, that he acts and works in each creature, that he directs each thing to its end and brings all into line with it, and finally that nothing happens without his knowledge or against his will. Let those keep far away who posit in God's providence I know not what contingency, which is the next step to Epicureanism. We admit indeed that many things happen to us beyond the will and purpose of the mind, and that many things occur in the nature of things which could have happened otherwise; but what has this to do with God, who sees and governs all things, so that, if you regard his providence, nothing happens rashly or by chance? Shall we measure him by our own mind, and, lest we say anything about him that seems absurd to our reason, thrust him from the helm of the world? Such things are unworthy of Christian ears. Let us therefore be persuaded that God is almighty, that he pervades heaven and earth, that he governs all things, and that nothing happens without his will; which, indeed (as Augustine of old used to say), is not always known to us, but is always just.

units.la: Vsus autem huius considerationis nobis esto, non vt illius arcana scrutari, & quæcunq; fiunt, ad nostræ rationis calculum revocare velimus: sed vt primum memores, nos in Dei conspectu agere, cuius oculos & aures nemo fallere aut latere potest, tam in dictis quàm factis nostris omnibus innocentiæ & sanctitati studeamus. Deinde vt hinc consolationem petamus in aduersis. Quia enim absque eius voluntate nihil fit, illo permittente nos tyranni persequuntur, fortunis spoliant, sedibus patriis eiiciunt, in vincula & carceres rapiunt, occidunt denique & omne crudelitatis genus in nos exercent. Similiter eius voluntas est, vt cum morbis diuturnis luctemur, vt egestate premamur, vt esuriamus, algeamus, calumniis circumueniamur, periclitemur, aut quicquid præterea homini incommodum aut noxium accidere potest, sustineamus. At quia idem ille Pater indulgentissimus, iudex item iustissimus, adhæc ipsa est sapientia, procul dubio nihil nobis accidere sinet, quàm quod nobis utile & salutare fuerit, neq; quisquam de eius iustitia conqueri poterit. Dei ergo manum in omni afflictionum genere agnoscamus, & leuissima mox apparebunt, quæ primo intuitu grauissima & prorsus intolerabilia esse videbantur. Hac consolatione olim Josephus carcerem, seruitutem, calumnias & exilium diuturnum superauit, quòd se non sine certo Dei consilio in Ægyptum peruenìsse cogitaret. Hæc ipsa lobum quoque armauit, vt opum direptionem, agrorum vastationem, liberorum dulcissimorum miserabilem interitum patienter ferret. Sciebat enim hæc omnia sibi prius à Deo gratuita liberalitate donata, nunc autem iusto iudicio rursus erepta esse. Et sane qui hoc ipsum in suis periculis & aduersis cogitant, nunquam impatientia superabuntur, neq; aduersus Deum murmurabunt. Adhæc fidem nostram inter precandum hæc consideratio confirmat, quando cogitamus Deum nos laborantes videre, & proinde audire etiam ad se clamantium preces. Imò vt Deum ex fide innocet impossibile est, quisquis de eius Prouidentia dubitauerit. Mox enim cogitationes obrepent, Num te miserum & contemptissimum ille respiceret? num tui curam susci-peret Deus, cùm te intimi tui negligant? num qui circa mundi totius gubernationem occupatus est, sese ad tuas miserias sublevandas demitteret? At inanes esse eorum preces, qui inter dubitationes eiusmodi fluctuant, Scripturæ non vno loco docent. Recte ergo Christus ad Prouidentiam Patris cœlestis discipulos remittit, in quam nos quoque recumbere decet. Itaque meminerimus nos ad cœlestem & immortalem vitam creatos esse, & proinde fluxæ huius & mortalis ıactuaram patienter feramus: & quia huius etiam custos est Deus, qui illius dies iam olim in numerato habet, de illa non plus æquo solliciti simus. Nam vt Apostolus ait, nullus sibiipsi viuit, & nullus sibiipsi moritur. Est enim siue viuimus, Domino viuimus: siue morimur, Domino morimur. Siue igitur viuamus siue moriamur, Domini sumus. Adhoc enim Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit & reuixit, vt tam mortuus quàm viuentibus dominetur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let this be the use of this consideration for us: not that we should wish to search out his secrets and bring everything that happens back to the reckoning of our own reason, but first, that we remember that we act in the sight of God, whose eyes and ears no one can deceive or escape, and that in all our words and deeds we strive for innocence and holiness. Then, that we seek comfort from it in adversity. For since nothing happens apart from his will, it is by his permission that tyrants persecute us, strip us of our property, drive us from our ancestral homes, drag us into chains and prisons, finally kill us, and inflict every kind of cruelty upon us. Likewise it is his will that we struggle with lingering diseases, that we be pressed by want, that we hunger and freeze, that we be surrounded by slanders, endangered, or endure whatever else can befall a man as an inconvenience or harm. But since that same most indulgent Father, who is also most just judge, and indeed is wisdom itself, will without doubt allow nothing to happen to us except what is useful and salutary for us, no one will be able to complain of his justice. Let us therefore acknowledge the hand of God in every kind of affliction, and soon those things will appear very light which at first glance seemed most heavy and utterly intolerable. By this consolation Joseph once overcame prison, slavery, slander and long exile, because he reflected that he had come into Egypt not without the certain counsel of God. This same thought armed Job too, so that he patiently bore the plundering of his goods, the devastation of his fields, and the wretched death of his most beloved children. For he knew that all these things had first been given to him by God out of free generosity, and now by just judgment taken back again. And indeed those who think this very thing in their dangers and adversities will never be overcome by impatience, nor will they murmur against God. Moreover, this consideration strengthens our faith while we pray, when we think that God sees us labouring and therefore hears the prayers of those who cry out to him. Indeed, it is impossible to think rightly of God if one has doubted his providence. For soon thoughts creep in: Would he look upon you, a wretched and most contemptible man? Would God take up the care of you, when your own intimates neglect you? Would he who is occupied with the governance of the whole world lower himself to relieve your miseries? But the Scriptures teach in more than one place that the prayers of those who waver amid doubts of this kind are empty. Rightly therefore Christ sends his disciples back to the providence of the heavenly Father, on which we too ought to lean. Let us therefore remember that we were created for a heavenly and immortal life, and so let us patiently bear the troubles of this fleeting and mortal life; and since God, who has long since numbered its days, is also its guardian, let us not be anxious about it more than is right. For, as the Apostle says, no one lives to himself, and no one dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; and whether we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live or die, therefore, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ both died and rose and returned to life, that he might rule over both the dead and the living. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXVII.

units.la: Dico autem vobis: Quisquis me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eum Filius quoq; hominis confitebitur coram Angelis Dei. Qui vero negauerit me in conspectu hominum, is abnegabitur in conspectu Angelorum Dei. Et quisquis dicet verbum in Filium hominis, ei remittetur: Ei vero qui in Spiritum sanctum blasphemauerit, non remittetur. Cùm autem adduxerint vos ad Synagogas, & ad magistratus ac potestates, ne solliciti estote, quomodo aut quid pro defensione allaturi, aut quid dicturi sitis. Spiritus enim sanctus docebit vos eo ipso momento, quæ oporteat dicere.
units.tr: "I tell you: whoever confesses me before men, the Son of Man will also confess before the angels of God. But whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven. When they bring you before the synagogues, and before the magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious how or what you are to answer in your defence, or what you are to say. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say."

units.la: QVemadmodum homo felicitatis in hoc seculo appetens est, & hanc fere suorum studiorum atq; actionum finem siue scopum constituit: ita eam in primis in religione quaerere, imo etiam certo sperare solet. Quia enim nos per hanc Deo, qui omnus boni fons est, conungi audit, mox carnis sensum secutus spem magnarum opum, honorum, otij & pacis animo concipit, neglectis bonis coelestibus & aeternis, quae in se credentibus Deus offert. Est autem error hic nocentissimus, quia in causa est, ut plerique aduersis, quae praeter omnem expectationem incidunt, offensi, de religione ex huius seculi euentu iudicent, & a fide turpiter deficiant. Prudenter ergo Christus Dominus discipulos suos, qui fidei doctores esse debebant, aduersus omnes tentationes armat & instruit. Et initio quidem eos neglecta omni pompa & inanis ostentationis fuco, integritati studere & ab ipso acceptam Veritatis doctrinam bona fide tradere iussit. Quia vero hoc non sine periculo fieri potest, eo quod mundus hic Veritatis lucem indignissime ferat, rationes adhibet validissimas, quibus confirmentur. Prima est, quod qui ad vitam aeternam & beatam immortalitatem destinati sunt, nequaquam sibi ab hominibus timere debeant, qui non nisi corpus trucidare, & vitam hanc fluxam eripere possunt. Altera ex Dei Providentia desumitur, in quam illos recumbere iubet, quando fieri non possit, ut suorum vitam ille negligat, qui & auiculus otiosis prospicit, & capitis nostri pilos numeratos habet. Caeterum, ne quis solus Apostolus & horum in docendi munere succedentibus haec dicta putaret, nunc in genere omnibus doctrinam hanc applicat, docens, ab vnoquoq; nostrum liberam & ingenuam fidei confessionem requiri, neq; salvos fore eos, qui ipsum coram hoc mundo negauerint.
units.tr: Just as man seeks happiness in this world, and usually sets this as the chief end or aim of his studies and actions, so he is wont above all to seek it in religion, and even to hope for it with confidence. For since he hears that through religion he is joined to God, who is the fountain of all good, he at once, following the senses of the flesh, conceives in his mind the hope of great wealth, honours, leisure and peace, neglecting the heavenly and eternal goods which God offers to those who believe in him. This error is most harmful, because it is the cause of why many, offended by adversities that befall them beyond all expectation, judge of religion from the outcome in this world and shamefully fall away from the faith. Christ the Lord therefore wisely arms and instructs his disciples, who were to be teachers of the faith, against all temptations. At the outset he commanded them, setting aside all pomp and the empty show of display, to aim at integrity and to hand on in good faith the doctrine of truth received from him. But since this cannot be done without danger, because this world bears the light of truth most unworthily, he brings forward very strong reasons by which they may be strengthened. The first is that those who are destined for eternal life and blessed immortality ought in no way to fear men, who can only kill the body and take away this fleeting life. The second is drawn from the providence of God, on which he bids them rely; for it cannot be that he who watches over the sparrows that sell for nothing, and has even the hairs of our head numbered, neglects the lives of his own. Moreover, lest anyone think that these words were spoken only to the Apostle and to those who would succeed them in the office of teaching, he now applies this doctrine to all in general, teaching that a free and open confession is required of each one of us, and that those who deny him before this world will not be saved.

units.la: Sic enim ait: Quisquis me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eum Filius quoq; hominis confitebitur coram Angelis Dei: Qui vero negauerit me in conspectu hominum, is abnegabitur in conspectu Angelorum Dei. Comprehenditur hic (ut modo diximus) generale praeceptum, quod ad omnes homines pertinet, qui Christiani haberi & in Christo seruari volunt. Est hoc, ut eum libere & ingenue confiteamur, neq; nos eius apud quenquam pudeat. Ita enim haec verba apud Marcum enuntiantur. Non ergo sufficit, ut intra animos nostros de fide recte instituti simus, sed huius confessionem accedere oportet. Nam ut pater eum filium ferre non potest, neq; herus seruum, quem sui pudere nouit, & marito intolerabile fuerit uxorem habere, quae eius uxor videri nolit: Ita indigni sunt, qui pro Dei filijs agnoscantur, quos Patris coelestis & Filij eius unigeniti pudet, neq; Christi serui & sponsa censeri merentur, qui ipsi se hac dignitate abdicant, dum illum apud eos abnegant, quos eius hostes esse nouerunt. Et quia nos ex mundo selegit, ut totos sibi consecraret, nimium iniqui & ingrati sunt, qui ut mundo placeant, illum suum Dominum & seruatorem agnoscere dedignantur. Damnat itaque Christus hoc loco omnes eos, qui fidei confessionem inter res medias & indifferentes numerant, & simul Christo ac mundo seruire volunt: quales hodie Libertini & Dauidiani sunt, qui ubi ipsis commodu & utile est, Christum & fidem in hunc pleno ore profitentur: at ubi periculum imminere vident, eam turpiter dissimulant, vel etiam diserte negant. Et hi quidem fide, quam in animo habeant, gloriantur, neq; quicquam praeterea a nobis requiri putant. Sed longe aliter hic Christus pronuntiat, & notum est illud Pauli: Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus: Si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus eum excitauit a mortuis, seruaberis. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. Rom. 10.
units.tr: For he says thus: "Whoever confesses me before men, the Son of Man will also confess before the angels of God; but whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God." Here is comprehended (as we have just said) a general precept, which pertains to all men who wish to be considered Christians and to be saved in Christ. It is this: that we confess him freely and openly, and that we are not ashamed of him before anyone. For these words are set out in the same way in Mark. It is therefore not enough that we are rightly instructed in the faith within our hearts; we must also add its confession. For as a father cannot bear a son, nor a master a servant whom he is ashamed of, and as it would be intolerable for a husband to have a wife who does not wish to be seen as his wife, so those are unworthy to be acknowledged as children of God who are ashamed of the heavenly Father and of his only-begotten Son, nor do they deserve to be counted as servants and bride of Christ, who themselves renounce this dignity while they deny him before those whom they know to be his enemies. And since he chose us out of the world to consecrate us wholly to himself, those are far too unjust and ungrateful who, that they may please the world, disdain to acknowledge him as their Lord and Saviour. Christ therefore in this place condemns all those who count the confession of the faith among things indifferent and neutral, and who wish to serve both Christ and the world; such are today the Libertines and the Davidians, who, when it is convenient and profitable for them, profess Christ and the faith with full mouth, but when they see danger impending, shamefully dissemble it or even deny it outright. These men boast of the faith that they hold in their heart, and think that nothing further is required of us. But Christ speaks quite differently here, and that saying of Paul is well known: "This is the word of faith which we preach: if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Rom. 10.

units.la: Caeterum ne fidei confessio vitiosa fit & imperfecta, & eiusdem abnegatio facilius cauari possit, teneamus oportet quid sit Christum confiteri aut abnegare. Illud itaq; est, eum ingenue coram quibusuis pro humani generis unico redemptore agnoscere & praedicare, omnia deniq; profiteri publice, quae per Euangelium de illo traduntur. Itaq; confessionis regula ex Euangelio peti debet, quod ipse apud Marcum, & supra Capite nono, non obscure docet, ubi se & sermones suos coniungit, dicens: Quemcunq; puduerit mei & meorum sermonum, &c. Et Paulus fidem suam profesturus aiebat: Non me pudet Euangelij Iesu Christi: est enim potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Constat autem confessio vera verbi & factis. Verborum confessio est, qualis Petri fuit, qui quid discipuli de Christo sentirent interrogatus, omnium nomine respondit: Tu es CHRISTVS ille, Filius Dei viuentis. Cui reliquorum etiam Apostolorum & Martyrum omnium confessiones consentiunt. Et hic exigitur, ut & de persona siue essentia Christi, & de eius de officio recte pronuntiemus. Et in persona quidem una atq; indiuisa Deum simul & hominem fateri oportet. Quoad officium vero quod idem ille Sacerdos sit æternus & Rex, quem Deus Pater æterno suo decreto constitue-rit super Zion montem suum sanctum. Ad Sacerdotium pertinet, ut doctorem catholicum æternæ veritatis agnoscamus, & talem quidem, qui seipsum pro nobis in ara crucis obtulerit, & peccato-rum remissionem meruerit nobis sempiternam, quique perfecto salutis negotio in cœlos subuectus no-ster apud Patrem Mediator sit & aduocatus. Regis autem officium præstitit idem, quando nos ex diaboli tyrannide asseruit, & adhuc Regem agit fidelem & bonum, dum Ecclesiam suam aduer-sus omnes hostes tam visibiles quam invisibiles tuetur, dum eandem legibus bonis & sanctis regit, iustitiam facit & iudicium in puniendis hostibus & seruandis suis, dum denique liberalitate plus quam regia regni cœlestis thesauros inter nos distribuit, nosque ditat omni benedictione spirituali. Hæc omnia in illo fateri oportet eos, qui veram & perfectam confessionem verbis edere volunt. Vbi in primis obseruandum, ut ista omnia illi soli tribuantur, neue quæ eius sunt in alios partia-mur. In hoc enim multi hodie peccant, qui se officio suo probe defunctos putant, si ista obiter de Christo fateantur, cum interim hæc ipsa Dei quoque cœlitibus tribuant, & ita illum magna ex parte suo honore spolient. At neminem ille in sua gloriæ consortium admittit, & hoc olim Martyres pro-be obseruarunt: qui hoc potissimum nomine horrendis supplicijs excruciati sunt, quod uno Christo contenti nullos alios Deos & seruatores voluerunt agnoscere. Factis autem illum fatebimur, si tota vita Christum loquatur, si apud illum solum quæramus quæ ad salutem nostram spectant, neque aliquid admittamus quod eius merito deroget.
units.tr: But lest the confession of the faith be faulty and imperfect, and lest its denial be more easily committed, we must hold what it is to confess or to deny Christ. It is this: to acknowledge and proclaim him openly before anyone whatsoever as the sole redeemer of the human race, and in short to profess publicly everything that is handed down about him through the Gospel. Therefore the rule of confession ought to be sought from the Gospel, which he himself, in Mark and above in chapter nine, plainly teaches, where he joins himself and his words together, saying: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, etc." And Paul, about to set forth his faith, said: "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Jesus Christ; for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." Now the confession of Christ consists of words and deeds. The confession in words is such as that of Peter, who, when asked what the disciples thought of Christ, answered in the name of all: "You are that CHRIST, the Son of the living God." With this the confessions of the rest of the Apostles and of all the Martyrs agree. Here it is also required that we speak rightly both of the person or essence of Christ and of his office. In respect of the person, we must confess him to be at once God and man in one undivided person. As for the office, we must confess that the same one is the eternal Priest and King, whom God the Father by his eternal decree has set up upon his holy mountain Zion. To the priestly office belongs the acknowledgement of him as the catholic teacher of eternal truth, and indeed of one who offered himself for us on the altar of the cross, and who obtained for us the everlasting forgiveness of sins, and who, having completed the work of salvation, was taken up into heaven and is our Mediator and Advocate before the Father. The kingly office he performed when he rescued us from the tyranny of the devil, and he still acts as a faithful and good King while he defends his Church against all enemies, visible and invisible, while he rules it by good and holy laws, while he executes justice and judgement in punishing its enemies and saving his own, and finally while he distributes among us, with a liberality more than royal, the treasures of the heavenly kingdom and enriches us with every spiritual blessing. All these things those must confess in him who wish to make a true and perfect confession in words. Here, first of all, it must be observed that all these things are to be ascribed to him alone, and that we do not transfer to others what belongs to him. For in this many today sin, who think they have discharged their duty well if they confess these things about Christ in passing, while in the meantime they ascribe these same things to the heavenly beings of God as well, and so in large part strip him of his honour. But he admits no one to the fellowship of his glory, and the Martyrs of old observed this well: they were tortured with dreadful punishments chiefly on this account, that, being content with Christ alone, they would acknowledge no other gods and saviours. We shall confess him in deeds if we let Christ speak through our whole life, if we seek with him alone what pertains to our salvation, and if we admit nothing that detracts from his merit.

units.la: Ex his iam colligi potest, quid sit Christum & fidem in hunc abnegare. Fit hoc quoque non uno modo. Crassissimum vero abnegationis genus est, quando Dei Filius esse negatur & unicus humani generis redemptor, simulque Euangelium ipsius falsi arguitur, denique si nobis nihil cum eo commercij intercedere dicamus. Ita autem illum alij ex prophano contemptu & malicia negant, ut olim Iudæi coram Pilato, & impius ille omnis religionis illusor Julianus Apostata: alij autem ex metu quod Petro inter Sacerdotum famulos accidisse scimus. Vtrumque hodie nimis vulgare est, dum alij procul abiecto diuini cultus studio, mundi amicitiâ atque voluptates sectantur, alij autem ad quasuis impiorum minas consternati, illorum postulationibus nimium seruiliter indulgent. Factis etiam Christus negatur multiuariam. Primùm, cum contra Christianæ professionis leges alienis sacris communicamus, cœtus papisticos accedimus, Missas audimus, apud simulachra procumbimus, aut quo cunque honore illa veneramur: cum item sacra pro defunctis facimus, aut illis adstamus in hominum gratiam. Quibus etiam adnumerari debent, qui per Deos aut Diuos iurant, quod olim à Martyribus in primis requisitum fuisse, historiæ Ecclesiasticæ testantur. Quia enim hæc omnia cum fidei ingenio & legibus pugnant, non possunt non ignaui huius dissimulatores aut abnegatores dici, quotquot ali quid horum faciunt. Deinde abnegatur Christus, quando in aduersis & periculis alibi quam apud illum solum opem & auxilium quærimus. Faciunt hoc qui Diuos inuocant & illis vota nuncupant: qui in morbis aut rerum amissione Magos & diuinos consulunt: qui deniq; in hominibus plus spei habent quàm in Deo, quæ nobis Christus placatu & propitiu reddidit. Nam has abnegationis species esse, Deus in Prophetis passim docet. Eos enim defectionis impiæ accusat, qui etsi ipsum ex parte fate-rentur, Deos tamen alienos inuocabant. Et Ochoziæ, qui ex graui morbo decubens ad Baalzebub Dei- um Ekrom legatos mittebat, Elias dici mandauit: Anno est Deus in Israele, quòd vos consultum mit-titis ad Baalzebub? Quæ verba satis docent, de Deo prius spe omne eos abiecisse, qui alio confugiunt in periculis. Ieremias autem maledictum pronuntiat, qui spem suam ponit in homine, & Asa Rex hoc nomine reprehenditur, quod ex pedibus laborans medicorum potius quam Dei opem quæsiuisset. Fit preterea abnegatio moribus & vitæ conuersatione, quando ore quidem profitemur, vitam autem viuimus ab eius regula alienissimam, neque obedimus Euangelio, quod verum & sanctum esse dicimus. De talibus Paulus pronuntiat: Deum fatentur se scire, verum factis eundem negant, cum sint abominabiles & immorigeri, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi. Et sanè fieri non potest, ut Christum suum redemptorem esse, & eundem omnis carnis iudicem fore credant, qui ita viuunt, ut propter ipsos nomen eius & Euangelium male audiat. Hæc igitur omnia Christus prohibet, & vult ut relictis procul superstitionibus & vitijs, ipsum tam ore quàm vita ingenuè profiteamur. Est enim hæc non postrema cultus diuini pars, & ij demum fidem suam in hoc mundo pie & utiliter exercent, qui liberam sui seruatoris confessionem super stitionibus etc, corruptis mundi studijs fortiter opponunt, & si opus sit, etiam sanguine suo illi testimonium ferunt.
units.tr: From these things it can now be gathered what it is to deny Christ and the faith in him. This also happens in more than one way. The grossest kind of denial is when the Son of God is denied to be the only redeemer of the human race, when his Gospel is declared false, and finally when we say that we have no fellowship with him at all. Some deny him in this way from profane contempt and malice, as the Jews once did before Pilate, and as that impious mocker of all religion, Julian the Apostate, did. Others deny him from fear, as we know happened to Peter among the servants of the high priest. Both are far too common today: some, having cast off all zeal for divine worship, pursue the friendship and pleasures of the world; others, dismayed by the threats of the impious, give in far too slavishly to their demands. Christ is also denied by deeds, in many ways. First, when against the laws of the Christian profession we share in alien rites: we attend Papist assemblies, hear Masses, prostrate ourselves before images, or honour them in any way; likewise when we perform rites for the dead, or stand by at them to please men. To these must be added those who swear by gods or saints, which the histories of the Church testify was especially demanded of the martyrs in former times. For since all these things clash with the nature and laws of the faith, everyone who does any of them cannot but be called a cowardly dissembler or denier of it. Next, Christ is denied when in adversities and dangers we seek help and aid anywhere other than from him alone. Those do this who invoke saints and make vows to them; who in sickness or loss consult magicians and diviners; who, finally, place more hope in men than in God, whom Christ has made placated and propitious to us. For God teaches throughout the Prophets that these are kinds of denial. He accuses of impious apostasy those who, although they partly acknowledged him, nevertheless invoked foreign gods. And when Ahaziah, lying sick from a grave disease, sent messengers to Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, Elijah was ordered to say: "Is there no God in Israel, that you send to consult Baal-zebub?" These words sufficiently teach that those who flee elsewhere in dangers have first cast off all hope in God. Jeremiah pronounces a curse on him who puts his hope in man, and King Asa is reproved on this account, because when suffering in his feet he sought the help of physicians rather than of God. Denial also occurs in conduct and manner of life, when with our mouth we profess, but live a life most alien to its rule, and do not obey the Gospel, which we say is true and holy. Of such people Paul pronounces: they profess that they know God, but they deny him by their deeds, since they are abominable and disobedient, and reprobate for every good work. Indeed, it cannot be that those who live in such a way that his name and Gospel are ill spoken of on account of them believe that Christ is their redeemer and that he will be the judge of every flesh.
