Christ therefore forbids all these things, and wills that, having put far away superstitions and vices, we openly profess him both with mouth and life. For this is no small part of divine worship; and those, finally, practise their faith in this world piously and profitably who freely confess their Saviour, and strongly oppose superstitions and the corrupt pursuits of the world, and, if need be, bear witness to him even with their blood.

units.la: Quia vero hoc carni durum & graue videtur propter impiorum petulantiam & tyrannorum rabiem, qui veros Christi confessores non oderunt modo, verumetiam extinctos volunt, praeceptum suum ille promissione magnifica & comminatione terribili confirmat. Nam quisquis (inquit) me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eum Filius quoque hominis confitebitur coram Angelis Dei. Filium hominis sese dicit, ut ijs medeatur, qui vili eius specie ita offenduntur, ut eius ipsos pudeat, indeoque Angelorum quoque meminit. Quasi diceret: Etsi nunc non alius quam filius hominus imo hominum infimus & miserrimus esse videar, non est tamen quod aliquem mei pudeat. Nam simul aeternus ille Dei Filius sum, quem Daniel olim innumeris Angelorum myriadibus stipatum vidit, & qui in nouissimo die cum Angelis sanctis in gloria Patris venturus sum ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos: & tunc ego quoque vera fidei & pietatis testimonium feram ijs, qui me coram hominibus confessi fuerunt, imo eos pro fratribus & fidelissimis meae gloriae vindicibus agnoscam. Est hac am plissima promissio, quae omnem hominis felicitatem continet, vna cum omnibus, quae ad salutem aeter nam faciunt. Si enim olim sui nominis confessores Christus agnoscet, vtiqu iam quoque in certamine constitutos videt tanquam Agonothetes aliquis diligentissimus. Potest hoc verum nobis animos addere. Quem enim non pudeat remissius & ignauius agere in Filij Dei consessu? Aut quis de victoria desperet, qui cogitat illum non modo laborum & certaminum nostrorum spectatorem esse, verumetiam praesidem fidelem, qui pro sua gloria certantes suo fauore iuuat, & infirmioribus aut iam succubituris nouas vires sufficit, vel assultus hostis coercet, vt in omni pugna superiores fieri possint? Est enim (vt Paulus ait) fidelis & nostri amans, neq; nos supra quam ferre possimus tentari sinit. Quanta autem haec gloria futura est, quando in totius mundi, & quidem hostium suorum iam ad aeternas poenas destinatorum conspectu, adhaec coram sanctis Angelis & Patre suo coelesti, eorum fidem & virtutem Dei Filius publice commendabit, qui ipsum in hoc mundo ingenuè confessi fuerunt? Gaudent Imperatorum suorum triumphis milites, & eius honoris spe fortius pugnant. Atqui luius & iocus, imo inanis gloriae vmbra sunt triumphi huius saeculi prae illa gloria, qua in illo die veri Christi cultores obtinebunt. Finge regis potentissimi filium e pugna reuersum, coram patre, in frequenti procerum & nobilium totius regni consessu aliquos produxere, qui ab hostibus circumuentum protexerint, & non sine periculo & vulneribus liberarint. Quis non beatos dicet cuius hoc contingit? Quis non honesta & felicia iudicabit vulnera, quae tantum habent praeconem, & quibus merces quoque maxima iam parata est? Quanto igitur felicior eorum fors erit, quibus in magno illo die virtutis & fidei constantis testimonium deferet aeternus Dei filius? Nam quos hic tunc pro suis agnoscet, ij ipsius fratres atque coheredes erunt, & (vt discipulus dicebat) ad illius mensam beato illo immortalitatis nectare in aeternum fruentur.
units.tr: But since this seems hard and burdensome to the flesh, on account of the wantonness of the impious and the rage of tyrants, who not only hate the true confessors of Christ but want them dead as well, he confirms his precept with a magnificent promise and a terrible threat. For whoever (he says) confesses me before men, the Son of man will also confess before the Angels of God. He calls himself the Son of man so that he may heal those who are so offended by his lowly appearance that they are ashamed of him; and so he also mentions the Angels. As if he were saying: "Although now I may seem to be nothing other than the Son of man, nay, the lowliest and most wretched of men, there is no reason for anyone to be ashamed of me. For I am at the same time that eternal Son of God, whom Daniel once saw surrounded by countless myriads of Angels, and who at the last day will come in the glory of the Father with the holy Angels to judge the living and the dead; and then I too will bear true witness of faith and piety to those who have confessed me before men, nay, I will acknowledge them as brothers and most faithful vindicators of my glory." This is a most ample promise, which contains all human happiness together with everything that pertains to eternal salvation. For if Christ will acknowledge in the future those who confessed his name, surely he also sees now those who are set in the contest, as a most diligent president of the games. This can truly add courage to us. For who would not be ashamed to act more lazily and cowardly in the assembly of the Son of God? Or who would despair of victory, when he considers that Christ is not only a spectator of our labours and struggles, but also a faithful helper, who with his favour aids those contending for his glory, supplies new strength to the weaker or to those about to succumb, and checks the assault of the enemy, so that in every battle they may become victors? For (as Paul says) he is faithful and loves us, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. How great this glory will be, however, when before the whole world, and indeed before his enemies already destined to eternal punishment, and moreover before the holy Angels and his heavenly Father, the Son of God publicly commends the faith and virtue of those who freely confessed him in this world! Soldiers rejoice in the triumphs of their emperors and fight more bravely in hope of that honour. Yet the triumphs of this age are but a jest, nay, the empty shadow of glory, compared with that glory which the true worshippers of Christ will obtain on that day. Imagine the son of a most powerful king returning from battle; before his father, in the assembled gathering of the nobles of the whole kingdom, some men are brought forward who protected him when surrounded by enemies and delivered him, not without danger and wounds. Who would not call blessed the one to whom this happens? Who would not judge those wounds honourable and happy, which have so great a herald, and for which a very great reward is already prepared? How much happier, then, will be the lot of those to whom the eternal Son of God bears witness of a steadfast testimony of virtue and faith on that great day! For those whom he then acknowledges as his own will be his brothers and co-heirs, and (as the disciple said) they will enjoy for ever at his table that blessed nectar of immortality.

units.la: E contra, Qui negauerit me in conspectu hominum, is abnegabitur in conspectu angelorum Dei. Apud Marcum loco hominum ponit nationem adulteram et peccatricem, vt ostendat, non dignum esse mundum aut huius saeculi filios, quorum tantam rationem habeamus, vt propter eos ipsum abnegemus. Sunt enim adulteri & degeneres, qui & fidem Deo debitam dudum violarunt, & ingenii filiorum Dei nullo modo referunt, cum toti sceleribus & vitijs sint obsiti. Facit ergo hoc ad scelerus amplificationem, si propter tales aeternus Dei Filius negetur, qui nobis à Patre sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est. Ideo minatur, quod ipse etiam abnegaturus sit coram Angelis Dei eos, qui ipsum coram hominibus tam peruersis & improbis negare audet. Vt vero prioribus illis omnem felicitatem cum summa gloria coniunctam pollicetur: ita his omnem infelicitatem & extremam ignominiam minatur. Quia enim salus in illo vno habetur, ab hac excidant oportet, quosquunq; ille suo testimonio reijcit, ne in filiorum Dei & fratrum suorum numero censeantur. Et quae turpior atque infelicior ignominia homini accidere potest, quam si in conspectu omnium Angelorum & electorum Dei, pro Christi seruatoris nostri desertore habeatur, & eo nomine excludatur à regni coelestis consortio? Etenim quem ille abdicat, huic in hoc etiam saeculo omnes creaturae infensae sunt, & idem diabolo permittitur, qui infinitis modis ludificatum tande ad sempiternos infelicitates cruciatus abripit. Est ergo locus hic multa & diligenti consideratione dignissimus. Docet enim eos demum vere Christianos esse, qui fidem & vitam suam ita instituunt, ut eos Christus in adventu suo novissimo pro suis posit agnoscere: non qui nomine Christiano & Dei verbo atq; Sacramentis absque fide gloriantur. Studeamus ergo ijs rebus, in quibus veram Christi confessionem conspicere diximus, ea autem horreamus & abominemur, quibus ille abnegatur.
units.tr: On the contrary: "Whoever denies me before men, he will be denied before the Angels of God." In Mark he puts "this adulterous and sinful generation" in place of "men", to show that such people are not worthy, nor are the children of this age, for us to have such regard for them that we deny him on their account. For they are adulterers and degenerate, who have long since violated the faith owed to God, and in no way resemble the disposition of the children of God, since they are wholly beset with crimes and vices. It therefore increases the gravity of the crime if the eternal Son of God is denied on account of such people, he who has been made for us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Therefore he threatens that he too will deny, before the Angels of God, those who dare to deny him before men so perverse and wicked. Just as he promises the former every happiness joined with the highest glory, so to these he threatens every unhappiness and the utmost ignominy. For since salvation is had in that one alone, those whom he rejects by his testimony must necessarily fall from it, so that they are not counted among the sons of God and his brothers. And what more shameful and unhappy disgrace can befall a man than to be regarded, before all the Angels and elect of God, as a deserter of Christ our Saviour, and on that account to be excluded from the fellowship of the heavenly kingdom? For all creatures are hostile in this life to the one whom he disowns, and he is handed over to the devil, who, having mocked him in countless ways, at last drags him off to everlasting torments of misery. This passage is therefore well worthy of much and diligent consideration. For it teaches that they alone are truly Christians who so order their faith and life that Christ at his final coming may acknowledge them as his own; not those who boast of the Christian name, the Word of God and the Sacraments without faith. Let us therefore be zealous for those things in which we have said the true confession of Christ is seen, but let us shun and abhor those by which he is denied.

units.la: Quia vero de his multi leuissime iudicant, quibus etiam indignum & iniquum videtur tam graue supplicium ijs statui, qui Christum vel ex metu vel alicuius luculenti commodi causa abnegant, amplius ille docet, quam grave & immane hoc scelus sit, & simul comminationis sua rationem reddit. Sic autem ait: Et quisquis dicet verbum in Filium hominis, ei remittetur: Ei vero, qui in Spiritum sanctum blasphemauerit, non remittetur. Distinguit inter eos, qui ipsum ex ignorantia reij ciunt & contumeliosus habent, & alteros illos, qui cum Dei Filium & humani generis seruatorem esse norint, nihilominus vel lucri vel periculi alicuius vitandi causa, vel deuota malitia, eum abnegant. Nam in Filium hominis conuitium dicere aut peccare dicuntur, qui nondum eius cognitione illuminati sunt, & proinde eundem Dei Filium esse ignorant, nec quicquam hominE maius in illo agnoscunt. Vt si quis regis filium, absque omni comitatu & pannis lacerus male tectum, erronem dicat ex ignorantia, quod minime facturus erat, si Regis filium esse sciret. Ad hunc modum multi olim Christum negauerunt & eidem conuitiati sunt, ut multi Iudaeorum, qui illum Pilato traditum ad crucis supplicium seditionis clamoribus postulauere, quos Petrus hoc per ignorantiam fecisse testatur, & ideo plurimos ex illis seruatos fuisse legimus. In quo numero ij quoque, qui illum in crucem suffixerunt, censendi sunt, pro quibus ipse Dominus intercedens ait: Pater remitte eis, nesciunt enim quid faciant. Et Paulus: Si cognouissent, nequaquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent. Quin hic ipse Apostolus non modo aduersus Filium hominis multa contumeliose dixit & fecit, sed eiusdem Ecclesiam quoque hostiliter & crudelissime persecutus est. Idem tamen gratiam inuenit apud Deum quia patriae legis zelo excaecatus & ignorans haec omnia fecit. Tales hodie multi sunt, qui vel Papistica superstitionis tenebris adhuc immersi, vel Mahumetica delirijs fascinati fidem Christianam oderunt, & de Euangelij doctrina pessime loquuntur, id autem zelo bono, sed non secundum scientiam faciunt. Et his quidem omnibus in praesenti Christus aeternae salutis spem facit, quando eos remissionem sui peccati confessi posse testatur. Non ergo de illis facile desperare, multo minus autem eos temere damnare, sed potius (quod Christus & Paulus fecerunt) pro illis apud Deum intercede re, & eorum salutem precibus nostris adiuuare debemus. Est autem hoc magnum diuinae benignitatis argumentum, quod cum aeterno supplicio dignus sit, qui in hominem quemcunque vel ex odio, vel ira vel superbo contemptu contumeliosus est, conuitia tamen quae in filium suum unigenitum dicuntur, benigne remittit, & in gratiam recipit eos, a quibus grauissime laesus est. Quod ut in tentationibus conscientiae nos plurimum consolari & in fide confirmare potest: ita officij quoque nos admonet, ne rigidiores simus in eos, qui nos aliquo dicto aut facto laeserunt.
units.tr: Because many people judge these matters very lightly, and think it unworthy and unjust that so grave a punishment should be laid on those who deny Christ, whether from fear or for the sake of some striking advantage, he goes on to show how grave and monstrous this crime is, and at the same time gives the reason for his threat. He speaks thus: "And whoever shall speak a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever shall blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him." He distinguishes between those who reject him and revile him out of ignorance, and those others who, though they know that he is the Son of God and the Saviour of mankind, nevertheless deny him for gain, or to avoid some danger, or from settled malice. For those are said to speak against the Son of man or to sin who have not yet been enlightened by the knowledge of him, and so do not know that he is the Son of God, and recognise nothing greater in him than a man. It is as if someone, seeing a king's son without any retinue and badly clothed in torn rags, called him a vagabond through ignorance, which he would certainly not do if he knew him to be the king's son. In this way many once denied Christ and reviled him, as many of the Jews did, who with seditious shouts demanded that he be handed over by Pilate to the punishment of the cross. Peter testifies that they did this through ignorance, and we read that therefore very many of them were saved. Among this number those also must be counted who fastened him to the cross, and for whom the Lord himself interceded, saying: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And Paul: "Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." Indeed, this same apostle not only said and did many insulting things against the Son of man, but also persecuted his Church with hostility and the utmost cruelty. Yet he found grace with God, because, blinded by zeal for the law of his fathers, he did all these things in ignorance. Many such people are found today, who, either still immersed in the darkness of Papist superstition, or bewitched by the delusions of Mahumet, hate the Christian faith and speak very wickedly of the doctrine of the gospel; and they do this from a good zeal, but not according to knowledge. To all these Christ now offers the hope of eternal salvation, since he testifies that they can obtain forgiveness of their sin when they confess it. We ought therefore not to despair of them easily, much less to condemn them rashly, but rather, as Christ and Paul did, to intercede for them with God and to help their salvation by our prayers. Moreover, this is a great proof of divine kindness: though whoever reviles any man at all out of hatred, anger or proud contempt deserves eternal punishment, yet God graciously remits the insults spoken against his only-begotten Son, and receives into favour those by whom he has been most grievously wronged. This can greatly comfort us in the temptations of conscience and confirm us in faith; and it also admonishes us of our duty not to be too harsh towards those who have injured us by any word or deed.

units.la: Caeterum ijs, qui in ipsum per ignorantiam peccant, eos opponit, qui conuitium dicunt in Spiritum sanctum, & horum scelus nullam veniam aut remissionem habituram testatur. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi Spiritus sanctus Filio praestantior sit, aut hic ab illo diuelli possit: Sed in Spiritu sanctum contumeliosi esse dicuntur, qui per hunc Filij Dei cognitione illuminati, & intra conscientias suas conuicti, hunc & Deum verum & diaboli victorem atque olim promissum humani generis redemptorem esse, nihilominus tamen illum negant, & eius doctrinae contradicunt. Tales olim Pharisaei fuerunt, qui etsi doctrina & miraculis conuincerentur, Christum diuina virtute malos spiritus eijcere, eum tamen coniurationis cum Beelzebub factae accusabant. Talis olim Pharao quoq; fuit, qui etsi sciret Mosen & Aaronem Dei negotiu agere, & saepius Spiritus sancti fugestione supera tus se huic obtemperaturu esse polliceretur, mox tamen adingeniu redijt, & populu Dei tyrannide maioris oppressit. In horum etiam ordine Iulianus Apostata poni debet, qui Christum, quem prius publice professus fuerat, Galilaeum dicere solebat, & nihil no moliebatur, ut eius doctrinam atq; vaticinia falsi argueret. Quibus in praesenti Dominus omnes eos adnumerat, qui ut dignitates, honores, munda amicitiam, opes, vita deniq; retineant, fide in ipsum abnegant, superstitionibus & sacris alienu communicant, & ab eius Ecclesia manifestam faciunt secessionem. Et hos quidem in Spiritu sanctum blasphemos esse ait, quia hac facere non possunt, quin hunc falsi accusent, & qua ex eius illuminatione habuerunt, Christi cognitionem impie conculcent. Quod Paulus observans coram Rege Agrippa fatetur, se Christianos homines ad blasphemandum coegisse: nimirum quod videret cum fidei abnegatione blasphemiam in Spiritum sanctum coniunctam esse. De istis vero Christus pronuntiat, quod remissionem peccati nullam consequantur: quia (ut Paulus ait) non possunt renovari per poenitentiam. Ut enim terra quaedam, etsi pluviis & rore irrigetur, non tamen mollescit, neque fecunda redditur, quod apertum maledictionis veteris & sterilitatis incurabilis indicium est: ita illi quia ut verbum Dei audiant, amice moniantur, animos suos interdum vinci sentiant, adeo tamen non emendantur, ut potius contumaciores fiant, & undique rationes conquirant, quibus sibi ipsis delitias faciant & defectionem a fide tueantur. Tales hodie multos est videre in episcoporum & principum aulis, inter eos item, qui lucri & quaestus causa in ea loca concedunt, ubi veritatem profiteri non audent, & insuper sacris atque cultibus illicitis interesse coguntur. Qui non contenti ab Ecclesia Christi secessionem fecisse, insuper conditionem suam mirifice commendant, & sibi ipsi magnae prudentiae laudem tribuunt, qui rebus suis tam probe consuluerint. Sed quicquid illi dicant, in Spiritum tamen sanctum contumeliosi sunt, cuius dona tam secure aspernantur. Et de his nos pro suo erga homines amore Christus admonet, ut revelatam nobis sui cognitionem & fidei verae lucem magni facere discamus, & in eius confessione constanter perseveremus. Quam primum enim de illa levius sentire incipitur, euanescit paulatim Dei timor & fidei zelus: quo fit ut a parvus initiis ad scelus illud longe atrociissimum progrediamur, quod certam homini pernitiem & aeternam mortem affert.
units.tr: Moreover, he sets against those who sin against him through ignorance those who speak against the Holy Spirit, and he testifies that the guilt of these will have no pardon or forgiveness. This must not be understood as if the Holy Spirit were superior to the Son, or could be separated from him. Rather, those are said to be reviling the Holy Spirit who, having been enlightened by him to the knowledge of the Son of God and convicted in their own consciences, nevertheless deny that he is the true God, the conqueror of the devil and the long-promised redeemer of mankind, and contradict his doctrine. Such once were the Pharisees, who, although they were refuted by doctrine and miracles, accused Christ, who cast out evil spirits by divine power, of having made a compact with Beelzebub. Such also once was Pharaoh, who, though he knew that Moses and Aaron were carrying out God's business, and, overcome by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, often promised that he would obey, soon returned to his old cunning and oppressed the people of God with greater tyranny. Julian the Apostate also ought to be placed in this company, who used to call Christ, whom he had once publicly professed, "the Galilean," and who did nothing else but strive to prove his doctrine and prophecies false. These are the people whom the Lord in the present passage includes: all those who, in order to keep their dignities, honours, worldly friendship, wealth and, in the end, their lives, deny the faith in him, take part in superstitions and unlawful rites, and openly separate themselves from his Church. He says that these are blasphemers against the Holy Spirit, because they cannot do these things without slandering him, and impiously trample underfoot the knowledge of Christ which they have received through his enlightenment. Paul, observing this, confesses before King Agrippa that he compelled Christians to blaspheme, namely because he saw that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit was joined with the denial of faith. Of these people Christ pronounces that they obtain no forgiveness of sin, because (as Paul says) they cannot be renewed through repentance. As a certain land, though watered by rain and dew, does not soften or become fruitful, which is a plain sign of the old curse and incurable barrenness, so these people, though they hear the word of God, are kindly admonished, and sometimes feel their minds overcome, yet are not amended at all; rather they become more obstinate and seek reasons on every side by which they may pamper themselves and defend their defection from the faith. Many such people may be seen today in the courts of bishops and princes, and among those too who go to such places for gain and profit, where they dare not profess the truth and are moreover compelled to attend unlawful rites and worship. Not content to have withdrawn from the Church of Christ, they also commend their own position marvellously and claim for themselves the praise of great prudence, since they have looked after their affairs so well. But whatever they say, they are nonetheless reviling the Holy Spirit, whose gifts they so carelessly spurn. Concerning these people Christ, out of his love for men, admonishes us to learn to hold dear the knowledge of himself revealed to us and the light of true faith, and to persevere constantly in its confession. For as soon as one begins to think lightly of it, the fear of God and zeal for the faith gradually fade away; and so it comes about that, from small beginnings, we advance to that most atrocious crime, which brings certain destruction and eternal death upon man.

units.la: Porro multos a fidei libera atque ingenua confessione abster ret, quod sua infeliciae & infantia sibi conscij metuunt, ne confessionem suam aduersus hostes authoritate & rerum usu atque erudito ne praestantes tueri possint, & ita non sese ipsos modo, sed totam quoque fidei Christianae causam impiorum ludibrio exponant. Quapropter huic etiam obstaculo Dominus remedium praesens adhibet, dicens: Cum autem adduxerint vos ad Synagogas, & ad magistratus ac potestates, ne solliciti sitis, quid pro defensione allaturi, aut quid dicturi sitis, &c. Synagogas nominat, sub quibus nos Concilia quoque intelligere possumus, in quibus fere praesident, penes quos summa est sanctitatis & eruditionis existimatio. Deinde magistratuum meminit, quo nomine iudices intelligit, qui aliorum nomine & mandato iudicia publica exercent. His coniungit potestates, id est, supremos rerum dominos, quales sunt Reges, Imperatores & quotquot horum similes summum & merum imperium in suos obtinent. Tribus ergo verbis comprehendit quicquid in mundo magnificum & terribile habetur: & simul de sua forte fideles omnes admonet, fore nimirum ut capti coram talibus fiant, ut suae fidei ratione reedant: quod Matth. decimo cap. apertius dicit. Iubet autem ne propterea animis concidant, imo solicitos esse vetat quid dicturi aut quibus argumentis causam suam defensuri sint. Ubi nemo putauerit, Christum nos securos rerum esse velle, qui belluino fiupore omnia negligamus, quae nobis accidunt. Nam alibi serpentina prudentia nos hominum insidias cavere iubet. Sed anxiam illam animorum solicitudinem prohibet, quae perplexos & feruiliter timidos reddit, atque liberam veritatis confessionem quam maxime impedire solet. Vult ergo nos animo praesenti & ad omnem euentum parato esse, ne propria infirmitatis aut infeliciae sensu nos superari aut abster reri patiamur. Et praecepto promissionem consolationis dulcissimae plenam subiicit: Spiritus enim sanctus docebit vos eo ipso momento, quae oporteat dicere. Alibi hoc ipsum maiori verborum emphasi explicans ait: Non vos estis qui loquimini, sed Spiritus Patris vestri is est, qui loquitur in vobis. Est autem promissio haec plurimis exemplis confirmata. Nam si Apostolos spectemus, nihil illis imperitius & ab omni disciplinarum studio alienius fuit. At ijdem accepto Spiritu sancto, non apud vulgus modo hominum Euangelij doctrinam perspicue & commode praedicarunt, verumetiam in senatu Hierosolymitano Christi causam tanta constantia & dexteritate egerunt, ut omnibus admirationi essent qui illos homines idiotas & illiteratos antea fuisse sciebant. Quid autem de caeco illo dicemus, quem Ioannes cap. nono describit, qui cum a partu matris oculorum visu destitutus fuisset, & mendicando victum sibi parare cogeretur, tamen ob acceptum a Christo visus beneficium in Sacerdotum & Pharisaeorum confessum vocatus, in confitendo illo talem se praebuit, ut magnifici illi doctrinae & authoritatis sua oppugnatores omnibus ludibrio essent? In ecclesiasticis vero historijs multa huius generis exemrù exempla inueniuntur. Constat enim non semel mulieres, pueros, puellas vix dum nubiles acutissimis philosophorum & tyrannorum quæstionibus sic respondisse, vt illi non haberent quod opponerent, præter faces & gladios atque reliqua impia crudelitatis instrumenta. Et nostro sæculo omnes prope nationes eiusmodi exempla viderunt, & adhuc non sine multorum admiratione vident. Quæ omnia nos de huius promissionis veritate nequaquam dubitare sinut.
units.tr: Moreover, many are held back from a free and open confession of the faith because, being conscious of their own infelicity and inexperience, they fear that they cannot defend their confession against enemies with authority, practical experience and learned skill, and so they expose not only themselves but the whole cause of the Christian faith to the mockery of the ungodly. Therefore the Lord applies a ready remedy to this obstacle too, saying: "But when they bring you before synagogues, and magistrates and powers, do not be anxious about what you are to offer in your defence, or what you are to say," etc. He names synagogues, under which we may also understand councils, in which those generally preside who hold the highest reputation for holiness and learning. Then he mentions magistrates, by which name he means judges who hold public trials in the name and by the commission of others. To these he joins powers, that is, the supreme lords of affairs, such as kings, emperors and all who like them hold supreme and absolute command over their subjects. Thus in three words he comprehends whatever is great and terrible in the world; and at the same time he warns all the faithful of their lot, namely that they will certainly be brought captive before such men to give an account of their faith, which he says more plainly in Matthew chapter ten. He bids them not on that account lose heart; nay, he forbids them to be anxious about what they are to say or with what arguments they are to defend their cause. Let no one suppose that Christ wants us to be careless about affairs, so that in brutish stupidity we neglect whatever happens to us; for elsewhere he bids us guard against men's snares with serpent-like prudence. But he forbids that anxious solicitude of mind which makes men perplexed and slavishly fearful, and which is wont greatly to hinder the free confession of the truth. He therefore wills us to be present in spirit and ready for every outcome, so that we do not allow ourselves to be overcome or deterred by a sense of our own weakness or misfortune. To this precept he adds a promise full of the sweetest consolation: "For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say." Elsewhere, explaining the same thing with greater emphasis, he says: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." This promise is confirmed by very many examples. For if we look at the apostles, nothing was more unlearned than they, nor more foreign to all study of the disciplines. Yet these same men, having received the Holy Spirit, preached the doctrine of the gospel clearly and fittingly not only among the common people, but also before the senate at Jerusalem they pleaded Christ's cause with such constancy and skill that they were a cause of wonder to all who knew that these men had formerly been untaught and illiterate. But what shall we say of that blind man whom John describes in chapter nine? Although from his mother's womb he had been deprived of sight and was forced to beg for his living, yet, because of the sight he had received from Christ, he was summoned before the assembly of priests and Pharisees, and in his confession he showed himself such that those great opponents of his teaching and authority were a laughing-stock to all. In ecclesiastical histories many examples of this kind are found. For it is well established that more than once women, boys and girls scarcely of marriageable age answered the most acute questions of philosophers and tyrants in such a way that their opponents had nothing to set against them except torches, swords and the other impious instruments of cruelty. And in our own age nearly all nations have seen examples of this kind, and still see them, not without the wonder of many. All these things do not allow us to doubt at all the truth of this promise.

units.la: Debet igitur ex his doctrina siue consolatio generalis peti, Deum videlicet nequaquam suos ministros deserere, quorum opera & ministerio ad regnum suum propagandum vti decreuit. Nouit enim qui sinus, & quam multa nobis desint eorum, quæ ad tantam functionem sunt necessaria. Is ergo nos instruit, & eos qui (vt Paulus ait) ne ad cogitandum idonei erant, subito ad omnia idoneos & instructos facere consueuit. Sic Mosem olim ex tardioris linguæ & meticulosio homine facundum & animosum reddidit. Sic Bezaleelem sapientia, intelligentia & scientia donauit, vt ad mirificam & artificiosissimam tabernaculi atque sacrorum vasorum structuram posset sufficere. Similiter septuaginta illos seniores repente spiritus sui donis repleuit, quos Moses in administranda repub. socios esse volebat. Quibus multorum iudicum, qui populi vindices fuerunt, Dauidis, Solomonis, Prophetarum denique omnium exempla adnumerari poterant, in quibus omnibus similis Spiritus sancti virtus & præsens auxilium eluxit. Debent ergo promissionem hanc ad se transferre omnes loci & ordinis homines, vt in suo munere constantes sint & intrepidi. Expectent singuli legitimam vocationem, neque ipsi temere onera subeant, ad quæ illos Deus non destinauit. Vocati autem sedulo officium faciant, neque illis deerit Dominus, si quid per eos confectum volet, & quamuis euentus nostræ voluntati non semper respondeat, probatur tamen illi sanctus conatus noster, & sua semper apud illum parata erunt virtuti præmia. In primis autem hæc in fidei causa meditemur, & constantissimus in Iesu Christi confessione, vt hic quoq; nos pro fratribus & coheredibus suis agnoscat, cum venerit ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos in gloria Patris sui. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It follows, then, that from these things we may draw a general doctrine or consolation: namely, that God will by no means desert his ministers, whose labour and service he has resolved to use for propagating his kingdom. For he knows how things stand with us, and how much we lack of those things which are necessary for so great a task. He therefore instructs us, and he is accustomed to make those who (as Paul says) were not even fit to think, suddenly fit and equipped for everything. Thus once he made Moses, a man of slow tongue and rather timid, eloquent and courageous. Thus he endowed Bezalel with wisdom, understanding and knowledge, so that he could suffice for the wonderful and most skilful construction of the tabernacle and of the sacred vessels. In the same way he suddenly filled those seventy elders with the gifts of his Spirit, whom Moses wished to be his partners in administering the commonwealth. To these could be added the examples of many judges, who were the defenders of the people, of David, of Solomon, and finally of all the Prophets, in all of whom the same power of the Holy Spirit and his present help shone forth. Therefore all men of every rank and office ought to apply this promise to themselves, so that they may be steadfast and fearless in their duty. Let each await a lawful calling, and let them not rashly take upon themselves burdens to which God has not appointed them. But those who are called should diligently perform their office, and the Lord will not fail them if he wishes anything accomplished through them; and although the outcome does not always correspond to our will, yet our earnest endeavour is approved by him, and rewards are always ready for us with him. Above all, let us meditate on these things in the cause of the faith, and be most constant in the confession of Jesus Christ, so that he too may acknowledge us as his brothers and fellow heirs, when he comes to judge the living and the dead in the glory of his Father. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 128.

units.la: Dixit autem ei quidam è turba: Magister, dic fratri meo, vt partiatur mecum hæreditatem. Ipse vero dixit ei: Homo, quis me constituit iudicem aut partitorem super vos? Dixit igitur eis: Videte & cauete ab auaritia. Neque enim cum quispiam abundat, vita ipsi constat ex bonis suis. Dixit autem eis parabolam in hæc verba: Hominis cuiusdam ager vberes proventus tulit. Itaque ratiocinabatur apud se dicens, Quid faciam? nec enim habeo vbi cogam fructus meos. Et dixit: Hoc faciam, destruam horrea mea, & maiora ædificabo, & illic cogam fructus meos & bona mea: & dicam animæ meæ: Anima, habes multa bona reposita in multos annos: requiesce, comede, bibe, oblectare. Dixit autem ei Deus: Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt abs te: quæ vero parasti, cuius erunt? Ita est qui thesaurum congerit sibi, nec est in Deo dives.
units.tr: Then one of the crowd said to him, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." But he said to him, "Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?" And he said to them, "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life does not consist in the abundance of the things which he possesses." And he told them a parable, saying: "The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully. And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns and build greater, and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said to him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God."

units.la: Quoniam Dei Filius Iesus Christus propter nos in mundum venit, et eo vsq; seipsum demisit vt servi formam siue personam suscieperet optimo iure à nobis vicissim requirit, vt et nos eius non pudeat, vtq; ipsum coram quibusuis nostrum Dominum & seruatorem esse libere ac ingenuè profiteamur. Et quia hic multa nos impediunt, rationes nuper validissimas adduxit, quibus fides nostra confirmari poterit, ne vel mortis vel alterius alicuius periculi metu nos à confessione eius abstrerre ripiamur. Cæterum inter fidei obstacula, quibus eius confessio quoque impeditur, nullum vulgarius & efficacius siue nocentius est, quam auaritia & insatiabile opum huius sæculi studium. Vt enim hoc accensi plerunque diuitias per fas nefasque acquirunt: ita qui illas iam acquisierunt ij aut spem & fiduciam in ijs collocando idololatrae fiunt, aut illis ad luxum & fastum abutuntur, quo inebriati diuina & coelestia bona negligunt. Utrinque certe cum propter fidem & religionem opes in periculum veniunt, illam potius abnegare, quam has amittere volunt. Commodissime ergo Christus nouam orationem instituit, qua credentes diligenter & copiose admonet, ut in Dei solius providentiam recumbant, & forte sua contenti coelestia quaerant, ne ab hac nocentissima peste circumuenti salutis aeternae iacturam faciant.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, Jesus Christ, came into the world for our sake, and humbled himself so far as to take upon him the form or person of a servant, he may most justly require in return that we should not be ashamed of him, but that we should freely and openly profess him to be our Lord and Saviour before anyone whatsoever. And because many things hinder us here, he has lately brought forward most powerful reasons by which our faith can be strengthened, so that we may not be turned aside from confessing him through fear of death or of any other danger. Moreover, among the obstacles to faith by which its confession is also hindered, none is more common, or more effective or harmful, than covetousness and the insatiable pursuit of the riches of this world. For those who are fired by this often acquire wealth by fair means or foul; and those who have already acquired it, either become idolaters by placing their hope and trust in it, or abuse it for luxury and pride, and, drunk with these, neglect the divine and heavenly goods. On either side, certainly, when wealth is put in danger on account of faith and religion, they prefer to deny the former rather than lose the latter. Christ therefore most aptly set forth a new discourse, by which he diligently and fully admonishes believers to rely on the providence of God alone, and, content with what they have, to seek heavenly things, so that, ensnared by this most harmful plague, they do not suffer the loss of eternal salvation.

units.la: Occasionem de his differendi Christo praebuit auarus quidam, qui de grauissimis rebus dicente interburbat, importuno clamore petens, ut fratrem, a quo se fraudatum aut omnino deiectum queri tur, ad iustam patrimonij diuisionem cogat. Quod etsi importune simul & imprudenter faciat, alij tamen errores atque vitia grauiora concurrunt. Primo enim non leuiter delinquit in eo, quod solus opibus & a maioribus relicto patrimonio intentus, a feria & attenta verbi Dei auscultatione sine meditatione mentem suam auocari sinit. Est ergo fucatus Christi discipulus, & ex eorum audito rum numero, qui semel verbi a curis & solicitudine huius seculi suffocari patiuntur, ne dignum fructum ferat. Accedit huic vitio alter error, quod Christum terrenum principem & rerum temporalium iudicem fingit, cuius authoritate & iussu frater cogi possit & debeat. Itaque in illo non regni coelorum thesauros, sed huius seculi bona & eorundem tutam atque tranquillam possessionem quaesiuit. Quem errorem inter Iudaeos vulgarem omnino fuisse alibi diximus, nimirum quod Prophetarum oracula de regno Messiae secundum literam & carnis sensum acciperent, neglectis interea promissionibus bonorum coelestium, quae ille nobis offert. Est autem auarus hic & importunus Christi auditor typus omnium eorum, qui sub Christianae fidei atque religionis praetextu non aliud quam quae carnis sunt quaerunt. Hi etsi aliquando, vel etiam frequenter admodum, coetibus sacris intersint, & conciones ex verbo Dei audiant, non mouentur tamen iis, quae de salute aeterna & huius at quirenda ratione dicuntur. Nam aut animis suis peregrinantur, ut dictis minime aures praebeant, aut quaecunque audiunt, ad suorum affectuum calculum reuocant, quibus nisi satisfiat, omnia scurriliter & cum risu exibilant. Fuerunt tales multi Prophetarum temporibus, quos Michaeas reprehendens ait: Si vir esset ventum sequens & mendacium concinnans, & stillarem, id est, propheta rem de vino & sicera, tunc Propheta esset pro hoc populo. Hodie autem passim audiuntur, qui non minus impie quam impudenter a verbi administris postulare audent, ut conciones habeant blandas, utque ad belluinum potandi certamen, ad choreas & saltationes lasciuas, ad vsurariorum fraudes, ad bella mercenaria, & quae alia sunt huius generis connivcant. Plerique vero, ut noster hic sub Euangelij praetextu opes quaerunt, neque alio instituto illud amplectuntur, quam ut ex coenobiorum & Ecclesiarum bonis ditescant. Atqui omnes isti, quamuis interdum in fidei professione toti feruere videantur, mox tamen deficiunt, quando ea sibi negari aut eripi vident, quae ipsis unice cordi sunt. Quare hic antidoto praesenti & efficaci opus est, quod hac occasione oblata Christus adhibet.
units.tr: Christ was given the occasion for these matters by a certain greedy man, who, while he was speaking of most serious things, interrupted him with an importunate shout, demanding that he compel his brother, by whom he complains he has been cheated or altogether disinherited, to make a just division of the patrimony. Although he does this both importunately and imprudently, other and graver errors and vices also come together in him. For, first, he sins not lightly in that, being intent solely on wealth and on the patrimony left by his ancestors, he allows his mind to be distracted from the attentive hearing of the Word of God, without meditation. He is therefore a pretended disciple of Christ, and belongs to the number of those hearers who allow the Word to be choked by the cares and anxieties of this age, so that it does not bear worthy fruit. To this vice is added another error: he imagines Christ to be an earthly prince and judge of temporal things, by whose authority and command his brother can and must be compelled. Thus he sought in him not the treasures of the kingdom of heaven, but the goods of this age and their safe and tranquil possession. We have said elsewhere that this error was altogether common among the Jews, namely that they took the oracles of the Prophets about the kingdom of the Messiah according to the letter and the sense of the flesh, meanwhile neglecting the promises of heavenly goods which he offers us. Now this greedy and importunate hearer of Christ is a type of all those who, under the pretext of the Christian faith and religion, seek nothing but what belongs to the flesh. Although these sometimes, or even quite often, attend sacred assemblies and hear sermons from the Word of God, they are not moved by what is said about eternal salvation and the way to seek it. For either their minds wander elsewhere, so that they give no ear to what is said, or whatever they hear they bring back to the reckoning of their own passions, and if these are not satisfied, they mock and hiss everything with scurrility and laughter. There were many such in the times of the Prophets, of whom Micah, rebuking them, says: "If a man walking in the wind and fabricating lies should say, I will preach to you of wine and strong drink, he would be the prophet for this people." Today too, on every side, there are those who dare to ask, no less impiously than shamelessly, that the ministers of the Word should give flattering sermons, and should connive at drunken drinking contests, at wanton dances and revels, at the frauds of usurers, at mercenary wars, and at other things of this kind. Most, however, like this man, who seeks wealth under the pretext of the Gospel, embrace it with no other purpose than to grow rich from the goods of monasteries and churches. Yet all these people, although at times they seem to glow entirely in the profession of faith, soon fail when they see those things denied or snatched from them which are dearest to their hearts. Therefore a present and effective remedy is needed here, which Christ applies on this occasion offered to him.

units.la: Prius tamen auari iflius importunam postulationem graui responsione abs se reijcit, dicens: Heus tu, quis me vobis iudicem aut partitorem constituit? Atqui bonum opus est fratres ob haereditatem aut alias causas inter se discordes reconciliare, & ut id faciamus charitatis lex monet. Iustum quoque & aequum est, ne quem fraudari patiamur, sed pro virili curemus, ut vnicuique debitur quod suum est. Et in Lege Deus multa statuit de haereditatibus, ne ha ad alienos transferantur. Denique quanti patrimonia sua pij semper fecerint, vel vnius Nabothi exemplum docere potest, qui a patribus suis sibi relictam vineam Regi quoque negandum putauit. Non vult tamen huic liti se interponere Christus, neque partiunda haereditatis inter hos fratres munus subire. Quam vero ob causam? Num quod ipsi improbetur, quod alibi lex iubet? Aut quod Christianum hominem non decere ostendat, ut vel iudicem agat, vel haereditates diuidat, aut quibuscunque negotijs ciuilibus se immisceat? Quem sensum Anabaptistae ex eius facto siue exemplo eliciere conantur. At nihil horum illi in mentem venit, sed longe alias huius dicti rationes habuit. Primo enim cauere voluit, ne falsam Iudaorum de Regno Messiae opinionem confirmaret, & simul aduersarijs occasionem calumniandi praeberet, qui omnia eius attentissime obseruabant. Nam ut primum huic liti suam authoritatem interposuisset, mox multi ex rudioribus simile quid, vel etiam vel etiam maiora ab eo postulassent, improbi vero clamauissent, illum iura publica turbare, priuata iudicia instituere, & intolerabilem atq; seditionis suspectam introducere Reipublicae mutationem. Deinde inter docendi munus vel Ecclesiae ministerium, cui destinatus erat, & magistratus officium distinguere voluit, ne vel Apostolis vel horum successoribus ansam daret ea tractandi, quae ab ipsorum functione aliena sunt. Postremo eos arguit, qui Euangelij praetextu, & ministrorum authoritate vel fauore abutuntur, vt res suas agant & commodo priuato consulant. Quod genus hominum omnibus seculis frequentissimum fuit, & hodie passim cernitur. Quam multos enim est inuenire, qui cum Euangelij doctrinam improbe contemnant, & eius ministros odio prosequantur, si ta men ipsis cum aliquibus controuersia intercedit, aut aliquid comodi ab ijs sperare possunt, quos Euangelicae doctrinae studiosos & huius administrorum amicos esse norunt, illico ipsi quoq; eiusdem doctrinae studiū simulant, ministros accedunt, officia quaeuis pollicentur, domū suam inuitant, & nihil non faciūt quod ab horū obseruantissimo sperari poterat. At tūc magna cautione opus est ministris, ne improbis illis hypocritis facile morem gerant, & sua authoritate eos in suis cupiditatibus & pessimis studijs confirment. Nam nisi hic admodum circumspecte agant, fraudi erit pijs ipsorum intercessio, & multis calumniandi occasio datur, quasi illi quoque mundi huius amicitiam plures faciant quàm verbum Dei, quod ab ijs praedicatur. Hac (inquam) causa Christum mouerunt, vt responso hoc duriori auari huius petitionem abs se reiecerit.
units.tr: Yet first he rejects this greedy man's importunate request with a severe answer, saying: "Hey you, who made me a judge or divider over you?" And yet it is a good work, brothers, to reconcile those who are at odds with one another over an inheritance or other causes, and the law of charity urges us to do so. It is also just and fair that we not allow anyone to be defrauded, but that we take care, as far as we can, that each receives what is his own. And in the Law God laid down many things about inheritances, so that they should not pass to strangers. Finally, how much the pious have always valued their patrimonies, the example of Naboth alone can teach, who thought he must refuse even the king the vineyard left to him by his fathers. Yet Christ does not wish to interpose himself in this lawsuit, nor to undertake the office of dividing the inheritance between these brothers. For what reason, then? Is it because this is disapproved of, or because the law commands it elsewhere? Or does it show that it is not fitting for a Christian man to act as judge, or to divide inheritances, or to mix himself in any civil affairs? The Anabaptists try to draw this meaning from his deed or example. But none of these things came into his mind, and he had quite different reasons for this saying. First, he wished to take care not to confirm the false opinion of the Jews about the kingdom of the Messiah, and at the same time not to give his adversaries an occasion for slander, since they were observing his every action most attentively. For as soon as he had interposed his authority in this lawsuit, many of the cruder sort would immediately have demanded something similar from him, or even greater things from him, and the wicked would have cried out that he was disturbing public law, setting up private courts, and introducing an intolerable change of government, suspect of sedition. Next, he wished to distinguish between the office of teaching or the ministry of the Church, to which he was appointed, and the office of the magistrate, so that he would not give the Apostles or their successors an occasion for handling matters foreign to their function. Lastly, he rebukes those who, under the pretext of the Gospel and by abusing the authority or favour of ministers, pursue their own affairs and look to private advantage. This kind of man has been most frequent in all ages, and is seen everywhere today. For how many are there who, while they wickedly despise the doctrine of the Gospel and hate its ministers, yet, if some dispute arises between them and certain people, or if they can hope for some advantage from those whom they know to be zealous for the Gospel doctrine and friends of its ministers, straightway pretend zeal for that same doctrine themselves, approach the ministers, promise every service, invite them to their homes, and do nothing that could be hoped from the most devoted man. But then great caution is needed on the part of ministers, lest they readily humour those wicked hypocrites and by their authority confirm them in their desires and wicked pursuits. For unless they act very circumspectly here, their pious intercession will be to their discredit, and an occasion for slander is given to many, as if they too make more of the friendship of this world than of the Word of God which they preach. For this reason (I say) Christ was moved to reject the request of this greedy man with such a harsh answer.

units.la: Vehementer ergo & turpiter nimis falluntur Anabaptistae, qui iudicum ordinem & magistratum omnem huius exempli authoritate aboleri clamant. Nec enim semper quaecunque Christus fecit in generale exemplum trahi & ad omnes homines transferri debent. Sunt enim nonnulla, quae ad eius modo officium spectant, cui illum Pater caelestis destinauerat, quae si quilibet abfq; certa Dei vocatione imitari velit, non sine scelere id faciet. Eius generis est, quòd puer desertus parentibus Hierosolymae mansit, & in templo docuit, neq; ei curae fuit, quòd se ab illis magna cum solicitudine & acerbo animi dolore interea quaeri sciret. Quod vt faceret, Patris mandatum iubeat. At si idem alij pueri tentent, impietatis in parentes poenas dabunt. Ita in praesenti neq; iudicem agere neq; hereditatem inter fratres partiri voluit, non quia hoc per se malum sit, aut ab hominis Christiani officio alienum, sed quòd non ad ipsum ista pertinebant, qui vt Patris voluntatem nobis manifestaret, & nos sui corporis sacrificio à peccatis ac morte redimeret, regnum deniq; Dei spirituale inter homines instauraret, in mundum venerat. Paralogizant ergo Anabaptistae, perinde ac si quis disceret: Christus non exercuit artem sutoriam, neque agros coluit, neque domum administrauit: ergo ista Christianos minimè decent.
units.tr: Therefore the Anabaptists are greatly and shamefully mistaken when they cry out that by this example of Christ all judges and every magistracy are to be abolished. For not everything Christ did is to be drawn into a general example and transferred to all people. Some things pertain only to the office to which the heavenly Father had appointed him, and if anyone wished to imitate these without a clear calling from God, he would not do so without sin. Of this kind is the boy who, left behind by his parents, stayed in Jerusalem and taught in the temple, and was not concerned that his parents were meanwhile seeking him with great anxiety and bitter grief. He could do this because his Father commanded it. But if other boys were to attempt the same, they would pay the penalty for impiety towards their parents. So too, at present, he did not want to act as a judge or divide an inheritance between brothers, not because this is evil in itself or foreign to the duty of a Christian man, but because these things did not pertain to him, who had come into the world to reveal the Father's will to us, to redeem us from sin and death by the sacrifice of his body, and finally to establish the spiritual kingdom of God among men. The Anabaptists therefore reason falsely, just as if someone were to conclude: Christ did not practise the trade of a cobbler, nor cultivate fields, nor manage a household; therefore these things do not befit Christians.

units.la: Debet autem in primis hoc obseruari, quòd alienam functionem ille subire noluit. Ex eo enim generalis doctrina rectissimè petitur, vt singuli se intra suas metas contineant, neq; res aggrediantur à sua vocatione alienas, vnde alij occasione calumniandi arripere possint. Quod si fanatici illi obseruarent, minus ab illis turbarentur Ecclesiae. Nec enim familias suas desererent, neq; docendi munus priuata temeritate inuaderent, neque magistratus abolere & nouam mundi faciem introducere conarentur. Quae omnia cùm seditiosè nimis sub Euangelij praetextu faciant, hoc multis suspectum & exosum reddunt, apertis verò eiusdem hostibus amplissimam maledicendi materiam praebent. In primis autem hoc Christi exemplo Pontifices & Episcopi confutantur, qui cùm Christi in terris vicarij & Apostolorum successores haberi velint, negotijs tamen ab illorū functione alienissimis sese immiscent. Nec enim hereditates solum diuidūt inter fratres, sed alienas hereditates intercipiunt, & patrimonium quoddam Petri finxerunt, cuius nomine magnam Italiae partem Graecis Imperatoribus eripuerunt: neque eo contenti, in alia quoq; regna sibi ius & imperium vendicant, adeoq; orbis imperium pro sua libidine hinc inde transferunt. Quorum vestigia alij etiam Episcopi secuti, amplissimas ditiones, comitatus & ducatus cum vrbibus florentissimis ad se rapuerunt, in quibus more principū huius seculi dominantur. Sunt haec aliena prorsus ab Ecclesiastica functione, & non exemplo solum verumetiā disertis Christi verbis arguuntur, qui Apostolis dixit: Principes gentium imperitant, vos autem non sic, &c.
units.tr: But this must be observed above all: he was unwilling to take on another's function. From this a general doctrine is rightly drawn, that each person should keep within his own limits and not undertake affairs foreign to his calling, lest others seize the chance to slander. If those fanatics observed this, the Churches would be less troubled by them. For they would not desert their families, nor presume with private rashness to assume the office of teaching, nor attempt to abolish the magistrates and introduce a new face of the world. Since they do all these things too seditiously under the pretext of the gospel, they make it suspect and odious to many, while to the open enemies of the gospel they provide a very ample matter for slander. Above all, the Popes and bishops are refuted by this example of Christ. Although they wish to be regarded as Christ's vicars on earth and successors of the Apostles, they nevertheless meddle in affairs most alien to that office. For they not only divide inheritances between brothers, but also seize the inheritances of others, and they have invented a certain patrimony of Peter, in whose name they tore a large part of Italy from the Greek emperors. Not content with this, they also claim right and rule over other kingdoms, and so they transfer the rule of the world hither and thither at their own pleasure. Following their footsteps, other bishops too have seized for themselves very ample lordships, counties and duchies with the most flourishing cities, over which they rule in the manner of the princes of this age. These things are wholly alien to the ecclesiastical function, and they are condemned not only by example but also by the plain words of Christ, who said to the Apostles: The kings of the Gentiles rule over them, but you shall not be so, etc.

units.la: Obseruabis praeterea, hunc tam duriter à Christo reijci, qui ipsius authoritate & praetextu ad hereditatem, quae ad ipsum iure pertinebat, obtinendam abuti voluit, neglecto Dei verbo, quod ma
units.tr: You will also observe that he who wished to misuse Christ's authority and pretext to obtain an inheritance that rightly belonged to him is so harshly rejected by Christ, neglecting the word of God, which offered him greater

units.la: Christus non damnat actiones ciuiles.
units.tr: Christ does not condemn civil actions.

units.la: Nemo alienam functionem inuadat.
units.tr: Let no one usurp another's function.

units.la: Contra raptores. iora & aeterna bona ipsi offerebat. Quid ergo fiet iniquis & temerarijs raptoribus, qui fideiChristiana & Euangelij nomine palliati aliena inuadunt? Est hoc per se nefas, & ita olim per Prophetas omnibus illis vae illud horrendū denuntiauit, qui adaugent non sua, qui praedantur, qui domos domi bus & agros agris coiungunt. At vehementer augetur huius peccati atrocitas siue pondus, si Christum & Euangelium eius cupiditati nefariae praetexamus. Quis enim vir bonus ferat aliquem sui nominis aut etiam sigilli sui praetextu decipi vel fraudari? Et nos Christum, qui ipsissima iustitia est, hoc passurum putabimus, ut quis eius nomine, Euangelio item & Sacramentis Ecclesiae suae adspo liandos homines abutatur? Quod utinam prae aliis obseruarent, qui dum Euangelicae doctrinae pa- troni & propugnatores videri volunt, Iudas agunt, & quae olim pijssimi principes & maiores no- stri Ecclesijs cotulerunt, insatiabili rapacitate sibi vendicant. Sentient illi aliquando, quid sit cum Christo ludere, & eius verbo abuti.
units.tr: Against plunderers. greater and eternal goods were offered to him. What then will become of the wicked and rash plunderers who, cloaked under the name of the Christian faith and of the gospel, seize what belongs to others? This is wicked in itself, and so of old the Prophets pronounced that dreadful woe upon all those who add house to house and join field to field, who plunder. But the atrocity or weight of this sin is greatly increased if we use Christ and the gospel as a cover for such wicked greed. For what good man would bear being deceived or defrauded under the pretext of his own name or even his own seal? And shall we think that Christ, who is justice itself, will suffer men to be despoiled in his name, and by the abuse of his gospel and the sacraments of his Church? Would that they observed this above others, those who, while they wish to appear as patrons and defenders of the evangelical doctrine, play the Judas, and with insatiable rapacity claim for themselves what the most pious princes and our ancestors once bestowed upon the Churches. Some day they will feel what it means to trifle with Christ and to abuse his word.

units.la: Sed ad eius verba redeamus, qui post quā importunum iustum reiecit, nunc in generalem doctri- nam de auaritia digreditur, & (ut diximus) omnium nocentissimae cupiditati remedium adhibet. Propositio totius tractationis est: Videte & cauete ab auaritia. Lucas πλεονεξίας vocabulum po- suit, quod plus quiddam quam auaritia denotat. Nam immodica plura indies habendi cupiditatē significat, quae cum aliorum detrimento coniuncta est, quibus sua vel eripiuntur, vel iniquē detinen tur, & opponitur τῇ ἀντιπρὸσ εἰα, quae facit, ut homo sua sorte contentus nihil praeterea velit aut cu- piat, quam Paulus maximum quaestum esse dicit, si cum pietate vera coniungatur. Graui autē ad- monitione discipulos & totum populum compellat. Videte (inquit) & cauete. Cura igitur & magno studio hic opus esse innuit, ut cupiditatem hanc euitare & eius laqueos effugere possimus. Nec sine causa sic loquitur Dominus. Est enim vitium illud nobis innatum, & a pueris nobiscum succrescit atq; augetur. Docent hoc mores infantium atq; puerorum, qui aequalibus praestare volunt, & si quid inter eos diuidi oporteat, singuli ad portionem eam aspirant, quam reliquis maiorem aut meliorem esse arbitrantur. Neq; id mirum videri potest, cum primos parentes, quibus in summa rerum abun dantia & felicitate constitutus nihil omnino deerat, ad altiora animum adiecisse sciamus, quae illa infelicissimae ruinae causa fuit. Ex illis ergo hoc malum in omnem posteritatem propagatum est, ut nemo sua sorte contentus viuat, & ij quoq; plura appetant, qui ne ijs quidē omnibus possunt vti, quae iam possident. Cuius rei exempla in opulentissimis quibusq; imò in Regibus potentissimis quo- tidie videmus, qui cum terras suas ne omnes quidem lustrare, nedum regere possint, alienis tamen re- gnis subinde inhiant, ut vix orbis totus cupiditati ipsorum sufficiat. Recte ergo auari hydropicis conferuntur, de quibus poeta dixit: Quo plus sunt potae, plus sitiuntur aquae.
units.tr: But let us return to his words. Having rejected the importunate man's request, he now digresses into a general doctrine about covetousness, and, as we said, applies a remedy to the most harmful of all desires. The theme of the whole discourse is: Take heed and beware of covetousness. Luke has used the word πλεονεξία [pleonexia], which signifies something more than avarice. For it denotes an immoderate desire to have more and more each day, which is joined with the loss of others, whose goods are either snatched away or unjustly withheld. It is opposed to αὐτάρκεια [autarkeia], self-sufficiency, which makes a man content with his lot, wanting or desiring nothing beyond it. Paul calls this the greatest gain, if it is joined with true godliness. He addresses the disciples and the whole people with a grave warning: Take heed, he says, and beware. He thus indicates that care and great diligence are needed here, so that we may avoid this desire and escape its snares. Nor without reason does the Lord speak thus. For this vice is innate in us, and grows up and is increased with us from childhood. The behaviour of infants and boys teaches this, who want to excel their peers, and if anything has to be divided among them, each aspires to the portion which he thinks is larger or better than those of the others. Nor can this seem surprising, since we know that our first parents, who were established in the greatest abundance and happiness, lacking nothing at all, directed their minds to higher things, and this was the cause of their most unhappy fall. From them, therefore, this evil has been propagated to all posterity, so that no one lives content with his lot, and those who cannot even use all the things they already possess still crave more. We see examples of this every day among the most wealthy, and indeed among the most powerful kings, who, though they cannot survey, let alone rule, all their own lands, nevertheless keep longing for the realms of others, so that the whole world can scarcely satisfy their desire. Rightly, then, are covetous men compared to dropsical patients, of whom the poet said: The more they drink, the more they thirst for water.

units.la: Porrò admonitionem siue praeceptum suum Christus ratione confirmat, quae plurimum mouere potest, si diligentius consideretur. Neque enim (inquit) cum quispiam abundat, vita ipsi constat ex bonis suis. Vitae nomine non solum eam, quae proprie vita dicitur, sed simul omnem hominis in- columitatem & felicitatem, adhaec omnia vitae praesidia intelligit. Opponit autem hanc sententiam communi hominum opinioni, qui vitae beatitudinem in opum abundantia consistere putant, qui pro prius auaritiae & insatiabilis illius cupiditatis fons est. Itaque sensus est, Inane & superuacaneū esse ditescendi studium, & frustra seipsos circa hoc homines fatigare, cum neque ipsa vita, neque bo- nus felicitas in diuitijs consistat. Sunt enim haec externa modo vitae adminicula, quae per se non pro- sunt, nisi Dei benedictione nobis vtilia & salutaria fiant. Potest hoc facile probari ijs, qui vitae huius conditionem & diuitiarum vsum propius considerant. Primo enim vita nostra diuitijs super fluus minimē opus habet, cum natura paucis contenta sit, & ij quoq; non incommode viuant, quibus res domestica angustior contigit. Et si verum fateri libeat, commodius & tranquillius viuunt, qui suo labore victum necessarium sibi in diem parant, quam qui in opū abundantia vel luxu diffluunt, & sibijpsis morbos accersunt, vel curus & solicitudine assidua excruciantur. Deinde ex opibus nihil ad nos redit praeter vsum necessarium. Vt enim nudi nascimur, nec quicquā in mundum inferimus, ita vbi vitae nostrae cursum emensi fuerimus, hinc migrantes animae corpus sepulturae relinquunt, nihil autem ex omnibus bonis huius seculi nobiscum efferimus. Quare etsi infinita aureorum millia, im- mensa agrorum latifundia, domos innumeras & multa alia possideas, nihil inde ad te redit praeter victum & amictum, sub quo hospitij quoq; vsus continetur. Praeterea neque ad vitae cursum prolongandum aliquid seruiunt opes immodicæ. Sunt enim (vt Christus ait) horæ diei duodecim, & vbi no bis præfinita mortis hora aduenerit, omnino hinc migrandum est, neque vlla vitæ redemptio potest fieri. Quod Dauid his verbis prolixè docet: Ex ijs qui nituntur opulentia sua, & in multitudine di uitiarum suarum gloriantur, nemo fratrem suum vlla ratione redimere potest, neque Deo pretium redemptionis suæ persoluere. Nimij siquidem pretij est redimi à morte animas eorū vt æuo viuant perpetuo, & vitam in sempiternum proferant sepulchrum nunquam visuri. Etenim videre est, vt sapientes perinde moriantur ac stulti, & stupidi intereant, atq; opes suas alijs relinquant, &c. Sunt hæc tam manifesta, vt ampliori demonstratione nequaquam opus habeant. Quod si vero ad vitam æternam respiciamus, quæ sola vitæ nomine digna est, ad hanc consequendam adeò nihil conferunt diuitiæ, vt potius nos remorentur, quò minus ad eam peruenire possimus. Nam plerunq; malus & iniquus artibus acquiritur, nec temere veteri prouerbio dives aut iniquus aut iniqui hæres esse dicitur. Vbi autem iam acquisitæ & vehementer auctæ sunt, tunc vel luxus & fastus materiam præbent, & multorum scelerum causa sunt, vel idololatras reddunt eos, qui quam in Deo collocare debebant, fiduciam in illis repositam habent. Et hi quoque dum illis addicti sunt, infinitis curis & prophanis cogitationibus distrahuntur, vt de regno Dei & vita æterna vix vnquam serio cogitare possint. At si casus aliquis improuisus opes eripiat, Deum immortalem, quid non dicunt & faciunt, qui vitam suam & felicitatem in harum abundantia consistere putant? Illos certè omnis iactura impatien tissimos esse, & animi impotentiam modo diris conuitijs in homines, modò blasphemijs in Deum atrocissimis, modò vocibus desperationis plenis testari videbis. Quis ergo non fateatur, verissimè à Christo dictum esse, vitam homini non ex opibus immodicis constare? Cæterum quod breui sententia dixerat, nunc parabola eleganti illustrat, qua res omnis ceu in spe culo spectanda proponitur. Estq; illa eo illustrior & ad persuadendum efficacior, quia etsi fictam narrationem continere videatur, nihil tamen habet, quàm quod indies fieri consueuit. Proderit autem singulas partes ex ordine videre, vt plus inde ad nos vtilitatis redeat. Primum homo quidam dives proponitur, ex eorū ordine qui opes iustas possident. Nec enim de publicano aliquo, aut vsurario, aut sanguinario militæ prœda & hostiū spoliis ditato loquitur, sed de patrefamilias, qui agros coluit, & ex Dei benedictione prouentus vberrimos collegit. At quæ ita obtingunt opes, cum nullius iniuria aut damno obtingunt. Veruntamen in illis ipse peccauit, & Dei sententia damnatur, vt postea audiemus. Vbi admonemur, quàm periculosa sit opum administratio siue possessio. Si enim circa eas, quas nobis diuina benedictio largitur, salutis iactura fieri potest, quid de illis dicemus, qui iniquissimis modis & cum aliorum detrimento diuitias congerunt, & in ipso li mine (quod dicitur) offendunt? Debebant hoc diligenter obseruare fæneratores & vsurarij, qui mo nopolijs, monetæ mutationibus insidiosis, mercium adulteratione, & alijs infinitis artibus in iusti tia & charitatis leges aperte peccant. Placent illi sibi ipsis mirifice, & quæstus dulcedine illecti vix vnquam cogitant, se Dei oculos offendere. Sed passim eorum artes damnantur, & has in lege Dominus venenato serpentis morsui confert, eo quod præsens exitiū afferunt omnibus, quibus cum ipsis res est. Nec minori diligentia illis etiā hac meditanda erant, qui mercenarios & quosfus alios, quorum labore & opera vtuntur, defraudant, quorum peccatū ad Deum clamat, & quibus Iacobus Apostolus horribilem Dei maledictionem denuntiat. Item ij quoque, qui ex militia mercenaria, rapinis & sanguinis effusione ditescunt, quorum maximus numerus est hodie, & qui sibi præcipuam fortitudinis laudem vendicant, atq; patriæ communis propugnatores & defensores videri volunt. Sed in omnibus istorum domibus ignis ardet (vt Micheas ait) thesauri nimirum impij & iniusti, quibus in illos Dei ira accenditur. Discant ergo singuli ab omni iniquitate sibi cauere, & cum opes iustæ obtinguunt, has quoque propter nostræ naturæ vitiositatem spinarum instar esse meminerint, & vt ijs recte vtantur, cogitent. Videamus autem vt iste dives peccarit. Ratiocinabatur apud se dicens: Quid faciam? Nec enim habeo vbi cogam fructus meos. Et dixit: Hoc faciam: destruam horrea mea, & maiora ædificabo, & illuc cogam fructus meos, & bona mea, & dicam animæ meæ: Anima, habes multa bona, repositæ in annos multos: requiesce, comede, bibe, obleStare. Hæc verbis ingenij, mores, consilia & studia ditium huius seculi ceu in tabula Christus depingit. Primo non recte iudicat de vbere illo suarum terrarum proventu. Nam fructus hoc se suos dicit, in quo bifariam peccat. Suo enim labore & industria eos comparatos arbitratur, nec agnoscit Dei beneficium, ex cuius benedictione omnia proveniunt. Etenim ut Paulus ait, nihil est qui plantat, nec qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat, Deus. Deinde suos dicendo, sibi soli illorum usum vendicat, neque aliquam vel Dei vel hominum mentionem facit. Est hic fons, omnis abusus, quo circa divitias peccatur. Qui enim ita sentiunt, ij vel recondunt illas, ut nec sibi ipsis neque aliis sint usui: vel carnis cupiditatibus abrepti ex illis superbiunt, voluptuantur, luxuriantur, nec aliquam gloriae Dei aut proximorum egentium rationem habent. Admonemur itaque hoc loco, ut de opum largitore & earundem usu legitimo semper cogitemus. Dantur illae a Deo. Nam nisi hic sua benedictione terram fæcundet, & ipse domum ædificet, frustra nos mane surgimus (ut Dauid inquit) & circa rem domesticam fatigamur. Ut enim nihil in mundum inferimus, ita ne herbulam quidem aut culmum unum creare possumus. Dantur autem a Deo divitiæ ut œconomis & dispensatoribus, qui aliorum inopiam respicere, & eam sua abundantia sublevare debent, ut infra capite decimo sexto Christus apertius docebit. Ista qui ignorant aut negligunt, ij bonis suis nunquam recte utentur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ confirms his admonition or precept with a reason that can move us greatly if it is considered more carefully. For (he says) when someone abounds, his life does not consist of his goods. By "life" he understands not only that which is properly called life, but at the same time all of a person's safety and happiness, and in addition all the means of living. He sets this saying against the common opinion of men, who think that the blessedness of life consists in an abundance of wealth; this opinion is the source of avarice and that insatiable desire. The sense, therefore, is that the eagerness to grow rich is empty and superfluous, and that men wear themselves out in vain over it, since neither life itself nor true happiness consists in riches. For these things are only external aids to living, which of themselves do not profit us, but become useful and salutary to us only through God's blessing. This can easily be proved to those who consider more closely the condition of this life and the use of riches. First, our life has no great need of superfluous wealth, since nature is content with little, and those also live not uncomfortably whose domestic circumstances are rather narrow. And, to tell the truth, those live more comfortably and peacefully who by their own labour provide for their necessary sustenance day by day, than those who overflow in abundance or luxury of goods and bring diseases upon themselves, or are tormented by cares and constant anxiety. Next, nothing from our riches returns with us beyond what is necessary use. For just as we are born naked and bring nothing into the world, so when we have run the course of our life, the soul departs hence and leaves the body to burial, and we carry nothing out of all the goods of this age with us. Therefore, although you possess infinite thousands of gold coins, immense estates of lands, countless houses and many other things, nothing from them returns to you except food and clothing, under which the use of lodging is also included. Moreover, excessive riches do not help at all in prolonging the course of life. For (as Christ says) the hours of the day are twelve, and when the hour of death appointed for us has arrived, we must depart hence altogether, and no ransom of life can be made. David teaches this at length in these words: "None of those who trust in their wealth and boast in the multitude of their riches can in any way redeem his brother, nor pay to God the price of his redemption. For the redemption of their souls from death is a costly price, that they should live forever and never see the grave." For indeed one sees that the wise die just as the foolish do, and the stupid perish, and leave their riches to others, etc. These things are so plain that they need no lengthier demonstration. But if we look to eternal life, which alone is worthy of the name of life, riches contribute so little to obtaining it that they rather hold us back from being able to attain it. For wealth is usually acquired by wicked and unjust arts, and it is not without reason that the old proverb says the rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. And when wealth has been acquired and greatly increased, then it either provides matter for luxury and pride and becomes the cause of many sins, or it makes idolaters of those who have placed in riches the trust that they ought to have placed in God. And these too, while they are devoted to riches, are distracted by endless cares and profane thoughts, so that they can hardly ever think seriously about the kingdom of God and eternal life. But if some unforeseen mishap snatches away their wealth, good God, what do they not say and do, who think that their life and happiness consist in the abundance of these things? You will see them altogether impatient of any loss, and testifying their lack of self-control now by dreadful insults against men, now by most atrocious blasphemies against God, now by words full of despair. Who, then, would not confess that it was most truly said by Christ that a man's life does not consist in excessive riches? Moreover, what he had said in a brief sentence he now illustrates with an elegant parable, in which the whole matter is set forth as if to be viewed in a mirror. And this is all the clearer and more effective for persuading, because although it may seem to contain a fictional narrative, it contains nothing but what is customarily done every day. It will be useful, however, to look at the individual parts in order, so that more profit may return to us from it. First, a certain rich man is set forth, of the class of those who possess lawfully gained wealth. For he does not speak of some tax collector, or usurer, or a bloody soldier enriched by plunder and the spoils of enemies, but of a head of a household who tilled the fields and gathered very abundant produce by God's blessing. But wealth that comes in this way comes without wrong or loss to anyone. Yet in these very riches he sinned, and he is condemned by God's sentence, as we shall hear afterwards. Here we are warned how dangerous is the management or possession of riches. For if loss of salvation can occur with respect to those riches which the divine blessing bestows upon us, what shall we say of those who heap up wealth by the most unjust means and at another's loss, and stumble, as they say, on the very threshold? Money-lenders and usurers ought to have observed this carefully, who by monopolies, treacherous changes of coinage, adulteration of merchandise, and countless other arts openly sin against the laws of justice and charity. They please themselves wonderfully, and, enticed by the sweetness of gain, hardly ever think that they offend the eyes of God. But their arts are condemned on all sides, and in the law the Lord compares them to the poisonous bite of a serpent, because they bring present destruction to all with whom they have dealings. With no less care should those also have considered this, who defraud hired workers and other wage-earners whose labour and services they use, whose sin cries out to God, and upon whom the Apostle James pronounces the dreadful curse of God. Likewise also those who grow rich from mercenary soldiering, from plunder and the shedding of blood, a very great number of whom there are today, and who claim for themselves the special praise of courage and wish to be seen as the common champions and defenders of their country. But in all the houses of these men, a fire burns (as Micah says), namely the treasure of the impious and unjust, by which the wrath of God is kindled against them.
