Let each one therefore learn to guard himself from all iniquity, and when lawful riches come to him, let him remember, on account of the wickedness of our nature, that they are like thorns, and let him think about how to use them rightly. Let us now see how this rich man sinned. He reasoned within himself, saying: "What shall I do? For I have nowhere to gather my fruits." And he said: "I will do this: I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and there I will gather my fruits and my goods, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, be merry." Christ paints in these words the nature, morals, counsels and pursuits of the rich of this age, as if on a tablet. First, he judges wrongly about that abundant produce of his lands. For he calls the fruits "his own," in which he sins in two ways. For he thinks he has acquired them by his own labour and industry, and does not acknowledge God's benefit, from whose blessing all things come. For, as Paul says, "neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase." Next, by calling them his own, he claims their use for himself alone, and makes no mention of God or of men. This is the source of every abuse by which riches are sinned against. For those who think this way either hoard their wealth so that it is of use neither to themselves nor to others, or, carried away by the desires of the flesh, they grow proud, indulge in pleasures, and live in luxury, and have no regard for the glory of God or for their needy neighbours. We are therefore admonished in this place to think always about the giver of riches and their lawful use. They are given by God. For unless he fertilizes the earth with his blessing, and himself builds the house, we rise up early in vain (as David says) and wear ourselves out with domestic affairs. For just as we bring nothing into the world, so we cannot create even a little herb or a single stalk. Riches are given by God, moreover, so that we may be stewards and dispensers, who ought to look to the want of others and relieve it by their abundance, as Christ will teach more plainly in chapter sixteen below. Those who are ignorant of these things or neglect them will never use their goods rightly.

units.la: Deinde ratiocinatur apud se & consultat quid sit agendum. Sunt ergo tales rerum suarum incerti, & variis cogitationibus distrahuntur, ideoque nihil a pauperibus & egenis differunt. Hos enim egestas cogit de victu in diem parando cogitare: illi autem ut congerant & congesta seruent, omnis generis consilia ineunt. Imo potior est & felicior in hac parte pauperum conditio. Hi enim paruo contenti sunt, & ubi victum necessarium acquisierunt, a curis suis quiescunt: at illis quibus nulla est, dum nihil illis sufficit, & ne opes quæsitæ dilabantur metuunt. Itaque perpetuis curis æstuant, qua dies illis laboriosos, noctes autem insomnes reddunt, ut nec ea quiete fruantur, qua canes, iumenta & reliqua animalia gaudent. Et de hoc eleganter Solomon disserit his verbis: Qui amat argentum, non saturabitur argento: & qui amat divitias, nullum fructu percipiet: quæ quidem etiam inanitas est: Dum augentur opes, augentur etiam qui eas comedant: & quæ utilitas peruenit ad possessores ipsarum, quam ut oculis suis spectent? Dulcis est somnus operanti, sive parum sive multum comederit: diuiti autem satietas non concedit dormire, & c. Quæ omnia docent, quam imprudenter rebus suis consulant, qui diuitijs se totos addicunt, cum quæ has comitantur solicitudines, & corpus fatigent, & animi tranquillitatem turbent.
units.tr: Then he reasons with himself and takes counsel about what is to be done. Such men are therefore uncertain about their possessions, and they are pulled in different directions by various thoughts, and so they differ in nothing from the poor and the needy. For need compels the poor to think about getting food for each day, while the rich lay plans of every kind to gather and keep what they have gathered. Indeed, the condition of the poor is in this respect the better and happier. They are content with little, and when they have acquired their necessary food they rest from their cares; but the rich, for whom nothing is ever enough, fear that the wealth they have sought may slip away. Thus they seethe with constant cares, which make their days toilsome and their nights sleepless, so that they do not enjoy that rest which dogs, beasts of burden and other animals enjoy. And Solomon discusses this elegantly in these words: "He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, and he who loves riches will gain no fruit from them; this too is vanity. When goods increase, those who eat them increase too; and what profit comes to their possessors, except that they look on them with their eyes? Sleep is sweet to the labourer, whether he has eaten little or much, but the fullness of the rich does not allow him to sleep," and so on. All these things teach how unwisely they look after their affairs who devote themselves wholly to riches, since the anxieties that accompany them both wear out the body and disturb the tranquillity of the mind.

units.la: Postremo concludit dies iste. Hoc faciam, inquit: Destruam horrea mea, & maiora ædificabo, & illic cogam fructus meos, & bona mea: & dicam animæ meæ, Anima, habes multa bona, & c. Duo statuit facienda. Primum, quod horreis veteribus destructis noua & maiora velit extruere, quæ tantum anni proventu capere possint. At quid hoc opus erat, cum vetera hucusque ipsi potuerint sufficere? Cur no ad pauperes respicit, quorum domus simul & ventres omnino vacui multa capere poterant? Alterum, quod otiu & voluptates sibi porro pollicetur. Dicam animæ meæ (inquit) Anima, habes multa bona repositæ in annos multos: requiesce, comede, bibe, obleotare. Est hic belluinus plane error, quod non alium usum diuitiarum agnoscit, quam quem bellue & pecudes ex prædæ & pabuli abundantia percipiunt. Neque hic quoque aliquam Dei mentionem facit, cui gratias agere & eius spiritum petere debuisset, ut eo gubernatus bonus concessis recte uteretur. Itaque Dei obliuio securitate peperit & stultam vitæ in plurimos annos prorogandæ fiduciam. Etenim dum de otio, de edendo, bibendo & oblectationibus solummodo verba facit, satis innuit, se fortis suæ mortalis prorsus esse oblitum. Solus item ex bonis illis voluptuari vult, immemor se illorum dispensatorem a Deo constitutum esse. Et hæc quidem in illo Christus reprehendit, qui alioqui moderatam & cum pietate coniunctam rei domesticæ curam non damnat: cuius exempla etiam in sanctissimis patribus scriptura nobis proponit. Debent autem ista nos admonere, ut de nostri seculi moribus discamus iudicare. Nam hodie etiam congerendis terræ fructibus publice & priuatim studetur: & in eum fine noua horrea, granaria, apothecæ & cellæ vinariæ passim extruuntur, cum interim innumerabiles pauperum turbæ obe-rent, quibus victus quoque necessarius deest, quos pleriq; negligunt. Imo abundantia reconditorum bonorum Dei immemores reddit, & eò stupiditatis multos adducit, ut se mortales esse non amplius cogitent, sed vitæ suæ rationes in annos infinitos usq; extendat. Hinc sequitur voluptuandi studium, otium ignauum, comessationes, ebrietas, luxus, libido & quæcunq; carnis inexplebilis cupiditas suadet. Et qui hîs student, hodie optimi censeri possunt, si cum illis conferantur, qui opibus suis vsuras exercent, & artibus iniquissimis quosuis circumueniunt & opprimunt. Sunt ergo pleriq; hoc diuite peiores, & ijs moribus viuunt, quos nouissimi seculi hominibus Christus tribuit.
units.tr: Finally that day comes to a conclusion. "I will do this," he says: "I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and there I will gather my fruits and my goods; and I will say to my soul, 'Soul, you have many goods,' and so on." He resolves on two things to be done. The first is that, with the old barns pulled down, he wishes to build new and larger ones, which can hold only the yield of a single year. But what was the need for this, since the old ones had so far been able to suffice for him? Why does he not look to the poor, whose houses and stomachs, all of them empty, could hold much? The second is that he promises himself further leisure and pleasures: "I will say to my soul, 'Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry.'" This is plainly a beastly error, in that he recognises no other use of riches than that which beasts and cattle derive from the abundance of prey and fodder. Nor does he here make any mention of God, to whom he ought to have given thanks and whose Spirit he ought to have asked, so that, guided by that Spirit, he might use what had been granted him rightly and well. Thus forgetfulness of God produced security and a foolish confidence that life would be prolonged for many years. For while he speaks only of leisure, of eating, drinking and pleasures, he sufficiently hints that he has entirely forgotten his mortality. He alone also wishes to take his pleasure in those goods, unmindful that he has been appointed by God their steward. Christ rebukes him for these things, though he does not otherwise condemn a moderate care of household affairs joined with godliness; Scripture sets before us examples of this even in the most holy fathers. These things ought to admonish us to learn from them how to judge the manners of our own age. For today too, both publicly and privately, zeal is given to gathering in the fruits of the earth, and to this end new barns, granaries, storehouses and wine-cellars are built everywhere, while meanwhile countless crowds of the poor languish, lacking even their necessary food, whom most people neglect. Indeed, the abundance of stored-up goods makes many forgetful of the goodness of God, and brings many to such stupidity that they no longer think of themselves as mortal, but extend the plans of their lives to infinite years. From this follows the pursuit of pleasure, idle sloth, carousing, drunkenness, luxury, lust, and whatever insatiable desire of the flesh persuades. And those who devote themselves to these things may today be counted the best of men, if they are compared with those who exercise usury with their wealth and by the most unjust arts circumvent and oppress whomever they can. So most men are worse than this rich man, and they live by those manners which Christ assigns to the men of the last age.

units.la: Sed deliberationis istius & totius negotij exitum videamus, quem his verbis Dominus expo-nit: Dixit autem ei Deus: Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt abs te, quæ vero parauisti, cuius erunt? Continentur his multa dignißima obseruatu. Primùm illum Deus compellat, de quo ipse ne cogitabat quidem. Non ergo ignorat hic nostras cogitationes & consilia, & quamuis ipsi rerum secu-ri illum negligamus, non tamen hic nos negligit, sed vindice oculo in nostra omnia requirit. Deinde stultum siue dementem vocat, quæ cæco mundi iudicio opponitur. Huic enim, qui tales sunt, mortalium sapientissimi putantur, vt qui dum viuunt, bene viuere curant, seq; ab omni curarum molestia eximunt. Sed Dei sententia omnium stultissimi sunt, quia rebus caducis intenti & fluxis huius seculi voluptatibus immersi, æterna regni cœlorum gaudia amittunt. Tertiò quid ipsum maneat, docet. Tu (inquit) agrorum prouentus in multos annos habes reconditos, & voluptates perpetuas tibi pollice-ris: sed hac ipsa nocte repetetur abs te anima tua, & moriendum tibi erit, adeoq; migrabit hinc anima tua, quam ad securum voluptuandi studium modo exhortatus es. Fingit autem angelos exactorum rigidissimorum similes, quia talibus nihil huius opinantibus & plane inuitis mors obrepit, & tunc de-bitum illud naturæ necessario persoluendum est, cùm neq; opes, neq; honores, neq; potentia vlla nos ab eo liberare possint. Alia autem est piorum ratio, qui cùm se mortales & in hoc mundo peregrinos esse norint, nunquam nö vigilant, & ipsi sponte animas suas Deo comendant, adeoq; cupiunt dissolui, vt cum Christo in cœlis viuere possint. Porrò aliud adhuc addit Dominus, quod auaros opum coacer-uatores pessimè habet. Quæ vero parauisti (inquit) cuius erunt? Quasi diceret: Quæ tibi & Deo & vi-ta æterna chariora fuerunt, ex quibus item tibi felicitate & omnis generis voluptates pollicitus es: Illa (inquam) ita nunc relinquenda erunt, vt nescias ad quos peruentura sint. Congerunt quidem multi, vt liberis & nepotibus suis prospiciant. Sed vanissimus ille labor est. Fit enim sæpissimè vt cogestæ illæ opes turpiter dilapidentur, & lenonibus, scortis, aleatoribus, vsurarijs & fœneratoribus cedat, quæ illi magnis laboribus, vel etiam genij sui fraudatione parauerunt. Et huc illa Salomonis pertinet: Est malum, quod vidi sub Sole, idq; principatu inter homines obtinet. Est vir, cui Deus diuitias dedit, & opes, & honores, vt nulla re careat, qua animus eius delectetur ex omnibus quæ posset expetere, nec tamen instituit eum Deus dominum, vt comedat ex illis, sed externus quispiam ea devorabit. Eccle. 6.
units.tr: But let us look at the outcome of that deliberation and of the whole affair, which the Lord sets out in these words: "But God said to him, 'Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?'" Many things most worthy of notice are contained in these words. First, God addresses him, whom he himself did not even think of. Therefore God does not ignore our thoughts and plans here, and although we neglect him while we are secure in our possessions, he does not neglect us here, but with an avenging eye he inquires into all our affairs. Next, he calls him foolish or demented, which is set against the blind judgment of the world. For to such men the wisest of mortals are thought to be those who, while they live, take care to live well and free themselves from all the trouble of cares. But in the judgment of God they are the most foolish of all, because, intent on fleeting things and immersed in the pleasures of this age, they lose the eternal joys of the kingdom of heaven. Thirdly, he teaches what awaits him. "You," he says, "have the produce of your fields stored up for many years, and you promise yourself perpetual pleasures; but this very night your soul will be demanded from you, and you must die, and so your soul, which you have just urged to a carefree pursuit of pleasure, will depart hence." He imagines angels like the most rigid exactors, because death creeps upon such men, who expect nothing of the kind and are wholly unwilling, and then that debt owed to nature must necessarily be paid, since neither wealth, nor honours, nor any power can free us from it. But the way of the godly is different: since they know that they are mortal and strangers in this world, they never fail to keep watch, and they commend their souls to God of their own accord, and so they desire to be dissolved so that they may live with Christ in heaven. Furthermore, the Lord adds something else, by which he holds the greedy hoarders of wealth in the worst regard. "But the things you have prepared," he says, "whose will they be?" As if he said: the things which were dearer to you than God and eternal life, from which you also promised yourself happiness and every kind of pleasure: those things (I say) must now be left behind in such a way that you do not know into whose hands they will come. Indeed many gather up, so that they may provide for their children and grandchildren. But that labour is most vain. For it very often happens that the heaped-up wealth is shamefully squandered, and passes to pimps, harlots, gamblers, usurers and moneylenders, which they acquired with great labour, or even by defrauding their own genius. To this belongs that saying of Solomon: "There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it holds sway among men: a man to whom God has given riches, wealth and honours, so that he lacks nothing his soul desires of all that he could wish for; yet God does not appoint him lord to eat of them, but a stranger devours them." Ecclesiastes 6.

units.la: Poterant hæc multis exemplis demonstrari, sed præstat parabolæ totius vsum videre, quem Do-minus infert his verbis: Ita est qui thesaurum congerit sibi, nec est in Deo dines. Generalem doctri-nam ex his colligit, eandem esse omnium conditionem, qui sibijpsis diuitias coaceruant, non autem sunt in Deo diuites. Nō ergo diuites per se simpliciter propter diuitias damnantur, sed ij soli, qui sibijpsis congerunt. Faciunt hoc qui non expectata Dei benedictione opes corradunt, in quibus fiduciam col-locant, & quasi ipsis solis date sint, quosuis alios securi negligunt. Hi quæ sperant ex opibus suis fru-stum, nunquam percipiunt. Itaq; omne illorum studium inane & labor irritus est. His autem opponit eos, qui in Deo diuites sunt, quod Paulus in priori ad Timotheum exponit, dicens: Ijs qui diuites sunt in hoc seculo, denuntia ne efferantur animo, neque spem ponant in diuitijs incertis, sed in Deo viuo, qui præbet nobis omnia copiose ad fruendum: Vt alijs benefaciant, vt diuites sint operibus bonis, fa-ciles ad impertiendum, facilis conuiuis: recondentes sibijpsis fundamentum bonum in posterum, vt apprehendant æternam vitam. Sunt igitur in Deo diuites, qui humiliter & modeste de seipsis sen-tientes, non diuitijs cor apponunt, sed spem omnem cùm præsentis tum futuræ vitæ in vno Deo re-positam habent, diuitijs autem suis sobrie vtuntur, & pauperes omni officiorum genere iuuant. Hæc ergo singuli serio meditentur, vt olim in magno illo die iudicij ex eorum numero sint, quos Chri-stus Iesus propter charitatis & misericordiæ opera commendabit, & Regni sui cœlestis cohæredes faciet. Illi debetur benediction, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things could be shown by many examples, but it is better to see the use of the whole parable, which the Lord draws from it in these words: "So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God." From this he draws a general teaching: that the condition of all is the same who heap up riches for themselves, and who are not rich toward God. Therefore it is not that the rich are simply condemned for their riches in themselves, but only those who store up for themselves. They do this who acquire wealth without expecting God's blessing, and place their trust in it, and carelessly neglect all others, as if the goods were given to them alone. Such men never obtain the fruit they hope for from their possessions. So all their labour is empty and their toil is in vain. He sets against these those who are rich toward God, as Paul explains in his first letter to Timothy, saying: "Charge those who are rich in this age not to be haughty in mind, nor to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things richly to enjoy; that they may do good, that they may be rich in good works, ready to give, willing to share; storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life." Therefore those are rich toward God who, thinking humbly and modestly of themselves, do not set their heart on riches, but place all their hope, both for the present and the future life, in the one God, and who use their riches soberly and help the poor with every kind of service. Let each therefore meditate seriously on these things, so that on that great day of judgment they may be among those whom Christ Jesus will commend for works of charity and mercy, and will make heirs of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXIX.

units.la: Dixit autem discipulis suis: Propterea dico vobis, ne soliciti estote de anima vestra, quid esuri sitis, neq; de corpore, quà re sitis induendi: Anima plus est quàm alimentum, & corpus quàm vestitus. Considerate coruos: nec enim seminant, neque metunt, quibus non est cella neque horreum, & Deus alit eos. Quanto vos præstatis volucribus? Quis autem ex vobis solicitè cogitando potest apponere ad staturam suam cubitum vnum? Itaque si ne id quidem quod minimum est potestis, quid de cæteris soliciti estis? Considerate lilia, quomodo crescant: non fatigantur, neque nent: dico autem vobis, ne Solomonem quidem in omni gloria sua amictum fuisse vt vnum ex iis. Quòd si herbam, quæ hodie est in agro, & cras in clibanum mittitur, Deus ita circumuestit, quanto magis vos o exigua fide prediti? Vos igitur ne quæritè quid esuri sitis, aut quid bibituri: & ne suspenso animo estote. Hæc enim omnia gentes requirunt; Pater autem vester nouit vos istis indigere. Quin potius quærite Regnum Dei, & hæc omnia adiicientur vobis.
units.tr: And he said to his disciples: "Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall put on. Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and God feeds them. How much better are you than the birds? Who among you, by being anxious, can add one cubit to his stature? So if you cannot even do the least thing, why are you anxious about the rest? Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin. I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith? So do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink, and do not be of anxious mind. For the nations seek all these things; but your Father knows that you need them. Rather, seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you."

units.la: Si homo ad Dei gloriam & regni cœlestis possessionem creatus sit, ea tamen est ingenij nostri prauitas, vt plerique in sola huius seculi bona intenti, de ijs acquirendis cogitent, æterna autem et cœlestia negligant. Est hæc salutis remora nocentissima. Impossibile enim est, vnum duobus dominis multùm inter se dissidentibus seruire, Deo nimirum & mammonæ, cùm ille nos totos sibi vendicet. Deinde cupiditas illa multorum scelerum radix est: quia illa inflammatis media illicita Satan obijcit, vt fieri nequeat, quin in tentationes & illius laqueos incidant, qui ditescere volunt. Adhac idololatriæ species est, si quæ in vno Deo collocari debebat, fiducia in opibus repositam habeamus; Ideo Christus Iesus de hoc vitio discipulos suos admodum diligenter admonet: & vt huic medeatur, nuper communè vulgi errorem oppugnauit, docens hominis vitam & felicitatem non in opum abundantia, sed in eo potius consistere, vt quis in Deo dives sit. Quia verò propter innatam nobis habendi cupiditatem, nulla diligentia hic nimia aut superuacanea esse potest, nunc ipsam huius mali radicem aggreditur, quæ est cura & solicitudo de victu & amictu parando, sub quibus omnia alia continentur, quæ nostræ necessitati seruiunt. Nam sub horum prætextu fere auaritiæ & opibus congerendis studetur. Docet ergo curam omnem in Deum reijcere, cuius Prouidentiam magnificè commendat, quam qui recte considerant, ij aduersus omne tentationum genus abunde instructi sunt.
units.tr: Although man was created for the glory of God and for the possession of the heavenly kingdom, our nature is so perverse that most people, intent only on the goods of this age, think about acquiring them and neglect the eternal and heavenly things. This is a most harmful hindrance to salvation. For it is impossible to serve two masters who are very much at odds with each other, namely God and Mammon, since the one claims us wholly for himself. Moreover, that desire is the root of many sins, because Satan puts before those who want to grow rich, inflamed by it, the illicit means, so that they cannot help falling into temptations and his snares. Besides, if we place our trust in riches, it is a kind of idolatry, since trust ought to be placed in the one God alone. Therefore Christ warns his disciples very diligently about this vice. And to remedy it, he recently attacked the common error of the crowd, teaching that the life and happiness of a man consist not in the abundance of wealth, but rather in being rich in God. But because of the desire of having that is innate in us, no diligence here can be excessive or superfluous, so he now goes after the very root of this evil, which is the care and anxiety about providing food and clothing, under which all other things are included that serve our necessities. For under the pretext of these, people usually strive for greed and for piling up wealth. He therefore teaches that every care should be cast upon God, whose providence he commends magnificently; those who consider it rightly are amply equipped against every kind of temptation.

units.la: Propositio & summa huius doctrinæ est: Ne soliciti estote de anima, id est, vita vestra, quid esuri sitis, neq; de corpore, qua re sitis induendi. Solicitudine prohibet, qua plerique ob hæc vitæ mortalis subsidia distrahuntur. At quia hic in vtramq; partem peccatur, dum alij auariores sunt, alij nimium securi seipsos & suos impiè negligunt, diligentius videre oportet, quid hoc præcepto Christus sibi velit. Vbi obseruabimus duplicem esse curam aut solicitudinem, qua homines in hac vita tenentur. Alia est sobria & legitima, imò necessaria quoq;, vt omnino vitari aut abijci nec possit nec debeat. Dei enim mandatum est: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Et Apostoli non vno loco docent, Christianorum esse, vt vitæ suæ rationem ita instituat, ne quem grauent, sed potius alijs subuenire possint, & eos ethnicis atq; infidelibus deteriores esse scribunt, qui suis nō prospiciunt. Id verò abesse labore fieri non potest, cui cura & solicitudo aliqua coniuncta est. Sunt ità sanctissimorum hominum exempla, qui rei domesticæ curâ diligentè habuerunt, inter quos celeberrimi sunt Abrahamus, Isaacus, Iacobus, Iosephus, qui toti regno sua cura & prouidentia prospexit, ne famis tempore populo vitus deesset. Et annonæ curâ principibus in primis commendatam esse debere, ipse rerum vsus quotidianus docet. De hac cura non agitur in præsenti, neq; eam Sacra litera prohibent, cùm ex eorum numero sit, quibus nos Deus coercet, ne animo elati & nostra fortunæ immemores lasciuiamus. Alia autem solicitudo est immoderata, qua fit vt ex diffidentia anxie nimis opibus accumulandis studeamus, quasi neque Deus nostri curam habeat aliquam, neq; vspiam sit in rerum natura, quod nobis possit sufficere. Hæc auaritiæ & malorum omnium quæ ex hac nascuntur, fons atq; origo est. Hinc enim fit, quòd nulla opum abundantia homines cotenti, plura semper appetunt, & ipsa copia magis accenditur, vt plura congerere & coaceruare velint. Illa ergo à Christianis hominibus Dominus alienissima esse vult: quorum est, cauere quidem ne cui sint oneri, & proinde honesto labore sibi ipsis necessaria parare: Interim verò seipsos & sua omnia Deo committere, absq; cuius benedictione nihil nostrum curis vel industria proficiet. Nihil ergo hic locus malæ frugis hominib. patrocinatur, qui sua turpiter dissipat, deinde otiosi & in
units.tr: The proposition and summary of this teaching is: Do not be anxious about your life, that is, your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, with what you shall clothe yourselves. He forbids the anxiety by which most people are distracted on account of these supports of mortal life. But since sin is committed in both directions, some being too greedy, others too careless, impiously neglecting themselves and their own, we must look more carefully at what Christ means by this precept. Here we observe that there are two kinds of care or anxiety by which men are held in this life. One is sober and lawful, indeed also necessary, so that it neither can nor ought to be avoided or cast aside altogether. For it is God's command: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." And the Apostles teach in more than one place that it is the duty of Christians to order their life so that they do not burden anyone, but rather may be able to help others, and they write that those who do not provide for their own are worse than the heathen and unbelievers. But this cannot be done without labour, to which some care and anxiety is joined. There are thus examples of most holy men who took diligent care of household affairs, among whom the most famous are Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, who by his care and foresight provided for the whole kingdom, so that in time of famine the people should not lack food. And the daily experience of affairs itself teaches that the care of the grain supply should be entrusted above all to rulers. This care is not the subject at present, nor do the Holy Scriptures forbid it, since it belongs to those things by which God restrains us, lest we, puffed up in mind and forgetful of our fortune, grow wanton. The other anxiety, however, is immoderate, by which it happens that out of distrust we too anxiously strive to accumulate wealth, as if God had no care for us at all, or as if there were nothing in nature that could suffice for us. This is the source and origin of greed and of all the evils that arise from it. For hence it happens that people, content with no abundance of goods, always desire more, and the very plenty kindles them further, so that they want to heap up and hoard even more. Therefore the Lord wants this to be most alien to Christian people, whose duty it is indeed to take care not to be a burden to anyone, and accordingly to obtain by honest labour what is necessary for themselves; but meanwhile to commit themselves and all their things to God, without whose blessing nothing of ours will profit from our cares or industry. Therefore this passage gives no support to bad stewards, who shamefully squander their own, and then, idle and...

units.la: Vitæ præsentis solicitudo prohibetur.
units.tr: The anxiety about the present life is forbidden.

units.la: 2. Thess. 3. 1. Tim. 5. & inertes oberrant, publicè quidem Ecclesijs, priuatim verò bonus omnibus graues & molesti, dum ex alieno viuere volunt. Hos Paulus ἀτάκτους, id est, inordinatos dicit, eò quod nullis legibus sese contineri sinunt, & naturæ quoq; ordine violant, quæ iubet, ut quisq; sibi ipsi & suis honestis rationibus prospiciat, & huius curæ exempla in feris quoq; immanissimus proponit, quæ catulos suos lactare & alere solent, donec ipsi sibi prospicere possint. Indigni sunt ergo illi, qui in Repub. bene constituta, ne dum in Ecclesia ferantur. Viderunt hoc sapientissimi quiq; inter gentes, qui ob grauem & prudentem Reipub. administrationem commendantur. Apud Athenienses enim diligenter in vnûquenque quæ inquiri solebat, qua arte aut quo quæstu viueret, & otiosi in ius vocabantur, vt inertiæ & ignauiæ pœnas darent. Massilienses verò neminem in ciuitatem suam admittebant, qui non artem aliquam teneret, qua se honestè aleret: & in eo tam attenti & seueri fuerunt, vt non solum mimos & histriones, verumetiam omnes eos procul arcerent, qui sub aliquo religionis prætextu inertiæ alimenta quærebant, quod hodie à fratribus (quos vocant mendicantes) in primis fieri solet.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 3; 1 Tim. 5. ...and wander about idle and inactive, publicly a burden to the congregations, and privately heavy and troublesome to all good people, since they want to live at the expense of others. Paul calls these ataktous [ἀτάκτους], that is, disorderly, because they allow themselves to be restrained by no laws, and they also violate the order of nature, which requires that each one provide for himself and his own by honest means. Even the most savage beasts set this example of care: they suckle and feed their young until the young can provide for themselves. Those who are carried along in a well-ordered commonwealth, and not only in the Church, are therefore unworthy. The wisest men among the nations have seen this, those who are commended for the serious and prudent administration of the commonwealth. For among the Athenians, each person was carefully asked by what art or what trade he lived, and the idle were summoned to court to pay the penalty for sloth and laziness. The Massilians admitted into their city no one who did not practise some craft by which he might support himself honestly; and in this they were so strict and severe that they kept away not only mimes and actors, but also all those who under some pretext of religion sought food by idleness, which today is especially done by the brothers whom they call mendicants.

units.la: Porro rationes videamus, quibus suum hoc præceptum Christus probat, & quarum pleraq; ex Patris cœlestis prouidentia desumpta sunt. Prima generalior est, & ea tam victu quàm amictu hominis comprehendit. Anima (inquit) plus est quam alimentum, & corpus quam vestitus. Apud Matthæum hæc per interrogationem enuntiantur, vt magis moneat, & nos proprij oris testimonio convincat. Est autem argumentum à comparatis, cuius sensus est: Deus, qui quod maius & præstantius est, dedit, minora & viliora non negabit: Atqui ille vitam dedit, quæ alimentum longè superat, corpus item cum suis membris formauit, quod vestibus longè præstat. Nunc ergo, negaret ide ille, quæ vitæ seruandæ & corpori aduersus cœli iniurias tegendo necessaria sunt? Ita vero admonet, ne tam iniquè de Deo sentiamus, quasi ut sua dona & suas creaturas negligat. Nam aut absq; causa vitæ & corporis nobis ab illo dati meminit. Prodest enim in huius consideratione crebrò & diligenter versari, quod olim sanctissimi Patres & cultores Dei fecerunt. Dauid certè nō vno loco Deum suum Deum fuisse fatetur ita inde ab vtero matris, & ab illo se formatum, inq; luce hanc eductum. Ista enim consideratio efficacissima consolationis argumenta aduersus omne tentationum genus nobis exhibet, maximè si generationis non stirpe ratione & admirabile atq; ad omnia vitæ huius negotia optime seruientem corporis humani fabricam diligenter expendamus. Quis enim nō inde colligat, hominem Deo curæ esse, cum is sese ad ea quoq; demittat, quæ in nostro corpore contemptissima videntur? Simul autem officij nostri per illam consideratione admonemur. Quia enim Deus nobis vitam & corpus dedit, & (vt Paulus ex vete ri Poeta dixit) in illo viuimus, monemur & sumus, satis constat nos illi nostra omnia debere, & pro indenimium ingratos & iniquos esse, qui propter carnis studia & res huius seculi illum negligunt.
units.tr: Next let us look at the reasons by which Christ proves this his precept, most of which are taken from the providence of the heavenly Father. The first is more general, and it comprehends both the food and the clothing of man. "Life," he says, "is more than food, and the body more than clothing." In Matthew these things are stated by way of question, so as to admonish more strongly and to convince us by the testimony of our own mouth. It is an argument from comparison, whose sense is this: God, who has given what is greater and more excellent, will not deny what is smaller and less valuable. But he has given life, which far surpasses food, and he has also formed the body with its members, which far excels clothing. Would he then deny what is necessary for preserving life and for covering the body against the injuries of the sky? Thus he admonishes us not to think so unfairly of God, as if he neglected his gifts and his creatures. For either he is mindful of the life and body given to us by him without cause. For it is profitable to dwell often and diligently on this consideration, as the most holy Fathers and worshippers of God did of old. David certainly, in more than one place, confesses that his God had been his God from the womb of his mother, and that he had been formed by him and brought forth into this light. For this consideration presents us with most effective arguments of consolation against every kind of temptation, especially if we carefully weigh the fabric of the human body, which is not the product of chance, admirable and best suited to all the affairs of this life. For who does not infer from this that man is a care to God, since God condescends even to those things that seem most contemptible in our body? At the same time we are reminded of our duty by this consideration. For since God has given us life and body, and (as Paul said from an ancient poet) in him we live, move, and have our being, it is quite clear that we owe him all our things, and that those are excessively ungrateful and unjust who, for the sake of the flesh and the affairs of this age, neglect him.

units.la: Cæterum quod in genere de victu & amictu dixit Dominus, id nunc singulis applicat: & exēplis euidentissimis probat, etiā minora hæc ad Dei prouidentiam pertinere, qui ea nunquā sit negaturus iis, qui in sua vocatione ambulat. Et quoad victu ait: Considerate coruos: nec enim seminat neq; metunt, quibus non est cella neq; horreum, & tamen Deus alit eos. Poterat patrum exempla allegare, vt Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, qui in terris peregrinis durissimæ farris temporibus à Deo liberalissimè acceperunt quæ vitæ subsidia sunt. Et in primis huc pertinebat Israelitarum in deserto agentium exemplum, quos totus annus quadraginta absq; semente & messe aluit pane, quæ cœlitus pluebat, vt vita doceret (sicuti Moses interpretatur) hominem non solo pane vsitato & ordinario viuere, sed infinitas esse Deo huius alendi rationes, & ad hoc sufficiens esse quicquid ille in eū vsum destinauerit. Nota sunt etiam Mosis & Eliæ exempla, quorum vterq; 40. dies absq; omni cibo transegit, hunc verò corui etiam aluerunt, qui quotidie mane & vespere panes atq; carnes ad ipsum deferebant. Et huius generis multa alia in scripturis habentur. Sed quia exempla eiusmodi, si nobis applicentur, nō semper nobis conueniunt, & in semetipsis errores & vitia multa homines deprehendunt, quæ illos prohibet sperare, quòd miracula in ipsorum gratiam Deus edere, aut peculiari aliqua ratione ipsos etiā seruare velit, coruos adducit, vorax & infaustum (vt vulgo putatur) atq; plerisque inuisum auitij genus, ne quam nobis tergiuersandi aut de diuina bonitate dubitandi occasionem relinquat: & simul ad scripturas discipulos remittit, quæ eodem exemplo Dei beneficentiam nobis commendat. Nam ipsum Iobo olim inter operum suorum commemorationem quæ captum humanum superant, his etiā verbis vsum fuisse legimus: An tu leænæ vænaberis prædam, & pastum sufficientem exhibebis catulis eius, cùm in cubilibus iacent atq; insidiantur in lustro? Quis parat suam prædam coruo, cùm eius pulli ad Deum clamant, & cibo carentes oberrant? Et Dauid in Psalmis de Deo ait: Qui dat pecori suum paflum, & pullis coruorum, qui ipsum inuocant. Ad hæc ergo loca alludit Dominus, vt discipulos ad attentiorem veterum scripturarum lectionem atq; meditationem excitet. Apud Matthæum vero omnium volucrum cæli meminit, quæ per æstatem temere circumuolitantes nihil colligunt, neq; penum aliquem recondunt, ex quo possint hyberno tempore viuere. Inde autem nos consolationem petere docet, ne Dei in victu largiendo nobis maligniore fore putemus. Ideo infert: Quanto vos præstatis volucribus? Quasi diceret: Etsi omnes aues vna cum reliquis animatibus vniuersis in vnū conueniant, non tamen vnius modo hominis dignitate possunt æquare, cum omnia in huius vsum sint condita. Cum vero Deus aues otiosas & inertes alat, & ita quidem, vt pullis coruorum a parentibus derelictis & confuso clamore ad illū crocitatibus prospiciat, & byeme fere pinguiores sint auiculæ, quibus nullus penus reconditus est, quam iniquum & absurdum fuerit de illius liberalitate dubitare, quasi is hominem negligere velit, qui secundum ipsius imaginem creatus est?
units.tr: Moreover, what the Lord said in general about food and clothing, he now applies to particular cases, and he proves by the most evident examples that even these lesser things belong to God's providence, since he will never deny them to those who walk in their calling. As for food, he says: "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them." He could have cited the examples of the fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who in foreign lands, in times of the hardest famine, received from God most generously the means of sustaining life. Above all, the example of the Israelites living in the desert was relevant here. For a whole year, forty years, God fed them without sowing or harvest, with bread that rained from heaven, so that they might learn (as Moses explains) that man does not live by ordinary and customary bread alone, but that God has countless ways of feeding him, and that whatever he has appointed for that purpose is sufficient. The examples of Moses and Elijah are also well known: each of them passed forty days without any food, and yet ravens fed Elijah, bringing him bread and meat morning and evening. There are many other examples of this kind in the Scriptures. But because such examples, if applied to us, do not always fit us, and because people find in themselves many errors and vices which forbid them to hope that God will work miracles for their sake or wish in some special way to preserve them, Christ brings forward the raven, a greedy bird and (as is commonly thought) unlucky, and hated by most people, so that he leaves us no excuse for shirking or for doubting God's goodness. At the same time he sends his disciples back to the Scriptures, which commend God's bounty to us by the same example. For we read that Job, in his enumeration of God's works which surpass human understanding, used these words: "Will you hunt prey for the lioness, and supply enough food for her cubs, when they lie in their dens and lurk in the thicket? Who provides food for the raven, when its young cry out to God and wander about without food?" And David in the Psalms says of God: "He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens which call upon him." Christ therefore alludes to these passages, to rouse his disciples to a more attentive reading and meditation on the ancient Scriptures. In Matthew, however, he mentions all the birds of the air, which in summer flutter about carelessly, gathering nothing and storing no provision from which they might live in winter. From this he teaches us to take comfort, lest we think that God will be less generous in providing us with food. Hence he adds: "Are you not much better than they?" As if to say: even if all birds, together with all the other living creatures, were gathered into one place, they could not equal the worth of one man alone, since all things were created for his use. But when God feeds idle and unthinking birds, and indeed so that he looks upon the cries of the young ravens abandoned by their parents, who croak loudly to him, and when the little birds that have no hidden store are often fatter in winter, how unjust and absurd it would be to doubt his generosity, as if he were willing to neglect the man who was created in his own image!

units.la: Debet autem sæpe & diligenter a nobis considerari hac paterna Dei prouidentia, qui ad minima quoque se demittit, adeò vt neq; coruorum pullos negligat. Prædicat hanc paßim in scripturis Spiritus sancti, & huc in primis pertinent, quæ in postrema parte libri Iobi & Psalmis aliquot habentur. Nam vt aliâs monuimus, non alia efficacior ratio est, quæ nos & in aduersis consolari, & simul in officio continere possit, ne affectuum & prauarum cupiditatum æstu abrepti exorbitemus. At hic maximū nostræ corruptionis & vitiositatis argumentū cernitur. Agnoscūt enim Dei imperiū omnes creaturæ, & forte sua contenta officiū faciunt. Norunt hirundo, turtur, grus & ciconia tempus suum (vt apud Ieremiam dicit Dominus) quo ad nos redire, & rursus alio abire debent: & quia ita Deo visum est boues cornibus & robore præstantes, equi vngulis & dentibus armati, asini quantumuis stolidi & contumaces, homini suo obsequium præstant, imo aues et pisces ad prædam sese ingerunt, & bellua immanissima ab illo sese cicurari patiuntur. At solus homo sua conditionis immemor recalcitrat, vt suum officium Deo creatori minus præstet. Discamus ergo frequenter ad animalium aliorum exempla respicere, vt in diuina prouidentia cognitione confirmati, Deo melius fidamus & fidelius obtemperemus.
units.tr: This fatherly providence of God, who condescends even to the smallest things, so that he does not neglect even the young of the ravens, ought to be often and carefully considered by us. The Holy Spirit proclaims it everywhere in the Scriptures, and especially relevant are those passages in the last part of the book of Job and in several of the Psalms. For, as we have elsewhere observed, there is no more effective reason which can both console us in adversity and at the same time keep us in our duty, so that we do not go astray, carried away by the heat of passions and depraved desires. Yet here we see the greatest proof of our corruption and wickedness. For all creatures acknowledge God's command, and perhaps they perform their duty, content with what is theirs. The swallow, the turtle-dove, the crane and the stork know their time (as the Lord says through Jeremiah) when they must return to us and again depart elsewhere. And because God has so willed it, oxen, excelling in horns and strength, horses armed with hooves and teeth, and asses, however dull and stubborn, render obedience to their master; nay, birds and fish throw themselves into the hunter's hands, and the most savage beast allows itself to be tamed by him. Man alone, forgetful of his condition, kicks back, so that he performs his duty to God his Creator less well. Let us therefore learn to look often at the examples of other animals, so that, strengthened in the knowledge of divine providence, we may trust God better and obey him more faithfully.

units.la: Quia vero multos ea persuasio seducit, quod sua industria & viribus res cofici oportere & posse arbitrantur, & ideo minus in Dei prouidentia respiciunt, aliud argumentum subiicit, quo omnem curam atq; solicitudinem nostram inutilem esse, & nos frustra fatigari docet. Sic enim ait: Quis autem ex vobis solicitè cogitando, potest apponere ad staturam suam cubitum vnum? Itaq; si ne id quidem quod minimum est potestis, quid de cæteris solicitè estis? In humani corporis constitutione minimum est statura, vt quæ nec ad præsentem vitam neq; ad æternam salutem quicquam confert. Nā nō minus commodè viuunt parui quam magni, apud Deum autem nulla statura nostræ ratio est, quoad dona eius, quæ tam parùs quā grandibus atq; procerib; confert. Ideo olim Samuelis inter Isai filios regem quærenti dicebat: Ne respicias ad formam eius, neq; ad procéritatem staturæ eius: non enim quod videt homo (homo siquidē videt quod oculis obuersatur) sed Dominus cor intuetur. Porro corporis proprij staturā mutare, et ei aliquid vel auferre vel addere nemo potest, imò (vt alibi Christus ait) ne capillū quidē vnicū vel albū vel nigrū facere possumus. Quæ ergo stultitia est circa ea fatiga-ri, quæ et longè grauiora & multò minus in nostra potestate sunt? Num enim nos terra fœcundare dere, seminibus vim generandi inferre, tempestates cōmodas et necessarias de cælo elicere, ventorū flatus tēperare, è terra segetes, ex dissortis vitib. vuas, et ex arborū fragilib. ramus omnis generis poma producere poterim? Nihil ergo tutius & cōmodi fuerit, quā in solius Dei prouidētia recubere.
units.tr: But because many are led astray by the persuasion that things must and can be accomplished by their own industry and strength, and therefore pay less regard to God's providence, he adds another argument, by which he teaches that all our care and anxiety is useless and that we toil in vain. For he says: "Which of you, by taking thought, can add one cubit to his stature? If then you are not able even to do that which is least, why are you anxious about the rest?" In the constitution of the human body, stature is the least thing, since it contributes nothing either to the present life or to eternal salvation. For short people live no less comfortably than tall ones, and before God there is no account taken of stature, in respect of his gifts, which he bestows as much on the small as on the great and tall. Therefore long ago God said to Samuel, when he was seeking a king among the sons of Jesse: "Do not look on his appearance, or on the height of his stature; for the Lord does not see as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart." Moreover, no one can change the stature of his own body, or take anything from it or add anything to it; indeed (as Christ says elsewhere) we cannot make even a single hair white or black. What folly, then, is it to labour over things which are far more serious and much less in our power? For can we fertilise the earth, impart the power of generation to seeds, draw seasonable and necessary weather from heaven, temper the blowing of the winds, produce crops from the earth, grapes from unpruned vines, and fruit of every kind from the brittle branches of trees? Nothing, therefore, is safer or more fitting than to rest in the providence of God alone.

units.la: Cum autem quæ ad corporis & vitæ huius mortalis sustentationem faciunt, Christus in nostro arbitrio & potestate esse negat, idq; nos quoq; fateri cogamur, nō minus stultus quam impius & in solens illorum error est, qui æterna salutis hæreditate ex hominis libero arbitrio & viribus atque operum eius meritis pendere contendunt. Num enim se totos regenerare & innouare poterūt, qui ne corporis quidem staturam aut capillorum colorem mutare possunt? Vel num in illis quæ natura bu manam longe excedunt, aliquid proficiunt suis viribus, qui ne actiones quidem naturales in sua po-testate habent? Nam vt dormiat iube eum, quem aut mordaces curæ aut aduersa valetudo noctes insomnes ducere cogit. Certè frustra iusseris, etiamsi ipse tibi obreperare quam maximè cupiat. Eá dem
units.tr: Since Christ denies that the things which serve to sustain this mortal body and life are in our choice and power, and since we too are compelled to confess this, the error of those is no less foolish than it is impious and insolent, who contend that the inheritance of eternal salvation depends on the free will and strength of man and on the merits of his works. For will those who cannot even change the stature of their body or the colour of their hair be able to regenerate and renew themselves wholly? Or do those who do not even have control over natural actions accomplish anything by their own strength in matters which far exceed nature? For bid a man sleep, when gnawing cares or ill health keep him awake through the night. You will certainly bid in vain, even if he himself most eagerly desires to sleep. The same ... holds for almost all actions, because God is the one who does this, because he directs the ways and steps of man.

units.la: {1. Sam. 16.} Matth. 5. dem ess actionum fere omnium ratio, quia Deus est, quia vias & gressus hominis disponit. Itaque salutem in eius gratia consistere credamus, & ita illius certi erimus, cum qui alio respiciunt, semper incertis cogitationibus iactati fluctuent.
units.tr: {1. Sam. 16.} Matth. 5. The reason for nearly all of our actions is the same: because God is God, and because he orders the ways and steps of man. So let us believe that our salvation rests in his grace, and then we will be secure in him, whereas those who look elsewhere are always tossed about by uncertain thoughts like waves.

units.la: Cæterum pergit Christus Iesus, & de vestitu quoq; exemplum ex rerum natura adducit, vt illius curam & studium nimium prohibeat. Et sane nemo illius in his tradendis diligentia mirabitur, qui cogitauerit hic etiam in primis euidens corrupta ac peruersæ nostræ naturæ argumentum elucere. Nam vestium originem ex peccato esse constat. Vt ergo facinorosum vincula & compedes de sceleribus admonent: ita nos quoties induimur et exuimur, de primorum parentum infelici lapsu & inde in nos propagato peccato miserijsq; ex hoc quotidie nascentibus cogitare debebamus, vt in Dei conspectu humiliati veræ pœnitentiæ studeremus. Id autem adeò non fit à plerisq; hominum, vt potius circa immodicam vestitus & ornatus corporis curā occupati, reliqua omnia negligant, vt in illis potissimum luxu & fastu peccent. Et vt pauperiores nimia solicitudine peccant, dū metuunt ne desint aliquando indumenta, quæ in veterum & attritorum locum succedant: ita qui opulentiores sunt, mollitiei & peregrinitati student, & dum quisq; alij præstare cupit, terras & maria omnia fatigat. Est vtrunq; peccatum graue admodum, & multa in superbos & molles illos vestium ostentatores à Prophetis dicuntur: prioribus autem illis, quos aut egestas aut præpostera rerum huius seculi cura plus æquo solicitos reddit, Christus in præsenti consolatione adhibet, dicens: Cōsiderate lilia, quomodo crescant: non fatigantur neque nent: dico autem vobis, ne Solomonem quidem in omni gloria sua amictum fuisse vt vnum ex ijs, &c. Summa omnium est, quod hos quoque ad Dei prouidentiam remittit, cui amictus noster non minus quam vitæ curæ sit. Et vt prius non celebrium amicorum atque cultorum Dei exempla, sed coruos & volucres otiosas adduxit: ita hic quoque non eorum meminit, in quorum vestitu Dei bonitas mirabiliter sese exeruit, quales primi parentes fuerūt, quibus ille ipse vestes parauit. Israelitæ item in deserto, quorum vestes totis annis quadraginta neq; vetustate computruerunt, neq; vsu quotidiano attritæ sunt: sed lilia allegat, sub quibus genus omne florū comprehendit. Nam in Matthæo lilia aut flores agri nominantur, quos nulla hominum cura aut industria educat, & colit, sicuti alijs nonnullis fieri solet, qui in hortis delicatioribus solent plantari. Rē vero mirificè aplificat, & verbis vtitur, quæ singula animos mouere possūt. Primò cōsiderate (inquit) lilia. At quis non excitetur, quando se à Dei Filio ad rem aliquam spectandam vocari audit? Quid vero in liliis aut floribus adeo spectatu dignum est? Videte (inquit) quomodo crescant. Et sanè mirabilis est florum generatio, si vt primum ex terra prodeant, quam fragili stylo innixi ventis & pluuijs resistāt, vt disruptis caulyculis folia distendant, & alia huius generis consideres. Vnde vero sistabet? Nō fatigantur (ait Christus) neq; nent, imò ne possunt quidē aliquid operis facere. Verū tamen vestiuntur, & ita quidem, vt ne Solomonis quidem vestitus, quo in sua maiestatis publica declaratione vti solebat, vel vni illorum conferri possit. Atqui illum splendissimum fuisse oportuit, cum Reginam Sabæ seruorum eius vestes cum admiratione obseruauisse legamus. Et sanè nullus regū cultus flores æquare potest, siue formam eorum, si colorum splendorem & admirabilem compositionem spectemus: vt iam de odore iucundissimo & medendi virtute, qua pleriq; commendantur nihil dicamus. Quomodo autem flores æquarent sericum aut acu pictæ vestes, quando illos pro exemplari habent, qui istis texendis occupantur? Quid vero inde Christus colligit? Rursus à minori ad maius argumentum ducens ait: Quod si herbam, quæ hodie est in agro, & cras in clibanum mittitur Deus ita circumuiestit, quanto magis vos, ô exigua fide prædití? Verba hæc per se clara sunt, nec expositione aliqua opus habent. Obseruanda autem in his est diligenter paterna Dei bonitas, qua creaturas omnibus, etiā vilißimis, tam mirabiliter prospicit. Quid enim floribus magis caducum & vanius? Per illos tertè rerum huius seculi instabilē conditione, & gloriā humanæ aut carnalis vanitatē Spiritus sanctus adumbrat. Omnis caro fœnū (clamat Isaias) & omnis gloria eius flos agri. Et Iobus de homine misero & mortali dicit: Vt flosculus oritur & succiditur. Et Dauid: Hominis ætas gramini similis est, floreteq; vt flos in agro: Qui nullus erit, cum eum ventus perflauerit, &c. Ita samè fouet & vestit ornatq; flores Deus, vt nos de eius prouidentia admonere & in fide cōfirmare possint. Quis ergo eius bonitatem non exscrutetur & colat? Quis non ab illo vno pendeat? Quis itē non detestetur illorum vasaniam, qui simulachris opus esse aiunt, quæ Deum & eius beneficia nobis in mentem revocent, quando vnius flosculi temere nascentis centemplatio nobis potest sufficere?
units.tr: Christ goes on, and to restrain our excessive care and concern he also offers an example from nature concerning clothing. Indeed, no one will marvel at his diligence in teaching this if he considers that here, too, the corrupt and perverse character of our nature is especially evident. For it is established that clothing had its origin in sin. Just as chains and fetters remind a criminal of his crimes, so whenever we dress and undress we ought to think of the unhappy fall of our first parents, the sin propagated from them into us, and the miseries that arise from it every day, so that humbled before the sight of God we may strive for true repentance. But most people do not do this. Instead they are so occupied with an excessive care for clothing and bodily adornment that they neglect everything else, and they sin chiefly in luxury and pride. Just as the poorer sin through overanxious concern, fearing that they may at some time lack garments to replace those that are old and worn, so the wealthier devote themselves to softness and fine display, and while each wants to outdo the others, they wear out lands and seas. Both sins are very grave, and the Prophets speak against the proud and effeminate displayers of clothing in many places. But to those who are made more anxious than is right, either by poverty or by a misguided concern for the affairs of this world, Christ offers consolation in the present passage, saying: "Consider the lilies, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin. But I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these," and so on. The sum of it all is that he refers these people too to the providence of God, for whom our clothing is no less a matter of care than our life. And just as earlier he cited not the examples of famous friends and worshippers of God but the ravens and the idle birds, so here too he does not mention those in whose clothing the goodness of God has shown itself wonderfully, such as our first parents, for whom he himself made garments. Likewise the Israelites in the wilderness, whose clothes for forty whole years neither decayed with age nor wore out with daily use, are not mentioned. Instead he points to the lilies, under which he includes every kind of flower. In Matthew the lilies, or the flowers of the field, are named; no human care or industry raises or tends them, unlike some other plants that are usually set in more delicate gardens. He magnifies the matter greatly and uses words each of which can stir the mind. "First," he says, "consider the lilies." But who would not be roused when he hears himself called by the Son of God to look at something? What, indeed, is so worthy of looking at in lilies or flowers? "See," he says, "how they grow." And truly the generation of flowers is wonderful: how, as soon as they come forth from the earth, resting on a fragile stalk, they withstand the winds and rains, how they break open their little stems and spread out their leaves, and other things of this kind that you may consider. But where would this end? "They do not toil," says Christ, "nor do they spin"; indeed they cannot even do any work. Yet they are clothed, and so splendidly that not even the clothing of Solomon, which he wore when he publicly displayed his majesty, could be compared with any one of them. And yet Solomon's must have been most splendid, since we read that the Queen of Sheba marvelled at the garments of his servants. Indeed no royal finery can equal flowers, whether we look at their form, the brilliance of their colours, or their admirable arrangement; not to mention their most pleasant scent and the healing power for which many are commended. But how could flowers rival silk or embroidered garments, when people take as their model for weaving those very flowers? What, then, does Christ infer from this? Reasoning again from the lesser to the greater, he says: "If God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?" These words are clear in themselves and need no explanation. But in them we must carefully observe the Father's goodness of God, by which he so wondrously cares for all creatures, even the most worthless. For what is more fleeting and vain than flowers? Through them the Holy Spirit shadows forth the unstable condition of the things of this world and the vanity of human or carnal glory. "All flesh is grass," cries Isaiah, "and all its glory is like the flower of the field." And Job says of wretched and mortal man: "He comes forth like a flower and is cut down." And David: "The days of man are like grass; he flourishes like a flower in the field, which is gone when the wind has passed over it." So God so nourishes, clothes and adorns the flowers that they may remind us of his providence and confirm us in faith. Who, then, would not search out and cherish his goodness? Who would not depend on him alone? Who would not also detest the madness of those who say that images are needed to call God and his benefits to our minds, when the contemplation of a single flower that springs up by chance can be enough for us?

units.la: Porro priusquam progrediamur, observare nos conuenit correptionem illam satis acrem, qua si dei imbecillitatem discipulis suis Christus exprobrat. Illa enim docet, eos etsi sua iam pridem reliquis- sent, curis tamen & solicitudine adhuc tentatos fuisse, quae animos eorū distraxerunt, vt ijs minus attenderet, quae ab illo ipsis dicebantur. Habet ergo fides sua augmenta, nec statim ad summā per sectionem ascendunt, qui semel Christo nomen dederunt. De nullius ergo salute propter vitia quaedā aut fidei infirmitatem temere est desperandum. Interim admonemur, omnes illas solicitudines atque curas, quibus propter victum & amictum plerique excruciantur, ex diffidentia enasci, & fidei minus adhuc firmae certissimum esse argumentum. Nunquam enim curis immoderatus locum dabit qui Deum sua prouidentia nos alere, vestire & seruare ex animo credit. Et vt infantes ab vna matre pendent, in eius solius gremio acquiescunt, & hanc solam expetunt: ita filij Dei se totos eius prouidentiae committunt, & (quod Dauid iubet) in hunc sarcinas reiiciunt; de cuius fide non possunt dubitare. Psal. 55.
units.tr: Before we go further, we should notice the rather sharp rebuke with which Christ reproaches his disciples for their weakness of faith. For it teaches that although they had long since left their possessions behind, they were still troubled by cares and anxieties, which distracted their minds so that they paid less attention to what he was saying to them. Faith therefore has its growth, and those who have once given their name to Christ do not immediately rise to the highest perfection. Therefore no one's salvation should be rashly despaired of because of certain faults or the weakness of his faith. Meanwhile we are reminded that all those anxieties and cares, with which many are tormented for the sake of food and clothing, spring from distrust and are a most certain sign of a faith that is still not firm. For a man who sincerely believes that God feeds, clothes and preserves us by his providence will never give place to immoderate cares. And just as infants hang upon one mother, rest in her lap alone, and seek her only, so the children of God commit themselves wholly to his providence and cast their burdens upon him, as David bids, and they cannot doubt his faithfulness. Psal. 55.

units.la: Redit autem ad victum Dominus, quia de hoc plus quam alijs solicitos esse nouit eos, qui non omnibus necessarijs abundant. Vos igitur (inquit) ne quaerite (anxiè nimirum & solicitè) quid esuri sitis aut quid bibituri, & ne suspenso animo estote. Qua locutione ad eorum mores & ingenium alludit, qui non in Dei prouidentiam respiciunt, sed curis & cogitationibus suis indulgent. Hi enim sem per animi pendent, & varijs consilijs distracti nunquam certū quid & solidum de suis rebus possunt statuere. Hanc verò animorum fluctuationem Christus à suis discipulis alienissimam esse vult, & vt huic medeatur, duo argumenta prioribus adijcit. Primum ab exrmplo fidei aduerso sumitur, cum dicit: Haec enim omnia gentes mundi requirunt, qui nimirum nulla Dei veri cognitione, & multò minus fide instructi sunt. Hi enim suis viribus atq; industria haec acquiri oportere arbitrantur, & proinde curis & anxijs hisce cogitationibus non possunt non distrahi, quando non statim ad manū esse vident necessaria vitae subsidia. Ita verò docet, nimium adhuc crassos & ignorantes esse, & ne prima quidem Christianae fidei principia eos tenere, qui ijsdem curis locum dant. Quomodo enim Deum & Patrem & omnipotentem esse credet, qui illum nos alere velle & posse nondum intelligit? Aut num ab hoc Filium vnigenitum nobis in panem vitae aeternae datum esse vnquam credet, qui an panem quotidianum nobis ille daturus sit, dubitat? Qua ratione item sibi de aeternis & coelestibus bonis spem certam faciet, qui temporaria haec & quotidiana nondum sperare didicit? Recte erago & merito tales gentibus prophanus Christus confert.
units.tr: The Lord now returns to food, because he knows that those who do not abound in all necessities are more anxious about this than about anything else. "Therefore," he says, "do not seek" (anxiously and worriedly, of course) "what you will eat or what you will drink, and do not be of anxious mind." By this expression he alludes to the habits and disposition of those who do not look to God's providence but indulge their own cares and thoughts. For such people always hang in suspense, and, pulled apart by various plans, they can never settle anything certain and solid about their affairs. Christ wants this wavering of mind to be most alien to his disciples, and to remedy it he adds two arguments to the earlier ones. The first is taken from the contrary example of unbelief, when he says: "For the Gentiles of the world seek all these things," people who are without any knowledge of the true God, and still less instructed in faith. For they think these things must be acquired by their own strength and industry, and therefore they cannot but be drawn away by cares and anxious thoughts of this kind, when they do not see at once the necessary supports of life at hand. Christ teaches in this way that those who give place to the same cares are still too gross and ignorant, and that they do not hold even the first principles of the Christian faith. For how will one believe that God is Father and almighty, if he does not yet understand that God is willing and able to feed us? Or will he ever believe that the only-begotten Son has been given to us by him as the bread of eternal life, if he doubts whether God will give us our daily bread? By what reasoning, too, will he make for himself a sure hope of eternal and heavenly goods, if he has not yet learned to hope for these temporary and daily things? Rightly and deservedly, therefore, Christ compares such people with the profane Gentiles.

units.la: Alterum argumentum rursus ex Dei prouidentia petit, quo magis in hac vna acquiescere discamus. Dicit enim: Pater autem vester nouit vos istis indigere. Breuis sed multae consolationis plena sententia. Nam si propius inspiciatur, triplex in ea argumentum latere videbis. Primum est, quod de Deo loquens, hunc patrem nostrum dicit. Quis ergo de eius bonitate & beneficentia dubitet? Secundum in eo est, quod illum nouisse aut scire dicit. Nihil enim hunc latet, quia omnia penetrat; & oculi eius per omnem terram discurrunt. Quid verò nouit? Vos istis indigere. Est haec tertia ratio, qua nos solatur. Ita enim inter homines comparatum est, vt si parentes norint filijs peregrè agenti bus aliquid deesse, mox quacunq; possunt ratione illis opem ferant. At coelestis ille Pater, cuius bonitas & misericordia coelum transcendit, nos in hac lachrymarum valle peregrinantes videt, & vi- stu, vestitu, domicilio alisq; vitae subsidijs opus habere nouit. Nunquam ergo illa negabit, quoad nos hic viuere volet. Quomodo enim filios suos ille negligeret, cuius proprium opus est ijs succurrere, qui in necessitate constituti sunt? Docent haec quā felix & beata sit credentium conditio, de qua pter innatam carni nostrae socordiam plerique rarius cogitant. Patrem habent in coelis, qui vt illos hic laborantes videt & nouit: ita scit quoq; quibus rebus indigeant. Imò cum nos melius cognitos habeat, quam nos ipsi, melius etiam quae nobis vtilia & salutaria sint intelligit, & vt ea nobis largiatur nunquam non paratus est. Ab hoc igitur cum omnia nostra pendeant, ei omnem nostri curam relinquere debemus, ne inani & noxio labore nosipsos fatigemus.
units.tr: Next he draws a second argument from God's providence, so that we may learn to rest the more firmly in this one. For he says: "But your Father knows that you have need of these things." A short saying, but full of great comfort. For if we look at it more closely, we will see that it contains a threefold argument. The first is that, speaking of God, he calls him our Father. Who then could doubt his goodness and kindness? The second is that he says God knows or understands these things. For nothing is hidden from him, since he penetrates all things, and his eyes run through the whole earth. But what does he know? That you have need of these things. This is the third reason by which he comforts us. For it is so ordered among men that if parents know their children, who are away from home, lack something, they straightway bring them help by whatever means they can. But that heavenly Father, whose goodness and mercy surpass the heavens, sees us wandering in this valley of tears, and knows that we need food, clothing, shelter and other supports of life. He will therefore never deny them to us, as long as he wills that we live here. For how would he neglect his own sons, whose proper work it is to help those who are in need? These things teach how happy and blessed is the condition of believers, which on account of the sloth natural to our flesh most people think about too rarely. They have a Father in heaven, who sees and knows them labouring here, and so also knows what they need. Indeed, since he knows us better than we know ourselves, he also understands better what is useful and wholesome for us, and he is always ready to bestow these things upon us. Since therefore all our affairs depend on him, we ought to leave all our care to him, so that we do not weary ourselves with vain and harmful toil.

units.la: Porro doctrinae huius vsum ipse Dominus tradit, dum infert: Quin potius quaerite regnū Dei, & haec omnia adijcientur vobis. Per regnū Dei tota nostrae redeptionis & salutis ratio intelligitur, cuius hic finis est, vt destructo diaboli & peccati regno, in nobis regnet Deus nosq; ei obediamus, tandem ad regnum illud cœleste transferamur, quod sui sanguinis pretio Christus nobis acquisiuit. Quærunt regnum hoc, qui Filium Dei vera fide amplexi, sese illius voluntati accomodant, & vocationem suam, cui ipsos Deus destinauit, sedulò sequuntur. Is in præsenti pollicetur Dominus, quod nihil ipsis defuturum sit eorum, quæ ad vitam hanc tuendam necessaria sunt. Cui promissioni illud Dauidis conuenit: Iuuenis fui, & nunc senui, nec vidi iustum derelictum, aut posteros eius mendicantes panem. Et Paulus pietatem cum animo sua forte contento magnum quæstum esse dicit, vt quæ promissiones præsentis & futuræ vitæ habeat. Exempla cum vetera tum recentia passim occurrunt quibus hoc probari potest, & prodest diligenter obseruare quæ piis inter medios persecutionum fluctus accidunt, & hoc à Christo verissimè dictum esse patebit. Debet autem doctrina hæc ad omnis loci & ordinis homines extendi. Qui igitur Rempub. administrant, ij ante omnia curent, vt Deus regnet, huic credant, leges ipsius voluntati consentientes condant, easq; constanter tueantur, ijsdem verò populus obtemperet, nec dubium est, quin omnia habituri sint à Deo quæ ad pacem & conseruationem Reipublicæ faciunt. Idem patresfamilias, opifices, agricolæ & quicunque alij nominari possunt, obseruent, & ipsi quoque Dei benedictionem sentient, quæ omnia illorum fausta & auspicia reddet. Nec enim suos fallere potest Iesus Christus, qui ipsissima est veritas: Cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Lord himself sets out the use of this teaching when he adds: "But rather seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you." By the kingdom of God is understood the whole plan of our redemption and salvation, whose aim is that, with the kingdom of the devil and of sin destroyed, God may reign in us and we may obey him, and at last be transferred to that heavenly kingdom which Christ has won for us at the price of his own blood. They seek this kingdom who embrace the Son of God with true faith, conform themselves to his will, and diligently follow the calling to which God has destined them. To these the Lord promises in the present that nothing will be lacking to them of those things which are necessary for sustaining this life. To this promise that saying of David agrees: "I have been young, and now I am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his descendants begging for bread." And Paul says that godliness with contentment of mind is great gain, since it has the promises of the present and the future life. Examples, both old and recent, occur everywhere by which this can be proved, and it is useful to observe carefully what befalls the godly amid the waves of persecution, and it will become plain that Christ spoke most truly. But this teaching ought to be extended to men of every place and order. Therefore those who administer the commonwealth should above all take care that God reigns, believe in him, enact laws agreeing with his will, and maintain them constantly, and the people should obey them. And there is no doubt that they will have from God all things that serve the peace and preservation of the commonwealth. Likewise let heads of households, craftsmen, farmers and whoever else may be named observe these things, and they too will feel the blessing of God, which will make all their undertakings and enterprises prosperous. For Jesus Christ, who is very truth itself, cannot deceive his own: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY 130.

units.la: Ne timeas o parue grex: nam visum est Patri vestro dare vobis Regnum. Vendite bona vestra & date eleemosynam. Parate vobis crumenas, quæ non veterascunt, thesaurum in cœlis qui nunquam deficiat: quo fur non appropinquat, & vbi tinea non corrumpit. Vbi enim thesaurus vester est, illic & cor vestrum erit.
units.tr: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give alms. Make for yourselves purses which do not grow old, a treasure in heaven that never fails, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."

units.la: Quoniam Dominus noster Iesus Christus discipulos suos ad constantiam in vera fide & ingenuam eius confessionem gratuiter hortatus est, omnia etiam remouet, quæ nos hic abstterrere aut impedire possunt. Inter quæ postremo loco auaritia producitur, à qua multis & grauissimis rationibus debortatus est, eò quod vix aliud sit, quod efficacius nos à Deo auocet. Ostendit ergo contra vulgi opinionem, opes ad veram hominis felicitatem nihil conferre, neque vitam hanc tueri posse, quando mortis hora instat, quæ fere incautis & nihil tale sperantibus obrepit. Item opum possessionem dubiam esse, nec aliquem scire posse, cui iam morituris ea relinquat, quæ suis curis atque laboribus acquisiuit. Et quia plerosque vitus & vestitus cura solicitos habet, de hac nuper multis & diligenter monuit docens, hanc omnino inutilem & superuacaneam esse, cum nostra industria ne in minimis quidem aliquid possit, Deus autem cuius prouidentia ad coruos & flores vsque extenditur, suos nunquam sit neglecturus. Caeterum vt olim Cato Censorius populo Romano ob frumenti distributionem tumultuanti dicebat, difficile est verba facere ventri auribus carenti: Ideo Christus Dominus ipsum, quam discipulis nuper fecit, prima huius loci parte confirmat, deinde ad beneficentiæ studium exhortatur, vt ostendat, Christianos homines huic potius vacare, quam opibus congerendis intentos esse debere.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ freely exhorted his disciples to steadfastness in the true faith and to a sincere confession of it, he also removes everything that could frighten us here or hinder us. Among these, covetousness is mentioned last, and he dissuades us from it with many weighty reasons, since scarcely anything else draws us away from God more effectively. Against the opinion of the crowd, he therefore shows that wealth contributes nothing to a person's true happiness, and cannot protect this life when the hour of death is at hand, which usually creeps upon the careless and those who expect nothing of the kind. Likewise, the possession of wealth is uncertain, and no one can know to whom a dying man should leave what he has acquired by his cares and labours. And because many are anxious about food and clothing, he recently warned them about this at length, teaching that such anxiety is wholly useless and superfluous, since our diligence cannot achieve anything even in the smallest matters, while God, whose providence extends even to the ravens and the flowers, will never neglect his own. Moreover, as Cato the Censor once said to the Roman people, who were rioting over the distribution of grain, it is hard to make speeches to a belly that has no ears. Therefore Christ our Lord confirms what he has just said to his disciples in the first part of this passage, and then urges them to zeal in doing good, to show that Christians ought to devote themselves to this rather than be intent on heaping up wealth.

units.la: Primum breui & pathetica plane sententia absoluit, sic dicens: Ne timeas o parue grex: nam visum est (vel placuit) Patri vestro dare vobis regnum. Cohærent ista cum iis quæ aduersus nimiam & immoderatam vitus curam dixerat, & docent, non debere eos sibi in hoc seculo ab egestate timere, quibus Deus regni sui cœlestis hæreditatem æterno suo decreto destinauerit. Cur enim huius vitæ subsidia, quæ ne belluis quidem & volucribus negantur, non sperent à Patre cœlesti, qui se maiora & æterna bona accepturos esse nouerunt? Quia verò multa alia sunt, quæ pios terrent, vtpote fidelium paucitas, hostium vires & potentia, perpetuæ item eorundem insidiæ & sanguinariæ machinationes, multaq; alia huius generis, debet hinc generalis consolatio peti, qua nos aduersus omnes tentationum species confirmemus. Quæ vt efficacior sit, singulæ huius dicti partes erunt excutiendæ.
units.tr: First he concludes with a brief and plainly moving sentence, saying: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure (or will) to give you the kingdom." These words agree with what he had said against excessive and immoderate concern for food, and they teach that those whom God has destined by his eternal decree to inherit his heavenly kingdom ought not to fear want in this world. For why should they not hope for the support of this life from their heavenly Father, which is not denied even to beasts and birds, when they know they are to receive greater and eternal goods? But since there are many other things that terrify the godly, such as the small number of the faithful, the strength and power of their enemies, their constant plots and bloody schemes, and many other things of this kind, a general consolation must be drawn from here, by which we may strengthen ourselves against every kind of temptation.
