So that it may be more effective, each part of this saying will be examined.

units.la: Et primo quidem videre oportet, quos nam Dominus alloquatur, & quo nomine aut titulo eos compellet. Atqui ad discipulos hunc sermonem habitum fuisse supra Lucas ostendit. In horum numero tunc censebantur duodecim Apostoli cum septuaginta discipulis, de quibus capite decimo essedictum. Accesserunt his aliqui comites ex Galilaea, inter quos fere illustriores fuerunt aliquot mulieres, de quibus infra capite vigesimo tertio dicetur. Hos simul omnes alloquens amice admodum, eos pusillum gregem dicit.
units.tr: And first we must see whom the Lord addresses, and by what name or title he calls them. Now Luke shows above that this discourse was addressed to the disciples. Among these were then counted the twelve Apostles together with the seventy disciples, of whom it was said in the tenth chapter. Some companions from Galilee joined them, among whom the more notable were several women, of whom it will be spoken below in the twenty-third chapter. Addressing all of them together in a very friendly way, he calls them a little flock.

units.la: Vbi ante omnia obseruabis, Christi fideles gregem vocari. Nam dulcissimae consolationis plena est huius vocabuli consideratio. Vbi enim grex est, illic pastor quoque sit oportet, cum sine illo oues dispergi soleant, vt quae pro sua stoliditate in vnum convenire & gregis vnitate tueri non possint, nisi a pastore cogantur. Ergo qualescunque sint Christiani, pauci aut multi, illustres aut obscuri, diuites aut pauperes, firmi denique aut infirmi, grex tamen sunt, & pastorem habent, aeternum scilicet Dei Filium, quem Pater iam olim, & quidem ab aeterno, huic muneri destinauit. De hoc enim Isaias vaticinatus est: Ecce Deus veniet, ecce Dominus Deus veniet in robore, & brachium suum dominabitur per se: ecce merces eius cum eo, & opus eius ante ipsum. Pascet gregem suum vt pastor, & brachio suo congregabit agnos, in gremio suo feret, foetas autem suauiter ducet. Et ipse in Euangelio non semel se pastorem esse profitetur. Qualis autem pastor est? Sapiens nimirum & rei pastoritiae gnarus, non stultus, vt ille quem incurabilibus & poenitere nescijs Deus per Zachariam minatur. Nouit enim Christus oues suas, & quod de Cyro (qui eius typum gessit) scribitur, eum militum suorum omnium nomina tenuisse, hoc in primis in Christo locum habet, qui oui suarum nomina in coelis ascripta habet, & singulas etiam nominatim vocat. Nouit etiam pascua salubria, in quibus oues adolescere possint. Deinde fidelis est pastor, qui animam suam pro ouibus posuit, vt eas ex immanis illius leonis, diaboli nimirum faucibus eriperet, qui aeternum perditas volebat. Adhaec potentissimus & inuictus pastor est, ex cuius manu oues nemo potest rapere. Nam nemo potest (inquit) eas rapere ex manu Patris mei, ego autem & Pater vnum sumus. Quibus si addas, quae de seipso idem ille per Ezechielem dicit, nullum in eo fidissimi pastoris officium desiderabis. Vide Ezech. 34.
units.tr: Here, above all, you will observe that the faithful of Christ are called a flock. For the consideration of this word is full of the sweetest comfort. For where there is a flock, there must also be a shepherd, since sheep are usually scattered without him; by their own stupidity they cannot come together into one and be kept safe in the unity of the flock unless they are gathered by a shepherd. Therefore, whatever Christians may be, few or many, distinguished or obscure, rich or poor, strong or weak, they are nevertheless a flock, and they have a shepherd, namely the eternal Son of God, whom the Father appointed to this office long ago, indeed from eternity. Of him Isaiah prophesied: "Behold, God will come, behold the Lord God will come with strength, and his arm will rule for him; behold his reward is with him and his work before him. He will feed his flock like a shepherd, and with his arm he will gather the lambs, carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young." And he himself in the Gospel declares more than once that he is the shepherd. What sort of shepherd is he? Wise indeed, and skilled in the shepherd's task, not foolish like that one whom God threatens through Zechariah as incurable and unable to repent. For Christ knows his sheep, and what is written of Cyrus (who bore his type), that he knew the names of all his soldiers, holds first of all in Christ, who has the names of his sheep written in heaven, and calls each one of them by name. He also knows the wholesome pastures in which the sheep can grow. Then he is a faithful shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep, so that he might snatch them from the jaws of that fierce lion, namely the devil, who wished to destroy them for ever. Moreover, he is a most powerful and invincible shepherd, from whose hand no one can snatch the sheep. For, he says, no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand, and I and the Father are one. If you add to these the things that he himself says of himself through Ezekiel, you will find in him no duty of a most faithful shepherd lacking. See Ezek. 34.

units.la: At simul nos etiam nostri officij haec gregis & ouium nomina admonent. Harum enim est vocem pastoris sui nouisse, audita sequi, gregis vnitate tueri, neque hinc inde dispergi. Itaque nostrum quoque erit, pastorem vnicum agnoscere, huius verbum audire, impostorum vero & seductorum doctrinas vitare, Ecclesiae societate colere, a sectis nobis cauere, in periculis item omnibus ad vnum Christum confugere, & in hoc solo opem & salutem omnem sperare. Ita demum grex Filij Dei erimus, qui pro suis nunquam agnoscet eos, qui ipso relicto hinc inde dispergunt, & incerti doctrinis agitati fluctuant, neque ipsius verbo obediunt.
units.tr: But at the same time these names of flock and sheep also remind us of our own duty. For it is the part of sheep to know the voice of their shepherd, to follow when they hear it, to keep to the unity of the flock, and not to be scattered here and there. So it will be our part too to acknowledge him as the one shepherd, to hear his word, to avoid the teachings of impostors and deceivers, to cultivate fellowship with the Church, to beware of sects, and in all dangers to flee to Christ alone, and to hope for all help and salvation in him alone. Only thus shall we at last be the flock of the Son of God, whom he will never acknowledge as his own when they have abandoned him and scatter here and there, tossed about and wavering by uncertain doctrines, and do not obey his word.

units.la: Sed audiamus etiam, qualis grex sint Christi cultores: Paruus nimirum siue exiguus, tamen numero (si cum mundo aut huius seculi filijs conferantur) quam aestimatione. Nam etsi interdum longe lateque extendantur Ecclesiae pomaeria, & ad hanc nationes multae et populosissimae colligantur, tamen si mundum spectamus, semper verum esse deprehendetur, quod Christus dixit: Multos quidem esse vocatos, electos autem paucos. Est enim mundus hic totus in malo constitutus, & ideo plerique carnis sapientiam & desideria secuti in proprium exitium ruunt: vt iam de hypocritis nihil dicamus, qui cum Christum ore profiteantur, cum mundo tamen colludunt, & amicos habent a fide prorsus alienos. Vt vero cum impijs & prophanis collatione facta piorum grex admodum pusillus est: ita idem nullius in mundo existimationis sunt, & ab alijs quidem odio habentur, ab alijs aut stulti & dementes esse iudicantur, qui soli sapere & diuersam ab alijs salutis rationem sequi velint. Et hanc quidem Ecclesiae sortem ab ipsa rerum origine fuisse constat. Ante diluuium certe in immensum auctus est infelicis Caini posteritas, quae artium inuentione, vrbium aedificatione, potentia & opibus floruit, decrescente interim Sethi progenie & plerisque etiam ex ea degenerantibus, adeo vt patribus sanctis omnibus in hac vita defunctis, solus Noe cum octo animabus in arca seruatus Ecclesiae seminarium fuerit. Hoc ipsum de Abrahami & filiorum eius temporibus dici potest. Nec meliorem fuisse rerum conditionem Prophetis docentibus, eorum sermones abunde testantur. Isaias enim clamat: Nisi Dominus nobis aliquas seruasset reliquias, vt Sodoma & Gomorrha fuissemus. Et alibi se cum paucis discipulis portenti instar in Israele esse queritur. Idem de Christo & redemptionis per ipsum factae beneficio vaticinaturus, praefatur, paucos fore qui huic praedicationi credant, & Dei virtutem in Filio reuelatam agnoscant. Quod quàm verè ab illo dictum sit, Euan-gelica historia satis docet. Etsi enim Euangelium per totum orbem Apostoli prædicarint, & hinc inde Ecclesias constituerint, maior tamen gentium atq; Iudæorum pars in ignorantiæ & incredulitatis tenebris permansit, & Romani Imperatores per annos fere trecentos vsq; ad Constantini Magni tempora, Ecclesiam crudelissimè persecuti sunt. De nostris temporibus quid attinet dicere, quando res ipsa loquitur, pusillum esse verè credentium gregem, si cum reliqua totius mundi multitudine conferantur? Sunt autem vetera exempla probè observanda propter eos, qui quando de fide & religione agitur, ad hominum multitudinem, potentiam & authoritatem respiciunt. At si hæc ad veritatem aliquid momenti conferunt, Ægyptiorum Magos Mosi, Baalis sacerdotes Eliæ, Pharisæos deniq; & Scribas ipsi Christo & Apostolis anteponere oportebit. Quin ergo Dei consilium observemus, qui (vt Paulus docet) humilia & stulta huius mundi deligit, vt istius fastum deprimat, nosq; in illo vno gloriari dicamus. De Ecclesia autem ex Dei Verbo iudicari debet, ex quo illa nascitur: non ex hominum authoritate, quam Deus non magni facit.
units.tr: But let us also hear what sort of flock the worshippers of Christ are: small indeed, or few, yet in number (if they are compared with the world or with the children of this age) they are small, and in estimation even smaller. For although at times the boundaries of the Church are extended far and wide, and many and very populous nations are gathered to it, nevertheless, if we look at the world, what Christ said will always be found to be true: many are indeed called, but few are chosen. For this whole world is set in evil, and therefore most people, following the wisdom and desires of the flesh, rush to their own destruction; not to mention hypocrites, who while they profess Christ with their mouths, nevertheless collude with the world and have as friends men wholly alien to the faith. And just as the flock of the godly is very small when compared with the impious and profane, so the same godly have no esteem in the world; some hate them, and others judge them foolish and mad, because they alone wish to be wise and to follow a way of salvation different from others. And it is certain that this has been the lot of the Church from the very beginning of things. Before the Flood, indeed, the posterity of unhappy Cain increased immensely, and flourished through the invention of the arts, the building of cities, power and riches, while meanwhile the line of Seth declined, and many of them degenerated, so that when all the holy fathers had died in this life, Noah alone with eight souls in the ark was the seed-bed of the Church. The same can be said of the times of Abraham and his sons. That the condition of things was no better under the teaching of the prophets, their sermons amply bear witness. For Isaiah cries out: "Unless the Lord had left us some remnant, we would have been like Sodom and Gomorrah." And elsewhere he complains that he, with a few disciples, was like a portent in Israel. The same man, about to prophesy about Christ and the benefit of redemption made through him, foretells that few would believe this preaching and acknowledge the power of God revealed in the Son. How truly this was said by him, the Gospel history teaches enough. For although the Apostles preached the Gospel throughout the whole world and founded churches here and there, nevertheless the greater part of the Gentiles and Jews remained in the darkness of ignorance and unbelief, and the Roman emperors, for almost three hundred years, down to the time of Constantine the Great, most cruelly persecuted the Church. As for our own times, what need is there to say that, since the thing itself speaks, the flock of those who truly believe is small when compared with the rest of the multitude of the whole world? Yet old examples must be carefully observed, on account of those who, when matters of faith and religion are under discussion, look to the number, power and authority of men. But if these things contribute anything to the truth, it will be necessary to place the magicians of Egypt above Moses, the priests of Baal above Elijah, and finally the Pharisees and Scribes above Christ himself and the Apostles. Why then should we not observe the counsel of God, who (as Paul teaches) chooses the lowly and foolish things of this world, in order to humble its pride, and so that we may say that we glory in him alone? But the Church must be judged from the Word of God, from which it is born, and not from the authority of men, which God does not value much.

units.la: Quid autem gregi suo & singulis fidelibus Christus præcipit? Ne timeas, inquit. At hoc præcepto non obscure innuit, non defore vnquam timoris causam atq; materiam, si carnis iudicium audire velimus. Quid enim de hoc admonere opus erat, nisi essent, quæ nos terrere & fortissimus quibusque metum incutere possunt? Et sanè vt Satan regno suo difficulter cedit, ita mundus hic Veritatis lucem odit, neq; eos ferre potest, qui hanc secuti ab ipso secessionem faciunt. Hinc ergo omnis generis afflictiones atq; pericula oriuntur, quibus olim pij grauissimè exercitati sunt, & quæ hodie etiam ipsi experimur. Sed hic nos timere vetat Dominus. Quod nō ita accipi debet, quasi nos lapides aut truncos esse velit, qui nullis aduersis moveamur, sed ne metu nos ita superari patiamur præcipit, vt vel fidem negemus, vel aliqua in re nostrum negligamus officium. Estq; præceptum hoc perquam necessarium observatu. Nam vt in bello si timor militum animos occupet, nullo pudore aut periculo etiam in acie retineri possunt: ita in fidei negotio timor conceptus homines sui officii prorsus immemores & rerum omnium incertos reddit, simulq; pudorem omnem excutit, sicuti in Petri abnegatoris & multorum aliorum exemplis esse videre. Ideò præceptum hoc frequenter Deus ijs etiam olim inculcauit, qui inuicta animi constantia muniti videbantur: ex quorum numero Moses fuit, Iosua, Ieremias & alij quidam Prophetæ. Nobis ergo hoc ipsum dici putemus, & quoties terrorem aliquem Satan aut mundus concitant, consolationis huius recordatione fidem lad̃scentem fulciamus: meminerimus itèm nimium ignaui & degeneris animi argumentum esse, si ijs nos per terreri sinamus, de quibus toties sumus admoniti, quæ & nobis iampridem præmeditata esse debebant. Quis enim militem in castris ferat, quem classici tantùs terret, & qui non potius hoc audito pugnandi ardorem animo concipit?
units.tr: But what does Christ command his flock and each of the faithful? "Fear not," he says. By this command he clearly indicates that there will never be lack of cause or material for fear, if we are willing to listen to the judgment of the flesh. For why would it have been necessary to give this warning, unless there were things that could terrify us and strike fear even into the bravest? Indeed, just as Satan yields his kingdom with difficulty, so this world hates the light of truth and cannot bear those who follow it and withdraw from the world. From this arise afflictions and dangers of every kind, by which the godly were severely tried in former times, and which we ourselves experience today. Yet here the Lord forbids us to fear. This must not be understood as if he wished us to be stones or logs, unmoved by any adversity; rather, he commands that we not allow ourselves to be so overcome by fear that we either deny the faith or neglect our duty in any matter. This precept is very necessary to observe. For just as in war, if fear takes hold of the soldiers' minds, they cannot be held in the battle line by any sense of shame or danger, so in the matter of faith, fear that has taken hold makes people utterly forgetful of their duty and uncertain of everything, and at the same time shakes off all sense of shame, as we can see from the examples of Peter, who denied his Lord, and of many others. Therefore God often impressed this command even on those who seemed armed with an invincible steadfastness of spirit, among whom were Moses, Joshua, Jeremiah and certain other prophets. Let us therefore consider that this has been said to us as well, and whenever Satan or the world stirs up some terror, let us strengthen our faltering faith by remembering this consolation. Let us also remember that it is a sign of a very slothful and degenerate spirit if we allow ourselves to be terrified by those things about which we have been warned so often, and which ought to have been considered in advance long ago. For who would bring a soldier into the camp if he is terrified by the mere sound of the trumpet, and who would not rather, on hearing it, feel his eagerness to fight kindled?

units.la: Porrò rationem sui præcepti adducit Dominus: Nam visum est Patri vestro dare vobis Regnum. Id verò de Regno cœlorum dicit, cuius nomine vniuersa hominum salus & beata immortalitas intelligitur, in qua omnis dolor & gemitus cessabit, & omnis lachryma abstergetur, nec aliquid erit, quod nos terrere possit, aut quod metuere debeamus. Habent autem singula verba emphasim. Rursus enim Dei Patris meminit, & hunc nostrum Patrem vocat, quò minus de eius bona erga nos volun-tate dubitemus. Imò dum Patrem suum nobiscum communem facit, nos ex iure suos regni illius coheredes fore docet. Deinde Patri vestro (inquit) visum est, siue placuit. In Græco verbum εὐδόκησεν ponitur, quod beneuolentiam siue misericordiam gratuitã denotat, cuius non alia causa sit, quàm quod ita placeat Deo, qui homines cupiat saluos fieri, & ita nos dilexerit, vt Filium quoq; vnigenitum pro nobis daret. Ad illam verò nos remittit, vt intelligamus salutem nostram non ex nostris meritis pendere, sed in libera & gratuita misericordia Dei fundatam esse, & proinde nostra indignitatis sensu non tereamur. Adhæc irrevocabile Dei decretum hæc vox exprimit. Si enim ita placuit aut visum est Deo omnipotenti, cui in omnes creaturas ius est & imperiū, & qui ideò Dominus exercituū dicitur, quis obstabit, quò minus quod decreuit perficiat? Domino exercituū aliquid constituente (inquit Isaias) quis illud faciet irritum? Et Dauid: Consilium Domini in æternum perstat, & decreta cordis eius per omnia sæcula. Quid autem visum est Patri? Vobis dare Regnum, qui ni mirum paruus & contemptissimus grex estis, & quos hic mundus vix dignos tenset quos terra ferat, L l quiq̃ comuni cum alijs hominibus aura fruantur. Vobis, inquam, Regnum dare placuit, vt mecum eius gloria atq; felicitate fruamini. Exprimitur hic magna Christianorum dignitas, quos Dei Filius (vt in Apocalypsi scribitur) Reges fecit, non quidem terrenos, sed tales qui mundo, peccato, carne propria & eius desiderijs superiores facti, olim in coelis cum ipso regnabunt. Debet nos illius consideratio consolari, ne vllis aduersis succumbamus. Cur enim huius seculi infamia multum moueatur, qui se coelestis & aeternae gloriae haeredem fore audit? Cur egestate metuat, qui regni Dei thesaurus ad se pertinere credit? Cur famem & sitim indigne ferat, qui olim ad mensam Iesu Christi beato immortalitatis nectare & ambrosia saturabitur? Cur exilium formidet, qui patriam & regnum in coelis habet? Cur item credentium paucitate offendatur, qui in magno illo die cum omnibus electis & innumeris Angelorum myriadibus in coelis viuet? Denique cur mors illis acerba & grauis videatur, qui vitam aeternam sibi promissam & paratam sciunt? Aut cur hostium fidei minus & dirus conspectu consternetur, qui Christo redemptore gaudet, qui in medio inimicorum suorum dominatur? Vides ergo breui hac sententia consolationem multiplicem contineri, quae sola nobis aduersus omnia potest sufficere, quae carni terrorem & formidinem incutiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord gives the reason for his command: "For it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom." He speaks here of the kingdom of heaven, by whose name is understood the whole salvation of mankind and blessed immortality, in which all pain and groaning will cease, and every tear will be wiped away, and there will be nothing that can terrify us or that we ought to fear. Moreover, each of these words carries emphasis. Again he mentions God the Father, and calls him our Father, so that we may not doubt his good will toward us. Indeed, by making the Father common to himself and to us, he teaches that we are by right his co-heirs of that kingdom. Next, "it has pleased your Father" (he says), or "it has seemed good." In the Greek the word eudokēsen [εὐδόκησεν] is used, which denotes goodwill or free mercy, whose only cause is that it pleases God, who desires men to be saved and has so loved us that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. By this word he refers us to that goodwill, so that we may understand that our salvation does not depend on our merits, but is founded on the free and gratuitous mercy of God, and therefore we should not be worn down by a sense of our unworthiness. Furthermore, this expression conveys the irrevocable decree of God. For if it has so pleased or seemed good to almighty God, who has right and dominion over all creatures and who is therefore called the Lord of hosts, who will stand in the way, so that he does not accomplish what he has decreed? "When the Lord of hosts has determined something" (says Isaiah), "who will make it void?" And David: "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, and the thoughts of his heart to all generations." But what has seemed good to the Father? To give you the kingdom, who are certainly a small and most despised flock, whom this world scarcely thinks worthy of the earth that bears them, and who enjoy the same air as other men. To you, I say, it has pleased him to give the kingdom, so that you may share with me in its glory and happiness. Here is expressed the great dignity of Christians, whom the Son of God (as is written in the Apocalypse) has made kings, not indeed earthly kings, but such as, raised above the world, sin, their own flesh and its desires, will one day reign with him in heaven. Consideration of this ought to console us, so that we do not yield to any adversity. For why should a man be much moved by the disgrace of this age, when he hears that he will be heir of heavenly and eternal glory? Why should he fear poverty, who believes that the treasure of the kingdom of God belongs to him? Why should he endure hunger and thirst unworthily, when one day at the table of Jesus Christ he will be filled with the blessed nectar and ambrosia of immortality? Why should he dread exile, who has a fatherland and kingdom in heaven? Likewise, why should he be offended by the small number of believers, who in that great day will live in heaven with all the elect and countless myriads of angels? Finally, why should death seem bitter and grievous to those who know that eternal life has been promised and prepared for them? Or why should he be dismayed by the sight of the enemies of the faith, however fierce, who rejoices in Christ the Redeemer, who reigns in the midst of his enemies? You see, then, that this single sentence contains a manifold consolation, which alone can suffice for us against all those things that strike terror and dread into the flesh.

units.la: Vsus diuitiarum
units.tr: The use of riches

units.la: Caeterum quia de opum vanitate & incertitudine supra Dominus disseruit, simulq; de victu & reliquis necessarijs solicitos esse prohibuit, poterant hinc quaestiones duae enasci. Prima, quis ergo diuitiarum huius seculi vsus sit, quas ex Dei benedictione interdum sanctissimis quoque dari videmus? Altera, num omnino nefas sit aliquem sibi ipsi & suis prospicere? Ad utrumque ergo Dominus respondet, & ita quidem, vt & verum bonorum temporariorum vsum tradat, & simul ostendat, qua ratione homo sibi commodissime prospicere & diuitias solidas, & fere felices comparare possit. Ad primam quaestionem pertinet praeceptum hoc: Vendite bona vestra, & date eleemosynam. Quorum verborum sensus germanus diligenter inuestigari debet, eo quod omnibus seculis inuenti sint, qui de opibus male iudicarunt, quasi per se noxia & indignae sint, quae ab ijs possideantur, qui virtuti & pietati operam dare instituerunt. Nam gentium in historijs Crates Thebanus narratur immensum auri pondus abiecisse, cum animum ad philosophiam appulisset. Inter Christianos autem homines olim reperti fuerunt, quibus nefas videbatur, aliquid proprium possidere. Hodie Monachi paupertatem voluntariam vouent, & nonnulli eorum religio est pecuniam manibus contrectare: Anabaptistae autem Platonicam bonorum omnium communionem pertinaciter urgent, & Christianos esse negant eos, qui non omnibus relictis hinc inde vagantur, & alijs oneri sunt. Sed infinitae rationes sunt, quibus omnium istorum sententia confutantur. Primo enim Scripturae Sacrae veres terrae prouentus & diuitias inter Dei benedictiones numerant, quibus cultorum suorum pietatem ille soleat etiam in hoc seculo remunerare. Deinde ditissimos suos fecisse constat multos ex sanctissimis Dei cultoribus, & inter hos Abrahamum quoque, quem credentium omnium patrem Apostolus vocat. Sed & fuerunt tam in Lege quam Euangelio prohibetur, quod frustra fieret, si quid proprium habere non liceret. Adhaec diuitibus praecepta dantur, vt opibus suis vti debeant, sicut supra audiuimus. Postremo repugnat illorum sententia Ecclesiae primitiua mos, in qua bonorum communio magis quam vllis vnquam temporibus locum habuit. Nec enim tunc quisquam cogebatur, vt sua bona in commune deponeret, sed cuiq; liberum erat de suis prout ipsi videbatur constituere, sicut Petri verba ad Ananiam diserte docent. Et multi tunc suas domus & alias facultates retinuerunt. Quid, quod ne vendere quidem licuisset, si quid proprium habere non liceret? Ita enim alijs peccandi fuissent authores, quod ab homine Christiano alienissimum esse debet. Non ergo secundum literam Christi verba vrgeri, nec generale praeceptum ex ijsdem colligi potest, nisi illum toti scripturae contradicere, velimus putare. Quid ergo sibi vult? Vt rum diuitiarum vsum tradit, qui est, vt beneficentia erga quosuis Iudeos amus, maxime autem eos, qui nostra ope indigent. Quia autem multum nos remoratur opu vsus, verbis vehementioribus vtitur, vt ostendat, adeo non negligendos esse miseros & egenos, vt si reddituus annui, & ea quibus abundamus, non sufficiant illis iuuandis, non grauemur praedia quoq; & alia bona vendere. Itaq; vt dendi verbo animi promptitudinem requirit. Quae enim vanum exponimus, ea omnino cupimus dirabi, & emptores nobis obtingere gaudemus. Et hoc quidem in beneficentia in primis requiritur. Nam hilarem datorem diligit Dominus, & egentibus quoq; magis grata sunt nostra officia, sinos illa prompto & alacri animo præstare videat. Ideo Dauid dispergendi verbo utitur, quando de homine vere pij & iusti liberalitate erga pauperes sermonem facit. Et huc pertinet, quod alibi Christus monet, ne sinistra manus norit quid dextera faciat, id est, ne quis sinister & maleuolus affectus concurrat, quo nostra beneficentia vitietur. Deinde vt nostra bona vendamus iubet, ita innuens nos ex proprijs facultatibus, non ex alienis largiri debere, quod ipsum Tobias quoq; diligenter filio suo mandauit. Nec enim Deo probatur ex alieno facta liberalitas: quia quod nostrum non est, legitimis dominis restituere debemus, quod nisi fiat, furti arguimur. Quod Zachæus obseruauit, dum pollicetur, quod restitutione secundum Legem facta, dimidium suorum bonorum pauperibus elargiri velit. Nihil ergo proficiunt homines iniqui, qui vbi contra humanitatis leges vsuras, rapinas, fraudibus, sanguinis denique effusione diuites facti sunt, partem aliquam pauperibus decidunt, quasi cum Deo pacisci velint, vt reliqua præda ipsis frui permittat. Quid enim hoc aliud est, quàm illum in sceleris societatem vocare, quod nemo vir bonus patienter ferre posset? Postremò, Date (inquit) eleemosynam. Hæc Græcis à misericordia nomen habet, & fontem verę beneficentiæ exprimit, qui est alienæ misericordiæ respectus, & ex hac enascens animi commotio. Non ergo eleemosynas dant, qui vt ab hominibus conspiciantur & sibi laudem parent, vel alicuius priuati commodi causa egenis aliquid largiuntur. At simul admonemur, in quos beneficentiam exercere debeamus. In omnes videlicet, qui miseri & egentes nostram opem requirunt, vel ea opus habent: de quo in Samaritani parabola prolixè dictum est. In eo enim nos Dei Patris nostri exemplum imitari conuenit, qui erga omnes beneficus est, & (vt in Psalmis scribitur) aperit manum suam, & omnia implet benedictione, omniumque animantium desiderium saturat. Præ aliis tamen nobis commendati esse debent domestici fidei, ne cum publico Christianæ religionis ludibrio egestatis exempla fiant. Fuerunt in hoc diligentissimi primitiuæ Ecclesiæ fideles, qui exteris quoque & proculdissitis sua liberalitate subuenerunt. At quid hodie fiat, nimis notum est, & multorum lachrymis deploratur.
units.tr: Since the Lord has spoken above about the vanity and uncertainty of wealth, and has also forbidden us to be anxious about food and other necessities, two questions could arise from this. The first is what the proper use of the riches of this age is, since we see that God sometimes gives them even to the most holy. The second is whether it is altogether wrong for a person to provide for himself and his own. The Lord answers both, and in such a way that he both teaches the true use of temporal goods and shows how a person may most conveniently provide for himself and acquire solid and almost happy riches. To the first question belongs this precept: "Sell what you have, and give alms." The true sense of these words must be carefully investigated, because in every age there have been people who have judged wealth badly, as if it were in itself harmful and unworthy to be possessed by those who have set themselves to pursue virtue and piety. Among the Gentiles, for example, we read in the histories that Crates of Thebes threw away a huge weight of gold when he turned his mind to philosophy. Among Christians too there were once those who thought it wrong to own anything privately. Today monks vow voluntary poverty, and some of them consider it a religious scruple even to handle money. The Anabaptists, meanwhile, stubbornly press the Platonic communion of all goods, and deny that those are Christians who do not leave everything behind, wander about from place to place, and become a burden to others. But there are countless reasons by which the opinions of all these people are refuted. First, the Holy Scriptures count the fruits of the earth and riches among God's blessings, by which he is accustomed to reward the piety of his worshippers even in this age. Next, it is plain that many of the most holy worshippers of God became very rich, and among them Abraham too, whom the Apostle calls the father of all believers. Moreover, the Law and the Gospel both forbid theft and fraud, which would be pointless if it were not permitted to have anything of one's own. Besides, instructions are given to the rich that they should use their riches, as we heard above. Finally, the practice of the primitive Church contradicts their opinion, for in that Church the communion of goods had a place more than at any other time. For no one was then compelled to put his goods into a common fund; rather, each was free to arrange his own property as he himself saw fit, as Peter's words to Ananias plainly teach. And many then kept their houses and other property. Moreover, if it were not permitted to have anything of one's own, could one even sell? For then others would have been made authors of sin, which ought to be utterly alien to a Christian man. Therefore the words of Christ cannot be pressed according to the letter, nor can a general precept be drawn from them, unless we wish to suppose that he contradicts the whole of Scripture. What, then, does he mean? He teaches the true use of riches, which is that we show kindness to any of the needy, but especially to those who require our help. And because the use of wealth often holds us back, he uses stronger words, to show that the poor and needy are not to be neglected to such an extent that, if our annual income and the things in which we abound are not enough to help them, we should not hesitate to sell even estates and other goods. Thus, as with the word "sell", the word "give" requires readiness of mind. For the things we put up for sale we certainly want to be sold off, and we rejoice to find buyers. And this readiness is especially required in beneficence. For the Lord loves a cheerful giver, and our services are more welcome even to the needy when they see that we render them with a prompt and eager mind. For this reason David uses the word "scatter" when he speaks of the generosity toward the poor of a man who is truly pious and just. And to this belongs what Christ says elsewhere, that the left hand should not know what the right hand does; that is, that no sinister and ill-willed feeling should mingle in, by which our beneficence would be spoiled. Next, when he bids us sell our goods, he signals that we ought to give from our own resources, not from what belongs to others, which Tobit also diligently charged his son. For God does not approve a gift made from what is another's: what is not ours we must restore to its lawful owners, and if we do not, we are charged with theft. Zacchaeus observed this, when he promised that, once restitution had been made according to the Law, he would give half of his goods to the poor. Wicked men therefore accomplish nothing when, having grown rich against the laws of humanity by usury, robbery, fraud, and finally the shedding of blood, they give some part to the poor, as if they wished to bargain with God that he would allow them to enjoy the rest of the plunder. For what is this but calling God into partnership in crime, something no good man could patiently endure? Finally, he says, "Give alms." This word in Greek takes its name from mercy, and expresses the source of true beneficence, which is regard for another's misery and the emotion of heart that springs from it. Therefore those who give alms in order to be seen by men and win praise for themselves, or who give something to the needy for some private advantage, are not giving alms at all. At the same time we are reminded toward whom we ought to exercise beneficence: namely toward all who are wretched and needy and seek our help, or stand in need of it. This was treated at length in the parable of the Good Samaritan. For in this we ought to imitate the example of God our Father, who is kind to all, and (as is written in the Psalms) opens his hand and fills all things with blessing, and satisfies the desire of every living creature. Nevertheless, those who are of the household of faith ought to be commended to us above others, lest examples of want be made to the public mockery of the Christian religion. The faithful of the primitive Church were most diligent in this, and they gave help by their generosity even to strangers and those very far away. But what is done today is only too well known, and is lamented with the tears of many.

units.la: Quia autem carni graue & iniquum videtur sua alijs largiri, & (quod dicitur) proprium genium fraudare, vt aliorum inopiæ succurras, alteram quoq; doctrinam subijcit Christus, quæ & amplissimæ retributionis promissionem continet, & simul ostendit, eam demum certissimam tutissimamq; solidas diuitias comparandi rationem esse, si egentibus liberaliter largiamur ea, quibus opus habent. Parate (inquit) vobis crumenas, quæ non veterascunt, id est, recondite vestra sic vt qmitti non possint, sicuti amittuntur quæcunque in crumenas vetustate consumptas & pertusas homines reponunt. Et huius modum vel rationem mox exponit: Thesaurum videlicet parate in cœlis, qui nunquam deficiat: quo fur non appropinquat, & vbi tinea non corrumpit. Pulchrè autem Dominus infelicem diuitiarum huius seculi conditionem exprimit, quando furum & tinearum, & (vt Matthæus annotauit) eruginis quoque facit mentionem. Ita enim docet, illas infinitis casibus obnoxias esse, nec vnquam tam bene custodiri posse, quin aliqua tandem earum iactura fiat. Nam vt nihil aliud accidat, metalla rubigine exeduntur, vestes pretiosæ à tineis & vermicolis arroduntur, fruges in horreis conditæ à muribus, & alijs animalculis devorantur, vina in doliis acescunt & fugiunt, pecora morbis contabescunt. Sed hisce incommodis accedunt tempestates, quæ opulentos terra mariq; infestant: obrepunt fures: qui clam pecunias, vestes & quæcunq; alia auferunt: irruūt violenti raptores: qui omnia dissipant: oriuntur subita incendia, quæ ditissimos quoque ad extremam egestatem adducunt: lites mouent sycophantæ, & insidiosis causidicorum artibus adiuti aliena bona ad se transferunt: filij item prodigi aut rixatores maxima eorum parte parentes interdum spoliant. Taceo nunc eos, qui diuitias sibi quasi ex manibus effluere sentiunt, neq; ipsi rationem possunt reddere, qua illas amittant. Tot, inquam, insidijs & casibus obnoxiæ sunt opes, vt non temere veterū quidam aurum præmetu pallere dixerint. Verè ergo in crumenas pertusas recondunt sua, quicunque abiecto pietatis studio diuitijs coaceruandis inuigilant. Nam etsi nihil horum accidat, ipsis tamen quando minimè putant moriendum esse, & eiusmodi opes raro ad tertium vsque hæredē deueniunt. Quæ ergo stultitia, vel dementia potius est, teipsum fatigare, vt opes tineis, furibus, erugini, incendijs alijsq; casibus congeras, quarum possessio periculosa est, iactura autem animum incredibili dolore excruciat? Verissimè enim Satyricus dixit: Ploratur lachrymis amissa pecunia verè. Quid ergo (inquis) faciam? Quod Christus iubet, ut thesaurū nobis in cœlis recondamus. Id ve-rò faciunt, qui procul relictis huius seculi curis & insano diiescendi studio, ȳni Deo fidunt, vitā ca-lestem viuere studēt, opes autem & quæcunq; præterea habent, in Dei manus deponunt, & ab eius prouidentia atq; benedictione toti pendēt. Qui ita affecti sunt, ij si opus sit et sic Dei vocatio iubeat, opes suas propter ipsum alacri mente relinquunt, sicuti olim Abrahamū, Mosem, Apostolos & mul-tos alios fecisse legimus. Iide dum eis illarū possessio cœditur, liberaliter egentibus quibusuis succur-runt, & quoad animi voluntate omnia sua cum reliquis Christi membris communia habent. Itaq; in crumenas minimè pertusas neq; vetustate pereuntes, sed in ipsius Dei æterni atq; immortalis sinum sua reponunt, qui remunerator est fidelissimus, neq; suis quicquam deseri patitur. Et huc promissio-nes Christi pertinent: Quisquis reliquerit domos, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut vxorem, aut filios, aut agros propter nomen meum, centuplum recipiet, & vitæ æternæ hæredi-tate fruetur. Item quod in nonissimo suo aduentu ad iudicium suis dicet: Amen amen dico vobis, quod fecistis vni ex hisce fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Quibus cōsentit Solomon, qui Domino eū fœnerari dicit, qui pauperi largitur. At vtinam in horum consideratione frequentiores hodie esse-mus. Quàm multos enim est videre, qui tunc demū se rebus suis prospexisse arbitrantur, si pecunias suas dent ad vsurā, & apud fœneratores deponant, à quibus redditus maiores quàm vulgò soleat re-cipiunt. At quantò satius erat facultates omnes apud Deum deponere, quàm neglecto verę pietatis officio insuper peccatis etiā alienis communicare? Cyrus olim Crœso suadenti, ut pecunias accumula-ret, respondebat: Vt thesauros apud me collectos habeā iubes, ut propter eos inuidiæ sim & odio, fi-damq; custodibus mercenarijs, quos ijs præfecerim: at ego dum amicos diuites reddo, hos puto mihi esse thesauros & custodes simul cum meipsius tum meorum bonorum. Et poëta prophanus ait:
units.tr: But because it seems grievous and unfair to the flesh to give its own to others, and (as the saying goes) to cheat one's own genius in order to relieve the poverty of others, Christ adds another teaching, which contains both a promise of very ample reward, and at the same time shows that the most certain and safest way to acquire solid riches is to give generously to the needy what they require. "Make for yourselves purses," he says, "which do not grow old," that is, store up your treasure so that it cannot be lost, as whatever people put away in purses that wear out with age and become full of holes is lost. And he soon explains the manner or method of this: namely, lay up a treasure in heaven that never fails, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. The Lord expresses beautifully the unhappy condition of the riches of this age when he mentions thieves and moths, and (as Matthew noted) rust too. For he teaches that these riches are exposed to endless accidents, and that they can never be kept so safely that some loss of them does not at last occur. For even if nothing else happens, metals are eaten away by rust, costly garments are gnawed by moths and grubs, grain stored in barns is devoured by mice and other little creatures, wine in casks turns sour and leaks away, and cattle waste away from disease. Added to these troubles are storms that harass the wealthy by land and sea; thieves creep in, who secretly carry off money, clothing, and whatever else; violent plunderers rush in, who scatter everything; sudden fires break out, which reduce even the richest to utter want; sycophants stir up lawsuits, and aided by the crafty tricks of advocates, they transfer others' goods to themselves; and prodigal or quarrelsome sons, for the most part, sometimes despoil their parents. I say nothing now of those who feel their riches slipping, as it were, through their fingers, and cannot themselves give any account of how they are lost. Such, I say, are the snares and accidents to which wealth is exposed, that the ancient writer rightly said that gold often turns pale with fear. Truly, then, those who, having cast off the pursuit of piety, keep watch to heap up riches, store their goods in purses full of holes. For even if none of these things happens to them, they will still have to die when they least expect it, and such riches rarely pass to a third heir. What folly, or rather madness, is it then to wear yourself out heaping up riches for moths, thieves, rust, fires, and other accidents, a possession that is dangerous, and whose loss tortures the mind with incredible grief? For the satirist spoke most truly: "Money lost is truly wept over with tears." "What then," you ask, "shall I do?" What Christ commands: lay up a treasure for yourselves in heaven. Those truly do this who, having left far behind the cares of this age and the mad pursuit of getting rich, trust in the living God, strive to live a heavenly life, and place their wealth and whatever else they have into the hands of God, depending wholly on his providence and blessing. Those who are so disposed, if the call of God requires it, leave their riches for his sake with a willing mind, just as we read that Abraham, Moses, the Apostles, and many others did of old. And while the possession of these things is taken from them, they generously help the needy of every kind, and in their willing mind they hold all that they have in common with the rest of Christ's members. And so they put their goods not into purses that are not full of holes and do not perish with age, but into the bosom of the eternal and immortal God himself, who is the most faithful rewarder, and who allows nothing entrusted to him to be lost. To this belong the promises of Christ: "Whoever has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life." Likewise what he will say to his own at his final coming to judgment: "Truly, truly I say to you, what you did to one of these least brothers of mine, you did to me." Solomon agrees with these, who says that he who gives to the poor lends to the Lord. But would that we were more frequent today in considering these things! For how many are there to be seen who think they have then provided for their goods, if they lend their money at interest and deposit it with moneylenders, from whom they receive greater returns than is usual! But how much more fitting it would be to deposit all one's resources with God, rather than, neglecting the true duty of piety, to share in the sins of others as well! Cyrus once answered Croesus, who urged him to accumulate money: "You bid me have treasures gathered and kept by me, so that I may be an object of envy and hatred on their account, and trust them to mercenary guardians whom I have set over them; but I, while I make my friends rich, consider these to be my treasures and my guardians, both of myself and of my goods." And a secular poet says:

units.la: Extra fortunam est, quicquid donatur amicis:
units.tr: Whatever is given to friends lies beyond the reach of fortune;

units.la: Quas dederis, solas semper habebis opes.
units.tr: the riches you have given away are the only wealth you will always keep.

units.la: Quòd si isti ea demum cum lucro certo depositā putarunt, quæ amicis dantur, nimium crassi & igno-rantes sunt, qui sua in Christi amicos & fratres conferre nolunt, ne aliquando ipsis desit vnde vi-uant. Sed magnas suæ stultitiæ pœnas dabunt, quando ærugo & tineæ (vt Iacobus scribit) quæ bona & vestes ipsorum eroferunt, eos inhumanitatis conuincent, & Dei Filius in magno illo die sibi ne-gatum iudicabit, quod minimo ex suis fratribus illi negarunt.
units.tr: But if these people think that only what is given to friends is laid up with a sure profit, they are too gross and ignorant. They are unwilling to contribute their goods to the friends and brothers of Christ, lest they ever lack the means to live. Yet they will pay heavy penalties for their folly, when rust and moths (as James writes) consume their goods and clothing, and they are convicted of inhumanity. On that great day the Son of God will judge that what they refused to the least of his brothers was refused to him.

units.la: Sed ipsum Dominū audiamus sui præcepti ratione reddentē: Vbi enim thesaurus vester est, illic & cor vestrum erit. Quo dicto docet, necessarium omnino esse, ut thesauros nobis in cælo recon-damus, nisi à Deo prorsus deficere libeat. Thesauri enim nomine idē denotat, quod vulgo Summū bonum dicunt, & generalis hæc sententia est, atq; vsu aut experientia quotidiana probatur. Nam fieri non potest, quin cor & animum totum homo ei rei addicat, in qua summū bonum & felicita-tem suam constitere sibi ipsi persuasit. Itaq; qui hoc honoribus huius seculi tribuit, huius animam am-bito occupat: qui in voluptatibus beatitudinem collocat, eius mens circa comessationes, ludos, libidi-nies vagas & alia huius generis studia occupatur: qui verò ex multiplici rerū cognitione se felicem fore sperat, huius cogitationes & studia in librorū plurium lectione & rerum vsu vario versantur. Similiter qui Summum hominis bonum in diuitiis statuunt, horū corda his solis affixa sunt, deq; ijs accumulandis dies noctesq; cogitant. At cùm Deus cor totū sibi vendicet, seq; vnū tota anima & o-mnibus viribus diligi atq; coli velit, nunquā certè pro suis seruis eos agnoscet, qui cor suū rebus & studijs alijs mancipauerunt. Rectè ergo Christus iubet thesaurū in cœlis reconditū habere, vt eius desiderio inflāmati, relictis huius seculi studijs cœlestia meditemur, & vitā viuamus nostra profes-sione digna. Quo sensu Paulus quoq; cùm Colos.ad vitæ cœlestis studiū hortaretur, Christū ipsum in cœlis monstrat, in quo vita nostra adeoq; summū bonū hominū, abscondituš sit. Interea admonet nos locus iste, quàm multiplex peccatum sit auaritia. Hæc enim causa est, vt contra charitatis leges fra-tres egenos negligamus, vt contra ius & æquum alienā inuadamus, & nobilissimā hominis partem, mentem siue animum turpi seruitute grauemus. Eadem omnia pietatis exercitia impedit, preces ni-mirū & Verbi diuini studiū, dum cordis nostri cogitationes etiā inter illa alio auocat. Deniq; idolo-latras reddit, vt opes Dei loco nobis sint, quando spem & fiduciam omnē in his habemus collocatā. Fugiamus ergo tam noxia & multiplicem pestem, & thesaurū in cœlis recondamus, quo fruemur, si Iesum
units.tr: But let us hear the Lord himself giving the reason for his command: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." By this saying he teaches that we must absolutely store up treasures for ourselves in heaven, unless we are willing to fall away from God altogether. By "treasure" he means what the common people call the chief good. This is a general truth, and it is proved by daily use and experience. For it cannot be that a man devotes his heart and whole mind to the thing in which he has persuaded himself that his chief good and happiness lie. So whoever places this in the honours of this age occupies his soul with ambition; whoever locates blessedness in pleasures has his mind taken up with feasting, games, wanton lusts and other pursuits of this kind; whoever hopes to become happy through the wide knowledge of many things has his thoughts and studies occupied in reading many books and in various experience of things. Likewise, those who place the chief good of man in riches have their hearts fastened to these alone, and they think day and night about piling them up. But since God claims the whole heart for himself, and wishes to be loved and worshipped as the one and only object of the whole soul and all our strength, he will certainly never acknowledge as his servants those who have given their hearts over to other things and pursuits. Christ rightly commands us to have a treasure laid up in heaven, so that, inflamed with desire for it, we may set aside the pursuits of this age and meditate on heavenly things, and live a life worthy of our profession. Paul too, in the same sense, when he urged the Colossians to the pursuit of the heavenly life, pointed to Christ himself in heaven, in whom our life and so the chief good of men is hidden. Meanwhile this passage warns us how manifold a sin covetousness is. For it is the cause of our neglecting needy brothers against the laws of charity, of our seizing what belongs to others against right and justice, and of burdening the noblest part of man, his mind or soul, with shameful slavery. It also hinders all the exercises of piety, namely prayer and the study of the divine Word, since it draws the thoughts of our heart away even during these. Finally, it makes us idolaters, so that riches take the place of God for us, when we place all our hope and trust in them. Let us therefore flee so harmful and manifold a plague, and store up our treasure in heaven, where we shall enjoy it, if we have embraced Jesus

units.la: Coloss. 3. fi Iesum Christum fide constanti & per charitatem agente amplexi fuerimus, qui arca illa fœderis est, in qua omnes thesauros scientiæ & cognitionis, gratiæ item suæ & regni cælorum vitæq; æternæ nobis Pater proposuit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Coloss. 3. If we have embraced Jesus Christ with constant faith and working through love, who is that ark of the covenant in which the Father has set before us all the treasures of knowledge and understanding, and likewise of his grace, the kingdom of heaven and eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXI.

units.la: Sint lumbi vestri præcincti, & lucernæ accensæ: & vos similes estote iis, qui expectant quando dominus suus reuersurus sit à nuptiis: vt cum venerit ac pulsauerit, statim aperiant ei. Beati serui illi, quos cùm venerit dominus, inueniet vigilantes. Amen dico vobis, quòd præcinget se, & faciet vt discumbant, & prodiens ministrabit eis. Et si venerit secunda vigilia, & si tertia vigilia venerit, atque ita inuenerit, beati sunt serui illi. Hoc autem scitote, si sciret paterfamilias, qua hora fur venturus sit, vigi laret, nec sineret perfodi domum suam. Et vos igitur estote parati: quia qua hora non putatis Filius hominis veniet.
units.tr: Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning; and be you like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open to him immediately. Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he cometh, shall find watching. Amen I say to you, that he will gird himself, and make them sit down to meat, and passing will minister unto them. And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find them so, blessed are those servants. But this know ye, that if the goodman of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would watch, and not suffer his house to be broken open. Be you also then ready, for at what hour you think not, the Son of man will come.

units.la: Dominus & seruator noster, Iesus Christus, non solum æternæ salutis rationem perspicuè tradit, & vt eam fide constanti amplectamur monet: verumetiā fideliter vitijs omnibus medetur, quæ nos à salutis via reuocare, & synceram fidei professionem impedire solent. Apparet hoc tum alibi, tum in tota eius doctrina, quæ hoc Capite describitur. Quia enim ad fidei constantiam & eius confessionem hortatus erat, mox obstacula remouit, quæ multis causam præbent, vt à fide omnino deficiant, aut saltem ignavo & seruili metu superati eam turpiter dissimulent. At quia illa remouisse non satis est propter innatam nobis socordiam, quæ in rebus diuinis nunquam non obrepit, denuo ad adhortationes nunc redit, vt omnibus huius mundi curis atq; studijs procul abiectis, singuli suum officium faciant, neue vlla mora aut difficultate sese superari patiantur, quo minus in statione sibi à Deo commissa maneant. Continet autem locus iste vniuersam vitæ nostræ, quam in terris agimus, conditionem elegantibus parabolis adumbratam, & proinde dignissimus est, quem diligenter consideremus.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ not only sets out clearly the way of eternal salvation and admonishes us to embrace it with a steadfast faith, but also faithfully heals all those vices which are wont to call us back from the way of salvation and to hinder a sincere profession of faith. This appears both elsewhere and throughout the whole of his teaching which is described in this chapter. For since he had urged us to constancy of faith and to its confession, he at once removed the obstacles which provide many people with a reason to fall away from the faith altogether, or at least, overcome by a lazy and servile fear, to dissemble it shamefully. But because removing these is not enough, on account of the sloth innate in us, which always creeps into divine matters, he now returns again to exhortations, so that, with all the cares and pursuits of this world cast far away, each one may do his duty, and that no delay or difficulty may allow him to be overcome, so that he does not remain in the station committed to him by God. This passage, moreover, sets forth in elegant parables the whole condition of our life which we lead on earth, and therefore it is most worthy that we consider it diligently.

units.la: Prima parabola de seruis est herum suum expectantibus, quando à nuptiis domum reuertatur. Vbi, vt diximus, vitæ nostræ imago aut typus proponitur. Serui enim illi sunt, quotquot Christo nomen dederunt, & eum cum fide sunt amplexi. Ipse autem herus est, quem à nuptiis reuersurum expectamus. Nam vbi redemptionis nostræ negotium totum perfecit, ex mundo hoc in cœlos ascendit, & eò carnem, quam ex nobis assumpserat, subuexit. Solet autem nuptijs conferri vita cœlestis & immortalis, cùm quòd nullus in ea dolori, luctui aut lachrymis locus est, sed solidi & perpetui gaudij plena sunt omnia, tum quòd æternus Dei Filius illic Ecclesiam, quæ sponsa eius dicitur, sibi vere coniunget, vt bonorum ipsius omnium consors & particeps fiat. Imò iam nunc in cœlis nuptias illas beatissimas agit cum omnibus pijs & credentibus, qui ab ipso rerum exordio in hunc vsque diem in fide vera decesserunt, & ad beatas æternæ vitæ sedes collecti sunt. Et frequenter hac nuptiarum parabola Christus tam apud Prophetas quàm in Euangelio vitur, vt nos futuri gaudij consideratione ad patientiam & constantiam in vera fide excitet. Et in præsenti aperte docet, se nos non ita reliquisse, etiamsi corpus suum ex hoc mundo abstulerit, vt nullam nostri curam habeat, qui in terris hisce cum infinitis periculis quotidie luctamur. Nam quoad huius seculi vitam semper nobis adest suo Spiritu, quem nobis aduocatum siue patronum & consolatorem dedit: simul[a] Ecclesiam sedulò regit & gubernat, atque singulos in periculis & aduersis laborantes videt, & viribus subinde nouis armat, ne afflictionum pondere opprimantur. Quoad vero futuri seculi vitam, ad singulos venit suo tempore, vt eorum animas ad se colligat, olim autem cum gloria & maiestate venturus est ad iudicium, vt impios quidem sui nominis hostes & perfidos defectores æternis inferorum cruciatibus mancipet, fideles autem seruos suos ad nuptias illas æternas transferat, vbi tam corpore quàm anima in æternum viuant atque gaudeant. Ita ipse seipse exponit, quando in vltima Cœna discipulis dicit: In domo Patris mei habitationes multæ sunt:
units.tr: The first parable is of servants waiting for their lord, when he will return home from the wedding. Here, as we have said, a picture or type of our life is set before us. For those servants are all who have given their name to Christ and have embraced him with faith. The lord himself is he whom we expect to return from the wedding. For when he had completed the whole business of our redemption, he ascended from this world into heaven, and there carried up the flesh which he had taken from us. Now the heavenly and immortal life is usually compared to a wedding, both because there is no place in it for pain, mourning or tears, but all things are full of solid and perpetual joy, and because the eternal Son of God will there truly join to himself the Church, which is called his bride, so that she may become a partaker and sharer in all his goods. Indeed, even now in heaven he holds that most blessed wedding with all the godly and believers who from the beginning of the world until this day have died in true faith and have been gathered to the blessed seats of eternal life. And Christ frequently uses this parable of the wedding, both among the Prophets and in the Gospel, to rouse us by the consideration of future joy to patience and constancy in the true faith. And in the present passage he clearly teaches that he has not so left us, even though he has taken his body out of this world, that he has no care for us who daily struggle on this earth with endless dangers. For as regards the life of this age, he is always present with us by his Spirit, whom he gave us as advocate or patron and comforter; at the same time he diligently rules and governs the Church, and sees each one labouring in dangers and adversities, and from time to time arms them with new strength, lest they be crushed by the weight of afflictions. As regards the life of the age to come, he comes to each one at his own time, to gather their souls to himself; but at length he will come to judgment with glory and majesty, to deliver the impious, indeed the enemies of his name and treacherous deserters, to the eternal torments of hell, but to carry his faithful servants over to that eternal wedding, where they will live and rejoice for ever, both in body and in soul. He himself explains this when, at the last supper, he says to the disciples: In my Father's house there are many mansions;

units.la: Christus ad nuptias abijt. quod si secus effet, dixissem vobis. Vado vobis paraturus locum: & cum profectus fuero, & parauero vobis locum, rursus veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum: ut vbi ego sum, & vos sitis. Et Paulus ipsam aduentus Christi nostræq; ad illum assumptionis historiam describens ait: Ipse Dominus cum hortationis clamore ac voce Archangeli & tuba Dei descendet è cælo: & qui mortui fuerint in Christo resurgent primùm: deinde nos viui, qui reliqui erimus, rapiemur simul cum eis in nubibus in occursum Domini in aërem, & ita semper cum Domino erimus. Et hæc quidem omnibus seculis omnium sanctorum ipses fuit, quia sese in tentationibus cofolati sunt (vt sæpe alias diximus) & hanc in præsenti Christus confirmat.
units.tr: Christ went away to the wedding. If it were otherwise, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you; and when I have gone and have prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also. And Paul, describing the coming of Christ and the history of our being taken up to him, says: The Lord himself with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so shall we be always with the Lord. And indeed this has been the comfort of all the saints in every age, since they were consoled in their temptations (as we have often said elsewhere), and Christ confirms it here in the present passage.

units.la: Præcipuum tamen hic est, quòd officij nostri nos admonet, & hoc paucis capitibus comprehendit. Inter quæ primum est, quòd similes iubet esse seruis, qui expectant quando dominus suus à nuptijs redeat. Ergo licet ex hoc mundo Christus quoad corpus suum abierit, non tamen nos rerum securos & otiosos esse vult, sed vt bonus paterfamilias seruulos suos quàm maximè operi intentos esse & res omnes diligentius solito curare iubet, quando ipse peregre proficiscitur: ita à nobis quoq; eandem sedulitatem & industriam Dominus requirit. Expectandi autem verbo obedientiam cum patientia constanti requirit, qua omnino opus est. Nam differt suum aduentum Dominus, siue singulos priuatim, siue vniuersalem totius mundi consummationem consideres. Et frequenter accidit, vt propter continuos labores, pericula & metum perpetuū pios huius vitæ tædere incipiat, & mortem quàm ocyßime approperare velint, quod Eliam quoq; aliquando passum fuisse scimus. Dauid etiam grauißimis morbi diuturni doloribus excruciatus clamabat: Indica mihi Domine finem meum, & quis nam sit terminus dierum meorum, vt sciam quàm diu mihi in miseriis viuendum sit. Similiter quando pij mundum hunc indies in peius proficere, impios aduersus Ecclesiam ferocire, Christi culatores crudeliter opprimi, legum disciplinam dissipari, deniq; diabolum in membris suis tantùmnon triumphare vident, fere communi voce cum Propheta clamant, Quousq; tandem Domine via impiorum prosperatur? Quousq; nostri obliuisceris? Quousq; Domine, qui es iustus & verax, non iudicas, ac vindicas sanguine nostrum de his, qui habitant in terra? Et hi simul omnes Christum quàm celerrimè venire vellent, vt semel malis omnibus finem imponeret. At tunc quàm maximè fidei obedientia opus est, vt ea admoniti non murmuremus, neq; Deo præscribamus, sed patienter expectemus eius aduentū. Et huc pertinent illa Dauidis, quibus seipsum confirmauit, dicens: Expecta Dominum, forte fit & roboretur cor tuum, expecta Dominum. Item, Vtiq; ad Deum silens respicit anima. Sicut se dicit, non quoad preces, in quibus nos nunquam non assiduos esse oportet, sed quòd linguam cohibuit, ne aduersus Deum murmuraret, aut illi temere præscriberet. Quid verò Dauidè inter tot triστissimos casus & noua indies pericula tam patientè reddidit? Audi ipsum amplius dicentem: Ab ipso salus mea: Vtiq; ipse est petra mea & salus mea, ipse arx sublimis mea: ideo non labascam admodum graviter. Quibus nos addere possumus, quòd Paulus Deum fidelem esse scribit, qui nos supra vires tentari non patiatur, sed cum tentatione viam quoq; euasionis monstret. Hæc qui diligenter expendunt tam in priuatis quàm publicis Ecclesiæ totius calamitatibus, iis non admodum graue erit salutiferum Domini aduentum expectare, qui quo diutius differtur, eò iucundior nobis redditur, & gloriam Dei magis illustrat.
units.tr: Yet the chief thing here is that he reminds us of our duty, and he sums this up in a few verses. Among these the first is that he bids us be like servants who wait for their lord to return from the wedding. Therefore, although Christ has departed from this world as regards his body, he does not wish us to be careless and idle about our affairs; rather, just as a good householder orders his little servants to be most intent upon their work and to look after all things more carefully than usual when he himself goes abroad, so the Lord requires the same diligence and industry from us too. Yet the waiting requires of us obedience to his word, together with constant patience, which is altogether necessary. For the Lord delays his coming, whether you consider each person individually or the final consummation of the whole world. And it often happens that, because of continual labours, dangers and constant fear, the godly begin to be weary of this life and want death to come as quickly as possible, which we know Elijah also once suffered. David too, tormented by the most grievous pains of a long illness, cried out: Lord, show me my end, and what is the measure of my days, that I may know how long I must live in miseries. Likewise, when the godly see this world daily growing worse, the impious raging against the Church, the worshippers of Christ cruelly oppressed, the discipline of the laws dissipated, and finally the devil all but triumphing in his members, they cry out almost with one voice with the Prophet: How long, Lord, will the way of the impious prosper? How long will you forget us? How long, Lord, who are just and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? And all of them would wish that Christ come as quickly as possible, so that he might once for all put an end to all evils. But then the obedience of faith is most necessary, so that, being admonished by it, we do not murmur, nor prescribe to God, but patiently wait for his coming. To this belong those words of David, by which he strengthened himself, saying: Wait for the Lord; perhaps your heart will be made strong and firm; wait for the Lord. Likewise: Surely my soul waits upon God in silence. He says this not as regards prayers, in which we ought always to be constant, but because he restrained his tongue, lest he murmur against God or rashly prescribe to him. But what made David so patient amid so many most sorrowful events and daily new dangers? Hear him saying further: My salvation is from him; surely he is my rock and my salvation, my high fortress; therefore I shall not be moved greatly. To these we may add that Paul writes that God is faithful, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but with the temptation also shows the way of escape. Those who carefully weigh these things, both in the private and in the public calamities of the whole Church, will not find it very hard to wait for the saving coming of the Lord, which, the longer it is deferred, the more pleasant it becomes to us, and the more it illustrates the glory of God.

units.la: At multum in eo situm est, vt illum rectè & vt pios decet expectemus. Nam inuenias seruulos, qui herum quidem reditur um sciunt, & eius aduentum expectant, attamè securi nimis interea otio indulgent, aut etiam turpißima quæq; designant. Ideò Christus à suis seruis duo requirit. Primum est, vt lumbis succincti sint. Loquitur autem pro more Orientalium, qui longioribus vestibus vtuntur, quas vel iter facturi, vel aliquod obituri succingere solent, vt sint expediti ores. Vult ergo nos semper ad iter paratos esse, vt quandocunq; venerit, ipsi obuiam prodeamus. Nam in hisce terris peregrini sumus, neq; hic habemus ciuitatem permanentem, patria autem & municipatus nostrer in cælis est, vbi nobis à Christo locum paratum esse paulò ante diximus. Semper ergo nos vt terius progredi, semper item in opere Domini esse conuenit, quod est (vt ipse interpretatur) vt reliquis huius mundi studijs omnibusq; quæ carni & ventri seruiunt, panem illum viuificum quæramus, quem ipse nobis in ipso offert, & vitam viuamus cælestem. Debet huc referri, quod infra monet, vt uxoris Lothi meminerimus, ne idem nobis, quod illis accidat. Nam vt hæc cum Sodoma egressa est. egressa ducibus Angelis à tergo respiceret, vitam minimè seruauit, sed in statuam salis commutata est: ita qui per Christum è mundo hoc impuro euocantur, si aliquò vsque progressi ad huius delitias atq; voluptates respiciant, magno suo cum dedecore salutis & vitæ æternæ iacturam faciunt.
units.tr: But much depends on how we wait for him: rightly, as befits the godly. For you will find servants who know their master will return and who look for his coming, yet who in the meantime grow too careless and indulge in idleness, or even plan the most shameful things. Therefore Christ requires two things of his servants. The first is that they be girded in their loins. He speaks in the manner of the Orientals, who wear long garments, which they are accustomed to gather up when about to travel or to undertake some task, so that they may be unencumbered. He wills, then, that we always be ready for the journey, so that whenever he comes we may go out to meet him. For we are strangers in this land and have no lasting city here, but our homeland and citizenship are in heaven, where, as we said a little before, a place has been prepared for us by Christ. It is fitting, therefore, that we always press on as travellers and always be engaged in the work of the Lord. This work is, as he himself explains, that, setting aside all other pursuits of this world and everything that serves the flesh and the belly, we seek that living bread which he himself offers us in himself, and live a heavenly life. To this belongs his further warning that we remember Lot's wife, lest the same thing happen to us as happened to her. For just as she, when she had gone out of Sodom under the guidance of the angels, looked back over her shoulder, did not keep her life at all but was turned into a pillar of salt, so those who are called out of this impure world through Christ, if, having gone some distance, they look back at the delights and pleasures of this world, suffer, to their great shame, the loss of salvation and eternal life.

units.la: Quia verò mundus hic tenebris & caligine totus est obsitus, lucerna opus erit, ne eo longius aberremus, quò festinantius pergimus. Nam quibus hoc accidit, eos satius esset pedem sistere, aut quàm tardissimè progredi. Iubet ergo Dominus, vt lucernas in manibus habeamus. Lucernæ autem parabola verbum Dei denotari, supra docuimus: & notum est illud Dauidis: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lux semitarum nostrarum. Lucernam verò hanc Christus nos non in ore aut capite, sed manibus gestare iubet, vt doceat, non sufficere otiosam eius professionem, sed omnes vitæ nostræ actiones secundum illius regulam institui & dirigi debere. Est hoc obseruatu in primis necessarium. Est enim hoc homini natura insitum, quod in iis etiam ex semetipso sapere vult, quæ ad Deum & æternæ salutis negotium spectant. Quàm primum verò sibi ipsi indulget, tunc aut proprij animi intentione, aut aliorum placitis ac traditionibus seductus à veritatis via deflectit, & indies maioribus errorum Labyrinthis atq; tenebris inuoluitur. Accidit hoc olim gentium philosophis, vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit. Et Iudæorum sacerdotes atq; doctores hac ratione seductos fuisse scimus, qui deinde toti populo errorum atq; superstitionum fuerunt authores. Quid verò nouissimis hisce temporibus inter Christiani nominis professores acciderit, notius est, quàm vt multus commemorari oporteat. Postquam enim in scholis loco verbi Dei Philosophorum libri prælegi cæperunt, nec quisquam ad Theologiæ studium est admissus, nisi prius illorum placitis bene imbutus, imò exercitatus esset, nulla postea apud tales lucernæ illius fuit vtilitas. In hanc enim illi suas tenebras intulerunt, & Dei verbum secundum philosophiæ dogmata interpretati sunt, à quibus dissentire nefas videbatur. Hinc ergo errores de liberoarbitrio, de hominis viribus, operum nostrorum merito, satisfactionibus, igne lustrali aut purgatorio, Diuorum cœlitum intercessione & aliis infinitis exorti sunt, quæ omnia olim inter gentes solis nominibus mutatis recepta fuerunt. Et quia tantum hominis arbitrio atq; facultatibus datum est, singuli ex semetipsis nouos cultus instituere & nouas salutis vias ingredi cœperunt, quæ sectarum causa fuit, in quas distracti & scissi sunt, qui sub vno capite Christo vnum corpus, id est, grex vnus & vna ecclesia esse debebant. Quin hodie adhuc plurimos in superstitionum tenebris hæc persuasio detinet, quod cultus sacros apud Deum ex cordis nostri intentione æstimari, & proinde vnumquenq; in sua religione seruari posse arbitrantur. Est ergo necessaria hæc admonitio, vt non modo ad opus Domini & ad iter regni cœlorum accinctì simus, verum etiam curemus, vt nostris actionibus verbum Dei præluceat, quod nos aberrare non sinet. Nam ni si illud sequamur, de nobis quoq; dicetur, quod Christus ex Propheta repetiit: Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas hominum. Isa. 29. Matth. 15.
units.tr: Since this world is wholly covered with darkness and gloom, a lamp will be needed, lest we wander the farther the more hastily we hurry. For those to whom this happens would do better to halt their step or to advance as slowly as possible. The Lord therefore bids us have lamps in our hands. We have taught above that by the parable of the lamp the Word of God is meant, and the saying of David is well known: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." Christ bids us carry this lamp not in the mouth or on the head but in the hands, to teach that an idle profession of it is not enough, but that all the actions of our life must be shaped and directed by its rule. This is especially necessary to observe. For it is natural to man that he wishes to be wise by himself even in those matters which concern God and the business of eternal salvation. As soon as he indulges himself, then, led either by the bent of his own mind or by the opinions and traditions of others, he turns aside from the way of truth and day by day is entangled in ever greater labyrinths of error and darkness. This happened once to the philosophers of the Gentiles, as Paul writes to the Romans. We know that the priests and teachers of the Jews were led astray in the same way, and then became the authors of errors and superstitions for the whole people. What has happened in these latest times among the professors of the Christian name is too well known to need much mention. For after the books of the philosophers began to be read in the schools in place of the Word of God, and no one was admitted to the study of theology unless he had first been thoroughly steeped, indeed trained, in their opinions, that lamp was of no further use among such people. For they brought their own darkness into it and interpreted God's Word according to the doctrines of philosophy, from which it seemed wrong to dissent. Hence arose errors about free will, about the powers of man, the merit of our works, satisfactions, cleansing or purgatorial fire, the intercession of the blessed saints, and countless others, all of which were once received among the Gentiles under changed names only. And because so much was given to man's judgement and abilities, individuals began to devise new forms of worship from themselves and to enter new ways of salvation. This was the cause of the sects into which those who ought to be one body under one head, Christ, that is one flock and one Church, were torn and split. Indeed, even today this persuasion still holds very many in the darkness of superstition, since they think that sacred worship is judged before God by the intention of our heart, and that therefore each may be saved in his own religion. This admonition is therefore necessary: that we should not only be girded for the work of the Lord and for the way to the kingdom of heaven, but should also take care that the Word of God shines before our actions, for it will not let us go astray. For if we do not follow it, what Christ quoted from the Prophet will be said of us too: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." Isa. 29. Matth. 15.

units.la: Tertiò requiritur, vt domino venienti & pulsanti aperiamus. Pulsat autem Christus ad ostium cordis nostri per Verbum suum, quo se totum & omnium bonorum suorum communionem nobis offert. Et huc pertinet, quod Laodicensium Ecclesiæ in Apocalypsi dicitur: Ecce sto ad ostium & pulso: si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit ostium, ingrediar ad illum, & cœnabo cum eo, & ipse quoq; meu. Item quod in Euangelio Christus ait: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit: & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, et manstionem apud ipsum faciemus. Itaq; hic in primis studio & industria opus est, ne vel pulsantem Dominum excludamus, quod impij & pœnitere nescij faciunt: vel in eo admittendo cunctatores simus, quales multi hodie passim cernuntur. Sunt enim, qui Christum seruatorem suum esse, & Euangelio verba vitæ æternæ contineri, ideoq; cultum externum & omnes vitæ actiones secundum illud institui debere fatentur: interim verò cunctatores agunt, & absq; animarum periculo rem differri posse putant. Peccatur in hoc publicè & priuatim. Publicè, dum Ecclesiarum reformatio extrahitur, & occasiones commodiores vel tempora minus turbulenta aut periculosa expectant, qui illa maturare debebant. Priuatim verò quando post agnitam veritatem quidam in superstitionibus adhuc hærent, fidem dissimulant, vt interim rebus suis possint prospicere, priusquam ex iis locus discedunt, in quibus fidè profiteri non audent, sacris autem illicitis communicare coguntur. Priuatim quoq; peccant, qui per Dei verbum intra conscientias suas scelerum conuicti, pœnitentiam tamen differunt, prius nimirum ea perfecturi, quæ ex suo commodo fore
units.tr: Thirdly, it is required that we open to the Lord when he comes and knocks. Christ knocks at the door of our heart through his Word, by which he offers himself wholly to us and the fellowship of all his good things. To this pertains what is said in the Apocalypse of the Church of the Laodiceans: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and will sup with him, and he with me." Likewise what Christ says in the Gospel: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him." Therefore here above all there is need of care and diligence, lest we either shut out the Lord who knocks, as the impious and the unrepentant do, or be hesitant in admitting him, as many today are seen to be everywhere. For there are those who confess that Christ is their Saviour and that the words of eternal life are contained in the Gospel, and who therefore admit that external worship and all the actions of life ought to be ordered according to it; yet in the meantime they delay, and think the matter can be put off without danger to souls. This sin is committed both publicly and privately. Publicly, while the reformation of the Churches is drawn out, and men wait for more convenient occasions or for less turbulent and dangerous times, when they ought rather to hasten them.
