Privately, when, after the truth has been recognised, some still cling to superstitions and dissemble their faith, so that meanwhile they may look after their affairs before they leave those places where they do not dare to profess the faith openly, yet are compelled to take part in unlawful rites. Those also sin privately who, convicted in their consciences of their sins through the Word of God, nevertheless defer repentance, intending, of course, first to bring to completion those things which they think will be to their advantage.

units.la: Lucerna. Psal. 119. Aperire oportet Christo pulsanti. Apoc. 3. Ioan. 14. existimant. Hi omnes dum bene agendi occasiones meliores expectant, optimas negligunt, quas ill-lis Dominus offert, & pulsantem excludunt. Vt autem dignas & iustas iras berus concipit, si à servus vel omnino excludatur, vel pulsans diutius negligatur, illis interim suo genti indulgentibus: ita non potest non illis irasci Deus, qui suam gratiam & salutem æternam per verbum suum offerentem noluit admittere. Ideo apud Prophetam de talibus ait: Fiet vt quemadmodum ego clamaui, & non audierunt: ita & ipsi clamabunt, & non exaudiam eos. Et in Euangelio excluduntur à nuptiis satuæ virgines, quæ sine oleo aduentantes, sponsum, dum tempus erat, neglexerunt. Pertinent autem ista ad omnes loci & ordinis homines. Meminerint ergo singuli, se Dei seruos esse, & proinde ad omne obsequium semper parati sint, neque huius seculi sordibus immorentur. Obseruent autem Dei verbum, ne suæ voluntatis aut intentionis placita sequendo exorbitent. Et si quando aberrarunt, Dominum ipsos revocantem audiant, & in viam redeant: similiter, si quando huius immemores, eum quasi excluserunt, pulsanti aperiant, vt denuo apud ipsos locum habeat. Hæc si faciant qui in Ecclesiæ ministerio sunt, aut qui rempub. administrant, singuli item priuatim, nunquam à salutis via aberrabunt.
units.tr: Lamp. Ps. 119. One must open to Christ when he knocks. Rev. 3. John 14. Those who think so, all of them, while they wait for better opportunities of doing well, neglect the best ones, which the Lord offers them, and shut out the one who knocks. But just as a master conceives a just and fitting anger if a servant is either shut out altogether or the one knocking is neglected for a long time while the servant indulges his own pleasures, so God cannot but be angry with those who were unwilling to admit his grace and eternal salvation, offered through his Word. Therefore the Prophet says of such people: "It shall come to pass that, as I called and they did not hear, so they shall call and I will not hear them." And in the Gospel the foolish virgins, who came without oil, neglected the bridegroom while there was still time, and were shut out of the wedding. These things pertain to all people of every place and rank. Let each one therefore remember that he is a servant of God, and so should always be ready for every obedience and not linger in the filth of this age. Let them observe the Word of God, lest by following the dictates of their own will or intention they go astray. And if at any time they have wandered, let them hear the Lord calling them back and return to the way; likewise, if at any time, forgetful of him, they have as it were shut him out, let them open to him when he knocks, so that he may again have a place among them. If those who are in the ministry of the Church, or who administer the commonwealth, do this, and each individual likewise in private, they will never wander from the way of salvation.

units.la: Porrò pulsare etiam dicitur Dominus, quando fatalis illa hora imminet, & animas nostras ex huius corporis ergastulo euocat. Quod gentium quoque sapientes intellexisse, Horatius hic verbis docet: Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas, Regumq; turres. Tunc quoque nos exci tari, imò in omnia momenta paratos esse conuenit, vt alacri animo vitam hanc ærumnosam relinquamus & optemus dissolui, vt cum Christo in cœlis viuere liceat. Et quia tunc in primis nobis in sidiatur Satan, vt aut mortis terroribus, aut peccatorum commissorum conscientia in desperationem adducat, lucerna verbi quam maximè est opus, vt ea illuminati videamus, neq; mortem Christia no hominis formidabilem esse, neque hunc de peccatorum remissione & gratia Dei desperare debere. Solent quidam morituris candelas in manus dare ardentes, quasi hæc ad eorum salutem aliquid conferant. Sed maiores atque densiores sunt peccati & mortis tenebræ, quam vt lucernæ sebaceæ aut cereæ discuti possint. At si Deum audiamus loquentem, qui nobis in Filio suo gratuitam peccatorum remissionem offert, & mortem credentibus non peccati pœnam, sed transitum ex hac mortali vita ad immortalem esse docet, mox nouam lucem animis nostris exoriri sentimus, quæ & salutem certos & mortem nobis iucundam reddit. Et qui Dei verbum, dum viuunt & valent, semper ob oculos habent, ijs nō inexpectata mors obrepit, sed in omnes horas eius memores, Dominum per hanc fores pulsantem mox agnoscunt, & eidem aperiunt, cum sancto illo Simeone clamantes: Nunc dimittis seruum tuum Domine in pace, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord is also said to knock when that fateful hour is at hand and calls our souls out of the prison-house of this body. Horace teaches in these words that the wise men of the Gentiles understood this too: "Pale death knocks with impartial foot at the cottages of the poor and the towers of kings." Accordingly, we ought to be roused even now, and to be ready at every moment, so that we may leave this troublesome life with a cheerful spirit and long to be released, in order to live with Christ in heaven. And because Satan lies in wait for us chiefly at that time, to drive us into despair either by the terrors of death or by the awareness of sins committed, we have the greatest need of the lamp of the Word, so that, enlightened by it, we may see that death is not terrifying to a Christian, nor should he despair of the forgiveness of sins and of the grace of God. Some people give burning candles into the hands of the dying, as if these contributed something to their salvation. But the darkness of sin and death is too great and too thick to be dispelled by tallow or wax lamps. But if we listen to God speaking, who offers us in his Son the free forgiveness of sins, and who teaches that for believers death is not the punishment of sin but a passage from this mortal life to an immortal one, we soon feel a new light rising in our souls, which makes both our salvation certain and our death welcome to us. Those who always keep the Word of God before their eyes while they live and are well are not overtaken by death unexpectedly; mindful of it at every hour, they recognise the Lord knocking at this door and at once open to him, crying out with the holy Simeon: "Now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace," and so on.

units.la: Cæterum quia in hus natura tardiores ac segniores sumus, rationes aut argumenta subijcit Christus, quibus nos vrgeat. Primum ab vtili sumitur, & amplissimam promissionem habet. Beati (inquit) serui illi, quos cum venerit Dominus, inueniet vigilantes. Et mox beatitudinis huius conditionem explicans addit: Amen dico vobis, quod præcinget se, & faciet, vt discumbant, & pro diens ministrabit eis. Loquitur autem pro ratione huius seculi, in quo heri humaniores seruorum fidelium obsequia agnoscunt, & licet hi omnia ex debito faciant, tamen se illis vicißim gratos præbent, vt magis in officio contineant. Iubet hoc communis humanitatis sensus, vt quia homines sunt serui, & eiusdem nobiscum naturæ participes, illis quoque non vt iumentis abutamur, sed humanitatis officia ipsis quoque præstemus. Admonet de hoc Paulus, qui cum sua officia seruis præscripsisset: heru quoque dicit: Vos domini æquitatem & æqualitatem seruis exhibete, scientes vos quoque Dominum habere in cœlis. Et commendatur in historijs Alexandri Magni humanitas, qui cum quo dam loco niuali tempestate oppressus, senio iam confestum militem, nimio frigore obstupefactum, ipse sublimi & igni propinqua sede sedens, animadueerteret, mox non fortuna, sed ætatis vtriusque æstimatione facta, descendit, & illis manibus, quibus opes Darij afflixerat, corpus frigore duplicatum in suam sedem imposuit. Quò etiam referri possunt multorum exempla, qui seruos fideles libertate donarunt, & omni humanitatis officio prosecuti sunt. Porro quoad verborum Christi sensum, nemo hunc iam in cœlesti gloria residentem aliquid seruile facere putabit: pollicetur autem quod parem gratiam reddere velit ijs, qui in eius seruitio fideles fuerint. Id autem bifariam facit. Primo dum suum meritum illis communicat, & eorum participes reddit, quæ olim forma serui assumpta, nostrae salutis ergo fecit. Nam vt discipulorum pedes abluit, sic nos à peccatis purgauit proprio sanguine. Mensam item nobis instruxit lautissimam, ad quam suo corpore & sanguine nos pascit & alit ad vitam æternam. Horum ergo beneficiorum participes erimus, si ad eius obsequium parati simus, & ipsum pulsantem atq; monentè admittamus. Deinde amplior & perfecta omnibus numerus retributio in cœlis sequetur, vbi nos ex huius vitæ laboribus ereptos ad suā mensam discumbere faciet, id est, requie æterna donabit, & bona sua cœlestia nobiscū communia habebit. Estq; hoc observatu dignißimū, imò necessarium, ne huius seculi miserijs superati deficiamus. Facilè autem illas omnes vincemus, si nobis retributionem in cœlis præparatam esse firmiter credamus. Cum enim nunc multa faciamus & feramus spe alicuius cōmodi temporarij, quæ carni dura & acerba sunt, nihil intolerabile illis videri poterit, qui æternæ illius remunerationis spem animo suo verè conceperunt. Hæc enim certa est & infallibilis, neq; de ea dubitare cuiquam licet. Nam promissiones sunt infinitæ, non hominū, sed Dei qui ipsa est veritas. Et hac spe seruatos esse constat omnes quorū fides & pietas in scripturis cōmendatur. Sed & Dei iustitia hoc exigit, vt sua virtuti præmia reddantur. Quod cum in hoc seculo rarius fiat, & pelerunq; pij multis periculis, laboribus & curis exerceantur, in cœlis retributionem fieri necesse est, nisi Deum iniustū dicere libeat. Est hæc efficacißima consolatio, quæ omnes huius seculi labores nobis leues & iucundos reddit: & hanc cœlestis vox in Apoc lypsi confirmat: clamans: Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur: Etiam dicit Spiritus, quoniam requiescunt à laboribus suis, & opera eorum sequuntur eos. Facit autem ad consolationis istius confirmationem, quod addit: Et si venerit secunda vigilia, & si tertia vigilia venerit, atq; ita inuenerit, beati sunt serui illi. Vbi rursum pro illius seculi more loquitur, quo excubias nocturnas in quaterna horarum spacia diuidebant, vnde vigilia prima, secunda, tertia & quarta dicebantur. Sensus ergo est, ijs qui credunt & in officio suo diligentes sunt, neq; mortis horam neq; postremum Domini aduentum tristem aut inauspicatum posse accidere. Nam quandocunque Deo visum fuerit, vel animas eorum hinc euocare, vel toti mundo finem imponere, illos paratos inueniet, & proinde hora illa eis beata & felix erit, vt quæ ipsorum laboribus finem optatum adferet, vt modò diximus.
units.tr: But since we are slow and sluggish by nature, Christ adds reasons or arguments by which he may urge us on. The first is taken from advantage and holds out a very great promise: "Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching." And soon explaining the condition of this blessedness, he adds: "Truly I say to you, that he will gird himself, and make them sit down to eat, and will go round and serve them." He speaks according to the custom of this age, in which masters nowadays show more kindness in the services of faithful servants, and although these men do everything from duty, they nevertheless show themselves grateful to them in return, so that they may be held more firmly to their duty. The common sense of humanity bids us, since servants are men and share the same nature as ourselves, not to abuse them like beasts of burden, but to render them the offices of humanity too. Paul gives this admonition, who, after prescribing their duties to servants, also says to masters: "Masters, give your servants what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven." And the humanity of Alexander the Great is commended in histories: when, at a certain place, in a snowstorm, he saw a soldier worn out with age and numbed by the bitter cold, he himself, sitting in a lofty seat near the fire, at once got down, without considering rank but only the age of each, and with those hands which had crushed the power of Darius, he placed the body, doubled up with cold, in his own seat. Examples of many who gave freedom to faithful servants and treated them with every courtesy of humanity may also be cited here. Furthermore, as regards the meaning of Christ's words, no one will think that he who now sits in heavenly glory does anything servile; rather, he promises that he will repay in like measure those who have been faithful in his service. He does this in two ways. First, while he shares his merit with them and makes them partakers of those things which he once did, taking the form of a servant, for our salvation. For as he washed the feet of his disciples, so he has cleansed us from sins by his own blood. He has also set before us a most sumptuous table, at which he feeds and nourishes us with his body and blood unto eternal life. Therefore we shall be partakers of these benefits if we are ready for his service and admit him when he knocks and warns us. Then, a fuller and perfect recompense will follow for all in heaven, where he will make us, rescued from the labours of this life, sit down at his table, that is, he will grant us eternal rest and will hold his heavenly goods in common with us. This is most worthy of notice, indeed necessary, lest we give up, overcome by the miseries of this age. We shall easily overcome all of them if we firmly believe that a reward is prepared for us in heaven. For since we now do and endure many things, in hope of some temporary advantage, things hard and bitter to the flesh, nothing will seem intolerable to those who have truly conceived in their minds the hope of that eternal reward. For this hope is certain and infallible, and no one may doubt it. For the promises are infinite, not of men but of God, who is truth itself. And it is clear that all whose faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures were kept by this hope. But also the justice of God requires that rewards be given to his virtue. Since this seldom happens in this age, and the godly are often exercised by many dangers, labours and cares, a retribution must take place in heaven, unless we are willing to call God unjust. This is a most effective consolation, which makes all the labours of this age light and pleasant for us; and the heavenly voice in the Apocalypse confirms it, crying out: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord." Also the Spirit says that "they rest from their labours, and their works follow them." What he adds also helps to confirm this consolation: "And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants." Here again he speaks according to the custom of that age, when they divided the night watches into four spans of time, whence they were called the first, second, third and fourth watches. The sense, therefore, is that for those who believe and are diligent in their duty, neither the hour of death nor the last coming of the Lord can be sad or ill-omened. For whenever it shall please God either to call their souls hence or to put an end to the whole world, he will find them ready, and therefore that hour will be blessed and happy for them, since it will bring the desired end to their labours, as we have just said.

units.la: Secundum argumentum ab exemplo sumit, quod est eiusmodi: Hoc autem scitote, si sciret paterfamilias, qua hora fur venturus sit, vigilaret, nec sineret perfodi domum suam. Subest hic comparatio à minori ad maius. Quasi dicat: Tanta rei domesticæ cura tenet patersfamilias, vt si de suis aduentu admoneantur, totas noctes potius vigilare, quam iacturam rerum suarum aliquam facere velint. Quantò magis ergo vobis vigilandum est, de quorum animabus & salute æterna hic agitur? Simul autem hus verbis perstringitur humani ingenij peruersitas & præpostera cura. Iniis quæ corpori & huic seculo seruiunt, nihil planè negligimus. Agricolæ tempora arationis, sementis, messis & vindemiæ, lunæ item incrementa & decrementa diligenter obseruant. Nautæ etiam ventos & tempestates futuras prospiciunt. Patresfamilias congerunt, ades & horrea probè claudunt, vigilant quoque, & totas noctes sæpe insomnes ducunt, ne quid damni accipiant. In morbis pro valetudine recuperanda quiduis facimus & feriimus. Interim verò potiorem nostri partem, animas nimirum, & quæ ad salutem æternam faciunt, securi negligimus. Nec enim vocem Domini pulsantis audimus: neque visitationis nostræ tempus agnoscimus: & cum non ignoremus, diabolum nobis perpetuò insidias struere, vt incautos opprimat, perpetuò tamen dormimus & sterci mus, quasi nihil nobis periculi vspiam sit timendum. Vult ergo Dominus, vt si rationibus è Dei verbo petitis minus moueamur, saltem hominum huius seculi exemplis excitemur. Turpe enim fuerit, nos in æternæ salutis negotio negligentiores deprehendi illis, qui pro rebus temporarijs & breui periturìs, tantum studij, curæ atq; laboris impendunt.
units.tr: The second argument is taken from an example, and is of this kind: "But know this, that if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would keep watch and not allow his house to be broken into." Here there is a comparison from the less to the greater, as if he were to say: the householder is held by such care for his domestic property that, if they are warned of a thief's coming, they would rather keep watch all night than suffer any loss of their goods. How much more, then, must you keep watch, since it is your souls and eternal salvation that are at stake here? At the same time, by these words the perversity and perverse care of the human mind is rebuked. In the things which serve the body and this age we neglect absolutely nothing. Farmers carefully observe the times of ploughing, sowing, harvest and vintage, and likewise the waxing and waning of the moon. Sailors also foresee the winds and storms to come. Householders lay up stores, and carefully shut their houses and granaries, and they keep watch too, often spending whole nights sleepless, lest they suffer any harm. In sickness we do and endure anything to recover our health. Meanwhile, however, we carelessly neglect the greater part of ourselves, that is, our souls, and what pertains to eternal salvation. For we do not hear the voice of the Lord knocking, nor do we recognise the time of our visitation; and although we are not ignorant that the devil is always laying snares for us, to catch us off our guard, we nevertheless sleep and snore continually, as if there were no danger anywhere to be feared. The Lord therefore wills that, if we are not moved enough by reasons drawn from the Word of God, we should at least be roused by the examples of the people of this age. For it would be shameful if we were found more negligent in the business of eternal salvation than those who spend so much zeal, care and labour on temporal things that will soon perish.

units.la: Cohæret hïs tertium argumentum à necessario: Et vos igitur estote parati, quia qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet. Qui herum certò venturum esse sciunt, diem verò & horam aduentus eius ignorant, eos perpetuò vigilare & paratos esse necesse est, ne ex improuiso ille aduéniens negligentiores, & officij immemores inueniat. At qui eadem est omnium nostrū conditio, siue de mortis hora, siue de nouissimo Christi aduentu hæc verba intelligas. Illa enim in omnes ætates cadit, & via est omnis terræ, quam omnes ingredi coguntur, quotquot viuunt, cuiuscunque sint conditionis aut ordinis. At hora mortis adeò dubia & incerta est, vt paucos inuenias, quibus illa non prater omnem expectationem obrepat. Plerunque enim fit, vt qui aut negotijs plurimis & inextricabilibus distinentur, aut rebus omnibus compositis vitam sibi ipsis quietam & tranquillam promittunt, morte minimè sperata hinc auferantur: vt iam de illis nihil dicam, quos subitaneus aliquis casus vno quasi momento abripit. Horam verò aduentus Domini Angeli quoque ignorant, & pro inde hanc quoque nihil huius opinantibus impijs superuenturam esse, Christus alibi diluuij, & Sodomarum exemplo docet. Et Paulus scribit: Scitis fratres, diem illum Domini, vt furem in nocte, ita venturum esse. Cum enim dicent, Pax & tuta omnia: tunc repentinum eis imminet exitium, sicuti dolor partus mulieri vterum ferenti, nec effugient. Quibus plane consentiunt, quae Petrus in posteriori sua epistola Cap. tertio tradit. Est autem hoc non vulgare diuinae bonitatis & fidei argumentum. Nouit Deus quam socordes & securi simus, & quod fere differimus ea, quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt. Necessitate ergo nos ad vigilandum astringit, & tam mortis quam finis huius saeculi horam incertam & omnibus ignotam esse voluit, vt in omnes horas intenti simus, & nunquam non vigilemus. Quod vt diligentius faciamus, quotidianis exemplis nos ad mortis considerationem excitat, dummodo hos, modo illos subito tollit, qui quam diutissime victuri videbantur. Quoadve nouissimum Domini aduentum, signa multa & illustria habemus ex ipsius ore, quae illi non procul abesse docent. Minimè ergo audiendi sunt, qui illum plane in dubium vocant, eo quod hucusque dilatus sit, multis ex patribus eum amide optantibus. Nam vt Petrus ait: Non tardat Dominus qui promisit (vt nonnulli tarditatem hanc esse ducunt) sed patiens est erga nos, nolens vllos perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam tendere. Et qui nunc aduentum suum differt, vt poenitentiae tempus concedat peccatoribus, idem vbi malitia mundi praevaluerit, illum accelerabit propter electos suos ne & ipsi seducantur & pereant. Horum itaque memores, semper in statione nostra instructi & parati simus, vigilemus item & diuini verbi lucernam sequamur constanter: vt nos omni momento fidelium seruorum similes inueniat Dominus noster Iesus Christus, & secum ad nuptias illas coelestes transferat, vbi laborum omnium retributionem accipiemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Connected with these is a third argument, drawn from what is necessary: "Therefore you also be ready, for at an hour you do not expect, the Son of man will come." Those who know that the Lord will certainly come, but do not know the day and hour of his coming, must needs watch and stand ready always, lest he come upon them unexpectedly and find them more careless and forgetful of their duty. And this holds for all of us alike, whether you understand these words of the hour of death or of the last coming of Christ. For the one falls upon all ages, and it is the way of all the earth, which everyone must walk, however many live, of whatever condition or rank. But the hour of death is so uncertain and doubtful that you will find few to whom it does not creep up beyond all expectation. For it generally happens that those who are either occupied with very many and tangled affairs, or who, having settled all things, promise themselves a quiet and tranquil life, are snatched away by death when it is least hoped for. I say nothing here of those whom some sudden accident carries off in a single moment. Moreover, the angels too do not know the hour of the Lord's coming, and Christ teaches elsewhere, by the example of the flood and of Sodom, that it will also come upon the wicked, who suspect nothing of the kind. And Paul writes: "You yourselves know, brethren, that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. For when they say, 'Peace and all is safe,' then sudden destruction hangs over them, as the pain of childbirth comes upon a woman with child, and they will not escape." Peter, in the third chapter of his second epistle, clearly agrees with these things. Now this is no ordinary proof of divine goodness and of faithfulness. God knows how careless and secure we are, and how we commonly defer the things that lead to eternal salvation. So he binds us by necessity to watchfulness, and has willed that the hour both of death and of the end of this age be uncertain and unknown to all, so that we may be attentive at every hour and never cease to watch. That we may do this more diligently, he stirs us up to the consideration of death by daily examples, taking away now one and now another suddenly, who seemed likely to live longest. And concerning the last coming of the Lord, we have many clear signs from his own mouth, which teach that it is not far off. Those therefore are by no means to be listened to who call it wholly into doubt because it has been delayed until now, many of the fathers having ardently longed for it. For as Peter says: "The Lord does not delay what he has promised" (as some think this slowness to be), "but is patient toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." And he who now defers his coming, so that a time of repentance may be granted to sinners, will hasten it when the wickedness of the world has prevailed, for the sake of his elect, lest they too be led astray and perish. Mindful of these things, then, let us always be found at our post, equipped and ready, and let us also keep watch and constantly follow the lamp of the divine word, so that our Lord Jesus Christ may find us at every moment like faithful servants, and may bring us with him to those heavenly nuptials, where we shall receive the reward of all our labours. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXII.
units.tr: Homily 132.

units.la: Dixit autem ei Petrus: Domine, nobis dicis istam parabolam, an etiam omnibus? Dixit autem Dominus: Quis nam fidus dispensator ac prudens, quem Dominus praeficiet familitio suo, vt in tempore det demensum? Beatus seruus ille, quem Dominus quum venerit, inuenerit ita facientem. Vere dico vobis, omnibus suis bonis praeficiet eum. Quod si dixerit seruus ille in corde suo: Tardat dominus meus aduentum: coeperitque verberare seruos & ancillas, & edere & bibere & inebriari: veniet dominus serui illius die quo non expectat, & qua hora non nouit, & diuidet eum, partemque cum infidelibus ei assignabit.
units.tr: Then Peter said to him, "Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone?" And the Lord said, "Who then is the faithful and wise steward whom the master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, will find doing so. Truly I tell you, he will set him over all his possessions. But if that servant says in his heart, 'My master is delaying his coming,' and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and assign him a place with the unfaithful."

units.la: IN ijs quae proximè praecesserunt, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, in genere de omnium eorum officijs disseruit qui eius serui esse & haberi volunt. Iussit autem illos semper succinctos & ad opus suum paratos esse, aduentui suum sedulò expectare, actiones verò omnes secundum lucernam aut regulam verbi Dei instituere. Sunt praecepta haec aequa & iusta, nec ab aliquo improbari possunt, nisi qui omne pietatis sensum exuerit. Veruntamen tanta est nostrae naturae vitiositas, vt in ijs quoque negligentiores simus quae honesta & salutaria esse fatemur. Ideo Deus omnibus seculis verbi sui praecones dedit qui vt ipsos admoneant quidam nos urgeant & ad officium praestandum subinde hortentur. Quia ergo horum magnus vsus est, idem vero plurimum nocent, si in suo munere negligentiores fuerint, nunc de illis etiam Christus disserit. Vsus autem loci huius est duplex. Primò enim Ecclesiae ministros suae dignitatis simul & officij admonet. Deinde alios omnes de illis & toto munere ecclesiastico recte iudicare docet: quod in primis est necessarium. Nam nisi in hoc probè instructi sint homines, nunquam illos patienter ferent, & dum eorum admonitiones aut correptiones reijciunt, in ipsum Deum peccabunt, qui verbi sui contemptum inultum non finit.
units.tr: In the passage that immediately precedes this, our Lord Jesus Christ spoke in general about the duties of all who want to be, and be considered, his servants. He commanded them always to be girded and ready for their work, to wait diligently for his coming, and to order all their actions by the lamp or rule of God's Word. These precepts are fair and just, and no one can reject them except one who has cast off all sense of piety. Yet human nature is so prone to vice that we are even more careless in those things which we admit are honourable and beneficial. Therefore God in every age has given heralds of his Word, who warn us, urge us on, and from time to time exhort us to perform our duty. Since their use is great, and since they do great harm if they are careless in their office, Christ now speaks also about them. The use of this passage is twofold. First, it reminds the ministers of the Church of their dignity and their office. Second, it teaches all others to judge rightly concerning these men and the whole ecclesiastical ministry, which is above all necessary. For unless people are thoroughly instructed in this, they will never bear with ministers patiently, and while they reject their admonitions or rebukes, they will sin against God himself, who does not let contempt of his Word go unpunished.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi Petrus praebuit, qui cum perpetuas vigilias à Christi servis exigi audiret, quaerit, an haec ipsis dicantur, aut num ad alios etiam omnes pertineant? Eo enim vitio Apostoli priusquam Spiritu Sancto donarentur, laborarunt, ut quemadmodum in Christo regnum terrenum speraverunt: ita sibi ipsis gradum altiorem pollicit sunt, in quo à communi hominum sorte exempti, alijs omnibus praestarent, & absq; molestia dignitatibus amplissimis quiete & tranquille fruerentur. Itaq; nunc etiam Petrus iniquè cum ipsis agi putat, si ad labores & curas assiduas vocentur, neque à vulgo reliquo Christianorum differant. Habemus ergo hic typum eorum qui hodie etiam sibi plus licere putant quam alijs, & supra omnes homines eminere volunt. Est horum persuasio nocentissima: quia qui eam conceperunt, ij & alios praese contemnunt, & in suo munere deficides fiunt, quasi illos Dominus in dignitatem quandam otiosam subuexerit. Tutius ergo & salutarius est, ut quaecunq; ex Dei verbo audimus, nobis etiam putemus dici, etiamsi de alterius ordinis aut conditionis hominibus sermo fit. Ea enim verbi natura est, ut singula eius praecepta, singulae admonitiones, hortationes, correptiones, omnibus applicari possint, ut omnium institutioni & consolationi seruiant.
units.tr: Peter gave occasion for this discussion. Hearing that constant watchfulness was demanded of Christ's servants, he asks whether this is said to them or whether it also pertains to all others. For the Apostles, before they were endowed with the Holy Spirit, laboured under this fault: just as they hoped for an earthly kingdom in Christ, so they promised themselves a higher rank, in which, exempt from the common lot of humanity, they would excel all others and enjoy the most ample dignities in quiet and tranquillity without trouble. So now too Peter thinks it unjust for them to be summoned to continual labours and cares, and not to differ from the rest of the Christian people. Here, then, we have a type of those who even today think they may claim more for themselves than others, and wish to stand out above all men. This conviction is most harmful, because those who have conceived it despise others, and become negligent in their office, as if the Lord had raised them to some idle dignity. It is therefore safer and more beneficial to think that whatever we hear from God's Word is said to us as well, even when the discourse concerns men of another order or condition. For this is the nature of the Word, that each of its precepts, each admonition, exhortation and rebuke can be applied to all, so that it serves the instruction and consolation of everyone.

units.la: Apparet hoc in praesenti tractatione. Quod enim de omnium Christianorum officio Dominus dicerat, nunc Apostolus sic applicat, ut ostendat, hoc in primis ab ipsis exigi, ut vigilent & munus suum magno studio administrent, eo quod non tam de ipsorum salute agatur, quam multorum aliorum, quorum cura ipsis sit credita. Unde rursus potest generalis doctrina peti, idem ab alijs etiam requiri, qui aliquem sublimiorem dignitatis gradum in populo Dei tenent, sive illi in magistratu sint constituti, sive patresfamilias sint, aut scholis praefecti pueros, quos non temere Reipub. & ecclesiae sibi dixeris, instituere debent. Nam si omnes si negligentiores sint, ad multos alios damnum redundat, & proinde Deo poenas graviores dabunt. Ideo Christus de Ecclesiastico munere graviter disserit, & ut magis moveat, fidum ministrum cum perfido & scelerato confert, & rem totam parabola ex re domestica petita illustrat. Prioris partis haec summa & sensus est: Quemadmodum dives aliquis peregre abiturus, alicui ex servis totius familiae curam committit & ab illo fidem atque prudentiam in domo administranda requirit: Ita ego iam brevi ex hoc mundo abiturus, vobis meae domus atq; familiae, quae Ecclesia est, curam commendo, & à vobis peto, ut fideles & prudentes sitis, & singulis prospiciatis, ne quis vestra incuria pereat. Ut enim felix erit oeconomus, quem bevirus reuersus officium fideliter fecisse deprehenderit, & illi ampliora multò credentur: ita vos quoq; beati eritis, si quod vobis mandatum fideliter exequamini. Nam & functionis vestrae rationem mihi ad iudicium redeunti reddere poteritis, & aeterni regni caelestis bonis mecum fruemini. At quia haec omnia comprehenduntur, quae de munere Ecclesiastico dici possunt, utile fuerit singulas huius parabolae partes sive circumstantias ex ordine considerare.
units.tr: This appears in the present discussion. For what the Lord had said about the duty of all Christians, the Apostle now applies in such a way as to show that this above all is required of them: that they be watchful and administer their office with great zeal, since the matter concerns not so much their own salvation as that of many others, whose care has been entrusted to them. Hence again a general doctrine may be drawn: the same is required of others also who hold some higher rank of dignity among the people of God, whether they are set in the magistracy, or are heads of households, or are placed over schools, where they must teach the children, whom you may not rashly call the property of the Commonwealth and the Church. For if all of these are negligent, much harm falls upon many others, and therefore they will pay heavier penalties to God. Therefore Christ speaks gravely about the ecclesiastical office, and, to move the hearers more, he compares the faithful minister with the treacherous and wicked one, and he illustrates the whole matter by a parable taken from domestic affairs. The sum and sense of the first part is this: just as a certain rich man, about to go abroad, commits the care of his whole household to one of his servants, and requires of him faithfulness and prudence in managing the house, so I, about to depart from this world before long, commend to you the care of my house and family, which is the Church, and I ask of you that you be faithful and prudent, and look after each one, so that none of you perishes through your neglect. For as the steward will be happy whom the master, on returning, finds to have done his duty faithfully, and to whom much greater things will be entrusted, so you too will be blessed if you carry out faithfully what has been entrusted to you. For you will be able to render an account of your office to me when I return for judgement, and you will enjoy with me the goods of the eternal heavenly kingdom. But since all those things are included which can be said about the ecclesiastical office, it will be useful to consider in order the single parts or circumstances of this parable.

units.la: Primò igitur ministerij huius authorem videamus. Est is ipse Christus, qui per diuitem illum patremfamilias adumbratur. Hic enim Ecclesiae suae caput, dominus, Rex & Sacerdos est, & ideo haec Dei domus dicitur. Docet hoc Paulus euidenter, quando illum in altum ascendisse, & dona Spiritus sui inter homines distribuere scribit, ut alios quidem daret Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios item Pastores & doctores ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerij, ad aedificationem (inquam) corporis sui. Et idem in Synodo Milelana Asiae ministris dicit: Attendite vobis ipsis & toti gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit suo sanguine. Quod ut ab omnibus intelligeretur, in utroque testamento multos ipse Deus immediate, & interdum non sine miraculo vocauit: & apud Ieremiam graviter de audaculis quibusdam queritur: quod cum ab ipso non missi essent, nihilominus tamen currerent ad praedicandum. Et Paulus dicit: Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Est hoc diligenter obseruandum, ut sciamus, quo loco haberi debeant verbi administri: Nimirum quod à Deo instituti, & huius serui, adeoque in eius domo, Ecclesia, mysteriorum illius (ut Paulus ait) oeconomi sive dispensatores sint. Neque hic aliquem moueat, quod non hodie etiam, ut olim, omnes ab ipso Deo immediatè vocantur, & miraculis com-
units.tr: First, then, let us see the author of this ministry. It is Christ himself, who is shadowed forth by that rich master of the household. For he is the head, lord, king and priest of his Church, and therefore it is called God's house. Paul clearly teaches this, when he writes that Christ ascended on high and distributed the gifts of his Spirit among men, so that he gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some also pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up (I say) of his body. And in the Synod of Miletus he says the same to the ministers of Asia: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood." So that this might be understood by all, God himself in both Testaments called many immediately, and sometimes not without a miracle; and in Jeremiah he complains bitterly of certain bold men who, though they had not been sent by him, nevertheless ran to preach. And Paul says: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" This must be carefully observed, so that we know in what position the ministers of the Word ought to be held: namely, that they are instituted by God and are his servants, and therefore stewards, or dispensers, as Paul says, of his mysteries, in his house, which is the Church. Nor should it trouble anyone that today not all are called immediately by God himself, as of old, and that they are not commended by miracles.

units.la: Ephes. 4. mendantur. Eadem enim ministerij Ecclesiastici ratio est, quæ aliorum ordinum, quos inter homines Deus instituit. Exempli gratia, primos parentes ipse coniugio iunxit, vt fe coniugij authorem esse doceret, & de hoc leges dedit. Qui ergo hodie matrimonium legitimè contrahunt, bi quoque Dei instituto gloriari possunt, etiamsi non ab ipso Deo, sed huius nomine ab Ecclesiæ ministro folenni cum benedictione coniunguntur. Sic Mosem olim reipub. Ifraelitica præfecit, huic successor sub ftituit Iofuam, Iudices item suo Spiritu excitauit, Dauidem quoque constituit regem, denique sua iudicia iudicibus enuntianda credidit, vt ostenderet, magistratum & omnem huius potestatem ex ipso esse. Quotquot ergo hodie ad rempub. legitimè vocantur & eam fecundum Dei leges administrant, ij non minus ferui Dei sunt: quam veteres illi, & ipsis quoque obedientia debetur, vt Paulus ad Romanos docet. Ita olim quidem Prophetæ & Apostoli immediatè à Deo vocati iunt, vt hunc ministerij huius authorem esse constaret, interim vero Ecclesiæ potestas data est eligendi pastores & de ea re Canones Apostolici in epistolis ad Timoth. & Titum extant. Quicunq; ergo fecundum bos eliguntur, ij pro legitimis ministris & Dei ferui agnosci debent, modo suum officium faciant. Et de hoc admonebat olim manuum impositio, quæ ex sacrificantium ritu desumpta consecrationis symbolum erat, quo docebatur, illos iam totos Deo & ecclesiæ suæ ministerio cofecratos esse debere. Horum diligens cognitio primum ipsos ministros admonet, ne abfq; vocatione legitima tantum onus subeant temerè, vocati autem curent, ne sua leuitate & corruptis moribus ministerij authoritatem prostituant, ita vt propter ipsos verbum Domini male audiat. Quantum enim illud scelus fit, & quam grauiter talibus irascatur Deus, exempla filiorum Eli & eorum sacerdotum abunde docent, de quibus per Malachiam conqueritur. Deinde auditores quoque admonentur, ne quem ministrorum Ecclesiæ, qui Dei verbum fideliter & liberè prædicat, propter vilem & abiectam speciē contemnant. Nam vt Cap. decimo dictum est, contemptus ille in ipsum Deum redundat, & minifitrus explosis pœnæ scelerum magis aggrauantur, sicuti omnium seculorum exempla docent.
units.tr: Eph. 4. For the reason of the ecclesiastical ministry is the same as that of the other orders which God has established among men. For example, he himself joined the first parents in marriage, so that he might show himself to be the author of marriage, and he gave laws concerning it. Therefore those who today lawfully contract matrimony can also glory in God's institution, even though they are joined not by God himself but in his name by a minister of the Church with solemn blessing. So of old he set Moses over the Israelite commonwealth, and appointed Joshua to succeed him; he also raised up judges by his Spirit, and established David as king; finally he entrusted his judgements to be pronounced by the judges, so as to show that the magistracy and all its power come from him. Therefore all who today are lawfully called to the commonwealth and administer it according to God's laws are no less servants of God than those ancients, and obedience is owed to them as Paul teaches to the Romans. Thus, while the Prophets and Apostles were then called immediately by God, so that it might be established that he was the author of this ministry, the power of electing pastors has nevertheless been given to the Church, and the Apostolic canons about this matter exist in the epistles to Timothy and Titus. Therefore whoever are chosen according to these canons ought to be acknowledged as lawful ministers and servants of God, provided they do their office. The laying on of hands, taken from the rite of sacrificing priests and a symbol of consecration, once served to remind of this, teaching that such men ought to be wholly consecrated to God and to the ministry of his Church. Careful knowledge of these things first admonishes the ministers themselves not to undertake so great a burden rashly, without lawful calling, and, once called, to take care not to prostitute the authority of the ministry by their levity and corrupt morals, so that the Word of the Lord is badly spoken of because of them. How great a crime that is, and how gravely God is angered by such men, the examples of the sons of Eli and of those priests, about whom he complains through Malachi, abundantly teach. Next, the hearers too are admonished not to despise any minister of the Church who preaches God's Word faithfully and freely because of his poor and humble appearance. For, as was said in the tenth chapter, that contempt redounds upon God himself, and the ministers of the Church, once the wrongs are cast out, are the more burdened with the punishments of their sins, as the examples of all ages teach.

units.la: Secundo videre oportet, quo nomine illos Christus dignetur. Seruos dicit, & quidam seruos æco nomos fiue dispensatores, quia illis domus suæ curam & (vt paulò ante diximus) miniferiorum regni fui & salutis æternæ dispensationem commisit. Debet hoc quoque diligenter obseruari, quod est domui Dei præficiantur, ferui tamen sunt, non domini, qui pro suo arbitrio in Ecclesia quicquam agere debeant. Vnus enim Ecclesiæ Dominus, caput & sponsus est, quem Petrus ἀρχιποιμένα id est, pastorum principem dicit. Qui cum gloriam suam det nemini, omnes huic subesse, ei obedire, & in ecclesia, quæ eius sponsa est, non plus iuris & imperij sibi fumere debent; quàm ipsis ab illo fit datum. Ideo olim Prophetæ cerdo Dei mandato astricti fuerunt, vt verbu ex ore Dei iumerent, & duriter accusantur, qui sub huius muneris prætextu res suas agebant. Et Apostolus non liberū fuit quidus pro suo nutu statuere, sed quæ à Domino acceperant, docere debuerunt. Seruit hoc confutan dis Pontificibus, qui cum ferui feruorum dici velint, interim crudelem in Ecclesia tyrannidem exercent, & non solum contra Christi præceptum in huius seculi regna sibi potestatem vendicant, verum etiam in religione pro sua libidine leges condunt, & in ijs quæ ad animæ spectant, superbè dominantur. Sed & singulorum admonitioni hoc feruit, ne ecclesiarum ministris plus quam par est tribuant (quod olim Corinthij fecerunt) neque illos pro salutis authoribus habeant, sed Dei seruos esse agnoscant, quibus eatenus parendum fit, quatenus Dei verbum docent. Nam fi qui diuersum tradunt, ij non merentur audiri, etiamsi Angeli cœlestes fuerint. Vide Galat. 1.
units.tr: Secondly, we must see by what name Christ designates them. He calls them servants, and some call them stewards or dispensers, because he has committed to them the care of his house and, as we said a little earlier, the stewardship of the ministries of his kingdom and of eternal salvation. This must also be carefully observed: although they are set over the house of God, they are servants, not lords, and they ought not to do anything in the Church at their own pleasure. For the Church has one Lord, head and bridegroom, whom Peter calls the Prince of Shepherds [ἀρχιποιμένα], that is, the chief shepherd. Since he gives his glory to no one, all are subject to him and must obey him, and in the Church, which is his spouse, they must not assume any more right and authority for themselves than has been given them by him. For this reason the prophets of old were bound by the command of God to take the word from the mouth of God, and those who used this office as a pretext for pursuing their own affairs are harshly accused. The Apostle too was not free to lay down whatever he pleased, but had to teach what he had received from the Lord. This serves to refute the Pontiffs, who wish to be called the servants of servants, and yet in the meantime exercise a cruel tyranny in the Church; not only do they claim for themselves power over the kingdoms of this world, contrary to Christ's precept, but they also make laws in religion at their own lust, and lord it proudly over the things that pertain to the soul. This also serves the admonition of individuals, that they should not attribute to the ministers of the churches more than is fitting (as the Corinthians once did), nor regard them as the authors of salvation, but acknowledge that they are servants of God, to be obeyed only so far as they teach God's word. For if anyone teaches otherwise, such men do not deserve to be heard, even if they were heavenly angels. See Galatians 1.

units.la: Tertium in hac tractatione est, vt quibus verbi fui ministros Dominus præfecerit, intelligamus. Famulitium hic nominat, quo nomine omnes, qui ad domum fiue Ecclesiam Dei pertinent intelliguntur. Nam ij omnes cuiuscunque loci sint aut ordinis, Dei ferui & famuli sunt. Ideo apud Ezechielem domus Iuda vel Israel nominatur, & Paulus fe Timotheo scribere dicit, vt sciat, quomodo versari debeat in domo Dei. Comprehendit autem hæc vox omnes hominum ordines, principes, subditos, heros & seruos, senes & pueros, mares & fœminas, doctos & indoctos, diuites & pauperes, nobiles & ignobiles. Nam vt Paulus docet, non aliquis apud Deum perfonarū respectus est. Ideo Ieremiæ dicebatur: Constitui te super gentes & regna. Item: Ecce ego facio te hodie ciuitatem munitam, columnam ferream, & murum æneum contra omnem terram, contra reges Iuda, contra principes eius, & contra vniuersum populum terra. Et Christus Apostolis mandauit
units.tr: The third point in this discussion is that we should understand to whom the Lord has given charge of his word as ministers. Here he names them a household, a name under which all who belong to the house or Church of God are understood. For all of them, of whatever place or rank, are servants and household slaves of God. Therefore in Ezekiel the house of Judah or of Israel is named, and Paul says that he writes to Timothy so that he may know how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God. This word, moreover, embraces all orders of men: rulers and subjects, freemen and slaves, old and young, males and females, learned and unlearned, rich and poor, noble and base. For, as Paul teaches, there is no respect of persons with God. Therefore it was said to Jeremiah: "I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms." Likewise: "Behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar and a brazen wall against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, and the whole people of the land." And Christ commanded the Apostles

units.la: Ierem. 1. danit, ut Euangelium omni creaturae praedicarent. Ergo ministri nemine negligere aut vilem atq; contemptu dignum censere debent, pro quo Dei Filius mori dignatus est, & qui inter Ecclesiae membra aut Christi domesticos numeratur. Quin potius cogitent, in magna domo (ut Apostolus ait) omnis generis vasa esse, aurea, argentea, anea, ferrea, lignea, testacea, de omnibus autem ratione esse reddenda ei, qui domus administratione ab hero susceptit. Et boni pastoris est non solum oves pingues pascere, sed macilentis quoq; prospicere, imo errantes quaerere, vulneratas & sauciás obligare, inualidas mederi, omnia denique agere, quae ad singularum salutem faciunt. Obseruarunt hoc olim Prophetae diligenter, ut in illorum sermonibus est videre. Et Ioannes Baptista omnibus promiscue concionatus est, deinde singulis abs se consilium petentibus fideliter indicauit, quid eos facere conueniret. Idem Christus fecit, cuius exemplum & mandatum Apostoli secuti, omnis loci, aetatis & sexus hominibus sua officia praescripserunt. Debet ad hoc ministros excitare, quod impij quoq; sanguinem eorum manu Deus requiret, si in illo admonendo negligentiores fuerint. Quas ergo poenas non merentur, qui salutis & veritatis cognoscendae cupidos negligunt, & interea rebus vacant a sua functione alienis? At simul docet locus iste, omnes homines teneri, ut Dei verbum audiant & hoc annuntianti ministro obtemperent. Nam ut omnibus doctrina & institutione opus est: ita nemo cuiuscunq; sit loci aut ordinis, se immunem & ab aliorum numero exemptum dicere potest, nisi simul ex Dei familia velit expungi. Est ergo nimium impudens & effrenis illorum arrogantia, qui Ecclesiarum ministros nihil ad ipsos pertinentia tractare clamant, neq; suos mores & studia prava ab illis argui atq; corripi patiuntur. Insurgunt hi aduersus ipsum Deum, & seipsos abdicant, ne ex filiorum eius numero censeantur, unde non aliud quam praesens exitium & sempiternus interitus sequi poterit. Nam qui ex Deo est (inquit Christus) audit verbum meum. Et Pharisaeos diaboli filios esse dicit, quod illud audire dedignarentur. Ioan. 8. cap.
units.tr: Jer. 1. to preach the Gospel to every creature. Therefore ministers ought not to neglect anyone or to judge anyone base and worthy of contempt, for whom the Son of God deigned to die, and who is numbered among the members of the Church or the household of Christ. Rather let them consider that in a great house (as the Apostle says) there are vessels of every kind, gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, earthenware, and that they must give account of all of them to him who has received the administration of the house from the master. It is the duty of a good shepherd not only to feed the fat sheep, but also to look after the weak, indeed to seek out the straying, to bind up the wounded and the injured, to heal the infirm, and in short to do everything that contributes to the salvation of each one. The prophets of old observed this carefully, as may be seen in their sermons. And John the Baptist preached to all in common, and then faithfully showed each individual who sought counsel from him what he ought to do. Christ did the same, and the Apostles, following his example and command, prescribed duties for men of every place, age and sex. This should stir ministers up, since God will require the blood of those even of the ungodly at their hand if they have been negligent in admonishing them. What punishments, then, do they not deserve who neglect those who desire salvation and the knowledge of the truth, and in the meantime give themselves to affairs foreign to their own office? At the same time this passage also teaches that all men are bound to hear the word of God and to obey the minister who announces it. For just as all need teaching and instruction, so no one, of whatever place or rank, can say that he is exempt and excluded from the number of the others, unless he wishes at the same time to be struck off from the family of God. Therefore the arrogance of those is very shameless and unbridled, who cry out that the ministers of the churches deal with matters that do not concern them, and who will not allow their wicked morals and pursuits to be reproved and corrected by them. Such men rise up against God himself and disown themselves, so that they will not be counted among his sons; from this nothing can follow but present ruin and everlasting destruction. For "he who is of God," says Christ, "hears my word." And he says that the Pharisees are sons of the devil, because they disdained to hear it. John 8.

units.la: Quarto proprium & praecipuum dispensatoris Ecclesiastici officium exprimitur: quod est, ut familiae Domini in tempore det demensum. Fuit autem demensum certa frumenti mensura, quam singulis mensibus heri serui admetiebantur in totius mensis vitium. Sensus ergo est, quod ministri Ecclesiae cibum singulis depromere & distribuere debeant. Loquitur autem non de cibo corruptibili quo homines ad vitam hanc temporariam & mortalem aluntur: sed de aeterno & caelesti, quo ad vitam caelestem atque aeternam pascimur. Est is verbum Dei, de quo apud Isaiam loquens Dominus clamat: O vos omnes, qui sitis, venite ad aquas: & vos quibus non est pecunia, venite, comparate, & comedite. Emite, inquam, sine argento & sine pretio vinum & lac. Cur expenditis pecuniam pro non pane? & laborem vestrum pro eo quod non satiat? Et mox ipsum exponens addit: Audite audiendo me, & comedite bonum, & in pinguedine oblectet se anima vestra: Inclinate aurem vestram, & ad me venite, audite, & viuet anima vestra, &c. De cibo igitur & potu agit, qui audiendo editur & bibitur: unde constat, hunc non alium quam verbum esse, cum solae voces auditu percipiantur. Praecipuum ergo ministri Ecclesiae munus est, docere aut praedicare verbum Dei: in quo possit Prophetas & Ioannem Baptistam Christus quoq; in primis occupatus fuit, qui se ideo in mundum venisse testatur. Verbum vero hoc proponere debet in tempore, id est, pro ratione temporum, locorum, & ingeniorum, quibus cum illi res est, & ita accommodare, ut ex eo quam plurimi aedificentur ad salutem aeternam. Id Paulus vocat, Recte secare verbum Domini. Quod ipse summa diligentia praestitit, quando omnibus omnia factus est, ut omnes lucrifaceret: & Corinthios lacte abs se enutritos fuisse testatur, cum solidiorem cibum nondum possent capere. Idem vero Galatas durius tractat, eo quod illud eorum leuitas, & huic coniuncta stupiditas mereretur. Et debet hoc propter eos obseruari, qui verbum Dei simpliciter annuntiari, nullius autem moribus applicari debere clamant: & qui nihil praeter promissiones de gratia Dei & suauem de humani generis redemptione & Iesu Christi merito doctrinam audire cupiunt. Quod perinde est, ac si aegrotus medico praescribat, & dulcia leniaq; pharmaca aut molles unctiones adhiberi velit, quando vstione aut sectione opus est. Ut autem medici saepe inuitis amariora pharmaca ingerunt, & reluctantes vrunt atq; secant: ita verbi administrum no illorum delicatulas aures respicere, sed ad ministerij sui finem constanter tendere oportet, qui est, ut homines in Christo poenitentiam simul & remissione peccatorum assequantur. Et de hoc Paulus Timotheum suum magna cum gravitate admonet, dicens: Obtestor ego coram Deo & Do-
units.tr: Fourthly, the proper and chief office of the ecclesiastical steward is set forth: that he gives the household of the Lord its measure of food in due season. Now the measure was a fixed quantity of grain, which the servants of the household used to measure out each month for the whole month's supply. The sense, then, is that the ministers of the Church ought to bring forth and distribute food to each person. But it speaks not of the perishable food by which men are nourished for this temporary and mortal life, but of the eternal and heavenly food by which we are fed for the heavenly and eternal life. This food is the word of God, of which the Lord, speaking through Isaiah, cries: "O all you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat. Buy, I say, without money and without price, wine and milk. Why do you spend money for what is not bread, and your labour for that which does not satisfy?" And soon, explaining it, he adds: "Hear me, hearing, and eat what is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Incline your ear and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live," etc. He speaks, then, of food and drink which is eaten and drunk by hearing; whence it is plain that this is nothing other than the word, since only voices are perceived by hearing. The chief duty of the ministers of the Church, therefore, is to teach or preach the word of God, in which Christ too was chiefly occupied, as were the prophets and John the Baptist, and he himself testifies that he came into the world for this reason. Moreover, this word the minister ought to set forth in due season, that is, according to the circumstances of the times, places and dispositions of those with whom he has to deal, and to adapt it so that very many may be built up to eternal salvation. This Paul calls "rightly dividing the word of the Lord." He himself did this with the greatest diligence when he became all things to all men, that he might gain all; and he testifies that he had fed the Corinthians with milk, since they could not yet take solid food. He treats the Galatians more harshly, because their levity, and the stupidity joined with it, deserved this. And this must be observed on account of those who cry out that the word of God ought to be announced simply, without being applied to anyone's morals, and who wish to hear nothing but promises about the grace of God and a sweet doctrine of the redemption of mankind and the merit of Jesus Christ. This is just as if a sick man were to prescribe to his physician, and wished soft and sweet medicines or gentle ointments to be applied, when cauterising or cutting is needed. And just as physicians often force bitter medicines upon unwilling patients, and burn and cut them although they resist, so the minister of the word ought not to regard the dainty ears of such people, but must steadily aim at the end of his ministry, which is that men may obtain in Christ both repentance and at the same time the forgiveness of sins. And on this point Paul admonishes his Timothy with great seriousness, saying: "I charge you before God and the Lord..."

units.la: 2. Tim. 4. mino Iesu Christo, qui iudicaturus est viuos & mortuos in illustri illo suo aduentu & regno suo: Prædica sermonem, insta tempestiue & intempestiue, argue, obiurga, exhortare cum omni lenitate & doctrina. Intempestiuum quoq; esse iubet, non Christi mandato contradicens, sed vt offendat pro eorum etiam ingenio prædicationem accommodari oportere, qui præfractiores sunt, & eam minus patienter ferunt. Ideo huius dicti rationem subijcit: Nam erit tempus, cum sanam doctrinam non tolerabunt: sed auribus prurientes ipsi sibi pro suis cupiditatibus coacernabunt doctores, &c. Ergo non hominum desiderijs indulgere, sed quod à Deo in mandatis habet, minister exequi debet.
units.tr: 2. Tim. 4. "I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the living and the dead at his glorious appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching." He also bids him be urgent out of season, not contradicting Christ's command, but to show that preaching must be adapted even to the temperament of those who are more stubborn and bear it less patiently. So he gives the reason for this saying: "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but having itching ears they will heap up for themselves teachers according to their own lusts, etc." Therefore the minister must not indulge men's desires, but carry out what he has been commanded by God.

units.la: Et huc pertinet, quòd dotes quoq; animi aut virtutes Christus commemorat, quibus illum instructum esse conuenit. Dicit enim: Quis nam est fidus dispensator ac prudens? Primo fidem in rebus agendis requirit, quam Paulus quoq; præ omnibus alijs in dispensatore requiri ait. Nam si hac deficiatur, iam aut fur erit, aut heri bona negligentia sua dissipabit. At fidi sunt dispensatores in domo Dei, qui studiorum suorum omnium finem sibi proponunt gloriam illius & Ecclesiæ ædificationem. Quod tunc illos facere patebit, si in multis Christo adducendis & gloria Dei promouenda industrij sint, nec quicquam ferre possint, quo vel hæc obscuratur, aut homines à salute in Christo parta abstrahuntur: qualia in primis sunt falsa doctrina, superstitiones, illiciti cultus, idololatria aperta & scelerum licentia. Hæc igitur fidi ministri diruunt, extirpant & eradicant, sicuti Ieremiæ olim Dominus mandauit. Vnde sequitur parùm fideles Deo & hominibus esse eos, qui cum falsis doctoribus colluduntur, qui superstitiones fouent, qui ad cultus nefarios & idololatricos conniuent, & in scelaribus arguendis canes muti sunt. At ne zelus fidei coniunctus transfuerfos abripiat, prudentem quoq; & prouidum esse vult Dominus suæ domus dispensatorem, qui quid quoque loco & tempore docere debeat, & quid ædificationi seruiat, videre possit. Vbi ante omnia diligenti scripturarum cognitione opus est, ex quibus doctrinam omnem hauriri oportet. Ideo Paulus Timotheum, quem à pueris in Scripturis enutritum esse sciebat, nihilominus lectioni incumbere iubet. Deinde vigilans & diligens omnium circumstantiarum obseruatio requiritur, pro quarum ratione doctrinam attemperet. Non ergo de carnis & mundi prudentia loquitur Christus, cui si ministri studeant, fere perfidi fiunt, & dum mundo placere volunt, Dei serui esse non possunt. Prudentia igitur opus est, quæ cum fide coniuncta sit, imò quæ hanc quasi ducem sequatur, & qua non tam alijs, quam sibijpsis attendant (vt Paulus ait) ne quid inconsultius agant cum Ecclesiæ incommodo.
units.tr: This is also the point of the qualities of mind or virtues which Christ mentions, with which it is fitting that the steward be equipped. For he says: "Who then is the faithful and wise steward?" First he requires faithfulness in carrying out his duties, which Paul also says is required of a steward above all else. For if this is lacking, he will either be a thief or, through his own carelessness, squander his master's goods. Now the stewards in God's house are faithful when they set before themselves as the goal of all their labours the glory of God and the building up of the Church. This will be plain if they are diligent in bringing many to Christ and in advancing the glory of God, and if they can tolerate nothing that either obscures this or draws men away from the salvation obtained in Christ. Chief among such things are false doctrine, superstitions, unlawful worship, open idolatry and licence in sin. Faithful ministers therefore tear these down, uproot them and eradicate them, as the Lord once commanded Jeremiah. Hence it follows that those who play along with false teachers, who foster superstitions, who wink at wicked and idolatrous worship, and who are dumb dogs in rebuking sins, are scarcely faithful to God or to men. But so that a zeal for the faith does not carry him off into extremes, the Lord also wants his house-steward to be prudent and provident, able to see what he ought to teach in each place and at each time, and what serves for edification. Here above all there is need of diligent knowledge of the Scriptures, from which all teaching must be drawn. So Paul bids Timothy, whom he knew to have been nourished in the Scriptures from childhood, nevertheless to devote himself to reading. Then a watchful and diligent observation of all the circumstances is required, so that he may adapt his teaching to them. Christ therefore is not speaking of the prudence of the flesh and of the world. If ministers strive after this, they almost inevitably become unfaithful, and while they wish to please the world they cannot be servants of God. Prudence is therefore needed, joined with faith, or rather following faith as its guide, by which they attend not so much to others as to themselves (as Paul says), lest they do anything too rashly to the harm of the Church.

units.la: Quia verò tota hac functio laboris & odij plena est, amplissimi præmij promissione ministros excitat Dominus, dicens: Beatus seruus ille, quem Dominus, cùm venerit, inueniet sic facientem: Vere dico vobis, omnibus suis bonis præficiet eum. Primò beatum dicit, & hoc mundi atq; carnis iudicio opponit, quo tales fere omnium mortalium miserrimi putantur. Idem enim illis fit, quod fidis æconomis in perfida & petulanti familia. Vt enim hi dum heri sui commodis studeant, illam aduersus se pro uocant, & domesticos omnes inimicos habent: ita qui in Ecclesiæ ministerio fideles sunt, abijs fere acerbissimis odijs infestantur, pro quorum salute ipsi dies noctesq; excubat. Ideo Elias mori cupiebat, ne porrò hoc saxum voluere cogeretur. Et Ieremias clamabat: Væ mihi o mater mea, quòd me peperi sti, virum litigatorem, & virum controuersiæ vniuersæ terræ: non fæneraui, neq; fænori innexus sum, veruntamen omnes me contemnunt. Sed non debet corruptum mundi iudicium aliquos mouere, qui officium suum diligenter faciunt. Reuera enim beati sunt, vt de illis caro sentiat. Nam Christo seruiunt liberalissimo remuneratori, qui omnibus bonis suis eos præficiet. Dicitur hoc ἀνθρωποπρεπῶς, id est, pro hominum sensu & more, qui serui quorum fidem perspectam habent, pluriu̇m & maiorum rerum administrationem solent committere. Exponitur autem infra cap.22. vbi Apostolus secum ad eandem mensam in regno Patris sui discubituros, id est, bonorum cœlestium vna participes & cosortes futuros esse pollicetur. Et cum Daniele de fine seculi huius differes Angelus, inter alia ait: Porrò doctores splendebunt, vt splendor firmamenti: & qui multos ad iustitiam adducunt, vt stellæ sempiternis temporibus. Quæ ita de Ecclesiæ ministris dicuntur, vt nō minus ijs quoq; omnibus accommodari possint, qui vel in Repub. vel Scholis, vel familijs suis gloriā Dei promouebunt, aut etiā priuatim aliquos ad pœnitentiam & fidem in Christū excitant. Imò attentis quoq; verbi auditoribus, qui ei obtemperant, Regnū Dei promittitur, & quod in cœlis cum Christo bonorū cœlestium hæredes futuri sint. Vide Ioan.17.
units.tr: But since this whole office is full of toil and hatred, the Lord rouses ministers with the promise of a very great reward, saying: "Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing. Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his goods." First he calls him blessed, and sets this against the judgment of the world and the flesh, by which such men are generally thought the most wretched of all mortals. For it happens to them just as it does to faithful stewards in a faithless and unruly household. When these look to the advantage of their master, the household stirs itself against them, and all the servants become their enemies. So those who are faithful in the ministry of the Church are assailed with the bitterest hatreds, from the very people for whose salvation they keep watch day and night. Therefore Elijah wished to die, lest he be forced to roll this stone any longer. And Jeremiah cried out: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet all men curse me." But the corrupt judgment of the world ought not to disturb those who faithfully do their duty. For they are truly blessed, however the flesh may feel about them. For they serve Christ, the most generous rewarder, who will set them over all his goods. This is said ἀνθρωποπρεπῶς [in a manner suited to men], that is, according to human feeling and custom, which is accustomed to entrust the management of many and greater affairs to servants whose fidelity has been proved. It is explained further on in chapter 22, where the Apostle promises that those who have followed him will sit with him at the same table in the kingdom of his Father, that is, will be partakers and fellow heirs of the heavenly goods. And when the angel, speaking to Daniel about the end of this age, says among other things: "Moreover the teachers shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who bring many to righteousness as the stars for everlasting ages." These things are said of the ministers of the Church in such a way that they can be applied no less to all those who advance the glory of God in the commonwealth, in schools or in their households, or who even privately stir some to repentance and faith in Christ. Indeed, to the hearers of the word who attend to it and obey it, the kingdom of God is promised, and that they will be heirs with Christ of heavenly goods in heaven. See John 17.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua dispensatorem perfidum atque nequam describit, & huius mores simul ac poenam, quae ipsum manet, fido & prudenti seruo opponit, ut magis moueat. Sic autem ait: Quòd si dixerit seruus ille in corde suo: Tardat dominus meus aduentu, &c. Orditur à causa omnis mali & licentiae, quae est, quòd in corde suo dicit, id est, persuadet sibi, herum vel nondum, vel etiam omnino non rediturum esse. Quo loco malae frugis seruorum ingenium atq; mores exprimuntur. Hi quia ad oculū modò seruiunt, heri discessu gaudent, & seduli sunt in omnibus parandis, quae illi ad professionem sunt necessaria. Vt primum verò illum iam longius recessisse sciunt, mox illius reditum in multos menses aut annos reiciunt, aut eum omnino vix unquam redire posse sibi pollicentur. Quae causa est, quòd neglecto suo officio carnis cupiditatibus indulgent, & ad omnem nequitiam se proiiciunt, ut postea audiemus. Idem Christus Ecclesiae ministrus accidere dicit, ut falsis persuasionibus se decipiat, nisi animos vero & serio Dei timore muniant.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other part of this passage, in which he describes the unfaithful and wicked steward, and sets his manners and the punishment that awaits him against the faithful and prudent servant, so as to move us more. He says: "But if that servant shall say in his heart, My lord delays his coming, etc." He begins with the cause of all evil and licence, which is that he says in his heart, that is, persuades himself, that his master will either not yet return or not return at all. Here the nature and manners of bad servants are set forth. Since they serve only before the eyes, they rejoice when the master is gone, and they are diligent in preparing whatever is needed for their own profit. But as soon as they know that he has gone far away, they put off his return for many months or years, or promise themselves that he will hardly ever be able to come back. The result is that, neglecting their duty, they indulge the lusts of the flesh and throw themselves into every wickedness, as we shall hear afterwards. Christ says that the same thing happens to a minister of the Church: he deceives himself with false persuasions, unless his mind is fortified with true and serious fear of God.

units.la: Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, omnis impietatis & licentiae scelerum praecipuam causam esse, falsò conceptas de Deo & eius Prouidentia opiniones. Nam vt vera Dei cognitio fidè parit, eius item dilectionem & ingenuum timorem, quem serium illi obsequendi studium necessariò sequitur: Ita falsae de illo opiniones fidem extinguunt, & hac extincta amorem quoq; Dei ex animis auferunt, superstitionum verò causa sunt & idololatriae, quam plerunq; effrenus morum corruptio comitatur, vt Paulus gentium exemplo ad Romanos docet. Inter opiniones autem huiusmodi omnium nocentissima est eorum, qui aut Deum omnino nullum esse dicunt, aut (quod in idem recidit) illum res hominū & quae in terris geruntur, curare negant. Hi enim, cuiuscunq; sint loci & ordinis, in omne scelus praecipites ruunt. Ideo Dauid impietatis fontem & progressum describturus ait: Dixit Nabal (id est, homo stolidus & mentis depravatae) in corde suo, Non est Deus. Et mox subiicit: Corrupta & abominanda studia sectantur, nemo est qui quod bonum est faciat, &c. Et alibi, cùm de tyrannicis sui seculi moribus conqueritur essel, eorum scelicet, qui populum Dei affligebant, viduas & aduenas occidebant, & pupillos interimebant, etiam infert: Interim dicunt, Dominus non videt, neq; Deus Iacob intelligit, &c. Discant ergo singuli recta de Deo sententijs assuescere, & ex Scripturis sacris edocti firmiter credant Deū esse, qui omnia creavit & omnia gubernet: qui nos in terris bisce laborantes & tumultuantes videat, afflictorum clamores audiat, & eorundem lachrymas in suarum rationum libros ascribat: qui zelotes sit & sceleribus irascatur, & qui iudicium sit facturus olim, in quo scelerum poenas exoluere oporteat omnes eos, qui se contumaciores & incurabiles praebent. Qui ista frequenter meditantur, & simul quae quotidie fiunt iudiciorum Dei exempla obseruant, ij neq; carnis propriae socordia, neq; mundi huius exemplo decipi poterunt, quò minus fidelium seruorum instar ad illius aduentum semper parati sint.
units.tr: From this a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that the chief cause of all impiety and licence in sin is false opinions conceived about God and his providence. For just as the true knowledge of God brings forth faith, and likewise love of him and a free fear, which necessarily follows upon a serious desire to obey him, so false opinions about him extinguish faith, and once faith is extinguished they also remove the love of God from men's minds. Such opinions are the cause of superstitions and idolatry, which is usually accompanied by a headlong corruption of morals, as Paul teaches in Romans by the example of the Gentiles. Among opinions of this kind, the most harmful is that of those who either say that there is no God at all, or (which comes to the same thing) deny that he cares for the affairs of men and what goes on on earth. For such people, of whatever place or rank they are, rush headlong into every crime. So David, wishing to describe the source and progress of impiety, says: "Nabal (that is, a foolish man of depraved mind) said in his heart, There is no God." And soon after he adds: "They pursue corrupt and abominable pursuits; there is none who does what is good, etc." And elsewhere, when he complains of the tyrannical manners of his own age, namely of those who afflicted the people of God, killed widows and strangers and murdered orphans, he also adds: "Meanwhile they say, The Lord does not see, neither does the God of Jacob understand, etc." Let each one therefore learn to be accustomed to right opinions about God, and, taught from the holy Scriptures, let him firmly believe that there is a God who created all things and governs all things; who sees us labouring and struggling here on earth, hears the cries of the afflicted, and records their tears in the books of his accounts; who is a zealot and is angry at sins; and who will one day hold a judgment in which all those must pay the penalties of their sins who show themselves stubborn and incurable. Those who frequently meditate on these things, and at the same time observe the examples of God's judgments that happen every day, will be deceived neither by the sloth of their own flesh nor by the example of this world, so that they may always be ready, like faithful servants, for his coming.

units.la: Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, qui impietatis progressum exponens, perfidi & nequam serui mores & facta describit, & duobus membris seu cribus omnia eius scelera comprehendit. Primum est, quòd sua potestate crudeliter abutens in conseruos, quos alere debebat, tyrannidem exercet, & seruos atque ancillas percutit. Solent hoc fere seruili ingenij homines, qui ex infima conditione in aliquem sublimiorem dignitatis gradum euehuntur, ut non temere prouerbio dicatur, nulla imperia duriora & minus tolerabilia esse, quàm pauperum & seruorum. Alterum est, quòd non solum familiam & res heri sui negligit, verumetiam luxu & intemperantia illius bona dilapidat. Cui tertium coniunctum est, quòd malorum consortia sectatur, & cum ebriosis comessatur ac potat. Quod ipsum quoq; malae frugis serui facere consueuerunt: & cùm serui sit res heri sui ut proprias curare, honori & commodo eius pro virili consulere, diuersum plane faciunt, & quasi ad dissipandam rem domesticam conducti sint, omnia dilapidant, nocturnis comessationibus se dedunt, & sui similes nequam intra heriles aedes adducunt, aut heri penum ad illos exportant, quae certissima familiarum pestis est.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ's words, in which he describes the progress of impiety, the manners and deeds of the wicked and faithless servant, and sums up all his crimes under two, or rather three, heads. The first is that he cruelly abuses his power over his fellow servants, whom he ought to feed, exercises tyranny over them, and beats the menservants and maidservants. Men of servile disposition who are raised from the lowest station to some higher rank of dignity commonly behave this way, and the proverb is not idly spoken: no rule is harsher or less tolerable than that of the poor over their servants. The second is that he not only neglects the household and property of his master but also squanders his goods in luxury and intemperance. Joined to this is the third: he keeps company with bad men and feasts and drinks with drunkards. Bad servants are wont to do exactly this. Although the property of a master should be cared for as one's own and his honour and advantage promoted to the best of one's ability, they do the opposite. As if hired to ruin the household, they squander everything, give themselves over to nightly carousing, and bring their wicked fellows into the master's house, or carry the master's provisions out to them. This is the surest plague of a household.

units.la: Porrò sub hoc typo perfidos Ecclesiae ministros graphicè Dominus depingit, in quibus haec omnia licet inuenire. Olim certè Prophetarum temporibus falsi doctores in bos crudelem tyrannidem exercuerunt.
