Nam sub Achabo Rege Zedeckias quidam impostor nequissimus Michea verbum Domini annuntiante ignominiose in faciem percutit. Amos Prophetam Amasias Sacerdos iolum vertere iubet, & obedire nolentem apud Ieroboamum Regem seditionis accusat. Ieremias quoq; non alios graviores hostes sensit, quàm Hananiam & alios falsos doctores, qui se veros Ecclesiae antistites & pastores esse profitebantur. Et reliquos Prophetas idem passos esse, eorum sermones satis euidenter docent. Sed & totum populum Dei illi percussere, quando falsa sua doctrina seductis multorum malorum, & tandem excidij atq; exilij Babylonici fuerunt authores. Pertinet huc quod Mich.scribit: Sic dicit Dominus contra prophetas, qui seducunt populum meum: Mordent dentibus suis, & clamant, Pax: & si quis non dederit in os eorum, sanctificant contra eum bellum. Quibus ver bis simul gulae & ventris quoq; studium eis exprobrat, quod evidentius Isaias facit, dicens: Pastores ipsi nihil intelligunt, omnes suam viam spectant, quisq; ad emolumentum suum a summo eius. Venite (aiunt) vinum adferam, ut perpotemus ad ebrietatem usq; atq; adeo sicut hodie, ita & cras abundantia magna valde. Quales autem olim in veteri testamento falsi antistites fuerunt, tales in Novo quoq; temporibus Christi & Apostolorum fuisse, Evangelica historia docet. Eò usq; progressa fuit Sacerdotum & Pharisaeorum audacia, ut ipsi Dei Filio insidiarentur, & eum suis artibus atq; calumniis ad infamem crucis mortem adducerent. Populum vero traditionibus iniquis & nocentissimis grauarunt. Insuper Ecclesiae bona, decimas, primitias & quaecunq; alia conferebantur, ad se rapuerunt, & ex illis ditati sunt, multis interim contra legem Dei mendicantibus, quibus publice & priuatim prospici debebat. Interim cum Sadducaeis Epicureismi sectatoribus, cum Herodianis item & Romanis praesidibus colludebant, ut veritatis praecones facilius possent opprimere.
units.tr: Under this figure the Lord vividly portrays the faithless ministers of the Church, in whom all these vices may be found. In the days of the Prophets, false teachers certainly exercised cruel tyranny over the godly. Under King Ahab, the wicked impostor Zedekiah struck Micaiah in the face with contempt when he announced the word of the Lord. Amaziah the priest ordered Amos to leave and, when he refused to obey, accused him of sedition before King Jeroboam. Jeremiah likewise felt no heavier enemies than Hananiah and the other false teachers, who professed to be the true leaders and ministers of the Church. The writings of the other Prophets show clearly that they suffered the same. These men also struck the whole people of God, since by their false doctrine many were seduced into evil and were finally the authors of the destruction and the Babylonian exile. To this belongs what Micah writes: "Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray: they bite with their teeth and cry, 'Peace'; and if anyone does not put something into their mouths, they proclaim war against him" (Mich. 3.). With these words he also rebukes them for their zeal for the belly and gullet, which Isaiah does more plainly, saying: "The shepherds themselves understand nothing; they all look to their own way, each for his own gain from its beginning. 'Come,' they say, 'I will fetch wine, and we will drink ourselves full of strong drink; tomorrow will be like today, very abundant'" (Isa. 56.). Evangelical history shows that such were the false leaders of the Old Testament, and that such also were those of the New Testament, in the time of Christ and the Apostles. The audacity of the priests and Pharisees went so far that they laid snares for the Son of God himself and, by their arts and calumnies, brought him to the infamous death of the cross. They burdened the people with wicked and most harmful traditions. Moreover, they seized for themselves the goods of the Church, the tithes, the firstfruits and whatever else was contributed, and grew rich from them, while meanwhile many who ought to have been provided for publicly and privately went begging against the law of God. In the meantime they colluded with the Sadducees, followers of Epicurean doctrine, and likewise with the Herodians and the Roman governors, so that they could more easily crush the heralds of the truth.

units.la: Docent ista nos iudicare de iis, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus in Dei domo omne ius & imperium vsurparunt, Pontificibus nimirum & Episcopis, in quibus eosdem mores & eadem studia est videre. Primò enim tyrannide Ecclesiam oppresserunt, quoad animas & corpora atq; fortunas hominum. Quos enim verbo Dei pascere debebat, eos traditionibus impijs de salute incertos & dubios fecerunt, eò autè praetextu fortunis quoq; spoliarunt, quando tota religio ipsis quaestus facta est. Quod si qui fideles serui Dei ipsorum iniquitate arguere ausi sunt, mox ad vim conuersi, illos carceribus, vinculis, ferro item & igne coercuerunt. Tanta denique eorum rabies & insolentia iam saeculis aliquot fuit, ut ne Regibus quidem & Imperatoribus pepercerint, sed hos quoq; suis excommunicationibus flagellarint, seditionibus & bellis exagitarint, sibi supplices fieri coegerint, & eorum colla pedibus imparis calcarint. Exempla huius tonitrumeliae in Heinricho IIII. Friderico I. & II. & multis alijs extant, quorum vitae etiam no putarunt esse parcendum. Et quid hodie faciant, quamq; multorum bellorum atq; seditionum authores sint, vulgo notum est, ut ijs commemorandis non opus sit insistere. Interim ijdem toti carnis studijs & voluptatibus immersi res Ecclesiae negligunt, ventri autem & gulae studeant, venantur, ludunt, perpotant scortantur, thoros alienos polluunt, adhaec libidinis aestro extimulati ea designant nonnulli, quae pudor est dicere. Et cum Ecclesiae antistites videri & haberi velint, plerunq; eos in deliciis habent, qui ut inter Ecclesiae membra numerentur indigni sunt: interdum cum Turcis colluduntur, ut suae tyrannidi consulant. Sic Friderichu Barbarossam ab Alexand.III. Turcis proditum fuisse historiae testantur. Et simili in Carolu Francorum regem Alexandri V I. perfidia patrum memoria extitit. Cum enim ille in Neapolim cum exercitu tenderet, eoq; bello confecto in Graeciam traijcere decreuisset, ut eam ex Turcarum tyrannide vindicaret, & ad id bellum Baiazetis Turcici Imperatoris fratre Gemē, qui patria pulsus et extorris Romae in custodia detinebatur, vt decreuisset, Pontifex hæc Regis consilia Baiazeti prodidit, neq; antea Carolo Gemem tradidit, quàm ei venenum lentum propinauisset, ex quo ad Caietam mortuus est. Et huius generis exempla infinita adduci poterant, si quis singulorum Pontificum, Cardinalium & Episcoporum vitas veliet excutere. Quis ergo dubitet eos illorum loco debere haberi, quos hic Christus sub iniquissimi dispensatoris persona describit? Est autem deplorata mundi infelicitas, qui cum ista non modo videat, verumetiam magno suo malo sentiat, illos tamen fert, imo tyrannidem eorum publica authoritate defendit, & pro illis pugnat aduersus omnes, qui ipsis subesse nolunt.
units.tr: These things teach us to judge those who in these latest times have usurped all right and power in the house of God, namely the Popes and bishops, in whom the same manners and the same pursuits may be seen. First, they have oppressed the Church with tyranny, both as to the souls, bodies and fortunes of men. Those whom they ought to feed with the Word of God, they have made uncertain and doubtful about salvation by impious traditions, and under that pretext they have also stripped them of their goods, since all religion has become a source of gain for them. If any faithful servants of God have dared to rebuke their wickedness, they have straightway turned to violence and restrained them with prisons, chains, and also with iron and fire. Finally, their rage and insolence have been so great for some centuries that they have not spared even kings and emperors, but have scourged them too with their excommunications, harassed them with seditions and wars, forced them to become suppliants to themselves, and trampled their necks under their feet. Examples of this thunderbolt are found in Henry IV, Frederick I and II, and many others, whose lives they did not think should be spared. And what they do today, and how many wars and seditions they are the authors of, is commonly known, so there is no need to dwell on recounting these things. Meanwhile these same men, wholly immersed in the pursuits and pleasures of the flesh, neglect the affairs of the Church, but devote themselves to the belly and the gullet. They hunt, they gamble, they drink to excess, they whore, they defile other men's beds; moreover, stirred by the heat of lust, some of them plan things that are shameful even to speak of. And although they wish to be seen and regarded as leaders of the Church, they often keep in their favour those who are unworthy to be counted among the members of the Church. At times they even collude with the Turks in order to secure their tyranny. Histories testify that Frederick Barbarossa was betrayed to the Turks by Alexander III. In our own memory there was a similar treachery of the Pope, Alexander VI, against Charles, king of the French. When that king was marching with his army toward Naples, and after finishing that war had decided to cross into Greece to deliver it from the tyranny of the Turks, the Pope betrayed the king's plans to Bajazet, the Turkish emperor. For this war Djem, the brother of Bajazet, had been driven from his homeland and held in custody at Rome. The Pope did not hand Djem over to Charles until he had given him a slow poison, from which Djem died at Gaeta. Countless examples of this kind could be adduced if anyone wished to examine the lives of individual Popes, cardinals and bishops. Who then could doubt that these men must be taken to be in the place of those whom Christ here describes under the person of the most unjust steward? Yet it is the wretched condition of the world that, although it not only sees these things but feels them to its great harm, it nonetheless endures these men, indeed it defends their tyranny by public authority and fights for them against all who refuse to be subject to them.

units.la: At non inter Pontifices modo & Episcopos dispensatores illi nequam inueniuntur, sed apud eos etiam, prob dolor, qui Euangelij doctrinā puriorem profitentur. Quàm procul enim ab istorum moribus absunt Superintendentes quidam, qui in multas Ecclesias sibi ius sumunt, & non solum illis contra Petri praeceptum, verumetiam earum ministris superbè dominantur? Et cum multorum corruptos mores facilè ferant, eos tamen ferre nequeunt, qui vetus illud Papisticae de re Sacramentaria doctrinae fermentum improbant, & simplicem veteris Ecclesiae sententiam tradunt. Quàm primùm enim istis verbulum aliquod excidit, quo crassa ipsorum opinio perstringitur, mox ceu Catones quidã è cœlo delapsi eos ad suum quasi tribunal citant, nec ratione doctrinæ ab eis exigunt, sed vt nondum conuiëti errorem & culpam agnoscant petunt, & in hominum quorundam verbis iurare cogunt, quorum authoritate ipsi supra omnes primitiuæ Ecclesiæ doctores atq; Martyres eminere volunt. Quòd si illi obedire detrectent, ad amicum colloquiũ aut disputationẽ sese offerant, & vt rationes ipsorum audiantur postulent: tunc noui isti omnium doctrinarum Censores maiori rabie accensi apud principes eos accusant, & odiôsis Sacramentariorum ac Suermerorum nominibus grauatos ab Ecclesiarum ministerio deturbant, & cum vxoribus atq; dulcissimis liberis in exilium eijciunt. Annon hoc est conseruos & ancillas in domo Dei percutere? Adde hîs, quòd ijdem illi amplißimus stipendijs ditati cum ebriosis aulicis comessantur & ludunt, fame interim tantùmnon pereuntibus multis verbi ministris, qui tenuissimo salario, tanquam pecudum pastores conducti, in diem vičitant. Sed ne illi quidem soli reprehensionem merentur, cùm inter vulgus quoq; ministrorum non pauci sint, qui deposita fere omni cura gregis sibi crediti, frequentius in publicis diuersorijs inter ebriosorum comessationes, quàm domi inter libros & Scripturæ sacræ meditationem visuntur. Et hi quoq; cùm turpissimè ipsi viuant, & Euangelicæ doctrinæ labes sint, interim superbè nimis suo in quosuis imperio abutuntur, & quouis supplicio dignos esse putant omnes, qui ipsorum authoritatem contemnunt, quam ipsi iampridem suis vitijs prostituerunt. Sunt hæc seculi corruptissimi argumenta, cui interitus haud dubiè imminet, cùm ad ista pleriq; conniueant, & improbi illi scurræ fidelibus verbi dispensatoribus præferantur.
units.tr: But those wicked stewards are found not only among the Popes and bishops, but also, to our grief, among those who profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel. How far removed from the manners of the Papists are certain superintendents, who claim for themselves authority over many churches and lord it over them not only, contrary to Peter's precept, but also over their ministers! And although they easily tolerate the corrupt morals of many, they cannot bear those who reject the old leaven of Papist doctrine concerning the sacraments and teach the simple opinion of the ancient Church. For as soon as some little word escapes these men which exposes their crass opinion, straightway, like Catos who have fallen from heaven, they summon those who said it to their own tribunal, and they do not demand an account of the doctrine but ask that the one not yet convicted acknowledge error and fault, and they compel him to swear to the words of certain men, by whose authority they themselves wish to stand above all the teachers and martyrs of the primitive Church. But if the other refuses to obey, they offer themselves for a friendly conference or disputation and demand that their reasons be heard. Then these new censors of all doctrines, inflamed with greater rage, accuse them before the princes, and, branding them with the hateful names of Sacramentarians and Swenckfeldians, drive them from the ministry of the churches, and cast them into exile with their wives and dearest children. Is this not beating the menservants and maidservants in the house of God? Add to this that these same men, enriched with the most ample stipends, feast and gamble with drunken courtiers, while many ministers of the Word are almost starving, hired for the smallest wage like shepherds of cattle, and live from day to day. But not even those men alone deserve blame, since among the common run of ministers there are not a few who, having laid aside almost all care of the flock entrusted to them, are seen more often in public inns amid the carousing of drunkards than at home among their books and meditating on Holy Scripture. These men too, although they live most shamefully and are a stain on the evangelical doctrine, meanwhile abuse their authority over whomever they like too arrogantly, and think that all who despise their authority, which they themselves long ago prostituted by their vices, deserve any punishment. These are the marks of a most corrupt age, which doubtless faces ruin, since so many connive at these things and worthless buffoons are preferred to the faithful dispensers of the Word.

units.la: Cæterùm ne quis illorum impunitate, qua nunc gaudent, offendatur, pœnam grauem illis Domi-nus denuntiat. Veniet (inquit) dominus serui illius die quo non expectat, & qua hora non nouit, & dissecabit eum, partemq; cum infidis ei assignabit. Primò improuisum & repentinũ aduentum suum illis minatur, qui eò terribilior erit, quò minus illi de eo cogitant, vt nuper ex Paulo docuimus. Deinde pœnas daturos dicit, quæ ex veteri more etiam adhuc hodie de proditoribus sumi cõsueuerunt. Dissecabit enim (inquit) illum, & eius partem siue sortem ei tribuet cum malæ fidei hominibus. Apud Matthæum addit: Illic erit fletus & stridor dentium: quod de æternis inferorũ cruciatibus intelligi debere, ex aliis locis apparet. Etenim indigni sunt, qui cum pijs ad Regni cœlestis societatem admittantur, quicunq; Dei Ecclesiã in terris turbant. Magno igitur istis constabit sua licentia & securitas. Porrò quod de illis dicitur, ad alios quoq; extendi potest. Discant ergo principes viri, ne Dei populum iniqua tyrannide opprimant, & exactionibus immodicis excorient aut deglubant. Idem à luxu & intemperantia sibi caueant: neq; cum impijs colludant, vt aliquid contra Dei leges faciant in illorum gratiam. Nam nisi hæc cauerint, easdem pœnas cum improbis Ecclesiarum ministris subibunt. Omnes verò, cuiuscunq; loci sint, aduentus Iesu Christi memores, ita viuant, vt hunc cum gaudio excipere possint, & ab eo ad Regni æterni hæreditatem atq; possessionem colligantur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone be offended by the impunity which they now enjoy, the Lord threatens them with a heavy punishment. "The lord of that servant," he says, "will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and assign him his portion with the unfaithful." First, he threatens them with his sudden and unforeseen coming, which will be all the more terrible the less they think about it, as we taught recently from Paul. Then he says they will suffer the punishments which, according to the ancient custom, are even today still usually inflicted on traitors. For he will cut him in pieces (he says), and will assign him his portion or lot with men of bad faith. In Matthew he adds: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," which ought to be understood of the eternal torments of hell, as is clear from other passages. Indeed, those who trouble the Church of God on earth are unworthy to be admitted with the godly into the fellowship of the heavenly kingdom. Their license and security will therefore cost them dearly. Moreover, what is said of them can be extended to others also. Let princes learn, then, not to oppress the people of God with unjust tyranny, nor to flay and skin them with excessive exactions. Let them likewise guard themselves against luxury and intemperance, and not collude with the wicked, to do anything against God's laws for their sake. For unless they take heed of these things, they will undergo the same punishments together with the wicked ministers of the Churches. But all, wherever they are, should remember the coming of Jesus Christ and so live that they may receive him with joy, and be gathered by him to the inheritance and possession of the eternal kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXIII.

units.la: Ille autem seruus, qui nouit voluntatẽ Domini, nec se comparauit, nec fecit ex voluntate eius, cædetur multis plagis. Qui verò nõ nouit, & fecit digna plagis, cædetur paucis. Porrò cuicunq; multũ datũ est, ab eo multum repetetur: & apud quem deposuerunt multa, ab eo amplíus reposcent.
units.tr: That servant who knew his master's will, but did not prepare himself or act according to it, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he who did not know it, yet did things deserving of stripes, shall be beaten with few. Moreover, from everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom they entrusted much, they will demand all the more.

units.la: Quoniam Deus à nobis exigit, vt omnes vitæ nostræ actiones secundùm suæ voluntatis regulam instituamus, omnibus seculis verbi sui ministros & prædicones dedit, quorum ministerio voluntatẽ suam nobis reuelat. Est hoc inter eius beneficia longè præstantissimum: quia & nos sibi amicorũ loco esse testatur, & simul mentes illuminat, vt salutis in Christo exhibitæ participes fieri possimus. At quia ministri etiam homines, & proinde erroribus & vitijs obnoxij sunt, frequenter illos officij sui admonet. Et Christus quàmuis de hoc sæpius apud discipulos suos disseruisset, idë tamen hoc etiam loco singulari cum grauitate & diligentia facit: vtq; magis moueat, nuper elegan-tissima parabola verbi praecones œconomis aut dispensatoribus assimilauit, eo quod per illos salutis æternæ mysteria Ecclesiæ distribuuntur, & fidis quidem suo, officio probè fungentibus amplissima præmia promisit, infidis autem atq; domus Dei turbatoribus minatus est, quod ceu proditores gloriæ Dei & publicæ salutis dissecandi ad sempiternos inferorum cruciatus damnandi sint. Id ve-rò quia nonnullis durum nimis videri poterat, sententiam hanc suam modò duobus argumentis gra-uissimis, & ex communi sensu hominum petitis confirmat. Sunt autem hæc eiusmodi, vt ad omnes homines transferri possint: quamobrem diligentius à singulis debent considerari.
units.tr: Since God requires of us that we order all the actions of our lives according to the rule of his will, he has given in every age ministers and preachers of his word, through whose ministry he reveals his will to us. This is by far the most excellent of his benefits, because it both testifies that he regards us as friends and at the same time enlightens our minds, so that we may become partakers of the salvation offered in Christ. But because ministers are also human, and therefore liable to errors and vices, he frequently reminds them of their duty. And although Christ had discussed this more than once with his disciples, he nevertheless deals with it here too with singular seriousness and care. And so that he might move them more, he recently compared the preachers of the word to stewards or dispensers, because through them the mysteries of eternal salvation are distributed to the Church. He promised very great rewards to those who faithfully perform their duty, but threatened the unfaithful, and those who disturb the house of God, that as betrayers of the glory of God and of the public welfare they are to be cut in pieces and condemned to everlasting torments in hell. Since this might seem too harsh to some, he now confirms this sentence with two very weighty arguments drawn from the common sense of mankind. These are of such a kind that they can be applied to all people, and therefore they must be considered more carefully by each one.

units.la: Primum his verbis proponit: Ille autem seruus, qui nouit voluntatem Domini sui: nec se com-parauit: nec fecit ex voluntate eius, cædetur multis plagis, &c. Conuenit dictum hoc cum eo, quod in lege qui deliquerant, pro sui sceleris ratione, plagis multis aut paucioribus cædi iubentur. Cùm enim omnium consensu constet grauiorem esse eius culpam, qui de heri sui voluntate probè instru-ctus, non ignorantia aut imprudentia, sed improbo contemptu illam transgreditur, quàm eius, qui ignarus & imprudens delinquit: illum etiam grauius puniri debere fatendum erit. Etenim cùm ne ignorantia quidem nos apud Deum excusset (vt postea audiemus) quæ obsecro potest excusatio illis reliqua esse, qui omni illius timore abiecto impudenter aduersus illum proterutiunt, aut saltem in suo munere exequendo sunt negligentiores? Id verò in primis ad Ecclesiæ ministros & verbi Dei prae-cones pertinet. Norunt hi illius voluntatem esse, vt homines salui fiant & ad veritatis cognitio-nem adducantur. Norunt item ministerij huius finem esse, vt homines ad Christi corpus colligan-tur, & in eius fide ædificati sub illo inter se coalescant. Sciunt præterea sui officij esse, vt in Scriptu-rarum meditatione sedulij sint, & ex illis desumptam doctrinam bona fide & prudenter populo an-nuntient, neq; aliquem negligant, quem in salutis negotio vel desidem & cunctatorem, vel contuma-cem viderint. Neq; etiam illos latet quæ præmia fidis doctoribus parata sint, quæ rursus pœnæ infi-dos manent. Quomodo enim ignorarent quod Ezechieli dicitur: Nisi diserte monueris impium ex-me, vt conuertatur à via sua mala, ipse quidem in impietate sua morietur, sanguinem verò eius de manu tua requiram? Et illud Pauli, Væ mihi si non euangelizem? Habent deniq; exempla innu-merabilia tam veterū quàm noui testamenti, quibus promissiones & minæ ista confirmantur. Quòd si igitur hæc omnia illos non mouent, vt in officio suo diligentes sint, quis non videt dignos esse, qui plagis plurimis grauissimisq; multentur? Atqui accedit bis omnibus, quòd negligentia quidem sua multorum pœnitentiam atq; salutem impediunt, malo autem vitæ exemplo scandalum præbent lon-gè nocentissimum. Nam qui illos de cœlorum gaudijs deq; pœnis infernalibus splendidè quidem differentes audiunt, flagitiosam verò & timoris Dei experte vitam viuere vident, non possunt non de doctrinæ ipsorum veritate dubitare, & paulatim ipsi quoque sceleribus & peccandi licentiæ assue-scunt. Itaq; propter illos male audit verbum Domini, & multis exitij authores sunt, qui salutis ad-ministri esse debebant. Qui ergo hæc scientes faciunt, imò (quod dubium esse non potest) contra pro-priam conscientiam scelerato Dei contemptu peccant, nulla pœna de illis iumi potest, quæ tanti sce-lerus magnitudini respondeat. Et hæc quidem omnia Christus breui hoc dicto comprehendit, cuius memoria nunquam excidere debet ijs, qui ad Ecclesiæ ministerium vocati sunt. Huius certè confi-deratio Paulum excitauit, vt in opere Euangelij indefessus fuerit, & omnium Ecclesiarum curam suis humeris incumbere putaret, neq; tamen de suo hoc studio gloriaretur, eò quòd sciret se necessita-te & Dei mandato vrgeri, & hæc omnia ex officio facere. Quod ipsum de reliquis etiam Apostolis & Prophetis dicere possumus. Et si ista diligentius expenderent omnes hodie, quibus Ecclesia-rum cura commissa est, haud dubiè & has melius constitutas haberemus; & singuli maiores in pie-tate progressus facerent.
units.tr: First he sets this forth in these words: "That servant who knew his master's will, and did not prepare himself nor act according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes," and so on. This saying agrees with the law, under which those who had offended were ordered to be beaten with more or fewer stripes according to the measure of their crime. For since everyone agrees that the fault of one who, thoroughly instructed in his master's will, transgresses it not through ignorance or inadvertence but through wicked contempt, is greater than the fault of one who sins in ignorance and without thought, it must be admitted that the former ought to be punished more severely. For since not even ignorance excuses us before God (as we shall hear later), what excuse, I beg you, can remain for those who, having cast off all fear of him, shamelessly rebel against him, or at least are more careless in carrying out their office? This applies above all to the ministers of the Church and the preachers of God's word. They know that it is God's will that people be saved and brought to the knowledge of the truth. They also know that the end of this ministry is that people be gathered into the body of Christ and, being built up in his faith, grow together under him. Moreover, they know it is their duty to be diligent in meditating on the Scriptures, and to announce to the people in good faith and wisely the doctrine drawn from them, and not to neglect anyone whom they see to be either slothful and hesitant, or stubborn, in the matter of salvation. Nor are they unaware what rewards are prepared for faithful teachers, and what punishments remain for the unfaithful. For how could they be ignorant of what is said to Ezekiel: "If you do not clearly warn the wicked man that he should turn from his evil way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand"? And of Paul's words: "Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel"? Finally, both the Old and the New Testament have countless examples by which these promises and threats are confirmed. If then all these things do not move them to be diligent in their office, who does not see that they deserve to be punished with very many and very grievous stripes? Yet to all this is added that by their carelessness they hinder the repentance and salvation of many, and by a bad example of life they give a scandal that is by far the most harmful. For those who hear them speak brilliantly of the joys of heaven and the pains of hell, but see them living a dissolute life without the fear of God, cannot help doubting the truth of their teaching, and gradually they themselves grow accustomed to sins and to the license of sinning. Thus the word of the Lord is badly spoken of on their account, and they become the authors of ruin for many, when they ought to have been ministers of salvation. Therefore, those who do these things knowing them, indeed (which cannot be doubted) who sin against their own conscience with wicked contempt of God, no punishment can be devised for them that matches the greatness of so great a crime. Christ comprehended all these things in this brief saying, and it must never slip from the memory of those who have been called to the ministry of the Church. Indeed, the consideration of this roused Paul, so that he was tireless in the work of the gospel, and thought that the care of all the Churches lay upon his shoulders; yet he did not boast of this zeal of his, because he knew that he was driven by necessity and by God's command, and that he did all these things out of duty. We may say the same of the other Apostles and Prophets as well. And if all those to whom the care of the Churches is entrusted today weighed these things more carefully, we would undoubtedly have these Churches better ordered too, and each individual would make greater progress in godliness.

units.la: Quia verò hoc Christi dictum generalem doctrinam continet, quæ ad omnis ordinis homines debet extendi, quædam diligentius erunt cōsideranda, vt qui rudiores sunt plenius intelligant, quid ab ipsis fieri debeat. Inter quæ primum est, quæ sit generalis illa Dei voluntas, cui omnes studere conuenit, & num ea nobis sit reuelata. Sunt enim fanatici quidam & pessimi impostores, qui vt sibi ad sua dogmata viam sternant, nondum plenè constare aiunt, quid Deus velit, & ne Apostolorum quidem temporibus Veritatis cognitionem satis adhuc patefactam fuisse. Ita vero mendacij arguunt Deum, qui per Mosem Israelitis dixit: Praeceptum istud, quod ego tibi praecipio hodie, non est abscondituni tibi, neque remotum. Non est in coelis, ut dicas: Quis ascendet nobis in coelum, ut illud nobis afferat, annuncietque nobis ut illud faciamus? Nec est ultra mare, ut dicas: Quis traijciet nobis mare, & afferat, nobis annunciet, ut ipsum faciamus? Sed valde propinquum est tibi verbum in ore tuo & in corde tuo, ut facias illud. Ecce posui hodie ante te vitam & bonum, mortem deniq; & malum, &c. Et Paulus scripturas a Deo inspiratas & utiles esse dicit, ut homo Dei perfectus fiat, & ad omne bonum opus instructus. At quomodo hoc praestare poterunt, si non intelligantur, & quae in illis continentur Veritas non adhuc manifestata est. Quibus adde; quod quae fusius in Lege & tota scriptura traduntur, Deus ipse in compendia & epitomes breviores contraxit, ut il literati quoq; homines & pueri voluntatem eius intelligere possent. Huc decalogus pertinet, & quae habentur, atq; alij similes loci. Ut vero cum veteri Lege Euangelij doctrinam apertius coniungamus, poterit tota Dei voluntas, cuius cognitio nobis necessaria est tribus capitibus comprehendi. Primum est, ut uni Deo fidamus, & ex fide hac illam diligamus ex toto corde, timeamus, colamus, & apud ipsum, ceu unicum omnis boni fontem, quaeramus quaecunq; nobis necessaria & utilia sunt. Est hoc primum & praecipuum foederis cum Abrahamo instaurati caput. Idem in primo Decalogi praecepto diligentissime inculcatur. Et Christum ideo in mundum venisse scimus, ut in illo Pater omnes suae gratiae thesauros aperiret, nosq; in eo omnem salutem nobis repositam esse sciremus. Alterum ergo divinae voluntatis caput est, ut per hunc Mediatorem ad Deum contendamus, & illum vera atq; constanti fide amplexemur. Haec est enim voluntas eius, qui misit me (inquit ille) ut omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. Tertium, ut secundum charitatis legem sanctè & innocenter viuamus. In his (inquam) voluntas illa Dei continetur, cui nos studere vult Christus: quae cum passim in sacris literis perspicuè tradantur, & tam vulgaria sint hodie, ut in omnibus linguis decantentur, adhaec picturis quoque illustrentur: nimium impudentes sunt, qui illam obscuriorem esse aiunt, quam ut certo cognosci queat.
units.tr: But since this saying of Christ contains a general doctrine, which must be extended to men of every rank, some points will have to be considered more carefully, so that those who are less learned may understand more fully what must be done by them. Among these, the first is what that general will of God is, to which all ought to strive, and whether it has been revealed to us. For there are certain fanatics and most wicked impostors who, in order to pave the way for their own dogmas, say that it is not yet fully clear what God wills, and that even in the time of the Apostles the knowledge of the truth had not been sufficiently disclosed. Yet in this way they accuse God of lying, who said through Moses to the Israelites: "This commandment which I command you today is not hidden from you, nor is it far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, to bring it to us and declare it to us, that we may do it? Nor is it beyond the sea, that you should say, Who shall cross the sea for us, and bring it to us and declare it to us, that we may do it? But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it. See, I have set before you today life and good, death also and evil," etc. And Paul says that the Scriptures are inspired by God and useful, so that the man of God may be made perfect and equipped for every good work. But how will they be able to accomplish this if they are not understood, and the truth contained in them has not yet been made manifest? To these add this: what is set forth at greater length in the Law and in all Scripture, God himself has drawn together into shorter summaries and epitomes, so that even unlearned men and children might understand his will. To this belong the Decalogue, and the other passages of this kind. But so that we may join the doctrine of the gospel more clearly with the old Law, the whole will of God, whose knowledge is necessary for us, can be comprehended under three heads. The first is that we trust in the one God alone, and from this faith love him with our whole heart, fear him, worship him, and seek from him, as from the one fountain of all good, whatever things are necessary and useful for us. This is the first and chief head of the covenant renewed with Abraham. The same is most diligently impressed in the first precept of the Decalogue. And we know that Christ came into the world for this reason, that in him the Father might open all the treasures of his grace, and that we might know that all salvation has been laid up for us in him. The second head of the divine will, therefore, is that we strive toward God through this Mediator, and embrace him with a true and steadfast faith. For this is the will of him who sent me, says he, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life. The third is that we live holily and innocently according to the law of charity. In these three things (I say) that will of God is contained, to which Christ wills us to apply ourselves. Since it is set forth everywhere plainly in the sacred writings, and is so commonplace today that it is sung in all languages, and is moreover illustrated by pictures, those are most shameless who say that it is too obscure to be known with certainty.

units.la: Caeterum ut nos huic accomodare debeamus, & quae huius exequendae ratio sit, teneamus oportet. Exprimit hanc Christus, quando de malo illo seruo dicit, quod neq; se comparauerit, neq; fecerit ex voluntate heri sui. Duo ergo requiruntur. Primum est praeparatio, qua homo se totum huic studio dedit, ut voluntati divinae satisfaciat. Nam nisi animus totus huc destinetur, perfunctorie modo omnia faciet, neq; Deo probari poterit. Et huc pertinent, quae de abnegatione sui ipsius, de mortificatione carnis, de regeneratione & innovatione hominis alibi traduntur. Quoad enim carni habenas laxamus, & eius desideriis indulgemus, nullus apud nos divinae voluntati locus erit. Concupiscit enim caro contra spiritum, & illa dominante hic opprimitur. Multum autem hic profuerit, si ad audiendum Dei verbum animus rectè praeparatus & discendi cupidus accedamus. Tunc enim semen Verbi verè excipiemus, & hoc in nobis radices agere poterit. Quod si simul preces accedant feriae & ardentes, procul dubio carnis cupiditates restingui, corda mutari & voluntatis divinae stimulo accendi sentiemus. At hic nequaquam subsistere debemus, quasi officio omni simus defuncti: sed quod animo concepimus, id factis praestare oportet. Non enim in otiosa meditatione, aut externa professione vel sermone consistit Regnum Dei, sed in virtute, quae totum hominem transformat, & se in omnibus eius studijs atque actionibus exerit. Et hoc est, quod Davidem, qui Legem Dei dies & noctes meditatur, arbori fecundissimae confert, quae quovis tempore fert fructus suos. Psalmo primo.
units.tr: Moreover, we must hold to how we ought to apply this to ourselves and what the manner of carrying it out is. Christ expresses this when he speaks of that wicked servant, who neither prepared himself nor acted according to the will of his lord. Two things are therefore required. The first is preparation, by which a person gives himself wholly to this pursuit, so that he may satisfy the divine will. For unless the mind is wholly directed to this, he will do everything in a perfunctory way and will not be able to please God. To this belong the things taught elsewhere about self-denial, the mortification of the flesh, and the regeneration and renewal of the man. For as long as we loosen the reins on the flesh and indulge its desires, there will be no place for the divine will among us. The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and while it rules, the Spirit is oppressed here. It will be of great benefit, however, if we approach the hearing of God's Word with a mind rightly prepared and eager to learn. For then we will truly receive the seed of the Word, and it can take root in us. And if fervent and earnest prayers are added, we will undoubtedly feel the desires of the flesh being quenched, our hearts changed, and kindled by the goad of the divine will. Yet we must by no means stop here, as if we had finished every duty; what we have conceived in the mind, we must also perform in deeds. For the kingdom of God does not consist in idle meditation, or in outward profession or speech, but in power, which transforms the whole man and shows itself in all his pursuits and actions. This is what the Psalmist means when he compares David, who meditates on the law of God day and night, to a most fruitful tree, which bears its fruit at every season. Psalm 1.

units.la: Ut vero Ecclesiarum ministri grauius puniuntur, si ipsis probè cognitam Dei voluntatem securi negligant, inq; officio suo remissiores, vel etiam proterui praevaricatores sint: ita omnes alij poenas acerbiores merentur, qui cum Verbo divino illuminati quid credi, vtq; Deus coli & quomodo vita omnis instituti debeat, abunde norint, nihilominus tamen mundo ac carni indulgent, & reclamante conscientia in Dei voluntatem peccant. Est enim hoc animi prophani & ab omni numinis reverentia alieni argumentum, quo excusationis praetextus omnis adimitur. Peccavit in hoc gravissimè Iudaeorum gens, de qua Christus dicit: Si non venissem & locutus eis essem, peccatum non haberent: Nunc autem non habent, quod praetexant peccato suo. Et sanè illos grauissimè punitos esse constat. Etsi enim multa & horrenda extent iudiciorum Dei exempla, quae in alias gentes edi ta sunt, nullum tamen poenarum atrocitate ac diuturnitate illud aequat, quo in Iudaeos animad- uertit, qui post clades maximas, post vrbis & templi excidium & terrae totius vastationem, per omnes gentes dispersi, iam annis amplius mille quingentis repub. simul & sacris ordinarijs destitu- entur, & simul omnium ludibrio atque iniurijs sunt expositi. Sunt tamen multorum quoque alio- rum exempla, quae huic Christi dicto fidem faciunt, inter quae memorabilia admodum sunt, quae in Asiae, Aegypti, Aphricae & Graeciae Ecclesijs videmus. Fuerunt enim isti homines in Christiana fi de ac religione probe instituti per ipsos Apostolos & horum successores. At quia aduersus cognitā Dei voluntatem curiosis hominibus locum dedere, qui impijs disputationibus fidei principia conuel lere & religionis fundamenta oppugnare ausi sunt, adhaec a cultus diuini simplicitate recesserunt, & incurabili scelerū licentia fidē Christianā prophanarunt; grauissimè in illos Dei ira exarsit, qui cru deli Turcarum tyrannidi eas terras subiecit, in quibus olim Apostolorū voces audita fuerunt. Et nescio quàm procul à nobis absit eadem poena, quando & eadem inter nos scelera regnant, & crescē te indies Turcici imperij potentia Christianus orbis arctioribus indies finibus concluditur. Debe- bant in horum consideratione diligentius versari, qui quam animo conceperunt fidem, & de cuius veritate satis instructi sunt, in hominum gratia abnegant: qui cultus illicitos admittunt, & contra propriam conscientiam sese illis polluunt: qui item effreni licentia in turpissima quaeque flagitia ru- unt, à quorum turpitudine communis etiam sensus abhorret. Est eiusmodi hominum magnus nu- merus vbiq; gentium: plerique tamen quasi quae faciunt nullius momenti sint, impietati suae colophone imponunt, dum petulantes linguas aduersus Deum laxant, & huius praecepta singula vnà cū Ver- bi diuini admonitionibus & correptionibus scurriliter eludunt & rideant. Sunt hi ex illusorum nu- mero, quos Spiritus sanctus in scripturis non vno loco grauissimè reprehendit. Accedunt tamen hu quoq; alij peiores, qui non contenti eo, quod obedientiae iugum & omnis disciplinae frenum excusse- runt, insuper aduersus Deum & Verbum eius hostiliter insurgunt, neq; ea accusari aut corripi pa- tiuntur, à quibus olim quotquot inter gentes solam naturae legem secuti sunt, abhorruerunt. De Chri stiani nominis & Euangelij professoribus loquor, inter quos gigantes isti & Cyclopes passim inue- niuntur, quorum impia audacia fit, vt tutius agant, qui toti flagitijs & sceleribus sunt obruti, quā qui illa ex Dei Verbo reprehendunt. Est hoc exitij ad fores nostras excubantus certissimum argu mentum, quod non alia ratione effugere poterimus, quam si nos totos diuinae voluntati per fidei obe dientiam subijciamus, &c.
units.tr: Just as the ministers of the churches are punished more severely if they carelessly neglect the will of God, which they have thoroughly learned, and become more remiss in their office or even shameless transgressors, so all others deserve harsher penalties, who, enlightened by the divine Word, know full well what is to be believed, how God is to be worshipped, and how the whole of life ought to be ordered, and nevertheless indulge the world and the flesh, and sin against the will of God while their conscience protests. For this is a mark of a profane mind, alien to all reverence for the divine majesty, and it removes every pretext for excuse. The Jewish nation sinned most gravely in this, of whom Christ says: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin" (John 15:22). And indeed those people were punished most severely, as is clear. For although many terrible examples of God's judgments exist, which have been displayed against other nations, none equals in the atrocity and duration of its punishments that which has fallen upon the Jews, who after the greatest defeats, after the destruction of the city and the temple and the devastation of the whole land, dispersed among all nations, have now for more than fifteen hundred years been deprived of both commonwealth and regular worship, and at the same time have been exposed to the mockery and injuries of all. There are, however, also many other examples that bear out this saying of Christ, among which those we see in the churches of Asia, Egypt, Africa and Greece are most memorable. For these people were well instructed in the Christian faith and religion by the Apostles themselves and their successors. But because they gave room to curious men against the known will of God, who dared to overthrow the principles of the faith with impious disputations and to assail the foundations of religion, and moreover departed from the simplicity of divine worship, and profaned the Christian faith by an incurable license of wickedness, the wrath of God blazed most fiercely against them, and subjected those lands, where once the voices of the Apostles were heard, to the cruel tyranny of the Turks. And I do not know how far from us the same punishment is, since the same crimes reign among us, and the power of the Turkish empire, growing daily, shuts the Christian world into ever narrower borders. Those who, having conceived the faith in their minds and being sufficiently instructed in its truth, deny it for the sake of human favour, should have dwelt more carefully on the consideration of these things; likewise those who admit illicit forms of worship and pollute themselves with them against their own conscience; likewise those who rush with unbridled license into every most shameful disgrace, from whose baseness even common feeling shrinks. Of such people there is a great number everywhere in the world. Most of them, however, as if what they do were of no importance, put a finishing touch on their impiety, while they loosen their insolent tongues against God, and mock and scoff at each of his precepts together with the admonitions and rebukes of the divine Word. These belong to the number of the scoffers whom the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures reproves most severely in more than one place. Yet there are also others worse than these, who, not content that they have shaken off the yoke of obedience and the bridle of all discipline, moreover rise up with hostility against God and his Word, and will not suffer themselves to be accused or corrected by those things from which all who, among the nations, have followed the law of nature alone have shrunk. I speak of the professors of the Christian name and the Gospel, among whom those giants and Cyclopes are found everywhere, whose impious audacity makes it safer for those who are wholly overwhelmed by disgraces and crimes to act, than for those who rebuke these from the Word of God. This is a most certain sign that the destruction is standing at our doors, and that we will be able to escape it by no other means than by subjecting ourselves wholly to the divine will through obedience of faith, etc.

units.la: Porro obijciat aliquis: Si qui Dei voluntatem nouerunt, nō autem ei obtemperant grauius pu- niuntur, praestat illam ignorare & Verbum eius, ex quo ea discitur, negligere. Et iane hodie nō pau- cos est inuenire, qui inter nostri seculi de religione & Dei cultu controuersias, nihil tutius esse arbi- trantur, quàm rerum sacrarum ignorantiam, seq; apud Deum abunde excusatos putant, si in patrum religione, siue ea vera siue falsa fuerit, simpliciter pergant. Et hi fere disputationes de religione ad homines otiosos pertinere, ac superuacaneas esse dicunt. Sed & in manifestis sceleribus ad ignoran tiae praetextum, quasi ad clypeum Aiacis confugiunt. Hu ergo aliam sententiā opponit Dominus: Qui vero non nouit, & fecit digna plagis, caedetur paucis. Faciunt haec quidem ad prioris confirma tionem, interim docent, eum quoq; non impune laturum esse, qui diuinae voluntatis ignarus ea defig narit, quae poenas merentur. At ne cui hoc durius dictum videatur; tenere oportet duplicem esse co- gnitionem Dei & voluntatis ipsius. Vna est perfecta, quae per verbum eius in Scripturis manife statum traditur, & in primis per Christum reuelata est, secundum illud Ioannis: Deum nemo vi dit vnquā: sed Filius ille Vnigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse nobis exposuit. Et ipse Christus ait: Omnia quae accepi à Patre meo, nota feci vobis. Haec igitur cognitio diuinae voluntatis plene & perfectè continet omnia, quae nobis ad salutē aeternā necessaria sunt: quia Christum simul appre- hendit, in quo omnes scientiae thesauri repositi sunt, & qui nobis quoque à Patre sapientia factus est. Et de hac cognitione prior sententia exponi debet, de qua hucusq; diximus. Altera est imper- fectior, quam Deus omnium hominum animis insculpsit, & quae notitias generales continet, de Deo & religione, de vitae innocentia, de colenda mutua dilectione, aliisq; rebus ad huius vitae vsum necef sarijs. Hanc vulgo legem naturae vocant, & voluit eam Deus ex peculiari gratia in hominibus reliquam esse posse Adami lapsum, quo melius in officio continerentur, & non in infinitum grassare tur peccandi licentia cum vniuersali humani generis exitio. Ex illa enim homines prudentes & virtutis studio prae aliis praediti leges bonas & Reipub. vtiles promulgarunt, quales apud omnes fere gentes fuisse, historici testantur. De hac Paulus in epistola ad Romanos disserit, quando ait gentes quae Legem Moysis non acceperunt, sibi ipsis Legem esse, & opus Legis in cordibus suis scriptum ostendere, quando suis legibus scelera prohibent & puniunt, opera vero egregia & virtutis plena honoribus & praemijs exornant. At quia haec cognitio (vt idem Paulus docet) partim quorundam curiositate, & ex ea enatus superstitionibus corrupta atq; obscurata, quorundam vero temeritate & licentia fere tota extincta fuit, prorsus nulla censeri potest, si cum priori illa conferatur. Et hanc praesupponit (vt aiunt) Christus hoc altero membro de seruo loquens, qui voluntatis diuinae ignarus poenis aut plagis digna fecerit. Nam eos intelligit, qui notitias quidem illas generales cordibus in scriptas habent, ipsum vero salutis aeternae authorem, & quae solis electis patent regni coelorum mysteria ignorant. Et hos non quidem tam graviter vt priores illos punitum iri, non tamen ab omni poena liberos & immunes fore dicit. Sufficit enim ad eos convincendos Lex naturae, idque eo magis quod ipsorum conscientia huic testimonium defert, & a proprijs cogitationibus accusantur, si quid praeter officium fecerunt, excusantur autem, quando suo munere diligenter defuncti sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, someone may object: if those who know the will of God but do not obey it are punished more severely, it is better to be ignorant of it and to neglect the Word from which it is learned. And indeed today it is not hard to find not a few who, amid the controversies of our age about religion and the worship of God, think nothing safer than ignorance of sacred things, and believe themselves sufficiently excused before God if they simply continue in the religion of their fathers, whether that religion be true or false. And such people commonly say that disputations about religion pertain to idle men and are superfluous. But even in manifest crimes they flee to the pretext of ignorance, as if to the shield of Ajax. The Lord therefore sets against this another sentiment: "He who did not know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes" (Luke 12:48). These words indeed serve to confirm the former statement, while at the same time they teach that he too will not go unpunished who, being ignorant of the divine will, commits deeds that deserve punishment. But lest this seem too harsh to anyone, we must hold that there is a twofold knowledge of God and of his will. One is perfect, which is set forth plainly in Scripture through his Word, and was above all revealed through Christ, according to the saying of John: "No one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known to us." And Christ himself says: "All that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." This knowledge of the divine will therefore fully and perfectly contains all that is necessary for us to eternal salvation, because it grasps Christ at the same time, in whom all treasures of knowledge are laid up, and who has also been made wisdom to us from the Father. And it is of this knowledge that the former statement ought to be explained, which we have discussed up to this point. The other is more imperfect, which God has engraved on the minds of all men, and which contains general notions concerning God and religion, concerning the innocence of life, the cultivation of mutual love, and other things necessary for the use of this life. Commonly they call this the law of nature, and God, out of special grace, willed that it should remain among men even after the fall of Adam, so that they might be kept better in duty, and that the license of sinning should not rage without limit to the universal destruction of the human race. For from this law wise men, and those endowed beyond others with a zeal for virtue, have promulgated good laws useful to the commonwealth, such as historians testify existed among almost all nations. Paul discourses of this in his epistle to the Romans, when he says that the Gentiles, who have not received the law of Moses, are a law to themselves, and show the work of the law written in their hearts, since by their laws they forbid and punish crimes, and adorn excellent works full of virtue with honours and rewards. But because this knowledge (as the same Paul teaches) has been partly corrupted and obscured by the curiosity of some and the superstitions that arose from it, and has been almost wholly extinguished by the rashness and license of others, it can be counted as nothing at all when compared with the former knowledge. And this, as they say, Christ presupposes when, in this second member, he speaks of the servant who, ignorant of the divine will, did things worthy of stripes or punishments. For he means those who indeed have those general notions inscribed on their hearts, but are ignorant of the Author of eternal salvation himself and of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, which lie open only to the elect. And he says that these will indeed be punished, not so severely as those former ones, yet they will not be free and exempt from all punishment. For the law of nature is sufficient to convict them, and all the more so because their own conscience bears witness to this, and they are accused by their own thoughts if they have done anything beyond their duty, but are excused when they have diligently discharged their office.

units.la: Vnde sequitur apud Dei tribunal neminem excusari, sed omnes homines coram illo peccati reos & poenis dignos esse: frustra denique ad ignorantiae praetextum eos confugere, & Deum iniquitatis aut seueritatis nimiae accusare, qui a propria conscientia & cogitationibus cordis sui conuincuntur. Etenim cum nos a seruis nostris requiramus, ne quid temere pro suo arbitrio faciant, sed de nostra voluntate inquirant, eamq; obseruent: quanto magis hoc Deo debemus, vt procul relictis nostris placitis, eius voluntati nos accomodemus, quae sola bona, sancta & salutaris est? Et quam obsecro ignorantiam praetexere possumus, quando ille (vt supra monuimus) voluntatem suam omnem nobis fidelissime manifestauit? Negligentia ergo potius est quam ignorantia, quam praetexi-mus, & illa quidem cum Dei contemptu coniuncta, cui tam parum honoris deferimus, vt quid ille a nobis exigat non quaeramus. Quod saepe cogitare decebat eos, qui cum Ecclesiarum ministri & pastores haberi & esse velint, falsa tamen doctrina & vanissimis superstitionibus populum infelicem circunducunt, deque eo accusati, se meliora ignorare, & proinde vetera instituta partum retinere aiunt. Placent illi sibi ipsis egregie ista excusatione, qua nihil vanius & putidius excogitari potest. Possunt quidem isto praetextu aliqua ex parte excusari, qui ante manifestatam Euangelij lucem communibus tenebris immersi, adhaec monitoribus simul & libris destituti fuerunt, ex quibus meliora discerent. At quid hoc ad nostri seculi homines pertinet, qui omnia habent, quae ipsis ad Veritatis cognitionem adiumento esse poterant? Audiuntur enim passim Euangelij praecones, libri sacri in omnes linguas translati in omnium manibus versantur, de religione & Dei cultu disputant non docti modo & illustres viri, verumetiam opifices, agricolae, nautae, mercatores, mulieres denique & pueri. Quod ergo illi ignorantes subinde manent, id inexcusabilis ofcitantiae argumentum est. Quia enim ipsorum munus circa aeternae salutis negotium versatur, & hoc cum multarum animarum periculo in controuersia est, illorum erat, non veterem saliuam populo pertinaciter obtrudere, sed posito omni affectu rei veritatem inuestigare, & (quod Christus Iudaorum Scribis dicebat) scripturas diligentius scrutari, in quibus vitae aeternae consequendae ratio vera traditur. Non dam natur statim qui nauticam artem ignorat, quando haec non omnium est, nec vt eam omnes norint opus est: At si quis eam profitetur, & vectores cum suis mercibus in nauim receptos in altum educit, postea autem ventis aduersis flantibus & tempestate periculosa mare turbantibus se illius ignarum esse ostendit, nae ille poena potius quam venia & commiseratione dignus est. At quid hic iudicari potest aliud de ijs, qui ad Ecclesiae gubernacula sedent, & quidem multis inuitis & reluctantibus, in tantis autem sententiarum de religione diuersissimarum fluctibus ignorantiam suam sponte profitentur, & causam hanc ad alios reijciunt, qui de ea decernere debeant? Atqui singulorum pastorum est o boni, pascua bona nouisse, & Christi principis pastorum vocem tenere, vt ea oues ducant & gregis ecclesiastici vnitatem conseruent. Omnibus item in hoc munere constitutis dicitur: Labia sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & Legem ex ore eius requirent;
units.tr: It follows that no one is excused before God's judgement, but all people stand before him as guilty of sin and deserving of punishment. In short, it is in vain that they flee to the pretext of ignorance and accuse God of injustice or excessive severity, when their own conscience and the thoughts of their heart convict them. For when we require our servants not to act rashly at their own discretion, but to inquire into our will and observe it, how much more ought we to do this toward God: to set aside our own pleasures and accommodate ourselves to his will, which alone is good, holy and saving? And what ignorance, I ask, can we plead, since he (as we noted above) has most faithfully made his whole will known to us? It is negligence rather than ignorance that we put forward as a pretext, and that negligence is joined with contempt for God, to whom we pay such little honour that we do not seek what he requires of us. Those who wish to be called and to be ministers and pastors of the Churches, yet lead an unhappy people about with false doctrine and most vain superstitions, ought often to have considered this. When accused of it, they say that they are ignorant of better things and therefore keep the old institutions in place. They are remarkably pleased with themselves over this excuse, than which nothing more empty and foolish can be devised. Indeed, those who were immersed in common darkness before the light of the gospel was made manifest, and who were also without teachers and books from which they might learn better things, may be excused in some measure by this pretext. But what does this have to do with the people of our age, who have all the things that could help them to know the truth? For gospel preachers are heard everywhere, holy books translated into all languages are in everyone's hands, and about religion and the worship of God dispute not only learned and distinguished men but also craftsmen, farmers, sailors, merchants, women and even children. Therefore, that these men remain ignorant is a proof of inexcusable sloth. For since their office is concerned with the business of eternal salvation, and this is at issue with the danger of many souls, it was their duty not to obstinately thrust old slobber upon the people, but, setting aside all feeling, to investigate the truth of the matter and (as Christ told the scribes of the Jews) to search the Scriptures more diligently, in which the true way of obtaining eternal life is handed down. A man who does not know the art of navigation is not condemned at once, since it is not for everyone, nor is it necessary that everyone should know it. But if someone professes it, takes passengers with their goods on board and leads them out to sea, and afterwards, when adverse winds blow and a dangerous tempest stirs the sea, shows that he is ignorant of it, that man deserves punishment rather than pardon and pity. What else can be judged here about those who sit at the helm of the Church, and that against the wishes and resistance of many, yet who in such a tide of most diverse opinions about religion freely profess their ignorance and shift this cause onto others, who ought to decide it? And yet it is the duty of each pastor, good men, to know good pastures and to hold fast to the voice of Christ, the chief of pastors, so that he may lead the sheep there and preserve the unity of the ecclesiastical flock. To all who are set in this office it is likewise said: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth."

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. Frustra ergo ad aliorum iudicia controuersiam hanc reijcitis, de cuius veritate vos vestræ fidei cõ missos debebatis edocere. Sunt tamen peiores his, qui ne doceri quidem volunt, imò oblatam veritatem lucem hostiliter persequuntur. Est horum maximus numerus hodie, qui hoc sibi gloriæ & laudi ducunt, quod à nemine suos errores argui, à nemine item doceri, admoneri, neq; alicuius de religione disputationes admittere soleant. Atqui hæc gloria illis cum Mahumete communis est, qui suos hominibus hanc legê culit, ne cum aliquo de religione disputent. Videbat enim astutissimus impostor, eam esse suorum dogmatum absurditatem, vt nullis vel scripturis vel rationibus probabilibus defendi possint. Quod ipsum cum hodie etiam multi videant, quibus falsa religio vberrimus quastus est, hanc vnam rationem sibi reliquam esse intelligunt, qua quastum suum retineant. Sed cum bi neque primis illis, neq; alteris conferri possint, de quibus hoc loco agitur, sed aperti veritatis hostes sint, horribiles procul dubio pœnas dabunt, neque de eis multum sperari potest, cum sibijpsis data opera tenebras offundunt, & salutis ostium præcludant, quod illis multi patefacere conantur.
units.tr: {y} Ioan. 3. Therefore it is in vain that you refer this controversy to the judgements of others, about whose truth you ought to have taught those committed to your faith. Yet there are worse than these, who do not even want to be taught, but hostilely persecute the light when it is offered. Today the greatest number of such people are found, who count it a glory and a praise that no one argues their errors, no one teaches or admonishes them, and that they are accustomed to admit no disputations about religion with anyone. Yet this glory is shared with Mahomet, who laid down this law for his followers, that they should not dispute about religion with anyone. For that most cunning impostor saw that his doctrines were so absurd that they could be defended by no Scripture or probable reasons. Since many people today also see this, for whom false religion is a most abundant source of gain, they understand that this one way is left to them by which to keep their gain. But since these men cannot be compared with those first ones, nor with the second group, of whom we are speaking in this place, but are open enemies of the truth, they will undoubtedly pay terrible penalties, and not much can be hoped for them, since they deliberately spread darkness over themselves and close the door of salvation, which many try to open for them.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque argumentum videamus, quo suam sententiam Christus confirmat, sic dicens: Cuicunq; multum datum est, ab eo multum repetetur: & apud quem deposuerunt multa, ab eo amplius reposcent. Sumitur hoc quoq; ex communi hominum more, & cum Lege naturæ conuenit. Cum enim hunc sensum in brutis animalibus esse videamus, vt suos benefactores agnoscant, & is- dem bonam gratiam referant: adhæc cum rudis tellus agricolarum labori atq; industriæ respondeat, adeò vt quò diligentius colitur, eò vberiorem proventum ferat, messemq; habeat copiosiorem, qui se- mentem fecit liberaliter: æquum est, vt homines quoq; eorum respondeant fidei & liberalitati, qui in ipsos aliqua beneficia contulerunt, neq; maligni aut fraudulenti sint eorum, quæ adipsos deponun- tur, custodes. Id verò commodissime Christus ad Ecclesiarum ministros transfert, de quorum officio hucusq; disseruit. Vt enim illos in sublimiorem dignitatis gradum Deus collocauit, & suæ voluntatis apud alios interpretes constituit: ita eosdem donis quoq; amplioribus exornat, vt functioni suæ satisfacere possint. Nam si illos spectes, homines sunt & ijsdem cum aliis hominibus affectionibus obnoxij: & vt Paulus de seipso & reliquis sui seculi doctoribus fatetur, ex semetipsis ad nihil idonei sunt, sed ex Deo habent quicquid in ipsis præclarum est, & ad ministerium, quod eis creditum est, vtile. Cur ergo non ab eis idem ille rationem exigat? Et quis non videat supplicio dignos esse eos, qui & propriæ dignitatis & gratiæ ipsis à Deo factæ immemores, dona sua vel perfidè in vsus alienos transferunt, vel turpi ignauia perire sinunt? Pertinet autem ad huius loci illustrationem parabola de talentis, quæ Matth. 25. describitur.
units.tr: But let us also look at the other argument by which Christ confirms his opinion, speaking thus: "To whom much has been given, of him much will be required; and with whom they have deposited much, of him they will demand the more." This too is taken from the common custom of men, and it agrees with the law of nature. For we see this sense even in brute animals, that they recognise their benefactors and return the same goodwill. Moreover, the untilled earth responds to the labour and industry of farmers, so that the more diligently it is cultivated, the more abundant the yield it bears and the greater the harvest it gives to the one who sowed generously. So it is right that men too should answer the faith and generosity of those who have conferred some benefits upon them, and not be malicious or fraudulent guardians of the things entrusted to them. Christ applies this most fittingly to the ministers of the Churches, of whose office he has discoursed up to this point. For as God has placed them on a higher rank of dignity and appointed them interpreters of his will to others, so he also adorns them with larger gifts, so that they may be able to fulfil their function. For if you look at them, they are men, subject to the same passions as other men; and as Paul confesses of himself and of the other teachers of his age, they are of themselves not sufficient for anything, but whatever is excellent in them they have from God, and whatever is useful for the ministry entrusted to them. Why then should he not demand an account of it from them? And who does not see that those deserve punishment who, forgetful both of their own dignity and of the grace God has shown them, either pervert their gifts to other men's uses or allow them to perish through shameful idleness? The parable of the talents, described in Matth. 25., also serves to illustrate this place.

units.la: At debet hinc doctrina generalis peti, neminem ob suæ functionis excellentiam & dotes à Deo acceptas superbire & infoletius efferri, sed potius terreri atq; humiliari debere. Vt enim ex alto gra- uior est casus: ita maior & periculosior peccandi occasio illis in singula momenta offertur, qui in al- tiori dignitatis gradu constituti sunt: & eò diligentius seueriusq; ab eis rationem exigit Deus, quò pluribus atq; præstantioribus donis eos cumulauit. Meminerint huius diligenter ministri Ecclesia- rum, de quibus in primis hic agitur. Vocat hos Christus lucem mundi & salem terræ, eò quod Verbi sui lucerna & vitæ exemplo omnibus præluceant, & singulis pia admonitione atq; doctrina mederi debent, ne in vitijs coputrescant. Curent ergo nequid negligant, neue vel otij sui, vel quastus maio- rem habeant rationem, quam gloriæ Dei & publicæ salutis. Nisi enim officium fecerint, eò maiori infamia multabuntur, quò maior est dignitas, inquam euectii sunt. Exemplo sint illis Iudaorum antistites, quibus per prophetam Dominus minatur: Si non audieritis, neq; posueritis super cor, vt detis gloriam nomini meo, dicit Dominus exercituum, mittam in vos execrationem, atq; maledicta benedictionibus vestris: quin maledixi iam, quia non ponitis super cor. En ego increpabo vobis se- men, & spargam stercus in facies vestras: stercus (inquam) dierum vestrorum solennium, tolleique vos ad se: & scietis, quod ad vos mandatum istud miserim, &c. Quod autem his dicitur, hoc ipsum prin- cipes viri & quotquot magistratu gerunt, ad se quoq; pertinere sciant. Dignatur hos potentia simul & dignitate summa Deus, quando suum quoq; nomen illis communicat. Gratiam ergo ei referant dignam & eius gloriam vicissim prouebant, & in primis caueant, ne cui vel in religione scandalo sint, vel vitæ morum exemplo aliquem seducant atq; corrumpant. Quid enim tales maneat, Solo- mones, Ieroboami, Achabi & multorum aliorum exempla abunde docent. Et notum est illud Sa- pientis
units.tr: But from this a general teaching ought to be drawn: that no one should be puffed up or unduly elated on account of the excellence of his office and the gifts received from God, but rather should be terrified and humbled. For as a fall from a height is more severe, so a greater and more dangerous occasion of sinning is offered at every moment to those placed in a higher rank of dignity; and God demands an account from them the more diligently and strictly, the more abundantly and excellently he has loaded them with gifts. Let the ministers of the Churches, of whom this is chiefly speaking, keep this diligently in mind. Christ calls them the light of the world and the salt of the earth, because by the lamp of his Word and the example of their life they ought to shine before all, and to heal each one with pious admonition and teaching, lest they rot in vices. Let them therefore take care not to neglect anything, nor to have more regard for their leisure or their gain than for the glory of God and the public salvation. For if they do not perform their duty, they will be punished with the greater infamy, the greater their dignity, I say, the loftier the height to which they have been raised. Let the high priests of the Jews be an example to them, to whom the Lord threatens through the prophet: "If you will not hear, and will not lay it to heart to give glory to my name, saith the Lord of hosts, I will send a curse upon you and curse your blessings; indeed I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart. Behold, I will rebuke your seed and spread dung upon your faces, the dung (I say) of your solemn days, and one shall take you away with it; and you shall know that I have sent this commandment to you," etc. Whatever is said to them, princes and all who hold magistracy should know applies to them too. God honours these men with power and the highest dignity, when he also shares his own name with them. Let them therefore return a worthy thanks to him and in turn promote his glory, and above all take care not to be a stumbling block to anyone in religion, or to lead anyone astray and corrupt them by the example of their conduct. For what the end of such men will be, the examples of Solomon, Jeroboam, Ahab and many others teach abundantly. And that saying of the Wise Man is well known:

units.la: Malach. 2. pientiŝ dictum: Potentes potenter punientur. Transferunt quoque ad se dictum hoc Christi diuites & cogitent quantum Deo debeant, qui illos eximit molestijs, quæ paupertati multæ & grauissimæ coniunctæ sunt: & proinde officij sui memores diuitijs ad prouehendam illius gloriam & fratrum inopum subuentionem vtantur, vt illi olim possint rationem reddere. Seruit etiam doctrina hæc in uenibus, quibus parentes & institutores fidei obtigerunt, atq; alia ad virtutem siue eruditionem ad minicula. Nam ab his quoq; rationem olim repetet Dominus, nec impunè ferent, si tantorum beneficiorum ingrati conteptores fuisse deprehendentur. Et vt tandem dicendi finem faciamus, curent omnes, vt Deo, qui suam voluntatem nobis fidelissimè reuelat, sese accommodent, & ab illo acceptis donis vsuram illam sanctam exerceant, qua multi alij ad salutis societatem adducuntur, vt olim cum bonis & fidis seruis ingredi possint in gaudium Domini nostri Iesu Christi: Cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Malach. 2. As the saying of Wisdom has it: "The mighty shall be mightily punished." Let the rich also apply to themselves this saying of Christ, and consider how much they owe to God, who frees them from the troubles that are bound up with poverty, many and very grievous. Let them therefore, mindful of their office, use their riches to advance God's glory and to relieve their needy brothers, so that they may one day be able to give an account. This teaching also applies to those who have been given parents and teachers of the faith, and to other helps towards virtue or learning. For the Lord will demand an account of these also, and they will not go unpunished if they are found to have been ungrateful and contemptuous of such great benefits. And, to bring my speech to an end, let all take care to accommodate themselves to God, who most faithfully reveals his will to us, and, having received his gifts from him, to exercise that holy usury by which many others are brought into fellowship of salvation, so that, like the good and faithful servants, they may one day enter into the joy of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXIIII.

units.la: Ignem veni missurus in terrã, & quid volo si iam accensus est? Sed baptismo oportet me baptizari: & quomodo costringor, vsque quo perficiatur? Putatis me venisse pacem daturum in terra? non dico vobis, imò dissidium. Erunt enim ex hoc tempore quinq; in vna domo dissidentes: tres aduersus duos, & duo aduersus tres. Dissidebit pater aduersus filium, & filius aduersus patrem: mater aduersus filiam, & filia aduersus matrem: socrus aduersus nurum suam, & nurus aduersus socrum suam.
units.tr: "I have come to send fire on the earth, and what do I want if it is already kindled? But I must be baptized with a baptism, and how am I constrained until it is accomplished? Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? I tell you, no, but rather division. For from now on there will be five in one house divided: three against two, and two against three. The father will be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law."

units.la: Multis & diligenter hucusque Dominus & redemptor noster, Iesus Christus, de Ecclesia sua & Verbi Dei ministris disseruit, simulque in genere omnes admonuit, vt fidelium ac frugi seruorum instar semper ad omne officium parati sint, & secundum Verbi illius regulam actiones suas omnes instituant. His cómodissimè subijciuntur quæ modò recitauimus, in quibus de Verbi sui aut Euangelij effectu amplus disserit, docens, quid hoc tam in pijs quam impijs agat, & quam turbulenta totius mundi conditio futura sit, quando hoc passim prædicabitur. Est ergo locus hic multa ac diligenti consideratione dignißimus. Nam scandalum remouet Christus, ad quod plerique offendunt, quando ex Euangelij prædicatione turbas ac tumultus publicos, adhæc inter priuatos homines, qui prius coniunctissimi erant, dissidia acerrima atq; implacabiles inimicitias oriri videnť. Admonemur præterea, quo animo ad Christum accedere, & vt nos ad certamina hæc subeunda præparare debeamus.
units.tr: Up to this point our Lord and Redeemer, Jesus Christ, has spoken at length and carefully about his Church and the ministers of his Word, and at the same time has admonished everyone in general that faithful and sensible servants should always be ready for every duty and should order all their actions according to the rule of that Word. What we have just read is most fittingly joined to these teachings. In them he speaks at greater length about the effect of his Word or Gospel, teaching what it will do among the godly and the ungodly alike, and how turbulent the condition of the whole world will be when this is preached everywhere. This passage is therefore most worthy of much careful consideration. For Christ removes a stumbling block, at which many take offence when, from the preaching of the Gospel, they see public riots and tumults arise, and, even among private persons who were formerly closest, the bitterest quarrels and implacable enmities. We are also admonished with what disposition we ought to come to Christ, and how we ought to prepare ourselves to undergo these conflicts.

units.la: Principio cur in mundum hunc venerit docet: vt nimirum totius orbis mutationem aut innoua tionem inuehat per Euangelij sui doctrinam. Iguem (inquit) veni missurus in terram, & quid volo si iam accensus est? Quibus verbis hoc omnino dicere videtur: Quoniam mundus hic totus corruptus & depravatus est, adeò, vt nisi mutatio quædam violentior fiat, omnes periturí essent, ego ex æterno Patris decreto veni, vt huius innouationis author sim, neq; aliud perinde in votis habeo, quàm vt ignis ille ardeat, quo tota mundi facies innouabitur. At cum iam nunc accensus sit, sicuti ex quorundam studio, qui me sequuntur, & aliorum contumacia, qui me oppressum volunt, coniici potest, quid præterea volo? Iam enim confectum videri poterat id cuius gratia veni. Caterum sunt hæcignis istius & mutationis principia tantum. Nam per totum terrarum orbem extendatur oportet: quod non prius fiet, quam ego mortem subiero. Tunc enim exaltatus omnia ad me trahám, & eam, quæ nunc est, mundi faciem abolebo.
units.tr: First, he teaches why he has come into this world: namely, to bring about a change or renewal of the whole world through the teaching of his Gospel. "I have come," he says, "to send fire on the earth, and what do I want if it is already kindled?" By these words he seems to say this: Since this whole world is corrupt and depraved, to such an extent that, unless some more violent change takes place, all would perish, I have come by the eternal decree of the Father to be the author of this renewal, and I have no other desire than that that fire should burn by which the whole face of the world will be renewed. But since it is already kindled, as can be inferred both from the zeal of some who follow me and from the obstinacy of others who want me crushed, what else do I want? For what I came for might already seem accomplished. But these are only the beginnings of that fire and that change. For it must spread through the whole orbit of the earth, and this will not happen until I have undergone death. For then, lifted up, I will draw all things to myself, and I will abolish the present face of the world.

units.la: Porrò ignem dicit Verbum Dei, idq; ab effectu, eò quod per illud innouationem hanc orbis si-rioportet. Estque hæc Metaphora siue similitudo frequens admodum in scripturis, & ipse Dominus apud Ieremiam ait: Annon Verbum meum est sicut ignis, & sicut malleus petras dissi-pans? Etenim multa sunt in igne, quæ Verbi naturam egregiè exprimunt. Primum, vt inter elementa nullum illo purius est: ita Verbum Dei purum & mundum est, cumq; omnes aliæ doctrinæ
units.tr: Moreover, he calls the Word of God "fire," and does so from its effect, because through it this renewal of the world must come about.
