This metaphor or likeness is quite common in the Scriptures, and the Lord himself says through Jeremiah: "Is not my word like fire, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?" Indeed, there are many things in fire that express the nature of the Word very well. First, as among the elements none is purer than fire, so the Word of God is pure and clean, while all other teachings contain the dross of human traditions mixed in. The doctrine of the divine Word alone is free from every error and, as David says, is like silver refined seven times and purified.

units.la: Cur Christus in mundum venerit.
units.tr: Why Christ came into the world.

units.la: Verbum Dei dicitur ignis. Ierem. 23. scoriam humanarum traditionum admixtam habeant, solius Verbi diuini doctrina ab omni errore libera, & (vt Dauid inquit) argento septies excocto & purgato similis est. Deinde vt ignis calore suo omnia fouet ac vegetat, membris item torporem eximit: ita Dei Verbum animis conceptum Dei amorem accendit, spem atque fidem nostram fouet & confirmat, adhac industrios reddit ad omnia exequenda, quae nostri sunt officij. Tertiò vt ignis splendorem sibi coniunctum habet, quo tenebras discutit & lucem rebus infert: ita Dei verbum mentes illuminat, vt Deum atque voluntatem eius agnoscere, & per huius mundi tenebras inoffenso pede ambulare possimus: quo nomine Christus supra illud lucernam dixit. Quartò, vt ignis neque celari neque concludi potest, quò minus erumpat: ita Dei verbum occultare, aut semel animo conceptum reprimere impossibile est. Efficaciter enim agit, vt etiam qui natura vel timidiores vel remissiores sunt, eius virtute cogantur officium facere. Exemplum huius efficaciae in Ieremia habemus, qui incurabili populi & principum atque sacerdotum contumacia tantumnon vitus aliquando dicebat: Quandoquidem Verbum Domini mihi probro vertitur, & omnibus diebus vituperio, statui mentionem eius porro non facere, neque posthac loqui in nomine eius. Sed quid idem ille mox subiecit? At fiebat illud (inquit) in corde meo & in ossibus meis tanquam conclusi ignis incendium, vt sustentando laborarem nec possem, &c. Et haec illa vis est, quae in missione Spiritus sancti per igneas linguas adumbrata, Apostolos & horum germanos successores monuit, vt contra regum & principum edicta & crudeles minas Euangelium constantissimè praedicarint, & omnes difficultates atque pericula superauerint.
units.tr: The Word of God is called fire. Jer. 23. Next, as fire warms and quickens all things by its heat, and also drives out sluggishness from the limbs, so the Word of God, once conceived in souls, kindles the love of God, nourishes and strengthens our hope and faith, and moreover makes us diligent to carry out all the duties that belong to us. Third, as fire has a brightness joined to it, by which it scatters darkness and brings light to things, so the Word of God illuminates minds, so that we may recognize God and his will and walk without stumbling through the darkness of this world; for this reason Christ said that it is a lamp. Fourth, as fire cannot be hidden or shut in so that it does not break out, so it is impossible to conceal the Word of God or to suppress it once it has been conceived in the mind. For it works effectively, so that even those who by nature are more timid or more lax are compelled by its power to do their duty. We have an example of this efficacy in Jeremiah, who, against the incurable obstinacy of the people, and of the princes and priests, at one point almost said with a broken spirit: "Since the Word of the Lord has become a reproach to me and a mockery all the day long, I have resolved no longer to mention it, nor to speak any more in his name." But what did the same man add immediately afterwards? "But it was in my heart and in my bones like a fire shut up, so that I was weary with forbearing and could not," and so on. This is the power that was foreshadowed in the sending of the Holy Spirit through tongues of fire, and which admonished the Apostles and their true successors to preach the Gospel most constantly against the edicts of kings and princes and their cruel threats, and to overcome all difficulties and dangers.

units.la: Quod ipsum etiam hodie faciunt, quicunque ignem hunc diuinum in cordibus suis accensum habent. Postremò quemadmodum ignis res mirifice transmutat, dum quasdam absumit prorsus, vt paleas & stipulas: quasdam in cineres redigit, vt ligna: nonnullas indurat, vt lutum & ex hoc confecta vasa: alias liquefacit, vt ceram: alias insuper excoquit & purgat, vt aurum, argentum & similia metalla: Ita verbum Dei mutationem rebus humanis admirabilem & variam affert. Nam alij quidem hoc audito & animis concepto toti innouantur: alij etiamsi non eo vsq; proficiant, non nihil tamen mollescunt & tractabiliores fiunt: alij vero indurantur, vel potius in rabiem accenduntur, dum illud prauis suis cupiditatibus atque studijs scelerati aduersati sentiunt. Et quo minus iisti effectus praedicationem Euangelij sequantur, nemo prohibere potest. Nam vt ij qui ex electorum numero sunt, voce sui pastoris agnoscunt, & hanc secuti ex femine illo renascuntur: ita prophani & reprobi aduersus illud insurgunt, & quotidie in peius proficiunt, non quidem Euangelij vitio (quod in illo nullum est) sed propria culpa & ingenij sui innata prauitate, quà verbum salutis respuunt. Et huc in primis facit, quod in praesenti de igne, quem in terram sit missurus, Dominus dicit. Nam vt sequentia docent, subitam rerum mutationem cum acerrimis eorum dissidijs coniunctam intellegit, qui prius inter se consentiebant. Nec temere hoc illum dixisse patebit, si quae post eius Ascensionem acciderunt, consideremus. Nam caelitus accepto Spiritu sancto Apostoli Euangelium in toto orbe terrarum praedicarunt, cuius praedicatione tam electi quam reprobi accensi sunt: illi quidem vt relictis superstitionibus & falsis Dijs, Deum verum in spiritu & veritate colerent: hi vero vt superstitiones & receptos cultus tuerentur: interim tamen Euangelicus ille ignis per omnia obstacula erupit, & incendio longè lateque grassanti similes Deos illos fictitios vna cum suis simulachris & idololatria absumpsit: adeò, vt ex triginta millibus Deorum, quos in orbe cultos fuisse Diuus Augustinus ex Varrone prodidit, vix paucorum nomina extent, & ij quoque non alio in honore sint, quam quem illis Astrologi, vanissimum & impudentissimum hominum genus, tribuunt. Taceo nunc morum mutationes non minori admiratione dignas, quando homines, qui luxu & libidine diffluebant, subito sobrij & temperantes, ex auaris liberales & benefici, ex sanguinariis ar morum & bellorum sectatoribus mites & mansueti facti sunt. Quod multis admirationi fuisse scimus, qui diuini istius ignis virtutem ignorabant. Et quantum hic etiam hodie possit, in multis videmus, qui non fido animo ad Euangelij partes transeunt. E contra autem arguuntur hic falsi, qui cunque illud ore quidem profitentur & iactant, nullum vero vel gloriae Dei zelum, vel morum mutationem in melius ostendunt. Inde de turbis & motibus in orbe oriturus Christus omnes homines admonet, vt illis non offendantur, sed potius agnoscant in illis Verbi diuini virtutem, & huic obtemperent. Qui vero in Ecclesia ministerio versantur, ij Christum imitari debent, neque ad vitandas turbas das turbas Veritatum dissimulare, sed potius maiori spiritus virtute aduersus mundi contumaciam luctari.
units.tr: And this is what those still do today who have this divine fire kindled in their hearts. Lastly, just as fire marvellously transforms things, consuming some altogether, like chaff and stubble, reducing some to ashes, like wood, hardening some, like clay and the vessels made from it, melting others, like wax, and moreover refining and purifying others, like gold, silver and similar metals, so the Word of God brings about a wonderful and varied change in human affairs. For some, when they hear it and receive it in their minds, are wholly renewed; others, even if they do not advance that far, nevertheless soften somewhat and become more tractable; but others are hardened, or rather are inflamed into rage, when they perceive that it opposes their wicked desires and evil pursuits. And no one can prevent these effects from following the preaching of the Gospel. For just as those who belong to the number of the elect recognize the voice of their shepherd, follow it, and are born again from that seed, so the profane and the reprobate rise up against it and daily grow worse, not indeed through any fault of the Gospel (for there is none in it), but through their own guilt and the innate perversity of their nature, by which they reject the word of salvation. And to this point especially bears what the Lord says in the present passage about the fire he is about to send on the earth. For, as what follows shows, he understands a sudden upheaval of affairs joined with the bitterest quarrels of those who had previously been in agreement with one another. Nor will it be clear that he spoke this rashly if we consider what happened after his Ascension. For, having received the Holy Spirit from heaven, the Apostles preached the Gospel throughout the whole world, and by this preaching both the elect and the reprobate were kindled: the former so that, leaving behind superstitions and false gods, they might worship the true God in spirit and truth; the latter so that they might defend superstitions and the accepted forms of worship. Meanwhile that Gospel fire broke out through all obstacles, and, like a fire spreading far and wide, consumed those fictitious gods together with their images and idolatry. So much so that out of the thirty thousand gods, which Augustine, the divine, tells us from Varro were worshipped in the world, scarcely the names of a few survive, and even these are held in no higher honour than that which the astrologers, the most vain and shameless race of men, assign to them. I pass over now the changes of manners, no less worthy of wonder, when men who had been dissolute in luxury and lust became suddenly sober and temperate, when the greedy became generous and beneficent, and when the bloodthirsty pursuers of war and slaughter became gentle and meek. We know that these things were a matter of wonder to many who did not know the power of that divine fire. And how much it can still do even today we see in many who pass over to the side of the Gospel with a sincere mind. On the other hand, those are exposed here as false who profess and boast of the Gospel with their mouths, but show no zeal for the glory of God and no change of life for the better. Therefore, Christ, speaking of the tumults and disturbances that are about to arise in the world, admonishes all men not to take offence at them, but rather to recognize in them the power of the divine Word, and to obey it. But those who are engaged in the ministry of the Church ought to imitate Christ, and not to dissemble the truth in order to avoid tumults, but rather to struggle against the obstinacy of the world with greater strength of spirit.

units.la: Et huc in primis pertinet votum illud Christi ardentissimum, quo ipsius patris caelestis voluntas exprimitur: quae est, ut ignis ille Euangelicus in toto orbe terrarum ardeat. Nam ut Paulus ait, vult ille omnes homines saluos fieri, & in Veritatis cognitionem venire. Ideo ab ipsa rerum origine patribus prisci locutus est multiuariam, & Verbi sui luce eo clarius subinde accendit, quo magus auctae sunt superstitionum & humanarum traditionum tenebrae. Et quamuis olim lux ista intra Iudaici populi fines concluderetur, eandem tamen ad gentes quoq; extendi tandem oportere promisit per Prophetas: quod Apostolorum ministerio factum est, qui (ut paulo ante diximus) ex Christi mandato Euangelium ad extremos usq; mundi cardines diuulgauerunt. Unde nos colligere possumus, nullum Deo cultum magis acceptum aut gratum esse, quam ut Verbum suum quam latissime propagetur, & huius praedicatione quam plurimi ad illius cognitionem & aeternae salutis haereditatem adducantur. Quo Paulus respiciens, gentes, quibus ipse Euangelium praedicabat, oblationem fidei victimam Deo gratam & per Spiritum sanctificatam dicit. Itaq; Dei hostes sunt, & cum eo bellum quodammodo gerunt, qui Verbi doctrinam oderunt, & ne hoc diuulgetur obstare audent. Suntenim hi ipsi, quos Dauid aduersus Deum & Unctum eius insurrecturos praedixit, ut huius vincula disrumpant, & iugum eius reiiciant, deniq; regnum eius euertant & destruant. Sed nihil proficiunt omnes isti. Ridet enim eorum conatus atq; consilia Dominus, & ignem Verbi sui flatu Spiritus accendit ubicunq; vult: neq; impediri potest Dei consilium, qui ut passim ardeat, decreuit.
units.tr: This is especially the case with that most ardent wish of Christ, which expresses the will of the heavenly Father himself: that the Gospel's fire should burn throughout the whole world. For, as Paul says, God wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Therefore from the very beginning of things he spoke to the fathers in many ways, and he kindled his light from his Word ever more brightly as the darkness of superstitions and human traditions grew thicker. Although that light was once confined within the borders of the Jewish people, he promised through the prophets that it would at last be extended to the Gentiles also. This was accomplished by the ministry of the apostles, who, as we said a little earlier, by Christ's command spread the Gospel to the farthest corners of the earth. From this we may gather that no worship is more acceptable or pleasing to God than that his Word be spread as widely as possible and that through its preaching as many people as possible be brought to the knowledge of it and to the inheritance of eternal salvation. Paul, looking to this, calls the Gentiles, to whom he preached the Gospel, an offering of faith, a sacrifice acceptable to God and sanctified by the Spirit. So those who hate the teaching of the Word and dare to stand in the way of its being published are God's enemies, and in a sense wage war against him. These are the very people whom David foretold would rise up against God and his Anointed, to break their bonds and throw off their yoke, and finally to overturn and destroy his kingdom. But all these men achieve nothing. The Lord laughs at their attempts and plans, and he kindles the fire of his Word by the breath of his Spirit wherever he wills. God's purpose, that it should burn everywhere, cannot be hindered, since he has decreed it.

units.la: Porro redeamus ad verba Christi, qui tempus etiam indicat, quo ignis ille debeat accendi, & ita tacitae obiectioni occurrit. Diceret enim aliquis: Si venisti, ut Euangelij ignem in tota terra accendas, cur in obscuro hoc Iudaeae angulo moram trahis, & non potius orbem terrarum lustrans ubiq; inter gentes doces? Respondet ergo: Sed baptismo oportet me baptizari, & quomodo constringor, vsq; quo perficiatur? Id vero de morte sua dicit, quam ipsum prius subire oporteat. Baptismum autem vocat mortem, quia instar transitus est per maxima discrimina ad vitae aeternae possessionem. Ut enim qui baptizantur, in aquas immersi perire videntur, sed ijdem mox iterum emergunt: ita pij in morte videri possunt communem cum impijs fortem subire, quibus illa peccati poena, & proinde aeternorum cruciatuum initium est, sed quia Christo insiti & in hoc iam pridem peccato mortui sunt, per illam transeunt ad vitam aeternam. Quod in primis in ipso Dei Filio in carne manifestato locum habuit, qui per diram & infamem mortem crucis in gloriam Patris ingressus est. His autem verbis ille innuit, hoc Dei consilium esse, ut ipse quidem solis Iudaeis praedicet, & perditas Israelis oues reducere atq; colligere stdeat, mortuus autem & ex morte resuscitatus inq; coelestem gloriam euectus per Apostolos Spiritus sui virtute armatos totum orbem terrarum illuminet. Ita vero ostendit graues istos motus & horribilem mundi totius mutationem sua morte sanciri oportere, & se primum fore, qui pericula illa sentiat. Et hoc illud est, quod olim per Zachariam Deus praedixerat: En ego adduco seruum meum, Germen.Ecce enim lapis, quem posui coram Iehosua: super lapidem unum septem oculi, & ego sculpo sculpturam eius, ait Dominus exercituum, & auferam iniquitatem terrae uno die. Quo loco Christus primo Germen dicitur, eo quod ex stirpe seu trunco potius Isai vel Dauidicae posteritatis excreuit, cum hac ad extremam egestatem redacta esset, & humano iudicio nihil magnificum de ea posset sperari. Eundem vero mox lapidem dicit, quem ipse in conspectu summi Pontificis Iehosuae posuerit, ceu fundamentum Ecclesiae & salutis totius, quod toto illo Sacerdotio adumbretur. Ideo septem, id est, omnium electorum oculos in hunc lapidem respicere ait, quem tamen prius secundum aeterni sui consilij decretum caelari aut sculpi, id est, vulnerari & occidi oporteat, ut eius merito mundi peccatum sine iniquitas expietur. Et huius generis multa apud Prophetas habentur, quae omnia Dominus suis discipulis nunc in mentem reuocat. Ut vero istud impletum sit, vnus Actorum liber abunde docet, ut longiori demonstratione non sit opus. Consideremus hic potius, quanti a nobis fieri debeat lux Euangelica, quae non prius mundo illucescere potuit, quam Dei Filius sua morte illi ostium patefaceret. Ex eo enim apparet nimium ingratos esse diuinae bonitatis aestimatores, qui illam fastidiunt, & tenebras amant, ut prauis suis studijs liberius possint indulgere. Sed hi, ut par est, fere in tenebris pereunt. Nos ergo dum lux illa salutifera nobis affulget, in ea ambulemus, ne nos tenebrae apprehendant.
units.tr: Let us return, then, to the words of Christ, who also indicates the time when that fire ought to be kindled, and so meets an objection that is left unspoken. For someone might say: "If you have come to kindle the fire of the Gospel throughout the whole earth, why do you linger in this obscure corner of Judea, and do not rather go through the whole world and teach among the nations?" He therefore replies: "But I must be baptized with a baptism, and how I am straitened until it is accomplished!" He says this of his death, which he must first undergo. He calls his death a baptism because it is a passage through the greatest dangers into the possession of eternal life. For just as those who are baptized, when they are plunged under the water, seem to perish, yet soon come up again, so the godly in death may seem to undergo the same fate as the wicked, for whom that death is the punishment of sin and so the beginning of eternal torments; but because they are implanted in Christ and have already died to sin, they pass through death into eternal life. This was true first of all of the Son of God himself, made manifest in the flesh, who entered into the glory of the Father through the dreadful and infamous death of the cross. By these words, moreover, he hints that it is God's purpose that he should first preach to the Jews alone, and go to gather and bring back the lost sheep of Israel; but that, having died and been raised from the dead and taken up into heavenly glory, he should enlighten the whole world through his apostles, armed with the power of his Spirit. He shows, too, that these grave disturbances and the dreadful upheaval of the whole world must be sanctioned by his death, and that he himself will be the first to feel those perils. This is what God had foretold long before through Zechariah: "Behold, I will bring my servant, the Branch. For behold, the stone that I have set before Joshua: upon one stone are seven eyes; and I will engrave its engraving, says the Lord of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of the land in one day." In this passage Christ is first called the Branch, because he sprang up from the stock, or rather the trunk, of Jesse or the Davidic posterity, when that line had been reduced to extreme poverty and nothing great could be hoped for from it by human judgment. But the same stone he then calls the one that he himself placed before the face of the high priest Joshua, as the foundation of the Church and of all salvation, which is shadowed by that whole priesthood. Therefore he says that the seven, that is, the eyes of all the elect, look upon this stone, which nevertheless must first, according to the decree of his eternal counsel, be engraved or carved, that is, wounded and slain, so that by his merit the sin and iniquity of the world may be expiated. Many things of this kind are found among the prophets, and the Lord now brings all of them back to the minds of his disciples. That these things were fulfilled, one book of the Acts sufficiently teaches, so that there is no need for a longer demonstration. Let us rather consider here how highly the light of the Gospel should be valued by us, a light that could not dawn upon the world until the Son of God opened the door for it by his death. For from this it appears that those who despise it and love darkness, so that they may indulge more freely in their wicked pursuits, are far too ungrateful judges of the divine goodness. But such men, as is fitting, mostly perish in darkness. Therefore, while that saving light shines upon us, let us walk in it, lest darkness overtake us.

units.la: Est praeterea hic observandum, quòd se constringi vel coartari & angi dicit, donec baptismo illo mortis baptizetur, & ignem istum paßim accendat. Exprimit illa locutione magnas gravesq; animi angustias, quae ipsum undique coartabant. Vrgebatur enim aeterno Patris decreto, cuius hanc voluntatem fuisse ante diximus. Movebat item humani generis amor, cui salutem restitutam voluit, & ideo in ultima coena se ingenti eius epuli edendi desiderio accensum fuisse testatur. Ex altera autem parte terruit illum mortis dirae & infamis recordatio, quam ipsi acerbissimam fuisse constat. Quia enim verum hominem assumpsit, & nostras infirmitates sentire debuit, non potuit non ad mortis recordationem exhorrescere, in qua Dei ira elucet adversus peccata & omnes eos, qui his sunt dediti. Fatetur hoc ipsum alibi disertis verbis. Nam ad olivarum montem, cùm iam mortis hora instaret, animam suam contristari dicit usque ad mortem, & mox eandem deprecatur, tantaq; fuit huius tristitiae & anxietatis vehementia, ut sanguineum sudorem ei exprimeret. Et apud Ioannem, cùm de morte sua & eius fructu, qui ad credentes redit, dissereret, illius consideratione territus inter alia dicit: Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater conserva me ab hac hora: sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Pater glorifica nomen tuum. Quae verba diligenti & multa consideratione dignissima sunt. Nam primò euidens nostrae infirmitatis, quam ille suscepit, testimonium continent, quo eum fidelem faterdotem esse docemur, qui nobis condolere possit: quod unum in omni tentatione nos plurimum consolatur. Deinde illam exprimunt, quae frequenter in nobis inter Spiritum & Carnem oritur, & quid tunc facere conueniat, docent. Licet ergo de carnis infirmitate conqueri, nec per se peccatum est mortem aut alia pericula timere, aut etiam deprecari. At videre oportet, ut quemadmodum Christus ad Patris decretum respexit, qui illum ideo in mundum miserat, ut nos suae mortis merito seruaret, & ideo hoc potissimum petijt, ut Patris nomen illustraretur: ita nos quoque cogitemus, nihil nobis absque diuinae prouidentiae consilio accidere, & proinde huic nos totos submittamus, neque tam de nobis ipsis atque salute nostra, quàm de gloria Dei solicïti simus, ne impatientia aut aliis affectibus superati aliquid dicamus aut faciamus, quo illa obscuretur, aut propter quod eius nomen sine Verbum malè audiat. Vbi plurimùm proderit, si Christi exemplum nobis ob oculos ponamus, & in coelestis gloria meditatione frequenter versemur, quae parata est omnibus, qui in finem usque perseueraverint. Cur enim graue alicui videatur aut iniquum ea pati, quae Filius Dei redemptionis & salutis ergò prior sustinuit? Aut quem non excitet aeterna & coelestis gloriae praemium, ut huius spe quaeuis discrimina iubeat, & labores quosuis ferat? Neque terreat nos carnis propria infirmitas, quae tunc maximè se exerit, quando minimè oportebat. Vincet enim hanc Spiritus, qui in nobis habitat, & in Christo poterunt omnia, qui ex semetipsis plus quàm manci & claudi sunt. Qui enim nos ad certamina vocat, & horum spectator est, nos quoque in his laborantes videt, & iam iam succubituros nouis viribus instruit, quibus superare possumus quaecunque saluti nostrae obstare videbantur.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed here that he says he is constrained, or confined and distressed, until he is baptized with that baptism of death, and kindles that fire everywhere. By this expression he conveys the great and grievous anguish of his mind, which pressed upon him on every side. For he was urged by the eternal decree of the Father, whose will we said before was this. The love of the human race also moved him, for whose salvation he wished to be restored; and therefore he testifies that at the last supper he was kindled with an enormous desire to eat that feast. On the other hand, the memory of a dreadful and infamous death terrified him, which is known to have been most bitter to him. For since he had taken on true manhood and was bound to feel our infirmities, he could not but shudder at the recollection of death, in which the wrath of God against sin and against all who are given over to it is revealed. He confesses this himself in plain words elsewhere. For at the Mount of Olives, when the hour of death was at hand, he says that his soul was sorrowful unto death, and soon he prays that this cup may pass from him; and so great was the vehemence of this sorrow and anguish that it forced from him a bloody sweat. And in John, when he was speaking of his death and of its fruit, which returns to believers, he was dismayed at the thought of it and said, among other things: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this cause I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name." These words deserve the most careful and thorough consideration. For first they contain clear evidence of the infirmity of our nature, which he took upon himself, by which we are taught that he is a faithful priest who can sympathize with us, and this alone greatly comforts us in every temptation. Next they express that conflict which often arises in us between the Spirit and the flesh, and they teach what we ought to do then. It is therefore permissible to complain of the weakness of the flesh, and it is not in itself sinful to fear death or other dangers, or even to pray against them. But we must take care, as Christ looked to the Father's decree, who had sent him into the world so that by the merit of his death he might save us, and therefore asked above all that the Father's name be glorified, that we likewise consider that nothing happens to us apart from the counsel of divine providence, and therefore submit ourselves wholly to it. We should be concerned not so much for ourselves and our own salvation as for the glory of God, lest, overcome by impatience or other passions, we say or do anything by which that glory is obscured or by which his name is ill spoken of. Here it will greatly help if we set Christ's example before our eyes and often dwell in meditation on the heavenly glory, which is prepared for all who persevere to the end. For why should it seem grievous or unjust to anyone to suffer those things which the Son of God first endured for our redemption and salvation? Or who would not be stirred by the reward of eternal and heavenly glory, so that by hope in it he would undertake any dangers and bear any labors? Nor should the peculiar weakness of the flesh terrify us, which shows itself most strongly just when it should least do so. For the Spirit who dwells in us will overcome it, and in Christ all things are possible for those who in themselves are weaker than the lame and the maimed. For he who calls us to the contests and watches them, sees us also labouring in them, and, when we are about to give way, supplies us with new strength, by which we can overcome whatever seemed to stand in the way of our salvation.

units.la: Caeterùm ne alienos solùm & exteros, aut eos qui veteres inimicitias certis de causis fouent, sibi hostes fore putarent discipuli, amplius exponit Dominus quò vsq; ignis iste exarsurus sit apud impios: eò vsq; nimirum, ut abruptis naturae & communis humanitatis vinculis ij quoq; aduersus eos hostiliter insurgant, qui ipsis cognationis & affinitatis iure coniunctissimi sint. Ita verò communi Iudaeorum errori occurrit, qui ex prophetarum oraculis malè intellectis enatus fuerat. Quia enim illi Regnum Messiae & piorum sub hoc felicitatem per similia & parabolas à regno huius seculi desumptas describunt, & pacem atque concordiam admirabilem pollicentur, quam lupi cum ouibus & agnus, vt cum lobis, leones cum reliquis pecoribus, basilisci deniq; & venenatissimi serpentes cum pueris & infantibus culturi sint: pleriq; illa secundùm literam de felicitate huius seculi intelligentes sibi ipsis liberationem ex Romanae tyrannidis seruitio, adhaec victoriam contra hostes, & postea pacem vniuersalem & omnia tuta atque laeta promittebant. Quo errore Apostolos quoque imbutos fuisse, alibi ostendimus, & Euangelistae non vno loco testantur. Quae causa fuit, quòd plerique contempta & vili Christi specie offensi, cum pro Messia & patribus promisso res dempsore demptore non possent agnoscere. Quamobrem diligenti admonitione opus fuit, & hodie ea non minus necessaria est, cùm multi in Christo & Euangelio eius non cœlestia & æterna bona, sed diuitias, honores, amicitias & pacem huius mundi quærant: qui deinde turbis & seditionibus ad illius prædicationem exorientibus, adhæc domesticis multorum dissidijs, publicis item persecutionibus & infelicium piorum forte, quam in hoc seculo fere sustinent, ita offenduntur, ut de Euangelij ac Verbi Dei veritate dubitent, & à fide resiliant, quam prius amplexuri videbantur. Itaque ne quid nobis huius accidat, attentiùs animis Christum de sui Regni & Ecclesiæ statu, quoad præsens seculum, differentem audiamus. Putatis (inquit) me venisse pacem daturum in terra? Non, dico vobis, imò diuisionem. Quasi diceret: Scio quæ multorum, adeoque omnium veστrum sententia sit de Regno Messiæ, & quid nonnulli ex me sperent, quasi Regnum in hisce terris pacificum & lætum constituturus sim. Sed longè aliter se res habent. Nam pacis quidem princeps sum, sicuti Prophetæ prædixerunt, & pacem daturus veni, sed meam pacem, non autem pacem huius mundi. Imo quoad hunc, dissensiones grauissimæ & dissidia implacabilia exorientur inter eos quoque, qui vix vnquam dissentire posse videbantur. Erunt enim ex hoc tempore quinque in vna domo dissidentes, tres adversus duos, & duo adversus tres. Quod alibi breuius enuntiat, dicens: Erunt inimici hominis domestici eius. Et hic speciem quoque exponens addit: Dissidebit pater aduersus filium, & filius aduersus patrem: mater aduersus filiam, & filia aduersus matrem: socrus aduersus nurum suam, & nurus aduersus socrum suam. Tres hominum ordines enumerat, sub quibus omnes alios humanæ societatis & coniunctionis gradus comprehendit. Primus est patrum & filiorum: alter matrum & filiarum. Coniunxit hos mutuo amore & naturalibus affectionum vinculis Deus, quæ Græcis στοργαὶ dicuntur. Et sanè, quoad naturæ Lex non tota extinguitur, non possunt non illi sese mutuò amare, cùm liberi parentibus suam originem, adeoque vitam ipsam debeant: hi verò sese in illis quodammodo renasci & reuiuiscere videant. Similis est inter socrus & nurus ratio, cùm hæ filiarum loco sint, & nepotes pariant, in quibus optata generis propagatio conspicitur. At nullum naturæ vinculum tam arctum, nullam coniunctionem tam iucundam, nullam societatem tam necessariam fore Christus ait, quæ non dissiliat & abrumpatur, quando Euangelicus ille ignis ardere incipit.
units.tr: But so that the disciples would not think that only strangers and outsiders, or those who nurse old enmities for specific reasons, would be their enemies, the Lord goes further and explains how far this fire will spread among the wicked: so far, namely, that they will break the bonds of nature and common humanity and rise up hostilely even against those who are most closely joined to them by the ties of kinship and marriage. This answers the common error of the Jews, which arose from a wrong understanding of the prophetic oracles. For the prophets describe the kingdom of the Messiah and the happiness of the godly under it by likenesses and parables drawn from the kingdoms of this world, and promise a wonderful peace and harmony: the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the kid, the lion with the other cattle, and finally the basilisk and the most poisonous serpents playing with boys and infants. Most of the Jews understood these things literally, as referring to the happiness of this age, and they promised themselves deliverance from the slavery of Roman tyranny, then victory over their enemies, and afterwards a universal peace and everything safe and joyful. We have shown elsewhere that the apostles also were imbued with this error, and the evangelists testify to it in more than one place. This was the reason why many were offended by the contemptible and lowly appearance of Christ, and could not recognise in the Redeemer what had been promised to the fathers through the Messiah. Therefore careful warning was needed then, and it is no less necessary today, since many seek in Christ and His Gospel not heavenly and eternal goods but the riches, honours, friendships and peace of this world. When tumults and seditions arise at the preaching of Christ, and when there are domestic quarrels in many families, and public persecutions, and the misfortunes which the godly generally endure in this age, they are so offended that they doubt the truth of the Gospel and of the Word of God, and fall away from the faith which they seemed about to embrace. So, lest anything of this happen to us, let us listen more attentively to Christ, as He speaks of the state of His kingdom and Church in the present age. "Do you think," He says, "that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division." It is as if He said: I know what the opinion of many, indeed of all of you, is about the kingdom of the Messiah, and what some hope from me, as if I were going to establish a kingdom in these lands that is peaceful and joyful. But things are quite otherwise. For I am indeed the Prince of Peace, as the prophets foretold, and I have come to give peace, but my peace, not the peace of this world. Indeed, as far as this world is concerned, the most serious dissensions and irreconcilable quarrels will arise even among those who seemed scarcely ever able to disagree. For from this time there will be five divided in one house, three against two and two against three. He states this more briefly elsewhere, saying: "A man's enemies will be those of his own household." And explaining the particular forms of this, He adds: "The father will be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." He lists three orders of people, under which He includes all the other degrees of human society and connection. The first is that of fathers and sons; the second, that of mothers and daughters. God has joined these together by mutual love and the natural bonds of affection, which the Greeks call [στοργαί]. And indeed, so long as the law of nature is not wholly extinguished, they cannot but love one another, since children owe their origin and even their life to their parents, while parents see themselves in some way reborn and revived in their children. The relation between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law is similar, since these stand in the place of daughters and bear grandchildren, in whom the desired propagation of the family is seen. Yet Christ says that no bond of nature is so tight, no union so pleasant, no fellowship so necessary, that it will not be torn apart and broken when that Gospel fire begins to burn.

units.la: At hic meminisse oportet, illum de differentionibus ac dissidijs inter electos & reprobos, fideles & infideles exorituros loqui, quorum propria causa est, non Euangelium, sed obstinata & incurabilis impiorum ac reproborum malitia, qui se illi hostiliter opponunt. Nam si Euangelium spectes, pacis & charitatis doctrinam continet, qua hostes quoque diligere & eorum salutem precibus nostris iuuare iubemur. Et qui illam vere intra animos suos admittunt, ij mox extinctis odij atque inuidiæ flammis, & procul abiectà vindictæ cupiditate, eos etiam summo amore complectuntur, quos (si humana spectes) iustis de causis odisse poterant. Vnde ergo dissidiorum tanti ignes nascuntur? Ex impiorum (vt diximus) contumacia & rebellione. Hi enim quia toti in malo iacent (vt de mundo Ioannes pronuntiat) & operibus pessimis atque apertis flagitijs assuevèrunt, neque lucem ipsos arguentem, neque ignem conscientias ipsorum adurentem ferre possunt, & proinde omnino extinctum volunt. Quod cùm perficere nequeant, rabiem suam aduersus pios conuertunt, apud quos ignis ille ardet & lucet. Hinc ergo dissensiones prodeunt, & præter animi voluntatem cum improbis illis dissidere coguntur, fideles Christi cultores, cùm neque agnitam veritatem abnegare, neque illorum libidini indulgere possunt. Itaque ab illis quidem dissentiunt, sed ita, ut eos nihilominus amplent, saluti ipsorum consultum cupiant, & eorundem interitum pijs atque minimè fictis lachrymis deplorent. Sed implacabilis est impiorum furor, qui se non aliter suam felicitatem tueri posse arbitrantur, nisi illos simul omnes è medio tollant. Quapropter pax illa, quam Prophetæ in Christo pollicentur, inter eos solos fore, qui ipsum cum fide apprehendunt, qua animati in vnum corpus coalescunt: alijs verò idem ille barbarum author est, non sua, sed ipsorum culpa, qui se ei contumaciter opponere non verentur. Est hoc ingens corruptæ & vitiosæ naturæ nostræ argumentum, cuius exempla ab ipso mundi exordio infinita reperiuntur. Cœpit enim hoc dissidium in primogenito Adami, Caino, qui Abelum fratrem crudeli parricidio occidit, non alia quàm religionis & fidei causa, quòd hunc propter huius puritatem Deo acceptum esse, se autem propter impiam hypocrisim ab eo
units.tr: Here, however, we must remember that He is speaking of the divisions and quarrels that will arise between the elect and the reprobate, the faithful and the unbelieving, whose real cause is not the Gospel but the obstinate and incurable malice of the wicked and reprobate, who oppose it hostilely. For if you look at the Gospel, it contains the teaching of peace and charity, by which we are commanded to love even our enemies and to help their salvation with our prayers. And those who truly admit this teaching into their hearts, once the flames of hatred and envy are quenched and the desire for revenge is cast far away, embrace with the greatest love even those whom, if you look at human considerations, they could justly have hated. Whence, then, do such great fires of dissension arise? From the stubbornness and rebellion of the wicked, as we have said. For since they lie wholly in evil (as John says of the world), and have grown accustomed to the worst deeds and open crimes, they can bear neither the light that convicts them nor the fire that burns in their consciences, and therefore they wish it utterly extinguished. When they cannot accomplish this, they turn their rage against the godly, in whom that fire burns and shines. Hence dissensions arise, and faithful worshippers of Christ, who can neither deny the truth they have acknowledged nor indulge the lusts of those others, are forced against their will to disagree with those wicked men. Thus they do indeed dissent from them, yet in such a way that they nevertheless love them, desire their salvation, and lament their ruin with pious and wholly unfeigned tears. But the fury of the wicked is implacable; they think they cannot preserve their own happiness unless they remove all the others from the midst. Therefore that peace which the prophets promise in Christ will exist only among those who grasp Him with faith, by which, being animated, they grow together into one body; but for the others the same Christ is the cause of strife, not through His own fault but through theirs, since they do not hesitate to oppose Him stubbornly. This is a great proof of the corrupt and vicious nature we have, and examples of it are found without number from the very beginning of the world. For this division began with the firstborn of Adam, Cain, who killed his brother Abel in a cruel murder, for no other cause than religion and faith: because he saw that Abel was accepted by God on account of his uprightness, while he himself was not approved on account of his impious hypocrisy.

units.la: Euangelium non propria causa dissidiorum. dem minus probari videret. Deinde crescete indies magis humano genere, dissidia quoq; maiora & frequentiora exorta sunt. Et si Apostolorum tempora inspiciamus, haec à Christo verissime prædicta esse patebit. Sed non opus est longa veterum historiarū commemoratione, quando quæ hodie fiunt, hus possunt fide facere. Quot enim filios à patribus abdicatos, quot filias exhæredatas, quot socrus à nuribus derelictas, quot nurus à soceris & socribus domo expulsas, quot coniugia rescissa iam annis aliquot vidimus? Quòd si causam quæras, non aliam, quàm religionis inuenies quòd nimirum bi qui dem Veritatis lucem sequuntur, illi verò quò minus id fiat, conantur probibere. Sunt hæc dura & iniqua admodum, sed vlterius quoq; impietas crudelis grassata est, quando fratres à fratribus, illu- stres item personæ à suis consanguineis, filij à parentibus propter fidem in Iesum Christum casi sunt. Taceo nunc eos, qui vt Euangelij doctrinam euerterent, veteres & communes hostes, adhæc barbaras gentes non minus crudelitate quam publicus ac nefandis flagitijs infames in patriæ viscera adduxerunt. Atqui vtinam vel nunc cessaret tanta impietas, & non quotidie adhuc fierent, quæ fine lachrymis non possunt commemorari. Dum verò ista fiunt, nos in hæc Christi verba respicere conuenit, ne tanquam nouis atq; insolitis offendamur, sed potius fidei constantia armati aduersus mun di impietatem atque audaciam luctemur.
units.tr: The Gospel is not the proper cause of the divisions. Then, as the human race grew day by day, the divisions too became greater and more frequent. And if we look at the times of the apostles, it will be plain that these things were most truly foretold by Christ. But there is no need for a long recital of the histories of the past, since what happens today can bear witness to them. For how many sons have we seen disinherited by their fathers, how many daughters cut off from their inheritance, how many mothers-in-law abandoned by their daughters-in-law, how many daughters-in-law expelled from the house by their fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law, how many marriages broken off in recent years? And if you ask the cause, you will find none other than religion: namely, that some follow the light of truth, while others try to prevent them from doing so. These things are very hard and unjust, but further, a cruel impiety has also raged, when brothers have been cast out by brothers, illustrious persons by their own kinsmen, and sons by their parents, because of faith in Jesus Christ. I say nothing now of those who, in order to overturn the doctrine of the Gospel, brought into their country's bowels the old and common enemies, and barbarous peoples no less infamous for cruelty than for public and abominable crimes. Yet would that such great impiety would now cease, and that those things which cannot be recounted without tears were not still happening every day. While these things are being done, it is fitting for us to look to these words of Christ, lest we be offended as by something new and unusual, but rather, armed with constancy of faith, we should struggle against the impiety and audacity of the world.

units.la: Accusant quidem nos impij Euangelicæ Veritatis hostes, quòd huius prædicatione pax publica turbata, concordia rescissa & consensus omnis in religione abruptus sit. At quid aliud fit hodie, quàm cuius causa se Christus venisse dicit? Est quidem plausibile pacis nomen, sed non omnis pax bona, neque omnis concordia sancta & salutaris est. Colunt inter se pacem prædones, concordiam fouent socij vsurarij, & inter scortatores atque scorta mirificus est consensus, vt alter in altero quasi viuere videatur. Quis verò prudens & bonus ista probauerit? Et nonne lau- dem meretur, qui istos dirimit, vt & scelerum finis fiat, & aliqui saltem ad frugem meliorem re- ducantur? Idem ergo in religione obseruari debet. Nam neque ibi probari potest consensus in su- perstitionibus aut cultibus illicitis, nisi gentium idolomaniam, Mahumetistarum deliria & Iu- dæorum fabulas probare velimus: sed quod Christus iam morituros precatur, vt in ipso consentia- mus atque vnum simus videre oportet. Hypocritæ autem & superstitiosis humanarum traditio- num obseruatoribus minimè consentire debemus, etiamsi parentes, soceri, coniuges, fratres aut aliis nominibus nobis coniunctissimi fuerint. Nam vt D. Ambrosius scribit, prima religionis causa est secunda pietatis, ideoq; Deo potius quàm hominibus obedire decet. Quare inexcusabilis illo- rum error est, qui hodie inter dissensiones & controuersias de fide & religione, multa aduersarijs concedenda esse putant, vt publica pax atque concordia seruetur. Quorum sententia tunc demum admitti posset, si Dei Verbum nostri iuris esse probarent prius, nosque de Dei culcu statuendi po- testatem habere ostenderent. Quod cùm nemo possit demonstrare, quid reliquum est, quàm vt nos ad certamina & crucem præparemus, & Christum Iesum ducem sequamur, qui eos ad Regnum suum cœleste transferet, qui in finem vsque perseuerauerint. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The enemies of the Gospel truth, the impious, indeed accuse us that by its preaching public peace has been disturbed, concord broken, and all agreement in religion torn apart. But what else is happening today than that for which Christ says he came? The name of peace is indeed attractive, but not every peace is good, nor is every concord holy and salutary. Robbers keep peace among themselves, partners in usury foster concord, and among fornicators and their whores there is a remarkable agreement, so that one seems to live in the other. But what wise and good man would approve of these things? Does not he deserve praise who separates such men, so that both the end of their crimes comes about and at least some are brought back to a better way of life? The same must be observed in religion. For agreement in superstitions or illicit worship cannot be approved there either, unless we wish to approve the idolatry of the nations, the delusions of the Mahumetists and the fables of the Jews. Rather, we must see that we agree in him and are one, as Christ prays for those who are about to die. We ought in no way to agree with hypocrites and with those who observe superstitious human traditions, even if they are our parents, fathers-in-law, spouses, brothers, or bound to us by any other closest ties. For, as St Ambrose writes, the first concern of religion is the second concern of piety, and therefore it is fitting to obey God rather than men. Hence inexcusable is the error of those who today, amid disputes and controversies about faith and religion, think that many things must be conceded to our adversaries in order that public peace and concord may be preserved. Their opinion could only be admitted if they first proved that the Word of God is at our disposal, and showed that we have the power to decide about the worship of God. Since no one can demonstrate this, what remains but that we prepare ourselves for conflicts and the cross, and follow Jesus Christ as our leader, who will transfer to his heavenly kingdom those who persevere to the end. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXV.
units.tr: Homily CXXXV.

units.la: Dicebat autem etiam turbæ: Cum videritis nubem exorientem ab Occasu, statim dicitis, Imber veniet: & ita fit. Et cum Austrum flantem, dicitis, Æstas erit: & fit æstus. Hypocritæ, faciem cœli & terræ nostis probare: hoc autem tempus qui fit vt non probetis? Cur autem & per vosipsos non iudicatis quod iustum est? Quando enim abis cum ad- uersario tuo ad magistratum, da operam in via vt liberēris ab eo: ne per trahat te ad iudicem, & iudex te tradat exactori, & exactor conijciat te in carcerem. Dico tibi, non exibis illinc vsquequo vltimum etiam minu- tum reddideris.
units.tr: And he also said to the crowds: "When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, 'A shower is coming,' and so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, 'There will be heat,' and there is. Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you do not interpret this time? Why do you not even judge for yourselves what is right? For when you go with your adversary before the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be rid of him, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last penny."

units.la: Vàmuis Deus omnis ordinis & loci homines velit saluos fieri & in veritatis cognitionem peruenire, nec aliquid eorum praetermittat, quae ad salutem nostram promouendam aut conseruandam faciunt, ea tamen est plerorumq; peruersitas atq; ingenij malitia, vt neq; Dei beneuolentiam infinitis argumentis sese exerentem agnoscant, neq; oblatam sibi salutis rationem amplectantur. Conqueritur de hoc ille passim apud Prophetas, quando se mane surrexisse & tota die manus expandisse dicit ad populum rebellem & contumacem. Et de hoc in praesenti etiam Christus agit. Postquam enim docuit, hanc esse Dei Patris voluntatem, vt ignis Euangelij in toto terrarum orbe ardeat, mox etiam praedicit, quàm improbè quamq; contumaciter plurimi aduersus hunc pugnaturi sint: adeo, vt omnis charitatis & naturalium quoq; animi affectionum immemores, eos etiam persequantur, quos cognationis & affinitatis vinculum ipsis arctissimè coniunxit. De illis verò suos praemonet, ne turbis & dissidijs eiusmodi offendantur, sed potius voluntati diuinae sese accommodent, & salutis doctrinā gratis animis excipiant. At quia hic natura tardiores sumus, & ex ijs quibus tunc Christus loquebatur, pleriq; incurabiles erant, admonitioni huic grauem increpationem subijcit, qua & horum contumaciam accusat, & pios quid ipsi facere debeant, docet. Quae vt rectius intelligantur, locus hic ex Matth. Cap. 16. erit farciendus.
units.tr: Although God wishes men of every rank and place to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and omits nothing that serves to promote or preserve our salvation, yet such is the perversity of most people and the malice of their minds that they neither acknowledge God's goodwill, displayed by countless proofs, nor embrace the way of salvation offered to them. The Lord complains of this throughout the Prophets, when he says that he rose early and stretched out his hands all day to a rebellious and stubborn people. Christ too is dealing with this very matter here. For after teaching that it is the will of God the Father that the fire of the Gospel should burn throughout the whole world, he at once foretells how wickedly and how obstinately very many will fight against it, so that, forgetting all love and even natural affection, they will persecute those whom the bond of kinship and marriage has joined to them most closely. He warns his own people not to be offended by such tumults and divisions, but rather to conform themselves to the divine will and to receive the doctrine of salvation with willing hearts. But because we are slow by nature, and many of those to whom Christ was then speaking were incurable, he adds a grave rebuke to this warning, by which he both accuses their obstinacy and teaches the godly what they themselves ought to do. So that these things may be understood more rightly, this passage must be filled out from Matthew chapter 16.

units.la: Nam occasionem, quae illum mouit, vt durius eos tractaret, omittit Lucas, quae apud Matthaeum exprimitur. Illo enim populum instituente, Pharisaei & Sadducaei conspiratione facta eum aggressi sunt: & primo quidem (vt Marcus annotauit) disputationem contra illum instituerunt, vbi verò nihil proficiunt, signum aliquod coelitus fieri postulant, quo probet, se a Deo missum, & doctrinam suam diuinam atque coelestem esse, cui omnes credere & obedire debeant. Astutè autem hoc petunt, quo olim serui Dei & Prophetae sibi fidem conciliarunt. Mosis certè doctrina signis coelestibus, columna nimirum nubis & ignis, Manna item coelitus dato, & ijs quae in monte Sinai acciderunt, comprobata fuit. Samuel quoque populi ingratitudinem & contumaciam tonitruis & pluuijs subitò exortis, cum coelum prius serenissimum esset, redarguit. Et Elias non modo ad montem Carmeli Baalis cultum igne coelitus impetrato confutauit, verum etiam prophanos & imperiosos Regis Ochoziae nuntios ad se missos flammis coelestibus exusit. Quae cum nō ignorarent Pharisaei & Sadducaei, consultò simile quid fieri volunt, vt suam contumaciam prisci exemplis defendant atque excusent.
units.tr: For Luke leaves out the occasion that moved Christ to treat them more harshly, which Matthew sets out. For while he was instructing the people, the Pharisees and Sadducees joined in a conspiracy and attacked him. At first (as Mark noted) they disputed against him, but when they gained nothing they demanded some sign from heaven, by which he might prove that he was sent by God and that his teaching was divine and heavenly, something all ought to believe and obey. They ask this cunningly, because by such means the servants of God and the prophets of old won faith for themselves. Indeed the teaching of Moses was confirmed by heavenly signs: namely the pillar of cloud and fire, the manna given from heaven, and the things that happened on Mount Sinai. Samuel too rebuked the people's ingratitude and obstinacy with thunder and rain suddenly arising when the sky had been perfectly clear. And Elijah not only refuted the worship of Baal on Mount Carmel by fire obtained from heaven, but also consumed with heavenly flames the profane and arrogant messengers of King Ahaziah who were sent to him. Since the Pharisees and Sadducees were not unaware of these things, they deliberately wish something similar to happen, so that they may defend and excuse their obstinacy by ancient examples.

units.la: Rursus autem elucet hic hostium Veritatis malitia atq; improbitas. Audiuerunt isti hucusque Christum docentem, qui totam salutis humanae rationem non minus perspicuè quàm fideliter tradebat: neq; eius doctrinam vllis vel scripturae testimonijs vel argumentis idoneis confutare possunt: imò cum hoc saepius tentassent, semper non sine ignominia victi succubuerunt. Non tamen cedunt Veritati. Sed nouas subinde cauillandi occasiones quaerunt, vt populo suspectū & inuisum reddant. Maiori tamen impudentia eius miracula contemnunt atq; in dubium vocare audent, quàmuis nulla in illis fraus siue impostura a quoquam posset deprehendi, & quae populus publicè praedicabat, eò quòd multis salutaria essent. Quo exemplo admonemur, Veritatis doctrinā a nemine tam clarè & perspicuè proponi, quin aduersarios atq; contradictores habeat. Quid enim de sua industria & dexteritate sibijpsis homines polliceantur, quando Dei Filius, qui aeterna est Dei sapientia, nō omnibus persuadere potuit, vt illam amplecterentur? Et hic quidem admiratione in primis dignum est, eos Veritati prae alijs obstrepere, qui eius studium publicè profitentur, & praecipuam doctrinae atq; pietatis existimationem sustinent. Tales enim istos fuisse, alibi diximus. Sed hoc ita euenturum esse, olim Prophetae praedixerunt. Isaias certè de Christo vaticinaturus, ab initio statim de paucitate credentium conqueritur. Quis credidit (inquit) praedicationi nostrae? & brachium Domini cui reuelatum est? Dauid verò lapidem hunc ab ipsis architectis reprobatum iri ait, qui in caput anguli a Deo constitutus sit. Et quod Christo in terris agenti accidit, hoc ipsum Apostoli quoq; passim experti sunt. Patet hoc abunde ex toto Actorum lib. cuius exempla hic commemorare nimis longum foret, & sufficere potest quod Iudaei Paulo Romam deducto dicunt, sibi compertum esse, quòd Christianorum secta passim ab omnibus contradicatur. Habes ergo quod ijs respondeas, qui hodie istud nobis obijciunt, quod Euangelij doctrina apud plerosq; male audiat, & ijs inuisa sit, qui in hoc mundo dignitate & sapientia reliquos praestant. Nec enim hoc nouum est, aut insolens: imò hinc colligimus in illa Veritatis lucem proponi, quam mundus ferre non potest, eò quòd opera eius mala sint. Et quomodo doctrinam illam, quæ gloriam omnem uni Deo vendicat, ij probarent, qui mundi gloriâ affectant, de Dei auem gloria vix unquam cogitant?
units.tr: Again here the malice and wickedness of the enemies of the Truth is evident. Those men had heard Christ teaching until now; he set out the whole way of human salvation no less clearly than faithfully. Nor can they refute his doctrine by any testimony of Scripture or by any suitable argument. Indeed, although they had tried this often, they were always defeated and gave way, not without disgrace. Yet they do not yield to the Truth. Instead they keep seeking fresh occasions for cavilling, so as to make him suspect and hateful to the people. With still greater shamelessness they despise his miracles and dare to call them into doubt, although no fraud or imposture in them could be detected by anyone, and although the people openly proclaimed them, because they were beneficial to many. From this example we are warned that the doctrine of the Truth is never set forth so clearly and plainly by anyone that it does not have adversaries and contradictors. For what can men promise themselves from their own diligence and skill, when the Son of God, who is the eternal wisdom of God, could not persuade everyone to embrace it? And indeed it is especially worthy of wonder that those who publicly profess zeal for the Truth and hold the chief reputation for doctrine and piety are the ones who clamour against it more than others. For we have said elsewhere that such men these were. But the Prophets long ago foretold that this would happen. Isaiah, about to prophesy of Christ, complains at the very outset of the small number of believers: "Who has believed our preaching? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" David says that this stone will be rejected by the very builders, though it has been set by God as the head of the corner. And what happened to Christ while he was on earth, the Apostles too experienced everywhere. This is abundantly clear from the whole book of Acts, whose examples would be too long to recall here; it is enough that the Jews, when Paul was brought to Rome, said that they had learned that the sect of the Christians is everywhere spoken against by all. You therefore have an answer for those who today object to us that the doctrine of the Gospel is ill spoken of by most people and is hateful to those who excel the rest in this world by dignity and wisdom. For this is neither new nor unusual. Indeed, from this we gather that the light of the Truth is set forth which the world cannot bear, because its works are evil. And how would those who seek the glory of the world, and hardly ever think of the glory of God, approve that doctrine which claims all glory for the one God?

units.la: Porrò Christum audiamus, quem Marcus in spiritu suo altè ingemuisse scribit, nimirum quòd Patris sui bonitatem ab istis tam malitiosè conculcari, & ipsos sponte in proprium exitium ruere simulq; multos alios secum abripere videret. Est hoc animi plane paterni argumentum. Nam ut fidelis pater liberorum interitu dolet, quem ipsi neq; videre neq; cauere volunt: ita Filius Dei non semel animi sui dolorem ex hostium malitia & perditione conceptum testatus est, cùm illi securi nimis omnes admonitiones contemnerent. In præsenti autem pius iste & iustus dolor illum movet, ut aduersarios suos graviter increpet, sic dicens: Cum videritis nubem exorientem ab Occasu, statim dicitis, Imber venit: & ita fit. Et cum austrum flantem, dicitis, Æstus erit: & fit æstus. Hypocritæ faciem cœli & terræ nostis probare: hoc autem tempus quî fit ut non probetis? Hypocritas dicit, quia pietatis ac veritatis studium simulabant, cùm omnia insidiose facerent, & ius quæstionibus non aliud quàm Veritatis oppressionem molirentur. De duobus autem illos accusat. Primum est, incurabilis & voluntaria cæcitas, qua sibi ipsis malitiosè oculos claudant, ne virtutem suam aperte satis in doctrina & miraculis sese exerentem agnoscant. Deinde, eos esse ostendit, qui in luce meridia na tenebras quærant, ne Veritati cedere cogantur. Alterum, quòd huius seculi commodis addicti, quæcunq; illa promouere possunt, diligenter obseruent, negligant autem ea, quæ ad Regnum Dei & æternam veramq; hominis salutem faciunt. Utrumq; vero confirmat & illustrat exemplo ex communi vulgi usu petito, cuius hic sensus est: Petitis ut signo aliquo cœlesti probem, me à Deo missum & diu à patribus expectatum Messiam esse. Ita vero dum incredulitate vestram accusare vultis, malitiosam & voluntariam ignorantiam siue cæcitatem egregièproditis. Nam ea est vestri ingenij solertia atq; industria, ut ex signis naturalibus futuras tempestates cognoscere possitis, & eas etiam prædicere. Quæ ergo malitia est, ex iis quæ ob oculos versantur & quotidie fiunt, nō iudicare de præsenti temporum istorum statu & conditione, vosq; illi accommodare? Unde vero ista cæcitas suam originem ducit? Non aliunde certè, quàm quòd cœlestia bona securi negligitis, & huius solùm vitæ commodis intenti, Veritatis lucem auersamini, quæ studijs vestris pessimis aduersatur.
units.tr: Next let us hear Christ, whom Mark writes groaned deeply in his spirit: namely because he saw his Father's goodness so wickedly trampled underfoot by these men, and saw them rushing of their own accord to their own destruction and dragging many others along with them. This is plainly a sign of a fatherly heart. For as a faithful father grieves at the ruin of his children, who neither see nor wish to guard against it, so the Son of God more than once bore witness to the sorrow of his mind, conceived from the malice and perdition of his enemies, since they, too secure, scorned every warning. In the present passage, however, this pious and just sorrow moves him to rebuke his adversaries severely, saying: "When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, 'A shower is coming,' and so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, 'There will be heat,' and there is. Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you do not interpret this time?" He calls them hypocrites because they feigned a zeal for godliness and truth, while they did everything insidiously, and their questions aimed at nothing but the oppression of the Truth. He accuses them of two things. The first is an incurable and wilful blindness, by which they maliciously shut their own eyes, so that they do not acknowledge his power, displayed clearly enough in doctrine and miracles. Next, he shows that they are men who seek darkness in the midday light, so that they will not be forced to yield to the Truth. The second is that, devoted to the advantages of this age, they diligently observe whatever can advance these, but neglect those things that pertain to the kingdom of God and to the eternal and true salvation of man. He confirms and illustrates both with an example taken from the common usage of the people, whose sense is this: "You ask me to prove by some heavenly sign that I am the Messiah sent by God and long expected by the fathers. Yet in accusing your unbelief you plainly display your malicious and wilful ignorance or blindness. For such is the cleverness and diligence of your minds that from natural signs you can recognise coming storms and even predict them. What malice, then, is it not to judge from what lies before your eyes and happens every day the present state and condition of these times, and to accommodate yourselves to it? But whence does this blindness take its origin? Surely from nowhere else than that you carelessly neglect heavenly goods, and, intent only on the advantages of this life, you turn away from the light of the Truth, which opposes your wicked pursuits.

units.la: Loquitur autè Dominus de iis, quæ Messiæ temporibus euentura esse olim Prophetæ prædixerant. Inter quæ primum erat Iacobi oraculum, qui iam moriturus ex Spiritus sancti suggestione dicit, sceptrū & regiam potestatem non prius auferendam fore à Iuda, quàm in foribus iam adsit Schilo, id est, Seruator ille promissus, ad quem gentes quoq; confluere oporteat. Sed apertius Daniel tempus illud monstrauit, tunc nasciturū illū prædicens, quando Monarchia quarta, Romana scilicet iã stabilita & cõfirmata fuerit. Et Isaias eũ ex trunco Isai instar surculi aut germinis noui emersurum ait, id est, tunc nasciturū, quando Dauidis familia omni dignitate spoliata ad egestatē & miseram illam conditionem denuo redacta fuerit, qualis fuit Isai, quem rusticū fuisse & suo labore vitã tasse legimus. His adde quod de Elia præcursore & voce præconis in deserto clamantis idē Isaias & Malachias tradunt. Sed & dissidiorū atq; inimicitiarum inter coniunctissimos Mich.meminit: neq; reticentur miracula, quibus diuinam virtutē ille declaraturus fit. Nam Isaias populum, quem multa tristia manebant, consolaturus inter alia dicit: Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit nos: Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur: tunc claudus instar cerui saltabit, & inbila bit lingua muti. Et huius generis multa apud Prophetas habentur, quæ vulgo notissima erant, adeò ut multi in singulas horas Regni Dei instaurationē expectarent, sicuti de Simeone, Iosepho Arima thæo, Anna prophetissa Lucas testatur. Apud Ioannē verò publicè in templo multi dixerunt: Cùm venerit Christus, num maiora signa ædet, quā iste? Interim pleriq; auaritia, ambitione & Veritatis odio excæcati, ista minimè obseruabant, neq; pro Messia & promisso seruatore Iesum hunc agnoscebant, in quo hæc omnia quotidie implebantur. Merito igitur Christus malitiosam & voluntariam cæcitatem siue ignorantiam illis exprobrat, ob quam breui pœnas graues daturi sint. Similis expro bratio apud Ieremiam extat, vbi volucrum exemplis Iudæorum stupiditatem & socordiam Deus arguit, dicens: Ciconia in aëre nouit sua stata tempora: turtur, grus & hirundo obseruant tempus profectionis suæ: at populus meus non cognouit iudicium Domini. Et Christus infra Hierosolymam cum cum tota gente nouo & inaudito exemplo excindendam fore dicit, eò quod non agno scanit tempus suae visitationis.
units.tr: The Lord speaks of those things which the Prophets had long before foretold would come to pass in the times of the Messiah. Among these the first was the prophecy of Jacob, who, about to die, declared under the prompting of the Holy Spirit that the sceptre and royal power would not be taken from Judah until Shiloh, that is, that promised Saviour to whom the nations must also flock, was already at the gates. But Daniel showed the time more plainly, foretelling that he would be born when the fourth monarchy, namely the Roman, had already been established and confirmed. And Isaiah says that he would come forth from the stump of Jesse like a shoot or a new sprout, that is, that he would be born when the family of David had been stripped of all dignity and reduced again to poverty and that wretched condition in which Jesse was, whom we read was a countryman who earned his living by his own labour. To these add that Isaiah and Malachi also write about Elijah the forerunner and the voice of the herald crying in the desert. Micah also mentions the discords and enmities between those closest to one another. Nor are the miracles by which he would show forth divine power passed over. For Isaiah, when he would comfort a people beset by many sorrows, says among other things: God himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unsealed; then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb will sing for joy. There are many things of this kind in the Prophets, which were very well known among the people, so that many looked for the restoration of the kingdom of God every hour, as Luke bears witness of Simeon, Joseph of Arimathea, and Anna the prophetess. But in John's account many publicly said in the temple: When Christ comes, will he do greater signs than this man? Meanwhile most, blinded by greed, ambition and hatred of the truth, did not observe these things, nor did they acknowledge this Jesus as the Messiah and promised Saviour, in whom all these things were being fulfilled every day. Christ therefore rightly reproaches them for their malicious and wilful blindness or ignorance, on account of which they would soon pay heavy penalties. A similar rebuke stands in Jeremiah, where by the examples of birds God charges the Jews with stupidity and dullness, saying: The stork in the air knows its appointed times; the turtle-dove, the crane and the swallow observe the time of their migration; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. And Christ, further on, says that Jerusalem, together with the whole nation, will be destroyed in a new and unheard-of manner, because it did not recognise the time of his visitation.

units.la: Porro vt hæc paternam Dei bonitatem nobis commendant, qui omnibus seculis gratiæ suæ certa signa extare voluit, vt hanc omnes amplecti & salutem consequi possent: ita simul humani inge-nij peruersitatem atque improbitatem arguunt. In iis enim quæ corpori & carnis cupiditatibus ser viunt nihil negligimus, & mira est hominum iudustria in excogitandis rationibus, quibus aut sua commoda promoueant, aut carnis libidini atq; voluptatibus satisfaciant. Tempora sementis, messis & vindemiæ diligenter agricolæ obseruant. Nautæ ventorum & tempestatum signa norunt, & ijdem per immensum Oceanum syderum ductu naues ad littora certa dirigunt. Piscatores ex imis lacuum & fluuiorum vadis atque maris abysso pisces extrahunt. Venatores ferarum lustra inquirunt, & ex his illas eijcere solent, vt præda petita potiantur. Quid verò non faciunt & ferunt auari aut voluptatibus dediti, quibus neque tellus vniuersa sufficit, quò minus per maria quoque lucrum aut voluptatum materiam quærant? Taceo amatores, quos libido & ingeniosos & ad quæ-us indignissima ferenda paratos reddit. At in iis, quæ ad regnum Dei & salutem æternam spe-ctant, ferè cæci, ignaui & omnis laboris impatientissimi sumus. Nam, etsi omnem illius rationem nobis Deus per verbum suum in Scripturis reueler, & ea nullis argutijs inuoluta, sed facilis atque perspicua sit: plerique tamen de eius obscuritate conquerun-tur, & quasi nihil certum de hominis sa-lute vnquam traditum sit, hinc inde dubij respiciunt & nouas definitiones expectant. Quod si verò aliquid pro religione audendum est, ibi timedissimos & ignauissimos esse videbis, qui si de priuato ipsorum honore aut lucro agatur, cœlum terra potius miscere vellent, quam de suo iure vel latum vnguem cedere. Neque hic solum tam stupidos & ignauos se plerique præbent, sed in obseruandis etiam iræ Dei & iudiciorum eius inditis hæc ipsa socordia regnat. Quis enim non videat & sentit bodie horribiles tempestates imminere, quibus totum orbem terrarum concuti oporteat? Quis ignorat turbas & motus omnium populorum, quibus inter se commiscuntur, qui vnanimi studio suæ gentis incolumitati prospicere debebant? Quis non audit Dei vocem, qua ad pænitentiam omnes inuitat, & in hac sola effugium & salutem nos inuenturos esse docet? At quotus quisque est, qui ista diligentius obseruet, aut isdem moueatur, vt de pænitentia serio cogitet? Idem de fine seculorum & nouissimo Christi ad iudicium aduentu dicere possumus. Nam quocunq; oculos vertas, signa occurrent, quæ illum non procul abesse docent, nosq; excitant, vt fidelium seruorum instar succinctí & ad illum excipiendum parati simus. In religione dissensiones & scismata sunt. Cum Pseudoprophe-tæ pseudochristi etiam audiuntur, qui Iesu Christi honorem & gloriam in se transserunt. Sed & ipse Christus monstratur in certis locis, in deserto, in cellulis aut ædiculis penarijs, quæ vulgo Cibo-ria vocant. Sedet in templo, Dei Filius ille perditionis, qui se supra omne nomen extollit. Audiun-tur falsi doctores, qui dæmoniorum dogmata prædicant, dum cibos à Deo nobis datos prohibent, & connubium damnant, in quo sanctissimi quiq; vixerunt. In Ecclesiam quoque iam pridem Chana-næi mercatores irrepserunt, qui non sacra modo omnia venalia habent, verumetiam fidei sermonibus populi simplicis animas negotiantur, & Christum redemptorem suum aperte negant, dum nomina alia sibi ipsis accersunt. Et hæc quidem circa religionem euentura esse nouissimis tempo-ribus, Christus & Apostoli prædixerunt. Quod si reliquam mundi faciem inspicias, hanc quoque cum illorum vaticiniis conuenire videbis. Sunt enim omnia turbarum plena, bellicis rumoribus orbis totus strepit, insurgit gens alia aduersus aliam, fides nusquam tuta est, extincta friget cha-ritas, fames & rerum omnium caritas infelix vulgus misere affligit, neque vnquam minuitur semel auctum rei cuiuscunque pretium: græssatur pestis continua, & noui atque prius inauditi morbi indies exoriuntur. Accedunt hus signa in cœlo, prodigia in terris & omnis generis ostenta, quibus iram suam Deus denunciat. At inter hæc omnia plus quam supina securitas & admonitionum omnium contemptus mentes hominum occupat, nec quisquam ferè est, qui vel à verbi ministris argui, vel ab amicissimis admoneri, vel publica magistratus authoritate coerceri velit: denique ij plane nostro seculo omnium hominum mores sunt, quos Noæ & Lothi tempo-ribus fuisse Christus ait. Spes autem reformationis aut emendationis nulla esse potest, quando in pueris quoque huius corruptionis & contumaciæ exempla passim cernere licet. Itaque increpatio ista non minus hodie nobis seruit, quam olim Iudaeorum genti, cuius duritiam & stupiditatem pleriq; superant, dum ea quoq; officiunt er nimis negligunt, quae vitae praesentis exitium & fortunarum omnium iacturam possunt afferre.
units.tr: Moreover, just as these things commend to us the fatherly goodness of God, who in every age wished to have sure signs of his grace, so that all might embrace it and obtain salvation, so at the same time they expose the perversity and wickedness of the human mind. For in those matters which serve the body and the lusts of the flesh we neglect nothing, and there is a remarkable diligence of men in devising means by which they may either advance their own advantages or satisfy the lust and pleasures of the flesh. Farmers carefully observe the seasons of sowing, harvest and vintage. Sailors know the signs of the winds and storms, and by guiding their ships by the stars they steer them across the vast ocean to certain shores. Fishermen draw fish from the depths of lakes and rivers and from the abyss of the sea. Hunters search out the lairs of wild beasts, and commonly drive them out from these so that they may gain the prey they seek. And what do greedy men or men given over to pleasures not do and endure, for whom the whole earth is not enough, so that they seek gain and the matter of their pleasures even across the seas? I say nothing of lovers, whom lust makes ingenious and ready to bear the most unworthy things in pursuit of their desire. But in those things which pertain to the kingdom of God and eternal salvation, we are almost blind, idle, and most impatient of all labour. For although God reveals to us through his Word in the Scriptures the whole method of it, and it is not wrapped up in any subtleties, but is easy and plain, yet many complain of its obscurity, and as if nothing certain had ever been handed down about the salvation of man, they look hither and thither in doubt and wait for new definitions. But if anything must be ventured for religion, you will see them most timid and most idle; whereas if their own private honour or gain is at stake, they would rather turn heaven and earth upside down than yield a hair's breadth of their right. Nor do most people show themselves so dull and idle only here, but in observing the wrath of God and the judgments he has appointed, this very same sluggishness reigns. For who does not see and feel that horrible storms now hang over us, by which the whole world must be shaken? Who is ignorant of the disturbances and movements of all peoples, by which they are thrown into confusion among themselves, when they ought with united zeal to look after the safety of their own nation? Who does not hear the voice of God, by which he invites all to repentance, and teaches that in this alone will we find refuge and salvation? Yet how few there are who observe these things more carefully, or are moved by them to think seriously about repentance! The same we may say about the end of the ages and Christ's final coming to judgment. For wherever you turn your eyes, signs present themselves which teach that he is not far off, and rouse us to be like faithful servants, girded and ready to receive him. There are dissensions and schisms in religion. False prophets and false christs are also heard, who transfer to themselves the honour and glory of Jesus Christ. And Christ himself is pointed to in certain places: in the desert, in little cells or small chapels for storing food, which are commonly called ciboria. That son of perdition sits in the temple, who exalts himself above every name. False teachers are heard, who preach the doctrines of demons, while they forbid the foods given us by God and condemn marriage, in which the holiest men have lived. Into the Church too there have long since crept Canaanite merchants, who not only have all sacred things for sale, but also barter the souls of the simple people with their words of faith, and openly deny Christ their Redeemer while they take other names to themselves. These things indeed, that they would come to pass in religion in the last times, Christ and the Apostles foretold. But if you look at the rest of the world's face, you will see that this too agrees with their predictions. For everything is full of tumults; the whole world rings with rumours of war; one nation rises against another; faith is nowhere safe; charity is extinguished and grows cold; famine and the unhappy dearness of all things miserably afflict the common people, and the price of any commodity, once raised, never falls again; a continual pestilence rages, and new and previously unheard-of diseases arise daily. To these are added signs in heaven, portents on earth, and omens of every kind, by which God announces his wrath. Yet amid all these things a more than sluggish security and contempt of all warnings seize men's minds, and there is scarcely anyone who wishes to be rebuked by the ministers of the Word, or admonished by his closest friends, or restrained by the public authority of the magistrate. Finally, these are plainly the manners of all men in our age, which Christ says existed in the times of Noah and Lot. Moreover, no hope of reformation or amendment can exist, since examples of this corruption and obstinacy can be seen everywhere even among children.
