Therefore this rebuke serves us today no less than it did the Jewish nation of old, whose hardness and stupidity many surpass, since they neglect even those things which can bring destruction to the present life and the loss of all their fortunes.

units.la: Caeterum pergit Dominus, & fontem quoque omnis mali ostendit, simulque tacita obiectioni re spondet. Nam diceret aliquis: Quomodo ego de temporis statu & conditione iudicarem, qui rerum omnino rudis atque imperitus sum? Et solent fere ad ignorantiae excusationem confugere, qui doctrinam atque admonitiones omnes suis cupiditatibus postponunt. Dicit ergo Christus. Cur autem & per vos ipsos non iudicatis quod iustum est, id est, quid vos facere deceat? Quasi diceret: Age concedo hoc, vos tam rudes esse, ut Messiae vobis exhibiti indicia agnoscere & de huius temporis statu iudicare non possitis. Sed cur quaeso non animum attenditis, ut ex ijs, quae homines frugi & cordati faciunt documentum sumatis, quid nunc vobis facto fit opus. Et mox exemplum subiicit e foro petitum, quod ut vulgare sic omnibus notum est. Eo autem docet nocentissimae huius socordiae causam esse, quod homines non inspiciunt seipsos, nec quae ipsis in vsu quotidiano sunt considerant, quae sola quoq; eos admonere poterant, ut de diuinis & ijs quae ad aeternam salutem faciunt, recte iudicarent. Est hoc vitium fere innatum omnibus, ut quamvis ad Dei gloriam & futurorum caelestium bonorum possessionem destinati sint, tamen perinde ut bruta animalia praesentibus modo ducantur & in terrenis quoq; non magnam eorum, quae futura sunt, rationem habeant. Fieri ergo nequit, ut qui tales sunt, de diuinis recte iudicent.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord goes on to show the fountain of all evil, and at the same time answers an objection that has not been spoken. Someone might say: "How can I judge the state and condition of the times, when I am altogether untrained and inexperienced in these matters?" People who put their desires ahead of all teaching and admonition usually take refuge in this excuse of ignorance. So Christ says: "Why do you not also judge for yourselves what is right, that is, what it is fitting for you to do?" As if he were saying: "Grant that you are so unskilled that you cannot recognise the signs of the Messiah shown to you, or judge the state of this time. But why, I ask, do you not pay attention, so that you may learn from what sensible and prudent people do what you now need to do?" Right after this he adds an example taken from the forum, one as common as it is familiar to everyone. By it he teaches that the most harmful cause of this folly is that people do not look into themselves, nor consider what lies before them in daily life. These things alone could have taught them to judge rightly about divine matters and those that pertain to eternal salvation. This fault is almost innate in all people: although they are destined for the glory of God and the possession of heavenly goods, they are nonetheless led by present things alone, like brute animals, and even in earthly affairs they take little account of what is to come. It is therefore impossible that those who are such should judge rightly about divine things.

units.la: Admonet autem nos in genere hoc Christi dictum, immerito aliquos de salutis aeterna negotio conqueri, quasi hoc intricatum & obscurum sit, quod non nisi ab acutissimis ingenijs intelligi queat. Nam ut fateamur, nonnulla in scripturis contineri, quorum sensus non omnibus patet, ea tamen eiusmodi sunt, ut sine salutis iactura ignorari possint. Quae vero ad illam consequendam cognitu & creditu necessaria sunt, ea perspicuitate & methodo proponuntur, ut pueris quoque & agricolis tradi queant. Adhaec in semetipsis & quotidiano vsu multa habent homines, quae totum illud Regni Dei mysterium illustrant, & huius amplexandi rationem tradunt. Dum enim sementem aut messem faciunt agricolae, de verbi Dei natura & effectis admonentur, & simul discunt, quae praemia pios & ex verbi semine renatos (qui instar boni frumenti sunt) quae item poena impios manent, qui paleis inanibus conferuntur. Sic pastores propria persona, quam sustinent, & oues in Christi veri animarum pastoris consideratione adducere, simulque admonere possunt, ut hunc sequm audiant ac sequantur. In oeconomia patribus familias occurrunt, quae docent quid eos facere oporteat, qui in Dei domo locum habere cupiunt. Quoties item nuptiae celebrantur, toties nobis aptissima, quae nobis cum Christo intercedit coniunctio, & quod illi debemus officium in mentem venire potest. Sic panis, fontes, lucerna, petra, ostium, vites, & innumera alia Christum nobis adumbrant, & nos ad illum digne excipiendum hortantur. Quis ergo iustus querelis locus est reliquus? Aut quam praeterea definitionem expectamus, quae omnes de religione controversias componat aut e medio tollat? Sunt haec autem contra eos quoq; observanda, qui imaginibus patrocinantur hoc argumento, quod libri sint hominum illiteratorum, quos illarum contemplatione excitari deque Dei beneficijs in Christo exhibitis admoneri oporteat. Atqui imaginum, quas Deus ipse suo verbo consecrauit, plena sunt omnia, ut hominum manibus novas fingere nequaquam opus sit. Illarum ergo mysteria atque typos Ecclesiarum ministri diligenter populo exponant, & se plus proficere sentiet, quam si in omnibus locis, cum publicis tum prophanis statuae erigantur, aut imagines Christi sive seruorum suorum depingantur. Nam ut illae contra Dei praeceptum fiunt, & forma mendaci commendantur, ita non nisi mendacia & falsos cultus ex illis homines discunt, ut alibi ex Propheta docuimus. Vide Habak. 2.
units.tr: Moreover, this saying of Christ warns us in general that some people complain without cause about the business of eternal salvation, as if it were so entangled and obscure that it could be understood only by the sharpest minds. For, granting that some things in the Scriptures contain meanings that are not open to everyone, these are nonetheless of such a kind that they can be unknown without loss of salvation. But those things that are necessary to know and to believe in order to attain it are set forth with such clarity and order that they can be taught even to children and farmers. Besides, people have in themselves and in daily life many things that illustrate the whole mystery of the Kingdom of God and teach the way of embracing it. For while farmers sow or reap, they are reminded of the nature and effects of the word of God, and at the same time learn what rewards await the pious and those reborn by the seed of the word (who are like good grain), and likewise what punishment remains for the impious, who are compared to empty chaff. So ministers, by the very office they hold, can lead their sheep to consider Christ, the true shepherd of souls, and at the same time urge them to hear and follow him. In household management, the fathers of families meet with things that teach what those must do who wish to have a place in the house of God. Whenever weddings are celebrated, the most fitting union that exists between us and Christ, and the duty we owe him, can come to mind. So bread, springs, a lamp, a rock, a door, vines, and countless other things set forth Christ to us and urge us to receive him worthily. What room, then, is left for complaint? Or what other definition do we expect that would settle all the controversies about religion, or remove them from the midst? These things must also be kept in mind against those who defend images on this argument: that images are books for the unlettered, by whose contemplation people ought to be stirred up and reminded of the benefits of God exhibited in Christ. Yet the images that God himself has consecrated in his word are everywhere, so there is by no means any need to fashion new ones with human hands. Let the ministers of the Churches therefore diligently expound to the people the mysteries and types of those images, and they will feel that they profit far more than if statues were erected in all places, both public and profane, or pictures of Christ or of his servants were painted. For just as images are made against the command of God and recommended by a lying form, so people learn from them nothing but lies and false worship, as we have shown elsewhere from the Prophet. See Habakkuk 2.

units.la: Nunc exemplum videamus, quo Dominus doctrinam & admonitionem suam confirmat, sic dicens: Quando enim abis cum aduersario tuo ad magistratum, da operam in via ut liberetur ab eo: ne pertrahat te ad iudicem, & iudex te tradat exactori, & exactor coniiciat te in carcerem. Dico tibi non exibis illinc, vsquequo vltimum etiam minutum reddideris. Est exemplum hoc ab ijs desumptum, qui ob rem pecuniariam aut aes alienum a creditoribus suis in ius vocantur. Et quam vis docere velit, in salutis negotio eam rationem obseruari debere, quam in casu eiusmodi homines frugi & cordati sequuntur, tamen sub praeceptionis formula parabolam totam proponit, vt partim ijs simul occurrat, qui libertatis Christianae praetextu ad captandam immunitatem abutuntur, & neminem quicquam debere contendunt, partim vt de charitatis officio omnes admoneat, ne temera rijs litibus seipsos & fortunas suas omnes in discrimen adducant. Et in hunc fine eadem apud Matthaeum quinto capite dicuntur. Quoad vero huius loci statum, ita mihi dicere videtur: Si quis te propter debitam sibi pecuniam in ius vocet, tunc homo frugi & prudens fueris, procul dubio in ipsa etiam via, dum ad forum itur, operam dabis, vt cum illo aliqua ratione transigas. Nam qui id negligunt ijudicum sententijs damnati exactoribus aut publicis ministris traduntur, qui eos in neruum aut carcerem trahunt, vnde euadere non possunt, nisi totum debitum ad extremum vsque quadrantem dissoluerint. Atqui hoc ipsum in re maioris momenti, aeternae nimirum salutis negotio, cuius ego Mediator & author sum, observari debebat. Adumbratur autem hoc exemplo vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio, cuius singulas partes inspexisse proderit.
units.tr: Now let us look at the example by which the Lord confirms his teaching and admonition, saying: "When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be freed from him, lest he drag you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison. I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last penny." This example is drawn from those who are summoned to court by their creditors over money or debt. And although he wishes to teach that in the business of salvation the same plan must be followed that sensible and prudent people follow in a case of this kind, nonetheless, under the form of a precept, he sets forth the whole parable: partly so that it may meet at once those who abuse the pretext of Christian liberty to seek immunity, and insist that they owe nothing to anyone; partly so that he may warn all people of the duty of charity, lest they rashly bring themselves and all their fortunes into danger through quarrels and lawsuits. To this same end the same things are said in Matthew, chapter 5. As to the state of this passage, he seems to me to say: "If anyone summons you to court over money he is owed, then, if you are a sensible and prudent man, you will without doubt, even on the way as you go to the forum, make an effort to settle matters with him somehow. For those who neglect this are condemned by the judges' sentences and handed over to the officers or public servants, who drag them into fetters or prison, from which they cannot escape unless they pay the whole debt down to the last farthing." Yet this very thing ought to have been observed in a matter of greater weight, namely the business of eternal salvation, of which I am the Mediator and author. Now, in this example the whole plan of our salvation is foreshadowed, and it will be useful to examine its individual parts.

units.la: Primo igitur loco obseruemus, quod redemptionis & salutis nostrae negotium per debitoris & creditoris parabolam adumbratur. Est hoc frequens admodum in Scripturis. Et huc pertinet, quod in Oratione Dominica petimus, vt Pater caelestis nobis debita nostra remittat, sicuti nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Quod vt fiat, Christus eleganti parabola apud Matthaeum cap. 18. exponit. Ita vero nostrae conditionis admonemur, quae si per se & nuda consideretur, sane miserrima est. Nam omnes in aere Dei & huius debitores sumus, idque multis nominibus. Is enim noster creator est, qui vt olim Adamum ex vili luto formauit, & eidem inspirauit animam viuentem: ita nos quoque (vt Dauid testatur) ratione admirabili & quae omnem humani ingenij captum excedit, in matris vtero formare, & illic ceu in sepulchro delitescentibus animam inspirare, & cum tempus est illinc educere solet. Idem nos a pueris & teneris vnguiculis tuetur, custodit & seruat, ne inter pericula & casus varios, quibus aetatula illa obnoxia est, pereamus. Adhaec terram, aquam, ignem, aerem, animalia denique omnia in nobis alendis occupata esse vult. Neque his contentus, caelestes quoque spiritus, Angelos nimirum, vitae nostrae custodes dedit, qui nobis adsunt, nos ducunt, & saepe praeter animi nostri voluntatem seruant, ne pericula nobis incognita incurramus. Deo igitur debemus quod viui-mus, sumus, & inter innumera rerum humanarum discrimina incolumes manemus. Magna sunt haec & praeclara beneficia, sed maiora sequuntur. Nam ne huius vitae breui curriculo eius gratia coarctetur, nos in Filio suo vnigenito adoptauit, & hunc pro nobis tradidit, vt eius morte at sanguine a peccatorum nexibus liberati, eius filii & regni caelestis haeredes efficeremur. Quis vero hanc illius bonitatem atque beneficentiam gratuitam dignis verbis explicet? Quis item nos illius debitores esse negabit? Debemus autem ei non aurum, non argentum, non vestes, non victimas animalium (nec enim externis hisce & corporalibus subsidijs opus habet, qui Spiritus est, & in Spiritu atque veritate vult coli) sed vt ipsi vni fidamus, ipsum ex toto animo diligamus supra omnia, atque praeceptis eius animo sincero minimeque fucato obtemperemus requirit. Comprehendunt haec proximi quoque dilectionem & vitae totius innocentiam atque sanctitatem: denique huc omnis nostri debiti summa redit, vt (quod Paulus admonet) mortificemus membra nostra terrestria, & nos illi sanctissimam hostiam viuentem. Et haec quidem a nobis ille exigit in foedere cum Abrahamo facto, in Lege & Prophetis, neque aliud vnquam Christus & Apostoli eius nomine postulauerunt. At si in nosipsos descendamus, & qui simus propius consideremus, iam nos in his exoluendis cunctatores & mala nomina esse patebit, ideoque dignos, qui Legis sententiam subeant, quae maledictionem & mortem aeternam omnibus minatur, qui officium suum Deo non praestant. Et haec quidem nostrum omnium est conditio.
units.tr: First, then, let us observe that the business of our redemption and salvation is shadowed forth by the parable of the debtor and the creditor. This is very frequent in the Scriptures. To this belongs what we ask in the Lord's Prayer: that our heavenly Father forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. That this may happen, Christ explains in an elegant parable in Matthew, chapter 18. In this way we are reminded of our condition, which, if considered in itself and naked, is certainly most wretched. For we are all debtors in the sight of God and to him, and that on many counts. He is our creator, who, just as he once formed Adam from base clay and breathed into him a living soul, so also (as David testifies) forms us in our mother's womb by a wonderful method that surpasses all human understanding, and breathes a soul into us while we lie hidden there as if in a grave, and brings us out from there when the time comes. The same God protects, guards and preserves us from our earliest years and tender nails, so that among the dangers and various accidents to which that tender age is exposed, we do not perish. Besides this, he has ordained that earth, water, fire, air, and indeed all animals, be busy in nourishing us. And not content with these, he has also given us heavenly spirits, namely angels, as guardians of our life, who are present with us, lead us, and often keep us, even against our will, from falling into dangers unknown to us. We owe to God, then, that we live, that we exist, and that among the countless hazards of human affairs we remain unharmed. These are great and remarkable benefits, but greater ones follow. For lest his grace be confined within the brief course of this life, he has adopted us in his only Son and delivered him up for us, so that, freed from the bonds of sins by his death and blood, we might become heirs of his Son and of the heavenly kingdom. But who can explain worthily this goodness and gratuitous beneficence of his? Who, again, will deny that we are his debtors? Yet we owe him not gold, not silver, not garments, not sacrificial animals (for he who is Spirit has no need of these external and bodily supports, and wishes to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth), but he requires that we trust in him alone, love him above all with our whole heart, and obey his precepts with a sincere and unfeigned mind. These include love of neighbour and the innocence and holiness of the whole of life. In short, the sum of all our debt comes to this: that (as Paul admonishes) we mortify our earthly members and offer ourselves to him as a holy and living sacrifice. And indeed he demands these things of us in the covenant made with Abraham, in the Law and the Prophets, and Christ and his Apostles have never asked anything else in his name. But if we descend into ourselves and consider more closely what we are, it will become plain that we are slow and bad payers in discharging these things, and therefore worthy to undergo the sentence of the Law, which threatens curse and eternal death to all who do not render their duty to God. And this, indeed, is the condition of us all.

units.la: Quid ergo hic nobis agendum fuerit, vt sententiam hanc duram effugiamus? Docet id paucis verbis Dominus. Da (inquit) operam in via, vt liberetis ab eo. Primum vt negotium hoc curemus admonet, dum in via sumus, id est, dum haec vita durat, & priusquam nobis mors obrepit, quae omnem bene agendi occasionem abrumpere & auferre solet. Et recte vitae nostrae curriculum viae confert, quando illam peregrinationis instar esse omnis Scriptura docet, & res ipsa abunde testatur. At sic loquendo procrastinatores esse vetat, quales multi sunt, qui salutis aeternae curam magno suo malo de die in diem reijciunt atque suspendunt, dum sibi ipsis adhuc multos vitæ annos pollicentur, intra quos pœnitentiam agere & cum Deo reconciliari possint. Atqui vanissimæ sunt eiusmodi persuasiones, quando quotidianis exemplis docemur, vitæ huius finem incertissimum esse, & nos plerunque ad metam propius venisse quam putemus. Quam multi enim dum & opibus florent, & honoribus superbiunt, & valetudine prosperrima fruuntur, subito & improvviso aliquo casu pereunt? Omnis ergo procrastinatio in hac causa periculi plena & noxia est, & ideo alibi etiam Christus nos perpetuo vigilare iubet, eò quod nesciamus, quando nobis hora illa fatalis instet, quæ vitæ nostræ finem imponat. Deinde docet etiam Dominus, quid fieri debeat, dum adhuc in via sumus. Da operam (inquit) ut libereris ab eo. Id apud Matthæum clarius exponit, dicens: Benevolus esto, id est, amice cum illo transfige, ut cum eo reconcilieris & in gratiam redeas. At quomodo cum Deo transfigere & ei reconciliari poterimus, qui & filii iræ sumus, & nihil ex nobis ipsis habemus, quod ei satisfaciat? Nam ut David ait, superat nos ratio iniquitatum nostrarum, & si nobiscum Deus iure agat, toti perijmus. Hic ergo Mediatore opus erit, cuius reflectu illæ iram suam remittat, & nos debito illo liberet, quod ipsi dissoluere non possumus. Quis vero ille? Unus Iesus Christus, æternus Dei Filius, qui ex Patris decreto homo factus, nostras iniquitates in se transtulit, & eàdem morte suâ merito in ara crucis expiavit. Hic nobis (ut in Actis Apostoli dicunt) & pœnitentiam & peccatorum remissionem largitur: hic nos ex verbo sui semine per Spiritum sanctum regenerat in filios Dei, & qui illum fide vera apprehendunt, ij & Deo placent & Filij eius cohæredes fiunt. Docet hoc Pater cœlestis, quando de illo de cœlis testatur, hunc esse Filium suum dilectum, in quo nobis placatus atque reconciliatus sit. Vult ergo in præsenti Dominus, ut cum Dei iudicium nobis semper instet, omni mora abrupta de illo nobis reconciliando cogitemus, & ut ipsum vera fide amplexi in eo vitam viviamus novam, & carnis membra mortificemus. Et hæc unica illa ratio est, qua à peccatorum debitis liberari & æterna damnationis sententiam subterfugere possumus: quam cum passim sacræ litteræ tradant, nolumus nunc prolixius agere.
units.tr: What, then, must we do here to escape this harsh sentence? The Lord teaches this in a few words: "Make an effort on the way, that you may be freed from him." First, he urges us to take this matter in hand while we are on the way, that is, while this life lasts and before death steals up on us, since death usually cuts off and takes away every opportunity to act well. Rightly does he compare the course of our life to a road, since all Scripture teaches that it is a pilgrimage, and experience itself bears ample witness to it. But by speaking thus he forbids us to be procrastinators, of whom there are many who, to their great harm, put off and defer from day to day the care of eternal salvation, promising themselves many more years of life within which they may repent and be reconciled to God. Yet such assurances are most empty, since daily examples teach us that the end of this life is most uncertain, and that we have often come nearer the goal than we think. How many, while they flourish in wealth, take pride in their honours, and enjoy the most robust health, suddenly perish by some unforeseen accident? Every delay in this matter is therefore full of danger and harmful, and for this reason Christ elsewhere bids us watch constantly, because we do not know when that fatal hour is at hand which will set an end to our life. Next, the Lord also teaches what ought to be done while we are still on the way. "Make an effort," he says, "that you may be freed from him." Matthew expounds this more clearly, saying: "Be well disposed," that is, come to terms with him as a friend, so that you may be reconciled to him and return into favour. But how can we come to terms with God and be reconciled to him, we who are children of wrath and have nothing of our own that could satisfy him? For, as David says, the reckoning of our iniquities overwhelms us, and if God should deal with us by strict right, we are all lost. Here, then, we need a Mediator, by whose intercession he may lay aside his wrath and free us from that debt which we ourselves cannot pay. Who is this? The one Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, who, by the Father's decree, was made man, took our iniquities upon himself, and by that same death of his expiated them, deservedly, on the altar of the cross. From him, as the Acts of the Apostles say, come both repentance and the forgiveness of sins; by the word of his seed, through the Holy Spirit, he regenerates us as sons of God, and those who lay hold of him by true faith both please God and become fellow heirs of his Son. The heavenly Father teaches this when he bears witness from heaven that this one is his beloved Son, in whom he is appeased and reconciled to us. The Lord therefore wills, in the present time, that since the judgment of God is always impending over us, we should, with every delay cast aside, think about being reconciled to him, and that, embracing him with true faith, we should live a new life in him and mortify the members of the flesh. This is the one reason by which we can be freed from the debts of sin and escape the sentence of eternal damnation; since the sacred letters teach this everywhere, we do not wish to treat it at greater length here.

units.la: Ut vero carnem nostram cunctatricem magis excitet Christus, pœnam minatur ijs, qui hic negligentiores fuerint: & idem eis euenire docet, quod illis, qui contemptis admonitionibus & postulationibus legitimis creditores suos eludere & debiti dissolutionem contemptim, vel etiam scurriliter extrahere audent. Nam ut hi illos ad iustam iram provocant, & interdum vel invitos cogunt ius suum persequi: quod est, ut exactoribus publicis rem omnem committant, qui si illi negligentes & cunctatores esse pergant, eos in carceres abducunt, unde non nisi omni debito plenè dissoluto exire possunt: Ita Deus improbos illos sua gratiæ contemptores, qui eius longanimitate ad peccandi licentiam abuntur, iusta sua ira vlcisci solet, & si in peccatis suis moriantur, eos suo exactori, diabolo tradit, qui eos ad tartara abreptos vinculis seu catenis tenebrarum constringit, ut illic iustitiæ Dei satisfaciant, quam dum in huius vitæ itinere sùæ curriculo essent, contemptui habuerunt. Est autem hæc Christi admonitio diligenti & assidua consideratione dignissima. Etenim si unum hoc sæpiùs expenderent homines, pœnitentia & gratia tempus post hanc vitam nullum reliquum esse, sed æternos inferorum cruciatus ijs destinatos esse, qui in sceleribus pergunt, & gratiæ Dei Mediatorem, Iesum Christum aspernantur: sentirent profectò non tanti faciendas esse huius sæculi voluptates & carnis cæcæ studia, ut quisquam propter illa Dei iram contra se provocare debeat.
units.tr: But so that Christ may stir our sluggish flesh more strongly, he threatens punishment to those who prove more careless in this life, and he teaches that what happens to them is what happens to those who, scorning warnings and lawful demands, dare to mock their creditors and to drag out the payment of their debt with contempt, or even with buffoonery. For these men provoke the creditors to just anger, and sometimes compel them, even against their will, to pursue their right; that is, they hand the whole matter over to the public officers of debt, who, if the debtors persist in negligence and delay, lead them off to prison, from which they cannot leave until the whole debt has been paid in full. So God is wont to avenge with his just wrath those wicked contemners of his grace who abuse his long-suffering as a licence to sin; and if they die in their sins, he hands them over to their exactor, the devil, who, having dragged them down to hell, binds them with the chains and fetters of darkness, so that there they may satisfy the justice of God, which they held in contempt while they were on the course of this life's journey. Now this admonition of Christ is most worthy of diligent and constant consideration. For if men would more often weigh this one thing, that there is no time left after this life for repentance and grace, but that eternal torments of hell are appointed for those who persist in wickedness and despise Jesus Christ, the Mediator of God's grace, they would surely feel that the pleasures of this age and the pursuits of the blind flesh are not to be valued so highly that anyone should provoke the wrath of God against himself for their sake.

units.la: Porro ut reliquam doctrinam Christi omnem Antichristiani doctores vel obscurarunt vel corruperunt: ita hanc quoque tantumnon aboleuerunt, ut pauci de illa cogitarint. Finxerunt enim Purgatorium ignem, in quo animæ corporis vinculo solutæ omnis generis cruciatus patiantur, & ubi iustitiæ Dei satisfecerint, inde liberatæ ad beatorum sedes transferantur. Inter alia autem, quibus suum commentum confirmant, hunc quoque locum adducunt, & argumentum eiusmodi colligunt: Ex inferis nulla est redemptio: At Christus de carcere loquitur, unde aliquando egressuri sint peccatores: quando nimirum ultimum quadrantem sive minutum reddiderint: Ergo locus est inter cœlos & inferos medius, ubi animæ à peccatis expiantur, quorum pœnitentiam homines, dum in vitæ essent, neglexerunt. Habet hoc apud simplices & imperitos aliquam veri speciem, & erroris in
units.tr: Furthermore, although the Antichristian teachers have either obscured or corrupted all the rest of Christ's doctrine, they have so nearly abolished this too that few think about it. For they invented a purgatorial fire, in which souls, released from the bond of the body, suffer every kind of torment and, once they have satisfied the justice of God, are thence freed and transferred to the seats of the blessed. Among other arguments by which they confirm their invention, they also cite this passage and draw an argument of this kind: "There is no redemption from hell; but Christ speaks of a prison from which sinners will at some time come out, namely when they have paid the last farthing or mite; therefore there is a middle place between heaven and hell, where souls are cleansed from sins, for which men, while they were in life, neglected to make repentance." This has, for simple and inexperienced people, a certain air of truth, and of error

units.la: Pfalm.65. res in Ecclesiam plurimos nocentissimosque inuexit. Nam simul sacra excogitarunt, quibus anima in igne illo laborantes liberari possint. Sacris hisce coniunxerunt Indulgentias Romanas, peregrinationes ad Diuorum simulachra, operum item nostrorum merita. Quo factum est, ut quae uni Christo debetur gloria, partim in Purgatorium ignem, partim in superstitiosa sacra & hominum opera transferetur. Accessit aliud malum, quod plerique huius tam necessariae admonitionis obliti licentius peccarunt, eo quod suam ex Purgatorio redemptionem Missarum multiplici repetitione, sacrificulorum conductitijs preculis, aqua lustrali, cereorum fulgore, donationibus & anathematis in templo suspensis, aliisque eiusmodi rebus accelerari posse crederent. Fuit hoc Monachis & sacrificulis quaestuosissimum aucupium, & hic lapis ille philosophicus aut quinta essentia dici potest, in qua inuenienda Alchymistarum ingenia tot iam saeculis frustra laborauerunt. Sed si Christi verba propius considerentur, fallacia facile patebit, qua illi ea in alium sensum detorserunt. Primo enim iubet nos salutis aeternae causam agere, & cum Deo in gratiam redire, dum in huius vitae via sumus. Ergo nullum salutis curandae locum nobis relinquit, vbi e vitae exceßerimus. Deinde non exituros dicit ex illo carcere, qui simul eo detrusi fuerint, donec pro omnibus suis debitis satisfecerint. At vt hoc fiat impossibile est, eo quod peccata non temporarias poenas, sed aeternam mortem merentur. Quare sequitur Christum haec non alio sensu dicere, quam quo creditor, quem debitoris scurrilitas iusta ira accendit, ei iam in vincula abducendo ait: Non exibis inde donec obulum quoque vltimum dissoluerris: cum non ignoret, illum nec habere vnde ipsi satisfaciat, neque etiam a quoquam aliud accipere posse. Est ergo istorum hominum commentum vanissimum. Nos potius in huius loci statum respiciamus, neque extrahamus admissorum peccatorum poenitentiam, sed de Deo nobis placando in tempore cogitemus: quoad vero aeternae salutis spem, redemptoris nostri Iesu Christi verbis credamus, qui vt latroni in mortis articulo ipsum invocanti dixit, Hodie mecum eris in paradiso: ita omnibus qui in ipsum credunt, pollicetur, quod non in iudicium aliquod, sed a morte transituri sint in vitam aeternam. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Psalm 65. and it has introduced into the Church very many and most harmful errors. For at the same time they devised sacred rites by which souls labouring in that fire might be freed. To these rites they joined Roman indulgences, pilgrimages to the images of the saints, and also the merits of our works. As a result, the glory that is owed to Christ alone has been transferred partly to purgatorial fire, partly to superstitious rites and to the works of men. Another evil arose: many, forgetting this so necessary admonition, sinned more freely, because they believed that their redemption from purgatory could be hastened by the multiplied repetition of Masses, by the paid prayers of hired priests, by holy water, by the glow of candles, by gifts, by votive offerings hung in the temple, and by other things of this kind. This was a most profitable fishing ground for monks and priests, and this may be called their philosopher's stone or quintessence, in finding which the wits of the alchemists have laboured in vain for so many ages. But if the words of Christ are considered more closely, the deceit by which they twisted them into another sense will easily be seen. For, first, he bids us attend to the cause of eternal salvation and to return into favour with God while we are on the way of this life. Therefore he leaves no place for securing salvation once we have departed from life. Next, he says that those who have been thrust into that prison will not come out of it until they have satisfied for all their debts. But this is impossible, since sins deserve not temporary punishments but eternal death. Hence it follows that Christ does not speak in any other sense than that in which a creditor, whose anger has been kindled by the debtor's buffoonery, says to him as he leads him off to chains: "You shall not go out from there until you have paid even the last penny," although he knows that the debtor has nothing from which to satisfy him and cannot receive anything from anyone else. Therefore the invention of these men is most empty. Rather, let us look to the state of this passage: let us not prolong repentance for the sins we have committed, but think in due time about appeasing God; and as for the hope of eternal salvation, let us believe the words of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, who said to the thief invoking him at the point of death, "Today you will be with me in paradise." So he promises to all who believe in him that they will pass not into any judgment, but from death into eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXVI.

units.la: ADfuerunt autem eo ipso tempore quidam annuntiantes ei de Galilaeis, quorum sanguinem Pilatus miscuerat cum ipsorum sacrificijs. Et respondens Iesus dixit eis: Putatis hos Galilaeos prae omnibus Galilaeis peccatores fuisse, quoniam talia passi sunt? Non, dico vobis: imo nisi resipiscatis, omnes itidem peribitis. Aut illos decem & octo, super quos cecidit turris in Siloam, & trucidauit eos, putatis debitores fuisse prae omnibus hominibus qui habitant in Hierusalem? Non, dico vobis: imo nisi resipiscatis omnes itidem peribitis. Dixit autem hanc parabolam: Ficum habebat quidam plantatam in vinea sua, & venit quaerens fructum in ea, neque inuenit. Dixit autem vinitori: Ecce anni tres sunt, ex quo venio quaerens fructum in ficu ista, & non inuenio: Excinde eam: quorsum etiam terram inutilem reddit? Ille vero respondens dixit ei: Domine, dimitte eam etiam hoc anno, vsquequo fodero circa eam, & mittam stercus. Et si quidem tulerit fructum, dimittes: sin minus, in futurum excindes eam.
units.tr: At that same time there were some present who told him of the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And Jesus answered and said to them: Do you suppose that these Galileans were greater sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, no; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, do you think that they were debtors above all the men who dwell in Jerusalem? I tell you, no; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. And he spoke this parable: A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, and found none. Then he said to the vinedresser: Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none. Cut it down; why does it also use up the ground? But he answered and said to him: Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. And if it bears fruit, well; but if not, after that you shall cut it down.

units.la: DIligenter admodum & prolixè Dominus & seruator noster Iesus Christus in iis quæ præcesserunt, de Euangelij doctrina disseruit: cuius hæc summa est, ut homines à peccatis ad Deum conuersi priorís vitæ pœnitentiam agant, & ipsum constanti fide apprehendant, in quo uno nobis peccatorum remissio parta & cœlestis Pater placatus est. At quia in pœnitentiæ negotio natura segnes & cunctatores sumus, vehemens fuit in illa exigenda Dominus. Nam ad signa remisit auditores, ex quibus cognoscant imminere iam diem illum, quando omnes ad suum tribunal sisti & omnium quæ fecerunt rationem reddere oporteat. Addit hus credito rūs & debitoris parabolā, quæ docet quid contumaces & pœnitere nescios procrastinatores maneat. Caterum constat, Deum nos non solum Verbo suo, verumetiam crebris & grauibus iudiciorum suorum exemplis ad pœnitentiam excitare: quæ cum plerique aut omnino non obseruent, aut etiam pro sua libidine perperam interpretentur, commodè Christus hoc loco docet, ut de illis iudicare & ijsdem salubriter uti debeamus. Est igitur doctrina hæc nostris temporibus non minus necessaria quam vtilis, quando infinitis quidem exemplis iram suam Deus declarat, pleriq; tamen illa plus quam belluino stupore negligunt, neq; eorum considerationem ad se pertinere arbitrantur: imò ex ijs fere deteriores fiunt, dum ex eo calumniandi & miseris insultandi occasionem arripiunt ex quo vitæ rectius instituendæ documentum petere debebant. Duo autem exempla hic proponuntur, alterum publicum, alterum priuatum, quibus parabola generalem de pœnitentia doctrinam continens subijcitur.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ has discoursed very diligently and at length, in the passages that went before, on the doctrine of the gospel. Its sum is this: that men, converted from their sins to God, should repent of their former life and lay hold on him with a steadfast faith, in whom alone the remission of sins has been won for us and the heavenly Father has been appeased. But because we are by nature sluggish and dilatory in the business of repentance, the Lord was vehement in demanding it. For he sent his hearers away to signs by which they might know that the day was now at hand when all must be brought before his judgment seat and must give an account of all they have done. He adds the parable of the creditor and the debtor, which teaches what awaits the stubborn and the procrastinators who will not repent. Moreover, it is clear that God stirs us to repentance not only by his Word but also by frequent and grievous examples of his judgments. Most people either do not observe these at all, or even interpret them wrongly as they please; Christ here fittingly teaches us how we ought to judge them and use them profitably. This doctrine is therefore no less necessary and useful in our own times, when God declares his wrath by countless examples, yet most people neglect them with more than brutish stupor, and think that their consideration does not concern them. Indeed, many of them become worse for these things, while they seize upon an occasion for slandering and mocking the wretched, from which they ought rather to have taken a lesson for ordering their lives more rightly. Two examples are set before us here, one public and one private, and the parable containing the general doctrine of repentance is added to them.

units.la: Occasionem de his differendi Christo præbuerunt quidam non sine numinis ductu superuenientes, qui eo tempore factam Galilæorum stragem nuntiauerunt, quorum sanguinem Pilatus cum ipsorum sacrificijs miscuerat. Cuius facti etsi nulla, quod sciam, in historijs mentio fiat (nisi quod de Iuda Galilæo in Actis Gamaliel narrat, huc referre volumus) ex illorum tamen temporum statu & Iudæorum moribus atque consilijs quæ passim describuntur, satis apparet, Galilæos illos seditio se sub prætextu libertatis recuperandæ collectos fuisse. Cum enim hanc per intestina dissidia Iudæi amisissent, & graui Romanorum præsidum iugo premerentur, indies tumultuari & omnem vindicandæ libertatis pristinæ occasionem auidè magis quam prudenter arripere solebant. Neque deerant impostores, qui vulgi simplicitate abutebantur, & sese eiusmodi consiliorum duces præbebant. Hinc ergo seditiones quotidie nouæ exoriebantur, quas Romani præsides facile reprimere poterant, cum militum præsidia per vrbes fere singulas disposita haberent. Quod in præsenti etiam factum est. Et videntur isti, ut felicius res succederet, à re diuina & sacrificijs cœpisse, à Pilato autem cum militibus repente superueniente inter ipsa sacra trucidati fuisse cæsi, adeò ut circa aras occumbentium sanguis cum pecorum immolatorum sanguine confunderetur. Quam rem cum plerique indignissimam putarent, alijs Galilæorum seditiosam temeritatem, alijs Pilati crudelem impietatem accusantibus, nuntium hoc quidam ad Christum attulerunt, ut huius de toto hoc facto iudicium audirent.
units.tr: Certain men who came up at that time, not without a prompting from the divine will, gave Christ the occasion for discussing these things: they reported the slaughter of the Galileans that had then taken place, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. Although, so far as I know, no mention of this deed is made in the histories (except that Gamaliel, in the Acts, speaks of Judas the Galilean, and we wish to refer this to that), yet from the condition of those times, and from the customs and designs of the Jews which are described everywhere, it sufficiently appears that those Galileans had been gathered into a sedition under the pretext of recovering their liberty. For when the Jews had lost this liberty through internal dissensions, and were oppressed under the heavy yoke of the Roman governors, they were accustomed to stir up tumults daily, and to seize eagerly, rather than prudently, every opportunity of vindicating their former freedom. Nor were there lacking impostors who abused the simplicity of the common people and presented themselves as leaders of such plans. Hence new seditions arose every day, which the Roman governors could easily suppress, since they kept garrisons stationed in almost every city. This also happened on the present occasion. And it seems that these men, so that the affair might go more happily, had begun at the divine service and the sacrifices, but that Pilate, with his soldiers suddenly coming upon them, had slain them among the sacred rites, so that the blood of those falling about the altars was mixed with the blood of the victims being offered. Since many thought this a most unworthy thing, some blaming the seditious rashness of the Galileans and others the cruel impiety of Pilate, certain men brought this news to Christ, so that they might hear his judgment on the whole deed.

units.la: At priusquam longius progrediamur, non inutile fuerit in Iudæorum exemplo considerare, quis fere status & qui mores esse soleant populi, qui amissa libertate pristina alienæ aut peregrinæ tyrannidis iugo premitur. Iudæos enim in libertatem non semel asseruerat Deus, ut suum peculium essent, & miraculum conseri poterat, gentem illam inter grauissimos totius orbis motus libertatem suam cum religione & legibus diuinitus traditis retinere potuisse. Sed quæ humani ingenij est improbitas, tantum Dei beneficium vix vnquam rectè æstimauerunt. Nam vt patres illorum in deserto aduersus Mosem, primum libertatis suæ vindicem tumultuati sunt, ita deinceps suæ fortis pertæsi posteri Regem ceruicibus suis imposuerunt, & tandem quasi vnus non sufficeret ipsis deglu bendis, in duo regna scissi sunt, quæ diuisio bellorum ciuilium causa fuit, & tandem vtriq; regno exitium peperit, quando Israelitæ quidem ab Assyrijs, Iudæi vero à Babylonijs deuicti & in exilium abducti sunt. E Babylone vero hi cum alijs multis reuersi posterum urbem & rempub. instauratam mox ad ingenium redierunt, & posteà multa indigne & impiè ab ipsis facta, postremo duorum fratrum. Aristobuli & Hircani, ambitione in partes distracti, Romanus tunc contra Parthos belligerantibus Iudæam opprimendi occasionem dederunt. Ab horum autem præsidibus & hinc inde dispositis
units.tr: But before we proceed further, it will not be unprofitable to consider, in the example of the Jews, what condition and what morals are usually found in a people that, having lost its former liberty, is oppressed under the yoke of foreign or alien tyranny. For God had once and again set the Jews free, that they might be his own peculiar people, and it could be a marvel that that nation, amid the most grievous upheavals of the whole world, could have kept its liberty together with the religion and laws divinely handed down to it. But such is the wickedness of the human mind that they have scarcely ever rightly valued so great a benefit of God. For just as their fathers in the desert murmured against Moses, the first champion of their liberty, so afterwards their descendants, weary of their own strength, placed a king upon their necks; and at last, as if one were not enough to devour them, they were split into two kingdoms. This division was the cause of civil wars, and at length brought ruin to both kingdoms, when the Israelites were overcome by the Assyrians and the Jews by the Babylonians, and were led away into exile. Returning from Babylon with many others, these men soon restored their city and commonwealth, but afterwards went back to their old disposition, and many unworthy and impious things were done by them; finally, when two brothers, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, were divided into factions by ambition, they gave the Romans, who were then at war with the Parthians, an occasion to oppress Judea. But from the governors of these men, placed here and there,

units.la: Galilæi à Pilato cæsi.
units.tr: The Galileans slain by Pilate.

units.la: Conditio populi qui libertate amisit. dispositis præsidijs, cùm multa indignè & crudeliter quotidie fierent, sentire cœperunt quantum bo-num amisissent, & amissam libertatem novis subinde seditionibus recuperare conati sunt, quarum infelix semper exitus fuit, & quibus Romani tandem irritati urbem cum templo devastarunt, & infelicis populi reliquias per omnes gentes dispers- erunt. Solet hoc ipsum omnibus accidere, qui pri-vatas cupiditates libertati patriæ præferunt, & non agnoscunt Dei beneficium, qui à tyrannide li-beros atque immunes esse voluit. Exempla enim similia in Græcis, Lacedæmonijs & multis aliis gentibus historiæ proponunt. Et Romanis, cùm potentia & opibus quàm maximè florerent, pau-corum avaritia atque ambitio, quorum consilijs atque promissionibus populus sese in partes dis-trahi passus est, libertatem abstulit, & tyrannidem inuexit intolerabilem, qua oppressi Impe-ratoribus, quorum plerique propter libidinem & crudelitatem nefariam monstra naturæ dici po-terant, parere coacti sunt, qui prius bonis legibus & legitimi Senatus imperio subesse nolebant. Vtinam verò inistorum consideratione diligentius versarentur, quibus hodie etiam patriæ liber-tas sordet, & qui luxu atque peregrini fastus studio abrepti cum exteris colludunt, & vt sibijpsis priuatim consulant, publicæ libertatis oppressores in propriæ patriæ viscera adducunt. Falluntur isti omnes spe sua, neque sibijpsis consulunt, sed tandem cum alijs oppressi sese infelices & miseros esse sentiunt. Accedit huic malo, quòd dum libertatem turpiter proditam seditionibus recupera-re conantur, fere in suis illis consilijs pereunt, & iugum seruitutis indies graujus atque intolera-bilius reddunt. Nec enim seditionibus quicquam proficitur, quàmuis hæ sub plausibili religionis prætextu excitentur, quem Galilæos quoque istos captauisse apparet. Quare initijs potius tanti mali resistendum est, & hunc operas suas omnu loci & ordinis homines conferre decet. Itaque Ec-clesiarum ministri publica & priuata Dei beneficia populo diligenter commendent, & eundem assi-duis admonitionibus in officio contineant, & docent paci & concordiæ studere. Qui verò magistra-tum gerunt, doctrinam veritatis & puriorem cultum Dei sedulò tueantur, ins sancte dicant, bo-nestati studeant, disciplinam verbi Dei patienter ferant, curent denique, ne quis vel iudicio-rum iniquitate vel prauo ipsorum exemplo provocatus tumultuandi occasionem habeat. Popu-lus autem utrisque obediat, & omnem reipublicæ mutationem periculosam esse cogitet, ideoque patienter ferat quaeuis incommoda, ne dum leuiora imprudentius depellere studet, graviora sibi ac-cersat. His artibus libertas retinetur, quam tuo vitio amissam per seditiones nunquam recupe-raueris. Nam Dei iudicijs nemo resistere potest, & notum est illud Christi: Qui gladium acripit, gladio peribit.
units.tr: The condition of a people that has lost its liberty. ...with garrisons placed everywhere, while many unworthy and cruel things were being done daily, they began to feel how great a good they had lost, and they tried to recover their lost liberty by new seditions from time to time. The outcome of these was always unhappy, and at last the Romans, roused to anger by them, devastated the city together with the temple, and scattered the remnants of the unhappy people among all nations. This same thing is wont to happen to all who prefer private desires to the liberty of their country, and do not acknowledge the benefit of God, who willed that they should be free and exempt from tyranny. For histories set forth similar examples among the Greeks, the Lacedaemonians and many other nations. And among the Romans, when they flourished most greatly in power and wealth, the avarice and ambition of a few men, by whose counsels and promises the people allowed itself to be split into factions, took away their liberty and introduced an intolerable tyranny, under which they were forced to obey emperors, many of whom, on account of their lust and wicked cruelty, could be called monsters of nature; they who formerly would not submit to good laws and the authority of a lawful Senate. Would that those who today also think their country's liberty worthless, and who, carried away by luxury and the desire for foreign display, collude with outsiders, would consider these things more carefully. In order to look after themselves privately, they bring the oppressors of public liberty into the very bowels of their own homeland. All of these men are deceived in their hope, and they do not in fact look after themselves; at last, oppressed along with others, they feel that they are unhappy and wretched. To this evil is added the fact that, while they try to recover by sedition a liberty shamefully betrayed, they mostly perish in those very plans, and make the yoke of servitude heavier and more intolerable every day. For nothing is gained by seditions, however they may be stirred up under a plausible pretext of religion, which those Galileans also seem to have sought. Therefore one should rather resist such a great evil at its beginnings, and men of every place and rank ought to devote their efforts to this. Accordingly, let the ministers of the Churches diligently commend to the people the public and private benefits of God, keep the people in their duty by constant admonitions, and teach them to pursue peace and concord. Let those who bear the magistracy carefully defend the doctrine of truth and the purer worship of God, judge justly, aim at honesty, patiently bear the discipline of God's Word, and see to it, finally, that no one has an occasion for tumult, whether provoked by the iniquity of judgments or by the wicked example of the magistrates themselves. Let the people obey both, and consider that every change in the commonwealth is dangerous; therefore let them patiently bear whatever inconveniences come, lest, while they imprudently strive to drive off lesser evils, they bring greater ones upon themselves. By these arts liberty is kept; once lost through your own fault, you will never recover it by seditions. For no one can resist the judgments of God, and that saying of Christ is well known: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad huius loci historiam, & vulgi de illa iudicium audiamus. Veniunt ad Chri-stum nonnulli, & rem ei nuntiant, utq; ex eius responsione apparet, Galilæos istos præ omnibus alijs peccatores fuisse putant, qui sua temeritate & tumultuandi libidine cladem istam meruerint. Quo exemplo admonemur, ut fere vulgus de aliorum calamitatibus iudicare soleat. Est natura Lex omnium animis inscripta, qua edocti Deum iustum esse noverunt, qui hominum peccata dignis supplicijs multare soleat. At quia philautia morbo excæcati plerique sibijpsis placent, bifariam erra-tur, quoties Deus in alios iustæ seueritatis exempla edit. Primò enim pauci in semetipsos descen-dunt, ut quid ipsi mereantur cogitent. Deinde ex impunitate, qua ipsi fruuntur spem inanem con-cipiunt, quasi ipsorum moribus Deus delectetur, neque eis in mentem venit, illum exemplis eius-modi omnes homines ad pœnitentiam excitare. Hinc fit, ut in aliorum peccatis inuestigandis ocu-latissimi & acerrimi censores sint, & illis etiam scurrilius insultent, quos consolationibus pijs sub-leuare debebant. Et tanta est humani ingenij licentia, ut de illis quoque male suspicemur, imò damnemus quoque eos, in quibus nullum scelus reprehensione dignum sese profert. Exemplum hu-ius rei in Iobi amicis historia sacra proponit, qui ex calamitatibus repente immissis eum accusandi occasionem arripuerunt, cuius fides atque integritas toti Orienti nota atque perspecta erat. Et di-scipuli apud Ioannem, cùm mendicum quendam, qui ex natiuitate cæcus erat, conspicarentur, non de occulta iudiciorum diuinorum ratione cogitant, sed quasi nulla alia cæcitatis istius causa reddi posset, quærunt, num ipse aut parentes eius suis peccatis meruerint, ut talis nasceretur. Idem pleri-que faciunt, quando aut veteres historias legunt, aut sui seculi hominum calamitates atque aduer-sos casus intuentur. Ita verò in charitatis legem peccatur, & augetur afflictorum miseria, dum ipsis calamitatis esse non licet nisi insuper pro flagitiosis & sceleratis habeantur. Adhæc securitatem parit malum hoc, ut aliorum exempla nihil ad nos pertinere putemus, neque emendemus, etiamsi manifesta iræ Dei argumenta in oculos nostros incurrant, quibus ad pœnitentiam nos excitari oportebat.
units.tr: But let us return to the history of this passage and hear the crowd's judgment of it. Some people come to Christ and report the matter to him, and from his reply it is clear that they thought those Galileans were greater sinners than all the others, and that by their own recklessness and their lust for rebellion they had deserved that disaster. From this example we are reminded that the common people are generally accustomed to judge the misfortunes of others in this way. The law of nature is written on every mind, and through it people know that God is just and is wont to punish the sins of men with fitting penalties. But because most people are blinded by the disease of self-love and are pleased with themselves, men go wrong in two ways whenever God displays examples of his just severity toward others. First, few descend into themselves to consider what they themselves deserve. Second, from the impunity they enjoy they form a vain hope, as if God took pleasure in their conduct, and it never occurs to them that God, by examples of this kind, is calling all men to repentance. Hence it happens that in searching out the sins of others they are the sharpest and most keen-eyed censors, and they mock with buffoonery those whom they ought to have comforted with pious consolations. Human intellect is so presumptuous that we even form bad suspicions about people, indeed condemn even those in whom no crime worthy of reproach appears. The sacred history sets before us an example of this in the friends of Job, who, when calamities were suddenly sent upon him, seized the chance to accuse him, though his faith and integrity were known and well attested throughout the whole East. And when the disciples in John saw a beggar who had been blind from birth, they did not reflect on the hidden reasons of the divine judgments, but, as though no other cause of that blindness could be given, they asked whether he himself or his parents had sinned so that he should be born thus. Many people do the same when they read ancient histories or look at the calamities and adverse fortunes of men of their own age. In this way the law of charity is violated, and the misery of the afflicted is increased, since they are not permitted to suffer misfortune unless they are also regarded as wicked and criminal. Moreover, this evil brings security, so that we think the examples of others have nothing to do with us, and we do not amend our lives, even when the plain signs of God's wrath strike our eyes, by which we ought to have been roused to repentance.

units.la: Audiamus ergo Iesu Christi responsum, cuius partes sunt duæ. Prima corrupto & falso de aliorum calamitatibus iudicio medetur, dicens: Putatis ne hos Galilæos, præ omnibus Galilæis peccatores fuisse, quoniam talia passi sunt? Quasi diceret: Fateor quidem illos peccauisse, & hoc veletiam graviori supplicio dignos fuisse: At præ omnibus aliis hoc illos meruisse, ut qui aliis sceleratiores fuerint, id vero constanter nego. Nullam ergo illis injultandi occasionem habetis, neque opus est eorum sceleribus inuestigandus vos diutius intuere. Continet autem hæc pars generalem doctrinam, qua admonemur, omnes homines in Dei iudicio peccatores & quibusque supplicijs dignos esse, quæ de aliis ille sumit. Nec enim naturalis solum & hereditaria vitiositas nobis inhæret, verumetiam eius fructus sese in nostris cogitationibus, desideriis, dictis & factis quotidie exerunt. Et quamuis peccatum aliud alio grauius sit, minimum tamen atque leuissimum mortem æternam atque perpetuos inferorum cruciatus meretur. Quis ergo temporarijs calamitatibus aut pœnis indignos dicet eos, qui ut æternos supplicijs multentur meruerunt? Agnouerunt hoc optimi & sanctissimi quique, quorum preces in scripturis extant: Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo Domine: Si enim iniquitates obseruaueris, quis subsistet? Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c. Et prodest in communi huius miseriæ consideratione crebro & diligenter versari, ne temere de aliorum calamitatibus pronuntiemus, sed fraterna pietate ijs condoleamus, qui diuinitus puniuntur. Cur enim aliis insultent, qui se eadem meruisse, & propter communem humani generis sortem ijsdem casibus obnoxios esse meminerunt?
units.tr: Let us therefore hear the answer of Jesus Christ, which has two parts. The first corrects the corrupt and false judgment about the misfortunes of others, when he says: "Do you think that these Galileans were greater sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things?" It is as if he said: I grant that they sinned, and that they deserved even a heavier punishment; but that they deserved it above all others, so that they were more wicked than the rest, that I firmly deny. You therefore have no occasion to mock them, nor need you look so long into their crimes. This part, however, contains a general teaching, by which we are reminded that all men are sinners before the judgment of God and deserve whatever punishments he inflicts on others. For not only does natural and hereditary corruption cling to us, but its fruits also show themselves every day in our thoughts, desires, words and deeds. And although one sin is more grievous than another, the smallest and lightest sin still deserves eternal death and the everlasting torments of hell. Who, then, will say that those who deserved to be punished forever are unworthy of temporal calamities or penalties? The best and holiest men have acknowledged this, and their prayers remain in the Scriptures: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord; for if thou shouldest mark iniquities, who shall stand?" and "Forgive us our debts," and so on. It is also useful to dwell often and carefully on the common consideration of this misery, so that we do not rashly pronounce on the misfortunes of others, but feel brotherly compassion for those whom God punishes. For why should they mock others who remember that they themselves have deserved the same things and are exposed to the same chances because of the common lot of mankind?

units.la: Altera parte exempli huius & omnium similium vsum Christus tradit, dum sic infert: Nisi resipiscatis, omnes itidem peribitis. Quibus verbis testatur, Deum non tam Galilæos istos punire, quam portendere & præmonere voluisse, quid de tota Iudæorum gente futurum sit, nisi matura pœnitentia ad illum conuertantur. Est ergo hic proprius & salutaris iudiciorum Dei vsus, ut quæcunque aliis accidunt, nobis in exemplum fieri cogitemus. Nisi enim alios excitare vellet Deus, occulte peccata punire poterat, ut minime opus esset iram suam cœlitus manifestare. Quoties ergo impij homines puniuntur, quos manifestis sceleribus Dei iram prouocauisse satis constat, non tamen in illis pedem sistere, neque solum Dei iustitiam qua in illis puniendis vsus est, prædicare debemus, sed simul nostram quoque vitam atque mores excutere, vbi fortasse similia aut etiam graviora vitia deprehendemus, quæ nobis etiam pœnitentia opus esse docebunt. Quod si autem pios videamus affligi, mox succurrat quod Petrus ait, iudicium Domini à domo eius ferè incipere, & illud Christi: Si hoc fit in viridi, quid fiet in arido? Ista consideratione fiet, ut neque in charitatis legés peccemus, neque securitate oppressi exempla iudiciorum Dei negligamus, sed quæcunque aliis accidunt, nostræ institutioni seruiant. Transferamus ergo hanc doctrinam ad nostri seculi exempla, quæ plurima in vtramque partem extant. Puniuntur aperti Euangelicæ veritatis hostes seditionibus, bellis externis atque ciuilibus, direptionibus & infinitis aliis malis: adeò, ut idem illis videamus accidere, quod olim Iudæi, qui Christum regem suum agnoscere dedignati sunt. Puniuntur item qui Euangelio locum dant, & huius doctrinam profitentur, eo quod sua professioni minus respondeant, & partim superstitionum plurimarum reliquijs, partim vitæ morum, licentia fidem Christianam polluant. Possunt hic plerique causas pœnarum in aliorum moribus atque studijs deprehendere, & de illis pleno ore passim differunt: qui si in seipsos descenderent, se quoque Christi regnum subterfugere, Deo itē ingratos, superstitionū contumaces defensores, & infinitis sceleribus pollutos esse sentirent. At quia pauci manticam suam inspiciunt, sed à tergo pendentem securè neglgunt, fit ut pleriq; in peius quotidie proficiant, & iram Dei nouis subinde sceleribus prouocent. Quo ties ergo huius generis exempla cernimus, semper nobis hoc Christi dictum in mentem veniat: Nisi resipiscatis omnes itidem peribitis.
units.tr: Christ gives the other part of this example and of all similar ones, when he goes on thus: "Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish." By these words he testifies that God wished not so much to punish those Galileans as to forewarn and portend what would become of the whole nation of the Jews unless they turned to him in timely repentance. Therefore the proper and wholesome use of God's judgments is this: that whatever befalls others, we should consider it made an example for us. For if God had wished only to rouse others, he could have punished sins in secret, so that there would have been no need to make his wrath known from heaven. Whenever wicked men are punished, men who clearly provoked God's wrath by manifest crimes, we must not stop at them, nor only proclaim the justice of God that he displayed in punishing them, but at the same time also examine our own lives and conduct, where we will perhaps find similar or even graver vices, which will teach us that we too need repentance. But if we see the godly afflicted, let us immediately recall what Peter says, that the judgment of the Lord begins mostly at his own house, and Christ's saying: "If they do this in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?" By this consideration it will come about that we neither sin against the law of charity, nor, overwhelmed by security, neglect the examples of God's judgments, but whatever befalls others serves our instruction. Let us therefore apply this teaching to the examples of our own age, which are abundant on both sides. Open enemies of the truth of the Gospel are punished by seditions, by foreign and civil wars, by plundering and by countless other evils, so that we see befalling them the same thing that once befell the Jews, who disdained to acknowledge Christ as their king. Those also are punished who give room to the Gospel and profess its doctrine, because they do not live up to their profession, and partly pollute the Christian faith with remnants of many superstitions, partly with licence of life and morals. Many of them can detect the causes of punishments in the morals and pursuits of others, and talk about them freely and at length; yet if they descended into themselves, they would feel that they too flee from the kingdom of Christ, are ungrateful to God, stubborn defenders of superstitions, and polluted with countless crimes. But since few look into their own wallet, and carelessly neglect the one hanging behind their back, it happens that most people daily grow worse and provoke the wrath of God with fresh sins. Whenever, therefore, we see examples of this kind, let this saying of Christ always come to mind: "Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish."

units.la: Sequitur alterum exemplum, quod ipse Dominus allegat. Et hoc priuatum & fortuitum videri poterat. Nam turris ad Siloam (fuit is riuus qui in vrbem placido cursu defluens piscinam efficiebat aquæductui seruientem, vt ex Isaia & Ioannis nono Capite apparet) repente col lapsa viros decem & octo oppresserat, de quorum miserabili interitu diuersa hominum iudicia fuisse non esset dubium, plerisque existimantibus eos ob singularia quædam & atrocia scelera diuinitus sic punitos fuisse. Negat ergo hoc quoque Christus, & quod de Galilæis dixerat hîc repetit, dicens: Illos decem & octo, super quos cecidit turris in Siloam, & trucidauit eos, num putatis debitores fuisse præ omnibus hominibus, qui habitant in Hierusalem? Non, dico vobis: imò nisi resipiscatis, omnes itidem peribitis.
units.tr: There follows a second example, which the Lord himself cites. This too might seem a private and accidental matter. For a tower at Siloam (this was a stream which flowed gently into the city and formed a pool serving as a water-conduit, as appears from Isaiah and from chapter nine of John) suddenly collapsed and crushed eighteen men. There was no doubt that people's judgments about their miserable deaths were varied, since most thought that they had been punished by God in this way on account of some singular and atrocious crimes. Christ therefore denies this too, and repeats here what he had said about the Galileans, saying: "Those eighteen, on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, do you think they were debtors above all the men who dwell in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish."

units.la: Quo loco in primis obseruari debet, quòd in exemplum trahit Christus, quod prophanus hominibus & carnis prudentiæ fortuitum siue contingens videri solet, & eo quoque doctrinam generalem elicit, qua omnes ad maturam pœnitentiam hortatur. Constat ex hoc, nemini quicquam fortuitò & sine certo diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio accidere. Nouit enim Deus omnes homines, & (vt apud Prophetam ait) manibus suis insculptos habet, capitis item pilos numerat, & ne passerculos quidem absque suo consensu aut voluntate perire patitur. Aut quomodo illo vel inscio vel inuito aliquid fiat, qui vbique præsens adest, qui omnia videt, & cuius nutus ad quodvis opus hominum impediendum vel promouendum sufficit? Quod D. Augustinus obseruans, liberè fatetur sibi displicere, quod in nonnullis libris fortunæ & fortuiti vocabilis vsus esset, & hoc omne ad Dei prouidentiam referri debere docet. Huius nos meminisse conuenit in repentinis calamitatibus, quæ præter omnem expectationem incidunt: vt cum domus aut arboris ruina aliquem opprimit, aut cum quis ex casu aut lapsu subitò moritur, vel etiam ab alio per imprudentiam & præter animi voluntatem occiditur, dum vel ligna simul secant (quo exemplo Deus in Lege de asylis vtitur) vel quodcunque opus aliud faciunt. In eiusmodi (inquam) casibus, neque iudicium nostrum temere præcipitare, neque eos qui ita pereunt mox damnare debemus, nisi eorum impietas & incurabilis aduersus Deum contumacia certus argumentum perspecta sit, neque (quod fere moderatiores solent) talia in fortunam aut diei horam inauspicatam referre, sed potius arcanum iudicium Dei agnoscere atque exoculari; qui vel illos hac ratione ad Regni sui cœlestis possessionem transferre, vel nobis exemplum proponere voluit, in quo incertam vitæ nostræ conditionem agnoscere, nosque in singulas horas ad omnem euentum præparare discamus, ne quid simile nobis inopinantibus accidat. Nam (vt paulò ante dictum est) iumus omnes iisdem casibus obnoxii, neque vlla tam tristis & insolens calamitas incidere potest, quam non ipsi quoque meruerimus, si iuo iure in nos Deus vti velit. Quò dergo baptizenus tuti & immunes fuimus, id nos diuina bonitati debere fateamur, quæ nostræ infirmitati parcere voluerit, ne supra vires nostras tentati succumbamus: Est hæc consideratio longè vtilissima, & huius occasiones atque materiam Deus nobis subinde offert, quò facilius linguæ petulantiam frænare, & alienis malis ad nostram emendationem vti possimus.
units.tr: Here, first of all, it should be noted that Christ takes as his example something that worldly people, guided by the wisdom of the flesh, usually regard as chance or accident, and from it he draws a general teaching by which he urges everyone to timely repentance. From this it is clear that nothing happens by chance, without the certain counsel of divine providence. God knows all people and, as the Prophet says, has them engraved on his hands; he also numbers the hairs of our heads, and he does not allow even the little sparrows to perish without his consent or will. Or how could anything be done without his knowledge or against his will, when he is present everywhere, sees all things, and his nod is enough to hinder or advance any human work? St Augustine, observing this, freely confesses that he disliked the fact that in some books the words fortune and chance had been used, and he teaches that all such things must be referred to God's providence. We should remember this in sudden calamities that befall beyond all expectation: when the collapse of a house or a tree crushes someone, or when someone dies suddenly by accident or a fall, or is even killed by another through carelessness and against his will, while they are sawing wood together (an example God uses in the Law concerning cities of refuge), or while doing any other work. In cases of this kind, I say, we ought neither rashly pass judgment nor immediately condemn those who perish in such ways, unless their impiety and incurable obstinacy against God have been clearly shown to be a sure proof. Nor should we (as the more moderate people usually do) ascribe such things to fortune or to an unlucky day, but rather acknowledge and reverence the hidden judgment of God, who wished either to transfer those men by this means to the possession of his heavenly kingdom, or to set an example before us, in which we may learn to recognise the uncertain condition of our life and prepare ourselves hour by hour for every outcome, lest something similar happen to us when we least expect it. For, as was said a little above, we are all liable to the same accidents, and no calamity, however sad and unusual, can befall us that we ourselves have not deserved, if God were willing to use his right against us. Therefore, whenever we have been safe and free from such things, we should confess that we owe it to the divine goodness, which has been willing to spare our weakness, so that we are not overcome by temptations beyond our strength. This consideration is most useful, and God offers us its occasions and material from time to time, so that we may more easily restrain the wantonness of the tongue and make use of other people's misfortunes for our own correction.

units.la: Porrò doctrinam hanc parabola de ficu sterili Christus illustrat atq; confirmat, cuius statuus aut finis est, Deū non semper subitò omnes eos perdere, qui excidio digni sunt, sed erga illos quoq; multa longanimitate & clementia vti, & pœnas quas meruerunt differre, si forte conuersi pœnitentiam agant: eosdem verò ob moram hanc non debere sibi ipsis impunitatem perpetuam polliceri, quando hoc firmum & semper ratum Dei decretum sit, vt pœnitere nescij & suæ bonitatis contemptores tandem miserè pereant, & ab Ecclesiæ suæ cœsortio eiecti æternis cruciatibus tam anima quàm corpore multentur. Conuenit autem probè cum præcedentibus exemplis hæc doctrina, quia alteri adhuc vitio medetur, quo multi peccant, quando vel seipsos vel alios improuisa aliqua calamitate obrui sentiunt. Tunc enim aduersus Deum linguas laxant, & cur non simili iudicio in multos alios vtatur quærunt, qui similia aut etiam graviora flagitia designarint? Adhæc ex aliorum impunitate occasionem arripiunt contemnendi exempla iudiciorum Dei, sic vt omnia fortuito ferri, neq; diuinitus gubernari dicant. Admonet ergo Dominus impios & steriles sui nominis professores, etsi ad tempus locum suum tueri videantur & lætis rerum successibus floreant, non tamè hoc illis perpetuum fore, sed iam nunc diem constitutum esse, quando contumaciæ suæ dignas pœnas exoluant: ideoq; illorum prosperitate neminem offendi, multò minus autem Dei iudicia accusari debere. Sed præstat singulas huius parabolæ partes ex ordine considerare.
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ illustrates and confirms this teaching by the parable of the barren fig tree. Its purpose or end is that God does not always suddenly destroy all who deserve destruction, but also shows them much long-suffering and clemency, and defers the punishments they have earned, in case they perhaps turn back and repent. Yet those same people should not promise themselves perpetual impunity because of this delay, since it is God's firm and always valid decree that those who do not know how to repent, and who despise his goodness, should at last perish wretchedly, and, cast out from the fellowship of his Church, be tormented with eternal torments in both soul and body. This teaching fits well with the preceding examples, because it also heals another fault, by which many sin when they feel themselves or others overwhelmed by some unforeseen calamity. For then they loosen their tongues against God, and ask why he does not use the same judgment on many others who have committed similar or even graver crimes. Moreover, from the impunity of others they seize the occasion to despise the examples of God's judgments, so that they say everything is carried along by chance and not governed by God. The Lord therefore warns the impious and barren professors of his name that, although for a time they may seem to hold their place and flourish with happy successes, this will not last for them. Rather, a day has already been appointed when they will pay the punishments due to their obstinacy. Therefore no one should be offended by their prosperity, much less accuse God's judgments. But it is better to consider the individual parts of this parable in order.

units.la: Ficus plantata in vinea quamuis gentem & quemuis hominem in Ecclesiæ societatem adoptatum siue insitum denotat. Ecclesiam enim vineam esse Dei ex Isaia & aliis Christi parabolis notius est, quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Habet hæc vinea vitem vnicam, ipsum Christum, eius palmites dicuntur omnes, qui per fidem ei sunt insiti & nomen ipsius profitentur. Vt verò in vineis nemo bonus agricola arborem fert sterilem, quæ & succum terræ attrahat & vmbra sua vitibus noceat, fructum verò nullum ferat, quo damna illa farciantur: Ita neque Deus in Ecclesiæ suæ consortio eos perpetuò tolerat, qui inani professione Christiana titulo turgidi nõ aliud præstant, quàm quòd Ecclesiæ bona ad se rapere conantur, exemplo suo pijs omnibus nocent, nullum verò fidei & charitatis fructum ex se pariunt, quo vel Dei nomen honoretur, vel alij homines in fide ædificentur ac meliores fiant.
units.tr: The fig tree planted in the vineyard signifies any nation or person adopted or grafted into the fellowship of the Church. That the Church is God's vineyard, from Isaiah and from other parables of Christ, is too well known to need demonstration. This vineyard has one vine, Christ himself, and all who are grafted into him through faith and profess his name are called its branches. But just as in vineyards no good farmer keeps a barren tree, which both draws moisture from the soil and harms the vines with its shade, yet bears no fruit to make up for these losses, so God does not endure in the fellowship of his Church those who, puffed up with the empty title of Christian profession, do nothing except try to seize the goods of the Church for themselves, harm all the godly by their example, and produce no fruit of faith and love, by which God's name might be honoured or other people built up in faith and made better.

units.la: Quid ergo facit Deus? Inuisit frequentius vineam suam, neque ignauos & socordes patresfamilias imitatur, qui prædia sua prorsus negligunt: sed eos potius, qui cum oculo beri agros maximè impinguari norint, ferus in illis opus facientibus subinde adesse, & vt omnia rectè atque fideliter fiant prospicere solent. Et cur Ecclesiam, qua nihil in toto mundo charius & pretiosius habet, aut huius membra Deus negligeret, qui suam prouidentiam ad pecora, ad feras immanes, ad auiculas & coruorum pullos, denique ad res inanimatas quoque extendit? Venit autem fere tribus annis continuò & fructum quærit. Qua locutione eius bonitatem & longanimitatem Christus exprimit, quæ tanta est, vt quàmuis semel & iterum spe sua frustretur, non tamen mox securim stringat & infrugiferas excindat. Pugnat enim cum nostra duritie & contumacia Dominus, & omnes rationes huius vincendæ & emollienda adhibet. Exempla huius studij & industriæ passim occurrunt. Sic olim Iudæorum gentem tribus quasi vicibus inuisit. Primò nimirum per Mosem, quando ex Ægyptiaca seruitute vindicatis Legem dedit, quæ in singulis præceptis fructus à nobis requirit nostra professione dignos & Deo gratos. Deinde cùm Legem illi negligerent, & Sacerdotes legitimi, quos huius custodes & exactores constituerat, fere in suo officio cessarent, extraordinarie Prophetas excitauit, qui mira cum grauitate tam illos quàm totum populum officij sui admonuerunt. At hîs quoque non multùm proficientibus apud duræ ceruicis gentem, tandē Filium vnigenitum misit, si forte huius reuerentia moti sese tractabiliores atque morigeros præberent. Sed huius quoque studium inutile & irritum fuisse, Euangelica historia abundè docet. Et quod in Iudæis factum fuit, hoc ipsum in gentibus quoque alijs obseruatum fuisse constat. Ab hïs fructus innocentiæ & pietatis primùm per Legem naturæ requisiuit, quæ singulorum animis inscripta eos quid facerent quidue cauerent admonuit. Accessit mox aliqua diuina Legis per Mosem descriptæ cognitio, quando Iudæos varijs exilijs in gentes fere omnes dispersit, qui multos in veri Dei & voluntatis eius cognitionem adduxerunt. Secuta est postremò Euangelij prædicatio, quæ totum orbem terrarum breui paucorum annorum spacio percurrit, & vbique ecclesias constituit, in quibus in veri Dei cultu & omnibus pietatis officijs instituerentur, qui prius sub tenebrarum potestate degentes ignorantiæ tenebris immersi fuerant.
