Quòd si autem singulos homines priuatim inspicias, eandem Dei industriam deprehendes, qui terquaterq; illos inuisit & fructus quærit, quibus delectari queat. Nec enim vlla hominis ætas est cui sese non accommodet, dum modò per Verbi prædicationem, modò occultis propriæ conscientiæ suggestionibus, modò per amicos prudentes & fidos, sæpe etiam per inimicos officij admonet. Porrò vt olim Iudæorum gentem sterilem inuenit & omnium admonitionum contemptricem: ita plerique etiam hodie nullos pietatis fructus ferunt, sed inani professionis Christianæ fiducia decepti, Christum factis suis abnegant, quem ore profitentur. Et vt gentes quæque sua habent peculiaria scelera, quæ eradicare difficile est: ita nulla ætas est, quæ non suis vitijs proprijs laboret, quibus iustitia & pietatis fructus impeditur. Ad omnes ergo pertinet, quod in præsenti bonus ille paterfamilias vinitori aut colono suo dicit: Ecce anni tres sunt, ex quo venio quærens fructum in ficu ista, & non inuenio. Excinde igitur eam: quorsum etiam terram inutilem reddit? Est enim Deus iustus iudex & verax, qui neque apertam impietatem, neque fucatam & ementitam pietatis speciem impunitam abire sinit. Et conuenit dictum hoc cum illo alio Christi: Quæcunque arbor non fert fructum bonum, exciditur & in ignem conijcitur.
units.tr: What then does God do? He visits his vineyard more often. He does not imitate lazy and careless householders who utterly neglect their estates, but rather those who, knowing that fields are greatly enriched by the master's eye, are wont to be present from time to time among those doing the work and to see that everything is done rightly and faithfully. And why would God neglect the Church, which he holds dearer and more precious than anything else in the whole world, or its members, when he extends his providence to cattle, to wild beasts, to little birds and the young of ravens, and finally even to inanimate things? He comes, moreover, for about three years continually and seeks fruit. By this expression Christ shows God's goodness and long-suffering, which is so great that, although he is often disappointed in his hope, once and again, he does not at once draw the axe and cut down the unfruitful trees. For the Lord struggles against our hardness and obstinacy and uses every means of overcoming and softening it. Examples of this care and diligence occur everywhere. Thus he formerly visited the nation of the Jews, as it were, three times. First, indeed, through Moses, when after freeing them from Egyptian slavery he gave the Law, which in each precept requires from us fruits worthy of our profession and pleasing to God. Then, when they neglected the Law, and the lawful priests, whom he had appointed as its guardians and enforcers, had largely ceased from their office, he raised up extraordinary prophets, who admonished both them and the whole people of their duty with remarkable seriousness. But since these too accomplished little among a people of stiff neck, at last he sent his only-begotten Son, in case perhaps, moved by reverence for him, they might show themselves more tractable and compliant. But that this effort too was useless and fruitless the Gospel history amply teaches. And what was done among the Jews, it is clear, was also observed among the other nations. From these he first required the fruits of innocence and piety through the law of nature, which, written in the minds of individuals, admonished them what to do and what to avoid. Soon after came some knowledge of the divine Law described by Moses, when he scattered the Jews by various exiles among almost all nations, and they brought many to knowledge of the true God and of his will. Last of all followed the preaching of the Gospel, which ran through the whole world within a short space of a few years and everywhere established churches, in which those who had previously lived under the power of darkness and been immersed in the shadows of ignorance were instructed in the true worship of God and in all the duties of piety. But if you look at individual people privately, you will find the same diligence of God, who visits them three or four times and seeks the fruits in which he may delight. For there is no age of man to which he does not adapt himself: now through the preaching of the Word, now through the hidden promptings of one's own conscience, now through prudent and faithful friends, and often also through enemies, he admonishes us of our duty. Moreover, just as he once found the nation of the Jews barren and scornful of all admonitions, so many even today bear no fruits of piety, but, deceived by the empty confidence of Christian profession, they deny by their deeds the Christ whom they profess with their mouths. And just as each nation has its own peculiar sins, which are hard to root out, so there is no age that does not suffer from its own vices, by which the fruit of righteousness and piety is hindered. Therefore what that good householder says to his vinedresser or farmer in this passage applies to everyone: "Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down; why does it also make the ground useless?" For God is a just and true judge, who allows neither open impiety nor feigned and counterfeit appearances of piety to go unpunished. And this saying agrees with that other saying of Christ: "Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire."

units.la: Quid ergo remoratur Dei iudicium, quò minus steriles istæ ficus subinde excidantur & male pe-reant? Exprimit huius moræ causam Dominus, quando colonum pro ficu intercessisse ait, & herodixisse: Domine, dimitte eam etiā hoc anno, vsque quo fodero circa eam & misero stercus: Et si qui-dem tulerit fructum, dimittes: sin minus, in futurum excides eam. Colonus hic est Dei Filius Iesus Christus, quem suæ Vineæ aut Ecclesiæ Pater sacerdotem constituit. Hic quia nostras infirmitates expertus est, fidelem agit intercessorem, vt Dei iram à nobis auertat. Sed conditiones obseruare oportet, quibus suam hanc intercessionem temperat, vt iustitiæ Dei nihil omnino derogetur. Nam primò suam industriam promittit, qua sterilitati nostræ velit mederi. Fodiam (inquit) circa fi-cumistam, & mittam stercus. Fodit autem circum nos Dominus, quando cruce & afflictionibus nos exercet, quæ nobis non minus vtiles sunt, quàm arboribus fossio esse soleat. Vt enim hæc radices purgat, & ne præfocatæ arboribus ariditatem pariant atque interitum, cauet: ita fidei radix cruce purgatur, & eadem vegetatur ne deficiat, & nos eius virtute destituti vitam veram amittamus, quæ bonorum fructuum causa est. Similiter nos stercorat Christus, quando Euangelij doctrinam adhibet per ministros suos, qui ideo & rigare dicuntur, quod affectuum ardore Verbo restinguunt, & eos qui iam aridi prorsus atque exucci erant, fœcundos & ad omne opus bonum idoneos reddüt. Et in his quidem Christum mirè sedulum & industrium esse constat. Nam & dona Spiritus sui liberaliter distribuit, ne doctoribus idoneis Ecclesia destituatur, & suos omnes ad crucem vocat, quà carnis petulantiam coercet, & ad preces atque reliqua verę pietatis exercitia ardentiores reddit. At simul altera adhuc conditio proponitur, qua apud Patrem pro ficu illa sterili intercedit, dicens: Si quidem tulerit fructum, dimittes: sin minus, in futurum excides eam. Non ergo nequitia improborum hominum, qui incurabili malitia peccant, Christus patronus est: sed peccatorùs & inani pietatis fuco gloriantium vitam sic quærit, vt eosdem proprio ore damnet ad exitium, si tales esse pergant. Sunt igitur hic nobis duo hæc diligenter obseruanda. Primum, Christi intercessione fieri, quòd non semper illico puniuntur & exciduntur, qui hoc iam pridem suis sceleribus meruerunt. Et quia Deus misericors est & humani generis amans, iram suam quantùmuis iustam differre solet, ne iis qui resipiscunt ianuam salutis præcludat. Quod vt singulos priuatim cosolatur, ita admonet simul, ne temere de alicuius hominis salute desperemus. Quàm enim efficax sit Christi apud Patrem intercessio, eorum exemplo patet, qui ipsum in Crucem suffixerunt, & Pilato traditum turpissimè abnegarunt: ex quorum numero non paucos conuersos & salutis æternæ hæredes factos esse scimus. Alterum est, quòd Deus non perpetuò parcit steriltibus in sua vinea arboribus. Quia enim hypocritæ & palàm scelerati ipsam quoq; terram Ecclesiæ inutilem reddunt, dum multos alios suo exemplo seducunt, & religionem ipsam impiè prophanatam in contemptum trahunt, iusto illius iudicio exciduntur, vbi se incurabiles esse sufficientibus argumentis declarauerunt. Exempla, quibus hoc probari poterat, multa passim occurrunt, & quid totis Ecclesijs in Oriente olim acciderit, quid item priuatim multi patiantur, qui suum in Ecclesia locum non probè tutati sunt, plerisq; satis notum est. Itaq; huius parabolæ doctrinam singuli ad se transferant. Cogitent qua conditione in Ecclesiam adoptati sint. Ferant patienter à Deo submissos fructuum exactores. In primis autem colono Vineæ istius, Domino Iesu Christo, sese morigeros & obsequentes præbeant, vt huius disciplina & institutione meliores & indies fœcundiores facti, cum eodem in cælis tandem viuant & regnent: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Why then does God's judgment delay, so that these barren fig trees are not cut down at once and perish miserably? The Lord himself states the cause of this delay, when he says that the vinedresser interceded for the fig tree and said: "Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. And if it bears fruit, well; but if not, you will cut it down in the future." This vinedresser is the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom the Father has appointed as priest over his vineyard, that is, over the Church. Because he has experienced our weaknesses, he acts as a faithful intercessor, to turn away God's wrath from us. But we must observe the conditions by which he tempers this intercession, so that nothing whatever is taken from the justice of God. For first he promises his own diligence, by which he is willing to heal our barrenness. "I will dig around it," he says, "and put on manure." The Lord digs around us when he exercises us with the cross and afflictions, which are no less useful to us than digging is customarily to trees. For just as digging cleans the roots and guards against the trees being choked and bearing dryness and destruction, so the root of faith is cleansed by the cross, and is kept growing lest it fail, and lest we, deprived of its strength, lose the true life which is the cause of good fruits. In the same way Christ manures us, when he applies the teaching of the Gospel through his ministers, who are also said to water, because by the Word they quench the heat of the passions and make fruitful and fit for every good work those who had already become utterly dry and parched. In these things it is plain that Christ is wonderfully diligent and active. For he also distributes the gifts of his Spirit generously, so that the Church is not left without fit teachers, and he calls all his people to the cross, by which he restrains the wantonness of the flesh and makes them more ardent in prayer and the other exercises of true piety. But at the same time another condition is set forth, by which he intercedes with the Father for that barren fig tree, saying: "If it bears fruit, well; but if not, you will cut it down in the future." Christ is therefore not the patron of the wickedness of wicked men, who sin with incurable malice; rather, he seeks the life of sinners who glory in an empty show of piety in such a way that he condemns them by his own mouth to destruction, if they persist in being such. There are therefore two things here that we must carefully observe. The first is that, by the intercession of Christ, it comes about that those who have long since deserved it by their crimes are not always punished and cut down at once. And because God is merciful and loves the human race, he is accustomed to delay his wrath, however just it may be, so that he does not shut the door of salvation against those who repent. As this consoles each person individually, so it also warns that we should not rashly despair of anyone's salvation. For how effective Christ's intercession before the Father is, is shown by the example of those who nailed him to the cross and shamefully denied him when he had been handed over to Pilate; and we know that not a few of these were converted and made heirs of eternal salvation. The second is that God does not spare barren trees in his vineyard forever. For since hypocrites and openly wicked men also make the very soil of the Church useless, while they lead many others astray by their example and drag the religion itself, impiously profaned, into contempt, they are cut down by his just judgment, when they have shown by sufficient arguments that they are incurable. Examples by which this could be proved occur everywhere, and what once happened to whole Churches in the East, and what many individuals still suffer who have not properly maintained their place in the Church, is known to most people well enough. Therefore let each one apply the teaching of this parable to himself. Let them consider on what condition they have been adopted into the Church. Let them bear patiently the tax-collectors of fruit sent by God. Above all, let them show themselves compliant and obedient to the vinedresser of this vineyard, the Lord Jesus Christ, so that, made better by his discipline and instruction and more fruitful day by day, they may at last live and reign with him in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXVII.

units.la: Docebat autem in quadā synagoga Sabbato. Et ecce adfuit mulier habens spiritum inualitudinis ab annis decem & octo, eratq; incurua, nec prorsus sese poterat recuruare. Ipsam autem cum vidisset Iesus, aduocauit, & dixit ei: Mulier, absoluta es ab inualitudine tua. Et imposuit ei manus: & illico surrecta est, & glorificabat Deum.
units.tr: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over and could not straighten herself up at all. When Jesus saw her, he called her to him and said to her: "Woman, you are freed from your infirmity." And he laid his hands on her, and at once she stood upright and glorified God.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus Ecclesiam, quae per Euangelij praedicationem ex omnibus gentibus colligitur, suum peculium & sibi consecratam esse vult: ita postulat quoque, vt quotquot huius membra censeri volunt, se tales esse vita & moribus testentur. Quae causa est, quòd Ecclesiae Rex & Sacerdos, Iesus Christus, passim poenitentiam docet, & ab ea fere praedicandi initium facit. Pertinent huc quae in ijs, quae proximè praecesserunt, audiimus, vbi non obiter modò Iudaeorum genti poenitentiam suasit, sed quia contumaciores esse sciebat, minus quoque & exemplo grauissimis vsus est, adhaec ficus parabola docuit, quid steriles & poenitere nescios maneat. His ordine commodissimo Lucas historiam de muliere incurua per Christum curata, & Synagogae principis de illo facto iudicium subiicit. Ea enim docetur, vnde nobis virtus illa obtingat, quae nos ad bona opera fecundos atque idoneos facit, simulq; sterilis ficus exemplum proponitur in hypocrita illo, qui praeter inanem & foliorum similem pietatis ostentationem nihil habebat. In praesenti tamen priorem modò partem historiae consideMbimus.
units.tr: Just as God wills that the Church, which is gathered from all nations through the preaching of the Gospel, be his own people and consecrated to himself, so he also requires that all who want to be counted as her members show by their life and conduct that they are such. This is the reason why Jesus Christ, the King and Priest of the Church, teaches repentance everywhere and almost always begins his preaching with it. To this belong the things we heard in the passage just before, where he not only urged repentance in passing on the Jewish people, but, because he knew they were the more stubborn, he also used the most serious examples. Besides this, he taught by the parable of the fig tree what awaits the barren and those who do not know how to repent. In the most fitting order, Luke places after these the story of the woman bent over, healed by Christ, and the ruler of the synagogue's judgment on that deed. For here we are taught where that power comes from which makes us fruitful and fit for good works, and at the same time the barren fig tree is set before us as an example in that hypocrite who, apart from an empty show of piety like leaves, had nothing. For the present, however, we shall consider only the first part of the story.

units.la: Principiò persona describitur, in qua miraculum editum est. Fuit ea multis modis miserrima. Nam spiritu inualitudinis aut infirmitatis detentam fuisse Lucas scribit, quod postea Christus exponens, eam Satanae vinculis constrictam fuisse dicit. Ergo illam diabolo vexandam Deus tradidit, communi humani generis hosti, qui vt ab initio homicida fuit, ita ex eo summam voluptatem capit, si quos eius potestati Deus permittit, nouis & horrendis exemplis affligere queat, sicuti in Iob etiam historia est videre, & in multis daemoniacis, quorum indomitos furores & miserrimam conditionem Euangelistae describunt. Deinde morbi species exprimitur, quae fuit corporis totius incuratio, & talis quidem, vt non posset pro communi hominum more caput attollere, aut erecto corpore incedere, sed brutorum animantium instar prona terram solam spectaret. Accessit morbo, quem Satanae vis incurabilem faciebat diuturnitas, spem quoq; salutis omnem adimens. Nam annis totis decem & octo iam inualitudine ista laborabat.
units.tr: First, the person in whom the miracle was performed is described. She was in many ways most wretched. For Luke writes that she was held by a spirit of infirmity or weakness, which Christ later explained by saying that she had been bound by Satan. So God handed her over to be tormented by the devil, the common enemy of the human race, who from the beginning was a murderer, and who takes the greatest delight from this, if God permits him to afflict those under his power with new and dreadful examples. This can be seen in the history of Job, and in many demoniacs, whose untamed frenzies and miserable condition the evangelists describe. Next, the kind of illness is set out: it was a crippling of the whole body, and of such a sort that she could not lift her head as people ordinarily do, or walk with her body upright, but, like the brute animals, looked only at the ground with her face bowed down. To this illness, which the power of Satan made incurable through its long duration, was added the loss of every hope of recovery. For she had already suffered from this affliction for eighteen whole years.

units.la: Et haec quidem huius mulieris conditio fuit quoad corpus, in qua communis omnium hominum typus proponitur, qui nam & quales sint quoad animam, priusquam illis Christus remedium adhibet. Etenim quando diabolus primos parentes suis mellitis promissionibus illectos in peccatum adduxit, eadem opera sibi in omnem illorum posteritatem ius & imperium acquisiuit. Adam enim amissa & obliterata Dei imagine, ad quam initio conditus fuerat, & totus peccator factus, non alios quàm sui similes filios gignere potuit: quod Moses non obscurè exprimit, quando illum in suo simulachro & secundum suam imaginem, corruptam videlicet & peccatricem, filios genuisse scribit. Et huic consentiens Paulus, peccatum per vnum hominem ingressum esse ait, adeo vt omnes quotquot ex Adamo descendunt, peccatores facti sint. Agnouerunt hoc in semetipsis etiam sanctissimi quique, inter quos Dauid se in iniquitate conceptum & in peccato formatum esse fatetur. At vbi peccatum regnat, ibi diabolus regnum obtinet, quem hoc nomine mundi huius principem Scripturae vocant. Hic autem cum in Veritate non steterit, & turpiA Deo defectione facta a pristina dignitate exciderit, hoc vnum iam agit, vt sui similes faciat omnes, quos in suam potestatem redegit. Est autem ille immundus & impurus spiritus, scelerum & nequitiae author, terrenarum rerum amans, caelestium contemptor & Dei inimicus. Tales ergo suos facit, quorum animis se insinuat. Et huius operatione fit, vt homo animalis non intelligat ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Ex corrupto autem intellectu voluntas praua & a diuinis atque caelestibus abhorrens nascatur oportet. Itaque vt qui corpore incuruo sunt terram modò intuentur: sic quoad corruptam carnis rationem & ex primis parentibus quasi hereditario iure in nos deriuatam totius naturae vitiositatem sequimur, neque Deum omnis boni fontem amare, neque eundem in spiritu & veritate colere, neq; ad caelestia animos attollere, neque virtuti & sanctimoniae studere possumus: sed impuro Satanae spiritu & carnis infelici caeco iudicio prauisq; desiderijs decepti, in solis terrenis haeremus. Et si quid de Deo cogitamus, id omne erroneum, absurdum & ab illius ingenio atq; natura alienissimum est: & quia eundem ex nostro ingenio fingimus, cultus quoq; institutimus, quibus daemones potius quàm ille, delectantur, sicuti de gentibus Paulus testatur. Sequuntur mox omnis generis peccata & scelera, in quorum sterquilinio vt porci volutamur, & tunc de-mum mum nos felices esse iudicamus, si illis pro nostra libidine indulgere liceat. Exempla huius mali pas-sim occurrunt, & quanta sit naturae corruptio sancti quoque in semetipsis experiuntur, à quibus ten-tandis minimè abstinet Satan, qui ipsum quoque Dei Filium aggredi non est veritus. Estq; malum hoc vetustum atq; diuturnum, ut quod ex conceptione (ut diximus) nobis inhaeret. Itaq; ut im-medicabilia fere sunt corporis vitia, quae aut in vtero matris nobis innascuntur, aut in partu acci-dunt, ita innatae nobis naturae vitiositati nemo hominum mederi potest.
units.tr: This was indeed the woman's condition as regards the body, in which the common type of all men is set before us, as to what and of what kind they are in soul before Christ applies a remedy to them. For when the devil led our first parents into sin, enticing them with honeyed promises, by the same act he acquired for himself right and dominion over all their posterity. For Adam, having lost and erased the image of God in which he had been created at the beginning, and having become wholly sinful, could beget only sons like himself. Moses expresses this not obscurely when he writes that Adam begot sons in his own likeness and according to his own image, namely corrupt and sinful. Paul agrees with this when he says that sin entered through one man, so that all who are descended from Adam have become sinners. Even the most holy men have recognised this in themselves; among them David confesses that he was conceived in iniquity and formed in sin. But where sin reigns, there the devil holds the kingdom, whom the Scriptures call by this name, "the prince of this world." Yet since he did not stand in the truth, and by a shameful revolt against God has fallen from his former dignity, he now has one aim only: to make all those whom he has brought under his power like himself. He is an unclean and impure spirit, the author of crimes and wickedness, a lover of earthly things, a despiser of heavenly ones, and an enemy of God. So he makes such men his own as he insinuates himself into their minds. By his working it happens that the natural man does not understand the things of the Spirit of God. But from a corrupted understanding a perverse will must necessarily arise, one that shrinks from what is divine and heavenly. Therefore, just as those who are bent over in body look only at the ground, so, as regards the corrupt reasoning of the flesh and the vicious nature of the whole man, which has come down to us from our first parents as if by hereditary right, we follow the same course. We can neither love God, the fountain of all good, nor worship him in spirit and truth, nor raise our minds to heavenly things, nor strive after virtue and holiness. Instead, deceived by the impure spirit of Satan, by the wretched blind judgment of the flesh, and by evil desires, we cling to earthly things alone. And if we think anything about God, all of it is mistaken, absurd, and wholly alien to his nature and character. Because we fashion him according to our own mind, we also devise forms of worship in which demons rather than he take delight, as Paul testifies about the Gentiles. Soon follow sins and crimes of every kind, in whose dung heap we wallow like pigs, and then at last we judge ourselves happy if we are allowed to indulge in them as our lust wishes. Examples of this evil occur everywhere, and even the saints find in themselves how great the corruption of nature is. Satan does not hold back from tempting them, for he did not shrink from attacking the Son of God himself. This evil is ancient and lasting, since it clings to us from conception, as we have said. And so, just as physical defects are almost incurable, since they are either born in us in the mother's womb or occur at birth, so no one can heal the innate vice of our nature.

units.la: Vbi ergo medicina aut salus quaeri debet? Apud illum solum, qui isti mulieri remedium adhi-buit. Est is aeternus Dei Filius, qui ex Maria Virgine hominem assumpsit, & ipso nomine Iesu medicum & Seruatorem nostrum se esse profitetur. Hic in Synagoga docuit, in quam mulier quo-que haec venerat, & ea visa opem illi absq; mora tulit. Proderit autem, si ordinem, quo in illa curan-da vsus est, aliquanto diligentius consideremus. Si enim qui valetudinis suae rationem habent, stu-diose obseruant qua methodo & ordine periti medici in difficilioribus morbis curandis progrediun-tur: quanto magis nos Christum vnicum humanae salutis authorem atq; administrum obseruare de-cet, ut huic nos accomodare discamus.
units.tr: Where then must medicine or salvation be sought? With him alone who applied a remedy to this woman. He is the eternal Son of God, who took man from the Virgin Mary, and by his very name Jesus he declares himself our physician and Saviour. He taught in the synagogue, into which this woman too had come, and seeing her he brought her help without delay. It will be profitable, however, if we consider somewhat more carefully the order which he followed in her cure. For if those who look after their health carefully observe the method and order by which skilled physicians proceed in curing more difficult diseases, how much more should we observe Christ, the only author and minister of human salvation, so that we may learn to conform ourselves to him.

units.la: Primò illam vidisse dicitur. Atqui alios quoq; procul dubio vidit, qui in Synagoga congregati ipsum docentem audiebant. At hic singularis bonitas & misericordia affectus notatur, qua miseram & afflictam respexit, ut ipsi subueniret. Atqui eo tempore in praecipuae dignitatis & maximè necessa-rio docendi munere versabatur, cuius ergo se in mundum venisse alibi fatetur, & à quo ne à matre quidem & fratribus suis requisitus alias discedere voluit. Ita vero de initio & fonte salutis nostrae nos spiritus sanctus admonet. Est is incredibilis & plus quàm paterna Dei bonitas, qui etsi in al-to habitet (ut Psalt es ille regius canit) eiusque gloria caelus sublimior sit, adhaec totius mundi gu-bernationem administret, demittit tamen se, ut pauperrimos & miserrimos quosque respiciat, & opem optatam, vel etiam non requisitam interdum illis ferat. Ita Adamum corpore & anima nudum vidit, & improbi transgressoris miserius, fugientem & latebras quarentem ipse quaesiit prior. Eadem bonitate Abrahamum inter idololatras agentem respexit, & ne eorum exemplo se-ducius periret curauit. Ad eundem modum filios Israel Aegyptiorum tyrannidè crudeliter oppressos & (quod omni seruitute miserius erat) eorundem superstitionibus excaecatos iam & corruptos vidit, deque illis liberandis cum Mose egit. Quid? nonne eiusdem gratiae & bonitatis fuit, quod Dauidem adulterum & homicidam, salutis autem suae securum nimis contemptorem & nefarijs libidinibus, ceu re bene confecta gaudentem vidit, & de illo in viam reducendo consilium cepit? Extant huius generis exempla plurima in Scripturis, quae omnia recitare longum foret: sufficiat autem omnium loco, quod totum genus humanum peccati seruitio & mortis tyrannide oppressum ex alto vidit Dei Filius, & ut nos seruaret, ex sinu Patris ad nos descendere & in mundum hunc longè miserrimum ve-nire dignatus est: & quod nos ab eodem quotidie respici sentimus, dum nobismet ipsis inter peccandum delitias facimus, & vix quicquam de salute nostra cogitamus. Haec ut vitam nostram & salutem omnem in mera Dei bonitate fundatam esse docent, omnemque meriti nostri respectum procul exclu-dunt: ita consolationem efficacissimam habent, qua fidem nostram in omni tentationum genere con-firmemus. Cur enim conscientiae terroribus superati in peccatis suis desperent, qui peccatores à Deo non negligi aut hostiliter repelli, sed oculis plus quam paternis respici audiunt? Cur salutem suam in dubium vocent, qui dilectum illum Dei Filium, in quo omnes sapientiae & scientiae thesauri re-conditi sunt, sibi medicum destinatum esse norunt? Vel cur in egestate, exilio, morbis aut quibus-cunque alijs miserijs animum despondeant, qui pauperes & afflictos à Deo in primis respici tot scrip-turae testimonijs & exemplis cum antiquis tum recentibus & quotidianis edocentur? Horum itaque consideratio spem nostram atq; fidem fulcire debet, ne vel desperemus, vel impatientia superati mur-muremus aduersus Deum, vel etiam tempus & modum auxilij ferendi eidem praescribamus. Hu-ius potius voluntati nos subijci decet, & ei salutis nostrae curam committere, qui cum nostri sit aman-tissimus, nullam eius promouendae occasionem negliget.
units.tr: First, it is said that he saw her. Yet without doubt he also saw others who were gathered in the synagogue listening to him teaching. But here a singular goodness and an affection of mercy is noted, by which he regarded the wretched and afflicted woman so as to help her. Yet at that time he was engaged in the most distinguished office and in the duty of teaching that was most necessary, the very office for which, as he elsewhere says, he came into the world, and from which he would not turn aside even when his mother and brothers asked for him. Thus the Holy Spirit admonishes us about the beginning and source of our salvation. It is the incredible and more than fatherly goodness of God which, although he dwells on high (as the royal Psalmist sings), and although his glory is higher than the heavens, and although he administers the government of the whole world, nevertheless stoops down so as to regard the poorest and most wretched, and at times brings them the help they desire, or even help they have not asked for. So he saw Adam naked in body and soul, and, more pitiable than the wicked transgressor who fled and sought hiding places, he himself sought him first. By the same goodness he regarded Abraham living among idolaters, and took care that he should not perish, led astray by their example. In the same way he saw the sons of Israel cruelly oppressed by the tyranny of the Egyptians and, what was more wretched than any slavery, blinded and now corrupted by their superstitions, and he dealt with Moses about freeing them. What then? Was it not of the same grace and goodness that he saw David, an adulterer and murderer, too careless of his own salvation and rejoicing in wicked lusts as if in a deed well done, and that he took counsel to bring him back to the way? There are very many examples of this kind in the Scriptures, and it would be long to recite them all. Yet it will suffice, in place of all of them, that the Son of God looked down from on high upon the whole human race, oppressed by the slavery of sin and the tyranny of death, and deigned to come down from the bosom of the Father to us and to enter this world, most wretched by far, in order to save us. And we feel that he regards us every day, even while we indulge ourselves in pleasures as we sin, and scarcely think anything about our salvation. These truths teach that our life and all our salvation are founded in the pure goodness of God, and they wholly exclude every regard for our own merit. So they also provide a most effective consolation by which we may strengthen our faith in every kind of temptation. For why should those overcome by the terrors of conscience despair of their sins, when they hear that sinners are not neglected by God nor repelled as enemies, but are regarded with eyes more than fatherly? Why should those doubt their salvation who know that the beloved Son of God, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, has been appointed as their physician? Or why should those who are taught by so many testimonies and examples of Scripture, both ancient, recent, and daily, that God especially regards the poor and afflicted, lose heart in poverty, exile, sickness, or whatever other miseries? Therefore the consideration of these things ought to support our hope and faith, so that we neither despair, nor, overcome by impatience, murmur against God, nor even prescribe to him the time and manner of bringing help. It is rather fitting for us to submit to his will, and to commit the care of our salvation to him who, since he loves us most dearly, will neglect no opportunity of advancing it.

units.la: Deinde aduocat mulierem inualidam Dominus ad se. Est enim bonus ille pastor, qui oues suas nouit, & singulas nomine etiam vocat. Et hic nobis secundus ad salutem gradus est, quod à Deo efficaciter vocamur, alioqui nunquam ad eum accessuri. Nam eorum similes sumus, qui ne aegrotare videantur, medicum non adeunt, vel illum sponte venientem ex medicinae impatientia reijciunt. Vt ergo vocemur diuinitus, imo vt trahamur opus est, Christo teste, qui dicit: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit illum. At hic etiam probe suo officio Dominus fungitur. Vt enim iam vocauit, ita frequenter in Scripturis omnes homines ad se vocat, & ad se venientibus certam salutis spem facit. Huc referri debet, quod apud Isaiam clamat: O vos omnes qui sititis venite ad aquas, & hi quibus non est pecunia, venite, comparate, & comedite: emite sine argento & sine precio vinum & lac, &c. Generalis etiam est vocatio, quam singuli ad se trahere possunt, illa Christi: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego vos refocillabo. Item: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat. Vocat nos etiam viva voce per praecones suos, quoties Euangelium praedicatur. Et priuata atque occulta vocatio dici potest, quoties nobis Spiritus sanctus animam vellicat & animis nostris bonas cogitationes insinuat, quibus ad verbi Dei & salutis nostrae studium excitamur. At quocunque modo vocemur, nostrum fuerit vocantem Deum audire & sequi, ne eius mandato reluctantes simul salutem, quam ille nobis liberalissime offert, excludamus.
units.tr: Then the Lord calls the weak woman to himself. For he is that good shepherd who knows his sheep and calls each of them by name. This is the second step towards salvation for us: we are effectually called by God, since otherwise we would never come to him. We are like those who, so as not to appear sick, do not go to the physician, or who, out of impatience with medicine, reject him even when he comes of his own accord. So if we are to be called by God, indeed drawn, as Christ bears witness when he says: "No one can come to me unless my Father draws him." And the Lord also performs his own office well here. For just as he has called, so in the Scriptures he frequently calls all people to himself, and he gives a sure hope of salvation to those who come to him. To this belongs what he cries out through Isaiah: "Oh, all you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, come, buy and eat; buy wine and milk without money and without price, etc." The call is also general, and each person can take it to himself, as in Christ's words: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you." Likewise: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." He also calls us by his heralds with the living voice whenever the Gospel is preached. And a private and hidden call may be spoken of, whenever the Holy Spirit pricks our souls and instils good thoughts in our minds, by which we are stirred to the study of God's Word and of our salvation. But however we are called, it is for us to hear and follow the God who calls, lest by resisting his command we shut out the salvation which he offers us most generously.

units.la: Excitet ergo nos huius exempli siue miraculi consideratio. Nam ad se accedentem mulierem Christus illico sanat, quod his verbis Lucas scribit: Dixit ei, Mulier, absoluta es ab infirmitate tua: & imposuit ei manus, & illico surrecta est. Duo dicuntur, quibus & Christi virtus & modus siue ordo continetur, quo in nobis seruandis vti solet. Primum est, quod verbo salutem praesentem pollicetur: Mulier (inquit) absoluta es ab infirmitate tua. Iam absolutam esse pronuntiat, cum nihil minus adhuc appareret. Sed pro imperio loquitur, vt se potentem rerum Dominum esse ostendat, qui tam morbos quam vitam & mortem in sua manu habeat, & tunc quoque salutem praesentem nutu at que verbo suo nobis conferre possit, quando carnis rationi nulla huius spes affulget. Et est hic Dei mos iam inde a prima rerum origine usurpatus, quod per verbum nos seruat. Sic Adamo verbum salutis propositum, quando pollicitus est semen mulieris, cuius merito & virtute caput serpentis conteri oporteat. Et Abrahamo salutem certam attulit promissio: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. Quia enim huic credidit, fides haec ipsi imputata est ad iustitiam, & simul diem Iesu Christi vidit, cuius merito seruatus est. Pertinet huc quoque illud Psalmi dictum, quo de ijs, qui morbis confecti ad Deum clamant, pronuntiat: Misit verbum suum & sanauit eos. Quod Paulus observans dicebat, Euangelium esse potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Cui conuenit Angelite stimonium, qui Cornelium Centurionem, vt Petrum accerseret, admonens ait: Is tibi loquetur verba, per quae seruetur tu & domus tua. Etenim si reges huius seculi suam erga seruos suos beneficam voluntatem verbo uno declarare solent, quod irritum esse nolunt: quanto magis cum Filij Dei, Sacerdotes & regis aeterni verbo salutifica virtus coniuncta est? Faciunt haec ad Euangelij commendationem, & eos confutant validissime qui huius praedicationem contemnunt, & eius studium inutile esse arbitrantur. Qui dum ordinem salutis a Deo institutum & tot seculis confirmatum nolunt admittere, a salute omni excidunt.
units.tr: Let the consideration of this example or miracle stir us up. For Christ immediately heals the woman who came to him, as Luke writes in these words: "He said to her, 'Woman, you are loosed from your infirmity'; and he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight." Two things are said, in which both the power of Christ and the manner or order that he is accustomed to use in preserving us are contained. The first is that he promises present salvation by a word: "Woman," he says, "you are loosed from your infirmity." He pronounces her already loosed when nothing of the kind yet appeared. But he speaks with authority, to show that he is the powerful Lord of all things, who holds diseases as well as life and death in his hand, and who can bestow present salvation on us by his nod and his word even when no hope of it shines on human reason. And this is God's custom, used from the very beginning of things, that he preserves us by the word. Thus he set before Adam the word of salvation when he promised the seed of the woman, by whose merit and power the head of the serpent was to be crushed. And to Abraham the promise brought certain salvation: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." For because he believed this, his faith was imputed to him for righteousness, and at the same time he saw the day of Jesus Christ, by whose merit he was saved. To this also belongs that saying of the Psalm, in which it is declared of those who, worn out with diseases, cry to God: "He sent his word and healed them." Paul, observing this, said that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. The testimony of the angel agrees with this, who, when he bade Cornelius the centurion send for Peter, said: "He will speak to you words by which you and your household will be saved." For if the kings of this age are accustomed to declare their beneficent will towards their servants by a single word, which they do not want to be void, how much more is saving power joined to the word of the Son of God, the priest and eternal king? These things serve to commend the Gospel, and they most forcefully refute those who despise its preaching and think its study useless. While they refuse to admit the order of salvation instituted by God and confirmed through so many ages, they fall away from all salvation.

units.la: Alterum est, quod manus mulieri Dominus imposuit. Vsus est hoc ritu sine gestu etiam in mul tis alijs curandis, quo communicatio figuratur, per quam ille nobis coniungitur oportet. Nam nisi id fiat, nulla ex ipso salus sperari potest. Quid enim a nobis alienus proderit? At communicationi huic in primis incarnatio seruit, de qua Ioannes Euangelista pronuntiat: Verbum caro factum est, & habitauit in nobis. Qua ratione etiam Emanuel dicitur, quod idem est ac si dicas: NOBISCVM DEVS. Vinculum huius coniunctionis fides est, quae Spiritus sancti virtute in nobis generata animos nostros illustrat & supra mundum hunc corruptibilem, adeoque supra omnes coelos euehit, vt illum apprehendamus, & eidem inseramur, vt ipse quidem in nobis, nos autem in illo viuamus. Quae vt verbo traduntur, ita externis quoque signis adumbrari & confirmari solent, vt nostrae infirmitati consulatur, qua impediti ad tam sublimia mysteria percipienda tardiores sumus. Baptismo igitur in Ecclesiae societatem adoptamur, quae Christi corpus est, vt ex ipso capite omnium electorum vitae spiritum hauriamus. In Coena autem obsignatur redemptionis per mortem illius beneficium, & simul ostenditur ipsum esse panem illum vitae, qui ideo de coelo venerit, vt nos ad vitam aeternam pascat. Et hoc causa est, quod in Sacramentis ipsi Christo communicare dicimur: Vbi tamen nos nihil carnale & crassum (vt olim Capernaitae fecerunt) imaginari decet, cum tota hac ratio hæc ratio communicandi spiritualis sit, neq; nos eius aliter quam per fidem participes efficiamur. Non ergo in externis symbolis hærere, sed potius fidei contemplatione in rem ipsam, quæ his adumbratur atq; obsignatur intenti esse debemus. Nam vt multis no profuit, quod vel ipsi Christi cõtrectauerunt, vel ab ipso cõtrectati sint (vt in Iudæ proditoris & aliorū, qui fide destituti fuerunt exemplis cernitur) ita multò minus Symbola corporis & sanguinis eius proderunt, si ea absq; fide vsurpemus. At quia de his alibi copiosius est dictum, hæc nunc breuius perstrinxisse satis sit. Interim tenere oportet, hanc esse salutis consequendæ rationem vnicam, vt Christum in Euangelio nobis loquentem audiamus, & eundem se nobis quasi manibus porrectis & ad nos protensis offerentem admittamus. Nam vt mulier ista, dum hoc facit, illico surrecta & à maligno illo infirmitatis spiritu liberata est: ita mox suos quoq; animos ex terra sterquilinio in cælos erigi, & Satana procul discedere sentient, quotquot illius exemplum imitati fuerint. Nec enim illius est aliquid in eos, qui Christi peculium facti sunt. Et vt huic nos consecremus, nos huic mulieri exhibitum beneficium excitare debet, in quo tam illustre suæ tam gratiæ quam potentiæ specimen adidit. Gratia enim & bonitatis singularis argumentum est, quod illam respicit, & visam ad se vocat, & accedenti manus imponere dignatur. Potentiæ autem & virtutis diuinæ opus fuit, quod verba & promissionem eius absq; mora effectus sequitur, & nullo alio fulcro adiuta erectos ad sydera vulcus attollit, quæ ab annis decem & octo incurua repserat.
units.tr: The second thing is that the Lord laid his hands on the woman. He used this rite, without any gesture, in healing many others too, by which communion is figured, through which he must be joined to us. For unless this happens, no salvation can be hoped for from him. For what would it profit us if he were alien to us? This communion is above all served by the incarnation, of which the Evangelist John declares: "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us." For this reason he is also called Emmanuel, which is the same as saying: GOD WITH US. The bond of this union is faith, which, generated in us by the power of the Holy Spirit, illuminates our souls and lifts them above this corruptible world, and indeed above all the heavens, so that we may lay hold of him and be grafted into him, so that he lives in us and we in him. And just as these things are delivered by the word, so they are usually also shadowed forth and confirmed by external signs, so that our weakness may be provided for, since we are hindered and slower to perceive such sublime mysteries. Therefore by baptism we are adopted into the fellowship of the Church, which is the body of Christ, so that from the head himself we may draw the Spirit of life for all the elect. In the Supper, moreover, the benefit of his redemption through his death is sealed to us, and at the same time it is shown that he himself is that bread of life, which came down from heaven so that he might feed us to eternal life. And for this reason we are said to communicate with Christ himself in the sacraments. Yet we ought not to imagine anything carnal and gross in this (as the Capernaites once did), since this whole manner of communicating is spiritual, and we become partakers of him only through faith. Therefore we ought not to cling to the external symbols, but rather, by contemplating faith, to be intent on the thing itself, which is shadowed forth and sealed by these. For just as it did not profit many that they had touched Christ, or had been touched by him (as is seen in the examples of Judas the traitor and of others who were destitute of faith), so much less will the symbols of his body and blood profit us if we use them without faith. But since these things have been discussed more fully elsewhere, it is enough to have touched on them briefly here. Meanwhile we must hold that this is the one way of obtaining salvation: that we hear Christ speaking to us in the Gospel, and admit him as he offers himself to us, as it were with hands stretched out and held towards us. For just as that woman, in doing this, immediately rose up and was freed from that evil spirit of infirmity, so as many as imitate her example will soon feel their souls also raised from the earth and the dunghill to heaven, and Satan departing far away. For nothing of his has any hold on those who have become Christ's own possession. And to consecrate ourselves to him, the benefit shown to this woman ought to stir us up, in which he has added so illustrious a specimen of both his grace and his power. For it is a sign of grace and singular goodness that he looks upon her, calls her to himself when seen, and deigns to lay his hands on her as she approaches. But it was a work of divine power and strength that her healing followed his word and promise without delay, and, helped by no other prop, he lifted up her bent back, which for eighteen years had been crawling bowed down, so that it looked up to the stars.

units.la: Porro vt huius miraculi doctrina fructuosior fit, diligentius consideranda erit mulieris exemplum, vt quid hæc ante & post restitutæ salutis beneficium fecerit, videamus. Occurrit hic primum quod die Sabbati Synagogam ingressa est, vbi ex veteri more Lex Dei & veterum Prophetarum sermones prælegebantur, & preces publicæ fiebant. Fuit ergo verbi Dei amans & pietatis studiosa, quòd electis proprium esse Christus docet, apud Ioannem dicens: Qui ex Deo est, audit verba mea. Item: Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt. Amplius vero mulieris huius pietatem commendat ad versa eius valetudo. Quam enim molestum & laboriosum ei fuerit domo egredi & in publicum prodire, facile æstimabunt, qui vel vnico alicuius membri morbo laborant. Adhæc toto corpore incurua molestiam omnem superat. Magnū ergo in illa fuerit oportet verbi Dei studium, in quo procul dubio consolatione multam & recreatione à morbo grauissimo inueniebat, vt cum Dauide posset dicere: Magis expetibilia sunt verba Domini quam aurum præstantissimum, & dulciora fauis melle stillantibus. Est hoc (vt ante diximus) quoad nos, salutis nostræ principium. Quia enim hanc nobis per verbum Deus offert, nunquam eam assequentur, qui illud fastidiunt vel oderunt. Et simul à nobis rogari vult Deus, cum preces proprijssimum sint exercicium fidei, qua ille in primis delectatur. Pudeat autem suæ ignauiæ eos, qui cum corpore sint sano & integro, nunquam tamen vel quàrarissimè ad cætus sacros veniunt, & quasi sibijpsis sufficere possint ad omnia, vnà cum verbo Dei preces quoq; cum publicas tum priuatas negligunt. Solent illi multa prætexere, quibus sese excusent sed sufficit illis confutandis & conuincendis muliercula huius exemplum, quam neq; corporis miserabilis conditio, neq; labor & itineris molestia, neq; Sacerdotum & Scribarum indocta anaritia abterrere potuit, quò minus ad cætus sacros proreperet, vt verbū Dei recitari audiret, & cum aliorū precibus suas quoq; coniungeret. Non neglexit ergo eam Dominus, & suæ ordinationi sese accomodantem ita sanauit, vt multis alijs ad salutem aspirantibus potuerit esse exemplo, & nos quoque hodie erudiat.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that the teaching of this miracle may be more fruitful, we must consider the woman's example more carefully, and see what she did before and after the benefit of her restored health. The first thing that stands out is that on the Sabbath day she entered the synagogue, where, according to the ancient custom, the Law of God and the sermons of the old Prophets were read aloud and public prayers were offered. She was therefore a lover of God's Word and devoted to godliness, which Christ teaches is the mark of the elect, when he says in John: "He who is of God hears my words." And again: "My sheep hear my voice." Moreover, her piety is commended by her condition. Those who suffer from even a single ailing limb will readily judge how troublesome and laborious it was for her to leave her house and go out in public. Bent over with her whole body, she overcame every hardship. She must therefore have had a great zeal for the Word of God, in which without doubt she found much comfort and refreshment from her very grievous illness, so that with David she could say: "The words of the Lord are more to be desired than the finest gold, and sweeter than honey dripping from the comb." As we said before, this is for us the beginning of our salvation. For since God offers us salvation through the Word, those who despise or hate it will never attain it. At the same time God wishes to be asked by us, since prayer is the most proper exercise of faith, in which he above all delights. Those people should be ashamed of their laziness who, though they are sound and whole in body, never or very rarely come to the sacred assemblies, and, as if they could suffice for everything by themselves, neglect both the Word of God and prayers, both public and private. They are wont to offer many excuses to clear themselves; but to refute and convict them, the example of this poor woman is enough, for neither the wretched state of her body, nor the labour and trouble of the journey, nor the unlearned avarice of the priests and scribes could deter her from making her way to the sacred assemblies, to hear the Word of God read and to join her own prayers with those of others. The Lord therefore did not neglect her, and, accommodating herself to his ordinance, she was so healed that she could be an example to many others who aspire to salvation, and he teaches us too today.

units.la: Deinde oblatū ex insperato Dei beneficiū alacri & propto animo excipit. Argumenta huius sunt duo. Vnū, quod à Christo vocata mox ad eū accedit, neq; incessus sui absurdi & miserabilis ipsam pudet coram tota ecclesia, vt propius ei coiungatur, quæ docente hucusq; cū voluptate audiuerat. Alterū quod audita salutis promissione illico surrigitur, & terræ in diu assuetos oculos in cælū attoilit. Sunt hæc quoque imitanda nobis, si salutis in Christo participes velimus fieri. Et in primis videre oportet, ne nos pudeat illum vocantem audire ac sequi, quod quàmplurimi hodie obstaculo esse solet, quò minus salui fiant. Sunt enim non pauci, qui etsi aurem sibi à Spiritu Christi vellicari sentiant, neq; etiā animo ad illū sequendū prorsus alieno sint, mundū tamē & vitæ prioris socios tàti faciunt, vt eos deserere & subitā morum mutationem facere ipsis indecorum & inhonestū videatur. Est autem pudor hic plus quàm præposterus, adhæc noxius & cū præsenti exitio coniunctus est, cùm pœnitentiæ
units.tr: Next, she receives the unexpected benefit of God offered to her with a ready and eager mind. There are two signs of this. The first is that, when called by Christ, she immediately comes to him, and is not ashamed of her strange and wretched gait before the whole congregation, so that she may draw nearer to him whom she had until then listened to with pleasure as he taught. The second is that, as soon as she hears the promise of salvation, she rises at once and lifts her eyes, long accustomed to the ground, up to heaven. These things too we must imitate, if we wish to become partakers of salvation in Christ. Above all we must take care that we are not ashamed to hear and follow him when he calls, which is often an obstacle to many today, preventing them from being saved. For there are not a few who, though they feel the Spirit of Christ tugging at their ear, and are not altogether unwilling in their mind to follow him, yet value the world and their former companions so highly that to abandon them and make a sudden change of life seems to them unseemly and dishonourable. This shame is more than foolish; moreover it is harmful and joined with present destruction, since it stands in the way of repentance

units.la: Officia eorum, qui seruari volunt.
units.tr: The duties of those who wish to be saved.

units.la: 1. Studiū verbi
units.tr: 1. The study of the Word.

units.la: 2. Alacritas ad dei & obedientia. tentia obstet, & à Christo unico salutis authore abducat. Non puduit olim Polemonem Atheniensem iuuenem, ebrietate & morum licentia infamem, subitò coronas conuiuales ex capite detrahere, corporis totius cultum mutare & morum emendationem polliceri, cum à conuiuio luxurioso rediens Xenocratem philosophum de temperantia & modestia differentem audiuisset. At hodie qui Christiani dici volunt, rem pudore dignam putant, si Christum ad vitae genus melius & salutarius ipsos vocantem audiant. Discant ergo omnes caecum hoc & peruersum iudicium corrigere, & cogitent se ad vitam caelestem conditos esse, cuius nobis doctor & author Christus est. Huius igitur voce audita à somno expergefiant, animos humi defixos attollant, & deserti huius mundi studijs caelestia meditentur, seque totos medico huic fidissimo accomodent: ne ab ipso oblatum aeternae salutis beneficium spreuisse videantur.
units.tr: 2. Readiness towards God and obedience. ...stands in the way and draws them away from Christ, the only author of salvation. Long ago Polemon the Athenian, a young man notorious for drunkenness and licentious conduct, was not ashamed to take the garlands from his head at once, to change his whole manner of dress and to promise amendment of life, when, returning from a riotous banquet, he heard the philosopher Xenocrates discourse on temperance and moderation. But today those who want to be called Christians think it a thing to be ashamed of if they hear Christ calling them to a better and more wholesome way of life. Let all therefore learn to correct this blind and perverse judgement, and let them consider that they were made for a heavenly life, of which Christ is our teacher and author. Let them therefore, on hearing his voice, awake from sleep, lift up their minds fixed to the ground, and, abandoning the pursuits of this deserted world, meditate on heavenly things, and entrust themselves wholly to this most faithful physician, so that they do not seem to have spurned the benefit of eternal salvation offered to them by him.

units.la: Postremò mulier, vbi salutem sibi restitutam sentit, Deum publice glorificat, & huic beneficiô illud omne transcribit. Et quidem inter eos hoc facit, quorum multos de Christo pessimè sentire & eum odisse non poterat ignorare. Ita vero Dei mandato obedit, qui vt se inuocari vult, & ipsum in inuocantibus opem pollicetur, ita ab ijsdem requirit, vt liberati ipsum dignis laudibus vehant. Est hoc nobis probè obseruandum, quibus salutem aeternam Christus attulit, cum plus quàm incuria sub tenebrarum potestate premeremur. Si enim hominibus beneficioribus gratiam bonam debemus, quanto magis Dei Filio, qui vt nobis subueniret extrema & tristissima quaeque perpeti voluit? Ideo gratiarum actionem publicam Dauid in Psalmis vouet, quoties in aliquo graviori periculo constitutus Dei opem implorat. Et facit illa ad fidei confessionem, cuius nemine pudere debet, qui aeternae vitae haeres fieri voluerit. Quam serio enim illam à nobis exigat Dominus, non vno loco audiuimus. At videndum simul, ne illa otiosa sit, & verbis nudis atque inanibus constet, sed vt vita atque mores nostri illi respondeant. Ita enim vere glorificatur Deus, quando nostro exemplo plures alij in illius cognitionem & ad veri cultus studium adducuntur. Faxit ille, vt horum meditatione accensi mulierem istam imitem ur, & salutis per Iesum Christum partae digni & legitimi haeredes efficiamur. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, when the woman feels her health restored, she glorifies God publicly and ascribes the whole matter to this benefit. She does this among those, many of whom she could not fail to know thought very badly of Christ and hated him. Thus she obeys the command of God, who wishes to be called upon, and promises his help to those who call upon him, and who requires of those so delivered that they bear him worthy praises. This we must carefully observe, we to whom Christ has brought eternal salvation, since we were oppressed under the power of darkness by more than mere carelessness. For if we owe good thanks to men who do us good, how much more to the Son of God, who was willing to suffer the most extreme and bitterest things so that he might help us? For this reason David in the Psalms vows public thanksgiving whenever he, placed in some greater danger, implores the help of God. And this serves the confession of faith, of which no one ought to be ashamed who wishes to become an heir of eternal life. For we have heard in more than one place how seriously the Lord requires it from us. But we must also take care that it is not idle, and does not consist of bare and empty words, but that our life and conduct correspond to it. For God is truly glorified when, by our example, many others are brought to the knowledge of him and to zeal for true worship. May he grant that, kindled by meditation on these things, we imitate that woman, and are made worthy and lawful heirs of the salvation obtained through Jesus Christ. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXXXVIII.

units.la: Respondens autem praefectus Synagogae, indignans quod Sabbato sanaret Iesus, dixit turbae: Sex dies sunt quibus oportet operari: his ergo venite & sanamini: & non die Sabbati. Respondit ergo ei Dominus & dixit: Hypocrita, vnusquisque vestrum Sabbato non ne soluit bouem suum aut asinum à praesepi, & ducit aquatum? Hanc autem filiam Abrahami quam vinxerat Satanas, ecce decem & octo annos, non oportuit vinculo isto solui die Sabbati? Et cum haec diceret, pudore afficiebantur omnes qui se opponebant ei: sed tota turba gaudebat super omnibus rebus, quae fiebant ab eo.
units.tr: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the crowd: "There are six days on which work ought to be done; come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day." The Lord answered him and said: "Hypocrite, does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his ass from the manger and lead it away to water? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, to be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?" When he said these things, all who opposed him were put to shame, but the whole crowd rejoiced at all the wonderful things done by him.

units.la: Postquam Dominus noster Iesus Christus Iudaeorum gentem & cum his simul omnes homines grauissimis rationibus & exemplo eo ipso tempore admitus ad poenitentiam hortatus est, mox miraculo in mulieris incurvae curatione facto docuit, unde nolus, qui natura steriles & ad bona opera inepti sumus, virtus illa obtingat, quae poenitentiae studium excitat & fecundos reddit, vt nostra professione dignos fructus feramus. Est enim quoad animam (vt nuper diximus) eadem omnium nostrum conditio quae huius mulieris fuit. Sed vt ea Christi verbo & contactu sanatur: ita nos quoque illius virtute restituimur, qui per Verbum se nobis offert, & ideo homo factus est, vt quaecunque in ipso sunt nobis communicaret. Itaque fide percepitis facit, vt ex verbi femine renati omnia possimus, quae prius nobis factu impossibilia erant. Hinc ergo bonorum fructuum fecundissima seges nascitur, vt animis ex terra & mundi huius sordibus erectis caelestia meditemur, & toti in hoc simus, vt Deus in dictis & factis nostris omnibus glorificetur. Hu Lucas in praesenti principis Synagogae de hoc Christi facto iudicium subiicit, in quo fici isti us sterilis exemplum proponitur, de quo nuper audiuimus, & in quo praeter folia, id est, externam pietatis & sanctimoniae fucatae speciem nihil inuenitur. At cum simul multa alia hic locus contineat, de singulis eius partibus ex ordine erit dicendum.
units.tr: After our Lord Jesus Christ had urged the nation of the Jews, and with them all people, to repentance by the weightiest reasons and by his own example at that very time, he then taught, by the miracle of healing the bent woman, whence we who are barren by nature and unfit for good works may obtain that power which stirs up the zeal for repentance and makes us fruitful, so that we may bear fruits worthy of our profession. For our condition as to the soul is (as we lately said) the same as that of this woman. But just as she was healed by Christ's word and touch, so we too are restored by his power, who offers himself to us through the Word, and who for this reason became man, that he might share with us whatever is in him. Thus, by faith received, the Word's seed makes us, being born again, able to do all those things which before were impossible for us. From this there springs the most fruitful harvest of good fruits, so that, our minds being lifted from the earth and the filth of this world, we may meditate on heavenly things, and make it our whole aim that God be glorified in all our words and deeds. Now Luke, in the present account of the ruler of the synagogue, adds his judgement on this deed of Christ, in which the example of that barren fig tree, of which we heard lately, is set forth, and in which, apart from leaves, that is, the outward appearance of piety and of counterfeit holiness, nothing is found. But since this passage also contains many other things at once, we shall speak of its individual parts in order.

units.la: Principio de principe Synagogae dicitur, quod Christi factum iniquè tulerit, & indignabundus populum corripuerit, qui illius opem die Sabbati quaerebat. Vidit ergo miraculum in muliere miseram editum, & illud nec dissimulare, nec negare, multò minus autem reprehendere aut damnare potest. Nam vt illustre erat diuinae virtutis & gratiae testimonium: ita per se pium & laude dignum est miseris succurrere, & malis diuturnis fatigatos atq; depressos leuare. Adhaec Christi virtutem veritus cum illo congredi non audet, neq; eum coram Ecclesia in disputationis arenam aut certamen protrahere. Itaq; ad rudem plebeculam conuersus eos accusat violati Sabbati, qui vt sanaren-tur ad illum conuenerant. Sex (inquit) dies sunt, quibus oportet operari: His ergo venite & sanamini, non autem die Sabbati. In quibus verbis imperitiam & ignorantiam ne istius nebulonis, an potius effrontem cum hypocrisi coniunctam audaciam mirari debeamus, nescio. Ignorantia enim est quod in solam literam Legis intentus, verum huius sensum non videt neq; intelligit. Stupiditas autem & caecitas dici meretur, quod inter opera seruilia & vera atq; salutaria pietatis exercitia, non potest discernere, quorum illa quidem prohibentur, haec autem nunquam magis quàm die Sabbati fieri debent. Et quid obsecro hic factum fuerat, quod inter opera prophana aut à Sabbati religione alienæ referri posset? In Synagogam venerat haec mulier, vt Dei verbum audiret, & publicis ecclesiae precibus interesset. A Christo item accersita ad ipsum progressa erat, vt ei obediret, qui tunc doctrinae officio fungebatur. Nec praeterea quicquam fecit, quam quod oblatum sibi ex gratiae salutis restitutae beneficium laeto & grato animo excepit, & Deo publicè gratias egit. Quid vero in his omnibus reprehensione dignum est? Aut an non haec sunt veri cultus exercitia, propter quae dies Sabbati in festum vtus & eius obseruatio nobis à Deo mandata est? Idem fateamur oportet, si Christi factum excutiamus, de quo non aliud dicitur, quàm quod docuerit, & mulierem solo verbo & manuum impositione sanarit. Fuit ergo hic Synagogae princeps ipso Mida & Murna stolidior, cum eius iudicio Sabbatum violent, qui Dei verbum vel docent, aut ad proximum laborantem manus amicas extendunt. At huic stoliditati atque ignorantiae audacia detestabilis coniuncta est, qua in populum inuehitur nulla reprehensione dignum, & ita proverbio vulgari fidem facit, quo nihil insolicia arrogantius siue audacius esse dicitur. Unde autem haec enata est? Ex religionis fuco & hypocrisi, qua istius loci homines iam pridem apud populum infelicem sibi authoritatem & in Ecclesiam summum ius atque imperium acquisierant. Quia enim homines fallebant, Deum quoque falli posse arbitrabantur: & proinde nihil ab se tam absurdum fieri sibi iam pridem persuaserant, quod simulata hac pietatis & religionis specie non posset defendi.
units.tr: First, it is said of the ruler of the synagogue that he took ill the deed of Christ and, indignant, rebuked the people who sought his help on the Sabbath day. He saw, therefore, the miracle wrought on the wretched woman, and he can neither conceal it, nor deny it, much less reprove or condemn it. For just as it was a splendid testimony to divine power and grace, so it is in itself pious and worthy of praise to help the miserable, and to relieve those worn out and depressed by long-standing troubles. Moreover, fearing the power of Christ, he does not dare to engage with him or to drag him before the Church into the arena of debate or contest. So, turning to the uneducated common folk, he accuses of breaking the Sabbath those who had come to him to be healed. "There are six days," he says, "on which work ought to be done. Come on those days, therefore, and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day." In these words I do not know whether we ought to marvel more at the ignorance and inexperience of this scoundrel, or rather at his brazen boldness joined with hypocrisy. For it is ignorance to be so intent on the mere letter of the Law that one does not see or understand its sense. But he deserves to be called stupid and blind, because he cannot distinguish between servile works and the true and saving exercises of piety; of these the former are forbidden, while the latter ought never to be done more than on the Sabbath day. And what, I ask, had been done here that could be reckoned among profane works, or as alien to the sanctity of the Sabbath? This woman had come into the synagogue to hear God's Word and to take part in the public prayers of the Church. Likewise, summoned by Christ, she had come forward to him in order to obey him, who at that time was discharging the office of teaching. Nor did she do anything else beyond receiving with a glad and grateful heart the benefit of restored salvation offered to her, and giving thanks to God publicly. What, indeed, in all these things is worthy of blame? Or are these not the true exercises of worship, for the sake of which the day of the Sabbath was appointed as a feast and its observance was commanded us by God? We must admit the same, if we examine Christ's deed, of which nothing else is said than that he taught and healed the woman by his word alone and the laying on of hands. So this ruler of the synagogue was more foolish than Midas and Murna, since in his judgement they violate the Sabbath who either teach God's Word or stretch out friendly hands to a neighbour in trouble. But with this stupidity and ignorance there is joined a detestable boldness, by which he attacks the people, though in nothing deserving reproof, and so he lends credence to the common proverb, which says that nothing is more arrogant or more audacious than ignorance. But whence did this arise? From the varnish of religion and from hypocrisy, by which the men of that place had long since acquired for themselves authority over the unhappy people, and the highest right and power over the Church. For since they deceived men, they thought that God too could be deceived; and accordingly they had long ago persuaded themselves that nothing could be so absurd for them to do that it could not be defended under this pretended appearance of piety and religion.

units.la: Est autem haec viua hypocrisis imago, ex qua omnium hypocritarum mores atque ingenium aestimare possumus. Nouerunt hi plerunque veritatem, cum ea vel inuitis se fe ingerat, & ipsos proprie conscientiae testimonio conuincat. Veruntamen non cedunt, eò quod suo bono & quaestui timent, quem ex pietatis ementita specie habent verberrimum. Itaque in illis maximè impletur, quod Isaias improbis verbi Dei contemptoribus denuntiat, fore vt audiant quidem auribus, sed non intelligant: & quando videant, neq; tamen agnoscant: quales hodie multos videmus, qui dum ex religione ludos fingunt theatricos, diuino Dei iudicio in crassam hanc & voluntatem caecitatem siue ignorantiam praecipitantur. Et accedit huic malo aliud, quod audaciae improbae ac impudenti metus coniunctus est, quem dissimulare non possunt, quantumuis ferociant. Solebant quidem Iudaei hypocritae magno cum fastu apud populum imperitum sese venditare, & coram illo nihil non audere. At idem cum Christo palam & aperio Marte congredi non audebant: sed vel omnem cum eo disputationem declinabant, vel ex insidijs per quaestiones captiosas illum agrè diebantur. Idem metus hodie etiam hypocritas exagitat. Quia enim in tenebris praecipuum & fortissimum sui regni praesidium esse sciunt, non possunt non timere veritatis lucem, quae omnem ignorantiae caliginem penetrat, & vulgi oculos illustrat, vt eos agnoscant, & agnitos contemnant atque detestentur, quos prius pro sanctis aut Semideis venerabantur. Itaq; si quod ab illa periculum imminere videnr, mox ad populum rudem atque rerum imperitum conuersi cum omnibus iis expoſtulant, qui veritatis doctrinae aures praebent, & de illa rectius sentire incipiunt: Adhaec anxie cauent, ne ad liberam & publicam disceptationem res perueniat. Fit iStud hodie tam aperte, ut nemo negare posit. Clamant enim ex omnibus pulpitis Monachi & sacrifici aduersus Euangelij doctrinam & populi leuitatem accusant, qui nouis istis doctoribus (sic de nobis loquuntur) atque haereticis locum det. At si quis vel ex doctorum numero, vel etiam ex vulgo se offerat, qui cum ipsis de tota hac controuersia colloquium aut disputationem publicam petat, mox fugiunt quaerunt, & congressum omnem deuitant, ne populus ampliorem habeat veritatis cognoscendae occasionem. Maior est autem Pontificum impudentia, qui ne causae cognitionem subterfugere videantur, Concilia in dicunt generalia, ad quae omnes tam Episcopos quam principes conuenire iubent, & in iis cuiq; libertum tutumō fore pollicentur, ut suae doctrinae & fidei rationem reddat. Interim vero iniquis praeiudicijs istud omne agunt, dum ad reddendam rationem eos vocant, quos iam ante nondum audiuerunt damnauerunt, & seipsos actores, testes & iudices faciunt: ita denique rem omnem agunt, ut veritatis cognitio ad vulgus nunquam possit peruenire: nec causae huius cognitionem vlli permittunt quam quos sibi prius iuramento peculiari obstrinxerunt. Ne quid tamen sceleris desit, in omnibus istis Dei zelum & diuini cultus atque publicae salutis studium praetexunt. Haec vero ita vrgent, ut omissis praecipuis capitibus ex quibus Dei cultus & hominum salus dependent, in externis modo haereant, quae inani potius ostentationi quam pietati seruiunt. Sic nostra ista de solo otio Sabbati agit, & hoc tale fingit, quo proprius quoq; Sabbati vsus in vniuersum aboleatur. Ita hodie Monachi & qui eorum partes sequuntur, ad imperitum vulgus ferias & dies sacros, ieiunia, castitatem, paupertatem voluntariam, carnis mortificationem, obedientiam & sexcenta alia perpetuo in ore habent: ista autem omnia non nisi externa & hypocritica specie metiuntur, & sub feriarum nomine vel otium ignauum, vel superstitiosum Diuorum cultum intelligunt: ieiunia autem inutili ciborum discrimine, castitatem impuro suo caelibatu, paupertatem quaestuosa & impudenti mendicitate, carnis castigationem ciliciorum vsu & alijs exercitijs corporalibus, obedientiam immunitate licentiosa definiunt, sub cuius praetextu parentibus, magistratibus legitimis, ecclesiarum pastoribus, omnibus deniq; debitum obsequium negant, quibus non Lex diuina obedire iubet. Nihil autem ijdem dicunt de ieiunio vero, quod per Isaiam nobis Deus commendat, nihil de otio sacro, quod nos vni Deo addicit: nihil de fide & castitate coniugali, quam patres olim in legitima liberorum procreatione obseruarunt, & quae thorum coniugalem omni pollutione liberat: nihil de communione bonorum Christiana, quae & suum cuiq; ius integrum seruat, & verae beneficentiae mater est: nihil de carnis mortificatione, quae gladio spiritus perficitur, nihil de obedientia vera, quae & Deo reddere iubet quae Dei sunt, & Caesari quae sunt Caesaris. Et hi omnes reuera fici sunt non steriles solum, verumetiam noxiae. Nam & terram Dominicae vineae occupant, in qua sibi summum imperium vendicarunt, & simul obstant ne alij fructus ferant, dum quosuis a vera pietate ad inanes ceremonias remittunt, quae neq; gloriae Dei neq; saluti hominum seruiunt. Quales fuisse Iudaeorum antistites supra audiuimus, qui cum clauem scientiae haberent, nec ipsi ingrediebantur in regnum caelorum, neq; alios ingredientes bant. Et tales nouissimis temporibus regnaturos esse Paulus praedixit, quos infelix mundus sibi ac cumulaturus sit, ut eorum traditionibus & blanditiis delibutus veritatis doctrinam non admittat, quae carni & morum licentiae assuetis durior & intolerabilior esse videtur. Quod cum multis in locis hodie fiat, neq; exempla desint eorum, qui ab illis decepti corpore & anima pereunt, eo magis nos adniti ac vigilare decet, ne idem nobis accidat. Neminem ergo titulorum magnificus splendor aut quantumuis speciosus sanctitatis fucus mouere debet, ut aliquem temere audiat & sequatur. Sed rem ipsam omnes considerent, & spiritus sive doctrinas omnes ad verbi Dei examen revocent. Quod si cum hoc pugnent, noxiae censeantur, & qui eas inuebunt, in eorum architectorum numero habeantur, qui pretiosum illum lapidem fundamenti reprobare audent.
units.tr: This is indeed a living image of hypocrisy, and from it we can judge the morals and character of all hypocrites. They commonly know the truth, even when it forces itself upon them against their will and convicts them by the testimony of their own conscience. Yet they do not give way, because they fear for their own advantage and their profit, which they draw most abundantly from the feigned appearance of piety. So what Isaiah threatens against the wicked despisers of God's word is fulfilled most fully in them: they will hear with their ears but not understand, and they will see but not perceive. We see many such people today who, while they make a theatre out of religion, are cast by God's just judgment into the gross blindness or ignorance of their own will. Another evil is joined to this: a shameless audacity mixed with a fear that they cannot hide, however fiercely they bluster. Admittedly the Jewish hypocrites used to show off with great pomp before the unlearned people and to dare anything in their sight. But when it came to Christ, they did not dare to meet him in open and fair combat. They either avoided all discussion with him or tried to wear him down with captious questions laid as traps. The same fear troubles hypocrites today. Since they know that their chief and strongest defence is darkness, they cannot help fearing the light of truth, which penetrates all the mist of ignorance and enlightens the eyes of the common people, so that they recognise those whom they had formerly revered as saints or demigods, and having recognised them, despise and detest them. So if they see any danger threatening from that light, they immediately turn to the rude and inexperienced people and complain against all who give an ear to the doctrine of truth and begin to think more rightly about it. Moreover, they anxiously take care that the matter does not come to free and public debate. Today this is done so openly that no one can deny it. From every pulpit the monks and priests cry out against the doctrine of the Gospel and accuse the people of levity for giving a hearing to these new teachers and heretics (so they speak of us). But if anyone, whether from the number of the learned or even from the common people, offers himself and asks for a conference or public disputation with them on this whole controversy, they at once flee, make excuses and avoid every meeting, so that the people will not have a greater opportunity of learning the truth. The impudence of the Pontiffs is greater still. So that they may seem not to shun the investigation of the cause, they speak of general councils, to which they command all bishops and princes to come, and they promise that in them each man will be free and safe to give an account of his doctrine and faith. Meanwhile they carry out all this with unjust prejudgment: they summon to give an account those whom they have already condemned without first hearing them, and they make themselves the parties, witnesses and judges. In the end they so manage the whole affair that knowledge of the truth can never reach the common people, and they allow no one to know the cause except those whom they have previously bound by a special oath. Yet, lest any wickedness be lacking, in all these things they put forward zeal for God, the worship of God and concern for public welfare. But they press these matters so hard that, leaving aside the principal heads on which the worship of God and the salvation of men depend, they cling only to external things, which serve empty show rather than piety. Thus our opponents make a fuss about the mere leisure of the Sabbath, and they invent something of that kind by which the proper use of the Sabbath is altogether abolished.
