So today the monks and those who follow their side always have in their mouths for the unlearned crowd holy days and feast days, fasts, chastity, voluntary poverty, mortification of the flesh, obedience and six hundred other things. But they measure all these things only by their outward and hypocritical appearance. Under the name of holy days they understand either idle leisure or superstitious worship of the saints. They define fasting by a useless distinction of foods, chastity by their impure celibacy, poverty by a profitable and shameless begging, mortification of the flesh by the wearing of hair shirts and other bodily exercises, and obedience by a licentious exemption, under the pretext of which they deny due submission to parents, to lawful magistrates, to the pastors of the churches and, finally, to all those whom the divine Law commands us to obey. Yet these same men say nothing of the true fasting which God commends to us through Isaiah, nothing of the holy rest which binds us to the one God alone, nothing of the faith and conjugal chastity which the fathers of old kept in the lawful procreation of children and which frees the marriage bed from all defilement, nothing of Christian fellowship in goods, which both preserves the full right of each man and is the mother of true beneficence, nothing of the mortification of the flesh, which is accomplished by the sword of the Spirit, nothing of true obedience, which bids us render to God the things that are God's and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. And all these men are truly fig trees, not only barren but even harmful. For they occupy the soil of the Lord's vineyard, in which they have claimed for themselves supreme power, and at the same time they hinder others from bearing fruit, while they turn people away from true piety to empty ceremonies, which serve neither the glory of God nor the salvation of men. We have heard above what kind of leaders the Jews had, who, though they held the key of knowledge, neither entered the kingdom of heaven themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter to do so. And Paul foretold that such men would reign in the last times, whom the wretched world will heap up for itself, so that, steeped in their traditions and flatteries, it will not admit the doctrine of truth, which seems harder and more intolerable to those accustomed to the flesh and to licence of morals. Since this happens in many places today, and examples are not lacking of those who, deceived by them, perish in body and soul, we ought all the more to strive and be watchful that the same does not happen to us. Therefore let no one be moved by the splendid magnificence of titles or by whatever showy veneer of holiness, so as to hear and follow anyone rashly. Rather, let everyone consider the thing itself, and bring all spirits or doctrines to the test of the word of God. If they clash with this, let them be judged harmful, and those who bring them in should be counted among those builders who dare to reject that precious stone of the foundation.

units.la: Porro ad Christum veniamus, qui simplici plebi, quam insolens iste princeps Synagogae suae dulcis dictus protelare & procul ab illo arcere conabatur, egregie patrocinatus est, & huius nequitiam atq; iudicij temeritatem probe detexit. Nec enim ille suos vnquam deserit, quisquis tandem sit qui eis molestiam exhibet. Nam fidelis pastor nihil acerbius esse putat & intolerabilius, quam si qui oues ues ab ipso abducere conentur. Ita alibi discipulos tuetur, quos Pharisaei accusabat, quod illotis manibus ad mensam accubuissent. Simili fide postea Mariae suum patrocinium praebuit, cum ab ipsis Apostolis temere reprehenderetur, eo quod maximi pretij unguento caput eius & corpus totum perfudisset. Debet hoc fidos Christi seruos consolari, quando in grauissimus periculus famae aut vitae suae, se omni humano praesidio destitutos esse videt. Nam vbi pater meus & mater mea (inquit Dauid) me deserunt, Dominus adest mihi. Neque patronum alium sibi anxiè quaerere debent, quibus spiritum sanctum paracleti & aduocati loco aeternus Dei filius destinauit. Simul autem omnes Ecclesiarum pastores exemplum hoc officij sui admonere debent: ne videlicet personatos illos alienae fidei dominatores in rudem populum grassari patiantur, sed lupos ouillis pellibus tectos liberè arguant, seq; improbis eorum conatibus opponant. Sed Christum ipsum loquentem audiamus.
units.tr: But let us come to Christ, who nobly defended the simple common people, whom that insolent ruler of his synagogue, called gentle, tried to push aside and keep far from him, and who thoroughly exposed his wickedness and the rashness of his judgment. For he never deserts his own, whoever it is that causes them trouble. A faithful shepherd thinks nothing more bitter and intolerable than when anyone tries to lead his sheep away from him. So elsewhere he protected the disciples whom the Pharisees accused because they sat down to eat with unwashed hands. Later, with the same faithfulness, he gave his protection to Mary, when she was rashly rebuked by the Apostles themselves because she had poured very costly ointment over his head and whole body. This ought to comfort the faithful servants of Christ, when they see themselves deprived of all human help in the greatest danger to their reputation or their life. For, as David says, "When my father and my mother forsake me, the Lord takes me up." Nor ought they anxiously to seek another patron, since the eternal Son of God has appointed the Holy Spirit in the place of Paraclete and Advocate. At the same time all the pastors of the churches ought to be reminded of this example of their office: that they should not allow those masked lords of another's faith to rage against the simple people, but should boldly expose those wolves covered in sheepskins and set themselves against their wicked attempts. But let us hear Christ himself speaking.

units.la: Hypocrita (inquit) vnusquisque vestrum Sabbato nonne soluit bouem suum aut asinum à praesepi, & ducit aquatum? Hanc autem filiam Abrahami, quam vinxerat Satanas ecce decem & octo annos, non oportuit soluì die Sabbati? Primò hypocritam dicit, & ita eum maximi sceleris accusat. Quia enim hypocrita est, qui specie falsa alium sese simulat, quàm reuera sit, perinde hoc est, ac si mendacem dixisset. At mendacij pater est diabolus, & huius filij sunt, quotquot mendacij studènt & veritatem oderunt. Et hoc quidem de omni mendaciorum genere dici potest. Quòd si qui verò hypocritae sunt in iis, quae ad religionem spectant, & Dei nomine ad velanda mendacia sua abutuntur, horum scelus cum summa impietate coniunctum est. Nam tales Spiritui sancto mentiuntur, & (quod nemo vir bonus ferre potest) suis fraudibus nomen Dei praetexunt. Poterat ergo Christus conuitiator videri, quando hoc nomine eum compellat, cuius summa erat in illa synagoga authoritas. Sed non statim conuitium dicit, qui ex officio vnumquemque eum dicit qui est. Et ministrorum verbi est peccata arguere, & vnumquemque in suijpsius cognitionem inducere, vt vitia sua detestari discant, & poenitentiam seriam meditentur. Id verò in hypocritis omnino fieri oportet, qui simulata pietatis & sanctimoniae specie sibipsis quidem delitias faciunt; alijs autem multis imponunt, qui ipsorum cum doctrina tum exemplo seducuntur. Itaque huic etiam tarnam detrahi necesse fuit, vt magis animo perculleretur, & auditores eius authoritati minus tribui debere intelligeret. Et ad monentur hoc exemplo omnes Ecclesiarum pastores, qua ratione ipsi quoq; eos tractare debeant, qui cum doctrinae & religionis primi antistites haberi volunt, Christo tanquam & veritati sese impudenter opponunt. Sunt hi liberè arguendi, ne qui illorum authoritate & magnifico titulorum splendore seducti pereant. Quod enim hic fecit Dominus, hoc eum saepe aliàs fecisse scimus, & idem ante illum ex spiritus impulsu Prophetae fecerunt, quorum omnium exemplum Apostoli imitati sunt, quibus non satis fuit sui seculi impostores arguisse, nisi de iis etiam admonerent, quos nouissimos temporibus exorituros esse sciebant. Hos autem suis nominibus ita descripserunt, vt nihil omiserint, quod eos pijs inuisos & exosos posset reddere. Nam magnum illum Christi aduersarium Paulus filium perditionis dicit, & hominem peccati, qui diabolica virtute instructus sese exaltaturus sit supra omne numen. Et alibi eos, qui coniugij & ciborum nobis à Deo concessorum vsum prohibent, daemoniorum doctrinâ annuntiare scribit. Nimium ergo iniqui sunt, qui hodie dicendi leges fidei Euangelij ministris praescribunt, & indignum putant, si qui ista faciunt, liberius arguantur. Nam nō solum in Dei verbum & spiritum sanctum sibi ius sumunt (quae plus quam diabolica est arrogantia) ve rumetiam populum Christianum ab interitu eripi nolunt, & scandalum ponunt caeci, quorum institutioni potius & saluti consulere debebant.
units.tr: "Hypocrite," he says, "does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his ass from the manger and lead it to water? Ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, be loosed on the Sabbath day?" First he calls them hypocrites, and so charges them with the greatest wickedness. For a hypocrite is one who falsely pretends to be other than he really is, which amounts to calling them liars. But the devil is the father of lies, and all who devote themselves to lying and hate the truth are his children. This may be said of every kind of lie. But if there are hypocrites in matters that concern religion, who abuse the name of God to cover their lies, their crime is joined with the greatest impiety. For such people lie to the Holy Spirit and, what no good man can bear, they put the name of God in front of their frauds. Christ might therefore seem a reviler when he addresses them by this name, since they held the highest authority in that synagogue. But he does not at once utter a reproach; he calls each person by what he is, as his office requires. It is the task of ministers of the Word to rebuke sins and to lead each person to self-knowledge, so that they learn to detest their faults and seriously consider repentance. This must certainly be done with hypocrites, who, under a pretended appearance of piety and holiness, indulge themselves, yet deceive many others, who are led astray by their teaching and their example. Therefore it was also necessary that this woman's ruler be stripped of his mask, so that he might be struck more deeply in mind and his hearers might understand that his authority ought to count for less. By this example all ministers of the churches are also admonished how they themselves should deal with those who wish to be regarded as the chief leaders of teaching and religion, yet shamelessly set themselves against Christ and the truth. Such men must be rebuked openly, lest those who are misled by their authority and the splendour of their grand titles perish. For what the Lord did here, we know he did often on other occasions, and the same was done before him by the prophets, moved by the Spirit. The apostles imitated all this, and they did not think it enough to have refuted the impostors of their own age, but warned also against those whom they knew would arise in the last times. These they described by their names in such a way that they omitted nothing that might make them hateful and odious to the godly. For Paul calls that great adversary of Christ the son of perdition and the man of sin, who, endowed with diabolical power, will exalt himself above every divinity. And elsewhere he writes that those who forbid the use of marriage and of foods granted to us by God teach the doctrines of demons. Therefore they are far too unjust who today prescribe to the ministers of the gospel of faith the rules of how they must speak, and think it unworthy that, if such men do these things, they should be rebuked more freely. For they not only claim for themselves a right over the word of God and the Holy Spirit (an arrogance more than diabolical), but they are also unwilling that the Christian people be snatched from destruction, and they place a stumbling block, blind as they are, when they ought rather to have cared for the instruction and salvation of those people.

units.la: Sed pergit Dominus & causam suam tuetur, docens eiusmodi operibus nequaquam violari Sabbati religionem: Id autem exemplo vulgari & ex quotidiano vsu petito probat. Vnusquisque vestrum die Sabbati (inquit) soluit iumenta sua à praesepi, & aquatum ducit, neque id Lex diuina prohibet, eò quòd sic fieri necesse sit, & necessitati lex non sit posita: Cur ergo accusor ego, qui filiam Abrahami decem & octo annorum spatio diaboli vinculis astrictam solui hodie, vt dulcissimis consolationis diuinae aquis tandem ipsa quoque recreetur? Amplificatur verò argumentum hoc comparatione. Nam inter se conferuntur bos siue asina & filia Abrahami: deinde capistrù, quo iumenta ad praesepe astringuntur, & vincula diaboli. At quàm ingens discrimen sit inter iumenta & Abrahami filios, id est, electos Dei, nemo non nouit. Imò ne verbis quidem exprimi potest, quantum
units.tr: But the Lord goes on and defends his cause, teaching that the observance of the Sabbath is in no way violated by works of this kind. He proves this by a common example, drawn from everyday practice: "Does not each one of you on the Sabbath (he says) loose his ox or his ass from the manger and lead it to water? And the divine Law does not forbid this, because it is necessary to do so, and the law is not laid down for necessity. Why then am I blamed, who on this day have loosed a daughter of Abraham, bound for eighteen years by the bonds of the devil, so that at last she too may be refreshed with the sweetest waters of divine consolation?" The argument is strengthened by a comparison. Ox or ass is set against the daughter of Abraham, and the halter by which the animals are tied to the manger is set against the bonds of the devil. But how great the difference is between beasts and the sons of Abraham, that is, the elect of God, everyone knows. Indeed, it cannot even be expressed in words how much

units.la: Christus suum factum tuetur
units.tr: Christ defends his deed

units.la: vel minimus ex filiorum Dei numero omnibus animantibus praestet, cum pro illis vnigenitus Dei Filius mortem infamem subire & proprium sanguinem effundere dignatus sit. Similiter non minus fere inter se differunt capistrum & vincula Satanae. Illo enim iumenta ad praesepe alligantur, vbi pabulum suum habent, & ideo alligantur, ne in stabulo inter se pugnent & se mutuo laedant. At Satan suis vinculis ideo astringit homines, vt ab Ecclesiae praesepi & Verbi Dei pabulo retrahat, & ipsdem impatientia, murmuris, scelerum denique maximorum ansam praebeat, quibus exitium tam sibi ipsis quam aliis accersant. Ex his autem efficacissime concluditur: Si iumentum a praesepi soluere & aquatum ducere licet die Sabbati, multo magis homine ad Dei imaginem conditum & qui Ecclesiae Dei membrum est, Sabbato licebit vinculis diaboli liberare, neque in eo cunctari debent, quibus hoc faciendi facultas offertur, quando in eiusmodi causa omnis mora pernitiosa est. Simile argumentum Christus Matthaei duodecimo capite adducit, vbi hominem, cuius manus exaruerat, die Sabbati curauit: & infra capite decimo quarto tale quid audiemus, vbi hydropici Sabbato curati historia describitur.
units.tr: the least of the sons of God excels all living creatures, since the only-begotten Son of God deigned to undergo an infamous death and to pour out his own blood for them. Likewise the halter and the bonds of Satan differ not much less from one another. For beasts are tied to the manger where they have their fodder, and they are tied so that they do not fight among themselves in the stable and harm one another. But Satan binds men with his chains so that he may draw them away from the manger of the Church and the food of the Word of God, and so that by impatience, murmuring, and finally the greatest wickedness he may provide an occasion of ruin both for themselves and for others. From this the following is most effectively concluded: if it is lawful on the Sabbath day to loose an ox from the manger and lead it to water, much more will it be lawful on the Sabbath to free from the bonds of the devil a man made in the image of God and a member of the Church of God. Nor should those to whom the opportunity of doing this is offered delay in it, since in a cause of this kind every delay is harmful. Christ brings forward a similar argument in the twelfth chapter of Matthew, where he healed on the Sabbath the man whose hand had withered; and below, in the fourteenth chapter, we shall hear something of the same kind, where the story of the dropsical man healed on the Sabbath is described.

units.la: Sed priusquam de huius quaestionis aut controuersiae statu plura dicamus, diligenter obseruari debet Christi locutio, qua filiam Abraham dicit mulierem, quam diabolus quoad corpus per annos decem & octo suis vinculis astrictam habuerat. Ita enim dicitur, non quod secundum carnis generationem ex Abraham genere nata esset, sed ad electionis gratiam respicit Dominus, qua illam Pater caelestis inter germanos Abrahami filios & regni sui haeredes aeterno suo consilio adoptarat. Ad eundem modum Paulus non vno loco eos, qui ex gentibus crediderant, primum sub potestate tenebrarum, adhaec a Republica Israelis abalienatos, extraneos a pactis promissionum & Dei expertes in mundo fuisse scribit, cum ijdem illi tunc quoque apud Deum in electorum numero essent. Et hoc illud est, quod Christus apud Ioannem se oues alias, praeter Iudaeos, habere ait, quas vocari oporteat: ita nimirum electos ex gentibus vocans, qui tunc a societate Ecclesiae adhuc alieni erant. Non ergo ex praesenti statu de quoquam temere pronuntiandum est, cum quo loco apud Deum sit nescimus. Multo minus damnandi statim sunt, quos a diabolo exagitari & vexari videmus. Nam hoc etiam electus suis certo consilio accidere Deus patitur, quando vel carnis eorum petulantia coercere, vel fidem exercere, vel etiam aliis eos in exemplum proponere decreuit. Patet hoc in huius mulieris historia, in qua etsi Satan tanto tempore summum imperium habere visus sit, eadem tamen in Christi manu fuit, qui ne quid anima eius pateretur, eam fideliter custodiuit. Simile est Iobi exemplum & multorum aliorum, quos Scriptura nobis proponunt. Non temere ergo Apostoli olim homines contumaces & impaenitentes in Satanae potestate tradebant ad carnis interitum, vt spiritus seruaretur in die Domini, sicuti in Corinthio illo incesto videmus factum fuisse. Et quamuis hodie Ecclesiarum ministri non armati sine simili aut eadem Spiritus virtute, Deus tamen illud ipsum quotidie facit, dum morbis diuturnis aut aliis flagellis, in quibus Satana ministro vtitur, eos domat & frangit, qui incurabili vel malitia vel socordia ad exitium tendunt. Tunc autem nobis patientia & sano fidei iudicio opus est, ne nos ideo a Deo desertos & Satanae omnino mancipatos esse putemus. Nam etsi interdum Dominus omnem diutius differat, interea tamen spiritu suo nobis adest, neque nos supra vires tentari patitur, & quando salus nostra id exigit, omni flagello liberatos in integrum restituit.
units.tr: But before we say more about the state of this question or controversy, the manner of Christ's speaking must be carefully observed, in which he calls the woman a daughter of Abraham, whom the devil had kept bound in her body with his chains for eighteen years. For he says this not because she was born of the lineage of Abraham according to the generation of the flesh, but he looks to the grace of election, by which the heavenly Father, in his eternal counsel, had adopted her among the true sons of Abraham and heirs of his kingdom. In the same way Paul, in more than one place, writes that those who came to faith from the Gentiles were first under the power of darkness, moreover alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, and without God in the world, although those same people were then also among the number of the elect with God. And this is what Christ means in John when he says that he has other sheep, besides the Jews, which must be called: thus he calls the elect from the Gentiles, who as yet were strangers to the fellowship of the Church. Therefore we must not rashly pronounce anyone's standing with God from his present state, since we do not know what place he has with God. Much less are those whom we see harassed and vexed by the devil to be condemned at once. For God also allows this to happen to his elect by a certain counsel, when he has decided either to restrain their wantonness of the flesh, or to exercise their faith, or even to set them before others as an example. This is evident in the history of this woman, in whom, although Satan seemed for so long a time to hold supreme power, she nevertheless remained in the hand of Christ, who faithfully guarded her so that nothing might harm her soul. Similar is the example of Job and of many others whom Scripture sets before us. Therefore the apostles did not rashly hand over stubborn and impenitent men in former times to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord, as we see was done in the case of that incestuous man at Corinth. And although today the ministers of the churches do not act with a similar or the same power of the Spirit, God nevertheless does this same thing every day, when, by lingering sicknesses or other scourges, in which he uses Satan as his servant, he subdues and breaks those who are heading for ruin through incurable malice or carelessness. At such times we need patience and a sound judgment of faith, lest we think that we have been deserted by God and wholly handed over to Satan. For although the Lord sometimes delays his help for a long time, yet in the meantime he is present with us by his Spirit, and he does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, and when our salvation requires it, he frees us from every scourge and restores us to wholeness.

units.la: Porro verum Sabbati vel diei Dominici vsum paucis hisce verbis Christus tradit. Est huius institutio vetustissima, vt quae ad primam mundi creationem refertur, & hominis lapsum praecesserit, nec dubium est quin illum prisci patres religiosissime obseruarint. In Lege deinceps Deus illius obseruationem saepissime & magna cum gravitate commendat, adeo vt in eius transgressores poenam capitis decernat. Prophetae item Sabbati violationem inter excidij Hierosolymitani & Babylonici exilij causas numerant. Quod Nehemiam mouit, vt post reditum ab illo exilio & vrbe iam rursus instaurata hunc sanctissime coli vellet, & eiusdem obseruationem contra vicinos, armata quoque manu, nisi ab eius prophanatione abstinerent, se vindicaturum esse minitaretur. Sed neque Legis diuinae authoritas, neque principum piorum & fidelium doctorum diligentia atque seueritas vllu seculis efficere potuit, quin semper peccatum fit aut superstitione aut prophano contemptu. Et Christi tempore per humanas traditiones Rabbini Iudaeorum rem eo deduxerant, vt vniuersa Sabbati obseruatio in ceremonijs & praeceptiunculis non minus ridiculis quam inutilibus consisteret, adeo vt nefas putarent eo die pulicem saltantem capere. Inter Christianos autem homines in superstitionis locum prophanus contemptus subijt: nimirū quòd qui ex gentibus oriundi dies festos prius conuiuijs, choreis & ludis transfegerant, hoc ipsum diebus Dominicis sibi licere putarent. Quare multa in Patrum sermonibus leguntur, quibus pestulantia illam accusant: & extant leges Imperatoriae, quibus eadem seuerissimè prohibetur. Quid hodie fiat, nemo pius non videt, & quidem non sine dolore. Est ergo hic locus multa consideratione dignissimus, quo verum & proprium Sabbati vsum Christus tradit: qui est: vt eo die tam nosipsos quàm alios soluamus à vinculis diaboli. Sunt haec potissimum peccata, quibus homines ille constringit, vt ad pietatis exercitia neq; pedes neq; manus mouere, imò ne oculos quidem ad caelestium bonorum contemplatione attollere possint. Soluuntur vincula ista per Verbi Dei studium & preces ad Deum ardentes. His etiam pietas & beneficentia atque dilectio fraterna excitatur. Et haec praecipua otij huius sacri ratio est, vt verbo Dei & precibus vacare possint, quos alijs diebus communis omnium hominum necessitas circa ea, quae corpori curando & rei domesticae seruiunt, occupatos tenet. At si nostrorum temporum mores spectemus, nunquâ diabolo magis quàm hoc die seruitur, dum illius vincula plerique sibijpsis accerjunt, & simul alijs eadem inijcere iata-gunt. Alij enim auaritiae laqueu conflricti rationes suas ineunt, quando coetibus sacris adesse debe-bant, vel mercantur, vel debita ab alijs exigunt, simulq; seruos & ancillas in aliquo opere detinent, ne vel vnū diem otiosos alere cogantur. Alij libidine irretiti scorta sectantur, & tunc maximè cor-pus & animam pollunt, quando toti sanctimonia studere debebant. Plerique Bacchofestum agût, qui mos ita obtinuit, vt nunquâ plures temulenti & ebrij conspiciantur, quàm diebus Dominicis, et tunc maximè hospitia publica, tabernae meritoriae, domus priuatae vino madent, incondito ebrio-rum clamore & cantu strepunt, qui plerunque in rixas, pugnas & caedes desinit. Qui verò optimi sunt, ij vel aucupio sese exercent, vel ferarum & leporum vulpiumque lustra indagant, aut ignaui domi desidēt, vt neque conciones sacras adeant, neque Scripturas ipsi legant, & nulla prorsus ope-rum atq; beneficiorum Dei meditatione animos recreent. Sunt haec tam manifesta, vt extremae im-pudentiae sit ea negare. Non est ergo, quòd calamitatum tam publicarum quàm priuatarum, quae nos vndiq; vrgent, causas admiremur aut curiosius inquiramus, quando haec sola ad prouocandam Dei iram potest sufficere.
units.tr: Now Christ teaches the true use of the Sabbath, or the Lord's Day, in a few words. Its institution is very ancient: it goes back to the first creation of the world and preceded man's fall, and there is no doubt that the holy fathers observed it most devoutly. Later, in the Law, God commends its observance very often and with great solemnity, so much so that he decrees the death penalty for those who break it. The prophets likewise count the violation of the Sabbath among the causes of the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Babylonian exile. This moved Nehemiah, after his return from that exile and when the city had been restored, to want the day kept most holy, and he threatened that, with armed force if need be, he would avenge its profanation against his neighbours unless they abstained from profaning it. But neither the authority of the divine Law nor the diligence and severity of godly princes and faithful teachers has in any age been able to prevent sin, which always takes the form either of superstition or of profane contempt. In Christ's time the Rabbis of the Jews, through human traditions, had brought the matter to such a point that the whole observance of the Sabbath consisted in ceremonies and little precepts no less ridiculous than useless, so much so that they thought it a sin to catch a dancing flea on that day. Among Christians, on the other hand, profane contempt has taken the place of superstition: namely, because those who were born of the Gentiles had previously spent their feast days in banquets, dances and games, they thought they might do the same on the Lord's Days. Hence many passages in the sermons of the Fathers are read which accuse this licence, and there are imperial laws which most severely forbid it. What happens today no godly person fails to see, and indeed not without grief. This passage, then, is most worthy of close consideration, in which Christ teaches the true and proper use of the Sabbath, which is this: that on that day we loose both ourselves and others from the bonds of the devil. Chief among the sins by which he binds men are those which so hold them that they can move neither feet nor hands to the exercises of piety, nor even lift their eyes to the contemplation of heavenly goods. These bonds are loosed through zealous study of the Word of God and fervent prayer to God. By these also piety, beneficence and brotherly love are roused. And this is the principal reason for this holy rest: that those whom the common necessity of all men on other days keeps occupied with caring for the body and household affairs may be free for the Word of God and for prayer. But if we look at the customs of our times, the devil is never served more than on this day, while most people bring his chains upon themselves and eagerly try to put the same on others. For some, caught in the snare of greed, make their calculations when they ought to be present at the sacred assemblies: they either trade, or demand debts from others, and at the same time keep their male and female servants at some work, so that they are not forced to keep even one day idle. Others, entangled by lust, pursue prostitutes, and then they most defile body and soul when they ought to be wholly given to holiness. Many keep the festival of Bacchus, a custom that has so taken hold that more drunkards and inebriates are never seen than on the Lord's Days; and then especially the public inns, the brothels and private houses drip with wine and resound with the disorderly shouting and singing of the drunkards, which usually ends in quarrels, fights and slaughter. Those who are the best of them either take up fowling, or hunt the lairs of wild beasts, hares and foxes, or sit idle at home, so that they neither attend the sacred sermons nor read the Scriptures themselves, and refresh their minds with no meditation at all on the works and benefits of God. These things are so obvious that it is the height of shamelessness to deny them. There is therefore no reason for us to marvel at, or to inquire too curiously into, the causes of calamities, both public and private, which press on us on every side, since these alone may be enough to provoke the anger of God.

units.la: Restat vt totius negotij finem aut exitum videamus, quem his verbis Lucas describit. Et cùm hac diceret, pudore afficiebantur omnes, qui se opponebat ei: sed tota turba gaudebat super omnibus gloriosis rebus, quae fiebant ab eo. Proponuntur hic nobis duo hominum genera. Vnum est aduersa riorum Christi, quorum ducem aut antesignanum dicere possumus Principem synagogae, qui primus hanc litem mouerat. Hi simul omnes pudore afficiuntur, quando se publicè & coram toto populo ita conuincì audiunt, vt nihil possint respondere. Et sanè merito illos suae stoliditatis pudet, qui ne id quidem potuerunt intelligere, de quo proprijs exemplis quotidie admonebantur. Sed quamuis ipsos pudeat, non tamen cedunt, sed Christum pertinaci atque incurabili odio prosequuntur, quae cau-sa fuit, quòd omnia eius dicta & facta subinde calumniati sunt. Est hoc proprium hypocritu: Quia enim gloriae priuatae studio tument, mox pudorem abstergunt, & quamuis occasionem auide arri-piunt, qua veritatis lucem obscurari posse sperant. Alterum genus est hominum vulgarium, qui gaudent audito Christo, & ei publicè congratulantur, quòd hypocritae impudentem arrogantiā tam feliciter repressērit. Apparet in hoc exemplo quanta sit vis diuinae Veritatis. Nam etsi hostes ha-beat acerrimos, potentia & authoritate instructos & qui cedere ipsi nesciunt, eosdem tamen intra conscientias suas conuincere possunt, vt inuitos quoque suae ignorantiae & temeritatis pudeat: vt eorum confusione atque ignominia gaudeant, qui illos prius pro Dijs adorare solebant. Est ergo in felicissima hypocritarum conditio, quia dum se iam regnū obtinuisse putant, subitò detegitur ipsorum fraudibus, eos etiam sibi inimicos esse sentiunt, à quibus paulò ante colebantur. Exempla huius gene-ris hodie passim cernuntur. Triumphant quidem Episcopi & praesules personati, dum nemo est qui se ipsis opponat: quàm primùm verò luce veritatis arguuntur, mox aduersus eos omnis loci & ordinis homines conclamant, & quod antea mente repostū celabant, odiū detegunt. Nimium ergo stulti sunt, qui vulgi momentaneo fauore decepti veritatem abs se vinci aut opprimi posse sperant. Discant potius omnes huic cedere & gloriam Deo dare, quando se intra animos suos conuinci sen-
units.tr: It remains for us to see the end or outcome of the whole affair, which Luke describes in these words: "And when he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him." Two kinds of men are set before us here. The first is the adversaries of Christ, whose leader or chief spokesman we may call the ruler of the synagogue, who first stirred up this quarrel. All of them are put to shame when they hear themselves so publicly and before the whole people convicted that they can make no answer. And certainly they deserve to be ashamed of their stupidity, since they could not even understand what they were being taught daily by their own examples. Yet although they are ashamed, they do not give way, but pursue Christ with stubborn and incurable hatred; the reason was that they kept slandering all his words and deeds. This is the mark of hypocrites: because they swell with desire for private glory, they soon wipe away their shame, and though they eagerly seize any opportunity by which they hope the light of truth may be obscured. The other kind of men are the common people, who rejoice when they hear of Christ and openly congratulate him, because he has so happily repressed the shameless arrogance of the hypocrites. In this example the power of divine Truth appears. For although it has most bitter enemies, armed with power and authority, who do not know how to yield, it can nonetheless convict them within their own consciences, so that even against their will they are ashamed of their ignorance and rashness, and the common people rejoice at the confusion and disgrace of those whom they had formerly been accustomed to worship as gods. The condition of hypocrites is therefore most unhappy in this respect: while they think they have already secured their kingdom, they are suddenly exposed by their own frauds, and they feel that those by whom they were honoured a little before are now their enemies. Examples of this kind are seen everywhere today. Bishops and masked prelates indeed triumph as long as no one opposes them; but as soon as they are convicted by the light of truth, men of every place and rank immediately cry out against them, and they reveal the hatred that they had previously hidden and kept buried in their minds. Those, then, are very foolish who, deceived by the momentary favour of the crowd, hope that the truth can be overcome or suppressed by them. Rather let all learn to yield to it and to give glory to God, when they feel themselves convicted within their own minds; let them finally rejoice when they see Jesus Christ superior to his enemies. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: Effectus actio-nis huius. tiunt: gaudeant denique, quando Iesum Christum hostibus suis superiorem esse vident. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The effect of this action. Let them at last rejoice, when they see that Jesus Christ is superior to his enemies. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 139.

units.la: Dixit autem Iesus: Cui rei simile est Regnum Dei? & cui illud assimilabo? Simile est grano sinapis, quod acceptum quispiam misit in hortu suum: & creuit, & euasit in arborem magnam, & volucres caeli nidulati sunt in eius ramis. Et rursum dixit: Cui rei assimilabo Regnum Dei? Simile est fermento, quod acceptum mulier condidit in farinae satis tribus, vsquequo fermentaretur tota. Et transibat singulas urbes & vicos, docens & iter faciens Hierosolymam.
units.tr: And Jesus said, "To what is the Kingdom of God like? And to what shall I liken it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden; and it grew and became a large tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches." And again he said, "To what shall I liken the Kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened." And he went through the cities and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem.

units.la: Inter Dei opera nullum praestantius, illustrius atque admirabilius est, quam quod Filium suum unigenitum & dilectum nobis Seruatorem dedit, qui & mortis suae merito nos redemit, & salutem sanguinis sui pretio partam per Euangelium omnibus liberalissimè offert. Idem tamen hoc omne ita administrauit, ut nihil contemptius aut ignobilius videri queat, si res humani iudicij calculo aestimetur. Nam ut Dei Filius Iesus Christus, ex virgine pauperecula in stabulo nasci voluit & in terris pauper atque contemptissimus vixit: Ita Euangelij sui doctrina non solum simplex & nullis verborum phaleris commendabilis, sed propter hostes quos habet acerrimos & qui hanc comitantur motus atque turbas, plerisque noxia & proinde odio digna putatur. Offendit hoc multos hodie, nec dubium est, quin olim quoque multi offensi fuerint, quando ipsum Dominum potentissimus quibusque exosum esse, & eius doctrinam quotidie oppugnari videbant. Itaque cum nuper quidam Synagogae princeps sese ei opposuisset, & populum quoq; abstterrere conatus esset, ne apud illum opem suae salutem quaererent, ex eo occasione sumpta parabolas binas proponit, quibus populo & auditoribus suis animum facit, ne humilibus hisce Regni sui exordijs offendantur, neq; etiam hostium minis aut conatibus sese perterrefieri sinant. Docet enim eam esse Euangelicae doctrinae vim, ut praeter omne hominum expectationem succrescat, & inuitus aduersarijs omnibus sese quam latissime diffundat. Est ergo consolatio ista nobis etiam hodie plus quam necessaria, quando Antichristus omnes vires atque extremos conatus exerit, ut surgentem Euangelij lucem extinguat, aut saltem intra angusti anguli fines concludat.
units.tr: Among the works of God none is more excellent, more illustrious or more admirable than that he gave us his only-begotten and beloved Son as Saviour, who by the merit of his death redeemed us, and who through the Gospel offers to all the salvation won at the price of his blood most generously. Yet he has so administered all this that nothing can seem more contemptible or ignoble, if the matter is weighed by the reckoning of human judgment. For just as the Son of God, Jesus Christ, chose to be born in a stable of a poor little virgin and lived on earth poor and most despised, so the doctrine of his Gospel is not only plain and commendable without any verbal ornaments, but, because of the most bitter enemies it has and the disturbances and tumults that accompany it, it is thought by many to be harmful and therefore worthy of hatred. This offends many today, and there is no doubt that long ago too many were offended, when they saw the Lord himself hated by the most powerful and his teaching attacked every day. So when recently a certain ruler of the synagogue set himself against him and tried to terrify the people as well, so that they would not seek help and salvation from him, he took occasion from this and put forward two parables, by which he encourages the people and his hearers not to be offended by these humble beginnings of his kingdom, nor to let themselves be terrified by the threats or attempts of enemies. For he teaches that it is the power of the Gospel doctrine to grow beyond all human expectation and, despite all adversaries, to spread itself as widely as possible. This consolation is therefore more than necessary for us even today, when Antichrist exerts all his strength and every last effort to extinguish the rising light of the Gospel, or at least to shut it within the bounds of a narrow corner.

units.la: Primam parabolam ex re hortulana petit, & ab interrogatione admirationis plena exordiatur, ut auditores attentiores reddat. Cui rei (inquit) simile est regnum Dei? & cui illud assimilabo? Vocat autem Regnum Dei ipsum Euangelium, siue huius praedicationem, eo quod per hanc nobis Regnum suum Deus offert, cuius initium hic est totius hominis innouatio, qua illum totum Deo vindicat, finis autem & complementum in caelo habetur, vbi credentes Christus sibi cohaeredes adoptat. Et hoc sensu Dominus ipse & Apostoli Regnum Dei praedicauisse dicuntur. In praesenti autem sibi ipsi respondens ait: Simile est grano sinapis, quod acceptum quispiam misit in hortum suum: & creuit, & euasit in arborem magnam, & volucres caeli nidulati sunt in eius ramis. Quo loco tota grani sinapis natura consideranda erit. Nam etsi Christus duo solum attingat, tamen reliqua etiam, quae illi insunt, ad illustrandam Euangelicae doctrinae virtute plurimum faciunt. Et parum quidem est, nec magni momentirees videri poterat, nisi vim suam effectus non vulgaribus proderet. Natura enim calidum & siccum est, & ideo acre admodum, quod mox ab ijs sentitur, qui illud vel manibus vel dentibus conterunt. Adhaec purgandi vim habet, ex capite phlegma eijcit, & serpentium atque scorpionum ictibus medetur. Et quod in praesenti Christus potissimum attingit, etsi inter seminarium minimum sit, tam felix tamen est eius proventus, ut semel in hortis semente eius facta, ipsum sibi ipsi semen atque sationem subministret, & in altum surgens ramosq; latissime diffundens omnes plantas hortenses longè superet, adeo ut auium nidos sustinere possit.
units.tr: He takes the first parable from the garden, and begins with a question full of wonder, to make his hearers more attentive. "To what," he says, "is the Kingdom of God like? And to what shall I liken it?" Now he calls the Kingdom of God the Gospel itself, or its preaching, because through it God offers us his Kingdom. Its beginning here is the renewal of the whole man, by which God claims him wholly for himself; its end and completion is had in heaven, where Christ adopts believers as his co-heirs. In this sense the Lord himself and the apostles are said to have preached the Kingdom of God. In the present passage, answering himself, he says: "It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden; and it grew and became a large tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches." Here the whole nature of the mustard seed must be considered. For although Christ touches on only two points, the other qualities it has also contribute greatly to illustrating the power of the Gospel doctrine. And indeed it is a small thing, and would seem of little importance, were it not that its effects reveal its power, which is not ordinary. For by nature it is hot and dry, and therefore very sharp, as those feel at once who crush it with their hands or teeth. Besides, it has the power to purge: it expels phlegm from the head, and it heals the bites of serpents and scorpions. And what Christ especially touches on in the present passage: although it is the smallest of seeds, its growth is so fruitful that once its seed has been sown in the garden, it supplies its own seed and sowing, and rising high and spreading its branches very widely, it far surpasses all garden plants, so that it can bear the nests of birds.

units.la: Ista vero Euangelij naturam atque conditionem nobis seu in tabula depictam adumbrant, vel potius perfectissime exprimunt. Nam hoc quoque, si externa speciem consideres, carnis iudicio nullius pretij aut virtutis esse putabitur. Argumentum enim eius est Iesus Christus, de quo olim Isaias vaticinatus est: Non est ei forma neque decor: videbimus eum, sed non est ei aspectus ut cupiamus illum: Despectus est & abiectus inter viros, vir dolorum, & qui infirmitatem expertus est: erit vt aliquis, à quo quis faciem abscònderet, &c. Quae omnia cum iis consentiunt, quae de illo ab Euangelistis traduntur. Non temere ergo Paulus dixit: Nos praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudaeis quidem scandalum, Graecis verò stultitiam. Et vtinam hodie hoc solum nobis dicere liceret: sed eò vsque progressa est hominum impietas, vt Christiani quoque nominis professoribus plerique idem possit dici, quorum alij Christi crucem & vili specie offenduntur, alij doctrinam eius sannis & ludibriis eludunt, multi verò hostiliter erga eam affecti sunt. Sed & dicendi genus est simplex & humile, nullus humanae eloquentiae coloribus phaleratum. Ministri siue praecones fere homines obscuri, contempti, & propter huius praedicationem liberiorem exosi. Ea denique horum est sors atque conditio, vt cum alios omnes sua fides & industria commendet, soli Euangelij praecones eò magis odio habeantur, quò fidelius in creditam sibi prouinciam incumbunt. Itaque cum illius praedicatione crux atque persecutiones semper coniunctae sunt, quae in auditores quoque redundant. Vt enim Verbi Dei lucem mundus odit, quia per hanc opera eius prava arguuntur: ita neque eos ferre potest, qui luce ista fruuntur, & suo etiam exemplo impios atque prophanos homines accusant. Fit ergo quod Paulus dicit, vt persecutionem patiantur quicunque volunt in Christo pie viuere. Etsi verò haec in mundo Euangelij sors sit, virtus tamen eius maxima & effectus mirifici sunt. Nam calore habet & acrimoniam, quibus totum hominem penetrat, animos caelestium bonorum amore accendit, carnis desideria aduruit & consumit, eorundem superflua studia exiccat: & ideo alibi sali & gladio confertur. Quod vt apud pios illud commendat, ita impios in odium eius excitat, vt modò diximus. Deinde vt ipsum purum est & argento septies per ignem purgato simile: ita in homine purgando plurimum potest. Nam redundantes humanae sapientiae humores eijcit, carnis desideria abstergit, & veteris serpentis morsui medetur, quo Adam ictus peccatum & mortem ad omnem posteritatem quasi haereditario iure transmisit. Quia enim Christum praedicat, qui nobis à Deo Patre sapientia, iustitia & satisfactio datus est, quotquot illi verè credunt, ijs propter Christum fide apprehensum peccata non imputantur amplius, & ijdem ignorantiae tenebris exempti luce filiorum Dei salutari fruuntur. Unde sequitur, vt quoad mores innocentiae & sanctimoniae studeant, & quas ipsis mundus & natura carnis corruptae labes aspergunt, poenitentia quotidiana abluant. Denique totum hominem immutat & regenerat semen Euangelij, sicuti in eorum exemplis est videre, qui olim ei crediderunt, & hodie illud non ficta fide recipiunt. Vt verò sinapi semel seminatum postea seipsum seminat & propagat: ita admissa semel Euangelij doctrina propriis viribus (vt ita dicam) indies latius diffunditur, & ad plures subinde sese extendens nouos quotidie Christo cultores parat. Factum hoc Apostolorum temporibus, quando incredibili successu paucorum annorum spatio totum orbem terrarum percurrit. Et huc in primis pertinent, quae de mirificis Ecclesiarum aliquot incrementis traduntur. Vocatur in Macedoniam per Angelum Paulus, & haud dubiè ipsem Euangelij in ea propagandi maximam concepit. At Philippus sola Lydia purpuraria cum paucis alijs eum docentem audit, & Christo nomen dat. Mox inde in carcerem rapitur & virgis caeditur, quod carceris custodi lucrifaciendo occasionem praebuit. Et hoc tam tenui fidei Christianae initio facto ex ea urbe discedit. Caeterum pauca haec semina tanto cum fenore protenerunt, vt Ecclesiam illic constituerint, cuius fidem, constantiam atque liberalitatem Paulus prae multis alijs praedicat. Quod ipsum de Thessalonicensibus, Ephesijs, Corinthijs & infinitis alijs dici potest. Et sunt nostri seculi exempla, quae istius fidem faciant. Quàm enim contemptum fuerit lucis Euangelicae exordium apud Germanos, & quam leuem adeò ridiculam eius proferendae occasionem habuerint Lutherus apud Saxones, & in Helueriorum gente Zuinglius, cum paucis alijs, quorum vix nomina prius audita fuerant, nemo ignorat. At ex tam paruo semine arbor illa nata est, quae breui temporis spatio ramos suos ad omnes Europae nationes extendit, & nouam (vt sic loquar) toti orbi terrarum faciem induxit. Ita denique factum est, vt nunc sub illius vmbra nidulentur, qui prius auium instar vagabantur per omnis generis superstitiones, neque locum in venire poterant, in quo animae & conscientiae ipsorum quiescerent. Est ergo Euangelij doctrina, quae carnis & mundi iudicio contemptissima videtur, omnium disciplinarum praestantissima nobilissimaque, siue argumenti excellentia, siue tradendi modum, siue effectus, siue etiam eiusdem administros atque sectatores consideres. Argumentum enim eius est Christus Iesus, aeternus Dei Filius, quem etsi reijciant qui Ecclesiæ architecti habere volunt, lapis tamen ille pretiosus est, qui & ædificium totu su- stinet, & in caput auguli assurgit. Tradendi modus est simplex, quem pueri quoque, mulieres, suto- res, cerdones, nautæ, agricolæ percipere possunt, cum paucis capitibus comprehendatur quæcunq; ad salutem cognitu & creditu necessaria sunt. Nec enim inuidet nobis istorum cognitionem Spiritus Sanctus, sed vt hanc plures assequantur, omnium captui se accomodat. Effectus autem huius doctrinæ tam priuatim quàm publicè incredibiles sunt, quos eò magis admirari oportet, quòd ijs minis- tris vritur Christus, qui nulla humana authoritate commendantur. Diuinam ergo virtutem esse oportet, quæ in illis se exerit. Poterat his vetustas & diuturnitas huius doctrinæ addi, quæ vt æ- terno Dei decreto nititur, ita in Paradiso posita primi parentis lapsum vulgari cæpit, & ab eo tem- pore nunquam prorsus extincta est, durabit autem Christo teste vsq; ad finem mundi.
units.tr: These things depict for us, as on a painted panel, or rather express most perfectly, the nature and condition of the Gospel. For this too, if you look at its outward appearance, will be judged by the judgment of the flesh to be of no worth or power. Its subject is Jesus Christ, of whom Isaiah long ago prophesied: "He has no form or comeliness; we shall see him, but he has no appearance that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected among men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity; and he will be as one from whom a man hides his face," and so on. All these things agree with what the evangelists hand down about him. Paul therefore did not speak rashly when he said: "We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness." And would that today we could say only this! But human impiety has advanced so far that many of those who profess the name of Christian can be said to be the same: some are offended by the cross of Christ in its base appearance, others mock his doctrine with sneers and jeers, and many are hostilely disposed towards it. Moreover, the manner of speaking is simple and humble, adorned with no colours of human eloquence. The ministers or heralds are for the most part obscure and despised men, and hated more freely on account of this preaching. Finally, this is the lot and condition of these men: whereas their faith and diligence commend them to all others, the heralds of the Gospel alone are held in greater hatred the more faithfully they apply themselves to the province entrusted to them. Thus the cross and persecutions are always joined with its preaching, and they overflow upon the hearers as well. For just as the world hates the light of the Word of God, because by it its wicked works are exposed, so it cannot bear those either who enjoy that light and, even by their example, accuse impious and profane men. So it comes about, as Paul says, that all who want to live piously in Christ suffer persecution. And although this is the lot of the Gospel in the world, its power is nevertheless very great and its effects marvellous. For it has heat and sharpness, by which it penetrates the whole man; it kindles minds with love of heavenly goods, burns up and consumes the desires of the flesh, and dries up their superfluous pursuits. And therefore elsewhere it is compared to salt and to a sword. As this commends it to the godly, so it stirs up hatred of it in the impious, as we have just said. Then, just as it is pure and like silver purified seven times in the fire, so it has great power in purifying man. For it expels the overflowing humours of human wisdom, wipes away the desires of the flesh, and heals the bite of the old serpent, by which Adam, struck, transmitted sin and death to all posterity as if by hereditary right. For because it preaches Christ, who has been given to us by God the Father as wisdom, righteousness and satisfaction, whoever truly believes in him, to them, apprehended by faith in Christ, sins are no longer imputed, and they, freed from the shadows of ignorance, enjoy the saving light of the sons of God. Hence it follows that they should strive for innocence and holiness of life, and wash away daily, by repentance, the stains that the world and the corrupt nature of the flesh cast upon them. Finally, the seed of the Gospel changes and regenerates the whole man, as can be seen in the examples of those who long ago believed in it and today receive it with a faith that is not feigned. And just as the mustard seed, once sown, afterwards sows and propagates itself, so the Gospel doctrine, once admitted, spreads more widely each day by its own powers, so to speak, and extending itself again and again to more people, daily prepares new worshippers for Christ. This happened in the times of the apostles, when within a few years it ran through the whole world with incredible success. And to this especially pertain the things that are handed down concerning the remarkable growth of several churches. Paul is called into Macedonia by an angel, and without doubt he conceived the greatest hope of spreading the Gospel there. But Philippi, with a few others, hears him teaching, and only Lydia, a seller of purple, gives her name to Christ. Soon after, he is dragged into prison and beaten with rods, because he provided an occasion for the jailer to gain. And with the Christian faith so slight at its beginning, he departs from that city. But these few seeds afterwards yielded such increase that they established a church there, whose faith, steadfastness and generosity Paul commends above many others. The same can be said of the Thessalonians, the Ephesians, the Corinthians and countless others. And there are examples from our own age that confirm this. Nobody is unaware how little regard was had for the beginning of the Gospel light among the Germans, and how slight and even ridiculous an occasion for spreading it Luther had among the Saxons, and Zwingli among the people of the Helvetii, together with a few others whose names had scarcely been heard before. Yet from such a small seed that tree has grown, which in a short time has extended its branches to all the nations of Europe and has given, so to speak, a new face to the whole world. Thus, finally, it has come about that those now nest under its shade who once wandered like birds through every kind of superstition and could find no place where their souls and consciences might rest. The doctrine of the Gospel, therefore, which seems most contemptible by the judgment of flesh and world, is the most excellent and noblest of all teachings, whether you consider the excellence of its subject, or its manner of delivery, or its effects, or even its ministers and followers. For its subject is Christ Jesus, the eternal Son of God, whom those reject who wish to be architects of the Church; yet he is that precious stone which both sustains the whole building and rises up into the head of the corner. Its manner of delivery is simple, such that boys, women, shoemakers, cobblers, sailors and farmers can grasp it, since everything necessary for salvation to know and believe is comprehended in a few heads. For the Holy Spirit does not begrudge us the knowledge of these things, but, so that more may attain it, he adapts himself to everyone's capacity. Moreover, the effects of this doctrine, both private and public, are incredible, and all the more to be wondered at because Christ uses for them ministers who are commended by no human authority. It must therefore be the divine power that shows itself in them. The antiquity and long duration of this doctrine could also be added, which, resting on the eternal decree of God, began to be spread abroad from the fall of the first parent in Paradise, and from that time has never been wholly extinguished; and it will endure, with Christ as witness, until the end of the world.

units.la: Hæc vt huius doctrinæ dignitatem & studium nobis commendant, ita officij quoque omnes eos admonent, qui illam profitentur: quod est, vt ipsi quoque granum sinapis vita & moribus refe- rant. Itaque ante omnia suæ tenuitatis sibi conscij humilitati & modestiæ studeant, neque huius mundi fastu delectentur, vt ambitioso splendore seipsos supra alios omnes attollant. Calere autè & feruere debent zelo gloriæ Dei & veræ pietatis, idq; dictis, factis & omni vita testentur. Item Chri- sti sanguine purgati & abluti à peccatorum sordibus, nequaquam illis penes se locum dent amplius, sed procul abiectis humanæ sapientiæ noxijs humoribus & fœdis carnis suæ desiderijs innocentiam & sanctimoniam suam constantissimè tueantur. In primis autem ramos suos ad quosuis alios dif- fundant, vt & Regnum Dei indies latius propagetur, & apud ipsos nidum aut sedes tutas inue- niant, qui propter fidem in Christum à patrio solo exulare coguntur. Minimè ergo audiant neq; ad- mittat malæ fidei colonos, qui huius arbusti ramos, quasi nimium luxuriantes, detruncare conatur: dum ministris Ecclesiarum dicendi scribendique libertatem eripere studeant, & typographicam ar- tem, quæ in doni linguarum, quo olim Apostoli claruerunt, locum successit, suppressam & extinctam volunt. Quin potius singuli Christianæ communionis memores, se omnibus hominibus debitores esse cogitent, & pro suæ vocationis ratione, talento suo, quod à Domino acceperunt, vsuram illam sanctis- simam exerceant, qua plures quotidie Christo lucrifiant, in quibus Dei gloria illustretur. Sunt hæc diligenter ijs meditanda, quibus hoc turbulentissimo sæculo datur, vt pace & otio abundent, atque Euangelij doctrina tutò frui possint, cuius liberam prædicationem multi alij vix sanguine suo tuen- tur. In eum enim finem Deus Ecclesiæ suæ omnibus sæculis sedem aliquam tutiorem concedere so- let, vt non desint, qui alijs periclitantibus consilio atque auxilio suo adesse, & suis sedibus eiectos recipere queant. Quod singulare Dei beneficium si illi agnoscant, seque fidos & beneficos præbeant, tunc demum res suas stabilient, & perpetuo Dei fauore protegentur. Qui verò tanti beneficij ingra- ti æstimatores sunt, sibi solis viuunt, & insuper otio suo ad libidines & impura carnis studia abu- tuntur, horribiles suæ impietatis pœnas dabunt, quas nunquam effugient. Et hæc quidem in pri- mam huius loci parabolam dicta sint.
units.tr: These things, as they commend to us the dignity and zeal of this doctrine, also remind all who profess it of their duty: that they too should express the grain of mustard seed in their life and conduct. Above all, therefore, those who are conscious of their own littleness should cultivate humility and modesty, and not delight in the pomp of this world so as to raise themselves above all others with ambitious display. They ought to glow and burn with zeal for the glory of God and true piety, and bear witness to this by their words, deeds and whole life. Likewise, having been cleansed and washed from the filth of sins by the blood of Christ, they should by no means give such things a place in themselves any longer. Rather, casting far away the harmful humours of human wisdom and the foul desires of the flesh, they should most steadfastly guard their innocence and holiness. Above all, let them spread their branches to others, so that the kingdom of God may be propagated more widely day by day, and so that those who are compelled to go into exile from their native soil for faith in Christ may find among them a nest or safe seats. Let them therefore by no means listen to, or admit, the ill-minded settlers who try to lop off the branches of this tree as if they were growing too luxuriantly, while they strive to snatch from the ministers of the Churches the freedom to speak and write, and wish the printing art, which has taken the place of the gift of tongues by which the Apostles once shone, to be suppressed and extinguished. Rather, let each one, mindful of Christian fellowship, think that he is a debtor to all men, and, according to the nature of his calling, exercise with his talent, which he has received from the Lord, that most holy usury by which many are won for Christ every day, and in whom the glory of God is made known. These things are to be carefully considered by those who, in this most turbulent age, are granted to abound in peace and leisure and can safely enjoy the doctrine of the Gospel, whose free preaching many others scarcely defend with their blood. For to this end God is wont to grant his Church in every age some safer seat, so that there may not be lacking those who can stand by others in danger with counsel and help, and receive those driven from their own homes. If they acknowledge this singular benefit of God, and show themselves faithful and beneficent, then at last they will establish their affairs and be protected by the perpetual favour of God. But those who are ungrateful judges of so great a benefit, who live for themselves alone and moreover abuse their leisure for lusts and impure pursuits of the flesh, will pay horrible penalties for their impiety, which they will never escape. And let these things be said as the first parable of this passage.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram, quam à fermenti natura petit, & cuius idem qui prioris sensus est. Proponit hanc quoq; non sine admiratione specie Dominus, sic dicens: Cui rei assimilabo Re- gnum Dei? Simile est fermento, quod acceptum mulier condidit in farinæ satis tribus vsquequò fer- mentaretur tota. Quo loco nemini scrupulum mouere debet, quòd alibi fermentum in malam partem sumitur pro hypocrisi & falsa doctrina, item pro peccato & naturæ vitiositate atq; pessimis eius ef- sectis: vt cum Christus discipulos monet, vt sibi caveant à fermento Pharisæorum & Herodis: & Apostolus clamat: Expurgate vetus fermentum. Scimus enim multa esse in rerum natura, ex qui- bus pro diuersorum effectuum ratione similitudines tam in bonam quàm in malam partem peti pos- sunt: neq; etiam opus est, vt quæcunque alicui rei insunt, cum argumento similitudinis conueniant: & ideo similia ferè omnia claudicare dicuntur. Equidem in præsenti ad vim solam fermenti Chri- stus respicit, qua massam aut farinæ conspersionem maximam penetrat, vt ei saporem nouum magnq; gratum conferat. Itaq; verborum eius hic sensus est: Quemadmodum fermentum res vi- lis & nullius efficaciæ esse videtur, veruntamen si tribus aut etiam pluribus farinæ satis misceatur, mirifica vi totâ illam massam peruadit, & ex ea coctos panes sapore iucundo condit, vt & palato melius sapiant, & stomacho totiq; corpori salubriores sint: Ita Euangelij verbu primo quidem ase stu contemptibile & infirmum videtur, sed in aliqua gente aut vrbe praedicatum in singulas horas latius serpit, plures subinde in Christi cognitionē trahit, quos ex se renatos per Spiritus Sancti virtutem plane alios facit, ut qui prius filij irae & ad nullum opus bonum idonei erant, mox & Deo accepti & pulcherrimis virtutibus insignes sint, ad quos aeternae salutis haereditas pertinet. Est ergo hic illud etiam diligenter obseruandum, quod per Euangelium nobis virtus illa offertur, quae nos fecundos & ad opera Deo grata idoneos, adeoque Christi consortes facit, in quo vno salus omnis habetur. In nobis ergo nihil est, quod gloriari possimus, & omnibus vere loquitur Paulus: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Interim nostri officij est, sancto illo fermento locum dare, quo vetus & noxium peccati fermentū pellitur, ut in Christo Iesu noua massa sive conspersio, & (ut Ignatius martyr dicebat) Dei triticum, imo Deo ipsi panes mundi ac synceri efficiamur.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the second, which takes its image from the nature of leaven, and which has the same sense as the first. The Lord also sets this forth, not without wonder, saying: "To what shall I liken the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Here no one should be troubled that elsewhere leaven is taken in a bad sense, for hypocrisy and false doctrine, and likewise for sin and the vitiated nature of man and its worst effects: as when Christ warns the disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, and the Apostle cries out, "Purge out the old leaven." For we know that there are many things in nature from which, according to the different effects, comparisons can be drawn in a good sense as well as a bad one; nor is it necessary that everything that belongs to a thing should agree with the point of the comparison, and therefore almost all comparisons are said to limp. Indeed, in the present case Christ looks only to the power of the leaven, by which it penetrates the greatest mass or quantity of meal, and imparts to it a new and very agreeable savour. So the sense of his words is this: just as leaven seems a thing of little worth and no efficacy, yet if it is mixed with three or even more measures of meal, it pervades that whole mass with a wonderful power, and seasons the bread baked from it with a pleasant taste, so that it is better to the palate and more wholesome for the stomach and the whole body. So too the word of the Gospel at first sight seems contemptible and weak, yet when it is preached in some nation or city it creeps wider from hour to hour, and draws more and more into the knowledge of Christ; those whom it has regenerated through the power of the Holy Spirit it makes entirely other people, so that those who were before children of wrath and fit for no good work are soon both acceptable to God and distinguished by most excellent virtues, and to them belongs the inheritance of eternal salvation. Here, therefore, this also is to be carefully observed: that through the Gospel that power is offered to us which makes us fruitful and fit for works pleasing to God, and thus partakers with Christ, in whom alone all salvation is found. Therefore there is nothing in us of which we can glory, and Paul speaks truly to all: "What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" Meanwhile it is our duty to give place to that holy leaven, by which the old and harmful leaven of sin is driven out, so that in Christ Jesus we may be made a new mass or lump, and (as Ignatius the martyr used to say) the wheat of God, nay, bread of God itself, pure and unleavened.

units.la: Caeterum in vtriusque parabolae finem sive scopum, quem Christus sibi propositum habuit, & de quo sub initium huius sermonis quaedam diximus, nos in primis intentos esse oportet. Est vs, ne quae tenuia & contempta Euangelij aut regni Dei in hoc mundo exordia offendant, & nemo impiorum ludibrijs moueatur, qui ex illis nobis insultandi occasionem arripiunt. Quia enim totum hoc negotiū Dei est, neque ab humana authoritate sive potentia dependet, stultē nimis faciunt, qui illud ex primo intuitu & praesenti facie aestimant. Finem potius diuini consilij inspiciamus, quem Paulus hunc esse docet, ut per ea quae in hoc mundo humilia, ignobilia, stulta et quasi nulla sunt, vniuersus mundi fastus simul & humanae sapientiae turgidus splendor pudefiat, & omnis gloria ipsi soli detur. Itaq; ridēt quidē impij Veritatis hostes, quando in potentissimis regnis & ferocissimis nationibus reformationem religionis homines aliqui obscuri & imbelles, neque vlla authoritate publica muniti, multiuntur, & nos ex illorum studio atque conatu fructum non paenitendum speramus. At quia rem istam carnis ac mundi iudicio metiuntur, quod in diuinis caecum & plus quam stultum est, turpissi mēseipsos fallunt, & plerunque suipsorum eos pudet, quod ante victoriam triumphos iactarint, & Paeana cecinerint. Non autem irrita est spes nostra, vt ut illi fremant & sanguine atque incendijs omnia misceant: quia fieri non potest, ut vel sanguis martyrum, quo Ecclesiae ager rigatur, fructu omni careat, vel Euangelij semen reprimatur, ut nō suo tempore germinet, & messis alicuius spem certam faciat. Docet hoc Dominus apud Marcum alio etiam simili, sic dicens: Ita est Regnum Dei, ut si quispiam iaciat semen in terra, & dormiat & exurgat nocte & die, & semen germinet at que exurgat quando ipse nescit: Sponte enim terra fructum fert, primum herbam, deinde spicam, inde plenum frumentum in spica, &c. Qua parabola nos Christus de Euangelica semente securos esse iubet: quoad huius mundi furores. Vt enim agricolae, vbi sementem fecerunt, nihil praeterea possunt addere, & proinde dormiunt & surgunt, id est, alias res agunt ad rem domesticam pertinentes, & interim somno etiam & quiete concessa fruuntur: Ita fidos verbi administros, & qui illud iam pridem receperunt facere conuenit, ut vbi ipsi suum in hac semente officium fecerunt, rem omnem Deo committant, & in reliquis diligentes sint, in quibus ipsorum industria requiritur. Nam vt semen terrae mandatum huius virtute per Dei benedictionem vegetatum sponte germinat, & quamus nunc quidem niuibus obrutum lateat, modo pruinis aduratur, mox imbrium fluentis quasi suffocetur, saepe etiam grandine horribili sternatur, suis tamen incrementis augetur, donec ad maturitatem perductum agricolam messe lata exhilarat. Ita Dei Verbum vbi semel praedicatum, & vel à pauculis atque vilissimis homuncionibus receptum fuerit, propria virtute germinat, & quamuis omnis generis obstacula mundus & Satan obiiciant, succrescit tamen, neque angustioris agelli finibus concludi potest, & tandem fructus fert omni spe & expectatione vberiores. Sunt haec omnium saeculorum exemplis confirmata, & (ut supra dictum est) multa nostri seculi exempla exstant, quae hodie aduersus Antichristi atque complicum eius conatus nos consolari & confirmare possunt. Quod si vero infelicius in aliqua gente res succedit, id quoque certa cum ratione & iusto iudicio fieri permittit Deus: idem tamen suorum spem minimè frustratur, quos interna crucis & afflictionum Filij sui participes factos ad se colligit, & eosdem olim in magno illo die non sine summa impiorum consternatione atq; ignominia pro suis agnoscet.
units.tr: Moreover, we ought chiefly to attend to the end or aim of both parables, which Christ had set before himself, and about which we said something at the beginning of this sermon. It is this: that the humble and despised beginnings of the Gospel, or of the kingdom of God, in this world should not give offence, and that no one should be moved by the mockery of the ungodly, who seize on these things as an occasion of insulting us. For since this whole business belongs to God, and does not depend on human authority or power, they are very foolish who judge it from the first glance and from its present appearance. Rather let us look to the end of the divine counsel, which Paul teaches to be this: that through those things in this world which are humble, ignoble, foolish, and as it were nothing, all the pride of the world and the swollen splendour of human wisdom may be put to shame, and all glory be given to him alone. So indeed the impious enemies of the truth laugh when, in the most powerful kingdoms and the fiercest nations, certain obscure and unwarlike men, protected by no public authority, undertake the reformation of religion, and we hope, from their zeal and effort, for a fruit not to be regretted. But because they measure this matter by the judgement of the flesh and the world, which in divine things is blind and more than foolish, they most shamefully deceive themselves, and often are ashamed of themselves that they boasted of triumphs and sang the Paean before the victory. Yet our hope is not vain, even though they rage and mix everything with blood and fires: for it cannot happen that either the blood of the martyrs, by which the field of the Church is watered, should be without any fruit, or that the seed of the Gospel should be held back so that it does not sprout in its time and give a sure hope of some harvest. The Lord teaches this in Mark by another similar parable, saying: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow up when he himself does not know. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear," etc. By this parable Christ bids us be secure about the Gospel seed as far as the rage of this world is concerned. For as farmers, when they have sown, can add nothing further, and therefore sleep and rise, that is, attend to other business belonging to their household, and meanwhile enjoy sleep and rest granted to them, so it is fitting for the faithful ministers of the word, and for those who have long since received it, that when they have done their own duty in this sowing, they should commit the whole matter to God, and be diligent in the remaining things in which their own industry is required. For just as seed entrusted to the earth sprouts of its own accord, by the power of God's blessing, and although for now it lies hidden, buried under the snow, then is scorched by frosts, soon is almost suffocated by the floods of rains, and often is flattened by terrible hail, yet it is increased by its own growth until, brought to maturity, it gladdens the farmer with a rich harvest; so the Word of God, once it has been preached and received even by a few and the most humble little people, sprouts by its own power, and although the world and Satan may throw in every kind of obstacle, it grows up nonetheless, and cannot be confined within the limits of a narrow little field, and at last bears fruit more abundant than all hope and expectation. These things are confirmed by the examples of all ages, and (as was said above) many examples of our own age exist, which today can comfort and strengthen us against the efforts of Antichrist and his accomplices. But if in some nation matters turn out more unhappily, God also allows this for a certain reason and by a just judgement; yet he does not in the least disappoint the hope of his own, whom he gathers to himself as sharers in the inner cross and afflictions of his Son, and these he will acknowledge in that great day as his own, to the great dismay and shame of the ungodly.

units.la: Finis vtriusque parabolae.
units.tr: The end of both parables.

units.la: Porro postremam huius loci partem audiamus, qua summatim Lucas describit, quae potissima Iesu Christi in professione hac, de qua capite nono dicere coepit, studia fuerint, sic dicens: Et transibat singulas urbes & vicos docens & iter faciens Hierosolymam. Eo autem illum contendisse supra dictum est, quod dies assumptionis suae instaret. Est hoc evidens obedientiae argumentum, qua aeterno Patris decreto se accommodavit, & quo semel testatum voluit se animam suam spontè pro nobis tradidisse. Inter eundum vero ad singulas urbes & vicos diverti, ut in illis doceret. Quod ipsum sae pe annotat Evangelista, & ipse alibi se in hoc a Patre missum esse testatur. Rursus ergo nobis suo exemplo Evangelij dignitatem commendat, & ministerij ecclesiastici contemptores arguit, quorum hodie infinitus est numerus. Nam etsi vix vllum vitae genus sit, quod non multis arrideat, & cui no suos liberos addicat qui illis prosipere cupiunt: vix tamen millesimus quisque inveniatur, qui suis impensis filium alat, quem in bonis atque sacris literis institui curet, ut aliquando ecclesiae Christi servire possit. Imo plerisque ignominiosum videtur, si filium aut affinem habeant Verbi Dei ministrum. At quid isti aliud faciunt, quam quod Dei Filium fastidiunt, quando hoc aliis vitio vertunt, circa quod ille quam maxime fuit occupatus? Mireetur ingratitudo haec graves poenas, & huic debemus, quod multi fidis ministris destituuntur, multi se dignos habent, qui aut canes muti sunt, aut malo exemplo Ecclesias dissipant, & multos secum in exitium trahunt.
units.tr: Let us now hear the last part of this passage, in which Luke sums up briefly what were the chief concerns of Jesus Christ in this public profession, which he began to speak of in chapter nine, saying: "And he went through every city and village, teaching, and journeying toward Jerusalem." It has been said above that he was hastening there because the day of his being taken up was at hand. This is clear evidence of obedience, by which he conformed himself to the eternal decree of the Father, and by which he wished it to be attested once for all that he gave up his soul freely for us. In travelling to each city and village he turned aside to teach in them. The Evangelist often notes this, and Christ himself elsewhere testifies that he was sent by the Father for this purpose. So again he commends to us, by his own example, the dignity of the Gospel, and rebukes the despisers of the ecclesiastical ministry, whose number today is endless. For although there is hardly any way of life that does not please many, and to which parents do not devote their children who wish to prosper by it, yet scarcely one in a thousand is found who, at his own expense, feeds a son whom he takes care to have trained in good and sacred letters, so that he may one day be able to serve the Church of Christ. Indeed, to many it seems shameful if they have a son or a son-in-law who is a minister of the Word of God. But what else do such people do than despise the Son of God, when they find fault with that very thing with which he was most of all occupied? Let this ingratitude be marked with grievous punishments; and for this reason we owe it that many are deprived of faithful ministers, while many who are considered worthy are either dumb dogs or, by bad example, scatter the churches and drag many with them into destruction.

units.la: At in Christi facto non oscitanter observari debet, quod Hierosolymam versus iter faciens, ubi se moriturum & prius dira quaeque passurum esse sciebat, tam sedulus est in praedicando & docendo. Atqui eum Pharisaei & Sacerdotibus non aliam ob causam exosum fuisse scimus, quam quod Veritatis doctrina eorum impostturas argueret, & ita ipsorum quaestui atque honori multum derogaret. Pergit tamen in munere sibi a Deo Patre commisso, & suo exemplo docet, quam sedulo & constanter nos quoque esse debeamus in iis exequendis, quae nobis divinitus mandata sunt. Si enim imminens dirae ac infamis mortis supplicium non abstterruit Filium Dei, quin officium fideliter faceret, nimium professio molles & ignavos se esse ostendunt, qui laborem omnem subterfugiunt, & quous strepitus aut minus leuissimus terrentur. Meminerimus ergo non satis esse, si quid bene coeptum aut inchoatum est, sed eos demum probari Deo & salvos fore, qui in finem usque perseverant. Neque coronatur statim qui certat, nisi legitime certaverit. Viderunt hoc veteres Prophetae, quorum aliqui per annos quadraginta, alij quinquaginta & sexaginta, vel etiam plures (ut ex regum historia colligere licet) hoc saxum voluerunt, etiamsi sibi nihil quam irritos labores & dira pericula polliceri possent apud gentem ingratam atque contumacem, quam Dei sententia iam pridem damnatam esse non ignorabant. Idem de Apostolis, & in primis Paulo, possumus dicere, si quae Lucas in Actis de illo prodidit, diligentius inspiciamus. Hos aut non solum Verbi praeconies, verumetiam alij quoque omnes in suis functionibus imitari debent.
