Etenim ijs qui Rempub. administrant, hoc in primis necessarium esse, Saulis, Solomonis, Uziae & similium exempla docent, qui in medio quasi cursu defecerunt, & a Deo graviter puniti sunt. Et quoad fidei negotium & vitae totius consuetudinem, nunquam salutem erunt, qui non in finem usque constantes manserint. Quis enim mercede dignos dixerit eos seruos, qui sibi ipsis ferias faciunt hero nolente, aut opus non absolutum temere deseruunt? Itaque buius loci considerate ratione confirmati nullis laboribus aut periculis nos fatigari patiamur, ut quando finis vitae huius nobis instat, singuli cum Paulo possimus dicere: Certamen illud praeclarum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi: Quod superest, repositum est mihi iustitiae corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus Iesus in illo die, iustus iudex: non solum autem mihi, sed & omnibus, qui expetierint illius adventum. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But in the deed of Christ we must not observe carelessly that, as he made his way toward Jerusalem, where he knew he would die and first suffer all kinds of dreadful things, he was so diligent in preaching and teaching. Yet we know that the Pharisees and priests hated him for no other reason than that the teaching of truth exposed their deceits and so greatly detracted from their gain and honour. Nevertheless he persisted in the office committed to him by God the Father, and by his example he teaches how diligently and steadfastly we too ought to carry out those things which have been entrusted to us by God. For if the threat of a dreadful and infamous death did not deter the Son of God from faithfully doing his duty, those who shrink from every labour and are frightened by any noise, however slight, show themselves to be too soft and lazy for their profession. Let us therefore remember that it is not enough if something has been well begun or undertaken, but that those alone are approved by God and will be saved who persevere to the end. Nor is he who competes crowned at once, unless he has competed lawfully. The ancient Prophets saw this, some of whom, for forty years, others for fifty and sixty, or even more (as can be gathered from the history of the kings), held out in this task, although they could promise themselves nothing but fruitless labours and dreadful dangers among a people ungrateful and stubborn, whom they knew had long since been condemned by the sentence of God. We can say the same of the Apostles, and above all of Paul, if we examine more carefully what Luke has related about him in the Acts. These men, and all others as well, ought to imitate in their functions not only the heralds of the Word. For that this is especially necessary for those who govern the commonwealth, the examples of Saul, Solomon, Uzziah and the like teach, who failed in the middle of their course and were severely punished by God. And as regards the matter of faith and the whole course of life, those will never be saved who have not remained steadfast to the end. For who would call those servants worthy of their wages who take holidays for themselves against their master's will, or rashly abandon a task not finished? Therefore, strengthened by the considered reasoning of this passage, let us not allow ourselves to be worn down by any labours or dangers, so that when the end of this life is at hand, each of us may be able to say with Paul: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord Jesus, the righteous judge, will give me in that day; and not to me only, but also to all who have longed for his appearing." To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXL.
units.tr: HOMILY CXL.

units.la: Dixit autem ei quidam: Domine, num pauci sunt qui serventur? Ipse autem dixit eis: Contendite intrare per angustam portam: quia multi dico vobis, studebunt intrare, & non poterunt: Ex quo videlicet surrexerit paterfamilias, & occluserit ostium, & coeperitis foris stare, & pulsare ostium, dicentes, Domine Domine aperi nobis. Qui respondens spondens dicet vobis : Nescio vnde vos sitis. Tunc incipietis dicere: Edimus in tui conspectu, & bibimus: & in plateis nostris docuisti. Et dicet: Dico vobis, nescio vnde vos sitis: abscedite à me omnes, qui facitis quod iniustũ est. Illic erit fletus & stridor dentium, cum videritis Abraham & Isaacum & Iacobum & omnes Prophetas in Regno Dei, vos autem expelli foras. Et venient multi ab Oriente & Occidente, & Borea & Austro, & discumbent in Regno Dei. Et ecce sunt vltimi, qui erunt primi: & sunt primi, qui erunt vltimi.
units.tr: Then one said to him, "Lord, are there few that be saved?" And he said to them, "Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able. When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us; he shall answer and say to you, I know you not whence ye are. Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out. And they shall come from the east and west, and from the north and south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last."

units.la: OLim quidem Deus æterna salutis promissiones prisci patribus ita reuelauit, vt eas ad omnes gentes pertinere satis euidenter pateat: Idem tamen Iudaeorum gentem præ omnibus aliis elegit, cum qua familiarius versatus esset, vt in illis ostenderet, quæ nam ipsius voluntas, quæ item vera & vnica salutis ratio sit, quam omnes sectari debeant. Vt autem in eo eluxit singularis eius bonitas: ita in illis contumaciæ & ingratitudinis extremæ exemplum habemus, cuius simile nullum aliud extat. Nam & Mosem improbè aspernati sunt, cuius ministerio ex Ægyptica seruitute liberati Legem & cultus diuini rationem acceperant, & cum Prophetis perpetuo pugnarunt, qui eos in officio & vero salutis tramite retinere studebant. Neq; eo contenti, maiori audacia & impietate ad uersus æternum Dei Filium insurrexerunt, quando is in carne manifestatus ipsis primis Verbi vi tæ æternæ prædicauit. Nam etsi magno studio atq; diligentia illeomnes vrbes & vicos obiret docés simul & doctrinam suam operibus miraculosis confirmans, adeo tamen non potuit frangere contumaces eorum animos, vt odio illius exacerbati quotidie in peius profecerint. Quapropter cum inde fessum Iesu Christi erga illam gentem studium & eorunde incurabilem ingratitudinem Lucas hucusque multis exemplis expositset, nunc illum poenas graues & diras eis minitantè describit. Vbi ne mo putauerit, quæ hic dicuntur ad illos solos pertinere. Quia enim hos (vt diximus) omnibus populis exemplo esse voluit, in primis ad nos ista pertinent, qui in illorum locum adoptati, nunc Dei populus aut Ecclesia dicimur. Itaq; huius loci nobis vsus hic esto, vt infelici & tristi illorum exemplo admoniti, vel territi potius, nos Christo Domino tractabiles atq; morigeros præbeamus.
units.tr: Of old God revealed the promises of eternal salvation to the fathers in such a way that it is quite plain they pertained to all nations. Yet he chose the Jewish nation above all others, to live among them more intimately, so that in them he might show what his will is, and what the true and only way of salvation is, which all should follow. As his singular goodness shone forth in this, so in them we have an example of extreme stubbornness and ingratitude, of which no other like it exists. For they shamefully spurned Moses, through whose ministry they had been freed from Egyptian slavery and had received the Law and the manner of divine worship; and they fought continually against the prophets, who strove to keep them in their duty and on the true path of salvation. Not content with this, they rose up with greater audacity and impiety against the eternal Son of God, when he, manifested in the flesh, first preached to them the living power of the eternal Word. For although he went through all the cities and villages with great zeal and diligence, teaching and at the same time confirming his doctrine by miraculous works, he nevertheless could not break their stubborn minds, so that, embittered by hatred of him, they grew worse every day. Therefore, since Luke had hitherto set forth with many examples Jesus Christ's tireless concern for that nation and their incurable ingratitude, he now describes the heavy and dreadful punishments with which he threatens them. Let no one think that what is said here pertains only to them. For since he wished them (as we have said) to be an example to all peoples, these things apply above all to us, who have been adopted into their place and are now called the people of God or the Church. Therefore let us make use of this passage in such a way that, warned, or rather terrified, by their unhappy and sad example, we may show ourselves docile and obedient to the Lord Christ.

units.la: Præmittitur autem occasio, quæ illum, vt de his dissereret mouit. Dū enim Euangelij doctrinam per omnes vrbes ac vicos celebriores spargit, quidam huius consideratione abreptus, de eorum numero quæstionem mouet, qui salutis æternæ participes futuri sint. Domine (inquit) num pauci sunt qui seruentur? Videtur autem hic quæstionis huius argumentum sumpsisse ex ipsius Christi doctrina. Prædicabat vt primo poenitentiam, & hanc non in simulatis ieiuniis & inanibus ceremoniis, sed in totius hominis mortificatione & innouatione, vel (vt ipse ait) in abnegatione sui ipsius et regeneratione cōsistere docebat: fructus aut illius esse ostendebat perpetuū et perfectū innocentiæ, sanctimoniæ et beneficetiæ erga quosuis studium. Quæ omnia si recte considerentur, hominis vires longe superant. Addebat his secū do loco promissione de peccatorū remissione & regno Dei, quod omnibus patet, qui ipsum vere & constanti fide amplexantur. Hæc cum ille quisquis fuit, cū paucitate discipulorū Christi conferret, non potuit non offendi, & ideo num pauci seruandi sint quæritur. Et videtur non tam curiosi hominis quàm impij fuisse hæc quæstio, qui Christū mendacij arguere & simul omnibus inuisum facere voluerit. Nam si saluandorū numerū ingentē fore respondisset, in promptu erat excipere: Atqui paucissimi te sequuntur, & ideo homines abs te tuaq; doctrina seruari possunt. Sin paucos fore dicat, indigne ferent omnes maiorē hominum partem damnari, nec quisquam inter illos censeri volet. Deniq; omnino videtur iste ex eorum numero fuisse, qui in homines potius quā Dei verbū respiciūt. Hi vt sibi delitias faciant, Dei bonitatē magnificè commendant, neq; verisimile esse aiunt, quod vs plures perire quàm seruari velit, cum misericordia eius in omnibus operibus & iudicijs ipsius emineat. Tandem vero peccandi dulcedine & mundi amore inescati palam testari audent, se cū multis damnari, quā cum paucis seruari malle. Exemplum tantæ impietatis memorabile in Rhatboldo Frisiorum Principe, qui Caroli Martelli temporibus regnauit, historici proponunt. Cum enim Frisij ad fidem Christianorum cogerentur, & ipse Baptismum se recepturum esse simulans pedem alterum in lauacrum sacrum iam impositset, ad Episcopum conuersus interrogauit, plures ne ex defunctis, apud inferos, aut in cælis agerent? Eo autem respondente, maiorem esse apud inferos agentium numerū: illico pedem retraxit dicens: Igitur & ego multitudinem sequar. Et tales quidē hodie multos esse, si non verba eorū, certè facta & mores abunde testatur. Plerique enim multitudinis consensum Verbo Dei & omnibus iis præferunt, qui laboriosam hanc & mundo inuisam Christi sectam sequendo ab aliis dissentiunt. Alij verò à principum authoritate pendent, & in fide amplectenda cunctantur, quoad illos ab ea abhorrere vident. Multi quæstiones de electione & prædestinatione mouet curiosas potius quàm necessarias, & dum de singulorum salute aut damnatione interrogant, rem omnem velin dubium vocant, vel vulgi ludibrio exponunt. Est præterea vitium hoc sanctis etiam commune, quod ut primùm de personis hominū agitur, & ipsi quid facere debeant admonentur, ad alios potius respicere solet, quàm de sua functione aut forte cogitare. Exemplum huius rei in Petro habemus, qui cum à Christo admoneretur, quid iam seniefset euenturum, non ad seriam martyrij meditationem aut preces ardentes, sed ad Ioannem dilectum Christi discipulum conuersus ait: Domine, hic autem quid? Est hæc ad modum noxia curiositas, cuius initijs obstare debent, qui ad maiorē impietatē progredi nolunt. Quo ties ergo admiratio ista animos nostros subit, quid de his aut illis futurū sit? nobis idè quod Petro à Christo dici putemus. Si eos omnes manere velim quales sunt, quid hoc ad te? tu me sequere.
units.tr: The occasion which moved him to discourse on these matters is set forth first. For while he was spreading the doctrine of the gospel through all the more notable cities and villages, someone, carried away by consideration of it, raised a question about the number of those who would be sharers in eternal salvation: "Lord," he said, "are there few who are saved?" He seems to have taken the substance of this question from the teaching of Christ himself. He preached repentance first, and taught that it consists not in feigned fasts and empty ceremonies, but in the mortification and renewal of the whole man, or (as he himself says) in denying oneself and being born again; and he showed that its fruit is a perpetual and perfect innocence, holiness, and zeal for doing good to anyone. If all these things are rightly considered, they far exceed human strength. Besides these, in the second place he added the promise of the forgiveness of sins and the kingdom of God, which lies open to all who embrace it with a true and steadfast faith. When that man, whoever he was, compared these things with the small number of Christ's disciples, he could not but be troubled, and therefore asks whether few are to be saved. And this question seems to have come not so much from a curious man as from an impious one, who wished to convict Christ of falsehood and at the same time make him hated by all. For if Christ had answered that the number of those to be saved would be great, it would have been easy to retort: "But very few follow you, and so men can be saved by you and your doctrine." But if he said they would be few, all would take it hard that the greater part of mankind should be condemned, and no one would wish to be counted among them. Finally, this man altogether seems to have been one of those who look to men rather than to the word of God. To please themselves, these men extol the goodness of God magnificently, and say it is not likely that he wishes more to perish than to be saved, since his mercy shines forth in all his works and judgments. At last, however, enticed by the sweetness of sin and the love of the world, they dare to declare openly that they would rather be damned with many than saved with a few. The historians set forth a memorable example of such impiety in Radbod, prince of the Frisians, who reigned in the times of Charles Martel. For when the Frisians were being compelled to accept the faith of the Christians, he, pretending that he would receive baptism, had already placed one foot in the holy font, but turned to the bishop and asked whether more of the dead were in hell or in heaven. When the bishop answered that the number of those in hell was greater, he at once drew back his foot, saying: "Then I will follow the multitude." And that there are many such people today, their deeds and manners, if not their words, abundantly bear witness. For most men prefer the consensus of the multitude to the Word of God and to all those who, by following this toilsome sect of Christ, which is hateful to the world, differ from others. Others depend on the authority of princes, and hesitate to embrace the faith until they see those princes shrink from it. Many raise curious rather than necessary questions about election and predestination, and while they inquire into the salvation or damnation of individuals, they either call the whole matter into doubt or expose it to the mockery of the crowd. Moreover, this fault is common even among the saints: as soon as there is talk about the persons of men, and they are reminded of what they themselves ought to do, they are wont to look to others rather than to think about their own office or fate. We have an example of this in Peter, who, when Christ warned him what would happen to him in old age, did not turn to serious meditation on martyrdom or to fervent prayer, but turned to John, the beloved disciple of Christ, and said: "Lord, what about this man?" This is a harmful curiosity, and those who do not wish to advance to greater impiety ought to check it at its beginnings. Therefore, whenever this wonder comes into our minds, what will become of this man or that, let us think that Christ says to us what he said to Peter: "If I will that he remain as he is, what is that to you? Follow thou me."

units.la: Conuenit cum hoc dicto quod in præsenti curioso isti respondetur. Quia enim quæstiones eiusmodi salutem impediunt potius quàm promouent, non directè neq; illi soli respondet Dominus: sed ad totā populi multitudinē sermone dirigens, singulos docet, quid ipsos facere conueniat, & argumentu effi cacissimus cunctabundos illos propriæ salutis procrastinatores vrget: atq; ea occasione in Iudaica ge tis impietate digreditur, illam à regno Dei excludendam, gentes autem prophanas in eorum locum succeßuras esse docens. Sunt aut singulæ huius loci partes dignißimæ, quæ diligentius inspiciantur.
units.tr: This saying agrees with what is answered in the present passage to that curious man. For since questions of this kind hinder salvation rather than promote it, the Lord does not answer directly, nor only that man, but addresses his discourse to the whole multitude of the people, teaching each one what it is fitting for them to do, and with a most effective argument he presses those hesitant procrastinators of their own salvation. On this occasion he digresses into the impiety of the Jewish nation, teaching that it is to be shut out of the kingdom of God, and that profane nations will succeed in their place. Each part of this passage is most worthy to be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primò sic ait: Contendite intrare per angustam portā, &c. Plenius hæc apud Matth. cap. 7. ex ponuntur, vbi duas portas fingit, quarū vna lata & spaciosa dicitur, ad interitū ducens: altera angusta & arcta, per quam ad vitā fit aditus. Et tale quid gentiū quoq; philosophi naturæ lege illumi nati viderunt, quando virtutis viam, quæ ad felicitatē & gloriam verā deducit, asperam atq; supe ratu difficillimam, vitiorum verò tritam & facilem esse dixerunt. Quo etiam referri debet, quod de litera Pythagoræ à poetis traditur. Quia autem porta, quæ ad interitum ducit, non solū lata & cari ni iucunda est, verumetiam mundi authoritate & multitudine commendatur, Christus cōtendere nos iubet, vt per alteram illam, quæ angustior est, ingrediamur. Ita verò docet difficultates plurimas nobis propositas esse, cum quibus nos luctari oporteat, simulq; admonet, ne multitudinis exemplū se quamur, quæ vitiorum illecebris capta ad interitum tendit. Facit hoc ad frenandam eorū curiositatem, qui in alios semper respicere solent, & docemur, singulos potius de propria salute & quid ipsos facere deceat cogitare debere, quàm in alios inquirere.
units.tr: First, he says: "Strive to enter by the narrow gate," etc. Matthew 7 sets this out more fully, where he imagines two gates: one called wide and spacious, leading to destruction; the other narrow and strait, through which there is an entrance to life. Even the philosophers of the Gentiles, enlightened by the law of nature, saw something similar when they said that the way of virtue, which leads to true happiness and glory, is rough, steep and very difficult, but the way of vices is worn smooth and easy. The story that the poets tell about the letter of Pythagoras should also be referred here. But because the gate that leads to destruction is not only wide and pleasant, but also commended by the authority and the multitude of the world, Christ bids us strive to enter through the other, which is narrower. He teaches that very many difficulties are set before us, with which we must struggle, and at the same time he warns us not to follow the example of the multitude, which, captured by the allurements of vice, heads towards destruction. This serves to curb the curiosity of those who are always accustomed to look at others, and we are taught that each of us ought to think about his own salvation and what is fitting for himself to do, rather than inquire into others.

units.la: Hic autem necesse est, vt quæ nam illa porta vitæ sit, probè teneamus, ne nos Satan decipiat, qui mirifica & profunda astutia portas non minus angustas & arctas fabricauit, quæ ad exitium ducunt, veram autē salutis ianuam hoc nomine multis suspectam facit, quod nimium patens & tran situ facillima, adhæc carni iucundior existat. Nam si regulas Monachorum inspicias, quid illis dif ficilius & asperius? quid item eremitica vita ad coercendam carnis petulantiā efficacius videri po test? At non quid carni videatur, sed quid Christus Iesus, qui nobis à Patre doctor & magister datus est, nos sectare conuenit. Is autē alibi clamat: Ego sum ostium: per me si quis introierit, seruabi tur: & ingredietur & egredietur, & pascua inueniet. Itē: Ego sum via & veritas & vita: nemo ve nit ad Patrē nisi per me. Et eodē scala illa, quā in somnis Iacobus vidit, referri debet, quæ ex terra in cælū vsq; protensa Christum adumbrauit, qui terrā cœlis coiunxit, quando Patri placuit per illū sibi reconciliare tam quæ in terra quàm quæ in cœlo sunt. Ergo idè ille porta est, de qua hic agitur, & per eam ingrediuntur, qui ipsum vera fide amplexi, eius regulæ insistunt, quā omnibus discipulis suis communē præscripsit dicens: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucē suā quo tidie & sequatur me. Quo dicto primū obedientia fidei exigitur, qua fit, vt homo procul abiectis car nis desiderijs vnà cū sensu & intellectu suo omni, se totū Dei verbo subijciat. Deinde alacrē & con stantem in ferenda cruce patientiam præcipit Dominus: Postremo fidem requirit, quæ nos in ipsum vnū respicere doceat, & simul ad exēpli sui imitationē nos excitet, quo ipse nobis præiuit. Diximus da hu
units.tr: Here, however, it is necessary that we hold firmly which gate of life this is, lest Satan deceive us, who by a wonderful and deep cunning has built gates no less narrow and strait, which lead to ruin, while he makes the true door of salvation suspect to many on this account: that it is too open and very easy to pass through, and moreover more pleasing to the flesh. For if you look at the rules of the monks, what could be more difficult and harsh? What, again, could seem more effective for restraining the wantonness of the flesh than the life of the hermit? But we ought to follow not what seems good to the flesh, but what Christ Jesus, who has been given to us by the Father as teacher and master, does. He cries out elsewhere: "I am the door: by me if anyone enters in, he shall be saved, and he shall go in and go out, and find pasture." Likewise: "I am the way, the truth and the life: no one comes to the Father except by me." And that ladder which Jacob saw in his sleep should be referred here, which, stretched from earth to heaven, foreshadowed Christ, who joined earth to the heavens, when it pleased the Father to reconcile to himself through him all things that are in earth as well as those that are in heaven. Therefore he is the gate of which we are speaking here, and through it enter those who, embracing him with true faith, abide by his rule, which he prescribed to all his disciples in common, saying: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me." By these words, first, the obedience of faith is required, by which a man, having cast far away the desires of the flesh, together with all his feeling and understanding, submits himself wholly to the word of God. Next, the Lord commands a patience that is ready and steadfast in bearing the cross. Lastly, he requires faith, which teaches us to look to him alone, and at the same time stirs us up to imitate the example which he himself has gone before us in. We have said this much already

units.la: Refponsio Christi.
units.tr: The answer of Christ.

units.la: Ingredi iubet per portam angustam.
units.tr: He bids them enter by the narrow gate.

units.la: Porta vitæ Christus.
units.tr: Christ the gate of life.

units.la: Ioan. 10. 14. Gen. 18. Coloss. 1. de his alibi fusius, & ideo hic consulto sumus breviores. Hoc autem in primis teneamus, portam vitae nobis in uno Christo patefactam esse, & proinde neminem audiri debere, qui nobis aliud salutis ostium, aut viam aliam monstrare audet, qua ad Patrem veniatur.
units.tr: John 10:14. Gen. 18. Col. 1. These things we have treated more fully elsewhere, and so here we have deliberately been briefer. But let us hold first of all that the gate of life has been opened to us in Christ alone, and therefore that no one should be heard who dares to show us another gate of salvation, or another way by which one may come to the Father.

units.la: Cur vero porta haec angusta & transitu difficilis dicitur, cum Christus omnibus pateat, nec aliquem reijciat ad se venientem, & insuper dicat, Iugum meum facile est, & onus meum leve est? Sed in praesenti ad hominum iudicium atque mores respicit, qui suo vitio viam hanc sibi asperam & arctam faciunt. Sunt inter hos alij hypocritae, alij prorsus carnales & mundo dediti: verisq; autem porta salutis angustissima est. Illi enim ut per eam ingrediantur adduci non possunt, sed suorum operum meritis confisi superstitiones subinde accumulant, quarum fiducia turgidi ita a Christo abhorrent, ut eius praedicatione offendantur, veletiam flultam aut bonis moribus inimicam putent eam doctrinam, quae illi uni confidere nos iubet. Ita vero ostium, quod late patens omnes recipere & ad regni caelestis haereditatem simul transmittere posset, ipsi humanarum traditionum & superstitio sanarium ceremoniarum fiducia sibi obstruunt, & idem cum Iudaeis patiuntur, qui (ut Paulus ait) cum propriam iustitiam constituere vellent, a iustitia Dei exciderant, quam is nobis in Filio suo offert. Non minus autem angusta est porta haec mundo & carni addicta. Hi enim salutis rationem sibi monstrari vellent, quae carni arrideret, & hanc tractaret indulgentius. At longe aliam audiunt esse regulam Christi, qui non inanes ritus, non simulatam sanctimoniae speciem, sed totius hominis innovationem, carnis mortificationem & sui exempli imitationem requirit: adhaec de cruce verba fecit, quae non solum nos ferre, sed alacri animo in nos suscipere iubet. Quae omnia ut carni dura & ingrata, sic etiam praestitu impossibilia sunt. Itaque sive fucatos illos iustitiae propriae ostentatores, sive carni & mundo servientes spectemus, vitae porta humano iudicio angusta est, & pauci per eam ingrediuntur. Ne ergo aliorum exemplis seducamur, nobis cum mundi illecebris, imo cum propria carne eius prudentia luctandum est, ut calcare possimus quaecunq; nos remorari solent. Hoc olim Abraham & alios patres fecisse legimus, & hic animus Martyribus fuit qui invicta fidei constantia per angustias & difficultates omnes ad regni caelestis possessionem penetrauerunt. Turpissime autem fallentur, qui ubi iam iter ingressi sunt, subinde ad mundi exemplum respiciunt, & hoc detenti pedem figunt, quasi ab illo differentire nefas sit. Quia vero caro vix persuaderi potest, ut illis fidem habeat, argumenta validissima subijcit Dominus, quibus illam vrget atq; extimulat.
units.tr: But why is this gate called narrow and difficult to pass through, since Christ lies open to all, and rejects no one who comes to him, and moreover says, "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light"? But at present he is looking at the judgement and the manners of men, who by their own fault make this way rough and narrow for themselves. Among these there are some who are hypocrites, others altogether carnal and given over to the world; and yet the gate of salvation is most narrow to them. For the former cannot be brought to enter through it, but, trusting in the merits of their works, they continually heap up superstitions, and swollen with confidence in these they so shrink from Christ that they are offended by his preaching, or even think that doctrine foolish or hostile to good morals which bids us trust in him alone. Thus the door, which, open wide, could receive all and send them on together to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, they themselves block up by their trust in human traditions and the superstitious ceremonies of their own devising; and they suffer the same as the Jews, who (as Paul says) when they wished to establish their own righteousness, fell away from the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son. But no less narrow is the gate of those who are given over to the world and the flesh. For these would have a way of salvation shown to them which would please the flesh and treat it more indulgently. But they hear that the rule of Christ is quite different, who requires not empty rites nor a feigned appearance of holiness, but the renewal of the whole man, the mortification of the flesh and the imitation of his example; moreover he spoke of the cross, which he bids us not only bear but take up with a ready mind. All these things are as hard and unwelcome to the flesh as they are, in practice, impossible. Therefore, whether we look at those brazen displayers of their own righteousness or at those who serve the flesh and the world, the gate of life is narrow by human judgement, and few enter through it. Lest we be led astray by the examples of others, we must struggle with the allurements of the world, and indeed with our own flesh, with its prudence, so that we may trample underfoot whatever is wont to hold us back. We read that Abraham and the other fathers did this of old, and this was the spirit of the martyrs, who with unconquered constancy of faith pressed through all straits and difficulties to the possession of the heavenly kingdom. But those are most shamefully deceived who, once they have entered upon the way, keep looking back to the example of the world, and stop there with their foot fixed, as if it were a sin to depart from it. But because the flesh can scarcely be persuaded to have faith, the Lord adds most powerful arguments by which he presses and spurs it on.

units.la: Primo spem inanem confutat, qua plerique seipsos decipiunt, dum viam in caelos facilem esse & nunquam non patere sibi persuadent. Dicit ergo: Quia multi, dico vobis, studebunt intrare & non poterunt. Quasi dicat: Iussi ut contendatis intrare per angustam portam, & neq; multitudinem sectemini, neq; curam salutis aeternae differatis, sed potius absque mora hanc, dum offertur, studeatis apprehendere. Id vero non temere monui. Nam etsi quidam sibi ipsis delitias faciant, & pro suae voluntatis arbitrio ingressuros putent ad regni caelestis possessionem, quandocunque ipsis libuerit: est tamen haec illorum spes non incerta modo, verumetiam periculosa. Nam multis hoc accidet, ut magno quidem conatu ad salutem aspirent, eam tamen obtinere non possint. Vobis ergo videndum erit ne qui seipsos, vel alios vana hac persuasione decipiant, dum oblatam salutis occasionem praeterlabi sinunt. Sufficit autem unus hic locus iis confutandis, qui vires hominis eo usque extollunt, ut in vius potestate sitam esse dicant salutem, modo eam amplecti velit. Atqui nos ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneos esse ex nobismetipsis Paulus ait. Et ut demus nos voluntatem in nostra manu habere, tamen ne hoc quidem ad salutem sufficere Christus diserte pronuntiat. Multi (inquit) studebunt intrare, & non poterunt. Et huius rei exempla in iis videmus, qui desperatione exagitati nihil perinde volunt & cupiunt quam ut Christi participes fiant, nihil autem proficiunt, nisi Deus ex singulari misericordia ipsis succurrat.
units.tr: First he refutes the empty hope by which many deceive themselves, while they persuade themselves that the way to heaven is easy and is never closed to them. So he says: "For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able." As if he were saying: "I bade you strive to enter by the narrow gate, and neither follow the multitude nor put off the care of eternal salvation, but rather, without delay, eagerly seize this while it is offered." And I did not give this warning rashly. For although some pamper themselves and think that they will enter into possession of the heavenly kingdom whenever it pleases them, according to the judgement of their own will, yet their hope is not only uncertain but also dangerous. For it will happen to many that they strive with great effort towards salvation, and yet cannot obtain it. Therefore you must see to it that you do not deceive yourselves or others by this vain persuasion, and allow the offered occasion of salvation to slip past. One passage is enough, however, to refute those who so exalt the powers of man that they say salvation lies in a man's own power, provided only he is willing to embrace it. Yet Paul says that we are not even fit of ourselves to think anything. And even granting that we have the will in our own hand, Christ plainly declares that not even this is enough for salvation. "Many," he says, "will seek to enter, and will not be able." And we see examples of this in those who, driven by despair, want nothing so much and desire nothing so much as to become partakers of Christ, yet make no progress unless God, out of singular mercy, comes to their aid.

units.la: Caeterum diligentius exponit, quod uno verbo dixerat, & quando conatus iste irritus aut fraudulentus fit, docet hoc verbis: Ex quo videlicet surrexerit paterfamilias, & occluserit ostium, & cepit foris stare & pulsare ostium, dicentes: Domine Domine, aperi nobis: Qui respondens dicet vobis, Nescio unde vos sitis, &c. Deus sub patrisfamilias persona describit, quod in scripturis admodum frequens est. Ita enim & illius bonitas commendatur, & nos de nostro officio admonemur: quod hoc loco in primis Christus spectat. Ut enim bonus paterfamilias domus suae curam habet, adeo diligentem, vt interdum excussò somno de nocte surgat, & pessulo ostij obdito malæ frugis famulos excludat, qui præter eius mandatum domo egressi vel in tabernas & ganeas perporrò, vel per plateas atq; vicos grassantur: Ita Deus Pater, etsi interdum dormire videatur, quando nobis omne salutis occasionem negligentibus ad nostram petulantiam conniuet, suo tamen tempore surgit ad iudicandum, & ex familia sua excludit eos, qui professioni suæ non respondent. Patet quidem semper in Christo ostium gratiæ Dei & salutis omnibus, qui feria pœnitentia adipsum conuertuntur: ijs autem occludi-tur, qui aut incurabili pertinacia bonitatem Dei superant, dum agnitæ veritati reluctando in Spiritum sanctum peccant, aut pœnitere nescij in suis peccatis moriuntur. Nä vt prioribus illis remissio peccatorum negatur: ita alteri illi nullam habent postquam è viuis discesserunt cum Deo in gratiam redeundi occasionem. Vides ergo Deum cum paterna bonitate & indulgentia seueritatem coniungere, quando illam contemni videt, & (vt historicus Romanus ait) tarditatē vindicta supplicij gravitate compensare. Extant eius generis exempla iam inde à prima mundi origine, quæ cum alibi commemorauerimus, eadem nunc repetere non opus est. Neq; desunt hodie, quæ nos ad serium salutis studium excitare poterant, nisi cum pudore & communi intellectu plerique omnes etiam mali sensum depositissent. Veruntamen quæ in hoc sæculo impijs & incurabilibus procrastinatoribus accidunt, ludus & iocus sunt præillis, quæ in altero sæculo patientur, vt paulò post audiemus. Interim extinguitur huius loci authoritate Purgatorium ille ignis, adeoq; maxima doctrinæ Papisticæ pars palæ euertitur, quæ defunctis quoq; salutis spem facit, vt ab ijs tributum exigere possint homines auari, qui religionem omnem quæstu metiuntur. Atqui admonet Christus, ne dum adhuc in vita superstites sumus, nosipsos spe inani decipiamus: quanto minus ergo spem salutis post mortem usq; extendere debemus, quasi vel nostris cruciatibus, vel hæredum nostrorum operibus meritorijs Deus placari possit; vt semel occlusum domus suæ cælestis ostium nobis patefaciat.
units.tr: Moreover, he explains more carefully what he had said in a single word, and shows in words when this attempt fails or is fraudulent: "From the time that the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, 'Lord, Lord, open to us'; he will answer and say to you, 'I do not know where you are from,' etc." God is described under the person of the master of the house, which is very common in Scripture. For in this way both his goodness is commended and we are reminded of our duty, which Christ chiefly has in view in this passage. As a good master of the house takes such careful charge of his household that he sometimes rises from sleep at night, bars the door and shuts out the worthless servants who, against his command, have gone out and wander far and wide into taverns and brothels, or through the streets and lanes, so God the Father, although he may seem sometimes to sleep while we neglect every opportunity of salvation and he winks at our wantonness, nevertheless rises at his appointed time to judge and shuts out from his household those who do not live up to their calling. The door of God's grace and of salvation stands always open in Christ to all who turn to him in time of repentance; but it is shut against those who, either through incurable obstinacy, overcome God's goodness, sinning against the Holy Spirit by resisting the truth they have recognised, or who die in their sins without knowing how to repent. For as the former are denied forgiveness of sins, so the latter have no opportunity of being reconciled to God once they have departed from the living. You see, then, that God joins severity to his fatherly goodness and indulgence, when he sees himself despised; and (as the Roman historian says) makes up for the slowness of vengeance by the severity of the punishment. Examples of this kind exist from the very beginning of the world; but since we have mentioned them elsewhere, there is no need to repeat them now. Nor are there lacking today things which could arouse us to a serious concern for salvation, were it not that nearly all people, even the wicked, had laid aside shame and common sense. Yet what happens in this age to the wicked and incurable procrastinators is mere sport and jest compared with what they will suffer in the next age, as we shall hear shortly. Meanwhile, by the authority of this passage, that fire of Purgatory is extinguished, and in this way the greater part of Papist doctrine is overthrown, which also gives hope of salvation to the dead, so that greedy men, who measure all religion by profit, may exact payments from them. Yet Christ warns us not to deceive ourselves with empty hope while we are still alive in this life: how much less, then, ought we to extend the hope of salvation beyond death, as if God could be appeased by our sufferings or by the meritorious works of our heirs, so as to open for us the door of his heavenly house once it has been shut.

units.la: Porrò quia ipsi cum hypocritis res erat, qui etiamsi in scelere deprehendantur, se tamen excusare & operum suorum merita prætexere audent, aut priuilegia quædam sibi vendicare, ex quibus immunitatem quandam sibi ipsis pollicentur: ipsos per Profopœiam paterfamilias respondentes & suis operibus gloriantes inducit: Edimus in tui conspectu & bibimus, & in plateis nostris docuisti. Pertinent ista proprie ad Iudæos, quos scimus hac potissimum fiducia elatos fuisse, quod se solos Dei populum & Ecclesiam esse putarent, cum illi obstrictus esset. Horum ergo voces erant: Nos sumus vt nea Dei, grex Dei, populus Dei, electum illud peculium, quod vt sibi ex omnibus gentibus selegit, & Regnum sacerdotale. Nobis ille se familiarius quam vllis alijs populis reuelauit: nobis legem dedit, nos illum in nostris Synagogis & plateis docentem audiuimus: nobis cultum illum magnificum instituit, qui solus in orbe ei probatur: nos secundum eius præcepta sacrificamus, nos ex sacrificijs & libaminibus epulas sacras instituimus, & coram ipso (sicuti iussit) edimus & bibimus atq; dies lætos agimus: nobis denique promissus est Messias, Rex & Sacerdos æternus. Num ergo nos ignoraret Deus? Num nos excluderet promissionum veterum immemor? Num populum suum abijciat cuius sunt patres, testamenta, fœdus, & qui hucusque solus cultum eius verum exercuit? Hanc gloriationem Iudæorum fuisse omnibus seculis, non solum Prophetarum sermones, verumtamen ea testantur, quæ Ioanni Baptistæ & ipsi Christo de patre suo Abrahamo obiecerunt. Sed Dominus hanc inutilem prorsus fore docet, quando patrem familias priorem sententiam ijsdem verbis repetentem & simul ipsos duriori responso reijcientem inducit: Nam dicet vobis, inquit: Dico vobis, nescio unde vos sitis: abscedite à me omnes qui facitis quod iniustum est. Et apud Matthæum præmittitur: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine Domine, introibit in Regnum cælorum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui est in cœlis. Quibus verbis diserte docet, neq; externa fidei professionem, neque ritus vllos aut ceremonias, neq; vlla opera, quæ absq; fide fiunt, ad salutem acquirendam sufficere: sed hanc omnem in eo consistere, vt nos Patris cœlestis voluntati accommodemus. Est autem hæc, vt Filium suum dilectum audiamus, huic vni fidamus, & eius regulam sequi cuti nosipsos abnegemus, in cruce ferenda alacres atque constantes simus, & exemplum illius, quo nobis præiuit, sedulò imitemur.
units.tr: Furthermore, since he was dealing with hypocrites, who, even when caught in wickedness, dare to make excuses and put forward the merits of their works, or claim certain privileges for themselves, by which they promise themselves a kind of immunity, he introduces the master of the house, by prosopopoeia, answering them and boasting of their works: "We have eaten and drunk in your presence, and you have taught in our streets." These words properly apply to the Jews, whom we know were especially puffed up by this confidence, because they thought they alone were God's people and Church, to whom he was bound. Their words, therefore, were these: "We are the sons of God, the flock of God, the people of God, that chosen possession which he selected for himself from all nations, and a royal priesthood. He revealed himself to us more intimately than to any other people: he gave us the law; we heard him teaching in our synagogues and streets; he instituted for us that magnificent worship which alone in the world is approved by him; we sacrifice according to his precepts; from the sacrifices and libations we hold sacred feasts, and in his presence (as he commanded) we eat and drink and keep joyful days; finally, the Messiah, the eternal King and Priest, was promised to us. Would God then be ignorant of us? Would he exclude us, forgetful of the ancient promises? Would he cast off his people, whose are the fathers, the testaments, the covenant, and who alone until now have practised his true worship?" That this boasting of the Jews existed in all ages is attested not only by the words of the Prophets, but also by what they objected to John the Baptist and to Christ himself concerning their father Abraham. But the Lord shows that this boasting will be altogether useless, when he introduces the master of the house repeating his former sentence in the same words, and at the same time rejecting them with a harsher answer: "He will say to you," he says, "I tell you, I do not know where you are from: depart from me, all you who do what is unjust." And in Matthew it is prefaced: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." By these words he clearly teaches that neither an outward profession of faith, nor any rites or ceremonies, nor any works which are done without faith, are enough to obtain salvation; but that all this consists in our conforming ourselves to the will of the heavenly Father. Now this will is that we hear his beloved Son, trust in him alone, and follow his rule, deny ourselves, be ready and steadfast in bearing the cross, and diligently imitate the example which he has gone before us in.

units.la: Quod ergo hic Iudæis dicitur, non minus ad nos, qui Christiano nomine gloriamur putemus pertinere. Nam eadem fiducia multos etiam hodie dementat, vt sibi immunitatem ex falsa fidei professione sessione & externo atque hypocritico Sacramentorum vsu polluceantur. Silent hi quoq; Christo ad poenitentiam seriam ipsos exhortanti vel aperto ore vel intra animum suum respondere: Aliqui in Christi nomen baptizati sumus, de mensa Domini edimus & bibimus, Ecclesiae titulo & nomine censemur, Euangelio locum damus, quod in nostris templis praedicatur, intra privatas aedes legitur & canitur, in plateis & foro passim sonat. Num ergo nos non agnoscat ille, qui neminem vnquam fastidiuit? Num nobis abiectis Antichristo locum dabit, aut Iudaeorum delirijs vel Turcica barbarie omnem orbem obrui patietur? Sed nequicquam haec ab ijs dicuntur, qui nominis sui professioni non respondent, sed suis desiderijs addicti per omnem iniustitiam & iniquitatem volutantur. At si haec nos Deo non possunt comendare, quae si nudam literam spectes, ex eius praescripto, sed absq; fide sunt: quid ergo de superstitiosis illis humanarum traditionum obseruatoribus dicemus, qui suas sordes & stercora Deo obtrudere audent clamantes, Nos Missae sacrificio quotidie afflimus, ad Christi & Diuorum imagines cernui procumbimus, illis cerea accendimus, anathemata ijsdem consecra mus, peregrinationes suscipimus longinquas laboris atq; periculi plenas, adhaec feriamur, ieiuna mus, cilicijs induimur, humi dormimus, cucullati, funibus cincti, nudipedes aut fenestratis vel lig neis soleis muniti incedimus, de nocte ad psalmodias surgimus, a coniugijs abstinemus, flagellis & virgis carnem nostram coercemus, in syluis desertis aut claustris vitam degimus, deniq; vitae genus sequimur a mundi huius consuetudine & moribus alienissimum? Haec (inquam) sunt, quae nostri se culi hypocritae fiduciam faciunt, vt sibi omnia tuta & perpetuum Dei fauorem promittant. Sed iam pridem illis per Prophetam respondit Dominus: Quis requisiuit ista de manibus vestris? Item: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Quibus enim scripturis probabunt, haec a Deo praecepta esse? Et quomodo ex fide possunt fieri, quae nullo Dei verbo nituntur, in quod vnum fides respicit? At quod non ex fide fit, peccatum est. Rom.14.
units.tr: What is said here to the Jews, therefore, let us think applies no less to us, who glory in the Christian name. For the same confidence drives many even today to madness, so that they flatter themselves with immunity from a false profession of faith, from a session in the Church, and from an outward and hypocritical use of the sacraments. These people too, when Christ urges them to serious repentance, keep silent, or answer within their own minds: "We have been baptised in the name of Christ; we eat and drink at the table of the Lord; we are counted by the title and name of the Church; we give a place to the gospel, which is preached in our churches, read and sung in private houses, and sounds everywhere in the streets and the marketplace. Will he not then acknowledge us, who has never despised anyone? Will he cast us off and give place to Antichrist, or allow the whole world to be overwhelmed by the follies of the Jews or the Turkish barbarism?" But these things are said in vain by those who do not live up to the profession of their name, but, given over to their desires, wallow in every injustice and iniquity. And if these things cannot commend us to God—things which, if you look only at the bare letter, are according to his prescription, but are without faith—what shall we say of those superstitious observers of human traditions, who dare to thrust their filth and dung upon God, crying out: "We offer the sacrifice of the Mass every day; we prostrate ourselves before the images of Christ and of the saints; we light wax candles before them; we dedicate votive offerings to them; we undertake long pilgrimages full of toil and danger; moreover, we fast on days of abstinence, we clothe ourselves in haircloth, we sleep on the ground, we go about hooded, girded with ropes, barefoot, or protected by wicker or wooden soles; we rise at night for psalmody; we abstain from marriage; we restrain our flesh with whips and rods; we live our lives in deserted woods or cloisters; and finally we follow a way of life most alien to the customs and manners of this world?" These things, I say, are what the hypocrites of our age make the ground of their confidence, so that they promise themselves that all things are safe and God's favour perpetual. But long ago the Lord answered them through the Prophet: "Who required these things at your hands?" Again: "They worship me in vain, teaching doctrines which are the commandments of men." For by what Scriptures will they prove that these things have been commanded by God? And how can those things be done from faith which rest on no word of God, to which faith alone looks? But whatever is not done from faith is sin. Rom. 14.

units.la: Sed ad Christi verba redeamus, qui hypocritas, quibus non aliud hominum genus consumacius & incurabilius est, poenarum atrocitate territans subdit: Illic erit fletus & stridor dentium, cum videritis Abrahamum & Isaacum & Iacobum & omnes Prophetas in regno Dei, vos autem expelli foras, &c. Multa simul congerit, quae ad supplicij magnitudinem faciunt. Primo fletum & stridorem dentium minatur, qua locutione frequenter inferorum cruciatus describi, vt hos non leues esse neque nihil praeter otiosam a Regno Dei exclusionem afferre, sed acutissimis doloribus ad animam simul & corpus penetrare ostendat. Etenim cum vtraque hominis pars peccati particeps & ministra sit, vtramque plecti oportet, nisi Deum iniustum dicere velimus. Itaque anima perpetuo irae Dei sensu cruciabitur, qui fletum & gemitus extorquebit. Corpus autem ardoribus diris adustum horrebit, & dentium quoque stridore dolorem intollerabilem testabitur. Erit autem cruciatus ille eo gravior, quod perpetuus vel aeternus erit, quem nulla liberatione spes levare aut mitigare poterit. Nam vt alibi ex Propheta dicit Dominus, vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Christ, who, terrifying the hypocrites (a kind of men more obstinate and incurable than any other) with the atrocity of punishments, adds: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the Prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves cast out." He heaps up many things at once that add to the greatness of the punishment. First, he threatens weeping and gnashing of teeth, an expression by which the torments of the lower world are often described, to show that these are no light matter, nor merely the idle exclusion from the kingdom of God, but that they pierce the soul and body at once with most severe pains. For since each part of man shares in and serves sin, each must be punished, unless we are willing to call God unjust. Thus the soul will be tormented with a perpetual sense of the wrath of God, which will wring from it weeping and groaning. The body, scorched by dreadful burnings, will shudder, and the grinding of teeth will bear witness to its intolerable pain. That torment will be all the heavier because it will be perpetual, or eternal, and no hope of deliverance will be able to lighten or soften it. For, as the Lord says elsewhere, citing the Prophet, "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched."

units.la: Secundo, Haec tunc vobis euenient (inquit) cum videritis Abrahamum & Isaacum & Iacobum & omnes Prophetas in Regno Dei, vos autem expelli foras. Facit hoc multum ad miseriae illius amplificationem. Acuit enim vehementer animi dolorem, quando alios in honore & gloria constitutos feliciter agere, nos autem miseros & calamitosos esse videmus: eo magis ille intenditur, si tales videamus eos, quos aut odio habuimus semper, aut quorum admonitiones contempsimus, aut quorum nomine nequicquam gloriati sumus. Quae omnia Iudaeis conueniunt. Prophetas enim oderant, admonitiones & minas eorum aspernabantur, Abrahami & patrum aliorum nomen hypocritica & inani confidentia suis sceleribus praetexebant. Non poterit ergo non incredibilis esse cruciatus ille, quem sentient, quando hos quidem in caelestem gloriam recipi, se vero in totius mundi & Angelorum conspectu, vt degeneres & spurios filios, a patrum societate repelli & excludi videbunt. Proderat hic patrum mentionem facere, ne generis fiducia porro seipsos fallerent, & vt omnes scirent, non promiscuam eorum qui ad exitium tendunt multitudinem, sed potius sanctorum patrum fidem atq; exemplum spectandum esse ijs, qui seruari volunt. Quod ipsum hodie obseruare debebant, qui Diuos quidem in ore habent, eorum autem mores, doctrinam & exemplum sequuntur, qui a fide Diuorum prorsus sunt alieni. Additur bis tertium: Et venient multi ab Oriente & Occidente & Borea & Austro, & discumbent in regno Dei. Quibus verbis non solùm Iudaeos repudium passuros, sed in eorum locum gentes adoptandas fore docet: quod ipsum Prophetae etiam veteres non semel minati fuerant. Fuit autem hoc cum summa Iudaicae gentis ignominia coniunctum. Eo enim patuit intolerabilem planè fuisse eorum impietatem, quando eos ipsos in Regni sui haereditatem Deus succedere voluit, qui hucusq; pro prophanis habiti, & ab omni Ecclesiae societate & veri Dei cognitione alieni sub tenebrarum potestate non minus turpem quàm miseram peccati seruitutem seruierant. Voluit autem Dominus (sicuti olim per Mosem praedixerat) zelotypia sancta Iudaeos provocare, vt ad ipsum conuersi se à gentibus prophanis praeueniri non paterentur. Et simul eorum spem & fiduciam confutat, qui Deum ita sibi obstrictum esse arbitrabantur, vt ipsis reiectis nullam porrò Ecclesiam fore putaret. Docet ergo, non defuturos vnquam Deo quos vocet, & iam nunc per totum orbem praedestinatum esse electorum numerum, qui in Regni Dei haereditatem subituri sint. Idem Baptista quoq; Pharisaeos monuit, quando Deum ex lapidibus Abrahamo filios excitaturum esse promisit. Quod nobis etiam in mentem venire debet, quando eadem perfuasio nos quoq; confidentiores & Deo minus obsequentes reddit. Nec enim deficient in vniuersum Christiani, etiamsi nos, qui hoc nomine nunc gloriamur, dignas nostra ingratitudinis & impietatis poenas demus. Nam & de Iudaeorum reiectione ne Paulus ad Romanos non obscurè vaticinatur, & fortasse inter Turcas maiori cum fructu Euangelium praedicabitur, quàm inter pseudochristianos, qui vel in Antichristi verba iurarunt, vel Epicuri discipuli facti cum Deo sacra simul omnia contemnunt.
units.tr: Second, he says: "This will happen to you when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the Prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves cast out." This greatly adds to the magnitude of that misery. For it sharpens the pain of the mind intensely when we see others placed in honour and glory and living happily, while we are wretched and miserable; and it is increased still more if we see those whom we have always hated, or whose admonitions we have despised, or in whose name we have vainly boasted. All of this applies to the Jews. For they hated the Prophets and scorned their admonitions and threats, and they covered their crimes with the name of Abraham and the other fathers, with hypocritical and empty confidence. That torment, then, cannot fail to be incredible, which they will feel when they see these men received into heavenly glory, while they themselves, in the sight of the whole world and of the Angels, are repelled and shut out from the company of the fathers, as degenerate and bastard sons. It was useful here to mention the fathers, so that they would no longer deceive themselves by trust in their lineage, and so that all might know that those who wish to be saved must look not to the promiscuous multitude of those who rush to destruction, but rather to the faith and example of the holy fathers. This very thing they ought to observe today, those who have the saints on their lips but follow the morals, teaching and example of those who are wholly estranged from the faith of the saints. He adds a third time: "And many will come from the East and the West and the North and the South, and will sit down in the kingdom of God." By these words he teaches that not only will the Jews be rejected, but that the Gentiles will be adopted in their place, which the ancient Prophets had also threatened more than once. This, however, was joined with the great disgrace of the Jewish nation. For it became plain that their impiety had been utterly intolerable, when God wished the very people who until now had been regarded as profane, and who, alienated from all fellowship of the Church and from the knowledge of the true God, had served under the power of darkness a slavery of sin no less shameful than wretched, to succeed to the inheritance of his kingdom. The Lord, moreover, wished (as he had foretold long before through Moses) to provoke the Jews to holy jealousy, so that, turning to him, they would not allow themselves to be outstripped by the profane Gentiles. And at the same time he refutes their hope and confidence, who thought that God was so bound to them that, once they were rejected, he would think there would be no Church anymore. He teaches, therefore, that there will never be a lack of those whom God may call, and that even now the number of the elect who are to share the inheritance of the kingdom of God is predestined throughout the whole world. John the Baptist also warned the Pharisees when he promised that God could raise up children to Abraham from stones. This ought to come to our minds too, since the same persuasion makes us also too confident and less obedient to God. For Christians will by no means fail altogether, even if we, who now glory in this name, pay the penalties due to our ingratitude and impiety. For Paul also prophesies not obscurely in the Epistle to the Romans concerning the rejection of the Jews; and perhaps the Gospel will be preached among the Turks with greater fruit than among the pseudo-Christians, who have either sworn to the words of Antichrist or, having become disciples of Epicurus, despise all sacred things together with God.

units.la: Postremò addit Dominus: Et sunt vltimi, qui erunt primi: & sunt primi, qui erunt vltimi. Primos dicit Iudaeos, quia cum horum patre Abrahamo Deus foedus salutis, quod in diluuio abolitum videri poterat, instaurauit, & ijsdem ipse primis per Euangelij praedicationem & miracula innotuit. Vltimi sunt, qui postea ex gentibus vocati crediderunt. Ista autem sententia, quae saepe ab illo repetitur, amplius adhuc deprimit Iudaeorum superciliùm, qui aduersus omnes gentes suis praerogatiuis superbiebant. Ostendit enim fore vicissitudinem rerum, vt qui nunc alieni sunt à repub. Israelis, primum in ea locum obtineant, in postremum autem reijciantur qui secundùm carnem ex Abrahamo nati sunt. Factum hoc duplici ratione. Nam quoad multitudinem & dignitatem, ij qui ex gentibus descendunt Christiani, eos longè superant, qui ex Iudaeis crediderunt. Imò raro bonae frugis sunt Iudaei, qui Christo per baptismum nomen dant, cùm plerique ad manifestam idololatriam, quae in Papatu regnat, conuertantur (quod imminentem & Cyclopicum legis per Mosem datae contemptum arguit) aut saltem nihil praeter quaestum quaerant, multi etiam ex eo voluptatem captent, quòd Christianis hominibus illudere, & nostris Sacramentis abuti possint. Deinde quoad ordinem quoq; implebitur hoc Christi dictum. Nam, vt Paulus scribit, vbi plenitudo gentium intrauerit, tunc rursus vocabuntur Iudaei, vt ita totus Israel, tam ij qui secundùm carnem, quàm alteri qui per fidem Israelitae facti sunt, seruentur. Semper autem meminisse nos decet, ista ad nos quoq; pertinere, neque nobis Deum parsurum esse, qui ex oleastro defracti & in sanctam patrum stirpem insiti sumus, si Iudaeorum caecitatem & contumaciam imitemur. Itaq; qui sibi ipsi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Ete nim ruinae grauis praeludia multa sunt, & exemplis multis nos Deus excitat quotidie. Vigilemus ergo, & grati simus Deo, fidei verò professionem vitae ac morum sanctimonia confirmemus, vt in magno illo die nos profratribus & coharedibus suis agnoscere possit aeternus Dei Filius, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally the Lord adds: "And the last will be first, and the first will be last." By the first he means the Jews, because God renewed with their father Abraham the covenant of salvation, which might seem to have been abolished at the Flood, and because he himself was made known first to them through the preaching of the Gospel and through miracles. The last are those who afterwards believed, called from the Gentiles. Now this saying, which he repeats often, humbles still more the arrogance of the Jews, who boasted of their privileges against all the nations. For it shows that there will be a reversal of affairs, so that those who are now strangers to the commonwealth of Israel will obtain the first place in it, while those who were born of Abraham according to the flesh will be cast into the last place. This happens for a twofold reason. For as to number and dignity, those who descend from the Gentiles and are Christians far surpass those of the Jews who have believed. Indeed, the Jews who give their name to Christ through baptism are rarely of good fruit, since most of them turn to manifest idolatry, which reigns in the Papacy (which shows an impending and Cyclopean contempt for the law given through Moses), or at least seek nothing beyond gain; and many also take pleasure from it, because they are able to mock Christians and abuse our sacraments. Then, as regards order too, this saying of Christ will be fulfilled. For, as Paul writes, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then the Jews will again be called, so that all Israel, both those who are such according to the flesh and the others who have become Israelites through faith, may be saved. We ought always to remember, however, that these things pertain to us also, and that God will not spare us, who have been broken off from the wild olive and grafted into the holy stock of the fathers, if we imitate the blindness and obstinacy of the Jews. Therefore let him who seems to himself to stand see that he does not fall. For there are many forerunners of a grievous ruin, and God rouses us daily with many examples. Let us therefore be watchful and thankful to God, and let us confirm our profession of faith by the holiness of our life and morals, so that in that great day the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, may acknowledge us as brothers and co-heirs of his own: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLI.

units.la: Eo ipso die accesserunt quidam Pharisaeorum dicentes ei: Exi, & abi hinc: nam Herodes vult te trucidare. Tunc ait eis: Profecti dicite vulpi illi: Ecce, eiciam daemonia, & sanationes peragam hodie & cras, & tertia die consummabor. Veruntamen oportet me hodie & cras & perendie iter facere: quia fieri non potest, vt Propheta pereat extra Hierusalem. Hierusalem, Hierusalem, quæ trucidas Prophetas, & lapi-das eos qui ad te missi sunt, quoties volui congregare liberos tuos, quem-admodum gallina pulliciem suam sub alas & noluistis. Ecce relinqui-tur vobis domus vestra deserta. Amen autem dico vobis, non videbitis me, vsque dum venerit tempus vt dicatis: Benedictus qui venit in no-mine Domini.
units.tr: On that same day some of the Pharisees came and said to him: "Get out and leave this place, for Herod wants to kill you." He said to them: "Go and tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I shall be finished. Nevertheless, I must journey today, tomorrow and the next day, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing. Behold, your house is left to you desolate. I tell you truly, you shall not see me until the time comes when you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

units.la: Quemadmodum doctor & seruator noster, Iesus Christus, cùm primùm docere inciperet, omnes ad poenitentiam atque vitæ priores emendationem hortatus est: ita quando mortis hora instabat, eandem doctrinam passim magno & singulari studio inculcauit. Et hoc quidem capi-te exempla simul & similia multa in eum finem adduxit, vt offenderet nullam nobis salutis spem reliquam esse, nisi dum hæc vita durat ad Deum verè conuertamur. Doctrinam verò hanc Iudæis potissimùm accommodans, quos inani generis & externi cultus fiducia deceptos nimiùm in re ma-xime necessaria cunctari videbat, grauiter monuit, vt dum tempus est, cum Deo in gratiam redire studeant, & nisi id faciant, eos à Regno illius omnino excludendos fore minatus est. Sequitur nunc, quàm parum doctrina hac profecerit apud eos, qui in illa gente sanctissimi habebantur: deinde vt ea occasione toti populo, in primis tamen Hierosolymæ horrendum excidium atque dissipa-tionem miserrimam denuntiarit, quibus Deus in hoc etiam seculo ipsorum contumaciam & ingra-titudinem statuerit vlcisci.
units.tr: Just as our teacher and saviour, Jesus Christ, when he first began to teach, urged everyone to repentance and to the amendment of their former lives, so when the hour of his death was at hand, he impressed the same teaching everywhere with great and singular earnestness. In this chapter he brought forward examples, together with many similar ones, for the purpose of showing that there is no hope of salvation left for us unless we turn truly to God while this life lasts. Adapting this teaching especially to the Jews, whom he saw were too slow in the most necessary matter, deceived by the vain confidence of a merely outward worship, he solemnly warned them to seek to be reconciled with God while there is time, and threatened that if they did not do so they would be shut out altogether from his kingdom. There follows now how little this teaching had profited among those who were regarded as most holy in that nation; then, on that occasion, how he announced a dreadful destruction and most wretched dispersion for the whole people, but especially for Jerusalem, whom God would in this age also punish for their obstinacy and ingratitude.

units.la: Ad primùm huius loci caput pertinet quod de Pharisæis scribitur, qui nouam de his dicendi occasionem Christo præbuerunt. Eo ipso die (ait Lucas) accesserunt quidam Pharisæorum dicen-tes: Exi, & abi hinc: nam Herodes vult te trucidare. Videntur isti ex eorum numero fuisse, qui ipsius amici videri volebant. Certè amici officium est, aliquem de imminenti periculo certiorem facere, & vt sibi prospiciat admonere. Sed falsam atque simulatam fuisse hanc admonitionem, ex Domini responso abunde patet, quo illam non sine iusta indignatione reiecit. Afluté autem illi & subdole fugam ei suadent, vt porrò negotium ipsis facere desinat. Scimus enim eum nusquam pluries & constantiores habuisse discipulos, quàm in Galilæa, in qua vt plurimùm versatus est, & vnde Apostoli quoque oriundi fuerunt. Et quia fortassis Sacerdotibus quoque minus licebat in regno Herodis, qui Iudæorum potentiam non sine causa suspectam habebat, eò res spectare videbatur, vt plerisque Christo iam credentibus, & eius doctrina indies latiùs serpente gens illa tota à Sacerdotibus & Scribis aperte deficeret. Quia ergo in illis locis aliquid violentius tentare minimè tutum erat, & proinde eum aperta vi cyjcere non possunt, ad dolos & mendacia confugi terrorem illi incutere volunt, vt sponte discedens populum illum ipsis denuo in statum priorem reducendum relinquat. Neque ignorare poterant homines astutissimi, quantum hoc authoritati illius derogaturum esset, si turpi fuga sibi consuleret, & in latebras aliquas se reciperet. Itaque vt suum regnum stabiliant, consulunt, vt quam otiosissimè se alio conferat, & ad hoc Herodis Regis nomine abuntur, quem Christo minus propitium esse verisimile erat, cùm eius præcursorem, Ioannem Baptistam, non ita pridem crudeliter & iniustè iugulasset decollari. Est hoc odij vehementissimi & implacabilis argumentum, quod iflos homines ex ambitione & auaritia con-cepisse, alias diximus. Nam si Christum spectemus, adeò non dignus erat odio, vt potius omnium hominum amorem atque fauorem mereretur: cùm non solùm nemini noceret, & ab omni abstine-ret maleficio, verumetiam promiscuè omnibus benefaceret, partim docendo, partim miracula ac-dendo, quibus immedicabiles multorum morbos curabat. Veruntamen tanto illius odio flagrant Pharisæi, vt & eum eiectum & populum tanto benefactore destitui velint, ne ipsorum fraudi-bus in vniuersum detectis, eorum authoritas tota concidat, & quæstus nefarius, quem ex sacris fa-ciebant, euertatur. Fuit hæc plus quàm sacrilega impietas, quæ etiam hodie apud omnes eos regnat, qui fucata sanctimonia specie sese venditant, eo autem prætextu non aliud quàm inanem gloriam inter homines & priuatum quæstum venantur. Non possunt tales vllis beneficijs placari. Nam vt veritatis lux eos offendit, ita quæ in plures alios conferuntur, salutis æternæ dona illos prorsus in rabiem adigunt.
units.tr: To the first part of this passage belongs what is written about the Pharisees, who gave Christ a new occasion for speaking about them. "On that same day," says Luke, "some of the Pharisees came and said: Get out and leave this place, for Herod wants to kill you." These men seem to have been among those who wished to appear as his friends. Certainly it is the duty of a friend to warn someone of an impending danger and to advise him to look after himself. But that this warning was false and feigned is abundantly clear from the Lord's reply, by which he rejected it not without just indignation. These men, however, craftily and deceitfully urge him to flee, so that he would stop causing them trouble. For we know that he never had more numerous and more constant disciples anywhere than in Galilee, where he mostly lived, and whence the apostles too were born. And perhaps because the priests too had less freedom in the kingdom of Herod, who had good reason to regard the power of the Jews with suspicion, it seemed that the situation was going in this direction: since many were already believing in Christ, and his teaching was spreading more widely every day, that whole nation would openly fall away from the priests and scribes. Since therefore it was by no means safe to attempt anything more violent in those regions, and so they could not drive him out by open force, they resort to deceit and lies, wishing to strike terror into him, so that he would withdraw of his own accord and leave the people to be brought back to their former state under them. Nor could these most crafty men fail to see how much this would detract from his authority, if he looked after himself by a shameful flight and withdrew into some hiding place. So, to strengthen their own rule, they advise him to betake himself elsewhere as quietly as possible, and to this end they use the name of King Herod, who was not likely to be well disposed towards Christ, since not long before he had cruelly and unjustly had his forerunner, John the Baptist, beheaded. This is a proof of the most violent and implacable hatred, which, as we have said elsewhere, these men conceived out of ambition and greed. For if we look at Christ, he was so far from deserving hatred that he rather deserved the love and favour of all people: he not only harmed no one and abstained from every wrong, but also did good to all without distinction, partly by teaching and partly by performing miracles, by which he cured the incurable diseases of many. Yet the Pharisees burn with such hatred for him that they want him expelled and the people deprived of so great a benefactor, lest, once their frauds were fully exposed, their whole authority should collapse and the wicked profit which they made from sacred things should be overturned. This was an impiety more than sacrilegious, and it still reigns today among all those who put themselves on sale under a false appearance of holiness, but who under that pretext hunt for nothing else than empty glory among people and private gain. Such men cannot be placated by any kindnesses. For just as the light of truth offends them, so the gifts of eternal salvation, when they are bestowed on many others, drive them utterly into a frenzy.

units.la: Pharisæi Christo fugam suadent.
units.tr: The Pharisees urge Christ to flee.

units.la: Quia verò ijdem non semper possunt quod volunt, iram atque odium nonnunquam egregiè dis- simulant, & quod aperta vi non potest perfici, id sub falso amicitiæ prætextu ad finem optatum de- ducere cônantur. Et est hoc egregium atque singulare diaboli stratagema, quo suos ministros in- struit, vt inanibus & fictis terriculamentis eos ab officio reuocet, quos regno suo obesse videt. Quod enim isti hic faciunt, hoc ipsum sæpe aliâs factum esse scimus, & huic prorsus simile est, quod de Amasia Vitulini cultus antistite in Bethel scribitur. Is enim cùm Amos Prophetam extinctum cuperet, primò quidem eum apud Ieroboamum Regem grauissimè accusat, & læsæ ma- iestatis reum agere studet. Amos (inquit) conspirauit contra te in medio domus Israelis, nec poterit ipsa tellus omnes eius sermones sustinere, &c. At quando Regis animum ira atque indi- gnatione accendi non posse videt, mox amicum simulans Prophetam accedit; & vt sibi mature consulat, monet, dicens: Vade ô Videns, & fuge in terram Iuda, & illic panem edito atque ibi- dem propheta: in Bethel autem nec posthac prophetes: quoniam Sanctuarium est Regis, & do- mus Regis est. Videntur hæc ex animo amico & benevolo profecta: cùm & locum tutiorem osten- dat, vbi maiori cum fructu docere possit, & simul causas indicet, quæ obstent quò minus in Israe- lis regno, & quidem in Bethel maximè, aliquid proficiat: imò periculosum esse innuit illic ali- quid moliri, vbi cultus exerceatur Regum publica authoritate & liberalitate iampridem con- firmatus, & vbi conatus eius non possit celari, cùm illic Regis sedes sit, neque desint Regibus Corycæi, qui omnia obseruent, & ijsdem omnia renuntient, quæ in vulgo fiunt. Sed si rem ipsam propius contemplerùs, hoc vnum quærit crudelis hypocrita, vt Amos hoc nuntio territus pro- fugiat, seque ipsum atque doctrinam suam omnium ludibrio exponat, adhæc fidem faciat calum- niæ suæ, qua illum vt res nouas seditiose molientem accusauerat. Est borum infinitus numerus hodie, qui vbi Euangelij doctrinam in aliqua gente ita receptam atque confirmatam esse vident, vt eam aperta vi eiici non posse sentiant, ad artes eiusmodi conuersi, se ad ministrorum verbi amano tes & publicæ salutis quàm maximè studiosos esse simulant. Itaque de illis quidem honorificè lo- quuntur, studium eorum commendant, ad mensam suam non raro inuitant: interim verò se tam ipsis priuatim quàm toti reipub. timere dicunt, & frequenter sermones instituunt de temporum nostro- rum iniquitate, vicinorum & sociorum ingenio atque moribus, quibus omnino aliquid dari opor- teat, ne quæ turbæ graviores oriantur, quæ toti quidem genti & reipub. malum dent, in primis au- tem in præconum Euangelij capita redundent. Sed & priuatim interdum cum illis agunt, vt cir- cumspectè & prudenter res suas instituant, neq; rigidius atq; seuerius vrgeant id, quod non possit obtineri. Adhæc pericula fingunt, & de diris quorundam conatibus non sine gemitu loquuntur, vt plus fidei inueniant. At quorsum ista omnia tendunt? Eò nimirum, vt Ecclesiæ ministri timore perculsi frigidius agant Domini negotium, aut etiam aliò sese conferant, & turpi metu sibijpsis & doctrinæ suæ fidem atque authoritatem omnem derogent: Vel vt principes atque magistratus ter- riculamentis eiusmodi fratri, doctoribus abire nolentibus dicendi leges præscribant, spiritus liber- tatem restinguant, & eosdem ab omni scriptione abstinere iubeant, ne hac aduersarij irritentur. Ita vero tenebriones isti sub ementito amicitiæ & salutis publicæ prætextu plus postulare audēt, quàm ipsi hostes facerent, si rerum omnino potirentur. Sunt ergo diligenter tales obseruandi, & in eorum dolis arguendus verbi administros sedulos atq; intrepidos esse conuenit, ne qui artibus illis despi- libertatem Euangelij amittant & Antichristianæ tyrannidi denuo subijciantur, dum sibijpsis & aliis temere voluut consulere.
units.tr: But since these men cannot always do what they want, they sometimes skilfully conceal their anger and hatred, and they try to bring about under the false pretence of friendship what cannot be accomplished by open force. This is a remarkable and singular stratagem of the devil, by which he instructs his ministers to call back from their office, by empty and feigned frights, those whom he sees standing in the way of his kingdom. For what these men do here, we know has often been done elsewhere, and it is quite like what is written of Amaziah, the priest of the calf-worship at Bethel. For when he wished the prophet Amos to be put to death, he first accuses him very gravely before King Jeroboam and strives to make him guilty of treason. "Amos," he says, "has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land itself cannot bear all his words," and so on. But when he sees that the king's mind cannot be inflamed with anger and indignation, he at once approaches the prophet, pretending to be his friend, and, in order to give him timely counsel, he warns him, saying: "Go away, O seer, and flee into the land of Judah, and there eat your bread and prophesy there; but at Bethel do not prophesy any more, for it is the king's sanctuary and the king's house." This seems to have come from a friendly and kindly spirit, since he points out a safer place where he could teach with greater profit, and at the same time indicates the reasons why he would achieve little in the kingdom of Israel, and especially at Bethel: indeed, he hints that it is dangerous to attempt anything there, where the worship has long since been confirmed by the public authority and generosity of the kings, and where his efforts cannot be hidden, since the king's seat is there, and there are no lack of informers who watch everything and report to the kings everything that happens among the common people. But if we look at the matter more closely, this cruel hypocrite seeks only one thing: that Amos, terrified by this message, should flee, and that he should expose himself and his teaching to everyone's mockery, and moreover give credibility to his slander, by which he had accused him of plotting revolution.
