There is an endless number of such men today, who, when they see that the teaching of the gospel has been so received and established in some nation that they feel it cannot be cast out by open force, turn to arts of this kind, and pretend to be most devoted lovers of the ministers of the Word and most zealous for the public welfare. So they speak honourably of them, commend their zeal, and not seldom invite them to their table; yet meanwhile they say that they fear for them both privately and for the whole commonwealth, and they often engage in talk about the wickedness of our times, about the disposition and habits of our neighbours and allies, to whom something must certainly be given, lest greater disturbances arise which would bring harm to the whole nation and commonwealth, and fall especially on the heads of the heralds of the gospel. But at times they also deal with these men privately, urging them to conduct their affairs cautiously and prudently, and not to press with excessive rigour and severity what cannot be obtained. Moreover, they invent dangers and speak with groans about the dreadful attempts of certain people, so that they may gain more trust. But to what end do all these things tend? Surely to this: that the ministers of the Church, struck with fear, should carry on the Lord's work more coldly, or even withdraw elsewhere, and by shameful fear should take away from themselves and their teaching all trust and authority; or that princes and magistrates, using such frights, should prescribe laws for the teachers who are unwilling to depart, should quench the freedom of the spirit, and should order them to abstain from all writing, lest they provoke the adversaries. In this way those scoundrels, under the pretext of a feigned friendship and of public welfare, dare to demand more than the enemies themselves would do if they had complete power over affairs. Such men must therefore be carefully watched, and it is fitting that the faithful and fearless servants of the Word should expose their deceits, lest, being deceived by those arts, they lose the freedom of the gospel and are again subjected to Antichristian tyranny, while they rashly wish to look after themselves and others.

units.la: Docet hoc in præsenti Christus suo exemplo. Nam subdolos hosce & perfidos monitores grau- responso reijciens ait: Profecti dicite vulpi illi: Ecce eijciam dæmonia, & sanationes peragā hodiè & cras, & tertia die consummabor: Veruntamen oportet me hodie & cras & perendie iter facere: quia fieri non potest, vt pereat Propheta extra Hierusalem. Primùm ipsos abire iubet abs se, quæ illum vt se alió recipēret, monuerant: eo ipso indicans, quàm parum eorum consilio tribuat. Deinde quia illi Herodis nomen prætexebant, ad eum illos remittit, & Vulpem nominat, nimirum pro- pter astutiam & calliditatem, qua instructum fuisse eius facta & mores satis testantur. Nam ille ipse est, qui Ioannem Baptistam, quam in pretio habere & eius doctrina se delectari diu simularat, crudeliter in carcere occidi curauit sub iurisiurandi temere dati prætextu: quæ extera- bilis oīnā bilis omnino fuit astutia cum iniquitate summa coniuncta. Et credibile est, eum multa de Christo per insidias opprimendo cogitauisse, cum apertam vim illi inferre non auderet. Huc enim referri potest, quod illo capto & ad se misso gauisus est, & cum non alia ratione ei nocere posset, candida veste indutum ludibrio habuit. Vulpinae etiam astutiae argumentum est, quòd Philippi fratris vxorem, violato & hospitij & cognationis iure, suis blanditiis deceptam abduxit, ac sibi per incestas nuptias coniunxit. Cuius simile est, quod in vxoris fratrem Herodem Aggrippam designauit, quem Caio Caligulae exosum & inuisum facere conatus est, vt regno eum exueret. Sed tunc vt vulpes laqueo capta sibi ipsi exilium & ignominiam accersiuit. Quae omnia cum Dominus non ignoraret, vulpem dixit, vt indignum ostenderet, in cuius gratiam faceret aliquid. Suo autem exemplo docet, qua dicendi libertate administri verbi Dei in arguendis hominibus sceleratis & hostibus Dei vti debeant. Detrabenda enim omnino illis est larua, qua sese occultant, vt minus nocere possint, & vt nemo eorum exemplis malis offendatur. Nec est quod aliquis personae dignitatem obijciat, quasi propter hanc immunis sit. Nam quò nocentius est, quod ab illustribus viris datur scandalum, eò liberius illi argui debent: quod olim Prophetae, & postea hos Apostoli quoque fecerunt.
units.tr: Christ teaches this at present by his own example. For, rejecting the crafty and treacherous advice with a stern answer, he says: "Go and tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I shall be perfected. Nevertheless I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after, for it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem." First he bids them depart from him, those who had urged him to withdraw elsewhere, thereby showing how little he values their counsel. Then, since they put forward Herod's name, he sends them back to him and calls him a fox, plainly because of his cunning and craftiness, which his deeds and character sufficiently attest. For he is the one who had long pretended to hold John the Baptist in high esteem and to delight in his teaching, yet cruelly had him put to death in prison under the pretext of a rashly sworn oath; that was utterly detestable cunning, joined with the greatest wickedness. And it is credible that he devised many schemes against Christ to crush him by treachery, since he did not dare to inflict open violence on him. To this may be referred the fact that, when Christ was seized and sent to him, he rejoiced, and since he could not harm him in any other way, he had him dressed in a white robe and held him up to mockery. It is also a proof of his foxlike cunning that he lured away his brother Philip's wife, deceiving her with his flatteries and violating the rights of hospitality and kinship, and joined her to himself in an incestuous marriage. Similar to this is his plot against his wife's brother, Herod Agrippa, whom he tried to make hateful and odious to Gaius Caligula, so as to strip him of his kingdom; but then, like a fox caught in a snare, he brought exile and disgrace upon himself. Since the Lord was aware of all these things, he called him a fox, to show how unworthy he was of any consideration on his account. By his own example, however, he teaches with what freedom of speech the ministers of the Word of God ought to rebuke wicked men and enemies of God. For the mask by which they hide themselves, so that they may do less harm, must be completely stripped away, so that no one is offended by their evil examples. Nor should anyone object the dignity of a person, as if he were thereby exempt. For the more harmful the scandal given by illustrious men, the more freely they ought to be rebuked; this the Prophets did of old, and afterwards the Apostles too.

units.la: Quid verò illud est, quod Herodi renuntiari voluit Dominus? Ecce (inquit) eijciam daemonia & sanationes peragam hodie & cras, & tertia die consummabor, &c. Comprehendit hïs verbis causas, propter quas non posset neque debeat Herodis minis aut conatibus moueri, vt ab officio suo discedat. Primam ex Dei Patris prouidentia petit, quae certos vitae in terris agendae dies iam pridem ipsi constituerit, quos ad suum finem decurrere oporteat. Ex quo colligit, neq; Herodem neque quenquam alium ipsum occidere posse, donec finem aut metam hanc attigerit. Et huc faciunt omnes loci Euangelici, in quibus horae mentio fit, qua debuerit mori: vt cum Ioannes ait: Studebant eum prehendere, sed nemo iniecit ei manum, quia nondum venerat hora eius. Et ipse alicubi Patrem orat: Conserua me ab hac hora, sed propterea veni in horam hanc. Item: Sciens Iesus venisse horam ipsius, vt transfiret ex hoc mundo ad Patrem, &c. Altera à breuitate temporis, quod ipsi adhuc reliquum fit, sumitur: Nam hodie & cras (ait) eijciam daemonia & sanationes peragam, & tertia die consummabor. Quasi diceret: Compleui fere cursum vitae meae, vt vix pauculi dies adhuc restent, quibus elapsis consummabor, id est, plenè perficiam, quae per me effici vult Pater. Nam peccatum mundi mortis meae merito expiabo, mortem & inferos resurrectione vincam, de diabolo & vniuersis salutis humanae hostibus per Ascensionem triumphum agam, & in caelos euectus ad dextram Patris confidebo Rex & Sacerdos aeternus, cuius scabello pedum inimicos omnes subijci oportebit: deniq; eos etiam qui in me credunt perfectos & consummatos reddam, vt iustificati & filij Dei facti, eiusdem Regni & gloriae coheredes sint. Quàm verò absurdum & inconsultum foret, me nunc deficere, & à Patre commissum munus deserere, cùm meta in propinquo adsit, & iam vno atque altero passu possit attingi? His tertia additur: Veruntamen oportet me hodie & cras & perendie iter facere. A necessario haec desumpta est, & hunc sensum habet: Etsi ego ignauo metu superatus velim officium negligere, tamen vt id faciam non licet. Quia enim Patris hoc aeternum decretum est, necesse fuerit vt suum habeat in me complementum. Nam illo aliquid statuente, quis illud irritum faciet? quis eius consilia impediet, quo minus suum habeant effectum? Postrema causa ex loci conditione deducitur: quia non posset in Galilaea aliquid mali accidere sibi, eò quòd Hierosolyma suae neci destinata sit, quae Prophetarum caedibus & sanguini ita assueuerit, vt vix fieri possit, Prophetam aliquem alibi trucidari.
units.tr: But what is it that the Lord wished to be reported to Herod? "Behold," he says, "I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I shall be perfected," and so on. In these words he sets out the reasons why he could neither be nor ought to be moved by Herod's threats or attempts to abandon his task. The first he draws from the providence of God the Father, who had long ago fixed for him the set days for living out his life on earth, which he must run through to their end. From this he infers that neither Herod nor anyone else can kill him until he has reached that end or goal. To this point bear all the Gospel passages in which mention is made of the hour in which he was to die: as when John says, "They sought to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come." And he himself somewhere prays to the Father: "Keep me from this hour; but for this reason I came to this hour." Likewise: "Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father," and so on. The second reason is taken from the shortness of the time still left to him: "For today and tomorrow," he says, "I shall cast out demons and perform cures, and on the third day I shall be perfected." As if he were saying: "I have almost completed the course of my life, so that only a few days remain, after which I shall be perfected, that is, I shall fully accomplish what the Father wills to be accomplished through me. For I shall atone for the sin of the world by the merit of my death, I shall conquer death and hell by my resurrection, I shall win a triumph over the devil and all the enemies of human salvation by my Ascension, and, carried up into heaven, I shall sit at the right hand of the Father as King and eternal Priest, at whose footstool all his enemies must be placed; and finally I shall make perfect and complete even those who believe in me, so that, justified and made sons of God, they may be co-heirs of the same kingdom and glory. How absurd and ill-advised it would be for me now to fail and to abandon the office entrusted to me by the Father, when the goal is near at hand and can be reached with one or two more steps!" To this is added a third reason: "Nevertheless I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after." This is taken from necessity and has this sense: "Even if I, overcome by cowardly fear, should wish to neglect my duty, it is still not permitted me to do so. For since this is the eternal decree of the Father, it must necessarily have its fulfilment in me. For when he has decided something, who will make it void? Who will hinder his counsels from having their effect?" The last reason is drawn from the condition of the place: that nothing evil could befall him in Galilee, because Jerusalem was destined for his death, a city which had become so accustomed to the slaughter and blood of the Prophets that it was scarcely possible for a prophet to be killed anywhere else.

units.la: Ita verò simul scandalo medetur, quod apud infirmiores enascí poterat, quando eum visuri erunt in ea vrbe pro scelerato & impio damnari atque occidi, quam Deus sui cultus sedem fecerat, & quae ideo Ciuitas Sancta dicebatur. Fuit hoc horrendum iudicium Dei, qui Filij sui sanguine mensuram iniquorum impleri voluit, vt mox dignas suae impietatis poenas darent. Quo exemplo docemur, quàm parum locorum sanctitati & priscae dignitati tribui debeat. Nec enim alicui vrbi aut genti Deus alligatus est, quo minus gratiam omnem ab ijs auferat, qui hanc improbè asper-nantur. Frustra ergo Romam suam nobis iactant Pontifices, cuius fidem Paulus commendauerit, in qua primus Ecclesiae antistes fuerit Petrus, à quo legitima Episcoporum successio ad nostra vsque tempora numeretur. Nam vt haec omnia illis demus (quae tamen maxima ex parte confitta & falsa sunt) nunquam tamen inde colligi poterit, Romanum Pontificem Ecclesiarum omnium caput & vi-carium Christi esse, cui omnes necessario obedire debeant, & qui errare non possit. Quia enim ab ea fide, quam Paulus commendat, iam pridem defecerunt, eandem hodie ferro & igne persequuntur, & maiorem Pontificum partem iam seculis aliquot Simoniacis artibus, multos etiam aperta vi, in eius sedis fastigium ascendisse constat, quid obsecro de illa civitate nobis amplius, quàm de Hierosolyma, possumus polliceri? Annon enim iam olim Apostolorum & episcoporum sanctissimorum sanguine maduit? Annon illuc, ceu ad publicam carnificinam ex toto terrarum orbe pertracti sunt beati Martyres, ut illic vel bestiis obiicerentur, aut aliis supplicijs crudelissimis excruciati perirent? Annon hodie adhuc ex ea urbe procedunt fulmina excommunicationum, sanguinaria de Evangelica veritatis oppressione consilia, & Legati à latere (ut ipsi loquuntur) qui in omnium Regum aulis versantur, & illos aduersus Christi fideles accendunt? Annon Pontificum artibus potentissimi Monarchae hactenus commissi bella gesserunt, in quibus plus sanguinis Christiani fusum est, quàm olim truculentissimi Ecclesiae hostes effuderint? Annon hodie Pontificum promissionibus, consiliis, pecunijs, bella civilia foventur, quibus florentissima regna vastantur, exhauriuntur & pereunt? Desinant ergo nobis eius urbis dignitatem iactare, quae qualis qualis olim fuerit, nunc tamen cum sanguinaria Hierosolymorum civitate omnia communia habet. Discant potius ij quos honore tanto Deus dignatur, ut verbo & cultui suo apud ipsos locum esse velit, illius beneficium agnoscere, & tam horrendis exemplis territi, dignitate suam constanti gloriae Dei & verae pietatis studio tueantur. Nam quo altius evectuntur aliquae civitates aut nationes, eo graviori & ignominiosiori ruina cadunt, si gratiam sibi à Deo factam turpiter prophanent atque polluant, ut alibi in Capernai, Bethsaida & Corozaini exemplis vidimus.
units.tr: In this way he at the same time remedies a scandal which could have arisen among the weaker, when they would see him condemned and put to death as a wicked and impious man in that city which God had made the seat of his worship, and which for that reason was called the Holy City. This was a terrible judgment of God, who willed that the measure of the wicked be filled up with the blood of his Son, so that they might soon pay the penalties worthy of their impiety. From this example we are taught how little should be ascribed to the holiness of places and to former dignity. For God is bound to no city or nation so as not to take away all grace from those who wickedly spurn it. In vain, therefore, do the Pontiffs boast to us of their Rome, whose faith Paul commended, in which Peter was the first bishop of the Church, from whom the lawful succession of bishops is counted down to our own times. For even if we grant them all these things (which yet are for the most part invented and false), it can never be concluded from them that the Roman Pontiff is the head of all churches and the vicar of Christ, whom all must necessarily obey, and who cannot err. For since they have long since fallen away from the faith which Paul commends, they now persecute that same faith with sword and fire; and since it is established that for some centuries the greater part of the Pontiffs have ascended to the summit of that see by simoniacal arts, and many by open force, what, I beg you, can we promise ourselves more concerning that city than concerning Jerusalem? Has it not long since been drenched with the blood of Apostles and most holy bishops? Were not the blessed martyrs dragged there from the whole world, as to a public slaughterhouse, so that they might be thrown to the beasts there or perish, tortured by other most cruel punishments? Do not the thunderbolts of excommunication still issue from that city today, and bloody plans for the suppression of the Gospel truth, and legates "a latere" (as they themselves call them), who move about in the courts of all kings and inflame them against the faithful of Christ? Have not the most powerful monarchs, entrusted to the arts of the Pontiffs, hitherto waged wars, in which more Christian blood has been shed than the most savage enemies of the Church once poured out? Are not civil wars fostered today by the promises, counsels and money of the Pontiffs, by which most flourishing kingdoms are laid waste, drained and perish? Let them therefore cease to boast to us of the dignity of that city, which, whatever it once was, now shares everything in common with the bloody city of Jerusalem. Rather, let those whom God deigns to honour with so great an office, that he wishes his Word and his worship to have a place among them, learn to acknowledge his benefit, and, terrified by such horrible examples, let them defend their dignity by a constant zeal for the glory of God and true piety. For the higher that any cities or nations are raised, the heavier and more shameful is their fall, if they basely profane and pollute the grace given them by God, as we have seen elsewhere in the examples of Capernaum, Bethsaida and Chorazin.

units.la: Porrò quod praecipuum huius loci caput est, suo exemplo nos Christus docet, quà constantia à Deo creditam nobis functionem obire debeamus. Nam si universam vitae eius in terris transactae historiam consideres, nihil praeter continuos labores, potentissimorum inimicitias, callidissimorum hominum insidias, & nova indies pericula videbis, quibus illum satan vel perdere vel ab officio suo revocare conatus est. At neque labores eum defatigare, neque vllorum hominum inimicitiae & insidiae, neque iam capiti imminentia pericula terrere potuerunt, ut stationem suam desereret: imò quo propius adesse vidit horam illam fatalem, quae dira & infamis necis supplicio destinata erat, eò fortior & animosior omnium hostium consiliis atque terroribus se opposuit. Debent exemplum eius imitari, quotquot cum ipso regnare & salutem per illum partae haeredes fieri cupiunt. Quod tunc demum poterunt praestare, si ijsdem rationibus atque argumentis fidem suam confirment, quibus illum in praesenti vsum fuisse audimus. Discant ergo in Dei providentiam respicere, qui & dies vitae nostrae & capitis capillos numerauit, adhaecworti nostrae suum tempus & locum constituit. Etenim ut duodecim horae diei sunt (sicuti alibi dicit Dominus) ita priusquam nostrae vitae hora duodecima adveniat, nemo nobis nocere aut illam eripere poterit. Quin ergo in tam proui-di Patris tutela acquiescimus, qui solo nutu nos tueri, hostium conatus impedire, vel etiam animos eorum mutare potest? Cogitent etiam singuli, breve esse huius vitae spatium, & in singula momenta ad suum finem propius decurrere: adeoque nosipsos ignorare quàm procul ab illo absimus, plerunque autem fieri, ut iam finis instet, & extrema hora nos hinc evocet, quando nihil minus sperabamus. Quare nimium imprudentes & ignaui sunt, qui cùm ex anteactae vitae annis conijcere possint, se maiorem partem sui temporis iam transegisse, deficiunt tamen, & tunc cursum sistunt, quando aeternae vitae brauium iam iam praebensuri erant. Potuit olim senectus M. Catritium confirmare, ut Cn. Carboni iniquum quid petenti sese opponeret, & huic minitanti se multos habere gladios, responderet, Et ego annos: Quantò maior ergo Christianorum fiducia esse debet, qui annos suos in Dei manu, & vitae huius tempus breve esse sciunt, quam aeterna excipiet, si in finem usque perseuerauerimus? Debet praeterea nobis semper in mentem venire, oportere nos omnino cursum nostrum perficere. Qui enim nos sumus, qui Dei decreto resistamus, aut ei officium nostrum negemus in illis rebus, quas nostro ministerio confectas vult? Num ut hominum consiliis obtemperemus, cum illo pugnabimus? Vel num eo honore nos spoliabimus, quo seruos spontaneos & alacres ille dignatur? Obseruarunt hoc diligenter Apostoli, qui olim Senatui Hierosolymitano silentium
units.tr: Moreover, the chief point of this passage is that Christ teaches us by his own example with what steadfastness we ought to discharge the office entrusted to us by God. For if you consider the whole history of his life on earth, you will see nothing but continual labours, the enmities of the most powerful, the plots of the most crafty men, and new dangers every day, by which Satan tried either to destroy him or to call him away from his duty. Yet neither his labours wore him down, nor the enmities and plots of any men, nor the dangers now hanging over his head, could frighten him into abandoning his post. Rather, the nearer he saw that fatal hour approaching, the hour appointed for the bitter and infamous punishment of death, the more resolutely and courageously he set himself against all the schemes and terrors of his enemies. All who wish to reign with him and to become heirs of the salvation won through him ought to imitate his example. They will be able to do this only if they strengthen their faith by the same reasons and arguments by which we hear he was sustained in his own time. Let them therefore learn to look to the providence of God, who has numbered both the days of our life and the hairs of our head, and has also fixed the time and place of our word. For just as there are twelve hours in the day (as the Lord says elsewhere), so no one can harm us or snatch us away before the twelfth hour of our life arrives. Why, then, should we not rest in the protection of so provident a Father, who by a mere nod can keep us safe, check the attempts of our enemies, or even change their minds? Let each one also consider that the span of this life is brief, and that with every moment it runs closer to its end; and that we do not know how far we are from that end, but that it often happens that the end is already upon us, and the last hour calls us away when we least expect it. Therefore they are very foolish and slothful who, though from the years of their past life they can infer that they have already spent the greater part of their time, nevertheless fail, and halt their course just when they were about to offer the prize of eternal life. Old age once enabled Marcus Catritius to stand firm against Gnaeus Carbo when he sought something unjust, and to answer him, when Carbo threatened that he had many swords, "And I have my years." How much greater, then, ought the confidence of Christians to be, who know that their years are in God's hand, and that the time of this life is short, and that eternal life will receive them if we persevere to the end? Moreover, we should always keep in mind that we must by all means complete our course. For who are we, that we should resist the decree of God, or deny him our duty in those matters which he wills to be accomplished by our ministry? Shall we fight against him in order to obey the counsels of men? Or shall we strip ourselves of that honour with which he deigns to honour his willing and eager servants? The Apostles observed this carefully, who once answered the Council of Jerusalem when it ordered them to keep silent: "Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye." "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." And Paul wrote: "If I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of; for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel." All men of every place and rank ought to apply these things to themselves, and in their affairs to join prudence with a godly and certain trust in God, which alone can keep us in our duty, so that we do not stray by following the dictates of our flesh.

units.la: Ioan. 11. silentium ipsis mandanti responderunt: An iustum sit vobis potius obedire quàm Deo, vos iudicate? Non possumus enim quae audivimus, & quae vidimus, non loqui. Et Paulus scribebat: Si euangelicem, non est quod glorier: necessitas enim mihi incumbit: Vae autem mihi est, nisi euangelicem. Debent ista sibi accomodare omnis loci & ordinis homines, & in rebus agendis cum prudentia pia fiduciam certam in Deum coniungere, quae sola nos in officio continere potest, ne nostrae carnis rationes secuti exorbitemus.
units.tr: Ioan. 11. Ioan. 11. Ioan. 11. Ioan. 11. (The Apostles, when the Council ordered them to be silent, answered: "Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.") And Paul wrote: "If I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of; for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel." All men of every place and order ought to apply these words to themselves, and in their dealings to join godly prudence with a sure trust in God, which alone can hold us to our duty, so that we do not go astray by following the reasonings of our flesh.

units.la: Caterum exijs, quae de Hierosolyma dixerat, occasione sumpta, totum sermonem ad illam convertit, ut imminens illi iudicium Dei aperte denuntiet, & omnem scandali materiam remoueat, quae simplicium fidem poterat labefactare. Vtitur autem pathetica prorsus exclamatione: Hierusalem, Hierusalem, quae trucidas Prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt: quoties volui congregare liberos tuos, quemadmodum gallina pulliciem suam sub alas? & noluistis, &c. Sunt verba haec plana & perspicua admodum, sed res multa consideratione dignas continent. Primò enim Dei bonitatem & studium plus quàm paternum commendant, quo saluti huius vrbis consulere iam diu conatus sit. Deinde illorum incurabilem contumaciam arguit. Tertiò poenas praedicit graves atque horrendas.
units.tr: Moreover, taking occasion from what he had said about Jerusalem, Christ turns the whole discourse to that city, so that he may openly announce the judgment of God hanging over it, and remove every cause of offence that could shake the faith of simple people. He uses a thoroughly passionate exclamation: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets and stonest those who are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her brood under her wings, and ye would not!" etc. These words are very plain and clear, but they contain matters worthy of much consideration. For first, they commend the goodness of God and his more than fatherly care, with which he has long tried to provide for the safety of this city. Second, they charge the people with their incurable obstinacy. Third, they foretell grave and dreadful punishments.

units.la: Ordicur autem à Dei bonitate, ut euidentior sit eorum culpa, & ut inexcusabiles esse ostendat. Et cum infinita beneficia recitare posset, quibus suam gratiam erga illos declarauerat, Prophetarum in primis meminit, qui ab ipso missi Verbum suum illis praedicarint. Et hos quidem ipsis nunquam defuisse constat. Nam si ad primos vsque gentis illius progenitores ascendamus, hos Prophetas fuisse inueniemus. Hoc enim nomine Abrahamum Deus exornat, & notum est illud Psalmi, quo idem Chananaeos terruit, ne quam illis vim facerent: Nolite tangere Christos meos, & ne quid malifaciatis Prophetis meis. Postea per Mosem & Aaronem non solum ex Aegypto liberauit filios Israelis, sed vnà cum cultu externo Verbi sui doctrinam inter eos vulgauit, cuius communes & perpetuos praecones atque interpretes esse voluit Sacerdotes, quos ex reliquis tribubus atque familijs sibi in hunc vsum segregauerat. Et cum isti aliquando in suo munere cessarent, vel saltem negligentiores essent, extraordinarie ex diuersis tribubus Prophetas excitauit, qui singulari Spiritus virtute armati totum populum & ipsos quoque antistites atque principes de officio suo admonerent. Successit his tandem Ioannes, cuius eò maior debuit esse authoritas, quod eius missionem veteres Prophetae olim praedixerant. Veruntamen quasi nihil vnquam fecisset, tandem ipse Dei Filius venit, qui incomparabili studio omnia fecit, quae admirandum aliquem populum facta necessaria sunt. Idem quoque postea Apostolos reliquit, qui ab ipso traditam salutis doctrinam vrgerent, & modis omnibus instarent apud eos, qui hactenus se nimium contumaces praebuerant. In quem verò finem haec omnia facta sunt? Volui (inquit) congregare liberos tuos, quemadmodum gallina pulliciem suam sub alas. Est hic praedicationis Verbi proprius finis aut scopus, quod per illam nos Deus ad se colligit, adeoque sub vmbram alarum suarum confugiamus inuitat. Quod vt singularem eius erga nos bonitatem commendat: ita hic similitudine illustratur, quam ita proponit Christus, vt singula verba Emphasim & pondus habeant. Nam ait, Quoties volui. Quasi dicat: Non nunc demum meum in vos studium declarare cepi, sed à multis seculis totus in hoc fui, vt vestrae saluti consulerem, vt de mea voluntate non possitis dubitare. Volui autem cogere vel congregare, ne more aliarum gentium in sectas & superstitiones varias distracti errarent. Et quidem ad me congregare volui, qui & summum bonum & omnis bonifons sum vnicus. Neque obiter & quasi aliud agens hoc feci, sed vt gallina pulliciem suam glocitando inuitat sub alas: ita ego Verbi mei voce vos inuitaui, non vt vile aliquod obsequium mihi praestaretis, sed vt sub alas meas abscondit mihi quàm arctissimè coniungeremini, & sub mea protectione tuti degeretis. Faciunt haec omnia ad diuinae bonitatis amplificationem, quam nunquam satis admirari poterimus, si illius maiestatem cum nostra plus quàm misera conditione conferamus. Amoris & studij ingens est argumentum, quod qui nullius est indigens, nostri curam qualemcunque suscipit, & propter nos mundum hunc cum omnibus, quae illo continentur, conseruat atque regit. Maius verò, quod qui ipsa iustitia & sanctitas est, nos filiorum loco habere dignatur, qui natura peccatores & omni supplicio digni sumus. Imò non patrem modò nostrum se esse profitetur, sed matris quoque affectum induit, quo nullus est inter homines tenerior & vehementior. Superat tamen haec omnia, quod gallina, aui vilißimae, sese confert, & ita sese ad pulueres vsque demittit, vt nos seruet. Etenim non sictam esse hanc comparationem, res ipsa testatur. Vt enim gallinae innata vel naturalis vis fouendi inest: ita Deus propriam sibi habet virtutem, quae omnibus fouendis atque conseruandis sufficit. Et vt gallina suum ergo pullos studium mirifice declarat, dum propter hos & genium suum defraudat, & pro illis acriter pugnat, imò corpus suum miluo rapacibus obijcit, vt eos sub alis suis absconditos tueatur: ita Deus in Filio suo haec omnia praestitit, qui propter nos extremam egestatem passus sitiuit, esuriuit, alsit, & tandem se totum pro nobis tradidit in mortem, vt nos redimeret, pasceret, tueretur, & regni sui coheredes faceret. Quae beneficia cum iam pridem per promissiones & Verbum suum Iudaeorum genti obtulisset quam libe ralissimè, merito ista nunc à Domino dicuntur: quae à nobis ita accipi debent, vt multo magis nobis ea conuenire cogitemus, quibus perfecta salus iam pridem in Christo exhibita est, vt nos ei gratos & obsequentes praebeamus. Auget enim culpam nostram magnitudo diuinae gratiae, nisi eam qua de cet reuerentia agnoscamus.
units.tr: He begins with the goodness of God, so that their guilt may be more evident and so that he may show that they are inexcusable. And although he could recite the countless benefits by which he had declared his grace toward them, he makes mention above all of the prophets, whom he sent to preach his Word to them. It is certain that these were never lacking to them. For if we go back to the first forefathers of that nation, we shall find that they were prophets. Indeed, God adorns Abraham with this title, and that well-known verse of the Psalm, by which he terrified the Canaanites so that they would do them no harm, is famous: "Touch not my anointed, and do my prophets no harm." Afterwards, through Moses and Aaron, he not only freed the sons of Israel from Egypt, but along with the outward worship he spread the teaching of his Word among them; and he wished the priests, whom he had set apart for this use from the remaining tribes and families, to be its common and perpetual heralds and interpreters. And when these at times neglected their office, or at least were more careless, he raised up prophets extraordinarily from various tribes, who, armed with a singular power of the Spirit, admonished the whole people and their leaders and rulers too to return to their duty. At last John succeeded these, whose authority ought to have been all the greater because the ancient prophets had long before foretold his mission. Yet, as if he had done nothing at all, the Son of God himself finally came, who with incomparable zeal did all those things which were necessary to be done for an admirable people. Afterwards he also left the Apostles, who were to press upon them the doctrine of salvation delivered by him, and to insist on it in every way with those who until now had shown themselves too stubborn. But to what end were all these things done? "I would have gathered thy children together," he says, "as a hen gathers her brood under her wings." This is the proper end or aim of the preaching of the Word: that by it God gathers us to himself, and invites us to take refuge under the shadow of his wings. As this commends his singular goodness toward us, so it is illustrated here by a comparison, which Christ puts forward in such a way that each word has emphasis and weight. For he says, "how often would I have"; as if he were saying: "I have not only now begun to declare my zeal toward you, but for many ages I have been wholly intent on this, to provide for your salvation, so that you may not doubt my will. Moreover, I wished to gather you together, lest, scattered into various sects and superstitions after the manner of other nations, you should wander astray. And indeed I wished to gather you to myself, who alone am the highest good and the fountain of all goodness. Nor did I do this in passing, as if busy with something else, but as a hen by clucking invites her brood under her wings, so I have invited you by the voice of my Word, not so that you would render me some paltry service, but so that you would be joined to me as closely as possible under my wings, and live safe under my protection." All these things serve to magnify the goodness of God, which we can never sufficiently admire if we compare his majesty with our most wretched condition. It is a great proof of love and care that he, who lacks nothing, takes up any care at all for us, and for our sake preserves and rules this world with all that is contained in it. Greater still is that he, who is justice and holiness itself, deigns to hold us in the place of sons, we who by nature are sinners and deserving of every punishment. Indeed, he not only professes himself to be our Father, but also puts on a mother's affection, than which there is none more tender and fervent among men. Yet what surpasses all these things is that he likens himself to a hen, a most worthless bird, and so lowers himself even to the dust in order to keep us safe. For the reality itself shows that this comparison is no feigned one. As the hen has an innate and natural power of brooding, so God has a power of his own which is sufficient for cherishing and preserving all things. And just as the hen wonderfully displays her affection for her chicks, when for their sake she neglects her own nourishment and fights fiercely for them, and even exposes her body to the rapacious kite so as to guard them hidden under her wings, so God has done all these things in his Son, who for our sake suffered the utmost poverty, was thirsty, hungry, and cold, and at last gave himself wholly for us to death, so that he might redeem us, feed us, protect us, and make us co-heirs of his kingdom. Since he had long ago offered these benefits to the Jewish nation through promises and his Word, most generously, it is rightly said now by the Lord; and they ought to be received by us in such a way that we consider them to belong to us much more, to whom perfect salvation has already been shown forth in Christ, so that we may show ourselves grateful and obedient to him. For the greatness of divine grace increases our guilt, unless we acknowledge it with due reverence.

units.la: Et huc Hierosolymitanae vrbis exemplum pertinet, cuius ingratitudinem Dominus horum beneficiorum commemoratione exaggerat. Quo loco praecipuum & omnis mali caput atq; fons est, quod ipsos ad Deum colligi & seruari noluisse dicit. Ergo cum Dei voluntate illi pugnarunt: quod vt nimium frequenter fit, ita ingens est indicium, quo nostrae naturae corruptio & prauitas arguitur. Nec enim solum nihil boni ex semetipso habet homo, verumetiam quam Deus eis ex gratia offert, salutem fastidit & respuit, perinde vt qui stoma chi cruditate laborant cibos optimos & saluberrimos respuere, noxios autem appetere consueuerunt. Id vero in praesenti Christus attingit, vt per ditionem (sicut olim per Prophetam dixerat) ex ipsis esse ostendat, & Deum omni culpa liberet. Quod autem noluerint salutem amplecti, aut Deo ipsos vocanti morem gerere, factis eorum probat.
units.tr: This also bears on the example of the city of Jerusalem, whose ingratitude the Lord magnifies by recalling these benefits. The chief point here, the head and source of all the evil, is that he says they were unwilling to be gathered and saved by God. So they fought against the will of God. This happens all too often, and it is a great sign by which the corruption and perversity of our nature is proved. Man has nothing good in himself, and moreover he loathes and spurns the salvation that God offers him by grace, just as people with a queasy stomach refuse the best and most wholesome food and crave what is harmful. Christ touches on this now, so that, as he once said through the prophet, he may show that the ruin comes from themselves and free God from all blame. His deeds prove that they did not want to embrace salvation or to obey God when he called them.

units.la: Nam Prophetas hastenus Hierosolymae trucidatos, & à Deo missos voluntatis suae interpretes ibidem lapidatos fuisse dicit. Est hoc notius ex sacra historia, quam vt multis demonstrari oporteat, & supra sub finem vndecimi Cap. ideo illis exprobrauit. Neque hoc olim modo fecere, sed ipsum quoque Filium Dei gentibus crucifigendum tradiderunt, & eadem rabie in eius quoque Apostolos grassati sunt. At quia isti omnes nullo scelere aut maleficio infames, sed fidissimi poenitentiae & salutis gratuitae praecones fuerunt, quis non videat illos ad Deum congregari noluisse? Docemur autem horum exemplo, Veritatis odium & quae aduersus huius ministros instituuntur persecutiones, extremae ac deploratae malitiae argumentum esse. Quid enim de aegroto speres, qui & medicum odit, & medicinam omnem respuit? Aut quis non de filio nequam desperet, qui patrem exsuum habet, eius admonitiones cum ludibrio reijcit? At quid hodie frequentius fit? Etenim si mundi mores spe- stemus, atrocissima quidem scelera passim regnant, soli tamen pro sceleratis & quouis supplicio dignis iudicantur fideles Verbi Dei interpretes. In hos alij ferro & igne seuiunt: alij qui Euangelij studium profitentur, eosdem tamè oderunt, vt qui soli dissidiorum authores sint, aut saltem profanaticis habent, quorum morositate nemo moueri debeat. At neminem piorum ista debent offendere. Est enim hoc mundi huius ingenium, qui ita ad propriam pernitiem & exitium ruit, cum interim beati ac felices sint qui in Domino moriuntur, & suo prius officio fideliter defuncti sunt.
units.tr: For he says that the prophets, sent by God as interpreters of his will, were killed in Jerusalem and stoned there until then. This is too well known from sacred history to need proof with many examples, and above, at the end of the eleventh chapter, he rebuked them for it. Nor did they do this only once. They even handed over the Son of God himself to the Gentiles to be crucified, and they raged with the same fury against his apostles. Yet all of these were infamous for no crime or wrongdoing, but were most faithful preachers of repentance and of free salvation. Who would not see that they were unwilling to be gathered to God? We are taught by their example that hatred of the truth, and the persecutions set up against its ministers, are a sign of extreme and hopeless wickedness. For what can you hope of a sick man who hates the doctor and rejects all medicine? Or who would not despair of a worthless son who has a father and mocks his admonitions? Yet what happens more often today? For if we look at the customs of the world, the most atrocious crimes reign everywhere, and yet only the faithful interpreters of God's Word are judged criminals and deserving of any punishment. Some rage against them with sword and fire. Others, who profess zeal for the gospel, nonetheless hate the same men, as if they alone were the authors of dissensions, or at least they regard them as fanatics whose stubbornness ought to move no one. But these things ought to offend no godly person. Such is the nature of this world, which rushes headlong to its own destruction and ruin, while those who die in the Lord, and have first faithfully discharged their duty, are blessed and happy.

units.la: Sequitur grauissima poena comminatio, quam de Iudaeis sumpturus sit Deus. Ecce inquit )relinquitur vobis domus vestra deserta: Amen autem dico vobis, non videbitis me, vsq; dum venerit tempus, vt dicatis: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini. Primò excidium illis minatur, & quamuis hoc ad totam vrbem & omnem terram ipsorum referri debeat, quae cum omnibus vrbibus suis Romanorum armis miserè vastata est, in primis tamen domus meminit, per quam templum intelligi debere non est dubium. Et hanc ipsorum domum dicit, vt innuat eam à Deo nō amplius pro sua agnosci, eo quod illam ex domo precationis, speluncâ latronum fecerint. Item relinquitur vobis, inquit: Quasi diceret: Quoniam templum, relicto & contempto vero eius vsu, in vestrū vsum conuerti stis, & alij quidem in hoc spem & fiduciam omnem tollocant, & sub eius praetextu atrocissima quae flagitia designant. alij vero tam templo quàm toto cultu externo ad suum quastum & ambitionem abutuntur, Deus illud vobis relinquet, vt eo quale nunc est fruamini, & suae gratiae praesentiam pro tiam procul ab illo auferet. Itaque desertum vobis relinquetur, ut non possitis illo amplius fidere; ubi nullum eius vestigium extare videritis. Fuit hoc horrendum iustitiae divinae exemplum, quando domum eius mandato extructam, promissionibus amplissimis commendatam, adhuc Filii sui & nostri redemptoris typum, à prophanis militibus incendi & excindi passus est: & ita quidem, ut nunquam instaurari potuerit (sicut alibi prolixè ostendimus) & nunc annis circiter mille quingentis in cineribus & ruinis iaceat. Quo argumento Deus toti orbi demonstrare voluit, se nulli loco aut genti propter externos ritus & pristinam gloriam obstrictum esse, quo minus contumaces & poenitere nescios male perdat. Discant ergo hic omnes homines, quae illa flabella sint, quibus Dei ira accenditur quaeque item causae sint seditionum, bellorum civilium, excidiorum denique, quibus regna florentissima & urbes celeberrimae intereunt: Non equidem (ut prophani homines & huius saeculi sapientia tur gidi loquuntur) libera Verbi Dei praedicatio, & Ecclesiarum ex hac nascens reformatio: sed Verbi contemptus, odia ministrorum, persequutiones piorum & incurabilis in retinendis superstitionibus atque peccandi libidine contumacia. Haec sunt, quae Dei iram provocant, & gentibus exitium afferunt: quod ille tam in lege quam Prophetis passim testatur, & huc exempla pertinent, quae in omnium prope gentium historiis plurima occurrunt. Quae omnia si hodie expendamus, facile patebit, quid nobis sperandum sit, quando illa vbiq; regnant, ut paulo ante diximus.
units.tr: There follows the most grievous threat of punishment that God is about to inflict on the Jews. "Behold," he says, "your house is left to you desolate. Truly I say to you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." First he threatens them with destruction. Although this must be referred to the whole city and all their land, which was miserably laid waste with all its towns by the Roman arms, he especially mentions the house, by which the temple must surely be understood. He calls it "your house" to signify that God no longer acknowledges it as his own, because they have made it from a house of prayer a den of robbers. Likewise, he says, "it is left to you." It is as if he said: Since you have turned the temple, abandoning and despising its true use, to your own use, and since some place all their hope and trust in it and cover up the most atrocious wickedness under its pretext, while others abuse both the temple and the whole external worship for their own gain and ambition, God will leave it to you, so that you may enjoy it as it now is, and he will take far away from it the presence of his grace. Thus it will be left to you as a desert, so that you cannot trust in it any longer, when you see no trace of him there. This was a dreadful example of divine justice, when God allowed his house, built by his command and commended by the greatest promises, a type of his Son and our Redeemer, to be burned and destroyed by profane soldiers. It was destroyed in such a way that it could never be restored (as we have shown at length elsewhere), and now for about fifteen hundred years it has lain in ashes and ruins. By this argument God wished to show the whole world that he is bound to no place or nation, on account of external rites or former glory, so as not to destroy utterly those who are stubborn and do not know how to repent. Let all men here learn what those bellows are by which the wrath of God is kindled, and likewise what causes sedition, civil wars, and finally destruction, by which the most flourishing kingdoms and the most famous cities perish. Not, indeed, as profane men and the wisdom of this age foolishly speak, the free preaching of God's Word and the reform of the churches arising from it, but contempt of the Word, hatred of the ministers, persecution of the godly, and an incurable obstinacy in holding on to superstitions and in the lust for sinning. These are what provoke God's anger and bring destruction on nations, as he bears witness everywhere in the law and the prophets, and the examples that occur in almost every nation's history pertain to this. If we weigh all these things today, it will be easy to see what we may hope for, since these things reign everywhere, as we said a little while ago.

units.la: Sed addit adhuc gravius quid Dominus dicens: Amen autem dico vobis, non videbitis me, vsque dum venerit tempus, ut dicatis: Benedictus, qui venit in nomine Domini. Quae verba à nonnullis exponuntur, quod se non ante cum illis in gratiam reditrum esse minetur, quam ipsi ex animo ad eum converti fuerint. Sed cum horum sententia pugnat, quod Domino hic cum incurabilibus res est, & quidem praecipue cum Hierosolyma, quae aeterna maledictione ad irreparabile excidium damnatam esse constat. Rectius ergo de postremo Christi adventu intelliguntur, cuius denuntiatione postea quoq; Sacerdotes & Seniores Hierosolymitanos terruit, cum captivus in eorum concilio de sua doctrina & conditione interrogaretur. Nec nobis absurdum videri debet, quod illis verba tribuit, quae in Psalmis habentur, & quibus vere pij olim Christi sui redemptoris adventum optabunt atque celebrabunt. Nam hypocritas in novissimo etiam die ingenium minimè mutaturos esse, ex ijs apparet quae de illis Christus apud Matthaeum cap.7. & 25. dicit. Sed seram nimis & inutilem fore poenitentiam hic ostendit, licet eam blanditijs & acclamationibus honorificis palliare conentur. Itaq; qui talis sunt, nihil praeter aeterna inferorum supplicia possunt sperare, nisi dum in hac vita degunt ad Deum serio conver tantur. Excitet autem nos tota huius loci consideratio, ut quoties alas suas ille expandit, ad eum nos recipiamus. Haec enim unica est vera salutis ratio & via. Dicitur autem ille alas suas extendere, quoties per Euangelium nos invitat, ut Iesum Christum amplexemur, qui nobis salutis author & mediator est unicus. Huic ergo fidere, ad eundem per fidei unitatem congregari, & nostra illi obsequia praestare debemus, ut olim in magno illo die, non turbatis & territis animis (ut hypocritae tacent) sed laeta certaq; salutis fiducia exclamare nobis liceat: Benedictus, qui venit in nomine Domini. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But the Lord adds something still more grievous when he says: "Truly I say to you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Some explain these words to mean that he threatens not to be reconciled with them until they have turned to him from the heart. But this opinion conflicts with the context, since the Lord is here dealing with incurable people, and especially with Jerusalem, which is known to have been condemned by an eternal curse to irreparable destruction. It is therefore more correctly understood of Christ's final coming, by whose announcement he later also terrified the chief priests and elders of Jerusalem, when, as a prisoner, he was questioned in their council about his teaching and his position. Nor should it seem absurd to us that he gives them words found in the Psalms, with which truly godly people of old wished for and celebrated the coming of Christ, their Redeemer. For that hypocrites will not change their disposition even on the last day is clear from what Christ says of them in Matthew chapters 7 and 25. But here he shows that repentance will be too late and useless, even if they try to disguise it with flattery and honorific acclamations. Therefore those who are such can hope for nothing but the eternal punishments of hell, unless while they live in this life they seriously turn to God. Let the whole consideration of this passage stir us up, so that whenever he spreads his wings, we may take refuge with him. For this is the only true way and method of salvation. Christ is said to spread his wings whenever he invites us through the gospel to embrace Jesus Christ, who is our only author and mediator of salvation. Therefore we must trust in him, be gathered to him through the unity of faith, and render him our obedience, so that on that great day, with our minds not troubled and terrified (as the hypocrites are silent), but with a joyful and certain confidence of salvation, we may be permitted to cry out: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.tr: CAPUT XIIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXLII.

units.la: ET factum est, cum veniret in domum cuiusdam ex primoribus Pharisaeis Sabbato ad capiendum cibum, ipsi observabant eum. Et ecce quidam hydropicus erat coram eo. Tum respondens Iesus dixit Legis interpretibus & Pharisaeis in haec verba: Licet ne sanare sabbato? Ipsi vero tacuerunt. Tum ipse prehensum eum sanavit ac dimisit. Et respondens eis dixit: Cuius vestrum asinus aut bos in puteum cadet, qui non statim extrahat eum die Sabbati? Et non poterant ad ista respondere.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath, that they watched him. And behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy. And Jesus, answering, spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day? But they held their peace. And he took him, and healed him, and let him go. And he answered and said unto them: Which of you shall have an ass or an ox fallen into a pit, and will not straightway pull him out on the Sabbath day? And they could not answer him again to these things.

units.la: Cap. X IIII.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: VOniam Dominus noster Iesus Christus hucusq; multis de poenitentia & salutari ad Deũ conuersione disseruit, simulq; exemplis & argumentis grauissimis Iudaeorũ gentem, & cum his nos omnes, ad seriũ illius studium exhortatus est: commodè nunc Lucas hoc capite non nulla eius facta & dicta commemorat, quae erroribus atq; vitijs medentur, quibus poenitentia quam maximè impeditur, quibus ite Iudaei fere retinebantur, quò minus illam sibi necessariam putar ent. Primò enim rursus de Sabbato agit, vt illos de ext ernis omnibus rectè iudicare doceat, ne eorum fiducia dementati, nihil porrò sibi facto opus esse putarent. Deinde cum superbia initium sit peccati, hanc quoq; retundit, & humilitatem atq; modestiam nobis commendat. Tertiò veram dilectionem tradit, docens eius officia sic nos praestare debere, ne sub eorum praetextu nostrum commodum quaeramus. Postremò quid vocante nos Deo fieri debeat, docet, ne vocationi eius reluctantes illam nobis faciamus inutilem. In praesenti, quae de Sabbato dicuntur, videbimus.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ has hitherto discoursed at length on repentance and on the saving conversion to God, and has at the same time exhorted the Jewish nation, and with them all of us, to the earnest pursuit of it by examples and by the weightiest arguments, Luke now fitly records in this chapter some of his deeds and sayings, which heal the errors and vices that most hinder repentance, and by which the Jews were largely held back from thinking it necessary for themselves. First, he again deals with the Sabbath, to teach them to judge rightly of all external matters, lest, made foolish by their confidence in these, they should think that nothing further needed to be done for themselves. Then, since pride is the beginning of sin, he also beats it down and commends humility and modesty to us. Thirdly, he sets forth true love, teaching that we ought to perform its duties in such a way that we do not seek our own advantage under their pretext. Lastly, he teaches what must be done when God calls us, lest by resisting his call we make it useless to ourselves. For the present, we shall see what is said about the Sabbath.

units.la: Quia autem non ignorabat Dominus, Iudaeos in huius aliorumq; ritum obseruatione cum superstitiosa eorum fiducia incurabilem contumaciam coniunxisse, non verbis solis docet, in quo Sabbati religio consistat, verumetiam facto miraculoso doctrinam hanc suam confirmat: cuius idem finis & scopus est, qui prioris, quod sub initium proximi cap. in muliere incurua aditum fuisse audiimus: nimirum dilectionis & verae pietatis officia propter Sabbatum & alias huius generis ceremonias nequaquam intermitti debere. Etsi vero in huius miraculi descriptione Lucas breuitati studeat, tamen in recensendis circumstantijs, quae alicuius momenti sunt, diligentissimus est.
units.tr: Now, since the Lord was not unaware that the Jews, in their observance of this and of other rites, had joined an incurable obstinacy to their superstitious confidence, he does not teach by words alone in what the religion of the Sabbath consists, but confirms this doctrine by a miraculous deed. The aim and purpose of this is the same as that of the earlier miracle, which we heard was introduced at the beginning of the previous chapter in the case of the bent woman: namely, that the duties of love and true piety must by no means be omitted on account of the Sabbath or other ceremonies of this kind. And although in describing this miracle Luke strives for brevity, nevertheless in recounting the circumstances that are of some importance he is most careful.

units.la: Et primò locum cum tempore annotans, Christum Sabbato in domum cuiusdam principis Pharisæorum ingressum esse scribit, vt cibum illic caperet. Quod haud dubiè no impudenter ab eo factum est, vt erronum more non vocatus irrumperet, sed inuitatus eò venit cum multis aliis, qui ad idem conuiuium vocati fuerant. Et videri poterat Pharisæus iste humanitatis atq; amicitiae officium facere dum Christum honorario conuiuio adhibet, sed insidiose & hostiliter istud omne factum fuisse, vno verbo indicatur, quando eos illum obseruauisse, Euangelista scribit. Nec enim in eius verba intenti fuerunt, aut mores obseruarunt, vt ex ipso aliquid discerent, aut virtutis exemplum caperent: sed vt aliquam ipsius accusandi & perdendi occasionem haberent. Fuit hoc non inhumanum modo, sed plane barbarum quoque, & tantis viris indignissimum facinus. Constat enim, apud omnes gentes ex communi more, eiusdem mensae communionem amicitiae symbolum, vel etiam vinculum quoddam atque mutui amoris fomentum semper fuisse. Et quanto in pretio atque honore apud ethnicos quoque hospitalitatis ius fuerit, ex eo apparet, quod in bellis etiam apertius illud violari nefas duxerunt, adeo vt hostibus parcerent, quos hospites paternos aliquando fuisse intelligebant. Sed & Iouem solebant ξένιον vocare, quod Deum hospitibus iura dare (vt poeta loquitur) & horum violatores ulciscì crederent. Neque superstitiosam fuisse hanc illorum persuasionem, ex plus ex scriptura sacra desumptis probari potest. Abrahamum certè hospitalitatis studiosissimum fuisse legimus: nimirum, quod illam Deo in primis placuisse. Rursus etsi infinita & nefanda fuerint Sodomaeorum scelera, poenas tamen diu distulit Dominus, si forte ad ipsum conuersi emendarentur: at postquam violato hospitij iure, Lothi domum oppugnare, & eius hospites ad extremam ignominiam postulare ausi sunt, mox omnem moram abrupit, & primo flatim diluculo flammis caelitus immissis illos cum tota finitima regione perdidit. Quid? annon ipse Dei Filius hospitalitatis officia in magno illo die iudicij commendabit, eos autem detestabitur, qui illa neglexerint? Fuit ergo plus quàm barbara crudelitas, quod sub conuiuij honorarij praetextu isti insidias Christo struxerunt.
units.tr: And first, noting the place together with the time, he writes that Christ entered on the Sabbath the house of a certain leader of the Pharisees to take food there. This was undoubtedly not done by him without some forethought, since he did not force his way in uninvited, like a vagabond, but came there as a guest, invited together with many others who had been summoned to the same feast. And this Pharisee might seem to be performing the office of kindness and friendship in receiving Christ at a festive banquet; but that all this was done insidiously and with hostility is indicated in a single word, when the evangelist writes that "they watched him." For they were not attentive to his words, nor did they observe his manners so as to learn something from him or take an example of virtue; rather, they sought an occasion to accuse and destroy him. This was a deed not merely inhumane but plainly barbarous too, and most unworthy of such men. For it is established that among all nations, by common custom, sharing a table has always been a sign of friendship, or even a certain bond and fostering of mutual love. And how highly the right of hospitality was esteemed even among the heathen appears from this: that they thought it a sin to violate it even in wars, so much so that they spared enemies whom they knew had once been their hereditary guests. Indeed they used to call Jupiter Xenios, because they believed that God gives laws to guests (as the poet says) and avenges those who violate them. Nor can it be proved from the holy Scripture alone that this belief of theirs was superstitious. We read that Abraham was most zealous in hospitality, namely because it was especially pleasing to God. Again, although the crimes of the Sodomites were boundless and unspeakable, the Lord nevertheless long deferred their punishment, in case perhaps they might be converted to him and amend themselves. But after, having violated the right of hospitality, they dared to assault the house of Lot and demand his guests for the utmost shame, he at once broke off all delay, and at the first light of dawn he destroyed them, together with the whole neighbouring region, by fire sent from heaven. What then? Will not the Son of God himself commend the duties of hospitality on that great day of judgment, and condemn those who have neglected them? It was therefore more than barbarous cruelty that they laid this snare for Christ under the pretext of an honourable banquet.

units.la: At non inutile fuerit illos propius inspicere, vt & incurabilem hypocritarum malitiam & è contra Dei bonitatem agnoscere discamus. Pharisæos enim illo tempore pro sanctissimis habitos fuisse, iam saepe diximus: veruntamen, nulli illi graviores Christi hostes fuerunt, cuius odio ita flagrarunt, vt toties ab illo victi, subinde tamen ad nouas artes conuersi sint, & pugnam aduersus eum instaurarint. Interim quando opus est, odium istud celare, & amicitiam simulare possunt, vt fraude doloque in periculum adducant, quem argumentis & rationibus non poterant convincere. Est hoc hypocritarum omnium ingenium. Sanctitatis nomen apud rude vulgus externo fuco sibi acquirunt, & cum illa prae aliis omnibus glorientur, eum tamen ferre nullo modo possunt qui ipsa sanctitas est, & per quem unum homines sanctificantur. Ita vero fit, ut dum propria dignitate niituntur, à salute in universum excidant. Et quamvis se miseros & infelices esse propriae conscientiae testimonio edoceantur, & non raro publice etiam convincantur, ijsdem tamen nihil est audacius in veritate oppugnanda. Nam etsi ad tempus quiescant, & pacem pollicentur, non tamen desinunt vanari occasiones, quibus se aliquid profecturos esse sperant. Semper ergo adversus eos in excubijs stent veritatis studiosi, neque illorum blanditijs quicquam tribuant, sed tunc in primis sua specie habeant eorum consilia, quando nihil periculi ab eis imminere videtur. Et pudeat omnes eos suae ignaviae, qui cum Christi nomen profiteantur, tamen eius causam, qua nulla honestior & sanctior, quaeque cum salute nostra coniuncta est, non simili zelo atque studio agunt, sed ab his se sese vinci patiuntur, qui & propriae salutis & gloriae Dei studio iam pridem excussi, nihil praeter auram popularem & quaestum privatum quaerunt.
units.tr: But it will not be unprofitable to look at them more closely, so that we may recognise both the incurable malice of hypocrites and, on the other hand, the goodness of God. For we have often said already that the Pharisees at that time were regarded as most holy; yet none were more serious enemies of Christ, and they burned with such hatred of him that, though so often defeated by him, they nevertheless kept turning to new arts and renewed the struggle against him. Meanwhile, when the occasion requires, they can hide that hatred and feign friendship, so that they may bring into danger by fraud and guile the man whom they could not convince by arguments and reasons. This is the nature of all hypocrites. They acquire for themselves the name of holiness among the uneducated crowd by outward show, and though they boast of it above all others, they cannot at all bear him who is holiness itself, and through whom alone men are sanctified. And so it happens that, while they lean on their own dignity, they fall away entirely from salvation. And although they are taught by the testimony of their own conscience that they are wretched and unhappy, and not seldom are also publicly convicted, yet nothing is more bold than they in attacking the truth. For even if for a time they keep quiet and promise peace, they do not cease to seek occasions by which they hope to achieve something. Therefore let those who are zealous for the truth always stand on watch against them, and give nothing to their flatteries, but especially regard their plans with suspicion when no danger seems to threaten from them. And let all those be ashamed of their cowardice who, though they profess the name of Christ, nevertheless do not pursue his cause, which is none more honourable or holier, and which is bound up with our salvation, with a similar zeal and eagerness, but allow themselves to be beaten by those who, having long since been shaken off from concern for their own salvation and for the glory of God, seek nothing but popular applause and private gain.

units.la: Sed ipsius etiam Christi Iesu factum consideremus, qui ad eos ingreditur, quos hostes suos esse & omnia insidiose facere, non potuit ignorare. Id vero nequaquam fecit, ut seruiliter adulando eos sibi magis propitios redderet, aut aliud quoddam commodum temporarium ex illis venaretur, sed quia in mundum venerat, ut eos salvos faceret qui perierant, istud omne ex officio fecit, & quia Pharisaeos prae aliis excaecatos & obstinatos esse sciebat, non publice modo eos cum aliis docere & arguere, sed privatam quoque institutionem adhibere voluit. Ideo frequenter ad illos diverit, cum ijsdem edit & omnem occasionem captat, qua vel doctrina sua vel miraculis eos lucrifacere possit. Et eodem referri debet, quod Nicodemum, qui eiusdem ordinis erat, noctu ad se venientem tanquam amicè & fideliter instituit. Sunt haec praeclara bonitatis & facilitatis incomparabilis argumenta, quando ijs sese tam amicum & benevolum praebuit, qui eius vitae irrequieto plane studio insidias struebant. Debent autem ex ijs consolationem petere pij, quando fidem suam intra suas conscientias nonnihil tentari sentiunt. Cur enim infirmos ille negligeret, qui erga obstinatos & induratos officium fecit? Aut num eos aspernari poterit, qui eius gratiam & opem implorant, qui hanc hostibus quoque acerrimis tam clementer, & plerunque nihil huius petentibus, offerre dignatur? Neminem ergo Satanicae suggestiones salutis suae dubium & incertum reddant. Nemo item propriae infirmitatis sensu terreatur. Mendax enim est Satan, & quos abs se vinci omnino non posse videt, eos inanibus terriculamentis exagitare studet, ut vel momentaneam ex illorum anxietate & solicitudine voluptatem capiat. At eosdem non deserit Christus, qui ideo infirmitates nostras in se susceptit, & ab eodem tentari voluit, ut Pontificem atque mediatorem fidelem esse sciremus, qui nobis condolere possit, & instar indulgentissimi parentis nostrae imbecillitati ignoscere. Hoc modo caveant singuli, ne eius facilitate abutantur, & quam ille ipsis sponte offert, gratiam contemnant. Nam qui id faciunt, ij tandem severum impietatis vindicem sentiunt, quem magistrum & servatorem suum agnoscere noluerunt. Exemplum huius rei memorabile est Pharao, cuius contumacia postquam diu frustra luctatus esset Deus, tandem rubri maris fluctibus emollitum fateri coegit, sibi cum Iehova, Deo omnium authore, negotium esse. Et quid Pharisaeus incurabilibus, quid Sacerdotibus poenitere nescijs, quid denique toti Iudaeorum genti acciderit, historia testantur, & nos nuper quaedam huc pertinentia diximus. Quae exempla utinam hodie diligentius expenderent, quos eodem favore & honore Christus dignatur, ut non inuitatus quoque ad ipsos diverit per Verbi sui praedicationem, qua & seipsum illis totum offert, & eosdem ad regni sui omniumque bonorum caelestium possessionem vocat. Sed quae nostri seculi ingratitudo est, non temere pij & cordati omnes horribilem totius orbis mutationem metuunt, cum Verbum illud salutis Cyclopico sane contemptu reijci, & ipsum Christum in suis membris passim pelli & affligi videant.
units.tr: But let us also consider the deed of Christ Jesus himself, who goes in to those whom he could not fail to know were his enemies and were acting insidiously in everything. He did not do this to win their favour by fawning flattery, nor to hunt from them some other temporary advantage; rather, because he had come into the world to save those who had perished, he did all this out of his office, and because he knew the Pharisees to be blinder and more obstinate than others, he wished not only to teach and rebuke them publicly with the rest, but also to apply private instruction. Therefore he often turned aside to them, dined with them, and seized every opportunity by which he might win them over, either by his teaching or by his miracles. To the same purpose belongs the fact that he instructed Nicodemus, who was of the same order, when he came to him by night, as a friend and faithfully. These are excellent proofs of his incomparable goodness and kindness, since he showed himself so friendly and benevolent to those who were laying snares for his life with a restless zeal. And the godly ought to draw consolation from them when they feel their faith somewhat tried within their consciences. For why would he neglect the sick, who performed his office toward the stubborn and hardened? Or will he be able to spurn those who implore his grace and help, he who deigns to offer this so graciously even to his most bitter enemies, and very often to those who do not ask for it at all? Therefore let no satanic suggestions make anyone doubtful and uncertain of his salvation. Nor let anyone be terrified by a sense of his own weakness. For Satan is a liar, and those whom he sees he cannot altogether overcome, he strives to harass with empty terrors, so that he may gain a momentary pleasure from their anxiety and distress. But Christ does not abandon those very people; he therefore took our weaknesses upon himself, and willed to be tempted by the same things, so that we might know him to be a faithful high priest and mediator, who can feel for us and, like the most indulgent parent, pardon our frailty. Let each therefore take care not to abuse his kindness, and not to despise the grace which he offers them of his own accord. For those who do this at last feel the stern avenger of impiety, whom they refused to acknowledge as their master and saviour. A memorable example of this is Pharaoh, whose obstinacy, after God had long struggled with it in vain, he at last compelled, softened by the waves of the Red Sea, to confess that he had to do with Iehova, the author of all things. And history bears witness what befell the incurable Pharisees, the priests who knew not how to repent, and finally the whole Jewish nation; and we have lately said some things pertinent to this. Would that they now weighed these examples more carefully, those whom Christ deigns to honour with the same favour and kindness, so that he comes to them too, though uninvited, through the preaching of his Word, in which he offers himself wholly to them and calls them to the possession of his kingdom and of all heavenly goods. But such is the ingratitude of our age that all the godly and thoughtful fear, not without reason, a horrible overturning of the whole world, when they see that word of salvation rejected with truly Cyclopean contempt, and Christ himself everywhere driven out and afflicted in his members.

units.la: Admonet nos praeterea suo exemplo Dominus, qua conditione nos quoque cum ijs familiarius possimus conuersari, quos à fide in Christum & doctrina eius animo alieno esse scimus. In eo enim plurimi peccant, qui privati commodi & mundi illecebris sese vinci patiuntur, ut illorum amicitiam ambiant, seruiliter sese illis submittant, ijsdem in multis assentiantur, omnia denique simulent & dissimulent in eorum gratiam, ut illis magis propitijs possint uti. Et hi fere Christi exemplo se tuentur, & Christianam charitatem praetexunt, cuius sit de omnibus bene sperare, hostes diligere.
units.tr: The Lord also teaches us, by his own example, on what terms we may associate more closely with those whom we know to be estranged from faith in Christ and from his doctrine. Many go wrong here: they allow themselves to be overcome by private advantage and the allurements of the world, so that they court the friendship of such people, submit to them like slaves, agree with them in many things, and in short pretend and dissemble everything to win their favour, so that they may enjoy their goodwill more. Most of these shelter themselves under Christ's example and pretend it is Christian charity, which is to hope well of everyone and to love one's enemies.

units.la: omnibus item sese amicum atque beneuolum prabere. At quam turpiter illi exemplo Christi abu- tantur, mox apparebit, si eorum mores cum hoc conferas. Hic enim ex officio fecit quicquid fecit, & quia medicus humani generis in mundum venerat, nullos quocunque morbo laborantes, & ne phreneticos quidem aut mente captos negligere debuit. Quem vero officij titulum illi possunt praetexere? Num Christiani hominis esse dicent, cum huius hostibus colludere, consilia sua conferre, & eorunde studijs atq; moribus sese accomodare? At quibus scripturis siue exemplis id probabunt? Deinde Christus non suum commodum, sed eorum salutem quaesiuit quibus cum versatus est: Isti vero si nulla priuati commodi spes affulgeat, facile ab eiusmodi commercijs abstinebunt. Christus in Pharisaeorum gratiam nihil dissimulauit, neque vel docendi munus intermisit, neque vllam miracula edendi, aut illos etiam seuerius arguendi occasionem neglexit: Nostri vero illi omnia dissimulant, de fide requisiti tacent, vitia & errores nullos arguunt, corruptos quorumuis mores & aperta in Christum atque Euangelium eius conuitia suo silentio probant, exemplo denique suo illos in impietate confirmat, & multos in ignorantia tenebris detinent, qui ex ijs emergere poterant, si illi suo erga eos officio fungerentur. Desinant ergo isti exemplo Christi suam ignauiam atque perfidiam celare: desinant dilectionis fraternae studium iactare, cum ijs exitij authores sint, quibus lucrifacien dis se totos debebant impendere. Qui autem serio tam propriae quam alienae salutis studio tenentur ij ex Babylone (vt Christus monet) discedant, Antichristiano nidore fragrantes culinas deserant, & non necessaria cum Christi aduersarijs commercia declinet, ne idem ipsis, quod olim Petro in Caiapheae atrio ad prunas Pontificias se calefacienti, accidat. Quod si haec neglexerint, nae illis aliquando familiaritas ista magno constabit.
units.tr: Likewise he shows himself friendly and kind to all. But how shamefully these men abuse Christ's example will soon be clear, if you compare their conduct with it. He did whatever he did out of duty, and because he had come into the world as the physician of the human race, he ought not to neglect anyone suffering from any disease, not even the frenzied or the mentally deranged. But what title of duty can they put forward? Will they say it belongs to a Christian man to collude with Christ's enemies, to confer with them about their plans, and to adapt himself to their pursuits and manners? And by what Scriptures or examples will they prove it? Further, Christ sought not his own advantage but the salvation of those among whom he lived; these men, however, if no hope of private gain shines on them, will easily abstain from such dealings. Christ did not dissemble anything to win the Pharisees' favour; he neither gave up his teaching office, nor neglected the working of miracles, nor let slip any opportunity of rebuking them more sharply. Our men, by contrast, dissemble everything: when questioned about the faith they keep silent, they rebuke no faults or errors, and by their silence they approve the corrupt morals of anyone at all and the open insults against Christ and his Gospel. Finally, by their example they confirm the others in impiety, and they keep many in the darkness of ignorance who could have been brought out of it, had those men performed their duty towards them. Let them therefore stop hiding their idleness and treachery behind Christ's example; let them stop boasting of their zeal for brotherly love, when they are the authors of the ruin of those whom they ought to have devoted themselves wholly to winning. But those who are seriously concerned for their own salvation and that of others should, as Christ warns, depart from Babylon, leave the Antichristian-smelling kitchens behind, and avoid unnecessary dealings with Christ's adversaries, lest what once happened to Peter should happen to them, when he warmed himself at the Papists' fire in the courtyard of Caiaphas. But if they neglect these things, that familiarity of theirs will one day cost them dearly.

units.la: Porro ipsam Christi actionem & miraculi hic editi historiam videamus. Occurrit hic primus nobis hydropicus, quem coram illo fuisse Lucas scribit. Videtur autem ex inuestria vel in eius cubiculo conuiuium instructum, vel hunc priusquam Christus veniret in triclinium translatum fuisse, vt aliquam occasionem ei obijcerent, propter quam ipsum violati sabbati possent accusare. Quam enim superstitiosi fuerint in eius obseruatione, alibi diximus. Facile ergo illis erat ex hoc argumento calumniari struere, quibus populi animos ab ipso alienarent, & simul eum in periculum adducerent. Sed ex aduerso illustrior fit huius potentia, qui illorum insidiosa consilia in ipsos retorquet, vt ex ijs ignominiam referant, quibus illum irretire voluerunt. Nam vt primum miseri hunc consp exit, ipse prior Legis interpretes atque Pharisaeos aggressus, quaestionem proponit: Licet ne sanare Sabbato? Conuenit haec cum ea, qua alibi publice in Synagoga monit, quum quidam manum aridam habens adesset. Nam tunc quoq; ipsum obseruantibus Pharisaeis dixit: Licet ne Sabbatis benefacere, an malefacere, hominem seruare, an trucidare? At sic quarendo partim offensionem cauere voluit, ne quid ipsum temere fecisse possent dicere: partim eos intra conscientias ipsorum conuincit, quare iudicium subterfugere non poterant. Quis enim negaret Sabbato licitum esse homini laboranti benefacere, & eundem seruare, quando nullum opus est; quo propius ad Dei ingenium atque mores accedant homines, sicut gentium quoque philosophi annotarunt? Et ipsos hoc ipsum intellexisse, ex eorum silentio apparet. Quia enim illud non possunt negare, affirmando autem illius causam defendi & iuuari sentiunt, nihil tutius sibi fore arbitrantur, quam omnino tacere. Quid vero turpius fieri poterat, quam Legis interpretes & sanctitatis exiflimatione celebres viros subito obmutescere, neque habere quod responderent ad quaestionem de re vsitatissima, & quae in omnium ore tunc versabatur, ipsis eandem subinde exagitantibus? Sed ita hypocritarum arrogantiam Deus vlcisci solet, vt eorum insciitia omnibus nota fiat, quando agnitam veritatem agnoscere nolunt. Non tamen eorum malitioso silentio sic offenditur Christus, vt propter hoc vel hydropici salutem negligat, vel ipsos docere dedignetur. Nam illis tacentibus, ipse non quidem verbis primum, sed facto respondet, & dum aegrotantem manu prehensum sanat, satis aperte docet, quid de propositta quaestione fit sentiendum. Nec tamen eo contentus, mox argumentum subijcit ex publica consuetudine & communi hominum sensu desumptum, quo probat licere Sabbato Salutem laborantibus conferre.
