Rursus autem interrogatione vtitur, vt proprio iudicio conuincti magis erubescant. Cuius (inquit) vestrum bos aut asinus in puteum cadet, qui non statim extrahat eum die Sabbatii? Ex eo autem quius colligere poterit, multo magis licere homini morbo letali & doloribus assiduis fatigato opem feramus. Sed quia argumentū huic simile in proximo capite nuper vidimus, nunc non opus fuerit in hoc examinando aut etiam confirmando diutius immo rari: quare rem ipsam potius consideremus.
units.tr: Next let us look at Christ's action itself and the story of the miracle performed here. The first person we meet is the man with dropsy, whom Luke writes was before him. It seems that either a banquet had been prepared in the house or in his bedroom, or that this man was brought into the dining room before Christ came, so that they might have some occasion against him, on account of which they could accuse him of breaking the Sabbath. For how superstitious they were in observing it, we have said elsewhere. It was therefore easy for them to plot slander from this pretext, by which they could turn the people's minds away from him and at the same time bring him into danger. But on the contrary, his power is shown more brightly, for he turns their insidious plans back upon themselves, so that they carry away shame from the very things by which they wished to ensnare him. For as soon as he perceives their wretched plot, he himself first addresses the interpreters of the Law and the Pharisees and puts the question: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? This agrees with what he said publicly in the synagogue elsewhere, when a man with a withered hand was present. For then too, while the Pharisees were watching him, he said: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it? By asking thus he wished partly to guard against offence, so that they could not say he had acted rashly, and partly to convict them by their own consciences, so that they could not escape judgement. For who would deny that it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good to a suffering man and to save him, since this is no labour; men draw nearer to God's nature and ways in this, as even the philosophers of the nations have noted? That they themselves understood this is clear from their silence. For since they cannot deny it, yet feel that by affirming it the cause would be defended and supported, they judge that nothing is safer for them than to keep utterly silent. What could be more shameful than that the interpreters of the Law, men famed for their reputation of holiness, should suddenly fall dumb, and have no answer to a question about a very common matter, which at that time was on everyone's lips, while he kept pressing it upon them again and again? But God is accustomed to punish the arrogance of hypocrites in this way, so that their ignorance becomes known to all, when they refuse to acknowledge the truth once it is recognised. Yet Christ is not so offended by their malicious silence that he neglects the healing of the man with dropsy on account of it, or disdains to teach them. For while they are silent, he answers first not in words but in deed, and while he takes hold of the sick man by the hand and heals him, he teaches quite plainly what is to be thought about the question proposed. Nor is he content with that alone: he soon adds an argument drawn from common custom and the shared sense of mankind, by which he proves that it is lawful on the Sabbath to bring help to those who suffer. Again he uses a question, so that they may be the more ashamed, convicted by their own judgement: Which of you, he says, will not at once pull out his ox or ass that has fallen into a well, even on the Sabbath day? And from that one may infer that much more it is lawful to bring help to a man worn down by a deadly disease and constant pains. But since we saw an argument similar to this in the preceding chapter only recently, there is no need now to linger longer over examining or confirming it here; let us rather consider the matter itself.

units.la: Et primò quidem non ofcitanter obseruari debet, quòd de Sabbato toties in Scripturis agitur. Nam si externa omnia, quæ ad Dei cultū spectant, ex ordine consideres, nihil reperies, cuius obseruatio tam serio tamá, crebrò inculcetur. Etsi enim hoc proprio exemplo Deus in rerum omnium creatione pijs abunde commendauisset, & iam multis seculis in vsu fuisset, de eodem tamen postea proprium præceptum dedit, quod vt in prima tabula locum quartum habet, ita verbis plurimis & diligentissima omnium circunstantiarum enumeratione proponitur, ne quis in eo aliquam inueniret tergiuersandi occasionem. Postea rursus in Legis expositione hoc ipsum vbiq; repetitur. Et Prophetæ in eius mentione frequentissimi sunt, & Sabbati violationem aut prophanatione inter atrocissima flagitia numerant, propter quæ Deus vrbem cum templo excideriţ, & populum in Babylonem passus sit abduci. Quibus adde, quòd cùm in deserto agentibus Israelitis Circuncisio infantium totus annus quadraginta sine scelere neglecta esset, Sabbati tamen transgressione Deus capitali supplicio puniri voluit. Vnde apparet rem hanc esse magni momenti, cuius vsum verum omnes inquirere, & de eo frequenter cogitare debeant. Et hîc nos Christi exemplū excitare debet, qui & ipse de illo toties disputauit. Vt autē Pharisaicas superstitiones passim arguit, ita quid in illo nobis obseruandum sit, & quis nobis otij aut quietis illius sacræ finis siue scopus esse debeat, subinde docet. Et in præsenti quidem vno verbo (vt dicitur) rem omnem comprehendit, dum licere docet, vt homo salvetur, aut salutis beneficium conferatur morbo periculosò laborantibus. Itaque proprium Sabbati opus est, saluti tam nostræ quàm aliorum consulere: & quia hæc ad totum hominē extenditur, neque anima neque corpus hîc à quoquam negligi debet. At ne sub hoc prætextu vel superstitione peccemus, vt olim Iudæi: vel avaritia & intemperantia, vt hodie homines prophani solent, in quo nam vera hominis salus consistat, probè teneamus oportet. Ad animæ salutem religionis & fidei exercitia pertinent, quæ sunt, vt Dei verbum audiamus, opera & beneficia eius meditemur, eiusdem nomen cum gratiarum actione prædicemus, precemur deniq; tam pro nobisipsis quàm alijs hominibus, & abstineamus à carnis operibus prauis, quibus & animæ nostræ grauantur, & Dei ira accendi-tur. Et hic sanè præcipuus Sabbati vsus est, propter quem dies ille Deo sanctus esse passim dicitur. Quod primitiuæ Ecclesiæ patres obseruasse parent, quando ne Iudæorum superstitionibus communicare viderentur, sacram hanc quietem in diem quidem proximum transtulêre, sed eundem Dominicum dixerunt, vt eum totum Domino consecratum esse debere docerent. Ad corporis verò salutem facit quies, quæ tam hominibus quàm iumentis hoc die præcipitur: & necessario quidem, quia quod caret alterna requie (vt Poeta ait) durabile non est: & quia nec ea quæ ad animæ salutem pertinere modò diximus, perfici possunt ab ijs, qui circa res huius seculi & corpori seruientes occupantur. Estque hoc non vulgare bonitatis & clementiæ argumentum, quòd cum Deus vniuersum vitæ nostræ tempus sibi vendicare posset, sex tamen dies nostris vsibus concessit, vt ea curare possimus, quæ ad rem domesticam faciunt: & rursus vt nostræ cupiditati modum poneret, & ne æternæ salutis cura in nobis tota extinguereţur, diem vnum sibi consecratum esse voluit, quo & corpus & anima otio non minus necessario quàm sanctô reficeretur. Ex his autem cuius colligere promptum est, Sabbati præcepto neque diuina opera, neque ea, quorum intermissio cum certa hominis pernicie coniuncta est, prohiberi: quin potius mandari omnibus, vt sicuti hoc die Deo sese consecrant, ita tunc potissimum charitatis Christianæ meminerint, & hanc pro sua virili beneficentiæ operibus testentur. Ideo quoties de festis celebrioribus Moses loquitur, semper monet, vt pauperum & peregrinorum inter ipsos habitantium meminerint, vt hi ipsorum liberalitate recreati cum ipsis in Domino gaudendi occasionem habeant. Et Paulus de collectione pecuniarum, quæ ad egenos Syriæ ac Iudææ fratres mittendæ erant scribens, admonet, vt diebus sabbati quisque seponat in eum vsum quod ipsi per Dei benignitatem licuerit. Ex his autem firmissimè concluditur, quod sub initium huius Sermonis monuimus, Christium ideo hanc de Sabbato tractatione hoc loco repetisse, vt inanem omnium ceremoniarum fiduciam è medio tollat, qua tunc Iudæi impediebantur, quo minus doctrinam de vera pœnitentia admitterent. Cur enim de hac soliciti essent, qui se abunde omni pietatis officio defunctos putabant, si Sabbatum in ignauo otio transfigerent, & sacris obiter interfuissent. Docet ergo longè alia esse verae pietatis exercitia: & cùm hic Sabbatum cedere debuerit, quo inter omnia externa nihil sanctius, nihil magis necessarium, nihil deniq; maiori cum seueritate à Deo mandatum erat, quanto magis alij ritus omnes ad eundem scopum dirigi debuerunt, ne his aliqui in tenti illa praestantiora & magis necessaria negligerent? Meminisse autem hic oportet, eandem doctrinam ad nos quoq; pertinere, vt externis ritibus non tantum tribuamus, quasi in horum obseruatione vel religio vera vel salus nostra consistat. Vtamur ergo illis ex Domini mandato, vt nobis ad verae pietatis exercitia adiumento sint, salutis verò spe atq; fiduciam in sola Dei gratia repositam habeamus, idq; non tam verbis quàm poenitentiae assiduae & obedientiae verae studio testemur. Sed vrinam doctrina haec hodie non perinde à Christiani nominis professoribus, vt olim à Iudaeis explorata: quando alij quidem inanibus atque frigidissimis ceremonijs fidunt, alij verò tam hi quàm die Dominico ad carnis licentiam abutuntur, & tunc maximè diabolo seruiunt, quando toti Deo consecrati esse debebant.
units.tr: And first of all, it must be observed carefully that the Scriptures speak of the Sabbath so often. For if you consider in order all the external matters that pertain to the worship of God, you will find none whose observance is urged so seriously and so repeatedly. Although God had already commended this by his own example at the creation of all things, and it had been in use for many ages, he later gave a separate command about it. It holds the fourth place in the first table, and it is set forth in many words and with the most careful enumeration of every circumstance, so that no one might find in it an occasion for evasion. Afterwards it is repeated everywhere in the exposition of the Law. The Prophets mention it very frequently, and they count the violation or profanation of the Sabbath among the most atrocious crimes, on account of which God allowed the city and the temple to be destroyed and the people to be led away into Babylon. Add to these that, while the Israelites were in the desert, circumcision of infants was neglected for a whole forty years without punishment, yet God wished the breaking of the Sabbath to be punished by death. From this it is clear that the matter is of great importance, and that all people ought to inquire into its true use and think about it often. Here the example of Christ too should move us, for he himself also discussed it so often. And while he everywhere refutes the Pharisaic superstitions, he also teaches from time to time what we ought to observe in it, and what the purpose or aim of that holy rest and leisure should be for us. In the present passage he comprehends the whole matter, so to speak, in one word, when he teaches that it is lawful to save a man, or to confer the benefit of salvation on those who suffer from a dangerous illness. Therefore the proper work of the Sabbath is to care for our own salvation and that of others, and since this extends to the whole man, neither soul nor body should be neglected by anyone. But so that we do not sin under this pretext, either by superstition, as the Jews did formerly, or by greed and intemperance, as profane people commonly do today, we must hold firmly to where true human salvation consists. For the salvation of the soul, the exercises of religion and faith are needed: that we hear the Word of God, meditate on his works and benefits, proclaim his name with thanksgiving, and finally pray both for ourselves and for other people, and that we abstain from the wicked works of the flesh, by which our souls are burdened and the wrath of God is kindled. And this is indeed the chief use of the Sabbath, on account of which that day is everywhere said to be holy to God. The Fathers of the early Church are reported to have observed this; when, so as not to seem to share in the superstitions of the Jews, they transferred this holy rest to the following day, yet called it the Lord's Day, so that they might teach that the whole day ought to be consecrated to the Lord. For the salvation of the body, rest serves, which is commanded on this day for men and beasts alike; and this is necessary, because what lacks alternating rest (as the poet says) does not endure, and because those things which we have just said pertain to the salvation of the soul cannot be carried out by those who are occupied with the affairs of this age and serve the body. And this is no ordinary proof of goodness and mercy: although God could claim for himself the whole time of our life, he has nevertheless granted us six days for our own uses, so that we may attend to the things that concern our household affairs; and again, to set a limit to our desire, and so that the care of eternal salvation might not be wholly extinguished in us, he wished one day to be consecrated to himself, on which both body and soul might be refreshed by leisure no less necessary than holy. From these things anyone can easily gather that the commandment of the Sabbath forbids neither divine works nor those duties whose omission is bound up with certain ruin to a human being; rather, it enjoins on all that, just as they devote themselves to God on this day, so then especially they should remember Christian love and bear witness to it by their works of kindness, as far as each is able. Therefore, whenever Moses speaks of the more solemn feasts, he always reminds them to remember the poor and the strangers living among them, so that these, refreshed by their generosity, may have an occasion to rejoice in the Lord together with them. And Paul, writing about the collection of money to be sent to the needy brothers in Syria and Judea, advises that on the Sabbath day each person should set aside for that purpose whatever God's goodness has allowed him. From these things it is most firmly concluded what we noted at the beginning of this sermon: that Christ repeated his discussion of the Sabbath at this point so as to remove from the midst the empty confidence in all ceremonies, by which the Jews were then hindered from admitting the doctrine of true repentance. For why would those be anxious about this who thought they had sufficiently discharged every duty of piety, if they spent the Sabbath in idle leisure and had incidentally been present at the sacred rites? He therefore teaches that the exercises of true piety are quite different. And since the Sabbath, among all the external things, was the holiest, the most necessary, and finally the one commanded by God with the greatest strictness, should not all the other rites be directed to the same end, lest some, occupied with these, neglect those more excellent and more necessary things? Here it is right to remember that the same doctrine also applies to us: that we should not attribute so much to external rites, as if true religion or our salvation consisted in their observance. Let us therefore use them in accordance with the Lord's command, so that they may be helps to us in the exercises of true piety, but let us place our hope and confidence of salvation in the grace of God alone, and let us witness to this not so much by words as by constant repentance and by the earnest pursuit of true obedience. But would that this doctrine were not today as little explored by the professors of the Christian name as it was formerly by the Jews: since some trust in empty and utterly cold ceremonies, while others abuse both these and the Lord's Day for licence of the flesh, and serve the devil most of all at the very time when they ought to have been wholly consecrated to God.

units.la: Caeterum vt alia Christi facta miraculosa fere docet, quae sit nostrae salutis ratio: ita in hoc quoque eadem doctrina adumbratur. Et in hydropico quidem typum nostrae conditionis longe corruptissimae habemus euidentissimum. Solet morbus ille ex inflammatione & corruptione membrorum vitalium, pulmonis inprimis atq; hepatis & lienis obstipatione oriri. Quibus corruptis neque stomachus officio suo fungitur, ideoq; cibus non in alimentum, sed phlegma purulentum atq; saniosum conuertitur. Hinc ergo tussis praecordia infestans & concutiens nascitur: hinc humores corrupti per totum corpus defluunt, & viscaeribus inflammatis reliqua etiam membra replent atq; inflant. Sequitur mox sitis non alium potum quàm noxium appetens, & quae nec hoc quidem extinguere potest. Nam vt Poeta dixit, Quo plus sunt potae, plus sitiuntur aquae. Et cùm praesens mors hydropicus quasi ob oculos versetur, plerunq; tamen sibi salutem pollicentur, neq; patienter satis eos ferunt, qui ipsos de mortis appropinquantis hora admonent. Eadem prorsus est conditio hominis propter innatam nobis naturae vitiositatem, quam vulgo peccatum originale dicunt. Per illam enim intellectus corruptus non percipit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei: voluntas item vitiata nisi malum appetit, à bono autem abhorret: Regnant ergo carnis cupiditates, quae totum hominem rerum illicitarum amore inflammant, qui adeo non restingui poterit si ei indulgere incipias, vt potius magis accendatur. Exemplo sunt auari, libidinosi, ebriosi, vindictae cupidi, & quicunque alij praui desiderijs habenas laxant. Et quàmuis ipsius omnibus verbum Dei mortem denuntiet, & non desinunt exempla multorum quibus peccata exitio fuerunt, illi tamen sibi ipsis tuta & salua omnia promittunt, & eos oderunt qui ipsos liberius admonent. Remedium ergo in nobis nullum est, & perimus iam, nisi nobis Christus opem ferat. Ad hunc ergo contendamus, qui vt hydropico isti, quem insidiose in eius conspectum collocarant Pharisaei, salutem attulit: ita multò magis ijs fidelis medicus erit, qui ad ipsum animo contrito accedunt, & ab eo curari petunt. Hic vnus nos regenerat & viribus nouis instruit: hic à vitiorum phlegmate purgat & emundat: hic deniq; cupiditates noxias restinguit, & caelestis vita defendio accensos seruat atq; tuetur, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the other miraculous deeds of Christ largely teach what the reason of our salvation is, so this same doctrine is also foreshadowed in this one. In the dropsical man we have a most evident type of our condition, which is far more corrupt. That disease usually arises from the inflammation and corruption of the vital organs, above all from an obstruction of the lungs, liver and spleen. When these are corrupted, the stomach neither performs its function, and so the food is not turned into nourishment but into a purulent and foul phlegm. Hence a cough is born, which harasses and shakes the chest; hence corrupt humours flow through the whole body, and with the inflamed viscera they fill and swell the remaining limbs as well. Next follows a thirst that craves no drink but a harmful one, and which cannot even quench itself with this. For as the poet said: the more of water one drinks, the more one thirsts. And although death from dropsy is present, as it were before their eyes, they nevertheless commonly promise themselves recovery, and they scarcely bear patiently those who warn them of the approaching hour of death. The condition of man is exactly the same, on account of the inborn corruption of our nature, which is commonly called original sin. For through it the corrupted understanding does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; likewise the vitiated will seeks only evil and shrinks from good. Thus the desires of the flesh reign, which inflame the whole man with love of forbidden things, and this love cannot be extinguished if you begin to indulge it, but rather is kindled all the more. Examples are the covetous, the lustful, the drunkards, those who are greedy for revenge, and all others who loosen the reins to their wicked desires. And although the Word of God announces death to all of them, and the examples of many whom sins have destroyed never cease, they nevertheless promise themselves that everything is safe and sound, and they hate those who admonish them more freely. There is therefore no remedy in us, and we are already perishing unless Christ brings help to us. Let us therefore draw near to him, who brought salvation to that dropsical man, whom the Pharisees had insidiously placed in his sight; and in the same way he will be a faithful physician to those who approach him with a contrite heart and ask to be healed by him. He alone regenerates us and furnishes us with new strength; he purges and cleanses us from the phlegm of vices; he finally quenches harmful desires, and preserves and guards those kindled by the zeal of heavenly life, etc.

units.la: Restat huius historiae clausula, qua dicitur, non potuisse Pharisaeos ad Christi quaestionem aliquid respondere. Tanta veritatis vis est, vt pertinacissimis quoq; hostibus silentium imponat. Attamen licet nunc tacere cogantur, neq; in faciem illi resistere audeant, non tamen perpetò quieuerunt, sed quamprimùm occasio data est, ad nouas insidias coeuerunt, vt eum neci traderent. Nunquam ergo securitati locum dare debent pij, etiamsi interdum impiorum furor extinctus esse videatur. Nam solet nonnunquam Deus Halcyonia concedere Ecclesiae suae, ne perpetuis laboribus pij omnino frangantur: Nunquam tamen intra animos suos impij quieuerunt, sed vt mare aestuant, & occasione oblata nouos conatus proferunt. Dormiebant quidem ad Oliueti montis discipuli: sed non dormiecant interea Pontifices, Iudas & milites, qui in Christi necem conspirauerant. Debent nos ista exempla excitare, vt perpetuo vigilemus, & ad pugnam parati stemus, ne nos ex improuiso Satan obruat. De victoria autem minimè desperare nos decet, quam nobis iampridem peperit Iesus Christus, in quo & nos vincemus, si fidem in ipsum constantem seruauerimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: It remains to note the closing sentence of this history, in which it is said that the Pharisees could make no answer to Christ's question. So great is the power of truth that it silences even the most stubborn enemies. Yet although they are now compelled to keep silent and dare not resist him to his face, they did not remain quiet for good. As soon as an opportunity was given, they came together again to lay new snares, so that they might hand him over to death. Godly people must therefore never give place to complacency, even when the fury of the wicked seems at times to have been quenched. For God sometimes grants his Church a halcyon calm, so that the godly are not utterly broken by unending labours; yet the wicked never fell quiet in their hearts, but like the sea they keep seething, and whenever an occasion offers they put forth fresh attempts. The disciples indeed slept on the Mount of Olives, but the high priests, Judas and the soldiers, who had conspired against Christ's life, did not sleep in the meantime. These examples ought to rouse us, so that we keep constant watch and stand ready for battle, lest Satan overwhelm us unawares. Nor ought we at all to despair of the victory which Jesus Christ won for us long ago, and in which we too shall conquer, provided we keep our faith in him steadfast. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 143.

units.la: Dixit autem parabolam iis qui vocati fuerant, attendens quomodo primos accubitus eligerent, dicens eis: Cum vocatus fueris ab aliquo ad nuptias, ne accumbito primo loco: ne forte honoratior te sit vocatus ab eo, & is qui te & illum vocavit, veniens dicat tibi: Da huic locum, et tunc incipias cum pudore ultimum locum obtinere. Sed cum vocatus fueris, vade discubitum in ultimum locum: ut cum venerit qui te vocavit, dicat tibi: Amice, ascende superius. Tunc erit tibi gloria in conspectu eorum, qui tecum discumbunt. Nam omnis qui se extollit, deprimetur: & qui se depresserit, extolletur.
units.tr: He also told a parable to those who had been invited, noticing how they chose the first places at the table, and said to them: "When someone invites you to a wedding, do not take the first place, in case someone more honoured than you has been invited by him, and the one who invited you both comes and says to you, 'Give this man your place,' and then you begin with shame to take the last place. But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher.' Then you will have glory in the sight of those who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."

units.la: QVoniam Dei Filius ideo in mundum venit, ut nos salvos faceret, undequaque occasione captat nos admonendi de iis, quae ad salutem consequenda cognitu necessaria sunt. Argumentum huius studii evidens sunt parabolae, quibus doctrinam suam illustrat. Eas enim ex rebus passim obviis & quae in frequenti hominum usu sunt desumit, ut quocunque oculos circumferamus, aliquid occurrat, quod nobis occasionem praebeat ea meditandi, quae ad salutem nostram faciunt. Adde his quod ut passim in Synagogis, in vicis publicis, in locis desertis populum ad se confluentem docuit: ita quoties ipsum ad convivia sua aliqui invitarunt: non tam cibo sumendo intentus fuit, quam ut accumbentium animas verbo Dei ipse pasceret, & salutem conferret iis, qui eius desiderio tenebantur. Exemplum eius rei supra cap. 7. vidimus, quando a Simone quodam Pharisaeo invitatus mulierem peccatricem in gratiam recepit, & inde occasione sumpta hospitem suum de vera salutis ratione admonuit. Huic recte adnumerauieris primam huius capitis partem, qua narratur, quid fecerit, cum alius quidam inter Pharisaeos primarius ipsum ad mensam suam vocavisset. Primo enim hominem ex aqua intercute letaliter laborantem curavit, & eo facto partim superstitiosum de Sabbati & aliarum ceremoniarum observatione errorem confutavit, quo tunc maior Iudaeorum pars impediebatur, quo minus de spirituali cultu & vera poenitentia solliciti essent: partim se medicum esse ostendit, qui solus vitiis nostris omnibus mederi posset, & propterea ad ipsum debere confugere omnes, qui servari volunt. At non contentus hoc miraculo se illis patefecisse, qui ipsum hostiliter & insidiose observabant, nunc iisdem beneficium confert, & eo vitio eos liberare studet, ex quo veritatis odium & saniorum doctrinae contemptus aliaque infinita enascebantur. Erat illud ambitio & inanis gloriae studium, quod hodie etiam multis obstat, quo minus credant, & relictis superstitionibus Deum in spiritu & veritate colant. Est autem exemplum hoc Christi probe observandum. Ex eo enim bonitas illius perspicitur, cuius cognitio afflictis conscientiis dulcissimam consolationem affert: Adhac doctrinam eius confirmat, qua hostes quoque diligere & de ipsis bene mereri iubemur.
units.tr: Since the Son of God came into the world so that he might save us, he seizes every opportunity to remind us of the things that must be known in order to attain salvation. Evidence of this purpose is found in the parables with which he illustrates his teaching. For he draws them from things that lie everywhere to hand and are in common human use, so that wherever we turn our eyes something presents itself that gives us occasion to meditate on the things that serve our salvation. Add to this that, just as he taught the people who flocked to him everywhere, in the synagogues, in the public streets and in deserted places, so whenever certain men invited him to their banquets, he was less intent on taking food than on feeding the souls of those who reclined with him by the Word of God, and on bringing salvation to those who were held by longing for him. We saw an example of this above, in chapter 7, when he was invited by a certain Pharisee, Simon, and received a sinful woman into favour, and then, taking occasion from this, admonished his host about the true way of salvation. To this you may fittingly add the first part of this chapter, which tells what he did when another man, a leading figure among the Pharisees, had invited him to his table. For first he healed a man who was mortally sick with dropsy, and by that deed he refuted in part the superstitious error about keeping the Sabbath and other ceremonies, which at that time hindered most of the Jews from being concerned about spiritual worship and true repentance. In part he showed himself to be the physician who alone can heal all our vices, and for that reason everyone who wishes to be saved must flee to him. But not content to have revealed himself by this miracle to those who watched him with hostility and treachery, he now confers a benefit on the same men and strives to free them from that vice out of which hatred of the truth, contempt for sounder teaching and countless other evils were born. That vice was ambition and the pursuit of empty glory, which even today hinders many from believing and from worshipping God in spirit and truth, abandoning superstitions. This example of Christ is to be carefully observed. For from it his goodness is seen, and the knowledge of that goodness brings the sweetest comfort to troubled consciences. Moreover, it confirms his teaching, by which we are commanded to love even our enemies and to do good to them.

units.la: Caeterum ut praesentis admonitionis status recte intelligatur, & ex ea ad nos fructus uberior redeat, ante omnia Pharisaeorum ambitio diligentius erit inspicienda. Hic enim una solummodo species notatur, quod nimirum in conviviis primos accubitus captarint, id quod cum morum quoque civilitate pugnabat. Et quamvis ex eo Dominus occasionem ipsos admonendi arripuerit, certum tamen est, eum longius prospexisse: nimirum, ut omnis huius mali fontem obturaret, eam videlicet animi superbiam, qua adversus ipsum Deum efferebantur. Nam certum est, eos propriam iustitiam constituisse, ut qui propter suorum operum merita atque dignitatem ad Dei tribunal consistere possent. Quod ut facilius quibusque persuaderent, externa sanctimoniae specie mirifice se venditabant, cum fimbrias lege Dei inscriptas dilatarent, de religione & vitae innocentia crebro disserrerent, in sacrificiis liberales essent, decimas minutissimarum quoque rerum persoluerent, morum austeritate singulari uterentur, adhaec ieiuniis & precibus frequentius vacarent, eleemosynas denique in publico distribuerent. Quae omnia illos, ut hominum iudicio probarentur & pro sanctis haberentur, fecisse Christus alibi testatur: imo non tam ab omnibus probari, quam supra omnes efferri & cunctis dominari cupiebant. Quomodo enim aliquos hominum ipsis superiores ferre poterant ij, quos in Dei conspectu superbire non pudebat? Itaque in moribus quoque & totius vitae consuetudine ambitiosi illi spiritus sese exerebant, ut in Synagogis in sublimiori loco considere vellent, & in conuiuijs primi accumberent, deniq; in omnibus quae agenda erant primatu ambirent. Et quod ambitiosis omnibus solet accidere, apud ipsos etiam locum habuit. Nam etsi eandem sectam omnes tenerent, & idem omnes vitae institutum sequerentur, ambitione tamen inter seipsos commissi sunt, & quia singuli prae aliis omnibus eminere cupiebant, non potuerunt non inter ipsos nouae indies concertationes exoriri. Et tale quid illos in hac principij sui domo designauisse, Lucas non obscure docet, quando Christum animaduertisse scribit, qua ambitione ad primos accubitus contenderent, neq; expectarent vt pro conuiuatoris arbitrio collocarentur. Et hi fuerunt sancti illi & rigidissimi omnium censores, qui Christi paulo ante ex insidijs obruere conati fuerant, si vel minimo opere Sab bati religionem violaret, cum ipsi tam corpus quam animum ambitione fatigarent, qua nihil laboriosius, nihil inquietius excogitari potest.
units.tr: But so that the state of this present admonition may be rightly understood, and so that a richer fruit may come back to us from it, first of all the ambition of the Pharisees must be examined more closely. For here only one form of it is noted, namely that at banquets they sought the first places, which was also at odds with good manners. And although the Lord took occasion from this to admonish them, it is certain that he looked further ahead: namely, that he might close the source of all this evil, which is that pride of mind by which they were puffed up against God himself. For it is certain that they set up their own righteousness, as if on account of the merits and worth of their works they could stand before the tribunal of God. To persuade people of this more easily, they paraded themselves wonderfully in an outward show of holiness: they enlarged the fringes inscribed with God's law, talked often about religion and innocence of life, were generous in sacrifices, paid tithes even of the smallest things, practised a singular austerity of manners, devoted themselves more frequently to fasting and prayers, and finally distributed alms in public. Christ elsewhere bears witness that they did all these things so that they would be approved by human judgement and regarded as holy. Indeed they wanted not so much to be approved by all as to be exalted above all and to rule over everyone. For how could those men bear to have anyone above them, who were not ashamed to be proud in the sight of God? So in their conduct and in the whole habit of their lives those ambitious spirits put themselves forward: they wanted to sit in a higher place in the synagogues, to recline first at banquets, and finally to seek the first rank in all the things that had to be done. And what usually happens to all the ambitious also happened among them. For although all held the same sect and followed the same way of life, they were nevertheless set against one another by ambition, and since each wished to stand out above all the others, new contests were bound to arise among them day by day. Luke clearly teaches that they showed something of this sort already in the house of their beginnings, when he writes that Christ noticed with what ambition they struggled for the first places, and did not wait to be placed according to the host's judgement. And these were those holy and most rigid censors of all, who had recently tried to trap Christ, if he violated the observance of the Sabbath even in the smallest work, while they themselves wore out both body and mind with ambition, than which nothing more troublesome and restless can be devised.

units.la: Recte ergo ille eos arguit, & quia idem omnium morbus erat aut vitium, omnes quoque simul aggrediutur, & quid fieri ab ipsis debeat monet. Propositio seu summa aut status admonitionis est, Vnumquenque humilitati & modestiae potius studere debere, quam vt priuata temeritate supra alios efferri cupiat. Id probat argumento, quo nullam aliud ambitiosis deprimendis commodius & efficacius haberi potest. Nam omnis (inquit) qui se extollit, deprimetur: & qui se depresserit, extolletur. Quasi diceret: Cum nihil gloria antiquius habeatis, & supra omnes velitis eminere, etiam atque etiam videndum vobis erit, ne per eam viam ingrediamini, quae ad praecipitium infamiae & ignominiae ducit: sed illi insistatis, quae homines vere extollit & gloriosos reddit. Ea autem est modestiae & humilitatis studium. Ita enim inter homines est comparatum, vt quo quis modestior est, & quo magis sese ad quaeuis officia omnibus praestanda demittit, eo magis ab omnibus diligatur & maiori fit in pretio: exosi autem sint & contemnantur superbi & confidentes, qui quasi soli honore digni sint, omnibus praeferri volunt. Id vero similitudine siue exemplo ex re praesenti, conuiuiorum scilicet consuetudine, desumpto illustrat. In his enim frequenter fieri solet, vt qui propria arrogantia primum locum occupant, alio hospite honoratiore superueniente, ei locum dare iubeantur, & non sine pudore atque ignominia infra eos etiam collocentur, qui ipsis multo inferiores sunt: rursus, qui sua sponte ad extremum mensae angulum accumbunt, ij fere a conuiuatore altius ascendere, & locum honoratiorem occupare iubentur, id quod ipsis vere gloriosum est. Hic omnium eorum sensus est, quae hic a Christo dicuntur. Non debent tamen ea sic accipi, quasi sub humilitatis praetextu gloriam inter homines vanari, & ideo nos demittere debeamus, vt supra alios extollamur. Eiusmodi enim humiliatio a Pharisaica ambitione nihil differt, cui per omnia similis est; qua Monachi hodie sese venditant, dum hominis totius mortificationem, voluntariam pauperatatem, contemptum huius seculi, obedientiam & submissionem aut humilitatem extremam profitentur, ijs autem artibus in aulas Regum obrepunt, primum inter illorum consultores locum occupant, & tandem ad Episcopatus & Pontificatum vsq; inexplebili gloriae cupiditate ascendunt. Atqui nihil huius hic Dominus iubet, sed (vt initio monuimus) occasionem modo ex conuiuiorum consuetudine sumit docendi, quales nos in ipsius Dei conspectu gerere debeamus, vt nimirum vere humiliati ab illius gratia toti pendeamus, qui nobis ad veram & immortalem gloriam gradus futurus sit. Eorum ergo commemoratione, quae inter homines fieri solent, ambitiosos terret, vt eo magis Dei iudicium timeant, qui superbiam omnem detestatur, & cui facile est, vnumquenque ex suprema dignitatis gradu deturbare. Quia vero locus hic totus planus est, & iam satis constat, quo nam Christus haec dicendo respexerit, res ipsae potius considerandae sunt, de quibus hic agitur.
units.tr: Rightly, then, he rebukes them, and since the same disease or vice was in all of them, he attacks them all together and tells them what they ought to do. The proposition, or the sum and point of the admonition, is this: everyone ought to strive for humility and modesty rather than desire, by private rashness, to be lifted above others. He proves it by an argument, and no more suitable or effective one can be had for humbling the ambitious: "For everyone," he says, "who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." It is as if he said: since you hold nothing more precious than glory, and wish to stand out above all, you must look again and again to make sure that you do not walk along that road which leads to the precipice of infamy and disgrace, but that you keep to the one which truly lifts men up and makes them glorious. That road is the pursuit of modesty and humility. For it is so ordered among men that the more modest a man is, and the more he lowers himself to perform any duties for everyone, the more he is loved by all and the higher he is valued. Proud and arrogant men, who want to be placed above everyone as if they alone deserved honour, are hated and despised. He illustrates this by a likeness or example taken from the present matter, namely the custom of banquets. For in them it often happens that those who have taken the first place by their own arrogance, when a more honoured guest arrives, are ordered to give him their place, and with shame and disgrace are seated below even those who are far inferior to them. Conversely, those who of their own accord recline at the far corner of the table are commonly bidden by the host to come up higher and take a more honoured place, which is truly glorious for them. This is the whole sense of what Christ says here. Yet these words must not be taken as if, under the pretext of humility, one should seek glory among men, and therefore lower oneself in order to be exalted above others. For such humbling differs in no way from Pharisaic ambition; it is altogether like it, and it is the very thing by which monks today put themselves on display, while they profess the mortification of the whole man, voluntary poverty, contempt for this world, obedience, and utmost submission or humility; yet by these arts they creep into the courts of kings, take the first place among their advisers, and at last climb to bishoprics and the papacy, with an insatiable desire for glory. And yet the Lord here commands nothing of this kind, but (as we noted at the beginning) he only takes occasion from the custom of banquets to teach what sort of people we ought to be in the sight of God himself: namely, that truly humbled by his grace, we should depend wholly on him, who will be for us the step to true and immortal glory. Therefore, by recalling what usually happens among men, he frightens the ambitious, so that they may fear the judgement of God all the more, for God detests all pride, and it is easy for him to cast down everyone from the highest rank of dignity. But since this whole passage is plain, and it is already sufficiently clear for whom Christ intended these words, the matters themselves that are discussed here should be considered more closely.

units.la: Videamus ergo ante omnia, quae nam superbia illa sit, quam Christus damnat, quae rursus vera humilitas siue modestia, quam tantopere commendat. Nam etsi omnes fateantur, superbiam scelus aut vitium esse detestabile, pauci tamen de eo recte iudicant, vt illud tam in semetipsis quam alijs possint agnoscere. Superbire autem Latinus voce ex praepositione super & verbo eo, is, ire composita dicuntur, qui supra alios vadere aut emergere cupiunt, aut seipsos vana persuasione extollunt, quasi alijs sint praestantiores. Hinc superbia deriuatur, quae vox elationem animi significat, qua homo impulsus vel inflatus sibi arrogat quod non habet, aut quae habet Dei dona, ijs cum aliorum
units.tr: Let us therefore first consider what that pride is which Christ condemns, and again what true humility or modesty is, which he commends so highly. For although everyone admits that pride is a detestable sin or vice, few judge it rightly enough to recognise it both in themselves and in others. The Latin verb superbire is compounded from the preposition super and the verb eo, is, ire, and those are said to be proud who desire to go above others or to rise over them, or who puff themselves up with empty conceit, as if they were better than others. From this comes superbia, a word that signifies an elation of the mind, by which a man, driven or puffed up, claims for himself what he does not have, or misuses the gifts of God with contempt for others.

units.la: {y} Christus humilitatem suadet. aliorum contemptu abutitur. Patet autē vitium hoc latißimè, vt ex ijs apparet, quæ nuper de Pha- risæis diximus. Et omnium teterrima nocentißimaq; superbia est, qua aduersus Deum homo extol- litur. Faciunt hoc, qui iustitiam propriā iactant, & iuorum operum meritis se seruari posse conten- dunt: qui item sanctimoniā & innocentiam perfectam sibi tribuunt. Quid enim isti faciunt aliud, quàm quòd sibi arrogant quæ solius Dei sunt, qui vt solus ex seipso iustus sanctus & æternus est: ita solus etiam quos vult iustificat, sanctificat, & vita æterna donat? Proximi istos sequuntur, qui etsi hoc fateantur, & Dei donum esse dicant quicquid habent, gratuitam tamen illius liberalitatem non agnoscunt, sed dignitate quandam sibi fingunt, quam in ipsis Deus resplexerit, vt eos donis præstan- tioribus exornaret. Quæ persuasio vt vanißima est, ita temerarios & audaces reddit, vt nō conten- ti sua sorte, ad altiorē gradum subinde aspirent, & (quod olim primis parentibus Satan persuasit) Deo similes esse cupiant. Atqui omnes isti cum Deo bellum suscipiunt, cùm & gratiam atq; miseri- cordiam eius aspernentur, & contra ipsius voluntatem plus sibi ipsis tribuant, quàm ab eo accepe- rint, adhæc imperium quoq; eius contemnant. Huic autem superbiæ omnes superstitiones debemus cum toto cultu hypocritico, quo homines confisi, se gratia aliqua singulari nequaquam opus habere arbitrantur. Et quod irrefragabile est superbiæ plus quàm diabolicæ argumentum, omnes isti ver- bum Dei non modò contemnunt atq; scurriliter eludunt, verumetiam oderunt & hostiliter infestan- tur, quando per illud se grauius vrgeri & eius luce arrogantiā suam argui, adeoq; inanem illam sal- sæ sanctitatis atq; dignitatis laruam sibi detrahi sentiunt. Hinc ergo omnibus seculis Prophetarum persecutiones & indignißimæ cædes exortæ sunt: & vt Christum illo potißimùm nomine Pharisæi extinctum voluerunt: ita hodie etiam quæcunq; aduersus fidos Christi cultores geruntur bella, tam ciuilia quàm extera, arrogantibus illis & superbis hypocritis debemus, qui veteres illos imitantur. Et hæc quidē superbia est, quam pleriq; spiritualem dixerunt, quia in spiritualibus Dei donis potis- mùm sese exerit, & falsa spiritus humiliati cordisq; contriti specie palliatur. Est deinde alia cras- sior, quam carnalem possumus dicere, & qua ij quoq; turgent, qui de spiritualibus Dei donis nihil so- liciti, cultum quoq; Dei omnem aperte contemnunt, & toti circa res huius seculi occupantur. Et ista ferè per totam vitæ consuetudinem extenditur, atq; causa est, vt externis Dei donis, vel etiam ani- mi dotibus, quibus prophanos quoq; homines & à fidei professione alienißimos interdum Deus dig- natur, confisi, nihil non sibi arrogent, vt supra omnes alios eminere velint. Hanc vulgo Ambitio- nem dicunt, & immoderatam gloriæ atq; honorum siue dignitatum cupiditatem esse definiunt. Qui verò hac laborant, ij opum abundantia insolentius efferuntur, eandē vestitu splendidiori & minus stato, victu sumptuoso, ædificijs magnificis & sublimioribus, seruorum atque clientum turba, de- niq; cultu, incessu, gestibus & verbis, à communi loquendi consuetudine alienis & altum quiddam spirantibus testantur. Idem in foro, Senatu, templis, theatris, conuiuijs primo loco sedere, in pompis & processionibus supra alios conspici, omnium oculos in se conuerti, omniumq; digitus monstrari, & (vt semel dicam) se solos videri volunt, à quibus publica salus dependeat, qui soli sapiant, soli rebus consulere possint, & proinde soli digni sint, qui ab omnibus colantur, & in alios omnes imperium atq; dominium habeant.
units.tr: Christ recommends humility. Pride is spread very widely, as appears from what we said recently about the Pharisees. And the most hateful and most harmful pride is that by which a man exalts himself against God. Those do this who boast of their own righteousness and contend that they can be saved by the merits of their good works; likewise those who attribute to themselves holiness and perfect innocence. For what else do such people do than claim for themselves what belongs to God alone, who alone is righteous, holy and eternal of himself, and who alone also justifies, sanctifies and gives eternal life to whom he wills? Next to these follow those who, although they confess this and say that whatever they have is God's gift, nevertheless do not acknowledge his free generosity, but imagine for themselves some dignity, which God has seen in them, so that he adorned them with more excellent gifts. This persuasion, as it is most empty, so makes men rash and bold, that, not content with their lot, they keep aspiring to a higher rank and desire (as Satan once persuaded our first parents) to be like God. Yet all such people wage war against God, since they both despise his grace and mercy and, contrary to his will, attribute more to themselves than they have received from him, and moreover scorn his authority. To this pride we owe all superstitions, together with the whole hypocritical worship, in which men, trusting in themselves, think they have no need of any singular grace. And, what is an unanswerable proof of pride more than diabolical, all such people not only despise the Word of God and mock it scornfully, but also hate it and attack it with hostility, since they feel that through it they are pressed more heavily, their arrogance is exposed by its light, and that empty mask of false holiness and dignity is torn from them. Hence from all ages have arisen the persecutions of the Prophets and most unworthy murders; and just as the Pharisees wished Christ to be destroyed especially under that name, so today we owe all the wars waged against the faithful worshippers of Christ, both civil and foreign, to those arrogant and proud hypocrites who imitate those ancient ones. And this is the pride which many have called spiritual, because it chiefly shows itself in the spiritual gifts of God and is cloaked under the false appearance of a humbled spirit and a contrite heart. There is then another, grosser kind, which we may call carnal, and by which those also swell who, not at all concerned about the spiritual gifts of God, openly despise all worship of God and are wholly occupied with the things of this world. This extends over almost the whole course of life, and it is the cause that, trusting in external gifts of God, or even in endowments of mind, which God sometimes deigns to bestow upon profane men too, utterly alien to the profession of faith, they claim everything for themselves and wish to stand out above all others. This they commonly call ambition, and define it as an immoderate desire for glory and honours or dignities. Those who suffer from this, moreover, being puffed up more insolently by an abundance of wealth, bear witness to it by splendid and unusual clothing, sumptuous food, magnificent and lofty buildings, a crowd of servants and dependants, and finally by a bearing, gait, gestures and words alien to ordinary speech and breathing something lofty. Likewise they wish to sit in the first place in the forum, the senate, the temples, the theatres and the banquets; to be seen above others in processions and parades; to draw all eyes to themselves and have all fingers pointed at them; and (to say it once for all) they wish to be regarded as the only ones on whom public welfare depends, who alone have wisdom, alone can take thought for affairs, and therefore alone deserve to be honoured by all and to hold rule and dominion over all others.

units.la: Et de hīs quidem omnibus hæc Christi admonitio intelligi debet, & omnes superbiæ species ne-cessariò fugiendæ sunt ijs, qui nomen illius atque fidem in illum profitentur, vt se nihil perinde dece- re cogitent, quàm vt humilitati & modestiæ studeant. Quæ tamen ista sit, & in quibus rebus consi- stat, ex ijs facilè patet, quæ de superbia hucusque diximus. Vt enim hæc animi eleuatio est, ita hu- militatis nomine illius depressio significatur, qua homo sese demittit, vt de suo potius erga Deum & homines officio, quàm de gradu dignitatis sublimiori cogitet. Non ergo in vestitu sordidiori, non in incessu & gestu ad simulandam animi deiectionem, neque in vlla specie externa consistit, sed in eo, vt homo seipsum abneget atque exinaniat, neq; carnis ad altiora semper aspirantis affectibus ob- temperet. Verè ergo humiliantur, qui de semetipsis modestè sentiunt, coram Deo se peccatores esse agnoscunt, miseriam suam fatentur, & abiecta omni propriæ dignitatis fiducia ad illius misericor- diam confugiunt. Item, qui donis ab illo acceptis non efferuntur vt proprijs, sed gratuitæ liberalita- tis ea esse sciunt, & proinde eorum consideratione excitati, ijsdem rectè vti student. Huius modestiæ & humiliationis effectus sunt, quòd sua sorte contenti, absq; Dei vocatione ad nullos honores aut dignitates sublimiores aspirant, quòd verbo Dei delectantur, & per hoc suo officio edoceri atq; admoneri cupiūr: quòd cum omnibus pacificè viuunt, nemini sese præferunt, honore omnes præueniūt, vt qui alios se præstantiores esse putent: quòd nulla opum fiducia elati, nulla ciuilium honorum aut munerum dignitate ebrij, nullo rerum huius seculi splendore decepti, in omnibus suis dictis & factis modestiam exerunt, & ad omnia dilectionis Christianæ officia quibusuis præstanda nunquam non prompti atq; parati sint: & vt ipsi omnibus consultum esse cupiunt, ita aliorum quoq; sententias patienter audiunt, atq; meliora dicentibus libenter obtemperant.
units.tr: Christ's admonition must be understood to concern all these things, and all kinds of pride must necessarily be shunned by those who profess his name and faith in him, so that they think nothing more becoming to them than to devote themselves to humility and modesty. What this humility is, and in what it consists, is easily clear from what we have said so far about pride. For just as pride is an elevation of the mind, so humility, by its name, signifies a lowering by which a man abases himself, so that he thinks rather of his duty towards God and men than of a higher rank of dignity. It therefore does not consist in shabbier clothing, in gait and gesture feigned to show a dejected mind, nor in any outward appearance, but in this: that a man denies and empties himself and does not yield to the desires of the flesh, which always aspire to higher things. Truly they humble themselves who think modestly of themselves, acknowledge that they are sinners before God, confess their misery, and, having cast off all confidence in their own dignity, flee to his mercy. Likewise, those who are not puffed up by the gifts they have received from him as if they were their own, but know them to be of his free generosity, and therefore, stirred by that consideration, strive to use them rightly. The effects of this modesty and humility are that, content with their lot, they aspire to no honours or higher dignities without God's calling; that they delight in the Word of God and desire to be taught and admonished by its office; that they live peacefully with all, prefer themselves to no one, and surpass all in honouring them, as those who think others better than themselves; that, not elated by confidence in wealth, not intoxicated by the dignity of civil honours or offices, not deceived by any splendour of the things of this world, they show modesty in all their words and deeds, and are always ready and prepared to perform the duties of Christian love to anyone whatever; and that, as they desire that everyone be cared for, so they also patiently hear the opinions of others and willingly obey those who speak better.

units.la: Hæc ergo sunt, de quibus nos Christus in præsenti admonet, quæ sic à nobis considerari debent, vt singuli ea ad se pertinere certò sibi persuadeant. Nam etsi vnam modò causam sine rationem hic afferat, propter quam superbia vitari, modestia autem sine humilitas coli debeat, sunt tamen infinitæ aliæ, quæ nos cogunt, si quidem salus nostra nobis cordi est. Etenim exigit hoc primum ipsa nominis Christiani professio. Quàm enim turpe fuerit, eos insolentius efferri, & vel contra Deum vel homines superbire, qui Christo gloriantur, quo nemo vnquam modestior, humilior atque abiectior in terris vitus est? Intolerabilis est seruorum superbia, qui supra heros eminere volunt: discipuloru item, qui magistros suos superare cupiunt. At quanto intolerabilius peccant, qui supra æternum Dei filium, quem suum Dominum & magistrum esse fatentur, sese extollunt, & neque admonitionibus, neque exemplo illius adduci possunt, vt de semetipsis modestius sentiant? Semper ergo in auribus nostris sonent illius verba, dicentis: Tollite iugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quòd mitis sum & humilis corde. Deinde ipsa fides nos idem docet. Huius enim proprium est, in solam Dei misericordiam propter Christi meritum respicere, & in hoc vno omnem salutis fiduciam collocare. Quomodo autem id faciet, quem propria dignitatis fiducia dementat? Adhæc fides vinculum illud est Christianæ communionis, quæ nos omnes eiusdem Patrus Dei filios, & eiusdem corporis Christi, Ecclesiæ nimirum membra facit. Quis ergo fide præditum dicet eum, qui supra eos insolentius assurgere nititur, quos pro fratribus & commembris suis (si nouo vocabulo vti licet) agnoscere debebat? Adde hu, quòd superbiam peccati initium esse Scriptura docent, & quòd eadem plurimorum & atrocium vitiorum fæcundissima mater est. Nam vt superba diuini honoris affectatione primi parentes peccauerunt: ita Cain eorundè primogenitus non aliam ob causam Abelum fratrem immani parricidio sustulit, quàm quòd hunc sibi à Deo præferri dolebat. Et hodie hæc eadem omnis inuidiæ, odij, simultatum, homicidiorum, bellorum denique præcipua causa est, quòd alij alios contemnunt, & se solos dignos iudicant, qui donis Dei & honoribus huius seculi excellant. Quid verò in morbis & afflictionibus diuinitus immissis impatientes & murmuratores facit? quid vindictæ cupiditate iniurijs affectos accendit? nisi quòd de semetipsis arrogantius sentiunt, & indignos se arbitrantur, in quos vel Deus animaduertere, vel quisquam hominum aliquid audere debeat? Taceo nunc donorum Dei turpissimum abusum, qui ex superbia enascens per omnem vitam atq; omnes hominis actiones sese diffundit. E contra autem humilitas siue modestia mutuæ charitatis fidelissima nutrix est, qua Paulus Legem totam impleri, & proinde eandem virtutum omnium parentem esse docet. Ideo Christus, cùm nouum & eximium illud de dilectione fraterna siue mutua præceptum discipulis commendare vellet, prius eò vsque demisit se vt eorum omnium pedes ablueret, sicque suo exemplo doceret, neminem posthac alicuius officij pudere debere, quo proximum iuuari posse videt. Et exempla sunt quotidiana, quæ docent ad placandos simul & retinendos in amore homines, nihil efficacius esse officiosa modestia & humilitate: cùm ex aduerso inter ambitiosos & superbos neque Charitas Christiana radices agere, neque concordia diu subsistere aut durare possit. Ex quibus hoc quoque colligitur, humilitati omnes eos studere debere, qui vel Rempublicam vel Ecclesiam seruatam volunt. Constat enim vtriusque salutem, quoad hominum studia, potissimum ex animorum consensione in ijs quæ recta & bona sunt, pendere. Atqui neque animus verè consentient vnquam, neque consilia sua syncerè in commune conferent, imò neque consilijs sanis acquiescent, quotquot supra omnes alios eminere conantur. Hinc ergo acerbæ contentiones in Senatu interque verbi administros, hinc simultates, odia, insidiæ, iniuriæ omnis generis, & tandem aperta dissidia nascuntur, quæ quasi ex capite in populi totum
units.tr: These, then, are the things Christ admonishes us about here. We should consider them so that each of us is firmly persuaded that they pertain to himself. For although he gives only one cause or reason here for avoiding pride and cultivating modesty, or rather humility, there are countless others that compel us, if our salvation is truly dear to us. First, the very profession of the Christian name requires this. How shameful it is for those who glory in Christ, than whom no one on earth was ever more modest, humble and lowly, to carry themselves insolently and to be proud either against God or against men! The pride of slaves who want to rise above their masters is intolerable, and so is that of disciples who want to surpass their teachers. But how much more intolerably do those sin who exalt themselves above the eternal Son of God, whom they confess as their Lord and Master, and who cannot be brought, either by his admonitions or by his example, to think more modestly of themselves! Let his words always sound in our ears: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." Then faith itself teaches the same thing. For it is faith's own task to look only to God's mercy, on account of Christ's merit, and to place all its confidence of salvation in that alone. But how can someone do this when confidence in his own dignity has driven him out of his mind? Moreover, faith is that bond of Christian fellowship which makes us all sons of the same Father God and members of the same body of Christ, namely the Church. Who, then, would call a man endowed with faith one who strives to rise more insolently above those whom he ought to acknowledge as brothers and fellow members (if I may use a new word)? Add that Scripture teaches that pride is the beginning of sin, and that it is the most fruitful mother of very many and atrocious vices. For just as our first parents sinned through proud desire for divine honour, so Cain, their firstborn, killed his brother Abel in a monstrous murder for no other reason than that he grieved that God preferred Abel to himself. And today this same thing is the chief cause of all envy, hatred, enmities, murders, and finally of wars: that some despise others and judge themselves alone worthy to excel in the gifts of God and the honours of this age. But what makes people impatient and murmuring in the diseases and afflictions sent by God? What inflames those who have been wronged with the desire for vengeance, except that they think too highly of themselves and consider themselves unworthy that God should punish them, or that anyone should dare to act against them? I say nothing now of the most shameful abuse of God's gifts, which springs from pride and spreads through the whole of life and every human action. On the other hand, humility or modesty is the most faithful nurse of mutual charity, by which Paul teaches that the whole Law is fulfilled and that it is therefore the parent of all virtues. Hence Christ, wishing to commend to his disciples that new and outstanding precept of brotherly or mutual love, first humbled himself so far as to wash the feet of all of them, and so taught by his example that from then on no one should be ashamed of any service by which he sees he can help his neighbour. There are daily examples which show that nothing is more effective for winning over and keeping men in love than dutiful modesty and humility. On the contrary, among the ambitious and proud, Christian charity cannot take root, nor can concord long endure. From these things this too is concluded: all those who want either the commonwealth or the Church preserved ought to strive after humility. For it is established that the safety of both, so far as human efforts go, depends chiefly on agreement of minds in what is right and good. But minds will never truly agree, nor will they sincerely contribute their counsels to the common good; indeed, they will not even yield to sound counsel, however many strive to rise above all others. Hence come bitter contentions in the Senate and among the ministers of the Word; hence come enmities, hatreds, plots, injuries of every kind, and finally open dissensions, which, spreading as it were from the head into the whole body of the people, produce factions and partisan zeal. By these, commonwealths and most powerful kingdoms have been scattered and utterly overthrown, as the histories of all nations bear witness.

units.la: Matth. 11. / Eccle. 10. / Rom. 13. totius corpus diffusa factiones & partium studia pariunt, quibus respublicas & regna potentissima dissipata & prorsus euersa esse, omnium gentium historiae testantur. Romanam certe Rempublicam atque libertatem duorum in illa excellentium ducum Iulij Caesaris & Pompeij, ambitio perdidit, cum hic neminem se superiorem, ille vero ne parem quidem ferre vellet. Quantum autem Ecclesiae totiusque rei Christianae nocuerit olim Episcoporum superbia, norunt omnes, qui historiam Ecclesiasticam vel obiter percurrerunt. Illa certe & haereses peperit, quibus Ecclesiae vnitas sciissa est, & persequutoribus tyrannis saeuiendi occasionem dedit, tandem vero partu plus satis infelici atque inauspicatissimo Antichristum enixa est, qui in templo Dei throno suo collocato se ipsum supra omne numen extulit, & euerso veri Dei cultu superstitionum absurdissimarum chaos inuexit, quo tam animae quam corpora hominum grauissime affliguntur. Et vtinam hodie nulla exempla extarent eorum, qui superbia & ambitione extimulati sordes Papisticas tuentur, ne quid ipsorum existimationi decedat, si relictis erroribus in aliorum sententiam eant: qui veritatem purius tradunt.
units.tr: Matth. 11. / Eccle. 10. / Rom. 13. Certainly the ambition of the two outstanding leaders of that time, Julius Caesar and Pompey, destroyed the Roman commonwealth and its liberty, since the one would tolerate no one above himself, and the other would not tolerate even an equal. How much the pride of bishops once harmed the Church and the whole Christian cause, all know who have run through ecclesiastical history even in passing. It indeed gave birth to heresies, by which the unity of the Church was torn apart, and it gave persecuting tyrants an occasion to rage. Finally, bringing forth an offspring that was far too unhappy and ill-omened, it gave birth to Antichrist, who, setting up his throne in the temple of God, exalted himself above every divinity. Overthrowing the true worship of God, he introduced a chaos of most absurd superstitions, by which both the souls and the bodies of men are most grievously afflicted. And would that today there were no examples of those who, goaded by pride and ambition, defend the Papistical filth, lest anything be lost of their reputation if, abandoning their errors, they went over to the opinion of those who deliver the truth more purely.

units.la: Sunt haec rationes grauissimae, quibus aliae etiam adijci poterant, quae Christianis hominibus nihil decentius, vtilius, magisque necessarium esse probant, quam humilitatis & modestiae studium: sed ne prolixiores simus, vnam illam paulo propius excutiamus, qua in praesenti super-bos Christus territat, dicens: Nam omnis qui se extollit, deprimetur, & qui se depresserit aut humiliauerit, exaltabitur. Est haec generalis sententia, quae ex Dei natura atque ingenio desumpta est. Solet enim vs humiles & abiectos respicere, fastidire autem superbos & arrogantes, sicuti multis Scripturae sacrae testimonijs docemur. In Psalmis certe multa huius generis occurrunt. Domi-nus (inquit Dauid) sublimis existit, & quod humile est intuetur: & quod altum est, eminus vel a longe agnoscit. Item: Dominus euehit mansuetos, deprimit impios vsque ad terram. At quis magis impius, quam qui se aduersus illum extollit? Et rursus: Quis similis est Domino Deo nostro, qui in alto praesidet, seque demittit, vt inspiciat quaecunque sunt in caelo & in terra? Qui erigit tenuem ex pulvere, & pauperem e stercore euehit: Vt collocet eum cum principibus populi sui, &c. Consentit his Solomon dicens. Praeiuit ruinam exaltatio, & commutationem praecedit animi elatio. Melius est animo deiici cum humilibus, quam praedam partiri cum elatis. Quibus adde quod Maria Virgo canit: Detraxit potentes de sedibus, & exaltauit humiles. Quae omnia Petrus Apostolus non ignorans scribebat: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus vero dat gratiam. Sunt haec infinitis exemplis confirmata. Annon primi parentes cum diuinitatem ambitiose affectarent, in sordes & miserias extremas deturbati sunt? Annon Cain fratre sue praestare volens, aeternam ignominiam sibi accersiuit, hic autem nomen gloriosum & immortale assecutus est? Quid vero de Saule & Dauide dicemus? Annon illum perdidit arrogantia, hunc autem humilitas & modestia Deo gratum & acceptum fecit? Adde his horrenda iudiciorum Dei exempla, quibus Senacheribi Assyriorum tyranni, Baltazaris Babylonij, & ante hunc Nabuchodonozoris, Herodis Agrippae, multorumque Regum fastum immanem repressit. At quid veterum commemoratione opus est, quando quotidie fiunt quae his possunt fidem facere? Imo ea est arrogantia & superborum conditio, vt si nulla calamitas illis superueniat, ipsi propria culpa sibi ignominiam atque pernitiem accersant, & se hominum abiectissimos esse testentur. Magni enim & vere excellentis animi argumentum est, virtuti operam dare, res caducas & fluxas non magni facere, vulgi stolidi iudicia contemnere, caelestia sectari & aduersa omnia constanter sufferre. At quid horum ambitiosi & arrogantes faciunt? Imo annon omnia his contraria faciunt, quando virtutis studio neglecto de sola gloria huius seculi cogitant, res fluxas & inflabiles admirantur, vulgo seruiliter se submittunt, & eorum manus prensare & fauorem ambire solent, qui neque de republica neque de priuatis rebus possunt iudicare, denique quando terrenus affixi nihil altius sapiunt, & in calamitatibus muliebri eiulatu & querelis iniquissimis animos degeneres produnt? Quis ergo eos dignos iudicet, quos homines cordati & sapientes in pretio habeant? Accedit his, quod arroganti suo aestu odia multorum sibi conciliat, & ideo fere in hoc seculo ignominia publica notantur. Taceo quod cum diaboli ingenium & mores referant, cum eodem ad inferos detrusi aeternum dolebunt, nisi ante obitum suũ vere humiliati ad Dei gratiam confugiant. Docent hac quid de nostri seculi hominibus iudices, quando immanis arrogantia passim regnat. Pontifices enim non contenti Ecclesiasticis muneris dignitate, diuinos honores sibi vendicant. Episcopi & Abbates regnum in ecclesia affectant, & calcato Dei verbo pro sua libidine omnia instituunt. Principes & qui in magistratu sunt, nihil non sibi licere putant, & subditorum non fortunas modo insolenter diripiunt, verumetiam eorundem capitibus superbè nimis insultant. Sed ne vulgus quidem hominum Dei verbo subesse vult, & paucos esse videre, qui per hoc se argui & corrigi patiantur. Hinc ergo prodeunt tot iudiciorum Dei exempla, quibus incurabilem mundi contumaciam Deus contundit, & periculum est, ne breui duriora sequantur.
units.tr: These are very weighty reasons, to which others could also be added, which prove that nothing is more fitting, more useful, or more necessary for Christians than the pursuit of humility and modesty. But lest we be too long, let us examine more closely that one reason with which Christ now terrifies the proud, saying: "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles or lowers himself will be exalted." This is a general saying, drawn from the nature and disposition of God. For he is wont to look upon the humble and lowly, but to despise the proud and arrogant, as we are taught by many testimonies of holy Scripture. The Psalms certainly contain many things of this kind. "The Lord," says David, "is on high, yet he regards what is lowly, and he knows what is lofty from afar." Again: "The Lord lifts up the meek, and casts the wicked down to the ground." And who is more wicked than the one who exalts himself against him? And again: "Who is like the Lord our God, who sits enthroned on high, yet stoops down to look upon what is in heaven and on earth? He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dunghill, to set him among the princes of his people," and so on. Solomon agrees with these, saying: "Exaltation goes before ruin, and a haughty spirit comes before a fall. It is better to be of humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud." To these add what the Virgin Mary sings: "He has put down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble." Peter the Apostle, who was not unaware of all this, wrote: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." These things are confirmed by countless examples. Did not our first parents, when they ambitiously aspired to divinity, get thrown down into the utmost filth and misery? Did not Cain, wanting to be above his brother, bring eternal disgrace upon himself, while Abel obtained a glorious and immortal name? What shall we say of Saul and David? Did not arrogance destroy the one, while humility and modesty made the other pleasing and acceptable to God? Add to these the dreadful examples of God's judgments, by which he crushed the monstrous pride of the Assyrian tyrant Sennacherib, of Belshazzar of Babylon, and before him of Nebuchadnezzar, of Herod Agrippa, and of many kings. But why do we need to recall the ancients, when every day there happen things that can give credence to these? Indeed, such is the condition of the arrogant and proud that, even if no calamity befalls them, they bring shame and ruin upon themselves by their own fault, and they bear witness that they are the most abject of men. For it is the mark of a great and truly excellent mind to devote itself to virtue, not to value fleeting and transitory things, to despise the judgments of the foolish crowd, to pursue heavenly things, and to bear all adversity steadfastly. But what do the ambitious and arrogant do of these things? Indeed, do they not do all the opposite? When they neglect the pursuit of virtue and think only of the glory of this world, they admire fleeting and empty things, submit slavishly to the crowd, and are accustomed to grasp hands and court the favour of those who can judge neither about the commonwealth nor about private affairs. Finally, when fixed on earthly things they savour nothing higher, and in calamities they reveal their degenerate spirits with womanish wailing and most unjust complaints. Who, then, would judge worthy those whom wise and sensible men hold in esteem? Add to this that by their arrogant heat they win the hatred of many, and so are for the most part branded with public disgrace in this age. I say nothing of the fact that, since they resemble the devil in nature and manners, they will grieve eternally with him when they are cast down into hell, unless before death they truly humble themselves and flee to the grace of God. These things teach us what we should think of the men of our own age, since monstrous arrogance reigns everywhere. For the popes, not content with the dignity of ecclesiastical office, claim divine honours for themselves. Bishops and abbots aspire to royal power in the Church, and, trampling the Word of God underfoot, establish everything as they please. Princes and those in magistracy think nothing is forbidden to them, and not only insolently plunder the fortunes of their subjects but also insult their heads excessively arrogantly. But not even the common crowd wants to be subject to the Word of God, and there are few to be seen who allow themselves to be reproved and corrected by it. Hence come so many examples of God's judgments, by which God crushes the incurable obstinacy of the world, and there is danger lest harsher things soon follow.

units.la: Quapropter nunquam nobis excidere debet huius loci doctrina, ut humilitati & modestiæ studeamus. Id verò etiam reluctante carnis & naturæ nostræ vitioso ingenio poterimus, si primum nosipsos, deinde res quibus plerique superbiunt, postremo Dei maiestatem propius consideremus. Nam si hominem per se, qualis suapte natura est, consideres, omnium creatorum miserrimum esse videbis. Quid huius natalibus tristius & sordidius? Quanta a primis unguiculis corpusculi humani imbecillitas? Quod animalculum, vel insectum quoque, tam parum in seipso præsidij & virium habet? Quod nam ex brutis omnibus tot morbis atque periculis est obnoxium? Sunt hæc admodum misera, at miserior multo est anima conditio, quæ peccatorum vinculis atque sarcinis grauata, nisi Dei manu subleuetur, ad cœlestia suspicere non potest. Quid ergo in nobis aliud est, quam extrema perniries? Et ut lætior interdum nobis fortuna arrideat, quid illa instabilius? quid mortis tacitè obrepentis hora incertius & velocius? Qua igitur stultitia est arrogantius de semetipso sentire? At sunt mihi (inquis) opes, honoribus publicis infinitos alios supero, est firma corporis valetudo, forma integra, applaudit vulgus, & pace atque otio abundo. Audio ô bone. Sed quid in his omnibus stabile, quid solidum, quid perpetuum est? Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Fluxa & incerta est opum possessio, honores & dignitates ex vulgi mutabilis iudicio pendent, valetudo facillime & præter expectationem decтpyitur, forma bonum fragile & sæpe turpitudinis ex trema causa est, voluptates plerunque dolores & ignominiam pariunt: denique si cum Salomone omnia inspicias, quæ sub sole sunt, exclamabis tandem: Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas. Quod si simul cogites, nos in Dei conspectu viuere, qui corda & renes scrutatur, qui index scelerum seuerus, imo ignis consumens est, certè non poteris non de teipso humilimè sentire, & toto animo trepidare, quod olim Abrahamum, Dauidem, Paulum & sanctissimos quosq; passos fuisse scimus. Horum consideratio nos excitare debet, ut superbiæ spiritum fracto & excusso eum affectum induamus, qui in Christo Iesu fuit, ut ad eius exemplum humiliati, cum eodem olim in gloriam cœlestem euehamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore the teaching of this passage must never slip from our minds: we ought to devote ourselves to humility and modesty. We shall be able to do this even though our sinful nature and flesh resist, if we first consider ourselves, then the things in which most people take pride, and last of all the majesty of God. For if you consider man by himself, as he is by his own nature, you will see that he is the most wretched of all creatures. What is more miserable and more squalid than his birth? How feeble is the human body from its very first little nails? What little creature, or even what insect, has so little help and strength in itself? Which of all the brute animals is subject to so many diseases and dangers? These things are wretched enough, but the condition of the soul is far more wretched: weighed down by the chains and burdens of sins, it cannot lift its eyes to heavenly things unless the hand of God raises it up. What, then, is there in us but utter ruin? And even if fortune sometimes smiles on us more cheerfully, what is more unstable than fortune? What is more uncertain and more swift than the hour of death, which creeps up unnoticed? By what folly, then, is it more arrogant to think highly of oneself? But you say: "I have wealth; I surpass countless others in public honours; my health is sound, my appearance unimpaired; the crowd applauds me, and I abound in peace and leisure." I hear you, my good sir. But what in all these things is stable, what is solid, what is lasting? "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the field." The possession of wealth is slippery and uncertain; honours and dignities hang on the changeable judgment of the crowd; health is most easily and unexpectedly destroyed; beauty is a fragile good and is often the greatest cause of shame; pleasures for the most part bring pain and disgrace. In short, if with Solomon you survey all that is under the sun, you will at last cry out: "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity." But if at the same time you reflect that we live in the sight of God, who searches hearts and reins, who is a strict judge of sins, indeed a consuming fire, then you certainly cannot fail to think very humbly of yourself and to tremble in your whole soul, as we know Abraham, David, Paul and all the most holy men once did. The consideration of these examples ought to rouse us, so that, with the spirit of pride broken and shaken off, we may put on that disposition which was in Christ Jesus, so that, humbled after his example, we may with him be exalted one day into heavenly glory. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 144.

units.la: Dicebat autem etiam ei qui ipsum vocauerat: Cum facis prandium aut cœnam, ne vocato amicos tuos, neq; fratres tuos, neq; cognatos tuos, neq; vicinos diuites: ne quando & ipsi te vicissim vocent, ac retribuatur tibi gratia. Sed cum facis epulũ, voca pauperes, mancos, claudos, cæcos: Et beatus eris, quia non possunt retribuere tibi: retribuetur enim tibi in resurrectione iustorum. Hæc autem cum audisset quidam ex iis, qui simul accumbebant, dixit ei: Beatus, qui comedet panem in regno Dei.
units.tr: He also said to the man who had invited him: "When you make a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, nor your brothers, nor your relatives, nor your rich neighbours, lest they invite you in return and you be repaid.
