But when you make a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just." When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, "Blessed is he who will eat bread in the kingdom of God."

units.la: Præcipuum & proprium Domini nostri Iesu Christi officium est, miseros mortales cum Deo Patre in gratiam reducere, ut huic reconciliati æternæ salutis hæredes fiant. Id verò nö obiter modò præstitit, quando in cruce moriens peccata nostra expiauit, quæ nos à Deo alienos faciebant: sed doctrinam quoq; suã ita nobis attemperat, ut omnibus vitiis medeatur, quæ nos in veræ pietatis & salutis studio remorari possunt. Quod vt multis alijs in locis fecit, ita maxime in hoc cap.præ-stat, vbi cum apertis hostibus agens, omnia salutis obstacula ex ordine tollit. Nam primum à cul-tu Dei exorsus, superstitiosam ceremoniarum fiduciam confutauit, docens, non istarum obserua-tionem vmbratilem & ostentationi potissimum seruientem, sed multò magis vera solidæ pietatis ac beneficentiæ officia à nobis requiri. Deinde cum illos ambitione & gloriæ priuatæ studio quam ma-xime impediri sciret, quò minus crederent, huic etiam malo remedium adhibuit, & non sine graui comminatione æternæ ignominiæ ipsis humilitatem commendauit. His nunc commodissimè subij-cit doctrinam de dilectione & beneficentia, quæ inter fidei & veræ pœnitentiæ opera siue effecta pri-mas tenet. Et quia circa illa quoque plurimum peccabant Iudæi, imò & hodiè ferè sub eius præ-textu pleriq; sua commoda quærunt, graviter monet ille, quid hic præcipuè obseruari & fieri debeat.
units.tr: It is the chief and proper office of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring wretched mortals back into favour with God the Father, so that, being reconciled to him, they may become heirs of eternal salvation. He did not accomplish this only in passing, when dying on the cross he expiated our sins, which made us strangers to God; he also so adapts his teaching to us that he heals every vice which can hold us back from the pursuit of true piety and salvation. As he does in many other places, so in this chapter especially he does it, where, dealing with open enemies, he removes in order every obstacle to salvation. For first, beginning from the worship of God, he refuted the superstitious confidence in ceremonies, teaching that it is not the shadowy observance of these, serving chiefly to display, but much more the duties of true and solid piety and beneficence that are required of us. Then, knowing that they were especially hindered by ambition and the pursuit of private glory, so that they could not believe, he also applied a remedy to this evil, and commended humility to them, not without a grave warning of eternal disgrace. Now he most fittingly adds to these the teaching about love and beneficence, which holds the first place among the works that flow from faith and true repentance. And because the Jews also sinned very much in these matters, and even today many, almost under this pretext, seek their own advantage, he warns gravely what ought especially to be observed and done here.

units.la: Rursus autem ex re præsenti occasione sumpta veram conuiuiorum rationem tradit, quæ do-ctrina inde ad omnia charitatis & beneficentiæ officia extendi debet. Videbat enim plerosque Iu-dæorum non solum priuati commodi studio peccare, verumetiam in conuiuijs omni lautitiarum ge-nere & apparatus magnifici splendore sese ostentare, adeoque in eleemosynis quoque distribuendis (vt apud Matthæum annotatur) gloriam & auram popularem captare. Quo vitio cum procul du-bio princeps iste Pharisæorum laboraret, ad cuius mensam cum multis alijs fuerat inuitatus, to-tum sermonem ad illum in primis dirigit, vt simulatum eius officium vero & solido beneficio re-pendat. Nec enim melior gratia ijs quoque, qui nobis ex animo benefaciunt, referri potest, quàm si erroribus liberentur, & fideliter instituantur in ijs, sine quibus salus æterna constare non po-test. Itaque Dominus ante omnia vitio medetur, quo tota beneficentiæ ratio turbari solet: deinde quid fieri debeat docet, & suam doctrinam magnifica præmij amplißimi atque æterni promissione confirmat.
units.tr: Again, taking occasion from the present circumstance, he gives the true rule of feasting, and this teaching ought then to be extended to all the duties of charity and beneficence. For he saw that most of the Jews sinned not only from the pursuit of private advantage, but also showed themselves off at their banquets with every kind of luxury and the splendour of a magnificent display, and so, even in distributing alms (as is noted in Matthew), sought glory and popular applause. Since without doubt that leader of the Pharisees was troubled by this vice, and had been invited with many others to his table, he directs the whole discourse chiefly at him, so that he may repay his pretended kindness with a true and solid benefit. For no better return can be made even to those who do us good from a sincere heart than that they be freed from errors and faithfully taught in those things without which eternal salvation cannot stand. Therefore the Lord first of all heals the vice by which the whole reckoning of beneficence is usually disturbed; then he teaches what ought to be done, and confirms his teaching with the magnificent promise of a most ample and eternal reward.

units.la: Ad primam huius orationis partem pertinent hæc verba: Cùm facis prandium aut cœnam, ne vocato amicos tuos, neque fratres tuos, neque cognatos tuos, neque vicinos divites, ne quando & ipsi te vicissim vocent, ac retribuatur tibi gratia. Quo loco probe tenendum est, non damnari à Christo hospitalitatis officia, quæ amicis fratribus, cognatis aut vicinis opulentioribus & in ali-qua dignitate constitutis exhibentur. Scriptura enim passim humanitatem & gratitudinem nobis commendat, ingratos vero & inhumanos detestatur. Et vt Christus nusquam docuit, ingratitu-dinem: ita homines ἀςόργως, qui nullo cognationis respectu ducuntur, & ab eo etiam amore alieni sunt, quo natura nos eos prosequi iubet, qui nobis propius coniuncti sunt, inter nouissimi seculi pe-stes numerat Paulus Apostolus, & ne illorum mores imitemur admonet. Sed & naturæ lex est, vt bonam gratiam quibuscunque referamus, & amorem inter nos mutuis officijs foueamus. Vide-runt hoc olim omnes, qui inter gentes sapientia & virtute excelluerunt: apud quos hospitalitas tan-to in pretio fuit, vt huius præsidem dixerint summum illum Iouem, sicuti alibi diximus. Itaque plus quam barbarum esset, hospitalitatis officium amicis negare, quod peregrinis etiam atque ignotis debetur. Quod si hominis ingenium spectemus, nos ad societatem & amicitiam natura proclives & propensos esse constat, & inde factum esse, vt olim in ciuitates coirent, qui prius dispersi vagaban-tur. Ad societatem verò vel ineundam vel feruandam conuiuia honesta & amica plurimum con-ferre, nemo negauerit, qui vel mediocrem habet rerum humanarum vsum. Cato certè inter Romanos non tam grauissimus morum censor, quam paterfamilias frugalis & prouidus, mensam amico-rum parentem atque procreatricem dicere solebat. Et ipsa conuiuij vox vitæ significat, qua nihil iucundius, nihil vtilius, nihil deniq; magis necessarium est, cum sine illa neq; priuatæ amicitiæ, neq; ciuitatum concordia, imò nec quæ in Christi Ecclesia habetur salutis æterna communio siue societas consistere potest. Quapropter honoraria conuiuia sanctissimis quoq; patribus olim in ve-su fuisse legimus. Abrahamus cum Isaacum Sara ablactauisset, conuiuium magnum instruxit ami-cis suis, vt acceptum à Deo beneficiū publicè prædicaret. Isaacus quoq; Abimelechū regem cum ma-gno amicorum eius numero & militiæ præfecto Phicole, epulo splendidiore excepit. Idem postea Io-sephus fecit, cum ad ipsum fratres eius emendi frumenti causa in Ægyptum venissent. At quid ex emplis alijs opus est? quando ipse Christus ad conuiuia honoraria accessit: quod nunquam facturus erat, si illa Deo Patri improbari sciuisset, eòq; magis ab illis abstinuisset, quod suos aduersarios inde calumniandi & ipsum traducendi occasionem arripere non ignoraret. Adde tamen hīs omnibus, quod inter cultus diuini exercitia aliquus conuiuiorum eiusmodi vsus fuit. Qui enim sacrificia Eucharistica pro acceptis à Deo beneficijs offerebant, ij ex illorum carnibus conuiuia instruere, & ad illa amicos inuitare solebant, vt hos suae laetitiae testes & congratulatores haberent. Quę morem adeò non improbauit Deus, vt potius per Mosem festorum publicorum rationem tradiderit, & inter alia iusserit Israelitas in suo conspectu epulari. Quò referri potest Samuelis historia, qui Saulem epulo eiusmodi excepit, & eidem inter inuitatos primum locum dedit, quod eum à Deo Regem Israelis designatum esse cognouisset. Possent huius generis multa recenseri, quae abundè docent, non debere Christi verba ad statum alienum detorqueri, ne ciuilitatis & humanitatis pars praecipua aboleatur inter homines, quorum aliqui auaritia ducti omnem deuitandae impensae occasionem faciè arripiunt, aliqui vero in nimia & inhumana austeritate summam religionis consistere putant, & tunc demum suam authoritatem saluam fore sibi persuadent, si in conuiuiu difficiles & ipsi nemine domum suam inuitent, & ad nullius mensam se inuitari patiantur. In qua sententia olim aliqui inter gentes fuerunt, qui conuiuia cum magnanimitate pugnare arbitrati sunt, eò quod in illis morum grauitas vix retineri posset, & qui illa frequentant, multa dissimulare cogantur, & ita in suspicionem animi seruilis & abiecti veniant. Quod Periclem monuit, vt postquam ad Rempublicam accessit, nullius vnquam conuiuijs interfuerit, ne authoritati ipsius aliquid decederet. Fatemur quidem id fieri non raro, si luxuriosis epulis sese admisceant qui in Ecclesia & Republica praesunt. At nos de conuiuijs honestis & amicitiae seruandae causa institutis loquimur, quae damnari non possunt, nisi amicitias magna ex parte abolere, & cum inhumanitate coniunctam barbariem inducere velimus.
units.tr: To the first part of this discourse belong these words: When you make a lunch or a supper, do not invite your friends, nor your brothers, nor your relatives, nor your rich neighbours, lest they in turn invite you, and a return be made to you. Here it must be well held that Christ does not condemn the offices of hospitality which are shown to friends, brothers, relatives, or to richer neighbours who hold some dignity. For Scripture everywhere commends to us humanity and gratitude, and detests the ungrateful and the inhuman. And just as Christ nowhere taught ingratitude, so Paul the Apostle counts among the plagues of the last age men who are ἄστοργοι [without natural affection], who are guided by no regard for kinship and are estranged even from that love by which nature bids us cherish those who are most closely joined to us, and he warns us not to imitate their manners. Moreover it is also a law of nature that we return a good turn to whomever we can, and that we cherish love among ourselves by mutual services. All who excelled among the nations in wisdom and virtue have seen this: among them hospitality was held in such esteem that they said its guardian was that highest Jupiter, as we have said elsewhere. Therefore it would be more than barbarous to deny to friends the duty of hospitality, which is owed even to strangers and unknown persons. And if we consider the nature of man, it is plain that we are by nature inclined and disposed to fellowship and friendship, and from this it came about that those who once wandered dispersed came together into cities. Now no one who has even a moderate experience of human affairs would deny that honourable and friendly banquets contribute greatly both to entering into and to preserving fellowship. Cato, certainly, among the Romans, not so much the most severe censor of morals as a thrifty and provident head of a household, used to say that the table of friends is the parent and the begetter of friendship. And the very word for a banquet, convivium, signifies life, and nothing is more pleasant, nothing more useful, nothing finally more necessary than this, since without it neither private friendships nor the harmony of cities, nor even the communion or fellowship of eternal salvation which is had in the Church of Christ, can stand. Wherefore we read that honourable banquets were in use even among the most holy fathers of old. When Abraham had weaned Isaac from Sarah, he prepared a great feast for his friends, so that he might publicly proclaim the blessing he had received from God. Isaac also received Abimelech the king with a large number of his friends, and Phicol, the commander of his army, with a more splendid feast. Joseph afterwards did the same, when his brothers came to him in Egypt to buy grain. But why need we other examples, when Christ himself came to honourable banquets? He would never have done so if he had known that these were disapproved by God the Father, and he would the more have abstained from them, since he was not unaware that his adversaries would seize from them the occasion of slandering and disparaging him. Add to all these things, moreover, that a banquet of this kind was part of the exercises of the divine worship. For those who offered eucharistic sacrifices for the benefits received from God used to prepare banquets from the flesh of these, and to invite friends to them, so that they might have these as witnesses and fellow-rejoicers of their gladness. God did not so disapprove of this custom that he rather, through Moses, laid down the rule of public feasts, and among other things commanded the Israelites to feast in his sight. To this may be referred the story of Samuel, who received Saul at a feast of this kind, and gave him the first place among the guests, because he had learned that Saul had been designated by God as king of Israel. Many things of this kind could be recounted, which abundantly teach that the words of Christ ought not to be twisted to a foreign purpose, lest the principal part of civility and humanity be abolished among men; some of whom, led by avarice, eagerly seize every occasion of avoiding expense, while others, in excessive and inhuman austerity, think that the sum of religion consists in this, and persuade themselves that their authority will then be safe, if they themselves invite no one to their home in a banquet, and suffer themselves to be invited to no one's table. In this opinion there were once some among the nations who judged that banquets were at odds with greatness of soul, because the gravity of morals could scarcely be kept at them, and those who frequent them are forced to dissemble many things, and thus fall under the suspicion of a servile and abject spirit. This is what warned Pericles, after he entered public affairs, never to attend anyone's banquets, lest anything should be taken from his authority. We certainly grant that this happens not rarely, if those who preside in the Church and the commonwealth mix themselves with luxurious feasts. But we are speaking of honourable banquets instituted for the sake of keeping friendship, which cannot be condemned unless we wish to abolish friendships for the most part and introduce barbarism joined with inhumanity.

units.la: Quid ergo Christum hoc loco agere dicemus? Hoc ipsum nimirum, quod saepe aliàs facit, vt ex re vulgari & minoris momenti occasione sumpta, animos ad sublimiora euehat, & erroribus meadeatur, quibus multi impliciti circa fidei & salutis aeternae mysteria hallucinantur. Sic cū de manum ablutione quaestionem Pharisaei mouissent, ille non de hac curiosius disputat, sed de vera & interna hominis tam purificatione quam pollutione sermonem instituit: & simile quid in causa de iuni-nijs factum fuisse scimus, vt nunc multa alia omittamus. Ita in praesenti sub conuiuiorum exemplo siue parabola, quid in charitatis officijs & beneficentiae potissimum cauteri debeat docet, quid item fieri debeat, vt illa solida sint, & Deo vere probentur. Debent autem ea cauteri, in quibus Iudaeos tunc temporis peccauisse, paulò ante diximus: priuati nimirum commodi aut retributionis ampliorus spes, vel gloriae & aurae popularis cupiditas. Qui enim vt plura recipiant beneficiunt, ij sub beneficentiae praetextu quaestum turpem faciunt. Quid autem inhonestius & inciuilius fingi potest, quam vili aliquo officio alios cogere, vt maiora quasi ex debito reddant, à quibus nihil huius petere auderes? Et cum eiusmodi officia hominibus sordeant, num ea probare poterit Deus, qui nos absq; omni mercedis temporariae respectu à Iua gratia pendere vult? Qui vero hoc artificio laudem venantur, ij (vt alibi Christus monet) iam receperunt mercedem suam, neque habent, quo apud Deum glorientur, qui misericordiam & voluntariam beneficentiam requirit, sicuti in Samaritani parabola videmus. Peccant ergo in Christi praeceptum, quotquot non nisi in publico eleemosynas faciunt, vt apud plures beneficentiae laudem mereantur: quotquot item in templis quoque illarum memoriam extare volunt, aut in alijs locis publicis: quibus adnumerari debent, qui suae liberalitatis praecones coduncunt poetastros & scripturiendi scabie prurientes, & ita tantum non tubarum clangore sua officia apud posteros quoq; diuulgari cupiunt. Adde his eos, qui in pios & eximios Christi seruos beneficia plurima conferunt, vt horum fauore atq; patrocinio iuuentur apud principes viros, qui illos in honore & pretio habent. Et tales quidem suis temporibus plurimos fuisse Chrysostomus queritur, hodie autē infinitus est illorum numerus in locis ijs, vbi Christianae religionis libertas regnat. Qui vt non nisi priuatum commodum quaerunt, vt nimirum vel honoribus publicis augeantur, vel ad munera quaestuosa sibi via parent: ita ministrorum Ecclesiae fauore nimis turpiter abutuntur, & saepe hīs inuidiā atq; odium conciliant. Peccant deniq; hoc loco omnes qui sumptus quidem magnos faciunt in alijs vel honorandis vel iuuandis, in eo autem nihil praeter gloriam priuata aut retributionem quaerunt. Itaq; si ad hanc regulam singuli sua officia, quibus charitatem erga illos declarare videntur, examinent, mox videbunt quantum illis decedat, & quam exiguam adeo nullam de illis gloriam di occasionem habeant.
units.tr: What, then, shall we say Christ is doing in this place? Surely this very thing which he often does elsewhere: taking an occasion from a common matter of small importance, he lifts minds to higher things and remedies the errors by which many, entangled in the mysteries of faith and eternal salvation, go astray. So when the Pharisees raised the question about washing the hands, he did not dispute about that more closely, but discoursed on the true and inward purification and pollution of man. We know something similar happened in the matter of fasting, not to mention many other things now. So in the present passage, under the example of a banquet or parable, he teaches what above all must be guarded against in deeds of charity and beneficence, and also what must be done so that those deeds are solid and truly approved by God. The faults in which we said a little earlier the Jews of that time sinned must be guarded against: namely, the hope of private gain or of a larger return, or the desire for glory and popular applause. For those who do good so that they may receive more make a shameful profit under the pretext of beneficence. What could be more dishonourable and uncivil to imagine than to compel others, by some base service, to repay greater things as if they were a debt, when you would not dare to ask anything of the kind from them? And since such services are contemptible to men, will God, who wishes us to depend on his grace without any regard to temporal reward, be able to approve them? Those who hunt for praise by this trick, as Christ warns elsewhere, have already received their reward, and have no ground for glorying before God, who requires mercy and voluntary beneficence, as we see in the parable of the Samaritan. They sin against Christ's precept, then, all who give alms only in public so that they may earn the praise of beneficence before many; likewise all who want the memory of their gifts to remain in churches or in other public places. Among these must be counted those who hire heralds of their liberality, poetasters itching with the scab of writing, and who so wish their deeds to be spread to posterity almost with the blare of trumpets. Add to these those who confer many benefits on pious and distinguished servants of Christ so that they may be helped by the favour and patronage of these men among the princes who hold them in honour and esteem. Chrysostom complains that there were many such people in his own times, and today their number is endless in places where the liberty of the Christian religion reigns. Those who seek nothing but private advantage, namely that they may be raised by public honours or prepare for themselves a path to lucrative offices, abuse so shamefully the favour of the ministers of the Church, and often win hatred and odium for them. Finally, all who make large expenses in honouring or helping others, but in this seek nothing except private glory or return, also sin here. So if each one examines by this rule his own duties, by which he seems to show charity toward those people, he will soon see how much is lost to him, and how small, indeed how non-existent, is the occasion he has for glory from them.

units.la: Quid ergo hic observari & fieri debet? Cùm facis epulum (inquit Dominus) voca pauperes, mancos, claudos, cæcos, &c. Sensus est, benefaciendum esse illis, qui nostræ opis sunt indigi, quamuis nullam retributionis spes affulgeat. Quid enim ex pauper aliud speres, quam ut vno beneficio illectus plura abs te petat? Quid ex manco, claudo & cæco tibi polliceare præter laborem atque molestiam cum fastidio coniunctam? At nihilominus illis præstari debet dilectionis officia, idque eo magis, quod & ipsi nihil sibi conferre possunt, & plerumque ab aliis negliguntur. Admonet de hoc ipsa dilectionis vox, quæ relationem habet ad alios. Quomodo enim illa locum habebit, si nemo sit quem diligas? At quis magis dignus dilectione, quam qui aliorum auxilio carere non potest, & proinde à tua beneficentia totus pendet? Vult ergo Dominus, ut non nostri, sed aliorum rationem habeamus, quoties benefici in aliquos esse aut videri volumus. Quod ipsum supra per Samaritani parabolam aperti us docuit. Apud Matthæum vero Dei Patris exemplum nobis imitandum proponit, quod unum nos abunde docere, & omnium argumentorum loco esse potest. Si enim filii Dei censeri & regni eius hæredes esse cupimus, non poterimus illius exemplum contemnere, sed ut eius ingenio atque moribus nos accommodemus necesse est. Atqui is totus quantus est, charitas est: & quamuis dilectionis suæ exempla passim edat, & illa in omnibus mundi partibus occurrant, magis tamen illustria & frequentiora sunt, quibus illam erga homines miserrimos & omni præsidio destitutos declarat. Quo nomine pater viduarum & orphanorum, patronus peregrinorum, afflictorum vindex & servator in Scripturis dicitur. Quid, quòd indignos & filios iræ dilexit, & quotidie salutem in Christo illis offert, qui æternam mortem merentur? Et deniq; eo in nos affectu prædictus est, ut quando pœnas à nobis eius iustitia necessario exigit, hanc tamen misericordia sua temperet, & non aliud finem sibi proponat, quam ut à peccatis converti serenemur? Quò Psaltes respiciens eos beatos dicit, quos Dominus castigat. Et rursus: Bonum mihi Domine, quod humiliasti me. Et tales quidem nos quo quæ Christus esse iubet, ut tam benefici Patris filii germani simus.
units.tr: What, then, ought to be observed and done here? "When you make a feast," says the Lord, "invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind," and so on. The sense is that we should do good to those who are in need of our help, even though no hope of return shines forth. For what else could you hope from a poor man than that, enticed by one benefit, he will ask more of you? What could you promise yourself from the maimed, the lame and the blind, except labour and trouble joined with disgust? Yet acts of love must nevertheless be rendered to them, all the more because they themselves can confer nothing on you, and for the most part are neglected by others. The very word "love" admonishes us of this, since it has a relation to others. For how will it have a place if there is no one whom you love? But who is more worthy of love than one who cannot do without the help of others, and therefore depends wholly on your beneficence? The Lord therefore wills that we have regard not to ourselves but to others whenever we want to be, or to seem to be, beneficent to some. This he taught more openly before through the parable of the Samaritan. In Matthew, however, he sets before us the example of God the Father to be imitated, which can teach us enough by itself and serve in place of all arguments. For if we wish to be counted sons of God and heirs of his kingdom, we cannot despise his example, but must of necessity accommodate ourselves to his nature and manners. Yet he is wholly, altogether, love; and although he displays examples of his love everywhere, and they meet us in all parts of the world, those by which he declares that love toward the most wretched men, destitute of all help, are more illustrious and more frequent. On this account in the Scriptures he is called the father of widows and orphans, the patron of strangers, the avenger and saviour of the afflicted. What of the fact that he loved the unworthy and the children of wrath, and daily offers salvation in Christ to those who deserve eternal death? And finally, is he so disposed toward us that, when his justice necessarily exacts punishments from us, he tempers these with his mercy, and proposes to himself no other end than that we may be gently turned from our sins? Looking to this, the Psalmist calls those blessed whom the Lord chastens. And again: "It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me." Such, indeed, we ought to be, as Christ bids, so that we may be true brothers' sons of so beneficent a Father.

units.la: At elucet hic non seculi modò nostri deplorata conditio, verumetiam vniuersalis ingenij nostri prauitas atque malitia. Nam cum Christiani dici & haberi velimus, quorum propria nota atque tessera est mutua dilectio, eam tamen ferè negligimus in pauperibus & egenis, qui nobis præ aliis commendati esse debebant: ut hic nimis aperte illud videas quod Christus de nouissimorum temporum hominibus dixit, fore ut charitas prosus frigeat atque extinguatur. Argumentum quo duritiem & inhumanitatem suam plerique excusant, præcipuum est, quod tantæ egentium multitudini alendæ nemo sufficiat, cum plerisque inopia & mendicitas quæstus factus sit. Sed vtinam non idem de diuitiis dici posset, quarum multi non alium vsum norunt, quam quod vsuris & impo- sturis illas quotidie augent, & auaritia insatiabili accensi quæstum ex quæstu faciunt. Quam ve- rò friuolum sit, quod pauperes ali posse negant, ex eo satis apparet, quod plerique in res nihili & in- honestas mira prodigalitate opes ingentes profundunt, & nimij sunt erga eos, qui seipsos alere po- terant. Quid enim de conuiuiorum luxu & mensis plus quàm Sybaricis dici potest, quod nostri seculi intemperantia non longè superet? Quid de immodico vestium ornatu, quo viri animos mu- lebres, mulieres autem cum fastu ferociam plus quam virilem & meretriciam impudentiam pro- dunt? Quid de insanis ædificiorum structuris, in quas passim opes tam publicæ quàm priuatæ in- utiliter consumuntur? Interim qui tanta prodigalitate Baccho, Veneri, mundo & huius princi- pi diabolo seruiunt, in solos pauperes parcissimi & pumice aridiores sunt, imò hoc solum perditum, aut saltem malè collocatum arbitrantur, quod in illos confertur. Non ergo hos alendi facultas, sed voluntas plerisque deest, quæ mox in illis noua nasceretur, si charitatis igne animi ipsorum arderent.
units.tr: But here there shines forth not only the deplorable condition of our age, but also the depravity and malice of our nature in general. For although we wish to be called and considered Christians, whose proper mark and badge is mutual love, we nevertheless almost neglect it toward the poor and needy, who ought to have been commended to us above others; so that here you may see all too plainly what Christ said about the men of the last times, that love would altogether grow cold and be extinguished. The argument by which most excuse their hardness and inhumanity is chiefly this: that no one is sufficient to feed so great a multitude of the needy, since for most, poverty and begging have become a trade. But would that the same could not be said of riches, of which many know no other use than that they increase them daily by usury and deceit, and, inflamed by insatiable greed, make profit upon profit! How frivolous it is that they deny the poor can be fed appears sufficiently from this: that most pour out great wealth on trifling and dishonourable things with wonderful prodigality, and are overly generous toward those who were able to feed themselves. For what can be said of the luxury of banquets and tables, more than Sybaritic, which the intemperance of our age does not far surpass? What of the immoderate adornment of clothes, by which men display womanish minds, and women, with pride, a ferocity more than manly and a whorish impudence? What of the insane structures of buildings, on which public and private wealth alike is uselessly consumed everywhere? Meanwhile those who serve Bacchus, Venus, the world and the devil, the prince of this world, with such prodigality are most sparing and drier than pumice toward the poor alone, and they think this the only thing lost, or at least badly spent, which is bestowed on them. So it is not the means of feeding them that most lack, but the will, which would soon be born in them if the fire of charity burned in their hearts.

units.la: Quia verò hæc frustra ijs dicuntur, qui præter quæstum aut honorem vel mundi applausum nihil spectant, grauem & nostræ vitiositati in primis conuenientem rationem Christus suæ doctrinæ subijcit, dicens: Et beatus eris, quia non possunt retribuere tibi: retribuetur enim tibi in resurrectione iustorum. Quasi diceret: Non est quod beneficia, quæ in pauperes contuleris, te amissurum aut malè collocaturum esse timeas. Tam enim hoc abest, ut hanc non postremam tuæ felicitatis partem putare debeas. Quia enim illi non possunt dignas gratias referre, remuneratorem habebis Deum, qui illa cum fœnore retribuet. Neque etiam te moueat, si in hoc seculo retributionem plane nullam recipias, tunc enim vberior tibi obtinget in resurrectione iustorum idest, eo die, quo omnes homines à mortuis resuscitati ad Dei tribunal sistentur, tu vero inter iustos & legitimos Dei cultores censeberis, qui regni illius cœlestis & æterni hæreditatem adibunt. Debent huc referri promissiones, quibus passim Spiritus sanctus Deum ipsum pro pauperibus vadem aut fideiussorem nobis sistit. In Lege certè non vno loco illos ea conditione commendat, quod se eos locupletare velle promittit, qui in illos benefici fuerint. Et notum est illud Solomonis: Domino fœneratur quisquis benefacit pauperi: secundum beneficium eius rependetur ei. Apud Isaiam vero clamat: Si effuderis esurienti animam tuam, & animam afflictam satiaueris, tunc orietur in tenebris lux tua, & erit caligo tua sicut meridies: Et deducet te Dominus semper, & saturam reddet in siccitatibus animam tuam, & ossa tua saginabit, &c. Plenissimè autem hæc omnia ab ipso Christo confirmantur, qui in magno illo die sibi factum iudicabit, quicquid in pauperes suos collatum fuerit. Sunt ergo nimium vecordes, qui illos negligunt, eò quod ex eis retributionem nullam sperare possunt: his autem, imò terà, quàterà, stulti sunt, qui ab hominibus mendacissimus gratias dignas ex pectant, Dei autem promissionibus diffidunt, qui ipsa est veritas.
units.tr: Since these things are said in vain to those who look for nothing beyond gain, honour or worldly applause, Christ attaches to his teaching a weighty reason, one especially suited to our own wickedness, saying: "And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just." It is as if he said: "You need not fear that the benefits you have bestowed on the poor will be lost or wasted. Indeed, so far is this from being so, that you should not regard this as the last part of your happiness. For since those poor people cannot make fitting return, you will have God as your rewarder, who will repay you with interest. Nor should it trouble you if you receive no repayment at all in this age, for then a fuller reward will be yours at the resurrection of the just, that is, on the day when all people raised from the dead will stand before God's judgement seat, and you will be counted among the just and lawful worshippers of God, who will enter into the inheritance of that heavenly and eternal kingdom." To this belong the promises by which the Holy Spirit everywhere sets God himself before us as surety and guarantor for the poor. In the Law, certainly, in more than one place he commends them on this condition: that he promises to enrich those who have done good to them. And the saying of Solomon is well known: "Whoever does good to the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him according to his good deed." In Isaiah he cries out: "If you pour out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light shall rise in darkness, and your gloom shall be as the noonday. And the Lord shall guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make your bones fat," and so on. All these things are most fully confirmed by Christ himself, who on that great day will count as done to himself whatever has been bestowed on his poor. Those, therefore, are exceedingly foolish who neglect the poor because they can hope for no repayment from them. But far more foolish, indeed fourfold foolish, are those who look for worthy thanks from men, who are most deceitful, and distrust the promises of God, who is truth itself.

units.la: Porro potest ex hoc loco firmissimum argumentum peti, quo nouissimus Christi ad iudicium ad uentus & vita æterna asseratur. Nam vt retributionem habeant ta iusti quam iniusti, pij & impij ipsa Dei iustitia exigit. Quia enim iustitiæ est suum cuique tribuere, & sceleratos quidem pro meritis multare, bonos autem præmijs dignos honorare, Deum iniustū dicere oportebit, nisi illud ipsum præstet. At in hoc seculo remunerationem dignam non semper, sed quàm rarissimè fieri videmus. Ferè enim impij diuitijs & honoribus affluunt, impunitate scelerum gaudent, & pro sua libidine res suas agunt: pijs interea laborantibus & aduersa omnis generis sustinetibus: Quæ res non semel fidei Dei cultoribus adeò molesta fuit, vt de eius iustitia grauiter conquesti sint. Aliud ergo seculum sequatur oportet, quo Deus omnibus iustè rependat pro ijs, quæ in hac vita fecerunt. Et ideo Christus hic nos ad resurrectionem iustorum remittit, ne de Dei iustitia dubitemus, si quando non statim vir tutus præmia accipimus, aut impios atq; crudeles non confessim puniri videmus. Est hæc consideratio vtilissima, adhæc digna & necessaria, quæ crebro nobis in mentem veniat. Nam vt à sceleribus nos vehementer absterret, ita animos & voluntatem nostram confirmat, ne benefaciendo defatigemur. Accidit hoc multis, qui mundum hunc suis benefactoribus semper ingratissimum fuisse nouerunt, & qui pessimam gratiam sibi quoque referri sentiunt ab illis, de quibus meliora sunt meriti. Cogitemus ergo, nos remuneratorem in cœlis habere Deum, qui virtuti sua præmia defieri nunquâ patietur: vicissim autem gratiis supplicijs multabit inhumanos & duros illos, qui aliorum miserias siccis oculis intuentur, vel etiam ex illis res suas augendi occasionem arripiunt. Sed & paupe res hinc consolationem petere possunt. Nam etsi ipsorum inopia pauci moueantur, videt tamen hanc Deus, qui patientiam ipsorum æternus regni sui thesaurus remunerabit.
units.tr: Moreover, from this passage a most firm argument can be drawn, by which the final coming of Christ to judgement and eternal life is established. For God's own justice demands that both the righteous and the unrighteous, the godly and the ungodly, receive a repayment. For since it is the part of justice to render to each his due, to punish the wicked according to their deserts and to honour the good with rewards, we must call God unjust unless he himself brings this about. Yet in this age we see that a worthy repayment is not always made, but very rarely. For the ungodly for the most part abound in riches and honours, rejoice in impunity for their crimes, and manage their affairs as their lust directs, while the godly labour and endure adversities of every kind. This has more than once troubled the worshippers of God so greatly that they have complained bitterly about his justice. Another age must therefore follow, in which God will justly repay all men for what they have done in this life. And so Christ here refers us to the resurrection of the just, lest we doubt God's justice when we do not at once receive a reward, or when we see the impious and cruel not punished at once. This consideration is most useful, and worthy and necessary to be often brought to mind. For while it strongly deters us from wickedness, so it strengthens our minds and will, that we may not grow weary in doing good. This happens to many who know that this world has always been most ungrateful to its benefactors, and who feel that the worst thanks is returned to them by those to whom they have done the best. Let us therefore consider that we have God in heaven as our rewarder, who will never allow the rewards of virtue to perish; and on the other hand he will punish with fitting torments those inhuman and hard men who look upon the miseries of others with dry eyes, or even seize the chance to increase their own wealth from them. But the poor too may draw consolation from this. For although few are moved by their want, God sees it, and he who is the eternal treasure of his kingdom will reward their patience.

units.la: Cæterum quando Christus resurrectionis iustorum mentionem fecit, in qua beneficentia sua præmia acceptauri sint, qui in pauperes sunt liberales, quidam ex ijs qui simul accumbebant, ex eo occasionem arripiens exclamauit: Beatus, qui comedet panem in regno Dei. Videtur vs, quisquis fuerit, non omnino prophanus & impius verbi Dei irrisor fuisse. Nam qui tales sunt, ij tam minas quàm promissiones de futuro seculo & nouissima illa retributione cum cachinnis excipere & impudenter exibilare solent. Hic vero meditatione alterius vitæ abreptus, eos demum beatos fore pronunciat, qui hanc assecuti gloria in cœlis vera & immortali fruentur. Locutione autē vtitur, quæ præsenti argumento optimè conueniebat, cum de beneficentia sub couiuiorum parabola Dominus hucusque disseruisset. Et frequens est locutio ista in Scripturis, adeo vt Christus quoque credentes omnium gentium cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo accubituros dicat. Et in vltima cœna discipulis ait: Vos ij estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis. Ego igitur paciscor vobis prout pactus est mihi Pater meus, regnum: vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo, &c. Quibus verbis non aliud quam cœlestis gloriæ & felicitatis societatem intelligit. Et tale quid gentium quoque sapientes innuisse videntur, quando cœlites ambrosia vesci, & neʇar bibere dixerunt, cum ꝯraque ytraque vox immortalitatem & conditionem nulli corruptioni obnoxiam significet. Secuti sunt postea quidam crassiores & ventris gulæq; mancipia, qui conuiuia in cœlis agitari finxerunt, qualia impurus etiam Mahumetes somniauit. Qui error licet inter Iudæos non habuerit locum, & pro inde conuiuia ipse hæc verba sano sensu dixisse videatur, Christus tamen ex illis occasionem sumit, Iudæos simul omnes reprehendendi, qui cum æternæ salutis studium profiterentur, illam tamen non recipiebant, imò vocati quoque & inuitati ad epulas illas cælestes accedere detrectabant: vt in sequenti sermone dicetur.
units.tr: Moreover, when Christ made mention of the resurrection of the just, in which those who are generous to the poor will receive the rewards of their beneficence, one of those who were reclining at table with him, seizing the occasion, cried out: "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." He seems, whoever he was, not to have been wholly profane, nor an impious mocker of the word of God. For such men are accustomed to receive with laughter, and shamelessly to hiss at, both the threats and the promises concerning the future age and that final retribution. But this man, carried away by thought of the other life, declares that those will at last be blessed who obtain this glory and enjoy the true and immortal life in heaven. He uses a form of speech which fitted the present subject very well, since the Lord had hitherto discoursed about beneficence under the parable of a banquet. And this manner of speaking is frequent in the Scriptures, so much so that Christ also says that believers of all nations will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And at the last supper he says to his disciples: "You are those who have remained with me in my temptations. I therefore covenant with you, as my Father has covenanted with me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom," and so on. By these words he means nothing other than the fellowship of heavenly glory and blessedness. And something of the same kind the wise men of the Gentiles also seem to have hinted, when they said that the heavenly ones feast on ambrosia and drink nectar, since both words signify immortality and a condition subject to no corruption. Afterwards certain grosser men, slaves of belly and gullet, imagined that banquets were held in heaven, such as the impure Mahomet also dreamed of. Although this error had no place among the Jews, and although he himself seems to have used these words in a sound sense, Christ nevertheless takes from them an occasion to rebuke all the Jews together, who, while professing zeal for eternal salvation, nevertheless did not receive it; indeed, though called and invited to those heavenly feasts, they refused to come, as will be told in the following sermon.

units.la: Nunc non ofcitanter obseruari debet, commune quoddam salutis desiderium omnibus hominibus insitum esse, cuius indicia non raro in impijs & prophanis quoque apparent, si quando illorum conscientias Deus tangit. Tunc enim terrores sentiunt, & eos beatos dicunt, quos tranquillos & salutis securos esse vident. Quid, quòd qui cœlos & inferos impudenter negant, damnatorum tamen gregi adnumerari nolunt, & iniquissime ferunt eos, qui ex Dei verbo æterna supplicia ipsis minantur? Vnde vero hoc? ex eo nimirum, quod occulta Spiritus suggestione aliquis Vitæ futuræ sensus vel inuitus obrepit. At qui eo impietatis nondum progressi sunt, ij salutem æternam serio desiderant, plerique autem in eius assequendæ ratione falluntur, dum ex carnis ratione & sensu hanc rem æstimant, quæ omnem humani ingenij captum excedit. Et hæc fere superstitionum causa est, quibus in felix mundus omnibus seculis in diuersas sectas scissus & distractus, à vero Regni Dei tramite aberrauit. Discamus ergo huius conuiuiæ exemplo, non sufficere ardentissimum Vitæ æternæ desiderium, & quæ ex hoc nascitur, bonam animi nostri intentione: sed necesse esse, vt tota illius ratio nobis perspecta fit, vt eam viam ingrediamur, quæ sola nos ad illam deducit. Est illa æternus Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, quem qui sequitur, is non ambulabit in tenebris, & in illo optata salute fruetur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now it must be observed, not carelessly, that a certain common desire for salvation is implanted in all men, whose signs appear not seldom even in the impious and profane, when God touches their consciences. For then they feel terrors, and call blessed those whom they see to be tranquil and secure in their salvation. What of this, that those who impudently deny heaven and hell nevertheless refuse to be numbered among the company of the damned, and most unjustly bear those who threaten them with eternal punishments from the word of God? Whence does this come? Doubtless from this: that some sense of the future life creeps upon them, against their will, by a hidden prompting of the Spirit. But those who have not yet advanced so far into impiety earnestly desire eternal salvation; yet most of them go astray in the way of attaining it, while they judge this matter by the reasoning and senses of the flesh, though it exceeds the whole grasp of the human mind. And this is nearly the cause of the superstitions by which the unhappy world, in every age, split and divided into diverse sects, has strayed from the true path of the kingdom of God. Let us learn therefore from the example of this banquet that the most ardent desire for eternal life, and the good intention of our mind which arises from it, are not enough; but it is necessary that the whole manner of it be made clear to us, so that we may enter that way which alone leads us to it. That way is the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, whoever follows him shall not walk in darkness, and in him shall enjoy the salvation he desires. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLV.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLV.

units.la: Iesus autem dixit ei: Homo quidam fecit cœnam magnam, & vocauit multos, misitq; seruum suum hora cœnæ, vt diceret vocatis: Venite, quia iam parata sunt omnia. Et omnes cœperunt vno ore se excusare. Primus dixit ei: Agrum emi, & necesse habeo exire, & eum inspicere: rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alter dixit: Iuga boum emi quinque, proficiscor ad probandum ea: rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alius dixit: Vxorem duxi, & propterea non possum venire. Cum igitur seruus aduenisset, annunciauit ista Domino suo. Tunc iratus paterfamilias dixit seruo suo: Abi cito in plateas & vicos urbis, & pauperes ac mancos claudosq; & cæcos huc introducito. Et ait seruus: Domine, factum est vt imperasti, & adhuc locus est. Tunc ait Dominus seruo: Abi in vias & sepes, & coge ingredi, vt impleatur domus mea. Dico enim vobis, neminem virorum illorum, qui vocati fuerant, gustaturum cœnam meam.
units.tr: Then Jesus said to him: "A certain man made a great supper and invited many, and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who were invited: 'Come, for all things are now ready.' And they all with one accord began to make excuse. The first said to him: 'I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it; I pray you, have me excused.' And another said: 'I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them; I pray you, have me excused.' And another said: 'I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.' So when the servant came, he told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant: 'Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind.' And the servant said: 'Lord, it is done as you commanded, and still there is room.' Then the lord said to the servant: 'Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I say to you, that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.'"

units.la: Quoniam homo per peccatum non solum à felicitate pristina excidit, verumetiam præclaram illam intellectus lucem & pleniorem rerum cælestium cognitionem amisit, qua initio illum Deus donauit: manet quidem in omnibus naturale quoddam salutis æternæ desiderium, huius autem assequendæ rationem videre non possunt, nisi cœlitus illuminentur. Quæ causa est, quòd multi de Regno Dei præclarè differunt, & quàm ardenti eius studio flagrent, verbis grauibus & plerunque non sine gemitu pronuntiatis testentur, cùm interim Dei ipsos inuitantis gratiam contemnant atque fastidiant. Laborarunt hoc vitio in primis Iudæi, quâmuis Regnum Dei ad se solos putarent pertinere: & eius exemplum non omnino obscurum nuper vidimus in eo, qui Christi verbis de Resurrectione iustorum excitatus, inter discumbentes exclamauit: Beatus, qui comedet panem in Regno Dei. Ideo Dominus illi nunc ita respondet, vt in eius persona generalem Iudaici populi ingratitudinem & cotumax gratia Dei fastidium reprehendat, simulque poenas dignas denuntiet: quod nimirum ipsis a Regno coelorum exclusis, gentes vocari & in illorum locum surrogari oporteat. Rursus autem parabola ex re praesenti petita videtur, qua aeternum Dei consilium de hominum salute comprehendit, causas item ostendit, quibus plerique auocati illud aspernantur, & quae poenae contemptores eiusmodi manent. Parabolae partes sunt duae. Prima proprie ad Iudaeos pertinet: Altera de Gentium vocatione disserit, & qua conditione omnes a Deo vocentur, docet. Quia vero Lucas breuior est, quaedam ex Matthaeo sarcienda erunt, quae suo loco videbimus.
units.tr: Because man, through sin, has not only fallen from his former happiness, but has also lost that clear light of understanding and that fuller knowledge of heavenly things with which God endowed him at the beginning, there remains in all men a certain natural desire for eternal salvation; yet they cannot see the way of attaining it unless they are enlightened from heaven. This is why many speak well of the Kingdom of God, and by their grave words, often uttered not without groaning, bear witness how fiercely they burn with zeal for it, while at the same time they despise and scorn the grace of God that invites them. The Jews suffered chiefly from this vice, although they thought the Kingdom of God belonged to them alone; and we recently saw an unobscure example of it in the man who, roused by Christ's words about the resurrection of the righteous, cried out among those reclining at table: "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the Kingdom of God." Therefore the Lord now answers him in such a way that, in his person, he rebukes the general ingratitude of the Jewish people and their stubborn contempt of the grace of God, and at the same time announces the punishment they deserve: namely, that they, being shut out from the Kingdom of heaven, must be called away, and the Gentiles substituted in their place. Again, the parable seems to be drawn from a present matter, in which he sets forth the eternal counsel of God concerning the salvation of men, and also shows the causes by which many are turned away and despise it, and what punishments remain for such despisers. The parable has two parts. The first properly pertains to the Jews; the second treats of the calling of the Gentiles, and teaches on what condition all are called by God. But because Luke is briefer, some things must be supplied from Matthew, which we shall see in their place.

units.la: Principio aeternum Dei de hominibus feruandis consilium exponit, quando hominem quendam coenam magnam fecisse ait: Et hominem dicit Deum Patrem, non quod is homo factus sit, sed quod humano prorsus more & amice nobiscum agit. Matthaeus Regem quendam filio suo nuptias fecisse scribit. Ergo de coena nuptiali hic agitur, & huic salutem & beatitudinem aeternam, quae in coelis fruemur, Dominus confert: quia in eo maxime consistit, vt cum Christo, vnico sponso nostro, spiritualis coniugij vinculo sociemur: & quamuis coniunctio ista nunc incipiat, sub vesperum tamen & finem mundi demum perficietur, quando ille tam corpora quam animas nostras ad se recipiet in coelos, vt aeternum cum ipso viuamus & regnemus. Et debet hoc non ofcitanter obseruari, ne morae impatientia superati ante tempus liberari, & priusquam certamen nostrum decertaueri-mus, triumphare velimus. Nam vt sanguinis sui pretio nos Dei Filius acquisiuit, vt sibi sponsam faceret: ita nobis quoque coniunctio illa multis laboribus, periculis, cruce & plerunque sanguine etiam multo constat. In his ergo nos durare, & sponsi aduentum, quem tota haec mundi fabrica cum gemitu desiderat, patienter expectare decet.
units.tr: At the beginning he sets forth the eternal counsel of God concerning the saving of men, when he says that a certain man made a great supper. He calls God the Father a man, not because he became man, but because he deals with us in a thoroughly human manner and in friendship. Matthew writes that a certain king made a wedding feast for his son. So here it is a marriage supper, and the Lord bestows upon it salvation and eternal blessedness, which we shall enjoy in heaven; for this consists chiefly in our being joined in the bond of spiritual marriage with Christ, our only bridegroom. And although this union now begins, it will nevertheless be completed only at evening and at the end of the world, when he will receive us, both bodies and souls, into heaven, so that we may live and reign with him for ever. And this ought to be observed carefully, lest, overcome by impatience at the delay, we wish to be freed before the time and to triumph before we have finished our contest. For just as the Son of God acquired us at the price of his own blood, to make us his bride, so that union costs us many labours, dangers, the cross, and very often much blood as well. It is fitting, therefore, that we endure in these things and patiently await the coming of the bridegroom, for whom this whole fabric of the world longs with groaning.

units.la: Nec temere coenam hanc iampridem paratam fuisse Christus ait. Ea enim locutione aeternum electionis & praedestinationis decretum denotatur, de quo Apostoli testantur, quod & Christum nobis Seruatorem destinarit, & nos in illo elegerit, priusquam mundus hic conderetur. Et ipse Dominus in nouissimo iudicio suis cultoribus dicet: Venite benedicti Patris mei, & possidete Regnum paratum vobis a iactis mundi fundamentis. Commendant haec Dei bonitatem, & salutem nobis ex mera gratia obtingere docent, ne quid nostro arbitrio aut viribus, vel etiam operum nostrorum meritis tribuamus. Quid enim ad salutem nostram conferre potuimus, cum nondum creati fuimus: imo priusquam hic mundus corruptibilis existeret? Aut nunc in nobis aliquid praeuidere potuit Deus, quod tantam salutem mereretur, qui quanti quanti sumus, peccatores sumus, & qui in aeterno exitio mansuri eramus, nisi ille nostri miseritus Filium destinasset, cuius merito redempti ad Regni sui haereditatem veniremus?
units.tr: Nor did Christ say without reason that this supper had been prepared long ago. For by that expression the eternal decree of election and predestination is signified, of which the Apostles testify, that he both appointed Christ as our Saviour and chose us in him before this world was founded. And the Lord himself at the last judgment will say to his worshippers: "Come, blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." These words commend the goodness of God and teach that salvation comes to us from pure grace, so that we attribute nothing to our own will or strength, or even to the merits of our works. For what could we contribute to our salvation, when we had not yet been created? Nay, even before this corruptible world existed? Or what could God foresee in us now that would deserve so great a salvation? We are all sinners, however great or small we are, and we would have remained in eternal destruction, unless he, having pity on us, had appointed his Son, by whose merit we, being redeemed, would come to the inheritance of his kingdom.

units.la: Quamuis vero omnium saeculorum atque gentium credentes iam inde ab aeterno ad nuptias illas coelestes electi & conscripti sint, ordine tamen certo in illis vocandis Deus est visus, & a Iudaeis initium fieri voluit, vt in illis sua cum bonitatis tum iustitiae exempla toti orbi terrarum proponeret. Idin praesenti hus verbis Dominus exponit: Vocauit multos, misitque seruum suum hora coenae, vt diceret vocatis: Venite, quia iam parata sunt omnia: Apud Matthaeum plures serui & saepius missi fuisse dicuntur. Etenim iam olim coepit Deus suam gratiam erga Iudaeos variis modis declarare, postquam cum Abrahamo foedere inito eius posteros reliquos gentibus antepositus, & eodem postea per Mosem & Prophetas vocauit, qui vt numero plures, ita per omnia saecula diffributi fuerunt, ne vlli vocationis istius laetissimae expertes essent. Nam durauit haec ad ipsum Christum vsque, qui praecursorem habuit Ioannem Baptistam, quem totum in hoc fuisse constat, vt quam plurimos Christo adducerer. Sed & ipse Dominus in illis vocandis & alliciendis assiduus fuit, & hinc discipulos Apostolos dedit, qui ipsi quoque salutis doctrinam Iudaeis primum praedicauerunt. Est hoc praeclarum bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui seruos suos selectissimos vnà cum Filio suo dilectio toti saeculis in illis vocandis occupatos esse voluit. At cum non minus benignus erga nos quoque fit, etiam atque etiam cauere nos decet, ne Iudaeorum similes hanc eius gratiam aspernemur.
units.tr: Although believers of all ages and nations have been chosen and enrolled for those heavenly nuptials from eternity, yet God seemed to proceed in a fixed order in calling them, and he willed that the beginning be made with the Jews, so that in them he might set forth to the whole world examples of both his goodness and his justice. The Lord expresses this in the present words: "He called many, and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who were invited: 'Come, for all things are now ready.'" In Matthew, several servants are said to have been sent, and more often. For God began long ago to declare his grace towards the Jews in various ways, after he had made a covenant with Abraham, preferring his remaining posterity to the nations, and afterwards called them by the same means through Moses and the Prophets; and these, as they were many in number, so were they distributed through all ages, so that none might be without a share in this most joyful calling. For this continued down to Christ himself, who had John the Baptist as his forerunner, whose whole task, as is well known, was to lead as many as possible to Christ. But the Lord himself also was constant in calling and drawing them, and from them he gave the Apostles as disciples, who themselves also first preached the doctrine of salvation to the Jews. This is a remarkable proof of the goodness of God, who wished his most select servants, together with his beloved Son, to be occupied through all ages in calling them. But since he is no less kind towards us also, we ought all the more to beware lest, like the Jews, we despise this grace of his.

units.la: Sed modum quoque vocationis huius videre praestat: Venite (inquiunt) quia iam parata sunt omnia. Ita vero officij illos admonuerunt, quod à nobis quoque exigitur. Est hoc, ut veniamus ad Christum in quo nobis parata sunt, quaecunque ad nostram salutem pertinent. Et sic quidem olim Prophetae clamabant: O vos qui sititis, venite ad aquas: & bi quibus non est pecunia, venite. Et ipsius Christi vox in Euangelio auditur: Venite ad me qui laboratis & onerati estis, &c. Item, Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Venitur autem ad illum sola fide, quae animos nostros euehit, ut relictis terrenis illi coniungamur. Ita ipse hoc mysterium interpretatur apud Ioannem, dicens: Qui venit ad me, nequaquam esuriet: & qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam.
units.tr: But it is also worth seeing the manner of this calling: "Come," they say, "for all things are now ready." Thus they admonished those invited of the duty that is also required of us. It is this: that we come to Christ, in whom are ready all those things that pertain to our salvation. So indeed in former times the Prophets cried out: "O you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come." And the voice of Christ himself is heard in the Gospel: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, etc." Likewise: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Now we come to him by faith alone, which lifts up our minds, so that, leaving earthly things, we may be joined to him. Thus he himself interprets this mystery in John, saying: "He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst."

units.la: At non negligenter considerari debet ratio, qua Dei serui Iudaeos, & cum bis omnes homines excitant, ut ad nuptias istas festinent: Quia iam parata sunt (aiunt) omnia. Etenim in Christo Iesu parata & confecta sunt, atque plenissime nobis exhibentur, quaecunque animas esurientes & sitientes saturare atque recreare possunt. Ille enim nobis à Deo Patre factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Ille panis vitae est, qui caelo ad nos delapsus carnem suam dedit pro mundi vita. Ille fons est gratiae uberrimus, qui affluentis conscientiae ardores solus restinguit. Ille agnus Dei est, qui peccatum mundi tollit. Ille denique lux, via, veritas & salus ipsa est, & ut haec omnia in se habet, ita omnibus eadem liberaliter communicat, qui ad ipsum accedunt. Debet ergo haec vox in omnium nostrum auribus atque animis sonare, ne vocati mores nostros neglectamus, neque illos audiamus, qui nobis extra Christum noua salutis adminicula monstrant, quibus meritum illius magna ex parte euacuatur. Parata sunt in illo iam inde ab aeterno, quaecunque ad coenam illam nuptialem & caelestem requiruntur. Ergo nimium stolidi sunt coci illi, qui novis ferculis illam vel augere vel ornare conantur: imo fere venefici sunt, dum humanarum traditionum & nocentissimarum superstitionum toxica admiscent, quae multos salutis incertos faciunt, plerisque autem exitium afferunt. Plus autem quam miseri & calamitosi sunt, qui cum in Christo iam omnia parata & instructa esse audiant, impuris illis sordium impurissimarum sartoribus atque cubicularijs squalidissimis locum dant: quasi vero ab illis aliquid fingi possit Christo suavius, delicatius atque salubrius.
units.tr: But we must consider carefully the reason why the servants of God urge the Jews, and with them all people, to hurry to these wedding feasts: "Because everything is now ready" (they say). For in Christ Jesus everything is ready and complete, and is offered to us in the fullest measure, everything that can satisfy and refresh hungry and thirsty souls. For he has been made by God the Father our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He is the bread of life, who came down from heaven and gave his flesh for the life of the world. He is the most abundant fountain of grace, the only one who quenches the burning of a troubled conscience. He is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Finally, he is the light, the way, the truth and salvation itself, and as he has all these things in himself, so he shares them freely with all who come to him. This voice, then, ought to sound in the ears and minds of all of us, so that we do not neglect the invitation, nor listen to those who show us new aids to salvation apart from Christ, by which the merit of his work is for the most part emptied out. Everything needed for that heavenly wedding feast has been prepared in him from eternity. Therefore those cooks are very foolish who try either to add to that feast or to adorn it with new dishes. Indeed they are almost poisoners, when they mix in the poisons of human traditions and most harmful superstitions, which make many uncertain of their salvation and bring ruin to most. But they are more than wretched and miserable who, when they hear that everything is already prepared and furnished in Christ, give place to those filthy tailors of impurities and most squalid chamberlains, as if anything could be devised that is sweeter, more delicate and more wholesome than Christ.

units.la: Porro videamus Iudaeorum ingratitudinem & stolidam contumaciam, qua oblatam sibi Dei gratiam repulerunt. Comprehendit hanc vno verbo Dominus, dicens: Et omnes coeperunt vno ore, & quasi ex pacto & constituto (tantundem enim significat locutio Graeca, qua Lucas vtitur) se excusare. Et hi quidem reliqui meliores, imo optimi in illa gente fuerunt. Nam apud Matthaeum aliqui seruos, à quibus vocabantur, contumeliis affecisse & trucidauisse dicuntur. Crescit enim suis augmentis siue gradibus impietas, & qui initio Dei gratiam obiter fastidiunt, ij tandem si fortius vrgeantur, furore accensi eius praeconibus vim quoque inferunt. In praesenti Christo satis fuit docere, Iudaeos propria culpa à salute excidisse, cum Deus quidem hanc illis liberaliter obtulerit, ipsi vero eam noluerint ampleti, imo aduersus huius praeconium hostiliter insurrexerint. Quod ipsum de omnibus alijs dici potest: quando quotquot pereunt, vel supino contemptu Dei gratiam negligunt, vel contumeliose fastidiunt, vel etiam plus quam gigantea temeritate oppugnant.
units.tr: Let us now look at the ingratitude and foolish obstinacy of the Jews, by which they rejected the grace of God offered to them. The Lord sums this up in one word, saying: "And they all began with one voice, as if by agreement and design, to make excuses" (for the Greek expression Luke uses means exactly this). And these were the better, indeed the best, of that nation who were left. For in Matthew some are said to have insulted and killed the servants who had been sent to call them. Impiety grows by its own increments and steps: those who at first casually scorn the grace of God, if they are pressed more strongly, are inflamed with rage and even use violence against its heralds. In the present passage it was enough for Christ to teach that the Jews fell from salvation through their own fault, since God indeed offered it to them freely, but they would not embrace it, and rather rose up in hostility against its proclamation. The same can be said of all others: whoever perish either neglect the grace of God with careless contempt, or scorn it insolently, or even attack it with more than gigantic recklessness.

units.la: Caeterum priores illos audiamus, qui excusationis honestos praetextus quaesiuerunt, ne prophani gratiae Dei contemptores esse putarentur. Primus dixit: Agrum emi, & necesse habeo exire, & eum inspicere: rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alter dixit: Iuga boum emi quinque, & proficiscor ad probandum ea: rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alius dixit: Vxorem duxi, & propterea non possum venire. Nominantur hic tria hominum genera, quibus omnes eos comprehendit Dominus, qui rerum huius seculi curis siue studijs, & quidem per se licitis atque concessis, se auocari patiuntur, quo minus ad Regnum Dei accedant. Primum eorum est, qui agros emunt, in quo numerari debent omnes, quos rei domesticae cura impedit. Etenim agricultura per se laudem meretur, cum eam primis parentibus Deus mandauerit, & huius institutum sit, ut homo in sudore vultus sui panem suum comedat. Nec minus licita sunt alia opificia, quibus boni patresfamilias tam sibijpsis quàm suis prospiciunt. Et Paulus infidelibus deteriores esse dicit eos, qui nulla suorum domesticorum cura tanguntur. Sed hic de illis sermo est, quos anxia nimis & irrequieta cura distrahit, dum ut (Propheta loquitur) domus domibus, & agros agris coniungunt, & rei domesticae ita addicti sunt, ut prae hac regnum Dei negligant. Est horum ingens numerus hodie, quos studium hoc ita captivos detinet, ut ne Dominicus quidem diebus ad coetus sacros veniant, neque verbum Dei audiant, si quae lucri faciendi spes sese offerat. Secundum genus eos habet, qui boves emunt: quo omnes denotantur, qui ex mercatura qualicunque quaestum faciunt. Licet hoc quoque, & rerum usus docet, necessaria esse commercia inter homines, quando non omnis fert omnia tellus: neque iustum aut aequum esset, aliquem in aliorum gratiam mercibus aliunde inferendis absque omni lucro defatigari. At rursus hic quoque eos perstringit Christus, qui facultatibus suis augendis ita intenti sunt, ut nulla prorsus vitae & salutis aeternae cura tangantur, neque Apostoli regulam observant, qui eos qui emunt ita affectos esse iubet, quasi nihil possideant: & eos qui hoc mundo utuntur viuere docet, ne eo abutantur. Et isti quoque plurimi hodie passim inveniuntur, quibus suavissimus est lucri odor ex re qualibet, & qui multis mensibus aut annis conciones sacras prorsus negligere malunt, quam leuem rerum suarum iacturam facere. Tertio genere continentur qui uxores duxerunt, & ideo non possunt venire. Quo loco non simpliciter damnantur omnes, qui uxoribus coniugij vinculo copulantur (hoc enim sanctum & thorus coniugalis impolutus est), daemoniorum autem doctrina ab Apostolo dicitur, quae nubere prohibet) sed qui uxorii nimis sunt, & ut vel eas obtineant quas volunt, aut uxoribus commodioribus utantur, religionem minus curant, & frequenter propter coniuges lucris alienis communicant. Et isti quidem omnes excusatos se haberi cupiunt, & rationes praetexunt graves atque minime contemnendas si carnis iudicium in hac causa aliquid valeret. Primi enim necessitate se urgeri dicunt: alteri utilitatem adducunt, cui fere in commercijs necessitas quoq; coniuncta est: postremi impossibilitatem allegant, ad quam (ut vulgo aiunt) nemo debet obstringi. Et satis constat quam magnificis verbis quamq; gravibus argumentis suas excusationes amplificare & exornare soleant, qui hodie in religione ambidextri sunt, & in utrunque latus claudicant. Multi denique tanto artificio illud faciunt, ut tunc maxime gloriam Dei & salutem propriam curare videantur, quando ut sua privata commoda retineant, Regnum caelorum prorsus negligunt. At docet hoc loco Christus inutiles esse iństas delitias, quas sibi ipsis faciunt homines carni & mundoediti. Ut enim his impedimentis Iudaei detenti salutis suae iacturam fecerunt: ita nihil melius sibi polliceri poterunt, quotquot hodie eosdem laqueos sibi iniici patiuntur. Meminerimus ergo speciem huius mundi euanidam esse, & proinde indignam, cuius gratia vocationem Dei negligamus. Itaque regulam eam sequamur in rerum huius saeculi usu, quam ex Pauli ad Corinth. Epistola adduximus.
units.tr: But let us listen to those first guests, who sought honest pretexts for excuse, so that they would not be thought profane despisers of the grace of God. The first said: "I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it; I pray you, hold me excused." And another said: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them; I pray you, hold me excused." And another said: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Three kinds of men are named here, and under them the Lord comprehends all those who allow themselves to be drawn away from coming to the kingdom of God by the cares or pursuits of this world, even by things that are in themselves lawful and permitted. The first kind is of those who buy fields, under which all should be counted whom the care of domestic affairs hinders. For agriculture is in itself praiseworthy, since God commanded it to our first parents, and it is his ordinance that man should eat his bread in the sweat of his face. Other trades are no less lawful, by which good heads of households provide for themselves and for their own. And Paul says that those who are not moved by any care for their households are worse than unbelievers. But here the discussion concerns those whom an anxious and restless care distracts, who, as the prophet says, join house to house and field to field, and are so devoted to domestic affairs that for their sake they neglect the kingdom of God. Today there is a vast number of these, whom this pursuit holds so captive that they do not come to the sacred assemblies even on the Lord's days, nor hear the word of God, if any hope of gain presents itself. The second kind includes those who buy oxen; by this all are designated who make a profit from trade of whatever sort. This too is lawful, and experience of affairs teaches that trade between men is necessary, since not every land bears every thing; nor would it be just or fair for someone to labour without any gain to bring goods from elsewhere for the benefit of others. Yet here again Christ strikes at those who are so intent on increasing their wealth that they are not touched by any care for life and eternal salvation, and do not observe the Apostle's rule, which bids those who buy to be as if they possessed nothing, and teaches those who use this world to live so as not to abuse it. Very many such people are found everywhere today, for whom the sweet smell of gain from any thing whatever is most pleasant, and who prefer to neglect sacred sermons for many months or years rather than suffer a slight loss of their property. The third kind comprises those who have taken wives, and therefore cannot come. Here not all who are joined to wives by the bond of marriage are condemned (for this is holy, and the marriage bed is undefiled; it is the teaching of demons, which the Apostle names, that forbids marriage). Rather, those are condemned who are excessively fond of their wives, and who, in order either to obtain the wives they desire or to enjoy more comfortable ones, care little for religion, and often for the sake of their spouses share in other people's gains. All of these wish to be held excused, and they put forward reasons that are serious and by no means to be despised, if the judgement of the flesh had any weight in this matter. The first say they are pressed by necessity; the second bring forward profit, to which necessity is almost always joined in trade; the last allege an impossibility, to which (as people commonly say) no one ought to be bound. And it is well known with what grand words and weighty arguments they are accustomed to magnify and adorn their excuses, those who today are double-minded in religion and limp on both sides. Finally, many do this with such skill that they seem to seek the glory of God and their own salvation most of all at the very moment when, in order to keep their private advantages, they wholly neglect the kingdom of heaven. But Christ teaches in this place that these delights, which men born of the flesh and the world make for themselves, are useless. For as the Jews, held back by these hindrances, suffered the loss of their salvation, so those who today allow the same snares to be laid for them can promise themselves nothing better. Let us therefore remember that the appearance of this world is fleeting, and so unworthy of being the reason for neglecting the call of God. Accordingly let us follow in our use of the things of this age the rule which we cited from Paul's letter to the Corinthians.

units.la: Cum vero tantae tamque efficaces sint huius mundi illecebrae, ut earum quoque rerum studia, quae per se licitae & necessariae sunt, nos a via salutis revocent, quanto maiori cura & diligentia cauteri debent, quae disertus Dei verbus damnantur? Nocet nimium rei domesticae studium: quid ergo fiet, si auaritia inescati fraudes & impostures exerceamus? Si usus iniquis eos grauemus, qui nostra beneficentia debebant subleuari? Si item ex sanguine & belli non necessarijs quaestum captemus? Impedit multos coniugalis amor, qui & honestus & ad vitam bene instituendam necessarius est: quid igitur sperare possunt, qui libidines vagas sectantur, & scortatione atque adulteriis foedis sese polluunt? Procul ergo arceri debent, qui homines in perditissimis scelerum studijs seruari posse sibi persuadent: quasi vero aliqua inter Christum & Belial coniunctio, aut inter Regnum Dei & diaboli seruitium aliqua societas esse possit. Etenim cum tanta sit nostrae naturae & ingenij corruptio seu prauitas, ut ex ijs obstacula aeternae salutis nobis faciamus, quae Deus ut vitae honestae & piae transigendae adminicula sint, instituit, quis aliud quam praesens exitium ex ijs sperare potest, qua & Dei verbo & naturae legibus prohibentur? Semper ergo vigilemus, & Christi doctrinam sequamur, qui eos demum suos discipulos & Regni caelorum haeredes fore docet, qui per Spiritus virtutem renati carnem mortificant, seque ipsos abnegant.
units.tr: But since the allurements of this world are so great and so powerful that even the pursuits of those things which are in themselves lawful and necessary call us back from the way of salvation, with how much greater care and diligence must we guard against those things which the plain word of God condemns? Excessive devotion to domestic affairs does harm: what then will happen if, enticed by greed, we practise frauds and swindles? If we burden with unjust usury those who ought to have been relieved by our kindness? If we likewise make profit from blood and from war that is not necessary? Marital love, which is both honourable and necessary for living a good life, hinders many: what, then, can those hope for who pursue wandering lusts and defile themselves with whoredom and foul adulteries? Those who persuade themselves that men can be kept safe in the most destructive pursuits of sin must be kept far away: as if there could be any union between Christ and Belial, or any fellowship between the kingdom of God and servitude to the devil. For since our nature and disposition is so corrupt and depraved that we make out of the things God instituted as aids to living an honourable and pious life obstacles to our eternal salvation, what else can anyone hope from them than present destruction, when they are forbidden both by the word of God and by the laws of nature? Let us therefore always be watchful, and follow the teaching of Christ, who says that those alone will be his disciples and heirs of the kingdom of heaven who, born again by the power of the Spirit, mortify the flesh and deny themselves.

units.la: Excitet nos ad hoc studium Iudaicæ gentis exemplum, cui pœnas horrendas in præsenti Dominus denuntiat. Nam serui ad herum redijsse, & ei nuntiauisse dicitur, quid inuitati responderint. Quod non eo sensu accipi debet, quasi internuntijs vllis Deus opus habeat: sed vt sciamus eum nihil eorum ignorare, quæ inter suæ gratiæ præcones & eiusdem contemptores fiunt. Deinde iratus est vehementer, & quidem merito. Si enim hominibus stomachum mouet ingratitudo, qua se abijs sper ni sentiunt, de quibus optimè sunt meriti, num quis Deum iniustũ dixerit, si aduersus suæ gratiæ & Regni contemptores excandescat? Vidit hoc Ioannes Baptista, qui iræ huius causam simul & veœmentiam expressurus dicebat: Qui non paret Filio, non videbit vitam: sed ira Dei manet super eum. Ergo non tam leuis est incredulitatis & spreti Euangelij culpa, quàm multi existimant. Quid enim ira Dei grauius fingi potest? Fremitus leonis (inquit Solomon) est ira Regis. Quid igitur de Deo irato dicemus, de quo Propheta scribit: Terra ardet ex illius aspectu, & totus orbis vna cum degentibus in eo? Coram facie indignationis eius quis persistet? In furore eius quis durabit? Effunditur vt ignis furor eius, & filices ab eo dissoluuntur, &c. Quid, quòd electus intolerabile prorsus est salutiferam Dei ipsos in ira sua castigantis manum sentire, sicuti Dauid non vno loco testatur? Quid ergo ijs miserius & infelicius esse potest, super quos ira illa perpetuò manet? Id vero Christi contemptoribus Baptista ex Spiritus sancti suggestione minatur: neq; melius quid sperari potest, eò quòd tales non solùm gratiam Dei fastidiunt, verumetiam ipsum mendacij arguunt, quasi de Filio falsò testatus sit, & nos ad epulas fictitias & inanes inuitat. Idcò apud Matthæum Rex iste missis exercitibus suis homicidas illos atq; ingratos trucidauisse atque vrbem eorum incendisse dicitur. Quibus verbis totius gentis & vrbis Hierosolymæ excidium denuntiat, quod non multò post secutum esse scimus. In præsenti addit: Dico vobis neminem virorum illorum, qui inuitati fuerant, gustaturum cœnam meam. Quæ comminatio priori illa grauior est, quia illos à Regni cœlorum hæreditate excludit, & vniuersam salutis spem semel aufert.
