Vbi nos meminisse oportet, hæc ita Iudis denuntiari, vt non minus nobis quoque seruiant, qui in illorum locum successimus, si simili ingratitudine & contumacia iram Dei prouocemus. Qui enim naturalibus ramis non pepercit, multò minus ijs parcet, qui ex oleastro defracti & in stirpem sanctam insiti tantum eius beneficium non agnoscunt. Pereunt ergo hi quoque quoad corpus & fortunas omnes: & (quod grauius multò est) exclusi à mensa Christi & omni salutis spe destituti famem illam diram sentiunt, qua animæ quoque illorum contabescunt.
units.tr: The example of the Jewish nation should stir us to this diligence, for whom the Lord now threatens dreadful punishments. For the servants are said to have returned to their master and reported to him what the invited men answered. This should not be taken to mean that God needs any messengers, but so that we may know that he is ignorant of nothing that happens between the heralds of his grace and its despisers. Then he was greatly angered, and rightly so. For if men are provoked to anger by the ingratitude of those by whom they feel themselves spurned, to whom they have done the greatest service, will anyone call God unjust if he flares up against the despisers of his grace and kingdom? John the Baptist saw this, and in order to express both the cause and the vehemence of this wrath he said: "He who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him." So the guilt of unbelief and of despising the gospel is not so slight as many think. For what heavier thing can be imagined than the wrath of God? "The roaring of a lion," says Solomon, "is the anger of a king." What then shall we say of an angry God, of whom the prophet writes: "The earth burns at his presence, and the whole world together with those who dwell in it. Before the face of his indignation who can stand? In his fury who can endure? His fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken up by him," and so on? Moreover, is it not utterly intolerable for the elect to feel the saving hand of God chastising them in his anger, as David testifies in more than one place? What then can be more wretched and unhappy than those upon whom that wrath abides for ever? This is what John, prompted by the Holy Spirit, threatens to the despisers of Christ; nor can anything better be hoped for, since such people not only scorn God's grace but also accuse him of lying, as if he had testified falsely about the Son, and invite us to fictitious and empty feasts. Therefore in Matthew this king is said to have sent his armies, to have slain those murderous and ungrateful men and burned their city. In these words he foretells the destruction of the whole nation and of the city of Jerusalem, which we know followed not long after. In the present passage he adds: "I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper." This threat is heavier than the former, because it excludes them from the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven and at once takes away all hope of salvation. Here we must remember that these things are threatened to the Jews in such a way that they serve no less for us, who have succeeded into their place, if we provoke God's wrath by like ingratitude and obstinacy. For he who did not spare the natural branches will much less spare those who, broken off from the wild olive and grafted into the holy stock, do not acknowledge his benefit. So these too perish, all of them, in body and fortune; and (what is much graver) shut out from the table of Christ and deprived of all hope of salvation, they feel that dreadful hunger by which their souls too waste away.

units.la: Porrò ne quis æternum illud Dei decretum labefactatum aut omnino irritum factum putaret, eò quòd Iudæi accedere noluerunt, qui soli aliis omnibus præteritis inuitati & vocati esse videban-tur: alteram parabolæ huius partem interserit Dominus, qua de gentium vocatione disserit. Facit hæc Iudæus ad pœnæ suæ amplificationem, quia illa ipsorum ingratitudinem ex parte vltus est Deus, quando alios in illorum locum surrogauit. Idem enim passi sunt quod mulier adultera, quæ non solùm ab ædibus & consuetudine mariti repellitur, sed aliam ab eo dustam esse videt, quàm in pretio habet & diligit. Et ita olim per Mosem minatus fuerat Deus, dicens: Ipsi me prouocaue-runt ad indignationem in eo, qui non est Deus, ad iracundiam me irritarunt vanitatibus suis: & ego illos quoque prouocabo in eo qui non est populus, in gente stulta irritabo eos. Et huius generis multa in Prophetarum scriptis occurrunt: quorum omnium consideratio nos admonet, nihil Dei gratiæ & Regno eius decedere, etiamsi illud improbè aspernentur, qui præ alijs id amplecti debebant. Nec enim vllì genti aut ordini hominum ita ille alligatus est aut obstrictus, vt non possit illud aliò transferre, si quos ingratos & iniquos suæ bonitatis æstimatores esse sentiat. Et vt in magna domo non perit cœna iam parata, etiamsi ex inuitatorum numero multi emaneant: ita multò facilius est Deo conuiuas inuenire, quos suæ mensæ participes faciat. Nemi-nem ergo terreat multorum incredulitas & defectio: nemo etiam præsenti sua dignitate efferatur, vt Deum sibi perpetuò obstrictum fore putet. Sed huius etiam alterius partis singula capita excutiamus.
units.tr: Furthermore, lest anyone should think that God's eternal decree was weakened or made wholly void because the Jews refused to come, they who alone, all others passed over, seemed to have been invited and called, the Lord inserts the other part of this parable, in which he speaks of the calling of the Gentiles. This tells against the Jews, to magnify their punishment, since God has in part avenged their ingratitude when he substituted others in their place. For they have suffered what an adulterous wife suffers, who is not only cast out of her husband's house and company, but sees another taken by him, whom he values and loves. So God had long before threatened through Moses, saying: "They have provoked me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have moved me to anger with their vanities; and I will provoke them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will anger them with a foolish nation." Many things of this kind occur in the writings of the prophets, and consideration of all of them admonishes us that nothing is lost to God's grace or to his kingdom, even if those who ought to have embraced it before others shamefully spurn it. For he is not so bound or tied to any nation or order of men that he cannot transfer it elsewhere, if he perceives them to be ungrateful and unjust judges of his goodness. And just as in a great house a meal already prepared is not wasted, even if many of those invited fall away, so it is far easier for God to find guests whom he may make partakers of his table. Let no one therefore be frightened by the unbelief and defection of many; and let no one be puffed up by his present dignity, as if he thought God would be bound to him for ever. But let us also examine the individual points of this other part.

units.la: Primùm dicitur seruo: Abi citò in vicos & plateas vrbis, & pauperes ac mancos, claudosque & cæcos huc introducito. Per vicos & plateas, loca ab Israelitarũ Republica exclusa intelligit, & proinde fore docet, vt in viam gentium diuertant salutis æternæ pracones, quod hucusque non licuerat, vt Christi verba ad Apostolos Matth.decimo Cap.testantur. Iubet autem pauperes ac mancos, claudos item & caecos introduci, idq; de gentibus dicit, non solum ex Iudaeorum iudicio aut fensuloquens, qui omnes populos contemptui habebant: sed vt simul innuat, quae omnium conditio hucusq; fuerit, qui extra Ecclesiae suae pomeria sub tenebrarum potestate vixerunt. Erant hi revera pauperes & omnibus donis spiritualibus destituti, nihil eorum comparare sibi poterant, quae ad vitam caelestem atque aeternam necessaria sunt. Itaque famelici per suorum Philosophorum vias vagabantur, quae miseros & infelices simul in sectas diuersas distrahebat. Adhaec manci, claudi & caeci erat, cum vires non haberent aliquas, quibus ea facere possent quae Deo probantur, neq; in vijs eius ambularent, imo ne viderent quidem Regni caelestis mysteria. Accedebant his malis oraculorum ambigua responsa, cultus illiciti & magna ex parte prophani & crudeles, effrenis denique peccandi licentia. Quid multis? ea omnino fuit gentium conditio, quam Paulus ad Ephesios his verbis describit: Memententote vos quondam Gentes in carne fuisse absq; Christo, abalienatos a Republica Israelis: extraneos a pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, & Dei expertes in mundo. Veruntamen tales colligi & per Euangelium ad nuptias illas caelestes & vere beatas vocari voluit Deus: vt & suae bonitatis specimen luculentum daret, & simul ostenderet eos demum idoneos esse ad Regnum Dei, qui suae inopiae sensu ita tanguntur, vt eam dissimulare nullo modo possint: qui item se caecos, claudos & mancos esse agnoscunt. Hi enim bonitatem eius magni faciunt, Christum medicum admittunt, & eius consilijs obtemperant, cum e contra hypocritae iustitiarij gratiam Dei perinde vt ipsis minime necessariam fastidiant, medicum excludant, & ad eius manum sine contactu fremant atque tumultuentur. Docet hoc alibi Christus Pharisaeorum & publicanorum atque meretricum exemplo, quando hos illis anteire dicit in Regno Dei. Et hodie videmus facilius esse homines militiae & flagitijs manifestis deditos conuertere, quam Monachum aliquem, quem propria iustitia & sanctimonia fiducia inflat.
units.tr: First the servant is told: "Go quickly into the streets and squares of the city, and bring in here the poor and maimed, the lame and the blind." By the streets and squares he means places shut out from the commonwealth of Israel, and so he teaches that the heralds of eternal salvation will turn aside into the way of the Gentiles, which had not been lawful until then, as Christ's words to the Apostles in Matthew chapter 10 attest. He bids the poor, maimed, lame and blind be brought in, and he says this of the Gentiles, speaking not merely from the judgment or opinion of the Jews, who held all peoples in contempt, but also to hint at what the condition of all had been until then who lived outside the bounds of his Church under the power of darkness. These were indeed poor and destitute of all spiritual gifts; they could acquire for themselves none of the things necessary for heavenly and eternal life. So they wandered hungry along the paths of their own philosophers, which drew the wretched and unhappy at the same time into divergent sects. Besides, they were maimed, lame and blind, since they had no strength by which they could do what pleases God, nor did they walk in his ways, nor even see the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom. To these evils were added the ambiguous answers of oracles, unlawful worship, for the most part profane and cruel, and finally an unbridled licence to sin. To be brief, such was the condition of the Gentiles, which Paul describes to the Ephesians in these words: "Remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world." Nevertheless God willed such people to be gathered and called through the gospel to those heavenly and truly blessed nuptials, both to give a clear sign of his goodness and at the same time to show that those are at last fit for the kingdom of God who are so touched by a sense of their poverty that they cannot in any way dissemble it, who likewise acknowledge themselves to be blind, lame and maimed. For these esteem his goodness highly, admit Christ as physician and obey his counsels; whereas on the contrary the hypocritical self-righteous, as if God's grace were in no way necessary to them, scorn it, shut out the physician, and fume and riot at his hand without touching it. Christ teaches this elsewhere by the example of the Pharisees, the tax collectors and the prostitutes, when he says that these go before them into the kingdom of God. And today we see that it is easier to convert men given to soldiering and open vices than some monk, whom confidence in his own righteousness and holiness puffs up.

units.la: Sed pergamus in parabolae expositione, qua admirabilis illa Patris caelestis bonitas erga mundum hunc magis illustratur. Cum enim possit vocatos pauperes, claudos, mancos & caecos adhuc locus vacaret, dicit seruo: Abi in vias & sepes, & coge ingredi, vt impleatur domus mea. Vbi rursus de ijs agitur, qui a Iudaeorum Republica exclusi per diuersas suarum opinionum vias, vel alia potius, erraverunt, & ad sepes peccatorum, quae nos a Deo dirimunt, securi quieuerunt, inque desiderijs suis pravis voluptuati sunt. Hos cogi vult, vt domus impleatur. Habet enim certum suo rum electorum numerum Deus, quem omnino compleri oportet, neque in Ecclesia sua locum alium vacare vult. Obseruabis autem, quod cum priores solummodo vocati sint, hos cogi oportuit vt ingrederentur. Ita enim admonet, non eodem omnes ingenio praeditos esse, & proinde non eadem docendi ratione apud omnes vti debere eos, quibus verbi praedicatio commissa est. Sunt enim quibus simplex doctrina sufficit. Alij insuper admonitione crebriori opus habent. Multis necessaria est adhortatio grauior. Apud aliquos autem nihil proficias, nisi obiurgatione & increpatione vehementiori vtaris, & eos ad Dei tribunal citando cogas, vt a vijs suis peruersis conuertantur. Quod Paulus obseruans, Timotheum iubet tempestiue & intempestiue instare: arguere item, obiurgare & exhortari, prout auditorum ingenia opus habere videbit. Vehementer ergo fallluntur, qui Veritatis doctrinam simpliciter & absque omni errorum aut scelerum redargutione proponi volunt. Quid enim illa proficias, quando multi ne increpatione quidem liberiori monentur, & nisi publica quoque magistratus authoritas accedat, quae reluctantes cogat relicti aperte superstitionibus & flagitijs intra Ecclesiae septa ingredi & Dei verbum audire? Vidit hoc olim Diuus Augustinus in Donatistas, & ideo eos ciuili etiam potestate coercendos esse censuit. Et hodie constat multos pia Christianorum principum seueritate seruari, qui in erroribus suis perirent, & multos, alios seducerent, nisi publicis edictis & poenarum metu coercerentur. Et frequenter fit, vt qui inuiti coguntur ad Ecclesiae coetus, postea cum voluptate Verbum salutis audiant, vbi illius dulcedinem semel gustauerunt.
units.tr: But let us go on with the exposition of the parable, in which that wonderful goodness of the heavenly Father towards this world is set forth more clearly. For although there was still room after the poor, the lame, the maimed and the blind had been called, he tells the servant: "Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." Here again it is a question of those who, excluded from the commonwealth of the Jews, have wandered along various paths of their own opinions, or rather along other paths, and have securely settled at the hedges of sins, which separate us from God, and have delighted in their wicked desires. He wants these to be compelled, so that the house may be filled. For God has a definite number of his elect, which must by all means be completed, and he does not wish any other place in his Church to remain empty. You will observe, moreover, that since the former were only invited, these had to be compelled to enter. For he thereby warns that not all are endowed with the same disposition, and that therefore those to whom the preaching of the Word has been entrusted ought not to use the same method of teaching with everyone. For some are satisfied with simple teaching. Others need more frequent admonition. Many need a more serious exhortation. With some, however, you will accomplish nothing unless you use more vehement rebuke and reproof, and by summoning them to God's tribunal compel them to turn from their perverse ways. Paul observed this, and so he bids Timothy to press on in season and out of season, also to reprove, rebuke and exhort, as he sees the hearers' dispositions require. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who want the doctrine of truth to be set forth simply, without any refutation of errors or sins. For what would you accomplish when many are not warned even by a freer rebuke, and unless the public authority of the magistrate also comes in, to compel the unwilling, who have been left openly in superstitions and crimes, to enter within the walls of the Church and hear the Word of God? St Augustine saw this long ago in the case of the Donatists, and therefore judged that they should be restrained even by civil power. And today it is clear that many are kept safe by the pious severity of Christian princes, who would otherwise perish in their errors, and who would lead many others astray, unless they were restrained by public edicts and the fear of punishment. And it often happens that those who are unwillingly compelled to the assemblies of the Church afterwards hear the Word of salvation with delight, once they have tasted its sweetness.

units.la: Adijcitur autem istis apud Matthaeum, quid cum illo actum sit, qui sine veste nuptiali ingressus ad coenam illam accubuit. Iussit eum Rex ligatis manibus & pedibus eius in tenebras exteriores con-
units.tr: Matthew adds to these things what happened to the man who entered the wedding feast without a wedding garment and reclined at that banquet. The King ordered that he be bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness

units.la: Eph 5. res conijci. Quo loco adumbratur, inter eos etiã, qui ex gentibus Iudæis surrogandi sint, fore semper aliquos, qui suæ professioni minus respondeant, quos tandem rursus eijci oporteat, ne suis sordibus Ecclesiam polluant. Itaque admonet, ut qui ad nuptias illas accedere instituerunt, non sine veste nuptiali veniant. Est hæc ipse Christus, secundum illud Apostoli: Quicunque in Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Dicitur is vestis nostra, quia nobis à Deo Patre, sapientia, iustitia, & sanctificatio factus est, adeo ut suo merito nostra vitia tegat, suis autem virtutibus atque donis nos ornet, ut in Patris conspectu comparere possimus. Induitur autem fide, quæ nos illi inserit, & cuius effectus est, quod tota nostra vita, actiones item & studia illum loquuntur atq; referunt. Est igitur cœna ista miraculorum plena, cum unus & idem Christus noster cibus, potus & vestis fit, & tanta cum liberalitate ad hæc omnia sese offerat hominibus indignissimis, qui non solum negligi, sed exterminari quoq; merebantur. Quò magis nos anniti decet, ut ad eius mensam non indigni accedamus. Vocat enim adhuc hodie per Euangelij prædicationem omnes homines. Vocatione hanc multi contemnunt, qui optimi & sanctissimi haberi volunt. Multi nudæ professionis titulo turgidi sufficere arbitrantur, si cœtibus sacris intersint, Sacramentis Ecclesiæ communicent, & se Christianos esse dicant, licet interim quam ore profitentur, factis negent. Possunt bi aliquandiu inter Christi convivas locum aliquem obtinere, quorum oculos fallere non admodum difficile est. Sed quando ipse Dominus ingredietur, ut qui nam & quales venerint, spectet, tunc sordes suas occultare non poterunt, & illo ipsos examinante obmutescent. Quid enim Deo respondeant, qui à propria conscientia accusantur? Meminerint ergo omnes, nos ea conditione ad salutis æternæ hæreditatem vocari, ut procul relictis sordibus pristinus Iesum Christum induamus, qui nostram carnem mortalem assumere dignatus est, ut nos Dei Filios & regni sui cohæredes faceret. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Eph. 5. (thrown out). In this passage it is foreshadowed that among those who are to be admitted from the Gentiles and the Jews there will always be some who fall short of their profession, and who must in the end be cast out again, lest they pollute the Church with their filth. Accordingly he admonishes that those who have resolved to come to those wedding feasts should not come without a wedding garment. This is Christ himself, according to the saying of the Apostle: "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." That garment is said to be ours because God the Father has made him our wisdom, righteousness and sanctification, so that by his merit he covers our vices, and by his virtues and gifts adorns us, that we may appear in the sight of the Father. He is put on by faith, which grafts us into him, and the result of which is that our whole life, and our actions and pursuits likewise, speak and refer to him. This feast, therefore, is full of wonders, since the one and the same Christ becomes our food, drink and clothing, and with such generosity he offers himself for all these things to men most unworthy, who deserved not merely to be neglected but also to be destroyed. All the more reason, then, that we should strive to approach his table not unworthily. For even today, through the preaching of the Gospel, he calls all men. Many despise this calling, though they wish to be thought the best and most holy. Many, puffed up with the mere title of profession, think it enough to attend the sacred assemblies, to share in the Sacraments of the Church, and to say that they are Christians, although in the meantime they deny by their deeds what they profess with their mouths. These may for some time obtain a place among Christ's guests, and it is not very difficult to deceive their eyes. But when the Lord himself comes in to see who and what sort of people have come, then they will not be able to hide their filth, and under his scrutiny they will be struck dumb. For what will they answer God, who are accused by their own conscience? Let all therefore remember that we are called to the inheritance of eternal salvation on this condition: that, having put aside the filth of our former life, we put on Jesus Christ, who deigned to take upon himself our mortal flesh, so that he might make us sons of God and co-heirs of his kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLVI.

units.la: Ibat autem turba multa cum eo: & conuersus dixit eis: Si quis venit ad me, & non odit patrem suum, & matrem, & vxorem, & liberos, & fratres & sorores, atque adeo etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Et quisquis non portat crucem suam, & non sequitur me, non potest meus esse discipulus.
units.tr: Now a great crowd went with him, and he turned and said to them: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. And whoever does not carry his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple."

units.la: DOminus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus, in parabola cœnæ nuptialis de Iudaicæ gentis repudio & gentium vocatione ita disseruit, ut simul omnia complexus sit, quæ de regno Dei & æternæ salutis negotio dici possunt, aut nobis cognitu necessaria sunt. Docet enim hanc nobis æterno Dei decreto ex gratuita misericordia præparatam, & nos priusquam mundus hic crearetur, in ipso inuitatos, id est electos esse, ut eius consortes efficiamur. Ostendit deinde hoc Dei decretum per Euangelij prædicationem revelari, qua etiam vocamur, adeoq; cogimur interdum, ut per multa obstacula ad illam penetremus. Ad hac præcipuas quoque remoras expositi, quibus plerique hominum detinentur, quò minus vocationi diuinæ obtemperent: Sunt hæ avaritia & immodicum rei domesticæ studium, voluptatum item huius seculi illecebræ. Vnde apparet salutem quidem nobis ex gratia absque vllo nostrorum meritorum respectu offerri, perditionis autem causam in nobis hærere, qui res vanas & inutiles illi præferimus. Deniq; quales esse oporteat eos docuit, qui in beatis illis nuptijs locum suum retinere volunt, ne denuo repulsi in tenebras exteriores eijciantur. Quam partem quia Lucas breuitatis studio omisit, consulto Christi verba subijcit, quæ modo recitauimus, quibus aperte traditur, qui nam veri & Germani illius discipuli sint, quidue eos facere conueniat, qui ipsum cum fructu audire, & salutis, quam nobis acquisiuit, hæredes fieri cupiunt.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, in the parable of the wedding feast, discoursed on the rejection of the Jewish nation and the calling of the Gentiles in such a way that he embraced at once everything that can be said about the kingdom of God and the business of eternal salvation, or that is necessary for us to know. For he teaches that this kingdom was prepared for us by God's eternal decree, out of free mercy, and that before this world was created we were invited in him, that is, chosen, so that we might become his partners. He then shows that this decree of God is revealed through the preaching of the Gospel, by which we are also called, and that we are sometimes compelled to press through many obstacles to reach it. He also sets out the chief hindrances by which most people are held back from obeying the divine calling. These are avarice, an excessive devotion to domestic affairs, and likewise the allurements of the pleasures of this age. From this it is evident that salvation is indeed offered to us by grace, without any regard to our merits, but that the cause of perdition lies within us, since we prefer empty and useless things to it. Finally, he taught what sort of people those must be who wish to keep their place at that blessed wedding, lest they be rejected again and cast out into the outer darkness. Because Luke, in his concern for brevity, omitted this part, he appends the words of Christ that we have just recited, in which it is plainly taught who are the true and genuine disciples of that Lord, and what those ought to do who wish to hear him to good profit and to become heirs of the salvation he has won for us.

units.la: Occasionem vero huius doctrinæ seu admonitionis vno verbo exprimit Euangelista, quando multam populi turbam illi affuisse scribit, ad quos conuersus ista dixit. At quæ causa eum mouit, ut de bis, quæ carni durissima & iniquissima videntur, apud eos verba faceret, qui tanto studio ipsum sequebantur, & potius promissis magnificis & blanditiis in officio debebant retineri?
units.tr: The evangelist expresses in a single word the occasion of this doctrine or admonition, when he writes that a large crowd of people was present, and it was to them that he turned and spoke these things. But what reason moved him to speak about those things that seem harshest and most unjust to the flesh, to people who followed him with such eagerness, and who ought rather to have been held to their duty by great promises and flattery?

units.la: Gal. 3. Nimirum ea, quod plerique non ex animo sequerentur, neque salutis aeternae aut regni Dei studio arderent, sed quae carnis sunt quaererent. Patet hoc satis euidenter ex iis quae non multo post acciderunt. Etenim verisimile est multos se illi coniunxisse, quod audirent tempus illud ita instare, quo iniunctum sibi a patre munus absoluere ipsum oportteat: et quia in illo regnum terrenum, victoriis, epulis et gloria florentissimum somniabant, singuli sibi ipsis montes aureos pollicebantur. At omnes illi, cum a discipulo proditum in Sacerdotum manus venisse et praesidis quoque Romani sententia damnatum esse viderent, turpi defectione facta nimis aperte offenderunt, quis illis antea animus fuisset. Grauem ergo et iustam causam habuit de his differendi, quorum nos nunquam non meminisse oportebat. Hoc enim illud scandalum est, ad quod plerique offenduntur, qui Christum profitentur: quod nimirum terrena potius quam caelestia spectant. In hoc ipsos quoque Apostolos peccauisse non semel diximus. Et hodie vix quicquam vulgarius est. Huic autem errori debemus, quod multi perfide deficiunt a fide, quando huius constantiam quam maxime testari debebant: quod item multi doctri nam Euangelij calumniantur, et ne a manifesta quidem atq; atrocissimis conuitijs sibi temperant. Semper ergo nobis in mentem veniat, Regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo, neque huius seculi opes, honores atq; voluptates ab eo debere sperari, qui ipse in terris pauper et omnium egenus, adhuc inglorius vixit et omne genus miseriae sustinuit. Sed ipsum loquentem audiamus, qui duabus regulis totam hanc causam comprehendit.
units.tr: Gal. 3. Surely because most of them did not follow him from the heart, nor burned with zeal for eternal salvation or the kingdom of God, but sought the things of the flesh. This is clear enough from what happened not long afterwards. For it is likely that many joined him because they heard that the time was drawing near when he would have to complete the task laid upon him by the Father, and because they dreamed that in his kingdom, most flourishing with victories, feasts and glory, each would be promised golden mountains for himself. But when all of them saw that he had been betrayed by a disciple, had come into the hands of the priests, and had been condemned by the sentence of the Roman governor, they made a shameful defection and revealed all too plainly what their attitude had been before. He therefore had a grave and just reason for speaking of those things that we ought never to have forgotten. For this is the stumbling block at which many who profess Christ take offence: namely, that they look to earthly things rather than heavenly. We have said more than once that the apostles themselves sinned in this respect. And today nothing is more common. Yet from this error it comes that many faithless people fall away from the faith precisely when they ought most of all to bear witness to its constancy; and likewise that many slander the doctrine of the Gospel and do not restrain themselves even from open and most atrocious insults. Let us therefore always keep in mind that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and that the riches, honours and pleasures of this age ought not to be hoped for from him who himself lived on earth poor, in need of everything, without glory, and endured every kind of misery. But let us hear him speaking, who comprehends this whole matter in two rules.

units.la: Prima est: Si quis venit ad me, et non odit patrem suum et matrem, et uxorem et liberos, et fratres et sorores, atque adeo etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Sunt haec verba non ofcitanter excutienda, ne vel nobisipsis blandiamur pernitiose, dum ab officio nostro discedimus, vel sub pietatis praetextu impij efficiamur. Nec enim hoc iubet Dominus, ut extinctus naturalibus animi affectionibus, quas Graeci στοργὰς vocant, parentes iniusto odio prosequamur, coniugem cum liberis concilicemus, fratres et sorores crudeliter negligamus, aut praecipiti temeritate vitae nostrae cursum violenter abrumpamus. Nam ut in veteri Lege Deus pietatem in parentes magnifice commendat: ita Christum huius studiosissimum fuisse constat, qui et patritio patri Iosephi subditus fuit, et iam moriturus matris Virginis rationem habuit. Idem Pharisaeos et omnes humanarum traditionum obseruatores hoc nomine damnat, quod sub pietatis et cultus diuini praetextu liberorum erga parentes officia impedirent. Eadem est amoris atq; fidei coniugalis ratio. Quod enim olim in Paradiso sanciuit Deus, Christus in Euangelio sua authoritate confirmat, iubens, ut homo parentes deferat et uxori suae adglutinetur. Qua ratione autem liberos abijcere aut inhumaniter negligere iuberet, qui proprius naturalis illius amoris, quo eos prosequimur, author est et qui per Paulum pronunciat, eum infidelì esse deteriorem, qui suis domesticis non prospiciat? Cur item vterinos fratres odisse et deserere doceret, qui alienos quoque et nobis incognitos amore frater no iubet complecti? Adde his, quod ipse vitae suae non semel fuga consuluit, quando ipsi ante fatalem illam horam hostes insidias struebant. Turpiter ergo et impie hoc loco abiiciuntur, qui sub religionis praetextu parentibus debitum obsequium negant, coniuges et liberos deserunt, et erga eos duri atq; inhumani sunt, quos cognationis vinculo sibi coniunctos prae aliis diligere debebant. Pecc cant in hoc Monachi, qui tunc demum mundo mortuos se esse putant, si parentes negligant, et extreme periclitantes siccis oculis intueantur. Idem quoque coniugum et liberorum cura tangi non possunt, cum nullas sibi legitimo coniugij vinculo obstrictas habeant, neq; liberos legitimos procreent, sed vaga libidine thoros alienos promiscue polluant. Insistunt horum vestigijs Anabaptistae, qui insuper vitam quoque impie profundunt, dum absque necessitate ad tormenta et mortis suppli cia se offerunt: quod olim Donatistas simili cum insania fecisse legimus. Sunt autem haec impia palam, et non a Christianae modo religionis professione, verumetiam a communi humanitatis sensu aliena.
units.tr: The first is: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple." These words are not to be passed over carelessly, lest we flatter ourselves destructively, as we depart from our duty, or become impious under the pretext of piety. For the Lord does not command that, with the natural affections of the mind, which the Greeks call στοργαί, extinguished, we should cruelly pursue our parents with unjust hatred, fail to show affection to our wife and children, neglect our brothers and sisters without mercy, or with headlong rashness violently break off the course of our life. For just as in the Old Law God commends piety towards parents with great emphasis, so it is established that Christ was most devoted to this, for he was subject to Joseph his earthly father, and even when about to die he took thought for his mother, the Virgin. The same Christ condemns the Pharisees and all observers of human traditions on this ground, that under the pretext of piety and divine worship they hindered the duties of children towards their parents. The principle of love and of conjugal faith is the same. For what God once decreed in Paradise, Christ confirms in the Gospel by his own authority, commanding that a man should leave his parents and cleave to his wife. But by what reasoning would he command us to cast off children or to neglect them inhumanly, he who is the author of that natural love by which we cherish them, and who through Paul declares that one who does not provide for his own household is worse than an unbeliever? Why would he teach us to hate and desert our full brothers, when he bids us embrace with brotherly love even strangers and those unknown to us? Add to these things that he himself more than once sought safety by flight, when his enemies were laying snares for him before that fated hour. Therefore those who, under the pretext of religion, deny the obedience owed to parents, desert wives and children, and are harsh and inhuman towards those whom they ought to love above others as bound to them by the tie of kinship, are here shamefully and impiously cast off. The monks sin in this, who then at last think themselves dead to the world when they neglect their parents and look on dry-eyed while they are in extreme danger. Likewise those who have no care for wives and children cannot be touched by this, since they have no bond of lawful marriage binding them, and do not beget lawful children, but in wandering lust pollute the beds of others indiscriminately. The Anabaptists follow in their footsteps, who moreover squander their lives impiously, offering themselves without necessity to torments and to execution, which we read the Donatists once did in similar madness. These things, however, are openly impious, and alien not only to the profession of the Christian religion but also to the common sense of humanity.

units.la: Quid ergo Christum hoc loco docere et a suis exigere dicemus? Hoc nimirum, ut ipsum omnibus, qui nobis coniunctissimi sunt et qui naturae legibus commendantur, praeferamus, imo tantum non odio habeamus, si quando res eo deueniat, ut aut ipsum abnegare, aut ab illis diuelli oporteat. Itaque per comparationem ista dicuntur, ut neminem nobis tam charum aut amicum habeamus, ut in eius gratiam velimus a Christo deficere, qui nos sui sanguinis pretio sibi acquisiuit. Etenim cum
units.tr: What, then, shall we say Christ teaches and requires of his people in this place? Surely this: that he is to be preferred to all those who are most closely joined to us and who are commended to us by the laws of nature, indeed that we should hold them in something not far short of hatred, if ever the matter comes to such a pass that we must either deny him or be torn away from them. Thus these things are said by way of comparison, so that we should not hold anyone so dear or so friendly to us that for his sake we would be willing to fall away from Christ, who acquired us for himself at the price of his own blood. For since

units.la: Nota: marginal notes read: "Christus non damnat ςυγγὰς", "Luc. 2. Ioan 19. Matth. 15.", "Christus omnibus debet praeferri." cum inter homines certi coniunctionis & cognationis gradus sint, quorum respectu aliquos prae aliis diligere debemus, aequum est vt supra omnes Christus emineat, qui nobis vnicus caput nostrum est, & qui nos Dei patris sui filios fecit. Denique hoc ille vult, vt eos etiam affectus, qui per se laude digni sunt, in officio contineamus, ne nos a fide & pietate, quam ipsi debemus, transfuerfos abripiant. Et hunc sensum ipse indicat, quando apud Matthaeum hanc sententiam sic exprimit: Qui amat patrem & matrem supra me, non est me dignus: & qui amat filium aut filiam supra me, non est me dignus. In praesenti autem durius & gravius loquitur, vt carnem sibi tenerius blandientem magis terreat, & odio dignos esse ostendat omnes affectus, quibus ab illo abstrahimur. Quod autem hic iubemur, id iam olim multos praestitisse scimus, quorum fides & pietas in scripturis commendatur. Sic enim Abrahamus, pater credentium, natale solum cum domo paterna & cognatis omnibus odio habuit, quando ab illis potius discedere, quam Dei vocationem negligere maluit. Idem filium Isaaci odisse dici poterat, quando eum propria manu iugulare & Deo victimam offerre volebat. Simili ratione Moses aulicas delitias, opes, honores, vitam denique propriam odio prosequutus est, quando nulla istorum omnium ratione habita Dei vocationi obediuit, qui ipsum populi sui vindicem constituerat. Apostoli item inhumani & crudeles fortasse multis visi sunt, quando vxores, familiam, parentes senio confectos, suos denique omnes reliquerunt, vt Christo discipuli & comites indiuulsi adhaererent. Et Paulus omnia pro damnosis & noxiis habebat, quae in mundo praestantissima putantur, vt Christum vere apprehenderet. Idem cum ex Spiritus revelatione sciret, vincula & afflictiones omnis generis sibi Hierosolymis paratas esse, magno tamen animo, & multis nequicquam eum debortantibus, eo perrexit, nimirum, quod (vt in celebri illa ministrorum Asiae Synodo ipse testatur) neque vitam propriam sibi charam haberet, modo cursum suum absolueret, & ministerio, quod a Christo acceperat, digne defungeretur. Eadem omnium Martyrum sententia fuit, qui nunquam tot tamen horribiles exquisitissimorum tormentorum cruciatus ferre & superare potuissent, nisi corpus & vitam suam prae Christo odissent. Ita ergo omnes erga se affectos esse vult, qui salutis aeternae in ipso participes fieri cupiunt. Nam diserte ait: Si quis venit ad me, & non odit patrem suum & matrem, & vxorem & liberos, & fratres & sorores, atque adeo etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Nemo igitur sibi ipsi delitias faciat, quasi ista non ad se, sed ad solos Apostolos & horum in verbi ministerio successores pertineant. Nulla enim hic est inter Christianos homines immunitas, & quisquis ille sit, qui Christi discipulum se profitetur, hunc animum induat oportet nisi falsi velit argui. Vult enim Deus, vt ipsum diligamus ex toto corde, ex tota anima & omnibus nostris facultatibus. Id vero nunquam praestabunt, quicunque vel vitam suam, vel aliquos hominum tanti faciunt, vt propter eos fidem abnegent. Atqui non possunt non id facere, qui carnis rationem atque huic coniunctos affectus in consilium admittunt. Itaque bos per fidei obedientiam subigere oportet, ne in re omnium maxime necessaria nobis impedimento sint. Quod vnum si recte consideretur, satis docet, Christianam religionem non in externa fidei professione aut Sacramentorum ecclesiae vsu consistere, sed in eo potius, vt homo totus quantus est, Deo mancipatus sit, neque vllis vel ilicebris vel periculis se a Christo diuelli patiatur. Potest etiam hoc loco iis respondari, qui in iis etiam quae ad religionem spectant, magistratui obedendum esse clamant. Solent hi multum de regum & principum authoritate differere, vt eos extra culpam esse doceant, qui in rebus illicitis contra propriam conscientiam illis obediunt. Atqui nos quoque libenter fatemur illorum potestate ex Deo esse, qui suum quoq; nomen illis communicare dignatur: interim vero no debet negari, illam certis quoq; limitibus esse circumscriptam, neq; illos aliquod ius habere in hominum conscientias, vt has ad cultus illicitos cogant. Ita ergo illis obtemperandum est, vt (quod Christus alibi admonet) Deo suum ius apud nos integrum maneat. Quod ipsum olim prophetae, Apostoli & Martyres sanctissimi probe observarunt. Imo hic maxime opus est hac Christi regula, vt nos eius germanos discipulos esse probemus. Etenim si parentes, vxorem, liberos & fratres odio dignos iudicare debemus, si nos a Christo diuellere conetur: quanto magis principibus obedientiam negare decet, qui vt fide abnegemus & prophanis cultibus nos polluamus mandat? Cedunt leges civiles, vt Consul vrbis in adulterio deprehensos a marito vxoris occidatur: & iniurias notarias, quib. sopyai naturales violantur, tyrannorum cæde ylcifci licet. Sic Harpagus iure excusatur, qui cum Cyrus coniurauit aduersus Astyagem Regem, qui ipsi filium proprium comedendum apposuerat. Et multorum aliorum fortitudo probatur, qui uxorum & filiarum stupra aduersus principes suos vindicarunt. Potest his adnumerari primus fœderis Heluetici author & fortissimus libertatis veteris vindex, Guilhelmus Tellius, qui tyrannum occidit, qui ipsum ex filij vertice pomum sagitta decutere coegerat. Hæc cum in rebus propbanis & ad corpus solum spectantibus licita sint, quæ ratio iubebit Regibus tunc simpliciter obedire, quando illi aduersus Deum insurgunt, & nos in hunc atq; Filium suum vnigenitum impios esse cogunt? Nemo igitur vanissimos homines audiat, qui impiâ à fide defectionem obedientiæ prætextu palliant, quam magistratui deberi aiunt. Videant tamen omnes, ne quid temere & absque causa necessaria tentent, & priuatas iniurias sub religionis prætextu vlciscantur.
units.tr: Note: marginal notes read: "Christ does not condemn kinsmen [συγγενεῖς]", "Luke 2; John 19; Matt. 15", "Christ is to be preferred to all." Since there are fixed degrees of kinship and connection among men, in respect of which we ought to love some more than others, it is right that Christ should stand above all, since he alone is our head and has made us sons of God his Father. Finally, he wills that even those affections which are praiseworthy in themselves be kept in check, lest they turn us aside and drag us away from the faith and piety which we owe him. He himself indicates this sense when he expresses the saying in Matthew thus: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." Here, however, he speaks more harshly and severely, so as to frighten the flesh, which caresses itself too tenderly, and to show that all affections by which we are drawn away from him deserve hatred. Now, we know that many have already done in former times what is commanded here, and their faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures. Thus Abraham, father of the faithful, hated his native land, his father's house and all his kin, when he chose to depart from them rather than neglect God's calling. The son of Isaac could likewise be said to have been hated by him, when he wished to slay him with his own hand and offer him to God as a victim. In the same way Moses spurned courtly luxuries, wealth, honours, and finally his own life, when, taking no account of any of these, he obeyed the calling of God, who had appointed him the deliverer of his people. The apostles too seemed perhaps to many inhuman and cruel, when they left their wives, families, parents worn with age, and finally all they had, so as to cling inseparably to Christ as his disciples and companions. And Paul counted as loss and harm all things that are thought most excellent in the world, so that he might truly lay hold of Christ. The same man, knowing by revelation of the Spirit that chains and afflictions of every kind awaited him at Jerusalem, nevertheless went on there with a great spirit, though many dissuaded him in vain; for, as he himself testifies in that famous synod of the ministers of Asia, he did not hold his own life dear, provided he finished his course and worthily discharged the ministry which he had received from Christ. This was the judgment of all the martyrs, who could never have borne and overcome such dreadful torments of the most exquisite kind unless they hated their own body and life in comparison with Christ. Thus he wishes all who desire to become partakers of eternal salvation in him to be disposed towards himself in this way. For he says plainly: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple." Let no one therefore indulge himself, as if these things pertained not to himself but only to the apostles and their successors in the ministry of the Word. For there is no exemption here among Christian people, and whoever he is that professes himself a disciple of Christ must put on this disposition, unless he wishes to be proved false. For God wills that we love him with our whole heart, our whole soul and all our faculties. Yet those will never do this who hold either their own life or certain men in such esteem that they deny the faith for their sake. And they cannot but do so who admit the reasoning of the flesh and the affections joined to it into their counsels. Therefore the ox must be tamed by the obedience of faith, lest these things hinder us in the matter that is of all most necessary. If this single point is rightly considered, it sufficiently teaches that the Christian religion consists not in the outward profession of faith or in the use of the Church's sacraments, but rather in this, that a man, wholly as he is, be given over to God and suffer himself to be torn away from Christ neither by allurements nor by dangers. This can also be answered here to those who cry out that magistrates are to be obeyed even in matters that concern religion. Such men are accustomed to discourse at length on the authority of kings and princes, in order to teach that those are free from blame who obey them in unlawful things against their own conscience. Yet we too gladly confess that the power of those who are also graciously pleased to share with them his own name is from God; but meanwhile it must not be denied that this power is circumscribed by certain limits, and that they have no right over men's consciences to compel them to unlawful worship. Thus they are to be obeyed in such a way that (as Christ elsewhere admonishes) the right of God remains whole among us. The prophets, apostles and most holy martyrs of old observed this well. Indeed, here above all there is need of this rule of Christ, that we may prove ourselves his true disciples. For if we ought to judge father, wife, children and brothers worthy of hatred when they try to tear us away from Christ, how much more ought we to refuse obedience to princes who command us to deny the faith and defile ourselves with profane worship? Civil laws yield, so that the consul of a city may have a man caught in adultery put to death by the husband of the woman; and when natural modesty [σωφροσύναι] is violated by such notorious wrongs, the killing of tyrants is permitted. Thus Harpagus is rightly excused, who conspired with Cyrus against King Astyages, who had set before him his own son to be eaten. And the courage of many others is approved, who avenged the rapes of their wives and daughters against their princes. To these may be added the first author of the Swiss covenant and the bravest champion of ancient liberty, William Tell, who killed the tyrant who had forced him to shoot an apple from his son's head with an arrow. If these things are lawful in profane matters that concern the body alone, what reason will bid us simply to obey kings when they rise up against God and force us to become impious toward him and his only-begotten Son? Let no one therefore listen to the most empty men, who cover up impious defection from the faith with the pretext of the obedience which they say is owed to the magistrate. Yet let all take care not to attempt anything rashly and without necessary cause, and not to avenge private injuries under the pretext of religion.

units.la: Quia verò carni durum & in primis arduum est quod Christus iubet, & certamen non leue nobis proponitur, nō inutile fuerit scire, quibus præsidijs & adminiculis res tanta confici possit. Vbi ante omnia regeneratione opus est, quæ nos totos innouet: quia nisi id fiat, hæc nunquam præstabimus. At hanc nobis superne obtingere, & solius Spiritus virtute perfici notius est, quam vt demonstrari oporteat. Nostri autem officij fuerit, precibus assiduis apud Deum instare, vt animi viribus nos instruat, affectus immoderatos coerceat, & viuo Filij sui amore corda nostra accendat. Deinde non parum nobis proderit crebra & diligens nostræ vocationis consideratio, quæ bifariam fieri debet. Est enim publica, quam cum omnibus credentibus communem habemus: vt nimirum Christiani, id est vnii Dei, & proinde reges atq; Sacerdotes simus, qui mundo & affectibus omnibus dominentur, & seipsos Deo sistant viuentem hostiam. Est alia priuata, cuius ratio singulis olim reddenda erit, quæ pro functionum diuersitate non omnibus eadem est. Quod si utraq; probè quis expenderit, mox videbit, quam parum tribui debeat hominibus, cum yiring, ita nos sibi Deus vendicet, vt vix vlli alij rei vacare possimus. Addamus his humanæ naturæ atq; conditionis, adhæc rerum huius seculi considerationem. Illic enim inueniemus, alios quidem hominū indignos esse, in quorum gratiam aliquid fiat: eos autem qui nobis propter artius vel cognationis vel coniugij vinculum commendatissimi esse debent, non opus habere, vt propter illos Christum abnegemus. Nā etsi nostra ope & defensione destituantur, reuera tamen orphani & viduæ dici non possunt, cùm Deū habeant Patrem, tutorem, maritum vel sponsum, eos autem omnes Dei Filius profratribus & coheredibus suis agnoscat. Itaq; dum ipsi ex viuis emigramus, illos sub Dei protectione relinquimus, quæ eis abundè sufficiet, donec perfecto sua etiam vita cursu ad beatorū cœlestes sedes colligentur. Hæc qui non oscitanter expendunt, ijs non admodum grane erit omnibus longum valere dicere, dū modo Christum retineant, in quo omnis salus atq; felicitas habetur.
units.tr: But since what Christ commands is hard and especially difficult for the flesh, and a no light struggle is set before us, it will not be unprofitable to know by what safeguards and aids so great a task can be accomplished. Here, before all else, there is need of regeneration, which renews us wholly, for unless this happens we shall never accomplish these things. That this comes to us from above, and is brought about by the power of the Spirit alone, is better known than that it needs to be demonstrated. It will be our duty to press on before God with constant prayers, that he may strengthen us with the powers of the soul, restrain immoderate affections, and kindle our hearts with the living love of his Son. Next, no little profit will come to us from frequent and diligent consideration of our calling, which must be done in two ways. The one is public, which we hold in common with all believers: namely, that as Christians, that is, of the one God, we are kings and priests, who rule the world and all affections, and present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice. The other is private, the reckoning of which will one day be rendered by each man, and which is not the same for all because of the diversity of offices. If someone weighs both of these carefully, he will soon see how little should be given to men, since God so claims us for himself that we can scarcely be free for any other business. To these let us add the consideration of human nature and condition, and besides this, of the things of this age. For there we shall find that, indeed, some men are unworthy that anything be done for their sake, but that those who ought to be most commended to us by the closer bond of kinship or marriage do not need us to deny Christ on their account. For even if they are deprived of our help and defence, they cannot truly be called orphans and widows, since they have God as their Father, protector, husband or bridegroom, and the Son of God acknowledges all of them as his brothers and co-heirs. Therefore, when we ourselves depart from the living, we leave them under God's protection, which will be more than sufficient for them, until, their own course of life finished, they are gathered to the heavenly seats of the blessed. Those who weigh these things carefully will not find it very hard to bid all a long farewell, provided only that they keep Christ, in whom all salvation and happiness is found.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram regulam, quam suis sectatoribus ille his verbis præscribit: Et quisquis non portat crucem suam, & non sequitur me, non potest meus esse discipulus. Rursus ad hanc quoque necessitatis lege nos obstringit, ne liberum nobis esse putemus ipsius præcepto obedire vel minus. Nam discipulos suos nos fore negat, nisi quod hic iubet faciamus. Duo autem præcipit quæ in genere comprehendunt præcipua hominis Christiani officia. Primum est, vt quisque suam crucem portet. At crucis nomine omnia intelligi alibi diximus, quæ homini aduersa atque molesta accidunt: qualia sunt paupertas, fames, morbi omnis generis, infamia, persecutio, captiuitas, exilium, iniuriæ, oppressio, solicitudines variæ, conscientiæ terrores, & quæcunque alia possunt nominari. Quibus etiā publica mala accenseri debent, tempestates noxiæ, bella, incendia, depredationes, vrbium excidia, inundationes, pestilentia, & si quæ alia totas ciuitates aut gentes exercent. Solent ista apud Prophetas calix Domini dici, eò quod ab illo quasi propinantur, & quidem certa cū mensura & ratione. Christus verò crucem vocat, vt communionis quæ nobis cum ipso intercedit admoneamur. Itaq; vox ista tam institutioni quam consolationi nostræ plurimum seruit. Docet enim patienter ferenda esse, quæ nobis à Deo imponuntur, neque desperare aliquem debere de illius gratia & auxilio: quia nunquam ille eos negligere poterit, quos Filij sui dilecti in cruce ferenda socios esse vidit. Vt verò tales simus, altero opus est, vt scilicet ipsum sequamur. Quod cum corpore fieri non possit, animo & exempli eius imitatione fiat oportet. Hic ergo fides exigitur, quæ sola animos nostros
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other rule, which he sets down for his followers in these words: "And whoever does not carry his cross and follow me, cannot be my disciple." Again, by this law of necessity he binds us, so that we do not think it free to us to obey his precept more or less. For he says that we will not be his disciples unless we do what he commands here. He prescribes two things, which together comprise the chief duties of a Christian. The first is that each one should carry his cross. We have said elsewhere that by the name of cross we understand everything that befalls a man as adverse and troublesome: such as poverty, hunger, diseases of every kind, infamy, persecution, captivity, exile, injuries, oppression, various anxieties, terrors of conscience, and whatever else can be named. Public calamities should also be counted among these: harmful storms, wars, fires, plunderings, the destruction of cities, floods, pestilence, and any other afflictions that harass whole cities or nations. The Prophets are accustomed to call such things the cup of the Lord, because they are, as it were, poured out to us by him, and indeed in a certain measure and proportion. Christ, however, calls it the cross, so that we may be reminded of the fellowship that exists between us and him. Thus this word serves greatly both our instruction and our consolation. For it teaches that what is laid upon us by God is to be borne patiently, and that no one ought to despair of his grace and help, because he can never neglect those whom he has seen to be companions of his beloved Son in bearing the cross. But that we may be such, a second thing is needed, namely that we follow him. Since this cannot be done in body, it must be done in spirit and by imitating his example. Here, therefore, faith is required, which alone

units.la: Cap. XIIII. si cum suis seruiunt etiam ftros supra cælum euehit, vt Christum assequamur, & huius spiritu animemur. Excitat deinde hac in nobis illum imitandi studium: quo fit vt discipuli eius germani vitam atq; mores, adeoque actiones suas omnes ad illius exemplum componant. Elucet in eo obedientia summa, quam nec mortis quidem acerbissimæ recordatio impedire potuit: innocentia omnibus numeris absoluta, in qua reliqua hendenda ne hostes quidem oculatissimi aliquam occasionem habuerunt: patientia invicta, quæ per omnes cruciatus victrix euasit: humilitas extrema, qualem ne in seruulo quidem a bene dissimo innocentia: charitas perfecta, quæ omnibus iniurijs & contumelijs superior facta hostium quoque saluti consulere studuit. Sed & ciuilis iustitiæ exemplo perfectissimo nobis præiuit, quando sub censu nascivoluit non sine maximo virginis matris incommodo, & censum ipse persoluit, & Cæsari dare debuit quæ ei iure debentur. Hæc quicunque præstant, ij Christum vere sequuntur, & eiusdem discipuli sunt veri.
units.tr: Chapter XIIII. ... if with his own they serve, he lifts even their hearts above heaven, so that we may attain Christ and be animated by his Spirit. Then he stirs in us the desire to imitate him, so that his true disciples shape their life and manners, and indeed all their actions, after his example. In him shines forth the highest obedience, which not even the recollection of the most bitter death could hinder; innocence altogether complete, in which not even the most keen-eyed enemies found any occasion to blame him; patience unconquered, which emerged victorious through all torments; utmost humility, such as even the most innocent servant would scarcely show; perfect charity, which, though it was superior to all injuries and insults, took care for the salvation even of its enemies. He also went before us in the most perfect example of civil justice, when, being born under the census, he rolled himself up, not without the greatest inconvenience to his virgin mother, and both paid the tax himself and gave to Caesar what was rightly owed to him. Whoever performs these things truly follows Christ, and is a true disciple of his.

units.la: At quia hæc omnia cum cruce coniuncta sunt, qua nihil molestius & acerbius carni accidere potest, rationibus quoque certis nos excitari & confirmari oportet, vt ad ista alacriores simus. In ter quas merito primam numerauerit prouidentiæ Dei considerationem, sine cuius nutu nihil nobis accidere potest. At quia vt iustus, bonus, sapiens & noster amantissimus est, nullam nobis iniuriam facit, & simul certa cum ratione omnia ad eum finem dirigit, vt salutis æternæ haeredes efficiamur. Quæ ergo causa iusta excogitari poterit, qua nos excusemus, si aduersus illum murmurare libeat. Adde huic ingenij nostri vitiositatem, quæ nisi crucis fræno coerceatur, aduersus spiritum prouocare nunquam desinet. Quid quod æquum est, vt Christi Iesu in cruce ferenda socij sint, qui regni & gloriæ eius consortes fieri cupiunt? Cur enim cum Imperatore triumphaturi milites, qui pugnæ & belli discrimina cum illo subire detrectarunt? Accedat his omnibus amplissimi præmij, quod nobis in cælis repositum est, meditatio, & mox videbimus huius spem ad omnia ea sufficere, quæ carni iniqua & prorsus intolerabilia esse videntur. Possent ista multis verbis illustrari, & exemplis quoque grauissimis confirmari, sed breuiores hic sumus, cum alibi de his abunde sit dictum. Admonet nos autem diligens huius loci consideratio, quam procul adhuc à Christianæ religionis scopo absint, qui toti carnis cupiditatibus immersi, ne à sceleribus quidem manifestis & atrocibus abstinent, & mundo infelici potius quam Christo placere studeant. Gloriantur hi quidem Christiani nominis professione, sed reuera absq; veste nuptiali ad nuptias illas beatas irrepunt: in quibus erit aliquando locum aliquem habeant, suo tamen tempore Iuam in illos sententiam Dominus proferet, & tunc ad æternos tenebrarum exteriorum cruciatus damnabuntur, vbi erit fletus & stridor dentium. Itaq; horum memores, carnis affectus tam prauos quam bonos subigere discamus per fidei obedientiam, & supra omnia in animis nostris emineat Iesus Christus: Cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But since all these things are joined with the cross, than which nothing can befall the flesh more grievously and bitterly, we must also be stirred and strengthened by sound reasons, so that we may be more eager toward these things. Among these, rightly the first to be numbered is the consideration of God's providence, without whose will nothing can befall us. For he is just, good, wise, and our most loving Father; he does us no wrong, and at the same time he directs all things by a certain plan toward this end, that we may be made heirs of eternal salvation. What just cause, then, can be devised by which we might excuse ourselves if we are inclined to murmur against him? Add to this the faultiness of our nature, which, unless it is restrained by the bridle of the cross, will never cease to rebel against the Spirit. What of the fact that it is only fair that those be companions of Christ Jesus in bearing the cross who desire to share his kingdom and glory? For with what soldiers would the Emperor triumph, if they refused to undergo with him the dangers of battle and war? To all these things add the meditation on the most ample reward laid up for us in heaven, and soon we shall see that the hope of it suffices for all those things which seem hostile to the flesh and utterly intolerable. These matters could be illustrated with many words and confirmed with very weighty examples, but we are briefer here, since they have been dealt with fully elsewhere. Yet the careful consideration of this passage warns us how far from the aim of the Christian religion those are who, wholly immersed in the lusts of the flesh, do not refrain even from manifest and atrocious crimes, and who strive to please the unhappy world rather than Christ. These people indeed boast of the profession of the Christian name, but in truth they creep into those blessed nuptials without the wedding garment; they may at some time have a place among them, yet at his own time the Lord will pronounce sentence against them, and then they will be condemned to the eternal torments of outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Therefore, mindful of these things, let us learn to subdue the affections of the flesh, both bad and good, through obedience of faith, and above all let Jesus Christ stand out in our minds, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLVII.

units.la: Quis enim ex vobis, si velit turrim ædificare, non prius sedens computat sumptus, an habeat quæ ad perfectionem operis requiruntur? Ne postquam posuerit fundamentum, & non potuerit perficere, omnes qui spectarint incipiant ei illudere, dicentes: Homo iste coepit ædificare, & non potuit perficere. Aut quis Rex proficiscens vt committat prælium aduersus alterum regem, sedens prius non consultat, an possit cum decem millibus occurrere ei, qui cum viginti millibus venit aduersus ipsum? Alioqui cum adhuc ille procul est, legatione missa rogat ea quæ ad pacem pertinent. Sic ergo quisquis vestrum non valedicit omnibus bonis suis, non potest meus esse discipulus.
units.tr: For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, to see whether he has what is needed to finish the work? Otherwise, once he has laid the foundation and cannot finish, everyone who sees it will begin to mock him, saying, "This man began to build and could not finish." Or what king, setting out to wage war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand men the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while the other is still far off, he sends an embassy and asks for the terms of peace. So then, whoever of you does not renounce all his possessions cannot be my disciple.

units.la: Proponit quidem & liberaliter offert nobis Deus in Filio suo Iesu Christo vniuersos suæ gratiæ atq; bonitatis thesauros, & in eodem viam quoq; aperit, qua in illorum possessionem veniamus: sed ea est nostri ingenij prauitas, vt vel non ample stamur hunc vnicum salutis æternæ mediatorem, vel illius nomine & præpositera meriti eius fiducia iurpiter abutamur, sic vt nobis offendiculi lapis fiat, qui vitæ huius mortalis dux, & æternæ author esse debebat. Causa tâti mali præcipua est quod neglectis bonis spiritualibus plerique in illo longè alia, quàm oportebat, quærere solet. Eo enim fit, vt vana temporariorum commodorum spe decepti, Euangelicum illud semen in corda petricosa excipiant, & vbi spe sua sese frustrari vident, turpiter deficiant à Christo, quando constantia fidei in primis opus erat. Est ergo necessaria admodum Christi doctrina, quæ nuper tradere cœpit, & quæ docet, quibus causis potissimum homines à salutis via reuocetur, quales item esse oporteat eos, qui ip sius veri sectatores & discipuli esse volunt. Requiritur ab his, vt abnegatis propriis affectibus, simul omnibus ijs renuntient, quæ nos abipso diuellunt: Deinde vt aduersa quæuis patienter ferat, & se to tos ad eius exemplum conforment. Id nunc parabolis elegantissimis illustrat, quibus vtilem admoni tionem comprehendit, vt seipsos prius probe explorent qui ipsi nomen dare volunt, ne postea in me dio cursu deficientes se omnibus ridendos propinent cum certa propriæ salutis iactura.
units.tr: God indeed sets forth and freely offers to us in his Son Jesus Christ all the treasures of his grace and goodness, and in him he also opens the way by which we may come into their possession. But such is the perversity of our nature that either we do not embrace this one mediator of eternal salvation, or we shamefully abuse his name and the confidence in his merit, so that he becomes for us a stone of stumbling, which ought to have been the guide of this mortal life and the author of eternal life. The chief cause of so great an evil is that, neglecting spiritual goods, most people seek in him something quite different from what they ought. For this reason, deceived by the vain hope of temporary advantages, they receive that gospel seed on stony hearts, and when they see their hope frustrated, they shamefully fall away from Christ, when steadfastness of faith was above all needed. The teaching of Christ, which he has only recently begun to deliver, is therefore very necessary; it teaches for what causes above all men are called back from the way of salvation, and also what sort of people ought to be those who wish to be true followers and disciples of him. It is required of them that, having denied their own affections, they at the same time renounce all those things which tear them away from him; and then that they bear patiently whatever adversities come, and conform themselves wholly to his example. He now illustrates this with most elegant parables, in which he gives a useful warning, that those who wish to enlist under his name should first test themselves thoroughly, lest afterwards, failing in the middle of the course, they expose themselves to ridicule from all and suffer the certain loss of their own salvation.

units.la: Primam parabolam ab ædificantibus sumit, & sensus est: Quemadmodum vir prudens & cor- datus ædificium turris nô inchoat, nisi subductis prius rationibus, num sumptibus aut impensis, quæ facienda sunt, posset sufficere: ita si quis ad me venire & fidè in me profiteri velit, prius in seipsum descendat, & animum suum diligenter exploret, ne forte postea tanti operis difficultate superatus nô sine publica infamia illud vix dum inchoatum relinquat. Quo loco ante omnia obseruabis, eos qui Christiani nominis professionem faciunt, illis conferri qui turrim ædificant. Est similitudo hæc vsi tata admodum in scripturis, & notum est illud Pauli: Dei ædificatio vos estis. Ratio eius duplex afferri potest. Vna, quod tales Dei templum sunt (vt idem Paulus annotat) domus nimirum Dei spiritualis, quam ille cum thesauris & bonis suis omnibus inhabitare dignatur, quem cæli cœlorum non capiunt. Altera quod ijdem instar turris altæ & inexpugnabilis sunt, dum & mundo & huius principi fortissimè resistunt, neque se ab instituto tam pio & sancto dimoueri patiuntur. Vt vero ædificatio res est plena laboris & molestiæ, necessaria tamen, eò quod sine ea homines tutò & commodè non possunt viuere: ita carni durum & acerbum est, si quis ex semetipso Dei templum aut turrim sacram ædificare velit, veruntamen vt id fiat necesse est, quia nisi tales simus, neque honestè in Dei conspectu viuere, neq; inter tot tam graues mundi huius & diaboli insidias tutò degere poterimus: imò (vt alibi Christus monet) si nos otiosos & à vera pietate fluctio alienos aut salutis sue curos Satan inueniat, mox assumptis plurimis impuris spiritibus sibi ipsi in nobis domicilium parat, ex quo præsens exitium homini nascitur. Rursus vbi turris clam & occultè extrui non potest, & qui id faciunt, hominum & quidem vilissimi cuiusq; ex vulgo iudicium non possunt subterfugere: ita cum Christiani nominis professio aperte & publicè fiat, non possunt latere qui hanc faciunt, sed omnium oculis, ceu turris aliqua altissima aut vrbs in montis vertice sita, expositi, varia multumq; inter se diuersa hominum iudicia subire coguntur, in quibus fere omnium andacissimi sunt, qui de religione & æternæ salutis negotio quam minimum iudicare possunt. Quod vnum, est si nulla alia causa accederet, illos excitare debet, vt diligenter & prudenter res omnes instituant, ne (quod ineptus & temerarijs ædificatoribus solet accidere) cum publica ignominia salutis propriæ faciant iactura irreparabilem.
units.tr: He takes the first parable from builders, and the sense is this: just as a prudent and wise man does not begin the construction of a tower unless, having first reckoned the costs and expenses that must be met, he can be sure of meeting them, so if anyone wishes to come to me and profess faith in me, let him first go down into himself and carefully examine his own mind, lest perhaps afterwards, overcome by the difficulty of so great a work, he abandons it, scarcely begun, and not without public disgrace. Here, above all, you should observe that those who make profession of the Christian name are compared with those who build a tower. This likeness is much used in the Scriptures, and the saying of Paul is well known: "You are God's building." This can be explained in two ways. First, because such people are God's temple (as Paul also notes), that is, a spiritual house of God, which he deigns to inhabit with all his treasures and goods, whom the heavens of heavens cannot contain. Second, because they are like a high and impregnable tower, since they resist most firmly both the world and its prince, and do not allow themselves to be moved from so pious and holy a purpose. But just as building is a work full of toil and trouble, yet necessary, because without it men cannot live safely and comfortably, so it is hard and bitter for the flesh if anyone wishes to build out of himself a temple of God or a sacred tower. Nevertheless, for this to happen it is necessary, because unless we are such, we shall be able neither to live honourably in God's sight nor to dwell safely amid so many grave snares of this world and the devil. Indeed (as Christ warns elsewhere), if Satan finds us idle, estranged from true piety, or careless of our salvation, he soon takes many unclean spirits to himself and prepares a dwelling for himself in us, from which present ruin is born for the man. Again, just as a tower cannot be raised secretly and in hiding, and those who build it cannot escape the judgment of men, even of the very lowest of the common people, so when the profession of the Christian name is made openly and publicly, those who make it cannot lie hidden. Instead, exposed to everyone's eyes like some very high tower or a city set on a mountain top, they are compelled to undergo the varied and widely differing judgments of men. Among these, almost the most bold are those who are least able to judge about religion and the matter of eternal salvation. This alone, even if no other cause were added, ought to rouse them to arrange all things diligently and prudently, lest (as usually happens to foolish and rash builders) they suffer, with public disgrace, an irreparable loss of their own salvation.

units.la: Hic autem duo præcipuè requiruntur. Primum, vt fundamentum ædificij collocetur firmum & solidum. Id enim ante omnia curant architecti prudentes, quia qui supra terram nudam aut arenam moles ingentes extruunt, sumptus plane faciunt inutiles. Nam aut paulatim illæ subsidunt, & rimas agunt, quibus ædificia eiusmodi deformantur: aut aquarum inundationibus violentis & ventorum vndiq; ruentium turbine atq; procella euertuntur. Fundamentum verò vnicum est Christus Iesus, extra quem (vt Paulus testatur) aliud poni non potest, & idem prophetarum atq; Apostolorum fundamentum dicitur, quia illum vnum bi omnes prædicauerunt. Etenim per Isaiam Deus ipse ait: En ego fundo in Zion lapidem, lapidem probationis, angularem, pretiosum, solidissimum fundamentum: & qui squis credit in eum, non pudefiet. Quem locum Apostoli de Christo diserte exponunt, vt qui ipsum dixisse sciebant: Super hanc petram (seipsum nimirum denotans) ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum aduersus eam non prævalebunt. Neq; hic parasitorum Romanenfium figmentum admittimus, qui hæc verba de Petro dicta esse cotendunt. Næ ipsius Petri authoritate cofutantur, qui in Senatu Hierosolymitano liberè testatur, Christū esse lapidem illum pretiosum quem
units.tr: Two things are chiefly required here. First, that the foundation of the building be laid firm and solid. For wise architects take this care above all, because those who raise huge structures on bare ground or sand make the expense entirely useless. For either the structures gradually sink and crack, so that buildings of this kind are disfigured, or they are overturned by violent floods of water and by the whirlwind and storm of winds rushing from every side. But the only foundation is Jesus Christ, besides whom (as Paul testifies) no other can be laid, and the same is called the foundation of the prophets and apostles, because they all preached him alone. For God himself says through Isaiah: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a most solid foundation; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." The Apostles expressly expound this passage of Christ, since they knew that he himself had said: "Upon this rock (meaning himself) I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." Nor do we admit here the fiction of the Roman parasites, who contend that these words were spoken of Peter. For they are refuted by Peter's own authority, since he freely testifies before the council at Jerusalem that Christ is that precious stone which

units.la: Fundamentum Christus. quem architecti reprobarint: ita Iudaicos Sacerdotes nominans, qui Ecclesiæ instauratores & fundatores volebant haberi. Et idem in Epistola priori locum Isaiæ, quem modò adduximus, de Christo luculenter exponens, omnes grauissimè hortatur, vt super ipsum ceu viui lapides ædificentur in domum spiritualem, & sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias, Deo acceptas per Iesum Christum. Hæc ergo omnium prima cura esse debet, ne fundamentum alienum iaciant, dum salutis spem atque fiduciam alibi habent collocatam. Faciunt hoc non modò Turcæ & Iudæi, qui à Christi fide prorsus alieni sunt, verumetiam inter nos multi, qui illum magnificè prædicant, salutem verò in Diuorum intercessione, in Pontificum bullis, & suorum operum meritis inueniri sibi persuaserunt. Putant hi ista cum Christo coniungi posse: sed est hoc commentum friuolum, cùm neque in gloriæ suæ societatem, quoad nostræ redemptionis negotium, quenquam admittat, neq; Ecclesia, quæ vnica est & ideo Catholica, id est, vniuersalis dicitur, diuersis fundamentis imponi possit. Itaq; non aliud isti homines proficiunt, quàm quòd structuræ suæ ruinam horribilem aliquando sentient, quando in grauiori tentationum palæstra, aut in mortis articulo, certam salutis fiduciam non possunt concipere.
units.tr: Christ the foundation. which the builders rejected, thus naming the Jewish priests, who wanted to be regarded as the restorers and founders of the Church. In his first Epistle, expounding powerfully the passage of Isaiah just cited concerning Christ, he also earnestly exhorts all to be built upon him like living stones into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore the first care of all should be that they do not lay another foundation, while they place their hope and confidence of salvation elsewhere. Not only the Turks and Jews do this, who are wholly alien to faith in Christ, but also many among us who preach him magnificently, yet have persuaded themselves that salvation is found in the intercession of the saints, in papal bulls, and in the merits of their own works. They think these things can be joined with Christ; but this is a frivolous invention, since he admits no one into the fellowship of his glory in the business of our redemption, nor can the Church, which is one and therefore called Catholic, that is universal, be set upon different foundations. So these people achieve nothing other than that they will at some time feel the dreadful ruin of their structure, when, in the sterner arena of temptations or at the point of death, they cannot conceive a certain confidence of salvation.

units.la: Deinde alterum requiritur, de quo in præsenti nos Christus admonet: vt nimirum supputatis prius ædificij huius sumptibus videamus, an nostræ facultates illis possint sufficere. At hic de illis sermo est, de quibus nuper dixit: Si quis venit ad me, & non odit patrem suum ac matrem, & vxorem & liberos, & fratres & sorores, adeoq; etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. In aliis quidem structuris multa pecunia est opus, & fere rationes omnes, etsi diligentissimè subducantur, impensæ postea superant. At in hoc spirituali ædificio non de pecunijs & fortunis agitur, sed qui nobis coniunctissimi sunt homines, parentes nimirum, vxor cum dulcissimis liberis, fratres, sorores, amici, denique sanguis & vita nostra in rationes impensarum veniunt.
