Nam cum cruce coniuncta est Christiani nominis professio, & qui secundum huius leges vitam instituunt, ij plerunque extorres facti à parentum & coniugum atque liberorum complexu auelluntur, & à fratribus atque amicis deseruntur, vel etiam hos sibi hostes acerrimos fieri sentiunt. Denique nihil tam durum, tam crudele, tam acerbum excogitari potest, quod non superent pericula illa, quibus fideles Christi cultores in hoc seculo exercentur. Hic ergo, vt alibi diximus, nostrij ipsius abnegatione, carnis mortificatione, patientia constanti, adhæc totius mundi & omnium quæ in hoc præstantissima habentur, contemptu opus est. Nisi enim his facultatibus instructi simus, mox nos instituti nostri pœnitebit, & bene cœptam fidei verae professionem deseremus, vt primùm nobis parentum mina, coniugum querelæ, suauissimorum pignorum lamentationes, exilij infamia & ipsius vita præsens periculum in oculos incurrent.
units.tr: Next comes the other requirement, about which Christ warns us in this passage: namely, that we first reckon up the costs of this building and see whether our resources can meet them. But here he is speaking of those things he mentioned a little earlier: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple." In other buildings much money is needed, and however carefully the accounts are drawn up, the expenses usually exceed them later. But in this spiritual building the question is not one of money and property. Rather, those who are closest to us, namely parents, a wife with dearest children, brothers, sisters and friends, and finally our very blood and life, all come into the reckoning of expenses. For the profession of the Christian name is joined to the cross, and those who order their lives according to its laws are for the most part made exiles and torn from the embrace of parents, wives and children, and deserted by brothers and friends, or they even find these become their bitterest enemies. In short, nothing so hard, so cruel or so bitter can be imagined that those dangers do not surpass, with which the faithful worshippers of Christ are tried in this age. Here, therefore, as we have said elsewhere, there is need of self-denial, mortification of the flesh, steadfast patience and, besides these, contempt of the whole world and of all those things held most precious in it. For unless we are equipped with these resources, we will soon regret our undertaking and abandon the true profession of faith once well begun, as soon as the threats of parents, the complaints of wives, the laments of our dearest pledges, the disgrace of exile and the present danger to life itself come before our eyes.

units.la: Exempla huius ignaviæ & pusillanimitatis multa extant, & hodie non pauca aduntur publicè & priuatim, dum leuissima aliqua fortunarum iactura, aut etiam solo metu infamiæ aut mortis turpem à Christo defectionem faciunt, qui adificij sui fastigium supra ipsos cœlos educturi esse paulò ante videbantur. Est hoc non solum cum ignominia publica coniunctum, sed multis scandalo est, qui istorum exemplis confirmari debuissent, & illis ipsis exitium affert, qui fidei suæ confessionem tantis cum impensis nolunt facere. Nec enim temerè à Christo dictum est: Nemo qui vbi manum aratro admouit, respexerit à tergo, idoneus est ad Regnum Dei. Vult ergo, ne temeraria leuitate prorumpamus, sed prius ad istam regulam nosipsos & facultates nostras omnes examinemus. In hoc autem vehementer falluntur, qui Regnum Christi de hoc mundo esse sibi persuaserunt, & proinde sibi ipsis opes, honores, pacem & otium, victorias deniq; splendidissimas promittunt. Sunt hi reuera stultissimi homines, quasi verò vt ista nobis acquireret Dei Filius cœlo descenderit & homo fit factus, quæ prophanis huius seculi filijs & ab omni cognitione Dei alienis cumulatissimè obtingunt. Nos potius præmij multò præstatioris spes excitare debet, cœlestis nimirum patriæ hæreditas, & plena æterni gaudij cœlorum palatia, in quibus nobis Christus sui sanguinis pretio sedes certas præparauit. Hæc si rectè & digne æstimemus, vilissimum nobis videbitur vitam ipsam per mille mortes profundere, nedum hominum consuetudini renuntiare, modò in illorum possessionem veniamus.
units.tr: There are many examples of this cowardice and faintheartedness, and today not a few occur publicly and privately, when people, at the mere loss of some slight property, or even from fear alone of disgrace or death, make a shameful defection from Christ, though shortly before they seemed about to raise the roof of their building above the very heavens. This is not only attended by public disgrace, but is a scandal to many who ought to have been strengthened by the examples of such men, and it brings ruin on those very people who are unwilling to confess their faith at such great cost. Nor did Christ speak rashly when he said: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." He wants us not to rush forward in reckless levity, but first to examine ourselves and all our resources by this rule. But those are greatly deceived who have persuaded themselves that the kingdom of Christ is of this world, and who therefore promise themselves riches, honours, peace and leisure, and finally most splendid victories. These are truly most foolish people, as if the Son of God had come down from heaven and been made man so that he might win for us those things which are abundantly bestowed on the profane sons of this age, who are estranged from all knowledge of God. Rather, the hope of a far better reward ought to stir us up: namely, the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, and the palaces of heaven full of eternal joy, in which Christ has prepared for us certain dwelling-places at the price of his own blood. If we weigh these things rightly and worthily, it will seem the cheapest thing to pour out our life through a thousand deaths, let alone to renounce the customs of men, provided we come into possession of those things.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt alteram quoque parabolam consideremus, quam ex re militari petit Domi-
units.tr: But it is time that we consider the other parable as well, which he takes from military affairs,

units.la: {s} Ioan. 14. nr, & quæ huic negotio mirificè conuenit. Scimus enim principes prudentes & populi amantes ȃellis non necessarijs toto animo abhorrere, cùm omne bellum mala innumera secum trahat, illa vero plerunque regnis florentissimis ruinam & excidium afferant. At si res quorundam iniustitia & improbitate eò adducatur, vt armis omnino experiri oporteat, magna cum circumspectione & diligenti consilio bellum suscipiunt. Nam non solùm vires suas considerant, verumetiam rationem secum ineunt, num cum paruis copijs hostem cum maioribus aduentantem sustinere & profligare possint, nec temere summam rei aleæ prælij, cuius euentus fere dubius & incertus est, committunt. Hæc ergo & quæcunque alia in istam consideracionem veniunt, Christus ad hanc causam applicans, ita dicere videtur: Cùm tanta industria tamen grauibus atque profundis consilijs reges huius seculi bella suscipiant atque gerant, in quibus de regnorum finibus, acceptis iniurijs, aut alijs rebus temporarijs & caducis agitur: quantò cautiores & diligentiores eos esse decet, qui meum nomen profesi bellum suscipiunt cum publico & veteri humani generis hoste, in quo æterna animarum salus in periculum venit?
units.tr: Ioan. 14. and which fits this matter wonderfully. For we know that wise princes and people-loving rulers, with their whole heart, shrink from unnecessary wars, since every war drags countless evils in its train, and those wars commonly bring ruin and destruction even upon the most flourishing kingdoms. But if the injustice and wickedness of some people drive matters to the point where they must try arms, they undertake war with great caution and careful counsel. For they consider not only their own strength, but also reckon with themselves whether, with small forces, they can withstand and overthrow an enemy advancing with greater ones, and they do not rashly stake the whole matter on the hazard of battle, whose outcome is almost doubtful and uncertain. So Christ, applying to this cause these and whatever other things come into such consideration, seems to say: If kings of this age undertake and wage wars with such diligence and with weighty and deep counsels, wars in which the question concerns the borders of kingdoms, received injuries, or other temporary and perishable matters, how much more cautious and diligent ought those to be who take up my name and wage war against the public and ancient enemy of the human race, in which the eternal salvation of souls is put in peril?

units.la: Est autem hic multa consideratione dignum, vitam Christiani hominis bello aut prælio conferri. Nam etsi de quouis dici possit, vitam hominis in terra militiam esse, proprie tamen hoc pijs & Christum profesus conuenit. Habent enim hi communem hostem diabolum, qui vt primos parentes suos telis melleo veneno tinctis prostrauit: ita nunquam non rugientis leonis instar oberrans quærit quos perdat ac devoret. Potentiam huius & vires Spiritus sanctus in scripturis non dissimulat, quando eum principem mundi & Deum huius seculi dicit. Crudelitas ex operibus eius plus satis perspicua est, quando præter cædes, vrbium excidia, agrorum vastationes, incendia, stupra & infinita alia huius generis nihil spirat, quæ singula non corporibus solis nocent, sed animas quoque ad tartara & æternos cruciatus adducunt. Arma eidem passim ad manum sunt, cùm & inter homines maior pars in illius castris militet, & ijs etiam, quæ in nobis sunt, contra nos abutatur: qualia sunt innata nobis totius naturæ vitiositas, cupiditates item quæ ex hac enascuntur, intellectus prauus, voluntas ad malum proclivis, sensuum organa, quæ omnia mirificis artibus desiderijs carnis subijcit, vt huic vni aduersus spiritum seruiant. Adde his mundum hunc totum, qui cùm totus in malo iaceat, vel malorum exemplorum illecebris & voluptatum laqueis, vel diris comminationibus & horrendis supplicijs cultores Christi oppugnat, vt deserta sua statione diabolo locum dent. Nullam ergo pacem, nullum otium illi sperare possunt, quoad vitam hanc mortalem in terris vixerint.
units.tr: Here, moreover, there is much worth considering: the life of a Christian is compared to a war or a battle. For although it may be said of anyone that the life of man on earth is a warfare, this applies properly to the godly and to those who profess Christ. For they have a common enemy, the devil, who, just as he overthrew our first parents with darts smeared with honeyed poison, so, wandering like a roaring lion, never ceases to seek whom he may destroy and devour. The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures does not hide this one's power and strength, when he calls him the prince of the world and the god of this age. His cruelty is clear enough from his works, since he breathes nothing but murders, the destruction of cities, the devastation of fields, fires, debauchery and countless other things of this kind, each of which harms not only bodies but also leads souls to hell and to eternal torments. He has weapons at hand everywhere, since most people serve in his camp, and he misuses against us even those things which are in us: such as the innate corruption of our whole nature, the desires that spring from it, a depraved understanding, a will inclined to evil, and the organs of the senses, all of which he subjects to the desires of the flesh by wonderful arts, so that they serve him alone against the Spirit. Add to these the whole world, which, though it lies entirely in evil, attacks the worshippers of Christ either by the allurements of bad examples and the snares of pleasures, or by dreadful threats and horrible punishments, so that they abandon their post and give place to the devil. Therefore they can hope for no peace or leisure while they live this mortal life on earth.

units.la: Quid ergo faciendum, ne in pugna succumbamus? Primò cum armis omnino opus sit, num ijs instructi simus videndum est. Nimium enim temerarius fuerit, qui inermis hosti armato & in armis exercitatissimo volet occurrere. Deinde num armis illis ita possimus vti videre oportet, vt nobis ad hostem deuincendum sufficiant. Noluit Dauid armis Saulinis indutus cum Goliatho congredi, quòd se illis impediri & grauari potius quàm adiuuari & defendi sentiret: Ita nos etiam atque etiam curare decet, vt arma habeamus, quæ & nobis conueniant, & quibus deuinci possint omnia salutis nostræ obstacula. Describit ea Paulus Apostolus ad Ephesios his verbis: Assumite vniuersam armaturam Dei, vt possitis stare aduersus insidias diaboli. Quoniam non est nobis luctaa aduersus carnem & sanguinem: sed aduersus imperia, aduersus potestates, aduersus mundi dominos rectores tenebrarum seculi huius, aduersus spiritualies malitias, quæ sunt in sublimi. Quapropter assumite armaturam illam Dei, vt possitis resistere tempore aduerso, & omnibus confectis stare. State igitur lumbis circuncinctis Veritate, & induti thorace Iustitiæ, calceatis pedibus præparatione Euangelij pacis: adhæc assumpto scuto fidei, quo possitis omnia iacula mali illius ignita extingere: galeamque salutis accipite, & gladium Spiritus, quie est Verbum Dei: omni obsecratione & deprecatione orantes omni tempore per Spiritum, & illi ipsi inuigilantes cum omni perseuerantia & deprecatione pro omnibus sanctis, &c. Est hic Apostoli locus dignissimus, quem semper in ore habeamus, & animo voluamus atque meditemur summa qua possumus diligentia. Nam primò hostem describit, vt nos ad arma excitet, ne securitate oppressi succumbamus. Ne gat autem nobis cum carne & sanguine rem esse, non vt carnem aut veterem hominem ab hac pugna excludat, à quo nos quàm maximè oppugnari sentimus: sed vt hostis diaboli conditionem atque naturam exprimat, quæ non mortalis, caduca & infirma, sed perpetua & potentissima est{.}. Ideo dæmones postea malitias spirituales dicit, & ijsdem imperia atque potestates tribuit, adeoq; κοσμο-κρατορας, id est, mundi potentes (vt D. Hilarij verbo vtar) & rectores tenebrarum huius seculi esse ait. At ne his auditis terreamur, armaturam nobis monstrat, qua & nos defendere, & hostes tantos superare possimus: & hanc Dei armaturam dicit, quia ab hoc datur, & eiusdem virtute ad omnia potens atque efficax est{,} quæ in hac pugna fieri oportet. Quod vt melius intelligatur, singulas eius partes ex ordine commemorat. Et à balteo orditur, quod militaris dignitatis insigne olim fuit, vt posteris temporibus torques aurei equestris ordinis testimonium esse cœperunt. Ab illo autem orditur, quia à nobis ipsis initium pugnæ fieri oportet, vt intestinos hostes, qui proditoria arte cum diaolo colludunt, ante omnia subigamus: affectus nimirum pravos & cupiditates illicitas. State igitur (inquit) lumbis circuncinctu Veritate. Recte autem & prudenter Veritatem primo loco nominat, quia nihil hac fortius est & potentius; nec etiam magis idoneum ad obtinendam huius pugnæ victoriam. Vt enim diabolus mendax est, & mendacijs maximè pugnat, ita veritatis lucem ferre nequit, quæ eius impostura & artes detegunt. Similiter cupiditates pravæ suis illecebris nihil aduersus eos possunt, qui Veritatis cognitione instructi de peccatis, de mundo, de voluptatibus, de hominum singulorum officijs rectè iudicant. Prima igitur nobis Veritatis cura fit, & huius luce atque fulgore omnes, quas diabolus nobis offundit, huius seculi tenebræ discutiantur. Deinde thoracem nominat, quo pectus & tota corporis pars anterior munitur. Huius loco iustitiam nobis commendat, qua nisi tegamur, causam nostram aduersus Satanâ non obtinebimus, qui nos peccatis conuictos facile subiget. At quia in illa nobis nulla est, ea intelligi debet, quæ nobis per Euangelium in Christo Iesu offertur, quem nobis à Deo iustitiam factum esse, Paulus alibi testatur. Et sanè vnus ille abundè sufficit, vt iniquitates nostras suo merito auferat, & nostræ etiam naturæ vitio sitatem tegat, ne quid huius nobis imputetur. Adhæc qui huius per fidem verè participes sunt facti, ijdem iustitiæ studeant, & tàm Deo quàm hominibus debita officia præstant. Quamuis ergo parentes honorandos, coniugem cum liberis tenerrimè diligendam, fratres item fouendos, & vitæ nostræ rationem diligentem habendam esse sciant, quia tamen nos totos Deo obstrictos esse, & hunc super omnia ex toto corde & omnibus viribus diligi debere intelligunt, non graue illis fuerit omnibus ijs renuntiare, quibus se ab eius dilectione sentiunt reuocari. At quia in pugna subinde progredi, hostem vrgere & insequi oportet, pedibus quoque armaturam suam Apostolus tribuit, & nos calceatos esse vult præparatione Euangelij pacis. Ita verò loquitur, quia per Euangelium & vocamur & præparamur, vt salutis viam ingressi per omnia aduersa eluctemur. Consultò autem Euangelium pacis dicit, vt sciamus nos cum Deo reconciliatos esse, & proinde inter media arma & belli terrores certam pacis in Christo spem habere. Sed & finem indicat, qui nobis in hac pugna propositus esse debet: vt nimirum Deo propitio vtamur, & cum hominibus quoq; omnibus pacem colamus, quantum in nobis est. Cæterùm quia vndiq; tela volant, & ea non acuta modo, verumetiam ignita, quibus viscera quoq; & medulla (vt ita dicam) aduruntur, quando charissima pignora & homines nobis coniunctissimos relinquere, adeoq; famæ & vitæ nostræ curam omnem abijcere cogimur, scuto etiam nos armat Apostolus: fide scilicet in Iesum Christum, quæ sola telis illis & excipiendis & eludendis atq; resting uendis potest sufficere. Quia enim nos totos Christo inserit, & hunc nobis quoq; vnit, fit vt in eo omnia possimus, & proinde desideria quoq; carnis omnia reslinguamus, quæ nobis hoc certamè sustinentibus obstaculo sunt. Cur enim illis moueatur aut vincatur, qui totus Christi amore ardet, præ quo illi sordent, quæcunq; carni & mundo præclara aut magnifica videntur? Aut quomodo Satanæ vel minas vel pollicitationes admittat, qui Dei verbo credit, & in hoc Veritatem omnem nobis propositam esse notiit? Quia verò caput in primis petit Satan, vt vulnera lethalia nobis infligat, galeam nobis Paulus imponit salutis, vel τὸ σωτήριον: quo nomine iustus ille & pius senex Simeon Christum appellat, vt pote salutis vnicum authorem atq; mediatorem. Hoc autem caput & sensus omnes vnà cum intellectu nostro tegi atq; muniri necesse est: quia eum nobis Pater dedit, vt sapientia nostra fit, & qui in illum vnum intenti sunt, ij neq; pernitiosè errare, neque diaboli telis vllis expugnari possunt. Porrò parum proficit miles, qui tela quidem hostium fortiter excipit, & ad illorum impressionem intrepidus consistit, non habet autem quo illos feriat, iugulet & profligethe: ergo ne quid in eo nobis desit, dexteram quoque gladio Spiritus, id est, Verbo Dei Apostolus armat. Merito autem hoc gladio confertur. Viuus enim est (vt ad Hebræos habetur) sermo Dei, & efficax, & penetrantior quouis gladio ancipiti: ac pertingit vsque ad diuisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumque & medullarum, & discretor est cogitationum & intentionum cordis. Quæ omnia vere dici non ignorant, quicunque Verbum illud attenti audiunt vel legunt. Sed & diabolo gladius hic in primis terribilis est, quia eius sophismata, impostituras & dolos arguit. Nequit ergo ille diutius consistere contra eos, qui illum assidue vibrant. Exemplum huius rei in historia Christi ab illo tentati videmus: unde peti debent, quæ ad pleniorem huius loci expositionem faciunt. Hoc vnum in præsenti monuisse sufficiat, Christianis hominibus nihil perinde necessarium esse, quàm vt Dei Verbum crebrò audiant, inque eius meditatione dies noctesque versentur. Videtur quidem hoc multis superuacaneum esse, quia se abunde instructos putant: at idem postea sibi multa deesse sentiunt, si quando certamen acrius & grauius exoritur. Rursus autem qui Verbi studiosiores sunt, iij tunc illorum opportuna recordatione plurimùm iuuantur, quæ ipsis cum ea audirent, non vsque adeò necessaria esse visa sunt. At quia vires nostræ nullæ sunt, neque armis iistis vti possumus, nisi Dei gratia & virtute adiuuemur, ex qua omnis huius pugnæ euentus atque victoria dependet, postremò nos ad preces assiduas Paulus remittit, quibus ea petere iubet à Deo quæ & nobis & omnibus sanctis siue credentibus necessaria sunt. Etsi enim singulis sua certamina proposita sint, communis tamen est Christianorum omnium militia, & ideo commilitones iure dicuntur. Quare non propriam solùm salutem singuli quærere, sed alios etiam suo studio adiuuare, proqué illis apud Deum precibus assiduis intercedere debent. Et hæc quidem de armis nostris dicta sint, quibus nos instructos esse oportet, si germani & constantes Christi Iesu discipuli esse velimus: quia sine his nunquam ea præstabimus, quæ ille nuper à suis requisiuit.
units.tr: What then must be done so that we do not succumb in the battle? First, since we certainly need arms, we must see whether we are equipped with them. For he would be very rash who, unarmed, wished to meet an armed enemy who is highly skilled in warfare. Second, we must see whether we can use those arms in such a way that they suffice for us to overcome the enemy. David, clothed in Saul's armour, would not fight with Goliath, because he felt that those arms hindered and weighed him down rather than helped and protected him. So we too ought to take great care, again and again, to have arms that both suit us and by which all the obstacles to our salvation can be overcome. The apostle Paul describes them in these words to the Ephesians: "Take up the whole armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Therefore take up that armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and, having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness, and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all, taking the shield of faith, with which you may quench all the fiery darts of that wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints," etc. This is a most worthy passage of the apostle, which we should always have on our lips, and turn over in our minds, and meditate upon with the greatest diligence we can. For first he describes the enemy, in order to rouse us to arms, lest, overcome by complacency, we succumb. He says that our struggle is not with flesh and blood, not so as to exclude the flesh or the old man from this fight, by which we feel ourselves most fiercely attacked; rather, he is setting out the condition and nature of the devil's enemies, which is not mortal, frail and weak, but everlasting and most powerful. Therefore he later calls the demons "spiritual wickednesses," and attributes to them dominions and powers, and says that they are "world-rulers [κοσμοκράτορας]," that is, the mighty of the world (to use the word of St Hilary), and rulers of the darkness of this age. But so that we are not terrified by hearing this, he shows us the armour by which we can both defend ourselves and overcome such great foes; and he calls it God's armour because it is given by God and, by his power, is powerful and effective for all that must be done in this battle. So that this may be better understood, he recounts each of its parts in order. He begins with the belt, which was once the mark of military rank, just as in later times the golden torque became the token of the equestrian order. He begins with this because the battle must begin with ourselves, so that we first subdue the internal enemies who collude with the devil by treacherous skill, namely depraved affections and unlawful desires. "Stand therefore," he says, "with your loins girt about with truth." He rightly and wisely names truth first, because nothing is stronger or more powerful than it, nor more fitted to win the victory in this struggle. For just as the devil is a liar and fights chiefly with lies, so he cannot bear the light of truth, which uncovers his deceit and wiles. Likewise, depraved desires can do nothing against those who, armed with the knowledge of the truth, judge rightly about sins, about the world, about pleasures, and about the duties of each person. Our first care, then, is for the truth, and by its light and brilliance all the darkness of this world which the devil pours over us is to be dispelled. Next he names the breastplate, by which the chest and the whole front part of the body is protected. In its place he commends righteousness to us; unless we are covered by it, we shall not win our cause against Satan, who will easily subdue us when we are convicted of sins. But since we have no righteousness of our own, it must be understood as that which is offered to us through the gospel in Christ Jesus, whom Paul elsewhere testifies has been made righteousness to us by God. And certainly that one alone is more than sufficient to take away our iniquities by his merit, and to cover the faultiness of our nature too, so that nothing of it is imputed to us. Moreover, those who have truly become partakers of this righteousness through faith should also pursue righteousness and perform their duties both to God and to men. So although they know that parents must be honoured, a wife and children must be loved most tenderly, brothers must likewise be cherished, and a careful regard for our life must be kept, yet since they understand that we are wholly bound to God, and that he must be loved above all, with the whole heart and all our strength, it will not be hard for them to renounce all those things by which they feel themselves called back from his love. But because in battle one must keep advancing, pressing and pursuing the enemy, the apostle also assigns to the feet their armour, and wills us to be shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace. He speaks thus because through the gospel we are both called and prepared to enter the way of salvation and to struggle through all adversities. He deliberately says "the gospel of peace," so that we know we have been reconciled to God, and therefore, amid the weapons and terrors of war, have a sure hope of peace in Christ. But he also indicates the aim that ought to be set before us in this battle: namely, that we may enjoy God's favour and cultivate peace with all men as far as in us lies. Furthermore, since missiles fly on every side, and not only sharp ones but fiery ones, by which the very bowels and marrow (so to speak) are set aflame, when we are forced to leave behind our dearest pledges and those most closely joined to us, and to cast off all care for our reputation and life, the apostle also arms us with a shield: namely faith in Jesus Christ, which alone can suffice both to receive and to ward off those missiles and to repel them. For since it engrafts us wholly into Christ and unites him to us also, it comes about that we can do all things in him, and therefore leave behind all the desires of the flesh, which are obstacles to us as we endure this conflict. For why should he be moved or overcome by them who burns wholly with the love of Christ, before whom all things that seem splendid or magnificent to the flesh and the world become worthless? Or how should he admit either the threats or the promises of Satan who believes God's word, and knows that all truth has been set before us in it? But since Satan chiefly aims at the head, to inflict deadly wounds on us, Paul places on us the helmet of salvation, or τὸ σωτήριον [the saving one]; by this name the righteous and pious old man Simeon calls Christ, as the sole author and mediator of salvation. This head and all the senses, together with our understanding, must necessarily be covered and protected, because the Father has given him to us to be our wisdom; and those who are intent on him alone can neither be destroyed by ruinous error nor be overcome by any of the devil's missiles. Moreover, a soldier who bravely receives the enemy's missiles and stands fearless against their attack accomplishes little if he has no means of striking, slaying and routing them. Therefore, lest anything be lacking to us in this respect, the apostle also arms our right hand with the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of God. And this sword is rightly chosen. For the word of God is living, and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, as it is written in Hebrews; it reaches even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and it is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. All who listen attentively to or read that word do not fail to see that these things are truly said. But this sword is especially dreadful to the devil, because it exposes his sophisms, impostures and tricks. He therefore cannot hold out for long against those who wield it constantly. We see an example of this in the history of Christ tempted by him; from there, what helps toward a fuller explanation of this passage should be sought. It is enough here to remind you of this one point: nothing is so necessary for Christians as to hear the word of God often and to be occupied with its meditation day and night. Many think this superfluous, because they believe they are sufficiently instructed; but afterwards they feel that they lack much when a sharper and heavier struggle arises. Conversely, those who are more devoted to the word are greatly helped at such times by the timely recollection of things which, when they heard them, did not seem so very necessary to them. But since our strength is nothing, and we cannot use those arms unless we are aided by the grace and power of God, on which the whole outcome and victory of this battle depends, Paul finally sends us back to constant prayers, by which he bids us ask from God those things that are necessary both for us and for all the saints, that is, for believers. For although each has his own struggles set before him, the warfare of all Christians is common, and therefore they are rightly called fellow soldiers. Hence each must seek not only his own salvation, but also help others by his zeal, and intercede for them with God in continual prayers. And let these things be said about our arms, with which we ought to be equipped if we wish to be genuine and steadfast disciples of Jesus Christ; for without them we shall never accomplish those things which he recently required of his own.

units.la: Porrò etsi nos vt prudentes architectos sumptus supputare iubeat, priusquam ædificium hoc spirituale inchoemus, & vires nostras explorare priusquam huic militiæ sanctissimæ nomen demus: non tamen hæc ita accipi debent, quasi nobis liceat cessare, aut etiam cum hoste diabolo eiusque coniuratis pacisci, si nos infirmiores esse videmus, quàm vt tantis rebus possimus sufficere. Solent quidem nonnulli hoc effugio vti, vt suæ ignauiæ patrocinium inueniant: sed hi mentem Christi & huius admonitionis scopum minus obseruant. Nec enim ista proponit, vt nos terreat, & eos remoretur, qui alacri animo ad ipsum festinant: sed vt rem probè secum deliberent monet, ne alacritas illa ex falsa spe bonorum huius seculi aut propriæ virtutis fiducia procedat, qua frustrati postea tur piter terga vertamus, & ita omnis nostri studij fructus evanescat. Ideo in fine subijcit: Sic quisquis vestrûm non valedicit omnibus bonis suis, non potest meus esse discipulus. Rursus ergo quid facto opus sit docet, & nos ad id præstandum præparari vult, ne tantum opus imprudenter & non prius exploratis viribus nostris aggrediamur. Ex eo autem non sequitur, ab illo abstinendum esse ijs, qui se minus instructos vident: & in hoc ædificandi & militiæ parabola non coeuniunt cum spirituali illa ædificatione atq; militia, de qua hic agitur. Nam in alteris illis prudentis est abstinere ab ædificando, si impensas suis facultatibus maiores fore videat, cum hoste item de pacis honestæ, aut saltem tolerabilis conditionibus agere, si se imparem esse deprehendat. At vt nos supra Christum ædificemur & nostrum ædificium absoluatur, vt item aduersus hostem diabolum perpetuò pugnemus necesse est: quia aliter non poterimus salutem vel retinere vel consequi: Itaque nullis impensis nos abterreri patiamur, etiamsi cum fortunis omnibus parentes quoque, vxorem, liberos, fratres, sorores abijcere oporteat: neque etiam vllis periculis, quæ Satan obijcit, nos patiamur adduci, vt cum eo pacem aut indutias aliquas faciamus, qui & Christi hostis est, & tunc maximè nobis nocet, quando amicitiâ simulat. Lacedæmonij, fortissimi libertatis suæ vindices, olim hostibus iniquissimas pacis conditiones præscribentibus respondisse feruntur: Si iubeamur duriora morte, potius moriemur. At quæcunque à nobis Satan & mundus exigunt, mille mortibus duriora sunt: cum Christi abnegationem petant, quæ cum præsenti æterna mortis periculo coniuncta est. Potius ergo parentes & coniunctissimos quosque relinquamus, imò cum sanguine vitam quoque profundamus potius, quàm turpi illa defectione pacem faciamus cum eo hoste, qui sub pacis prætextu hoc unum agit, ut Dei inimicos faciat. Arguunt hæc nostri seculi hominum ignaviam, quorum alij rerum securi genio indulgent, & vix unquam aduersus diabolum in arenam descendunt: alij verò cum pericula imminent, ad impia pacta se demittunt, & Christum cum Belial, lucem cum tenebris conciliare conantur: multi, qui iam aliquo usque progressi videbantur, subitò deficiunt. Non possunt hi omnes Christi discipuli esse, qui neminem pro suo agnoscet, quem ipsius puderit coram mundo hoc prano & adultero. Nec est, quòd te infirmiorem esse dicas, quàm ut tantas impensas atque pericula possis sustinere. Nam non nostris viribus hoc ædificium aut bellum conficitur. Nostram solummodo operam & nostrorum corporum usum ad illa Deus requirit, vires autem & facultates ipse largitur, quæ nobis necessariæ sunt. Non negemus ergo illi operam nostram, oremus autem indesinenter, ut suo Verbo & Spiritu nos armare dignetur, ut omnibus obstaculis superatis fortes & constantes simus in Christo Iesu Domino & Seruatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, although a prudent architect bids us reckon the costs before we begin this spiritual building, and test our strength before we enlist in this most holy warfare, these words must not be taken to mean that we may be idle, or even make a bargain with the enemy, the devil, and his confederates, if we see ourselves too weak for such great matters. Some indeed use this escape to find a defence for their own cowardice, but such people pay too little heed to the mind of Christ and the purpose of this admonition. For he does not set these things before us to frighten us and hold back those who hasten eagerly to him. Rather, he bids them weigh the matter carefully with themselves, lest that eagerness spring from a false hope of worldly goods or from confidence in their own virtue, so that, once disappointed, they shamefully turn their backs and all the fruit of their effort vanishes. Therefore he adds at the end: "So whoever of you does not renounce all his possessions cannot be my disciple." Again, then, he teaches what must be done and wishes us to be prepared to do it, lest we undertake so great a work rashly and without first testing our strength. It does not follow, however, that those who see themselves less equipped should hold back from it. In this parable of building and warfare they do not correspond to that spiritual building and warfare of which we speak here. For in the former cases it is the mark of a prudent man to refrain from building if he sees the costs will exceed his means, and likewise to negotiate with the enemy for honourable, or at least bearable, terms of peace if he finds himself unequal to the fight. But we must be built up upon Christ and see our building completed, and we must fight against the enemy, the devil, without ceasing, for otherwise we cannot keep or attain salvation. Therefore let us not allow ourselves to be frightened off by any expense, even if we must cast away, together with all our fortunes, our parents also, wife, children, brothers and sisters. Nor let us allow ourselves to be drawn by any dangers Satan throws in our way into making peace or any truce with him, who is Christ's enemy and does us the greatest harm precisely when he feigns friendship. The Lacedaemonians, the bravest defenders of their liberty, are said once to have answered enemies who dictated most unjust terms of peace: "If we are ordered to do things harder than death, we will rather die." But whatever Satan and the world demand of us is a thousand times harder than death, for they demand the denial of Christ, which is joined with the present danger of eternal death. Rather, then, let us leave behind parents and all those closest to us; indeed, let us rather pour out our life along with our blood than make that shameful desertion and peace with that enemy, who under the pretext of peace does this one thing: he makes enemies of God. These things condemn the cowardice of the men of our age. Some, secure in their affairs, indulge their own inclinations and scarcely ever descend into the arena against the devil; others, when dangers threaten, lower themselves to impious pacts and try to reconcile Christ with Belial and light with darkness; and many who seemed to have advanced some way suddenly fall away. None of these can be disciples of Christ, for he will not acknowledge as his own anyone whom he is ashamed of before this perverse and adulterous world. Nor should you say that you are too weak to bear such expenses and dangers. For this building and this war are not carried out by our own strength. God requires of us only our labour and the use of our bodies for these things; strength and resources he himself bestows, and these we need. Let us not, then, deny him our labour, but pray without ceasing that he deign to arm us with his Word and Spirit, so that, all obstacles overcome, we may be brave and steadfast in Christ Jesus, our Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLVIII.

units.la: Bonus est sal: si verò sal infatuatus fuerit, quo condietur? Neque ad terram neque ad sterquilinium appositus est, foras eum abiiciunt. Qui habet aures ad audiendum, audiat.
units.tr: "Salt is good; but if salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be seasoned? It is fit neither for the land nor for the dunghill; men cast it out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

units.la: Quoniam hominum salus in eo potissimum consistit, ut unigenitum Dei Filium Iesum Christum fide vera complectamur, & in eodem constanter in finem usque perseueremus: non tamen nos ille tanta diligentia admonet, nihil nobis tam charum, tam eximium, tam pretiosum debere censeri, quod non sponte relinquamus, imò ut noxium & odio dignum detestemur, si nos ab ipso revocet, aut salutis viam ingressos aliquo modo remoretur. Ut autem hoc facilius fiat præstitu, neue insolens nobis videatur, iubet, ut initio statim quando fidem profiteri volumus, diligenter prius labores, curas, pericula & quæcunque cum ista professione coniuncta sunt expendamus, cumq; his viribus atque facultates nostras conferamus, nosq; ijs muniamus præsidijs, quæ ad opus hoc laboriosum & periculi plenum necessaria sunt. Ad quem scopum ta quoque referri debent, quæ modò recitauimus. Nam argumento ab hominum Christianorum conditione, ad quam vocati sunt, petito, docet cauendum esse, ne qui abiecta fide & calcata Dei gratia, quam semel degustauerunt, non solum seipsos perdant, verumetiam alios corrumpant: quos exemplo suo seruare & in officio continere debebant. Quia verò breuior est Lucas, locus iste ex ijs supplendus erit, quæ Matthæi quinto & Marci nono cap. habentur.
units.tr: Since the salvation of men consists chiefly in embracing with true faith the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, and in persevering constantly in him to the end, Christ nevertheless does not warn us with such great care that we should count nothing so dear, so precious and so valuable to us that we would not willingly give it up. Rather, we should detest as harmful and worthy of hatred whatever would call us back from him, or in any way delay us once we have entered the way of salvation. So that this may be done more easily, and so that it may not seem strange to us, he bids us, at the very start when we wish to profess the faith, first to weigh carefully the labours, cares and dangers, and whatever else is bound up with that profession. We should then set our strength and resources against these, and arm ourselves with those safeguards which are necessary for this laborious work, full of danger. To this same aim the things we have just recited must also be referred. For from the argument drawn from the condition of Christians, to which they have been called, he teaches that care must be taken lest those who have cast off the faith and trampled underfoot the grace of God, which they once tasted, destroy not only themselves but also corrupt others, whom they ought to save and keep in their duty by their example. But because Luke is briefer, this passage must be supplemented from what is found in Matthew chapter 5 and Mark chapter 9.

units.la: Et quia salis parabola vtitur, ante omnia obseruabis, per illum discipulos suos & cum his Christianos omnes intelligi debere, per quos terram siue mundum totum seruari oporteat. Ita verò illi dicuntur propter Verbum Dei, ex quo regenerantur ut filij Dei sint, & cuius naturam referunt, quæ cum sale prorsus conuenit. Est sal natura calidus: ita Dei verbum reuera calidum est, imò æstuans atque feruens, adeò ut suo calore intimos sensus atque ipsas quoque hominum mentes penetret & accendat. Ideo frequenter in scripturis igni conseritur. Nam apud Ieremiam dicit Deus: Annon verbum meum est sicut ignis, & sicut malleus dissipans petram? Et rursus: Ecce ego reddam verba mea in ore tuo ignem, & populum istum ligna, & devorabit eos. Nam ut Dei verbo piorum corda salubriter accenduntur & à sordibus purgantur: ita illo ipso impij devorantur, & tandem magno suo malo sentiunt in Dei ministris cum verbo coniunctam esse virtutem, quæ sufficiat ad reprimendam ipsorum ferociam: quando nimirum Deus vindictam persequitur, quam per illos minatus est. Et huc etiam pertinet, quod in Apocalypsi dicitur de igne, qui ex ore testium Christi egressurus sit, ut ipsorum hostes devoret. Et in præsenti parabola apud Marcum ignem cum sale coniungit, dicens: Omnis homo igne salietur, & omnis victima sale salietur. Deinde sal cum calidus sit, exiccandi vim habet, & proinde scabiei pruritum ex humorum abundantia nascentem tollit, adhaec à corruptione seruat, & ideo perpetuitatis symbolum est, vt à sale denominentur, quae firma stabilia & perpetua esse debent. Sic pactum salis, id est statutum perpetuum dicitur apud Mosem, quo Leuitis sacerdotium & quae inde recipere debebant stipendia Deus assignauit. Et foedus salis cum Dauide Deus fecisse dicitur, quando promissiones dedit de regno, quod in sua posteritate perpetuum & firmum manere debeat. Conueniunt haec quoque cum Dei Verbo. Quia enim ignitum est, non potest ab eo abesse vis diuina, quae superfluos cupiditatum carnis nostrae humores exiccat, peccandi pruritum reflinguit, & ne illo absumamur defendit. Nam vt illud aeternum est, neque vnquam mutatur, multo minus autem aboletur: ita homines quoque seruat, ne in scelaribus computrescant, & eosdem vitae aeternae haeredes facit. Praeterea sale cibi condiuntur, vt sapore suauiori commendentur, & in stomacho facilius concoquantur: Sic Dei Verbum nos, qui natura insipidi & plus quàm fatui sumus, Deo gratos & acceptos reddit, simulque nobis adiumento est, vt durissima quaeque, & quae prorsus intolerabilia videbantur, concoquere & animo constanti sufferre possimus. Postremò magnus in sacrificijs salis vsus fuit olim, & Lex apud Mosem extat: Omne munus sacrificij tui cibarij sale condias, nec vnquam desit sal foederis Dei tui in cibarijs tuis sacrificijs: sed in omni munere tuo salem adhibebis. Id vero in primis Verbo Dei conuenit, sine quo nulli cultus, nulla dicta aut facta nostra Deo placere possunt. Quod ergo veteres dixerunt, nihil sole & sale vtilius esse, hoc verius multo de Verbo Dei potest dici, quo & ad vitam hanc rectè instituendam, & ad conciliandum nobis Dei fauorem, nihil vtilius, nihil magis necessarium est: & ideo (vt paulò ante ex Marco annotauimus) omnes homines hoc igne coelesti saliri oportere Christus dixit.
units.tr: And because he uses the parable of salt, you will observe first of all that by it his disciples are meant, and with them all Christians, through whom the earth, or the whole world, ought to be preserved. They are so called on account of the Word of God, by which they are regenerated to be sons of God, and whose nature they bear, which agrees thoroughly with salt. Salt is by nature hot. So the Word of God is truly hot, indeed burning and glowing, so that by its heat it penetrates and kindles men's innermost feelings and even their very minds. Therefore in the Scriptures it is often compared to fire. For in Jeremiah God says: "Is not my word like fire, and like a hammer that breaks the rock?" And again: "Behold, I will make my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them." Just as the hearts of the godly are salutarily kindled and purged of filth by the Word of God, so the wicked are devoured by that same word. At length, to their great harm, they perceive that in the ministers of God there is joined with the Word a power sufficient to restrain their ferocity, namely when God pursues the vengeance which he threatened through them. To this also pertains what is said in the Apocalypse about the fire which will go out of the mouth of the witnesses of Christ to devour their enemies. And in the present parable, in Mark, he joins fire with salt, saying: "Every man shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt." Then, since salt is hot, it has the power of drying, and so it removes the itching of scabies arising from an abundance of humours. Moreover, it keeps things from corruption, and so it is a symbol of perpetuity; this is why things that ought to be firm, stable and lasting are named from salt. Thus the "covenant of salt", that is, a perpetual statute, is mentioned in Moses, by which God assigned to the Levites the priesthood and the stipends they were to receive from it. And God is said to have made a "covenant of salt" with David when he gave promises about the kingdom, which ought to remain perpetual and firm in his posterity. These things also agree with the Word of God. For since it is fiery, the divine power cannot be absent from it; that power dries up the superfluous humours of our fleshly desires, quenches the itching of sin, and defends us from being consumed by it. For as that Word is eternal, never changes, and much less is abolished, so it also preserves men from rotting in wickedness, and makes them heirs of eternal life. Moreover, food is seasoned with salt so that it may be commended by a sweeter taste and digested more easily in the stomach. So the Word of God makes us, who by nature are insipid and more than foolish, pleasing and acceptable to God, and at the same time it helps us to digest whatever is most harsh, and what seemed utterly intolerable, and to bear it with a steadfast mind. Lastly, salt was of old greatly used in sacrifices, and the Law in Moses stands: "Every offering of your sacrifice you shall season with salt; nor shall the salt of the covenant of your God ever be lacking from your sacrificial food; in every offering you shall add salt." This agrees above all with the Word of God, without which no worship, and no words or deeds of ours, can please God. So what the ancients said, that nothing is more useful than sun and salt, can be said much more truly of the Word of God, by which nothing is more useful and nothing more necessary, both for rightly ordering this life and for winning God's favour for us. Therefore (as we noted a little earlier from Mark) Christ said that all men ought to be salted with this heavenly fire.

units.la: Quia verò quod Verbo suo proprium est, ad homines transfert, non obscurè docet, quales esse oporteat omnes eos, qui ipsi nomen dederunt. In genere enim hoc ab omnibus requiritur, vt diuini illius salis naturam referant. Itaque ante omnia verò & constanti amore Dei ardere debent, vt nihil eius gloria antiquius habeant, eundem omnibus alijs rebus praeferant, neque ab illo diuelli patiantur. Quod vt minori negotio fieri possit, carnis cupiditates inutiles & noxias reflinguant, vt simul expurgatis corruptae naturae sordibus, intolerabilis ille & molestissimus peccati pruritus reprimatur. Neque illis satis fit, ipsos corruptionis & perditionis periculum effugisse, sed curent interim vt suis sermonibus atque totius vita exemplo alios quoque condiant, vt incorrupti sint, & Deo probentur. Nam qui hoc faciunt, proprie sal terrae dicuntur: quia & multis alijs ad salutem adiumento sunt, & propter ipsos saepe populi toti & respublicae seruantur, sicuti in Sodomaorum historia Deus cum Abrahamo colloquens, diserte docet. Denique in hoc praecipuè omnes incumbant, vt sale isto saluberrimo conditi, seipsos Deo sistant hostiam viuentem, qua ille delectari possit. Elucet autem in his magna Christianorum dignitas, quos tanto honore Deus dignatur: & simul eorum arguitur improbitas, qui nominis quidem Christiani professione gloriantur, nihil autem horum praestant, imò his contraria plane faciunt. Est illorum magnus numerus hodie inter eos etiam, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profitentur. Quam multos enim est videre, qui adeò non calent Dei amore, vt nihil inter res huius seculi tam vile & contemptum sit, quod non illi praeferant: nemo item hominum tam improbus reperiatur, in cuius gratiam non aliquid faciant à Christiana professione alienum. Quàm parum autem plerique in expurgandis turpissimarum cupiditatum sordibus profecerint, effrenis illa peccandi licentia satis docet, quae vbique locorum regnat. Quid verò de illis dicemus, qui suo exemplo non solùm alios inficiunt, verumetiam authores sunt, vt propter ipsos Dei Verbum male audiat, & multi pedem referant, qui iam ad illud accessuri erant? Qui verò seipsos Deo hostiam viuentem sistant, paucissimi sunt, cùm maior pars se totos peccato & mundo mancipauerint. Hinc ergo est, quòd plerique & seipsos perdunt, & alios quoq; corrumpunt.
units.tr: But because he transfers to men what is proper to his Word, he clearly teaches what all those who have given their name to him ought to be like. In general this is required of all: that they should bear the nature of that divine salt. Above all, therefore, they ought to burn with a constant love of God, so that they hold nothing more precious than his glory, prefer him to all other things, and suffer themselves never to be torn from him. So that this may be done with less trouble, they should restrain the useless and harmful desires of the flesh, so that, once the filth of corrupt nature is also purged, that intolerable and most troublesome itch of sin may be checked. Nor is it enough for them to have escaped the danger of corruption and perdition. They should also take care, meanwhile, to season others as well, by their speech and by the example of their whole life, so that those others may be incorrupt and approved by God. For those who do this are properly called the salt of the earth: they are a help to salvation for many others, and often whole peoples and commonwealths are preserved on their account, as God, speaking with Abraham in the history of Sodom, clearly teaches. Finally, all should strive above all to be seasoned with this most wholesome salt, so that they may present themselves to God as a living sacrifice, in which he may take delight. In this the great dignity of Christians, whom God honours with such high distinction, shines forth; and at the same time the wickedness of those is exposed who glory in the profession of the Christian name but perform none of these things, and indeed do the very opposite. Today their number is large, even among those who profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel. For how many are there to be seen who so little burn with the love of God that nothing among the things of this age is so base and contemptible that they do not prefer it! Likewise, no man is so wicked that they will not do for his sake something alien to the Christian profession. And how little most have advanced in purging the filth of their most shameful desires is sufficiently shown by the unbridled licence of sinning which reigns everywhere. But what shall we say of those who, by their example, not only infect others but are also the cause that the Word of God is ill spoken of on their account, so that many who were just about to draw near to it turn back? Those who present themselves to God as a living sacrifice are very few, since the greater part have given themselves wholly over to sin and the world. Hence it is that most both destroy themselves and corrupt others too.

units.la: Porrò quod in genere de omnibus Christianis dicitur, hoc singuli etiam pro suae vocationis ratione ad se priuatim transferre discant, vt quoad eos, quibus cum ipsis res est, salus instar sint, quo condiantur atque seruentur. In quo ordine primus locus merito ministrus Ecclesiae & Verbi praeconibus debetur, quibus prae alijs potissimum conuenit, quod apud Matthaeum discipulis siue Apostolis dicitur: Vos estis sal terræ. Debent ergo hi suæ curæ creditos diligenter salire, ne in vitijs aut super stitionibus computrescant. Quò in primis pertinet pœnitentiæ prædicatio, quæ & peccata publice arguit, & quid quisque facere debeat docet. Commendauit hanc olim Deus Prophetis magna cum gravitate, & Apostolos ab hac docendi initium facere iussit Christus, utriq; autem in illa inculcan da & vrgenda non diligentes modò, sed acres etiam & feruentissimi fuerunt. At ne in scelerum a- pertorum locum pestile ns propriæ iustitiæ & meriti fiducia succedat, quæ vt sanies quædam homi num mentes totas inficit, vt instar carnis iam pridem putrefactæ contabescant: ex altera parte gra tiam Dei prædicare & remissionem peccatorum in solius Christi merito monstrare oportet: vt fides in hominum animis accendatur, quæ sola nos Deo sapidos & acceptos reddit. Quod si cum doctrinæ puriorîs sale vitæ etiam piæ & Christianæ exemplum doctores coniungant, tum renera sal terræ & multa laude dignißimi sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, what is said in general of all Christians, each person should also learn to apply privately to himself according to his own calling, so that for those with whom he has dealings he may be salt, by which they are seasoned and preserved. In this order the first place is rightly owed to the ministers of the Church and the heralds of the Word, to whom especially belongs what is said to the disciples, or Apostles, in Matthew: "You are the salt of the earth." They ought therefore to salt diligently those entrusted to their care, lest they rot in vices or superstitions. To this especially pertains the preaching of repentance, which both publicly reproves sins and teaches what each person ought to do. God long ago commended this to the Prophets with great seriousness, and Christ ordered the Apostles to make this the beginning of their teaching. Both have been not only diligent but also keen and most fervent in inculcating and urging it. But lest in place of open wickedness a pestilent confidence in one's own righteousness and merit should take over, which like a kind of festering pus infects men's minds entirely, so that they waste away like flesh long since putrefied, on the other hand it is necessary to preach the grace of God and to show the forgiveness of sins in the merit of Christ alone, so that faith may be kindled in men's hearts, which alone makes us savoury and acceptable to God. But if teachers join to the salt of purer doctrine the example of a pious and Christian life, then they are truly the salt of the earth and most worthy of great praise.

units.la: Similiter hic sui etiam officij admonentur, qui reipub. gubernaculis præsident. Nam vt absque sale vitiis hominum salutaris non potest parari: ita sine magistratu neque pax publica conseruari neque homines in officio contineri possunt, vt bene & commodè viuant. Ergo illi quoque sale Euan gelico conditi ardere debent, vt operam suam cum Ecclesiæ ministris coniungant, gloriam Dei promouere studeant, in legibus vero & iudicijs suis omnibus salù illius acrimoniam salutarem re- ferant, vt cordatus & pius quisque intelligat, ipsos Dei negotium bona fide agere. Et quia maxima exemplorum vis est, vitæ morumque suorum rationem habeant diligentem, vt proprio exemplo leges bonas confirment, & sibijpsis authoritatem concilient quam ipsorum conditio requirit: Qui tales sunt, ij ciuitatum & reipub. sal dici merentur, & tam seipsos quàm alios seruant. Stultissimi autem & ingratissimi hominum sunt, qui tales non venerantur, & in Ecclesia quidem ministros verbi ignauos, in repub. autem magistratus negligentes & infatuatos habere cupiunt, qui ad omni um facta connirent.
units.tr: In the same way those also are reminded of their duty who preside over the helm of the commonwealth. For just as without salt the healing of men's vices cannot be secured, so without the magistracy neither public peace can be preserved nor men kept in their duty so that they may live well and conveniently. Therefore these also ought to be seasoned with the Gospel salt and to burn with zeal, so that they join their work with the ministers of the Church, strive to advance the glory of God, and in their laws and judgments refer all the wholesome sharpness of that salt, so that every sensible and pious person may understand that they are conducting God's business in good faith. And since the force of example is very great, they should take diligent account of the course of their life and morals, so that by their own example they may confirm good laws and win for themselves the authority which their station requires. Those who are such deserve to be called the salt of cities and commonwealths, and they preserve both themselves and others. But the most foolish and ungrateful of men are those who do not venerate such people, and who wish to have in the Church idle ministers of the Word, and in the commonwealth magistrates who are negligent and foolish, who turn a blind eye to everyone's deeds.

units.la: Quod de Ecclesiarum ministris & magistratum gerentibus dicitur, non minus ad parentes & eos omnes pertinet, qui in instituendis pueris parentum officio funguntur. Debent hi quoque memi nisse, se salem totius familiæ esse, quam nisi prudenter gubernent, & disciplina diligenti coerceant, mox licentia sequetur, quæ liberos, seruos, ancillas quoq; & omnes alios domesticos corrũpet. Curent ergo suæ fidei commissos in vera Dei cognitione & pietate institui, peculantiam item & improbos eorundem mores pro virili corrigant, dicta scurrilia & impia proferri non patiantur, cantilenas lasciuas & quæcunq; alia sunt libidinis irritamenta procul excludant. Et hic quoque nõ tam doctri na & institutione, quàm exemplo opus esse meminerint. Quia enim parentum mores pleriq; imitan- tur, nihil pietati & bonis moribus magis officit, quam si mali exempli authores sint illi, quos merito alij omnes respiciunt & obseruant. Debet ista consideratio scholarum quoq; præfectos excitare, vt salem hunc spirent, ne sua vel negligentia vel improbitate eos corrumpant, quos iure spem totius reipub, dixeris. Et huc referri debent quæcunq; in lege de pueris in Dei cognitione & veræ pietatis exercitijs rectè instituendis traduntur.
units.tr: What is said of the ministers of the Churches and of those who bear magistracy applies no less to parents and to all those who fulfil the parental office in the training of children. These too should remember that they are the salt of the whole household; unless they govern it prudently and restrain it with diligent discipline, licence will soon follow, which will corrupt children, servants, maidservants, and all the other members of the household. Let them therefore take care that those committed to their faith are instructed in the true knowledge and piety of God, and as far as they can correct their greed and wicked morals; let them not permit scurrilous and impious words to be uttered, and let them banish far away songs of wantonness and whatever else is an incitement to lust. And let them remember that here too what is needed is not so much teaching and instruction as example. For since most people imitate their parents' morals, nothing hinders piety and good morals more than when those are authors of bad example whom all others rightly regard and observe. This consideration ought also to rouse the heads of schools, so that they breathe this salt and do not corrupt, through their negligence or wickedness, those whom you may rightly call the hope of the whole commonwealth. And to this should be referred whatever the Law hands down about rightly instructing children in the knowledge of God and in the exercises of true piety.

units.la: Vt verò ista fortius persuadeat Dominus, apud Marcum toti huic doctrinæ rationem ab vti- litate subijcit dicens: Habete in vobis ipsis salem, & pacem habete inter vos inuicem. Duo coniungit vt simul ijs respondeat, qui nimio & præpostero pacis aut concordiæ studio abrepti sale isto minus vtendum esse putant, ne inde dissensiones & turbæ oriantur. Etenim passim inueniuntur, qui & di- sciplinam omnem oderunt, & admonitionum omnium impatientes sunt. Sed propter aliquos deplo- rata malitiæ homines non intermitti debet quod ab omnibus Deus requirit officium. Nec enim in omnibus idem accidit. Imò si rem rectè æstimemus, ita coniunctæ sunt inter se disciplina Christiana & pax mutua, vt hanc proprie ex illa nasci dicendum sit. Nam si verbi administri & qui Rem- publicam gubernant, salùs istius acrimonia prudenter vtantur, multorù proteruiam & improbita- tem coercent, qui ad turbas proni sunt. Et in familijs patrum seueritate & grauitate pacem inter domesticos conseruari videmus. Inter priuatos vero homines ad amicitiam vel conciliandam vel retinendam nihil vtilius & efficacius est, quàm si liberè admoneantur qui aliquid præter ossi- cium faciunt. Nam etsi nonnulli id primò impatientius ferant, ijdem tamen (nisi cum humani- tate sensum quoque communem exuerunt) postea re diligentius expensa amici officium agnoscunt.
units.tr: So that the Lord might persuade these things more strongly, in Mark he adds to this whole teaching a reason from its usefulness, saying: "Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves one with another." He joins two things so that he may answer at once those who, carried away by an excessive and misplaced zeal for peace or concord, think that this salt should be used less, lest dissensions and tumults arise from it. For everywhere there are found people who both hate all discipline and cannot bear any admonition. But because of some men whose malice is past cure, the duty which God requires of all should not be abandoned. Nor does the same thing happen in all cases. Indeed, if we judge the matter rightly, Christian discipline and mutual peace are so bound together that it must be said that peace is properly born from discipline. For if the ministers of the Word and those who govern the commonwealth use the sharpness of that salt prudently, they restrain the insolence and wickedness of many who are prone to tumults. And we see that in households peace among the members is preserved by the severity and gravity of the fathers. Among private persons, nothing is more useful or effective for either winning or keeping friendship than to be admonished frankly when one does something beyond one's duty. For even if some at first bear it more impatiently, yet afterwards, unless they have cast off common feeling along with humanity, when they have weighed the matter more carefully they acknowledge the friend's service, and they love those whose correction was salutary for them. But those who admonish nobody to his face, so as not to offend, usually bite behind people's backs and by secret slanders harm others' reputation, and so become the authors of the gravest quarrels and enmities. Rightly, therefore, Christ inserts this saying, by which he teaches that we ought to use that Gospel salt, and at the same time he promises us from it the most excellent fruit, namely peace.

units.la: Magistratus.
units.tr: Magistrates.

units.la: Parentes & pædagogi.
units.tr: Parents and schoolmasters.

units.la: Disciplina paci seruit. & eos redamant, quorum correctio ipsis salutaris fuit. At qui in faciem quidem neminem admonent, ne què offendant, ij ferè absentes mordent, & occultis obtrectationibus aliorū famam laedunt, & sic grauissimorum dissidiorum atque simultatum authores sunt. Recte ergo hanc sententiā Christus interserit, qua docet vt sale isto Euangelico vti debeamus, & simul ex eo nobis fructu praestan tissimum, pacem nimirum pollicetur.
units.tr: Discipline serves peace. And they love those whose correction was wholesome for them. But those who admonish nobody to his face, so as not to offend, bite people for the most part when they are absent, and by hidden backbiting harm the good name of others, and so are the authors of the gravest dissensions and enmities. Rightly, therefore, Christ inserts this sentence, by which he teaches that we ought to use this Gospel salt, and at the same time promises us from it the most excellent fruit, namely peace.

units.la: Caeterum si ista omnia penitius considerentur, mox elucebit misera & infelix nostrorum temporum conditio, quando non vulgo solum suum officium plerique negligunt, verumetiā qui totius terrae sal esse debebant, ipsi insulsi & infatuati sunt. Nam vt à ministris Ecclesiarum exordiamur, quàm multi inter hos sunt canes muti, qui latrare non possunt, dum omnibus placere studeant, & omnem odij & inuidiae occasionem declinant? Quid verò de illis dicemus, qui loco salis Euangelici pulueres venenatos humanarum traditionum aspergunt, & superstitionibus frigidissimis eos dementant, quos Dei verbo erudire & in verae pietatis officio continere debebant. Sunt hi nō Christi æcononi, sed potius auari sicalitores, dum sub verbi diuini praetextu ex iis tributum colligunt & quaestum faciunt, quae ipsi ex suo cerebro comminiscuntur. Adde hīs, quod ijdem ferè mali exempli authores sunt aliis, dum vel ebrietati indulgent, vel libidinis foedae mancipia sunt, vel toti circa opes accumulandas occupantur. Et vtinam non multi tales haberentur inter eos quoque, qui in reformatiōne Ecclesiis docent. Quod si ad principes viros & eos, qui in magistratu sunt, oculos conuertas, idē videbis. Nam plerique quis sal ille diuinus sit nesciunt, & aut nulla prorsus religionis cura tangun tur, aut in illa perinde vt in prophanis rebus sibi omnia licere putant. Itaq; religionem quaestū metiuntur, & Ecclesiarum quidem prouentus ipsi intercipiunt, illarum verò ministris dicendi leges praescribunt, vel etiam tacere cogunt. In repub. autem vel leges omnino nullas condunt, quibus morum licentia frenetur, vel bene conditas negligunt & abolent, aut saltem suo exemplo eas violant & vulgo contemptas faciunt. Sunt ergo homines reuera insulsi, & vtinam non toti reipub. exitiales essent. Eadem ferè est patrumfamiliās, infelicitas, quorum maior pars de religione & sanctaliberorum institutione vix vnquam cogitat, multi verò insuper liberos suos pessimis artibus instituunt, & à primis annis ad superbam & luxuriosam vestium ostentationem, ad intemperantiam, libidinem, fraudes, impostturas, deniq; ad crudelitatem & sanguinariam bellandi rabiem afflucfaciunt. Quibus plerunq; hoc etiam accedit, quod proprio exemplo corrumpunt eos, quos ad pietatem instituere debebant. Quis ergo tales non dixerit salem infatuatum, imò vix hoc etiam nomine dignos esse, cum ne externam quidem salis speciem referant? Hinc ergo enascitur quae apud omnes hominum ordines regnat effrenis morum licentia, & immanis atq; plus quam Cyclopicus religionis contemptus. Quid enim aliud fiat, quando qui alios ad Christi fidem adducere, & suo insuper exemplo terram omnem salire debebant, plurimos in superstitionibus detinent, à veritatis studio abstrerent, & pessimis exemplis passim omnes inficiunt?
units.tr: Moreover, if all these things are considered more deeply, there will soon shine forth the wretched and unhappy condition of our times, when not only do most people neglect their duty among the common folk, but even those who ought to be the salt of the whole earth are themselves unsalted and foolish. For to begin with the ministers of the Churches: how many among them are dumb dogs, who cannot bark, while they strive to please everybody and avoid every occasion of hatred and envy? And what shall we say of those who, instead of the salt of the Gospel, sprinkle poisonous dust of human traditions, and drive out of their senses with the coldest superstitions those whom they ought to instruct in the Word of God and keep in the duty of true piety? They are not stewards of Christ but rather avaricious extortioners, while under the pretext of the divine word they collect tribute from people and make gain from things which they themselves have invented out of their own brains. Add to these that the same men are for the most part bad examples to others, since they either indulge in drunkenness, or are slaves of foul lust, or are wholly occupied with piling up wealth. And would that many such were not found among those also who teach in the reformed Churches. And if you turn your eyes to the princes and those who hold magistracy, you will see the same. For most of them do not know what that divine salt is, and either are touched by no care for religion at all, or in religion think that everything is permitted to them just as in profane affairs. Thus they measure religion by profit: they themselves intercept the revenues of the Churches, and prescribe laws of speaking to the ministers of those Churches, or even force them to be silent. In the commonwealth, either they enact no laws at all by which licence of morals may be restrained, or they neglect and abolish those well enacted, or at least by their own example they violate them and make them despised by the common people. Therefore they are truly unsalted men, and would that they were not utterly destructive to the whole commonwealth. The unhappiness of the heads of families is much the same, the greater part of whom scarcely ever think about religion and the holy upbringing of their children; and many moreover train their children by the worst arts, and from their earliest years drive them to proud and luxurious display of clothing, to intemperance, lust, frauds, deceits, and finally to cruelty and the bloody frenzy of war. To these it often adds that they corrupt by their own example those whom they ought to have trained to piety. Who, then, would not call such men unsalted salt, and scarcely even worthy of this name, since they do not even show the outward appearance of salt? Hence arises that unbridled licence of morals which reigns among all orders of men, and that monstrous religious contempt, more than Cyclopean. For what else must happen, when those who ought to lead others to faith in Christ, and moreover by their own example to season the whole earth, keep most people in superstitions, turn them away from the pursuit of truth, and everywhere infect all with the worst examples?

units.la: Sunt hi reuera omnium hominum infelicissimi, vt ex huius loci verbis patet. Addit enim Christus: Si verò sal infatuatus fuerit, quo condietur? Neque ad terram, neque ad sterquilinium appositus est: foras eum abijciunt. Tria dicit, quibus istorum infelix conditio & quae eos manent poenae comprehenduntur. Primum, si sal infatuatus fuerit (inquit) quo ipse condietur? Interrogatione vtitur; vt fortior sit negatio, qua docere vult nihil esse, quo tales corrigi possint. Nam vt salis acrimonia semel amissa & extincta non potest restitui: ita incurabiles sunt, qui quam ex Dei Verbo habuerunt, acrimoniam euanescere patiuntur, eamq; ipsi restinguunt. Quia enim solum Dei verbū nos salit & illi acceptos reddit, certè qui illo excusso ad pristinam corruptionem redeunt, ijs nihil in tota rerum natura reliquum est, quo possint reparari. Sunt enim ex eorum numero, quos Apostolus per poenitentiam renouari posse negat. Nā vt terrae maledictae indicium est, si licet caelitus rigetur & studiosè colatur, nihilominus tamen nihil praeter spinas & tribulos profert: ita incurabiles plane sunt, qui nec efficacissimo illo & saluberrimo sale verbi Dei corrigi & in officio retineri possunt. Exempla passim occurrunt, euidentissima autem sunt, quae in illustrioribus personis proponuntur. Quem enim ex pseudoprophetis & pseudoapostolis vnquam emendatum fuisse legimus? Certè post quam Romani episcopi ab Apostolorum exemplo degenerauerunt, & sal infatuatus facti sunt, nemo mortalium, imò ne Imperatorum quidem potentissimorum, eos in ordinem redigere potuit. Quod ipsum
units.tr: Those men are truly the most unhappy of all people, as the words of this passage make plain. For Christ adds: "But if the salt has lost its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? It is neither fit for the land nor for the dunghill; men cast it out." He says three things, by which the unhappy condition of these people and the punishments that await them are comprehended. First, "if the salt has lost its savour" (he says), "wherewith shall it be salted?" He uses a question so that the denial is stronger, by which he means to teach that nothing remains by which such people can be corrected. For just as the sharpness of salt, once lost and extinguished, cannot be restored, so those are incurable who allow the sharpness they had received from God's Word to fade away and who themselves quench it. For since only the Word of God salts us and makes us acceptable to him, certainly those who, having shaken off that Word, return to their former corruption have nothing left in the whole of nature by which they can be repaired. They belong to the number of those whom the Apostle says cannot be renewed through repentance. For just as the sign of a cursed land is that, though it is watered from heaven and carefully cultivated, it nevertheless produces nothing but thorns and thistles, so those are wholly incurable who cannot be corrected and kept in their duty even by that most effective and wholesome salt of God's Word. Examples occur everywhere, but the most obvious are those set forth in more illustrious persons. For what false prophet or false apostle have we ever read to have been amended? Certainly, after the bishops of Rome degenerated from the example of the Apostles and became salt that had lost its savour, no mortal, not even the most powerful emperors, could bring them back into order.

units.la: Corruptio nostri seculi.
units.tr: The corruption of our age.

units.la: Sali infatuato quid fiat?
units.tr: What happens to salt that has lost its savour?

units.la: Heb. 6. ipsum de apostatis omnibus dici posse, qui fide abnegata salem illum infatuari sinunt, quo prius cosecrati fuerant. Sunt enim peiores multo ijs, qui nulla habent adhuc fidei principia. Ita principes quoque viri, si reliquis vitijs contemptum verbi Dei coniungant, corrigi non possunt. Qua enim ratione id fiat, quando illud reijciunt, quod solum illis praestantius est & efficacius? aut num hominum authoritate moucbuntur, quibus Dei omnipotentis & verbi eius authoritas sordet? Deinde salem infatuatum prorsus inutilem, & ne ad terram quidem aut sterquilinium, appositum esse dicit Christus. Nam sterilitatem inducit, nec aliquid ex seipso procreat. Itaque etsi aliarum rerum omnium, etiamsi corrumpantur, aliquis usus sit, salis tamen nullus esse potest, vbi acrimoniam suam amisit. Hoc ipsum omnibus solet accidere, qui Euangelij sale conditi suam dignitatem semel prostituerunt. Digni enim sunt, qui omni simul authoritate amissa omnibus exosi & infames sint.
units.tr: Heb. 6. This can be said of all apostates, who, having denied the faith, allow that salt by which they had earlier been consecrated to lose its savour. For they are far worse than those who as yet have no principles of faith. So too princes, if they join contempt for the Word of God to their other vices, cannot be corrected. For by what means can this happen, when they reject that which alone is more excellent and effective for them? Or will they be moved by the authority of men, when the authority of almighty God and of his Word is worthless to them? Next, Christ says that salt which has lost its savour is wholly useless, and fit neither for the land nor for the dunghill. For it brings on barrenness and produces nothing from itself. Therefore, although all other things, even when they have decayed, still have some use, salt that has lost its sharpness can have no use at all. This happens to all who, once seasoned with the salt of the Gospel, have prostituted their dignity. For they deserve, having lost all authority at once, to be hated and infamous to everyone.

units.la: Exempla quae huc faciunt, in quibusdam nostri seculi doctis est videre, qui cum non vulgarem haberent Euangelicae veritatis cognitionem, ut ex eorum libris apparet, eam tamen aperte profiteri aut Ecclesiae Christi se coniungere noluerunt, ne potentes & illustres viros, quorum fauore sustentabantur offenderent. Quid vero illis accidit? Euanuit paulatim apud illos salis istius acrimonia, ipsi vero cum suis scriptis, quorum immortalitati consultum volebant, prorsus inutiles facti sunt, cum & hostibus suspecti sint, & neque nos illis vti possimus, qui partes nostras tam turpiter deserue runt. Recte igitur Christus tertium adijcit, quod salem infatuatum foras eijciant, ut conculcetur a quibusvis. Notatur ea locutione extremus contemptus, quo digni sunt omnino, qui Dei gratiam non maioris faciunt, quam quod ea gustata seipsos tame prophanant. Possunt huc referri, quae apud Malachiam infidis & ignauis Sacerdotibus Deus minatur. Sensit hoc Christi iudicium Ecebolius Sophista Constantinopolitanus, qui cum prius inter Christianos prae alijs ferucre videretur, sub Iuliano a fide defecit. Cum enim hoc extincto ad Ecclesiam redire cuperet, propriae conscientiae testimonio conuictus ante templi fores prosternebatur, altum clamans: παπαπαπ με το αλας το αλατ, id est, calcate me salem insensatum. At quod fidei abnegatoribus accidit, hoc etiam in Reipub. principibus viris, & in re domestica patribus familias accidere solet, qui salem infatuatum referunt, & authoritatem suam ipsi prosternunt, qua illos Deus armauit. Erat hoc probe meditandum Ecclesiae & Reipub. praesidibus, parentibus item & scholarum praefectis, qui omnes de collapsa omnium ordinum authoritate queruntur. At quomodo ea consistere potest, cum ipsi sal infatuatus sint, & suam dignitatem turpissime prostituant?
units.tr: Examples that bear on this can be seen among some learned men of our age, who, although they had no common knowledge of evangelical truth, as their books show, nevertheless were unwilling to profess it openly or to join the Church of Christ, lest they offend the powerful and illustrious men by whose favour they were supported. What then happened to them?
