The sharpness of that salt faded away little by little among them, and they themselves, with their writings, whose immortality they wished to secure, became wholly useless, since they are suspected by their enemies, and we cannot make use of them, because they have so shamefully deserted our cause. Rightly, therefore, Christ adds a third point: that they cast the salt that has lost its savour outside, so that it may be trampled underfoot by anyone. By this expression is marked the utmost contempt, which they thoroughly deserve who value the grace of God no more than to taste it and then profane themselves. To this may be referred what God threatens against the faithless and idle priests in Malachi. The judgment of Christ was felt by Ecebolius the sophist of Constantinople, who, though he had seemed before to shine among the Christians above others, fell away from the faith under Julian. For when after Julian's death he wished to return to the Church, convicted by the testimony of his own conscience, he lay prostrate before the doors of the temple, crying out loudly: "Trample me, the salt that has lost its savour" [παπαπαπ με το αλας το αλατ]. But what happens to those who deny the faith also tends to happen to the princes of commonwealths, and to heads of households in their own homes, who become salt that has lost its savour and cast down their own authority, with which God has armed them. The rulers of the Church and of the commonwealth, and likewise parents and the heads of schools, ought to have pondered this well, since all of them complain of the collapse of authority in every rank. But how can it stand, when they themselves have become salt that has lost its savour and shamefully prostitute their own dignity?

units.la: Quia vero doctrina haec magni momenti est, graui epiphonemate eam commendat. Qui habet aures ad audiendum, audiat. Quo dicto omnes ad illius meditationem diligentem excitantur, & cauetur, ne quis iocularem esse, aut eam nihil ad se pertinere putet. Non temere autem aurium meminit. Nam etsi de auditu solo dicere videatur, longius tamen prospicit: Vt nimirum facultates omnes intendamus in ijs considerandis, ex quibus vniuersum hominis Christiani officium dependet. Vt enim aures dantur ad audiendum, oculi ad videndum, ita ratio & intellectus dantur ad ea percipienda quae corporis sensus excedunt, & ad totius hominis salutem pertinent. Et qui donis ita sibi datis digne veruntur, ij indies in melius proficiunt: excaecatio autem horribilis & induratio cum aeterna morte coniuncta eos manet, qui videntibus oculis videre nolunt, & audientes no audiunt, adeoque quod sciunt nesciunt. Faxit Deus Opt. Max. ut sale verbi sui vere imbuti, Christum Iesum vita & moribus referamus, & cum eodem in coelis olim regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Since this teaching is of great importance, he commends it with a weighty exclamation: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." By this saying all are roused to diligent meditation upon it, and care is taken that no one thinks it a jest or that it has nothing to do with him. He does not mention ears without reason. For although he seems to speak of hearing alone, he looks further ahead: namely, that we should direct all our faculties to considering those things on which the whole duty of a Christian depends. For just as ears are given for hearing and eyes for seeing, so reason and understanding are given for perceiving those things which exceed the senses of the body and pertain to the salvation of the whole man. Those who use the gifts so given to them worthily make progress daily into better things, but a terrible blindness and hardening, joined with eternal death, remain for those who, though their eyes see, are unwilling to see, and who, though they hear, do not listen, and so do not know what they know. May God, best and greatest, grant that, truly seasoned with the salt of his Word, we may show forth Christ Jesus in life and conduct, and reign with him in heaven hereafter, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLIX.

units.la: Accedebant autem ad eum omnes publicani & peccatores, vt eum audirent. Et murmurabant Pharisaei & Scribae, dicentes: Iste peccatores recipit, & vescitur cum eis: Ipse vero locutus est ad eos hanc parabolam, dicens: Quis ex vobis, si habeat centum oues, & perdiderit
units.tr: Now all the tax collectors and sinners drew near to him to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying: This man receives sinners and eats with them. But he spoke to them this parable, saying: What man among you, having a hundred sheep, and having lost one of them,

units.la: {*} Attentionem requirit. vnam exillis, non relinquit illas nonaginta nouem in deserto, & pergit ad eam quae perijt, vsque dum eam inueniat? Et inuentam imponit in humeros suos gaudens, veniensque domum conuocat amicos & vicinos, dicens eis: Gratulamini mihi, nam inueni ouem meam quae perierat. Dico vobis ita fore gaudium in coelo super vno peccatore resipiscente magis, quam super nonaginta nouem iustis, quibus non opus est resipiscentia. Aut quae mulier, si habeat drachmas decem, & perdiderit drachmam vnam, non accendit lucernam ac verrit domum, quaeritque accurate, vsquequo eam inueniat? Et cum inuenerit, conuocat amicas & vicinas, dicens: Gratulamini mihi, nam inueni drachmam quam perdideram. Ita dico vobis, gaudium est apud Angelos Dei super vno peccatore resipiscente.
units.tr: {*} It requires attention. does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders rejoicing, and coming home he calls together friends and neighbours, saying to them: Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. I tell you that there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous who have no need of repentance. Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her women friends and neighbours, saying: Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma that I had lost. So I tell you, there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents.

units.la: Dixit autem hucusque Iesus Christus de suorum discipulorum officijs, quae sunt, vt seipsos abnegent, crucem suam patienter ferant, & ipsum constanti fide atque diligenti sui exemplimitatione sequantur. Et haec quidem tanta cum gravitate requirit, vt infamem & irreparabilem aeternae salutis iacturam omnibus minetur, qui non toti in hoc sunt, vt ipsis sufficere & ea praestare possint. At poterant illa infirmiores & male sibi conscios non parum terrere, quasi ille neminem pro suo agnoscat, qui non omnibus numeris perfectus sit, aut in gratiam non recipiat eos, qui semel eius iugum excusserunt. Commode ergo nunc toto hoc Cap. doctrinam de poenitentia, de Dei misericordia & gratuita peccatorum remissione subijcit, cuius summa est: Je peccatores adeo non aspernari, vt potius propter illos in hunc mundum venerit, Dei vero misericordiam & peccatorum remissionem omnibus paratam esse, qui per poenitentiam ad ipsius gregem, Ecclesiam, reuertuntur.
units.tr: Up to this point Jesus Christ has spoken of the duties of his disciples: that they deny themselves, bear their cross patiently, and follow him with steadfast faith and diligent imitation of his example. He demands these things with such seriousness that he threatens disgraceful and irreparable loss of eternal salvation to all who are not wholly intent on being able to meet and perform them. Yet these words could greatly frighten the weaker and those with guilty consciences, as if he acknowledged as his own none who were not perfect in every respect, or received again into favour those who had once shaken off his yoke. So now, fittingly, throughout this whole chapter he sets out the teaching about repentance, about God's mercy and the free forgiveness of sins, the sum of which is this: that the Lord does not so despise sinners that he came into this world rather for their sake, and that God's mercy and forgiveness of sins are ready for all who return through repentance to his flock, the Church.

units.la: Praemittit autem pro more suo Lucas doctrinae huius occasionem, quae fuit, quod ad Christum omnes istius loci publicani & qui alijs peccatis infames erant, accesserunt. Factum hoc saepius, to quod in illo consolationem & conscientiae pace inueniebant. Id vero non potuerunt ferre Pharisaei & Scribae, qui vt propriae iustitiae fiducia efferebantur, ita ex peccatis vulgi & afflictis multorum conscientijs quaestum faciebant, cum eos ad sacrificia & alia legis opera remitterent. Mox ergo huc concursum hominum manifestis vitijs laborantium illi exprobrant, dicentes: Ille peccatores recipit, & vescitur cum eis. Et haec dicendo non tam praesens factum carpere, quam ipsum omnibus suspectum & inuisum facere instituunt, quasi sua doctrina & exemplo hominibus scelerati patrocinetur, atque indulgentia nimia eos praefractiores reddat, qui seuerius erant coercendi. Offenduntur ergo doctrina gratiae & misericordiae Dei, quod omnibus proprium est, qui in salutis negotio humanam rationem in consilium adhibent. Tametsi Deus doctrinam illam & gratuitae misericordiae promissiones in ipso Paradiso primis parentibus praedicauerit, & eadem postea omnibus seculis illustrauerit atque exemplis plurimis confirmarit: haeret tamen in illis subinde carnis ratio, & Deum quidem misericordem esse fatetur, sed eius misericordia eos solummodo frui putat, qui iustitiae studient, aut in quibus meritum aliquod inuenitur, quod aliqua saltem ratione ipsorum delicta compenset. Nec enim de eo cogitat humana sapientia, quod misericordiae & gratiae amplitudo illustrior multo appareret in miseris peccatoribus, quam in ijs qui aliquo iustitiae titulo palliantur. Hinc est, quod Pharisaei olim nunquam non contra Christum murmurarunt, & hodie plurimos Euangelij doctrina hoc nomine offendit, quod gratiae praedicatione iustitiam Dei aboleri, & inter homines securitatem atque peccandi licentiam plantari metuunt. Et hoc quidem hodie nobis multi palam obijciunt, eorumque clamoribus simpliciores fere offensi de Euangelio minus honorifice sentire, aut saltem animis suis fluctuare incipiunt.
units.tr: Luke, as is his custom, prefaces the occasion of this teaching, which was that all the tax collectors and those otherwise infamous for sins in that place drew near to Christ. This happened often, because they found consolation and peace of conscience in him. But the Pharisees and scribes could not bear this. Puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, they profited from the sins of the common people and the troubled consciences of many, since they sent them back to sacrifices and other works of the law. So at once they reproach him for this gathering of men labouring under obvious vices, saying: This man receives sinners and eats with them. In saying this they aimed not so much to find fault with the present deed as to make him suspect and hateful to all, as if by his teaching and example he were defending wicked men, and by excessive indulgence making more stubborn those who ought to have been restrained more severely. So they take offence at the teaching of God's grace and mercy, which is characteristic of all who in the business of salvation take human reason as their counsellor. Although God proclaimed that teaching and the promises of his free mercy to our first parents in Paradise itself, and afterwards illuminated them in every age and confirmed them with very many examples, nevertheless human reason keeps clinging to these things from time to time. It confesses that God is merciful, but thinks his mercy is enjoyed only by those who pursue righteousness, or in whom some merit is found that at least in some way makes up for their offences. For human wisdom does not consider that the greatness of mercy and grace appears far more glorious in wretched sinners than in those who are covered by some title of righteousness. Hence it is that the Pharisees of old never ceased to murmur against Christ, and today the teaching of the gospel offends very many on this account: they fear that by the preaching of grace the righteousness of God is abolished, and that security and licence to sin are planted among men. Many now openly raise this objection to us, and the simpler sort, offended by their outcries, nearly all begin to think less honourably of the gospel, or at least to waver in their minds.

units.la: Est ergo diligenti consideratione dignissima Christi responsio, quam horum cauillis opponit, cuius duplex status est. Primo enim docet, se nihil praeter officium fatere, dum peccatores ad se colligit: quando boni pastoris sit oues errantes quaerere, & ad gregem reducere, bona autem & frugi materfamilias in vnius drachmae amissae recuperatione studium suum omne intendat. Deinde hypocrisim illorum arguit, adeoque malitiam eorum accusat, qui remissionem peccatorum gratuitam & salutem ijs tem ijs inuideant, quibus potius congratulari deberent. Et quia haec magni momenti sunt, parabolis elegantissimis doctrinam hanc illustrat, quae vt Dei gratiam nobis commendant, ita vniuersam salutis nostrae ordinem egregie depingunt, & Ecclesiarum pastores, adeoque omnes homines sui erga peccatores officij admonent. In praesenti duas parabolas connectit, quas & nos breuitatis causa coniunctim exponemus hoc ordine: Primum hominis peccatoris conditionem videbimus: deinde de Dei erga peccatores studio & vniuersa salutis ratione dicetur. Postremo quis nobis erga eos animus esse debeat, in quorum conuersione gratiae Dei exemplum peculiare habemus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ's answer to these cavillers deserves most careful consideration, and it has a twofold character. First, he teaches that in gathering sinners to himself he does nothing beyond his duty: it belongs to a good shepherd to seek straying sheep and bring them back to the flock, and it belongs to a good and thrifty housewife to direct all her care to recovering one lost drachma. Then he exposes their hypocrisy, and so accuses the malice of those who grudge free forgiveness of sins and salvation to those whom they ought rather to congratulate. And because these matters are of great weight, he illustrates this teaching with most elegant parables, which both commend God's grace to us and admirably portray the whole order of our salvation, and remind the pastors of the Churches, and indeed all men, of their duty towards sinners. In the present passage he joins two parables, which we too, for the sake of brevity, will expound together in this order: first we shall see the condition of the sinner; then it will be said what is God's concern for sinners and the whole manner of our salvation; lastly, what attitude we ought to have towards them, since in their conversion we have a singular example of God's grace.

units.la: Quoad primum, oui perditae aut erranti & drachmae amissae peccatores confert Christus. Loquitur enim de iis, qui non simpliciter ex innata nobis naturae prauitate peccant (quod sanctis quoque & fidis Dei cultoribus solet accidere) verum de illis, qui a Deo prorsus alieni extra Ecclesiae eius septa vagantur, & quorum salus, si illos solos spectes, prorsus deplorata est. Probe autem & propriissime utraque similitudo huic argumento conuenit. Numis enim aut drachmis antiquo more (cuius authorem primum Ianum fuisse veteres scriptores prodiderunt) principum aut etiam Deorum imagines atque nomina imprimuntur. Ita ad suam imaginem Deus initio hominem condidit, & suum nomen nobis quodammodo insculpsit, dum nos suos filios & suum opus vocare dignatur. At imaginem illam primi parentes in seipsis vastarunt, quando diuini mandati transgressores facti sunt, & eadem opera seipsos & posteritatem omnem perdiderunt. Recte ergo drachmis amissis aut perditis similes dicit Christus, cum hominis, in quo Dei imago obliterata est, ita domo eius non maior vsus sit quam in familia aliqua amissi numi esse potest. Deinde vt ouis animal stolidum est & futuri ignarum atque negligens: consilio item destituitur, seque ipsam adeo inuare aut seruare non potest, vt si semel gregem deseruerit, ad eum non possit reuerti, neque pastorem quaerat ipsa, sed vt ab eo quaeratur necesse sit: Ita homines post amissam puriorem rationis lucem naturali stolidi sunt, neque ea percipere possunt quae sunt spiritus Dei: adhaec praesentibus solis intenti de salute futura vix vnquam cogitant, & si semel a Deo auersi sint, ad eum sponte nunquam reuertuntur, nisi ipse eos quaerat, & ad suae Ecclesiae gregem reducat. Imo vt ouis ouem per praecipitia quoque ruentem sequitur & temerario saltu sese perdit: ita homines mundi in suum exitium ruentis exemplum sequi solent: & quamuis in peccatorum praecipitiis multos iam pridem periisse, multos item quotidie perire videant, nihilominus tamen ipsi quoque plus quam stolida temeritate ijsdem peccatis sese mancipant, & eiusdem exitii sibi ipsis auctores sunt. Exempla quibus id probetur, non opus est adducere, cum quotidie fiant, quae istis fidem faciunt. Ideo Isaias quoque perditam & deploratam humani generis conditionem describurus ait: Nos omnes tanquam oues erravimus, quisque in viam suam respexit. Est horum cognitio admodum necessaria, adeoque salutis nostrae principium est: Quia enim tales sumus, nihil ad illam ex nobis ipsis possumus conferre, sed ad Dei gratiam confugiamus oportet, qui eam nobis in Filio suo offert. Itaque prima haec pars eos confutat, qui hominis vires praedicant, & ad operum merita remittunt eos, qui peccatorum suorum conscientia grauantur: quem nocentissimum errorem esse, non vno loco demonstrauimus.
units.tr: As to the first point, Christ compares sinners to a lost sheep and to a lost drachma. For he speaks of those who do not sin merely from the innate corruption of our nature (which also tends to happen to the saints and faithful worshippers of God), but of those who wander entirely estranged from God, outside the fold of his Church, and whose salvation, if you look at them alone, is utterly hopeless. Both comparisons fit this matter most aptly and appropriately. For in the ancient manner, coins or drachmas bear the images and names of princes or even of gods (the ancient writers record that Janus was the first author of this practice). So God at the beginning made man in his own image, and in some measure engraved his name upon us, when he deigns to call us his sons and his work. But our first parents laid waste that image in themselves when they became transgressors of the divine command, and by the same act destroyed themselves and all their posterity. Rightly, then, Christ calls men like lost or perished drachmas, since in the man in whom the image of God has been effaced, its use for his household is no greater than a lost coin can be in some family. Next, as a sheep is a stupid animal, ignorant of what lies ahead and careless, and is also without counsel, and cannot help or save itself, so that once it has deserted the flock it cannot return to it, nor does it seek the shepherd itself, but it must be sought by him: so men, after the purer light of reason has been lost, are by nature stupid, and cannot perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. Moreover, intent only on present things, they hardly ever think of future salvation, and if once they have turned away from God, they never return to him of their own accord, unless he himself seeks them and brings them back to the flock of his Church. Indeed, just as a sheep follows a sheep that is rushing over a precipice and destroys itself by a reckless leap, so the people of the world are accustomed to follow the example of those who rush to their own ruin; and although they see that many have already perished long ago in the precipices of sin, and many die every day, nevertheless they too, with more than foolish rashness, surrender themselves to the same sins and become the authors of the same ruin for themselves. There is no need to bring forward examples to prove this, since daily occurrences bear witness to it. So Isaiah too, about to describe the lost and despaired-of condition of the human race, says: We all like sheep have gone astray; each has turned to his own way. The knowledge of these things is most necessary, and indeed it is the beginning of our salvation: for since we are such, we can contribute nothing to it from ourselves, but we must flee to the grace of God, who offers it to us in his Son. Therefore this first part refutes those who extol the powers of man and send back to the merits of works those who are burdened by the consciousness of their sins; which error we have shown in more than one place to be most harmful.

units.la: Nunc ad alteram partem accedamus, quae ardentissimum & plus quam paternum Dei studium erga peccatores, & totam salutis nostrae rationem atque ordinem adumbrat. Vbi primo loco occurrit, quod qui infelicem nostram conditionem nouerat, minime eos neglexit, sed pastorem nobis iam inde ab aeterno constituit, Filium suum vnigenitum, cuius opera & labore seruaremur. Expontit hoc Dei consilium Ezechiel Propheta, qui illum de gregis sui dispersione conquerentem his verbis inducit: Errauit grex meus in omnibus montibus, atque in omni colle excelso, in omni superficie terrae dispersus est, grex meus, nec est qui quaerat aut requirat. Postea multa vero, quae ibidem contra iniquos & male fidos pastores dicuntur, tandem subiicit: Ego seruabo oues meas, vt non pateant vltra direptioni, & iudicabo inter pecus & pecus. Et suscitabo super eas pastorem vnum, qui pascat eas, Dauidem seruum meum: is pascet eas, & is erit eis Pastor. Ego autem Dominus ero eis Deus, seruus meus Dauid princeps in medio earum. Per Dauidem vero Christum intelligit, quem ex Dauidis semine hominem nasciturum esse alibi promiserat. Et huius generis multa apud Prophetas habentur. Isaias certe idem his verbis dicit:
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other part, which sets out God's most ardent and more than fatherly zeal toward sinners and the whole plan and order of our salvation. Here we first meet the fact that God, who knew our unhappy condition, did not neglect us at all, but from eternity appointed as our shepherd his only-begotten Son, by whose work and labour we would be saved. The prophet Ezekiel expounds this counsel of God, introducing him complaining of the scattering of his flock in these words: "My flock has gone astray on all the mountains and on every high hill; my flock is scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there is none who seeks or searches for them." Afterwards he says much against the wicked and faithless shepherds, and at last adds: "I will save my sheep, so that they are no longer exposed to plunder, and I will judge between sheep and sheep. And I will set up over them one shepherd, who will feed them, my servant David: he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. And I the Lord will be their God, and my servant David a prince in their midst." By David he means Christ, whom he had elsewhere promised would be born a man from the seed of David. Many things of this kind are found among the prophets. Isaiah certainly says the same thing in these words:

units.la: E Deus vester,ecce Eominus Deus veniet in robore, & brachium eius dominabitur perse e merces eius cum eo,& opus eius ante ipsum.Pascet gregem suum vt pastor,& brachio suo con gregabit agnos,inque gremio suo feret,fœtas autem suauiter ducet,&c.Concurrunt hic multa ma ximæ bonitatis argumenta. Huius enim est,quod nos priusquam, essemus respexit : quod propria salutis securos & nihil de ipsa cogitantes videt & nostra perditione dolet,quod pastorem ijs desti- nauit,qui seipsos pascere & seruare non poterant. Superat autem hæc omnia, quod cum nemo ho- minum siue Angelorum huic muneri obeundo posset sufficere, Filium suum vnigenitum & dile- ctum,pastorem dedit, qui in Euangelio tam hic quam alibi se eum esse profitetur, ne quis talem sibi imaginetur,quem nostri pudeat:imo qui & homo fieri,& seruuli abiectissimi formulam assume te voluit,ne diuina eius maiestate terreamur. Hæc vt nobis paternam Dei bonitatem commen- dant:ita nos officij admonent,vt vnum hunc pastorem agnoscamus,& sequamur vocem eius, non autem audiamus infelices mercenarios,qui vt quæstum ex hominibus faciant,eos per mille amba- ges circunducunt.
units.tr: "Behold, the Lord God will come with strength, and his arm shall rule for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. He shall feed his flock like a shepherd, and gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young," etc. Many arguments of the greatest goodness meet here. For it is the mark of this goodness that he looked upon us before we existed; that he sees those who are careless of their own salvation and think nothing of it, and grieves over our destruction; and that he appointed a shepherd for those who could not feed and keep themselves. But above all this is the fact that, since no man or angel could be sufficient for this office, he gave his only-begotten and beloved Son as shepherd, who in the Gospel professes himself to be this shepherd both here and elsewhere, lest anyone imagine such a one as he would be ashamed of. Indeed, he willed to become a man and to take the form of a most abject servant, so that we would not be terrified by his divine majesty. As these things commend to us the fatherly goodness of God, so they also remind us of our duty: that we should acknowledge this one shepherd and follow his voice, and not listen to the wretched hired men, who lead people around through a thousand windings in order to make gain from them.

units.la: At hic proderit diligentius inspicere quæ hic dicuntur, vt videamus nullum in eo boni pasto- ris officium desiderari. Primum de certo ouium numero & certa drachmarum summa loquitur. Habet ergo oues suas Christus numeratas, quod in diligenti & fido pastore in primis requiritur. Quomodo enim omnes curabit & seruabit,qui quam multas habeat, nescit? Facit huc quod ille apud Ioannem ait:Ego sum pastor bonus,& agnosco oues meas,& cognoscor à meis. Et sane fie- ri non potest,vt aliquem suorum Christus ignoret, cum ipse liber vitæ sit,in quo electorum om- nium nomina conscripta sunt. Nam in illo nos elegit Pater (vt Paulus ait) priusquam mun- dus hic crearetur. Deinde non eas modo oues ille nouit, quæ gregi suæ coniunctæ manent, & ipsius vocem sequuntur, verumetiam eas,quæ vel à grege suo sese alienauerunt, vel nunquam adhuc in illum assumptæ hinc inde vagantur, vt pro perditis & prorsus alienis haberi possint. Quæ enim hominum oculos latent,ea ille videt, & non solum quales nunc sint homines, verumetiam quales futuri sint,& ad quid prædestinati sint,perspicit. Ideo rursus apud Ioannem oues suas dicit eos ex gentibus, qui nulla adhuc veri Dei cognitione illustrati in superstitionum & idololatriæ vepretis oberrabant,suo autem tempore ad Ecclesiæ suæ societatem debebant vocari. Tertiò non solum nouit,sed si vel vnam ex ijs perdiderit,mox relictis alijs nonaginta nouem in loco tutiori, perdi- tam quærit per montes & valles,nec prius cessat,quam illam inuenerit. Vt ergo bonus pastor ossi- cij sui esse nouit, ex quibus nullam perdere:ita Christus singulatum curam habet, singulas quærit & seruat. Exempla studij huius multa ab origine rerum sunt edita. Sic primos parentes quæsiuit Dominus,cum illi fugerent & latebras quærerent,in quibus occultarentur,& qui ab Adamo in- uocari debebat,ipse clamauit: Adam vbi es? Eiusdem bonitatis est, quod Abrahamum in Chal- dæa cum idolorum cultoribus agentem quæsiuit, vt totum sibi vendicaret. Quæsiuit item per Mo- sem eos,qui per totam Ægyptum dispersi durißima cum corporum tum animarum tyrannide preme bantur. Pertinet eodem quod cum Dauide factum esse legimus. Cum enim hic post libidinis fœdæ cupiditates erraret,& à Dei vijs deuiasset,per Nathanum quæsitus est, qui ipsum in viam redu- xit. Quid verò cum tota Iudæorum gente egerit,ex ijs apparet,quæ paulò ante ex Ezechiele addu ximus:Illustrius tamen huius studij argumentum in gentium vocatione habetur. Cum enim tem- pus illud aduenijset,quo regnū Dei in toto orbe instaurari oportebat, bonus ille pastor,qui vt filios Dei dispersos colligeret in mundum venerat, accensa verbi sui face totum orbem terrarum lustra- uit,& in medijs tenebris latentes oues quæsiuit. Taceo nunc singularia exempla,quæ vbique gen- tium edita sunt. Et quod olim factum est,hoc ipsum etiam hodie fieri videmus. Quam multi enim quotidie relicto Christi grege per superstitiones, mendacia, & omnis generis scelera vagantur? quam multi item obliterata prorsus quæ in ipsis extare debebat Dei imagine, seipsos perdunt, vt pro Christi nomine signatis non possint amplius agnosci? At istos ab illo quæri constat,dum per Euangelium eos illuminat,vocat & trahit.Quo loco simul nobis deploranda venit multorum per- uersitas,qui ab illo inueniri nolunt,& vt Adam olim ficuum folijs testus latebras quæsiuit: ita illi vel in peccatorum lutum sese demergunt, vel ad superstitiosa figmenta conuersi sub cucullus,cili- cijs & frigidißimarum ceremoniarum velis delitescunt,& iniuriam sibi maximam fieri clamant, si quis per Dei verbum deprehensos inde extrahere conetur.
units.tr: But it will be useful here to look more carefully at what is said, so that we may see that no duty of a good shepherd is lacking in him. First, he speaks of a certain number of sheep and a certain sum of drachmas. Christ therefore has his sheep counted, which is above all required of a diligent and faithful shepherd. For how will he care for and keep all of them, if he does not know how many he has? This agrees with what he says in John: "I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and am known by mine." And indeed it cannot happen that Christ should be ignorant of any of his own, since he himself is the book of life, in which the names of all the elect are written. For in him the Father chose us (as Paul says) before the world was made. Next, he knows not only those sheep which remain joined to his flock and follow his voice, but also those which have either strayed from his flock or, not yet having been received into it, wander here and there, so that they might be regarded as lost and wholly alien. For what is hidden from the eyes of men, he sees; and he perceives not only what men are now, but also what they will be, and to what they have been predestined. Therefore again in John he calls his sheep those from the Gentiles, who, though not yet enlightened by any knowledge of the true God, were wandering in the thickets of superstition and idolatry, but who in their time were to be called into the fellowship of his Church. Thirdly, he not only knows them, but if he should lose even one of them, he at once leaves the other ninety-nine in a safer place and seeks the lost one over mountains and valleys, and does not stop until he has found it. Just as a good shepherd knows that none of his duty is to lose any of them, so Christ has a care for each one individually, seeks and keeps each one. There are many examples of this concern from the beginning of things. Thus the Lord sought our first parents, when they fled and looked for hiding places in which to conceal themselves, and he who was to be called upon by Adam himself cried out: "Adam, where are you?" It belongs to the same goodness that he sought Abraham, who was living in Chaldea among the worshippers of idols, so that he might claim him wholly for himself. He also sought through Moses those who were scattered throughout all Egypt and oppressed by the most cruel tyranny, both of body and of soul. To the same thing belongs what we read was done with David. For when he had wandered after the foul desires of lust and had turned aside from the ways of God, he was sought out through Nathan, who brought him back onto the way. But what he has done with the whole nation of the Jews appears from those things which we cited a little earlier from Ezekiel. Yet the more illustrious proof of this concern is found in the calling of the Gentiles. For when that time had come, in which the kingdom of God had to be established throughout the whole world, that good shepherd, who had come into the world to gather the scattered children of God, kindled the torch of his word, searched the whole circle of the earth, and sought the sheep lying hidden in the midst of darkness. I pass over now the particular examples that have been produced everywhere among the nations. And what was done long ago, we see is done even today. For how many every day, having left the flock of Christ, wander through superstitions, lies, and every kind of wickedness? How many also, with the image of God that ought to be in them utterly effaced, destroy themselves, so that, being marked with the name of Christ no longer, they can no longer be recognised? But it is plain that these are sought by him, while through the Gospel he enlightens, calls, and draws them. At this point there also falls to us to lament the perversity of many, who do not wish to be found by him, and who, like Adam of old who sought to hide himself under fig leaves, either plunge themselves into the mire of sin, or, turned to superstitious fictions, hide under cowls, hair shirts, and the veils of the most cold ceremonies, and cry out that the greatest injury is done to them if anyone tries to drag them out from there after they have been caught by the word of God.

units.la: Quid autem cum oue iam inuenta bonus ille pastor agit? Num laboris impatientia & ira præcipiti abreptus ei conuitiatur, trepidantem percutit, conculcat aut humi allidit? Nequaquam, sed in humeros suos sublatam gestat, adeoq; in sinu suo fouet, vt olim Isaias prædixit. Et hæc quidem Christo optimè conueniunt, qui nullum vnquam peccatorem, qui se ab ipso inueniri passus est, durius tractauit, sed amicissimè suscepit, adeò vt eius facilitas multis suspecta esset, vt initio audiuimus. Reuera autem humerus suus nos gestauit, quando onus peccatorum, quo nos grauabamur, in se transtulit, & sua mortis merito expiauit, ne nobis porrò imputentur. Gestare etiam nos dicitur, quando infirmos indulgentius tractat, & ijs qui ad sequendum vires nullas habent, spiritu suo adest, quo subleuati in salutis viam pergunt. Arguit hæc pars eos, qui sibi apud Christum Mediatoribus diuis opus esse putant, eò quod illum erga peccatores durum & seuerum iudicem fingunt. At qui non venit ille in hunc mundum, vt iudicet, sed vt mundus per ipsum seruetur. Olim quidem iudicem aget, quando in nubibus cœli throno collocato tam piis quàm impijs rependet. Interea suorum fidelis Pontifex est, qui infirmitates nostras nouit, & pro nobis apud Patrem intercedit, ad se autem intrepidos venire iubet omnes, qui peccatorum sensu grauati laborant.
units.tr: But what does that good shepherd do when he has found the sheep? Does he, carried away by impatience at the labour and by headlong anger, rebuke it, strike the trembling creature, trample it, or dash it to the ground? Not at all; he carries it on his shoulders, and so cherishes it in his bosom, as Isaiah foretold long ago. And indeed these things agree most well with Christ, who never treated any sinner who has allowed himself to be found by him more harshly, but received him most kindly, so that his gentleness was suspected by many, as we heard at the beginning. In truth, his shoulder bore us when he transferred to himself the burden of sins by which we were weighed down, and atoned for them by the merit of his death, so that they should no longer be imputed to us. He is also said to carry us when he deals more gently with the weak, and stands by with his Spirit those who have no strength to follow, so that, lifted up by him, they go on in the way of salvation. This part refutes those who think that they need the divine Mediators besides Christ, because they imagine him to be a hard and severe judge toward sinners. But he did not come into this world to judge, but so that the world might be saved through him. Indeed, he will one day act as judge, when, seated on the throne in the clouds of heaven, he will repay both the pious and the impious. Meanwhile he is the faithful High Priest of his people, who knows our infirmities and intercedes for us with the Father, and he bids all who labour burdened with the sense of their sins to come to him without fear.

units.la: Porrò non modò in humeros attollit pastor iste ouem perditam, sed eandem domum portat, vt gregi suo rursus coniungatur. Ergo non vagari finit suos, sed per verbum suum eos ad Ecclesiæ suæ societatem colligit, vt posthac ipsius peculium maneant. Nam vt vnus pastor, sic vnus grex & vnum ouile est, extra quod salus nusquam inuenitur. Quod vnum eos abunde refellit, qui per Euangelij prædicationem Ecclesiæ vnitatem scindi, sectas inuehi, adeoque peccandi licentia plantari voci ferantur. Nam ea conditione nos Christus quærit, & in humeris atque sinu suo gestat, vt relictis superstitionibus simul & tota prioris vitæ consuetudine, ipsi soli consecrati simus, & nos vere conuersos esse reipsa & factis testemur. Et huc pertinet, quod respipiscenti peccatori vtramque parabolam Christus applicat, ne quis ipsum eorum contumaciæ patrocinari putet, qui absque pœnitentia in erroribus & sceleribus suis pergunt.
units.tr: Moreover, this shepherd does not merely lift the lost sheep onto his shoulders but carries it home, so that it may be joined again to his flock. He therefore does not let his own wander, but through his Word gathers them into the fellowship of his Church, so that from then on they remain his own possession. For as there is one shepherd, so there is one flock and one fold, outside of which salvation is found nowhere. This single point thoroughly refutes those who complain that through the preaching of the Gospel the unity of the Church is torn apart, sects are introduced, and so a licence to sin is planted. For Christ seeks us on this condition, and carries us on his shoulders and in his bosom, so that, having left behind superstitions and the whole custom of our former life, we may be consecrated to him alone, and by our deeds and actual conduct bear witness that we have truly been converted. To this also belongs the fact that Christ applies both parables to the sinner who repents, lest anyone think that he is lending support to those who persist in their errors and wickedness without repentance.

units.la: Itaque nobis hoc loco consideranda venit tota pœnitentiæ ratio, quam proprie conuersionem ad Deum esse alibi diximus. Constat ea fere tribus partibus, Contritione, Fiducia gratiæ Dei in Christo nobis factæ, & Obedientia fidei. Contritio est, quando ira Dei agnita expauescimus, & toto animo dolemus, quòd Patrem tam bonum, benignum & iustum offenderimus. Nascitur illa ex peccati agnitione, & vtraque admodum est necessaria. Nam cum peccata carni nostræ arrideant, & illis natura delectemur, nunquam illius reliquis de emendatione vitæ cogitabimus, nisi illorum fœditas nobis perspecta sit, & nos irati Dei manu grauari sentiamus. Vnde certò colligimus, eos adhuc pœnitere nescios esse, qui nullo Dei timore aut iræ ipsius sensu percelluntur: quod non obscure Paulus docet, quando de gentibus pronuntiat: Qui postquam dedoluerunt, semetipsos proterua dediderunt ad patrandum impuritatem omnem certatim. Et hodie videmus scelerum licentiam non aliunde nasci apud plerosq;, quàm quòd Deum nullum esse sibi persuadent, qui peccatis offendatur, & in ea pœnus animaduertat. Itaq; securi quiduis designant, modò nullo pœnarum ciuilium timore abstrerreantur. Prodest igitur semper in promptu habere argumenta, quæ nos de Dei ira & peccatorum pœnis admoneant. Et hic magnus legis vsus est, quæ minas graues & horribiles proponit, quibus ille suam iram, maledictionem, inopiam, famem, bella, regnorum euersiones, exilium, mortem denique sempiternam omnibus denuntiat, qui præcepta eius transgrediuntur. Nec facile minas istas contemnere poterimus, si exempla simul considerremus, quibus iam inde à rerum exordio confirmatæ sunt, & indies non sine multorum magno malo confirmantur. Imò si singuli seipsos & quæ ipsi aliquando passi sunt, vel etiamnum patiuntur, paulò diligentius considerent, mox cum Dauide fatebuntur, se Dei iram sentire, & propter iniquitatem suam castigari. Inter alia autem iræ suæ argumenta, cumprimis euidens & terrificum Deus in Filij sui indigna & dira morte ædidit. Quis enim illum peccata vel negligere vel indulgentius in nobis puniturum esse putet, qui vt illa digno supplicio expiarentur, Filium dilectum & vnigenitum in cruce suspensum atrocissimis doloribus confici, conuitijs improbissimorum hominum obrui, & tandem inter duos latrones ex-
units.tr: Accordingly, the whole nature of repentance must be considered here, which we have elsewhere said is properly conversion to God. It consists roughly of three parts: contrition, trust in the grace of God made ours in Christ, and obedience of faith. Contrition is when, recognising the wrath of God, we are struck with dread and grieve with our whole soul that we have offended so good, kind and just a Father. It arises from the knowledge of sin, and both are absolutely necessary. For since sins flatter our flesh, and we take pleasure in them by nature, we will never think of amending our life unless their foulness has been clearly seen by us and we feel ourselves weighed down by the hand of an angry God. From this we rightly conclude that those are still ignorant of repentance who are not struck by any fear of God or any sense of his wrath; as Paul clearly teaches when he says of the Gentiles: "Who, being past feeling, have given themselves over to wantonness, to work all uncleanness with greediness." And today we see that licence in wickedness arises among most people from nothing else than their persuading themselves that there is no God who is offended by sins and punishes them. And so, secure, they undertake whatever they please, provided they are not deterred by any fear of civil penalties. It is therefore always useful to have at hand arguments that warn us about the wrath of God and the punishments of sins. Here the great use of the law appears, which sets out severe and dreadful threats, by which it proclaims to all who transgress its precepts its wrath, curse, want, famine, wars, the overthrow of kingdoms, exile, and finally everlasting death. Nor will we easily be able to despise these threats if we also consider the examples by which they have been confirmed from the very beginning of things, and are daily confirmed, not without great harm to many. Indeed, if each person considers a little more carefully himself and what he has suffered at some time or still suffers, he will soon confess with David that he feels God's wrath and is chastised for his iniquity. Among his other tokens of wrath, God displayed most clearly and terribly the unworthy and dreadful death of his Son. For who would think that he would either overlook sins or punish them in us too leniently, when, so that they might be atoned for with the due penalty, he willed that his beloved and only-begotten Son should be hanged on the cross, worn down by most atrocious pains, overwhelmed by the insults of the most wicked men, and at last made to breathe out

units.la: V u pirare voluit. Enimuero qui hoc vnum non ofcitanter expendunt, de peccatis leuiter indicare non poterunt, & mox irae diuinae sensu perterrefient, vnde vera animi contritio & (vt Pauli verbo vtar) dolor secundum Deum nascitur.
units.tr: ...breathe his last between two thieves. Indeed, whoever weighs this one thing carefully will not be able to judge lightly about sins, and will soon be terrified by a sense of the divine wrath, from which true contrition of mind arises, and (to use the word of Paul) godly sorrow.

units.la: Caeterum ne dolor ille terrorem nimium pariat, neue eo superati Deum odisse & fugere incipiamus, quae proxima ad desperationem & exitium via est, fiducia gratiae Dei in Christo factae opus erit, quae animum territum consoletur, fluctuantem ceu anchora vere sacra confirmet, & conscientiae ac ipsum restinguat. Excitant hanc promissiones Euangelicae, quae in veteri etiam testamento occurrunt, quales sunt: Ego ego deleo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur, & viuat. Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum traderet, vt omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Quibus adde mandatum & aeternum decretum Dei, qui iubet, vt per fidem in Filium suum iustitiam & peccatorum remissionem obtineamus, & hanc ab illo postulemus. Quod si vel legis minae, vel peccatorum nostrorum multitudo aut magnitudo nos terreat, illis quidem promissiones de quibus diximus, his autem Dei gratiam & misericordiam opponamus, quae inexhausta est, & illic maxime exuberat, vbi peccatum abundat. Accedat his consideratio exemplorum, quae multa passim occurrunt, & his omnibus coniungamus preces, vt Deus fidem nostram augeat, & infirmitati succurrat, ne vllis tentationibus superemur.
units.tr: But lest that sorrow produce too much terror, and lest, overcome by it, we begin to hate God and flee from him, which is the road nearest to despair and ruin, there will be need of trust in the grace of God made ours in Christ, which may console the frightened mind, steady it as a truly sacred anchor when it is tossed about, and quench the terror of conscience. The gospel promises, which are also found in the Old Testament, stir up this trust, such as these: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and that for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins." "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live." "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." To these add the command and eternal decree of God, who bids us to obtain righteousness and forgiveness of sins through faith in his Son, and to ask for them from him. And if the threats of the law, or the multitude or magnitude of our sins, frighten us, let us set against the threats the promises of which we have spoken, and against the sins the grace and mercy of God, which is inexhaustible and most abounds exactly where sin abounds. Let the consideration of the examples, which occur in many places everywhere, be added to these, and let us join all these with prayers, that God may increase our faith and come to the aid of our weakness, so that we are not overcome by any temptations.

units.la: Ac ne caro promissionum & exemplorum gratiae fiducia efferatur, & haec in securitatem primo, deinde in nouam licentiam peccandi degeneret, finem nostrae redemptionis semper ob oculos habere conuenit, qui est, vt ex femine verbi per spiritus virtutem renati & innouati sanctè viuamus, neque porro peccatum patiamur regnare in membris nostris, sed affectus carnis vna cum ratione & intellectu nostro per fidei obedientiam subigamus, vt Deo audientes simus. Hic autem firmo & constanti animi proposito opus est, vt recte viuamus, neque aliquid faciamus repugnante conscientia. Iuuat propositum illud inuocatio Dei, in qua nos assiduos esse oportet, vt is suo Spiritu nos regat atque in officio contineat. Et haec quidem paenitentia vera est, quae non leuibus initijs perficitur, sed assidua & continua praxi (vt ita loquar) constat: quia semper aliquid occurrit quod emendationem requirit, & cum quo nos luctari conuenit. Author illius verus est bonus ille pastor, Christus Iesus, qui per illam nos ad sui gregis societatem reducit, in qua manere non poterunt, nisi qui illi perpetuo studeunt, & infelix peccati seruitium abominantur.
units.tr: And lest the flesh, puffed up by the confidence in the promises and examples of grace, degenerate into security and then into a new licence to sin, we ought always to keep before our eyes the purpose of our redemption, which is that, born again and renewed by the power of the Spirit from the seed of the Word, we should live holily, and that we should not allow sin to reign any longer in our members, but through obedient faith subdue the affections of the flesh together with our reason and understanding, so that we may be obedient to God. Here, however, a firm and steady resolve of mind is needed, so that we live rightly and do nothing against the testimony of conscience. The invocation of God helps this resolve, and we ought to be constant in it, so that he may rule us by his Spirit and keep us in our duty. And this is true repentance, which is not accomplished by slight beginnings, but consists in constant and continual practice, so to speak, because something always arises that requires correction and with which we must struggle. Its true author is that good shepherd, Christ Jesus, who through it leads us back into the fellowship of his flock, in which only those can remain who strive for him continually and abhor the unhappy slavery of sin.

units.la: Porro quia de his differendi occasionem Christo Pharisaei & Scribae dederant, qui publicanos & apertos peccatores in gratiam recipi indignos ferebant, hunc illorum errorem corrigit, & congratulandum potius esse docet ijs, qui a peccatis conuersi in viam redeunt. Nam qui oium perdidit inuenit (inquit) conuocat amicos & vicinos, & dicit eis: Gratulamini mihi, nam inueni ouem meam, quae perierat. Et quae drachmam amissam reperit, similiter amicas & vicinas conuocat, vt ipsi congratulentur. Ista autem humano more de semetipso Christus loquitur, vt affectum & studium, quo nos prosequitur, melius exprimat. Scelerus enim eorum recuperatione, quae amisimus, magis gaudere quam ijs, quae nobis semper salua manserunt: quia ex amissione illorum conceptus dolor gaudium illud intendit & auget. Simul autem nostri nos officij admonet. Si enim amici & vicini ijs congratulantur merito, qui sua recuperauerunt, & vt id illi faciant iure ab eis exigitur, quanto aequius est, vt nos Christo congratulemur, si quos ad ipsum conuerti, & (quod vt super omnia optat) salutis in ipso participes fieri videmus? Quis enim nos eius amicos, quos illi coniunctos dixerint, nisi ijs gaudeamus, ex quibus ipse maximam voluptatem percipit? Quod vt melius doceat, quid in coelis fiat ostendit. Dico vobis (inquit) ita fore gaudium in coelo super vno peccatore resipiscente maius, quam super nonaginta nouem iustis, quibus non opus est resipiscentia. Iustos dicit eos, qui non alieni sunt a suo grege, quamuis alioqui suos nauos habeant, quos iugi paenitentia elui oportet, & his peccatores opponit, eos nimirum intelligens, qui prorsus perditi erant, nisi per ipsum quaesiti & inuenti essent. At horum conuersione coelites gaudere aits vt horum exemplo Pharisaicos illos spiritus confutet, qui illis Dei gratiam atque salutem inui- dent. Quod vero dictum hoc nonnulli ad Diuos extendunt, vt eos res nostras nouisse & pro nobis intercedere probent, nimis dilutum & friuolum est. Nam simpliciter in coelo gaudium fore dicit, si vnus modo peccator resipiscat: qui vero gaudituri sint, postea denotantur in drachmae parabola, Angeli Dei nimirum. Quid ergo Diuos hic ingerere opus est, de quibus nullus est sermo? De Angelorum autem studio erga nos dubitare non possumus, cum Dei ministri sint, qui propter eos mittuntur, qui haeredes sunt salutis. Et non possunt illi non gaudere nostra resipiscentia, cum per hanc Dei gloria illustretur, & regnum eius augeatur, cuius illi studiosissimi sunt. Obseruemus potius hoc loco, quanta sit hominis per Christum reparati dignitas. Gaudet eius salute aeternus Dei Filius, & tam huic quam illi congratulantur Angeli. Quod vt nos in tentationibus grauissimis consolari ita etiam excitare debet, ne dignitatem hanc iterum prophanemus scelerum licentia, sed tanto Christi studio & tanto pretio partam fide constanti & vitae sanctitate conseruemus. Admonent praeterea haec Christi verba, quam alieni sint ab eius affectu & bonorum spiritunum ingenio, qui infamia & perditione hominum potius quam eorum conuersione & salute gaudent: qui item multis scandalo sunt, vt a salute excidant. Sunt illi pestes humani generis, & hostes Regni caelorum, qui sua improbitate (quantum in ipsis est) Christum & Angelos tristitia & maerore afficiunt. Quod vtinam diligentius & frequentius meditarentur qui hodie Euangelij professione superbiunt, sua autem licentia & nequitia Papistas superant, & multos abstrerunt, ne ad bonum illum pastorem Christum & ad Ecclesiae societatem colligantur. Dabunt hi olim graues poenas, de quibus alibi est dictum. In primis autem ad se transferant Christi exemplum Ecclesiarum pastores, & ex eo discant de suo officio iudicare. Meminerint ipsorum esse non solum pascere obiter creditum sibi gregem, sed singulas oues ita curari ab ipsis debere, vt nulla sua culpa amissas quaerere, dispersas colligere & humeris quoque suis & in sinu gestare debeant. Nam singulas de illorum manu requiret Christus Dominus. Est ergo munus ipsorum plenum laboris & periculi, & cum studio indefesso singularem quoque industriam requirit. Iuuent hos suo saltem fauore reliqui Christiani, quos gratiae Dei consideratio non minus excitare debet, vt ipsi quoque omnium hominum saluti consultum cupiant. Si qui vero ad hanc nihil conferre possunt, pia saltem congratulatione testentur se illa ex animo gaudere, simul & Deum Patrem precibus assiduis fatigent, vt is Regnum Filij sui indies protendere & quam plurimos ad eius societatem pertrahere dignetur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now, since the Pharisees and Scribes had given Christ an occasion to debate these matters, because they held that publicans and open sinners were unworthy to be received back into favour, he corrects this error and teaches that those who turn from their sins and return to the right way should rather be congratulated. "For," he says, "what man of you, having lost one of his sheep, does not leave the ninety-nine and go after the one that is lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he calls together his friends and neighbours and says to them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost.'" Likewise, when a woman has found a lost drachma, she calls together her women friends and neighbours so that they may rejoice with her. Christ speaks of himself in these human terms so that he may express more clearly the affection and care with which he pursues us. For we rejoice more over the recovery of what we have lost than over what has always remained safe with us, since the grief conceived from its loss heightens and increases that joy. At the same time, he reminds us of our duty. If friends and neighbours rightly rejoice with those who have recovered what was theirs, and if they are rightly required to do so, how much more fitting is it that we should rejoice with Christ when we see some being converted to him and (which above all things he desires) made partakers of salvation in him? For whom should we rejoice with, as his friends whom he calls his own, if not with those in whom he himself takes the greatest delight? That he may teach this more fully, he shows what happens in heaven: "I tell you," he says, "that there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance." He calls those righteous who are not estranged from his flock, although they also have their own stains, which must be washed away by continual repentance; and he sets sinners over against them, meaning those who were utterly lost unless they had been sought and found by him. Yet he says that the heavenly beings rejoice at their conversion, so that by their example he may refute those Pharisaical spirits who begrudge them God's grace and salvation. But that some extend this saying to the saints, to prove that they know our affairs and intercede for us, is too weak and trifling. For he says simply that there will be joy in heaven if even one sinner repents; who will rejoice is shown afterwards in the parable of the drachma, namely the angels of God. Why, then, is there any need to bring in the saints here, when no mention is made of them? Yet we cannot doubt the zeal of the angels towards us, since they are ministers of God, sent on account of those who are heirs of salvation. Nor can they fail to rejoice in our repentance, since by it the glory of God is made manifest and his kingdom is enlarged, and they are most eager for that kingdom. Let us rather observe in this place how great is the dignity of man restored through Christ. The eternal Son of God rejoices in his salvation, and the angels rejoice with both him and them. This should comfort us in the most severe temptations, and also stir us up, so that we do not again profane this dignity by licence in sin, but keep it, won by such zeal and at such a price of Christ, by a steadfast faith and holiness of life. Moreover, these words of Christ show how alien from his affection and from the disposition of good spirits are those who rejoice in the disgrace and ruin of men rather than in their conversion and salvation, and who also become a stumbling-block to many, so that they fall away from salvation. Such men are plagues of the human race and enemies of the kingdom of heaven, who by their wickedness (so far as lies in them) bring sorrow and grief upon Christ and the angels. Would that those who today boast of their profession of the Gospel, yet surpass the Papists in their licence and wickedness, and who have drawn many away so that they are not gathered to that good Shepherd Christ and to the fellowship of the Church, would meditate on this more diligently and more often! Those men will one day pay heavy penalties, of which we have spoken elsewhere. Above all, let the ministers of the Churches apply Christ's example to themselves, and learn from it to judge their own office. Let them remember that it is their duty not only to feed the flock entrusted to them in passing, but that each single sheep must be so cared for by them that they seek out those lost through no fault of their own, gather those scattered, and carry them on their shoulders and in their bosom. For Christ the Lord will require each one at their hand. Their office is therefore full of labour and danger, and it demands singular diligence along with untiring zeal. Let the rest of the Christians help these ministers at least by their favour; the consideration of God's grace ought to stir them no less, so that they too desire the welfare of all men. If any cannot contribute anything to this, let them at least bear witness by a devout congratulation that they rejoice in these things from their heart, and at the same time weary God the Father with constant prayers, that he may deign to extend the kingdom of his Son day by day and draw very many into its fellowship. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CL.
units.tr: HOMILY CL.

units.la: Ait autem: Homo quidam habebat duos filios: quorum iunior dixit patri: Pater, da mihi partem substantiae mihi contingentem. Et diuisit illis facultates. Post dies autem non multos cum omnia coegisset iunior ille filius, peregre profectus est in regionem longinquam: & illic dissipauit substantiam suam profuse viuendo. Omnibus vero ab eo consumptis, orta est fames valida in regione illa, & ipse coepit victu deficì. Abijt igitur & adhaesit vni ex ciuibus regionis illius, qui misit eum in agros suos, vt pasceret porcos. Et desiderabat implere ventrem suum siliquis, quas edebant porci: & nemo ei dabat.
units.tr: And he said, "A certain man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me.' And he divided his property between them. Not many days later, the younger son gathered everything together and went off to a distant country, and there he squandered his substance in reckless living. When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he longed to fill his belly with the carob pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him any."

units.la: Vemadmodum Deus primis parentibus, cum foedissime lapsi mortem meruissent, poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum gratuitam praedicauit: ita doctrinam illam posteris temporibus quoque toti mundo proposuit, & vult idem vt per hanc ij quoque ad ipsum colligantur, qui iam perijsse & exitio aeterno digni esse videri poterant. Perpetuo enim ratum erit quod per Ezechielem {a}ebielem pronuntiat: Viuo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt resipiscat & viuat. Et ne quid de eo dubitaremus, Filium dedit, qui peccatores blandè ad se invitat & recipit, omnes autem eos feveriter increpat, qui propriæ iustitiæ fiducia superbi illos fastidiunt, adeoque gratiam, quam illis Deus facit, invident. Pertinet huc totum istud caput, quo doctrinam istam aduersus Pharisæos parabolis elegantissimus illustrat: quarum duas nuper vidimus. Subijcitur hu confirmationis loco tertia, quæ totum hoc negotium prolixè tractatur, & tanquam in tabella spectandum proponitur. Partes eius sunt duæ. Priori docetur, quanta sit Dei in peccatis condonandis & peccatoribus recipiendis facilitas. Altera iustitiarij coniutantur, qui illos recipi indignè ferunt, & prædicationem gratiæ calumniis suis vellicant. In prima parte omnia traduntur, quæ de salutis nostræ ratione & ordine dici possunt. Describitur enim hominis conditio, qualis nimirum ille sit sua natura, quidue ei accidat, si sua rationis & cupiditatis ductum sequatur. Deinde vera pœnitentiæ ratio traditur. Inde Dei peccata condonantis & peccatores in gratiam recipientis bonitas adumbratur. In præsenti de primo agemus, & sic quidem, vt initio ea excutiamus, quæ in ipsa parabolæ historia secundum literam considerari possunt: eadem vero postea ad hominis conditionem applicabimus.
units.tr: Just as God, when our first parents had fallen most shamefully and deserved death, proclaimed repentance and the free forgiveness of sins, so he has set this same teaching before the whole world in later times too, and he wills that through it even those who might seem already lost and worthy of eternal destruction are gathered to himself. For what he declares through Ezekiel will always stand: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he repent and live." And so that we would have no doubt about this, he gave his Son, who gently invites sinners to himself and receives them, but who sternly rebukes those who, proud in their confidence in their own righteousness, despise them and so begrudge the grace that God shows them. To this belongs that whole chapter, in which he most elegantly illustrates this teaching against the Pharisees by parables, two of which we have just seen. A third is added as a confirmation, which treats this whole matter at length and is set forth to be looked at as if on a tablet. It has two parts. In the first it is taught how great God's readiness is to pardon sins and receive sinners. In the second the self-righteous are rebuked, who take it badly that such people are received and who sneer at the preaching of grace with their slanders. In the first part everything is set out that can be said about the manner and order of our salvation. For the condition of man is described, namely what he is by nature, and what befalls him if he follows the lead of his reason and desire. Then the true manner of repentance is given. After that the goodness of God, who forgives sins and receives sinners into favour, is sketched. At present we shall deal with the first part, and in such a way that first we examine those things that can be considered according to the letter in the story of the parable itself; afterwards we shall apply the same things to the condition of man.

units.la: Inducitur vir dives & illustris, cui duo fuerunt filij: alter frugi & patri obediens, alter protervus & luxu perditus. Hic audacter patrem accedit, & ab eo postulat partem bonorum, quæ ex hereditate ad ipsum pertineat. Qua impetrata & accepta, abit peregrè, pecuniam omnem luxu & intemperantia consumit, & tandem omnibus exutus, cùm fames publica, & ea quidem validissima, in ea regione orta esset, cuiusdam seruitio se addicere cogitur, qui ipsum ad porcos ablegat, inter quos sordibus, fœtore & fame tantum non totus conficitur.
units.tr: A man is introduced who was rich and distinguished, and he had two sons: one thrifty and obedient to his father, the other headstrong and ruined by luxury. This one boldly approaches his father and asks him for the part of the goods that would pass to him from the inheritance. Having obtained and received it, he goes abroad, spends all his money in luxury and intemperance, and at last, stripped of everything, when a public famine, and a very severe one, had arisen in that region, he is compelled to hire himself out to a certain man, who sends him off to the pigs, among whom he is all but worn down by filth, stench and hunger.

units.la: Quo loco nobis ante omnia parentum fors atque conditio, quamferè vulgò experiuntur, consideranda venit. Nam qui hic introducitur, procul dubio ex optimis fuit, cùm ipsius Dei personam illi Christus imponat. Idem filios habuit duos, solummodo, eoque felicior videri poterat, cùm liberorum multitudo multis obstet, ne illos commodè educare, aut eis dignè instituendis sufficere possint. Veruntamen ex his qui natu minor est, pessima frugis homo omnia facit impudentissimè, quæ de deplorata indolis iuuene dici possunt. Idem sanctissimus viri nou semel accidisse legimus. Nam si ad Adamum usque ascendamus, ex duobus filijs primogenitum non solum consumacem fuisse, sed eò impietatis progressum fuisse videbimus, vt omni humanitatis sensu extincto, fratre crudelissimè trucidaverit, & acerbissimis lusibus causam dederit parentibus, quos peccati conscientia & ex illo enatæ miseriæ plus fatis excruciabant. Nec multò melior Noæ conditio fuit, cuius filium minorem neque patris institutio fidelis & diligens, neque horrendæ iustitiæ Dei in diluuio edictum exemplum emolliri potuit, quin parenti vino & somno deuicto petulanter nimis insultaret, & eundem ignominia extrema afficeret. Quid de Abrahamo dicemus, qui etiam Deo teste in filijs & domesticis suis omnibus bene instituendis fidelissimus fuit? Nonne hic etiam Ismaelem habuit filium, illusorem & intolerabilis proteruiæ hominem, qui vnà cum matre ex ædibus eiici merebatur? Poterant his adnumerari Isaac, Iacob, Samuel, Dauid & infiniti alij: quorum exempla obseruari prodest, ne vel offendamur si quid huius nobis quoque accidit, sed potius feramus patienter fortem, quæ nobis cum tantis viris communis est: vel suspectos temere habeamus parentes, quasi hi nequitiæ filiorum authores sint.
units.tr: Here, before all else, we must consider the lot and condition of the parents, which is what most people commonly experience. For the man introduced here was without doubt one of the best, since Christ puts on him the person of God himself. He had only two sons, and he might seem the more fortunate for this, since a large number of children is a hindrance, so that parents cannot bring them up well or be adequate to instruct them properly. Yet of these two, the younger is a man of the worst character, who does everything most shamelessly that can be said of a youth of hopelessly corrupt disposition. We read that this same thing has happened to the most holy men more than once. For if we go back even as far as Adam, we shall see that of his two sons the firstborn was not only obstinate but advanced so far in wickedness that, with all human feeling extinguished, he most cruelly slew his brother, and gave his parents the bitterest grief, who were tormented beyond measure by the consciousness of sin and the misery that sprang from it. Nor was Noah's situation much better: neither his faithful and diligent upbringing by his father nor the example of God's dreadful justice shown in the flood could soften his younger son, who wantonly insulted his parent, overcome by wine and sleep, and subjected him to extreme disgrace. What shall we say of Abraham, who, as God himself bears witness, was most faithful in bringing up his sons and all his household well? Did he not also have a son Ishmael, a mocker and a man of intolerable insolence, who deserved to be cast out of the house together with his mother? Isaac, Jacob, Samuel, David and countless others could be added to these, whose examples it is useful to observe, so that we are not offended if something of this kind happens to us as well, but rather bear patiently the lot that we share with such great men; or so that we do not rashly hold parents under suspicion, as if they were the authors of their children's wickedness.

units.la: Sed quid iste filius fecerit, videamus. Occurrit hic primùm, quòd de patris imperio excutiendo cogitat, vt qui non putat sibi bene fore, nisi quàm longissimè ab illo absit, ne eum suæ vitæ & morum censorem habeat. At non aliquam fuisse huius iustituti causam iustam aut grauem, ipse postea proprio ore testatur, quando patris bonitatem & liberalitatem prædicat, qua in mercenarios vti soleat. Ergo sola proteruiendi libidine & impunitatis spe motus abitum parat. Deinde hæreditatem sibi ante tempus dari petit, & patri de parte bonorum, quæ ad ipsum pertineat, verba facit, cùm in bona paterna nihil adhuc iuris haberet. Nam defunctus demum parentibus filij in bonorum aut facultatum, quas illi reliquerunt, possessionem veniunt. Est ergo postulatio hæc non minus iniqua quàm impudens. Accedit hu ingratitudo & impietas inexcusabilis, quòd patrem iam senescentem deserit, officia debita eidem negat, & insuper magna bonorum parte spoliat. Tales hodie passim inueniuntur, qui hoc vnum agunt, vt paterna disciplinæ iugum exeuniant, & ex eo sibi ipsis omnia fausta & laeta pollicentur. Vt enim aues & ferae, quàmuis in caueis optimè tractentur, libertatem tamen affectant: ita iuuenes licet patrum indulgentiam maximam experiantur, & omnibus abundent, quae ad voluptatem honestam & alias huius vitae commoditates faciunt, nihil tamen licentia beatius & felicius esse putant. Et excusabilis quidem est auium atq; ferarum cupiditas, quae non aliud expetunt, quàm quod illis Deus dedit: sed venia nulla digni sunt, qui cum ex Dei institutô parentes obseruare & colere debebant, illis subesse nolunt. Interim solent isti semper ius aliquod praetexere. Sunt enim qui haereditatem maternam à patribus exigunt. Alij parentes negligentiâ accusant, vt qui rem domesticam pessimè administrent: quod olim Sophoclis filij fecerunt. Inueniuntur item, qui iustitiam in patribus desiderant, quasi non aequali iure erga liberos suos vtantur. Et hi omnes interea mirifica iactitant de sua industria, quae rem augere & omnia melius administrare velint, si quando ipsis locus fiat. Sunt autem haec summae ingratitudinis argumenta, quam Deus inultam non sinet. Nam qui longaeuos annos pollicitus est ijs, qui parentes in honore & pretio habent: idem eos etiam seueriter punit, qui in illos impij sunt, & impietate illa ipsis tristitiam & moerorem afferunt.
units.tr: But let us see what this son did. First of all it occurs that he thinks about shaking off his father's authority, since he does not think he will do well unless he is as far away from him as possible, so that he will not have him as the judge of his life and conduct. But that there was no just or serious reason for this decision, he himself later testifies in his own words, when he proclaims his father's goodness and generosity, with which he is accustomed to treat even hired men. So, moved by nothing but a desire for wantonness and the hope of impunity, he prepares to leave. Then he asks that his inheritance be given to him before the proper time, and he speaks to his father about the part of the goods that belongs to him, although he had as yet no right in his father's property. For sons come into possession of their parents' goods and property only when they have died. This request is therefore no less unjust than it is shameless. To it is added ingratitude and inexcusable impiety: he deserts his father, now growing old, denies him the duties he owes, and moreover strips him of a large part of his goods. Such men are found everywhere today, who do only this one thing, namely to throw off the yoke of parental discipline, and from this promise themselves every happy and joyful thing. For just as birds and wild beasts, however well they are treated in cages, nonetheless long for liberty, so young men, though they experience the greatest indulgence of their fathers and abound in everything that serves honest pleasure and the other conveniences of this life, still think that nothing is happier or more blessed than licence. The desire of birds and beasts is indeed excusable, since they seek nothing but what God has given them; but those are deserving of no pardon who, when by God's ordinance they ought to honour and cherish their parents, are unwilling to be subject to them. Meanwhile such men are accustomed always to put forward some pretext of right. For there are some who demand their maternal inheritance from their fathers. Others accuse their parents of negligence, as if they managed the household badly; which the sons of Sophocles once did. There are also those who look for justice in their fathers, as if they did not use the same right towards their own children. And all of these meanwhile boast wonderfully of their own industry, saying that they would like to increase the estate and manage everything better, if ever the opportunity came to them. But these are signs of the greatest ingratitude, which God will not leave unpunished. For he who has promised long life to those who hold their parents in honour and esteem also severely punishes those who are impious towards them, and whose impiety brings sorrow and grief upon them.

units.la: Id verò Christus in praesenti non obscurè docet, dum quid huic nostro Acolasto euenerit, narrat. Primùm ex solo natali abit, & seipsum spontaneo exilio multat, quo viri boni & honesti nihil grauius & molestius esse arbitrantur. Quid illic fit? Opes patrias & honestè à patre partas atque seruatas turpissimè prodit, intemperanter viuendo: & quae patri abstulerat, profundit in ganeonesʼ, lenones, scorta, mimos, aleatores, ambubaias, cupediarios, sartores, tibicines, ebriosos & impuros homines, quos non immeritò reipub. pestes dixerit, & quos Propheta locustis confert, quòd publicas & priuatas opes deuorent. Et fertur quidem inter longinquae regionis homines infelix ille iuuenis, quàm diu tantus sumptibus potest sufficere. Vbi verò omnibus dilapidatis, & ipse iam egere incipit, & fames publica ex parcissimo terrae proventu rerumque inopia exorta late iam regnat, mox miser eijcitur, & seruus heri duri & iniqui factus conditionem sustinet ipsis porcis infelicior. Solet hoc plerunque accidere iuuenibus, qui parentum disciplinam & monita ferre dedignantur. Quia enim per se minus sapiunt, & consilio maturo destituuntur, totos abripit pessimorum affectuum libido, qui in illis vehementissimi & prorsus immoderati sunt. Fieri ergo non potest; quin se totos mundi & carnis voluptatibus dedant. Ita verò in homines nihili & malae frugis incidunt, qui ipsorum facilitate ad suam libidinem abutuntur, & incautos pecunijs emungunt. Et ista quidem fieri fere patiuntur qui reipub. gubernaculis assident, quorum erat intemperantiam omnem publica legum authoritate coercere. Sed cessantibus illis, non tamen cessat aut dormitat Dei iudicium, qui & improbos istos concoctores priuatim, & totos populos publicè punit, qui ista fieri patiuntur. Illi enim fere ad inopiam extremam redacti, fastidio & odio sunt ijs, qui ipsis priùs seruiliter blandiebantur, & ipsos pro semideis quibusdam colebant. Et isti simul omnes Dei iram aduersus se prouocant, qui immanem luxum & disciplinae omnis contemptum sterilitate agrorum, inopia & fame castigat. Exempla quibus hoc probetur, non opus est adducere, quia historias legentibus passim occurrunt, & multa fiunt quotidie, quae istis fidem faciunt. Multis enim hodie idem accidit, quod de isto pessimo boni parentis filio dicitur. Noluit in domo paterna libertate frui, & à seruis paternis obseruari ac coli: nunc autem in terra peregrina durissimam seruitutem seruire cogitur. Patris indulgentissimi imperium ferre detrectauit, nunc alienum herum sibi accersit, eumque durum & immitem. Durum illi visum est inter patris domesticos habitare, & cum hominibus amicissimis atque honestis vitam degere: dignus ergo est, qui ex impurissimorum nebulonum & scortorum contubernio infamiam sibi conciliet, & tandem porcorum socius & contuina, imò seruus fiat. Panes delicatissimos fastidiuit, quibus in patris aedibus mercenarij abundabant: nunc siliquas & furfures vorat, nec est qui tantum illi det, quantum latrans praefame stomachus requirebat. Est haec communis fors prodigorum, qui honestiori disciplina se coerceri nolunt. Ad inopiam enim extremam redacti à socijs deseruntur, quos fere illorum pudet adeò, vt procul conspectus ijs alio declinent, ne eos vel salutare vel alloqui cogantur. Ergo ex patria fere profugiunt, & serui fiunt crudelissimorum hominum, ducum militiae, quos capitaneos vocant: qui vili pretio conducti, non ad porcos, sed ad bellum educunt, vbi mille discrimina vitae subeunt. Itaque qui optimis parentibus
units.tr: Christ indeed teaches this plainly in the present passage, where he tells what befell our Acolastus. First he leaves his native soil and punishes himself with voluntary exile, which good and honourable men regard as nothing more grievous or troublesome. What happens there? He shamefully betrays the wealth inherited from his father, honestly gained and kept, by living intemperately. What he had taken from his father he pours out on gluttons, pimps, whores, mimes, gamblers, ambubaiae, confectioners, tailors, pipers, drunkards and impure men, whom one may not unfairly call the plagues of the commonwealth, and whom the Prophet compares to locusts because they devour public and private wealth. It is said that among the people of a distant region that unhappy young man kept up his spending for as long as his money could last. But when everything has been squandered, and he himself begins to lack, and a public famine arising from the meagre yield of the land and the scarcity of goods now spreads widely, the wretch is soon thrown out. Made a slave to a hard and unjust master, he endures a condition more wretched than the pigs themselves. This usually happens to young men who disdain to bear their parents' discipline and admonitions. Because they know little in themselves and lack mature counsel, the lust of the worst passions carries them off entirely; in them these passions are most violent and altogether immoderate. It is therefore impossible that they should not give themselves wholly to the pleasures of the world and the flesh. And so they fall among worthless men of bad character, who exploit their easy nature for their own lust and fleece them of their money while they are off guard. Those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth generally allow these things to happen, though it was their duty to restrain all intemperance by the public authority of the laws. But while they are idle, the judgement of God neither ceases nor sleeps. It punishes these wicked squanderers privately and whole peoples publicly, who allow such things to happen.
