For those men, reduced nearly to extreme poverty, become objects of disgust and hatred to those who formerly fawned on them as slaves and worshipped them as demigods. All of them together provoke the anger of God against themselves, who chastises immense luxury and contempt for all discipline with barren fields, want and famine. There is no need to adduce examples to prove this, since histories meet readers everywhere, and many things happen every day which bear witness to it. For today the same thing happens to many as is said of that wicked son of a good father. He did not want to enjoy liberty in his father's house, and to be attended and served by his father's servants; now in a foreign land he is compelled to serve the hardest slavery. He refused to bear the rule of a most indulgent father; now he has summoned a strange master for himself, and a harsh and cruel one. He thought it hard to live among his father's household and to spend his life with most friendly and honourable men; so he is worthy to win infamy for himself from the company of the most impure scoundrels and whores, and at last to become a companion of pigs, indeed their slave. He despised the most delicate bread, of which hired servants had plenty in his father's house; now he devours husks and bran, nor is there anyone who gives him as much as his barking stomach demanded in its hunger. This is the common lot of prodigals who will not be restrained by a more honourable discipline. Reduced to extreme poverty, they are deserted by their companions, whom they are generally so ashamed to face that they turn aside, out of sight, lest they be forced to greet or speak to them. So they generally flee their country and become slaves of the most cruel men, the leaders of armies whom they call captains. Hired for a paltry price, these men lead them not to pigs but to war, where they undergo a thousand dangers to life. And so those who would not obey their most excellent parents, and who would obey the lawful command of a godly magistrate, are compelled to obey those bloodthirsty men. Those who would not live honourably at home perish amid the weapons, worn down by hunger, cold and disease, or are cruelly slaughtered abroad. While the captains grow fat on their blood, these men either perish altogether or at last return home poor, starving, naked and infamous. These things are now so common and familiar that there is no city or village in which public examples of such men cannot be seen. The consideration of them ought to warn young people not to hate discipline, which is wholly necessary at this age, and to bear patiently the lawful commands of parents and magistrates. For although these commands sometimes seem hard and unjust, they are nevertheless salutary and contribute greatly to ordering life well, and so they also bear the happiest fruit.

units.la: Filiorum inobedientium poena. & legitimo pij magistratus imperio parere voluerunt, sanguinarijs istis obsequi coguntur: qui domi suæ honestè viuere noluerunt, foris inter media arma fame, frigore, morbis confecti moriuntur, aut crudeliter trucidantur. Et cum ex illorum sanguineditescant capitanei, ipsi vel toti pereunt, vel inopes, famelici, nudi & infames tandem domum redeunt. Sunt hæc tam vulgaria & visitata hodie, vt nulla ciuitas aut pagus extet, in quo non publica eiusmodi hominum exempla cernere liceat. Debet autem horum consideratio iuuenes monere, ne disciplinam oderint, quæ huic ætati prorsus necessaria est, & vt patienter ferant legitima parentum & magistratuum imperia. Nam etsi hæc interdum dura & iniqua videntur, salutaria tamen sunt, & plurimum momenti conferunt ad vitam bene instituendam, vnde fructum quoq; ferunt lætissimum.
units.tr: The punishment of disobedient sons. Those who would not obey their excellent parents and the lawful command of a godly magistrate are forced to obey those bloody men; those who would not live honourably at home perish abroad in the midst of arms, worn down by hunger, cold and disease, or are cruelly butchered. And while the captains grow fat on their blood, these men either perish altogether or return home at last poor, starving, naked and infamous. These things are so commonplace and familiar today that no city or village exists in which public examples of such men cannot be seen. Moreover, the consideration of these things ought to warn young people not to hate that discipline which is wholly necessary at their age, and to bear patiently the lawful commands of parents and magistrates. For although these commands sometimes seem hard and unjust, they are salutary and contribute much to bringing up life well, and so they also bear a most joyful fruit.

units.la: Porrò ad parabolæ argumentum accedamus, quod Christo hæc dicenti propositum fuit, qui prima hac parte infelicem & miserrimam hominis peccatoris conditionem describit. Nam homo iste sine pater Deus est. Habet ii in sua domo, id est, in electorum numero, seu Eccl. sia, duos filios, per quos duo hominum genera denotantur. Primum eos habet, qui vt filij frugi & obsequentes disciplina se contineri sinunt, & vitam suam honestè transigunt. Altero genere ij continentur, qui excusso omnis disciplinæ iugo pro sua libidine proteruiunt, nec prius ad officium redeunt, quàm à Deo seuerius castigentur. Et in his quidem omnia fiunt, quæ de filio prodigo & intemperante bacchanus dicta sunt.
units.tr: Let us now come to the subject of the parable, which was the purpose of Christ in speaking these words, and which in this first part describes the unhappy and most wretched condition of the sinful man. For this man is without his Father, God. He has in his house, that is, in the number of the elect or in the Church, two sons, by whom two kinds of men are denoted. The first kind are those who, as obedient and dutiful sons, allow themselves to be restrained by discipline and live their lives honourably. The second kind are those who, having shaken off the yoke of all discipline, run wild at their own pleasure, and do not return to their duty until they are chastised more severely by God. In these men everything happens that has been said of the prodigal and riotous son.

units.la: Initium mali ac infelicitatis omnis est, quòd Dei disciplinæ subijci nolunt, neque se vnquam felices fore sibi persuadent, nisi huius iugo confractò & abiecto possint pro suo arbitrio viuere. Per-suasionem hanc vehementer in illis auget & confirmat mundi exemplum, quando impios impunè proteruire & feliciter agere, pios autem perpetuis calamitatibus atque periculis exerceri vident. Nam vt pueri, qui à bonis parentibus artiori disciplina in officio continentur, ipsis multò beatiores putant esse alios, quibus per patrum negligentiam & incuriam quidus pro suo arbitrio facere licet: ita plerique hominum eorum felicitatem prædicant, qui nulla legum authoritate, nullo pœnarum metu, nullis item aduersis coercentur, seipsos autem cum tota filiorum Dei generatione (vt Asaphi Prophetæ verbis vtar) infelices adeoq; reprobatos à Deo esse arbitrantur, eò quòd se cum illis arctius in ordinem cogi, & perpetuò affligi cernant. Vt ergo sibi consulant, ex seipsis sapere volunt, seq; abunde instructos putant esse, vt ad omnia sibi sufficiant, quæ ad vitam bene gubernandam pertinent: Itaque contempta Dei voluntate, quam is nobis in verbo suo reuelat, pro suo arbitrio omnia instituunt, & tantùmnon à Deo petunt, vt ipsos suo sensu abundare & propriæ rationis aut intellectus ductum sequi permittat. Quid verò hoc aliud est, quàm debitam sibi hæreditatis partem postulare à Deo, qui nemini quicquam debet? Fuit hoc Adamo peccati & omnis miseriæ initium, quòd se plus sapere putauit quàm Deum, & ideo contra huius præceptum ad diuinitatis fastigium proprijs viribus atq; sua industria ascendere voluit. Ad hunc lapidem Israelitæ etiam non semel offenderunt: quem gentibus quoq; omnis erroris principium fuisse Paulus in 1. cap. ad Roman. aperte docet. Sed & hodie hæc omnium superstitionum, adhæc scelerum & nequitiæ omnis prima causa est: quòd plerique rem se indignam putant, si intra domum Dei, id est, ecclesiæ septa con-tineantur, vbi ipsos verbi diuini legibus parere, & hs suam rationem & intellectum cum omnibus carnis desiderijs subijcere oporteat. Nam quando ita affectos videt Deus, iusto iudicio tales sibijpsis permittit, vt facultatibus naturalibus, quas cum alijs hominibus communes habent, tanquam suis vtantur, simulq; suam manum ipsis subducit.
units.tr: The beginning of all evil and unhappiness is that they are unwilling to submit to the discipline of God, and never persuade themselves that they will be happy unless, with this yoke broken and cast off, they can live at their own discretion. This persuasion is strongly increased and confirmed in them by the example of the world, when they see the impious rage with impunity and prosper, while the godly are exercised by constant calamities and dangers. For just as boys who are kept in obedience by strict discipline from good parents think that others are far happier, to whom through the negligence and carelessness of their fathers it is permitted to do as they please, so most men proclaim the happiness of those who are restrained by no authority of laws, no fear of punishment, no adversity; while they themselves, together with the whole generation of the sons of God (to use the words of the prophet Asaph), think they are unhappy and therefore rejected by God, because they see themselves being more closely brought into order and constantly afflicted. So, to look after themselves, they want to be wise from their own resources, and they think they are sufficiently equipped to meet all that pertains to governing life well. Therefore, having despised the will of God, which he reveals to us in his word, they order everything by their own judgement, and they ask of God hardly anything more than to let them abound in their own sense and follow the guidance of their own reason or understanding. But what is this other than to demand from God the portion of the inheritance owed to them, when he owes nothing to anyone? This was the beginning of sin and of all misery for Adam, that he thought himself wiser than God, and therefore, against his command, wished to ascend by his own strength and industry to the height of divinity. On this stone the Israelites also stumbled more than once; and that it was the beginning of all error for the Gentiles too, Paul clearly teaches in the first chapter of Romans. But even today this is the first cause of all superstitions, and besides of all wickedness and every kind of iniquity: that many think it beneath them to be contained within the house of God, that is, within the fold of the Church, where they ought to obey the laws of the divine Word and subject their reason and understanding, together with all the desires of the flesh, to it. For when God sees people so disposed, by his just judgement he permits them to be such to themselves, so that they use the natural faculties which they have in common with other men as if they were their own, and at the same time he withdraws his hand from them.

units.la: Quid verò fit, quando hoc quasi impetrarunt, vt absque meliori disciplina pro suo arbitrio viuant? Abeunt in regionem longinquam, id est, procul discedunt ab Ecclesia Dei, quæ vere est terra viuentium (vt Dauid loquitur) & in qua suum πολίτευμα sive municipium habent ecclesi, quoad in terris hisce viuunt. At quia Ecclesia Dei domus est, qui illic habitare dignatur, ab eo simul elongantur, seq; totos mundo addicunt. Ex eo sequitur, quòd dum huic placere student, facultates sibi à Deo datas turpissimè dilapident. Rationis enim acumen consumunt atque attenuant in rebus partim inutilibus, partim perniciosis & noxijs. Mentem, quæ Dei sacrarium esse debebat, ab eo alienant, & ipsi quoque mente alienantur, dum absque ratione & pudore omnia faciunt. Fit ergo vt corporis vires & membra omnia diaboli vasa atque organa fiant, quæ iusti-tia arma tiæ arma esse debebant. Similiter fortunæ etiam bona non minus turpiter dissipant, dum illis ad scelera omnis generis pro affectuum suorum libidine abutuntur. Fieri ergo non potest, quin tandem omnibus bonis tam animi quam corporis spoliati ad extremam inopiam redigantur. Neq; hic mihi aliquis eos obijciat, qui diuitijs interea affluunt, & ideo beati putantur. Nec enim diuites aut diui tiarum possessores dici debent, qui ipsi à diuitijs possidentur, aut quibus hæ non aliud sunt, quam gladius in furentis manu, eò quod eas in proprium exitium conuertunt. Qualescunque ergo illi esse videantur, reuera tamen pauperes & omnium mortalium miserrimi sunt, cum neq; huius vitæ commodis fruantur, neq; de futura bene sperare possint.
units.tr: But what happens when they have, as it were, obtained this, that they live by their own will without better discipline? They depart into a distant region, that is, they withdraw far from the Church of God, which is truly the land of the living (as David speaks), and in which they have their citizenship [πολίτευμα] or home, for as long as they live on this earth. But because the Church is the house of God, and he who deigns to dwell there is at the same time removed from them, they surrender themselves wholly to the world. It follows that while they strive to please the world, they squander shamefully the faculties given them by God. For they consume and wear down the keenness of their reason on things partly useless, partly harmful and noxious. They alienate from God the mind, which ought to have been the sanctuary of God, and they themselves are alienated in mind, while they do everything without reason or shame. Thus it comes about that the powers of the body and all its members become the vessels and instruments of the devil, which ought to have been the weapons of righteousness. Likewise they squander the goods of fortune no less shamefully, while they abuse them for crimes of every kind at the bidding of their passions. It cannot but happen, therefore, that at last, stripped of all goods both of soul and body, they are reduced to extreme poverty. Nor let anyone here object to me those who meanwhile abound in riches and are therefore thought blessed. For those should not be called rich or possessors of riches who are themselves possessed by their riches, or for whom these are nothing but a sword in the hand of a madman, because they turn them to their own destruction. Whatever they may seem to be, therefore, they are in truth poor and the most wretched of all mortals, since they enjoy neither the comforts of this life nor can they hope well for the life to come.

units.la: Id verò ea quæ sequuntur plenius docent, quibus iniquorum hominum pœnæ describuntur, quas in hoc seculo ferunt. Nam ipsis quoque fames oritur, qua sui Verbi & disciplinæ contemptum Deus vlciscitur. Nam in angustias illas redacti sentire incipiunt iudicium Dei, qui terrores conscientiæ horribiles ipsis obijcit. Et occasionem istam minime negligit Satan, qui vt prius peccati blanditijs inescatos in nassam pertraxit: ita nunc terrores illos mirificè auger, vt in desperationis præcipitium miseros detrudat. Tunc ergo fames illa animarum eos infestat, quam Deus per Amos Prophetam Verbi sui contemptoribus minatur. Nam etsi se miseros esse sentiant, & sibi consultum velint, nihilominus consilij, nullam consolationem, nullum salutis præsidium in semetipsis inuenire possunt. Quid enim hic faciat carnis ratio, quæ in diuinis iam antea cæcutiebat, & nunc affectuum pessimorum tyrannide prorsus oppressa iacet? Quod autem vnicum restabat Dei Verbum, quo hominum mentes illustrari & confirmari possunt, hoc illi iam pridem abiecerunt: quo fit, vt nec ipsi eius cum aliquo fructu recordari, aut eius prædicationem attentis animis audire possint. Idem ergo isti homines faciunt, quod de filio hoc prodigo dicitur. Nam consilio & auxilio omni destituti, adiungunt vel addicunt se hero alieno in terra illa longinqua: Id est, extra ecclesiæ septa vagantes conscientiæ & fidei dominos siue tyrannos sibi sponte accersunt, & temere quemuis recipiunt, ex quo aliquid sperari posse videtur. Ita verò prorsus fiunt diaboli mancipia, qui prius in iis modò peccare videbantur, quæ ad externæ vitæ consuetudinem faciunt. Est autem ille herorum omnium iniquissimus, qui à Christo abstractos fere ad porcos remittit, vt subulci infelices & fœdi fiant, qui in Dei domo inter huius filios locum suum retinere noluerunt. Porcorum autem nomine homines impuri denotantur, qui vel sub religionis prætextu vitam prophanam degunt (quales fere sunt sacrificuli, Monachi & omnes superstitionum & idololatriæ ministri) vel in apertis flagitijs absque omni pudore volutantur. In priores incidunt, in quibus adhuc aliquis timoris Dei stimulus reliquus est, quo excitantur, vt salutis æternæ desiderium atque studium non possint omnino deponere: Alteris verò accedunt, qui excusso omni timore Dei, cælum & inferos negare incipiunt, & quia æternæ vitæ spem omnem in animis suis iampridem extinxerunt, plus quam Cypselico omnis numinis contemptu abrepti cum Sardanapalo clamant:
units.tr: What follows teaches this more fully, where the punishments of wicked men are described, which they suffer in this age. For hunger arises for them too, by which God avenges the contempt of his Word and discipline. For, brought into those straits, they begin to feel the judgment of God, who sets before them dreadful terrors of conscience. And Satan, who first drew them into the net, enticed by the flatteries of sin, does not neglect this opportunity at all: so now he wonderfully increases those terrors, so as to thrust the wretched into the precipice of despair. Then indeed that famine of souls, with which God threatens the despisers of his Word through the prophet Amos, harasses them. For even if they feel themselves wretched and wish to be provided for, they can nevertheless find no counsel, no consolation, no safeguard of salvation in themselves. For what can human reason do here, which was already blind in divine matters, and now lies utterly oppressed by the tyranny of the worst passions? And the one thing that remained, the Word of God, by which the minds of men can be enlightened and strengthened, this they had long since cast away; so that they cannot recall it with any profit, nor hear its preaching with attentive minds. These men therefore do what is said of this prodigal son. For, destitute of all counsel and help, they attach or bind themselves to a foreign master in that distant land: that is, wandering outside the fold of the Church, they voluntarily summon to themselves lords or tyrants of conscience and faith, and rashly receive whoever seems to offer some hope. And thus they truly become slaves of the devil, who before seemed to sin in these things only, which pertain to the customs of outward life. Now that master of all masters is most unjust, who sends back those drawn away from Christ almost to the swine, so that they become wretched and filthy swineherds, since they were unwilling to keep their place in the house of God among the sons of this house. By the name of swine are denoted impure men, who either lead a profane life under the pretext of religion (such are for the most part the little priests, the monks, and all the ministers of superstitions and idolatry), or wallow without any shame in open crimes. Into the former kind fall those in whom some remaining goad of the fear of God still exists, by which they are stirred so that they cannot altogether lay aside the desire and zeal for eternal salvation. But to the latter belong those who, having shaken off all fear of God, begin to deny heaven and hell, and, because they have long since extinguished every hope of eternal life in their minds, carried away by a contempt of every deity more than Cypselus's, cry out with Sardanapalus:

units.la: Ede, bibe, lude, post mortem nulla voluptas.
units.tr: Eat, drink, play; there is no pleasure after death.

units.la: In quoscunque ergo infelices illi bonorum Dei concoctores incidant, in porcos incidunt, quos suis quidem impensis & laboribus pascunt, ipsi vero apud illos nihil quam siliquas & furfures inueniunt & ne his quidem ad satietatem frui possunt. Reuera enim siliquæ & furfures sunt hominum traditiones & quicunq; secundum has instituuntur cultus, vt animas esurientes & æstuantes recreent. Nam præter inanem speciem pietatis nihil habent, quæ etsi oculos hominum aliquo splendore perstringat, conscientiæ tamen terrores non tollit, sed potius auget & horribiliores reddit. Alteri verò illi, quos scelerum libido trahit, vt horum magistris se coniungant, ne siliquas quidem habent aut furfures, sed in fœdissimis stercoribus volutantur, & ne sic quidem libidinæ suæ possunt satisfacere. Sunt ergo omnes isti omnibus modis miseri atque infelices, adeo vt lusus & iocus videri possint quæ de filio isto prodigo dicuntur, præ ijs quæ isti sustinent.
units.tr: Into whatever hands these wretched men fall, those who digest the good things of God, they fall into swine, whom indeed they feed at their own expense and labour, yet they themselves find nothing among them but husks and bran, and cannot even enjoy these to the full. For indeed the husks and bran are the traditions of men and whatever worship is instituted according to them, to refresh souls hungry and burning. For apart from an empty appearance of piety they have nothing; and even if it dazzles men's eyes with some splendour, it does not remove the terrors of conscience, but rather increases them and makes them more dreadful. But as for those others whom the lust of crimes draws, so that they join themselves to the masters of these, they do not even have husks or bran, but wallow in the most foul dung, and not even so can they satisfy their lust. All these men, therefore, are wretched and unhappy in every way, so that what is said of this prodigal son may seem mere play and jest, compared with what these men suffer.

units.la: Ita verò Deus Verbi sui & legitimæ disciplinæ contemptum atq; inobedientiam in hoc etiam seculo vlciscitur, & id quidem iustas & graues ob causas facit. Primò enim hoc iustitia requirit, vt improbi illi puniantur, & de seipso ille pronuntiat, quod peccatum quidem condonet, non autem impunitum dimittat, sed patrum iniquitatem in filijs visitet, si hi illorum similes esse pergant. Deinde ut poenis eiusmodi hominum licentia coerceatur necesse est, ne prorsus indomita & intolerabilis fiat. Nam ut Poeta olim dicebat: Oderunt peccare boni virtutis amore, Oderunt peccare mali formidine poenae.
units.tr: In this way God avenges, even in this age, contempt and disobedience toward his Word and lawful discipline, and he does so for just and grave reasons. For first, justice requires that those wicked men be punished, and he himself declares that he indeed pardons sin, but does not let it go unpunished, but visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, if these persist in being like them. Next, it is necessary that the licence of such men be restrained by punishments of this kind, lest it become altogether unbridled and intolerable. For as a poet of old said: Good men shun sin from love of virtue; bad men shun sin from fear of punishment.

units.la: Postremo aduersus & miserijs ad poenitentiam excitantur, qui de ea vix cogitant, quando ipsis omnia pro votis succedunt. Vexatio enim (ut Isaias ait) dat intellectum. Et notum est illud Ieremiae: Castigauisti me Domine, & eruditus sum. Quod huic etiam concoctori nostro accidisse audiemus, ut inter porcos de patris optimi liberalitate & fide, deq; sua nequitia rectius iudicare disceret, qui in schola ingenuorum filiorum Dei minores antea progressus fecerat. Et haec quidem de miseria hominis peccatoris, qui se totum a Deo alienauit, nunc dicta sint. Vsus autem horum esto, ut sibi ipsis omnes caveant, & in Dei domo, Ecclesia, sese contineant, illi seruiant totus animus, ut caelesti pane fruantur & saturentur, qui est Christus Iesus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, those who hardly think of repentance are roused to it by miseries, when all things turn out according to their wishes. For affliction (as Isaiah says) gives understanding. And that saying of Jeremiah is well known: You have chastised me, O Lord, and I have been taught. We shall hear that this our swineherd also experienced this, so that among the swine he might learn to judge more rightly of the generosity and faithfulness of the best father, and of his own wickedness, he who had made less progress earlier in the school of the free sons of God. And these things have been said concerning the misery of the sinful man who has wholly alienated himself from God. Let the use of them be that all take care for themselves, and keep themselves within the house of God, the Church; let the whole soul serve him, that they may enjoy and be satisfied with the heavenly bread, which is Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLI.

units.la: Cum autem ad se redijsset, dixit: Quot mercenarij patris mei abundant panibus, ego vero fame pereo. Surgens proficiscar ad patrem meum, & dicam ei: Pater peccavi in caelum & aduersum te: nec amplius sum dignus vocari filius tuus: fac me ut unum ex mercenarijs tuis. Surgens ergo venit ad patrem suum.
units.tr: But when he came to himself, he said: "How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, while I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants.'" So he arose and came to his father.

units.la: Inter parabolas, quibus Dominus & Seruator noster, Iesus Christus, doctrinam suam illustrat semper celeberrima & prae alijs in usu fuit haec, quae de filio prodigo habetur: & quidem merito, cum totum Euangelium & universam salutis humanae rationem comprehendat. Constat enim illud doctrina poenitentiae & remissionis peccatorum. Sub poenitentia autem ipsum peccatum, huius poena & vera ad Deum conversio continetur. Remissio peccatorum e contra Dei gratiam, iustificationis nostrae negotium & omnem hominis felicitatem completitur. Atqui omnia haec per parabolam istam Christus ceu in tabella nobis spectanda proponit. Nam in prima eius parte peccati originem & progressum vidimus. In secunda, eiusdem poena adumbratur, quae est, quod diaboli mancipia facit, & tandem conscientias hominum terroribus gravissimis & dolore incredibili excruciat. Sequitur modo pars tertia, quae vera poenitentiae rationem describit, adeoque depingit ordinem, quo in gratiam cum Deo redimus. Itaq; singula diligentius excuti debent.
units.tr: Among the parables by which our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, illustrates his teaching, this one about the prodigal son has always been the most celebrated and the most used, and rightly so, since it comprehends the whole Gospel and the entire plan of human salvation. For it deals with the doctrine of repentance and the forgiveness of sins. Repentance includes both sin itself, its punishment, and the true conversion to God. The forgiveness of sins, on the other hand, comprises the grace of God, the business of our justification, and all of man's happiness. Christ sets all of this before us in this parable, as if in a picture to be gazed upon. For in its first part we have seen the origin and progress of sin. In the second, the punishment of sin is sketched: it makes men slaves of the devil and at last tortures their consciences with the most grievous terrors and with incredible anguish. Now follows the third part, which describes the true nature of repentance and so portrays the order by which we are restored to favour with God. Each of these things must therefore be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primum in se redijsse, & dixisse fertur: Quot mercenarij patris mei abundant panibus, ego vero fame pereo? Notatur his verbis agnitio peccati, quae iam animo eius affulgere coepit. Recte autem hac oriente peccatores in se redire dicuntur, quia quam diu cupiditatibus suis excaecati manent, extra se quodammodo vagantur, ut neque seipsos, neque Deum agnoscant, multo minus autem intelligant, quid huic ex officio debeant. Est ergo hoc verae & salutaris poenitentiae initium, si homo ad se reuersus cogitet, unde exciderit, & quae nunc ipsius sit conditio, quodq; miseriam omnem, qua premitur, non alij causae quam peccandi licentiae acceptae ferre possit. Exprimit haec omnia paucis verbis hisce Christus. Nam ex praesenti conditione plus quam infelici miser iste magnitudinem peccati aestimat, & se propterea miserum esse sentit, quod carnis cupiditatibus tantum indulserit. Deinde non potuit non prioris suae conditionis, quam in aedibus paternis ut filius herilis optimam habuit, recordari, cum ei in mentem veniat, quantam liberalitatem in mercenarios suos pater exercet: quod ad commendandam huius bonitatem plurimum facit. Quin in ista meditatione non probe exercentur, poenitere ex animo non possunt, eo quod ut peccatum nobis blanditur, ita oculos quoque perstringit, ut quasuis alias calamitatum causas nobis fingamus, modo ne quid nobis ex merito pro peccatis accidere, cogamur fateri.
units.tr: First, it is said that he came to himself and said: "How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, while I perish with hunger?" These words express the recognition of sin, which has begun to dawn upon his mind. And rightly, when this recognition arises, sinners are said to come to themselves, because as long as they remain blinded by their desires they wander, as it were, outside themselves, so that they know neither themselves nor God, and much less understand what they owe to him by their duty. This, then, is the beginning of true and saving repentance: when a man, coming back to himself, considers from what he has fallen, what his present condition is, and that he can attribute all the misery that oppresses him to nothing but the licence he has taken to sin. Christ expresses all of this in a few words. For from his present condition this wretched man, who is more than unhappy, estimates the greatness of his sin, and he feels himself wretched because he has indulged so much in the desires of the flesh. Then he could not help remembering his former condition, which he enjoyed in his father's house as the master's son, in the best of circumstances, when it came into his mind how great a generosity his father shows to his hired servants. This contributes greatly to commending the father's goodness. Indeed, those who do not properly engage in such meditation cannot repent from the heart, because sin both flatters us and dazzles our eyes, so that we invent for ourselves all sorts of other causes for our calamities, provided we are not compelled to admit that anything happens to us as the deserved wages of our sins.

units.la: At hic teneamus oportet, unde hoc nobis obtingat, quod ad nos redimus, & de Dei ira simul atque atq; paterna indulgentia cogitamus. Nam multi hoc omne in nostro arbitrio situm esse sibi persuadent, & quosdam ex prisci patribus dixisse scimus: Velis modo, & Deus praeoccurrit. Quos ego vicissim interrogo, quomodo velle possit homo aliquid boni, qui suo intellectu non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, & cuius cor cum figmentis suis omnibus pravum est ab ineunte aetate? Paulus certè, nos ex nobisipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneos esse scribit, Deum autem esse, qui in nobis operetur velle & facere. Et Christi vox est: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Ut ergo infans, cuius populites nondum confirmati sunt, assurgere & se ad iter parare non possunt: ita neq; nos ex peccatorum luto ad nos possumus redire, & seriam salutis curam atq; meditationem animo concipere, nisi manu porrigat Deus, & suo Spiritu nos excitet. Itaq; hoc ipsum gratuitum divinae misericordiae beneficium est, quod ad nos reversi de Deo placando cogitamus.
units.tr: But here we must hold fast to the source of this, that we come back to ourselves and think of the wrath of God and, at the same time, of his fatherly indulgence. For many persuade themselves that all of this lies within our own power, and we know that some of the ancient Fathers said: "Only will it, and God runs to meet you." To them I in turn put the question: how can a man will anything good, when by his own understanding he does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, and whose heart is wicked with all its imaginings from his earliest age? Paul certainly writes that we of ourselves are not even fit to think anything, but that it is God who works in us both to will and to do. And the word of Christ is: "Without me you can do nothing." Therefore, just as an infant, whose knees are not yet strengthened, cannot rise up and prepare itself for the journey, so neither can we return to ourselves out of the mire of sins, and conceive in our minds a serious care and meditation of salvation, unless God stretches out his hand and stirs us up by his Spirit. Thus it is itself a free benefit of divine mercy that, having come back to ourselves, we think about appeasing God.

units.la: At hic duo observari debent, quibus in nobis conuertendis Deus solet uti: media nimirum ex terna & interior animi illuminatio. Inter illa primus locus Verbo debetur, quo voluntate suam no bis ille revelat nosq; nostri officij admonet. Proximae sunt admonitiones privatae, quas vel amici vel inimici nobis adhibent: illi quidem nostri honoris & commodi studio, hi verò exprobrandi & conuiciandi libidine abrepti. Accedunt hu signa irae Dei & poenarum imminentium praesagia, quae multa & varia saepe in coelo, aere, aquarum intempestivis inundationibus, & infinitis aliis rebus proponuntur. Et quia natura duriores atq; contumaciores sumus, nō raro calamitatibus improvisis & aliquo tristiori casu veterum hunc nocentissimum nobis Deus excutit. Veruntamen omnibus istis nihil proficitur, nisi suo spiritu animos nostros illuminet, & corda moveat, vitta diligentius expendant. Alioqui enim monitores, ut qui nos oderint, suspectos habemus: alia verò omnia vel in causas naturales à philosophis olim excogitatas reijcimus, vel fortuita esse, & nihil ad nos pertinere putamus. Utrunq; in hoc inuene prodigo cernimus. Nam panis atq; deliciarum saturitas, quibus in patris domo abundabat, ferocem & refragatorem fecerat, ut paternis legibus porrò nolit subijci. Secuta est mox luxuriandi & voluptuandi licentia apud peregrinos, quae securum & socordem fecit, ut quotidie in peius proficeret, & facultates omnes dilapidaret. Ut ergo saluti eius consulatur, Deus primò inopia multat, quae causa est, ut ab illis ipsis ejiciatur, qui eum antea ut Heroem & Semideum coluerant, cum aliqua lucri spes affulgeret. Incipiam seruitus se juitur non minus foeda quam gravis & misera. Comitatur hanc fames dira, quae ad furtu res & quisquilias illum adigit, qui panes & lautitias patriae culinae fastidierat. Inter mala autem hae monitores quidem ex amicorum numero nulli sunt, porcos autem sodales & conuiuas habet, qui intolerabili faetore & molestissimo grunnitu ei ob sirepunt, & ne quisquilijs quidè atq; siliquis eum pacifice vesci patiuntur. Et tales quidem concionatores atq; magistros audire merebatur, qui vitam portenta in foedissimis voluptatibus vixerat. Sunt autem haec media, quibus animum eius excitat Deus, ut de seipso diligentius incipiat cogitare, & seriam salutis suae curam suscipiat. Quod ut citius faciat, Spiritus quoque animi aures illi vellicat ut tantae miseriae causas veras discat cognoscere. Et hoc quidem ordine cum suis ab ipsa usq; rerum origine Deus egit, quod in Adami etiam lapsu perspicuè cernitur. Nonne enim propriae nuditatis conspectus & irae divinae sensus, qui conscientiam eius infestabat, media fuerunt, quae Dei & mandati divini memoriam ei refricuerunt, quam paulò ante totam ex animo ejecerat? Accessit non multò post Dei ipsum quaerentis vox: Adam ubi es? qua eum excitavit, ut non de fuga sola & latebris quas frustra quaerebat, cogitaret: sed potius rationem secum inire, unde excidisset, & quo delapsus esset, quibus denique medijs ad hanc miseriam esset adductus. Nec tamen his contentus fuit Deus, sed eidem duros agriculturae labores imposuit, Euam partim doloribus acutissimis multaauit, utrunque à paradiso ejectum exilij molestijs exercuit, ut perpetuam de suo peccato & priori felicitate occasionem cogitandi haberent. Quid autem de indigna Abeli caede dicemus, quem infando parricidio Cain sustulit? Annon hunc quoque gravissimum stimulum fuisse putabimus, ut illius consideratione excitati intelligerent, quanta sit peccati vis, quando naturae corruptae iam in filios suos propagatae tam dirum & horrendum spectimen videbant? Simile quid cum David factum fuisse legimus. Media enim externa fuerunt, quibus securum & confidentem nimis Dominus perterruit, Nathani Prophetae non minus artificiosa quam gravis admonitio, & quae mox secuta sunt, stuprum Thamari filiae oblatum, Amnonis filij caedes, Absolomica seditio, bellum ci uile, filij charissimi infelix & Tragicus obitus & infinita alia, quae bellum istud comitata sunt. At ne ista vel inefficacia essent, vel conscientiam desperationis terroribus superatam in salutis periculum adducerent, no defuit interea Spiritus sancti suggestio, qui oculos eius illustrabat, ut & peccati sui magnitudinem cognosceret, & de calamitatum istarum causis recte iudicaret, atque his omnibus ceu adminiculis saluberrimis iuuaretur, ut cum Deo posset in gratiam redire. Adde his exemplis Petrum Apostolum, cui cum Christum abnegauisset, galli cantus occasionem dedit, ut illius ad ipsum respicientis bonitatem obseruaret, & ad se reuersus omnes Domini admonitiones in mentem reuocaret, & cum illo cuperet reconciliari. Possent huius generis infinita exempla adduci, sed plurimus non est opus, cum singuli ista in semetipsis quotidie experiantur.
units.tr: But here two things must be observed, which God is accustomed to use in turning us: namely, the outward means and the inward illumination of the mind. Among these the first place is owed to the Word, by which he reveals his will to us and reminds us of our duty. Next are the private admonitions which either friends or enemies address to us: the former out of zeal for our honour and advantage, the latter carried away by the desire to reproach and revile us. To these are added the signs of God's wrath and the omens of impending punishments, which are often set forth in many and varied forms in the heavens and the air, in untimely floods of waters, and in countless other things. And because we are by nature harder and more obstinate, God often shakes off this most harmful sluggishness from us by unforeseen calamities and some sadder misfortune. Yet nothing is gained by all these things unless he illumines our minds by his Spirit, moves our hearts, and makes us weigh these things more carefully. For otherwise we regard those who admonish us as suspect, as men who hate us, and we either reject all other things as causes arising from nature, as the philosophers once devised, or we think they are accidental and have nothing to do with us. We see both of these in this prodigal young man. For the abundance of bread and delights, with which he abounded in his father's house, had made him proud and defiant, so that he was unwilling to submit any longer to his father's laws. Soon there followed a licence to live riotously and indulge in pleasures among strangers, which made him careless and heedless, so that every day he went from bad to worse and squandered all his means. So, to provide for his salvation, God first afflicts him with poverty, which is the reason he is cast out by those very people who had previously honoured him as a hero and a demigod, as long as some hope of gain shone upon him. Then servitude follows, no less foul than it is heavy and wretched. Dire hunger accompanies it, which drives him to eat husks and refuse, he who had despised the bread and dainties of his father's kitchen. Among these evils, indeed, he has no friends from among those who might admonish him; instead he has pigs as his companions and table-mates, which creep upon him with intolerable stench and most disgusting grunting, and do not even allow him to eat the husks and pods in peace. And he deserved to hear such preachers and teachers, since he had lived a life of monstrous and most foul pleasures. These, then, are the means by which God stirs up his mind, so that he begins to think more carefully about himself and takes up a serious care for his salvation. So that he may do this more quickly, the Spirit also pricks the ears of his mind, so that he may learn to recognise the true causes of so great a misery. And God has dealt in this same order with his people from the very origin of things, which is plainly seen in the fall of Adam as well. For was not the sight of his own nakedness, and the sense of the divine wrath that troubled his conscience, the means that refreshed in him the memory of God and of the divine command, which a little before he had entirely cast out of his mind? Not long after, there came the voice of God seeking him: "Adam, where are you?" This roused him so that he thought not only of his flight and of the hiding-places in which he vainly sought shelter, but rather of how he should reckon with himself: from what he had fallen, into what he had slipped, and by what means at last he had been brought to this misery. Nor was God content with these things, but he laid hard labour of tilling the ground upon Adam, and afflicted Eve with most severe pains, and exercised both of them, cast out of paradise, with the troubles of exile, so that they might have a perpetual occasion of thinking about their sin and their former happiness. But what shall we say of the unworthy slaughter of Abel, whom Cain killed with unspeakable murder? Shall we not think that this too was a most serious goad, so that, stirred by its consideration, they might understand how great is the power of sin, when they saw so dire and horrible an example of their corrupted nature propagated into their own sons? We read that something similar happened with David. For the external means by which the Lord terrified him, too secure and too confident, were the admonition of the prophet Nathan, no less skilful than grave, and what followed soon after: the outrage done to his daughter Tamar, the murder of his son Amnon, the rebellion of Absalom, the civil war, the unhappy and tragic death of his dearest son, and countless other things that accompanied that war. But lest these things should prove ineffective, or leave his conscience overcome by terrors of despair and brought into peril of salvation, the suggestion of the Holy Spirit was not lacking in the meantime; it illumined his eyes, so that he might both recognise the greatness of his sin and judge rightly about the causes of these calamities, and so be helped by all these things as most salutary aids, that he might be able to return to favour with God. Add to these examples the apostle Peter, whom the crowing of the cock gave occasion, after he had denied Christ, to observe the Lord's goodness looking upon him; and, coming back to himself, he recalled to mind all the admonitions of the Lord, and desired to be reconciled to him. Countless examples of this kind could be brought forward, but there is no need of very many, since each one of us experiences these things in himself every day.

units.la: Hic potius sui officij omnes meminisse conuenit, ut in his Dei bonitatem agnoscant, & medijs istis atque ordini, quo in nobis reducendis vtitur, se accommodent. Sibi ergo dici meminerint, quod Laodicensium Ecclesiae in Apocalypsi dicitur: Ecce sto ad ostium & pulso: Si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit ianuam, intrabo ad illum, & coenabo cum illo, & ipse mecum. Reuera enim ista pulsantis Dei voces sunt, quibus securos & dormientes expergefacere solet, ut de ipso admittendo cogitent, & se in viam reduci patiantur. Aperiant ergo illi animarum aures quicunque pulsantem audiunt. Fit hoc, quando Verbum audiunt diligenter, & quae illud comitantur signa obseruant, calamitates non fortuitas esse putant, sed in his iustum Dei iudicium agnoscunt, & earundem causas veras in seipsis & vita antea acta inquirunt. Qui ista non ofcitanter faciunt, mox vident, se non habere aliquam murmurandi causam, etiamsi graviter ipsos Deus vrgeat, & quasi repetitis ictibus contundat. Nam ne sic quidem ingenij nostri duritiem emolliri & contumacia frangi potest. Veruntamen qui ista patientius ferunt, & Dei paternam manum agnoscunt, horum animis Spiritus cogitationes sanctas & salutares suggerit, quibus admoniti intelligunt, quanto potior sit sors vilissimorum seruorum in domo Dei, quam eorum, qui extra hanc licenter vagantes, diaboli porcos pascunt. Et sane potest hic non omnino stupidus modica diligentia sufficere, ut apertis animi oculis, rei veritatem cernant. Quis enim non videat, quanto beatius & quietius viuant, qui intra Ecclesiae septa se continent, & illic Deum in Spiritu & Veritate ritu simplicissimo colunt, quam qui illa relicta in superstitionibus oberrant, cultibus quotidie nouis fatigantur, ex quibus ad ipsos quidem nihil praeter labores, molestias & assiduos conscientiae aestuantis cruciatus, lucrum vero ingens ad impostores sacrificos & monachos redit, quos non imm erito diaboli porcos dixeris? Idem iudicabis si coniuges honestos & mutuae fidei tenaces cum impuris scortatoribus & adulteris confer as. Illi enim molestiarum omnium solatia certa & efficacissima quotidie percipiunt, cum in Dei vocatione viuant: hi vero cum suis similibus porcis in Satanae sterquilinio volutantur, & plerunque facultates omnes turpiter dilapidant, morbos foedos & atroces contrahunt, & tandem infames etiam fatis ab omnibus contemnuntur, qui non omnem honestatis curam abiecerunt. Confer item bonum & frugi patrem familias, qui cum pietate animum sua sorte contentum (ut Pauli verbis vtar) conjunxit, cum auaro vsurario, & mox videbis, hunc quidem insanis laboribus, immodicis vigiliis, curis mordacibus & infinitis alijs molestijs in infelici Satanae seruitio confici, alterum vero istum in diem viuere vitam tranquillam, & Dei benedictione frui, denique ex suis laboribus voluptatem percipere. Quod ipsum fateri cogeris, si omnia alia vitae genera percurras. Vere enim panibus & caelestibus donis abundant, quotquot in Dei domo fideliter seruiunt, fame interim pereuntibus ijs, qui diabolum cum suis porcis pietati & Dei beatissimo seruitio praeferunt.
units.tr: Here it is fitting that all should remember their duty, so that they recognise God's goodness in these things and accommodate themselves to these means and to the order by which he uses to bring us back. Let them remember that what is said in the Apocalypse to the church of the Laodiceans applies to them: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and sup with him, and he with me." These are indeed the voices of God knocking, by which he is accustomed to rouse the secure and sleeping, so that they may think about admitting him and allow themselves to be led back onto the way. Let those who hear him knocking therefore open the ears of their souls. This happens when they listen diligently to the Word and observe the signs that accompany it, when they think that calamities are not accidental but recognise in them God's just judgement, and when they inquire into the true causes of these in themselves and in the life lived before. Those who do not do this carelessly soon see that they have no cause for complaint, even if God presses them hard and beats them as if with repeated blows. For not even so can the hardness of our nature be softened and our stubbornness broken. Yet those who bear these things more patiently, and acknowledge the Father's hand of God, have holy and salutary thoughts suggested to their minds by the Spirit, and, admonished by them, they understand how much better is the lot of the lowliest servants in God's house than of those who wander freely outside it and feed the swine of the devil. And indeed even a not wholly dull person can, with modest diligence, see the truth of the matter once the eyes of the mind are opened. For who does not see how much more blessedly and quietly they live who keep themselves within the fences of the Church and there worship God in spirit and truth with the simplest rite, than those who, having left it, wander in superstitions and are daily wearied by new forms of worship, from which nothing comes back to them but labours, troubles and constant torments of a seething conscience, while a huge profit goes to impostor priests and monks, whom you might not undeservedly call the swine of the devil? You will judge the same if you compare honest spouses, faithful to their mutual trust, with impure whoremongers and adulterers. For the former daily receive sure and most effective consolations for all their troubles, since they live in God's calling; the latter wallow with their like, the swine, in the dunghill of Satan, and for the most part squander all their substance shamefully, contract foul and atrocious diseases and at last, infamous, are despised by all, even by those who have not cast off all care for honesty. Likewise compare a good and thrifty head of household, who has joined a mind content with its lot to godliness (to use Paul's words), with the greedy usurer, and soon you will see the one worn down by insane labours, immoderate watchings, gnawing cares and countless other troubles in the unhappy service of Satan, while the other lives the day tranquilly, enjoys God's blessing and finally derives pleasure from his labours. You will be forced to confess this yourself if you run through all the other ways of life. For truly, those who serve faithfully in God's house abound in bread and heavenly gifts, while meanwhile those who prefer the devil with his swine to piety and the most blessed service of God perish with hunger.

units.la: Ex his autem omnibus apparet, quae causa sit, cur multi ad poenitentiam salutarem nunquam perueniant. Ea nimirum, quod Deum pulsantem negligunt, & medijs quibus ille vtitur se accommodare dedignantur. Quam multos enim est videre, qui vt Verbum Dei audiant adduci non possunt, qui amicorum admonitiones improbe eludunt, signa irae Dei scurriliter contemnunt & ridGent, calamitatibus autem circumuenti, veras harum causas non respiciunt, sed vndique exempla corradunt, quibus se tueantur, ne se dignas sceleribus suis poenas pati cogantur fateri? Sunt his magis deplorati, qui cum Verbo Dei se conuictos esse, & eiusdem iudicio vrgeri & spem liberationis omnem sibi ereptam sentiunt, fremere & in voces horrendas atq; blasphemas ruere non verentur: cuius impietatis exempla in Caino, Saule, Juliano, & hodie in multis extant, qui ex prophano omnis discipline plinæ concemptu sibi laudem supremam pollicentur. Quid ergo in omnibus illis Spiritus Dei prosi-ciat? aut num quis hoc petere ausit, ut is se ipsis reluctantibus in animos plus quàm porcinos & fa--distimum diaboli sterquilinium intrudat? Itaq; in peius isti omnes proficiunt, neq; vnquam ad se reuertuntur, & tandem in desperationis præcipitium adducti pereunt.
units.tr: From all these things it appears what the cause is why many never come to saving repentance. It is namely that they neglect God knocking and disdain to accommodate themselves to the means by which he works. For how many are there to be seen who cannot be brought to hear the Word of God, who wickedly evade the admonitions of friends, scurrilously despise and laugh at the signs of God's wrath, and, beset by calamities, do not look at their true causes, but gather examples from everywhere by which to protect themselves, so that they are not compelled to confess that they suffer punishments worthy of their crimes? More hopeless still are those who, feeling that they are convicted by the Word of God and pressed by its judgement, and that all hope of deliverance has been snatched from them, do not hesitate to rage and rush into horrible and blasphemous outcries. Examples of this impiety exist in Cain, Saul and Julian, and today in many, who promise themselves the highest glory from the contempt of all profane discipline. What then does the Spirit of God accomplish in all those? Or would anyone dare to ask that, while they resist themselves, he should thrust into their minds something more than swinish, and the most loathsome dunghill of the devil? And so all these grow worse, never return to themselves, and at last, driven into the precipice of despair, perish.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad nostrum subulcum, quem calamitatis sensus rectius iudicare docuit. Nam non solum queritur de sua infelicitate, sed consilio sano secum inito addit: Surgens proficiscar ad patrem meum. Paucis verbis duo comprehendit obseruatu in primis necessaria. Primum est, con-ditionis præsentis odium & vitæ totius emendatio. Nec enim ait: Quandoquidem me & amicus de-stitutum & mihi omnia elementa infesta esse sentio, neq; alia melioris fortis spes mihi affulget, age-dum fatus superq; in hoc porcorum sterquilinio volutabor, aut aliquo profugiam, & rapinis, furtis, impostuts meam leuabo inopiam: denique ne à cædibus quidem abstinebo, vt vel melius mihi pro-ficiam, vel vitam infelicem semel finiam. Nihil horum ille dicit, neque fratri aut aliis patris sui domesticis fortem meliorem inuidet, quod multi faciunt, qui vbi sibi ipsis calamitates accersue-runt, vna secum omnes homines calamitosos esse vellent, & odio dignos arbitrantur, quorquoe feli-cius aut beatius viuere audiunt. Quin potius noster hic ad patrem redire, & huius disciplinæ sr ruri-sus subijcere statuit, cuius iugum antea improbè excusserat. Alterum huic consilio coniunctum est, Spes bona de patris clementia & facilitate. Nam nisi illa confirmatus fuisset, de reditu ad illum ne cogitasset quidem.
units.tr: But let us return to our swineherd, whom the sense of calamity taught to judge more rightly. For he not only complains of his unhappiness, but with sound counsel taken within himself adds: "Rising, I will go to my father." In a few words he comprehends two things especially necessary to observe. The first is hatred of the present condition and the amendment of the whole life. For he does not say: "Since my friend has abandoned me and I feel that all the elements are hostile to me, and no other hope of a better fortune shines on me, come, let me wallow in this dunghill of swine, or let me flee somewhere and relieve my poverty with robberies, thefts and frauds; finally I will not refrain even from murder, so that either I may do better for myself or end my unhappy life once and for all." He says none of these things, nor does he begrudge his brother or the others of his father's household their better fortune, which many do, who, when they have brought calamities upon themselves, would wish all wretched men to be together with them, and think hateful those whom they hear live more happily or blessedly. Rather, this man of ours resolves to return to the father and again to submit to that discipline whose yoke he had previously shaken off wickedly. Another thing joined to this counsel is good hope in the father's clemency and kindness. For unless he had been strengthened by that, he would not even have thought of returning to him.

units.la: Sunt hæc præcipua veræ & salutaris pœnitentiæ capita, sine quibus hæc non consistit. Quomo-do enim relictis peccatis ad Deum reuertetur, quem nullus scelerum admissorum & vitæ anteactæ pudor tangit? Rursus, quæ ratio mouebit, vt ad illum redeat, qui non bene sperat de eius bonitate & misericordia? At nihil horum præstabimus absq; fide. Hæc enim sola animos supra terrena om-nia euebit, & de Dei clementia certos facit, dum ad hanc nobis aditum fatu esse docet per Christū Iesum, qui nobis ab illo iustitia & sanctificatio datus est. Eadem vitæ prioris & mundi huius tæ-dium in nobis generat, quod non potest non oboriri illis, qui immensam Dei bonitatem & ineffabi-lem, quæ in cœlis nobis repositæ est, felicitatem diligentius intra animos suos expendunt. Et quam uis mores solitos & studia priora relinquere carni durum sit, fides tamen ita nos Christo inserit, vt eius Spiritu animati in ipso possimus omnia. Itaq; in pœnitentia in primis fide opus est, quæ vt de-speratiois periculum sola repellit, ita virtutum omnium fœcundissima mater est, & nos ad seriæ vitæ emendationem excitat, facit denique, vt in Christo renati fructum multum feramus. Quæ cau-sa est, quod hic non modo peccatorum remissionem, verumetiam pœnitentiam in suo nomine prae-dicare iussit. Et nocentissima illorum doctrina est, qui pœnitentiam quidem multis vrgent, nullam autem fidei mentionem faciunt, sine qua illa aut nulla erit, aut salutaris esse non poterit. Nam si fi-dem auferas à eo, qui iam viua & feria peccatorum cognitione & diuini iudicij sensu terretur, quis obstabit, quò minus cum Caino, Saule, Iuda & similibus desperationis voragine absorbeatur? Da-uidem certè non aliud seruauit, quam quod cum suis peccatis multitudinem gratiæ & miserationis Dei conferens, has omnibus illis superiores esse videret. Et Petrum hoc ipsum ab interitu eripuit, quod in Christi ipsum respicientis paterno intuitu bonitatem Dei gratuitam agnouit, quæ dolentem & in lachrymas amarissimas effusum ipse bona impleuit. Multa igitur & diligenti promissionum Dei & exemplorum gratiæ eius meditatione nobis opus est: quæ cum non semel iam alibi comme-morauerimus, & scripturas legentibus passim occurrant, nolumus eorundem repetitioni nunc diuti-us insistere.
units.tr: These are the chief heads of true and saving repentance, without which it does not stand. For how will someone who has left his sins return to God, if no shame for the crimes committed and the life lived before touches him? Again, what reason will move him to return to one who he does not hope well of, as to his goodness and mercy? But we will accomplish none of these things without faith. For faith alone lifts minds above all earthly things and makes them certain of God's clemency, while it teaches that access to this is open to us through Christ Jesus, who has been given to us by him as righteousness and sanctification. The same faith generates in us a weariness of our former life and of this world, which cannot fail to arise in those who weigh more diligently within their souls the immense and ineffable goodness of God and the happiness laid up for us in heaven. And although it is hard for the flesh to leave behind customary habits and former pursuits, faith nevertheless so grafts us into Christ that, animated by his Spirit, we can do all things in him. So in repentance there is first of all need of faith, which alone repels the danger of despair, and thus is the most fruitful mother of all virtues; it rouses us to a serious amendment of life and finally makes us, reborn in Christ, bear much fruit. This is why he commanded that not only the remission of sins but also repentance be preached in his name. And that teaching is most harmful which urges repentance on many but makes no mention of faith, without which repentance will either be nothing or cannot be saving. For if you take away faith from one who is already terrified by a living and sharp knowledge of his sins and by a sense of divine judgement, who will stand in the way, so that he is not swallowed in the whirlpool of despair along with Cain, Saul, Judas and similar men? David certainly kept to nothing else than this: comparing the multitude of God's grace and compassion with his sins, he saw that these were superior to all of them. And Peter was rescued from perdition by this very thing, that, looking at Christ, he recognised the free goodness of God with a fatherly gaze, which filled him with good things when he was grieving and poured out into bitterest tears. Therefore we have need of much and diligent meditation on the promises of God and the examples of his grace; since we have already recalled these not once elsewhere, and they occur everywhere to those who read the Scriptures, we do not wish now to dwell longer on their repetition.

units.la: Cæterum in hac pœnitentiæ parte duo præcipitia diligenter cauere oportet. Primum est hypo-crisis, quæ facit, vt pœnitentiam aut fucatam aut momentaneam agamus. Reprehendit hoc vitium passim Deus per prophetas in Iudæorum gente, & huc præcipuè pertinet, quod per Hoseam dicit: Quid faciam tibi ô Ephraim? Quid faciam tibi ô Iuda? Pietas vestra est vt nubes matutina, & ve-luti ros manè veniens & abiens. Similibus elegantissimis hypocritas depingit. Vt enim nubes ma-tutina, etsi terræ arenti & sitienti pluuias polliceantur, ad Solis tamen exortum euanescunt: ita illi interdum calamitatibus coacti pœnitentiæ consilium ineunt, vt magno cum conatu nescio quid fa-cturi videantur: sed mox nouis cupiditatum ardoribus inflammati curam hanc omnem abijciunt & ad pristina studia reuertuntur. Vt item æstiuo tempore roris gutte terram siticulosam nonnihil irrigant, & ex summis graminum apicibus instar vnionum dependet, non autem durabiles sunt, & vel vento exorto decutiuntur, vel solaribus radijs exiccantur: ita hypocritæ pœnitentia publicam sæpe mirifico cum apparatu instituunt: hanc supplicationibus publicis, solenni pompa, vestitu theatrico, gestibus ad summam animi deuotionem artificiosè compositis, ieiunijs & alijs huiusmodi cere monijs profitentur: sed omnia ista non nisi ros sunt mututinus, neque diutius durant, quam irę Dei sensus, quem ex animis suis statim excutiunt, quàm primum pœnis & calamitatibus liberantur. Et talem quidè Iudæorū pœnitentiam olim fuisse certò constat. Hodie autem ista tam vulgaria sunt, siue publicos omnium hominum mores, siue singulos priuatim inspicias, vt multa demonstratione non sit opus. Sed meminerint isti homines, Deum neque externo fuco decipi posse, neq; eorum resipi-scentia delectari, quos seruilis timor ad ipsum placandum cogit, mox autem vt canes ad vomitum redeunt.
units.tr: Moreover, in this part of repentance we must take careful care to avoid two precipices. The first is hypocrisy, which makes us repent either in pretence or only for a moment. God rebukes this vice everywhere through the prophets among the Jewish people, and above all what he says through Hosea pertains to it: "What shall I do to you, O Ephraim? What shall I do to you, O Judah? Your goodness is like the morning cloud, and like the early dew that goes away." He depicts hypocrites with these very apt similes. For just as the morning cloud promises rain to the dry and thirsty earth but vanishes at the rising of the sun, so such people sometimes, compelled by calamities, form a plan of repentance and seem, with great effort, to be about to do something; but soon, inflamed again by the fires of their desires, they cast off all this care and return to their former pursuits. Likewise, in summer, drops of dew moisten the thirsty ground a little and hang from the tips of the grass like pearls, yet they do not last: either a wind arises and shakes them off, or the rays of the sun dry them up. So hypocrites often undertake public repentance with wonderful display: they profess it by public supplications, solemn pomp, theatrical clothing, gestures artfully arranged to show the highest devotion, by fasts and other ceremonies of this kind. But all these things are only morning dew, and they last no longer than the sense of God's wrath, which they shake from their minds as soon as they are freed from punishments and calamities. And that the repentance of the Jews was once of this sort is certain. Today, however, such things are so commonplace, whether you look at the public morals of all people or at individuals in private, that there is no need for a long demonstration. But let these people remember that God can be deceived neither by outward paint, nor is he delighted by the repentance of those whom servile fear compels to placate him, and who soon return, like dogs, to their vomit.

units.la: At non minus periculi etiam serio pœnitentibus ex altero præcipitio imminet, quod est iustitiæ propriæ aut etiam alienæ fiducia. Hæc enim olim satisfactiones peperit, quibus homines superstitio si peccata sua expiari posse existimauerunt. Est autem hæc vanissima persuasio. Quæ enim corporalis exercitatio, quæ disciplina siue castigatio, quod hominis cuiuscunq; opus, quod meritū, pœnas quas peccando meruimus, expiare poterit, cum illa omnia breuissimo tempore perficiantur, hæ autē æternæ sint? Aut num Dei iram placabunt illa, quæ non alio quam humanarum traditionum fundamento niituntur, quas ille iampridem damnauit, dicens: Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas hominū? Et vt de operibus per se bonis & sanctis dicamus, ne his quidem nos fidere conuenit, cum ea non propria virtute faciamus (Dei enim in nobis agentis opus sunt) & eadem imperfecta sint, eò quod ex innata nobis naturæ nostræ prauitate aliquid vitij contrahunt. Adde hũ, quod qui suis satisfactionibus fidunt, ij Christi merito derogant, & dum suam iustitiam stabilire volunt, à Dei iustitia excidunt, quam si nobis in Filio suo vnigenito offert. Ita ergo nos pœnitentiam agere & hanc fructibus dignis testari debemus, vt interea nihil nobisipsis aut nostrorum operum meritis tribuamus, sed salutis fiduciam omnem in solius Dei gratuita misericordia collocemus.
units.tr: But no less danger threatens those who truly repent from the other precipice, which is confidence in one's own righteousness or even in another's. For this once gave birth to satisfactions, by which superstitious people thought their sins could be expiated. Yet this persuasion is most vain. For what bodily exercise, what discipline or chastisement, what work or merit of any human being will be able to expiate the punishments we have deserved by sinning, when all those things are accomplished in the briefest time, while the punishments are eternal? Or will those things placate God's wrath which rest on no foundation other than human traditions, which he condemned long ago, saying: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men"? And to speak even of works that are good and holy in themselves, it is not fitting for us to trust even in these, since we do them not by our own power (for they are the work of God working in us), and since they are imperfect, because they contract some fault from the innate corruption of our nature. Add to this that those who trust in their satisfactions detract from the merit of Christ, and while they wish to establish their own righteousness, they fall away from the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his only-begotten Son. Therefore we ought to repent in such a way, and bear witness to this by worthy fruits, that meanwhile we attribute nothing to ourselves or to the merits of our works, but place all our hope of salvation in the free mercy of God alone.

units.la: Sequitur pœnitentia, quam noster hic iam animo concepit, effectus. Est is seria meditatio de patre placando, cuius gratia iam nihil antiquius habet. In illa autē primum locū habet peccatorum confessio cum ardentibus precibus coniuncta, quibus se in gratiam recipi postulat. Hanc enim formulam animo concipit, & eo ipso testatur, quod & serio hoc negotium agat, & non impudenter in patris conspectum se ingerere conetur, quem tot tantis iniurijs affecerat. Est enim peccatorum confessio admodum necessaria. Nam qui illa fateri nolunt, non obscurè animi sui confidentiā produnt, qua inebriati sibijpsis multum adhuc tribunt, neq; se meruisse putant, vt tam duriter à Deo tractentur. Quia autem fiducia hæc vanissima est, vt quæ nullis Dei promissionibus nitatur, sieri non potest, quin isti grauioribus conscientiæ terroribus pressi miserabiliter intra animos suos æstuent, eoq; infeliciores sint, quò diutius peccata sua tegunt atq; dissimulant. Frustra enim (vt D. Ambrosius ait) velis occultare Deum, qui falli non potest, & cuius oculi cordis arcana penetrant. Expertus est hoc olim Dauid, qui quidipsi aliquando in hac tentationum palestra acciderit, exponens dicit: Dum quotidie tacitus mecum cogito, dum voce infremo, contabuerunt ossa mea. Nam dies noctesq; aggrauabatur super me manus tua, versus est succus meus in siccitates æstiuas. Sed vbi peccatum meum tibi notum feci, & iniquitatem meam non celaui: cum cogitarem, Fatebor contra me transgressionem meam Domino: tu remisisti iniquitatem peccati mei. Quibus per omnia consentiunt, quæ Ioannes Apostolus scribit: Si dixerimus, peccatum non habemus, nosipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est: Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, vt remittat nobis peccata nostra & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate.
units.tr: Next comes the effect of repentance, which the one we are considering has now conceived in his mind. It is a earnest purpose of appeasing the Father, whose favour he now values above all else. In this, the first place belongs to the confession of sins, joined with burning prayers, by which he asks to be received back into favour. For he conceives this form of words in his mind, and by that very fact shows both that he is treating this matter in earnest and that he is trying not to thrust himself shamelessly into the sight of the Father whom he had wronged with so many and great injuries. For the confession of sins is altogether necessary. For those who are unwilling to confess them reveal, not obscurely, the confidence of their mind, by which, intoxicated with themselves, they still ascribe much to themselves and think they have not deserved to be treated so harshly by God. But because this confidence is most vain, since it rests on no promises of God, it cannot happen that such people, pressed by heavier terrors of conscience, do not wretchedly seethe within their minds; and they are the more unhappy the longer they hide and conceal their sins. For (as Ambrose says) it is in vain that you wish to hide from God, who cannot be deceived, and whose eyes penetrate the secrets of the heart. David once experienced this, who had himself once fallen into this wrestling-ground of temptations, and he describes it, saying: "While I kept silent day by day, while I groaned all day long, my bones wasted away. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was turned into the drought of summer. But when I made my sin known to you, and did not hide my iniquity, when I said, I will confess my transgressions to the Lord, you forgave the iniquity of my sin." With these things agree in every respect what the Apostle John writes: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

units.la: Sed videamus confessionis formulam, quam filius iste prodigus animo concepit. Pater (inquit) peccaui in cœlum & aduersum te: neq; amplius sum dignus vocari filius tuus: fac me vt vnum ex mercenarijs tuis. Breuis confessio, sed quæ multa comprehendit, & proinde digna, cuius singulæ partes diligentius examinentur.
units.tr: But let us look at the form of confession that this prodigal son conceived in his mind. "Father," he says, "I have sinned against heaven and before you; and I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants." A brief confession, but one that comprehends much, and therefore worthy of having each of its parts examined more carefully.

units.la: Primò solius patris meminit. Ergo restà ad hunc abire & huic sua delicta confiteri voluit, nō ad aliquem patris vicinum aut amicum confugere. Et est hoc magnum bonitatis & clementiae Dei argumentum, qui etsi plurimis grauissimisq; peccatis offendatur, pater tamen à nobis agnosci & dici gaudet. Admonemur autem, nos quoq; peccata non alij, quàm huic confiteri debere, eò quòd solus hic ea remittendi ius habet. Vt ergo stultus merito censetur, qui medicinam quaerit apud eum, qui neq; medendi arte, neq; etiam pharmacis aut remedijs instructus est: ita nō stulti modò, sed terq; quaterq; infelices sunt, qui in periculosissimis animae morbis ad eos confugiunt, qui his mederi nō possunt. Faciunt hoc, qui Sacrificos & Monachos sibi deligunt, in quorum aures delicta sua fatentur, & ab ijsdem horum remissionem, siue absolutionem (vt ipsi loquuntur) postulant. Abutuntur illi ad erroris sui defensionē Iacobi authoritate, qui dixit: Cōfitemini alij alij offensas aut delicta. Sed quid hoc ad Sacerdotes, cùm de mutua iniuriarum aut offensarū confessione Apostolus loquatur, qua fit, vt in gratiā redeant, qui prius inter se dissidebāt? Et nō vident stupidissimi homines, ex illo loco cōfessionē illā, quā Sacrifici exigunt, nō aliter astrui posse, quàm vt ipsi vicissim in laicorū aures sua delicta deponāt. Nos ergo hunc nostrū imitemur, quod sanctissimos quosq; omnibus seculis fecisse cōstat.
units.tr: First, he remembers the Father alone. Therefore he resolved to go to him and confess his offences to him, not to flee to some neighbour or friend of the father. This is a great proof of God's goodness and mercy, who, although he is offended by very many and very grave sins, nevertheless rejoices to be acknowledged and called Father by us. We are also reminded that we ought to confess our sins to no one other than him, because he alone has the right to forgive them. Just as a fool is rightly judged who seeks medicine from one who is skilled neither in the art of healing nor equipped with drugs or remedies, so those are not only foolish but doubly and trebly unhappy who, in the most dangerous diseases of the soul, flee to those who cannot cure them. Those do this who choose for themselves priests and monks, into whose ears they confess their sins, and from whom they ask for remission, or absolution (as they themselves call it). They abuse the authority of James, who said: "Confess your faults one to another," to defend their error. But what has this to do with priests, since the Apostle is speaking of a mutual confession of injuries and offences, by which those who previously were at odds with one another are brought back into favour? And the most stupid men do not see that from that passage that confession which the priests demand cannot be built up except by their in turn laying their sins down in the ears of the laity. Therefore let us imitate this son of ours, as is certain that all the most holy men in every age have done.

units.la: Quomodo autem fatetur peccata sua filius iste infelix? Num omnia ex ordine recenset, vt quid toto illo tempore, quo à patris aedibus abfuit, fecerit, quidue in singulis vrbibus designarit, ex ordine exponat? Nequaquā. Etenim vt id verè fiat, impossibile est. Delicta enim (inquit Dauid) quis intelligit? Et vafrū est cor hominis & inscrutabile: quis cognoscet illud? Itaq; vno verbo omnia peccata sua simul comprehendit, neq; ea in aurem susurrat, sed clara voce clamat: Peccaui in cœlum & aduersum te. Paucis atrocitatem & magnitudinem peccati exprimit, quod in primis opus est fa⁠cto, vt eò feruentiori poenitentiae studio accendamur, & simul Dei cùm bonitatem tum potentiam commendemus, qui peccatis nostris vinci non potest. In cœlum autē peccare dicimur multis ob causas. Primò, quòd etsi homines iniuria afficimus, in his tamen Deus ipse laeditur, qui ne quid huius facinoris prohibet. Et hoc quàm maximè in ijs locū habet, qui impij sunt in parentes, & quosuis alios, qui ex Dei instituto aliquod ius in ipsos obtinent. Deinde in cœlum peccare dicuntur homines, quia eorum peccata in cœlum clamant, sicuti de sanguine Abel per Cainum effuso, de Sodomaeis item & Niniuitis Scriptura loquitur. Tertia huius locutionis ratio est, quia peccata cum naturae ordine pugnant, cui creaturae omnes obediunt, & quidem in primis cœli quoad motū perpetuum & certum atq; alias influentias siue effectus. Quis enim non fateatur hanc iniuriam fieri ab homine, qui cum horum seruitio & obsequio vtatur ex singulari Dei beneficio, ipse solus huic minus obtemperat? Adde his, quòd peccando dona cœlestia prophanantur atq; minuuntur, deniq; quòd cœlo teste, adeoq; in ipsius Dei cōspectu peccatur. Prodest ergo hoc in singulis peccatis obseruare, ne illa extenuando simul Dei gratiam non satis digne aestimemus, & in poenitentia etiam simus languidiores.
units.tr: But how does this unhappy son confess his sins? Does he recount them all in order, setting out in sequence what he did during the whole time he was away from his father's house, and what he committed in each city? By no means. For it is impossible to do this truly. For "who understands his errors?" asks David; and "the heart of man is deceitful and inscrutable: who shall know it?" So in one word he comprehends all his sins together, and he does not whisper them into an ear, but cries out in a clear voice: "I have sinned against heaven and before you." In a few words he expresses the atrocity and magnitude of sin, which is above all necessary for the deed, so that we may be kindled to a more fervent zeal for repentance, and at the same time commend both the goodness and the power of God, who cannot be overcome by our sins. We are said to sin against heaven for many reasons. First, because although we injure men, God himself is nevertheless wounded in them, since he forbids any such wrong. This applies most of all to those who are impious towards parents and any others who by God's appointment hold some right over them. Next, men are said to sin against heaven because their sins cry out to heaven, as Scripture speaks of the blood of Abel shed by Cain, and likewise of the Sodomites and Ninevites. A third reason for this way of speaking is that sins fight against the order of nature, to which all creatures are obedient, and especially the heavens in their perpetual and fixed motion and in their other influences or effects. For who would not admit that this is a wrong done by a man who, while he enjoys their service and obedience by the singular benefit of God, alone is less obedient to them? Add to these things that by sinning the heavenly gifts are profaned and diminished; and finally, that sin is committed with heaven as witness, and so in the very sight of God himself. It is therefore useful to observe this in each sin, lest by minimising them we at the same time fail to esteem God's grace sufficiently worthily, and become more sluggish in repentance too.

units.la: Praeterea ad extremam humilitatē nostrer hic sese deijcit, dicens: Neq; amplius sum dignus vocari filius tuus. Id verò in primis fiat oportet. Quia enim superbis & confidentibus Deus resistit, nūquam huic probabuntur, qui non toti in eius conspectu humiliati fuerint. Id verò prae alijs peccatores facere debent, qui Dei oculos atrocioribus delictis offenderunt. Et quantū hic noceat confidentia & superbia Pharisaica, tam Iudaeorum veterum, quàm multorum aliorum exemplis admonemur. Quàm stultè autem faciant, qui sese confidentius efferunt, vnius hic locus abunde admonet, qui tantam peccati atrocitatē esse docet, vt indignos faciat, qui filij Dei nominemur. Ergo à Deo sepa-rat (quod omnis miseriae & infelicitatis initiū atq; summa est) & proinde à regni quoq; caelestis haereditate excludit. Quàm ergo infelices sunt, qui adhuc superbiūt in Dei conspectu, & sua merita iactāt?
units.tr: Moreover, the prodigal here humbles himself to the utmost, saying: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son." This humility must come first of all, because God resists the proud and the self-confident, and he will never approve of those who have not humbled themselves completely before his sight. Sinners who have offended God's eyes by more heinous crimes ought to do this above all others. The examples of the Pharisee's confidence and pride, both of the ancient Jews and of many others, warn us how much harm such confidence and pride do.
