One passage here warns abundantly how foolish those are who boast of themselves so confidently. It teaches that sin is so grievous that it makes us unworthy to be called sons of God. Therefore it separates us from God, which is the beginning and the sum of all misery and unhappiness, and so it also shuts us out of the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. How unhappy, then, are those who still take pride in God's sight and boast of their own merits!

units.la: Addit his postremò filius iste: Fac me vt vnū ex mercenarijs tuis. Quibus verbis obedientiam pollicetur omnibus numeris perfectā. Quasi diceret: Non peto vt pristinae dignitati restituar, quam turpiter prostitui: sed vt domi tuae mihi versari liceat, precor: quod vnū si mihi obtingat, nullā fortem quantumuis durā & acerbā subire detrectō. Imò me beatū exi-stimabo, si vel inter mercenarios locum habeam. Ita olim Dauidem affectum fuisse legimus, qui tunc quoq; se ad obsequiū omne Deo paratū fore testabatur, si se ab illo reijci audiret. Nec aliter ipsi quoq; de nobis statuere poterimus, si cogitemus, nihil nobis tā graue & dirū accidere posse, quin grauiora & durioria meruerimus. Itaq; patienter omnē fortunam sustinere debemus, & sufficiat nobis, si in Dei domo locū possimus qualemcunq; obtinere. Nam vt idem Dauid dicebat, satius est ad limen domus Dei desidere, quàm in
units.tr: Finally, this son adds: "Make me as one of your hired servants." With these words he promises obedience in every respect perfect. It is as if he said: "I do not ask to be restored to my former dignity, which I shamefully forfeited; I only pray that I may be allowed to dwell in your house. If I obtain only this, I refuse to undergo no fortune, however hard and bitter it may be. Indeed, I shall count myself blessed if I have a place even among the hired servants." We read that David was once disposed in the same way, when he declared that he would be ready for all obedience to God, if he heard that he was rejected by him. Nor can we judge ourselves otherwise, if we consider that nothing so heavy and dire can befall us that we have not deserved things heavier and harsher still. Therefore we ought to bear every lot patiently, and it should suffice us if we can obtain some place, of whatever kind, in the house of God. For, as the same David said, it is better to sit at the threshold of the house of God than to be seen, proud, in the tents of the wicked, amid much glory.

units.la: Xx atrijs impiorum multa gloria superbum conspici. Admonet autem nos locus iste, eos qui poenitentiam veram agunt, nō ideò spem otij perpetui concipere & sibijpsis omnia læta polliceri debere, quasi nihil aduersi vnquam patiantur qui cum Deo semel in gratia redierunt. Etenim de Adami poenitentia quis dubitet, quando illum benedicti seminis promissione Deus confirmare dignatus est? eunde ta men hic laboribus & infinitis calamitatibus exerceri voluit. Et Dauidi dixerat Nathā: Transtu lit Deus peccatum tuum: Secuta tamen sunt, quæ idem minatus fuit, neq; ab eius domo gladius vn- quàm recessit. Quod ipsum de multis alijs dici potest, & hodie multis exemplis quotidie cōfirmatur. Id verò neminem offendere debet, vt propterea de Dei gratia & misericordia dubitet. Nam vt ita fiat necesse est propter inhærentem nobis naturæ nostræ vitiositatem, quam multa & seuera disciplina coercẽri oportet. Adhæc exempla extare opus est, quibus alij terreantur, & Dei iustitia excusetur. Si quid ergo huius accidit, cogitemus, nos dignos esse, qui vt mercenarij tractemur, qui cum heriles filij simus, dignitatem nostram minus tuemur.
units.tr: This passage also reminds us that those who truly repent should not therefore conceive a hope of perpetual ease and promise themselves all joys, as if those who have once returned to grace with God never suffered anything adverse. For who could doubt Adam's repentance, since God deigned to confirm him with the promise of the blessed seed? Yet God nonetheless wished him to be exercised here with labours and countless calamities. And Nathan had said to David: "God has taken away your sin"; yet those things followed which the same prophet had threatened, and the sword never departed from his house. This can be said of many others, and today it is daily confirmed by many examples. Yet this ought to offend no one, so that on that account he should doubt God's grace and mercy. For that such things happen is necessary, on account of the vice of our nature which dwells within us, and which must be restrained by strict and severe discipline. Moreover, there must be examples to frighten others and to vindicate God's justice. If, therefore, something of this kind befalls us, let us consider that we deserve to be treated as hired servants, since, though we are sons, we take too little care of our dignity.

units.la: Vt verò dicendi finem faciamus, quod iste animo concepit, illico reipsa præstat. Surgit enim, & venit ad patrem suum. Non ergo in inani speculatione poenitentia consistit, neq; ista dicere satis est, sed vt ad patrem reuertamur oportet. Surgat ergo qui prius in luto iacentes peccatis suis securi indormiebant: & ad Ecclesiæ gremium confugiant, vbi Patrem cum Filio & Spiritu sancto inue- nient. In horum meditatione hodie versemur, quando vndiq; pericula imminent. Descendamus in nosipsos, agnoscamus peccata nostra, quæ multa & grauia sunt: recurramus ad Dei gratiam: confi- teamur nos miseros esse, humiliemur autem, & ad omne obsequium parati simus. Ita nobis salutifer illucescet Iesus Christus, in quo Pater nobis iampridem placatus est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: To bring our discourse to an end: what the son conceived in his mind, he immediately carries out in deed. For he arises and comes to his father. Repentance therefore does not consist in an empty speculation, nor is it enough to say these things; we must return to our Father. Let those who lay in the mud and slept securely in their sins now arise, and let them flee to the bosom of the Church, where they will find the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let us be occupied in meditation on these things today, when dangers threaten on every side. Let us descend into ourselves, acknowledge our sins, which are many and grievous, and have recourse to God's grace. Let us confess that we are wretched, let us humble ourselves, and be ready for every obedience. So will Jesus Christ, in whom the Father has long since been reconciled to us, rise upon us as our salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLII.

units.la: Cum autem adhuc longè abesset, vidit eum pater ipsius, ac misericor- dia motus est: & accurrens incidit in collum eius, & deosculatus est eū. Dixit autem ei filius: Pater peccaui in cœlum & aduersum te, nec jam- plius sum dignus vocari filius tuus. Dixit verò pater ad seruos suos: Pro- ferte stolam illam primam, & induite eum, & date anulum in manum e- ius, & calceos in pedes: & adductum vitulum illum saginatum macta te, & vescentes oblectemur: Quia filius ille meus mortuus erat, & reuixit: perierat, & inuentus est. Coeperunt igitur lætari.
units.tr: But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. Then the son said to him: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son." But the father said to his servants: "Bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and be merry, because this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." And so they began to rejoice.

units.la: Q Vemadmodū nihil nocentius & detestabilius est peccato, quod nos à Deo alienat, & dam- nationi atq; morti æternæ subijcit: Ita nihil vtilius salutarius & expetibilius est vera pœ- nitentia, per quam ad Deum reuersi, cum illo in gratiam redimus, & vitæ bonorum cœlestium effi- cimur hæredes. Fatentur hoc ex communi sensu omnes, qui non omnē Dei metum in animis suis ex- tinxerunt: veruntamen circa poenitentiam à multis graviter & pernitiosè erratur. Alij enim pecca- ta quidem agnoscunt, sed eorū grauitate territi, de Dei bonitate & gratia desperant: quod olim Cai- no & Iudæ accidisse legimus. Alij verò non ad Deum conuertuntur, sed vel suis vel aliorum operi- bus atq; meritis confidunt: qui dum animarum sitim eo qui non est potus (vt apud Isaiam Deus lo- quitur) refrinquere conantur, illam magis accendunt, & miserius torquentur. Adde hu deplorate malitiæ homines, qui vt de pœnitentia vel cogitent adduci non possunt. At omnibus iste remedium præsentissimum ista parabola Iesus Christus adhibet. Nam primo peccati originē atq; progressum describit, quo facilius illud cauere, aut pedem ab eo retrahere possimus. Deinde infelicē eorum con- ditionem exprimit, qui huius mancipia facti sunt: vt eius odium in nobis exciteret. Tertia parte con- uersionis veræ typus proponitur, in quo nuper vidimus omnia, quæ salutarem poenitentiam actu- rus necessaria sunt. Sequitur nunc pars quarta, quæ reconciliatione hominis peccatoris cum Deo, & huius admirabilem erga eos, qui ad ipsum conuertuntur, bonitatem depingit. Quæ vt pœnitentia no- stra Deum delectari, & proinde hanc non inutilem esse docet: ita efficacissimā consolationem affert ijs, qui desperationis tela ignita sentiunt: adhæc quid eos deceat ostendit, qui verè conuersi sunt. Orditur autē hanc partem Dominus à prima reconciliationis causa quam his verbis exponit: Cùm autem adhuc longè abesset filius ille perditus, vidit eum pater ipsius, ac misericordia motus est. Exprimitur his gratuita & paterna Dei bonitas, cuius certæ notæ indicantur. Prima est, quòd filium, qui adhuc procul aberat, ipse prior videt. Unde enim hoc? Nimirum, quòd cum desiderio eius reditum expectauit, & ideò quasi in specula aliqua constitutus in illum intentus fuit. Deinde illo vi so misericordia motus est, vel (vt Lucas scripsit) ἐσπλαγχνίσθη, quod totis visceribus commotum fuisse significat. Respondet enim Græca vox Hebræa Rachan, & Rachem, qua σπλὴν, id est, natu ralis illa affectio exprimitur, qua parentes erga liberos in periculo aut miseria maxima constitutos affici solent. Exemplum huius in meretrice, quæ apud Solomonis tribunal aduersus socia suam pro filio suo contendit, in historia sacra habetur. Cùm enim Rex infantem dissecari & utrique partem dari iussisset, eius viscera commota esse aut incaluisse dicuntur, adeò vt filium potius alteri concedere vellet, quàm in eius crudelem necem consentire: quo indicio Solomon illam eius matrem esse deprehendit. Hunc verò affectum Deo patri Christus in præsenti tribuit, quod alibi quoq; in Scripturis fieri consueuit. Nam in Psalmo scribitur: Sicuti pater liberorum suorum miseretur: ita Dominus miseretur eorum, qui ipsum timent. Et per Ieremiam ipse populi sui liberationem & reditum ex Babylone promittens inter alia dicit: Annon pretiosus filius est mihi Ephraim? annon natus delicatulus? Omnino enim adhuc memor eius sum iam inde cùm primùm ei loquerer: unde & viscera mea commouentur super eum, omnino miserebor eius, dicit Dominus. Neq; nobis de hoc paterno Dei affectu dubitare licet. Si enim homines, qui natura iracundi & iniuriarum impatientes sunt, paternus amor vincit & mouet, vt filiorum contumacium miseriis tangantur: quanto magis hoc nos de Deo sperare debemus, cuius misericordia sempiterna est, & omnia opera eius superat? Ipse certè apud Isaiam amorem suum, quo nos prosequitur vehementiorem multò esse testatur, quàm naturales illas parentum affectiones, de quibus ante diximus.
units.tr: Just as nothing is more harmful and detestable than sin, which alienates us from God and subjects us to condemnation and eternal death, so nothing is more useful, saving, and desirable than true repentance, through which we return to God, are reconciled to him, and are made heirs of the good things of heaven. All who have not extinguished every fear of God in their minds agree on this from common sense. Nevertheless, many go badly and destructively astray concerning repentance. Some acknowledge their sins, but, terrified by their gravity, they despair of God's goodness and grace, as we read happened long ago to Cain and Judas. Others do not turn to God at all, but trust in their own works or in the works and merits of others. While they try to quench the thirst of their souls with what is not drink (as God speaks through Isaiah), they only inflame it more and are tormented more wretchedly. Add to these the people of deplorable wickedness who cannot even be brought to think about repentance. Jesus Christ applies the most effective remedy to all of them in this parable. First, he describes the origin and progress of sin, so that we may more easily guard against it or draw our foot back from it. Then he sets out the wretched condition of those who have become its slaves, so that hatred of it may be stirred up in us. In the third part, a picture of true conversion is presented, in which we have recently seen everything that is necessary for a man who is going to repent in a saving way. Now follows the fourth part, which portrays the reconciliation of the sinful man with God and God's wonderful goodness toward those who turn to him. Just as it teaches that our repentance pleases God, and therefore is not useless, so it brings the most effective consolation to those who feel the fiery darts of despair. Moreover, it shows what befits those who have truly been converted. The Lord begins this part with the first cause of reconciliation, which he expresses in these words: "But while the lost son was still a long way off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion." By this, God's free and fatherly goodness is set forth, and its certain marks are indicated. The first is that he sees the son, who was still far off, before the son sees him. How so? Surely because he waited for his return with longing, and so, as if stationed on some watchtower, he kept his eyes fixed on him. Then, when he had seen him, he was moved with compassion, or (as Luke wrote) "was moved in his bowels" [ἐσπλαγχνίσθη], which signifies that he was stirred in his whole inner being. For the Greek word answers to the Hebrew word rachan and rachem, by which is expressed the natural affection [σπλὴν] with which parents are usually moved toward their children when they are in the greatest danger or distress. An example of this is found in sacred history, in the case of the harlot who, before Solomon's tribunal, contended against her companion for her son. For when the king ordered the infant to be cut in two and a half given to each, her bowels are said to have been moved and to have grown warm, so that she preferred to give her son to the other woman rather than consent to his cruel death. By this sign Solomon discovered that she was his mother. Christ now attributes this same affection to God the Father, as is also customary elsewhere in the Scriptures. For in a Psalm it is written: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him." And through Jeremiah, promising the liberation and return of his people from Babylon, he says among other things: "Is not Ephraim my precious son? Is he not a delightful child? For indeed I still remember him, ever since I first spoke to him; therefore my bowels are moved for him; I will surely have mercy on him, says the Lord." Nor may we doubt this fatherly affection of God. For if human beings, who by nature are quick to anger and impatient of wrongs, are conquered and moved by paternal love, so that they are touched by the miseries of their stubborn sons, how much more ought we to hope this of God, whose mercy is everlasting and surpasses all his works? Indeed, he himself testifies through Isaiah that the love with which he pursues us is far more vehement than those natural affections of parents of which we spoke before.

units.la: Non tenicre autem huius primo statim loco Christus hic meminit. Ita enim docet, reconciliationem cum Deo ex qua omnis nostra salus dependet, nobis ex mera & gratuita misericordia obtinere. Eadem est enim omnium nostrum, quæ filij huius concoctoris conditio. Nam abs se alienatos & procul seiunctos Deus prior respicit, & quia pater est indulgentissimus, mox nostri miseretur, priusquam nos nostram miseriā exponamus, aut ipsius opem precibus multis & artificiosis implore-mus. Vt enim patri sufficit, si filium in flumine aut incendio periclitantem videat, & patris nomen ab illo inclamari ac repeti audiat: ita periculis & calamitatibus nostris Deus abunde mouetur, & satis illi fuerit, si nos de pœnitentia & nostræ miseriæ confessione solicitos esse, iamq; animis nostris pias atque serias de his cogitationes concepisse intelligat. Videt enim animi nostri recessus, & ideò (vt apud Isaiam ait) priusquam clamemus, exaudit nos. Et hæc illa bonitas est, quam Dauid prædicat dicens: Cùm cogitarem, Fatebor contra me transgressionem meam Domino, tu remisisti iniquitatē peccati mei. Exempla quibus ista confirmentur, plurima adduci poterant. Annon enim nos omnes à longè vidit Deus, quando priusquam hic mundus crearetur, conditionē nostram infelicem, in quam deuenturi eramus, considerans, nostri miseritus, æterno suo decreto Filium suum nobis redemptorem prædestinauit? Annon procul abs se alienatos respexit Israelis filios, quando Pharaonis tyrannide oppressos, & Ægyptiorum superstitionibus immersos liberauit, & sibi ex illis peculium fecit? Sic à longè gentes vidit, quando sub tenebrarum potestate laborantibus Apostolos submisit, qui salutis Verbum illis prædicarent. Et vt de priuatis hominibus loquamur, nonne Adamum eminus vidit, quando fugientem & latebras quærentem retraxit, vt promissionem de semine mulieris audiret? Annon à longè Abrahamum vidit, quando inter idololatras agentem euocauit, vt cum eo salutis fœdus instauraret? Annon Dauidem iam procul extra salutis viam vagantem vidit, quando Nathanum misit, qui securum in viam remitteret? Sic Petrum prior Christus respexit, cùm ille iam turpis abnegator factus illi tergum obuertisset. Sed quid horum commemoratione opus est, quando singuli hanc Dei gratiam in seipsis quotidie experiuntur. Prodest autē gratuitam hanc Patris cœlestis dilectionem atq; misericordiam crebrò meditari. Est enim hæc præcipua & vnica salutis nostræ spes, quæ sola animos ob peccatorum magnitudinem fluctuantes confirmare & erigere potest. Nam quoad in suas vires aut suorum operum merita homines respiciunt, sa iutiùs certi fieri non possunt, cum hæc quidem omnino nulla, illæ autem non solùm debilitatæ, verum etiam corruptæ & ad sola peccata efficaces sint. Minimè ergo audiri debent, qui ex hoc loco elicere conantur, principium reconciliationis cum Deo ex nobis esse, eò quòd miserum illum tunc demùm respexerit pater, cum ille iam de pœnitentia seriò cogitauisset, & iter ingressus esset, vt ad patrem rediret. Nam supra diximus pœnitentiam quoq; à Deo nobis dari, neque de illa nos cogitare posse, nisi suo Spiritu animos nostros ille excitet. Quid enim hic faciat homo, qui ex semetipso ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneus est? Et supra in ouis parabola audiuimus, Deum esse, qui nos quærit, & ad gregem suum reducit, qui alioqui nunquam iter ingressuri eramus, vt ad ipsum colligeremur.
units.tr: Christ does not, however, mention this in the first place. For he teaches that reconciliation with God, on which all our salvation depends, is obtained by us from pure and free mercy. For the condition of all of us is the same as that of this son of the householder. God first looks upon us when we are estranged from him and far separated, and because he is the most indulgent of fathers, he soon has compassion on us, before we set out our misery or implore his help with many and elaborate prayers. Just as it is enough for a father to see his son in peril in a river or a fire, and to hear his name called out and repeated by the son, so God is abundantly moved by our dangers and calamities, and it is enough for him to perceive that we are anxious about repentance and the confession of our misery, and that we have already conceived in our minds pious and earnest thoughts about these things. For he sees the recesses of our mind, and therefore (as he says through Isaiah) he hears us before we call. This is the goodness that David proclaims when he says: "When I thought, 'I will confess my transgression to the Lord,' you forgave the iniquity of my sin." Very many examples could be brought forward to confirm this. Did not God see all of us from afar, when, before this world was created, considering the unhappy condition into which we were about to fall, he had mercy on us and, by his eternal decree, predestined his Son to be our Redeemer? Did he not look upon the sons of Israel, estranged and far away, when he delivered them from the tyranny of Pharaoh and from the superstitions of the Egyptians, in which they were immersed, and made a peculiar people for himself out of them? So from afar he saw the nations when he sent the apostles to those who labored under the power of darkness, to preach to them the word of salvation. And, to speak of private persons, did he not see Adam from afar, when he drew him back as he fled and sought hiding places, so that he might hear the promise about the seed of the woman? Did he not see Abraham from afar, when he called him out from among the idolaters to establish with him the covenant of salvation? Did he not see David already wandering far outside the way of salvation, when he sent Nathan to bring him back to the path, though he was secure? So Christ looked upon Peter first, when Peter, having become a shameful denier, had turned his back on him. But why do we need to recall these things, when each one of us daily experiences this grace of God in himself? Yet it is profitable to meditate often on this free love and mercy of the heavenly Father. For it is the chief and only hope of our salvation, the only thing able to strengthen and raise up souls that waver because of the greatness of their sins. For as long as people look to their own strength or to the merits of their works, they cannot be made certain, since the former is altogether nothing, and the latter are not only weakened but even corrupted and effective only for sins. Therefore those should by no means be heard who try to draw from this passage the claim that the beginning of reconciliation with God comes from us, because the father looked upon the wretched son only when the son had already seriously thought about repentance and had set out on the way to return to his father. For we said above that repentance too is given to us by God, and that we cannot even think about it unless he stirs up our minds by his Spirit. For what can a man do here, who of himself is not even fit to think? And above, in the parable of the sheep, we heard that it is God who seeks us and leads us back to his flock, we who otherwise would never have set out on the way, so that we might be gathered to him.

units.la: Quid autem visò filio pater ipse fecit? Num in otiosa commiseratione subsistit, aut illachrymasse contentus illum præterea neglexit? Nequaquam, quin potius ei occurrit, ne quis ipsum adsei iturum impediret, aut ille ipso viso, terrore nouo perculsus pedem referret. Ita omnibus hominibus obuiam excurrit Deus in Filio suo, qui in mundum hunc venit, vt miseros in gratiam reciperet. Et quotidie nobis publicè & priuatim occurrit, quando per Verbum suum gratiam suam nobis offert, & simul animus nostris Spiritum suggerit, qui conscientiæ terrores discutit, & spe bona nos implet atque confirmat. Exemplo hoc demonstrare nequaquam opus est, quando hanc gratiam Dei omnes fateri cogentur, qui quid cum ipsis agatur quotidie non ofcitanter obseruauerint. Nunc potius meminerimus nostri officij esse, ne nobis occurrentem ipsi auersemur, & illi humeros aut tergum obuertamus, quod olim Iudæos atq; Israelitas fecisse scimus. Faciunt hoc, qui gratiæ prædicationem, vt superuacaneam & sibi minimè necessariam, respuunt. Item qui pœnitentiam ipsis offerentem non admittunt, & non modò ad Verbum Dei aures obturant, verumetiam Spiritus sancti sugestiones & propriæ conscientiæ testimonium eludere & extinguere conantur. Est hic impietatis colophon, & compendium est, quo ad desperationis præcipitium homines adducuntur. Non potest enim sopiri conscientiæ stimulus, quin cum minimè sperès recurrat. At si cor nostrum nos condemnet, quomodo Dei iudicium sustinebimus, qui & potentior est, & quem nihil eorum latet, quæ nos adhuc ignoramus? Vide 1. Ioan. 3.
units.tr: But what did the father himself do when he saw his son? Did he stop at idle pity, or was he content to weep and then neglect him? Not at all. Rather, he ran to meet him, lest anyone prevent him from coming, or lest the son, on seeing him, be struck by fresh terror and draw back. So God runs out to meet all people in his Son, who came into this world to receive wretched sinners into grace. And every day he meets us, both publicly and privately, when he offers us his grace through his Word, and at the same time suggests his Spirit to our minds, who dispels the terrors of conscience and fills us with good hope and strengthens us. There is no need to prove this by example, since all will be compelled to confess this grace of God if they have observed carefully every day what is being done with them. Let us rather remember that it is our duty not to turn away from him when he meets us, nor to turn our shoulders or backs to him, as we know the Jews and Israelites once did. Those do this who reject the preaching of grace as superfluous and not at all necessary for themselves. Likewise do those who do not admit the repentance offered to them, and who not only stop their ears to the Word of God but also try to elude and extinguish the promptings of the Holy Spirit and the testimony of their own conscience. This is the crown of impiety, and it is the shortcut by which people are led to the precipice of despair. For the sting of conscience cannot be lulled to sleep but it returns when we least expect it. But if our heart condemns us, how shall we stand the judgment of God, who is both more powerful and knows all those things that we are still ignorant of? See 1 John 3.

units.la: Sequitur in patris exemplo, quòd in collum filij iuciderit & complexus eum fit osculatus. Est hoc nouum tenerrimæ dilectionis argumentum, quæ à nobis melius cognosceretur, si habitum filij animo repetamus, qui non alius esse potuit, quàm qualis subulcorum esse solet. Ergo lacerum sordidum & squalidum, imò male olentem & fœtore grauem complectitur & deosculatur. His autem summus & paternus Dei amor plenius exprimitur, quem erga nos per Filium suum vnigenitum declarauit. In hoc enim nos, qui præter grauissimum fœtorem inter diaboli porcos, aut potius eius cloacas, contractum, & laceros squalentesq; pannos, nihil in eius conspectum afferebamus, tenerrimè complexus est, quando naturam nostram ille assumpsit, vt ipsi prorsus vniremur. Reuera enim magnus sit oportet peccati fœtor, qui in cœlum vsque ascendit, & Dei non nares modò, verumetiam oculos offendit. Quid verò nostram iustitiam esse dicemus aliud, quàm vestem laceram, quæ corpus ne tegere quidem nedum ornare potest? Isaias certè centonibus sordidissimis, vel etiam pannis mulieris fluxum menstruum patientis illam confert. Veruntamen nō abstterruerunt ista optimū illum patrem, quin nobis in Filio suo occurrere & nos completi dignatus sit. Coniunxit complexui isti osculaquoque, quod inter homines præcipuum amicitiæ & amoris maximi symbolum habetur. Quia enim per os spiritus ducitur, & eodem animi nostri cogitationes atque arcana manifestamus, per oris coniunctionem recte spiritus atque animorum coniunctio significatur. Ideò in excellentissimo illo Solomonis Cantico Ecclesia Christum orat, vt ipsam osculetur osculis oris sui, id est, suum amorem suis vsitatis signis atque indicijs testetur, & ita de Dei gratia & salute sua certam atque securam faciat. Et ita Diuus Ambrosius locum illum intellexit, qui in Psalm. 118. explicatione scribit: Osculatur nos Dei Verbum, quando sensum nostrum Spiritus cognitionis illuminat. Loquitur enim de læta illa & salutifera cognitione Dei, qua eius erga nos beneficam voluntatem percipimus. At quod Ecclesia orat, & quod in huius indulgentissimi Patris typo adumbratur, hoc Deus quotidie præstat, & ita quidem, vt plus quàm stipites sint, qui eius bonitatem non agnoscunt, ferrum autem & Adamantem duritie superent, quos tanti amoris tot indicia nō mouent atque emolliunt. Annon enim osculum Dei est, quando ait: Viuo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuerconuertatur & viuat? Quis item non osculum Dei suavissimum agnoscat in Christi verbis? Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam? Osculum Dei dulcissimum est, quod caelitus nobis offert clamans: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Sic ipse Filius, sponsus animarum nostrarum, oculo laetissimo & ardentissimi amoris pleno nos invitat, cum ait: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos. Item: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat. Possunt etiam inter oscula Dei censeri Sacramenta, quibus promissiones gratuitas & universum nostrae redemptionis atque salutis beneficium obsignat. Et revera nos complectitur arctissime & exosculatur Dominus, quando per Baptismum nos in Ecclesiae suae gremium recipit, ut sponsa suae membra & honorum ipsius omnium haeredes efficiamur. Idem in Coena sua facit Dei Filius, quando se eum esse confirmat, qui sua carne & sanguine nos alat & feruet ad vitam aeternam. Possumus his adnumerare quotidiana beneficia Dei, quibus suum amorem nobis testatur, & quae plura sunt, quam ut verbis explicari possint. Utinam vero oscula haec Dei omnes agnoscerent, & ijs ad ipsum omnes redamandum accenderentur. Sed quae nostra est infelicitas & ingenij corruptio, quam plurimi reperiuntur, qui dum ista per Evangelij praedicationem ad se deferri audiunt, non aliter rabie nova inflammantur, quam si quid hostiliter adversus se tentari viderent? Ambiunt illi fere magni illius Babylonici scorti, matris fornicationum, oscula, quae philtris & veneficijs suis inescatos ad exitium & infamiam sempiternam deducit.
units.tr: Next, in the father's example, he fell on his son's neck and embraced him and kissed him. This is a new proof of the tenderest love, which we would understand better if we call to mind the son's condition, which could be nothing other than that of swineherds. So he embraces and kisses him in his torn, filthy and squalid state, indeed in his foul-smelling and noisome condition. In this his supreme and fatherly love of God is more fully expressed, which he has shown towards us through his only-begotten Son. For in this he tenderly embraced us, who, apart from the very grievous stench we had contracted among the swine of the devil, or rather his sewers, and our torn and filthy rags, brought nothing into his sight, when he assumed our nature so that we might be wholly united to him. For truly the stench of sin must be great, since it ascends even to heaven and offends God not only in his nostrils but also in his eyes. And what shall we say our righteousness is but a torn garment, which cannot even cover the body, much less adorn it? Isaiah indeed compares it to the most filthy rags, or even to the cloth of a woman suffering a menstrual flow. Yet these things did not frighten that most excellent father away, so that he did not deign to meet us in his Son and embrace us. To the embrace he added a kiss, which among men is held to be the chief sign of friendship and the greatest love. For since the breath of the spirit is drawn through the mouth, and through the mouth we reveal the thoughts and secrets of our minds, the joining of the mouths rightly signifies the joining of spirits and minds. That is why in the most excellent Song of Solomon the Church asks Christ to kiss her with the kisses of his mouth, that is, to attest his love by his customary signs and indications, and so to make her certain and secure of God's grace and her own salvation. Blessed Ambrose also understood that passage thus, in his explanation of Psalm 118, where he writes: "The Word of God kisses us when the Spirit of knowledge illuminates our sense." For he speaks of that joyful and saving knowledge of God by which we perceive his kindly will towards us. But what the Church prays for, and what is foreshadowed in the type of this most indulgent father, God does every day; and indeed those who do not acknowledge his goodness are more than tree-stumps, and those whom so many tokens of such love do not move and soften surpass iron and adamant in hardness. For is not the kiss of God in his words: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live"? Who also does not recognise the sweetest kiss of God in the words of Christ: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life"? The kiss of God is most sweet, which he offers to us from heaven, crying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." So the Son himself, the bridegroom of our souls, invites us with a most joyful look and full of most ardent love, when he says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Likewise: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." The sacraments too can be counted among the kisses of God, by which he seals to us his free promises and the whole benefit of our redemption and salvation. And truly the Lord embraces us most closely and kisses us, when through Baptism he receives us into the bosom of his Church, that we may be made members of his bride and heirs of all his honours. The Son of God does the same in his Supper, when he assures us that he is the one who nourishes and quickens us to eternal life with his flesh and blood. We may add to these the daily benefits of God, by which he attests his love towards us, and which are too many to be explained in words. Would that all acknowledged these kisses of God and were kindled by them to love him in return! But what is our misfortune and the corruption of our nature, that very many are found who, when they hear these things brought to them by the preaching of the Gospel, are inflamed with a new rage, just as if they saw something hostile being attempted against them? They seek the kisses of that great Babylonian harlot, the mother of fornications, which, with her love-potions and sorceries, leads those she has enticed to destruction and everlasting infamy.

units.la: Audivimus hucusque magna & stupenda amoris divini argumenta, sed maiora sequuntur. Priusquam enim orationem animo conceptam filius ille miserabilis totam absoluat, servos inclamat pater, & dicit eis: Proferte stolam illam primam, & induite eum, & date annulum in manum eius, & calceos in pedes: & adductum vitulum illum saginatum macta-te, ut vescentes oblectemur. Atqui durus aliquis Demea nunc sibi exprobrandi occasionem datam gauisus esset, aut saltem se durior rem simulavisset, & non nisi conditionibus durissimis recepisset filium, ut eo obsequentior in posterum vteretur. Sed nihil istorum hic audimus: imo absque mora in filio vestiendo & ornando servos omnes occupatos esse vult, & ita eum ornare iubet, ut omnibus constare posset, eum posthac non pro extero aut rebelli, vel mercenario aliquo vili, sed pro filio herili agnosci debere. Ista autem parte docemur, Deum ita nos in gratiam suam recipere, ut (quod olim ex Sibyllinis carminibus Poeta male ad Pollionis sui filium detorsit) Si qua manent scelerиc vestigia nostri, irrita sint prorsus, nec nobis imputet illa. Imo domus prioribus nos rursus instruit & ornat, adeoque in pristinam dignitatem restituit. Et huc pertinet tam diligens vestium atque ornatus illius expositio. Primo enim stolam illam primam proferre iubet, ut ea induatur. Per hanc recte innocentiam & sanctimoniam veram intelligimus. Prima autem dicitur, non solum κατ' ἐξοχὴν, propter excellentiam suam, sed quod ea primum parentem nostrum Deus ornaverat, quando ad suam imaginem & similitudinem eum creavit: cuius effectus erat, ut quamvis corpore nudus esset, non tamen ipsum puderet. Sed amisit vestem hanc Adamus, quando diaboli consilium secutus ex arbore vetita comedit. Tunc enim ex innocente & sancto peccator & reus laesae maiestatis factus nuditatem suam vidit, & huius testimonio convictus nova tegmina & latebras quaesiuit frustra, quibus se a Dei conspectu occultaret. At restituit priorem illam vestem ad se converis Deus in filio suo Iesu Christo, quem pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos per ipsum eius iustitia efficeremur. Imo hic nobis sapientia, iustitia & sanctificatio factus est, dum eius obedientia atque merito tegimur, ut nostrae iniquitates apud Deum porro non amplius in rationem veniant. Idem ille etiam nos regenerat, quo fit, ut veteri homine depositio novum induamus, & mortificatis carnis nostrae desideriis vitam viuamus novam, quae nominus no stri professioni respondeat. Ideo Paulus dicebat: Quicunque in Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Et haec illa vestis nuptialis est, sine qua ad Ecclesiae societatem nemo ingredi, nemo etiam in ea perdurare potest, etiamsi ad tempus in externo illius coetu aliquem locum obtineat. Debet hoc propter eos observari, qui doctrinam de gratuita Dei misericordia bonis operibus inimicam esse, & hominibus ad licentiam peccandi viam sternere dicunt. Nec enim de eo nobis cum aliquo lis est, num bona opera fieri debeant: sed num operibus nostris remissionem peccatorum & salutem merea-mur? Ex his postremum hoc negamus, & quidem gravissimis rationibus adductis, quas alibi comamemoranimus: illud vero omnino necessarium esse docemus, quando fieri non potest, quin fructusferant suae professione dignos, qui in vite illa vera, Iesu Christo, insiti, cum eius Spiritu, succo nimirum vitali & vegetativo, participant. Scimus item eos qui iustitiam faciunt, iustos esse & Christum nobis non solum gratuitae iustificationis esse authorem, sed in eodem nos etiam peccato mori, ut eius Verbo ac Spiritu ad vitae novitatem excitemur. Quia deniq; iustificati ex fide pacem habent cum Deo, idem conscientiae puritate retineant oportet, quae in peccandi licentia consistere nullo modo potest.
units.tr: Thus far we have heard great and wonderful proofs of divine love, but greater ones follow. For before that wretched son has finished the speech he had conceived in his mind, the father calls to his servants and says to them: "Bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; and bring the fattened calf and kill it, that we may eat and be merry." Surely some harsh Demea would now have rejoiced at being given an occasion to reproach him, or would at least have feigned greater sternness and received his son only on the harshest conditions, so that he might be more obedient in future. But we hear nothing of that here. Rather, without delay he wants all his servants to be busy in clothing and adorning the son, and he orders him to be so adorned that it might be plain to everyone that he ought from now on to be acknowledged not as a stranger, a rebel or some worthless hireling, but as a son of the household. By this part we are taught that God receives us into his favour in such a way that (as a poet once wrongly twisted the Sibylline verses to apply to his patron Pollio's son) "if any traces of our wickedness remain, they are utterly annulled, and he does not impute them to us." Nay, the house restores and adorns us with its former things, and so restores us to our former dignity. To this pertains that so careful description of his garments and adornment. For first he bids them bring out the first robe, so that he may be clothed in it. By this we rightly understand innocence and true holiness. It is called "first" not only by way of pre-eminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], on account of its excellence, but because God had clothed our first parent with it when he created him in his own image and likeness; and its effect was that, although he was naked in body, he was not ashamed. But Adam lost this robe when, following the counsel of the devil, he ate from the forbidden tree. For then, from innocent and holy, he became a sinner and guilty of treason against majesty, and he saw his nakedness, and convicted by this testimony he sought in vain new coverings and hiding places by which he might conceal himself from the sight of God. But God restored that former robe to those who turn to him in his Son Jesus Christ, who for our sake was made sin, so that through him we might be made his righteousness. Indeed, he has been made for us wisdom, righteousness and sanctification, since we are covered by his obedience and merit, so that our iniquities no longer come into account before God. The same Christ also regenerates us, so that, laying aside the old man, we put on the new, and having mortified the desires of our flesh we live a new life, which corresponds to our profession of the name. Therefore Paul said: "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." And this is the wedding garment, without which no one can enter into fellowship with the Church, and no one can even persevere in it, even if for a time he holds some place in its external assembly. This must be observed on account of those who say that the doctrine of God's free mercy is hostile to good works and paves the way for men to a licence to sin. For the question between us is not whether good works ought to be done, but whether by our works we deserve the forgiveness of sins and salvation. We deny the latter, and indeed on the most weighty grounds, which we have recalled elsewhere; but we teach that the former is entirely necessary, since it cannot fail that those who are grafted into that true vine, Jesus Christ, and share with his Spirit, that is to say his living and life-giving sap, bear fruits worthy of their profession. We know likewise that those who do righteousness are righteous, and that Christ is for us not only the author of free justification, but also that in him we die to the same sin, so that we are raised by his Word and Spirit to newness of life. Finally, since those justified by faith have peace with God, they ought to keep the same purity of conscience, which can in no way consist in a licence to sin.

units.la: Sed ad patrem illum bonum redeamus, qui ut filio annulus quoq; in manum detur, servus mandat. Annulorum usum antiquissimum esse constat ex historia Moysis, apud quem Iudas Thamari annulum pignoris loco dedisse scribitur. Vsus autem eorum duplex fuit. Primo enim virtutis & honoris insigne erat: & ideo apud Romanos antiquitus legatis, qui ad exteras gentes ituri erant, publice dabantur annuli, ut dignitatis esset testimonium: neq; alij ijs utebantur, quam qui illos ex ea causa publice accepissent. Posteris temporibus equestris ordinis insigne annuli factum est, ut bis a plebe distinguerentur. Ideo nulli nisi libero annulum gestare fas erat, neq; plures uno habere licebat, imo plures bis uti viro infame erat, ut ex Gracchi verbis in Maeuium colligitur: Considerate Quirites sinistram eius: en, cuius authoritatem sequimini, qui propter mulierum cupiditatem ut mulier est orna tus. Certe virtutis symbolum fuisse annulos, mos quoq; vetustus docet, quo illi in digito sinistrae manus qui minimo proximus est, gestabantur. Quia enim ex eo nervus tenuissimus ad cor usque extendi creditur, cor ipsum, qui virtutis fons habetur, coronare ad hunc modum videbantur, qui illi annulum inferebant. Deinde fidei & obligationis symbolum annuli fuerus, & ideo a sponso sponsae annulus mittebatur, & simul mos obtinuit, ut illis sigilla quoque insculperentur. Hodie quia luxus omnium mores corrupit, fere non nisi ostentationis causa promiscue ab indignissimis quoq; gestantur, & saepe annulus signatorijs superbiunt, qui vel literas prorsus ignorant, vel quod obsignent nihil habent. Quoad vero huius loci sensum, filio annulum dari iubet pater, ut eum pristinae dignitati restitutum esse ostendat, & gratiam suam illi quasi obsignet. Solet hoc ipsum Deus quoque facere illis, qui a peccatis ad ipsum converterunt. Vt enim eos dignitate filiorum suorum exornat, ita ijsdem Spiritum suum confert, quem υἱοθεσίας sive adoptionis spiritum, & proinde salutis quoq; arrhabonem Apostolus nominat. Et recte idem a nobis annulus dici potest, quia vinculum est, quo nos sibi desponsat Deus, & quo gratiam suam in cordibus nostris obsignat, ut de ea amplius non possimus dubitare. Ideo D. Ambrosius annulum syncerae fidei signaculum esse interpretatur, quod no aliud, quam Spiritum illum dicere possumus, in quo clamamus Abba pater. Ista vero ut ineffabilem Dei bonitatem nobis commendant ita eorum commentum confutant, qui hominem salutis suae certum fieri posse negant & proinde de Dei gratia semper dubitandum esse docent. Ergo si illos audiamus, incerta & fallacia sunt omnia ea, quibus suam gratiam nobis Deus offert, & maior erit conscientia fluctuantis vis, quam Spiritus sancti, quem credentium cordibus Christus insinuat. Atqui huius effectum est, quod cum Paulo nobis exclamare licet: Quis nos separabit a dilectione Dei? num oppressio? num angustia? num persecutio, &c. Vide Rom. 8.
units.tr: But let us return to that good father, who, when the servant is ordered to put a ring on the son's hand as well. It is well established that the use of rings is very ancient, as we learn from the history of Moses, where Judah is written as having given Tamar a ring as a pledge. Their use was twofold. First, the ring was a mark of virtue and honour, and so among the Romans of old rings were given publicly to envoys who were about to go to foreign nations, as a testimony of their dignity; and no one used them except those who had received them publicly for that reason. In later times the ring became the badge of the equestrian order, by which they were distinguished from the common people. For this reason no one but a freeborn man was permitted to wear a ring, nor was it allowed to have more than one; indeed, for a man to use more than one was disgraceful, as is gathered from the words of Gracchus against Maevius: "Consider, Quirites, his left hand: look, you follow the authority of a man who, from desire for women, is adorned like a woman." Certainly the custom of ancient times shows that rings were a symbol of virtue, since they were worn on the finger of the left hand next to the smallest. For a very slender sinew is believed to run from that finger to the heart, and so those who put the ring on it seemed to crown the heart itself, which is held to be the fountain of virtue. Secondly, the ring was a symbol of faith and obligation, and for this reason the bridegroom sent a ring to the bride, and at the same time the custom arose of having seals engraved on them as well. Today, since luxury has corrupted all manners, rings are for the most part worn, merely for show, even by the most unworthy, and often men who are utterly ignorant of letters, or who have nothing to seal, are proud of their signet rings. As for the meaning of this place, the father orders a ring to be given to the son, to show that he has been restored to his former dignity, and as it were to set his seal upon his favour. God is wont to do this very thing for those who have turned from their sins to him. For just as he adorns them with the dignity of his sons, so he bestows on them his Spirit, whom the Apostle calls the Spirit of adoption, and therefore also the pledge of salvation. And rightly the same thing may be called a ring by us, because it is the bond by which God betroths us to himself, and by which he seals his grace in our hearts, so that we can no longer doubt it. For this reason Ambrose rightly interprets the ring as the seal of sincere faith, which we can call nothing other than that Spirit in whom we cry, "Abba, Father." These things commend to us the ineffable goodness of God, and at the same time refute the invention of those who deny that a man can be certain of his salvation, and therefore teach that one must always doubt God's grace. If we listen to them, then all those things by which God offers us his grace are uncertain and deceptive, and the wavering conscience will be stronger than the Holy Spirit, whom Christ instils into the hearts of believers. Yet the effect of this is that we may cry out with Paul: "Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution?" etc. See Rom. 8.

units.la: Postremo calceamenta quoque pedibus filij reducis adduntur, quibus poenitentia verae effectus notantur. Per pedes enim affectus hominis significari constat, & ideo illos Christus quotidie ablu vult ab ijs quoque, quos ipse suo sanguine mundavit. At quia nunquam omnino elui possunt, quo minus locum apud nos habeant, ut diligentius coerceantur opus est, ne nos per errorum & superstitionum auia, aut vitiorum spineta transfuersos abripiant. Id vero per Euangelij praedicationem fit, quae & pedes nostros munit, ne offendamus: & in vijs praeceptorum Dei dirigit, ut intra vocationis nostrae fines ambulemus, & ea studeamus praestare, quae a nobis ille exigit. Et hunc sensum ex Pauli verbis colligimus, qui nos pedibus calceatos & aditer paratos esse iubet praeparatione Euangelij pacis. Itaque calcei isti totum vitae Christianae cursum adumbrant, in quo in primis praelucere debet fidei confessio, quae tunc demum syncera & salutaris erit, si ei mores & dicta factaq; nostra omnia respondeant.
units.tr: Last of all, shoes are also put on the feet of the returned son, by which the effects of true repentance are noted. For it is well known that the feet signify the affections of a man, and therefore Christ wishes them to be washed every day, even of those things which he himself has cleansed by his own blood. But since they can never be entirely washed clean, and there is no reason why they should not still have a place among us, there is need for them to be restrained more carefully, lest they carry us off sideways through the pathless ways of errors and superstitions, or through the thickets of vices. This is done indeed through the preaching of the Gospel, which both protects our feet lest we stumble, and directs us in the paths of God's precepts, so that we walk within the bounds of our calling and strive to perform those things which he requires of us. And we gather this sense from the words of Paul, who bids us to be shod on our feet and ready to go, with the preparation of the Gospel of peace. Therefore these shoes sketch out the whole course of the Christian life, in which the confession of faith ought above all to shine forth; and it will be sincere and saving only if our morals and all our words and deeds correspond to it.

units.la: Est autem locus hic dignissimus, qui non semel modo a nobis diligentius consideretur, sed quem perpetuo meditemur & animo nostro voluamus: Docet enim quibus notis eos dignoscamus, qui vere ad Deum conversi sunt, Gloriantur eo nomine plerique, & ij quoque, qui ab illo adhuc longissime absunt: & nos sæpe nobisipsis surpiter imponimus, vt nos vere iam resipuisse putemus, quando in te-ri adhuc luto hæremus. At quia hoc triplici ornatu filius iste donatur, vbi ad patre reuersus est, satis constat, nondū cum cœlesti Patre eos in gratia redijsse, qui neq; veste illa nuptiali amicti sunt, qua vitæ innocentiam & conscientiæ puritatem denotari diximus, neq; salutis Arrhabonem, Spiri-tu sanctum, intra animos suos receperunt, neq; in sua vocatione pedibus inoffensis ambulant. Habet ergo hic Lydium lapidem omnis generis & loci homines, ad quem vitam atque fidem suam examinent, ne in otiosa meditatione subsistant, & seipsos vanis persuasionibus decipiant.
units.tr: This place, moreover, is most worthy, not to be considered by us more carefully only once, but to be constantly meditated upon and turned over in our minds. For it teaches by what marks we may recognise those who have truly been converted to God. Many boast of that name, and also those who are still very far from him; and we often impose upon ourselves rashly, so that we think we have already truly repented, when we still stick in the mud of the earth. But since this son, when he returned to his father, was given this threefold adornment, it is quite plain that those who have not yet returned into grace with the heavenly Father are those who are not clothed in that wedding garment, by which we have said the innocence of life and purity of conscience are denoted, nor have they received within their souls the pledge of salvation, the Holy Spirit, nor do they walk with unhindered feet in their calling. Here, then, is the touchstone for men of every kind and station, by which they may test their life and faith, so that they do not rest in idle meditation and deceive themselves with vain persuasions.

units.la: At priusquam hinc discedamus, videre præstat, quis ista nobis largiatur, aut qua ratione nobis obtingant. Vbi obseruabis omnem hunc ornatum ex patris domo atq; thesauris depromptum fuisse, hunc autem seruis suis mandauisse, vt illum proferrent atque eo filium induerent. Ergo ni-hil hic nostrum est, sed à Deo nobis confertur pristina innocentia atque dignitas. Huius item donum est Spiritus ille, quo corda nostra obsignantur, & qui salutis nostræ arrhabo est. Idem ille nos munit, confirmat & dirigit, vt secundum Euangelij sui canonem in vocatione nostra ambulemus. In his autem conferendis suorum seruorum opera vtitur, eorum videlicet, qui verbi eius administrisunt, per quod omnia ista ad nos deferuntur. Et hos quoque ille vocat, ad munus suum obeundum excitat, verba sua ipsorum ori inserit, vt ex suis thesauris ea depromere norint, quæ ad nostræ restitutionem necessaria sunt. Ideo hos Christus alibi sub œconomorum persona describit, & eosdem Apostolus mysteriorū Dei dispensatores dicit. Facit hoc administerij Ecclesiastici commendatio-nem, & nos admonet, vt ordini huic, quem Deus instituit nos accommodemus. Nam qui eo contem-pto sua figmenta sequuntur, ij cum illo nunquam in gratiam redibunt.
units.tr: But before we depart from here, it is worth seeing who bestows these things upon us, or by what means they come to us. Here you will observe that all this adornment was brought out from the father's house and treasuries, and that he ordered his servants to bring it forth and clothe the son with it. Therefore nothing here is ours, but our former innocence and dignity are conferred on us by God. Also the gift of that Spirit by which our hearts are sealed, and who is the pledge of our salvation, is his. He himself protects, strengthens and directs us, so that we walk in our calling according to the rule of his Gospel. In conferring these things he uses the work of his servants, namely of those who serve his Word, through whom all these things are brought to us. He also calls these men, stirs them up to discharge their office, puts his words into their mouths, so that they know how to bring forth from his treasures those things which are necessary for our restoration. Therefore Christ elsewhere describes these men under the persona of stewards, and the Apostle calls the same men dispensers of the mysteries of God. This commends the ecclesiastical ministry, and admonishes us to accommodate ourselves to this order which God has instituted. For those who, despising it, follow their own fictions will never return into favour with him.

units.la: Porrò non fatus est patri illi indulgentissimo filium vestitu digno ornauisse, sed aliud quoque seruis mandat. Adducîtum (inquit) vitulum illum saginatum mactate, vt vescentes oblectemur. Ergo epulum quoque instituit, cui Musicum concentū & choros adhibitos fuisse, postea audiemus. Adumbratur conuiuio isto felicitas vera & lætitia perpetua, qua qui verè conuersi sunt, tam in hac vita quàm futura fruuntur. Nam non potest illis non iucundissima esse bonitatis & gratiæ diuinæ recordatio: & ideo quasi continuum epulum agentes in Deo semper exultant, & poculo salutis cum Dauide sumpto in perpetua beneficiorū eius commemoratione gaudent. Neq; cum vita hac mortali gaudiū istud finitur, sed vbi ex corporis huius ergastulo liberati sunt, ad beatæ immortalitatis se-des colliguntur, vt in cœlis cū Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo ad filij Dei mensa accumbant, vbi cum Angelis sanctis & omnibus electis gaudio æterno exultabunt. Interim hic vituli saginati mentio fit, vt salutis & felicitatis huius vera ratio adumbretur. Hic enim Christus est, qui pro peccatis nostris hostia factus gaudium illud nobis meruit. Nam eius morte redempti sumus, eiusdem verò vi-ta nobis iustitiam sempiternam vnà cū pristina dignitate atq; vita cœlesti restituit. Saginatus ve-rò dicitur, non solum quod dilectus ille Dei filius & delicatissimus æternæ vitæ cibus est, verum-etiam quod eum Pater æterno suo decreto prædestinauit, priusquam mundi huius fundamenta iace-rentur, vt noster redemptor fieret. In hoc igitur salus omnis habetur, & idem ille cum sponsus noster sit, simul nobis in seipso conuiuium illud nuptiale exhibet, à quo luctus & dolor omnis excluditur, ani-mi autem gaudio cœlesti & nunquam morituro recreantur.
units.tr: Moreover, the father, being very indulgent, was not content to have adorned his son with worthy clothing, but also orders his servants to do something else. "Bring," he says, "that fattened calf and kill it, so that we may eat and be merry." Therefore he also arranged a feast, to which, as we shall hear later, music and choirs were added. By this banquet is shadowed forth true happiness and perpetual joy, which those who are truly converted enjoy both in this life and in the future. For the remembrance of God's goodness and grace cannot fail to be most pleasant to them; and therefore, as if continually feasting, they always exult in God, and with David, having taken up the cup of salvation, they rejoice in the perpetual remembrance of his benefits. Nor is that joy ended with this mortal life; but when they are freed from the prison-house of this body, they are gathered into the abodes of blessed immortality, so that in heaven, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, they sit down at the table of the Son of God, where with the holy angels and all the elect they will exult in eternal joy. Meanwhile mention is made here of the fattened calf, so that the true ground of this salvation and happiness may be shadowed forth. For it is Christ who, made a sacrifice for our sins, merited that joy for us. For we have been redeemed by his death, and by his life he has restored to us everlasting righteousness, together with our former dignity and heavenly life. He is called "fattened," not only because that beloved Son of God is also the most delicate food of eternal life, but also because the Father, by his eternal decree, predestined him, before the foundations of this world were laid, to become our redeemer. In him, therefore, all salvation is found; and since he is our bridegroom, he at the same time shows us in himself that nuptial feast, from which all mourning and sorrow are shut out, and our souls are refreshed with heavenly joy that will never die.

units.la: Cæterum ne quid temere aut leuiter factum putetur, causam sui instituti pater subijcit: Quia filius iste meus mortuus erat, & reuixit: perierat, & inuentus est. Faciunt ista ad expositio-nem parabolarum de one perdita & amissa drachma: quibus docuit, quàm gaudeat Deus eorum cō-uersione, qui in erroribus & vitiis iam toti periisse videbantur: imò iam perierant, nisi gratuita illius misericordia ad Ecclesiæ gremium rursus colligerentur. Et dum simul omnes domesticos læ-tari cœpisse dicit cum patre illo tam benigno, iterum Pharisæos perstringit, qui suæ iustitiæ & digni-tatis fiducia ebrij, salutem peccatoribus inuidebant, & ex eo dolorem concipiebant, quo Deus & Angeli omnesque germani filij Dei delectantur. At simul paucis hisce verbis Christus peccati & veræ pœnitentiæ effectā comprehendit. Peccatum occidit & perdit: Pœnitentia autem reditus in vitam est, & per eandem quasi inuenimur rursus à Deo, qui prius amissi & procul ab illo vagi aberrabamus. Adhæc discrimē indicatur inter electos et reprobos, Peccati vtriq;, & tam bi quàm illi
units.tr: Moreover, lest anything be thought to have been done rashly or lightly, the father sets out the reason for his action: "Because this son of mine was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found." These words bear on the explanation of the parables of the lost sheep and the lost drachma, by which he taught how greatly God rejoices at the conversion of those who seemed to have utterly perished in their errors and vices; indeed they had already perished, unless by his free mercy they were gathered back again into the bosom of the Church. And in saying that all the household began to rejoice together with that so kindly father, he again rebukes the Pharisees, who, drunk with confidence in their own righteousness and dignity, begrudged salvation to sinners and conceived grief at that which gladdens God, the angels and all the true sons of God. At the same time, in these few words Christ sums up the effect of sin and of true repentance. Sin kills and destroys; repentance, however, is a return to life, and through it we are, as it were, found again by God, we who before were lost and wandering far from him. Furthermore, a distinction is indicated between the elect and the reprobate, as to the sin of each, and of both these and those.

units.la: Cap. XV.
units.tr: Chapter XV.

units.la: pro mortuis & perditis haberi debent, si ex conditione hominum communi iudicium fiat. At illi rediuiui ex peccatu resurgunt, & ad Deum conuersi feruantur, hi vero in morte perpetuo manent, & nec volunt quidem inueniri, cum sceleribus & proprio interitu gaudeant. Reprobi enim truncis eradicatis & aridis similes sunt, ex quibus fructus frustra fructū sperēt. Electi vero semen Dei in se habent, & arborum instar sunt, quae etsi byberno tempore intermoriantur, nouo tamen vere ineunte iucco vitali vegetantur, & quasi reuiuiscentes parturiunt, & nouos fructus generant.
units.tr: they ought to be regarded as dead and lost, if judgment is made by the common condition of men. But the others, having risen again from sin, are turned to God and saved; these, however, remain constantly in death, and do not even wish to be found, since they rejoice in their crimes and their own destruction. For the reprobate are like trunks cut down and dried up, from which one vainly hopes for fruit. The elect, however, have the seed of God in themselves, and are like trees which, though they die back in winter, are nevertheless quickened by the living sap when the new spring begins, and, as if coming back to life, they bear new fruits and produce them.

units.la: Minimè ergo doctrina haec de gratuita reconciliatione cum Deo ijs patrocinatur, qui illa ad tarnis suae licentiā abutuntur. Finis enim tam poenitentiae quàm reconciliationis nostrae est, ut qui prius in peccatis mortui fuimus, vitam nouam viuamus, & fructus feramus nostra professione dignos. Intellexit hoc olim Dauid, qui cum omnem spem salutis in gratuita Dei misericordia collocatam haberet, sic tamen orabat: Cor mundum crea in me Deus, & Spiritum rectum innoua in visceribus meis. Ne proijcias me à facie tua & Spiritum tuum sanctum ne auferas à me. Redde mihi laetitiam salutaris tui, & spiritu spontaneo confirma me. Qua precatione totum reconciliationis nostrae mysterium & eius effecta breuiter explicat. Primum inter haec est cordis mundities, quam deleto in nobis peccato sequi necesse est. Secundo loco spiritus rectus aut firmus nominatur, qui salutū certos facit, ne de Dei gratia dubitemus. Sequitur mox spiritus sanctificationis, qui nos gubernat, ut & Deum innocemus, & vitam omnem sanctè instituamus. His subijcit laetitiam salutaris Dei & spiritum spontaneum. Qui enim priora illa se accepisse sentiunt, hi in salute per Deum exhibita laetantur, & voluntario spiritus motu se totos illius voluntati subijciunt per fidem, obedientiam. Sit ergo haec nobis quoq; precum nostrarum regula, & fide firma amplectamur gratiae huius media torem, qui est aeternum Dei Filius Iesus Christus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This doctrine of free reconciliation with God, therefore, by no means gives any support to those who abuse it as a licence for their own flesh. For the end both of our repentance and of our reconciliation is that we who were formerly dead in sins should live a new life and bear fruits worthy of our profession. David understood this long ago: although he had placed all his hope of salvation in the free mercy of God, he nevertheless prayed thus: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my bowels. Cast me not away from your face, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a willing spirit." In this prayer he briefly sets out the whole mystery of our reconciliation and its effects. First among these is purity of heart, which must follow once sin has been blotted out in us. In the second place a right or steadfast spirit is named, which makes our salvation certain, so that we do not doubt the grace of God. Next comes at once the spirit of sanctification, which governs us, so that we both call upon God and order our whole life holily. To these he adds the joy of God's salvation and a willing spirit. For those who feel that they have received the former gifts rejoice in the salvation offered by God, and by a voluntary movement of the spirit they submit themselves wholly to his will, through faith and obedience. Let this, then, be for us also the rule of our prayers, and let us firmly embrace with faith the mediator of this grace, who is the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 153.

units.la: Erat autem filius eius senior in agro, qui ut veniens appropinquauit domui, audiuit concentum & choros: & cum vnum ex pueris vocasset, percontatus est, quid istud esset. Is vero dixit ei: Frater tuus venit, & mactauit pater tuus vitulum illum saginatum, quod valentem illum receperit. Indignatus est autem ille, nec voluit introire. Pater ergo eius egressus hortatus est cum. Ipse vero respondens dixit patri: Ecce tot annos seruio tibi, nec vnquam mandatum tuum sum transgressus: nec vnquam dedisti mihi haedum, ut cum amicis meis oblectarer. Sed cum filius iste tuus, qui deuorauit facultates tuas cum meretricibus, venit, mactasti ei vitulum illum saginatum. Ipse vero dixit ei: Fili, tu semper mecum es, & omnia mea tua sunt: Oblectari autem & gaudere te oportebat, quod frater tuus hic mortuus erat & reuixit: perieratq; & inuentus est.
units.tr: Now his elder son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And calling one of the servants, he asked what these things meant. And he said to him: Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fatted calf, because he has received him back safe and sound. But he was angry and would not go in. So his father came out and begged him. But he answered and said to his father: Look, for so many years I have served you, and never have I transgressed your command; and you never gave me a young goat, that I might make merry with my friends. But when this son of yours, who has devoured your property with harlots, came, you killed the fatted calf for him. But he said to him: Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting that we should make merry and rejoice, because this your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.

units.la: Nihil quidem homini tam necessarium est, quàm gratuita Dei misericordia, per quam in nobis in Christo Iesu peccata nostra remittit, & nobis vitam aeternam largitur: ea est autem humani ingenij prauitas, ut illam sibi liberaliter oblatam pauci digne excipiant. Sunt enim nonnulli qui cum omni pietatu sensu extinctio in omne scelus praecipiti licentia ruant, iampridem sibi persuaserunt, Deum qui mortalia curet nullum esse, & proinde nos illius gratia nequaquam opus habere. His iam opponit se hypocritarum turba, qui suorum operum merito & propria iustitia tofisi, haec ita ostentant, ut gratia praedicationem, quasi superuacaneam & nihil ad se pertinentem facile negligant. Et horum quidem tanta est improbitas, ut tanquam canes in praesepi alijs quoque inuidendo benignitatem Dei, quaipsi frui dedignantur. Verisq; Domin u hac parabola medetur. Nam prioribus illis perspicuè offendit quae sit peccati conditio, & quòd Deus disciplinae contemptum atque violationem non dimittat impunè abire. Ne quis tamen ex eo in desperationem delabatur, immensam Dei bonitatem depingit, qua ad se conuersos indulgentia plus quàm paterna excipit. His nunc vltima pars parabolæ subtexitur, qua eorum confidentiam atque morositatem reprehendit, qui suæ iustitiæ fiducia turgidi, indignè ferunt peccatoribus peccata sua remitti, & gratiæ Dei exempla malignis atque inuidis oculis intuentur. Typum istorum facit fratrem prodigi illius maiorem natu, per quem aliqui Iudæorum populum adumbrari arbitrantur. Quorum sententia tolerabilis quidem est, si quis hos cum gentibus conferat. Sed si quis totum huius capitis contextum diligentius consideret, videbit Christum generaliorem doctrinam proponere. Nam scribas atque pharisæos cum publicanis & peccatoribus manifestus confert, qui simul omnes viring, ex Iudæis erant. Vt ergo prodigus ille omnium personam sustinet, qui palam disciplina Dei iugum excutiunt, & nefaria licentia illius dona turpiter prophanant: ita alter iste, de quo nunc agetur, omnium hypocritarum ingenium atque mores exprimit, qui se solos dignos esse putant, vt pro Dei filijs & Regni eius haeredibus habeantur. Quia verò tales non in sola Iudæorum gente Pharisæi atque Scribæ fuerunt, sed hodie etiam passim inueniuntur, & ijdem Euangelij doctrinæ insolenter nimis obstrepunt, proderit quæ de isto dicuntur diligentius inspicere, vt de illorum moribus ex ipsius Christi verbis discamus iudicare.
units.tr: Nothing is so necessary to man as God's free mercy, by which he forgives our sins in Christ Jesus and grants us eternal life. Yet such is the perversity of the human mind that few worthily receive this when it is offered freely. For there are some who, with all sense of piety extinguished, rush headlong into every crime with unbridled licence, and have long since persuaded themselves that there is no God who cares for mortal things, and that therefore we have no need at all of his grace. Against these there now stands the crowd of hypocrites, who, puffed up with the merit of their own works and their own righteousness, make these so conspicuous that they easily neglect the preaching of grace as superfluous and having nothing to do with them. And of these men such is the wickedness that, like dogs in a manger, they grudge others the kindness of God, which they themselves disdain to enjoy. The Lord heals this with this parable. For the earlier part clearly strikes at what the condition of sin is, and shows that God does not allow the contempt and violation of his discipline to go unpunished. Lest anyone, however, fall into despair from this, he depicts God's immense goodness, by which he receives those who turn to him with more than fatherly indulgence. To these the last part of the parable is now added, in which he rebukes the confidence and surliness of those who, swollen with trust in their own righteousness, take it ill that sins are forgiven to sinners, and look upon the examples of God's grace with malicious and envious eyes. He makes the elder brother of that prodigal the type of these men, and some think that by him the Jewish people is foreshadowed. Their view is tolerable indeed, if someone compares these men with the Gentiles. But if someone considers the whole context of this chapter more carefully, he will see that Christ sets forth a more general teaching. For he plainly compares the scribes and Pharisees with the publicans and sinners, who were all alike Jews. So just as that prodigal bears the person of all those who openly shake off the yoke of God's discipline and shamefully abuse his gifts with wicked licence, so this other man, of whom we shall now speak, expresses the nature and manners of all hypocrites, who think that they alone are worthy to be regarded as sons of God and heirs of his kingdom. But since such Pharisees and scribes were not only in the Jewish nation, but are found everywhere even today, and insolently clamour against the doctrine of the Gospel, it will be useful to examine more carefully what is said of this man, so that from Christ's own words we may learn to judge their morals.

units.la: Erat (inquit) filius eius senior in agro, qui vt veniens appropinquauit domui, audiuit concentum & choros, &c. Primum vbi fuerit filius iste indicatur, & vnde aduenerit. In agro autem fuit: qua locutione eorum studia Christus exprimit, qui salutem proprijs suorum operum meritis obtinere satagunt. Laborant hi in agro, terrenis nimirum operibus occupati, cum ignorent ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Quia enim nesciunt vniuersa humani generis salute ex æterno Dei decreto pendere, qui nostri miserctus Filium suum nobis Seruatorem vnicum prædestinauit ex semetipsis cultum instituunt, quibus illum placari & Regnum eius obtineri posse sibi persuadent. Itaq; alij quidem castitatem vouent, quam coelibatu definiunt, & eo ipso coniugium impuritatis accusant. Alij vitæ solitariæ genus sequuntur, & in locis ab hominum consuetudine remotioribus degunt, vt mundum reliquisse videantur. Alij vitam monasticam in cænobijs agunt, & ab aliis vestitu quoq; distingui volunt, quasi ad salutem aliquid faciat. Sunt qui iejunijs & ferijs vacant, & in otio ignavo vel ciborum discrimine superstitioso Dei cultum consistere sibi persuadent. Sunt qui toti ex simulachrorum cultu pendent, neq; illus quæ domi habent contenti per terras & maria vagantur, & inani labore seipsos conficiunt, vt peregrinis idolis nuncupata vota persoluant. Inueniuntur etiam, qui suis viribus diffisi, alios mercede conducunt, qui pro ipsis preces demurmurent, cantent, Missas celebrent, & alia infinita faciant, quæ nulla diuini verbi authoritate nituntur. Taceo nunc cilicia, chameunias, aliarum extructiones, monasteriorum fundationes, donationes, indulgentiarum contractus, fraternitates, exequias & sacra pro defunctis, cum sexcentis alijs, quæ homines superstitiosi excogitauerunt. Atqui omnia ista in exercitatione corporali consistunt, quam Paulus paululum vtilitatis habere scribit, & cum terrena opera sint, quæ humanis viribus confici possunt, vt ijs coelum quis mereatur impossibile est. Nemo enim ascendit in coelum, sua virtute, nisi qui è coelo descendit, Iesus Christus, qui ex verbi sui semine renatos nouos viribus instruit, vt & ipsi per fidem coheuebantur, & in ipso bonorum coelestium participes fiant. Et cum ex operibus Legis nemo iustificari queat, stultum fuerit aliquod salutis meritum in illis collocare, quæ secundum humanas traditiones fiunt, quas Dei sententia iam pridem damnatas esse constat.
units.tr: "He was," he says, "his elder son in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing," and so on. First, the place where this son was is indicated, and where he had come from. He was in the field, and by this expression Christ describes those who strive to obtain salvation by the merits of their own works. They toil in the field, of course, busy with earthly works, since they do not know the things of the Spirit of God. For, not knowing that the salvation of the whole human race depends on the eternal decree of God, who in his mercy predestined his Son to be our only Saviour, they set up a worship of their own devising, by which they persuade themselves that he can be appeased and his kingdom obtained. So some vow chastity, which they define as celibacy, and by that very act accuse marriage of impurity. Others follow a solitary way of life, and dwell in places remote from human society, as if they had left the world. Others live a monastic life in cloisters, and wish to be distinguished from others even by their dress, as if this made any difference to salvation. There are those who devote themselves to fasts and feast days, and persuade themselves that the worship of God consists in idle inactivity or in superstitious distinctions of food. There are those who depend wholly on the worship of images, and, not content with what they have at home, wander over lands and seas, and wear themselves out with empty labour, so that they may pay the vows they have made to foreign idols. There are also those who, distrustful of their own strength, hire others for money, who mumble prayers on their behalf, chant, celebrate Masses, and do countless other things which rest on no authority of the divine Word. I say nothing now of hair shirts, of chamaeunias, of the building of other things, the foundation of monasteries, donations, the contracts for indulgences, fraternities, funeral rites and masses for the dead, and six hundred other things which superstitious men have devised. Yet all these things consist in bodily exercise, which Paul writes is of little profit, and since they are earthly works which can be accomplished by human strength, it is impossible for anyone to merit heaven by them. For no one ascends into heaven by his own virtue, except him who came down from heaven, Jesus Christ, who from the seed of his word strengthens the reborn as new men with power, so that they too may be joined to him through faith and become sharers in the heavenly goods in him. And since no one can be justified by the works of the Law, it would be foolish to place any merit of salvation in those things which are done according to human traditions, which, as is well known, have long since been condemned by the sentence of God.

units.la: Deinde audit iste concentum Musicorum & choros in aedibus paternis. Vbi nemo laesciuas & petulantes saltationes animo concipere debet, quæ hodie chorearum & chororum nomine palliantur. Longè alia enim fuit horum ratio apud veteres. Chori enim non ex maribus & puellis simul conflabant, sed secundum sexum distinguebantur. Præcipuum in illis erat carminum concentus, ad quorum rhythmos gressum quoque moderabantur. Carminum verò argumentum cum re præsenti conueniebat, vt in Tragœdijs est videre. Itaque pro illorum tempore consuetudine Christus loquitur, & per concentum illum atque choros laetitiam credentium adumbrat, quæ ex diuinæ bonitatis consideratione nascitur, & in quam pij effunduntur si quæ illius exempla singularia videant in illis, quorum salus iam omnino desperata esse videbatur. Et sanè iucundissimus est chori illius Ecclesiastici concentus. In illo enim ipse Dei spiritus, quasi choragus aut chorodidascalus gratuitæ misericordiæ prædicatione præire solet, quâ ille nobis in Filio suo vnigenito exhibet. Respondent illi credentes cum gratiarum actione, & vicissim ipsi quoque bonitatis illius laudes decantant. Hinc conscientiæ gaudium & tripudium oritur, in quo simul omnes totus animis exultant, adeò vt quamus gaudiū illud Satan persecutionibus & afflictionibus omnis generis turbare conetur, nihil tamen proficiat. Qui enim ex fide iustificati pacem habent cum Deo, in aduersis quoque gaudent, imò afflictionibus gloriantur, vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit. Et ista quidem palàm fiunt in ecclesia, vt hypocritæ etiā & hostes gratiæ Dei ea audiant & videat.
