Sic in conspectu Pharisæorum Matthæus & Zachæus cū suis exultarunt, & huius capitis initio illis videntibus publicanos & peccatores ad Christum confluxisse audiuimus, vt eius doctrinam audirent, quæ istius lætitiæ causam atq; materiam exhibet. Nec enim dissimulare possunt pij gratuitæ misericordiæ Dei beneficium, & in eo etiam huius bonitas elucet, qui nouis quotidie exemplis hostes quoque inuitat, vt quam alij iam sentiunt, gratiam ipsi quoque ampliettantur. Quod si ea vel tunc quoque contempserint, vel inde arripuerint aduersus illum murmurandi occasionem, eo ipso confidentiam nulla venia dignam ostendunt.
units.tr: Next, this man hears the concert of musicians and dancing in his father's house. Here no one should conceive in his mind the wanton and impudent dances which today are covered under the name of choral dances and choirs. For the practice of these was quite different among the ancients. For choirs were not formed of men and girls together, but were separated according to sex. The chief feature of them was the singing of songs, to whose rhythms they also regulated their steps. Moreover, the subject of the songs agreed with the present matter, as can be seen in the tragedies. So Christ speaks in accordance with the custom of his time, and by that concert and those choirs he shadows forth the joy of believers, which arises from the consideration of divine goodness, and into which the godly pour themselves out when they see in those whose salvation seemed utterly hopeless some singular examples of it. And indeed that choir of the Church has a most pleasant concert. In it the Spirit of God himself, like a choir-leader or choir-trainer, is accustomed to go before with the preaching of free mercy, which he offers us in his only-begotten Son. The believers answer him with thanksgiving, and in turn they also sing the praises of that goodness. Hence arises the joy and exultation of conscience, in which all together rejoice with their whole minds, so that although Satan tries to disturb that joy with persecutions and afflictions of every kind, he achieves nothing. For those who are justified by faith have peace with God, and they rejoice even in adversities, indeed they glory in afflictions, as Paul writes to the Romans. And these things are indeed made public in the Church, so that hypocrites and enemies of God's grace also hear and see them. Thus in the sight of the Pharisees Matthew and Zacchaeus rejoiced with their friends; and at the beginning of this chapter we have heard that publicans and sinners flocked to Christ while the Pharisees looked on, so that they might hear his teaching, which provides the cause and matter of that joy. For the godly cannot hide the benefit of God's free mercy, and in it also his goodness shines forth, which day by day invites even enemies with new examples, so that they too may embrace the grace which others already feel. But if they despise it even then, or seize from it an occasion for murmuring against him, they thereby show a confidence that deserves no pardon.

units.la: Id verò plerisque accidit, quod suæ iustitiæ fiducia inebriauit, quod fratris huius seniorum exemplo Christus docet. Audit is concentum & alia lætitiæ insolitæ indicia in paternis ædibus, quæ ipsum excitare debebant, vt rectà ingrediens se gaudij communis socium adiungeret. Sed homo tetricus prius causam huius rei cognoscere vult, quasi verò pater aliquid præter rationem domi suæ fieri pateretur. Illa autem cognita, mox indignatur, neque vult ingredi. Quid verò eum mouerit, paulò post ex eius ad patrem verbis intelligemus. Ista autem exemplo arrogans hypocritarum animus exprimitur, qui in Dei opera atque iudicia confidentissime inquirunt, & quasi illo sanctiores atque honestiores sint, nihil minus ferre possunt, quam si illum gratiam suam peccatoribus communicare, & cum his familiarius agere videant. Exempla huius generis in Iudæorum Pharisæis Euangeliæ multa proponunt, & hodie infinita extant, ex quibus temerariam eiusmodi hominum confidentiam possumus agnoscere. Nam in exempla gratuitæ misericordiæ curiosius inquirere, & ea ad suæ rationis calculum reuocare solent. Vbi mox occurrit, iniquum & absurdum esse, vt inæqua libris æqualia dentur præmia, id est, vt regni cœlorum hæredes cum iustitiæ & honestatis publicæ studiosis fiant ij, qui prius vitijs multis polluti & infames vixerunt. Et quia neque latentem sub sanctitatis specie humani ingenij prauitatem, neque Dei misericordiam rectè agnoscunt, ista considerazione abrepti huius prædicationem re præhendere, & Deum ipsum (vt postea sequetur jaccusa re non verentur. Deniq; eò tandem deueniunt, quod neq; cum ecclesijs illis communicare volunt, quæ peccatores recipiunt, neque etiam cœlum illud ingredi, in quo peccatoribus locum esse videntur: imò etiam hanc salutis rationem detestantur, quæ sceleratis & flagitiosis hominibus aditum facit ad thronum gratiæ, vt ij quoq; vitæ & gaudij æterni hæredes fiant. In isto hominum genere, neftro seculo facile primatum habent Anabaptistæ, qui dum à nobis secessioni faciunt, & scismatis autho res sunt, hoc potissimum argumento sese excusant, quod nos ecclesias pollutas habere aiunt, in quibus homines vitijsediti & flagitijs infames admittantur, vt euangelium aut gratiæ Dei prædicatio nem audiant, & huius sigillus, id est, Sacramentus communicent. Quasi verò in nostra potestate sit, gratiam Dei angustioribus finibus includere, aut eorū conscientias altius scrutari, qui peccata sua confitentur, & pœnitentiæ doctrinam admittunt. Stulti revera homines, qui nulla necessitate adacti iudicij de aliorū conscientijs sibi vendicant, in quo omnes eos periculose errare oportet, qui cordium arcana nō possunt inspicere. Atqui hoc solius Dei opus esse notius est, quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Ignorantia verò suam simul egregiè produnt, dum ex aliorum peccatis pollutionem metuunt, si cœtus sacros ingrediantur, in quibus non scelerum, sed sacrorum communionem haberi cōstat. Ca terum dum suæ innocentiæ & sanctitati quam maximè consulitum volunt, canes referunt. Vt enim bi inuidia præ aliis animalibus laborant: ita incomparabilis sit oportet iistorum inuidia, quæ eos adeo fascinat & dementat, vt seipsos potius à Dei domo excludere malint, quàm cum alijs diuina bonitatis beneficia percipere, quos suæ consuetudine semel indignos esse sibi persuaserunt. units.tr: Now this happens to most people, and it is what the confidence in their own righteousness has made drunk, as Christ teaches through the example of this elder brother. He hears music and other unusual signs of rejoicing in his father's house, which ought to have roused him to go straight in and join the common joy. But the surly man first wants to learn the reason for it, as though his father would allow anything in his own house to happen without good reason. When he has learned it, he at once becomes indignant and refuses to go in. What moved him we shall understand shortly from his words to his father. This example expresses the arrogant mind of hypocrites, who inquire most boldly into the works and judgments of God, and, as if they were holier and more honourable than that man, can least of all bear to see God share his grace with sinners and deal more familiarly with them. The Gospels set before us many examples of this kind among the Pharisees of the Jews, and today there are endless ones, from which we can recognise the rash confidence of such men. For they are accustomed to inquire too curiously into the examples of free mercy and to bring them back to the reckoning of their own reason. There they immediately come upon the thought that it is unjust and absurd that equal rewards should be given for unequal deserts, that is, that those who have lived earlier, polluted by many vices and infamous, should become heirs of the kingdom of heaven together with those who have zealously pursued justice and public honesty. And because they recognise neither the wickedness of the human mind lurking beneath the appearance of holiness, nor the mercy of God rightly, carried away by this consideration they do not hesitate to find fault with this preaching, and even with God himself (as will follow afterwards). At last they come to the point where they are unwilling to communicate with those churches which receive sinners, and do not even wish to enter that heaven in which sinners seem to have a place. Indeed they even detest this way of salvation, which opens access to the throne of grace for wicked and shameful men, so that these too may become heirs of life and eternal joy. In this kind of men, in our age the Anabaptists easily hold the first place. While they secede from us and are the authors of the schism, they excuse themselves chiefly on this ground: that they say we have polluted churches, in which men stained with vices and infamous for their crimes are admitted to hear the gospel or the preaching of the grace of God, and to partake of its seal, that is, the sacrament. As if it were in our power to confine the grace of God within narrower limits, or to search more deeply the consciences of those who confess their sins and accept the doctrine of repentance! Truly foolish men, who, though under no necessity, claim for themselves a judgment on the consciences of others, a judgment in which all must err dangerously who cannot see into the secrets of hearts. Yet that this is the work of God alone is too well known to need demonstration. By their ignorance they also reveal their own folly very plainly, when they fear pollution from the sins of others if they enter assemblies of the sacred, in which it is plain that what is shared is not wickedness but holy things. Meanwhile, while they wish to look most carefully to their own innocence and holiness, they bark like dogs. For just as dogs suffer from envy more than other animals, so the envy of these men must be incomparable, which so bewitches and maddens them that they prefer to shut themselves out of God's house rather than receive the benefits of divine goodness along with others whom they have once persuaded themselves are unworthy of their company. And as

units.la: { } Hypocritæ exemplū gratiæ offenduntur.
units.tr: Hypocrites are offended by the example of grace.

units.la: { } Anabaptistæ. canes fere campanarum sonitum, tubarum clangorem & concentum plurium cantorum ferre non possunt, sed tristi & molesto vlulatu illis obstrepunt: ita isti homines gratuitae misericordiae diuulgatione, coelestis tubae omnes homines ad Dei regnum vocantis laetissimo clangore & dulcissimo Prophetarum, Apostolorum & credentium omnium concentu offenduntur, qui vno ore & corde bonitatem Dei praedicant, & ad huius laudes nouis quotidie exemplis excitantur. Quae autem ingenij peruersitas est, ex eo dolorem & inuidiae occasionem arripere, unde consolationis argumenta peti debebant?
units.tr: Anabaptists. Dogs cannot bear the sound of church bells, the blare of trumpets and the harmony of many singers, but howl at them in a sad and disagreeable way; so these men are offended by the proclamation of free mercy, the most joyful blast of the heavenly trumpet calling all men to the kingdom of God, and by the most sweet harmony of all the Prophets, Apostles and believers, who with one mouth and heart proclaim the goodness of God and are roused every day by new examples to praise it. What perversity of mind is it to seize upon grief and an occasion for envy from the very thing from which the grounds of consolation ought to be sought?

units.la: Sed relictis luiudis isti gratiae Dei oseoribus, ad huius bonitatem considerandam redeamus, quam nouo argumento nobis Christus commendat. Nam patrem ad filium ingredi nolentem foras exiuisse, & illum hortatum fuisse dicit, ut & ipse ingressus cum aliis gauderet. Ipsius vero admirabilem Dei manstuetudinem exprimit, qua malignos suae gratiae aestimatores prosequitur, qui odio potius & contemptu digni erant. Poterat equidem pater iste optimo iure cum filio superbo & confidenti expostulare, qui morositate sua gaudium totius familiae iustum & honestum, turbabat: sed precibus cum illo agere digiatur. Ita non semel Deum fecisse legimus. Huc enim pertinent paternae illae admonitiones & adhortationes non minus blandae quam graues, quibus per Prophetas apud veterem Iudaeorum gentem olim usus est. Quid vero de Filio Dei, Iesu Christo dicemus, qui gratiam Patris sui non modo in genere praedicauit, verumetiam multa priuatim cum Pharisaeis egit, qui illam confidenter nimis explodebant? Ita sane hac causa illi cordi fuit, ut ne a lachrymis quidem sibi temperauerit, quibus infelicem Hierosolymitanae urbis sortem deflevit, in qua illud hominum genus dominabatur. Facit hoc ipsum hodie etiam, quando assidua verbi sui praedicatione eos ad se vocat, quos suorum operum fiducia in erroribus & superstitionibus detineri videt. Sed & ex illorum grege multos quotidie illuminat & trahit, ut eorum exemplo alij moueantur. Est hac diuinae bonitatis consideratio plena dulcissima consolationis: Qui enim hostes & iniquissimos suae gratiae censores tanta benignitate inuitat, num eos negligere aut odisse poterit, qui totis animis ad illam anhelant?
units.tr: But leaving aside these enemies of the grace of God, let us return to considering its goodness, which Christ commends to us with a new illustration. For he says that the father went out to the son who was unwilling to enter, and urged him to come in and rejoice with the others. He expresses the admirable gentleness of God, with which he treats those who wickedly undervalue his grace, men who deserved hatred and contempt rather. Indeed that father could with perfect right have remonstrated with his proud and presumptuous son, who by his peevishness was disturbing the just and honourable joy of the whole household; but he deigns to deal with him by entreaty. So we read that God has done this more than once. To this belong those fatherly admonitions and exhortations, no less gentle than weighty, with which he once dealt through the Prophets with the ancient Jewish nation. But what shall we say of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who not only preached his Father's grace in general, but also dealt privately with many Pharisees, who too confidently rejected it? So truly was this matter dear to his heart that he did not even restrain himself from tears, with which he lamented the unhappy fate of the city of Jerusalem, in which that kind of men held sway. He does the same today also, when by the constant preaching of his word he calls to himself those whom he sees held in errors and superstitions by their confidence in their works. And from their flock he also enlightens and draws many every day, so that others may be moved by their example. This consideration of divine goodness is full of the sweetest consolation: for he who invites with such kindness enemies and the most unjust censors of his grace, will he be able to neglect or hate those who long for it with their whole souls?

units.la: Porro fili maioris responsum audiamus, quem ita patri loquentem Christus inducit: Ecce tot annos seruio tibi, nec vnquam mandatum tuum sum transgressus: nec vnquam dedisti mihi haedum, ut cum amicis meis oblectarer: Sed cum filius iste tuus, qui deuorauit facultates tuas cum meretricibus, venit, mactasti ei vitulum illum saginatum. Depingitur hic nobis intolerabilis hypocritarum superbia, qui ne rogari quidem a Deo adduci possunt, ut eius bonitatem agnoscant, & hanc fratribus inuidere desinant. Sed praestat singula illius verba propius inspicere. Primo suas virtutes iactat, & quod ex officio fecit perinde narrat, ac si beneficium gratuitum in patrem contulisset. Deinde patrem ingratitudinis & iniustitiae accusat, ut qui ne haedum quidem vnquam ipsi dederit, ut cum amicis oblectari posset. Atqui plura alia dederat pater, qui ipsum genuerat, educauerat, fauore summo erat prosecutus, & per quem ipsi quotidie licebat cum amicis paternis versari quibus haud dubie gratus & in honore fuit. Neque eo contentus, fratris vitam & mores corruptos contumeliose proscindit, & illum patri rursus inuisum vel exosum facere conatur. Et quod turpius est, patrem nequitiae fautorem & patronum facit, quasi vitulum saginatum ideo in eius gratiam mactarit, quod sua omnia turpiter prodegisset. Itaq; cum odio fratris impietatem quoq; in patrem optime de se meritum coniungit. Et cum fratrem accusat, qui patris bona cum meretricibus abligurierit, ipse sibi in totam domum & ipsum patrem ius sumit atq; imperium, adeo ut per ipsum ei ne vitulum quidem mactare liceat.
units.tr: Further, let us hear the reply of the elder son, whom Christ introduces speaking thus to his father: "Behold, these many years I serve you, and never have I transgressed your commandment; yet you never gave me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends. But when this son of yours, who has devoured your substance with harlots, came, you killed for him the fatted calf." Here is depicted for us the intolerable pride of hypocrites, who cannot even be induced by God's asking to acknowledge his goodness and to cease envying their brothers. But it is better to look more closely at each of his words. First he boasts of his virtues, and speaks of what he did out of duty as though he had conferred a free benefit on his father. Then he accuses his father of ingratitude and injustice, since he never gave him even a kid, that he might enjoy himself with his friends. Yet the father had given him many other things: he who had begotten him, reared him, had shown him the greatest favour, and through whom it was daily permitted him to associate with his father's friends, by whom he was doubtless esteemed and held in honour. Not content with this, he insultingly tears apart his brother's life and corrupt morals, and tries to make the father hostile to him again or hateful. And, what is more shameful, he makes the father a patron and defender of wickedness, as if he had killed the fatted calf for the sake of that man's favour only because he had wastefully squandered all his goods. Thus, together with hatred of his brother, he couples impiety also toward his father, who had deserved so well of him. And while he accuses his brother of having squandered his father's goods with harlots, he claims for himself a right and authority over the whole house and over the father himself, so that through him it is not even permitted to kill a calf.

units.la: Est hic euidentissimus typus, in quo hypocritarum mores atque ingenium spectare licet, qui cum omnibus hominibus sanctiores haberi velint, plus omnibus peccant. Nam initio iustitiae specie sese magnifice venditant, dum quid faciant & quid hucusque fecerint multis exponunt. Horum enim voces sunt: Ecce tot annis tibi iam seruimus Domine, tot annis in coenobijs ructullati sub disciplina arctissima viximus, vigiliis, ieiunijs & curis assiduis nos maceramus, pro Ecclesiae conseruatione foli laboramus, genium nostrum fraudamus, vitae honestatem enixe tuemur, denique iam inde a pueris in Lege tua instituti tibi obedimus, adeo ut nos nemo facile transgressionis reos possit agere. Sic Pharisaeos olim locutos esse in Euangelio legimus, & hodie hanc multorum sententiam. esse insolens illa propriorum meritorum fiducia abundè testatur. Quid enim non facere audent, qui preculas quoque suas Deo adnumerant, quasi cum eo aliquando rationem inituri? Atqui omnia ista salsissima sunt. Quo ore enim se Deo obedire dicunt, cum maior eorum pars quae faciunt, contra Dei praescriptum ab illo fiat, & hominum potius quam Dei serui sint? Quae autem impudentia est Legis impletionem iactare, cum ne unicum quidem praeceptum quisquam perfectè observare possit, & ideo sanctissimi quoque orent: Ne introras Domine cum seruis tuis in iudicium: item Remitte nobis debita nostra? &c. Quàm vero immane scelus est, in Dei conspectu mendacem deprehendi, & tamen huic mendacia velle obtrudere? Vnum ergo istud sufficiebat conuincendis illis quos propriae iustitiae fiducia inflat. Sed aliud grauius adhuc ex ea nascitur: quod nimirum Deum iniustitiae & ingratitudinis accusant. Quia enim sua illa opera tanti faciunt, leuiculum ipsis videtur quicquid in ipsos Deus confert, imò se ab illo iniquissimè negligi queruntur, si vel sibi non omnia ex animi arbitrio succedere, vel alios felicius agere & illo propitio vti videant. Ieiunauimus (inquiunt) & tu non vides: affligimus animas nostras, & tu ignoras. Item: Frustra seruitur Deo: Quae enim vtilitas, quod custodiam eius custodiuimus, & quod humilitati coram Domino exercituum incedimus? Imò beatos dicimus superbos: & qui impietatem faciunt aedificantur, & qui Deum tentant, liberantur. At dum ista tam impudenter contra Deum deblaterant hypocritae, suo sese indicio produnt: quod nimirum nihil hucusque de illo meriti sint, & proinde inania esse ipsorum opera, quae apud homines imperitos illi tanti aestimant, vt coelum ipsis deberi iactitent. At qui eò vsque progressi sunt, vt aduersus Deum linguas suas laxare audeant, ijdem nulli mortalium parcere norunt. Ideò si quos felicius agere, & à Deo in gratiam receptos esse vident, qui prius licentius viuebant, tunc quasi noua iniuria affecti, istorum vitia omnibus in mentem reuocant, verbis contumeliosissimis amplificant, & quae Deus sua bonitate texit ipsi insidiosè & odiosè nimis retegunt, imò haec etiam ipsi Deo exprobrant, quasi is scelerum fautor sit atq; patronus. Est hoc alienissimum à charitatis ingenio, quae (vt Diuus Petrus ex Solomone docet) peccata proximi, licet multa & grauia sint, tegere & dissimulare solet, deq; ijs corrigendis potius cogitare, quam vt aliquem per illa infamem fieri velit. Itaq; omnes isti ex eorum numero sunt, quos Christus ait festucam quidem videre in oculo fratris sui, in proprijs autem oculis trabes non obseruare. Nam quae aperta sunt vitia & ab illis ipsis agnoscuntur, qui ijs laborant, tanto odio exagitare solent, vt illos nulla venia dignos iudicent, cum ipsi multò atrociora intra animos suos secure foueant, qualia sunt, propriae iustitiae fiducia planè Pharisaica, dubitatio de gratia Dei, arrogans factorum eius reprehensio, obmurmurationis plena impatientia, suipsius admiratio, aliorum fastidiosa despectio, inuidia, odium, ambitio & superbia, qua decepti atq; inebriati, & coelos sibi solis debere arbitrantur, & omnibus alijs domi nari volunt. Interim tanta huius inuidiae atque superbiae vis est, vt perpetuò foris stent, & seipsos à coelestis Patris domo excludant, ne gratiae & bonitatis exempla videre cogantur, quibus ille ad se conuersos recipit, & simul plures alios inuitat. Atqui haec est Sanctitas illa egregia, qua hypocritae sese palliant, digna planè, quae apertis publicanorum & meretricum flagitijs postponatur, vt alibi Christus docet.
units.tr: This is a most evident type, in which we may observe the character and disposition of hypocrites, who, though they wish to be thought holier than all other men, sin more than all. At first they boast of themselves with a show of righteousness, setting out to many what they do and what they have done up to now. Their words are these: "Look, Lord, for so many years we have served you; for so many years we have lived in monasteries, shut away under the strictest discipline. We wear ourselves out with vigils, fasts and constant cares. We labour alone for the preservation of the Church. We deny our own inclinations and zealously guard the honesty of our lives. Finally, instructed in your Law from boyhood, we obey you, so that no one can easily accuse us of transgression." So we read that the Pharisees once spoke in the Gospel, and today the great confidence in their own merits, which is so common among many, bears full witness to the same opinion. For what will they not dare to do, who reckon even their little prayers to God, as if they were about to settle accounts with him? Yet all these claims are utterly absurd. With what mouth do they say they obey God, when most of what they do is done contrary to God's command, and they are servants of men rather than of God? And what shameless boasting it is to claim the fulfilment of the Law, when no one can keep even a single precept perfectly; for this reason the most holy men also pray, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord," and likewise, "Forgive us our debts," and so on. How monstrous a crime it is, moreover, to be caught lying in the sight of God and yet still to wish to foist lies upon him! That alone would have been enough to convict those whom confidence in their own righteousness puffs up. But a graver error arises from it: they accuse God of injustice and ingratitude. For because they value their own works so highly, whatever God bestows upon them seems to them a trifle; indeed they complain that they are most unjustly neglected, if they do not see everything turn out as they wish for themselves, or if they see others prospering more happily and enjoying God's favour. "We have fasted," they say, "and you do not see it; we have afflicted our souls, and you take no notice." Again: "It is in vain to serve God. For what profit is it that we have kept his charge, and that we have walked in humility before the Lord of hosts? Rather we call the proud blessed; those who work wickedness are built up, and those who tempt God are set free." But while hypocrites babble these things so shamelessly against God, they betray themselves by their own testimony: namely, that they have deserved nothing from him so far, and that therefore their works, which they value so highly before unlearned men, are empty, so that they boast that heaven is owed to them. Yet they have advanced so far that they dare to loose their tongues against God, and at the same time they spare no mortal. Hence, if they see others, who formerly lived more licentiously, doing better and being received into favour by God, then, as though wronged by a new injury, they recall the faults of those people to everyone's mind, magnify them with the most insulting words, and treacherously and spitefully expose what God has covered with his goodness; indeed they even reproach God himself with these things, as if he were a patron and promoter of crimes. This is utterly alien to the nature of love, which (as the blessed Peter teaches from Solomon) is accustomed to cover and overlook the sins of a neighbour, however many and grave they may be, and to think rather about correcting them than to wish anyone to be made infamous by them. Therefore all these men belong to the number of those whom Christ says see the mote in their brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in their own eyes. For the faults that are open and acknowledged by those who suffer from them they are accustomed to assail with such hatred that they judge such men worthy of no pardon, while they themselves securely cherish within their own minds much more atrocious things, such as a Pharisaic confidence in their own righteousness, doubt about the grace of God, arrogant criticism of his deeds, impatience full of murmuring, self-admiration, contemptuous disdain for others, envy, hatred, ambition and pride; deceived and intoxicated by these, they think that heaven is owed to themselves alone, and they want to lord it over all others at home. Meanwhile such is the force of this envy and pride that they always stand outside and shut themselves out from the house of the heavenly Father, so that they are not compelled to see the examples of grace and goodness by which he receives those who turn to him and at the same time invites many others. Yet this is that outstanding holiness with which hypocrites cloak themselves, truly worthy to be placed behind the open wickedness of tax collectors and harlots, as Christ teaches elsewhere.

units.la: Sed Patris responsum audiamus, quo tota ista actio concluditur. Fili (inquit) tu semper mecum es, & omnia mea tua sunt; Oblectari autem & gaudere te oportebat, quod frater tuus hic mortuus erat, & reuixit: periensque & inuentus est. Responsi huius partes duae sunt: Priora animum filij exacerbatum mitigat: altera eundem officij admonet. Vtraque rationem adducit, qua docet, ipsum iniuste conqueri de indulgentia sua, qua filium ad se reuersum excep erat. Ad primam partem haec verba pertinent: Fili, tu semper mecum es, & omnia mea tua sunt. Filij nomine eum dignatur, qui de ipso tanquam iniquissimo dispensatore questus erat. Quod nouum est bonitatis Dei testimonium, cuius tanta vis est, vt non facilè se patrem nostrum esse obliuiscatur, aut nos pro filijs suis agnoscere dedignetur. Exempla huius in Prophetis passim extant, per quos Iapius blandissimè eos appellat, & populum suum dicit, qui millies abdicari meruerant.
units.tr: But let us hear the Father's answer, with which the whole of that dispute is concluded. "Son," he says, "you are always with me, and all my things are yours. But it was right that you should be glad and rejoice, because this your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found." This answer has two parts: the first softens the son's embittered mind, the second reminds him of his duty. Both give a reason by which he shows that the son complains unjustly about his indulgence, by which he received the son who had returned to him. To the first part belong these words: "Son, you are always with me, and all my things are yours." He addresses him as son, although he had complained of him as a most unjust steward. This is a new testimony to God's goodness, whose power is so great that he does not easily forget to be our Father, nor does he disdain to acknowledge us as his sons. Examples of this are found everywhere in the Prophets, by whom the LORD most tenderly addresses them and calls them his people, although they had deserved to be disinherited a thousand times.

units.la: Apud Micheam certè, etsi litem aduersus eos instituat, non tamen immemor sui amoris sic ordi- tur: Populo mi, quid feci tibi? aut qua nam re molestus tibi fui? Item, Populo mi, recordare quaso, quid consultarit contra te Balak, &c. Quod autem in praesenti dicitur, Tu semper mecum es, & omnia mea tua sunt: non ita accipi debet, quòd momentanea modò esse debuerit gratia illa quæ filio prodigo iam facta erat, & idem in posterum ab hæreditate paternorum bonorum exclusus esse debuerit: aut quòd Deus, etsi manifestos peccatores in gratiam recipiat, hos tamen hypocritas iustitiarios præferat, quos alteris illis exclusis secum perpetuo seruare velit. Sed Concessionis speciem habent verba ista. Quasi dicat: Etsi vera essent quæ dicis fili, tamen nulla tibi esset causa iusta de me conquerendi. Annon enim tu mecum fuisti hucusque? annon mei amoris fructum percepisti? annon tu interea, dum miser ille foris esuriuit, sitiuit, algsit, domi meæ fatur & felix vixisti? Annon te ad huc hæredem agnosco, & habiturus sum, modò tu teipsum tua insolentia non abdicaueris? Nimium ergo morosus & iniquus es, qui indulgentia mea in fratre tuo offenderis, cùm illa tibi nequaquam fraudi sit, nec tibi inde quicquam decedat. Quin ergo procul abiecta æmulatione illa cæca, communis illius lætitiæ socium te adiungis? Et hus alteram rationem ex charitatis fraternæ ingenio desumptam subijcit, quod est, ut fratrum restitutione homines gaudeant, non contristentur aut ringantur. Atqui tuus ille frater (inquit) mortuus erat, & reuixit: perierat, & inuentus est. Quare te quoque, siquidem germanus eius frater, atque meus filius es, nobiscum gaudere decebat, &c.
units.tr: In Micah, certainly, although he brings a lawsuit against them, he nevertheless begins without forgetting his love, saying: "O my people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I troubled you? ..." and again: "O my people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised against you, ..." But what is said here, "You are always with me, and all my things are yours, should not be understood to mean that the grace already granted to the prodigal son was only momentary, and that he was to be excluded from his father's inheritance in future; nor that God, although he receives manifest sinners into favour, prefers these self-righteous hypocrites, whom he wishes to keep with himself for ever while the others are shut out. Rather these words have the appearance of a concession, as if he said: "Even if what you say, son, were true, you would still have no just cause to complain of me. For have you not been with me until now? Have you not enjoyed the fruit of my love? Meanwhile, while that wretched brother was starving, thirsting and freezing outside, did you not live well and happily fed in my house? Do I not still acknowledge you as heir, and will I not continue to do so, provided you do not disinherit yourself by your own arrogance? You are therefore too peevish and unjust, if you have taken offence at my indulgence towards your brother, when it is in no way a loss to you, nor does anything of yours decrease because of it. Why then, setting aside that blind rivalry, do you not join yourself as a partner in this common joy?" Then he adds a second reason, drawn from the nature of brotherly love: that men should rejoice at the restoration of their brothers, not be saddened or grieve. "But," he says, "that brother of yours was dead, and has come to life again; he had perished, and has been found. Therefore you too, since you are his brother and my son, ought to rejoice with us, etc."

units.la: Ita verò Dominus parabolam hanc totam ad suum statum siue scopum refert, quem huius cap. initio propositum. Est ut, quod qui germani filij Dei sunt, peccatoribus ad Deum conuersis huius gratiam non inuidere, sed potius illis gratulari & eorum salute gaudere debeant. Exigit hoc gloriæ Dei studium, quod omnibus nobis commendatissimum esse debet. Nec enim illa maiori cum fructu propagatur & illustratur, quàm si noui quotidie discipuli accedant, qui relicto diaboli atque peccati seruitio, Dei regnum ampletuntur, & eius bonitatem publicè prædicant. Sunt tamē & aliæ rationes, quibus carnis ratio magis mouetur, & quas ideo Christus in præsenti adducit. Prima est, quòd ne sanctissimi quidem aliquam quiritandi causam habent, cùm ipsis nihil decedat ex promisso æternæ beatitudinis præmio, etiamsi ad illud multa quotidie millia eorum admittantur, qui prius apertis flagitijs dediti fuerunt. Est enim eadem omnium electorum hæreditas, cùm eos Christus suos cohæredes fecerit. Et mirificum atq; ineffabile est hæreditatis illius cœlestis mysterium. Nam etsi noui quotidie ad eius ius admittantur, non tamen in partes illa distrahitur, sed singuli totam possident, tota fruuntur, neque aliquod ex suis particulonibus detrimentum sentiunt. Vt enim inexhaustus est diuinæ bonitatis fons: ita omnibus patet, qui ad illum accedunt, & ij simul omnes & singuli in conspectu Dei societate bonorum atque gaudiorum fruuntur. Quæ ergo ratio mouet etiam sanctissimos, vt aliquos admitti doleant? Non alia certè quàm inuidia, quam si in cordibus suis regnare patiantur, iam non amplius sancti, sed potius diaboli mancipia sunt, qui hominibus felicitatem inuidet: & quidē maiore iure, cùm ipse ab illa excidérit. Ad omnes ergo pertinet, quod inuido operario & murmuratori cœlestis ille Paterfamilias dicit: Amice non facio tibi iniuriam. Nonne denario pactus es mecum? Tolle quod tuum est, & abi: Volo autem huic postremo dare, sicut & tibi. Annon licet mihi quod volo facere in rebus meis? Num oculus tuus malignus est, quia ego benignus sum? Est autem huius rationis multiplex visus in ijs etiam, quæ ad huius seculi bona spectant: ne videlicet illis inuideamus, qui hos abundant, cùm nobis deteriores, & proinde ijs indigni esse videantur. Fallitur enim frequenter nostrum iudicium, & quamuis non fallamur in iudicandis aliorum moribus, suum tamen ius Deo integrum manet, neque nobis licet de illo conqueri, si abs[?]q; nostro damno multis alijs benefaciat. Ideo Cainum olim hoc argumento monuit, vt contra Abelum fratrem conceptam inuidiam deponeret.
units.tr: Thus the Lord refers this whole parable back to its purpose or aim, which he set out at the beginning of this chapter. Those who are true children of God ought not to begrudge grace to sinners who turn to God, but should instead congratulate them and rejoice in their salvation. The zeal for God's glory demands this, and it ought to be most commended to all of us. For that glory is not spread and made illustrious with greater fruit than when new disciples come forward daily, who, having left the service of the devil and of sin, enter the kingdom of God and publicly proclaim his goodness. There are, however, other reasons by which fleshly reason is more moved, and which Christ therefore brings forward here. The first is that not even the most holy have any cause for complaint, since nothing is taken from the promised reward of eternal blessedness, even if many thousands of those who previously gave themselves over to open crimes are admitted to it every day. For the inheritance of all the elect is the same, since Christ has made them his fellow heirs. The mystery of that heavenly inheritance is wonderful and beyond words. For even if new people are admitted daily to its right, it is not divided into parts; rather, each one possesses the whole, enjoys the whole, and suffers no loss from the portions of others. Just as the fountain of divine goodness is inexhaustible, so it lies open to all who come to it, and all of them together, and each one, enjoy in the sight of God the fellowship of goods and joys. What reason, then, moves even the most holy to grieve that some are admitted? Certainly none other than envy; if they allow it to reign in their hearts, they are no longer holy but slaves of the devil, who begrudges men their happiness, and with greater right, since he himself has fallen from it. Therefore what that heavenly Householder says to the envious and grumbling labourer applies to everyone: "Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give to this last man just as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I like with my own things? Is your eye evil because I am good?" This reason also has a wider application to the goods of this present age, namely that we should not begrudge those who abound in them when they seem worse than we are and therefore unworthy of them. For our judgment often errs, and although we are not wrong in judging the morals of others, God's own right remains whole, nor may we complain about him if he does good to many others without loss to us. Therefore he once warned Cain with this argument, that he should lay aside the envy he had conceived against his brother Abel.

units.la: Sed alia etiam ratio est, cuius in præsenti Christus meminit: Nimirùm duros & ab humanitatis sensu alienos esse, qui non lætantur fratrum suorum restitutione atque salute. Etenim iubet hoc natura Lex, ex qua affectiones illæ vehementissimæ nascuntur, quas Græci σοργὰς dixerunt, quæ nos mouent, vt eorum interitu & pericula non possimus sine acerbissimo dolore & gemitu intueri, qui sanguinis propinquitate nobis coniuncti sunt. Atqui arctior est multò spiritualis illa cognatio, quæ credentibus in Christo intercedit. Quis ergo Christianos esse dixerit, qui aliquos ab interitu revocari & cum Deo in gratiam redire iniquius ferunt? Interim semper nobis occurrat, quòd hîs dicitur: Filius hic meus mortuus erat, & reuixit: perierat, & inuentus est. Eo enim admonemur, Dei gratiam non alijs expositam esse, neque alios communem hanc totius Ecclesiæ congratulationem mereri, quàm eos qui ex peccatis resurgunt, & in Christo vitam nouam viuunt: qui item à Deo salutem nostram quaerente se inueniri patiuntur, vt ad eius familiam redeant. Nihil ergo patrocinatur locus hic contumacibus & poenitere nescijs. Quin potius ad illos pertinent primae huius parabolae partes, quae peccati conditionem & infelices eorum poenas exprimunt, quae illius serui parata sunt. At quos serio poenitentiae sensus tangit, ij gratiae Dei fores sibi patere non dubitent. Qui vero hactenus à grauioribus vitijs immunes fuerunt, ij istorum conuersione gaudeant, & quotidie quosuis alios adducere studeant ad poenitentiam, vt nouis indies incrementis Regnum Dei augescat, & quàm plurimi seruentur in Christo Iesu, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But there is also another reason, which Christ mentions here: namely, that those who do not rejoice at the restoration and salvation of their brothers are hard and alien to human feeling. For natural law commands this, and from it arise those most vehement affections, which the Greeks called στοργαί [storgai], which move us so that we cannot look upon the destruction and dangers of those joined to us by blood kinship without the most bitter grief and groaning. Yet that spiritual kinship which exists between believers in Christ is far closer. Who, then, would call those Christians who bear it with ill grace that some are called back from destruction and return into grace with God? Meanwhile let this always come to our minds, what is said here: "This son of mine was dead, and has come to life; he was lost, and has been found." For we are reminded by this that God's grace is not set forth for others, nor do others deserve this common congratulation of the whole Church, except those who rise from sins and live a new life in Christ: who likewise allow themselves to be found by God, who seeks our salvation, so that they return to his household. This passage therefore lends no support to the obstinate and to those who do not know how to repent. Rather, the first parts of this parable pertain to them, which express the condition of sin and the unhappy punishments prepared for that servant. But those whom a earnest sense of repentance touches should not doubt that the doors of God's grace stand open to them. Those, however, who until now have been free from graver vices should rejoice at their conversion, and strive daily to bring any others whomsoever to repentance, so that the Kingdom of God may grow with new increases each day and as many as possible be kept safe in Christ Jesus our Lord: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVI. HOMILIA CLIIII.
units.tr: Chapter 16. Homily 154.

units.la: Dixit autem etiam discipulis suis: Fuit homo quidam, diues, qui habebat dispensatorem, & is delatus est apud eum, vt qui dissiparet ipsius bona. Vocauit igitur eum, & dixit ei: Quid hoc audio de te? redde rationem dispensationis tuae: nō enim poteris amplius esse dispensator. Dixit autem apud se dispensator: Quid faciam, cùm dominus meus auferat à me dispensationem? Fodere non possum, mendicare pudet. Noui quid sim facturus, vt cum amotus fuero à dispensatione, recipiat me ali qui in domus suas. Conuocatis igitur singulis debitoribus domini sui, dixit primo: Quantū debes domino meo? Is ait. Centum batos olei. Tum ille dixit ei: Accipe tabulas tuas, & sede cito, & scribe quinquaginta. Deinde alij dixit: Tu vero quantum debes? Is autem ait, Centum coros tritici. Tum ipse dixit ei: Accipe tabulas tuas, & scribe octoginta. Et laudauit dominus dispensatorem iniustum, quòd prudenter fecisset: Quoniam filij huius seculi prudentiores sunt filijs lucis in suo genere.
units.tr: And he said also unto his disciples: There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods. And he called him, and said unto him: How is it that I hear this of thee? Give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward. Then the steward said within himself: What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses. So he called every one of his lord's debtors unto him, and said unto the first: How much owest thou unto my lord? And he said: An hundred baths of oil. And he said unto him: Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty. Then said he to another: And how much owest thou? And he said: An hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him: Take thy bill, and write fourscore. And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.

units.la: Diligenter hucusq; Christus Iesus de Euangelio & singulis huius partibus, poenitentia nimirum & remissione peccatorum, disseruit. Et illam quidem omnibus necessariam esse docuit, qui cum Deo reconciliari & salutem consequi volunt: hanc autem omnibus expositam esse ostendit, qui à peccatis ad Deum serio conuertuntur. Atqui non in nuda aut inani professione ista consistunt, neq; Deus suos cultores vult otiosos esse: ideo commodè nunc de praecipuo hominis Christiani officio, dilectione & beneficentia, disputat. Quae vt in opū abundantia amplissimam habet sese exercendi materiam: ita in illis maximè peccatur. Quapropter de his diligenter disserit aduersus auaritiam & luxū, in quibus opum abusus potissimum consistit. Et in praesenti quidem beneficentiae studium eleganti parabola nobis commendat, cuius hic scopus & haec summa est: Eos, qui diuitias habent, non suis cupiditatibus indulgere, sed potius recta illarum dispensatione animarum quoq; suarum saluti in futurum prospicere debere: vt quando à nobis Deus rationes exigit, dignum & optatum ex nostra beneficentia fructum percipiamus. Figuratur autem tota haec tractatio per comparationem, quae docet, inexcusabilem esse illorum ignauiam, qui in iis, quae ad aeternam vitam spectant, non eodem studio & industria vtuntur, qua homines mundo dediti ea curare solent, quae corporis necessitati, aut etiam voluptati foli, seruiunt. Quia vero singulae partes simul multa alia continent, quae cognitu vtilissima sunt, de omnibus ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Thus far Christ Jesus has treated diligently of the Gospel and of its individual parts, namely repentance and the forgiveness of sins. He has taught that repentance is necessary for all who wish to be reconciled to God and to obtain salvation, and he has shown that it lies open to all who seriously turn from their sins to God. Yet these things do not consist in a bare or empty profession, nor does God want his worshippers to be idle. Therefore he now fittingly discourses on the chief duty of a Christian, love and beneficence. Just as wealth offers a very wide field for exercising these, so it is in the use of wealth that people especially sin. For this reason he treats these matters carefully, arguing against avarice and luxury, in which the abuse of riches chiefly consists. In the present passage he commends to us the zeal for beneficence by an elegant parable, whose aim and substance is this: that those who have riches should not indulge their own desires, but should rather, by the right management of them, look ahead to the salvation of their souls in the future, so that when God calls us to account we may receive from our beneficence a worthy and desired fruit. This whole discussion is set forth by means of a comparison, which teaches that those are inexcusable who in matters concerning eternal life do not use the same zeal and diligence that worldly-minded people customarily bring to things serving the needs of the body or even mere pleasure. Since, however, each part contains many other matters that are most useful to know, we shall speak of all of them in order.

units.la: Principiò homo diues aut opulentus inducitur, qui opum suarum dispensatorem habuit. Quae parte tota diuitiarum aut bonorum huius seculi ratio adumbratur. Nam diues ille homo Deus est, quem omnium bonorum tam spiritualium quàm corporalium fontem atq; largitorem esse, non solùm sacrae literae docent, verumetiam gentium philosophi olim agnouerunt. Dispensatores huius sunt homines, & ij in primis, quos ille prae aliis diuites & bonis variis instructos fecit. Nā vt dispensator proprium propriū habet nihil,sed alterius bona suæ fidei credita administrat: ita omnes nos nihil possidemus, quod possimus nostrum dicere (quia nudi ex utero matris nascimur, nec aliquid in mundum inferi mus) Deus autē ex gratuita bonitate inter nos dona sua distribuit, alijs quidem opes, alijs honores atq; dignitates, alijs sapientiam, alijs corporis vires, alijs aliud prout ipsi visum fuerit. Imò ne hæc quidem æquali mensura omnibus confert, sed certo iudicio agit, ut qui nos probè cognitos habet, & quantum cuique committi debeat, intelligit. Est hoc obseruatu & consideratu dignissimum: quia nos officij admonet, & ne donis qualibuscunque efferamur nos coercet. Nam omnibus occini potest Paulinum illud: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quòd si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi nō acceperus? In quem finem verò dona Dei accipimus? Num ut nobis solis priuatim illa seruiant? Certè ut non nobis, sed alijs nascimur (quod omnibus seculis sapientissimi quique intellexerunt) ita nobis non solis Deus sua dona largitur, sed dispensatores esse vult, qui illis ad sui nominis illustrationem & multorum aliorum utilitatem utamur. Admonet nos de isto corporis nostri fabrica aut constitutio. Nam quia corpus unū est, membra, & si diuersa & alia alijs præstantiora sint, singula tamen quicquid habent in commune deponunt, ut totius corporis valetudo seruetur, & membris laborantibus succurratur. Ita cùm unum sit omnium credentium Ecclesia, quæ ex membris multum inter se diuer sis constituitur (si Dei dona consideres) æquum est, ut hic quoq; omnes omnia inter se communia faciant, non quidem iniusta confusione, quæ ex rerum suarum possessione aliquem deijciat, sed amica dispensatione, quam nobis Deus commisit. Debent ergo illud ad se priuatim transferre omnis ordinis & loci homines, ut se Dei dispensatores, & proinde aliorum omnium in eius domo agentium seruos esse meminerint. Nam si unum hoc non ofcitanter considerent, adeò nō superbibunt opibus aut quibuscunq; alijs bonis, ut potius eò humiliores fiant, quò plura se à Domino accepisse vident. Semper enim illis in mentem veniet, quòd de pluribus rationem reddere cogentur.
units.tr: First, a rich or wealthy man is introduced, who had a steward over his goods. In this part the reckoning of the riches or goods of this world is outlined. For that rich man is God, who is known not only by the holy letters to be the fount and giver of all good things, both spiritual and bodily, but was also long ago acknowledged by the philosophers of the nations. The stewards of this man are human beings, and above all those whom he has made richer than others and furnished with various gifts. For just as a steward has nothing of his own, but administers the goods of another entrusted to his faithfulness, so we all possess nothing that we can call our own, since we are born naked from our mother's womb and bring nothing into the world. God, however, out of free goodness distributes his gifts among us: to some wealth, to others honours and dignities, to others wisdom, to others bodily strength, to others something else, as seemed good to him. Indeed he does not even grant these things to everyone in equal measure, but acts by a sure judgement, knowing us thoroughly and understanding how much should be entrusted to each. This is most worthy of observation and reflection, because it reminds us of our duty and restrains us from being puffed up by whatever gifts we have. For to all of us may be sung that saying of Paul: "What hast thou that thou didst not receive? And if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it?" For what purpose, then, do we receive the gifts of God? Surely not so that they may serve us alone, in private? Certainly we are born not for ourselves but for others (as the wisest men of every age have understood), and so God gives his gifts not to us alone, but wants us to be stewards, so that we may use them for the glory of his name and the benefit of many others. The very structure and constitution of our body admonishes us of this. For the body is one, and though its members are diverse and some are more excellent than others, each member nevertheless contributes whatever it has for the common good, so that the health of the whole body is preserved and the suffering members are helped. So too, since the Church of all believers is one, and is made up of members quite different from one another, if you consider the gifts of God, it is right that all here too should hold all things in common among themselves; not indeed by an unjust confusion that would cast anyone down from the possession of his own property, but by a friendly stewardship, which God has committed to us. Therefore people of every rank and place ought to apply this to themselves personally, remembering that they are stewards of God and, accordingly, servants of all the others who serve in his house. For if they consider this one thing carefully, they will not be so puffed up by wealth or by any other goods, but will rather become the more humble the more they see they have received from the Lord. For it will always come into their minds that they will be compelled to give an account for many things.

units.la: Sed è contra videamus, quis nam & qualis hic dispensator fuerit: Iniquus nimirum & perfidus. Nam bona heri suæ fidei credita dissipauit, & tandem apud herum eo nomine delatus est. Quo loco diuitum huius seculi conditio nobis depingitur. Non sufficiunt hi rebus suis curandis, & quò plures sunt diuitiæ, eò pluribus seruis opus habent, per quos sua & recipiant & dispensent. Ita verò onus & molestiam magnam ex eo sentiunt, in quo infelix & stultus mundus summam felicitatis partem consistere putat. Nam præter id, quòd ipsi seruos prospicere, & proinde ipsis inseruire coguntur, ab ijsdem plerunque contemni solent: Vnde mox fraudes, impostura, furta & omnis generis expilationes nascuntur, quas nunquam omnes effugere possunt. Et cùm omni populo in ore sint, quæ à seruis fraudulenter & iniustè fiunt, illi ferè postremi ea rescisc unt, cuius mali causa est, quòd vel ignaui & stupidi nimis parasitos & assentatores frugi seruis præferunt: vel insolentiores æquo se plus satis sapere sibi iampridem persuaserunt, neq; de rebus suis à quoquam volunt admoneri. Sed & vulgi vitio multum hic delinquitur. Nam ut pleriq; leuissima quæque obseruant & traducunt: ita rarissimè ad eos rem referunt, ad quos ea in primis pertinet. Ergo postremi ferè rescisc unt patresfamilias, quæ à filijs & seruis suis improbè dissignantur. Est hæc tanta diuitum infelicitas, ut sola sufficere posset rectè consideratæ, ne opes tanto studio corradamus, quibus tot curæ totq; incommoda coniuncta sunt.
units.tr: But on the other hand let us see who and what kind of steward this was: wicked indeed and faithless. For he squandered the goods entrusted to his faithfulness and was at last accused of this before his lord. In this place the condition of the rich of this world is portrayed for us. Such people are not sufficient for managing their own affairs, and the more wealth they have, the more servants they need, through whom they both receive and dispense their goods. Yet they feel great burden and trouble from this very thing in which the foolish and unhappy world thinks the chief part of happiness consists. For besides the fact that they are forced to provide servants for themselves and so to serve them, they are usually despised by those same servants. Hence soon come frauds, deceit, thefts and every kind of plundering, which they can never all escape. And although everyone talks of what is done fraudulently and unjustly by servants, the masters are almost always the last to find it out. The cause of this evil is that either the lazy and stupid prefer parasites and flatterers to honest servants, or the more insolent have long persuaded themselves that they know more than enough and do not want to be warned about their affairs by anyone. But also through the fault of the common people much wrong is done here. For while most people notice and spread about even the slightest matters, they very rarely report them to those to whom they especially pertain. Therefore fathers of families are almost always the last to learn of the wicked deceptions practised upon them by their sons and servants. This great unhappiness of the rich is such that it alone could suffice, if rightly considered, to keep us from gathering wealth with such great eagerness, since so many cares and so many discomforts are joined to it.

units.la: Simul autem in isto dispensatore omnium eorum typus proponitur, qui donis à Deo datis abuntur. Est hoc vitium vulgare admodum: Qui enim diuitijs per se iustis & legitimè partis abundant, ij aut non contenti illis quas habent, insatiabili auaritiæ studio quotidie illas augere satagunt, & sibi solis ea congerunt atq; possident, quæ multorum aliorum vsibus debebant seruire: aut luxu fœdo omnia dissipant, dum suo fastui, gulæ, libidini, ambitioni, aliisq; prauis cupiditatibus satisfacere studeant. Et illi se egregiè excusatos arbitrantur, si diuitias suas esse dicant, & sibi licere, ut eis pro suo arbitrio utantur. At nihil habent illi, quod iure suum dicere possint, & simul ea, quæ Deus dedit, iniustè & turpiter dissipant, dum ea alienis vsibus seruire cogunt. Eadem principum culpa est, qui authoritate & potestate diuinitus data suas res agunt, publicas negligunt: vel ut ipsi otio suo consulant, populum officiarijs committunt, quorum rapacitate totus expilatur. Et hi quoque se extra culpam esse putant, si penes se potestatem & ius esse vociferentur de omnibus pro suo arbitrio statuendi. Sed hi quoq; præstantissima Dei dona dissipant, ut iam de populo nihil dicam, quem Deus {a}vlim de ipsorum manibus requiret. Idem de iis dicere possumus, qui valetudine, forma & viribus corporis, sapientia & eloquentia, aliisq; tam corporis quam ingenij animiq; bonis profusae carnis arbitrio abutuntur. Quia enim illa in vsus inhonestos & Deo inimicos converterunt, & eorum improbi dissipatores sunt, dignas olim poenas Domino exoluent. Hic ergo magna & universalis (ut sic loquar) mundi improbitas arguitur, quando paucissimos esse videre, qui domus suis recte vtantur, ut & Dei gloriam promoveant, & proximi commodis atque saluti consultum velint.
units.tr: At the same time, in this steward a type is set before us of all those who abuse the gifts given them by God. This vice is very common. For those who abound in riches lawfully and justly acquired either are not content with what they have, and with insatiable greed strive every day to increase them, heaping up and possessing for themselves alone what ought to serve the use of many others; or they squander everything in foul luxury, while they seek to satisfy their pride, gluttony, lust, ambition and other wicked desires. And they think they are well excused if they say that their riches are their own and that it is lawful for them to use them as they please. But those men have nothing that they can rightly call their own, and at the same time they shamefully and unjustly squander what God has given, while they compel it to serve other people's uses. The same fault belongs to princes, who manage their own affairs with the authority and power given them by God, but neglect the public good; or who, in order to consult their own leisure, entrust the people to officials, through whose greed the whole population is plundered. And these too think themselves free of blame if they loudly claim that the power and right to decide everything at their own discretion belong to them. But these men too squander the most excellent gifts of God, not to mention the people, whom God will one day require from their hands. We may say the same of those who abuse, by lavish indulgence of the flesh, health, beauty and bodily strength, wisdom and eloquence, and other goods of body, mind and soul, whether of talent or of spirit. For since they have turned those gifts to dishonourable uses and ones hostile to God, and are wicked squanderers of them, they will one day pay to the Lord the penalties they deserve. Here, then, a great and universal wickedness of the world (if I may so speak) is exposed, since we see that very few use their households rightly, so as both to advance the glory of God and to wish to promote the advantage and salvation of their neighbour.

units.la: Sed videamus quid cum suo ipsto dispensatore herus egerit, ut ex eo discamus quid a Deo expectare debeant omnes ij, qui illius mores imitantur. Vocatur ab hero, qui cum eo expostulans ait: Quid hoc audio de te? Quasi dicat: Haec ne fides tua est? Ita ne rerum mearum curam geris? Et mox addit, Redde rationem dispensationis tuae: non enim poteris amplius esse dispensator. Ita ergo rationem suae administrationis ab illo exigit, ut simul eum ab officio removeat. Solet hoc ipsum omnibus accidere, qui Dei negotia fide mala agunt. Rata enim erit omnibus saeculis sententia, quam per Ieremiam pronuntiat: Maledictus, qui fecerit opus Domini maligne. Et hic primum occurrit, quod tales diu latere non possunt, imo ne momento quidem oculos Dei effugere. Nam etsi ad tempus multa dissimulet, omnia tamen videt & audit, ut aliorum relatione ipsi nequaquam sit opus. Facit huc quod idem per eundem Prophetam dicit: Ego Dominus & cor perscrutor, & renes exploro, ut reddam cuique iuxta viam suam, & secundum fructum studiorum suorum. Quod vnum sufficere debebat ad excitandum eos, qui sibi ex eo impunitatem perpetuam pollicentur, quod Deus res humanas aut prorsus ignoret, aut saltem negligat. At neutrum de illo cogitari debere, hic locus docet. Nam qui huius dispensatoris improbitatem resciuit, simul ab eodem suae dispensationis rationem exigit. In quo cum seueritate iustitiam quoque suam declarat. Nam etsi iniquitatem impunitam non sinat, iudicium tamen non solet praecipitare. Huius autem meminisse debent quotquot vel opum abundantia affluunt, aut alijs Dei donis ornati sunt. Reddent aliquando suae dispensationis rationem, quando a moriturus animam repositet Deus, quando item in magno illo die Christus pauperum causam suscipiet, & sibi factum iudicabit quicquid cum illis factum fuerit. Sed & Ecclesiarum ministri & qui magistratus gerunt, de hoc ipso frequenter cogitare debent, a quibus suae functionis rationem sic Deus exiget, ut eorum quoque sanguinem ex ipsorum manibus requisiturus sit, qui eorum incuria aut negligentia perierunt. Semper ergo in nostris animis atque auribus vox ista sonet, ut nobis dici putemus, Redde rationem dispensationis tuae. Nec enim rationes modo a nobis exigit Deus, verumetiam ex gradu suo eos deturbat, quos malae fidei dispensatores esse deprehendit. Aufert ergo illis bona sua, quibus male vsi sunt, adeoque infamia notatos a Regno suo in universum excludit. Hinc est, quod diuitiae vel palam diripiuntur: aut per intemperantiam dilapidantur, vel etiam sensim euanescunt, ut raro ad tertium haeredem perueniant immodicae illae opes, quae in aliqua familia perpetuae fore videbantur. Idem fit in iis, qui in publicis functionibus parum fidi sunt. Multos certe ex Ecclesiae ministris exauthorari videmus iusto Dei iudicio, ut inglorij & omnibus exosi fiant, qui vt in honore & pretio essent, malis hominibus blandiendo sua authoritatem turpi silentio aut indulgentia seruili prostituerunt. Cuius rei exempla in Heli sacerdote & ijs, qui post Babylonicum exilium in afferenda Dei gloria ignauiores fuerunt, scripturae sacrae proponunt. Principes quoque viros non raro idem pati cernimus, & in historijs exempla eorum passim occurrunt, qui quod in repub. perfidi aut negligentiores aequo fuerunt, hominum contemptissimi facti sunt. Nec enim alicui mortalium Deus obstrictus est, ut eius opera non possit carere: sed facile illi est invenire quorum ministerio vtatur, & quos ad functiones suas obeundas donis necessarijs instruat. Nemo igitur seipsum inani perfuasione fallat.
units.tr: But let us see what the lord did with his own steward, so that we may learn what all those who imitate his ways should expect from God. The steward is called by his lord, who challenges him: "What is this I hear about you?" As if he were saying, "Is this your loyalty? Is this how you look after my affairs?" And straightaway he adds, "Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward." So he demands an account of his administration and at the same time removes him from office. The same thing usually happens to all who carry out God's business with bad faith. The sentence that Jeremiah pronounces will hold for all ages: "Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully." And here we first notice that such people cannot stay hidden for long, indeed cannot escape God's eyes even for a moment. For although he may overlook much for a time, he sees and hears everything, so that he has no need of reports from others. To the same point is what he says through the same prophet: "I, the Lord, search the heart and try the reins, to give to each man according to his way and according to the fruit of his deeds." This one statement should have been enough to rouse those who promise themselves perpetual impunity because they suppose that God either knows nothing of human affairs or at least takes no notice of them. This passage teaches that neither of these is to be thought of him. For he who has learned of the wickedness of this steward at the same time demands an account of his stewardship from him. In this he also shows his justice with severity. For although he does not allow iniquity to go unpunished, he is not accustomed to rush into judgment. Yet all who abound in wealth, or are endowed with other gifts of God, must remember this. They will one day render an account of their stewardship, when God requires the soul from those who are dying, and likewise on that great day when Christ will take up the cause of the poor and will judge whatever has been done to them as done to himself. But the ministers of the Churches and those who hold magistracies must also often think about this very thing. God will require an account of their office from them, so that he will also demand the blood of those who perished through their carelessness or negligence at their hands. Let this voice therefore always sound in our minds and ears, so that we may think it is said to us: "Give an account of your stewardship." For God not only demands accounts from us, but also casts down from their station those whom he finds to be stewards of bad faith. Therefore he takes away from them the goods they have misused, and so, marked with infamy, he shuts them out entirely from his kingdom. Hence it is that riches are either openly plundered, or squandered through intemperance, or even slowly vanish away, so that those immense fortunes which seemed destined to last forever in some family rarely reach a third heir. The same happens to those who are of little trust in public offices. We certainly see many ministers of the Church deprived of their authority by the just judgment of God, so that they become without glory and hated by all. Though they wished to be held in honour and esteem, by flattering wicked men and by shameful silence or servile indulgence they have surrendered their authority. Holy Scripture sets before us examples of this in Eli the priest, and in those who after the Babylonian exile were too lazy in asserting the glory of God. We also see princes not infrequently suffer the same, and in histories examples of them are everywhere, of those who, because they were too treacherous or too negligent in the commonwealth, became utterly despised by men. For God is bound to no mortal, so that he could not do without his work; rather it is easy for him to find those through whose ministry he may act, and to equip them with the gifts necessary for performing their functions. Let no one, therefore, deceive himself with empty confidence.

units.la: Continet praeterea totus iste locus doctrinam obseruatu vtilem & necessariam ijs, qui rempub. administrant. Horum ante omnia est, ut ipsi negotia sua curent, neque eorum gubernationem aliis committant, ut ipsi quid rerum geratur, ignorent. Quia tales ignorantia minime excusat, si quod malum dent. Nam cum capitis instar sint in populo, nomen istud nunquam merebuntur, nisi videant, audiant, sapiant, ea deniq; prospiciant, quae reipub. salutaria & necessaria sunt. At quae nostri saeculi calamitas est, hodie plerique Reges & principes vltimi fere resciscunt, quae ipsorum ministri iniuste, iniquè, & interdum crudeliter faciunt: neque prius manum admouent, quam malum prorsus est immedicabile. Deinde si quid ad ipsos deferatur, ne praecipitent iudicium. Est hoc vulgare vitium eorum, qui suo otio & negligentia res in discrimen adduxerunt. Tunc enim non tam reipub. amore, quàm vindictae privatae studio in quosuis capitalibus poenis animaduertunt, vt bonorem suum aliquo modo tueantur, quem prius officiunter nimis neglexerunt. Aequi diligenter prius causae cognosci, & postea demum sententiae ferri debent. Vbi plerunque opus est, vt altera quoque pars audiatur, & ne animum affectu aliquo priuato aut praeiudicio occupatum habeamus. Postremo pro dignitate puniant eos, quos aliquid praeter officium fecisse vident. Quod vt in omnibus hominibus absque omni personarum respectu obseruari debet: ita maximè in iis, qui supremi magistratus nomine rebus praefecti sunt: eò quòd horum exempla, si impunita abeant, plures alios corrumpunt, & licentiam publicam inducunt. Quod ne fiat, initiò cauere proderit, ne qui alij rebus praficiantur, quàm quorum fides & integritas prius satis perspecta est. At hodie in utroque peccatur, dum temere publicis functionibus adhibentur, qui suas res nunquam cum laude administrarunt: & idem feruntur indulgenter nimis, etiamsi rempub. simul omnem dissipent, & cum exitiali licentia communem confusionem introducant.
units.tr: Moreover, this whole passage contains a teaching useful and necessary to be observed by those who administer the commonwealth. The first duty of such men is to attend to their own affairs, and not to commit the government to others and so remain ignorant of what is being done. For such ignorance is in no way an excuse if they cause some harm. Since they stand as the head among the people, they will never deserve that name unless they see, hear, understand, and finally provide for those things which are salutary and necessary for the commonwealth. But what a calamity of our age it is: today most kings and princes learn last of all what their ministers unjustly, iniquitously, and sometimes cruelly do; and they do not lay a hand to it before the evil has become utterly incurable. Next, if anything is reported to them, they should not rush to judgment. This is a common fault of those who, through their idleness and negligence, have brought affairs into danger. For then they punish any capital offences not so much out of love for the commonwealth as out of a desire for private vengeance, so that they may somehow defend the honour which they had earlier too carelessly neglected. Causes ought to be examined carefully first, and only afterwards should sentence be passed. Often it is necessary that the other party also be heard, and that we not hold our minds occupied by some private affection or prejudice. Finally, they should punish, in proportion to its gravity, those whom they see to have done anything beyond their duty. This should be observed in all men without any regard for persons, but most of all in those who have been placed in charge of affairs in the name of the supreme magistrate. For if the examples of these men go unpunished, they corrupt many others and introduce public licence. To prevent this, it will help at the outset to take care that no one is set over affairs except those whose faithfulness and integrity have been sufficiently tested beforehand. But today both things are done wrongly, while men who have never administered their own affairs with credit are rashly admitted to public offices; and the same men are borne with too indulgently, even when they squander the whole commonwealth and introduce common confusion with destructive licence.

units.la: Sed proderit dispensatorem hunc iniustum audire, quale ipse de rebus suis consilium secum ineat. Quid faciam (inquit) cùm dominus meus auferat à me dispensationem? Vnde verò ista consilij incertitudo? Addit: Fodere non possum, mendicare pudet. Fatetur ergo ignauiam cum detestabili superbia vel ambitione coniunctam. Quia enim in otio & rerum abundantia hucusque enutritus fuerat, à labore non potuit non abhorrere. At cùm nihil haberet aliud unde viveret, mendicandum illi fuisset, & oppiatim stipes aut victus quaerendus. Eius autem non poterat non pudere eum, qui hactenus ex alieno superbierat. Quid ergo restat tibi o infelix? Nomi (inquit) quid faciam, vt cùm amicus fuero à dispensatione, recipiant me aliqui in domus suas. Nouis ergo artibus amicos sibi parare vult, qui egentem recipiant & sua ope subleuent. At quae illae artes fuerint, paulo post audiemus. Nunc prius obseruandi nobis veniunt inertium concoctorum & abliguritorum mores, quos hoc exemplo tanquam in tabula depictos Christus nobis proponit. Primum rerum omnium incerti sunt, nec aliquam inire possunt honestè viuendi rationem, si vitae genus sit mutandum, cui iam diu assueuerunt. At quae huius mali causa est? Quia fodere non possunt, mendicare autem pudet. Laboris enim omnis impatientes sunt, vt qui nunquam aliquod opus suis manibus fecerint. Eo ipso autem se degeneres esse produnt, quando ad laborem omnes nati sumus, & in primo parente omnibus nobis dictum sit: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Quis ergo suae fortis aut etiam vocationis Dei memores esse dicat eos, qui à labore non aliter quàm à scelere aliquo aut re hominibus ingenuis indigna abhorrent? Atqui id faciunt reuera, quicunque assueuerunt ex alieno in rerum omnium abundantia viuere. Idem verò interea pauperes videri nolunt, & proinde mendicare eos pudet. Imò plerosque horum superbire adhuc, & maiorum opibus, stemmatum antiquitate, generis nobilitate & nescio quibus aliis hominum ambitiosorum figmentis gloriari videmus. Ergo rursum hoc illus reliquum est, vt ad malas artes conuertantur, quas interim honestatis & amicitiae titulis palliant. Est hoc hominum genus hodie vbique obuium, & idem praecipui malorum fere omnium auctores sunt. Sunt enim ignaui & inertes plurimi, qui laborare neque possunt, neque volunt. Sunt quos nobilitatis opinio inebriat, vt labores manuarios aut seruitia sibi dedecori fore existiment: & bi fere eò vsque stultitiae progrediuntur, vt familiae suae toti ignominiam fieri clament, si liberos suos opificibus manuarijs instituendos dare iubeantur. Interim vtriq; edere & bibere volunt: imò belluari, voluptates omnis generis sequi, vestitu sese ostentare, & supra omnes alios eminere volunt. Hinc ergo consilia illa ineunt & fere communis omnium istorum quaestio est: Quid faciam? Nobili familia oriundus sum, nobilibus semper conuixi, sumptus magnos illud vita genus requirit quod solum me decet. Istos verò neque patrimonij tenuitas sustinere potest, neq; vt manuum labore aut ostiatim mendicando illos mihi parem, decorum est. Num ergo furabor? At vt mihi abundant omnia suppetant necesse est. At quae fere est deliberationum eiusmodi conclusio? Ea nimirum, vt dum omnem infamiam subterfugere volunt, & in primis à furti crimine sibi timent, quod in primis infame & exosum est, ad suas artes conuertuntur, quae etsi non censeantur furti nomine, suspendio tamen magis dignae sunt quàm ipsum. Alij enim ad rempub. admissi publicas leges & iura violat, iudicia venalia habent, & mirificu exactionibus quosuis expilant. Alij in bellum profugius & militiam mercenariam sectantur, ut huius titulo sua furta, rapinas, homicidia, sacrilegia deniq; & quaecunque atrocissima scelera tegant. Alij seditiosas legu & reipub. mutationes moliuntur, quod olim cum suis coniuratus apud Romanos Catilina fecit. Alij quibus ad ista non satis animi est, etsi mendici videri nolint, ex publico tamen sibi dari volunt quod ipsis satis sit. Itaq; ex atakton illorum numero fiunt, de quibus in epistolis ad Thessalonicenses Paulus scribit, qui nullis legibus siue politicis siue ecclesiasticis subditi absque omni disciplina atq; ordine viuunt, & quae in alios usus collecta sunt, bona publica ipsi otiosi & ignavi ventres devorant. Et tales quidem bodie plures passim esse videmus, quam Christianae professioni vtile aut decorum sit: imo periculum est, ne quando isti & respub. & Ecclesias simul omnes evertant, ac dissipent, nisi remedium breui adhibeatur.
units.tr: But it will be useful to hear what plan this unjust steward devises for himself regarding his affairs. "What shall I do," he says, "since my lord is taking the stewardship away from me? And whence this uncertainty of plan?" He adds, "I cannot dig, I am ashamed to beg." He therefore confesses a sloth joined with detestable pride or ambition. For since he had been nurtured until now in idleness and abundance of goods, he could not but shrink from labour. But since he had nothing else to live on, he would have had to beg and seek alms or food door to door. And he could not but be ashamed, having till now lived proudly on what belonged to others. "What, then, is left for you, unhappy man?" "I know what I shall do," he says, "so that when I have been removed from the stewardship, some people may receive me into their houses." He therefore wishes to make friends for himself by new arts, who will take in the needy man and relieve him with their help. But what those arts were we shall hear shortly. For now we must first observe the habits of the idle, the wasteful, and the gluttonous, whom Christ sets before us in this example as if painted on a tablet. First of all, such men are uncertain of everything, and cannot find any honest way of living if the kind of life to which they have long been accustomed must be changed. And what is the cause of this evil? It is that they cannot dig, and are ashamed to beg. For they are impatient of all labour, as men who have never done any work with their own hands. And by this very fact they show themselves to be degenerate, since we are all born for labour, and to all of us in the first parent it was said: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." Who, then, mindful of his own strength, or even of God's calling, could say that those men shrink from labour as from some crime or from a thing unworthy of free men? Yet indeed all who have grown accustomed to live at others' expense, in abundance of everything, do exactly this. Meanwhile they do not wish to appear poor, and therefore they are ashamed to beg. Indeed we see most of them still proud, and boasting of their ancestors' wealth, the antiquity of their pedigree, the nobility of their birth, and I know not what other figments of ambitious men. Therefore what is left for them is once again to turn to wicked arts, which they cover in the meantime with the titles of honour and friendship. This kind of men is found everywhere today, and they are almost the chief authors of nearly all evils. For there are many who are lazy and idle, who neither can nor will labour. There are those whom the opinion of nobility intoxicates, so that they think manual labour or service would be a disgrace to them; and some of these advance so far into folly that they cry out that their whole family will be dishonoured if they are ordered to put their children to be trained as manual workers. Meanwhile they want to eat and drink with the rest, indeed to gorge themselves, to pursue pleasures of every kind, to display themselves in clothing, and to stand out above all others. Hence they form those plans, and the common question of all of them is this: "What shall I do? I am descended from a noble family, I have always lived among nobles, and that way of life, which alone befits me, requires great expense.
