The slenderness of my patrimony cannot support these things, nor is it fitting for me to match them by labour of my hands or by begging from door to door. Shall I then steal? But I must have all things in abundance." And what is usually the conclusion of such deliberations? Namely, that while they want to escape all infamy, and above all fear the charge of theft, which is especially disgraceful and hateful, they turn to their own arts. These, although they are not counted under the name of theft, nevertheless deserve the gallows more than theft itself does. For some, admitted to the commonwealth, violate public laws and rights, hold judgments for sale, and plunder everyone by marvellous extortions. Others flee to war and pursue mercenary soldiering, so that under its title they may conceal their thefts, robberies, murders, sacrileges, and finally whatever most atrocious crimes. Others plot seditious changes of laws and of the commonwealth, as Catiline once did at Rome with his conspirators. Others, to whom there is not enough spirit for these things, even though they do not want to seem beggars, still want to be given from the public purse what is enough for them. And so they become of the number of the disorderly [ἀτάκτων], of whom Paul writes in his letters to the Thessalonians, who, subject to no laws, whether civil or ecclesiastical, live without any discipline or order, and idle and lazy bellies devour the public goods that have been collected for other uses. And we see many such men everywhere today, more than is useful or fitting for the Christian profession. Indeed there is danger lest at some time such men overthrow and wreck both the commonwealth and the Churches all together, unless a remedy is applied soon.

units.la: At quod nam illud fuerit? Primum in Dei promissiones singuli respiciat, qui in sua vocatione ambulantibus abunde pollicetur, quae ad vitam commode & honeste transfigendam necessaria sunt. Eas ergo sibi ipsis singuli applicent, neque dubitent de earum veritate, quae olim plurimis exemplis demonstrata est, & quotidie multis confirmatur. Iuuenis fui (inquit Dauid) & iam senui, nec vidi iustum derelictum, neque posteros eius mendicantes panem. Deinde singuli vocationi diuinae sese ac commodent, neque ignauum otium sequantur, sed labore aliquo honesto victum sibi parare satagant. Fecerunt hoc olim sanctissimi patres, quorum labores benedictione liberalissima Deus probauit. Et cur hodie alicuius operis pudeat Christianos homines, qui patrem credentium Abrahamum, Isaacum item, Iacobum, Mosem, Dauidem agros coluisse & pecora pauisse audiunt? qui deniq; aeternum Dei filium, iam homine factum in pauperis fabri Iosephi domo inter quotidianos labores aduetum esse norunt? Aut cur iuuenes patritij & ad rempub. nati ignominiosum sibi ducat, si aut agri culturae intenti sint, aut alijs sese laboribus exerceant, quando constat tunc maxime veteri reipub. floruisse, & imperio atq; potentia auctas esse, quando ab aratro in curiam Patres veniebant, & ex triumphalibus curribus ad agros suos reuertebantur? Quam potius turpe est eos in ignauo otio consenescere, qui Christum suum seruatorem profitentur, cuius vita omnis laborum & negotiorum plena fuit, & qui Apostolis praeceptoribus gloriantur, qui piscando, texendo & alijs opificijs victum sibi parauerunt? Horum igitur consideratione omnes excitati, etiam ignaui fugiant, & mox sentient, artibus hisce malis & inhonestis nequaquam sibi opus esse, quibus hodie multi sibiipsis consulunt. Accedat his magistratuum industria, quorum est ad labores & opera honesta suos adiuefacere, leges sumptuarias tueri, luxui & intemperantiae modum statuere, otiosis aditum ad rempub. praecludere: quod olim Athenienses & Massilienses, homines sapientia & virtute celeberrimos, non minori cum fructu quam laude fecisse scimus. Apud illos enim Areopagita quid quisque ciuium faceret, aut quo nam quaestu sustentaretur, diligentissime inquirere solebant. Hi vero ab otio ita abhorruerunt, ut neque Mimis & histrionibus locum darent, neq; intra vrbem admitterent eos, qui sub alicuius religionis simulatione inertiae alimenta quaerebant. Quorum exempla si hodie principes & vrbium magistratus sequerentur, breui Respub. & Ecclesias magis videremus florere.
units.tr: But what, then, is that way? First, each person should look to God's promises, which He generously offers to those who walk in their calling, for living a life that is decent and honourable. Let each one apply these promises to himself and not doubt their truth, which was long ago shown by very many examples and is confirmed every day by many. "I have been young," says David, "and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his descendants begging for bread." Next, each person should apply himself to his divine calling and not pursue idle sloth, but strive to provide for himself a livelihood by some honest labour. The most holy Fathers did this long ago, and God approved their labours with the most generous blessing. And why should Christians be ashamed of any kind of work, when they hear that Abraham, the father of believers, and likewise Isaac, Jacob, Moses and David tilled fields and tended flocks, and when they know that the eternal Son of God, now made man, came into the home of the poor carpenter Joseph and lived among daily labours? Or why should young men of patrician birth, born for the commonwealth, count it disgraceful to be devoted to tilling the land or to exercise themselves in other labours, since it is certain that the ancient commonwealth flourished most when its fathers came to the senate from the plough and returned to their fields from triumphal chariots, and grew in empire and power? How much more shameful it is that those who profess Christ as their Saviour, whose whole life was full of toil and business, and who boast of the Apostles as their teachers, who by fishing, weaving and other trades earned their living, should grow old in idle sloth! Therefore, let all who are stirred by the consideration of these things, even the lazy, flee, and they will soon feel that there is no need for those base and dishonourable arts by which many today provide for themselves. Let the diligence of magistrates be added to these, whose duty it is to accustom their people to labour and honest work, to uphold sumptuary laws, to set limits on luxury and intemperance, and to close the doors of public office to idlers. We know that the Athenians and the Massilians, peoples most famous for wisdom and virtue, did this long ago with no less profit than praise. For among them the Areopagus used to inquire most carefully what each citizen did and by what gain he supported himself. And they so abhorred idleness that they gave no place to mimes and actors, nor admitted within the city those who sought the means of idleness under the pretence of some religion. If princes and the magistrates of cities followed these examples today, we would soon see the commonwealth and the Churches flourish more.

units.la: Porro redeamus ad nostrum illum, qui quod animo conceperat consilium, facto exequitur. Nam ad se vocatus omnibus sui heri debitoribus, singulis ex summa, quam debebant, aliquid detrahit. Et primum quidem, qui batos sive cados olei centum debebat, nouas tabulas vel nouum obligationum instrumentum conscribere iubet, quo quinquaginta tantum continentur. Idem postea cum reliquis fecit, ut omnes illos tato beneficio sibi obstringeret, & ex alieno sibi amicos pararet, qui ipsum adiuuarent. Vbi rursum malae fidei dispensatorum artes exprimuntur, quas non in cum finem Christus describit, ut aliquis eas imitetur, sed potius ut sibi ab illis cauere possint, quibus cum illis res est. At hodie tanta est astutia illorum hominum, ut ne Lynceis quidem oculis omnes eorum fraudes & dolos possint deprehendi: & cum nemini quicquam remittant, sed potius summo rigore extremum quoque quadrantem exigant, ita tamen sibi ipsis prospicere norunt, ut suorum magistratuum impensis sibi amicos parent, & cum illos etiam turpissime fallant, tamen fidelissimi & integerrimi dicantur. Dispensator eiusmodi Iudas fuit, qui ideo unguenti pretiosi super Christi caput effusi unctionem aegre tulit, quod praeclaram defraudandi occasionem sibi ex manibus elapsam esse videret. Et huius discipuli atque successores sunt, qui vel in Ecclesia vel Repub. pecunias aut quacunque alia bona sibi credita
units.tr: But let us return to that man of ours, who carries out with deed what he had conceived in mind. For, having summoned all his lord's debtors, he takes something off the sum that each owed. And first, to the man who owed a hundred baths, or jars, of oil, he orders that new tablets, or a new bond, be drawn up, in which only fifty are stated. He did the same afterwards with the rest, so that he might bind all of them to himself by such a favour and make for himself, out of another's property, friends who would help him. Here again the tricks of dishonest stewards are laid bare, which Christ does not describe so that anyone should imitate them, but rather so that we may guard against those with whom we have to deal. Yet today the cunning of such men is so great that not even with lynx eyes can all their frauds and tricks be detected. And although they remit nothing to anyone, but rather exact even the last farthing with the utmost rigour, they nevertheless know how to look after themselves so well that, at the expense of their superiors, they make friends for themselves, and although they deceive even those very men most shamefully, they are still called most faithful and upright. Such a steward was Judas, who for this reason took it hard that precious ointment was poured over Christ's head, because he saw that a splendid opportunity to defraud had slipped from his hands. His disciples and successors are those who, whether in the Church or in the commonwealth, steal money or whatever other goods have been entrusted to them

units.la: disd dita suffurantur: quod non uno modo (ut diximus) solet fieri. Nam inter expensorum rationes saepe adscribunt, quod ipsi nunquam dederunt, aut inter accepta minus consignant quam acceperunt. Sa-pe etiam ab iis, quos meticulosiores esse vident, multa extorquent publicae authoritatis praetextu, quae postea sibi ipsis reseruant. Taceo nunc fraudes in contractibus, in monetae & numorum ratio-nibus, in frugum distractione, & sexcenta alia, quibus possunt oculatissimis quoque fucum facere, ut sub reipub. praetextu res suas agant. At meminisse idem debebant, frustra ea homines celari, quae Dei oculis patent, qui occultissima quaeque videt. Et qui olim Iudam peculatorem, & Ananiam, qui in propriis pecuniis fraudem commisit, exemplis novis atque horrendis puniuit, nunquam impunitos dimittet eos, qui illorum vestigiis insistunt. At quod de illis dicitur, non minus ad eos pertinet, qui priuatim seruiunt, quales sunt famuli domestici & famulae vel ancillae. Nam istorum quoq; vocatio a Domino est, a quo reportabunt (ut Paulus ait) quicquid boni aut mali fecerint. Serviat ergo cum simplicitate cordis, & cum timore ac tremore, neq; ad oculum modo seruiant, ut qui hominibus placere studeant, sed ut serui Christi ex animo faciant, quae vult Deus. Vide Ephes. 6.
units.tr: ... (as we have said, this is not done in one way only). For among the entries of expenses they often record what they never gave, or among receipts they enter less than they received. Often, too, from those whom they see to be more timid, they extort many things under the pretext of public authority, which they afterwards keep for themselves. I say nothing now of frauds in contracts, in the accounting of money and coin, in the sale of grain, and in six hundred other things by which they can deceive even the most watchful, so that under the pretext of the commonwealth they may carry on their own affairs. Yet these men ought to remember that it is in vain that men hide what lies open to the eyes of God, who sees the most hidden things. And He who long ago punished Judas the embezzler, and Ananias, who committed fraud in his own money, with new and dreadful examples, will never let go unpunished those who walk in their footsteps. But what is said of those men pertains no less to those who serve in private households, such as domestic servants, maidservants and handmaids. For their calling too is from the Lord, from whom, as Paul says, they will receive whatever good or evil they have done. Let them therefore serve with simplicity of heart, and with fear and trembling, and not serve only before the eyes, as men who seek to please men, but as servants of Christ do from the heart what God wills. See Eph. 6.

units.la: Restat postrema parabolae pars, qua eius argumentu atq; scopus continetur. Et laudauit dominus (inquit) dispensatorem iniustum, quod prudenter fecisset. Laudatisse eum dicitur herus, non quod fraudes & impostura probentur Deo, sed quod ex hominum sensu atque more Christus loquitur. Ita laudare dicimur ea, quae admiratione prosequimur, aut in quibus astutiam & prudentiam eorum per Sarcasmum probamus, qui revera vituperio digni sunt. Et mox gnomen generalem subjicit, quod omnes excitat, ut sibi a filiis huius seculi cauent. Nam sic ait: Quoniam filij huius seculi prudentiores sunt filiis lucis in suo genere. Quae sententia reprehensionis speciem habet, ac si diceret: Mirum sane est filios lucis, id est, homines a Deo consecratos & Verbi atq; Spiritus luce illustratos, tanta stupidos & socordes esse in iis, quae ad salutem aeternam spectant, cum huic mundo dediti tanta solertia atq; industria res suas agant, ne huius mortalis vitae praesidiis destituantur. Quin ergo experg. ..., vt ipsi quoq; quos suorum bonorum dispensatores Deus constituit, vobis amicos paretis, quorum opera vobis aliquando utilis atq; salutaris sit. At quia parabola totius sententiae atq; scopum postea ipse Dominus exponet, ista modo sufficiant. Nunc autem obseruemus Christum nobis commune vitium exprobrare, quo fit, ut res huius seculi maiori studio agamus, quam vitae aeternae negotium. Exempla in omni vita plurima occurrunt. Quid enim non faciunt auari ut opum aceruos cogerant? Per terras & maria discurrunt, mille discrimina vitae subeunt, noctes insomnes ducunt, laboribus totam familiam fatigant, seipsos curis conficiunt. At quantos ijdem in verae & coelestis sapientiae studio progressus facerent, si vel decimam laborum istorum partem huic serio impenderent? At hic fere frigent, & nimium illis videtur quicquid Deus exigit. Ide de ambitiosis & aurae popularis captatoribus dicere licet, qui seruitutem omnium inhonestissimam subeunt, & vulgo ignobili, quem vere bestiam multorum capitum veteres dixerunt, turpissime assentantur: qui interim eximijs Dei seruis, piis nimirum magistratibus & fidis verbi diuini doctoribus parere detrectat, qui ipsos ad caelestem & aeternam gloriam euehere studeant. Quid vero de impuris scortatoribus dicemus, quos illicitus amor eo redigit, ut omnes animi & corporis vires incredibili industria intendant ad libidini suae satisfaciendum? at ijdem in coelestium bonorum amore prorsus frigent, neq; illa putant digna esse, quorum causa aliquid faciant. Quod si veritatis Euangelicae hostes spectemus, quid hos labo riosius, ingeniosius & pertinacius in oppugnanda luce illa, qua tantopere oderunt, stertentibus inter ea & omnem laborem subterfugentibus pijs, qui veritatis studium profitentur? Excitet nos istorum consideratio, ut nos tam turpis socordiae pudeat, & ne ex nostris moribus hostium ingenia atq; consilia iudicemus. Nunquam enim illi dormiunt & omnem extinguendae doctrinae puriorus occasionem venantur. Vigilemus ergo etiam nos, & fidem nostram publice testemur beneficentia in fratres egenos, innocentia vitae & cultus puritate, ut olim coelestis regni haeredes simus cum Christo Iesu, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of the parable, which contains its argument and aim. "And the lord," he says, "praised the unjust steward, because he had acted prudently." The lord is said to have praised him not because fraud and deceit are approved by God, but because Christ speaks according to human feeling and custom. Thus we are said to praise those things which we follow with admiration, or those in which we commend the cunning and prudence of men who, in truth, deserve blame, by way of sarcasm. And soon after he adds a general maxim which rouses everyone to beware of the sons of this world. For he says: "For the sons of this world are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation." This saying has the appearance of a rebuke, as if he were saying: It is truly strange that the sons of light, that is, men consecrated to God and illumined by the light of the Word and the Spirit, should be so dull and careless in those things which concern eternal salvation, when those given over to this world carry on their affairs with such skill and diligence, lest they be deprived of the protections of this mortal life. Therefore, make for yourselves friends, even from those whom God has appointed as stewards of His goods, by whose help you may at some time be served and saved. But since the Lord Himself will afterwards explain the whole meaning and aim of the parable, let these few words suffice for now. Let us observe, however, that Christ reproaches us with a common fault, by which we pursue the things of this age with greater zeal than the business of eternal life. Examples abound in every life. For what do not the greedy do to heap up piles of wealth? They run over lands and seas, undergo a thousand dangers to life, lie awake through sleepless nights, wear out their whole households with toil, and waste themselves with cares. But how much progress would these same men make in the pursuit of true and heavenly wisdom if they devoted even a tenth part of those labours to this earnestly! But here they grow cold, and whatever God demands seems to them far too much. The same may be said of the ambitious and of those who hunt after popular applause, who submit to the most dishonourable servitude and most basely flatter the common mob, which the ancients rightly called a beast with many heads; yet meanwhile they refuse to obey God's choice servants, namely pious magistrates and faithful teachers of the divine Word, who strive to raise them to heavenly and eternal glory. And what shall we say of the impure whoremongers, whom unlawful love drives to bend all the powers of mind and body, with incredible industry, to satisfy their lust? Yet these same men grow utterly cold in the love of heavenly goods, and do not think those things worth doing anything for. But if we look at the enemies of the Gospel truth, what do they do with more toil, ingenuity and stubbornness in attacking that light which they so greatly hate, while meanwhile the pious, who profess a zeal for the truth, snore and shun every labour? Let the consideration of these men stir us up, so that we may be ashamed of such shameful sloth, and so that we do not judge their minds and counsels from our own habits. For they never sleep, and they hunt for every opportunity to extinguish the purer doctrine. Let us therefore also be watchful, and publicly bear witness to our faith by generosity towards needy brethren, by innocence of life and purity of worship, so that we may one day be heirs of the heavenly kingdom with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLV.
units.tr: HOMILY CLV.

units.la: Et ego vobis dico, Facite vobis amicos ex mammona iniquitatis, ut cum defeceritis, recipiant vos in aeterna tabernacula. Qui fidelis est in minimo, etiam in magno fidelis est: & qui in minimo iniustus est, etiam in magno est iniustus. Si ergo in iniusto mammona fideles non fuistis, verum mammona quis credet vobis? Et si in alieno fideles non fuistis, quod vestrum est quis dabit vobis? Nullus seruus potest duobus dominis seruire: Aut enim vnum odio habebit, & alterum diliget: aut vni adhaerebit, & alterum contemnet. Non potestis Deo seruire & mammonae.
units.tr: "And I say to you, make for yourselves friends by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. He who is faithful in the least is faithful also in much, and he who is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust the true riches to you? And if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own? No servant can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon."

units.la: Quoniam Deus teste Ioanne Apostolo ipsissima charitas est, & in nos continuo atque irremissio benefaciendi studio bona sua confert: nos quoque sui similes esse vult, & proinde nihil a nobis frequentius & diligentius exigit, quam dilectionem & beneficentiam mutuam. Extant huius voluntatis testimonia passim in Lege & prophetis, quibus per omnia Christus Iesus consentit, sicuti cum alibi tum in praesenti hac eius concione videmus. Quia autem ea est nostrae naturae prauitas, ut opum huius saeculi administratio, quae nobis ad beneficentiae studium adiumento esse debebat, nos quam maxime remoretur, de illis & vero earum vsu ante omnia disserit, & ut doctrina haec animis nostris altius atque tenacius haereat, ea parabola eleganti vestitam proponit. Docet enim nos Dei dispensatores esse: unde sequitur opes ab illo dari, & ita quidem, ut penes eum maneat proprietas, nobis autem illarum dispensatio sola committatur, & proinde neminem debere eas sibi quasi proprias vendicare, sed in eum vsum conferre, quem Deus tradidit, ne dum illis vel per auariam, vel per luxum & saltum abutimur, nosipsos bonis caelestibus atque aeternis spoliemus. Id vero nunc Christus pluribus exponit atque confirmat.
units.tr: Since God, as the Apostle John witnesses, is love itself, he constantly and without ceasing bestows his goods by an eagerness to do good. He also wills that we be like him, and therefore he requires nothing from us more often or more diligently than mutual love and beneficence. Testimonies to this will are found everywhere in the Law and the Prophets, with which Christ Jesus agrees in every respect, as we see both elsewhere and in this present sermon of his. But because it is our nature's perversity that the management of the wealth of this world, which ought to help us in the eagerness to do good, delays us most of all, he first discusses those riches and their true use, and, so that this teaching may cling more deeply and firmly to our minds, he sets it forth clothed in an elegant parable. For he teaches us that we are stewards of God. From this it follows that riches are given by him, in such a way that ownership remains with him, while only their management is entrusted to us. Therefore no one should claim them for himself as if they were his own, but should put them to the use God has appointed, lest by avarice or by luxury and dissipation we abuse them and strip ourselves of the heavenly and eternal goods. Christ now sets out and confirms this at greater length.

units.la: Et initio quidem totius parabolae scopum & vsum paucis verbis indicat: Et ego vobis dico, Facite vobis amicos ex mammona iniquitatis, ut cum defeceritis recipiant vos in aeterna tabernacula. Quasi diceret: Auditis quam solertia sibi prospiciant, qui opum alienarum dispensatores ab hominibus constituti sunt. Hi quam primum se ab illa functione amouendos fore resciscunt, mox sibi ex alieno amicos parant, quorum beneficentia deinceps subleuentur. Quanto magis ergo vos omnes anniti decet, ut diuitiis, quae vobis a Deo creditae sunt, amicos vobis conciliteris, cum quibus olim aeternas beatae immortalitatis sedes incolatis? Sunt autem in paucis hisce verbis, quibus tota diuitiarum huius saeculi ratio continetur, quaedam diligentius consideranda, de quibus ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: And at the start of the whole parable he indicates its aim and use in a few words: "And I say to you, make for yourselves friends by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings." As if he were saying: You see with what cleverness those men provide for themselves who have been appointed by men as stewards of other people's wealth. As soon as they learn that they are about to be removed from that office, they at once make friends for themselves out of what is another's, by whose kindness they are afterwards supported. How much more, then, ought you all to strive to win for yourselves friends by the riches that have been entrusted to you by God, friends with whom you may one day dwell in the eternal abodes of blessed immortality? In these few words, which contain the whole account of the riches of this world, there are some points to be considered more carefully, and we shall speak of them in order.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum, quod illas Mammona iniquitatis Christus appellat. Atqui Mammona Syriacam vocem esse Hieronymus scribit, quae idem significat, quod Graecus πλοῦτος, quem ipsi Deum diuitiarum finxerunt. Diuus Augustinus Punica lingua, quae cum Syriaca magnam affinitatem habuit, eadem voce lucrum denotari testatur. Et credibile est, Christum eo vocabulo vti voluisse, quod tunc inter Iudaeos vulgare erat, & diuitiis nescio quid magnum tribuebat, cum τοῖς πλήκτω Graecorum responderet. Ideo ut animos stulta & pernitiosa opum admiratione atque cupiditate liberet, Mammona iniquitatis dicere voluit. Atqui certum est, cum hoc loco non agere de male & iniquè partis opibus. Nam liberalitatem & beneficentiam in pauperes nobis commendat, quae Deo non probatur, si eam ex alieno aut iniuste acquisitis exerceamus. Qui enim in Lege probibuit, ne quis in quocunque voto mercedem meretricis aut pretium canis inferat in domum Domini, eadem ratione prohibet, ne ex rapinis aut furtis vel sanguinis pretio eleemosynas faciamus, quae inter sacrificia censeri merentur, eo quod sibi factum aestimat Dei Filius quicquid in pauperes suos confertur. Ideo Tobias filio suo dicebat: De facultatibus tuis exerce beneficentiam. Et Zachaeus cum ad Christum conuersus esset, se male partorum restitutionem quadruplam facturum, & insuper dimidium suarum facultatum in pauperes erogaturum esse pollicebatur. Cur ergo (inquis) Christus Mammona iniquitatis dicit? Ab effectu nimirum & propter multiplicem abusum, qui apud eos cernitur, qui animos suos fide & pietate vera non probè munierunt. Nam si ea, ex quibus diuitiae constant, confidere res, utpote agros, pecora, aurum argentumque et quaecunque alia sunt huius generis: omnia ista Dei creaturae & eiusdem dona sunt, quibus suorum quoque fidem atque pietatem in hoc etiam saeculo interdum remunerat, ut in Abrahami, Iosephi & multorum aliorum exemplis apparet. Sed ex nostra natura vitio abusus multiplex nascitur, & quia in illam incidunt, irritamenta multorum fiunt (ut veteris Poetae verbis ytar)
units.tr: The first thing that meets us here is that Christ calls them "the mammon of unrighteousness." Now Jerome writes that Mammon is a Syriac word, which means the same as the Greek ploutos, which they made into a god of riches. Saint Augustine testifies that in the Punic language, which had a great affinity with Syriac, the same word denotes gain. And it is credible that Christ wished to use that term, which was then common among the Jews, and which attributed some great power to riches, since it corresponded to the Greek word [τῷ πλούτῳ]. So, in order to free minds from the foolish and destructive admiration and desire for wealth, he chose to call it the mammon of unrighteousness. It is certain, however, that he is not speaking here of wealth gained wrongly and unjustly. For he commends to us liberality and beneficence towards the poor, and this is not pleasing to God if we exercise it with what has been acquired from another's property or unjustly. For in the Law he forbade anyone, in any vow whatever, to bring into the house of the Lord the wages of a harlot or the price of a dog; by the same reasoning he forbids us to give alms from plunder, theft, or the price of blood, since the Son of God counts as done to himself whatever is given to his poor, and such gifts deserve to be reckoned among sacrifices. Therefore Tobit said to his son: "From your substance give alms." And Zacchaeus, when he had been converted to Christ, promised that he would make fourfold restitution of what he had gained wrongfully, and would moreover give half of his goods to the poor. "Why then," you ask, "does Christ call it the mammon of unrighteousness?" Plainly from its effect, and because of the manifold abuse that is seen among those who have not properly fortified their minds with true faith and piety. For if we consider the things of which riches consist, namely fields, flocks, gold and silver, and whatever else is of this kind, all these are creatures of God and gifts of his, by which he sometimes rewards the faith and piety of his people even in this world, as appears in the examples of Abraham, Joseph and many others. But from the vice of our nature a manifold abuse arises, and because men fall into it, they become the incitements of many (to use the words of an old poet).

units.la: Argumentum parabolae praecedentis.
units.tr: Argument of the preceding parable.

units.la: Mammona iniquitatis. ytar) & multis sceleribus occasionem atque materiam præbent. Vulgare etenim est, quod illarum abundantia confidentes reddit: at confidentiam mox sequitur fastus & insolentia, inhumanitas & superbia aliorum hominum contemptus, luxus, libido, petulantia morum, quibus omnibus fere comes adest avaritia & insatiabilis illas augendi cupiditas. Nam vt per se arrident carni, ita accessione sua huius desideria indies accendunt, & licet aliqui in ijs tractandis prodigaliores sint, ijdem tamen sua profusione coguntur, vt fere tenaciores sint vbi minime oportebat, vt luxui & intemperantiæ suæ possint satisfacere. Et quia apud sanctos quoque vitijs ipsis interdum locus est, non tamen hæ etiam, quæ iustis rationibus partæ sunt, aut ex peculiari Dei benedictione obtigerunt, iniquitatis diuitiæ dicuntur. Quibus addere licet, quod etsi sancti sibijpsis diligenter caueant, & illis rectissime vtantur, non idem tamen semper hæredum animus est, qui vt primum in liberam earum possessionem veniunt, desiderijs suis indulgere, & multa aduersus charitatis & innocentiæ leges pa-trare incipiunt. Quæ causa est, quod alibi Scriptura diuitias laqueum & spinas dicit, eo quod ob in-hærentem nobis naturæ corruptionem periculosa est earum tractatio, quæ si per se æstimetur, diuinæ bonitatis præclarum donum sunt. Possunt etiam iniquæ dici, quod caducæ & fluxæ sunt, & ideo fe-re eos præter omnem expectationem fallunt, qui sibi in illis certum & perpetuum vitæ præsidium constituerunt: qua de re supra capite duodecimo plura diximus. Vt enim non semper præstant felicitatem, quam prima fronte pollicentur, cum comites habeant curas, laborem, metum & infinita alia, quæ sæpe vitam ipsam nobis amaram reddunt: ita plerunque suos cultores atque custodes subito deserunt, qui eas animabus suis chariores habebant. Et de hus quidem diligentius dicimus propter eos, qui cum ob pauperta-tem, cum qua ipsi conflictantur, morosiores sint, diuites omnes temere damnant & studiosè omnia ea corradunt, quæcunque in diuitiarum vituperium tam in sacris quam prophanis scriptoribus dicuntur. Hi vero meminisse debebant, corruptos diuitum mores ita reprehendi ac tra-duci debere, ne qua interea Deo iniuria fiat, neque huius dona præclara & vtilia propter nostram prauitatem damnentur. Sed & diuites nunquam non cogitent, quo epitheto æterna Dei sapientia di-uitias ornet. Huius enim consideratio faciet, vt neq; anxiè nimis illas acquirere cupiant, neque ijs-dem animos suos applicent: adhæc eosdem in officio continebit, ne earum fiducia in charitatem fra-ternam & sanctitatem vitæ insolenter peccent.
units.tr: Mammon of unrighteousness. (to use the words of an old poet) and they furnish occasion and material for many crimes. For it is commonly known that their abundance makes men confident; and confidence is soon followed by pride and insolence, inhumanity and arrogance, contempt for other men, luxury, lust, and wantonness of morals, almost all of which are accompanied by avarice and an insatiable desire to increase them. For just as they smile upon the flesh of themselves, so by their addition they kindle these desires day by day; and although some are more prodigal in handling them, the same men are nonetheless compelled by their own profusion to be almost stingier where it least ought to be, so that they may satisfy their luxury and intemperance. And because even among the saints vices sometimes find a place, those riches are not called riches of unrighteousness, even though they were gained by just means or came by the special blessing of God. To these things it may be added that, although the saints carefully guard themselves and use these goods most rightly, the mind of their heirs is not always the same: as soon as they come into free possession of them, they begin to indulge their desires and to commit many acts against the laws of charity and innocence. This is why Scripture elsewhere calls riches a snare and thorns, because, on account of the corruption of nature that clings to us, the handling of them is dangerous; yet if they are considered in themselves, they are an excellent gift of divine goodness. They may also be called unrighteous because they are perishable and fleeting, and so they very often deceive, beyond all expectation, those who have set up in them a sure and lasting protection for their life; concerning which matter we have said more above, in chapter twelve. For just as they do not always give the happiness they promise at first sight, since they bring with them cares, labour, fear and countless other things that often make life itself bitter to us, so they generally desert suddenly those who cultivated and guarded them, and who held them dearer than their own souls. And we say these things more carefully on account of those who, being rather peevish because of the poverty with which they themselves struggle, rashly condemn all the rich and eagerly gather together everything that is said against riches, whether in sacred or in profane writers. Yet these men ought to remember that the corrupt morals of the rich should be rebuked and exposed in such a way that no wrong is done meanwhile to God, and that his splendid and useful gifts are not condemned on account of our perversity. But let the rich also never fail to consider with what epithet the eternal wisdom of God adorns riches. For the consideration of this will ensure that they neither desire to acquire them too anxiously nor attach their minds to them; and further, it will keep them within their duty, lest, trusting in them, they sin arrogantly against brotherly charity and the holiness of life.

units.la: Proderit ergo nunc verum quoque & licitum vsum diuitiarum propius intueri, quo minus à nobis peccetur. Est autem hic etiam multiplex. Primò nostræ necessitati seruire debent. Nec enim ita earum dispensatores nos facit Deus, vt omnis fructus ad alios redeat, nos vero nihil inde præmij recipiamus. Sed vt dispensatores ex sua functione mercedem habent, unde viuunt, ita nobis quoque victum & alia necessaria huius vitæ subsidia ex opibus à Deo datis recipere licet. Minimè ergo peccant, qui diuitijs suis fruuntur, & ex illis commodum viuunt, modò in alijs etiam sui officij probè sint memores. Id enim sanctissimos quosq; cultores Dei olim fecisse legimus. Deinde cum nos totos & omnia nostra Deo debeamus, huius quoque cultus diuitijs nostris adiuuari & prouehi debet. Atqui ipse quidem neque auro & argento, neq; vestibus aut pecoribus nostris opus habet: gratis-simus autem illi cultus est, si verbi sui doctrina longè lateque diuulgetur, si ecclesiæ conseruen-tur, & legitimus Sacramentorum vsus retineatur. Quæ omnia cum absque scholis, verbi præco-nibus & Ecclesiarum ministris fieri non possint, non poterimus diuitijs nostris melius vti, quam si scholas & in his agentium studia adiuuemus, & Verbi administros foueamus, ne qui inopia pres-si Ecclesiam relinquere & aliam vitæ rationem inire cogantur. Ideo olim Deus Sacerdotibus & Leuitis ex terra totius prouentibus decimas atque primitias reddere, & in publico populi cen-su vnumquenque qui in censum veniebat, dimidium siclum in cultum tabernaculi sacri aut tem-pli dare iußit. Quod olim Christiani principes obseruarunt, & decimas Ecclesijs hinc inde at-tribuerunt, quod non aliam conseruandi ministerij Ecclesiasticii & externi cultus rationem com-modiorem inuenire posse viderent. Tertius diuitiarum vsus est in ijs, quæ ad Rempub. pertinent. Quia enim multa sunt, quæ non nisi publicis impensis fieri possunt, siue ædificia publica, vrbium munitiones, vias, fontes, iuris administrationem, legationes, bellicum apparatum & infinita alia, quæ ad Reipublicæ conseruationem necessaria sunt, siue magistratuum & publicorum ministrorum stipendia pendemus, optimo sanè iure exigitur, vt singuli pro suarum facultatum ratione quod publica authoritate constitutum & in quauis gente receptum est, contribuant. Admonet de hoc Christus, quando Caesari reddere iubet quae sunt Caesaris, & ipse sub censu nasci & tam suo quam Petri nomine didrachma dare voluit, ne quis suo exemplo abuteretur, aut sub libertatis Christiana praetextu immunitatem sibi vendicaret. Et notum est illud Pauli: Reddite omnibus quod debetis: cui tributum debetur, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal. Itaque graue illorum scelus est, qui in iis fraudulenter agunt, & ijdem in legitimum diuitiarum vsum non sine totius reipub. incommodo peccant. Postremo pauperum quoque subuentioni opes nostrae inseruire debent, ut nostra abundantia aliorum inopiam subleuet atque farciat. Et de isto potissimum facultatum vsu Dominus in praesenti loquitur. Exigit hunc passim scriptura sacra, & in Lege pauperibus ita prospectum voluit Deus ne qui essent, qui ab opulentioribus neglecti victum suum ab alijs emendicare cogerentur. Et idem multas rationes ostendit, quibus tam publice quem priuatim illis subueniri possit. Propheta etiam de beneficentia in pauperes saepe concionantur, & eam omnibus sacrificijs & ieiunijs longe praeferunt. Christus item, ne quae nobis restaret tergiuersandi occasio, illos sibi substituit, & ut in eos conferamus iussit, quae in ipsum vellemus conferre, si adhuc in terris ageret. Quorum omnium Apostoli memores, hoc sui officij in primis esse putauerunt, ut ipsi causam egentium susciperent, & cum in Iudaeorum gente Sacerdotum partim incuria, partim auaritia & rapacitate res eo deuenisset, ut contra Legem Dei mendicorum plena essent omnia, qui & vias publicas & templi fores obsidebant: Apostoli id effectum dederunt, ut in primitiua Ecclesia nullus haberetur, cui vitae subsidia deesset, aut qui ostiatim panem flipemue peteret: & ijdem ecclesias passim hortati sunt, ut exterorum quoque inopiae succurrerent. Iubet hoc communis humanitatis sensus, ut eorum misereamur, qui cum eius dem naturae nobiscum consortes sint, durius tamen tractantur. Neque poterimus non eorum miseria tangi, si cogitemus a nobis quoque nihil humani alienum esse, & nobis idem posse accidere, quod illis accidit. Et ista quidem gentium philosophi viderunt, qui eos demum proxime ad Deorum similitudinem dixerunt accedere, qui quàm plurimis benefaciunt. At diligentiores in hus esse conuenit Christianos homines, quos Deus ipse suo Verbo ad ista officia excitat, & qui in Christo Iesu in vnum corpus coaluerunt, quique nisi vno spiritu ducantur, corporis istius membra censeri non possunt. At quis eodem spiritu eos duci & animari dixerit, qui suis modo rebus intenti, aliorum miserias securè negligunt? Non temerè ergo de pauperum subuentione Christus saepe concionatur: quae doctrina & si ad omnes homines extendi debeat, in primis tamen ad eos pertinet, qui diuitijs pluribus à Deo donati sunt. Hi ergo meminerint, se Dei dispensatores esse, qui certo iudicio alios alijs opulentiores & pauperiores facit, ut mutuae beneficentiae inter nos locus sit: adeoque ut ad illius istius necessitatis vinculo astringi nos sentiamus, cum nemo sibi ipsi solus sufficiat, sed alter alterius opera & auxilio habeat opus. Turpe & iniquum iudicatur, si quis dispensator ab hominibus constitutus, aliena bona vel negligentius tractet, vel etiam fraudulenter diripiat. At quanto turpius scelus & maiori supplico dignum est, in dispensatione diuinitus commissa perfidum & iniustum de prahendi.
units.tr: It will therefore be useful now to look more closely at the true and lawful use of riches, so that we sin less. This use is also manifold. First, they ought to serve our own necessity. God does not make us stewards of them in such a way that all the fruit goes to others while we receive no reward from it. Just as stewards have wages from their office, by which they live, so we too may receive from the wealth given by God our food and the other necessities of this life. Those who enjoy their riches and live on them by no means sin, provided they are also mindful of their duty to others. We read that the holiest worshippers of God did this in the past. Next, since we owe ourselves and all we have to God, his worship too ought to be aided and advanced by our riches. Yet he has no need of our gold, silver, clothing or livestock. His worship is most pleasing to him if the teaching of his Word is spread far and wide, if the churches are preserved, and if the lawful use of the sacraments is maintained. Since all these things cannot be done without schools, preachers of the Word and ministers of the churches, we cannot use our riches better than by helping the schools and those who labour in them, and by supporting the ministers of the Word, so that they are not forced by poverty to leave the Church and take up some other way of life. For this reason God once ordered the priests and Levites to be given tithes and firstfruits from the produce of the whole land, and ordered each man who was enrolled in the public census to give half a shekel for the worship of the holy tabernacle or temple. Christian princes later observed this, and assigned tithes to the churches here and there, because they saw that no more suitable way could be found of maintaining the ministry of the Church and external worship. The third use of riches concerns those things that pertain to the commonwealth. For there are many things that can be done only at public expense: public buildings, city fortifications, roads, springs, the administration of justice, embassies, military equipment and countless other things necessary for the preservation of the commonwealth. We also pay the salaries of magistrates and public officials. Most certainly, by the best right, each person is required, according to his means, to contribute to what has been established by public authority and accepted in every nation. Christ gives instruction on this when he bids us render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and when he himself was born under the census and wished to pay the didrachma in his own name and in Peter's, so that no one might abuse his example or claim exemption for himself under the pretext of Christian liberty. And that saying of Paul is well known: Render to all what you owe: to whom tribute is owed, tribute; to whom custom, custom. Therefore grave is the wickedness of those who act fraudulently in these matters, and who by so doing sin against the lawful use of riches, to the no small harm of the whole commonwealth. Lastly, our resources ought also to serve the relief of the poor, so that our abundance may lighten and fill the want of others. It is chiefly of this use of possessions that the Lord speaks in the present passage. Holy Scripture demands it everywhere, and in the Law God provided for the poor in such a way that there should be none who, neglected by the wealthier, were compelled to beg their food from others. He also shows many ways in which help can be given to them, both publicly and privately. The prophets too often preach about beneficence towards the poor, and they set it far above all sacrifices and fastings. Likewise Christ, so that we might have no opening for evasion, has placed the poor in his own stead, and has commanded that what we would wish to bestow upon him, were he still on earth, we should bestow upon them. Mindful of all this, the apostles judged that the first of their duties was to take up the cause of the needy themselves. When, among the Jewish nation, through the negligence of some priests and the greed and rapacity of others, matters had reached such a point that, contrary to the Law of God, everything was full of beggars who besieged the public roads and the doors of the temple, the apostles brought it about that in the primitive Church there was no one who lacked the means of life, or who went from door to door begging bread or a coin. And these same apostles urged the churches everywhere to relieve the want of strangers too. The common sense of humanity bids us pity those who, though they are sharers of the same nature with us, are treated more harshly. Nor can we fail to be moved by their misery, if we consider that nothing human is foreign to us, and that what has happened to them could happen to us as well. The philosophers of the nations saw this, and they said that those come closest to the likeness of the gods who do good to the greatest number. But it is fitting that Christians should be more diligent in these things, since God himself stirs them up to these duties by his Word, and since they have grown together in Christ Jesus into one body, and cannot be counted members of that body unless they are led by one Spirit. Yet who would say that they are led and animated by that same Spirit, if they, intent only upon their own affairs, carelessly neglect the miseries of others? It is not without reason, then, that Christ so often preaches about the relief of the poor. Although this teaching ought to extend to all men, it nevertheless pertains chiefly to those whom God has endowed with greater riches. Let these therefore remember that they are stewards of God, who by his certain judgment makes some richer and others poorer, so that there may be room for mutual beneficence among us; and so that we may feel ourselves bound together by the tie of this need, since no one is sufficient for himself alone, but each has need of another's labour and help. It is judged base and unjust if a steward appointed by men treats another's goods carelessly, or even plunders them dishonestly. How much more base a crime, and how much more deserving of punishment, is it to be faithless and unjust in a stewardship committed to us by God!

units.la: Sed de eo etiam nos hic apertius admonet Christus, quando beneficii amplissimi praemij promissionem ita proponit, ut simul doceat, quid de duris illis & inhumanis fratrum egentium contemptoribus Pater caelestis iam pridem decreuerit. Facite (inquit) vobis amicos ex mammona iniquitatis, ut cum defeceritis recipiant vos in aeterna tabernacula. Cum defeceritis, inquit, ut partim ad dispensatoris parabolam alludat, qui ab officio amotus ad egestatem venturus erat, nisi praepositus sua beneficentia sibi aliquorum animos conciliauisset, à quibus suscipe retur: partim vero nos communis nostra fortis admonet, ut nos mortales esse meminerimus, qui vt nihil nobis insolens accidat, cum aeta te tamen deficimus, neque permanentem habemus ciuitatem in terris, vbi nunc cum labore & multiplici molestia peregrinamur. Vult ergo, ita res nostras instituamus, ut cum huius vitae curriculu emensi fuerimus, locum in caelesti patria iam praeparatum habeamus, in quem cum aliis pijs, atq; adeo cum illis ipsis colligamur, quos in hoc saeculo egentes nostra beneficentia subleuauimus. Ex eo autem aliud elici debet, nullam caelestis vitae & felicitatis spem illis reliquam esse, qui adamantina cordis duritia omnium calamitates atq; egestatem dispiciunt, & sua abundantia ad explendam ingluuiem, adfastum & libidinem foedè abutuntur.
units.tr: But Christ here also warns us more plainly about this, when he sets forth the promise of a most ample reward for beneficence, and at the same time teaches what the heavenly Father has long since decreed concerning those hard and inhuman despisers of their needy brethren. "Make for yourselves friends," he says, "of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail they may receive you into the everlasting dwellings." "When you fail," he says: partly he alludes to the parable of the steward who, removed from his office, was about to come to want unless, while still in charge, he had won the goodwill of some by his beneficence, by whom he might be received. Partly, however, he reminds us of our common mortality, that we should remember that we are mortals, who, though nothing unusual happens to us, nevertheless fail as we age, and have no abiding city on earth, where now we wander with toil and manifold trouble. He wishes us, therefore, so to order our affairs that when we have run the course of this life we may have a place already prepared in the heavenly fatherland, into which we may be gathered together with other godly people, and even with those very men whom in this age, in need, we have relieved by our beneficence. From this, moreover, another thing must be drawn: that there is no hope of heavenly life and happiness left for those who, with hearts of adamant, look upon the calamities and want of all, and foully misuse their abundance to satisfy their gluttony, their pride and their lust.

units.la: Caeterum
units.tr: Moreover

units.la: Caterum occurrunt hoc loco quæstiones duæ. Vna, an sancti cœlites nos in vitæ æternæ consortium recipiendi ius habeant, aut vt recipiamur, suis apud Deum precibus impetrent? Altera, num operibus charitatis & beneficentiæ cœlos mereri possimus? Controuertitur de vtraq; hodie passim, & scimus aduersarios nostros huius loci authoritate plurimū niti, eò quod verba Christi tale quid dicere videntur. At cum idem ille sibijpsi minimè contradicat, alibi autem diserte pronuntiet, salu-tem & vitam æternam nobis ex mera & gratuita Dei misericordia dari, huius autem apprehen-dendæ rationem nullam esse aliam quàm fidem, qua ipsi vnimur atque inserimur: necessario nobis sensus quærendus erit, qui cum fidei analogia conueniat, & omnem contradictionis speciem tollat. Et primò quidem quoad sanctos cœlites, hi neque recipiendi in cœlos ius habent, sed omne hoc Christo relinquunt, cui soli omnis potestas data est in cœlo & in terra: neque etiam nostri apud Deum deprecatores sunt, cum hanc quoque gloriam sibi vendicet Christus, qui solus Filius ille dilectus est in quo Patri esset satisfactum. Et meminisse oportet, Christum hic de illis solis loqui, quos in terris agentes nostra liberalitate adiuuimus. Hi nos in æterna tabernacula ad se recipere dicuntur, quan-do in illis nostræ fidei testimonium extat, quæ sola nos cœlorum hæredes facit in Christo. Adhæc vt Christum ipsum alere, vestire, inuisere, hospitio excipere & iuuare dicuntur, qui pauperes illius ossi-cijs istis subleuant: ita hi ipsi nos in tabernacula æterna recipiunt, quando Christus nos illorum co-hæredes & contubernales (vt ita loquar) in cœlis facit: à quibus omnino excluduntur, quotquot sua inhumanitate ostendunt se à fide esse alienos.
units.tr: Moreover, two questions arise here. The first is whether the holy inhabitants of heaven have a right to receive us into the fellowship of eternal life, or whether, by their prayers before God, they obtain that we be received. The second is whether we can merit heaven by works of charity and beneficence. Both are disputed today on every side, and we know that our opponents rely heavily on the authority of this passage, because the words of Christ seem to say something of the kind. But since the same Christ does not contradict himself, and elsewhere plainly declares that salvation and eternal life are given to us from the mere and free mercy of God, and that the only way of laying hold of it is faith, by which we are united and grafted into him, we must necessarily seek a sense that agrees with the analogy of faith and removes every appearance of contradiction. First, then, as regards the saints in heaven: they have no right to receive anyone into heaven, but leave all this to Christ, to whom alone all power in heaven and on earth has been given. Nor are they our intercessors before God, since Christ claims this glory for himself too, he who alone is that beloved Son in whom the Father was satisfied. And we must remember that Christ here speaks only of those whom we help by our liberality while they are living on earth. These are said to receive us into the eternal tabernacles, because in them there is the testimony of our faith, which alone makes us heirs of heaven in Christ. Moreover, just as those who relieve the poor with these services are said to feed, clothe, visit, entertain and help Christ himself, so these same poor receive us into the eternal tabernacles when Christ makes us their co-heirs and, so to speak, fellow-dwellers in heaven. From that company, however, are wholly excluded all who by their inhumanity show that they are alien from faith.

units.la: Quoad alteram quæstionem de operibus beneficentiæ aut charitatis, facilis etiam est solutio. Nã vt demus meritum aliquod ijs tribui, qui electis benefaciunt, quos suo tempore Christus in cœlos ad se recipiet, iam hoc ipsum omnibus alijs negabitur, qui eleemosynã faciunt in indignos, quos pro suis Christus non agnoscit. Atqui constat beneficentia nostra ex nostri animi instituto æstimari, & Deo gratam esse, si propter Christi nomen eam exerceamus, licet multi nos fallant, qui hoc falso & frau-dulenter prætexunt. Quod nisi nobis probè persuasum sit, mox charitate frigere & beneficentia stu-dium extingui sentiemus, si qui nobis vel leuissima ex causa suspecti sint. Quod ergo alibi monuimus hic quoq; obseruandum erit, in operibus eiusmodi ad fidem respici debere, sine qua Deo probari non possunt. Nam quod non ex fide fit, peccatum est: & vt per solum Christum fide apprehensum nobis ad thronum gratiæ accessus patet: ita opera quoq; nulla in Dei conspectu consistere possunt, quàm quæ ex fide ista emanant. Itaq; omnis meriti gloria ad Christum redit, propter quem & nos & opera nostra Patri placent, vt imperfectionem, quæ illis coniuncta est, nobis non imputet. Et cum illa ipsa in nobis Dei spiritus operetur, ille suum opus in nobis remunerat (quod non vno loco D. Augustinus docet) nobis autem hoc ipsum adscribit ex gratia, vt ad benefaciendum magis excitemur.
units.tr: As for the second question, concerning works of beneficence or charity, the answer is also easy. For even if we grant that some merit is attributed to those who do good to the elect, whom Christ in due time will receive into heaven to himself, it will then be denied to all others who give alms to the unworthy, whom Christ does not acknowledge as his own. Yet it is certain that our beneficence is judged by the disposition of our mind, and is pleasing to God if we practise it for the sake of Christ's name, although many people deceive us, pretending this falsely and fraudulently. Unless we are thoroughly persuaded of this, we shall soon feel our charity grow cold and our zeal for beneficence die out, if those whom we help are suspect for even the slightest reason. Therefore, what we have taught elsewhere must be observed here as well: in works of this kind, regard must be had to faith, without which they cannot be approved by God. For whatever is not done from faith is sin; and just as access to the throne of grace lies open to us through Christ alone, laid hold of by faith, so works also can stand in the sight of God only if they flow from that faith. Thus all the glory of merit returns to Christ, on account of whom both we and our works are pleasing to the Father, so that he does not impute to us the imperfection that clings to them. And since God's Spirit himself works those very things in us, he rewards his own work in us (as St Augustine teaches in more than one place), yet he ascribes this to us by grace, so that we may be the more stirred up to do good.

units.la: Sed vt adrem ipsam redeamus, est hoc eximium diuinæ bonitatis argumentū, quod quæ in pauperes conferuntur officia tam cumulatè rependit, vt pro terrenis cœlestia, pro temporalibus æterna retribuat. Nūquā enim hoc faceret, nisi miseros nos mortales ineffabili amore complecteretur, & eos cuperet regni sui cœlestis consortes habere, qui ne hac quidem vita in terris digni sumus. Et non de-sunt exempla, quæ docent ad multos etiã in hoc sæculo magno cum fœnore officia illa redijsse, quæ in Dei seruos egentes contulerunt. Sareptana vidua Eliam, quæ Achabi tyrānus ex Israele eiecerat, ho-spitio excipit, & vicissim huius ministerio ad Dei veri Ecclesiã adducitur, & nũc in cœlis viuit ac regnat. Eodē tempore Abdias prætorio præfectus Prophetas in speluncis abscōsos alit et tuetur: nec dubium est, quin fidei suæ fructum in cœlis habeat, in ecclesia certè eius nomē magnificè celebratur.
units.tr: But to return to the matter itself: it is a remarkable proof of divine goodness that it repays the services rendered to the poor so abundantly, that for earthly things it gives heavenly ones, and for temporal things eternal ones. For God would never do this, unless he embraced us wretched mortals with ineffable love and wished to have as companions of his heavenly kingdom those who are not even worthy of life on earth. Nor are there lacking examples which teach that in this age also those services rendered to the needy servants of God have returned to many with great interest. The widow of Sarepta received Elijah into her house, whom the tyrant Ahab had driven out of Israel, and in return, through his ministry, she was brought into the Church of the true God, and now lives and reigns in heaven. At the same time Obadiah, prefect of the palace, fed and protected the prophets hidden in caves. There is no doubt that he has the fruit of his faith in heaven, and certainly in the Church his name is celebrated with great honour.

units.la: Sed quid exemplū opus est, quando vniuersales promissiones vbiq; occurrūt, quibus fidē suam omni-bus obstringit Deus, qui in pauperes misericordiam exercent? Apud Isaiā ait: Frange esurienti pa-nem tuū, afflictos & vagos domū deducito: si viderus nudum, tege eū, & à carne tua ne te abscondas, id est, ne pudeat te proximi aut cognati tui pauperis. Tūc erumpet velut aurora lux tua, & sanitas tua protinus germinabit: iustitia anteibit facie tuâ, & gloria Domini colliget te. Cōsentit hus quod in præsenti Christus promittit: quod nimirū benefici amicos sibi parēt veros Dei cultores, & proin-de ecclesiæ Dei mēbra fiant, cū quibus tandē in cœlis quoq; sint regnaturi. Arguit autē istorū consi-deratio multorū inhumanitatem, quos neq; communis hominū sors, neq; præsens fratrū egentium ca-lamitas, neq; promissionū diuinarū liberalitas atq; amplitudo mouet, vt ijs succurrant, quorū opera fortassis ipsis etiam aliquando vtilis esse poterat. Ita vero isti seipsos à regno Dei excludunt, dum eos tam facile negligunt, qui eius veri cives sunt. Causa tanti mali est philautia, quae plerosque ex caecat, vt non videant se Deo fenerari, quando egenis benefaciunt, & quod hunc remuneratorem habituri sint. Quapropter Christus rationes aliquot è vulgo petitas, adeoque sententias prouerbiales subjicit, quibus veternum hunc nobis excutiat.
units.tr: But why do we need examples, when universal promises meet us everywhere, by which God binds his faith to all who show mercy to the poor? In Isaiah he says: "Break thy bread to the hungry, and bring the afflicted and the wandering into thy house; if thou seest the naked, cover him, and hide not thyself from thine own flesh," that is, be not ashamed of your neighbour or kinsman who is poor. "Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thy health shall spring forth speedily; righteousness shall go before thee, and the glory of the Lord shall gather thee." This agrees with what Christ promises in the present passage: namely, that those who do good make for themselves true friends, worshippers of God, and thus become members of the Church of God, with whom at last they will also reign in heaven. Yet the consideration of these things shows the inhumanity of many, whom neither the common lot of men, nor the present calamity of needy brothers, nor the liberality and greatness of God's promises moves to help those whose services might perhaps at some time be useful to themselves. Thus they exclude themselves from the kingdom of God, while they so easily neglect those who are its true citizens. The cause of so great an evil is self-love, which blinds most people so that they do not see that they are lending to God when they do good to the needy, and that they will have him as their rewarder. Therefore Christ adds some reasons taken from common life, and proverbial sayings, by which he may shake us out of this drowsiness.

units.la: Prima est: Qui fidelis est in minimo, etiam in magno fidelis est: & qui in minimo iniustus est, etiam in magno est iniustus. Sensus est: qui rebus maioribus praefici volunt, ij paruas fideliter ad ministrare debent. Quis enim ea quae maioris momenti sunt ei committat, qui in minimis negligens & malae fidei seruus esse deprehenditur? At nihil inter homines vilius & minoris pretij est quam diuitiae. Nam quae in his pretiosissima habentur, aurum videlicet & argentum, quid aliud quàm terrae excrementa sunt, ad solum luxum & fraudes idonea, quibus hominum vita commodius carere poterat: cum per se ad hanc conferuandam nihil conferant, insuper autem praecipua sint causa maxi morum scelerum, quibus infelix hic mundus turbatur? Si quis ergo his ita addictus fuerit, vt negle cto illorum vsu, in quem Deus ea destinauit, ea petulanter dissipat, aut malis artibus opes in vniuersum omnes in vsum alienum conuertit, nec illae indignus est, qui ad veros illos & caelestes aeternae beatitudinis thesauros admittatur.
units.tr: The first is: "He that is faithful in the least is faithful also in much; and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much." The sense is this: those who wish to be set over greater things ought to administer small things faithfully. For who would entrust what is of greater importance to one who is found to be careless and dishonest in small matters? Yet among men nothing is baser or of less worth than riches. For what are the things held most precious among them, namely gold and silver, but the dung of the earth, fit only for luxury and fraud, which human life could far more conveniently do without, since they contribute nothing to its preservation, and moreover are the chief cause of the greatest wickedness by which this unhappy world is disturbed? If anyone is so attached to these that, neglecting their use for which God intended them, he squanders them wantonly, or by wicked arts turns all his wealth to the use of others, he is not worthy to be admitted to those true and heavenly treasures of eternal blessedness.

units.la: Potest autem huius sententiae multiplex vsus esse in alijs vitae generibus. Paulus certè diaconus hanc non obscurè applicat, quando eos qui bene ministrauerint, gradum sibi bonum acquirere ait, vt ad maiora promoueantur. Et rursus de episcopis agens, eos ad gubernandam Dei Ecclesiam minime idoneos fore scribit, qui domui suae praeesse non possunt. Debent ergo huius sententiae omnes me minisse, vt in quacunq; vocatione cogitent se Deo seruire, & hanc eius voluntatem esse, vt quod in mandatis acceperunt, fideliter exequantur. Dauid cùm opilionem ageret, eam fidem praestitit, vt ouium causa, imò propter agnum vnicum cum vrsis & leonibus congrederetur: mox ergo ad militiā pro populo Dei obeundam promotus est. Et cum hic quoq; omnia boni militis officia strenuè obiret, dignus se ostendit esse, qui ad regiā dignitatē eueheretur. Debebant in horum meditatione diligentius versari, qui se à Deo negligi queruntur, & indignè secum agi putant, si non ad dignitates aut feliciorem vitae conditionem prouehantur. Nam si in seipsos descenderent, & pristinos mores examinarent, mox viderent nullam sibi iniuriam fieri, sed potius sibi precibus opus esse apud Deum, ne is dignas ab illis negligentiae poenas exigat. Habent praeterea hic regulam generalem principes viri, quam obseruent, si quando publici ministri, prouinciarum praefecti, quaestores, dispensatores bonorum Ecclesiae, aut quicunque alij in Republ constituendi sunt: Vt nimirum eos deligant, quorum fides atque probitas in minoribus officijs, aut etiam in propriae domus administratione, prius satis cognita & perspecta est. At hodieferè ad publica munera adhibentur, qui prius infami luxu sua pro degerunt, quibus & reipub. & Ecclesiarum dissipationem maxima ex parte debemus.
units.tr: The application of this saying may be manifold in other kinds of life. Paul certainly applies it plainly when he says that those who serve well acquire for themselves a good standing, so that they may be promoted to greater things. And again, speaking of bishops, he writes that those cannot be fit to govern the Church of God who cannot rule their own household. All should therefore remember this saying, so that in whatever calling they are placed they may consider that they serve God, and that this is his will: that they faithfully carry out what they have received in charge. When David was tending sheep, he showed such faithfulness that for the sake of the sheep, indeed for the sake of the one lamb, he would go out against bears and lions; soon afterwards he was advanced to bear arms for the people of God. And since he also there carried out faithfully all the duties of a good soldier, he showed himself worthy to be raised to royal dignity. Those who complain that God neglects them, and think they are treated unworthily if they are not promoted to honours or to a happier condition of life, ought to dwell more diligently on these examples. For if they went down into themselves and examined their former conduct, they would soon see that no wrong is being done to them, but that rather they need to pray to God, lest he exact from them the due penalty of their negligence. Moreover, princes and men in authority have here a general rule which they should observe whenever public ministers are to be appointed, governors of provinces, quaestors, stewards of the goods of the Church, or anyone else to be installed in the commonwealth: namely, that they should choose those whose faith and integrity have first been sufficiently tested and proved in lesser offices, or even in the management of their own household. But nowadays public offices are for the most part given to those who have previously spent their lives in infamous luxury, and to them we owe, for the most part, the ruin of the commonwealth and of the Churches.

units.la: Secunda ratio est, quam ex priori concludit, dicens: Si in iniusto mammona fideles non fuistis, verum mammona quis credet vobis? Iniustum mammona hic dicit pro diuitijs mendacibus & fluxis, quae possessorem fallunt & se sua frustrantur, vt supra diximus, & ideo illis veras opes opponit, caelestes nimirum & diuinas intelligens, quae sola stabiles & aeternae sunt. Et eodem sensu subijcit: Si in alieno fideles non fuistis, quod verum est quis dabit vobis? Vbi alienae diuitiae dicuntur, quas vulgo fortunae bona dicunt, & alienas proprijssimè vocat, eo quod neque nobiscum nascuntur (nudi enim in mundum ex matris vtro venimus) neque reuera nostrae sunt, cum earum dispensatores modò simus & neq; dispensatio illa in nostra potestate sit, sed plerunq; à nobis etiam inuitis at que reluctantibus transferatur. His opponuntur verae, quas modò nostras dicit: quia qui illas semel verè apprehenderunt, ij meliorem partē (vt de Maria dixit supra) elegerūt, quae ab illis nunquam auferetur. Nam vt filij Dei & legitimi haeredes illas possident. Ideo apud Matthaeum eo nomine eas commendat, quod neq; à tineis aut aerugine corrumpi, neq; à furibus diripi possint. Quid, quod ne in morte quidem eas amittimus, sed potius in plenam venimus possessionem? Verè igitur de illis Christiani homines dicere possunt, quod olim Bias de sapientia & alijs animi bonis pronunciauit, cùm capta ab hostibus Priene patria, alijs rerum preciosissimarum pondere onustis, ipse vacuus abibat, dicens: Ego verò bona mea mecum porto. Potuit ergo pro alienis agnoscere ea, quae fortunae tunæ casibus obnoxia sunt: sola autem sua putauit esse, quæ à nemine eripi poterant. Arguitur hoc exemplo multorum peruersitas (ne quid grauius dicam) qui de solis alienis & caducis opibus solici ti, ea nihili faciunt, quæ vt nobis propria & perpetua essent, Christus sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit.
units.tr: The second reason is the one he draws from the previous one, saying: "If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will trust you with the true riches?" By "unrighteous mammon" he means here the deceitful and fleeting riches, which deceive their possessor and cheat him of what is his, as we said above; and so he sets against them the true riches, understanding the heavenly and divine ones, which alone are stable and eternal. In the same sense he adds: "If you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?" Here "that which is another's" means the riches which the common people call the goods of fortune. He calls them "another's" most properly, because they are not born with us (for we come naked into the world from our mother's womb), and they are not truly ours either, since we are only their stewards, and that stewardship is not in our power, but is often transferred from us even against our will and resistance. Opposed to these are the true riches, which he calls "our own": for those who have truly laid hold of them have chosen the better part (as he said above of Mary), and it will never be taken from them. For as sons of God and lawful heirs they possess them. Therefore in Matthew he commends them on this ground, that they cannot be corrupted by moths or rust, nor snatched away by thieves. And what of the fact that we do not lose them even in death, but rather come into full possession of them? Christian people may therefore truly say of them what Bias once declared of wisdom and the other goods of the mind, when his homeland Priene was captured by the enemy and the others, laden with the weight of their most precious possessions, were leaving, while he himself departed empty-handed, saying: "But I carry my goods with me." So he could recognise as another's those things which are exposed to the chances of fortune, and he thought only those were his own which no one could snatch away. By this example is shown the perversity of many (not to say anything harsher), who, anxious only about the other's and perishing wealth, make nothing of those things which Christ acquired by the price of his blood to be ours and everlasting.

units.la: Tertia ratio sequitur, quæ plus quiddam continet. Nam illis eam opponit, qui diuitiis ita se feser uire posse sibi persuadent, vt simul Deo quoque cultum suum exhibeant, & pariter huius seculi & æternæ vitæ bonis fruantur. Hos igitur generali sententia, quæ tunc quoq; in omnium ore fuisse vi- detur, confutat, dicens: Nullus seruus potest duobus dominis seruire: ijs nimirum, qui ingenio, moribus & iussis inter se pugnant. Nam vt vnum odio habebit, & alterum diliget: aut vni adhærebit, & alterum contemnet. Et quia hæc communi sensu confirmantur, sententiam istam præsenti causæ accommodans infert: Non potestis Deo seruire & mammonæ. Cuius dicti veritas etsi in paucorum animis fidem inueniat, irrefragabilis tamen est, cum Deus & Mammon siue Plutus tam præceptis quàm operibus dissideant. Deus enim iubet thesaurum in cœlis parare, Mammon vt in terris hisce nobis prospiciamus præcipit. Dei mandatū est iuuare pauperes & egentium misereri: Mammon clamat, proximus tibi ipsi esto, & cur alios iuuando teipsum negligas? Deus mandat, ne quem fraudemus: Mammon in dolis, impostoris, furtis & rapinis laudem induestriæ & lucrum inueniri docet. Deus vt in se solo spem omnem collocemus præcipit, non autem in opibus perituris & momentaneis: Mammon spem vitæ & felicitatis omnem in diuitiis monstrat. Dei voluntas est, vt opibus sobriè & temperanter vtamur, & vitam viuamus honestam & sanctam: Mammon verò nos luxuriari & voluptuari vult, & omnibus alijs contemptis immani fastu efferri. Denique, Deus suo Spiritu in nobis proximi dilectionem, verbi sui studium, fidei constantiā, pacem conscientiæ gi- gnit: At Mammon inuidiæ ac odij flammis animos accendit, verbi semē spinis suis suffocat, fidem extinguit, idololatras, iniustos, impostores & raptores facit, & conscientias immanibus curis cur- bat, atq; salutis incertas facit. Verissimè ergo dicitur, eos non posse Deo seruire, qui diuitiis animos suos mancipauerunt. Dicit enim quidem fuisse fatemur multos eximios Dei cultores, at eosdem diuitiis non seruiuisse, sed potius hus præfuisse & pie ijsdem vsos fuisse, omnia illorum facta testantur. Quid ergo restat fratres, quàm vt mundo & huius seculi bonis longum valere dicentes: totos nos Deo consecremus, ab hoc datas opes gratis animis excipiamus, illis pie vtamur, vt non nostræ modò necessitati seruiant, verumetiam per nos Ecclesia, Respublica & pauperes iuuentur? Ita nobis amicos parabimus fidelissimos. Nam electis Dei omnibus associati in æterna tabernacula recipiemur, vbi immortali gaudio exultabimus cum Domino & redemptore nostro Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The third reason follows, which contains something more. For he sets it against those who persuade themselves that they can so serve riches as at the same time to render their worship to God, and equally enjoy the goods of this age and of eternal life. Therefore he refutes these with a general saying, which seems to have been on everyone's lips even then, saying: "No servant can serve two masters": namely those who are at odds with one another in disposition, morals and commands. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other. And because these things are confirmed by common sense, he applies this saying to the present case and concludes: "You cannot serve God and mammon." Although the truth of this saying may find belief in the minds of few, it is nonetheless irrefutable, since God and Mammon, or Plutus, disagree both in their precepts and in their works. For God commands us to lay up treasure in heaven; Mammon bids us provide for ourselves in these earthly things. It is God's command to help the poor and to have pity on the needy; Mammon cries, "Be a neighbour to yourself, and why neglect yourself by helping others?" God commands that we defraud no one; Mammon teaches that gain and profit are to be found in deceits, cheating, thefts and robberies. God bids us place all our hope in himself alone, not in perishing and momentary riches; Mammon shows that all hope of life and happiness lies in riches. It is God's will that we use goods soberly and temperately, and live an honest and holy life; but Mammon wants us to revel and indulge ourselves, and, with all others despised, to be lifted up in monstrous pride. Finally, God by his Spirit begets in us love of neighbour, zeal for his word, constancy of faith, and peace of conscience; but Mammon kindles hearts with the flames of envy and hatred, chokes the seed of the word with his thorns, extinguishes faith, makes idolaters, unjust men, cheats and robbers, and racks consciences with monstrous cares, and makes salvation uncertain. It is therefore most truly said that those who have given their souls over to riches cannot serve God. For we grant that there were many distinguished worshippers of God, but the facts of all of them testify that they did not serve riches, but rather ruled over them and used them devoutly. What remains, then, brethren, but that, bidding farewell to the world and the goods of this age, we consecrate ourselves wholly to God, receive with grateful minds the riches given by him, and use them piously, so that they serve not only our own need but also, through us, the Church, the commonwealth and the poor are helped? Thus we shall make for ourselves most faithful friends. For, joined to all the elect of God, we shall be received into the eternal tabernacles, where we shall exult with immortal joy with the Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLVI.

units.la: Audiebant autem hæc omnia etiam Pharisæi, qui erant auari: & deridebant eum excipiebant. Tunc dixit eis: Vos estis qui iustificatis vosipsos in hominum conspectu: Deus autem nouit corda vestra: Quia quod apud homines sublime est, abominationi est in conspectu Dei. Lex & Prophetæ vsque ad Ioannem: ab eo tempore regnum Dei annunciatur, & quiuis in illud vi irrumpit. Facilius est autem cœlum & terram præterire, quàm Legis vnum apicem excidere. Quisquis dimittit vxorem suam, & alteram ducit, mœchatur: & qui à viro dimissam ducit, mœchatur.
units.tr: Now the Pharisees, who were covetous, heard all these things, and they derided him. And he said to them: You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts, for what is lofty among men is an abomination in the sight of God. The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses violently into it. It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall. Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

units.la: Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, ideo in mundum venit & homo factus est, vt nos ex peccatis & ab æterna damnationis sententia liberatos Patri suo cœlesti reconciliaret, & Regni sui cohæredes faceret. Quapropter totus in hoc est, vt nos à studijs mundi & carnis nostræ ad cœlestia reuocet. Et eò pertinet quæcunq; ab illo de nostra regeneratione, nostri abnegatione, veteris hominis mortificatione, de pœnitentia deniq; & conuersione ad Deum passim dicuntur. At quia inter Regni Dei atq; salutis impedimenta nullum efficacius & nocentius est auaritia, qua & fides in Deum impeditur, & proximi dilectio extinguitur, nō temere aduersus illam hoc cap, tam diligenter disserit. Et primò quidem offendit quæ sit opum huius seculi & ipsorum diuitum conditio, quos Deus non illarum dominos, sed dispensatores constituerit, & quos illi rationem reddere oporteat suæ dispensationis. Huic loco grauissimas rationes subiecit, quibus omnes hortatus est, vt fidi sint dispensatores bonorum quæ à Deo acceperunt. Tandem testatus est, fieri non posse, vt simul Dei cultores simus, & Mammonæ aut diuitiis seruiamus. Debent ista omnia sic audiri & accipi, vt ea nobis dici, & non minus ad nos pertinere putemus, quàm ad eos, quos tunc auditores habuit. Quia verò in hoc plurimùm peccatur, commodè ea quæ nunc recitauimus Lucas subijcit, quæ nobis exemplum proponunt, quo docemur, quid in toto hoc negotio potissimùm caueri debeat.
units.tr: The Son of God, Jesus Christ, therefore came into the world and became man, so that he might free us from sins and from the eternal sentence of damnation, reconcile us to his heavenly Father, and make us heirs of his kingdom. For this reason his whole aim is to call us back from the pursuits of the world and of our flesh to heavenly things.
