To this end belong all the things he says everywhere about our regeneration, our self-denial, the mortification of the old man, and finally repentance and conversion to God. But since among the hindrances to the kingdom of God and to salvation none is more effective and harmful than covetousness, which impedes faith in God and extinguishes love of neighbour, he does not without reason argue so carefully against it in this chapter. First of all he shows what the condition of the riches of this age is, and of the rich themselves, whom God has appointed not as their lords but as their stewards, and to whom it is right that they should render an account of their stewardship. To this passage he attached very weighty reasons, by which he exhorts all to be faithful stewards of the goods they have received from God. Finally he testifies that it is impossible for us to be worshippers of God and at the same time to serve Mammon or riches. All these things should be heard and received in such a way that we think they are said to us, and that they pertain to us no less than to those whom he then had as hearers. But since men sin most in this matter, Luke fittingly adds what we have just recited, which sets before us an example by which we are taught what must above all be guarded against in this whole business.

units.la: Describit enim initio, vt Pharisæi doctrinam hanc acceperint, & quid illis Christus responderit. De illis dicitur, quòd ipsum differentè audierint, sed eius doctrinam Iannis exceperint. Causa additur, quòd auari essent. Ergo vt cum vicus suum tangi nō possunt ferre, & eo ipso quòd doctrinam Christi derident atque scurriliter eludunt, verbis eius suo exemplo fidem astruunt, quòd nimirùm Deo obedire & seruire non possint, quorum corda auaritiæ studium occupauit: imò ijdem ne audire quidem possunt, quæ aduersus ipsos dicuntur. Vt enim ventri, qui auribus caret (quod Cato olim in publica concione dixit) frustra de sobrietate & temperantia verba fecerris: ita de opum contemptu & legitimo earundem vsu differentem nunquam audient auari, quos earum cupiditas non surdos modò, verùmetiam omnino cæcos fecit. Quod autem de illis dicitur, de omnibus sentire debemus, qui ad aliquod vitium animum appulerunt: & hæc causa est præcipua, ob quam Euangelij doctrina passim ridetur, subsannatur atque eluditur: quòd nimirum nemo pro sui defensione laborat, & quàmuis de alijs differentes verbi administros vtcunque ferat, mox animi sui impatientiam prodit, si ipsum pungi & sua vitia perstringi sentiat. Hic tamen duo hominum genera est videre. Primi sunt, qui cum risu & iannis verbum excipiunt, & hi quidem optimi censeri poterant, si cum multis alijs conferantur. At derisionis huius causa est, quòd verbum ad carnis suæ rationem examinant, & mundi huius iudicium sequuntur. Carni enim proprium est, quòd peccatis delectatur, & proinde eius blanditijs atque illecebris facilè capitur. Non potest ergo sibi ipsi persuadere, Deum adeò seuerum & rigidum esse, vt nos voluptatibus in vniuersum fraudare, & eos qui in terris adhuc degunt cælestibus solis vacare velit. Adhæc quia maiorem hominum partem vitijs deditam esse videt, nimiùm iniquus & temerarius esse videtur, qui illos simul omnes damnare audeat. Isaque etsi sibi ab odio veritatis nonnihil temperet, neque huius ministros conuitijs proscindat, ridet tamen & fanaticos putat, qui ex sua morositate Deum æstiment, & longè alium fingant, quàm reuera sit. Exempla hodie passim extant in scortatoribus, adulteris, ebriosis, vsurarijs militibus mercenarijs, Epicureis denique omnibus, qui quæ de mundi fine & nouissimo Christi aduentu dicuntur, mira scurrilitate exagitare consueuerunt, sicuti de illis olim Petrus prædixit. Cæterùm hi peiores & magis caendi sunt, qui non contenti risu & ludibrijs, insuper odij & iræ flammas aduersus fidos monitores concipiunt. Vt enim qui phrenesi laborant, in medicos furunt pharmaca propinantes: ita illi perditos volunt omnes eos, quos studijs suis pessimis contradicere audiunt. Nam hos pro acerrimis hostibus habent, vt in Achabi iudicio de Elia, in Iudæorum item aduersus Ieremiam altercantium exemplo videmus. Et vtinam non hodie passim isiorum similes haberemus. Sunt hi pessimi mortalium, de quorum salute vix quicquam sperari potest. Quia enim ea oppugnant hostiliter, quæ communi sensu probantur, non possunt non in propriam conscientiam peccare, & proinde ijs adnumerari merentur, quos Paulus in reprobum sensum datos esse scribit. Interim non debent sibiipsis blanditias facere priores illi, quibus lusus iocusque videtur Dei verbum, & tunc demum le egregie facetos atque iucundos congerrones esse putant, si ex scripturis scommata & dicteria concinnare, & his inter sui similes risum excitare possint. Hic enim Pharisaicus ludus est, quem Deus tandem seriis & grauibus pœnis in risum plane Sardonium conuertit. Imò isti ipsi dum ludibrijs eiusmodi assuescunt, tandem aperti hostes fiunt, si quando fortius vrgeantur. Et ideo Spiritus sanctus passim multa graviter aduersus illusores eiusmodi pronuntiat, Dauid verò eum felicem & beatum dicit, qui ab irrisorum consessu sibi cauet. Psal. 1.
units.tr: For at the beginning he describes how the Pharisees received this teaching and what Christ answered them. It is said of them that they heard him with contempt, but they had received the teaching of John. The cause is added: they were covetous. Therefore, as people who cannot bear to have their sore touched, and by the very fact that they deride Christ's teaching and mock it with buffoonery, they confirm by their own example the words he has spoken, namely that those whose hearts are occupied with the pursuit of covetousness cannot obey or serve God. Indeed they cannot even bear to hear what is said against themselves. For as Cato once said in a public assembly, one speaks in vain about sobriety and temperance to a belly that has no ears; so covetous men, whom the desire for wealth has made not only deaf but altogether blind, will never listen to someone who discourses on contempt of riches and their lawful use. What is said of them, we ought to think of all who have given their minds to any vice. This is the chief reason why the doctrine of the gospel is everywhere mocked, scorned and ridiculed: namely, that no one labours in his own defence, and although men may tolerate, in some fashion, ministers of the Word who speak about others, they soon betray their impatience of mind if they feel that they themselves are being pricked and their own vices laid bare. Yet here we may see two kinds of people. The first are those who receive the Word with laughter and jeering; these might be judged the best if they were compared with many others. But the cause of their derision is that they test the Word by the judgment of their flesh and follow the verdict of this world. For it is characteristic of the flesh to delight in sins, and therefore it is easily captured by its flatteries and allurements. It cannot therefore persuade itself that God is so severe and stern that he wishes to deprive us altogether of pleasures, and to have those who still live on earth devote themselves only to heavenly things. Moreover, since it sees that the greater part of mankind is given over to vices, it seems to itself too unjust and rash to dare to condemn them all together. And so, although it restrains itself somewhat from hatred of the truth, and does not tear its ministers with insults, it nevertheless laughs and thinks that they are fanatics who, out of their own moroseness, imagine a God and fashion one quite different from what he really is. Examples are to be found today everywhere among fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, usurers, soldiers, mercenaries, and finally all the Epicureans, who are accustomed to harass with wonderful buffoonery what is said about the end of the world and the last coming of Christ, just as Peter foretold of them long ago. However, those who are not content with laughter and mockery, but moreover conceive the flames of hatred and anger against faithful admonishers, are worse and more to be avoided. For just as those who suffer from frenzy rage against physicians who offer them medicines, so these men wish all those destroyed who they hear are opposing their wicked pursuits. For they regard these as their bitterest enemies, as we see in the judgment of Ahab about Elijah, and in the example of the Jews quarrelling against Jeremiah. And would that we did not today have everywhere men like them! They are the worst of mortals, and scarcely anything can be hoped for their salvation. For since they attack with hostility those things which are approved by common sense, they cannot but sin against their own conscience, and therefore they deserve to be counted among those whom Paul writes were given over to a reprobate mind. Meanwhile, those first ones, to whom the Word of God seems a game and a joke, must not flatter themselves; they think they are then finally truly witty and pleasant companions when they can concoct jests and witticisms out of the Scriptures and stir up laughter among their like. For this is the Pharisaic game, which God at last turns into utterly sardonic laughter by serious and grievous punishments. Indeed, those very men, while they grow accustomed to such mockeries, at last become open enemies whenever they are pressed more strongly. And therefore the Holy Spirit everywhere pronounces many heavy things against such mockers, and David calls happy and blessed the man who guards himself against the assembly of scoffers. Psalm 1.

units.la: Sed nunc Christum audiamus, qui isiorum iannis minimè cedit, sed aduersus illos altius insurgens suæ doctrinæ authoritatem tuetur, & simul hypocritis detrahit laruam, qua apud rude & imperitum peritum vulgus sese ostentabant. Ita vero exemplum præbet omnibus verbi administris, quos eadem constantia armatos esse decet, ne se vllis aduersariorum ludibrijs aut minis superari ac perterrefieri patiantur. Quod olim Prophetas & Apostolos admodum diligenter fecisse scimus. Verba Christi sunt: Vos estis qui iustificatis vosipsos in hominum conspectu: Deus autem novit corda vestra: quia quod apud homines sublime est, abominationi est in conspectu Dei. Sensus est: Vos quidem omnia vestra in eum finem facitis, vt vos iustos & sanctos esse ostendatis, & tales hominum iudicio habeamini: Ideo crebris lotionibus, ieiunijs, precationibus & eleemosynis in publico vacatis, vestitu quoque peculiari & gestibus mirificis, adhac sacrificijs & oblationibus, sanctitatis laude captatis. Quasi vero illa in externis eiusmodi laruis consistat. At vanissimus & irritus plane hic vester labor est: Deus enim non externo fuco aut inanibus ceremonijs ducitur, sed cor & animum totum sibi vendicat: & vt hunc cum omnibus facultatibus hominis tam externis quam internis requirit: ita cordium quoque arcana intuetur, neque aliquid in homine tam abstrusum atque occultum est, quod non videat. Adhac tam abest vt hominum iudicijs quicquam tribuat, vt potius in eius conspectu abominationi sit, quod apud homines eximiu & immortali laude dignum habetur. Debet autem postremum hoc membrum non de virtute & huius præclaris exemplis intelligi, quæ homines cordati, & non prorsus impij solent magni facere, imo quæ hostibus interdum admirationi sunt: sed deijs Dominus loquitur, quæ hominum huic mundo addictorum iudicio eximia sunt, maximè autem illis, quæ homines ex suo sensu circa religionem & Dei cultum instituunt. In ijs enim maximè a Pharisæis peccabatur, quos humanarum traditionum obseruantissimos fuisse constat.
units.tr: But now let us hear Christ, who by no means yields to their jeering, but rising up against them more loftily defends the authority of his doctrine, and at the same time strips the hypocrites of the mask by which they presented themselves to the rude and inexperienced common people as skilled and learned. Thus he gives an example to all ministers of the Word, who ought to be armed with the same constancy, so that they do not allow themselves to be overcome or terrified by any mockeries or threats of their adversaries. We know that the Prophets and Apostles did this very diligently long ago. The words of Christ are: You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is lofty among men is an abomination in the sight of God. The meaning is this: You indeed do all your things with this end in view, that you may show yourselves to be righteous and holy, and be regarded as such by the judgment of men. Therefore you devote yourselves in public to frequent washings, fasts, prayers and almsgivings, and also to peculiar clothing and wonderful gestures; moreover, you seek the praise of holiness by sacrifices and offerings. As if such things consisted in outward masks of this kind! But this your labour is altogether vain and worthless: for God is not moved by outward paint or empty ceremonies, but claims for himself the heart and the whole soul, and requires this with all the faculties of man, both external and internal; and so he beholds the hidden secrets of hearts, and there is nothing in man so deep and concealed that he does not see it. Moreover, he is so far from giving anything to the judgments of men that rather, in his sight, what is considered outstanding and worthy of immortal praise among men is an abomination. This last clause must not be understood as referring to virtue and its excellent examples, which thoughtful men who are not wholly impious are accustomed to esteem highly, and which sometimes even excite admiration in enemies; rather, the Lord speaks of those things which are outstanding in the judgment of men who are given over to this world, and especially of those things which men devise from their own sense concerning religion and the worship of God. For the Pharisees sinned most in these matters, who are known to have been most observant of human traditions.

units.la: Debet autem ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, ne de vllo hominum instituto ex carnis aut no stra rationis sensu secundùm externa speciem iudicemus, sed in Dei verbum simus intenti, quod nobis actionum & consiliorum omnium vnica regula esse debet. Magnum enim inter homines & Deum discrimen est, & vt animalis homo ea nõ percipit quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: ita si sibijpsi permittatur, ea admirabitur & adorabit, quæ Deus quàm maximè abominatur. In hoc igitur sapientia vera constitit (quam rerum humanarum atque diuinarum causarumque quibus illæ continentur, scientiam esse, veteres philosophi definierunt) vt de omnibus rebus ex verbo Dei iudicare & pronuntiare possimus, quod nos falli aut errare nõ sinet. Obseruari ergo debet in religione. Ibi carnis iudicio arridēt Ceremoniarum magnificentia, operum electitiorum gloriatio, multorum seculorum consensus, maiorum exemplum & Regum authoritas. At quid de omnibus illis pronuntiat Deus? Ceremonias vanitatis damnat, & animos fide vera illuminatos requirit. Ad quid mihi (inquit) multitudo sacrificiorum vestrorum? Holocausta arietum & adipem saginatorum fastidio, boum cruorem, agnorum & hircorum non amo, &c. Idem corporalia exercitia nihili facit, vt quæ ad vera pietate nihil faciant. Ideo de ieiunijs interrogatus olim respondit: Cùm comeditis & bibitis, annõ vobis comeditis & bibitis? Item: Num huiusmodi ieiunium est quod ego elegi, vt ad diem homo affligat animam suam, vt retorqueat caput suum tanquam hamum, saccum & puluerem sternat? Num hoc ieiunium & diem gratum Domino appellabis? Annon hoc ieiunium eligo? aperire nexus impios, soluere fasciculos iugi, liberos dimittere oppressos? &c. Similiter neq; secul orum multorum consensu, neq; vllorum hominum exemplis, aut etiam Regum authoritate Deus mouetur, cùm vetustissima omniū & à sanctissimis hominib. obseruata sit ea fides, cuius summa & fundamenta in prima promissione Adamo de semine mulieris facta continentur: Vere ergo in Dei conspectu abominabile est omne illud, quo homines super stitiosi sese venditant. At non minus hoc ad vitā quoq; & reliqua hominū studia debet transferri. Hic enim apud mundū summo in pretio sunt opes, honores, amicitiæ & fœdera, rei militaris gloria, victoriarum successus, regnorum propagatio, & quæ alia sunt huius generis. Et quidem tanti ista fiunt, vt pleriq; propterea ab officio discedant, & Deo debitum obsequium negent. Sed quod nam de istis omnibus est Dei iudicium? Opes mammona iniquitatis Christus vocat, & eas de, si iniquis modis quæsitæ sint, ignem esse dicit in ædibus, qui omnia deuoret. Honores autem ad salutem nobis maximo impedimento esse testatur, quando Scribas & Pharisæos in se credere posse negat, eò quòd gloriam abs se inuicem vænentur, Dei verò gloriā negligant. Similiter per Iacobum Spiritus pronuntiat, amicitiam huius mundi inimicitiam esse cum Deo. Quàm parui autem idem ille faciat militaris rei peritiam, belli magnificum apparatum & alia in quibus pleriq; spem victoriæ omnem consistere arbitrantur, Dauid docet, cum ait: Res fallax est equus, & multo licet praeditus fit robore, nō tamen seruabit. Item: Non probat Dominus fortitudinem equi, neq; delectatur tibijs viri: Delecta tur autem timentibus ipsum, quiq; eius bonitatem expectant. Et huc referri debent potentissimorum Regum atq; populorū exempla, qui post longos victoriarū successus ab hostibus numero paucioribus & cōtemptissimis nullo negotio deuicti sunt, cum iam inuictissimi esse viderentur. Quibus adde hor-ribiles illas Dei comminationes, quibus maledictione & exitium omnibus denuntiat, qui terras alie-nas vastant, sanguinis effusione gaudet, populorū fines turbant & tollunt. ex praedis item ditescunt, & qua non sua sunt domi suae coaceruant. Deniq; verissimè à Christo dicitur, in Dei cospectu abomi-nationi esse & danari, quaecunq; infelix mundus admirari & praecipua salutis praesidia putare solet.
units.tr: From this passage a general doctrine should be drawn: we must not judge any human institution by the standard of the flesh or our own reason, judging by its outward appearance. Instead we should attend to the Word of God, which ought to be the sole rule for all our actions and plans. There is a great difference between humans and God, and as the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, so if he is left to himself he will admire and worship what God most utterly abhors. True wisdom therefore consists in this: that we can judge and pronounce on all things by the Word of God, which will keep us from being deceived or led astray. The ancient philosophers defined wisdom as the knowledge of human and divine things and of the causes contained in them, and this is the wisdom we must observe in religion. There, the judgment of the flesh is pleased by the splendour of ceremonies, the boasting of chosen works, the consensus of many ages, the example of our ancestors and the authority of kings. But what does God pronounce about all these things? He condemns empty ceremonies and seeks minds enlightened by true faith. "What to me," he says, "is the multitude of your sacrifices? I am sick of whole burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bullocks, lambs and goats," and so on. Likewise he makes nothing of bodily exercises, since they contribute nothing to true piety. So when he was asked once about fasting, he answered: "When you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?" Again: "Is this the fast that I have chosen, that a man should afflict his soul for a day, bow his head like a hook, and spread sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this fast and this day acceptable to the Lord? Is not this the fast I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, to let the oppressed go free?" and so on. Likewise God is not moved by the consensus of many ages, by the examples of any people, or even by the authority of kings. The faith whose sum and foundations are contained in the first promise made to Adam concerning the seed of the woman is the most ancient of all and has been observed by the holiest of men. Truly, then, in God's sight everything is abominable by which superstitious men display themselves. Yet this must be applied no less to life and to the other pursuits of men. For in the world wealth, honours, friendships and alliances, the glory of war, the success of victories and the extension of kingdoms, and other things of this kind, are held in the highest esteem. Indeed they are valued so highly that many men on account of them depart from duty and refuse the obedience owed to God. But what is God's judgment on all these things? Christ calls riches the mammon of unrighteousness, and says that if they are gained by wicked means they are a fire in the house that will consume everything. He testifies that honours are the greatest hindrance to salvation, since he says that the Scribes and Pharisees cannot believe in him, because they seek glory from one another and neglect the glory that comes from God. Likewise, through James the Spirit declares that friendship with this world is enmity with God. How little that same Spirit values skill in war, the magnificent preparation for battle, and the other things in which most men think all hope of victory consists, David teaches when he says: "The horse is a vain thing for safety; neither shall he deliver any by his great strength." Again: "The Lord takes no pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor delights in the legs of a man; but the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, who hope in his mercy." To this must also be referred the examples of the most powerful kings and peoples, who after long successes in war were overcome without any trouble by enemies fewer in number and utterly despised, when they seemed already invincible. Add to these those dreadful threats of God, by which he denounces curse and destruction on all who lay waste foreign lands, delight in the shedding of blood, disturb and remove the boundaries of peoples, grow rich from plunder, and heap up at home what is not their own. Finally, it is most truly said by Christ that whatever the unhappy world is wont to admire and to consider the chief safeguards of salvation is an abomination and a thing damned in the sight of God.

units.la: Habes igitur hoc loco, quod ijs respondeas, qui hodie nunquam non in ore habent, opus esse vt mundo nos accomodemus, eius amicitiam colamus, & foedera cum illis quoq; feriamus, qui à religio-ne vera abhorrent: Nam nisi id fiat, pericula vndiq; nobis imminere, quae deuitari nullo modo pos-sint. Et vt suam sententiam omnibus persuadeant, multis amplificare solent opum splendorem, ho-nores, gloriam, authoritatem, potentiam & victorias eorum, quos à nobis coli & obseruari volunt. Quid autē illis aliud respondeas, quàm quod hic Christus dicit: Quod apud homines sublime est, a-bominationi est in conspectu Dei? Ex eo autem sequitur, non modo inanem esse istorum omnium fi-dutiam, sed simul Deo abominabiles fieri eos, qui propter ista ab illius praeceptis discedunt, & fidem illi datā fallunt. At si Deo abominationi simus, quis nos aduersus eum defendere? quis ab eius ira seruare poterit? Num opes? Atqui fluxae & caducae sunt, neq; his animae possunt à morte redimi. Num hominum auxilia & foedera? At omnis caro foenum: & maledictus, qui fidit homini, & fa-cit carnem brachium suum. Num fastus & insolens humanae gloriae vel authoritatis fiducia? Sed Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Vel num abscondemur à conspectu eius, ne nos ipse inueniat? Atqui terram & caelum ille implet, & vbiq; praesens adest. Et vt vno verbo om-nia dicamus, vt ijs qui Deum diligunt omnia adiumento sunt ad bonum: ita ijs, quos ille iusto iudi-cio abominatur & odit, omnia exitio sunt. Itaq; huius sententiae memores, neq; fucatae sanctimoniae fiducia efferri, neque in vllis hominum aut mundi praesidijs sperare, sed in vnum Deum respicere, & ab huius nutu atq; voluntate toti pendere debemus.
units.tr: Here, then, you have an answer to those who today never cease to have on their lips that we must accommodate ourselves to the world, cultivate its friendship, and make alliances even with those who shrink from the true religion, for unless this is done, dangers hang over us on every side that can in no way be avoided. And to persuade everyone of their opinion, they are wont to magnify at length the splendour of wealth, the honours, glory, authority, power and victories of those whom they want us to honour and observe. But what else can you answer them than what Christ says here: "What is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God"? From this it follows not only that all their confidence is empty, but also that those who depart from God's precepts for the sake of such things, and break the faith pledged to him, become abominable to him. But if we are an abomination to God, who will defend us against him? Who will be able to keep us from his wrath? Will riches? But they are fleeting and perishable, and by them souls cannot be redeemed from death. Will the help and alliances of men? But "all flesh is grass," and "cursed is he who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm." Will pride and the arrogant confidence of human glory or authority? But "God resists the proud, and gives grace to the humble." Or shall we hide ourselves from his sight, lest he find us? But he fills heaven and earth and is present everywhere. And to say everything in one word: as all things work together for good for those who love God, so all things are for destruction to those whom in his just judgment he abhors and hates. Therefore, mindful of this sentence, we ought neither to be puffed up with the confidence of feigned holiness, nor to place our hope in any human or worldly protection, but to look to the one God and depend wholly on his nod and will.

units.la: Caeterum ad Christum redeamus, qui cum vt nos seruet in mundū venerit, increpationes quoq; suas ita moderatur, vt hos homines emendari, & simul certam salutis spem concipere possint. Ideo ijs fere vitijs occurere & mederi studet, quibus maximè impedimur, ne doctrina salutis apud nos locum habeat. Idem ergo in praesenti quoq; facit. Quia enim Pharisaei Legis & Prophetarū studio sissimi videri volebant, & ipsum eo nomine in primis oderant, quod Mosis & Prophetarum hostem esse, sibi iampridem persuasissent: adhaec eam ob causam populi quoq; ad Christum concursu offende-bantur, breuem de Lege, huius vsu & abrogatione admonitiunculam interserit, qua simul & seip-sum excusat & populum, qui studio tam ardenti in ipsum ferebatur. Lex (inquit) & Propheta vsq; ad Ioannem: ab eo tempore Regnū Dei annunciatur, & quiuis in illud vi irrumpit. Quibus verbis alibi quoq; alia occasione vtitur, in praesenti aut hoc omnino dicere videtur: Scio vos Legi & huius Ceremonijs addictissimos esse, & vobis de me iampridē persuasisse, quasi de Mose & Prophetis mi-nus honorificè sentiam. At multùm fallimini ô boni. Ego enim & Legis & Prophetarum vsum hu-cusq; fuisse fateor praeclarū & multiplicē: quia promissiones de benedicto illo semine & humani gene-ris redeptione, deq; Regni Dei instauratione illustrauerunt atq; confirmarunt, simulq; docent, quid ijs facto opus sit, qui tantis istis bonis frui volunt. Habuit ergo vsus iste certū finē, quē Ioannes Bapti-sta vobis adduxit. Is enim iam adesse docuit promissum illum humani generis seruatorē, & agnum illum Dei digito monstrauit, qui expiatis mundi peccatis & deuicta atq; euersa diaboli tyrannide, Regnum Dei instaurraturus sit. Quid ergo miramini, si multi vobis & veteris cultus ceremonijs re-lictis me sequantur, & tantumnon vi quadā & importunitate magna in Regnū Dei irrumpant, cu-ius virtutem iam intra animos suos sentiunt? Quin vos quoq; horum exemplo excitati, rem omnem penes vos diligetius expendite, & videte ne in hoc salutis studio postremi sitis, qui alijs omnibus ve-stro exemplo debebatis praeire. Hic mihi istorum verborū sensus simplicissimus & argumento Chri-sti appositissimus esse videtur. Nec enim illis assentiri possum, qui Euangelistas ex illius sermonibus sententias temere congessisse, & vt scopas dissolutas prorulisse arbitrantur. Toto certè hoc capite continuam Christi concionē describi satis constat, cui hæc de Lege digressiuncula optimè conuenit, cùm ea Pharisæi validissimè confutentur & vrgeantur, qui illius doctrinam scurriliter irridebant. Sunt autem in his quædam diligentius inspicienda.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who came into the world to save us, and who so moderates his rebukes that these men may be corrected and at the same time may conceive a sure hope of salvation. Therefore he strives to meet and remedy those faults above all by which we are hindered from allowing the doctrine of salvation a place among us. He does the same thing now. For since the Pharisees wished to be seen as most devoted to the Law and the Prophets, and hated him above all for this reason, because they had long been persuaded that he was an enemy of Moses and the Prophets, and since the people too were offended by their crowding to Christ for this reason, he inserts a brief digression about the Law, its use and its abrogation, by which he excuses both himself and the people who were carried along with such fervent zeal towards him. "The Law and the Prophets," he says, "lasted until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses into it." In other places, on other occasions, he uses these words in another way, but here he seems to mean simply this: "I know that you are most devoted to the Law and its ceremonies, and you have long been persuaded about me, as if I thought less honourably of Moses and the Prophets. But you are very much mistaken, my friends. For I confess that the use of the Law and the Prophets has so far been excellent and manifold, because they illustrated and confirmed the promises about that blessed seed and the redemption of the human race and the restoration of the kingdom of God, and at the same time they teach what must be done by those who wish to enjoy such great blessings. This use therefore had a definite end, which John the Baptist brought to you. For he showed that the promised Saviour of the human race was now at hand, and pointed out with God's finger that Lamb who, having expiated the sins of the world and overthrown and destroyed the tyranny of the devil, was about to restore the kingdom of God. Why then do you wonder if many, having abandoned the ceremonies of the old worship, follow me, and almost force their way into the kingdom of God with a certain violence and great eagerness, since they already feel its power within their souls? Indeed, you too, roused by their example, should weigh the whole matter more carefully, and see that you are not the last in this zeal for salvation, you who ought to have gone before all others by your example." This, to me, is the plainest sense of these words and the one most suited to Christ's argument. For I cannot agree with those who think that the Evangelists rashly gathered sayings from his discourses and tossed them out like loose brushwood. It is quite clear that this whole chapter describes a continuous sermon of Christ, into which this short digression about the Law fits very well, since the Pharisees, who scoffingly mocked his teaching, are most powerfully refuted and pressed by it. There are, however, some points in these words that must be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primum est, quod Legem & Prophetas ad Ioannē vsq; durauisse ait. Ita verò hunc primū facit noui Testamenti præconem, vt hoc cum veteri coniungat: quam connexionē D. Marcus perspicuè ostendit, quando Euangelium Iesu Christi ita cœpisse scribit, vt olim in Prophetis fuerat prædictum. Id verò non ita accipi debet, quasi in illius aduentu Lex cū Prophetis omnino abolita sit, aut quòd nullus vel illius vel horū vsus nobis hodie esse debeat (nam de hoc Dominus mox ipse testabitur) sed dicto isto admonemur, finem & scopum Legis, adeoq; totius veteris Testamenti, esse Iesum Christum. Ita huius dicti sententiā ipse exponit, quando Mosem de ipso scripsisse testatur, & ex mortuis resuscitatus discipulis ait: Hi sunt sermones, quos locutus sum ad vos, cùm adhuc essem vobiscū: quòd scilicet oporteret impleri omnia, quæ scripta sunt in Lege Mosis, & Prophetis, & Psalmis de me. Posset hoc prolixè demonstrari, nisi passim de his dicendi occasio sese offerret. In Mose certè primū locū habent promissiones, quas omnes in Christo Iesu esse Etiā & Amen, Paulus testatur. Eadem est omnium typorum & ceremoniarū ratio, quæ non alium quam Christum, vnicam pro peccatis hostiam adumbrarunt. Et ipsa Lex dum omnes homines peccati reos agit & dānatos esse docet, non obscurè ostendit, nobis alia iustitia & redemptione opus esse, quæ in solo Christo habetur. Quid? an-non Moses post omnium, quæ in lege continentur, promulgatione, ad Magnū illum Prophetā remittit, quem omnes audire debeant? Quòd si quis omnia Prophetarū testimonia producere velit, totus dies illis recitandis non sufficeret. Tam enim abest, vt illi æternā salutē alibi quàm in Christo nobis commonstrent, vt hunc temporalium quoq; beneficiorū, quæ Deus olim Iudæis contulit Mediatorem vnicum esse doceant. De Psalmis quid dicere attinet, quando præcipuus horum Scriptor Dauid Christi typum gessit? Hæc vt inanem esse docent omnem ceremoniarum & operum nostrorum fiducialm: ita ostendunt simul, eam fidem & religionem, quæ solo Christo nititur, omnium vetustissimam atq; certissimam esse, neq; aliam salutis rationem in Ecclesia prædicari debere.
units.tr: First, he says that the Law and the Prophets lasted until John. In this way he makes John the herald of the New Testament, so that he joins it to the Old. Mark makes the same connection plainly when he writes that the Gospel of Jesus Christ began just as it had been foretold in the Prophets. This must not be taken to mean that at Christ's coming the Law and the Prophets were utterly abolished, or that no use of them should be ours today. The Lord himself will testify about this shortly. Rather, these words remind us that the end and goal of the Law, and so of the whole Old Testament, is Jesus Christ. He himself explains the meaning of this saying when, after his resurrection, he testifies that Moses wrote about him, and says to his disciples: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me." This could be demonstrated at length, were there not occasions to speak of these matters everywhere. Certainly in Moses the promises hold first place, and Paul testifies that all of them are "Yea and Amen" in Christ Jesus. The same is true of all the types and ceremonies, which foreshadowed none other than Christ, the one sacrifice for sins. The Law itself, while it declares all men guilty of sin and shows them to be condemned, makes it clear enough that we need another righteousness and redemption, which is found in Christ alone. What then? Does not Moses, after the promulgation of everything contained in the Law, send us on to that great Prophet whom all must hear? If anyone wished to produce all the testimonies of the Prophets, a whole day would not suffice to recite them. So far are they from showing us eternal salvation anywhere but in Christ, that they teach that he is also the sole Mediator of the temporal benefits which God formerly bestowed on the Jews. As for the Psalms, what need is there to say anything, since their chief author, David, bore the type of Christ? These writings teach that all confidence in ceremonies and in our own works is empty, and at the same time they show that the faith and religion which rests on Christ alone is the most ancient and most certain of all, and that no other way of salvation should be preached in the Church.

units.la: Deinde non temere dictum putemus, à Ioanne Regni Dei prædicatione cœpisse. Solet ita Euangelium dici, vt alibi etiam annotauimus. Ratio nominis est, quòd Christum prædicat, qui destructa diaboli tyrānnide Dei Regnum instaurauit. Habet hoc dulcissimā consolatione, quæ nos aduersus diaboli minas atq; conscientiæ terrores confirmat, quibus nos ille turbare satagit. Quid enim in nos possit ille quem iampridem foras eiectum esse, Christus testatur, & qui se ab hoc deuictū esse non semel confessus est? Hunc ergo clypeum opponamus, & nos in Dei Regno esse meminerimus, quoties quadruplator ille fingit sibi in nos aliquod ius esse & imperiū. At simul officij quoq; istud nos admonet, vt memores nos Regni Dei ciues esse diaboli iugum procul à nobis reiciamus, & locum nullum demus peccatorum atq; pessimarum cupiditatum illecebris, quibus nos in pristinam seruitutem retrahere conatur. Hic ergo regeneratione, nostri abnegatione, carnis mortificatione opus est. Hic sanctimonia vera exigitur, sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Hic charitati locus detur oportet, ne Regni Dei vnitatem dissidijs nostris turbemus. Deniq; cùm multa nos quotidie auocent, nunquā non precari nos conuenit, vt Regnum suum Deus in nobis suo Spiritu & verbo instauret.
units.tr: Next, let us not think it was without reason that John began by preaching the Kingdom of God. The Gospel is commonly so described, as we have also noted elsewhere. The reason for the name is that it preaches Christ, who, having destroyed the tyranny of the devil, restored the Kingdom of God. This carries a most sweet consolation, which strengthens us against the threats of the devil and the terrors of conscience, with which he strives to disturb us. For what can he do against us, that one whom Christ testifies was long ago cast out, and who has more than once confessed that he has been conquered by him? Let us therefore hold up this shield, and remember that we are in the Kingdom of God whenever that cheat pretends that he has some right and power over us. At the same time this also reminds us of our duty: mindful that we are citizens of the Kingdom of God, we should cast the yoke of the devil far from us, and give no place to the allurements of sins and of the worst desires, by which he tries to draw us back into our former slavery. Here, therefore, there is need of regeneration, of self-denial, and of mortification of the flesh. Here true holiness is required, without which no one will see God. Here room must be given to love, lest we disturb the unity of the Kingdom of God by our dissensions. Finally, since many things call us away every day, we ought never to cease praying that God would restore his Kingdom in us by his Spirit and Word.

units.la: Tertiò prædicationis huius vim Christus indicat, quando in Dei regnū omnes vi irrumpere ait. Apud Matthæū, violenti (inquit) rapiūt illud. Id verò de publicanis, meretricibus & alijs peccatoribus dicit, qui omnes mirifico studio ad ipsum confluebant, vt gratiæ Dei, quā ipse offerebat, participes fierent. Idem de gentibus quoq; intelligi debet, quæ turmatim ad Christū paulò post confluxerunt. Et sanè magnā esse oportuit Spiritus vim, quæ flagitijs obrutos illuminauit, vt in Christo pœnitentiæ locū & simul peccatorū remissione sibi offerri, certò scirent. Ineffabilis itē fuerit necesse est Dei potentia, quæ homines obscuros, imbelles & inermes confirmauit, vt contra Imperatorū edicta, contra Sacerdotū decreta, contra Proconsulū & Præsidū crudeles cōminationes, in Ecclesiæ Christi gremiū irruerent, & neq; periculis grauissimis, neq; supplicijs horrendis & exquisitis retineri aut absterreri possent, quò minus fidē in Christū inter medios gladios & rogos ardentes profiterentur. Exempla huius feruoris hodie multa in omnibus prope nationibus vidimus, quæ cùm omnibus nota sint, non spūs est eorū commemorationi diutius insistere. Nec aliter fieri potest, cùm Euangelium ani mis hominum conceptu totos sibi vendicet, & instar fermenti omnes sensus penetret, adeoq; homines nouos faciat, qui Dei voluntate & fide in Christo nihil antiquius habent. Vt autem Dominus hoc loco aliorum exemplo Pharisaeos excitare vult, ne ipsi aliis tardiores aut ignauiores sint: ita nos quoq; moueri conuenit eorum exemplis, qui per tot rerum discrimina perq; mille labores irrumpunt, vt in Euangelij communionē perueniāt, & fidei libertate fruantur. Quod vtinq; nos diligentius meditaremur, qui otio quasi abundamus, dū in huius mūdi theatro passim suorū electorū certamina Deus exhibet. Vt enim hic suorum studio & feruore delectatur: ita non potest nō eos dānare, qui hic otiosos spectatores agunt, vel etiā in peius proficiunt. De illis certè alibi dicit Christus: Erunt primi nouissimi, & c.
units.tr: Thirdly, Christ indicates the force of this preaching when he says that everyone forces his way into the Kingdom of God. In Matthew he says: "The violent take it by force." He says this of tax collectors, prostitutes and other sinners, who all flocked to him with remarkable eagerness, so that they might share in the grace of God which he offered. The same must also be understood of the Gentiles, who a little later flocked to Christ in crowds. And certainly the power of the Spirit must have been great, which enlightened those sunk in wickedness, so that they might know for certain that repentance is offered to them in Christ, and with it the forgiveness of sins. The power of God too must have been beyond words, which strengthened men who were obscure, weak and unarmed, so that, against the edicts of emperors, the decrees of priests, and the cruel threats of proconsuls and governors, they rushed into the bosom of the Church of Christ, and could be held back or frightened neither by the gravest dangers nor by dreadful and exquisite tortures, so that they professed faith in Christ even amid swords and blazing pyres. Today we have seen many examples of this zeal among almost all nations; since they are known to everyone, there is no need to dwell on their recounting at length. Nor can it be otherwise, since the Gospel claims men's minds wholly for itself, penetrates all their senses like leaven, and so makes men new, who, by the will of God and through faith in Christ, hold nothing more precious. Now, in this passage the Lord wishes to rouse the Pharisees by the example of others, so that they may not be slower or more sluggish than others. In the same way we too ought to be moved by the examples of those who, through so many dangers and countless labours, press on until they reach fellowship in the Gospel and enjoy the freedom of faith. We who, as it were, abound in leisure should consider this all the more diligently, since God displays on the stage of this world the struggles of his elect everywhere. For just as he delights in their zeal and fervour, so he cannot fail to condemn those who act here as idle spectators, or even grow worse. Of such people Christ speaks elsewhere: "The first will be last," and so on.

units.la: At poterat hoc Christi pronuntiatū Pharisaei falso sensu accipere, quasi nulla posthac valere deberat Legis & Prophetarum authoritas. Vt enim multi hodie Euangelij doctrinā bonus operibus inmica esse clamant, eò quòd salute in gratuita Dei misericordia nobis comonstrat: ita tunc Christum aduersarij, Mosis & Prophetarum authoritate impie labefactare vociferabantur, vt omnibus exosum & inuisum redderent. Id vero constantissimè negat, dicens: Facilius est aut cælum & terra praeterire quàm Legis vnū apicem excidere. Facit ad huius dicti interpretationē, quod apud Matthæū pluribus verbis dicitur: Ne existimetis, quòd venerim vt dissoluam Legem & Prophetas: nō veni vt dissoluam, sed vt impleam. Amen quippe dico vobis, vsq; dum praeterierit cælum & terra, iota vnum aut vnus apex nequaquā praeterierit ex Lege, vsq; dum omnia facta fuerint. Fatetur hic, vel potius testatur, se Legis authoritate inuiolabile agnoscere, imò nihil in tota hac cælorum & terrarum machina tam firmum & stabile esse, quàm Lex Dei sit. Quia enim hæc Dei voluntate constat, quæ sibi ipsi semper constat, illa mutari & aboleri nunquam poterit. Et quàmuis quædam in ea habeantur, quæ ad tempus correctionis abrogari debuerunt, id tamen non antea factū est, quàm cum ipsa quoq; fine suum attigissent, & in Christo essent impleta. Quo loco tota Legis ratio considerada venit, id quod paucis & breuiter absoluī potest. Diuiditur illa in Moralē, Ceremonialē & Iudicialē. Moralis est, quæ praecepta de moribus & omnibus vitæ actionibus tradit, à quibus fides in Deū & verus huius cultus separari non possunt. Epitome illius est decalogus & alij loci, qui de vno Deo diligendo & de proximi dilectione habentur. Ceremonialis de externo Dei cultu agit, qui olim in ceremonijs & ritibus certis consistebat, Circuncisione nimirū, feriis, sacrificijs, suffitu, purificationū formis variis, & alijs eiusmodi: quæ omnia partim promissionum diuinarū sigilla erant, partim bomines sui officij admonebant. Iudicialem dixerunt eam partē, quæ ad forum pertinet, de hereditatibus, coniugio & diuortijs, pœnis fontiū & multis alijs, quorū nonnulla ad solā Iudæorum rempub. accomodata fuerunt, quæ ab omnibus alijs populis palàm distincta esse debebat. Quoad vero impletionem & abrogationē Legis aut singularum partium, vtroq; in Christo solo habetur. Ceremonialia enim in eo suum complementū habuerunt, quando in morte sua & resurrectione omnia ea fere facta sunt, quæ in illis adumbrabantur: & quia iam reipsa praestitum est quicquid vmbrae illae promitte bant, nullus porrò illarū est vsus in Ecclesia, & proinde ita abrogatæ sunt, vt sine Christi contumelia & meriti eius euacuatione reduci aut instaurari nō possint, sicut Apostolus de circuncisione ad Galatas & in epist. ad Hebræos de toto sacerdotio & cultu Leuitico testatur. Abrogatio ergo Ceremonialis Legis facta est, nō quidē ignominiosa, sed cūprimis honorifica, quia sic impleta sunt quæ cunq; in ea tradebantur, vt ne vnus quidē apex & vnum iota excideret. In Iudicialibus ea modo abrogata sunt, quæ ad solā Iudæorū remp. pertinebāt. Quia enim hæc in Christo cessare debuit propter ingratitudinem & contumaciā, qua aduersus Dei Filium peccauerunt, illorū posthac nulla potuit esse vtilitas. Quæ vero inter illa cū Lege naturæ conueniunt, & alijs quoq; secundū hanc viuentibus comunia sunt, vnā cum tota Lege Morali, ea adhuc rata sunt, nec vnquā abrogari aut tolli debet. Abrogata aut est maledictio & damnatio quæ olim omnes eos manebat, qui non omnia praestarent, quæ in libro Legis continentur. Nā vt Paulus ait, Christus nos redemit ab execratione Legis, dū pro nobis factus est execratio. Quæ omnia si paulò attentius expendantur, facile apparebit, verum Legis vsum in Christo Iesu adeo nō aboleri, vt non alibi suum complementū habeat. Quibus adde, quòd in illo renatis Spiritus adoptionis datur, quo confirmati ea facimus, quæ viribus nostris prius perfici non poterant: & quàmuis quotidie sæpius labamur, eiusdē tande virtute resurgimus ad vitā nouitatem. Manet igitur semper rata & sacrosancta Legis authoritas, neq; ex illa quicquā excidit, cùm nos pædagogi instar ad Christum deducat, in quo nobis perfecta iustitia & redemptio exhibetur. Vt vero doctrina ista consolationem affert dulcissimā in tentationibus conscientiæ, ne Lagu minus atq; damnationibus terreamur: Ita peccandi licentiae obstat, quam multi sub libertatis Christianae praetextu venantur. Ita enim maledictionem Legis Christus sustulit, ut rata semper esse vellit praecepta, quae habentur de uno Deo colendo, de veri cultus ratione, de peccato, vitae innocentia, fraterna dilectione et aliis eiusmodi: quae nisi sedulo observemus, illius liberti nunquam erimus.
units.tr: But the Pharisees could have taken this saying of Christ in a false sense, as though the authority of the Law and the Prophets ought thenceforth to have no force. For just as many today cry out that the doctrine of the Gospel is hostile to good works, because it shows us salvation in the free mercy of God, so then his adversaries loudly claimed that Christ impiously undermined the authority of Moses and the Prophets, in order to make him hateful and odious to all. But he firmly denies this, saying: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall." What helps to explain this saying is what Matthew records in more words: "Do not think that I have come to dissolve the Law and the Prophets; I have not come to dissolve, but to fulfil. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will by any means pass from the Law, until all things have been done." Here he declares, or rather testifies, that he acknowledges the authority of the Law as inviolable; indeed, that nothing in this whole machine of heaven and earth is as firm and stable as the Law of God is. For since it stands on the will of God, which always remains consistent with itself, it can never be changed or abolished. And although some things in it were to be abrogated for a time of correction, this was not done before they had reached their own end and been fulfilled in Christ. At this point the whole account of the Law must be considered, which can be settled briefly and in a few words. It is divided into the Moral, the Ceremonial and the Judicial. The Moral is that which lays down precepts about morals and all the actions of life, from which faith in God and true worship of him cannot be separated. Its summary is the Decalogue, and other passages which concern the love of the one God and the love of neighbour. The Ceremonial deals with the external worship of God, which formerly consisted in certain ceremonies and rites: namely circumcision, festivals, sacrifices, incense, the various forms of purification, and others of this kind. All of these were partly seals of God's promises and partly reminders to men of their duty. They called the Judicial part that which pertains to the courts: concerning inheritances, marriage and divorce, penalties for crimes, and many other matters, some of which were adapted to the commonwealth of the Jews alone, and which had to be clearly distinguished from all other peoples. As for the fulfilling and abrogation of the Law, or of its individual parts, both are found in Christ alone. For the ceremonial precepts had their complement in him, since in his death and resurrection almost all those things were accomplished which had been foreshadowed in them. And because what those shadows promised has now actually been granted, there is no further use of them in the Church, and so they have been abrogated in such a way that they cannot be restored or re-established without dishonour to Christ and the emptying of his merit, as the Apostle testifies about circumcision to the Galatians, and in the Epistle to the Hebrews about the whole priesthood and Levitical worship. The abrogation of the Ceremonial Law was therefore made, not in a shameful way, but above all in an honourable way, because whatever was taught in it has been so fulfilled that not one stroke or one iota has fallen. In the Judicial laws only those were abrogated which pertained to the commonwealth of the Jews alone. For since this had to cease in Christ on account of the ingratitude and obstinacy with which they sinned against the Son of God, no usefulness of it could remain afterwards. But those things in them which agree with the Law of nature, and which are also common to other peoples living according to it, together with the whole Moral Law, are still in force and must never be abrogated or removed. The curse and condemnation which once hung over all who did not perform everything contained in the book of the Law have been abrogated. For as Paul says, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, when he became a curse for us. If all these things are weighed a little more carefully, it will easily appear that the true use of the Law is so far from being abolished in Christ Jesus that it finds its complement nowhere else. To these add that, to those reborn in him, the Spirit of adoption is given, by which, being strengthened, we do those things which previously could not be accomplished by our own strength; and although we fall more often every day, by his power we rise again to a new life. The authority of the Law therefore remains always valid and sacrosanct, and nothing is removed from it, since, like a tutor, it leads us to Christ, in whom perfect righteousness and redemption are given to us. But while this doctrine brings a most sweet consolation in the temptations of conscience, so that we are not terrified by the snares and condemnations of the Law, it also stands in the way of that licence to sin which many hunt under the pretext of Christian liberty. For Christ so removed the curse of the Law that he wished its precepts always to remain in force, those concerning the worship of the one God, the proper manner of true worship, sin, innocence of life, brotherly love and others of this kind. Unless we diligently observe these, we shall never be free from its bondage.

units.la: Porro ne quod dubium in hominum animis relinquat, exemplo docet, legem abs se non abrogari, sed confirmari. Dicit enim: Quisquis dimittit uxorem suam, et alteram ducit, moechatur: et qui a viro dimissam ducit, moechatur. Conuenit hoc cum praeceptorum quorundam pleniori expositione quae apud Matthaeum quinto cap. habetur. Ut enim illic eos confutat, qui solo litterali legis sensu ducti, se abunde innocentes esse arbitrabantur, si a manifestis et actualibus (ut loquitur) flagitiis abstinerent, etiam si animi foedissimus cogitationib. et desiderijs distracti a Deo et voluntate eius prorsus abhorret: Ita hic dispensationem illam corrigit, quam Moses propter duritiam cordis ipsorum (ut alibi dicit) in coniugij legib. permiserat, quoad divortia, et qua illi quoties libeat nimis utebantur. De qua cum alibi dixerimus, nunc sufficiat monuisse, licentiam repudiorum cum Dei voluntate pugnare, et illa coniugij vinculum in primis violari. Quis enim adulterum fieri negabit, qui aliam duxerit uxorem, priusquam legitimum cum priori divortium fecerit? Licet enim humano iure, aut dispensatione potius divortium fiat, manet tamen apud Deum firma et rata prioris coniugij necessitudo: quia hominis nequaquam ius est separare ea, quae Deus coniunxit. Similiter qui illegitime a viro eiecta ducit, revera moechatur, cum illa in Dei conspectu adhuc viri prioris uxor censeatur. At cum utrumque inter Iudaeos nimium frequens esset, non obscure pharisaeos et scribas Christi pstringit, qui cum acerrimi Legis vindices haberi vellet, ista sic fieri patiebatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest he leave any doubt in people's minds, he shows by example that the law is not abrogated by him but confirmed. For he says: "Whoever dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery, and whoever takes a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery" [Matth. 19.9; Luc. 16.18]. This agrees with the fuller exposition of certain precepts that is found in Matthew, chapter five. There he refutes those who, led by the bare literal sense of the law, thought themselves thoroughly innocent if they abstained from manifest and outward (as he puts it) crimes, even though their minds, filled with the foulest thoughts and desires, were utterly estranged from God and his will. Likewise here he corrects that dispensation which Moses, because of the hardness of their hearts (as he says elsewhere), had allowed in the laws of marriage concerning divorce, and which they used far too freely whenever they pleased. Since we have spoken of this elsewhere, it is enough now to remind you that the licence of divorce is contrary to the will of God, and that it above all violates the bond of marriage. For who will deny that a man becomes an adulterer when he takes another wife before he has made a lawful divorce from the first? For although a divorce is made by human law, or rather by dispensation, the bond of the earlier marriage remains firm and valid before God, because it is in no way man's right to separate those whom God has joined. Similarly, a woman who is taken by a man after being unlawfully put away truly commits adultery, since in the sight of God she is still regarded as the wife of her former husband. But since both were very common among the Jews, he plainly rebukes the Pharisees and scribes, who, wishing to be regarded as the most zealous defenders of the Law, tolerated such things being done.

units.la: Non temere autem factum putabimus, quod cum infinita alia huius generis exempla posset adducere hoc tamen ut voluit, quod ex coniugio petitur et ad huius instaurationem pertinebat. Patet ex eo matrimonij dignitas, et qua illud Deo cura sit: quam ut deniq; referat, ut illud recte contrahatur atque seruetur. Quia enim ex illo dependet legitima humani generis propagatio, vita quoq; hominum sine illo nunquam bene instituetur, et indies experimur, verissimum esse illud Dei dictum: Non est bonum, ut homo solus sit. Quod causa est, quod ut Deus illud in ipso statim rerum initio instituit: ita eius observatio nem gentibus vniuersis occulto naturae sensu commendauit: ut semper sacrosanctum et honorabile fuerit apud omnes, qui non prorsus in belluas degenerarunt. Docent hoc omnium gentium historici, qui grauissimos regnorum motus, periculosissimas reipub. mutationes, horribiles potentissimorum regum caedes, bella denique cum externarum ciuilia ex adulteriis, chori alieni violatione et vagis libidinibus originem duxisse scribunt. Est ergo incurabilis et detestanda nostri seculi hominum petulantia, quae neq; exemplis, neq; aeternae mortis comminationibus coerceri potest.
units.tr: We should not think it happened by chance that, although he could have adduced countless other examples of this kind, he chose this one, which is drawn from marriage and pertains to its maintenance. From this the dignity of matrimony is evident, and how much God cares for it; and, finally, he would have it entered into and kept rightly. For since the lawful propagation of the human race depends upon it, human life can never be well ordered without it, and we daily experience how true is that saying of God: "It is not good for man to be alone" [Gen. 2.18]. This is why God instituted it at the very beginning of things, and why he commended its observance to all nations by a hidden sense of nature, so that it has always been held sacred and honourable among all who have not wholly degenerated into beasts. All the historians of the nations teach this, who write that the most grievous upheavals of kingdoms, the most perilous changes in commonwealths, the horrible slaughters of the most powerful kings, and finally wars, both foreign and civil, took their origin from adulteries, from the violation of another's bed, and from wandering lusts. The wantonness of men in our age is therefore incurable and detestable; it can be restrained neither by examples nor by threats of eternal death.

units.la: Nec minus in repudijs aut divortijs peccatur, in quib. olim inter gentes licentia non minus turpi quam iniusta et iniqua multi visi sunt. Inter Christianos autem hodie multi similiter peccant, et quamus causam sufficientem esse censent, ad dissoluendum coniugij vinculum: et hi fere Iudaeis iniquiores sunt. Illi enim salte libellum repudij dabant, quo uxorum dimissarum pudicitia et honori consulebatur, at nostri illi fere cum aliqua infamiae nota dimittunt. Quorum licentia ut omnibus bonis iure displicet: ita multos mouet, ut in alteram partem peccent, et Pontificum sententiam sequantur, qui omne repudium illicitum esse tradiderunt. Fuit hoc iugum intolerabile pijs et honestis hominibus, qui adulteras uxores retinere, aut fornicationis periculum subire coacti sunt. Ita vero adulterij ab uxore comissi poenas viri luunt, et rursum adulterorum loco innoxiae foeminae multantur, illis interea impune per omne libidinis genus grassantibus. Media ergo via incedendum est, ut neq; licentia repudiorum locum habeat, neq; omne ius bonis eripiatur, quod ipse Deus illis concesserit. Atqui duas legitimi divortij causas Scriptura ostendit. Prima est adulterium. Cur enim no dimittatur, quae coniugij vinculum ipsa iam abrupit? aut cur eum maritum ferat Christiana mulier, qui fidem data turpiter fallit? Certe qui illud licere negant, ij non coniugii, sed fornicationis et adulteriorum patroni sunt. Altera causa est Religionis, si infidelis coniugi fideli cohabitare nolit, et ab eo discedat. Quid enim hic faciat Christianus, qui Christi paretibus, coniugi, liberis longe praeferri debere didicit? Paulus certe ait: Quod si infidelis discedit, discedat. Non est seruituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi rebus. Sed quia Dominus hac causam tantum exempli causa adducit, non opus est nunc ei diutius immorari. Discamus nos vniuersam Euangelij doctrinam magni facere, ne eam cum Pharisaeis, ut nihil ad nos pertinentem rideamus. Studeamus autem pietati et sanctitati verae: salutis vero fiduciam omnem repositam habeat. mus in gratuita Dei misericordia, qui Filium suum Iesum Christum pro nobis dedit, ut nostra sit iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Sin is no less committed in repudiations or divorces, in which of old among the nations a licence was seen to be no less shameful than unjust and iniquitous. Among Christians today, many likewise sin in this way: although they think that any cause is sufficient to dissolve the bond of marriage, and these people are almost more unjust than the Jews. For the Jews at least gave a bill of divorce, by which the chastity and honour of the dismissed wives were safeguarded, whereas our people for the most part put their wives away with some mark of infamy. Such licence displeases all good people rightly; yet it moves many to sin in the other direction, and to follow the opinion of the Pontiffs, who have taught that every divorce is unlawful. This yoke has been intolerable to godly and honest men, who have been forced either to keep adulterous wives or to undergo the danger of fornication. Thus the penalties for adultery committed by a wife fall upon the husbands, and in turn innocent women are punished in place of the adulterers, while those men rage on unpunished through every kind of lust. We must therefore go by the middle way, so that neither the licence of repudiation has a place, nor is every right taken from good people which God himself has granted them. Yet Scripture shows two lawful causes of divorce. The first is adultery. For why should she not be put away who has herself already broken the bond of marriage? Or why should a Christian woman bear a husband who shamefully breaks his faith? Certainly those who deny that this is lawful are defenders not of marriage but of fornication and adulteries. The other cause is religion: if an unbelieving spouse is unwilling to live with a believing one and departs from him. For what should the Christian do here, who has learned that Christ must be preferred far above parents, spouse, and children? Paul certainly says: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. A brother or sister is not under bondage in such matters" [1 Cor. 7.15]. But since the Lord adduces this cause only by way of example, there is no need to dwell on it any longer now. Let us learn to hold the whole doctrine of the Gospel in high esteem, and not to mock it with the Pharisees as something that does not concern us. Let us, however, strive for piety and true holiness, and let us place all our confidence of salvation in the free mercy of God, who gave his Son Jesus Christ for us, that he might be our righteousness, sanctification and redemption. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 157.

units.la: Caeterum quidam erat dives, & induebatur purpura & byssो, & se obłecta bat quotidie splendide. Erat autē quidam mendicus nomine Lazarus, qui pro ianua eius erat ad vestibulum eius, ulcerosus, & desiderans saturari micis, quae cadebant è mensa diuitis: sed & canes veniebant ac lingebant eius ulcera.
units.tr: There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who was laid at his gate, full of sores, and desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus, multa hucusque de avaritia aut immodico opum studio, deque vero earundem usu disseruit, qui est, ut non modo nostrae necessitati seruiat, sed ut simul benefici simus in pauperes, & ita nos eorum societati insinuemus, qui vera ecclesiae membra sunt, ut olim cum illis in caelo viviamus. Est doctrina haec simplex, & communis sensus testimonio probatur: Vehementer autem illi obstat iudicium vulgi. Plerique enim divites ex huius saeculi fortuna iudicant, & proinde illos felices atque beatos dicunt, paupertate autem nihil infelicius, nihil miserius aut calamitosius esse sentiunt. Hinc fit, quod capitali paupertatis odio inflammati, nullas verbi Dei admonitiones audiunt, neque rationibus ullis se persuaderi patiuntur, ut mediocritati & beneficentiae studeant: sed potius insatiabili habendi cupiditate divitiarum acervos congerendos inuigilent: quae multorum atque maximorum scelerum causa est. Nam qui ditescere volunt (ut Paulus ait) incidunt in tentationem & laqueum, & in cupiditates multas amentes & damnosas: quae demergunt homines in exitium & interitum. Qua propter Christus pro suo more doctrinam hanc sua eleganti parabola, vel potius rei gestae narratione (ut quibusdam videtur, in quorum sententia D. quoq; Ambrosius fuisse apparet) illustrat: qua caecum vulgi iudicium confutatur, & multa alia continentur cognitu & observatu necessaria. Hic enim discemus, quae nam fere sint diuitum vitia, quae opes illis exitiales reddunt. Quae poenae eosdem maneant. Rursum, quae pauperum sors sit atque conditio. Quid item de defunctis pie & orthodoxe sentire debeamus. Admonemur praeterea poenitentiam nō debere post mortem usque differri, & ex solis scripturis petere dū esse salutis consilium. De quib. omnib. suo loco dicetur. Nunc de divitis & Lazari personis agemus.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ has hitherto discoursed at length on avarice and on an immoderate zeal for riches, and on their right use. That use is not only to serve our own needs, but also to make us beneficent to the poor, and so to join us to their fellowship, who are the true members of the Church, so that we may one day live with them in heaven. This teaching is simple, and is confirmed by the testimony of common sense. But the judgment of the crowd strongly opposes it. For most people judge by the fortune of this world, and therefore call the rich happy and blessed, while they feel that nothing is more unhappy, more wretched, or more calamitous than poverty. Hence it comes about that, inflamed with a deadly hatred of poverty, they hear none of the warnings of the Word of God, and they allow themselves to be persuaded by no arguments to pursue moderation and beneficence. Instead they strive to heap up piles of riches with an insatiable desire to possess, and this is the cause of many and very great crimes. For those who want to be rich (as Paul says) fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge men into ruin and destruction. For this reason Christ, after his usual manner, illustrates this teaching by his elegant parable, or rather by a narrative of an actual event (as it seems to some, and in the opinion of which St. Ambrose also evidently was), by which the blind judgment of the crowd is refuted, and many other things necessary to know and to observe are contained. For here we shall learn what the vices of the rich are, which make their wealth ruinous to them, and what punishments await them. Again, what the lot and condition of the poor is. Likewise, what we ought to think piously and orthodoxly about the dead. We are also admonished that repentance ought not to be deferred until after death, and that the counsel of salvation is to be sought from the Scriptures alone while there is still time. All these things will be discussed in their proper place. Now we shall deal with the persons of the rich man and of Lazarus.

units.la: In divite typus summae felicitatis proponitur, qualis hac hominib. in hoc saeculo obtingere potest. Itaque diligentius consideranda erit primū tota eius conditio: deinde studia quoq; & mores, quibus pec cauit. Ad primum pertinet, quod simpliciter diuite dicit, neque alicuius publicae dignitatis aut functionis meminit. Itaque homo privatus ille fuit, & vita privatam vixit. Est haec non postrema felicitatis pars, eo quod non laboribus modo, verumetiam curis atque periculis assiduis exercentur, quicunq; rebus praesunt, & publica aliqua functione sustinent. Quod nō imprudenter Rex ille barbarus observavit, qui cū oblatū diadema multū diuq; contemplatus esset, tandē exclamavit: ô nobile potius & pretiosum quam felice pannū, quae ne humi quidem iacentem tolleret, quisquis sciret quot & quantis curis atq; solicitudinibus refertus sis. Placent quidem sibi ipsis Reges in sua magnificentia & opū atq; potentiae ostentatione, & Semidei quidā esse videntur: sed quam mordaces curas quamq; acerbos cruciatus intra animos suos sentiant, exquisita illa corporum suorum custodia non obscure testantur: dū fere barbaros & peregrinos milites acciersunt, quos multa pecunia conducunt, ut ab ipsorum vita seruetur intra suos parietes, ubi omnia tutissima esse debebant. Nihil nunc de illis dicimus, quibus proprij liberi, uxores, fratres suspecti sunt, & qui ne vrgente quidem fame cibū capere audēt, nisi ab alijs praegustatum, ne forte venenum hauriant. Potuit ergo noster hic vere beatus ceseri, qui procul negotijs vitam privatam egit, & proinde liberiorem suarum diuitiarum vsum habere potuit. Adde ita diuitem dici, ut neq; de opibus iniuste partis accusetur. Nec enim fenerator aut furarius, non miles, non raptor, non sacrilegus, non impostor vel defraudator dicitur. Talem ergo aestimare possumus, qui opes possederit iustas & bono iure ad se pertinentes: qualis alter ille fuit, de quo cap. duodecimo est dictum. Sunt haec in eum fine nobis observanda, ut discamus in illarum quoq; opū administratione peccari posse, quae optimo iure aut titulo a nobis possidentur: & proinde eos vehementer falli, qui sibi in illis quicquid libet licere putant. Esset quidē aliqua iflius persuasionis ratio, si quid ex nobis ipsis haberemus, quod iure possemus nostrum dicere: Sed cum opes a Deo dentur, nobis autem earum dispensatio modo credita sit (ut supra audiuimus) stulta & pernitiosa est insolētia, quae nos impellit, ut a Deo datis bonis petulantius abutamur. Ergo nostri huius exemplum intueamur, de quo etsi nihil adhuc dici potest, quod vituperium mereatur, abusu tamen in proprium exitium sibi vertit opes, quas ex Dei liberalitate acceperat. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui & pessimus artibus ditescunt, & illius mores atque studia imitantur?
units.tr: In the rich man is set forth a picture of the highest happiness, such as can fall to men in this world. Therefore his whole condition must first be considered more carefully, and then also his pursuits and the morals by which he sinned. To the first point belongs the fact that he is simply called a rich man, and no mention is made of any public dignity or office. He was therefore a private man, and lived a private life. This is no small part of happiness, because those who preside over affairs and bear some public office are exercised not only by labours but also by constant cares and dangers. This was not unwisely observed by that barbarian king, who, when a diadem was offered to him, looked at it for a long time and at last exclaimed: "O noble and precious rag rather than a happy one, which no one would pick up even from the ground, if he knew how full you are of so many and such great cares and anxieties!" Kings indeed take pleasure in themselves in their magnificence and in the display of their wealth and power, and they seem to be demigods: but how biting their cares and how bitter their torments are within their souls, that exquisite guarding of their bodies bears clear witness. For they often summon foreign and barbarian soldiers, whom they hire at great expense, so that their life may be kept safe within their own walls, where everything ought to have been most secure. I say nothing now of those whose own children, wives, and brothers are suspected, and who dare not take food, even when pressed by hunger, unless it has first been tasted by others, lest perhaps they swallow poison. So this man of ours, who truly could be called blessed, could live far from affairs a private life, and therefore could have a freer use of his riches. Add that he is called rich in such a way that he is not accused of having unjustly acquired his wealth. For he is not called a usurer or a thief, not a soldier, not a plunderer, not a sacrilegious man, not a cheat or defrauder. We may therefore judge him to be one who possessed wealth that was just and rightly belonging to him, as was that other man of whom it was said in the twelfth chapter. These things are to be noted by us for this purpose: that we may learn that sin can be committed even in the management of those riches which we possess by the best right or title, and that therefore they are greatly mistaken who think that they may do whatever they please with them. There would indeed be some reason for that persuasion, if we had anything from ourselves which we could rightly call our own. But since riches are given by God, and only the stewardship of them has been entrusted to us (as we heard above), it is foolish and pernicious arrogance that drives us to abuse the goods given by God more wantonly. Let us then look upon the example of this man, against whom, although nothing can yet be said that deserves blame, nevertheless his abuse turned to his own destruction the wealth which he had received from the liberality of God. What then will become of those who grow rich by the worst arts, and imitate his morals and pursuits?

units.la: Sed videamus, quae illa fuerint? Induebatur purpura & bysso, & se obtegebat quotidie splendide. Primum vestitus mollior & ornatior illi tribuitur. Purpura enim tinctura excellentior, pretium & dignitatem summam apud veteres conciliavit. Byssus autem lini quoddam genus apud Aegyptios & Orientales fuit, cuius materia ex arboribus colligebatur. Deinde splendidius obtectum fuisse dicit, quo membro vitiu & omnia alia totius vitae studia comprehendit, & sensus est, quod cibus vi|us fit lautioribus, adhaec ludis deditus hoc unum quaesierit, ut vitam in tripudiis & magnificentia transfigeret. Atqui interdum splendidius vestiri per se peccatum non est, modo conditionis & dignitatis ratio habeatur: & scimus quid in vestitu Joseph, David, Salomon, Hestera regina fecerint, quorum omnium pietas in scripturis celebratur. Ita neque in genere damnantur conuivia lautiora, neque etiam gaudia, quibus animos interdum recreari utile & necesse est. Quin Moses ipse iubet, ut diebus festis, qui victimas obtulerant, epulentur & laetetur coram Domino. In quo ergo ipse peccavit? Vno verbo id Christus indicat, quando haec illum QVOTIDIE fecisse ait. Nam ut temporis ratio permittit, ut aliquando splendidius & laetius vivamus: ita non minus eadem illa requirit, ut interdum ieiunijs vacemus, sacco vestiamur & (ut scriptura loquuntur) animas nostras affligamus. Qui ergo quotidie vestitu molliori superbiunt, & quotidie lautius epulantur, ij satis ostendunt, se nimium securos animi esse nec multum moveri iudiciorum Dei exemplis, quibus hic mundi petulantia coerce satagit. Ita duo non vulgaria vitia dives iste coniunxit, Securitatem nimirum atque Luxum sive Intemperantiam. Ex his tertium manavit, pauperum contemptus, & quod Lazarum famelicum atque ulceribus obsitum, qui ad eius vestibulum prostratus iacebat, facile neglexit, adeo ut ne reliquis quidem aut micis ex mensa sua cadentibus eius famem atque inopiam releuare dignaretur: imo canibus, qui eius vulnera lingebant, esset durior.
units.tr: But let us see what those were. He was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day. First, a softer and more ornate clothing is attributed to him. For purple, a more excellent dye, won the highest price and dignity among the ancients. Byssus, however, was a kind of linen among the Egyptians and Orientals, whose material was gathered from trees. Then he says that he was clothed more splendidly, a phrase which comprehends in one member his vice and all the other pursuits of his whole life; and the sense is that, because his food was made more luxurious, and because he was given to revelry, he sought only this, that he might spend his life in feasting and magnificence. And yet to be dressed more splendidly is not in itself a sin, provided that regard is had to one's station and rank; and we know what Joseph, David, Solomon, and Queen Esther did in their clothing, whose piety is celebrated in the Scriptures. So neither are more lavish banquets condemned in general, nor those joys by which men's minds may sometimes be refreshed, and which are useful and necessary. Indeed Moses himself commands that on festival days those who had offered sacrifices should feast and rejoice before the Lord. In what, then, did he himself sin? Christ indicates this in one word, when he says that the man did these things EVERY DAY. For just as the circumstances of time allow us sometimes to live more splendidly and joyfully, so they no less require that at other times we should give ourselves to fasting, be clothed in sackcloth, and (as the Scriptures put it) afflict our souls. Therefore those who every day pride themselves on softer clothing, and every day feast more luxuriously, show well enough that they are too secure in mind and are little moved by the examples of God's judgments, by which this passage seeks to restrain the wantonness of the world. Thus this rich man joined two vices that are not ordinary: namely, security and luxury, or intemperance. From these a third sprang forth, the contempt of the poor, and that he easily neglected Lazarus, who lay prostrate at his gate, hungry and covered with sores, so that he did not even deign to relieve his hunger and want with the leftovers or crumbs falling from his table: indeed he was harder than the dogs which licked his wounds.

units.la: Isto autem exemplo divitum vitia Christus adumbrat, quibus plerunque iram Dei provocant, & divitias sibi ipsis exitiales reddunt. Primum inter illa est securitas cum confidentia coniuncta, quam divitijs perpetuam fere comitem esse, aut saltem ex illis nasci, Germani vulgari proverbio testantur. Ut enim egestas impatientes facit & murmuratores: ita difficile est cavere, ne cristas attollant, qui opes possident ampliores, & earum aceruos indies augeri videt. Mali aut vitij huius praecipua causa est, caecum atque peruersum de divitijs iudicium. Quia enim has sibi proprias esse, adhaec aeternas & in ipsdem veram hominis felicitatem consistere sibi ipsis persuadent, non possunt non simul putare, se extra omnem telum tactum constitutos esse, si aurum & argentum plurimum possideant, latifundijs maximis & amplissimis dominentur, serus stipati incedat, & propter opes atque splendorem insolitum ab omnibus digito monstretur. Itaque praesens vitij huius remedium fuerit, si nos nihil in terris proprium possidere, sed dispensatores modo esse cogitemus eorum, quae Deus nobis gratuita misericordia largitur. Tunc enim mox succurret, olim reddendam esse rationem Deo, ubi nulla exillarum abundantia ad nos utilitas redibit: quin potius ea ipsa aduersus nos testabitur, ut Iacobus docet. Adde hiis, quod fluxae & caducae sunt, & proinde ad hominis felicitatem nihil possunt conferre. Quae omnia si diligenter expendantur, mox omnem ex animis securitatem eijcient, & de veri dispensatione solicitos reddent eos, qui prius sibi ipsis omnia tuta promittebant.
