units.tr: Christ depicts the sins of the rich by this example, the sins that usually provoke God's wrath and make their riches deadly to themselves. The first of these is complacency joined with confidence, which the Germans testify by a common proverb is almost always the constant companion of wealth, or at least springs from it. For just as poverty makes people impatient and grumbling, so those who possess greater riches and see their heaps grow daily find it hard to avoid holding their heads high. The chief cause of this evil and vice is a blind and perverse judgment about riches. Because people persuade themselves that riches are their own, and that true human happiness is eternal and rests in them, they cannot help thinking that they are placed beyond every missile, if they possess much gold and silver, rule over vast and extensive estates, walk about with a crowd of servants, and, on account of their wealth and unusual splendour, are pointed out with the finger by everyone. So the remedy for this vice will be present if we reflect that we possess nothing in the world as our own, but are only stewards of the things God freely gives us in his mercy. For then it will immediately occur to us that an account must one day be rendered to God, when no abundance of these things will bring any benefit back to us; rather, they themselves will bear witness against us, as James teaches. Add to this that such things are fleeting and perishable, and therefore can contribute nothing to human happiness. If all these things are carefully weighed, they will soon drive complacency out of minds and make anxious about faithful stewardship those who before promised themselves everything was safe.

units.la: Alterum vitiu, quo diuites plerunque laborant, luxus est, qui ex priori illo nascitur. Nam qui opes sibi proprias esse sibi persuaserunt, ij illarum vsum ad se solos pertinere putant. At cum natura parcis contenta sit, & necessitati pauca possint sufficere, plura luxui dare oportet eos, qui diuitijs soli volunt uti. Varias itaque eius species excogitat insatiabilis hominum cupiditas, quae si semel ei indulgeas modum non inuenit. Hinc ergo luxuriosa in vestitu mollities sese exerit, quae & naturae & Christi legibus repugnat. Quia enim vestitus origo ex peccato est, nimis absurdi ac imprudentes sunt, qui illis superbiunt, & quid obsecro bi aliud faciunt, quam si quis facinorosus ex catenis & laqueis, quibus vincitur, gloriam quaerat? Quae vero amentia est, Christianum hominem vestitu luxuriari, qui omnem salutis suae fiduciam in Christo collocatam habet, qui ut vestes habuit paucissimas, ita easdem propter nos militibus prophanis praedam fieri voluit, & nudus in cruce pependit, ut primam innocentiæ vestem nobis recuperaret? Quæ cum verissimè dicantur, & merito molliculos illos pudore suffundere debeant, pleriq; tamen diuitum non contenti sumptuosiori vestitu, parum se fecisse existimant, nisi peregrinis quoq; vestium formis sese ostentent, & has quoq; indies mutent, ne quid cum aliis commune habeant. Ridiculum sane hominum genus, qui dignitatem maiorem sibi ipsis ex pannis pollicentur, quasi hi animum mutare & huius dotes augere possint. Atqui (quod proverbio dicitur) Simia manet Simia, etiamsi aurea gestet insignia. Comitatur luxum hunc intemperantia in victu, gulæ studium, ex quo fœdus & belluinus donorum Dei abusus nascitur cum ebrietate, quam merito omnium scelerum atq; turpitudinis parentem dixeris. Et quia huic etiā cupiditati finis statui non potest, non minus peregrinas & nouas lautitias quotidie quærunt, qui illi semel cœperunt indulgere. Itaq; maria & terras omnes fatigant, ut non tam cibos quam gulæ irritamenta conquirant, quibus palati fastidio medeantur. Et dum ex illis voluptatem magnam sperant, sua intemperantia tam corporis, quam ingenij vires debilitant, & sibi ipsis morbos omnis generis accersunt.
units.tr: The second vice, to which the rich are usually prone, is luxury, which arises from the first. For those who have persuaded themselves that their riches are their own think that the use of them belongs to themselves alone. But since nature is content with little, and a few things can suffice for necessity, those who wish to enjoy their riches alone must give more to luxury. Thus insatiable human desire devises its various forms, and if you once indulge it, it finds no limit. Hence there arises effeminacy in dress, which is contrary both to the laws of nature and to the laws of Christ. For since the origin of clothing lies in sin, those are most absurd and foolish who take pride in them. What else, I ask you, do they do but what a criminal would do if he sought glory from the chains and snares by which he is bound? And what madness it is for a Christian, who has placed all his confidence of salvation in Christ, to indulge in luxurious clothing, when Christ, who had very few garments, chose for our sake that they should become plunder for profane soldiers, and hung naked on the cross, so that he might restore to us the first garment of innocence! Although these things are said most truly, and ought rightly to make those effeminate fops blush with shame, yet most of the rich, not content with more costly clothing, think they have done little unless they also display themselves in foreign styles of dress, and change these styles daily, lest they have anything in common with others. Truly a ridiculous kind of people, who promise themselves greater dignity from their rags, as if they could change their minds and increase their qualities by this means! Yet (as the proverb says) the ape remains an ape, even if it wears golden trappings. Intemperance in food accompanies this luxury, the zeal for gluttony, from which arises the foul and brutish abuse of God's gifts together with drunkenness, which one may rightly call the parent of all crimes and baseness. And since this desire too cannot be set a limit, those who once began to indulge it seek daily no less foreign and new delicacies. So they wear out lands and seas, seeking not so much food as stimulants for the gullet, by which they may remedy the disgust of the palate. And while they hope for great pleasure from these, by their intemperance they weaken the strength of both body and mind, and bring upon themselves diseases of every kind.

units.la: Coniunctus est vitijs hisce pauperum contemptus, quos fere nihil ad se pertinere putat. Quomodo enim aliorum rationem aliquam habent, quos securitas iam pridem occupauit, & quorū cogitationes circa vestium ambitiosam ostentationem, conuiuiorum luxum, superbas inutilium ædificiorum structuras, theatra, ludos, spectacula & alia sexcenta huius generis distrahuntur, quibus paupertas ipsa inimica est? Itaq; qui inter illos alijs meliores sunt, securi pauperes atq; egenos negligunt, & Sacerdotem atq; Leuitam, de quibus in Samaritani parabola dictum est, imitantur qui saucium & à latronibus spoliatum præterierunt, neq; eius curam ad se pertinere sunt arbitrati. Et hanc ostendi tantiam crudelem in isto etiam diuite epulone Christus perstringit, quando Lazarum ad vestibulū eius proiectū iacuisse ait, nullam vero vel beneficij in ipsum collati, vel alicuius iniuriæ facit mentionem. Atqui eo nomine multi sibi ipsis placent, seq; apud Deum abunde excusatos esse arbitrantur, si ab iniurijs abstineant, etiamsi interea pauperes omnes negligant. Quasi vero non satis iniurius sit, qui egeni debitum officium negat: aut non satis noceat, qui eum fame perire finit, quem sua ope subleuare poterat. Et quid aliud in Sodomæis Deus per Ezechielem reprehendit, quàm quæ de hoc nostro diuite narrantur? Ecce (inquit) hæc fuit iniquitas Sodomæ sororis tuæ, fastus, saturitas panis, felicitas, otium, & manum pauperis atq; egeni non firmauit. Quò etiā referri debet, quod Christus in nonissimo die actionem suam proprie aduersus eos instituet, qui esurientem non cibarunt, sitienti non dederunt potum, nudum non vestierunt, peregrinum non exceperunt hospitio, ægrotantem aut captiuum non inuiserunt, neq; consolati sunt. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui non contenti neglexisse pauperes, insuper eos odiose accusant, eorum vitia maligne notant, ut alios quoq; à benefibentia abstrerent, adhæc ab ostijs & domibus suis procul arcent, vel etiam illis claudunt vrbium portas, quæ interea mimis, scurris, bistrionibus & meretricibus impudentissimis patet? Quid deniq; sperare possunt ab his, quorum durites ne in his quidē modū habet, sed insuper suis fraudibus, impostura, rapinis & tyrannide ad extremā egestate redigunt, quorū fortunas tueri debebant? Damnatur dives ille, quod neglecto Lazaro ipse vestitu superbiuit, & laute epulatus est, seq; ipsum ludis & omni voluptatis genere oblectauit. Num ergo impune feret, qui ut molliter vestiri, epulari, ludere & voluptuari possint, multos quotidie pauperes faciunt, & non solum ex ædibus paternis, verumetiam ex solo natali eijciunt? Atqui hi illi sunt, qui hodie mortalium in hoc mundo beatissimi censentur, & quorum typum nobis in isto sumptuoso epulone Christus proponit. Sunt hi reuera omnium infelicissimi, cum tota felicitatis ipsorum existimatio ab opibus dependeat, quibus nihil est instabilius, & quæ illis tot tantorum scelerum occasiones atq; materiam suppeditant.
units.tr: Joined with these vices is contempt for the poor, whom they generally think has nothing to do with them. For how can they take any account of others, when security has long since occupied them, and their thoughts are distracted by the ambitious display of clothing, the luxury of banquets, the proud construction of useless buildings, theatres, games, spectacles, and countless other things of this kind, to which poverty itself is hostile? So those who are somewhat better than the rest, being secure, neglect the poor and needy, and imitate the priest and the Levite, of whom it is spoken in the parable of the Samaritan, who passed by the man wounded and stripped by robbers, and judged that his care did not concern them. Christ also censures this same cruel indifference in that rich glutton, when he says that Lazarus lay cast down at his gate, yet makes no mention of any benefit conferred on him or of any wrong done to him. Yet many are pleased with themselves on this account, and think they are fully excused before God if they abstain from injuries, even though meanwhile they neglect all the poor. As if one who denies the duty owed to the needy were not sufficiently unjust, or one who allows a man to perish of hunger whom he could have relieved with his help did not sufficiently harm him! And what else did God rebuke in the Sodomites through Ezekiel than what is recounted of this rich man of ours? "Behold," he says, "this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread, prosperity, idleness, and she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy." To this also belongs the fact that on the last day Christ will bring his action directly against those who did not feed the hungry, did not give drink to the thirsty, did not clothe the naked, did not receive the stranger into their hospitality, did not visit the sick or the prisoner, and did not console them. What then will become of those who, not content with having neglected the poor, further accuse them spitefully, maliciously note their faults, so that they may turn others also away from beneficence, and moreover keep them far from their doors and houses, or even close the gates of the cities against them, while meanwhile those gates stand open to mimes, buffoons, actors and most shameless harlots? Finally, what can the poor hope from those whose hardness does not even keep measure with these, but who, by their frauds, trickery, robberies and tyranny, reduce to extreme want those whose fortunes they ought to protect? That rich man is condemned because, neglecting Lazarus, he himself took pride in his clothing, feasted sumptuously, and delighted himself with games and every kind of pleasure. Will then those escape unpunished who, so that they may be softly clothed, feast, play and indulge in pleasures, make many poor every day, and drive them out not only from their paternal homes but even from their native soil? Yet these are the people who today are judged the most blessed of mortals in this world, and whose type Christ sets before us in that sumptuous glutton. In truth they are the most unhappy of all, since the entire estimation of their happiness depends on riches, which are nothing more unstable, and which supply them with so many occasions and material for such great crimes.

units.la: Sed videamus ex altera parte Lazarum, qui eorum est typus, quos mundus hic solos infelices & miseros iudicare solet. In quo primum nobis occurrit nomen, quo illi Christus dignatur, qui diuitis nomen nullum expressit. Ita vero in ipso limine ostendit, Dei iudicium ab hominum sententia multum differre. Hi enim solos diuites immortali gloria dignos esse existimant, nec satis esse videtur, si nomē eorū cum aliqua honoris significatione celebrent, nisi titulos quoq; addant ambitionis plenos, quorum aliqui nimij, aliqui indigni & absurdi, multi inepti, omnes vero salsissimi sunt. Sed & ipsi diuites, ut nomina suo ad posteritatem transmittant, stemmata sua ex ordine domi suæ collocare, gentis insignia in teplis, hospitijs publicis, ad sepulchra deniq; suspendere solent: & insuper seruiliter ingenij scriptores amplißimù donis inuitare, quos suarum laudum præcones habeant. Et hæc quidē ad tem pus aliquod multi admirantur: sed plerunq; præter omnem expectationem omnia ista intercidunt, vt aut nulla extet vel nominis ipsorum memoria, aut ea fœtida & ignominiosa maneat. Quod Dauid obseruans dicebat: Vidi impium sese diffundentem instar lauri frondosæ: Et transiui, & ecce non erat: quæsiui eum, & non est inuentus. At longè alia est piorū sors, qui etsi in hoc mundo obscuri & ignobiles sint, in cœlis tamē eorū nomina adscripta sunt: & proinde immortalem atq; æternam laudem habent. Ideo Christus, qui diuitem illum molliculum & ambitiosum ne nominare quidē dignatus est, mendici pauperrimi nomen diligenter exprimit. At quale nā hoc fuit? Lazarus, quod idem est cum Eleazari nomine, virumq; vero Deum adiutorem vel Dei adiutorium significat. Videtur huic allusio subesse ad vulgarem morem, quo mendicis stipem aut panē petentibus respondetur: Adiuuet te Deus. At quod illi ab inhumanis & duris dicitur, id Dominus consolationis loco ipsis esse vult, eò quod omnes illi, qui hominū ope destituuntur, reuera Lazari sint, id est tales, quibus Deus adiutor & patronus esse velit. Huc enim illud Psalmi pertinet: Beatus cuius auxilium est Deus Iacob, & cuius spes est apud Dominum Deum suum. Itaq; ipso nomine statim Christus eum felicem & beatum pronuntiat, qui propter egestatem miserrimus erat hominum iudicio.
units.tr: But let us look on the other side, at Lazarus, who is the type of those whom this world is accustomed to judge alone unhappy and wretched. Here the first thing that meets us is the name by which Christ honours him, while he gave the rich man no name at all. Thus from the very threshold he shows that God's judgment differs greatly from the verdict of men. For these think that only the rich are worthy of immortal glory, and it seems not enough for them to celebrate their names with some sign of honour, unless they add titles full of ambition, some of which are excessive, some unworthy and absurd, many foolish, and all most ridiculous. Moreover, the rich themselves, so that they may hand down their names to posterity, are accustomed to set up their genealogies in order in their houses, to hang the insignia of their family in temples, public inns, and finally at tombs; and besides, they slavishly invite writers of talent with the most generous gifts, so that they may have heralds of their praises. For a while many admire these things; but for the most part, contrary to all expectation, all these things perish, so that either no memory of their name survives, or it remains foul and disgraceful. David, observing this, said: "I saw the wicked spreading himself like a green laurel tree; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and he was not found." But the lot of the godly is very different: although in this world they are obscure and ignoble, yet their names are written in heaven, and therefore they have immortal and eternal praise. Hence Christ, who did not even deign to name that effeminate and ambitious rich man, carefully expresses the name of the most destitute beggar. And what sort of name is this? Lazarus, which is the same as the name Eleazar, and means "God is a helper" or "the help of God." There seems to be an allusion here to the common custom by which beggars asking for alms or bread are answered, "May God help you." What the hard and inhuman say to them, the Lord wishes to be a consolation to them, because all those who are deprived of human help are truly Lazaruses, that is, such as God wishes to be helper and patron to. For to this belongs that verse of the Psalm: "Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, and whose hope is in the Lord his God." So by the very name Christ at once pronounces him happy and blessed, who by the judgment of men was most wretched on account of his poverty.

units.la: Præstat tamen paulò diligentius Lazari huius conditionē inspicere. Primùm non pauper modò, sed πτωχὸς fuisse dicitur: quæ vox proprie eum significat, qui omnium indigus ne labore quidem manuū sibijpsi victum parare potest, sed aliorum opem implorare cogitur: quos vulgò mendicos dicimus. Est horum conditio miserrima, quia illis non solum cum paupertate, verumetiam cū mundo res est, in quo plures semper immites & inhumani sunt, qui ipsos oderunt, & indignos esse iudicant quibus aliquis opem ferat. Et quod reliqua mala superat, vitæ etiam innocentia & morū probitas in isto hominum ordine plurimū periclitatur. Quia enim paupertas, si per se consideretur, malesuada est, tales autem ab omnibus ferè negliguntur, nec vlla vel Ecclesiastica vel politica disciplina continentur, facilis illis in omnē licentiam lapsus est, & ferè eò usq; delabuntur, vt ex inopia sua impunitatem sibijpsis polliceantur, & non ipsi modò pessimè viuant, verumetiā liberos suos male educent, & tales posteros relinquant, quos neq; religio neq; magistratuum authoritas mouet, cum nulla apud eos sit illarum rerum cognitio, quibus homines in officio cōtineri possunt. Quæ causa est, quod Deus olim pauperes quidē suo populo nunquam defuturos esse testatus est, & eosdem commendatissimos esse voluit, simul autem grauiter monuit, ne mendicos esse patiātur. Quod ipsum Apostoli probè considerantes, in primitiua Ecclesia res ita instituerunt, ne quis egenus esset, qui viritim stipem aut ostiatim panē emendicare cogeretur. Et Paulus in epistolis ad Thessalonicenses multa graviter dicit τῶν ἀτάκτων, id est, de inordinatis illis hominibus, qui cum nec priuatim rem domesticam obeant, nec publicè politicis legibus aut Ecclesiasticis viuant, ex publicis tamen Ecclesiæ bonis & priuatis piorum eleemosynis sibi dari volunt, quod ipsorum ignauiæ & licentiæ possit sufficere. Quoties ergo in euangelica historia mendicorum fit mentio, id in Iudæorū opprobrium fieri cogitemus, quorum Sacerdotes & Seniores publica bona ad se rapuerant, & nulla habita pauperum cura eos vagari & oberrare patiebātur. Quod vtinā non etiam hodie apud multos fieret, qui Euangelicæ doctrinæ professione superbiunt. Illis enim ferè debemus magnam illam mendicorum turbam, qui hinc inde famelici oberrant, vias omnes obsident, clamore & querelis omnes obtundunt, ex Ecclesiarum bonis interea ditescentibus & voluptuatibus illis, qui vt inter Ecclesiæ membra numerentur multis nominibus indigni sunt. Sentient isti aliquando graue Dei iudiciū. Interim nō obstabit illorum inhumanitas atq; rapacitas, quo minus Deo grati sint, qui per illos mendicare cogun tur, modò isti fidem in Deū retineant, patientiæ & vitæ innocentiæ studeant, quod hunc Lazarum fecisse paulo post audiemus.
units.tr: It is worth looking a little more carefully at this Lazarus's condition. First, he is said to have been not merely poor but πτωχὸς [ptōchos], a word that properly denotes someone who lacks everything and cannot even earn his living by the labour of his hands, but is forced to beg help from others. We commonly call such people beggars. Their condition is most wretched, because they have to deal not only with poverty but with the world, in which there are always many harsh and inhuman people who hate them and judge them unworthy of anyone's help. And, beyond all the other evils, the innocence of their life and the uprightness of their morals are greatly endangered in this class of people. Poverty, considered in itself, is conducive to bad counsel, and such people are for the most part neglected by everyone and restrained by neither church nor civil discipline. So they slip easily into every kind of licence, and often sink so far that, from their want, they promise themselves impunity. Not only do they live very badly themselves, but they also bring up their children badly and leave behind such offspring as are moved neither by religion nor by the authority of magistrates, since they have no knowledge of those things by which men can be kept in their duty. This is why God, though he once declared that there would never be lack of poor among his people and wished them to be commended, at the same time solemnly warned that beggars should not be allowed to exist. The Apostles, considering this carefully, arranged matters in the primitive Church so that no one would be in need, forced to beg a coin from person to person or bread from door to door. And Paul, in his epistles to the Thessalonians, speaks sternly of the τῶν ἀτάκτων [tōn ataktōn], that is, of those disorderly men who neither attend to their own household affairs in private nor live under the public political laws or church rules, and yet want to be supported from the public goods of the Church and from the private alms of the godly, as if these could satisfy their idleness and licence. Whenever, then, mention is made in the gospel story of beggars, let us think that this is recorded to the shame of the Jews, whose priests and elders had seized the public goods for themselves and, with no care for the poor, allowed them to wander and roam about. Would that this did not happen even today among many who boast of their profession of the gospel doctrine! For we owe to them that great crowd of beggars who wander hungry from place to place, besiege every road, and wear everyone down with clamour and complaints, while the goods of the Churches meanwhile make rich those voluptuaries who, though in many respects unworthy to be numbered among the members of the Church, ... Those men will one day feel the heavy judgment of God. Meanwhile, their inhumanity and rapacity will not stand in the way of those who are compelled to beg through them being pleasing to God, provided they keep their faith in God and pursue patience and innocence of life, as we shall hear a little later that this Lazarus did.

units.la: Nunc vt ad hunc redeamus, extremæ eius inopiæ aliud incōmodum longè maius accessit, aduersa nimirū corporis valetudo, & ea quidē non vulgaris, aut in qua aliqua restitutionis spes posset haberi. Nam totus vlceribus obsitus fuit, quorum sanies totum corpus & ipsas quoq; medullas iam eò vsq; depasta erat, vt non multo post vitam suam finierit. Et cum alios morbos ferè cibi fastidium comitetur, iste simul cum fame etiam conslictatus est, quam vulgò extremum malorum omnium esse aiunt. Adde his, quod & famelicus & vlceribus contabescens, neq; propria domum, neq; hospitium aut cubiculum meritorium habuit, in quo se contineret: sed ad diuitis huius abliguritoris ve stibulum proiectus iacuit, prae fame non lautitias & rariores aliquas dapes (quas fere aegroti appe tunt) sed micas petens e mensa cadentes, quas obrepens libenter collecturus erat, modo eo fuisset admissus. Facit praeterea ad cumulum istius miseriae, quod solus illic iacet, neque socium habet egestatis, ex quo vel consolatione vel consilium aliquod petere possit. A diuite autem & eius familia, quae procul dubio numerosissima fuit, ita inhumaniter & immisericorditer negligitur, ut ne micas quidem modicas effl agitare possit, & canes omnibus illis humaniores & officiosiores erga se sentiat. Hi enim veniebat, & lingebant eius vlcera. Quo spectaculo Christus no huius modo epulonis, sed omnium eorum duritiem atq; crudelitatem arguit, qui procul abiecto omni humanitatis sensu nulla vllius hominis miseria tanguntur. Hi certe non solum in charitatem & communionem Christianam peccant, sed naturae etiam leges violant. Cum enim in pauperrimis hominibus imo in mendicis sanie & tabo diffluentibus, humanae naturae dignitatem animalia bruta, canes, equi, volucres, & interdum ferae etiam agnoscant, quis obsecro naturae sensum aliquem in illis reliquum esse dixerit, qui eiusdem secum naturae consortes tam facile negligunt, ut neq; commiseratione aliqua spontanea, neq; animalium brutorum exemplo moveantur? Quoties ergo canes aut iumenta aliquid officij egenis atque mendicantibus praestare cernimus, toties aduersus nos testes produci, aut a Deo iudices constitui cogitemus, quorum exemplis condemnemur.
units.tr: Now, to return to him: a further evil, much greater than his extreme poverty, was added, namely a grave illness of the body, and not a common one, nor one in which any hope of recovery could be entertained. For he was covered all over with ulcers, whose matter had by now eaten away his whole body, even his very marrow, so that not long after he finished his life. Although loss of appetite usually accompanies other diseases, he was afflicted at the same time with hunger, which people commonly call the worst of all evils. Add to this that, being both hungry and wasting away with ulcers, he had neither a home of his own, nor a lodging, nor a room to shelter in; he lay thrown down at the vestibule of this rich glutton, longing, because of his hunger, not for delicacies and rarer dishes (which sick people usually crave), but for the crumbs falling from the table, which he would gladly have gathered up, creeping in, had he only been admitted. What adds to the height of his misery is that he lies there alone, and has no companion in his want from whom he could seek either comfort or some counsel. But he is neglected by the rich man and his household, who were doubtless very numerous, so inhumanly and pitilessly that he could not even scrape together a few small crumbs, and he felt the dogs to be more humane and obliging towards him than all those people. For they came and licked his ulcers. By this spectacle Christ condemns not only the hardness and cruelty of this feaster, but of all those who, having cast off every sense of humanity, are not moved by any misery of any man. Such people not only sin against Christian charity and fellowship, but also violate the laws of nature. For since brute animals, dogs, horses, birds, and sometimes even wild beasts, recognise the dignity of human nature in the poorest men, indeed in beggars dripping with pus and filth, who could say, I beg you, that any sense of nature remains in those who so easily neglect their fellows of the same nature, that they are moved neither by any spontaneous pity nor by the example of brute animals? Whenever, then, we see dogs or beasts of burden render some service to the needy and the beggars, let us think that they are produced as witnesses against us, or appointed by God as judges, by whose examples we shall be condemned.

units.la: Etenim hoc exemplo commune speculum nobis Deus proponere voluit, in quo hominum mores, & quid hodie publice atq; priuatim fiat contemplemur. Quid enim aliud faciunt principes, quos ne graviores quidem sui populi calamitates movent, ut de ope ferenda cogitent? Regnant vbiq; terrarum vsurarij, qui monopolijs suis & imposituris plurimos quotidie adegestatem redigunt, & rerum omnium pretium ita auxerunt, ut vix atrum panem ex laboribus suis habeant, qui dies noctesq; fatigantur. Clamat ergo passim misera civium & agricolarum turba, plenae sunt querelarum curia omnes, tribunalia & iudicum subsellia ijsdem resonant atq; strepunt. Infiniti praedonum istorum artibus prostrati principum opem implorant; magistratuum genua supplices prehendunt. At quotus quisque est, qui illorum miseretur, qui vsuris modum statuat, qui praedones publicos coerceat? Imo beatos possemus dicere pauperes, si saltem quae ex aliorum liberalitate illis debentur, & quae multo sudore acquirunt, ipsis salva manerent. Sed & bona Ecclesiarum multi ad se rapiunt, & insuper missos nouos exactionibus, tributis, vectigalibus quotidie deglubunt, & a famelica opificum, agricolarum, vpilionum, subulcorum, viduarum & orphanorum turba exigunt pecunias, quas deinde in ludos, spectacula, venationem, aleam, scorta, mimos, insana aedificia, sanguinarios milites, parasitos & nouarum voluptatum inuentores turpiter profundunt. Quis ergo illos hoc epulone inhumaniores & iniustiores esse negauerit? Hic certe canibus permittebat, ut Lazari vlcera lingerent. At si quis hodie pauperum & populi tot modis afflicti causam suscipiat, mox erunt qui minacibus edictis illum deterreant.
units.tr: For God wished to set before us this example as a common mirror, in which we may contemplate the morals of men and what is done today both publicly and privately. For what else do princes do, who are not moved even by the more serious calamities of their people to think about bringing help? Usurers reign everywhere on earth, who by their monopolies and exactions reduce very many to want every day, and have so raised the price of all things that men who are worn out day and night by their labours scarcely have black bread from their toil. So the wretched crowd of citizens and farmers cries out everywhere; all the courts are full of complaints, and the tribunals and the benches of the judges ring and resound with them. Countless numbers, crushed by the arts of these plunderers, implore the help of princes; they fall as suppliants at the knees of magistrates. But how few are there who take pity on them, who set a limit to usury, who restrain public plunderers? Indeed, we could call the poor blessed, if at least what is owed to them from the generosity of others, and what they acquire with much sweat, remained safe for them. But many also seize the goods of the Churches for themselves, and, besides, pluck the new arrivals bare every day with exactions, taxes and tolls, and they demand money from the hungry crowd of workers, farmers, labourers, swineherds, widows and orphans, which they then shamefully squander on games, shows, hunting, dice, prostitutes, mimes, insane buildings, bloodthirsty soldiers, parasites, and inventors of new pleasures. Who, then, would deny that these men are more inhuman and more unjust than that feaster? He at least allowed the dogs to lick Lazarus's ulcers. But if anyone today takes up the cause of the poor and of a people afflicted in so many ways, there will soon be men who will frighten him off with threatening edicts.

units.la: Veruntamen lusus & iocus sunt ista, si cum ijs conferantur, quae in ecclesiam Christi designantur. Nam & haec in mundo sedibus incertis vagatur, & multis in locis famelica saltem micas aliquas saniores doctrinae expetit. Adhaec morbus atque vitijs plurimis debilitata opem atque medelam postulat: & ad ipsa Pontificum atque Regum limina misere prostrata iam multis annis eos suis clamoribus atque gemitibus fatigauit, qui ipsius nutritij, patroni, vindices & medici esse debebant. Sed nequicquam haec omnia. Ridentis Ecclesiae morbos Pontifices, & felices illos vulgi miseri errores esse aiunt, per quos ipsi dominentur. Idem propius accedenti & manum medicam poscenti pedes deosculandos propinant. Reges, aut securi clamores eius negligunt, aut cum Pontificibus coniuratione facta querelas istas ferro & igne, aut etiam bellis publicis sopire satagunt. Pauci aliqui canes a Deo excitati Ecclesiae vulnera lingunt, dum verbi doctrinam & ex hac desumptas afflictarum conscientiarum consolationes adhibent. At ne hi quidem istud absq; periculo faciunt: & plerunq; pro tam pio & necessario officio vincula, exilium, bonorum omnium direptionem & horrenda supplicia reportant. Et haec quidem publice fieri nemo negauerit, nisi qui in luce meridiana caecutire velit: imo vtinam ista negari possent, & ego potius mendacij arguerer, non autem tot infelices animae de salute sua periclitarentur.
units.tr: Yet these things are mere sport and jest if they are compared with those that concern the Church of Christ. For she too wanders in the world with no fixed abode, and in many places, hungry, seeks at least some crumbs of wholesome doctrine. Moreover, she, weakened by disease and many vices, asks for help and remedy, and, miserably prostrated at the very thresholds of the Pontiffs and kings, has for many years wearied with her cries and groans those who ought to have been her nurses, patrons, defenders and physicians. But all this is in vain. The Pontiffs say that the diseases of the Church are laughable, and that they are the happy errors of the wretched crowd by which they themselves rule. And to anyone who comes closer and asks for a physician's hand, they offer the feet to be kissed. The kings either ignore her cries as if they were nothing, or, by conspiring with the Pontiffs, they strive to quell these complaints with the sword and fire, or even with public wars. A few dogs, roused by God, lick the wounds of the Church, while they apply the doctrine of the Word and the consolations drawn from it to troubled consciences. But even these do not do so without danger; and for such a pious and necessary duty they usually bring back chains, exile, the plundering of all their goods, and dreadful punishments. And no one will deny that these things are done publicly, unless he wishes to go blind in broad daylight. Indeed, would that these things could be denied, and that I might rather be proved a liar, and that so many unhappy souls were not in peril of their salvation.

units.la: Quod
units.tr: That

units.la: Quòd si verò ad huius seculi pauperes atque mendicos reuertamur, & quid priuatim in singulos plerique designent videamus, mox Lazarus ille ad fores diuitis & voluptuarij lurconis vestibulum prostratus occurret. Quis enim non videat innumerabilem illorum multitudinem, quos aut principum iniquae exactiones, aut militum rapacium crudelitas, aut incendia publica, aut tempestates, & naufragia, aut etiam propria negligentia siue prodigalitas mendicos fecit? Sunt hi omnes publica exempla, quibus à nobis omnibus primò quidem poenitentiam & vitae anteactae emendationem, deinde opem atq; auxilium Christus ipse flagitat. Iacent hi ad templorum fores prostrati, ad vrbium portas, ad magnatum palatia, adhaec oftiatim pulsant, stipem & panem, adeoq; micas ex mensa diuitum, & laceros attritosq; pannos, contemptas pretiosissimarum vestium reliquias magno & miserabili clamore postulant. Ad hos vero multi aures obturant, multi facies auertunt, multi ijsdem vias publicas & communem aerem inuident: omnium vero vna vox est, neminem tot mendicis alendis sufficere. Quàm multi autem interea quàmq; immodici sumptus fiunt in luxuriosa conuiuia, in turpes ludos, in theatrorum apparatus, in vestes fastuosas & inhonestas, in aleam, in scorta, lenones, scurras, gelopaeos, citharistrias & impuros Penelopes sponsos, qui cum fruges consumere nati sint, neque vllum opus honestum faciant, tamen feruntur & aluntur, imò conuiuijs publicis cum omnium applausu intersunt, & tandem priuatim argenteis nobilium insignibus, publicè autem vestibus honorarijs & viatico donati discedunt. Et istis quidem sumptibus plerique se sufficere arbitrantur, & indignè ferunt, si quis eos illis leuare velit: quàm primum verò de pauperibus alendis & in ordinem redigendis quaestio proponitur, omnes rem impossibilem tentari vociferantur. Quis ergo non exclamet, O mores, ô tempora? Intueamur ergo diligentius hoc nostri seculi speculum, ne dum diuitis istius mores imitamur, cum eodem poenas demus Deo, qui pauperibus factas iniurias, inultas non finit.
units.tr: But if we turn to the poor and beggars of this age, and look at what most people point to when they consider individuals, that Lazarus lying prostrate at the door and vestibule of the rich, self-indulgent glutton will immediately come to mind. For who does not see the countless multitude whom the unjust exactions of princes, the cruelty of rapacious soldiers, public fires, storms and shipwrecks, or even their own carelessness and prodigality, have reduced to begging? All these are public examples, by which Christ himself demands from all of us, first, repentance and amendment of the past life, and then help and assistance. These people lie prostrate at the doors of churches, at the gates of cities, and at the palaces of great men. They knock at every door and beg with a loud and pitiful cry for alms and bread, for the crumbs from the rich men's tables, and for torn and worn rags, the discarded remnants of very costly clothing. To these many stop their ears, many turn away their faces, and many begrudge them the public roads and the common air. Yet the one cry of all is that no one is able to feed so many beggars. Meanwhile, how many and how extravagant are the expenses on luxurious feasts, on shameful games, on the trappings of the theatres, on proud and immodest clothing, on dice, on whores, pimps, buffoons, dancers, harpists, and the shameless suitors of impure Penelopes! These men, who were born only to consume the fruits of the earth and do no honest work, are nevertheless supported and maintained. Indeed, they attend public banquets to general applause, and at last they depart, presented privately with silver tokens of nobility and publicly with honorary robes and travel money. Most people think these expenses are adequate, and they take it badly if anyone wishes to lighten them for those expenses. But as soon as the question is raised of feeding the poor and bringing them into order, everyone cries out that the thing is impossible to attempt. Who then would not exclaim, "O manners! O times!" Let us therefore look more carefully into this mirror of our age, lest, while we imitate the manners of that rich man, we pay the same penalty to God, who does not leave unavenged the wrongs done to the poor.

units.la: Porrò priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, Lazari nostri mores & studia inspicere oportet, vt eius exemplo inopes discant, quae ipsorum sint officia. Nam etsi Christus de illo nihil expresse dicat, ex aliis tamen circunstantijs facile colligi potest, qualis fuerit. Quia enim illi morienti adsunt Angeli, quos electorum ministros esse Apostolus testatur, & animam eius in sinum Abrahami deferunt: satis constat eum germanum Abrahami filium fuisse, quo nomine electos Dei & verè credentes Spiritus sanctus in scripturis ornare solet. Fidem certè operibus euidentissimè declarauit, patientia nimirum & charitate, quas virtutes in illo praeclaras & perfectissimas fuisse oportet. Quàm enim multa audiuimus, quae eius patientiam superare poterant, nisi inuicta fide & spe suffulta fuisset? Et quàm multos hodie, qui in fide robustissimi habentur, murmurare, de suis afflictionibus impatienter quiritari audimus, qui ne decimam quidem eorum partem patiuntur, quae ille perpessus est? Adhaec quàm multas quamque graues causas habuit, quae ipsum mouere poterant, vt diuitii isti opes atque fortunas suas inuideret, & tam ipsi quàm toti eius familiae maledicteret, à quibus tam inhumaniter negligebatur? Solent hoc fere pauperes, adeò vt sapius absque omni causa quibusuis conuitientur, & diuites quosque exitio dignos esse iudicent. At longè alia beati istius mendici mens fuit, qui suam fortem patienter ferendo, neminè suae miseriae socium, aut etiam seipso miseriorem fieri optauit. Imitentur hoc exemplum pauperes, & ante omnia fide in Deum habeant inconcussam, neque se propter egestatem ab illo negligi putent. Respiciant autem in fidei huius Mediatorem Iesum Christum, qui vnus nobis Dei gratiam impetrauit, ne ex paupertate (quod multi faciunt) meritum fingant. Vt enim diuitiae neminem damnant, qui inter illas pietati studet: ita neque egestas aliquè seruat, qui à fide alienus fuerit. Fidem verò testentur patientia & dilectione. Itaque neque de Deo improbè conquerantur, neque alicui meliorem fortem inuideant: quin potius tam publicam quàm priuatam omnium salutem Deo suis precibus quàm possunt fidelissimè commendent. Hae si fecerint, vberrimū ex sua inopia fructū reportabunt. Erit enim ea ipsis saluberrima disciplina, qua carnis cupiditates coerceant: palaestra item patientiae, in qua fidem suam magna cum laude exerceant: & vbi in finem vsq; perseuerauerint, salutis per Iesum Christum participes fient, qui cùm dives esset, propter nos pauper factus est, vt nos illius paupertate ditesceremus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, before we make an end of speaking, we ought to look into the character and conduct of our Lazarus, so that the poor may learn from his example what their duties are. For although Christ says nothing expressly about him, what sort of man he was can easily be gathered from the other circumstances. For since angels attend him as he dies, and the Apostle testifies that they are ministers of the elect, and carry his soul into Abraham's bosom, it is quite clear that he was a true son of Abraham, a name by which the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures is accustomed to honour the elect of God and true believers. He certainly showed his faith most plainly by his works, namely by patience and love, virtues which must have been outstanding and most perfect in him. For how many things have we heard that could have overcome his patience, had he not been sustained by an unconquered faith and hope? And how many today, who are considered most robust in faith, do we hear murmuring and complaining impatiently about their afflictions, though they do not suffer even a tenth part of what he endured? Besides, how many and how grave were the causes that could have moved him to envy that rich man his wealth and fortune, and to curse him and all his household, by whom he was so inhumanely neglected? Poor people commonly do this, so much so that they often revile whomever they meet without any cause, and judge all the rich to deserve destruction. But the mind of this blessed beggar was far different. He bore his lot patiently, and wished neither that anyone should share his misery nor that he himself should become more wretched. Let the poor imitate this example, and above all let them hold to God with an unshaken faith, and not think that they are neglected by him on account of their poverty. Let them look to Jesus Christ, the Mediator of this faith, who alone obtained for us the grace of God, so that they do not, as many do, make a merit out of their poverty. For just as riches condemn no one who strives for godliness among them, so neither does poverty save anyone who is a stranger to faith. Let them bear witness to their faith by patience and love. Thus they should neither complain wrongly about God nor envy anyone a better lot, but rather commend, as faithfully as they can, the welfare of all, both public and private, to God in their prayers. If they do this, they will reap the most abundant fruit from their poverty. For it will be for them a most wholesome discipline by which to restrain the lusts of the flesh, a training ground of patience in which they may exercise their faith with great praise, and, if they persevere to the end, they will become partakers of salvation through Jesus Christ, who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be made rich. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: a 1.Cor.8.
units.tr: a 1.Cor.8.

units.la: Factum est autem vt moreretur mendicus, & asportaretur ab Angelis in sinum Abrahami. Mortuus est autem etiam dies ille, ac sepultus est. Et apud inferos sublatis oculis suis, cum esset in tormentis, vidit Abrahamum procul, & Lazarum in sinu eius. Tum ipse clamans dixit: Pater Abraham miserere mei, & mitte Lazarum, vt intingat extremum digitum suum in aquam, & refrigeret linguam meam: quoniam crucior in ista flamma. Dixit autem Abraham: Fili, memento te bona tua recepisse in vita tua, & Lazarum similiter mala, nunc autem hic solatio fruitur, tu vero cruciaris. Et ad haec omnia, inter nos & vos hiatus ingens constitutus est: vt hi qui volunt hinc transire ad vos, non possint, neque isthinc huc transire.
units.tr: And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died, and was buried. And in hell, lifting up his eyes, when he was in torments, he saw Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. But Abraham said: Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. And besides all this, a great gulf is fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.

units.la: Quoniam homo ex terra originem ducit, terrenis quoque studijs solummodo intentus caelestia & aeterna bona negligit, & ne sensu quidem & intellectu percipere potest ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Et haec causa est, quod plerique communi errore decepti in diuitijs summam felicitatem consistere, paupertate autem nihil miserius aut calamitosius esse putant. Parit hic error aliud, vt ege statem quacunque ratione effugere conentur, diuitias autem per fas & nefas congerant. Adhaec quia futurae & aeternae vitae cura nulla tanguntur, vsum quoque diuitiarum nullum nouerunt, quam qui huius vitae commodis seruit, ideoque, aut illis indormiunt, vt nec ipsi aliquem ex eis fructum percipiant, aut ijsdem ad luxum, fastum & turpissima carnalium voluptatum studia abutuntur. Quapropter vt tanto tamque multiplici malo remedium esset, Christus Iesus historiam de diuite quodam epulone, & mendico Lazaro proponit, qua de hominis felicitate & miseria non ex huius seculi conditione iudicare, sed vltra in seculum futurum prospicere docet. Ab vna enim parte diuite producit, qui si mundi iudicium audiamus, omnibus numeris beatissimus videri poterat. Huic opponit mendicum, quo vix aliquid miserius & calamitosius posset fingi. Atqui hunc vere beatum & felicem, illum vero infelicissimum & miserrimum fuisse, vtriusque exitus ostendit, de quo nunc dicetur.
units.tr: Since man takes his origin from the earth, he who is intent only on earthly pursuits neglects heavenly and eternal goods, and cannot perceive even by sense and understanding the things that are of the Spirit of God. This is the reason why most people, deceived by a common error, think that the highest happiness consists in riches, and that nothing is more wretched or calamitous than poverty. This error produces another: they try to escape poverty by any means, and heap up riches by right or wrong. Moreover, because they are not touched by any care for the future and eternal life, they know no use of riches except that which serves the comforts of this life. Therefore they either sleep upon their wealth, so that they do not themselves reap any fruit from it, or they abuse it for luxury, pride and the most shameful pursuits of carnal pleasures. Therefore, so that there might be a remedy for so great and so manifold an evil, Christ Jesus sets before us the story of a certain rich glutton and the beggar Lazarus, by which he teaches us to judge of man's happiness and misery not from the condition of this age, but to look further on into the age to come. On the one side he sets forth the rich man, who, if we listen to the judgment of the world, might seem most blessed in every respect. Against him he sets the beggar, than whom hardly anything more wretched and calamitous could be imagined. Yet he shows, from the outcome of both, which will now be told, that the one was truly blessed and happy, and the other most unhappy and most miserable.

units.la: Lazari mortem paucis verbis describit: Et factum est, vt moreretur mendicus, & asportaretur ab Angelis in sinum Abrahami. Concurrunt in breui hoc dicto multa, quae ad summam hominis felicitatem faciunt. Primum est, quod qui mendicus, famelicus, ulcerosus & ignominiose ab omnibus neglectus ad diuitis vestibulum iacuerat, moritur, & moriendo semel liberatur ab omnibus molestijs, quae vitam ipsam illi amarum fecerant. Qua ergo ratione infelix dicetur, qui corporis morbidi & afflictissimi vinculis liberatus, optatum malorum omnium finem inuenit? Beatus dicitur, qui ex carcere euadit subito, in quo perituru videbatur. Cur ergo miseru dicamus, qui ex corporis huius ergastulo extrahitur, in quo nihil praeter tristissima quaeque nobis possumus polliceri? Atqui mors omnibus mortalibus communis est, & quantacunque fuerit alicuius hominis calamitas, ea tamen finem suum aliquando attinget, ideoque ex huius vitae laboribus siue aduersis nemo iudicari potest, cum qualis nam exitus ille futurus sit, ignoremus. In horum meditatione diligentius versari debent, quos afflictionis diuturnitas & longior huius vitae mora offendit. Fieri enim non potest, vt perpetua sit aliqua nostra in hisce terris calamitas, cum vita ipsa mortalis sit. Diuturna quidem carnis iudicio videntur afflictiones, sed revera diuturnitas ista momentanea est, & singulis momentis ad suum finem decurrit. Itaque quod alibi quoque monuimus, eadem est nostra, quae navigantium conditio. Vt enim illi in instituto itinere in singulas horas proficiunt, siue in naui dormiant, siue vigilent, siue sedeant, siue iaceant, & eadem fluminis rapacitas aequali motu sanos & aegrotos, laetos atque tristes secum auehit: ita eiusdem temporis navigio omnes vehimur, quod perpetuo & semper sibi constanti cursu tam eos qui secundis ventis feruntur abripit, quam eos, quibus omnis fortuna aduersa esse videtur. Itaque mora illa omnis, quae nos anxios facit, imaginaria est, nec digna cuius nomine nosipsos discruciemus.
units.tr: He describes Lazarus's death in few words: "And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom." Many things that contribute to man's highest happiness come together in this brief saying. First, he who had lain as a beggar, hungry, full of sores, and shamefully neglected by all, at the rich man's vestibule, dies; and by dying he is at once freed from all the troubles that had made his very life bitter to him. By what reasoning, then, would he be called unhappy, who, freed from the chains of a diseased and most afflicted body, has found the longed-for end of all his evils? He is called blessed who suddenly escapes from a prison in which he seemed bound to perish. Why, then, should we call wretched the one who is drawn out of this prison-house of the body, in which we can promise ourselves nothing but the saddest things? And yet death is common to all mortals, and however great a man's calamity may be, it will at some time reach its end. Therefore no one can be judged by the labours or adversities of this life, since we do not know what that outcome will be. Those whom the long duration of affliction and the lengthy delay of this life distress ought to dwell more carefully on this reflection. For it cannot be that any calamity of ours in this earth should be perpetual, since life itself is mortal. The afflictions seem long according to the judgment of the flesh, but in truth that length is momentary, and runs to its end at every moment. Therefore, as we have also observed elsewhere, our condition is that of sailors. For as they make progress on their chosen journey every hour, whether they sleep in the ship, keep watch, sit, or lie down, and the same rapid river carries sick and healthy, joyful and sad alike with equal motion, so we are all carried on the same vessel of time, which by its perpetual and always constant course snatches away alike those who are borne on with favourable winds and those to whom every fortune seems adverse. Thus all that delay which makes us anxious is imaginary, and not worth the name of a reason for us to torment ourselves.

units.la: Secundo ab Angelis asportatur Lazarus: id quod Synecdochicè de eius anima dicitur, quae potior & immortalis siue incorruptibilis hominis pars est. Vide ergo mirifica rerum vicissitudinem. Paulo
units.tr: Second, Lazarus is carried away by the angels. This is said by synecdoche of his soul, which is the nobler and immortal, or incorruptible, part of a man. See then the remarkable change of circumstances. A little

units.la: Lazarus mortem declaratur felicissimus fuisse.
units.tr: Lazarus's death is declared to have been most fortunate.

units.la: Lazarus ab Angelis asportatur. Paulo ante nemo hominū illi aliquod officium præstare voluit, & alijs quidem vlcerum fluentium saniem, alijs intolerabilem eorundem fœtorem abominantibus, fortasis nemo morienti adfuit, qui vel caput eius molliter reclinaret, vel æternæ salutis promissionibus in extremo agone luctantem confirmaret, vel iam mortui oculos clauderet. At idem ille nunc Angelos ministros habet, qui & morienti adfuerunt, & iamiam ex corporis carcere exituram animam aduersus diaboli insidias seruarunt, inque sedes beatæ immortalitatis detulerunt. Quo loco incomparabilis piorum dignitas consideranda venit, de qua nemo dubitare debet, vtut mundo huic despicatui sint. Nam ad hominis quidem seruitium tota hæc mundi machina condita est, cum omnibus quæ illa continentur. Et in impijs quoque communem hanc humanæ naturæ dignitatem belluæ etiam agnoscunt, & ideo illos metuunt, seque ab illis cicurari & regi patiuntur. At electus & fidis Dei cultoribus Angeli quoque in ministerium destinati sunt. Angelus Domini (inquit Psalmus) castrametatur circa eos qui timent, & eripit eos. Et ad omnes Dei filios pertinet, quod de Iesu Christo dicitur: Angelis suis tuo nomine præcipiet, vt in omnibus vijs tuis te custodiant: manibus gestabunt te, ne pes tuus ad lapidem offendat. Exempla, quæ promissionibus istis fidem faciant, passim occurrunt Scripturas legentibus, quæ cū non vno loco recitauerimus, ea in præsenti breuitatis studio omittimus. Vnū tamen non possumus præterire, minimè dubitandum esse, quin nobis morientibus Angeli assistant, qui & malos Spiritus procul arceant, & animas nostras ad vitæ æternæ possessione deferant. Cùm enim in leuioribus periculis illi nobis adsint, quæ ratio eos absterreret, ne in extremis agentes iuuarent? Christo certè ob mortis iam astantis recordationem grauissimè consternato Angelus Domini apparuit: vt eo exemplo discamus illum ijs quoque cum gaudio apparituram esse, qui vera Christi membra fuerint. Neq; desunt exempla nostro seculo, quæ vt istud credamus, nos mouere debent. Vnde enim ista multorum in morte alacritas? vnde gaudium & voces consolationis plenæ? vnde animæ iam iam exire gestientis tripudium, quod in multis cernimus, nisi quòd læto Angelorum conspectu exhilarantur, & iam nunc in Spiritu ineffabilis illius gaudij gustum percipiunt, quod Deum diligentibus Isaias præparatum esse scribit? Possem ego exempla commemorare, quæ in hominibus planè illiteratis & simplicissimis ædita vidi, qui in ipsa mortis hora tanta animi & oris alacritate exultarunt, vt nisi subitò expirauissent, ab omni prorsus ægritudine liberati videri poterant. Debent ista eos consolari, quos aut grauiora pericula circumstant, aut quibus vel solis vel procul à suorum complexu agentibus mors inopina obrepit. Cogitent illi se Deo curæ esse, neque officio suo defuturos esse Angelos, quos hominū salute exultare supra audiuimus. Petant etiam hinc consolationem, qui suos peregre diem suum obijsse audiunt, omni hominum seruitio destitutos. Quid enim hoc saluti illorū officere potuit, si in fide Christi obdormierunt, cùm Angeli Lazaro ad superbum impij diuitis palatium morienti tam fidele obsequium præstiterint? Discant potius omnes homines tantam Dei bonitatem agnoscere, & hanc suam dignitatem assiduo atque serio innocentiæ atque pietatis studio tueantur.
units.tr: Lazarus is carried away by the angels. A little earlier no one among men was willing to render him any service. Some shrank from the discharge of his ulcers, others from the intolerable stench of them. Perhaps no one was present at his dying who would gently rest his head, or strengthen him with the promises of eternal salvation as he struggled in his last agony, or close his eyes once he was dead. But now the same man has angels as his ministers, who were present at his dying, who guarded his soul, about to leave the prison of the body, against the snares of the devil, and who carried it into the abode of blessed immortality. Here the incomparable dignity of the godly deserves consideration, a dignity about which no one ought to doubt, however much they are despised by this world. For this whole machine of the world, with all that it contains, was made for the service of man. Even wild beasts acknowledge this common dignity of human nature in the wicked, and therefore they fear them and allow themselves to be tamed and ruled by them. But the angels too are appointed for the ministry of the chosen and faithful worshippers of God. "The angel of the Lord," says the Psalm, "encamps round about those who fear him, and delivers them" (Ps. 34). And what is said of Jesus Christ pertains to all the sons of God: "He will give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways; they shall bear you in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone" (Ps. 91). Examples which give credit to these promises occur everywhere to those who read the Scriptures. Since I have cited these in more than one place, in the present concern for brevity I omit them. Yet there is one thing I cannot pass over: there is no doubt that the angels stand by us as we die, both to keep wicked spirits far away and to carry our souls to the possession of eternal life. For if they are present with us in lesser dangers, what reason would deter them from helping us in our final hour? Certainly, when Christ was greatly dismayed at the thought of death now at hand, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, so that from this example we may learn that he will also appear with joy to those who are true members of Christ. Nor are there lacking examples in our own age which ought to move us to believe this. For whence comes that cheerfulness of many in death? Whence their joy and voices full of consolation? Whence the exultation of souls eager to leave the body, which we see in many, unless it is that they are cheered by the joyful sight of the angels, and already now in the Spirit taste that inexpressible joy which Isaiah writes has been prepared for those who love God? I could recount examples which I have seen occurring among men who were quite unlearned and most simple, who in the very hour of death exulted with such cheerfulness of mind and voice that, had they not suddenly expired, they might have seemed entirely freed from all sickness. These things ought to console those who are surrounded by more serious dangers, or to whom death creeps unexpectedly when they are alone or far from the embrace of their own people. Let them consider that they are cared for by God, and that the angels, whom we have heard rejoice in the salvation of men, will not fail in their duty. Let those also take consolation from this who hear that their own people have died abroad, deprived of all the service of men. For what could this have hindered for their salvation, if they fell asleep in the faith of Christ, since the angels rendered such faithful service to Lazarus as he died at the gate of the proud palace of the wicked rich man? Rather, let all men learn to acknowledge so great a goodness of God, and let them guard this dignity of theirs by a constant and earnest pursuit of innocence and piety.

units.la: Tertiò locus quoq; exprimitur, quo Lazarum Angeli asportauerunt: nimirum in sinum Abrahami. Disputatum de hoc sinu olim inter Theologos, quibusdam illum apud inferos, alijs vero in cœlis ipsum constituentibus. Augustinus vbi nam sit, se ignorare non dissimulat, apud inferos tamen illum esse constanter negat ex authoritate verborum Abrahami, de quibus postea dicetur. Eundem tamen secretæ quietis habitationem esse definit, & in eo beatorum spiritus viuere atque Dei læto conspectu frui testatur, de Nebridio suo scribens: Nunc ille viuit in sinu Abrahæ. Et mox addit: Quicquid illud est, quod illo significatur sinu, ibi Nebridius meus viuit, dulcis amicus meus, tuus autem Domine adoptiuus ex liberto filius ibi viuit. Nam quis alius tali animæ locus? Iam non ponit aurem ad os meum, sed spirituale os ad fontem tuum, & bibit quantum potest sapientiam pro auiditate sua, sine fine felix, &c. Porrò Abrahami sinum non aliud quàm domum patris cœlestis dicere possumus, in qua Christus nobis mansionem parauit, sicuti ipse apud Iohannem testatur. Nam idem ille in Matthæo dicit: Multi ab Oriente & Occidente venient, & discumbent cum Abrahamo & Isaaco & Iacobo in Regno cœlorum. Ergo in sinum Abrahami deferri idem est, quod in Regni cœlorum possessionem recipi, & ad eorum cætum colligi, qui Abrahami fidem imitati promissionibus de Christo redemptore crediderunt. Locum verò illum extra hunc mundum corruptibilem & omnibus cœlis superiorem esse, ex ijs apparet, quæ de Christi ascensione Apostoli prodiderunt. Itaque in cœlos & æterna beatitudinis sedem Lazarus receptus est. Quis vero nunc illum miserum & infelicem esse dixerit, quòd paulò ante ad vestibulum diuitis belluonis iacuit, neq; superbum huius limen transfilire ausus fuit? Quin potius rursus obseruemus lætam hanc vicissitudinem, quòd in æterno Regni cœlorum palatio iam triumphat, cui cum in terris ageret, priuatæ etiam miserorum hominicionum ædes non patebant. Certè si communis sensus iudicium audire & sequi libeat, felicem fuisse fatebimur eam egestatem, per quam ille ad Regni æterni hæreditatem admissus & cœlorum eius factus est, cui in terris locus negabatur.
units.tr: Third, the place is also named to which the angels carried Lazarus: namely, into Abraham's bosom. Among the theologians there was once a dispute about this bosom, some placing it in the underworld, others in heaven itself. Augustine does not hide that he does not know where it is, yet he steadfastly denies that it is in the underworld, on the authority of Abraham's words, which will be discussed later. Nevertheless he defines it as a dwelling of secret rest, and testifies that in it the spirits of the blessed live and enjoy the joyful sight of God, writing of his Nebridius: "Now he lives in Abraham's bosom." And soon he adds: "Whatever that bosom signifies, there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, and your adopted son, freed from servitude, Lord, lives there. For what other place is there for such a soul? Now he does not put his ear to my mouth, but his spiritual mouth to your fountain, and he drinks as much wisdom as he can, according to his desire, happy without end," and so on. Moreover, we can say that Abraham's bosom is nothing other than the house of the heavenly Father, in which Christ has prepared a dwelling for us, as he himself testifies in John. For in Matthew he says the same: "Many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven." Therefore to be carried into Abraham's bosom is the same as to be received into possession of the kingdom of heaven, and to be gathered into the company of those who, imitating the faith of Abraham, believed the promises concerning Christ the Redeemer. That this place lies beyond this corruptible world and above all the heavens appears from what the Apostles have related of Christ's ascension. Thus Lazarus was received into the heavens and the seat of eternal blessedness. Who, then, would call him wretched and unhappy because a little before he lay at the threshold of the rich beast, not daring to cross the proud man's doorstep? Rather let us again observe this joyful change: he now triumphs in the eternal palace of the kingdom of heaven, to which, while he lived on earth, even the private houses of poor men were not open to him. Certainly, if it pleases us to hear and follow the judgment of common sense, we shall confess that that poverty was happy, through which he was admitted to the inheritance of the eternal kingdom and made a citizen of the heavens, when on earth a place was denied him.

units.la: Venit autem hoc loco nobis consideranda animarum conditio, de quibus olim multa multi disputarunt, quorum errores hodie quidam postliminio reducunt, vt præ aliis sapere videantur, aut contra conscientiæ terrores sibijpsis delitias faciant. Quia vero illorum sententia indignæ sunt quæ recitetur, nos ijs insistemus, quæ certis Verbi Dei testimonijs cognosci possunt. Illa vero animas, quoad essentiam spiritus, quoad conditionem, immortales esse docent. Spiritus enim vocabulo Christus iam moriturus vtitur, de sua anima loquens: & præceptoris exemplum Stephanus secutus est, quando inter vndique volitantium lapidum grandines clamauit: Domine Iesu suscipe spiritum meum. Immortales autem esse, multis Scripturæ testimonijs probari potest. Veteres enim ad patres suos colligi dicebantur, & Christus Abrahamum, Isaacum & Iacobum viuere dicit, quod non aliter quam de animabus illorum potest intelligi. Quo sensu quoque Paulus dissolui cupiebat, & cum Christo esse. Sed quid opus est testimonia congerere, cùm de animarum immortalitate dubitare non possit, nisi qui aut Scripturæ libros nunquam inspexit, aut omnē pietatis sensum iampridem ex animo eiecit? Recipiuntur autem illæ, vbi ex hoc corpore migrant in certum locum: impiorum quidem ad inferos, vt mox in diuitis exemplo videbimus: piorum autem in sedes à Christo nobis paratas. De vtrisq; testimonia passim habentur. Ezechiel enim diserte inferni meminit, in quem colligantur omnes, qui posuerunt terrorem suum in terra viuentium. Christus autem de suis pronuntiat: Amen dico vobis, qui audit verba mea, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam: & in iudicium non veniet, sed à morte transiuit in vitam. Ad cuius promissionis confirmationem plurimum facit Lazari nostri exemplum, vt & latronis, cui in cruce Christus dixit: Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Ista nobis in mentem venire debent, quoties aut terrenorum studio bonorum, aut acerba mortis recordatione tentamur. Cur enim terrenus totus inhiet, qui ad cœlestia conditus, patrem, patrimonium & patriam in cœlis habet? Cur vero mortis formidine vincatur, qui hanc non modo finem malorum huius seculi, sed felicem ex lachrymarum valle ad patriam cœlestem transitum esse nouit?
units.tr: Here we must consider the condition of souls, about which many disputed long ago, and whose errors some now bring back again, so that they may seem wiser than others, or else, against the terrors of conscience, they make pleasures for themselves. But since their opinions are unworthy of being recited, we shall keep to those things which can be known from the certain testimonies of the Word of God. These teach that souls, as to their essence and their condition, are immortal. For Christ, about to die, uses the word "spirit" when speaking of his own soul, and Stephen followed the example of his teacher when, amid the hail of stones flying on every side, he cried: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." That they are immortal can be proved by many testimonies of Scripture. For the men of old were said to be gathered to their fathers, and Christ says that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live, which cannot be understood otherwise than of their souls. In this sense also Paul desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ. But why is there need to heap up testimonies, when no one can doubt the immortality of souls except one who has never looked into the books of Scripture, or who has long since cast out every sense of piety from his mind? Souls are received, however, when they depart from this body into a certain place: the souls of the wicked indeed into the underworld, as we shall soon see from the example of the rich man; the souls of the godly into the abodes prepared for us by Christ. Testimonies about both are found everywhere. For Ezekiel expressly speaks of hell, into which are gathered all who have set their terror in the land of the living. Christ, moreover, pronounces about his own: "Truly I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; and he shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life." To the confirmation of this promise our Lazarus's example contributes greatly, as does that of the thief to whom Christ said on the cross: "Today you will be with me in Paradise." These things ought to come to our minds whenever we are tempted either by the eager pursuit of earthly goods or by the bitter remembrance of death. For why should he gasp entirely for earthly things who was made for heavenly ones, and who has his father, inheritance and fatherland in heaven? And why should he be overcome by the dread of death who knows that death is not only the end of the evils of this age, but a happy passage out of the valley of tears to the heavenly fatherland?

units.la: Porrò ad diuitis quoque obitum tandem accedamus, de quo Christus hæc dicit: Mortuus est autem etiam diues ille, & sepultus est. Paucis verbis res maximi momenti comprehendit. Primùm, quòd diues etiam ille (emphasim habet demonstratiua particula, ILLE) mortuus fit. Quid (inquis) audio? Num diues ille, qui quotidie purpura & byssoo induebatur, qui inter conuiuia lautissima & perpetuos ludos oblectabatur, qui in ædibus magnificis, inter seruorum turbam, amicorum concursum, clientum applausum & totius vulgi admirationem Deorum vitam agebat, itáne mortuus est, & moriendo deliciis, voluptatibus, luxui, fastui & ambitioni finem imposuit? Quid ni? Mortuus est, inquam: neq; eius mortem pluribus verbis Dei Filius indicat, quàm quibus paulò ante de Lazari obitu vsus fuerat. Ita vero docet, mortem omnibus communem esse, neque vllis viribus aut rationibus posse impediri. Est enim via omnis terræ, quam nobis primi parentis transgressio strauit, vt Paulus ad Romanos testatur. Ideo quod Poëta quoque obseruauit, Pallida mors æquo pede pulsat pauperum tabernas, Regumq; turres. Et vt egenus improuisa obrepit, ita diuites quoque præter expectationem inuadit, vt supra capite duodecimo audiuimus. Id vero illis grauissimum est, & non potest non terribile videri. Ita enim rationes eorum subitò turbantur, quas illi in multos annos vsq; extenderant. Deinde felicitati illorum finis imponitur, & vt ab huius seculi bonis ægrè diuellantur, ita nulla futurorum spe confirmari & inuitari possunt, cùm partim illa ignorent, partim vnà cum morte horribiles conscientiæ & diuini iudicij terrores sibi obrepere sentiant, quos prius nō sine securitate eludere solebat, nunc autē nullis rationibus, nulla hominū authoritate, nullis gemitibus aut lachrymis possunt discutere. Nihil ergo quàm tristissimus mortis horror eos exagitat, & tunc ob oculos versantur ab ipsis oppressi miseri homines, quos iniquissimus modis spoliarunt: tunc sese ingerunt viduae & pupilli per ipsos ex patrimonio suo deiecti: tunc in auribus ipsorum resonant prius neglecti pauperum clamores: tunc conscientia illis exprobrat libidines, luxum, fastum, blasphemias & infinita alia scelera, quae aduersus Deum & homines designarunt. Et haec quidem initia modo sunt malorum: quia non vani sunt illi terrores, sed sequitur hos damnatio, & animas corporis vinculo solutas crudelis & aeternus apud inferos cruciatus excipit, ut paulo post audiemus. Exci tent nos ista, ut quando res nobis secundae affluunt, frequenter in mortis consideratione versemur, quae ut certissime nobis obrepet, ita moriendi horam incertam & nobis incognitam esse voluit Deus, ut sciremus, nobis nunquam non vigilandum esse, ne terrenis studijs immersi aeternae salutis iacturam faciamus.
units.tr: Let us now come to the death of the rich man, of which Christ says: "The rich man also died, and was buried." In a few words he sets out a matter of the greatest importance. First, that this rich man (the demonstrative particle THAT gives emphasis) also died. "What's this I hear?" you may say. "Did that rich man, who was dressed daily in purple and fine linen, who was entertained with the most lavish banquets and constant games, who lived like a god in his splendid house, surrounded by a crowd of servants, a throng of friends, the applause of his clients and the admiration of the whole populace, did he really die, and by dying put an end to his pleasures, luxuries, pomp and ambition?" Why not? He died, I say. The Son of God does not describe his death in more words than he used a little earlier for Lazarus's death. And he teaches that death is common to all and cannot be prevented by any strength or reasoning. For the way of all the earth is the path that the transgression of our first parent laid down, as Paul testifies to the Romans. So too the poet observed: "Pale death knocks with equal foot at the huts of the poor and the towers of kings." Death creeps up on the beggar unawares, and so it also strikes the rich beyond their expectation, as we heard above in chapter twelve. For them this is the most grievous thing, and it cannot but seem terrible. Their calculations, which they had extended over many years, are suddenly overturned. Then their happiness is brought to an end, and although they are hardly torn away from the goods of this world, they cannot be strengthened or encouraged by any hope of the future, since they either do not know those things or, together with death, feel horrible pangs of conscience and the terrors of divine judgment creeping upon them. Earlier they used to brush these aside without concern, but now they cannot dispel them by any reasoning, any human authority, any groans or tears. So nothing but the most dreadful horror of death harasses them. Then before their eyes appear the wretched people whom they crushed by the most unjust means; then the widows and orphans they drove from their property force themselves upon them; then in their ears resound the cries of the poor that they had earlier ignored; then conscience reproaches them for their lusts, luxury, pride, blasphemies and countless other crimes they had devised against God and man. And these are only the beginnings of evils, for those terrors are not empty; damnation follows them, and a cruel and eternal torment among the dead receives their souls, loosed from the bond of the body, as we shall hear shortly. Let these things rouse us, so that when prosperity flows in upon us, we often dwell on the thought of death. Death will creep upon us most surely, yet God willed that the hour of dying should be uncertain and unknown to us, so that we would know we must always keep watch, lest, immersed in earthly pursuits, we suffer the loss of eternal salvation.

units.la: Alterum de diuite hoc narratur, quod sepultus sit. Id vero de Lazaro non dixit Dominus: nimirum, quia corpus eius vel ignominiose abiectum, vel negligenter terra obrutum fuit: Illius vero funus magnifice & non sine pompa ductum fuisse innuit. Ita vero solet fieri, ut qui vitam suam in fastu & luxu, vel etiam sceleribus maximis transegerunt, post mortem quoq; superbire velint. Vbi vnum hoc illorum conditioni optime conuenit, quod qui iam morituri conscientiae terrores senserunt, & animi dolorem acerbissimum turpi eiulatu testati sunt, praeficos & praeficas, adhaec monachorum & sacrificulorum turbam conducunt, qui & ipsi lugubri cantu, atro vestitu & gestibus ad maximi luctus significatione compositus, illos miseros & infelices esse testantur. Imo cum sacra quoq; pro illis fiant, quae damnationis ipsorum publicum sunt testimonium: ipsorum corpora Mausoleus includuntur superbis, quibus imagines eorum armatae incumbunt: quasi nimirum adhuc crudelitate spirent, quorum animae apud inferos torquentur. Sunt haec ridicula admodum, siquidem in re tam seria aliquis risui locus esse reliquus. Meminerint ergo Christiani homines, sepulturas quantumuis magnificas animarum saluti nihil conferre, sed potius ambitionis & vitae absq; poenitentia transactae testimonium esse. Itaq; iam morituri animas fide vera muniant, peccatorum remissione a Deo ardeter flagitent, seq; ipsos certa gratiae per Christum nobis partae fiducia illi commendent. Qui vero illorum funera ducunt, humanae sortis memores, non eos qui iam vita defuncti in caelis gaudent, lugeant, sed potius mortis recordatione seipsos ad vitae caelestis meditationem excitent, defunctorum autem corpora ita sepeliant, ut nihil ambitioni detur, nihil etiam superstitiose fiat, quod merito Christi vel minima ex parte deroget. Et honorifice quidem sepeliri debent corpora, quae dum viuerent, Spiritus Sancti templa fuerunt, & quae olim ad caelestis vitae possessionem Christus suscitabit: caeteri tamen oportet omnia, quae vel animos adhuc mundo addictos arguunt, aut fidem labefactare possunt.
units.tr: The second thing told of this rich man is that he was buried. The Lord did not say this of Lazarus; no doubt because Lazarus's body was either cast out with ignominy or buried carelessly in the earth. But he hints that the funeral of the rich man was conducted with great display and not without pomp. And indeed it is usual that those who have spent their lives in pride and luxury, or even in the greatest crimes, wish to show their arrogance after death too. In this one thing their condition agrees very well with theirs: those who, about to die, have felt the terrors of conscience and bore witness to their bitter anguish with shameful wailing, hire mourning women and men, and a crowd of monks and little priests, who by their dismal chanting, black clothing and gestures arranged to signify the greatest grief, also testify that those wretches are miserable and unhappy. Indeed, even while sacred rites are performed for them, which are a public testimony to their damnation, their bodies are enclosed in proud mausoleums, on which their armed images lie, as if they still breathed cruelty, though their souls are being tormented among the dead. These things are utterly ridiculous, since in so serious a matter there should be any room left for laughter. Let Christians therefore remember that however magnificent their tombs, they contribute nothing to the salvation of souls, but rather are a witness to ambition and a life spent without repentance. Let those who are about to die fortify their souls with true faith, fervently ask God for the forgiveness of sins, and commend themselves to him with the sure trust in the grace procured for us through Christ. As for those who lead the funerals of such people, let them, mindful of the human lot, not mourn those who have already departed this life and rejoice in heaven, but rather, by the remembrance of death, stir themselves to the meditation on the heavenly life. Let them bury the bodies of the dead in such a way that nothing is given to ambition and nothing superstitious is done that would in the least detract from the merit of Christ. Bodies that, while they lived, were temples of the Holy Spirit, and which Christ will one day raise to possess the heavenly life, ought indeed to be buried with honour. Yet everything that either betrays souls still attached to the world or can weaken faith must be avoided.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad animam huius epulonis, ut videamus, quae eius conditio post mortem in altero seculo fuerit. Hanc ita describit Christus: Et apud inferos sublatus oculis suis, cum esset in tormentis, vidit Abrahamum procul, & Lazarum in sinu eius.
