Tum ipse clamans dixit: Pater Abraham miserere mei, & mitte Lazarum, ut intingat extremum digitum suum in aquam, & refrigeret linguam meam: quoniam crucior in ista flamma, &c. Vbi rursus multa concurrunt, quae miserrimam eius conditionem fuisse docent. Et primo quidem locus notatur, in quem anima eius a morte migrauerit. Fuit vt in inferno, quem supplicijs damnatorum destinatum esse scriptura non vno loco testantur. Et tenendum est probe aduersus Epicuraeos illusores, esse certum locum in pijs praeparatum, in quem animae ipsorum statim a morte, post resurrectionem autem corpora quoq; colligantur.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the soul of this feaster, to see what its condition was after death, in the other age. Christ describes it thus: "And in hell, being in torments, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried out and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame, etc." Here again many things come together that show his condition to have been most wretched. And first of all the place is noted to which his soul migrated at death. It was hell, which the Scriptures in more than one place declare to be appointed for the punishments of the damned. And it must be firmly held, against the Epicurean mockers, that there is a certain place prepared for the godly, into which their souls are gathered at once after death, and their bodies too after the resurrection.

units.la: De hoc Moses loquitur, quando Core, Dathanum & Abironem terrae hiatu absorptos esse, ac vi-uos cum omnibus suis ad infernum descendisse scribit. Isaias vero eius non meminit modo, verumetiam illum describit, quando Assyrij tyranni supplicium exponens, inter alia sic ait: Praeparata est praeterea ab heri Thopheth, haec etiam pro Rege praeparata est: quam profundam & amplam fecit, pe netrale eius ignis, vis lignorum ingens, quae flatus Domini, ceu sulphureus torrens, incendit. Pertinent eodem, quae apud Ezechielem Cap.23. & Danielis 7. leguntur. Et Christus Dominus saepissime de inferno loquitur, & in nouissimi iudicij descriptione se impijs dicturu ait: Discedite a me maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Ad quorum omnium confirmationem facit hic locus, quem si quis eludere velit, quod parabolica sit narratio, is simul totum narrationis huius argumentum negabit, & Christum impostoribus similem finget, qui inanibus terriculamentis simplices hominum imperitorum mentes deludunt. At hodie multos esse videre, qui mirifica & plus quàm scurrili dicacitate omnia ista negant. Sunt ij revera de quibus in Psalmis scribitur: Dixit stolidus in corde suo, Non est Deus. Sed quia Deum simpliciter negare nimis durum est, & ab eo communis etiam sensus ita abhorret, ut inter Ethnicos olim capitis supplicio digni habiti sint, qui illud facere sunt ausi: nostri illi diabolum & inferos negant, quod perinde est. Ita enim scelerum poena tolluntur, & proinde Dei iustitia negatur, quam si sustuleris, non magis Deus dici merebitur, quàm Regus nomine dignus est, qui omnem iuris administrationem negligit. Itaque quod hic de epulone habetur, illum in inferno fuisse, simpliciter accipi debet, quòd ut Lazarus in sinu Abrahami inter beatorum spiritus fuit, ita ille ab horum coetu exclusus, adeoque à facie Dei reiectus & ad tartara detrusus fuerit.
units.tr: Moses speaks of this when he writes that Korah, Dathan and Abiram were swallowed up by a gaping of the earth and descended alive with all their households into hell. Isaiah not only mentions it but also describes it, when, setting out the punishment of the tyrant of Assyria, he says among other things: "Tophet has been prepared from of old; it is prepared also for the king; its pit is deep and wide; its fire and its wood are abundant; the breath of the Lord, like a sulphurous torrent, kindles it." To the same point belong the passages in Ezekiel chapter 23 and Daniel chapter 7. And the Lord Christ very often speaks of hell, and in the description of the last judgment he says he will say to the impious: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." This passage serves to confirm all of these things. If anyone wishes to mock it, on the ground that it is a parabolic narration, he will at the same time deny the whole argument of this story and make Christ like the impostors who deceive the simple minds of ignorant men with empty frights. Yet today we see many who deny all these things with wonderful and more than buffoonish wit. These are truly those of whom the Psalms write: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God." But because it is too harsh simply to deny God, and common sense itself so abhors this that among the heathen of old those who dared to do it were judged worthy of capital punishment, our people deny the devil and hell instead, which amounts to the same thing. For in this way the punishment of sins is removed, and therefore God's justice is denied; and if you take this away, God no more deserves the name of God than a man who neglects all administration of justice deserves the name of king. Therefore what is said here of the feaster, that he was in hell, must be taken plainly: just as Lazarus was in Abraham's bosom among the spirits of the blessed, so he, excluded from their company, was cast out from the face of God and thrust down to the depths.

units.la: Quid verò illic patitur? Miserè & variè torquetur. Primùm sublatis oculis suis, cùm esset in tormentis vidit Abrahamum procul, & Lazarum in sinu eius. In tormentis fuisse dicitur, quae & gravissima & perpetua esse, alibi Christus docet his verbis: Vbi ignis non extinguitur, & vermis eorum non moritur. Ad supplicij verò gravitatem facit, quòd procul vidit Abrahamum, ita nimirum loci distantia spem salutis omnem negante. Item quòd in eius sinu Lazarum vidit, cuius conspectus ipsi inhumanitatem exprobrabat, qua in famelicum & ulcerosum ante vestibulum ipsius iacentem vsus fuerat. Deinde cruciatum suum non uno indicio prodit. Nam Abrahamum inclamat, & Lazari opem implorat, ut is summo digito in aquam intinctò vel unica aquae guttula liguam arentem & inflammatam refrigeret. Et addit: Quoniam crucior in ista flamma. Vbi ergo nunc mutatoriae vestes, quibus & frigoris & æstus molestiâ solebat declinare? Vbi domus in varia cubicula pro anni ratione distincta? Vbi unguentorum fragrantium odor? Vbi vinorum genera infinita? Vbi artificiosae dapes? vbi condimenta, quibus olim edendi & bibendi appetitu provocare solebat? Horribilem sanè & omni sensu humano superiorem fuisse oportet cruciatum illum, qui homini voluptuario, fastuoso & ambitioso pauperum contemptori voces istas extorquere potuit, quibus & tormentorum suorum acerbitatem confessus, & non tam Abrahamo quàm Lazaro prius tam indignè & inhumaniter abs se contempto supplex factus est. Et observa hic quoque miram & iustissimam rerum vicissitudinem. Lazarum intra vestibuli limen admittere dedignatus est: nunc ipse procul à Regni coelorum palatijs exclusus in inferno agit. Micas è mensa cadentes Lazaro negavit: ab eo autem nunc guttam aquae sibi aspergi cupit. Inter delitias corpus & animum variis delitijs recreavit: nunc totus flammis undique circundatus torquetur. Lazarum ulceribus obsitum & tabo diffluentem conspectu suo indignum iudicavit: nunc eundem coelesti gloria ornatū videre cogitur. Ista verò seuerum iustumq; Dei iudicium exprimunt, quo ille impiorum crudelitatem atque scelera punire solet. Quod enim isti accidit, hoc omnibus eventurum esse Scripturae docent, qui huius vestigijs insistunt, Vident ergo impij inter sua tormenta eos beatos & felices esse, quos hic vel superbè neglexerunt, vel etiam crudeliter persecuti sunt: quia de re supra quoq; Cap.13. Dominus disseruit. Deinde retributionem sententiam dignam & suis moribus respondentem. Vt enim qui misericordiam exercuerunt, mercedem suam minimè amittunt: Ita iudicium aut damnatio absque misericordia erit eis, qui misericordiam non praestitit. Quapropter omni solatio illi destituuntur, neque aliquid vident, quàm quo ipsorum dolor atque cruciatus augentur. Interim admonet nos totus iste locus, quàm turpiter iudicio suo fallantur, qui ex huius seculi conditione de hominum felicitate aut infelicitate iudicant. Vt enim cùm in vitiis agerent dives iste & Lazarus, hic quidem mortalium miserrimus, ille verò omnium beatissimus esse videbatur: Ita postquam hac vita defuncti sunt, dives à Regno Dei reiectus horribiliter cruciatur, Lazarus autem æternus coelorum gaudijs fruitur. Neminem ergo huius seculi illecebrae capiant, neminem quae hic nobis occurrunt certamina abstererent: sed in hoc potius omnes incumbant, ut vitae huius curriculum constanti & serio pietatis atque innocentiae studio emensi, olim in coelis viuant atque exultent.
units.tr: But what does he suffer there? He is tormented wretchedly and in many ways. First, when he was in torment he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus in Abraham's bosom. He is said to be in torments, which Christ elsewhere teaches are both most severe and everlasting, in these words: "where the fire is not quenched, and their worm dies not." The distance of the place adds to the severity of the punishment, since it means that every hope of salvation is denied him by the gap. Likewise, that he saw Lazarus in Abraham's bosom, whose sight upbraided him with the inhumanity he had shown to the hungry and ulcerous man lying before his gate. Then he betrays his anguish by more than one sign. For he calls out to Abraham and implores Lazarus's help, that he might dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his parched and burning tongue with a single drop. And he adds: "for I am tormented in this flame." Where now are those changes of clothing with which he used to ward off the discomfort of both cold and heat? Where is the house divided into various rooms according to the season of the year? Where is the scent of fragrant ointments? Where are the endless kinds of wine? Where are the elaborate banquets? Where are the seasonings with which he used once to stir up his appetite for eating and drinking? That torment must surely have been dreadful and beyond all human feeling, which could wring from a man given to pleasure, proud and ambitious, a despiser of the poor, words such as these, by which he confessed the bitterness of his torments and became a suppliant, not so much to Abraham as to Lazarus, whom he had earlier so shamefully and inhumanly despised. And observe here also the wonderful and most just reversal of things. He disdained to admit Lazarus within the threshold of his vestibule; now he himself, shut out far from the palaces of the kingdom of heaven, is in hell. He denied Lazarus the crumbs falling from his table; now he longs for a drop of water to be sprinkled on him by Lazarus. Among his delights he refreshed body and soul with various pleasures; now he is tormented, wholly surrounded on every side by flames. He judged Lazarus, covered with sores and dissolving in pus, unworthy of his sight; now he is forced to see that same man adorned with heavenly glory. These things express the severe and just judgment of God, by which he is accustomed to punish the cruelty and wickedness of the ungodly. For Scripture teaches that what befell him will befall all who follow in his footsteps. The wicked therefore see, amid their torments, that those whom they proudly neglected here, or even cruelly persecuted, are blessed and happy; on this matter the Lord also discoursed above, in chapter 13. Then comes a sentence of retribution worthy of and corresponding to their conduct. For just as those who have shown mercy do not at all lose their reward, so judgment, or condemnation without mercy, will fall upon those who have not shown mercy. Therefore they are deprived of all comfort, and they see nothing but what increases their grief and torment. Meanwhile this whole passage warns us how shamefully they are deceived in their judgment who judge the happiness or unhappiness of men by the condition of this world. For just as, while they were living in sin, that rich man and Lazarus, the one indeed the most wretched of mortals, the other seemingly the most blessed of all, so after they departed from this life, the rich man, rejected from the kingdom of God, is horribly tormented, while Lazarus enjoys the eternal joys of heaven. Let no allurements of this age therefore capture anyone, nor let the struggles that meet us here dismay anyone; rather let all strive in this, that, having run the course of this life with a steadfast and earnest zeal for piety and innocence, they may live and rejoice one day in heaven.

units.la: Sed Abrahamum audiamus, qui epuloni isti graviter respondet, amicè tamē & verbis minimè contumeliosis, ut eo exemplo discamus, non scurriliter insultandum esse iis, qui dignas suorum scelerum poenas exoluunt. Et huc etiam referri debet, quòd non Lazarus, sed ipse Abrahamus respondens inducitur. Estq; exemplum hoc iudicibus imitandum, ut tunc quoque gravitatis suae meminerint, quanrint, quando illis cum hominibus quouis supplicio digni res esset. Fili (inquit) memento, te bona tua recepisse in vita tua, & Lazarum similiter mala: nunc autem hic solatio fruitur, tu vero cruciaris. Et ad haec omnia inter nos & vos hiatus ingens constitutus est, &c. Responsionis huius partes sunt duae. Prima iustum Dei iudicium exponit, digne vnicuique rependentis secundum ea, quae in vita hac gesserit. Quo loco pulchra comparatione vtitur. Tu recepisti bona tua in vita tua, id est, tu felicitatem omnem collocauisti in bonis terrenis, quae tibi copiosissime affluxerunt, & quibus addictus, vel immersus potius, nullam vel Dei vel hominum rationem habuisti: Merito ergo nunc ista pateris. E contra Lazari vita aerumnarum & calamitatum plenissima fuit: aequum ergo est, vt is nunc solatio & quiete optata fruatur.
units.tr: But let us listen to Abraham, who answers that rich man severely, yet kindly and in words by no means insulting, so that from this example we may learn not to mock with buffoonery those who pay the due penalties of their crimes. This also should be taken as the reason why it is Abraham himself, and not Lazarus, who is introduced as replying. This example is also to be imitated by judges, so that they remember their dignity even then, when they have to deal with men who deserve any punishment. "Son," he says, "remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. And besides all this, a great chasm is set between us and you," and so on. The reply has two parts. The first sets out the just judgment of God, which repays each person worthily according to what he has done in this life. Here he uses a fine comparison. "You received your good things in your life": that is, you placed all your happiness in earthly goods, which flowed to you most abundantly, and to which you were devoted, or rather immersed, having no regard for God or men. It is therefore rightly that you now suffer these things. On the other hand, Lazarus's life was full of hardships and calamities; it is therefore fitting that he now enjoys the comfort and rest he longed for.

units.la: Debent autem diligenter obseruari vicissitudinis huius causae verae & propriae: ne vel meritu statuamus in huius seculi afflictionibus, aut temere quosuis damnemus, qui in hoc seculo felicius vi uunt. Vt enim huius vitae afflictiones nullo modo conferri possunt cum bonis illis aeternis & incomparabilibus, quae nobis in caelo repositae sunt: ita minime putandum est, quod ea nostris laboribus aut molestiis mereamur. Et non raro fit, vt pij in hoc seculo bonis affluant & feliciter agat, e contra impij cum calamitatibus assiduis conflictentur: Deo nimirum vtrisque gustum aliquem futurae conditionis propinante, vt & ipsi de rebus suis diligentius cogitent, & alij exemplis eorum excitentur. Et huc promissiones atque mina pertinent, quas in Lege & Prophetis habemus. Nec temere a Paulo dictum est, pietatem cum praesentis tum futurae vitae promissiones habere. Inde vero elicitur impietati poenas quoque tam hic quam in alio seculo paratas esse. Itaque quod hic de diuitis felicitate dicitur, quam nunc merito cruciatus infernalis excipiat, ad illius abusum restringi debet. Nec enim ideo ille ad inferos damnatus fuit, quod opibus, otio & rebus secundis abundauisset: sed quod fortuna elatus totum se luxui & fastui tradidit, neglecta pietate & beneficentia, quae tales potissimum decent. Similiter felicitatis aeternae causa pro via Lazaro fuit non paupertas & aduersa valetudo, sed quod Dei promissionibus credidit, onus ab eo sibi impositum patienter tulit, seque totum per fidei obedientiam voluntati diuinae submisit. Itaque vt impios laetior fortuna inebriat, & officij sui immemores facit: ita pijs afflictiones adiumento sunt, vt in pietate magis proficiant. Et hinc retri butio illa dependet, cuius in praesenti Abrahamus meminit. Debet tamen ex his generali doctrina peti, perpetuam hanc esse rerum vicissitudinem, vt qui in felici statu alios affligunt, tandem ipsi quoque afflictionem sustineant: & rursum relaxationem habeant quicunque affliguntur. Vide Paulum in posteriore ad Thessalonicen. cap. 1.
units.tr: Yet the true and proper causes of this reversal must be carefully observed, so that we neither think that the afflictions of this age are deserved, nor rashly condemn whoever lives more happily in this age. For just as the afflictions of this life can in no way be compared with those eternal and incomparable goods which are laid up for us in heaven, so it must by no means be thought that we merit these by our labours or troubles. And it often happens that the godly abound in goods in this age and live happily, while the ungodly are constantly struggling with calamities; God, of course, giving each a taste of the future condition, so that they themselves may think more carefully about their own affairs, and others may be stirred up by their examples. The promises and threats which we have in the Law and the Prophets pertain to this too. Nor did Paul speak rashly when he said that godliness has promises both of the present and of the future life. From this it follows that punishments are prepared for ungodliness both here and in the other age. Therefore what is said here of the rich man's happiness, which is now rightly followed by infernal torment, must be restricted to its abuse. For he was not condemned to the depths because he abounded in wealth, leisure and prosperity, but because, puffed up by fortune, he gave himself wholly to luxury and pride, neglecting piety and beneficence, which such men above all ought to show. Similarly, the cause of Lazarus's eternal happiness was not his poverty and ill health, but that he believed God's promises, bore patiently the burden laid upon him, and submitted himself wholly to the divine will through obedient faith. Thus, just as a more favourable fortune intoxicates the ungodly and makes them forgetful of their duty, so afflictions serve the godly to make them grow more in piety. And that recompense of which Abraham speaks at present depends upon this. Yet from these things a general doctrine must be drawn: this reversal of things is perpetual, so that those who afflict others while in a happy state will in the end themselves undergo affliction, and conversely, whoever are afflicted will have relief. See Paul in his second letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 1.

units.la: Restat altera responsionis huius pars, qua omnem liberationis aut fortis melioris spem negat, dicens: & ad haec omnia inter nos & vos hiatus ingens constitutus est, vt bi qui volunt hinc transire ad vos, non possint, neque iisdem hinc huc transire. Hiatus nomine magnam intercapedinem aut distantiam loci vtriusque denotat, qua alter ab altero separetur. Longe aliter ergo Abrahamus ipse de seculi & vitae alterius conditione siue statu loquitur, quam hodie phanatici quidam & contentiosi homines, qui neque caelum neque inferos locorum nomina esse, neque inter illa aliquam distantiam esse contendunt. Scio tamen quid illi respondeant, parabolam scilicet narrari. Sed quid dicent, si ego rem vere gestam, & quae filio Dei non potuit ignota esse, recitari contendam? Quibus argumentis obsecro me erroris conuincent? Deinde cum hic de maximi momenti articulo agatur, de immutabili nimirum forte aut conditione eorum, qui hac vita defuncti & in alterum seculum translati sunt, quus obsecro sanae mentis, Abrahamum dicet argumento parabolico vsum esse, cuius verba aliter quam sonent, accipi debeant? Certe ipse Christus ingentem locorum distantiam expressit, quando Abrahamum procul visum fuisse dixit a diuite. Et in praesenti hiatus ille constitutus & fundatus esse dicitur, aeterno nimirum Dei decreto. Itaque omissis quaestionibus, quibus scripturae sacrae veritas labefactatur, teneamus firmiter, eos qui ex hac vita migrant, perpetua & irreuocabili Dei sententia vel in caelestes beatae immortalitatis sedes recipi, vel ad inferos detrudi. Et in huius consideratione diligentius versandum est, quia hic duo insignes errores confutantur.
units.tr: There remains the second part of this reply, in which he denies any hope of release or of a better state, saying: "And besides all this, a great chasm is set between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us." The word "chasm" denotes a great interval or distance of place by which the one is separated from the other. Abraham himself therefore speaks quite differently about the condition or state of the age to come and of the other life than some fanatical and contentious men do today, who contend that heaven and hell are not names of places, nor is there any distance between them. Yet I know what they answer: that a parable is being related. But what will they say if I maintain that a real event is recounted, one which cannot have been unknown to the Son of God? By what arguments, I ask, will they convince me of error? Moreover, since this concerns an article of the greatest importance, namely the unchangeable condition of those who have departed from this life and passed into the other age, what sane man, I ask, will say that Abraham used a parabolic argument, whose words ought to be taken otherwise than they sound? Certainly Christ himself expressed a great distance of places when he said that Abraham was seen afar off by the rich man. And here that chasm is said to be set and fixed, namely by the eternal decree of God. Therefore, setting aside the questions by which the truth of Holy Scripture is undermined, let us hold firmly that those who depart from this life are received, by the perpetual and irrevocable sentence of God, either into the heavenly seats of blessed immortality or are thrust down into hell. And in considering this we must dwell on it more carefully, because two notable errors are refuted here.

units.la: Primus eorum est, qui Diuos invocandos esse contendunt, eo quod illorum intercessione & merito tam in hac praesenti quam futura vita iuuari possimus. Solent hi inter alia argumenta epulonis
units.tr: The first of these errors is held by those who contend that the saints (Divi) are to be invoked, because through their intercession and merit we can be helped both in this present life and in the life to come. Those who hold this usually bring forward, among other arguments, the example of the rich man (epulo) in the parable.

units.la: huius exemplum producere. Sed eo suam stoliditatem produnt. Quis enim hominis impij & damnati exemplum imitari velit in ijs, quae ad aeternam salutem faciunt? Etenim quam parum illorum verbis tribui debeat, ex alijs locis apparet, in quibus Dominus exponit, quam inepte & imprudenter ijdem in nouissimo iudicio suam iustitiam atq; dignitatem iactaturi sint. Deinde quid impetrat infelix ille, dum & Abrahami & Lazari opem implorat? Nihil prorsus. Imò Abrahamus negat, illi aliquam salutem aut relaxationem afferri posse. Quod de omnibus intelligi debet, qui iam in coelis agunt. Nam vt alibi diximus, illi eos non norunt, qui adhuc in terris degunt, neq; aliqua rerum huius seculi cura tanguntur. Alteros autem illos, qui iam ad aeternas poenas damnati sunt, neq; possunt neq; volunt iuuare. Causa in promptu est: Quia Dei voluntas sola in coelis omnia moderatur, & in hac cum laude & gratiarum actione Angeli & Dini coelites acquiescunt. Ideo inter precandum dicimus: Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in coelo, sic etiam in terra. Quibus adde, quod Deus Sanctos, non suarum rerum curatores fecit, sed regni sui & beatitudinis consortes, manente perpetuo mandati huius authoritate: In die afflictionis tuae inuoca me, &c. Psalm. 50.
units.tr: But by doing so they betray their own folly. For who would wish to imitate the example of a wicked and damned man in matters that pertain to eternal salvation? How little credit should be given to their words appears from other passages, in which the Lord shows how foolishly and imprudently these same men will boast of their righteousness and dignity at the last judgment. Next, what does that unhappy man obtain while he begs for the help of both Abraham and Lazarus? Nothing at all. Indeed Abraham denies that any relief or respite can be brought to him. This must be understood of all who now dwell in heaven. For, as we have said elsewhere, they do not know those who still live on earth, nor are they moved by any concern for the affairs of this world. As for those others who have already been condemned to eternal punishment, they can neither help them nor wish to. The reason is ready at hand: the will of God alone governs all things in heaven, and in this will the angels and the heavenly inhabitants rest, with praise and thanksgiving. Therefore in prayer we say: Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. To these things add that God made the saints not overseers of his affairs but partners in his kingdom and blessedness, the authority of this command remaining forever: "Call upon me in the day of trouble," etc. Ps. 50.

units.la: Alter eorum error est, qui salutis suae curam post mortem vsque differunt, & eam vel haeredibus mandant, vel sacrificulis aut monachis. Etenim duo soli loci sunt, in quos defunctorum animae colliguntur: Coelum & infernus. Tertium locum, Purgatorium ignem, Scriptura prorsus ignorat, & nihil nisi hominum superstitiosorum atque χπρωσπλάσματων figmentum est. Eorum vero conditio, qui vel in coelis vel apud inferos agunt, immutabilis est. Frustra igitur homines, qui in terris superstites manserunt, semel latam Dei sententiam reuocare conantur. Adde quod ne coelites quidem Diui eos iuuare possunt, qui infernalibus poenis iam cruciantur: sicuti in Abrahami verbis euidentissime apparet. Quid ergo impurus sacrificus aut monachus proficeret tale quid moliendo? Vel nui sepulchris aspersa aqua lustralis eos recrearet, qui in inferno ardent, cum diues iste a Lazaro ne quicquam aquae guttulam vnicam petierit? Itaque cogitent singuli, mortis tempus omnibus definitum esse, & in morte animas ad suos locos colligi, vnde nunquam discessurae sint: inutiles autem esse omnes labores atque impensas, quae pro mortuis fiunt. Quare operemur bonum, dum tempus est: salutis vero fiduciam omnem in vno Iesu Christo collocemus, cuius sanguis nos ab omni peccato emundat, & ad mensam patris sui gaudio aeterno recreat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The second of these errors is held by those who put off the care of their salvation until after death, and entrust it either to their heirs, or to priests and monks. For there are only two places into which the souls of the dead are gathered: heaven and hell. Scripture entirely ignores a third place, a purgatorial fire, and it is nothing but the figment of superstitious men and of deceivers (πρωσπλάσματων?). The condition of those who dwell either in heaven or among the dead is unchangeable. Therefore men who remain alive on earth try in vain to recall the sentence of God once pronounced. Add that the saints in heaven cannot help those who are already tormented by infernal punishments, as is most clearly seen from the words of Abraham. What then would an impure priest or monk achieve by attempting such a thing? Would water sprinkled over graves refresh those who burn in hell, when that rich man from Lazarus did not ask for even a single drop of water? Therefore let each one consider that the time of death is appointed for all, and that at death souls are gathered to their own places, from which they will never depart; and that all the labours and expenses that are made for the dead are useless. Let us therefore do good while there is time; and let us place all our trust of salvation in the one Jesus Christ, whose blood cleanses us from every sin and restores us at his Father's table to eternal joy. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLIX.

units.la: Dixit autem ille: Rogo ergo te pater, vt eum mittas in domum patris mei. Habeo enim quinque fratres: vt testificetur eis, ne & ipsi veniant in hunc locum tormenti. Dicit ei Abraham: Habent Moysem & Prophetas, audiant eos. Ille vero dixit: Non pater Abraham: sed si quis ex mortuis abierit ad eos, resipiscent. Abraham autem dixit ei: Si Moysem & Prophetas non audiunt, neque si quidem quispiam ex mortuis resurrexerit, assentientur.
units.tr: Then he said: "I beg you therefore, father, to send him to my father's house. For I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, lest they too come to this place of torment." Abraham said to him: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." But he said: "No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent." Abraham said to him: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead."

units.la: Aeternus Dei Filius Iesus Christus, qui vt miseros nos seruaret, in mundum venit, doctrinam quoque omnem ad eum scopum dirigit, vt ostendat, quid facere quidq; vitare aut intermittere debeant, qui serio aeternae salutis studio tenentur. Obseruat hoc ipsum in historica narratione, quae de diuite & Lazaro mendico contexuit. Ea enim ei vitio medetur, quo homines a vera & aeterna salutis via quam maxime reuocantur: Corrupto nimirum iudicio de felicitate. Docet enim hanc non in opum abundantia aut vllis huius seculi commodis consistere, sed in fide, pietate & beneficentia. Ita vero simul diuites & pauperes sui officij admonet. Vt bi quidem non obmurmurent Deo, neque impiorum successibus inuideant, aut etiam illis offendantur, sed onus sibi impositum patienter ferant: illi vero spem suam non in diuitijs fluxis & perituris collocent, sed in Deo viuo & aeterno, atque creditam sibi dispensationem bona fide administrent. Caeterum quia hic, vt in alijs quoque rebus, iugi & assidua doctrina opus est, sine qua homines in officio contineri non possunt: simul autem sub tem sub prætextu doctrinæ nobis Satan non minus astuè quàm pernitiosè insidiatur, vltima huius narrationis parte de illa quoque disserit, docens, unde nam bene & beatè viuendi ratio peti debeat, simulq; omnes alias discendi rationes confutat, quas ex diaboli suggestione homines curiosi & superstitiosi inuexerunt.
units.tr: The eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, who came into the world to save us wretched people, directs all his teaching to this aim: to show what those who are seriously intent on eternal salvation ought to do, what they ought to avoid, and what they ought to leave undone. He observes this very thing in the historical narrative he composed about the rich man and the beggar Lazarus. For it heals that fault by which people are most of all turned away from the true and eternal way of salvation, namely a corrupt judgment about happiness. For he teaches that happiness does not consist in an abundance of wealth or in any advantages of this age, but in faith, piety and beneficence. In this way he also reminds both rich and poor of their duty. The rich should not grumble against God, nor envy the prosperity of the wicked, nor be offended by them, but bear patiently the burden laid on them; the poor should not place their hope in fleeting and perishable riches, but in the living and eternal God, and should faithfully administer the stewardship entrusted to them. Moreover, since here, as in other matters, constant and frequent teaching is needed, without which people cannot be kept in their duty, and since Satan lays traps for us under the pretext of teaching, no less craftily than destructively, the last part of this narrative discusses that too. It teaches whence the rule of living well and happily must be sought, and at the same time it refutes all the other methods of learning which curious and superstitious people have introduced at the devil's suggestion.

units.la: Principio tractationis huius occasio præmittitur. Dives cum suæ salutis spem nullam audiret reliquam esse, de fratrum salute anxius redditur, quos ex seipso æstimat. Nam vt ex verbis eius evidentissimè apparet, cum in vita esset, non fidem habuit iis, quæ in scripturis de futura vita, de cœlo & inferis, de præmiis piorum & pœnis impiorum dicuntur: quamuis in filiorum Abrahami numero censeretur. Itaque huius modo seculi bonus intentus, præsentibus delitiis animum expleuit, sui tura autem prorsus neglexit. Quia ergo fratres sui similes esse sciebat, nunc illis consultum vellet: & ideo petit, vt ad eos mittatur Lazarus, quem haud dubie illi nouerant, qui illos de futuri seculi statu admoneat, vt conuertantur. Quo loco rursus aduersarij nostri abutuntur, vt probet mortuos nostræ salutis curam habere, & proinde illos à nobis debere inuocari. Sed quod nuper respondimus, hic repeti debet, proponi nimirum hominis impij & ad æterna supplicia damnati exemplum, ex quo religionis & salutis dogmata petere, non ridiculum modò, verumetiam nefarium est, & cum graui scandalo coniunctum. Neq; tamen temerè negauerim, impijs omnia ea in mentem venire, quæ dolorem & cruciatum illorum augere possunt. Quid verò hoc ad beatorum spiritus? quos si nostra cura & solicitudine angi dicamus, iam multum derogabimus eorum felicitati, quam perfectam & omnibus numeris absolutam esse, Scripturæ docent. Itaque & si illos nostri memores esse demus, fatendum tamen erit recordationem hanc eorum modò esse, quæ dum in vitus agerent facta sunt, nec quicquam continere, quod molestiam possit afferre, qua ipsorum beatitudo atque gaudium turbetur. In qua sententia olim Beatus quoque Augustinus fuit, qui etsi Nebridium in cœlo sui memorem esse fateatur, idem tamen in libro De cura pro mortuis habenda diserte negat, animas defunctorum nobis apparere, aut se nostris immiscere negotijs. Nam inter alia scribit: Si rebus viuentium interessent animæ mortuorum, & ipsæ nos quando eas videmus alloquerentur, in somnis, vt de alijs tacerem, meipsum pia mater nulla nocte deserteret, quæ terra marique secuta est vt mecum viueret. Abit enim vt facta sit vita feliciore crudelis, vsque adeò, vt quando aliquid angit cor meum, me triste filium non consoletur, quem dilexit vnicè, quem nunquam voluit mœstum videre. Sed profectò quod sacer Psalmus personat: verum est: Quoniam pater meus & mater mea dereliquerunt me, Dominus autem assumpsit me. Si ergo dereliquerunt nos patres nostri, quomodo nostris curis & rebus interfuint? Si autem parentes non interfuint, qui sunt alij mortuorum, qui nouerunt quid agamus, quidue patiamur? Isaias Propheta dicit: Tu es enim pater noster, quia Abraham nos nescuit, & Israel non cognouit nos. Si tanti Patriarchæ quid erga populum ex his procreatum ageretur, ignorauerunt, quibus Deus credentibus populus ipse de stirpe illorum promissus est, quomodo mortuorum rebus atque actibus cognoscendis adiuuandisq; miscentur? Hæc omnia Augustini sunt, quæ ideo recitauimus, vt omnes intelligant, nos non noui dogmatis in ecclesia authores esse, sed eorum sententiam sequi, qui ex scripturis de mortuorum conditione magis sobriè & diligentius disseruerunt, quam posteris temporibus factum sit, quando auaritia & ambitio cum superstitionibus barbarâ omnes scripturæ ignorantiam innexerunt. Quapropter hoc epulonis nostri exemplum non debet latius extendi, neq; ad animas in cœlis gaudentes trahi, quod ille ideo passus est, vt eius tormenta atq; cruciatus augerentur.
units.tr: The occasion of this discussion is set out at the beginning. The rich man, hearing that no hope of his own salvation remains, becomes anxious about the salvation of his brothers, whom he judges by himself. For, as is most clearly evident from his words, while he was alive he did not believe what the Scriptures say about the future life, about heaven and hell, about the rewards of the pious and the punishments of the impious, although he was counted among the sons of Abraham. Thus, intent on the good things of this age, he satisfied his mind with present delights and utterly neglected what was to come. Since he knew his brothers were like himself, he now wishes to provide for them, and therefore he asks that Lazarus, whom they undoubtedly knew, be sent to them to warn them about the state of the future age, so that they may be converted. Here again our adversaries misuse the passage to prove that the dead have care for our salvation and therefore ought to be invoked by us. But what we answered recently must be repeated here: the example of a wicked man condemned to eternal punishment is set forth, and to seek the doctrines of religion and salvation from it is not only ridiculous but wicked, and attended with grave scandal. Yet I would not rashly deny that all those things which can increase the pain and torment of the impious come into their minds. But what has this to do with the spirits of the blessed? If we say they are troubled by our care and anxiety, we will greatly detract from their happiness, which the Scriptures teach is perfect and complete in every respect. Therefore, even if we grant that they remember us, it must be admitted that this remembrance concerns only those things which happened while they were living, and contains nothing which could bring annoyance disturbing their blessedness and joy. Blessed Augustine too was of this opinion, who, although he admits that Nebridius is mindful of him in heaven, nevertheless in his book On the care to be had for the dead plainly denies that the souls of the departed appear to us or mix themselves in our affairs. For among other things he writes: "If the souls of the dead were present in the affairs of the living, and spoke to us when we saw them, my pious mother would not have deserted me in dreams on any night, to say nothing of others, she who followed me over land and sea so that she might live with me. Far from it: her life has become happier, not crueller, so much so that when something grieves my heart, she does not console her son, whom she loved uniquely and whom she never wished to see sad." But surely what the sacred Psalm sounds is true: "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up." If then our fathers have forsaken us, how do they take part in our cares and affairs? And if parents do not take part, who are the other dead who know what we do or suffer? The prophet Isaiah says: "For you are our father, for Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us." If such great patriarchs were ignorant of what was done to the people descended from them, to whom God promised that the people would be born from their stock, how are the dead mixed up with knowing and helping the affairs and actions of the living? All these things are Augustine's, which I have recited so that everyone may understand that we are not the authors of a new doctrine in the Church, but follow the opinion of those who discussed the condition of the dead from the Scriptures more soberly and carefully than was done in later times, when avarice and ambition, together with superstitions, bound all Scripture in barbarous ignorance. Wherefore this example of our feasting rich man should not be extended more widely, nor drawn to the souls rejoicing in heaven, since he suffered it so that his torments and agony might be increased.

units.la: Nunc illud potius consideremus, quod proprie ad hunc locum pertinet, quid nimirum maneat impios illos & securos illusores, qui contempto & procul abiecto Dei verbo omnia ea rident, quæ de futuro seculo & animarum immortalitate, de corporum resurrectione, de æternis piorum præmijs & nunquam finiendis impiorum cruciatibus dicuntur. Fuerunt tales omnibus seculis, & nota est hæc Poetarum quorundam sententia: Scilicet hic superis labor est, hæc cura quietos sollicitat: nouissimis autem temporibus istud hominum genus vulgo regnaturum Christus & Apostoli prædixerunt. Vnde enim securitas illa nascitur, quam illis Dominus tribuit, quando similes fore dicit iis, qui Noæ & Lothi temporibus vixerunt? Ex eo nimirum, quod non credent vnquam venturum in dicem illū, ad cuius tribunal omnes homines sistendi sint. Petrus autē Apostolus diserte & clarius idexprimit,sic scribens: Veniet extremis diebus irrisores,qui in suis ipsorum cupiditatibus incedât & dicant: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? Nam ex quo patres nostri obdormierunt,omnia ita permanent ab initio creationis. Quibus Paulus subscribit,dicens: Cum dixerint, Pax & tuta omnia:tunc repentinum eis imminet exitium,sicuti dolor partus mulieri vterum ferenti,nec effugient. Atqui audiuntur voces ista hodie passim,& vtinam non inter eos etiam sonarent,qui summi Ecclesiæ antistites haberi volunt.Et quamuis multi à verbis hisce scurrilibus sibi temperent, ne toti impij esse putentur,ijdé tamen vita & moribus satis aperte testantur,hanc persuasionem animis ipsorum penitus insculptam esse. Cur enim aliter de illis sentiamus, qui omni cœlestis & futuræ vitæ cogitatione abiecta,genio suo indulgent securi,& ne quid illos turbet,aut conciones sacras omnino nullas audiunt,aut eos sibi doctores deligunt,qui inani blandiloquentia aures auditorum demulcent, manifesta autem & libera scelerum redargutione in conscientias eorum minimè penetrant? Quin hi ipsi propriæ etiâ conscientiæ testimonia eludunt, quò securius suis desideriis seruire possint. At ijdé suo tempore, velint nolint, coguntur sentire ea, quæ nunquam euentura esse credere noluerunt:& iam morituri non solum eiulatu belluino animi sui horribiles terrores testantur, verum etiam tunc magni facere incipiunt eos,quorum monita prius contempserunt,imò quos propter liberiores admonitiones odio capitali persecuti sunt. Quid verò,nisi Deus eorum ex singulari gratia misereatur, vt in extremis saltem constituti verè credant & resipiscant,apud inferos patiantur,exemplum infelicis istius diuitis satis docet. Qui enim paulò ante Lazari ministerium postularat, vt ù vel vnica aquæ guttula linguam eius refocillaret,idem nunc eum suis fratribus, æquè nimirum superbis & ambitiosis,doctorem mitti cupit,quem prius intra vestibulum admittere dedignatus fuerat.
units.tr: Let us now consider rather that which pertains properly to this place: namely what awaits those impious and careless mockers who, scorning and casting away the Word of God, laugh at everything that is said about the future age and the immortality of souls, the resurrection of bodies, the eternal rewards of the pious and the never-ending torments of the impious. Such people have existed in every age, and that saying of certain poets is well known: "Surely this is the toil of the gods above, this is the care that disturbs the quiet." But Christ and the Apostles foretold that in the last times this kind of people would reign widely. For whence does that security arise which the Lord ascribes to them, when he says they will be like those who lived in the times of Noah and Lot? Surely from this: that they will never believe that the coming judgment will take place, before whose tribunal all people must stand. The Apostle Peter expresses it plainly and more clearly, writing thus: "In the last days there will come scoffers, walking according to their own lusts, and saying: Where is the promise of his coming? For since our fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation." Paul agrees with them, saying: "When they say, Peace and safety, then sudden destruction hangs over them, as the pain of childbirth comes upon a woman with child, and they will not escape." And indeed these voices are heard everywhere today, and would that they did not sound even among those who wish to be regarded as the chief bishops of the Church. And although many refrain from these scurrilous words, lest they be thought wholly impious, yet by their life and morals they testify quite clearly that this persuasion is deeply engraved in their minds. For why should we think otherwise of those who, casting off all thought of the heavenly and future life, indulge their own inclinations securely, and, lest anything disturb them, either hear no sacred sermons at all, or choose for themselves teachers who soothe the ears of their hearers with empty flattery, but do not in fact penetrate their consciences with plain and open rebuke of sins? Indeed these very people also evade the testimony of their own conscience, so that they may serve their desires more securely. Yet in due time, whether they wish or not, they are compelled to feel those things which they refused to believe would ever come to pass; and now, about to die, they not only show the terrors of their mind by bestial howling, but also begin to set great store by those whose warnings they had previously despised, and whom they had persecuted with deadly hatred for their more free admonitions. What, indeed, unless God in his singular grace has mercy on them, so that at least in their last moments they truly believe and repent, they suffer among the dead, this unhappy rich man sufficiently teaches. For he who a little before had asked for Lazarus's service, that a single drop of water might cool his tongue, now desires that a teacher be sent to his brothers, who are equally proud and ambitious, a teacher whom he had earlier disdained to admit even within his vestibule.

units.la: Debent exempla eiusmodi,quorū multa quotidie videre licet,nos excitare, vt aures nostras obturemus ad impias illusorum istorum voces, quibus ipsissimus impietatis fons referatur. Firmiter autem animis nostris persuasum sit, Deum esse,qui omnia regat,omnia videat,& vbiq; præsens sit. Si enim hoc ex admirabili ista totius mundi machina intelligere potuerunt multi, qui animos suos paulò altius supra carnis sensum euexerunt,meritò suæ stupiditatis pudere debet Christianos homines,quos Deus ipse verbo suo quotidie docet & excitat. Deinde vlterius progressi,cogitemus hoc omnino postulare Dei iustitiam, vt vita post hanc mortalem alia immortalis & æterna sequatur. Constat enim illum remuneratorem esse,& nisi talem fateamur,iniustum quoque & iniquum simul esse dicamus oportet. Atqui non semper neque erga omnes in hac vita remuneratoris officio fungitur, sed multi inter scelera & vitam pœnitere nesciam pace & felicitate perpetua fruuntur, multa interim ferentibus & patientibus ijs,qui illum timent & inuocant. Aliud ergo seculum sit necesse est, in quo bi quidè promissa pietatis præmia accipiât,illi verò dignas sceleribus suis pœnas luant. Hæc si frequenter & attentius paulò meditemur,mox nos extimulari sentiemus, vt contemptus huius mundi studijs,nos totos accomodemus diuinæ voluntati & cœlestia bona sectemur, quæ sola nos vere beatos facient. Nam & mors nobis neque insperata neque terribilis obrepet, neque morituri anxiè tumultuabimur,animæ autem corporis carcere soluta nihil patientur,quod dolorem aut cruciatum illis afferat,sed cum Christo in cœlis æternum gaudebunt.
units.tr: Examples of this kind, of which many can be seen every day, ought to rouse us to stop our ears against the impious voices of these mockers, from which the very fount of impiety flows. Let it be firmly fixed in our minds that God is the one who governs all things, sees all things, and is present everywhere. For if many who raised their minds a little above the sense of the flesh could understand this from the marvellous machine of the whole world, Christians, whom God himself teaches and stirs daily by his Word, ought surely to be ashamed of their stupidity. Going further, let us consider that God's justice demands that this mortal life be followed by another, immortal and eternal. For it is established that he is the rewarder, and unless we confess him to be such, we must say he is also unjust and iniquitous. Yet he does not always fulfil the office of rewarder in this life, nor toward all; many who live in sin and do not know how to repent enjoy perpetual peace and happiness, while those who fear and call upon him endure many hardships in the meantime. Therefore another age must necessarily exist, in which the promised rewards of piety are received by the one and the due punishments for their crimes are paid by the others. If we meditate on these things often and with some attention, we shall soon feel ourselves stirred to despise the pursuits of this world, to devote ourselves wholly to the divine will, and to seek heavenly goods, which alone will make us truly blessed. For death will not creep upon us unexpected or terrible, nor will we, about to die, be anxiously agitated; the soul, freed from the prison of the body, will suffer nothing that could bring pain or torment, but will rejoice eternally with Christ in heaven.

units.la: Porro Abrahamum diuiti respondentem audiamus: Habent Mosem (inquit) & Prophetas,eas audiant. Indignus erat,cui amplius responderetur,respondet tamen,vt magis appareat eorum vanitas,qui hodie adhuc ista imitantur,& sibi doctores ex altero orbe dari volunt,quoniam reuelatione discât,quid in cœlis & quid apud inferos rerum agatur. Ergo simpliciter quidè negat,quod ille petebat,simul autem ostendit postulationem eius superuacaneam esse,cum fratribus abundè prospectum sit, vt qui doctores habeant Lazaro multò præstantiores: Mosem nimirum fidelissimum illum in domo Dei seruum,in quo verè fastum est teste toto populo Israelitico, quod Poetæ prophani de Minoe suo fabulati sunt,quem Iouis ὀαοιςλών,id est,collocutorem finxerunt,Quis verò eius colloquij testis vnquam productus est? At Moses spectante & audiente toto populo ad Dei colloquium euocatus est, & cum eo per dies quadraginta versatus eas leges attulit, quibus ipsissima Dei voluntas exprimitur,& quarum authoritas omnibus seculis firma & rata esse debet. Huic postea successores dati sunt Prophetæ, quos vt legis suæ interpretes essent Deus excitauit,& Spiritu suo instruxit. Ad hos ergo diuitis istius fratres Abraham remittit, vt ostendat eos non solum modo, modò seculi hominibus seruiuisse, sed eius doctrinæ fuisse ministros, quæ posterù quoq; omnibus vitæ & salutis rationem tradere debeat.
units.tr: Next let us hear Abraham answering the rich man: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." He was unworthy to be answered further, yet he answers, so that the vanity of those is made more apparent who even today imitate such things and want teachers sent to them from the other world, so that by revelation they might learn what is happening in heaven and in hell. So he simply denies what the man asked, and at the same time shows that his request was superfluous, since sufficient provision has been made for the brothers through teachers far superior to Lazarus: namely Moses, that most faithful servant in God's house, in whom, with the whole Israelite people as witness, there truly was what the profane poets fabled of their Minos, whom they called Jove's [ὀαοιςλών], that is, his interlocutor. But who was ever produced as a witness of that conversation? Yet Moses, with the whole people watching and listening, was called into conversation with God, remained with him for forty days, and brought those laws by which God's very will is expressed, and whose authority ought to remain firm and valid in every age. After him prophets were given as successors, whom God raised up to be interpreters of his law and instructed with his Spirit. To these, therefore, Abraham sends the rich man's brothers, to show that they had served not merely the passing needs of one age, but were ministers of that teaching which ought afterwards to hand down the rule of life and salvation to all.

units.la: Admonemur igitur hoc loco, unde nobis etiam hodie doctrina petenda sit. Ex Scripturis ni- mirum per Mosem & Prophetas traditu. Potuerunt illæ olim veteri populo sufficere, quia Christum pollicebantur, & ad eum omnes deducebant. Ut verò omnibus constaret, hunc mundo exhi-bitum esse, neque alium expectari debere, Apostolicos quoque libros veteribus illis Spiritus sanctus coniungi voluit: ideoque nostra fors potior & præstantior est quam veterum olim fuerit, qui solis promissionibus atque prophetijs ducebantur. Authoritas autem totius scripturæ infinitis argumentis iam olim probata est. De Mose certè dubitare non possumus, cum occulta quadam Dei virtute factum sit, ut illius libri apud eos etiam fidem inueniant, qui à religione & vera illius cognitione sunt alienissimi. Dei certè consilio excitatus Ptolemæus Philadelphus magnis muneribus ex Iudæa euocauit interpretes, qui Mosis historiam Græco sermone exponerent, quod illus contineri reliquisset historiam certam de mundi creatione & humanarum rerum progressu. Inter Iudæos autem etsi magna esset Sadducæorum improbitas atq; impudentia, qua in scripturæ veteris libros sibi iudicium atque censuram sumebant, ijdem tamen Mosi quicquam derogare ausi non sunt. Et hodie librorum eius summam authoritatem esse constat inter Turcas quantumuis barbaros & acerrimos crucis Christi hostes. Eandem verò fidem Prophetas mereri Christus ipse docet, qui illos cum Mose coniungit, & tam ex hoc quàm illis suarum concionum argumenta desumpsit: Apud Ioannem certè Iudæus ille dicit: Scrutamini scripturas (nam vos videmini vobis in illis vitam æternam habere) & illæ sunt quæ testificantur de me. Et paulò post, Si credidissetis Mosi, crediditis mihi: de me enim ille scripsit. Paulus autem in posteriori ad Timoth. ait: Tota Scriptura diuinitus est inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iustitia: Ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. In quibus verbis duo diligenter obseruari debent. Primum, quod scriptura authore facit Spiritum Dei. Quod Petrus exponens ait: Non enim voluntate hominis allata est olim Prophetia: sed acti à Spiritu sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Ergo Dei verbum scriptura continent, & has audire atq; legere debent, quicunque Deum ipsum loquentem audire cupiunt. Alterum est, quod scripturis omnia tradi testatur, quæ ad hominem vel instituendum vel in officio retinendum necessaria sunt. Nam utilis est (inquit) ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quæ est in iustitia. Doctrinæ nomine dogmata fidei & salutis intelligit, quæ in scripturis omnia contineri nemo negauerit, quam qui totam salutis rationem in dubium vocare cupiat. Doctrinam verò hanc non simpliciter tradi, sed ita proponi oportet, ut simul ea arguantur errores, quibus multi à veritatis via abducuntur. Rursus cum peccatorum etiam ille cebræ multos transfuersos abripiant, illis etiā corrigendis & in officio retinendis scripturas suffice re dicit. Deniq; eadem ad institutionem in iustitia utiles esse ait, ut illis contineri doceat quicquid ad vitā pie & iustè instituendā cognitu necessarium est. Et ne qua esset tergiuersandi occasio, hunc illarum vsum & finem esse testatur, ut homo Dei, id est, quisquis Deo seruire & placere cupit, perfectus fiat, & ad omne opus bonum perfectè instruatur. Pleonasmo uti voluit Apostolus, ut omnibus os obturaret, qui nobis aliud quoddam verbum Dei reconditum fingunt, quod non ex scripturis, sed reuelationibus certis addiscere oporteat. Quid enim discendum præter scripturas ei reliquum est qui si illas probè imbiberit & rectè teneat, etiam Dei iudicio perfectus censetur? Est ergo multa ob seruatione dignissima. Dei bonitas, qui verbum suum non voce modo viua proponi, sed scriptis ac litteris comprehendi voluit, libros etiam scripturæ (ut alibi monuimus) in hunc vsque diem non sine miraculo seruauit, ut quoties libet illum de rebus abstrusissimis, de huius vitæ officijs, de futuræ statu, de cælis, de inferis, de præmijs item & pœnis, denique de vniuersa Regni cælorum administratione, loquentem audire liceat. Magna igitur est eorum ingratitudo, qui tantum beneficium Dei contemnunt: maior ite eorū improbitas, qui ne quid suis affectibus contrarium audiat, aures suas obturat: execrabilis autem multorum impietas, qui scripturis fidem derogant, & scurriliter omnia eludunt, imò studiosè conquirunt argumenta, quibus illarū authoritate euertere possint. Sunt hi (ut alias diximus) perfidorum villicorum similes, qui post multam berorum beneficentiam, qua diu usi sunt, rationum libros improbè vellicant, & ita falsi insimulant eos, quibus omne gratitudinis officium debent. Sem per ergo nobisipsis hoc Abrahami dictum applicemus, quoties aliqua dubitatio in animis nostris ob oritur, aut nos curiositatis vitio titillari sentimus, nobis (inquam) tunc occinamus: Mosem habes & Prophetas, imò ipsum Dei Filium & Apostolos, quos hic orbis totius doctores esse voluit, hos audito, & in illis quae ipsi tradiderunt, perfistito, &c.
units.tr: Here, then, we are reminded from where we must seek doctrine even today: namely from the Scriptures, handed down through Moses and the Prophets. Those could indeed suffice for the old people, because they promised Christ and led everyone to him. But so that it might be plain to all that he has been shown to the world, and that no other should be expected, the Holy Spirit willed that the apostolic books also be joined to those ancient ones; therefore our lot is perhaps better and more excellent than that of the ancients, who were guided only by promises and prophecies. The authority of the whole of Scripture has, however, already long been proved by countless arguments. Concerning Moses we certainly cannot doubt, since by some hidden power of God it has come about that his books find credence even among those who are most alien to his religion and true knowledge. Certainly by God's counsel Ptolemy Philadelphus was stirred up to summon interpreters from Judaea with great gifts, who should set out the history of Moses in Greek, because he had left a sure account of the creation of the world and of the progress of human affairs contained in it. Among the Jews, although the Sadducees' wickedness and shamelessness were great, by which they claimed for themselves judgement and censure over the books of the Old Testament, yet they did not dare to detract anything from Moses. And today it is established that the highest authority of his books is recognised among the Turks, however barbarous and fierce enemies of the cross of Christ they are. Christ himself teaches that the Prophets deserve the same faith, for he joins them with Moses, and drew the arguments of his sermons from them as much as from these: indeed in John that Jew says, "Search the Scriptures (for you seem to have eternal life in them), and these are they which testify of me." And a little after: "If you had believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me." Paul, moreover, in the second letter to Timothy says: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work." In these words two things ought to be carefully observed. First, that Scripture has the Spirit of God as its author. Peter, expounding this, says: "For prophecy came not at any time by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." Therefore Scripture contains the Word of God, and whoever wishes to hear God himself speaking must hear and read it. The second is that Scripture testifies that everything necessary for a man either to be instructed or kept in his duty is handed down in it. For it is profitable, he says, for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. By "teaching" he understands the doctrines of faith and salvation, which no one will deny are all contained in the Scriptures, unless he wishes to call the whole account of salvation into doubt. This doctrine ought not simply to be delivered, but set forth in such a way that at the same time the errors by which many are led away from the way of truth are refuted. Again, since the lusts of sin also carry many off crookedly, he says the Scriptures suffice for correcting these too and keeping men in their duty. Finally, he says they are useful for instruction in righteousness, so that he teaches that whatever is needful to know for living piously and justly is contained in them. And lest there be any occasion for evasion, he testifies that this is their use and end: that the man of God, that is, whoever desires to serve and please God, may be made perfect and thoroughly equipped for every good work. The Apostle chose to use a pleonasm so as to stop the mouths of all who invent for us some other hidden Word of God, which must be learned not from the Scriptures but from certain revelations. For what is left to learn beyond the Scriptures for one who has thoroughly imbibed them and holds them rightly, and who is accounted perfect by God's judgement? There is therefore much that is most worthy of observation. God's goodness, who willed that his Word be set forth not only by the living voice but also be comprehended in writings and letters, has preserved the books of Scripture to this day, not without a miracle (as we have noted elsewhere), so that whenever it pleases us we may hear him speaking about the most abstruse matters: about the duties of this life, about the state of the future, about heaven and hell, likewise about rewards and punishments, and finally about the whole administration of the kingdom of heaven. Great, therefore, is the ingratitude of those who despise so great a benefit of God; greater still the wickedness of those who stop their ears lest they hear anything contrary to their desires; and detestable the impiety of many who detract from the faith due to the Scriptures and mock everything in a buffoonish way, nay rather diligently seek out arguments by which they might overthrow their authority. These men (as we have said elsewhere) are like dishonest stewards who, after long enjoying their master's bounty, wrongly pluck at the account books, and so falsely accuse those to whom they owe every duty of gratitude. Let us therefore always apply to ourselves this saying of Abraham, whenever some doubt arises in our minds, or we feel ourselves tickled by the vice of curiosity: let us (I say) then say to ourselves: "You have Moses and the Prophets"; nay, the Son of God himself and the Apostles, whom he willed to be the teachers of the whole world: hear these, and persist in what they themselves have handed down, etc.

units.la: Caeterum non sufficiens visa est diuiti nostro Mosis & Prophetarum doctrina. Manet enim semper sui similis impietas, & incurabili pertinacia aduersus Deum tunc quoque luctatur, quando se constrictam & iusto eius iudicio oppressam esse sentit. Docet hoc ipsum alibi quoque Dominus, quando impios in nouissimo die sententiae eius postremae & irreuocabiliogganientes inducit: Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem, aut sitientem, aut hospitem, aut nudum, aut inualidum, aut in carcere, & non ministrauimus tibi? Vt vero isti seipsos excusando iudicem illum iustissimum accusant: ita dives hic simile quid Abrahamo respondat: Non pater Abraham, sed si quis ex mortuis abierit ad eos, resipiscent. Quid enim hoc aliud erat, quàm Deum ipsum contumaciae fratrum authorem facere, & in hunc perditionis atque exitij ipsorum causam transferre, quia non ea ratione erga eos vita tur, qua facile emendari possint? Sed & suae damnationis culpam non omnino obscure in Deum reijcit, quasi ipse quoque vitae suae rationem aliter instituturus fuisset, si quem habuisset monitorem ex inferis aut ex superis redeuntem. Audiuntur etiam hodie multa huius generis, & multi qui sibi egregiè sapere videntur, dicere audent: Cum abundè omnibus constet, neque Deus ignoret, plerosque contumaciores esse quàm vt scripturis fidem habeant, verbi praedicatione emendentur, aut à ministris illis morosis & contentiosis admoneri atque reprehendi velint: cur nō alia via rem aggreditur? At qui facile illi foret, vel prodigijs subitis verbi contemptores terrere, vel aliquos ex defunctorum numero illis probè notos emittere, qui quae ex scripturis traduntur suo testimonio confirmaret: nec illi desunt Angeli, qui noua & insolita docendi ratione hominum mentes commouere poterant. At quorsum ista omnia tendunt? Vt suam atq; aliorum contumaciam excusent, Deum autem fingant, qui hominum exitio delectetur.
units.tr: Moreover, the teaching of Moses and the Prophets did not seem sufficient to our rich man. Unbelief always remains like itself, and with incurable obstinacy it struggles against God even when it feels itself bound and oppressed by his just judgment. The Lord teaches the same thing elsewhere, when he brings in the wicked on the last day, groaning at his final and irrevocable sentence: "Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?" Just as those men, in excusing themselves, accuse that most just judge, so this rich man answers Abraham in a similar way: "No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent." For what else was this than to make God himself the author of his brothers' stubbornness, and to transfer to him the cause of their ruin and destruction, because he did not live toward them in a way by which they could easily be amended? But he also casts the blame for his own damnation, not very obscurely, upon God, as if he too would have ordered his life differently had he had a warner returning from the dead or from above. Many things of this kind are heard even today, and many who seem to themselves remarkably wise dare to say: since it is perfectly clear to all, and God does not fail to know, that most people are too stubborn to trust the Scriptures, and do not want to be corrected by the preaching of the word or admonished and rebuked by those tiresome and contentious ministers, why does he not take another way? But it would be easy for him to terrify the despisers of the word with sudden portents, or to send some of the dead, well known to them, who might confirm by their testimony what is handed down in the Scriptures; nor are angels lacking, who could move men's minds by a new and unusual method of teaching. But where do all these things lead? To excuse their own and others' obstinacy, and to imagine a God who delights in the destruction of men.

units.la: Sed omnibus istis Abrahamus respondet: Si Mosem & Prophetas non audiunt, nec si quidem quispiam ex mortuis extitetur, assentietur. Rationes huius dicti multae afferri possunt. Nam si Mosis & Prophetarum libri excutiantur, quid obsecro in illis reperietur, quod nō cum naturae legibus & communi hominum paulò cordatiorum sensu conueniat? Paulus equidem Gentes olim eam ipsam legem in cordibus suis inscriptam habuisse testatur, quam Moses Dei digito in tabulis lapideis descriptam Israelitis promulgauit: quod ab illo verissimè dictum esse, in eius loci expositione prolixè demonstrauimus. Si qui ergo Mosi credere dedignantur, eos certum est naturae legem negare, & cum propria conscientia certamen suscepisse. Adde huic argumento vaticiniorum veritatem infallibilem, de quorum fide amplius dubitare non licet, cum pleraque iam olim impleta sint, & quae adhuc reliqua sunt, quotidie impleatur. Quibus ergo fidem adhibebunt, qui ea negare audent, quae in omnium oculis, ore & manibus versantur? Aut quis illos dignos esse dixerit, in quibus instituendis Deus noua ratione vtatur? Quae vero eorum impudentia est, qui à Deo petere audent, quod à viro bono & bonesto postulare, nimis inciuile & iniquum diceretur, vt nimirum propter viles & nullius pretij seruulos, imo propter contumaces responsatores totam suae domus administratione mutaret? Ac cedit hus omnibus, quod nunquam tutum esset mortuorum apparitionibus & nouis quotidie reuelationibus fidere. Nam & Satan Iesu in Angelum lucis transformare nouit, & idem sanctorum personam interdum assumit, vt facilius curiosis & incautis, vel aliquo affectu vehementiori laborantibus imponat. Sicuti in Samuelis & Saulis historia est videre. Et quam multi per apparitiones & reuelationes eiusmodi delusi sint & miserè decepti nō sine aperto animarum suarum periculo, notius est, quàm vt multorum exemplorum commemoratione demonstrari oporteat. Ergo vt nostrae saluti Deus consuleret, certam doctrinae formam extare voluit literis mandatam, ad quam in omni casu recurrere & eam tutò sequi possemus.
units.tr: But Abraham answers all these objections: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded, even if someone should rise from the dead." Many reasons can be given for this saying. For if the books of Moses and the Prophets are examined, what, I ask, will be found in them that does not agree with the laws of nature and the common sense of fairly thoughtful people? Paul indeed testifies that the Gentiles long ago had that same law written in their hearts which Moses promulgated to the Israelites, written with the finger of God on tablets of stone; that this was said most truly by him, we have demonstrated at length in the exposition of that passage. If therefore some refuse to believe Moses, it is certain that they deny the natural law and have entered into conflict with their own conscience. Add to this argument the infallible truth of the prophecies, whose trustworthiness there is no longer room to doubt, since many have already been fulfilled long ago, and those that remain are being fulfilled every day. To whom, then, will those give credence who dare to deny what is in the sight, mouth and hands of all? Or who would say that those are worthy for whose instruction God should use a new method? What impudence it is of those who dare to ask of God what would be called too uncivil and unjust to ask of a good and honest man: namely, that for the sake of cheap and worthless slaves, or rather stubborn answerers, he should change the whole administration of his household! And besides all this, it would never be safe to trust in apparitions of the dead and new revelations every day. For Satan also knows how to transform himself into an angel of light, and sometimes assumes the person of the saints, so that he may more easily deceive the curious and the incautious, or those labouring under some more violent passion, as may be seen in the history of Samuel and Saul. And how many have been deluded and wretchedly deceived through apparitions and revelations of this kind, not without manifest peril to their souls, is too well known to need demonstrating by the recounting of many examples. Therefore, so that God might provide for our salvation, he willed that a certain form of doctrine be committed to writing, to which we could have recourse in every case and follow safely.

units.la: Ex his ergo omnes in genere discant, non aliud Dei verbum quaeri debere, quam quod in Scripturis continetur. Cum enim in his certa & omnibus numeris absoluta credendi atq; viuendi regula proponatur, inexcusabilis stultitia, vel etiam execrabilis curiositas est alias revelationes expectare. Itaq; confutantur huius loci authoritate omnes rationes discendi, quae absq; scripturis instituuntur. Fuerunt haec omnibus seculis infinitae & multiplices inter se diversae. Inter gentes artes fatidicas Persarum sapientes, quos illi Magos dicebant, primi professi sunt, inter quas antiquitus sex fere species fuerunt, Necromantia, pyromantia, aeromantia, hydromantia, geomantia, & chiromantia. Necromantia utebantur, qui ex defunctis rescire volebant rerum eventus: & illi aut spiritus defunctorum, aut etiam eorundem corpora excitare se profitebantur, a quibus de omnibus admonerentur. Exemplum huius apud Lucanum habetur, ubi Erichto Thessalica maga mortui hominis cadaver excitauisse scribitur, quod belli civilis eventum Pompeij filio ex ordine recitauit. Et tantus huius artis usus fuit, ut in populo Dei tandem locum habuerit, ut Saulis historia testatur, qui Samuelem excitari voluit per veneficam quandam, ut ex illo disceret quid sibi in praelio contra Philistaeos esset eventurum. Pyromantia dixerunt divinationem, quae per ignem fit, dum fulgurum fulminum aut aliarum impressionum ignearum vis inuestigatur. Quo & tonitrua referri possunt, quae Latini homines felicia putabant, si a sinistra parte audirentur, ut Cicero in hoc Ennij versu observauit, Cum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena: cum e contra Homerus Aiacem de Troianorum ferocitate cum Achille loquentem inducens tonituris dexteris laetum quid portendi innuat. Aeromantia erat, quae ventos, avium volatus, insolitas tempestates & alia huius generis observabat. Hydromantia circa aquas versabatur, geomantia ex terrae hiatibus, chiromantia ex linearum, quae in manibus visuntur, inspectione hominis sua fata praedicebat. Accesserunt posteris temporibus infinitae aliae species, aruspicina, fortes Praenestinae, oracula omnis generis, quibus Satan infelices gentes misere delusit. Nostro autem tempore in hoc ordine primus locus ijs debetur, qui Astrologiam iudiciariam profitentur tanta audacia, ut hominis vitia & virtutes, mortem & vitam, adhaec regnorum motus & mutationes, imo ipsam quoque religionem astris subijciant. Damnantur hi omnes per Legem Dei, & Prophetae non solum gentium divinatoribus amarulenter insultant, verumetiam omnes artium eiusmodi professores a Christi regno excindendos & procul relegandos esse testantur. Veruntamen tanta superstitionis & curiositatis humanae vis est, ut inter Christianos homines, qui veteris illius artis impostoras facile observarunt, alia locum inuenerint non minus periculosae, inter quas vetustissima habentur, apparitiones Angelorum & revelationes, quibus multi decepti ea admiserunt & fecerunt, quae cum Dei Verbo aperte pugnant. Nam ut paulo ante diximus, posse se in Angelum lucis Satan quoque transformare. Necesse quod hic mihi aliquis vetera exempla obiciat. Olim enim apud Prisicos patres & Prophetas multus apparitionum & revelationum usus fuit, qui hodie nullus est, cum iampridem scripta sint quaecunque nos scire necesse est. Etsi hodie Angeli doctores darentur, aut ea docerent, quae Apostoli per Euangelium olim tradiderunt, aut ab his diversa. Si eadem, inutilis & superuacanea erit haec mutata doctrinae ratio. Si diversa autem praedicarent, iam illis fidem habere Paulus prohibet. Paulo post animarum quoq; apparitiones ceperunt, de quibus multum etiam Augustini temporibus disputatum fuisse, ex illius libro De cura pro mortuis gerenda apparet. Initio tamen de illis fere solis agebatur, quae in somnis apparent. Id vero Sanctus ille Pater ridiculum esse docet ad animarum substantiam referre, cum qui adhuc in vivis sunt, procul autem a nobis distant, saepe in somnis nobiscum colloqui, nos de multis admonere, aut alia nobiscum agere videantur. Tandem vero crescente indies superstitione, vigilantibus quoq; spectra obijci coeperunt, ex quibus ignis Purgatorij calefactores quaestum fecerunt longe uberrimum; & ipse Satan mira finxit, quia hoc breuissimum compendium esse videbat, per quod homines a Verbi Dei doctrina abducerentur. Atqui animas semel a corporibus egressas vel incertis locis vagari, vel ad nos redire, cum Christi doctrina aperte pugnat, & ad erroris huius confutationem vnicum hoc Abrahami responsum sufficere poterat. Ergo quicquid huius obijcitur, id aut hominum dolo & artibus fit, aut diabolica impostura est, cui interdum aliquid permittit Dominus, ut efficaci errore eos puniat, qui Veritati nolunt credere. Nobis ergo persuasum sit, omnes quae extra Scripturas instituuntur docendi rationes, illicitas & errorum irritamenta esse, & ideo Isaiam audimus dicentem: Si dixerint vobis, Scisicitamini a Pythonicis diuinis, qui musitant & susurrant. Annon gens quaeq; suos Deos consulit? Num pro vivis ad mortuos? Ad Legem & testimonium: & qui non dixerint secundum verbum hoc, ijs non erit lux matutina. Denique celebremus gratis animis Dei bonitatem, qui ut olim variis modis cum patribus collocutus est: sic tandem Filium suum misit, qui voluntatem eius omnem exponeret. Hic cum nobis etiam hodie loquatur per Scripturas, audiamus illum, ut eo magistro & doctore vsi per huius vitae tenebras secure pede ambulemus, tandem vero salutis & vitae aeternae participes efficiamur, quam nobis suo merito acquisivit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: From these things, then, let everyone learn in general that no other word of God is to be sought than what is contained in the Scriptures. For since in them a certain and in every respect complete rule of believing and living is set forth, it is an inexcusable folly, or even an accursed curiosity, to look for other revelations. Thus by the authority of this passage all the methods of learning that are pursued apart from the Scriptures are refuted. These have been infinite and manifold in every age, differing greatly among themselves. Among the nations, the Persian wise men, whom they called Magi, were the first to profess the magical arts, and of these there were in ancient times about six kinds: necromancy, pyromancy, aeromancy, hydromancy, geomancy and chiromancy. Those who practised necromancy wished to learn the outcomes of events from the dead, and they professed that they could raise either the spirits of the dead or even their bodies, from whom they might be instructed about everything. An example of this is found in Lucan, where it is written that Erichtho, the Thessalian witch, raised the corpse of a dead man, who then recited in order to Pompey's son the outcome of the civil war. And the use of this art was so great that at last it found a place among the people of God, as the history of Saul testifies, who wished Samuel to be raised through a certain sorceress, so that he might learn from him what would happen to him in battle against the Philistines. They called pyromancy the divination that is done through fire, when the force of lightning bolts or other fiery impressions is investigated. To this may also be referred thunder, which the Latin people thought propitious if it was heard from the left, as Cicero observed in this verse of Ennius: "When it thundered on the left, the weather being serene, it was well." Homer, on the other hand, introducing Ajax speaking with Achilles about the ferocity of the Trojans, indicates that thunder on the right portends something joyful. Aeromancy was that which observed the winds, the flights of birds, unusual storms and other things of this kind. Hydromancy was concerned with waters, geomancy with the openings of the earth, and chiromancy foretold a man's fate from inspection of the lines that are seen in the hands. In later times there were added infinite other kinds: haruspicy, the Praenestine lots, oracles of every sort, by which Satan miserably deluded unhappy nations.
