In our own time, however, the first place in this order belongs to those who profess judicial astrology with such audacity that they subject human vices and virtues, death and life, and moreover the movements and changes of kingdoms, and indeed religion itself, to the stars. All these are condemned by the law of God, and the Prophets not only bitterly mock the diviners of the nations, but also testify that all practitioners of such arts are to be cut off from the kingdom of Christ and banished far away. Nevertheless, so great is the force of human superstition and curiosity that among Christians, who have easily observed the impostures of that ancient art, other practices have found a place no less dangerous. Among these the most ancient are considered to be apparitions of angels and revelations, by which many, deceived, have admitted and done things that openly clash with the word of God. For, as we said a little before, Satan too can transform himself into an angel of light. It is necessary that someone here should object to me old examples. For formerly among the ancient fathers and prophets there was frequent use of apparitions and revelations, which today is no longer the case, since all that we must know has long since been written down. Even if angels were given as teachers today, they would either teach what the apostles once handed down through the Gospel, or something different from it. If the same, this changed method of teaching would be useless and superfluous; if they were to preach something different, Paul forbids us to give them credence. A little after Paul's time apparitions of souls also began, concerning which much was disputed even in the times of Augustine, as appears from his book On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead. At first, however, the discussion concerned almost only those things that appear in dreams. But that holy Father teaches that it is absurd to attribute to the substance of souls the fact that those who are still alive, though far from us, often seem in dreams to converse with us, to admonish us about many things, or to deal with us in other ways. At length, however, superstition growing day by day, spectres began to be presented even to the waking, and from these the warmers of the fire of Purgatory made a very rich profit; and Satan himself devised wonders, since he saw this to be a very short shortcut by which men might be led away from the doctrine of the word of God. Yet that souls, once they have gone out of their bodies, should either wander in uncertain places or return to us, clearly fights against the doctrine of Christ, and this one answer of Abraham could have sufficed to refute this error. Therefore, whatever of this kind is put forward, it is either done by the trickery and arts of men, or it is a diabolical imposture, which the Lord sometimes permits, so that he may punish by an effective error those who are unwilling to believe the truth. Let us therefore be persuaded that all teaching methods pursued outside the Scriptures are unlawful and incitements to error; and so we hear Isaiah saying: "If they say to you, Seek of the Pythonic spirits and the diviners, who mutter and whisper, should not a people seek its gods? On behalf of the living, to the dead? To the law and to the testimony! Whoever does not speak according to this word, for them there will be no morning light." Finally, let us celebrate with grateful hearts the goodness of God, who, as he once spoke to the fathers in various ways, at last sent his Son, who would set forth his whole will. Since he still speaks to us today through the Scriptures, let us hear him, so that, using him as our teacher and instructor, we may walk securely through the darkness of this life, and at last be made partakers of salvation and eternal life, which he acquired for us by his own merit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: HOMILIA CLX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLX.

units.la: Ait autem discipulis: Fieri non potest quin eveniant scandala: sed vae illi per quem eveniunt. Expedit ei si mola asinaria circumponatur collo eius, & abiectus fuerit in mare, quam ut offendat unum ex parvis istis. Cavete vobis. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, obiurga eum: & si resipuerit, remitte ei. Et si septies in die peccaverit, & septies in die reverterur ad te, dicens: Poenitet me; remittes ei.
units.tr: He said also to his disciples: It is impossible but that offences will come; but woe to him through whom they come. It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should offend one of these little ones. Take heed to yourselves. If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him. And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent, thou shalt forgive him.

units.la: Proximo Capite Christus Iesus multa graviter dixit contra avaritiam & petulantem opum huius seculi abusum. Et quia in his plerique summa suae felicitatis collocant, errorem hunc nocentissimum diligenter confutavit, docens quam miseri & infelices sint post finitum huius vitae cursum, qui inter opes luxuriae et voluptatibus. Dediti, fidei & charitatis officia negligunt. Porro ut doctrina haec tunc a Pharisaeis cum risu & sannis excepta fuit, eo quod cum avaritia inanem superstitiosae persuasionis fiduciam coniunxerant, & omnem abusum opum sacrificiis atque oblationibus expiari posse arbitrabantur: Ita hodie etiam ab omnibus ridetur, qui carni & mundo diediti, sibi ipsis iampridem persuaserunt, Deum minuta ista non curare, adhaec incerta esse & dubia, quaecunque de fine huius seculi, de vita futura, de animarum immortalitate, caelo deniq; & inferis dicuntur. Et si qui meliores sunt, hi quoq; rapinas suas, imposituras, faslum & luxum abunde expiari existimant, si ex male partis aliquam summulam Deo decidant, quae vel in ignavos sacriculos, aut etiam in pauperes erogetur. Est autem hoc plenum scandali, simulq; multa alia quotidie fiunt, quae Evangelij doctrinam magno cum scandalo remorantur apud eos, qui minus adhuc instructi sunt: Ideo Dominus ad discipulos conversus admonitionem de scandalis subiicit, qua docet, fieri non posse, quin illa pijs multa & gravia objiciantur, simul autem poenam horum authoritate denuntiat, & eorum cavendorum rationem tradit. Quorum omnium confirmationi serviit postrema pars huius Capitis, qua de novissimorum temporum moribus atque statu disserit.
units.tr: In the previous chapter Christ Jesus spoke many severe words against avarice and the wanton abuse of the riches of this world. And because many place the sum of their happiness in these things, he diligently refuted this most harmful error, teaching how wretched and unhappy they are after the course of this life is finished, those who, among their riches, luxuries and pleasures, neglect the duties of faith and love. Moreover, just as this teaching was then received by the Pharisees with laughter and mockery, since they had joined avarice with a vain confidence in superstitious persuasion and believed that every abuse of wealth could be atoned for by sacrifices and offerings, so today too it is ridiculed by all who, given over to the flesh and the world, have long ago persuaded themselves that God does not care about these trifles, and that whatever is said about the end of this age, the future life, the immortality of souls, and finally heaven and hell, is uncertain and doubtful. And even those who are the better sort think that their robberies, frauds, deceits and luxury are amply atoned for if they give some small sum to God out of ill-gotten gains, which is distributed either to idle little priests or even to the poor. This is full of offence, and at the same time many other things happen every day which hinder the teaching of the Gospel, with great offence, among those who are still less instructed. Therefore the Lord, turning to the disciples, adds a warning about offences, in which he teaches that it is impossible but that many grave offences will be laid before the godly, and at the same time, with his authority, he threatens punishment for them and gives the manner of guarding against them. The last part of this chapter, in which he discourses on the customs and state of the last times, serves to confirm all these things.

units.la: Priusquam vero ad Christi verba accedamus, de scandalis quaedam in genere dicenda sunt. Scandali vox Graeca est, et Latinis impedimentu, obstaculu vel offendiculu significat. Proprie autem de illis dicitur, ad quae iter faciendo offendimus, a deo ut vel casus sequatur, aut aliqua laesio, quae ut minus possimus progredi nos impedit. Per Metaphoram vero vox ista ad hominis vitam et mores transfertur, & ut in Scripturis vita viae cofertur, ita scandalu seu offendiculu dici solet omne dictu aut factu, quod in pietatis via ambulates remoratur, aut lapsus occasione praebet. Sunt haec multa & varia, adhaec varie etiam obiici solet, ta in religione quam reliqua hominis vita. Et sane nocentissima sunt, quae in religione et Dei cultu nos impediunt, aut erroris causam praebet, eo quod ex religione universa hominis salus dependet. At hic primu locu habet falsa doctrina, quae simplices a veritatis via abducit, et superstitionib. implicat, ut non possint pgredi, quo maxime volebat. Proximus locus principib. debetur, qui edictis publicis et proprio exemplo superstitiones et illicitos cultus inuehut, imo etiam inuitis obtrudut, vel quod Veritatis ignari zelo praepostero feruntur, vel sub religionis praetextu regnu suu stabilire conatur, ut olim Ieroboam primus Israelis rex & Herodes fecerut: quorum vestigijs bodie multi insistut, qui superstitiones Papisticas non alia ob causam apud suos tanta pertinacia tuentur, quam ut Pontificu & aliorum regu auxilijs suffulti tyrannide in suos tutius exercere possint. Scandala quoq; in religione non leuia, sunt consortia non necessaria cū impijs & coniugia imparia, quæ in Lege Deus olim seueriter prohibuit. Fit enim vt vel sociorum causa, vel vt coniuge commo-diore vtantur, pij multa faciant, quæ cum fidei professione minus conueniunt. Similiter scandalum dant veræ religionis sectatores imperitis, quando vel apertis superstitionibus communicant, vel in re-bus medijs atq; indifferentibus libertate sua licentius vtuntur, nulla infirmorum ratione habita. Ex emplo in Corinthijs Paulus proponit, qui idolothytorum esum libertatis Christianæ prætextu excusa-bant, cum interim dæmoniorum cultui communicaret. Et huc pertinet omnia ea, quæ hodie Euangelicæ fidei professores in suspicionē adducunt, quasi à Papatu & idololatria minus abhorreant: vt cum a-lienis à fide filiæ elocantur, filij idololatris instituendi committuntur. Encæniorum & Bacchanalium festa frequentantur, multa deniq; fiunt & dicuntur, quibus vel superstitiones aperte probāt, vel sal-tem leuiores esse ducunt, quàm vt propter illas cum quoquam aliquis debeat contendere. Quæ omnia cum infirmiores vident, non possunt non offendi, vt vel odisse incipiant languidos & tepidos istos Euangelij professores, vel eorundem exemplum secuti, ipsi quoq; multa faciant reclamante consci-entia, ex quibus periculum salutis ipsis imminet. Non autē minor est in reliqua hominis vita scan-dalorum numerus, siue sermonem aut verba, siue facta hominum inspicias. Ad sermonem pertinent scurriles facetiæ, illusorum de cælo & inferis fabulæ, obscæna dicta, conuitia, execrationes, & quæ-cunq; alia animos hominum ad desiderIa praua accendere, aut pessimarum cogitationum materiam sive argumentum præbere possunt. Est etenim maxima verborum vis, & vt nostri animi index est sermo, ita in aliorum quoq; animis efficaciter agit: quod Paulus obseruans ethnici Poetæ versum dignum putauit, quem sua authoritate cōfirmaret: Corrumpunt mores bonos colloquia praua. Præ aliis tamen plurimum possunt cantilenæ ab hominibus libidini deditis factæ, fabulæ item de amato-ribus, quæ vt propter argumentum carni iucundæ sunt, ita verborum elegantia et numerorum sua-uitate hominum mentes facile abripiunt. Nec temere Platoni visum est poetas à republica bene constituta eijcere, cum illos non alia tractare videret, quàm quæ bonis moribus officiunt, & religio-nem quoq; in contemptum adducunt. Porrò ex factis quoq; hominum scandala plurima nascuntur, eorum in primis, qui authoritatem & existimationem virtutis & sapientiæ sustinent. Nam si isti vel in religione vel moribus aliquid præter officium faciant, mox imitatores inueniunt, qui iam si-bi licere putant, quæ prius illicita esse sciebant: at qui meliores & honestatis amantes sunt, non pos-sunt nō eos odisse, quos publicæ licentiæ authores esse vident. At quæ nostri seculi calamitas est, hic ferè scandalorum seges vberrima emergit: quando parentes in liberorum conspectu multa indecen-ter, multa turpiter & impiè faciunt: qui verò Ecclesiarum ministri sunt, & qui rempublicam guber-nant, suo exemplo ebrietatem, aleam, vsuras & publicam licentiam stabiliunt: rursus senes quoq; iu-niores ad libidinem & morum leuitatem alliciunt. Similiter diuites pauperibus offendiculum præ-bent, quos suo fastu & luxu eò adducunt, vt suam paupertatē impatientius ferant, & aduersus De-um murmurent, quasi hic dona sua indignè et iniquè distribuat. Taceo infinitas alias scandalorum species, quæ partim alijs obijciūt homines, partim multi arripiunt, cum nullæ detur, vt calumniandi occasione habeat. Et de his quidē omnibus Christus iā disserit, breuiter quidē, sed mira cū grauitate.
units.tr: Before we come to the words of Christ, some things must be said about offences in general. The word "scandal" is Greek, and in Latin it means an impediment, obstacle or stumbling-block. Properly it is said of those things against which we strike when making our way, so that either we fall or suffer some injury which hinders us from advancing. But by metaphor this word is transferred to a person's life and conduct, and just as in Scripture life is compared to a way, so any saying or doing that delays a man walking in the way of godliness, or offers occasion of falling, is commonly called a scandal or stumbling-block. These are many and various, and they are offered in various ways, both in religion and in the rest of human life. Indeed those are most harmful which hinder us in religion and the worship of God, or give cause of error, because the whole salvation of man depends on religion. But here first place belongs to false doctrine, which leads simple people away from the way of truth and entangles them in superstitions, so that they cannot go forward at all, which is what it most wants. The next place is owed to rulers, who by public edicts and their own example introduce superstitions and unlawful forms of worship, and even force them on unwilling people, either because they are carried away by preposterous zeal without knowledge of the truth, or because they try to establish their own kingdom under the pretext of religion, as Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, and Herod did long ago. Many today follow in their footsteps, who defend Papist superstitions among their own people with such obstinacy for no other reason than that, supported by the help of the Pontiffs and other kings, they may exercise tyranny over their subjects more safely. Scandals in religion that are not slight are also unnecessary associations with the wicked, and unequal marriages, which God once severely forbade in the Law. For it happens that godly people, either for the sake of partners or to use a more convenient spouse, do many things that agree poorly with the profession of faith. Likewise the adherents of true religion give scandal to the unlearned when either they take part in open superstitions, or use their liberty too freely in matters indifferent and neutral, with no regard for the weak. Paul sets before us the example of the Corinthians, who excused eating meat offered to idols under the pretext of Christian liberty, while at the same time they took part in the worship of demons. To this belongs everything that today the professors of the evangelical faith bring under suspicion, as if they were not sufficiently averse to Papistry and idolatry: when daughters are given in marriage to men alien from the faith, and sons are committed to idolaters to be educated; when the feasts of dedication and the Bacchanalia are frequented; and finally when many things are done and said by which they either openly approve superstitions or at least consider them too trivial for anyone to contend about. When the weaker brethren see all these things, they cannot but be offended, so that they either begin to hate these lukewarm and languid professors of the Gospel, or, following their example, themselves also do many things against the protest of conscience, from which danger to their salvation hangs over them. Nor is the number of scandals in the rest of human life smaller, whether you look at men's speech or their deeds. To speech belong buffoonish jests, fables mocking heaven and hell, obscene words, reproaches, curses, and whatever else can kindle people's minds to wicked desires or provide the matter and subject for evil thoughts. For the power of words is very great, and just as speech is an index of our mind, so it works effectively on the minds of others. Paul, observing this, thought a verse of a heathen poet worth confirming by his own authority: "Evil conversations corrupt good manners." Yet songs made by men given over to lust have the greatest power, and likewise stories about lovers, which, as they are pleasing to the flesh because of their subject, so by the elegance of their words and the sweetness of their rhythm easily carry away men's minds. Nor did Plato think it without reason that poets should be cast out of a well-ordered commonwealth, since he saw that they treat nothing but what harms good morals and brings religion into contempt. Moreover, many scandals also arise from people's deeds, especially from those who bear the authority and reputation of virtue and wisdom. For if these men do anything in religion or morals beyond their duty, soon they find imitators who now think it allowed what they had known to be forbidden before; but those who are better and love honesty cannot but hate those whom they see to be the authors of public licence. And what a calamity of our age it is that here a very rich crop of scandals springs up: when parents in the sight of their children do many things indecently, many things basely and impiously; when those who are ministers of the Churches and who govern the commonwealth establish, by their example, drunkenness, gambling, usury and public licence; and again, when older men entice younger ones to lust and levity of morals. Likewise the rich provide a stumbling-block to the poor, whom by their pride and luxury they lead to bear their poverty more impatiently and to murmur against God, as if he distributed his gifts unworthily and unjustly. I pass over the countless other kinds of scandal, some of which men throw in each other's way and some of which many seize upon, since there is never any lack of occasion for slander. Christ is already discoursing about all these things, briefly indeed, but with wonderful weight.

units.la: Primò autē periculū ex scandalis mundo imminens prædicit, ne de re leuicula aut superuacanea loqui videatur: Fieri non potest (inquit) quin eueniāt scandala. Quod apud Matth. durioribus ver-bis expressurus clamat: Væ mundo à scandalis: necesse est enim vt veniāt scandala. Quo loco nō opus est ad prouidentiæ diuinæ arcana penetrare, vt ex ijs fatale necessitatē statuamus, quæ homines cul-pa liberet, Deum autē tanti mali faciat authorē. Quin potius nos ipsos excutiamus, & dicti huius ra-tione ex peruersa & incurabili hominum malitia pendere intelligemus. Hi enim, quoad suam ratione sequuntur, diuina & cælestia non sapiunt, imò illa oderunt atq; abominantur. Fit ergo, vt impij & contumaces Dei hostes passim scandala inueniant, ad quæ impingāt, etiāsi nihil huius vel Deus vel quispiā alius obijciat. Sic Caino ambitionis & inuidiæ mācipio scādalū fuit fauor Dei, quo hic Abe-lum prosequebatur. Esauo itā Iacobi simplex integritas, quæ ipsum Deo et hominibus cōmendabat: huius autem filijs Iosephi probitas atq; industria, & quod eum à patre tenerius diligi viderent. Sic Pharaonē offendit populi Dei incredibilis propagatio, & hodie multos est videre, qui scandala sibi ipsis fabricant ex aliorum felicitate, in qua Dei bonitatē agnoscere; & eius cōsideratione ad huius
units.tr: Primò autē periculū ex scandalis mundo imminens prædicit, ne de re leuicula aut superuacanea loqui videatur: "It is not possible," he says, "that offences should not come." In Matthew, wishing to express this in harsher words, he cries: "Woe to the world because of offences! For it must needs be that offences come." In this place there is no need to penetrate the secret counsels of divine providence in order to set up from them a fatal necessity, which would free men from blame and make God the author of so great an evil. Rather let us examine ourselves, and we shall understand from the reason of this saying that the evil depends on the perverse and incurable malice of men. For these, so far as their reason goes, do not savour things divine and heavenly; nay, they hate and abominate them. So it comes about that the impious and stubborn enemies of God find scandals everywhere to stumble over, even when neither God nor anyone else puts anything of the kind before them. Thus for Cain the favour of God, with which God looked on Abel, was a scandal; for Esau the simple integrity of Jacob, which commended him to God and men; and for Jacob's sons the uprightness and industry of Joseph, and the fact that they saw him loved more tenderly by their father. So the incredible increase of the people of God offended Pharaoh. And today one may see many who make scandals for themselves out of the good fortune of others, in which they ought to recognise the goodness of God, and from its consideration be stirred up to

units.la: Scandala esse necesse est. simul atq; fratrum dilectione accendi deberent. Num vero id Deo fraudi esse aut vitio verti debet, quòd isti maligno suo oculo eius beneficentiam intueri non possunt? Hodie certè pessimum illud est hominum genus, qui ex Euangelij doctrina studiose scandala conquirunt, quibus & suâ & aliorum fidè impediant. Alios enim simplex & ab omni fuco alienum docendi genus offendit: aliis indignum & bonis moribus inimicum videtur, gratiam Dei in Christo peccatoribus prædicari: plerique ad crucem et persecutiones impingùt, quas Euangelij comites perpetuos esse vident: sunt qui dissensiones nobis ex probrant, quibus inter se committuntur præcipui huius doctrinæ instauratores: & ista quidem omnia sic exagitant, quasi noua hæc sint, nec vnquam visa aut cognita in mundo. Sed cùm hos omnes prater causam sibi ipsis scandala fingere alibi demonstrauerimus, nō opus est nunc illorum improbitatem pluribus confutare. Sed cùm tanta sit hominum improbitas, vt scandala inueniant, vbi nulla sunt; non possunt non ijdem multa quotidie facere & dicere, quibus rudes & infirmi offenduntur, vt aut nullos aut minores in regno Dei progressus faciant. Etenim tanta est vbiq; morum licentia, tam effrenis linguarum petulantia, tam horribilis opinionum absurdissimarum confusio, vt optimos quoq; offendi oporteat, nisi indesinenter in Christi verbum respiciat, qui hæc omnia nouissimis temporibus ita euentura esse prædixit. Adde his felices impiorum successus, victorias, opes, honores, dignitates, quibus ita efferuntur, vt pij interdum nouis cogitationibus & rei indignitate extimulati clament: Quò vsq; Domine clamo, & non exaudis? Qui fit, vt via impiorum prosperetur, & feliciter agant omnes, qui impudentissimè prævaricantur? Non sunt eis nexus ad mortem, quin pingues sunt & præualidi: Nulla eos, vt reliquos mortales, premit molestia, malorum communium immunes sunt, &c. Et hæc quidem pij & sancti homines impiorum successibus offensi dicunt, vt in Ieremia, Asaphi & similium verbis est videre. At qui Dei timore animis suis expuerunt, ij maiori impudentia animorum offensionem produnt, & dicunt: Frustra seruitur Deo: Quæ enim vtilitas, quòd custodiam eius custo diuimus? & quòd humiliati coram Domino exercituum incedimus? Et nunc beatos dicimus superbos, quin & impietatem patrantes ædificantur, & qui Deum tentant, liberantur. Hæc (inquam) & multa alia huius generis hodie passim audiuntur: & cùm hominum ingenia non mutentur, scandalorum finem nemo sperare aut sibi ipsi turò polliceri potest: quin cum Christo fateamur oportet, fieri non posse quin eueniant scandala. Permittit autem ista Deus iusto iudicio, vt electorum suorum fidem exerceat, hypocritas autem arguat, adeoq; ab Ecclesiæ suæ gremio excutiat, in qua sæpe locum primum obtinere videntur. Quo sensu Paulus hæreses (quæ inter scandala facile primatum habent) oportere esse ait: vt qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant. 1. Corinth. 11. Hic autem non tam vtile quàm necessarium obseruatu est, nihil periculosius esse, quàm vel in fidei & religionis causa, vel vitæ consuetudine & moribus, mundi huius exemplum sequi. Quia enim mundus scandalorum plenus est, & fieri non potest, quin illa eueniant, imò etiam augeantur in hac mūdi quotidie in peius proficientis senecta, incerto gressu feratur oportet, & ad singulos passus offendat, quisquis multitudinem sequi instituit. Debet hoc ijs responderi, qui hodie hoc vnum in ore habent, non discedendum esse à maiorum exemplis, multitudinis consensu & magnorum principum auctoritate. Optima sanè ratio, si neq; hos falli posse, neq; maiores nostros vnquam falsos fuisse constaret. At cum Christo teste mundus tenebris gaudeat, & plures sint qui per latam viam ad interitum ruunt, quàm qui per arctam & asperam vitæ semitam incedunt, non poterunt non errare, quicunque illos sequi in animum inducunt. Et hic verissimè impletur, quod alibi dicit Dominus: Si cæcus cæco viæ dux fuerit, ambo cadunt in foueam. Itaque in vnum Iesum Christum intenti simus, qui via est, veritas & vita, & qui in Euangelio nos ad se inuitans clamat: Ego sum lux mundi: qui sequitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ. Porrò ne quis ex necessitate illa scandalorum, quā Christus statuit, sibi ipsi delitias faceret, et per illam vel seipsum vel alios excusaret, idem graue Dei iudicium & horribiles poenas illorum authoribus denuntiat, dicens: Væ illi, per quem scandala eueniunt. Conuenit hoc dictum cum Legis sententia: Maledictus, qui cæcũ errare aut impingere facit in itinere: & dicet vniuersus populus, Amen. Comprehendit autem hæc imprecatio omnem infelicitatem hominis quoad corpus & animam. Vt enim ex Dei benedictione vniuersa hominis salus atq; felicitas dependet, neq; vlla creatura ei nocere potest, quem ille suo amore & fauore in Filio suo Iesu Christo complectitur: ita infelicissimus fit oportet, & omnium malorum generi obnoxios, quisquis Deum sibi aduersum habet, & eius maledictione premitur. Ideo Moses maledictionem istam postea per partes siue species exponens dicit: Maledictus eris in urbe, maledictus in agro. Maledicta erit sporta tua, & reliquiae tuae. Maledictus fructus ventris tui, & fructus terrae tuae, foetus boum tuorum, & greges ouium tuarum. Maledictus in introitu tuo, maledictus in exitu tuo, &c. Et ideo væ illud horrendum non nisi deploratis & extrema quaeq; iam meritis Christus intonat, utpote Pharisaeis & Scribis, quorum contumacia plane indomita & incurabilis erat: & Bethsaidae, Corozaimo & Capernao, quae nullis eius siue admonitionibus siue miraculis adrepisci entiam adduci potuerant. Et ut in praesenti poenam amplificet, addit: Expedit ei si mola asinaria circumponeretur collo eius, & abiectus fuerit in mare, quam ut offendat unum ex paruis istis. Fuit hoc supplicij genus non graue modo, sed ignominiosissimum quoq; non multum dissimile ei, quo parricidae apud Romanos multabantur. Ut enim hi cum vipera, cane, simia, serpente & gallo gallinaceo culeo insuti in profluentem abijciebantur, ut indigni, quos vel terra, vel ignis, vel aer, vel aqua propius attingerent: ita qui cum lapide molari ex collo alligato in mare demergebantur, omnium iudicio indigni erant, quorum corpus vnquam aeri aut luci restitueretur. Quod si vero grauius quid de scandalorum authoribus Deus statuit, poenas eorum ne cum vita quidem perdiram & infamē mortem finiri sed aeternas esse oportet. Itaq; infernalibus supplicijs excruciandos fore innuit Christus, dum ista pronuntiat.
units.tr: brotherly love at once. Yet is this to be laid to God's charge, or counted as a fault, that these men cannot look upon his beneficence with their envious eye? Certainly today there is a most wicked kind of men who eagerly seek out scandals from the doctrine of the gospel, by which they may hinder both their own faith and that of others. For the plain manner of teaching, free from all disguise, offends some; to others it seems unworthy and hostile to good morals that the grace of God in Christ should be preached to sinners; many stumble at the cross and the persecutions, which they see to be the constant companions of the gospel; some reproach us with the dissensions among the chief restorers of this doctrine. And all these things they harp upon as if they were new, and never seen or known in the world. But since we have shown elsewhere that all these men, without cause, invent scandals for themselves, there is no need now to refute their wickedness at length. Yet since human wickedness is so great that men find scandals where there are none, they cannot but daily say and do many things by which the untutored and the weak are offended, so that they make no progress, or only little progress, in the kingdom of God. For there is everywhere such licence of morals, such unbridled wantonness of tongues, such a horrible confusion of most absurd opinions, that even the best must be offended, unless they constantly look to the word of Christ, who foretold that all these things would come to pass in the last times. Add to these the happy successes of the impious: victories, wealth, honours, dignities, by which they are so puffed up that the godly, sometimes goaded by these new thoughts and by the unworthiness of the thing, cry out: "How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?" "Why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why do all who deal most shamelessly live at ease? There are no bands in their death, but they are fat and strong. They are not in trouble as other men, neither are they plagued like other men," and so on. And these things the godly and holy, offended by the successes of the impious, say, as may be seen in the words of Jeremiah and Asaph and the like. But those who have cast off the fear of God from their minds display their offence of spirit with greater impudence, and say: "It is in vain to serve God. What profit is it that we have kept his charge, and that we have walked humbly before the Lord of hosts? And now we call the proud blessed; yea, those who work wickedness are set up, and those who tempt God are delivered." These things, I say, and many other things of this kind, are heard everywhere today; and since the natures of men do not change, no one can hope for an end of scandals, or promise it to himself with any certainty. Rather we must confess with Christ that it is not possible that scandals should not come. God permits these things by his just judgment, that he may exercise the faith of his elect, but may convict the hypocrites, and thus cast them out of the bosom of his Church, in which they often seem to hold the first place. In this sense Paul says that heresies (which easily hold first place among scandals) must be: "that those who are approved may be made manifest" (1 Cor. 11). Here it is not so much useful as necessary to observe that nothing is more dangerous than to follow the example of this world, whether in the cause of faith and religion or in the habit and manners of life. For since the world is full of scandals, and it is not possible that these should not come, nay, since they are even increased in this old age of the world, which daily grows worse, whoever undertakes to follow the multitude must go with an uncertain step and stumble at every pace. This must be answered to those who today have this one thing constantly on their lips: that one must not depart from the examples of our ancestors, from the consent of the multitude and the authority of great princes. Certainly this would be an excellent reason, if it were established that these men could not be deceived, and that our forefathers had never been false. But since, by the witness of Christ, the world rejoices in darkness, and there are more who rush to destruction by the broad way than who walk by the narrow and rough path of life, those who resolve to follow them cannot but go astray. And here what the Lord says elsewhere is most truly fulfilled: "If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the pit." Let us therefore fix our eyes on Jesus Christ alone, who is the way, the truth and the life, and who in the gospel, inviting us to himself, cries: "I am the light of the world: he who follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." Furthermore, lest anyone make for himself a pleasure out of that necessity of scandals which Christ laid down, and excuse either himself or others by it, the same Christ denounces a grievous judgment of God and dreadful punishments against their authors, saying: "Woe to that man by whom the offences come." This saying agrees with the sentence of the Law: "Cursed is he who makes the blind to err or stumble in the way; and all the people shall say, Amen." This curse comprehends every unhappiness of man, in body and soul. For as all the salvation and happiness of man depend on the blessing of God, and no creature can harm the one whom he embraces in his love and favour in his Son Jesus Christ, so he must become most unhappy, and liable to every kind of evil, who has God against him and is oppressed by his curse. Therefore Moses, afterwards explaining this curse part by part or in its kinds, says: "Thou shalt be cursed in the city, cursed in the field. Cursed shall be thy basket and thy store. Cursed shall be the fruit of thy body, and the fruit of thy land, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep. Cursed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and cursed when thou goest out," and so on. And so Christ thunders that dreadful woe only against men already abandoned and deserving the utmost, such as the Pharisees and Scribes, whose stubbornness was utterly untamed and incurable, and Bethsaida, Chorazin and Capernaum, which could not be brought to repentance by any of his admonitions or miracles. And to increase the punishment in the present, he adds: "It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones." This kind of punishment was not only grievous but also most ignominious, not very unlike that with which parricides were punished among the Romans. For as these were sewn into a sack with a viper, a dog, an ape, a serpent and a cock, and cast into a running river, as unworthy to be touched by earth, fire, air or water, so those who were sunk in the sea with a millstone tied to their neck were, in the judgment of all, unworthy ever to have their bodies restored to air or light. But if God has decided something still more grievous about the authors of scandals, their punishment must not be ended with life, nor their infamous death, but must be eternal. Therefore Christ, in pronouncing these things, indicates that they will be tormented with infernal punishments.

units.la: Causas tam durae & grauis sententiae Scriptura saepe commemorat, praecipuas autem Paulus breuiter comprehendit, vbi de illis differens, qui in idolorum templis ad epulas ex sacrificiorum carnibus in Deorum honorem institutas accumbebant, inter alia sic scribit: Tua ista scientia frater, qui infirmus est propter quem Christus mortuus est, peribit. Ita autem peccantes in fratres, & vulnerantes ipsorum conscientiam infirmam, in Christum peccatis. Coniunguntur hic duo grauissima scelera, quibus & charitas Christiana violatur, & in Christum ipsum peccatur. Nam frater (inquit) qui tuo exemplo ad idem scelus adductus est, perit: nimirum quoad animam, cuius salus consistere non potest, quam primum fit fidei naufragium. Cum autem tuo exemplo pereat, tu vtiq; illum occidis, & propterea parricidij reus es. Sed & culpam amplificat, quod infirmus perditur, quem ex charitatis officio erigere & seruare debebamus. Deinde cum ille pereat, propter quem Christus mortuus est, in hunc ipsum peccatur: quia meritum eius exinanitur, & maiori apud te loco esse ostendis gulae studiū, quam sanguinis Christi pretium, quo frater ille tuus redemptus fuerat. Quid vero ab homine grauius, quid sceleratius, quid fidei professione indignius designari poterat? Maledictū pronuntiat Lex Dei eum, qui caeco erroris aut lapsus causam praebet. Quo ergo supplicio no digitus est, qui ignorantem & infirmum fide suo exemplo in barathrū aeterni exitij praecipitat? Nec tamē hic subsistit adhuc tanti sceleris indignitas. Nam simul & Dei gloria minuitur, & contagio ad multos alios serpit. Quod autem de isto scandalo Paulus pronuntiauit, id in omnibus alijs locum habet. Nam cum omne peccatū mortem aeternam mereatur, fratres suos (quantum in ipsis est) omnes ij perdunt, quicunq; illis alicuius peccati authores sunt. Nemo igitur Christum nimij rigoris accusare poterit.
units.tr: Scripture often records the causes of so harsh and grave a sentence, but Paul briefly sums up the chief ones. Discussing those who reclined at meals in the temples of idols, on meat from sacrifices instituted in honour of the gods, he writes among other things: "Your knowledge, brother, the weak one for whom Christ died, will perish. Thus sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ." Two most grievous crimes are joined here, by which both Christian love is violated and Christ himself is sinned against. For the brother (he says) who has been led by your example to the same sin perishes: surely as to his soul, whose salvation cannot stand once faith has been shipwrecked. But since he perishes by your example, you indeed kill him, and so you are guilty of murder. He also magnifies the fault in that the weak one is destroyed, whom we ought to have raised up and preserved by the duty of love. Then, since he perishes for whom Christ died, sin is committed against Christ himself: his merit is made empty, and you show that your concern for gluttony weighs more with you than the price of Christ's blood by which your brother was redeemed. What could be designated as heavier, more wicked, or more unworthy of a profession of faith than this? The Law of God pronounces a curse on him who gives occasion of blind error or fall. What punishment, then, is not deserved by the one who, by his own example, hurls the ignorant and weak in faith into the abyss of eternal ruin? Nor does the indignity of so great a crime stop here. For at the same time the glory of God is diminished, and the contagion creeps on to many others. What Paul pronounced about this scandal holds good in all other cases too. For since every sin deserves eternal death, all those who are authors of any sin to their brothers destroy them (as far as lies in them). No one, therefore, will be able to accuse Christ of excessive rigour.

units.la: Nos potius istorum consideratio excitet, ut in tota vita & morum consuetudine prouidi simus, nec quicquam temere aut inconsulto faciamus, sed (ut Apostolus monet) salutem nostram operemur cum timore & tremore. Quid enim tam facile est, quam vel dicto vel facto aliquem offendere? Faciunt hoc optimi quiq;, quando minime volunt, quam primum suis modo rebus intenti, aliorum salutem nihil ad se pertinere putant. Ideo Deus toties admonet, ut ori nostro custodiam ponamus, & linguam frenemus, ne quid temere effutiat. Et Christus nos de quouis verbo otioso rationem red dituros esse ait, ut nos attentos reddat, ne quid dicamus, absq; diligenti praemeditatione, multo minus autem faciamus, quo alij possint offendi aut peiores fieri. Debebant ista frequentius meditari securi illi & insolentes, qui cum omnes homines contemnant, non aliquam habent suorum dictorum aut factorum rationem: imo non putant aliquem dignum esse, in cuius gratia ab aliquo vel dicto vel facto abstineant. Et quis (inquiunt) ille cerdo, sutor aut mendicus, quem ego reuereri debeo, quo minus meis diuitijs pro meo arbitrio vtar? Num propter peregrinos errones ego a saltationibus, compotationibus, ludis & iocis abstinebo? Quin potius illi ad sua redeant, si nostris moribus offenduntur. Hac & similia multa audimus hodie ab illis dici, qui in morum licentia gloriam suam, & voluptatem omnem consistere putant. Sed ego illos cogitare velim, Christũ hic non diuitũ,non nõ-bilium,non ciuium tuorum,aut quorumuis aliorum mentionem facere, quibus aliquo iure vel necef-sitatis vel propinquitatis obstricti sumus: sed paruorum aut pusillorum, qui à plerisque impunè con-temnuntur. Nec enim vt vilis aut alienus æstimari poterit aliquis,pro quo æternus Dei Filius mo-ri dignatus est{ç}. Ideò non ex nostro,sed Dei .u licio homines æstimare debemus, & minus peccabi-mus. Est hucfacit grauis illa admonitio,cui ipsa breuitas vim addit: Cauete vobis. Perinde enim hoc est,ac si dixisset: Audio, & iampridem audiui,quid multi praetexant. Sed quid verbis aut ratio-nibus opus est in re manifesta? Si vestra salus vobis cordi est,cauete vobis, ne què offendatis vestro exemplo,vel aliorum dictis facilisue offendamini. Quia enim Deus verbo suo salutis viam planam & facilem sternit,inexcusabilis erit vterq;,qui vel ipse offendit, vel alijs offendendi occasionè præ-ber. At cauendi ratio vnica est Fides:quæ quia Dei Verbo nititur, facit, vt nos illi totos subijcia-mus, neque vllorum moueamur exemplis, qui nos ab illo reuocant. Quotquot ergo huius ductum se-quuntur,hi & ipsi quotidie in melius proficiunt, & ἀπροσκοπτοι viuunt, vt nemo ex ipsis scandali occasionem habeat:quod à Christianis Paulus quàm maximè requirit. Vide 1.Corinth.10.
units.tr: Rather, let consideration of these things stir us, that in our whole life and habit of conduct we be prudent, and do nothing rashly or thoughtlessly, but (as the Apostle admonishes) work out our salvation with fear and trembling. For what is so easy as to offend someone by word or deed? The best people do this, when they least wish to, as soon as they are intent only on their own affairs and think the salvation of others has nothing to do with them. Therefore God so often admonishes us to set a guard before our mouth and to bridle our tongue, lest it utter anything rashly. And Christ says that we shall give account of every idle word, so as to make us attentive, that we say nothing without diligent premeditation, and much less do anything by which others may be offended or made worse. Those secure and insolent men ought to have meditated on these things more often, who, while they despise all people, have no regard for their words or deeds; indeed they do not think anyone worthy of whose favour they should refrain from any word or deed. "And who," they say, "is that cobbler, shoemaker or beggar, whom I must revere, so that I may not use my riches at my own discretion? Shall I, on account of foreign wanderers, abstain from dances, drinking parties, games and jokes? Rather let them return home if they take offence at our customs." We hear many such things said today by those who think their glory and all their pleasure consists in license of manners. But I would have them consider that Christ here makes mention not of the rich, not of the noble, not of your fellow citizens or any others to whom we are bound by some right of necessity or kinship, but of the little and the humble, who are commonly despised with impunity. For no one can be esteemed as worthless or a stranger, for whom the eternal Son of God deigned to die. Therefore we ought to esteem men not by our own judgment but by God's, and we shall sin less. That grave admonition, to which the very brevity adds force, bears on this: "Take heed to yourselves." For it is just as if he had said: "I hear, and I have long since heard, what many put forward. But why need words or arguments in a manifest matter? If your salvation is dear to you, take heed to yourselves, lest you give offence by your example, or be easily offended by the words of others." For since God, by his word, lays down a plain and easy way of salvation, both will be inexcusable: he who himself gives offence, and he who provides occasion of offence to others. But the one way of taking heed is faith, which, because it rests on the Word of God, makes us submit ourselves wholly to it, and not be moved by the examples of any who call us back from it. Therefore all who follow its guidance daily make progress for the better, and live blamelessly [ἀπροσκοπτοι], so that none of them has occasion of scandal, which Paul above all requires of Christians. See 1.Corinth.10.

units.la: Cæterum hic duplex scrupulus incidit. Alij enim eos, à quibus vel ipsi vel alij offensi sunt,mox temere damnant, & eos vel hostiliter oderunt, vel saltem negligunt vt indignos,quibus cum aliquid habeant commercij. Alijs vero non satis est{ç} scandalum dedisse aliquibus,insuper aduersus monito-res suos insurgunt, & eos à quibus corripiuntur,conuitijs proscindunt & hostium loco habent. Ita vero charitas vtrinque turbatur ,neque è medio tolluntur scandala, sed potius augentur indies,& tam propria quàm aliorum culpa pereunt , qui seruari poterant, si charitatis lex rectius expende-retur. Quare vtilem & necessariam doctrinam Christus subijcit de fratribus admonendis & in gratiam recipiendis,si resipiscant. Docet enim eos,qui peccarunt aut nos offenderunt, neque negli-gi,neque odiosius exagitari, sed potius de errore suo admoneri debere, prout salutis eorum ratio po-stulare videtur. Vnde alterum sequitur , admonitiones quoq; eiusmodi patienter ferri debere,ne eas spernendo in charitatem peccemus, & viam salutis nobisipsis præcludamus. Sic autem ait:Si pecca-uerit in te frater tuus,obiurga eum: & si resipuerit,remitte ei. Et si septies in die peccauerit, & sep-ties vno die reuertatur ad te,dicens: Pœnitet me,remittes ei.
units.tr: Moreover, a twofold difficulty arises here. For some immediately and rashly condemn those by whom they or others have been offended, and either hate them with hostility or at least neglect them as unworthy of any dealings with them. Others, however, think it is not enough to have given scandal to some; in addition they rise up against their admonishers, tear to pieces with insults those who rebuke them, and treat them as enemies. Thus charity is disturbed on both sides, and scandals are not removed but rather grow daily, and people perish both by their own fault and by that of others, who could have been saved if the law of charity were weighed more rightly. Wherefore Christ adds a useful and necessary teaching about admonishing brethren and receiving them back into favour if they repent. For he teaches that those who have sinned against us or offended us must neither be neglected nor harshly pursued, but rather admonished about their error, as the reason of their salvation seems to require. From this follows the other point: such admonitions too must be borne patiently, lest by spurning them we sin against charity and close off the way of salvation for ourselves. He says: "If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in one day returns to you saying, 'I repent,' you shall forgive him."

units.la: Hic autem ante omnia videndũ est,de quibus peccatis Christus agat,& cum quibus loquatur. Sunt enim qui huius loci prætextu omniũ scelerum impunitatē atq; licentiam inuehere studeffent,dum quæ hic dicuntur,ad Verbi administros & Ecclesiarum pastores,ad magistratus item et iudices,ad parentes deniq; & quosuis alios extendunt, quorum est peccantes punire & disciplina seueriori coer-cere. At Christus cum discipulis suis,vt cum hominibus priuatis loquitur: Non ergo quicquâ ex hoc loco personis publicis præscribi debet,quo ipsorũ functio impediatur. Deinde diserte ait: Si peccaue-rit INTE frater tuus. De ijs ergo peccatis agit, ex quibus iniuria aliqua ad nos redundat,& quo-rum condonatio in nostra potestate est,adeò vt illa nemo alius lædatur aut saltè impediatur,quò mi-nus suum ius persequi possit. Intra hos ergo cancellos seu limites hanc Christi admonitionem conti-neamus,ne inde eliciamus quod ab eius instituto est alienissimum. Non enim abolere voluit hic spe-ciales eorum functiones , quibus disciplinæ executio cùm publica tum priuata diuinitus mandatur: sed vindictam priuatam prohibet,& simul commodissimam rationem præscribit, qua eos qui in nos peccauerunt corrigere & in viam reuocare possimus, ne quod ex illis enatum est scandalum,latius serpat. Itaque conuenit hæc doctrina cum eo , quod in Lege Deus præcepit : Ne oderis in corde tuo fratrẽ tuum:sed arguendo argue,id est, diligenter & seriò reprehende & corripe proximũ tuum,ne feras propter eũ peccatũ. Interim nõ obstat hoc,quò minus singuli officiũ faciant pro suæ vocationis aut functionis ratione. Itaq; minister Ecclesiæ publicè coràm omnibus eos arguat , qui publicè mul-tos offenderunt : magistratus item publica authoritate malos & improbos coerceat, & pro delicti ratione quosuis puniat : parentes ius suum contra liberos immorigeros atque contumaces seriò tue-antur,ne quando horum nequitia ipsis imputetur,quod olim Eli sacerdoti factū fuisse legimus. Quæ propter miserè & pueriliter falluntur,qui sub prætextu misericordiæ & indulgentiæ, quæ ab homi-nibus priuatis exigitur,sceleratis et publicorum scandalorũ authoribus patrocinatur, et publicam licentiam inuehunt. Imò si verum dicere libeat, pugnant illi cum instituto Christi, qui fratres nostra correptione.
units.tr: Here, however, before all things we must see which sins Christ is speaking of, and to whom he is speaking. For there are those who, under the pretext of this passage, have tried to introduce impunity and licence for all wrongdoing, extending what is said here to the ministers of the Word and pastors of the churches, likewise to magistrates and judges, and finally to parents and any others whose task it is to punish sinners and restrain them by a stricter discipline. But Christ speaks with his disciples as with private persons. Nothing from this passage, therefore, ought to be prescribed to public persons, by which their office would be hindered. Next he says expressly: "If your brother sins against YOU." He therefore speaks of those sins from which some injury redounds to us, and whose pardon is in our power, so that no one else is harmed or at least hindered from pursuing his right. Within these bounds or limits, then, let us confine this admonition of Christ, lest we draw from it what is most alien to his purpose. For he did not wish here to abolish the special offices by which the execution of discipline, both public and private, is divinely committed; he forbids private revenge, and at the same time prescribes a most convenient method by which we may correct those who have sinned against us and call them back to the way, so that the scandal arising from them may not spread more widely. Thus this teaching agrees with what God commanded in the Law: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall surely rebuke your neighbour, that is, diligently and seriously reprove and correct him, so that you do not bear sin because of him." Meanwhile this does not prevent individuals from performing their duty according to the nature of their calling or office. Therefore let the minister of the Church rebuke publicly, before all, those who have publicly offended many; likewise let the magistrate, with public authority, restrain the evil and the wicked and punish whoever according to the nature of the offence; let parents seriously defend their right against disobedient and stubborn children, lest at some time their wickedness be imputed to themselves, as we read was once done to Eli the priest. Those men are wretchedly and childishly deceived who, under the pretext of mercy and indulgence, which is required of private persons, shelter criminals and authors of public scandals, and introduce public licence. Indeed, if it is right to speak the truth, they are at odds with the institution of Christ, who wishes brethren to be corrected by our rebuke.

units.la: Leuit.19. correptione & seueritate corrigi vult, nos autem in ferendis priuatis iniurijs ad patientiam & dilectionem fraternam exercere.
units.tr: Leviticus 19: he wants us to be corrected with reproof and severity, but we are to exercise ourselves, in bearing private injuries, in patience and brotherly love.

units.la: Sed videamus ipsum praeceptū. Si peccauerit in te (inquit) frater tuus, obiurga eum. Ergo non feruiliter dissimulare, aut turpiter conniuere debemus ad ea quae in nos contra charitatis & aequitatis leges designantur. Cauendū quidem, ne temere diffamemus fratrē, aut cum eius contumelia publicemus quae in nos comisit (ideo apud Matthaeū ait: Argue eum inter te & illū solum) interim vero non parci debet eius petulantiae, quo minus libere & serio arguatur, vt vel agnito peccato suo resipiscat statim, vel in posterum habeat resipiscendi occasionem. Et ibidem addit: Si te audierit, lucratus es fratrem tuum. In praesenti vero dicit: Si resipuerit, remitte ei. Quod propter eos dictum est, qui in eos adhuc sibi multum licere putant, qui culpam suam agnoscunt. Vult ergo, vt talibus ex animo remittamus: & vt id fiat aequum est, cum nostra obiurgatio siue admonitio iam suū fine attigerit. Nā nisi resipiscentem in gratiam recipiamus, obiurgatio illa non ex amore eius, sed ex animo inuidiae & odij pleno profecta fuisse videbitur. Ideo ne qua nobis reliqua sit tergiuersandi occasio, addit: Et si septies in die peccauerit, & septies vno die reuertatur ad te dicens: Poenitet me, remittes ei. Vult ergo nos Christus dilectionis affectu ita ardere, vt pluribus etiam iniurijs & saepius vno die repetitis nos vinci minime patiamur, sed semper faciles simus omnibus, qui se peccasse fatentur.
units.tr: But let us look at the precept itself. "If your brother sins against you" (he says) "rebuke him." Therefore we ought not to dissemble slavishly or connive shamefully at those things which are committed against us in violation of the laws of charity and fairness. Care must indeed be taken that we do not rashly defame our brother, or make public with his disgrace what he has done against us (for this reason he says in Matthew: "Reprove him between you and him alone"). Meanwhile, however, his wantonness should not be spared, so that he may be reproved freely and earnestly, either to recognise his sin at once and repent, or to have an opportunity of repenting in the future. And in the same place he adds: "If he hears you, you have gained your brother." But in the present passage he says: "If he repents, forgive him." This is said on account of those who still think they may do much against us, even when they acknowledge their fault. He wills, therefore, that we forgive such people from the heart; and it is fitting that we do so when our rebuke or admonition has already reached its end. For unless we receive the penitent back into favour, that rebuke will appear to have come not from love for him but from a spirit full of envy and hatred. Therefore, lest any occasion for evasion be left to us, he adds: "And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day he returns to you saying, 'I repent,' you shall forgive him." Christ therefore wills us to burn with such affection of love that we do not allow ourselves to be overcome even by many injuries, repeated more often even in one day, but always be ready to forgive all who confess that they have sinned.

units.la: At quia multorū contumacia maior est, quam vt priuata admonitione corrigi possint, quid cum illis fieri debeat, apud Matthaeū docet: Sin vero te non audierit, accipe tecū adhuc vnum aut duos: vt in ore duorū aut trium testium stabile sit omne verbum. Ergo ne tunc quidem abijciendus frater, etiāsi eū erga te duriorē esse sentias: neq; tuae authoritatis contemptus tanti fieri debet, vt dignū putes qui abs te negligatur. Quin potius adhibendi sunt alij duo aut tres, qui & ipsi illū admoneant, si forte horum authoritate mouebatur: aut si hanc quoq; contemnat, illi testiū loco sint, quibus eius contumacia coūincatur, tua autē indulgentia atq; bonitas commendetur. Est hoc ijs diligentius meditandū qui si quem obiter monuerūt, nihil praeterea sibi tentandum esse putant, quasi officio suo plene defuncti sint. At indefessa est charitas in fratris salute quaerenda, & ideo ne tunc quidē cessare nos oportet, si secundum quoq; conatum nobis infelicius succedere, & simul testium adhibitorū authoritatem vilipendi videamus. Nam addit Christus: Quod si neglexerit eos audire, dic Ecclesiae. Loquitur autem pro eius seculi ratione. Ecclesiae enim nomine appellabatur Septuaginta duorum Seniorū Senatus quē Graeci συνέδριον, Iudaei autē corrupto vocabulo Sanhedrim dicebāt. Fuerat penes istū ordinem summa authoritas post reditum ex Babylone: sed postquā Romanirerū in Iudaea potiti, eum primo per Herodē, deinde per praesides suos administrauerunt, Synedrij illius authoritas maxima ex parte imminuta est. Aliqua tamen erat propter veterem dignitate apud eos, qui Iudaicae gentis gloriam non omnino oppressam cupiebant. Iubet ergo Christus, vt si iniuriae a fratre nobis factae intolerabiles sint, ipse autem priuatis paucorū admonitionibus ad mentē meliorem adduci non possit, ad publicam authoritatem confugiamus, si forte illius metu & reuerentia corrigatur. Quod vnum satis ostendit, quam fallantur, qui neminem seuerius corripi aut corrigi volunt, & eam ab hominibus Christianis requirunt indulgentiam, quae cum scelerum impunitate coniuncta sit. Atqui Christus ne hic quidem subsistit, sed quo loco habendi sint docet ij, qui publicam quoque ordinariorum iudicum authoritatem contemnunt. Nam subijcit: Quod si Ecclesiam audire neglexerit, sit tibi velut ethnicus & publicanus. Quibus verbis ostendit, indignū esse, quem pro fratre agnoscas, sed aut Dei iudicio tale permitti, aut ita cū eo agi debere, quem admodū cū homine ab Ecclesia alieno agere licet.
units.tr: But because the obstinacy of many is too great to be corrected by private admonition, he teaches in Matthew what ought to be done with them: "But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." Therefore, even then the brother is not to be cast off, even if you perceive him to be harsher toward you; nor should contempt for your authority be made so great that you think he deserves to be neglected by you. Rather, two or three others are to be brought in, who may themselves admonish him, in case he was perhaps moved by their authority; or, if he despises this too, they should serve as witnesses by whom his obstinacy is convicted, while your indulgence and goodness are commended. Those who, having admonished someone in passing, think they should attempt nothing further, as if they had fully discharged their duty, ought to consider this more carefully. But love is untiring in seeking the brother's salvation, and therefore we ought not to cease even then, if we see that our second attempt also turns out unhappily, and at the same time the authority of the witnesses who were brought in is held cheap. For Christ adds: "But if he refuses to listen to them, tell the Church." He speaks, however, according to the custom of that age. For by the name of Church was called the Senate of the Seventy-two Elders, which the Greeks called συνέδριον [synedrion], and which the Jews, with a corrupted word, called Sanhedrim. After the return from Babylon, supreme authority rested with this body; but after the Romans gained control of Judea, they administered it first through Herod and then through their own governors, and the authority of that Sanhedrin was for the most part diminished. Yet it still retained some standing among those who did not wholly wish the glory of the Jewish nation to be crushed. Christ therefore commands that if the injuries done to us by a brother are intolerable, and he cannot be brought to a better mind by the private admonitions of a few, we should have recourse to public authority, in case he may perhaps be corrected through fear and reverence for it. This alone sufficiently shows how wrong are those who want no one to be rebuked or corrected more severely, and who demand of Christian people that indulgence which is joined with impunity for crimes. Yet Christ does not stop even here, but teaches how those are to be regarded who despise the public authority of the ordinary judges as well. For he adds: "But if he refuses to listen to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." By these words he shows that a man whom you cannot acknowledge as a brother is unworthy of that name, but that either he is allowed by God's judgment to remain such, or that one should deal with him as one may deal with a man who is alien to the Church.

units.la: Et hic mihi tam huius loci quàm eorū, quae apud Matthaeū habentur, sensus videtur (simplicissimus esse, et argumento praesenti in primis congruere. Anabaptistae autē hic suā Excommunicationē sta-biliri putat, quod quam firmis rationibus fiat, adhuc nō video. Nā quod de priuatis iniurijs dicitur, hoc illi ad oīa peccata publica extendūt. Deinde Senatū ecclesiasticū fingūt, quale ego à Deo nuspiam institutū esse legi. Quae enim de Senioribus dicūtur, qui Apostolorū tēpore fuerūt, ad nos minimē spectat, qui magistratus habemus Christianos, quorū est in quoruuis mores inquirere et scādala punire. At magistratus (inquiunt) nō semper facit officiū: Ergo alio Senatu opus est qui hunc in ordinē cogat. Ego vero hanc consequentiā nego, quòd nuspiam legerim vel Prophetas vel Apostolos tale quid ausos fuisse: imò cauisse potius diligenter, ne quam populo aduersus magistratū tumultuandi occasionem sionem darent. Ferenda potius sunt regnorum huius saeculi vitia, dummodo sub illis Ecclesia Christi locum habeat: ne dum laboriosi lepores iura dare volunt, Ecclesiam totam dissipent. Postremo, ut hic Excommunicationem instituí fateamur, non tamen ea talis fuerit, quae a sacrorum communione eos excludat, qui illa frui cupiunt. Nam sit tibi (inquit) ut ethnicus & publicanus. Atqui ethnicos & publicanos in templum Dei admissos fuisse, nemo negauerit, nisi qui cum Iudaeis insanire velit, qui Paulum hoc nomine accusarunt, quod incircuncisos in templum adduxisset. Nota est enim Salomonis precatio in templi dedicatione facta, in qua hoc etiam habetur: Sed & alienum, qui non est de populo tuo Israel, qui e longinqua regione propter nomen tuum venerit (audient enim nomen tuum magnum, manum tuam robustam, atque brachium tuum extensum, venientque oraturi in domo ista) audies tu in caelis, in habitaculo manssionis tuae, &c. Et in sequenti Cap. publicanum cum Pharisaeo simul in templo comparuisse audiemus. Quare etiamsi pro ethnicis & publicanis aliqui habendi sint, non tamen ex eo colligi poterit, quod a coetibus sacris, a verbi Dei doctrina, a precibus publicis, & per Consequens ne a Sacramentis quidem temere arceri debeant, cum haec infra Dei verbum longe subsidant, cuius non nisi appendices atque sigilla sunt, quorum nullus usus erit, si verbum & promissiones ab illis auferas. Denique ego excommunicationem, quae a coetibus sacris excludat, in Scripturis nullam inuenio, nisi quae secundum Legem Mosis propter immunditiem aliquam corporalem fiebat, & qua Pharisaei non minus tyrannice quam impie usi sunt in eos, qui Christum sequebantur: quos a Synagogis exclusos fuisse legimus. Itaque Christi doctrina non latius, quam ille voluit, extendi debet. Discant autem singuli, illum non temerarijs excommunicationibus fratrum, sed potius pia erga eos qui peccarunt indulgentia delectari, & velle ut per nos reducantur, qui ipsius ab Ecclesia discesserunt: quod ouibus eius interdum accidere satis constat.
units.tr: And to me the sense of this passage, as well as of what is found in Matthew, seems most simple and especially well suited to the present subject. But the Anabaptists here think that their excommunication is established; how this is done on firm grounds I still do not see. For what is said of private injuries, they extend to all public sins. Then they invent an ecclesiastical senate, of a kind that I have never read was instituted by God anywhere. For what is said of the elders, who existed in the time of the Apostles, does not at all concern us, who have Christian magistrates, whose office it is to inquire into the morals of any persons whatever and to punish scandals. But (they say) the magistrate does not always perform his duty; therefore another senate is needed to bring him into line. Indeed I deny this consequence, because I have nowhere read that either the Prophets or the Apostles ventured anything of the kind; rather, they took careful pains to avoid giving the people any occasion for tumult against the magistrate. The faults of the kingdoms of this age must rather be borne, provided that under them the Church of Christ has a place; lest, while troublesome gnats wish to give laws, they scatter the whole Church. Finally, even if we concede that excommunication is instituted here, it would not be of the kind that excludes from fellowship in sacred things those who desire to enjoy them. For let him be to you (he says) as a heathen and a tax collector. Yet that heathens and tax collectors were admitted into the temple of God, no one would deny, except one who wishes to rave along with the Jews, who accused Paul on this very ground, because he had brought uncircumcised people into the temple. For the prayer of Solomon at the dedication of the temple is well known, in which this also is found: "Moreover the stranger, who is not of your people Israel, who comes from a far country for your name's sake (for they will hear of your great name, and your strong hand, and your outstretched arm), and who comes to pray in this house, hear you in heaven, in the dwelling place of your habitation, etc." And in the following chapter we hear that the tax collector appeared in the temple together with the Pharisee. Wherefore, even if some are to be regarded as heathens and tax collectors, it cannot therefore be concluded that they ought rashly to be kept from sacred assemblies, from the doctrine of the Word of God, from public prayers, and consequently not even from the Sacraments, since these are far inferior to the Word of God, of which they are only appendages and seals, and which would have no use if you took away the word and the promises from them. Finally, I find in the Scriptures no excommunication that excludes from sacred assemblies, except that which was made according to the Law of Moses on account of some bodily uncleanness, and which the Pharisees used no less tyrannically than impiously against those who followed Christ; and we read that these were cast out of the synagogues. Therefore the doctrine of Christ ought not to be extended further than he himself wished. But let each one learn that he delights not in the rash excommunications of brothers, but rather in a pious indulgence toward those who have sinned, and wills that those who have departed from his Church be brought back through us; which, as is well established, sometimes happens to his sheep.

units.la: At quia natura nostri ipsorum amantes, & ideo vindictae cupidi sumus, nec facile offensas illis remittimus, qui in nos peccauerunt, rationibus iustis & idoneis nos extimulari oportet. Erit inter has non inefficax nostrae vitiositatis diligentior consideratio. Ex ea enim patebit, Deum non sine causa permittere interdum, ut iniurijs & damnis afficiamur, cum ut nos castiget, tum ut nostram imperfectionem agnoscamus, quae nos hucusque latuit. Haec certe meditatio olim Davidem monit, ut Semei conuitia patienter ferret, quibus hic infelicem & a filio proprio pulsum indignissime obruebat. Eadem illa admonebit, in nos quoq; cadere posse, quod nunc in fratre quouis supplicio dignum esse iudicamus. Quam ergo veniam tunc nobis dari vellemus, eam nunc fratri demus aequum est. Deinde hoc etiam in mentem veniat, nos dum peccata aliis remittimus, maximum ex ea indulgentia fructum percipere. Nam per eam omnium crudelissima periculosissimaque carnificina liberamur: odio nimirum, vindictae cupiditate & invidia, de qua verissime Poeta dixit: Invidia Siculi non inuenere tyranni Tormentum maius. Haec enim & curis assiduis discrutiat, & periculosa consilia suggerit, & ipsam vitam nobis amaram reddit. At qui hac procul explosa cum inimicis vere in gratiam redeunt, ij tanto pietatis progressu gaudent, & seipsos cura atque solicitudine liberant. Adde his propriam salutem, quae vnicuique commendatissima esse debet, & quae retineri non poterit, nisi in condonandis iniurijs faciles simus. Nam qui vindictam persequuntur, sacrilegio sese polluunt, dum quod solius Dei est sibi vendicant. Ipse enim dixit: Mihi vindictam, ego retribuam. Idem preces quoque suas quodammodo exarmant, & inutiles, imo sibi ipsis exitiales faciunt. Precantur enim Deum: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicuti nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Cum ergo ipsi remittere nolint, ut eodem iuris rigore aduersus ipsos Deus vtatur, postulat. Nec id frustra postulari, imo Deum, licet nihil huius petant, inhumanitate illam aeternis supplicijs multare, Christus eleganti parabola apud Matthaeum in loco supra citato docet. In horum igitur consideratione diligentes & assidui simus: & qui alijs iniuriam fecerunt, ij admonitiones atque correptiones fraternas patienter ferant, culpam agnoscant, & ut sibi ea remittatur pie petant: qui vero iniurias & damnum passi sunt, dilectionis & patientiae memores sint, & fraterna felicitate quibusuis ignoscant. Erit hoc officium utrinque Deo gratissimum. Nam & infelicem scandalorum segetem maximae ex parte resecat, & nos germanos Iesu Christi discipulos esse ostendit, ad quos Regni per ipsum paratae hereditas pertineat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But because by nature we love ourselves, and are therefore eager for revenge, and do not readily forgive those who have sinned against us, we ought to be stirred up by just and suitable reasons. Among these, a more careful consideration of our own faultiness will not be without effect. For from it will appear that God does not permit, sometimes without cause, that we be harmed and wronged, both to chastise us and to make us recognise our imperfection, which until now has lain hidden from us. Certainly this reflection once warned David to bear patiently the insults of Shimei, by whom he, being unhappy and driven out by his own son, was most unworthily reviled. The same reflection will remind us that what we now judge a fellow man deserves any punishment may also fall upon us. It is only fair, therefore, that we now grant our brother the pardon we would then wish to be granted to us. Next, let this also come to mind: while we remit the sins of others, we receive the greatest fruit from that forgiveness. For through it we are freed from the most cruel and dangerous torment of all, namely hatred, the lust for revenge and envy, of which the poet spoke most truly: "The tyrants of Sicily have not found a greater torment than envy." For this constantly tears us apart with anxieties, suggests dangerous plans, and makes our very life bitter to us. But those who cast this far away and truly return into favour with their enemies rejoice in such advance in godliness, and free themselves from care and anxiety. Add to these our own salvation, which ought to be most commended to each one of us, and which cannot be retained unless we are ready to pardon injuries. For those who pursue vengeance pollute themselves with sacrilege, while they claim for themselves what belongs to God alone. For he himself said: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay." The same people also in a manner disarm their own prayers, and make them useless, nay, deadly to themselves. For they pray to God: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Therefore, since they are unwilling to forgive, they ask that God deal with them by the same rigour of law. Nor is this asked in vain; rather, that God, even though they ask for nothing of this kind, punishes such inhumanity with eternal punishments, Christ teaches in an elegant parable in Matthew in the passage cited above. Let us therefore be diligent and attentive in considering these things: and those who have done wrong to others should patiently bear fraternal admonitions and rebukes, acknowledge their fault, and piously seek that it be forgiven them; but those who have suffered injuries and loss should remember love and patience, and out of brotherly happiness pardon whoever they may be. This duty will be most pleasing to God on both sides. For it cuts away for the most part the unhappy harvest of offences, and shows us to be true disciples of Jesus Christ, to whom the inheritance of the kingdom prepared through him belongs. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXI.

units.la: Tunc dixerunt Apostoli Domino: Adde nobis fidem. Dixit autem Dominus: Si haberetis fidem quantulum est granū sinapis, diceretis huic sycamino: Eradicator & plantator in mari: & obediret vobis. Quis autem vestrum habet seruum arantē aut pascentem, qui regressō ab agro dicat statim: Prodi, ac discumbe? Imo nonne dicit ei: Para quod cœnem, & præcinctus ministra mihi vsque dum edero & bibero: & postea edito & bibito tu? Num gratiam habet seruo illi, quia fecit quæ ipsi præcepta fuerant? non puto. Ita & vos cum feceritis omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Serui inutiles sumus, quod debuimus facere, fecimus.
units.tr: Then the apostles said to the Lord, "Increase our faith." And the Lord said, "If you had faith as a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this sycamine tree, 'Be uprooted and planted in the sea,' and it would obey you. But which of you, having a servant plowing or keeping sheep, will say to him when he comes in from the field, 'Come at once and sit down to eat'? Will he not rather say to him, 'Prepare my supper, and gird yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; after that you shall eat and drink'? Does he thank that servant because he did what he was commanded? I think not. So also you, when you have done all that is commanded you, say, 'We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.'"

units.la: Dominus & redemptor noster Iesus Christus, nuper huius Cap. initio duos insignes locos tractauit: alterum de scandalis, vbi docuit quam graue quamq; multiplex periculum ex illis nascatur, & vt nosipsos in vtranq; partem caveamus hortatus est, ne vel ipsi alios offendamus, vel temere illis misceamur, qui nobis scandalum dare possunt: alterum de condonandis offensis, ne quis ex iis quæ de scandalis dicta sunt, odij occasionem arripiat, & sub zeli vehementioris prætextu fratrem vel negligat vel etiam perdat, cuius emendationi debebat studere. Porro si ista cum nostro ingenio & viribus nostris conferemus, ea præstitu impossibilia esse sentiemus. Nam vt ipsi ad malum natura proclives sumus: ita scandali quoq; occasione, vbi nulla datur, facile arripimus. Accedit his philautiæ malum, quæ vindictæ cupidos facit, & charitati fraternæ in primis obstat. Quare hic nobis aliena virtute opus est, quæ vitiosæ nostræ naturæ medeatur, & viribus nouis instruat, vt ad ea præstanda idonei simus, à quibus hominis ingenium quàm maximè abhorret. De illa igitur in præsenti Christus agit, & hanc docet esse Fidem, cuius virtute animatis atq; confirmatis nihil impossibile sit. Inde vero de fidei operibus differens docet, quid de illis sentire debeamus, ne fides in confidentiam degeneret, quæ facit, vt aduersus Dei gratiā sese insoleter extollat, qui præ aliis humiliari debebat.
units.tr: Our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, at the beginning of this chapter, lately treated two notable topics. The first was about offences, where he taught how grave and how manifold the danger arising from them is, and urged us to guard ourselves against both extremes: neither to give offence to others ourselves, nor to mix rashly with those who can give us offence. The second was about forgiving offences, so that no one, taking occasion of hatred from what was said about offences, should, under the pretext of a more vehement zeal, neglect or even destroy a brother whose correction he ought to have pursued. Now if we compare these precepts with our own natural ability and strength, we will judge them impossible to perform. For just as we are naturally prone to evil, so we readily seize on an occasion of offence even where none is given. To this is added the evil of self-love, which makes men eager for vengeance and above all stands in the way of brotherly love. Therefore we need a virtue not our own, which may heal our corrupt nature and furnish us with new strength, so that we may be fit to perform those things from which the human mind shrinks most. Christ therefore is now speaking of that virtue, and teaches that it is Faith, by whose power those who are quickened and strengthened can do nothing impossible. Then, discussing the works of faith, he teaches what we ought to think of them, lest faith degenerate into self-confidence, which makes a man insolently exalt himself against the grace of God, when he ought rather to be humbled above all others.

units.la: Occasionem huius doctrinæ Christo Apostoli dederunt. Audierant hi illum de rebus maximi momenti & arduis differentem, & has cum suis viribus conferunt. Mox autem sentiunt, sibi non solum vires deesse, quibus faciant quæ Deus iubet, verumetiam vix adduci posse aliquem, vt eius verbis aut mandatis fidem habeat. Itaque in extremis angustijs quodammodo luctantes, dum Christo obedire volunt, ad id verò se minus adhuc instructos esse sentiunt, non sine gemitu & magni doloris significatione exclamant: Domine adde nobis fidem. Quasi dicat: Audimus Domine quid à nobis exigas, & debitum tibi obsequium præstare cupimus: sed quæ est humanæ naturæ calamitas, nos tantis rebus impares esse videmus. Atq; vtinam firmo animi assensu ijs credere possemus, quæ abs te dicuntur. Quia ergo nos multa auocant, tu quæso da quod iubes: fidem (inquam) in animis nostris accendito, ne quid de tua doctrina dubitemus, & qua armati vincamus omnia, quæ nostram obedientiam remorantur.
units.tr: The apostles gave Christ the occasion for this teaching. They had heard him speak of matters of the greatest moment and difficulty, and they compare them with their own strength. Soon, however, they perceive that they lack not only the powers to do what God commands, but that they can scarcely be brought to trust anyone's word or commands. So, struggling in some sort in extreme distress, while they wish to obey Christ, yet feeling themselves still less equipped for this, they cry out, not without groaning and a sign of great sorrow: "Lord, increase our faith." As if they said: "We hear, Lord, what you require of us, and we desire to render the obedience owed to you; but what a calamity of human nature it is that we see ourselves unequal to such great things. Would that we could believe with a firm assent of mind what is said by you.
