Since, therefore, many things draw us away, do you, we beg, give what you command: kindle faith, I say, in our minds, so that we may not doubt anything of your teaching, and that, armed with it, we may overcome all the things that delay our obedience."

units.la: Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo admonemur, vt à nobis verbum Dei audiri, vtq; nos eo affici conueniat. Apostolis certè hæc tam seria & ardens precatio nunquam excidisset, nisi quæ à Christo dicebantur, ad se pertinere putassent. Itaq; nos etiam ea, quæ ex Scripturis depromuntur, ad nos pertinere putemus. Quia enim in hunc finem Scriptura diuinitus inspirata & data est, vt homo Dei perfectus fiat, et perfectè ad omne opus bonum instruatur: non possunt huius doctrinā abs se alienam putare, quotquot homines Dei, id est, veri huius cultores esse & haberi cupiunt. Ergo nosipsos accomodemus quæcunq; dicuntur, vt ex iis discamus, quantū nobis adhuc deest. Hæc enim cognitio, aut potius infirmitatis nostræ sensus, studiū proficiendi et errores vel vitia emendadi in nobis accendet, imo ad preces seriās nos excitabit, quas Deus negligere non poterit, cū ea petamus, quæ voluntati eius consentanea sunt & quæ ille dare cupit. At si discipulorū exemplū cū nostri seculi moribus conferamus, mox videbimus, quæ incurabilis illius licētiæ causa sit, qua hodie Dei verbū contemnitur. Nō desunt eqdē qui doceat, moneat, hortetur, increpent, tempestiue deniq; & intempestiue insistet: quin nisi manifesta veritatem negare libeat, fatendum est, Deum non minori benevolentia omnes nationes prosequi, quàm olim Israëlitas suos. Nam ex filijs nostris excitat prophetas, & manè surgens de malis imminentibus admonet, ad poenitentiam hortatur, & ad se conversis gratiuam peccatorum remissionem & salutem aeternam pollicetur. At qui Apostolorum exemplum imitentur, paucissimi sunt. Multi ad verbi praedicationem aures obturant: multi coetus sacros fugiunt: multi doctrinam veritatis odeuntur, conuitijs diris proscindunt, adhaec ferro & igne persequuntur. Qui verò optimi sunt hodie, eos fere imitantur, de quibus apud Ezechielem Deus sic loquitur: Et tu fili hominis, filij populi tui oblo quuntur tibi iuxta parietes, & in ostijs domorum loquitur alius ad alium, quisque videlicet ad proximum suum dicendo: Venite quaeso, & audite quod nam verbum egressum sit à Domino: & veniunt secundum ingressum populi (id est, multi & confertim, ut populus aliquis conuenire solet) sedentque coram te populus meus, et audiunt sermones tuos, quos tamen non faciunt: quoniam cantiones vel sub sannationes ore suo concinnant: sed post auaritiam eorum vadit cor eorum. Et ecce tu es eis instar cantionis amatoriae, quae suaui & eleganti melodia resonat: audiuntq; verba tua, sed ea non faciunt, &c. Quis verò in hisce Dei verbis non agnoscat eorum mores & voces, qui hodie Euangelij doctrinam & huius studium profitentur?
units.tr: This is a memorable example, by which we are admonished that the word of God ought to be heard by us, and that we ought to be affected by it. Certainly the apostles would never have uttered this so earnest and fervent prayer, unless they had thought that what was said by Christ pertained to them. So we too should think that what is drawn from the Scriptures pertains to us. For since Scripture was divinely inspired and given to this end, that the man of God may be made perfect and be thoroughly furnished unto every good work, those who desire to be and to be regarded as men of God, that is, true worshippers of him, cannot consider this teaching foreign to themselves. Therefore let us apply to ourselves whatever is said, so that we may learn from it how much we still lack. For this knowledge, or rather the sense of our weakness, will kindle in us a zeal to make progress and to correct our errors and vices; indeed, it will stir us up to earnest prayers, which God will not be able to neglect, since we ask for what agrees with his will and what he wishes to give. But if we compare the example of the disciples with the morals of our own age, we will soon see what is the cause of that incurable licence by which the word of God is despised today. Indeed, there are not lacking those who teach, admonish, exhort, and rebuke, who press on in season and out of season. Yet, unless one wishes to deny the truth plainly, it must be admitted that God embraces all nations with no less goodwill than he once did his Israelites. For he raises up prophets from among our sons, and rising early he warns of the evils that are at hand, urges us to repentance, and promises to those who turn to him the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation. But those who imitate the example of the apostles are very few. Many stop their ears at the preaching of the word; many flee the sacred assemblies; many hate the doctrine of truth, tear it apart with dreadful reproaches, and moreover persecute it with sword and fire. Those who are today the best mostly imitate those of whom God speaks thus through Ezekiel: "And you, son of man, the sons of your people speak of you beside the walls and at the doors of the houses, one saying to another, each to his neighbour: 'Come, I pray you, and hear what word has come forth from the Lord.' And they come in throngs as the people usually gather, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but they do not do them; for with their mouth they make songs, or mockeries, but their heart goes after their covetousness. And behold, you are to them like a love song sung with a sweet and graceful melody; they hear your words, but do not do them," etc. Who, then, in these words of God does not recognise the manners and voices of those who today profess the doctrine of the Gospel and zeal for it?

units.la: Caeterùm ipsam Apostolorum petitionem paulò diligentius vnà cum ijs inspiciamus, quae in illa nobis sunt obseruanda. Primum in his est, sine fide nihil eorum praestari posse, quae à nobis exigit Deus, & proinde neminem quoq; absq; fide illi placere posse: sicuti Paulus ad Hebraeos disertè testatur. Pugnat enim cum omnibus Dei praeceptis carnis nostrae sensus. Lex siquidem (vt Apostolus ait) spiritualis est, & totum hominem sub Spiritus Dei obedientiam adducere studet: homo autem carnalis est, venundatus sub peccatum. Concupiscit itaq; caro aduersus spiritum, & Legi Dei non subijcitur, imò ne potest quidem. Fatebuntur hoc omnes, quotquot in Legis speculo seipsos diligentius contemplantur, & suas vires ad singula eius praecepta, ceu ad lydium lapidem explorant. Sola fides totum hominis intellectum illuminat, rationem & sensus omnes verbo Dei subijcit, & nouis viribus nos donat, quibus carnis desideria vincere, & animum nostrum ad Dei seruitiu appellere possumus. Atqui vno hoc argumento confutari possunt, quicunq; nostrorum operum meritis aliquid tribuunt, cum peccatum sit quicquid sine fide fit. Rom. 14.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us examine more carefully, together with them, the very petition of the apostles, and what in it is to be observed by us. First of all, in it we see that without faith nothing can be performed of what God requires of us, and therefore that no one can please him without faith either, as Paul plainly testifies to the Hebrews. For the sense of the flesh is at war with all the precepts of God. The law, as the Apostle says, is spiritual, and it strives to bring the whole man under the obedience of the Spirit of God; but man is carnal, sold under sin. The flesh therefore lusts against the Spirit, and is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. All who look more carefully at themselves in the mirror of the law, and test their own strength against each of its precepts as against a touchstone, will confess this. Faith alone illuminates the whole intellect of man, subjects reason and all the senses to the word of God, and gives us new strength by which we can overcome the desires of the flesh and direct our mind to the service of God. Yet by this one argument can be refuted all who ascribe anything to the merits of our works, since whatever is done without faith is sin. Rom. 14.

units.la: Vnde autem fides illa, quae sola innatae nobis vitiositati medetur? Sunt quidam qui in nostro arbitrio situm esse aiunt, vt credamus, vel minus. Alij initium saltem fidei ex nobis, huius verò augmentum atque profectum à Deo dari contendunt. Sed vtrosque suo exemplo Apostoli confutant. Audiuerunt hi longo tempore Christum, qui cùm eos ex toto hominum genere elegisset, & amicorum loco haberet, nihil eorum illos celauit, quae à Patre sibi manifestata erant. Imò beatos dicit, quibus ea videre & audire datum sit, quae multi Prophetae & iusti olim videre atque audire nequicquam desiderauerint. Veruntamen ad preces confugiunt, & suae tarditatis sensu territi Dominum rogant, vt fidem illis addat. Nec pro augmento solum orant (quod multi veteris interpretis translatione decepti arbitrantur) sed ipsam fidem sibi addi petunt, ad ea nimirum, quae hucusque didicerant. Itaque fides Dei donum est, qui & animis nostris eam inserit, & eandem in nobis auget, adhaec confirmat, vt in finem vsque constantes perseueremus. Ideo Christus credentes suos θεοδίδακτος, id est, Dei discipulos vel à Deo edoctos nominat & ibidem addit: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Et Petro, qui ipsum liberè confessus erat, idem respondit: Beatus es Simon, quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed Pater meus qui in coelis est. Non debent tamen ista sic accipi, quasi inertes & otiosi expectare debeamus, quando fidem nobis nihil huius opinantibus Deus inserat: sed cùm is ordinarijs medijs vti soleat, ad ea nos accommodemus oportet. Fides (inquit Paulus) ex auditu est: auditus verò per verbum Dei. Et in priori ad Corinthios: Ministri Dei sumus, per quos credidistis, quantum vnicuique dedit Deus. En fidem illis à Deo datam esse docet, sed hunc ad eam rem Apostolorum ministerio vsum esse testatur. Et hunc ordinem iam inde ab origine rerum obseruatum fuisse omnes fatebuntur, qui scripturas sacras non omnino ofcitanter legerunt. Quapropter etiamsi fidem Dei donum gratuitum esse dicamus, nemini tamè desidiae & ignaui otij sumus authores. Qui enim doni huius participes fieri volent, ij ordini sese accommodent oportet, quo ille in fide nobis largienda vti consueuit. Audiant ergo verbū Dei sedulò, legat Scripturas, in his dies noctesq; meditentur, & huic studio preces coniungant (quod Apostolos fecisse audimus) & mox non pœniten dos progressus sentient.
units.tr: But whence comes that faith which alone heals our innate viciousness? Some say that it lies in our own power whether we believe or not. Others contend that at least the beginning of faith comes from us, but its increase and progress from God. The Apostles refute both by their example. These men heard Christ for a long time, and since he had chosen them from the whole human race and held them as friends, he concealed nothing from them of what the Father had revealed to him. Indeed, he calls blessed those to whom it has been given to see and hear the things which many prophets and righteous men longed in vain to see and hear. Yet they flee to prayer, and, terrified by their sense of their own slowness, they ask the Lord to add faith to them. Nor do they pray only for an increase (which many, deceived by the translation of the old interpreter, suppose), but they ask that faith itself be added to them, namely for those things which they had learned up to now. Therefore faith is the gift of God, who both implants it in our minds, increases it in us, and further confirms it, so that we persevere steadfast to the end. Hence Christ calls his believers θεοδίδακτος [theodidaktos], that is, taught by God or disciples of God, and in the same place adds: No one comes to me unless my Father draws him. And to Peter, who had freely confessed him, he gave the same answer: Blessed are you, Simon, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Yet these things must not be understood as if we ought to wait idle and inactive, while God implants faith in us when we are not expecting it at all. Rather, since he is accustomed to use ordinary means, we must adapt ourselves to them. Faith (says Paul) comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. And in the first letter to the Corinthians: We are ministers of God, through whom you believed, as God gave to each one. See, he teaches that faith was given by God, but testifies that for this purpose he used the ministry of the Apostles. And all who have read the holy Scriptures not wholly carelessly will admit that this order has been observed from the beginning of things. Therefore, even if we say that faith is a free gift of God, we are nonetheless not the authors of idleness or lazy inactivity to anyone. For those who wish to become partakers of this gift must accommodate themselves to the order by which he is accustomed to bestow faith upon us. Let them therefore hear the word of God diligently, read the Scriptures, meditate on them day and night, and join prayers to this study (as we hear the Apostles did), and soon they will perceive progress that they will not regret.

units.la: Excitet nos ad ista Iesu Christi responsio, quæ eiusmodi est: Si habueritis fidem quantulum est granum sinapis, diceretis huic sycamio, Eradicator & plantator in mari: & obediret vobis. Quibus verbis, non modò probat hanc Apostolorum petitionem, sed eorundem desiderium adhuc magis accendit, dum fidei mirabiles effectus describit. Sensus enim huius dicti est, fidei nihil impossibile esse, et eos qui hac prædicti sunt, ea præstare posse, quæ naturæ rerum repugnant, & nullis hominū viribus aut industria possunt perfici. Id vero parabola docet, in qua duo impossibilia coniungit: Vnum, vt arbor seipsam eradicet, non alia vi quàm hominis credentis iussu impulsa vel adiuta; Alterum, vt seipsam transplantet, & quidem in mare, & in vnda instabili inter perpetuas fluctuum collisiones firmas radices agat. Apud Matthæum & Marcum per aliam occasionē de fidei virtute & eius effectis differens, montis exemplo vtitur: Si dixeritis (inquit) monti huic, Migra hinc & in mare proji citor; mox obediet vobis. Et sunt hæ quidem comparationes hyperbolicæ, si rerum naturam spectes: at si diuinæ virtutis in credentibus agentis potentiam consideres, nihil hic hyperbolicū suerit. Nam & hæc ipsa, quæ hic dicuntur, & his multò maiora olim facta fuisse, & quotidie fieri constat. Sunt enim homines mistar arborum, quæ nisi transplantentur, fructum nullum ferunt. Regeneratione & innouatione nobis opus est. Vt vero homo seipsum regeneret aut innouet, tam impossibile est, quàm arborem proprio motu transferri & alibi radices agere. Fit tamen illud per fidem, vt qui oleastri steri lis germina & rami inutiles erant, in oleam illam pinguem, quàm Deus in Abrahamo sibi præparauit, insiti, fructus ferant vberrimos. Et cùm Ecclesia in hoc mundo inter perpetuos & periculosissimos orbis terrarum motus fluctuet, & in singula momenta naufragium factura videatur, pij tamen fidei radices in Christo firmissimas & profundissimas agunt, vt nullo ventorum vndique ruentium turbine, nullo collidentium fluctuum assultu, nullis denique mundi & principis eius conatibus è sua statione possint deijci. Idem de montibus dicere possumus, qui nunquam non ceruicibus & humeris pio rum maximi & grauissimi incumbunt, vt illos reuera Atlanti similes esse dixeris, quem Poëtæ totam cælorum machinam humeris suis sustinere fabulantur. Mons enim molestissimus est caro, cuius pondere pressus Paulus clamat: Miserum me, quis me liberabit ex corpore isto mortis? Montis quoq; ardui instar est mundus, qui vt exemplo suo nos premit, ita authoritate, potentia, tyrannide, minis & horrendis conatibus planè intolerabilis efficitur. Quid vero de diabolo dicā, qui vt Encela dus & Typhæus quispiam indefesso studio horribiles montium moles supra piorum humeros congerit, si quo modo eos à Deo abstrahere possit, & fidem in illis extinguere? At vincit hæc montes istos omnes, imò per Dei verbum illis imperat, & excussos in mare præcipitat, vt ne vestigia quidem motis illius appareant, quæ paulò ante ad nubes vsq; extollebatur. Rectè ergo Ioānes dicebat: Hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, nempe fides nostra, &c. Exempla huius rei in Scripturis & historijs passim occurrunt. Per fidem Moses immanem illum montem, Pharaonem, & minaces Ægyptiorū scopulos in mare deiecit. Per fidem Iofua Chananæorum vrbes & arces, montium instar exaltatas, euertit. Per fidem Dauid ingentem illum Goliam deiicit. Per fidem omnia Saulis obstacula è medio sustulit. Huc denique pertinent quæcunq; Apostolus ad Hebræos congerit exempla eorum, qui res maximas & humanis viribus impossibiles solius fidei virtute confecerunt. At quid opus est vetera commemorare, cùm nostro sæculo his similia multa sint facta? Quos enim & quantæ molis montes è medio sustulerunt sancti Dei homines, qui sæculis aliquot sepultam & superstitionibus obrutam veritatis lucē instaurauerunt? Quot montibus superiores sacti sunt principes viri, qui cum illis ad Ecclesiæ reformationem animū appulerunt? Ædita sunt tunc multa præclarę fidei opera, quæ immortalem laudem merentur. Hodie ad quemuis rumorem temere exortū trepidamus, quia fide destituimur. Veruntamē non debet nos terrere hæc fidei imbecillitas. Nam quantulacunq; sit, ad Christum apprehendendum sufficit, & in hoc omnem mundi potentiam longè superat. Docet hoc non obscurè Dominus, dum eam grano sinapis confert, de cuius natura & virtute cùm Cap. XIII. dixerimus, non opus est eadem hic repetere. Discant potius omnes, vt hac fidei commendatione excitati nunquam non cum Apostolis clament, vt Deus illam in animis ipsorum accendat, augeat & confirmet, vt ad uensus omnis generis scandula consistere & mundi huius certaminibus sufficere possint.
units.tr: The answer of Jesus Christ should spur us on to these things, which runs as follows: If you have faith as small as a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this sycamine tree, "Be uprooted and planted in the sea," and it would obey you. By these words he not only approves this petition of the Apostles, but kindles their desire even more, while he describes the wonderful effects of faith. For the sense of this saying is that nothing is impossible for faith, and that those who are endowed with it can accomplish things that are contrary to the nature of things and cannot be done by any human strength or industry. The parable teaches this, in which he joins two impossibilities: one, that a tree should uproot itself, moved or helped by nothing other than the command of a believing man; the other, that it should transplant itself, and indeed into the sea, and strike firm roots in a restless wave amid the perpetual clashing of waves. In Matthew and Mark, speaking of the power of faith and its effects on another occasion, he uses the example of a mountain: If you say (he says) to this mountain, "Be removed from here and cast into the sea," it will immediately obey you. These comparisons are indeed hyperbolical if you look at the nature of things; but if you consider the power of divine virtue working in believers, nothing here will be hyperbolical. For it is certain that these very things said here, and much greater things than these, have been done in the past and are done every day. Men are indeed like trees, which bear no fruit unless they are transplanted. We need regeneration and renewal. But for a man to regenerate or renew himself is as impossible as for a tree to be moved by its own motion and strike roots elsewhere. Yet this is accomplished through faith: wild olive shoots that were barren and useless branches are grafted into that rich olive which God prepared for himself in Abraham, and they bear most abundant fruit. And although the Church in this world wavers amid perpetual and most dangerous upheavals of the globe, and seems about to suffer shipwreck at every moment, yet the godly send down most firm and deep roots in Christ, so that they cannot be cast from their station by any whirlwind of winds rushing from every side, by any assault of colliding waves, or finally by any attempts of the world and its prince. The same we may say of the mountains, which always weigh most heavily and grievously upon the necks and shoulders of the godly, so that you may truly call them like Atlas, whom the poets fable to sustain the whole machinery of the heavens on his shoulders. For the most troublesome mountain is the flesh, under whose weight Paul, pressed down, cries out: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The world is also like a lofty mountain, which presses us by its example, and is made utterly intolerable by its authority, power, tyranny, threats and dreadful assaults. And what shall I say of the devil, who, like Enceladus or some Typhoeus, with tireless zeal heaps horrible masses of mountains upon the shoulders of the pious, if in any way he could draw them away from God and extinguish faith in them? Yet faith overcomes all these mountains, and indeed commands them through the word of God, and casts them shaken into the sea, so that not even traces of their motion appear, though they were a moment before raised up to the clouds. Rightly, therefore, John said: This is the victory that overcomes the world, namely our faith, etc. Examples of this matter occur everywhere in the Scriptures and in histories. Through faith Moses cast that huge mountain, Pharaoh, and the threatening rocks of the Egyptians into the sea. Through faith Joshua overthrew the cities and citadels of the Canaanites, raised up like mountains. Through faith David struck down that huge Goliath. Through faith he removed all the obstacles of Saul from the way. Finally, to this belong all the examples which the Apostle collects in the letter to the Hebrews, of those who accomplished very great things, impossible to human strength, by the power of faith alone. But why need we recall ancient things, since many similar things have been done in our own age? How great and of what size were the mountains that the holy men of God removed, who restored the light of truth, buried for some centuries and overwhelmed by superstitions? How many princes were raised above mountains, who joined their minds with them for the reformation of the Church? Many excellent works of faith were then produced, which deserve immortal praise. Today we tremble at every rumour that arises rashly, because we lack faith. Yet this weakness of faith ought not to terrify us. For however small it may be, it is sufficient for laying hold of Christ, and in this it far surpasses all the power of the world. The Lord teaches this plainly when he compares it to a grain of mustard seed; since we have spoken of its nature and power in chapter XIII, there is no need to repeat the same things here. Rather, let all learn, stirred up by this commendation of faith, never to cease crying out with the Apostles that God would kindle, increase and confirm it in their minds, so that they may withstand every kind of stumbling-block and be sufficient for the struggles of this world.

units.la: Caterùm dum fides prædicatur, bifariam ferè homines offendunt. Alij enim quia per illam omnia confici audiunt, ex eo securitate concipiunt, nec quicquam sibi facendu esse arbitrantur: & hi fidem mortuâ, id est, nudam & inanem fidei professionem loco veræ fidei ostentant. Alij verò tanta fidei virtute & eiusdem operibus tam præclaris insolescunt adeò, ut suis meritis atque viribus acceptum ferant quod nobis Deus ex gratuita misericordia largitur. Quapropter Christus doctrinæ de fide parabolam ex vulgari hominum consuetudine desumptam subijcit, qua utriq; errori medetur. Quis autem vestrûm (inquit) habet seruum arantem aut pascentem, qui regressio ab agro dicat statim: Prodi, aut discumbe? Imò, nonne dicet ei: Para quod cœnem & præcinctus ministra mihi usque dum edero & bibero: & postea edito & bibito tu? Num gratiam habet seruo illi, quia fecit quæ illi præcepta fuerunt? Nô puto. Sic & vos, &c. Quo loco ut res fit magis perspicua, obseruare oportet, Christum de seruis loqui, qualis antiquitus fuerunt, qui aut bello capti, aut ære empti erant à suis heris, & mancipia, quasi manu capti dicebantur. Erat in hos heris summa potestas, adeò ut his seipsos & labores suos omnes deberent, ipsis autem heri vicissim nullo debiti iure tenerentur. Et hero quidem eiusmodi Christus Deum confert, nos autem mancipijs similes facit, quia filij Dei sanguine redempti nos & nostra omnia illi debemus. Ex eo autem duo elicit, de quibus singulis ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: But while faith is being preached, men take offence in roughly two ways. Some, hearing that everything is accomplished through faith, grow complacent on that account and think nothing more is required of them. They display a dead faith, that is, a bare and empty profession of faith, in place of true faith. Others swell with pride at the great power of faith and its splendid works, so much so that they credit to their own merits and strength what God bestows on us from free mercy. For this reason Christ, to heal both errors, sets before us a parable about faith drawn from ordinary human custom: "Which of you, having a servant ploughing or feeding cattle, will say to him when he comes in from the field, 'Come at once and sit down to eat'? Will he not rather say to him, 'Prepare my supper, and gird yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; afterwards you may eat and drink'? Does he thank that servant because he did what he was commanded? I think not. So also you, etc." In this passage, to make the matter clearer, we must notice that Christ is speaking of servants such as existed in ancient times, who were either taken in war or bought with money by their masters, and were called chattels, as if "taken by the hand." Masters held supreme power over them, so that they owed their masters themselves and all their labours, while the masters in turn were bound by no legal obligation to them. Christ compares God to such a master, and makes us like chattels, because we, redeemed by the blood of the Son of God, owe him ourselves and all that we have. From this he draws two conclusions, each of which we shall take in turn.

units.la: Alterum est de officio hominis Christiani, adeoque omnis hominis, qui Dei seruus censeri cupit. Fingitur enim seruus, qui vbi totum diem arando aut pascendo consumpsit, vespere domum reuersus non antea accumbit, ut edat & bibat, priusquam hero cœnam parauerit, & cœnanti ministrauerit: adeo ut ipse vix ante multam noctem cœnare possit. Ea parte autem innuit Dominus, nos vitam nostram omnem Deo debere, vsque ad nostrum vesperum, id est, vsque ad mortis horam, quæ illi finem imponet. Non ergo desides & otiosos facit fides, neque nos in inani quadam persuasione acquiescere iubet, quod fere faciunt, qui vitam contemplatiuam profitentur. Atqui Ecclesia Dei aruū, Dei vinea, Dei domus, Dei militia est, & vita Christiani hominis peregrinatio est, qua ex hoc exilio & valle lachrymarum ad patriam cœlestem contendimus. Deus itaque in suo aruo & vinea non otiosis contemplatoribus, sed operarijs opus habet, neque in peregrinatione illa quicquam proficitur contemplando, sed progressu & labore opus est, ut in singulas horas aliquò vsque promoueamus. Et ut non probatur seruus, qui postquam per aliquot horas opus fecit, inde se ad somnum componit, aut otio se dedit. Sed ut ad vesperum vsque perseueret necesse est, & tunc quoque cœnam hero paret, priusquam ipse ad mensam accumbat; Ita nunquam fideles & sedulì serui Dei censebuntur, qui vbi semel aliquid laude dignum fecere, ipsi sibi ferias indicunt, & ad quietem se componunt, priusquam vitæ suæ finem attigerunt. Itaq; nullus hic ignauiæ aut desidiæ locus est, & tam abest, ut nos ab operibus bonis fides reuocet, ut potius nos Deo obstrictos teneat, quoad vitæ huius spiritum ducimus. Etenim ea etiam est hominis natura, ut omnino quiescere non possit, & ideo vel Deo vel Diabolo seruiamus oportet. Si qui ergo de quiete & otio paciscuntur, neque se Deo porrò obstrictos esse sibi persuadent, ij reliquum vitæ tempus diabolo impendant oportet. Quodetiamsi illi se facere pernegent, ego tamen hoc reuera fieri dico. Nam ut scelus nullum adhuc designarint, tamen illud ipsum otium, cui seipsos dediderunt, Diabolo cultus gratissimus est, cùm nullum interea Deo obsequium præstent, illi autem amplissimam occasionem præbeant ipsos circumuenien- di. Quod quàm facile fiat, multorum exempla docent, qui post multa præclarè facta tandem turpiter succubuere, postquam se omni officio defunctos esse sibi persuaserunt.
units.tr: The first concerns the duty of a Christian, and so of every man who wishes to be counted a servant of God. The servant described is one who, having spent the whole day ploughing or feeding cattle, returns home in the evening and does not sit down to eat and drink until he has prepared his master's supper and waited on him at table, so that he himself can scarcely dine until late at night. In this the Lord signifies that we owe God our whole life, right up to our evening, that is, up to the hour of death, which will put an end to it. Faith therefore does not make us idle and slothful, nor does it bid us rest in some empty assurance, as those do who profess the contemplative life. Yet the Church of God is God's field, God's vineyard, God's house, God's army, and the life of a Christian is a pilgrimage, by which we press on from this exile and vale of tears towards our heavenly fatherland. God therefore has need in his field and vineyard not of idle contemplatives but of workers; nor does anything advance us on that pilgrimage by contemplation alone, but progress and labour are needed, so that we move ourselves forward every hour. Just as a servant is not approved who, after working for a few hours, then composes himself for sleep or gives himself over to idleness, but must persevere until evening, and even then prepare his master's supper before he sits down to table himself, so those will never be counted faithful and diligent servants of God who, once they have done something praiseworthy, declare holiday for themselves and settle into rest before they have reached the end of their life. There is therefore no place here for laziness or sloth. Far from faith calling us back from good works, it binds us more firmly to God for as long as we draw the breath of this life. Indeed, human nature is such that it cannot be altogether at rest, and so we must serve either God or the Devil. Those who bargain for rest and leisure, and persuade themselves that they are no longer bound to God, must therefore spend the rest of their life on the Devil. Even if they deny that they do so, I say that in truth this is what happens. For even if they have not yet committed any crime, that very leisure to which they have given themselves is most pleasing to the Devil, since in the meantime they render no obedience to God, and they offer the Devil a very great opportunity to ensnare them. How easily this happens many examples teach, of men who, after doing many excellent things, at last shamefully fell, once they had persuaded themselves that they had discharged every duty.

units.la: In hac autem parte simul admonemur, quæ nam sint bona opera, quæ Deo probentur. Nam vt diximus, seruus fingitur, qui ex heri iussu aut arauit aut gregem pauit, & ex agro domum reuersus eidè cœnam parat, opera igitur bona non erunt, nisi quæ ex Dei mandato fiunt ab ijs, qui se totos illius seruitio addixerunt. Nominantur autem opera, quæ proprie seruorum sunt. Quare ea vnusquisque facere debet, quæ suæ vocationi conueniunt, neque temere in alienam functionem manus extendat, cùm singulis in sua conditione nunquam defuturum sit quod agant. Itaque qui ad rempub. vocati sunt, populum suæ fidei creditum diligenter excolant & pascant. Opus hic aratro, ut nouis sulcis ductis Dei nouale fiant, qui diuspinis & sentibus obsiti fructum nullum tulerunt. Ergo legibus bonis peccandi licentiam coerceant, & disciplinæ iugo contineant omnes, qui posse suæ carnis desideria exorbitare volunt. Adhæc se ποιμένας λαῶν, idest, populi pastores esse meminerint: & ideo ct rent, vt gregis vnitas seruetur, singuli suo iure vti & bonis concessis tutò frui possint: in primis autem populi salutem priuato suo cömodo antiquiorem ducant. Qui verò Ecclesiarum ministri sunt, ij quoque in Dei aruo (vt Paulus ait) se laborare cogitent: vbi eradicatione & plantatione, extirpatione & insitione opus fit, vt olim Ieremiæ Deus dicebat: Strenuè ergo laborem hunc obeant, vt simul Deo cœnam parent suauissimam, dum quàm plurimos illi adducunt. Hoc enim illud ferculum est, quo ille in primis delectatur. Similiter parentes & qui iuuentuti instituendæ præfecti sunt, hunc quoq; agellum Dei esse meminerint, & curent vt in teneros animos ea plantent & inserant, quorum fructus illum aliquando oblectare possit. Eadem est opificum, agricolarum, priuatorum denique hominum omnium ratio, qui similiter seipsos excolere, prauas cupiditates ex corde suo excindere virtutis semina concipere, & ea magno studio educare debent, vt aliquando fructum Deo gratum ferant. Omnibus denique suorum studiorum, atq; actionum hic finis propositus esto, vt Dei sanctissimum demonstrat, qui non aliud quam nostram salutem esurire & sitire solet. Atqui hæc illa opera sunt, quæ à nobis Deus exigit, & quæ sola bona dici merentur, quia ex fide fiunt cum multorum commodo, & simul Dei gloriam promouent. Cum his si omnia fere eorum opera conferas, qui meritis proprijs cœlum conscendere volunt, non modo meritum illis nullum subesse, sed ne digna quidem esse patebit, quæ bona dicantur. Pleraq; enim nullo Dei mandato fiunt, sed inanibus hominum traditionibus nituntur, & proinde nec ex fide fiunt, quia hæc nulla esse potest, vbi verbum Dei nullum est. Deinde nemo ex illis aliquid commodi percipit. Quid enim alios iuuat, si tu ieiunijs teipsum macerés, si cilicio supra nudu corpus vestiaris, si cælebs viuas, humi dormias, vel noctes insomnes ducas, si Psalmorum integros modios præcipiti murmure profundas, cereis & lampadibus templa omnia illustres, fune nodoso ilia, calceis fenestratis pedes constringas? Certè licet hæc omnia magno cum labore facias, nihilominus tamen per se famelici esuriunt, sitibundi sitiunt, nudi algent, exteri & peregrini incertis sedibus oberrant, nec etiam quisquam tuo exemplo emendatur. Num verò ex istis delectatione Deus capiat, qui eis minimè indiget, & si indigeret, illis absq; tua opera posset potiri? Gloriantur ergo omnes isti, vt lubet, Spiritualium, Clericorum, Mortificatorum, Sanctorum denique titulis, ego tamen virum Senatorium sancte ius dicentem, opificem absq; fraude opus facientem, rustican agros suos cum Dei inuocatione & gratiarum actione colentem, matremfamilias liberos procreantem & domum suam fideliter administrantem, pueros & puellas sub parentum disciplina honestè viuentes, omnibus istis sanctiores esse dixero. Illi enim quicquid agunt, ex Dei mandato agunt: istis verò omnibus dicitur: Quis requisiuit ista ex manibus vestris?
units.tr: In this part we are also reminded what good works are, those which are approved by God. For, as we have said, the servant described is one who, at his master's command, has either ploughed or fed the flock, and who, returning home from the field, prepares supper for him. Therefore only those works will be good which are done by command of God, by those who have devoted themselves wholly to his service. Works are named here that properly belong to servants. Each person ought therefore to do those things which fit his calling, and not rashly stretch out his hand to another's office, since there will never be lack of something for each to do in his own station. Accordingly, those who are called to the commonwealth should diligently cultivate and feed the people entrusted to their faith. Here the plough is needed, so that, with new furrows drawn, the field of God may be made new, which, overgrown with thorns and briars, has borne no fruit. Let them therefore restrain the licence to sin by good laws, and hold all within the yoke of discipline who wish to let loose the desires of their flesh. Moreover, let them remember that they are shepherds of the people [ποιμένας λαῶν], that is, shepherds of the people; and so let them take care that the unity of the flock is preserved, that individuals may enjoy their own rights and securely possess the goods granted to them; and above all let them count the safety of the people as more important than their own private advantage. Those who are ministers of the Churches should likewise consider that they labour in God's field (as Paul says), where uprooting and planting, pulling down and grafting are needed, as God once said to Jeremiah. Let them therefore undertake this labour with vigour, so that they may prepare for God a most pleasant supper, while they bring as many as possible to him. For this is the dish in which he above all delights. Similarly, parents and those set over the education of youth should remember that this little field too is God's, and should take care to plant and graft into tender minds those things whose fruit may one day delight him. The same reasoning applies to craftsmen, farmers, and indeed to all private persons, who likewise ought to cultivate themselves, to root out depraved desires from their heart, to conceive the seeds of virtue and to nurture them with great zeal, so that one day they may bear fruit acceptable to God. Finally, let this be the proposed end of all their studies and actions, which the most holy will of God demonstrates, since he is wont to hunger and thirst for nothing but our salvation. These are indeed the works which God requires of us, and which alone deserve to be called good, because they are done from faith, for the benefit of many, and at the same time advance the glory of God. If, beside these, you compare almost all the works of those who wish to climb to heaven by their own merits, it will be plain that they have no merit at all, and are not even worthy of being called good. For most of them are done by no command of God, but rest on empty human traditions, and therefore are not done from faith either, since faith cannot exist where the Word of God is absent. Moreover, no one derives any advantage from them. For what good is it to others if you mortify yourself with fasts, if you clothe your bare body with a hair shirt, if you live celibate, sleep on the ground, or pass sleepless nights, if you pour out whole bushels of Psalms with rapid mumbling, if you light up all the churches with wax candles and lamps, if you bind your loins with a knotted cord and your feet with perforated sandals? Certainly, even if you do all these things with great labour, nevertheless the hungry still go hungry, the thirsty still thirst, the naked still shiver, strangers and foreigners wander without settled homes, and no one is corrected by your example. Would God take pleasure from these things, he who has no need of them, and even if he had need, could obtain them without your effort? All those men, then, boast as they please of the titles of Spiritual, Clerics, Mortifiers, and finally Saints; yet I shall say that a senator who justly administers the law, a craftsman who works without fraud, a farmer who tills his fields with invocation of God and thanksgiving, a mother of a family who bears children and faithfully manages her household, and boys and girls who live honourably under their parents' discipline, are more holy than all of them. For these people, whatever they do, they do by command of God; but to those others it is said: "Who required these things at your hands?"

units.la: Alterum quod ex hac parabola Christus elicit, ad operum nostrorum meritum spectat, & quo loco illa haberi debeat, docet his verbis: Num gratiam habet seruo illi, quia fecit quæ ipse præcepta fuerant? Non puto. Ita & vos cum feceritis omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Serui inutiles sumus: quod debuimus facere fecimus. Quæstio huius loci est: Num ea faciendo, quæ in lege nobis Deus præcipit, aliquid de ipso mereamur? Id verò diserte Christus negat. Vt enim herus mancipio suo gratiam non habet, neque ei ideo obstrictus redditur, etiamsi totum diem aret, pascat, aut opus aliquod ab ipso mandatum faciat: ita neque vobis (inquit Christus) Pater meus quicquam debet, etiamsi ad finem vitæ vsque & extremum mortis articulum in eius præceptis seduli ac strenui fueritis. Causa huius pronuntiati est, quòd quæcunque facimus, ex debito facimus. Deo enim debemus quòdin rerum natura sumus, quòd spiritum vitalem ducimus, quòd mouemur: denique nosipsos & nostra omnia ille sibi optimo iure vendicat, vt pote nòster pater, opifex & dominus. Quid ergo nobis reliquum est, quod pro nostro vendicare, & Deo impendere possimus, vt is nobis debitor fiat? Damnari quidem & æterno exitio addici meremur, nisi præcepta Dei faciamus, quia sic officium debitum ei negamus: vt verò eorundem obseruatione quicquam mereamur impossibile est, eò quòd nihil ex nostro illi damus, quæ nos totos sibi iam obstrictos habet. Quibus adde, quòd neque nostra dicere possumus opera, quæ ex Dei mandato bene & rectè facimus. Ex nobis ipsis enim nihil boni habemus, & (vt Paulus inquit) ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus: sed Deus est, qui in nobis agit tam velle quàm facere. Vnde idem Apostolus dicebat: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Quòd si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Quòd si verò serui inutiles sumus, etiamsi omnia faciamus, quæ nobis in lege præcepta sunt, qui obsecro aut quales dici meremur, quando ne millesimam
units.tr: The second point Christ draws from this parable concerns the merit of our works, and he shows in these words where it ought to be placed: "Does he thank that servant because he did what he was commanded? I think not. So also you, when you have done all that is commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done only what we were bound to do." The question here is whether, by doing what God commands us in the law, we earn anything from him. Christ plainly denies this. A master does not owe thanks to his slave, nor is he thereby bound to him, even if the slave ploughs, feeds the flock, or does any task the master has assigned for the whole day. So too (says Christ) my Father owes you nothing, even if you have been diligent and earnest in obeying his commands to the last moment of your life and to the final hour of death. The reason for this statement is that whatever we do, we do out of obligation. We owe God our very existence, the vital breath we draw, and our power of movement. In short, he rightly claims for himself ourselves and all that we have, as our Father, Maker and Lord. What then is left that we can claim as our own and offer to God, so that he would become our debtor? We deserve to be condemned and handed over to eternal destruction, unless we keep God's commands, for by failing to keep them we deny him the obedience we owe. But that we could earn anything by keeping them is impossible, since we give him nothing of our own, for he already holds us wholly bound to himself. Add to this that we cannot even call our works our own, those good and right deeds we do by God's command. For we have nothing good of ourselves, and (as Paul says) we are not even capable of thinking anything of our own; it is God who works in us both to will and to do. Hence the same Apostle said: "What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" If then we are unprofitable servants even when we do everything the law commands us, who, I beg you, are we to be called, when we do not even perform the thousandth part of what God requires of us?

units.la: Ccc mam quidem partem eorum facimus, quae à nobis Deus requirit? Quem enim hominum dabis, qui vel vnius praecepti perfecta observatione gloriari possit? Nā vt supra diximus, lex spiritualis est, & ita totum hominem Deo vendicat, vt ne cogitare quidem aut cupere fas sit ea, quae in illa prohibentur. Quis verò est, qui cogitationum celerrimos discursus continere, aut subito emicantes cupiditatum scintillas reprimere possit? Et vt minutiora haec omittam (quae tamen & ipsa mortem merentur) quis obsecro se nullo dicto aut facto vnquam peccauisse, dicere audet? Certè qui hoc dixerit, eo ipso peccatum committet aeterno inferorum cruciatu luendum. Ioannes enim Apostolus ait: Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Et quasi parum dixisset, addit: Si dixerimus nos non peccasse, mendacem facimus eum, & sermo eius non est in nobis. Mentiuntur ergo, qui se peccasse aut peccati reatu teneri negant. At mendacij pater est diabolus, cuius illi ipsi iam filij sunt. Est hoc graue admodum, sed multo gravius, imò inexpiabile scelus est, quòd idem Deum mendacij arguunt, dum illud negare audent, quod ille per omnes Scripturas testatur. Quid verò verbis opus est? Nisi plus quàm diabolica superbia nos totos dementauerit, omnes cum Iacobo Apostolo fateri cogemur: In multis labimur omnes. Ergo si nos spectes, non inutiles modò serui, sed noxij etiam, sed perfidi, sed domus Dei turbatores, & indegni sumus, quorum opera Deus vel in minimis & abiectissimis rebus vtatur. Teneamus itaq; huius loci capita diligenter. Primum est, nihil boni absque fide fieri, hanc autem Dei donum esse, apud quem pro illa consequenda precibus assiduis intentos esse conuenit. Alterum, non habere nos quo apud Deum gloriemur, etiamsi omnia praestemus, quae is in lege sua nobis praescribit. Ex quo tertium sequitur, morte aeterna omnes homines dignos esse, cùm nemo inueniatur, qui non Dei leges infinitis delictis violet. Quid ergo nobis restat, si quidem seruari volumus, quàm vt nostris viribus & meritis diffisi, ad thronum gratiae recurramus, & constanti fide amplexemur Iesum Christum, qui nobis à Deo Patre factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio et redemptio. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Not even a thousandth part of what God requires from us. For who among men can you name who could boast of the perfect observance of even one commandment? As we said above, the law is spiritual, and it claims the whole man for God, so that it is not even lawful to think or desire those things which it forbids. And who is there who can restrain the swift rush of thoughts, or suppress the sudden sparks of desire as they flash up? And, to pass over smaller matters (which nonetheless also deserve death), who, I ask, dares to say that he has never sinned in word or deed? Certainly whoever says this commits a sin by that very saying, a sin to be paid for with eternal torment in hell. For the Apostle John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." And as if he had not said enough, he adds: "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us." Those, then, who deny that they have sinned or are held guilty of sin are liars. But the father of lies is the devil, whose children they already are. This is a very grave matter, but far graver, indeed an unforgivable crime, is that they also charge God himself with lying, while they dare to deny what he attests through all the Scriptures. But why need I use many words? Unless a more than devilish pride has driven us all out of our minds, we shall all be forced to confess with the Apostle James: "In many things we all stumble." So if you look at us, we are not only unprofitable servants but also harmful, faithless, disturbers of the house of God, and unworthy that God should use our work even in the smallest and most despised matters. Let us therefore hold carefully to the main heads of this passage. First, nothing good is done without faith, and this faith is God's gift, from whom it is fitting that we seek it with constant prayer. Second, we have nothing in which we may glory before God, even if we perform all that he prescribes to us in his law. From this follows a third point: all men deserve eternal death, since no one is found who does not violate God's laws with countless offences. What then remains for us, if we wish to be saved, but to distrust our own strength and merits, to run to the throne of grace, and to embrace with steadfast faith Jesus Christ, who has been made for us by God the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXII.
units.tr: HOMILY 162.

units.la: Et factum est inter eundum Hierosolymam, ipse transibat per mediā Samariam et Galilaeam. Et cùm ingrederetur in quendam vicum, occurrerunt ei decem viri leprosi, qui steterunt procul, & extulerunt vocem dicentes: Iesu magister miserere nostri. Et cùm eos vidisset, dixit eis. Profecti ostendite vos sacerdotibus. Et factum est, vt inter eundum purgati sint. Vnus autem ex ipsis, vt vidit se sanatum esse, reuertit glorificans Deum voce magna. Et procidit in faciem ad pedes eius, gratias ei agens: erat autem ille Samaritanus. Respondens autem Iesus dixit: Nonne decem illi purgati sunt? nouem autem illi vbi sunt? Non sunt reperti qui redierint vt tribuerent gloriam Deo, nisi alienigena iste. Et dixit ei: Surge, & abi: Fides tua te seruauit.
units.tr: And it came to pass, as they went to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered into a certain village, there met him ten men that were lepers, who stood afar off: and they lifted up their voices, and said, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. And when he saw them, he said unto them, Go shew yourselves unto the priests. And it came to pass, that as they went, they were cleansed. And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, and fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan. And Jesus answering said, Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? There are not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger. And he said unto him, Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole.

units.la: Audiuimus in proximo Sermone Iesum Christum pulchrè & graviter de fide & eius virtute atq; operibus siue effectis differentem. Docuit autem per illam ea confici, quae omnes hominis vires superant, eo quòd corruptae naturae medetur, & omnem carnis sensum atque intellectum vnà cum affectibus & desiderijs nostris obedientiae Dei & verbi eius subijcit. Ne quem verò praeclara illa & eximia fidei opera insolentiorem facerent, neue quis loco fidei inane persuasionem animo concuperet, parabolam subiecit, quà omnium eorum officia complectitur, qui per fidem Dei serui facti sunt, simulq; docet nullam eos quoq; gloriandi occasionem habere, qui illa fidelissimè faciunt. Quo enim merito superbire possunt, qui cum serui sint, ex debito omnia faciunt? Imò cùm nos ex nobismetipsis Deo seruitium nullum praestare possimus, ei potius nos gratias agere debemus, quòd nos seruorum loco habere dignatur. Est doctrina haec non tam vtilis quàm necessaria coguicu, ideoque in Scripturis passim repetitur, & eandem Christus in praesenti facto miraculoso illustrat atque confirmat. Historiam
units.tr: We heard in the previous sermon how Jesus Christ spoke finely and weightily about faith, its power and its works or effects. He taught that by faith those things are accomplished which surpass all human strength, because faith heals our corrupted nature and subjects every sense and understanding of the flesh, together with our affections and desires, to the obedience of God and his word. Lest those remarkable and outstanding works of faith should make anyone more arrogant, or lest anyone should covet an empty persuasion in place of faith, he added a parable, in which he embraces the duties of all those who have been made servants of God through faith, and at the same time teaches that those who perform these duties most faithfully have no occasion to boast. For with what merit can they be proud, who, though they are servants, do everything out of duty? Indeed, since we can render God no service from ourselves, we ought rather to give him thanks that he deigns to count us in the place of servants. This teaching is not so much useful as necessary to know, and therefore it is repeated everywhere in the Scriptures; and Christ, in the present miraculous deed, illustrates and confirms the same. The history

units.la: Doctrinam de fide confirmat miraculo. Historiam vero eius sic describit Lucas, vt eius multiplex vsus nobis esse possit. Nam impura & infelix hominum conditio in decem leprosis adumbratur. Deinde medicus noster ostenditur Christus, qui ad se venientes purgat & seruat. Samaritani autem exemplo purgati docentur, quid nam ipsi Christo debeant: in reliquis vero nouem tam Iudæis quàm alijs omnibus sua ingratitudo exprobratur, qui Christi beneficium non agnoscunt, et libertate sua ad carnis otium fouendum abutuntur. Quæ omnia vt rectius intelligamus, singulas historiæ partes ex ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: He confirms the doctrine of faith by a miracle. Luke describes the history in such a way that it can serve us in many ways. For the impure and wretched condition of mankind is shadowed forth in the ten lepers. Then Christ is shown to be our physician, who cleanses and saves those who come to him. The Samaritan, cleansed, teaches us what we owe to Christ himself; but in the other nine, their ingratitude is rebuked, both that of the Jews and that of all others, who do not acknowledge Christ's benefit and abuse their freedom to indulge the leisure of the flesh. So that we may understand all these things more rightly, let us look at the individual parts of the history in order.

units.la: Primùm de tempore & loco Euangelista nos admonet, docens, quando & vbi hoc miraculum Christus fecerit: Nimirum quando per mediam Samariam ex Galilæa Hierosolymam proficiscebatur, vt illic seipsum pro mundi vita traderet. Est hoc magnum bonitatis argumentum, quam neque imminens dirae mortis periculum, neque præbenota hominum ingratitudo vincere potuit, quò minus promiscuè omnibus benefaceret, & à Patre sibi creditam functionem in finem vsque constanter obiret. Suo igitur exemplo confirmat, quod proximæ parabolæ primum caput est, nos videlicet totum diem, id est, omnem vitam ad extremum vsq; mortis articulum in Dei vocatione laborare & huic debitum obsequium præstare debere. Ad fidei vero confirmationem facit, quòd salutem omnibus subinde offert, & tantumnon inter indignissimos quaerit, quibus benefaciat. Indigni enim illo erant, tam Iudæi quàm Samaritani, vt alibi demonstrauimus.
units.tr: First, the Evangelist reminds us of the time and place, teaching us when and where Christ performed this miracle: namely, when he was travelling from Galilee to Jerusalem through the midst of Samaria, so as there to give himself up for the life of the world. This is a great proof of his goodness, which neither the imminent danger of a dreadful death nor the well-known ingratitude of men could overcome, so that he would not do good to all alike, and would constantly carry out to the end the office entrusted to him by the Father. By his example, therefore, he confirms what is the first point of the parable just before, namely that we ought to labour all the day, that is, through all of life up to the final moment of death, in the calling of God, and render this due obedience to him. It also serves to confirm faith that he offers salvation to all in turn, and seeks out, almost without distinction, those on whom he may do good. For both the Jews and the Samaritans were unworthy of him, as we have shown elsewhere.

units.la: Secundò eos producit Lucas, in quibus miraculum hoc fuit æditum. Fuerunt autem decem viri leprosi, qui vicum quendam ingressuro occurrerunt. Atqui lepram inter peccati pœnas scriptura numerat, quas Deus iratus hominibus infligit. Moses enim legis transgressoribus dicit: Percutiet te Dominus vlcere Ægyptiaco, ficu, scabie fluida & scabie sicca, ita vt sanari non possis. Et singularia huius plagæ exempla extant in Maria sorore Mosis, quæ quòd contra hunc contumacius loqueretur, lepra à Domino percussa est: in Giezi item Helisæi famulo & Vzia rege, quorum hic propter arrogantem muneris sacerdotalis vsurpationem, ille verò quòd donis heri sui spiritualibus ad quæstum priuatum abuti vellet, leprosus factus est. Veruntamen in lepra naturæ etiam nostræ corruptionem adumbrari, & in leprosis nos omnes de miserabili & infelici generis humani conditione admoneri, alibi diximus. Illa enim ex sanguine adusto & corrupto nascitur, & ideo per totum corpus serpendo membra depascitur, & faciem aspectu fœdam totumq; homine anhelitu grauem reddit, quæ causa est, quòd qui illa laborant, ab hominum consortijs & consuetudine exclusi seorsim vitam degunt. Atqui eadem peccati vis est, eademq; omnium conditio, quibus illud imperat. Nam ex primis parentibus quasi hæreditario iure in nos propagatum medullis & cordi nostro inhæret, & ideo mox omnes hominis facultates inficit, vt intellectus non percipiat ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, voluntas autem à diuinis & cœlestibus abhorreat, totus deniq; homo cupiditatibus pessimis inflammatus æstuet, & cogitationibus partim iniustis partim fœdis diffluat. Itaq; per totam hominis vitam malum hoc diffunditur, & in omnibus actionibus, quantumuis in speciem honestis, eius indicia apparent, quæ vt Dei oculos offendunt, ita alijs quoq; peccandi causam præbent, & alij alios suo exemplo inficiunt. Effectus autem omnium est, quòd nisi Deus gratuita misericordia nobis succurrat, ab eius conspectu & Ecclesia exclusi æternum perimus. De istis ergo nos admoneri cogitemus, quoties leprosi occurrunt. Sunt enim commune speculum, in quo nos Deus communem humanæ naturæ infelicitatem contemplari vult, vt eò studiosius salutis nostræ curam suscipiamus.
units.tr: Second, Luke brings forward the persons upon whom this miracle was performed. There were ten lepers, who met him as he was about to enter a certain village. Now Scripture counts leprosy among the punishments of sin, which God, in anger, inflicts upon men. For Moses says to the transgressors of the law: The Lord will smite you with the botch of Egypt, with the emerods, with the scab and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed. And there are notable examples of this plague: in Miriam, the sister of Moses, who, because she spoke more stubbornly against him, was struck with leprosy by the Lord; likewise in Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, and in King Uzziah, of whom the one became a leper because of his arrogant usurpation of the priestly office, and the other because he wished to abuse the spiritual gifts of his master for private gain. Yet we have elsewhere said that in leprosy the corruption of our own nature is also shadowed forth, and that in lepers we are all reminded of the wretched and unhappy condition of the human race. For leprosy arises from blood that is burnt and corrupted, and therefore, creeping through the whole body, it eats away the limbs, makes the face loathsome to look upon and the whole man foul in breath; for this reason those who suffer from it live apart, shut out from the company and society of men. Yet this is the same force of sin, and the same condition of all those over whom it rules. For it has been propagated to us from our first parents, as if by hereditary right; it clings to our marrow and our heart, and therefore soon infects all the faculties of man: so that the understanding does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, the will shrinks from things divine and heavenly, and finally the whole man, inflamed with the worst desires, seethes and pours forth thoughts partly unjust and partly foul. Thus this evil spreads through the whole of human life, and its signs appear in all actions, however honourable they may seem in appearance; and these signs, as they offend the eyes of God, so also provide others with a cause for sinning, and one infects another by his example. The result for all is that, unless God succours us by his free mercy, we perish eternally, shut out from his sight and from the Church. Let us therefore think of these things and be reminded of them whenever lepers come before us. For they are a common mirror, in which God wishes us to contemplate the common unhappiness of human nature, so that we may take up the care of our salvation all the more zealously.

units.la: Merentur autem diligentiorem consideratione decem isti, quia suo exemplo simul docent quid eos facere oporteat, qui peccati noxa liberari et Ecclesiæ Dei restitui cupiunt. Nam etsi nouem ex illis postea ingratitudine peccent, principia tamen fidei egregia habuerunt, quæ minimè contemni debent, ideo quòd non in finem vsque perseuerarunt. Id enim ipsorum leuitati tribuendum est, non fidei, quæ veris & proprijs indicijs sese exeruit: ideoq; quid fecerint probè est obseruandum. Primum est, quòd morbum suum & eius vim rectè agnouerunt: patet hoc exeo, quòd salutem tam sedulò & anxiè quæsiuerunt. Est hic primus ad salutem gradus. Vt enim qui morbum non agnoscunt, sed dissimulant, ijdem neq; medicum neq; remedium vllum admittunt: ita quoad nos peccatores esse non intelligimus, imò tales nos esse dissimulamus, vel etiā aperte negamus, salutis studium in nobis locum habere non potest. Quia verò vitium illud nobis commune est, vt (quod olim primi parentes fecerunt) peri ʒomata quæramus, quibus turpitudo nostra tegatur: ideò legis speculum inuitis Deus obijcit, vt in illo nosipsos contemplemur, & peccatorum sensu coacti de salute nostra serio cogitemus. Deinde ad solum Christum decem illi contendunt, de cuius bonitate, virtute & miraculis haud dubie multa audiuerant. Est hoc euidens fidei argumentum, quam ex auditu illo conceperunt. Nisi enim bonitatis & virtutis Christi fiducia animos illorum confirmauisset, nunquam apud illum quaesituri fuissent, quod nulla hominum industria dari posse sciebant. Hic ergo nobis quoque sufficiat, neque de eius vel potentia vel beneficia erga nos voluntate dubitemus, cum dilectus ille sit Dei Filius, cui omnis potestas in coelo & in terra data est, & qui vt nos Patri suo reconciliaret in mundum venit, atque salutis nostrae causa inopiam, labores omnis generis & mortem infamem sustinuit. Et cum ista solus ille pro nobis fecerit, vehementer errant, qui salute alibi quaerunt. Tertio leprosi illi procul stetisse dicuntur, & in altum sublata voce clamauisse: Iesu magister miserere nostri. Procul steterunt, ne quid in Dei legem peccarent, quia expresse cautum erat, vt leprosi non solum separarentur, verumetiam morbum suum habitu & voce profiterentur, si quando in publicum prodibant, vt minus esset ab illis periculi. Ita enim apud Mosem Deus loquitur: Leprosus in quo fuerit macula, huius vestimenta lacera sint, & caput eius nudum, mentum vero super tegat & clamet, Immundus immundus. Huius ergo memores non temere aut impudenter se in Christi conspectum & confertissimam illam hominum turbam ingerunt, quae ipsum comitabatur. Ita vero non obscure ostendunt se nequaquam ex eorum numero esse, quos calamitas impudentes facit, & qui suos morbos quibusuis affricare cupiunt, vt plures suae miseriae socios habeant. Pulchre autem in his declaratur fidei ingenium. Est haec certa & constans misericordiae Dei fiducia per Christum. Firmiter ergo credit, illum nobis propitium fore: attamen non procax est aut impudens, sed modesta & humilis. Nec enim propriae infirmitatis & imperfectionis immemores facit: sed potius huius agnitionem in nobis auget, quae humilitatis extremae causa est. Exemplum in Dauide habemus, qui cum multitudinem miserationum sibi apud Deum repositam esse firmiter crederet, clamat tamen: Transgressiones meas agnosco, & peccatum meum assidue mihi obuersatur. Item, En ego in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Et huius generis multa in Scripturis occurrunt. Non impedit autem ista animorum consternatio inuocationem diuinae misericordiae. Quia enim fides de ea dubitare non potest, excitat humiliatos illos & contritos animos, vt clament: Iesu magister miserere nostri: Domine propitius esto mihi peccatori. Miserere mei Deus secundum misericordiam tuam, secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum dele peccata mea. Ex quibus apparet, a fide adhuc nimium alienos esse, quos propriae dignitatis aut iustitiae fiducia inflat, & quibus ridiculum videtur ad solius misericordiae Dei thronum confugere, nulla proprij meriti aut nostrarum satisfactionum mentione facta.
units.tr: Those ten, however, deserve closer consideration, because by their example they teach at the same time what those ought to do who desire to be freed from the harm of sin and restored to the Church of God. For although nine of them afterwards sinned through ingratitude, they nevertheless had excellent beginnings of faith, which must not be despised, because they did not persevere to the end. This must be attributed to their fickleness, not to faith, which showed itself by true and genuine signs; therefore we must carefully observe what they did. First, they rightly recognised their disease and its power: this is clear from the fact that they sought salvation so earnestly and anxiously. This is the first step towards salvation. For just as those who do not recognise a disease, but conceal it, admit neither a physician nor any remedy, so, as long as we do not understand that we are sinners, or rather pretend that we are not such, or even openly deny it, there can be no place in us for a zeal for salvation. But because that vice is common to us all, that we seek (as our first parents once did) coverings of fig leaves with which to hide our shame, God therefore sets before us, against our will, the mirror of the law, so that we may behold ourselves in it, and, compelled by the sense of sin, think seriously about our salvation. Next, those ten strive towards Christ alone, of whose goodness, power and miracles they had doubtless heard much. This is a clear evidence of the faith they conceived from that hearing. For unless confidence in the goodness and power of Christ had strengthened their minds, they would never have sought help from him, since they knew that no human effort could provide it. Let it therefore be enough for us also, not to doubt either his power or his will to do us good, since he is that beloved Son of God, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, and who came into the world to reconcile us to his Father, and for our salvation endured poverty, labours of every kind and an infamous death. And since he alone has done these things for us, those greatly err who seek salvation elsewhere. Third, those lepers are said to have stood afar off, and to have cried out with a raised voice: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. They stood afar off so that they would not sin against the law of God, for it was expressly provided that lepers should not only be separated, but also, whenever they came out in public, should declare their disease by their dress and by their voice, so that there would be less danger from them. For thus God speaks through Moses: The leper in whom the plague is, his clothes shall be rent, and his head bare, and he shall put a covering upon his upper lip, and shall cry, Unclean, unclean. Mindful of this, they do not rashly or shamelessly thrust themselves into the sight of Christ and into that very dense crowd of men that accompanied him. And in this way they show clearly that they are by no means of the number of those whom calamity makes shameless, and who wish to rub their diseases against anyone at all, so that they may have more companions in their misery. Now in these things the nature of faith is admirably displayed. It is a certain and steadfast confidence in the mercy of God through Christ. Therefore it firmly believes that he will be gracious to us; yet it is not forward or shameless, but modest and humble. For it does not make us forgetful of our own weakness and imperfection; rather, it increases our recognition of these, which is the cause of the deepest humility. We have an example in David, who, though he firmly believed that a multitude of mercies was laid up for him with God, nevertheless cries out: I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Likewise: Behold, I was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Many things of this kind occur in the Scriptures. Yet this consternation of spirit does not hinder the calling upon God's mercy. For since faith cannot doubt that mercy, it rouses those humbled and contrite hearts to cry out: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us; Lord, be merciful to me a sinner; Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy mercy: according to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. From these things it appears that those are still far removed from faith, who are puffed up with confidence in their own dignity or righteousness, and to whom it seems ridiculous to flee to the throne of the mercy of God alone, with no mention of any merit of their own or of our satisfactions.

units.la: Sed ad Christum accedamus, qui istorum fidem miraculo publico comprobauit. Nam mox ad sacerdotes abire iubet, vt se illis ostendant. Ita vero purgationis aut sanitatis spem illis facit, vel potius illam aperte pollicetur. Nam vt alibi diximus, sacerdotibus inspectio leprosorum diuinitus mandata erat, vt penes illos esset lepra infectos excludere, mundos item aut purgatos in hominum contuberniu admittere. Instituti huius causa fuit, quod qui corporis immunditia laborabat, a sacrorum & tabernaculi communione excludebantur. Quia ergo ista exclusio proprie ad sacerdotes pertinebat, horum etiam fuit de lepra & eius purgatione iudicare. Voluit aut Christus abs se mundatos ad sacerdotes remittere, primu ne quis leges publicas ab ipso turbari diceret: deinde vt gratitudinis erga Deum admoneret eos, qui tantu beneficiu acceperat, (iubebantur enim ijdem sacrificia gratulatoria Deo offerre) tertio, vt sacerdotes proprio testimonio couincerentur, si ipsum Messiam aut humani generis seruatorem esse negarent. Qua fronte enim id negare poterant, qui prius tam multos eius virtute a lepra mundatos esse, publice testati fuerant? Nihil ergo facit locus iste pro aduersarijs nostris, qui confessione auriculare ex eo eliciut. Christus enim no leprosos Sacerdotibus transmisit, vt horum ministerio purgarentur: sed iam purgatos, propter ciuile ordinem, illorum testimonio ciuitatibus et hominum consortio restitui voluit. Et si omnino hic aliquis Allegoriae locus est, no alia hinc elici potest, quam quod abs se institutum Ecclesiae suae ministerium confirmat. Quia enim fidem hominum non a signis, quae interdum ab impostoribus quoq; fiunt, pendere oportet, sed eandem verbo Dei confirmari atque gubernari necesse est, non possunt neque debent Ecclesiae ministerium contemnere, qui fidei fructum aliquem iam perceperunt. Confutatur ergo hic eorum contumacia, qui cum fide in Christum, & propter illam peccatorum quoque remissione & salute certa glorientur, coetus tamen sacros vnà cum concionibus verbi Dei & omnibus alijs Ecclesiæ exercitijs fastidiunt.
units.tr: But let us come to Christ, who confirmed the faith of these men by a public miracle. For at once he orders them to go to the priests, so that they may show themselves to them. In this way he gives them hope of cleansing and health, or rather openly promises it. For, as we have said elsewhere, the inspection of lepers had been divinely committed to the priests, so that it was in their power to exclude the infected and likewise to admit the clean or cleansed into fellowship with men. The reason for this institution was that those who suffered from bodily uncleanness were excluded from communion in holy things and in the tabernacle. Since this exclusion pertained properly to the priests, it was also their task to judge about leprosy and its cleansing. Christ wished to send the cleansed men back to the priests: first, so that no one could say that he had disturbed the public laws; second, to remind those who had received so great a benefit of their gratitude to God (for they were commanded to offer thank-offerings to God); third, so that the priests might be convicted by their own testimony, if they denied that he was the Messiah or the saviour of the human race. For with what face could they deny it, who had earlier publicly testified that so many had been cleansed from leprosy by his power? Nothing in this passage therefore supports our opponents, who draw auricular confession from it. For Christ did not send the lepers to the priests so that they might be cleansed by their ministry; rather, having already been cleansed, they were to be restored to the cities and to human society, by the priests' testimony, on account of civil order. And if there is any allegorical sense here at all, nothing else can be drawn from it than that it confirms the ministry of the Church instituted by him. For since the faith of men must not depend on signs, which are sometimes done even by impostors, but must be confirmed and governed by the Word of God, those who have already perceived some fruit of faith can neither despise nor ought they to despise the ministry of the Church. Here, then, is refuted the obstinacy of those who glory in faith in Christ and in the certain salvation and forgiveness of sins that comes through it, yet scorn the sacred assemblies, together with the sermons of the Word of God and all the other exercises of the Church.

units.la: Cæterùm quia de his sæpe aliâs dictum est, ad leprosos istos reuertamur, qui accepto Christi mandato mox abierunt, vt sese sacerdotibus ostenderent. Est hoc nouum fidei non vulgaris argumentum. Nec enim adhuc purgati erant, sed facies & corpora ipsorum adhuc scabies fœda occupabat. Abeunt tamen, sic iubente Christo, vt sese pro purgatis & mundis ostendant apud eos, quorum hostiles in illum animos non poterant ignorare. Unde vero hoc? Nimirum quod ex verbis eius spem salutis certam concepissent, neq; dubitarent se plenè purgatos fore, priusquam in Sacerdotum conspectum venirent. Hinc ergo obedientia illa secuta est, qua omnes rationes contempserunt, quas caro obijcere poterat, quò minus temere obediendo seipsos omnium ludibrio exponerent. Nec defuit successus tantæ fidei. Nam inter eundum purgati sunt. Excitemur ergo huius exempli consideratione, vt neque de promissionibus Dei, neq; mandatis eius dubitemus. Qui enim veritas ipsa est, promittendo neminem ludificat aut fallit. Et cùm idem nobis optimè consultum velit, adhæc possit etiam præstare, quæcunque pollicetur, non est periculum, ne quis ludibrium fiat, qui se totum ei subiecerit per fidei obedientiam.
units.tr: But since these things have often been said elsewhere, let us return to those lepers, who, having received Christ's command, at once went away to show themselves to the priests. This is a new and no ordinary argument of faith. For they were not yet cleansed; their faces and bodies were still covered with foul scabs. Yet, at Christ's bidding, they go away to present themselves as clean and cleansed before men whose hostile minds towards him they could not fail to know. Whence did this come? Surely from the fact that they had conceived a certain hope of salvation from his words, and did not doubt that they would be fully cleansed before they came into the sight of the priests. Hence came that obedience, by which they disregarded all the objections that the flesh could raise, lest by obeying rashly they should expose themselves to the mockery of all. Nor did such faith lack its outcome. For on the way they were cleansed. Let us therefore be stirred by the consideration of this example, so that we doubt neither the promises of God nor his commands. For he who is truth itself deceives and mocks no one by promising. And since he also wishes the best for us and is able to perform whatever he promises, there is no danger that anyone who has submitted himself wholly to him through obedient faith will become a laughing-stock.

units.la: In primis autem hoc loco miraculorum omnium finem & vsum obseruare oportet. Sunt illa doctrinæ Christi Iesu testimonia, neque aliam ob causam facta sunt, quàm vt reipsa testaretur, se verè eum esse, quem se esse docebat. Ideo apud Ioannem Iudæis dixit: Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater, vt ea perficerem, ipsa (inquam) opera quæ ego facio, testantur de me, quòd Pater misit me. Et alibi: Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi: Sin verò facio, etiamsi mihi non credatis, operibus credite: vt cognoscatis & credatis, quòd Pater in me est, & ego in eo. Nec tamen nuda sunt doctrinæ testimonia Christi miracula, sed exempla quoq; & sigilla sunt promissionum Euangelij, quibus fidem nostram debemus confirmare, ne dubitemus, illum eadè bonitate, qua olim erga se inuocantes vsus est, nobis quoq; opem laturum esse, si illum fide non fucata petamus. Itaque vt morbi omnis generis, inopia, fames, bella, seditiones, pestilentia, mors, & quæcunque aliæ afflictiones nos in huius vitæ palæstra exercent, nos de peccato, naturæ nostræ vitiositate & ira Dei admonent: ita quoties Iesum Christum morbos miraculosè depulisse, aut ex alijs periculis suos seruauisse audimus, illum nobis à Deo datum aut missum esse credamus, vt peccato abolito mortis imperium frangeret, & nos patri reconciliaret. Et prodest miraculosas morborum mirabilium sanationes, quæ olim ab illo factæ sunt, diligentius inspicere, vt ex illis fiduciam certam concipiamus, Christum tam nobis priuatim quàm toti Ecclesiæ salutem afferre posse, quando res in extremas angustias deuenerunt, vt nulla in humanis spes salutis sit reliqua.
units.tr: In the first place, however, in this place we must observe the end and use of all miracles. They are testimonies of the teaching of Jesus Christ, and they were done for no other reason than to show by deed that he is truly the one he taught himself to be. Therefore he said to the Jews in John: The works which the Father has given me to accomplish, these very works (I say) which I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. And elsewhere: If I do not the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works: that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him. Yet the miracles of Christ are not bare testimonies of his teaching; they are also examples and seals of the promises of the Gospel, by which we ought to confirm our faith, lest we doubt that he will bring help to us also with the same goodness with which he formerly dealt with those who called upon him, if we ask him with unfeigned faith. Therefore, just as diseases of every kind, want, hunger, wars, seditions, pestilence, death, and whatever other afflictions exercise us in the arena of this life, remind us of sin, the corruption of our nature and the wrath of God, so, whenever we hear that Jesus Christ drove out diseases by miracle, or saved his own from other dangers, let us believe that he has been given or sent to us by God, so that, sin being abolished, he might break the power of death and reconcile us to the Father. It is also profitable to examine more carefully the miraculous healings of marvellous diseases that he once performed, so that from them we may conceive a sure confidence that Christ can bring salvation to us privately, and to the whole Church, when affairs have come to the utmost straits and no human hope of salvation remains.

units.la: Sed vt pergamus in historia, quid leprosi isti fecerunt, quando inter eundum purgati sunt? Nouem illi, qui omnes ex Iudæorum gente erant, ad Sacerdotes pergunt, & Christi tantum non obliti pro tanto beneficio gratias ei agunt nullas.
