Vnus solus, quem Samaritanum fuisse Lucas scribit, vt primùm se sanatum vidit, mox ex itinere reuersus clara voce Deum glorificat, & ad Christi pedes procidens gratias illi agit quàm potest maximas. Ita verò Iudæorum ingratitudo adumbratur, fore nimirum, vt quàmuis salutem ipsis quoq; Dei Filius offerat, pauci tamen futuri sint, qui eius beneficium agnoscant, sed plerosque Sacerdotio & cultui Mosaico addictos fore, vt propriæ iustitiæ fiducia gratiam Dei & Christi meritum obscurent. Quod quanta pertinacia fecerint, Actorum liber & Apostolorum scripta prolixè indicant. Fuit autem hæc repudij illorum causa, vt abrupto fœdere cum Abrahamo initi vinculo, Deus gratiam suam ad gentes transtulerit, ipsi verò, cum Christo, quem recipere dedignati sunt, templum quoque & sacerdotium & totum illum cultum amiserint, quem cum fortunarum omnium, imò corporum quoq; & animarum iactura non minus impiè quàm pertinaciter defendere satagerunt.
units.tr: But to go on with the narrative: what did those lepers do when they were cleansed on the way? Nine of them, who were all of the Jewish nation, went on to the priests, and, not even mindful of Christ, they gave him no thanks for so great a benefit. Only one, whom Luke writes was a Samaritan, as soon as he saw himself healed, returned from the journey at once, glorified God with a loud voice, and, falling at Christ's feet, gave him thanks as warmly as he could. Thus the ingratitude of the Jews is foreshadowed: that, although the Son of God offers salvation to them too, few will nevertheless be found who acknowledge his benefit, and that most will be devoted to the priesthood and the Mosaic worship, so that through confidence in their own righteousness they obscure the grace of God and the merit of Christ. How stubbornly they did this the Book of Acts and the writings of the apostles set out at length. The reason for their rejection was that, the covenant made with Abraham having been broken, God transferred his grace to the Gentiles; but they themselves, having refused to receive Christ, lost the temple, the priesthood and the whole of that worship, which they strove to defend no less impiously than stubbornly, at the cost of all their possessions, indeed also of their bodies and souls.

units.la: Exhibetur præterea hic generale exemplum cæcitatis & infirmitatis nostræ, qua fit, vt pauci se Deo pro acceptis beneficijs gratos præbeant, pleriq; autem postquam ex periculis & afflictionibus liberati sunt, Dei obliuiscantur, & relabantur in ea ipsa scelera, quæ prius ipsis afflictionum causa fuerunt. Vt enim morborum diuturnitas, inopia, fames, oppressio & extrema quæque pericula nos excitant, vt Dei opem imploremus, ei obedientiam & omnia nostra voueamus: ita prosperior vale tudo, diuitiæ, saturitas, libertas et felix consiliorum nostrorum successus, Dei immemores, adhæc securos & ingratos reddunt, deniq; causa sunt, vt in priora scelera relabamur, vel etiam quotidie proficiamus in peius. Exemplum huius vitij non semel Israelitæ dederunt, qui quoties in deserto graues puniti sunt, Dei opem implorare, peccata confiteri, Mosi supplices fieri solebât, liberati autem, semper ad contumaciam & murmura redierunt. Quod ipsum illos postea quoq; Iudicum temporibus factitauisse constat. Faciunt idem multi priuatim. Saul certè toties liberatus a Deo, semper relapsus est, & peccata accumulauit. Et vt ad vulgaria descendamus, quotus quisq; est, qui post messem & vindemiam factam, aut ex morbo restitutus ad Deum reuertatur, et huic ex animo gratias agat? Est autem vitium hoc etiam hominum iudicio detestabile, & ferè vindictæ desiderio accenduntur, qui ab ingratis se toties falli sentiunt. Quanto autem magis Deum tales abominari putabimus, qui præter gratiarum actionem nihil à nobis pro maximis beneficijs requirit?
units.tr: Moreover, a general example of our blindness and weakness is set forth here, by which it comes about that few show themselves grateful to God for benefits received, while most, once freed from dangers and afflictions, forget God and slip back into those very sins which were earlier the cause of their afflictions. For just as the long duration of disease, want, hunger, oppression and every extreme danger stir us up to implore God's help and to vow obedience and all that we have to him, so a more prosperous health, riches, plenty, freedom and the happy success of our plans make us forgetful of God, and moreover secure and ungrateful, and finally are the cause of our relapsing into former sins, or even of our growing worse every day. The Israelites gave an example of this fault more than once: whenever they were severely punished in the desert, they used to implore God's help, confess their sins, and become suppliants to Moses; but once freed, they always returned to stubbornness and murmuring. It is agreed that they did the same thing afterwards, in the times of the Judges. Many men do the same in private. Saul, certainly, though so often delivered by God, always relapsed and piled up sins. And to come down to common things: how few are there who, after the harvest and vintage are gathered in, or after they have recovered from sickness, turn back to God and give him thanks from the heart? Yet this fault is detestable even by human judgment, and men are almost inflamed with a desire for revenge when they feel that they have been so often deceived by the ungrateful. How much more, then, shall we think that God abominates those who, beyond the thanksgiving, require nothing from us for the greatest benefits?

units.la: Christus certè, etsi mansuetudine & bonitate omnes vincat, quotquot vnquam in terris visi sunt, in præsenti tamen non dissimulat sibi nouem illorum ingratitudinem quàm maximè displicere. Nam non sine acerba illius exprobratione ait: Nonne decem illi purgati sunt? nouem autem illi vbi sunt? Non sunt reperti qui redierint, vt tribuerent gloriam Deo, nisi alienigena iste. Quæ verba sic ab illo pronuntiantur, vt tam nouem illis quàm toti Iudæorum genti ingratitudinem exprobret, & quas merebantur pœnas denuntiet. Alienigenam enim nominat, vt in mentem ipsis reuocet singularem Dei gratiam, qui ipsorum patres, præteritis omnibus alijs gentibus, sibi delegerat, vt ex illis progenitum populum sibi peculium faceret, et inter illos constitueret regnum illud sacerdotale, ex quo totius mundi salus dependebat. Et vt nouem istorum ingratitudo clarius & non sine gentis totius ignominia eluxit in Samaritani exemplo: ita non multò post illustrior, imò execrabilior facta est Iudæorum pertinacia & improbitas, qui fide & pietate à gentibus prophanis & à repub. Israelis hucusque exclusis se vinci passi sunt.
units.tr: Christ, certainly, though he surpasses in gentleness and goodness all who have ever been seen on earth, does not conceal in the present passage that the ingratitude of those nine displeases him most of all. For he says, not without bitter reproach: "Were not ten made clean? But where are the nine? Have none been found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?" These words are uttered by him in such a way that he reproaches the nine, and the whole Jewish nation with them, for ingratitude, and declares the punishments they deserved. For he names him a foreigner in order to recall to their minds the singular grace of God, who, passing over all the other nations, had chosen their fathers for himself, so that from them he might make a people for his own possession, and among them establish that kingly priesthood from which the salvation of the whole world depended. And just as the ingratitude of those nine shone out more clearly, and not without disgrace to the whole nation, in the example of the Samaritan, so not long afterwards the stubbornness and wickedness of the Jews became more notable, indeed more detestable, since they allowed themselves to be outdone in faith and piety by profane nations, who had hitherto been excluded from the commonwealth of Israel.

units.la: Porrò addit Christus in præsenti breue dictum, quo causas salutis simul atq; perditionis aperte satis indicat. Nam ad Samaritanū conuersus dicit ei: Surge, & abi: fides tua te seruauit. Surgere iubet, & abire, vt mentem magnitudine beneficij accepti et digna eius æstimatione deiectam erigat atq; confirmet. Rursus verò, vt quod hic factum erat, multorū institutioni seruiret, addit: Fides tua te seruauit. Annon verò (inquis) de alijs nouem idem dici poterat, qui & ipsi crediderunt, & ex lepra seruati sunt? Sed obseruari debet, Christum hic de totius hominis, id est: de corporis simul & animæ salute loqui, & proinde Samaritani huius fidem ab aliorū fide distinguere. Etenim decem illos omnes Christo credidisse supra verè diximus, neq; id aliquis negauerit, qui effectus fidei obseruarit, quibus eam nō obscurè declarauerunt. In eo autem differunt, quòd nouem illorum fides euanuit, vbi se sanitati restitutos esse viderunt, & proinde Christo sibi non adeo in posterum opus fore putarunt: Samaritanus autem cū fide perseuerantiam coniunxit. Vnde apparet, eius fidem non in otiosa virtutis Christi prædicatione aut eiusdem miraculis, sed in Spiritu regenerationis fuisse fundatam, quæ illum mouit, vt acceptū à Christo beneficium digne æstimaret, & sui officij esse intelligeret se totum illi consecrare, & vitam omnem ad eius gloriā celebrandam instituere. Itaq; priores quidem illi corporis salutem temporariam ex fide sua, quæ & ipsa temporaria & euanida fuit, retulerunt: Samaritanus autem corpore simul et anima seruatus est, quia per fidei constantiā in eo perseuerauit, in quo totius hominis salus habetur. Vnde colligitur, externa beneficia Christi sæpe hypocritis quoq; et temporarijs illis conferri, quos ille in sementis parabola προσκαιρὸς vocat, eo quòd pro temporis ratione, & prout ipsis commodum videtur, fidem aut profitentur aut dissimulant: illa ipsa autem ad animarum salutē ijs solis adiumento esse, qui fide viua & constanti ea excipiunt, & se Deo gratos præbent, adeò vt se totos huic sistant viuentem hostiam, neq; vllis rationibus se ab eo patiantur diuelli. Hic ergo nobis totius historiæ vsus esto, vt primò quidem nos natura miseros & infelices, adeoq; in Dei conspectu leprosorum instar esse agnoscamus: deinde nobisipsis & aliorum hominū siue viribus siue meritis diffisi spem salutis omnem in vno Iesu Christo collocemus, & ab eo salutem petamus: postremò, eius beneficio seruati gratias illi agamus, imò ita nos ei mantipemus, vt ipsi soli & viuamus & moriamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ adds in the present passage a short saying by which he plainly enough indicates the causes both of salvation and of ruin. For, turning to the Samaritan, he says to him: "Arise, and go; your faith has saved you." He bids him rise and go, so that he may lift up and strengthen a mind cast down by the greatness of the benefit received and by the fitting estimate of it. Again, so that what was done here might serve the instruction of many, he adds: "Your faith has saved you." But (you will say) could the same not have been said of the other nine, who also believed and were saved from leprosy? It must be observed, however, that Christ here speaks of the salvation of the whole man, that is, of body and soul together, and therefore distinguishes the faith of this Samaritan from the faith of the others. For we have truly said above that all ten believed in Christ, and no one will deny it who has observed the effects of their faith, by which they clearly declared it. But they differ in this: the faith of the nine vanished as soon as they saw themselves restored to health, and so they thought they would no longer have need of Christ; the Samaritan, however, joined perseverance to his faith. Hence it is clear that his faith was founded not on an idle proclamation of Christ's power or on his miracles, but on the Spirit of regeneration, which moved him to estimate rightly the benefit received from Christ, and to understand that it was his duty to consecrate himself wholly to him and to order his whole life to the celebration of his glory. Thus those others indeed obtained from their faith a temporary bodily health, and that faith was itself temporary and fleeting; but the Samaritan was saved in body and soul together, because through the constancy of his faith he persevered in that in which the whole salvation of man is held. Hence it is gathered that Christ's external benefits are often conferred even on hypocrites and on those temporary believers whom he calls "for a time" [πρόσκαιρος] in the parable of the sower, because they either profess or dissemble faith according to the circumstances of the time and as it seems advantageous to them; but that those same benefits serve for the salvation of souls only to those who receive them with a living and steadfast faith, and show themselves pleasing to God, so that they present themselves wholly to him as a living sacrifice and suffer themselves by no means to be torn away from him. Let us therefore make use of the whole of this history here, so that first we may acknowledge that by nature we are wretched and unhappy, and in the sight of God like lepers; then, distrusting ourselves and the strength or merits of other men, we may place all our hope of salvation in the one Jesus Christ and seek salvation from him; lastly, having been saved by his benefit, we may give thanks to him, and indeed so bind ourselves to him that we may live and die for him alone. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA
units.tr: HOMILY

units.la: Interrogatus autē à Pharisæis, quando venturum esset regnum Dei: Respondit eis ac dixit: Non veniet regnū Dei cum obseruatione: neq; dicēt, Ecce hic, aut ecce illic. Ecce enim regnū Dei intra vos est. Dixit autē discipulis: Veniet tempus, cū desiderabitis videre vnū ex diebus Filij hominis, nec videbitis. Et dicēt vobis: Ecce hic, aut Ecce illic: sed ne abite, neq; prosequimini. Nā sicut fulgur coruscās ex vna regione, quæ sub cœlo est, in alteram quæ sub cœlo est, splendet: ita erit & Filius hominis in die suo. Sed prius oportet eum multa pati & reprobari à natione ista.
units.tr: When the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, 'Look, here it is!' or 'There it is!' For behold, the kingdom of God is within you." He said to the disciples: "The time will come when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, 'Look, here it is!' or 'Look, there it is!' Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning, flashing out of one part of the sky, shines to the other part under heaven, so will the Son of man be in his day. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation."

units.la: Quoniam Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, cùm mortis suæ hora immineret, discipulos de omnibus admonere & instituere voluit, quæ ipsis ad cauenda scandala, quæ multa & grauia euentura esse sciebat, cognitu necessaria erant, multa hucusq; de præcipuo Euangelicæ doctrinæ articulo disseruit, de fide nimirum & eius effectis, sub quibus omnia Christiani hominis officia comprehenduntur: Doctrinam verò suam miraculis plurimis confirmauit, inter quæ admodum illustre ac memorabile est, quod in decem Leprosis æditū fuisse nuper audiuimus. Cæterum præcipua salutis remora apud meliores quoque tunc temporis erat, quòd Regni Dei conditionem & eius inter homines instaurandi rationem plerique Iudæorum ignorabant, & proinde inanibus figmentis eludebantur. Quapropter de hoc etiam sermonem nunc instituit, qui ad finē Capitis vsq; extenditur. Est autē doctrina hæc nobis maximè necessaria. Nam licet eam Christus discipulis suis, qui tunc erant, accommodet, vt aduersus pericula eos instruat, quæ toti Iudæorum genti post suum è terris discessum imminebant: ita tamen ista tractat, vt non minus nostris temporibus seruiant, quibus in Hierosolyma & Iudaicæ gentis excidio prælusum fuit.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, Jesus Christ, when the hour of his death was near, wished to admonish and instruct his disciples about all those things which they needed to know in order to guard against the stumbling-blocks that he knew would come, many and grievous, he had up to this point discoursed at length on the chief article of the Gospel teaching, namely faith and its effects, under which all the duties of the Christian man are comprehended. He also confirmed his teaching by very many miracles, among which the most famous and memorable is that which we recently heard was performed on the ten lepers. Moreover, the chief obstacle to salvation at that time, even among the better sort, was that most of the Jews were ignorant of the nature of the kingdom of God and of the manner in which it was to be established among men, and so they were deluded by empty fancies. Therefore he now begins a discourse on this very subject, which extends to the end of the chapter. This teaching is most necessary for us. For although Christ adapts it to the disciples who were then present, in order to instruct them against the dangers that threatened the whole Jewish nation after his departure from the earth, he treats these matters in such a way that they serve no less our own times, in which the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish nation was foreshadowed.

units.la: Occasionem de his differendi Pharisæi dederunt, qui Dominum interrogauerunt, quando Regnum Dei esset venturum. Credibile autem est, quæstionem hanc per ludibrium ab illis motā fuisse, vt coram vulgo doctrinam eius omnē vanitatis arguerent. Scimus enim omnes eius temporis conciones de Regno Dei fuisse. Nam Ioannē Baptistam clamauisse scribitur: Resipiscite, in propinquo est enim Regnum cœlorum. Concionum verò Christi argumentum Marcus iisdem ferè verbis comprehendit: Impletum est tempus, & instat Regnum Dei: resipiscite, & credite Euangelio. Et supra Apostolos quoq; ad prædicandum Regnum Dei missos fuisse audiuimus. Solent autem Prophetæ redemptionis & salutis humanæ negotium, cuius author esse debuit promissus ille Messias, Iesus Christus, Regnum Dei dicere, eò quòd illius hic finis est, vt destructa diaboli tyrannide homines in libertatem asserantur, & in illis Deus regnet suo Verbo & Spiritu, donec huius vitæ cursum emensi ad regni cœlestis & æterni possessionem veniant. Id cum non intelligerent Iudæorum Scribæ & Sacerdotes, regnū terrenum & temporarium somniabant, & prophetias secundùm literam interpretabantur. Quæ causa fuit, quòd omnium animi in regni terreni spem erecti, Messiam eiusmodi animo concipperent, qui Iudæos in libertatem pristinam vendicaret, & inter illos regnū constitueret, in quo ipsi victoriis, opibus & potentia vniuersis hostibus suis essent formidabiles. Cùm ergo Christus tam prijs verbis quàm Apostolorum suorum concionibus, regnum illud Dei promissum iam præforibus esse quotidie clamaret, nulla autem interea fieret rerum mutatio, Pharisæi, vt illum vulgo exosum facerent, aut saltem ludibrijs omnium exponerent, quæstionem hanc in publico non sine acerba irrisione mouerunt: Quasi dicerent: Tu quidem Regnum Dei numquam non in ore habes, & te huius instauratorem venisse multi arbitrantur, quos tu promissionibus & miraculorum ostentatione lactas: Quin ergo definis tandem certum tempus, quo Regnum hoc instarari oporteat? aut dicito saltem quousq; expectare debeant, quos hucusq; suspensos habuisti? Quis enim tibi porrò fidem habeat, cùm nulla vspiam regni noui spes appareat, & vulgi conditio indies deterior fiat?
units.tr: The Pharisees gave the occasion for this discussion, when they asked the Lord when the kingdom of God would come. It is credible that they raised this question in mockery, so that before the common people they might prove his whole teaching to be vanity. For we know that all the sermons of that time were about the kingdom of God. It is written that John the Baptist cried out: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Mark summarises the theme of Christ's preaching in almost the same words: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe the Gospel." And we have heard above that the apostles too were sent out to preach the kingdom of God. The prophets are accustomed to call the work of redemption and human salvation, whose author was to be the promised Messiah, Jesus Christ, the kingdom of God, because its purpose is that, with the tyranny of the devil destroyed, men may be set free, and that God may reign in them by his Word and Spirit, until, having finished the course of this life, they come into possession of the heavenly and eternal kingdom. Since the scribes and priests of the Jews did not understand this, they dreamed of an earthly and temporal kingdom and interpreted the prophecies according to the letter. This was the reason why the minds of all were raised in hope of an earthly kingdom, and they conceived of a Messiah of such a kind as would restore the Jews to their former liberty and establish among them a kingdom in which they themselves would be feared by all their enemies for their victories, wealth and power. Therefore, since Christ was crying out daily, both by his own words and by the sermons of his apostles, that the promised kingdom of God was now at the doors, and yet no change of affairs took place in the meantime, the Pharisees, in order to make him hated by the people, or at least to expose him to the mockery of all, raised this question in public, not without bitter derision. As if they were saying: "You indeed always have the kingdom of God on your lips, and many think that you have come as its restorer, whom you delight with promises and a display of miracles. Why then do you not at last fix a certain time when this kingdom ought to be restored? Or at least tell us how long those whom you have kept in suspense until now must wait. For who will any longer put faith in you, when no hope of a new kingdom appears anywhere, and the condition of the people grows worse day by day?"

units.la: Debet autem in his obseruari diaboli astutia, qui Christi Iesu cognitionem tunc maximè obscurat, quando eius gloriam promouere videtur. Quia enim ipse in animas nostras sibi imperium vendicat, Christum in corpora & fortunas nostras regnum obtinere facile ferret, modò ipsi meliorem nostri partem cederet. Imò vt hanc obtineret, Christum Regem, quales in hoc seculo habentur, facere voluit, quando in montem altum subducto omnia huius mundi regna ostendit, & dixit: Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si prostratus me adoraueris. At quia illum cæco ambitionis affectu non potuit vincere, sed se ab illo vinci sensit, false hominibus talem persuadere conatur, ut nimirum relictis cælestium bonorum studijs, in illo non nisi terrena & temporalia quærant. Ideo Iudæos hac regni terreni expectatione dementauit, quæ tantum in eis potuit, ut Regnum Dei reiecerint & in crucem egerint eum, qui hoc ipsis erat instauraturus. Quin hac vna spe auitæ libertatis & regni terreni adhuc hodie delusi, ad Christi mentionem tantùmno exhorrescunt, adeoq; diris horrendis eum prosequuntur, quæ eorum patres tanto cum desiderio expectauerunt. At quid de Iudæis dico, quando inter Christianos homines inuenti sunt, qui simili errore se deludi paterentur? Olim certè Chiliastæ fuerunt, qui authore Papiaregnum Christi post resurrectionem in terris corporaliter futurum crediderunt: & ante hunc Cerinthus, Christum à resurrectione tradidit secundum huius seculi morem Hierosolymis regnaturum esse, et tunc homines ijsdem cupiditatibus atq; studijs obnoxios fore, quibus hodie distrahuntur. At quorum opinione non omnino absunt, qui Prophetarum vaticinia, quibus illi pacem vniuersalem & vitam felicem in Christo pollicentur, secundùm literam interpretantur, & Regnum Dei ad huc venisse negant, eò quòd totum orbem terrarum bellis atq; seditionibus turbari, in primis autem Ecclesiam adhuc duris periculis exerceri vident. Insistunt horum vestigijs Anabaptistæ, qui sub Christianæ libertatis prætextu magistratus & ius gladij abolere conantur, quasi hic minimè opus sit, Christo nimirum scilicet mirificè defendente. Quid vero de Pontificibus dicemus, qui quod alij infelicius tentauerunt, miris artibus obtinuerunt, ut nimirum vicariorum Christi titulo superbi totius mundi imperium ad se transferrent, & potentissimos reges pedibus suis subijcerent? Quod quid aliud est, quàm regnum Christi in terrenum commutare, & hunc talem fingere, qualem olim Chiliastæ & Iudæi somniauerunt? Quòd si nostros homines inspicias, qui puriori Veritatis euangelicæ & Christi cognitione gloriantur, quàm multos in illis reperies, qui sub Euangelij prætextu non aliud quàm opes, honores, pacem huius seculi, & (quod turpissimum est) peccandi licentiam atq; impunitatem quærunt? Et hi quidem omnes diaboli ludibrijs circumducuntur, qui eiusmodi persuasionibus infelices inescare solet, ut de cælestibus & æternis bonis cogitare desinant.
units.tr: In these matters we must observe the cunning of the devil, who obscures the knowledge of Christ Jesus most of all just when he seems to promote his glory. For since he claims dominion over our souls for himself, he would easily bear with Christ holding a kingdom over our bodies and fortunes, provided that he himself were granted the better part of us. Indeed, in order to obtain this, he wished to make Christ a king of the kind that are found in this world, when he led him up into a high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of this world, and said: "All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me." But because he could not overcome Christ with a blind desire for ambition, and felt himself to be overcome by him, he tries to persuade men falsely that they should, namely, set aside the pursuit of heavenly goods and seek in Christ nothing but earthly and temporal things. Thus he drove the Jews mad with this expectation of an earthly kingdom, which had such power over them that they rejected the kingdom of God and brought to the cross him who was about to restore it to them. Moreover, still today they are deluded by this one hope of ancestral liberty and an earthly kingdom, and at the mention of Christ they do not shudder, but pursue him with such dreadful curses as their fathers longed for with such desire. But why do I speak of the Jews, when among Christian men there have been found some who suffered themselves to be deceived by a similar error? Certainly in former times there were Chiliasts, who, with Papias as their author, believed that after the resurrection the kingdom of Christ would be bodily on earth; and before him Cerinthus taught that after the resurrection Christ would reign at Jerusalem in the manner of this age, and that men would then be subject to the same desires and pursuits by which they are distracted today. Nor are they far from the same opinion who interpret literally the prophecies in which a universal peace and a happy life in Christ are promised, and deny that the kingdom of God has yet come, because they see the whole world troubled by wars and seditions, and above all the Church still exercised by harsh dangers. The Anabaptists follow in their footsteps, who under the pretext of Christian liberty try to abolish the magistrate and the right of the sword, as if it were scarcely needed, since Christ, of course, defends his people wondrously. But what shall we say of the Pontiffs, who obtained by wonderful arts what others attempted less fortunately, namely, that by the title of vicars of Christ they proudly transferred to themselves the empire of the whole world and placed the most powerful kings beneath their feet? What is this other than to change the kingdom of Christ into an earthly one, and to imagine him such as the Chiliasts and Jews once dreamed of? But if you look at our own people, who boast of a purer knowledge of the Gospel truth and of Christ, how many will you find among them who, under the pretext of the Gospel, seek nothing but wealth, honours, the peace of this age and (what is most shameful) licence and impunity for sinning? And all these are indeed led around by the mockeries of the devil, who is accustomed to entice the unhappy with such persuasions, so that they cease to think of heavenly and eternal goods.

units.la: Audiamus ergo ipsum Christum, qui etsi quæstionem hanc Pharisæi per ludibrium mouissent, grauiter tamen respondet, & paucis verbis primò errorem Iudaici populi communem refellit, deinde regni sui rationem explicat: Sic enim dicit: Non veniet Regnum Dei cum observatione: neq; dicent, Ecce hic, aut Ecce illic. Ecce enim Regnum Dei intra vos est. Negat Regnum Dei venturum cum observatione. Atqui in Prophetis multa proponuntur, ex quibus veteres Christi aduentum primum præ foribus esse, agnoscere debuerunt: & ipse Dominus nos signis instruxit, quorum diligens obseruatio admonet non procul abesse diem redemptionis nostræ, quo Regnum Dei, quod nunc cœpit, verè compleri, & salute totius hominis perfici oporteat. Sed in præsenti de splendore aut apparatu Christus loquitur, quale Iudæi iam pridem animo conceperant. Putabāt enim præcursuros anteambulones quosdam, qui in eius aduentum omnia magnificè præpararent. Ipsum verò Messiam armis & militum copijs stipatum fingebant, qui deiectis Romanorum præsidijs Regni sedem Hierosolymæ esset constituturus: & alia huius generis multa sibijpsis persuaserant, quæ in huius seculi regnis solent fieri. Ea verò omnia negat Dominus, dicens: Non veniet Regnum Dei cum observatione. Et ideo per expositionem addit: Neque dicent, Ecce hic: aut, Ecce illic. Id est, non habebit sedem certam sede vel Hierosolymæ, vel Samariæ, aut in vlla alia vrbe in terris celebriori. Conueniunt his, quæ in Prophetis habentur, qui etiamsi regnum Christi per comparationes & similia ex regnis huius seculi petita describant, multa tamen intermiscent, ex quibus illius tenuitatem & aspectum contemptibilem deprehendere licet. Dauid certè ait: De torrente in via bibet. Et notum est Zachariæ vaticinium: En Rex tuus veniet tibi, iustus & seruator ipse, pauper, qui vehetur asino & pullo asinæ. Quibus addere licet totum Isaiæ Caput quinquagesimum tertium, quo totam ferè mortis eius historiam cum illius fructu Spiritus sanctus clarissimè prædixit. Quorum omnium confirmationi seruit, quod ipsemet à Pilato de regno interrogatus respondit: Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: Si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei certarent, ne traderer Iudæis: nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc.
units.tr: Let us therefore hear Christ himself, who, although the Pharisees had raised this question in mockery, nevertheless answers it seriously, and in a few words first refutes the error common to the Jewish people, and then explains the nature of his kingdom. For he says: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, 'Look, here it is!' or 'Look, there it is!' For behold, the kingdom of God is within you." He denies that the kingdom of God will come with observation. And yet in the Prophets many things are set forth from which the ancients ought to have recognised that the first coming of Christ was at the doors; and the Lord himself has instructed us with signs, by the careful observation of which we are reminded that the day of our redemption is not far off, on which the kingdom of God, which has now begun, ought to be truly completed, and the salvation of the whole man perfected. But in the present passage Christ is speaking of a splendour or display of the kind the Jews had long since conceived in their minds. For they thought that certain forerunners would go before him, who would prepare everything magnificently for his coming. They imagined the Messiah himself surrounded by arms and troops of soldiers, who, having cast down the Roman garrisons, would establish the seat of his kingdom at Jerusalem; and they had persuaded themselves of many other things of this kind, such as usually happen in the kingdoms of this age. The Lord denies all these things, saying: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation." And therefore by way of explanation he adds: "Nor will they say, 'Look, here it is!' or 'Look, there it is!'" That is, it will not have a fixed seat either at Jerusalem or at Samaria, or in any other city on earth that is more famous. These words agree with what is found in the Prophets, who, although they describe the kingdom of Christ by comparisons and likenesses drawn from the kingdoms of this age, nevertheless mingle in many things from which its lowliness and contemptible appearance may be perceived. David certainly says: "He shall drink of the brook in the way." And the prophecy of Zechariah is well known: "Behold, your King will come to you, just and a saviour himself, poor, riding on an ass and on the colt of an ass." To these may be added the whole fifty-third chapter of Isaiah, in which the Holy Spirit most clearly foretold almost the whole history of his death together with its fruit. What serves to confirm all these things is that he himself, when asked by Pilate about his kingdom, answered: "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here.

units.la: Debet ex his generalis doctrina peti, Regnum Dei, quod Euangelio praedicatur, & ex quo vni uersa nostrae salutis ratio dependet, non habere Metropolim certam aut sedem fixam, ad quam ceu ad commune totius orbis oraculum omnes debeant concurrere. Olim quidē externi cultus, & sacrificiorum certum locum esse voluit Deus, ad quem vt ad commune gentis totius parochiam Iudaei ex omnibus tribubus conuenirent: sed id partim vnitatis conseruandae studio constitutum fuit, partim vt ad vnius Christi Iesu sacrificium omnes respicere discerent, qui Hierosolymis sui corporis victima peccatum mundi expiaturus erat. At vmbris illis iam olim sublatis, nullum alium locum Christus designauit, qui regni sui aut Ecclesiae sedes sit principalis: sed vt haec per totum orbem terrarum extenditur: ita quoad Christum & eius meritum, ille omnibus Ecclesijs praesens adest, suo spiritu omnes gubernat, & suo merito partā salutem omnibus ex aequo impertit. Neq; haec Domini voluntas fuit, vt omnes gentes Hierosolymā conuenirent, sed vt Apostoli inde digressi Regnū Dei vbiq; terrarum praedicarent, & in omnibus locis tam celebrioribus quàm obscuris Ecclesias sibi colligerent. Extant de hoc Prophetarum promissiones, qualis est quae in Psalmis habetur: Dominus e Zion emittet virgam potentiae suae. Et illa Isaiae, quam ijsdem verbis Micheas repetijt: E Zion exibit Lex, & Verbum Domini de Ierusalem. Quibus omnino consentit postremum Christi mandatū, quo Apostolis dixit: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae. Item: Vos eritis mihi testes Hierosolymae, & in tota Iudaea, in Samaria, & vsq; ad fines terrae. Quae omnia non temere dicta fuisse, Actorum Apostolicorum liber abunde declarat. Ista eorum audaciam fortissimè refel lunt, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus Ecclesiae & religionis Christianae sedē Romae constituerunt, eò quòd illius Ecclesiae cathedram Petrus, princeps Apostolorum, tenuerit, ex quo Pontificum Romanorum perpetua successio deducatur. Atqui Apostolorū principem fingunt Petrum, qui se aliorum collegam & συμπρεσβύτερον dixit, neq; aliter dicere potuit, nisi Christo vellet contradicere, qui primatus affectationem ab illis omnibus alienissimam esse voluit. Deinde Petrum primum Romanae Ecclesiae episcopum fuisse fingunt, quem vnquam Romae fuisse vix probari potest: certè illum tot annis illic docuisse, quot illi dicunt, totius historiae Apostolicae contextu aut serie & scriptorum Apostolicorum authoritate negari potest, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Successione ergo Pontificum ab ipso Petro deducunt, quae omnino nulla est. Et quàmuis ea probari posset, quid obsecro ea ad defendendū Ecclesiae Romanae primatū faceret? Annon enim Dauidis successores, imò posteri fuerunt Achaz, Manasses, Ioakim & Zedechias? Aaroni verò & pijs sacerdotibus alijs successerūt Annas, Caiaphas, Alexander & aliae gentis Iudaicae pestes. Est ergo putidissimum commentū quicquid illi fingunt, vt iam de eo nihil dicam, quòd & Petro grauem iniuriā faciunt, quasi is relicta Apostolica sun-ctione vnius vrbis Episcopus fuerit per totos annos viginti quinq; suo otio potius quā Christi mandato intentus: & Christi Regnū vni loco astringunt, quod is per totum orbem extendi voluit. Quin ipsum Spiritum sanctum haec iniuria redundat, quem illi homines ad Romanam cathedram, vt olim gentes suum Apollinem ad Delphicum oraculū, alligant. Sed oportet vt eiusmodi arundineis fulcris nitantur, qui semel aduersus Veritatem proteruire instituerunt.
units.tr: From these things a general doctrine may be drawn: the Kingdom of God, which is preached in the Gospel and on which the whole order of our salvation depends, has no fixed metropolis or set seat to which all must flock as to a common oracle for the whole world. Indeed, God once willed that there be a fixed place for external worship and sacrifices, to which the Jews from all the tribes would gather as to a common assembly of the whole nation. But this was established partly to preserve unity, and partly so that all would learn to look to the one sacrifice of Christ Jesus, since at Jerusalem he was to be offered as a victim of his own body to expiate the sin of the world. But with those shadows now long since removed, Christ has appointed no other place as the principal seat of his kingdom or of his Church. Rather, just as the Church extends throughout the whole earth, so with respect to Christ and his merit, he is present to all churches, governs all by his Spirit, and bestows on all alike the salvation won by his merit. Nor was it the Lord's will that all nations should gather at Jerusalem; rather, the Apostles were to depart from there and preach the Kingdom of God everywhere on earth, and gather churches for themselves in all places, both the more famous and the obscure. There are prophetic promises about this, such as the one in the Psalms: "The Lord will send forth the rod of his power out of Zion." And that of Isaiah, which Micah repeated in the same words: "Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." The final command of Christ wholly agrees with these, in which he said to the Apostles: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature." Likewise: "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." That these things were not said rashly, the book of the Acts of the Apostles abundantly shows. Those men refute most strongly the audacity of those who in these latest times have set up the seat of the Church and of the Christian religion at Rome, on the ground that Peter, the prince of the Apostles, held the chair of that Church, from which the perpetual succession of the Roman Pontiffs is derived. Yet they make Peter the prince of the Apostles, though he called himself a fellow elder with the others ["συμπρεσβύτερος"], and he could not have said this unless he wished to contradict Christ, who willed that the pursuit of primacy be wholly alien to all of them. Next, they pretend that Peter was the first bishop of the Roman Church, though it can hardly be proved that he was ever at Rome at all; certainly that he taught there for as many years as they claim can be denied on the basis of the whole course and sequence of Apostolic history and the authority of the Apostolic writings, as we have shown elsewhere. Therefore, they derive the succession of Pontiffs from Peter himself, which is entirely non-existent. And even if it could be proved, what, I ask you, would it contribute to defending the primacy of the Roman Church? For were not the successors of David, indeed his descendants, Ahaz, Manasseh, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah? And after Aaron and the other godly priests came Annas, Caiaphas, Alexander and other plagues of the Jewish nation. So whatever they invent is a most rotten fiction. I say nothing more of this, but they also do grave injury to Peter, as if, having abandoned his Apostolic office, he had been bishop of one city for twenty-five years, intent on his leisure rather than on Christ's command; and they confine Christ's kingdom to one place, though he willed it to be extended throughout the whole world. Indeed, this injury reaches even the Holy Spirit himself, whom those men bind to the Roman chair, just as the nations once bound their Apollo to the Delphic oracle. But those who once resolved to act defiantly against the Truth must lean on such reed props.

units.la: At non contentus Iudaeorum errorem confutauisse Christus, simul etiam regni sui rationem ex- ponit, & illos non obscurè hortatur, vt se illi accommodent. Ecce enim (inquit) Regnum Dei intra vos est. Quasi diceret: Inepta & superuacanea quaestio, interrogare quando venturum sit Regnum Dei, cùm illud iam in medio vestri sit, & ita se omnium oculis & sensibus ingerat, vt nisi talpis caeciores & caudicibus stupidiores effetis, non possetis non aliud animaduertere. Ita verò ignorantiam crassam & nimiam stupiditatem ipsis exprobrat, qui cùm populi duces & doctores haberi velint, vt absentem quaerant, qui ipsis quotidie adsit & colloquatur. Similis exprobratio apud Ioannem habetur, qui cùm Christum dixisset eam lucem esse, quae suo in mundum aduentu omnem hominem illuminet, mox tamen addit, illum non mundo solum, verumetiam suis incognitum fuisse, quibus seipsum familiarissimè manifestabat. In sua (inquit) venit, & sui eum non receperunt.
units.tr: But Christ, not content to have refuted the error of the Jews, at the same time sets out the nature of his kingdom and not obscurely urges them to adapt themselves to it. "For behold," he says, "the Kingdom of God is within you." It is as if he were saying: "It is a foolish and superfluous question to ask when the Kingdom of God will come, since it is already in the midst of you, and it so presses itself on everyone's eyes and senses that, unless you were blinder than moles and more stupid than stumps, you could not fail to notice it." Indeed, he rebukes them for their gross ignorance and extreme stupidity, since though they wish to be considered leaders and teachers of the people, they seek one who is absent, while he is present and speaks with them every day. A similar rebuke is found in John, who, after saying that Christ was the light which, by coming into the world, enlightens every man, immediately adds that he was unknown not only to the world but also to his own people, to whom he manifested himself most familiarly. "He came to his own," he says, "and his own did not receive him."

units.la: Sed proderit hic diligentius videre, quae tunc fuerit inter Iudaeos rerum conditio, vt ex ea intelligamus, quae Regni Dei ratio sit in terris, & quib9 indicijs nos illud hodie agnoscere possimus. Dominabatur, tunc in illis locis Romani, qui Iudaeae praesidem dederant, & praesidia per vrbes dispo-suerat. In sacris verò omnis potestas penes Sacerdotes et Scribas, maximè autē penes Pharisaeos erat, qui præsidū authoritate defendebantur. Erat ergo infelicissima miseri populi conditio. Interista autem publica mala Dei Filius pro nobis homo factus emersit, qui Regnum Dei iam adesse clamabat, & ad hoc excipiendum omnes hortabatur. Doctrinæ eius capita erant, Pænitentia & Remissio peccatorum, vtramq; autem in suo nomine prædicabat, se nimirum eum esse docens, cuius virtute nos ex verbi semine renasci & mortificata atq; abnegata carne nouum hominē induere oporteat, vt per fidem in ipsum iustificati vitā æternam in regno illo Dei æterno atq; cœlesti consequamur. Doctrinam hanc miraculis confirmabat, cū dæmonia eiiceret, morbis omnibus solo dicto aut nutu mederetur, leprosos mundaret; vita nimirum docens, se eum esse, qui mundi huius principē deuincat, naturæ nostræ vitiosæ medeatur, veteris vestigia culpæ deleat, à peccatis omnibus purget, & iustitiā sempiternam (vt Daniel loquitur) cum salute vera atq; perfecta nobis reducat. Hæc (inquā) omnia cum tunc faceret Christus, & cum Veritatis doctrina æternæ vitæ beneficium omnibus offerret, Regnū Dei in tra illos esse ait. Ex quo colligimus, Regnum Dei apud omnes etiam hodie esse, quibus per Euangelij doctrinam in Christi nomine pœnitentia & peccatorū remissio prædicatur: etiamsi externa tam Reipub. quàm Ecclesiæ constitutio turbulentissima atq; miserrima sit. Nec enim terrenum est Regnum istud, neq; in ritibus aut ceremoniarum splendore aut fortunatis huius seculi successibus consistit: sed in Spiritus virtute, quæ hominum mentes innouat, & Deo subijcit per fidei obedientiam. Hinc ergo consolationē petāt, quicunq; dura tyrannide premuntur, & ideo se à Regno Dei exclusos esse putant. Nec enim animæ libertatem seruitus corporis impedit: & potest in te Regnū suum ob tinere Deus, licet in iis, inter quos tu versaris, diabolus et tenebrarū princeps dominetur. Sed & eos locus iste consutant, qui Regnum Dei consistere posse negant, nisi reipub. formā mutent, magistratus è medio tollant, & omnia pro suo arbitrio constituant. Sunt hi plerunq; maximarū turbarum authores, & dum Regnum Dei inconsulta & ambitiosa temeritate prouehere studet, fere ab alijs feliciter iacta eius fundamenta ipsi conuellunt & dissipant. Discant ergo omnes causam hanc prudenter & modestè agere, agnoscat singulare Dei beneficium, qui inter nouissimorum temporū periculosissimos motus passim Ecclesiæ suæ hospites & hospitia qualiacunq; inuenit, & vt in nostris quoq; regionibus doctrinam illam conseruet oremus, per quam suum Regnum instauratur atq; seruatur.
units.tr: But it will be worthwhile to look more carefully here at what the condition of affairs among the Jews was at that time, so that from it we may understand what the nature of the Kingdom of God is on earth, and by what signs we may recognise it today. At that time the Romans ruled in those regions; they had given Judaea a governor and had stationed garrisons in the cities. In sacred matters, all power lay with the priests and scribes, and most of all with the Pharisees, who were protected by the authority of the governors. The condition of the wretched people was therefore most unhappy. Amid these public evils the Son of God, made man for us, appeared, proclaiming that the Kingdom of God was now at hand and exhorting all to receive it. The heads of his teaching were repentance and the forgiveness of sins, and he preached both in his own name, teaching, of course, that he was the one by whose power we ought to be born again from the seed of the Word, and, with the flesh mortified and denied, put on the new man, so that through faith in him, being justified, we may obtain eternal life in that eternal and heavenly kingdom of God. He confirmed this teaching with miracles: he cast out demons, healed all diseases by a word or a nod alone, and cleansed lepers. By his life he taught, of course, that he was the one who overcomes the prince of this world, heals our vicious nature, erases the traces of ancient guilt, purges us of all sins, and restores to us everlasting righteousness (as Daniel puts it) together with true and perfect salvation. When Christ was doing all these things, and when by the doctrine of truth he was offering the benefit of eternal life to all, he said that the Kingdom of God was among them. From this we gather that the Kingdom of God is today also among all those to whom repentance and the forgiveness of sins are preached in the name of Christ through the doctrine of the Gospel, even if the external constitution both of the commonwealth and of the Church is most turbulent and wretched. For that kingdom is not earthly, nor does it consist in the splendour of rites and ceremonies or in the fortunate successes of this age; it consists in the power of the Spirit, which renews the minds of men and subjects them to God through obedience of faith. Let therefore whoever are oppressed by harsh tyranny, and for that reason think they are excluded from the Kingdom of God, seek consolation here. For bodily servitude does not hinder the freedom of the soul, and God can hold his kingdom in you, even though the devil, the prince of darkness, rules among those with whom you live. But this passage also confutes those who deny that the Kingdom of God can exist unless they change the form of the commonwealth, remove the magistrates, and arrange everything at their own discretion. These men are usually the authors of the greatest disturbances, and while they strive with unconsidered and ambitious rashness to advance the Kingdom of God, they themselves overthrow and scatter the foundations that others have happily laid. Let all therefore learn to pursue this cause prudently and modestly, and let them acknowledge the singular benefit of God, who, amid the most dangerous upheavals of these latest times, has found everywhere some guests and dwellings for his Church, whatever they may be. And let us pray that he would also preserve in our own regions that doctrine through which his Kingdom is restored and kept safe.

units.la: Porrò nō ignorabat Christus, se de tantis tamq; arduis mysterijs frustra verba facere apud Pharisæos, quibus iampridē lusus iocusq; esse cœperat, quicquid in Scripturis de Regno Dei cœlesti tradi tur, cū ipsi præter opes, honores & voluptates huius seculi nihil saperent. Ideo relictis illis qui revera canes & porci erant, ad discipulos sermonem conuertit, quos primùm de periculis admoner, quibus infelicem Iudæorum gentem propter impium & prophanum Regni Dei contemptū, adhæc propter incurabilem ingratitudinem atq; contumaciam iactari oporteat. Deinde consilio tam illos quàm omnes credentes instruit. Postremò redit ad mortis suæ mentionem, quam sæpius apud eos fecerat, vt huius recordatio conceptum in animis illorum de Regno Dei terreno errorem confutet.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ did not fail to see that he was speaking in vain to the Pharisees about such great and difficult mysteries. For some time they had been treating with mockery and jest whatever is taught in the Scriptures about the heavenly Kingdom of God, since they cared for nothing beyond the riches, honours and pleasures of this age. So, leaving aside those who were in truth dogs and swine, he turned his speech to the disciples. He first warns them of the dangers by which the unhappy Jewish nation must be tossed about, on account of its impious and profane contempt for the Kingdom of God and its incurable ingratitude and obstinacy. Then he instructs them, and all believers, with counsel. Finally, he returns to the mention of his death, which he had made to them more than once, so that the remembrance of it might refute the earthly error conceived in their minds about the Kingdom of God.

units.la: Pericula & turbulentissimam rerum conditionem primùm in genere comprehendit, dum often dit, in quas angustias ipsi deuenturi, & quis ipsis animus futurus sit. Veniet tempus (inquit) cùm de siderabitis videre vnum ex diebus Filij hominis, nec videbitis. Dies filij hominis tempus illud dicit, quod in priori suo aduentu homo factus in terris transegit, et sensus verborum est. Nunc quidem à plerisq; contemnor & negligor, & vix vlli gratiam atq; saluificam Regni Dei virtutem in me sese manifestantē agnoscere dignantur: sed breui eueniet, vt vos, quos mihi ceu singulares amicos & seruos selegi, propter vndiq; surgentia pericula & horribiles mundi motus, vel vnum diem mecum vt nunc familiarius conuersari, & me consultore & consolatore vti optetis: id verò vobis cōtingere nō poterit. Et ista quidē discipulis dicit, vt ex comparatione hostes intelligant, quantò grauiora & duriora ipsi passuri sint: simul autem suos excitat, vt felicitate illa, qua tunc vt domestici eius discipuli fruebantur, bene vti studeant, & quod alibi dicit, ambulent dum lucem habeant, ne subitò à tenebris obruantur. Et sanè non potuit discipulis superuacanea videri hæc admonitio, cùm eos nimiùm secu ros tanti beneficij æstimatores fuisse constet, adeo vt de illorū side actum fuerit, nisi Dominus illos sua manu quasi è cœlo protensa erexisset, & tandem misso Spiritu suo magis confirmasset. Nec du- bium est, hoc solicitum videndi eius desiderium ipsorum animos vehementer discruciauisse, quando illo in cruce mortuo & sepulto in latebris absconsi iacuerunt, vt præ metu Iudæorum ne fores quidē domus aperire nedum prodire auderent. Quoties itē hæc verba non sine acerbißimo dolore illis in mentem venisse putabimus, quando totam Iudæam quotidianis seditiosorum hominū furoribus tur bari, multos passim cædi, pios in exilium eijci, & tandem Romanorum arma in patriā dulcißimam inferri, agros & vicos vastari, oppida excindi, horribiles infelicis populi strages fieri, & tandē miserias reliquias per totum orbem dispersas vagari viderunt? Taceo nūc, quæ ad ipsos propius spectarunt, quando vbiq; locorum sibi insidias strui, carceres & vincula passim parata esse, & nunquā non sua capita ab impijs Christi hostibus peti sentiebant. Ah quoties tunc recordati sunt dulcißimæ illius consuetudinis, in qua Dei Filiū coram videre, audire, contrectare soliti fuerant. Quoties suæ socordiæ & negligentiæ illos pœnituisse putas? Est enim hoc humani ingenij proprium, vt quæ dum præsentia sunt fastidimus, aut salutē oscitanter nimis negligimus, ea cum gemitu, dolore, eiulatu requiramus, vt à nobis ablata aut amissa fuerint. Veruntamen quæ tunc Apostoli passi sunt, ludus censeri possunt, si cum ijs conferantur, quæ reliquis Iudæis & impijs Christi aduersarijs acciderunt: quos non solum bellici terrores, cædes, oppidorum excidia, fames & dirißima quæq; pericula exagitarunt, verumetiam propriæ conscientiæ carnificina exercuit, cum Deum sibi iratum esse, & Filij sui sanguine ex manibus ipsorum requirere, calamitates vero ißas pœnarum infernalium præludia esse sentirēt. Quis dubitet tunc quoq; illos Christi sæpißimè recordatos fuisse, & hunc solicitis animis requisiuisse, frustra tamen, cum fide vera destituerētur, neq; preces pias in Dei conspectum afferrent, sed belluino vlulatu sanctis eius auribus obstreperent?
units.tr: He first sets out the dangers and the very turbulent state of affairs in general, when he says what straits they will fall into and what their state of mind will be. "The time will come," he says, "when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and you will not see it." The days of the Son of man signify that time which, as man made on earth, he spent during his first coming; and the sense of the words is this: "Now indeed I am despised and neglected by many, and scarcely any deign to acknowledge in me the grace and saving power of the Kingdom of God manifesting itself. But soon it will happen that you, whom I have chosen as my special friends and servants, will wish to have even one day with me, to converse with me more familiarly now, and to use me as counsellor and comforter, because of the dangers rising on every side and the terrible upheavals of the world. Yet this will not be possible for you." He says these things to the disciples so that, by comparison, they may understand how much more grievous and harsh the things are that they themselves will suffer. At the same time he rouses his own, so that they may take care to make good use of that happiness which they then enjoyed as his household disciples, and, as he says elsewhere, "walk while they have the light, lest they be suddenly overtaken by darkness." Indeed, this warning could not have seemed superfluous to the disciples, since it is certain that they were too secure and too poor judges of so great a benefit, so much so that their faith would have failed, had not the Lord raised them up with his hand, as if stretched out from heaven, and at last strengthened them further by sending his Spirit. Nor is there any doubt that this anxious desire to see him tormented their minds greatly, when, with him dead on the cross and buried, they lay hidden in hiding, so that, for fear of the Jews, they did not dare even to open the doors of the house, much less go out. How often, we may suppose, did these words come to their minds, not without the most bitter grief, when they saw all Judea disturbed by the daily frenzies of seditious men, many killed everywhere, the pious driven into exile, and at last the arms of the Romans brought into their most sweet fatherland, the fields and villages laid waste, the towns razed, horrible slaughters of the unhappy people made, and the miserable remnants scattered through the whole world and wandering? I say nothing now of those things which touched them more closely, when they felt that snares were laid for them in every place, that prisons and chains were prepared everywhere, and that their heads were never not sought by the impious enemies of Christ. Ah, how often then did they recall that most sweet custom, in which they had been accustomed to see, hear and handle the Son of God in person! Do you think they regretted their sloth and negligence often? For it is the peculiar trait of the human mind that we despise what is present, or neglect our salvation too carelessly, and then we seek it back with groaning, grief and wailing, once it has been taken or lost from us. Yet what the Apostles then suffered may be counted as sport, if it is compared with what befell the rest of the Jews and the impious adversaries of Christ. Not only did warlike terrors, slaughters, the destruction of towns, famine and every most dreadful danger harass them, but also the torture of their own conscience tormented them, when they felt that God was angry with them and was demanding the blood of his Son at their hands, and that these calamities were the prelude to the punishments of hell. Who can doubt that then too they often remembered Christ, and sought him with anxious minds, yet in vain, since they were deprived of true faith and did not bring pious prayers before the sight of God, but with bestial howling pressed upon his holy ears?

units.la: Admonent ista quid omnibus eueniat, qui per Euangelij prædicationem sibi oblatum Regnum Dei reijciunt. Est peccatum hoc nimis vulgare inter eos etiam, qui Christum pleno ore profitentur. Clamant illi, Adueniat Regnum tuum. Quando autem hoc Deus illis offert, & ad eius communionē vocat per pœnitentiæ doctrinam, illud auersantur, & iniuriam sibi fieri putant, quādo iubentur ex cussō diaboli & mundi seruitio, Deum admittere, vt suo verbo & spiritu in illis regnet. Pollicentur isti sibijpsis omnia læta, si mundo sese conformes faciant. Sed spe sua miserrimè falluntur. Nam non solum æternæ vitæ, quam nullam esse credunt, iacturam faciunt, verumetiam in hoc mundo mortaliū calamitosißimi fiunt. Quia enim nobis Deus in solo Christo reconciliatus est, fieri non potest, quin ira Dei & maledictio omnibus ijs incumbat, qui Christi prædicationem reijciunt. At qui Deum sibi iratum habet, huic omnes Angeli & homines, elementa deniq; omnia & creaturæ omnes infestæ sunt. Exemplū eius rei euidens est admodū, quod in Iudæis proponitur. Debuit ex his Dei Filius homo nasci, & ideo gentē illā ipse amore plus quàm paterno prosecutus est, & beneficijs amplißimis ornauit. Quàm primùm autē hunc aspernati sunt, abstulit ab eis regnum suum Deus, ipsi verò amissa vrbe & templo, iam per annos amplius mille, quingentos vagantur, Deo & hominibus exosi, & omni restitutionis spe destituti. Similia exempla in multis Græcia & Asiæ populis extant, inter quos cum olim Apostoli Ecclesias florentißimas constituerint, hodie sub impuro Mahumetistarum iugo seruitutem non minus ignominiosam quàm miseram seruiunt. Et vtinā non magis vicina exempla videremus, quibus propter spretam Euangelij doctrinam regna celeberrima conquassantur, & tam exteris quàm ciuilibus bellis sese mutuò conficiunt. Debent ista eos terrere, quibus cum pace Euangelio frui datum est, ne similia mala, aut etiam his graviora, ipsi quoq; aliquando patiantur.
units.tr: These things warn what will happen to all who reject the Kingdom of God offered to them through the preaching of the Gospel. This sin is far too common even among those who profess Christ with full mouth. They cry, "Let your Kingdom come." But when God offers it to them and calls them to its fellowship through the teaching of repentance, they shrink from it and think they are being wronged, when they are commanded, having shaken off the servitude of the devil and the world, to admit God, that he may reign in them by his word and Spirit. Such people promise themselves all happy things if they make themselves conformable to the world. But they are most miserably deceived in their hope. For they not only suffer the loss of eternal life, which they believe does not exist, but in this world also they become most wretched of mortals. For since God has been reconciled to us in Christ alone, it cannot be but that the wrath and curse of God rest upon all those who reject the preaching of Christ. But he who has God angry with him, against him all the angels and men, indeed all the elements and all creatures, are hostile. The example of this is quite plain in what is set before us in the Jews. The Son of God was to be born a man from them, and therefore he himself loved that nation more than a father, and adorned it with the greatest benefits. But as soon as they spurned him, God took away his kingdom from them, and they themselves, their city and temple lost, have now for more than fifteen hundred years wandered, hated by God and men, and destitute of every hope of restoration. Similar examples exist among many peoples of Greece and Asia, among whom the Apostles once established most flourishing churches, and who today serve under the impure yoke of the Mahumetans a servitude no less shameful than wretched. And would that we did not see closer examples, by which, on account of the scorned doctrine of the Gospel, most famous kingdoms are shaken and wear themselves down by mutual wars, both foreign and civil. These things ought to terrify those to whom it has been granted to enjoy the Gospel in peace, lest they too one day suffer similar evils, or even worse than these.

units.la: Sed ad Christū redeamus qui sui dicti ratione sic reddit, vt simul doceat, à quo periculo maximè sibi debeant cauere pij, quando motus istos & turbas oriri vident. Nimirum quòd impostores inter pericula futuri sint plurimi, qui redemptorem promissum hinc inde monstrent, & noua quotidie salutis consilia fingendo omnes consilij & auxilij incertos reddant. Nam dicent vobis: Ecce hic: aut, Ecce illic. Apud Matthæum & Marcum hæc pluribus exponuntur. Tunc si quis dixerit vobis: Ecce hic Christus, aut illic: ne credatis. Surget enim pseudochristi, & pseudoprophetæ, & ædet signa magna & prodigia: ita vt seducant, si fieri possit, etiam electos. Ecce prædixi vobis. Si ergo dixerint vobis: Ecce in deserto est: ne egrediamini. Ecce in cœcla ibus, aut penarijs cellis (has enim pro priè vox Græca indicat) ne credatis. Pseudochristos dicit eos, qui se Messiæ aut Seruatoris promissi nomine vendebant, quales multos fuisse ante vrbis & gentis totius excidium, in Marco nostro ex Iosepho annotauimus. Et digni erant Iudæi, quibus impostores & Magi illi exitium struerent, cum verum Christum tam multis tamen salutaribus signis doctrinam suam commendantem Homil. 107. et 110. agnoscere & ampletti noluissent. Similia exempla omnibus seculis sunt edita. Sic Pharao & Ægyptij à Magis suis delusi sunt, qui Mosem & Aaronem noluerunt audire. Et multis Iudæ atq; Israelis regibus, qui Dei seruos contumeliosius tractarunt, exitio fuerunt pseudoprophetæ, quos illi in pretio habebāt. Nouissimis autē temporibus idem accidisse, nemo ignorat, qui Ecclesiæ historiā obiter modò inspexit. Postquā enim mundo sordere cœpit purior & simplicior Christi doctrina, mox impo sturis ianua patuit, & Orientē quidem Mahumetici furores turbarunt, in Occidente autem Ecclesiæ imperium sibi vendicarunt Pontifices, quorum astutia & tyrannide factum est, vt veraChristi cognitione ex hominum animis deleta, nouum quendā & prioribus seculis inauditum Christum plenū sequerentur: qui nimirū ex aqua & farina in sartagine factus, & quinq; verbis consecratus pro peccatis viuorum atq; mortuorum quotidie sacrificaretur. Cœpit hoc iniquitatis mysterium agitari sub annum Christi 844. quo tempore Romanam sedem tenuit Sergius, quem prius fatali & portentoso nomine Os porci dictum fuisse tradunt historici. Nec meliore fato Sergij nomen accepit, cùm annis ante ipsum circiter ducentis Sergius Monachus Orieti Mahumetē dedisset. Cæterum vbi Christum eiusmodi (vt diximus) nobis Pontifices fabricarunt, indies crescere magis cœpit tam ipsorum quàm aliorum Sacerdotum potentia, quos illi ad eius ministerium consecrabant. Et parum illis vi- sum est, si Christum interim dum sacra fiunt corporaliter adesse populus crederet, sed ne ipsorum sem per opera requireretur, tale finxerūt, qui semel factus diutius duraret, & proprio loco inclusus à quo- uis prætereunte salutari ac adorari posset. Loca illa ciboria dixerunt, quæ Græcè rectissimè τεμένια dixeris, quo vocabulo Matthæus vtitur. Author illorū fuit Honorius III. sub annū Christi 1225. quo tempore Franciscanorum quoq; & Dominicanorum ordines cœperūt, & Pontificū authoritate confirmati sunt. Et ne quid deesset fictitio illi Christo, eidem Vrbanus IIII. anno 1264. diem sacrum fecit, quem Festum corporis Christi ridiculè nominant, eo ipso nimirum profitentes, se corpus sine spiritu colere. Quibus verò turbis interea orbis terrarum collisus, quot familiæ illustres figmentis iis ad inopiam redactæ, quot animarum millia horribiliter excruciata sint, longum foret commemorare. Sentimus adhuc hodie imposituram illā: & præcipuæ nostri seculi turbæ, quibus Ecclesiæ inter sese committuntur, ab iis potissimum excitari solent, qui Christum iam in cælis regnantem simplici vul- go in terris monstrant, & tantùmnon his ipsis verbis vtuntur: Ecce hic, Ecce illic.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who, by the manner of his saying, so answers that at the same time he teaches from what danger the godly ought most of all to guard themselves, when they see such movements and disturbances arising. Namely, that there will be very many impostors among the dangers, who point to the promised Redeemer here and there, and by inventing new plans of salvation every day make everyone uncertain of counsel and help. For they will say to you: "Behold, here," or "Behold, there." In Matthew and Mark these things are set out at greater length: "Then if anyone shall say to you, 'Behold, here is Christ,' or 'there,' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise, and will show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if it were possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you beforehand. If therefore they say to you, 'Behold, he is in the desert,' do not go out; 'Behold, he is in the inner chambers' or 'the storerooms' (for the Greek word signifies these more precisely), do not believe it." He calls false christs those who sold themselves under the name of the promised Messiah or Saviour, of whom we have noted in our Mark, from Josephus, that there were many before the destruction of the city and of the whole nation. And the Jews deserved that impostors and those magicians should prepare their ruin, since they were unwilling to acknowledge and embrace the true Christ commending his doctrine by so many saving signs. See Homil. 107 and 110. Similar examples have been put forth in all ages. So Pharaoh and the Egyptians were deceived by their magicians, who would not hear Moses and Aaron. And to many kings of Judah and Israel, who treated the servants of God more insolently, the false prophets, whom they held in esteem, were a cause of destruction. That the same has happened in the latest times, no one is ignorant who has merely glanced at the history of the Church. For after the purer and simpler doctrine of Christ began to be despised by the world, straightway the door was opened to impostures; and on the one hand the Mahumetan furies disturbed the East, while in the West the Pontiffs claimed for themselves the dominion of the Church, by whose cunning and tyranny it came about that, the true knowledge of Christ having been blotted out of men's minds, they followed a new Christ, one unknown in earlier ages, who, forsooth, made out of flour and water in a frying pan and consecrated by five words, was offered daily as a sacrifice for the sins of the living and the dead. This mystery of iniquity began to be stirred under the year of Christ 844, when Sergius held the Roman see, whom historians report had earlier been called by the fateful and monstrous name Pig's Snout. Nor did he receive a better fate in the name Sergius, since about two hundred years before him a monk Sergius had given Mahumet to the Orient. Moreover, when the Pontiffs had fashioned such a Christ for us, as we have said, the power of the priests, both of themselves and of the others whom they consecrated to his ministry, began to grow more and more every day. And it seemed too little to them if the people believed that Christ was bodily present meanwhile while the rites were performed; but, lest their work should always be required, they devised such a Christ who, once made, would last longer and, shut up in his own place, could be saluted and adored by any passer-by. They called those places ciboria, which in Greek you would most rightly call temenia [τεμένια], a word Matthew uses. The author of these was Honorius III, under the year of Christ 1225, at which time the orders of the Franciscans and the Dominicans also began and were confirmed by papal authority. And lest anything be lacking to that fictitious Christ, Urban IV in the year 1264 made the same a sacred day, which they ridiculously call the Feast of Corpus Christi, thereby of course professing that they worship a body without a spirit. How many tumults the world was thrown into meanwhile, how many illustrous families were reduced to poverty by those figments, how many thousands of souls were horribly tortured, would be a long matter to recount. We still feel that imposture today: and the chief disturbances of our age, by which the churches are set against one another, are for the most part stirred up by those who point out to the simple common people a Christ now reigning in heaven, and use almost these very words: "Behold, here; behold, there."

units.la: Non minus ergo nobis, quàm discipulis, seruit Domini consilium, quod duobus verbis Lucas comprehendit: Sed ne abite, neq; prosequimini: ita admonens, vt ne obiter quidem impositorum illorum voces sequamur, nedum studiū aliquod impendamus, quod nos vel minimum illis tribuere testetur. Causam præcepti huius addit: Nam sicut fulgur coruscans ex vna regione quæ sub cælo est, in alteram quæ sub cælo est, splendet: ita erit & Filius hominis in die suo. Sensus est, non alium eius adventum expectari debere, quàm illustrem illum, quo ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos veniet: aduentum verò illum subitum fore instar fulguris, vt neq; digito eminus aut cominus monstrari, neq; certus illi locus designari posset. Quæ verba si diligentius expendantur, sola sufficere possunt ad confutandos duos insignes errores, quibus crassa illa corporis Christi præsentia in Cœna statuitur, & Christi meritum certis locis alligatur, quæ persuasio peregrinationum superstitionem peperit, de qua alibi prolixè diximus.
units.tr: It is therefore no less a counsel for us than for the disciples of the Lord, which Luke sums up in two words: "But do not go away, nor follow them." He thus warns us not even in passing to follow those false voices, much less to give any attention to them, since that very thing would testify that we attribute some small credit to them. He adds the reason for this command: "For as the lightning, flashing out of one part under heaven, shines to the other part under heaven, so will the Son of Man be in his day." The meaning is that we ought not to expect any other coming of him than the illustrious one by which he will come to judge the living and the dead; and that his coming will be sudden, like lightning, so that it cannot be pointed out with a finger, either from afar or near at hand, and no certain place can be assigned for it. If these words are weighed more carefully, they are sufficient by themselves to refute two notable errors: the first, by which that crude bodily presence of Christ is set up in the Supper, and the second, by which the merit of Christ is tied to certain places. This persuasion gave birth to the superstition of pilgrimages, of which we have spoken at length elsewhere.

units.la: Cæterùm ne discipuli suspicarentur, Christum nō ita multò post regni sui maiestatem tanta cum gloria & virtute manifestaturum esse, quod errore terreni regni expectatione rursus confirmare potuisset, diserte docet, quid ipse prius passurus sit, dicēs: Sed prius oportet me multa pati, & reprobari à natione ista. Quasi diceret: Tam abest, vt huius seculi more inter Iudæos regnaturus sim, vt potius me ab illis reiici, contumeliosissimè tractari, & diram atq; infamē mortem in cruce perpeti oportet. Rursus ergo admonemur, Regnum Dei in terris cum cruce coniunctum esse, adeoq; ipsum Dei Filium, qui illius Mediator atq; instaurator est, per crucem in illud esse ingressum. Et hoc illud est, quod omnes scripturæ passim inculcant, & in cuius meditatione nos indefinetet versari conuenit. Eo enim admonemur, nobis quoad in carne viuimus, per multa certamina eluctandum esse ad cœlestem patriam. Ad ea ergo præparemur, & oremus Deum Patrem, vt regnum suum in nobis instauret, & viribus nouis instruat, quibus confirmati Filium eius Iesum Christum sequi, & cum eodē cœlestē illud & immortale gaudium obtinere possimus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, lest the disciples should suspect that Christ would reveal the majesty of his kingdom with great glory and power not long after, a thing which the error of an earthly kingdom could again have confirmed in their expectation, he plainly teaches what he himself must first suffer, saying: "But first it is necessary for me to suffer many things and to be rejected by this generation." As if he said: So far is it from being the case that I shall reign among the Jews after the manner of this age, that rather I must be rejected by them, treated with the greatest contumely, and endure a dreadful and infamous death on the cross. Therefore we are again admonished that the kingdom of God on earth is joined with the cross, and that the Son of God himself, who is its Mediator and restorer, entered into it through the cross. And this is what all the Scriptures inculcate everywhere, and in the meditation on which we ought to be constantly occupied. For we are admonished by it that, as long as we live in the flesh, we must struggle through many conflicts to reach the heavenly fatherland. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for these, and let us pray God the Father that he would restore his kingdom in us and furnish us with new strength, by which, being confirmed, we may be able to follow his Son Jesus Christ and obtain with him that heavenly and immortal joy. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXIIII.

units.la: Et prout factum est in diebus Noe, ita erit etiam in diebus Filij hominis: edebant, bibebant, uxores ducebant & dabantur nuptum, ad eū usque diem, quo introiuit Noa in arcam, venitqʒ diluuium, & perdidit omnes. Similiter etiam ut accidit in diebus Loti: edebant, bibebāt, emebant, vendebant, plantabant, ædificabant. Quo autem die Lot exiuit Sodomis, pluit igne & sulphure è cœlo, & omnes perdidit. Secundum hæc erit dies, quo Filius hominis reuelabitur.
units.tr: "And as it was in the days of Noah, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man: they were eating and drinking, they were marrying and being given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Likewise also as it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day that Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all. According to these things will be the day on which the Son of man is revealed."

units.la: VT homo ex innato suiipsius amore in omnibus aliis rebus siue actionibus suum commodum & præsentis vitæ felicitatem quærit: ita id cum primis circa religionem facere solet. Est hæc causa multorum scandalorum, dum alij sub religionis prætextu carnis licentia secuti impuris mundi studijs sese accomodant: alij vero in persecutionibus à fide turpiter deficiunt. Non temere ergo Christus de Regno suo apud discipulos frequenter disserit. Et nuper quidem docuit differre, illud non terrenum aut temporarium, sed spirituale esse, & in eo consistere, ut dum hanc vitā viuimus, ipsum suo Verbo & Spiritu in nobis patiamur regnare, defuncti autem hac vita cum eodem in cœlis regnemus æternum. Quia vero caro ab his natura abhorret, mox pœnas commemorauit, quæ Regni sui contemptoribus iam paratæ sint: ut nimirum non modo æterna & cœlestia bona amittant (quæ facile contemnunt, cum non credant aliam vitam vnquam futuram esse) verumetiam in hoc sæculo calamitatibus omnis generis obruti, simul consolatione omni destituantur, & impostoribus præda fiant, qui ipsos vanis & noxijs promissionibus ludificent. Quod ut olim Iudæis euenit, ita hodie multis accidit, qui Veritatis doctrinam fastidiunt. Porrò ne quid nobis deesset in re maximi momenti, transit modo ad describendos nouissimorum temporum mores, quibus pœnam quoque denuntiat, improuisum videlicet & ipsis horribilem totius mundi finem, quem subterfugere nullo modo possint. Finis autem & vsus loci istius est, ut præmoniti nos communi exemplo non patiamur seduci, ne cum infelicibus istis eadem impiæ securitatis pœnas luamus. Ut vero tota hæc commemoratio illustrior sit, & animos natura stupidos efficacius moueat, similibus, seu potius exemplis agit iudiciorum Dei, quibus olim homines incurabiles & pœnitere nescios multauit. Possunt illa, cum eadem fere sint, simul comprehendi: sed cum Christus de singulis peculiarem sermonem fecerit, nos quoque singula diligentius considerare non pigeat. Ea enim in his est hominum stupiditas, ut nulla diligentia animia aut superuacanea esse possit.
units.tr: As a man, from his innate self-love, seeks his own advantage and the happiness of this present life in all other matters and actions, so he is especially wont to do the same in matters of religion. This is the cause of many scandals: some, under the pretext of religion, follow the license of the flesh and accommodate themselves to the impure pursuits of the world, while others shamefully fall away from the faith in persecutions. It is not without reason, then, that Christ so often speaks to his disciples about his Kingdom. Recently he taught that this Kingdom is not earthly or temporary but spiritual, and that it consists in this: while we live this life he allows himself to reign in us by his Word and Spirit, and after we have departed this life we shall reign with him in heaven for ever. But because the flesh naturally shrinks from these things, he soon mentioned the punishments already prepared for the despisers of his Kingdom: namely, that they will lose not only the eternal and heavenly goods, which they easily scorn because they do not believe that another life will ever come, but also that, overwhelmed in this world by calamities of every kind, they will at the same time be deprived of all consolation and become the prey of impostors who will mock them with empty and harmful promises. As this happened once to the Jews, so today it happens to many who despise the doctrine of the truth.
