Moreover, lest anything be lacking to us in a matter of the greatest importance, he now turns to describe the morals of the last times, and at the same time threatens punishment, namely the sudden end of the whole world, which is terrible to them and which they can by no means escape. The purpose and use of this passage is that, being forewarned by the common example, we should not allow ourselves to be seduced, lest we pay the same penalties of impious security along with those unhappy people. To make this whole recollection more vivid, and to move minds that are naturally dull more effectively, he also brings forward similar examples, or rather examples, of the judgments of God, by which he once punished men who were incurable and unable to repent. These can be taken together, since they are almost the same; but since Christ made a particular discourse about each, let us not be unwilling to consider each more carefully. For such is human stupidity that no diligence in these matters can be superfluous.

units.la: Primum est primi seculi aut noui mundi hominum, qui ante diluuium vixerunt. Prout factum est (inquit) in diebus Noæ, ita erit etiam in diebus Filij hominis. Vocat autem dies Filij hominis totum illud tempus, quod à suo natali vsq; ad finem mundi decurrit. Vt enim tempus Patriarcharum est illa ætas mundi, in qua ante legem latam patres floruerunt, ex quibus genus humanum in omnes terras propagatum est, & cum quibus fœdus atque promissiones salutis Deus subinde instaurauit: & rursus dies Mosis & Legis tempus illud denotat, quo Lex per Mosis ministerium promulgata regnauit: ita dies Filij hominis dicitur tempus illud nouissimum, quo Dei Filius in carne manifestatus ea omnia compleuit, quæ olim promissa & typis variis adumbrata fuerūt: & extenditur sæculum istud ad finem vsque, in quo ipse venturus est ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, ut redemptione nostram prorsus absoluat, corporibus quoq; nostris beata immortalitate in gloria cœlesti gaudentibus. Debet ergo hæc locutio obseruari diligenter aduersus eos, qui adhuc nouas quasdam mundi mutationes expectant, quales olim fuerunt, quæ in diluuio, in Legis promulgatione, & sub primum Christi aduentum factæ sunt. Quæ persuasio ut olim Chiliastis aut Millenarijs stultissimi erroris occasionem dedit: ita Mahumeti quoque fenestram aperuit, ut toti Orienti abs se confictas fabulas non minus impias quàm superstitiosas & noxias inueheret. Cùm enim Mosem Dei seruum & Prophetam magnum, hoc autem maiorem fateretur esse Iesum Christum, nunquam se tertium et omnium maximum Prophetam esse, vllis hominibus potuisset persuadere, si cogitassent totum illud nouissimum tempus, vsque ad consummationem sæculi ad Christum pertinere, neque aliquam vel
units.tr: The first is that of the people of the first age, or the new world, who lived before the flood. "As it happened," he says, "in the days of Noah, so it will be also in the days of the Son of man." Now he calls the days of the Son of man the whole time which runs from his birth to the end of the world. For just as the time of the Patriarchs is that age of the world in which the fathers flourished before the law was given, from whom the human race was spread over all lands, and with whom God repeatedly renewed the covenant and the promises of salvation; and again, the days of Moses and of the Law denote that period in which the Law, promulgated through the ministry of Moses, reigned: so the days of the Son of man are said to be that final time in which the Son of God, made manifest in the flesh, fulfilled all those things that had been promised of old and foreshadowed by various types; and this age extends to the end, in which he himself will come to judge the living and the dead, so that he may completely free our redemption, our bodies also rejoicing in heavenly glory with blessed immortality. This manner of speaking must therefore be observed carefully against those who still expect some new changes of the world, such as once occurred at the flood, at the promulgation of the Law, and at the first coming of Christ. As this persuasion once gave occasion of the most foolish error to the Chiliasts or Millenarians, so it also opened a window for Mahomet, so that he might bring into the whole East fables invented by himself, no less impious than superstitious and harmful. For since he admitted that Moses was the servant of God and a great Prophet, but that Jesus Christ was greater than this one, he could never have persuaded men that he was the third and greatest of all Prophets, if they had considered that the whole of that last time, until the consummation of the age, pertains to Christ, and that no further change either of doctrine or of external worship ought to be expected.

units.la: Ddd doctrinæ vel externi cultus mutationem porrò debere expectari. Nos itaq; aliorum exemplo cautio res facti, omnes eos caueamus, qui nobis nouũ quid & hucusque inauditũ obtrudere conantur. Nulla enim in hac mundi senescentis & quotidie in peius proficientis ætate postrema mutatio in melius sperari potest, quàm quæ in nouissimo Christi aduentu fiet, qui & machinæ mundi huius & corruptis hominum moribus finem imponet, suos autem ad se recipiet, vt æternùm cum ipso viuant.
units.tr: Therefore let us, taking warning from the example of others, beware of all those who try to thrust upon us something new and hitherto unheard of. For in this age of a world that is growing old and daily going from bad to worse, no final change for the better can be hoped for, other than that which will take place at the last coming of Christ, who will both put an end to the machinery of this world and to the corrupt morals of men, and will take his own to himself, that they may live with him for ever.

units.la: Quia verò eandem hominũ conditionem fore dicit, quæ olim temporibus Noæ ante diluuium fuit, proderit paulò diligentius illorum temporum historiam obseruauisse, vt & de nostri seculi moribus iudicare, & ab ijs nobis cauere possimus, quæ illis olim exitium attulerunt. Describitur hæc à Mose satis prolixè ipsius etiam Dei verbis, quibus si quæ in præsenti Christus dicit, adijcias, nihil deerit, quod ad illius cognitionem faciat. Summatim tamen præcipua capita perstringemus. Primò immanis Dei contemptus regnauit apud omnis loci et ordinis homines. Nam etiamsi Noam haberet præconem iustitiæ Dei, nemo tamẽ illum audiebat: sed toti caro erant, adeò vt nulla prorsus in illis spiritus Dei virtus siue operatio eluceret. Quod Deus ipse nõ obscurè his verbis testatur: Non contendet aut rixabitur Spiritus meus perpetuò cum homine, id est, non fatigabo aut discruciabo posthac meipsum propter hominẽ, in quo corrigendo me nihil proficere video, eò quòd caro sit, id est, totus carni & prauis eius cupiditatibus seruiat. At studia carnis, quibus tunc omnes vacauerũt, in præsenti Christus commemorat, dicens: Edebant, bibebant, vxores ducebant & dabantur nuptum, ad eum vsq; diem, quo introiit Noa in arcam, &c. Atqui edere, bibere, cõiugio copulari malanon sunt, neq; ullis legibus diuinis prohibita: imò dæmoniorum doctrinam dicit Apostolus, quæ ista prohibet: neq; aliter dici meretur, cùm illa ad conseruandum genus humanũ non minus necessaria sint quàm vtilia. Sed impia securitas notatur, & quòd Dei simul atq; iudiciorum siue comminationum eius immemores, voluptatibus magis quàm necessitati studuerint. Argumentum huius euidens est in cõiugijs imparibus, quæ tũc in quotidiano vsu fuisse, Moses apertè satis innuit, sic scribens: Cum cæpissent homines multiplicari super terram, natæq; illis essent filiæ: viderunt filij Dei filias hominum, quòd elegantes essent, & duxerunt sibi vxores ex omnibus, quas elegerant: Filios Dei dicit Sethi posteros, inter quos purior Dei cognitio atq; cultus hucusq; permansisset, cùm Cain & huius posteri iampridem à Dei conspectu reiecti proprium vitæ genus sibi ipsis delegissent: & hi Filij hominũ dicuntur, eò quòd extincto in illis prorsus filiorũ Dei semine, nihil quàm homines, id est, corrupti & peccatores essent. Quamuis ergo inter duas istas progenies discrimẽ satis luculentum posuisset Deus, eò tamen vsque securitas omnium progressa est, vt qui Dei veri cultum sincerioreм profitebantur, vxores sibi duceret ex Caini genere, superstitiosas, fastui, luxui et libidini deditas, & ita carnis suæ desideria religioni longè præferrent. Ex coniugijs autem eiusmodi progeniti sunt Nephilim, id est, homines defectores, quos ἀθεῖς dicere licebit. Quia enim à parentibus diuersarum religionum professoribus æducabantur, in diuersas quoq; sententias distracti nihil de Deo & eius cultu certum statuere poterant: & ideo paulatim euanescente in animis eorum omni Dei cognitione & timore, ad manifestam impietatem prolabebantur, quæ deinde nefandissimorum scelerum, omnis denique iniu stitiæ & violentiæ causa erat. Neq; intra paucos hæc pestis sese continuit, sed per totũ orbem propagata omnium mentes longè lateq; peruasit. Ideo Moses addidit: Et vidit Deus terram, & ecce corrupta fuit: nam omnis caro corruperat viam suam super terram. Qua locutione docet, apud omnes hominum ordines nihil sanum, nihil integrum, nihil iustum aut sanctũ fuisse. Et hæc quidem illorum studia fuerunt in eum vsque diem, quo Noa in arcam cum suis ingressus est, diluuium verò ex improuiso immissum omnes perdidit. Nihil ergo vel admonitiones piissimi serui Dei, vel eiusdẽ exemplum eos mouit, cùm viderent virum multa authoritate grauem, commune quoddam & ingens malum animo præuidere, seq; ipsum ad illud euitandum præparare. Fuit ergo hoc malitiæ incurabilis argumentum, vt de alijs iam nihil dicatur, quæ ipsos mouere debuissent,
units.tr: But since he says that the condition of men will be the same as it was once in the days of Noah before the flood, it will be useful to have observed the history of those times a little more carefully, so that we may both judge the morals of our own age and guard ourselves against those things which once brought ruin upon them. Moses describes this at considerable length, in the very words of God, and if you add to these what Christ says in the present passage, nothing will be lacking that pertains to knowledge of it. Nevertheless, we shall touch briefly upon the chief points. First, a monstrous contempt for God reigned among men of every place and rank. For although Noah had as a herald of God's justice, nevertheless no one listened to him; rather, all were flesh, so that no virtue or operation of the Spirit of God shone forth in them at all. God himself bears witness to this not obscurely in these words: "My Spirit shall not contend or strive with man for ever, that is, I shall no longer wear out or torment myself on account of man, in whose correction I see that I accomplish nothing, because he is flesh, that is, wholly given over to the flesh and its wicked desires." But the pursuits of the flesh, with which all men were then occupied, Christ mentions in the present passage, saying: "They were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, etc." And yet to eat, to drink and to be joined in marriage are not evil in themselves, nor forbidden by any divine law; indeed, the Apostle calls the doctrine of demons that which forbids these things; nor do they deserve to be called otherwise, since they are no less necessary for preserving the human race than useful. But the impious security is what is condemned, and the fact that, forgetful of God and of his judgments or threats at the same time, they devoted themselves more to pleasures than to necessity. Evidence of this is clear in the unequal marriages, which Moses plainly enough indicates were then in everyday use, writing thus: "When men had begun to multiply upon the earth, and daughters had been born to them, the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose." By the sons of God he means the posterity of Seth, among whom the purer knowledge and worship of God had persisted until then, since Cain and his posterity had long been cast out from the sight of God and had chosen for themselves a manner of life of their own; and these are called the sons of men, because, the seed of the sons of God having been utterly extinguished in them, they were nothing but men, that is, corrupt and sinners. Although God had therefore set a clear enough distinction between these two lines, yet the security of all went so far that those who professed a purer worship of the true God took for themselves wives from the race of Cain, superstitious, given to pride, luxury and lust, and so they placed the desires of their flesh far above religion. Now from marriages of this kind were born the Nephilim, that is, men who were deserters, whom one may call godless [ἄθεοι]. For since they were brought up by parents who professed different religions, they were drawn in different directions and could establish nothing certain about God and his worship; and so, as all knowledge and fear of God gradually faded from their minds, they slipped into open impiety, which afterwards was the cause of the most wicked crimes and finally of every kind of injustice and violence. Nor was this plague confined within a few people, but spreading through the whole world it invaded the minds of all far and wide. Therefore Moses added: "And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupted; for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth." By this expression he teaches that among all orders of men nothing was sound, nothing whole, nothing just or holy. And these, indeed, were their pursuits until the day when Noah entered the ark with his household, and the flood, sent upon them unexpectedly, destroyed them all. Nothing, then, moved them, neither the admonitions of the most pious servant of God nor his example, although they saw a man of great authority and gravity foresee a common and huge evil in his mind and prepare himself to avoid it. This, therefore, was the proof of an incurable wickedness, so that nothing need be said of other things which ought to have moved them,

units.la: At si ista ad nostrum seculum transferamus, eosdem mores & eadem studia hodie etiã regnare videbis. Prædicatur equidem Dei verbum, & vbique locorum audiuntur præcones iustitiæ, & quod mirum est, plerique intra conscientias suas conuicti, illos vera dicere fatentur. Nam quoscum que hominum cœtus siue publicos in foro, siue priuatos ingrediaris, multos de vniuersali & intolerabili omnium ordinum corruptione conqueri audies, quam ingens aliquod malum breui sequatur oportet. eportet. Sed quotus quisq; est, qui vitam suam emendet, mores suos corrigat, vel ad reformationem publicam animũ serió adiciat? Carni certè & desiderijs carnalibus omnes student, & pleriq; etiam Euangelij prætextu ad suam licentiã abutuntur: vt de illis nunc nihil dicam, qui quam omnes deplorant communem omnium ordinum confusionem, à solis Verbi administris ne attingi quidem volunt. Regnant ergo passim quæ hoc loco Christus prædixit: comessandi & belluandi studium insatiabile, ebrietas exemplo carens, securitas profundissima, intemperantia omnis generis, & effrenis libido. In matrimonijs quæ gentes olim sacrosancta haberi voluerunt, hodie nulla siue Dei siue religionis ratio habetur, sed in illis contrahendis consultores iam optimi putantur libido & auaritia. Itaq; cum impijs Euangelicæ veritatis hostibus per coniugij vinculũ coalescunt, qui illius cultores & sectatores volunt censeri, & (quod grauiter olim Paulus prohibuit) iugum ducunt cum incredulis aut infidelibus. Non possunt autem in eiusmodi coniugijs liberi rectè institui aut in veri Dei cultu erudiri, cùm semper in alterutro parente exemplum diuersum occurrat. Itaque augetur indies tergiuersatorum numerus, qui cùm religionem aut omnino nullam intra animos suos habeant, aut illam putent esse indifferentem, omnia pro mundi infelicis arbitrio, & prout ipsis commodũ esse videtur, dicunt atque faciunt. Fit ergo quod de Noæ temporibus Moses scripsit, vt omnis caro, id est, omnis loci & ordinis homines vitam suam corrumpant, dum à vocatione sua discedunt, vel saltem posthabita gloria Dei & publica salute suis modò commodis atque pessimis cupiditatibus student. Potentissimi Reges bellis non necessarijs inter se committuntur, & cæteros principes in partes trahunt. Pontifices per suos emissarios ad illa classicum canunt & frigidam suffundunt. Inter eos qui Euangelium profitentur, Ecclesiarum ministri vel inter sese hostiliter disceptant de rebus nihili, seque inuicem dilacerant, vel otio deditï belluantur, et morum leuitate, luxu et fastu ab improbissimis huius seculi filijs nihil differunt. Inter priuatos homines alij vsuras exercent voracissimas, alij vsuris opprimuntur atq; deuorantur, vtrinque verò omnes libidine, luxu, petulantia & nequitia diffluunt, & cùm in solo scelerum immanissimorum studio consentiant, interea odijs ringuntur, cõuitijs, litibus, iurgijs, pugnis, turbis cùm publicis tum priuatis omnia miscent. Et quàmuis præter Verbi commonitiones multa indies audiantur & omnium oculis videantur, quæ iam Dei toti mundo iam imminere portendunt, communis tamen veternus omnium animos ita oppressit, vt de pœnis euitandis nemo cogitet, durabilem verò omnes sibi polliceantur rerum huius seculi conditionem. Imò quasi non satis scelerum in mundo sit, publicè audiuntur impij illi derisores, qui (vt Petrus prædixit) mirificis ludibrijs in dubium vocant omnem doctrinam, quam de fine huius seculi, de mortuorum resurrectione & animarum immortalitate, de cælestis vitæ gaudijs & horrendis infernalium pœnarum tormentis, Christus & Apostoli tradiderunt.
units.tr: But if we carry these things over to our own age, you will see the same manners and the same pursuits reigning today as well. The Word of God is indeed preached, and everywhere heralds of righteousness are heard, and, remarkably, many people, convicted within their own consciences, admit that they speak the truth. For whatever gatherings of men you enter, public in the marketplace or private, you will hear many lamenting the universal and intolerable corruption of all orders, which must soon be followed by some great evil. But how few there are who amend their life, correct their morals, or seriously apply their minds to public reform? Certainly all strive after the flesh and carnal desires, and many even abuse the pretext of the Gospel to indulge their own licence. I say nothing now of those who, while they all deplore the common confusion of every order, do not want even the ministers of the Word to be touched. So everywhere reign the things Christ foretold in this place: an insatiable zeal for feasting and gluttony, drunkenness without precedent, the deepest security, intemperance of every kind, and unbridled lust. In marriages, which the nations of old wished to be held most sacred, today no regard for God or religion is had; instead, lust and greed are thought to be the best advisers in arranging them. And so people join in the bond of marriage with the impious enemies of evangelical truth, though they wish to be counted its worshippers and followers, and (as Paul gravely forbade) they draw the yoke with unbelievers or infidels. Children in such marriages cannot be rightly brought up or instructed in the true worship of God, since a contrary example always meets them in one parent or the other. And so the number of time-servers grows daily; having either no religion at all within their minds, or thinking it a matter of indifference, they say and do everything according to the whim of the unhappy world and as seems convenient to themselves. So it happens, as Moses wrote of the times of Noah, that all flesh, that is, men of every place and order, corrupt their lives while they depart from their calling, or at least, setting aside the glory of God and the public good, pursue only their own advantage and their worst desires. The most powerful kings are drawn into unnecessary wars against one another and draw the other princes into their parties. The Pontiffs, through their emissaries, sound the trumpet for these wars and pour cold water on the peace. Among those who profess the Gospel, the ministers of the churches either wrangle hostilely among themselves over trifles and tear one another apart, or, given over to idleness, indulge in gluttony, and in levity of manners, luxury and arrogance they differ in nothing from the most wicked sons of this age. Among private persons, some practise the most voracious usury, others are crushed and devoured by usury; on both sides all overflow with lust, luxury, wantonness and wickedness, and while they agree in their sole zeal for the most monstrous crimes, meanwhile they are torn by hatreds and mix everything with public and private reproaches, lawsuits, quarrels, fights and disturbances. And although, besides the admonitions of the Word, many things are heard daily and seen before the eyes of all, which already portend God's judgement hanging over the whole world, nevertheless a common lethargy has so oppressed the minds of all that no one thinks about escaping punishment, and everyone promises himself a lasting state of the affairs of this age. Indeed, as if there were not enough wickedness in the world, those impious scoffers are heard openly who (as Peter foretold) with marvellous mockery call into doubt all the teaching that Christ and the Apostles handed down: concerning the end of this age, the resurrection of the dead and the immortality of souls, the joys of heavenly life, and the dreadful torments of the punishments of hell.

units.la: Mouentur hac vniuersali totius mundi corruptione pij non parum, & interdũ Deum putant æquo neglegentiorem esse, qui ista tam diu fieri patiatur: multi etiam exemplo multitudinis abstracti in vero Dei cultu & omnibus, quæ ad æternam salutem spectant, remissius agere incipiunt. At hiis vitijs remedium adhibet Christus, quando pœnam quoq; commemorat, qua primi mundi securitatem atq; licentiam Deus tandem compescuit: Venit diluuium (inquit) & perdidit omnes. Paucis verbis horribilem totius mundi interitum comprehendit. Veniendi enim verbo improuisam & subitam pœnam denotat, quæ nihil tale opinantibus accidit. Et quæ nam illa? Diluuiũ, id est, vniuersalis aquarum omniũ tam earum quæ in mari sunt quàm fluuiorum, lacuum & torrentium inundatio. Nam hæ omnes (vt Moses scribit) tã imbribus cœlestibus quàm propriorum fontium redundantia auctæ omnes campos, vrbes, vicos, ædificia deniq; omnia tã publica quàm priuata operuerũt, imò montiũ quoq; cacumina superarunt. Additur, Et perdidit omnes, diuites nimirum & pauperes, viros & fœminas, nobiles & ignobiles, iuuenes & senes. Neminem ergo generis nobilitas seruauit, nemini diuitiæ profuerũt, nemini vita in delitijs et voluptatibus transacta, nemini ætas aut corporis vires, nemini mundi authoritas vel honores auxilio fuerunt: quò minus vnũ diluuiũ tam vitæ ipsorũ, quàm delitijs et petulantiæ finem imponeret. Solus Noa per fidè admonitus (vt in Epistola ad Hebræos scribitur) Dei timore concepto arcam præparauit, cuius beneficio cum suis filijs eorumq; vxoribus seruatus est, vt tam generis humani quàm Ecclesiæ Dei seminarium extaret. Fuit ista horribilis rerum facies, quæ haud dubiè sanctissimũ quoq; virum vehementer terruit: nec fieri potest, quin ho-
units.tr: Godly people are not a little moved by this universal corruption of the whole world, and sometimes they think God is too careless to allow these things to continue for so long. Many, too, drawn away by the example of the multitude, begin to act more negligently in the true worship of God and in all the things that concern eternal salvation. But Christ applies a remedy to these vices when he also recalls the punishment by which God at last restrained the security and licence of the first world: "The flood came," he says, "and destroyed them all." In a few words he sums up the dreadful destruction of the whole world. The word "came" denotes a punishment that is unforeseen and sudden, and that falls upon those who suspect nothing of the kind. And what was it? A flood, that is, a universal inundation of all the waters, both those in the sea and those of rivers, lakes and torrents. For all these, as Moses writes, swollen both by the heavenly rains and by the overflowing of their own springs, covered all the fields, cities, villages and buildings, public and private alike, and even rose above the tops of the mountains. It is added, "and destroyed them all": rich and poor certainly, men and women, noble and commoners, young and old. So nobility of birth saved no one, riches profited no one, a life spent in pleasures and delights helped no one, age or bodily strength helped no one, the authority or honours of the world helped no one; so that one flood put an end to their lives no less than to their delights and wantonness. Only Noah, warned through faith (as is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews), having conceived a fear of God, prepared the ark, by whose benefit he was saved with his sons and their wives, so that there might remain a seed both of the human race and of the Church of God. That was a dreadful sight of things, which surely terrified even the most holy man greatly; nor can it be that

units.la: Hebr.11. die eorum animi exhorrescant, qui exemplum illud iudicij diuini diligentius secum expendunt. At non in illo nos subsistere oportet, sed animi cogitationes, in nosipsos couertere, vt discamus idem nouissimis quoque temporibus euenturum esse, vt vniuersa haec mundi machina vno incendio conflagret cum omnibus, quae nunc nobis admirationi sunt, & subitum exitium eos abripiat, qui sibi in multos annos omnia laeta, adhaec posteris suis aeternitatem mundi pollicentur. Nam vt Paulus scribit, cum dixerint, Pax pax, repentinus illis imminebit interitus, vt partus dolores praegnanti muleri. Et Petrus: Veniet noctu, sicut fur, dies ille Domini: quo caeli cum stridore praeteribunt, elementa vero aestuantia soluentur, terraq; et quae in ea sunt opera exurentur. Tunc (vt apud Matthaeum Christus ait) plangent omnes tribus terrae, & videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus caeli cum potestate & gloria multa. Debet istorum recordatio nunquam non animis nostris obuersari, & facile cauebimus, ne infelicis mundi exemplo seducamur. Nam simul hoc quoq; occurret, Noam cum suis in arca sola vitae praesidium habuisse: quo exemplo simul adumbratum fuit, in extremo illo fine huius seculi non alios saluos fore, quam qui relicto mundo & huius studijs, Ecclesiae Christi sese coniunxerint, quam is vt dilectam sponsam inter huius mundi turbas & pericula seruat, & cum in gloria sua apparuerit, Regni sui caelestis & aeternae vitae consortem habebit.
units.tr: Heb. 11. the hearts of those who weigh that example of divine judgement more carefully with themselves should not tremble. But we ought not to dwell upon that alone; we should turn the thoughts of our minds upon ourselves, so that we may learn that the same will happen in the last times as well: this whole machine of the world will be consumed by one fire, together with all the things that are now objects of our admiration, and sudden destruction will snatch away those who promise themselves all happiness for many years and, besides, eternity of the world for their posterity. For as Paul writes, when they say, "Peace, peace," sudden destruction will hang over them, like labour pains upon a pregnant woman. And Peter: "The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the elements, burning, will be dissolved, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up." Then (as Christ says in Matthew) "all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory." The remembrance of these things ought never to leave our minds, and we will easily take care not to be led astray by the example of the unhappy world. For at the same time this also will come to mind: Noah with his family had the sole protection of life in the ark; by this example it was also foreshadowed that at that final end of this age none will be saved except those who, having left the world and its pursuits, have joined themselves to the Church of Christ, which he preserves, as his beloved bride, amid the tumults and dangers of this world, and when he appears in his glory, he will have as partner of his heavenly kingdom and eternal life.

units.la: Porro alterum quoque exemplum videamus, quod ex historia temporum Loti & Abrahami adducit, & proprie ad Sodomaeos atque Gomorrhaeos pertinet. Mores horum ijsdem fere verbis describit, quibus antea vsus erat. Edebant (inquit) bibebat, emebant, vendebant, plantabant, aedificabant. Sunt & haec omnia per se licita, sed abusum, quem nimia securitas peperat, reprehendit, de quo Deus ipse per Ezechielem sic disserit: Ecce haec fuit iniquitas Sodomae sororis tuae: fastus, abundantia panis, felicitas, otium: haec habuit ipsa & filiae eius, sed & manum pauperis & egeni non firmauit. Cum q; sic fastuosae essent, designarunt abominanda quaedam in conspectu meo: quas abieci, cum illa vidissem. Ederunt ergo & biberunt, non vt decet, sed cum agros haberent fertilissimos, quos Scriptura paradiso Domini confert, & insuper felicitate & otio abundarent, saturitas illa in luxum nefarium degeneravit, vt ebrietati & immodico voluptatum studio addicti domus Dei turpiter aburentur. Luxum comitata est superbia & immanis fastus, qui contemptum pauperum & peregrinorum, adhaec odium quoq; piarum admonitionum peperit. Cuius rei egregium specimen pridie quam perirent, dederunt. Cum enim Angeli humana specie velati Sodomam vespere venissent, nemo qui eos exciperet hospitio inuentus est, praeter vnum Lotum qui & ipse peregrinus erat. Cives autem non contenti barbara inhospitalitate, insuper cum iam bene potiti essent, quasi publico tumultu orto domum Loti obsederunt, & hospites ad foedam & detestandam libidinem sibi tradi postularunt. Neque hoc paucorum scelus fuit, sed omnium: quando senes quoque & pueros, adeoque populum vniuersum ab extremis partibus vrbis confluxisse Moses scribit. Fuit ergo incomparabilis istorum hominum malitia, cui securitas accesserat, quam in praesenti Dominus plantandi et aedificandi verbis comprehendit. His enim innuit, eos quamuis in singulas horas Dei iram contra se prouocarent, vitae tamen suae rationes perinde instituisse, ac si perpetuo victuri essent, & extra omnem telifactum essent constituti. Contumacia vero incurabilis argumentum luculentissimum fuit, quod cum non ita pridem ab hostibus bello victi & captiui abducerentur, Abrahami autem beneficio liberati atque sedibus suis restituti essent, non modo ad mores suos & scelera pristina redierunt, sed Lotu quoq; odio hostili prosecuti sunt, cuius patruus tam praeclarae restitutionis author ipsis fuerat. Ita deniq; omnium illorum mentes libido nefaria obsederat, vt Lotum iam abiturum ne generi quidem sequi voluerint, quibus eius filiae iam desponsatae erant.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us also consider another example, which he adduces from the history of the times of Lot and Abraham, and which pertains specifically to the Sodomites and Gomorrhites. He describes their manners in almost the same words he had used before: "They were eating," he says, "drinking, buying, selling, planting, building." All these things are lawful in themselves, but he rebukes the abuse that excessive security had produced, about which God himself speaks through Ezekiel as follows: "Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, abundance of bread, prosperity, idleness; she and her daughters had these, but they did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. And being thus haughty, they committed abominable things in my sight, which I cast away when I saw them." They therefore ate and drank, not as is fitting, but since they had most fertile fields, which Scripture compares to the paradise of the Lord, and moreover abounded in prosperity and idleness, that satiety degenerated into wicked luxury, so that, given over to drunkenness and an immoderate zeal for pleasures, they shamefully defiled the house of God. Luxury was accompanied by pride and monstrous arrogance, which bred contempt for the poor and strangers and, besides, hatred even of pious admonitions. They gave an outstanding example of this the day before they perished. For when the angels came to Sodom in the evening, veiled in human form, no one was found to receive them into hospitality except Lot alone, who was himself a stranger. But the citizens, not content with barbarous inhospitality, and moreover, when they had already got the upper hand, as if a public tumult had arisen, besieged Lot's house and demanded that the guests be handed over to them for foul and detestable lust. Nor was this the crime of a few, but of all: since Moses writes that old men and boys, and indeed the whole people, had flocked together from the farthest parts of the city. So the wickedness of these men was beyond compare, and security was added to it, which the Lord expressed in the words "planting and building." For by these words he signifies that, although they provoked God's wrath against themselves every hour, they nevertheless arranged the plans of their lives as if they were going to live forever and were set beyond every blow. Their obstinacy, which could not be cured, was a most striking proof of this: when not long before they had been conquered in war by enemies and led away captive, and had been freed by the benefit of Abraham and restored to their homes, they not only returned to their manners and former crimes, but also pursued Lot with hostile hatred, whose uncle Abraham had been the author of that splendid restoration to them. Thus at last unspeakable lust had so possessed the minds of all of them that they did not even want to follow Lot, though he was now about to depart, not even his sons-in-law, to whom his daughters were already betrothed.

units.la: Conueniunt ista quoque nouissimorum temporum, in quae nos incidimus, studijs atque moribus. Regnat enim apud omnes homines luxus & nefarius abusus frugum cum manifesto Dei contemptu coniunctus. Est illi comes fastus & superbia, quam plerique vestitu indecoro, disciplinae & legum contemptu testantur. Otio autem ita omnes gaudent, vt a manuarijs opificijs plerique abhorreant, in otio autem ignauo atq; malesuado nobilitatem & gloriam praecipuam consistere putent. Et tolerabile videri poterat a superbis & otiosis & luxu perditis pauperes contemni atq; negligi, nisi praeterea partim vsurarijs artibus, partim sycophantico iuris legumque praetextu prorsus opprimerentur, & multis autem per vim diriperentur, qui bella mercenaria quaestum honestissimum esse ducunt. Libidi binde vero apud omnis loci & ordinis homines peccatur. Scortatio publicè defenditur, quam inter Christianos ne nominari quidem voluit Apostolus. Adulterium lusus & iocus putatur, & adulteri in foro, in Senatu, in cathedra sacra rerum gubernaculis assident. Et vtinam ab horrendo Sodomiæ flagitio immunes essent, qui inter Christianos Ecclesiæ proceres & summi religionis atq; fidei antistites haberi volunt. Interim verò cum ista omnia fiant, quæ gentes olim exitij mox secuturi causas esse intellexerunt, plerique tamen sibijpsis læta omnia pollicentur, hortos, vineta, agros conserunt, palatia ipsi cælo minantia extruunt, reddituus annuos in dies augent, vt à miseris agricolis & ciuibus noua rapacitate corradant, quod ipsorum luxui & libidini sufficiat. Adhuc tamen sua erga nos bonitatis memor Deus, suo officio egregiè fungitur. Nam & Verbi præcones excitat tanquam nostrates quàm peregrinos, & iudiciorum suorum exempla quotidie exhibet: adhæc vt Lotum propter religionem peregrinantem Sodomis induxit, ita passim exules hodie visuntur, qui purioris fidei & doctrinæ causa patrijs sedibus eiecti, suo exemplo docent: quid nos maneat, nisi in tempore resipiscamus. Sed nequic quam ista omnia. Imò plerique vix dum emersi ex aliquo graviori periculo redeunt ad studia carnis pessima, & fere fortuita dicunt esse ea, quibus Deus ipsorum petulantiam castigare voluit.
units.tr: These things also agree with the studies and morals of our most recent times, in which we have fallen. Luxury and the wicked abuse of good things, joined with open contempt for God, hold sway among all men. Pride and haughtiness accompany it, which most people display through indecent dress and contempt for discipline and the laws. Everyone delights so much in leisure that most shrink from manual trades, and they think nobility and especial glory consist in idle and vicious leisure. It might be tolerable that the poor are despised and neglected by the proud, the idle, and those ruined by luxury, if they were not also utterly crushed, partly by usury and partly under the pretext of law and by the sycophantic chicanery of lawyers, and if many were not robbed by force by those who count mercenary wars the most honourable form of gain. Lust is indulged everywhere, among men of every place and rank. Fornication is openly defended, though the Apostle did not wish it even to be named among Christians. Adultery is regarded as a game and a joke, and adulterers sit in the courts, in the senate, and in the sacred chair, at the helm of affairs. Would that those who wish to be counted among Christians as leaders of the Church and chief bishops of religion and faith were free from the horrible sin of Sodom! Meanwhile, though all these things are happening, which nations of old understood to be the causes of destruction soon to follow, most people nonetheless promise themselves everything happy: they plant gardens, vineyards, and fields, they build palaces that threaten the sky, they increase their annual revenues day by day, and they amass by fresh rapacity from wretched farmers and citizens whatever suffices for their luxury and lust. Yet God, still mindful of his goodness toward us, performs his duty well. For he raises up preachers of the Word, both our own countrymen and foreigners, and he displays daily examples of his judgements. Moreover, just as he led Lot, a pilgrim on account of religion, to Sodom, so today exiles are seen everywhere, who, driven from their native homes for the sake of purer faith and doctrine, teach by their example what awaits us, unless we repent in time. But all these things are in vain. Indeed, many, scarcely emerged from some more serious danger, return to the most wicked pursuits of the flesh, and they say that those things by which God wished to chastise their wantonness were nearly accidental.

units.la: Quoniam verò nostra hæc tempora cum Sodomæorum moribus atque studijs tam probè conueniunt, ad nos etiam pertinere putemus, quod de pœna illorum horrenda dicitur. Quo autem die (inquit Dominus) Lot exiuit Sodomis, pluit igne & sulphure è cœlo, & omnes perdidit. Et addit: Secundum hæc erit dies, quo Filius hominis reuelabitur. Fuit hoc non obscurum nouissimæ consummationis mundi præludium, quod Petrus Apostolus de impijs nouissimi iudicij contemptoribus loquens, diserte his verbis docet: Illud sponte ipsos latet, quòd cœli iam olim extiterunt per Dei sermone, & terra ex aqua & in aqua consistens. Quamobrem qui tunc erat mundus, aqua inundatus periit: qui verò nunc sunt cœli ac terra, eodem sermone repositi, seruantur igni in diem damnationis & exitij impiorum hominum. Fuit autem exemplum illud in Sodomis ædituum cum primis horribile, cuius perpetuam memoriam lacum Asphaltitim, quem Mare mortuum Scriptura nominat, Deus extare voluit, quam à prophanis quoque scriptoribus obseruatam esse, ex Strabone apparet. Quia verò subitum fuit illud incendium, et paucis horis vrbes plurimas cum agris adiacentibus consumpsit, rectè exemplum eius ad nouissimum illum Christi aduentum refertur, quando similiter ex improuiso tota mundi machina conflagrabit, & impios repentinus interitus abripiet.
units.tr: Since, however, our present times agree so well with the morals and pursuits of the Sodomites, let us think that what is said about their dreadful punishment pertains to us too. The Lord says: "On the day that Lot went out of Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all" (Luke 17:29). And he adds: "After the same manner shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed" (Luke 17:30). This was an unmistakable prelude to the final consummation of the world. The Apostle Peter, speaking of the impious scorners of the last judgement, teaches this plainly in these words: "For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water; whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgement and perdition of ungodly men" (2 Pet. 3:5-7). That example in Sodom was indeed most terrible, and God willed that its perpetual memory should remain in the lake Asphaltites, which Scripture calls the Dead Sea. That profane writers also observed it is clear from Strabo. Since that fire was sudden, and in a few hours consumed very many cities together with the adjacent fields, its example is rightly referred to that last coming of Christ, when in the same way the whole machinery of the world will be set on fire unexpectedly, and sudden destruction will snatch away the impious.

units.la: At quia hæc in suorum quoq; vsum Christus dixit, non temere dici putabimus, eo die pluisse igne & sulphure, quo Lot è Sodomis exiuit. Et id quidem Moses diligenter inculcat, qui illum ab Angelis eductum esse, & propter eum Zoar oppidum ex incendio illo seruatum fuisse scribit. Est exemplum hoc multa obseruatione dignissimum. Vt enim Deus propter suos cultores toti mundo benefacit, & sæpe in illorum gratiam regna & ciuitates amplissimas conseruat: ita his subductis aut è medio sublatis, impios punit. Ante quidem (vt diximus) propter Lotum Sodomæi ex hostium manu asserti, & suæ ciuitati restituti sunt: nunc autem eodem ex vrbe egresso, illa cœlestibus flammis exuri tur. Simile quid Hierosolymis accidit, quādo Ecclesia, quæ illic erat, oraculo admonita Pellam emigrauit, mox autem à Romanis illa obsessa, & tandem miserabiliter euersa est. Et de hoc Isaias quæritur, quando iustum colligi dicit priusquam dies illi mali veniant, quibus impiorum incurabilem malitiam Deus punire statuit. Ista nos admoneant, vt pios nobis commendatos habeamus. Simul autem consolationi seruiat exemplum Loti. Eo enim Petrus docet, posse Deum suos ex tentatione eripere, & tunc etiam seruare, quando vniuersali exitio pœnitere nescios perdit. Est enim (vt Propheta ait) apud Deum discrimen inter pium & impium, quod multis alijs quoq; exemplis demonstratum est, de quibus sæpe aliâs diximus. Itaque huius admonitionis memores, non patiamur nos publico mundi infelicis exemplo abripi, sed Noam atque Lotum secuti Deo fidem seruemus illibatam, neque dubitemus de promissionibus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui & huius seculi calamitates pro nostra imbecillitate temperabit, & nos tandem in beatæ immortalitatis portum ad se recipiet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But since Christ spoke these things also for the use of his own people, we shall think it not without reason that it rained fire and brimstone on the day Lot went out of Sodom. Moses carefully emphasises this, writing that Lot was led out by angels, and that on his account the town of Zoar was preserved from that burning. This example is most worthy of careful attention. For just as God, for the sake of his worshippers, does good to the whole world, and often preserves kingdoms and very great cities for their sake, so, when these are withdrawn or taken from the midst, he punishes the impious. Before (as we have said), the Sodomites were rescued from the hand of their enemies and restored to their city on account of Lot; but now, when he had gone out of that city, it is burned up by heavenly flames. Something similar happened at Jerusalem, when the Church that was there, warned by an oracle, emigrated to Pella; soon afterwards the city was besieged by the Romans, and at last miserably overthrown. Isaiah complains of this too, when he says that the righteous is taken away before those evil days come, in which God has decided to punish the incurable malice of the wicked (Isa. 57:1). Let these things admonish us to hold the godly as commended to us. At the same time, the example of Lot serves for consolation. For through it Peter teaches that God can rescue his own from temptation, and preserve them even when he destroys with universal ruin those who do not know how to repent. For (as the Prophet says) there is a distinction before God between the righteous and the wicked, which has been shown by many other examples, of which we have often spoken elsewhere. Therefore, mindful of this warning, let us not allow ourselves to be swept away by the common example of an unhappy world, but following Noah and Lot, let us keep our faith in God unimpaired, and let us not doubt the promises of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will temper the calamities of this age in proportion to our weakness, and at last will receive us into the harbour of blessed immortality. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXV
units.tr: HOMILY CLXV

units.la: In illo die si quis fuerit supra domum, & vasa eius in ipsa domo, ne descendat ad ea sumenda: & qui in agro, similiter non reuertatur retro. Memores estote uxoris Loti. Quicunq; quaesierit animam suam seruare, perdet eam, & quicunque eam perdiderit, viuificabit eam. Dico vobis, illa nocte erunt duo in lecto uno: unus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Duae erunt molentes simul: una assumetur, altera relinquetur. Duo erunt in agro; unus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Tunc respondentes dicunt ei: Ubi Domine? Ipse vero dixit eis: Ubi corpus, illuc cogentur & aquilae.
units.tr: In that day, if anyone is upon the housetop, and his goods are in the house, let him not go down to take them; and likewise let him who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife. Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will preserve it alive. I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together: one will be taken and the other left. Two will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left. Then they answer and say to him, "Where, Lord?" But he said to them, "Where the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered."

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus de nouissimis temporibus & suo ad extremum iudicium aduentu magna diligentia disserit, idq; duas potissimum ob causas. Prima est, ut doceat, Regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, neq; in illo terrena bona aut temporariam felicitatem quaeri debere. Et huc pertinent quaecunque de periculis & corruptissimis posteri seculi moribus hucusque dicta sunt, quibus multi etiam alij loci conueniunt, qui eadem prolixius exponunt. Paulus certe in posteriori ad Timoth. cap. tertio scribit: Illud autem scito, quod in postremis diebus instabunt tempora molesta. Erunt enim homines sui amantes, auari, gloriosi, superbi, maledici, parentibus immorigeri, ingrati, impij, charitatis expertes, nescij foederis, calumniatores, intemperantes, immites, minime amantes bonorum, proditores, praecipites, inflati, voluptatum amantes potius quam amantes Dei, habentes effigiem pietatis, sed qui vim eius abnegarint, &c. Quam vero periculosum sit pijs Dei cultoribus inter tales viuere, quius facile aestimare potest: & non possunt non vehementer falli, quicunq; sibi in hoc seculo omnia tuta & laeta pollicentur. Vult autem nos de his admoneri Christus, ne ijs offenda mur, si nobis praeter expectationem accidant. Altera causa est, ut horum consideratio nos ad vigilantiam et seriam pietatis studium excitet, ne huius mundi exemplo abrepti vel tantorum scelerum socij efficiamur, vel securitate absorbeamur. Est hoc eximium bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui non contentus de praesentibus nos admonuisse, futura quoque mala praedicit, ut omnibus ijs consulat, qui vsq; ad mundi consummationem victuri sunt. Debet huc referri, locus quem modo recitauimus, in quo praeceptis saluberrimis suos instruit, quae inter nouissimorum temporum horribiles motus obseruare debeant, & eadem rationibus quoque grauissimis confirmat.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ discusses the last times and his coming to the final judgment with great care, and he does so for two main reasons. The first is to teach that his kingdom is not of this world, and that earthly goods and temporary happiness ought not to be sought in it. To this belongs everything said so far about the dangers and the most corrupt morals of the last age, and many other passages agree with it, which set out the same things at greater length. Paul certainly writes in his second letter to Timothy, chapter three: "Know this, that in the last days grievous times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, without love, unforgiving, slanderers, intemperate, brutal, not lovers of the good, betrayers, reckless, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, holding to a form of godliness but denying its power," etc. How dangerous it is for the godly worshippers of God to live among such people, anyone can easily judge; and those who promise themselves that everything in this age will be safe and happy cannot but be greatly deceived. Christ wishes us to be warned of these things, so that we are not offended when they befall us contrary to our expectation. The second reason is that the consideration of these things should stir us to watchfulness and to earnest zeal for godliness, so that we are not carried away by the example of this world and become partners in such great wickedness, or be swallowed up by complacency. This is a remarkable proof of God's goodness, who, not content to warn us about present evils, also foretells future ones, so that he may provide for all those who are going to live until the end of the world. The passage we have just recited belongs here, in which he instructs his people with most wholesome precepts about what they ought to observe amid the terrible upheavals of the last times, and confirms the same with most weighty reasons.

units.la: Summa praeceptorum Christi est: In illo die si quis fuerit supra domum, & vasa eius in ipsa domo, ne descendat ad ea sumenda: & qui in agro, similiter non reuertatur retro. Sunt haec figuratae locutiones, quarum sensus est, vnumquenq; suae vocationi debere intentu esse, & in ea sic pergere, ut ne minimum quidem se huius mundi negotijs immisceat: imo omnibus ijs, quae in mundo praeclara & necessaria habemus, ita renunciandum esse, ut nullam eorum habeamus rationem, dummodo caelestia & aeterna bona possimus obtinere. Vasa enim dicuntur, Hebraica phrasi, non ea modo quae ad suppellectilem pertinent, verumetiam vestes & quaecunq; corporibus seruiunt. Quo loco cum primis obseruari debet, Christum neq; discipulis suis priuatis, neque vulgo Christianorum peculiare quoddam & nouum vitae genus praescribere, sed hoc ab omnibus in genere exigi, ne mundi huius studijs immergantur, sed omnium quae a tergo sunt obliti per suam vocationem ad caelestis Regni haereditatem magno & irremissio studio contendant. Nam ut aliàs monuimus, variae multumque inter se diuersae hominum vocationes sunt, quas Christus sua doctrina minime abrogat, neq; ut abrogentur opus est, cum in ipso, quoad salutis aeternae negotium, non sit mas aut foemina, non seruus aut liber, & proinde non doctus aut indoctus, non opifex aut agricola, non sutor aut nauta, &c. Hoc autem ab omnibus, cuiuscunque sint loci aut ordinis, requirit, ut singuli in ea vocatione aut vitae genere, in quo vocati sunt (de honestis & per se licitis loquor) maneant, & in eo suum officium constanter faciant. Itaque qui iam supra domum ascenderunt, & in sua vocatione ad fastigium virtutis euecti sunt, ij curent ne turpiter ad huius mundi studia relabantur. Qui item adhuc in agro sunt, & aliquos saltem progressus fecerunt, ij non respiciant ad ea quae a tergo sunt, sed ad metam sibi propositam perpetuò contendant. Hic enim omnium vocationum finis generalis est, ut huius vitae vsibus seruiant secundum charitatis & iustitiae legem, interim vero studia nostra omnia ad gloriam Dei & aeternae salutis haereditatem dirigat. Istam ergo regulâ omnes homines pro suae vocationis ratione sibijpsis applicare debet. Confutatur ergo huius loci authoritate illorum superstitiosus error, qui ut corruptissimos postremi saeculi mores & horum contagionem fugiant, relicto vitae prioris genere aut statu, in defer- tum profugiunt, aut in monasteria sese occultant, & novae regulae legibus astricti insolitam vitae ra- tionem vestitu, gestibus & ceremonijs peculiaribus profitentur. Ita vero se mundum fugere & mun- do mori sibijpsis persuadent. Atqui mundus est, vbicunque carnis affectus atque mundi studia sunt. Quae cum in animis huminum sedem suam habeant, neque aliter quam per fidem & spiritum regenerationis mortificentur, mundum nobiscum circumferimus sive in eremo, sive in monasterio, si- ue quocunque alio loco viuamus. Exemplo nobis esse possunt Lot, & filiae eius. Nam cum deletis Sodomis prae metu ex Zoare oppido discedentes in spelunca quadam montis sibi domicilium dele- gissent, magis in mundo fuerunt, quam cum inter sceleratissimos Sodomarum cives viuerent. Filiae enim, quae virginitatis suae florem hucusque inuiolatum seruarant, illic de concubitu cum patre con- silium ineunt, ipse autem vino nimio deuictus tam seipsum quam filias proprias foedo incestu polluit. Et quid plerunque accidere soleat ijs, qui in eremo vitam degunt, monachis item & monialibus in- tra arctissimos monasteriorum muros conclusis, notius est quam ut multis demonstrari opoteat. Nam ut nihil dicatur de foeda illorum libidine, qua pessime vruntur, nusquam certe magis re- gnant inuidia, aemulatio, odium, ira, obtrectatio, contentiones, ambitio & reliqua vitia, quae proprissima mundi & carnis opera sunt. In seipsis ergo mundum mortificent, & impurae carnis desideria fugiant, imo conculcent, quicunque relicto mundo ad patriam caelestem inoffenso pede contendere volunt. Qua in re plurimum auxilij illis adferet, si quam a Deo habent vocatio- nem semper sibi ob oculos ponant. Nec enim aliquod ordinarium vitae genus tam vile & leuicu- lum est, quod non totum hominem sibi vendicet, si quis suo officio digne fungi velit: neque mul- tum otij erit in sua vocatione seriò occupatis, ut simul mundo seruire & carnis suae desiderijs satis- facere possint.
units.tr: The sum of Christ's precepts is this: "In that day, if anyone is upon the housetop, and his goods are in the house, let him not go down to take them; and likewise let him who is in the field not turn back." These are figurative expressions, whose sense is that each person ought to be intent upon his own calling and to persevere in it in such a way that he does not mix himself even slightly in the affairs of this world; indeed, that we must renounce all those things in the world which we hold dear and necessary, so that we take no account of them, provided that we can obtain heavenly and eternal goods. For by a Hebrew idiom "goods" (vasa) are called not only those things which belong to household furniture, but also clothes and whatever serves the body. In this passage we must observe above all that Christ does not prescribe a peculiar and new way of life either to his private disciples or to the common crowd of Christians, but requires this of all people in general: that they not be immersed in the pursuits of this world, but, forgetting all that lies behind them, strive with great and unremitting zeal, through their calling, for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. For, as we have said on other occasions, there are various and very different callings among people, which Christ by his teaching does not abolish, nor is it necessary that they be abolished, since in the matter of eternal salvation there is neither male nor female, neither slave nor free, and therefore neither learned nor unlearned, neither craftsman nor farmer, neither cobbler nor sailor, etc. He requires of all people, of whatever place or rank, that each remain in that calling or way of life in which he has been called (I speak of honest callings which are lawful in themselves), and there faithfully perform his duty. Accordingly, those who have already climbed onto the housetop, and have been raised by their calling to the height of virtue, should take care not to fall back shamefully into the pursuits of this world. Likewise, those who are still in the field, and have made at least some progress, should not look back at what lies behind them, but should strive continually toward the goal set before them. For this is the general end of all callings: that we serve the uses of this life according to the law of love and justice, while at the same time directing all our pursuits to the glory of God and the inheritance of eternal salvation. Every person ought therefore to apply this rule to himself according to the nature of his calling. Hence the superstitious error of those is refuted by the authority of this passage: they, in order to flee the most corrupt morals of the last age and the contagion of them, abandon their former way of life or station, and flee into the desert, or hide themselves in monasteries, and bound by the laws of a new rule, profess an unusual manner of life by their dress, gestures, and peculiar ceremonies. And so they persuade themselves that they flee the world and die to the world. Yet the world is wherever the affections of the flesh and the pursuits of the world are. Since these have their seat in human minds, and cannot be mortified except through faith and the Spirit of regeneration, we carry the world with us, whether we live in the wilderness, in a monastery, or in any other place. Lot and his daughters can serve us as an example. For when Sodom had been destroyed, and they, fearing the city of Zoar, had chosen for themselves a dwelling in a certain cave of a mountain, they were more in the world than when they lived among the most wicked citizens of Sodom. For the daughters, who had hitherto preserved the flower of their virginity unviolated, there form a plan to lie with their father; and he himself, overcome by much wine, polluted both himself and his own daughters with foul incest. And what is wont to happen for the most part to those who live their life in the desert, and likewise to monks and nuns shut up within the closest walls of monasteries, is better known than that it need be demonstrated to many. For, to say nothing of their foul lust, which they practise most wickedly, envy, rivalry, hatred, anger, slander, strife, ambition, and the other vices, which are the very proper works of the world and the flesh, certainly reign nowhere more. Therefore, whoever wishes to make his way to the heavenly homeland with an unhindered foot, leaving the world behind, let him mortify the world in himself, and flee, or rather trample underfoot, the desires of the impure flesh. In this matter it will bring them great help if they always keep before their eyes the calling they have from God. For no ordinary way of life is so mean and trifling that it does not claim the whole person for itself, if someone wishes to discharge his duty worthily; nor will there be much leisure for those seriously occupied in their calling, so that they could at the same time serve the world and satisfy the desires of their flesh.

units.la: Quia vero hic nos multa retrahunt, qualia sunt diuitiarum huius saeculi illecebrae, quae & ana- ritiam & diffidentiam in nobis gignunt, vitae item huius cupiditas, dulcissima cum hominibus con- iunctissimis consuetudo, singulis istis occurrit Dominus, & rationibus validissimis illa omnia oppu- gnat. Et primo quidem ijs, qui opum iacturam impatientius ferunt, eo quod Dei gratia diffisi in il- lis spem & fiduciam omnem collocant, vxoris Loti exemplum proponit. Memores (inquit) estote vxoris Loti. Quid vero ista fecit, quidue passa est? Si historiae circumstantias consideres, illam opes in Sodoma relictas maioris fecisse patebit, quam praeclarum illud liberationis beneficium, quod per Angelorum ministerium Deus toti eius familiae conferebat. Nam cum marito & sibi dictum sciret: Serua vitam tuam, neque respectes post te, neque consistas in tota ista planitie, &c. Ipsa ta- men aliquo vsque progressa, a tergo respexit: nimirum sulphureae pluuiae stridore, ignis & fulgurum micantium splendore, ardentium tectorum crepitu, domuum ruentium fragore, virorum hinc inde discurrentium horrendis clamoribus & miserabili mulierum atque paruulorum eiulatu excitata, quae omnia domum amissam cum supellectile chara & reliquis bonis illi in mentem reuocauerunt: adeo vt non tam corporeis oculis quam animo iam diffidentiae pleno in Sodomam respexerit, id quod nunquam fecisset, si Dei beneficium, quo tunc fruebatur, digne aestimasset. Quam multos enim tunc in Sodomis fuisse putas, qui vitam suam libenter omnium fortunarum suarum iactura redem- pturi fuissent, si id facere licuisset: cum illa opes iam in caelesti incendio pereuntes vitae propriae ante- poneret? Idem ergo ei, quod postea Israelitis in Aegyptum ad ollas carnium respicientibus accidit. Et exempla huius generis hodie multa in ijs habemus, qui exhibitum in Christo salutis aeternae beneficium facile contemnunt, modo bonis suis in hoc saeculo frui possint. Quid vero de illis dicemus, quos non pudet publice profiteri, se propter fidem in Christum & Euangelium eius, neque cum ali- quo disceptare, neque fortunarum suarum quantulamcunque iacturam facere velle? Sunt hi lon- ge deteriori loco, quam Loti vxor fuerit, quae respexisse solum ad Sodomam dicitur: imo Loti generis peiores sunt, qui emigrantem socerum sequi noluerunt, quod nihil huius euenturum putarent: cum isti iam eductii ex mundo hoc ad eum redeant, etiamsi illum turpissimis immanis- simorum scelerum cupiditatibus aestuare, & diuinae vindictae ignem non vno loco iam incensum esse videant. Vult autem hos omnes Christus vxori Loti meminisse, vt nimirum perpetuò cogitent, quale exemplum in illam Deus ediderit, & quid ipsis sit sperandum, si tales esse pergant. Muta ta est illa in statuam salis. Ita verò perpetuum & incorruptibile monumentum vindictae Dei fa-ctam fuisse innuitur. Quia enim sal à corruptione seruat, perpetuitatis symbolum est, vt locutiones multae in scripturis docent. Nam foedus salis pro perpetuo Deus dicit apud Mosem. Vel etiā secundum literam intelligi potest, quod in statuam salis metallici mutata sit, quem ita indurescere constat in fodinis aliquibus, vt crystalli similis factus nunquam postea soluitur aut liquefiat. Plinius certè author est, Carris Arabiae oppido muros & domus ex massis salis aedificari. Et notae sunt etiam nostris hominibus in fodinis Poloniae salis gemmae (quas vocant) quae instar crystalli indurate suum in medicina vsum habent. Non igitur incredibile est in eiusmodi statuam Loti vxorem abijsse, cuius materia salem metallicum aut crystallinum (vt sic dicam) referret. Sed vtro sensu Mo- fis verba accipias, in idem recidet, voluisse nimirum Deum in hoc exemplo perpetuam memoriam extare, qua posteri omnes admonerentur, non cunctandum esse ijs, qui per Deum euocati iter aeternae salutis iam semel ingressi sunt: deniq; omnes eos mundum à tergo relinquere & ad coelestia respicere oportere, qui Dei iram effugere velint, quando ille venit adiudicandum impios. Constat enim, iactu ram salutis aeternae eos facere, qui Deo simul & mundo aut Mammonae seruire volunt, quia id factu impossibile est, vt supra demonstrauimus. Quoniam verò ad mundi & opum huius saeculi studium natura proclives sumus, & plerunque metuimus, ne satis fit nobis, quo vitam nostram sustentemus, proderit animos certa promissionum Dei fiducia confirmare: quae eo firmior atque certior erit, si simul cogitemus, quàm fluxa & incerta sit diuitiarum possessio, & quòd in earum abundantia hominis vita siue incolumitas minimè consistit. Vide Luc. 12. Sed ad alterum salutis impedimentum transit, vitae nimirum praesentis cupiditatem, quae vt multis turpissimorum facinorum causa est: ita fidem in Christum & felicitatem hominis veram vehementer impedit. Dicit ergo: Quicunque quaesierit animam suam seruare, perdet eam: & quicunque eam perdiderit, viuificabit eam. Habetur eadem sententia supra nono capite, vbi de vita secundum suam regulam & exemplum instituenda disserit. Est autem bimembris, & prima parte de illis loquitur, qui cum fidei abnegatione & vocationis suae intermissione vitae suae consulunt, id est, qui ne vitae periculum subire cogantur, fidem veram abnegant, & non faciunt officium in eo, ad quod peculiariter à Deo destinati sunt. Qui id faciunt, ij revera animam perdunt, quia Christum amittunt, in quo vno vita & salus habetur. Ipse enim ait: Quemcunq; mei & sermonum meorum puduerit coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero, eius etiam Filium hominis pudebit cum venerit in gloria sua cum Angelis sanctis. Quibus adde, quòd ijdem ne de huius quidem saeculi vita certi sunt: sed aut subita morte tolluntur, quando se otio suo optimè consuluisse putant: aut vitā viuunt inter horribiles conscientiae terrores atq; cruciatus ipsa morte miseriorem. E contra quisquis animam perdit (quae altera huius sententiae pars est) nimirum propter Christum, & verae fidei confessionem, is viuificabit eam. In Graeco est verbum ζωογονεῖν, quod foetum viuum parere significat: & causae praesenti pulcherrimè conuenit. Verè enim qui pro Christo & pietate moriuntur, animas suas ad vitam pariunt siue gignunt. Nā illo ipso teste à morte transeunt in vitam, & ad illum colliguntur ipsorum animae, quae in resurrectione corporibus restituentur, vt totus homo aeternae vitae & regni coelestis gaudijs fruatur. Qui ista considerant, hos praesentis vitae cupiditas minimè retinebit, quò minus ad omnia pro Christo facienda atq; ferenda parati sint. Cur enim illis graue videatur vitam profundere, quae tunc demum immortalis fit, dum mortali huic finis imponitur? Aut cur propter huius saeculi bona vitam hanc mortalem retinere cupiant, cùm & haec fluxa sit, illa autem ad hanc diutius seruandam niuil prosint? Discant potius omnes homines ex hisce Christi verbis, non aliam esse rationem commodiorem siue tutiorem conseruandi vitam & quaecunq; alia nobis chara atq; pretiosa sunt, quàm vt omnia nostra ad diuinae voluntatis nutum componamus, & in eius manu deponamus, quaecunq; is à nobis exigit. Vt enim fidelis est, neq; nos supra vires tentari sinit: Ita renumerator quoq; est liberalissimus, qui apud se depositā cum faenore reddere consueuit. Exempla, quibus istud probari possit, passim in scripturis cùm sacris tum prophanis occurrunt, quae cum experientia quotidiana confirmentur, non opus est illis commemorandis diutius insistere. Caterum
units.tr: Since, however, many things here hold us back, such as the allurements of the riches of this world, which breed both greed and distrust in us, and likewise the love of this life and the sweetest custom of living with our closest kin, the Lord meets each of these and fights against all of them with very strong arguments. And first, to those who bear the loss of their wealth too impatiently, because in distrust of God's grace they place all their hope and confidence in such things, he sets before them the example of Lot's wife. "Remember," he says, "Lot's wife." But what did she do, or what did she suffer? If you consider the circumstances of the story, it will be plain that she valued the wealth left behind in Sodom more than that splendid benefit of deliverance which God, through the ministry of the angels, was granting to her whole household. For she knew that she and her husband had been told: "Save your life; do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in all this plain" (etc.). Yet she went on some distance and then looked back. No doubt she was roused by the hissing of the sulphurous rain, the glare of fire and flashing lightning, the crackling of burning roofs, the crash of falling houses, the dreadful cries of men running hither and thither, and the pitiful wailing of women and little children; all of these brought back to her mind the house she had lost, with its dear furnishings and her other goods. So she looked back toward Sodom, not so much with her bodily eyes as with a mind already full of distrust. She would never have done this if she had rightly valued the blessing of God which she then enjoyed. For how many people do you think there were then in Sodom who would gladly have redeemed their lives by giving up all their property, if they had been allowed to do so, since she preferred her wealth, which was already perishing in the heavenly fire, to her own life? So it happened to her as it later happened to the Israelites, who looked back to the pots of meat in Egypt. Today too we have many examples of this kind in those who lightly despise the eternal salvation offered in Christ, provided they can enjoy their goods in this world. But what shall we say of those who are not ashamed to profess publicly that, for the sake of faith in Christ and his Gospel, they are unwilling either to dispute with anyone or to make even the smallest loss of their fortunes? They stand in a far worse position than Lot's wife, who is said only to have looked back toward Sodom. Indeed, they are worse than the kinsmen of Lot who refused to follow their father-in-law when he was leaving, because they thought nothing of the kind would happen; for these people, though already led out of this world, return to it, even though they see that it burns with the most shameful lusts for the most monstrous crimes, and that the fire of divine vengeance has already been kindled in more than one place. Christ, however, wants all these people to remember Lot's wife, so that they may always consider what example God has set in her case, and what they themselves may expect if they persist in being such people. She was turned into a pillar of salt. This signifies that she was made a lasting and incorruptible monument of God's vengeance. For since salt preserves from corruption, it is a symbol of perpetuity, as many expressions in Scripture teach; for God speaks in Moses of a covenant of salt, meaning an everlasting one. Or, taken literally, it can be understood that she was changed into a statue of metallic salt, since it is known that in some mines such salt hardens so that it becomes like crystal and is never afterwards dissolved or melted. Pliny certainly records that houses and walls are built of blocks of salt in the Arabian town of Carra. Our own people also know the salt gems (as they are called) in the Polish mines, which harden like crystal and have their use in medicine. It is therefore not incredible that Lot's wife passed into a statue of such a kind, whose material resembled metallic or crystalline salt, if I may so put it. But whichever sense you take the words of Moses in, it comes to the same thing: God wanted this example to stand as a lasting memorial, by which all posterity might be warned not to hesitate when they have been called by God and have once entered upon the way of eternal salvation; and finally, that all who wish to escape God's wrath, when he comes to judge the wicked, must leave the world behind them and look up to heavenly things. For it is certain that those who wish to serve God and the world, or Mammon, at the same time, bring the loss of eternal salvation upon themselves, because this is impossible to do, as we have shown above. But since we are by nature inclined to the pursuit of the world and its wealth, and often fear that what we need to sustain our lives will not be enough for us, it will profit us to strengthen our minds with a firm confidence in God's promises. This confidence will be all the firmer and surer if we also consider how uncertain and fleeting the possession of riches is, and that a person's life or safety does not at all depend on abundance of such things. See Luke 12. But he turns to the other impediment to salvation, namely the desire for the present life, which, just as it is the cause of many most shameful deeds, so it strongly hinders faith in Christ and the true happiness of man. So he says: "Whoever seeks to save his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will make it alive" [ζωογονεῖν]. The same saying is found above in chapter nine, where he discusses how life is to be ordered according to his rule and example. It has two parts. The first part speaks of those who, by denying the faith and abandoning their calling, look after their own life; that is, who, so that they are not forced to face danger to their lives, deny the true faith and do not perform the duty to which they have been specially destined by God. Those who do this truly lose their souls, because they lose Christ, in whom alone life and salvation are found. For he himself says: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words before this wicked and adulterous generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in his glory with the holy angels." To these add that such people are not even sure of the life of this world; for they are either carried off by a sudden death, when they think they have made the best provision for their ease, or they live amid the dreadful terrors and torments of conscience, more wretched than death itself. On the other hand, whoever loses his soul (which is the other part of this saying), that is, for Christ's sake and the confession of true faith, will make it alive. The Greek word is ζωογονεῖν, which means to bring forth a living offspring, and it agrees most beautifully with the present case. For truly those who die for Christ and godliness bring their souls forth into life, or beget them. For by his own testimony they pass from death into life, and their souls are gathered to him, to be restored to their bodies in the resurrection, so that the whole man may enjoy the joys of eternal life and the heavenly kingdom. Those who consider these things will not be held back by the desire for the present life from being prepared to do and to bear all things for Christ. For why should it seem a hard thing to them to pour out their life, which only then becomes immortal when an end is put to this mortal life? Or why should they wish to keep this mortal life for the sake of the goods of this world, since these are fleeting, while those goods are of no help in preserving this life any longer? Rather, let all people learn from these words of Christ that there is no better or safer way of preserving life, and whatever else is dear and precious to us, than to put all our things in order at the nod of the divine will, and to place in his hand whatever he demands from us. For as he is faithful, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, so he is also the most generous repayer, who is accustomed to return with interest what has been deposited with him. Examples that could prove this are found everywhere in Scripture, both sacred and profane, and they are confirmed by daily experience; there is no need to dwell longer on recounting them. Moreover

units.la: Cæterùm multos est videre, quos non tam diuitiæ aut vitæ huius cupiditas, quàm coniunctissimorum hominũ dulcissima consuetudo detinet, quò minus mundo renunciare & se totos ad cœlestiũ honorum studium componere possint. Nam non durum modò, sed inhumanum, sed barbarum, sed id quum videtur, ab ijs diuelli, quibus vel propter coniugij aut alterius fœderis vinculum, vel propter studiorum similitudinem, vel iucundissimum & diuturnum commercium non parũ debes. Ergo isti quoq; remedium adhibet, quando ostendit diuisionem aut separationem omnino necessariam esse, neq; nos vnquam posse obstare, quin ea fiat inter eos, qui nõ pari fide & studio Deum colunt, viur in alijs conuersant. Suos enim ad se colligit Dominus relictis in interitu ijs, qui maiorem suorum desiderium quàm Regni sui rationẽ habuerunt. Sic autẽ dicit: Dico vobis, illa nocte erunt duo in vno lecto: vnus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Duæ erunt molētes simul: vna assumetur, altera relinquetur. Duo erunt in agro: vnus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Quid ergo profuerit cũ eo indiuulsam in hoc seculo consuetudinem seruare velle, à quo vel sub mortis horam, vel in nouissimo Christi aduentu diuellaris oportet, nisi cum illo æternum perire velis? Certè si vnum hoc rectius omnes expenderent, nunquam tanti facerent hominum impiorum aut fide alienorum consortia.
units.tr: Yet it is easy to see that many people are held back, not so much by riches or love of this life, as by the sweetest companionship of those closest to them, so that they cannot renounce the world and devote themselves wholly to the pursuit of heavenly honours. For it is not only hard but inhuman, barbarous, and, as it seems, unnatural to be torn away from those to whom we owe a great deal, whether by the bond of marriage or some other covenant, or by likeness of studies, or by a most pleasant and lasting fellowship. So Christ also applies a remedy here, when he shows that division or separation is altogether necessary, and that we can never prevent it from happening between those who do not worship God with equal faith and zeal, but live together with others. For the Lord gathers his own to himself, leaving behind in destruction those who have valued their own desires more than the reason of his kingdom. He speaks thus: "I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken, the other left. Two women will be grinding together: one will be taken, the other left. Two will be in the field: one will be taken, the other left." What good, then, will it do to wish to keep an unbroken attachment in this world to one from whom you must be torn away at the hour of death or at Christ's last coming, unless you wish to perish with him for ever? Certainly, if everyone weighed this one thing more carefully, they would never set such store by the company of wicked men or of those estranged from the faith.

units.la: Simul autem his verbis docet Christus, quæ nam nouissimi iudicij ratio siue executio futura sit: ea nimirum, vt absque omni personarum respectu, inter eiusdem loci & ordinis homines alij quidem seruentur, alij verò damnentur, prout crediderunt, aut fide atque pietate fuerunt destituti. Istud innuit Dominus, quando duorum in vno lecto iacentium, duarum simul in vno pistrino molentium, duorum item in eodem agro laborantium meminit, quorum alterum ad se recipere velit, alterũ exitio sempiterno relinquere. Confutantur igitur huius loci authoritate, qui vel coniugium vel quæcunque alia vitæ genera damnant, quasi in ijs Deo seruire & seruari impossibile sit: qui itè hominis salutem paupertate & duro manuum labore, aut seruitute metiuntur. Hic enim inter eiusdem thori consortes, vel coniuges, aliquos assumptum iri audimus. Est enim thorus coniugum immaculatus, cùm illum Deus & instituerit & sanctificarit. Imò adeò non officit saluti coniugium, vt pij Christi cultores salui futuri sint, etiamsi coniuges æterno exitio destinatos habeant: modò non communicent illorum impietati. Quod Paulus non obscurè alio argumento docet, quando liberos, qui ex imparibus coniugijs procreantur, & quorũ alteruter modò parens fidelis est, sanctos esse testatur. Similiter ex vilissimis mancipijs aliquos damnationi obnoxios fore, Christus dicit.
