Scimus enim antiquitus pistrini laborem non grauem modò, sed cum aliqua ignominiæ specie coniunctum fuisse, cùm in illud serui contumaciores detruderentur, qui heros suos aliquo scelere aut delicto graviori offenderant. Attamẽ ex illis quoque, qui in eodem pistrino & sub eiusdem heri imperio laborant, aliqui ad cœlestis Regni hereditatem assumentur, alij relinquentur, vt æternas suæ contumaciæ pœnas luant. Vt enim liberas per se neminem damnat, qui ea bene vsus fuerit: ita neq; seruitus suo merito aliquem seruat, nisi in conditione seruili idem Christi libertus sit. Idem de diuitijs & paupertate dicimus. Solius enim Iesu Christi paupertas meritum coniunctum habet, qui cùm omnium Dominus esset, pauper factus est, vt nos Regni cœlestis thesauris ditaret. Et vt principes viri, qui iniusta tyrannide terrorem suum in terra posuerunt (vt Prophetæ verbis vtar) ad tartara rapientur: ita illos multi ex subditis eorum comitabuntur, qui vel scelerum ipsis ministri fuerint, vel suis affectibus abrepti vitam vixerunt impiam & prophanam. Neminem ergo suæ conditionis fiducia decipiat: sed qui ad res arduas vocati & in altiori gradu constituti sunt, periculi semper meminerint, quod ex alto cadentibus imminet, eaque diligentius officio suo fungantur: quibus verò humilior & abiectior sors obtigit, ij animis persidem supra cœlũ euectis in Christo consolatione quærant, & huius merito se seruari firmiter credant. Et vt semel omnia dicam, quisque in sua vocatione pietati studeat, & ita in hoc mundo viuant omnes, vt eo non abutantur, neq; animos suos prauis illius studijs immergant. Itaq; qui coniuges sunt, fœderis sui vinculum sanctè seruent, & Deo liberos procreare studeant: cœlibes verò animi & corporis castitatem sedulò tueantur. Heri ergo seruos humani & benigni: hi verò ergo illos fideles sint. Diuites in Dei cõspectu humilientur & beneficentiæ studeant: pauperes et inopes paupertatis incommoda patienter ferant, nemini meliorem fortem invideant, multò minus autem conentur malis artibus aut etiam apertis sceleribus sibijpsis cõsulere. Ita deniq; viuant omnes: ne magnus ille dies ipsos in flagitio aliquo deprehendat. Quia vero Christus alios quidem assumptum iri, alios vero in exitio relictum iri dixerat, discipulos nova cura solicitos habuit, quo nam pios assumi oportteat, aut ubi nam portus ille sive asylum sit, in quod se recipere debeant inter periculosissimos novissimi seculi motus, qui salutis iacturam nolunt facere. Quaerunt ergo: Ubi Domine, scilicet ista fient? Aut ubi nam nobis tutus et securus esse licebit? Respondet illis Christus proverbiali sententia: Ubi corpus aut cadaver, illuc cogentur et aquilae. Aquilis pios confert, quae ut acutissimum vident, ita olfactu quoque plurimum valent: et mira vel etiam incredibilia videri poterant, quae de illis historici tradunt, nisi ipsius Dei verbis confirmarentur, qui de sua providentia et omnipotentia apud Iobum differens inter alia dicit de aquila: Habitat in petra, et moratur in praeruptis saxis et loco inaccessso: inde speculatur, ut cibum inveniat, cuius oculi prospiciunt longinquas res: pulli eius sanguinem lambunt, et ubicunque sunt cadavera eum locum frequentant. Ad hanc ergo aquilarum naturam respiciens Dominus, vult ut sui oculis fidei in ipsum respiciant, et spiritus olfactu ex praecedentibus signis adventum suum instare cognoscant, seque praeparent, ut ad ipsum colligantur, qui solus credentium omnium esca aut cibus est, et qui eosdem fideli patrocinio protegit. Et de his quidem nunquam non nos cogitare decet, ne salutis nostrae portum alibi quam in Christo quaeramus. De hoc enim in Psalmis dicitur: Petra mea et arx mea tu es. Item Deus nobis suffugium et robur est, premente adversitate auxilium praesentissimum. Et patent alae eius semper omnibus, qui sub illas recipi et illic latere cupiunt. Vere tamen et perfecte implebitur, quod hic dicit, quando in novissimo die ad eius adventum mortui resurgent, et qui in ipso pie vixerunt corporibus quoque suis in eius occursum per aerem rapientur, ut semper cum illo sint. Et conuenit hoc eius promissioni: Vado paraturus vobis locum: et si abiero ad parandum vobis locum, redibo et assumam vos ad meipsum: ut ubi ego sum, et vos sitis. Ex quibus certo colligitur, eos non posse in filiorum Dei et haeredum Regni eius numero censeri, quicunque, vel in periculis alio respiciunt, vel iam morituri animas suas nescio quibus aliis commendant. Discant ergo omnes inter horribiles motus nostrorum temporum et effrenem mundi totius licentiam cum deceptabili omnis loci et ordinis hominum securitate coniunctam, animos suos constanti promissioni Dei fiducia confirmare, vocationem eius sequi, et procul relicto mundo et eius studiis in unum Iesum Christum respicere, qui et huius saeculi pericula vel amoliri, vel leviora reddere poterit, et tandem omnes, qui ipsi fidunt, ad Regni sui coelestis consortium colliget, ut cum ipso aeternum viviant atque gaudeant. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time, by these words Christ teaches what the manner and execution of the final judgment will be: namely, that without any regard for persons, some of those of the same place and station will be saved, and others condemned, according as they have believed or been destitute of faith and piety. The Lord indicates this when he speaks of two lying in one bed, two grinding together in one mill, and likewise two labouring in the same field, one of whom he will receive to himself, and the other he will leave to everlasting destruction. Therefore those are refuted by the authority of this passage who condemn marriage or any other way of life, as if it were impossible to serve God or be saved in them; who measure a man's salvation by poverty, hard manual labour, or servitude. For here we hear that some will be taken from among those who share the same bed, whether spouses or not. The marriage bed is undefiled, since God both instituted and sanctified it. Indeed marriage so little hinders salvation that the godly worshippers of Christ will be saved even if their spouses are destined for everlasting destruction, provided they do not share in their impiety. Paul teaches this not obscurely by another argument, when he declares that children born of unequal marriages, of which one parent alone is faithful, are holy. Similarly Christ says that some of the lowliest slaves will be liable to condemnation. For we know that in ancient times labour at the mill was not only heavy but also attended with a certain mark of disgrace, since the more stubborn slaves were thrust into it, those who had offended their masters by some crime or more serious fault. Yet even among those who labour in the same mill and under the same master's rule, some will be taken up to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, and others left, to pay the eternal penalty of their stubbornness. For just as freedom condemns no one in itself, to one who has used it well, so servitude by its own merit saves no one, unless in the servile condition a man is also Christ's freedman. We say the same about riches and poverty. For the poverty of Jesus Christ alone has merit attached to it, since he, though Lord of all, became poor so that he might enrich us with the treasures of the heavenly kingdom. And just as princes who have set their terror upon the earth by unjust tyranny (to use the words of the prophet) will be swept down to the depths, so many of their subjects will accompany them, those who were either ministers of their crimes or, carried away by their passions, lived an impious and profane life. Let no one, then, be deceived by confidence in his station; but let those who are called to difficult tasks and placed in a higher rank always remember the danger that hangs over those who fall from a height, and carry out their duty all the more diligently. As for those to whom a lowlier and humbler lot has fallen, let them, lifting their minds above the heavens by faith, seek consolation in Christ, and firmly believe that they are kept safe by his merit. And to say everything in a word: let each person strive for godliness in his own calling, and let all so live in this world that they do not abuse it, nor plunge their minds into its pursuits to their harm. Therefore let those who are married keep the bond of their covenant holy, and strive to bear children for God; but let the unmarried carefully guard the chastity of body and mind. Let masters be humane and kind to their servants, and let servants be faithful to them. Let the rich humble themselves in the sight of God and devote themselves to beneficence; let the poor and needy bear the hardships of poverty patiently, envy no one a better lot, and much less attempt to provide for themselves by wicked arts or even open crimes. Let all live in this way, so that that great day may not find them caught in some disgrace. But because Christ had said that some would be taken and others left to destruction, the disciples, anxious with a new concern, asked which of the godly ought to be taken, or where that harbour or refuge might be into which they should withdraw amid the most dangerous movements of the last age, since they did not wish to suffer loss of salvation. So they ask: "Where, Lord, will these things happen? Or where will it be permitted for us to be safe and secure?" Christ answers them with a proverbial saying: "Where the body or carcass is, there the eagles will also be gathered." He compares the godly to eagles, which see most keenly and also have a very strong sense of smell; and the marvels that the historians report about them might seem wonderful or even incredible, were they not confirmed by the words of God himself, who, speaking of his providence and omnipotence to Job, says among other things of the eagle: "It dwells in the rock and makes its home on the crags and in an inaccessible place; from there it watches for food, its eyes see things afar off; its young lick up blood, and wherever there are carcases, there it resorts." Looking to this nature of eagles, the Lord wills that his own should look to him with the eyes of faith, and that with the spirit's sense of smell, from the preceding signs, they should recognise that his coming is at hand, and prepare themselves to be gathered to him, who alone is the food and bread of all believers, and who protects them with faithful patronage. We ought always to think on these things, lest we seek the harbour of our salvation anywhere but in Christ. Of him it is said in the Psalms: "You are my rock and my fortress." Likewise, God is our refuge and strength, our most present help when adversity presses. And his wings are always open to all who wish to be received beneath them and to hide there. Yet what he says here will be truly and fully fulfilled when, on the last day, at his coming, the dead will rise, and those who have lived godly in him will be caught up with their bodies also through the air to meet him, so that they may always be with him. This agrees with his promise: "I go to prepare a place for you; and if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be too." From these things it is clearly gathered that those cannot be counted among the sons of God and heirs of his kingdom who look elsewhere in dangers, or who, about to die, commend their souls to I know not what others. Let all therefore learn, amid the terrible upheavals of our times and the unbridled licence of the whole world, which is joined with a deceptive sense of security among every place and rank of men, to strengthen their minds by confidence in God's constant promise, to follow his calling, and, leaving the world and its pursuits far behind, to look to Jesus Christ alone, who can either remove the dangers of this age or make them lighter, and who will at last gather all who trust in him into the fellowship of his heavenly kingdom, so that they may live and rejoice with him for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Dixit autem eis etiam parabolam, hoc spectante, quod oportet semper precari, nec segnescere, dicens: Iudex quidam erat in quadam urbe, qui Deum non timebat, nec hominem reverebatur. Erat autem in illa urbe quaedam vidua, quae venit ad eum dicens: Vindica me ab adversario meo. Ille autem noluit per multum tempus. Postea vero dixit apud se: Et si Deum non timeo, nec hominem revereor: tamen quia molestiam mihi exhibet vidua ista, vindicabo eam, ne ad extremum veniens obtundat me. Ait autem Dominus: audite quid iudex ille iniustus dicat. Deus autem non vindicabit electos suos, clamantes ad ipsum die ac nocte, etiamsi iram differat super ipsis? Dico vobis, vindicabit eos cito. Veruntamen Filius hominis cum venerit, num reperturus est fidem in terra?
units.tr: He also told them a parable, to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart, saying: "There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God and did not respect man. And there was a widow in that city who came to him, saying, 'Avenge me of my adversary.' For a while he would not. But afterward he said to himself, 'Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow troubles me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.'" And the Lord said, "Hear what the unjust judge says. And will not God avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth?"

units.la: Omnibus quidem saeculis iam inde a prima rerum origine pii cultores Dei multis calamitatibus pressi et variis fortunae casibus iactati sunt, periculosissimam tamen fere docet Christus illorum conditionem novissimo tempore, eo quod abundante passim iniquitate fides & charitas extinguentur. Et voluit de his ille nos praemonere, ne forsan nobis meliora polliciti postea turbis & aduersis ex improuiso incidentibus offendamur. Idem vero in semetipso portum felicitatis monstrauit, ad quem confugere debeant, qui ex periculis seruari volunt. Caeterum ne quid nobis defit, nunc viam quoque & rationem nobis monstrat, quam secuti eius protectionis beneficio frui poterimus: Preces nimirum ex fide manantes & vere ardentes, in quibus nos constanter perseuerare iubet, etiamsi malis aliquanto diuturnioribus premamur. Quia vero multa sunt quae fidem precantium oppugnant atque remorantur (vt quando Deum longe alijs & maioribus negotijs occupatum esse, aut nos indigniores esse nobis persuademus, quam qui ab eo exaudiri mereamur, vel etiam mora auxilij diuturniori offendimur) commodè parabolam proponit, qua omnibus istis impedimentis medetur. Eius enim status vel argumentum est, Deum, etiamsi interdum difficilior nobisque infensior videatur, nos item hominum calamitosissimi, adhaec ope et auxilio indigni sumus, non defuturum nobis, quo minus preces nostras exaudiat, modo in ijs inuicta fidei constantia perseueremus, vt vero id rectius & maiori cum fructu intelligamus, partes parabolae singulas ex ordine videre oportet.
units.tr: In every age from the very beginning of things, the godly worshippers of God have been oppressed by many calamities and tossed about by the varied chances of fortune. Yet Christ teaches that their condition will be most perilous near the last time, because iniquity will everywhere abound, and faith and charity will be extinguished. He wished to forewarn us of these things, lest, having been promised better things, we should afterward be offended when troubles and adversities fall upon us unexpectedly. Moreover, he has shown in himself the harbour of happiness to which those must flee who wish to be saved from dangers. But that nothing may be lacking to us, he now shows us also the way and the method by which, by following it, we may enjoy the benefit of his protection: namely, prayers springing from faith and truly fervent, in which he bids us persevere constantly, even if we are pressed by evils somewhat lasting. Since there are indeed many things which assail and hinder the faith of those who pray (as when we persuade ourselves that God is occupied with other and greater affairs, or that we are too unworthy to deserve to be heard by him, or when we are offended by the longer delay of help), he suitably sets forth a parable by which he heals all these impediments. For its scope or argument is this: that God, although he may sometimes seem more difficult and less favourable to us, and although we are most wretched men and unworthy of help, will not fail to hear our prayers, provided we persevere in them with unconquered constancy of faith. But that we may understand this more rightly and with greater profit, it is necessary to see the individual parts of the parable in order.

units.la: Prima Deum sub persona iudicis, & quidem impij atque iniusti, describit. Id vero non per aequiparationem intelligi debet, vt Deum talem esse putemus, sed per comparationem, qua vti voluit Dominus, vt argumentum à comparatis esset efficacius, cuius summa est: Si assidua & importuna auxilij legitimi imploratio apud tyrannos & prophanos, Dei simul atque hominum contemptores, non semper infructuosa est: quanto maior precum efficacia erit apud Deum, qui vt iustus iniquitatis vindex, ita ad seruandum natura propensus est? Est ergo huius parabolae argumentum eius simile, quod supra audiuimus: Si vos cum sitis mali, nostris bona dona dare liberis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester caelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum ijs, qui ab eo petierint? Nam hic quoque inter nos, qui natura magligni sumus, & Deum liberalissimum omnis boni largitorem comparatio fit, vt maiorem ex ea precandi fiduciam concipiamus.
units.tr: First, he describes God under the person of a judge, and indeed of a wicked and unjust one. This ought not to be understood by way of equality, as if we thought God to be such, but by way of comparison, which the Lord chose to use, so that the argument from things compared might be more effective. Its sum is this: if the constant and importunate imploring of lawful help is not always fruitless before tyrants and profane men, who are despisers of both God and men, how much greater will the efficacy of prayer be before God, who, as a just avenger of iniquity, is likewise by nature inclined to save? The argument of this parable is therefore similar to what we heard above: "If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?" For here too a comparison is made between us, who by nature are evil, and God, the most generous giver of every good, so that we may conceive from it a greater confidence in praying.

units.la: Vt vero ex ipsa etiam historica parabolae narratione aliqua ad nos vtilitas redeat, obseruari debet iudicis iniqui descriptio, de quo duo dicuntur: Vnum, quod à timore Dei alienus fuerit; alterum: quod superbia & immani confidentia elatus pudorem omni absterso, quorumuis de se iudicia contemp-serit. Continentur duobus hisce summa iniustitiae & impietatis. Nam Dei timorem verae sapientiae, & proinde iustitiae etiam (quae sine illa non potest consistere) fontem esse, sapientissimus Solomon testatur. Quid ergo vel consilij vel iudicij aequi ab eo sperabis, qui Dei reuerentia nulla tenetur? Poeta certè ethnicus cum iustitia Dei timorem conexum esse vidit, dicens: Discite iustitiam moniti, & non temnere diuos. Sunt tamen aliqui, qui etiamsi Deum esse vix credant, hominum tamen reuerentia & pudore aliquo aliquantulum in officio continentur, vt in Saule cernimus: qui cum Dei mandatum secure & absque omni numinis reuerentia transgressus esset, hominum tamen iudicia veritus Samueli dicebat: Peccaui: sed nunc quaeso istum honorem mihi exhibe coram senioribus populi mei, coram Israele, & reuertere mecum, vt adorem Dominum Deum tuum. Quod si ergo neque hominum neque Dei reuerentia aliqui tanguntur, quid illi non facient, quod malesuada libido iubet? Etsi in principes viros atq; iudices confidens ista securitas cadat, quid aliud quam cum omni iniustitia coniunctam tyrannidem expectabimus? Exempla talium hominum historiae in Cambyse, Atreo, Nerone, Caligula & similibus monstris exhibent: & vtinam nulli essent hodie iudices, quibus haec Christi definitio conueniret. Quam multos enim est videre, qui adeo nullo Dei timore tanguntur, vt seipsos Deorum loco esse putent: non quidem eo sensu, quo Scripturae iudices & principes Deos dicunt, sed quod penes se de re quauis quiduis pro suo arbitrio statuendi potestatem esse volunt: Olim quidem tyrannorum vox erat: Sic volo, sic iubeo: sit pro ratione voluntas: At quid ab ista differunt, qui hodie de iure appellati clamant: Et quid nam est ius? Annon ius dici debet, quod nos statuerimus? Nos ne legibus parere aequum est, & non potius vt Leges prout nobis commodum fuerit, moderemur? Addunt nonnulli, nimium stultos esse eos, qui seipsos legum vinculis astringant, cum ea dissoluendi habeant potestatem. At qui ita sentiunt, ij neq; Deum timent, neq; hominum reuerentia mouentur: fieri ergo non potest, quin multa contra ius & aequum faciant, & tandem sui illius regni, seu tyrannidis potius, finem videant infelicissimum.
units.tr: So that some usefulness may also come to us from the very historical narrative of the parable, we must observe the description of the unjust judge, of whom two things are said: first, that he was a stranger to the fear of God; second, that, puffed up with pride and monstrous self-confidence, he cast off all shame and despised the judgments of anyone about himself. These two contain the sum of injustice and impiety. For the most wise Solomon testifies that the fear of God is the fountain of true wisdom, and therefore of justice also, which cannot stand without it. What counsel or what fair judgment, then, will you hope for from one who is held by no reverence for God? Certainly the heathen poet saw that the fear of God is joined with justice, saying: "Learn justice, being warned, and not to despise the gods." Yet there are some who, although they scarcely believe that God exists, are nevertheless somewhat restrained in their duty by reverence for men and by some sense of shame, as we see in Saul. When he had transgressed the command of God carelessly and without any reverence for the divine will, yet fearing the judgments of men, he said to Samuel: "I have sinned; but now, I beg you, honour me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may worship the Lord your God." If, then, some are moved neither by reverence for men nor by reverence for God, what will they not do that a wicked lust commands? And if this carelessness falls upon princes and judges who trust in it, what else shall we expect than tyranny joined with all injustice? The histories show examples of such men in Cambyses, Atreus, Nero, Caligula and similar monsters; and would that there were no judges today to whom this definition of Christ applies! For how many may be seen who are so untouched by any fear of God that they think themselves to be in the place of gods, not indeed in that sense in which the judges and princes of Scripture are called gods, but because they wish to have the power in themselves of deciding whatever they like about any matter at their own pleasure. Formerly this was the voice of tyrants: "Thus I will, thus I command; let my will be my reason." But how do those differ from this who today, called to account for their right, cry out: "And what is right?" Is not that to be called right which we ourselves have decided? Is it fair that we should obey the laws, and not rather regulate the laws as it suits us? Some add that they are too foolish who bind themselves with the chains of laws, since they have the power to loosen them. But those who think in this way neither fear God nor are moved by reverence for men. It cannot therefore be but that they do many things against right and equity, and at last they see the most unhappy end of that kingdom, or rather tyranny, of theirs.

units.la: Discant ergo hic quid sui sit officij, quicunque Rempub. administrant, aut in publicis iudicijs praesident. Meminerint ergo iudicium (vt Moses inquit) non hominis alicuius, sed ipsius Dei esse, qui proprie iudex vniuersæ terræ dicitur. Cogitent item, se huius ministros esse, qui ex peculiari gratia ipsos in eam dignitatem euexerit, & authoritate donarit, vt iudiciorum suorum sint executores. Non ergo sua placita proferre, aut leges pro suo arbitrio flectere vel torquere, sed secundum illas iudicium iustum & rectum facere debent. Nec vnquam excidat ex animis illorum, quod in Psalmo habetur: Deus constitit in coetu Deorum, in medio Deorum ille iudicem agit. Et ad se dici putent: Num vere quod iustum est pronunciatis? recte ne iudicatis o filij hominum? Item: Quo vsque tandem iudicabitis iniquè, & facies impiorum suscipietis? Addant his se, licet cæteris authoritate & potentia præstent, mortales tamen esse, qui olim Deo rationem reddituri sint. Quod ipsum quoque ille per Prophetam grauissimè admonet dicens: Equidem dixeram, Vos Dij estis, & vos omnes Filij altissimi: Veruntamen sicut homines moriemini, & sicut vnus ex tyrannis cadetis. Et sanè non desunt exempla, quibus & olim testatus est Deus, & hodie adhuc testatur, quàm facilè & leuiter fere ex improviso eorum potentia & authoritas corruat, qui ea ad suam libidinem violenter abutuntur. Horum itaque memores ante omnia quidem Dei gloriam pro virili proseqvantur, deinde populi sui curam habeant diligentem, neque negligant eorum clamores, qui sibi ius dici petunt, & apud ipsos opem quærunt. Nam qui viduarum, pupillorum, peregrinorum & quorumuis qui iniuriam patiuntur querelas surda aure prætereunt, vt eosdem ad Dei tribunal confugere & huius vltricem manum inuocare cogunt, qui illos minimè negliget, sicuti in Lege testatur. Quod Sapiens ille Sirachi filius non ofcitan ter obseruauit, sic scribens: Dominus iudex est, nec habet personæ rationem aduersus inopem: sed iniuriam passi precationem exaudiet. Supplicationem pupilli minimè negliget, nec preces fundentem viduam. Nonne cum lachrymæ viduæ ad maxillam eius defluunt, ad cælum vsq; redundant? & Dominus libenter exaudit eas? Oratio afflicti nubes penetrat, non conquiescit nec desistit, donec peruenerit ad altissimum. Cæterum Dominus non permanebit in mora, nec patientia super eis præstabit omnipotens, donec lumbos immitium conquassarit, gentesq; multarit supplicio, donec subtulerit turbam iniuriosorum & iniustorum sceptra confregerit, &c. Possent ista multis exemplis confirmari, quæ docent hoc multis regibus mortem, regnis autem potentissimis ruinam aut mutationes periculosas peperisse, quod indigne afflictorum iniurias contemnerent. Eam ob causam Philippum, cum medius inter duos Alexandros, generum & filium incederet, à Pausania occisum fuisse, Iustinus author est. Et Demetrius eo potissimum animos Macedonum abs se alienauit, quod multorum supplices libellos, ipsis spectantibus, in profluentem abiecisset. Sed sufficere debebat Christianis principibus, quod Christus impij & ab omni tam Dei quàm hominum reverentia alieni iudicis exemplum proposuerit, talem describit, qui viduæ afflictæ causam neglexerit. Sed ipsam quoque viduam videamus, quæ altera huius parabolæ pars est. Habuit illa aduersarium grauem, qui vel hæreditatem eius intercepit, vel bona eripuit, aut alijs grauioribus iniurijs eam oppressit. Ergo iudicem adit, & Legum præsidium implorat, & vindicari petit à suo illo aduersario. Id verò cuius oppressio licere, Scriptura non vno loco testatur. Quorsum enim magistratum & iudices constituisset Deus, si ab illis ius petere, aut Leges implorare nefas esset? Ergo (quod alibi monuimus) de priuata & illegitima vindicta intelligi debet, quod dicitur: Ne resistatis malo, &c. Et sanctorum exempla habemus, qui armato etiam præsidio potius defendi, quàm hostiū libidini se subijcere voluerunt, sicuti de Paulo Lucas in Actis scribit. Nemo igitur phanaticos audiat, qui duo Christianos homines iure & legibus vti prohibent, impiorum & iniuriosorum audaciam confirmant, multis autem authores sunt, vt iniuriarum pondere superati vindictæ cupiditatem admittant, & hanc quouis modo persequantur. Cæterum adumbrat simul hoc exemplo Christus, quæ fere viduarum atque orphanorum in hoc mundo sors sit. Patitur illa iniuriā, & proinde vt publica authoritate defendatur opus habet. Sed illam iudex ille facilè negligit. Solet hoc plerunque accidere. Quia enim homines natura alieni appetentes sunt, frequenter aliorum fortunas vel violenter, vel simulato iuris prætextu inuadunt. Id autem fere accidit viduis atque orphanis, eò quòd tutores aut omnino nullos habent, aut eos habent, qui propter illos nullius hominis inuidiam sive odium sibi acersere volunt. Itaque auxilio & patrocinio trotinio destituti, omnium iniurias ferre coguntur. Et quàmuis magistratus præcipuè propter eos in stitutus sit, qui sibiipsis & rebus suis defendendis non sufficiunt, ab ipsis tamen iudicibus negligun- tur, eò quòd lucrum quidem ex illis nullum sperari potest, causæ autem eorum cum inuidia & odio coniunctæ sunt. Exemplis hoc demonstrare non est opus, quando res ipsa loquitur, & in rebuspublicis etiam optimè constitutis interdum superante bonas leges improborum malitia, quædam huius generis fiunt. At non ideò desperare debent, qui & omnium iniurijs se expositos, & tribunalia omnia sibi clausa esse atq; negari sentiunt. Est enim viduarum, orphanorum, peregrinorū & afflictorum omnium pater & vindex Deus, qui vt hos omnes sibi cōmendatissimos habet: ita de illis passim leges dat, & eos qui magistratum gerunt, horum præcipuam rationem habere iubet. Quòd si hi in officio cessent, non tamen cessat ille, qui sine iudicibus suos vindicare potest, inultos aut non sinit eos abire, qui quod ijs debetur patrocinium denegant. Non ergo vilis & contempta eorum conditio, qui iniuriam pati untur, iudicibus imponat, vt eos impunè negligi posse putent. Quod enim mundi iudicio contemptum est, id Deus maximi æstimare solet: imò miseri illi hi ipsi sunt, quorū vindicem se ille esse profitetur.
units.tr: Let those who administer the commonwealth, or preside over public courts, learn what their duty is. Let them remember that judgment (as Moses says) belongs not to any man but to God himself, who is properly called the judge of the whole earth. Let them also consider that they are ministers of God, who by his special grace has raised them to that dignity and endowed them with authority so that they may carry out his judgments. Therefore they must not put forward their own opinions, nor bend or twist the laws according to their own will, but must render just and right judgment according to them. Let the words in the Psalm never leave their minds: "God stands in the assembly of the gods; in the midst of the gods he judges." Let them take as spoken to themselves: "Do you indeed speak what is just? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?" Likewise: "How long will you judge unjustly, and accept the faces of the wicked?" Let them add that, although they excel others in authority and power, they are nonetheless mortal, and will one day have to render an account to God. The prophet also warns them most seriously of this, saying: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes." Indeed, there are no lack of examples by which God has shown, both in former times and still today, how easily and lightly the power and authority of those who violently abuse it for their own lust often collapse, and that suddenly. Mindful of these things, let rulers above all pursue the glory of God to the best of their ability; then let them take diligent care of their people, and not neglect the cries of those who ask for justice and seek help from them. For those who turn a deaf ear to the complaints of widows, orphans, strangers and all who suffer wrong, compel them to flee to God's tribunal and call upon his avenging hand, and he will by no means neglect them, as the Law testifies. The wise son of Sirach observed this not carelessly, writing thus: "The Lord is judge, and with him there is no respect of persons against the poor; but he will hear the prayer of one who suffers wrong. He will not neglect the supplication of the fatherless, nor the widow who pours out her complaint. Do not her tears run down her cheek, and do they not rise even to heaven? And does not the Lord gladly hear them? The prayer of the afflicted pierces the clouds; it does not rest nor cease until it reaches the Most High. Moreover the Lord will not linger, nor will the Almighty show patience towards them, until he has broken the loins of the merciless, and punished the nations with punishment, until he has taken away the multitude of the insolent and broken the sceptres of the unjust," and so on. These things could be confirmed by many examples, which teach that for many kings the scorn of the unjust wrongs done to the afflicted brought death, and for the most powerful kingdoms ruin or dangerous upheavals. For this reason, Justin is the authority that Philip was killed by Pausanias when he walked between the two Alexanders, his son-in-law and his son. And Demetrius alienated the minds of the Macedonians chiefly by throwing the petitions of many suppliants into the flowing river while they looked on. But it ought to have been enough for Christian princes that Christ, setting before them the example of an impious judge who had no reverence either for God or for men, described one who neglected the cause of a afflicted widow. But let us look also at the widow herself, who is the other part of this parable. She had a grievous adversary, who either had seized her inheritance, or snatched away her goods, or oppressed her with other more serious wrongs. So she goes to the judge, implores the protection of the laws, and seeks to be avenged on that adversary. Now Scripture testifies in more than one place that it is lawful to seek redress from such oppression. For why would God have appointed magistrates and judges, if it were wrong to ask them for justice or to implore the laws? Therefore (as we have elsewhere pointed out) what is said, "Do not resist evil," etc., must be understood of private and unlawful vengeance. We also have the examples of saints who preferred to be defended even by an armed guard rather than submit to the lust of enemies, as Luke writes of Paul in the Acts. Let no one, then, listen to the fanatics who forbid Christian men to use right and the laws, who confirm the boldness of the impious and the wrongdoers, and who on the other hand advise many to yield to the weight of injuries and to desire vengeance, and to pursue it by any means. Moreover, Christ shows by this example what is generally the lot of widows and orphans in this world. They suffer wrong, and so they need to be defended by public authority. But that judge easily neglects them. This usually happens. For since men are by nature greedy for what belongs to others, they often invade the fortunes of others, either by violence or under a pretext of pretended right. This happens especially to widows and orphans, because they either have no guardians at all, or have guardians who do not wish to incur the hatred or ill will of anyone on their account. Thus, destitute of help and protection, they are compelled to bear the wrongs of all. And although the magistracy is established chiefly for the sake of those who are not sufficient to defend themselves and their property, nevertheless they are neglected by the judges themselves, because no gain can be expected from them, while their causes are bound up with envy and hatred. There is no need to demonstrate this by examples, since the thing speaks for itself; and even in commonwealths that are very well ordered, such things sometimes happen, when the wickedness of the wicked overcomes good laws. Yet those who feel themselves exposed to the injuries of all, and all tribunals closed and denied to them, ought not on that account to despair. For God is the Father and avenger of widows, orphans, strangers and all the afflicted; as he holds all these most dear to himself, so he gives laws concerning them everywhere, and commands those who hold the magistracy to have their chief regard for them. But if the magistrates fail in their duty, he who can avenge his own without judges does not cease; he does not allow those to depart unpunished who deny the protection that is owed to them. Therefore let the lowly and despised condition of those who suffer wrong not lead judges to think they can neglect them with impunity. For what is despised in the judgment of the world, God is accustomed to value most highly; indeed, those wretched people are the very ones whose avenger he professes himself to be.

units.la: Sequitur postrema parabolæ pars, quæ statum totius causæ, quam Christus tractat, comprehen dit. Cùm enim iudex ille ad clamorem viduæ aures diu obturauisset, ipsa verò indies ei molestior fie ret, & vbiq; occurreret quærelam suam ingeminans, ille tandem intra seipsum dicit: Etsi Deum non timeo neq; hominem reuereor, tamen quia molestiam mihi exhibet ista vidua, vindicabo eam, ne ad extremum veniens obtundat me, id est, verbis obruat & plane fatigatum subigat. Potuit ergo assi duo & importuno clamore tantum efficere muliercula ista apud prophanum hominem, vt quàmuis se neq; Dei neq; hominum respectu ad officiū faciendum moueri fateatur, simul tamen id præstet sui ipsius causæ, vt nimirum semel infestis illis clamoribus liberetur. Ex eo autem Dominus statum parabolæ magna cum grauitate infert, dicens: Audite, quid iudex ille iniustus dicat. Deus autē non vin dicabit electos suos clamantes ad ipsum die ac noc̃te, etiamsi iram differat super ipsis? Quasi diceret: Cùm vidua ista iudicem iniustum & immitem suis querelis tandem vincere potuerit, quantò magis Deus assiduis & irremissis precibus superari poterit, vt opem ferat, etiamsi aliquò vsque cunctatus fuerit? Est autem validum in primis & multiplex comparationis huius argumentum, eò quòd sin gula verba inter se mutuò opponuntur. Nam iudex tyrannicus cum Deo confertur: vbi primùm oc currit, quòd ille quidem homo, & proinde natura malus, hic autem pater est bonus & fidus: deinde quòd ille immitis ac impius tyrannus, hic misericors est: item quòd illi molestum est supplicantium querelas & postulationes audire, Deus autem ijsdem delectatur, & quosuis ad se inuocandum promissionibus quoque amplißimis inuitat. In die (inquit) tribulationis tuæ inuocame, & liberabo te. Item: Priusquā inuocent, ego respondebo: & adhuc illis loquentibus ego exaudiā. Et ipse Dei Filius ait: Petite, & dabitur vobis, quærite, & inuenietis: pulsate, & aperietur vobis. Nō autē vanas esse promissiones istas, exemplis infinitis iam inde ab exordio mundi probatum est, quæ si omnia comme morare velim, totus dies nobis non sufficeret. Nec longa illorum commemoratione opus est, quando neminem tam miserum aut infelicem esse puto, qui non ipse hanc Dei Patris facilitatem expertus sit: nisi forte aliquem dederis prophanum Cyclopem, qui de Deo inuocando ne cogitauit quidem.
units.tr: There follows the last part of the parable, which comprehends the state of the whole cause that Christ treats. For when that judge had long stopped his ears at the widow's cry, and she, daily more troublesome to him, met him everywhere repeating her complaint, at last he says to himself: "Although I do not fear God nor reverence man, yet because this widow causes me trouble, I will avenge her, lest at last by coming she wear me out," that is, overwhelm me with words and utterly weary me and bring me down. So this little woman, by her persistent and importunate clamour, was able to achieve so much with a profane man that, although he confesses that he is not moved to do his duty by any regard for God or men, nevertheless he does this for her own cause, namely, that he may at last be freed from her troublesome cries. From this the Lord then draws the state of the parable with great seriousness, saying: "Hear what the unjust judge says. And will not God avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, even though he delays his anger over them?" As if he were saying: since this widow was at last able to overcome an unjust and merciless judge by her complaints, how much more will God be overcome by constant and unceasing prayers, so as to bring help, even if he has delayed for some time? Now the argument of this comparison is strong and manifold in the first place, because each word is set over against the others. For the tyrannical judge is compared with God: where first it is evident that the one is indeed a man, and therefore by nature wicked, while the other is a good and faithful Father; then that the one is a harsh and impious tyrant, while the other is merciful; likewise that it is irksome to the one to hear the complaints and petitions of supplicants, whereas God delights in them, and invites everyone to call upon him even with the most ample promises. "In the day of your trouble," he says, "call upon me, and I will deliver you." Likewise: "Before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear." And the Son of God himself says: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you." That these promises are not empty has been proved by infinite examples from the very beginning of the world, and if I were to recount them all, a whole day would not suffice us. Nor is there any need for a long recital of them, since I think there is no one so miserable or unhappy who has not himself experienced this kindness of God the Father, unless perhaps you should name some profane Cyclops who never even thought of calling upon God.

units.la: In præsenti autem peculiarem considerationem meretur, quòd Deus suos electos tandem vindi cet ad se die ac noctè clamantes, etiamsi iram suam aliquandiu in causa illorum differat. Quia enim ille iudex est vniuersæ terræ (vt Abraham ait) cum iudicio autem vindicta coniuncta est, hanc ne gligere non poterit, nisi simul iudicem agere desinat. Ideò Deum vltionum vocant Sancti in Psal- mo clamantes: Domine Deus vltionum, Deus vltionum conspicuus apparet. Attolle te ô iudex ter- ra, redde talionē superbis. Cùm autē talis reuera sit, quoad omnes homines, quod manifestè omnium gentium historiæ testantur, multò magis electos suos vindicabit, quos æterno suo decreto sibi delegit, quosque tandem Filijsui sanguine redemit, vt eos sibi peculium, imò Filios suos & Regni sui cælestis hæredes faceret. De his certè per Zachariā pronuntiat: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Et apud eundem Prophetam Ecclesia lapidi oneris confertur, quem omnes quidem è medio tollere conentur, nemo autem absq; aliquo luculento damno illi manum admoueat. Neq; debet hic fidem no stram labefactare mora illa, quam interdum Deus facit: huius enim causa est, non quòd nos Deus vel momento vno ignoret siue negligat: sed quia ipse patiens & longanimis iram suam differt, vt & improbis illis respiscendi occasionem praebeat, & simul patientiam atq; fidem suorum exerceat. Hoc vbi probè factum fuerit, impij autem pergant incurabili contumacia aduersus illum luctari, tarditatem illam vindictæ gravitate compensat. Exempla huius plurima in omnibus historijs occurrunt. Prodeant inter hæc primo loco filij Israelis, quos annis circiter centum & amplius (si Mosis ætatem cum tota illa historia conferas) Pharao plus quàm barbara tyrannide afflixit. Itaq; Deus sui populi simul, & fœderis cum Abrahamo facti oblitus videri poterat. Sed cùm iam ad extremum perveniisset tyranni crudelitas, & Israelitæ inter durissima ista onera ad Deum suspirarent atque clamarent, ascendit ad eum clamor illorum, & recordatus est fœderis sui, id est, se huius probè memorem esse, reipsa testatus est, & Mosi apud Madianitas agenti dicit: Videndo vidi afflictionem populi mei, qui est in Ægypto, & audivi clamorem eorum propter exactores quos habent, atq; scio dolores eorum: ideò descendi, vt liberem eos de manu Ægyptiorum, &c. Quàm dira autem & horrenda vindictæ exempla in Pharaonem & totam Ægyptum edita sint, nemo est qui ignoret. Eadem quodillic fecit in populi sui vindicatione Deus, hoc ipsum postea non semel temporibus Iudicum contra Ammonitas, Chananæos, Madianitas, Philistæos, & tandem contra Babylonios quoque factitatum est, cùm hi illum totis septuaginta annis in exilio & captiuitate detinuissent. Neq; in novo Testamento mutavit ingenium suum Deus, sed hic quoq; vltricem manum non semel exeruit. Et vt rursus à Iudæis exordiamur, sciunt omnes, quanta cum impietate exhibitû sibi generis humani redemptorem reiecerint, quàm implacabili odio eundem persecuti sint, quàm iniustè simul & crudeliter in crucem egerint, quam denique indomita rabie in Apostolos eius & toto orbe surgentem Euangelij doctrinam sœuierint. Gemuerunt diu & clamarunt interea pij, & videbatur Deus ista non curare: sed subitò illuxit dies ille vltionis, quo & Filij sui & sanctorum eius sanguinem de impijs illorum manibus requisiuit, & infelices horrendo & exemplo carente excidio perdidit. Nec feliciorfuit Herodis posteritas, quæ patris exemplum secuta Iudæorum furores adiuuit. Quid autem de Roma et Romanis Imperatoribus dicemus, quorum crudelitatem in electos suos tam diris tamq; illustribus exemplis Deus vltus est, vt si nulla alia extarent, hæc sola Christi verbis possent fidem facere? Nero enim, qui primus in illos gladiû acuit, vt Romæ abs se incensæ crimen (vt Cornelius Tacitus scribit) in Christianos deriuaret, sicq; ipsum odio & invidia liberaret, tandem à Senatu hostis iudicatus sibi ipsi manum intulit, cumiam moriturus ne percussorem quidem inuenire posset, qui illum vel amore vel odio occideret. Vnde dicebat: Itáne neminem amicum vel inimicum habeo? Secutus est eius vestigia Domitianus, quem servi sui domestici crudeliter trucidarunt. Traiani verò in fideles edicta crudelia & impios conatus mox secuta sunt domus aureæ conflagratio, Tyberis inundatio, pestis, fames & terræmotus, quibus aliquot Græciæ & Asiæ vrbes corruerunt. Non terruerunt ista M. Antoninum Verum, quin & ipse contra Ecclesiam insurgeret: sed hunc quoque pestè, quæ Italiam horribiliter vastauit atque oppida multa prorsus exhausit, adhæc Germanorum irruptionibus Deus coercuit. Similiter grauem Dei vindictam sensit L. Septimius Seuerus: quem bella ciuilia exagitarunt propter fusum Christianum sanguinem, & qui procul à Roma Eboraci moriens vocem hanc desperationis plenam edidit, πάντα ἐγένοµην, καὶ ἐδὲν ἐµοὶ λυσιτελεῖ, id est, omnia fui, & nihil mihi prodest. Nam cum fine vitæ & rerum humanarum fragilitate simul Dei iram sentiebat, qua infelix animaiam exagitabatur. Nec in eo subsitit vindicta divina, sed Tragicæ calamitates vxorem & filios eius exercuerunt. Getam enim ex matris collo pendentem Bassianus frater occidit, hæc autem cùm postea tam crudele parricidium priuigno nu-pfisset, & is à satellite corporis custode iugulatus esset, illa quoq; supra cadauer illius ad se delatum seipsam interfecit. Quid Iulius Maximinus, qui post institutam contra Dei electos persecutionem, apud Aquileiam seditione militari oppressus vnà cum filio perijt, omnibus acclamantibus, Ex pessimo genere ne catulum quidem relinqui debere? Quid Decius, qui in barbarico solo paludis voragine absorptus est, vt ne corpus quidem eius inueniri potuerit, cùm primùm filium contra hostes acriter pugnantem amisisset? Quàm verò horrendum vltionis diuinæ exemplum Licinius Valerianus factus est, qui à Sapore Persarum rege captus, huic aliquandiu equum conscensuro scabelli loco fuit, qui tandem iam seni post multa ludibria pellem à ceruice ad pedes detraxit? Valerium quoque Aurelianum crudelia aduersus Christianos edicta vulgantem, Deus primùm fulmino fulmine ante pedes delapso terruit, sed poenitere nescium mox suorum insidijs oppressum è medio sublatus est. Adde his Diocletianum & Maximianum, qui cum multa iniustè & crudeliter per multos annos aduersus Ecclesiam designauissent cum collegis suis Maxentio & Maximino, illi quidem uno die imperio sese abdicarunt, vel dolore, quòd perficinon posse viderent ea, quae moliti fuerant, vel Constantini metu, & Diocletianus insuper sibipsi mortem consciuit. Maximianus autem cum genero Constantino insidias struxeret, à filia, quae maritum patri praeferebat, proditus & Maßilia occisus est: Maxentius autem ad pontē Miluium à Constantino victus in praecipiti fuga, Pharaonis exemplo, in flumine periit: nec multò post Maximinus à Licinio Constantini auspicijs victus, phthriasi inter diros totius corporis dolores mortuus est. Et hi quidem omnes intra annos circiter ducentos quinquaginta & unum (si ab ultimo Neronis ad decimum annum Constantini numeres, qui Ecclesiae pacem dedit) regnarunt, et tam horrenda irae Dei exempla facti sunt. Quibus non multò post Licinius accessit, qui cum nouas minas contra Christianos spiraret, duobus praelijs victus & imperio exutus aliquandiu Thessalonicae priuatus vixit, sed tandem, cum res nouas moliretur, à Constantini praesidio ibidem interfectus est. Adde his Iulianum, cuius obitus plus quàm Tragicus & postrema vox, non tam contumaciae incurabilis quàm desperationis horrendae testis, abunde docent, Deum nunquam officio deesse, quò minus suos ex impiorum manibus vindicet. Nec tamen Imperatores soli vindictam diuinam senserunt, sed Romae etiam, quae Christianorum supplicijs diu oblectata fuerat, tandem rependere coepit Deus, quando populis barbaris atque crudelissimis diripiendam atque lacerandam propinauit. Coepit ea calamitas anno à natali Christi CCCCXII. & vsque ad annum DLI. progressa est per annos centum triginta & nouem, intra quos sexies à barbaris aut exteris capta, omnia ea perpessa est, quae in urbe capta hostiliter fieri consueuerunt. Nam anno quadringentesimo & duodecimo illam duce Alarycho Visigotthi coeperunt & diripuerunt. Inde sub annum CCCCLVI. à Vandalis duce Genserycho occupata & direpta est. Idem post annos quindecim ei accidit per Odoacrum Herulorum Regem. Rursus vix quatuordecim annis elapsis illa potitur Theodorychus Ostrogotthorum rex. Et cum ab istis calamitatibus aliquantulum respirauissent, eam Imperatori Iustiniano recuperauit Bellisarius, quod anno DXXXVIII. factum esse historici tradunt. At anno ab ea instauratione duodecimo per proditionem capit illam Totilas, captam & direptam vastat & incendit, & habitatoribus eiectis vacuam reddit, ne vno quidem mortalium illic relicto. Quam cum sequenti anno Bellisarius recuperauisset, eandem tamen ipse Byzantium profectus, Totilae rursum occupandam reliquit. Itaque vrbs quondam rerum domina, totius mundi & barbarissimarum gentium ludibrium facta fuit, sic nimirum vindicante Deo suorum sanguinem, qui in ea per multos annos effusus fuerat. Taceo nunc Hunnos & Longobardos, qui & ipsi illam terroribus grauissimis exagitarunt. Taceo infelicem eius conditionem, quae in hodiernū usq; diem premitur, dum amisso Imperio (cuius umbratili titulo Pontifices superbiunt) & abolita Senatus authoritate, Paparum libidini seruit, pijs omnibus exosa. Et si quae nostro secu-lo tam Romae quam multis alijs regnis acciderūt cōsideres, mox videbis adhuc veram ratamq; esse Christi sententiam, qua Deum pronuntiat vindicaturum electos suos, qui adipsum die ac nocte clamant. Iltorum ergo consideratione seipsos consolentur atque confirment, quotquot vel publicis totius Ecclesiae calamitatibus premuntur, vel priuatim iniurias improborum patiuntur. Nam etsi Deus (vt supra diximus) aliquandiu vindictam differat, suo tamen tempore manum exerit, vt iustus laetetur, et pedes suos (vt Dauid ait) in sanguine impiorum abluat, dicendo: Certè iustum ma-net suus fructus, certè est Deus, qui facit iudicium in terra. Interea nostri officij esse memineri-mus, moram quantamcunque patienter ferre, & cum carnis impatientia luctari, ne in precibus fatigemur, aut spe liberationis prorsus extincta murmuremus, si non illico nostris votis Deus annuat. Vbi non parum profuerit cogitare, quoties nos quoque illum nos admonentem & magnis clamoribus poenitentiam & emendationem vitae requirentem contempserimus. Nam solet hoc interdum optimis etiam accidere, vt in pace & otio securiores facti, Deum in Verbo suo loquentem minus audiant, & ferè vix correptione aut increpatione duriori se excitari patiantur, vt quae sui officij sunt faciant. Quae ergo nobis iustae querelae causa reliqua est, si ad nostros quoq; clamores aliquandiu ille surdus esse videatur? Adde his, quòd mora ista nobis vtilissima est, quia fidem nostram exercet & huius obedientiae carnem subijcit: quòd denique facit ad illustrandam gloriam Dei, cuius potentia & iustitia, eò clarius elucet, quò minus in humanis spei est{c} reliquum.
units.tr: In the present matter, a particular consideration deserves attention: God will at last avenge his elect, who cry out to him day and night, even if he postpones his anger against their enemies for a while. For since he is the judge of the whole earth (as Abraham says), and vengeance is bound up with judgment, he cannot neglect this duty unless he also ceases to act as judge. That is why the saints in the Psalms call him "the God of vengeances," crying: "O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongs, O God, to whom vengeance belongs, shine forth. Lift up yourself, O judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud" [Psal. 94.]. Since he is truly such toward all people, as the histories of all nations bear witness plainly, he will much more avenge his own elect, whom he chose for himself by his eternal decree, and whom at last he redeemed with the blood of his Son, so that he might make them his own special people, indeed his sons and heirs of his heavenly kingdom. Of these he certainly declares through Zechariah: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye" [Zech. 2.]. And in the same prophet the Church is compared to a stone of burden, which all indeed try to remove from the midst, yet no one can lay a hand on it without some plain loss [Zech. 12.]. Nor should the delay which God sometimes allows shake our faith. Its cause is not that God ignores or neglects us even for a moment, but that he, being patient and long-suffering, holds back his anger so that he may give the wicked an opportunity to repent, and at the same time exercise the patience and faith of his people. When this has been done well, and the wicked persist in struggling against him with incurable obstinacy, he compensates for that delay by the severity of his vengeance. Many examples of this occur in all histories. First among these, let the children of Israel come forward, whom Pharaoh afflicted with more than barbaric tyranny for about one hundred years and more (if you compare Moses' age with that whole history). And so God might seem to have forgotten both his people and the covenant he made with Abraham. But when the cruelty of the tyrant had reached its limit, and the Israelites sighed and cried out to God amid these most severe burdens, their cry came up to him, and he remembered his covenant. That is, he showed in fact that he was mindful of it, and said to Moses, who was living among the Midianites: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, and I know their sorrows. Therefore I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians," and so on [Exod. 3.]. Who does not know how dire and horrible were the examples of vengeance executed upon Pharaoh and all Egypt? God did the same in avenging his people afterward, not once only, in the times of the judges against the Ammonites, Canaanites, Midianites and Philistines, and at last also against the Babylonians, when they had held the people in exile and captivity for a full seventy years. Nor did God change his disposition in the New Testament, but here too he stretched out his avenging hand more than once. And to begin again with the Jews: everyone knows with what impiety they rejected the Redeemer offered to the human race, how relentlessly they pursued him with hatred, how unjustly and cruelly they put him on the cross, and finally with what untamed rage they raged against his Apostles and the doctrine of the Gospel rising throughout the world. The godly groaned for a long time and cried out meanwhile, and God seemed not to care about these things. But suddenly that day of vengeance dawned, on which he required the blood of his Son and of his saints from the wicked hands of those people, and destroyed the unhappy nation by a destruction terrible and without parallel. The posterity of Herod did not fare better, for it followed its father's example and aided the fury of the Jews. But what shall we say of Rome and the Roman emperors, whose cruelty against his elect God avenged with such dire and notable examples that, even if no others existed, these alone could establish the faith by the words of Christ? For Nero, who first sharpened the sword against them, in order to shift onto the Christians the blame for the fire he had set in Rome (as Cornelius Tacitus writes), and so free himself from hatred and envy, was finally judged a public enemy by the Senate, and laid hands on himself, since, though about to die, he could not even find an executioner to kill him either out of love or hatred. Whence he said: "Have I then no friend or enemy at all?" Domitian followed in his footsteps, and was cruelly butchered by his own household servants. Soon after the cruel edicts of Trajan against the faithful and his impious attempts came the burning of the Golden House, the flooding of the Tiber, plague, famine and earthquakes, by which several cities of Greece and Asia collapsed. These things did not frighten Marcus Antoninus Verus, who even rose up against the Church himself; but God restrained him too, by the plague which horribly laid waste Italy and utterly drained many towns, and also by the invasions of the Germans. In a similar way L. Septimius Severus felt the heavy vengeance of God: civil wars harassed him on account of the Christian blood he had shed, and dying at York, far from Rome, he uttered this word full of despair: "I have become all things, and nothing profits me" [πάντα ἐγένομην, καὶ οὐδὲν ἐμοὶ λυσιτελεῖ]. For at the end of his life and amid the fragility of human affairs he was feeling the anger of God, by which the unhappy soul was tormented. Nor did divine vengeance stop there, but tragic calamities afflicted his wife and sons. For his brother Bassianus killed Geta while he hung from their mother's neck. Later she married the murderer as her stepson, and when he was throttled by a bodyguard, she too killed herself over his corpse, which had been brought to her. What of Julius Maximinus, who, after instigating persecution against God's elect, was overwhelmed by a military mutiny at Aquileia and perished together with his son, while all cried out: "The wicked brood should not even leave a whelp behind"? What of Decius, who was swallowed up in a bog on barbarian soil, so that his body could not even be found, after he had first lost his son, who was fighting bravely against the enemy? And what a horrible example of divine vengeance Valerian became, who, captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, served as a footstool for him when he was about to mount a horse, and who at last, after many mockeries, when he was already old, had his skin stripped from his neck to his feet? God also terrified Valerius Aurelianus, who was publishing cruel edicts against the Christians, first by a thunderbolt falling at his feet; but since he was unwilling to repent, he was soon overwhelmed by the plots of his own men and removed from the midst. Add Diocletian and Maximian, who, after they had planned many unjust and cruel measures against the Church for many years together with their colleagues Maxentius and Maximinus, abdicated the throne in one day, the former out of grief that he could not accomplish what he had attempted, the latter out of fear of Constantine. Diocletian moreover took his own life. Maximian, who was plotting against his son-in-law Constantine, was betrayed by his daughter, who preferred her husband to her father, and was killed at Massilia. Maxentius, defeated by Constantine at the Milvian Bridge, perished in the river in headlong flight, as Pharaoh did. Not long afterward Maximinus, defeated by Licinius under Constantine's auspices, died of phthiriasis amid dreadful pains throughout his whole body. All these men reigned within about two hundred and fifty-one years (if you count from the last year of Nero to the tenth year of Constantine, who gave peace to the Church), and became such horrible examples of God's wrath. Not long after them came Licinius, who, while breathing fresh threats against the Christians, was defeated in two battles and deprived of his empire. He lived for a time as a private man at Thessalonica, but at last, when he was plotting new schemes, he was killed there by Constantine's guards. Add Julian, whose death, more tragic than tragedy, and whose last word, bear witness not so much to incurable obstinacy as to dreadful despair, and abundantly teach that God never fails in his duty to avenge his own from the hands of the wicked. Nor did the emperors alone feel divine vengeance. At Rome too, which had long delighted in the punishment of Christians, God began at last to repay, when he handed it over to be plundered and torn apart by barbarous and most cruel peoples. That calamity began in the year 412 after the birth of Christ, and it continued through 139 years, until the year 551, during which time Rome was six times captured by barbarians or foreigners and suffered everything that is customarily done to a city taken by an enemy. For in the year 412 the Visigoths under their leader Alaric began to attack and plunder it. Then, about the year 456, it was seized and plundered by the Vandals under their leader Genseric. The same thing happened fifteen years later through Odoacer, king of the Heruli. Again, scarcely fourteen years had passed when Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, took possession of it. When they had drawn some breath after these calamities, Belisarius recovered it for the emperor Justinian, which historians record as having happened in the year 538. But in the twelfth year after this restoration, Totila took it by treachery; having captured and plundered it, he laid it waste and burned it, and drove out its inhabitants, leaving not a single mortal there. When Belisarius recovered it the following year, he himself went off to Byzantium and left it to be taken again by Totila. And so the city, once mistress of the world, became a plaything of the whole world and of the most barbarous peoples. Thus indeed God avenged the blood of his people, which had been shed there over many years. I say nothing now of the Huns and Lombards, who also harassed it with most grievous terrors. I say nothing of its wretched condition, which still oppresses it to this day, while, the empire having been lost (whose shadowy title the popes boast of) and the authority of the Senate abolished, it serves the lust of the Popes, hateful to all the godly. And if you consider what has happened in our own age, both at Rome and in many other kingdoms, you will soon see that the saying of Christ is still true and valid, in which he declares that God will avenge his elect, who cry out to him day and night. Let all who are oppressed either by public calamities of the whole Church or privately suffer the injuries of the wicked therefore comfort and strengthen themselves by considering these things. For although God (as we said above) postpones vengeance for a while, yet in his own time he stretches out his hand, so that the righteous may rejoice and wash his feet in the blood of the wicked, as David says, saying: "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth" [Psal. 58.]. Meanwhile let us remember that it is our duty to bear patiently whatever delay there is, and to struggle against the impatience of the flesh, lest we grow weary in prayer, or, with hope of deliverance utterly extinguished, murmur if God does not immediately grant our prayers. It will greatly help to consider how often we too have despised him when he admonished us and with loud cries required repentance and amendment of life. For this sometimes happens even to the best people: made more careless by peace and leisure, they hear less well God speaking in his Word, and they hardly allow themselves to be roused except by a sharp rebuke or reproof, so that they may do what belongs to their duty. What, then, is left as a just cause for our complaint, if he seems deaf even to our own cries for a while? Add to this that this delay is most useful to us, because it exercises our faith and subdues the flesh to this obedience; and finally, that it serves to make the glory of God shine forth, since his power and justice shine all the more clearly the less hope remains in human affairs.

units.la: Porrò ad Christi verba redeamus, qui non obscurè docet, non sine graui causa fieri, quòd Deus nouissimis temporibus opem suam diutius differat, cùm plerique sibijpsis obstent, quo minus illa frui queant: & simul ostendit, eò feruentius nos precibus instare debere, quò maiorem videmus esse mundi huius in suum interitum ruentis socordiam. Dicit enim: Veruntamen Filius hominis cùm venerit, num reperturus est{c} fidem in terra? Ostendit fidem inter homines postremis temporibus rarissimam fore, quae causa sit futura, ob quam pluribus malis exerceantur, qui vnicum istud salutis praesidium tam ofcitanter negligunt. Habet verò fidei vocabulum significationem multiplicem & variam. Proprie fiduciam certam in Deum per Christum denotat, qua illius promissiones firmo animi assensu apprehendimus. Deinde pro doctrina quoque fidei sumitur. Item pro confessione Iesu Christi, quem illa solum redemptorem agnoscit. Est etiam fides inter homines, quam Cicero dictorum conuentorumq; constantiam & veritatè definit, & ex Stoicorum sententia sic appellatam credit, quia fiat quod dictum est. Atqui omnibus istis significationibus hoc Christi dictum applicari poterit. Quis enim non videt Christianam fidem quae solius Dei gratia per Christum nititur, in angustos fines redactam esse, Turcis & alijs Mahumetanae superstitionis sectatoribus maiorem orbis terrarum partem occupantibus? Vt iam nihil dicamus de Pontificijs & Romanae sedis adoratoribus, de Anabaptistis, Libertinis, Seruetanis & infinitis alijs sectis inter Christianos passim regnantibus. Per hos fit, vt vera doctrina de Christo multis in locis explodatur, conculcetur, & ferro atque igne oppugnentur, qui illam solam sibi sequendam proponunt. Accedit praeterea, quòd alij fidem in vnum Christum disertis verbis abnegant: alij verò cum illam ore profiteantur, eandem tamen vitae licentia & morum improbitate impijssimorum hostium ludibrijs exponant. Quòd si ad hominum commercia respicias, illic quoque fides rarissima est. Quae enim ratio hominibus fideles faciat eos, quibus lusus & iocus est Deo fidem datam fallere? Sunt ergo diffidentiae & perfidiae omnia plena. Nam vt à capite exordiamur, quàm rari sunt inter principes, qui populi pacem atq; salutem fideliter curent, & non potius illum immoderatis exactionibus exhauriant, bellis non necessarijs fatigent, et insuper publicanorum atq; vsurariorum artibus deglubendum exponant? Rursum quàm paucos ex subditorum numero pijs quoq; magistratibus fideles reperias, si licentiam suam bonis legibus paulò seuerius coercenti sentiant? Similiter si Ecclesiarum ministros considereris, maior eorum pars lucro studet, et huius gratia impijs blandiuntur, & Ecclesias facilè deserunt, si quae maioris stipendij spes aliunde affulserit. E contra, qui fidos pastores obseruare & diligere debebant, eos odisse et inuidia prosequi, imò interdum pacem huius mundi illorum proditione redimere consueuerunt. Eadem est{c} ratio inter heros & seruos, in foederibus, contractibus, et omnibus alijs hominum commercijs: adeò vt quod Poeta de ferrea aetate dixit, nos de nostri seculi hominibus possimus dicere: Iam pridem fugëre pudor, verumque fidesque: In quorum subiere locum fraudesque doliqué, Insidiaeque, & vis, & amor sceleratus habendi. Viuitur ex rapto: non hospes ab hospite tutus, Non socer a genero, fratrum quoque gratia rara est{c}. Imminet exitio vir coniugis, illa mariti, Lurida terribiles miscent aconita nouercae, Filius ante diem patrios inquirit in annos:
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Christ, who plainly teaches that there is a serious reason why God delays his help for so long in the last times, since many people stand in their own way and cannot enjoy it. At the same time he shows that we ought to press on in prayer all the more eagerly the more we see the sloth of this world rushing towards its own destruction. For he says: "Nevertheless, when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" (Luke 18:8). He indicates that faith will be extremely rare among men in the last times, and what the cause will be for which many are punished with evils, since they so carelessly neglect this one safeguard of salvation. The word "faith" has many and varied meanings. Properly, it denotes a sure trust in God through Christ, by which we grasp his promises with a firm assent of the mind. Then it is also taken for the doctrine of faith. Likewise it is taken for the confession of Jesus Christ, whom faith acknowledges alone as Redeemer. There is also faith among men, which Cicero defines as the constancy and truthfulness of words and agreements, and he believes it was so named after the Stoics' opinion, because what has been said is done. Yet this saying of Christ can be applied to all these meanings. For who does not see that the Christian faith, which rests on the grace of God alone through Christ, has been reduced to narrow limits, while the Turks and the other followers of the Mahumetan superstition occupy the greater part of the world? To say nothing yet of the Papists and the adorers of the Roman see, or of the Anabaptists, Libertines, Servetians and countless other sects that rule everywhere among Christians. Through these it comes about that the true doctrine concerning Christ is in many places hissed down, trampled underfoot, and assailed with sword and fire, by those who propose to follow only that doctrine for themselves. Besides, some openly deny faith in Christ alone, while others, though they profess it with their mouths, nevertheless expose it to the mockery of the most ungodly enemies by their licence of life and wickedness of manners. And if you look at the dealings of men, faith is extremely rare there too. For what reason would make men faithful to one another, when those who make a game and a joke of breaking faith given to God? So everything is full of distrust and treachery. For to begin at the head: how rare are the princes who faithfully care for the peace and welfare of the people, and do not rather drain them dry with immoderate exactions, wear them out with unnecessary wars, and, besides, hand them over to be stripped by the arts of tax-farmers and usurers? Again, how few faithful subjects you would find among the people, even under pious magistrates, if they feel their licence restrained a little too severely by good laws? Likewise, if you consider the ministers of the Churches, the greater part of them pursue gain, and for its sake they flatter the wicked, and they readily desert the Churches if some hope of a larger stipend has shone upon them from elsewhere. On the contrary, those who ought to have observed and loved faithful ministers have been accustomed to hate them and pursue them with envy, and at times even to buy the peace of this world by their betrayal. The same is the case between masters and servants, in covenants, contracts, and all the other dealings of men; so much so that what the poet said of the iron age we may say of the men of our own age: "Long since have shame and truth and faith fled away; in their place have come deceits and guile, plots, violence, and the accursed love of possessions. They live by plunder: no guest is safe from his host, no father-in-law from his son-in-law; even brotherly affection is rare. The husband threatens his wife's death, the wife her husband's; pale stepmothers mix terrible poisons; the son inquires into his father's years before their time."

units.la: Victa iacet pietas, &c. Haec cum omnia hodie fiant, & ferè impunè fiant, quis non Christum hîc verè locutum esse fateatur, Filius hominis cùm venerit, num reperturus est fidem in terra? Quis item miretur, multorum preces minus exaudiri, & optatam salutem diutius differri? Quid verò hîc faciant homines Christiani, quorum animos purior verae fidei & veritatis cognitio illustrauit? Num e mundo emigrabunt? Num & ipsi spe salutis abiecta eandem cū alijs viam ingredientur, vt vitam tutius transfigant? Minimè. Sed vt nuper dictum est, singuli vocationi suae insistant, stationem suam sedulò tueantur, salutis portum tutum sibi in Christo paratum esse credant, Deum autem assiduis precibus fatigent, vt is rebus vbiq; in peius prolabentibus manu admoueat, hostium impiorum conatus frangat, Ecclesiæ suæ reliquias seruet: vt denique maturet aduentum Filij sui Iesu Christi, qui tantis miseriis finem imponat, et nos in æternæ felicitatis portum ad se recipiat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: "Piety lies vanquished," and so on. Since all these things are done today, and for the most part done with impunity, who would not confess that Christ spoke truly here: "When the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" Who likewise would be surprised that the prayers of many are less heard, and the longed-for salvation deferred for longer? But what should Christian men do here, whose minds the purer knowledge of true faith and truth has enlightened? Will they emigrate from the world? Will they too, with hope of salvation abandoned, enter the same way as the others, so as to pass their life more safely? By no means. But, as was said recently, let each keep to his own calling, diligently guard his post, believe that the harbour of salvation is safely prepared for him in Christ, and wear out God with constant prayers, that he may put his hand to things that are everywhere sliding into worse, break the attempts of the impious enemies, preserve the remnants of his Church; and finally hasten the coming of his Son Jesus Christ, who may put an end to such great miseries and receive us to himself in the harbour of eternal happiness. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 167.

units.la: Dixit autem etiam quibusdam, qui sibi persuaserant se iustos esse, & pro nihilo habebant reliquos, parabolā istam. Duo homines ascenderant in templum vt precarentur, vnus Pharisæus, & alter Publicanus. Pharisæus stans hæc apud se precabatur: Deus, gratias ago tibi, quod non sim vt reliqui homines, rapaces, iniusti, mœchi, vel etiam vt iste publicanus. Ieiuno bis in hebdomade, decimo quæcunque possideo. Publicanus autem procul stans nolebat vel oculos in cœlum attollere: sed percutiebat pectus suum, dicens: Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori. Dico vobis, descendit iste iustificatus domum suam potius quàm ille. Quia quicunque se extollit, deprimetur, & qui se deprimit, extolletur.
units.tr: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and looked down on everyone else: "Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed this within himself: 'God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust men, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.' But the tax collector, standing far off, would not so much as lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner.' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."

units.la: Quemadmodum inter fidei & veræ pietatis exercitia preces in primis commendantur: ita Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus, cùm de nouissimorum temporum periculis disseruisset, portum & asylum tutissimum in precibus assiduis monstrauit. At duo fere sunt, quæ preces Deo ingratas, & proinde inanes reddunt: Suijpsius nimirum aut operum atque meritorum proprium fiducia, & superbus aliorum contemptus. Etenim etsi monstro simile videri possit, hominem mortalem & propter peccata ira Dei atque damnationi æternæ obnoxium, in Dei conspectu sese ostentare, est tamen hic communis morbus, cuius (vt & multorum aliorum) causa est, quòd plerique Deum ex suo ingenio & proprijs moribus æstimant. Quia ergo apud homines aliquid impetraturi nostra in illos officia & merita allegamus, idem sibi coram Deo quoq; non licere solum, verum etiam necessarium esse multi arbitrantur, & ideo sua opera vel aperte iactant, vel saltem intra animos suos fiduciam in illis collocant. Nascitur ex eo alterum vitium, quòd ijdem reliquos omnes præse contemnunt. Nec enim fieri potest vt aliquem mortalium magni faciat, qui in Dei conspectu sese venditare, & cùm eius gratia quodammodo bellum suscipere audet. Quapropter ijs, quæ de precandi assiduitate dixerat, commodè huius loci doctrinam Christus subijcit, qua monet, preces nostras Deo minimè acceptos fore, nisi ex animo verè humiliato & peccatorum seria agnitione contritô proficiscantur.
units.tr: Just as prayers are especially commended among the exercises of faith and true godliness, so our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, after speaking of the dangers of the last times, pointed to prayer, persevering and constant, as the safest harbour and refuge. Yet there are almost two things which make prayers unpleasing to God and therefore empty: namely, confidence in oneself, in one's own works and merits, and proud contempt of others. For although it may seem monstrous that a mortal man, who on account of his sins is liable to the wrath of God and to eternal damnation, should display himself before the sight of God, this is nonetheless a common disease, whose cause (as with many others) is that most people judge God by their own disposition and their own ways. So, because when we are about to obtain something from men we plead our services and merits to them, many think that it is not only permitted but even necessary to do the same before God, and therefore they either openly boast of their works or at least place their confidence in them within their hearts. From this arises the second vice, that the same people despise all others. For it cannot happen that someone who dares to show himself off before the sight of God, and as it were to wage war against his grace, values any mortal at all. Therefore, after what he had said about the constancy of prayer, Christ fittingly adds the teaching of this passage, by which he warns that our prayers will by no means be acceptable to God unless they proceed from a heart truly humbled and from a serious recognition and contrition of sins.

units.la: Occasione huius admonitionis ex ijs petit, qui iampridem sibi persuaserant, se iustos esse, & hac fiducia turgidi reliquos homines non sine contumelia publica fastidiebant.
