Erat talium magnus numerus illo tempore, cùm inter Iudæos rerum quodammodo potirentur Pharisæi, quos in Legis operibus & propria iustitia salutis suæ fiduciam collocauisse, iam sæpe diximus: Quorum doctrina ex ijsdem fontibus, morali nimirum ethnicorum philosophia, nouissimis temporibus in Ecclesiam deriuata, errores & superstitiones infinitas peperit, quibus Veritatis doctrina partim miserè adulterata, partim obruta atq; sepulta fuit. Est ergo hæc admonitio Christi etiā nobis cognitu vtilissima, quam vt altius animis auditorū insideret, eleganti parabola comprehendit, qua simul famosissima illa de hominis iustificatione quæstio luculentissimè explicatur. Producuntur enim duo, qui etsi eodem precandi ardore & cultus diuini studio accensi esse videantur, conditione tamen, ingenio & moribus plurimùm inter se differunt. Alter enim est Pharisæus, propriæ iustitiæ fiducia turgidus, alter verò Publicanus, qui cùm neq; peccata sua diffiteri, neq; vllum in proprijs suorum operū meritis præsidiū invenire posset, ad solius Dei misericordiam confugit, & ita gratuitam peccatorum suorum remissionem assecutus est. Sed præstat vtrunq; seorsim inspicere, & de vtroq; ipsius Christi iudicium audire.
units.tr: On the occasion of this warning he takes his example from those who had long persuaded themselves that they were righteous, and, puffed up with this confidence, looked down upon the rest of men with public insult. There was a great number of such people at that time, when among the Jews the Pharisees more or less held power; as we have often said already, they had placed their hope of salvation in the works of the Law and in their own righteousness. Their teaching, derived in these latter times into the Church from the same sources, namely the moral philosophy of the heathens, has produced infinite errors and superstitions, by which the doctrine of truth was partly miserably corrupted and partly overwhelmed and buried. This admonition of Christ is therefore most useful for us also to know; and so that it might sink more deeply into the minds of his hearers, he set it out in an elegant parable, by which at the same time that most famous question about the justification of man is most clearly explained. For two men are brought forward who, although they seem to be inflamed with the same zeal in prayer and the same eagerness for divine worship, nevertheless differ greatly from one another in condition, disposition and manners. The one is a Pharisee, puffed up with confidence in his own righteousness; the other is a tax collector, who, since he could neither deny his sins nor find any support in the merits of his own works, fled to the mercy of God alone, and so obtained the free remission of his sins. But it is better to look at each of them separately, and to hear Christ's own judgement on each.

units.la: In primo humanæ iustitiæ, & quæ ex hac nascitur, operum fiduciæ typus nobis exhibetur. Itaq; quæ ille fecerit ex ordine consideranda veniunt. Inter quæ primū est, quòd in templū Domini ascendit: nimirum secundùm Dei institutionē, qui ita præceperat, & veteris Ecclesiæ more. Voluit enim
units.tr: In the first, a figure of human righteousness and of the confidence in works that arises from it is set before us. Let us therefore consider in order what he did. The first thing is that he went up into the temple of the Lord, certainly according to God's institution, who had so commanded, and in keeping with the custom of the old Church. For God willed that his people be frequent in sacred assemblies, and therefore he also consecrated the temple built by Solomon, not without a miracle, by which he showed that he wished to hear the prayers of those who called upon his help there.

units.la: Deus populum suum in caeribus sacris frequentem esse, & ideo templum quoque à Solomone ædifica|tum non sine miraculo consecrauit, quo testatus est, se illorum preces exaudire velle, qui in illo opem suam invocarent. Quae causa fuit, quod omnibus seculis Iudaei ad illud ex longinquis etiam regionibus confluxerunt, & ipsi Apostoli quotidie eò abierunt, ut precationibus publicis interessent, sicuti in Actorum libro esse videre. Itaque laudem meretur, quod Pharisaeus iste in templum ascendit.
units.tr: This was the reason why the Jews from every age flocked to it, even from distant regions, and the Apostles themselves went there daily to take part in the public prayers, as may be seen in the book of Acts. Therefore this Pharisee deserves praise for going up into the temple.

units.la: Deinde preces facturus non apertis verbis aut ad hypocrisim fictis susurris atque demurmuratio|nibus utitur, quod in aliis istius ordinis Christus apud Matthaeum reprehendit: sed intra animum suum cum Deo colloquium instituit. Tertio non publicus suarum virtutum praeco est, sed Deo gratias agit pro donis, quibus se ab illo ornatum esse agnoscebat. Quarto opera habet per se bona & sancta, quae cum Legis divinae regula coueniunt, & quae ipse Deus per Isaiam nobis commendat, dicens: Cessate male facere, & discite bene facere. Abstinet enim à malo, cum neque alienaa rapiat, neq; aliquem defraudet vel quicquam iniuste agat, neque thori coniugalis sanctitatem violet. Adhaec bonis operibus studet, dum (ut modò diximus) templum Domini frequentat, Deum ritu in Lege tradito colit, & credibile est beneficentiam quoque illum exercuisse, cum alibi hanc Christus Pharisaeis tribuat. Adde his, quod bis in hebdomade ieiunet, & decimas persoluat ex bonis suis omnibus. Et has quidem ex peculiari mandato Dei omnes dare debebant, ut ex illis Leuitae atque parentes alerentur: ieiunia vero ordinaria nulla Deus praescripserat, praeter quam quod septimo mense in die expiationis animas affligere & carni solita substantia subtrahere iubebantur.
units.tr: Next, when about to pray, he does not use open words, nor feigned whisperings and mutterings for the sake of hypocrisy, which Christ in Matthew rebukes in others of that order; but he holds converse with God within his own mind. Third, he is not a public herald of his own virtues, but gives thanks to God for the gifts with which he knew himself to be adorned by him. Fourth, he has works that are good and holy in themselves, which agree with the rule of the divine Law, and which God himself commends to us through Isaiah, saying: "Cease to do evil, and learn to do good." For he abstains from evil, since he neither plunders another's goods, nor defrauds anyone or does anything unjustly, nor violates the sanctity of the marriage bed. Besides, he devotes himself to good works, since (as we have just said) he frequents the temple of the Lord and worships God in the manner handed down in the Law; and it is credible that he also practised beneficence, since Christ elsewhere ascribes this to the Pharisees. Add to these that he fasts twice a week and pays tithes of all his goods. Indeed, by a special command of God all were bound to give these tithes, so that the Levites and the poor might be fed from them; but God had prescribed no ordinary fasts, except that on the Day of Atonement in the seventh month they were commanded to afflict their souls and withdraw the customary sustenance from the flesh.

units.la: At Pharisaeos frequentius ieiunauisse ex Christi etiam verbis apparet, quae Matthaei sexto capite habentur. Et aliqui veterum illos singulis hebdomadibus die secundo et quinto id fecisse tradunt. Dum ergo huius mentionem facit, se plus quiddam hucusque praestitisse arbitratur, quàm Deus in Lege requirat. Quod vero obseruatu in primis dignum est, etsi haec intra animum suum secum cogitet, nihil tamen suis viribus aut propriae industriae tribuit, sed in omnibus istis Dei gratiam agnoscit, cuius virtute haec praestet. Ideo dicit: Deus, gratias ago tibi, quod nõ sim ut reliqui homines, &c. Ergo in eo etiam aliis Pharisaeis melior fuisse videtur, qui hominem cum philosophis gentium αὐτεξούσιον, id est, sui iuris & potestatis esse fingebant: libertate sui arbitrij gloriabantur, & proinde sibi ipsis acceptum ferebant si quid recte facerent. Itaque habuit Pharisaeus iste multa, quae per se laudem merentur, in quibus typum verae iustitiae operum nobis Christus proponit. Licet enim nihil horum nos iustificet apud Dei tribunal, ab omnibus tamen haec pietatis exercitia requiruntur, ut religioni studeant, Sabbatum sanctificent, coetus sacros adeant, Deum cum gratiarum actione inuocent, à sceleribus manifestis simul & occultis abstineant, vnicuique reddant quod debetur, & inter haec omnia carnem lasciuientem temperantiae fraeno coerceant. Haec enim cum Legibus naturae conueniunt, & qui ista vel omnino negligunt vel etiam reprehendunt, eos non temere Pharisaeis & ethnicis deteriores esse dixeris.
units.tr: But that the Pharisees fasted more often appears also from the words of Christ, which are found in the sixth chapter of Matthew. And some of the ancients report that they did so on the second and fifth day of each week. Therefore, when he mentions this, he thinks he has done something more than what God requires in the Law. What is especially worthy of notice is that, although he thinks these things within his own mind, he attributes nothing to his own strength or his own diligence, but in all these things acknowledges the grace of God, by whose power he accomplishes them. Therefore he says: "God, I thank you that I am not like other men," and so on. In this he seems to have been better than the other Pharisees, who pretended that man was αὐτεξούσιον [autexousion], that is, master of his own right and power, together with the philosophers of the nations; they boasted of the freedom of their own will, and therefore credited themselves with whatever they did rightly. And so this Pharisee had many things which deserve praise in themselves, and in these Christ sets before us a type of the true righteousness of works. For although none of these things justifies us before the judgement seat of God, nevertheless all men require these exercises of piety: that they pursue religion, sanctify the Sabbath, attend sacred assemblies, call upon God with thanksgiving, abstain from manifest and hidden crimes, render to each what is due, and in all these things restrain the wanton flesh with the bridle of temperance. For these agree with the laws of nature, and those who either altogether neglect or even reprove these things, you could not rashly call worse than the Pharisees and the heathens.

units.la: Quid ergo illud est, in quo iste peccauit, & propter quod in Dei conspectu non est iustificatus? Vno verbo explicari potest. Nam propriae iustitiae fiducia illi obstitit, qua deceptus contra Deum simul & homines superbiuit. Nam etsi Deo gratias agat, id tamen obiter & perfunctorie facit, & simulata potius vel imaginaria quàm seria est haec gratiarum actio, qualis interdum à diuitibus solet fieri, qui cùm se Deo gratias debere fateantur, interim se propria industria diuitias tantas acquisiuisse sibi persuadent, ijsdem ut proprijs efferuntur, & in illis spem omnem collocant: quae etiam causa est, quod neq; egestatis suae pristinae sunt memores, neq; animos suos ad humilitatem & modestiam componunt. Et talem hunc quoq; fuisse facile ex eo apparet, quod nullam innatae omnibus hominibus vitiositatis mentionem facit, quod peccata sua non fatetur, & proinde nec remissionem illorum à Deo petit: sed quasi sarta tecta sint omnia, de operibus suis gloriando sibi ipsis delitias facit: adhaec omnes simul homines prae se contemnit & damnat, cum potius cogitare deberet, abs se quoque nihil humani alienum esse, se deniq; in domo Dei adhuc seruum esse inutilem, etiamsi omnia fecisset, quae in Lege reperiuntur. Ergo non satis fuerit, Dei gratiam in genere fateri, imò illi gloriam dare, quod ipsius opus sit quicquid à nobis boni fit, nisi simul omne ex nostro animo expuamus operum nostrorum fiduciam. Est enim haec simulata gratiae diuinae praedicatio, si interea aliquod salutis meritum operibus nostris tribuamus. Ita enim Deum quoque nobis duplici nomine debitorem facimus, qui & debuerit nobis eam virtutem largiri, quæ nos alijs præstantiores fecit, & insuper opera nostra, quæ inde enata sunt, præmijs remunerare debeat. Sunt ergo eiusmodi hominum cultus non solum inutiles, verumetiam Deo abominabiles, cùm illis neq; timor Dei coniunctus sit, neq; pœnitentia & fide commendentur, neq; etiam illius misericordiam inuocent. Cur enim Deum timeat, qui peccatu, quo ille offenditur, nullum in se agnoscit. Cur pœnitentiam vel simulet saltem, qui se per omnia inu-stum esse sibi persuasit? Aut quis Deo fidere dicet eu, qui propriæ iustitiæ fiducia nititur? Ista verò simul invocationem Dei excludunt, quæ si timorem, pœnitentiam & fidem sustuleris, aut omnino nulla, aut non nisi frigidissima erit & imaginaria.
units.tr: What, then, was it in which this man sinned, and on account of which he was not justified in the sight of God? It can be explained in one word. Confidence in his own righteousness stood in his way, and deceived by it he grew proud against God and men alike. For although he gives thanks to God, he does so in passing and perfunctorily, and this thanksgiving is feigned or imaginary rather than earnest. It is like the thanksgiving that rich men sometimes make: they confess that they owe thanks to God, yet meanwhile persuade themselves that they have acquired such great wealth by their own industry, and they take pride in it as their own and place all their hope in it. This is also why they neither remember their former poverty nor bring their minds to humility and modesty. That this man was such a person is easily seen from the fact that he makes no mention of the inborn corruption common to all men, and that he does not confess his sins and therefore does not ask God for their forgiveness. As if everything were in good order, he delights himself by boasting of his works. Besides, he despises and condemns all other men together with himself, whereas he ought rather to have reflected that nothing human is foreign to him, and that in God's house he is still an unprofitable servant, even if he had done everything that is found in the Law. So it is not enough to acknowledge God's grace in general, or even to give him glory for the fact that whatever good we do is his work, unless at the same time we cast out of our minds all confidence in our works. For this proclamation of divine grace is feigned if, meanwhile, we ascribe some merit of salvation to our works. Thus we make God our debtor on a double count: he who ought both to have bestowed on us that virtue which has made us superior to others, and moreover ought to reward with prizes the works that have sprung from it. Therefore the worship of such men is not only useless but even abominable to God, since the fear of God is not joined to it, nor are they commended by repentance and faith, nor do they call upon his mercy. For why should he fear God who recognises no sin in himself by which God is offended? Why should he even pretend to repentance who has persuaded himself that he is righteous in every respect? Or who will say that he trusts God who relies on confidence in his own righteousness? Such confidence at the same time excludes the invocation of God; and if you remove fear, repentance and faith, the invocation will be either none at all or only most cold and imaginary.

units.la: At cùm huius Pharisæi iustitia siue meritū nullū fuerit, quàm miserè & quàm turpiter seipsos fallunt, qui cùm nihil horum allegare possint, tamè aduersus Deum simul & homines efferuntur? Id verò nimis impudenter faciunt, qui in Papatu suorū operum iustitiā iactant. Nā nulla prorsus facta gratiæ Dei aut gratuitæ misericordiæ mentione suas vires prædicant: operū autè bonorū loco commemorant Missæ sacrificium, ferias, peregrinationes, votum cælibatus, voluntariam paupertatē, templorum & altariū fundationes, donationes collegijs factas, sacra pro defunctis, ieiunia quæ ciborum delectu metiuntur, preculas certo numero et summa cū festinatione præcipitatas, portentosas vestiū formas & sexcenta alia, quæ nemo sanctorū veteris aut Noui testamenti vnquā sibi facienda putauit, & quæ non alia quàm humanarū traditionū authoritate nituntur. Ista tamen in Dei cōspectu sic iactat, vt cœlum sibi propterea deberi putent: alios verò omnes tanta cū superbia præse cōtemnunt, vt se solos clerum, id est, hæreditatem & peculium Domini esse dicant, totum verò populū reliquum prophano vocabulo laicos appellent: tantumnon Iudæos imitati, qui gentes omnes per contumeliam Goijm dicere consueuerunt: imò locum quoq; in templis sibi proprium vendicarunt, quo vulgus Christianorum cancellis ferreis, & plerunq; etiam gradibus sublimioribus excluditur. Nec his omnibus contenti, opera supererogationis finxerunt, quorum merita in alios redundent, qui illa pecunijs redimunt. Quis verò istos homines negauerit omnibus Pharisæis insolentiores atq; confidentiores esse? Aut num illis vnquam in mentem venire putas illud Christi: Si feceritis omnia, quæ vobis præcepta sunt, dicite, Serui inutiles sumus? Quomodo enim se inutiles seruos esse dicerent, qui se multis alijs salutem suis operibus mereri posse, sibi persuaserunt? At non habent quod omnibus istis insultent quidam ex nostris, qui cùm neque vera neque simulata opera habeant, quibus aliquam pietatis speciem prætexant, sed in apertis sceleribus vitam transigant, fide tamen & Euangelij cognitione gloriantur: neque pudet illos suæ confidentiæ, qua in cœtibus sacris prima subsellia occupant, sacramentis Ecclesiæ communicant, Euangelicæ item doctrinæ vindices videri & haberi volunt, cùm in iustissimi sint hominum, cùm ex rapto viuant, vsuras iniquissimas exigant, fallant, defraudent, adhæc intemperantia, luxu & libidine diffluant, & ne à sacris quidem Ecclesiæ opibus manus abstinent. Arbitrantur illi nudam fidei ac nominis Christiani professionem sufficere, sed omnibus illis dicitur, quod olim hypocritis Deus respondit: Quid tibi vis, quòd commemoras ceremonias meas? Cur ore tuo fœdus meum iactas, cùm odio habeas disciplinam, & verba mea poste abijcias? Os tuum addixisti malo, & lingua tua dolum concinnat. Sedes, & contra fratrem tuum loqueris, filium matris tuæ probro afficis. Hæc fecisti, cumq; ego dissimulo, fingis me plane tibi similem esse. Disceptaboitaque tecum, & ordine proponam ante oculos tuos. Istud quæso intelligite qui obliti estis Dei, ne cùm rapiam, non sit qui eripiat. Psal. 50.
units.tr: But since the righteousness or merit of this Pharisee was nothing, how wretchedly and how shamefully do they deceive themselves, who, though they can allege none of these things, nevertheless exalt themselves against God and men? Those do so most impudently who in Papacy boast of the righteousness of their works. For they make no mention at all of the grace of God or of his free mercy, but in place of good works they recount the sacrifice of the Mass, holy days, pilgrimages, the vow of celibacy, voluntary poverty, the founding of temples and altars, gifts made to colleges, masses for the dead, fasts measured by a choice of foods, little prayers rattled off in a set number and with great haste, monstrous forms of clothing, and six hundred other things which no saint of the Old or New Testament ever thought should be done, and which rest on nothing but the authority of human traditions. Yet they boast of these things in God's sight so that they think heaven is owed to them on that account; and all others they despise with such pride that they call themselves alone the clergy, that is, the inheritance and the portion of the Lord, and call the rest of the people by the profane name of laity. They are only just short of imitating the Jews, who were accustomed to call all nations by the insulting name of Goyim. Indeed they have also claimed for themselves a place of their own in the temples, from which the common crowd of Christians is shut out by iron railings and, for the most part, by higher steps. Not content with all this, they have invented works of supererogation, whose merits overflow to others, who buy them with money. Who would deny that these men are more insolent and more confident than all the Pharisees? Or do you think it ever came into their minds that saying of Christ: "When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants"? For how could they call themselves unprofitable servants, who have persuaded themselves that they can merit salvation for many others by their works? But there are some among us who have no reason to insult all these people. They have neither true nor feigned works with which to put on some appearance of piety; they spend their lives in open crimes, yet they glory in faith and in knowledge of the Gospel. They are not ashamed of their confidence: they occupy the front seats in the sacred assemblies, they take part in the sacraments of the Church, and they wish to be seen and regarded as defenders of the evangelical doctrine, although they are most unjust of men, live by robbery, exact most iniquitous usury, cheat and defraud, and besides, they overflow with intemperance, luxury and lust, and do not even keep their hands off the goods of the Church. They think that a bare profession of faith and of the Christian name is enough. But to all of them what God once answered the hypocrites applies: "What do you mean by reciting my ordinances? Why do you boast of my covenant with your mouth, when you hate discipline and cast my words behind you? You give your mouth over to evil, and your tongue weaves deceit. You sit and speak against your brother, you bring reproach upon your mother's son. You have done these things, and because I keep silent you think I am altogether like you. But I will reprove you and set them in order before your eyes. Understand this, you who forget God, lest I tear you in pieces and there be none to deliver you." Psalm 50.

units.la: Cæterùm Pharisæo hypocritæ publicanus opponitur, verę iustitiæ exemplū, eius nimirum, quæ in Dei iudicio sola potest consistere, & quæ preces nostras Deo gratas atque acceptas reddit. Estq; comparatio hæc carnis iudicio non mira solum sed etiam absurda. Nam quæ publicanorum cōditio & studia eo tempore fuerint, alibi diximus: Iudæis certè omnibus exosi erant, non propter auaritiā modò, verumetiam quòd Romanæ tyrannidis ministri essent; & iugum illius per se durum & graue, ipsi suis exactionibus iniquis & subdolis intolerabile prorsus redderent. Talè ergo Pharisæo opponere perinde fuit, ac si quis hodie cum eremita barbarum & sanguinarium militem, cum viro honesto & graui, lenonem impurum conferret. Sed ita fieri oportebat, vt Pharisæorum hypocrisis & confidentia fortius confutaretur, & omnibus constaret, quàm abominabilis Deo sit propriæ iustitiæ fiducia. Ne tamen quis ex eo scelerum excusationem captet, quid de publicano dicatur videamus.
units.tr: Moreover, the publican is set against the Pharisee hypocrite, as an example of true righteousness, namely of that righteousness which alone can stand in God's judgment, and which makes our prayers pleasing and acceptable to God. This comparison is not only remarkable but even absurd by the judgment of the flesh. For what the condition and occupations of the publicans were at that time I have said elsewhere: they were certainly hateful to all the Jews, not only for their greed but also because they were ministers of Roman tyranny, and by their unjust and deceitful exactions they made its yoke, hard and heavy in itself, utterly intolerable. To set such a man against the Pharisee was therefore just as if someone today were to compare a barbarous and bloodthirsty soldier with a hermit, or a filthy pimp with an honest and serious man. But it had to be done in this way, so that the hypocrisy and confidence of the Pharisees might be more strongly refuted, and it might be clear to all how abominable to God is confidence in one's own righteousness. Yet let us see what is said of the publican, lest anyone catch from this an excuse for his crimes.

units.la: Papistæ Pharisaei insolentiores.
units.tr: The Papists are more insolent Pharisees.

units.la: Publicanus vera iustitiæ exemplum.
units.tr: The publican is a true example of righteousness.

units.la: Cap. XVIII. Primùm procul stetisse dicitur, nimirum ab altari vel propiciatorio, quod præsentiæ & gratiæ Dei Sacramentum erat, & quod ne oculos quidem attollere voluerit. Unde verò hæc formido exorta est? Vel quæ pudoris huius causa fuit? Non alia certè, quàm vera & seria peccatorum agnitio, quæ in animo eius sensum iræ Dei & veram contritionem excitavit. Etenim fieri non potest, quin iram Dei sentiant, quicunque peccata sua veré agnoscunt. Adhæc cognitionis huius perpetuus comes est pudor, quod Paulus apertè docet, de iis loquens, qui ad Christum conversi eorum, quæ aliquando designauerunt, recordantur. Quem (inquit) tunc fructum habebatis eorum, de quibus nunc erubescitis? Id est, quorum tanta est fœditas & indignitas, ut sine pudore non possitis eorum meminisse? Omnium certè, qui in seipsos descendunt, & quot modis clementissimum illū Patrem offenderint seriò cogitant, vox vna est: Peccavi Pater in cœlum & in te, neque dignus sum posthac vocari filius tuus. Et Dauid querebatur, peccatum suum semper sibi obuersari: nimirum, quod & pudorem nouum ipsi subinde offunderet, & animum iræ diuinæ sensu perterrefaceret. Est autem hoc iustitiæ veræ & totius salutis initium, vt iam sæpe diximus, Seipsum videlicet nouisse. Ex eo enim vera humilitas nascitur, quæ facit, vt de remedio gratiæ Dei solicitii nosipsos damnando illius iudicium præueniamus. Exempla huius cognitionis in sanctissimis hominibus passim occurrunt, & quia caro propter innatam sibi confidentiam ab ea abhorret, Legis speculum omnibus Deus propositum, quod qui intuentur, ij velint nolint coguntur se miseros & infelices agnoscere. Habet ergo publicanus ille salutis principium, & quamvis operum iustitia penes Pharisæum maior sit, in eo tamen superat hunc illè, quòd peccati agnitione humiliatus primum iustitiæ verae gradum iam attigit, cùm Pharisæus sua confidentia excæcatus seipsum ab illa longissimè alienaret.
units.tr: Chapter XVIII. First, he is said to have stood far off, namely from the altar or mercy seat, which was a sacrament of God's presence and grace, and that he did not even wish to lift up his eyes. But from where did this fear arise? Or what was the cause of this shame? Certainly none other than a true and serious recognition of sins, which stirred in his mind a sense of God's wrath and true contrition. For it is impossible that those who truly acknowledge their sins should not feel God's wrath. Moreover, the constant companion of this knowledge is shame, as Paul clearly teaches, speaking of those who, converted to Christ, recall the things they once practised: "What fruit did you then have from those things of which you are now ashamed?" That is, whose foulness and unworthiness are so great that you cannot call them to mind without shame? Certainly all who go down into themselves and seriously consider in how many ways they have offended that most merciful Father say with one voice: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son." And David complained that his sin was always before him: namely because it both repeatedly brought fresh shame upon him and terrified his mind with a sense of divine wrath. Now this is the beginning of true righteousness and of all salvation, as we have often said, namely to know oneself. For from this true humility is born, which makes us, anxious about the remedy of God's grace, anticipate his judgment by condemning ourselves. Examples of this knowledge occur everywhere among the most holy men. Because the flesh shrinks from it on account of its inborn confidence, God has set before all the mirror of the Law, and those who look into it, whether they wish or not, are compelled to acknowledge themselves miserable and unhappy. So that publican has the beginning of salvation; and although the righteousness of works is greater in the Pharisee, yet in this the publican surpasses him: humbled by the recognition of sin, he has now reached the first step of true righteousness, whereas the Pharisee, blinded by his confidence, estranged himself as far as possible from it.

units.la: Deinde pœnitentia vitæ prioris seria tangitur, quod non tam verbis quàm gestu testatur. Nā percutit pectus suum, quo animi acerbissimus dolor notatur, qui vt de vita totius emendatione cogitans filium ineamus efficit. Est hic alter ad iustitiam gradus necessarius omnino: quia nisi seria de pœnitentia cogitatio peccati agnitionem sequatur, hæc non multùm proderit: imò noxia erit: quia securitas noua obrepens paulatim agnitionem illam ex animis nostris delet, tandem verò cum desperatione eadem reuertitur, eò quòd conscientiam omnino extinguere impossibile est. Id verò Pharisæis olim accidit, & hodie omnibus accidere solet, quos propriæ iustitiæ fiducia dementat, vt de pœnitentia ne cogitent quidem, sed huius doctrinam sibi superuacaneam esse arbitrantur. Simul autem eos quoque exemplum hoc publicani arguit, qui peccata quidem sua agnoscunt atque fatentur, in iisdem verò absque pœnitentia pergunt, dum in theatrica quadam expiatione & fictitijs satisfactionibus acquiescunt, vt olim Iudæi, qui sacrificijs, ieiunijs & aliis quibusdam ceremonijs sidebant.
units.tr: Next, the seriousness of repentance for the former life is touched upon, which he shows more by gesture than by words. For he beats his breast, a sign of the most bitter grief of mind, which, reflecting on the amendment of the whole life, brings us to enter upon a new course. This is another step to righteousness that is absolutely necessary, because unless serious thought of repentance follows the recognition of sin, the recognition will do little good; indeed it will be harmful, since a new security creeping in gradually deletes that recognition from our minds, and at last it returns together with despair, because it is wholly impossible to extinguish conscience. This indeed happened to the Pharisees of old, and happens to all today who are maddened by confidence in their own righteousness, so that they do not even think of repentance but judge its teaching superfluous to themselves. At the same time this example of the publican also rebukes those who acknowledge and confess their sins but persist in them without repentance, resting in some theatrical expiation and fictitious satisfactions, as the Jews of old relied on sacrifices, fasts and other ceremonies.

units.la: Tertiò ad solius Dei misericordiam publicanus confugiens clamat: Deus, propitius esto mihi peccatori. Vicit ergo in lucta illa conscientiæ fides, quæ illum monit & confirmauit, vt quàmuis se propter peccata morte & exitio sempiterno dignū sentiret, nec aliquid videret, quo Dei iram posset restinguere, non tamen desperaret, sed in gratuita misericordia salutis præsidium quæreret. Et debet hic diligenter obseruari, quòd simpliciter petit, vt sibi ignoscatur, nihil autē iactat, neq; vllis satisfactionibus gloriatur. Sciuit ergo cum Dauide, Deum sacrificijs non opus habere, & peccata inanibus ceremonijs non posse expiari, in hominis autem viribus nihil esse, quod ad Dei tribunal possit cōsistere: ideoq; idem facit, quod optimi quiq; Dei cultores omnibus seculis fecerūt, & quod solum intra æstuantis conscientiæ certamina nos iuuare potest. Hoc igitur ordine progrediantur, quotquot hodie salutis suæ consultum cupiunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, the publican, fleeing to the mercy of God alone, cries: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." Faith, which admonished and strengthened him, thus prevailed in that struggle of conscience, so that although he felt himself worthy of death and eternal destruction on account of his sins, and saw nothing by which he could quench God's wrath, he did not despair, but sought the safeguard of salvation in free mercy. And it must be carefully observed here that he simply asks to be pardoned, boasts of nothing, and glories in no satisfactions. He knew, therefore, with David, that God has no need of sacrifices, that sins cannot be expiated by empty ceremonies, and that nothing in human strength can stand before God's tribunal; and so he does what all the best worshippers of God have done in every age, and what alone can help us amid the struggles of a seething conscience. Let all who today desire to consult their salvation proceed in this order.

units.la: Sequitur enim Christi Iesu de vtroq; iudicium, graue admodum & multa observatione dignum. Dico vobis, descendit iste iustificatus domum suam potius quàm ille. Quæ comparatio non ita accipi debet, quasi Pharisæum quoque iustificatum fuisse ex operibus suis, Christus sentiat, idem tamen præferat publicanum: sed de Dei iudicio hic agitur, & iustitia operum cum iustitia fidei conferuntur, quam Paulus iustitiam Dei dicit, quia nobis à Deo per Euangelium in Christo offertur, & sola in eius iudicio consistit. Etenim habuit iustitiam humanam Pharisæus, quæ hominum iudicio magnifica & laude dignissima videri poterat, cùm nullius sceleris reus esset, & vitam viueret innocuam. Sed quid illa ad Dei tribunal profuit, vbi cordium & cogitationum, imò ipsius naturæ vitiosæ examen fit? Planè nihil, cum secundū hanc in peccatis conceptus & natus esset, cogitationibus pessimis distraheretur, cupiditatibus prauis arderet, & sua illa confidentia sese Deo abominabilem atq; exosum faceret. Publicanus autem, cùm humana aut operum iustitia destitueretur, ad Dei misericor-diam conuersus huius iustitiam fide vera apprehendit, quæ peccatorum remissione & imputatione iustitiæ Filij Dei gratuita constat. Itaque improprie iustificatus dicitur Pharisæus, quia humano iudicio talis videbatur: verè autem iustificatus fuit publicanus, quia pro iusto illum habuit Deus, à cuius solius iudicio salus nostra dependet. Facit ergo exemplum hoc ad illustrandam & confirman-dam doctrinam de iustificatione fidei, quam vnanimi consensu Apostoli tradunt. Nam si Publi-canum spectes, peccatorem quidem fuisse constat & morte dignum, neque nouam qualitatem ac-cepisse. Iustificatus tamen fuit, eò quod propter fiduciam gratuitæ misericordiæ Deus illi peccata non amplius imputauit, sed iustitiæ suæ in Filio suo nobis exhibitæ consortem siue participem fecit. Itaque ex gratuita peccatorum remissione iustificatio nostra dependet, & ideo fide iustificari dici-mur, quòd hac sola Christus apprehenditur, in quo Pater placatus peccatis nostris ignoscit, & se no-bis propitium præbet.
units.tr: For there follows Christ Jesus' judgment on both, very weighty and deserving of much attention: "I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that one." This comparison should not be understood as if Christ thought the Pharisee also had been justified by his works, yet still preferred the publican. Rather, the judgment of God is at issue here, and the righteousness of works is set against the righteousness of faith, which Paul calls the righteousness of God, because it is offered to us by God through the Gospel in Christ, and rests alone in his judgment. The Pharisee had human righteousness, which in the judgment of men could seem splendid and most worthy of praise, since he was guilty of no crime and lived an innocent life. But what did that profit before God's tribunal, where the examination is made of hearts and thoughts, indeed of corrupt nature itself? Plainly nothing, since according to that nature he had been conceived and born in sins, was distracted by wicked thoughts, burned with depraved desires, and that very confidence made him abominable and hateful to God. The publican, however, lacking human or works-righteousness, turned to God's mercy and grasped its righteousness by true faith, which consists in the free remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of the Son of God. Thus the Pharisee is called justified improperly, because he seemed such by human judgment; but the publican was truly justified, because God, from whose judgment alone our salvation depends, held him as righteous. This example therefore serves to illustrate and confirm the doctrine of justification by faith, which the Apostles deliver with one consent. For if you look at the publican, it is clear that he was a sinner and deserving of death, nor had he received a new quality. Yet he was justified, because on account of his trust in free mercy God no longer imputed his sins to him, but made him a partaker and sharer of his righteousness, exhibited to us in his Son. Thus our justification depends on the free remission of sins, and we are therefore said to be justified by faith, because by faith alone Christ is apprehended, in whom the Father, appeased, pardons our sins and shows himself favourable to us.

units.la: Porrò concludit doctrinam hanc Dominus Epiphonemate seu vniuersali sententia, qua etiam Capite decimo quarto vsus fuit: Quia quicunque se extollit, deprimetur: & qui se deprimit, extol-letur. Conuenit dictum hoc cum naturæ legibus aut communi sensu, & tam hominum quàm Dei iu-dicio ratum habetur. Coram hominibus enim sese extollunt, qui supra alios efferuntur, & quasi soli sapiant, soli laude & honore digni sint, alios omnes præse contemnunt. Qui ita sentiunt, ferè omni-bus inuisi & exosi fiunt, & quàmuis ad tempus superbiant, & multi metu potius quàm amore addu-cti eos reuerentur, occasione tamen oblata ex alto detruduntur, & eos quoque hostes sentiunt, quo-rum authoritate in primis nitebantur. E contra ad lucrifaciendum animos hominum nihil efficacius est officio sa humilitate, quam Christus, discipulorum pedes abluens, proprio exemplo nobis commen-dat. At hîc de Dei iudicio Dominus loquitur, qui & ipse (vt Petrus ait) superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam: quod facile apparet, si Esauum cum Iacobo, Iosephum cum ambitiosis fratri-bus, Dauidem cum Saule conferas. In præsenti tamen vniuersalem doctrinam Christus ad salutis æternæ & iustificationis nostræ negotiù accommodat, in quo nihil superbia exitialius, nihil item ve-ra humiliatione vtilius & salutarius est. Superbia autem in hac causa est, sine Dei timore seipsum admirari & magni facere, donis Dei extolli, propriæ virtutis fiducia niti, neque in Dei verbum re-spicere, sed pro suo arbitrio vitam & actiones omnes instituere. Est hæc superbia execrabilis, quia aduersus Dei gratiam effertur, & ἐθελοθρησκείαν parit, vt relicto Dei verbo ex nobis ipsis cultus nouos & illicitos instituamus. E contra humilitas vera est, Deum reuereri, dona eius agnoscere, pro-priæ indignitatis sensu affici, & non alio quàm gratuitæ misericordiæ præsidio niti. Hæc quia cum fide coniuncta sunt, & veram obedientiam in nobis excitant, Deo gratos atq; acceptos faciunt. Itaq; nobis totius huius doctrinæ vsus esto, vt procul relicta nostrorum siue operum siue meritorum fidu-cia, nostram indignitatem & peccata, quæ multa & grauia sunt agnoscamus: non desperemus au-tem de gratia Dei, quæ inexhausta est, & sub eius potenti manu humiliati studeamus innocentiæ & charitati fraternæ, cuius exemplum nobis viuum est Iesus Christus, salutis nostræ Mediator v-nicus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord concludes this doctrine with an epiphonema, or general saying, which he also used in chapter fourteen: "Whoever exalts himself will be brought low, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." This saying agrees with the laws of nature and common sense, and is held valid by the judgment of men as well as of God. For those exalt themselves before men who raise themselves above others, and as if they alone are wise, alone worthy of praise and honour, despise all the rest in comparison with themselves. Those who think so become almost hated and detested by everyone, and although for a time they grow proud, and many, led more by fear than by love, revere them, yet when the opportunity arises they are thrust down from on high, and they find as enemies even those on whose authority they especially relied. On the contrary, nothing is more effective for winning men's hearts than the duty of humility, which Christ commends to us by his own example in washing the disciples' feet. But here the Lord speaks of God's judgment, who also himself (as Peter says) resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; this is easily seen if you compare Esau with Jacob, Joseph with his ambitious brothers, and David with Saul. Yet in the present case Christ applies this universal doctrine to the business of eternal salvation and our justification, in which nothing is more destructive than pride, and nothing more useful and salutary than true humility. Pride in this matter is to admire and magnify oneself without the fear of God, to be puffed up by God's gifts, to rely on confidence in one's own virtue, and not to heed God's Word, but to order all one's life and actions at one's own discretion. This pride is detestable, because it is lifted up against God's grace, and it begets self-devised worship, so that, leaving God's Word, we institute new and unlawful cults of our own. True humility, on the contrary, is to revere God, acknowledge his gifts, be affected by a sense of one's own unworthiness, and rest on no other aid than free mercy. Since these are joined with faith and stir up true obedience in us, they make us pleasing and acceptable to God. Therefore let us make use of this whole doctrine, so that, far from trusting in our works or merits, we acknowledge our unworthiness and our sins, which are many and grave; yet let us not despair of God's grace, which is inexhaustible, and, humbled under his mighty hand, let us strive for innocence and brotherly love, whose living example is Jesus Christ, our one Mediator of salvation, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 168.

units.la: Adferebant autem ad eum etiam infantes, vt eos tangeret. Cum autem hoc vidissent discipuli, obiurgarunt eos. Iesus vero cum pue-rulos aduocasset, dixit: Sinite puerulos venire ad me, & eos non pro-hibete: talium enim est Regnum Dei. Amen dico vobis, quicunq; non acceperit Regnum Dei tanquam puerulus, nequaquam intro-bit in illud.
units.tr: And they brought infants also to him, that he might touch them. But when the disciples saw this, they rebuked them. Jesus, however, calling the little children to him, said: "Suffer the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them, for of such is the kingdom of God. Verily I say unto you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, shall in no way enter into it."

units.la: Docuit nuper eleganti parabola Christus Iesus, iustitiam operum nostrorum in conspectu Dei nullâ esse, salutem verò nobis ex gratuita misericordia obtingere, si eâ fide vera amplectamur. Ita vero monuit, neminem vel sua dignitate & meritis gloriari, vel alios praesse contemnere debere, sed potius in Dei gratiam recumbere, cuius fores omnibus patent, qui vero eius desiderio tenentur. Hanc doctrinam, quia non minus necessaria quam utilis & consolationis plena est, nunc exemplo illustrat & confirmat. Paruulos enim, qui ad ipsum deferebantur, etiamsi nullo propriae iustitiae merito commendarentur, benigne excipit, Regnum Dei ad illos pertinere docet, adeoque nobis illos magistros praeficit, quos imitemur. Itaque altius nunc assurgit Christus, & promissionem gratuitae misericordiae ad eos etiam extendit, qui per aetatem de illa non cogitant, neque sentire possunt quam illa opus habeant. Ut ergo dulcissimae consolationis plena est huius loci historia, ita doctrinam quoque utilem habet de pueris, quo nimirum loco apud Deum habeantur, & quid officij illis debeant parentes, aut alij omnes, quorum curae illi commissi sunt. Partes historiae tres sunt, quas breuiter percurremus.
units.tr: Christ Jesus lately taught, in an elegant parable, that there is no righteousness of our works in the sight of God, and that salvation comes to us from free mercy, if we embrace it with true faith. He warned, moreover, that no one should glory in his own dignity and merits, or despise others who are set over him, but should rather lean upon the grace of God, whose doors stand open to all who are held by desire for it. Because this doctrine is no less necessary than useful and full of consolation, he now illustrates and confirms it by example. For he kindly receives the little children who were brought to him, even though they were commended by no merit of their own righteousness, and he teaches that the kingdom of God belongs to them, and so he sets them before us as teachers whom we should imitate. Therefore Christ now rises to a higher point, and extends the promise of free mercy even to those who, because of their age, do not think of it and cannot feel how much they need it. Thus, as the story of this place is full of the sweetest consolation, so it also contains useful teaching about children: namely, in what position they stand before God, and what duty parents, or all others to whose care they are committed, owe them. The story has three parts, which we will briefly run through.

units.la: Prima de parentibus est, qui infantes quoque ad Christum attulerunt, ut eos tangeret. Matthaeus, ne quis de vulgari attactu locum intelligeret, impositionis manuum meminit, quae cum benedictione & fausta imprecatione fiebat, & consecrationis symbolum erat, sicuti ex sacrificandi ritu apparet, in quo manuum impositione victima Deo consecrabatur. Monuit istos procul dubio σοφγν, id est, naturalis illa & communis affectio, qua parentes liberis suis optime consultum esse cupiunt: & quam Deus consulto animis omnium inseruit: quia necessaria omnino est propter grauissimas & multiplices educationis molestias, quae cum fere nulla cum gratia coniunctae sint, intolerabiles essent, nisi amor ille naturalis leues & iucundas faceret. Est autem exemplum istorum parentum omnibus imitandum, qui suis infantibus tunc optime prospectum fore putarunt, si eos ad Christum afferrent, ut per hunc Deo consecrarentur. Peccant enim in eo plurimi, qui ex se genitos ad ea vitae genera siue conditiones detrudunt, in quibus non possunt non perire. Faciunt hoc, qui vitae Monasticae eos mancipant, quae praeter ignauum otium & putidissimas superstitiones nihil habet: qui item ad militiam assuefaciunt, & illos in castris, id est, in schola scelerum & impietatis educari siue institui volunt. Quibus merito eos adnumerauerris, qui imparibus coniugijs irretitos variis tentationum periculis obijciunt, quibus fides illorum labefactatur, & plerunque euertitur. Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui hominibus vsurarijs instituendos committunt, aut socios illis adiungunt improbos, quorum consuetudine & exemplo corrumpantur? Peccant isti omnes in naturae legem & sacrilegio se polluunt, cum Dei depositum tam mala fide custodiant, qui ea conditione liberos dare solet, ut ad nominis sui gloriam aeducentur.
units.tr: The first concerns the parents, who also brought the infants to Christ, that he might touch them. Matthew, lest anyone understand a common touch, mentions the laying on of hands, which was done with blessing and a favourable invocation, and was a symbol of consecration, as is clear from the rite of sacrifice, in which the victim was consecrated to God by the laying on of hands. Doubtless that natural and common affection [στοργή] admonished them, by which parents desire the best for their children, and which God wisely planted in the minds of all. It is absolutely necessary, on account of the very heavy and manifold troubles of bringing up children, which, since they are almost never joined with any pleasure, would be intolerable unless that natural love made them light and agreeable. The example of these parents, however, is to be imitated by all, since they thought their infants would be best cared for if they brought them to Christ, so that they might be consecrated to God through him. For many sin in this, that they thrust the children they have begotten into those ways of life or conditions in which they cannot help but perish. They do this who hand them over to monastic life, which has nothing but idle leisure and most foul superstitions; likewise those who train them for the army and wish them to be brought up or instructed in the camp, that is, in the school of crimes and impiety. Those too are rightly counted among them who, when they are entangled in unequal marriages, expose them to various dangers of temptation, by which their faith is weakened and for the most part overthrown. And what shall we say of those who commit their children to be educated by usurers, or join to them wicked companions, by whose company and example they are corrupted? All these sin against the law of nature, and they pollute themselves with sacrilege, since they keep so badly the deposit of God, who is accustomed to give children on the condition that they be brought up for the glory of his name.

units.la: Istorum ergo exemplum imitentur Christiani homines. Quod enim isti fecerunt, fidei opus fuit, imperfectae quidem adhuc, sed quam suis augmentis creuisse, credibile est. Nam etiamsi de Christo magnifice sentiant, nondum tamen eo vsque progressi sunt, ut aeternum Dei filium agnoscant, qui absque contactu diuina virtute salutem omnem conferre possit. Veruntamen fortis est fides eorum, cum in publico eam facto isto profiteantur, neque Sacerdotum & Pharisaeorum iudicium atque minas timeant, quos tam illius quam sectatorum eius hostes acerrimos esse non poterant ignorare. Est igitur hoc quoque plenum consolationis, quod illos non fastidit Dominus, sed eis benigne morem gerendo fidem eorum fouet atque confirmat. Id vero omnibus ille pollicetur, neque de eius promissione dubitare nos conuenit, quae tot exemplis iam confirmata est. Discamus modo mundi minas atque conatus sperare, neque propter pericula vndiq; imminentia succumbamus: oremus autem indesinenter Deum, ut is fidem vacillantem suo Spiritu fulciat atque confirmet.
units.tr: Let Christian people therefore imitate the example of these. For what they did was an act of faith, imperfect indeed as yet, but which it is credible grew by its own increase. For even if they think greatly of Christ, they have not yet advanced so far as to acknowledge the eternal Son of God, who could bring all salvation without touch and by divine power. Nevertheless their faith is strong, since they profess it publicly by this deed, and do not fear the judgment and threats of the priests and Pharisees, whom they could not fail to know were the most bitter enemies both of him and of his followers. This too, then, is full of consolation, that the Lord does not despise them, but by kindly granting their wish he nourishes and strengthens their faith. He promises this to all, and we ought not to doubt his promise, which has already been confirmed by so many examples. Let us only learn to hope against the threats and efforts of the world, and not give way on account of the dangers hanging over us on every side; and let us pray without ceasing that God may uphold and strengthen our wavering faith by his Spirit.

units.la: Secunda parte discipulorum de hoc facto iudicium describitur. Cum hoc vidissent (inquit Lucas) discipuli obiurgauerunt eos. Paucis verbis, vel vno potius, quam illis hoc displicuerit, docet, quando dignos putarunt parentes illos, qui publice obiurgarentur. Et sane, si quis carnis rationem audiat, non temere hoc ab illis factum fuisse putabit: Primo enim cum morbis nullis infantes isti obnoxij essent, nulla causa esse videbatur, ob quam ad Christum afferri deberent. Nam doctrinae, quae multos attrahebat, illi per aetatem nondum erant capaces: Deinde cum discipuli in Christi regnum terrenum, victoriis & multa maiestate illustre somniarent, indignum illis visum est, virum tantum & maioribus negotijs destinatum circa pueros occupari, quorum cura ad nutrices & mulierculas potius quam ad viros pertinet. Dum vero istis rationibus locum dant, turpissime falluntur, & quantum in ipsis est, à Christo infantes excludunt, qui non minima Ecclesiæ pars sunt, & in quibus Dei gratia quàm maximè elucet. Quo exemplo admonemur, hanc multorum grauissimorum̄ errorum causam esse, si Christum ex carnis nostræ sensu æstimemus, & secundùm hunc iudicemus de æternæ salutis & Regni cælorum mysterijs. Nam qui hic carnem in cõsilium adhibent, mox sibi Christum fingunt nouum & diuersum ab eo, qui à Prophetis & Apostolis describitur. Faciunt id hodie, quotquot vel Missæ sacrificium, vel Diuorum intercessionem, vel Romani Pontificis (quem Christi vicarium esse contendunt) primatum propugnant. Quæ enim ratio hos omnes moueat, nisi quòd carnis sensus non videt, quomodo vna Christi mors sufficiens pro totius mundi peccatis victima esse potuerit: quodmodo item vnus ille sufficiat, vt pro omnibus Mediator & intercessor sit apud Patrem: aut vt in cœlis residens, nihilominus Ecclesiam regere, & Spiritus virtute seruare possit? Itaque nihil in toto religionis negotio tam vtile tamen necessarium est, quàm vt Christum talem esse nobis persuadeamus, qualem Scriptura proponit, carnis verò sensibus atque iudicio nullum locum demus in iis, quæ ad æternæ salutis negotium aut Christi Regnum pertinent, quod ipse de hoc mundo esse negat.
units.tr: In the second part, the judgment of the disciples on this deed is described. "When the disciples saw this," says Luke, "they rebuked them." In few words, or rather in one, he shows how much this displeased them, and when they thought those parents worthy to be publicly rebuked. And indeed, if anyone listens to the reasoning of the flesh, he will think that they did not do this rashly. For first, since these infants were subject to no diseases, there seemed to be no cause why they should be brought to Christ. For they were not yet capable, by reason of their age, of the teaching which drew many. Then, since the disciples dreamed of an earthly kingdom of Christ, illustrious with victories and great majesty, it seemed unworthy to them that a man so great and destined for greater business should be occupied with little children, whose care belongs rather to nurses and women than to men. But while they give place to these reasons, they are most shamefully deceived, and, as far as in them lies, they shut infants out from Christ, who are no small part of the Church, and in whom the grace of God shines most brightly. By this example we are admonished that this is the cause of many very serious errors, if we judge Christ by the sense of the flesh, and by that judge concerning the mysteries of eternal salvation and the kingdom of heaven. For those who here take counsel from the flesh soon fashion for themselves a Christ who is new and different from him who is described by the prophets and apostles. All do this today who defend either the sacrifice of the Mass, or the intercession of the saints, or the primacy of the Roman Pontiff (whom they contend is the vicar of Christ). For what reasoning moves all these, except that the sense of the flesh does not see how the one death of Christ could be a sufficient sacrifice for the sins of the whole world; or how, likewise, that one man could suffice to be Mediator and intercessor for all before the Father; or how he, sitting in heaven, could nevertheless rule the Church and preserve it by the power of his Spirit? Therefore nothing in the whole business of religion is so useful, and yet so necessary, as that we should be persuaded that Christ is such as Scripture sets him forth; but we should give no place to the senses and judgment of the flesh in those matters which pertain to the business of eternal salvation or the kingdom of Christ, which he himself denies belongs to this world.

units.la: Interim debet hoc loco obseruari singulare diaboli stratagema, quo ille infantium saluti omnibus sæculis insidias struxit, vt sub religionis quoque specie eos perderet, quos humani generis simul & Ecclesiæ seminarium esse nouit. Ideo olim gentes adeam dementiam adduxit, vt filios Diis suis immolarent, quæ impietas tandem apud Iudæos quoque locum inuenit, vt in parricidio et sanguinis innoxij effusione salutem quærerent. Hinc graues illæ Leges, quibus Deus exitium omnibus minatur, qui de semine suo sacrificium Moloncho fecerint. Hic per Apostolos confectum cupit, vt Christi meritum & gratiam non ad pueruulos vsque extendi putemus: quod quid aliud est, quàm illos à salute prorsus excludere? Postremis temporibus vota monastica & regulas monachorum excogitauit, ad hæc monasteria fabricauit, in quibus voto castitatis astricti pueri & puellæ, postea per omnem aetatem vel crudelissimè vruntur, vel in omni libidinis genere cum certo animarum periculo volutantur. Quibus omnibus nostro tempore accesserunt furores Anabaptistarum, qui infantibus baptismum negando, eos à Christi Ecclesia excludunt, & quantum in ipsis est, diaboli insidijs obijciunt. Sed agnoscamus veteris illius hostis dolos, nec vnquam nobis excidat, liberos à Deo dari, & huic in primis curæ esse, quemadmodum Christus in præsenti docet.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in this place, the singular stratagem of the devil should be noted, by which he has laid snares for the salvation of infants in all ages, so that under the very appearance of religion he might destroy those whom he knows to be the seed-bed both of the human race and of the Church. Thus of old he drove the nations into such madness that they sacrificed their sons to their gods; and this impiety at last found a place among the Jews too, so that they sought salvation in parricide and the shedding of innocent blood. Hence those grave laws by which God threatens destruction to all who have given sacrifice of their seed to Moloch. Here the devil desires, through the Apostles, that we should think the merit and grace of Christ do not extend even to little children; and what else is this than to exclude them utterly from salvation? In more recent times he devised monastic vows and the rules of monks, and built monasteries for these, in which boys and girls bound by a vow of chastity are afterwards abused, either most cruelly through their whole lives, or wallow in every kind of lust with a certain danger to their souls. To all these things, in our own time, have been added the frenzies of the Anabaptists, who, by denying baptism to infants, exclude them from the Church of Christ, and, as far as in them lies, expose them to the snares of the devil. But let us recognise the tricks of that old enemy, and let it never slip from our minds that children are given by God, and that he cares for them above all, as Christ teaches in the present passage.

units.la: Sequitur enim tertia huius historiæ pars, qua quid ille de toto hoc negotio pronuntiarit, narratur. Et ipsum quidem discipulis indignatum fuisse Marcus scribit. Vehementer ergo illi displicuerit oportet eorum temeritas, qua ipsi parentes pios obiurgarunt: & sanè merito, cùm & infantium saluti obstarent, et parentum fidem labefactarent, quâ potius sermone & exemplo confirmare debuissent. Deinde Parentes simul cum puerulis ad se vocat, dicens: Sinite puerulos venire ad me, & eos nõ prohibete. Et causam siue rationem addit: Talium enim est Regnum Dei. Præterea exemplum eorum omnibus imitandum proponit, addens: Amen dico vobis, quicunq; non acceperit Regnum Dei tanquam puerulus, nequaquã introibit in illud. Quasi dicat: Tã abest, vt à me & Regno meo isti arceri debeant, vt potius nemo nisi qui eorum similis fuerit, salutis capax esse queat. Et quod verbis dicit, reipsa cõfirmat. Nã vt Marcus annotat, in vllnas eos accepit, & manib. impositis benedixit illis.
units.tr: Next comes the third part of this story, which tells what Christ pronounced on the whole matter. Mark writes that he was indignant with the disciples. Their rudeness in rebuking the pious parents must have displeased him greatly, and rightly so, since they were standing in the way of the infants' salvation and undermining the parents' faith, which they ought rather to have strengthened by word and example. Then he calls the parents and the little children to himself, saying: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." He adds a reason: "For of such is the kingdom of God." Moreover, he sets their example before everyone to imitate, adding: "Verily I say unto you, whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, shall in no wise enter therein." It is as if he said: far be it from me and my kingdom to keep these children out; rather, no one can be capable of salvation unless he is like them. And what he says in words, he confirms in deed. For, as Mark notes, he took them up in his arms and laid his hands on them and blessed them.

units.la: Quo loco primùm docemur, infantes Christo adduci debere. Quod enim hic adducitur argumentum, ad omnes extendi debet, qui ex parentibus fide præditis nascuntur. Nam Christi sententia est, ad se adduci debere omnes eos, quorum est Regnum Dei. Cuius dicti ratio potest afferri, quòd ille Regni huius princeps & caput est, sicuti in Psalmo dicitur: Ego constitui Regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum. Atqui Regnum Dei infantium est, qui ex parentibus Christianis nascuntur, secundùm promissionem Abrahamo factam, Ero Deus tuus, & seminis tui. Ergo ijdem Christo debent adduci. Quia verò doctrinæ & prædicationis, qua adultiores in fide instituuntur & vocantur, pueruli non sunt capaces, nõ alia ratio reliqua est, per quam Christo adduci possint, quàm vt per baptismum in album Ecclesiæ adscribantur, quæ Christi corpus atque sponsa est. Vt ergo recens nati quoque ad Christum perueniant, baptizari debent, sicuti olim Iudæorum infantes masculi octauo die circuncidebantur. Et posset vnum hoc argumentum sufficere contra Anabaptistas, nisi hi scientes volentes errarent, & cum impudenti temeritate contumacia incurabilem comunxissent.
units.tr: At this point we are first taught that infants ought to be brought to Christ. The argument this passage offers extends to all who are born of parents endowed with faith. For it is Christ's saying that all those to whom the kingdom of God belongs ought to be brought to him. The reason for this saying can be given: he is the prince and head of this kingdom, as is said in the Psalm: "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." But the kingdom of God belongs to the infants who are born of Christian parents, according to the promise made to Abraham: "I will be your God, and the God of your seed." Therefore these same children ought to be brought to Christ. But since children are not capable of the teaching and preaching by which adults are instructed and called to faith, there remains no other way by which they can be brought to Christ than to be enrolled through baptism in the register of the Church, which is Christ's body and bride. So, that newborns too may come to Christ, they ought to be baptized, just as the male infants of the Jews were circumcised on the eighth day. This one argument might be enough against the Anabaptists, were it not that they err knowingly and willingly, and have joined an incurable obstinacy to shameless rashness.

units.la: Diabolus infantium hostis.
units.tr: The devil is the enemy of infants.

units.la: Christus infantes suscipit.
units.tr: Christ receives infants.

units.la: Infantes debent Christo adduci.
units.tr: Infants ought to be brought to Christ.

units.la: Psal. 2. Cap. XVIII. At quia ad illorum obiectiones in Marco nostro respondimus, nolumus hic plura addere.
units.tr: Psalm 2. Chapter XVIII. But since we have already answered their objections on the basis of our passage in Mark, we do not wish to add more here.

units.la: Obseruemus nunc hoc etiam, denuo nobis infantes aut puerulos in exemplum proponi. At regulam, quam hic sequamur, Paulus praescribit, in priori ad Corinthios Cap. 14. dicens: Ne sitis pueri intelligentia, sed malitia pueri, intelligetia vero adulti sitis. Cui sententiae illud Christi consentit, qui nos cū columbina simplicitate serpentinam prudentiam coniungere iubet. Sunt autem in infantibus multa, quae nos imitari conuenit: vtpote humilitas, simplicitas fraudis nescia, facilitas in condonandis offensis, & quòd mundi huius turbulentis motibus minime mouentur, quò minus suum ingenium retineant. Quae omnia à nobis etiam requiri, alibi diximus. In primis tamen huc pertinet obedientia, quam ab infantibus facile impetraueris, si huic à teneris assuefiant, in primis vero parentum pro missionibus non aegre fidem adhibent, seq; his duci patiuntur ad multa, quae ipsorum desideriis minus conueniunt. Ita fidei obedientia nobis quoque in primis opus est: quia nisi per hanc carnis nostrae sensus & affectiones omnes verbo Dei subijciamus, ad Regni illius caelestis hereditatem nequaquam poterimus peruenire. At si ista in nobis quaeras, nulla prorsus inuenies: imò nos ab his natura abhorrere constat. Itaq; regeneratione nobis opus est, vt ex femine verbi aeterni & immortalis renati infantes efficiamur, qui lac illud Sermonis seu Euangelij syncerū appetant, & per illud in viros perfectos adolescant. Ex quibus omnibus colligitur, salutem nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia contingere, cum nemo mortalium sit, qui ista suis viribus possit praestare. In hanc ergo totis animis intenti simus, & magni faciamus Dei bonitatem, qui ex filijs irae sibi nos delegit, vt in Filio suo Iesu Christo renati & Spiritu adoptionis donati caelestis Regni hereditatem cum illo possideamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now also observe that, once again, infants or little children are set before us as an example. The rule which we should follow here is prescribed by Paul in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14, where he says: "Brethren, be not children in understanding; howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be ye men." Christ's saying agrees with this, bidding us join serpentine prudence with the simplicity of the dove. Now there are many things in infants which we ought to imitate: namely humility, simplicity that knows no deceit, readiness to pardon offences, and the fact that they are not greatly moved by the turbulent upheavals of this world, so that they keep their native disposition. We have said elsewhere that all of these are required of us too. Yet above all, obedience belongs here, which you may easily obtain from infants if they are accustomed to it from tender years; above all, they readily give faith to their parents' promises, and allow themselves to be led by them in many things that do not well suit their own desires. Thus we too have most of all need of obedience of faith, for unless through it we subject all the senses and affections of our flesh to the word of God, we shall by no means be able to attain the inheritance of that heavenly kingdom. But if you look for these things in yourselves, you will find none at all; indeed it is plain that we shrink from them by nature. Therefore we need regeneration, so that, born again of the seed of the eternal and immortal word, we may become infants, who desire that milk of the pure Sermon or Gospel and grow through it into mature men. From all these things it is gathered that salvation comes to us from the free mercy of God, since there is no mortal who could accomplish these things by his own strength. Let us then be wholly intent upon this, and let us hold the goodness of God in high esteem, who has chosen us from the children of wrath for himself, so that, reborn in his Son Jesus Christ and endowed with the Spirit of adoption, we may possess with him the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXIX.
units.tr: Homily CLXIX.

units.la: Tunc interrogauit eum quidam ex primoribus dicens: Magister bone, quid faciendo vitam aeternam possidebo? Dixit autem ei Iesus: Cur me dicis bonum? Nemo bonus nisi vnus, nempe Deus. Mandata nosti: Ne moechare, Ne occidito, Ne furare, Ne falsum testimonium dicito. Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam. Ille autem dixit: Haec omnia obseruaui à iuuentute mea. Iesus vero his auditis dixit ei: Adhuc vnum tibi deest: quaecunque habes vende, & distribue pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in coelo, & veni, sequere me. At ille his auditis valde tristis factus est: Nam diues erat valde. Cum autem vidisset Iesus eum valde tristem factum, dixit: Quàm difficile qui pecunias habent, in Regnum Dei introibunt. Facilius est enim camelum per foramen acus transire, quàm diuitem introire in Regnum Dei. Qui vero hoc audierant, dixerunt: Et quis poterit saluus fieri? Ipse autem dixit: Quae impossibilia sunt apud homines, possibilia sunt apud Deum.
units.tr: Then a certain ruler asked him, saying, "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why callest thou me good? None is good, save one, that is, God. Thou knowest the commandments: Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honour thy father and thy mother." And he said, "All these have I kept from my youth up." Now when Jesus heard these things, he said to him, "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me." And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful, for he was very rich. And when Jesus saw that he was very sorrowful, he said, "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." And they that heard it said, "Who then can be saved?" And he said, "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God."

units.la: Quamuis homo quoad innatam nobis naturae vitiositatem, quae ex primis parentibus in nos deriuata est, totus corruptus sit, manet tamen in illo naturalis quaedam salutis & felicitatis recuperandae cupiditas. Eadem tamen nihil prodest, nisi Dei verbo dirigatur: eò quòd animalis homo (vt Paulus ait) non percipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Posset hoc philosophorum exemplis probari, qui cum homines acutissimi fuerint, & in rerum naturalium causis multa deprehenderint, quae innumeros alios latebant: circa quaestionem tamen de summo bono omnes hallucinati, & in sententias diuersissimas scissi sunt. Sed in primis memorabile est exemplum, quod modò recitauimus. Proponitur enim hic quidam, quem serio salutis aeternae desiderio arsisse, & in vera pietate à pueris institutum fuisse, neque vulgares in illius studio progressus fecisse, circumstantiae omnes indicant. Eundem tamen primò humanae traditiones communi errore excaecarunt, vt verum Legis Dei finem & vsum videre non potuerit: deinde verò de hoc edoctum diuitiarum amor retinuit, quò minus in Christi schola proficeret. Quia autem curabilem fuisse verisimile est, ita cum eo egit Dominus, ut quae de vera salutis assequendae ratione, deinde de diuitijs & auaritia, maxima salutis remora, dicuntur, omnium nostrum institutioni simul & consolationi seruiant. Est ergo locus hic totus multa consideratione dignissimus: in qua tamen breuiores erimus propter ea quae in Marci explanatione fusius dicta sunt.
units.tr: Although man, as regards the innate sinfulness of our nature, which has been derived to us from our first parents, is wholly corrupt, a certain natural desire for recovering salvation and happiness nonetheless remains in him. Yet this desire profits nothing unless it is directed by the Word of God, because the natural man (as Paul says) does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. This could be proved from the examples of the philosophers, who, though they were most acute men and discovered many things about the causes of natural things that were hidden from countless others, nevertheless all went astray in the question of the highest good and were torn apart into the most diverse opinions. But the example we have just recited is especially memorable. For all the circumstances show that this man was seriously burning with desire for eternal salvation, had been trained in true piety from boyhood, and had made no ordinary progress in that pursuit. Yet first the human traditions, through common error, blinded him, so that he could not see the true end and use of God's Law; then, once he had been taught about this, the love of riches held him back from making progress in Christ's school. Since it is likely that he was curable, the Lord dealt with him in such a way that what is said about the true way of attaining salvation, and then about riches and avarice, the greatest hindrance to salvation, serves at once the instruction and the comfort of all of us. This whole passage is therefore most worthy of much consideration; yet we shall be briefer here, on account of what was said at length in the exposition of Mark.

units.la: Principio conditionem illius exprimit, qui praecipua huius actionis persona est, & Christo de his differendi occasionem siue argumentum dedit. Fuit is ex primoribus & magnatum numero, ad- hanc diuitijs multis praeditus. Matthaeus iuuenem fuisse scribit, quod ipsum ad eius commendationem facit: quia non vulgarem oportet fuisse hominem, qui in iuuenili aetate inter principes populi locum habuit. Est autem obseruatu valde dignum, quod cum talis sit, de vita aeterna interrogat. Eo enim animum pium & religiosum prodit, quem neque honores neque diuitiae huius seculi inescare potuerunt, ut futurae vitae & Regni Dei nullam rationem haberet, quod plerunque ijs accidere solet, qui alijs in mundo praestant. Et si diligenter rem omnem expendamus, nemo omnium, qui huc vsque Christum secuti sunt, cum isto conferri dignus est. Vulgus enim hominum a signis modo externis pependit, ex quibus vtilitatem priuatam capiebat. Apostolos regni terreni spes lactauit. Multos curiositas attraxit. At quem vitae aeternae studium ad illum audiendum excitarit, neminem praeter hunc vnum fuisse legimus: neminem item, qui & in publico & tanta quidem cum reuerentia de illa ipsum sit percontatus. Nam ad genua eius procidit, & magistri boni nomine illum ornat. Discant igitur hoc exemplo omnes homines, in primis autem iuuenes & qui publicas dignitates gerunt, quod nam illorum praecipuum studium esse debeat. Sunt quidem non pauci, qui curam regionis & Regni Dei ad iuuenilem aetatem nihil pertinere sibi persuadent, & proinde hanc in extremam senectam reijciunt, quasi sufficiat diaboli castra tunc demum reliquisse, quando vires nos deficiunt, ut illi militare non possimus. Plerique etiam principum virorum maiestate indignum esse arbitrantur, ut ipsi ijs se immiscant, quae ad Regnum Dei & aeternam salutem pertinent. Sed vtrique non minus pernitiose quam turpiter falluntur. Quia enim nos totos Deo debemus, nullum vitae tempus est, quod non illius cultui tribui debeat. Et cum iuuenes perinde ut senes moriantur, etiam illi de vita aeterna cogitent necesse est, nisi huius iacturam facere libeat. Adde, quod cum iuuenilis aetas cupiditatibus maxime feruea t, fraeno arctiori eam cohibere oportet: quod tunc commodissime fiet, si futurae sortis memores cogitent, aliam vitam restare, in qua nos vel aeternum gaudituri simus cum Dei Filio, vel nunquam finiendos inferorum cruciatus passuri. Quoad principes viros, eadem cogitatio illis perquam necessaria est, partim ut Deo bonam gratiam referant, qui in tantam dignitatem illos euexit: partim ut caelestium bonorum & vitae futurae feria cogitatione in officio contineantur. Quia nisi id fiat, facile abutentur illa potestate, qua se praeditos vident. Nam cum natura ad malum proclives simus, nihil tam facile est quam in omne scelus ruere, si impunitatis spes proponatur. Et si nostri seculi mores diligentius expendamus, haec fere omnis corruptionis causa est, quod & iuuenes pessime instituuntur, & ijdem ad rerum gubernacula adhibiti sibi nihil non licere putant. Fere enim omnium animis insidet insolentia, quam in Dionysij Syracusanorum tyranni filio historici describunt. Is cum a patre acrius obiurgaretur, quod eius cuiusdam vxorem constupraret, & inter alia ei diceret pater, An quid huius vnquam abs me factum audiuisti? mox illi respondit: Id vero abs te factum non est, quia patrem Regem non habuisti. Etenim ut hic propter patrem Regem omnia sibi licere putabat: ita hodie imperij dignitate & impunitatis spe plerique efferuntur, ut pro sua libidine omnia faciant. Qui non alia ratione facilius continebuntur, quam si de aeterna vita diligentius & frequentius cogitent.
units.tr: First, he sets out the condition of the man who is the chief person in this action and who gave Christ the occasion or subject for speaking about these matters. He was one of the rulers and of the number of the great men, and endowed with much wealth. Matthew writes that he was a young man, which tends to his commendation, for a man who held a place among the leaders of the people in his youth must not have been an ordinary person. It is also very worthy of notice that, being such a man, he asks about eternal life. For by this he shows a devout and religious mind, one whom neither honours nor the riches of this age could entice, so that he had no regard for the future life and the kingdom of God, which usually happens to those who excel others in the world. And if we weigh the whole matter carefully, none of all who have followed Christ until now is worthy to be compared with this man. For the crowd of men depended only on outward signs, from which they gained private advantage. The hope of an earthly kingdom deceived the apostles. Curiosity drew many. But we read that no one except this one man was moved by the desire for eternal life to hear him; and no one else asked him about it in public and with such reverence. For he fell down at his knees and honoured him with the title of good master. Let all men therefore learn from this example, and especially young men and those who hold public offices, what their chief concern ought to be. There are indeed not a few who persuade themselves that concern for the kingdom and the rule of God has nothing to do with youthful age, and so they put it off to extreme old age, as if it were enough to leave the camp of the devil only when our strength fails us and we can no longer fight for him. Many also think it unworthy of the dignity of great men to meddle themselves with those things that pertain to the kingdom of God and eternal salvation. But both groups are deceived no less ruinously than shamefully. For since we owe ourselves wholly to God, there is no time of life that should not be given to his worship. And since young people die just as old people do, they must necessarily think of eternal life too, unless they are willing to lose it. Add to this that since youthful age is especially fervent in its desires, it must be restrained with a tighter bridle; and this will be done most conveniently if they remember their future lot and consider that another life remains, in which we shall either rejoice forever with the Son of God or suffer the torments of hell, which will never end. As for great men, the same thought is very necessary for them: partly so that they may give thanks to God, who raised them to such a dignity, and partly so that by frequent thought of heavenly goods and the future life they may be kept in their duty. For unless this is done, they will easily abuse that power which they see they possess. For since we are naturally prone to evil, nothing is so easy as to rush into every crime when the hope of impunity is set before us. And if we weigh the morals of our own age more carefully, this is almost the whole cause of corruption: that young men are very badly brought up, and those who are placed at the helm of affairs think that nothing is forbidden to them. For almost everyone's mind is haunted by that insolence which the historians describe in the son of Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse.
