When his father rebuked him sharply because he was debauching the wife of a certain man, and among other things the father said to him, "Have you ever heard that I did anything of this kind?" he at once replied, "Indeed you never did such a thing, because you did not have a king for a father." For just as this man thought he might do everything because his father was king, so today many are puffed up by the dignity of office and the hope of impunity, so that they do whatever their lust dictates. They will not be restrained more easily by any other means than if they think more diligently and more often about eternal life.

units.la: Obseruari praeterea in huius nostri exemplo debet, quod de vita aeterna interrogaturus, Christum adiit, non Iudaeorum Scribas aut Pharisaeos, quorum tunc praecipua erat authoritas. Causam huius facti non aliam video, quam quod illos diu nequicquam audiuisset, nec aliquid profecisset per humanas traditiones, quibus illi verum Legis sensum obscurabant. Admonemur, ut ipsi quoque in causa religionis atque Regni Dei vnum Iesum Christum audiamus. Hic enim ab aeterno in sinu Patris est, venit autem in mundum hunc, ut nobis annunciaret quaecunque a Patre accepit: & eundem nobis ille doctorem catholicum siue vniuersalem constituit, quem omnes audire debeant, qui salutem consequi cupiunt. At hodie plerique ex philosophorum libris, vel eorum scriptis discere volunt Regni cœlorum mysteria, qui humanam philosophiam Scripturis sacris longè præferunt. Quid ergo mirum est, si plerique minus proficiant, & in tenebris miserè tumultuentur?
units.tr: Moreover, in the example of this man it must be observed that, wishing to ask about eternal life, he went to Christ, not to the scribes or Pharisees of the Jews, whose authority was then pre-eminent. I see no other reason for this than that he had listened to them for a long time to no avail, and had gained nothing through human traditions, by which they obscured the true sense of the Law. We are warned that we too, in matters of religion and the kingdom of God, should hear only Jesus Christ. For he has been in the bosom of the Father from eternity, and he came into this world to announce to us whatever he received from the Father; and he has appointed him to us as the catholic, or universal, teacher, whom all who desire to obtain salvation ought to hear. But today many want to learn the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven from the books of philosophers, or from their writings, who put human philosophy far above the holy Scriptures. What wonder, then, is it if most make little progress and wretchedly stumble about in darkness?

units.la: Sed ipsam quoq; quæstionem examinemus. Magister bone (inquit) quid faciendo vitam æternam possidebo? Subest quæstioni huic Iudaicus error. Quia enim Lege perperam intellecta iustitiam & salutem sibi pollicebantur, de solis operibus soliciti erant: nec interim observabant adhærentem nobis, imò cordi & medullis insidentem naturæ nostræ corruptionem, qua impediti nihil boni vel cogitare, nedum velle aut facere possumus. Ideo hic quoq; non quærit, quæ nam vitæ æternæ consequendæ ratio sit, aut penes quem illa inveniatur, sed quid ipse facere debeat, ut eam possit obtinere. Similis omnium eorum error est hodie, qui de salute deliberaturi ab operibus suis & errorum meritis initium faciunt. Offendunt hi in ipso limine, quod aiunt, neq; aliquid proficiunt, donec in seipsos descenderint, ut quantum sibi deest intelligant. Ideo Christus, ut huic consulat, latentem illam noxam in lucem protrahit sua responsione, quæ bimembris est.
units.tr: But let us also examine the question itself. "Good Teacher," he says, "what must I do to possess eternal life?" This question carries a Jewish error with it. Because they misread the Law and promised themselves righteousness and salvation from it, they were anxious only about works, and meanwhile did not notice the corruption of our nature that clings to us, or rather sits deep in our heart and marrow, by which we are so hindered that we can neither think, let alone will or do, anything good. So here too he does not ask by what means eternal life is to be obtained, or with whom it is found, but what he himself must do to obtain it. The error of all those who today begin to deliberate about salvation from their own works and the merits of their own deeds is similar. They stumble on the very threshold, as they say, and make no progress until they go down into themselves and understand how much they lack. Therefore Christ, to provide for this man, draws out into the light the hidden fault by his answer, which has two parts.

units.la: Prima parte aliam quæstionem iuveni proponit: Cur me dicis bonum? Nemo bonus nisi unus, nempe Deus. Boni titulum detrectat, non ut se vel bonum vel Deum esse neget, sed ut illi alteram cogitandi occasionem præbeat. Quasi diceret: Quæris, quid faciendo vitam æternam possidere queas? Atqui solius boni titulus, quo me ornas, te docere poterat rem omnem. Communis enim hæc est omnibus hominibus cognitio, ea quæ bona sunt fieri debere ab iis, qui Deo probari & cum illo æternum vivere cupiunt. Atqui solus Deus bonus est, cùm homines natura corrupti & cordis humani figmenta ab ineunte ætate mala sint. Ergo nihil bonum fuerit, nisi quod ille iusserit, & quod cum eius voluntate bona & sancta conveniit. Adhæc ut bonum quid facias impossibile erit, nisi eius virtute & gratia excitaris. Ita verò Christus communem omnium hominum ofcitantiam arguit, qui cùm solum Deum verè bonum adeoque summum bonum esse vulgò fateantur, tamen non illum solum audiunt, non illi soli fidunt, neque ab illo uno petunt quæ ad salutem & vitam æternam ipsis necessaria sunt. Et hæc fere causa est, quòd cæcis suis opinionibus seducti miserè oberrant atque vagantur.
units.tr: In the first part he puts another question to the young man: "Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, namely God." He rejects the title of good, not to deny that he is good or God, but to give the young man another occasion for thought. As if he were saying: "You ask what you must do to possess eternal life? Yet the title of good with which you adorn me could have taught you the whole matter. For this knowledge is common to all men: that those who wish to please God and live with him forever must do what is good. But God alone is good, since men by nature are corrupt and the imaginations of the human heart are evil from earliest youth. Therefore nothing will be good except what he has commanded and what agrees with his good and holy will. Moreover, you will be unable to do anything good unless you are roused by his power and grace." Thus Christ rebukes the common drowsiness of all men, who, although they commonly confess that God alone is truly good and therefore the supreme good, nevertheless do not listen to him alone, do not trust him alone, and do not ask of him alone what is necessary for their salvation and eternal life. This is almost the reason why, led astray by their blind opinions, they wander miserably and go astray.

units.la: Altera parte directè ad iuvenis quæstionem respondet, dicens: Mandata nosti: Ne mæchare, Ne occidito, Ne furare, Ne falsum testimonium dicito, Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam. Quasi diceret: Quid opus est quærere quid facias? Atqui iampridem Deus voluntatem suam disertis præceptis expresserit. Quin ergo illis insistis, & facis quæ ille iubet? Ubi quis interrogaverit. Cur qui alibi vitam æternam in se credentibus pollicetur, iltum ad Legis opera remittat? Vel num diversæ sunt vitæ & salutis consequendæ rationes, una nimirum per fidem, altera per opera? Nequaquam. Nam non est nomen sub cælo hominibus datum, per quod oporteat nos salvos fieri, præter Iesum Christum: huius autem apprehendendi ratio nulla est quàm fides, ut passim Scripturæ docent. Iltum ergo ad Legis opera ablegat, ut latentem naturæ vitiositatem arguat, quam in seipso ille nondum agnoscebat. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd omissis primæ tabulæ præceptis, quæ sublimiora sunt, et aperte ipsum hominis animum sibi vendicant, secundam modò tabulam adducit, cuius præcepta ut omnibus nota sunt, ita præstitu facillima videtur. Cùm enim paulò post horum contemplatione in charitatis exercitio perfecto offendat, ad cuius mentionem ille totus confiter natur, evidentissimè docet, sal li omnes eos, qui suis viribus sive operibus vitam æternam assequi conantur, & proinde alia via esse ingrediendum. Minimè ergo locus iste iis patrocinatur, qui operum iustitiam & meritum hic stabiliri putant, eò quòd dictum sit, Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Nam hoc Christi dictum verissimum esse ipsi quoq; fatemur, & illud Mosis quoq; agnoscimus, qui de Dei statutis & iudiciis loquens dicebat: Quæ qui fecerit, in eis vivet. At nos inferimus: Atqui mandata Dei nemo facere & plenè præstare potest. Ergo nemo etiam suorum operum iustitia seruabitur. Num ergo (inquis) nos manibus præceptis & vanis promissionibus lactat Deus? Minimè. Imò præcipit ista, ut nostræ in illis infirmitatè agnoscamus, & ita confugere cogamur ad Christū Iesum, qui nobis iustitia & satisfactio datus est. Est præterea usus Legis nō contemnendus, quòd de Dei voluntate nos admonet, bonorum operum regulam præscribit, ne electitia quædam & superstitiosa ex nobis ipsis fingamus: quòd quòd item cauet, ne quis fidei prætextu ad licentiã abutatur. Nec enim huius doctrina bonis operibus inimica est, sed potius ad eanos obstringit, vt quam ore profitemur fidem, factis quoque & totius vitæ actionibus testemur. Si enim qui Christo nomen dederunt, licitis quoq; renuntiare debent, propter illum, quanto magis ijdem ab illis abstinere debent, quæ Deo inuisa & exosa esse constat?
units.tr: In the second part he answers the young man's question directly, saying: "You know the commandments: Do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honour your father and your mother." As if he were saying: "What need is there to ask what you should do? Surely God long ago expressed his will in plain precepts. Why then do you not keep to them and do what he commands?" If anyone should ask why he sends him back to the works of the Law, when elsewhere he promises eternal life to those who believe in him, are there perhaps different ways of obtaining life and salvation, one through faith and the other through works? By no means. For there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved except Jesus Christ, and there is no way of laying hold of him except faith, as the Scriptures teach everywhere. So he sends him back to the works of the Law in order to convict him of the hidden corruption of nature, which as yet he did not recognise in himself. This is also the reason why, leaving aside the precepts of the first tablet, which are loftier and plainly claim the very inner mind of man for themselves, he brings forward only the second tablet, whose precepts, since they are known to everyone, seem very easy to perform. For when, a little later, he stumbles over the perfect exercise of love, at the mention of which he is utterly cast down, he most clearly teaches that all who try to attain eternal life by their own strength or works are lost, and that another way must therefore be entered. Therefore this passage gives no support to those who think that the righteousness and merit of works is established here, because it is said: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." For we ourselves also confess that this saying of Christ is most true, and we acknowledge that saying of Moses too, who, speaking of God's statutes and judgments, said: "Whoever does them shall live in them." But we infer: "Yet no one can perform God's commandments and fulfil them fully. Therefore no one will be saved by the righteousness of his own works." "Does God then (you ask) feed us with impossible precepts and empty promises?" By no means. Rather he commands these things so that we may recognise our weakness in them, and so be compelled to flee to Jesus Christ, who has been given to us as righteousness and satisfaction. Moreover, the use of the Law is not to be despised: it reminds us of the will of God, prescribes the rule of good works, and keeps us from devising for ourselves self-chosen and superstitious forms of worship. It also guards against anyone abusing faith as a pretext for licence. For this doctrine is not hostile to good works; rather, it binds us to them, so that the faith we profess with our mouths we also bear witness to by our deeds and by the whole course of our lives. For if those who have given their name to Christ ought to renounce even lawful things on his account, how much more ought they to abstain from those things which are known to be hateful and detestable to God?

units.la: Porrò iuuenem Christo respondentem audiamus. Hæc omnia (inquit) obseruaui à iuuentute mea. Et apud Matthæum addit: Quid adhuc mihi deest? Est hoc responsum alacre, imò insolens nimiùm: & quàm turpiter vana persuasione seipsum deceperit, postea videbimus. Veruntamen præclarum hoc est vitæ transactæ testimonium, quòd saltem de externa præceptorum Dei obserua tione gloriari potuit. Nam verè hoc ab eo dictum fuisse, ex eo patet, quòd eum Christus nullius mendacij arguit, imò eundem (vt Marcus annotat) dilexit. Quem enim hodie dabis huius loci & ordinis iuuenem, imò virum iam ætate grauem, vel etiam Monachum sanctitatis specie venerabilem, qui istud de seipso verè dicere possit? Plures certè (quæ nostri seculi calamitas est) reperies, qui præcepta Dei ex ordine ne recitare quidem, nedum de illorum obseruatione gloriari possint. At hîc peculiari consideratione dignum est, quòd quid porrò faciat, quærit: imò quòd qui in præceptis Domini & operum iustitia tantum studium hucusque impenderat, Christum de consequenda vita æterna adhuc interrogat. Eo enim exemplo docemur, conscientiam nullis operibus externis placari posse, quò minus iudicij diuini terroribus infestetur. Vt vt enim illis sibi placeant homines, imperfectionem tamen suam subinde sentiunt, & nunquam non occursat Dei iudicium, cuius sensu intra animos suos conuincuntur. Est autem in hoc iuuene istud etiam laude dignum, quòd suæ imperfectionis sibi conscius proficere cupit, & quid sibi adhuc desit interrogat. Suo igitur exemplo eorum o-scitantiã arguit, qui cùm nihil adhuc fecerint, tamen quasi re bene gesta securi sunt & sibiipsis blan diuntur. Eos si quis accuset, abunde satis factu putant, si dicere possint: Et quid mali feci hactenus? Quid designaui? Sed vicissim interrogari poterant: Quid verò boni fecisti? Quasi verò non summa reprehensione dignus sit, qui in agro Domini securus otiatur, & tempus atq; ætatem malè collocat? Et si serui inutiles sumus, licet omnia faciamus, quæ nobis præcipiuntur, quo loco habendi sunt, qui contenti à maleficio abstinuisse, nihil insuper boni faciunt?
units.tr: Let us next hear the young man answering Christ. "All these things," he says, "I have kept from my youth." And in Matthew he adds: "What do I still lack?" This answer is eager, indeed excessively bold, and we shall see later how shamefully he deceived himself by a vain persuasion. Nevertheless, this is a notable testimony to a life lived, since at least he could boast of his outward observance of God's precepts. That he really said this is clear from the fact that Christ does not charge him with any falsehood, and indeed, as Mark notes, loved him. For whom will you find today, of this rank and order, a young man, or indeed a man already grave in years, or even a monk venerable for his appearance of holiness, who could truly say this of himself? You will certainly find many (which is a calamity of our age) who cannot even recite the commandments of God in order, much less boast of keeping them. But here it is worth special consideration that he asks what he should further do, and that he, who had devoted such zeal hitherto to the precepts of the Lord and to the righteousness of works, still asks Christ about obtaining eternal life. For by this example we are taught that a conscience cannot be quieted by any outward works, so that it is not harassed by the terrors of divine judgment. For although men are pleased with themselves, they still from time to time feel their imperfection, and the judgment of God always meets them, by the sense of which they are convicted within their own minds. Moreover, in this young man there is also something worthy of praise: being aware of his imperfection, he wishes to make progress, and asks what he still lacks. By his example, therefore, he rebukes the drowsiness of those who, although they have done nothing yet, are nonetheless secure, as if they had done well, and flatter themselves. If anyone accuses them, they think it is enough satisfaction if they can say: "What wrong have I done so far? What have I committed?" But in turn they could be asked: "What good have you done?" As if he who idles securely in the Lord's field and wastes his time and his life were not worthy of the utmost rebuke! And if we are unprofitable servants, although we do all that is commanded us, in what place are they to be held who, content to have abstained from wrongdoing, do nothing further that is good?

units.la: Quid verò Christus hoc responso audito? Marcus ait: Intuitus illum dilexit eum. Est enim indulgentissimus doctor, qui arundinem quassatam non comminuit, neque linum fumigans extinguit. Itaque etsi arrogantiorem æquo esse videret, quia tamen huius vitij causa erat communis illius seculi ignorantia, non potuit illi displicere studium pietatis, quod inter reliqua eius vitia emicabat. Et credibile est, non inefficacem fuisse hanc Christi dilectionem, & fortassis tandem ad fidem & Ecclesiam eum accessisse, qui nunc tristis abijt. Christus certè, ne tales temere iudicemus, suo exemplo docet. Nam amicè illum compellans ait: Adhuc vnum tibi deest: quæcunque habes vende, & distribue pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in cœlo: & veni sequere me. Quasi diceret: Vi deris tibi multum præstitisse hucusque, & tuum illud institutum laudo. Sed vnum adhuc tibi deest, & quidem præcipuum: nimirum fides viua & efficax, qua reliquis rebus huius seculi omnibus, ab vno Deo pendeas, huic vni fidas per me, qui vnicus ille Mediator sum, quem iŝ olim patribus promisit, & de quo Moses & prophetæ sunt vaticinati. Itaque ne quid tibi desit, vende quæcunque habes, & distribue pauperibus, & veni, sequere me. Non partem aliquam bonorum, sed simul omnia vendere, pecuniam verò inde colleƈtam in pauperes distribuere iubet. Quod quia carni graue est, præceptum promissione mitigat, dicens: Habebis thesaurum in cœlo. Cur enim pigeat terrena expendere, si certa cœlestium spes sit proposita? Et addit deinde aliud. Veni, sequere me. Quo loco finem & scopum Christi probè obseruari necesse est. Hunc enim quia multi non respiciunt, generale præceptum hîc dari putant, & Christianam perfectionem in eo sitam esse contendunt. At nihil hîc in genere omnibus præcipi, aliorum exemplis demonstrari potest, quibus per Christum licuit sua retinere, licet ipsius discipuli essent germani: in quorum numero Lazarus Bethaniensis fuit, Zacchæus item, Nicodemus, Iofephus Arimathæus & infiniti alij. Nec tale quid vnquam Apostoli à diuitibus requisiuerunt. Vnde apparet, neque perfectionem Christiani hominis in eo sitam esse: nisi talem fingamus, quæ nonnullis præcipiatur, alijs non item.
units.tr: But what did Christ do when he heard this answer? Mark says: "Looking upon him, he loved him." For he is a most indulgent teacher, who does not break a bruised reed or quench a smoking flax. So although he saw that the young man was more arrogant than he should be, yet, since the ignorance common to that age was the cause of this fault, the zeal for piety that shone out among his other faults could not displease Christ. It is credible that this love of Christ was not without effect, and that perhaps the man who now went away sad at last came to the faith and the Church. Christ certainly teaches us by his own example not to judge such men rashly. For, addressing him kindly, he says: "One thing you still lack: sell whatever you have, and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." It is as if he said: "You seem to have done much up to now, and I praise that resolution of yours. But one thing is still lacking to you, and indeed the chief thing: namely, a living and effective faith, by which you depend on the one God in all the other things of this age, and trust in this one through me, who am that unique Mediator whom he promised of old to the fathers, and of whom Moses and the prophets prophesied. So that nothing may be lacking to you, sell whatever you have, distribute it to the poor, and come, follow me." He does not bid him sell some part of his goods but all at once, and distribute the money gathered from them to the poor. Because this is hard for the flesh, he softens the command with a promise, saying: "You will have treasure in heaven." For why should one grudge to spend earthly things if the sure hope of heavenly things is set before him? Then he adds something else: "Come, follow me." Here we must carefully observe Christ's purpose and aim. Because many do not look to this, they think a general command is given here, and they contend that Christian perfection consists in it. But it can be shown from the examples of others that nothing is commanded here to all in general: through Christ they were permitted to keep their own possessions, although they were true disciples of his. Among their number were Lazarus of Bethany, Zacchaeus likewise, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, and countless others. Nor did the apostles ever demand any such thing from the rich. Hence it is clear that the perfection of a Christian man does not consist in this, unless we imagine a perfection that is commanded to some and not to others.

units.la: Quid igitur hoc præcepto vult Christus? Medicum imitatur, qui si cum ægroto confidentiòr sibi rem esse videat, consultò aliquid iubet, in quo infirmitatē suam ille sentiat, & hac agnita se ipsi præbeat obsequentiorem. Ita Christus, quia hic se ad Legem implendam satis instructum esse, imo se iam illi satisfecisse arbitrabatur, altius in animum eius penetrat, vt ostendat Lege non externam modò obedientiam, sed animum totum requiri, adeò, vt si Deus velit nos relictis omnibus se vnum sequi, & quæcunq; habemus aliis distribuere, nos ad hoc paratos & promptos præbeamus. Etenim iubet Lex, vt Deum diligamus ex toto corde & omnibus viribus, proximum verò vt nosipsos. Ab vtroq; autem se adhuc longius abesse bonus iste iuuenis ignorabat: ideoq; animum eius tali præcepto tentari oportuit, quo experiretur, quantum adhuc ipsi deesset. Et hoc Christi institutum fuisse, ex eo apparet, quod addit: Veni sequere me. Ergo ne hoc quidem satis fuerit ad consequendum vitam æternam, si quis sua omnia pauperibus distribueret, nisi insuper Christum sequatur, & in hoc nobis ob latam gratiam Dei fide constanti apprehendat: quem verum Legis totius vsum atq; finem esse, alibi ex Paulo ostendimus. Non ergo hæc Domini verba secundum literam exponi, & ex illis vniuer salis doctrina aut regula peti debet, ne illum sibi ipsi contrarium fingamus. Sufficiat nobis quoad salutis rationem, vt illum quidem credamus eum esse, quem Scripturæ docent; & in eo vno acquiescamus: fidem verò hanc dilectione testemur cùm erga ipsum, tum erga fratres egenos, quos eiusdem fidei vinculum nobis deuinxit. Quia enim hos ille sibi substituit, vt in illos conferamus, quæ in ipsum essemus impensuri, si hodie corpoream in terris vitam ageret; non alio euidentiori indicio quàm charitatis operibus demonstrari potest, quàm magnos in fide fecerimus progressus.
units.tr: What then does Christ mean by this command? He imitates a physician who, when he sees that he has to deal with a patient who is too confident, deliberately prescribes something in which the patient may feel his own weakness, and, having recognised this, becomes more compliant to him. So Christ, because this man thought himself sufficiently equipped to fulfil the Law, and even believed he had already satisfied it, penetrates more deeply into his mind, to show that the Law requires not merely external obedience but the whole heart, so that, if God wishes us to leave everything and follow him alone and to distribute to others whatever we have, we should show ourselves ready and prompt for this. For the Law commands that we love God with the whole heart and with all our strength, and our neighbour as ourselves. This good young man did not know that he was still far from both; therefore his mind had to be tested by such a command, by which he might learn how much he still lacked. And that this was Christ's intention appears from what he adds: "Come, follow me." So even this would not be enough to obtain eternal life, if someone were to distribute all his goods to the poor, unless he also follows Christ and, by the grace of God that has been offered, grasps him in steadfast faith. We have shown elsewhere from Paul that Christ is the true use and end of the whole Law. Therefore these words of the Lord should not be expounded according to the letter, nor should a general teaching or rule be drawn from them, lest we make him contrary to himself. For as far as the reason of salvation is concerned, it is enough for us to believe that he is the one whom the Scriptures teach, and to rest in him alone. And let us bear witness to this faith by love, both towards him and towards our needy brethren, whom the bond of the same faith has bound to us. For since he has substituted these brethren for himself, so that we may bestow upon them what we would have bestowed upon him had he been living a bodily life on earth today, there is no clearer proof of how great progress we have made in faith than the works of charity.

units.la: Et sanè quàm multum adhuc isti iuueni defuerit, Euangelista docet, qui eum hoc Christi mandato perterritum fuisse, & valde tristem abiisse scribit. Et causam addit: Nam diues erat valde. Atqui Abrahamum quoque diuitem fuisse scimus, qui tamen Chaldæam patriam alacri mente reliquit. Et Mosi non ita graue fuit Ægypti thesauros cum aulæ regiæ delitijs relinquere. Sed illi non tam opibus huius seculi diuites fuerunt, quàm fide & pietate, qua vt in vnum Deum respicerent mouebantur. Iste verò, quoniam à semetipso & suarum virium fiducia pendebat, non potuit non ex eo dolorem concipere, quod eius cupiditati in primis reluctabatur. Et ita pudefieri solent, quicunque suis viribus atque operibus fidunt. Adhuc tamen animi pij specimen in illo elucet, quando non aliquam murmurandi aut conuitiandi ansam arripit, vt dicat: Itáne mihi soli iniungitur, quod nulli hactenus mandatum fuit? Tam multos tecum trahis comites, in quorum numero fœmina illustres & viri opulenti sunt, quibus ad suas facultates regressus patet. An ergo ego solus dignus vi deor, quem nouo & peculiari præcepto ludifices? Talia certe multi dixissent, & hodie huius generis multa audiuntur ex ijs, à quibus non nisi communia Christiani hominis officia requiruntur. At longè aliter noster hic, quem indoluisse & valde tristatum fuisse audimus. Intellexit ergo, Christum nihil iniquum aut indignum abs se postulare: at simul se infirmiorem esse sensit, quàm qui tam graui mandato possit sufficere. Hinc igitur tristitia illa enata est, quam cum carnis ingenio luctans pietas peperit. Quo argumento iterum adducor, vt de illius salute nõ possim non bene sperare: quia non verisimile videtur, Christum, qui sanandis inualidis & infirmis venerat, tam pio affectui defuisse, quem suus Spiritus in illo excitarat.
units.tr: And indeed the Evangelist shows how much this young man still lacked, when he writes that he was dismayed at this command of Christ and went away very sad. And he adds the reason: "For he was very rich." Yet we know that Abraham also was rich, and yet he left his native Chaldaea with a willing mind. And it was not so hard for Moses to leave the treasures of Egypt with the delights of the royal court. But those men were rich not so much in the wealth of this age as in faith and piety, by which they were moved to look to the one God. This man, however, since he depended on himself and on trust in his own powers, could not help being distressed at what most opposed his desires. And so are all those put to shame who trust in their own strength and works. Yet a sign of a pious mind still shines in him, since he does not seize on any occasion to murmur or revile, saying: "Is this enjoined on me alone, what has not been commanded to anyone until now? You bring many companions with you, among whom are distinguished women and wealthy men, to whom a return to their own resources is open. Am I alone thought worthy, that you should mock me with a new and peculiar command?" Many would certainly have said such things, and today many such complaints are heard from those who are required only to perform the common duties of a Christian man. But our man here, who we hear was grieved and greatly saddened, acted very differently. Therefore he understood that Christ was asking nothing unjust or unworthy of him, but at the same time he felt that he was too weak to be equal to so heavy a command. Hence came that sadness, which piety, struggling with the nature of the flesh, produced. By this argument I am again led to hope well of his salvation, since it does not seem likely that Christ, who came to heal the weak and the sick, would have been wanting to such a pious feeling, which his Spirit had stirred up in him.

units.la: At quia huic diuitiæ impedimento fuerunt, quò minus statim per veram salutis viam ingrederetur, Christus in generalem doctrinam de diuitijs & diuitibus digreditur, qua periculosam eorum conditionem sic exponit, vt simul ijsdem spem salutis faciat. Et primò quidem ad discipulos conuersus nõ sine admirantis & dolentis specie ait: Quàm difficilè qui pecunias habent, in Regnum Dei introibunt, id est, quàm graue est diuitibus Euangelij vocationem sequi, & in illo oblatam ipsis salutem ampleƈti. Et mox istud ipsum per comparationem amplificat, dicens: Facilius est enim camelum per foramen acus transire, quàm diuitem introire in Regnum Dei. Dura sanè & grauis vox, maximè si cogites ista ab eo dici, qui ipsissima est veritas, & quidem dileƈtis discipulis dici, quos procul dubio noluit inanibus terriculamentis ludificare. At hic diligentius nobis considerandum venit, de quibus diuitibus ille loquatur. Nam (vt aliàs monuimus) diuitiæ ex Dei benedictione obtingunt (de iustis & legitimè partis loquor) & illis multos abundauisse scimus, quorum fides
units.tr: But because riches were an obstacle to this man, so that he did not at once enter by the true way of salvation, Christ turns aside into a general teaching about riches and the rich, in which he sets out their dangerous condition in such a way that at the same time he gives them hope of salvation. And first, turning to the disciples, he says, not without a look of wonder and grief: "How hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God!" that is, how difficult it is for the rich to follow the call of the gospel and to embrace the salvation offered to them in it. And soon he amplifies this very point by a comparison, saying: "For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." This is indeed a harsh and weighty saying, especially if you consider that it was spoken by him who is the very truth, and spoken to beloved disciples, whom he surely did not wish to mock with empty terrors. But here we must consider more carefully which rich men he is speaking of. For (as we have noted elsewhere) riches come by the blessing of God (I am speaking of wealth justly and lawfully gained), and we know that many men of abundant riches were, whose faith

units.la: Conditio diui- tū periculosa. fides & pietas in Scripturis probatur. Itaq; neminem huius dicti occasione temere damnare debemus, sed ipsum Christum illius interpretem fidelissimum audire, qui discipulis eo expauefactis (vt Marcus annotat) adiecit: Filij, quàm difficile est eos, qui confidunt opibus, in Regnū Dei ingredi? De his ergo dictum hoc intelligi debet, quos seruare non solum difficile, verumetiam impossibile est, quoad diuitijs fidunt. Primò enim Deo non possunt seruire (vt Christus supra docuit) imò idololatriæ reatu tenentur, cùm quæ in Deo collocata esse debebat fiducia, in diuitias incumbat. Itaq; ijdem has Deo longè præferunt, quod liquidò apparet, si quando vel opes amittere, vel fidem in Deum abnegare coguntur. Deinde nō contenti sunt tales ijs quæ habent, sed ea vel per auaram & sordidam parsimoniam augere, vel artibus planè illicitis plura acquirere studdesignt. Vnde vetus proverbiū enatum est, Omnis dives aut iniquus, aut iniqui hæres. Postremò nō sine murmure & fremitu amittuntur, siue aliquo casu ipsæ dilabantur, siue in mortis hora amittenda sint. Tunc enim locum verè habet, quo in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Quàm amara est ô mors tui memoria homini quieto in bonis suis, viro negotijs vacuo & felici, qui cibum adhuc sumere valet. De illis ergo cùm in præsenti Christus loquatur, videre omnes conuenit, ne diuitijs fidant, sed eorum memores sint, quæ Paulus in priori ad Timoth.6. Cap.de diuitum officijs tradidit.
units.tr: The danger of the rich's condition. Faith and piety are proved in the Scriptures. Therefore we ought not rashly to condemn anyone on the occasion of this saying, but to hear Christ himself, its most faithful interpreter, who, when the disciples were terrified (as Mark notes), added: "Children, how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the Kingdom of God!" This saying must therefore be understood of those whom it is not only difficult but impossible to save, insofar as they trust in riches. First, indeed, they cannot serve God (as Christ taught above); rather they are held guilty of idolatry, since the trust that ought to have been placed in God rests upon riches. Thus they put these far above God, which is clear if at any time they are forced either to lose their wealth or to deny their faith in God. Next, such people are not content with what they have, but either seek to increase it by avaricious and sordid thrift or strive to acquire more by plainly unlawful arts. Hence the old proverb arose: "Every rich man is either unjust, or the heir of an unjust man." Lastly, their wealth is not lost without grumbling and complaint, whether it slips away through some accident or has to be surrendered at the hour of death. Then indeed that saying of Ecclesiasticus truly applies: "How bitter is the remembrance of death to a man at rest in his possessions, to a man free from cares and prosperous, who is still able to take food!" Since Christ is speaking here of such people, all should see to it that they do not trust in riches, but remember those things which Paul delivered in his first letter to Timothy, chapter 6, concerning the duties of the rich.

units.la: Sed præstat discipulos Christi videre, & de hoc dicto loquentes audire. Hos Marcus adhuc magis animo perculsos fuisse scribit, & dixisse: Et quis poterit salus fieri? Ergo salutis negotium hucusque illis non adeò graue aut arduum visum fuit. At nunc, quando facultatum omnium voluntariam amissionem & animum ab omni rerum terrenarum fiducia alienum requiri audiunt, non possunt non percelli animo & consternari. Nam etsi ipsi diuitias nullas possiderent, sentiebant tamen cupiditatem illam atq; fiduciam opum, quæ hic damnatur, in suis etiam cordibus locum habere, & ideo ad se quoque pertinere quod dicebatur. Est autem exemplum hoc laude dignissimum. Ex eo enim apparet, quam alieni fuerint ab eorum moribus, qui diuitibus suas fortunas inuident, et paupertatis suæ fiducia sic efferuntur, vt diuites quidem omnes audacissimè condemnent, non autem animaduertant seipsos ijsdem affectibus laborare, qui illis suas opes exitiales reddunt. Sunt hi bis miseri, quia cum paupertate & inuidia conflictantur, & simul æternæ damnationis sententiam in sua quoq; capita accersunt.
units.tr: But it is well for us to look at the disciples of Christ and to hear them speaking about this saying. Mark writes that they were struck with even greater dismay and said: "And who then can be saved?" Thus the business of salvation had not seemed so grievous or hard to them until now. But now, when they hear that a voluntary surrender of all their goods is required, and a mind estranged from all trust in earthly things, they cannot but be stricken and dismayed in spirit. For even though they themselves possessed no riches, they felt that that greed and trust in wealth which is condemned here had a place also in their own hearts, and so what was said pertained to them too. This example is most worthy of praise. For it shows how far removed from their ways are those who envy the rich their fortunes and, relying on their own poverty, so exalt themselves that they boldly condemn all the rich, yet do not notice that they themselves labour under the same affections which make the riches of others ruinous to them. Such people are doubly wretched, because they wrestle with poverty and envy at once, and at the same time bring upon their own heads the sentence of eternal damnation.

units.la: Cæterùm piæ discipulorum consternationi Christus medetur, dicens: Quæ impossibilia sunt apud homines, possibilia sunt apud Deum. Apud Marcum hoc ita enuntiat: Apud homines hoc est impossibile, sed non apud Deum: nam omnia possibilia sunt apud Deum. Fatetur ergo neminem suis viribus seruari posse: quod de omnis loci & ordinis hominibus debet intelligi. Monet autem nō debere hoc ad aliquos ita restringi, vt eos propter opes suas seruari posse negemus. Quia enim Deo omnia possibilia sunt, facile illi fuerit, hos quoque ex Verbi sui semine per Spiritus virtutem regenerare, vt ea faciant, quæ veros Dei cultores decent. Confirmatur hoc dictum multorum exemplis, quibus diuitiæ adeò nullum impedimentum fuerunt, vt potius in illis pulcherrimarum virtutum, & in primis beneficentiæ egregiam materiam habuerint, sicut in Abrahamo, patre credentium, est videre: vt de multis alijs iam nihil dicamus. Est hæc præclara gratia Dei commendatio, quæ omnis generis hominibus patet. Discant modò singuli, vt suis viribus diffisi, & simul relicto rerum huius seculi studio, in illa vna salutis fiducia collocent, & per omne vitæ genus intrepida fide sequantur Iesum Christum, qui nobis à Deo Patre vitæ huius magister & exemplum perfectum, æternæ autem Mediator & author datus est. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ heals the pious dismay of the disciples, saying: "What is impossible with men is possible with God." In Mark he expresses it thus: "With men this is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God." He therefore confesses that no one can be saved by his own strength, which must be understood of men of every place and rank. But he warns that this must not be restricted to some so as to deny that they can be saved on account of their wealth. For since all things are possible with God, it will be easy for him to regenerate these also from the seed of his Word, by the power of the Spirit, so that they may do those things which become true worshippers of God. This saying is confirmed by many examples in which riches were no hindrance at all, but rather gave them an excellent material for the finest virtues, and above all for beneficence, as is seen in Abraham, the father of believers; to say nothing yet of many others. This is a notable commendation of the grace of God, which lies open to men of every kind. Let each one learn, distrusting his own strength and at the same time leaving aside the pursuit of the things of this age, to place his whole trust in that one salvation, and through every kind of life to follow Jesus Christ with fearless faith, who has been given to us by God the Father as the teacher of this life and its perfect example, and as Mediator and author of eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXX.

units.la: Dixit autem Petrus: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. Ipse verò dixit eis: Amen dico vobis, nemo est qui reliquerit domum, aut parentes, aut fratres, aut vxorem, aut liberos, Regni Dei causa, qui non recepturus sit multiplicia hoc tempore, & in seculo venturo vitam æternam. Iesus autem assumptis illis duodecim dixit eis: Ecce ascendimus Hierosolymam, & perficientur Filio hominis omnia, quae scripta sunt per Prophetas. Tradetur enim gentibus, & illudetur, & contumeliis afficietur, & conspuetur. Et postquam cum flagellauerint, trucidabunt: sed die tertia resurget. Ipsi vero nihil horum intellexerunt, eratque ista verba ipsis occulta, nec cognouerunt quae dicebantur.
units.tr: Then Peter said, "Behold, we have left all and followed you." But he said to them, "Truly I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times as much in this time, and in the age to come eternal life." Then Jesus took the twelve aside and said to them, "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that were written by the prophets concerning the Son of man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and insulted, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, but on the third day he will rise again." But they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was being said.

units.la: Etsi homo natura felicitatis atque salutis appetens sit, multa tamen sunt, quae illum in vera huius consequendae ratione impediunt. Inter ea primus fere locus diuitijs huius seculi debetur, sicut nuper in magnatis exemplo vidimus. Nam quamuis is non vulgares in pietatis studio progressus fecisset, tamen se in Regno Dei nimium adhuc frigere satis ostendit, quando ad Christi praeceptum toto animo consternatur, qui illum omnia diuendere & in pauperes distribuere iusserat, ut ad se sequendum expeditior esset atque alacrior. Et solet hoc frequenter fieri, ut qui optimi & feruentissimi videbantur, in fide nimis langueant, ut primum de amicis opibus relinquendis agitur: ut iam nihil de ijs dicamus, qui opum abundantia abutuntur ad ea, quibus tota Christiani nominis professio prophanatur. Non temere ergo fieri putemus, quod Christus Iesus de diuitijs toties disserit: qui ut nuper in Dei omnipotentis gratia spem salutis diuitibus adhuc reliquam esse docuit, quamuis periculi plenissima sit eorum conditio: ita in praesenti amplissimis promissionibus omnes eos confirmat, qui iacturam opum suarum propter ipsum facere coguntur: quibus mox vniuersalem doctrinam sub ijcit, qua aduersus omne crucis scandalum instruamur.
units.tr: Although man by nature desires happiness and salvation, there are nevertheless many things that hinder him in the true way of attaining it. Among these, the first place almost belongs to the riches of this age, as we recently saw in the example of the great man. For although he had made no ordinary progress in the pursuit of godliness, he nevertheless showed himself still too lukewarm in the kingdom of God, when at Christ's command he was struck with dismay in his whole mind, since Christ had bidden him sell all he had and distribute it to the poor, so that he might be freer and more eager to follow him. And it often happens that those who seemed the best and most fervent grow too weak in faith as soon as the question of giving up their dear possessions arises. Let us say nothing now of those who abuse their abundance of wealth for the things by which the whole profession of the Christian name is profaned. Let us not think it happens by chance that Christ Jesus speaks so often about riches. Just as he recently taught that, by the grace of almighty God, hope of salvation still remains for the rich, although their condition is full of danger, so now he encourages with the greatest promises all those who are compelled to suffer the loss of their possessions for his sake. Then he immediately adds a general teaching by which we may be armed against every stumbling-block of the cross.

units.la: Occasionem huic disputationi Petrus praebuit, qui omnium discipulorum nomine interrogat, quidnam ipsi sperare debeant, qui fortunas omnes iam pridem ipsius causa reliquerint. Quod si causam huius quaestionis quaeras, non alia reddi poterit, quam falsa & inanis de Regno Christi terreno persuasio, quam tunc ex communi errore conceptam omnium animis insedisse non semel diximus. Non dubium enim est, hoc illis praeter omnem expectationem accidisse, quod hoc tam duro mandato principem virum abs se abegerat Dominus, qui potius alliciendus esse videbatur, ut sua authoritate Regnum illud speratum promoueret. Absurdum praeterea videbatur esse, tam grauem ferre de periculosa diuitum conditione sententiam, cum ipsi animo suo non opes modo amplissimas, verumetiam dignitates, honores & imperia concepissent. Itaque inter spem & metum nunc fluctuans Petrus, Christo dicit: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te. Et apud Matthaeum addit quaestionem: Quid ergo erit nobis? Quasi diceret: Atqui sperabamus nos non vulgarem retributionem, qui tuam vocationem secuti nostra omnia reliquimus. At quid porro huius sperare licet, quando ipsum quidem omnia diuendere & egenis elargiri iubes, & simul opes huius seculi maximum impedimentum esse docet ijs, qui ad vitam aeternam contendunt? Scire itaque cupimus, quid de nobis futurum sit, quidue nobis sperare liceat? Latet sub hac quaestione non vnum modo innatae nobis vitiositatis argumentum. Primo enim apparet, discipulos spe regni terreni Christum secutos fuisse: quae hodie etiam plerosque trahit, qui pro Euangelio ne pedem quidem aut digitum vnum moverent, nisi diuitiarum honorum aut etiam licentiae carnis spe lactarentur. Deinde ambitiosum nimis est, quod non sine exprobrationis specie commemorant, quid pro Christo fecerint, idque omne nimis magno aestimant. Ecce (inquiunt) reliquimus omnia. Et quae obsecro erant illa omnia? Ruinosa nimirum piscatorum tuguria, paucae naniculae, retia lacera, hami, remi, & alia eiusmodi, quibus vitam suam aegre sustentabant. Nec se adhuc quicquam recepisse putant, cum toto illo tempore, quo cum Christo fuerant, nihil illis vnquam defuerit, sicuti in vltima Coena ipsi fatentur. Taceo nunc dulcissimam illam consuetudinem, qua cum aeterno Dei Filio fruebantur, miracula, conciones saluberrimas & non minus salutaria colloquia, in quibus ex illius ore caelestem sapientiam & vitae aeternae promissiones hauriebant. Quae omnia illos non pro dignitate aestimauisse, haec vna quaestio abunde docet. Est vero hoc etiam vulgare vitium, quod magni facimus quaecunque sub praetextu gloriae Dei & pietatis a nobis fiunt, & nescio quos montes aureos nobis deberi putamus, vilipendimus autem amplissima Spiritus sancti dona, quae quotidie recipimus. Accedit his tertium vitium, quod priusquam finem vocationis suae attigerint, de praemio quaerunt, adeoque triumphos sibi decerni volunt, prius quam in hostis conspectum venerint. Ita nostra quoque vota fere praecipitamus, & mercedem nobis solui petimus, quando nos potius de studij nostri perseverantia solicitos esse conveniebat. Veruntamen si nostros mores cum Apostolis conferamus, magnam prae nobis laudem merentur, qui quaestionem istam hucusque distulerunt: cum hodie plerique, priusquam Christo nomen dederint, aut priusquam Evangelium intra urbes suas admittant, de omnibus certiores fieri velint, quid nimirum periculi ex eo timendum sit, quid item lucri aut emolumenti sperari possit. Sunt haec salutis impedimenta nocentissima, quibus nos eorum exempla opponere debemus, qui eo nomine in Scripturis commendantur, quod absque omni disceptatione Deum vocantem secuti sunt. Primus in horum ordine merito censetur Abrahamus, credentium pater, qui nulla quaestione mota natale solum deseruit, cum se diuinitus vocari sentiret: imo filium quoque Isaacum, Deo iubente, absque mora, immolare voluit. Possunt huic adnumerari patres reliqui cum Prophetis, & multis alijs, qui Evangelij vocationem illico secuti sunt, & seipsos simul atque fortunas suas paternae Dei providentiae commiserunt.
units.tr: Peter gave the occasion for this discussion, asking in the name of all the disciples what they ought to hope for, who had long ago left all their fortunes for his sake. If you ask the cause of this question, no other can be given than the false and empty notion of a earthly kingdom of Christ, which, as we have said more than once, had taken hold of the minds of all from the common error of the time. There is no doubt that this happened to them contrary to all expectation, that the Lord had driven away from himself a leading man by so hard a command, when he seemed rather to be the one to be won over, so that by his authority he might advance that hoped-for kingdom. Moreover, it seemed absurd to pass so grave a judgment on the perilous condition of the rich, when they themselves had conceived in their minds not only great wealth but also dignities, honours and empires. And so Peter, now wavering between hope and fear, says to Christ: "Behold, we have left all and followed you." And in Matthew he adds the question: "What then shall we have?" As if he said: "Yet we hoped for no ordinary reward, we who left all our things to follow your call. But what can we hope for further, when you bid us sell everything and give to the needy, and at the same time teach that worldly riches are the greatest hindrance to those who strive for eternal life? We wish to know, then, what will become of us, and what we may hope for?" Beneath this question lies more than one proof of the vice innate in us. For first it appears that the disciples followed Christ in hope of an earthly kingdom; this hope draws many even today, who would not move a foot or a finger for the gospel unless they were buoyed up by the hope of riches, honours, or even licence of the flesh. Next, it is too self-regarding that they mention, not without a show of reproach, what they have done for Christ, and they value all of it far too highly. "Behold," they say, "we have left all." And what, I beg you, were those "all"? Surely the ruinous huts of fishermen, a few little boats, torn nets, hooks, oars, and other such things by which they laboured to sustain their lives. Nor do they think they have yet received anything, although during all that time they had been with Christ nothing was ever lacking to them, as they themselves confess at the last supper. I say nothing now of that sweetest fellowship they enjoyed with the eternal Son of God, the miracles, the most wholesome sermons, and the no less salutary conversations, from whose mouth they drew heavenly wisdom and the promises of eternal life. That they did not esteem all these things as they deserved is abundantly shown by this one question. Indeed this is also a common fault: we think much of whatever we do under the pretext of the glory of God and piety, and we imagine that we are owed I know not what golden mountains, while we make light of the very great gifts of the Holy Spirit that we receive every day. To these is added a third fault: before they have reached the end of their calling, they ask for a reward, and so want triumphs decreed to them before they have come into the sight of the enemy. So we too usually hurry our vows, and seek to have our wages paid, when we ought rather to be anxious about the perseverance of our labour. Nevertheless, if we compare our manners with those of the Apostles, those deserve great praise who have deferred that question until now; whereas today most people, before they give their name to Christ, or before they admit the gospel within their own cities, wish to be informed about everything: what danger, surely, is to be feared from it, and likewise what gain or advantage may be hoped for. These are the most hurtful hindrances to salvation, and against them we must set the examples of those who are commended in Scripture for this, that without any dispute they followed God when he called. Foremost in this order is rightly counted Abraham, the father of believers, who, without raising any question, left his native land when he felt himself called by God; indeed he was willing, at God's command, to sacrifice his son Isaac without delay. To these may be added the other fathers, together with the prophets and many others, who immediately followed the call of the gospel, and committed themselves and their fortunes together to the fatherly providence of God.

units.la: Quia vero Apostolorum exemplo multi hodie abutuntur, diligentius videre oportet, quomodo illi omnia sua reliquerint. Etenim cum hoc diceret Petrus, Apostoli suas adhuc domus habebant, nauiculas item, retia, & quaecunque prius possederant. Nam ipsum Petrum domum suam non semel diuertisse, & post Christi resurrectionem cum alijs in Galilaeam ad piscationem solitam redijsse scimus. Reliquerunt ergo sua, prout illud vocatio ipsorum exigebat, non autem proprietati rerum tiarunt, donec id quoque necessitas iniit: quando nimirum in orbem totum exire debebant, ut Evangelium omnibus populis praedicarent. Reliquerunt item quaecunque habebant, dum illis non apposuerunt animos suos, sed ut mutuo acceptis vsi sunt, quam diu hocipsis licuit. Nihil ergo patrocinij hic habent Monachi & Anabaptistae errones, qui Apostolorum imitatores haberi volunt, si vel patrimonio tenuissimo renuntient, aut uxoribus simul atque liberis relictis, vel Monasterium ingrediantur, vel alijs oneri sint, & docendi munus sibi propria temeritate vendicent, ad quod non sunt legitime vocati. Vt enim nihil huius simile Apostoli fecerunt: ita neque hanc voluerunt communem esse regulam, quae omnibus Christianis praescriberetur. Et Paulus Apostolus ἀτάκτους ἑαυτοὺς, id est, inordinatos homines, qui aliena quadra viuere instituerunt, arctiori disciplina coercere iubet, ut honesto aliquo labore victum quaerant, & alijs molesti esse desinant. Sufficiat ergo nobis, si quis animum ab opum amore auocet, & in vnam Dei vocationem intentus praesentibus bonis itaque, ut ea relinquere nunquam non paratus sit, quoties vel Dei gloria, vel propriae vocationis necessitas ita iubet. Hac ratione multi sua reliquisse dici possunt, qui illis adhuc cum fide & gratiarum actione fruuntur. E contra sua retinent saepe, qui ab illis praeter animi voluntatem aufulsi, ad ea subinde respiciunt. Enimuero Lothi vxor, etiamsi ex Sodomis egressa esset, fortunas tamen suas minime reliquerat, cum eas intra animum suum solicita gestaret, quae illam contra Dei mandatum ad illas respicere coegerunt. Et quis Israelitas Aegyptum vere reliquisse dixerit, qui illos ollas carnium, melones, allia & cepas subinde in corde & ore habuisse audit? Prima itaque nobis cura sit, ut animum a cupiditate & fiducia opum renocemus: ex eo enim alterum sequetur, ut eis dum licet pie vtamur, & quando Deus ita vult, easdem omnino alacri & minime inuito relinquamus, &c.
units.tr: Because many today abuse the example of the Apostles, we must look more carefully at how they left all their things. For when Peter said this, the Apostles still had their houses, their little boats, their nets, and whatever else they had possessed before. For we know that Peter himself lodged at his house more than once, and that after Christ's resurrection he returned with the others to Galilee to the fishing he was accustomed to. So they left their things insofar as their calling required it, but they did not give themselves over to the ownership of goods, until necessity imposed that too: namely, when they had to go out into the whole world to preach the gospel to all peoples. They also left whatever they had, in that they did not set their hearts upon it, but used it as things received on loan, for as long as it was permitted them. Therefore the monks and the Anabaptist fanatics have no support here, who want to be regarded as imitators of the Apostles if they renounce even a very slender patrimony, or leave behind wives and children, or enter a monastery, or become a burden to others, and claim for themselves by their own rashness the office of teaching, to which they have not been lawfully called. For the Apostles did nothing like this, and they did not wish this to be the common rule prescribed to all Christians. And the Apostle Paul bids that those who are ἀτάκτους ἑαυτοὺς [disorderly], that is, unruly men who have made it their custom to live at another's expense, be restrained by stricter discipline, so that they may seek their living by some honest labour and cease to be a burden to others. It is enough for us, then, if someone detaches his mind from the love of wealth, and, intent upon the one call of God, so uses present goods that he is always ready to give them up whenever the glory of God or the necessity of his own calling so demands. In this way many may be said to have left their things who still enjoy them with faith and thanksgiving. On the contrary, those often keep their things who have been torn from them against their will, and look back to them from time to time. Indeed, Lot's wife, although she had come out of Sodom, had certainly not left her fortunes, since she carried them anxiously in her mind, and these drove her, against God's command, to look back at them. And who would say that the Israelites truly left Egypt, when he hears that they kept the pots of meat, the melons, the garlic and the onions constantly in their heart and on their lips? Our first care, therefore, should be to call back our mind from the lust for and trust in wealth; for from this the other will follow, that we use these things devoutly while it is permitted, and when God so wills, leave them altogether with a cheerful and unreluctant spirit, etc.

units.la: Sed audire praestat Christum Petro ad hunc modum respondentem: Amen dico vobis, nemo est, qui reliquerit domum, aut parentes, aut fratres, aut vxorem, aut liberos, Regni Dei causa, qui non recepturus sit multiplicia hoc tempore, & in seculo venturo vitam aeternam. Quo loco ante omnia obseruari debet Christi lenitas atque mansuetudo. Etsi enim discipulorum quaestio reprehensione digna esset, & illi simul omnes propter vitia, quae supra commemorauimus, graue correptionem mererentur: infirmitatis tamen eorum rationem habet, & quia eos iam ante plus satis consternatos esse videbat, liberali potius promissione animos eorum nutantes erigit atque confirmat. Petant hinc communem consolationem, quotquot metuunt, ne ipsos propter vitia sua & inhaerentem imperfectionem Deus fastidiat. Idem vero sibi ipsis applicent Christi exemplum, ut simili lenitate fratres infirmiores ferant, & de illis confirmandis potius quam temere damnandis cogitent. Sunt autem in ista responsione duo obseruanda, quibus tertio loco apud Matthaeum & Marcum grauis admonitio adiciur ad reprimendam carnis securitatem.
units.tr: But it is better to hear Christ answering Peter in this manner: "Amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children, for the sake of the Kingdom of God, who will not receive manifold more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life." Here, before all else, the gentleness and mildness of Christ must be observed. For although the disciples' question deserved reproof, and they all together, on account of the faults we mentioned above, deserved a grave rebuke, yet he takes account of their weakness, and because he saw that they were already sufficiently dismayed, he lifts up and strengthens their wavering minds with a generous promise instead. Let all who fear that God may despise them on account of their faults and inherent imperfection take from this a common consolation. Let them likewise apply to themselves Christ's example, so that they bear weaker brethren with a similar gentleness and think of strengthening them rather than condemning them rashly. Now in this answer there are two things to be observed, and in the third place, in Matthew and Mark, a grave admonition is added to restrain the security of the flesh.

units.la: Primum est, vt videamus, quibus hic Christus loquatur. In Matthaeo quidem sermonem ad discipulos conuertit, & ipsis retributionem hanc liberalissimam pollicetur: eandem vero generalius ad omnes alios quoque extendi debere, qui Apostolorum fidem & exemplum imitantur, in praesenti apparet: cum dicat, Nemo est, qui reliquerit, &c. Discipulis autem eos connumerat, qui domum, parentes, fratres, vxorem, liberos relinquunt, causa Regni Dei. Apud Marcum ait, Mea causa & Euangelij: quod in idem recidit. Euangelio enim Christus praedicatur, qui Regnum Dei inter homines instaurauit, & nos ex potestate tenebrarum & infelici diaboli seruitio in libertatem filiorum Dei transtulit, vt is suo verbo & spiritu in nobis regnet, quoad in hoc seculo viximus, huius autem curriculi siue stadium emensos in Regnum suum caeleste transferat. Itaq; propter Regnum Dei sua relinquunt, qui vt Euangelij & fidei libertate fruantur, & Deo seruire possint, omnibus renuntiant, quae in hoc mundo habent. Neque superuacanea censeri debet tam diligens illorum omnium enumeratio. Voluit enim omnia nominare Christus, quae vel vtilitatis & necessitatis nomine, vel etiam pietatis praetextu commendantur. Ad prius pertinent domus & agri (quorum in Marco meminit) quibus omnia alia adnumerari debent, quae ad huius vitae vsum vtilia & necessaria sunt. Ad alterum, parentes, fratres, sorores, vxor, liberi: quos omnes naturae lex ita nobis obstringit, vt omnium iudicio impius videatur, qui illos temere reliquerit. Sed omnibus istis se & regnum suum Christus praeferre iubet, ne a mundi huius iudicio caeco pendeamus. Nihil ergo ad eos pertinet Christi promissio, qui vel luxu & prodigalitate, vel improuida rei domesticae administratione, & temerarijs contractibus sua dilapidant: vel superstitiosa aliqua persuasione decepti ad aliud vitae genus transeundo egestatem sibi ipsis absque vlla causa necessaria acceperunt. Nam etiamsi prioribus illis gratia Dei & vitae aeternae spes minime negari debeat, si inopiam suam patienter ferant, delictorum poenitentiam agant, & fidem in Deum retineant: nihil tamen ijsdem ex huius promissionis iure debetur, cum illis non mereantur accenseri, de quibus hic sermo est. Quoad vero superstitiosos illos, siue illi eremitae & Monachi, siue vagabundi errones sint, nulla ratione ad eos promissio ista pertinet, cum relicta vocatione legitima genus vitae sequantur diuinis legibus prohibitum, & quod a fine hominis ad quem hic creatus est, alienissimum esse merito dixeris. Et quid obsecro illi faciunt, quod non olim gentium philosophi, & in primis quidem Diogeniani aut Cynici, fecerint: & quod hodie multi inter Turcas faciunt, quorum milites artiori & seueriori disciplina, quam omnes isti fratres atque errones, coercentur? Neminem ergo vel amissionis bonorum, vel paupertatis fiducia decipiat. Nisi enim his legitima Dei vocatio accesserit, quam per fidei obedientiam sequamur, nihil erit, quo possimus gloriari.
units.tr: The first is that we see to whom Christ speaks here. In Matthew indeed he turns his speech to the disciples and promises them this most generous reward; but that the same should be extended more generally to all others who imitate the faith and example of the Apostles appears from the present passage, since he says, "There is no one who has left," etc. He counts among the disciples those who leave house, parents, brothers, wife, children, for the cause of the Kingdom of God. In Mark he says, "for my sake and the Gospel's," which comes to the same thing. For Christ, who has restored the Kingdom of God among men, is preached in the Gospel, and has transferred us from the power of darkness and the unhappy servitude of the devil into the liberty of the sons of God, so that he may reign in us by his word and Spirit as long as we live in this world, and, having finished this course or race, may transfer us into his heavenly Kingdom. Therefore they leave their possessions for the sake of the Kingdom of God who renounce everything they have in this world, so that they may enjoy the liberty of the Gospel and of faith and be able to serve God. Nor should so careful an enumeration of all these things be thought superfluous. For Christ wished to name everything that is commended either under the name of usefulness and necessity or even under the pretext of piety. To the former belong houses and fields (which he mentions in Mark), to which all other things must be added that are useful and necessary for the use of this life. To the latter belong parents, brothers, sisters, wife, and children, all of whom the law of nature binds us to in such a way that, in the judgement of all, he seems impious who has rashly left them. But Christ bids that he himself and his kingdom be preferred to all of these, so that we do not hang upon the blind judgement of this world. Therefore Christ's promise does not pertain to those who squander their goods through luxury and prodigality, or through improvident management of domestic affairs and rash contracts, or who, deceived by some superstitious persuasion and passing over to another way of life, have brought poverty upon themselves without any necessary cause. For although to those former the grace of God and the hope of eternal life ought by no means be denied, if they bear their want patiently, repent of their faults, and hold fast to faith in God, nothing is owed to them by right of this promise, since they do not deserve to be counted among those of whom this discourse speaks. As for those superstitious folk, whether they be hermits and monks or wandering vagrants, this promise in no way pertains to them, since, having abandoned a lawful calling, they follow a way of life forbidden by divine laws, and one which you may rightly call most alien to the end for which man was created. And what, I ask, do they do that the philosophers of the nations once did not do, especially the Diogenians or Cynics; and what do many among the Turks do today, whose soldiers are restrained by a stricter and harsher discipline than all those brothers and vagrants? Let no one therefore be deceived by confidence in the loss of goods or in poverty. For unless the lawful calling of God comes to them, which we follow through obedience of faith, there will be nothing in which we can glory.

units.la: Alterum huius responsionis caput est, praemij aut retributionis promissio quae duplex est. Primo enim eum, qui causa Regni Dei aliquid reliquerit, in hoc seculo multiplicia recepturum esse ait. In Matthaeo & Marco, centupla retributio exprimitur, numero finito pro infinito. Istud vero anxiae solicitudini opponit, quae rerum iacturam nobis grauiorem reddit, dum metuimus ne quid nobis aliquando desit eorum, quae ad vitae sustentationem faciunt. Pollicetur ergo nobis in lucro fore, si quid causa Euangelij & Regni Dei amittamus. At videtur cum promissione Christi pugnare experientia, quando multi patrijs sedibus pulsi oberrant, esuriunt, sitiunt, algent, plerisque exosi, multis etiam oneri sunt. Et scimus, quibus sannis olim promissionem istam Iulianus exagitarit, si quando de vi sibi facta deque illatis iniurijs Christiani homines apud eum conquesti sunt. Neque hodie desunt, qui cum risu & ludibrio eos prosequuntur, & scurriliter mordent, qui Dei misericordia freti, patriam potius cum fortunis suis omnibus relinquere malunt, quam turpi fidei abnegatione Regni Dei iacturam facere. Sed nihil isti omnes promissioni Christi derogat, cuius veritas semper rata manet, quod facile vident, qui rem diligentius expendunt. Etenim gentium sapientes eum demum vere diuitem dixerunt, qui nihil cupit, & sua forte contentus vixit. Id vero assequuntur, quicunque in vnum Deum respiciunt, & contemptis atque relictis omnibus, quae in mundo praeclara habentur, in illo sibi omnia repositia esse sciunt, quaecunque ad huius vitae vsum & aeternam salutem faciunt. Qui ergo centuplam retributionem eum accepisse negauerit, qui fortunarum omnium amissione αυτάρκειαν illam, id est, animum sua forte contentum sibi acquisiuit, quem nullo pretio, nullis item artibus, nulla industria homines sibi parare possunt? Nam siue immensos opum thesauros, siue honores & dignitates gnitates huius seculi, siue victorias & triumphos, siue regna & imperia mundi, siue voluptatum flu dia consideres, nihil in omnibus istis erit, quod hominis animum possit exatiare. Quid enim ista singula, aut etiam omnia simul coniuncta faciant, quando Alexandro Macedoni ne totius quidem orbis imperium sufficere potuit, ut bellis finem imponeret? At qui Deum fide vera apprehenderunt, & in eius gratia acquiescunt, ij omnem sortem patienter ferunt, iisdem omnia sufficiunt, & quia nihil praeterea cupiunt, soli etiam sunt divites. Verissime ergo multiplicia illis Deus retribuit, & quamuis mundo pauperrimi esse, & nihil prorsus habere videantur, apud illos tamen revera locum habet illud Solomonis: Melius est parum cum timore Dei, quam thesaurus magnus, cui tumultus ades est. Dum enim divites huius seculi non solum circa opes tumultuantur, verumetiam intra animos suos fremunt, & curis mordacibus distrahuntur, illi laeta & tranquilla conscientia modico illo fruuntur, quod ipsis in diem dat Deus, & simul aeternis caelorum thesauris gaudent, quorum fructum iam nunc intra animos suos sentiunt. Quod si vero literae verborum aut promissionis Christi insistere libeat, non poterit tunc quoque illa mendacij argui. Quia enim Christiani omnes in Christo fratres sunt, & uno eodemque Christi spiritu aguntur, non possunt eos negligere, quos propter fidei communis confessionem ad egestatem redactos esse vident. Fit ergo, ut hi non centum modo, sed mille & amplius patres, matres, fratres, sorores, liberos habeant, qui eos reliquerunt, quos carnis coniunctio ipsis copulauerat. Nam quocunque terrarum deveniant, germanos Dei filios reperiunt, qui illos amore plus quam fraterno amplectuntur, & omnia illis officia praestant, quae ex parentibus fratribus, liberis & coniunctissimis quibusque sperari poterant. Itaque ubique etiam gentium domus, agros & alia inveniunt, quae ad vitam hanc transfigendam sunt necessaria. Exempla, quibus istud confirmetur, passim occurrunt. Nam ut de Apostolis nihil dicamus, quibus nihil unquam defuit, quis nescit Iovinianum & Valentinianum ad Imperii fastigium evectos fuisse tandem, quos Iulianus primus propter fidem in Christum baltheo militari multatos in exilium relegauerat? Et quam multa fiunt quotidie, quae huic promissioni fidem faciunt? Utinam omnibus oculi essent, quibus ea viderent, & in fide confirmarentur.
units.tr: The second head of this answer is the promise of reward or recompense, which is twofold. For first he says that whoever has left something for the sake of the Kingdom of God will receive manifold in this age. In Matthew and Mark a hundredfold reward is expressed, a finite number for an infinite one. Now this sets itself against anxious care, which makes the loss of things weigh more heavily on us while we fear lest at some time we lack what serves the sustenance of life. He therefore promises that we shall be gainers if we lose anything for the sake of the Gospel and the Kingdom of God. But experience seems to clash with Christ's promise, when many, driven from their ancestral homes, wander, hunger, thirst, and go cold, hated by many and even a burden to many. And we know with what jeers Julian once mocked that promise, whenever Christian men complained to him of the violence done to them and the injuries inflicted. Nor today are there lacking those who pursue them with laughter and ridicule and bite them with buffoonery, though these people, relying on the mercy of God, prefer to leave their homeland with all their fortunes rather than suffer the loss of the Kingdom of God through shameful denial of the faith. But all of these take nothing from Christ's promise, whose truth always remains fixed, as those who weigh the matter more carefully easily see. For the wise men of the nations said that he is truly rich who desires nothing and lives content with what he has. Those who look to the one God, and, having despised and left behind all that is held illustrious in the world, know that everything which serves the use of this life and eternal salvation is laid up for them in him, attain this indeed. Who then will deny that he has received a hundredfold reward, who by the loss of all his fortunes has acquired for himself that self-sufficiency (αυτάρκεια), that is, a mind content with its lot, which men cannot procure for themselves by any price, nor by any arts, nor any industry? For whether you consider immense treasures of wealth, or the honours and dignities of this age, or victories and triumphs, or the kingdoms and empires of the world, or the flood of pleasures, nothing in all these will be able to satisfy the human mind. For what could these single things, or even all of them joined together, accomplish, when the rule of the whole world could not suffice for Alexander of Macedon to put an end to his wars? But those who have grasped God by true faith and rest in his grace bear every lot patiently; all things suffice for them, and because they desire nothing beyond, they alone are also rich. Most truly, therefore, God repays them manifold, and although they seem most poor to the world and to have nothing at all, yet in them there truly holds that saying of Solomon: "Better is a little with the fear of God than a great treasure where there is trouble with it." For while the rich of this age not only are in turmoil about wealth but also rage within their minds and are torn apart by biting cares, those others enjoy with a joyful and tranquil conscience that modest portion which God gives them day by day, and at the same time rejoice in the eternal treasures of heaven, whose fruit they already feel within their minds. But if one wishes to insist on the letter of Christ's words or promise, not even then can it be charged with falsehood. For since all Christians are brothers in Christ and are moved by one and the same Spirit of Christ, they cannot neglect those whom they see reduced to want on account of the common confession of faith. So it comes about that these people have not only a hundred but a thousand and more fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and children, in place of those whom they have left behind and whom the bond of flesh had joined to them. For wherever on earth they arrive, they find true sons of God, who embrace them with more than brotherly love and render all those services that might be hoped for from parents, brothers, children, and the closest kin. Thus everywhere, even among the nations, they find houses, fields, and other things necessary for getting through this life. Examples confirming this occur everywhere. For, not to speak of the Apostles, who never lacked anything, who does not know that Jovian and Valentinian were at last raised to the summit of the empire, although Julian had first stripped them of their military belts and relegated them into exile on account of their faith in Christ? And how many things happen every day that give credit to this promise? Would that all had eyes with which to see them and were confirmed in faith.

units.la: Altera promissionis parte vitam aeternam suis pollicetur, qua omnem hominis felicitatem comprehendi, alibi diximus: cuius initium est in hoc mundo, complementum vero in caelis erat, ubi sempiterno gaudio fruemur. Oportuit autem hanc quoque partem adjici, ne quis in huius seculi bonis acquiescat, & ne se deceptos arbitrentur, qui nullum aut per quam exiguum pietatis suae fructum in hoc seculo reportant. Etenim si huius praemij excellentiam consideremus, quae (ut Isaias testatur) omnem carnis sensum atque intellectum superat, tantam esse videbimus, ut eius spes atque diligens meditatio omnes huius seculi curas atque labores temperare, neque leves modo, verumetiam suaves & iucundos facere possit. Continet ergo promissio ista omnia, quae ad veram atque perfectam hominis felicitatem faciunt, quam qui periturus huius seculi bonis postponunt, ne illi indigni sunt, quos pro suis Deus agnoscat.
units.tr: The second part of the promise pledges eternal life to his people. We have said elsewhere that this life comprises all human happiness. Its beginning is in this world, but its completion is in heaven, where we shall enjoy everlasting joy. This part had to be added so that no one would rest content with the goods of this age, and so that those who gain little or no fruit of their godliness in this world would not think themselves deceived. If we consider the excellence of this reward, which (as Isaiah testifies) surpasses all the sense and understanding of flesh, we shall see that it is so great that the hope of it and its diligent meditation can soften all the cares and labours of this age, making them not merely light but even sweet and pleasant. This promise therefore contains everything that makes for true and perfect human happiness. Those who, for the sake of the goods of this age that will perish, set this aside are unworthy of being acknowledged by God as his own.

units.la: Porro, ut diximus, promissioni tam liberali apud Matthaeum & Marcum admonitionem adiicit graviem, dicens: Multi autem primi erunt ultimi, & ultimi primi. Qua sententia ijs mederi vult, qui aliquousque progressi in Regni Dei studio se iam ad perfectionem summam pervenisse putant, ideoque securi rerum omnes contemnunt, vel etiam temere damnant, quos abs se a tergo relictos aut nondum viam ingressos esse vident. Docet ergo Dominus non satis esse, si qui bene coeperint, nisi cursum suum absoluant, & indefesso studio ad metam sibi propositam contendant. Frequenter enim fit, ut qui primi videbantur, & Dei causam magno feruore agebant, subito deficiant, aut saltem ab illis praeueniantur, qui omnium postremi erant. Semper ergo meminerimus eius sententiae, qua cunctatori & ad res domesticas respectanti discipulo Christus dixit: Nemo qui manu sua admota aratro respexerit ad ea quae a tergo sunt, aptus est regno Dei. Luc.9.
units.tr: Moreover, as we said, Matthew and Mark attach a grave warning to this so generous promise, saying: "But many that are first shall be last, and the last first." This saying is meant to heal those who, having advanced some way in zeal for the kingdom of God, think they have already reached the highest perfection, and so, feeling secure, despise all others and even rashly condemn those whom they see left behind or not yet having entered the way. The Lord therefore teaches that it is not enough for some to make a good beginning unless they finish their course and press on to the goal set before them with unwearied zeal. For it often happens that those who seemed first, and who pursued the cause of God with great fervour, suddenly fail, or at least are overtaken by those who were last of all. Let us therefore always remember that saying with which Christ answered the disciple who hesitated and looked back to his household affairs: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back to the things behind is fit for the kingdom of God." Luke 9.

units.la: Caeterum quia ista cum discipulis tunc locutus est Dominus, quando Hierosolymam proficiscebatur, ubi seipsum pro mundi peccatis immolaturus erat, novum sermonem ille instruit, quo & trepidos consolatur, & adversus scandalum crucis illos instruit. De eo sic Lucas scribit: Iesus autem assumptis illis duodecim, dixit eis: Ecce ascendimus Hierosolymam & perficientur Filio hominis omnia, &c.
