Cum duodecim discipulis priuatim de his, quae ipsi eventura erat disserit: quia illi institutione præ aliis opus habebat, eò quòd (vt Marcus annotauit) timore non paruo correpti trepidarent. Sciebant enim Hierosolymæ hostes eius rerum potiri, & ibidem periculorum & insidiarum plena esse omnia. Et hi illi sunt, qui quasi confecta re omni de præmio paulò ante quæsiuerunt. Rursus ergo hic infirmitatis humanæ exemplum proponitur, cuius hic nobis vsus esse debet, vt ne nobis ipsis fidamus, aut nostræ salutis secuři alios temere damnemus. At non minus obseruari debet bonitas Christi, qui meticulosos milites non à signis suis reijcit, neque publica ignominia notat, sed amicè instituit atq; consolatur. Orationis istius partes duæ sunt.
units.tr: But because the Lord spoke these things to the disciples when he was setting out for Jerusalem, where he was to offer himself for the sins of the world, he prepares a new discourse by which he both comforts the fearful and instructs them against the scandal of the cross. Luke writes of it thus: "Then Jesus took the twelve and said to them: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written of the Son of man shall be accomplished," etc. He speaks privately with the twelve disciples about what was about to befall him, because they needed instruction more than the others, since (as Mark noted) they were seized with no small fear and trembled. For they knew that his enemies held power in Jerusalem and that everything there was full of dangers and snares. And these are the same men who, as if the whole matter were already settled, had shortly before asked about their reward. Here, then, an example of human weakness is set before us, and we ought to use it so that we do not trust in ourselves, nor rashly condemn others while we feel secure about our own salvation. Yet the goodness of Christ must be no less observed, for he does not cast off the fearful soldiers from his standards, nor brand them with public disgrace, but instructs and comforts them kindly. This discourse has two parts.

units.la: Prima consolationem habet validissimis argumentis suffultam. Ecce (inquit) ascendimus Hierosolymam, & perficientur Filio hominis omnia, quæ scripta sunt per Prophetas: Fidi Imperatoris instar periculum prædicit, & ita se non ignarum esse ostendit eorum, quæ ipsi sint eventura. Quo vt suam diuinitatem diserte declaratit, ita non obscurè innuit, inexcusabilem fore ipsorum timiditatem, si periculi eius socij esse nolint, cuius maior pars in ipsius solius caput sit redundatura. Deinde nihil temere eventurū esse decet, sed ea solum, quæ olim per Prophetas prædicta sunt. At constat hos Dei seruos fuisse, & proinde nihil prædixisse, quàm quod æterno Dei decreto constitutum esse, ex Spiritus sancti reuelatione didicerant. Sunt hæc efficacissima consolationis argumenta, quæ hodie sibi ipsis applicare debent, omnes, qui propter fidem in Christum in periculum veniunt. Cogitent primum, se ducem omnis certaminis habere ipsum Dei Filium, qui durissima pro nobis sustinuit olim, & hodie adhuc nobis sua virtute & Spiritu adest, vt omnibus ferendis possimus sufficere. Quis ergo sub hoc duce trepidet, quem in Euangelio clamantem audit: Venit princeps huius mundi, & in me non habet quicquam? Item, Confidite, ego vici mundum. Deinde meminerimus quoq; nihil nobis accidere fortuitum. In eius enim manu sumus, qui & dies vitæ nostræ & capillos omnes in numerato habet: cuius item prouidentia ad passerculos vsq; ad pullos coruorum, atque flores in agris absque omni hominum cultura nascentes extenditur. Quia vero ille humani generis amantissimus, imò Pater noster est, qui virium nostrarum tenuitatem probè nouit, minimè timendum erit, ne nos supra vires tentari patiatur. Illud potius probè omnes meditentur, quàm graue sceelus sit eius voluntati resistere, & collum subducere velle oneri, quod ille nobis certo consilio imponit. Venia indignus putatur, qui Senatusconsulto stare detrectat, aut publica authoritate confirmatam sententiam reijcit. Num ergo nos impune laturos putabimus, si crucem eam ferre detrectemus, quam summus ille Rex regum nobis ex æterno suo decreto imponit? Adde his, quòd cum afflictionum omnium ducem atq; socium habeamus, Iesum Christum, non alius nobis illarum finis erit, quàm qui ipsi fuit. Ipse per diram & infamem mortem in gloriam Patris sui ingressus est. Ergo nobis quoque in eodem ad cœlestem & æternam felicitatem aditus patebit, si cum illo in omni tentatione in finem vsque perseueremus. Vide infra Luc. 22. Vos ij estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis: Et ego dispono vobis, sicut mihi disposuit Pater regnum, &c. Quò Paulus respiciens dicebat: Si cum Christo affligimur, cum eodem regnabimus: si cum eo moriemur, cum eo viuemus.
units.tr: The first part offers comfort supported by very strong arguments. "Behold," he says, "we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of man shall be accomplished." Like a faithful commander, he foretells the danger, and shows that he is not ignorant of what is to befall them. In declaring his divinity so plainly, he also hints quite clearly that their timidity will be inexcusable if they are unwilling to share the danger with him, since the greater part of it is to fall upon his head alone. Next, nothing ought to happen by chance, but only those things that were foretold long ago by the prophets. It is certain that these were servants of God, and so they foretold nothing but what they had learned from the revelation of the Holy Spirit to be decreed by God's eternal counsel. These are most effective arguments of consolation, which all who come into danger for the sake of faith in Christ ought to apply to themselves today. First, let them consider that they have as leader of every conflict the Son of God himself, who once endured the hardest things for us, and who even now is present with us by his power and Spirit, so that we may be able to bear all things. Who, then, should tremble under such a leader, when he hears him crying in the gospel: "The prince of this world comes, and he has nothing in me"? Likewise: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." Next, let us remember that nothing happens to us by chance. We are in the hand of him who holds the days of our life and every hair of our head numbered; by his providence the sparrows and the young ravens are fed, and the flowers grow in the fields without any cultivation by men. And since he is the most loving of the human race, indeed our Father, who knows well the feebleness of our strength, there is no need to fear that he will allow us to be tempted beyond our powers. Rather, let everyone consider well how grievous a crime it is to resist his will and to wish to shake off the yoke that he lays upon us by his sure counsel. A man is thought unworthy of pardon who refuses to abide by a decree of the Senate or rejects a sentence confirmed by public authority. Shall we then suppose that we shall go unpunished if we refuse to bear the cross which the supreme King of kings lays upon us by his eternal decree? Add to this that since we have as leader and companion in all afflictions Jesus Christ, the end of these afflictions for us will be the same as it was for him. He entered into the glory of his Father through a dreadful and infamous death. So for us also there will be an open way into the same heavenly and eternal happiness, if we persevere with him to the end in every temptation. See below, Luke 22: "You are they who have continued with me in my temptations. And I appoint to you, as my Father has appointed to me, a kingdom," etc. With this in view Paul said: "If we suffer with Christ, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him."

units.la: Altera parte diligentius exponit, quæ nam illa sint, quæ ipsum Hierosolymis secundum Prophetarum veterū vaticinia pati aut sufferre oporteat. Tradetur (inquit) Filius hominis gentibus, & illudetur, & contumelijs afficietur, et conspuetur: Et postquam eum flagellauerint, trucidabunt, sed die tertia resurget. Habet hæc quoq; tam diligens omnium, quæ ipsi eventura sint, cōmemoratio, non obscurum diuinitatis testimonium, & ideo discipulorum fidem aduersus futurum crucis scandalum vehementer consolari potuit. Præcipua tamen illius causa mihi esse videtur, quòd de tota salutis ratione discipulos iterum admonere voluit: quod tunc in primis necessarium erat, ne propriæ iustitiæ & suorum operum fidutia efferrentur. Præstiterant enim illi, quod à magnate & opulento iuuene requisiuerat, atq; omnibus relictis rebus ipsum erant secuti. Laude etiam eximia illos Christus exornauerat, vt Matthæus prodidit: Amen dico vobis, vos qui secuti estis me, in regeneratione cum sederit Filius hominis in throno gloriæ suæ, sedebitis etiam vos super thronos duodecim iudicantes duodecim tribus Israelis. Quibus plures aliæ promissiones accesserunt, quas suo loco vidimus: Ne ergo (quod dixi) aduersus Dei gratiam cristas erigerent, vt qui iampridem amplissima præmia sibi deberi sibi ipsis persuaserant, paucis admonet, in quibusnam salus hominis consistat. Itaq; verborum istorum hic sensus est: Multa quidem hucusque præstitistis, & laudem meretur vestra virtus atq; constantia, quam mihi in hunc vsq; diem adhæsistis: sed non propterea vos gloriari aut efferri velim, vt qui ipsi vobis salutis æternæ sitis authores. Est enim illa maioris pretij, quàm vt vlla hominum industria aut operibus acquiri possit: & meum hoc opus est, quem Pater cælestis æterno decreto destinauit, vt mortis indignæ supplicio peccata mundi expiem, resurrectione autem gloriosa mortem atq; inferos deuincam, & vitam omnibus conferam, qui in me crediderint. Ex his autē doctrina generalis peti debet, salutem omnem in vno Christo haberi, neq; aliud nomen sub cælo hominibus datū esse, in quo seruari possint. Docent hoc vnanimi consensu Prophetæ & Apostoli, & hocipsum communis sensus testatur. Quis enim crediderit Deum, qui & iustissimus et sapientissimus est, hanc tam grauem atq; diram humanæ salutis recuperandæ rationem initurum fuisse, quæ non aliter quàm indigna Filij sui dilectissimi morte constare poterat, si vlla alia excogitari potuisset? In ea igitur nos bonitatem illius ita agnoscere decet, vt in vno Christo acquiescamus, procul relicta tam nostrorum meritorum quàm omnium aliorum hominum fiducia. Quia tamen de hoc diximus, & nunquam non de eo dicendi occasio occurrit, nolumus ista nunc prolixius prosequi.
units.tr: The second part sets out more carefully what those things are which, according to the ancient prophecies, he must suffer or endure at Jerusalem. "The Son of man," he says, "will be delivered to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and insulted, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, but on the third day he will rise again." This so careful foretelling of all that was to befall him likewise contains an unmistakable testimony to his divinity, and so it could greatly strengthen the disciples' faith against the coming scandal of the cross. Yet its chief purpose seems to me to be this: he wished to warn the disciples once more about the whole order of salvation, which was especially necessary then, lest they be puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness and their own works. For they had done what the rich young man had been asked to do: they had left everything and followed him. Christ had also honoured them with a remarkable commendation, as Matthew records: "Truly I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." Several other promises were added to this, which we have seen in their place. Therefore, so that they would not, as I have said, raise their crests against the grace of God, as men who had long ago persuaded themselves that very great rewards were owed to them, he briefly reminds them in what the salvation of man consists. The sense of his words, then, is this: "You have done many things up to now, and your virtue and steadfastness, by which you have clung to me until this day, deserve praise. Yet I do not wish you to glory or be puffed up on that account, as if you were the authors of your own eternal salvation. For that is of greater worth than any human industry or works can gain. It is my work, and the one whom the heavenly Father destined by his eternal decree to make expiation for the sins of the world by a punishment worthy of death, and by his glorious resurrection to overcome death and hell, and to bestow life on all who believe in me." From this, therefore, a general doctrine must be drawn: all salvation is to be had in Christ alone, and no other name under heaven has been given to men by which they may be saved. The prophets and apostles teach this with one accord, and common sense itself bears witness to it. For who would believe that God, who is most just and most wise, would have undertaken so grievous and dreadful a way of recovering human salvation, which could not have been achieved except by the unworthy death of his most beloved Son, if any other could have been devised? Therefore we ought to acknowledge his goodness in such a way that we rest in Christ alone, having utterly set aside all trust both in our own merits and in those of all other men. But since we have said these things, and there is never a lack of occasion to speak of it, we do not wish to pursue these matters at greater length now.

units.la: Audiamus vero de discipulis illis duodecim loquentem Lucam. Ipsi verò (inquit) nihil horum intellexerunt, eratq; ista verba ipsis occulta, nec cognouerunt quæ dicebantur. Multis rem vnã & eandem dicit, adeoq; Pleonasmis vtitur, vt plus quam stupidam ignorantiam exprimat. Nec enim contentus dixisse, quod nihil horum intellexerint, addit. Erantq; verba ista ipsis occulta. Et rursus: Nec ignorauerunt quæ dicebatur. Et quid obsecro in verbis istis tā occultū aut abstrusum erat? An nesciebant Filij hominis vocabulo ipsum Christum denotari? Erat certè hoc etiam hostibus illius notissimum, vt multis exemplis probari posset. An verò ignorabant, quid sit tradi gentibus, illudi, contumelijs affici, flagellari, conspui, deniq; trucidari? Aut quid obscuri inerat locutioni isti: Tertia die resurget? hæc certè omnia simplicia, aperta & clara sunt, neq; in sensum aliquem ambiguum possunt torqueri. Cur ergo illis occulta videntur? cur quæ his dicuntur non intelligunt? Quia falsa de Regno Christi terreno persuasione præoccupati & fascinati non possunt videre, quomodo ista ei conueniant, quem paulò post regni sedem Hierosolymis erecturum esse sibi persuaserant, deiectis Romanorum præsidijs, quibus tunc Iudæus populus grauabatur. Estq; hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quàm noxium sit falsis opinionibus imbui. Vt enim gustus organis corruptis omnia insipida esse aut acescere videtur: ita qui animos prauis persuasionib. occupatos habent, ijs obscura, absurda & impossibilia sunt, quæcunq; de Christi regno spirituali & salutis æternæ mysterijs traduntur. Quid ergo miramur, si hodie pauci Euangelio credat, quando infiniti errores atq; superstitiones ferè omnium animos iampridem fascinarunt? Nam vt de veteri superstitione nihil dicamus, nouæ quotidie sectæ prodeunt, & proprium (vt ita dicam) Christum sibi quiuis fingit. Taceo multorum furores, quibus agitati cælum terræ miscent, & pro sua libidine confundunt. Prodest autem illa diligenter obseruare, ne aliorum tarditas aut ignorantia nobis scandalo sit: Ipsi verò in Dei verbum atque promissiones intenti, Iesum Christum agnoscamus eum esse, qui suæ mortis & resurrectionis merito nobis salutem peperit, & cui nunc in cælis regnanti debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us hear Luke speaking of those twelve disciples. "But they," he says, "understood none of these things, and this saying was hidden from them, neither did they know the things that were said." He says the same thing many times over and uses pleonasms so as to express a more than stupid ignorance. For he is not content to have said that they understood none of these things; he adds, "and this saying was hidden from them." And again: "neither did they know what was said." And what, I ask you, was so hidden or obscure in these words? Did they not know that the name Son of Man denotes Christ himself? Indeed this was very well known even to his enemies, as many examples could prove. Or did they not know what it means to be delivered to the Gentiles, to be mocked, insulted, scourged, spat upon, and finally slain? Or what was obscure in that phrase, "On the third day he will rise again"? All these things are surely plain, clear and open, and cannot be twisted into any ambiguous sense. Why then do they seem hidden to them? Why do they not understand what is said to them? Because, preoccupied and bewitched by the false persuasion of an earthly kingdom of Christ, they cannot see how these things agree with him whom they had persuaded themselves would shortly set up the seat of his kingdom at Jerusalem, once the Roman garrisons, by which the Jewish people was then burdened, had been cast out. And this is a memorable example, by which we are taught how harmful it is to be imbued with false opinions. For just as to a palate with corrupted organs everything seems insipid or sour, so for those whose minds are occupied with wicked persuasions, whatever is taught about the spiritual kingdom of Christ and the mysteries of eternal salvation seems obscure, absurd and impossible. Why then are we surprised if few today believe the Gospel, when countless errors and superstitions have long since bewitched almost everyone's minds? For, to say nothing of the old superstition, new sects spring up every day, and each person makes up for himself (so to speak) a Christ of his own. I pass over the frenzies of many, by which they are driven to throw heaven and earth into confusion and to twist everything to their own lust. It is useful, however, to observe carefully that we are not made to stumble by the slowness or ignorance of others; but let us ourselves, intent upon God's Word and promises, acknowledge Jesus Christ as the one who by the merit of his death and resurrection has obtained salvation for us, and to whom, now reigning in heaven, be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXI.

units.la: Factum est autem dum ipse appropinquaret Iericho, cæcus quidam sedebat iuxta viam mendicans. Cum igitur is audisset turbam praetereuntem, percontabatur quid hoc esset. Nunciauerũt autem ei, Iesum Nazarenum transire. Tunc clamauit dicens: Iesu, Fili Dauid, miserere mei. Et qui præibant obiurgabant eum vt sileret. Ipse verò multo magis clamabat, Fili Dauid miserere mei. Iesus autem cum substitisset, iussit eum adduci ad se: & cum appropinquasset, interrogauit eum dicens: Quid tibi vis faciam? Ille verò dixit: Domine, vt visum recipiam. Et Iesus dixit ei: Recipito visum, fides tua te seruauit. Illico igitur visum recepit, ac sequebatur eum, glorificans Deum: & totus populus cum hoc vidisset, tribuit laudem Deo.
units.tr: It happened that as he drew near to Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting by the road begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this meant. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. Then he cried out, saying, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me." And those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me." Jesus stopped and ordered him to be brought to him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him, "What do you want me to do for you?" He said, "Lord, that I may receive my sight." Jesus said to him, "Receive your sight; your faith has saved you." Immediately he received his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And when all the people saw this, they gave praise to God.

units.la: Exposuit nuper Iesus Christus discipulis, quid ipsum Hierosolymis pati oporteat, & paucis verbis ostendit, salutem nostram omnem in suae mortis merito & resurrectionis virtute consistere. Caeterum quamvis diserte & absque omni verborum involucro ista propositerit, nihil tamen horum illi intellexerunt, eo quod falsa & erronea de Regno Christi terreno opinione excaecati haec ta profunda redemptionis nostrae mysteria cernere non possent. Eorum autem exemplo Spiritus Sanctus omnium nostrum caecitatem arguit, qui in divinis adeo nihil ex nobis ipsis sapimus, ut si quid conemur nostri ingenii solertia atque industria investigare, nosmetipsos inextricabilibus errorum Labyrinthis implicemus, sicut in Iudaeorum Rabbinis & gentium philosophis est videre. Et si uni cuius error ex communi omnium persuasione, quae tunc inter Iudaeos regnabat, conceptus, tantum in Apostolis potuit, quid tunc passuros nos putabimus, si cum carnis ratione omnes simul carnis sensus atque desideria concurrant? Itaque praesenti & prompto remedio nobis est opus, quod non aliud erit, quam ut Christum sequamur, qui lux mundi est, & suo in mundum adventu verum illum & salutiferum iustitiae Solem reduxit, qui nos in errorum & peccatorum tenebris errare non sinit. Commodissime ergo ijs, quae de discipulorum ignorantia dicta sunt, miraculi huius historia subijcitur, quo ille aperte probat, se lucem illam esse, quae sola mentes nostras veritatis & salutis cognitione illuminet. At cum eadem de multis alijs cognitu necessarijs nos admoneat, singulas partes percurramus.
units.tr: Not long ago Jesus Christ explained to his disciples what he must suffer at Jerusalem, and in a few words he showed that our whole salvation rests on the merit of his death and the power of his resurrection. Yet although he set these things out plainly and without any veil of words, they understood none of them, because they were blinded by a false and mistaken opinion about the earthly kingdom of Christ and could not discern these deep mysteries of our redemption. By their example the Holy Spirit also rebukes the blindness of all of us, who in divine matters have so little wisdom of our own that, if we try to investigate anything by the cleverness and diligence of our own minds, we entangle ourselves in inextricable labyrinths of error, as can be seen among the rabbis of the Jews and the philosophers of the Gentiles. And if one error, conceived from the common persuasion of all that then prevailed among the Jews, had such power even over the Apostles, what shall we think we will suffer, when all the desires and senses of the flesh rush together with the reasoning of the flesh? Therefore we need a present and ready remedy, which will be nothing other than to follow Christ, who is the light of the world, and by his coming into the world has restored that true and saving Sun of righteousness, who does not allow us to wander in the darkness of error and sin. It is most fitting, then, that the story of this miracle is set after what has been said about the ignorance of the disciples, since by it he plainly proves that he is that light which alone illuminates our minds with the knowledge of truth and salvation. And since it also warns us about many other things necessary to know, let us go through its individual parts.

units.la: Oritur a persona descriptione Lucas, in qua miraculum est editum. Gerit ea humani generis typum per omnia infelicis ac miseri. Caecus enim fuit, quam non leuem miseriam esse constat, cum inter hominis sensus visu nullus sit praestantior, & qui tam necessitati quam voluptati magis seruiat. Accedit calamitati huic inopia rerum omnium, quae infelicem coegit publice mendicando vitam sibi parare. Nam ut alias monuimus, etsi Deus in lege sua cauisset, ne mendicus esset in Israele, & rationem monstrauisset, qua inopes alerentur, sacerdotum tamen iniquitate & auaritia lex quoque illa abolita fuit, eo quod illi publica Ecclesiae bona sibi vendicabant, ut & suae & praesidum cupiditati satisfacerent, quorum authoritate adimpium suum quaestum tuendum ipsis opus erat. Et haec causa est, quod in Euangelica historia saepius fit mendicorum mentio, quos in Veteri testamento aut omnino nullos aut certe paucissimos et raros fuisse constat. Id vero admonemus, ut eorum cofutemus errorem, qui hodie mendicantium ordini patrocinantur, neque eos in ordinem cogi volunt; & utinam illud plerique non etiam priuati commodi & quaestus causa facerent, quem ex bonorum ecclesiasticorum dispensatione habent vberrimum. Quia tamen haec alterius loci sunt, nunc obseruemus, quod paulo ante dixi, in misero hoc omnium nostrum conditionem infelicissimam adumbrari, qui oculos mentis amisimus, ut diuina non possimus intueri: adhaec omnis virtutis egeni, & in Dei conspectu mendici sumus, periturι prorsus, nisi ille sua gratia & misericordia nostram egestatem sarciat.
units.tr: Luke begins with a description of the person on whom the miracle was performed. In him is shown the type of the whole human race, wretched and miserable in every way. For he was blind, which is plainly no small misery, since among the senses of man none is more excellent than sight, and none serves both necessity and pleasure more. To this calamity is added the lack of all things, which forced the unhappy man to get his living by begging in public. For, as we have pointed out elsewhere, although God in his law had provided that there should be no beggar in Israel, and had shown the means by which the needy were to be supported, yet through the wickedness and greed of the priests that law too was abolished, because they claimed the public goods of the Church for themselves, in order to satisfy both their own lust and that of the rulers, whose authority they needed to protect their own gain. This is the reason why the Gospel history so often mentions beggars, of whom in the Old Testament there were either none at all or certainly very few and rare. But we warn of this so that we may refute the error of those who today defend the order of mendicant friars and do not want them brought under rule; and would that most of them did not also do this for the sake of private gain and profit, which they have in abundance from the distribution of ecclesiastical goods. But since these matters belong to another place, let us now notice what I said a little while ago: in this wretched man is shadowed forth the most unhappy condition of all of us, who have lost the eyes of the mind, so that we cannot look upon divine things; and besides, we are destitute of all virtue, and in the sight of God we are beggars, sure to perish unless he, by his grace and mercy, makes up for our poverty.

units.la: Videamus ergo quid ille fecerit, ut quid nos quoque facere deceat discamus. Tribuuntur illi omnia verae fidei indicia siue argumenta, qua omnino opus est omnibus qui seruari cupiunt. Primo sedet iuxta viam, eo nimirum perductus, ut a praetereuntibus stipem peteret. Itaque audito strepitu maiori, quem ingens Christi illac transeuntis comitatus excitabat, quaerit quis nam ille sit, quem tam multi sequantur; & ut primum audit Iesum esse, alta voce eum inuocat. Unde apparet nomen Iesu ei non ignotum fuisse, de cuius miraculis & beneficentia haud dubie ex alijs multa audiuerat, & fortassis diu captarat ipsum conueniendi & implorandi occasionem. Est hoc salutis nostrae initium. Offert quidem se nobis Deus sponte per verbum suum, & promissionibus liberalissimis nos inuitat, idem tamen nos salutem sitire, & omnem eius assequendae occasionem diligenter quaerere & obseruare iubet, ne in re tanti momenti nobis ipsis vnquam desimus. Et huc seriae illae admonitiones pertinent: Quaerite Dominum dum inuenitur: inuocate eum dum prope est. Sedeamus ergo ad viam praeceptorum eius, & audiamus attente quid nobis ille loquatur. Studio huic autem coniungamus preces, quibus opem eius imploremus, qui illi gratissimus cultus est. Ista si qui negligunt, ij satis ostendunt, se non magno salutis studio teneri, & proinde non mirum est, si nihil proficiant. Quid ergo de illis dicemus, qui Dei gratiam fastidiunt, & Christum se ipsis liberaliter offerentem reijciunt: neue illum aliquando admittere cogantur, coetus sacros fugiunt, conciones nullas audiunt, Sacramentorum vsum detestantur, aut saltem impudenter negligunt? Indigni certe sunt tales, qui Spiritu Dei illuminentur & salui fiant: digni autem qui in sua caecitate pereant.
units.tr: Let us then see what he did, so that we may learn what it becomes us also to do. All the signs and marks of true faith, which are altogether needed by all who wish to be saved, are attributed to him. First, he sits by the road, plainly brought there so that he might beg alms from those passing by. So when he heard the great noise, which the large company accompanying Christ as he passed by made, he asked who that was whom so many followed; and as soon as he heard that it was Jesus, he called out to him with a loud voice. From this it appears that the name of Jesus was not unknown to him, and that he had doubtless heard much about his miracles and his kindness from others, and perhaps had for a long time been watching for an opportunity to meet him and beg for help. This is the beginning of our salvation. God indeed offers himself to us of his own accord through his word, and invites us with the most generous promises; yet he also bids us thirst for salvation ourselves, and diligently seek and watch for every opportunity of obtaining it, so that in a matter of such great importance we may never fail ourselves. To this belong those earnest admonitions: "Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near." Let us then sit by the way of his commands, and listen carefully to what he says to us. Let us join prayers to this zeal, by which we implore his help, which is the most pleasing worship to him. If some neglect these things, they sufficiently show that they are not held by any great eagerness for salvation, and so it is no wonder if they make no progress. What then shall we say of those who despise the grace of God and reject Christ, who offers himself to them freely; who, lest they be compelled at some time to admit him, flee the holy assemblies, hear no sermons, despise the use of the sacraments, or at least negligently and shamelessly neglect them? Such people are certainly unworthy to be enlightened by the Spirit of God and to be saved; they are worthy rather to perish in their blindness.

units.la: Deinde inuocat cæcus iste Iesum Christum, qui proprius fidei effectus est, vt iam sæpe diximus: inuocatione autem sua breuior complectitur quæcunque ad salutem necessaria sunt. Clamat enim: Iesu fili Dauid, miserere mei. Primò Christum inuocat, & hunc Filium Dauidis dicit, vt eum teste tur promissum illum & multis seculis expectatum seruatorem esse. Hunc enim ex Dauidis posteritate nascituram esse Prophetarum vaticinia docebant, in quibus aliquando Dauid ipse dicitur, & Isaias illū germen Iesse vocat. Fuit ergo hæc non obscura fidei confessio, quam miser iste ex eius miraculis & Spiritus sancti suggestione conceperat: & qua illuminatus animo suo acutius videt quàm Scribæ & Pharisæi, qui (vt olim per Isaiam Deus minatus fuerat) oculis videntibus cæcutiebant, audiendo non audiebant & scientes nesciebant, crassa nimirum & voluntaria ignorantia impediti. Ad hunc ergo nos quoque contendamus, qui vt propensus est ad iuuandum, & neminem ad se venientem reijcit. At hic in primis obseruari debet, quod suæ miseriæ sibi probè conscius, non sua opera aut merita qualiacunque iactat, sed solam misericordiā illius implorat: Iesu (inquit) fili Dauid, miserere mei. Agnouit ergo se non modò quoad corpus cæcum & mendicum esse, verumetiam animi cæcitate & virtutis inopia laborare, & proinde vniuersum salutis præsidium in sola misericordia Dei esse collocatum. Est hæc nostræ infirmitatis atque imperfectionis agnitio omnibus necessaria. Hæc enim sola seriū salutis studium in nobis excitat, & simul preces nostras Deo acceptas facit, quæ ipsi minimè probantur, si ex animo confidenti & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia inflato procedant, sicut in Pharisæi & publicani historia vidimus.
units.tr: Next this blind man calls upon Jesus Christ, which, as we have often said, is the proper effect of faith; and in his short invocation he embraces everything necessary for salvation. For he cries out: "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me." First, he invokes Christ and calls him the Son of David, so as to bear witness that he is the promised Saviour, expected for many ages. For the prophecies taught that he would be born from the posterity of David, in which sometimes David himself is named, and Isaiah calls him the shoot of Jesse. This, then, was no obscure confession of faith, which this wretched man had formed from his miracles and by the prompting of the Holy Spirit; and by it, enlightened in his mind, he sees more keenly than the scribes and Pharisees, who (as God once threatened through Isaiah) grew blind while seeing with their eyes, hearing without hearing, and knowing without knowing, being hindered by a gross and willful ignorance. To him, then, let us too strive to come, who is inclined to help and rejects no one who comes to him. But here above all it must be observed that he, being well aware of his misery, does not boast of his works or of any merits whatsoever, but implores only his mercy: "Jesus," he says, "Son of David, have mercy on me." He acknowledged, therefore, that he was blind and a beggar not only in body, but that he also suffered from blindness of mind and lack of virtue, and that therefore the whole safeguard of salvation was placed in the mercy of God alone. This acknowledgment of our weakness and imperfection is necessary for all. For it alone stirs up in us a serious zeal for salvation, and at the same time makes our prayers acceptable to God; these are not at all approved if they proceed from a heart that is confident and puffed up with trust in its own righteousness, as we saw in the story of the Pharisee and the publican.

units.la: Accedit tertium in cæci exemplo, sine quo priora illa omnia non profuissent, fortis nimirum & inuicta fidei constantia. Nam à populo obiurgatum fuisse Lucas scribit, ne Christi opem imploraret. Et credibile est multos offensos fuisse, quòd illum disertis verbis filium Dauidis & promissum Seruatorem diceret. Sciebant enim quàm hoc ingratū esset Pharisæis & Sacerdotibus, qui tunc rerum potiebantur. Alij etiam Christo aliquam moram iniici indignius ferebant. Multos fortasse suo morositas mouit, vt importuno mendici clamore offenderentur. Veruntamen pergit ille, v quasi certa men suscepisset cum illis omnibus, eò magis vocem suā intendit, quò magis illi increpando & obiurgando instant. Est hæc eius constantia imitatione dignissima. Quod enim isti accidit, omnibus fieri solet, qui Christum ex fide inuocant. Non potest enim hoc ferre mundus, qui cum totus in malo iaceat, veritatis lucem odit & extinctā cupit. Obstant item hypocritæ, quibus gratiæ & misericordiæ Dei imploratio intolerabilis videtur, eò quòd per hanc suorum meritorum & iustitiæ propriæ fiducia euerti sentiunt. Multi item qui eundem nobiscum Christum profitentur, nos modestiæ admonent, & prudenter interdum dissimulandam esse aiunt fidei confessionem, ne mundi odium & indignationem prouocemus. Terret interdum propria conscientia, quæ nos indignos esse clamat, qui à Deo exaudiamur. Adhæc quia interdum Deus opem diutius differt, ex eo diffidentia occasio nascitur, vt de illius erga nos voluntate dubitare incipiamus. Sed per omnia obstacula pergere nos conuenit. Cur enim mundi authoritas eos moueat, qui se non amplius ad huius societatem pertinere, sed ab eos selectos & separatos esse sciunt? Cur hypocritas iustitiarios audiamus, quibus nihil Deo magis inuisum atq; exosum est? Cur item fratrum consilia sequamur, qui carnis potius ratione quàm Dei verbo ducuntur? Aut num pluris faceremus nostræ conscientiæ iam fluctuantis suggestionem, quàm Dei promissiones, quibus suam nobis opem tam liberaliter pollicetur? Cur denique eius cunctatio nobis suspecta fit, qui & Pater est fidelissimus, & cum ipsa sit sapientia, melius quàm nos intelligit, quando nobis auxilium ferre debeat? Horum consideratine diligenti nos confirmemus, & viduae exemplum (quod huius capitis initio audiuimus) imitemur, vt fidei constantia superemus ea, quæ nullis hominum viribus confici possunt.
units.tr: A third quality is added in the example of the blind man, without which all those earlier things would have been of no avail: a strong and unconquered constancy of faith. Luke writes that he was rebuked by the people, so that he would not implore Christ's help. It is likely that many were offended because he called Christ in plain words the Son of David and the promised Saviour. They knew how unwelcome this was to the Pharisees and the priests, who then held power. Others took it worse that any delay was placed in the way of Christ. Perhaps many were moved by their own irritability, and were offended by the troublesome cry of a beggar. Yet he presses on, and as if he had resolved to hold out against them all, he raises his voice all the more, the more they insist on rebuking and scolding him. This constancy of his is most worthy of imitation. What happened to him happens to all who call on Christ in faith. The world cannot bear it: although it lies wholly in evil, it hates the light of truth and wishes it extinguished. The hypocrites also stand in the way, for the imploring of God's grace and mercy seems intolerable to them, because they feel that through it their confidence in their own merits and their own righteousness is overthrown. Many also who profess the same Christ as we do advise us to be moderate, and say that the confession of faith should sometimes be prudently concealed, so that we do not provoke the hatred and indignation of the world. Our own conscience sometimes terrifies us, crying out that we are unworthy to be heard by God. Moreover, because God sometimes delays his help for a long time, an occasion for distrust arises from this, so that we begin to doubt his will towards us. But we ought to press on through all these obstacles. Why should the authority of the world move those who know that they no longer belong to its fellowship, but have been chosen and separated from it? Why should we listen to the self-righteous hypocrites, to whom nothing is more hateful and odious than God? Why should we also follow the counsels of brothers who are led more by the reasoning of the flesh than by the Word of God? Or should we value the suggestion of our conscience, now wavering, more highly than the promises of God, by which he so generously pledges his help to us? Why, finally, should his delay be suspect to us, when he is a most faithful Father, and, being wisdom itself, understands better than we do when he ought to bring us help? Let us strengthen ourselves by diligent consideration of these things, and imitate the example of the widow (which we heard at the beginning of this chapter), so that by constancy of faith we may overcome those things which cannot be accomplished by any human strength.

units.la: Et seruiat hic nobis huius cæci exemplum, cuius tam seria tamque pertinax inuocatio fructu suo minimè caruit. Audit enim hanc inter turbæ strepitum & obiurgationum voces Christus, & mox gradum sistit, qui præteriturus videbatur. Quo loco partim Dei bonitas adumbratur, qui nullius clamorem fastidit; partim vis precationis ex vera fide proficiscentis exprimitur. Oratio afflicti (inquit Sapiens ille) nubes penetrat, non conquiescit, nec desistit, donec venerit ad Altissimum. Orando igitur impetramus, vt in auxilium nostrum Deus festinet, vtque nos benigne respiciat, qui nostri curam iampridē putabatur deposuisse. Exempla, quibus hoc demonstretur, alibi adduximus. Et multorū instar esse potest, quod hīc habemus. Nec enim subsistit modò Christus, sed cæcum hunc adse adducere iubet. At qui vno verbo absentem curare poterat. Sed docere voluit, necesse esse, vt ad ipsum propius accedat, qui animi oculos cœlesti & immortali luce illuminari cupiunt. Adipsum autem veniunt, quicunq; verbum eius studiose audiunt, & fidei alis supra mundum hunc euectis altiora & cœlestia quærunt. Simul etiā officij omnes eos admonet, qui ipsius sectatores haberi volunt: quod est, ne cui obstent, qui opem eius implorat, quin potius ad ipsam propius adducat, quoscunq; ad fidem inclinare vident. Vbi vero in conspectum eius ille adductus est, quærit quid sibi fieri velit. Poterat quæstio illa superuacanea & ridicula videri, sed necessaria fuisse patebit, si rē ipsam diligentius consideremus. Nam in vulgo mendicorum multi sunt, qui etsi ab omnibus opem magno & improbo clamore petant, ijdem tamē à morbis, quibus tenentur liberari minimè cupiunt, eò quòd ex illis quæstū faciant. Sunt bi eorū typus, qui veritatis cognitione illuminari nolunt, quia superstitionū tenebras sibi quæstuosas esse sentiunt. Deinde fidē istius adhuc clarius innotescere omnibus oportuit, ne Christum præclaro & illustri Filij Dauidis nomine ideò appellauisse putaretur, vt plus pecuniæ ab ipso & eius studiosis emungeret. Qui enim visum ab illo petit, non obscurè fatetur, se in illo aliquid homi ne maius agnoscere, neq; hoc ambitioni datum esse, quòd Dauidis Filium dixit. Id vero ad nos quoq; pertinet. Nam nostram quoq; fidem Deus nota esse vult omnibus: eò quòd eius libera confessio adil- lustrandam Dei gloriam facit, & alios quoq; excitat & trahit, vt de sua salute diligentius cogitet. Postremò quod ille petebat, liberalissimè largitur. Nā vno verbo visum illi reddit, et simul propter eos qui aderant, disertè exprimit medium, quo ille tantum Dei donū percipiebat. Fides tua (inquit) te seruauit. Icaque Dei verbo illuminamur, cuius lucerna et pedes nostri diriguntur (vt Dauid ait) & ea nobis reuelantur, quæ nostri ingenij captum superant: eodem etiam nobis Deus offert, quæcunque nobis ad salutem consequendam vtilia & necessaria sunt. At hic nobis fide opus est, sine qua verbum non potest intelligi, neq; etiam ratæ esse promissiones, quæ non aliter quam fide apprehendi possunt. Etenim contradicit verbo Dei carnis ratio, dum omnia ad suum calculum revocat: quam sola fides subigit, vt totus homo voluntati Dei sese submittat, & æternæ salutis capax fiat. At quia fides non nostri arbitrij est, sed à Deo datur (quod non vno loco scriptura docet) ex eo- nis aperte colligitur, totam nostræ salutis rationem ex gratuita Dei misericordia pendere.
units.tr: Let the example of this blind man also serve us, whose so earnest and persistent calling upon Christ did not lack its reward. For Christ hears his cry amid the noise of the crowd and the voices of those rebuking him, and at once stops, though he seemed about to pass by. In this passage the goodness of God is in part foreshadowed, for he scorns no one's cry; and in part the power of prayer arising from true faith is brought out. The prayer of the afflicted, says that wise man, penetrates the clouds; it does not rest, nor does it desist, until it reaches the Most High. By praying, therefore, we obtain that God hastens to our help and looks kindly upon us, though he was long thought to have laid aside his care for us. We have brought forward examples elsewhere to show this, and what we have here may stand for many. For Christ not only stops, but bids the blind man be brought to him. Yet he could have healed him from a distance with a single word. But he wished to teach that it is necessary for those who desire the eyes of their minds to be illumined with heavenly and immortal light to come closer to him. Now those come to him who listen diligently to his word, and with the wings of faith lifted above this world seek higher and heavenly things. At the same time he reminds all those who want to be counted as his followers of their duty: that is, that they should not stand in the way of anyone who implores his help, but rather bring closer to him all whom they see inclined to faith. When the man has been brought into his sight, Christ asks what he wishes to be done for him. That question might seem superfluous and ridiculous, but it will appear necessary if we consider the matter more carefully. For among the mass of beggars there are many who, although they ask everyone for help with loud and shameless clamour, do not at all wish to be freed from the diseases with which they are afflicted, because they make a profit from them. These are the type of those who do not wish to be enlightened by the knowledge of the truth, because they feel that the darkness of superstitions is profitable to them. Further, it was fitting that his faith should be made more clearly known to all, lest it be thought that he had called Christ by the illustrious and famous name of Son of David in order to squeeze more money out of him and his followers. For he who asks Christ for sight does not obscurely confess that he recognises in him something greater than a man, and that it was not from ambition that he called him the Son of David. This also pertains to us. For God wills that our faith too be known to all, because its free confession makes the glory of God shine forth, and also stirs up and draws others, so that they think more carefully about their own salvation. Finally, what he asked for, Christ bestows most generously. For with a single word he restores his sight to him, and at the same time, for the sake of those who were present, he plainly states the means by which the man received this so great gift of God: Your faith, he says, has saved you. Therefore we are enlightened by the Word of God, whose lamp and feet are directed (as David says), and by which those things are revealed to us that exceed the capacity of our understanding; and by the same word God offers us whatever is useful and necessary for obtaining salvation. But here we need faith, without which the word cannot be understood, nor the promises be valid, since they cannot be apprehended except by faith. For the reason of the flesh contradicts the Word of God, while it reduces everything to its own reckoning; faith alone subdues this, so that the whole man submits himself to the will of God and becomes capable of eternal salvation. But because faith is not of our choice, but is given by God (as Scripture teaches in more than one place), it is clearly gathered from this that the whole reckoning of our salvation depends upon the free mercy of God.

units.la: Cæterum ne quis hinc securitatem aliquā animo concipiat, et sub fidei prætextu otium quærat, non inutile fuerit videre, qualem cæcus iste inter se hæc omnia gesserit, quid item fecerit tanto bene ficio affectus. Occurrit hic primo loco, quod Marcus illū exilisse scribit, cùm se à Christo vocarias diret, & relicto etiam pallio ad eum festinauisse. Est hoc fidei alacris & vero zelo flagrantis euidentissimum argumentum: & eius exemplo admonemur, omnem moram eos abrumpere oportere, qui sa lutem in Christo cōsequi volunt, & procul à tergo relinquere veterem hominē cum omnibus iis, quæ huic iucunda aut magnifica videtur: qualia sunt, propriæ iustitiæ fiducia, opes, honores, dignitates, carnis sapientia, et quæcunq; alia sunt huius generis. Quæ omnia proprijssimè per huius mendici pal lium adumbrantur. Sunt enim reuera nullius pretij, cùm neq; in Dei conspectu atq; iudicio nos tueri vel regere possint, neq; etiam stabilia & firma sint, sed plerunq; tunc nos destituunt, quando ex illis magnum quid sperabamus. Deinde quod paulo ante diximus, quid petat interrogatus, non aliud pe- tit, quàm vt visum recipiat. Quo exemplo rursus admonemur, vt ipsi quoq; in Christo non alia quæ- ramus, quàm quæ æternæ salutis sunt: et in primis quidem, vt qui mundi lux est, cœlesti sapientia & salutifera Patris cœlestis atq; voluntatis eius cognitione mentes nostras illuminet, vt inoffenso pede per huius mundi tenebras ambulemus, & neq; exemplo eius prauo, neq; superstitionum aut errorum laqueis irretiamur. Qui ista quærunt, procul dubio quod quærunt inuenient. At qui carnalibus inten ti sunt, spe sua frustrabuntur. At quæ nostri seculi calamitas est, plerisq; cœlestia & æterna bona sor- dent, aut saltem ea non magni faciunt, nisi ea cum huius seculi bonis coniuncta esse videant. Postre- mò, vbi visum iste recepit, Christum cum alijs sequitur, & Deum glorificat. Vnde rursus apparet, eum maiora adhuc de Christo sperauisse, et nō tā corpore quàm mente fuisse illuminatū. Neq; hic præ terire debemus, quòd etsi mendicationi assueuisset, non tamen miraculo in sua persona ædito adquę stum abutitur, vt à turba populi, qui frequentissimus aderat, stipē & ampliora vitæ subsidia flagi- tet: quod hodie plurimi facere solet, qui se aliquo Dei beneficio insolito nobilitatos esse sentiunt. Sed noster hic vnum Christum animo suo cogitat, hunc vnum loquitur, et prioris vitae pertæsus ex sectatorum eius numero esse cupit: adhæc Deum publice prædicat, & huic gratias agit.
units.tr: Yet lest anyone conceive from this some security in his mind, and under the pretext of faith seek idleness, it will not be unprofitable to see what sort of man this blind man was in all these matters, and what he did after being so greatly benefited. Here first occurs what Mark writes, that he leapt up when he heard that he was being called by Christ, and that, leaving even his cloak, he hastened to him. This is a most evident argument of a faith that is eager and burning with true zeal; and by his example we are admonished that those who want to obtain salvation in Christ ought to break off every delay, and leave far behind their back the old man with all those things which seem pleasant or splendid to him: such as confidence in one's own righteousness, wealth, honours, dignities, the wisdom of the flesh, and whatever else is of this kind. All these are most aptly foreshadowed by the cloak of this beggar. For they are in truth of no worth, since they can neither protect nor govern us in the sight and judgement of God, nor are they stable and firm, but for the most part forsake us just when we hoped for something great from them. Next, as we said a little before, when he was asked what he sought, he sought nothing other than that he might receive his sight. By this example we are again admonished that we too should seek in Christ nothing other than what pertains to eternal salvation; and above all, that he, who is the light of the world, should enlighten our minds with the heavenly wisdom and the saving knowledge of the heavenly Father and of his will, so that we may walk through the darkness of this world with an unstumbling foot, and be entangled neither in his wicked example nor in the snares of superstitions or errors. Those who seek these things will without doubt find what they seek. But those who are intent on carnal things will be disappointed in their hope. And it is a calamity of our age that most people despise heavenly and eternal goods, or at least do not esteem them greatly unless they see them joined with the goods of this age. Finally, when he has received his sight, he follows Christ with the others and glorifies God. From this again it appears that he hoped for still greater things from Christ, and that he was illumined not so much in body as in mind. Nor ought we to pass over the fact that, although he had been accustomed to begging, he did not take advantage of the miracle wrought in his own person to beg alms and greater means of living from the crowd of people, who were present in great numbers; which very many today are wont to do, when they feel that they have been ennobled by some unusual benefit of God. But this man of ours thinks of Christ alone in his mind, speaks of him alone, and, weary of his former life, desires to be counted among his followers; moreover, he publicly proclaims God and gives thanks to him.

units.la: His præclarum miraculi huius effectum subiicit Lucas, qui ad populum redundauit. Hic enim cum illud vidisset, ipse etiam Deo laudem tribuit. Agnoscunt ergo in miraculis Christi virtute humana maiorem, quam nos quoq; in illis agnoscere debemus. Et quidem laude digni sunt, qui illud serio fecerunt. At ex sequenti narratione patebit, multos nimiùm leues & inconstantes fuisse, qui non multò post vel ab eo turpiter defecerunt, vel necis quoq; eius fuerunt authores. Quod exemplū obseruasse prodest, vt ne mundo fidamus, etiamsi is magno conatu & impetu ad prouehendā gloriam Dei ferri videatur. Est enim ferè torrentis instar ille impetus, qui repentinis pluuijs auctus ruit, mox autem subsidens cursum sistit, quòd fonte largiori & perenni destituatur. Quod verò præcipuum totius historiæ caput est, discamus lucem veritatis & vitæ æternæ nobis in Christo exhibitā esse. Illũ ergo sequamur, & relictis mundi tenebris filios lucis agamus, vt olim cum eo qui lux vera est, in cælis vivamus & regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: To this Luke adds the remarkable effect of the miracle: it spread through the people. For when they saw it, they too gave praise to God. They therefore recognised in Christ's miracles a power greater than human, which we too ought to recognise in them. And indeed those who did this earnestly deserve praise. But from the following narrative it will become clear that many were far too light and inconstant, and that not long after some shamefully fell away from him, while others were even the authors of his death. It is useful to observe this example, so that we do not trust in the world, even when it seems to be carried forward with great effort and impetus to advance the glory of God. For that impetus is almost like a torrent, which swells with sudden rains and rushes on, but soon subsides and halts its course, because it lacks a larger and perennial spring. But the chief point of the whole history is that we learn that the light of truth and of eternal life has been shown to us in Christ. Let us therefore follow him, and leaving behind the darkness of the world, live as sons of light, so that one day, with him who is the true light, we may live and reign in heaven. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIII.

units.la: IEsus autem ingressus Iericho, transibat: Et ecce quidam qui nomine vocabatur Zacchæus, princeps publicanorum, & diues, studebatq; videre quis esset Iesus: nec poterat præ turba, quòd statura paruus esset. Itaq; præcurrens ascendit in sycomorum, vt eum videret: quoniam futurum erat, vt illac transfiret. Vt autem venit ad eum locum, suspiciens Iesus, eum vidit, & dixit ei: Zacchæe, festinans descende: hodie enim domi tuæ oportet me manere. Tum is festinans descendit, & excepit eum gaudens. Et omnes cùm hoc vidissent, murmurabant, dicentes eum ingressum esse ad hominem peccatorem, vt ibi diuersaretur. Adstans autem Zacchæus dixit Domino: Ecce dimidium bonorum meorum Domine do pauperibus: & si quid cuiquam per calumniam eripui, reddo quadruplum. Dixit autem ei Iesus: Hodie salus domui huic contigit, eò quòd ipse quoque filius Abrahami est. Venit enim Filius hominis, vt quærat & seruet quod perierat.
units.tr: And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, who was the chief among the tax collectors, and he was rich. He sought to see who Jesus was, but could not for the crowd, because he was little of stature. So he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was to pass that way. When Jesus came to that place, he looked up, saw him, and said to him: "Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must stay at your house." So he hurried down and received him joyfully. And when all saw this, they murmured, saying that he had gone in to be the guest of a sinful man. But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: "Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore it fourfold." Then Jesus said to him: "Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost."

units.la: VONIAM Dei Filius, Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus ideo in mundum venit, vt qui non vident per ipsum illuminati videant: frequenter tam verbo quàm miraculis docet, qua ratione nos lucis & salutis, quæ in ipso habentur, participes fieri possimus. Et verbo quidem ostendit, fidem medium illud esse, quo ipsum cum suis donis omnibus apprehendimus: illud ipsum autem factis suis miraculosis probat. Quoties enim vel peccata aliquibus remittit, vel morbis quibuscunque medetur, semper solius fidei meminit, & hac illos seruari testatur. Exemplū eius rei nuper in cæci Hierichuntini historia vidimus. Vt autem ille, cùm inops & mendicus esset, Christi virtute atque beneficio visum recepit: ita nunc producitur Zacchæus, homo diues et opulentus, cuius mentem pari gratia ille illuminat & efficaciter trahit, vt ipsum communem omnis loci & ordinis hominum Seruatorem esse sciremus, adhæc vnam & eandem omnibus hominibus rationem propositam esse, qua ipsum & salutem in ipso amplectantur. Estq; hæc historia admodum memorabilis & consideratu dignissima. Nam simul et gratuitæ misericordiæ exemplum habet, qua Deus indignos quoque vocat, & pœnitentiæ veræ typum proponit, quo docemur, quid eos deceat, qui ex gratia & per fidem iustificati atque seruati sunt.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, came into the world so that those who do not see might be enlightened through him and see, he teaches often, both by word and by miracles, the way in which we may come to share in the light and salvation that are in him. By his word he shows that faith is the means by which we lay hold of him with all his gifts, and he confirms this by his miraculous deeds. For whenever he forgives sins to anyone or heals any sickness, he always mentions faith alone and testifies that they are saved by it. We saw an example of this recently in the story of the blind man of Jericho. As that man, though poor and a beggar, received his sight through the power and kindness of Christ, so now Zacchaeus is brought forward, a rich and wealthy man, whose mind Christ enlightens and draws effectually by the same grace. Thus we learn that he is the common Saviour of every place and rank of men, and that there is one and the same way set before all men by which they may embrace him and salvation in him. This story is very memorable and most worthy of consideration. For it offers an example of free mercy, by which God calls even the unworthy, and it sets before us a figure of true repentance, by which we are taught what befits those who have been justified and saved by grace and through faith.

units.la: Rursus autem à præcipuæ personæ descriptione Lucas orditur, quis nimirum fuerit ille, de quo hic agitur, & quid fecerit. Quoad primum, nomen illi fuit Zacchæus, & princeps publicanorum fuit, atq; admodum diues. Dum verò publicanorum principem siue magistrum dicit, vno verbo complectitur quicquid in aliquius infamiam dici poterat. Publicanos enim fuisse alibi diximus, qui telonia & vectigalia, sive quæcunq; huius generis ad Rempub. pertinet, certa aliqua pecuniæ summa redimebat, & illis in suam potestatem redactis, populū exactionibus insolitis atq; iniquis grauabant. Itaq; etsi per se non malum neq; impium opus sit, vectigalia exigere, isti tamen nō temere apud omnes pessime audiebant, quòd in populum Dei non minus iniustitia & iniquitate, quàm inhumanitate inexcusabili peccarent. Inter hos autem princeps quidam aut antesignanus fuit Zacchæus noster, propter impo sturas et crudelitatem insatiabilem adeò infamis, ut omnes fremāt et murmurēt, quando Christum videt ad illum ex itinere diuertere. Adhæc dives fuit: ex eo nimirū genere hominum, de quibus supra Christus admonuit, quòd magna cum difficultate in Regnum Dei ingrediantur. Et talem quidem hominem Christus sibi nunc deligit, ne de sua salute diuites facilè desperent, & ut suam misericordiam gratuitam nobis commendet, quæ salutis nostræ firmissima basis est.
units.tr: Luke begins again with a description of the principal person: who he was, namely the one of whom this is told, and what he did. As to the first, his name was Zacchaeus; he was chief of the tax collectors and very rich. By calling him the chief or master of the tax collectors, he sums up in one word whatever could be said to his discredit. We have said elsewhere that the tax collectors were those who bought for a fixed sum of money the tolls and customs duties, and whatever else of this kind belongs to the state. Once these had come into their power, they burdened the people with unusual and unjust exactions. So although collecting taxes is not in itself an evil or wicked work, these men were not without cause very ill spoken of by all, since they sinned against the people of God no less by injustice and iniquity than by inexcusable inhumanity. Among these men our Zacchaeus was a chief or leader, so notorious for his frauds and insatiable cruelty that all grumbled and murmured when they saw Christ turn aside to his house on the way. Besides, he was rich, one of that class of men of whom Christ above warned that they enter the kingdom of God with great difficulty. Christ now chooses such a man, so that the rich should not easily despair of their salvation, and so that he might commend to us his free mercy, which is the most secure foundation of our salvation.

units.la: Videamus igitur alterū, quod in eius descriptione annotatur, quid nimirū tunc fecerit, quando illum tanta gratia Dominus dignatus est. Studebat videre Iesum, de quo nimirum multa audierat singularis gratiæ & misericordiæ argumenta. Sive autem ad illud vel curiositas quædam prophana mouerit, qualem Herodi postea Lucas adscribet, sive fides, meritū tamen salutis nostræ hic nullum poterit statui. Quia enim nemo ad Christum venit, nisi Pater eum traxerit, illum quoq; non sine peculiari misericordia excitatū & instigatum fuisse oportet, ut id faceret, quod hic narratur. Nam cum statura pusillus esset, neq; Christum facile videret in confertissima hominū vndiq; circumfusorum frequentia, in arborem Sycomoreā ascendit, quæ ad eam viam fuerat plantata, per quā Christus erat transiturus. Est hoc nō vulgaris, sed ingentis et ardentissimi desiderij argumentum. Quia enim diuites & qui in publica dignitate constituti sunt, præ alijs eminere cupiunt, et ideo sese cum gratuitatis specie venditant, vehemens in Zacchæi animo studium exarserit oportet, quod virum opulentissimū & eius ordinis, qui (ut ex Cicerone alibi docuimus) apud Romanos honoratissimus erat, principem mouit, ut in tanta hominū tam peregrinorum quàm ciuium multitudine siue frequentia arborem conscenderet. Quid enim magis alienum ab eo, qui sibi maiorem, quàm vulgus hominū habeat, dignitatem & existimationē vendicat? Nec temere iistud ab Euangelista narratur. Eo enim exemplo admonemur, quid omnes eos facere conueniat, qui Christum coràm intueri, & salutari eius cognitione illuminari cupiūt. Quoad in huius mundi turba versamur, & illum sequimur, neq; Christum recte videre, neq; salutem in illo exhibitam percipere possumus. Sumus enim omnes quoad corporis staturam, id est, quoad vires nostri ingenij aut animi inferiores, quàm ut ad tantorū mysteriorum contemplationem nos erigere possimus. Adhæc mundus iste tenebrarū plenus est, & nouas quotidie nobis nebulas offundit, quibus magis excæcatur mens nostra, ut nihil eorum prospiciat, quæ ad nostram salutem necessaria sunt. Præcurrere ergo oportet, et in altiore Christi consideracionem eniti. Quod tunc commodissimè fiet, si Ecclesiæ nos coniungamus, cuius typum in sycomoro quidam nō omnino inepte obseruarūt. Est enim arbor illa partim fico partim moro similis, & ideò ànonnullis ficus Ægyptia, ab alijs Ægyptia morus dicitur. Fœcunda autē est admodum & succulaūleo abundat. Fructus itaq; gignit quotannis ter quaterq; copiosos, sed qui non maturescunt, nisi ferro aut vnguibus scalpantur, & deinde vngantur oleo. Est hæc pulcherrima Ecclesiæ externæ imago, in qua vox verbi Dei sonat, & sacramenta rite administrantur. Habet ea in mundo speciem mori, id est, stulti populi, cum veræ et cælestis sapientiæ schola sit, et diuinæ gratiæ dulcedine abundet, quæ in promissionibus Dei & in toto cultu externo elucet. Et quia eandem Spiritus Dei vegetat, quouis tempore fructus fert: qui tamen ut ad maturitatē Deo gratam perueniant sectione & oleo opus habent, id est, disciplina seueriori, quam consolationes spiritus mitiget atq; temperent. Illa enim carnis petulantia & securitas corrigitur, quæ frequenter in pijs quoq; locum habet: his autem fides stabiliitur & confirmatur, ne tentationibus succumbat. Quotquot ergo in illa arbore, Ecclesia nimirum consistunt, & eius doctrinæ atq; Sacramentis communicant, ijs datur, ut Iesum Christum verè videant, & eius cognitione illuminati ex tenebris huius mundi emergant.
units.tr: Let us therefore consider the other thing noted in his description: what he did at the time when the Lord deigned to show him such great grace. He was eager to see Jesus, of whom he had surely heard many proofs of singular grace and mercy. Whether some profane curiosity moved him to this, such as Luke later ascribes to Herod, or faith, no merit of our salvation can be assigned to it here. For since no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him, Zacchaeus must also have been roused and urged by a special mercy to do what is here related. For since he was small of stature and could not easily see Christ among the very dense crowd of men pressing on every side, he climbed a sycamore tree which had been planted along the road by which Christ was to pass. This is a sign not of ordinary but of huge and most ardent desire. For since the rich and those set in public office wish to stand out above others, and therefore display themselves with a show of kindness, a vehement zeal must have blazed in Zacchaeus's mind, which moved a man so wealthy, and of that order which (as we have shown elsewhere from Cicero) was most honoured among the Romans, to climb a tree in the midst of such a crowd of men, both foreign and native. For what is more foreign to one who claims for himself a greater dignity and reputation than the common people have? Nor does the Evangelist relate this without reason. For by this example we are admonished what all those ought to do who desire to behold Christ face to face and to be enlightened by the saving knowledge of him. As long as we live in the throng of this world and follow it, we can neither see Christ rightly nor receive the salvation offered in him. For we are all, as to stature of body, that is, as to the powers of our intellect and mind, too low to lift ourselves to the contemplation of such great mysteries. Moreover, this world is full of darkness and daily pours new mists over us, by which our mind is blinded all the more, so that it sees nothing of what is necessary for our salvation. We must therefore run ahead and strive toward the higher contemplation of Christ. This will be done most conveniently if we join ourselves to the Church, whose type some have not altogether unsuitably noticed in the sycamore. For that tree is partly like a fig and partly like a mulberry, and so some call it the Egyptian fig and others the Egyptian mulberry. It is very fruitful and abounds in juice and oil. Thus it bears plentiful fruit three or four times a year, but the fruit does not ripen unless it is cut with iron or fingernails and then anointed with oil. This is a most beautiful image of the external Church, in which the voice of the Word of God sounds and the sacraments are duly administered. In the world it has the appearance of a mulberry, that is, of a foolish people, although it is a school of true and heavenly wisdom and abounds in the sweetness of divine grace, which shines forth in the promises of God and in the whole external worship. And because the Spirit of God quickens it, it bears fruit at all times; yet for that fruit to come to maturity pleasing to God, it needs cutting and oil, that is, a stricter discipline, which the consolations of the Spirit soften and temper. For by discipline the wantonness and complacency of the flesh are corrected, which often have a place even among the godly, and by consolation faith is strengthened and confirmed, lest it succumb to temptations. Therefore, all who remain in that tree, namely the Church, and share in its doctrine and sacraments, are given to see Jesus Christ truly, and, enlightened by the knowledge of him, to rise out of the darkness of this world.

units.la: Faciunt ad horum confirmationem, quæ de Christo sequuntur. Is enim vbi ad eum locum venit, sublatis oculis Zacchæum vidit, & mox visum compellat, atque festinanter descendere iubet: quia apud ipsum velit diuertere. Suspexit in arborem Christus, cui Zacchæus insidebat. Iam ante ergo illum mouerat. Nam vt Paulus ait, nouit Dominus qui sunt sui, & eosdem quando tempus est vocat, vt Ecclesiæ vera membra facti hospitium ipsi præbeant. Habemus autem in his gratuitæ vocationis exemplum, quo docemur, salutem nobis absq; nostro merito ex misericordia mera contingere. Quid enim in Zacchæo fuisse putabimus, quo tantum beneficium meruerit? Christi quidem videndi desiderio arsit, & desiderium istud mirifico studio declarauit: sed nisi hunc affectum illi Deus indidisset nunquam id facturus erat. Quid enim in Christo erat, quod hominem auarū, raptorem iniustum, crudelem mouere poterat, vt illum videre cuperet? Nisi ergo Deus suo spiritu animum eius hoc affectu incendisset, & ignorantem impulisset, nulla vnquam eum subiisset seria de Christo & salute in eo consequenda cogitatio. Itaque quicquid hic Christus facit, gratuitæ misericordiæ attribui debet. Quod autē de Zacchæo dicitur, ad omnes nos ex æquo pertinet. Nam etiamsi non omnes publicani & peregrinæ tyrannidis contra fratres & cives nostros ministri simus, peccatores tamen sumus, & vitiorum illecebris irretiti nihil possumus ex nobis ipsis, quod nos ad Christum & salutem, quæ in illo habetur, perducat. Itaque nisi nos sua gratia Deus præueniat, & ipse nos quærat, summque nobis offerat commercium, iam toti perijmus. At non deest ille nobis, quin hæc omnia sedulò & optima fide præstet: quod alibi Adami, Abrahami, Dauidis & multorum aliorum exemplis docuimus, qui in Euangelica historia describuntur: quibus Zacchæum hunc merito inter primos adnumerauerit. Nemo igitur hypocritas iustitiarios audiat, qui nostri arbitrij libertatem & vires eo vsque extollunt, vt nos aut saltem nostris operibus mereri, aut salutem nosipsos ad gratiam excipiendam præparare contendant. Quomodo enim cœlos merebūtur qui æterno supplicio digni sunt? Aut quæ animi præparatio apud eos esse potest, qui ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sunt, & quorum cogitationes ab ineunte ætate prauæ sunt?
units.tr: What follows about Christ also serves to confirm these points. When he came to that place, he looked up, saw Zacchaeus, and at once addressed him, bidding him come down quickly, because he wished to stay at his house. Christ looked up at the tree in which Zacchaeus was sitting, so he had already stirred him up beforehand. As Paul says, the Lord knows who are his, and calls them when the time comes, so that, having become true members of the Church, they may offer him hospitality. In this we have an example of free calling, by which we are taught that salvation comes to us, without any merit of ours, from sheer mercy. For what can we suppose there was in Zacchaeus that earned so great a favour? He did burn with desire to see Christ, and he showed that desire with remarkable eagerness. But unless God had implanted this feeling in him, he would never have done so. For what was there in Christ that could move a greedy man, an unjust plunderer and a cruel man, to desire to see him? Unless God had kindled his mind with this feeling by his Spirit, and driven him on though he did not know it, no serious thought about Christ and about gaining salvation in him would ever have entered his mind. Therefore whatever Christ does here must be ascribed to free mercy. What is said of Zacchaeus applies equally to all of us. For even if we are not all tax-collectors and agents of foreign tyranny against our brothers and fellow citizens, we are still sinners, and entangled in the allurements of vice we can do nothing of ourselves that might lead us to Christ and to the salvation found in him. So unless God anticipates us with his grace, seeks us himself, and offers us the greatest fellowship, we are already utterly lost. But he is not lacking to us; he performs all these things diligently and in perfect faithfulness, as we have shown elsewhere by the examples of Adam, Abraham, David and many others who are described in the gospel history, among whom he has rightly numbered this Zacchaeus among the first. Let no one therefore listen to the hypocritical advocates of righteousness, who so exalt the freedom and powers of our will that they contend we merit by our works, or at least prepare ourselves for salvation so as to receive grace. For how could those who deserve eternal punishment merit heaven? Or what preparation of mind can there be in those who are not even fit to think, and whose thoughts have been depraved from early youth?

units.la: Prodest autem de his sæpe sermonem fieri, imò vt gratuitæ vocationis atque remissionis peccatorum doctrina in Ecclesijs pura & syncera constanter retineatur, multas ob causas nō modo vtile, verumetiam necessarium est. Primum, vt suus honos Christo Iesu habeatur, qui solus hoc testimonium meruit, quòd sit dilectus ille Filius, in quo Pater nobis placatus est. At quomodo honorem hunc illi reliquent integrū, qui peccata non propter eius solius meritū nobis ex gratia, sed propter nostra merita siue satisfactiones remitti contendunt? Deinde gratuitam remissionem doceri necesse est, vt conscientiæ certam atq; firmā consolationem habeant, quā sese in tentationibus sustineant. Illam enim habere non poterunt, sed ad nostram dignitatem aut nostra opera respiciant: quæ aut nulla sunt, aut manca atque vitiosa. Quod Paulus obseruans dicebat. Si ij qui ex Lege sunt, hæredes sunt, id est, si Regni cœlestis & salutis æternæ hæreditatem ij soli adibunt, qui Legi satisfaciunt: inanis facta est fides, & inanis reddita est promissio. Cuius dicti ratio est, quòd promissiones irritæ et nullæ sunt, quæcunq; conditionem coniunctam habent impossibilem præstitu. Exempli gratia: Quis non ridiculam & nullam promissionem dixerit, si cui aureos mille pollicearis ea conditione, vt vno die totū orbem terrarum obambulet, aut mare totum exhauriat? At legem operibus nostris implere, aut illi satisfacere, nō magis possibile est, quam maria omnia exhaurire, aut omnes terras vno die percurrere. Ni si ergo à remissionis peccatorum doctrina omnem nostrorum meritorum aut satisfactionum mentionem procul remoueas, promissiones omnes irritas & inutiles fecisti. Et ideo Paulus eodē loco infert: Propterea ex fide est hæreditas, id est, salus & hæreditas Regni cœlorum ad eos solos pertinet, qui Christum Iesum & in hoc nobis factam gratiam fide vera amplectuntur, vt sit per gratiam, & vt firma sit promissio toti semini, &c. Vnde colligitur eos humanæ salutis fundamenta conuellere, qui gratuitam peccatorum remissionem negant. Præterea vt illam firmiter teneamus oportet, siquidem Deum verè inuocare & cultum gratum illi præstare volumus. Qui enim de illius gratia dubitant, ij illum inuocare non possunt, cùm autem odisse: & conspectum eius fugere soleant, sicuti in Caini & Iudæ similiumq; exemplis est videre. Et huc illud Dauidis pertinet: Apud te clementia est, & propterea timeris. Id est, ideo te reuerenter colunt & inuocant homines, quia peccatis clementer & gratuita misericordia soles ignoscere. Est ergo turpissima & plus quàm sycophantica eorum calumnia, qui gratiæ prædicatione omnem Dei cultum vnà cum precibus & bonis operibus aboleri clamant: cùm nemo Deum ex animo & constanti fide inuocare, nemo eundem colere & illi verè obedire possit, nisi qui de eius gratuita misericordia certus fuerit.
units.tr: It is useful, and for many reasons not merely useful but necessary, to speak often about these matters, so that the teaching of free calling and the remission of sins may be constantly maintained in the Churches, pure and sincere. First, so that Christ Jesus may have his due honour, he who alone has earned this testimony, that he is the beloved Son in whom the Father is reconciled to us. But how will those leave this honour to him whole, who contend that sins are forgiven us by grace not for his merit alone, but for our merits or satisfactions? Next, free remission must be taught so that consciences may have a certain and firm consolation by which they can sustain themselves in temptations. For they cannot have that if they look to their own worthiness or to their works, which are either nothing or defective and faulty. Paul, observing this, said: "If those who are of the Law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise made of no effect" (Rom. 4:14). That is, if only those who satisfy the Law take up the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and eternal salvation, then faith is made empty and the promise void. The reason for this saying is that promises are null and void whenever they carry a condition attached that cannot be performed. For example, who would not call it a ridiculous and empty promise if you promised someone a thousand gold coins on condition that he walk round the whole earth in one day, or drain the whole sea? But to fulfil the law by our works, or to satisfy it, is no more possible than to drain all the seas or to run through all the lands in one day. Unless, then, you remove far from the doctrine of the remission of sins every mention of our merits or satisfactions, you have made all the promises void and useless. And so Paul infers in the same place: "Therefore the inheritance is of faith"; that is, salvation and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven belong only to those who embrace with true faith Christ Jesus and the grace given us in him, so that it is by grace, and so that the promise may be firm to the whole seed, etc. Hence it follows that those who deny the free forgiveness of sins overturn the foundations of human salvation. Moreover, we must hold this firmly if we wish to call upon God truly and render him acceptable worship. For those who doubt his grace cannot call upon him; rather they hate him and are accustomed to flee his sight, as can be seen in the examples of Cain and Judas and others like them. To this belongs also the saying of David: "With you is forgiveness, and therefore you are feared" (Ps. 130:4). That is, men therefore reverently worship and call upon you, because you are accustomed to pardon sins mercifully and by free mercy. The calumny of those is therefore most shameful and more than sycophantic, who cry out that by preaching grace all worship of God is abolished, along with prayers and good works; when no one can call upon God from the heart and with steadfast faith, no one can worship him and truly obey him, unless he is certain of his free mercy.

units.la: Caeterùm conuincuntur illi exemplo Zacchæi, quem illius fidutia non in otio ignauo atque secuto decinuit, sed vt ea faceret excitauit, quæ hodie vix vnquam abijs quoq; impetrauerîs, qui omnem salutem à suorû operum meritis pendere serió credunt. Inter ea primum est, quod audita Christi vocatione festinanter ex arbore descendit. Deinde excipit ad se diuertentem cum gaudio, neq; da sumptibus, qui non parui faciendi erant, neq; alijs molestijs conqueritur.
