Nam vt alias monuimus, non vulgare aut contemnendum officium fuit, tunc temporis Christum cum numerosissimo comitatu Hierosolymam contendentem excipere: vt iam de eo nihil dicam, quòd id cum inuidia & odio coniunctum erat, propter Sacerdotes & Pharisæos, qui illum extinctum volebant, & publica infamia excommunicationis eos multabat, qui fidem in ipsum profitebantur. Quod ergo homo auarus, qui hucusque quæstui iniusto & iniquo deditus populum vniuersum exactionibus extraordinarijs grauauit, Christum cum suis tam benignè & cum gaudij magni significatione (quam non fictam fuisse, ex ijs quæ sequuntur patebit) excipit, id certè conuersionis verae indicium est, quæ tam animum quàm mores atque studia eius mutauit.
units.tr: Moreover, those people are refuted by the example of Zacchaeus, whose trust in Christ did not keep him in lazy and careless idleness, but stirred him up to do those things which today you could hardly ever obtain even from those who seriously believe that all salvation depends on the merits of their works. Among these, first, when he heard Christ's call he hurried down from the tree. Then he received him joyfully into his house, and complained neither about the expense, which was not small, nor about other troubles. For, as we have noted elsewhere, it was no common or contemptible duty at that time to receive Christ, who was making for Jerusalem with a very large company; to say nothing of the fact that this was joined with envy and hatred, because of the priests and Pharisees, who wanted him dead, and who punished with public disgrace and excommunication those who professed faith in him. That this greedy man, who until now, given over to unjust and unfair gain, had burdened the whole people with extraordinary exactions, receives Christ and his company so kindly and with such a sign of great joy (that this joy was not feigned will be clear from what follows), this is certainly a sign of true conversion, which has changed his mind no less than his morals and pursuits.

units.la: Sequuntur enim opera eximia, quibus id testatur. Nam à nemine requisitus aut coactus Christo dicit: Ecce dimidium bonorum meorum Domine, do pauperibus: & si quid cuipiam per calumniam rapui, reddo quadruplum. Primò beneficentiam in pauperes vouet, quibus dimidium suarum facultatum velit distribuere. Et diserte de suis bonis loquitur, ne quis eum aliena & iniquis artibus partaipsum cum Deo partiri velle putet: vt hodie faciunt vsurarij, milites & quicunque ex alieno ditescunt. Sciebat enim Zacchæus Deo illud minimè probari, qui manus sanguine plenas detestatur, & pretium canis aut meretricis sibi offerri non vult. Obseruabis autem, quòd non omnia sua vendit Zacchæus, & in pauperes distribuit (quod à diuite illo & primate nuper dominus requisiuit) sed dimidiam modò illorum, quæ possidebat, partem: & tamen hoc officium Christus sibi gratum & acceptum habet. Ex eo igitur apparet, noluisse eum vniuersali præcepto omnes obstringere, sed (vt illic diximus) ad confidentem iuuenis illius animum respexisse, vt morbum in eo latentem argueret. Itaque si fide in Christum donati sumus, & charitate non simulata ducamur, in eleemosynis faciendis quisque sibi ipsi legem dare poterit, quàm multum ex suis facultatibus debeat pauperibus decidere. Et de hoc Paulus eleganter disserit, ad Corinthios scribens: Etenim si prius adsit promptus animus, is acceptus est pro eo quod habet aliquis, non pro eo quod non habet. Non enim vt alijs relaxatio fit, vobis autem oppressio: sed pari conditione hoc tempore vestra abundantia suppleat illorum defectum, &c. Quae verba satis docent, nimium temerarios esse, qui hodie omnibus leges ex suo capite praescribunt, quantum quisque dare, vel etiam vt omnibus relictis vitae genus temere mutare debeat.
units.tr: What follows are remarkable deeds by which he bears witness to this. For, without being asked or compelled by anyone, he says to Christ: "Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). First, he vows beneficence to the poor, to whom he wishes to distribute half of his means. He speaks expressly of his own goods, lest anyone think he wants to share with God what was gained from others' property and by unjust arts, as usurers, soldiers and all who grow rich at others' expense do today. For Zacchaeus knew that God by no means approves of this, since God detests hands full of blood and does not wish the price of a dog or a harlot to be offered to him. You will observe, however, that Zacchaeus does not sell all his goods and distribute them to the poor (which the Lord recently asked of that rich ruler), but only half of what he possessed; and yet Christ counts this duty pleasing and acceptable to himself. From this it is clear that he did not wish to bind all people by a universal precept, but (as we said there) looked to the over-confident mind of that young man, so as to expose the disease hidden in him. Therefore, if we have been given faith in Christ and are led by unfeigned love, each person in giving alms can set for himself a rule as to how much of his means he ought to give to the poor. Paul discusses this elegantly, writing to the Corinthians: "For if the willing mind is there first, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. For it is not that others should be relieved and you burdened, but by equal measure your abundance at this time should supply their want, etc." (2 Cor. 8:12–14). These words teach sufficiently that those are far too rash who today prescribe laws to everyone from their own head, how much each should give, or even that everyone should rashly abandon everything and change his way of life.

units.la: Porrò quia nemini dubium erat, Zacchæum opes suas pro communi publicanorum more modis iniquissimis auxisse, restitutionem pollicetur, & quidem quadruplam. Ita verò non obiter modò peccatum suum, sed eius quoque magnitudinem confitetur, adeoque docet, quo loco habeat ea, quæ hucusque contra iustitiam & charitatis leges designauerit. Nam in Lege fures quæ furto abstulerant, vel dupla vel quadrupla restituere iubebantur, pro furti ratione. Itaque furti seipsum accusat, neque se eleemosynis illis, quas liberalissimè faciebat, Deo gratum officium facere putat, nisi cuique quod suum est reddat, quoad illud fieri possit. Debebant ad hunc modum de suis etiam artibus iudicare vsurarij & fæneratores, monopolæ, sanguinarij milites, raptores, hæredipetæ, & quicunque alienas res vel violenter vel sub iuris praetextu rapiunt. Possunt quidem sese apud homines excusare, & propter opes ingentes in pretio habentur, sed in Dei conspectu fures sunt, neque eis illorum eleemosynas siue preces ratas habebit, nisi eius verbo mandatam restitutionem faciant. Docet hoc ipse Dominus, quando per Micheam omnes istorum hominum cultus reijciens, clamat: Audite virgam, & eum qui eam decernit: Annon adhuc ignis in domo impij? thesaurus nimirum iniustus? Et Epha perexiguum, ira plenum est? Num iustificabo cum bilance iniqua, & cum sacculo, in quo sunt lapides dolosi? Et apud Ezechielem inter poenitentiae opera restitutio eorum numeratur, quae per iniustitiam aliis erepta sunt. Vide Ezechielem Capite decimo octauo.
units.tr: Moreover, since no one doubted that Zacchaeus had increased his wealth by the most unjust means, as publicans commonly did, he promises restitution, and indeed fourfold. In doing so he confesses not only his sin in passing but also its magnitude, and he shows what place he gives to the things he has hitherto done against the laws of justice and love. For under the Law, thieves were ordered to restore what they had taken by theft, either double or fourfold, according to the nature of the theft. Zacchaeus therefore accuses himself of theft. He does not think that by those alms, which he gave most generously, he performs a service pleasing to God, unless he restores to each what is his, so far as that can be done. In the same way, usurers and moneylenders, monopolists, bloodthirsty soldiers, plunderers, fortune-hunters, and all who seize other people's goods either by violence or under the pretext of law, ought to judge their own practices. They may excuse themselves before men, and on account of their great wealth they may be held in esteem, but in the sight of God they are thieves, and he will not accept their alms or prayers unless they make restitution as his Word commands. The Lord himself teaches this when, through Micah, he rejects all the worship of such men and cries out: "Hear the rod, and him who appointed it. Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, and an unjust treasure? And a scant measure, full of wrath? Shall I justify the one with the false balance, and with the bag in which are deceitful weights?" And in Ezekiel, restoration of what has been taken from others by injustice is counted among the works of repentance. See Ezekiel chapter 18.

units.la: Porrò admonemur Zachæi exemplo, fidem in Christum minimè otiosam esse, & (quod paulò ante etiam monuimus) bona opera nequaquam ab ijs damnari, qui nos absque nostro merito, gratis, per solam fidem iustificari & seruari docent. Est enim fides arbor illa bona, qua vt in Dei bonitate radices agit, & huic vni nititur: ita Spiritus Sancti virtute vegetatur, vt omni tempore fructus ferat. Quo Christus respiciens dicebat: Qui manet in me, & ego in eo, hic fert fructum multum. Fieri enim non potest, vt in illis otiosus sit Spiritus Christi, quos ipse ex verbi æterni semine in Filios Dei regenuit. Ideo Iacobus fidem mortuam dicebat eam, quæ nullis operibus bonis conspicua est. Vt autem homo mortuus non nisi per Catachresim homo dicitur, cum revera nihil aliud quàm cadauer sit, mox à vermibus & putredine consumendum: ita fidei quidem vocabulum quibusdam abusiuè tribuitur, qui sola eius inani atque otiosa professione superbiunt. Quapropter idem Iacobus in eodem loco subijcit: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi ex operibus meis fidem meam. Et Christus iubet, vt opera nostra luceant in hominum conspectu, vt illorum contemplatione plures alij ad glorificandum Patrem nostrum qui in cælis est, excitentur. Procul ergo ab Ecclesiæ societate arcendi sunt, qui fidem quidem ore profitentur, factis autem negant: imo ita viuunt, vt propter ipsos nomen Christi male audiat.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of Zacchaeus admonishes us that faith in Christ is by no means idle, and (as we said a little earlier) that good works are in no way condemned by those who teach that we are justified and saved freely, by faith alone, without our merit. For faith is that good tree, which takes root in the goodness of God and rests wholly upon him, and it is so quickened by the power of the Holy Spirit that it bears fruit at all times. Looking to this, Christ said: "He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit." For it cannot be that the Spirit of Christ is idle in those whom he has regenerated as sons of God from the seed of the eternal Word. Therefore James called dead that faith which is not evident by any good works. Just as a dead man is called a man only by catachresis, since in truth he is nothing but a corpse, soon to be consumed by worms and rot, so the name of faith is misapplied to some who boast only of its empty and idle profession. For this reason James adds in the same place: "Show me your faith from your works, and I will show you my faith from my works." And Christ commands that our works shine before the eyes of men, so that many others, seeing them, may be stirred to glorify our Father who is in heaven. Those, therefore, who profess faith with their mouths but deny it by their deeds must be kept far from the fellowship of the Church; indeed, they so live that the name of Christ is ill spoken of on their account.

units.la: At simul videre oportet, quibus operibus fidem suam Zachæus testatus sit. Num sacrificijs? num donarijs in templo suspensis? num vestis mutatione, & habitu ad hypocrisim composito? num peregrinationibus? num ieiunijs status & electitio ciborum discrimine? Nihil horum audimus. Sed obedientia indicatur, qua Christum vocantem absque mora secutus est. Sequitur hanc gaudium nouum & singularis animi alacritas, quæ conuersionem totius hominis peperit, vt subitò ex auaro liberalis, ex raptore beneficus, ex lupo pastor fieret. Hæc ergo veræ fidei opera sunt, quibus sese conspicuam facit. Obedientia nimirum, quæ totum hominem Deo ita subijcit, vt procul relictis, imò calcatis etiam suis desiderijs atque rationibus, vtcunque splendidis & iustis in specie m, ab illius voluntate pendeat, nec quicquam bonum, sanctum, honestum, aut vtile putet, quàm quod cum illa videt conuenire. Est obedientiæ huic coniunctum gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Iustificati enim ex fide (inquit Paulus) pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: per quem etiam fide habemus aditum in gratiam hanc, per quam stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Quibus verbis Apostolus gaudium illud exprimit, quod ex reconciliationis cum Deo sensu atque fiducia in animis credentium nascitur, & cuius tanta virtus est, vt non solùm alacres & promptos faciat ad omne obsequium Deo præstandum, verumetiam omnes ærumnas atque afflictiones mitiget, quibus fideles adeò non succumbunt, vt illis etiam glorientur: eò quòd nihil illis suauius, nihil iucundius sit, quà pro Christia nomine aliquid facere aut pati. Hinc ergo totius hominis conuersio atque innouatio sequitur, quæ in charitatis operibus maximè elucet. Nam vt in vnum Christum fides recumbit: ita in eodem omnes eos, ceu fratres & eiusdem corporis membra complectitur, qui eundem Christum nobiscum profitentur: & ideo Paulus illam per dilectionem agere aut efficacem esse scribit. Agit autem dilectio inprimis erga eos, quos propter inopiam & miseram suam conditionem alieno auxilio opus habere videt. Ideo inter eius opera præcipua censentur, famelicis cibum & sitientibus potum præbere, nudos vestire, peregrinos hospitio excipere, captiuos consolari, ægrotantibus adesse, & si quæ alia sunt huius generis. Accedunt his quæ ad iustitiam pertinent, quæ vt suum vnicuique tribuit, ita restituit etiam quæ prius iniustè contra leges erepta fuerunt. Ita verò totum hominem fides inuouat, & hoc illud est, quod totius mundi oculos in Christi cultores conuertit: quia nō possunt videre prophani homines, vnde hæc tam subita mutatio procedat, eandem tamen improbare non possunt quicunque adhuc communi sensuduntur: sed velint nolinte, diuinam virtutem in illis cognoscere, quæ causa est, vt Deum glorificent, & sæpe ipsi quoque ea occasione ad Christum accedant. Istis ergo operibus studeant, qui pœnitentiam & conuersionem ad Deum profitentur. Quæ enim præter illam commenti sunt superstitiosi hominet, vanissima & nullius apud Deum momenti sunt, cùm non nisi hominum traditionibus nitantur.
units.tr: But at the same time we must consider by what works Zacchaeus bore witness to his faith. Was it by sacrifices? By gifts hung up in the temple? By a change of clothing and a manner of life put on for show? By pilgrimages? By fasts, fixed days, and distinctions of food? We hear none of these. What is indicated is obedience, by which he followed Christ calling him without delay. Following this came a new joy and a singular eagerness of mind, which brought about the conversion of his whole person, so that from a miser he suddenly became generous, from a plunderer a benefactor, and from a wolf a shepherd. These, then, are the works of true faith, by which it makes itself visible. This is obedience, which so subjects the whole man to God that, having put aside, indeed trampled underfoot, his own desires and reasonings, however splendid and just they may seem, he depends upon God's will and thinks nothing good, holy, honourable, or useful except what he sees agrees with that will. Joined to this obedience is joy in the Holy Spirit. For "being justified by faith," says Paul, "we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have by faith access into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God." In these words the Apostle expresses that joy which arises in the hearts of believers from a sense and confidence of reconciliation with God. Its power is such that it not only makes them eager and ready for all obedience to be rendered to God, but also softens all the troubles and afflictions by which the faithful are so far from being overcome that they even glory in them, because nothing is sweeter or more pleasing to them than to do or suffer something for the name of Christ. Hence follows the conversion and renewal of the whole man, which shines most clearly in works of love. For as faith rests on the one Christ, so in the same Christ it embraces all who confess the same Christ with us as brothers and members of the same body. Therefore Paul writes that faith works through love, or is effective through love. Love works especially toward those whom it sees, on account of their poverty and wretched condition, to need the help of others. Accordingly, among its chief works are counted giving food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving strangers into one's home, comforting prisoners, attending the sick, and whatever else is of this kind. To these are added the things that pertain to justice, which gives to each his own and also restores what was previously taken unjustly and contrary to the laws. In this way faith renews the whole man, and this is what turns the eyes of the whole world upon the worshippers of Christ. Profane men cannot see whence so sudden a change proceeds, yet they cannot disapprove of it, all those who are still guided by common sense; but whether they will or not, they recognise in these men a divine power, which is the cause that they glorify God, and often on this very occasion they themselves come to Christ. Let those therefore who profess repentance and conversion to God devote themselves to these works. For whatever superstitious men have invented apart from these is most vain and of no account before God, since it rests only on human traditions.

units.la: Cæterùm ijs, quæ inter Christum & Zacchæum sunt acta, Lucas ciuium Hierichuntinorum
units.tr: As for what took place between Christ and Zacchaeus, Luke, the citizens of Jericho

units.la: Cap. XIX.
units.tr: Chapter 19.

units.la: Vulgi de Christi & populi totius, qui illum sequebatur, iudicium de hoc eius facto interponit, sic scribens: Et omnes cum hoc vidissent murmurabant, dicentes eum ingressum esse ad hominem peccatorem, ut ibi diuerteret. Paucis verbis rem maximi momenti comprehendit. Nam displicuisse dicit Christi factum, non pauculis quibusdam, sed simul omnibus, qui ipsum in Zacchaei domum diuertisse videbant. Neque dubium est, eius rei famam subito per totam urbem diuulgatam fuisse, cum & Christus comitatum magnum haberet, & Zacchaeus omnibus notus esset. Ita vero displicuit omnibus, ut aperte etiam murmurarent, quod ad hominem peccatorem, id est, sceleratum & vitiis infamem diuertisset. Non dubitauerim ego passim de illo has aut similes his voces fuisse iactatas: En nouus iste veritatis doctor & poenitentiae praeco, quem multi suspiciunt, & solum dignum iudicant, qui audiatur. Quis vero ille sit, & quid de illo boni quisque sentire debeant, quis non videt? Si vitae innocentia tam illi cordi est, cur non cum optimis quibusque versatur? Cur quosuis in suum comitatum admitit? cur temere ad quosuis diuertit? Num in urbe populosa & celebri nemo illi dignus visus est, cuius hospitio uteretur, praeter Zacchaeum, publicanorum & raptorum antesignanum? Ergo ne ex illo liberationem & salutem sperabimus, qui cum iis colludit, qui peregrinae tyrannidis in populum Dei ministri sunt? Haec & multa alia huius generis tunc publice dicta fuisse non dubito, cum publicani (ut saepe diximus) omnibus inuisi & exosi essent. Neque illa ignorare potuit Christus, cui cordium quoque arcana patebant. At non movent illum maleuolorum aut imperitorum hominum sermones, quo minus officium suum faciat, quod ipsi mandauerat caelestis Pater: & suo exemplo omnes verbi ministros docet, qua constantia ipsi quoque per omnia scandala atque obstacula eluctari debeant, ne suo officio erga aliquem desint. Etenim ut cap. decimo quinto audiuimus, unius ouiculae salus tanti fieri debet, ut facile negligamus, quacunque nos ab eius inquisitione abstterrent.
units.tr: He records the judgment of the crowd, and of all the people who followed Christ, on this deed of his, writing thus: "And when all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had gone in to be a guest with a sinful man." In a few words he sums up a matter of the greatest weight. For he says that Christ's deed displeased not a few, but all together, who saw him lodging in Zacchaeus' house. There is no doubt that the report of this spread at once through the whole city, since Christ had a large company and Zacchaeus was known to everyone. And it displeased everyone so much that they openly murmured that he had lodged with a sinful man, that is, a wicked man infamous for his vices. I do not doubt that everywhere such words as these, or words like them, were bandied about concerning him: "Behold this new teacher of truth and herald of repentance, whom many admire and judge the only one worth hearing. But who he is, and what each man ought to think of him, who does not see? If innocence of life is so dear to him, why does he not keep company with the best people? Why does he admit anyone at all into his following? Why does he rashly lodge with whoever he pleases? In this populous and famous city, has no one seemed worthy to him to host him, except Zacchaeus, the foremost of tax collectors and robbers? Shall we then hope for deliverance and salvation from one who colludes with those who serve as ministers of a foreign tyranny over the people of God?" I do not doubt that these and many other such things were then said publicly, since the tax collectors (as we have often said) were hated and detested by all. Nor could Christ, to whom the secrets of hearts also lay open, be ignorant of them. But the talk of malicious or ignorant men does not move him from doing his duty, which the heavenly Father had laid upon him. By his example he teaches all ministers of the Word with what constancy they too must struggle through every scandal and obstacle, so that they do not fail in their duty toward anyone. For, as we heard in chapter fifteen, the salvation of one little sheep must be valued so highly that we easily disregard whatever frightens us away from seeking it.

units.la: Pulchre autem in hoc speculo adumbratur mundi infelicis ingenium. Qui inter Iudaeos Christum ferio & ex animo reciperent, paucissimi fuerunt: plerique autem Dei gratiam, quam ille offerebat, indignissime fastidierunt. Interim ijdem ferre no possunt, ut ab aliis recipiatur, & hi gratia ea fruantur, quam ipsi reijciebant. Solet hoc passim fieri, ut quam ipsi aspernantur gratiam Dei, homines impij, aliis quoque inuideant. Sunt eorum similes, qui cum morbo morosiores facti, videre non possunt, ut alij hilarius edant & bibant, cum ipsi cibum omnem fastidiant. Et vtinam hodie tales sola inuidia aut etiam linguae petulantia peccarent, a quibus autem abstinerent, quam fere, iis faciunt, qui Euangelium admittunt. Quanta vero sit eiusmodi hominum iniquitas, in istorum exemplo est videre. Diuerterat equidem ad Zacchaeum Christus, & non inuitatus sponte sibi eum hospitem delegerat. Nunc vero ea res tanti momenti erat, ut omnes murmurare, & totam urbem calumniis atque iniquis iudiciis impleri oportuerit? Atqui publicanorum conditio per se reprehensione nullam merebatur, cum vectigalia & telonia colligere peccatum non sit. At modum excedebat Zacchaeus, & multa hucusque contra ius & fas extorserat. Esto: num vero ideo Christus damnari debuit, priusquam constaret, quo animo & quare ad eum diuertisset? Cur non exitum totius negotij expectant, & interea iudicium suum suspendunt? Vel cur non Christi humanitatem potius praedicant, qui quosuis lucrifaciendi occasiones tam solicite quaerebat? Sed nihil videt hypocrisis veritatis odio excaecata: quae etiam causa est, quod hodie multi quosuis temere damnant, seq; hominum ineptissimos iniustissimosq; esse declarant, quando omnium optimi & sanctissimi haberi volunt.
units.tr: Moreover, in this mirror is pictured the nature of the unhappy world. Among the Jews very few received Christ gladly and from the heart, but most scornfully spurned the grace of God that he offered. Meanwhile these same men cannot bear that others should receive it, and that those others should enjoy the grace that they themselves rejected. This happens everywhere: wicked men, while they despise the grace of God, begrudge it to others as well. They are like those who, made more peevish by sickness, cannot bear that others eat and drink with more cheer, while they themselves loathe all food. And I wish that such men today sinned only by envy or by a wanton tongue; but they nearly all do the very things from which they ought to abstain, those who admit the Gospel. How great the wickedness of such men is can be seen in the example of these people. Christ had indeed lodged with Zacchaeus, and, uninvited, had of his own accord chosen him as his host. Was the matter now of such moment that everyone had to murmur, and the whole city had to be filled with slanders and unjust judgments? Yet the condition of tax collectors in itself deserved no reproach, since collecting tolls and taxes is not a sin. But Zacchaeus did exceed the bounds, and until then had extorted much contrary to right and law. Granted. But was Christ therefore bound to be condemned before it was established with what mind, and why, he had lodged with him? Why do they not await the outcome of the whole affair, and meanwhile suspend their judgment? Or why do they not rather proclaim the kindness of Christ, who so eagerly sought out every opportunity of winning people? But hypocrisy, blinded by hatred of the truth, sees nothing. This is also why many today rashly condemn whomever they please, and show themselves the most foolish and unjust of men, while they wish to be held the best and holiest of all.

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus, qui iniqua istorum iudicia nihil veritus fine & vsum sui facti infert, & Zacchaeo respondens ait: Hodie salus domui huic contigit, eo quod ipse quoque filius Abrahami est. Emphasim habet, quod de Zacchaeo loquens dicit: IPSE QVOQVE filius Abrahami est. Etsi enim ipsi respondeat, responsionem tamen astantibus, adeoq; omnibus accommodat, qui aduersus ipsum murmurabant, & sensus est: Vobis indignum videtur, quod ad hominem peccatore diuerterim. At qualiscunque hactenus fuerit, aut etiam nunc vobis esse videatur, tamen etiam ipse filius Abrahami est, non minus quam vos, qui titulum hunc vobis solis vendicatis. Filium autem Abrahami dicit propter fidem, qua eum apprehenderat, qui olim Abrahamo promissus fuit. Est enim Abraham omnium credentium pater, & eo nomine pater multarum gentium dicitur, sicuti Paulus ad Romanos docet. Ita vero simul causam salutis exprimit, ne quis hanc operibus tribuat, quibus Zacchæus post conuersionem istam claruit. Nec enim vllum opus est, quòd ex filijs iræ filios Abrahami faciat; sed hoc solius fidei effectum est, ideoq; Zacchæus non operibus salutem illam meruit, sed gratuita misericordia oblatam fide apprehendit. Sed de hac re iam sæpe multa diximus.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ, who, fearing nothing from these men's unjust judgments, carries his deed through to its purpose and answers Zacchaeus: "Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham." There is emphasis in what he says about Zacchaeus: HE TOO is a son of Abraham. For although he answers Zacchaeus, he nevertheless addresses the answer to the bystanders, and so to all who murmured against him, and the sense is this: "You think it unworthy that I lodged with a sinner. But whatever he has been until now, or even now seems to you, he too is a son of Abraham, no less than you, who claim this title for yourselves alone." He calls him a son of Abraham on account of the faith by which he had laid hold of him who was once promised to Abraham. For Abraham is the father of all believers, and on that account is called the father of many nations, as Paul teaches the Romans. At the same time he states the cause of salvation, so that no one attributes it to works, the works by which Zacchaeus shone after that conversion. For there is no work by which he makes sons of Abraham out of children of wrath; this is the effect of faith alone. Therefore Zacchaeus did not merit that salvation by works, but laid hold of it by faith, offered through free mercy. But we have already said much about this matter often enough.

units.la: Obseruabis autem, Christum salutis promissionem propter Zacchæum ad totam eius domum extendere. Hodie (inquit) salus domui huic contigit, eò quòd ipse quoq; filius Abrahami est. Num ergo (ais) fides aliena seruat aliquem? Minimè: nam notum est illud Prophetæ, Iustus fide sua viuet. Sed ad fœderis promissionem Christus respicit: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui. Et constat Abrahamum ex Dei mandato omnes, qui in sua familia erat, mares circuncidisse, vt fœderis gratia ad illos omnes extenderetur. Tanta est enim gratiæ & misericordiæ Dei amplitudo, vt non in patrefamilias subsistat, sed in omnes domesticos eius redundet. Quæ causa est, quòd supra Christus discipulos in ea domo manere iubet, in qua vel vnũ filium pacis inuenerint. Itaq; si Dei gratia spectemus, salus omnibus offertur, qui in domo sunt: quòd si verò quis ea non fruitur, id eius incredulitate & contumacia fit, qua salutẽ sibi liberaliter oblatã aspernatur. Ideo Apostoli quoq; familias totas baptizarunt, quarum capita ad fidem Christi conuertebantur. Quod eorum errore confutat, qui hodie infantibus Christianorũ baptismum negant, quos tamen Paulus sanctos dicere non est veritus, si alterum modò ex parentibus Christianum habeant. Est illorum audacia non iniqua modò, verumetiam cum sacrilegio coniuncta. Si enim Deus suam gratiam promiscuè toti familiæ offert, cur illi eos ab ea excludunt, qui eam minimè aspernantur, imò per ætatem ne aspernari quidem possunt? Atqui eandem (inquiunt) ne recipere quidem possunt. Id verò tu dicis ô bone: à nobis autẽ non sine ratione negatur, qui Christum scimus infantes in credentium numero habere. Neque nos moratur aliquid, quòd fidem profiteri non possunt. Plus enim promissioni Dei & gratiæ eius thesauro in exhausto, quàm professioni externæ tribuimus. Possunt enim nos fallere homines, cùm natura simulatores & mendaces sint: fallere autem non potest Deus, qui ipsa est Veritas.
units.tr: You will observe, moreover, that Christ extends the promise of salvation, made on account of Zacchaeus, to his whole household. "Today," he says, "salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham." Does someone else's faith (you ask) save anyone? By no means: for that saying of the Prophet is well known, "The just shall live by his faith." But Christ looks to the promise of the covenant: "I will be God to you and to your seed." And it is established that Abraham, by God's command, circumcised all the males who were in his household, so that the grace of the covenant might extend to all of them. For so great is the breadth of God's grace that it does not rest in the head of the family, but overflows upon all his household. This is why Christ above bids his disciples remain in that house in which they found even one son of peace. Therefore, if we regard God's grace, salvation is offered to all who are in the house; but if anyone does not enjoy it, this comes from his unbelief and obstinacy, by which he spurns the salvation liberally offered to him. For this reason the Apostles also baptized whole households, whose heads had been converted to faith in Christ. This refutes the error of those who today deny baptism to the infants of Christians, whom nevertheless Paul did not hesitate to call holy, if only one of the parents is a Christian. Their audacity is not only unjust but also joined with sacrilege. For if God offers his grace indiscriminately to the whole family, why do they exclude from it those who by no means spurn it, and who, by reason of their age, cannot even spurn it? "But," they say, "they cannot even receive it." Indeed you say so, good sir; but we deny it not without reason, since we know that Christ counts infants among the number of believers. Nor are we hindered by the fact that they cannot profess faith. For we give more weight to God's promise and to the treasury of his grace, which is not used up, than to an outward profession. Men can deceive us, since they are by nature pretenders and liars; but God, who is Truth itself, cannot deceive.

units.la: Porrò concludit totam hanc actionem Christus generali sententia, qua sæpe vsus est: Venit enim Filius hominis vt quærat & seruet quod perierat. Ita verò ab officio docet, nihil hic abs se factum esse, quo aliquis merito offendi debeat: adeoque proprio testimonio murmuratores istos conuincit: quasi diceret, Messiæ officium est perditos quærere & seruare. Quia ergo Zacchæum hunc ipsi inter perditos numeratis, cur mihi vitio vertitur, quòd eum quæro, vt conuersus seruetur? Est autem hæc propria Euangelij vox, quæ sola conscientijs territis consolationem solidam affert, & superstitiones confutat, quæ terrores gignunt, quibus infelices discrutiantur. Debet ergo ea semper in auribus nostris sonare: & cùm illam hodie nobis Deus subinde occinat, nos Zacchæum imitati, eius voluntati nos accomodemus per fidei obedientiam, vocantẽ sequamur cũ gaudio & alacritate, atq; relictis prioris vitæ studijs, toti innouemur. Ita nobis quoq; salus continget, & per fidem Abrahami filij facti Regnum cœleste possidebimus cum Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ concludes this whole action with a general saying, which he often used: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). In this way he teaches concerning his office that nothing has been done by him here for which anyone should rightly be offended; and so he convicts those murmurers by their own testimony, as if he were saying: "It is the office of the Messiah to seek and save the lost. Since you yourselves count this Zacchaeus among the lost, why is it held against me that I seek him, so that he may be saved by conversion?" This, moreover, is the proper voice of the Gospel, which alone brings solid consolation to frightened consciences and overturns those superstitions which produce terrors by which unhappy people are tormented. Therefore it ought always to sound in our ears; and since God still sings it to us from time to time, let us imitate Zacchaeus and accommodate ourselves to his will through obedient faith: let us follow the one calling us with joy and eagerness, and, leaving behind the pursuits of our former life, be renewed wholly. So salvation will also come to us, and through the faith of Abraham, having become sons, we shall possess the heavenly kingdom with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom is due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIII.

units.la: Hæc ipsis audientibus, pergens, dixit parabolam, eò quod esset prope Hierosolymam, & quod putarent fore, vt illico regnum Dei appareret. Dixit ergo: Homo quidam nobilis profectus est in regionem longinquam, vt acciperet sibi regnum, ac reuerteretur. Vocatis autem decem seruis suis, dedit eis decem minas, & dixit eis: Negotiamini donec veniam. Ciues autem eius oderant eum, miseruntq; legationem post eum, dicentes: Nolumus hunc regnare super nos.
units.tr: While they were still listening, he went on and told them a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God would appear at once. So he said: "A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself, and then to return. He called ten of his servants, gave them ten minas, and said to them, 'Do business until I come back.' But his citizens hated him, and they sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us.'"

units.la: Quemadmodũ æternus Dei Filius ideo in mundum venit & ex Maria virgine homo factus est, vt destructa per mortem & resurrectione suam diaboli tyrannide nos redimeret, vt Regnum æternũ tam sibi ipsi quàm in se credentibus obtineret: Ita de Regni sui mysterijs eiusq; maiestate cùm sæpe alias tum diligentissimè tunc disseruit, cùm mortis suæ horam iam instare sciret. Diligentiæ huius causæ fuerunt, quòd erroneas de Regno suo opiniones ex discipulorum animis eximenre voluit, & scandalo mederi, quod ex crucis & mortis suae ignominia exoriturũ esse sciebat. Et ad hoc argumentũ pertinent, quæcunq; deinceps vsq; ad finem cap. vigesimi primi commemoratur. Inter ea primum locum parabola ista obtinet, cuius primam partem modò recitauimus. Ea enim omnem Regni sui ratione summatim comprehendit: docens illud reuera cœleste esse, & proinde in hoc seculo non, vt huius mundi regna, maiestatem habere externam, sed per verbũ & Spiritum administrari: neq; crucè vnquam defore in hoc agentibus, eò quòd semper futuri sint, qui ipsum pro Rege suo nolent agnoscere: quorum rebellione & cotumacia nemo moueri debeat: se enim præfinito tempore venturum iudicem, vt feruis fidis promissa vitæ æternæ præmia retribuat, perfidos autẽ defectores atq; hostes sempiternis inferorum supplicijs multet. Est igitur parabola hæc dignissima, in cuius consideratione diligenter & crebrò versemur, ne mundi aduersus Christum et Euangelium eius tumultuantis exemplo offendamur, seduli autem & industrij simus in ijs, quæ nobis mandata sunt.
units.tr: Just as the eternal Son of God came into the world and was made man of the Virgin Mary so that, by destroying the tyranny of the devil through his death and resurrection, he might redeem us and obtain an everlasting kingdom both for himself and for those who believe in him, so he spoke about the mysteries of his kingdom and its majesty often on other occasions, but most carefully at this time, when he knew that the hour of his death was at hand. He had two reasons for such care. He wanted to remove the mistaken opinions about his kingdom from the minds of the disciples, and he wanted to remedy the offence that he knew would arise from the shame of his cross and death. The passage that follows, up to the end of chapter twenty-one, also belongs to this theme. Among these passages, this parable holds the first place, and I have just recited its first part. For it sums up the whole plan of his kingdom in brief, teaching that the kingdom is truly heavenly, and therefore in this age it does not have the external majesty of earthly kingdoms, but is administered through the Word and the Spirit. It teaches that those who act in this way will never lack a cross, because there will always be people who refuse to acknowledge him as their King. No one should be moved by their rebellion and obstinacy, for at a set time he will come as judge, to repay the faithful servants with the promised rewards of eternal life, and to punish the faithless deserters and enemies with everlasting torments of hell. This parable, therefore, is most worthy of our attention. We should consider it diligently and often, so that we are not offended by the example of the world raging against Christ and his Gospel, but are zealous and diligent in the tasks entrusted to us.

units.la: Cæterum hic quoq; Lucas occasionem huius actionis præmittit, vt eius scopum & vsum rectius intelligamus. Ideo enim Christum parabolam hanc recitauisse ait, quòd iam propius ad vrbem Hierosolymorum accessissent, pleriq; autem qui cum ipso erant, Regnũ eius iam nunc cum gloria & triumphis apparituru esse putarent. Scimus enim Hierosolymã non solum iam inde à Dauidis temporibus Regum prisco rũ sedem, verumetiam Ecclesiæ & Regni Christi typũ fuisse. De ea enim dictum fuerat: Hic est Deus, Deus noster in sempiternũ: ipse diriget nos admortem vsq;. Ite: Dominus elegit Zionem, & expetiuit eã sibi, dicens: Hæc requies mea est sempiterna, hic habitabo: quoniã expetiui eam. Sed & Regni Christi sedes quædam fuisse dici potest, eò quòd illic prædicationis Euangeli cæ initium fieri debuit, & inde egressi Apostoli verbum Dei in toto orbe prædicauerũt. Quod ipsum quoq; veteres Prophetæ olim prædixerant. Dauid enim de Christo canit: Dominus emittet sceptrũ potentiæ suæ de Zione. Et notum est illud Isaiæ & Michææ: Lex è Zione exibit, & verbum Domini de Hierusalem. Quia ergo discipuli regnum terrenum & temporale somniabant (vt iam sæpe dictum est), & Christum vrbi appropinquare, eoq; magno cum conatu contendere videbant, noua spes animos illorum titillare cœpit, vt iam nunc tempus illud præforibus esse putarent, quo Regnũ illud instaurari deberet. Quapropter vt diligentius admonerentur, omnino necesse erat.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke here also prefaces the occasion of this action, so that we may understand its purpose and use more correctly. He says that Christ told this parable because they had now come nearer to the city of Jerusalem, and most of those who were with him thought that his kingdom would now appear with glory and triumph. We know that Jerusalem was not only the seat of the ancient kings from the times of David onward, but was also a type of the Church and of the kingdom of Christ. Of it it was said: "This is God, our God forever; he will guide us even unto death" (Ps. 48:14). And again: "The Lord has chosen Zion and desired it for his dwelling, saying: This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it" (Ps. 132:13-14). But it can also be said that Jerusalem was a certain seat of Christ's kingdom, because the preaching of the Gospel had to begin there, and from there the apostles went out and proclaimed the Word of God throughout the whole world. The ancient prophets had also foretold this. David sings of Christ: "The Lord will send forth the sceptre of your power out of Zion" (Ps. 110:2). And the well-known words of Isaiah and Micah are familiar: "The law shall go out of Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Isa. 2:3; Mic. 4:2). Therefore, since the disciples were dreaming of an earthly and temporal kingdom (as has often been said already), and saw Christ drawing near to the city and hastening there with such great eagerness, a new hope began to tickle their minds, so that they thought that the time in which that kingdom must be restored was now at the doors. For this reason it was altogether necessary that they be admonished more carefully.

units.la: Est autem hoc stupiditatis maxima exemplum, quòd toties de morte admoniti, subinde ad cogitationes illas de regno terreno reuertuntur, in quo nõ vno modo ab illis peccatũ fuit. Nam de Christo & tota humanæ redemptionis causa perperã iudicant: & insuper victorias & triumphos spirant priusquam pugnauerint. Sed vtinã non hodie etiam error iste plerosq; dementaret, qui Christi doctrina & fide gloriantur. Vt enim homo animalis nõ sapit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei: ita in Christo quoq; terrena potius & temporalia bona, quàm cœlestia & aeterna quærers confuseuit. Ea igitur est multorum stupiditas, vt quamuis se totum qualis est, ille offerat cum omnibus ijs, quæ ad salutem æternam faciunt, illum tamen facile contemnant & negligat, nisi aliqua ipsis emolumenti terreni spes in præsenti affulgeat: Quæ causa est, quòd pauci Euangelium syncerè & cum fructu recipiunt. Nam si ea inueniant, quæ sola carni magnifica videntur, ijs solis immersi cœlestia negligunt: At si spes illa eos fallat, tum se deceptos esse quæruntur, & sæpe nõ contenti defecisse, insuper hostes aperti fiunt. Debet autem omnes isti meminisse, studia ipsorum Christum minimè latere. Nouit hic quid discipuli intra animos suos sperent & cogitent. Ad eundem modum hodie etiam omnes eos nouit, qui animo nõ syncero ad Euangelium eius accedunt. Et si reprehensione digni fuerunt, qui ex communi ignorantia olim peccauerunt, quas pœnas & quæ supplicia merentur, qui cum Christi in crucem suffixi nomine glorientur, eiusdem tamen professione ad impura carnis studia abutuntur? Si qui verò adhuc ignorantia & simplicitate peccant, ij parabolam istam probè considerent, qua Christus omnia coprehendit, quæ cognitu necessaria sunt ijs, qui eius Regno nõ inutiliter potiri volunt. Potest eain duas partes diuidi, ex quibus prior ea continet, quæ in terris hisce ante nouissimum illius aduentum accidere solent: altera, quid futurum sit docet, quando ille venerit ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos.
units.tr: Now this is a very great example of stupidity: although they had been warned so often about his death, they keep returning to those thoughts about an earthly kingdom, in which they erred in more ways than one. For they judged wrongly about Christ and about the whole cause of human redemption, and besides, they breathed out victories and triumphs before they had fought. Would that this error did not today also drive mad many who boast of the teaching and faith of Christ! For just as "the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2:14), so too many people seek earthly and temporal goods in Christ rather than heavenly and eternal ones. This is the stupidity of many: although he offers himself wholly as he is, with all the things that serve eternal salvation, they easily despise and neglect him, unless some hope of earthly advantage shines on them in the present. This is why few receive the Gospel sincerely and with fruit. If they find things that seem splendid to the flesh alone, they are so absorbed in these that they neglect the heavenly things. But if that hope deceives them, then they complain that they have been cheated, and often, not content to have fallen away, they even become open enemies. All such people should remember that Christ is by no means unaware of their pursuits. He knows what the disciples hoped and thought in their hearts. In the same way, today too he knows all those who approach his Gospel with an insincere heart. And if those who sinned long ago out of common ignorance deserved reproof, what punishments and what torments do they deserve who boast in the name of Christ crucified, and yet by that very profession abuse the Gospel for impure fleshly pursuits? But if there are some who still sin through ignorance and simplicity, let them carefully consider this parable, in which Christ comprehends all that is necessary to know for those who wish to possess his kingdom not to no profit. It can be divided into two parts. The first part contains what usually happens on earth before his final coming. The second teaches what will happen when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Prima pars, quam modò recitauimus, Regni eius in hoc seculo conditionem sic describit, vt eui dentissimè illorum errorem confutet, qui ipsum victorijs illustrẽ & cum maiestate, quæ apud mundi principes cernitur, regnaturũ fore somniat. Et quia illi in Hierosolymis subinde hærebat, quasi hæc Regni Messiæ sedes perpetua futura esset, se homini nobili confert, qui vt regnũ sibi acciperet, in longinquam regionem profectus, pecunias suas inter seruos distribuit, ut ijs negotientur. Quo loco haec consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: The first part, which I have just recited, describes the condition of his kingdom in this age in such a way that it most clearly refutes the error of those who dream that he will reign adorned with victories and with the majesty that is seen among the princes of the world. Because they kept fixing their minds on Jerusalem, as if it were to be the perpetual seat of the Messiah's kingdom, he turns to a nobleman who, in order to receive a kingdom for himself, went into a distant country, and before he left he distributed his money among his servants so that they might do business with it. Here the following points must be considered.

units.la: Primum, quòd Christus se hominem nobilem dicit. Et sanè reuera nobilis atque generosus est, siue diuinam siue humanam eius naturam spectes. Secundùm illam enim ab æterno ex Deo Patre genitus est: quod Micheas Propheta docet his verbis: Exitus eius ab initio, à diebus æternitatis. Et Isaias ait: Generationem eius quis enarrabit? Quoad verò humanam naturam, ex familia omnium quotquot vnquam in orbe fuerunt nobilissima prodijt, quæ certa & nunquam interrupta linea ab ipso Adamo, omnium nostrûm parente deducitur. Numerantur in ea sanctissimi patres, quicunque ad Noam vsq; vixerunt, per quem genus humanum, quod in diluvio perijsse videbatur, instauratum est: Sanctissimi illi Patriarchæ, Abrahamus, Isaacus & Iacobus, quibus cum salutis fœdus, itidem Deus instaurauit, & quorum Deum se dicere dignatur. Adde his Dauidem & ex eo progenitos Reges circiter viginti, qui per annos circiter quadringentos continuos regnauerunt. Taceo his internixtos Prophetas, inter quos ceu astra pulcherrima Isaias & Daniel fulserunt, vnà cum infinitis aliis, qui post reditum ex Babylone in illa gente claruerunt. Verè ergo nobilis homo est Iesus Christus, si vel solis rationibus humanis agatur. Quòd si virtus spectetur, quam Ethnicorum quoq; sapientes nobilitatè veram & vnicâ dixère, secundū hanc quoq; nihil illo nobilius & illustrius est: quia absq; omni vitiosa naturæ nostræ contagio ex intemerata virgine natus, ita vitâ trâsegit, vt ne hostes quidem infensissimi ipsum alicuius peccati arguere potuerint. Superat autè hæc omnia, quòd suam nobilitatem in eos quoq; transfundit, vt sui similes faciat, quod paucis inter huius sæculi nobilibus datur. Plerunq; enim degenerant, qui ex præclaris maioribus nascuntur, vt non temere vulgari proverbio dicatur: Heroum filij noxæ. At Christus Iesus ea conditione nobis à Deo Patre sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio deniq; factus est, vt omnes eos Dei filios faciat, quicunq; in ipsum credunt, & eosdem Regni sui coheredes habere dignetur. Imò ille est, qui nos Deo Patri suo Reges & Sacerdotes fecit, vt in Apocalypsi scribitur. Quis enim Reges esse neget eos, qui carni, mundo & diabolo dominantur? Quis verò non Sacerdotes dixerit, qui iuuencos labiorum suorum, id est, preces & gratiarum actionem quotidie offerunt, & qui seipsos Deo sistunt viuentes hostias, quem cultum Paulus Deo acceptissimum & solum vere rationalem esse docet? Et hæc quidem sola est nobilitas, quæ nos Deo simul & Angelis commendat: quæ vt non aliorum est, quàm qui Christo nomen dederunt, ita ad eam omnes aspirare decet, qui cum salute gloriam veram & sempiternam affectant. Stulti ergo reuera & miserrimi mortalium sunt, qui imaginum & stemmatum fiducia turgidi, inanibus titulis sese venditant, non autem in hoc incumbunt, vt germani filij Dei & Christi fratres sint.
units.tr: First, Christ calls himself a nobleman. And indeed he truly is noble and of high birth, whether you look at his divine nature or his human nature. For according to his divine nature he was begotten from eternity of God the Father, as the prophet Micah teaches in these words: "His goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" (Mic. 5:2). And Isaiah says: "Who will declare his generation?" (Isa. 53:8). As for his human nature, he came from the most noble family of all who have ever lived in the world, a family traced in an unbroken and certain line from Adam himself, the parent of us all. In this line are numbered the most holy fathers who lived down to Noah, through whom the human race, which seemed to have perished in the flood, was restored. There are also the most holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, with whom God likewise renewed the covenant of salvation, and whose God he deigns to be called. Add to these David and about twenty kings descended from him, who reigned continuously for about four hundred years. I say nothing of the prophets who came between them, among whom Isaiah and Daniel shone like most beautiful stars, together with countless others who became famous in that nation after the return from Babylon. Jesus Christ is therefore truly a nobleman, even if we consider only human reasons. But if we look at virtue, which even the wise men of the heathen called the only true nobility, then he is nothing less noble and illustrious in this respect too. For, born of the undefiled Virgin without any corrupting taint of our nature, he so lived that not even his most bitter enemies could accuse him of any sin. Yet what surpasses all this is that he also imparts his nobility to those who are his, so that he makes them like himself, which is granted to few among the nobles of this age. For those born of illustrious ancestors often degenerate, so that the common proverb is not said for nothing: "The sons of heroes are a disgrace." But Christ Jesus has been made by God the Father for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and finally redemption, so that he makes all who believe in him children of God and deigns to have them as co-heirs of his kingdom. Indeed, he is the one who made us kings and priests to his God and Father, as it is written in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1:6). For who would deny that they are kings who rule over the flesh, the world and the devil? And who would not call them priests who offer daily the calves of their lips, that is, prayers and thanksgiving, and who present themselves to God as living sacrifices, a worship that Paul teaches is most acceptable to God and the only truly reasonable service (Rom. 12:1)? This is the only nobility that commends us both to God and to the angels. It belongs to none but those who have given their name to Christ, and therefore everyone who seeks true and everlasting glory together with salvation ought to aspire to it. Truly foolish and most wretched of mortals, then, are those who, puffed up with confidence in images and family trees, advertise themselves with empty titles, and yet do not strive to be true sons of God and brothers of Christ.

units.la: Deinde se in regione longinquam abiturum dicit, vt accipiat sibi Regnum. Exponunt hoc nonnulli de tempore, quod inter eius mortem siue ascensionem atq; nouissimum aduentum intercedit, vt doceat, se diu abfuturum esse. At quia hic non tam de absentia Christi diuturna, quam de Regni sede agitur, quam discipuli (vt dictum est, & Lucas non obscure docet) Hierosolymæ collocabant: ego sicut Regni Christi, & eius sedem propriâ hac locutione denotari sentio. Ita ergo docet, Regnum eius non esse de hoc mundo, & perpetuâ atq; propriam eius sedem neq; Hierosolymæ, neq; Romæ, neq; in vllo certo loco terrarum, sed in ὑπεραιοις, id est, in ijs quæ supra cælos sunt (sic Apostolus exponit) esse ad dexteram Patris sui omnipotentis. Et hæc quidem longinqua regio dicitur, quia non modo diuturnum est tempus illud, quod ab eius Ascensione ad postremum eius reditum decurrit: verum etiam quia Regnum illud cœleste ab hoc mundo plurimum differt, & inter illius sedem supracœlestem & terras haec, in quibus nos viuimus, immensa est locorum distantia. Neque istud alicui arguetur, vt deri debet, quando & Scripturæ Euangelicæ testantur & Symboli Apostolici articuli hoc docent, Christum Iesum, postquâ totum nostræ redemptionis negotium in terris peregit, corpus suum in cœlos subuexisse, in Domum Patris sui, vt illos nobis quoq; patefaceret, & in illis locum nobis pararet, vbi cum ipso olim regnabimus. Scimus equidem, & firmissimè credimus, Christo omnè potestatem in cœlis & in terra datam esse. Scimus illum discipulis dixisse: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem sæculi & constanter credimus, eum Ecclesiæ suæ nunquam non adesse, hanc ab ipso gubernari & defendi, hostes quoq; eius ab illo coerceri atq; puniri, sed ista non corporis præsentia, sed virtute Spiritus fieri dicimus, ita nimirum illo ipsoȷ suæ præsentiæ modum definiente, quando discipu-
units.tr: Then he says that he will go away into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself. Some explain this as referring to the time between his death or ascension and his final coming, to teach that he will be absent for a long time. But since the passage concerns not so much the lengthy absence of Christ as the seat of the kingdom, which the disciples (as has been said, and as Luke teaches not obscurely) were placing at Jerusalem, I think that both the kingdom of Christ and his seat are signified by this phrase. So he teaches that his kingdom is not of this world, and that his perpetual and proper seat is neither at Jerusalem, nor at Rome, nor in any fixed place on earth, but in the heavenly places [ἐπουρανίοις], that is, in those things which are above the heavens (so the Apostle explains it), at the right hand of his almighty Father. This region is called distant not only because the time that runs from his Ascension to his last return is long, but also because that heavenly kingdom differs greatly from this world, and between that seat above the heavens and these lands in which we live there is an immense distance of places. Nor is this to be disputed by anyone, as it ought not to be, since the Gospel Scriptures testify and the articles of the Apostles' Creed teach that Christ Jesus, after he had completed the whole business of our redemption on earth, carried his body up into the heavens, into the house of his Father, to open those heavens to us also and to prepare a place for us there, where we shall one day reign with him. We know indeed, and firmly believe, that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ. We know that he said to his disciples: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age"; and we steadfastly believe that he is never absent from his Church, that it is governed and defended by him, and that his enemies are restrained and punished by him. But we say that these things are done not by bodily presence but by the power of the Spirit, his own presence being defined in this way, when he said to the disciples:

units.la: Regnum Christi non est de hoc mundo. lis dixit: Ego rogabo Patrem, & alium cõsolatorem dabit vobis, vt maneat vobifeum in æternum: nempe Spiritum illum Veritatis, &c. Item: Expedit vobis vt ego abeam: nam nisi abiero, Consola tor ille siue παράκλητος (quæ vox consultorem quoque & aduocatum significat, qui nobis in causa aliqua agenda consilio & authoritate sua adest) non veniet ad vos, &c. Et Paulus Apostolus eum supra omnes cœlos eueĉu̅ esse testatur, & inde ex alto Spiritus sui dona in homines distribuere, quo rum ministerio Ecclesiam suam colligat atque conseruet. Itaque siue de Regni Christi conditione & administratione, quæ tota spiritualis est & inuisibili virtute constat, siue de loco beatæ immortalita tis & propria Regni sede verba ista intelligas, reuera in longinquam regionem ille abijt. Et meo iudicio rectissime & vtiliter vtramque sententiam coniuxeris, vt primò quidem illis occurratur, qui Regnum Christi adhuc hodie terrenum fingunt, & sedem ei in terris tribuunt Romam, adeò vt de salutis necessitate esse dicant, vt omnis creatura Romano Pontifici obediat: deinde verò illorum error confutetur, qui corporalem eius in terris præsentiam statuunt, quam ille pasim negat, & quam Apostoli adeò ignorauerunt, vt Petrus magna cum authoritate testatur, illum OPORTERE in cœlis agere vsque ad tempus restitutionis omnium: Paulus autem tunc quoque, quando de Cœna eius mystica et vero eius vsu loquitur, corporalis absentiæ nõ obscurè meminerit, dicens: Annũtiate mortem Domini DONEC VENIT. Quam particulam, aut de toto Christo, Deo simul & Homine, aut de alterutra natura solummodo exponamus oportet. Si de toto interpreteris, totum Chri stum ab Ecclesia & Cœna illa excludes: quæ intolerabilis erit impietas. Si verò de eius diuinitate exponas, quasi eam venturam expectemus, inutilis erit corporis præsentia, si illa abstuleris, quæ sola eius merito gratiam & virtutem salutarem conciliat. Quid ergo restat, quam vt illum corpore suo extra hunc mundum corruptibilem in supracœlesti patria agere, Spiritu autem suo & diuina virtute nobiscum in terris agere, corda verò nostra per fidem supra cœlos euehi dicamus, vt eius corpore & sanguine alamur & pascamur ad vitam æternam? Neque ideo diuinam naturam ab humana auel limus, quasi hæc sola in cœlis resideat, illa autem per terras extensa Ecclesiam gubernet. Scimus enim de hac verissime dictum esse: Cœlum & terram ego impleo. Nulla igitur auulsione aut separatione o- pus est, cùm diuinitas Christi cœlum & terram impleat, & proinde ab humanitate in cœlis agente nunquam discedat. Quod autem aduersarij illa conuertunt, vt humanam quoque naturam esse pro- bent, vbicunque diuina est, id nos cum illis dicere non possumus: quia sic humanæ naturæ proprietas exinanitur, quod nullis Scripturæ testimonijs probari potest. Et ne quid ipsi fingere dicamur, Au- gustini verbis ad commentum illud respondemus: Non est consequens, vt quod in Deo est, ita sit vbique vt Deus: Nam vt de nobis veracissima scriptura dicit, quòd in illo viuimus, mouemur & sumus: nec tamen sicut ille vbique sumus: sed alter homo ille in Deo, quoniam alter & Deus ille in homine, proprio quodam & singulari modo: Vna enim persona Deus & homo est, & vtrunque est vnus Christus Iesus, vbique per id quod Deus, in cœlo autem per id quod homo, &c. Sed plura de his alibi. Sufficiat nunc, Christum ista locutione omnium eorum errorem refellere, qui Regnum eius hu mano sensu metiuntur, aut illud loco alicui certo in terris astringunt. Simul tamen quamuis se pere grinari à nobis dicat, sui tamen reditus disertam mentionem facit, vt testetur, se nos nequaquam ne gligere neq; propterea Ecclesiæ suæ curam depositisse.
units.tr: The kingdom of Christ is not of this world. "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you forever": namely that Spirit of Truth, and so on. Likewise: "It is expedient for you that I go away; for unless I go away, that Comforter, or Paraclete [παράκλητος] (a word which means also advocate and helper, one who stands by us in a case to be pleaded, with counsel and authority), will not come to you," and so on. And the Apostle Paul testifies that he has been raised above all the heavens, and from there on high distributes the gifts of his Spirit among men, by whose ministry he gathers and preserves his Church. Therefore, whether you understand these words of the condition and administration of Christ's kingdom, which is wholly spiritual and consists in invisible power, or of the place of blessed immortality and the proper seat of the kingdom, he has truly gone away into a distant region. In my judgement you will combine both views most rightly and profitably: first, so that one may meet those who still today imagine Christ's kingdom to be earthly, and assign him a seat on earth at Rome, so far that they say it is necessary for salvation that every creature obey the Roman Pontiff; and then so that the error of those is refuted who posit a bodily presence of his on earth, which he everywhere denies, and which the Apostles so little knew that Peter testifies with great authority that he MUST remain in heaven until the time of the restoration of all things. Paul too, when he speaks of the Lord's mystical Supper and its true use, does not obscurely recall his bodily absence, saying: "You proclaim the Lord's death UNTIL HE COMES." This phrase we must explain either of the whole Christ, God and man together, or of one nature alone. If you interpret it of the whole Christ, you will exclude the whole Christ from the Church and from that Supper, which would be an intolerable impiety. But if you explain it of his divinity, as if we were waiting for it to come, his bodily presence would be useless, if you took it away, which alone by its merit wins grace and saving power for us. What remains, then, but to say that he dwells with his body outside this corruptible world, in the heavenly fatherland, while by his Spirit and divine power he dwells with us on earth, and that our hearts are lifted above the heavens through faith, so that we may be nourished and fed by his body and blood unto eternal life? Nor, for this reason, do we separate the divine nature from the human, as if only the divine nature remained in heaven while the human, spread through the earth, governed the Church. For we know that of the divine nature it has been most truly said: "I fill heaven and earth." Therefore there is no need of any tearing away or separation, since the divinity of Christ fills heaven and earth, and so never departs from the humanity that acts in heaven. But as for what our opponents turn around, to prove that the human nature is also wherever the divine is, we cannot say this with them, because in that way the property of the human nature is emptied out, which cannot be proved by any testimony of Scripture. And lest we be thought to invent anything ourselves, we answer that fiction with the words of Augustine: "It does not follow that what is in God is everywhere in the same way as God is. For, as the most truthful Scripture says of us, that in him we live, move and are, yet we are not everywhere as he is; but that man is in God, and God in man, in a certain proper and singular way. For God and man are one person, and both together are one Christ Jesus, everywhere by what he is as God, but in heaven by what he is as man," and so on. But more on these matters elsewhere. For now it is enough that by this phrase Christ refutes the error of all those who measure his kingdom by human sense, or confine it to some fixed place on earth. At the same time, although he says that he is going away from us, he nonetheless makes explicit mention of his return, to testify that he by no means neglects us, nor for that reason has laid down the care of his Church.

units.la: Cæterum videamus, quam rationem interea in Regni sui administratione teneat. Vocatis (in- quit) decem seruis suis dedit eis decem minas, dixitque eis: Negotiamini donec veniam. Per seruos suos intelligit Apostolos & horum successores, quibus verbi Euangelici prædicatio commissa est, & quos Spiritus sui donis ille instruit, vt muneri suo possint sufficere: & vult vt ijs negotientur, vt quod dedit, olim cum lucro aut fænore recipiat. Et facit ad huius loci explicationem quod Apostolus ad Ephesios capite quarto scribit: Vnicuique nostrum data est gratia pro mensura doni Christi: Quapropter dicit, Cùm ascendisset in sublime, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dedit dona homini- bus. Et mox hoc exponès subijcit: Et ipse alios quidem dedit Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios autem Pastores & Doctores, ad coagmentationem Sanctorum, ad opus ministerij, ad ædificationem (inquam) corporis Christi, &c. Ergo (quod initio diximus) Regnum eius in hoc mundo, non cum externa maiestate coniunctum est, neq; armis & victorijs splendet: sed per Euangelij prædicationem & Spiritus virtutem administratur atque seruatur. De eo autem in præsenti
units.tr: Meanwhile let us see what plan he keeps in the administration of his kingdom. "He called his ten servants," he says, "and gave them ten minas, and said to them: Trade until I come." By his servants he means the Apostles and their successors, to whom the preaching of the Gospel Word has been committed, and whom he equips with the gifts of his Spirit so that they may be sufficient for their office; and he wills that they trade with these, so that he may receive back what he gave, in time, with profit or interest. This also helps to explain this passage: the Apostle writes to the Ephesians in chapter four: "To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ." Wherefore he says: "When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." And soon, explaining this, he adds: "And he himself gave some to be Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, and some Pastors and Teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up (I say) of the body of Christ," and so on. Therefore (as we said at the beginning) his kingdom in this world is not joined with external majesty, nor does it shine with arms and victories; but it is administered and preserved through the preaching of the Gospel and the power of the Spirit. But concerning this at present
Acts 3; 1 Cor. 11; John 14 and 16.

units.la: Epist.57. ad Dardanum.
units.tr: Epist. 57, to Dardanus.

units.la: Qua ratione regnum Christus in terris administret. præsenti ita disserit Dominus, vt paucis omnia comprehendat, quæcunq; de ministerio Ecclesiæ, & ministrorum officio dici possunt.
units.tr: In what way Christ governs his kingdom on earth. Here the Lord speaks in such a way as to sum up in a few words everything that can be said about the ministry of the Church and the duty of its ministers.

units.la: Primùm vocationis meminit, dicens: Vocatis decem seruis suis: Ergo vocatione legitima illis opus est, & missione quicunq; in hoc ministerio cum aliquo fructu versari volunt. Vt enim Legatus dici non potest, quem nemo misit: ita neq; Christi aut Ecclesiæ eius minister poterit censeri, qui non ab illo ad hoc munus vocatus & destinatus fuerit. Nam etiamsi verbum eius illi prædicent, absq; fructu tamen & nulla cum authoritate id faciunt: cùm legitimæ missionis testimonio destituti, eorum similes sint, qui legatos quidem se esse fingunt, non habent autem literas (quas Credentiæ vocant) quibus se hæc aut ista in mandatis habere præbent. Ideo de talibus apud Ieremiam conqueritur, dicens: Currebant & non mittebam eos. Et Apostolus dicebat: quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Quia enim munus hoc (vt aliàs diximus) periculi plenum est, non autem sibijpsis aliquid certum de Dei ope polliceri possunt, quicunq; illud absque Dei iussu aut vocatione legitima subeunt, fieri non potest, vt ijdem laboribus & periculis non succumbant, si quid grauius patiantur. Legitimæ autem vocationes censeri debent, non solùm extraordinariæ illæ, quibus Prophetæ & Apostoli olim immediatè vocati sunt, verùmetiam quæ ab Ecclesijs in nomine & Spiritu Christi congregatis fiunt, secundùm Canones verà Apostolicos, qui in libro Actorum, in Pauli epistolis ad Timoth. & Titum præscribuntur.
units.tr: He first mentions vocation, saying: "When he had called his ten servants" (Luke 19:13). So those who wish to serve in this ministry with any profit need a lawful calling and sending. Just as no one can be called an envoy whom nobody has sent, so no one can be counted a minister of Christ or of his Church who has not been called and appointed to this office by him. For even if such men preach his word, they do so without fruit and without authority, since they lack the witness of a lawful sending. They are like those who pretend to be envoys but have no letters (which they call credentials) showing that they hold this or that commission. So Jeremiah complains of such men, saying: "They ran, and I did not send them" (Jer. 23:21). And the Apostle said: "How shall they preach, unless they be sent?" (Rom. 10:15). Because this office (as we have said elsewhere) is full of danger, and men cannot promise themselves any certain help from God, it is impossible that those who take it up without God's command or lawful calling should not give way to labours and dangers if they suffer anything more serious. Yet lawful callings must be counted not only those extraordinary ones by which the Prophets and Apostles were once called immediately, but also those made by Churches gathered in the name and Spirit of Christ, according to the Apostolic canons, which are laid down in the Book of Acts and in Paul's epistles to Timothy and Titus.

units.la: Secundo loco pecuniam suam in seruos suos distribuisse dicitur homo ille nobilis. Et Lucas quidem vnicuiq; minam datam fuisse scribit: Matthæus verò vni quidé talenta quinq;, alteri duo, cuidam vnum datum fuisse ait, vt diuersitatem donorum Spiritus Sancti exprimat. In hoc ergo veriq; cum altero convenit, quòd ministros Ecclesiæ nihil ex seipsis habere docent, sed diuinitus accepisse quicquid habent: adhæc neminem à Deo ad hoc munus destinari, quem non mina sua instruat, id est, donis illis exornet, quæ ipsi ad functionem suam necessaria sunt. Etsi enim ministerium Ecclesiæ vnicum sit, & omnes ministri idem saxum volunt, alij tamen alijs plus laboris sustinent pro ratione locorum & hominum, quibus seruiunt. Ideo Paulus in priori ad Corinthios ait: Discrimina donorum sunt, sed idem Spiritus: Discrimina ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus: discrimina facultatum sunt, sed idem est Deus efficiens eas omnes in quibusuis. Prodest hoc diligenter obseruauisse: quia de multis cognitu necessarijs nos admonet. Primum est, quod ministri ex semetipsis nihil possunt. Ex nobisipsis (inquit Paulus) non sumus idonei, ne ad cogitandum quidem: sed quod idonei sumus, id ex Deo est. Id verò modestiæ illos admonere debet, ne propter ministerij excellentiam superbiant, aut sibi licere putent aliquid pro suo arbitrio facere, vel etiam Ecclesijs obtrudere, quod non à Domino acceperunt. Ideo enim suis donis illos instruit Dominus, vt suos prædicones & ministros agant, non autem aliquid ex suo cerebro instituant, Docete (inquit Christus) eos seruare, quæ ego vobis tradidi. Et Paulus: Quod à Domino accepi, tradidi vobis. Deinde mutui officij & dilectionis hæc donorum diuersitas ministros admonet. Quia enim eidem Domino omnes seruiunt, qui plus accepit inferiorem non contemnere, neq; hic illi inuidere, sed mutuas operas sibi tradere debent, vt opus Domini cum aliquo fructu perficiant. Facit huc parabola corporis humani & membrorum, quæ cùm alia alijs præstent, non tamen inter se contendunt, sed admirabili συμπαθείᾳ atq; consensione se mutuò tuentur & iuuant, vt corpus totum incolume seruetur. Singuli ergo quod acceperunt suam minam esse cogitent, neq; ad aliorum dona oculo maligno respiciant: sed hoc potius agant, vt quam plurimum conferant ad Communis Ecclesiæ ædificationem. Quia enim omnis donorum Dei fructus in vsu consistit, nequaquam illa sepulta latere, multò minus autem in vsus alienos, vel etiam contrarios conuerti debent: ne ad destructionem seruiant ea, quibus Ecclesia debebat adificari.
units.tr: In the second place, that nobleman is said to have distributed his money among his servants. Luke writes that a mina was given to each, while Matthew says that five talents were given to one, two to another, and one to a third, so as to express the diversity of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In this, then, the two accounts agree, namely that they teach that the ministers of the Church have nothing of their own but have received from God whatever they have; and further, that no one is appointed by God to this office whom he does not equip with his mina, that is, adorn with those gifts which are necessary for his task. For although the ministry of the Church is one, and all ministers pursue the same aim, yet some bear more labour than others, according to the places and the people they serve. So Paul says in the first letter to the Corinthians: "There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all in all" (1 Cor. 12:4-6). It is useful to have observed this carefully, because it reminds us of many things that must be known. The first is that ministers can do nothing of themselves. "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves," says Paul, "but our sufficiency is of God" (2 Cor. 3:5). This ought to teach them humility, so that they do not grow proud because of the excellence of their ministry, or think it lawful to do at their own pleasure anything, or even to force on the Churches anything they have not received from the Lord. For the Lord equips them with his gifts so that they may be his heralds and ministers, and not devise anything out of their own brain. "Teach them," says Christ, "to observe whatever I have commanded you" (Matt. 28:20). And Paul: "I delivered to you what I also received from the Lord" (1 Cor. 11:23). Next, this diversity of gifts reminds ministers of mutual duty and love. Since all serve the same Lord, the one who has received more must not despise the lesser, nor the lesser envy the greater, but they ought to lend each other mutual help, so that they may carry out the work of the Lord with some fruit. The parable of the human body and its members applies here: though some members excel others, they do not contend among themselves, but by a wonderful sympathy and agreement [συμπάθεια] they protect and help one another, so that the whole body is kept whole. Each, then, should consider that what he has received is his own mina, and should not look upon the gifts of others with an evil eye, but rather strive to contribute as much as possible to the building up of the common Church. For since the whole fruit of God's gifts lies in their use, they must not be buried and hidden, much less turned to other or even opposing uses, lest those things by which the Church ought to be built up serve for its destruction.

units.la: Tertiò officium ministrorum vno verbo definit, dicens: Negotiamini donec veniam. At quia pecuniam ab hero suo illi omnes acceperant, vtique non sibijpsis, sed illi negotiari debuerunt, & ita quidem vt huic ad sua reuerso possent rationem reddere. Loquitur autem Christus de negotiatione spirituali, quæ tota in eo consistit, vt plures quotidie Christo lucrifiant, qui & ipsi salutem consequantur, & sua vita atq; operibus Deū glorificent. Sic ipse Dominus exponit, discipulis dicens: Profecti μαθητεύσατε, id est, discipulos facite omnes gentes: hoc nimirum exigens, vt qui prius in diuersas sectas & superstitiones distracti erant, omnes ad se colligantur, ipsum præceptorem & magistrum suum agnoscant, & in ipso uno salutem quærant. Qua ratione in primitiua Ecclesia discipuli dicti fuerunt, qui postea Antiochiæ cœperunt Christianorum nomine appellari. Ut verò Christo homines lucrifiant, non simplici modo doctrina & prædicatione opus est, sed labor insuper multus & indefessa industria atq; cura requiritur. Nam ut poetæ verbis vtar: Impiger extremos currit mercator ad Indos, ut quæcunque ubique faciat, et huius amore illectus nullos labores et nulla pericula detrectat. At non minori studio in hac negotiatione spirituali opus est, eò quòd in illis ipsis, qui lucrifieri debent, multa obstacula sunt, & plerique à salute, quæ ipsis offertur, refugiunt. Illic ergo nihil non tædij devorandum est minystro, dum se omnium ingenijs accommodat. Admonet nos de eo Paulus proprio exemplo, quando se Iudæis Iudæum, infirmis infirmum, exlegibus exlegem, omnibus deniq; omnia factum esse scribit, ut saltem aliquos Christo lucri faceret. Eius ergo exemplum omnes ministri imitentur, & quamuis eadem doctrina semper prædicari debeat, eam tamen pro auditorum captu accommodent, ne quæ suis ineptijs aut importunitate abster reant. Peccant autem aduersus hoc Christi mandatum, qui turpi ignauia eos perire sinunt, quos diligenti prædicatione ad illum adducere debebant. Sunt hi temerarij dissipatores donorum Domini, & graues olim pænas dabunt, quando pereuntium sanguis de manu ipsorum requiretur. Mala etiam fide negotiantur, qui suæ gloriæ & priuato commodo addicti, sibi discipulos quærunt, & factiosis stultissimorum hominum titulis gaudent, qui se ab ipsis denominare consueuerunt: quod in Corinthiorum doctoribus olim Paulus reprehendit. Est ergo hoc Christi dictum dignissimum, quod in omnium ministrorum auribus sonet, quod oculis eorum semper obuersetur, quod in animis suis nunquam non meditentur. Eius enim diligens meditatio abunde eos admonebit, quid Domino & Ecclesiæ debeant, & quàm nullus locus segnitiei & socordiæ ipsis reliquus esse possit, si officio suo fideliter fungi velint.
