Debent etiam illius meminisse omnes alij, ne indigne ferant ministrorum industriam, sed potius cogitent suam salutem cum illa coniunctam esse: ipsos autem officium facere, dum serio instant omnibus, quos adhuc à Christo alienos esse, aut saltem in eius cultu frigidiores esse vident. Etenim nisi se lucrifieri patiantur, in suis superstitionibus aut peccatis pereant necesse est. Illi autem nisi in officio suo per omnia obstacula pergant, graues pœnas dabunt, sicuti in altera parabolæ huius parte audiemus.
units.tr: Thirdly, he defines the duty of the ministers in one word, saying: "Trade until I come" (Luke 19:13). But since all of them had received money from their master, they ought to trade not for themselves but for him, so that they could give an account to him when he returned. Christ speaks here of spiritual trading, which consists wholly in this: that every day more men are gained for Christ, who themselves obtain salvation and glorify God by their life and works. The Lord himself explains this to the disciples, saying: "Go and make disciples [μαθητεύσατε] of all nations" (Matt. 28:19). This plainly requires that those who had been divided before into diverse sects and superstitions should all be gathered to him, acknowledge him as their teacher and master, and seek salvation in him alone. It was for this reason that in the primitive Church those who afterwards began to be called Christians at Antioch were called disciples. Now, to gain men for Christ, not only simple teaching and preaching are needed, but also great labour and tireless industry and care. For, to use the words of the poet: "The eager merchant runs to the far-off Indians," so that he may do whatever he can anywhere, and, drawn on by love of gain, he shrinks from no toil and no danger. Yet no less zeal is needed in this spiritual trade, because among those very people who ought to be gained there are many obstacles, and most of them shrink from the salvation offered to them. Therefore the minister must swallow every weariness there, while he adapts himself to everyone's nature. Paul reminds us of this by his own example, when he writes that he became to the Jews a Jew, to the weak weak, to those outside the law as one outside the law, and in short to all things all things, so that he might at least gain some for Christ. Let all ministers, then, imitate his example, and although the same doctrine must always be preached, let them adapt it to the capacity of the hearers, so that they do not repel them by their own silliness or importunity. But those sin against this command of Christ who through shameful idleness allow to perish those whom they ought to have brought to him by diligent preaching. These are reckless squanderers of the Lord's gifts, and they will one day pay heavy penalties, when the blood of those who perish will be required at their hands. Those also trade in bad faith who, given over to their own glory and private advantage, seek disciples for themselves and rejoice in the factional titles of very foolish men who have been accustomed to name themselves after them; this Paul once rebuked in the teachers of the Corinthians. This saying of Christ is therefore most worthy to sound in the ears of all ministers, to be always before their eyes, and never to be absent from their minds. For its diligent meditation will sufficiently remind them what they owe to the Lord and the Church, and how no place for sloth and carelessness can remain for them, if they wish to discharge their office faithfully. All others, too, ought to remember it, so that they do not take ill the diligence of the ministers, but rather think that their own salvation is bound up with it; and that the ministers perform their duty when they earnestly press on all those whom they see still alien to Christ, or at least cooler in his worship. For unless they allow themselves to be gained, they must of necessity perish in their superstitions or sins. But the ministers, unless they persist in their office through every obstacle, will pay heavy penalties, as we shall hear in the other part of this parable.

units.la: Nunc quid impij defectores aduersus Christum moliantur videamus, dum ipse corpore suo ab sens ab Ecclesia prorsus peregrinari videtur. Id sic enuntiat: Ciues autem eius oderant ipsum, misera runt, legationem post eum, dicentes: Nolumus hunc regnare super nos. Paucis multa comprehendit, & eos in hoc mundo seditiosissimos fore docet in excutiendo iugo disciplinæ & Regni sui, qui huius ciues præ alijs esse debebant. Et sane idem hic accidere solet, quod huius seculi Regibus sæpe accidit. Eo enim vulgus ingenio præditum est, ut præsentis conditionis facile quosuis pigeat. Optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus: Sic etiam Reipub. formâ plerique fastidiunt, cui assueuerunt, & sibi ex mutatione feliciorem statum pollicentur. Hinc crebræ illæ & periculosæ rerumpub. mutationes, quæ multis populis exitio fuerunt, & qualis hodie multis in locis cernimus. His autem non mali modò principes iactantur, verumetiam boni interdum & sui populi amantes. Quo magis anniti & vigilare decet omnes magistratus, ne sua vel ignauia vel licentia aliquibus tumultuandi occasionem præbeant. Sed his nunc omissis, scopum & institutum Christi respiciamus, qui ut discipulorum errori, sibi ipsis omnia in hoc seculo læta & fausta pollicentium medeatur, eam potius Regni sui in terris conditionem fore docet, ut non solum exteros hostes sentiat, sed ciuium quoq; seditiosorum intestinis motibus concutiatur: ex quo cuiusis facile est conijcere, non extra periculum fore eos, quibus Regni istius administratio commissa est.
units.tr: Let us now see what the impious deserters plot against Christ, while he himself, in his body, seems to be quite estranged from the Church. They express it thus: "But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying: We will not have this man to reign over us." In a few words he takes in much, and teaches that these men, who ought to have been the most obedient citizens of his kingdom, would be the most seditious in throwing off the yoke of discipline and of his reign. And indeed what often happens to the kings of this age is wont to happen here as well. For the common people are so disposed by nature that they readily grow weary of any present condition. The lazy ox desires the saddle, the horse desires the plough. So too many men come to dislike the form of the commonwealth to which they have become accustomed, and promise themselves a happier state from change. Hence those frequent and dangerous overthrows of commonwealths, which have been the ruin of many peoples, and such as we see today in many places. Yet not only bad princes are harassed by these things, but sometimes good ones who love their peoples. So much the more should all magistrates strive and be watchful, lest by their either idleness or licence they give some men an opportunity to riot. But leaving these matters now aside, let us look at the aim and purpose of Christ, who, to cure the error of his disciples, who promised themselves everything happy and prosperous in this world, teaches rather that the condition of his kingdom on earth will be such that it will be shaken not only by foreign enemies but also by the internal stirrings of seditious citizens. From this anyone can easily conjecture that those to whom the administration of that kingdom is entrusted will not be free from danger.

units.la: Quod autem hic per parabolam docet Christus, id reuera mox ab eius Ascensione impleri cœpit. Ciues enim illius rectissimè dixeris Iudæos, qui ex sanctis patribus oriundi Legem à Deo acceperant cum amplissimis promissionibus, & inter quos cultus sui formam ille constituerat plenam mysteriorum, quibus tota salutis ratio continetur. Imò hos non ciuium & subditorum loco Christus habuit, sed pro fratribus suis agnouit, & ex illis ipsis carnem assumere dignatus est. At quid de illis apud Ioannem dicitur? In sua venit verbum illud æternum, & sui illud non receperunt. Et constat illos aduersus eum, qui coràm doctrina & miraculis seipsum quotidie manifestabat, iam inde ab initio statim prædicationis Euangelicæ tumultuatos esse, tandemque omnium promissionum & communis spei, quam ex patribus didicerant immemores, illum magna cum contentione in Pilati conspectu negauisse, cùm clamarent: Non habemus Regem, nisi Cæsarem. Postquā verò idem ille iam cœlos conscensurus Apostolos constituit, qui Regni eius prædicare & tam docendo quàm miraculorum virtute propagare cœperunt, mox aduersus illos insurrexerunt & eos hostiliter aggressi sunt. Nam in carcerē conjectos, & postea in Senatum productos minis grauibus terruerūt, iniurijs variis affecerunt, virgis cæciderunt, ita denique egerūt cum illis, vt Gamaliel, qui inter ipsos prudentia & consilio pollebat, timeret, ne cum Deo bellum apertum susciperent. Nec tamen in eo subsistit illorum rabies, sed mox Stephanus lapidum grandine obrutus, & post eius obitum Hierosolymæ persecutio instituta est, in qua tam viri quam mulieres ex ædibus violenter protracti, bonis aut fortunis omnibus multati, & tandem Ecclesia miserè dispersa est. Quid autem de eo dicemus, quòd non contenti Hierosolymam & Iudæam totam aduersus Christum commouisse, insuper vbiq; gentium Apostolis eius negotium fecerunt, ne gentibus eam doctrinam prædicarent, quam ipsi reiecerant? Quid verò hoc aliud fuit, quàm missis legatis post Christum seditionem & bellum apertum ei denuntiare? Quoties enim aliquem credentium aut discipulorum trucidauerunt, toties publicè protestati sunt, se illum Regem nolle agnoscere, neque ipsius legibus obedire.
units.tr: What Christ teaches here through the parable, indeed, began to be fulfilled right after his Ascension. For his citizens may most rightly be called the Jews, who, sprung from the holy fathers, had received the Law from God with the most ample promises, and among whom he had established the form of his worship, full of mysteries, in which the whole reason of salvation is contained. Indeed Christ did not hold these men in the place of citizens and subjects, but acknowledged them as his brothers, and deigned to assume flesh from them themselves. But what is said of them in John? "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." And it is clear that they rose in tumult against him, who was daily manifesting himself by teaching and miracles, from the very beginning of the Gospel preaching; and at last, forgetful of all the promises and the common hope which they had learned from the fathers, they vehemently denied him in the sight of Pilate, when they cried: "We have no king but Caesar." But after the same man, about to ascend into the heavens, had appointed the Apostles, who began to proclaim his kingdom and to propagate it both by teaching and by the power of miracles, straightway they rose up against them and attacked them with hostility. For they threw them into prison, and afterwards, when they were brought before the Senate, terrified them with severe threats, treated them with various injuries, beat them with rods; and finally they so dealt with them that Gamaliel, who excelled among them in prudence and counsel, feared lest they should undertake open war with God. Yet their rage did not stop there, but soon Stephen, overwhelmed by a hail of stones, and after his death a persecution was set on foot at Jerusalem, in which men and women alike were violently dragged from their houses, stripped of all their goods and fortunes, and at last the Church was miserably scattered. And what shall we say of this, that not content to have stirred up Jerusalem and all Judea against Christ, they moreover made trouble for his Apostles everywhere among the nations, forbidding them to preach to the Gentiles that doctrine which they themselves had rejected? What else was this than, by sending envoys after Christ, to denounce to him sedition and open war? For as often as they slaughtered any believer or disciple, so often did they publicly protest that they were unwilling to acknowledge him as king, or to obey his laws.

units.la: Porrò quod olim Iudæi fecerunt, hoc ipsum apud multos alios esse videre, & in hunc vsq; diem passim fieri solet. Etenim cives Christi omnes homines dici possunt, cùm illi dictum sit à Patre: Postula à me, daboq; gentes vt sint hereditas tua, & terminos terræ vt sint possessio tua. Itaq; cùm peracto in terris nostræ salutis negotio in cœlos abire vellet, Apostolis mandauit, vt in totum orbem digressi Euangelium omnibus populis prædicarent. Quod cùm illi facerent, mox vbiq; locorum emicuit veritatis odium, quod hucusque in animis hominum occultius latuerat: & non modò priuatim multi eum reiecerunt, verumetiam Romani Imperatores publicis edictis ipsi debitam negauerunt obedientiam, et ne quis ipsum coleret vetuerunt. Fuit hæc causa grauissimarum persecutionum, quæ Apostolos omnes & viros Apostolicos cum multis millibus piorum abstulerunt, & quibus Ecclesia per annos fere trecentos vsq; ad Constantini Magni tempora miserabiliter agitata fuit. Taceo nunc hæreticos, qui insidiosè Regnum eius aggressi sunt, vt illud everterent. Et quàmuis interdum Halcyonia seu inducias Ecclesiæ suæ Deus concesserit, nunquā tamen pax diuturna & solida fuit, quin mox insurgerent noui motus eorum, qui Christum super se nolebant regnare. Et hodie tales voces passim audiuntur, & quidem inter eos etiam, qui inter cives Christi primatum sibi vendicant. Quid enim aliud faciunt Pontifices, qui dum se Christi vicarios esse dicunt, eū cum suo Euangelio ab Ecclesia excludunt? Quid Episcopi, qui similiter sub nominis eius prætextu Ecclesiam fædè dilaniant, & lupos illos graues agunt, quos ex illo ordine orituros esse, olim Paulus prædixit? Quid principes & Reges, qui Filium Dei exosculari & Ecclesiæ eius nutritij esse debebant? Nonne plures horum magnam illam matrem scortationū exosculantur, ad eius pedes cernui procumbunt, Ecclesiam verò Christi ferro & igne persequuntur? Quid de priuatis hominibus dicemus, quorū similiter maior pars Christum Regem suum agnoscere dedignatur? Nam etsi quidam illum in Euangelio loquentem ferant, quoad Patris sui gratiam, peccatorum remissionem & æternam felicitatem illis pollicetur; idem tamē quàm primùm scelera sua accusari, seq; vrgeri sentiunt, vt Christo se se per fidei obedientiam subijciant, mox voces illas audire licet: Egone propter istam doctrinam vitæ genus mutabo, genium meum fraudabo, & amicorum dulcissimorum consuetudinem deseram? Nunquam faciam. Quid verò hoc aliud est, quàm Christo quasi in faciem dicere: Nolo te regnare super me, cùm iam pridem Baccho, Veneri, Marti, & furum mercatorumq; Deo Mercurio me obstrinxerim? Sunt hæc inter eos, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt, tam vulgaria, vt plerique sibi in Christum potius imperium vendicare soleant, quàm vt huic ipsi obedire velint. Est hoc incurabilis malitiæ argumentum, quo simul admonemur, ijs qui in Christo Iesu piè viuere volunt, non aliud quàm crucem & persecutionem in hoc mundo propositam esse, & proinde procul relicta Regni terreni spe, ad hanc nos præparari debere.
units.tr: Moreover, what the Jews once did, this same thing we see to be done among many others, and it is commonly done even to this day. For all men can be called citizens of Christ, since it was said to him by the Father: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession." Therefore, when he was about to depart into heaven, having completed the work of our salvation on earth, he commanded the Apostles to go out into the whole world and preach the Gospel to all peoples. When they did this, straightway in every place there broke out a hatred of the truth, which had lain more hidden in men's minds until then; and not only did many reject him privately, but the Roman Emperors also, by public edicts, denied him the obedience owed to him and forbade anyone to worship him. This was the cause of the most grievous persecutions, which carried off all the Apostles and apostolic men together with many thousands of the pious, and by which the Church was miserably harassed for almost three hundred years, down to the times of Constantine the Great. I now say nothing of the heretics, who insidiously attacked his kingdom in order to overthrow it. And although God has sometimes granted his Church a halcyon calm or truce, yet a lasting and solid peace never existed, but straightway new movements arose from those who did not wish Christ to reign over them. And today such voices are heard everywhere, and indeed among those too who claim the primacy among the citizens of Christ. For what else do the Pontiffs do, who, while they say that they are Christ's vicars, exclude him with his Gospel from the Church? What do the Bishops do, who in like manner under the pretext of his name foully tear the Church apart, and play the part of those grievous wolves whom Paul long ago foretold would arise from that order? What do the princes and kings do, who ought to kiss the Son of God and be nursing fathers to his Church? Do not many of them kiss that great mother of harlotries, fall prostrate with their faces at her feet, and meanwhile persecute the Church of Christ with sword and fire? What shall we say of private men, of whom the greater part likewise disdain to acknowledge Christ as their King? For although some bear with him speaking in the Gospel, promising them, as far as concerns the grace of his Father, the remission of sins and eternal blessedness, yet as soon as they feel their sins being accused and themselves being pressed, so that they must submit themselves to Christ by the obedience of faith, straightway one may hear those voices: "Shall I, for the sake of this doctrine, change my manner of life, defraud my genius, and forsake the most pleasant company of my friends? I will never do it." And what else is this than to say to Christ, as it were to his face: "I do not want you to reign over me, since long ago I have bound myself to Bacchus, Venus, Mars, and Mercury, the god of thieves and merchants"? Such things are so common among those who wish and are considered to be Christians, that most of them are wont to claim dominion over Christ for themselves rather than be willing to obey him. This is a proof of incurable malice, by which we are at the same time admonished that for those who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus there is nothing else set before them in this world but the cross and persecution, and therefore, with the hope of an earthly kingdom left far behind, we ought to prepare ourselves for this.

units.la: At simul elucet in his potentia Christi verè diuina, qui Regnum suum inuito mundo & huius principe propagat indies atque tuetur: idq; nullis huius seculi armis adiutus. Quis enim hoc olim sperare poterat, quando Iudæi cum gentibus aduersus illum conspirauerant, & suæ coniurationis duces atq; protectores habebat Romanos Imperatores, penes quos tunc totius fere erat orbis imperiū? Prævaluit tamen ille per Apostolos, quibus tunc temporis nulli erant ignobiliores aut imbecilliores homines. Et quod tunc factum fuit, aliis quoq; seculis postea accidisse scimus. Quibus omnibus si ea addas, quæ hoc nouissimo tempore facta sunt, quando Pontificum tyrannide atque superstitionibus obrutam Euangelij sui lucem instaurauit, nemo negare poterit, totum hoc negotium ex Dei consilio pendere, & humanis viribus neq; defendi neq; impediri, multo minus euerti posse. Debet ista fidei no stræ confirmandæ seruire, ne aliquorū impia defectione offendamur. Etsi enim nunc peregrinari videtur Iesus Christus, idem tamen Ecclesiæ suæ curam minimè deposuit, & olim in aduentu suo (vt in sequenti Sermone audiemus) fidis seruis præmia digna retribuet, hostes autem horrendis supplicijs coercebit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But at the same time there shines forth in these things the truly divine power of Christ, who propagates and defends his kingdom day by day, though the world and its prince are unwilling, and that without any arms of this age to help him. For who could have hoped for this long ago, when the Jews had conspired with the Gentiles against him, and had as the leaders and protectors of their conspiracy the Roman Emperors, in whose hands at that time lay almost the whole empire of the world? Yet he prevailed through the Apostles, who at that time had no men more obscure or weaker than themselves. And what was done then, we know has also happened in later ages. If you add to all these things those things which have been done in this most recent time, when he restored the light of his Gospel, overwhelmed by the tyranny and superstitions of the Pontiffs, no one will be able to deny that this whole business depends on the counsel of God, and can be neither defended nor hindered by human strength, much less overthrown. This ought to serve to confirm our faith, lest we be offended by the impious defection of some. For although Jesus Christ seems now to be a sojourner, yet he has by no means laid down the care of his Church, and at his coming (as we shall hear in the following Sermon) he will render worthy rewards to his faithful servants, but will restrain his enemies with dreadful punishments. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXIIII.

units.la: Et factum est cùm redijsset accepto regno, tunc iussit ad se vocari seruos illos, quibus dederat pecuniā: vt cognosceret quis quid negotiatus esset. Adfuit autem primus, dicens: Domine, mina tua decem minas lucrifecit. Ille autem ait ei: Bene habet serue bone: quia in minimo fuisti fidelis, habeto potestatem super decem vrbes. Et alter venit dicens: Domine, mina tua confecit quinque minas. Ille vero & isti dixit: Tu quoq; præesto quinque vrbibus. Et alius venit, dicens: Domine, ecce mina tua quam habui repositam in sudario. Timui enim te, quòd homo es austerus: aufers quod non deposuisti, & metis quod non seminasti. Tum ille dixit ei: Ex ore tuo te iudicabo, serue male: sciebas me hominem austerum esse, qui auferam quod non deposui, & metam quod non seminaui: Quare igitur non dedisti pecuniam meam apud mensam, & ego veniens cum vsuris eam exegissem. Et astantibus dixit. Tollite ab eo minam, & date ei qui decem minas habet. Illi vero dixerunt ei: Domine, habet decem minas. Et ille: Nam dico vobis, Omni habenti dabitur: ei autem qui non habet, etiam quod habet adimetur. Quin etiam meos illos inimicos, qui noluerunt me regnare super se, adducite huc & iugulate coram me. Et his dictis antegrediebatur, ascendens Hierosolymam.
units.tr: And it came to pass, when he had returned, having received the kingdom, that he commanded those servants to be called to him, to whom he had given the money, that he might know what each had gained by trading. The first came, saying: "Lord, your pound has gained ten pounds." And he said to him: "Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful in the least, have authority over ten cities." And another came, saying: "Lord, your pound has made five pounds." He said to him also: "You too shall be over five cities." And another came, saying: "Lord, here is your pound, which I kept laid up in a napkin. For I feared you, because you are a severe man: you take up what you did not lay down, and you reap what you did not sow." Then he said to him: "I will judge you out of your own mouth, wicked servant. You knew that I am a severe man, who take up what I did not lay down, and reap what I did not sow. Why, then, did you not put my money in the bank, so that when I came I might have demanded it back with interest?" And to those standing by he said: "Take the pound from him and give it to the one who has ten pounds." But they said to him: "Lord, he has ten pounds." And he said: "I tell you, to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Moreover, bring here those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, and slay them before me." And having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

units.la: Quoniam discipuli Iesu Christi communi de regno eius terreno errore tenebantur, ipse verò eundem errorem omnibus seculis regnaturum sciebat, vt nimirum pleriq; in ipso regnum, honores, opes & quæ alia sunt huius seculi bona quærant: sæpe in Euangelio de Regno suo disserit, & iam morti vicinus omnem eius conditionem parabola ista complecti voluit, ne quis porro erroris locus esset apud eos, qui ipsum audire volunt. Et prima quidem parte docuit, Regnum suum nō de hoc mundo esse, sed cœleste: neq; vt huius mundi regna armis administrari, aut victoriis & externa maiestate conspicuū esse, sed omnem eius gubernationem in Spiritu & verbo consistere, & ijs ab ipso committi, qui verbi prædicatione Ecclesias colligere, et ipsi nouos quotidie discipulos adducere debeant. Ita verò & carnales istas de Regno suo opiniones confutat, & omnes officij admonet, qui eius ciues haberi volunt. Porrò ne quis illum interea otiari & omnē suæ Ecclesiæ curam depositsse putaret, alteram parabolæ huius partem subijcit, qua de suo aduentu ad nouissimum iudicium disserit, & quid tunc futurum sit docet. Qui locus multa consideratione dignissimus est, quia omnes homines ad officium faciendum excitat, & dulcissimam consolationem ijs præbet, qui quòd in sua vocatione Christo fideles sunt, mundi huius odijs & persecutionibus grauissimis exagitantur.
units.tr: Since the disciples of Jesus Christ were held by the common error about his earthly kingdom, and he himself knew that this same error would reign in every age, so that many seek in him a kingdom, honours, wealth and the other goods of this age, he often speaks in the Gospel about his kingdom. And now, being near death, he wished to embrace its whole condition in this parable, so that no further occasion for error might remain among those who wish to hear him. In the first part he taught that his kingdom is not of this world but heavenly, and that it is not administered by arms, nor made conspicuous by victories and outward majesty, but that its whole government consists in the Spirit and the word, and is committed by him to those who ought to gather churches by the preaching of the word and bring new disciples to himself every day. Thus he refutes those carnal opinions about his kingdom, and admonishes all who wish to be counted his citizens about their duty. Moreover, lest anyone should think that in the meantime he is idle and has laid aside all care of his Church, he adds the second part of this parable, in which he speaks of his coming to the last judgement and teaches what will then happen. This passage is most worthy of careful consideration, because it stirs all men to do their duty, and it offers the sweetest consolation to those who, because they are faithful to Christ in their calling, are harassed by the hatreds and most grievous persecutions of this world.

units.la: Sic autē ille loquitur: Et factū est cum redijsset accepto Regno, tunc iussit ad se vocari seruos illos, quibus dederat pecuniam, vt cognosceret quis quid negotiatus esset, & ab illis (vt in Matthæo habetur) negotiationis suæ rationes exigeret. Differtē autem et Regni in cœlis accepti, & sui ad nos reditus mentione facit, vt partim spe bona suos impleat, partim excitet, ne eius obliti in suo officio torpeant. In priori enim sui à nobis discessus & Ascensionis fructum indicat: qui est, quòd cœlos no bis obtinuit, à quibus propter peccatum exclusi eramus, & (vt apud Ioannem pollicetur) in illis locum nobis parauit, in quo cum ipso viuamus atq; regnemus. Neminem ergo huius seculi turbæ mo-ueant, nemo item huius mundi minis terreatur, sed inter huius conatus & vndique surgentia peri-cula semper dulcissimi illius dicti recordemur, quod capite vndecimo audiuimus: Noli timere pusil-le grex: quia placuit Patri dare vobis Regnum.
units.tr: Now he speaks thus: "And it came to pass, when he had returned, having received the kingdom, that he commanded those servants to be called to him, to whom he had given the money, that he might know what each had gained by trading," and from them (as is found in Matthew) he demanded an account of their trading. He makes mention both of the kingdom received in heaven and of his return to us, so that he may partly fill his people with good hope, partly stir them up, lest, forgetful of him, they grow sluggish in their duty. For in the former he points out the fruit of his departure from us and of his Ascension, which is that he has obtained for us the heavens, from which we had been shut out on account of sin, and (as he promises in John) has prepared a place for us in them, in which we may live and reign with him. Therefore let no tumult of this age move anyone, and let no threat of this world terrify anyone; but amid the efforts of this life and the dangers arising on every side, let us always remember that most sweet saying which we heard in the eleventh chapter: "Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased the Father to give you the kingdom."

units.la: In altero autem membro finem sui reditus atque aduentus nouissimi exprimit, qui erit, vt omni hominum rationes inspiciat, in primis autem eorum, quos Ecclesiæ suæ gubernaculis adhibuit. Ergo etsi nunc procul hinc peregrinari putetur, neq; res mortalium curare, vindice tamen oculo o-mnia intuetur, & olim iudex veniet, vt ijs qui ipsi fideles fuerunt, promissa vitæ æternæ præmia do-net, rebelles verò & contumaces æternis inferorum supplicijs mancipet. Est huius aduentus fre-quens mentio in sacris literis. De eo enim Prophetæ olim vaticinati sunt, & eundem Daniel egre-giè descripsit, qualem in spiritu viderat. Et Christus non hic solùm, sed sæpè aliàs de illo disserit, & in Matthæo totum iudicij illius processum graphicè depingit. Apostoli quoq; eius sæpissimè memi-nerunt, quoties de rebus maximi momenti disputant, et vel contumaces aut securos terrere, vel pios in periculis grauioribus consolari instituerunt. Denique illum omnibus Christianis, doctis, indoctis, viris & fœminis, pueris & senibus ita notum esse voluit Spiritus sanctus, vt inter fidei Christianæ articulos eum adscripserit. Prodest enim in eius meditatione frequenter versari: quia vix aliud est, quo carnis socordia facilius excuti & contemptus verbi efficacius reprimi possit: quàm si cogite-mus, nunquam nos euasuros esse, quin cogamur iudicem seuerum & iustum ferre eum, quem Regem mitissimum & liberalissimum agnoscere dedignamur. Omnes enim ad eius tribunal sistentur, omni-um corda & conscientiæ illic revelabuntur, omnes denique tunc in suis corporibus recipient quæcun-que vel bene vel male fecerunt. Neq; tunc aliquid præsidij erit in opibus, honoribus & authoritate huius seculi, quia in aduentu illo Christi tota hæc corruptibilis mundi machina dissoluetur, & omnia quæ ea continentur liquefient: neq; etiam vllæ defensiones & exceptiones iuuabunt, eò quòd conscien-tiæ testimonio res agetur, quod negari vel eludi nulla ratione aut artificio potest. Hæc qui non osci-tanter expendunt, ij certè nunquam sibi permittent, vt otio ignauo aut voluptatibus dediti officium negligant, quod ipsis à Deo creditum est: quin pungentis ipsos conscientiæ stimulos sentient, qui eos otiari aut dormire non patientur. Nam etsi hominum iudicio domini rerum videantur, & multa au-thoritate atq; potentia præstent, cogitabunt tamen se Domini nostri Iesu Christi seruos esse, cui olim functionis suæ rationem reddere cogentur: quod ipsis eo difficilius erit factu, quò maiorem prouinci-am & plura dona ab illo acceperunt.
units.tr: In the second part, however, he expresses the end of his return and of his last coming, which will be that he inspects the accounts of all men, and especially of those whom he has placed in charge of the government of his Church. Therefore, although he is thought now to be far away and does not care for the affairs of mortals, yet he sees all things with a watchful eye, and one day he will come as judge, to grant the promised rewards of eternal life to those who have themselves been faithful, but to hand over the rebellious and obstinate to the eternal punishments of hell. Mention of this coming is frequent in the sacred writings. For the prophets once foretold it, and Daniel described it admirably, as he had seen it in the Spirit. And Christ speaks of it not only here but often elsewhere, and in Matthew he vividly depicts the whole course of that judgement. His apostles too most often remember it whenever they dispute about matters of the greatest moment, and they have undertaken either to terrify the stubborn and the secure, or to console the godly in more grievous dangers. Finally, the Holy Spirit wished it to be so well known to all Christians, learned and unlearned, men and women, boys and old men, that he has included it among the articles of the Christian faith. For it is profitable to dwell frequently upon its meditation, because there is scarcely anything by which the sloth of the flesh may more easily be shaken off and contempt of the word more effectually restrained, than if we consider that we shall never escape, but must be made to bear as judge the stern and just one whom we disdain to acknowledge as the gentlest and most generous King. For all will be brought before his tribunal; the hearts and consciences of all will be revealed there; and finally all will then receive in their bodies whatever they have done, whether good or bad. Nor will there then be any protection in the wealth, honours and authority of this age, because at that coming of Christ this whole corruptible machine of the world will be dissolved, and all the things contained in it will melt away. Nor will any defences or excuses help, since the matter will be decided by the testimony of conscience, which cannot be denied or evaded by any device or trickery. Those who weigh these things carefully will certainly never allow themselves to neglect the duty entrusted to them by God, giving themselves up to idle sloth or pleasures; rather, they will feel the goads of conscience pricking them, which will not suffer them to be idle or to sleep. For although in the judgement of men they may seem to be masters of affairs, and excel in great authority and power, yet they will reflect that they are servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom they will one day be compelled to render an account of their office; and this will be all the harder for them, the greater the province and the more numerous the gifts they have received from him.

units.la: Porrò audiamus quid factum sit, quando nobilis ille homo rationes cum seruis iniit, vt disca-mus quid olim sit euenturum, quando Dei Filius ad iudicium veniet. Inter seruos producuntur tres, quorum duo frugi, sed tamen impares sunt (primus enim in negotiatione sua felicior decem minas lu-cratus est, alter quinq; tantum) tertius autem ignauus acceptam ab hero pecuniam in sudario asser-uatam defodit, & se officio probè defunctum arbitratur, si illi quod suum est reddat. Adumbrantur his duo hominum genera inter eos, qui Christi serui habentur, & eius professione gaudent. Primum eorum est, qui pro suæ vocationis ratione Dei donis bene vtuntur, vt his & gloriam eius prouehant, & multorum quoq; aliorum saluti consulant. Alterum ignauos habet, qui solo dignitatis titulo aut nomine turgidi, interea vel otio suo consulunt, vel seruili metu impediti nihil audent eorum, quæ ex officio facere debebant.
units.tr: Let us next hear what was done when that noble man reckoned with his servants, so that we may learn what will one day happen when the Son of God comes to judgement. Three servants are brought forward, of whom two are good but nevertheless unequal (for the first, being more successful in his trading, gained ten pounds, the second only five), while the third, being idle, buried the money he had received from his master, kept in a napkin, and thinks he has discharged his office well if he returns to him what was his own. By these three figures are shadowed two kinds of men among those who are counted servants of Christ and rejoice in his profession. The first kind is of those who, according to the nature of their calling, make good use of God's gifts, so that by them they may advance his glory and also care for the salvation of many others. The other kind has idle men, who, puffed up only by the title or name of dignity, meanwhile either look after their own ease, or, hindered by servile fear, dare to do none of those things which they ought to have done by virtue of their office.

units.la: In primo genere, quod duos habet (vt modò diximus) quorum alius alio felicior fuit & maius lucrum fecit, obseruabimus, discrimina esse inter Christi ministros, & eos inter se gradibus quoq; cer-tis distare, vt alius alij præstet. Nec enim pari mensura Deus dona sua distribuit: non quod perso-narum respectu ducatur, sed quòd vnicuiq; (vt Matthæus annotauit) dare solet secundum suam fa-cultatem, id est, singulis ea dat, quæ functioni suæ, ad quam ipsum destinauit, seruiunt, & ad eam obeundam possunt sufficere. Vt enim nouit cui rei quisq; idoneus sit: ita donis quoq; necessarijs vnum quenque instruit. Docet hoc non vno loco Paulus, cuius verba cum nuper recitauerimus, eadem hic repetere non est opus. Hinc ergo fit, quòd alij alijs plus proficiunt in opere Domini: non quidè propria virtute, sed quòd Deus illorum opera ad res plures & excellentiores vti dignatur. Sic Paulus præ aliis electum illud organum Christi fuit, qui plus omnibus Apostolis laborauit, non quidem ipse (vt illius verbis vtar) sed gratia Dei, quæ cum illo erat. Et olim inter Prophetas alij alijs felicius & diutius docendi munus obierunt: quod ipsum hodie fieri nemo negabit, qui Ecclesiæ propagationem cum ijs, qui in ea laborant aut seruiunt, diligentius inspexerit. Non tamen ista inæqualitas alium terrere debet, vt animum despondeat, aut suum officium Deo minus gratum fore existimet, si ab alijs multis studio & successu vincatur. Quia enim omnes illius serui sunt, & hic in omnibus sua gratia & spiritu agit, omnium quoque officia sibi grata & accepta habet, qui syncero pietatis studio faciunt quod possunt: & ijsdem dona sua augere solet Deus, vt & ipsi magis proficiant, & plures alios quotidie ad salutis societatem adducant.
units.tr: On the first kind, which has two members (as we have just said), one of whom was more fortunate than the other and made greater gain, we shall observe that there are differences among Christ's ministers, and that they also stand at certain degrees apart from one another, so that one excels another. For God does not distribute his gifts in equal measure. This is not because he regards persons, but because to each one (as Matthew noted) he is accustomed to give according to his ability: that is, he gives to each the gifts that serve the office to which he has appointed him and that can suffice for discharging it. For just as he knows for what task each man is fit, so he equips each one with the gifts necessary for it. Paul teaches this in more than one place, and since we recently recited his words, there is no need to repeat them here. Hence it comes about that some make more progress than others in the Lord's work: not by their own virtue, but because God deigns to use their labours for more numerous and more excellent ends. Thus Paul was that chosen instrument of Christ, set above the others, who laboured more than all the Apostles, yet not himself (to use his own words) but by the grace of God which was with him. And in former times among the Prophets, some discharged the office of teaching more successfully and for longer than others. No one will deny that this same thing happens today, if he looks carefully at the growth of the Church together with those who labour or serve in it. Yet this inequality ought not to terrify another, so that he loses heart or thinks that his own office will be less pleasing to God if he is surpassed by many others in zeal and success. For since all are his servants, and since he works in all of them by his grace and Spirit, he holds the duties of all as pleasing and acceptable, provided they perform with sincere zeal of piety what they can. And God is accustomed to increase his gifts in the same people, so that they may themselves make more progress and every day bring many others into the fellowship of salvation.

units.la: Docet hoc in præsenti Christus, quando vtriq; præmium adscriptum fuisse ait. Primo enim dicitur: Bene habet serue bone, quia in minimo fuisti fidelis, habeto potestate super decem vrbes. Altery vero: Tu quoq; præsto quinq; vrbibus. Apud Matthæu generalius loquitur, vtriq; dicens: Intra in gaudium domini tui. Hic vrbes assignantur, vt ostendat in promptu sibi fore, quo fidelium labores in die illo rependat: & ad principum mores alludit, qui seruos quorum opera in pecuniarum & rerum minorum dispensatione vsi sunt, & quos sibi fideles atq; vtiles inuenerunt, solent vrbium & prouinciarum siue regionum gubernationi præficere. Paucis autē multa comprehendit, quæ præmij huius magnitudinem non obscurè exprimunt. Nam primò tam ipsos quàm studium eorum publicè commendat, dicens: Bene habet serue bone. Ita Christus olim in aduentu suo suorum seruorum fidem atq; opera in totius mundi conspectu probabit, quando illis dicet: Esuriui, et dedistis mihi cibū: sitiui, & dedistis mihi potum, &c. Quod vnum nobis sufficere debet aduersus iniqua impiorum de nobis iudicia, qui nobis obtrectant, si Euangelij doctrinam liberè prædicemus, Dei veri cultum contra superstitiones afferamus, & multos quotidie à peccatis & erroribus in viam salutis adducamus. Dicant illi nos importunos, dicaces, turbulentos, seditiosos, impostores, hæreticos, sacrilegos, et omne genus conuiciorum atq; maledictionum in capita nostra congerant: modò olim nobis detur lætam banc Iesu Christi voce audire: Bene habet, serue bone. Nec enim hæc inania verba sunt aut tituli inanes, quibus huius sæculi principes seruos ambitiosos remunerantur: qui secum magnificè actum putant, si post multos labores et infinita pericula, nobilitatis gradu aut equestris ordinis insignibus donetur, & immanem aliquā bestiam in tabella lignea, aut etiam in papyro vel fragili vitro cum fenestrata aut coronata galea ostentare possint. Sed maior est nostri Regis liberalitas, qui singulis olim dicet: Intra in gaudium domini tui. Et simul omnibus: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete Regnum paratum vobis ab iactis fundamentis mundi. Quod non aliud est, quàm quòd eiusdem felicitatis nos socios habere vult, in qua ipse nunc viuit & regnat ad dextram Patris sui omnipotetis. Ita enim alibi pollicetur, dicens: Volo, vt vbi ego sum, ibi etiā sit minister meus. Item: Volo Pater, vt vbi sum ego, ibi etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Nemini autē hic scrupulum injiciat, quòd vni quidem decem, alteri quinq; vrbes assignantur. Sunt enim præmiorū discrimina quidem, & (vt D. Augustinus ex Pauli verbis annotauit) alia est gloria Solis, alia Lunæ, & alia gloria stellarū, imò stella à stella differt in gloria: veruntamen omnibus datur denarius ille, quo vita æterna adumbratur, qui in vinea Domini quantulocunq; temporis spatio ad suæ vitæ finem vsq; laborauerunt: omnesq; in conspectu Dei satietate gaudiorum atq; bonorum cœlestium fruentur. Ea deniq; est cœlestis illius patriæ gloria & beatitas, vt cum Dauide omnes pij dicant: Malo ad limē domus Dei defidere, quàm habitare in tentoriis impiorum. Et facit ad præmij huius amplificationem, quod fideli seruo hic dicitur: Quia in minimo fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam. Minima enim dicit Euangelicæ prædicationis mu-nus & quæ huius ministris dona diuinitus conferuntur, vt illud digně possint obire. Atqui hæc eius-modi sunt, vt sine illis salus nostra nobis constare non possit: & ideo ea Dominus margarita & thesauro cōfert incomparabili, cuius obtinendi causa quis omnes fortunas aut facultates suas vendere debeat. Sed reuera pauca & parua sunt, si cum cœlestibus illis bonis & æternis conferantur, quæ (vt Propheta ait) oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, neq; in cor hominis ascenderunt. Ibi enim Deum videbimus facie ad faciem: ibi spiritus nostri in Domino exultabunt, corpora autem nostra gloriosò Christi corpori similia facta æternum viuent. Et sanè incomparabilem & omni intellectu excellentioexcellentiorem esse oportet eam felicitatem, quae non alio pretio redimi, nec alia industria aut labore acquiri potuit, quàm Filij Dei vnigeniti sanguine atq; merito. Etenim quando totam istam mundi machinam Deo ex nihilo producere visum fuit, vnicum verbum tanto operi potuit sufficere. Dicebat enim Deus, Fiat lux: & facta est lux. Item, Fiat firmamentum: & factum est. Et rursum, Congregentur aquae quae sub coelis sunt, in vnum locum, vt appareat arida: & factum est ita. Quod ipsum de omnibus alijs mundi partibus Moses perhibet. At quando amissam salutem reparari, & coelestis illius domus ianua iterum aperiri, Regnum deniq; illud acquiri oportuit, quo nos indignos Deus or-are & beare statuerat, tunc non verbis res acta est, sed Filii eius sanguine pretioso opus fuit. Quis ergo tam stupidus sit, vt ista cogitans, illius amore & desiderio non accendatur, & omnes vitae huius labores leues & iucundos, pericula item omnia facilia, imò nulla ducat, vt eo possit potiri?
units.tr: Christ teaches this in the present passage, when he says that a reward was assigned to each of the two. For first he is said: "Well done, good servant, because you were faithful in the least thing, have authority over ten cities." To the other: "You too are over five cities." In Matthew he speaks more generally, saying to both: "Enter into the joy of your lord." Here cities are assigned, to show that the reward for the faithful labours of those people will be ready for him on that day; and he alludes to the custom of princes, who are accustomed to set over the government of cities and provinces or regions those servants whose work they have used in the management of smaller sums and possessions, and whom they have found faithful and useful to themselves. He comprehends much in few words, which express the greatness of this reward not obscurely. For first he commends both them and their zeal publicly, saying: "Well done, good servant." So Christ will one day, at his coming, make known the faith and works of his servants in the sight of the whole world, when he says to them: "I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink," and so on. This alone ought to be enough for us against the unjust judgements of the impious about us, who detract from us, if we freely preach the doctrine of the Gospel, set forth the true worship of God against superstitions, and every day lead many from sins and errors into the way of salvation. Let them call us troublesome, abusive, turbulent, seditious, impostors, heretics, sacrilegious, and let them heap on our heads every kind of insult and curse: only let us one day hear this joyful voice of Jesus Christ: "Well done, good servant." For these are not empty words or idle titles, with which the princes of this age reward ambitious servants, who think they have been treated magnificently if, after many labours and endless dangers, they are granted the rank of nobility or the insignia of the equestrian order, and can display a fierce beast on a wooden panel, or even on papyrus or fragile glass, with a window-shaped or crowned helmet. But greater is the generosity of our King, who will one day say to each: "Enter into the joy of your lord." And to all together: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." This is nothing other than that he wishes us to be sharers in that same happiness in which he himself now lives and reigns at the right hand of his omnipotent Father. For so he promises elsewhere, saying: "I will that where I am, there my servant also may be." Again: "Father, I will that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me." Let no one here be troubled by the fact that to one ten cities, and to another five, are assigned. For there are indeed differences in rewards, and (as Augustine noted from the words of Paul) there is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, and another glory of the stars; indeed star differs from star in glory. Yet to all is given that denarius by which eternal life is foreshadowed, namely to those who laboured in the Lord's vineyard for whatever length of time up to the end of their life; and all will enjoy, in the sight of God, the satiety of joys and heavenly goods. Finally, such is the glory and blessedness of that heavenly homeland that all the godly say with David: "I would rather sit at the threshold of the house of God than dwell in the tents of the impious." And it contributes to the enlargement of this reward that to the faithful servant it is said here: "Because you were faithful in the least thing, I will set you over many things." For by "least things" he means the office of evangelical preaching and the gifts divinely conferred on its ministers, so that they can discharge it worthily. Yet these are of such a kind that without them our salvation cannot stand; and therefore the Lord confers them as a pearl and an incomparable treasure, for the sake of obtaining which one ought to sell all one's fortunes and possessions. But in truth these are few and small if they are compared with those heavenly and eternal goods, which (as the Prophet says) "eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man." For there we shall see God face to face; there our spirits will exult in the Lord, and our bodies, made like the glorious body of Christ, will live for ever. And indeed that happiness must be incomparable and more excellent than all understanding, since it could not be redeemed by any other price, nor acquired by any other industry or labour, than by the blood and merit of the only-begotten Son of God. For when it pleased God to produce this whole machine of the world out of nothing, a single word was enough for so great a work. For God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. Again, "Let there be a firmament," and it was so. And again, "Let the waters that are under the heavens be gathered into one place, so that the dry land may appear," and it was so. Moses reports the same of all the other parts of the world. But when lost salvation had to be restored, and the gate of that heavenly house opened again, and that kingdom finally acquired, to which God had determined to ordain and bless us, though we were unworthy, then the matter was not done by words, but there was need of his Son's precious blood. Who then is so stupid that, thinking on these things, he is not kindled with love and desire for that, and does not count all the labours of this life light and pleasant, and likewise all dangers easy, indeed none at all, so that he may gain it?

units.la: Sed transeamus ad alterum genus seruorum Christi, quorum typus est malae frugis & ignavus ille, quem tertio loco numerat. Nam alius (inquit) venit, & dixit: Domine, ecce mina tua, quam habui repositam in sudario. De hoc Matthaeus sic scribit: Qui vnum talentum acceperat, abiens defodit in terram, & abscondit pecuniam domini sui. Nunc verò idem, quando ille rationes à singulis exigit, acceptam pecuniam hero reddit, & suae ignaviae defensionem instituit mirificam. Timui te (inquit) quòd homo auerterus sis: Auferis quod non deposuisti & metis quod non seminasti. Itaque timens abij, abscondi talentum tuum in terra: ecce habes quod tuum est. Constat excusatio haec maxima ex parte criminis translatione: nam suae ignaviae culpam in heri austeritatem atque rigorem transfert, sibi verò frugi serui officium & prudentiam vendicat, qui pecuniam illius ita asseruerit, vt quamvis ea nullum fecerit lucrum, ipsi tamen extra damnum sit, cum sortem integram recipiat. Ita verò cum ignavia impudentiam summam coniungit.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the other kind of Christ's servants, whose type is that wicked and lazy man whom he mentions third. "Another came," he says, "and said: Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a napkin." Matthew writes of this man as follows: "He who had received one talent went away, dug a hole in the earth, and hid his master's money." Now, when the master calls each servant to account, this man returns the money he received and offers a remarkable defence of his laziness. "I feared you," he says, "because you are a harsh man: you take away what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow. So in my fear I went away and hid your talent in the earth. See, you have what is yours." This excuse rests mostly on shifting the blame. He puts the fault for his idleness on his master's severity and rigour, while claiming for himself the role and prudence of a thrifty servant, who guarded his master's money so carefully that, though it earned no profit, he himself suffered no loss, since he got back the whole principal. In this way he joins the greatest impudence to his laziness.

units.la: In huius autem exemplo ingenium & mores hypocritarum ceu in tabula depictos, Dominus nobis proponit. Primò non minus quàm alij dominum suum agnoscit, & ita seruum se esse profitetur. Ita hypocritae etiam Christum dominum dicere & seruos huius se profiteri solent: & in nouissimo die olim dicere audebunt: Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetauimus, & per nomen tuum daemonia eiecimus, & per nomen tuum multas virtutes fecimus? Imò vt male frugis serui ad quaeuis simulanda ferè bonis & industrijs doctiores sunt, & egregiè ad oculum seruire possunt: ita illi quoq; se ad omnia officia praestanda paratissimos esse fingunt, & si externam modò speciem consideres, eos pijs & fidis Christi seruis sanctiores multò esse putabis. Interim verò, vt ille in hero nihil quàm ingenium auserum & mores difficiles obseruat, imò eundem accusat, vt qui ad rem nimium attentus vndique lucrum colligat, nullum verò eius benignitatis mentionem facit, quia ipsum in familiam suam adoptauerat, & pecuniam suâ eius fidei crediderat: Ita hypocritae in Deo nihil praeter iustitiae rigorem agnoscunt, qui Legem dederit cui nemo mortalium sufficiat, qui obedientiam perfectam ab ijs quoq; exigat, quos donis ad hanc praestandam necessarijs non instruxit, qui deniq; morosior plus aequo nullis officijs sese deliniri aut placari patiatur. Quis enim nescit eorum voces, quas illis Isaias tribuit: Quare ieiunauimus, & tu non aspicis? affligimus animas nostras, & tu ignoras? Et hodie passim occurrunt, qui vt primùm Verbo Dei suarum virium fiduciam & operum merita euerti sentiunt, in eiusmodi voces erumpunt, quibus Deum iniquitatis accusant, qui cum hominibus ludat ea exigendo, quae ipsis praestitu impossibilia sint, & proinde interitu eorum delectetur. Inter omnia verò ista ne verbulo quidem vno eius gratiam praedicant, qui nos seruorum, imò filiorum loco habere dignatur, & voluntatem suam amicissimè reuelat, simulque Filium dilectum nobis offert, cuius virtute & merito omnis nostra infirmitas atque imperfectio farciatur. At quid impudentius fingi poterat, quàm hominem aduersus Deum insurgere, & de eius rigore atque morositate conqueri, qui nisi nos tenerrimè amaret & iniuriarum quoque tolerantissimus esset, tibi ne spiritus quidem esset ad voces illas proferendum, quibus illum accusas? Quid item iniquius, quàm de Legis onere conqueri, dissimulare autem Christi meritum, qui nobis ab illo satisfactio datus est, & spiritum illum adoptionis, quo adiuti & nouis viribus aucti omnia in illo possumus? Praeterea vt ignavus ille seruus contempto heri mandato, qui negotiari iusserat, nouum consilium init: neglecto item conseruorum exemplo, quos industrios videbat, nouam rationem excogitat, qua heri sui rebus consulat: Ita est hoc proprium hypocritis, quòd relicta vocatione Domini & procul abiectis eius mandatis nouum vitæ genus sibi eligunt, & in suis operibus electitijs mirificè sibijpsis placent. Etenim ad omnes homines vox ista Domini pertinet, Negotiamini donec veniam. Debent enim Verbi prædicatione instare ministri, vt plures quotidie Christo lucrifaciant. Magistratuum ess suum quoque populum eidem adducere, vt in vera pietate & legitimo Dei cultu omnes proficiant. Priuatos homines decet, vt coniugium sanctè colant, liberos ad Dei honorem educent, rem domesti cam fideliter curent, vt & ipsi cum suis absque aliorum molestia honestè viuant, & aliorum quoque inopiam sua liberalitate subleuare possint. Denique naturæ legibus hoc à nobis exigi constat, ne quis sibijpsi viuat, sed vt quisq; suas facultates & studium suum in commune deferat, & vno studio, vno spiritu & ore Deus in omnibus glorificetur. At longè alia hypocritarum mens est, qui tunc demum se officio functos esse existimant, si loco Verbi Dei psalmodiæ lingua peregrina instituatur, ad Missæ spectaculum homines vocentur, ferientur, ieiunent, ad Diuorum statuas discurrant, cereis & lam padibus templa exornent, anathemata suspendant: item relicto coiugio & procul abiecta Reipub. cura vitam monasticam quis viuat, nec sibijpsi nec cuiquam mortalium vtilis: si denique sub obe dientiæ, paupertatis voluntariæ & castitatis prætextu parentibus simul & magistratui legitimo debitum obsequium negent, inter diuitias amplissimas & aliorum labore partas otientur, thoris item alienis insidias struant, aut ea quoque occulte faciant, quæ ne verbis quidem eloqui fas est. Et hi tamen præ alijs serui Dei dici volunt, vt qui mundo mortui se totos huius seruitio consecrauerint. Mirificum sanè & nouum seruorum genus, qui nunquam seruiunt, & contemptis heri præceptis omnia pro suo arbitrio faciunt. Sed debent his etiam adnumerari, qui Euangelicæ Veritatis cognitione donati, & donis non vulgaribus instructi, otio suo potius quam gloriæ Dei & hominum saluti consulunt. In horum albo non pauci Ecclesiarum ministri sunt, qui in docendo frigidi hoc vnum agunt, ne alicuius odium in se provocent, & ideo prætermittis minis Dei, quibus ille peccatores territat, solius gratiæ prædicatione illis delitias faciunt, pusillos consuunt, quibus suauiter indormiant, qui seueriori iudiciorum irati Dei denuntiatione ad officium faciendum excitari debebant. Similes horum sunt qui in repub. ofcitantius agunt, morum licentiam induci patiuntur, & suo otio fruantur simulq; quæstum faciant, Dei gloriam simul & populi ipsorum fidei commissi salutem securi negligunt. Meretur his accenseri parentes quoq;, qui in liberis suis instituendis negligentiores sunt, aut quicunq; alia nimia indulgentia eos corrumpunt, quos in officio continere debebant. Et hi quidè se excusatos abunde putant, quòd à sceleribus gravioribus abstineant, quòd ad superstitiones & vitia neminem cogant, quòd deniq; etiamsi neminem lucrifaciant Christo, eiusdem tamen regno faueant, nec aliquę remorentur, quò minus ad illum accedat. Et hi plerunq; ex hominum contumacia & Dei prouidentia rationes decerpunt, quibus se excusent. Quid (inquiunt) faciamus ijs, qui nec Dei Verbo credere, nec bonis legibus obedire volunt? Quis inuitos coget? Dei hoc opus est, animos no nos creare, voluntatem in melius flectere & cœlestium desiderio eos accendere, qui nunc toti terrenis studijs immersi sunt. Quòd si hic illos efficaciter vocare & spiritus sui virtute trahere non vult, nos quod præterea faciamus non habemus. Num armis cogemus reluctantes? Num bella moueamus non necessaria, quorum exitus incertus, & plerunq; infelix est? Hæc & similia multa hodie audi- untur, & sunt rationes istæ carni admodum plausibiles, quia & otium nobis commendant, & multo rum odia declinant, quibus exagitantur, qui Christo fideliter seruiunt. Et qui ista dicere consueue- runt, hodie fere pro optimis & sapientissimis habentur.
units.tr: In this example the Lord sets before us, as if painted on a tablet, the character and manners of hypocrites. First, like the others, this servant acknowledges his master and so professes himself a servant. Hypocrites likewise are accustomed to call Christ Lord and to profess themselves his servants, and on the last day they will one day dare to say: "Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" Indeed, just as the wicked servant is skilled at feigning almost any of the good and diligent qualities, and can serve admirably in the eye of others, so they also pretend to be most ready to perform every duty; and if you look only at the outward appearance, you would think them far holier than the faithful and godly servants of Christ. Meanwhile, however, just as that servant in his master notices nothing but a harsh temper and difficult manners, and even accuses him of being too intent on business and gathering profit from every side, while making no mention of his kindness, though he had adopted him into his household and entrusted his money to his good faith, so hypocrites recognise in God nothing but the rigour of justice. They say he gave a Law which no mortal can keep, that he demands perfect obedience even from those whom he has not furnished with the gifts needed to render it, and that, in short, he is more morose than is right and allows himself to be softened or appeased by no services. Who does not know the complaints which Isaiah assigns to them? "Why have we fasted, and you do not look? We have afflicted our souls, and you take no notice?" And today there are everywhere people who, as soon as they feel the confidence in their own powers and the merits of their works overthrown by the Word of God, burst out into such complaints, accusing God of injustice, as if he mocks men by demanding what is impossible for them and so takes pleasure in their ruin. Yet in all this they do not mention, even in a single word, his grace, who deigns to regard us not as servants but as sons, who most kindly reveals his will and at the same time offers us his beloved Son, by whose power and merit all our weakness and imperfection is made good. But what more impudent thing could be imagined than a man rising up against God and complaining of his rigour and moroseness, when, had he not loved us most tenderly and been most patient of injuries, you would not even have the breath to utter those words with which you accuse him? What is more unjust than to complain about the burden of the Law while ignoring the merit of Christ, who was given to us as our satisfaction, and that Spirit of adoption by whose help, strengthened with new powers, we can do all things in him? Moreover, just as that idle servant, scorning his master's command to trade, devised a new plan, and, neglecting the example of his fellow servants whom he saw to be diligent, thought up a new method by which to look after his master's affairs, so it is characteristic of hypocrites that, abandoning the Lord's calling and casting his commands far aside, they choose for themselves a new way of life and take great delight in their own chosen works. For that word of the Lord, "Trade until I come," pertains to all men. Ministers of the Word ought to press on with the preaching of the Word, that more people may be won to Christ every day. Magistrates ought to bring their own people to the same end, that all may advance in true piety and lawful worship of God. Private persons ought to keep marriage holy, bring up their children to the honour of God, care faithfully for their household affairs, so that they may live honestly with their own without troubling others, and may also be able by their generosity to relieve the want of others. Finally, it is plain that the laws of nature require this of us: that no one lives for himself, but that each brings his abilities and zeal to the common good, and that God is glorified in all things with one zeal, one spirit and one mouth. But the mind of hypocrites is quite different. They think they have discharged their duty only when, in place of the Word of God, psalms are sung in a foreign tongue, when people are summoned to the spectacle of the Mass, beaten, made to fast, run about to the statues of the saints, and adorn their churches with wax candles and lamps, and hang up votive offerings. Likewise, having left marriage behind and cast off the care of the commonwealth, they live a monastic life, useful to neither themselves nor anyone else; and finally, under the pretext of obedience, voluntary poverty and chastity, they refuse the obedience they owe to their parents and to the lawful magistrate, while they live in idleness amid the vast riches won by the labour of others, lay snares for other men's beds, or secretly do even those things which it is not right even to name. Yet these people wish to be called servants of God before others, as those who, dead to the world, have consecrated themselves wholly to its service. A remarkable and new kind of servants indeed, who never serve, and who, scorning their master's precepts, do everything according to their own pleasure. But those must also be counted among these who, endowed with the knowledge of the Gospel truth and furnished with gifts not commonplace, consult their own leisure rather than the glory of God and the salvation of men. Among their number are not a few ministers of the churches who, cold in teaching, pursue this one aim: not to provoke anyone's hatred against themselves. Therefore they pass over the threats of God with which he terrifies sinners, and by preaching grace alone they pamper their hearers, sewing small pillows on which they may sleep softly, when they ought to have been roused to do their duty by a sterner proclamation of the judgments of an angry God. Similar to these are those who act lazily in the commonwealth, allow licence of morals to be introduced, enjoy their leisure and at the same time make a profit, and carelessly neglect the glory of God together with the salvation of the people entrusted to them. Parents also deserve to be reckoned among these, who are too negligent in bringing up their children, or who corrupt them by any other excessive indulgence, when they ought to have kept them under discipline. These people think they are amply excused because they abstain from grave crimes, because they force no one into superstition and vice, and because, even if they win no one for Christ, they at least favour his kingdom and do not hinder anyone from coming to him. And these people very often pluck out reasons for excusing themselves from men's obstinacy and God's providence. "What," they say, "are we to do with those who will neither believe the Word of God nor obey good laws? Who will compel the unwilling? It is God's work to create minds, to turn the will towards better things, and to kindle with desire for heavenly things those who are now wholly immersed in earthly pursuits. But if he does not wish to call them effectively here and draw them by the power of his Spirit, we have no means of doing anything further. Shall we compel the reluctant by arms? Shall we stir up unnecessary wars, whose outcome is uncertain and generally unhappy?" These and many similar arguments are heard today, and these reasons are very pleasing to the flesh, because they commend leisure to us and turn aside the hatred of many people by which those who serve Christ faithfully are harassed. And those who are accustomed to say such things are today generally regarded as the best and wisest of men.

units.la: Sed Iesu Christi, Filij Dei, de illis iudicium audiamus, quod olim in magno illo die aduersus eos pronuntiabit. Ex ore tuo (inquit) te iudicabo serue male: sciebas me hominem esse austerum, qui au- feram quod non deposui, & metâ quod non seminaui: Quare ergo non dedisti pecuniam meam apud mensam, & ego veniens cum vsuris eam exegissem? Primò seruum malum dicit. Non ergo ij soli in Ecclesia serui mali sunt, qui vel falsa doctrina vel alijs modis nocet aut malum dant: verumetiam qui Regnum Christi non promouent pro suæ vocationis & donorū, quæ acceperunt ratione. Etenim quis bonum seruum in agricultura dixerit eum, qui neq; arat, neq; sementem facit, neq; vites propa gare studet, sed otio & ignauiæ deditus terras segnes iacere, agros & vineas frutescere, pecora deni- fame perire finit? Vel annon satis malus hero mercatori seruus fuerit, qui omissa omni negotiatione merces simul omnes cum pecunijs sibi creditis in vnū colligit et conclusas seruat, etiam quando illas cum lucro poterat distrahere? Eadem ratione mali serui sunt in agro Domini & negotiatione illa spirituali, quotquot in officio suo torpent, & dona spiritus ignavo otio defodiunt, & nec propriam neque aliorum salutem prouehunt. At si isti mali serui sunt, quales obsecro eos esse dicemus, qui in agro Domini zizania superstitionum seminant, qui disciplinae septa ipsi perrumpunt, qui oues deglubunt & mactant, qui donis Spiritus sancti ad suum quaestum abutuntur, & negotiantur quidem, sed ea ratione, quam olim Simon Magus instituit, & quam Zacharias Propheta aperte damnat, quando Chananaeis aut mercatoribus locum in Ecclesia fore negat? Est horum magnus numerus hodie, & patronos ijdem habent potentia & authoritate graues: attamen nunquam effugient Dei iudicium.
units.tr: But let us hear the judgment that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, will one day pronounce against them on that great day. "Out of your own mouth," he says, "I will judge you, wicked servant. You knew that I am a harsh man, who takes up what I did not lay down and reaps what I did not sow. Why then did you not put my money on deposit, so that when I came I might have exacted it with interest?" First, he calls him a wicked servant. So it is not only those in the Church who do harm by false doctrine or by other means, or who give bad example, who are wicked servants, but also those who do not advance the kingdom of Christ according to their calling and the gifts they have received. Indeed, who would call a servant good in farming if he neither ploughs nor sows, takes no care to propagate the vines, but, given over to leisure and idleness, lets the land lie fallow, the fields and vineyards grow wild, and the cattle perish of hunger? Or would not a servant be wicked enough for a merchant master if, abandoning all trade, he gathered all the goods together with the money entrusted to him and kept them locked up, even though he could have sold them at a profit? By the same reasoning, all who grow sluggish in their office in the Lord's field and in that spiritual trade, who bury the gifts of the Spirit in lazy idleness, and who promote neither their own salvation nor that of others, are wicked servants. But if these are wicked servants, what shall we call, I beseech you, those who in the Lord's field sow the tares of superstition, who themselves break through the hedges of discipline, who flay and slaughter the sheep, who abuse the gifts of the Holy Spirit for their own gain, and who do trade, but in the manner that Simon Magus once devised, and which the prophet Zechariah openly condemns when he denies that there will be any room in the Church for the Canaanite or the merchant? There is a great number of these today, and they have as patrons men weighty in power and authority; yet they will never escape the judgment of God.

units.la: Deinde ex proprio ore & verbis proprijs seruus ille iudicatur. Si enim heri sui austeritatem & quam is ad lucrum attentus esset, nouerat: eo magis puniri meretur eius ignauia & otium, cui se se dedidit. Solet autem hoc vulgo accidere hypocritis, ut proprio ore seipsos accusent simul & condemnent. Queruntur de Dei seueritate & rigore, qui Legem dederit, quam nemo hominum vnquam praestare potuerit, & sibi iniuriam fieri clamant, si propter eius transgressionem damnentur. Sed haec dicendo seipsos accusant, & sui oris testimonio possunt conuinci. Si enim Dei seueritatem verae agnoscunt, cur non de illo placando & mitigando cogitant? Cur eius iram quaeritis & murmure iniquo subinde magis irritant? Si Legem praestitu impossibilem & suas vires infirmiores esse sentiunt, qua ut quis illi satisfacere queat, cur non ad eum confugiunt, quem idem ille nobis iustitiam & satisfactionem fecit, Iesum Christum videlicet? qui (ut Paulus ait) pro nobis peccatum factus est, ut nos iustitia Dei per ipsum efficeremur? cur item spreta iustitia Dei, quam hic nobis in Filio suo per Euangelium offert, suam iustitiam stabilire & venditare conantur, quae reuera nulla est, & cuius vanitate ipsi in propria conscientia quotidie experiuntur? Adde his, quod nostri seculi hypocritae ex suis precibus & Psalmodijs iudicabuntur. Cum enim nobiscum orent, Pater noster qui es in coelis: cum Symbolu fidei Apostolicae nobiscum commune habeant: cum Scripturis sacris, perinde ut nos, Dei Verbum contineri fateantur: Interim tamen Diuos inuocant, fide mirifice in creaturas omnis generis, in Romanas indulgentias, in suorum operum merita, in Purgatorij ignis lustrationem & sexcenta alia distrahunt, adhaec toti a Patrum canonibus, a Conciliorum decretis & incertis hominum traditionibus pendent, quae omnia vnanimi veteris ac noui Testamenti consensu damnantur. Quae ergo excusatio illis reliqua esse potest, qui seipsos suo ore accusant & damnant?
units.tr: Next, that servant is judged out of his own mouth and by his own words. For if he knew his master's severity and how intent he was on gain, then his idleness and laziness, to which he gave himself, deserve all the more punishment. This commonly happens to hypocrites: they accuse and condemn themselves by their own mouths. They complain of the severity and rigour of God, who gave a Law that no man has ever been able to keep, and they cry out that they are wronged if they are condemned for its transgression. But in saying this they accuse themselves, and they can be convicted by their own testimony. For if they truly acknowledge God's severity, why do they not think about appeasing and softening him? Why do they seek his anger and, by unjust murmuring, keep provoking it further? If they feel that the Law set before them is impossible to fulfil and that their own strength is too weak to satisfy it, why do they not flee to him whom the same God has made for us both righteousness and satisfaction, namely Jesus Christ? He, as Paul says, "was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Why, too, scorning the righteousness of God, which he here offers us in his Son through the Gospel, do they try to establish and peddle their own righteousness, which is really nothing, and whose vanity they experience every day in their own conscience? Add to these points that the hypocrites of our age will be judged by their own prayers and psalms. For when they pray with us, "Our Father, who art in heaven," when they hold the Apostles' Creed in common with us, and when they confess with us that the Word of God is contained in the holy Scriptures, yet meanwhile they invoke the saints, wonderfully turn their faith to creatures of every kind, to Roman indulgences, to the merits of their own works, to the cleansing of the fire of Purgatory and six hundred other things, and moreover depend entirely on the canons of the Fathers, the decrees of Councils and uncertain human traditions, all of which are condemned by the unanimous agreement of the Old and New Testaments. What excuse, then, can remain for those who accuse and condemn themselves by their own mouth?

units.la: At non satis est hero serui huius ignauiam verbis durioribus increpuisse, sed grauibus etiam poenis eundem subiicit. Nam astantibus dicit: Tollite ab eo minam, & date ei qui decem minas habet. Et cum hoc illis iniquum aut saltem absurdum videretur, ideoque responderent: Domine, habet decem minas: sententiae suae causas siue rationem hanc affert: Nam dico vobis, Omni habenti dabitur: ei autem qui non habet, etiam quod habet adimetur. Et apud Matthaeum addit his omnibus: Et inutilem seruum eijcite in tenebras exteriores: illic erit fletus & stridor dentium. Quo loco multa concurrunt, quae ad poenae atrocitatem faciunt. Primum est, quod minam ab eo Dominus aufert. Euenit hoc omnibus, qui vocationem suam non ea, qua debent, fide & industria obeunt. Illos enim e suo gradu Deus deijcit, ne vel in Ecclesia vel Repub. locum honorationem occupent, & eosdem donis quoque illis spoliat, quibus ad prouehendam ipsius gloriam vti noluerunt. Sic saepe ministros reijci videmus, ut cum ministerio authoritatem quoque omnem amittant, & eorum etiam odijs expositi sunt, quibus ipsi sua ignauia & proditorio silentio gratificari voluerunt. Exempla similia in ijs videmus, qui in Repub. administranda ignaui sunt, & gloriam Dei negligunt, ut infelici mundo placeant. Detrahit illos ex alto Deus, & donis, quibus antea ornati erant nudatos omnium risui & contemptui exponit. Et hoc cum prophetico illo dicto conuenit. Honorantes me honorabo: at qui me contumelia afficiunt, contumelijs afficientur. Accedit ad hanc ignominiam, quod minam ab illo abla tam non sibi seponit herus, sed alteri dat, qui decem minas lucratus fuerat. Facit hoc ad augendā ignominiam simul & dolore, qui ex ea nascitur. Et quam graue sit hominibus ambitiosis (quales sunt hypocritae) alios in eo dignitatis gradu videre, ex quo ipsi deiecti sunt, Saulis exemplu abunde docet, cui invidia & doloris impatientia tandem exitiu attulit. Simul autem fidis seruis Dominus animu facit, ne ignauorum exemplo se seducipatiatur, aut impatientiores fiant, si alijs securè otiantibus, aut etiam gemo indulgentibus, ipsi perpetuis curis atq; laboribus distineatur. Erit enim olim vicissitudo rerum, & non minus gloriosum quàm felicem atq; beatum finem suorum laborum attingent, quando aliorum ignauia industriæ ipsorum testimonium feret, & gloriam eorundem illustrabit. Id verò generali dicto probat: Omni habenti dabitur: ei autem qui non habet, etiam quod habet adimetur. Vsus est eadem sententia cap.8. vbi diximus quæ ad eius interpretationem faciunt.
units.tr: But it is not enough for the master to have rebuked this servant's idleness with harsher words; he also subjects him to severe penalties. For he says to the bystanders, "Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten minas." And when this seemed unjust, or at least absurd, to them, so that they answered, "Lord, he has ten minas," he gives the reason for his sentence: "For I tell you, to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away." In Matthew he adds to all this: "And cast the useless servant into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Many things come together in this passage that add to the atrocity of the punishment. First, the master takes the mina away from him. This happens to all who do not discharge their calling with the faith and diligence they ought. For God casts them down from their rank, so that they may not hold a place of honour either in the Church or in the commonwealth, and he also strips them of those gifts which they were unwilling to use for advancing his glory. Thus we often see ministers rejected, so that along with the ministry they lose all authority, and they are exposed to the hatred of those whom they had wished to please by their idleness and treacherous silence. We see similar examples in those who are lazy in administering the commonwealth and neglect the glory of God in order to please a wretched world. God drags them down from on high and, stripped of the gifts with which they were formerly adorned, exposes them to the laughter and contempt of all. This agrees with that prophetic saying: "Those who honour me I will honour, but those who treat me with contempt will be treated with contempt." To this disgrace is added the fact that the master does not keep for himself the mina he took away, but gives it to another, who had gained ten minas. This serves to increase both the shame and the grief that arises from it.
