And how grievous it is for ambitious men (such as hypocrites are) to see others in that rank of dignity from which they themselves have been thrown down, the example of Saul abundantly teaches, whom envy and impatience in grief at last brought to ruin. At the same time, the Lord encourages faithful servants not to let themselves be led astray by the example of the idle, nor to become more impatient if, while others sit idle in security or even indulge in sloth, they themselves are kept busy with constant cares and labours. For in time there will be a change of circumstances, and they will reach an end to their labours no less glorious than happy and blessed, when the idleness of others will bear witness to their diligence and illustrate their glory. He proves this with a general saying: "To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away." He used the same sentence in chapter 8, where we set out what bears on its interpretation.

units.la: Nunc obseruemus, hanc compendiosissimam tutissimamq; rationem esse, qua in Dei donis proficere & ad gradum honoratiorem ascendere atq; dignitatibus augeri possimus: si nos collata dona agnoscamus, iisdem bene vtamur, & actionum omnium finem atq; scopum nobis proponamus gloriam Dei & multorum salutem. Qui verò his neglectis per malas artes ad altiora tendunt, seipsos cum ignominia in exitium præcipites dare consueuerunt: cuius rei exempla plurima in prophanis etiam historijs habentur; qualia sunt Alcybiadis, Gracchorum, Marij, Pompeij & similium. At ne hic quidem subsistit iudicium Dei, quo seruos ignauos & inutiles punit: sed istiusmodi insuper in tenebras exteriores abijcere iubet, vbi est fletus & stridor dentium. Ea autem locutione statum eorum Christus denotare solet, qui ad æternos inferorum cruciatus damnati sunt. Vt enim Deus lucem inaccessam habitare dicitur, cuius olim participes fient, quotquot lucem, quæ nobis in Christo exhibita est, sedulò sequuntur: ita extra Christum meræ sunt tenebræ errorum, superstitionum & peccatorum, quarum princeps est Satan, qui iam olim ad catenas caliginis damnatus secum in æternas tenebras abstrahet eos, qui eius imperium & malas suggestiones admiserint. Exteriores autem dicuntur tenebræ illæ, quia procul extra Dei Regnum & beatæ immortalitatis sedem sunt; sicuti in epulonis diui tis & Lazari historia audiuimus. Per fletum verò & stridorem dentium æternos cruciatus intelligit, quibus tam corpore quàm anima multabuntur, quicunque in domo Dei inutiles, aut mali serui fuerint. Nobis autem istorum vsus esse debet, vt ad piam inductriam excitemur, & ipsi nobiscum quotidie rationem ineamus, nosq; ipsos examinemus ad nostræ functionis regulam: ne forte etiam ipsi otio & ignauia superati iisdem pœnis multemur.
units.tr: Now let us observe that this is the most compendious and safest way by which we can advance in God's gifts, rise to a more honourable rank and be increased in dignities: if we acknowledge the gifts conferred on us, use them well, and set before ourselves as the aim and goal of all our actions the glory of God and the salvation of many. But those who, neglecting these things, strive by wicked arts for higher positions usually hurl themselves with disgrace into ruin. Many examples of this are found even in profane histories, such as those of Alcibiades, the Gracchi, Marius, Pompey and others like them. But God's judgment does not stop even here, by which he punishes idle and useless servants; he further commands that such men be cast into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. By this expression Christ customarily denotes the state of those who are condemned to the eternal torments of hell. For just as God is said to dwell in unapproachable light, of which all who diligently follow the light shown to us in Christ will one day be partakers, so outside Christ there is nothing but the darkness of errors, superstitions and sins, whose prince is Satan, who, already long ago condemned to the chains of darkness, will drag with him into eternal darkness those who have admitted his rule and his evil suggestions. Those shadows are called outer because they lie far outside the kingdom of God and the seat of blessed immortality, as we heard in the history of the rich man and Lazarus. By weeping and gnashing of teeth he means eternal torments, with which both body and soul will be punished, as many as have been useless or wicked servants in the house of God. For us, however, the use of these examples ought to be to rouse us to pious diligence, to enter into reckoning with ourselves every day, and to examine ourselves by the rule of our office, lest perhaps we too, overcome by idleness and sloth, be punished with the same penalties.

units.la: Restat postrema parabolæ pars, qua quid seditiosis defectoribus & hostibus apertis eventurum sit, Dominus docet. Nam postquam cum seruis suis rationes subduxit, astantibus ait: Quin etiam meos illos inimicos, qui noluerunt me regnare supra se, adducite huc & iugulate coram me. Oportuit hoc addi, ne quis Christum in eos modo animaduersurum putaret, qui seruorum nomine censentur, impune autem omnia laturos esse, qui ab ipso prorsus alieni iugum eius iam pridem excusserunt. Et nim multos error istle decipit, eo quòd multos istorum in hoc sæculo triumphare & quasi extra omne teli iactum constitutos impunè aduersus illum proteruire vident. Docet ergo, se istorum quoque iudicem fore, & pœnas tandem daturos esse omnes eos, qui aduersus ipsum aliquid hostiliter moliuntur. Confirmatur hoc multis testimonijs, & in primis luculentum est, quod in Psal. secundo habetur. Describit illic Spiritus sanctus gentium ferocissimarum fremitus, vulgi concursum, regum & principum consilia, quorum omnium hic finis est, vt Christũ Dei è Regno suo expellant, disciplinæ vincula abrumpant, & iugum illud dulcissimum confringant, quo caro coercetur, vt spiritui & Deo obediat. Sed quid ijsdem illic respondetur? Qui sedet in cœlis ridet, Dominus subsanat eos. Tum loquetur ad eos in ira sua, & in furore suo terrebit eos. Ego verò constitui Regem meum super Zionem montem meum sanctum. Recensebo decretum: Dominus dixit mihi, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Postula à me, daboq; gentes, vt sint hereditas tua: & terminos terræ vt sint possessio tua. Sceptro ferreo cofringes eos: veluti vasa figulina comminues eos. En ferreo sceptro coterendos dicit eos, qui salutari sceptro Euangelij regi atq; coerceri nolunt. Et sceptri illius plus quàm ferrea, vel adamantina quoq; duritiem multi experti sunt, qui aduersus Christũ & Ecclesiam eius arma sua acuerunt: quorum exempla alibi recensuimus. At quàmuis aliquibus detur, vt huius sæculi vitam feliciter transfigant, & finiant, ijdem tamen Dei iudicium minimè effugient. Veniet enim suo tempore Iesus Christus, & per angelos suos à finibus orbis terrarum omnes homines colliget, qui ad ipsius tribunal sistentur, vbi pij quidem laudibus dignis & gloria ornabuntur, impij verò eius hostes verbi sui gladio mactati vna cum diabolo & pseudopropheta conijcientur in stagnum ignis & sulphuris, vbi die & nocte cruciabuntur in sempiterna secula. Vide Matth.25. Apoc.19.20.
units.tr: The last part of the parable remains, in which the Lord teaches what will befall the seditious rebels and open enemies. For after he had reckoned accounts with his servants, he said to those standing by: "Moreover, bring here those enemies of mine, who would not have me reign over them, and slaughter them before me." This had to be added, lest anyone think that Christ would punish only those who are reckoned among his servants, while those who have long since utterly withdrawn from him and shaken off his yoke would go unpunished. For this error deceives many, because they see many of these people in this age triumphing and, as if placed beyond the reach of any missile, defying him with impunity. He teaches, therefore, that he will be judge of these also, and that all who plot anything hostile against him will at last pay the penalty. This is confirmed by many testimonies, and the passage in Psalm 2 is especially clear. There the Holy Spirit describes the raging of the most fierce nations, the gathering of the common people, the counsels of kings and princes, whose whole aim is to drive Christ the Lord from his kingdom, to break the bonds of discipline, and to shatter that most sweet yoke by which the flesh is restrained so that it may obey the Spirit and God. But what is answered there to these same people? "He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord mocks them. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and terrify them in his fury. But I have set my King upon Zion, my holy mountain." I will recount the decree: "The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You will break them with an iron sceptre; you will crush them like potter's vessels." Behold, he says that those who are unwilling to be ruled and restrained by the saving sceptre of the Gospel are to be crushed with an iron sceptre. And many have experienced the hardness of that sceptre, harder than iron or even adamant, who have sharpened their weapons against Christ and his Church; we have recounted their examples elsewhere. But although some are permitted to pass the life of this age happily and to finish it, they will by no means escape the judgment of God. For Jesus Christ will come in his time, and through his angels will gather all men from the ends of the earth, and they will be brought before his tribunal. There the godly will be adorned with worthy praise and glory, but the impious, his enemies, slain by the sword of his word, will be cast together with the devil and the false prophet into the lake of fire and sulphur, where they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. See Matt. 25; Rev. 19, 20.

units.la: Porrò concludit narrationem istam Lucas his verbis: Et his dictis antegrediebatur Iesus, ascendens Hierosolymam. Quibus rursus eius constantiam & firmum propositum ea exequendi commendat. mendat, quæ à Patre in mandatis habebat. Nam vt sæpe vidimus, minimè ignorabat, quid ipsi Hie rosolymæ euenturum esset. Tendit tamen eò gradu indefesso, & quidem comitatum suum omnem, qui numerosissimus erat, præcedit ducis instar, vt omnibus exemplum præbeat, quod ipsi quoque sequamur vrgente nos Dei vocatione. Et hic nobis animum addere debet, quòd ille non exemplo solùm est nobis, verumetiam viam parauit facilem omnibus, qui in eius vocatione ambulare statuerint. Itaque eius memores intrepidè agamus negotium Domini, & procul relictis huius sæculi curis atque voluptatibus, Iesu Christi serui fimus fideles, vt in magno illo die honore & gloria sempiterna donati, in gaudium illius cœleste ingrediamur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke concludes that narrative with these words: "And having said these things, Jesus went on ahead, ascending to Jerusalem." By these words he again commends to them his constancy and firm resolve to carry out what he had received from the Father as commands. For, as we have often seen, he was by no means ignorant of what would befall him at Jerusalem. Yet he pressed on with tireless step, going ahead of all his companions, who were very numerous, like a leader, so that he might set an example for all, which we too should follow when the call of God urges us on. Here we ought to take heart, because he is not only an example to us but has also made the way easy for all who resolve to walk in his calling. Therefore, mindful of him, let us carry on the work of the Lord fearlessly, and, leaving far behind the cares and pleasures of this age, let us be faithful servants of Jesus Christ, so that, granted honour and eternal glory on that great day, we may enter into his heavenly joy. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXV.

units.la: Et factū est cum appropinquasset Bethphage & Bethaniæ ad montem qui vocatur Olearum, misit duos ex discipulis suis dicens: Abite in vicum, qui est ex aduerso: in quem ingressi inuenietis pullum alligatū, cui nemo vnquam hominum insedit, solutum eum adducite. Et si quis vos interrogauerit, Quare soluitis? Sic dicetis ei: Quoniam eo opus est Domino. Profecti autem qui missi erant, inuenerunt prout eis dixerat. Soluentibus autem eis pullum, dixerunt eis domini eius: Quare soluitis pullum? Ipsi verò dixerunt: Quoniam eo opus est Domino. Duxerunt igitur eum ad Iesum, & pallijs suis pullo iniectis, imposuerunt Iesum. Eunte autem ipso, substernebant pallia sua in via. Et cum appropinquaret ad descensum montis Olearum, cœpit omnis multitudo discipulorum gaudentium laudare Deum voce magna de omnibus quas viderant virtutibus, dicentes: Benedictus Rex ille, qui venit in nomine Domini: Pax in cœlo, & gloria in locis altissimis.
units.tr: And when they drew nigh to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples, saying: Go your way into the village over against you, in the which at your entering ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat: loose him, and bring him hither. And if any man ask you, Why do ye loose him? thus shall ye say unto him, Because the Lord hath need of him. And they that were sent went their way, and found even as he had said unto them. And as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt? And they said, The Lord hath need of him. And they brought him to Jesus: and they cast their garments upon the colt, and they set Jesus thereon. And as he went, they spread their clothes in the way. And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, saying: Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.

units.la: Postquam Dominus & redemptor noster, Iesus Christus, in parabola quæ proximè præcessit, omnem Regni sui conditionem diligenter exposuit, commodissimè illi doctrinæ Lucas historiæ huius de ingressu eius in vrbem natratione subjicit. Ea enim ille apertius demonstrare voluit, quod verbis docuerat, & duo agit. Primo se Regem esse docet, & ideo non vt solitus erat, pedes vrbem ingreditur, sed pullo asinæ insidens, vt se omnibus conspicuum præbeat: adhæc populi acclamationes admittit & probat, cum authoritate templum ingreditur, & ex eo auaros atque impios sacrorum nundinatores eijcit, & alia multa facit, quæ proprie ad Regem spectant. Nec alicui mirum videri debet, quòd hoc regni sui documentum in finem vsque suæ in hisce terris conuersationis differre voluit. Idenim postulabat eorum temporum status, ne populo plus satis ad res nouas procliui aliquam tumultuandi occasionem daret: simulque suo exemplo doceret, Regni sui specimen fere tunc in nobis quoq; luculentius apparere, quando morti vicini de illa simul & inferis triumphare incipimus. Alterum est, quòd hoc tam vili apparatu ostendit Regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde eos turpiter falli, qui huius sæculi splendore, opes & gloriam in illo quærunt. Interim multa alia in narratione ista concurrunt, quæ nos de multis cognitu necessarijs admonent, & ideo digna est, cuius singulæ partes diligentius considerentur.
units.tr: Our Lord and Redeemer, Jesus Christ, having in the parable immediately preceding set out carefully the whole condition of his kingdom, Luke appropriately joins to that teaching this account of his entry into the city. For he wished to show more plainly what he had taught in words, and he does two things. First, he shows that he is King: he therefore enters the city not on foot, as he was accustomed, but sitting on the colt of an ass, so that he might be seen by all; he further admits the acclamations of the people, and enters the temple with authority, and from it drives out the greedy and impious sellers of sacred things, and does many other things that properly belong to a king. Nor should anyone wonder that he chose to defer this proof of his kingdom until the end of his life in this world. For the condition of those times required that he not give the people, who were already too inclined to new things, any occasion for tumult; and at the same time he taught by his example that the sign of his kingdom shines most clearly in us also, when we begin to triumph over death, which is near, and over hell. The second point is that by so humble a display he shows that his kingdom is not of this world, and that therefore those are shamefully deceived who seek wealth and glory in it through the splendour of this age. Meanwhile many other things meet in this narrative which remind us of many matters that must be known, and so it is worthy that each of its parts be considered more carefully.

units.la: Prima ipsum Christum proponit, in quo si externam speciem intuearis, nihil præter extremam egestatem & inopiam reperies. Cum enim noui Reges vrbem præcipuam Regni sedem ingressuri equos & equites innumeros sibi parent, armis & omni ornatus genere conspicuos, noster hic ita omnibus istis destituitur, vt ipsi pullo asinæ precario opus sit. Ideo duos ex discipulis emittit, quibus ait: Abite in vicum, qui est ex aduerso: in quem ingressi inuenietis pullum alligatum, cui nemo vnquam hominum insedit: solutum eum adducite, & c. Et sunt hæc quidem carnis iudicio non contemptu modò digna, verumetiam ridicula: at si propius inspiciantur, Christum reuera Regem esse testantur, & earum virtutum specimen euidentissimum exhibent, quæ in Regibus præcipuæ sunt, & sine quibus regna feliciter administrari non possunt. Primam in his merito numeramus variarum rerum scientiam & sapientiam. Quid enim illis tam necessarium est, quàm vt sciant ea, quæ ad Reipub. administrationem pertinent: quæ nimirum populi ipsis crediti conditio, quod ingentum qui mores, quæ item Regum & principum officia, quibus legibus vitia coercere, honestatem morum prouehere, populi saluti consulere oporteat? Hæc qui ignorant, ij Regum quidem titulis superbire possunt, reuera autem nihil minus quàm reges sunt, cùm nihil eorum queant præstare, quæ ab illis exiguntur. Vidit hoc Solomon olim, qui cùm quiduis petendi optionem liberam ipsi fecisset Deus, neglectis omnibus, quæ plerique sola admiratione digna esse iudicant, dicebat: Ego puer sum parvus ignorans egredi & ingredi: & seruus tuus est in medio populi tui, quem elegisti: & quidem populus est multus, qui numerari non potest. Da igitur seruo tuo cor audiens, ad iudicandum populum tuum, vt discernam inter bonum & malum, &c. Quod votum ita Deo placuit, vt Solomonem non solum sapientia, verumetiam opibus & potentia Regum omnium præstantissimum fecerit. Præstat tamen illi verus hic noster Solomon, Iesus Christus, cui Pater Spiritum dedit non ad mensuram certam, sed cum plenitudine: Spiritum videlicet sapientiæ & intelligetiæ (vt Esaias prædixit) consilij item & scientiæ. Argumenta huius in Euangelica historia passim occurrunt, inter quæ non postremum debet censeri, quod hic habetur. Qui enim modo ex Galilæa hospes adueniebat, videt quid in vico illo fiat: imò nouit & prædicere potest, quid illic inuenturi sint discipuli vbi eo venerint. Id vero non humanæ solertiæ, sed sapientiæ diuinæ opus est. Quis enim mortalium, etsi multos alios scientia & rerum vsu superet, scire potest, quid ipso absente domi suæ geratur, quo loco pecora eius singula consistant, quid dicturi aut facturi sint eius domestici post horam vnam aut alteram? Hæc autem nos in Christo non admirari modò aut laudibus extollere, sed ad nostrum vsum transferre conuenit, vt ex iis consolationem & doctrinam petamus, quæ vitæ instituendæ seruiat. Etenim plurimum nos consolari potest omniscientiæ huius consideratio, quando in periculis, in morbis diturnioribus, in egestate & fame Satan atq; caro nobis suggerunt, nos à Christo prorsus derelictos, & hunc nostri immemorem esse. Qua ratione enim oues sanguinis sui pretio redemptas ille negligat, qui pullos asinorum respicit? Non dubitemus ergo, quin nos in periculis omnibus videat, calumnias hostium audiat, & eorundem conatus norit. Tutò igitur ad illius tribunal prouocare, ei nostras quere las exponere, & nostræ innocentiæ defensionem contra nostros persecutores instituere possumus: quod Dauidem non semel fecisse, ex Psalmis apparet. Est præterea hic efficacissimus stimulus ad virtutem & vitæ sanctitate tuendam, si omnes nostras actiones et studia eius oculus patère cogitemus, qui olim iudex venturus est.
units.tr: The first thing it sets before us is Christ himself, in whom, if you look at his outward appearance, you will find nothing but extreme poverty and want. For when new kings are about to enter the chief city, the seat of their realm, they provide for themselves countless horses and horsemen, conspicuous in arms and every kind of finery; but here is one who is so destitute of all these things that he needs the colt of an ass lent to him. So he sends out two of the disciples, saying to them: Go into the village over against you, in which at your entering you shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat: loose him and bring him, and so on. Now by human judgment these things are not only contemptible but even ridiculous; yet if they are looked at more closely, they bear witness that Christ is truly King, and they display the most evident sign of those virtues which are chief in kings, and without which kingdoms cannot be governed happily. We rightly count first among these the knowledge and wisdom of many things. For what is so necessary to them as to know those things which pertain to the administration of the commonwealth: namely, the condition of the people entrusted to them, the natures and manners of the people, likewise the duties of kings and princes, by what laws vices ought to be restrained, moral integrity advanced, and the welfare of the people cared for? Those who are ignorant of these things may indeed take pride in the titles of kings, but in truth they are nothing less than kings, since they can achieve none of the things that are demanded of them. Solomon long ago saw this, who, when God had given him a free choice of whatever he wished, neglecting all those things which most people judge worthy of admiration alone, said: "I am a little child, I know not how to go out or come in: and thy servant is in the midst of thy people which thou hast chosen, a great people, that cannot be numbered. Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad," etc. This prayer so pleased God that he made Solomon the most excellent of all kings, not only in wisdom but also in wealth and power. Yet our true Solomon, Jesus Christ, surpasses him, to whom the Father gave the Spirit not by a fixed measure but in fullness: namely the Spirit of wisdom and understanding (as Isaiah foretold), also of counsel and knowledge. Proofs of this occur everywhere in the Gospel history, and among them what is found here must not be counted least. For he who was coming as a stranger from Galilee sees what is happening in that village; indeed he knows and can foretell what the disciples will find there when they have arrived. But this is the work not of human skill but of divine wisdom. For what mortal, though he surpasses many others in knowledge and experience of affairs, can know what is going on at home in his absence, in what place each of his animals is standing, or what his household servants are going to say or do an hour or so later? We ought to apply these things to our own use in Christ, not merely to admire them and extol them with praises, so that from them we may seek consolation and teaching that serves for the ordering of our life. For the consideration of this omniscience can greatly comfort us, when, in dangers, in long illnesses, in poverty and hunger, Satan and the flesh suggest to us that we have been utterly abandoned by Christ and that he is forgetful of us. For how could he neglect the sheep redeemed at the price of his blood, if he takes notice of the colts of asses? Let us not doubt therefore that he sees us in all our dangers, hears the slanders of our enemies, and knows their attempts. We may therefore safely appeal to his judgment-seat, lay our complaints before him, and set up the defence of our innocence against our persecutors; as David did more than once, as appears from the Psalms. Moreover, here is a most effective spur to virtue and to guarding the holiness of life, if we consider that his eye, which will one day be the judge, looks upon all our actions and endeavours.

units.la: Cæterùm non potest Regibus sufficere sapientia cum scientia rerum coniuncta, nisi viribus potentia atque authoritate instructi sint, qua & suos in officio continere, & hostilem vim repellere possint. In eum certè finem magistratum gladio armatum esse, Paulus docet, & omniù animis hanc notitiam Deus inscripsit, vt principum authoritatem reuereantur. At in hoc etiam Rex noster, Iesus Christus, omnibus huius seculi regibus est superior, vt qui non edistis minacibus & aperta vi cogit (quàmuis & hoc possit, si ita necessitas postulet) sed in ipsa corda hominum ius habet & imperium, vt ex inuitis voluntarij fiant, & sua sponte ad omne obsequium præstandum parati sint, qui prius nihil minus factur i videbantur. Apparet hoc in eo, quòd ij, ad quos pullus iste asinæ pertinebat, audita eius voluntate mox acquiescunt, & ab hominibus peregrinis atq; ignotis eum abduci patiuntur: quod nunquam facturi fuerant, nisi corda eorum occulta virtute ille tetigisset. Sunt & alia eius generis exempla, quæ alibi recitauimus. Habet autem hoc quoq; dulcissimam consolationem. Qui enim istos mouere potuit, idem quorumuis animos flectere potest, vt quæ nobis ad huius vitæ vsum necessaria sunt liberaliter largiantur: vel etiam subitò ex inimicis amici fiant, & in lachrymas nostri causa erumpant, qui paulò ante in nostram necem animis acerbissimis coniurarant: quod olim Esau & Sauli accidisse legimus. Quòd si qui duriores sunt & prorsus implacabiles, tamen hos quoq; fræno suo continere solet, vt quod maximè volunt & quod posse videntur, minimè faciant. Sunt hæc exemplis infinitis probata, quæ commemorare nequaquam opus est, cùm multa quotidie fiant, quæ consolationem hanc nobis instaurare & confirmare possunt.
units.tr: Yet wisdom joined with knowledge of affairs cannot suffice for kings, unless they are also furnished with the strength of power and authority, by which they can both keep their subjects in obedience and repel hostile force. Paul teaches that the magistrate is armed with the sword to this very end, and God has written this knowledge on the minds of all, that they should reverence the authority of princes. But in this respect also our King, Jesus Christ, is superior to all the kings of this world: he does not compel by threatening edicts and open force (although he could do this too, if necessity so required), but he has right and rule over the very hearts of men, so that those who before seemed least likely to act make themselves willing, and of their own accord are ready to render every obedience. This appears in the fact that those to whom this colt belonged, once they hear his will, at once consent, and allow it to be led away by strangers and unknown men; which they would never have done unless he had touched their hidden hearts with his secret power. There are also other examples of this kind, which we have recounted elsewhere. Yet this too holds the sweetest consolation. For he who was able to move these men can bend the minds of anyone whatever, so that they generously give us what is necessary for the use of this life; or even that enemies suddenly become friends, and burst into tears for our sake, who a little before had conspired with the bitterest minds for our death: as we read happened long ago to Esau and to Saul. But if some are harsher and utterly implacable, he is accustomed to hold these too on a bridle, so that they do least of all what they most wish and what they seem able to do. These things are proved by countless examples, which there is no need to recall, since many such things happen every day, which can renew and confirm this consolation for us.

units.la: Secunda parte discipuli proponuntur, quibus asellum adducendi prouinciam ille mandauit. Obtemperant illi, & absq; murmure aut tergiuersatione officium faciunt, cùm non deessent rationes honestae & iustae in speciem, quibus se excusare poterant. Nec enim inhonestum modo verumetiã cum furti suspicione coniunctum, & proinde periculosum poterat videri, homines peregrinos nemine salutato aut rogato iumentum alienum & alligatum soluere atq; abducere. Sed didicerant illi iampridem omnes carnis sensus Christo subijcere, & huic in omnibus obedire. Estque hoc obedientiae fidei exemplum, quam omnibus necessariam esse, qui Christo nomen dederunt, saepe iam diximus: quia nisi haec carnis nostrae prudentiam atq; cupiditates subigat, nunquam officium faciemus, cùm illa Deo etiam respondare, & aduersus eum disputationes instituere non vereatur: quae execrabilis est cauda, & tandem in deploratam impietatem degenerat, nisi in tempore coerceatur.
units.tr: In the second part the disciples are introduced, to whom he entrusted the task of bringing the colt. They obey and perform the duty without murmuring or evasion, although there were not lacking reasons, apparently honourable and just, by which they could excuse themselves. For it could seem not only dishonourable but also, being linked with a suspicion of theft, dangerous, for strangers to untie and lead away another's animal, tied up, without greeting or asking anyone. But they had long since learned to subject all the desires of the flesh to Christ and to obey him in all things. And this is an example of the obedience of faith, which we have often said is necessary for all who have given their name to Christ: because unless this faith subdues the prudence and desires of our flesh, we will never perform our duty, since the flesh does not hesitate to answer back to God and to dispute against him. This is a detestable tail, which at last degenerates into a hopeless impiety, unless it is restrained in time.

units.la: Non autem inutilis vel è proposito historiae aliena est Allegoria, quam hic aliqui observarunt. Commune nimirum discipulorum Christi officium esse, vt ei asinos adducant, qui ipsum sessorem & rectorem patiantur. Asini autem reuera sunt omnes homines, si naturae vitiositatem, in qua concipiuntur & nascuntur, consideres. Vt enim asinus animal est stupidissimum, tardum et ignauum, in oneribus tamen ferendis robustissimum, contumax item & mirè refractarium: ita animalis homo in ijs, quae Spiritus Dei sunt, plus quàm stupidus est, nec tardus modò & ignauus in Dei mandatis obeundis, verumetiam refractor improbus, cùm è contra nullius laboris aut molestiae ipsum piget, quae in ferendis scelerum sarcinis subeunda est: & cùm Christum sessorem vix admittat, diaboli seruitio sponte sese subijcit. Tales asini olim Iudaei & gentes fuerunt, qui omnes Apostolorum ministerio ad Christum adducti sunt. Tales vtinam non hodie passim occurrerent. Nostri ergo officij esse
units.tr: Nor is the allegory, which some have noted here, useless or foreign to the purpose of the history. It is clearly the common duty of Christ's disciples to bring asses to him, so that they may suffer him as their rider and ruler. Indeed, all men are asses, if you consider the wickedness of nature in which they are conceived and born. For just as the ass is a most stupid, slow and lazy animal, yet most robust in bearing burdens, and also stubborn and wonderfully refractory, so the natural man, in the things that belong to the Spirit of God, is more than stupid. He is not only slow and lazy in carrying out God's commands, but also a shameless rebel, whereas on the contrary he feels no pain or trouble in bearing the burdens of sins. And though he hardly admits Christ as his rider, he willingly submits himself to the service of the devil. Such asses the Jews and the Gentiles once were, all of whom were brought to Christ by the ministry of the Apostles. Would that such asses did not everywhere meet us today. It is therefore our duty

units.la: Iustus. Proner.15.19. Lib.1.de vita Const. Obedientia discipulorum. Christo asini adduci debent. meminerimus, vt & nos ipsos Christo adducamus, & quoscunq; alios, quos vel à via salutis deflexisse, aut oneribus peccatorum succubuisse cernimus. Est hoc opus Deo gratissimum, qui non aliare magis quàm hominum salute delectatur. Et huc faciunt, quæ de boue & asino proximi subleuando & ad herum suum reducendo in Lege habentur. Exod.23. Deut.22.
units.tr: Just. Prov. 15.19. Book 1, On the Life of Constantine. The obedience of the disciples. Asses must be brought to Christ. to remember that we too should bring ourselves to Christ, and likewise whoever others we see to have turned aside from the way of salvation or to have sunk under the burdens of sins. This work is most pleasing to God, who delights in nothing more than in the salvation of men. And to this purpose belong the things that are said in the Law about helping a neighbour's ox and ass and bringing them back to their master. Exod. 23. Deut. 22.

units.la: At non minus laude digni sunt ij, à quibus Apostoli asellum illum abduxerunt. Cùm enim non absq; causa mirarentur, homines ignotos sanos pro imperio pullum soluere & abducere velle, tamen audito eorum responso, Quoniam opus est Domino, illum absq; omni difficultate eis concesserunt. Quem animum illis à Christo inditum fuisse diximus. Veruntamen eorum exemplo admonemur, ne quid ipsi quoq; Christo negemus, quo illum scimus opus habere. At ipse quidem si diuinam eius naturam spectes, nullius indiget, sed ipse potius omnium nostrum necessitatem sua liberalitate & omnipotentia subleuat. Quoad verò Regnum suum et eius in hoc seculo administrationem nostra opera & ministerio vti dignatur, vt illud per Verbi ministros prouehat, per pios principes tueatur, per singulos deniq; illustret atq; confirmet. Hic ergo quoties nostra vocatio nobis in mentem venit, semper nobis ab illo dici putemus: Dominus tuo labore, tua fide & industria opus habet. Ita simul admonebimur, nos qui illi nosipsos & omnia nostra debemus, nihil ei sine sacrilegio negare posse. Similiter cùm pauperes famelici, peregrini & exules Christi membra sint, ipsum nostram opem implorare existimemus, quoties illi ad nos clamant, seq; nostra beneficentia subleuari cupiunt. Quoties item propter fidem & Veritatis confessionem de fortunis nostris periclitamur, similiter in mentem veniat, Christum nostris facultatibus, nostro exilio, labore, molestijs opus habere, vt nimirum eius nomen nostra fide & patientia illustretur. Sed ô infelices nos: quando multi passim sunt, qui sua omnia Baccho, Veneri, mundo, diabolo sponte offerunt, pauci autem inueniuntur, qui hoc afflictissimo seculo, periclitantibus vbiq; Ecclesijs, hanc Christi vocem agnoscere, & ipsi obedire velint. Quid verò de illis dicemus, qui in membris suis esurienti & sitienti acetum tum felle propinant, dum illorum crucem conuitijs, calumnijs, opprobrijs & scurrilibus dictis atque insultationibus, ipsis acerbiorem & grauiorem reddunt?
units.tr: Yet those from whom the Apostles took away that colt deserve no less praise. For although they marvelled, not without cause, that men unknown to them, healthy, should by command want to untie and take away the colt, nevertheless, when they heard the reply, "The Lord has need of it," they gave it to them without any difficulty. We have said that this spirit was given to them by Christ. Yet by their example we are admonished not to deny Christ anything at all, since we know he has need of it. Indeed, if you regard his divine nature, he needs nothing, but rather he himself relieves the necessity of all of us by his bounty and omnipotence. Yet as to his kingdom and its administration in this age, he deigns to use our labour and ministry, so that he may advance it through the ministers of the Word, defend it through godly rulers, and finally illuminate and confirm it through each one of us. Therefore, whenever our calling comes to mind, let us always think that he says to us: "The Lord has need of your labour, your faith and your diligence." Thus we shall be reminded at the same time that we, who owe ourselves and all that we have to him, can refuse him nothing without sacrilege. Likewise, since the poor, the hungry, strangers and exiles are members of Christ, let us consider that he implores our help whenever they cry out to us and desire to be relieved by our kindness. Likewise, whenever on account of the faith and the confession of the truth we are put in danger of our fortunes, let it come to mind in the same way that Christ has need of our means, our exile, our labour and our troubles, that his name may be made illustrious by our faith and patience. But alas for us! Many are everywhere who willingly offer all they have to Bacchus, Venus, the world and the devil, yet few are found who in this most afflicted age, when the Churches are in danger everywhere, are willing to acknowledge this voice of Christ and obey it. But what shall we say of those who, in his members, give vinegar mixed with gall to the hungry and thirsty, while by reproaches, slanders, insults, scurrilous words and mockery they make their cross more bitter and heavier?

units.la: Sequitur tertia huius historiae pars, qua ipsa Christi profectio & tandem ingressus quoque in vrbem describitur. Nam asellum discipuli illi Christo adduxerunt, & huic iniectis pallijs suis eum imposuerunt, & goiam proficiscente alij quidem vestes suas, alij verò ramos palmarum in viam substrauerunt, omnis verò populus præcedens & sequens faustis acclamationibus eum deduxerunt clamantes: Hosanna Filio Dauid: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, &c. Quo loco ante omnia quærat aliquis, cur isto apparatu vrbem Regiam & cultus diuini sedem ingredi voluerit? Nam subest quidem his aliqua species Regis, sed ridicula planè, si ad nostrae rationis calculum reuocetur. Nam iumento quidem sublimis vehitur præter solitum morem, sed precariò, vt nuper diximus: & ita omnibus phaleris destituto, vt ne sellam quidem aut ephippia habuerit, & proinde discipulorum pallijs eum insterni oporteret. Habet præterea comitatum quidem numerosum, vt vnquam aliàs: sed qualem obsecro? Alij ex ipsa Galilæa ipsum secuti erant, homines ignoti & peregrini, cum mulierculis aliquot: alij in tota illa profectione ex vicis & oppidulis, per quæ transibat, temere confluxerant: quidam (vt Ioannes scribit) aduentantis fama excitati ex vrbe obuiam illi progressi sunt: sed & hi ex peregrinis fuerunt, qui iam ad festum illuc venerant. Nihil ergo in toto illo comitatu fuit, quod Regiam maiestatem referret, si occultam Christi virtutem auferas, qua illi omnes excitati & attracti fuerunt, & quam ijdem omnes fere ignorabant. Præterea acclamationes quidem fiunt magnificæ & ex Scripturis petitæ: sed à vulgo indocto & hominibus imperitis, quibus postea pueri accesserunt, qui illorum exemplum imitati sunt, vt Matthæus scribit: omnes verò illos palàm damnarunt Sacerdotes & Pharisæi, quorum tunc summa erat in ea gente authoritas. Ergo merito quis miretur, cur isto apparatu venire voluerit, qui suo nutu quosuis ad ornandum suum ingressum facile excitare poterat? Sed causam indicant Matthæus & Ioannes, qui hoc ita fieri oportuisse scribunt, vt impleretur, quod Zacharias olim prædixerat. Ita verò ad Dei decretum nos remittunt, quando constat, Prophetas sua vaticinia ex Spiritus sancti suggestione protulisse, qui de futuris illos admonuit, & in primis quidē ijs, quæ promissus ille redemptor facturus & passurus erat: Sic verò aduentum eius in vrbem Zacharias describit, vt non obscurè doceat, cur apparatu tam vilí
units.tr: The third part of this history follows, which describes Christ's journey itself and his final entry into the city. The disciples brought the young donkey to Christ, laid their cloaks on it, and set him upon it. As he went on his way, some spread their garments on the road and others spread palm branches, and the whole crowd, going before and following, escorted him with joyful acclamations, crying: "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," and so on. Here one should first ask why he chose to enter the royal city and the seat of divine worship with such a display. There is indeed some appearance of a king in this, but if it is weighed by our reason it is plainly ridiculous. He is carried high on a beast, contrary to his usual custom, but only on loan, as we said recently. He is so lacking in all trappings that he has no saddle or harness, so the disciples' cloaks had to serve as a covering. Moreover, his retinue is more numerous than ever before, but what sort of retinue, I ask? Some had followed him from Galilee itself, unknown and foreign men with a few women. Others had gathered haphazardly along the whole journey from the villages and small towns through which he passed. Some (as John writes), roused by the news of his coming, went out from the city to meet him, but these too were foreigners who had already come there for the feast. So in all that retinue there was nothing that resembled royal majesty, unless you take away the hidden power of Christ by which all of them were stirred and drawn, and which nearly all of them did not understand. Furthermore, the acclamations are indeed grand and taken from the Scriptures, but they came from the uneducated crowd and unskilled people, to whom afterwards boys joined themselves, imitating their example, as Matthew writes. The chief priests and Pharisees, whose authority among that people was then supreme, openly condemned all of them. Therefore, who could rightly wonder why he wished to come with such a display, when with a nod he could easily have stirred up whoever he liked to adorn his entrance? But Matthew and John indicate the reason, writing that this had to happen so that what Zechariah had foretold long ago might be fulfilled. They refer us in this way to the decree of God, since it is certain that the prophets uttered their prophecies by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, who warned them of future events, and first of all of those things which that promised Redeemer was to do and suffer. Zechariah describes his coming into the city in such a way that he clearly teaches why he chose such a mean and humble display.

units.la: Cur hoc habitu vrbem ingressus sit? vili & contempto vti voluerit: nimirum vt ostenderet, Regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, nec aliquid cum huius mundi regnis commune habere, quae fere armis acquiruntur & defenduntur, & proinde subditis magnifico apparatu equitum, satellitum & militum terrorem incutere solent. Ideo sic loquitur Propheta: Exulta vehementer filia Zion, iubila filia Hierusalem: en Rex tuus venit tibi, iustus & seruator ipse, pauper vel mitis, insidens asino, pullo scilicet asinorum. Quae omnia sic dicuntur, vt facile appareat, Regem hunc nemini grauem aut terribilem, sed potius beneficum & salutis publicae authorem esse. Et ideo confirmationis loco adijcitur: Excindam currus ex Ephraim, & equos ex Hierusalem, excinderur arcus bellicus, loquetur pacem gentibus, & imperium eius a mari ad mare extendetur. Adeo igitur non opus est ei armis, vt potius omnem apparatum bellicum procul remotum velit. Vt enim nos Patri reconciliat: ita inter nos quoq; mutuae dilectionis & pacis solidae atq; stabilis author est. De quibus omnibus, cum in Marco plura dicta sint, nunc ea breuius perstringimus. Ita vero Christus non modo discipulorum atq; totius populi Iudaici errorem confutare voluit, qui Regnum eius terrificum & armis atq; triumphis illustre fore somniabant: verum etiam personatos illos vicarios suos arguit, qui omnia eius exemplo & doctrinae contraria faciunt. Pontifices dico, qui omnia mundi regna ad se pertinere dicunt, Reges & Imperatores in sua verba iurare cogunt, eosdem ad osculà pedum euocant: adhaec aut multis auro ornatis, aut equis militaribus vehuntur: vel in sella pretiosissima baiulorum humeris sublimes gestantur, & omnes ex alto plus quam barbaro fastu despiciunt: pacis vero et concordiae capitales hostes sunt, orbemq; terrarum bellis continuis turbant, dum potentissimos Monarchas inter se nouis subinde occasionibus committunt: eo quod illorum dissidijs ipsi suam potentiam augere & quotidie suis terris aliquid adijcere, aut saltem sua facilius tueri possunt, dum illi inter se belligerantur. Quamuis autem haec omnia illi faciant, infelix tamen mundus pro illis pugnat, eos adorat & colit, neglecto Christo, salutis & pacis vnico authore. Sed neminem illius exemplum moueat, quo minus Christo ipsi adhaereamus: qui etsi nullo splendore aut terrore tyrannico sese venditet, imperium tamen diuina virtute per totum orbem extendit, & suos in medio hostium suorum facile tuetur.
units.tr: Why did he enter the city in this manner? He wished to use a poor and despised appearance, namely to show that his kingdom is not of this world and has nothing in common with the kingdoms of this world, which are generally acquired and defended by arms, and which therefore are accustomed to strike terror into their subjects by a splendid display of cavalry, guards and soldiers. So the prophet speaks thus: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you, just and himself a saviour, poor or meek, riding on an ass, that is, on a colt of asses." All these things are said in such a way that it easily appears that this King is terrible to no one, but rather is beneficent and the author of public salvation. And so, as a confirmation, it is added: "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off; he shall speak peace to the nations, and his dominion shall extend from sea to sea." Thus he has no need of arms, so that he would rather keep all warlike show far away. For as he reconciles us to the Father, so he is also the author of mutual love and of solid and lasting peace among us. Since many things were said about all these matters in Mark, we now touch on them more briefly. Christ wished in this way not only to refute the error of the disciples and of the whole Jewish people, who dreamed that his kingdom would be terrifying and renowned for arms and triumphs, but also to rebuke those masked vicars of his who do everything contrary to his example and teaching. I mean the pontiffs, who say that all the kingdoms of the world belong to them, who compel kings and emperors to swear to their words, who summon the same to kiss their feet; who, moreover, are carried either adorned with much gold or on military horses, or are borne aloft on the shoulders of bearers in a most precious chair, and look down on all from a height with more than barbarous pride. Yet they are the chief enemies of peace and concord, and they trouble the globe with continual wars, while they constantly set the most powerful monarchs against each other on new occasions, because by their quarrels they themselves can increase their power and daily add something to their lands, or at least defend their own more easily while those others are at war. Although they do all these things, the unhappy world nonetheless fights for them, adores and worships them, neglecting Christ, the sole author of salvation and peace. But let no one be moved by their example to refrain from clinging to Christ himself, who, although he does not display himself with any splendour or tyrannical terror, nevertheless extends his dominion through the whole world by divine power, and easily protects his own in the midst of their enemies.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, qua narratur, vt eum discipuli & totus populus in vrbem deduxerint. Et illi quidem (vt dictum est) Ieum asello, quem suis pallijs instrauerant, impositurunt. Alij ex vrbe eidem obuiam procedunt. Omnes vero vnanimi studio viam vestibus & arborum ramis sternunt, & simul acclamationibus laetis atq; solennibus prosequuntur. Hosanna Filio Dauid: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini: benedictum quod venit regnum in nomine Domini patris nostri Dauid. Hosanna in altissimis. Pax in caelo, & gloria in locis altissimis. Quae voces non temere in ore vulgi rudis & indocti nata, sed ex Psalmo centesimo decimo octauo desumptae sunt, quo solennis precatio pro Regno Messiae veri illius Dauidis Filij, instaurando continetur. Cui adijcitur Doxologia ex Angelorum Cantico, quo illi natalem Christi celebrauerunt, vt Cap.2. audiuimus. Sunt haec admiratione dignissima. Ignobilis populi turba impune tantum honorem ei defert, quem Pontifices & Seniores oderant. Homines item illiterati ex Scripturis eum publice celebrant, quem agnoscere non potuerunt hucusq;, qui Scripturarum cognitionem et clauem scientiae sibi solis vendicabant. Isto exemplo nos aduersus eorum calumnias tueamur, qui nobis nostrae partis hominū ignobilitatem exprobrant, & seditionis accusant eos, qui contra Regum edicta Christo honorem suum publice deferunt. Est illorum impudentia maior, quam vt multis confutari mereatur: seruiles autem animos produnt, quicunq; in hominum gratiam ea dissimulant, quae de Christo didicerunt. Interim meminerimus commune exemplum nobis proponi, quod omnes imitari oporteat, qui Christum se nobis per Euangelium offerentē digne & cum fructu aliquo excipere volunt. Agnoscant eum esse benedictum illud semen Abrahami, Regem item a Deo nobis datum, qui Regnū Dei inter nos instaurat, pacis item & gaudij aeterni nobis author est vnicus. Quem autem intra animos suos agnouerunt, eum publice inter eius hostes quoque profiteantur, neque eius ipsos pudeat, qui propter nos extrema quaeque pati dignatus est. Praeterea ipsi viam parent & vestes substernant: quod tunc proprie fit, quando veterem hominem exuunt, & hunc per fidei obedientiam illi subijciunt. Sunt haec rara hodie: & plures multò inuenias, qui illi aduentanti portas claudunt, vel etiam iam admissum eijciunt, quando nō omnia votis ipsorū respondent. Oremus ergo omnes, vt Deus Pater homi-
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, which tells how the disciples and the whole people led him into the city. The disciples, as has been said, set him on the young donkey which they had covered with their cloaks. Others go out from the city to meet him. All with one united zeal spread their garments and tree branches on the road, and at the same time follow him with joyful and solemn acclamations: "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the kingdom that comes in the name of the Lord our father David! Hosanna in the highest! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest places." These cries did not arise carelessly on the lips of the rude and unlearned crowd, but are taken from Psalm 118, in which a solemn prayer is contained for the restoration of the kingdom of the Messiah, that true Son of David. To this is added a doxology taken from the song of the angels, with which they celebrated the birth of Christ, as we heard in chapter 2. These things are most worthy of admiration. The lowly crowd of people pays with impunity such honour to him whom the pontiffs and elders hated. Likewise, unlearned men publicly celebrate from the Scriptures him whom they had not until now been able to recognise, although they had claimed for themselves alone the knowledge of the Scriptures and the key of learning. Let us, by this example, defend ourselves against the slanders of those who reproach us for the lowliness of the men of our party and accuse of sedition those who publicly render honour to Christ against the edicts of kings. Their impudence is too great to deserve to be refuted at length; but those who, to gain men's favour, conceal what they have learned about Christ betray servile minds. Meanwhile let us remember that a common example is set before us, which all ought to imitate who wish to receive Christ worthily and with some fruit when he offers himself to us through the gospel. Let them acknowledge that he is that blessed seed of Abraham, the King also given to us by God, who restores the kingdom of God among us, and who is the sole author of peace and of eternal joy for us. And whom they have acknowledged in their hearts, let them also publicly profess among his very enemies, and let them not be ashamed of him, who for our sake deigned to suffer every extremity. Moreover, they prepare the way and spread out garments, which is properly done when they put off the old man and subject him to Christ by obedience of faith. These things are rare today, and you will find far more who shut the gates against him as he comes, or even cast him out once admitted, when things do not answer to their desires. Let us therefore all pray that God the Father

units.la: Vt populus Christum deduxerit. num animos accendat Filij sui amore, vt Regnum illud benedictum et saluificum inter nos instau- rer, & aduersus impios hostium conatus tueatur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: How the people led Christ. would kindle the hearts of men with love for his Son, so that he may restore that blessed and saving kingdom among us, and defend it against the attempts of impious enemies. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXVI.

units.la: Tum quidam pharisaeorum e turba dixerunt ei: Magister, obiurga discipulos tuos. Et ipse respondens dixit eis: Dico vobis, si siluerint illi, mox lapides clamaturos. Et vt appropinquauit, visa vrbe fleuit super ea, dicens: Enimuero si vel tu noffes vel hoc saltem tuo die, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent. Sed occulta sunt nunc oculis tuis. Nam venient dies aduersum te, quo circumsicient inimici tui tibi vallum, & circumcingent te, & constringet vndique, te, solo aequabunt, & filios tuos intus: neque relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem: eo quod non noueris tempus illud visitationis tuae.
units.tr: Then some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, "Teacher, rebuke your disciples." He answered them, "I tell you, if these were silent, the stones would cry out at once." And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, "If you had known, even you, at least on this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a rampart around you, and surround you, and hem you in on every side, and they will level you to the ground, and your children within you; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation."

units.la: Sciebat Dominus noster Iesus Christus, mortem suam multis scandalo fore, qui difficulter credi- sturi essent, cum esse promissum illum humani generis redemptore & Regni Dei instauratorem, quem in cruce infami medium inter latrones pendere viderant. Ideo saepius de hoc priuatim cum se- lectis discipulis egit, & ipso in vrbem ingressu scandalum hoc aliqua ex parte remouere voluit. Nam vt nuper audiuimus, non vt solitus erat, cum paucis discipulis pedes aduenit, sed pullo asinae insi- dens & toti populo conspicuus numerosam comitatum secum traxit eorum, qui fanstis acclamatio- nibus populum totum in eius admirationem excitauerunt. Denique quamuis totus ille apparatus ni- hil magnificum aut regium praeferret, multa tamen fecit, quae ipsum vere Regem sapientia, po- tentia & iustitia prae aliis omnibus instructissimum, Regnum vero eius non terrenum, neque terri- bile, sed caeleste & saluificum esse docent. De quibus cum proxime dictum sit, nunc huius loci narratio consideranda nobis venit, qua docemur, vt pleriq. in mundo Christi aduentu & Regni eius manife- statione afficisoleant, & quae poenae omnibus ijs iam paratae sint, qui in illo se offerentem gratiam Dei contemnunt, aut etiam hostiliter persequuntur.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ knew that his death would be a stumbling block to many, who would find it hard to believe that the one promised as the redeemer of the human race and the restorer of the kingdom of God was the one they had seen hanging on a shameful cross between two robbers. For this reason he often spoke about it in private with his chosen disciples, and at his very entry into the city he wished in some measure to remove this stumbling block. For, as we heard recently, he did not come on foot with a few disciples, as was his custom, but riding on a colt of an ass, in full view of all the people, and he drew after him a large company of those who, with joyful acclamations, stirred the whole people to wonder at him. In short, although that whole display showed nothing grand or royal, he nevertheless did many things which teach that he is truly a King, more fully equipped than all others with wisdom, power and righteousness, and that his kingdom is not earthly or terrible, but heavenly and saving. Since we have spoken of these things recently, we now come to consider the account of this passage, by which we are taught what usually befalls most people in the world at the coming of Christ and the manifestation of his kingdom, and what punishments are already prepared for all those who despise the grace of God offered in him, or even persecute it with hostility.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet quod de Pharisaeis dicitur, qui illum monuerunt, vt discipulos sibi accla- mantes obiurgaret. Et illos quidem in turba hac aut comitatu Christi fuisse Lucas scribit, & haec illi dixisse, cum adhuc in via esset. Matthaeus vero puerorum meminit, qui postea in templo ijsdem vocibus illum celebrauerint, & quorum clamore Principes Sacerdotum & Scribae offensi eum simi- liter interrogauerint: Audis quid isti dicunt? Fuerunt ergo isti homines indefessi hostes Christi, neq. illos alicuius laboris piguit, vt aliquam vel calumniandi vel ipsum accusandi occasionem inuenire possent. Non puduit ergo eos, quo minus turbae huic immixti illum sequerentur: & postea puerorum quoque voces obseruant. Suo autem exemplo eorum arguunt ignauiam, qui cum Christum profitean- tur, tamen omnem laborem nimium & omne tempus male amissum & perditum putant, quod au- diendis concionibus eius impenditur: vt iam de illis nihil dicam, qui apertas & horribiles blasphe- mias surdis auribus praetereunt, imo ne prouocati quidem & in arenam protracti gloriam illius, qua decebat constantia, tuentur.
units.tr: As to the first point, there is what is said of the Pharisees, who warned him to rebuke the disciples who were acclaiming him. Luke writes that these men were in the crowd or company of Christ, and that they said this while he was still on the road. Matthew, however, mentions the children who afterwards praised him in the temple with the same cries, and whose shouting offended the chief priests and scribes, who likewise questioned him: "Do you hear what these are saying?" These men, then, were tireless enemies of Christ, and no labour wearied them, so that they might find some occasion either to slander him or to accuse him. Nor were they ashamed to mingle with that crowd in order to follow him; and afterwards they also watched the voices of the children. By their example, however, they condemn the sluggishness of those who, while they profess Christ, still think every labour excessive and all time spent in hearing his sermons to be wasted and lost. I say nothing now of those who pass over open and horrible blasphemies with deaf ears, or who, even when challenged and dragged into the arena, do not defend his glory with the constancy that befits it.

units.la: At quod hoc loco praecipuum est, admonemur isto exemplo, nunquam defore aemulos & hostes Christi, qui suum illi honorem inuidéant, & quidem tunc quando iam triumphare & omnium lau- dibus in caelos efferri videtur. Est enim signum illud contradictionis, de quo Simeon in spiritu va- ticinatus est. Sunt autem inter huius aemulos facile principes Pharisaei & Pontifices, quos partim propriae iustitiae fiducia inflat, partim ambitio & inanis gloriae studium excaecat, adhaec cupiditas quaestus extimulat, quem ex religione vexantur. Quia enim his vitiis ipsi laborant, non potest eis Christus non intolerabilis esse, qui humanam iustitiam omnem damnat, & larua detracta eorum su- perbiam atque auaritiam detegit. Idem tamen mira astutia odium veritatis simulato gloriae Dei zelo palliare possunt, & eos impiae arrogantiae insimulare, qui soli illius vindices sunt. Dum enim Christum satis pro imperio discipulos suos increpare iubent, dum item interrogant, an puerorum acclamantium voces audiat? non obscure illum perstringunt, quasi ambitiose nimis vulgi applausum capiet. captet, & non solùm rudis plebeculæ verùm etiam puerulorum simplicium laudibus delectetur. At dum hac suspicione illum grauant, pro sui nominis existimatione pugnant. Cùm enim ipsi hucusque in religione leges tulissent pro suo arbitrio, minimè ferre possunt, ut ipsorum authoritas vel minima ex parte labefactetur. Ea autem mox tota ruitura videbatur, si populo liceret Messiæ titulum & honorem ei deferre, quem ipsi cane & angue peius oderant, quem Samaritanum & diabolicum impo storem dicebant, eò quòd ipsorum dolos atq; tyrannidem argueret. Hæc igitur est illa Helena, pro qua isti homines pugnant, qui interea toti zelo gloriæ Dei ardere videri volunt. Imitantur horum mores hodie Monachi & purpurati præsules, qui iam aliquot seculis in Ecclesiam sibi omne ius & imperium vendicarunt. Quia enim hi quoque præcipuum præsidium in populi ignorantia habent, nihil minus ferre possunt, quam Veritatis lucem, qua vera Christi cognitio manifestata ipsorum quæ-stum & sastum euertit. Interea verò cum ipsi pro sua culina & gloria pugnent, nos ambitionis accu sare solent, qui Christo suum honorem vendicare studemus, & hoc unum agimus, ut ille supra omnes emineat, & solus agnoscatur esse promissus ille Rex gloriæ, quem Pater supra montem suum sanctum constituit. Obseruemus ergo vetera ista exempla, ne istorum calumniis moueamur, sed potius artes eorum detegamus, quibus imperito vulgo fucum faciunt.
units.tr: But what is especially important in this passage is that we are warned by this example that Christ will never lack rivals and enemies who begrudge him his honour, and indeed especially when he seems already to be triumphing and carried up to the heavens with the praise of all. For this is that sign of contradiction of which Simeon prophesied under the Spirit. Among his rivals the chief men are easily the Pharisees and the high priests: some of them are puffed up by confidence in their own righteousness, some are blinded by ambition and the eager pursuit of empty glory, and the desire for gain also spurs them on, by which they are troubled in the name of religion. Because they are afflicted by these vices themselves, Christ cannot but be intolerable to them, for he condemns all human righteousness and, the mask being torn away, lays bare their pride and greed. Yet by a remarkable cunning they can cover their hatred of the truth with a pretended zeal for the glory of God, and charge with impious arrogance those who are alone its defenders. For when they order Christ to rebuke his disciples sharply enough, and when they ask him whether he hears the voices of the children shouting, they plainly disparage him, as though he were too ambitiously seeking the applause of the crowd, and delighting in the praises not only of the rude common people but even of simple little children. And while they burden him with this suspicion, they fight for their own reputation. For since they had hitherto laid down laws in religion at their own pleasure, they can by no means bear that their authority should be weakened even in the least degree. And that authority seemed about to fall entirely if the people were allowed to give Christ the title and honour of the Messiah, whom they hated worse than dog and serpent, whom they called a Samaritan and a devilish impostor, because he exposed their deceits and tyranny. This, then, is that Helen for whom these men fight, while they wish to seem all aflame with zeal for the glory of God. The monks and purple-clad prelates of today imitate their ways, who for several centuries have claimed for themselves all right and power over the Church. For these men also have their chief protection in the ignorance of the people, and they can bear nothing less than the light of truth, by which the true knowledge of Christ, once made manifest, overthrows their gain and their pomp. Meanwhile, though they fight for their own kitchen and glory, they are accustomed to accuse us of ambition, we who strive to claim honour for Christ, and who aim at this one thing: that he should stand out above all, and be acknowledged alone as that promised King of glory whom the Father has set upon his holy mountain. Let us, then, observe these ancient examples, so that we are not moved by their calumnies, but rather unmask the arts by which they deceive the unlearned crowd.

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus his respondentem: Dico vobis (inquit) si siluerint isti, mox lapides clamaturos. Quibus verbis docet, non posse fieri, ut negotium hoc silentio sepeliatur. Quia enim Patris decretum sit nomè Filij glorificare, & publicis testimonijs indies illustrius facere, oleum & operam perdituros esse omnes eos, qui illud tegere & sub ignorantia tenebris detinere velint. Apud Mathæum verò ijs, qui puerorum acclamationes indignius ferebant, dicit: Quid ni? Nunquam legistis, Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem? Quibus verbis plus quàm puerilem ignorantiam, vel potius stupiditatem inexcusabilem illis exprobrat, qui cùm interpretes scripturarum & doctrinæ antistites haberi vellent, adhuc tamen ignorarent Dei consilium & morem, qui (ut in Psalmo octauo scribitur) pueruli & infantibus adeo delectatur, ut suum nomen per eos maximè illustrari velit. Et simul illos negligenti officij accusat, cùm ipsorum in primis esset, ei testimonium publicum deferre, & populum totum ad laudes ipsius decantandas excitare. In genere autem docet, Deum nunquam defuturum nominis & gloriæ suæ illustrationi, nec quicquam obstare posse, quo minus miraculose & præter omnium expectationem suæ gratiæ præcones excitet, si illi cessent, qui eam ex officio prædicare debebant. Debet hoc de tota Euangelij doctrina intelligi. Dei enim decretum est, quòd illius verbum de Hierusalem exire & totum orbem terrarum illustrare debuit. Et Christus ait: Oportet apud omnes gentes prædicari Euangelium. Quis ergo, quò minus id fiat obstabit? Quis Spiritui sancto resistet, quò minus vbi vult, spiret? Aut num Deo vnquam defuturos putabimus sui verbi præcones, qui omnium animos & linguas pro suo arbitrio formare potest? Olim certè cùm in officio segniores essent Sacerdotes, quorum labia scientiam custodire & populum verbo Dei instituere debebant, extraordinarie Prophetas excitauit, & ab aratro aut stiua Helisæum, à re pecuaria Amos, ex illustri & regia familia Isaiam, expiscatorum & publicanorum atque textorum siue cerdonum numero Apostolos vocare potuit, qui illud officium obirent. Quod ipsum hodie etiam fieri videmus, ut non expectata Pontificum aut Episcoporum ordinatione multi ad Euangelium prædicandum exurgant, & hoc illis inuitis mirifico cum successu annuntient. Ferunt hoc illi indignissimè, & legitimam vocationem in nobis desiderant, quasi verò ita sese illorum ordini obstrinxerit Deus, ut nemo legitimus Ecclesiæ minister censeri debeat, nisi quem ipsi ordinauerint. Et cur non potius Dei manum atque prouidentiam agnoscunt, qui necessario alios excitat Christi sui præcones, cessantibus illis, qui munus istud ad se solos pertinere existimant? Possunt quidem isti nobis negotium facere, & contra nos principum arma concitare possunt: Euangelij verò vocem prohibere nunquam potuerit. Nam ut hic Christus ait, tacentibus omnibus hominibus, lapides clamabunt. Quod reuera olim impletum est. Cùm enim nemo esset Hierosolymæ, qui Christi nomen & gloriam assereret, & Ecclesia tota oraculo admonita Pellam abijsseт, Romanorum legiones vrbem cinxerunt, & tunc horribiles petrarum ex castris eiaculationes, tectorum fragor, mœniorum ruinæ, & quæcunq; in obsessa aut capta vrbe fieri solent, quasi alta voce Christo Regi testimonium dederunt, hunc esse æternum Dei Filium & vnicum generis humani redemptorem, cuius contema Christi laudes sepeliri non possunt. ptum ille vlcisfcatur. Et hodie videmus elementa omnia aduersus Euangelij hostes conclamare,& horrendis portentis exitium illis denuntiare. Quorum consideratio terrorem quidem nobis incutere debet, ne in stupido admonitionum Christi contemptu obrigescamus: simul tamen consolationem iis|dem subesse meminerimus, quando Deus aperte testatur, se ecclesiae suae in hoc mundo laborantis curam habere, neque passurum unquam, vt verbum eius impune contemnatur.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ answering them: "I tell you," he says, "if these were silent, the stones would cry out at once." By these words he teaches that this matter cannot be buried in silence. For since it is the Father's decree to glorify the name of the Son, and to make it more illustrious day by day through public testimonies, all those who wish to hide it and keep it under the darkness of ignorance will be wasting their oil and labour. To those who took the children's acclamations more indignantly, he says in Matthew: "Why not? Have you never read, 'Out of the mouths of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise'?" By these words he rebukes them for more than childish ignorance, or rather for inexcusable stupidity, since, although they wished to be regarded as interpreters of the Scriptures and leaders of doctrine, they still did not know the counsel and custom of God, who (as is written in Psalm 8) delights so much in little children and infants that he wishes his name to be especially glorified through them. At the same time he accuses them of negligence in their office, since it was chiefly their duty to bear public witness to him and to stir the whole people to sing his praises. In general, he teaches that God will never lack means of illustrating his name and glory, and that nothing can hinder him from raising up, miraculously and beyond all expectation, heralds of his grace, if those who ought to proclaim it by office cease to do so. This must be understood of the whole doctrine of the gospel. For it is God's decree that his word should go out from Jerusalem and illuminate the whole world. And Christ said, "The gospel must first be preached among all nations." Who, then, will hinder this from happening? Who will resist the Holy Spirit, so that he may not blow where he wills? Or shall we think that God will ever lack heralds of his word, he who can shape the minds and tongues of all men at his pleasure? Indeed, in former times, when the priests, whose lips were to keep knowledge and instruct the people in the word of God, were rather slack in their office, he raised up prophets by an extraordinary act: from the plough or the oxgoad he called Elisha, from the herds Amos, from an illustrious and royal family Isaiah, and from the number of fishermen, tax collectors, weavers or cobblers he could call apostles to perform that office. We see this same thing happening today as well: without waiting for the ordination of the popes or bishops, many rise up to preach the gospel, and announce it with remarkable success, though this is against their will. They take this very ill, and they demand a lawful calling from us, as though God had so bound himself to their order that no one could be regarded as a lawful minister of the Church unless they had ordained him. And why do they not rather acknowledge the hand and providence of God, who of necessity raises up other heralds of his Christ when those who think this office belongs to them alone have ceased to act? They can indeed cause us trouble, and stir up the arms of princes against us; but they could never silence the voice of the gospel. For, as Christ here says, when all men are silent, the stones will cry out. And this was truly fulfilled once. For when there was no one in Jerusalem who would assert the name and glory of Christ, and the whole Church, warned by an oracle, had withdrawn to Pella, the Roman legions surrounded the city; and then the dreadful hurling of stones from the camps, the crash of roofs, the collapse of walls, and whatever usually happens in a besieged or captured city, bore witness with a loud voice to Christ the King, that he is the eternal Son of God and the only redeemer of the human race, whose contempt he will avenge. And today we see all the elements raising a clamour against the enemies of the gospel and threatening them with destruction by dreadful portents. The consideration of these things ought indeed to strike terror into us, lest we grow numb in a dull contempt of Christ's warnings; yet at the same time we should remember that consolation lies in them as well, since God openly testifies that he cares for his Church labouring in this world, and that he will never allow his word to be despised with impunity.

units.la: Faciūt ad horum confirmationē, quae deinceps Lucas narrat. Quia enim Christus nouerat, quid non multo post esset euenturum, vbi appropinquauit vrbi, fleuit super ea, dicens: Enimuero si vel tu noßes, vel hoc saltē tuo die, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent, &c. Describuntur haec ita, vt in illis manifesta habeamus fidelissimi Seruatoris simul & iustissimi Regis argumenta: & quia locus iste praeterea exemplum memorabile continet, quo Deus toti orbi terrarum irae suae magnitudinem ergaverbi sui hostes siue contemptores declarare voluit, vtile fuerit singulas eius partes diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: These things serve to confirm what Luke goes on to relate. For when Christ, having come near the city, knew what was going to happen not long after, he wept over it, saying: "If indeed you had known, even you, at least on this your day, the things that belong to your peace, etc." These words are set down in such a way that in them we have clear proofs both of the most faithful Saviour and of the most just King; and because this passage also contains a memorable example by which God wished to show the whole world the greatness of his wrath against the enemies and despisers of his Word, it will be useful to examine its individual parts more carefully.

units.la: Primum visa vrbe fleuisse super illa dicitur. Poterat hoc alicui mirum videri, & ab eius maiestate alienum, nisi eum verum hominē induisse Scriptura doceret, qui omnes nostrae naturae infirmitates in se recepit. Ne quam vero causam lachrymarum ex nobis ipsis fingeremus falsam, non Lucas modo eum super vrbe fleuisse dicit, sed idem ipse etiam testatur his verbis: Enimuero si vel tu noßes, vel hoc saltem tuo die, quae ad pacem tuā pertinent: Sed occulta sunt nunc oculis tuis. Quibus verbis duo agit. Primo animi sui dolore exprimit, qui ex commiseratione enascebatur, cū vrbis huius veterem dignitatem & mox venturum excidium, quo nullum vnquam in orbe miserabilius visum est, animo suo volueret. Fuit enim Plinio teste, vrbium totius Orientis celeberrima, & multum adeius ornatum Herodes contulerat, qui maximis impensis & mirifico studio templum aedificarat, quo vix vllum aliud magnificentius fuit. Adhaec iam inde a Dauidis temporibus vsque ad Babylonicum exilium, per annos circiter quadringentos & quinquaginta, Regni sedes fuerat. Superauit tamen haec omnia, quod illic cultus sui sedem Deus collocauit, & de illa dixit: Haec mea est requies in aeternum: hic habitabo, quoniam expetiui eam. Denique typus Ecclesiae fuit, quae frequenter Hierosolymae nomine appellatur, & illic primum collecta inde in totum orbem terrarum ad omnes gentes propagata est. Fuit ergo horribile illud Dei iudicium, talem tantamque vrbem tam miserabili exemplo perire. Non potuit ergo non toto animo commoueri & in lachrymas acerbissimas erumpere Christus, quando qui nihil antiquius habebat hominum salute, illā periturām prorsus cogitabat, quae prae aliis omnibus diuini cultus sacrarium & cultorum Dei asylum esse debuisset: Ideo dolorem hunc animi verbis quoque patheticis admodum testatur. Enimuero (inquit) si vel tu noßes, vel hoc saltem tuo die, &c. Confert vrbis huius ingratitudinem & contumaciam cum aliis, & eandem per temporis circumstantium amplificat. Quasi dicat: Tolerabile videri poterat, alias ciuitates me|sum redemptorem non agnoscere, & verbum illud gratiae aspernari: si vel tu, quae doctrina & cultus diuini sedes es, quā tot Prophetae sua praedicatione illustrarunt, & cui ego meipsum tam amice tam que varijs modis reuelaui, hanc Dei gratiam agnoscere, & ijs quae hucusq; contumaciter nimis fecisti contenta, vel saltem hoc tuo die, quo te peculiari bonitatis suae argumento ille visitat, rectius quid agatur expenderes. Certe si de his serio cogitares, non posses non de illis etiam cogitare diligentius, quae ad tuam pacem pertinent, id est, quae tibi ad tuendam tuam incolumitatem sunt necessaria. Ista vero dicendo patres fidos imitatur Christus, qui eo graviori dolore afficiuntur, quo propiorem vident filiorum calamitatem, quam illi suis ipsis sua prodigalitate & contumacia omnium admonitionum contemptu accersunt.
units.tr: First, it is said that when he saw the city he wept over it. This might seem strange to someone and foreign to his majesty, unless Scripture taught that he was a true man who took upon himself all the infirmities of our nature. Lest we invent a false cause for his tears out of our own heads, Luke not only says that he wept over the city, but Christ himself also testifies to this in these words: "If indeed you had known, even you, at least on this your day, the things that belong to your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes." With these words he does two things. First, he expresses the sorrow of his mind, which arose from compassion, as he turned over in his mind the former dignity of this city and the destruction soon to come, than which nothing more wretched has ever been seen in the world. For according to Pliny, it was the most famous of all the cities of the East, and Herod had greatly adorned it, having built with very great expense and remarkable zeal a temple, of which scarcely any other was more magnificent. Moreover, from the time of David until the Babylonian exile, for about four hundred and fifty years, it had been the seat of the kingdom. Yet it surpassed all these things in that God placed there the seat of his worship, and said of it: "This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it." Finally, it was a type of the Church, which is often called by the name Jerusalem, and from there first gathered, it was spread abroad into the whole world among all nations. That terrible judgment of God was therefore that such a great city, so distinguished, should perish in so miserable an example. Christ therefore could not but be moved with his whole soul and break out into most bitter tears, since he, who held nothing more dear than the salvation of men, was thinking of the city that was utterly about to perish, which above all others ought to have been the sanctuary of divine worship and the refuge of God's worshippers. Therefore he bears witness to this sorrow of mind also in words that are very full of feeling: "Indeed," he says, "if you had known, even you, at least on this your day, etc." He compares the ingratitude and obstinacy of this city with those of others, and magnifies it by the circumstances of the time.
