As if he were saying: It might seem tolerable that other cities did not acknowledge me as their Redeemer and scorned that word of grace; but if you, who are the seat of doctrine and of divine worship, whom so many Prophets have illustrated by their preaching, and to whom I have revealed myself in so friendly and so many ways, had recognised this grace of God, and had been content with those things which you have hitherto done too stubbornly, or at least on this your day, on which he visits you with a special proof of his goodness, had weighed more carefully what ought to be done. Certainly, if you had thought seriously about these things, you could not but think more carefully also about those things that belong to your peace, that is, that are necessary for you to preserve your safety. In saying these things, Christ imitates faithful fathers, who are afflicted with the greater sorrow the nearer they see the calamity of their children, which they by their own prodigality and obstinacy, by contempt of all admonitions, bring upon themselves.

units.la: Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, non temere dubitandum esse de gratia Dei, neue talem fingamus, qui vt sanguinarij tyranni solent, hominum exitio delectetur. Quis enim hoc vel cogitet, qui Christum reprobae gentis & ad omnem impietatem deuota vrbis interitum lachrymis prosecutum fuisse audiit? Etenim quem hic in illo videmus summae misericordiae affectum, eum Deus Pater non raro in Scripturis exerit. Eiusdem certe animi vox est, quae in Psalmis habetur: O si populus meus me audisset, si Israel in vijs meis ambulauisset: quàm breui inimicos eorum deiecissem, & contra infestantes eos vertissem manum meam, &c. Consentiunt his, quae per Isaiam idem dicit: O si ad praecepta mea attenderes, redundaret instar fluminis pax tua, & iustitia tua sicut fluctus maris. Cum ergo ille noßrum interitum, imo contumaciam nostram, quae huius causa est. ési deploret, nunquam profecto surdus erit ad eorum preces, qui ad ipsum conuersi gratiam & misericordiam eius inuocant. At hic simul cauendum erit, ne eius bonitate ad peccandi licentiam turpiter abutamur. Nam vt haec Christi lachrymae amoris erga nos maximi argumentum sunt: ita execrabilem Hierosolymitanorum ciuium impietatem arguunt, quae illum lachrymari coegit. Paterni amoris & indulgentiae signum est, flere visa filij rebellis & intemperantis contumacia: at fletus ille nisi filium moueat, & ad meliorem frugem reducat, eum quauis supplicio dignum esse oportet. Curemus ergo etiam atque etiam, ne ipsi quoque lachrymas Christi contra nos in testimonium iustae nostrae damnationis prouocemus. Flere quidem nunc non potest, quando in coelestem gloriam euectus eum locum obtinet, vbi olim noster etiam fletus cessabit, & omnis lachryma abstergetur: ut non poterit non ad iustam vindictam excitari, si se cum in terris hisce versaretur, frustra propterea nos fleuisse, esuriisse, sitiuisse, denique sanguinem quoque proprium profudisse videat. Horum itaque memores, horreamus & abominemur peccata, quae Dei filio tanti doloris causam olim fuisse scimus. Simul autem ad nos transferamus exemplum Christi, ne ipsi fratrum interitum siccis oculis intueamur, multo minus autem ijs insultemus, quorum commiseratio nos ad lachrymas prouocare debet.
units.tr: Now this is a memorable example, by which we are taught not to doubt rashly about the grace of God, nor to imagine such a God as, like bloodthirsty tyrants are wont to be, delights in the destruction of men. For who could think this, who has heard that Christ wept over the destruction of a rebellious nation and a city devoted to every impiety? For the affection of the highest mercy which we see here in him, God the Father often displays in the Scriptures. Certainly it is the voice of the same mind which is found in the Psalms: "O that my people had hearkened to me, that Israel had walked in my ways! How quickly would I have cast down their enemies, and turned my hand against those who oppressed them," etc. They agree with what the same God says through Isaiah: "O that you had attended to my commandments! Then your peace would have flowed like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea." Since then he deplores our destruction, nay our obstinacy, which is its cause, he will certainly never be deaf to the prayers of those who turn to him and call upon his grace and mercy. Yet here we must take care at the same time that we do not shamefully abuse his goodness for licence to sin. For as these tears of Christ are a proof of his greatest love towards us, so they also prove the detestable impiety of the citizens of Jerusalem, which compelled him to weep. It is a sign of fatherly love and indulgence to weep over the obstinacy and wantonness of a rebellious son; but that weeping, unless it moves the son and brings him back to better conduct, must mean that he is worthy of any punishment. Let us therefore take care again and again that we ourselves do not also call forth the tears of Christ against us as testimony to our just condemnation. He cannot indeed weep now, since he has been carried up into heavenly glory and holds that place where our own weeping too will one day cease, and every tear will be wiped away; so he cannot but be roused to just vengeance, if, while he was living in this earth, he should see that we had wept, fasted, thirsted, and finally shed even our own blood in vain. Therefore, mindful of these things, let us shudder at and abhor the sins which we know were once the cause of such great sorrow to the Son of God. At the same time, let us transfer the example of Christ to ourselves, that we may not look upon the destruction of our brothers with dry eyes, and much less insult those whose misfortune ought to move us to tears.

units.la: Sed alterum quoq; videamus, quod primis hisce verbis Dominus agit. Est hoc stupiditatis & socordiae exprobratio. Dicit enim: Sed occulta sunt nunc oculis tuis. Ergone (inquis) ignorantes peccauerunt, & proinde in illos iniquior fuit Deus, qui tam crudeli & horribili exemplo eos perdidit? Nequaquam. Quomodo enim Dei voluntatem ignorare poterant, qui promissiones salutis quotidie in ore habebant, & quibus lex nunquam non inculcabatur? Aut num Christum illos ignorauisse dicemus, qui iam annis aliquot inter illos versatus saluificam suam virtutem non tam doctrina quam factis miraculosis spectandam proposuerat? Quod si qui ignorantiam praetexere velint, vulgi Hierosolymitani vocibus conuincentur. Nam in publico, & quidem in templo a multis dictum fuisse Ioannes scribit: Christus cum venerit num signa plura edet ijs, quae hic edidit? Quapropter dum haec abscondita aut oculis eorum occulta esse dicit Christus, non culpam ipsorum extenuare vult, sed potius stuporem plus quam belluinum notat, quo impediti Deum sese illis offerentem non cernant, & neque gratiam eius neq; irae iam ardentis argumenta obseruent. Frequenter autem socordiam hanc Prophetae etiam accusant, quia deploratae malitiae indicium est, si qui Dei iudicia prorsus aspernentur, & omnia temere aut fortuito accidere sibi persuadeant. Apud Sophoniam Deus lucernis accensis se eos scrutari & inuisere velle ait, qui in fecibus suis coagulati dicunt intra corda sua: Dominus neq; benefacit, neque male. Et in Psalmis desperatae impietatis hominum voces sunt: Dominus non videt, neq; Deus Iacob intelligit. Vult ergo in praesenti verbis istis Christus docere, Hierosolymitanos ciues ipsos sui excidij sibi authores esse, & simul mederi scandalo, quod ex eorum ignorantia voluntaria nascebatur. Nam non dubium est, plerosque illius vrbis exemplo detentos fuisse, quo minus Christum amplecterentur, quem videbant ab ijs reijci, qui praecipuam doctrinae & sapientiae existimationem sustinebant. Vult ergo monere, ne quem eorum incredulitas aut contumacia offendat, qui horribili stupore excaecati sibi ipsis Dei iram atq; exitium iam pridem accersuerint. Quod ipsum nos quoq; cogitare oportet, si qui prae alijs sapere videntur, praedicationem gratiae exibilant, & incurabili contumacia in proprium interitum ruunt. Nam eo grauior poena eos manet, quo propius & illustrius Dei gratia illis affulgeat: neq; diu apud tales homines cessare potest vindicta Dei, qui suae misericordiae contemptores inultos abire non sinit.
units.tr: But let us also look at the other thing which the Lord does in these first words. This is a rebuke of stupidity and dullness. For he says: "But now they are hidden from your eyes." Are they then (you ask) sinned in ignorance, and therefore God was more unjust towards them, who destroyed them with so cruel and dreadful an example? By no means. For how could they be ignorant of the will of God, who had the promises of salvation daily in their mouths, and to whom the law was never not inculcated? Or shall we say that Christ was unknown to them, who had already for some years been living among them and had set forth his saving power to be beheld not so much by doctrine as by miraculous deeds? And if any wish to plead ignorance, they will be refuted by the voices of the people of Jerusalem. For John writes that in public, and indeed in the temple, many said: "When Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?" Therefore, when Christ says that these things are hidden or concealed from their eyes, he does not wish to lessen their guilt, but rather marks a stupor more than beastlike, by which, being blinded, they do not discern God offering himself to them, and do not observe either his grace or the signs of his wrath already burning. Now the Prophets often also accuse this dullness, because it is a sign of desperate wickedness when people despise the judgments of God altogether and persuade themselves that everything happens rashly or by chance. In Zephaniah God says that he wishes to search and visit with lamps those who, thickened in their dregs, say in their hearts: "The Lord neither does good nor evil." And in the Psalms are the voices of men of desperate impiety: "The Lord does not see, neither does the God of Jacob understand." Christ therefore wishes by these words to teach that the citizens of Jerusalem were themselves the authors of their own destruction, and at the same time to remedy the stumbling-block which arose from their wilful ignorance. For there is no doubt that many were held back by the example of that city from embracing Christ, since they saw him rejected by those who held the highest reputation for doctrine and wisdom. He therefore wishes to warn that no one should be offended by their unbelief or obstinacy, who, blinded by a dreadful stupor, have long since brought upon themselves the wrath and ruin of God. This we too ought to consider, if any who seem to be wiser than others hiss at the preaching of grace and rush headlong into their own destruction through incurable obstinacy. For the heavier punishment awaits them, the nearer and more brightly the grace of God shines upon them; nor can the vengeance of God long delay among such men, who does not allow the despisers of his mercy to go unpunished.

units.la: Et hoc faciunt quae sequuntur. Christus enim, qui miserabilem vrbis occasum ex misericordia paterna defleuerat, nunc quasi animo iterum collecto iudicis personam suscipit, & quas poenas de illa sumpturus sit Deus, pronuntiat. Nam veniet dies aduersum te, quo circumijcient inimici tui tibi vallum, & circumcingent te, & constringent vndique, teque solo aequabunt & filios tuos intus: neque relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem. Vbi primum pulchra & grauis diei aut temporis oppositio occurrit. Nam paulo ante conqueflus erat, quod hunc suum diem non obseruaret: vbi dies in bonam partem sumitur pro tempore gratiae, aut acceptollo tempore (vt Propheta loquitur) quo Deus gratiam suam hominibus offert. Hic vero diem vindictae intelligit, quem Ioel magnum & formidabilem dicit, eo quod nemo illum sustinere possit. Perinde ergo hoc est, ac si dixisset, Nunc quidem ô Hierosolyma, Deus suæ bonitatis memor, te inuisit amicè, & gratiam suam tibi offert: quam si agnoscères beata fores, & imminens tibi excidium posses subterfugere. At quia incurabili ingratitudine & proteruia cum illius bonitate bellum suscepisti, aliâ diem tibi dixit Deus, quo suum ius persequetur, & digno supplicio te multabit. Id vero omnes sibi dici putent, quoscunq; Deus Verbi sui luce & gratia prædicatione quasi ex alto inuisit. Qui enim plus quàm paterno affectu nos miseros complectitur, vt exitio iam pericuros subducat: idem iustus quoq;, & seuerus iudex esset, & gratiæ suæ contemptum magna cum seueritate vlciscitur. Sed præstat singula videre, quæ vrbi Hierosolymæ denuntiat, vt simul inspectis historijs in hac etiam parte Christi omniscientiam & Veritatem agnoscamus.
units.tr: This is what the following words do. Christ, who had lamented the miserable fall of the city out of fatherly compassion, now, as if he had gathered his spirit again, takes up the role of judge and declares what punishments God will inflict upon it. "For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side, and shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another." Here a striking and weighty contrast with time presents itself. A little earlier he had complained that the city did not recognise its own day. In a good sense, "day" means the time of grace, or, as the Prophet says, the accepted time, in which God offers his grace to men. Here, however, he means the day of vengeance, which Joel calls great and terrible, because no one can endure it. The sense is therefore the same as if he had said: "Now, O Jerusalem, God, mindful of his goodness, has visited you kindly and offers you his grace. If you recognised it you would be blessed, and you could escape the destruction that hangs over you. But because you have waged war against his goodness with incurable ingratitude and wantonness, God has appointed another day for you, on which he will pursue his right and punish you with a deserved penalty." Let all those whom God has visited from on high, as it were, with the light of his Word and the grace of preaching, consider that this is said to them as well. For he who embraces us wretched men with more than a father's affection, to rescue us from destruction that is already close, would also be a just and severe judge, and he avenges the contempt of his grace with great severity. But it is better to look at each thing that he foretells to the city of Jerusalem, so that, with the histories examined side by side, we may also acknowledge in this part the omniscience and truth of Christ.

units.la: Prædixerat ille Iudæis, fore, vt qui ipsum in nomine Patris sui veniente nollent recipere, alios essent recepturi, qui suo proprio nomine venirent, & priuatum commodum quærerent. Id vero mox à morte eius impleri cœpit. Cùm enim Romani præsides populum partim insatiabili auaritia, partim vi & iniustitia grauiter premerent, & ideo omnium animi nouo promissæ liberationis desiderio flagrarent, eam occasionem arripuerunt homines nequam & seditiosi, qui promissi illius Messiæ titulum sibi vendicabant. Itaque in suas partes trahebant illi infelicem populum: quæ tumultuum quotidie nouorum causa erant. Ceciderunt in illis multa millia Iudæorum, vnà cum impostoribus illis, quorum artibus seducebantur. Sed cùm seditionum nullus finis esset, tandem, vltimo Neronis anno cum legionibus in Iudæam mittitur Vespasianus, qui à Galilæa facto belli initio, totam ferro & igne vastat, inde vrbi Hierosolymæ imminet. In eius autem obsidione à militibus Imperator electus, Romam contendit, & bellum Tito filio committit. Fecit hic, quæcunque in vrbis munitissimæ obsidione ab imperatore bono & strenuo fieri solent, & quæ facturum Christus prædixerat.
units.tr: He had foretold to the Jews that, since they were unwilling to receive him when he came in his Father's name, they would receive others who came in their own name and sought private advantage. This began to be fulfilled soon after his death. For when the Roman governors oppressed the people grievously, partly with insatiable greed and partly with violence and injustice, and so everyone's mind burned with a new longing for the promised deliverance, wicked and seditious men seized the opportunity. They claimed for themselves the title of the promised Messiah. They drew the unhappy people to their side, and this was the daily cause of fresh uproars. Many thousands of Jews fell in these struggles, together with those impostors by whose arts they had been led astray. But since the seditions had no end, at last, in the final year of Nero, Vespasian was sent into Judaea with legions. Beginning the war from Galilee, he laid waste everything with sword and fire, and then bore down upon the city of Jerusalem. During its siege he was made emperor by the soldiers, hastened to Rome, and entrusted the war to his son Titus. Titus did all the things that a good and vigorous commander usually does in the siege of a most strongly fortified city, and all the things that Christ had foretold he would do.

units.la: Primò enim vallum circumiecit vrbi, quod Iosephus, fide dignissimus scriptor atque testis oculatus, his verbis describit: A Romanis duodecima Maij aggeres inchoati, vix vigesimanona perfecti sunt: cum totos dies septemdecim laborauissent. Ingentes enim aggeres quatuor iacti sunt: & vnus quidem qui erat ad Antoniam, & à quinta legione fuerat extructus contra medium stagnum, quod Struthium vocatur: alter vero à duodecima duodecim cubitis distans. Decima autem legio, quæ supra memoratis præstabat, in Septentrionali parte opus erexerat, vbi stagnum esset, quod Amygdalon dicitur. Sed & Quintadecima legio aggerem triginta cubitis descendentem fecit ad Pontificis monumentum. Facit etiam alterius aggeris & turrium aliquot per Romanos extructarum mentionem Iosephus, quæ omnia Christus hic vno verbo comprehendit: Deinde, circumcingent te, inquit.
units.tr: First of all, he cast a rampart about the city. Josephus, a most trustworthy writer and eyewitness, describes this in these words: "The Romans began the mounds on the twelfth of May and barely finished them by the twenty-ninth, though they had worked for seventeen whole days. Four great mounds were raised: one by the Antonia, built by the fifth legion opposite the middle pool, which is called Struthius; the other by the twelfth legion, twelve cubits away. The tenth legion, which excelled the aforementioned, had raised its work on the northern side, where there was a pool called Amygdalon. The fifteenth legion also made a mound descending thirty cubits to the tomb of the High Priest." Josephus also mentions another mound and several towers built by the Romans. Christ comprehends all of these in one word here: "Then they shall cast a trench about thee," he says, and "compass thee round."

units.la: Ad cuius explicationem facit, quod cum Iudæi eruptione facta, aggeres & munitiones Romanorum incendissent ac diruissent, Titus nouum & mirificum opus excogitans, totam vrbem muro inclusit, quem diuino impetu (vt Iosephus scribit) milites triduispatio per ambitum triginta & nouem stadiorum duxerunt, vnà cum tredecim castellis, in quibus excubiæ contra vrbem disponerentur. Ex eo secutum est, quod hic tertio loco Christus dicit: Et concringent vndique. Id vero de oppugnationibus crebris intelligi debet, quibus Romani inclusos cominus & eminus infestarunt: quæ eò graviores fuerunt, quod intra muros simul horribili lue, seditionibus item & fame plus quàm Saguntina consumebantur: quæ illos non modo ad cibos insolitos cogebat, verumetiam matres omni humanitatis sensu exutas detestabili crudelitate armabat, vt ex se natos infantes iugularent, & ignibus tostos auidis dentibus laniarent. Et huc cumprimis pertinet, quod Iosephus eiusdem libri cap. 14. scribit. Cum non superesset locus in vrbe, vbi sepelirentur cadauera, in fossas ex muro præcipitabant, quas circumiens Titus, vbi plenas cadaueribus vidit, altaque sanie tabefactis cadaueribus defluentes, ingemuit, & expansis manibus testabatur, hoc non suo opus esse. Addit his Dominus quartũ: Et æquabunt te solo. Quod ipsum iubente Tito factum esse idem Iosephus testatur, cum iam nullus cædi & rapinæ locus esset reliquus. Itaq; ex tota ciuitate, quæ in toto Oriente florentissima fuerat, tres solæ turres relictæ sunt, Phasselus, Hippicus & Mariamnes cũ parte muri ab Occidente: vt ex his ceu testibus constaret, quale quamq; munitam ciuitatê Romana virtus expugnauisset. In primis tamen memorabile est, quod hic Christus adiecit. Et non relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem. Fuit hoc perpetuum decretum Dei, vt nimirum vrbis huius & templi excidium irreparabile esset, sicuti in Marco nostro diximus. Passus est quidem Aelius Adrianus in ruinis Hierosolymæ vrbem nouam condi, quam ex suo nomine Æliam dixit, & Christianis habitandam permisit: templum tamen nemo vnquam potuit instaurare, etsi id Iudæi sæpe conati sint. Et vt multa alia omittamus, tradunt Ecclesiastici scriptores, Iulianum Apostatam, vt Christum falsi convinceret, Iudæis authorem fuisse, vt illius instaurationem aggrederentur: sed illos horrendis prodigijs impeditos & ab opere deterritos fuisse, quo minus illud perficerent. Itaque iam annis mille quingentis templum illud in ruinis iacet. Quæ enim de illo & Hierosolyma hodie fabulantur superstitiosi homines, qui Dei gratiam & Christi meritum illis locis alligant, tam putida & anilia sunt, vt refutatione nulla opus habeant. Cæterum ne quis Dei iram in muros modo & infensatos lapides desæuituram putaret, filiorum quoq; id est, ciuium & inquilinorum Christus diserte meminit, quos istis malis affligi & constringi oporteat. Et hoc ab illo verissimè dictum esse, ex iis patet, quæ supra de lue & fame intra vrbem grassante diximus. Quibus adijci debet, quod Iosephus de caesorum & captiuorum numero tradidit: illorum quidè decies centena, horum autem nonaginta septem millia numerans: quorū alij ad triumphum seruati, alij ad metalla, triremes & publica opera damnati, multi in ludis publicis cū bestijs aut gladiatoribus pugnare coacti miserabiliter perierunt. Et hæc quidem paulò diligentius & prolixius commemorauimus, vt euidentius pateat Christi Iesu Regis & Sacerdotis nostri Veritas & in hostibus vlciscendis potentia.
units.tr: To explain this, it is relevant that when the Jews made a sortie and set fire to and demolished the Romans' mounds and fortifications, Titus devised a new and remarkable work and enclosed the whole city with a wall. As Josephus writes, the soldiers, with divine speed, built it in three days, running it round the city for thirty-nine stadia, together with thirteen forts in which guards were stationed against the city. From this followed what Christ says third: "And they shall keep thee in on every side." This must be understood of the frequent assaults by which the Romans harassed those shut in, at close and at long range. These were the harder because within the walls the people were consumed at once by a dreadful plague, by seditions, and by famine, more than Saguntum had been. This famine forced them to unusual foods, and even drove mothers, stripped of all human feeling, to such detestable cruelty that they slaughtered the infants they had borne and tore them with greedy teeth after roasting them in fire. Josephus, in the fourteenth chapter of the same book, writes things that belong especially here: since there was no room in the city where corpses could be buried, they threw them from the wall into the ditches. Titus, going round and seeing them full of corpses and the bodies melting into deep putrid filth, groaned and, with outstretched hands, called God to witness that this was not his doing. To these Christ adds a fourth: "And they shall lay thee even with the ground." Josephus also testifies that this was done at Titus's command, when there was no longer any place left for slaughter and plunder. And so out of the whole city, which had been the most flourishing in the entire East, only three towers were left standing, Phasael, Hippicus and Mariamne, together with a part of the western wall, so that these, like witnesses, might show what a strongly fortified city Roman valour had conquered. Yet the most memorable thing is what Christ added here: "And they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another." This was the perpetual decree of God, that the destruction of this city and temple should be irreparable, as we said in our commentary on Mark. Aelius Hadrian did allow a new city to be built on the ruins of Jerusalem, which he named Aelia after himself, and he permitted Christians to live there. But no one was ever able to restore the temple, although the Jews often tried. To pass over many other things: ecclesiastical writers relate that Julian the Apostate, in order to convict Christ of falsehood, encouraged the Jews to undertake its restoration. But they were hindered by dreadful portents and turned away from the work, so that they could not complete it. Thus for now fifteen hundred years that temple has lain in ruins. As for the things that superstitious men today invent about it and about Jerusalem, binding God's grace and Christ's merit to those places, they are so foolish and childish that they need no refutation. Moreover, lest anyone think that the wrath of God would rage only against walls and stones that have been overthrown, Christ expressly mentions the children, that is, the citizens and inhabitants, who must be afflicted and shut in by these evils. That he spoke this most truly is clear from what we said above about the plague and famine raging within the city. To these should be added what Josephus records about the number of the slain and the captives: he counts one million one hundred thousand of the one and ninety-seven thousand of the other. Some of the captives were kept for the triumph, some condemned to the mines, the galleys and public works, and many were forced to fight with wild beasts or gladiators in the public games and perished wretchedly. We have recounted these things somewhat more carefully and at greater length so that the truth of Christ Jesus, our King and Priest, and his power in avenging himself upon his enemies, may appear more plainly.

units.la: Est autem excidij huius multiplex vsus. Primo enim testatur, promissum illum humani generis vindicē & redemptorem reuera exhibitum esse, & ea perfecisse, quæ ad nostram redemptionem pertinebant. Huc enim, stante adhuc Iudæorum Repub. nasci, mori & resuscitari debuisse, ex Daniele patet, qui post occisum Messiam demum vrbem à populo tuc orbis domino excindendam fore, olim prædixit. Docet item excidium hoc, Christum non venisse, vt in terris regnum more principum huius seculi constitueret: sed vt Dei regnum inter homines instauraret. Et solum hoc sufficit ad confutandum errorem eorum, qui regnum somniabant, cuius sedes futura esset Hierosolyma. Præterea est hoc abrogationis ceremoniarum Mosaicarum testimonium euidentissimum: quod toti mundo proponi admodum vtile & necessarium erat. Scimus enim quanta pertinacia Legem & huius ritus retinere conati olim fuerint non solum Iudæi, verumetiam multi eorum, qui Christo iam nomen dederant. Et quamuis veli scissio in morte Christi facta illos de hoc admonere poterat, & Apostoli graviter Legis iustitiam oppugnarent, nunquam tamen hæc persuasio ex quorundam animis eximi potuit, quo minus Legem cum Euangelio miscerent: & ideo ipsam officinam totius illius cultus Leuitici oportuit euerti, vt omnibus constaret, eius vsum porrò nullum esse in Ecclesia.
units.tr: This destruction had many uses. First, it shows that the promised deliverer and redeemer of the human race was truly sent, and that he accomplished what pertained to our redemption. Daniel makes it clear that he had to be born, die and rise again while the Jewish commonwealth was still standing, since Daniel foretold long before that after the Messiah was killed, the city would at last be destroyed by the people who then ruled the world. This destruction also teaches that Christ did not come to set up a kingdom on earth in the manner of the princes of this age, but to establish the kingdom of God among men. This alone is enough to refute the error of those who dreamed of a kingdom whose seat would be Jerusalem. Moreover, it is a most evident testimony that the Mosaic ceremonies have been abrogated, which it was very useful and necessary to set before the whole world. We know how stubbornly not only the Jews but also many who had already professed the name of Christ once tried to retain the Law and its rites. Although the tearing of the veil at Christ's death could have reminded them of this, and although the Apostles strongly attacked the righteousness of the Law, this conviction could never be removed from the minds of some, so that they still mixed the Law with the Gospel. For this reason, the very workshop of that whole Levitical worship had to be overthrown, so that it would be clear to all that its use was no longer valid in the Church.

units.la: Præcipuus tamen excidij istius vsus est, vt discamus Dei iram agnoscere, qua is peccata qui dem omnia, in primis autem Verbi sui contemptum & hostiles aduersus gratiæ suæ prædicationem conatus punire solet. Quod enim Iudæi passi sunt, hoc multis alijs iam inde ab origine rerum accidisse constat. Magna & multiplex fuit primi mundi malitia: sed diluuij pœnas tunc maximè in se prouocarunt, quando Noam iustitiæ præconem aspernati sunt. Ægyptios quoq; etsi luxu & intemperantia sua iampridem exitium meruissent, tunc demū horrendis exemplis Deus multauit, quando aduersus Ecclesiam Dei hostiliter insurrexerunt, in qua is Verbum suum prædicari & cultum verum exerceri volebat. Et si ad magnas illas Monarchias accedamus, Assyriacam nimirū, Babylonicam, Persicam & Græcam, omnibus illis persecutiones Ecclesiæ & Verbi Dei contemptum exitio fuisse patebit. De Romanis alibi diximus, nec vt eadem repetamus opus est, quando omnibus notum est, nulli Imperatori impunè abijsse, qui Christum auf us est aggredi, & eādem audaciam toti Imperio ruinam peperisse. Nec desunt exempla nostri seculi, quæ idem docet. In ea ergo mentis oculos dirigamus, & cogitemus quanti Deus suum Verbum & Ecclesiam faciat. Nam etiamsi dura & horrenda sint, quæ Euangelij & Filij Dei contemptoribus in hoc seculo accidunt, leuia tamen possunt videri præ illis, quæ ijdem æternùm patienter. Et Iudæi non solum euersa vrbe & prorsus sublata eorum politia extorres vagantur, & publicum iræ Dei exemplū sunt, verumetiam repudiati à Deo à promissionibus gratiæ exciderunt, & in sensum reprobum dati, contumacia incu rabili damnationem suam indies magis aggrauant. Semper ergo nobis Apostoli dictum obuersetur, quo huius exempli proprium vsum nobis commendat: Si Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, vide ne tibi quoque parcat. Admonet nos de eo ipse Christus, dum tantorum malorum causam denuo adducit & inculcat, dicens: Eò quod non noueris tempus illud visitationis tuæ. Solet autem Deus bifariam visitare homines. Primum, quando peccatorum remissionem gratuitam nobis offert, & ad pænitentiam hortatur, vt salutis in Filio exhibitæ participes reddamur. Et hanc visitationem Zacharias, in suo Cantico commendat his verbis: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quod inuiserit & redemerit populum suum. Et paulò post: Inuisit nos Oriens siue Germen (de Christo autem loquitur, quem hoc nomine Prophetæ designant) ex alto: vt appareat ijs, qui in tenebris & vmbra mortis positi sunt, ad dirigendum pedes nostros in viam pacis. Deinde visitare dicitur Deus, quando in peccata hominum inquirit, vt pœnas de illis iustas & dignas sumat. Quo sensu in Lege dicit: Ego Dominus Deus tuus fortis, Zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filijs, &c. Et in Sophonia: Eodem tempore lucernis scrutabor Hierosolymam, & visitabo viros, qui in fecibus suis coagulati, &c. In præsenti de primo visitationis genere loquitur, sic tamen vt alterum non omnino excludat, & sic duplice socordiam illis exprobrat. Vt enim non agnouerunt gratiam & bonitatem Dei, qui ipsos ad salutem inuitabat: ita nec tempus iræ obseruarunt, vt salutis huius indicijs visis à sceleribus abstinerent. Hæc verò exitij tam horribilis causam fore docet. Continetur autem his verbis sententia Dei generalis & perpetua, à qua is nunquam discedit. Vult hic (vt Paulus ait) homines saluos fieri & in Veritatis cognitionem venire; & ideo nos inuisit Verbo gratiæ, & ad vitæ emendationem hortatur. At idem gratiæ suæ contemptum seuerè vindicat, & contra securos aut contumaces admonitionum suarum contemptores lucernas illas accendit, de quibus modo ex Sophonia diximus. Sunt hæc nobis diligenter obseruanda nostro sæculo. Inuisit nos quotidie Deus & in Filio suo Iesu Christo salutem nobis offert gratuitam. Agnoscamus hanc eius bonitatem, & cùm simul infelicem mundum multis iræ suæ comminationibus territet, serio propriæ salutis studio accensi, illum vera fide amplectamur, vt eius Spiritu renouati vitam viuamus nouam, & per illius meritum seruemur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet the principal use of this destruction is that we learn to recognise the wrath of God, with which he is accustomed to punish all sins, but especially contempt for his Word and hostile attempts against the preaching of his grace. For it is established that what the Jews suffered had already happened to many others from the beginning of the world. The wickedness of the first world was great and manifold, but they provoked the punishments of the flood most of all when they despised Noah, the herald of righteousness. The Egyptians too had long deserved ruin for their luxury and intemperance, but God at last punished them with dreadful examples when they rose up in hostility against the Church of God, in which he wished his Word to be preached and the true worship to be practised. And if we come to those great monarchies, namely the Assyrian, the Babylonian, the Persian and the Greek, it will be plain that persecution of the Church and contempt of the Word of God brought ruin upon all of them. We have spoken of the Romans elsewhere, and there is no need to repeat it, since it is known to all that no emperor who dared to attack Christ went unpunished, and that the same audacity brought ruin upon the whole empire. Nor are there lacking examples from our own age that teach the same thing. Let us then direct the eyes of our minds to these things and consider how much God values his Word and his Church. For even if those things that befall the despisers of the Gospel and of the Son of God in this age are harsh and dreadful, they may seem light compared with those things which the same despisers will suffer eternally without end. And the Jews, not only with their city overthrown and their polity utterly destroyed, wander as exiles and are a public example of the wrath of God, but also, rejected by God, they have fallen from the promises of grace, and, given over to a reprobate mind, they daily increase their damnation by their incurable obstinacy. Therefore let the saying of the Apostle always be before us, in which he commends to us the proper use of this example: "If God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee." Christ himself warns us of this when he brings forward and presses again the cause of such great evils, saying: "Because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." God, however, is accustomed to visit men in two ways. The first is when he offers us the free forgiveness of sins and exhorts us to repentance, so that we may be made partakers of the salvation exhibited in the Son. Zacharias commends this visitation in his Canticle with these words: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he hath visited and redeemed his people." And a little later: "The dayspring from on high hath visited us" (he speaks of Christ, whom the prophets designate by this name, "the Branch" or "the Dayspring"), "to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace." The second way in which God is said to visit is when he searches out the sins of men in order to take just and fitting punishment for them. In this sense he says in the Law: "I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children," and so on. And in Zephaniah: "At that time I will search Jerusalem with candles, and I will punish the men that are settled on their lees," and so on. In the present passage he speaks of the first kind of visitation, yet in such a way that he does not altogether exclude the second, and so he reproaches them with a twofold carelessness. For just as they did not recognise the grace and goodness of God, who invited them to salvation, so neither did they observe the time of wrath, so that, seeing the signs of this salvation, they might have refrained from their wicked deeds. Yet he teaches that this is the cause of so dreadful a destruction. The general and perpetual sentence of God, from which he never departs, is contained in these words. He wishes here (as Paul says) that men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; therefore he visits us with the Word of grace and exhorts us to amend our lives. But he also severely avenges the contempt of his grace, and against the secure or obstinate despisers of his admonitions he kindles those lamps of which we have just spoken from Zephaniah. These things must be carefully observed by us in our age. God visits us every day and offers us free salvation in his Son Jesus Christ. Let us acknowledge this goodness of his, and, since at the same time he terrifies the unhappy world with many threats of his wrath, let us, kindled with a serious zeal for our own salvation, embrace him with true faith, so that, renewed by his Spirit, we may live a new life and be preserved through his merit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXVII.

units.la: Et ingressus in templū coepit eijcere eos, qui vendebant in eo & emebant, dicens eis: Scriptum est, Domus mea domus precationis est: vos autem fecistis eam speluncam latronum. Et docebat quotidie in templo. Principes autem Sacerdotum & Scribæ, & primores plebis studebant eum perdere: nec inueniebant quid facerent: Totus enim populus pendebat ab ipso, cum eum audiret.
units.tr: "And when he had entered the temple, he began to drive out those who sold and bought in it, saying to them: It is written, My house is the house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves. And he taught daily in the temple. But the chief priests and the scribes and the leading men of the people sought to destroy him, and they could not find what they might do, for all the people hung on him, listening to him."

units.la: Audiuimus ingressum regiū Domini nostri Iesu Christi in Hierosolymam, quem ita instituit & fecit, vt non obscure maiestatem suam atq; potentiam declararit, simulq; suo exemplo Reges & principes omnes officij admoneat. Vt enim omnisciētiæ, potentiæ & iustitiæ argumenta præbuit manifesta: sic bonitatis & clementiæ plus quàm paternæ exemplū est, quod ad vrbis conspectū lachrymas profudit, & eorum interitum deflere dignatus est, qui nō vno modo perdi meruerat. Ex eo igitur euidentissimè apparet, hominum sanguinem in oculis eius pretiosissimum esse, quod in bono Rege Spiritus sanctus in primis requirit. Sequitur nunc quid primū fecerit, vbi in vrbem peruenit: Quod nimirum templum ingressus ex eo omnes eiecerit, qui illic emebant aut vendebat, ipse verò ibi dem populum docuerit, & doctrinam suā (vt Matthæus annotat) miraculosa cæcorum & claudorum curatione confirmarit. Quo facto se reuera populi Dei siue Ecclesiæ Regem & Sacerdotum esse demonstrauit, cui Ecclesiæ & religionis reformandæ munus à Patre mandatum sit; simul autē suo exemplo docet, quid in reformationibus eiusmodi omnes eos facere conueniat, ad quos ea cura ex Dei mandato pertinet. Est ergo historia hæc digna, quæ sæpius consideretur, nec temere factum putabimus, quòd eam ab omnibus Euangelistis describi voluit Spiritus sanctus. Ita enim admonet, nobis quoq; non debere graue aut molestum videri, si frequentius eadem nobis proponatur.
units.tr: We have heard of the royal entry of our Lord Jesus Christ into Jerusalem. He arranged and carried it out in such a way that he plainly declared his majesty and power, and at the same time by his example admonishes all kings and princes of their duty. For just as he gave clear proofs of his omniscience, power and justice, so his goodness and mercy, more than fatherly, is shown in the fact that at the sight of the city he shed tears and deigned to lament the ruin of those who had deserved to perish in more ways than one. From this it therefore appears most clearly that the blood of men is most precious in his eyes, which the Holy Spirit above all requires in a good king. Next we see what he did first when he came into the city: entering the temple, he drove out all who were buying and selling there, while he himself taught the people in that place and confirmed his teaching (as Matthew notes) by miraculously healing the blind and the lame. By this act he truly showed himself to be the King of the people of God, or of the Church, and that the task of reforming the Church and religion had been committed to him by the Father. At the same time, by his example, he teaches what all those ought to do in such reformations, those to whom that care belongs by God's command. This history is therefore worthy of frequent consideration, and we shall not think it without reason that the Holy Spirit wished it to be described by all the Evangelists. For thus he warns us that we too should not think it grievous or troublesome if the same things are set before us more often.

units.la: Occurrit autem hic primo loco, quòd cùm iam vrbem ingressus esset, non in Antoniam (castel lum idfuit), quod Herodes magnus impensis instauratum in Antonij honorem ita denominauit) neque neq; in Prætorium, sed in templum diuertit. Eo autem facto rursus testatus est, Regnum suum non de hoc mundo esse, sed in mundum se venisse, ut Veritati testimonium ferat, huius doctrinam asse-rat, promissiones Dei impleat, & eius Regnum inter homines instauret. Quia verò ingressu hoc in vrbem se Regem esse testari voluit, interim suo exemplo aperte docet, templorum & religionis cu-ram ad principes quoq; & omnes eos pertinere, qui Rempub. administrant. Nam etiamsi cultum su-um Deus non armis huius sæculi, sed Verbi sui prædicatione & Spiritus virtute propagari velit: il-lius tamen curam magistratibus quàm maximè commendatam esse vult, & ab illis hoc requirit, ut illum inter suæ fidei creditum populum secundum sui verbi regulam constitui, & bene constitutum seruari ac retineri curent. Quorsum enim opus erat librum Legis diuinæ Regibus commendari, si re-ligionis cura nihil ad eos pertinet? Aut cur pœnæ blasphemis & falsis doctoribus constituuntur, si magistratus (cuius solius est pœnas de sontibus sumere) rebus aut negotiis ad religionem pertinen-tibus se non debet immiscere? Et vt ista omittamus, annon communis sensus & Lex naturæ hoc iu-bent, vt qui à Deo potestate & authoritate armati sunt, vicissim huius gloriam atq; honorem tueân-tur, sicq; ei bonam gratiam referant? Sed quid multis opus est, quando in veteri Testamento hoc po-tissimum nomine Dauid, Sololomon, Iosaphat, Ezechias, Iosias, Zorobabel & similes laudantur, quòd in religione rectè constituenda & abusibus seu superstitionibus abolendis operam strenuam na-rarunt? Et de Christi Ecclesia Isaias vaticinans, Reges eius nutritios & Reginas nutrices fo-re pollicetur. Sunt hæc obseruanda non solum propter Anabaptistas & horum similes fanaticos homines, qui omnem cum politicum tum ecclesiasticum ordinem è medio sublatum volunt; verumetiam propter Pontifices & Episcopos, qui in Ecclesia omnem potestatem ad se transtulerunt & ne-fas esse clamant, vt Reges atq; principes quicquam in illa constituant, aut ad reformandum cultum Dei manum admoueant: Id illud enim non nisi vniuersalis Concilij authoritate fieri oportere. Ita ve-rò malè vsurpatam tyrannidem peioribus artibus stabiliunt, & tanquam prophanos & impios ho-mines à religionis cura eos excludunt, quorum opera Deus omnibus sæculis ad coercendam Pontifi-cum licentiam & ad eorundem negligentiam corrigendam vtiliter est vsus. Imò cùm ipsi Imperato-rum donationibus partim fictis, partim impudenti ambitione et turpi hypocrisi extortis glorientur, ijsdem tamen minimè permissum esse clamant, vt in religione quacumque corrupta aliquid tentent. Ergò ne Ludouico licuit Romam Pontifici donare, & ad hoc Imperatoria authoritate vti: hodie au-tem Imperatori non licebit curare, vt tàm Romæ quàm alibi verus Dei cultus instauretur, & abu-sus è medio tollantur? Illis item ius erat superstitionibus Dei cultum peruertere, falsa doctrina con-scientias hominum turbare, eosdem pecuniis & fortunis omnibus emungere, animas deniq; in mor-tis æternæ periculum abducere: Regibus autem & alijs, quos magistratus authoritate Deus arma-uit, nefas fuerit, eorum licentiæ obstare, & vt veritatis doctrina cum vero cultu reducatur, prospice-re? Sed ita cornua sua Antichristus prodat oportet, cuius vox est, se à nemine reprehendi debere, e-tiamsi millia multa animarum cateruatim ad inferos rapiat. Excitent autem ista Christianos prin-cipes, ne sui populi salutem negligat. Hunc enim ex illorum manibus requiret Deus, neq; in eius con-spectu illis excusatio erit aliqua, si authoritatem suam tam seruiliter Pontificum pedibus calcan-dam subijciant, qua & Dei gloriam & publicam omnem salutem debebant tueri.
units.tr: But here, first of all, it is to be noted that when he had now entered the city, he turned aside not into the Antonia (a fortress there, which Herod the Great, having rebuilt it at great expense, named in honour of Antony), nor into the Praetorium, but into the temple. By doing so he again bore witness that his kingdom is not of this world, but that he came into the world to bear witness to the truth, to assert his doctrine, to fulfil the promises of God, and to establish his kingdom among men. But because by this entry into the city he wished to testify that he is King, he meanwhile teaches plainly by his example that the care of temples and of religion pertains to princes also, and to all who administer the commonwealth. For even though God wills that his worship be propagated not by the arms of this age, but by the preaching of his Word and the power of his Spirit, yet he wishes the care of it to be most earnestly committed to magistrates, and requires of them that they see to it that the people entrusted to their faith be constituted according to the rule of his Word, and, once well constituted, be kept and preserved. For why was it necessary for the book of the divine Law to be commended to kings, if the care of religion has nothing to do with them? Or why are punishments appointed for blasphemers and false teachers, if the magistrate (whose alone it is to exact punishment from the guilty) must not interfere in matters or affairs pertaining to religion? And to pass over these things, do not common sense and the law of nature command that those who are armed by God with power and authority should in turn defend his glory and honour, and so render him due thanks? But why need there be many words, when in the Old Testament David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah, Zerubbabel and others like them are praised chiefly for this, that they zealously laboured to establish true religion and to abolish abuses and superstitions? And Isaiah, prophesying of the Church of Christ, promises that its kings shall be its nursing fathers and its queens its nurses. These things are to be observed not only on account of the Anabaptists and similar fanatics, who wish every political and ecclesiastical order to be removed from the midst, but also on account of the Pontiffs and Bishops, who have transferred all power in the Church to themselves, and cry out that it is unlawful for kings and princes to establish anything in it, or to lay a hand to reforming the worship of God, since this, they say, ought to be done only by the authority of a universal Council. Thus they confirm by worse arts a tyranny wrongly seized, and as profane and impious men they exclude from the care of religion those by whose work God in all ages has usefully acted to curb the licence of the Pontiffs and to correct their negligence. Indeed, although they boast of the donations of the Emperors, partly fictitious, partly extorted by shameless ambition and foul hypocrisy, they nevertheless cry out that these same Emperors are by no means permitted to attempt anything in any corrupted religion. So was it lawful for Louis to give Rome to the Pontiff and to use imperial authority for this, but today it will not be lawful for the Emperor to take care that the true worship of God be restored both at Rome and elsewhere, and abuses be removed? Likewise it was their right to pervert the worship of God by superstitions, to disturb men's consciences with false doctrine, to drain them of their money and all their goods, and finally to lead souls into the peril of eternal death; but for kings and others whom God has armed with the authority of magistracy, would it be unlawful to oppose such licence, and to provide that the doctrine of truth be brought back together with true worship? But Antichrist must thus reveal his horns, whose voice is that he ought to be reproved by no one, even though he drags many thousands of souls in droves to hell. Let these things rouse Christian princes, lest they neglect the salvation of their people. For God will require it at their hands, and there will be no excuse for them in his sight if they so servilely submit their authority to be trampled under the feet of the Pontiffs, when they ought to defend both the glory of God and the whole public welfare.

units.la: Cæterùm quid Christus in templo fecerit, audiamus: Ingressus cœpit eijcere eos, qui vendebant in eo & emebant, &c. Summa omnium quæ dicuntur est, illum eiectis & abolitis ijs, quæ Sacerdotum auaritia atq; libidine contra Dei Verbum inuecta erant, ea sustinuisse, quæ in templis exerceri de-bent, quæq; ad verum cultum pertinent. Quod vt rectius intelligatur, paucis repetendum erit, qua-nam apud Iudæos templi prophanatio & cultus diuini corruptio fuerit. Fuit illud antiquitus in eum vsum Dei iussu ædificatum, vt illic colle&i Verbum audirent, preces publicè facerent, & quæ tunc in vsu erant sacra obirent. Vnicum verò esse voluit Deus, ne superstitionum diuersitate popu-lus in sectas distraheretur, sed facilius in fidei vnitate & eiusdē religionis siue cultus exercitio pos-set contineri. Erat ergo magna eius loci maiestas, et cùm illo tempore Iudæi per omnes gentes dispersi essent, quotidie ex remotissimis quoque terris illuc confluebant, qui Deo sacrificium aliquod vole-bant offerre. At cùm eodem tempore partim Romanorum præsidum rapacitate, partim Sacerdotum auaritia, Sacerdotium venale factum esset, hac Dei constitutione simul & populi undiq; confluentiū studio Sacerdotes ad quaestum suum abuti coeperunt. Itaq; oves, boves, columbas & quae alia sacrificijs seruire poterant, in templi atrio vendebantur, vt ex illorum emptione aliqua lucri pars ad ipsos rediret, & plures ad sacrificandum allicerentur. Adhaec propter peregrinos numulariorum etiam mensae aut abaci illic vtebantur: adeo vt templum iam nihil à foro prophano differret. Erat ergo haec turpis nimium loci sacri & totius cultus diuini prophanatio, quae sub plausibili religionis prouehendae praetextu priuato Sacerdotum quaestui seruiebat. Cum quasi conferas, quae posteremis temporibus in Christianorum templa inuecta sunt, non minorem, imo impudentiorem multo totius religionis prophanationem videbis: de qua cum saepe dictum sit, & omnium oculis obuersetur, non opus est nunc omnes negotiationes illius species enumerare.
units.tr: But let us hear what Christ did in the temple: "And when he had entered, he began to drive out those who sold and bought in it," etc. The sum of all that is said is that, when those things that the covenanted avarice and lust of the priests had introduced against the Word of God had been cast out and abolished, he restored what ought to be practised in temples and pertains to true worship. That this may be understood more correctly, it must be briefly recalled in what the profanation of the temple and the corruption of divine worship among the Jews consisted. Of old it was built by God's command for this use: that there the people might gather to hear the Word, make public prayers, and perform the sacred rites then in use. God willed that there be only one such place, so that the people should not be torn into sects by the diversity of superstitions, but might more easily be held together in the unity of faith and the practice of the same religion and worship. That place was therefore of great majesty, and although at that time the Jews were scattered through all nations, daily people flocked there even from the most remote lands who wished to offer some sacrifice to God. But when at the same time the priesthood had become a thing for sale, partly through the rapacity of the Roman governors, partly through the avarice of the priests, the priests began to abuse this ordinance of God, and the eagerness of the people flocking in from every side, for their own gain. And so sheep, oxen, doves and whatever else could serve for sacrifices were sold in the court of the temple, so that some part of the profit from their purchase might return to the priests themselves, and more people might be enticed to sacrifice. Besides, on account of foreign visitors, the tables or counters of money-changers were also used there, so that the temple now differed in no way from a profane marketplace. This was therefore a most shameful profanation of the sacred place and of all divine worship, which, under the plausible pretext of promoting religion, served the private profit of the priests. And if you compare what has been introduced into the temples of Christians in later times, you will see a profanation of all religion no less, indeed far more shameless: since this has often been said, and lies before the eyes of all, there is no need now to enumerate all the kinds of such dealing.

units.la: Videamus nunc potius Christi de his omnibus iudicium: quem ita offenderunt, vt non contentus verbis durioribus omnes increpasse, qui talia faciebant, manum quoque admonerit. Nam venditores simul atque emptores templo eiecit: quod alias quoque sub praedicationis suae initium flagello ex funibus facto illum fecisse, Ioannes scribit. Sed & mensas numulariorum euertit, & cathedras eorum confregit, qui ibidem columbas vendebant: Quae omnia absq; multorum detrimento fieri non potuerunt. Addit Marcus, quod per ipsum nemini licuerit aliquod vas aut instrumentum per templum deferre: adeo illud ab omnibus ijs repurgatum esse voluit, quae ad Dei cultum nihil faciunt. Neq; his subito factis profugit, sed in templo considens publice docere coepit, & doctrinam suam (vt initio diximus) operibus miraculosis confirmauit. Fuit ergo hoc inter omnia diuinae eius potentiae atq; maiestatis opera, quae hucusq; fecit, meo iudicio longe praestantissimum. Quis enim alius mortalium id sudim pune facere potuisset? Enimuero cum anno proxime sequenti Pilatus Caesaris imagines in templum intulisset, ingens populi concursus factus & publica seditio exorta est. Idem etiam maiori cum periculo accidit, cum pecuniam sacram è templo ablatam in aquaeductum insumpsisset. Nunc autem cum & templum temere violatum videri posset, & Sacerdotum authoritas contumeliose conculcata, & complures in corpore et fortunis damnum aut iniuriam passi essent, omnium tamen manus quiescunt, omnium ora silent, nec quisquam reperitur in seditiosissima gente, qui vim istam vi repellere, aut saltem impedire auisit. At cum praeter imbellem discipulorum turbam nemo Christo adesset, diuina vir tutus hoc opus fuit, quae mentes omnium terruit & manus continuit.
units.tr: Let us now consider instead Christ's judgment on all these things. He was so offended by them that, not content with harsher words against all who did such things, he also took action. He drove out the sellers and the buyers from the temple. John writes that he had done this earlier as well, at the start of his preaching, using a whip made of cords. He also overturned the tables of the money-changers and broke the seats of those who sold doves there. None of this could have been done without considerable damage to many people. Mark adds that he would not allow anyone to carry any vessel or implement through the temple. He wanted it cleansed of everything that had nothing to do with the worship of God. Nor did he flee once these things were done. He sat down in the temple and began to teach publicly, and he confirmed his teaching with miraculous works, as we said at the beginning. In my judgment, therefore, this was far the most outstanding of all the works of his divine power and majesty that he had performed up to that point. For what other mortal could have done this single-handedly? Indeed, when Pilate brought Caesar's images into the temple in the following year, a huge crowd gathered and a public uprising broke out. The same thing happened, with even greater danger, when he took sacred money out of the temple and spent it on an aqueduct. Yet now, although the temple may seem to have been violated rashly, the authority of the priests trampled shamefully, and many people suffered harm or injury to their bodies and property, all hands are still, all mouths are silent, and in this most seditious nation no one is found who dares to repel that violence by force, or at least to prevent it. But since no one was with Christ except a crowd of unarmed disciples, this work was done by his divine power alone, which terrified the minds of all and restrained their hands.

units.la: Disputatur hic à nonnullis, quo iure istud ille fecerit, & num alicui ex Verbi ministris aut privatis hominibus idem facere liceat? Et Christum quidem excusant, quod singulari quodam & Heroico motu rem tanta sit aggressus, & quod quae ita fiunt, diuinae virtutis opera sint. At mihi quoad Christum, disputatio ista superuacua & curiosa potius quam vtilis & necessaria videtur. Cur enim vt nudus homo consideratur, quem alieno motu excitari oportuerit, qui Deus quoque verus atque aeternus est, & proprio consilio atque instinctu facit omnia? Deinde cur de iure eius disputatur, cum eum à Deo Patre Regem & Sacerdotem destinatum fuisse constet, & iam olim à Malachia praedictum fuerit, illum ignis instar in templum venturum esse, vt filios Leui purget ac emundet? Suo igitur iure hic vsus est, & proinde alia excusatione non habet opus: Quin potius (vt ante monuimus) exemplum praebet Regibus & omnibus alijs, quos Deus imperio & authoritate armauit, vt ipsi quoque simili zelo ac feruore cultum verum tueantur, & ab omni superstitione atque idololatria repurgent.
units.tr: Some argue here about by what right he did this, and whether it is permitted to any minister of the Word or to private persons to do the same. They excuse Christ on the grounds that he undertook such a great matter by a singular and heroic impulse, and that what is done in this way is a work of divine power. But as far as Christ is concerned, this debate seems to me superfluous and curious rather than useful and necessary. Why should he be considered as a mere man, who would have needed to be stirred up by someone else's impulse, when he is also true and eternal God, and does all things by his own counsel and instinct? Further, why is his right disputed, when it is established that God the Father appointed him King and Priest, and when Malachi long ago foretold that he would come into the temple like a fire to purify and cleanse the sons of Levi? Therefore he exercised his own right here, and so has no need of any other excuse. Rather, as we noted before, he sets an example for kings and all others whom God has armed with command and authority, so that they too may defend the true worship with a similar zeal and fervour, and purge it of all superstition and idolatry.

units.la: Quoad vero priuatos homines, fatemur, hos nihil huius absque peculiari Dei mandato tentare debere: sed sufficiat eis, vt ipsi conscientiam puram seruent: publicas autem reformationes ijs relinquant, qui illas ex officio facere debent. Pium equidem est dolere ac ingemiscere, quando veri cultus loco superstitiones & idololatriam regnare vident (sicuti Paulum Athenienses idololatria doluisse legimus, sed tumultuandi occasionem neq; ipsi temere arripere neq; alijs praebere debent. Interim minime negamus, saepe fieri, vt priuati homines, & interdum idiotae etiam ac illiterati, eiusmodi facinora faciant, quae cum hoc Christi facto coeuniunt, & cum praesenti atque ineuitabili periculo coniuncta sunt: vt cum idola in locis publicis deiiciunt, doctores falsos palam in concionibus falsi arguunt, panem consecratum vt pro Christo adoretur, in processionibus publicis ex Episcoporum manibus excutiunt, aut etiam conculcant, quod nostro tempore non vno loco factum esse scimus. Quae omnia eiusmodi sunt, vt nemo illa temere iubere, aut aliquem ad ea hortari debeat: at si nemine iubente à viris bonis fiant, quorum pietas nobis satis perspecta est, & quos ratione sana semper vsos esse constat, ego tales minime damnauerim: sed peculiarem Spiritus Sancti motum in illis agnosco, qui eorum opera ad afferendam Dei gloriam & ad confundendam idololatrarum stupiditatem vti solet. Quòd si qui eos temeritatis accusant, ego potius spiritus Dei vim considerandam esse puto, qui in eiusmodi motibus verè Heroicis non permittit semper, vt omnia ad nostrae rationis calculum revocemus: potius autem reprehendi merentur ignaui principes & personati doctores vel potius canes muti, qui ea tam diu ferunt, quae authoritate publica tolli & aboleri debebant.
units.tr: As for private persons, we admit that they ought to attempt nothing of this kind without a special command of God. It is enough for them to keep their own conscience pure, and to leave public reforms to those who ought to carry them out by virtue of their office. It is indeed a godly thing to grieve and groan when we see superstitions and idolatry reigning in place of the true worship. We read that Paul was stirred in spirit by the idolatry of the Athenians, yet they ought neither rashly to seize the opportunity for tumult themselves nor give it to others. Meanwhile we by no means deny that it often happens that private persons, and sometimes even uneducated and unlettered ones, commit deeds of this kind, which agree with this deed of Christ and are bound up with a present and unavoidable danger. For example, when they throw down idols in public places, openly accuse false teachers in sermons, snatch the consecrated bread from the hands of bishops in public processions, so that it may be adored as Christ, or even trample it underfoot, as we know has happened in more than one place in our own time. All these things are of such a kind that no one should rashly command them or urge anyone to them. But if they are done by good men without anyone commanding them, men whose piety is well known to us and who are known always to have used sound reason, I would by no means condemn such men. Rather, I recognise in them a special motion of the Holy Spirit, which is wont to use their works to proclaim the glory of God and to confound the stupidity of idolaters. But if some accuse them of rashness, I think rather that the power of God's Spirit must be considered, which in such truly heroic impulses does not always allow us to bring everything back to the reckoning of our reason. Rather, it is the lazy princes and the masked teachers, or rather dumb dogs, who deserve reproach, for they tolerate those things which ought to have been removed and abolished by public authority.

units.la: Sed vt ad Christum redeamus, ne insanientium more ista facere videretur, consilij & facti sui rationem ex Scripturis affert. Scriptum est (inquit) Domus mea domus precationis est: vos autem fecistis eam speluncam latronum. Coniungit duos locos, quorum alter apud Isaiam Cap. 56. habetur de gentium vocatione, quas ad Ecclesiam & verum Dei cultum aliquando accedere oportet: alter extat Ieremiae septimo, vbi hypocritas accusat Dominus, qui tepli & externi cultus fiducia ad peccandi licentiam abutebantur, & impunitatem sibi ex eo promittebant, quòd in templo frequentes comparerent, & sacris publicis interessent. Vt enim latrones in speluncis suis fiduciam habent, eo audaciores sunt in perpetrandis sceleribus, si loca habeant munita aut occulta, quò se recipere possunt, vt tuto lateant: ita hypocritae ex simulato cultu & ceremoniarum obseruatione insolentem peccandi fiduciam solent concipere. Prophetae autem verbis vtitur Christus, vt malum hoc non recens, sed auitum & hereditarium istis esse ostendat. Quàmuis altius quoque insurgat, & sacerdotum doctrinam atq; mores accusat, qui templum reuera in latronum speluncam conuerterant. Qui enim non per Christum ingreditur, vere fur atque latro est: quia & illum sua gloria spoliat, & eos fortunis exuit, qui ipsi obediunt, adhaec animabus eorundem certum exitium struit. Atqui omnia haec ab illis fiebant, cum salutis ostia & vias longè alias monstrarent, religionem omnem sibi quaestum fecissent, & infelicem populum à Christo abstraherent: quod non aliud erat, quàm animas eorum iugulare & ad sempiternum exitium abripere. Continetur autem hoc Christi exemplo quicquid de reformatione religionis & Ecclesiae dici potest.
units.tr: But to return to Christ: lest he should seem to be acting like madmen, he gives the reason for his counsel and deed from the Scriptures. "It is written," he says, "My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves." He joins two passages. The first is found in Isaiah chapter 56, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, who must at some time come to the Church and the true worship of God. The other stands in Jeremiah chapter 7, where the Lord accuses hypocrites who, trusting in the temple and external worship, abused them as licence to sin, and promised themselves impunity because they came in great numbers to the temple and took part in public rites. For just as robbers feel bold in their caves, and are the more daring in committing crimes if they have fortified or hidden places to which they can retreat and lie safe, so hypocrites, from feigned worship and observance of ceremonies, are wont to conceive an insolent confidence in sinning. Christ uses the prophet's words to show that this evil is not recent but inherited and handed down from their forefathers. He rises even higher, and accuses the priests' teaching and morals, who had really turned the temple into a den of robbers. For whoever does not enter through Christ is truly a thief and a robber, because he both robs Christ of his glory and strips of their possessions those who obey him, and moreover prepares certain destruction for their souls. Yet all these things were done by them, since they showed the doors and ways of salvation quite differently, made all religion a source of gain for themselves, and drew the unhappy people away from Christ. This was nothing other than cutting their throats and dragging them off to eternal destruction. Whatever can be said about the reform of religion and the Church is contained in this example of Christ.

units.la: Et huius quidem curam atque studium ad magistratum legitimum in primis pertinere, iam ante diximus. Nunc obseruemus, quòd aeternus Dei Filius, cuius solius authoritas sufficere potest, facti sui rationem ex Scripturis adducit. Eo enim admonemur in reformandis aut constituendis Ecclesiis nihil ex priuato alicuius hominis arbitrio, sed omnia secundùm Verbi Dei praescriptum instituti ac fieri debere. Quia enim Ecclesia domus Dei est, nemo mortalium quantacunque authoritatis sit, in ea plus iuris aut imperij sibi sumere debet, quam ille dederit: ideoq; solius Dei Verbum audiatur. Obseruauit hoc olim Iosias Rex, qui cum ex Legis lectione intellexisset, quàm procul à viis Dei deflexisset populus, vestimenta sua scidit, & Legem diu amissam omnibus proponi voluit, vt secundùm hanc abusus omnes corrigerentur. Quem scopum etiam Christianis Regibus olim pro positum fuisse constat. Quapropter in ipso limine offendunt, qui hodie vel Concilio vniuersali opus esse clamitant, vel homines politica sapientia & eruditione praeditos diligendos dicunt, quibus hoc negotij detur, vt in nostri seculi controuersijs tolerabilem & moderatam doctrinae atque religionis formam conscribant, quae deinceps ab omnibus recipiatur. Quid enim Concilio opus est ijs, qui in Veteris & Noui testamenti libris verae Ecclesiae & omnium piorum, quotquot à mundi exordio fuerunt, consensum inueniunt, à quo nemini dissentire licet? Vel num interea de salute totius mundus periclitari & incertis opinionibus fluctuare debet, dum Patres illi mitrati sua dogmata parturiunt? Praeterea, quia tota haec causa ad conscientiam hominis pertinet, quae non alibi quàm in solius Dei Verbo acquiescit, frustra ijs hominum authoritas obtrudetur, qui quid Deus velit & iubeat, audire cupiunt.
units.tr: We have already said before that the care and zeal for this belongs first of all to the lawful magistrate. Now let us observe that the eternal Son of God, whose authority alone can suffice, brings forward the reason for his deed from the Scriptures. By this we are warned that in reforming or establishing Churches nothing should be instituted or done at the discretion of any private person, but everything according to the prescription of God's Word. For since the Church is the house of God, no mortal, however great his authority, ought to claim for himself more right or power in it than God has given him. Therefore the Word of God alone is to be heard. King Josiah observed this long ago. When he understood from the reading of the Law how far the people had turned aside from the ways of God, he tore his garments, and wished the Law, long lost, to be set before all, so that all abuses might be corrected according to it. It is well known that this aim was also set before Christian kings in former times. Therefore they stumble at the very threshold who now cry out that a general council is needed, or who say that men endowed with political wisdom and learning should be chosen to draw up, amid the controversies of our age, a tolerable and moderate form of doctrine and religion, which would then be received by all. For what need is there of a council for those who find in the books of the Old and New Testaments the consensus of the true Church and of all the godly, from the beginning of the world, from which no one may dissent? Or meanwhile should the salvation of the whole world be imperilled and tossed about by uncertain opinions, while those mitred Fathers give birth to their dogmas? Moreover, since this whole matter pertains to the conscience of man, which rests nowhere but in the Word of God alone, the authority of men is pressed upon those in vain who desire to hear what God wills and commands.

units.la: Deinde quid in reformationibus tolli, quidue substitui oporteat, Christus suo exemplo docet. Eijcit enim ex templo omnes qui vendebant & emebant, adhaec Sacerdotes hoc nomine graviter accusat, quòd ex templo Dei speluncam latronum fecissent. Damnantur ergo in religione & propter quae cunque ad quaestum instituta sunt. Cùm enim Deus nos gratuita misericordia seruet, quaestum à sua Ecclesia procul remotum esse vult. Et nimis temerarij sunt, qui hunc ex Spiritus Sancti donis facere in animum inducunt, cùm illa non sint in nostro arbitrio aut
units.tr: Next, Christ by his own example teaches what ought to be removed in reformations and what ought to be put in its place. He drove out of the temple all who were buying and selling, and he severely accused the priests of making God's temple a den of robbers. Therefore whatever is instituted for gain is condemned in religion. Since God preserves us by free mercy, he wills that profit be kept far from his Church. And those are very rash who think this can be made a matter of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, since those gifts are not in our power or control.

units.la: Kkk potestate. Constituit quidem Dominus, vt ex Euangelio viuant, quicunque hoc prædicant. At idem Spiritus sui dona aut Sacramenta vendere prohibet, & scimus quid Ghiezi seruo suo Elisæus, quiditem Simoni Mago Petrus olim dixerint, cùm illi simile quid tentarent. Pecunia tua (inquit Apostolus) tecum sit in perditionem, qui donum Dei putaris pecunijs acquiri. Non est tibi pars neque sors in ratione hac. Nec tamen eos solos eiecit Dominus ex templo, qui illic mercabantur, sed eos quoque prohibuit (vt diximus) qui vasa quæcunque per illud deferebant. Debent ergo in reformationibus omnia ea tolli, quæ vel ministrorū auaritiæ & quæstui priuato seruiunt, vel ad cultum Dei nihil faciunt. At si hæc regula obseruetur, quid obsecro ex toto Papatu reliquum manebit, vbi venalia sunt omnia, & ea etiam in honore summo & pretio habentur, quibus Dei cultus impeditur & euertitur? De simulachris loquor, de quibus olim Lactantius dicere non est veritus, Religionem omnino nullam esse, vbicunque simulachrum est. In illis ergo eijciendis olim strenuissimi fuerunt, quotquot à Spiritu sancto eo nomine commendantur, quòd veri Dei cultum à sordibus repurgauerint. Ezechias certè ne æneum quidem serpentem amplius ferendum putauit, quando Iudæi ex eo simulachrum fecerant, quod suffitu & cultu externo honorabant. Nec probrosum fuit inter Christianos aliquem εἰκονομάχον, id est, imaginum oppugnatorem aut destructorem dici, vsque ad Gregorij tertij tempora, qui sub annum nati Christi septingentesimum trigefimū nonum, Leonem Isaurum hoc nomine notauit, & excommunicationis fulmine ferijt, quòd imagines ex templis deleri iussisset. Sed neminem moueant hominum temeraria iudicia, quando quod facimus, Verbi Dei authoritate defendi potest.
units.tr: The Lord indeed ordained that those who preach the gospel should live by the gospel. But the same Spirit forbids selling his gifts or sacraments. We know what Elisha said to his servant Gehazi, and what Peter once said to Simon Magus when he attempted something similar. "May your money perish with you," said the Apostle, "because you thought the gift of God could be bought with money. You have no part or lot in this matter." Nor did the Lord drive out from the temple only those who did business there; he also forbade (as we have said) those who carried any vessels through it. Therefore in reformations all those things must be removed which either serve the greed of ministers and private profit, or contribute nothing to the worship of God. But if this rule is observed, what, I ask, will remain of the whole Papacy, where everything is for sale, and where those things are held in the highest honour and price which hinder and overturn the worship of God? I speak of images, of which Lactantius once did not hesitate to say that wherever there is an image there is no religion at all. Those who in removing them cleansed the true worship of God from defilement are commended by the Holy Spirit for this very reason, and they were once most zealous in it. Hezekiah certainly did not think the bronze serpent should be tolerated any longer, when the Jews had made an image of it and honoured it with incense and outward worship. Nor was it a reproach among Christians, down to the time of Gregory III, to be called an iconoclast, that is, an opponent or destroyer of images. In the year of Christ 739 Gregory branded Leo the Isaurian with this name and struck him with the thunderbolt of excommunication, because he had ordered images to be removed from the churches. But let not the rash judgments of men disturb anyone, since what we do can be defended by the authority of God's Word.

units.la: Porrò non sufficit sustulisse quæ Deo displicent & verum cultum impediunt, nisi substituantur ijs vera pietatis exercitia. Ea paucis hisce verbis comprehendit Christus: Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur. Continetur hic totum Ecclesiæ regimen siue gubernatio vnà cum vero cultu, qui huic necessariò coniunctus est. Nam oratio siue inuocatio absq; doctrina Verbi Dei cõsistere non potest. Quomodo inuocabunt cum (inquit Paulus) in quem non crediderunt? Quomodo autem credent ei, de quo nihil audiuerunt? Quomodo autē audient absq; prædicante? Itaq; Ecclesiæ gubernatio ex Verbi doctrina seu prædicatione Euangelij depēdet, quod ideò sceptrū potentiæ Christi dicitur. Et hæc causa est, quòd vt hic in docendo frequentissimus fuit antea: ita nunc quàm primùm negotiatores ex templo eiecit, mox populū docere incipit. Vnde colligimus Ecclesiam veram apud eos esse nō posse, apud quos Verbi prædicatio silet, & qui illo neglecto circa res inutiles aut inanes ceremonias occupantur. Cultus autem externus simul & internus fere in inuocatione consistit. Nam vt hæc ex fide nascitur: ita cum conscientiæ puritate confessionem quoq; coniunctam habet, quem cultum Deo gratissimum esse, omnis scriptura docet. Huc enim facit, quod in Psalmo veri cultus rationem tradit turus ait: In die tribulationis tuæ inuoca me, & liberabo te, tuq; me glorificabis. Et Christus eos demum veros Dei cultores esse testatur, qui illū adorāt in spiritu & veritate. Debet ergo hic locus nos ad inuocandū excitare, quando dubiū non est, preces nostras illi acceptas fore, cùm ijs maximè colatur atq; honoretur. Singuli item doctrinam hanc ad se transferre debent, vt seipsos veram Dei domum aut templum tunc demum fore meminerint, si Dei Verbo locum dent, et illum pura conscientia ex fide inuocent: Qui ista negligunt, non habent, quod de Dei cultu aut Ecclesiæ titulo glorientur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not enough to have removed what displeases God and hinders true worship, unless the true exercises of piety are put in its place. Christ sums these up in a few words: "My house shall be called a house of prayer." Here is contained the whole governance or government of the Church, together with the true worship that is necessarily joined to it. For prayer or invocation cannot exist apart from the doctrine of God's Word. "How shall they call upon him," says Paul, "in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" Therefore the governance of the Church depends on the teaching of the Word, or the preaching of the gospel, which is for this reason called the sceptre of Christ's power. And this is why, as Christ was very frequent in teaching before, so now, as soon as he had driven the merchants out of the temple, he at once began to teach the people. From this we gather that the true Church cannot be where the preaching of the Word is silent, and where people, neglecting it, occupy themselves with useless or empty ceremonies. Now external worship, as well as internal, consists almost entirely in invocation. For as this arises from faith, so it also has confession joined with it, along with purity of conscience; and all Scripture teaches that this worship is most pleasing to God. To this purpose is what the Psalm says when it sets out the manner of true worship: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." And Christ testifies that those are at last the true worshippers of God who worship him in spirit and truth. This passage ought therefore to stir us up to invoke him, since there is no doubt that our prayers will be acceptable to him when he is most worshipped and honoured by them.
