Likewise each one ought to apply this teaching to himself, remembering that they themselves will then be the true house or temple of God, if they give place to God's Word and call upon him from faith with a pure conscience. Those who neglect these things have nothing to boast of concerning the worship of God or the title of the Church.

units.la: Restat vltima huius loci pars, qua narratur, vt totum hoc Christi factum mundus exceperit, Principes Sacerdotum (inquit Lucas) & Scribæ & primores plebis, studebant eum perdere: nec inueniebant quid facerēt. Totus enim populus pendebat ab eo, cùm ipsum audiret. Quo loco tria dicūtur. Primum, qui nam Christi auditores fuerint, ex quibus tunc Ecclesia eius fuit collecta. Vbi præter vulgus & promiscuam populi ignobilis & imperiti turbam nemo nominatur. At solent Reges, quando vrbes regni primas ingrediuntur, nobilium & magstratuum corona stipari, & multa magnificè cum omniū ordinum applausu facere. Ergo Christus in eo etiam declarat Regnū suum non esse de hoc mundo, quòd non nisi ab obscuris et cõtemptissimis auditur. Veruntamē in eo elucet Euangelij eius virtus, quòd in infirmis & obscuris de illis triumphauit, qui in mundo omniū illustrissimi ac potentissimi habebantur. Quod obseruari debet, ne quem hodie offendat, si Ecclesia ex ijs potissimum confletur, qui à potentibus vix pro vulgi sece agnoscuntur. Ita enim Deus mundi huius superbia cõfundit, sicut Apostolus in priori ad Corinth. docet. Deinde secūdo loco ostēditur, quos nā hostes aut aduersarios Christus habuerit. Vbi nominantur Principes Sacerdotū & Scribæ, vnà cum primoribus populi. Opposuerunt ergo se illi omnes, qui vel in Ecclesia vel Repub. præ aliis excelluerūt. Nec leue fuit odium, quo illū persecuti sunt, sed eò vsq; exarsit, vt eum occidere studerent. In Græco Quærendi verbo vtitur Lucas, vt doceat, eos inter se de ratione ipsum interficiendi consultauisse: vt nimirum vel aperta vi trucidarent, vel occulte per insidias interciperent. Ita verò illorū nequitia & sanguinaria impietas detegitur. Quid enim multa deliberatione opus erat, si dignum mortis supplicio esse sciebant? Poterant enim aduersus eum iure ac legibus agere. At cùm id nolint, satis apparet, illos de iniusta vi cogitasse, vt vel templum quoq; in quo docebat, sanguine innoxio polluerent. Solent hoc ipsum etiam nostro tempore facere Pontifices, & qui cum his aduersus Veritatem conspirauerunt. Cùm enim nos hæresis accusent, non colloquijs aut disputationibus agunt, imò hoc solicitè cauent, ne res ad liberam & publicam disputationem deueniat; sed insidioso Conciliorum prætextu vtuntur, occultè autem Reges & Principes contra nos accendunt, neque pudet interdum per sicarios rem agere, vt eos è medio tollant, quos suæ tyrannidi præ aliis officere sentiunt. Sed quàm inanis fuerit hostium Christi conatus (quod postremum huius loci caput est) vno verbo Lucas indicat: Non inueniebant quid facerent. Itaque neque ratio aliqua vel in speciem honesta vel tuta, ne que aliquis tam improbus & deuotæ impietatis homo inueniri potuit, qui se illis tanti sceleris ministrum præberet. Et causa additur: Quia totus populus ab eo pendebat, et ipsum docentem audiebat. Hic principibus Sacerdotum & primoribus in Republica vulgus contemptibile, illorum autē consilijs & machinationibus doctrina Christi opponitur. At quid infirmius & inconstantius vulgo, si capite destituatur? quid Christi doctrina simplicius & contemptius, si ad nostræ rationis calculum examinetur? Potuerunt tamen ista sufficere contra omnes illos, qui eum occidere conabantur: adeoque metu plus quàm seruili retenti sunt, ne cruenta sua consilia exequi possent. Tam facile est Deo hostium suorum conatibus obstare: et solet ferè metus iste eorū corda occupare, qui tam Deum quàm homines securè cōtemnere videbantur. Exempla eius rei passim multa occurrunt. Imò hæc propria impiæ aduersus Verbum Dei tyrannidis pœna est, vt ignobile vulgus timeant, qui aduersus Deum plus quàm diabolica insolentia atque ferocia insurgunt.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, which tells how the world received this whole deed of Christ: "The chief priests," says Luke, "and the scribes and the leading men of the people sought to destroy him, and they could not find what they might do. For the whole people hung upon him when they heard him." Three things are stated here. First, who Christ's hearers were, from whom his Church was then gathered. Here, besides the common people and the mixed crowd of the lowly and unlearned, no one is named. Yet kings, when they enter the chief cities of their realm, are usually surrounded by a crown of nobles and magistrates, and they do many things magnificently to the applause of every rank. So Christ declares in this too that his kingdom is not of this world, since he is heard only by the obscure and most despised. Yet in this shines the power of his gospel, that among the weak and obscure he triumphed over those who were held most illustrious and powerful in the world. This must be observed, lest it offend anyone today if the Church is made up chiefly of those whom the powerful scarcely acknowledge as common folk. For thus God confounds the pride of this world, as the Apostle teaches in the first letter to the Corinthians. Secondly, it is shown who Christ's enemies or adversaries were. Here the chief priests and scribes are named, together with the leading men of the people. So all those set themselves against him who excelled others either in the Church or in the commonwealth. Nor was the hatred with which they pursued him slight; it blazed so fiercely that they sought to kill him. Luke uses the Greek word for "seek" to show that they took counsel among themselves about how to kill him: whether to slaughter him by open force or to trap him secretly by ambush. Thus their wickedness and bloodthirsty impiety is laid bare. For why was much deliberation needed if they knew he deserved the punishment of death? They could have proceeded against him by right and by law. But since they did not want this, it is sufficiently clear that they were planning unjust violence, so that they might pollute even the temple, where he taught, with innocent blood. The Pontiffs, and those who have conspired with them against the Truth, are accustomed to do this very thing in our own time. When they accuse us of heresy, they do not act through colloquies or disputations; rather they take great care that the matter never comes to free and public debate. Instead they use the insidious pretext of Councils, secretly stir up kings and princes against us, and are sometimes not ashamed to carry out the business through assassins, to remove from the midst those whom they feel stand in the way of their tyranny more than others. But how vain the attempt of Christ's enemies was (and this is the final point of this passage) Luke indicates in one word: "They did not find what they might do." So no reason, even one seemingly honest or safe, could be found, nor any man so wicked and devoted to impiety, who would offer himself as the minister of so great a crime. And a reason is added: "because the whole people hung upon him and heard him teaching." Here the contemptible common people are set against the chief priests and the leading men of the commonwealth, and the teaching of Christ against their counsels and schemes. But what is weaker and more inconstant than the common people when they are deprived of their head? And what is the teaching of Christ, simpler and more contemptible, when it is weighed by the reckoning of our reason? Yet those things were enough to withstand all who tried to kill him, and they were restrained by a fear more than servile, lest they should be able to carry out their bloody plans. So easy is it for God to block the attempts of his enemies; and that fear usually seizes the hearts of those who seemed to despise God as securely as men. Many examples of this occur everywhere. Indeed this is the proper punishment of impious tyranny against the Word of God: that those who rise against God with more than diabolical insolence and ferocity fear the common crowd.

units.la: Cæterum admonet nos huius historiæ conclusio, quid sibi polliceri debeant omnes ij, qui in resi- tuendo vero Dei cultu fidelem operam nauant. Vt enim falsi antistites quæstum suū minui nolunt; ita mundo dediti lucem Veritatis odisse solent, qua ipsorum mores improbi arguuntur. Hinc ergo odia, simultates, insidiæ & apertæ persecutiones nascuntur: quibus non solum Verbi administri, verumetiam pij principes peti solent, qui operi illi sanctissimo manum admouent. Expertus est hanc mundi malitiam Dauid sicuti in Psalmis non vno loco testatur. Et Ezechiæ non defuit Sobna, qui sanctis eius consilijs sese opponeret. Quid verò de Josia dicemus, sanctissimo principe, qui et populi sui perstitiosi contumacia, & principum malitia atq; consiliariorum perfidia impeditus est, quò minus proficeret in Dei cultu restituendo? Et quid hodie multis in locis fiat, non opus est commemorare, cùm omnibus nota sint. Neminem tamen hæc impiorum audacia terrere debet: quia non semper possunt quod volunt, aut quod posse putabantur. Et solet Deus tueri eos, qui in sua vocatione ambulant. Exempla quæ huc faciunt, alibi cōmemorauimus. Sed vt pessimè nobis res cedat, quoad huius seculi successum, beati tamen erimus, si pro causa tā bona & sancta aliquid sit ferendum. Quàm verò infelices sint, qui per Dei verbum reformari nolunt, multorum horribilis exitus probat. Olim Babylonis reformatores ijs adduxit Deus, qui Josiam & Prophetas audire noluerant. Et isti Romanorum armis miserè cum suo templo excisi sunt, quibus durum visum fuit Dei Filio obtemperare. Et quid hodie periculi à Turcis & ciuilibus bellis vndique immineat, nemo non videt. Excitet nos hæc exempla, vt fortes atque constantes simus in afferendo cultu Dei, neque terreamur infelicis mundi & impiorum præsulum conatibus, quos facilè eludet & franget is, qui mundum & huius principem iam olim deuicit, Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the conclusion of this history admonishes us what all those who labour faithfully in restoring the true worship of God ought to expect for themselves. For just as false prelates are unwilling to see their profit diminished, so those given over to the world are accustomed to hate the light of truth, by which their wicked morals are exposed. Hence hatreds, quarrels, plots and open persecutions arise, and they are directed not only against the ministers of the Word but even against godly princes who lay hand to that most holy work. David experienced this malice of the world, as he testifies in more than one place in the Psalms. And Hezekiah did not lack Shebna, who opposed his holy counsels. What shall we say of Josiah, most holy prince, who was hindered both by the stubborn superstition of his people, and by the malice of the princes and the treachery of his counsellors, so that he could not advance the restoration of God's worship? And what is done today in many places there is no need to recount, since it is known to all. Yet no one should be terrified by this audacity of the impious, for they cannot always do what they wish, or what they were thought able to do. God is accustomed to protect those who walk in their calling. Examples bearing on this we have recalled elsewhere. But although matters may turn out very badly for us as regards the success of this age, we shall nonetheless be blessed if something must be endured for so good and holy a cause. How wretched, however, are those who are unwilling to be reformed by the Word of God, the dreadful end of many proves. Once God brought the Babylonian reformers to ruin, those who had refused to hear Josiah and the prophets. And they were miserably cut off with their temple by the arms of the Romans, since it seemed hard to them to obey the Son of God. And no one fails to see what danger from the Turks and civil wars threatens on every side today. Let these examples stir us to be brave and steadfast in upholding the worship of God, and not to be frightened by the attempts of an unhappy world and of impious prelates, whom He will easily mock and break who long ago conquered the world and its prince, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXVIII.

units.la: ET factum est quodam dierum illorum, cùm ipse doceret populum in templo, & euangelizaret, superuenerunt principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ cum Senioribus, & dixerunt ei: Dic nobis qua authoritate ista facias, aut quis ille sit, qui dedit tibi istā authoritatem? Respondens autem dixit eis: Interrogabo vos & ego rem quandam: Dicite ergo mihi: Baptismus Ioannis è cœlo erat, an ex hominibus? At illi ratiocinati sunt apud se dicentes: Si dixerimus: E cœlo: dicet, Quare ergo non credidistis ei? Sin autem dixerimus: Ex hominibus: tota plebs lapidabit nos. Persuasum enim est ei, Ioannem Prophetam esse. Responderunt igitur se nescire vnde esset. Tum Iesus dixit eis: neque ego dico vobis, qua authoritate hæc faciam.
units.tr: And it came to pass on one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, that the chief priests and the scribes came upon him with the elders, and spoke to him, saying: Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority? But he answered and said to them: I will also ask you one question. Tell me: was the baptism of John from heaven, or from men? And they reasoned among themselves, saying: If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From men, all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet. So they answered that they did not know whence it was. Then Jesus said to them: Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.

units.la: Nter mundi huius vitia, quæ incurabilem & deploratam eius corruptionē & malitiam arguunt, præcipuum fere est ingratitudo, qua in eos peccat, qui vel publicæ saluti consulere volunt, vel priuatim quàm plurimis benefaciunt. Exempla quibus id probetur, in omnium gentium historijs occurrunt. Huc enim pertinent quæ apud Græcos de Aristide, Phocione, Miltiade, Cimone & similibus: apud Romanos de Camillo, Scipionibus, Cicerone, Pompeio atq; infinitis alijs leguntur, quibus ne mori quidem licuit in patria, quam consilio & armis saepius ab interitu seruauerant. De priuatis dicere non est opus, quando quotidie fiunt, quæ docent nihil tam vulgare esse, quàm hostes sentire eos, quibus quàm sæpissimè benefeceris. Superat tamen omnia exempla, quod in æternum Dei Filium mundus hic infelix designauit. Is enim cùm vt nos salvos faceret, homo factus esset, & salutem nostram studiorum atq; actionum suarum sccpum vnicum sibi propositum haberet, pessimam tamen gratiam inde retulit. Quod vt in totius vitæ eius historia patet, ita maximè in ijs cernitur, quæ proximè ante eius mortem acciderunt. Nam etsi Hierosolymæ acerbissima quæque passurum esse sciret, suam tamen erga eam ciuitatem benevolentiam multis argumentis declarauit, quando ad illius conspectum in lachrymas erupit, occasum eius verbis acerbissimi doloris testibus prædixit, templum a prophana nundinatione repurgauit, Veritatis doctrinam fideliter tradidit, & eandem miraculis publicis confirmauit. Omnibus verò hisce officijs non aliud meruit, quàm quòd vitæ eius insidias struxit ij, qui rerum apud illos potiebantur, à quibus procul dubio vel aperta vi vel per sicarios occisus fuisset, nisi illorum furorem Deus terrore & metu quodam occulto cohibuisset. Describuntur hæc propter nos, vt discamus, ad quæ certamina nos præparari oporteat, si in Euangelij ministerio, ex quo hominum salus dependet fideliter versari velimus: simulquè admonent, ne offendamur hominum ingratitudine & contumacia, sed cùm ea potius luctemur ad finem vsque nostræ vocationis: quod Christum constanter fecisse tota huius Capitis narratio docebit. Commemorat enim aliquot insidiosa colloquia Lucas, quibus Christum illaqueare & populo exosum, aut saltem contemptum facere conati sunt, quem nulla vi opprimi posse videbant. In omnibus autem illis partim eius sapientia plane diuina elucet, qua hostium insidias atque Sophisticam eluserit: partim bonitas plus quàm paterna cernitur, quæ eum continuit, ne à malè gratis & sanguinarijs hominibus discederet.
units.tr: Among the vices of this world, which show its corruption and malice to be incurable and hopeless, almost the chief is ingratitude, by which people sin against those who either wish to serve the public welfare or do good to very many in private. Examples proving this are found in the histories of all nations. To this belong the stories told among the Greeks of Aristides, Phocion, Miltiades, Cimon and others like them, and among the Romans of Camillus, the Scipios, Cicero, Pompey and countless others, who were not even allowed to die in the country which they had so often saved from destruction by their counsel and arms. There is no need to speak of private persons, since such things happen every day, and they teach that nothing is so common as for those whom you have benefited most often to come to regard you as an enemy. Yet all these examples are surpassed by what this unhappy world did to the eternal Son of God. For although he became man in order to save us, and although he had set our salvation as the single aim of all his studies and actions, he nevertheless received the worst thanks for it. This appears in the whole history of his life, and is seen most clearly in what happened just before his death. For although he knew that Jerusalem would suffer the most bitter things, he nevertheless declared his goodwill towards that city by many proofs: when he saw it he burst into tears, with words of bitter grief he foretold its downfall, he cleansed the temple of profane trading, he faithfully taught the doctrine of truth, and he confirmed it by public miracles. Yet for all these services he earned nothing but that those who held power among them plotted against his life, by whom he would undoubtedly have been killed, either by open force or through assassins, had God not restrained their fury by a certain hidden terror and fear. These things are recorded for our sake, so that we may learn for what conflicts we ought to prepare ourselves if we wish to serve faithfully in the ministry of the Gospel, on which the salvation of men depends. They also warn us not to be offended by the ingratitude and obstinacy of men, but rather to struggle against them until the end of our calling. That Christ did this steadfastly the whole narrative of this chapter will teach. For Luke relates several insidious conversations by which they tried to ensnare Christ and make him hateful, or at least contemptible, to the people, since they saw that he could not be overcome by force. In all of them, indeed, shines forth partly his wisdom, truly divine, by which he eluded the snares and sophistry of his enemies; and partly his goodness, more than fatherly, is seen, which restrained him from departing from men so wicked and bloodthirsty.

units.la: Vt verò hæc melius pateret, paucis præmittit Euangelista, quid toto illo tempore fecerit, quod ab eius ingressu in vrbem vsque ad mortis diem effluxit. Factum est (inquit) quodam dierum illorum, cùm ipse doceret populum in templo, & Euangelizaret. Ergo non primo tantùm die, quo in vrbem venerat, docuit: sed in eo frequentissimus fuit, & quàmuis propter ingratitudinem ciuium & magnatum insidias sub vesperam exire cogeretur, mane tamen ad docendi officium redijt. Adhæc cùm tanta ingratitudo atq; improbitas acerrimas inuectiuas & horribiles imminentis excidij commotiones mereretur, de eo tamen illos admonuisse contentus, nunc nihil quàm Euangelium prædicat, vt quod felix lætumq; gratia Dei nobis in ipso exhibita & salutis gratuitæ nuntium esse, iam sæpe dixi mus. Suo autem exemplo docet, doctrinam illam in Ecclesia constanter retineri debere, nec admit tendum esse, ut aliquorum improbitas, qui aduersus eam coniurarunt, bonis fraudi sit, qui eam esu riunt atque sitiunt. Et quia plerosque periculorum metus absterret, multa & diligenti consideratio ne dignum est Christi exemplum, qui cum in medio luporum versaretur, & mortis suæ horam in singula momenta appropinquare sciret, tanta tamen docendi sedulitate atque industria usus est. Nemo igitur propter periculum qualecunque à Deo sibi commissam vocatione deserere debet, quo ad eius obeundæ occasio sese offert. Nam ut sæpe iam diximus, facile potest Deus suos tueri, & ho stium ferocissimorum conatus atque consilia turbare. Id vero ad se transferre debent omnis loci & ordinis homines, ut se sub eius tutela esse meminerint, qui in corda hominum ius habet, et nihil nobis præter suæ voluntatis decretum euenire patitur.
units.tr: In order to make these things clearer, the evangelist first briefly sets out what Christ did during that whole time, from his entry into the city until the day of his death. It came to pass, he says, on one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel. Therefore he did not teach only on the first day, when he had come into the city, but he was most diligent in it, and although, because of the ingratitude of the citizens and the plots of the great men, he was compelled to leave at evening, he nevertheless returned in the morning to the duty of teaching. Moreover, although such great ingratitude and wickedness deserved the sharpest denunciations and the terrifying warnings of the coming destruction, he was content to have admonished them about these things, and now he proclaims nothing but the Gospel, which, as I have often said, is the happy and joyful news of the grace of God shown to us in him and the message of free salvation. By his example, however, he teaches that this doctrine must be constantly retained in the Church, and that it must not be allowed that the wickedness of some who have conspired against it should be a loss to good people, who hunger and thirst for it. And because the fear of dangers deters most people, the example of Christ is worthy of careful and diligent consideration, for although he lived among wolves, and knew that the hour of his death was drawing nearer every moment, he nevertheless used such great zeal and diligence in teaching. Therefore no one should desert the calling entrusted to him by God on account of any danger whatever, as long as the opportunity of discharging it presents itself. For, as we have often said already, God can easily protect his people and disturb the attempts and plans of the most fierce enemies. Men of every place and rank ought to apply this to themselves, so that they may remember that they are under the protection of him who has power over the hearts of men and suffers nothing to befall us except by the decree of his will.

units.la: Porrò transeamus ad Christi aduersarios, ut quid aduersus illum tentarint intelligamus. Sic autem scribit Lucas: Superuenerunt Principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ cum Senioribus, & dixerunt ei: Dic nobis, qua authoritate ista facias? aut quis ille sit, qui dedit tibi istam authoritatem? Primum ijdem nominantur, qui & nuper sub finem proximi Capitis. Et principes quidem Sacerdo tum erant, ad quos omnis religionis atque cultus diuini cura pertinebat, quorum summam in illo po pulo authoritate fuisse scimus. Scribæ autem doctrinæ antistites fuerunt, & quia ijdem annales quo que conseruabant, simul librariorum instar fuisse videntur, qui libros sacros abs se descriptos vulga bant. Summam certè eruditionis & scientiæ rerum sacrarum existimationem penes illos fuisse, vel ex eo apparet, quòd Herodes cum Sacerdotibus hos quoq; vocauit, quando de natali Messiæ loco edo ceri voluit. Seniores autem erant, quos Romani Seniores & Patres conscriptos dixerunt: & illi adhuc aliquam Synedrij eius speciem referebant, quod ex septuaginta Senioribus constabat, & penes quos summa erat eius gentis potestas. Ergo ut uno verbo rem dicamus, conspirarunt aduersus Chri stum primores omnes, tam spirituales quàm seculares, ut hodie loquuntur. Id vero in hoc mundo per petuum esse solet, ut omnium seculorum historiæ testantur. Non possunt enim Christum ferre Sacer dotes qui religionem sibi quæsitam fecerunt, & sua existimatione nihil antiquius habent. Idem Scri bis quoque & humana eruditione atque sapientia turgentibus planè intolerabilis est: quod hodie in Magistris nostris & plerisq; Iurisconsultis videmus, qui Christi cognitionem cum Legum scien tia non coniunxerunt. At quia isti se viribus destitui, rem verò hanc plenam periculi esse vident, magistratus & principes sibi coniungunt, ut armis quoq; si opus sit, suam existimationem tueantur. Atqui mirum videri poterat, Seniores istos, quorum erat populi iura & quod ex libertate adhuc re liquum erat tueri, Sacerdotibus sese coiunxisse, quos Herodes, publicus gentis illius hostis, extincta veterum Sacerdotum progenie, ex sece vulgi electos constituerat, & qui cum præsidibus prophanis colludentes populum sub religionis prætextu tyrannide grauissima premebant. Sed non est quod istos admiremur, quando iam sæculis aliquot inter Christianos idem est factitatum. Quis enim nescit, Romanos Pontifices ex Regum & Imperatorum oppressione creuisse, & ad se traxisse terras, quæ prius ad illos pertinebant? Quis item ignorat, quam multos Reges & Principes suis artibus cir cumuenerint? quàm multas Respublicas libertate sua spoliarint? Aut quis tam stupidus est, ut non sentiat, Reipublicæ nihil illorum potentia esse intolerabilius? Ut primùm enim in urbibus E pifcopi constituuntur, aut in illis Abbates cum infelici Monachorum auitio nidulantur, mox pu blicis & priuatis bonis insidias struunt, nec prius cessant, quam summam rerum potestatem ad se traxerint. Taceo nunc Imperatores Turcis proditos, taceo alios Pontificum pedibus insolenter cal catos, taceo tot iam seculis illorum artibus inter se commissos orbis terrarum Monarchas, & quæ cunque quotidie adhuc designant. Veruntamen etsi hæc omnibus nota sint, ea tamen est Regum stu piditas, ut cum illis aduersus Euangelij doctrinam coniurent, & ad stabiliendam eorum potentiam non solùm bella cum vicinis aut remotissimis quoque populis suscipiant, verumetiam in subditos suos ferro & igne grassentur. Est hic reuera spiritus ille fornicationis, qui oculos eorum perstringit, & animum quoq; aufert, ut nihil quod ipsis vel salutare vel noxium est, videre aut sentire possint. At solet plerunque Regibus accidere, quod istis accidisse nuper audiuimus, ut nimirum cum suis il lis impostoribus male pereant. Sed ipsum congressum spectemus, & quo astu rem hanc egerint. Dicunt ei: Dic nobis, qua authoritate ita facias? aut quis ille sit, qui dedit tibi istam authoritatem? Dic nobis, inquiunt: satis nimirum pro imperio, quasi hoc iure ab ipso exigant, & Christi sit eis omnium quae faciebat rationem reddere. Obseruabis autem, illos non de doctrinae veritate, aut de templi repurgatione, vel de miraculis eius quaestionem mouere, sed de sola authoritate, qua ordinatus & armatus haec faciat. Doctrinam enim oppugnare non audent, quam diuinam esse & cum Mose atque Prophetis conuenire non poterant negare, toties ab illo conuicti. Nundinationis autem in templo impietas tam crassa erat, ut quamuis frontem iamdudum perfricuissent, eam tamen vel uno verbulo tueri, aut Christum quod hanc eiecisset, accusare non auderent. At miracula accusare, ex quibus tam multi quotidie salutem percipiebant, extremae impudentiae fuisset. Quo ergo confugiunt? Nouum crimen fingunt: quod nimirum priuata audacia atque libidine extimulatus haec omnia agat, & a Deo institutum ordinem turbet. Astute autem ad se rapiunt dignitatem illam, qua olim Leuiticam tribum & eius familias Deus exornauerat. Scimus enim Deum primogenitorum omnium loco sibi Leuitas vendicauisse, ut eos cultus sui ministerio consecraret. Et alias quidem familias diuersis ministeriis destinauerat, penes Aaronem autem & eius posteritatem Sacerdotij administrationem esse voluit. Tanta vero authoritate hoc suum institutum confirmauit, ut nullum vnquam irae siue exemplum horribilius terribiliusque ediderit, quam quo Core cum coniuratis suis & domibus eorum terra ipsis dehiscente absorptus est. Cuius exempli seueritas postea Iudaeos ita in officio continuit, ut quamuis multis scelaribus aduersus Deum quotidie peccarent, Sacerdotium tamen intactum relinquerent. Vnus Vzias Rex repertus est, qui victoriis et potentia elatus in ara thymiamatis suffitum facere voluit, sed ob eam audaciam a Deo lepra percussus ordinis sacerdotalis authoritatem exemplo suo confirmauit. Adde his, quod cum cessantibus in docendi officio Sacerdotibus extraordinarij doctores a Deo excitarentur, Prophetae, nemini tamen nisi vocato diuinitus, munus illud obire licuit, & apud Ieremiam de illorum audacia grauiter queritur Deus, qui non miserat currebant. Itaque olim quidem Sacerdotum erat curare, ne quis docendi munus temere subiret, aut Sacerdotij ordinem priuata libidine siue ambitione turbaret. Quid vero hoc ad nostros istos, qui Christi tempore sacris praerant? Nam neque ex Aaronis filijs erant (quorum posteritatem ab Herode excisam fuisse, paulo ante diximus) neque Dei vocationem allegare poterant, cum Sacerdotium iampridem venale fecissent, & hoc quotannis ab auaris praesidibus redimerent. Ergo ipsi potius interrogari merebantur, qua authoritate aut iure sacrorum administrationem ad se rapuissent, ut sub huius praetextu Praesidum libidini seruirent? Verunt tamen hoc praeiudicio vtuntur, ut neminem pro legitimo Dei ministro aut doctore agnosci debere omnibus persuasum velint, quam qui ab ipsis vocatus aut missus sit: quod iy rannidis ipsorum potissimum fundamentum atque robur fuisse, ex Ioannis Baptistae historia apparet, ad quem in deserto docentem & baptizantem illico Inquisitores suos miserunt, qui quaererent quis nam esset, & cur docendi ac baptizandi munus sibi sumeret? Eodem igitur stratagemate nunc Christum quoque adoriuntur, & qua authoritate doceat, & cultum Dei constituat, quaerunt, nimirum vt omnibus suspectum reddant, quasi seditiose rebus nouis studeat, & tot seculis obseruatum ordinem Ecclesiae turbet. Interim cum ambitiosa illa audacia extremam impudentiam coniungunt, quando eius authoritatem in dubium vocare non erubescunt, quae tot signis iampridem confirmata erat, & nouis quotidie miraculis confirmabatur. Nec dum excidisse illis poterat, quod Christus illis dixerat non multo ante: Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi: Sin autem facio, etiamsi mihi non credatis, operibus credite: ut agnoscatis & credatis, quod Pater in me est, & ego in eo. Item: opera, quae dedit mihi Pater ut ea perficerem, ipsa (inquam) opera quae ego facio, testantur de me, quod Pater miserit me. Fuit ergo istorum hominum impudentia plus quam meretricia, qua adhuc illi ogganire audent: ijdem vero interea suae maliciae dignas poenas luunt. Dum enim pro suo honore et existimatione nimis ambitiose pugnant, suam stupiditatem produnt, qua impediti non possunt Dei virtutem in Christi operibus cernere, quam vilissimi quique in vulgo agnoscebant atque fatebantur.
units.tr: Let us now turn to Christ's adversaries, so that we may understand what they attempted against him. Luke writes as follows: "The chief priests and the scribes, with the elders, came upon him and said to him: Tell us, by what authority do you do these things? Or who is he who gave you this authority?" First, the same men are named who were mentioned at the end of the preceding chapter. The chief priests were the men to whom the whole care of religion and the divine worship belonged, and we know they held the highest authority among that people. The scribes were the experts in doctrine, and because they also kept the public records, they seem to have worked as copyists, who made and circulated copies of the sacred books. That they held the highest reputation for learning and knowledge of sacred things is clear enough from the fact that Herod summoned these men along with the priests when he wished to learn the place of the Messiah's birth. The elders were those whom the Romans called the Senior men and Fathers of the Senate, and they still preserved some image of the Sanhedrin, which consisted of seventy elders and in whose hands the supreme power of that nation lay. So, to put it in one word, all the leading men, both the spiritual and the secular (as people say today), conspired against Christ. This is always the way in this world, as the histories of all ages bear witness. For priests who have devised a religion of their own, and hold their own opinion above all else, cannot bear Christ. The scribes too, puffed up with human learning and wisdom, cannot endure him at all. We see this today among our doctors and most of the jurists, who have not joined the knowledge of Christ to the science of law. But because these men see that they lack strength, and that the matter is full of danger, they join the magistrates and princes to themselves, so that they may defend their reputation even with arms, if need be. Yet it might seem strange that these elders, whose duty it was to defend the rights of the people and whatever remained of their liberty, joined themselves to the priests, whom Herod, that public enemy of the nation, had set up from the common people after destroying the line of the old priests, and who, colluding with the profane governors, oppressed the people under the pretext of religion with the most severe tyranny. But we need not wonder at these men, since the same thing has been practised for several centuries among Christians. For who does not know that the Roman Pontiffs grew great through the oppression of kings and emperors, and drew to themselves lands that once belonged to those rulers? Who likewise is unaware how many kings and princes they have surrounded with their tricks? How many commonwealths they have stripped of their liberty? Or who is so dull that he does not feel that nothing is more intolerable to a commonwealth than their power? For as soon as bishops are set up in cities, or abbots settle in them to the unhappy loss of the monks, they soon lay snares for public and private goods, and they do not stop until they have drawn the supreme power to themselves. I say nothing now of emperors betrayed to the Turks, nor of others who have insolently fawned at the feet of the Pontiffs, nor of the monarchs of the world who for so many ages have been set against one another by their arts, nor of whatever else they still bring about every day. Yet although all these things are known to everyone, kings are so foolish that they conspire with the Pontiffs against the doctrine of the gospel, and in order to establish their power they not only wage wars against neighbouring or even the most distant peoples, but also rage with sword and fire against their own subjects. This is truly that spirit of fornication which blinds their eyes and takes away their understanding, so that they can neither see nor perceive what is either healthful or harmful to themselves. But it usually happens to kings what we have recently heard happened to these men, namely that they perish miserably together with their impostors. But let us look at the encounter itself and the cunning by which they carried out this business. They say to him: "Tell us, by what authority do you do these things? Or who is he who gave you this authority?" "Tell us," they say, plainly as if they were demanding it by right of their office, as if it were their due that he render an account of everything he did. You will observe that they raise no question about the truth of his doctrine, nor about the cleansing of the temple, nor about his miracles, but only about the authority by which he does these things, as one ordained and empowered. For they do not dare to attack his teaching, which they could not deny was divine and agreed with Moses and the Prophets, since they had so often been refuted by him. The impiety of the trading in the temple was so gross that, although they had long since hardened their foreheads, they did not dare to defend it even with a single word, or to accuse Christ for having driven it out. But to accuse the miracles, by which so many were daily receiving salvation, would have been the height of shamelessness. To what, then, do they flee? They invent a new charge: that he acts in all these things out of private audacity and lust, and disturbs the order instituted by God. Shrewdly, they also seize for themselves that dignity with which God had once honoured the tribe of Levi and its families. For we know that God claimed the Levites for himself in place of all the firstborn, so that he might consecrate them to the ministry of his worship. He had assigned the other families to different duties, but he willed that the administration of the priesthood should rest with Aaron and his posterity. He confirmed this institution with such authority that he never displayed a more dreadful and terrible example of his wrath than when Korah, with his conspirators and their households, was swallowed up as the earth opened under them. The severity of that example afterwards kept the Jews so much in check that, although they sinned daily against God in many wicked ways, they left the priesthood untouched. Only one king, Uzziah, was found who, puffed up by his victories and power, wished to offer incense upon the altar of incense; but for that boldness he was struck with leprosy by God, and by his example he confirmed the authority of the priestly order. Add to this that, while the priests neglected the duty of teaching, extraordinary teachers were raised up by God, the Prophets; yet no one was permitted to undertake that office unless he was called by God, and in Jeremiah God complains bitterly of their audacity: "They ran, though I had not sent them." Accordingly, in former times it was the task of the priests to see that no one rashly undertook the office of teaching, or disturbed the order of the priesthood through private lust or ambition. But what has this to do with those men who presided over sacred things at the time of Christ? For they were neither of the sons of Aaron (whose line, as we said a little earlier, Herod had cut off), nor could they plead a calling from God, since they had long made the priesthood a matter of sale, and every year bought it back from greedy governors. Therefore they themselves deserved rather to be asked by what authority or right they had seized the administration of sacred things, so that under this pretext they might serve the lust of the governors. Yet they use this prejudice, wishing to persuade everyone that no one should be acknowledged as a lawful minister or teacher of God except the one who has been called or sent by themselves. That this was the chief foundation and strength of their tyranny appears from the history of John the Baptist, to whom, while he was teaching and baptizing in the desert, they at once sent their inquisitors to ask who he was and why he took upon himself the office of teaching and baptizing. So now, by the same stratagem, they assail Christ as well, asking by what authority he teaches and establishes the worship of God, plainly so that they may make him suspect to everyone, as though he were seditiously pursuing novelties and disturbing the order of the Church that has been observed for so many ages. Meanwhile they join to that ambitious audacity the utmost shamelessness, since they do not blush to call into doubt an authority that had long been confirmed by so many signs and was being confirmed every day by fresh miracles. Nor could it yet have slipped from their minds what Christ had told them not long before: "If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in him." Likewise: "The works which the Father has given me to finish, these very works which I do, I say, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me." The impudence of these men, therefore, was more than harlot-like, and with it they still dare to boast; and in the meantime they pay the penalty their malice deserves. For while they fight too ambitiously for their own honour and reputation, they betray their own stupidity, by which they are so hindered that they cannot discern in Christ's works the power of God, which the very lowest among the common people acknowledged and confessed.

units.la: Continet autem historia haec speculum clarissimum, in quo posteremi seculi mores & quibus incrementis atque artibus Pontificum tyrannis propagata sit, spectare licet. Nam solis nominibus mutatis dotatis de istis verissimè dici potest, quod hucusque de Iudæorum Sacerdotibus dictum est. Olim enim Episcoporum electio penes Ecclesiam erat, quæ indicto etiam ieiunio & præmissis precibus publicis eum sortibus deligere solebat, quem Deus tanto muneri idoneum iudicauisset: sicuti in Matthiæ electione, & in Pauli ac Barnabæ ordinatione, quæ Antiochiæ facta fuit, cernimus. Cyprianus quoq; libro primo Epistola quarta sic scribit: Ipsa plebs maximè potestatem habet vel eligendi dignos sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi, &c. Et hunc morem Ecclesijs communem fuisse Ælius Lampridius in vita Alexandri Seueri testatur, sic scribens: Vbi aliquos voluisset rectores prouincijs dare, vel præpositos facere, vel procuratores, id est, rationales ordinare, nomina eorū proponebat, hortans populum, vt si quis quid haberet criminis, probaret manifestis rebus, si non probasset, subiret pœnam capitis. Dicebatq; graue esse, cùm id Iudæi & Christiani facerent in prædicandis Sacerdotibus qui ordinandi sunt, non fieri in prouinciarum rectoribus, quibus & fortunæ hominum committerentur & capita. Et huius generis exempla in Patrum orthodoxorum scriptis multa inueniuntur: inter quæ memorabilis est Diui Augustini narratio, qua exponit, quo ordine in totius Ecclesiæ conspe- etu & eiusdem publico consensu Eradium sibi collegam & successorem designauerit. Extant præterea Canones verè Apostolici in Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum, qui docent, quibus virtutibus instructos esse eos oporteat, qui ad Ecclesiæ ministerium ordinari debent. Quàm diu ergo mos iste duravit, & à Spiritu sancto præscripta electionis aut ordinationis ecclesiasticæ ratio seruata est, merito magna fuit ministerij dignitas & sacrosancta censeri debuit authoritas Episcoporū, vt hos obseruarent omnes, neq; aliquid in Ecclesia illis inuitis aut inscijs tentarent. Sed postquam illorum quoque animos ambitionis aut auaritiæ spiritus tentauit, mox res in peius labi cœperunt. Etenim cùm Romani quoq; Episcopi electio olim penes clerum & populum Romanum esset, & vel Imperatoris Constantinopolitani vel Exarchi eius, qui eius nomine in Italia cū imperio erat, authoritate confir- maretur, Constantinus Constantis Filius in Benedicti II. gratiam iure suo cedens statuit, vt quem clerus populusque Romanus cum equestris ordinis viris Episcopum creassent, is verus Christi in terris vicarius esse crederetur, nulla vel Imperatoris vel Exarchi approbatione expectata. Factum hoc sub annū nati Christi sexcentesimū septuagesimum. Coepit ab eo tempore confirmari Pontificum potentia, adeò vt Leo III. auderet Imperium ad Carolum magnum Francorū Regem transferre, Paschalis autè Papa, cùm à Ludouico Caroli fratre Romam cum adiacentibus terris & vrbibus dono accepisset, vicissim decretum fecit, ne quis laicus Ecclesias vel Ecclesiarum bona occupet aut disponat, & simul excommunicationis pœnam in eos statuit, qui alicuius ecclesiasticæ digni- tatis inuestituram à laico quocunq; acciperent. Secuta sunt mox indigniora: Nam Ioannes XIII. à Berengario armis petitus, cùm Francos ad opem ferendam tardiores videret, Imperium ad Ottho nem Saxonem transstulit, quem tamen prius iureiurando astrinxit, cuius formula in Decretis habetur: quod anno Domini D.CCCCLXVI. factum fuisse historici tradunt. Secutus est Anno circiter Millesimo Gregorius quintus, qui vt Imperium ad Germanos firmius ac stabilius esset, Electores instituit Principes tres & Episcopos totidem, penes quos eligendi Imperatoris potestas esset, ea tamen conditione, vt qui ab his electus est, tunc demum Imperator verus ac legitimus agnoscatur, cùm à Pontifice approbatus fuerit. Itaque tunc non abolito solùm verumetiam inuerso veteri more Imperatores à Pontificibus confutari cœperunt, cùm prius hi ab illis suæ ordinationis approbationem peterent. Nec satis fuit Pontificibus in Imperatores & Reges imperium obtinuisse, nisi Episcopos quoque omnes suæ tyrannidi subijcerent, et per hos in totum clerum (vt ipsi loquuntur) contra Petri Apostoli Canonem dominarentur. Itaque illos quoque in sua verba iurare coegerunt, & eius quoque iuramenti formulam in decreta sua retulerunt. Imitati sunt Pontificis exemplum Episcopi & reliqui præsules, qui Ecclesijs & Parochijs (vt vocant) passim insidiati sunt, & ius ordinandi ministros (quod illi ius patronatus, aut collaturam siue inuestituram dicunt) par- tim artibus mirificis, partim pecunijs adse transtulerunt. Breui ergo temporis spatio res eò deducta fuit, vt paucæ admodum Ecclesiæ inuenirentur, quæ pastoris elegendi ius haberent, sed pleræq; cum illo decimas quoq; & alios redditus ecclesiasticos amiserunt. Hinc omnis religionis corruptio in orbem Christianū ceu diluuio quodam inuecta est, Episcopis & Abbatibus fere eos ordinantibus, quorum seruitio prius aut vtiliter, aut etiam turpiter in rebus suis vsi erant, quàmuis neq; virtute neq; eruditione commendarentur. Et quia hi quoque Decanis suis, hi vero Episcopis fidem suam obstrin gere cogebantur, omnis Ecclesiarum gubernatio ceu coniuratione quadam ad Pontifices devoluta est. Unde accidit, ut ne ad infimum quidem muneris Ecclesiastici gradum admitteretur, qui non ac cepisset characterem bestiae, de qua in Apocalypsi sermo est. Isti vero homines, cum veterem & Apo stolicum Ecclesiae morem iampridem aboleuerint, & absque legitima vocatione imperium omne sibi vendicarint, nobis hodie negotium faciunt, & nefas esse arbitrantur, quenquam ad docendi munus promoueri, quem non ipsi ad hoc idoneum aut dignum iudicarint. Itaque cum Euangelij doctrinam oppugnare & confutare non possint, neque etiam horribiles abusus & sacrilegam Sacrorum nundi nationem defendere audeant, cum Iudaeorum Sacerdotibus eo refugiunt, quod vocationem ministro rum verbi, qui vel ab Ecclesijs vel pijs magistratibus ordinati sunt, in dubium vocat, & illos inter rogant, quo iure aut qua authoritate ad docendum prodeant & ad Ecclesiae reformationem manum admoueant? Et cum ipsi potius ad reddendam rationem cogi deberent, quo iure Ecclesias omnes op presserint, ius ordinandi illis eripuerint, & cum doctoribus ipsos etiam Reges in sua verba coegerint iurare: ipsi e contra ab ijs rationem exigunt, quorum vocationem non solum Ecclesiarum atq; piorum magistratuum authoritas commendat, verumetiam effectus ipse probat, quado sui ministerij sigilla proferre possunt, Ecclesias nimirum sua industria & mirifico atque felici successu ad verbi Dei normam reformatas. Et hic quidem multa magnifice dicunt de ordine Ecclesiae tot iam saeculis observa to, de successione item continua Pontificum, de Imperatorum & Regum authoritate, qui hanc illis dignitatem confirmarint, & alijs multis, quorum omnium hic finis est, ut Ecclesiae turbatores esse eiuncant eos, qui ipsorum tyrannidi resistunt, & veritatis doctrinam reducere veteremque Ecclesiae formam instaurare studeant. At nos non de temporis diuturnitate quaerimus, quae errores defendere non possent: neque successioni Pontificum aliquid tribuimus, quando omnibus saeculis constat saepe impios nebulones bonis pastoribus successisse; neque Regum authoritatem in ijs vellicamus, quae ad ipsorum curam atque officium proprie pertinent: sed potius dolemus, illos partim Pontificum dolis & hypocrisi circumuentos, partim vi aperta ac proditorijs artibus coactos esse ut ea illis daret, quae neque ipsi dare, neq; illi petere & accipere debuissent. Et quia omnibus hominum statutis antiquius est verbum Dei, huius authoritas nobis ad omnia sufficit.
units.tr: This history, however, is a very clear mirror in which one may see the morals of the last age and the means and arts by which the tyranny of the popes has been spread. For, with only the names changed, what has been said so far about the priests of the Jews can be said most truly of these men. In the past the election of bishops rested with the Church, which, after a fast had been proclaimed and public prayers offered, used to choose by lot the man whom God had judged fit for so great an office. We see this in the election of Matthias and in the ordination of Paul and Barnabas, which took place at Antioch. Cyprian also writes in the first book, epistle four: "The people themselves have the greatest power either of choosing worthy priests or of rejecting unworthy ones," etc. Aelius Lampridius, in the life of Alexander Severus, testifies that this custom was common to the churches, writing thus: "When he wished to give some governors to provinces, or to appoint presidents or procurators, that is, auditors of accounts, he would put forward their names, urging the people that if anyone had any charge against them, he should prove it by clear evidence; if he did not prove it, he would undergo the penalty of death. He said it was a serious matter that the Jews and Christians did this in choosing the priests who were to be ordained, but it was not done for the governors of provinces, to whom the fortunes and lives of men are entrusted." Many examples of this kind are found in the writings of the orthodox Fathers. Among them is the memorable account of the blessed Augustine, in which he explains the order by which, in the sight of the whole Church and with its public consent, he designated Eradius as his colleague and successor. Moreover, the truly apostolic canons exist in the epistles to Timothy and Titus, which teach what virtues those must be endowed with who are to be ordained to the ministry of the Church. Therefore, as long as this custom lasted, and the manner of ecclesiastical election or ordination prescribed by the Holy Spirit was observed, the dignity of the ministry was rightly great, and the authority of the bishops ought to have been regarded as sacrosanct, so that all observed them and no one attempted anything in the Church against their will or without their knowledge. But after the spirit of ambition or avarice also tempted their minds, things soon began to slide for the worse. For when the election of the Roman bishop had formerly rested with the clergy and people of Rome, and was confirmed by the authority of the Emperor of Constantinople or of his exarch, who held power in Italy in his name, Constantine, son of Constans, yielding his right in favour of Benedict II, decreed that whomever the clergy and people of Rome, together with the men of the equestrian order, had made bishop, he should be believed to be the true vicar of Christ on earth, without waiting for any approval either from the emperor or from the exarch. This was done in the year of Christ's birth 670. From that time the power of the Pontiffs began to be strengthened, so much so that Leo III dared to transfer the empire to Charles the Great, King of the Franks. Pascal, moreover, when he had received Rome with the surrounding lands and cities as a gift from Louis, brother of Charles, in turn issued a decree that no layman should seize or dispose of churches or church property, and at the same time established the penalty of excommunication against those who received the investiture of any ecclesiastical dignity from a layman. Worse things soon followed. John XIII, attacked with arms by Berengarius, and seeing the Franks too slow to bring aid, transferred the empire to Otto the Saxon, whom he nevertheless first bound by an oath, the formula of which is found in the Decretals. Historians report that this happened in the year of the Lord 966. About the year 1000 Gregory V followed, who, so that the empire might be firmer and more stable among the Germans, instituted three princes as electors and as many bishops, in whose hands would lie the power of electing the emperor. Yet on this condition: that the one elected by them should be acknowledged as the true and lawful emperor only once he had been approved by the Pontiff. Thus, not only was the old custom abolished but, indeed, reversed, and emperors began to be confirmed by the Pontiffs, whereas before they had sought approval of their appointment from them. Nor was it enough for the Pontiffs to have obtained power over emperors and kings, unless they also subjected all the bishops to their tyranny and, through these, lorded it over the whole clergy (as they themselves put it), contrary to the canon of the apostle Peter. Thus they also compelled the bishops to swear to their words, and they recorded the formula of this oath in their decrees. The bishops and the other prelates imitated the example of the Pontiff: they lay in wait everywhere for the churches and parishes (as they call them) and transferred to themselves, partly by wonderful arts and partly by money, the right of ordaining ministers, which they call the right of patronage, or the right of presentation or investiture. Within a short space of time things were brought to such a point that very few churches were found that had the right of choosing their minister; most of them lost along with it their tithes and other ecclesiastical revenues. From this, the corruption of all religion was brought over the Christian world as by a kind of flood, since bishops and abbots ordained almost those whom they had earlier used in their affairs, either usefully or even shamefully, although they were commended neither by virtue nor by learning. And because these men were forced to bind their faith to their deans, and those to bishops, the whole government of the churches was, as if by some conspiracy, handed over to the Pontiffs. Hence it came about that no one was admitted even to the lowest grade of ecclesiastical office who had not received the mark of the beast of which the Apocalypse speaks. But these men, since they had long ago abolished the old and apostolic custom of the Church, and without lawful calling had claimed for themselves every authority, now make trouble for us, and think it wrong for anyone to be promoted to the office of teaching whom they themselves have not judged fit or worthy for this. Therefore, since they cannot oppose and refute the doctrine of the Gospel, nor dare to defend the horrible abuses and the sacrilegious trade in holy things, they take refuge with the priests of the Jews, in that they call into doubt the calling of the ministers of the Word who have been ordained either by the Churches or by godly magistrates, and ask them: by what right or what authority do they come forward to teach and lay their hands on the reform of the Church? And although they themselves ought rather to be compelled to give an account by what right they have oppressed all the churches, taken away from them the right of ordination, and forced even kings to swear to their words as to teachers, they on the contrary demand an account from those whose calling is commended not only by the authority of the churches and of godly magistrates, but is also proved by the outcome itself, since they can display the seals of their ministry: namely, churches reformed to the rule of the Word of God by their diligence and by a remarkable and happy success. And here indeed they say many grand things about the order of the Church observed for so many ages, about the continuous succession of the Pontiffs, about the authority of the emperors and kings who confirmed this dignity for them, and about many other things, all of which aim at this: that those who resist their tyranny and strive to restore the doctrine of truth and to renew the old form of the Church should be cast out as disturbers of the Church. But we do not inquire into the length of time, which cannot defend errors; nor do we ascribe anything to the succession of the Pontiffs, since it is clear in every age that wicked scoundrels have often followed good ministers; nor do we find fault with the authority of kings in those matters which properly belong to their care and office. Rather, we grieve that they were partly deceived and beguiled by the tricks and hypocrisy of the Pontiffs, and partly, by open force and treacherous arts, compelled to give those things which neither they should have given, nor those men should have sought and received. And since the Word of God is older than all human statutes, its authority is sufficient for us in all things.

units.la: Et de eo nos in praesenti Christus quoque admonet. Nam etsi Sacerdotes illi ac Scribae indigni essent, quibus aperte responderetur, responsum tamen tale reddit, quo non obscure probat, se quicquid faciat, divina authoritate facere. Nam ipsorum quaestioni aliam opponit dicens: Interrogabo vos & ego rem quandam: Dicite igitur mihi, Baptismus Ioannis e caelo erat, an ex hominibus? Baptismi nomine totum Ioannis ministerium comprehendit, ea tamen locutione uti voluit, ut quoniam de vo catione lis erat, se quoque hoc pro indubitato fateri protestetur, nulli doctrinae aut ceremoniae in Ec clesia locum esse dandum, nisi divina ac caelesti authoritate confirmetur. Et quaestionis huius sensus est: Num Ioannem a Deo missum Prophetam aut verbi praeconem fuisse agnoscant, aut impostoris loco habeant, qui vel priuata animi libidine motus, vel ab alijs subornatus nouum doctrinae genus inuexerit, & suos discipulos siue auditores nouo atque prius inusitato Symbolo ab alijs distin xerit? De Ioanne autem quaerit, ut huius de se testimonia ipsis in mentem reuocet, quae ad soluen dam illorum quaestionem abunde poterant sufficere. Quasi dicat: Quaeritis qua authoritate ego ista faciam? Aut quid hoc quaerere opus est, quando (ut alia omnia taceam) iam pridem ab Ioan ne de eo edocti estis? Velim ego a vobis scire, quo loco illum habeatis. Verum ne Dei praeconem agnoscitis, aut impostorem improbum fuisse dicetis? Id vero vos nunquam dicturos puto, cum tan ta eius gravitas, tantus divini Spiritus ardor, tanta doctrinae virtus in eo eluxerit, ut Herodes quoque non vulgaris hominis indicia in illo potuerit agnoscere. Num vero quid is de me testatus sit, ignoratis? Annon legatis vestris ille dixit: Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua: sed in medio vestrum stat, quem vos nescitis? Ipse est, qui post me venit, qui praelatus est mihi: cuius solearum corri giam soluere ego non sum dignus? Itaque Christus hoc loco non aliter Sophistico vtitur, ut quaestio nem sibi propositam declinet, ne ad eam respondere togatur: sed ita respondet, ut aduersariorum ani mos magis vulneret veritatis confessione, quam si directe & palam dixisset quod res erat, sicut pau lo post videbimus.
units.tr: Christ also reminds us of this point in the present passage. Although those priests and scribes were unworthy of a straight answer, he gave them a reply that clearly shows that whatever he does, he does by divine authority. He sets another question against theirs, saying: "I will ask you one thing too. Tell me: was the baptism of John from heaven, or from men?" By the name of baptism he takes in the whole ministry of John, but he chose this expression so that, since the question concerned his calling, he might also declare that he himself holds this as beyond doubt: no doctrine or ceremony should have a place in the Church unless it is confirmed by divine and heavenly authority. The sense of the question is this: do they acknowledge John as a prophet and herald sent by God, or do they regard him as an impostor who, moved by private whim or put up to it by others, introduced a new kind of doctrine and separated his disciples or hearers from the rest by a novel creed never used before? Christ asks about John so that they may recall his testimony about himself, which could have been enough to resolve their question. It is as if he said: "You ask by what authority I do these things? Why do you even need to ask, when (to say nothing of everything else) you were long ago taught about this by John? I would like to know from you where you place him. Will you acknowledge that he was a herald of God, or will you say that he was a wicked impostor? I do not think you will ever say that, since such great seriousness, such great fervour of the divine Spirit, and such power of doctrine shone forth in him that even Herod could recognise in him signs of more than an ordinary man. But do you not know what he testified about me? Did he not say to your envoys: 'I indeed baptise you with water, but there stands among you one whom you do not know. He it is who comes after me, who has been preferred before me, whose sandal-thong I am not worthy to loose'?" Thus Christ does not here use a sophistical method to evade the question put to him, so as not to have to answer it. Rather, he answers in such a way as to wound his adversaries' minds more by confessing the truth than if he had said directly and openly what the matter was, as we shall see shortly.

units.la: Suo autem exemplo docet, vt cum apertis & praefractis hostibus veritatis agi debeat. Anteo mnia cauendū erit, ne turpi vel silentio vel dissimulatione veritatē prodamus: quod multi hodie faciunt, qui mirifica tergiuersatione propositas sibi quæstiones eludunt, ne cū bonorum suorum aut vi tæ periculo ad eas cogantur respondere. At simul meminerimus hic inprimis serpentina illa prudentia opus esse, quam in suis discipulis Christus requirit, ne nos temere in pericula non necessaria coniiciamus, interim tamen aduersariorum animos atq; consciencias feriamus, vt perplexi hereant, qui nos intricare conabantur. Potes̄ hoc commodissimè fieri hodie, si de nostra vocatione quæstionē mo uentibus similiter respōdeamus. Dicite vos, quid de Prophetarū scriptis, de Christi & Apostolorum doctrina, deq; toto Euangelij negotio sentiatis? Num hus Dei verbum & æternæ salutis doctrinam continerī, aut fabulas & hominum vanissimorū figmenta esse dicitis? At cum non possitis negare, illa ipsissimum verbum Dei esse, quod nam nostrum scelus est, si hoc plus satis longo tempore abscondituū denuo in lucem proferamus? Et vt nos nulla legitima vocatione niti fateamur, potior tamē no stra causa est quàm vestra, qui æterno silentio sepulta esse vultis, sine quorum cognitione salus hominum non potes̄ consistere. Dicite item, vnde hæc authoritas vobis obtigerit, quæ vos defendat, vt nemo in vestra statuta inquirere audeat, & vestra cunctatio omnibus fraudi esse debeat, qui de salute interea periclitantur, dum vos reformationem Ecclesiæ iam aliquot seculis optatam atque magno desiderio expectatam malitiosè & fraudulenter differtis, ne quid vestrae dignitati aut quæstui decedat? Hæc & alia huius generis si proferantur, non habebunt illi quod respondeant, nisi cum pudore sensum quoq; communem abstulerint. Hic certè mihi fortissimorum patrum nostrorum & Senatus Tigurini prudentia atq; in tuenda veritate constantia in mentem venit: qui cum ante annos quinquaginta Euangelij doctrinam admissent, deq; Ecclesiæ reformatione cogitarent, omnibus qui opus istud sanctissimum impedire conabantur, hoc vnum semper responderunt: Nos diuini verbi authoritatem secuti ista facimus: quod si quis ex illo nos convincere aut meliora edocere poterit, eū audire parati sumus. Potuit responsum hoc sufficere ad reprimendum multorum conatus, qui extrema quaque interdum moliri videbantur. Tanta verbi Dei & veritatis vis est, vt hostium quoq; corda penetret, & occulto pudore contumacissimos quosq; coerceat.
units.tr: By his example he also teaches that we must deal in this way with open and obstinate enemies of the truth. Above all we must take care not to betray the truth by shameful silence or dissimulation, as many do today, who, with wonderful evasiveness, dodge the questions put to them, so that they are not forced to answer at the risk of their goods or their lives. At the same time, let us remember that here, above all, that serpent-like prudence is needed which Christ requires of his disciples: we must not rashly cast ourselves into unnecessary dangers, yet meanwhile we must strike the minds and consciences of our adversaries, so that those who tried to entangle us stand perplexed. This can be done most conveniently today if, when they raise questions about our calling, we answer them in the same way. Tell us, you who ask, what do you think of the writings of the prophets, of the doctrine of Christ and the apostles, and of the whole business of the gospel? Do you say that these contain the word of God and the doctrine of eternal salvation, or that they are fables and the fictions of very vain men? But since you cannot deny that they are the very word of God, what wickedness is ours if, after so long a time of concealment, we bring it again into the light? And even if we confess that we rely on no lawful calling, our cause is nonetheless better than yours, who want what is necessary for the salvation of men to be buried in eternal silence. Tell us also, whence has this authority fallen to you, which defends you, so that no one dares to inquire into your decrees, and your delay must be a loss to all those who meanwhile are in peril of their salvation, while you maliciously and fraudulently postpone the reformation of the Church, longed for for many centuries and awaited with great desire, lest anything be lost to your dignity or your gain? If these and other arguments of this kind are put forward, they will have nothing to answer, unless they have lost even common sense along with their shame. Here there comes to my mind the wisdom of our most courageous fathers and of the Senate of Zurich, and their steadfastness in defending the truth. When they had admitted the doctrine of the gospel fifty years ago and were thinking about the reformation of the Church, they always gave this one answer to all who tried to hinder that most holy work: "We follow the authority of the word of God in doing these things; if anyone can convict us from it or teach us something better, we are ready to hear him." This answer was enough to check the attempts of many who sometimes seemed to be undertaking the most extreme measures. So great is the power of the word of God and of the truth that it penetrates even the hearts of enemies and restrains the most stubborn by a hidden shame.

units.la: Apparet hoc in Sacerdotum & Scribarum atque Seniorum exemplo, qui hac Christi responsione audita apud se ratiocinati sunt: Si dixerimus, E cælo, dicet nobis: Quare ergo nō credidistis ei? Sin autem dixerimus, Ex hominibus, tota plebs lapidabit nos. Persuasum est enim ei Ioannē Prophetā esse. Conuincuntur ergo ipsi propriæ conscientiæ testimonio, nō tamen hoc audiunt, sed ad suas rationes conuersi sese magis intricant, & dū omnia potius quàm Deum metuunt, seipsos omnium ludibrijs exponunt, id se scire negantes, quod iam toti populo, publicanis, cerdonibus, nautis & (vt pro verbo dicitur) lippis atque tonsoribus notum erat: simulque Christo honestissimam occasionem præbent sese ab ipsorum laqueis extricandi, imò etiam accusandi impiam eorum audaciam atque tyrannidem, sicuti in proximo Sermone audiemus. At hic nobis ingenium atq; mores falsorum antistitum ceu in tabula conspiciendi proponuntur. Ab vna parte gloriæ & dignitatis periculum subire timēt, si veritati testimonium ferant: ab altera populi furorem metuunt: de Dei gloria autem & populi salute nihil soliciti, vtranque securè negligunt. Et hoc illud est, quod Ecclesiasticos simul & politicos viros atque principes in salutis æternæ negotio maximè retardat, quod Dei timore & publicæ salutis studio iam pridem excussō, huius seculi gloriam quærunt, neq; suo quæstui aut priuatis commodis quicquam decedere volunt. Notū est enim illud Christi: Quomodo vos potestis credere, qui gloriam alij ab alijs captatis, & gloriam quæ à solo Deo proficiscitur, non quæritis? Fugiamus ergo nos hac nocentissimam salutis pestem, neq; quicquam eiusmodi hominum iudicijs tribuamus, sed in vnū Dei Filium intenti, eum audiamus & sequamur, cuius authoritas non Prophetarum modo & Ioannis atque Apostolorum testimonijs, verumetiam cœlestis Patris voce confirmata est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This appears in the example of the priests, scribes and elders, who, when they heard this answer of Christ, reasoned among themselves: "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From men,' the whole people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet." So they are convicted by the testimony of their own conscience, yet they do not accept this, but turning to their own reasonings they entangle themselves further. While they fear everything rather than God, they expose themselves to the mockery of all, denying that they know what was already known to the whole people, the tax collectors, cobblers, sailors and (as the saying goes) the bleary-eyed and the barbers. At the same time they give Christ a most honourable opportunity to free himself from their snares, and indeed to accuse their impious audacity and tyranny, as we shall hear in the next sermon. Here, however, the character and manners of the false prelates are set before us, as if displayed in a picture. On one side they fear to undergo a danger to their glory and dignity if they bear witness to the truth; on the other they dread the fury of the people. Yet they are carelessly indifferent to both, caring nothing for the glory of God or the salvation of the people. This is what chiefly holds back churchmen and civil rulers and princes alike in the business of eternal salvation: having long since cast off the fear of God and zeal for the public good, they seek the glory of this age and are unwilling that anything be lost to their gain or private advantage. For that saying of Christ is well known: "How can you believe, you who seek glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?" Let us therefore flee this most harmful plague to salvation, and let us not give any weight to the judgements of such men; rather, fixing our attention on the one Son of God, let us hear and follow him, whose authority was confirmed not only by the testimonies of the prophets, John and the apostles, but also by the voice of the heavenly Father. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 189.

units.la: Cœpit autem dicere ad plebem parabolam hanc: Quidam plantauit vineam, & elocauit eam agricolis, & peregre abfuit multum tempus. Et in tempore misit seruum ad illos agricolas, vt darent ex fructu vineae: hi vero illum caesum ablegarunt inanem. Ille vero perrexit alterum seruum mittere: at ipsi hunc quoque caesum & contumelia affectum ablegarunt inanem. Et perrexit mittere tertium: at illi & istum vulneratum eiecerunt. Dixit igitur Dominus vineae: Quid faciam? mittam Filium meum dilectum: forsitan cum hunc viderint, reuerebuntur. Viso autem eo agricolae collocuti sunt inter se, dicentes: Iste est haeres: venite, trucidemus eum, vt nostra fiat haereditas. Et eiectum eum extra vineam trucidarunt. Quid ergo faciet eis Dominus vineae? Veniet & perdet agricolas illos, & dabit vineam aliis. Hoc autem cum audiuissent, dixerunt, Absit. Ille vero intuitus eos, ait: Quid illud est ergo quod scriptum est: Quem lapidem reprobauerunt aedificantes, is factus est caput anguli? Quisquis ceciderit super illum lapidem, conquassabitur: super quem autem ceciderit, dispabit eum.
units.tr: He began to speak this parable to the people: A certain man planted a vineyard, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country for a long time. And at the season he sent a servant to the husbandmen, that they should give him of the fruit of the vineyard; but the husbandmen beat him and sent him away empty. And he proceeded to send another servant; but they beat him too, treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty. And he went on to send a third; but they wounded this one also and cast him out. Then the lord of the vineyard said: What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps when they see him, they will reverence him. But when the husbandmen saw him, they conferred among themselves, saying: This is the heir; come, let us kill him, that the inheritance may be ours. And they cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. What therefore will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those husbandmen and give the vineyard to others. When they heard this, they said: God forbid. But he looked at them and said: What then is this that is written: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner? Whoever falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; but on whomever it falls, it will grind him to powder.

units.la: Vdamus de toto mundo Iesus Christus recte pronuntiet, opera eius mala esse, & proinde veritatis lucem, quae per Euangelium nobis in ipso offertur, ferre non posse: nullos tamen idem ille acriores & vehementiores hostes habuit, quam Principes Sacerdotum, quorum quaestuosas artes atque tyrannidem arguebat. Abutebantur hi aduersus eum dignitate sua, quam vt legitimi Aaronis ac filiorum eius successores sibi ipsis iampridem vsurpauerant, ipsum vero (vt nuper audiuimus) populo suspectum facere conati sunt, quasi priuata temeritate & libidine munus docendi in uasisset, & sacris quoque manum admouendo ordinem Ecclesiae impudenter turbaret. Erat haec grauis & multiplicis scandali causa, nec dubium est multos vehementer offensos fuisse, quod illum ab iis indesinenter oppugnari viderent, penes quos praecipua erat in Ecclesia potestas atque eruditionis & pietatis existimatio. Commode ergo disputationi, quam proxime audiuimus parabolam istam de vinea & colonis subiicit, qua tria ex ordine agit. Primo docet, vnde primum exorta sit dignitas illa Sacerdotij, qua tantopere superbiant, & in quem finem hoc totum sit institutum. Deinde scelerata m ipsorum ingratitudinem accusat, qua iam olim in Deum peccare coeperint, & quae in ipsum porro sint designaturi. Tertio poenam minatur. Finis autem & scopus omnium est, vt & ipsis larvam detrahat, ne suos dolos celari posse sibi persuadeant & simul e medio auferat scandalum, quod ex more eius iam appropinquante, enasciturum esse sciebat. Quia vero simul hic tota Ecclesiasticae gubernationis ratio continetur, & quae de his dicuntur, nostri saeculi moribus in primis conueniunt, vtile fuerit huius parabolae partes singulas considerare.
units.tr: Granted that Jesus Christ rightly declared the whole world to be evil, and that for this reason it cannot bear the light of truth offered to us in him through the Gospel, yet he had no more bitter and violent enemies than the chief priests, whose profit-seeking arts and tyranny he exposed. These men abused against him the dignity which, as successors of the legitimate Aaron and his sons, they had long since usurped for themselves; and, as we heard recently, they tried to make him suspect to the people, as if he had assumed the office of teaching by private rashness and lust, and by impudently laying hands on sacred things were disturbing the order of the Church. This was a grave and manifold cause of scandal, and there is no doubt that many were deeply offended to see him attacked without ceasing by those in whose hands lay the chief power in the Church and the reputation for learning and piety. Fittingly, therefore, after the dispute we heard a little while ago, he adds this parable of the vineyard and the husbandmen, in which he treats three things in order. First, he teaches whence that dignity of the priesthood first arose, in which they so proudly boast, and to what end the whole thing was instituted. Then he accuses them of their wicked ingratitude, by which they had long before begun to sin against God, and of what they were going to do further against him. Third, he threatens punishment. The aim and purpose of all is both to strip off their mask, so that they may not persuade themselves that their deceits can be hidden, and at the same time to remove the scandal which he knew would arise from their conduct as he drew near. But since the whole rule of ecclesiastical government is contained here, and what is said about these men especially fits the manners of our own age, it will be useful to consider the individual parts of this parable.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet quod dicit: Quidam plantauit vineam, & elocauit eam agrocolis, & peregre abfuit multum tempus. Per vineam populus Iudaicus intelligitur, penes quem tunc fuisse titulum Ecclesiae satis constat. Estque parabola haec in Scripturis admodum frequens, quia Dei erga nos studium graphice adumbrat, & omnes eos officij admonet, qui Ecclesiae membra aut pars aliqua censeri volunt. Vt enim vinearum possessio pretiosissima, & earundem cultura admodum laboriosa est: ita non in alium finem & vsum coluntur, quam vt fructum ferant, & nisi hunc ferant, mox excinduntur vites, ne terram frustra occupent. In praesenti tamen praecipuum est, quod vineam hanc colonis elocatam fuisse Christus dicit. Per hos enim Sacerdotes intelligit, quos sui populi colonos Deus olim fecerat, vt illum diligenti Legis doctrina, legitimo sacrorum rituum vsu & exemplo quoque proprio ad pietatem excolerent, & ex eo fructus coligerent professione eorum dignos & quibus ille delectari posset. Sunt hi fides vera quae ex Dei veri & Filij eius cognitione dependet, sanctitatis & innocentiae studium, & dilectio fraterna siue mutua, qua Paulus totius Legis complementum esse dicit. Ista autem parte Christus Sacerdotibus supercilium detrahit, qui se colonos a Deo constitutos esse obliti, sibi ipsis imperium vendicabant in vinea Domini, & pro suo arbitrio, omnia omnia instituebant. Admonet ergo, non habere ipsos aliquam aduersus se superbiendi causam, neq; etiam se vllo iure cogi, vt illis suae vel doctrinae vel actionum suarum rationem reddat, cum Ecclesia Dei peculium atque vinea sit: sed potius ipsorum esse, vt suae conditionis memores, bonae fidei coloni sint, & de Dei potius gloria populiq; salute propaganda, quàm suis commodis & proprio honore cogitent. Et sane potuit vnum hoc sufficere ad confutanda illorum temeritatem, qui templi vsum pro phanarant, & totam cultus diuini formam mutarant, doctrinam item humanis traditionibus corrumperant. Obseruemus ergo hic simul omnes eos confutari, qui in Ecclesia hoc sibi ius sumunt & imperium, vt ex suo cerebro omnia constituant, nouas leges condant, articulos fidei nouos conscribant, cultus item formam mutent, & authoritate sua aduersus eos abutantur, qui veterē & à Deo traditam religionis & Ecclesiae formam reducere satagunt. Non est ergo, quod Pontifices nobis hodie catholicam Petri & perpetuam successionem obijciant. Nam vt haec omnia illis demus, & ipsos immediatè ab ipso Dei Filio instituros atque ordinatos esse fateamur, non tamen alios quàm colonos dicere possumus, qui non leges dare, sed à Christo accipere, nō in Ecclesiam dominari, sed ei potius seruire: non suam inde vtilitatem captare, sed omnia ad eius gloriam & honorem referre debeant, qui illam sui sanguinis pretio acquisiuit. Vnde etiam sequitur, reprehensione eosdem dignos esse, si quid praeter officium faciant. Nam vt olim magna quidem erat Sacerdotum authoritas & capitale esset eorum sententiae cōtumaciter reluctari, eos tamen à Prophetis acriter correptos & publicè etiam obiurgatos fuisse scimus, quando in suo munere vel negligentiores vel minus fidi fuerunt.
