Matthew and Mark noted that these spies were from the Herodians and the Pharisees, or rather disciples of the Pharisees. Both were most suited to ambush. For the Pharisees were held more holy than the rest, while the Herodians were not wholly alien to the Jewish religion; yet although with Herod they revered the majesty of the Roman Empire, they seemed to favour the advantages and liberty of the people; and, as is nearly peculiar to courtiers, they mixed their profession of religion with ambition and a pursuit of pleasures. Meanwhile there is no doubt that the Pharisees were most hostile to those others, since they hated courtly manners and burned more than the rest with zeal to recover liberty. Although therefore there was no small difference between these two groups of men, each nevertheless seemed fit in the eyes of the chief priests to be used against Christ, and in attacking him they could easily agree. It is characteristic of the wicked that, although they never agree among themselves in matters that concern the use of this life, but daily stir up quarrels, being overcome by ambition or avarice or other lusts, yet they conspire with unanimous consent against Christ, because his doctrine is equally hateful and detested by all. So have we not read that between the Sadducees and the Pharisees, men of most different sects, there was more than once peace, or at least a truce, so that they might attack Christ with united strength? Did they not think the bloodthirsty soldiers worthy of their friendship, when for seizing him they needed those who had previously been accustomed to slander him because he associated too familiarly with tax collectors? And who today does not know that monks, who wish to appear dead to the world, not infrequently conspire with the most impious soldiers, so that by their work they may abuse them against the brothers of Christ's worshippers? And these things might be tolerated, were they not made even more shameful in our own time, when Christian princes are not ashamed to make truces with the Turks, so as to turn their arms against the followers of the Evangelical truth; and would that men were not found who seek the aid of the enemies of the cross against those who have placed all their confidence of salvation in the merit of that one alone. Yet these things ought not to terrify anyone. For the Church speaks to all such men through Isaiah: "Make an alliance, O peoples, and you will be broken; give ear, you who are in distant lands, gird yourselves, and you will be broken; take counsel, and it will come to nothing; speak the word, but it will not stand, for God is with us." Meanwhile the conspiracies of the ungodly should stir us to agree in mind as well, and to speak one and the same thing in Christ Jesus. Finally, let us draw from this an argument by which we may confirm ourselves in his faith. For since this doctrine is equally hated by all the wicked, it must be the true and the only holy one.

units.la: At non minori astu Herodiani illi & Pharisæorum discipuli rem agunt, quàm à principibus Sacerdotum submissi fuerant. Nam mirificè dolum & insidias suas tegunt, vt facilius responsum eliciant, ex quo ipsum accusandi occasionem vaenentur. Magister (inquiunt) scimus te rectè dicere & docere, nec accipere personam, sed viam Dei in veritate docere. Tribuunt ei quaecunq; à bono & fido doctore exiguntur. Debet is viam Dei monstrare, id est, ea docere, quæ nos ad Deum deducunt, & nos illi acceptos faciunt. At ea non alibi quàm in sacris literis inueniuntur. Ex his ergo doctrinam suam petere, non circa vanas & ambiguas hominum traditiones vagari debet, quibus frustra Deus colitur. Deinde vt rectè omnia tradat, videndum est. Sunt enim qui Dei verbum docent, sed hoc ipsum non rectè secant, neq; cibum illum salutiferum suo tempore depromunt, vt doctrina homines ædificentur, & in via Dei dirigantur. Errant hic qui linguis peregrinis apud vulgus vtuntur, qui item gratiam & misericordiam Dei contumacibus & pœnitere nescijs prædicat, quos minis terreri oportebat: aut è contra minis & seueritate nimia vtuntur erga eos, quorum afflictas conscientias gratiæ doctrina debebant erigere. Itaque locorum & temporum diligenti obseruatione opus erit doctori. Neque tamen ista sufficiet, nisi à seruili personarum respectu alienus sit. Vt enim hic in iudicio aut foro omnia peruertit: ita si eundem ministri Ecclesiarū admittant, nihil in suo munere rectè facient: sed alios quidem vt sua cura indignos negligent, alios verò indulgentius tractabunt, quos vel metuunt vel sibi vtiles fore sperant: multos etiam nimio rigore perdent, quos priuatas ob causas oderunt. Meminerint ergo se publicos totius Ecclesiæ ministros esse, in qua omnis loci ac ordinis homines continentur: de quibus omnibus olim ratio reddenda erit Christo, qui suum sanguinem pro illis fudit. Sed quia hæc alterius loci sunt, ad insidiatores illos redeamus, qui ista omnia Christo tribuunt, quia nihil homine maius de illo sentiebant, sed talem putabant, qui blanditijs & laudibus fucatis posset excæcari, vt inconsultius aut inconsideratius aliquid effutiret. Discunt istas artes veritatis hostes à suo magistro Satana, qui & primos parentes illis decepit, & ijsdem Christum quoque aggredi ausus fuit in deserto, vt suo loco vidimus. Imò in huius schola Iudas versatus postea illum oculo prodidit. Et debent exempla ista obseruari, vt cautiores simus, si quando blandius nobiscum agunt ij, quos veritatis hostes esse satis constat. Interim hi quoque meminerint, se frustra ad artes istas confugere. Nam non solum nihil proficiunt aduersus Christum, verumetiam seipsos impietatis extremæ damnant, eum insidiosè tentando, quem magistri titulo dignantur, & omnibus fidi doctoris dotibus exornant. Accidit hoc ipsum multis hodie, qui dum nos persequuntur, interim Apostolorum fidem & doctrinam magnificè prædicant, ex quorum libris nos nostra proferimus. Tanta diuinæ istius lucis ac veritatis vis est, vt impij quoque ei suum testimonium non omnino possint negare.
units.tr: But the Herodians and the disciples of the Pharisees, who were sent by the chief priests, acted with no less cunning. They hid their trickery and snares very skilfully, so that they might more easily draw out an answer from which they could find a reason to accuse him. "Teacher," they said, "we know that you speak and teach rightly, and that you do not regard the person, but teach the way of God in truth." They ascribed to him everything that is required of a good and faithful teacher. He ought to show the way of God, that is, teach those things which lead us to God and make us acceptable to him. But these are found nowhere except in the Holy Scriptures. So he ought to draw his teaching from these, and not wander among the vain and ambiguous traditions of men, by which God is worshipped in vain. Next, one must see that he delivers everything rightly. For there are some who teach the word of God but do not cut it straight, and do not bring out that wholesome food at the proper time, so that people may be built up in doctrine and directed in the way of God. Those err who use foreign tongues before the common people, and likewise those who preach the grace and mercy of God to the obstinate and to those who do not know how to repent, when they ought rather to be terrified with threats; or, on the contrary, who use threats and excessive severity towards those whose troubled consciences the doctrine of grace ought to raise up. Therefore a teacher will need careful attention to places and times. Yet this will not suffice unless he is free from servile regard for persons. For just as this man perverts everything in a court of judgement or in the forum, so, if ministers of the Churches admit the same fault, they will do nothing rightly in their office; they will neglect some, whom they consider unworthy of their care, and treat others too leniently, whom they either fear or hope will be useful to them; and they will destroy many with excessive rigour, whom they hate for private reasons. Let them therefore remember that they are public ministers of the whole Church, which embraces men of every place and rank, and for all of whom an account will one day be rendered to Christ, who shed his blood for them. But since these matters belong elsewhere, let us return to those plotters who ascribed all these things to Christ, because they thought nothing greater of him than a man, and supposed him to be one who could be blinded by flattery and false praise, so that he would blurt out something ill-advised or thoughtless. Enemies of the truth learn these arts from their master Satan, who deceived our first parents and dared to attack Christ himself in the desert, as we saw in its place. Indeed, Judas, who was trained in this school, afterwards betrayed him with a kiss. These examples ought to be noted, so that we may be more cautious whenever those who are well known to be enemies of the truth deal with us too smoothly. Meanwhile, let them also remember that they resort to these arts in vain. For they not only achieve nothing against Christ, but also condemn themselves to the utmost impiety, by tempting insidiously him whom they honour with the title of teacher and adorn with all the gifts of a faithful teacher. This happens today to many who, while they persecute us, meanwhile magnificently proclaim the faith and doctrine of the Apostles, from whose books we bring forward our own. So great is the power of this divine light and truth that even the impious cannot altogether deny their testimony to it.

units.la: Christo veri doctoris partes tribuunt aduersarij.
units.tr: The adversaries assign to Christ the part of a true teacher.

units.la: Porrò quæstionem ipsam audiamus. Licet ne (inquiunt) nobis censum dare Cæsari, annon? Quæstionis cardo atque summa in particula, NOBIS, versatur. Nec enim tam iniquos aut tam impudentes fuisse putabimus, vt censum agendi & exigendi ius in quæstionem vocauerint. Quid enim Regibus debeatur, ex Mose & Samuele iampridem didicerant. Etiam multis seculis mos ille apud Romanos in vsu fuerat, vt cives quoq; in censum venirent. Nam T. Livius de eo sic scribit: Censum primus omnium Seruius Tullus Rex instituit, rem saluberrimam tanto futuro imperio: ex quo belli pacisque munia, non viritim vt ante, sed pro possessione pecuniarum cives obirent. Nā (vt hoc quoque propter rudiores annotemus) census agi dicitur, quando & numerus ciuium putatur, & singulorum facultates recensentur, vt imponendi tributa ratio possit iniri. Est ergo per se æquissima hæc ratio, vt ad communis reipub. conseruationem singuli conferant quantum per facultates ipsorum licet. Quod verò Romani Imperatores à Iudæis censum exigebant, ideo propter duas causas indignissimum & iniquissimum videbatur. Prima erat, quod cum Dei peculium & gens illa sancta atque sacerdotale regnum essent, nefas esse putabant prophanis principibus atque idololatris tributum dare. Altera, quod census iste olim Deo consecratus fuerat, vt inde sumptus sacrorum fierent, & ea conseruarentur, quæ ad Dei cultū pertinebāt. Sic enim ad Mosem dicit Dominus: Cum censum egeris secundum capita filiorum Israel, iuxta censum eorum dabunt singuli expiatione animæ suæ Domino, &c. Et paulo post: Hanc expiatoriam pecuniam à filijs Israel acceptam, trades in cultum tabernaculi constitutionis, vt sit filijs Israel ad monumentum coram Domino, vt propitius sit animabus vestris. Erat ergo Romanorum tyrannis cum sacrilegio coniuncta, cum Imperatores sibi ea vendicarent, quæ Deo debebantur; & ideo quærunt isti, an ipsis liceat in eo illis obedire, quod cum manifesta cultus diuini contumelia mandabatur. Et scimus iugum hoc vulgo Iudæorum grauissimum visum fuisse. Qui enim non multo post seditionem moverunt, quod Pilatus thesaurum templi in aquæductum insumpsisset, ex quo aliqua saltem ad totum populum vtilitas redibat, procul dubio iniquius tulerunt præcipuos redditus templi ab hominibus prophanis intercipi, & Romam deferri, cuius authoritate idololatria in toto orbe terrarum defendebatur. Fuit ergo quæstio ista multis modis insidiosa. Nam si censum Cæsari negandum esse dicat, optatam ipsum accusandi occasionem habebunt, vt qui seditiosa dogmata in populo spargat plus satis ad res nouas procliui. Quod si verò reddere iubeat, publicanis iniquiorem esse dicent, qui non modò Romanæ tyrannidis ministrum se faciat, verumetiam Dei cultum remoretur, idololatriam verò gentium prophanarum tueatur. Rursum si omnino taceat, populi salutem negligere videbitur, & boni fidiique doctoris existimationem amittet, vt qui metu aut personarum respectu impeditus veritatem dicere non ausit. Tot laqueos totā retia breuis hæc quæstio abscondita habet, quæ nemo alius effugere potuisset.
units.tr: But let us hear the question itself: "Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?" The crux and substance of the question turns on the small word "us." For we shall not suppose them so unjust or so shameless as to call into question the right of the rulers to levy and collect the census. They had long since learned from Moses and Samuel what is owed to kings. For many centuries that custom had been in use among the Romans, that citizens too should be enrolled in the census. Titus Livy writes of it thus: "Servius Tullius, king, was the first of all to institute the census, a most wholesome measure for an empire that was to become so great; from it citizens undertook the duties of war and peace not individually, as before, but according to the property of their wealth." For (to note this too for the less learned) the census is said to be taken when both the number of citizens is reckoned and each man's means are assessed, so that a rate of taxation may be fixed. This arrangement is therefore in itself most fair: that each man should contribute to the preservation of the common commonwealth as much as his means allow. But the reason why it seemed most unworthy and most unjust that the Roman emperors exacted the census from the Jews was twofold. The first was that, since that people was God's own possession, a holy nation and a kingdom of priests, they thought it wrong to pay tribute to profane and idolatrous rulers. The second was that this census had once been consecrated to God, so that from it the costs of the sacred rites might be met and those things maintained which pertained to the worship of God. For thus the Lord says to Moses: "When you take the census of the children of Israel according to their heads, then they shall each give, according to their census, a ransom for his soul to the Lord, etc." And a little later: "You shall take this money of atonement from the children of Israel and spend it on the service of the tabernacle of the congregation, that it may be a memorial to the children of Israel before the Lord, so that he may be merciful to your souls." Therefore the tyranny of the Romans was joined with sacrilege, since the emperors claimed for themselves what was owed to God; and so these men ask whether it is lawful for them to obey in this matter, which was commanded with a manifest insult to the worship of God. And we know that this yoke seemed most grievous to the common people of the Jews. For those who, not long afterwards, stirred up a sedition because Pilate had spent the treasury of the temple on an aqueduct, from which at least some benefit returned to the whole people, certainly took it worse that the chief revenues of the temple should be intercepted by profane men and carried off to Rome, by whose authority idolatry was defended throughout the whole world. This question was therefore insidious in many ways. For if Christ said that the census must be refused to Caesar, they would have the very occasion they desired for accusing him, as one who spread seditious doctrines among the people and was far too prone to revolution. But if he ordered it to be paid, they would say that he was a more unfavourable friend of the tax-collectors, who not only made himself a minister of Roman tyranny, but also hindered the worship of God and defended the idolatry of the profane nations. Again, if he kept silent altogether, he would seem to neglect the welfare of the people, and would lose the reputation of a good and faithful teacher, as one who, hindered by fear or by regard for persons, did not dare to speak the truth. So many snares, so many nets, were hidden in this short question, which no one else could have escaped.

units.la: At dum Christum irretire conantur, non solum nihil proficiunt, sed suam simul ignorantiam & præposterum templi atque religionis studium produnt. Promissiones enim de Messia secundum literam de regno terreno & libertate politica exponunt, quasi per illum Romanæ tyrannidis iugum frangi & auferri oporteat: nihil interim soliciti de liberatione ex peccatis & morte æterna, cui homines omnes sunt obnoxij. Deinde templum & externum cultum defendendum esse putant, ne huic debita pecunia in alios vsus conuertatur: interim illa humanis traditionibus & turpissima sacrorum omnium nundinatione prophanari passi sunt: imò Christum ideo extinctum volunt, quod is impias illas sordes & nocentissimas veri cultus pestes eiecisset. Similes ergo sunt isti Ioanni Pontifici, qui cum annis ante Christum natum trecentis sexaginta quatuor fratrem germanum, quo cum ei de sacerdotio lis erat, in ipso templo occidisset, Vagosem Persam impietatis accusauit, quod templum ingressus inde abstulisset spolia. Ita isti pro censu templi contendunt, cū illud iam pridem in speluncam latronum conuertissent. Atqui defendi debebat templum, non quoad ædificium aut redditus siue quamcunque pecuniam, quæ huic debebatur, sed quoad doctrinam & cultum, ne vel illa traditionibus falsis inficeretur, vel hic in quæstum superstitiosum degeneraret. Fuit ergo hæc nō minus turpis quàm exitialis ignorantia, vt infelix totius gentis exitium paulo post docuit. At hoc illud est quod patribus quoque olim imposuit, quod nimirum promissiones Dei non rectè intelligerent. Cum enim Prophetæ vrbi & templo excidium minarentur, & populum propter peccata enormia in Babylonē abducendum esse prædicerent, à plerisq; pro vanis & mendacibus habiti sunt, qui promissionem illis nem illis obijciebant: Hæc est mea requies in æternum: hic habitabo, quoniam expetiui eam. Item: Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, neque legislator de pedibus eius, donec veniat Schilo, & ad illum gentes confluent. Istis verò promissionibus male intellectis freti, prophetarum admonitiones contemnebant, quæ illis exitij causa fuit. Et hodie non paci promissiones Euangelicas de carnis libertate exponunt, & quæ in his nobis offertur, gratiam Dei de huius secnli opibus, honoribus, pace & otio interpretantur. Itaque nudam fidei professionem sufficere putant, & mendacij eos omnes accusant, qui propter scelera & ingratitudinem ipsi Dei iram atque pœnas denuntiant. Multi quoque, si quid aduersum patiuntur, se deceptos esse clamant ab Euangelij doctoribus, & cruce offensi à fide, quam professi erant, turpiter resiliunt. Nos ergo exemplis istis admoniti distinguere discamus inter mandata Dei & inter promissiones. Et illa quidem semper seruari debent, sed non eodem modo ab omnibus. Dei mandatum est, ut cultum eius tueamur. Id Reges & qui legitima potestate armati sunt, armis quoque (si ita necessitas iubeat) facere debent, ut strenui sint Ecclesiæ nutritij, quod olim Dauidem Ezechiam, Machabæos fratres, & postea Constantinum, Theodosium & plu res alios felicissimè fecisse legimus. Ut verò priuati homines aut Ecclesiarum ministri idem conentur nefas esse, nisi peculiaris vocatio accedat. Quod verò promissiones Dei, aliæ sunt de rebus spiri tualibus, ut de remissione peccatorum, reconciliatione per Christum, vita æterna: aliæ verò de rebus temporarijs, quæ ad huius seculi usum pertinent. Et illis quidem semper confidere & constanter insistere oportet: quia nunquam fallent: istis verò (ut Christus Marci decimo capite admonet) crucis conditio coniuncta est: quia benefacere quidem suis vult Deus, sed ea conditione, ut peccata eorum virgis paternis castiget, & carnis petulantiam aduersis, ceu fræno, coerceat. Si quid ergo eiusmodi accidit, patienter illud ferre, & simul Dei beneficium agnoscere oportet, qui cùm totos perdere posset, virga virorum & verberibus filiorum hominum (ut Dauidi olim promisit) erga nos vtitur, Quod si Iudæi obseruauissent, nunquam de excutiendo Romanorum iugo aut reddituum templi defensione temeraria cogitauissent, sed in suis istis calamitatibus Dei bonitatem prædicauissent, qui & patrias sedes & templi usum cum externi cultus & religionis libertate ipsis reliquerat, & ea contenti patienter tulissent reliqua seruitutis incommoda, quæ suis sceleribus atque ingratitudine meruerat.
units.tr: While they try to ensnare Christ, they not only achieve nothing but also reveal their own ignorance and their misguided zeal for the temple and religion. They expound the promises about the Messiah literally, as concerning an earthly kingdom and political freedom, as though through him the yoke of Roman tyranny must be broken and removed, while meanwhile they are not at all concerned about deliverance from sins and eternal death, to which all men are subject. Next, they think the temple and external worship must be defended, lest the money owed to it be diverted to other uses; yet they have allowed these same things to be profaned by human traditions and by the most shameful trading in all sacred things. Indeed, they want Christ put to death because he drove out those impious filths and most harmful pests of true worship. Such men are therefore like John the high priest, who, three hundred and sixty-four years before Christ's birth, killed in the temple itself his own brother, with whom he was in dispute over the priesthood, and then accused Bagoas the Persian of impiety, because Bagoas had entered the temple and carried off the spoils from there. So these men contend over the temple's revenue, although they had long since turned it into a den of robbers. Yet the temple ought to have been defended not in respect of its building or its income or whatever money was owed to it, but in respect of its teaching and worship, so that the teaching might not be infected by false traditions and the worship might not degenerate into superstitious gain. Their ignorance was therefore no less shameful than it was ruinous, as the wretched destruction of the whole nation soon taught. Yet this is the very error that once deceived the fathers too, namely that they did not rightly understand God's promises. For when the prophets threatened the city and temple with destruction, and foretold that the people were to be led away to Babylon on account of their monstrous sins, they were mostly regarded as vain and lying men, and the people threw in their faces the promise: "This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it" [Ps. 132:14]. Likewise: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come, and unto him shall the gathering of the people be" [Gen. 49:10]. Relying on these promises, misunderstood as they were, they despised the warnings of the prophets, and this was the cause of their ruin. And today, too, some expound the gospel promises as a freedom of the flesh, and interpret the grace of God that is offered to us in them as the wealth, honours, peace and leisure of this age. So they think a bare profession of faith is enough, and they accuse of lying all those who announce God's own anger and punishments on account of sins and ingratitude. Many also, if they suffer any adversity, cry out that they have been deceived by the teachers of the gospel, and, offended by the cross, shamefully fall away from the faith they had professed. Let us therefore, warned by these examples, learn to distinguish between God's commands and his promises. The commands must always be kept, but not in the same way by everyone. It is God's command that we defend his worship. Kings and those armed with lawful power ought to do this also with arms, if necessity so demands, so that they may be vigorous nurses of the Church; we read that David, Hezekiah, the Maccabean brothers, and afterwards Constantine, Theodosius and several others did this most happily. But for private persons or ministers of the Churches to attempt the same is wrong, unless a special calling is added. As for God's promises, some concern spiritual things, such as the forgiveness of sins, reconciliation through Christ, and eternal life; others concern temporal things, which pertain to the use of this age. We ought always to rely on the former and to persist in them constantly, because they will never fail us. But with the latter, as Christ warns in the tenth chapter of Mark, the condition of the cross is joined; for God indeed wishes to do good to his own, but on this condition, that he chastise their sins with a father's rod and restrain the wantonness of the flesh with adversities, as with a bridle. If therefore anything of this kind befalls us, we ought to bear it patiently and at the same time acknowledge God's kindness, who, though he could have destroyed us utterly, deals with us with the rod of men and the stripes of the sons of men, as he once promised to David [2 Sam. 7:14]. If the Jews had observed this, they would never have thought of shaking off the Roman yoke or of rashly defending the revenues of the temple. Instead, in these very calamities they would have proclaimed God's goodness, who had left them their native seats and the use of the temple along with the freedom of external worship and religion; and being content with these, they would have patiently borne the remaining burdens of servitude, which they had deserved by their own wickedness and ingratitude.

units.la: Sed ad Christum veniamus, quem aduersariorum calliditatem animaduertisse & eandem arguisse, Lucas scribit. Respondit enim: Quid me tentatis? Ita verò ostendit, se non ignorare, quòd sub dolo animo interrogent, ut ipsum capiendi occasionem inueniant. Est hoc euidens diuinitatis eius argumentum, cuius generis multa in historia Euangelica occurrunt. Debent ea nos consolari, ne causam fidei & religionis hostium astu atq; insidijs opprimi posse putemus. Quid enim illi vnquam instituent aut molientur, quod Christū lateat, qui luce sua in tenebras quoq; obstrusissimas penetrat, & cordium arcana scrutatur? Imò de eo verissimè dicitur, quod sapientes in ipsorum astutia comprehendat. At simul huius nos meminisse oportet, ne nostris cogitationibus siue consilijs plus æquo- indulgeamus: quod plerunque faciunt, qui Deum ista vel ignorare vel negligere sibi persuaserunt. Quoties ergo circa ea vagari mens incipit, quæ iniqua, iniusta & inhonesta sunt, simul in mentem quoque veniat, ea non posse Deum latere, qui vbique præsens adest. Quò àfacie tua fugiam? inquit Dauid. Si dicam. Tenebræ me contegent: etiam nox ipsa lux est circa me. Et ne tenebræ quidem a- liquid tibi occultant, & nox vt dies lucet, tenebræq;, & lux tibi iuxta habentur. Item: Nouit Domi nus cogitationes hominum, quòd vanæ sunt. Quibus adde, quòd eas Christus videt et nouit, ad cuius tribunal olim omnes nos sisti oportet.
units.tr: But let us come to Christ, whom Luke writes perceived the craftiness of his adversaries and rebuked it. For he answered: "Why do you tempt me?" [Luke 20:23]. In this way he showed that he did not fail to see that they were asking with a deceitful mind, so as to find an occasion to seize him. This is a clear proof of his divinity, and many instances of this kind occur in the gospel history. They ought to console us, so that we do not think the cause of faith and religion can be overcome by the cunning and snares of enemies. For what will they ever plan or attempt that is hidden from Christ, who penetrates with his light even the most obscure darkness and searches the secrets of hearts? Indeed, it is most truly said of him that he takes the wise in their own craftiness [1 Cor. 3:19]. But at the same time we must remember not to indulge our thoughts or counsels more than is right, which those commonly do who have persuaded themselves that God either does not know these things or does not care about them. Therefore, whenever the mind begins to wander over things that are wicked, unjust and dishonourable, let this also come to mind: that these cannot be hidden from God, who is present everywhere. "Whither shall I flee from thy presence?" says David. "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me. Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee, but the night shineth as the day; the darkness and the light are both alike to thee" [Ps. 139:7, 11–12]. Likewise: "The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men, that they are vanity" [Ps. 94:11]. To these add that Christ sees and knows them, and before whose judgment-seat we must all one day appear.

units.la: At simul docet nos suo exemplo Dominus, vt cum apertis hostibus veritatis sit agendum. No bis quidem impossibile est omnes eorum fraudes & quas intra animos suos versanc cogitationes deprehendere: attamen cautos & prouidos esse oportet, ne astutissimis hominibus nostra stupiditate aliquid confidentius tentandi occasionem præbeamus: & huc prudentia illa serpentina pertinet, quam Christus in suis requirit. Interea Deum precemur, vt hic improborum hominum dolos atque insidiosa consilia detegat, nostris autem animis ea suggerat, quæ vtilia & necessaria sunt ad veritatis defensionem. Quandocunque autem illorum improbitas nobis perspecta est, liberè & seriò illam arguamus, vt suos dolos nequaquam nos latere intelligant. Nisi enim id fiat, latebrarum spes aut fiducia audentiores reddit, ut proteruius omnium capitibus insultare conentur. Neq; hic personarum dignitati aut excellentiae aliquid dandum est: quando omnem hominum authoritatem longè superat veritas, quae nobis quàm maximè commendata esse debet: quod Prophetae olim & deinde Apostoli quoq; suo exemplo nos abunde docuerunt.
units.tr: At the same time the Lord teaches us by his own example that we must deal with open enemies of the truth. It is indeed impossible for us to detect all their frauds and the thoughts that stir in their minds; yet we ought to be cautious and watchful, lest by our dullness we give the most crafty men an occasion for attempting something more boldly; and to this belongs that serpentine prudence which Christ requires in his people [Matt. 10:16]. In the meantime let us pray God to reveal the deceits and insidious plans of wicked men, and to suggest to our minds what is useful and necessary for defending the truth. Whenever their wickedness has been plainly seen by us, let us expose it freely and earnestly, so that they understand their tricks do not escape us at all. For unless this is done, the hope or confidence of lying hidden makes them bolder, so that they try to insult everyone's head more shamelessly. Nor must anything be yielded here to the dignity or eminence of persons, since truth far surpasses all human authority, and truth ought to be commended to us above all things; the prophets of old, and afterwards the apostles also, taught us abundantly by their example.

units.la: Postquam verò aduersariorum dolos atque insidias Christus arguit, ad quaestionis propositae solutionem accedit, & hanc ex illorum ore mirifica & plane diuina prudentia elicit, & laqueo, quem ipsi abscónderant, eos capit. Ostendite (inquit) mihi denarium, cuius habet imaginem & inscriptionem? Nam (ut alibi annotauimus) ex veteri & vsitato more Romani Imperatores numis sua nomina atque imagines inscribere solebant: & hodie adhuc denarij eiusmodi multi visuntur, ex ruderibus collecti aut terra effossi. Respondent illi, Caesaris imagine & inscriptione signatum esse. Ex eo autem ille infert: Reddite igitur quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, & quae sunt Dei, Deo. Quasi diceret: Cum Caesaris numis aut moneta vtamini, ex eo constat, vos Caesaris imperio esse subiectos. Huic ergo reddite, quae Regibus aut magistratui ex iure debentur. Neque hic importunam de pristina vestrae gentis dignitate aut Dei cultu siue religione quaestionem moueritis. Non obstat enim Caesaris imperium siue iugum, quo minus animorum & conscientiae libertate fruamini, & quod Deo debetur obsequium simul praestetis. Ita verò praeposterum eorum zelum arguit, quo suum censum templo vindicare satagebant, quasi pecunijs Deus delectetur, neque sine his coli possit, neglectis interim praestantioribus illis officijs, sine quibus pietas & verus Dei cultus consistere non possunt. Etenim qui non vno loco sacrificia & oblationes, quas ipse per Mosem instituerat, reiecit, eo quòd circa has absque fide occuparentur: multo minus pecunijs nostris opus habet, quibus religionem potius euerti quam augeri scimus. Constat enim omnibus seculis cultum Dei corruptum fuisse, ut primùm diuitijs auctí fuerunt illius mystae siue antistites.
units.tr: But after Christ has exposed the deceits and snares of his adversaries, he comes to the solution of the question put to him, and with marvellous and plainly divine prudence draws it out of their own mouths, and catches them in the snare which they themselves had hidden. "Show me," he says, "a penny. Whose image and inscription has it?" For (as we have noted elsewhere) according to the old and customary practice, Roman emperors used to stamp their names and images on their coins; and even today many such denarii are seen, gathered from ruins or dug out of the earth. They answer that it bears the image and inscription of Caesar. From this he then infers: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's" [Matt. 22:21]. As if he were saying: since you use Caesar's coins and money, it is clear that you are subject to Caesar's rule. Therefore give to him what is due by right to kings or to the magistrate. Nor should you raise here an unseasonable question about your nation's former dignity or the worship or religion of God. For Caesar's rule or yoke does not stand in the way of your enjoying freedom of mind and conscience, and at the same time rendering the obedience due to God. In this way he rebukes the misguided zeal by which they strove to claim their revenue for the temple, as though God took pleasure in money, and could not be worshipped without it, while meanwhile the far more important duties, without which piety and true worship cannot exist, were neglected. For he who did not, in one place, reject sacrifices and oblations which he himself had instituted through Moses, because these were carried on without faith, has much less need of our money, by which we know religion is rather overthrown than increased. For it is agreed that in every age the worship of God has been corrupted as soon as those who were its priests or ministers grew rich.

units.la: Caeterum diligenti obseruatione dignum est, quòd inter Deum & Caesarem distinguens, vnicuique quod suum est, reddere iubet. Eo enim docemur, Christum non abolere politias, neq; obedientiam, quae magistratibus debetur. Olim quidem Donatistis nefarium visum fuit, Imperatores & prouinciarum praefectos in homines Christianos imperium habere: & horum vestigijs hodie Anabaptistae insistunt, qui simul impossibile esse clamant, ut quis simul & Christianus sit & magistratum gerat. Sed alibi istorum non minus insana quàm seditiosa dogmata confutauimus: & sufficit illis conuincendis vnicum hoc Christi dictum, quo ut suum magistratui ius asserit: ita perspicuè docet, etiam prophanis principibus, salua religione & Dei cultu, obedientiam praestari posse in ijs, quae ad ipsorum iurisdictionem pertinent. Obseruarunt hoc olim Prophetae etiam, inter quos Ieremias Babylonijs Regibus Iudaeos obedire iubet: imò hanc excidij vrbis atque templi, exilij item & seruitutis causam fuisse ostendit, quòd Zedechias cum vicinis regibus conspirasset aduersus Nabuchodonozorem, cui cum iureiurando fidem atque obedientiam promiserat. Et nota sunt quae Apostoli de subditorum fide atque obedientia erga suos magistratus tradiderunt. Paulus certè adeò noluit, ut quis in hac causa libertatem conscientiae praetexat, ut potius ostendat obediendum esse principibus propter conscientiam, eò quòd horum potestas à Deo instituta sit. Et illi consentiens Petrus ait: Subiecti estote cuiuis humanae ordinationi (ita verò politias & Reipub. constitutiones vocat, non quòd ab hominibus originem ducant, sed quòd ad homines, & ad vitae humanae vsum atque conseruationem in primis pertineant) propter Dominum, siue Regi, ut qui praesit: siue praesidibus, ut qui per eum mittantur cum ad vltionem maleficorum, tum ad laudem rectè agentium. Nihil ergo patrocinij merentur, sed ut pestes humani generis procul arcendi sunt Rerumpub. turbatores, qui religione & doctrinae Christianae praetextu ad licentiam scelerum & legum politicarum euertionem abutuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth careful attention that when Christ distinguishes between God and Caesar, he bids us render to each what is his. By this we are taught that Christ does not abolish civil government or the obedience owed to magistrates. The Donatists once thought it wicked that emperors and provincial governors should hold authority over Christian men, and the Anabaptists follow in their footsteps today, crying out that it is impossible for anyone to be both a Christian and a magistrate at once. But we have refuted elsewhere the doctrines of these men, which are no less mad than they are seditious. For their refutation, this one saying of Christ is enough: by it he asserts the magistrate's right and plainly teaches that obedience can be rendered even to godless princes, without harm to religion or the worship of God, in those matters that fall under their jurisdiction. The prophets too observed this. Among them Jeremiah bids the Jews obey the kings of Babylon, and he shows that the destruction of the city and temple, and likewise the exile and slavery, came about because Zedekiah had conspired with neighbouring kings against Nebuchadnezzar, to whom he had pledged faith and obedience under oath. And well known are the things the apostles handed down about the faith and obedience of subjects toward their magistrates. Paul certainly did not want anyone to pretend liberty of conscience in this matter; rather he shows that rulers must be obeyed for conscience's sake, because their power has been instituted by God. Peter agrees with him and says: "Be subject to every human ordinance" (so he calls the civil orders and constitutions of the commonwealth, not because they take their origin from men, but because they chiefly pertain to men and to the use and preservation of human life), "for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as those sent by him, both for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of those who do well." Those who abuse religion and the pretext of Christian doctrine to license their crimes and to overthrow the civil laws therefore deserve no protection, but must be driven far away like the plagues of the human race and the disturbers of the commonwealth.

units.la: Interim singulis profuerit distinctionem hanc Dei & Caesaris probè obseruare, ut ita utrique obedientiam praestemus, ne functiones siue officia ista confundamus, aut quod alterius est transferamus in alterum. Ut enim Iudaei in eo potissimùm peccarunt, quòd quae Caesari debebatur, pecuniam Deo reddere voluerunt, neglectis ijs officijs, quae hic requirit: ita hodie turpis & exitialis illorum error est, qui quae Dei sunt, principibus tribuunt, dum horum arbitrio atque libidini subijciunt religionem atque doctrinam, & sibi ab illis dicendi leges praescribi patiuntur, adeoque illicitos cultus illorum authoritate defendi & impune exerceri posse sibi persuadent. Atqui nequaquam ea Christi Iesu mens est, qui vt Cæsari demus iubet, quæ ad huius ius pertinent, Deo autem suum quoque in nobis ius saluum atque inuiolatum seruemus. Videant ergo diligenter singuli, quæ nam Cæsaris sint, & quæ magistratibus omnibus debeantur officia. Primum inter ea est, vt debito honore & reuerentia eos prosequamur, vt qui Dei in terris legati sint, & iudicia Dei enuntient, quo nomine Dij quoque dicuntur. Nihil ergo in eos insolenter aut contumeliose fiat. Nefas enim fuerit ijs honorem negare, quos Deus suo nomine exornare dignatus est. Neque hic licentiam nobis venemur ex illorum vitijs, quæ interdum enormia & sua functione alienissima designant. Nam qualescunque illi sint, Dei tamen ordo atque institutum honore dignum est. Quod Dauid obseruans in Saule tyranno, non ninus crudeli & impio quàm iniusto, Domini vnctionem agnouit. Debet autem honor ille non ab inuitis præstari, sed cum amore coniunctus esse, vt ex animo ijs faueamus, quos publicæ pacis custodes Deus constituit, & pro ijsdem preces faciamus, atque eorum conatus quouis officij genere adiuuemus. Hoc olim Iudæis in Babylonem abductis Ieremias præcipiebat, & Paulus ad Timotheum scribens, iubet, vt preces & supplicationes publicas fieri curet pro Regibus & quibusuis alijs, qui in eminentia constituti sint: quos illo seculo omnes ethnicos & à veri Dei cognitione alienissimos fuisse constat. Veteres autem Christianos in eo diligentissimos fuisse, Tertullianus scribit, & ex Ecclesiasticis historijs multa eius generis exempla adduci poterant. Præterea honorem atq; amorem ipsum obedientia testemur, ne quid contra leges ab ipsis promulgatas temere faciamus, nisi ea exigant, quæ Deo debentur, & quæ sine sacrilegio & impietate huic negari non possunt. Ad obedientiam census, tributa, vectigalia & alia huius generis pertinent, quæ Reipub. deberi supra often dimus. Nemo igitur in his persoluendis dolo malo vtatur, nemo furtim quæ illis debentur intercipiat, nemo propter illa tumultuetur. Quis enim non vt Reipub. & communis patriæ hostem detestetur eum, qui publicam pecuniam suffurari vel auertere, aut propter ea tumultuari ausit, sine quibus respub. administrari & seruari non potest?
units.tr: Meanwhile it will profit each of us to observe carefully this distinction between God and Caesar, so that we render obedience to both, and do not confuse these functions or duties, or transfer to one what belongs to the other. For just as the Jews sinned chiefly in this, that they wished to give to God the money that was owed to Caesar, while neglecting those duties which the latter requires, so today the shameful and ruinous error of those is equally great who assign to princes what is God's, subjecting religion and doctrine to their will and pleasure, allowing laws of teaching to be prescribed for them by those rulers, and persuading themselves that illicit forms of worship can be defended by their authority and practised with impunity. Yet this is by no means the mind of Christ Jesus, who bids us give to Caesar what pertains to his right, but also keep safe and inviolate in ourselves the right that belongs to God. Let each therefore carefully consider what things are Caesar's, and what duties are owed to all magistrates. The first of these is that we attend to them with due honour and reverence, as those who are ambassadors of God on earth and who pronounce the judgements of God, for which reason they are also called gods. Nothing, therefore, should be done toward them insolently or contemptuously. For it would be wicked to deny honour to those whom God has deigned to adorn with his own name. Nor should we seek here a licence for ourselves from their vices, which at times are monstrous and very foreign to their office. For whatever they are like, nevertheless the order and institution of God is worthy of honour. David observed this in Saul the tyrant, no less cruel and impious than unjust, and recognised in him the anointing of the Lord. Moreover, this honour ought not to be rendered unwillingly, but should be joined with love, so that we favour from the heart those whom God has appointed as guardians of public peace, pray for them, and assist their efforts in every kind of duty. Jeremiah enjoined this on the Jews carried away to Babylon, and Paul, writing to Timothy, bids that public prayers and supplications be made for kings and for all others who are set in high places. It is certain that in that age all of them were heathens and most alien from the knowledge of the true God. Tertullian writes that the ancient Christians were most diligent in this, and many examples of this kind could be brought from ecclesiastical histories. Furthermore, let us bear witness to honour and love by obedience itself, so that we do nothing rashly against the laws they have promulgated, unless those laws demand what is owed to God and what cannot be denied to them without sacrilege and impiety. To obedience belong the census, tributes, taxes and other things of this kind, which, as we said above, are owed to the commonwealth. Therefore let no one use deceit in paying these, let no one secretly intercept what is due to them, and let no one stir up tumult on account of them. For who would not detest, as an enemy of the commonwealth and of the common fatherland, the man who dared to embezzle or divert public money, or to stir up tumult because of it, when without such funds the commonwealth cannot be governed or preserved?

units.la: At multa (inquis) iniustè & iniquè exigunt principes, vtque habeant, quod ipsorum luxui & libidini sufficiat, crudeliter eorum fortunas diripiunt, qui necessarijs vitæ alimentis destituuntur. Est hoc quidem nostro seculo nimis vulgare, & fere apud Reges in pretio sunt, qui nouos exactionum modos & noua quotidie pecuniarum colligendarum aucupia excogitare nouerunt. Et debent hic sui officij illos admonere omnes, qui aut illis à consilijs sunt, aut ad quos ex iure regnorum cura veterumque priuilegiorum atque immunitatum conseruatio pertinet. Nemini autem priuato propterea tumultuari aut seditionem publicam excitare licet: sed meminerint, bonos principes & patriæ patres à Deo dari, ab eodem etiam excitari tyrannos, vt horum iniquitate & crudelitate puniantur, qui legibus bonis & verbo eius obedire nolunt. Ita Israelitis olim Reges in ira sua illum dedisse Hoseas scribit, & notum est illud Solomonis: Propter præuaricationem eorum, qui terram in colunt, mutantur aut transferuntur imperia. Agnoscant ergo miseri illi manum Dei, & patienter ferant incommoda illa imperiorum, quæ sua ingratitudine & contumacia sibipsis accersiuerunt. Simul tamen meminerint rigidi illi exactores, non impunè ipsis fore crudelitatem istam. Audit enim populi sui clamorem Deus, sentit egentium & inopum gemitus, & tandem manum suam exerit, vt ad se conuersos liberet, iniusta verò tyrannorum imperia aboleat. Et cõstat hos fere sibijpsis malum struere. Nam vt nihil aliud periculi oriatur, necesse est, vt exhaustis omnibus populi atque subditorum fortunis, ipsi quoque tandem egeant, & posteris regnum relinquant vacuum & viribus plane destitutum. Vidit hoc olim Traianus Imperator, qui immodicas exactiones detestatus fiscum solebat lienem dicere, quia & hoc crescente alia membra contabescunt: ita dum principes fiscum augere student, populum exhauriunt. At quæ nostri seculi infelicitas est, infelices subditi passim deglutiuntur, & ad extremam redigunter egestatem, nihilo interim crescentibus diuitijs principum, dum hi quæcunq; corradunt, vel turpiter prodigunt, vel à suis vicissim spoliantur.
units.tr: But (you say) princes demand many things unjustly and inequitably, and in order to have enough for their luxury and lust, they cruelly plunder the fortunes of those who are deprived of the necessary means of life. Indeed, in our age this is only too common, and kings for the most part are prized who know how to devise new modes of exaction and new contrivances for collecting money every day. Here all who are their counsellors, or to whom by right of the realm the care and preservation of the ancient privileges and immunities belong, ought to admonish them of their duty. But no private person may on that account stir up tumult or raise public sedition. Rather let them remember that good princes and fathers of the country are given by God, and that tyrants too are raised up by the same God, so that those who are unwilling to obey good laws and his word may be punished by their iniquity and cruelty. Thus Hosea writes that God in his anger once gave Israel kings, and that saying of Solomon is well known: "Because of the transgression of those who dwell in the land, kingdoms are changed and transferred." Let those wretched people therefore acknowledge the hand of God, and patiently bear the hardships of those rulers whom they have brought upon themselves by their ingratitude and obstinacy. At the same time, let those harsh exactors remember that this cruelty will not go unpunished. For God hears the cry of his people, feels the groaning of the needy and poor, and at last stretches forth his hand to free those who turn to him, and to abolish the unjust dominion of tyrants. And it is clear that these men for the most part build up evil for themselves. For, to say nothing of other dangers, it is necessary that, once the fortunes of the people and subjects are all drained, they themselves at last also become needy, and leave to their successors a kingdom empty and utterly deprived of strength. The Emperor Trajan saw this long ago; he detested immoderate exactions and used to call the treasury the spleen, because when it grows, the other limbs waste away. Thus while princes strive to enlarge the treasury, they drain the people dry. But such is the misery of our age that unhappy subjects are everywhere swallowed up and reduced to utter want, while the riches of princes do not grow at all, since whatever they gather they either shamefully squander or in turn are plundered by their own people.

units.la: Sed ad præsens argumentum reuerti quid Deo debeatur, videamus. Debemus autem huic nos totos corpore & anima, eò quod ab eo creati nihil habemus, quàm quod ex eius liberalitate accipimus. Multa tamen ille à nobis vult hominibus dari, qualia sunt, quæ modò de magistratu diximus; & eodem pertinent quæ parentibus, heris, coniugibus, liberis, alijs denique quibuscunque debentur officia. At quæ ille sibi soli vendicat, præcipua sunt, quæ ad eius cultum pertinent. In eo primæ partes sunt doctrinæ, sine qua ille non consistit. Videndum ergo ne quæ alia admittatur, quàm quæ ex Dei verbo desumpta sit. Scimus enim illum olim dixisse: Frustra me colunt docentes traditiones hominum. Ipsum ergo in suo verbo nobis loquentem audiamus, quo ante omnia fidem in se vnū requirit, clamans: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui te redemi, Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Fidei huius medium Filius traditur, qui nos illi reconciliauit, & qui solus inter eum & nos Mediator dici debet. Cum fide cultus coniunctus est, qui vt in spiritu & veritate consistit, ita ab illo sit mulachra atque imagines longissimè remoueri oportet, quibus Dei maiestas quàm maximè violatur, & quas hic passim damnat. Ad cultum confessio fidei pertinet, quam liberam, ingenuam & omnis doli expertem, deniq; ab omni simulatione aut dissimulatione alienam esse oportet. Sub illa precesque publicæ & nominis diuini inuocatio publica, adhæc iusiurandum pertinet, quod in eius solius nomine concipi debet & præstari: sicuti Danielis & multorum sanctissimorum Martyrum exempla docent: Imò fidei confessio ad totam vitam debet extendi, vt hæc tota Dei verbum & Christi Spiritum loquatur, & vt in viuentem hostiam nosipsos Deo consecremus, neq; eorum vlla faciamus, quæ eius sanctissimæ voluntati repugnant. Hæc & quæcunque alia sunt huius generis, ita à nobis Deo reddi debent, vt nihil eorum omittamus in hominis cuiuscunque gratiam, neque nos ab his officijs vel metu alicuius periculi, vel vllius commodi spe abduci patiamur. Vt primum enim Deus in partes venit, hic toti mundo & omnibus quæ in mundo magnifica & præclara habentur, præferri debet, eò quòd in illo sumus, viuimus & mouemur, & sine illo neque huius seculi vita, neque salus æterna nobis constare potest. Poterant hic enumerari exempla Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Martyrum denique omnium, quos in hoc constantissimos fuisse scimus: sed quia illa Scripturas & historias legentibus nunquam non occurrunt, ea breuitatis studio omittimus. Discat autem illa cum hoc Christi dicto diligentius conferre Reges & principes, ne facile ijs irascantur, qui in externis quidem omnibus fidem atque obedientiam ipsis præstant, in ijs autem quæ ad religionem & cultum pertinent, Deo fideles esse cupiunt, neque volunt ab eius verbo recedere. Putant aliqui Regum iustudin ipsorum contumeliam fieri, & rem mali exempli esse, si cui libertatem istam concedant: At quanto maiori contumelia seipsos afficiunt, si aduersus Deum insurgant? quanto item graviori periculo se se inuoluunt, si cum illo bellum suscipiant, aut saltem eum è regnorum suorum finibus eiectū velint? Aut num sibi fidos vnquam fore arbitrabuntur, qui Deo fideles non sunt? Quanto prudentius olim Constantius, Constantini Magni pater, suorum domesticorum atque militum animos atque fidem erga se eo argumento explorauit, vt quales in Deum essent videret? Nam propositā optione, vt aut dæmonibus siue Dijs sacrificarent, aut honoribus atque stipendijs exuti ab ipsius conspectu discederent, posteā omnes eos ex sui regni finibus eiecit, qui fidem suam alieno & idololatrico cultu abnegauerant. Nunquam enim Regi fideles fore dicebat eos, qui in summum illud æternumque numen ingrati fuissent. Sed quia hæc alterius loci sunt, nunc obiter attigisse sufficiat. Obseruemus autem ad mirabilem & verè diuinam Christi Iesu sapientiam, qui tam breui dicto tanta cum perspicuitate complexus est quæcunque de tota hominis vita, deque omnibus dici possunt, quæ vel hominibus vel Deo à nobis debentur.
units.tr: But let us return to the present subject and consider what is owed to God. We owe him ourselves entirely, body and soul, since we have nothing from him as our Creator except what we receive from his generosity. Yet he wills that many things be given to men, such as the duties we have just described regarding the magistrate, and likewise those owed to parents, masters, spouses, children, and finally to whomever else we are bound. But the things he claims for himself alone are the most important, namely those that pertain to his worship. Among these, the first place belongs to doctrine, without which he is not honoured. We must therefore take care that no doctrine is admitted except what is drawn from the Word of God. For we know that he once said: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the traditions of men." Let us, then, hear him speaking to us in his own Word, where before all else he demands faith in himself alone, crying: "I am the Lord your God, who redeemed you. You shall have no other gods before me." The Son is given as the mediator of this faith, who reconciled us to him, and who alone ought to be called the Mediator between him and us. Worship is joined to faith; and as it consists in spirit and truth, so images and idols must be entirely removed from it, since they grievously violate the majesty of God, and he condemns them on every side. To worship belongs the confession of faith, which ought to be free, open, and free of all deceit, and in short, far from all pretence or concealment. Under this heading belong public prayers and the public invocation of the divine name, and also the oath, which must be framed and sworn in his name alone, as the examples of Daniel and of many most holy martyrs teach. Indeed, the confession of faith ought to extend to the whole of life, so that the whole of it speaks the Word of God and the Spirit of Christ, and so that we consecrate ourselves to God as a living sacrifice, and do nothing that is contrary to his most holy will. These things, and whatever else is of this kind, must be rendered by us to God in such a way that we omit nothing of them for the favour of any man, nor allow ourselves to be drawn away from these duties either by fear of any danger or by hope of any advantage. For once God has come into view, he ought to be preferred to the whole world and to all that is held magnificent and splendid in the world, since in him we live, move and have our being, and without him neither the life of this age nor eternal salvation can stand for us. Examples could be listed here from the Prophets, the Apostles, and finally all the martyrs, whom we know to have been most steadfast in this; but since these are never absent from those who read the Scriptures and histories, we omit them for the sake of brevity. Let kings and princes, however, study this more carefully in comparison with this saying of Christ, so that they are not easily angered at those who, in all external matters, render them faith and obedience, but who, in what pertains to religion and worship, desire to be faithful to God and do not wish to depart from his Word. Some think it is an insult to the dignity of kings, and a matter of bad example, if they grant such liberty to anyone. But with how much greater insult do they dishonour themselves if they rise up against God? With how much graver peril do they entangle themselves if they take up war against him, or at least wish to drive him from the borders of their kingdoms? Or will they think that those will ever be faithful to them who are not faithful to God? How much more wisely did Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, once test the minds and loyalty of his household and soldiers towards himself by this means, so that he might see what they were like towards God! For, when the choice was offered them, either to sacrifice to demons or gods, or to depart from his sight stripped of honours and pay, he afterwards expelled from the borders of his kingdom all those who had renounced their faith by an alien and idolatrous worship. For he said that those who had been ungrateful to that supreme and eternal divinity would never be faithful to the king. But since these matters belong to another place, it is enough to have touched on them in passing here. Let us observe, moreover, the wonderful and truly divine wisdom of Christ Jesus, who in so brief a saying embraced with such clarity all that can be said about the whole of human life, and about all the things that we owe either to men or to God.

units.la: Agnouerunt hanc quàmuis inuiti, Herodiani illi & Pharisæi, qui ipsum tentare ausi fuerant. Nam addit Lucas: Itaque non potuerunt verba eius carpere coram populo; & mirati super eius responso, siluerunt. Magnum hoc est virtutis diuinæ argumentum, quod ne in verbis quidem aliquid inueniunt quod reprehendere possint, cùm nihil tam facile sit, & tam vulgare, quàm aliorum dicta calumniari. Itaque verè impletur hic illud Isaiæ: Et non est inuentus dolus in ore eius. Quæ causa est, quòd inexpectati responsi admiratione superati obmutescunt, qui ab eruditissimis & vaferrimis hominibus instructi in hanc disputationis arenam descenderant. Et solet hic esse omnium consiliorum exitus, quæ aduersus Deum ineuntur: vt seipsos suis sordibus polluant, quæ in cælum expuere audent. Quanta autem fuit istorum hominum improbitas, qui nihilominus illum paulò post apud Pilatum accusare non sunt veriti, quòd tributum Cæsari dandū esse negaret? Nihil ergo à calum niis impiorum tutum est: & scimus quam multa olim Christianis hominibus obiecta fuerint, quàm atrocibus criminibus grauentur hodie multi, qui pro Regibus suis animam & sanguinem pro fundere parati sunt. Sed aduersus illa nos fidei constantia armari oportet, nec dubitemus fore tem- pus, quando & nostram innocentiam Christus Iesus afferet, & calumniatores istos aeterna ignomi- nia multabit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Herodians and Pharisees, who had dared to test him, acknowledged this, though unwillingly. For Luke adds: "And so they could not catch his words before the people; and marvelling at his answer, they fell silent." This is a great proof of divine power, that they found nothing even in his words that they could find fault with, since nothing is so easy and so common as to slander the words of others. Thus that saying of Isaiah is truly fulfilled here: "And no deceit was found in his mouth." This is why those who had come down into this arena of disputation, trained by the most learned and crafty men, fall dumb, overcome by amazement at an unexpected answer. And this is usually the outcome of all the plans that are devised against God: they defile themselves with the filth they dare to spit into heaven. But how wicked were those men who, not long after, did not hesitate to accuse him before Pilate of forbidding the paying of tribute to Caesar! Nothing is therefore safe from the slanders of the wicked; and we know how many charges were once brought against Christians, and how many are now burdened with atrocious crimes, though they are ready to shed their soul and blood for their kings. But against these things we must arm ourselves with constancy of faith, and let us not doubt that a time will come when Christ Jesus will vindicate our innocence and will punish those slanderers with eternal disgrace. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXI.

units.la: Accedentes autem quidam Sadducaeorum, qui negant esse resurre- ctionem, interrogarunt eum dicentes: Magister, Moses scripsit nobis: Si cuius frater mortuus fuerit habens uxorem, & sine liberis mortuus fue- rit, ut eius frater accipiat uxorem illam, & excitet semen fratri suo. Sep- tem ergo fratres fuerunt, quorum primus accepta uxore mortuus est sine liberis. Accepit igitur eam secundus, qui & ipse mortuus est sine li- beris. Deinde tertius accepit eam: itidem autem & illi septem, nec reli- querunt liberos & mortui sunt. Post omnes autem mortua est & mulier. In resurrectione ergo cuius eorum erit uxor? Nam illi septem habuerunt eam uxorem. Et respondens dixit eis Iesus: Filii huius seculi ducunt uxores, & nuptum dantur: qui autem digni habiti fuerint, qui illud euum consequantur, & resurrectionem ex mortuis, neque ducunt uxores, neque nuptum dantur: Nec enim mori possunt amplius: pares enim Angelis sunt, & filii sunt Dei, cum sint filii resurrectionis. Mortuos autem excita- ri etiam Moses indicauit apud rubum, cum dicit Dominum Deum Abrahami, & Deum Isaaci, & Deum Iacobi. Nam Deus non est mortuo- rum, sed viuorum: Omnes enim ei viuunt. Respondentes autem ei quidam ex Scribis dixerunt: Magister, bene dixisti. Nec amplius audebant eum quicquam interrogare.
units.tr: Then some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, came to him and asked him, saying: "Master, Moses wrote to us: If a man's brother die, having a wife, and he die without children, that his brother should take his wife and raise up seed to his brother. Now there were seven brothers: and the first took a wife, and died without children. And the second took her, and he died childless. And the third took her; and in like manner the seven also left no children, and died. Last of all the woman died also. Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be? For the seven had her to wife." And Jesus answered and said to them: "The children of this world marry and are given in marriage. But they who are counted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage. For neither can they die any more: for they are equal to the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection. Now that the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not the God of the dead, but of the living: for all live to him." Then some of the scribes answered and said: "Master, you have spoken well." And they dared not ask him any more questions.

units.la: Quoniam homo natura ad peccandum proclivis est, & peccatis oblectatur, eade argui & corripi indignissime fert, & ideo aduersus veritatis doctrinam pertinacissime luctatur. Experti sunt hanc sui seculi hominum contumaciam Prophetae: nec meliores fuerunt ij, quibus cum Apostoli egerunt, cum in toto orbe Euangelium praedicarent. Hodie autem in manifestissima luce Verbi Dei maior hominum pars hoc unum agit, ut hoc aut violenter opprimat & extinguat, aut quacunque ratione ei fidem deroget, vulgo contemptum vel invisum reddat. Offendit hoc multos, qui doctrinam ex hominum authoritate aestimant: quo minus autem pij quoque offendantur, aeternus Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, eandem cum alijs Dei seruis forte subire voluit. Nam a baptismo statim in desertum, quasi in palaestram quandam digressus, tentationibus Satanicis se obiecit, quas grauissimas sustinuit. Inde vero toto eo tempore, quo docuit & doctrinam suam operibus miraculosis confirmauit, nunquam non hostium insidijs petitus est, qui aut ui aperta eum perdere, aut captiosis disputationibus irretire studuerunt: & quo propius ad mortis metam accesserit, eo pertinacius certamina illa ad uersarij eius instaurauerunt. Sunt in horum narratione Euangelistae admodum diligentes: quia non solum constantia & prudentia fidei exemplum in Christo exhibent, uerumetiam in illis multae quaestiones soluuntur de rebus non minus necessarijs quam utilibus cognitu. Quod ut in ijs congressibus uidimus, qui hucusque expositi sunt, ita in isto in primis patebit, qui modo est recitatus. Hic enim de praecipuo fidei nostrae articulo disputatur, nimirum de mortuorum resurrectione, sine qua Siculis gerrus uaniora erunt quaecunque, de religione, de uitae innocentia, de bonorum praemijs & malorum poenis dicuntur. Et illius certitudo aduersus eos asseritur qui ut authoritate praestabant in populo Dei, ita doctrinae etiam & iustitiae existimationem prae alijs sustinebant. Ne pigeat ergo nos historiam huius loci per singulas partes considerare.
units.tr: Because man is by nature prone to sin, and delights in sins, he bears it most unworthily to be reproved and corrected, and therefore he struggles most stubbornly against the teaching of truth. The Prophets experienced this obstinacy of the people of their age; nor were those any better with whom the Apostles dealt, when they preached the Gospel throughout the whole world. Today, in the very clear light of the Word of God, the greater part of mankind does this one thing: either it violently crushes and extinguishes this teaching, or by whatever means it disparages the faith and makes it commonly despised or hated. This offends many who judge doctrine by human authority; yet, so that the godly too might not be offended, the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, perhaps wished to undergo the same things as the other servants of God. For immediately after his baptism he withdrew into the desert, as into a kind of wrestling-ground, and exposed himself to Satan's temptations, which he endured most severely. Then, throughout the whole time in which he taught and confirmed his doctrine by miraculous works, he was never free from the snares of his enemies, who sought either to destroy him by open violence or to entangle him in captious disputations; and the nearer he drew to the goal of death, the more stubbornly his adversaries renewed those contests. The Evangelists are very diligent in their account of these things, because they set before us in Christ an example of constancy and prudence in the faith, and also because in these narratives many questions are resolved about matters no less necessary than useful to know. As we have seen in those encounters that have been expounded so far, so this will become especially clear in the one just read. For here is disputed the chief article of our faith, namely the resurrection of the dead, without which whatever is said about religion, the innocence of life, and the rewards of good and the punishments of evil will be as empty as chaff. And its certainty is maintained against those who, as they excelled in authority among the people of God, so also held the reputation for learning and righteousness above others. Let it not irk us, then, to consider the history of this passage part by part.

units.la: Et primum quidem aduersarios Christi uideamus, qui ab ijs, quos nuper uidimus plane diuersi fuerunt. Nuper enim Pharisaeorum discipuli assumptis in suas partes Herodianis quibusdam, de- censu Caesari soluendo quaestione mouerunt: hic vero his turpiter cedentibus in arenam descendunt quidam Sadducæorum, qui à Pharisæis ita dissidebant: ut non solùm simultates occultæ, verumetiam apertæ inimicitiæ & cœcertationes inter duos istos ordines sui sectas intercederent. Sadducæi enim alteris illis deteriores resurrectionem mortuorum negabant, & cum hac animarum quoq; immortalitatem, & quæcunque de spiritibus & Angelis tam bonis quàm malis dicuntur, reijciebant. Ex Scripturis quoque sacris solos Mosis libros agnoscebant, Prophetarum autem scripta asperna bantur. Interim iustitiæ studium præ aliis multis simulabant, quam colendam esse dicebant non alicuius futuri præmij spe, aut pœnæ metu, sed propter ea ipsam: quia per se & honesta, & utilis, & ad vitam bene feliciterque transigendam necessaria sit. Itaq; illos fere sequebantur opulentissimi quique, & quotquot mundo potius quàm Deo placere studebant. Similes istorum sunt hodie multi, qui vitæ quidem honestatem & iustitiam non omnino negligenter colunt, religionis autem sensu nullo ducuntur, ideoq; nos ridٍent, qui animarum immortalitate & corporum resurrectione gaudemus, & in futuræ æternæ, vitæ præmijs spem atque fiduciam collocamus. Fuit autem hæc teterrima facies rerum, quòd in ea gens, quæ Dei peculium esse debebat, & cui Legem cultumque suum crediderat Deus, tales reperti sunt, imò rerum gubernaculis adhibiti, qui ipsissima fidei atque pietatis fundamenta convellebant. At digni erant tam exitialibus monstris, qui Verbum Dei iampridem reiecerant, & sese in sectas scindi passi erant, cùm unus Dei populus & una Ecclesia esse deberent. Et novissimis temporibus inter Christi ani nominis professores idem factum esse cōstat, postquam simplex Veritatis doctrina multis sordere cœpit, ut alibi prolixius est demonstratum.
units.tr: And first let us look at the adversaries of Christ, who were quite different from those we have just seen. For a little earlier the disciples of the Pharisees, having enlisted some Herodians on their side, raised the question of paying tribute to Caesar; but now, since those men have been shamefully defeated, certain Sadducees step into the arena, who differed so much from the Pharisees that between these two orders there existed not only hidden grudges but open enmities and contentions, and sects of their own. For the Sadducees, worse than those others, denied the resurrection of the dead, and along with this they also rejected the immortality of the soul and whatever is said about spirits and angels, both good and bad. Of the sacred Scriptures they acknowledged only the books of Moses, while the writings of the Prophets they held in contempt. Meanwhile they pretended a zeal for righteousness above many others, which they said ought to be cultivated not from hope of any future reward or fear of punishment, but for its own sake, because it is in itself honourable, useful, and necessary for living well and happily. Therefore the most wealthy men, and all who were eager to please the world rather than God, mostly followed them. Many today are like them: they do not wholly neglect the honesty and righteousness of life, but are guided by no sense of religion; and so they laugh at us, who rejoice in the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, and place our hope and trust in the rewards of the life to come, which is eternal. This was a most hideous state of affairs, that in the nation which ought to have been God's own possession, and to which God had entrusted his Law and his worship, such men were found, and even admitted to the government of affairs, who overthrew the very foundations of faith and piety. But those were worthy of such pestilent monsters who had long ago rejected the Word of God and allowed themselves to be split into sects, when they ought to have been one people of God and one Church. And in the latest times it is established that the same thing has happened among those who bear the name of Christian, since the plain doctrine of the truth began to be despised by many, as has been demonstrated more fully elsewhere.

units.la: In præsenti autem portento simile uideri poterat, Sadducæos Pharisæis quasi succenturiatos factos esse, & hos ferre posse, ut ipsorum doctrina tam scurrilibus atq; impijs commentis in Christo oppugnetur. Licuit ergo tunc inter Iudæos præcipua fidei & religionis capita, imò cœlum & inferos ipsumq; Deum negare (quid enim de Deo reliquum fiet, si neque spiritus sunt aliqui, neque uirtutis præmia sperari, aut scelerum pœnæ timeri debet?) at Christo Iesu germanum Legis diuinæ sensum exponere; uerum externi cultus usum monstrare, & certam salutis rationem tradere non licuit. Ad miratione dignissima esset tam fœda istius populi corruptio & detestabilis licentia, nisi hodie idem multis in locis fieret. Gloriantur quidem pietatis zelo & gloriæ Dei studio Pontifices, sanctitatem singularem. Monachi profitentur, ex mortuis & horum carcere purgatorio seu lustrali igne quæstum maximum faciunt. Sacrificuli: at omnes isti facile ferre possunt homines blasphemos, qui per Deum & sacra omnia deierant, qui religionem omnem rident, qui postremum Christi aduentum, mortuorum resurrectionem, uitam æternam scurrili dicacitate in dubium uocant, aut apertè negant: at ijdem Euangelij præcones & auditores ferre nequeunt, qui in uno Christo sperare se dicut, & hunc unum salutis humanæ Mediatorem agnoscunt. Quid? nónne Iudæos ferri & apud principes aliquot in pretio haberi uidemus, Christianæ autem doctrinæ professores eijci, adhæc ferro & igne excindi? Negent ista qui possunt: & utinam uere negari possent, & ego mendax potius essem, & non infelix hoc seculum tanti sceleris reatu teneretur. Non est ergo, quòd deploratam Iudaici populi impietatem admiremur, in quorum oculis similia exempla quotidie uersantur: quin potius excitemur ad ardens atque assiduum defendendæ Veritatis studium, neque nobis ipsis inducias polliceamur, quando ex diuersis castris in singulas horas erumpunt, qui Christum in nobis extinctum uolunt.
units.tr: In the present portent it could seem that the Sadducees had become, as it were, reinforcements for the Pharisees, and that these could bear that their own doctrine should be assailed in Christ by such buffoonish and impious inventions. Thus at that time it was permitted among the Jews to deny the chief articles of faith and religion, indeed heaven and hell and God himself (for what would remain of God if there were no spirits, and no reward of virtue could be hoped for, nor punishment of wickedness feared?). But to expound to Christ Jesus the true sense of the divine Law, to show the proper use of external worship, and to teach a sure way of salvation, was not permitted. This foul corruption and detestable licence of that people would be most worthy of wonder, were it not that the same thing happens today in many places. The Pontiffs indeed boast of their singular holiness, with a zeal for piety and a concern for the glory of God. The monks profess it, and make the greatest gain from the dead and from their prison of purgatory, with its purifying fire. The little priests likewise: yet all these men can easily bear blasphemous men, who swear by God and all sacred things, who mock all religion, who with buffoonish wit call into doubt or openly deny the last coming of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal life; but those same men cannot bear the heralds and hearers of the Gospel, who say that they hope in Christ alone and acknowledge him as the one Mediator of human salvation. What? Do we not see the Jews tolerated, and held in high esteem by some princes, while the professors of Christian doctrine are cast out, and moreover cut down with sword and fire? Let those who can deny these things; and would that they truly could be denied, and that I were rather a liar, and this age were not held guilty of so great a crime. It is not, then, for us to marvel at the deplorable impiety of the Jewish people, before whose eyes similar examples occur every day. Rather we should be stirred to an ardent and unceasing zeal in defending the truth, and should not promise ourselves a truce, since those who want Christ extinguished in us break out from their various camps every hour.

units.la: Sed ad quæstionem accedamus, quam Sadducæi isti mouerunt. Moses (inquiunt) scripsit nobis: Si cuius frater mortuus fuerit habens uxorem, & sine liberis mortuus fuerit, ut eius frater accipiat uxorem illam, & excitet semen fratri suo: Septem ergo fratres fuerunt, quorum unus acepta uxore mortuus est sine liberis, &c. A Mose exordiuntur, ut causam suam impietatis crimine liberent. De resurrectione autem quæstionem mouent, quia Christum hanc asseruisse hactenus sciebant, nunc autem sperant eum odio Pharisaicæ sectæ in suas partes transituru, aut sic dicturum, non habiturum quod respondeat, & ita certam sibi de illo uictoriam pollicentur. Proponunt autem casum ex Lege, quæ Deut.25. habetur, ut quis fratris absque liberis defuncti uxorem ducat, & ex ea fratri semen suscitet, id est, liberos ex ea gignat, qui non suo, sed fratris nomine censeantur, & eam quæ defuncto illi debebatur, hæreditatem obtineat. Fuerunt istius Legis causæ uariæ in repub. Israelitica. Vnam & præcipuā Moses ipse indicat, ut defuncti illius nome non deleatur ex Israele. Faciebat ergo hoc ad conseruandum familias, ne quæ abolerentur. Est enim utilissimum in Republica familias ueteres extare, ex quibus ad rerum gubernacula adhibeantur, quorum maiores aliquot seculis feliciter & cum laude regnarunt. Vt enim hi gentilitiam authoritatem ad rempublicam afferunt, & maiorum uirtute commendantur: ita constat, homines nouos plerunque malum dedisse, quando aut imperium insolentius gesserunt, ut Marius fecit: aut nobilium odijs non sine reipublicæ detrimento exagitati sunt, quod Ciceroni accidisse constat. Non temere ergo Deus, qui Israeliticam rempublicam longo tempore ad Messiæ usque aduentum durare voluit, leges dedit quæ ad familiarum ueterum conseruationem facerent. Deinde quia familiæ sæpius egestate & inopia pereunt, simul prohibebat Lex ista, ne hereditates confunderentur. Videtur enim moris fuisse, ut uidua mariti absque liberis defuncti bonis succederet, & tale quid coniugij ius postulat, ne quæ una cum marito caro fuit, hoc mortuo pro aliena censeatur, eque domo deturbetur, in qua paulo ante matrisfamiliâs nomen sustinuit. Ne ergo uiro alteri nubens hereditatis partem in familiam alienam transferret, necesse fuit, ut defuncti mariti frater siue propinquus eam in uxorem duceret; & ea ratione tam uiduæ quam familiæ consulebatur. Præterea fratrum dissidijs Lex ea occurrebat, ne quis hereditatis obtinendæ sine fratrem extinctum cuperet. Et quia in ueteri illa Ecclesia atq; politia fere omnia typis sublimium mysteriorum Regni Dei referta fuerunt, aliqui ex ueteribus in isto more figuram resurrectionis observarunt, de qua Iudæos Dominus admonere voluerit, quando defunctis semen excitare & eorundem nomina in Israele conseruare iussit. Nec leue argumentum fuerit, si dicamus, fieri non posse, ut in Dei conspectu toti pereant, & nunquam resurrecturi moriantur, quorum nomina ne inter homines quidem delentur. Sunt qui alia etiam mysteria hic eruerunt, sed quia id argute magis quàm solide fecerunt, istas causas annotauisse sufficiat. Certè non leuiculam fuisse huius instituti rationem, uel ex eo patet, quòd publica ignominia notatus fuit, qui fratri defuncto semè excitare detrectabat. Nam ad iudices citabatur, & illic mulier calceum ei detrahens simul in faciem eius expuebat: quo ritu docebatur dignum esse, qui possessione caderet & infamis esset perpetuò.
