units.tr: But let us come to the question that these Sadducees raised. Moses (they say) wrote for us: If anyone's brother dies, having a wife, and he dies without children, let his brother take that wife and raise up seed for his brother: there were therefore seven brothers, of whom one, having taken a wife, died without children, etc. They begin from Moses so that they may free their cause from the charge of impiety. They raise the question of the resurrection because they knew that Christ had hitherto asserted it, and now they hope that, out of hatred for the Pharisaic sect, he will go over to their side, or will say something he cannot answer, and so they promise themselves certain victory over him. They propose a case from the Law, found in Deut. 25, that a man should take the wife of a brother who died without children and raise up seed for his brother from her, that is, beget children by her who would be counted not in his own name but in the brother's, and so obtain the inheritance that was owed to the dead man. The reasons for this Law in the Israelite commonwealth were various. Moses himself indicates one chief reason: that the name of that dead man should not be blotted out from Israel. It therefore served to preserve families, lest they be abolished. For it is most useful in a commonwealth that ancient families should survive, from whom men are chosen for the helm of affairs, whose ancestors have reigned for some centuries happily and with praise. For just as these bring the authority of their lineage to the state and are commended by the virtue of their forebears, so it is established that new men have generally done harm, either when they have governed more arrogantly, as Marius did, or when they have been harassed by the hatred of the nobles, not without damage to the commonwealth, which is known to have happened to Cicero. Not rashly, then, did God, who wished the Israelite commonwealth to endure for a long time, until the coming of the Messiah, give laws that would serve to preserve the ancient families. Next, since families often perish through poverty and want, this Law also forbade inheritances to be confused. For it seems to have been the custom that a widow whose husband died without children should succeed to his goods, and the right of marriage demands something of the kind, lest she who was one flesh with her husband should, on his death, be counted as belonging to another family and be thrust out of the house in which shortly before she had borne the name of mother of the household. So, lest by marrying another man she should transfer her share of the inheritance into an alien family, it was necessary that the brother or kinsman of the dead husband should take her as wife; and by this means provision was made both for the widow and for the family. Moreover, this Law met the quarrels of brothers, lest anyone should desire a brother's death in order to obtain the inheritance. And because in that ancient Church and polity almost everything was filled with types of the sublime mysteries of the Kingdom of God, some of the ancients observed in this custom a figure of the resurrection, about which the Lord wished to remind the Jews when he ordered that seed be raised up for the dead and their names be kept alive in Israel. Nor would it be a slight argument to say that those whose names are not even blotted out among men cannot perish utterly in God's sight and die never to rise again. There are those who have drawn out other mysteries here as well, but since they did so more cleverly than soundly, it is enough to have noted these reasons. That the reasoning behind this institution was no trifle is clear even from this: that a man who refused to raise up seed for his dead brother was marked with public disgrace. For he was summoned before the judges, and there the woman, pulling off his sandal, also spat in his face; by this rite it was taught that he deserved to lose his possession and to be infamous for ever.

units.la: Cæterum Sadducæi, qui nihil horum intelligebant, Lege ista ad struendam fallaciam abutuntur, & per eam putant mortuorum resurrectionem destrui, quæ (ut modò diximus) eius typum non obscurè continebat. Causa tanti erroris fuit, quòd (ut ex Christi responsione patebit) non distinguunt inter præsens hoc & futurum seculum, & eandem in futura uita rerum omnium faciem siue conditionem fore arbitrantur, quæ nunc est. Ex eo igitur colligunt, ut in resurrectione unicuique restituatur quod in terris hisce agens habuit. Itaque hoc errore præoccupati uidere non possunt, quid de illis futurum sit, qui uel uxores uel maritos plures habuerunt: & quia absurditas multa hic sese offert, non aliud compendium breuius & expeditius, quo hæc omnis semel tollatur, uident, quàm ut resurrectio in nniuersum negetur. Et hæc causa est, quòd casum istum de septem fratribus tam prolixè exponunt: & quod isti fecerunt, ex Legis authoritate factum esse ostendunt, ut euincant, resurrectionem fieri non posse, quin aut turpis confusio fiat, multis unam & eandem uxorem inte se communè habentibus, aut de iniuria sibi fleta conqueri possint reliqui, si ea uel primo marito, uel cuicunque alteri adiudicetur. Et hoc illud est, quod hodie multos decipit in tota Regni Dei consideratione, quòd nimirum huius mysteria carnis sensu metiuntur, & eo modo illud administrari putant, qui in regnis huius mundi obseruatur. Hinc Diuorum intercessio ortum habuit, hinc purgatorij ignis lustrationes prodierunt, hinc imaginum cultus manauit, & infinita alia, quæ Christiana religionem turpissimè deformauerunt. In primis autem obseruabis hoc loco, quàm uerissimè dictum sit: Dato uno inconuenienti sequitur aliud: imò multa ex uno sequuntur, & errorum absurdissimorum concatenatio mirifica texitur, quæ omnem religionis sensum in hominum cordibus abolet. Dum enim Sadducæi in futura uita nihil sublimius terrenis hisce studijs agnoscunt, eò deueniunt, ut illi mores turpiores tribuant, quàm quibus nunc utuntur. Et quia id absurdum & dictu inhonestum esse uident, resurrectionem prorsus negant. At quia hac negata, animarum quoque conditio in dubium uocatur, quas aut omnis pe restitutionis destitutas temere uagari, aut æterno somno sopiri oporteat: rursus hunc quoque nodum uno ictu abrumpi posse putant, si illas unà cum corpore mori dicant. Et quia obijci poterat: Quis ergo spirituum siue Angelorum usus est, si homines vitam in rerum pecudum instar agunt, & tam animam quàm corpore intereunt? rursus, ut quàm ocyssime sese expediant, spiritus simul omnes negant, & ita prophanis gentibus deteriores fiunt, in quibus aliqua fuit vitae futurae cognitio. Nam qui in illis sapientia claruerunt, ij Genios hominibus adesse confessi sunt, & defunctorum spiritus atq; animas ad campos Elysios aut alios locos laetiores colligi crediderunt, in quibus felicitate incredibili fruantur. Cicero certè dicere ausus fuit: Omnium animi immortales sunt, sed bonorum fortiumque divini. Item in oratione pro C. Rabirio : Bonorum virorum mentes mihi divinae atque aeternae videntur, & ex hominum vita ad Deorum religionem sanctimoniamque demigrare. Et rursus in Somnio Scipionis: Sic habeto, te non esse mortalem, sed corpus hoc. Idem denique in libro de Senectute has voces Catoni tribuit: Ego vestros patres P. Scipio, tuque C. Laeli, viros clarissimos mihique amicissimos vivere arbitror, & eam quidem vitam, quae est sola vita nominanda. Item: O praeclarum diem, cum ad illud animorum concilium coetumque profecisar, & cum ex hac turba & colluvione discedam. Proficiscar enim non ad eos solum viros, de quibus ante dixi, sed etiam ad Catonem meum, quo nemo vir melior natus est, nemo pietate praestantior: cuius a me corpus crematum est: quod contra decuit, ab illo meum. Animus vero non me deferens, sed respectans, in ea profecto loca discessit, quo mihi ipse cernebat esse veniendum. Haec & infinita alia huius generis apud scriptores prophanos inveniuntur, quorum ideo mentionem facimus, ut non solum Sadducaeorum, verumetiam nostri seculi hominum impia stoliditas arguatur, qui absurdissimis praeiudiciis occupati, in peius subinde degenerant, neque ea possunt videre, quae olim gentes non omnino ignoraverunt. Et debent horum exempla nos excitare, ne quid in divinis mysteriis animo concipiamus, quod in sacris literis nusquam traditur: sed in axiomata fidei Christianae totis animis intenti, expendamus diligenter quae de his Spiritus sanctus olim tradidit: & mox certa, vera & perspicua esse cernemus, quae prius absurda & impossibilia videbantur.
units.tr: But the Sadducees, who understood none of these things, abuse this Law to build a fallacy, and through it they think the resurrection of the dead is destroyed, although (as we have just said) it clearly contained its type. The cause of so great an error is that (as will be clear from Christ's reply) they do not distinguish between this present age and the age to come, and they think that in the future life the whole face or condition of things will be the same as it is now. From this they conclude that in the resurrection each person is restored to what he possessed while living on this earth. Therefore, preoccupied by this error, they cannot see what will become of those who have had several wives or several husbands; and since much absurdity presents itself here, they see no shorter or quicker way of removing all of it at once than to deny the resurrection altogether. This is why they set out the case of the seven brothers at such length, and why they show that what they did was done by the authority of the Law: to prove that the resurrection cannot happen without either a shameful confusion, with many men having one and the same wife in common, or the rest being able to complain of an injury done to them if she is adjudged either to the first husband or to any other. And this is what today deceives many in the whole consideration of the Kingdom of God: they measure these mysteries by the sense of the flesh, and think that it is administered in the way that is observed in the kingdoms of this world. Hence the intercession of the saints arose; hence came the lustrations of purgatorial fire; hence the cult of images flowed, and countless other things which have most foully deformed the Christian religion. Above all, here you will observe how very truly it was said: one absurdity granted, another follows; indeed many follow from one, and a marvellous chain of most absurd errors is woven, which abolishes every sense of religion from men's hearts. For while the Sadducees acknowledge nothing in the future life more sublime than these earthly pursuits, they come to attribute to it customs more shameful than those they now use. And because they see that this is absurd and dishonourable to speak of, they deny the resurrection altogether. But since, with this denied, the condition of souls too is called into doubt (for they must either be left wholly without restoration to wander at random, or be lulled to eternal sleep), they think this knot too can be cut at one blow, if they say that souls perish together with the body. And since it could be objected, "What then is the use of spirits or angels, if men live like beasts and perish both soul and body?", again, to extricate themselves as quickly as possible, they deny all spirits together, and so become worse than the profane nations, among whom there was some knowledge of the future life. For those who excelled in wisdom among them confessed that genii attend men, and believed that the spirits and souls of the dead are gathered to the Elysian fields or other more joyful places, where they enjoy incredible happiness. Cicero certainly dared to say: "The souls of all are immortal, but those of the good and brave are divine." Likewise in the speech for Rabirius: "The minds of good men seem to me divine and eternal, and to pass from human life to the religion and holiness of the gods." And again in the Dream of Scipio: "Know that you are not mortal, but this body is." Finally, in the book On Old Age, he assigns these words to Cato: "I think that your fathers, P. Scipio, and you, C. Laelius, most illustrious men and most dear to me, are alive, and that life which alone is rightly to be called life." Likewise: "O splendid day, when I shall set out for that assembly and gathering of souls, and depart from this crowd and filth. For I shall go not only to those men of whom I spoke before, but also to my Cato, than whom no better man was born, none more outstanding in piety; whose body I burned, when it should rather have been the other way round. But his spirit, not leaving me but looking back on me, has certainly departed to those places to which he saw I too must come." These and countless other things of this kind are found in the profane writers. We mention them so that the impious stupidity not only of the Sadducees but also of men of our own age may be exposed, who, occupied with the most absurd prejudices, degenerate ever further for the worse, and cannot see what the nations of old did not wholly ignore. And the examples of these should rouse us, lest we conceive anything in our minds about divine mysteries that is nowhere handed down in the sacred letters; but, intent with all our hearts on the axioms of the Christian faith, let us weigh carefully what the Holy Spirit once handed down about these matters, and soon we shall see that what seemed absurd and impossible before is certain, true and clear.

units.la: Admonet de hoc nos Christus Dominus, qui Sadducaeis respondens (ut Marcus annotavit) initio statim erroris ipsorum fontem recludens ait: Nonne propterea erratis, quòd nescitis scripturas, neque potentiam Dei? Quia enim homo animalis non percipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nisi in Scripturas respiciamus, in quibus suam voluntatem & Regni sui mysteria ille nobis revelat, non poterimus non novis subinde errorum Labyrinthis intricari. Etenim dum in nostras rationes intenti sumus, Dei voluntatem simul & omnipotentiam non animadvertimus, quae duo nos omni dubitatione & errore liberare poterant. Debent ergo duo ista semper coniungi, ut primò quidem Dei voluntatem inquiramus, deinde illum omnipotentem esse cogitemus, qui quod vult simul effectum dare possit. Ita fiet, ut voluntatis divinae cognitio nos errare non sinat, eiusdem verò omnipotentia omnem ex animis dubitationem eximat. Ubi tamen cavendum fuerit, ne omnipotentiam solam respiciendo iis fidem astruere conemur, de quibus nullum extat testimonium divinae voluntatis. In eo enim hodie turpiter hallucinantur, qui illo argumento omnipraesentiam corporis Christi asserunt, de quibus suo loco abunde diximus. Nunc ad praesens argumentum accedamus, in cuius tractatione Dominus duo agit.
units.tr: Christ the Lord warns us of this, when he answers the Sadducees (as Mark records) and, at the very start, lays open the source of their error: "Do you not therefore err, because you do not know the Scriptures, nor the power of God?" Since "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2.14), unless we look to the Scriptures, in which he reveals to us his own will and the mysteries of his kingdom, we shall not be able to avoid being entangled again and again in new labyrinths of error. For while we are intent on our own reasonings, we do not take notice of God's will and omnipotence together, and these two could free us from all doubt and error. These two things must therefore always be joined: first we should inquire into God's will, and then we should consider that he is almighty, able to bring about at once whatever he wills. In this way the knowledge of the divine will will keep us from straying, and his omnipotence will remove all doubt from our minds. Yet we must take care here not to try to establish beliefs by appealing to omnipotence alone, about matters for which there is no testimony of the divine will. Those who today wrongly assert the omnipresence of Christ's body by this argument make a shameful mistake, and we have spoken fully about this in its proper place. Now let us come to the present subject, in the treatment of which the Lord does two things.

units.la: Primùm turpem & absurdum aduersariorum errorem confutat, sic dicens: Filij huius seculi ducunt uxores & nuptum dantur: qui autem digni habiti fuerint, qui illud aeuum consequantur, & resurrectionem ex mortuis, neque ducunt uxores, neq; nuptum dantur. Nec enim mori possunt amplius, pares enim Angelis sunt, & filij sunt Dei, cum sint filij resurrectionis. Filios huius seculi dicit non eo sensu, quo filijs lucis opponuntur, qui mundo addicti divina & caelestia negligunt: sed eos, qui in hoc seculo vitam degunt mortalem & variis casibus obnoxiam. Et his filios resurrectionis opponit, qui olim incorruptibilitate donabuntur, ut amplius mori non possint, sed vitam cum ipso agent immortalem & aeternam. Distinguit ergo inter praesens hoc et futurum seculum, inter vitam hanc praesentem & futuram, ut vanum & absurdum commentum esse demonstret, quod ipsi derelicto suscitatorum statu sive conditione animo conceperant. Argumentum est huiusmodi: In praesenti seculo nuptiis & generatione opus est, ut humanum genus conserveatur, ne tandem totum deficiat, cùm omnes homines mortales sint. At in futuro seculo & resurrectione mortales esse desinent (quia corruptibile hoc induet incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induet immortalitatem) Ergo nullus nuptijs ac generationi locus erit amplius, & proinde nulla etiam de uxoribus aut maritis lis esse poterit. Ad argumenti huius confirmationem facit diligentior descriptio conditionis, qua refu- scitati fruentur. Nam illos posthac mori posse negat. Mors enim ipsa (ut Isaias inquit) abolebi-tur. Vt autem vitae nomine Scriptura omnem hominis felicitatem comprehendit: ita mortis vocabulo totum illud malorum agmen intelligitur, quod per peccatum ingressum est, & infelices nos per mille rerum discrimina tandem ad mortem deducit. Ergo haec simul omnia cessabunt, ut pijs neque fames aut sitis, neque æstus aut frigus, neque morbi, neque curæ ædaces, neque exilium, neque ulla pericula metuenda sint. Et hoc exemplo illustrat, dum nos Angelorum similes fore dicit: non quidem quo ad naturæ substantiam (bi enim spirituales essentiæ sunt, nos autem anima & corpore constamus, neque in resurrectione corpora suam naturam exuent, sed gloria & immortalitate donabuntur, ut ante diximus) sed quoad animarum affectiones, in quibus nihil erit, quod uel gaudium, quo tunc fruemur, turbare possit, illicitas atque foedas carnis huius peccatricis cupiditates spiret. Procul ergo facessant impuri Mahumetis deliria, qui ut Angelos olim mulieribus commixtos Nephilim genuisse fabulatur, qui diluuij authores fuerint: ita paradisum fingit, in quo uoluptatibus carnis indulgeant & omnibus delitijs abundent, qui ipsius leges obseruauerint. Addit enim tertium Christus, nos Dei filios fore. Etsi enim iam nunc tales sumus & adoptionis spiritu excitati Deum Patrem nostrum inuocemus, nondum tamen haec nostra dignitas omnibus conspicua est: at cum æternus ille Dei Filius apparuerit (ut Ioannes inquit) tunc toti mundo patebit qui si-mus: & ei similes erimus, eumque uidebimus sicuti est. Id uero omnem beatitudinis & felicitatis uerae summam comprehendit: Si enim Filij Dei erimus, utique fratres Christi & eiusdem cohaeredes quoque erimus, sicuti Paulus rectissime colligit. Poterant haec infinitis alijs promissionibus & scripturae testimonijs confirmari: sed quia Scripturas legentibus semper obuia sunt, & saepissime de illis dicendi locus occurrit, non opus fuerit eorum commemorationi diutius insistere. Nunc usum isto rum omnium obseruemus, qui duplex est. Primo consolationi seruiant in omni aduersorum genere, ne ullis periculis aut calamitatibus succumbamus, quibus tantæ felicitatis spes certa facta est ab eo, qui fallere nescit. Deinde aduersus mundi huius illecebras nos confirment, & in officio contineant, ne illis decepti à uia præceptorum Dei exorbitemus. Discamus ergo (quod hic Christus facit) inter præsens hoc & futurum seculum distinguere: et cogitemus simul, nos ad hoc conditos esse, in terris attem hisce peregrinos agere. Itaq; mundo hoc utamur, quoad Deo visum fuerit, eodem uero non abutamur. Deniq; cum huius seculi vita breuis, fluxa & momentanea, uenturi autem æterna & nulli corruptioni obnoxia sit, procul relictis huius vitæ curis atq; uoluptatibus, ad æternam illam contendamus. Quid enim ijs accedere soleat, qui mundi delitijs immersi bona cœlestia negligunt, in diuitis epulonis & Lazari mendici historia didicimus.
units.tr: First, he refutes the shameful and absurd error of his opponents, saying: "The sons of this world marry and are given in marriage; but those who are counted worthy to obtain that age, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they cannot die any more; for they are equal to the angels, and are the sons of God, being the sons of the resurrection" (Luke 20.34–36). By "the sons of this world" he does not mean in the sense in which they are opposed to the sons of light, who are given over to the world and neglect divine and heavenly things; he means those who in this world live a mortal life, exposed to various misfortunes. To these he opposes "the sons of the resurrection", who will one day be endowed with incorruptibility, so that they can no longer die, but will live with him an immortal and eternal life. He therefore distinguishes between this present age and the age to come, and between this present life and the future one, in order to show that the notion they had conceived, abandoning the state or condition of the risen, is a vain and absurd fiction. The argument runs thus: in the present age marriage and generation are needed, so that the human race may be preserved and not finally fail, since all men are mortal. But in the age to come, and in the resurrection, they will cease to be mortal (for this corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality). Therefore there will be no more place for marriage and generation, and consequently there can be no dispute about wives or husbands either. To confirm this argument, the fuller description of the condition which the risen will enjoy serves its purpose. For he denies that they can die after this. "Death itself," as Isaiah says, "shall be abolished." Now just as Scripture comprehends all human happiness under the name of life, so under the word death is understood the whole troop of evils which entered through sin and, through a thousand dangers, at last leads us, unhappy as we are, down to death. So all these things will cease together: the godly will have no hunger or thirst, no heat or cold, no sickness, no devouring cares, no exile, and no dangers to fear. He illustrates this by the example when he says that we shall be like the angels. He does not mean this as to the substance of their nature (for they are spiritual essences, whereas we consist of soul and body, and in the resurrection our bodies will not put off their nature, but will be endowed with glory and immortality, as we said before); he means it as to the affections of the soul, in which there will be nothing able to disturb the joy we shall then enjoy, and nothing breathing the unlawful and foul desires of this sinful flesh. Let the impure delusions of Mahomet, therefore, be far away, who fabricates that angels once mingled with women and begot the Nephilim, who were the authors of the flood; and likewise he imagines a paradise in which those who have kept his laws will indulge in the pleasures of the flesh and abound in every delight. Christ adds a third point: that we shall be the sons of God. For although even now we are such, and, stirred up by the Spirit of adoption, call upon God as our Father, yet this dignity of ours is not yet visible to all; but when that eternal Son of God shall appear (as John says), then it will be plain to the whole world what we are; and we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is (1 John 3.2). This indeed comprehends the whole sum of true blessedness and happiness. For if we shall be sons of God, then we shall certainly also be brothers of Christ and fellow heirs with him, as Paul rightly infers (Rom. 8.17). These points could be confirmed by countless other promises and testimonies of Scripture; but since they are always before the eyes of those who read the Scriptures, and an occasion for speaking of them very often arises, there is no need to dwell longer on their mention. Let us now observe the use of all these things, which is twofold. First, they should serve for consolation in every kind of adversity, so that we do not give way to any dangers or calamities, since the sure hope of so great a happiness has been given us by him who knows not how to deceive. Second, they should strengthen us against the allurements of this world and keep us in our duty, so that, deceived by them, we do not stray from the way of God's commands. Let us learn therefore (as Christ does here) to distinguish between this present age and the age to come, and let us at the same time consider that we were made for this, and that in this earth we live as strangers. Accordingly let us use this world as far as it shall please God, but not abuse it. Finally, since the life of this age is short, fleeting and momentary, while that which is to come is eternal and subject to no corruption, let us put aside the cares and pleasures of this life and press on to that eternal one. For what usually befalls those who, immersed in the delights of the world, neglect heavenly goods, we have learned from the story of the rich man who feasted sumptuously and of the beggar Lazarus.

units.la: Alterum tractationis huius Caput est, resurrectionis olim futurae demonstratio, quam his uer bis Christus comprehendit. Mortuos autem excitari etiam Moses indicauit apud rubrum, cum dicit: Dominum Deum Abrahami, Deum Isaaci & Deum Iacobi. Nam Deus non est mortuorum, sed uiuorum: Omnes enim ei uiuunt. Poterat infinita alia, & hoc multo clariora Scripturae testimonia producere, sed Mosis authoritate pugnat, quia huius solius scripta Sadducaei agnoscebant, ut initio diximus. Proderat etiam huius loci consideratio ad hoc, ut offenderet atrocem patribus prisci s iniuriam fieri, si resurrectio negetur, simulq; consolationes præcipuas Scripturæ eneruari. Harum enim omnium fundamentum in foedere illo consistit: quod cum Abrahamo initum Deus cum eius filijs Isaaco & Iacobo instaurauit. Si ergo isti perierunt, quibus foederis gratia primis oblata est, & quorum fides atque pietas tantopere Deo placuit, ut eorum Deum se dicere dignetur: quid obsecro sperare possunt posteri, qui illis nullo modo conferri merentur? Argumentum euidentiæ & perspicuitatis causa sic formari poterit: Deus est Deus viuorum, Deus est Deus Abrahami & Isaaci & Iacobi. Ergo Abrahamus & Isaacius & Iacobus viuunt. Argumenti vis in eo consistit, ut sciamus quid sit alicuius Deum esse, quam locutionum in scripturis frequentem esse constat. In Lege dicitur: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus. Et apud Ieremiam: Ero Deus illorum, ipsiq; erunt mihi populus, id est, Ego eorum protector & defensor ero, ipsi uero me eum agnoscent, & mihi obtemperabunt. Deus ergo hic relatiue dicitur respectu eorum, quorum Deus est: quo sensu ueteres quoque hominem homini Deum esse dixerunt. Vt ergo nemo herus esse poterit eorum qui nulli sunt: ita neque Deus illorum Deus esse poterit, qui in rerum natura esse desierunt. Atqui Deum Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi se esse profitetur: Ergo hi ipsi quamuis mortui sint, viuunt tamen: eò quòd animae illorum in sedes beatae immortalitatis receptae uita caelesti iam fruuntur, corpora autem in spe futurae resurrectionis quiescunt. Estq; argumentum hoc multò firmius, quàm primo aspectu esse videatur. Ita enim inter se foederis aeterni vinculo Deus & homines connectuntur, ut ille Deus noster esse desinat, adeoq; nullus sit, nisi mortuorum resurrectio nobis certa & salua maneat. Nec est quòd eos audiamus, qui sufficere putant, si animarum immortalitas statuatur. Nam ut Abrahamo toti, quando is corpore & anima constabat, dicebatur: Ego sum Deus tuus omnisufficiens: ita etiam dictum hoc, quo Mosem consolatus est postea, ad totum Abrahamum debet extendi. Et iniquus nec satis bonae fidei protector diceretur Deus, si dimidiam hominis partem perire sineret: & quidem eam, quae in hoc saeculo laboribus & aerumnis quàm maximè est obnoxia.
units.tr: The second point of this discussion is the demonstration of the resurrection that is to come, which Christ comprehends in these words. That the dead are raised, Moses also indicated at the bush, when he says: "The Lord God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." "For God is not the God of the dead, but of the living; for all live to him" (Luke 20.37–38). He could have brought forward countless other testimonies of Scripture, and much clearer ones, but he argues from the authority of Moses, because the Sadducees acknowledged only his writings, as we said at the beginning. The consideration of this passage was also useful for showing that it is a dreadful wrong done to the ancient fathers if the resurrection is denied, and at the same time for showing that the chief consolations of Scripture would be weakened. For the foundation of all these lies in that covenant which God, having been made with Abraham, renewed with his sons Isaac and Jacob. If then those perished to whom the grace of the covenant was first offered, and whose faith and piety so greatly pleased God that he deigned to call himself their God, what, I ask, can the posterity hope for, who in no way deserve to be compared with them? The argument may be formed, for the sake of clarity and plainness, thus: God is the God of the living; God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Therefore Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live. The force of the argument consists in knowing what it means to be someone's God, a manner of speaking which is known to be frequent in the Scriptures. In the Law it is said: "I am the Lord your God." And in Jeremiah: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (Jer. 31.33 and similar); that is, I will be their protector and defender, and they will acknowledge me and obey me. Therefore God is here called God in relation to those of whom he is God; in this sense the ancients also said that man is God to man. Just as no one can be the master of those who are nothing, so neither can God be the God of those who have ceased to exist in the nature of things. But he professes himself to be the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Therefore these men, although they are dead, nevertheless live: because their souls, received into the abodes of blessed immortality, now enjoy the heavenly life, while their bodies rest in the hope of the future resurrection. And this argument is much firmer than it may seem at first sight. For God and men are so bound together by the bond of the eternal covenant that he would cease to be our God, and so would be no God at all, unless the resurrection of the dead remains certain and secure for us. Nor should we listen to those who think it is enough if the immortality of the soul is established. For just as to Abraham as a whole, since he consisted of body and soul, it was said, "I am your God, all-sufficient" (Gen. 17.1), so also this saying, by which he afterwards comforted Moses, must be extended to the whole Abraham. And God would be called an unjust and not sufficiently trustworthy protector if he allowed half of a man to perish: and indeed that half which in this age is most exposed to labours and hardships.

units.la: Seruit autem hic locus multum ad asserendam nostrae salutis certitudinem, ne eorum cavillis seducamur, qui de illa ex carnis sensu iudicium faciunt. Hi enim quia Deum non aliter nobis propitium esse agnoscunt, quàm si uotis nostris omnibus annuat: ita in morte hominem totum perire & omnem restitutionis spem simul extingui arbitrantur. At longè aliter nos indicare docet Dei Filius, qui ut Abrahamum, Isaacum et Iacobum Deo uiuere dicit, qui ante annos plus mille septingentos mortem obierant: Ita in Euangelio pollicetur, eos qui Verbum eius audiunt, & secundum huius doctrinā credunt, à morte in uitam transfire. Et idem Marthae dicebat: Ego sum resurrectio & vita: qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, viuet: Et omnis qui viuit, & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum. Quo Paulus respiciens, perinde ac si totam rerum naturam deuicerimus, clamat: Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? Nam mihi persuasum habeo, quòd neque MORS, neque vita, &c. poterit nos separare à charitate Dei, quae est in Iesu Christo, Domino nostro. Sunt haec semper nobis meditanda, ne ullis aduersis terreamur, sed in ipso etiam mortis articulo spem in Christo habeamus inconcussam. Nam ubi mundo viuere desierimus, in uitae huius mortalis locum succedet caelestis & aeterna, cuius felicitas omnem intellectum superat.
units.tr: This passage is of great use in establishing the certainty of our salvation, so that we are not led astray by the quibbles of those who judge it by the sense of the flesh. For these people, because they acknowledge that God is not favourable to us unless he grants all our wishes, think that in death the whole man perishes and every hope of restoration is at once extinguished. But the Son of God teaches us quite otherwise. He says that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live to God, though they had died more than seventeen hundred years before. So in the Gospel he promises that those who hear his Word and believe according to his teaching pass from death into life. And he said the same to Martha: "I am the resurrection and the life: he who believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die for ever." Paul, looking to this, cries out as if we had conquered the whole nature of things: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, etc., will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Jesus Christ our Lord. These things must always be meditated upon by us, so that we are not terrified by any adversities, but have an unshaken hope in Christ even at the very moment of death. For when we have ceased to live to the world, there will take the place of this mortal life a heavenly and eternal one, whose happiness surpasses all understanding.

units.la: Porrò audiamus huius quoque certaminis sive congressus euentum. Matthaeus populum doctrina Christi perculsum fuisse scribit. Magnam ergo opportunit tunc fuisse Scripturarum ignorantiam, quando tantae admirationi fuit tam certa eius articuli assertio siue defensio, de quo nemo pius unquam dubitauit. Et hinc apparet, Pharisaeos hucusque aduersus Sadducaeorum sophismata nihil solidum afferre potuisse, Lucas uerò addit aliquos ex Scribis Veritati testimonium perhibuisse, dicentes: Magister, bene dixisti. Voluissent quidem illi Christum obmutuisse, ut populo contemptus fieri coepisset: sed tanta Veritatis lux est, ut reluctantium quoque animos penetret, & inuitis testimonium extorqueat. Accedit ad gloriam Christi, quòd nemo aduersariorum eum porrò interrogare audet. Quia enim toti ambitione ardebant, nec quicquam priuata gloria habebant antiquius, metuunt ne toties repulsi, omnium ludibrijs exponantur, aut suo silentio authoritatem & doctrinam Christi confirment. Quod autem tunc factum fuit, hodie non raro fieri uidemus, ut simplici Euangelij doctrina eorum ora obturentur, qui in mundo doctissimi & potentissimi habentur. Est enim inuictum Veritatis robur, eoq; magis emergit, quò pluribus telis oppugnatur. Non pudeat ergo nos illi testimonium ferre, fortes autem simus in Christo Iesu, qui neque nobis neque causae suae unquam deerit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us further hear the outcome of this struggle or encounter. Matthew writes that the people were struck by the teaching of Christ. Great ignorance of the Scriptures must then have prevailed, since the assertion or defence of this article, about which no godly person ever doubted, caused such wonder. And from this it appears that the Pharisees had until then been unable to bring anything solid against the sophistries of the Sadducees. But Luke adds that some of the scribes bore witness to the truth, saying: "Teacher, you have spoken well." They would indeed have wished Christ to be silent, so that he would begin to be despised by the people; but so great is the light of truth that it penetrates even the minds of those who resist, and extorts testimony from the unwilling. It adds to the glory of Christ that none of his adversaries dared to question him further. For since they burned entirely with ambition, and held nothing more precious than private glory, they feared that, having been repulsed so often, they would be exposed to the mockery of all, or by their silence would confirm the authority and teaching of Christ. What happened then, we often see happening today, that the mouths of those who are held to be the most learned and most powerful in the world are stopped by the simple doctrine of the Gospel. For the strength of truth is invincible, and it rises the more, the more it is assailed with many weapons. Let us not be ashamed, therefore, to bear witness to it; and let us be strong in Christ Jesus, who will never fail us or his cause. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXII
units.tr: Homily 182

units.la: Dixit autem eis: Quomodo dicunt Christum filium esse Dauidis, & ipse Dauid dicit in libro Psalmorum: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede à dextris meis, vsquedum posuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Dauid ergo Dominum eum vocat, & quomodo filius eius est? Audiente vero toto populo, dixit discipulis suis: Cauete à Scribis, qui voluntambulare stolati, & amant salutationes in foris, ac primos con-sessus in conuentibus, & primos accubitus in coenis. Qui deuorant do-mos viduarũ, & in speciem precibus longis vtuntur; liti auferent grauí us iudicium.
units.tr: And he said to them: How do they say that the Christ is the son of David, when David himself says in the book of Psalms: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool"? David therefore calls him Lord; how then is he his son? And while all the people were listening, he said to his disciples: Beware of the scribes, who like to walk about in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the chief places at feasts; who devour the houses of widows and, for show, make long prayers. These will receive the greater condemnation.

units.la: Postquam Lucas insidiosos aliquot Sacerdotum atq; Scribarum cum Iesu Christo congressus de scripsit, in quibus apparet, quibus artibus & dolis impij antistites & quotquot horum partes se quentur, aduersus veritatis doctrinam pugnent: subijcit commodissime hoc loco, vt idé toties prouoca-tus & toties victor tandem ipsos quoq; prouocauerit: non quidem animo malitioso & vindictæ cupi-do, sed amico & benevolo: neque aliam ob causam, quàm vt eos in vera Messiæ cognitione instituE-ret, cuius ignorantia ipsis omnium errorum simul atque omnis audaciæ contra veritatis doctrinam causa erat. Quia verò illos incurabili contumacia aduersus veritatè luctari, & ne conuictos quidem cedere sensit, plenis velis, quod aiunt, in illos inuehitur, & ad suos conuersus eos monet, vt ab eis sibi caueant, qui sub speciosó pastorum titulo vulpes & lupos agant, atq; cum gregis totius periculo suam gloriam atq; quaestum tueantur. Est ergo loci huius consideratio vtilissima: quia in vera Christi cognitione nos instituit, & simul docet qua ratione cum illis agere debeamus, qui non contenti propria impietate alios quoq; impediunt, ne salutem consequantur.
units.tr: After Luke has described several crafty encounters of Jesus Christ with the chief priests and scribes, in which it appears by what arts and tricks the impious leaders, and all who follow their party, fight against the doctrine of truth, he most fittingly adds at this point that he, who had been challenged so often and had always won, now at last challenged them in turn. He did this not out of a malicious spirit or a desire for revenge, but out of a friendly and kindly intent, and for no other reason than to instruct them in the true knowledge of the Messiah. Their ignorance of this was the cause of all their errors and of all their boldness against the doctrine of truth. But since he perceived that they struggled against the truth with an incurable obstinacy, and did not yield even when refuted, he attacks them with full sail, as they say, and turning to his own people he warns them to beware of those who, under the specious title of shepherds, act like foxes and wolves and, at the risk of the whole flock, defend their own glory and gain. Therefore, consideration of this passage is most useful: it instructs us in the true knowledge of Christ, and at the same time teaches us how we ought to deal with those who, not content with their own impiety, also hinder others from obtaining salvation.

units.la: Vt verò rem omnem rectius intelligamus, causa huius disputationis & totum Christi institutû aliquanto diligentius considerandum erit. Occasionem siue causam ei dedit communis Iudaeorum error, cuius primarij authores erant Scribae & Sacerdotes, qui populū consultò in ignorantiae tenebris detinebant. Nam etiamsi promissiones de Messia in omniũ ore essent, à paucis tamen rectè intelligebantur. Sciebat quidè ex Dauidis stirpe nasciturũ vindicem illum, qui populum in libertatem asserere & Regnum illud optatum instaurare deberet. Vt verò regnum terrenum somniabant, ita Messiam hominem nudum fore arbitrabantur, neq; aliquam habebant diuinæ illius virtutis, aut potius diuinitatis eius æternæ notitiam, qua illum instructum esse oportuit. Quæ causa erat, quòd non in opera Christi, luculenta diuinæ naturæ testimonia, intenti essent, sed regiî splendoris maiestatem requirerent, & proinde illum nõ possent pro Messia agnoscere, in quo nihil illius simile videbant. Quia ergo iam mortem aditurus erat, ex qua scandalum ingens sciebat nasciturum esse, errori illi opportunum remedium adhibere, & simul omnium nostrum fidem fulcire voluit.
units.tr: In order to understand the whole matter more correctly, the cause of this discussion and the whole course of Christ's teaching must be considered somewhat more carefully. The occasion or cause for it was the common error of the Jews, whose chief authors were the scribes and priests, who deliberately kept the people in the darkness of ignorance. For although the promises about the Messiah were on everyone's lips, few understood them rightly. They knew indeed that that avenger would be born from the stock of David, who was to free the people and restore that longed-for kingdom. But just as they dreamed of an earthly kingdom, so they believed the Messiah would be a mere man, and they had no knowledge of that divine power, or rather of his eternal divinity, with which he ought to have been endowed. This was why they were not attentive to the works of Christ, the clear testimonies of his divine nature, but sought the majesty of royal splendour; and therefore they could not acknowledge him as the Messiah, since they saw nothing like that in him. Therefore, since he was about to undergo death, from which he knew a great scandal would arise, he wished to apply a fitting remedy to that error and at the same time to strengthen the faith of all of us.

units.la: Est autem probè obseruanda diaboli in decipiendis hominibus astutia, aduersus quam verbi administros assiduè vigilare, & illius impostu ras arguere oportet. Non potuit ille omnem Messiæ notitiam ex Iudaeorum animis delere, multo minus efficere, vt spem aduentus eius abijcerent, quam ex patribus quasi iure hæreditario acceperant, & quæ promissionibus amplissimis confirmabatur. Vt ergo salutem ipsorum impediret, fictitium Messiam illis obtrusit, qui armis & militibus instru-ctus Romanos ex Iudæa eijceret, & regnum sibi pararet victorijs & opibus illustre, quale olim sub Dauide ac Solomone habuerant. Non enim ignorat astutus ille, homines diuina & cœlestia facilè negligere, si huius sæculi splendor ipsis obijciatur. Similis astutiæ fuit, quòd multis persuasit Christũ vel Ioannê Baptistam, vel Ieremiam, vel quencũq; alium ex veterum Prophetarum numero esse. Nam quidius ferre potest, modò illũ æternum Dei Filiū & æternæ salutis Mediatorẽ esse non credamus. Posteris ergo tëporibus inter Christianos quoq; hæreticos excitauit, quorũ alij illius diuinitatẽ, alij humanitate negarunt: vt veram eius cognitione obliteraret. Et hodie huius generis multæ fiunt, quibus vera Christi & salutis æternæ notitia impeditur. Et vt olim Iudæis imposuit, quòd in solum Dauidem intenti, ex cuius stirpe Messiam nasciturũ esse Prophetæ prædixerat, interim alios locos neglexerunt, qui de eiusdē diuina natura aperte testătur, & Regni eius conditionem egregiè describunt: ita hodie in religione plurimorũ atq; maximorũ errorũ causa est, quòd in controuersijs articulis nõ singulæ partes & quæcunq; de illis Scriptura tradit inspiciuntur, sed aliquos solùm locos homines cõtentiosis mordicus arripiũt et vrget, reiectis et explosis alijs, qui illos pleniꝰ instituere poterat. Sic Anabaptistæ de Baptismo verba facturi, ea modò proferunt, quæ ad fidei professionem, carnis mortificationem, regenerationē & alia huius generis mysteria pertinent, quæ non nisi in adultis possunt locum habere: at Dei gratiam, qui fœderis sui effectum atq; fructum ad infantes vsq; extendit. non agnoscunt, nec aliquam eius faciunt mentionem. Sic in Iustificationis articulo eos modo scripturae locos nonnulli corradunt, in quibus bona opera nobis commendantur, et ijsdem praemium aeternae salutis promittitur: illos autem quasi clausis oculis & surdis auribus praetereunt, qui nostrae naturae vitiositatem, gratuitam Dei misericordiam, fidem denique in Christum proponunt, quae unica bonorum operum causa atque origo est{C}. Istis ergo exemplis admoniti, discamus, non sufficere si unum & alterum Scripturae locum habeamus, quo causa siue sententia nostra defendi videtur: sed diligenti totius rei, de qua agitur cognitione & aliorum quoque locorum collatione opus esse, si veritatem rectius inspicere velimus.
units.tr: The craftiness of the devil in deceiving men must, however, be carefully observed, and against it the ministers of the Word must watch constantly and expose his deceptions. He could not wipe out all knowledge of the Messiah from the minds of the Jews, much less bring it about that they would abandon the hope of his coming, which they had received from their fathers as if by hereditary right, and which was confirmed by the most ample promises. So, in order to hinder their salvation, he thrust upon them a fictitious Messiah, one who, armed with weapons and soldiers, would drive the Romans out of Judea and win for himself a kingdom renowned for victories and wealth, such as they had once had under David and Solomon. For that crafty one does not fail to know that men easily neglect divine and heavenly things if the splendour of this age is set before them. A similar trick was his when he persuaded many that Christ was either John the Baptist, or Jeremiah, or some other from the number of the ancient prophets. For how can this be borne, unless we believe that he is the eternal Son of God and the Mediator of eternal salvation? Therefore in later times he stirred up heretics even among Christians, some of whom denied his divinity, others his humanity, so that he might blot out the true knowledge of him. And today many errors of this kind arise, by which the true knowledge of Christ and of eternal salvation is hindered. And just as he once deceived the Jews, who fixed their attention on David alone, from whose stock the prophets had foretold the Messiah would be born, and meanwhile neglected other passages which clearly bear witness to his divine nature and describe the condition of his kingdom excellently, so today the cause of very many and very great errors in religion is that in controverted articles, not each part nor whatever Scripture teaches about them is examined; instead, men with contentious spirit seize and press only a few passages with their teeth, rejecting and driving out the others, which could have instructed them more fully. Thus the Anabaptists, when they speak about baptism, bring forward only those words which pertain to the profession of faith, the mortification of the flesh, regeneration and other mysteries of this kind, which can have a place only in adults; but they do not acknowledge the grace of God, who extends the effect and fruit of his covenant even to infants, and make no mention of it. So too in the article of justification, some gather together only those passages of Scripture in which good works are commended to us and eternal salvation is promised as their reward; but they pass over, as if with closed eyes and deaf ears, those which set forth the corruption of our nature, the free mercy of God, and finally faith in Christ, which is the sole cause and origin of good works{C}. Warned, therefore, by these examples, let us learn that it is not enough to have one or two passages of Scripture by which our cause or opinion seems to be defended; but that careful knowledge of the whole matter under discussion, and comparison with other passages too, is needed if we wish to see the truth more correctly.

units.la: Porro accedamus ad Christum, qui ut paulo ante Sadducaeos, ita nunc omnes simul ad diligentiore Scripturarum considerationem remittit, ut de promisso illo populi vindice ac redemptore rectius sentire & iudicare discant. Sic enim quaestionem suam proponit: Quomodo dicunt Christum filium esse Dauidis? & ipse Dauid dixit in libro Psalmorum: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede a dextris meis, usque dum, &c. Quibus verbis non negat, Messiam Dauidis filium esse neque scribas & Iudaeos hoc nomine reprehendit, quod olim Dauidis filium dicerent: sed in eo illos errare docet, quod nihil homine maius de illo sentirent, neque aeternae atque caelestis vitae authorem, sed regem modo terrenum agnoscerent, qui pristinam libertatem ipsis esset instauraturus. Cum multos locos posset addu cere, quibus error iste confutatur, ipsius Dauidis authoritate pugnat, & hunc plus quiddam de Messia sperauisse offendit, & proinde ipsos tam huic quam illi iniuriam facere, qui circa terreni modo regni expectationem occupentur. Ducitur autem argumentum ex hominum consuetudine & communi sensu, qui cum naturae legibus per omniaconuenit, hoc modo. Neque aequum, neque naturae legibus conueniens, neque apud ullas gentes receptum est, ut patres filios suos pro dominis agnoscant, nedum ut hoc nomine posteros nondum in lucem hac aditos dignentur. Atqui Dauid Messiam illum fitue unctum Dei, quae praefinito demum tempore ex sua stirpe aut progenie nasciturum esse sciebat, Dominum suum dixit. Ergo aliquid homine maius & omnibus regnis huius saeculi excellentius in eo agnovit. Etenim si nihil aliud quam regem politicum fore credidisset, suum Dominum dicere non poterat, cum nemo haeres regni dominus illius dicatur, qui illud adhuc gubernat, et ipsemet reb. praesit. Ite, si Messias nihil praeter libertatem politicam & regnum terrenum conferre debuit, nihil utique profuisset Dauidi, qui illum multis saeculis praecessit. Magna quidem Scipionum, Aemiliorum, Pompeij, Caesaris, Augusti & similium apud Romanos gloria fuit, qui Imperium per totum ferè orbem propagarunt: at quae obsecro ex illis utilitas rediit ad Publicolas, Curios, Fabritios, Camillos & similes, quorum temporibus res Romana adhuc angustioribus finibus concludebatur? Et quis obsecro horum dominos fuisse dixerit postremos illos, qui imperij fines in Asia & Europam usque extenderunt? Quid ergo reliquum est, quam ut Dauidem dicamus in promisso illo Christo maiore dignitate atque excellentiam agnouisse? Quod nimirum bona caelestia, liberationem a peccato & morte atque vitam aeternam largiatur, quod divina potentia & virtute armatus aeternum Dei Regnum instauret: denique quod Dei Filius sit, qui tunc quoque priusquam in carne manifestatus esset, propuli sui protector atque Rex fuerit? Quod in Psalmo secundo apertius testatur, ubi Patrem ab aeterno Messiae illi promisso dicentem introducit: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Et Isaias Achaz Regem atque populum contra Syrorum & Israelitarum incursiones atque hostiles conatus consolaturus, ad promissum illum Dauidis Filium remittit, qui etiamsi suo demum tempore ex virgine nasci debeat: nunc tamen ipsis praesens adsit, ut hostes ipsorum deuincat & spolia Damasci diuidat: & ideo illi nomen Immanuelis tribuit, quod sonat, Nobiscum Deus. Et ista quidem omnia Christus hoc loco Iudaeorum Sacerdotibus atque Scribis in mentem reuocat, si forte oculos aperiant, & populum quoque totum in Messiae & promissae redemptionis negotio rectius instituant.
units.tr: Further, let us come to Christ, who, as a little before he sent the Sadducees back, so now sends all of them together back to a more diligent consideration of the Scriptures, so that they may learn to think and judge more rightly about that promised avenger and redeemer of the people. For thus he sets out his question: "How do they say that the Christ is the son of David? And David himself said in the book of Psalms: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until, etc." In these words he does not deny that the Messiah is the son of David, nor does he rebuke the scribes and Jews for calling him David's son in the past; rather, he teaches that they err in this, that they thought nothing greater of him than a man, and did not acknowledge him as the author of eternal and heavenly life, but only as an earthly king who was going to restore their former liberty. Although he could have adduced many passages by which this error is refuted, he fights with the authority of David himself, and shows that David hoped for something more than earthly in the Messiah; and therefore, that those who are occupied only with the expectation of an earthly kingdom do injury both to him and to David. The argument is drawn from human custom and common sense, which agrees with the laws of nature everywhere, in this way: It is neither fair, nor in accordance with the laws of nature, nor accepted among any nations, that fathers should acknowledge their sons as lords, much less that they should honour with this title descendants not yet born into the light. But David called the Messiah, the anointed of God, whom he knew would be born at a set time from his stock or line, his Lord. Therefore he recognised in him something greater than a man and more excellent than all the kingdoms of this age. For if he had believed that he would be only a political king, he could not have called him his Lord, since no heir to a kingdom is called lord by one who still governs it and presides over the state himself. Likewise, if the Messiah was to bring nothing beyond political liberty and an earthly kingdom, it would certainly have profited David nothing, who preceded him by many centuries. Great indeed was the glory among the Romans of the Scipios, Aemilii, Pompey, Caesar, Augustus and their like, who spread their empire across almost the whole world; but what, I ask, of advantage came from them to Publicola, Curius, Fabricius, Camillus and their like, in whose times the Roman state was still confined within narrower bounds? And who, I ask, would say that these men were the lords of those last ones, who extended the boundaries of the empire into Asia and Europe? What remains, then, but to say that David recognised in that promised Christ a greater dignity and excellence? Namely, that he bestows heavenly goods, deliverance from sin and death, and eternal life; that armed with divine power and might he restores the eternal kingdom of God; and finally that he is the Son of God, who, even before he was made manifest in the flesh, was the protector and King of his people. This he bears witness to more plainly in the second Psalm, where he introduces the Father speaking from eternity to that promised Messiah: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." And Isaiah, about to comfort King Ahaz and the people against the incursions and hostile attempts of the Syrians and Israelites, refers them to that promised son of David, who, although he was to be born of a virgin only at his own appointed time, yet should now be present to them, to overcome their enemies and divide the spoils of Damascus; and therefore he gives him the name Immanuel, which means "God with us." Christ in this passage calls all these things to the minds of the priests and scribes of the Jews, in case perhaps they might open their eyes and instruct the whole people more rightly in the matter of the Messiah and the promised redemption.

units.la: Porro hic nos meminisse oportet, Christu communem doctrinam proponere, qua simul discipulos suos aduersus mortis & crucis instantis scandalum praemunire & armare voluit: In eundem ergo usum nos quoque illam accommodare debemus, ut vera ipsius cognitione illuminati nullis huius saeculi minis aut machinationibus terreamur. Quia enim Regnum eius non est de hoc mundo, nullis etiam armis aut viribus mundi euerti poterit. Deinde quis eum ex regni solio deturbabit, qui ex aeterno Patris caelestis decreto ad dextram eius sedet, & in assumpta etiam carne in caelestem gloriam exaltatus omnem potestatem accepit in coelo & in terra? Aut num regno eius nocebunt hostes, quos scabelli instar pedibus eius subijci oportet? Quod quàm uerè dictum sit, tota mundi historia iam inde ab exordio rerum testatur. Christus enim ille est, qui olim Pharaonem, Chananaeos, Syros cum uicinis gentibus, adhæc Assyrios, Babylonios, Persas & Medos, Græcos & potentissimam illam Romam eius quoque imperium pedibus suis conculcauit, sicuti alibi prolixè demonstrauimus. Et hodie etiam eius ferreo sceptro comminuit atq; pedibus calcari uidemus multos, qui aduersus eum insurgere non uerentur. Nec hîc aliquem moueat, quòd interdum ipse hostibus suis succumbere uidetur, quando pij nominis ipsius cultores persecutionibus diris & omni calamitatum genere exercentur. Vt enim olim per crucem de mundo & huius principe triumphauit: ita sub crucis uexillo uincût, quicunq; illi per fidem uerè sunt insiti. Et in eo Regnum eius ab alijs huius sæculi regnis differt, quòd cùm hæc uix inter amicorum præsidia et triumphos continuos consistant, sæpius autem sua mole ruant (quod Romano Imperio & multis alijs accidisse legimus) ille inter medios hostes dominari consueuit. Cuius potentiæ euidens argumentum in Euangelij prædicatione olim dedit, quæ per obscuros discipulos paucorum annorum spatio per totum orbe terrarum felicissimo successu propagata est, invitis etiam & multùm reluctantibus omnibus ijs, qui tunc potentia & authoritate excellebât. Et postremis hisce temporibus idem factum esse uidemus. Nec tamen hic pedem fixit Christus uictor, sed olim quando in nubibus cœli ad iudicium ueniet, tunc ipsa etiam morte deuicta, diaboli cum pseudopropheta eiusq; coniuratis in stagnum ardes igne & sulphure præcipites dabit. Istorum consideratione nos confirmari oportet aduersus postremam hanc diaboli luctam, qua instante huius mundi fine Regnum Christi saltem aliqua ex parte concutere, & pios perterrefacere conatur. Nihil enim proficiet, neque eius minæ atq; machinationes eos ex statione sua deturbare poterunt, qui supra petram illam unica fide ædificati sunt, aduersus quam ne inferorum quidem portæ possunt aliquid.
units.tr: Moreover, we should remember here that Christ sets forth a common doctrine, by which he wanted to forearm and arm his disciples at once against the scandal of the death and cross that were about to come. We too ought to apply it to the same purpose, so that, enlightened by the true knowledge of him, we may not be terrified by any threats or schemes of this age. For since his kingdom is not of this world, it cannot be overthrown by any arms or powers of the world. Next, who will thrust him from the throne of his kingdom, he who by the eternal decree of the heavenly Father sits at his right hand, and who, having been exalted in his assumed flesh to heavenly glory, has received all power in heaven and on earth? Or will enemies harm his kingdom, when they must be placed under his feet like a footstool? How truly this has been said, the whole history of the world bears witness from the beginning of things. For it is that Christ who once trampled under his feet Pharaoh, the Canaanites, the Syrians with the neighbouring nations, besides the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians and Medes, the Greeks, and that most powerful Rome with its empire, as we have shown at length elsewhere. And today too he crushes them with his iron sceptre, and we see many trampled underfoot who do not fear to rise against him. Nor should anyone be moved here by the fact that he sometimes seems to yield to his enemies, when the worshippers of his holy name are harassed by dreadful persecutions and every kind of calamity. For just as once through the cross he triumphed over the world and its prince, so under the banner of the cross those conquer who are truly engrafted into him by faith. And in this his kingdom differs from the kingdoms of this age: these can scarcely stand amid the defences and continual triumphs of friends, and more often collapse under their own weight (as we read happened to the Roman Empire and many others), whereas he is accustomed to rule amid his enemies. He once gave clear proof of this power in the preaching of the Gospel, which, through obscure disciples, was spread throughout the whole world in a few years with the most happy success, even though all those who then excelled in power and authority were unwilling and strongly resisted. And in these latter times we see the same thing happening. Yet Christ the victor does not fix his foot here; but once, when he comes to judgment on the clouds of heaven, then, death itself having been conquered, he will cast the devil, the false prophet and their confederates headlong into the lake burning with fire and brimstone. We ought to be strengthened by consideration of these things against that final struggle of the devil, by which, as the end of this world draws near, he tries to shake the kingdom of Christ at least in some part and to terrify the godly. For he will gain nothing, nor will his threats and schemes be able to drive from their station those who have been built upon that rock by faith alone, against which not even the gates of hell can prevail.

units.la: Cæterùm hæc dicente Christo, nemo Sacerdotum aut Scribarum quicquam ei respondere potuit, sicut Matthæus annotauit. Erat enim quæstio ista non leuis aut expedita ijs, qui animum falsis & erroneis opinionibus præoccupatum habebant. Idem tamen suæ potius gloriæ quàm publicæ salutis studio addicti, ne interrogare quidem audent illum, & clariorem huius quæstionis sive argumenti explicationem petere, ne suam ignorantiam magis prodant. Quæ causa hodie etiam multis obstat, ut quàmuis se errare sentiant, neque se expedire possint à quæstionibus, quæ passim controuertuntur, dicere tamen nolunt, imò omnem discendi occasionem studiosè declinant, ne ipsorum authoritas uel minima ex parte labefactetur. Non tamen omni fructu doctrina ista caruit: nam populum illa delectatum & eius audiendi desiderio magis accensum fuisse Marcus ostendit. Quapropter ille audiente toto populo ad discipulos suos conuersus, Sacerdotum & Scribarum mores liberius arguit, ne uel discipuli idem cum his doctrinæ genus sectentur, vel populo graue aut nefas esse uideatur ab illis desiderere, qui summam in ea gente dignitatem sustinebant.
units.tr: Although Christ was saying these things, none of the priests or scribes could answer him, as Matthew has noted. This question was not an easy or simple one for those whose minds were preoccupied with false and erroneous opinions. Yet these men, devoted to the pursuit of their own glory rather than the public salvation, do not even dare to question him or to seek a clearer explanation of this question or argument, lest they reveal their ignorance more. This same cause still hinders many today: although they feel that they are in error, and cannot extricate themselves from the questions that are everywhere disputed, they nevertheless refuse to speak, and indeed carefully avoid every occasion of learning, lest their authority be weakened even in the smallest part. Yet this teaching was not without all fruit, for Mark shows that the people were delighted by it and were more kindled with the desire to hear him. Therefore, while the whole people listened, he turned to his disciples and rebuked the conduct of the priests and scribes more freely, so that the disciples should not follow this same kind of teaching from them, nor should it seem to the people a grave or wicked thing to take a different view from those who held the highest dignity in that nation.

units.la: Quo exemplo admonemur, non licere modò, uerumetiam necessarium esse, ut falsi antistites arguantur. Debet enim pluris fieri multorum salus quàm paucorum existimatio, qui authoritate sua adquæstum uel tyrannidem ambitiosam abutuntur, & ueritatis lucem extinctam uolunt. Obseruarunt hoc olim Prophetæ, quos in arguendis impostoribus acerrimos fuisse, ipsorum sermones testantur. Apostolis uero nõ satis fuit, si sui seculi impostores oppugnarèt, sed de ueturis quoq; nos admonerunt, ut posterorũ saluti consuleremus. Nec est quòd aliqui hîc nobis māsuetudinis & charitatis Christianæ leges obijciat. Quis enim māsuetior Christo? quis in charitate ardentior? quis patientior deniq; in ferendis iniurijs? quis itè erga peccatores indulgetior? Veruntamè idè illè, quādo ei cũ Pharisæis, Scribis ac sacerdotibus res est, omnis quodammodo patientiæ & mansuetudinis oblitus modũ excederet uideretur: neq; ei satis esset, si errores eorum & hypocrisim arguat, nisi eosdem diris quoq; devoueat, Væ illud horrendũ subinde minitando, quo omnis tam præsentis huius quàm futuræ uitæ calamitas comprehenditur. Sunt quidè multi, quibus istud indignum & minimè necessarium esse uidetur. Nam illos aut māsuetudine lucrifieri posse, aut omnino incurabiles esse aiût. Atqui illud falsissimũ est: quia multis alijs rationibus emolliri aut mitigari possūt, ut ueritati locũ det, quotquot Dei uerbũ ludibrio habet, aut etiã hostiliter insectatur. Et qui ita sentiût, hi seipso Deo sapientiores esse sibi persuadet, aut saltè se aliquid habere putat, quod uerbo Dei utilius & ad permouendũ hominũ animos efficaciùs sit. Ex altero autẽ illo minimè sequitur, tacendũ esse ijs quos Deus Ecclesiæ suæ pastores esse voluit. Nã ut plane incurabiles sint, imo etiam rabie maiori indies exasperentur lupi, arguere tamen eos & altis clamoribus exagitare oportet: idque ut ouium saluti consulatur, quarum fere tanta est stoliditas, ut sponte in illorum fauces atq; ungues incurrant, nec facile agnoscant, sub ouillis pellibus latentem lupinam rabiem. Quibus adde, quod hypocritis audacia crescit, si uel negligantur, uel se alijs terrori esse putent: ut iam de eo nihil dicam, quod pastores olim Deo rationem reddere cogentur omnium eorum, qui ipsorum incuria perierunt.
units.tr: By this example we are warned that it is not only permitted but necessary that false pastors be rebuked. For the salvation of many ought to be valued more than the reputation of a few, who abuse their authority for gain or for ambitious tyranny, and who want the light of truth extinguished. The prophets once observed this, and their own words testify that they were most fierce in rebuking impostors. But it was not enough for the apostles to attack the impostors of their own age; they also warned us about those who were to come, so that we might provide for the salvation of posterity. Nor is there anyone here who might object to us the laws of Christian gentleness and charity. For who was gentler than Christ? Who was more ardent in charity? Who was finally more patient in bearing injuries? Who was more indulgent towards sinners? Yet when he had to deal with the Pharisees, scribes and priests, he seemed in some sense to forget all patience and gentleness and to go beyond measure; and it was not enough for him to rebuke their errors and hypocrisy unless he also cursed them with dreadful words, repeatedly threatening that terrible Woe, by which every calamity of both this present life and the future is comprehended. There are indeed many who think this unworthy and by no means necessary. For they say that such men can either be won by gentleness, or are altogether incurable. But that is most false, since they can be softened or mitigated by many other means, so that truth may find a place in all those who mock the word of God or even attack it with hostility. And those who think this way persuade themselves that they are wiser than God himself, or at least think they have something more useful to the word of God and more effective for moving men's minds. But it by no means follows from the other point that those whom God wanted to be pastors of his Church should be silent. For even if they are wholly incurable, and the wolves grow daily more savage in their rage, nevertheless they must be rebuked and assailed with loud cries, and this for the salvation of the sheep, whose stupidity is so great that they run of their own accord into the jaws and claws of the wolves and do not readily recognise the wolfish rage hidden beneath the sheepskin. Add to this that the audacity of hypocrites grows if they are either neglected or think themselves a terror to others; not to mention that the pastors will one day be compelled to render account to God for all those who have perished through their negligence.

units.la: Sed ipsum Christum nobis omnibus loquentem audiamus: Cauete a Scribis, qui volunt ambulare stolati, & amant salutationes in foris, &c. Istud vero de illis dicit, qui veterum Sacerdotum successione, Legis diuinae doctrina & ipsius etiam Mosis cathedra (ut alibi ait) gloriabantur, & de quorum antecessoribus olim dictum fuerat: Labia sacerdotis custodient scientiam, Legemque ex ore eius requirent: Legatus enim est Domini exercituum. Et quia ut sibi ab illis caveant monet, non obscure ab eis secessionem facere iubet: quod quid aliud est, quam scisma suadere, quo nullum in Ecclesia crimen gravius atque atrocius putatur? At non omne scisma malum aut noxium esse, alibi Christus admonet, quando ait: Putatis quod pacem venerim missurus interram? Non dico vobis: sed separationem. Et videmus per Euangelij doctrinam, eos abs se invicem non sine dolore acerbissimo piorum diuelli, qui prius coniunctissimi erant. Ut vero necesse est Christi & veritatis causa a parentibus & fratribus discedere, imo liberis quoque & coniugibus longum valere dicere: ita maior necessitas nos urget, ut doctores falsos relinquamus, qui a Deo nos abstrahere, & veritatis lucem in animis nostris extinguere studeant. Neque nos hic quorumcunque titulis aut dignitatibus moueri decet, quibus inter homines excellunt. Deus enim suam Ecclesiam non hominibus, sed verbo suo subiecit, ut huius ductu & luce dirigatur: & eadem non hominum authoritate, sed solo Christo nititur, qui preciosus ille lapis est, quem in Zione fundavit Deus & quem Paulus fundamentum Prophetarum ac Apostolorum esse dicit. Ut primum ergo antistites religionis officij sui immemores a Christo eos abducunt, qui huic uni consecrati esse debent, nemo illorum authoritatem tanti faciat, ut propter ipsos a summo illo pastorum principe se auelli patiatur.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ himself speaking to us all: "Beware of the scribes, who desire to walk in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces," and so on. He says this about those who gloried in the succession of the ancient priests, in the teaching of the divine Law, and in the very seat of Moses (as he says elsewhere), and of whose predecessors it had once been said: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts" (Mal. 2.). And because he warns the people to beware of them, he plainly bids them withdraw from them; and what is this but to advise schism, which is thought the gravest and most atrocious crime in the Church? Yet Christ elsewhere reminds us that not every schism is evil or harmful, when he says: "Do you think that I have come to send peace on earth? I tell you, no, but rather division" (Matt. 10.). And we see through the doctrine of the Gospel that those who were most closely joined are torn apart from one another, to the bitter grief of the godly. Just as it is necessary to leave father and brothers for the sake of Christ and the truth, and even to bid a long farewell to children and spouses, so a greater necessity presses us to abandon false teachers, who strive to draw us away from God and to extinguish the light of truth in our minds. Nor ought we here to be moved by whatever titles or dignities they excel in among men. For God has subjected his Church not to men but to his word, that it may be directed by its guidance and light; and it rests not on the authority of men but on Christ alone, who is that precious stone which God laid as a foundation in Zion, and which Paul calls the foundation of the prophets and apostles. Therefore, as soon as the leaders of religion, forgetful of their office, lead away from Christ those who ought to be consecrated to him alone, no one should value their authority so highly as to allow himself to be torn away from that supreme Prince of pastors on their account.

units.la: Ut enim quae prouinciarum praesidibus debetur obedientia cessat, si hi Regibus suis male fidi Legum authoritatem aboleant & populum ad defectionem solicitent: ita neque ijs Ecclesiarum pastoribus obedientia debetur, qui loco verbi Dei humanas traditiones, & pro vero cultu superstitiones inuehunt. Est hoc propter eos obseruandum, qui nos scismatis nocentissimi authores & haereticos esse clamant, quod a Romana Ecclesia defecerimus, & Paulum nobis obiiciunt, qui Ecclesiae eius fidem olim in toto orbe annuntiatam fuisse testatur. At nos qualis olim fuerit, nunc non disputamus, imo optamus, ut vel vestigia aliqua prisca illius integritatis aliquando videre liceat: sed praesentem quae illic est rerum faciem intuemur: & quia nihil praeter hominum figmenta & cum prophano Dei contemptu coniunctam crassissimarum superstitionum Simoniam videre liceat, Christi admonitionem secuti, ex Babylone illa exiuimus, ne aliquando ijsdem cum illa plagis vapulemus. Scimus quidem nonnullos nimium securos sibi ipsis impunitatem polliceri, si non ipsi ex suo capite errores fingant, sed eos sequantur, qui duces & pastores Ecclesiae dicuntur, & pro legitimis ministris habentur. Sed nos illud Christi non temere dictum putamus: Si caecus caeco dux fuerint, ambo cadent in foueam. Et quia idem tam hic quam alibi clamat, ut nobis ab impostoribus caueamus, non poterunt extra culpam esse, qui supina ostentantia seipsos decipiunt, & ab alijs decipi patiuntur. Christianorum enim hominum est, non simplicem modo veritatis cognitionem tenere, sed iudicio instructos esse oportet, ut inter dogmata, quae proponuntur, discernere, & vera quidem amplecti, falsa autem auersari ac fugere possint. Admonet de eo Christus, quando ait: Oues meae uocem meam audiunt, & ego cognosco eas, & sequuntur me: Alienum autem non sequentur, sed fugient ab eo: quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Recte ergo Apostoli monuerunt: Omnia probate, quod bonum fuerit tenete. Item: Ne cuius spiritui crediderit is, sed probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. Quo loco Ioannes regulam quoque praescribit, ad quam spiritus, id est, doctrinae omnes probari debeant: & quia illam omnibus Christianis communem esse vult, nemini vitio vertri debet, si doctrinas ab ea discrepantes reiciat. Quo etiam referri debet, quod Paulus iudicium de prophetia penes eos esse vult, qui in Ecclesia sedent, id est, qui ut discipuli doctores audiunt. Vide 1. Corinth. 14. Et hoc debet referri quod Christus Scribas istos describit, ut ostendat dignos esse, à quibus sibi cauendum esse ij, quos seria salutis suæ cura tangit. Nam cauete (inquit) à Scribis, qui volunt ambulare stolati, & amant salutationes in foris, ac primos consessus in conuentibus, & primos accubitus in cœnis. Qui devorat domus viduarum & in speciem precibus longis utuntur. Summa est, eos neq; Dei gloriam neque hominum salutem quærere, sed hypocrisi, ambitioni & avaritiæ deditos, & proinde indignos esse qui audiantur. At quæ illis objicit crimina probat ex signis. Ad primum pertinet, quod eos stolis delectari ait. Græcis stola dicitur quæuis vestis ἀπὸ τῆς στέλλεσθαι, eò quod ad hominis ornatum atque decorum faciat. Latinis autem pro veste longiori usurpatur, quæ ad talos usque demissa totum corpus tegit: & apud Romanos non nisi nobilium matronarum vestitus erat. Tandem sic dici cœperunt vestes sacerdotum, eò quòd hæ quoque longiores essent, ut maior illorum dignitas atque auctoritas appareret. Et sane decet Ecclesiæ & doctrinæ antistites honestius vestiri, ut sic modestiam simul & morum grauitatem testentur: & multa reprehensione digni sunt, qui scurrili aut militari, vel etiam molliori habitu sacri ministerij dignitatem prostituunt. In Scribis tamen Iudæorum hoc Christus accusat, quòd stolis illis sanctitatem simularent, & ijs ad hypocrisim abuterentur. Nam ut apud Matthæum legimus, stolis suis fimbrias latiores addebant, quæ phylacteria dicebantur, eò quod in his præcipua Legis capita descripta gestarent: hæc autem illi dilatare & extendere consueuerant, ut at dentius pietatis studiū profiterentur. Poterat autè excusabilis videri hæc illorū ostentatio, cùm cer tam vestitus formam Deus summo Pontifici in Lege præscripsisset, & priuatis quoque hominibus mandauisset, ut Legis præcipua Capita in fimbriis vestium descripta gestarent, ut his vtis sui officij nunquam non admonerentur. Sed nihilominus istos tam duriter tractat Dominus, eò quòd nihil minus cogitarent, quàm quod Deus monuerat: omne verò hoc faciebant, ut sese apud imperitum populum inani fuco venditarent. Quod autem in vestitu faciebat, hoc ipsum in ieiunijs, in precibus, in eleemosynis, abolutionibus crebris & alijs infinitis fiebat: quæ omnia ad sanctimoniæ fucata ostentationem erant instituta. Nō temere autè ab eo orditur Christus, & alibi frequenter hypocritas dicit: quia ut populo imponebant simulato pietatis prætextu, ita eo nomine Deo in primis exosi erant. Is enim cùm veritas sit, in veritate etiā adorari atque coli vult, & proinde religioni verae nullus locus esse poterit, ubicunque simulatio siue hypocrisis regnat, quæ semper cū mendacio coniuncta est. Secundò ambitione quoq; et priuatæ gloriæ studiū, quo ardebant, ex signis describit, quádo eos salutationes in foris, et primos cōsessus in conuentibus, primosq; in cœnis accubitus amare dicit. Atqui salutare aut salutari per se neq; iniustū neq; inhonestū est. Sunt enim hæc officia charitatis, ad quæ hoc etiā perti net, ut quisq; alii honore præueniat. Sed hic de ambitiosis salutationū formulis sermo est, quas ambi tiosi affectare, & adulatores nimium seruiliter usurpare solent. Ideo apud Matthæum Rabbini titulus adducitur, quo sibi ipsis multifariam Legis cognitione & perfecta doctrinæ excellentiā uendicabant, ut supra omnes alios eminerent. Accedebant his titulis subsellioru gradus in conuentibus tam publicis quàm ecclesiasticis, & quòd ad conuiuia inuitati in summa mensa accumbere cupiebāt. Erat hæc intolerabilis ambitionis argumenta, quæ cùm nemine deceat, in primis tamen in illis turpissima est, qui omnibus alijs ad humilitatē & modestiam magistri esse debebant.
