Accedebat his malis quod hæc omnia superabat: falsa nimirū doctrina, et quæ ex hac nascebatur totius diuini cultus prophana tio. Speciem huius adducit preces, quæ ut maximè necessariæ nobis sunt, ita illis Deus præcipuè delectatur, si ex corde fide & charitate prædito proficiscantur. Quid verò illi? In publico orabant, ut Matth.6.cap.habetur, & simul preces suas alijs uendebat, ut mercenarij operam suam alijs elocare solent, idq; in eum finem, ut sub illarum prætextu domus viduarum devorarent, & ita non gloriæ mo-dò, uerumetiam quæstui suo consulerent. Id verò absq; falsa doctrina fieri nō poterat, cùm prius omni bus hoc persuaderi oporteret, ut salutem suam ipsorum conductitijs precationibus promoueri puta-rent. Quod autè precando fecerūt, hoc ipsum eos in toto cultu Dei fecisse apparet ex ijs, quæ Matth. 15.cap.dicuntur, & quod templū ab illis emporiū factū fuisse legimus. Et quāuis fraus ista ad totum populū extenderetur, in præsenti tamen uiduarū mentionem facit Dominus, partim quòd muliebris sexus ad superstitiones procliuior est, & præ alijs uiduæ facilius inseccatur: partim ut scelerū atroci tatem aggrauet, quo ijs potissimum insidiabātur, quarum eos misereri decuerat, & quas Deus omni-bus, qui uel in Repub. uel Ecclesia excellunt, uult esse commendatissimas. Amplificationi etiam feruit, quòd domus uiduarum ab illis devorari dicit, ut avaritiam insatiabilem & cum extrema crudelitate coniunctam eis exprobret. Fons omnis huius mali erat propriæ iustitiæ fiducia, quaineb ria ti populo etiam authores erant, ut salutem non in Dei misericordia, sed in suorum operum meritis quærerent, ut alibi prolixè diximus.
units.tr: Just as the obedience owed to provincial governors ceases when they, faithless to their kings, overthrow the authority of the laws and stir the people to revolt, so obedience is not owed to those ministers of the Churches who, in place of the Word of God, introduce human traditions and, in place of true worship, superstitions. This must be observed with regard to those who cry out that we are the most harmful authors of schism and heretics, because we have fallen away from the Roman Church, and who throw in our faces Paul, who testifies that the faith of that Church was once proclaimed throughout the whole world. But we are not now arguing about what that Church once was. Indeed, we wish that we might one day be allowed to see some traces of its ancient integrity. We are looking at the present state of affairs there, and since we can see nothing but human inventions and a Simony joined with profane contempt of God and the grossest superstitions, we have, following Christ's warning, come out of that Babylon, so that we might not one day be struck with the same plagues. We know indeed that some men are far too secure, promising themselves impunity if they do not invent errors on their own account but follow those who are called leaders and pastors of the Church and are held to be lawful ministers. But we think that saying of Christ was not spoken carelessly: "If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the pit." And since he cries out here, as elsewhere, that we should beware of impostors, those cannot be free of blame who deceive themselves through a lazy credulity and allow themselves to be deceived by others. For it is the duty of Christian men not merely to hold a simple knowledge of the truth, but to be furnished with judgment, so that they can distinguish among the doctrines that are put before them, embrace what is true, and shun and flee what is false. Christ gives this warning when he says: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. But they will not follow a stranger; they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers." Rightly, therefore, the Apostles admonished: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Likewise: "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God." In this passage John also prescribes a rule by which all spirits, that is, all doctrines, ought to be tested; and since he wishes this rule to be common to all Christians, no one should be blamed for rejecting doctrines that depart from it. To this too should be referred what Paul wills, that judgment on prophecy belongs to those who sit in the Church, that is, to those who hear the teachers as disciples. See 1 Corinthians 14. And this should also be referred to the fact that Christ describes those Scribes in order to show that they are worthy to be avoided by those whom a serious concern for their own salvation touches. For he says: "Beware of the Scribes, who love to walk about in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and the chief places at feasts; who devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers." The sum is that they sought neither the glory of God nor the salvation of men, but were given over to hypocrisy, ambition and greed, and therefore were unworthy to be heard. But he proves by signs the charges that he brings against them. The first concerns the fact that he says they delight in long robes. In Greek a stole is any garment, so called from stellesthai [ἀπὸ τῆς στέλλεσθαι], because it serves to adorn and dignify a man. Among the Latins, however, the word is used for a longer garment, which reaches down to the ankles and covers the whole body; and among the Romans it was the dress of noble matrons alone. Eventually the robes of priests began to be called by this name, because these too were longer, so that their greater dignity and authority might be evident. And indeed it becomes the ministers of the Church and the teachers of doctrine to dress more honourably, so that they may at the same time bear witness to their modesty and the gravity of their conduct; and those deserve severe reproof who debase the dignity of the sacred ministry with a buffoon's or a soldier's dress, or even with a more effeminate attire. Yet Christ accuses the Scribes of the Jews of this, that they feigned holiness by those robes and abused them for hypocrisy. For, as we read in Matthew, they used to make the fringes of their robes broader, which were called phylacteries, because on them they wore the principal chapters of the Law written out. They were accustomed to widen and extend these, so that they might profess a more eager zeal for piety. This display of theirs could perhaps seem excusable, since God had prescribed in the Law the exact form of the garment for the High Priest, and had also commanded private men to wear the principal chapters of the Law written on the fringes of their garments, so that they would never fail to be reminded of their duty by them. But nevertheless the Lord treats these men so harshly, because they thought nothing less of what God had enjoined, and they did all this so that they might display themselves in a vain varnish before an unlearned people. What they did in their dress, they did also in fasts, in prayers, in almsgiving, in frequent washings and in countless other things; all of which were instituted for a pretended display of holiness. Christ does not begin this charge lightly, and elsewhere he often calls them hypocrites, because, as they imposed upon the people under a feigned pretext of piety, so they were especially hateful to God on that account. For God, since he is truth, wishes to be worshipped and honoured also in truth; and therefore true religion can have no place wherever simulation or hypocrisy reigns, which is always joined with falsehood. Secondly, he describes by signs the ambition and the zeal for private glory with which they burned, when he says that they love greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the chief places at feasts. Yet to greet or to be greeted is not in itself unjust or dishonourable. These are duties of charity, and to them also belongs the practice of each one anticipating another with honour. But here the discussion is of ambitious forms of greeting, which ambitious men are accustomed to aim at, and which flatterers use with too much servility. Therefore in Matthew the title of Rabbi is mentioned, by which they claimed for themselves, on the ground of their manifold knowledge of the Law and their perfect excellence in doctrine, that they should stand out above all others. To these titles were added the rank of seats in assemblies, both public and ecclesiastical, and the desire, when invited to banquets, to recline at the head of the table. These were evidences of intolerable ambition; and while such ambition is unbecoming in anyone, it is most shameful in those who ought to have been teachers to all others in humility and modesty. Added to these evils was something that surpassed them all: false doctrine, and from it the profanation of the whole divine worship. He adduces prayer as an instance of this, which, as it is most necessary for us, so God especially delights in it, if it proceeds from a heart endowed with faith and charity. But what did they do? They prayed in public, as is found in Matthew 6, and at the same time they sold their prayers to others, as hired workmen are accustomed to hire out their labour to others; and they did this with the aim that under the pretext of those prayers they might devour widows' houses, and so look after not only their glory but also their gain. This could not have been done without false doctrine, since everyone had first to be persuaded that their salvation could be promoted by prayers bought from them. And that they did this in prayer, they clearly did in the whole worship of God, as is evident from what is said in Matthew 15, and we read that the Temple was made by them a marketplace. And although this fraud extended to the whole people, the Lord mentions widows in the present passage, partly because the female sex is more inclined to superstitions and widows are more easily ensnared than others, and partly to aggravate the atrocity of their crimes, since they lay in wait especially for those whom they ought to have pitied, and whom God wishes to be most commended by all who excel either in the commonwealth or in the Church. This also serves to amplify the charge, that he says they devoured widows' houses, so as to reproach them with insatiable greed joined with the utmost cruelty. The source of all this evil was confidence in their own righteousness, which also made them the authors for the people of seeking salvation not in the mercy of God but in the merits of their own works, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

units.la: Ista uero de Iudæorum Scribis ita dici cogitemus, ut discamus, omnes eos fugiendos esse, quicunque etiam hodie Dei cultum & doctrinam sua hypocrisi, ambitione & avaritia corrumpunt. Ex his ergo iudicemus de nostri sæculi impostoribus, qui cum successione apostolica glorientur, & sibi eo nomine in Ecclesia primatum vendicent, istorum tamen adeo sunt similes, ut Christi non minus de ipsis quàm illis locutus esse iurare possis. Quæ enim hypocrisis unquam in orbe terrarum fuit, quæ tot uestiu generibus atq; formis, tot ceremoniis & ritibus, tot uanissimarum superstitionum exercitijs sese uenditarit? In Scribis istis stolas reprehendit Christus, quibus maiorem sanctimoniæ speciem uænabantur. Quid ergo dicturus fuisset de theatrico sacrificio uestitu, quem ex Iudaismo in Ecclesiam Pontifices transtulerunt? de cucullis, liripipijs, humeralibus, cingulis, nodosis, calceis fenestratis ac ligneis, pileis quadratis, uarijs capillorum confuris, cilicijs deniq;, & sexcentis alijs, quibus improbissimi hypocritæ carnis mortificationem, uitæ innocentiam, divini amoris ardorem, humilitate, sanctitatem, omnisq; pietatis studium mentiuntur? De ambitione uero eorum quid dicere opus est, quam multis iam sæculis historiæ potentissimis quoq; Regibus intolerabile fuisse testantur? Et cur Regibus parcerent, qui quæ ad Christi folium meritu pertinent sibi uendicant, nequicquam illo per Prophetam clamante: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo? Auaritiam uero eorundem quis bonus non detestetur, quando nihil in tota rerum natura est, quod rapaces isti Chananæi non in suum quæstum converterint? ut iam nihil dicamus de interceptis patrimonijs aliorum, & uaferrimis artibus, quibus sub religionis prætextu nobilissimas frere omnium gentium familias ad egestatem redegerunt. Eo certè illorum fraudibus res Christiana eò deducta est, ut ubi il li dominantur, nemini gratis uel nasci uel mori liceat, imò ne per mortem quidem ungues eorum licet effugere. Et hi illi sunt, qui simul uiribus aucti, principes quoque & Reges in suas partes pertraxerunt, ut uolentes nolentes, ipsorum tyrannidem tueri cogantur: & ijdem passim piorum capitibus insultant, sibiq; omnia impune licere putant. Sed non dormitat iustus Deus, & (ut Christus hic minatur) gravius iudicium isti ferent, ubi mensuram suam impleuerint, & ille propter electos suos mundi huius ætatem decurtauerit. Neminem igitur illorum hypocrisis fallat, neminem fastus ille Persicus decipiat, neminem minæ & excommunicationum fulmina terreant: sed illis procul relictis ad unum Iesum Christum conuertamur, qui suo sanguine redemptam Ecclesiam ex illorum unquibus aliquando afferet, & in se credentes uera felicitate beabit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: We should understand what is said here about the scribes of the Jews in such a way as to learn that we must flee from all those who even today corrupt the worship and teaching of God by their hypocrisy, ambition and greed. Let us therefore judge by these men the impostors of our own age, who boast of apostolic succession and claim for themselves the primacy in the Church on that ground. Yet they are so like those scribes that you could swear Christ spoke no less of them than of the others. For what hypocrisy has ever existed in the world that has displayed itself in so many kinds and shapes of clothing, so many ceremonies and rites, so many exercises of the most empty superstitions? Christ rebuked those scribes for their long robes, by which they hunted after a greater appearance of holiness. What, then, would he have said about the theatrical sacrificial vestments which the Pontiffs have carried over from Judaism into the Church? About hoods, liripipes, shoulder cloths, girdles, knotted cords, perforated and wooden shoes, square caps, various tonsures of the hair, and finally hair shirts, and six hundred other things by which the most wicked hypocrites feign the mortification of the flesh, innocence of life, the fervour of divine love, humility, holiness and every zeal for piety? As for their ambition, what need is there to speak of it, when histories testify that for many centuries it has been intolerable even to the most powerful kings? And why would they spare kings, when they claim for themselves what belongs to the glory of Christ alone, though God cries out through the prophet in vain: "I am the Lord; that is my name, and I will not give my glory to another"? And as for the greed of these same men, who good man would not detest it, when in the whole of nature there is nothing that these rapacious Canaanites have not turned to their own profit? To say nothing yet of the seizing of others' inheritances, and of the most cunning arts by which, under the pretext of religion, they have reduced the most noble families of almost all nations to poverty. Truly, by their frauds the Christian cause has been brought to such a state that where they rule, no one may be born or die freely, and not even through death may anyone escape their claws. And these are the men who, having grown strong in power, have also drawn princes and kings to their side, so that, willing or unwilling, these rulers are forced to defend their tyranny; and the same men everywhere trample on the heads of the godly and think that they may do everything with impunity. But the righteous God does not sleep, and (as Christ threatens here) they will bear a heavier judgment when they have filled up their measure, and he will cut short the age of this world for the sake of his elect. Let no one, therefore, be deceived by their hypocrisy, let no one be taken in by that Persian pride, let no one be frightened by their threats and the thunderbolts of excommunications; but, leaving them far behind, let us turn to Jesus Christ alone, who will rescue the Church, redeemed by his blood, from their claws at last, and will bless with true happiness those who believe in him. To him alone belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXIII.

units.la: INtuitus autem vidit divites mittentes munera sua in gazophylacium. Vidit autem etiam quandam viduam pauperculam mittentem illuc minuta duo. Et dixit: Verè dico vobis, vidua hæc pauper misit amplius quàm omnes. Nam omnes hi ex eo, quod ipsis redundat, miserunt quod donarent Deo; hæc autem misit ex penuria sua totum victum, quem habebat.
units.tr: Looking up, he saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury. He also saw a poor widow putting in two small coins. And he said: Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For all these gave out of their abundance what they offered to God, but she out of her poverty put in all the living she had.

units.la: Magna cum gravitate nuper Iesus Christus totum populum monuit, ut à Scribis & Sacerdotibus sibi caveat, & huius admonitionis duas causas adduxit: Vnam, quòd priuatam gloriam diuinæ præferant, neque curent ut ministerium suum Deo probetur, sed ut ipsi apud omnes in honore & pretio sint. Alteram, quòd commodo priuato addicti salutem populi facilè negligant, imò sub falso religionis simulatæ & precum longarum prætextu domus uiduarum ac pupillorum ac papillorum devorent. Erat haec non tam grauis quàm necessaria admonitio, eò quòd qui tales doctores siue duces sequuntur, ij non possunt non cum illis in eandem foueam errorum & exitij incidere. Porrò periculum erat, ne qui his auditis Ecclesiæ ordinem turbarent, & ex corruptis antistitum moribus occasione sumpta, nihil porrò conferendum esse arbitrarentur ad cultū Dei & doctrinam, quæ duo omnibus piis commendatissima esse debent. Commodè ergo ijs, quæ præcesserunt, hanc historiam Lucas subtexit, qua docetur non propterea abolendas esse sacras illas pecuniarū collectas siue contributiones, quas Deus ipse instituit: monet item, quo affectu pij in illis duci, quiùe scopus omnibus propositus esse debeat. Itaq; non indigna est historia, cuius singulæ partes ex ordine considerentur.
units.tr: Not long ago Jesus Christ, with great seriousness, warned the whole people to beware of the scribes and priests, and he gave two reasons for this warning. The first was that they sought their own glory above the glory of God, and did not care that their ministry should be approved before God, but that they themselves should be held in honour and esteem by all. The second was that, being devoted to private gain, they easily neglected the welfare of the people, and indeed, under the pretext of a feigned religion and long prayers, devoured the houses of widows and orphans. This admonition was not so much grave as necessary, because those who follow such teachers or leaders cannot but fall with them into the same pit of error and ruin. Moreover, there was a danger that some, having heard these things, would disturb the order of the Church, and, taking occasion from the corrupt morals of the leaders, would judge that nothing further was to be contributed to the worship and doctrine of God, though these two things ought to be most commended to all the godly. Luke therefore fittingly appends this story to what has gone before, a story which teaches that those sacred collections or contributions of money, which God himself instituted, are not on that account to be abolished. It also teaches with what disposition the godly ought to give in them, and what aim ought to be set before all. So the story is not unworthy of attention, and its individual parts deserve to be considered in order.

units.la: Primum Christus diuites uidisse dicitur, qui munera sua in gazophylacium inferebant. Marcus cum consedisse scribit ex aduerso, ut spectator esset huius rei. Nihil ergo hic ab illo temere factum aut dictum est, eoq; diligentius attentiusq; audiri debent & obseruari quæ dicuntur. Fuit autem Gazophylacium (ut Iosephus libro septimo de bello Iudaico capite undecimo annotauit) locus certus in templo, sic dictus, quòd illuc pecuniæ & opes sacræ reponerentur: & arcæ erant complures, in quas donaria sua deponebant, qui aliquid in publicū templi usum conferre statuerant. Arcas hasce in Ioæ Regis Iuda historia descriptas inuenies. Habuit autem omnibus seculis Ecclesia publicas opes, quas à populo iusta & certa cum ratione collegit. Æquum enim esset, ut quando Dei cultus ex æquo ad omnes pertinet, omnium item saluti seruiunt sacra illa fidei atq; religionis externa exercitia, omnes quoque ad ea retinenda sumptus atq; impensas conferant. Ideo olim censum populi Deus instituit, in quo quicunq; annum ætatis uigesimū attigerant aut supergressi erant, siclum conferebant, ut ex ea pecunia sarta tecta tabernaculi aut templi instaurarentur. Quem morè postea quorundam incuria abolitum sub Ioa Rege reduxit Ioiada Sacerdos, & in eodem reducendo posterioris ex Babylone Nehemiam quoq; diligentissimum fuisse legimus. A quo tempore ad Christum usq; durauit, neq; ab eo improbatus fuit unquam, licet interdum in Sacerdotum auaritiam atq; rapacitatem seuerius & uehementius inuehatur. Taceo nunc quæ de decimis in Lege Mosis traduntur, quas an ce legem quoq; patrum tempore Sacerdotibus datas fuisse, ex Abrahami & Melchizedeki historia apparet: & quas bona fide reddendas esse Haggæus & Malachias aperte docent. Post Christi uero ascensionem in cœlos, in exordio nascentis Ecclesiæ, Apostolos quoq; cura ista non parum solicitos habuit, ut communē & publicum ærarium Ecclesiæ pararetur, ex quo & pauperes ali & alia perficipi possent, quæ ad Ecclesiam seruandam atque regendam sunt necessaria. Nec dubium est totis illis annis fere trecentis, quibus Christiani diris & continuis persecutionibus exagitati fuerunt usque ad Constantini Magni tempora, hunc morem obseruatum esse, ut Ecclesiæ singulæ suos ministros alerent ex ijs, quæ publicè pro uniuscuiusque fortunis aut facultatibus conferebantur. Ita enim Apostolorum temporibus factitatum fuisse, ex Pauli ad Corinthios uerbis apparet, quibus docet tam sibi quàm alijs licuisse, ut ab Ecclesijs uictum exigerent, ne hunc suo labore sibi parare cogerentur. Et nota est Macedonum liberalitas, qui Paulum apud alias Ecclesias agentem aluerunt, ut illis posset gratis inseruire. Neque aliter fieri potuit usque ad Constantini Imperium, cum ante hoc nunquam ea pace & tranquilitate usæ sint Ecclesiæ, ut certos redditus constituere possent, ex quibus sacrorum & ministrorum impensæ fierent. Ab eo tempore autem res in melius constitutæ sunt, & principum Christianorum nobiliumq; hominum liberalitate Ecclesiæ ditari cœperunt decimarum deinde collatio restituta est, sicuti uetustissimarum Ecclesiarum atque Collegiorum fundationes & quæ de his passim extant instrumenta seu tabulæ publicæ testantur. Et ista quidem scire opus est propter eos, qui sub religionis Ecclesiasticæ & Christianæ prætextu immunitatem quærunt, & ne decimas aut alios census agrorum domuumque reddere cogantur, horum omnium initia atque originem ad Papatum referunt, quasi Pontificum & Monachorum auaritia atque rapacitas in hac etiam parte Iudaismum nobis reduxerit. Fatemur quidem illorum artibus atq; dolis collegiorum atq; templorum opes in immensum auctas esse, & multos falsa doctrina & inanibus conscientiæ terriculamentis circumuentos bona sua, fraudatis legitimis haeredibus, harpyiarum istarum nidis atque lustris legauisse: id uero de omnibus decimis & antiquioribus Ecclesiarum redditibus nequaquam dici debet. Iustæ enim illæ opes sunt, utpote ab illis donatæ, qui eas donandi ius habebant, & quos Dei amor atque synterum pietatis studium, ut illas donarent, commouit. Neciam de iniquos tate aliquis conqueri potest merito, quando praedia & agri ea conditione per haereditatem aut contractum aliquem ad nos deveniunt, ut ex illis decimas aut quoscunque alios census ijs reddamus, quibus illa debentur. Neque hic audiri debent, qui corruptos antistitum sive ministrorum Ecclesiae mores turpemq; opum istarum abusum accusant. Nam etsi isti graviter peccent, & olim rationem Deo reddituri sint, qui sacrilegam eorum petulantiam non inultam sinet: nemo tamen propterea debito liberatur, quo semetipsum obstrinxit, quando praedia eiusmodi vel hereditario iure sibi vendicavit, vel emptione legitima acquisivit. Nam ut ad Prophetarum tempora redeamus, constat ex Haggai & Malachiae sermonibus, Sacerdotes tunc in officio suo admodum ignavos & perfidos fuisse: idem tamen populi ingratitudinem atque impostauras, quibus plerique in decimandis terrae proventibus utebantur, acerrime accusant. Quid vero de istis dicemus, quos paulo ante Christus accusavit, quod viduarum ac orphanorum domus devorent, & quos alibi lupos rapaces, fures ac latrones dixit? Num propter illos populum abstterret, ne quid in Gazophylacium conferant? num indignum esse clamat illis a populo luxuriae & superbiae fomenta subministrari? Imo potius viduae istius synceram pietatem & liberalitatem sanctissimam commendat, divitum vero sorditiem non obscure perstringit. Et quod initio monuimus, ut spectator, vel potius iudicis instar considet, ut tam de his quam de illis sententiam proferat: & ea occasione doceat, quid nobis in hac causa sit agendum. Nec quisquam dubitare debet, illum hodie etiam nostrarum actionum inspectorem esse: & qui olim Caesari prophano & impio reddere iussit, quae ad eum pertinebant, idem nequaquam vult, ut Evangelij sui & libertatis merito eius partae praetextu abutamur ad captandam immunitatem, qua debita aliis officia negemus.
units.tr: First, Christ is said to have seen the rich who were putting their gifts into the treasury. Mark writes that he sat down opposite, so that he might watch this. Nothing, therefore, was said or done by him rashly, and so what is said should be heard and observed all the more diligently and attentively. Now the Gazophylacium (as Josephus noted in the eleventh chapter of the seventh book of the Jewish War) was a fixed place in the temple, so called because money and sacred treasures were stored there; and there were several chests into which those who had resolved to contribute something to the public use of the temple placed their gifts. You will find these chests described in the history of Joash, king of Judah. The Church has always had public resources, which it gathered from the people by a just and fixed reckoning. For since the worship of God pertains equally to all, and those sacred external exercises of faith and religion serve the salvation of all, it would be fair that all should also contribute the expenses and costs of keeping them up. Therefore God once instituted a census of the people, in which whoever had reached or passed the twentieth year of age paid a shekel, so that from that money the tabernacle or temple might be repaired and kept in good condition. Later, this custom had fallen into disuse through the negligence of some, but under King Joash, Jehoiada the priest restored it; and we read that Nehemiah, after the return from Babylon, was also most diligent in restoring it. From that time down to Christ it continued, and it was never disapproved by him, although at times he attacked the avarice and rapacity of the priests more severely and vehemently. I pass over now what is handed down about the tithes in the law of Moses, and which, as the histories of Abraham and Melchizedek show, were given to priests even under the law of the fathers; and which Haggai and Malachi clearly teach must be paid in good faith. After Christ's ascension into heaven, at the beginning of the newborn Church, the Apostles too were not a little anxious about this matter, so that a common and public treasury of the Church might be provided, from which the poor could be supported and the other things could be supplied which are necessary for preserving and governing the Church. And there is no doubt that throughout those nearly three hundred years, during which Christians were harassed by dreadful and continual persecutions up to the time of Constantine the Great, this custom was observed, that each Church supported its own ministers from what was publicly contributed according to each person's means and resources. For that this was the practice in the times of the Apostles appears from Paul's words to the Corinthians, in which he teaches that it was lawful both for himself and for others to demand their sustenance from the Churches, so that they would not be forced to provide it for themselves by their own labour. And the generosity of the Macedonians is well known, who supported Paul while he was working among other Churches, so that he could serve them without charge. Nor could it have been otherwise until the empire of Constantine, since before this the Churches never enjoyed such peace and tranquillity that they could establish fixed revenues from which the costs of worship and ministers could be met. From that time, however, matters were set on a better footing, and through the generosity of Christian princes and noblemen the Churches began to be enriched; then the collection of tithes was restored, as the foundations of the most ancient Churches and colleges, and the public deeds and charters that survive about them everywhere, bear witness. These things indeed it is necessary to know because of those who, under the pretext of the ecclesiastical and Christian religion, seek immunity, and so that they may not be compelled to pay tithes or other taxes on their fields and houses. They trace the beginnings and origin of all these things to the Papacy, as though the avarice and rapacity of the Pontiffs and monks had in this respect also brought Judaism back upon us. We admit indeed that through their arts and tricks the wealth of colleges and temples was increased beyond measure, and that many, deceived by false doctrine and by empty terrors of conscience, bequeathed their goods to those nests and dens of harpies, defrauding their lawful heirs. But this must by no means be said of all tithes and of the older revenues of the Churches. For those riches are lawful, being given by those who had the right to give them, and who were moved to give them by love of God and a sincere zeal for piety. Nor can anyone rightly complain of injustice when estates and fields come to us by inheritance or some contract on the condition that we pay from them tithes or whatever other dues are owed to those to whom they belong. Nor should those be heard who accuse the corrupt morals of the leaders or ministers of the Church and the shameful abuse of these riches. For although they sin grievously, and one day will have to give account to God, who will not leave their sacrilegious wantonness unpunished, yet no one is on that account released from the debt by which he bound himself when he claimed such estates by hereditary right or acquired them by lawful purchase. For, to return to the times of the Prophets, it is clear from the sermons of Haggai and Malachi that the priests then were very slothful and faithless in their office; yet the same prophets most bitterly accuse the ingratitude of the people and the deceits by which many cheated in the tithing of the produce of the land. But what shall we say of those whom Christ accused a little before, because they devour the houses of widows and orphans, and whom elsewhere he called ravenous wolves, thieves and robbers? Does he on their account frighten the people away from putting anything into the treasury? Does he cry out that it is unworthy that the people should supply them with fuel for luxury and pride? Rather, he commends the sincere piety and most holy generosity of that widow, and plainly rebukes the meanness of the rich. And, as we said at the beginning, he sits as a spectator, or rather as a judge, so that he may pronounce sentence on both the one and the other, and on that occasion teach us what we ought to do in this matter. Nor should anyone doubt that he is today also the observer of our actions; and he who once ordered that what belonged to Caesar be given to Caesar, the profane and impious ruler, does not in any way want us to abuse the pretext of his Gospel and of the liberty gained by his merit in order to seek immunity by which we deny the duties owed to others.

units.la: Quia vero ista spectare solet, simul nos meminisse oportet, illum eos etiam videre, qui opes Ecclesiasticas, sacrilega audacia ad se rapiunt, aut saltem illas in usos illicitos atque prophanos convertunt. Itaque opus est, ut de earundem usu vero & legitimo frequenter cogitemus. Vulgo hodie Ecclesiastica bona dicuntur, quaecunque ad templorum aerarium pertinent, aut Collegijs debentur. Unde nos colligimus, non alium illorum usum esse debere, quam ut Ecclesiae necessitatibus serviant. Haec autem (ut alibi monuimus) duo habet prae alijs, quae sine pecuniis sive impensis sustentari non possunt: Religionem nimirum externam & pauperes, quos nobis Dei Filius tanto studio commendavit, ut quoad externa charitatis officia, eos sibi substituerent. Ad religionem doctrina & Sacramenta pertinent, utrunque vero coetus publicos requirit, qui ut non nisi certo statoque tempore colligi possunt, ita loco etiam certo & a prophanis usibus separato ad illos colligendos opus est. Ista vero omnia absque impensis parare & servare impossibile fuerit. Exigit praeterea natura Lex (ut alibi docuimus) ut qui Ecclesiae docendo serviunt, & sacris exercitijs vacat, ex illo suo ministerio victum sive stipendium legitimum recipiant. Turpe enim foret, agricolam ex agrorum cultu, pastorem ex ovibus, militem ex militia vivere, Ecclesiam vero, quae Dei arvum atque grex est, suis cultoribus atque pastoribus victum negare, vel eos negligere, qui nunquam non in acie consistunt, ut eius salutem adversus mundum et huius principem, diabolum, tueantur. Ut vero doctrina in Ecclesijs perpetua sit, scholis quoque opus est, in quibus instituti & eruditi homines Verbi administris iam ob aetatem rudes donatis, aut etiam facto suo defunctis succedant. Vidit hoc olim impius ille apostata Iulianus, qui Christianis interdicebat, ne vel gentium scholas adirent, vel ipsi proprias haberent, in quibus bonarum literarum & religionis principia traderentur. Ita enim sperabat fore, ut omni rerum cognitioni destituti fidem suam nullis vel scripturis vel argumentis idoneis tueri possent. Adeo sum ergo opus Ecclesiae id quoq; pertinet, ut ex illis stipendia constituantur bonarum artium & sacrae Theologiae professoribus, & iuvenes bonae indolis alantur, qui aliquando ad Verbi ministerium vocari possint. Quod quam necesse sit res ipsa docet, quando opulentiores fere ministerij pudet, & raro inveniuntur, qui suos ad hoc instituti urent, pauperiores vero tantis sumptibus non sufficiunt, nisi publice ad iuvenitur. Restant pauperes, quos nunquam defuturos esse in Ecclesia Christus palam testatur, et olim Moses quoque monuit. Et quia illi non minima Ecclesiae pars sunt, & idem Christi Iesu in hoc mundo pauperis ac egeni imaginem gerunt, non possunt a nobis negligi, nisi in illum impij simus, cuius discipulos atque cultores nos esse profitemur. Fuerunt illi Apostolis ita curae, ut sub initium primitivae Ecclesiae, ipsimet bonorum illorum administrationem in se reciperent, ex quibus illi alebantur: postea vero cum docendi necessitate se alio vocari sentirent, curam hanc non nisi perspectae fidei & probitatis hominibus committi voluerunt, quos a Spiritu Sancto gubernari atq; regi constaret. Et scimus vetustissimum hunc Ecclesiae morem esse, ut dominicis diebus collectae fiant in pauperum subventionem, atque illum ab Apostolis institutum esse, ex ultimo capite prioris ad Corinthios satis apparet. Cum autem pauperes unicuique privatim commendatissimi esse debeant, multo magis Ecclesiam totam decet, ut suos domesticos curet, & publicis eleemosynis eorum egestatem subleuet, quibus privatorum hominum beneficentia non sufficit. Ubi in primis cauere oportet, ne publica egestatis exempla fiant, qui eiusdem corporis nobiscum membra sunt sub capite Christo, quem perinde ut nos redemptorem atque Dominum suum profitentur. Ut enim hoc cum Dei Lege pugnat, qui ne mendicus sit in Israele graviter admodum prohibuit; ita scimus mendicatione bonis moribus vehementer officere, & eam nobis parere homines ἀτάκτως, qui nullo vel politicae vel Ecclesiasticae disciplinae freno continentur, & quos ideo Paulus vitare iubet, ne Ecclesiae opprobrio sint. At quia de his saepe aliàs diximus, nunc illud teneamus, proprium erarij Ecclesiastici usum esse, ut ex eo doctrinae antistites aut publici Ecclesiae ministri alantur una cum Scholarum professoribus & Theologiae candidatis: deinde ut ex eodem parentur atq; instaurentur loca sacra cum vasis & aliis ad Sacramentorum administrationem necessariis: postremo, ut pauperibus atque egenis subveniatur, ne in his ipse Christus esuriat atque algeat. Graue ergo illorum scelus & omni detestatione dignum sacrilegium est, opes illas in usum alienum convertere, sive id publicè sive privatim fiat. Est tamen illud nimis vulgare & frequens hodie. In Papatu enim illas sibi vendicant ignaui Pe-nelopes sponsi, qui cum soli nomen cleri ad se pertinere contendant, tamen neq; Ecclesiae serviunt, neque ita vivunt, ut pro germanis eius membris agnosci possint. Inter eos autem qui Euangelij nomine atq; doctrina gloriantur, & religionis reformatae sectatores videri volunt, impudentissimè thesauri illi sacri distrahuntur, multis illorū partem sibi privatim rapientibus, aliis quicquid reliquum est in fiscum congerentibus, ut ex illis insana aedificia extruant, arces condant, urbium munitiones extruant, aulicorum ignauam turbam alant, bombardas aliaque ad fundendum sanguinem Christianum excogitata arma fabricent, militibus deniq; sanguinarijs stipendia sua dissoluant. Fit ergo ut alijs ex Ecclesia ditescentibus, qui huius labes & maculae dici poterant, ministri eius fideles cum inopia & fame conflictentur, Scholae frigeant, doctissimi quiq; dilabantur, pauperes item cum turpissima Euangelicae doctrinae ignominia inter eos stipem & victu mendicent, qui illam pessimè oderunt, & prorsus extinctam volunt. Conqueruntur de his optimi quique, sed qui vitijs istis corrigendis manum admoueant pauci sunt: quia principibus viris durum videtur praedam illam ex manibus amittere, cuius dulcedine iampridem infecati sunt. At non dormitat Deus, qui ut olim in sacrilegos horrenda edidit iudiciorum suorum exempla, quae alibi recitauimus: ita postremis quoq; istis temporibus omnes eos puniet, qui Ecclesiarum opes vel violenter diripiunt, vel dolo malo dissipant. Et qui in praesenti tam diligens eorum spectator fuit, quae apud Gazophylacium fiebant, procul dubio istorum quoq; rapinas atq; impostouras videt, & olim male administratae dispensationis rationem ab illis exiget. Vt vero ista impijs illis opum sacrarum direptoribus dicuntur, ita non minus ad pauperes pertinent, qui ignauo otioditi labore omnem fugiunt: sed & ipsis pastoribus & doctrinae professoribus conueniunt, qui stipendia quidem ab Ecclesijs amplissima recipiunt, in officio autem suo nimium sunt negligentes, vel etiam suae conditionis obliti fastu atq; luxu cum opulentissimis quibusq; certant. Sed utinam tam facile esset omnium istorum vitia emendare, quam acerbè de illis conqueruntur, qui seriam Ecclesiarum & Rerumpub. reformationem expectant.
units.tr: Since this is the subject we ought always to keep in view, we should also remember that he sees those who seize the Church's wealth with sacrilegious audacity, or at least turn it to unlawful and profane uses. We must therefore often reflect on the true and lawful use of these goods. Today what is commonly called Church property is whatever belongs to the treasury of the temples or is owed to the colleges. From this we conclude that their use ought to be nothing other than to serve the needs of the Church. As we have noted elsewhere, these needs include two things above all others that cannot be maintained without money or expense: the external worship of religion, and the poor, whom the Son of God so earnestly commended to us that they might be his substitutes in the external duties of charity. Teaching and the sacraments belong to religion, and both require public assemblies. These cannot be gathered except at a fixed and appointed time, and so they also need a set place, separated from profane uses. All these things, however, cannot be provided and kept up without expense. Moreover, the law of nature requires (as we have taught elsewhere) that those who serve the Church by teaching and devote themselves to sacred duties should receive their living, that is, their lawful support, from that ministry. For it would be shameful for a farmer to live from tilling the fields, a shepherd from his sheep, a soldier from his service, and yet for the Church, which is God's field and flock, to deny sustenance to her cultivators and shepherds, or to neglect those who always stand in the battle line to defend her salvation against the world and its prince, the devil. So that doctrine may be perpetual in the churches, schools are also needed, in which learned men may be trained to succeed those minsters of the Word who have become too old and unfit, or who have finished their work. The impious apostate Julian saw this long ago. He forbade Christians to attend the schools of the Gentiles, or to have schools of their own in which the foundations of good letters and religion were taught. He hoped in this way that, lacking all knowledge of things, they would be unable to defend their faith with any suitable writings or arguments. Therefore it is also the task of the Church to fix stipends from these funds for teachers of the liberal arts and of sacred theology, and to support young men of good character who may one day be called to the ministry of the Word. How necessary this is the matter itself shows: the wealthier families are almost ashamed of the ministry, and rarely is anyone found who trains his own sons for it, while the poorer families cannot bear such expenses unless the young men are supported publicly. There remain the poor, whom Christ openly testifies will never be lacking in the Church, and whom Moses too warned us about long ago. And because they are no small part of the Church, and bear in this world the very image of Christ Jesus, who was poor and needy, they cannot be neglected by us unless we are impious toward him whose disciples and worshippers we profess to be. The Apostles cared for them so much that, at the beginning of the primitive Church, they themselves took on the administration of those goods from which the poor were fed. Later, when they felt themselves called elsewhere by the need to teach, they wished this care to be committed only to men of proven faith and integrity, whom it was plain were guided and ruled by the Holy Spirit. We know that this is the most ancient custom of the Church, that collections are made on the Lord's days for the relief of the poor, and that it was instituted by the Apostles is quite clear from the last chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians. But since the poor ought to be especially commended to each individual privately, much more does the whole Church owe it to them to look after its own members, and by public alms to relieve their want, which the beneficence of private persons does not suffice to meet. Here above all we must take care that members of the same body with us under the head Christ, whom they profess as their Redeemer and Lord just as we do, do not become public examples of poverty. For just as this conflicts with the law of God, who strictly forbade there to be beggars in Israel, so we know that begging greatly harms good morals and produces disorderly men [ἀτάκτως], who are restrained by no bridle of either civil or ecclesiastical discipline, and whom Paul therefore bids us avoid, lest they bring reproach upon the Church. But since we have often spoken of these matters elsewhere, let us now hold to this: the proper use of the ecclesiastical treasury is (1) that from it the teachers of doctrine, or the public ministers of the Church, be supported together with the professors of the schools and the candidates for theology; (2) that from it the sacred places be provided and restored, together with the vessels and other things necessary for the administration of the sacraments; and (3) finally, that help be given to the poor and needy, so that Christ himself may not hunger and thirst in them. It is therefore a grave crime and a sacrilege deserving all detestation to turn those resources to alien use, whether this is done publicly or privately. Yet this is far too common and frequent today. In the Papacy, the lazy suitors of Penelope lay claim to these goods; though they insist that only the name of the clergy belongs to them, they neither serve the Church nor live in such a way that they can be recognised as true members of her body. Among those who boast of the name and doctrine of the gospel, and wish to be seen as followers of the reformed religion, those sacred treasures are most shamelessly squandered: many privately seize a share for themselves, while others heap whatever remains into the public purse, so that from it they may build mad edifices, construct citadels, raise city fortifications, feed the idle crowd of courtiers, cast cannons and other weapons devised for shedding Christian blood, and finally pay their wages to bloodthirsty soldiers. And so it happens that, while others grow rich from the Church, who could be called its stains and blemishes, its faithful ministers struggle with want and hunger, the schools grow cold, the most learned men slip away, and the poor likewise beg alms and food, with the utmost shame to the gospel doctrine, from those who hate it most bitterly and want it utterly extinguished. The best men complain about these things, but few are those who lay a hand to correcting these vices, because it seems hard to the leading men to let go of the booty whose sweetness has long since infected them. But God does not sleep. Just as he long ago displayed terrible examples of his judgments against sacrilegious men, which we have recounted elsewhere, so in these last times too he will punish all those who either violently plunder the wealth of the Churches or waste it by fraud. And he who in the present age has watched so diligently what was done at the treasury will without doubt see the robberies and frauds of these men as well, and will demand from them an account of their mismanaged stewardship. Yet, just as these things are said of those impious plunderers of sacred goods, so they apply no less to the poor who, sunk in idle leisure, flee all labour; and they also apply to the ministers and teachers of doctrine themselves, who receive very generous stipends from the Churches but are too negligent in their office, or, forgetting their own station, vie in pride and luxury with the most opulent men. But would that it were as easy to correct all these faults as it is bitter to complain of them for those who await a serious reformation of the Churches and the commonwealth.

units.la: Porro ad huius loci historiam transeamus, ubi narratur, diuites quidem munera multa & magna in Gazophylacium misisse, uiduam vero quandam pauperculam eo contulisse minuta duo. Fuit hoc donum perquam exiguum, & indignum (si quis rem humano iudicio aestimet) quod inter sacra munera numeretur. At illud Christus qui non tam quid fieret quàm quo animo omnia fierent spectabat, magnis illis diuitiū donarijs praefert, dicens: Vere dico vobis, pauper haec vidua misit amplius quàm omnes. Poterat hoc παράδοξον & absurdum videri, perinde ac si quis duo plus esse diceret quàm decem: Sed (ut diximus) corda omnium istorum Christus inspexit, & ex animi intentione &
units.tr: Let us now turn to the history of this passage, where it is related that the rich put many large gifts into the treasury, but a certain poor widow put in two small coins. This gift was very small, and (if one judges the matter by human reckoning) unworthy to be counted among sacred offerings. But Christ, who looked not so much at what was done as at the spirit in which everything was done, prefers it to those great gifts of the rich, saying: "Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them." This might seem a paradox and absurd, as if someone should say that two is more than ten. But, as we said, Christ looked into the hearts of all these people and judged from the intention of their minds and the means each had.

units.la: Abusus bonorum Ecclesiae. facultatum cuiusq; ratione iudicium istud tulit. Ideo interpretationis loco subijcit: Nam omnes hi ex eo, quod ipsis redundat, miserunt quod donarunt Deo: hæc autem misit ex penuria sua totum victum quem habebat. Nec temere hæc à Christo dicta fuisse patebit, si rem ipsam propius inspiciamus. Scimus enim hanc communem esse regulam, dona omnia ex animo donantis æstimari debere, non ex eorum quæ donantur magnitudine aut tenuitate. Ideo bis dare dicitur, qui cito dat: & hilarè datorem diligit Dominus. Cum ergo diuites illi nō Dei cultúsue diuini studio munera sua in gazophylacium conijcerent, sed ambitione stimulati sese ostentarent, merito superati dicuntur fuisse auidua ipsa, quam nisi ardentissimus Dei amor accendisset, nunquam suum genium fuisset fraudatura, ut cultum illius adiuuaret. Deinde diuites illi non nisi partem aliquam ex suis facultatibus Deo decíderunt: ista uerò totum quod habebat contulit. Imò illi ea modò dederunt, quæ ipsis superflua erant: hæc uero substantiam simul omnem profudit. Quid uerò substantiam dico, quando uictum suum dedit, id est, hocipsum sine quo uictus ipsi nullus præterea reliquus erat? Quid uerò hoc aliud fuit, quam ipsam uitam ad prouehendū Dei cultum deponere? Vicit ergo mulierculæ huius pietas umbratilem illam omnium diuitum liberalitatem. Vicit omnem inopiæ & famis metum, quo multi superati nihil non sibi licere putant. Vicit scandalum omne, quod tunc ex corruptissimis sacerdotum moribus obijciebatur: qui certè tales erant, ut opulentissimos quosque, imò optimos quoq; absterrere possent, ne quid impijs istis & sacrilegis omnium sacrorum nundinatoribus largirentur. Sed non respexit uidua ista quid illi facerent, sed quid Deus iuberet cogitauit, quem dixisse sciebat: Nemo apparebit in conspectu Domini uacuus. Deut.16.
units.tr: Abuse of the goods of the Church. He passed that judgement according to the means of each person. So by way of explanation he adds: "For all these out of their abundance have put in gifts for God, but she out of her poverty has put in all the living that she had." Nor will it be clear that these words were spoken by Christ without reason, if we look more closely at the matter itself. For we know this to be the common rule: all gifts ought to be valued by the mind of the giver, not by the size or smallness of what is given. Hence he is said to give twice who gives quickly, and the Lord loves a cheerful giver. Therefore, since those rich men were putting their offerings into the treasury not out of zeal for God or for divine worship, but were showing off, stirred by ambition, they are rightly said to have been surpassed by her, whose ardent love of God alone could have moved her to give up her own livelihood, which she would never have forfeited unless to help that worship. Furthermore, those rich men gave only some part of their resources to God, but she gave up all that she had. Indeed, they gave only what was superfluous to them, but she poured out her entire substance. Why do I say substance, when she gave her living, that is, the very thing without which she had no other means of living? What else was this than to lay down life itself for the advancement of God's worship? So the piety of this poor woman outweighed the empty liberality of all the rich. It outweighed all fear of want and hunger, by which many, overcome, think nothing is allowed them. It outweighed every scandal that was then being thrown up against the most corrupt morals of the priests, who were certainly such that they could frighten away the most wealthy, indeed the best, from giving anything to those impious and sacrilegious dealers in all sacred things. But this widow did not regard what they would do, but thought about what God commanded, knowing that he had said: "No one shall appear before the Lord empty." Deut. 16.

units.la: Continet autem dictum illud Iesu Christi memorabilem doctrinam de oblationibus sacris, sub quarum titulo omnia ea quoque comprehenduntur, quæ egenis siue pauperibus dantur. Admonet enim nihil horum Deo gratum & acceptum fore, nisi quod ex animo uera fide & syncera charitate accenso emanat. Nam fieri non potest (inquit Apostolus) ut quis sine fide Deo placeat, imò peccátum est quicquid absque fide fit. Cùm uerò hæc à charitate non possit separari, absque fide fiat oportet, quod nō ex charitate, sed gloriæ priuatæ aut lucri siue commodi proprij studio fit. Ideo Christus alibi monet, ne dum eleemosynas largimur, sinistram manum eorum, quæ dextra facit, conscia fieri patiamur: hoc nimirum innuens, ut caueamus, ne quis prauus ambitionis aut auaritiæ affectus concurrens, opus illud per se sanctum & laude dignum inficiat. Discant igitur ex hoc loco diuites, ne suis largitionibus superbiant, aut eos temere contemnant, qui in speciem pauciora & minora conferunt. Quia enim illi ex iis modò largiuntur, quæ ipsis superflua sunt, & quæ alioqui uetustate, situ, putredine aut rubigine peritura erant, reuera nihil dant. Imò cùm ne illa quidem dent omnia, sed maiorem illorum partem in conuiuiorum luxu, uestium mollium fastu, ædificiorum inutilium superba ostentatione insumant, multa item in equos, canes, accipitres, mimos, scurras, lenones, scorta profundant, perfidi dispensatores, & iniustissimi bonorum alienorum usurpatores sunt: & proinde Deo nunquam probari poterunt.
units.tr: That saying of Jesus Christ contains a memorable teaching about sacred offerings, under whose heading are also included all those things that are given to the needy or the poor. For it warns that nothing of these is pleasing and acceptable to God unless it proceeds from a mind kindled with true faith and sincere love. For (says the Apostle) it is impossible that anyone should please God without faith; indeed whatever is done without faith is sin. But since this cannot be separated from love, whatever is not done from love must be done without faith, being done from a desire for private glory, or for gain or personal advantage. Therefore Christ elsewhere warns that when we give alms we should not allow the left hand to know what the right hand does; clearly signifying by this that we should take care lest some depraved affection of ambition or avarice intrude and stain that work, which is holy in itself and worthy of praise. Let the rich learn from this passage, then, not to be proud of their largesses, nor rashly to despise those who give less and smaller things in appearance. For since the rich give only out of what is superfluous to them, and what would otherwise perish by age, neglect, rot or rust, in truth they give nothing. Indeed, since they do not even give all of those things, but spend the greater part of them on the luxury of banquets, the show of soft clothing, and the proud display of useless buildings, and likewise pour out much on horses, dogs, hawks, actors, jesters, pimps and harlots, they are faithless stewards and most unjust usurpers of the goods of others, and therefore can never be approved by God.

units.la: Non minus autem pauperum quoque institutioni atq; consolationi dictum istud seruit. Ex illis enim multi immunitate sibi uendicant, nec se alicui debitores esse arbitrantur, eò quòd ipsi multis egeant, neque habeant quod alijs largiantur. Multos uerò hoc ipsum discruciat, & ideo se Deo minus acceptos esse putant. At quia pietatis atque charitatis officia animi promptitudine & alacritate æstimantur, uanum est quicquid illi prætexunt. Nam etsi neque pecuniam neque uitæ alimenta cuiquā conferre possis, studio tamen & amore Christum & huius membra prosequi potes, & saltem aliquo officiolo externo hanc animi tui promptitudinem testari. Quod si hoc etiam tibi negauit Dominus, cauere tamen potes, aut quàm minimè grauis, aut onerosus sis fratribus, neue ea tu in tercipias, quibus alij magis quàm tu opus habent. Conferes ergo tu quoque non contemnendum munus in Gazophylacium Ecclesiæ, si nihil inde auferas, sed proprio labore uitam tuam, quoad eius fieri potest. sustentes, ut alijs te egentioribus possit liberalius succurri. Et quicquid huius animo syncero feceris, Deo gratum atque acceptum erit. Denique si ne hoc quidem tibi licet, preces tamen habes, quibus & publicam Ecclesiæ & priuatam illorum salutem iuuare poteris, quorum beneficentia subleuaris: ut iam alia pietatis officia omittam, quæ neque egestate neque corporis aduersa ualetudine impediri possunt. Poterant hæc copiosius tractari, sed satius est, ut singuli ad opus accinagantur.
units.tr: This saying serves no less for the instruction and comfort of the poor. For many of them claim exemption for themselves, and think they are not indebted to anyone, because they themselves are in need of many things and have nothing to give to others. Indeed many are tormented by this very thing, and therefore think they are less acceptable to God. But since duties of piety and charity are valued by readiness and eagerness of mind, whatever they pretend is empty. For although you cannot contribute money or means of livelihood to anyone, you can nevertheless honour Christ and his members with zeal and love, and at least show this readiness of your mind by some small outward service. But if the Lord has denied you even this, you can still take care not to be a burden or a weight to your brothers, and not to seize those things which others need more than you. So you too will contribute a gift not to be despised into the treasury of the Church, if you take nothing from it, but sustain your life by your own labour, as far as that can be done, so that others who are poorer may be helped more generously. And whatever you do with a sincere mind of this kind will be pleasing and acceptable to God. Finally, if even this is not permitted you, you still have prayers, by which you can help both the public salvation of the Church and the private salvation of those by whose kindness you are relieved; to pass over other duties of piety, which neither poverty nor ill health of body can prevent. These matters could be treated more fully, but it is better that each should be girded for the work.

units.la: a. Cor. 9. gantur, & puro fidei atq; dilectionis studio ardentes seipsos & sua omnia Deo consecrent, huius cul- tum prouehant, egenis succurrant, & ad subleuandam omnium necessitate semper parati sint. Erit hoc officium gratissimū Iesu Christo, qui & in eo occupatos clementer respiciet, & olim æternæ uitæ præmijs illud compensabit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: a. Cor. 9. let them be girded, and, burning with a pure zeal of faith and love, consecrate themselves and all that they have to God, advance his worship, help the needy, and always be ready to relieve the necessity of all. This duty will be most pleasing to Jesus Christ, who will also mercifully look upon those who are busy in it, and will one day repay it with the rewards of eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXIIII.

units.la: Et quibusdam dicentibus de templo, quod pulchris lapidibus ac donarijs ornatum esset, dixit: Hæccine spectatis? venient dies, quibus non relinquetur lapis super lapidem, qui non destruatur. Interroga- uerunt autem eum dicentes: Magister, quando hæc erunt? & quod signum quando futurum est, ut ista fiant?
units.tr: And when some spoke of the temple, how it was adorned with beautiful stones and votive gifts, he said: "As for these things which you behold, the days will come in which not one stone will be left upon another that will not be thrown down." And they asked him, saying: "Master, when will these things be? And what sign will there be when these things are about to happen?"

units.la: QVamuis Deus totum cultum Leuiticum unà cum tabernaculo siue templo Iudæis eam potissimum ob causam instituisset, ut promissionum de Messia aut venturo humani generis redemptore sigilla essent, utq; hac quasi pædagogia ad illum deducerentur: plerique tamen templo & sacris externis ita addicti fuerunt, ut sub his adumbratam æternæ salutis rationem securi nimis negligerent, imò ut externa illa ipsis salua essent, Iesum Christum hostiliter persequerentur, & cum sua doctrina extinctum vellent. Multa igitur olim Prophetæ de templi & urbis excidio, multaitem de cultus istius externi abrogatione, deque Regno Christi per totum orbem propagando prædixerunt, ut scandalo occurrerent, quod inde infirmioribus & cultui illi assuetis obijciebatur, utque omnes ad illum amplectendum excitarent, in quo umbrarum omnium veritas reuelari atque exhiberi debebat. At quia hæc parum mouebant Sacerdotes, qui sacra omnia sibi quæstum fecerant, apud vulgus autem Prophetarum oracula ignorabantur, Dominus ea frequenter illis in mentem reuocauit, & non semel de templi excidio cōcionatus est hucusq;, ut pernitiosa illa cultu exterm fiducia omnium animos liberaret & simul Apostolorum ignorantiæ remedium afferret, qui terreni regni spe decepti aut præoccupati nihil de illo sublime aut cœleste sentiebant. At quia res ista maximi momenti erat, plerisq; etiam prorsus indignum uidebatur, tale quid mixtari urbi sanctissimæ & loco ab ipso Deo olim electo, atque tot testimonijs Spiritus sancti commendato, diligentionem de illa dissertatione instante iam mortis hora instituit, cuius argumentum ad finem mundi usque extendit, ut simul nobis quoq; consuleret, in quos fines seculorum inciderunt. Est igitur tota hæc doctrina non minus necessaria quàm utilis consideratu: in cuius tamen explicatione breuiores erimus, quia multa quæ huc transferri possunt, iam ante in Marco nostro sunt dicta.
units.tr: Although God had instituted the whole Levitical worship, together with the tabernacle or temple, for the Jews, chiefly for this reason: that they should be seals of the promises concerning the Messiah, or the future Redeemer of the human race, and that by means of these, as by a kind of schoolmaster, they might be led to him. Yet most of them were so devoted to the temple and to external rites that, under these, they carelessly neglected the picture of eternal salvation, indeed, so that they might keep those external things safe for themselves, they persecuted Jesus Christ with hostility and wished to extinguish him together with his teaching. Therefore the prophets long ago foretold many things about the destruction of the temple and the city, and many things about the abrogation of that external worship and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ throughout the whole world. They did this so that they might meet the stumbling block that was thrown in the way of the weaker people, who were accustomed to that worship, and so that they might stir all to embrace him, in whom the truth of all the shadows was to be revealed and displayed. But because these things moved the priests little, since they had made all sacred things a source of gain for themselves, and because the oracles of the prophets were unknown among the common people, the Lord frequently brought them back to mind, and until now he has preached more than once about the destruction of the temple, so that he might free the minds of all from that pernicious trust in external worship, and at the same time offer a remedy for the ignorance of the apostles, who, deceived or preoccupied with the hope of an earthly kingdom, thought nothing sublime or heavenly about it. But because this matter was of the greatest importance, and because it seemed to many altogether unworthy that such a thing should befall the most holy city and a place once chosen by God himself and commended by so many testimonies of the Holy Spirit, he set out to discuss it with care, at the very hour of his death, and he extended the subject of that discourse to the end of the world, so that he might also provide for us, into what ends the ages have fallen. This whole doctrine is therefore no less necessary to consider than useful. In explaining it, however, we shall be briefer, because many things that could be brought in here have already been said before in our commentary on Mark.

units.la: Occasionem de his differendi Christo discipuli dederunt, de templi magnificentia sermonem instituentes, quæ operosa lapidum structura & donarijs pretiosissimis spectabilis erat. Mouit autem istos partim triste illud de urbis excidio uaticinium, quod illa eminus uisa edidit, ut capite decimo nono audiuimus: partim quod (ut Matthæus annotauit) post acerrimam Sacerdotum atq; Scribarum correptionem dixerat: Ecce relinquitur uobis domus uestra deserta: Dico enim uobis, nequaquam me uidebitis ab hoc tempore, usque dum dicatis, Benedictus qui uenit in nomine Domini. Nam hoc dicto ceu indignabundus se foras proripuit, ut qui loco sanguinario & pœnitere nescijs extremum uale diceret. Itaque magnam de his cogitandi occasionem discipuli habuerunt, quibus & impossibile uidebatur tantam molem, quam munitionis etiam loco ab Herode extructam fuisse ex Iosephi historia patet, subitò euerti: imò indignum etiam putabant propter aliquorum ingratitudinem cultum illum aboleri, qui multorum seculorum uetustate, patrum exemplo, Dei authoritate & promissionum amplissimarum testimonijs confirmabatur. Denique non poterant animo concipere, unquam rem eò deduci posse, ut cultus ille auitus & eius splendor Christo cederet, quem propter uilem speciem plerisque contemptibilem, potentioribus uerò propter dicendi & corripendi libertatem exosum esse sciebant. Itaque illi iam ex templo digressio magnificas eius structras ostendunt, & non sine admiratione dicunt: Magister, uide quales lapides, & qualia ædificia. Et sanè erant ista admiratione dignissima, si quæ Iosephus de templi ædificatione tradidit, consideremus. Attrahebat praeterea illius splendor & religionis persuasio quàm plurimos ex longinquis regionibus, ut illic preces suas offerrent & sacra facerent, sicut ex Actorum capite secundo & Eunuchi Æthiopis historia, quae octavo capite narratur, colligi potest. Hi vero nō contenti sacrificijs solitis, insuper anathemata & donaria illic suspendebant, quibus templum magis exornabatur. Certè non multis annis ante Christi adventum in carnem tantae templi divitiae fuerunt, ut praesentis pecuniae bis mille talenta, & reliqui auri talenta octo millia unà cum trabe aurea immanis atque incomparabilis pretij Marcus Crassus inde abstulerit, qui non multò post à Parthis occisus tam impij sacrilegij poenas dedit. Non temere ergo discipuli, dum humanis rationibus minas Christi ponderarent, illas admirantur, & in verba ista erumpunt.
units.tr: The disciples gave Christ the occasion for speaking of these things, when they began a discussion about the magnificence of the temple, which was remarkable for its elaborate construction of stones and its most precious votive gifts. But what moved them was partly that gloomy prophecy about the destruction of the city, which the temple uttered when it was seen from a distance, as we heard in chapter nineteen; and partly that, as Matthew noted, he had said after the sharpest rebuke of the priests and scribes: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate. For I say to you, you will not see me from now on, until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." For with this saying he rushed out, as if indignant, and bade farewell to a place of bloodshed that did not know how to repent. And so the disciples had great cause to think about these things. It seemed to them impossible that so great a mass, which, as Josephus's history shows, had been built by Herod even as a fortress, should be suddenly overthrown. Indeed, they thought it unworthy that because of the ingratitude of some that worship should be abolished, a worship confirmed by the antiquity of many centuries, by the example of the fathers, by the authority of God, and by the testimony of most ample promises. Finally, they could not bring themselves to conceive that the matter could ever come to the point where that ancestral worship and its splendour would give way to Christ, whom they knew was hated by most, who regarded him as contemptible because of his lowly appearance, and by the more powerful, because of his freedom in speaking and rebuking. And so, as they went out of the temple, they pointed to its magnificent structures and said with wonder: "Master, see what stones, and what buildings!" And indeed these things were most worthy of wonder, if we consider what Josephus has handed down about the building of the temple. Moreover, its splendour and the persuasion of its religion drew very many from distant regions to offer their prayers there and to perform sacred rites there, as can be gathered from the second chapter of Acts and from the history of the Ethiopian eunuch, which is related in the eighth chapter. These people, not content with the customary sacrifices, also hung up there votive offerings and gifts, by which the temple was adorned even more. Certainly, not many years before the coming of Christ in the flesh, the riches of the temple were so great that Marcus Crassus carried off from it two thousand talents of present money, eight thousand talents of other gold, together with a golden beam of huge and incomparable value. Not long after, he was killed by the Parthians and paid the penalty for so impious a sacrilege. It is no wonder, then, that the disciples, while weighing the threats of Christ by human reasoning, marvelled at those buildings and broke out into these words.

units.la: Exhibent autè nobis memorabile humani ingenij exemplum. Etenim disertè locutus erat Dominus, & insuper causas indicarat, cur templum illud una cum urbe excindi oporteret: nimirum propter impiam religionis omnis prophanationem, falsam doctrinam, uenalia sacra & immanem uerbi Dei contemptum. Magis ergo admiratione dignum erat, Dei cultum in populo hoc ita corrumpi potuisse, qui illius peculium olim fuerat, & Messiam tot seculis tanto patrum desiderio expectatum ab illis ipsis non agnosci, qui eius testes atq; praecones esse debebant. At nihil horum mirantur Apostoli, ijsdem verò nix fieri posse videtur, ut tam magnifici aedificij moles corruat, & cultus ille aboleatur, in quo nihil praeter turpem quaestum uidere licebat. Equidem uel Solomonici templi destructio ipsis in mente uenire debuisset, ut de Christi verbis minus dubitarent. Poterat autem mira videri haec illorum oscitantia, nisi similis stupor hodie multorum animos occuparet. Multi enim quando Papatum non opibus modo, uerumetiam Regum potentia & armis muniri atq; defendi uident, stultitiae nos accusant, qui illum simplici Euangelij praedicatione expugnare & deijcere conemur: ideoque nunquam non nobis Episcoporum vires, Monasteriorum opes, Cardinalium maiestatem, Pontificum potentiam ostendunt, simulq; eorum exempla proferunt, qui olim in illis debellandis operam suam luserunt. Quasi verò negotium istud humanis viribus confici oporteat, & non olim iisdem armis gentium superstitiones euersae sint, quas multò fortioribus praesidijs suffultas fuisse scimus. Maiorem tamen reprehensionem eorum stoliditas meretur, quibus dolet ornatum illum theatricum templorum aboleri, Monachorum collegia dissipari, imagines & simulachra deijci, multa denique vastari & in nihilum redigi, quae superstitiosi homines maximis impensis fieri curauerunt. Atqui longè pretiosior est unius animae iactura. Cur ergo istis parcatur, quorum deceptione & impostturis infinita animarum millia iam seculis aliquot perierunt? Minimè igitur digni sunt isti qui audiantur. Doleat potius Christianis hominibus Veritatis doctrinam corrumpi, Dei cultum prophanari, uiua eiusdem templa & uiuas Iesu Christi imagines crudeliter destrui: gaudeant autem quantùmuis horribili ruina eorum, qui Luciferiana audacia sese aduersus Deum extollunt, ut Ecclesiam eius impia atque iniusta tyrannide opprimant.
units.tr: Moreover, they set before us a remarkable example of human intelligence. For the Lord had spoken plainly, and had also indicated the reasons why that temple, together with the city, had to be destroyed: namely, because of the impious profanation of all religion, false doctrine, venal sacred rites, and the monstrous contempt of the word of God. Therefore it was more worthy of wonder that the worship of God could have been so corrupted among this people, which had once been God's own possession, and that the Messiah, so long awaited by the fathers with such longing for so many centuries, was not recognised by those very people who ought to have been his witnesses and heralds. Yet the apostles marvel at none of these things. Rather, to these same men it seems almost impossible that the mass of so magnificent a building should collapse and that worship should be abolished, in which nothing could be seen except shameful gain. Indeed, the destruction of Solomon's temple should have come into their minds, so that they would have doubted the words of Christ less. And this dullness of theirs might seem remarkable, were it not that a similar stupor occupies the minds of many today. For many, when they see the Papacy defended and protected not only by wealth but also by the power and arms of kings, accuse us of folly, because we try to overthrow and cast it down by the simple preaching of the gospel. And so they always set before us the strength of bishops, the wealth of monasteries, the majesty of cardinals, and the power of popes, and at the same time they bring forward the examples of those who once spent their effort in waging war against them. As if, indeed, this business had to be accomplished by human strength, and as if the superstitions of the nations had not once been overthrown by these same weapons, though we know they were propped up by far stronger defences. Yet their stupidity deserves a greater reproach, those who grieve that that theatrical adornment of the temples is abolished, that the colleges of monks are dissolved, that images and statues are cast down, and, finally, that many things which superstitious men have taken great pains to make at great expense are laid waste and reduced to nothing. And yet the loss of a single soul is far more precious. Why, then, should those be spared, by whose deception and trickery infinite thousands of souls have already perished for some centuries? Therefore those who speak in this way are by no means worthy to be heard. Rather, Christian people should grieve that the doctrine of the truth is corrupted, that the worship of God is profaned, and that the living temples of God and the living images of Jesus Christ are cruelly destroyed. And let them rejoice, however dreadful the ruin of those who, with Luciferian audacity, raise themselves against God in order to oppress his Church with impious and unjust tyranny.

units.la: Et huc facit Christi responsio, qua discipulorum stultam admirationem confutat, & ut illos à praepostera illa templi & cultus Leviticj fiducia auocet, uno verbo ista omnia simul quasi absorbet. Quod ut maiori cum vehementia fiat, sub specie Concessionis iubet, ut structuram istam diligentius contemplentur, simul autem quid breui euenturum sit, docet. Haeccine (inquit) spectatis? Venient dies, quibus non relinquetur lapis super lapidem, qui nō destruatur. Grauis admodū sententia, qua discipuli nō potuerunt non uehementer percelli, quando (ut ex eorum quaestionibus mox apparebit) templum nunquam corruiturum putabant, quin ruinae pondus totum orbem concuteret, & simul finem totius mundi afferret. At quod hic pronuntiat Dominus, intra annos triginta octo factū est, sicuti alibi demonstrauimus: neque ab eo tempore templum illud unquam instaurari potuit. Nam quae hodie de locis Hierosolymae sacris dicuntur, putidissima Monachorum hominumque superstitiosorum figmenta sunt, quorum uanitas facile ab ijs deprehenditur, qui historias Ecclesiasticas uel obiter inspexerunt.
units.tr: Christ's answer bears on this too. In it he refutes the foolish wonder of the disciples, and to draw them away from that perverse trust in the temple and the Levitical worship, he swallows up all these things at once in a single word. So that this may be done with greater force, he bids them, under the appearance of concession, to contemplate that structure more carefully, and at the same time he teaches what will shortly happen. "As for these things which you behold," he says, "the days will come in which not one stone will be left upon another that will not be thrown down." This is a very grave statement, by which the disciples could not help being greatly struck, since (as their questions soon make clear) they thought the temple would never fall without the weight of its ruin shaking the whole world and at the same time bringing about the end of the whole world. But what the Lord here declares came to pass within thirty-eight years, as we have shown elsewhere, and from that time the temple could never be restored. For what is said today about the holy places of Jerusalem are the most foul fictions of monks and superstitious men, whose vanity is easily detected by those who have looked even briefly into ecclesiastical histories.

units.la: Quamobrem relictis ineptis illis superstitionum architectis, potius Christi Iesu veritatem atq; potentiam agnoscamus, & exempli huius, quo nullum à condito mundo tristius & horribilius aedificium est, causas diligentius scrutemur. Potest inter has merito censeri quòd cultum Leviticum hoc modo aboleri oportuit, cum tempus correctionis iam aduenisset: imò quia in illo retinendo pleriq; Idaeorum, dæorum, qui ad Christi fidem conuertebantur, pertinaciores erant, ipsam superstitionum officinam euerti necesse fuit, ne quæ reliqua esset illas exercendi occasio. At nō poterat hoc absq; urbis & populi tam lamentabili luctuosoque excidio fieri, ut autem sic fieret, Iudæorum ingratitudo & incurabilis contumacia merebatur, cum qua iam sæculis aliquot Prophetæ nequicquam luctati fuerat, & quam ipse Christus hucusq; neque docendi monendique assiduitate, neque miraculis saluberrimis frangere potuerat. Imò ut in sua uenientem non receperunt, sed Romanorum armis occidi curauerunt: ita eiusdem Apostolos crudeliter persecuti sunt, & in toto terrarum orbe aduersus nascentem Euangelij doctrinam tumultus concitauerunt, quibus eius cursum atque progressum impedirent. Itaque graviores pœnas ista contumacia merebatur, & (quod prouerbio dicitur) malo nodo malus cuneus quæ rendus erat, ut toti mundo exemplum proponeretur, quanti Deus faciat Filij sui prædicationem, & quibus pœnis coercere uelit omnes eos, qui simili contumacia aduersus illum pugnant. Experti sunt certè eandem Dei seueritatem multi alij, & in primis memorabilis est Romani Imperij calamitas atq; ruina, quam Imperatores sua audacia & impietate sibi accersiuerunt. Et nostro sæculo partim exteris partim ciuilibus bellis eos atteri & conficiuidemus, qui Euangelio Christi locum dare dedignantur.
