Nec meliorem sortem sperare nobis licet, quando mundus quotidie in peius proficit, & cùm teterrima monstra scelerum omnisque impietatis authores patienter ferat, eos solos exitio dignos iudicat, qui Deo creatori & redemptori suo fidele obsequium præstant. Nituntur quidem impij illi Thrasones inani potentiæ suæ persuasione, quæ infelices dementat, ut fœdera sua, opes, consilia, munitiones, splendorem denique & authoritatem suam Christo opponere audent: Sed arundineo baculo nituntur, neque mundi huius splendore ille perstringitur aut terretur, qui principem mundi iam olim deuicit, & nunc in cœlis ita triumphat, ut Ecclesiæ suæ curam minimè depositerit, sed eandem in medio suorum hostium conseruet atque tueatur. At quod apertis Christi hostibus dicitur, non minus ad se pertinere putent, qui Euangelij quidem doctrinam profitentur, disciplinam autem nullam ferre uolunt, & iugum omne conculcant, ut pro sua libidine uitam uiuere possint, in qua pietatis Christianæ uestigia nulla uidere possis. Est ingens horum numerus hodie, qui ut seipsos Christiano nomine indignos esse produnt, ita multorum quoq; aliorum progressum remorantur. Non deerit autem causæ suæ Dominus, & olim iudicio suo omnes eos coercebit, qui nunc neq; ipsi se iudicant, neq; ab alijs iudicari uel in ordinem cogi uolunt.
units.tr: Let us therefore set aside those foolish architects of superstition, and rather acknowledge the truth and power of Jesus Christ. And let us examine more carefully the causes of this example, since no building since the creation of the world has been more sad and dreadful. Among these causes it may fairly be reckoned that the Levitical worship had to be abolished in this way, since the time of correction had now come. Indeed, because many of the Jews who were converting to the faith of Christ were more stubborn in clinging to it, the very workshop of superstition had to be overturned, lest some remaining opportunity for practising it be left to them. But this could not be done without the most lamentable and mournful destruction of the city and people. That it should happen this way, the ingratitude and incurable obstinacy of the Jews deserved, the same obstinacy against which the prophets had struggled in vain for many centuries, and which Christ himself had not until now been able to break, either by his constant teaching and admonition or by his most healthful miracles. Indeed, since they did not receive him when he came to his own, they took care that he was put to death by the arms of the Romans. In the same way they cruelly persecuted his apostles, and stirred up tumults throughout the whole world against the nascent doctrine of the gospel, to hinder its course and progress. Therefore this obstinacy deserved heavier punishment, and (as the proverb says) a wedge had to be driven in to match the knotty log, so that an example might be set before the whole world of how highly God values the preaching of his Son, and with what punishments he wishes to restrain all those who fight against him with the same obstinacy. Certainly many others have experienced the same severity of God, and above all the calamity and ruin of the Roman Empire is memorable, which the emperors brought upon themselves by their audacity and impiety. And in our own age we have seen those who disdain to give place to the gospel of Christ crushed and destroyed, partly by foreign and partly by civil wars. Nor may we hope for a better lot, since the world grows worse every day, and while it patiently endures the most abominable monsters of crimes and the authors of every impiety, it judges those alone worthy of destruction who render faithful obedience to God, their creator and redeemer. Those impious braggarts indeed rely on the empty persuasion of their own power, which drives the wretched mad, so that they dare to set their alliances, wealth, counsels, fortifications, and finally their splendour and authority, against Christ. But they lean on a reed staff, and he who long ago conquered the prince of this world is not struck with terror or dismayed by the splendour of this world. He now triumphs in heaven in such a way that he has not in the least laid down the care of his Church, but preserves and defends it in the midst of its enemies. And what is said of the open enemies of Christ, those who profess indeed the doctrine of the gospel but are unwilling to bear any discipline, and trample underfoot every yoke so that they may live their lives as they please, in whom you can see no traces of Christian piety, should be thought to apply no less to themselves. The number of these is now huge, and by showing themselves unworthy of the Christian name, they also hold back the progress of many others. But the Lord will not lack a cause for his own, and one day by his judgment he will restrain all those who now neither judge themselves nor wish to be judged by others or brought into order.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Christi discipulos, quos illum interrogauisse Lucas scribit: Magister, quando hæc erunt? & quod signum quando futurum est ut ista fiant? Plura de hac parte annotarunt Marcus & Matthæus, quorum ille quidem & locum nominat, & eos, qui ipsum interrogauerunt: Petrum nimirum & Iacobum & Ioannem atque Andream: hic uero cum loco ipsam quoque quæstionem diligentius exponit, sic scribens: Sedente autem eo in monte Oliuarum accesserunt ad eum secretò discipuli dicentes: Dic nobis quando hæc erunt, & quod signum aduentus tui, & consummationis sæculi? Secretò agunt, quia propter efferatos in assueta superstitione animos Iudæorum, minimè tutum erat quicquam de templi excidio aut cultus illius abrogatione dicere, sicuti ex ijs appareret, quæ Stephano & Paulo postea acciderunt, quorum hic quidem per tumultum captus est, quod Ethnicos in templum introduxisset, ille uero lapidatus quoque, quòd quædam contra illud contumeliosius dixisse putaret. Quid, quòd ipsi Christo inter cætera crimina hoc per falsos testes fuit obiectum, quòd templi destructionem esset minatus? Prudenter ergo agunt discipuli, & suo exemplo docent, ne temere in publico moueamus quæstiones de rebus, quæ aut non necessariæ sunt cognitu omnibus, aut periculum non necessarium nobis ipsis uel alijs possunt conflare. Ex uno autem Christi dicto tres quæstiones illi eliciunt. Primam quando excidium istud templi futurum sit? Alteram, quo signo hæc futura esse, possint deprehendere? Tertiam, quando ipse ad iudicium uenire uelit & huic sæculo finem imponere? Poterat autem inepta nimis & absurda uideri postrema quæstio, sed causa huius fuit, quòd falsa Regni Christi in terris spe siue expectatione decepti, illum Hierosolymis regni sedem perpetuam habituris esse iampridem sibi persuaserant: Non possunt ergo aliam templi ruinam aut demolitionem animo concipere, nisi quæ simul totius mundi consummationem secum afferret. Et solet hoc fere omnibus accidere, qui terrena admirari assueuerunt, & sibi in illis aliquid stabile aut perpetuum pollicentur: multorum quoque confidentia eo usque interdum progreditur, ut
units.tr: But let us return to the disciples of Christ, whom Luke writes as having asked him: "Teacher, when will these things be? And what sign will there be when these things are about to happen?" Mark and Matthew have noted more about this part. Mark names the place and those who questioned him: namely Peter, James, John and Andrew. Luke, however, sets out the question itself more carefully along with the place, writing thus: "As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said: Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" They act secretly because, given the fierce minds of the Jews in their accustomed superstition, it was by no means safe to say anything about the destruction of the temple or the abolition of that worship. This is clear from what happened afterwards to Stephen and Paul. Stephen was seized in a tumult because he was thought to have brought Gentiles into the temple, and Paul was stoned because he was thought to have spoken somewhat insultingly against it. Indeed, was it not also laid against Christ himself, among other charges, by false witnesses, that he had threatened the destruction of the temple? The disciples therefore act prudently, and by their example they teach us not to raise rashly in public questions about things that either are not necessary for everyone to know, or may stir up a dangerous and unnecessary peril for ourselves or others. From one saying of Christ, however, they draw out three questions: (1) When will this destruction of the temple be? (2) By what sign may they recognise that these things are about to happen? (3) When will he himself wish to come to judgment and put an end to this age? The last question might seem too foolish and absurd, but the reason for it was that, deceived by the false hope or expectation of a kingdom of Christ on earth, they had long been persuaded that he would have a perpetual seat of his kingdom at Jerusalem. They therefore cannot conceive of any other ruin or demolition of the temple except one that would at the same time bring with it the end of the whole world. This generally happens to all who are accustomed to admire earthly things and promise themselves something stable or lasting in them. Sometimes the confidence of many also proceeds so far that

units.la: Discipuli de tempore excidij quærunt.
units.tr: The disciples ask about the time of the destruction.

units.la: Quæstio triplex. minas de regnorum huius seculi pœnis siue excidio cum risu atq; scurrilibus dicterijs excipiant, quae rentes: Quid si cœlum ruat?
units.tr: A threefold question. Those who hear threats of the punishments or overthrow of the kingdoms of this age receive them with laughter and jesting taunts, saying: "What if the heavens should fall?"

units.la: Non inhæsit autem tam prophana securitas in discipulorum cordibus, verum etiam idem nobis curiositatis humanæ exemplum præbent, quæ frequenter ex fidis Dei admonitionibus occasione de rebus inutilibus quærendi arripit. Quid enim proderat de tempore & signis templi destructione præituris quærere? Satius certè fuisset tam diræ sententiæ causas scrutari, & ratione evadendi ex tato periculo innestigare. Sed simili curiositate hodie etiam ubique peccatur. Prædicuntur pœnæ, quibus mundi scelera Deus punire statuerit: & ideo prædicuntur, ut eas ardenti pœnitentiæ studio avertamus, & ipsi priores occurramus Domino, ne quid durius in nos decernat. At plerique neglecta pœnitentiæ doctrina de temporum articulis, de supplicij genere & modo, deque infinitis aliis disputare incipiunt, quæ nihil conferunt ad hominis salutem. Similiter quando de novissimo Christi adventu sermo est, multi adinutiles quæstiones de tempore illius, de iudicij tunc futuri ratione atque forma, de conditione item vitæ cœlestis totiusque futuri seculi, conuertuntur, contemptis admonitionibus, quibus nos Dominus aduersus temporum nouissimorum scandala & pericula instruxit. Idem fit quado Dei percutientis manu mundus hic sentit, & uel bellis, uel fame, aut peste aliisq; plagis castigatur. Tunc enim plerique ad artes fatidicas conuersi, ab astrologis, ariolis & Magis consilia petunt, quæ ex Scripturis peti debebant. Sunt hæc aliena à religione Christiana, & simul pœnitentiæ obstant, quo minus ad Deum conuertantur, qui eum suis sceleribus adiram iustam provocauerunt. Nos ergo Iesum Christum audiamus, qui nobis à Patre cœlesti doctor datus est, quiq; de omnibus scitu necessarijs ita nos instruxit, ut falli non possint, quicunq; ipsum secuti fuerint. Ei debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet such worldly complacency did not take hold in the hearts of the disciples alone. They also provide us with the same example of human curiosity, which often seizes upon the faithful admonitions of God as an occasion to ask about useless things. For what would it profit to ask about the time and signs that would precede the destruction of the temple? It would certainly have been better to examine the causes of so dreadful a sentence, and to investigate the means of escaping so great a danger. But today the same curiosity is found everywhere. Punishments are foretold, with which God has determined to punish the sins of the world, and they are foretold so that we may avert them by an ardent zeal for repentance, and anticipate the Lord ourselves, lest he decree something harsher against us. Yet most people, neglecting the teaching of repentance, begin to dispute about the seasons of time, about the kind and manner of punishment, and about countless other matters that contribute nothing to the salvation of man. Similarly, when the subject is the last coming of Christ, many turn to useless questions about its time, about the manner and form of the judgment to come, and likewise about the condition of heavenly life and of the whole future age, while they despise the admonitions by which the Lord has equipped us against the scandals and dangers of the last times. The same happens when the world feels the hand of God striking it, and is chastised by wars, famine, plague or other blows. For then many turn to fortune-telling arts and seek counsel from astrologers, soothsayers and magicians, when they ought to seek it from the Scriptures. These things are foreign to the Christian religion, and at the same time they stand in the way of repentance, so that men are not converted to God, whom they have provoked to just wrath by their sins. Let us therefore hear Jesus Christ, who has been given to us by the heavenly Father as teacher, and who has instructed us in all things necessary to know, so that whoever follows him cannot be deceived. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXV.
units.tr: Homily 185.

units.la: Ipse vero dixit: Videte ne seducamini: Multi enim venient in nomine meo, dicentes: Ego sum Christus: & tempus illud appropinquauit. Ne igitur sequamini eos. Cum vero audiueritis bella & seditiones, ne terremini: oportet enim ista primùm fieri: sed non statim erit finis. Tunc dixit eis: Insurget gens in gentem, & regnum in regnum: & magni terræmotus erunt singulis locis, & fames ac pestilentiæ, & terriculamenta, & signa è cœlo magna erunt.
units.tr: And he himself said: "See that you are not deceived. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am Christ,' and 'the time has drawn near.' Therefore do not follow them. When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified, for these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once." Then he said to them: "Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes in various places, and famines and pestilences, and terrors and great signs from heaven."

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus olim in Iudaici populi exemplo, quem ex omnibus gentibus sibi in peculium selegerat, bonitatem & misericordiam suam, qua omnes homines complectitur, spectandam propositurus, ita in eiusdem reiectione et dissipatione omnium seculorum homines docet, quæ pœnæ eos omnes maneant, qui oblatam sibi in Iesu Christo gratiam contemnunt atque aspernantur. De illa ergo olim Prophetæ multa concionati sunt, Christus autem nuper paucis verbis omnia comprehendit, quæ ad istam causam faciunt. Dum enim urbi simul & templo excidium irreparabile denuntiat, non obscurè docet, ita perituros esse, ut cultum quoque illum, quo nunc glorientur, simul aboleri oporteat, ideoque neque Dei populum ipsos porro fore, qui hucusque titulum istum sibi præ aliis gentibus uendicarint. Fuit sententia ista admodum grauis, & discipulis quoque auditu difficilis uisa est, qui ideo quæstiones mouerunt, quando ista euentura sint, & quibus signis tanti mali initium possint agnoscere. Nec de solo templi et urbis excidio quærunt, sed huic mundi quoq; consummationem coniungunt: quia templum & cultum istum non prius aboleri posse putabant, quam totus hic orbis terrarum periret. Respondet ergo illis Dominus non minus placidè & benignè quam prudenter ac grauiter. Nam etsi ipsorum partim ignorantia partim curiositas grauem reprehensionem mereretur, parcit tamen ille infirmitati ipsorum, & ab inani regni terreni & lætæ pacis expectatione reuocatos de ijs admonet, quæ ipsis cognitu & obseruatu necessaria erant. Ne uidelicet impostores audiant, qui nouam populi liberationem polliceantur, neque cruce & periculosis huius mundi turbis offendantur, sed in agnita Veritatis ab ipso traditæ confessione constanter perseuerent. Et quia ipsi cum templi excidio quaestionem de huius saeculi consummatione coniunxerant, eius modi signa proponit, quae ad hanc quoq; extendi possunt, idq; certa cum ratione facit. Nam ut olim populi Iudaici liberationes ex Aegypto & Babylone redemptione totius humani generis adumbrauerunt, ita eiusdem exitium finis mundi huius typus esse debuit. Quapropter quacunq; de Iudaeis atq; Hierosolyma uel templo dicitur, sic à nobis considerari debet ut ea ad nostra quoq; tempora transferamus, & illorum consideratione ad gloriosum Iesu Christi aduentum praeparemur qui procul abesse non poterit.
units.tr: Just as God once set forth the Jewish people, whom he had chosen for himself as a special possession out of all nations, as an example to be looked upon, so that his goodness and mercy, which embraces all men, might be seen, so in the rejection and dispersion of that same people he teaches, for all ages, what punishments await all those who scorn and despise the grace in Jesus Christ that is offered to them. The Prophets preached much about that matter in former times, but Christ recently comprehended in a few words everything that pertains to this case. For when he foretold the irreparable destruction of both the city and the temple, he taught not obscurely that they would perish in such a way that the worship in which they now glory must also be abolished, and therefore that they themselves would no longer be God's people, they who hitherto have claimed this title for themselves above other nations. This statement was very weighty, and it seemed hard even for the disciples to hear. So they raised questions about when these things would happen and by what signs they might recognise the beginning of such great evil. They do not ask only about the destruction of the temple and the city, but join to it the consummation of this world as well, because they thought that the temple and that worship could not be abolished before the whole world perished. The Lord therefore answers them as kindly and gently as he is wise and serious. For although the ignorance of some of them and the curiosity of others deserved a severe rebuke, he spares their weakness, and recalls them from the empty expectation of an earthly kingdom and a happy peace, and warns them about those things which it was necessary for them to know and to observe. Namely, that they should not listen to impostors who promise a new deliverance of the people, nor be offended by the cross and the dangerous disturbances of this world, but should persevere constantly in confessing the Truth which he had delivered to them. And because they had joined the question about the consummation of this age to the destruction of the temple, he sets forth signs of such a kind that they can also be extended to the latter, and he does this for a sound reason. For just as the deliverances of the Jewish people from Egypt and Babylon once foreshadowed the redemption of the whole human race, so the ruin of that people ought to be a type of the end of this world. Therefore, whatever is said about the Jews, Jerusalem, or the temple, it must be considered by us in such a way that we apply it also to our own times, and by considering them we are prepared for the glorious coming of Jesus Christ, which cannot be far off.

units.la: Primò de impostoribus agit, & quid aduersus illos obseruari debeat, uno verbo monet, dicens: Videte ne seducamini. Ita uero offendit, nullum curiosis quaestionibus locum esse, quando pericula instent, quae unumquemque salutis propriae curam habere cogent; & quae nisi cauentur, toti populo exitium allatura sint. Et ne frustra monere uideatur, periculum quasi digito ostendit. Multi enim uenient (inquit) in nomine meo dicentes: Ego sum Christus; & tempus illud appropinquat. In nomine Christi uenire dicuntur, qui se ab eo missos esse gloriantur. Hic tamen non eos modo perstringit, uerumetiam alteros illos, qui impudentia audaciore elati, ipsius gloriam atq; officium sibi uendicant, dum se populi uindices & salutis authores esse pollicentur. Nam alias monuimus, Christi seu Messiae nomine Iudaei seruatorem illum olim patribus promissum intelligebant. Quod autem hoc loco Dominus praedixit, id reuera factum est. Nam ut Iosephus scribit, quam plurimi indies prodierunt, qui libertatis auitae & pristini regni pollicitationibus populo rerum nouarum authores fuerunt, ut nunc quidem in locis desertis, nunc prope urbem ad montem Oliuarum armati colligerentur, seq; in deiciendis Romanis praesidiis aliquid effecturos sperarent. Et Gamaliel (ut Lucas in Actis prodidit) Theudae cuiusdam & Iudae Galilaei meminit, qui tale quid conati sint: quibus adnumerari debet alter Galilaeus, qui non multò ante postremū Pauli in urbem aduentum quatuor millia sicariorum in desertum eduxit, ut ex Tribuni ad illum uerbis apparet. Fuerunt nebulones isti seditionum multarum authores, ex quibus tandem miserabilis totius gentis dispersio enata est. Iusto autem Dei iudicio fiebat, ut qui in Patris nomine in sua uenientem Dei Filium reiecerant, impostoribus locum darent, qui priuati commodi spe res nouas cum multorum interitu moliebantur. Nec tamen corporibus & fortunis solis illi nocuerunt, sed infelici populo causa fuerunt, ut toties decepti & ludificati tandem à Messiae nomine, ut omnium inauspicatissimo, abhorrerent, omnemq; salutis spem abijcerent: denique in Iesu Christi ueri redemptoris odio quotidie magis confirmarentur; in quo adhuc hodie infelices illi pertinacissime perseuerant.
units.tr: First he deals with impostors, and in one word gives the warning about what must be observed against them, saying: "See that you are not deceived." He indicates in this way that there is no room for curious questions when dangers are at hand, which will compel each one to take care of his own salvation, and which, unless they are guarded against, will bring destruction upon the whole people. And so that he might not seem to warn in vain, he points out the danger almost with his finger: "For many will come," he says, "in my name, saying, 'I am Christ'; and 'the time has drawn near.'" Those are said to come in the name of Christ who boast that they have been sent by him. Yet here he does not strike only these, but also those others who, puffed up with a more daring impudence, claim for themselves his glory and office, while they promise to be avengers of the people and authors of salvation. For we have said elsewhere that by the name of Christ or Messiah the Jews understood that Saviour who had once been promised to the fathers. What the Lord foretold in this passage has in truth come to pass. For, as Josephus writes, very many arose every day who, by promises of ancestral liberty and of the former kingdom, became authors of revolution among the people, so that they gathered armed men at one time in the desert and at another near the city, at Mount Olivet, hoping to achieve something in driving out the Roman garrisons. And Gamaliel (as Luke reported in Acts) mentions Theudas and a certain Judas the Galilean, who attempted something of the sort. To these should be added another Galilean, who, not long before Paul's last arrival in the city, led four thousand assassins out into the desert, as appears from the words of the tribune to him. These scoundrels were the authors of many seditions, from which at last came the miserable dispersion of the whole nation. But by the just judgment of God it came about that those who had rejected in the name of the Father the Son of God coming to them, gave room to impostors, who, driven by hope of private gain, prepared revolutions with the destruction of many. Nor did they harm only bodies and fortunes; they were also the cause for the unhappy people that, having been so often deceived and mocked, they finally shrank from the name of Messiah as the most ill-omened of all, and cast away every hope of salvation, and were at last confirmed more and more each day in hatred of Jesus Christ, the true Redeemer; in which unhappy hatred they still persevere most obstinately even today.

units.la: Est hoc memorabile, imò horrendum exemplum, quibus poenis Deus in Filij sui contemptores atq; hostes animaduertat: Ut nimirum excaecati impostoribus praeda fiant, qui blandi tijs, promissionibus, & saepe etiam minis eos adducunt, ut ea tententur, quae praesens exitium ipsis afferunt. Nam quod Iudaeis accidit, hoc ipsum Paulus nouissimis temporibus euenturū minatur, ut qui Veritatis doctrinam ferre nolunt, daemoniorum doctrinis circumueniantur, & in Antichristi laqueos incidant, qui partim aperta ui, partim dolis et falsa doctrina eos miserè seducat. Quod factū esse iam nemo non uidet. Nam ut de toto Oriente nihil dicamus, quem post haereticorum contra Christum non minus impiè quàm contumeliosè disputantium phalanges, tandē Mahumetica tyrannis totū oppressit: non minus horrenda sunt, quae in Occidente acciderunt. Postquam enim Romanorum adueteres superstitiones aspirantium audacia eò usq; excreuit, ut ab Imperatoribus Valentiniano, Theodosio & Arcadio, per Symmachum prisc um illum Deorum cultum & victoriae aram cū Vestalibus virginibus restitui peterent, & passim iam inter Christiani nominis professores omnium fere studia circa religionem frigerent: illico manum suam Deus exeruit, & urbe Romam Gothis, Vandalis & aliis barbarissimis nationibus diripiendā tradidit, quae tandē lacera & diuturnis calamitatibus fatigata Antichristo cessit, cuius tyrannis breui tempore per infelices orbis Christiani regiones extensa, Ecclesias simul omnes & regna in seruitutē turpissimā redegit. Venit is reuera in Christi nomine, quando quacunq; huius sunt sibi uendicat, & eius uicarium se esse gloriatur. Nam & Sacerdotium nouum instituit, in quo pro uiuentiū & defunctorū peccatis sacra fiunt, & regnum siue Imperiū excitauit, cuius potestia ipsis quoq; Imperatoribus & Regibus iam saeculis aliquot intolerabilis & formidolosa fuit. Taceo nunc impuros Monachos & rapaces Sacrificos, quibus parum uidetur superstitionibus uanissimis conscientias hominum grauauisse, nisi insuper libidine sua mulierculārum corporibus in sulcent, & in omnium fortunas manum inijciant. Gemūt subistorum fœda tyrannide omnis loci ac ordinis homines, & de eadem principes quoq; non obscurè conqueruntur: ferunt tamen illam magno cum nominis sui dedecore & fortunarum omnium dispendio: ita nimirum Filij sui & Euangelij contemptum uindicante Deo inter eos, qui oblatā in hoc salute immani & impio fastidio aspernantur.
units.tr: This is a memorable, indeed a horrible, example of the punishments by which God punishes the despisers and enemies of his Son: namely, that, blinded, they become the prey of impostors, who by flatteries, promises, and often even threats lead them to embrace those things which bring present destruction upon them. For what happened to the Jews, Paul threatens will happen in the last times as well, so that those who are unwilling to bear the teaching of the Truth are deceived by the teachings of demons and fall into the snares of Antichrist, who misleads them miserably, partly by open force, partly by trickery and false doctrine. That this has already happened, everyone sees. For, to say nothing of the whole East, which was afterwards overwhelmed entirely by Mahometan tyranny, after the battalions of heretics disputing against Christ no less impiously than insolently: the things which have happened in the West are no less dreadful. For after the audacity of those aspiring to the old superstitions of the Romans grew to such a point that they sought from the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, through Symmachus, the restoration of that ancient worship of the gods and the altar of Victory together with the Vestal virgins, and throughout the professors of the Christian name the zeal for religion was almost everywhere cooling, God immediately stretched out his hand and gave the city of Rome to be plundered by the Goths, Vandals and other most barbarous nations. At last, torn and worn out by long calamities, it yielded to Antichrist, whose tyranny, extended within a short time through the unhappy regions of the Christian world, reduced all the Churches together with kingdoms into most shameful slavery. He truly comes in the name of Christ, since he claims for himself whatever belongs to Christ and boasts that he is his vicar. For he has both established a new priesthood, in which sacrifices are offered for the sins of the living and the dead, and has raised up a realm or empire whose power for several centuries has been intolerable and dreadful even to emperors and kings themselves. I say nothing now of the impure monks and the rapacious sacrificing priests, who seem to burden men's consciences with superstitions that are most empty, unless they also insult the bodies of women with their lust and lay hands on the fortunes of all. Men of every place and rank groan under the foul tyranny of these subjects, and princes too openly complain about it. Yet they bear it with great dishonour to their name and with the loss of all their fortunes. Thus, of course, God avenges the contempt of his Son and of the Gospel among those who, with a vast and impious disdain, scorn the salvation offered in him.

units.la: At non debet commune exemplum infelicis mundi aliquem mouere, quo minus sibi etiam dici putét à Christo: Videte ne seducamini. Item: ne sequamini eos. Fallutur multi, quòd se extra culpam constitutos putant, si nō mala animi intentione eos sequantur, qui Christi nomine ad alios decipiendos abutuntur. Sed inanis est excusatio illa, eò quòd ne quosuis sequamur Christus prohibet, & hoc ouibus suis proprium esse dicit, quòd inter fidi pastoris & mercenarij uoce possint discernere. Idè per dilectū discipulū clamat: Dilecti, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis: sed probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. Neq; adeò difficile est in fidei & religionis causa uerum à falso discernere. Quia enim (ut Paulus admonet) nemo qui ex Dei Spiritu loquitur, Iesum potest anathema dicere, nemo item eundem, nisi Spiritu Dei agatur, Dominum profiteri potest: dubium non est, Veritatis doctores esse omnes eos, qui Iesum Dominum, id est, redemptorem, Regem & Sacerdotum Ecclesiæ suæ unicum esse docent, & eidem redemptionis atq; salutis nostræ gloriam omnem tribuunt: è contra autem impostores & mali ignis spiritus organa esse eos, qui illum laude sua spoliant, dum salutē alibi monstrant, nouā pro peccatis sacrificia fingunt, mediatores & aduocatos alios nobis obtrudunt. Quid enim est Iesum anathema dicere, si hoc non est? Ita enim mendacij arguitur, qui dixit: Ego sum uia, Veritas & Vita: Nemo uenit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Venite ad me qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo uos. Ego sum ostiū: per me si quis introierit, seruabitur. Consentit his Ioannes, quando in loco, què pauló ante adduximus subijcit: Per hoc cognoscite Spiritū Dei: Omnis Spiritus, qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carne uenisse, ex Deo est. At quicunq; Spiritus non confitetur Iesum Christum in carne uenisse, is ex Deo non est: sed hic est Spiritus ille Antichristi, &c. Neque hic mihi aliquis obijciat, aduersarios non minus quàm nos Filij Dei in carnem aduentum profiteri ac docere. Nec enim hic de rei gestæ historia nobis sermo est, sed de ipso rei effectu. Etenim frustra incarnationem Iesu Christi affirmauerit, qui ea negat, propter quæ illū in hunc mundū uenire & homine fieri oportuit. Quod quia nō aliam ob causam factū est, quàm ut peccata nostra in se transferret, pro ijsdem in arcrucis satisfaceret, patre nobis placaret, et eiusdē filios atq; coheredes suos nos efficeret: næuana atq; inutilis fuerit Christi Iesu in carne manifestati professio, si ista omnia alibi, quam apud illū quæsiueris. Hic ergo aures arrigant Christiani homines, & de particula, Solus, nobis litem esse meminerint. Ita enim hæc omnia nobis Christus meruit, ut nō aliud nomen sub cœlo hominibus datū sit, per quod seruari possimus, præter solum illum. Quod ut olim Apostoli omnes uno ore testati sunt: ita ipse per Prophetam clamat: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meū, & gloriā meam alteri non dabo. Quid ergo uerbis opus est? Si qui non unū Christum prædicant, sed quæ huius sunt, uel sibijpsis uel alijs quibuscunq; creaturis tribuunt, ij Christum nobis nouū fingunt, & proinde ex eorum numero sunt, quos sequi ille prohibet. Clamant aliqui, obediendum esse magistratui, & obedientiæ titulo eos excusari, qui ex principum mandato falsos doctores sequuntur. Sed hoc nouum Theologiæ genus est, quod si ad mittatur, Prophetas simul & Apostolos unà cum sanctissimo illo Martyrum choro damnabimus, qui omnes ideo cremati & horrendis suplicijs occisi sunt, quòd Deo potius quàm hominibus obedire maluerunt. Vide Actō. Cap. 4. & 5.
units.tr: But no one should be moved by the common example of the unhappy world into thinking that Christ does not also say to him, "Take heed that you are not led astray," and, "Do not follow them." Many are deceived in thinking they are free of blame if, without evil intent, they follow those who abuse Christ's name to deceive others. But that excuse is empty, since Christ forbids us to follow just anyone, and he says it is the mark of his sheep that they can tell the voice of the faithful shepherd from that of the hireling. So through his beloved disciple he cries: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God" (1 John 4:1). Nor is it so difficult to distinguish truth from falsehood in matters of faith and religion. For since, as Paul admonishes, no one who speaks by the Spirit of God can say "Jesus is anathema," and likewise no one can confess "Jesus is Lord" unless he is moved by the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 12:3), there is no doubt that all those are teachers of truth who teach that Jesus is the Lord, that is, the Redeemer, the King and the sole Priest of his Church, and who ascribe to him all the glory of our redemption and salvation. On the contrary, those who rob him of his praise, who point to salvation elsewhere, who invent new sacrifices for sins, and who thrust other mediators and advocates upon us, are the instruments of impostors and of the evil fiery spirit. For what is it to say "Jesus is anathema," if not this? He who said, "I am the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6), is thus convicted of lying. "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you" (Matt. 11:28). "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved" (John 10:10). John agrees with these, for when he adds, in the passage we quoted a little above: "By this know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God. But every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; this is the spirit of Antichrist," and so on (1 John 4:2–3). Let no one object here that our adversaries also profess and teach, no less than we do, that the Son of God came in the flesh. For our discussion here is not about the historical record of the event, but about its actual effect. Indeed, he affirms the incarnation of Jesus Christ in vain who denies those things for which it was necessary that he come into this world and become man. Since this was done for no other reason than that he might take our sins upon himself, make satisfaction for them on the cross, reconcile us to the Father, and make us his sons and co-heirs, the profession of Christ Jesus made manifest in the flesh will be empty and useless if you seek all these things anywhere other than in him. Let Christians therefore prick up their ears, and remember that our controversy with them turns on the little word "alone." For Christ has so merited all these things for us that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we may be saved, besides him alone. As all the Apostles once testified with one voice, so he himself cries through the Prophet: "I am the Lord; this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42:8). What need, then, is there of many words? If any men preach not Christ alone, but ascribe what belongs to him to themselves or to other creatures, they make for us a new Christ, and therefore they belong to the number of those whom he forbids us to follow. Some cry out that the magistrate must be obeyed, and that under the title of obedience those are excused who follow false teachers at the command of princes. But this is a new kind of theology. If it were admitted, we would have to condemn the Prophets and Apostles, together with that most holy company of Martyrs, all of whom were burned and killed with dreadful punishments because they chose to obey God rather than men. See Acts 4 and 5.

units.la: Sed ad alteram huius loci partē transeamus, qua de cruce & afflictionibus discipulos admonet, ne his ex improuiso incidentibus offendantur. Sic autem ait: Cùm audieritis bella & seditiones, ne terremini: Oportet enim ista fieri, sed non statim erit finis. Et mox periculi huius magnitudinem clarius exprimit, dicens: Insurget gens in gentem, & regnum in regnum, & magni terræmotus erūt sin gulis locis, & fames ac pestilentiæ, & terriculamenta: & signa è cœlo magna erūt. Atqui hæc etiam omnia priusquā urbs cum templo excinderetur, euenisse ex historijs abunde patet. In Iudæa seditiones indies nouæ exortæ sunt, quarū aliquas impostores illi excitarūt, de quibus ante diximus: multis autē occasione & initiū dederunt Romani præsides, qui uel auaritia uel odio getis Iudaicæ extimulati multa tentabant, quæ ipsis intolerabilia uidebātur. Pilatus certè cū altero mox à Christi morte anno Cæsaris imagines in templo collocauissęt, primam totius populi seditionem mouit. Nec multo post alterius, quoque tumultus fuit author, quando thesaurum templi siue pecunias sacras in aquæ-ductum insumpsit. Anno autem Claudij Imperatoris septimo sub præside Tiberio Alexandro, in die azymorum, tanta Hierosolymis seditio coorta est, ut circiter viginti millia hominum inter se compressorum perierint. Sub Felice autem præside latrones quoque per Iudæam horribiliter grassati sunt, quibus Magi seductores accesserunt, inter quos Ægyptius ille fuit, cuius nuper mentio facta est. Et Felice iam discedente ex Iudæa, per tumultum Cæsareæ ingens Iudæorum multitudo periit. Cum uero tot tantisq; calamitatibus non solum non frangerentur, verumetiā postremo armis sumptis ad uersus Cestium Florum insurgerent, bello initium dederunt, quod urbi & Templo excidium attulit. Adde his, quòd toto terrarum orbe tumultus dederunt, ut Euangelij prædicationem impedirent, sicut Lucas in Actis testatur. Feruente autem bello Iudaico, Romani mortuo Nerone inter se commissi de imperio certarunt, Galba, Ottone, Vitellio & Vespasiano ducibus. Terræmotuum quo que mentionem historiæ faciunt, ut famis quoque, sicuti alibi annotauimus. A quibus malis non potuit abesse lues & pestilentia, quæ bellorum uel comes uel pedisequa esse consueuit. Accesserunt his terrores maximi, qui quotidie noui obijciebantur: prodigia item & signa, quibus Deus iram suam cælitus quoque minitabatur: sed & in agro & in media urbe multa acciderunt, quæ cum alibi commemorauerimus eadem hic repetere non est opus. Ita uero tractari merebantur, qui pacis authorem Iesum Christum Barrabæ latroni & seditioso postposuerant, Euangelium pacis fastidiebant, & immerentes atq; sanctissimos homines, Iesu Christi seruos, indignis modis affligebant. Quòd si quis quæ iam sæculis aliquot facta sunt, & quæ quotidie fiunt, exponere instituat, is dicendi initium facilius quàm finem inuenerit, ideoq; oceanum illum bellorum, seditionum, malorum denique omnium ingredi nolumus, cui exhauriendo nullus labor suffecerit.
units.tr: But let us pass to the other part of this passage, in which he warns the disciples about the cross and afflictions, so that they may not be offended when these fall upon them unexpectedly. He speaks thus: "When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified; for these things must happen, but the end will not come at once." And soon after he expresses the magnitude of this danger more clearly, saying: "Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; there will be great earthquakes in various places, and famines and pestilences, and terrors, and great signs from heaven" (Luke 21:9–11). Yet from the histories it is abundantly plain that all these things also happened before the city was overthrown along with the temple. In Judea new seditions arose day after day, some of which were stirred up by those impostors of whom we spoke earlier. But the Roman governors gave occasion and beginning to many more, for they, goaded either by greed or by hatred of the Jewish nation, attempted many things that seemed intolerable to the Jews. Pilate, along with another, soon after Christ's death, placed the emperor's images in the temple, and so stirred up the first sedition of the whole people. Not long after, he was also the author of another tumult, when he spent the sacred treasure of the temple, or the sacred money, on an aqueduct. In the seventh year of the Emperor Claudius, under the governor Tiberius Alexander, at the feast of unleavened bread, so great a sedition arose at Jerusalem that about twenty thousand men perished, crushed together. Under the governor Felix, robbers also raged terribly through Judea, and deceiving magicians joined them, among whom was that Egyptian whose mention was made recently. And when Felix was leaving Judea, a huge multitude of Jews perished in a tumult at Caesarea. But since they were not broken by such great and numerous calamities, and at last took up arms and rose against Cestius Florus, they gave beginning to the war which brought destruction upon the city and the Temple. Add to these that they stirred up tumults throughout the whole world, to hinder the preaching of the gospel, as Luke bears witness in the Acts. While the Jewish war was raging, the Romans, after the death of Nero, fought among themselves for the empire, with Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian as their leaders. The historians also record earthquakes, as well as famine, as we have noted elsewhere. Plague and pestilence, which are wont to be the companions or followers of wars, could not be absent from these evils. To these were added the greatest terrors, which were presented fresh every day; also prodigies and signs by which God threatened his wrath even from heaven. And many things happened both in the countryside and in the middle of the city, which, since we have recounted them elsewhere, need not be repeated here. Indeed, they deserved to be treated thus who preferred Barabbas, a robber and seditious man, to Jesus Christ, the author of peace; who despised the gospel of peace and afflicted with unworthy treatment the innocent and most holy men, the servants of Jesus Christ. But if anyone should undertake to set out what has been done for several centuries past, and what is done every day, he will find it easier to find a beginning to his speech than an end. Therefore we do not wish to enter that ocean of wars, seditions, and in short of all evils, which no labour would suffice to exhaust.

units.la: Nunc obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd cùm paulò ante de seductoribus & Antichristis uerba fecisset, mox bella, seditiones atque tumultus publicos subijcit. Etenim horum malorum illos præcipuos in Iudæorum gente authores fuisse historiæ testantur. Et olim Ieremia docente, bellum Babylonicum extrahebat pseudoprophetæ, qui magnificis de ciuitatis sanctæ & regni Iudaici perpetuitate promissionibus Zedechiam & proceres aulicos accendebant, ne Nabuchodonosori se dederet. Quòd si gentium historias legamus, nonne maxima bella & grauissimas Reipub. mutationes plerunq; abillis excitatas fuisse uidebimus, qui sapientiæ & religionis existimatione eximij ad Deorum oracula & hominum superstitiosorum uaticinia omnes remittebant? Itaq; potentissimi reges non solum ex Sacerdotum suorum consilio, verumetiam nutu alicuius uenefica anus aut puellæ furiosæ, per quam diaboli spiritus loquebatur, bella solebant suscipere, quibus non raro seipsos in extremum discrimen adduxerunt. De Romanis Pontificibus quid opus est dicere? qui ut initio aliorum armis ad regnum suum instaurandum abusi sunt, Longobardorum nimirum contra Græcos, mox Francorum contra Longobardos: ita ab eo tempore nunquam destiterunt Imperij & Regnorum translationibus bella ex bellis serere. Quid uero de Concilijs ipsorum authoritate indictis dicemus, quorum exitus iam sæculis aliquot semper turbulentus fuit, ut nō temere tanquā proverbio iactetur: Omne Concilium parit bellum? Quod exemplorum commemoratione confirmari minimè opus est, cum Tridentinum Concilium iam annis uere uiginti quatuor grauissimorum bellorum faces accenderit, quibus primùm Germania nostra accensa fuit, nunc autē per annos octo infelix Gallia miserabiliter ardet. Quid, quòd ne pax quidē diuturna est unquam, quæ Pontificibus authoribus siue mediatoribus fit? Solet enim hiferè insidiosas conditiones interserere, ne illam turbandi occasio desit, si ita sibi utile atq; commodum esse uideant. At digni sunt, ut sanguinarijs illorum artibus ludificentur, qui manuetissimum illum pacis, uerę atque stabilis authorem, Iesum Christum, nolunt admittere. Prodest autem in istorum consideratione crebrò ac diligenter uersari eos, qui Euangelij cognitione iam illuminati sunt, ut Pontificum tendiculas atq; laqueos caueant, neue persecutionum aut turbarum metu illorum tyrannidi se iterum subijciant, quæ ipsis graviorum malorum causa sit.
units.tr: Now it is most worthy of notice that, having a little before spoken of seducers and Antichrists, he immediately adds wars, seditions and public tumults. For histories testify that the chief authors of these evils among the Jewish nation were precisely such men. Long ago, in the time of Jeremiah, false prophets prolonged the Babylonian war, inflaming Zedekiah and the court nobles with splendid promises of the perpetuity of the holy city and the kingdom of Judah, so that they would not surrender to Nebuchadnezzar. And if we read the histories of the nations, shall we not see that the greatest wars and the gravest upheavals in commonwealths were for the most part stirred up by those who, held eminent for wisdom and religion, referred everything to the oracles of the gods and to the prophecies of superstitious men? Thus the most powerful kings used to undertake wars not only on the counsel of their priests, but even at the nod of some poisonous old woman or a frenzied girl through whom a spirit of the devil spoke, and by this they often brought themselves into extreme peril. Why need I speak of the Roman Pontiffs? Just as at first they abused the arms of others to restore their own kingdom, namely of the Lombards against the Greeks and then of the Franks against the Lombards, so from that time on they never ceased to sow wars out of wars through transfers of empires and kingdoms. And what shall we say of the councils convened by their authority, whose outcome has for some centuries always been so turbulent that it is not rashly bandied about as a proverb: "Every council breeds war"? There is hardly any need to confirm this by examples, since the Council of Trent has now, for truly twenty-four years, kindled the torches of most grievous wars. By these Germany was first set on fire, and now for eight years unhappy France has been burning wretchedly. And what of the fact that peace is never even long-lasting when it is made under the Pontiffs as authors or mediators? For they are wont to insert treacherous conditions, so that there is no lack of occasion to disturb it, if they see it to be useful and convenient for themselves. But those deserve to be mocked by their bloody arts who refuse to admit Jesus Christ, that most gentle, true and stable author of peace. Moreover, it is profitable for those who are already enlightened by knowledge of the gospel to dwell often and diligently on the consideration of these men, so that they may beware of the Pontiffs' snares and nets, and not again submit themselves to their tyranny out of fear of persecutions or disturbances, which would be the cause of graver evils for them.

units.la: Et huc pertinet Christi admonitio, qui nos turbari aut terreri prohibet, si quid huius audiamus. Ne terreamini. Posset id partim præstitu impossibile, partim etiam inhumanum uideri. Quis enim non moueatur, quando orbe terrarum bellis & tumultibus ardere, & patriam dulcissimam eidem periculo iam impli
units.tr: And to this belongs Christ's admonition, who forbids us to be disturbed or terrified when we hear anything of this kind. "Do not be terrified." This might seem partly impossible and partly even inhuman. For who would not be moved, when he sees the whole world burning with wars and tumults, and his dearest country already involved in the same danger

units.la: Antichristi bellorum authores sunt. citam, aut certè uicinam esse uidet? Et ut aliorum calamitatibus commoueamur, pium atque Christianum est. Imò nisi ista irati Dei indicia nos perterrefaciant, nunquam ad serium pœnitentiæ studium accendemur, ut ad illum redeamus, à quo peccando discessimus. Cæterum Dominus admonitionem fiam ad officium restringit, cui discipulos suos destinauerat. Iubet ergo ut quàmuis ista fieri uideant, forti tamen & constanti animo per omnia seditionum atq; bellorum pericula eluctentur, neque desinant lætum illud Euangelij nuntium in medijs publicorum tumultuum terroribus & armorum strepitu diuulgare. Quod illos fecisse ex historijs constat. Porrò quod hic illis dicitur, sibi dictum putent hodie omnis loci & ordinis homines, & meminerint, Deo obsequium præstare debere tunc quoque, quando tota mundi facies diuersum suadare uidetur. Quid enim nobis hodie accidit, quod nō olim Apostoli quoque senserint, quorum uocationi non solùm temporum illorum turbæ, uerumetiam omnia ea obstabant, quæ in mundo potentissima & prorsus inuicta uidebātur? Perruperunt tamen illi sancta constantia, & felicissimus fuit rei difficillimæ euentus. Imitentur ergo illorum exemplum omnes ij, qui ad Ecclesiæ aut Reipub. gubernacula sedent: & illi quidem Verbi Dei tubâ inflare pergant, ut ad fidei constantiam omnes excitent, hi uerò intrepida animi fortitudine nauim sibi commissam per periculorum fluctus dirigant, nec quicquam metuant, quando Verbi Dei Cynosuram sequentibus omnis cursus expeditus & facilis tutusq; erit.
units.tr: or at least near it? And to be moved by the calamities of others is pious and Christian. Indeed, unless these tokens of God's anger terrify us, we will never be kindled to an earnest zeal for repentance, to return to him from whom we have departed by sinning. But the Lord confines his admonition to the duty for which he had destined his disciples. He bids them that, although they see these things happening, they should nonetheless struggle through all the dangers of seditions and wars with a brave and steady mind, and not cease to proclaim the joyful message of the gospel amid the terrors of public tumults and the clash of arms. That they did this is clear from the histories. Moreover, let all men of every place and rank take to themselves what is said here to them, and let them remember that they ought to render obedience to God even when the whole face of the world seems to suggest otherwise. For what has befallen us today that the Apostles did not also feel? To their calling stood in the way not only the disturbances of their times but also everything that seemed most powerful and utterly invincible in the world. Yet they broke through with holy constancy, and the outcome of a most difficult undertaking was most fortunate. Let all those who sit at the helm of the Church or the commonwealth therefore imitate their example: let the former keep blowing the trumpet of God's Word, to rouse everyone to constancy of faith; let the latter, with a fearless strength of spirit, steer the ship committed to them through the waves of dangers, and fear nothing, since for those who follow the Cynosure of God's Word every course will be clear, easy and safe.

units.la: Sed præstat rationes inspicere, quibus in præsenti discipulorum animos Christus confirmat. Oportet (inquit) ista primùm fieri, sed non statim erit finis. Primum ad Dei prouidentiam eos remittit, & ex communi sensu argumentum petit, quo docemur patienter ferendum esse quod mutari non potest. Nam qui sub onere luctantur & impatientius ferunt, quod omnino ferre coguntur, ij pondus magis aggrauant, & non modò laborum maiorum uerumetiam sæpe periculorū sibi authores sunt. Et quantum adiumenti in omni labore siue afflictione nobis affert patientia, quotidie experimur in ijs, qui uel morbis diuturnis, uel alijs aduersis exercentur. Patientiæ autem fortissimum fulcrum est {c} diuinæ prouidentiæ consideratio, quæ non solùm de necessitate decretorum Dei nos admonet, uerumetiam docet eius iudicia iusta, æqua, adhæc nobis salutaria esse, & proinde nullam nobis esse de illis quiritandi occasionem. Ne tamen certamen breuiusculum animo conciperent discipuli, & post unam atq; alteram luctam se omni officio defunctos putarent, de perpetuis laboribus eos admonet, quando finem malorum non statim appariturum, imò hæc malorum initia modò fore dicit. Quod de Iudæis uerissimè dictum fuisse euentus docuit: quando constat omnia, quæ ab ascensione Christi per annos circiter triginta sex passi sunt, lusum iocumq; fuisse præillis, quæ postea feruente iam bello & in urbis obsidione atque excidio acciderunt. Neque aliter fieri poterat, cùm ipsi indies contumaciores fierent, & cum Dei iustitia simul atq; longanimitate eluctarentur. Atqui idem de nostris temporibus possumus dicere. Crescit quotidie mundi impietas, & in peius subinde proficiunt, qui semel aduersus Euangelij doctrinam hostiles animos conceperunt. Apud eos autem, qui illam profitentur, exitialis securitas atque socordia regnat, in quam mox relabimur, etiamsi nos aliquando Deus seueriori flagello excitet. Quid ergo nobis polliceamur aliud, quàm necesse esse, ut periculis & turbis publicis nos Deus exerceat, neque finem fore malorum, donec ipse Christus gloriosò suo aduentu mundum hunc totum cum suis studijs depravatissimis aboleat? Discant ergo omnes in horum consideratione diligenter uersari, & æternæ Dei uoluntati sese subijciant, patienter autem ferant crucem Iesu Christi, ut olim eiusdem coheredes fiant: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But it is better to consider the reasons by which Christ now strengthens the minds of his disciples. "These things must come first," he says, "but the end will not be immediately." First, he refers them to God's providence, and from common sense he draws an argument by which we are taught to bear patiently what cannot be changed. For those who struggle under a burden and bear with impatience what they are utterly compelled to bear, only make the weight heavier, and become the authors not only of greater labours but often of greater dangers for themselves. And how much help patience brings us in every labour or affliction we learn daily from those who are exercised by lasting illnesses or other adversities. The strongest prop of patience, however, is the consideration of divine providence, which not only reminds us of the necessity of God's decrees, but also teaches that his judgements are just and fair and, moreover, salutary for us, and that therefore we have no occasion to complain about them. Lest, however, the disciples should conceive that the struggle would be brief, and should think that after one or two conflicts they had discharged their whole duty, he warns them of perpetual labours, saying that the end of evils will not appear at once, but that these are only the beginnings of evils. That this was most truly said of the Jews the outcome has shown: for it is established that all they suffered from the ascension of Christ for about thirty-six years was mere play and jest compared with what came afterwards, when the war was already raging and in the siege and destruction of the city. Nor could it have been otherwise, since they became more obstinate every day and struggled against the justice and at the same time the long-suffering of God. And we can say the same of our own times. The impiety of the world grows daily, and those who once conceived hostile minds against the doctrine of the gospel go on from bad to worse. Among those who profess it, however, a deadly security and sloth reign, into which we soon relapse, even if God at some time rouse us with a more severe scourge. What else, then, can we promise ourselves, than that God must exercise us with dangers and public tumults, and that there will be no end of evils until Christ himself, by his glorious coming, abolishes this whole world with its most depraved pursuits? Let all therefore learn to dwell diligently on the consideration of these things, submit themselves to the eternal will of God, and patiently bear the cross of Jesus Christ, that they may one day become his co-heirs: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXVI.

units.la: Sed ante hæc omnia iniicient vobis manus suas, & vos persequentur, tradentes in Synagogas & carceres, adductos ad Reges ac præsides nominis mei causa. Hæc autem cedent vobis in testimonium. Habete igitur fixum in cordibus vestris, non esse præmeditandâ defensionem. Ego enim dabo vobis os & sapientiam, cui nō poterunt contradicere neque resistere omnes qui se vobis opponēt. Trademini autem tem etiam à parentibus & fratribus & cognatis & amicis: & morte mulctabunt aliquos ex vobis. Et eritis exosi omnibus propter nomē meum. Sed pilus capitis vestri non peribit. Per patientiam vestram possidete animas vestras.
units.tr: "But before all these things they shall lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and bringing you before kings and governors for my name's sake. And this shall turn to you for a testimony. Settle it therefore in your hearts not to premeditate your defence. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all who oppose you shall not be able to gainsay or resist. You shall be betrayed even by parents, brothers, kinsfolk and friends, and some of you they will put to death. And you shall be hated by all men for my name's sake. But there shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls."

units.la: Quoniam discipuli de excidio templi Hierosolymitani & totius mundi consummatione quæ interrogationem moverant, Christus responsionem ita instituit, ut simul graviter de omnibus admoneat, quæ tam ipsos illo tempore scire oportuit, quàm nobis etiam hodie cognitu & observatu necessaria sunt. Et hactenus quidem de communibus periculis disseruit, quæ ex seductoribus, pseudochristis, seditionibus, bellis, fame, pestæ aliisq; huius generis calamitatibus nascitura sint. Caeterùm ne discipuli, quorum animos falsa de regno eius terreno persuasio iampridem occupaverat, se extra omne periculum constitutos fore putarent, nunc ad illos accedit, & quid ipsis incredito sibi munere euenturum sit docet. Erat autem ista admonitio admodum necessaria. Nam ut pericula improvisa magis terrent, ita portento simile videri poterat. Euangelij doctrinam, qua nihil simplicius, suavius & salutarius inveniri potest, ita omnibus exosam esse, ut adversus eam, ceu ad commune incendium restinguendum omnes concurrant. Id certè hodie multos terret, qui hoc saxum voluunt, multos item vehementer offendit, qui nondum eò usq; profecerunt, ut mundi iudicio nihil prorsus in hac causa tribuit debere intelligant. Ut ergo Apostolos olim de his admoneri necesse fuit, ita quæ ipsis dicuntur, non minus ad nos pertinere putemus. Quia enim mundus ingenium suum perpetuò retinet, eadem quoq; omnibus seculis erit seruorum Christi conditio: quos ideo ad perpetua certamina armari oportet. Nam etiamsi interdum Halcyonia quædam Ecclesiæ obtingunt, ut à laboribus respirare possit, nunc quam tamen illa diuturna sunt, plerunque ex improviso exorientibus ventis, quibus & mundus hic turbatur, & Ecclesia præ aliis oppugnatur.
units.tr: Since the disciples had asked about the destruction of the temple at Jerusalem and the end of the whole world, Christ framed his answer so that at the same time he warned them solemnly about everything that they needed to know then, and that we too need to know and heed today. So far he has spoken of the common dangers that will arise from deceivers, false Christs, seditions, wars, famine, plague and other calamities of this kind. But lest the disciples, whose minds had long been occupied by the false notion of a worldly kingdom, should think themselves placed beyond all danger, he now turns to them and tells them what will befall them because of the unexpected office laid upon them. This warning was indeed very necessary. For just as unforeseen dangers terrify us more, so this might have seemed a monstrous thing: that the teaching of the gospel, than which nothing can be found more simple, sweet and healthful, should be so hated by all that they would rush together against it, as if to put out a common fire. Certainly today this terrifies many who wish to keep clear of this stone, and it greatly offends many others who have not yet advanced so far as to understand that in this cause nothing at all should be yielded to the judgement of the world. Therefore, as the apostles once needed to be warned of these things, so let us think that what is said to them pertains no less to us. For since the world always keeps its nature, the condition of Christ's servants will likewise be the same in every age; they must therefore be armed for perpetual conflicts. For even if at times some halcyon calm falls to the Church, so that it may breathe after its labours, yet such calms are seldom lasting, since storms rise suddenly and by them this world is thrown into confusion and the Church is assailed more than the rest.

units.la: Porrò partem istam à diligenti temporis consignatione dominus orditur, dicens: Sed ante hæc omnia iniiciunt vobis manus, & c. Quasi diceret: Ne putetis vos eorum, quæ hucusq; dixi, otiosos modò spectatores fore, ut qui ex portu navales pugnas, aut inter fluctus atq; naufragia periclitantes spectare solent. Nam adeò vobis istud nō dabitur, ut potius à vobis malorum istorum initium futurum sit, & vos primi in arenam protrahendi sitis, qui hanc pugnam decertetis. Nam priusquam bellum illud fatale exardescat, quo urbem cum templo excindi oportet, aduersarij vestri, qui & mei hostes sunt, vobis manus iniicient, vosq; hostiliter persequentur: imò ad Synagogas citabunt & in carceres detrudent, inde ad Regum & præsidum tribunalia producent, ubi de criminibus capitalibus accusabimini. Adiista ergo vos præparari velim, & diligenter cauere, ne periculis tantis & indomito hostium furore offensi succumbatis. At hæc à Christo veri ssimè illis prædicta esse, Actorum liber prolixè testatur, qui ad huius loci expositionem nobis locupletissimi commentarij locus esse potest.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord begins this part with a careful marking of the time, saying: "But before all these things they shall lay their hands on you," and so on. As if he were saying: do not think that, after what I have said so far, you will be mere idle spectators, like those who are used to watch naval battles from a harbour, or sailors in peril amid waves and shipwreck. For this will not be granted you; rather, you will be the beginning of those evils, and you will be the first dragged into the arena to fight this battle. For before that fatal war breaks out, in which the city together with the temple must be destroyed, your adversaries, who are also enemies of me, will lay hands on you and pursue you as enemies do. Indeed they will summon you to the synagogues and thrust you into prisons, and from there they will bring you before the tribunals of kings and governors, where you will be accused of capital crimes. I wish you therefore to be prepared for these things and to take careful heed, lest, wounded by such great dangers and the untamed fury of your enemies, you give way. That these things were truly foretold to them by Christ, the book of Acts bears full witness at length, and it may serve us as a most copious commentary for the exposition of this passage.

units.la: Cæterùm miretur aliquis, cur regnorum atque urbium excidia ferè à priorum persecutione & grauissimis, quibus hi exercentur, afflictionibus initium sumant? Nam quod Apostolis accidit, hoc ipsum postea quoque accidisse scimus, ut Romani imperij ruinam horrendæ persecutiones præcesserint, quibus tota Ecclesia ubiq; terrarum graviter concussa atq; afflicta fuit. Et hodie huius generis exempla in regnis florentissimis uidimus, quæ Deus seueriori flagello castigare voluit. Sed ut ita fiat: partim Dei iustitia atq; honor, partim hominum salus exigit. Oportet enim, ut Petrus ait, iudicium à Domo Dei incipere, ne in suis indulgeter nimis ferre putetur scelera, quæ in alijs seuerissimè punit, & ita eius existimatio in periculum veniat. Deinde mundum totum excitare vult Dominus, ut quando impij se multò meliores tam indignè tractari uident, cogitare incipiant quid ipsi merean-tur, qui hucusq; peccata peccatis impiè accumulauerunt. Et huc illud Christi pertinet. Si hoc fit in uiridi, quid fiet in arido? Item quod Apostolus dicit: Si iustus vix seruatur, impius et peccator ubi comparebit? Tertiò suos à mundo separare solet Deus hoc persecutionum ventilabro, ut ille quidem dignas suæ impietatis pœnas exoluat, hi verò excussi veterno ad veram pœnitentiam expergefiant, ne cum impijs ac pœnitere nescijs condemnentur. Etenim quam difficulter sese ex mundo extricent atque diuellant etiam illi, qui ex illius sceleribus nullam voluptatem capiunt, Lothi exemplo docemur, quem per Angelos urgeri oportuit, ut infelices & iam exitio devotas Sodomas relinqueret. Adde his, quòd (ut Isaias annotauit) ante diem malum iusti colliguntur, ne uideant calamitates, & horrendos gentium atq; urbium occasus, quorum contemplatio eis morte ipsa acerbior esset. Unde colligimus, piorum dissipationes atque exilia, excidiorum præludia esse, quæ gentibus atque ciuitatibus imminent, quæ ad Deum conuerti nolunt. Ita Ecclesiam ex Hierosolyma dispergi, & tandem cum omnibus reliquijs Pellam migrare oportuit, ut Romanorum legionibus impios & sanguinarios Christi atq; fidelium carnifices obsidendi et crudeliter mactandi locus siue occasio daretur. Gaudent quidem & exultant impij ueritatis hostes, quando pios Christi cultores uel mori uident, uel sibi in illos quiduis audendi potestatem datam esse sentiunt. Sed nimium magno illis hoc gaudium constat, quia optimo præsidio nudatis uindicta Dei imminet, quæ diu non potest differri, quando nemo est reliquus, qui sua intercessione iram eius auertat siue restinguat.
units.tr: But someone may wonder why the overthrow of kingdoms and cities usually begins with persecution of the former kind and with the most grievous afflictions with which these are harassed. For we know that what happened to the apostles happened afterwards too: the ruin of the Roman empire was preceded by terrible persecutions, by which the whole Church was severely shaken and afflicted throughout the world. And today we have seen examples of this kind in most flourishing kingdoms, which God wished to chastise with a severer scourge. But that it should be so is required partly by the justice and honour of God, partly by the salvation of men. For, as Peter says, judgement must begin at the house of God, lest he seem to indulge too much the sins in his own people which he punishes most severely in others, and so his reputation be put in danger. Next, the Lord wishes to stir up the whole world, so that when the wicked see that much better men are treated so shamefully, they may begin to consider what they themselves deserve, who have so far impiously heaped sin upon sin. To this belongs also that saying of Christ: If this is done in the green wood, what will be done in the dry? Likewise what the Apostle says: If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? Thirdly, God is accustomed to separate his own from the world by this winnowing fan of persecutions, so that the one sort may pay the punishments their impiety deserves, while the others, shaken out of their drowsiness, may awake to true repentance, lest they be condemned together with the wicked and those who know not how to repent. For how hard it is for even those who take no pleasure in the world's wickedness to extricate and tear themselves free from it we are taught by the example of Lot, whom the angels had to urge to leave the unhappy Sodom, already devoted to destruction. Add to these that (as Isaiah observed) the righteous are gathered before the evil day, so that they may not see the calamities and the dreadful downfall of nations and cities, the contemplation of which would be more bitter to them than death itself. From this we gather that the scatterings and exiles of the godly are the preludes of the ruins which hang over the nations and cities that refuse to turn to God. Thus the Church had to be scattered from Jerusalem, and at last to migrate with all its remnants to Pella, so that the Roman legions might have a place or occasion to besiege and cruelly slaughter the impious and bloodthirsty butchers of Christ and of the faithful. Indeed the impious enemies of the truth rejoice and exult when they see the godly worshippers of Christ either die, or feel that power has been given them to dare anything against them. But this joy costs them far too dear, because, stripped of their best protection, they face the vengeance of God, which cannot long be deferred, since no one is left who might by his intercession turn away or quench his wrath.

units.la: Sed diligentius inspici debent quæ discipulis euentura esse Christus prædicit. Injicient (inquit) vobis manus, & persequentur vos. Deinde tradent in Synagogas, nimirum ut illic reddatis doctrinæ & fidei vestræ rationem. Adhæc in carceres abducent, ut qui iam hæresium abundè conuicti sitis. Postremò Regibus & præsidibus prouinciarum occidendos tradent. Quæ omnia ut olim Apostolis acciderunt: ita hodie ordo idem obseruatur in ijs persequendis, qui Christum purè ac constanter profitentur. Hostes eorum acerrimi & iurati sunt, qui in Synagogis præsident, quas ipsi Ecclesiam Christi esse dicunt. Instituunt hi ex suæ factionis hominibus inquisitores, qui non externos modò quorumuis mores atq; ritus obseruent, uerumetiam per suos Corycæos in occulta eorundem dicta & facta inquirant. Hi si quem suspectum habeant, mox illum apud suos antistites deferunt, uel etiam ipsi simul & testes & iudices fiunt. Et quàmuis nullo iustitiæ studio aut cura tangantur, tamen ordinem ac speciem aliquam iuris egregiè simulare possunt. Nam ad causarum Ecclesiasticarum indices eos citant, quos suspectos esse audiunt. Ibi eosdem diligenter de fide examinant, & non minus acutis quàm captiosis quæstionibus in illorum conscientias penetrant. Quòd si qui liberius ueritatem profiteantur, mox eos carceribus mancipant, & post omnis generis tormenta potestati seculari (ut ipsi loquuntur) mactandos tradunt. Nec alio ordine in Concilijs etiam, quæ illi generalia dicunt, proceditur: sicuti multis exemplis demonstrari poterat, nisi tam manifesta esset res ista, ut demonstratione nequaquam opus habeat. Itaq; sub iustitiæ & religionis prætextu pij opprimuntur ab illis, qui fidei ueræ vindices atq; assertores videri volunt. Est hoc moleston multis, & eo uno maximè offenduntur, quòd ea ratione famam quoque & honorem suum in discrimen adduci uident. At neminem istud mouere debet, qui Christum non solùm nos de istis admonuisse, sed eadem passum quoq; esse nouit, ut suo exemplo uiam, per quam nobis eundum est, sanctificaret.
units.tr: But what Christ foretells will befall the disciples ought to be examined more carefully. "They will lay hands on you," he says, "and persecute you." Then "they will deliver you up to the synagogues," clearly so that there you may give an account of your teaching and faith. Besides, "they will lead you into prisons," as men already sufficiently convicted of heresies. Lastly, "they will hand you over to kings and governors of provinces to be put to death." As all these things once happened to the apostles, so today the same order is observed in persecuting those who profess Christ purely and steadfastly. Their enemies are most bitter and sworn foes, who preside in the synagogues, which they themselves say are the Church of Christ. These men appoint inquisitors from among the men of their own faction, who not only observe the outward manners and rites of anyone whatever, but also through their Corycaean informers inquire into the secret words and deeds of the same. If they hold anyone suspect, they at once denounce him to their bishops, or even themselves become at once both witnesses and judges. And although they are moved by no zeal or care for justice, yet they can admirably simulate some order and appearance of law. For they summon before the judges of ecclesiastical causes those whom they hear to be suspect. There they carefully examine them on their faith, and with questions no less sharp than captious they penetrate into their consciences. But if any profess the truth more freely, they at once consign them to prisons, and after all kinds of torments they hand them over to the secular power (as they themselves put it) to be slaughtered. Nor do they proceed in any other order even in the councils which they call general; as could be shown by many examples, were not this matter so manifest that it needs no demonstration. And so, under the pretext of justice and religion, the godly are oppressed by those who wish to seem the defenders and champions of the true faith. This is troublesome to many, and they are offended chiefly by this one thing, that by such means they see their own good name and honour also put in jeopardy. But this ought to move no one who knows that Christ not only warned us of these things but also suffered the same, so that by his own example he might hallow the way along which we must go.

units.la: Singularem uero consolationem ipse in præsenti adhibet, quando hæc nos nominis sui causa passuros ait, & mox addit: Hæc aut cedent vobis in testimonium. Ergo quicquid impij illi prætexant, & quocunq; fuco suam tyrannidem palliare conentur, non alio tamen zelo, quàm ipsius Christi odia ducuntur, cuius lucem sibi intolerabilem esse putant, eò quòd per hanc ipsorum fraudes et impij conatus deteguntur. Est autem hoc summæ impietatis argumentū irrefragabile. Quia enim Dei Filius nostri causa in mundū uenit, idem propter nos in ara crucis seipsum pro mundi peccatis obtulit, & quam proprij sanguinis pretio meruit, salutem omnibus per Euangelij prædicationem liberalissimè offert, & ad illius possessionē nos quasi brachijs expansis inuitat, plus quàm diabolicus ille furor sit oportet, quo homines non modò salutis tantum authorem fastidiunt, & in proprium exitium ruunt, uerumetiam ferre nolunt, ut hunc alij agnoscant, & per illum parto uitæ æternæ beneficio fruantur. Simul aut hoc consolationem dulcissimā pijs affert, quòd crucis suæ infamiam sanctissimo & salutifero Iesu Christi nomine tegi, imò coronari audiunt. Cur enim illos alicuius periculi metus terreat? cur eosdem uinculorum, carcerū, suppliciorum deniq; ignominiosissimorum pudeat, qui se propter Dei Filiū ista perpeti, & hunc ipsum in suis corporibus affligi audiūt, qui eos olim in uitæ & gloriæ suæ cœlestis consortiū recipiet? Accedit huic consolationi altera, quòd hæc illis in testimonium fiunt. Apud Mar.pij ista ferre dicitur hostibus in testimoniū. Verūq; aut uerissimè dicitur. Hinc enim euides damnationis iustissimæ testimoniū referunt Christi hostes, quādo huius præcones tāta crudelitate persequuntur, qui ipsis uitæ æternæ uerba annuntiant. Etenim si puluis horū à pedibus aut uestimentis excussus (ut suo loco dictū est) adillos conuincedos sufficit, quid de ipso Martyrū sanguine dicemus. dicemus, qui (ut in Abeli historia cernitur) omnibus etiam tacentibus pro uindicta clamat ad Dominum? Porrò ipsis etiam serui Christi haec omnia in testimonium cedent. Quemadmodum enim ipsi sanguine suo testimonium ferunt Dei Filio, suamq; de hoc doctrinam hac ratione confirmat (quo nomine Martyres siue testes κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicuntur) ita uicissim hoc testimonio fidem suam Deo probant, seque dignos esse docent, quos Christus olim pro suis agnoscat, quando ueniet ad iudicandum uiuos & mortuos. Denique toti etiam Ecclesiae ostendunt, se bona fide & serio doctrinam salutis tradidisse. Et quanta huius testimonii uis sit apud posteros quoque, in Apostolorum & Prophetarum atq; Martyrum exemplis cernimus, quorum memoria hodie apud eos etiam sancta & venerabilis est, qui doctrinam & fidem illorum in nobis persequuntur. Horum consideratio diligens ministros uerbi omnes excitet, ut in suo munere fortes & constantes creditam sibi Euangelij praedicationem libere proponant, neq; ullis impiorum conuitijs, aut momentanea, quae ex illis nascitur, infamia moueantur: quando hanc apud posteros, gloriosissimum pietatis ipsorum testimonium excipiet, olim uero cum omnibus sanctis gloria & honore immortali fruentur.
units.tr: Christ himself offers a singular consolation in the present case, when he says that these things will happen to us for the sake of his name, and immediately adds: "This will turn out for you as a testimony." So whatever pretexts those wicked men put forward, and whatever coverings they try to lay over their tyranny, they are driven by nothing other than hatred of Christ himself. They think his light intolerable to them, because through it their frauds and impious attempts are exposed. And this is an irrefutable proof of the highest impiety. For since the Son of God came into the world for our sake, and for our sake offered himself on the altar of the cross for the sins of the world, and since he freely offers salvation to all through the preaching of the gospel, the salvation he earned at the price of his own blood, and invites us to take possession of it as though with outstretched arms, that devilish fury must be greater still, by which men not only despise the author of salvation and rush to their own destruction, but also refuse to bear that others should acknowledge him and enjoy, through him, the benefit of eternal life. At the same time, this brings the sweetest consolation to the godly, that the disgrace of his cross is covered, indeed crowned, by the most holy and saving name of Jesus Christ. For why should fear of any danger terrify them? Why should they be ashamed of chains, prisons, and finally the most ignominious punishments, when they hear that they suffer these things for the sake of the Son of God, and that he himself is afflicted in their bodies, and that he will one day receive them into the fellowship of his life and heavenly glory? To this consolation another is added: these things happen to them "for a testimony." In Mar.pij it is said that these things are borne "for a testimony against them" (to the enemies). And this is said most truly.
