For from this the enemies of Christ draw clear evidence of their most just condemnation, when they persecute with such cruelty the heralds of him who announce to them the words of eternal life. For if the dust shaken from the feet or garments of these men is enough to convict them (as was said in its place), what shall we say of the very blood of the martyrs, which (as is seen in the story of Abel) cries out to the Lord for vengeance even when everyone else is silent? Moreover, all these things will also turn out as a testimony for the servants of Christ themselves. For just as they bear witness to the Son of God with their own blood, and in this way confirm his doctrine (for which reason martyrs are called witnesses [μάρτυρες] par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]), so in turn by this testimony they prove their faith to God, and teach that they are worthy to be acknowledged by Christ as his own when he comes to judge the living and the dead. Finally, they also show the whole Church that they have handed down the doctrine of salvation in good faith and in earnest. And we see how great the power of this testimony is even among posterity, in the examples of the Apostles, Prophets and Martyrs, whose memory is holy and venerable today even among those who persecute their doctrine and faith in us. Careful consideration of them should stir up all ministers of the Word to be brave and steadfast in their office, to set forth freely the gospel committed to them, and not to be moved by any reproaches of the wicked, or by the momentary disgrace that arises from them, since posterity will receive this as the most glorious testimony to their godliness, and they will one day enjoy glory and immortal honour together with all the saints.

units.la: Porrò multos esse uidere, qui cùm ad quaeuis pericula & ad ipsam quoque mortem perferendam intrepidi sint, hoc uno tamen grauissimè anguntur, quòd metuunt, ne satis instructi sint ad diccendam causam, si quando in Concilijs aut principum cospectu fidei suae rationem reddere iubeantur. Timent ergo, ne sua ruditate aut ignorantia, aut saltem infantia sola, causae bonae & sanctae incommodent. Nec dubium est, discipulos non potuisse non commoueri, quando sibi illiteratis & indoctis cum acutissimis hominibus & cum Regibus potentissimis negotium fore audiebant. Quapropter huic etiam solicitudini remedium Christus adhibet, dicens: Habete igitur fixum in cordibus uestris, non esse praemeditandam defensionem, &c. Quae uerba non eò detorqueri debent, quasi illos rerum securos et temerarios esse uelit, qui inconsultò ad quiduis dicendum prorumpant. Nam alibi cautos esse iubet, & in periculis uitandis serpentinam prudentiam imitari. Sed in praesenti solicitudinem & anxietatem prohibet, quae in periculis improuisis animos eorum deijcere, & ipsos ab officio faciendo abterrere poterat. Vult enim, ut non tam quid ipsi possint praestare uideant, quàm quid ille possit, cuius ministri sint, qui nunquam passurus sit, ut causa sua propter ipsorum infantiam aut imperitiam periclitetur. Ideo promissionem praeclaram subijcit: Ego enim dabo uobis os & sapientiam, cui non poterunt contradicere neque resistere omnes qui seuobis opponent. Sensus est, ego animum simul & linguam instruam atque spiritu meo regam, ut prudenter & commodè ea dicatis, quae ad rem faciunt, & dictu in primis necessaria sunt. Apud Matthaeum eandem promissionem alio loco et tempore proferens adiecit: In illa hora dabitur uobis quid loquamini. In Marco autem ait: Quicquid datum fuerit uobis in illo momento, hoc loquamini. Non enim estis uos qui loquimini, sed Spiritus ille sanctus. Quod autem pollicetur, id fidelissimè praestitit postea, quando Apostoli in Concilio & Senatu Hierosolymitano fidei & doctrinae suae rationem tanta animi constantia & dicendi dexteritate reddiderunt, ut omnibus admirationi essent. Nihil nunc de Paulo dicemus, qui uix dum ex su-rentis populi manibus ereptus et duabus catenis alligatus, inter prophanos milites medius stans, ex tempore orationem habuit, quam diu magna cum attentione audierunt, qui paulò ante uix Tribuni authoritate et militum armis compesci potuerant, quò minus illum occiderent. Nec minori constantia idem postea coram Agrippa rege, Bernice regina, tribunis item militum & nobilissimis quibusq; totius gentis, ex uinculis causam dixit ita, ut prophano etiam Regi aliquam ueri confessionem extorqueret. Neque cum Apostolis huius promissionis fides & Spiritus sancti uirtus extincta est, sed posteris quoq; temporibus sese in martyribus exeruit, ut historiae Ecclesiasticae testantur. Et nostro seculo multa facta esse, multa item quotidie fieri uidemus, quae docent, promissionem hanc Christi ad nos quoq; pertinere, nec minus ueracem esse hodie quàm olim fuerit. Vnde enim mos ille nō tam crudelis quàm barbarus, quo impij Antichristianae tyrannidis satellites Christi testibus, dum ad rogos ducuntur, ora obturant, aut linguas candenti ferro perforant, uel etiam abscindunt, quàm quòd eorum constantiam & dicendi uim prius experti, metuunt, ne & innocentia suam omnibus testatam faciant, & multos ex spectatoribus ad fidem Christi conuertant? Sed quàm parum proficiant sua truculentia, res ipsa docet, quando ipsis inuitis ac reluctantibus Euangelij lux per omnia obstacula penetrat, & non raro pueris atque mulierculis in fide uera instituti ludibrium fiunt purpurati illi & bullati doctores, qui se solos sapere arbitrantur. Interim debet hinc communis consolatio peti, ne animum despondeant, quicunque se ad negotia ardua & uiribus suis maiora uocari sentiunt. Nam hos quoque donis idoneis & necessarijs Deus instruet, modo se illi obsequentes praebeant. Exempla huius rei in Mose, Iehosua, Dauide & multis alijs extant: & multa quotidie fiunt, quae nos in promissionis huius fide possunt confirmare.
units.tr: Moreover, we see that many, though they are fearless in the face of any dangers, and even in enduring death itself, are nevertheless most grievously troubled by this one thing: they fear that they will not be sufficiently prepared to plead their cause, if at any time they are ordered to give an account of their faith in councils or in the presence of princes. They fear, therefore, that by their roughness, or ignorance, or even mere inexperience, they may harm a good and holy cause. And there is no doubt that the disciples could not help being disturbed, when they heard that they would have to deal with the most sharp-witted men and the most powerful kings, while they themselves were unlettered and untaught. Therefore Christ also applies a remedy to this anxiety, saying: "Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to premeditate your defence," etc. These words ought not to be twisted as though he wanted those to be careless and rash who burst out to say anything without thought. For elsewhere he bids them be cautious, and to imitate serpentine prudence in avoiding dangers. But in the present passage he forbids that anxiety and worry which could cast down their minds in unforeseen dangers and frighten them from doing their duty. For he wants them to look not so much at what they themselves are able to accomplish as at what he is able to do, whose ministers they are, and who will never allow his cause to be endangered on account of their childishness or lack of skill. Therefore he adds this excellent promise: "For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all who oppose you will not be able to contradict or resist." The sense is: I will instruct both your mind and your tongue, and will govern them by my Spirit, so that you may speak prudently and fittingly those things that bear on the matter and are especially necessary to say. In Matthew, bringing forward the same promise at another place and time, he added: "In that hour it will be given to you what you should say." And in Mark he says: "Whatever is given to you in that moment, that speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit." Now what he promised he most faithfully performed afterwards, when the Apostles, before the Council and Senate of Jerusalem, gave an account of their faith and doctrine with such constancy of mind and skill in speaking that they were an object of admiration to all. We will say nothing now of Paul, who, hardly yet snatched from the hands of the raging people and bound with two chains, standing in the midst of the profane soldiers, spoke extempore, and for a long time they listened to him with great attention, though a little before they could scarcely be restrained, by the authority of the tribune and the soldiers' arms, from killing him. And with no less constancy, the same Paul afterwards pleaded his cause from his chains before King Agrippa, Queen Bernice, the military tribunes, and all the most noble men of the nation, so that he even wrung from the profane king some acknowledgment of the truth. Nor was the faithfulness of this promise and the power of the Holy Spirit extinguished with the Apostles; they also showed themselves in the martyrs in later times, as the ecclesiastical histories testify. And in our own age we see that many things have happened, and many things still happen daily, which teach that this promise of Christ pertains to us also, and is no less true today than it was in former times. For whence comes that custom, not so much cruel as barbarous, by which the wicked satellites of Antichristian tyranny stop the mouths of Christ's witnesses while they are led to the stakes, or pierce their tongues with red-hot iron, or even cut them off, except that, having first tested their constancy and power of speech, they fear that they may make their innocence known to all and convert many of the onlookers to the faith of Christ? But how little their savagery achieves is shown by the thing itself, since, against their will and despite their resistance, the light of the gospel penetrates through all obstacles, and often those purple-clad and bemedalled teachers, who think themselves alone wise, become a laughing-stock to boys and simple women instructed in the true faith. Meanwhile, from this a common consolation should be drawn, so that those who feel themselves called to difficult tasks greater than their own strength should not lose heart. For God will also furnish these men with suitable and necessary gifts, provided they make themselves obedient to him. Examples of this are found in Moses, Joshua, David, and many others; and many things happen every day that can confirm us in the faith of this promise.

units.la: At quasi parum dixisset Dominus de periculis & certaminibus, quae discipulos manebant, redit ad eorum expositionem, et ea nunc commemorat, quae bonis omnibus grauissima sunt: quando ni mirum se ijs etiam inuisos & exosos esse uident, quos ipsi neque sine scandalo relinquere, multo minus autem odisse possunt propter arctissimum cognationis aut consanguinitatis vinculum. Dicit enim: Trademini autem etiam a parentibus, et fratribus, et amicis, & cognatis. Et ne quis rabiem istam non durabilem fore putet, addit: Et morte multabunt aliquot ex vobis. Ergo non aliter quam sanguine odium illud exaturari poterit. Neque eo contentus subijcit: Et eritis exosi omnibus propter nomen meum. Id vero addi oportuit, ne quid praesidij inter homines sibi reliquum fore putarent: deinde ne propterea de Dei auxilio desperarent: quia impossibile est, ut Filius Dei eos in certamine deserat, qui propter ipsius nomen atque verbum periclitantur. Non dubium autem est, quin haec quoque facta sint, etiamsi sacra historia in singulis describendis sit parcior. Illud certe ex Actorum libro constat, Iudaeos, qui omnes inter se fratres dici atque censeri volebant, grauissimos Apostolorum hostes fuisse: adeo ut frequenter prophanas gentes aduersus illos concitarent.
units.tr: But as if the Lord had said too little about the dangers and conflicts that awaited the disciples, he returns to their description and now mentions what is most grievous to all good people: that they see themselves hated even by those whom, because of the closest bond of kinship or blood, they could neither abandon without scandal nor, much less, hate. For he says: "You will be betrayed even by parents, and brothers, and friends, and relatives." And lest anyone think that this rage will not last, he adds: "And they will put some of you to death." So that hatred can be satisfied only with blood. Not content with this, he adds: "And you will be hated by all men for my name's sake." This had to be added so that they would not think any help was left to them among men, and so that they would not then despair of God's aid, because it is impossible for the Son of God to abandon in the struggle those who are in danger for his name and word. There is no doubt that these things also happened, even though sacred history is sparing in describing each case. It is certainly clear from the book of Acts that the Jews, who wanted all to be called and regarded as brothers among themselves, were the most bitter enemies of the apostles, so much so that they often stirred up the heathen nations against them.

units.la: In quibus exemplis nos implacabile odium agnoscere debemus, quo impij aduersus Christum exardescunt: cuius tanta vis est, ut postquam illi indulgere coeperint, nullis rationibus placari immo neque naturae legibus coerceri possint, quo minus crudelissime in eos saeviant, quos ipsis artius aliquod cognationis vinculum devinxit. Cur enim ex se natos aut fratres siue consanguineos agnoscerent, qui aduersus caelestem Patrem & totius naturae creatorem insurgere non verentur? Exempla huius immanitatis multa extant iam inde a prima mundi origine: inter quae primus locus Caino debetur, qui Abelum fratrem, a quo nulla unquam iniuria provocatus fuerat, propter fidem in semen illud promissum & Dei cultum puriorem, trucidauit. Agitantur illius spiritu omnes illi, qui hodie proprios filios propter Christi confessionem abdicant, fratres germanos persequuntur, bella civilia movent, & antiquos hostes atque barbaras nationes in communis patriae viscera accersunt. Sentient isti aliquando graue Dei iudicium. Interim horum meminerint pij, ne temere ijs fidem habeant, quos aduersus Christum & Euangelium eius cum Antichristo coniurauisse sciunt. Simulant isti aliquando pacis studium, quando se inferiores esse uident. Sed fere insidiosa pax est, quam illi faciunt, sive palam improbi aut nequam hypocritae, sive quoad seculum viri boni fuerint. Illi enim prima quaque occasione ad axioma illud papisticum recurrunt, Haereticis non seruandam esse fidem: hi vero Pontificum minis atque anathematismis coguntur, ut fidem datam vel invriti violent. Qui huius perfidiae & immanitatis exempla requirit, nimis profecto stupidus est, cum quotidie huius generis multa fiant, ut vetera omnia omittamus, quae iam seculis aliquot, non in priuatos modo homines, verumetiam in potentissimos Reges atque Imperatores edita sunt. Caute ergo & circumspecte res suas gerant Christiani principes & Ecclesiarum pastores, ne negligentia aut facilitate nimia suae fidei creditos turpiter prodant impijs Christi hostibus, quibus nihil tam suave & iucundum est quam cum piorum sanguine ludere, & fidelium simplicitate ad suam tyrannidem stabiliendam abuti.
units.tr: In these examples we must recognise the implacable hatred with which the wicked blaze up against Christ. It is so great a force that, once they have begun to indulge it, it cannot be appeased by any reasons, nor even restrained by the laws of nature, so that they do not rage most cruelly against those whom some closer bond of kinship has tied to them. For why should they acknowledge as their own sons or brothers or kinsmen those who do not hesitate to rise up against the heavenly Father and the Creator of all nature? Examples of this savagery exist in abundance from the very beginning of the world, among which the first place is owed to Cain, who slew his brother Abel, who had never been provoked by any injury from him, because of his faith in the promised seed and his purer worship of God. All those are driven by his spirit who today disown their own sons on account of confession of Christ, persecute their own brothers, stir up civil wars, and summon old enemies and barbarous nations into the very vitals of their common fatherland. Those men will one day feel the heavy judgment of God. Meanwhile let the godly remember this, and not lightly trust those whom they know to have conspired with the Antichrist against Christ and his Gospel. These men sometimes feign a zeal for peace when they see themselves to be the weaker. But the peace they make is almost always treacherous, whether they are openly wicked or worthless hypocrites, or men who are good as far as the world is concerned. For at the first opportunity they run back to that Papist maxim, that faith is not to be kept with heretics; while the others, forced by the threats and anathemas of the Pontiffs, break a pledge given even against their will. Anyone who asks for examples of this faithlessness and savagery is surely very foolish, since many things of this kind happen every day, not to mention all the older cases, which were committed not only against private men but against the most powerful kings and emperors some centuries ago. Let Christian princes and the ministers of the Churches therefore conduct their affairs cautiously and circumspectly, lest through negligence or excessive ease they shamefully betray to the impious enemies of Christ those entrusted to their faith; for nothing is so sweet and pleasant to them as to toy with the blood of the godly and to abuse the simplicity of the faithful to establish their own tyranny.

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui locum istum noua consolatione concludit, & quid ab ipsis fieri debeat, amplius docet: Pilus capitis vestri (inquit) non peribit: Nimirum absque Patris mei voluntate sive consilio. Sic ipse dictum hoc Matth. 10. cap. exponit, dicens: Nonne duo passerculi assario veneunt, & unus ex eis non cadet humi sine Patre vestro? Vestri vero etiam capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. Ne igitur timueritis: multis passerculis praestatis vos. Ita vero ad Dei prouidentiam remittit, quae efficacissima consolationis argumenta suggerit omnibus, qui ea recte animo concipiunt. Quoad homines, aequius omnia ferunt, quotquot se amicis, aut parentibus, aut principibus suis curae esse sciunt. Cur ergo no gaudeat & exultet, qui se in Dei tutela & sub umbra alarum eius (ut in Psal. canitur) degere credunt, qui Pater est non minus fidelis quam potes, quique nostri nunquam obliuiscitur? Habet is nos (ut apud Isa. ait) in manib. suis insculptos, et proinde nihil perire potest illis, qui eius uocatione sequuntur Quaecunque Quæcunq; enim in hoc seculo amittunt, ea quasi in Dei manum deponunt, qui renumerator est liberalissimus. Fit ergo, ut pro umbratuli & momentanea huius seculi gloria solidam & immortalem, pro bonis terrenis cœlestia, pro vita hac caduca æternam et nullis casibus obnoxiam recipiant. Hæc qui minus expendunt, & res omnes fortuitò ferri sibi persuadent, ij ut in subeundis periculis trepidi sunt & cunctatores ignavi: ita si quid triste ipsis accidat, miserabiliter eiulant, & querelis iniquissimis te stantur, se nulla certa diuinæ bonitatis fidutia esse suffultos.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who closes this passage with a new consolation and teaches more fully what ought to be done by them: "Not a hair of your head," he says, "will perish." Of course, without the will or counsel of my Father. So he himself explains this saying in Matth. 10., saying: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing, and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father? But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore: you are of more value than many sparrows." In this way he refers them to the providence of God, which supplies the most effective arguments of consolation to all who rightly take them to heart. As far as men are concerned, all who know themselves to be cared for by friends, parents or their rulers bear everything more calmly. Why then should not he rejoice and exult who believes that he dwells under God's protection and in the shadow of his wings (as the Psalm sings), who is a Father no less faithful than powerful, and who never forgets us? He holds us (as Isaiah says) engraved on his hands, and therefore nothing can perish for those who follow his calling. Whatever they lose in this world, they deposit, as it were, into the hand of God, who is the most generous repayer. So it comes about that in place of the shadowy and momentary glory of this world they receive a solid and immortal glory, in place of earthly goods heavenly ones, and in place of this frail life an eternal life subject to no mischances. Those who weigh these things less, and persuade themselves that all things are carried along by chance, are fearful in facing dangers and cowardly hesitators; and so, if anything sad happens to them, they lament wretchedly and complain most unjustly that they have been supported by no certain trust in divine goodness.

units.la: Recte ergo Dominus infert: Per patientiam vestram possidete animas vestras. Breuis sententia, sed uere diuina & philosophica: ut quæ uno uerbo rem maximi momenti comprehendit. Docet enim quæ uera atque tutissima sit nosipsos & animas nostras seruandi ratio. Non ea nimirum, quam ij sequuntur, qui carnis & mundi rationem audiunt. Hi enim felicitatem sibi ex eo pollicentur, si à curis & molestiis liberi omnibus arrideant, si aduersa quæuis declinent, crucem ab humeris suis reiiciant, denique nihil sentiant, quod ipsis durum aut triste sit. Sed isti plerunque seipsos amittunt, dum pessimarum cupiditatum mancipia facti uitam & ignauo otio & turpi ueritatis agnitæ dissimulatione, aut etiam inter scelera manifesta transfigunt, simul autem à uitæ æternæ hereditate excidunt. At qui uera fide suffulti in Deum respiciunt, ij aduersa & pericula quæuis fortiter sustinent, & inuicto animi robore per omnia obstacula salutis eluctantur, & ita per patientiam suam felicitatem veram atque solidam apprehendunt. Nam inter omnes huius seculi casus conscientiarum tranquillitate fruuntur, & huius uitæ curriculum emensi ad cœlestis regni hereditatem transeunt. Ideò apud Matthæum in eodem argumento addit Dominus: Qui perseueraverit in finem, saluus erit. Nostrum fuerit ô fratres, ut his promissionibus confirmati statione nostram fortiter tueamur, & fide constanti atque patientia inuicta contendamus ad metam illam æternæ felicitatis, quam nobis suo sanguine meruit Iesus Christus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, the Lord concludes: "By your patience possess your souls." A brief saying, but truly divine and philosophical, comprehending in a single word a matter of the greatest importance. For it teaches the true and safest way of preserving ourselves and our souls: not, of course, the way followed by those who listen to the reasoning of the flesh and the world. For these promise themselves happiness from being free of cares and troubles, from having everything smile upon them, from avoiding every adversity, from throwing the cross off their shoulders, and, in short, from feeling nothing that is hard or sad for them. But such men for the most part lose themselves, becoming the slaves of the worst desires, and they spend their lives in idle sloth and shameful pretence of known truth, or even amid manifest crimes, and at the same time they fall from the inheritance of eternal life. But those who, supported by true faith, look to God, bear all adversities and dangers bravely, struggle through every obstacle to salvation with an unconquered strength of mind, and so by their patience lay hold on true and solid happiness. For amid all the chances of this world they enjoy tranquillity of conscience, and having run the course of this life they pass to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore the Lord adds in Matthew, on the same subject: "He who endures to the end will be saved." It is our part, brothers, to be strengthened by these promises, to hold our post bravely, and with steadfast faith and unconquered patience to strive towards that goal of eternal happiness which Jesus Christ merited for us by his blood, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 187.

units.la: Cum autem videritis Hierosolymam cingi ab exercitibus: tunc agnoscite appropinquare vastationem eius. Tunc qui in Iudæa sunt, fugiant in montes: & qui in medio eius, excedant: & qui in agris, non ingrediantur in eam. Nam hi sunt dies vltionis, vt impleantur omnia quæ scripta sunt. Væ autem vterum ferentibus & lactantibus in illis diebus. Erit enim necessitas magna in hac terra, & ira in populo isto. Et cadent acie gladij, & captiui ducentur in omnes gentes: & Hierosolyma calcabitur à gentibus, vsquequo impleantur tempora gentium.
units.tr: "But when you shall see Jerusalem compassed about with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh. Then let them which are in Judaea flee to the mountains; and let them which are in the midst of it depart out; and let not them that are in the countries enter thereinto. For these be the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled. But woe unto them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days! For there shall be great distress in the land, and wrath upon this people. And they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations: and Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled."

units.la: Etsi discipuli carnis potius curiositate quàm salutis æternæ studio abrepti quæstionem de urbis excidio & totius mundi consummatione aut fine mouerant, Christus tamen ita illis respondet, ut & superstitiosis ipsorum opinionibus medeatur, & de ijs eos admoneat, quæ ipsis cognitu & observatu necessaria erant. Est hoc magnum bonitatis ac mansuetudinis eius argumentum, quod patres pios imitatur, qui quàmuis filios suos multa iuuenilius & petulantius agere ac quaerere uidean-t, non tamen indignos iudicant, qui ab ipsis instituantur. Debet illius consideratio nobis animum addere, ne dubitemus, quin nos quoque non reiecturus sit ille, si de ijs serio quæramus; quæ nos scire refert. Exstat enim eius promissio: Quærite, & inuenietis. Cæterum postea multa, quæ hucusque audiimus, transfit ad caput quæstionis de urbis & templi uastatione, cum qua cultus legalis seu Leuitici abrogatio coniuncta erat, & quando hæc futura sit diserte docet: simul autem admonet de omnibus ijs, quæ ipsos tunc facere oporteat, si saluti suæ consultum uelint. Ista uerò sic considerari debent, ut eadem nobis etiam dici putemus, & proinde discamus imminentis iræ Dei signa agnoscere, & in declinandis pœnis ab illo nobis monstratam uiam sequamur.
units.tr: Although the disciples, carried away more by fleshly curiosity than by zeal for eternal salvation, raised the question about the destruction of the city and the consummation or end of the whole world, Christ nevertheless answers them in such a way that he both cures their superstitious opinions and admonishes them about those things which it was necessary for them to know and to observe. This is a great proof of his goodness and gentleness, and in it he imitates the godly fathers, who, although they see their sons acting and asking in a rather youthful and wanton manner, do not judge them unworthy to be instructed by them. Consideration of this should encourage us, so that we do not doubt that he too will not reject us, if we seriously ask about those things which it concerns us to know. For his promise stands: "Seek, and you shall find." Moreover, after passing over many things that we have heard so far, he turns to the main question, concerning the destruction of the city and the temple, with which the abolition of the legal or Levitical worship was joined, and he clearly teaches when this will happen; at the same time he warns about all those things which they then ought to do, if they wish to take thought for their own safety. These things, however, ought to be considered in such a way that we think the same things are also said to us, and so we may learn to recognise the signs of God's impending wrath, and in avoiding punishments follow the way shown us by him.

units.la: Principio signum proponit, ex quo intelligant excidium illud præ foribus adesse. Cum videritis
units.tr: First he sets forth a sign by which they might understand that this destruction was at the doors. "When you shall see"

units.la: Vide Marcum Homil. 109.
units.tr: See Mark, Homily 109.

units.la: Hierosolymam cingi ab exercitibus, tunc agnoscite appropinquare vastationem eius. Signo opus erat, quia incredibile & prorsus absurdum videbatur, urbem sanctam excindi cum templo, & eum cultum aboleri, quem ab ipso Deo traditum sanctissimè patres multis seculis magno studio exercuerant. Idèo quod Lucas distertis verbis enuntiat, id apud Matthæum & Marcum sic proponit, ut Danielis Prophetæ de hac re testimonium ipsis in mentem revocet, dicens: Cùm videritis abominationem desolationis, quæ dicta est à Daniele Propheta, stantem ubi non oportet, qui legit intelligat. Ita vero loquitur de obsidione urbis, quam Romanæ legiones oppugnaturæ sint, & quam secutura sit non tam crudelis quàm horrenda & abominabilis vastatio, cum totius cultus (ut modò diximus) exterminio coniuncta. Et sanè pijs omnibus non potuit non abominandum & execrabile videri, in ijs montibus Aquilas & signa Romana conspici, & horrenda litiorum atque tubarum classica exaudiri, de quibus olim Propheta dixerat: Quàm speciosi sunt super montes pedes evangelizantis, prædicantis pacem, evangelizantis bonum, &c. Scimus enim quàm acerbis lachrymis & querelis olim pij in Psalmis excidium urbis prosecuti sint, cùm eius instaurationem diuinitus promissam esse non ignorarent. At in præsenti de excidio agitur, ex quo urbs illa nunquam instaurata est. Itaque docet obsidionem istam non fore vulgarem, quales sunt, in quibus aut non capiuntur urbes, aut ita capiuntur, ut tamen salvæ maneant, aut saltem brevi post instaurentur: quod Hierosolymæ etiam interdum accidisse alibi annotavimus. Sed ubi eadem Romanorum armis eversa, & cum templo culus quoque abolitus & omnino sublatus fuit, nulla deinceps sperari potuit instauratio: eò quòd nullus porrò amplius usus esset templi & cultus istius, cum exhibitus esset Messias, quem ceremoniæ illæ adumbrabant. Ideo in morte Domini velum templi scissum est, quo non solùm docebatur, cultum istum iam debere cessare, verumetiam sublatum iam esse scutum illud, sub quo hucusque latuerant. Scimus enim rempublicam illam una cum templo debuisse durare, usque quò veniret promissus ille Seruator, in quo omnes prophetiæ atque promissiones impleri debebant. Abstulit autem velum istud Deus simulque omni protectione infelices nudavit, quia mensuram iniquitatis suæ impleuerat, cùm & Filium Dei crudeliter occidissent, & Apostolos persecuti essent, & Euangelij doctrinam, quam gentes passim omnes magno studio amplectabantur, ipsi extinctam vellent. Tempus ergo erat, ut ab incurabili & pœnitere nescia gente Deus sanguinem Filij & seruorum suorum tandem requireret, quod sæpe minatus fuerat.
units.tr: "Jerusalem compassed about with armies, then know that its desolation is at hand." A sign was needed, because it seemed incredible and utterly absurd that the holy city should be destroyed along with the temple, and that that worship be abolished which the fathers, handed down by God himself, had most devoutly practised with great zeal for many centuries. Therefore what Luke states in plain words, Matthew and Mark set forth in such a way as to bring to their minds the testimony of the prophet Daniel about this matter, saying: "When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing where it ought not (let him who reads understand)." He speaks in this way of the siege of the city, which the Roman legions were about to attack, and of the destruction that would follow, not merely cruel but dreadful and abominable, joined with the extermination of the whole worship (as we have just said). And surely to all the godly it could not but seem abominable and detestable that eagles and Roman standards should be seen on those mountains, and that the dreadful clamour of trumpets and horns should be heard, of which the prophet had once said: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings, who proclaims peace, who brings good news," and so on. For we know with what bitter tears and lamentations the godly in the Psalms once bewailed the destruction of the city, since they were not ignorant that its restoration had been divinely promised. But here the destruction in question is one from which the city was never restored. Therefore he teaches that this siege will not be an ordinary one, such as those in which either cities are not taken, or are taken yet remain safe, or at least are restored shortly afterwards; as we have noted elsewhere, this has sometimes happened to Jerusalem too. But where the city was overthrown by the arms of the Romans, and together with the temple that worship too was abolished and utterly removed, no restoration could thereafter be hoped for, because there would be no further use of the temple and that worship, since the Messiah, whom those ceremonies foreshadowed, had been revealed. Hence at the death of the Lord the veil of the temple was torn, which taught not only that that worship must now cease, but also that the shield under which they had hitherto lain hidden was now removed. For we know that that commonwealth, together with the temple, was bound to last until the promised Saviour came, in whom all prophecies and promises were to be fulfilled. But God took away that veil and at the same time stripped the unhappy people of all protection, because they had filled up the measure of their iniquity, since they had cruelly put to death the Son of God, had persecuted the apostles, and wished the doctrine of the gospel, which the nations everywhere eagerly embraced, to be extinguished. It was therefore time that God at last required the blood of his Son and his servants from a people incurable and unwilling to repent, as he had often threatened.

units.la: Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo (ut alibi quoq; monuimus) docemur, quid omnes eos maneat, qui aduersus veritatē hostiliter insurgunt, & gratuita misericordia sese ipsis offerente Christum nolunt excipere, ut in eo salui fiant. Solent tales ferè maiorū suorum potentia, virtute, successibus & alijs fauoris diuini indicijs siue argumentis gloriari, & ex ijs sibi perpetuā impunitate pollicentur. Atqui omnia ista Iudæi habuerūt, adeò ut nulla gens unquam fuerit, quæ cum illis conferri mereatur, ut iā de promissionibus Dei deq; Filio eius, qui ex ipsis homo natus est, nihil dicamus. Ea deniq; Hierosolymorū gloria atq; magnificentia erat, ut optimis quibusq; impossibile videretur eam urbē perire, quæ Dei protectione & tutela toties aduersus immanissimos hostes seruata, & Prophetarum quoq; hymnis atq; laudibus celebrata fuerat. At non profuerūt ista omnia, cùm cōtumacia et rebellione inuicta aduersus Dei uerbū luctarentur. Quid? annon eo ipso excidium totius gentis maturauerunt, quo illud arceri posse putabant? Notum est enim Caiaphæ consilium, qui nisi Christum è medio tollerent, Romanos uenturos dicebat, qui urbem & gentem totā uastarent. Atqui hoc illud scelus fuit, quod multis alijs additū bilancem illam diuinæ iustitiæ in exitiū ipsorum detraxit. Non temere ergo Christus obsidionem urbis docet extremæ uastationis signum fore. Et erat hoc dictū no bis hodie diligentius considerandum, ut de bellis ciuilibus iudicare discamus, quibus orbis Christianus miserrimè distrahitur: item de Turcarū expeditionibus, quæ iā multis annis eiusmodi fuerunt, ut singulæ aliquam partem terrarū nostrarum abstulerint, Turcici uerò imperij limites propagarint. Quid ergo sperari potest quàm quod otim Lactantius prædixit, fore ut Imperium in Orientem redeat, rursus autem seruiat Occidens? Mali tanti remedium unicum fuerit, si à peccatis ad Deum conuersi uitam morefq; nostros emendemus, & illum colamus in spiritu & veritate.
units.tr: This, moreover, is a memorable example, by which (as we have also noted elsewhere) we are taught what awaits all those who rise up in hostility against the truth, and who, when free mercy offers itself to them, are unwilling to receive Christ, that they may be saved in him. Such people are wont to glory in the power, virtue, successes and other tokens or arguments of divine favour of their forefathers, and from these they promise themselves perpetual impunity. Yet the Jews had all these things, so much so that there has never been any nation worthy to be compared with them, to say nothing yet of the promises of God and of his Son, who was born of them as a man. Finally, such was the glory and magnificence of Jerusalem that it seemed impossible to the best people that that city should perish, which had been so often preserved by God's protection and defence against most savage enemies, and had also been celebrated with the hymns and praises of the prophets. But all these things did not help them, since they struggled against the word of God with obstinate contumacy and rebellion. What then? Did they not hasten the destruction of the whole nation by that very means by which they thought it could be averted? For the counsel of Caiaphas is well known, who said that unless they removed Christ from the midst, the Romans would come and lay waste the city and the whole nation. Yet this was the crime which, added to many others, tipped the balance of divine justice against them to their ruin. It was not without reason, then, that Christ teaches that the siege of the city would be the sign of its final destruction. And this ought to be considered more carefully by us today, so that we may learn to judge the civil wars by which the Christian world is most miserably torn apart, and likewise the expeditions of the Turks, which for many years have been of such a kind that each has taken some part of our lands and enlarged the borders of the Turkish empire. What then can be hoped for, except what Lactantius long ago foretold, that the empire will return to the East, and the West will again be in servitude? The only remedy for so great an evil will be if, turning from our sins to God, we amend our life and manners, and worship him in spirit and in truth.

units.la: At non urbis modo excidiū prædicit Christus, uerumetiam quid bello isto iam accenso pij facere debeant, docet. Summa consilij est, ut fuga matura sibi cōsulant, ne eodem cum impijs & incurabilibus exitiū exitio implicentur. Id uero partium enumeratione exponit. Primò, qui in Iudæa sunt (inquit) fugiāt ad montes. Fuit enim Iudæa ab una parte Libano, ab alia montanis Arabiæ cinƈta. Iubet ergo, ut qui possunt sese in loca tutiora recipiant, uel etiam ex terra ista procul emigrent. Deinde, qui in medio urbis aut intra muros degunt, ij mox excedant. Tertiò, qui in agris sunt, ne ingrediantur in eam. Apud Marcum alia quoq; interseruntur: qui supra domum fuerit, ne descendat in domum, nec ingrediatur ut aliquid tollat è domo sua. Et qui fuerit in agro, ne reuertatur retro ad tollendum palium suum. Quibus omnibus fugam suadet celerem, & ne se ullis rebus impediri aut detineri patiantur, quò minus quàm longissimè abeant ex ijs locis, quibus Dei ira imminet. Debuerunt ergo ista tunc uerè fieri, & ideo quæ tunc fuit Hierosolymæ Ecclesia Pellam migrauit, sicuti iam non semel diximus. Rursus uerò elucet in his singulare bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui mala futura prædicit, non ut nos terreat, sed ut de ijs euitandis admoneat, simulq; liberum nobis facit, ut fuga nobis consulamus, quando nimirum id nobis per nostram uocationem licet facere, & salua religione aut fidei confessione fieri potest. Minimè ergo probari debet nimius ille Tertulliani rigor, qui Christianis hominibus fugam omnem negauit, neq; licere uult, ut quacunq; ratione persecutorum fidei furorem declinemus. Quem librum contra Ecclesiam scriptum esse D. Hieronymus ex Gennadio testatur. Quod enim ille uetat, hoc Apostolos & uiros Apostolicos non semel prudenter & utiliter fecisse scimus, ut se melioribus temporibus seruarent, quando neq; Dei uocatio peculiaris, neq; necessitas aliqua eos ad Martyrij certamen uocabat. Et ex historijs constat, pessimè cessisse Iudæis, quod hac Christi monitione contempta undiq; in urbem confluxerunt, in qua alij propter templum, alij proter munitiones se tutos fore putabant. Eorum enim multitudo obsidionis molestias atq; calamitates graniores fecit propter famem & luem in urbe grassantem, & ijdem omni effugio præclusò miserabiliter in hostium manus inciderunt.
units.tr: But Christ does not foretell only the destruction of the city; he also teaches what the godly ought to do now that this war has been kindled. The sum of his counsel is that they should take timely flight for their own safety, lest they be involved in the same ruin as the wicked and incurable. He sets this out by enumerating the parts. First (he says), "let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains." For Judaea was bounded on one side by Lebanon and on the other by the mountains of Arabia. He therefore bids those who are able to withdraw to safer places, or even to emigrate far from that land. Next, those who dwell in the middle of the city, or within its walls, should depart at once. Third, those who are in the fields should not enter it. In Mark other things are also inserted: "He who is on the housetop should not go down into the house, nor enter to take anything out of his house; and he who is in the field should not turn back to take his cloak." In all these things he urges swift flight, and that they should not allow themselves to be hindered or detained by any possessions, so that they may go as far as possible from the places on which God's wrath hangs. These things therefore had to be done truly at that time, and so the church that was then at Jerusalem migrated to Pella, as we have already said more than once. Again, in these words there shines out a singular argument of the goodness of God, who foretells future evils not in order to terrify us, but to warn us to avoid them; and at the same time he gives us freedom to take thought for our safety by flight, whenever, of course, our calling allows us to do so and it can be done without loss of religion or confession of faith. Therefore that excessive rigour of Tertullian, who denied Christians every kind of flight and would not allow us by any means to avoid the fury of persecutors of the faith, ought in no way to be approved. St Jerome, on the authority of Gennadius, bears witness that Tertullian wrote this book against the Church. For what he forbids, we know that the apostles and apostolic men have not once done prudently and usefully, namely, to preserve themselves for better times, when neither a special call of God nor any necessity summoned them to the contest of martyrdom. And from histories it is clear that it turned out very badly for the Jews, because, having disregarded this warning of Christ, they flocked together from every side into the city, where some thought they would be safe because of the temple, and others because of its fortifications. For their multitude made the troubles and calamities of the siege heavier, on account of the famine and pestilence raging in the city; and these same people, with every means of escape cut off, miserably fell into the hands of the enemy.

units.la: Vt autem ista tunc secundum literam fieri debuerunt, ita nos isto exemplo discimus, quid facere debeant quicunq; rebus suis consultum uolunt, quando Deus propter Filij sui contemptum & pertinacem falsæ doctrinæ atq; superstitionum defensionem uirgas suas exerit. Tunc qui in Iudea adhuc uersantur, id est, qui uel ceremonijs uel mundi huius præsidijs fidunt, ij ad montes confugiant: & eos quidem de quibus olim Dauid dicebat: Attollo oculos meos ad montes, unde nam ueniat auxilium meum: Auxilium meum à Domino conditore cœli & terræ. Etenim per montem Christum ipsum repræsentari, Daniel docet, qui lapidem illum, qui absq; manibus reuulsus Monarchias omnes contriuit, uidit excreuisse in montem magnum, qui totum terrarum orbem impleuit. Et idem petra illa inuicta est, cui Ecclesia innititur, & eius uiribus suffulta ipsas quoq; inferorum portas non pertimescit. Ad hunc ergo confugiant & in eo acquiescant pij, procul relicta omni aliorum præsidiorum fiducia. Deinde qui adhuc inter impios uersantur ab illis absq; mora discedant. Vt enim exorto iam in domo aliqua incendio omnis mora longior & periculosior est: ita uix tuti erunt, qui uel tantisper apud eos moram traxerint, quos iam Dei uindicta persequitur. Ideo Lothum olim ex Sodomis exire cogebant Angeli, & in Apocalypsi Babylonis ruinam prædicens Dominus clamat: Exite ex ea popule mi, ne participes sitis peccatorum eius, & de plagis eius ne participetis. Vehementer ergo errant, qui illud hodie superuacaneum esse arbitrantur, quasi aliqua inter Christum & Belial commu nio possit intercedere. Curent autem qui euaserunt, ne unquam ad sordes suas et hostium Christi commertia redeant. Nam id qui faciunt, horum postrema primis peiora fiunt, quod multorum apostatarum exemplis probari poterat. Disputant hodie multi, qua uia calamitates declinare aut auertere possimus, quæ toti mundo hodie passim imminent, & alij quidem in hominum auxilijs fortissimum præsidium situm esse putant, alijs uerò non alia commodior atq; expeditior ratio uidetur, quàm si relicta Euangelij doctrina ad pristinas superstitiones redeamus, & ita eos nobis placemus, quos nostra libertate hucusq; offendimus. Sed sunt hæc stultissima & pernitiosissima humanæ rationis figmeta. Quia quò longius à Deo recedimur, eò magis eius ira aduersus nos exardescit. Itaq; Christi consilium secuti cum Dauide dicamus: Animæ nostræ expectent Dominum, ipse enim est auxilium nostrum & clypeus noster. In ipso gaudebit cor nostrum, eò quòd sancto ipsius nomine nitimur. Psal.33.
units.tr: Just as these things had to happen then in the literal sense, so we learn from this example what those must do who wish to look after their own safety, when God, on account of the contempt of his Son and the stubborn defence of false doctrine and superstitions, brandishes his rods. Those who still dwell in Judea, that is, those who trust either in ceremonies or in the protections of this world, should flee to the mountains: and they should do so as those of whom David once said: "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come. My help comes from the Lord, the maker of heaven and earth." For Daniel teaches that the mountain represents Christ himself. He saw the stone that was cut out without hands and crushed all the monarchies grow into a great mountain that filled the whole earth. That same rock is unconquered, the rock on which the Church rests, and, supported by its strength, she does not fear even the gates of hell. So the godly should flee to him and rest in him, leaving behind all trust in other protections. Next, those who still live among the wicked should leave them without delay. For when a fire has already broken out in a house, any delay is longer and more dangerous; so those who linger even briefly among those whom God's vengeance is already pursuing will hardly be safe. This is why the angels once compelled Lot to leave Sodom, and in the Apocalypse, foretelling the ruin of Babylon, the Lord cries: "Come out of her, my people, lest you be partakers of her sins, and lest you receive of her plagues." Those therefore greatly err who think that this is pointless today, as if some fellowship could exist between Christ and Belial. Let those who have escaped take care never to return to their filth and to the dealings of Christ's enemies. For those who do this, their last state becomes worse than their first, as the examples of many apostates could prove. Many people today debate by what way we may avoid or turn aside the calamities that now hang over the whole world everywhere. Some think the strongest protection lies in human help; others think no more convenient or expedient course is available than, having abandoned the doctrine of the Gospel, to return to our former superstitions, and so to please those whom we have hitherto offended by our liberty. But these are the most foolish and pernicious fabrications of human reason. For the further we withdraw from God, the more his anger blazes against us. Therefore, following Christ's counsel, let us say with David: "Let our souls wait for the Lord, for he is our help and our shield. In him our heart shall rejoice, because we trust in his holy name." Ps. 33.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Christum, qui sui consilij rationem adducit: Nam hi sunt dies ultrionis, ut impleantur omnia quæ scripta sunt. Dies ultrionis uocat tempus illud, quo Iudæorum impietatem atq; contumaciam puniri, & sanguinem innoxium, quem multis seculis fuderunt, ab illis requiri oportuit. Et solet tempus illud Scriptura diem Domini dicere, ut doceat, esse Deo dies certos siue statos iudicij, quos nunquam effugere possint impij, etiam si interdū diutius differantur. Solent quidem Epicurei porci ex mora illa sibijpsis impunitatem polliceri: sed non minus misere quàm turpiter spe sua falluntur: quia (ut Romanus ille historicus scribit) tardo quidem pede aduindictam diuina ira procedit, sed tarditatem illam supplicij gravitate compensat. In præsenti verò vaticiniorum Scripturæ sacræ meminit Christus, non tam ut commination i suæ fidem faciat, quàm ut doceat, quò in tantis malis pij respicere, & unde consolationem petere debeant. Nimirum ex Dei providentia, qui ut nihil temere ferri aut fieri patitur: ita per Verbum suum causas malorum detegit, & salutis consilia certa atq; tuta suggerit. Et sanè multa erant in Prophetarum scriptis, quæ discipulos docere poterant, Iudæis nihil præter meritum, nihil item fortuitum accidere: et quæ simul illos consolabantur, cum audirent, nihil propterea derogari Regno Dei & Ecclesiæ, quò minus in Christo seruetur, quot quot huc sese cum fide & obedientia subijciunt. Ideo apud Matthæum diligentiorem eorum, quæ apud Danielem habentur, lectionem atq; meditationem discipulis commendat. Quod verò illos moner, hoc ipsum ad nos quoq; pertinere putemus. Itaq; inter nostri seculi turbas atq; pericula ad ea respiciamus, quæ de nouissimis temporibus à Christo & Apostolis prædicta sunt: & mox patebit quæ ex difficultatibus omnibus emergendi via sit tutissima.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who gives the reason for his counsel: "For these are the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled." He calls that time "the days of vengeance," the time when the impiety and obstinacy of the Jews had to be punished, and the innocent blood which they had shed through many ages had to be required of them. Scripture usually calls that time "the day of the Lord," to teach that God has fixed days, or appointed days, of judgment, which the wicked can never escape, even if they are sometimes deferred for a longer time. Indeed the Epicurean swine are wont to promise themselves impunity from that delay; but they are deceived in their hope no less wretchedly than shamefully, because (as that Roman historian writes) the wrath of God proceeds to vengeance with a slow foot, but makes up for its slowness by the severity of its punishment. Now Christ recalls the prophecies of Holy Scripture, not so much to confirm his warning as to teach where the godly should look in such great evils, and from where they ought to seek consolation. Surely, from the providence of God, who suffers nothing to happen or be done rashly, so through his Word he discloses the causes of evils and offers certain and safe counsels of salvation. And indeed there were many things in the writings of the prophets which could teach the disciples that nothing befell the Jews except by their deserts, and nothing by chance; and which at the same time consoled them, when they heard that the kingdom of God and the Church were in no way diminished, so that they are not preserved in Christ, however many submit themselves here with faith and obedience. Therefore, in Matthew he commends to the disciples a more diligent reading and meditation upon the things found in Daniel. And what he warns them of, let us think that this pertains to us as well. Therefore, amid the tumults and dangers of our age, let us look to those things which were foretold by Christ and the Apostles concerning the last times; and soon it will become clear what is the safest way out of all these difficulties.

units.la: Ut verò magis excitet discipulorum animos, tristissimum illius temporis statum, & totius populi clades non sine graui amplificationis specie ob oculos ponit. Væ (inquit) uterum ferentibus ac lactantibus in illis diebus. Alibi inter benedictionis Dei species non postrema numeratur fecunditas & numerosa soboles: sterilitate verò improbari & vituperij loco fuisse, in sanctissimarum fœminarum exemplis esse videre: Annâ nimirum matris Samuelis & Elizabeta, quæ tandem Ioannem Baptistam ex singulari Dei beneficio peperit. Grauem ergo esse oportet calamitatem, quæ homines mouet, ut steriles & orbi esse malint, quam in sobole numerosa & felici Dei benedictionem sentire. Et facit ad huius dicti confirmationem, quod Iosephus de Maria quadam narrat, quæ filium proprium iugulauit, ut eius carnibus paratis rabidam famem, qua agitabatur, placaret. Quod etsi fortasse à paucis aliis factitatum esse, auxit tamen omnium miseriam, quod liberos se non patriæ, sed hostibus peperisse viderent, & eos qui necem præsentem euadebant, in seruitutem rapi quauis morte acerbiore. Quod quàm graue sit generosioribus animis, in mulieribus Cymbricis est videre, quæ cum viros suos à Mario acie victos & ad internecionem cæsos esse, se verò hostium ludibrio & libidini subijciendas cernerent, seipsas mutuo & liberos suos occiderunt, ne quid grauius paterentur. Et huius generis exempla in historijs passim occurrunt, quæ docent, Deum hostium suorum peccata in liberis quoque ulcisci, sicut in Lege minatur. Obseruent ista parentes, qui posteris suis consultum esse cupiunt: & hos tunc demum felices fore sciant, si & ipsi Deo obtemperent, & ex se natos eidem consecrent.
units.tr: But in order to rouse the minds of the disciples more strongly, he sets before their eyes the most sorrowful state of that time and the destruction of the whole people, not without a heavy weight of exaggeration. "Woe," he says, "to those who are with child and to those who give suck in those days." Elsewhere fruitfulness and a numerous offspring are counted not least among the tokens of God's blessing, and barrenness was regarded as a reproach and a disgrace, as we see in the examples of the most holy women: namely Hannah, the mother of Samuel, and Elizabeth, who at last bore John the Baptist by a singular benefit of God. It must therefore be a grievous calamity which moves people to wish to be barren and childless rather than to feel God's blessing in a numerous and happy offspring. And what Josephus tells of a certain Mary confirms this saying: she slaughtered her own son and prepared his flesh to satisfy the raging hunger by which she was driven. Although perhaps this was done by few others, it nevertheless increased the misery of all, because they saw that they had borne children not for their country but for their enemies, and that those who escaped present death were dragged into slavery, a death more bitter than any. How grievous this is to more noble spirits may be seen among the Cimbrian women, who, when they saw that their husbands had been defeated by Marius in battle and slain to the last man, and that they themselves were to be subjected to the mockery and lust of the enemy, killed one another and their own children, so that they might suffer nothing worse. Examples of this kind occur everywhere in histories, and they teach that God avenges the sins of his enemies also upon their children, as he threatens in the Law. Let parents who wish to provide for their posterity observe these things: and let them know that they will then at last be happy, if they themselves obey God and consecrate to him those born of them.

units.la: Porrò addit Dominus quod ad huius loci explicationem facit: sic dicens: Erit enim necessitas magna in hac terra, & ira in populo isto. Debet hoc de Dei ira intelligi, per quam hostium furor accenditur, ut nullo sanguine rabies eorum satiari possit, ut neq; senum grandæuorum reuerentia, neq; muliebris sexus misericordia, neq; innocua puerorum & virginum ætate moueantur, sed in grandas quoq; matronas, in teneras virgines, in omnem deniq; sexum atque ætatem crudelitate & libidine sua sæuiant. Quæ omnia hoc breui dicto Christus comprehendit. Nec tamen hoc quoq; contentus addit: Et cadent acie gladij, & captiui ducentur in omnes gentes. Numerum cæsorum & captiuorum supra Cap. decimo nono ex Iosepho annotauimus. Est is tantus, ut rerum Iudaicarum ignaris possit incredibilis videri: quod Iosephum mouit, ut illius aliquam rationem reddendam esse putaret, ne populi sui cladem supra rei Veritatem amplificauisse videretur. At hic nobis in mentem venire debet Dei promissio, qui Abrahamo olim dixerat: Suspice quaso cælum, & numera, si potes, stellas: Sic erit semen tuum. Fuit hæc promissio admodum magnifica, cuius veritas in tota veteris Testamenti historia deprehenditur: & hodie adhuc eius manifesta argumenta extant. Nam licet in toto terrarum orbe dispersi sint Iudæi, neq; rempub. habeant certis legibus aut finibus circumscriptam, tanta tamen est eorum multitudo, ut omnes qui hodie sunt populos siue nationes numero facile uincilè uincant. Quid uerò illa profuit olim, cùm hora illa fatalis adesset, qua scelerum suorum pœnas debebant exulere? Nihil prorsus. Imò eò crudelior & miserabilior fuit clades, qua tanquam oues macti fuerunt: & hodie eò luctuosius & terribilius est diuinæ uindictæ exemplum, quod in eorum dispersione Deus toti orbi proponit. Ergo benedictiones quoq; Dei in maledictionem cedunt impijs, ut non solùm fructum ex illis nullum percipiant, uerumetiam eò infeliciores sint, quò magis promissiones Dei in ipsis elucescunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord adds what pertains to the explanation of this passage, saying thus: "For there shall be great distress in this land, and wrath upon this people." This must be understood of the wrath of God, by which the fury of the enemies is kindled, so that their rage can be satisfied by no bloodshed; so that neither reverence for grey-haired old men, nor pity for the female sex, nor the innocent age of boys and virgins moves them, but they rage with their cruelty and lust even against the great matrons, the tender virgins, and, in short, against every sex and age. Christ comprehends all these things in this brief saying. Yet not even content with this, he adds: "And they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led captive into all nations." We noted the number of the slain and captives from Josephus above, at chapter nineteen. It is so great that it may seem incredible to those ignorant of Jewish affairs; which moved Josephus to think that some account of it must be given, lest he should seem to have exaggerated the destruction of his people beyond the truth of the matter. But here the promise of God ought to come into our minds, which he once gave to Abraham: "Look now toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able: so shall your seed be." This promise was very magnificent, and its truth is seen throughout the whole history of the Old Testament; and even today its clear proofs remain. For although the Jews are scattered throughout the whole earth, and do not have a commonwealth circumscribed by fixed laws or borders, nevertheless their multitude is so great that they easily surpass in number all the peoples or nations that exist today. But what did this profit them formerly, when that fatal hour was at hand, in which they had to pay the penalties of their crimes? Nothing at all. Indeed the destruction was all the crueller and more wretched, in which they fell like sheep led to slaughter; and today the example of divine vengeance, which God sets before the whole world in their dispersion, is all the more sorrowful and terrible. Therefore the blessings of God also turn into a curse for the wicked, so that they not only receive no fruit from them, but are all the more unhappy, the more the promises of God shine forth in them.

units.la: Subijcit hîs Christus quod priora hæc omnia atrocitate sua superat: Et Hierosolyma calcabitur à gentibus, usq; quò implebuntur tempora gentium. Quod aliqui exponunt de tempore, quod gentium saluti & Iudæorum supplicio destinatum sit, & huc referunt quod in epistola ad Rom. 11. cap. de eorum restitutione dicitur, quà futurà dicit Apostolus, ubi plenitudo gentium ingressa fuerit. At quia illic non de politiæ Iudaicæ aut urbis Hierosolymorum instauratione sermo est, sed de vocatione ad salutem æternam, ego istis uerbis excidium irreparabile denotari existimo, quodq; urbs ista in ruinis mansura sit usq; ad consummationem sæculi. Negat ergo spem omnem instaurationis, & à gentibus (quas Iudæi ignominioso uocabulo Goijm dicunt) calcanda dicit, ut totius terræ illius prophanationem perpetuam exprimat. Scimus quidem homines superstitiosos de Hierosolyma & locis sacris multa fabulari, sed illa pudentissima Monachorum figmenta esse alibi demonstrauimus. Constat enim ex historijs, nullâ illic urbe unquam ab eo tempore condita fuisse, sed quæ hodie Hierosolyma nomine uenditatur, Bethera est, quam Ælius Adrianus muro cinctâ abs se Æliam nominauit. Fuerunt itè belli sacri incentores iam seculis aliquot Romani Pontifices, qui Christianos reges ad terram sanctam recuperandam hortati sunt, ut in Oriente usq; suam tyrannidem extenderent: sed quàm infeliciter con filia illa cesserint, historiæ testantur. Cæperunt quidem fictiti illâ Hierosolymam Gottfridus Bullonius & Baldoinus anno incarnati Filij Dei M.XCVIII. sed tandem post annos LXXXIX. Christiani amissam Turcis iterum cesserunt: nec tamen belli illius sacri tunc finis fuit, sed ad Friderici II. temporâ usq; durauit, qui cùm urbem illam anno M.CCXXVIII. recepisset, interea Pontificum dolis Apuliam amisit, & belli Neapolitani seminaiacta sunt, quo iam annis amplius trecentis Galli cum Hispanis comissi reliquas Christiani nominis gentes utrinq; in armorum societatem traxerunt: ita nimirum ulcisccente Deo Christianorum stultam superstitionem, qui de terra æterno exitio deuota recuperanda magis solliciti sunt, quam ut in suis terris Deo in fide uera seruiant. Neminem ergo hominum superstitiosorum fabulæ mouere debent. Excitet nos potius iustitiæ diuinæ consideratio, & Iudaicæ gentis exemplo territi, totis animis nos subijciamus Iesu Christo, cuius contemptu Deus tam seueriter ultus est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Christ adds to these things that the one which follows surpasses all the earlier ones in its atrocity: "And Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled." Some explain this as referring to a time appointed for the salvation of the Gentiles and the punishment of the Jews, and they relate to it what is said in Romans 11 about their restoration, when the Apostle, speaking of the future, says: "when the fullness of the Gentiles shall have come in." But since that passage is not about the restoration of the Jewish state or of the city of Jerusalem, but about calling to eternal salvation, I think that by these words an irreparable destruction is signified, and that this city will remain in ruins until the consummation of the age. He therefore denies all hope of restoration, and says that it will be trampled by the Gentiles (whom the Jews call by the insulting name Goyim), so as to express the perpetual desecration of that whole land. We know indeed that superstitious men tell many fables about Jerusalem and the holy places, but I have shown elsewhere that those are the most shameless fictions of the monks. For it is established from histories that no city was ever founded on that site from that time, and the place which today is sold under the name of Jerusalem is Bethera, which Aelius Hadrian, having surrounded it with a wall, named Aelia after himself. Roman Pontiffs for several centuries have also been the instigators of holy wars, exhorting Christian kings to recover the Holy Land, so that they might extend their own tyranny in the East; but histories bear witness how unhappily those undertakings turned out. Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin did indeed take that Jerusalem in the year of the incarnate Son of God 1098, but after eighty-nine years the Christians lost it again and yielded it to the Turks; nor was that holy war then ended, but lasted until the time of Frederick II, who, when he had recovered that city in the year 1228, meanwhile lost Apulia through the tricks of the Pontiffs, and the seeds of the Neapolitan war were sown, from which, now for more than three hundred years, the French, joined with the Spaniards, have drawn the remaining Christian nations on both sides into an alliance of arms. Thus God, no doubt, is avenging the foolish superstition of the Christians, who are more anxious to recover a land devoted to eternal destruction than to serve God in the true faith in their own lands. Therefore the fables of superstitious men ought to move no one. Rather let the consideration of divine justice stir us, and, struck with terror at the example of the Jewish nation, let us submit ourselves wholly to Jesus Christ, whose contempt God has punished so severely. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXVIII.

units.la: Tunc erunt signa in Sole & Luna & sideribus, & in terra angustia gentium in consilij inopia, resonante mari & salo: exanimatis hominibus præ timore & expectatione eorum quæ ventura sint super orbem terrarum. Nam potestates cœlorum agitabuntur. Et tunc videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nube cum potentia & gloria multa. Cum autem hæc fieri incipient, erigite & attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra.
units.tr: "Then there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress among the nations, in perplexity, with the sea and its waves roaring; men fainting for fear and in expectation of the things that are coming upon the world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. But when these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near."

units.la: Disseruit hucusq; Dominus & Seruator noster, Iesus Christus, de urbis Hierosolymæ & templi excidio, deq; signis quæ prius fieri oporteat, simulq; docuit, quid inter tanta pericula facere debeant pij, qui suæ saluti consulcum uolunt. Quibus absolutis nunc ad alteram quæstionem discipulorum transijt, quam ipsi de huius mundi fine proposuerant. Quo loco rursus à signis orditur, & turbulentissimum totius orbis terrarum statum, qui tunc futurus sit, exponit. Inde nouissimum suum adim dicium aduentum describit. Postremò breui ac salutari præcepto suos instruit, & aduersus omnia pericula efficacissimè consolatur. Quia autem hæc non tam propter discipulos quàm propter nos dicta sunt, in quos (ut Paulus ait) fines seculorum inciderunt, diligenter à nobis considerari debent, ne nostrorum temporum turbis moueamur, neue in huius uitæ delitijs animos defixos habeamus, sed intrepida fide atq; ita suffulti per omnia obstacula ad portum felicitatis nostræ eluctemur, quam suo aduentu gloriosò nobis Christus afferet.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, has so far discoursed on the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the temple, and on the signs that must come first. At the same time he has taught what the godly ought to do amid such great dangers, if they wish to look to their own salvation. Having finished these matters, he now turns to the second question of the disciples, which they had put to him about the end of this world. At this point he again begins with the signs, and sets out the most turbulent state of the whole world that will then be. Next he describes his final coming for judgement. Lastly he instructs his people with a brief and wholesome precept, and most effectively comforts them against all dangers. But since these things were said not so much for the disciples as for us, upon whom (as Paul says) the ends of the ages have come, they ought to be carefully considered by us. We must not be moved by the tumults of our own times, nor keep our minds fixed on the delights of this life. Instead, with fearless faith, sustained thus through every obstacle, we should struggle on to the haven of our happiness, which Christ will bring us at his glorious coming.

units.la: Primò signa multa & uaria exponit, quæ non ad paucos dies astringere, sed ad totum illud tempus extendere oportet, quod ab urbis excidio usque ad finem huius mundi decurret. Ideo enim apud Marcum ait: In diebus illis post afflictionem iltam Sol obscurabitur, &c. Et in Matthæo: Statim autem post {æ}afflictionem dierum istorum, &c. Et de his pios admoneri oportuit, ne in solius Iudaici populi calamitates intenti, in his mundum omnibus malis defunctum esse putarent, & sibi posthæc omnia læta pollicerentur. Vult ergo intelligant, noua certamina Ecclesiæ suæ propositæ esse, in quibus nos sudare oporteat, donec ipse aduentu suo redemptionem nostram perficiat. Dicit ergo: Tunc erunt signa in Sole & Luna & sideribus, & in terra angustia gentium in consilij inopia, resonante mari & salo, exanimatis hominibus præ timore & expectatione eorum quæ uenturα sint super orbem terrarum. Nam potestates cælorum commouebuntur. Quibus uerbis omnia nouissimorum temporum prodigia comprehendit, quibus Deus periculosas rerum mutationes & pœnas impijs atq; securis destinatas portendit. Quæ si quis omnia ex ordine recensere uelit, ingentis libri argumentum sibi propositum haberet, cui conscribendo uix multi menses possent sufficere. Nos igitur omissis ijs, quæ olim & ante nostra tempora acciderunt, ea obseruemus et meditemur, quæ ipsi multa & non tam prodigiosa quàm tristia & horrenda uidimus. Nam ut à cœlestibus illis & Meteoris exordiamur, nullum unquam seculum fuit, quo in Sole & Luna atque sideribus plura uisa sint fieri contra naturæ leges & ordinem. Quoties enim Soles plures uisi sunt? quoties Luna uel cælo discedere, uel atro cruore conspersa, aut etiam crucibus interpolata uisa est? quoties stellæ inter se concurrentes & quasi dimicantes tristia spectacula præbuerunt? Quis uerò Cometas omnes enumerauerit, qui intra annos circiter quadraginta plurimi & nunquam absq; tristi aliquo euentu apparuerunt? Quis item unquam cælum ipsum toties ardere uidit, quoties intra decennium illud arsisse uidimus? Taceo nunc alia, quæ uix absq; uiolenta orbium atq; potestatum cælestium concussione aut agitatione fieri posse uidentur. Nec minus nota sunt, quæ in mari acciderunt & aquis alijs. Illud enim non semel aut ter remotum uti adiutum, aut aliqua occultiori uirtute agitatum terras uicinas subito inundauit, loca multa horribiliter absorbuit, multa arenæ cumulis inuectis inculta & inhabitata fecit. Similia his in fluminibus quoque & lacubus fieri uidimus. Quibus si monstra ex hominibus & reliquis animalibus nata adnumeres, multa occurrent spectatu dira & horrenda. Et quamuis multorum ea sit impietas, ut ista omnia facile contemnant, uel etiam rideant, tamen inuitis quoq; & dissimulantibus terrores obrepunt, qui ipsis omnia infesta reddunt. Plerique uerò tantùmnon exanimantur metu, quando tristissimos rerum euentus spectant, & propter prodigia eiusmodi non possunt non longe tri stiora metuere. Et ut multa, quæ hic dici poterant omittamus, duo sunt, quæ hominum mentes uehementer discruciant, & plerosq; consilij inopia in angustias extremas adductos rerum omnium incertos reddunt: Bella nimirum, quæ alia ex alijs quotidie feruntur, & infelices illæ circa fidei & salutis dogmata concertationes, quibus inter se cum acerbissimis odijs & summa animorum contentione comittuntur, qui præcipuam doctrinæ & eruditionis existimationem suflinent. Nam si primum spectes, nulla gens extra periculum constituta est, quando non exteris modò bellis omnia turbantur, uerumetiam ciuilia arma passim strepunt & cladibus intestinis omnia miscentur, quas maxima ex parte Pontificum artibus proditorijs debemus, qui per Tridentinum Concilium nunc annis amplius uiginti, omnes Christiani orbis habitatores bellis atq; rumoribus bellorum exagitauerunt. Quis uerò bonus non expauesc at? quis non totus horreat, qui tetram hanc & plus quàm belluinam sanguinis fundendi rabiem cernit? Quis item rebus afflictissimis consilium inueniat? quis de suis rebus aliquid certum statuat, quando passim doli & fraudes regnant, neq; ijs fidere tutum est, quos uel cognationis uinculum, uel eiusdem fidei professio coniunxit? Poterant tamen ista aliquo modo ferri à pijs, qui iampridem didicerunt, quid de mundo sentire debeant, & qui se in terris hisce peregrinos esse norunt: sed multi horum non possunt non grauissimè offendi, quando salutis doctrinam, & Dei Verbum, quod nobis inter ista pericula facis instar prælucere debebat, odiosis doctorum contentionibus in dubium uocari, & disputationibus nunquam finiendis ita obscurari uident, ut quid credi aut quid sentiri debeat, incertum sit. Conqueruntur de hoc multi passim, & utinam istorum querelas attentius audirent, quos ambitio, & contendendi, uel potius conuitiandi libido transfuersos abripit, ut ex ijs certaminibus laudem quærant, quæ absque multorum scandalo decertari non possunt. Sed quia de his sæpe aliàs dictum est, sufficiat ista annotauisse, quæ ad afferendam huius naticinij veritatem faciunt. Nunc verò usum istorum obseruemus, qui in duobus consistit.
units.tr: First, he sets out many and varied signs, which must be restricted not to a few days but extended over the whole period that will run from the destruction of the city to the end of this world. For this reason he says in Mark: "In those days, after that affliction, the sun will be darkened," etc. And in Matthew: "Immediately after the affliction of those days," etc. The godly had to be warned about these things, lest, intent only on the calamities of the Jewish people, they should think the world had been finished off by all evils in those events, and should promise themselves all happy things thereafter. He wishes them therefore to understand that new conflicts are set before his Church, in which we must toil until he himself, by his coming, completes our redemption. So he says: "Then there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress among the nations, in perplexity, with the sea and its waves roaring; men fainting for fear and in expectation of the things that are coming upon the world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken." In these words he comprehends all the portents of the last times, by which God foreshadows dangerous changes in things and punishments destined for the impious and the secure. If anyone wished to recount all of these in order, he would have before him the subject of a huge book, which scarcely many months could suffice to write. Therefore, omitting those things which happened long ago and before our times, let us observe and meditate on those which we ourselves have seen: many, and not so much prodigious as sad and dreadful. To begin with those heavenly and meteoric phenomena: there has never been an age in which more things were seen to happen in the sun, moon and stars contrary to the laws and order of nature. For how often have several suns been seen? How often has the moon been seen to depart from the sky, or to be sprinkled with black blood, or even marked with crosses? How often have stars, running together and as it were fighting, presented sad spectacles? Who indeed could enumerate all the comets which, within about forty years, have appeared in great numbers, and never without some sad outcome? Who has ever seen the heaven itself burn as often as we saw it burn within that decade? I pass over other things now, which can hardly seem to happen without a violent shaking or disturbance of the heavenly spheres and powers. Those things that happened in the sea and other waters are no less well known. That sea, not once or thrice, being driven back or stirred by some hidden power, suddenly flooded the neighbouring lands, horribly swallowed up many places, and by heaping up sand made many uncultivated and uninhabited. Similar things we have seen happen in rivers and lakes too. If you add to these the monsters born of men and other animals, many dreadful and horrible sights will present themselves. And although the impiety of many is such that they easily scorn all these things, or even laugh at them, yet terrors creep upon even the unwilling and the dissembling, and make everything hostile to them. Indeed most are almost struck dead with fear when they behold the saddest events, and on account of such portents cannot but fear far sadder things. To omit many things that might be said here: there are two things which greatly torment men's minds and, bringing most people to the utmost straits through lack of counsel, leave them uncertain of everything. These are wars, which are waged daily one after another, and those unhappy disputes over the dogmas of faith and salvation, in which men contend among themselves with the bitterest hatreds and the greatest exertion of spirit, those who claim for themselves the chief reputation for doctrine and learning. For if you look first at war: no nation is placed beyond danger, since not only is everything thrown into confusion by foreign wars, but civil arms also clash everywhere and all things are mixed up in internal slaughter. For the most part we owe these to the treacherous arts of the Pontiffs, who, through the Council of Trent, for now more than twenty years have harassed all the inhabitants of the Christian world with wars and rumours of wars. What good man would not be terrified? Who would not shudder entirely, seeing this foul and more than beastly rage for shedding blood? Who likewise can find counsel in the most afflicted circumstances? Who can determine anything certain about his own affairs, when deceits and frauds reign everywhere, and it is unsafe to trust even those whom a bond of kinship or the profession of the same faith has joined? Yet these things could in some way be borne by the godly, who long ago learned what they ought to think of the world, and who know that they are strangers in these lands. But many of these cannot help being grievously offended when they see the doctrine of salvation and the Word of God, which ought to shine before us as a light amid these dangers, called into doubt by the hateful contentions of teachers, and so obscured by disputations never to be ended that it is uncertain what ought to be believed or thought. Many complain of this everywhere, and would that those who are carried off course by ambition and the lust for contending, or rather for reviling, would listen more attentively to these complaints, so that they might not seek praise from quarrels which cannot be fought out without scandal to many. But since this has often been said elsewhere, it is enough to have noted these things which bear on establishing the truth of this prophecy. Now let us observe the use of these things, which consists in two points.
