units.la: Primò enim admonet, nihil temere aut absq; certo prouidentiæ Dei consilio fieri, qui ut prodigijs securos ad seriam propriæ salutis curam excitat: ita doctorum quoq; contentiones incidere patitur, ut & multa diligentius uentilentur, quæ prius minus à plerisque obseruata fuerunt, & (ut Paulus inquit) qui probati sunt manifesti fiant. Discant de his cogitare pij, & non facile in errores abducentur. Namutut multa obscura sint, multa in contentionem & disputationem trahi possint, certa tamen sunt fidei Christianæ principia, quibus si qui constanter insistunt, ij in alijs pernitiose non poterunt errare. Deinde quando omnia quæ nobis tristia accidunt, peccatorum pœnas, aut saltem uirgas Dei esse constat, quibus ne quando grauius peccemus nos coercet, admonet nos prodigorum istorum consideratio, quanta sit apud Deum peccati atrocitas, & quidijs sit expectandum, qui illius iram sceleribus suis non desinunt prouocare. Nam ut propter hominem omnis hæc mundi machina condita est: ita omnes eius partes illis infestæ sunt, qui aduersus opificem & conditorem suum insurgere audent. Pertinent huc minæ Legis, in qua cœlum ferreum & terram saxeam Deus impijs transgressoribus minatur, adhæc ferarum incursionibus & infinitis alijs calamitatibus uexandos fore docet. Exemplain historijs multa extant, & multa quotidie fiunt, quæ minas istas nequaquam uanas esse docent. Et quid obsecro impij de elementis & mundi partibus sperarent, quando se à proprio corde infestari sentiunt? Nam ut nihil aliud accedat, cor illos fallit, & diris terroribus tunc excruciat, quando animo præsenti quàm maximè opus erat. Quod si (ut plerunque fit) conscientiæ dolores & accusationes accedant, nulla ab hominibus crudelissimis excogitata est carnificina, quæ cum illa conferri possit. Excitent nos ista, ut inter nouissimi sæculi turbas toto animo ad Deum conuertamur, quæ proxima & unica salutis via est. Neque hic eorum figmenta audiamus, qui uniuersalem quandam totius orbis conuersionem ad Deum & pacem ex ea altam atque stabilem sibi pollicentur: quorum fabulis multi decepti securius agunt, & scelerum pœnitentiam differunt, ne quid præproperè facere uideantur. At si Christi uerba attentius consideremus, perpetua erit hæc, quam hoc loco describit, mundi facies, neque unquam emollietur impiorum durities, quæ propriæ etiam conscientiæ terroribus exasperari solet, ideoq; tunc demum horribiliter plangent & in extremam desperationem (ut in Matthæo uidere est) conijcientur, quando Christum ad iudicium uenire uidebunt. Quod unum satis docet, quàm uanum sit, quod alteri illi de omnium gentium conuersione fabulantur.
units.tr: First, he admonishes that nothing happens rashly, or without the sure counsel of God's providence. As he rouses the careless by portents to a serious care for their own salvation, so he also allows the contentions of teachers to arise, so that many matters, which before were less observed by most, are sifted more carefully; and (as Paul says) those who are approved may become manifest. Let the godly learn to reflect on these things, and they will not easily be led into error. For although many things are obscure, and many can be drawn into dispute and contention, there are nonetheless sure principles of the Christian faith. If anyone holds firmly to these, he will not be able to err destructively in other matters. Next, since it is plain that all the things which befall us in sadness are punishments for sins, or at least rods of God by which he restrains us lest we ever sin more grievously, the consideration of these portents admonishes us how great the atrocity of sin is before God, and what is to be expected by those who do not cease to provoke his wrath by their crimes. For as this whole machinery of the world was made on account of man, so all its parts are hostile to those who dare to rise up against their Maker and Creator. To this belong the threats of the Law, in which God threatens impious transgressors with a heaven of iron and an earth of stone, and teaches that they will be harassed by the incursions of wild beasts and by countless other calamities. Many examples exist in histories, and many things happen every day, which show that these threats are by no means empty. And what, I beseech you, could the wicked hope from the elements and parts of the world, when they feel themselves harassed by their own heart? For, not to mention anything else, the heart deceives them, and then tortures them with dreadful terrors when a calm mind is most needed. But if (as commonly happens) the pangs and accusations of conscience are added, no torture devised by the cruellest men can be compared with it. Let these things rouse us, so that amid the tumults of the last age we may turn with our whole mind to God, who is the nearest and only way of salvation. Nor should we listen here to the fictions of those who promise themselves a universal conversion of the whole world to God, and a deep and stable peace from it. By their fables many are deceived, act more securely, and put off repentance for their crimes, lest they seem to do anything over-hastily. But if we consider the words of Christ more attentively, the aspect of the world which he describes here will be lasting, and the hardness of the wicked will never be softened. It is usually made harsher even by the terrors of their own conscience; therefore they will then at last wail dreadfully and be cast into extreme despair (as may be seen in Matthew) when they see Christ coming to judgement. This one thing sufficiently teaches how vain is that other fable of the conversion of all nations.

units.la: Et huc pertinet quod in præsenti Dominus subijcit: Et tunc uidebunt Filium hominis uenientem in nube cum potentia & gloria multa. Apud Matthæum ait: Tunc apparebit signum Filij hominis, & tunc plangent omnes tribus terræ. De signo aliquo peculiari loquitur, quod in cœlo apparituum esse uerisimile est. Cùm enim iudicijs Dei particularibus prodigia & portenta præmittere soleant, minimè dubitari debet, Christum singulari aliquo & memorabili signo suum nouissimum aduentum toti orbi significaturum esse. Neque ideo falsi arguuntur Apostoli, qui diem Domini ex improuiso instar furis uenturū esse aiunt. Hi enim hoc propter impios dicunt, qui præter omnem expectationem opprimentur, quando sibi ipsis omnia tuta & diuturnam scelerum impunitatem promittunt. Deinde temporis quidem articulus iam nobis incertus & incognitus est, sed id non obstat, quò minus iamiam instante aduentu illo Domini signum aliquod in cœlo conspiciatur, quod de illo totum mundum admoneat. Id uerò plerique ueterum de Crucis signo exponunt & fortassis non absque ratione, ut alibi diximus. Quia enim nunc quoque per Crucem Christus de impijs suis hostibus triumphat, credibile est tunc in primis trophæum illud crucis toti orbi conspicuum fore, quando plenam uictoriam reportabit, & suos quidem ad Regni sui æterni possessionem secum inducet, diabolum uerò cum seruis suis omnibus in igne inextinguibilem detrudet, abolita prius morte, per quam ille regnare uisus est.
units.tr: And to this belongs what the Lord adds at this point: "And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory." In Matthew he says: "Then shall appear the sign of the Son of man, and then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn." He speaks of some particular sign, which is likely to appear in heaven. For since God's particular judgments are usually preceded by prodigies and portents, we ought not to doubt that Christ will signify his last coming to the whole world by some singular and memorable sign. Nor on that account are the Apostles convicted of falsehood, who say that the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a thief. For they say this with regard to the impious, who will be overwhelmed beyond all expectation, when they promise themselves that all is safe and that their wickedness will go unpunished for a long time. Moreover, the moment of time is indeed uncertain and unknown to us, but this does not prevent a sign from being seen in heaven, at the very moment when that coming of the Lord is at hand, which will warn the whole world concerning it. Most of the ancients explain this sign as the sign of the Cross, and perhaps not without reason, as we have said elsewhere. For since even now Christ triumphs over his impious enemies by the Cross, it is credible that that trophy of the cross will then be most conspicuous to the whole world, when he wins complete victory, and brings his own into possession of his eternal kingdom, but casts the devil with all his servants into unquenchable fire, death having first been abolished, by which he seemed to reign.

units.la: At hic non temere dici putabimus: Et tunc uidebunt Filium hominis uenientem in nube cum potentia & gloria multa. Habent enim singula uerba emphasim, quæ isti argumento optime conuenit. Tunc (inquit) uidebunt: quando nimirum horribilis illa confusio passim omnia turbabit, & alij quidem securi genio indulgebunt, alij inter desperationis procellas luctabuntur, pij uerò redemptionem suam magno cum desiderio expectabunt. Tunc (inquam) juno momento isti simul omnes videbunt, quod ipsis videre conueniet. Et quid nam illud erit? Filius hominis. Ita uero seipsum dicere solet, & hic isto nomine cumprimis uti voluit, ut se ne in cœlesti quidem gloria hominem, quem semel assumpsit, depositurum esse ostendat. Et æquum est (quod D. Augustinus alicubi annotauit) ut ea forma ad iudicium ueniat, in qua passus & noster seruator factus est, & quam impij in illo contempserunt, atq; persecuti sunt. Huius enim conspectus ut pijs latissimus erit, ita terrorem atq; dolorem immanem impijs incutiet, quando iudicem cogentur uidere & ferre, quem pro Seruatore & uindice suo agnoscere noluerunt. Vbi uero illum uidebunt? In nube, quæ diuinæ præsentiæ atq; potentiæ symbolum est. In Psalmis enim de Deo canitur: Nubes & caligo circa ipsum sunt. Item: Qui fecit nubes uehiculum suum. Quia ergo nubes Christo tribuitur, simul eiusdem diuinam uirtutem atque maiestatem denotari cogitabimus. Ideo addit: Cum potentia & gloria multa: potentiâ nimirum & uirtutem omni humana maiorem intelligens. Et sane in comparabilem esse oportet eam gloriam, cuius ne gustum quidem discipuli illi selectissimi ferre potuerunt, coram quibus in monte Thabor clarificatus apparuit. Hæc infelicem hostium eius, quæ tunc erit, conditionem exprimunt. Quis enim non exhorresceat eius iudicis conspectum, quem abs se infinitis iniurijs læsum esse nouit? Quis non tremat coram eo, qui suo nutu terras & cœlum concutit? Terrentur sæpe qui nullius sceleris sibi conscij sunt, quando Reges cum armata satellitum turba prodire, & armis fulgentibus omnia coruscare uident. Quem ergo animum fore putabimus impijs illis qui Christum, quem in uerbo suo & membris suis hostiliter persecuti sunt, cælesti maiestate armatum & multis Angelorum myriadibus stipatum, thronum conscendere uidebunt, ex quo sententiam tonabit aduersus omnem carnem, quæ in æternum rata manebit? Quàm horribilis sit horum meditatio impijs, in eorum exemplis uidemus, qui scelerum conscientia uicti sibipsis mortem conscisc unt. Vincet tamen omnes istos terrores tanti iudicis conspectus, quando inuitis sese præsentem ingeret, & ut se actorem & iudicem audiant coget eos, qui ipsum salutem omnibus ex gratuita misericordia offerentem audire noluerunt. O si istorum consideratione diligentius uersarentur, quos mundi studium detinet, & suæ potentiæ fiducia inebriat. Obturant pleriq; istorum aures suas, & omnem de nouissimo iudicio meditationem ex animis suis excutiunt, ut liberius desiderijs pessimis & uoluptatibus turpissimis indulgeant. Sed ijdē nunquam subterfugient, quin Christum iudicem uidere & audire cogantur.
units.tr: But we shall think that these words are not said rashly here: "And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory." For each word has an emphasis which agrees very well with this argument. "Then," he says, "they will see": namely, when that dreadful confusion will everywhere disturb all things, and some will indulge their pleasures in carefree security, others will struggle amid the storms of despair, but the godly will await their redemption with great longing. "Then," I say, in a single moment all of them together will see what it befits them to see. And what will that be? "The Son of man." Indeed, he is accustomed to call himself this, and he chose especially to use this name, to show that he will not lay aside, even in heavenly glory, the man whom he once assumed. And it is fitting (as Augustine somewhere remarked) that he should come to judgment in that form in which he suffered and became our Saviour, and which the impious despised and persecuted in him. For as the sight of him will be most joyful to the godly, so it will strike terror and immense grief into the impious, when they are forced to see and endure as judge him whom they refused to acknowledge as their Saviour and Vindicator. But where will they see him? In a cloud, which is the symbol of the divine presence and power. For in the Psalms it is sung of God: "Clouds and darkness are round about him." Again: "He who makes the clouds his chariot." Because therefore clouds are ascribed to Christ, we shall consider that his divine power and majesty are at the same time denoted. Therefore he adds: "with power and great glory," understanding by power and strength something greater than all human power. And indeed that glory must be incomparable, the taste of which even those most select disciples could not bear, before whom he appeared transfigured on the mount Tabor. These words express the unhappy condition of his enemies which will then be. For who would not shudder at the sight of that judge whom he knows he has wronged by countless injuries? Who would not tremble before him, who shakes the earth and heaven at his nod? Often those who are conscious of no crime are terrified, when they see kings coming forth with an armed throng of attendants, and all things flashing with shining weapons. What then shall we think will be the state of mind of those impious men, who will see Christ, whom they hostilely persecuted in his word and in his members, armed with heavenly majesty and surrounded by myriads of angels, mounting the throne, from which he will thunder out sentence against all flesh, which will remain fixed for ever? How dreadful the contemplation of these things is to the impious, we see in the examples of those who, overcome by the consciousness of their crimes, have brought death upon themselves. Yet the sight of so great a judge will overcome all those terrors, when he presents himself to them against their will, and will compel those who refused to hear him offering salvation to all from free mercy, to hear him as their author and judge. O if only those whom the pursuit of the world holds, and whom confidence in their own power intoxicates, would more diligently dwell on the consideration of these things! Many of them stop their ears and shake out of their minds all meditation on the last judgment, so that they may indulge more freely in wicked desires and most shameful pleasures. But these men will never escape being compelled to see and hear Christ as judge.

units.la: At ne horum mentio pios quoq; terreret, hos ab infelici impiorum turba distinguit, & præcepto simul breui atq; consolatione dulcissima instruit, dicens: Cum autem hæc fieri incipient, erigite & attollite capita uestra: quoniam appropinquat redemptio uestra. Præceptum locutione proverbiali figurat, quando capita erigere & attollere iubet. Nam qui curis mordacibus, aut tristitia excruciantur, uel inertes & ignaui torpent, ij capite demisso sedent uel incedunt. Quo respiciens Christus hoc dicere uult: Dura & tristia sunt, quæ euentura auditis: sed non ideo uos animo concidere aut curis nimijs discrutiari, uel etiam ad desperationem adduci uelim, quasi impossibile sit inter tot pericula salutem propriam custodire. Quin potius animum colligite, & diuini auxilij mearum q; promissionum fiducia freti obuiam ite tantis malis, & ex his ipsis spem salutis certam concipite. Et mox huius præceptionis rationem consolationis plenam subijcit: Quoniam appropinquat redemptio uestra. Redemptionis uocabulo plenam & perfectam salutem intelligit totius hominis, quæ nemini in terris hisagenti obtingit. Nam expiauit quidem peccata nostra Dei Filius, & a morte æterna redemit, adhæc salutis arrhabonem dedit Spiritum sanctum, qui nobis regenerationis ac innouationis author est. Quia uero nunquam ita renascimur, quin innatæ uitiositatis reliquiæ in nobis maneant, & (quod Paulus de semetipso faretur) sanctissimi quoq; interdum per Legem peccati abripiantur, ut multa præter officium faciant: disciplina seueriori interdum nos coerceri opus est: adhæc carnis nostræ uitiositatem morte deleri atq; absorberi oportet, ut cælestis illius uitæ capaces efficiamur. Adhæc in mundi quoq; machina eius q; partibus singulis multa seruituris & corruptionis argumenta cernuntur, quæ ex peccato inuecta est. Ista uero omnia non prius cessabunt aut abolebuntur, quàm ubi nouissimus ille aduentus Dominici dies illuxerit. Tunc enim omnis creatura (ut Paulus inquit) à seruitute & uanitate, cui nunc subiecta suspirat, liberabitur: tunc abolebitur mors: tunc corpora quoq; resuscitata immortalitatem induent: tunc cœli innouabuntur: tunc lachryma abstergetur, cessabit item dolor & gemitus: tunc Christo per omnia similes erimus: tunc Deũ uidebimus facie ad faciem sicuti est, & in eius conspectu bonorum atq; gaudiorũ omnium satietate fruemur, deniq; bona illa ineffabilia possidebimus, quæ oculus non uidit, neq; auris audiuit, & quæ omnē cordis humani cogitationē superant. Hæc omnia redemptionis nomine Christus comprehendit, & quia ista appropinquat, nos tunc alacres & ad hanc excipiendam instructos esse iubet, dum infelix mundus circa curas inanes & scelerum studia tumultuatur. Ita uerò docet unum & eundē diem sui aduentus impijs quidem terribilem, pijs autem lætum & felicißimum fore: nimirum quòd his Seruator & redemptor, illis uerò iudex iustus & seuerus impietatis atq; scelerũ uindex uenturus sit. Latet autem sub his uerbis argumentum ualidißimum, quo & mortuorum resurrectio, & Christi ad iudicium aduentus probatur. Quia enim pios perfectè redemi, impios aut & pœnitere nescios uerè puniri oportet, (nisi Deũ iustitia simul et bonitate sua spoliare libeat) neutrũ uerò in hoc seculo fit, imò multa secus fieri uidemus, ut hi quidem feliciter agãt, illi uerò perpetuis certaminibus atq; laboribus exerceantur: necesse est alium diem constitutum iam esse, quo omnes homines in suis corporibus recipiant omne id quod aut bene aut male fecerunt. Sūt hæc alibi diligentius demonstrata. Nunc ergo sufficiat monuisse, fore omnino iudicium uniuersale, & huius diem impijs terribilem, pijs autē lætum atq; optatißimum fore. Quapropter procul reiectis mundi studijs atq; huius seculi uoluptatibus, pietati studeamus, ut cum gaudio & alacritate capita nostra attollere, & tam corporum quàm animarum nostrarum plena redemptione potiri possimus in magno illo die, quando cum Angelis & diuina potentia armatus ueniet Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But lest the mention of these things should terrify the godly also, he distinguishes them from the unhappy crowd of the impious, and instructs them at once with a brief precept and a most sweet consolation, saying: "But when these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near." He expresses the precept in a proverbial manner, when he bids them stand up and lift up their heads. For those who are tormented by gnawing cares or sadness, or who lie sluggish and idle, sit or walk with head bowed down. Looking to this, Christ wishes to say: "The things you hear are to come are hard and sad; yet I would not have you lose heart or be torn apart by excessive cares, or even be brought to despair, as if it were impossible amid so many dangers to keep your own salvation. Rather, gather your courage, and trusting in the help of God and in my promises, go to meet such great evils, and from these very things conceive a certain hope of salvation." And soon after he adds the reason for this precept, full of consolation: "because your redemption draws near." By the word redemption he understands the full and perfect salvation of the whole man, which falls to no one who is still living in this world. For the Son of God has indeed expiated our sins and redeemed us from eternal death; moreover, he has given the Holy Spirit as the pledge of salvation, who is the author of regeneration and renewal in us. But because we are never so reborn that remnants of innate wickedness do not remain in us, and (as Paul confesses of himself) even the most holy are sometimes carried away by the law of sin, so that they do many things beyond their duty, it is sometimes necessary for us to be restrained by a more severe discipline; moreover, the wickedness of our flesh must be destroyed and swallowed up by death, so that we may become capable of that heavenly life. Furthermore, in the machinery of the world and in each of its parts many signs of servitude and corruption are seen, which have been brought in by sin. But all these things will not cease or be abolished until that last day of the Lord's coming has dawned. For then every creature (as Paul says) will be freed from the servitude and vanity to which it now groans in subjection; then death will be abolished; then the bodies also, raised again, will put on immortality; then the heavens will be renewed; then every tear will be wiped away, and pain and groaning will likewise cease; then we shall be like Christ in all things; then we shall see God face to face as he is, and in his sight we shall enjoy the fullness of all good things and joys, and finally we shall possess those ineffable good things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, and which surpass all human thought. Christ comprehends all these things under the name of redemption, and because it is at hand, he bids us to be then cheerful and prepared to receive it, while the unhappy world is in tumult over empty cares and the pursuit of sins. Thus he teaches that one and the same day of his coming will be terrible to the impious, but joyful and most desirable to the godly: namely, because he will come as Saviour and Redeemer to these, but to those as a just and severe judge and avenger of impiety and wickedness. Moreover, under these words lies a most powerful argument, by which both the resurrection of the dead and the coming of Christ to judgment are proved. For since the godly must be perfectly redeemed, and the impious and those who know not how to repent must truly be punished (unless it please God to strip himself of his justice and goodness together), and neither of these comes to pass in this age, but on the contrary we see many things happening otherwise, namely that these men live happily while those are exercised in perpetual struggles and labours, it is necessary that another day has already been appointed, on which all men will receive in their bodies all that they have done, whether good or evil. These things have been demonstrated more diligently elsewhere. Now then it is enough to have warned that there will certainly be a universal judgment, and that its day will be terrible to the impious, but joyful and most desirable to the godly. Therefore, casting far away the pursuits of the world and the pleasures of this age, let us devote ourselves to piety, so that we may with joy and alacrity lift up our heads, and in that great day, when Jesus Christ comes armed with the angels and divine power, may obtain the full redemption of both our bodies and our souls: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXIX.

units.la: Dixit autem eis parabolam: Videte ficum et omnes arbores: cum iam emiserint gemmas, vos eas cernentes, per vos ipsos agnoscitis iam propè esse æstatē. Ita & vos cùm videritis hæc fieri; agnoscite propè esse Regnum Dei. Amen dico vobis, nequaquam præteriert hęc ætas, quousq; hęc omnia facta fuerint. Cœlum & terra præteribunt, verba autem mea nequaquam præteribunt.
units.tr: And he spoke to them a parable: "See the fig tree and all the trees. When they now put forth their buds, you see them and know of yourselves that summer is now near. So also you, when you see these things come to pass, know that the Kingdom of God is near. Verily I say to you, this generation shall by no means pass away until all these things have been done. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall by no means pass away."

units.la: Quoniam Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, toti humano generi doctor Catholicus siue uniuersalis datus est, non eos modò qui ipso in terris agente uixerunt instituit in iis, quæ ipsis cognitu necessaria erant, uerumetiam ea diligenter tradit, quæ ad totius posteritatis institutionem faciunt, & quorum usus nobis etiam hodie est magnus, si rectè à nobis considerentur. Exemplum huius fidei atq; diligentiæ euidens hoc Cap. Lucas proponit. Nam etiamsi discipulos, qui de urbis & templi excidio interrogauerant, instituere voluerit, in diligentiorem tamen tractationem de fine mundi & nouissimorum temporum statu periculosissimo digreditur, & omnes eos sui officij admoner, qui usq; ad postremi sui aduentus diem nascituri sunt. Cæterùm quando de istis sermo habetur, pleriq; uel omnino non credunt, uel uaticiniorum eiusmodi euentum in longum tempus, aut etiam in infinitum extrahentes, ea extenuant. Accedit huic leuitati manifesta improbitas atque audacia. Quia enim mundo hoc & eius studijs delectamur, intolerabilis & quouis supplicio digna multus uidetur ea doctrina, quæ de illius fine & interitu disserit. Etenim cùm Iudæi pro manifestis Dei hostibus eos persequerentur, qui de templi & cultus externi dissipatione loquebantur, & Romanis odio dignißimi uisi sint, qui eius urbis occasum prædicebant, quæ ab illis aurea & æterna dicebatur: quis dubitet mundi voluptatibus & studijs deditos, aduersus eos omnes pugnaturos esse omnibus seculis, qui illum cum omnibus, quæ eo continentur, periturum esse docent? Ex hoc fonte certè illusorum sermones promanant, quibus doctrinam hanc omnem eludere & in dubium uocare, imò falsi arguere satagunt. Ideò Christus, ne qui simpliciores horum discerijs atq; sophismatis decipiantur, suam hanc prophetiam argumentis solidis confirmat, quæ nos ita considerare decet, ut ea non solùm opponamus impijs illis scurris, quibus cum Deo ludere leuiculum uidetur, verumetiam eorum consideratione ad ardentius pietatis studium excitemur.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ was given to the whole human race as a Catholic, that is, universal, teacher, he has not only instructed those who lived while he was on earth in the things that were necessary for them to know, but he also carefully hands down those things which serve the instruction of all posterity, and whose use is still great for us today, if they are rightly considered by us. Luke sets before us a clear example of this faith and care in this chapter. For although he wished to instruct the disciples who had asked about the destruction of the city and the temple, he turns to a more careful treatment of the end of the world and the most perilous state of the last times, and he admonishes all those who are to be born until the day of his final coming of their duty. But when these matters are discussed, many either do not believe them at all, or they weaken them by stretching the fulfilment of such prophecies over a long time, or even into infinity. To this frivolity is added open wickedness and audacity. For since we delight in this world and its pursuits, the doctrine that treats of its end and destruction seems to many intolerable and deserving of any punishment. Indeed, when the Jews regarded as manifest enemies of God those who spoke of the destruction of the temple and of external worship, and when those were thought most worthy of hatred by the Romans who foretold the downfall of that city, which was called by them golden and eternal, who can doubt that those who are devoted to the pleasures and pursuits of the world will fight against all those who teach that it, with everything contained in it, is going to perish, in every age? From this source certainly come the mocking speeches by which they strive to mock this whole doctrine, to call it into doubt, and indeed to prove it false. Therefore Christ, lest the simpler sort be deceived by their quibbles and sophistries, confirms this his prophecy with solid arguments, which we ought so to consider that we not only oppose them to those impious buffoons, for whom it seems a trifle to play with God, but are also roused by their consideration to a more ardent zeal for piety.

units.la: Primum argumentū similitudine constat, qua docet, hæc tam certa esse, vt aliter fieri nō possit: vtq; efficacior sit demōstratio, ipsos testes sistit, adeoq; omnes homines, qui istud quotannis experiun tur. Sic enim ait: Videte ficū & omnes arbores: Cùm iam emiserunt gemmas, nos eas cernentes, per nos ipsos agnoscitis iam propè esse æstatem: Ita & vos cum videritis hæc fieri, agnoscite propè esse Regnum Dei. Sensus est, Nemini dubium aut impossibile, neque etiam obscurum debere videri id, cuius exempla singulis annis in rerū natura habentur. Cùm enim ineunte vere arbores parturiunt & succó uitali pleni gemmas extrudunt, nemo tam vecors est, qui non agnoscat æstatis iam appro- pinquantis indicium: nemo item tam slultus, qui quò minus illa neniat, obstare conetur. Est enim naturæ Lex inuiolta, cuius cursum nullæ uires humanæ impedire possunt: & notum est irrevocabile illud Dei decretum, quod post diluuiū protulit: Adhuc omnibus diebus terræ (id est, quàm diu terra erit) sementis & messis, frigus & æstus, æstas & hyems, dies & nox non cessabunt. Quamobrem etiam si dura & aspera hyems plantas atq; arbores omnino extinxisse putetur, cedit tamen suo tempore, et mox æstatis lætæ atq; fructiferæ indicia apparent certa atq; infallibilia. Eandem ergo scito te esse mundi huius conditionem, & piorum in primis, qui in illo degunt. Nam his quoque suum uer & æstatem suam destinauit Deus, qua nemo eos fraudare poterit.
units.tr: The first argument consists in a comparison, by which he teaches that these things are so certain that they cannot happen otherwise. And so that the demonstration may be more effective, he brings forward the witnesses themselves, and indeed all men, who experience this every year. For he says: "See the fig tree and all the trees: when they now put forth their buds, you, seeing them, know of yourselves that summer is now near. So also you, when you see these things come to pass, know that the Kingdom of God is near." The sense is this: what has examples in the nature of things every year ought to seem to no one doubtful, impossible, or even obscure. For when at the beginning of spring the trees bring forth and, full of vital sap, push out their buds, no one is so foolish as not to recognise the sign of summer now drawing near; nor is anyone so stupid as to try to hinder its coming. For the law of nature is inviolable, and no human strength can impede its course; and that irrevocable decree of God, which he pronounced after the flood, is well known: "While the earth remains (that is, as long as the earth endures), seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease." Wherefore, even if a harsh and rough winter is thought to have utterly destroyed the plants and trees, it nevertheless yields in its own time, and soon the certain and infallible signs of a joyful and fruitful summer appear. Therefore know that this is the condition of this world, and especially of the godly who live in it. For God has appointed for them also their spring and their summer, which no one will be able to take from them.

units.la: Est autem simile hoc diligenti meditatione dignißimum, eò quòd præsentis & futuri seculi statum nobis ceu in tabula depictum proponit. Etenim quam in hoc mundo uitam uiuunt pij, ea hyemi rectissimè confertur: imò hyems dici meretur totum illud ævum, quo mundi huius machina durabit, si piorum in terris agentium conditionem consideres. Vt enim hyems pruinis plantas adurit, niuibus operit, terram ipsam cum fluuijs gelu astringit, arbores folijs & succo spoliat, rebus deniq; omnibus torporem inducit molestissimum: Ita pios infinitæ & assiduæ tempestates malorum exercent, & uix unquā tempus fore putatur, quando fructu optatæ quietis fruantur. Quia enim mundo propter Euā gelij lucem, quæ apud illos fulget, exosi sunt, multorum quotidie conuitia, iniurias, probra & uim apertam sustinent. Nec minus uerè quam grauiter ab Apostolo dictum est: Omnes qui volunt piè uiuere in Christo Iesu, persecutionē patientur. Porrò ut in rerū natura hyemem æstas sequitur, cuius præcursor est uer lætum, quo terra et plantæ omnes parturiunt atq; germinant: Ita huius seculi tempestatibus olim nouissimus ille dies succedet, qui rectè æstati confertur, quia tunc messis illa fiet, qua pij quidē ut triticum bonū in cœlestis Regni horrea colligentur, impij verò palearū instar explosi in ignem æternū præcipitabuntur. Vt uero inter hyemem & æstatem uernū tempus intercedit, quod etsi facie mundi mirificè mutet, suis tamen quoq; tempestatibus obnoxiū est: Ita priusquam æstas illa æterna ueniat, afflictiones istæ grauiores exorientur, de quibus hucusq; Dominus locutus est ita. Is verò mensuram suam implent impij, Deus autem qui fidelis est, neq; nos supra quàm ferre possimus tentari patitur, dies illos abbreuiabit, sicuti alibi Christus pollicetur. Ex his nos consolatione petere conuenit, & quoties furiosos hostium Euangelij conatus cernimus, quoties piorū exilia, carceres, rogos & dira tormenta audimus, tunc nobis uer in mentem ueniat, & tot nos arborū parturientium gemmas cernere putemus, à quibus optatissimus ille Dominici aduentus dies procul abesse non poterit. Quàmuis autē hæc generalis consolatio sit, qua nouissimorum temporū calamitates Christus mitigat, nihil tamen obstat, quò minus singulí eam sibi priuatim accomodent, quoties uel egestate laboriosa, uel morbis grauioribus, uel quacunq; alia calamitate affliguntur. Nam illis quoq; lætior olim surget post nubila Phœbus, si fide constanti & patientia inuicta cum Christo perseuerent.
units.tr: This comparison, moreover, is most worthy of careful meditation, because it sets before us, as if painted on a tablet, the state of the present and the future age. For the life that the godly live in this world is most rightly compared to winter; indeed, that whole age during which the frame of this world will endure deserves to be called winter, if you consider the condition of the godly living on earth. For just as winter scorches plants with frost, covers them with snow, binds the earth itself and its rivers with ice, strips the trees of leaves and sap, and in short brings a most troublesome torpor upon all things, so endless and continual storms of evils harass the godly, and scarcely ever is there thought to be a time when they may enjoy the fruit of longed-for quiet. For since they are hated by the world on account of the light of the Gospel, which shines among them, they daily endure the reproaches, injuries, insults and open violence of many. Nor is it said less truly than seriously by the Apostle: "All who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." Moreover, just as in the nature of things summer follows winter, and its forerunner is the joyful spring, in which the earth and all plants bring forth and sprout, so after the storms of this age that last day will follow, which is rightly compared to summer, because then that harvest will take place, in which the godly, like good wheat, will be gathered into the barns of the heavenly Kingdom, while the wicked, cast out like chaff, will be thrown into eternal fire. And just as spring, which, though it wonderfully changes the face of the world, is nevertheless subject to its own storms, lies between winter and summer, so before that eternal summer comes, these heavier afflictions will arise, of which the Lord has so far spoken. "Indeed, the wicked fill up their measure. But God, who is faithful, does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, and he will shorten those days," as Christ promises elsewhere. From these things we ought to seek consolation; and whenever we see the furious attempts of the enemies of the Gospel, whenever we hear of the exiles, prisons, fires and dreadful torments of the godly, then let the spring come into our minds, and let us think that we see the buds of so many trees bringing forth, from which that most longed-for day of the Lord's coming cannot be far away. Although this is a general consolation, by which Christ softens the calamities of the last times, nothing hinders each one from applying it to himself privately, whenever he is afflicted by laborious poverty, by more grievous diseases, or by any other calamity. For the sun will one day rise more joyfully after the clouds for them too, if with steadfast faith and invincible patience they persevere with Christ.

units.la: Secundum argumentū à pronuntiatis desumptum dici potest. Nam iureiurando interposito testes sistit, uel potius ipso euentu, eorum quæ dixit ueritatē ipsos agnituros esse docet. Amen dico vobis (inquit) nequaquam præterierit hæc ætas, quò usq; hæc omnia facta fuerint. In Græco γενεὰ habetur, quod plerunq; pro generatione accipiunt. Intelligunt autem alij dictū hoc de toto humano genere, quod minimè periturum sit, priusquam ista suum habeat complementū. Mouet hos quod de nouissimo suo aduentu et huius seculi fine Christus in ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, disserui. Sed nihil obstat, quin de ijs, qui tunc uiuebant, illum nunc loqui dicamus, vt ijs occurrat, qui (vt initio monuimus) prædictiones eiusmodi rident, quia longius adhuc abesse sibi persuadent tempus illud, quo illas impleri oporteat. Itaq; ad ea, quæ de Hierosolymæ vastatione deq; hæc præcessuris calamitatibus dixerat, reuertens, hac asseueratione utitur: vt ostendat intra unius ætatis spaciū hæc euentura esse, adeò ut multi ex illis, qui nunc uiuunt, ista uisuri sint. Et ex historijs constat, illa omnia intra annos ab eius Ascensione quadraginta facta esse, & maiorem eorum, quae excidium illud gentis Iudaicae praecesserunt, partem ipsos discipulos suis oculis uidisse. Nihilominus autem dictum hoc eorum etiam confirmationi seruit, quae de nouissimorum temporum calamitosissimo statu & huius seculi consummatione dixit. Quia enim huius typus fuit Hierosolymae & templi conflagratio, recte concluditur, ea etiam suum euentum habitura esse, quae de illo sunt dicta, cum in primis illis tam certa fuerit diuini oraculi ueritas. Ita uero admonemur, ad nos in primis pertinere eorum considerationem, quae olim Iudaeis acciderunt, ut horum exemplo admoniti, impijs & contumacibus Christi hostibus paratas poenas declinemus. Ut uero Apostoli quidam & cum his non contemnenda Iudaeorum, qui iam ad Christum conuersi erant, multitudo inter tantas turbas & mille rerum discrimina mirifice seruati sunt: ita iam inde ab initio mundi Deus suam Ecclesiam seruauit inter horribiles rerum mutationes, regnorum collisiones & grauissimas calamitates, quibus hostium suorum contumaciam puniuit. Huc pertinent quae de Noa & eius familia arcae beneficio ex diluuio erepta, de Patriarchis inter Chanaeos defensis, de Israelitis in Aegypto miraculose auctis & inde eductis leguntur. Quibus addi possunt, quae in Assyria & in Babylone acciderunt, & deinceps quando inter Asiae totius & Europae tumultus & expeditiones utrinque factas Ecclesia semper incolumis mansit. Et nostro seculo huius generis multa uidimus: quae in eum finem obseruari debent, ne de Dei ope siue auxilio unquam dubitemus, neue (quod multi solent) propter imminentia pericula mundo infelici nos conformes faciamus, sed constantes simus in confessione Christi, cuius promissio est: Non relinquam uos orphanos; Ego uobiscum sum usque in consummationem seculi. Vide Ioan. 14. & 16. Item Matth. 28. cap.
units.tr: The second argument may be drawn from what is pronounced. For by adding an oath he calls the witnesses, or rather, he teaches by the event itself that they will know the truth of what he has said. "Verily I say to you," he says, "this generation shall by no means pass away until all these things have been done." In the Greek it is [γενεὰ], which they usually take to mean generation. Others, however, understand this saying of the whole human race, which will by no means perish before those things have their fulfilment. What moves these is that Christ, in the things that immediately precede, has discoursed about his final coming and the end of this age. But nothing prevents us from saying that he now speaks of those who were then living, so that he may meet those who (as we noted at the beginning) laugh at predictions of this kind, because they persuade themselves that the time when they must be fulfilled is still far off. Therefore, returning to what he had said about the destruction of Jerusalem and the calamities that were to precede it, he uses this solemn assurance, to show that these things will happen within the space of one generation, so that many of those who are now living will see them. And from histories it is clear that all those things came to pass within forty years of his Ascension, and that the disciples themselves saw with their own eyes the greater part of those things which preceded that destruction of the Jewish nation. Nevertheless, this saying also serves to confirm what he said about the most calamitous state of the last times and the consummation of this age. For since the burning of Jerusalem and the temple was a type of that, it is rightly concluded that those things which were said about that will also have their event, especially since the truth of the divine oracle was so certain in those earlier cases. In this way we are admonished that the consideration of those things which once happened to the Jews pertains chiefly to us, so that, warned by their example, we may avoid the punishments prepared for the impious and obstinate enemies of Christ. And just as certain Apostles, and with them not a small multitude of Jews who had already been converted to Christ, were wonderfully preserved amid such great tumults and a thousand dangers, so from the beginning of the world God has preserved his Church amid terrible changes of things, collisions of kingdoms and the gravest calamities, by which he punished the obstinacy of his enemies. To this belong the things that are read about Noah and his family, rescued from the flood by the benefit of the ark; about the patriarchs defended among the Canaanites; about the Israelites miraculously increased in Egypt and led out from there. To these can be added what happened in Assyria and in Babylon, and afterwards, when, amid the tumults and military expeditions made on both sides throughout Asia and Europe, the Church always remained unharmed. And in our own century we have seen many things of this kind, which ought to be observed to this end: that we never doubt the help or assistance of God, nor (as many are wont to do) conform ourselves to the unhappy world because of impending dangers, but that we remain steadfast in the confession of Christ, whose promise is: "I will not leave you orphans; I am with you always, even to the end of the age." See John 14 and 16, and Matthew chapter 28.

units.la: Tertium argumentum comparationem habet, & sic effertur: Caelum & terra praeteribunt, uerba autem mea nequaquam praeteribunt. Nominat duas totius machinae mundi huius partes longe solidissimas, & quae mutationibus quam minimum obnoxiae sunt: terra nimirum, quae suo pondere fundata totius mundi centrum dicitur; & caelum, quod perpetuo motu conseruatur, ut neque in contrarium moueri, neque ullo casu corrumpi possit. Estque hoc mirabile diuinae omnipotentiae opus, quod orbes caelestes tot iam seculis motu suo feruntur non minus certo quam constanti: cum quae ad horum imitationem magnis cum impensis & exquisita hominum ingeniosissimorum industria, uix paucis annis durare solent. De Archimede Syracusano traditur, quod mechanico artificio sphaeram uitreā fecerit, in qua dissimiles circulorum motus, quasi Deus aliquis terrenus, expresserit. Sed ut opus illud uitreum, ita uitrea quoque & fragilis fuit, quam inde reportauit gloria: & tandem infelici seni, qui patria à Romanis obsideri & capi uiderat, curiosa illa ingenij solertia necē attulit. At quae Deus condidit, caelum & terra, neque uetustate pereunt, neque usu atteruntur, & nullis casibus obnoxia sunt, nisi quibus aeternus ille opifex illa subijcit: Eadem tamen Christus cum uerbo suo confert, & hoc tunc quoque ratum firmumque fore testatur, cum illa interierint. Imò tunc maximè promissionū & oraculorum Dei omnium ueritas omnibus innotescet, quando sub nouissimum illius aduentum elementa omnia dissoluentur. Pertinent huc, quae in Psal. 102. item Isa. 51 & 54. cap. in eandem sententiam leguntur, & quod idem Propheta ex Dei mandato clamat: Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri: Exaruit fœnum, flos defluxit, Verbum Domini autem manet in aeternum. Isa. 40.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn by comparison, and runs thus: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away." He names the two most solid parts of the whole machinery of the world, the parts least liable to change: the earth, which is founded on its own weight and is said to be the centre of the whole world, and the heavens, which are kept in being by perpetual motion so that they can be moved in no contrary direction and corrupted by no accident. This is a marvellous work of divine omnipotence, that the heavenly spheres have been carried on their motion for so many ages, no less surely than constantly, whereas things made in imitation of them, at great expense and with the exquisite skill of the most ingenious men, usually last only a few years. It is said of Archimedes of Syracuse that by mechanical art he made a glass sphere in which he expressed the unlike motions of the circles, as if he were some earthly god. But as that glass work was itself brittle and fragile, so was the glory he gained from it; and at last that curious cleverness brought death to the unhappy old man, who had seen his homeland besieged and captured by the Romans. But what God created, heaven and earth, perish neither through age nor wear away through use, and are subject to no accidents except those to which that eternal Maker subjects them. Yet Christ sets these same things beside his word, and testifies that his word will be fixed and firm even when they have perished. Indeed, the truth of all God's promises and oracles will then be made known to all, when at his last coming all the elements are dissolved. To this belong the passages read to the same effect in Psalm 102, and in Isaiah 51 and 54, and what the same prophet cries out at God's command: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains for ever." Isa. 40.

units.la: Obseruari autē debet diligenter haec Verbi Dei certitudo & Veritas immutabilis, cui elementa quoque firmissima & ipsam rerum naturam cedere oportet, ne illius pronuntiatis aliquid derogetur. Exempla, quibus id probetur, multa passim in historijs extant. Promiserat Deus Abrahamo posteritatis suae liberationem ex Aegypto mirificam. Semen tuum peregrinum erit (inquit) in terra non sua & subijcient eos seruituti affligentē eos quadringentis annis. Veruntamen gentē, cui seruituri sunt, ego iudicabo, & post haec egredientur magna cum substantia. Tu uero ibis ad patres tuos in pace, & sepelieris in senectute bona: quarta autem generatione reuertentur huc. Oppositi se promissioni huic Pharao, Regum illius temporis potentissimus. Aduersatur eidem diabolus, qui Magos excitat, ut horum opera in Rege obfirmando siue indurando abutatur. Idem Israelitas laborum & calamitatum impatientia eò adducit, ut saluti propriae reluctentur, et aduersus Mosem atque Aaronem murmurent. Tandem iam iter ingressis mare obijcitur, & cum nauibus destituti essent, à tergo autem hostilibus armis premerentur: praesentem mortem omnia intentant. Sed ecce ipsa rerum natura cedit,
units.tr: This certainty of God's Word and its immutable truth ought to be carefully observed, since even the firmest elements and the very nature of things must yield to it, lest anything be taken away from its pronouncements. Many examples proving this are found scattered through the histories. God had promised Abraham a marvellous deliverance of his posterity from Egypt: "Your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will be made to serve and will be afflicted for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation they serve, and after these things they will come out with great substance. But you will go to your fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age; but in the fourth generation they will return here." Pharaoh, the most powerful king of that time, set himself against this promise. The devil also opposed it, stirring up the magicians to use their arts to harden and obstinate the king. The same devil, by the impatience of the Israelites at their labours and calamities, led them to resist their own salvation and to murmur against Moses and Aaron. At last, when they had set out on their journey, the sea blocked their way; and since they had no ships, and were pressed from behind by hostile arms, everything threatened immediate death. But behold, nature itself yields.

units.la: A comparatis. & ut Dei promissio locum habeat, aquæ diuisæ & procul abs se deductæ in cumulos seu montes u-trinq; assurgunt, et transitum præbent miseris, qui iam periturí uidebantur. Taceo nunc ea, quæ per annos quadraginta in deserto agentibus acciderūt, quæq; in terræ promissæ occupatione facta sunt: quando cœlum et terra, adeoq; omnes mundi partes unà cum Angelis promissioni Dei seruierunt, ne hæc aliqua ex parte labefactaretur. Idem in Dauide cernimus, cui Regnū promiserat Deus. Nam etsi aduersus illum primò Saul cum totius gentis principibus coniurauissēt, deinde his sublatis uici-næ gentes magno cum fremitu insurgerent, ratum tamen fuit Dei decretum, qui illum Regem con-stituerat super Zionem, montem suum sanctum. Quod si ad exilium Babylonicum respicias, quàm multa fuerunt, quæ Dei promissionem de reditu populi & urbis instauratione non modò impedie-bant, sed iam prorsus extinxisse uidebantur? Sed per omnes difficultates uiam inuenit Dominus, & potentissimam Monarchiam funditus euerti oportuit, ut illius promissio rata esset. Sed dies me deficeret, si quæcunq; huius generis exempla extant in historijs, commemorare uelim. Nos potius istorum usum consideremus, qui duplex est.
units.tr: For the sake of God's promise, the waters were divided and drawn far apart, and rose on either side in heaps or walls, and gave a passage to the wretched, who seemed already doomed to perish. I now pass over what befell those wandering for forty years in the desert, and what was done in the occupation of the promised land, when heaven and earth, indeed all parts of the world together with the angels, served God's promise, lest it be weakened in any respect. We see the same in David, to whom God had promised the kingdom. For although at first Saul, together with the chief men of the whole nation, conspired against him, and afterwards, when these had been removed, the neighbouring nations rose up with great uproar, nevertheless the decree of God stood firm, for he had appointed that king over Zion, his holy mountain. And if you look to the Babylonian exile, how many things there were that not only hindered God's promise of the people's return and the restoration of the city, but seemed to have utterly extinguished it? Yet through all difficulties the Lord found a way, and the most powerful monarchy had to be utterly overthrown, so that his promise might be fulfilled. But the day would fail me if I wished to recount all the examples of this kind that exist in histories. Let us rather consider the use of these, which is twofold.

units.la: Primus, ut ex ijs consolationem petamus in ijs, quæ ad priuatam nostram salutem & publicam Ecclesiæ conseruationem faciunt. Christi promissio est: Amen amen dico uobis, qui credit in me, ha-bet uitam æternam. Item: Vbi ego sum, illic erit & minister meus. Aduersatur his mundi incredulí cōtumacia, resistunt itē peccata nostra, & ipsa Dei iustitia obstare uidetur, ne quid huius fiat: deniq; carnis natura reluctatur, ne quæ ex terra originē cœpit in cœlis locum habeat. Sed nihil hæc omnia aduersus Christi promissionem poterunt, quæ ut nobis rata sit, ipsam rerū naturam immutari opor-tet, ut & ipsi in filios Dei renascamur, & mors transitus ad uitam fiat, & uirtus nostra in infirmi-tate perfectior appareat: deniq; cœlum & terram præterire & aboleri necesse est, ut corpora nostra nobis restituantur, & incorruptibilitate donata cœlos possideant. De Ecclesia itē promissio extat, quòd ne portæ quidem inferorū quicquam aduersus eam possint, & eidem dictum est: Ecce ego uo-biscum sum usq; in consummationem seculi. Luctantur aduersus hoc Christi decretum hæretici, ut eum ab Ecclesia sua eijciant: fremit insanus mundus, ut hanc totam aboleat: arma sumunt poten-tissimi Reges, ut illam expugnent: horrendus exquisitorum supplicioru tormentus singula eius mem-bra tyranni excarnificant, ut totam dissipent. Sed quàm parum aut nihil omnibus istis rationibus per annos iam mille quingentos effectum sit, res ipsa loquitur. Nam per omnes istas luctas salua eua sit Ecclesia, & in hunc usq; diem durat magna cum totius mundi admiratione, qui interea horrenda excidiorū exempla uidit in regnis potentissimis, quæ armis, fœderibus & authoritate munitissima fuerunt. Ista nos consolari & fidem nostram aduersus omnes mundi & principis eius conatus confir-mare debent. Quid enim isti proficiant, quando olim omnes mundi partes dissolui oportet, ut Eccle-sia tota simul cum Christo sponso suo in patria cœlesti gaudeat & regnet?
units.tr: The first is that from them we may draw consolation in those matters that concern our private salvation and the public preservation of the Church. Christ's promise is: "Truly, truly I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life." Also: "Where I am, there my minister also will be." The obstinacy of the unbelieving world opposes these promises; our sins resist them too, and God's own justice seems to stand in the way, lest any of this come to pass; finally the nature of the flesh struggles against it, since what took its origin from the earth should have a place in heaven. But all these things can do nothing against Christ's promise. For it to be fulfilled for us, the very nature of things must be changed, so that we too may be born again as sons of God, death may become a passage to life, our strength may appear more perfect in weakness; and finally heaven and earth must pass away and be done away with, so that our bodies may be restored to us and, once given incorruptibility, possess the heavens. There is likewise a promise concerning the Church, that the gates of hell shall prevail nothing against her, and it was said to her: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Heretics struggle against this decree of Christ, that they may cast him out of his Church; the mad world rages that it may utterly destroy her; mighty kings take up arms to storm her; tyrants with the dreadful torments of exquisite punishments tear her individual members apart, that they may scatter the whole. But how little, or nothing, has been accomplished by all these arguments over the now some fifteen hundred years, the thing itself speaks. For through all these struggles the Church has remained safe, and she endures to this day, to the great astonishment of the whole world, which meanwhile has seen dreadful examples of overthrow in the most powerful kingdoms, which had been fortified with arms, alliances and authority. These things ought to console us and confirm our faith against all the attempts of the world and its prince. For what will they achieve, since at last all parts of the world must be dissolved, so that the whole Church, together with Christ her bridegroom, may rejoice and reign in the heavenly fatherland?

units.la: At non minus ad uitæ morumque institutionē ista nobis seruire debent. Vt enim rata & firma erunt semper quæcunq; Christus promisit aut prædixit: ita certa quoq; & firma semper manebunt, quæcunq; idē de fide, de religione et de Dei cultu, de uitæ Christianæ officijs et moribus tradidit. Qui credit in me (inquit) habet uitā æternam: Item: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit: qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Accumulent ergo suorum operum merita hypocritæ, fatigentur cir-ca ceremonias Monachi & horum infelicia mancipia, nunquam tamen per ea salui fient, quæ cùm nullo Dei Verbo nituntur, ex fide fieri non possunt. Idē dicit: Deus Spiritus est, & eos qui adorant, in spiritu & Veritate oportet adorare. Erit ergo hæc perpetua diuini cultus regula, neq; Deus ul-los cultus probabit, qui ab illa dissentiunt, etiamsi plurimorum patrum & Conciliorum authoritate probentur. Similiter necesse esse docet ut renascamur, ut nosipsos abnegemus, ut carnem nostram mortificemus, deniq; impossibile dicit esse, ut Deo simul & Mammonæ seruiamus. Nisi ergo hæc ob-seruentur à nobis, Dei cultores non erimus. Item dilectionem mutuam nobis præcipiens, hanc dicit notam fore, ex qua discipuli eius agnoscantur. Quare omnes illi necessario studere debent, qui ex di-scipulorum eius numero censeri uolunt. Idem per Angelum suum in Apocalypsi pronuntiat: Bea-ti qui seruant mandata eius, ut sit eis ius in arbore uitæ, & per portas ingrediantur in urbem. Foris autem canes & uenefici, & scortatores, & homicidæ, & idololatræ, & quisquis amat & committit mendacium. Cuius generis multa in Apostolorum scriptis habentur. Disputat de his mundus, & ut ea eludat,
units.tr: But these things ought to serve no less for the instruction of life and morals. For just as whatever Christ promised or foretold will always be sure and firm, so too whatever he taught about faith, about religion and the worship of God, and about the duties and conduct of the Christian life, will always remain certain and firm. "Whoever believes in me (he says) has eternal life." Also: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned." Let hypocrites therefore pile up the merits of their works, and let monks and their unhappy slaves wear themselves out over ceremonies; they will never be saved by these things, which, since they rest on no word of God, cannot be done from faith. He says: "God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." This will therefore be the perpetual rule of divine worship, and God will approve no worship that dissents from it, even if it is commended by the authority of very many Fathers and councils. Similarly he teaches that we must be born again, that we deny ourselves and mortify our flesh; finally he declares it impossible to serve God and Mammon at once. Unless therefore these things are observed by us, we shall not be worshippers of God. Likewise, enjoining mutual love upon us, he says that this will be the mark by which his disciples are known. Therefore all who wish to be counted among his disciples must necessarily strive for it. He pronounces the same through his angel in the Apocalypse: "Blessed are those who keep his commandments, that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city through its gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers, the fornicators, murderers, idolaters, and whoever loves and practises lying." Many things of this kind are found in the writings of the Apostles. The world disputes about these, and in order to mock them,

units.la: Apoc. 22. eludat, nouas quotidie scelerum excusationes comminiscitur. Sed nihil proficiet aduersus Leges Regni Dei, quarum authoritas æterno eius decreto stabilitur. Atqui si iste rigor seruetur (inquis) maior hominum pars damnabitur. Quid tum ô bone? Ergo ne tu aut tui similes damnentur, Deum mendacem, aut omnino nullû fieri oportet? Valeat iustitia (dicebat ille) & pereat totus mundus. Quanto magis hunc totum perire conuenit, ut Dei Opt. Max. fides atq; authoritas salua maneat? Quòd si hoc alicui durum uidetur, is ab illo nobis monstratam salutis rationem sequatur, fidem ueram conlat, charitati fraternæ studeat, præceptis eius obediat. Hæc qui faciût, ij et inter huius uitæ certamina salui erunt, & olim in cælis niuent atq; regnabunt cum Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Apoc. 22. eludat, they devise new excuses for their sins every day. But they will gain nothing against the laws of God's kingdom, whose authority is fixed by his eternal decree. Yet, you say, if this strictness is maintained, most people will be condemned. What of it, my good sir? Must you and those like you not be condemned, and so God be made a liar, or else nobody must be condemned at all? Let justice prevail, as the saying goes, though the whole world perish. How much more fitting it is that this whole world perish, so that the faith and authority of God, the best and greatest, remain secure! But if this seems hard to anyone, let him follow the way of salvation that he has shown us, bring true faith, strive for brotherly love, and obey his precepts. Those who do these things will be saved amid the struggles of this life, and one day they will live and reign in heaven with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXC.
units.tr: HOMILY 190.

units.la: Cauete autem vobis, ne quando grauentur corda vestra crapula, & ebrietate, & curis huius vitæ: & repente vobis superueniat dies illæ. Nã vt laqueus inuadet in omnes, qui habitant in superficie totius terræ. Excubate igitur, omni tempore rogantes, vt digni habeamini, qui effugiatis ista omnia, quæ futura sunt, & consistatis coram Filio hominis. Docebat autè interdiu in templo, noctu verò exiens diuersabatur in monte, qui vocatur olearum. Et totus populus diluculo veniebat ad eum, vt eum audiret in templo.
units.tr: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and that day come upon you unawares. For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the face of the whole earth. Watch ye therefore, and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that shall come to pass, and to stand before the Son of man." And in the daytime he was teaching in the temple, and at night he went out and abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives. And all the people came early in the morning to him in the temple, to hear him.

units.la: INter admonitiones, quibus Dominus noster Iesus Christus suum erga omnes homines studium testatus est, non immeritò primum locum obtinet ista, in qua cum discipulis de urbibus & templi nastatione, deq; fine huius seculi & nouissimo suo ad iudicium aduentu disseruit. Ita enim hoc facit, ut non ipsorum curiositati satisfacere, sed de illis eos admonere studeat, quæ ipsis cognitu necessaria erant. Neque in illis subsistit, sed doctrinam hanc ad nos usq; extendit, quos simul omnes docet, quid nobis facto sit opus. Et debet doctrinæ huius fides apud nos infallibilis esse, quando ne pericula quidem dissimulat, quod plerunque impostores solent facere, ut plures in nassam trahant. A quorum moribus tam procul abest Christus, ut ex ordine ea quoque recenseat, quæ absterrere possent eos, qui mundi studijs & carnis rationi magis quàm diuinis atque cælestibus addicti sunt. Quia verò idem probè nouit, quàm supina securitate ea negligamus, quæ ad salutem nostram quàm maximè faciunt, locum hunc totum non minus fida quàm graui admonitione concludit, qua duo agit. Primùm docet, à quibus potissimùm nobis cauere debeamus. Deinde quid facere oporteat eos, qui salutem suam tueri voluerint. Quibus Lucas breuem narrationculam subijcit, qua illius in prouehenda multorum salute studium denuo commendat.
units.tr: Among the admonitions by which our Lord Jesus Christ showed his care for all men, this one rightly holds the first place, in which he spoke with his disciples about the destruction of the cities and of the temple, and about the end of this age and his last coming to judgement. He does this not to satisfy their curiosity but to warn them about those things which they needed to know. Nor does he stop at those things alone; he extends this teaching to us as well, teaching all of us together what we must do. The teaching ought to be wholly trustworthy to us, since he does not conceal even the dangers, which impostors commonly do, so as to draw more people into their net. Christ is so far from their ways that he goes through in order those things also which could frighten away those who are devoted more to worldly pursuits and the reasoning of the flesh than to divine and heavenly things. And since he knows well how carelessly in supine security we neglect those things which most of all serve our salvation, he concludes this whole passage with a warning that is as faithful as it is weighty, and in it he does two things. First, he teaches us from whom above all we ought to beware. Then, what those who wish to keep their salvation ought to do. Luke adds a short narrative to these, by which he again commends the earnestness of Jesus in advancing the salvation of many.

units.la: Primæ partis summa est: Cauete autem vobis, ne quando grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate, & curis huius vitæ. Quo loco ante omnia obseruabis, quòd ab ijs potissimùm cauere iubet, quæ nouissimis temporibus in primis regnatura esse sciebat. Nam supra Cap. 17. eos tunc hominum mores & ea mundi huius studia fore dixit, quæ olim temporibus Noæ & Lothi fuerunt, quando profundissima securitate omnium animi in præsentis vitæ studia demersi, nihil præter intemperantiam & libidinem atq; quæstum somniarunt. Nec illa Christo temere excidisse dicet, quisquis nostri seculi mores paulò attentius consideraverit. Vident enim boni omnes, & quidem cum dolore & gemitu uident, ebrietatem apud omnis sexus & ætatis homines regnare, adeo ut ne ij quidem ab hoc vitio immunes sint, qui alijs temperantiæ, sobrietatis & modestiæ exemplum esse debebant. De principibus loquor & reipub. gubernatoribus, de Ecclesiarum item ministris & scholarum præfectis. Nam etiamsi non desint inter hos viri graues & boni, qui honestatem colunt, plerique tamen, uel ut principibus rem gratam faciant, uel propria intemperantia & libidine abrepti, ad pocula desident, & procul relictis curis Ecclesiæ inter homines leuissimos helluantur, & diem eum sibi periisse putant, quo non probè madidi & distenti domum redeunt. Olim sui seculi pseudoprophetis Isaias hoc tribuebat, quòd de compotationibus & uino inter se sermones conferrent. At utinam hodie idem non ab illis quoque fieret, qui Verbum Domini annuntiant. De licentia autem potandi, quæ in Academijs passim obtu
units.tr: The sum of the first part is: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and cares of this life." Here you should first observe that he bids us beware above all of those things which he knew would prevail especially in the last times. For above, in chapter 17, he said that at that time there would be the manners of men and the pursuits of this world which were in the days of Noah and Lot, when, sunk in the deepest security, the minds of all were occupied with the pursuits of the present life, and dreamed of nothing but intemperance, lust and gain. Nor will anyone who considers the manners of our own age a little more carefully say that Christ spoke those words rashly. For all good people see, and indeed see with grief and groaning, that drunkenness reigns among people of every sex and age, so much so that even those who ought to have been an example of temperance, sobriety and moderation are not free from this vice. I speak of princes and rulers of commonwealths, and likewise of ministers of the Churches and heads of schools. For although there are not lacking among these grave and good men who cultivate honesty, yet many, either to do a favour to the princes or carried away by their own intemperance and lust, sit down at the cups, and, leaving the cares of the Church far behind, they revel with the most frivolous men, and think that day lost to them on which they do not return home thoroughly drunk and bloated. In former times Isaiah ascribed this to the false prophets of his own age, that they talked with one another about drinking bouts and wine. But would that today the same were not also done by those who proclaim the Word of the Lord. As for the licence of drinking which everywhere prevails in the universities, what is the use of speaking of it, since this evil seems to have become utterly incurable, when those men are more anxious about their gain than about the progress of their students, whose duty it was above all to maintain scholastic discipline?

units.la: { } nuit, quid attinet dicere, quando malum hoc prorsus immedicabile factum uidetur, cum de quaestu suo magis quam de discipulorum profectu solicitus sint, quorum erat disciplinam scholasticam maximè tueri? Solent isti fere, quando de hoc malo querimur, consuetudinem obijcere, & quia idem ubiq; fiat, se probè excusatos arbitrantur. At turpe est eos mundi huius exemplum suis moribus praetexere, quos ut sui discipuli sint, Christus ex mundo seleqit. Et cur mundo conformes fiant, qui parentes quoq; & fratres & uxorem & liberos odisse, imò seipsos abnegare debent, ut Christi discipuli esse possint? Quin ipsum audimus, qui etsi sciret (ut modo diximus) quid futurū esset hoc nouissimo tempore, tamen in praesenti clamat: Cauete uobis, ne quando grauentur corda uestra crapula & ebrietate, &c. Huius dicti authoritatem certè contemnere aut eludere nō poterimus, nisi nos Christi seruos esse uelimus negare. Sed de singulis aliquid dicamus diligentius.
units.tr: Those men are accustomed, when we complain of this evil, to object custom, and because it happens everywhere, they think themselves well excused. But it is shameful for them to shield with their manners the example of this world, when Christ chose them out of the world that they might be his disciples. And why should those who must hate their parents, brothers, wife and children, and indeed deny themselves, in order to be disciples of Christ, become conformed to the world? Indeed we hear Christ himself, who, although he knew (as we have just said) what would happen in this last time, nevertheless cries out in the present: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness," etc. We certainly cannot despise or evade the authority of this saying, unless we are willing to deny that we are servants of Christ. But let us say something more carefully about the individual points.

units.la: Primò crapulam & ebrietatē prohibet. Duabus uocibus rem unam denotat, nisi quòd intemperantiæ effecta illis distinguuntur. Cùm enim tam haec quàm illa ex nimia uini ingurgitatione nascantur, crapula tamè proprie dicitur, quae uertigine caput concutit, & proinde eam capitis luctam rectè dixeris. Aristoteles in Problematis inter ebrietatē & crapulam sic distinguere uidetur, ut illa cum mente sensum quoq; auferre dicat, haec autē etiamsi mens adhuc nobis constet, caput tamen affligat. Rectè autem utramq; coniungit Christus, ut omne uini usum nimium nobis noxium esse & Deo improbari doceat. Quod eorum sententiam confutat, qui se extra culpam esse sibi persuadēt, etiamsi nimium bibant, modò nullū de se praebeant mentis alienatæ argumentū. Atqui omnis uini abusus per se illicitus est, si nihil praeterea accedat. Quam ergo ueniam merentur, qui etsi insaniā aut furorem sibi nō accersant, caput tamen laedunt, intellectus & memoriae sedē, quod in toto corpore quasi regnū obtinet? Num innocente aliquis dixerit eum, qui alterius caput uulnerat? Cur ergo innocens putatur, qui proprū caput uiolentiori motu fatigat, & intemperanti uini usu sibijpsi uertiginē, paralysim & alios morbos grauissimos accersit, qui uitæ quoq; finem maturat, seu potius accelerat? Velsi istud licet, cur ergo leges eos damnat, qui quocunq; affectu prauo superati sibijpsis morte cōscisc unt? Sed ut ad Christi uerba redeamus, uidetur hunc locū ijs opponere, quae supra de Noæ & Lothi temporibus dixit: Edebant & bibebant, uxores ducebāt & dabantur nuptū, &c. Quo loco minimè damnantur cōuiuia honoraria, aut quae amicitiæ causa instituuntur (ea enim apud sanctissimos patres in usu fuisse scimus, neq; ab ijs ipse Christus abhorruit, ut suo loco diximus) sed luxu & intemperantiā denotat, qua illorum temporum homines Dei donis non sine scelere abusi sunt, & ne id fiat, prohibet.
units.tr: First he forbids surfeiting and drunkenness. He denotes one thing with two words, except that the effects of intemperance distinguish them. For since both of these arise from an excessive swallowing of wine, surfeiting is properly the name for that which shakes the head with giddiness, and so you might rightly call it a headache of the head. Aristotle, in the Problems, seems to distinguish between drunkenness and surfeiting in such a way that he says the former removes the sense together with the mind, while the latter, even when the mind still remains with us, afflicts the head. But Christ rightly joins both, to teach that every excessive use of wine is harmful to us and disapproved by God. This refutes the opinion of those who persuade themselves that they are free of blame even if they drink too much, provided they show no sign of a disordered mind. Yet every abuse of wine is in itself unlawful, if nothing else is added. What pardon then do those deserve who, though they do not bring madness or frenzy upon themselves, nevertheless injure the head, the seat of the understanding and memory, which holds sway in the whole body as a kind of kingdom? Would anyone say that a man who wounds another's head is innocent? Why then is he thought innocent who wears out his own head with a more violent motion, and by intemperate use of wine brings upon himself giddiness, paralysis and other most grievous diseases, and also hastens, or rather accelerates, the end of his life? And if this is allowed, why then do the laws condemn those who, overcome by any wicked passion, take their own lives? But to return to Christ's words: he seems to set this passage against what he said above about the times of Noah and Lot: "They ate and drank, they married wives and were given in marriage," etc. In this passage he does not condemn honourable feasts, or those held for the sake of friendship (for we know these were in use among the most holy fathers, and Christ himself did not shrink from them, as we said in its place), but he denotes luxury and intemperance, by which the people of those times abused God's gifts not without wickedness, and he forbids this.

units.la: Debet autē hic nō ofcitanter obseruari locutio: Cauete uobis, ne quando grauentur corda uestra crapula & ebrietate. Sunt enim, qui hanc eo nomine excusant, quòd in solo corpore haereat, minimè autem ad animum usq; pertingat, & proinde nō debeat inter peccata numerari, quae huius saluti officiunt. Imò unà cum uino aut crapula omnē quoq; culpam, quae admissa sit, edormiri atq; euanescere clamat. At longè aliter nos iudicare docet Christus, quādo corda quoq; crapula et ebrietate grauari dicit: Grauari enim dicuntur, quae nimio pondere pressa non possunt se ad sua sublimitatē erigere. Quod in animo hominis tunc fit, quando uitijs quibuscunq; premitur, ut assurgere nequeat ad rerum caelestium contemplationem, ut in Deō, qui bonū illud summum & aeternum est, se oblectet. Quid aut de corde aut animo grauius dici poterat? Aut quid excogitari poterat, quod hominis saluti magis inimicū, & à fine, ad quem ille conditus est, magis alienum sit? Verissimè aut hoc dici, res ipsa probat, si ebrietatis effecta cōsideremus. Primò enim ratione et intellectus usum aufert, in quo praecipua animæ rationalis functio consistit. Quod Hoseas obseruans illa scortationi coiungit, dicens: Scortatio & uinū potusq; inebrians, eripit cor. Ita nimirū plus quiddā dicens, quam Christus, qui cor grauari ait. Et quod Hoseas pronūtiat, id Isaias reipsa demonstrat, quādo de ijs, qui assiduis cōpotatio-nibus dediti sunt, loquens, inter alia hoc quoq; illis tribuit, quòd opus Domini non cōtemplentur, neq; opus manuū eius considerēt: quòd item repudient Legē Domini exercituū, et uerbum sancti Israelis cōtumeliosē blasphement. Atqui cōstat, hominem sola Dei notitia et religione à brutis differre, quod Lactantius nō minus uerè quā doctè docet, cuius uerba aliqua recitare lubet: Nonne ipsius corporis status & oris figura declarat, nō esse nos cum mutis pecudibus æquales? Illarū natura in humū pabulumq; prostrata est, nec habet quicquā cōmune cum cœlo, quod nō intuetur. Homo aut recto statu, ore sublimi ad cōtemplationem mundi excitatus, cōfert cum Deo uultum, et ratione ratio cognoscit.
units.tr: Here we must observe the phrasing carefully: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness." For some excuse this on the ground that it sticks only in the body and does not reach the soul at all, and therefore ought not to be counted among the sins which hinder salvation. Indeed they cry that with the wine or the surfeiting every guilt that has been committed is also slept off and vanishes. But Christ teaches us to judge far otherwise, when he says that the hearts too are overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness. For those things are said to be overcharged which, pressed down by excessive weight, cannot raise themselves to their height. This happens in the soul of a man when it is weighed down by whatever vices, so that it cannot rise to the contemplation of heavenly things, and take delight in God, who is that highest and eternal good. What could be said more heavily of the heart or the soul? Or what could be thought of that is more hostile to a man's salvation, and more alien to the end for which he was made? And that this is most truly said the thing itself proves, if we consider the effects of drunkenness. For first it takes away the use of reason and understanding, in which the chief function of the rational soul consists. Hosea, observing this, joins to it fornication, saying: "Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart." Thus he is certainly saying something more than Christ, who says the heart is overcharged. And what Hosea declares, Isaiah demonstrates in fact, when, speaking of those who are given over to continual drinking bouts, he attributes to them, among other things, this also: that they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the operation of his hands; that they reject the law of the Lord of hosts, and blaspheme the word of the Holy One of Israel with contumely. Yet it is certain that man differs from the brutes by the knowledge and worship of God alone, as Lactantius teaches no less truly than learnedly. It pleases me to recite some of his words: "Does not the very state of the body and the shape of the face declare that we are not equal to dumb beasts? Their nature is prostrate on the ground and on fodder, and it has nothing in common with heaven, which it does not behold.
