But man, with an upright stature and a face raised high to the contemplation of the world, sets his countenance against God, and reason knows reason."

units.la: Propterea nullum est animal (ut ait Cicero) praeter hominem, quod habeat aliquam notitiam Dei. Solus enim sapientia instructus est, ut religionem solus intelligat. Et est haec hominis atq; brutorum uel praecipua, uel sola distantia. Haec ille. Quis ergo eos ratione praeditos esse, aut homines esse dixerit, qui ad opera Dei non respiciunt: qui huius notitiam negligunt: qui deniq; in uerbo suo loquentem audire dedignantur? Taceo nunc ea, quae ebriosi in uulgaribus huius uitae actionibus praeter omnem rationē faciunt, quae tam multa sunt, ut nemo omnibus enumerandis sufficere possit: tam absurda item, ut quamuis plerique ea rideant, non tamen absq; gemitu & dolore cerni ac narrari possint ab illis, quae de hominis conditione tota paulò diligentius cogitant. Quorum omnium cum ipsimet sibi authores sint, & ad eadem subinde scientes volentes impingant, rectissime olim veteres Ebrietatem insaniam voluntariam esse dixerunt. Accedit huic malo aliud, quod rationis usu extincto pravis cupiditatibus habenas laxat, quas per hanc ceu fraeno coerceri oportebat. Fit ergo ut illae quasi effracti is clausrris qua data via ruant, & hominem per omnia brutis animalibus similem faciant. Qui enim prius animos iracundos et irritabiles celare, aut saltē continere poterant, ij ubi uino incaluerunt, in rabiem aguntur, & leonum atq; ursorum instar in eos furunt, à quibus uel unico uerbulo laesi sunt. Eadem est odij, libidinis & aliorum affectuum ratio, qui omnes erumpere & indomitum furere solent, ubi uino accensi fuerint. Exempla eius rei (ut quotidiana nunc omittamus) in sanctissimis hominibus inveniuntur: inter quae non tam memorabile quàm horrendum est, quod in Lotho proponitur: quae neq; educatio, neq; patrui Abrahami consuetudo, neq; religio, neq; recens in Sodomas editu irae divinae exemplum continere potuit, quin incestu turpissimo filias proprias coïupraret. Quae autem ta effrenis libidinis causa in viro grau & grandaevo? Ebrietas nimirum, quae ut rationis usum illi abstulerat: ita affectui quoq; aut cupiditati belluinae fraenum laxarat: Quis ergo per illa corda grauari negauerit? Ad de his, quod eadem rei domesticae pestis est nocentissima. Nam qui illi addicti sunt, ij procul abiectis curis coniuges, & ex se natos liberos negligunt, & in eo etiam brutis deteriores fiunt, quae catulos suos amare & aeducare consueuerunt: & opes omnes turpiter dilapidant. Ex eo autem infamia sequitur, et audax rerum nouarum cupiditas, quae saepius seditionum & tumultuum publicorum causa est, sicuti in Catilinae & sociorum coniuratione, aliisq; similibus exemplis est uidere. Nihil nunc de morbis acutissimis dicemus, quorum doloribus ebrioși illi superati aduersus Deum quoq; porcorum instar grunniunt, & saepe apertas proferunt blasphemias. Quid enim aliud facerent, qui opera Dei nunquam contemplati sunt, & ut tam absq; omni religione transegerunt? Accedit frequenter mors improuisa: dum uino madidi & distenti uel ex casu aliquo miserè pereunt, uel à socijs proprijs inter pocula confodiuntur, uel in aquas prolapsi, elemento sibi maxime inuiso, suffocantur, uel alijs casibus praeuenti infelicē animam absq; omni peccatorum suorum agnitione, absq; precibus & diuinae misericordiae invocatione exhalat. Quid nero de talibus aliud dici potest, quàm eos in peccatis suis mori? Quod Apost. obseruauit, quando illos in eorū catalogo non postremos numerat, quos ad Regne Dei hereditatē uenturos esse negat. Vides ergo non temere Christū hac locutione usum esse: Cauete uobis, ne quando corda uestra grauentur crapula & ebrietate: & simul uides quam turpiter fallantur, qui uitium istud leuiculū, aut etiā risu dignū putant, quo nullū homine indignius, nullū nocentius, nullum periculosius, nullum deniq; faecundius & proinde saluti corporū atq; animarum magis inimicum est. Ideo illud Proph. passim grauissimis concionibus incessunt, inter quos Isa. clamat: Vae his qui mane se accingunt, ut sectentur sicerā, prorogantes id ad crepusculum usq; uino eos incendente. Et mox poenam ijsde minitans addit: Ideo in captiuitatem abit populus meus, quòd cognitionem nullam habet, & gloria eius fame maceratur, & multitudo eius siti aret. Hinc inferi quoq; ingluuie suam dilatant, & os suum supra modū pandunt, ut descendat eo magnificentia eius, multitudo eius, & opulentia eius, & qui in his laetantur. Et alibi idem Propheta ait: Vae coronae superbiae temulentorū Ephraim, & deciduo flori decoris gloriae eius, quae super caput est uallis pinguium, percussorum à uino, &c. Et sapientissimus ille mortalium Solomon matris suae doctrinā dignissimam putauit, quam aeternae memoriae commendaret, quae inter alia hoc etiā continet. Ne regibus ô Lamuel uinū detur, neq; principib. sicera, ne poti obliuiscantur legis, aut peruertant causas afflictorū. Vidit nimirum prudentissima mulier, nunquā posse aut officij sui memores esse, aut quid in causis iustū iniustumue sit uidere, si uino dediti fuerint. Quod & Macedonica illa faemina obseruans, cum Philippus ebrius sententiam iniquam pronunciauisset, non tam facere quam graviter exclamavit, se ad Philippum provocare, sed sobrium. Quid vero de causis privatis & actionibus forensibus dicere attinet, quando constat ab ebriosis principibus ne ea quidem videri & observari posse, quae ad totius reipub. pacem atque salutem faciunt? Extant enim in omnibus historiis exempla, quae testantur potentissima regna & Respublicas florentissimas corruisse, quando ad gubernacula sederunt homines intemperantes & ventris mancipia. Ideo qui inter gentium legislatores prudentissimi habentur, principum ebrietatem in primis detestabilem & quovis supplicio dignam esse censuerunt. Plato certe scripsit, ebrium habere animum tyrannicum, quod omnibus pro libidine, non ex ulla ratione seu lege velit imperare. Idem gubernatorem ebriosum omnia subvertere dicebat, sive navigium, sive currum, sive exercitum, sive quamcunque rem suae fidei commissam. Quapropter, Carthaginenses, eode teste, magistratibus vino interdixerunt. Solon autem, qui inter septem Graeciae sapientes primus numeratur, capitis poenam constituit principi, si ebrius deprehenderetur. Pudeat ergo Christianos homines in re tanti momenti tam leves & impudentes esse, ut scelus hoc non minus belluinum quam exitiale non verbis quidem acrioribus reprehendi velint. Vos autem omnes, in quibus aliqua adhuc religiosae erga verbum Dei observantiae scintilla superest, per publicam salutem rogo & obtestor, ut tot veteribus & recentibus exemplis excitemini, & nunquam non memori mente versetis hanc Iesu Christi admonitionem, quae ut communi omnium saluti consulat, ait: Cave tibi, ne quando corda nostra gravantur crapula & ebrietate.
units.tr: Therefore there is no animal, as Cicero says, other than man that has any knowledge of God. For man alone is endowed with wisdom, so that he alone understands religion. This is the chief, or indeed the only, difference between man and the brute beasts. So Cicero. Who, then, would call those men rational, or say they are human, who do not regard the works of God, who neglect the knowledge of him, and who finally disdain to hear him speaking in his Word? I pass over now the things that drunkards do in the ordinary affairs of this life, against all reason. There are so many of these that no one could list them all, and they are so absurd that, although most people laugh at them, anyone who thinks even a little carefully about the whole condition of man cannot observe or relate them without groaning and grief. Since these men are themselves the authors of all this, and repeatedly rush knowingly and willingly into the same faults, the ancients rightly called drunkenness a voluntary madness. Another evil is added to this: once the use of reason is extinguished, men loosen the reins on wicked desires, which ought to be restrained as if by a bridle. The result is that these desires, like animals breaking out through unlocked gates, rush wherever they can and make a man altogether like the brute beasts. Men who before could hide their angry and irritable tempers, or at least keep them in check, when they have grown warm with wine, are driven into a frenzy and rage against those by whom they were hurt by a single word, like lions or bears. The same is true of hatred, lust and the other passions, which are wont to burst out and rage without restraint when they have been inflamed by wine. Examples of this (to leave aside the everyday ones) are found among the most holy men. Among them, the case of Lot is not so much memorable as horrible: neither his upbringing, nor the example of his uncle Abraham, nor his religion, nor the recent example of divine wrath against Sodom could restrain him, so that he committed the most shameful incest with his own daughters. But what was the cause of such unbridled lust in a grave and elderly man? Drunkenness, of course, which had taken from him the use of reason and so had loosed the reins on his passion and bestial desire. Who, then, could deny that such hearts are weighed down by it? Let me add this about these men: drunkenness is also the most harmful pest in the household. Those given to it cast off their cares, neglect their wives and the children born of them, and in this they become worse than brute beasts, which are accustomed to love and rear their young. They also shamefully squander all their wealth. From this follow infamy and a bold desire for revolution, which is often the cause of sedition and public tumults, as can be seen in the conspiracy of Catiline and his associates and in other similar examples. I say nothing now of the most severe illnesses, under whose pains these drunkards, overcome, grunt against God like pigs, and often utter open blasphemies. For what else would they do, who have never contemplated the works of God, and have spent their lives so without any religion? Sudden death also frequently comes: while they are soaked and bloated with wine, they either perish miserably by some accident, or are stabbed by their own companions over their cups, or, having fallen into the water, the element most hateful to them, they are suffocated, or, overtaken by other mishaps, they breathe out their unhappy souls without any acknowledgment of their sins, without prayer and without calling upon the mercy of God. What, then, can be said of such men except that they die in their sins? The Apostle observed this when he counted them not among the least of those whom he says will not inherit the kingdom of God. You see, therefore, that Christ did not use this expression without reason: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness." At the same time you see how shamefully those are deceived who think this vice trifling, or even a matter for laughter, when no man is more unworthy, none more harmful, none more dangerous, and finally none more fruitful of evil, and therefore none more hostile to the health of bodies and souls. Therefore the prophets everywhere assail this vice in the gravest sermons. Among them Isaiah cries out: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink, who linger on until the evening, while wine inflames them." And soon, threatening the same punishment, he adds: "Therefore my people go into captivity, because they have no knowledge, and their glory is wasted with hunger, and their multitude is parched with thirst. Hence Hell too enlarges its appetite and opens its mouth beyond measure, so that their splendour, their multitude and their wealth, and those who rejoice in them, go down into it." And elsewhere the same prophet says: "Woe to the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which lies on the head of the valley of the fat ones, of those overcome by wine," etc. And that most wise of mortals, Solomon, thought his mother's teaching most worthy to be commended to eternal memory, which among other things contains this: "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, to drink wine, nor for princes strong drink, lest they drink and forget the law, and pervert the cause of the afflicted." That wise woman clearly saw that those given to wine could never be mindful of their duty, nor see what is just or unjust in causes. The Macedonian woman also observed this. When Philip, being drunk, had pronounced an unjust sentence, she did not so much act as cry out vehemently that she appealed from Philip, but to Philip when sober. But why should I speak of private causes and legal proceedings, when it is well established that under drunken princes not even those things can be seen or attended to which bring peace and safety to the whole commonwealth? For in all histories there are examples attesting that the most powerful kingdoms and the most flourishing commonwealths have collapsed when intemperate men, slaves of their bellies, sat at the helm. Therefore those who are considered the wisest lawgivers among the nations judged that the drunkenness of princes is above all detestable and deserving of any punishment. Plato certainly wrote that a drunk man has a tyrannical soul, because he wants to rule everything according to his lust, not by any reason or law. The same Plato said that a drunken helmsman overturns everything, whether a ship, a chariot, an army, or any other thing entrusted to his good faith. For this reason, as the same authority attests, the Carthaginians forbade magistrates wine. Solon, who is counted first among the seven sages of Greece, established the penalty of death for a prince if he were caught drunk. Let Christian men, then, be ashamed to be so light and shameless in a matter of such importance, that they would not wish this crime, no less bestial than deadly, to be censured even with harsher words. But I beg and entreat you all, in whom some spark of religious observance of the Word of God still remains, for the sake of public safety, that you be stirred by so many examples, old and recent, and that you never fail to keep in a mindful heart this admonition of Jesus Christ, which, to provide for the common safety of all, he gives: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time our hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness."

units.la: Porro addit his aliud vitium, quod similiter vitari debeat: Curas nimirum vitae huius. Quo praecepto non damnat oeconomiam & moderatam, imo necessariam quoque curam rei domesticae, quam omnino deponere neque possumus neque debemus. Dei enim statutum est: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Et Paulus infideli deteriorem esse dicit eum, qui domesticis suis non prospicit. Hic ergo anxiam illam victus parandi solicitudinem damnari sciamus, quam apud Matthaeum gentibus tribuit, quae divinae providentiae cognitionem nullam habent. Gignit hanc in nobis avaritia, quam insatiabile acquirendi & habendi desiderium esse definiunt. Recte autem hanc ebrietati coniungit, quia multi ab hac quidem alieni sunt, qui tamen in diversam partem peccant, quando ipsorum cupiditati nihil sufficit, & ne frui quidem audent illis, quae ex Dei benedictione acceperunt, aut suis laboribus pararunt. Ergo hos admonet, corda non minus avaritia quam ebrietate gravari. Nam ut alibi monuimus, idololatria est, quia animum qui uni Deo debetur, divitiis vendicat, & in his confidere docet, cultum vero Dei quam maxime impedit, quando facit ut de divinis & aeternis bonis securi, ea sola curemus, quae huic saeculo serviunt. Quae causa est, quod eam malorum omnium radicem Paulus dicit, & laqueos ei tribuit pessimarum tentationum, quibus a Deo simul & omni pietatis studio abstrahuntur, quicunque illi indulgent. Poterant haec quoque plurimis exemplis probari, nisi non omnino stupidis sufficere possent ea, quae publice & privatim fiunt. Avaritia certe verbi Dei doctrinam corrupit, ius venale facit, disciplinam turbat, iniustitiae parit in contractibus, denique Ecclesias & Respub. evertit, neque fieri potest, ut aliquando caput aut animum ad Deum sive caelestium bonorum contemplationem attollat, qui ceruices suas hoc tam infelici pondere aggravarunt. Semper ergo meminerimus, nos in terris hisce peregrinos esse, patriam autem & patrimonium in caelis habere. Atqui huius vitae peregrinatio non multis indiget, cum ipsa natura paucis contenta sit, & ad eius finem singulis momentis decurramus. Eos, qui in extrema senecta opes solicite congerunt, flutissime facere olim philosophi intellexerunt, & Cicero eos viatorum similes esse dicebat, qui quo minus itineris ipsis reliquum est, eo magis de viatico soliciti sunt. At quanto stupidiores iudicabimus esse eos, qui non suam modo vitam, sed mundum hunc totum ad suum finem decurrere, et huius senectam extremam iam adesse vident, adhuc tamen annuos reditus congerunt, & terram iamiam perituram censibus quotidie novis gravant? Quis obsecro iisdem animus esse potest, quam quod sortis suae mortalis oblivi sibi vitam adhuc diuturnam pollicentur, aut Mahumeticum quid somniantes, opum & delitiarum usum aliquem in futuro etiam saeculo fore sibi persuadent? Nunquam possunt illi in pietate & Regni Dei studio proficere. Nos ergo huius dicti memores, animis in caelos sublatis excutiamus procul infelices illas ebrietatis & avaritiae sarcinas, ut liberius ijs vacemus, quae solida & aeternam felicitatem nobis pariunt.
units.tr: Moreover, he adds another vice which should likewise be avoided: the cares of this life. In this precept he does not condemn the careful and moderate, indeed necessary, care of household affairs, which we can neither altogether lay aside nor ought to. For it is God's decree: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." And Paul says that whoever does not provide for his own household is worse than an unbeliever. Let us know, then, that the anxious solicitude for getting food, which in Matthew he attributes to the Gentiles, who have no knowledge of divine providence, is what is condemned here. Avarice begets this anxiety in us, which men define as an insatiable desire to acquire and to have. Christ rightly joins this to drunkenness, because many who are free from drunkenness nonetheless sin in the opposite way, when nothing satisfies their greed, and they do not even dare to enjoy what they have received from God's blessing or obtained by their own labours. Therefore he warns these men that their hearts are weighed down no less by avarice than by drunkenness. For, as we have elsewhere observed, avarice is idolatry, because it claims for riches the heart that is owed to the one God alone, and teaches men to trust in them; and it greatly hinders the worship of God, since it makes us, secure about divine and eternal goods, care only for those things that serve this age. This is why Paul calls it the root of all evils, and attributes to it the snares of the worst temptations, by which all who indulge in it are drawn away at once from God and from every pursuit of piety. These things could also be proved by very many examples, were it not that what is done publicly and privately would suffice for all but the utterly stupid. Avarice certainly corrupts the doctrine of the Word of God, makes justice for sale, disturbs church discipline, produces injustice in contracts, and finally overturns churches and commonwealths. Nor can it happen that the head or the mind of those who have weighed down their necks with this so unhappy a burden is ever lifted up to God, or to the contemplation of heavenly goods. Let us therefore always remember that we are strangers in these lands, and that we have our homeland and our inheritance in heaven. Yet the pilgrimage of this life needs little, since nature itself is content with few things, and we run toward its end every moment. The philosophers of old understood that those who anxiously heap up wealth in extreme old age are most foolish, and Cicero said that they are like travellers who, the less of their journey remains, the more anxious they are about their provisions. But how much more foolish shall we judge those who, seeing not only their own life but this whole world running toward its end, and seeing that the extreme old age of this world is already at hand, still heap up yearly revenues and burden the earth, now about to perish, with fresh estates every day? Who, I beg you, can have such a mind, except those who, forgetful of their mortal lot, promise themselves a long life still, or, dreaming some Mahometan fancy, persuade themselves that there will be some use of wealth and pleasures even in the age to come? Such men can never make progress in piety and in zeal for the kingdom of God. Let us, then, mindful of this saying, lift our minds to heaven and shake off far from us those unhappy burdens of drunkenness and avarice, so that we may be more free to attend to those things which bring us solid and eternal happiness.

units.la: Caeterum admonitionem hanc Christus graviter admodum ratione confirmat, quae a necessario petitur. Nam periculi meminit, quod huius contemporibus maximum ac praesentissimum imminet: quia repente dies ille superuenturus sit. Et hoc ipsum simili ab aucupio desumpto explicans, addit: Nā ut laqueus inuadet in omnes, qui habitant in superficie totius terræ. Pulchrè autem ad securitatem, quæ nobis natura inhæret, alludit. Vt enim auicula rerum ignaræ & securæ circumuolitant, per arborum ramos decursant, modò in altum tendunt, modò in terram vsque sese demittunt, & cantu seipsas & auditores oblectant, nescia interim quot retia illis aucupes tendant, quot laqueos abscondāt, quot uimina uiscosa struant, à quibus ferè, quando minimū putant, capiuntur. Ita pleriq; hominum huius uitæ illecebris decepti discurrunt, ludunt, uoluptuantur, aut etiam inanibus curis atque labore inutili seipsos conficiunt, nihil interim uel de mortis hora cogitantes, quæ nihil huius expectantibus obrepit: neque sinem illum totius mundi considerantes, qui et ipse incautos aliquando opprimet.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ confirms this warning with a weighty argument, which is drawn from necessity. For he speaks of the danger that hangs over the people of his own time, a danger that is greatest and most immediate: because that day will come upon them suddenly. Explaining this by an image taken from fowling, he adds: For as a snare shall it come on all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. He alludes most aptly to the carelessness that is native to us. Little birds, heedless and unafraid, flit about and hop from branch to branch, now rising high, now swooping down to the ground, and they cheer themselves and their listeners with song. Meanwhile they do not know how many nets the fowlers are spreading for them, how many snares they are hiding, how many sticky twigs they are setting, and they are often caught when they least expect it. So too most men, deceived by the allurements of this life, run about, play, and indulge their pleasures, or else wear themselves out with empty cares and useless labour. Meanwhile they think nothing of the hour of death, which creeps upon those who do not expect it at all, nor do they consider that end of the whole world which will one day overtake the unwary.

units.la: Facit autem ad huius argumenti amplificationem, quòd diem islum instar laquei in omnes eos inuasurum dicit, qui habitant in superficie totius terræ. Ista enim locutione necessitatem siue malum inevitabile fore dicit omnibus, qui cupiditatibus suis & mundi studijs indulget. Possunt interdum auiculæ retia & tendiculas effugere, quia hæ non totas syluas, imò ne arbores quidem totas occupant, & ipsius etiam aeris usus illis liberior est. At dies illi Domini omnibus superueniet, & ad omnes iustitiæ atq; maiestatis eius virtus pertinget, & illius ministri, Angeli, à quatuor cardinibus mundi omnes ad illius tribunal cogent, ut illic digna suis factis præmia recipiant. Duo ergo hîc cõcurrunt, quæ nisi nos attentos reddant, næ plus quam stupidi sumus. Improuisus nimirum aduentus Domini & inevitabilis necessitas, cuius legibus omnes cuiuscunq; loci aut ordinis homines subiecti erunt. At quod de illo die dicitur, id nos ad mortis quoq; horam extendere debemus, cuius eadem planè est ratio. Solet hanc Scriptura uiam omnis terræ dicere, quia omnibus ex æquo incumbit moriendi necessitas. At eiusdem hora nihil incertius esse tam manifestum & notum est omnibus, ut stultus foret, qui in eo demonstrando uelit verba facere. Ita uerò nostræ saluti consulere voluit Deus ut nec inutili terrore aut pauore nosipsos conficiamus, neq; securi nimis ad extremum usq; ea differamus, quæ nobis nunquam non agenda sunt. Nostrum ergo fuerit in hoc etiam illius erga nos studium agnoscere, & horum consideratione rectè uti ad salutem nostram tuendam.
units.tr: Moreover, the image of the snare serves to strengthen this point, in that he says that day will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. By this expression he means that necessity, or an unavoidable evil, will fall on all who indulge their desires and the pursuits of the world. Small birds can sometimes escape nets and snares, because these do not cover whole woods, nor even whole trees, and the air itself is freer for them to use. But the day of the Lord will come upon everyone, and the power of his justice and majesty will reach every person; and his ministers, the angels, will gather everyone from the four corners of the world to his judgement seat, so that they may receive there rewards worthy of their deeds. Two things therefore come together here, which unless they make us attentive, we are more than stupid. Namely, the unexpected coming of the Lord and the inescapable necessity to which all people of every place and rank will be subject. Now what is said of that day we ought to extend also to the hour of death, for the reasoning is exactly the same. Scripture is accustomed to call this the way of all the earth, because the necessity of dying falls equally on all. And that the hour of death is entirely uncertain is so plain and well known to everyone that it would be foolish for anyone to make speeches to prove it. God wished to provide for our salvation in such a way that we should not wear ourselves out with useless terror or fear, nor, being too secure, put off until the very end those things which must always be done by us. It is therefore our part to recognise in this also his care for us, and to use the consideration of these things rightly for the safeguarding of our salvation.

units.la: Et huc referri debet altera huius Epilogi pars, qua quid à nobis fieri debeat, Dominus docet. Nec enim otiosos seruos ille vult habere, & proinde non satis fuerit omisisse ea, quæ prohibet, sed ut simul officium faciamus necesse est. Arguit hoc ignauos illos, qui nihil faciendo se excusatos fore putant, & proinde inutilem illum seruum imitantur: qui acceptum ab hero suo talentum humi defodit, ne quid in eius dispensationem peccaret. Quàm uerò ille Domino displicuerit, suo loco uidimus. Nunc ergo Christum dicentem audiamus: Excubate igitur, omni tempore rogantes, ut digni habeamini, qui effugiatis ista omnia, quæ futura sunt, & consistatis coram Filio hominis. Primò vigilare nos iubet, vel excubare. Vbi nemo de corporis vigilia agi putet, cum somnus singulare Dei beneficium sit, quo corpus totum irrigatur & uires instauDantur: sed ad animum hoc præceptum transferri debet, qui ut dormire dicitur, quando securitate & socordia quasi sepultus omnia negligit, nec quicquam pensi habet: ita vigilat idem, quando excusso hoc carnis ueterno ea curat & agit, quæ nobis ex officio agenda sunt. Et pertinet ad huius dicti expositionem parabola, quam supra Cap. duodecimo audiuimus, ubi nos seruis confert, qui heri sui reditum ex nuptijs expectant. Iam enim ipse in cœlis agit, ubi nuptiæ sunt perpetuæ & gaudium perpetuum. Inde uerò redibit olim in nubibus cæli ad iudicandum uiuos & mortuos, ut impios quidem puniat, electos autem suos ad se recipiat, & Regni sui cœlestis consortes reddat. Iubet ergo, ut hunc eius aduentū expectemus lumbis succinctis, qui iter ingredi uolentium & ad opus faciendum paratorum habitus est: utq; lucernas uerbi sui in manibus gestemus, quod omnibus nostris actionibus prælucere debet: deniq; ut pulsanti aperiamus. Pulsat quidem ille nunquam non cordis nostri ostium per uerbi prædicationem, cui nos locum dare conuenit, ut ad nos ingredi & Spiritu suo nos donare possit. Olim uerò in magno illo die pulsus longè grauior exaudietur, quando cum uoce Archangeli & tuba Dei (ut Paulus ait) de cœlo descendet, & ad suum tribunal omnium seculorum homines, quotquot unquam fuerunt ac fucuri sunt, citabit. Hîc ergo nos paratos esse conuenit, ne ex improuiso ille nobis superueniat: Vt enim aduentus ille terribilis erit impijs iudiciorum Dei contemptoribus: ita lætus ac felix illucéscet iis, qui animos suos iam pridem ad eum excipiendum præparauerunt: ut nuper abunde est dictum.
units.tr: The second part of this epilogue should also be referred to this point, in which the Lord teaches what must be done by us. For he does not wish to have idle servants, and therefore it is not enough to have left undone the things he forbids, but we must also at the same time perform our duty. This rebukes those sluggards who think they will be excused by doing nothing, and so they imitate that unprofitable servant who buried in the ground the talent he had received from his master, so that he would sin in its management. How much that servant displeased the Lord we have seen in its proper place. Now then let us hear Christ speaking: Watch therefore, and pray always, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are going to happen, and to stand before the Son of man. First, he bids us to be vigilant, or to keep watch. Let no one think that bodily wakefulness is meant here, since sleep is a singular blessing of God, by which the whole body is refreshed and its strength restored. Rather, this precept must be transferred to the mind, which is said to sleep when, as if buried in security and carelessness, it neglects everything and has no care for anything. In the same way it keeps watch when, having shaken off this drowsiness of the flesh, it attends to and performs those things which we are bound to do by our duty. The parable which we heard above in chapter twelve, where he compares us to servants who await their master's return from the wedding, belongs to the explanation of this saying. For he himself now acts in heaven, where the marriage is everlasting and the joy everlasting. Thence he will one day return in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead, so as to punish the wicked indeed, but to receive his elect to himself and make them partners of his heavenly kingdom. He therefore commands us to await his coming with loins girded, which is the posture of those who are about to set out on a journey and are prepared for work; and to hold his lamps of the word in our hands, for these ought to give light to all our actions; and finally, to open to him when he knocks. Indeed he knocks at the door of our heart continually through the preaching of the word, and we ought to give him room, so that he may enter to us and give us his Spirit. But one day, on that great day, his knock will be heard far more heavily, when with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God (as Paul says) he will descend from heaven, and will summon to his tribunal all the people of every age, as many as have ever lived or will yet live. Here therefore we ought to be ready, lest that day come upon us unexpectedly. For just as that terrible coming will be to the wicked, who despise the judgements of God, so it will dawn joyful and happy on those who have long since prepared their souls to receive him, as has been said at length a little while ago.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque nobis mandat Dominus, ut nimirum omni tempore rogemus, ut digni ha-beamur, qui effugiamus ista omnia quae futura sunt, &c. Nam ut absque Dei gratia nihil possumus, ita recurrit subinde carnis nostrae vitiositas, & nunquam non nobis insidias struit Satan, quibus non alia ratione commodius & felicius poterimus resistere, quam si nosipsos ac salutem nostram precibus assiduis Deo commendemus, & ab eo petamus vires, quae huic certamini sufficiant. At quia praecando plurimum peccatur, dum circa carnis vota & mundi studia occupamur, quis nobis precum finis aut scopus esse debeat, diserte exprimit Dominus, qui in duobus consistit. Primum est, ut digni habeamur qui effugiamus ista omnia, quae futura sunt. Qua locutione veram poenitentiam & conversionem ad Deum denotat. Constat enim hanc unicam esse rationem, per quam imminentes poenas & mala quaeque effugere possimus. Docet hoc ipse Dominus, quando in Prophetis hoc subinde ingeminat: Reuertimini ad me, & ego reuertar ad vos. Quam omnium concionum tam Propheticarum quam Apostolicarum summam esse, alibi prolixe demonstrauimus. Et exempla sunt nunquam spe sua falsos fuisse eos, qui poenarum comminatione perculsi se totos Deo subiecerunt: & ad hunc totis animis reuersi sunt. Nam etiamsi interdum non effugiant huius seculi calamitates, ijsdem tamen hae quoque adiumento sunt ad bonum, ut saluti ipsorum seruiant, quae aliis noxia & exitialia sunt. Seruit autem haec prima petitio ad hoc, ne ad inutilia aut illicita salutis media conuertamur, sed eam viam ingrediamur, quam Deus ipse in verbo suo praescribit. Altera petitio est, ut consistamus coram Filio hominis. Fit hoc bifariam. Nam in hoc seculo coram Domino stare & ambulare dicuntur, qui huic seruiunt, & ad eius iussa exequenda parati sunt. Hoc sensu apud Danielem myriades Angelorum coram illo stare viisae sunt. Deinde ad iudicium Dei hoc refertur, & inter se opponuntur Stare & cadere. Nam causa cadere Latinis dicitur, qui damnatur, stare autem qui illam iure & legibus obtinet. Verum sensus huius loci argumento probe conuenit. Nam ipsa necessitas iubet nos orare, ut Deus ita nos gubernet atque fulciat, ut quoad hic viuere datur, ipsi fideliter seruiamus, & olim in magno illo die ipsius conspectum atque iudicium pura conscientia & fide intrepida possimus sustinere. Negat hoc impijs Dauid in Psalmo primo dicens: Non stabunt impij in iudicio, neq; peccatores in coetu iustorum. Hac ergo bipertita petitione comprehendit Christus quaecunq; ad hominis felicitatem tam in hoc quam in futuro seculo necessaria sunt: & debet haec nobis esse summa votorum omnium adeoq; regula, secundum quam preces nostrae omnes dirigantur. Cum autem ista a Deo precibus petere iubeat Christus, non obscure omnem virium atque meriti nostri fiduciam iugulat, & omne salutis praesidium nobis in gratuita Dei misericordia consistere docet. Nam nisi ille nos dignetur pro suis agnoscere, neque in hac vita ipsi seruire, neque olim ad eius tribunal consistere poterimus. Quid vero in nobis est, cuius ergo nos ista gratia dignetur? Si iniquitates obseruaueris Domine (inquit Dauid) quis consistet? Item: ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo, &c. Et voluit de his nos in praesenti admonere Filius Dei, ne quis inter nouissimorum temporum turbas aliquid propriae suae dignitati aut iustitiae tribuat: sic hanc suam prophetiam admonitione non minus necessaria quam utilissima concludit.
units.tr: But the Lord also gives us a second command, namely that we should always pray, that we may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and so on. For just as we can do nothing without the grace of God, so the sinfulness of our flesh keeps recurring, and Satan never ceases to lay snares for us, against which we can resist in no more fitting or happy way than by commending ourselves and our salvation to God with constant prayers, and asking him for the strength that will suffice for this struggle. But because we sin greatly in praying, when we are occupied with the desires of the flesh and the pursuits of the world, the Lord clearly sets out what the aim and purpose of our prayers ought to be, which consists of two things. The first is that we may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come. By this expression he denotes true repentance and conversion to God. For it is established that this is the only way by which we can escape impending punishments and every evil. The Lord himself teaches this, when he repeats it often in the prophets: Return to me, and I will return to you. We have shown at length elsewhere that this is the sum of all the sermons of the prophets and the apostles. And there are examples of men who were never disappointed in their hope, who, struck by the threat of punishment, submitted themselves wholly to God and turned back to him with their whole souls. For even if they sometimes do not escape the calamities of this age, these same calamities nevertheless serve them for good, so that they promote their salvation, although for others they are harmful and deadly. This first petition serves to keep us from turning to useless or unlawful means of salvation, and to lead us to walk in the way which God himself prescribes in his word. The second petition is that we may stand before the Son of man. This happens in two ways. For in this age those are said to stand and walk before the Lord who serve him and are ready to carry out his commands. In this sense in Daniel myriads of angels are seen standing before him. Then this also refers to the judgement of God, and in this sense standing and falling are set against each other. For in Latin the one who is condemned is said to fall, but the one who wins his case by right and law is said to stand. And this meaning fits well with the subject of this passage. For necessity itself bids us pray that God may so govern and uphold us, that, as long as we are allowed to live here, we may serve him faithfully, and that on that great day we may be able to endure his sight and judgement with a clear conscience and fearless faith. David denies this to the wicked in the first Psalm, saying: The wicked shall not stand in the judgement, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. By this twofold petition, therefore, Christ comprehends everything necessary for the happiness of man both in this age and in the age to come, and this ought to be for us the sum of all our desires and so the rule by which all our prayers are directed. But since Christ bids us ask these things of God in prayer, he quite plainly cuts off all confidence in our own strength and merit, and teaches that all the safeguard of our salvation lies in the free mercy of God. For unless he deigns to acknowledge us as his own, we shall be able neither to serve him in this life nor to stand before his tribunal in that day. And what is there in us for which this grace should deign to regard us? If you should mark iniquities, O Lord (says David), who shall stand? Likewise: Enter not into judgement with your servant, and so on. The Son of God wished to warn us of these things at present, so that no one among the troubles of the last times should ascribe anything to his own dignity or righteousness; and so he concludes this prophecy of his with an admonition no less necessary than most useful.

units.la: Sequitur breuis narratiuncula, qua omnia ea comprehendit Lucas, quae Christus usq; ad eum diem deinceps fecit, quo ab hostibus suis captus & in mortem traditus est. Docebat (inquit) inter diu in templo, noctu vero exiens diuersabatur in monte, qui vocatur Olearum. Et totus populus diluculo veniebat ad eum, ut eum audiret in templo. Itaq; admonitionem hanc proprio exemplo confirmat. Totum enim diem docendo consumit, quam eius vocationem siue functionem fuisse, non uno loco diximus. Et ipse puer adhucid testatus est, quando inter doctores in templo sedens matri virgini cum ipso expostulanti dicit: An nesciebatis, quod in iis, quae Patris mei sunt, oporteat me esse? Quare etsi mortis horam sibi iam instare sciret neq; ignoraret hostium insidias, nihilo tamen segnior est in obeunda sua functione, ut qui hoc unum in uotis habebat, ut quam plurimos Patri lucrare-tur, & aduersus crucis scandalum simplicium animos confirmaret: Idem tamen, quia uerum hominem induerat, & in assumpta humanitate Sacerdotis munus sustinebat, noctu in montem exit: nimirum ut preces ad Patrem fundat, cui & seipsum commendauit, & pro discipulis suis intercesit, quos grauissimis tentationibus exagitandos breui fore sciebat. Ex alijs certe locis apparet praecipuam secessus sui causam semper fuisse preces, & quam serio pro discipulis precatus sit, ipse in ultima Cœna deinceps testabitur. Habent hæc dulcissimam consolationem, quia docent, quâ fideliter nostram quoq; salutem ille commendatam habeat. Simul autem officij admonemur, ut nihil antiquius habea mus uerbo Dei, in cuius prædicatione Filium eius æternum tam sedulum fuisse uidemus. Et huc pertinet quod de populo dicitur, qui mane ad illum in templo docentem confluxit, ut eum audiret. Peccarunt illi quidem inconstantia, quando mox ad Pontificum partes desciuerunt. Interim laude dignum est studium hoc, quo in præsentiflagrant. Hoc ipsum ergo imitemur, & inter nostri seculi grauissimos motus unum Iesum Christum audiamus, & eundem assiduis precibus fatigemus, ut Ecclesias in nostris quoq; regionibus seruare, nosq; omnes suo Spiritu regere dignetur, ut omnibus periculis superiores facti, olim in eius conspectu consistere possimus, cùm uenerit in gloria Patris sui cum Angelis suis sanctis. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: What follows is a short little narrative, in which Luke sums up everything that Christ did from then until the day on which he was seized by his enemies and handed over to death. "He was teaching," it says, "in the temple by day; but at night he went out and stayed on the mount called Olivet. And all the people came early in the morning to him in the temple, to hear him." So he confirms this admonition by his own example. For he spends the whole day in teaching, and we have said in more than one place that this was his calling or office. The boy himself also bore witness to it, when, sitting among the teachers in the temple, he said to his mother the Virgin, who was reproaching him: "Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?" Therefore, although he knew that the hour of his death was already at hand, and was not ignorant of the snares of his enemies, he was no less diligent in discharging his office, since his one wish was to win as many as possible for the Father and to strengthen the hearts of simple people against the scandal of the cross. Yet because he had put on true manhood, and in the humanity he had assumed bore the office of priest, he goes out into the mount at night: plainly to pour out prayers to the Father, to whom he had also commended himself, and to intercede for his disciples, whom he knew would soon be harassed by the gravest temptations. Certainly from other passages it appears that the chief reason for his withdrawal was always prayer, and how earnestly he prayed for his disciples he himself will afterwards testify at the Last Supper. These things hold the sweetest consolation, because they teach us how faithfully he has commended our salvation too to the Father. At the same time we are reminded of our duty: that we should hold nothing more precious than the Word of God, in the preaching of which we see his eternal Son so diligent. And to this belongs what is said of the people who gathered early to him as he taught in the temple, that they might hear him. They indeed sinned by their inconstancy, when soon afterwards they went over to the side of the high priests. Nevertheless, that zeal with which they burned at that time is worthy of praise. Let us therefore imitate this very thing: amid the gravest upheavals of our age, let us hear Jesus Christ alone, and let us weary him with constant prayers, that he may deign to preserve his Churches in our regions as well, and to rule us all by his Spirit, so that, having been made superior to all dangers, we may one day be able to stand in his sight, when he comes in the glory of his Father with his holy angels. To him alone be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCI.

units.la: APpropinquabat autem festum azymorum, quod dicitur Pascha. Et quærebant principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ, quomodo eum tollerent è medio. Timebant enim plebem. Introijt autem Satanas in Iudam cognominatum Iscariotem, qui erat è numero duodecim: Qui abiens collocutus est cum principibus Sacerdotum ac præfectis templo, quomodo ipsis eum traderet. Qui gauisi sunt, ac pacti sunt se daturos ei pecuniam: & ipse spopondit, quærebatq; opportunitatem, ut traderet eum ipsis absq; turba.
units.tr: Now the feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Passover, was drawing near. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking how they might put him to death, for they feared the people. Then Satan entered into Judas, surnamed Iscariot, who was one of the twelve. He went away and conferred with the chief priests and the captains of the temple about how he might betray him to them. They were glad and agreed to give him money. He consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them without a crowd.

units.la: INter opera Dei nullum admirabilius & præstantius est, quàm quòd Filium suum unigenitum ac sibi coæternum atq; coessentialem propter nos hominem uerù fieri uoluit, & eum de post infinitos labores atq; molestias, quas in terris agens perpessus est, pro nobis in mortem tradidit. Continetur in eo plena & perfecta Dei cognitio, quæ etiamsi ex omnibus aliis quoq; operibus hauriri possit, nullibi tamen clarius sese exerit, quàm hic, ubi omnes eius uirtutes tanquam in tabula nobis spectandæ proponuntur. Iustitiæ enim perfectissimæ exemplum est, quòd ne Filio quidem pepercit, ut peccatum dignis pœnis expiaretur. In eodem uerò misericordia plus quàm paterna elucet, quæ illum mouit ut Filium potius in infami cruce pendere, quàm nos in æternis inferorum cruciatibus uidere maluerit. Sapientiæ item sempiternæ opus est, quòd eam salutis ratione iniuit, qua & iustitiæ & misericordiæ eius satisfieret. Veritatem uerò eius infallibilè asserit, quæ promissis ijs quoq; deesse noluit, quæ sine Filij morte acerba impleri non poterant. Similiter omnipotentiam illius inuictam in eo cernimus, quod in assumpta carne, qua nihil miserius, infelicius atq; infirmius est, omnem aduersariam potestatem, peccatum scilicet, mortem, inferos, mundum mundiq; principem deiicit. Quæ omnia si rectè ac diligenter considerentur, de omnibus nos admonent, quæ nobis ad uitæ huius institutionem cognitu necessaria sunt, siue læta siue aduersa incidant. Quis enim peccati blanditias et carnis circa illud lascivientis rationes admittat, qui diuinæ iustitiæ rigore probè expenderit? Quis de Dei bonitate & misericordia dubitet, si exhibitam in Christo gratiam non ofcitanter agnoscat? Quis in rebus dubijs & perplexis animum despondeat, qui Dei sapientiam in animū reuocauerit? Vel num eundem promissionum suarum minus memorem fore putabimus, qui ueritati suæ tunc deesse noluit, quando de Filij sui uita & sanguine agebatur? Quàm uerò stultum & absurdū fuerit de Dei omnipotentia desperare propter nostram imbecillitatē aut hostiū uires siue potentiā, cùm Christus fragili & infirma carne uestitus de mundo & diabolo uictoriā tam præclarum reportauerit? Continet ergo historia hæc ueram sapientiam, quam rerum humanarū atq; diuinarum notitiam esse olim sapientissimi quiq; definierunt, et quæ sola nos armat, ut aduersus omnem fortunam fortes atq; intrepidi tenea mus stationē nobis à Deo creditam. Cæterùm præter istud duo adhuc alia hic proponuntur, ad quæ ceu scopum certum omnes istius historiæ partes dirigi debent, ut magis nostræ ædificationi seruiant.
units.tr: Among the works of God none is more wonderful or excellent than that he willed his only-begotten Son, who is co-eternal and co-essential with him, to become true man for our sake, and, after infinite toils and troubles which he endured while living on earth, to deliver him to death for us. In this is contained the full and perfect knowledge of God. Although this knowledge can be drawn from all his other works, it nowhere shines more clearly than here, where all his virtues are set before us as if on a tablet to be contemplated. For it is an example of most perfect justice that he did not spare even his Son, so that sin might be atoned for by fitting punishments. In the same act mercy shines forth more than fatherly, which moved him to choose that his Son should hang on the infamous cross rather than that we should see ourselves in the eternal torments of hell. It is also a work of everlasting wisdom that he devised a plan of salvation by which both his justice and his mercy were satisfied. And it asserts his infallible truth, for he was unwilling to fail in those promises which could not be fulfilled without the bitter death of his Son. Likewise we see his unconquered omnipotence in this, that in the assumed flesh, than which nothing is more wretched, unhappy and weak, he casts down every hostile power: sin, death, hell, the world and the prince of the world. If all these things are rightly and diligently considered, they admonish us about everything that we need to know for the ordering of this life, whether happy or adverse events befall us. For who would admit the allurements of sin and the lusts of the flesh that play about it, if he had duly weighed the strictness of divine justice? Who would doubt God's goodness and mercy, if he acknowledged without indifference the grace shown in Christ? Who would lose heart in doubtful and perplexing matters, if he had called to mind the wisdom of God? Or shall we think that he who was unwilling to fail in his truth when the life and blood of his Son were at stake will be less mindful of his promises? How foolish and absurd it would be to despair of God's omnipotence because of our own weakness or the strength and power of our enemies, when Christ, clothed in frail and feeble flesh, won so splendid a victory over the world and the devil! This history therefore contains true wisdom, which the wisest men have long defined as the knowledge of things human and divine, and which alone arms us to hold our post, given us by God, bravely and fearlessly against every fortune. Moreover, besides this, two further things are set forth here, to which all the parts of this history ought to be directed as to a fixed goal, so that they may serve more to our edification.

units.la: Primum est humani generis redemptio, quae tota hic fundatur, & quae aliter fieri non poterat. Nam, ut saepe dictum est, omnes homines peccatores sunt, peccatum autem noxa capitalis est, & proinde nulla eius expiatio absque sanguine potest fieri, sicuti Paulus ad Hebraeos admonet. Atqui non proderat nobis sacrificiorum siue pecorum sanguis, cum quibus nulla nobis naturae communio intercedit, neque aliquid sperari poterat, si qui sese pro publica humani generis salute sponte deuouissent, aut inuiti ex publico aliorum consensu abrepti fuissent, ut καθάρματα siue victimae expiatoriae fierent, quod olim gentibus in usu fuisse legimus. Itaque aeterno decreto Deus, priusquam mundus hic conderetur, Filium suum praedestinauit, ut ex virgine carnem veram assumeret, & ut frater atque uindex noster (quo nomine illum Iobus appellat) causam nostram suscipperet, atque sublata peccati noxa salutem nobis sempiternam pararet. Ad nos ergo historia haec omnis pertinet, & cum propter nos haec omnia facta sint, nos eorundem authores esse constat. Quod ideo admoneri oportet, ne in profscindendis Iudaeorum Sacerdotibus & militibus aliisque horum socijs occupati, ea negligamus, quae ad nos spectant: sed potius in nosipsos descendamus, ut nostra culpa agnita totis animis conteramur, credamus autem nos Iesu Christi morte redemptos esse, & tanti beneficij memores, nos Deo sistamus viuentem hostiam.
units.tr: The first is the redemption of the human race, which is wholly founded here, and which could not have been accomplished otherwise. For, as has often been said, all men are sinners, and sin is a capital crime, and therefore no expiation of it can be made without blood, as Paul admonishes the Hebrews. Yet the blood of sacrifices or of cattle would not have profited us, since no natural kinship lies between us and them, nor could anything be hoped for if some had voluntarily devoted themselves for the public salvation of the human race, or had been seized against their will by the common consent of others, so that they might become offscourings [καθάρματα], that is, expiatory victims, which we read was once the custom among the Gentiles. Therefore by an eternal decree God, before this world was founded, predestined his Son, so that he might assume true flesh from a virgin, and that he, as our brother and redeemer (by which name Job calls him), might take up our cause and, removing the guilt of sin, prepare eternal salvation for us. This whole history therefore pertains to us, and since all these things were done for our sake, it is plain that we are their authors. This must be pointed out, lest, while we are busy tearing into the priests of the Jews, the soldiers and their associates, we neglect the things that concern us. Rather we should descend into ourselves, so that, having acknowledged our fault, we may be crushed with our whole hearts, and believing that we have been redeemed by the death of Jesus Christ, and mindful of so great a benefit, we may present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice.

units.la: Alterum est exemplum, quo nobis Christus praeiuit. Nam ut Petrus ait, pro nobis ille passus est, relinquens nobis exemplum, cuius vestigijs nos insistamus. In illo igitur obseruari debet, quae nam totius Ecclesiae atque priorum omnium sors in terris hisce semper futura sit. Nam si me persecuti sunt (inquit ille) etiam uos persequentur: Si meum sermonem seruauerunt, uestrum quoque seruabunt. Quapropter nos ad illius imitationem praeparari conuenit, & nunquam non communis illius omnium Christianorum regulae meminisse: Qui vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Sunt autem in exemplo eius praecipua, quae nos imitari oportet: Obedientia, qua sese humiliauit usque ad mortem crucis, ut aeterno Patris decreto satisfieret: Patientia, qua armatus tanquam agnus ad macellum ductus est, & absque omni contradictione dirissima quaeque sustinuit: Fidei constantia, qua inter dolores acerbissimos perseuerauit, ut tunc quoque Deum suum dicere, quando propria caro atque hominis ratio eum prorsus ab illo derelictum esse dictabat: Charitas, qua hostes quoque complexus est, pro quibus preces fecit ad Patrem, & quos adhuc madentes suo sanguine in gratia recepit, cum intra animos suos copuncti adipsum conuerterentur. Istis virtutibus nos quoque insistere decet. Simul autem consoletur nos in omni fortuna, quod ille per crucem triumphauit, & ex mortuis resurrexit ad vitam caelestem atque immortalem. Nec enim dubium est, nos quoque victoria aduersus mundum & eius principem potituros esse, si ipsi per fidem insiti peccato moriamur, & in illo resurgamus ad vitam nouam atque nostra professione dignam. Et haec sunt praecipua capita, in quae nos potissimum intentos esse conuenit, ut ad ea referamus, quaecunque in historia hac tota tractantur. Itaque iis praemissis ad Euangelistae verba accedamus, quae modo recitauimus, quibus duo continentur. Nam tempus indicant, quo Dei Filius in mortem traditus est. Deinde mortis eius causas exponunt, uel eos potius monstrant, qui illius praecipui fuerunt ministri.
units.tr: The second is the example which Christ has gone before us in. For, as Peter says, he suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in his steps. Therefore in him we ought to observe what the lot of the whole Church and of all who went before will always be on this earth. For if they have persecuted me, he says, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my word, they will keep yours also. Wherefore it is fitting that we prepare ourselves to imitate him, and never forget that common rule of all Christians: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me. Among the things in his example which we ought especially to imitate are these: obedience, by which he humbled himself even to the death of the cross, so that the eternal decree of the Father might be satisfied; patience, by which, armed like a lamb led to the slaughter, he endured without any resistance the most dreadful things; constancy of faith, by which he persevered amid the most bitter pains, so that even then he called God his God, when his own flesh and human reason declared that he had been utterly forsaken by him; and love, by which he embraced even his enemies, for whom he prayed to the Father, and whom, still dripping with his blood, he received into grace when they turned to him with pricked hearts. We too ought to follow these virtues. At the same time, let it console us in every fortune that he triumphed through the cross and rose from the dead to a heavenly and immortal life. For there is no doubt that we too shall obtain victory over the world and its prince, if we die to sin through faith and rise again in him to a new life worthy of our profession. These are the chief heads on which we should especially fix our attention, so that we may refer to them whatever is treated in this whole history. Therefore, with these things premised, let us come to the words of the evangelist just recited, in which two things are contained. For they indicate the time at which the Son of God was delivered to death, and then they set forth the causes of his death, or rather point out those who were the chief agents of it.

units.la: Primum paucis Lucas expedit, dicens: Appropinquabat autem festum azymorum, quod dicitur Pascha. Marcus biduum modo abfuisse dicit a Pascha te. Nec otiosam aut superuacaneam esse hanc temporis notationem, ex Christi uerbis apparet, qui de illo discipulos admonuit (ut in Matth. legitur) dicens: Sciris quod intra duos dies Pascha fit, & Filius hominis traditur ut crucifigatur. Debuit igitur ex aeterno Patris decreto sub Paschatis festum Christus pati, ut ipsa temporis circumstantia nos de mortis illius fructu admoneret. Illud enim in memoriam liberationis Israelitarum ex Aegypto institutum & celebratum fuisse constat. Atqui omnium nostrum, uel potius totius humani generis, eandem conditionem fuisse sub dura peccati & diaboli seruitute, quae illorum sub Pharaonis tyrannide fuit, alibi prolixe demonstrauimus. Vt ergo illi, cum indignissimi essent, quorum causam Deus suscipere (sicuti ipsorum murmura & multa scelera testantur) ex gratia liberati sunt: & per Agni sanguinem seruati, ne ab Angelo vastatore occiderentur: Ita nos quoque omnes gratuita misericordia Deus seruauit per sanguinem Filij sui, qui per Euangelij praedicationem nobis aspergitur, quique per fidem receptus nos tuetur, ne quid in nos iuris habeat Angelus ille malus, qui iam inde ab initio homicida fuit, & nostrae etiam saluti subinde insidias struit. Quo Ioannes Baptista respexit, quando in Christum extenso digito dicebat: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Et Paulus: Pascha nostrum immolatum est, Iesus Christus. Sed & Propheta Micheas sui saeculi homines huius mysterij admonuit, quando Deum super scelus transire dixit, alludens nimirum ad transitum illum olim in Aegypto factum, quem nostrae redemptionis in Christo typum fuisse diximus.
units.tr: First, Luke briefly explains, saying: Now the feast of unleavened bread drew near, which is called the Passover. Mark says that it was only two days before the Passover. That this notice of time is not idle or superfluous appears from the words of Christ, who warned his disciples about it (as we read in Matthew), saying: You know that after two days the Passover is kept, and the Son of man is delivered up to be crucified. Christ therefore had to suffer at the feast of the Passover by the eternal decree of the Father, so that the very circumstance of time might remind us of the fruit of his death. For it is established that the feast was instituted and celebrated in memory of the liberation of the Israelites from Egypt. But we have shown at length elsewhere that all of us, or rather the whole human race, were in the same condition under the harsh slavery of sin and the devil as they were under the tyranny of Pharaoh. Therefore, just as they, though most unworthy (as their murmurings and many sins bear witness) of whose cause God would take up, were freed by grace, and were preserved through the blood of the Lamb so that the destroying angel would not kill them, so God has also preserved us all by his free mercy through the blood of his Son, which is sprinkled upon us through the preaching of the gospel, and which, received by faith, protects us so that that evil angel, who from the beginning was a murderer and continually lays snares even for our salvation, may have no right over us. To this John the Baptist looked when, pointing his finger at Christ, he said: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. And Paul: Our Passover, Jesus Christ, has been sacrificed. And the prophet Micah also warned the men of his age about this mystery, when he said that God passes over transgression, obviously alluding to that passing over once made in Egypt, which we have said was a type of our redemption in Christ.

units.la: Porrò non minus nostri etiam officij nos admonet epulum illud paschale, quod tunc certis cum ceremonijs agebatur. Nam habitu peregrinantium, qui iam ad iter parati sive accincti sunt, agnum illum festinanter comedebant, adhibitis herbis quibusdam amarioribus & panibus azymis aut infermentatis, à quibus festum hoc denominabatur, quia ut his per totos dies semper uescerentur, Deus sub capitis poena constituerat. Qui ritus etsi cum alijs legalibus sacris mutatus sit, doctrinam tamen continet, quam perpetuò observare debent, quicunque Christo, uero illo agno Dei, ad salutem frui volunt. Meminerint illi se in hoc mundo peregrinos esse, patriam verò in coelis habere ubi thesauri illi Regni coelestis repositi sunt, quos sanguinis sui pretio nobis Christus acquisivit. Itaque expurgato & procul reiecto veteri fermento hypocrisis, malitiae & nequitiae, totum vitae nostra tempus tanquam festum celebremus in panibus non fermentatis sinceritatis ac veritatis: item absque omni huius mundi respectu contendamus ad patriam coelestem, neque terreamur crucis amaritudine, quam facile concoquent qui in fide constantes ac sincepи fuerint. Nunquam ergo salutis uerae participes fient quot quot aut non in unum Christum intenti sunt, aut huius mundi studijs addicti crucem atque adversa omnia fugiunt, ut carnis affectibus pravis indulgere possint.
units.tr: Moreover, the paschal feast also reminds us of our own duty, since it was celebrated with certain ceremonies. They ate that lamb hurriedly, dressed like travellers who are already prepared or girded for the journey, with certain bitter herbs and with unleavened or unfermented bread, from which the feast takes its name, since God had commanded under pain of capital punishment that they should eat these every day throughout the feast. Although this rite has been changed along with the other legal sacred observances, it still contains a teaching that all who wish to enjoy salvation through Christ, that true Lamb of God, must always observe. Let them remember that they are strangers in this world, and that their homeland is in heaven, where those treasures of the heavenly kingdom are laid up, which Christ has won for us at the price of his blood. Therefore, let us cleanse out and cast far away the old leaven of hypocrisy, malice and wickedness, and celebrate the whole time of our life as a feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Likewise, without any regard for this world, let us press on towards our heavenly homeland, and let us not be terrified by the bitterness of the cross, which those who are steadfast and sincere in faith will easily digest. Therefore, those who either do not fix their eyes on Christ alone, or who, given over to the pursuits of this world, flee the cross and all adversity so that they may indulge their depraved fleshly desires, will never become partakers of true salvation.

units.la: Sed ad alteram huius loci partem accedamus, qua causa totius negotij huius exponuntur. Inter quas praecipua est, plus quam paterna Dei dilectio, qua is genus humanum prosecutus est, & cui non aliter subveniri poterat, ut modò monuimus. Hanc ipse Christus indicat, apud Ioannem dicens: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum, unigenitum illum traderet, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Est igitur tota haec historia in aeterno Dei decreto fundata, & ideo probè considerari debet: quia & certitudinem salutis nostrae asserit sive confirmat, & scandalo medetur, quod humana ratio ex crucis ignominia solet concipere. Docet praeterea, salutem nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtigisse, qui indignos nos dilexit, nostrum verò esse, ut vicissim illum diligamus ex toto corde, & nos eidem totos per fidei obedientiam consecremus. Caeterum accedunt hic aliqui ex hominibus, qui negotij huius ministri fuerunt, & qui non ut Dei decretum exequerentur, mortem Christi promouerunt, sed ut pravis suis affectibus satisfacerent. De his Evangelistae diligenter differunt: ut istorum exemplo discamus, quid nos in primis cavere oporteat, ne ad eosdem scopulos offendamus. Admonemur praeterea, homines malos atque improbos non excusari per Dei providentiam. Quia enim illi cupiditatibus malis ducuntur, haeret in eis peccati culpa: quòd verò eorundem opera Deus bene utitur ad exequendum sua decreta & ad promouendum communem hominum salutem, hoc illius sapientiae atque bonitatis opus est, quam nos agnoscere & praedicare convenit.
units.tr: But let us come to the other part of this passage, in which the cause of the whole matter is set out. The chief of these causes is God's more than fatherly love, by which he cared for the human race, and by which it could not otherwise be helped, as we have just said. Christ himself points to this in John, saying: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." This whole history is therefore founded on the eternal decree of God, and so it ought to be carefully considered, because it both asserts and confirms the certainty of our salvation, and heals the scandal which human reason is wont to conceive from the shame of the cross. It also teaches that our salvation has come to us from the free mercy of God, who loved us when we were unworthy, and that it is our part in turn to love him with our whole heart, and to consecrate ourselves wholly to him through obedient faith. Moreover, there come here some men who were ministers of this business, and who did not carry forward the death of Christ in order to carry out God's decree, but in order to satisfy their own depraved desires. The Evangelists carefully discuss these men, so that by their example we may learn what we above all must beware of, lest we stumble upon the same rocks. We are further admonished that wicked and depraved men are not excused by the providence of God. For since they are driven by evil lusts, the guilt of sin clings to them; but that God makes good use of their works to carry out his decrees and to advance the common salvation of men, this is a work of his wisdom and goodness, which we ought to acknowledge and proclaim.

units.la: Fuerunt autem inter authores sive ministros mortis Christi, primi Sacerdotes & Scribae Iudaeorum, de quibus sic dicit Lucas: Et quaerebant principes Sacerdotum & Scribae, quomodo eum tollerent è medio. Quaerendi verb diligentè & anxiam consultationem innuit, quam instituerunt, ut eum dolo malo, id est, praetextu aliquo criminis in speciem probabilis, uel etiam per insidias occiderent. Et ita hanc partem Matthaeus & Marcus exponunt. Quia verò ridiculum uideri poterat, uiros potentes & authoritate graues tam solicitos esse de perdendo homine obscuro & inermi, causa additur: quòd populum timuerint. Videbant enim hunc totum ab illo pendere, & fauoris popularis speciem sive argumentum non contemnendum uiderant in magnifico eius in urbem ingressu, quando cum multorum applausu & laetis acclamationibus deductus atq; exceptus fuit. Periculum ergo erat, ne quid violenter tentando seditionem concitarent, quae eò periculosior fuisset, quò plures undique ad festum Paschatis conueniebant. At poterat mirum uideri, hoc eos molitos fuisse, quorum erat populum Christo adducere, & de eò publicè testari. Sed alibi monuimus, uetere Sacerdotum ordinem ab Herode iampridem sublatum, & in eorum locum homines obscuros & ignaua ueneris mancipia substitutos fuisse, qui posteà sub Romanis praesidibus cum Sacerdotio sacra quoq; uenalia fecerunt, ut templum nihil à foro & nummulariorum officinis differret. Quod ut commodius fieret, ijdem Legis doEtrinam traditionibus superstitiosis & ineptis, uel potius impijs, corruperant. Non potuerunt ergo tales ueritatis lucem ferre, & quia Christus non uerbo solum artes atq; impostturas eorum arguebat, uerumetiam iam semel & iterum manum admouerat, & non sine publica ignominia illos ex templo eiecerat, de illo occidendo consilia conferre incipiunt. Quanta uero cum astutia & improbitate id secerint, Ioannes Euangelista capite undecimo narrat, ubi multa diximus, quae ad huius etiā loci expositionem faciunt. Nunc sufficiat obseruauisse acerrimos Christi ac veritatis Euangelicae hostes semper fore antistites Ecclesiae, quos ambitio & avaritia excaecauit, ut religionem sibi quaestum faciant, & sua figmenta loco uerbi Dei obtrudere ausint. Exempla huius generis multa omnibus seculis edita sunt, & semper lis fuit uerae sapientiae cum falsa & hypocritica. Nec hodie meliorem sortem sperari debere, ex Christi & Apostolorum uaticiniis apparet, quae de nouissimis temporibus prodiderunt. Etenim ut truculentissimi doctrinae sanioris hostes sunt, qui in Ecclesia primatum tenent: ita ijsdem omnino artibus in illa oppugnanda utuntur, quibus istos usos fuisse legimus. Nam concilia indicunt, ut publica authoritate rem transfigant. Deinde priuatis commodis publicam salutem praetexunt, imò zelum gloriae Dei fingunt, qui ipsos ad consilia sanguinaria excitet. Et noti sunt illorum sermones, quibus causam suam palliare & exornare confuserunt. Sed neminē ista offendere debent, quasi noua sint & insolita, cum olim eadem facta sint. Quin potius cōsoletur nos, quod istos et si authoritate & potentia praestarent, nō tamē immunes fuisse à metu uidemus: & quidem populum timuerunt, qui potius huic terrori esse debebant. Tam facile est Deo hostibus suis obicem ponere, quando fieri non potest, ut propriae conscientiae terrores effugiant, qui contra Deum & veritatem impia & scelerata temeritate conspirant. Quem uero non timeat, qui seipsum timet, & hostem infensissimum, ceu anguem & serpentem in sinu suo gestat? Cuius in primis meminisse debent, qui Rempub. gubernant, ne authoritatem suam prostituant & labefactent, uel etiam seipsos in pericula & turpem metum coniiciant, dum sua potestate insolentius abutuntur.
units.tr: Now among the authors or ministers of the death of Christ, the first were the chief priests and scribes of the Jews, of whom Luke speaks thus: "And the chief priests and scribes sought how they might take him out of the way." By "sought" he indicates their careful and anxious consultation, which they conducted so that they might kill him by evil stratagem, that is, under some pretext of a plausible crime, or even by treachery. Matthew and Mark also explain this part in the same way. But since it might seem ridiculous that powerful men, weighty in authority, should be so anxious about destroying an obscure and unarmed man, a reason is added: they feared the people. For they saw that all of them depended on him, and they had noticed in his splendid entry into the city, when he was escorted and welcomed with the applause and joyful acclamations of many, a sign or indication of popular favour not to be despised. There was therefore a danger that by attempting something violently they would stir up a sedition, which would have been all the more dangerous because so many were gathering from everywhere for the feast of the Passover. But it might seem strange that they undertook this, when it was their task to bring the people to Christ and to bear public witness concerning him. But we have elsewhere noted that the old order of priests had long before been removed by Herod, and that in their place men of obscure birth and servile, base-minded men had been set up, who afterwards under the Roman governors also turned the sacred office into a matter of sale, so that the temple differed in nothing from the marketplace and the offices of the money-changers. So that this might be done more conveniently, these same men had corrupted the doctrine of the Law with superstitious and foolish, or rather impious, traditions. Such men therefore could not bear the light of truth, and because Christ not only rebuked their tricks and frauds in words, but had already once and again laid hands on them and, not without public disgrace, had cast them out of the temple, they began to take counsel about killing him. How cunningly and wickedly they did this, John the Evangelist relates in chapter eleven, where we have said much that bears on the explanation of this passage too. For now it is enough to have observed that the bitterest enemies of Christ and of the Gospel truth will always be the prelates of the Church, whom ambition and avarice have blinded, so that they make a profit out of religion and dare to foist their own inventions in place of the Word of God. Many examples of this kind have been put forth in all ages, and there has always been a contest between true wisdom and false and hypocritical wisdom. Nor should we hope for a better lot today, as is clear from the prophecies of Christ and the Apostles, which they delivered concerning the last times. For just as those who hold the primacy in the Church are the most savage enemies of sound doctrine, so they use exactly the same arts to assail it that we read those men used. For they call councils so that they may settle the matter by public authority. Then they put forward public safety as a pretext for their private advantages, and even feign zeal for the glory of God, which stirs them to bloody counsels. And the speeches of those men are well known, by which they struggled to cloak and adorn their cause. But these things ought not to offend anyone, as if they were new and unusual, since the same things have happened before. Rather, let this console us: although those men excelled in authority and power, we see that they were not free from fear, and indeed they feared the people, who ought rather to have been a source of terror to them. So easily does God set an obstacle before his enemies, since it cannot happen that those who conspire against God and truth with impious and wicked rashness escape the terrors of their own conscience. And who will not fear him who fears himself, and carries within his bosom an enemy most hostile, like a snake and a serpent? Those who govern the commonwealth ought above all to remember this, lest they prostitute and weaken their authority, or even thrust themselves into danger and shameful fear, while they abuse their power too insolently.

units.la: Porro Sacerdotibus Iudas coiungitur, qui se illorum concilijs ducem praebuit, de quo Lucas haec tradit: Introijt autem Satanas in Iudam cognominatum Iscariotem, qui erat unus e numero duodecim. Qui abiens collocutus est cum principibus Sacerdotum ac praefectis templo, quomodo ipsis eum me traderet. Qui gauisi sunt, & pacti sunt se daturos ei pecuniam: & ipse spopondit, quaerebatq; opportunitatem, ut traderet eum ipsis absq; turba. Primum persona Iudae describitur, in qua descriptione praecipuum est, quod ex duodecim discipulorum numero fuit, quos Christus in eum finem selegerat, ut tanquam domestici testes essent doctrinae & miraculorum eius, mortis item atq; resurrectionis: quorum deniq; opera Euangelium per totum orbem terrarum praedicaretur, Iscariote uero dicunt Euangelistae, nimirum à patria aut natali solo, ut ab altero Iuda distinguant, quem Lebbaeū et Thaddaeū cognominatum fuisse scimus. Numeratur autem prior ille semper inter illos, qui iampridem emissi fuerant ad praedicandum, & qui in nomine Christi miracula multa et praeclara fecerant. Est hoc obseruandum, ut discamus, nullum hominum ordinem per omnia sanctum esse, ut nullus in illo naeuus, nullaue labes aut macula appareat. Quod enim huic sanctissimo choro accidit, quae Dei Filius peculiari studio & diligentia ex uniuerso genere humano sibi ceu peculium quoddam elegerat: hoc ipsum multis alijs accidisse scimus. Nam ut nihil dicamus de tota Israelitarum gente, quae etsi populus sanctus & regnum Sacerdotale dicatur, murmuratores tamen & rebelles & defectores habuit, qui aduersus Dei seruos hostiliter insurrexerunt: quis nescit, inter Iacobi filios fuisse, qui à patria virtute turpissime degenerarunt? & Dauidis posteros, ex quibus Dei Filius homo nasci debuit, nō paucos sceleribus atrocissimis laborauisse? Quid uero de primitiua Ecclesia dicemus, quae ut contentionibus & rixis exagitata est: ita Ananiam & Sapphiram aliosq; impios hypocritas habuit? Nemo igitur hodie offendatur, si eiusmodi pestes in Ecclesia conspiciat. Clamant quidē Anabaptistae Ecclesiam Christi ab Apostolo describi, ut quae sit absq; ruga & macula: & quia passim multos suae professioni minus respondere uident, mox Ecclesias damnant, & secessione facta nouā Ecclesiam ipsi cōstituere uolunt: quae temeritas hodie multis in locis grauissimorū motuū atq; turbarum causa fuit, quibus Ecclesiae non omnino male cōstitutae, subito euersae, aut priusquam constituerentur, in ipsa herba (quod aiunt) oppressae sunt: quod olim quoq; Donatistis ubiq; tumultuantibus factum esse, historici docent. Falluntur autem infelices illi, quòd homines dum in carne hac peccatrice & mortali uiuunt,
units.tr: Next to the priests is joined Judas, who made himself a leader for their councils. Of him Luke relates this: "And Satan entered into Judas, surnamed Iscariot, who was one of the twelve. He went away and conferred with the chief priests and the captains of the temple about how he might deliver him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money; and he promised, and sought an opportunity to betray him to them without a crowd." First, the person of Judas is described, and the principal thing in this description is that he was one of the number of the twelve disciples, whom Christ had chosen for this end, that as intimate witnesses they might be of his teaching and miracles, and likewise of his death and resurrection, and that through their work the Gospel might at last be preached throughout the whole world. The Evangelists call him Iscariot, no doubt to distinguish him from the other Judas, whom we know was surnamed Lebbaeus and Thaddaeus, from his homeland or birthplace. But that former man is always counted among those who had long before been sent out to preach, and who had done many notable miracles in the name of Christ. This ought to be observed, so that we may learn that no order of men is holy in every respect, so that no blemish, no stain or spot appears in it. For what happened to this most holy company, which the Son of God, with special zeal and care, had chosen for himself as a peculiar treasure out of the whole human race, we know has happened to many others as well.
