For, to say nothing of the whole nation of the Israelites, which, although it is called a holy people and a kingdom of priests, nevertheless had murmurers and rebels and deserters, who rose up with hostility against the servants of God: who does not know that among the sons of Jacob there were some who most shamefully degenerated from their father's virtue? And that not a few of the posterity of David, from whom the Son of God was to be born as man, laboured under most atrocious crimes? And what shall we say of the primitive Church, which was harassed by quarrels and strife, and yet had Ananias and Sapphira and other impious hypocrites? Therefore let no one today be offended if he sees such pests in the Church. The Anabaptists indeed cry out that the Church of Christ is described by the Apostle as being without spot or wrinkle; and because they see that many everywhere answer less well to their profession, at once they condemn the churches, and, making a secession, they wish to set up a new church of their own. This rashness has today been the cause of very serious disturbances and tumults in many places, by which churches that were not wholly ill-constituted have been suddenly overthrown, or, before they were established, have been crushed in the very grass (as they say). Historians teach that this was also done in the past, when the Donatists were raising tumults everywhere. But those unhappy men are mistaken in thinking that men, while they live in this sinful and mortal flesh, can attain to that perfection

units.la: ad eam perfectione peruenire posse arbitrantur, quam tunc demum attingemus, quando cum carne affectus quoq; deponere dabitur: item quod ad hominum opera et mores id restringunt, quod nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia imputatur. Etenim Ecclesia sine ruga & macula esse Paulus scribit, nõ quòd nos tales simus, sed quòd Deus pro talibus agnoscit eos, quos Filius eius Iesus Christus suo sanguine abluit, & qui huic per fidem insiti, eiusdem iustitiam induerunt. Itaq; neminem fanaticorum istorum intemperies moueat, qui dum omnes damnant, ipsi ferè scelere omnium atrocissimo se fe polluunt, cum Ecclesiam scindant, cuius unitatem Deus Filij sui morte instaurari voluit, & cuius uniculum est Spiritus Christi, qui & fidem & vitam eandem omnibus membris largitur. Quod autem de Ecclesia dicimus, id ad omnes hominum ordines & ad omnia vitae genera extendi debet: ne propter aliquos, qui officium non faciunt, ea damnemus, quae Deus bene instituit, et sine quibus vita haec non potest consistere. Peccant in eo, qui magistratum abolendum esse clamant, quòd multos sub hoc praetextu tyrannidem exercere uident: quòd item coniugiū damnant, quia pleriq; illo turpissime ab utuntur, aut etiam rixis quotidianis fatigantur. Atqui haec non magistratus & coniugij vitia sunt, sed hominum, qui Dei ordinem atq; voluntatem non observant. Quid uero iniquius est, quàm sapientissimū illum opificem propter eos reprehendere, qui eius operibus atq; institutis abutuntur pro sua libidine? Quin potius meminisse nos decet, quòd ut undecim discipulis non fraudi fuit proditoria Iudae improbitas: ita nemo pius damnari aut reprehendi debet propter vitae genus per se honestum, eò quòd alij in illo petulantiores sunt, & praeter officium multa faciunt.
units.tr: They suppose that a man in this mortal and sinful flesh can attain to that perfection which we shall reach only when we are finally given to lay aside the flesh with its affections. They also restrict to human works and conduct what is imputed to us from God's free mercy. For Paul writes that the Church is without spot or wrinkle, not because we are such, but because God acknowledges as such those whom his Son Jesus Christ has washed with his blood, and who, grafted into him by faith, have put on his righteousness. Let the intemperance of those fanatics not move anyone. While they condemn everyone, they themselves defile themselves with almost the most atrocious of all crimes, since they rend the Church, whose unity God willed to be restored by the death of his Son, and whose one bond is the Spirit of Christ, who bestows the same faith and life on all its members. But what we say about the Church must be extended to all orders of men and all kinds of life. We must not condemn, because of some who fail in their duty, those things which God has well ordained and without which this life cannot stand. They err who cry out that the magistracy must be abolished because they see many exercising tyranny under this pretext. Likewise they condemn marriage because many abuse it most shamefully, or are worn down by daily quarrels. Yet these are not faults of the magistracy or of marriage, but of men who do not observe God's order and will. What is more unjust than to blame that most wise Maker for those who abuse his works and institutions to suit their own lust? Rather we should remember that, just as the treacherous wickedness of Judas did not harm the eleven disciples, so no godly man ought to be condemned or censured because of a way of life that is honourable in itself, merely because others in it are more wanton and do many things beyond their duty.

units.la: At miretur aliquis, quae causa Iudam impulerit, ut ad tantum scelus animum appelleret? Sed Lucam audiamus, qui rem omne uno uerbo expedit dicens: Introijt Satanas in Iudam. Quod Ioan nes sic exponit: Cùm diabolus iam immisisset in cor Iudae Simonis Iscariotae, ut eum proderet. Satan ergo sive diabolus in eum introiuisse dicitur, quòd ipse illius suggestioni malae & impiae locum dedit. Qua autem ratione & quo ordine id factum sit, idem Ioannes duodecimo capite describit. Accendit in eo diabolus avaritiae cupiditatem & immoderatum suis rebus consulendi studium. Eo superatus furari coepit, & sacrilego ausu surripuit multa, quae à pijs Christi auditoribus conferebantur. Quod cùm aliquandiu occultius fecisset, neq; praeterea aliquid hostilius aduersus illū esset molitus, tandem in Coena, qua Simon quidam, cuius Bethaniensis, Christum excepit, noua occasio oblata animū auarum & insatiabilem exacerbauit, ut quasi atroci iniuria affectus esset, animū hostile induceret. Vbi multa concurrunt obseruatu dignissima, quae nunc consulto omittimus, eò quòd de illis in Marci & Ioannis expositione dixerimus.
units.tr: But someone may wonder what cause impelled Judas to direct his mind to so great a crime. Let us hear Luke, who explains the whole matter in one word, saying: "Satan entered into Judas." John expounds it thus: "When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him." Satan, or the devil, is therefore said to have entered into him because Judas himself gave place to that evil and impious suggestion. But John describes in the twelfth chapter by what means and in what order this happened. The devil kindled in him a desire for avarice and an immoderate zeal for looking after his own affairs. Overcome by this, he began to steal, and with sacrilegious daring he took away many of the gifts that were brought to Christ's godly hearers. Since he had done this rather secretly for some time, and had not yet attempted anything more hostile against him, at last at the supper which Simon of Bethany, in whose house Christ was received, gave, a new occasion was offered. This roused his greedy and insatiable mind, so that, as if he had been wronged in some atrocious way, he conceived a hostile purpose. Many things here are very worthy of notice, but we now deliberately pass them over, since we have discussed them in our exposition of Mark and John.

units.la: Nunc autē singularem consideratione meretur, quòd Satan, qui antiquus humani generis hostis & exitij nostri communis unicus author est, redemptionem & salutē nostram promouit, adeoq; huius minister factus est, dum Iudā accendit, ut Christum hostibus prodat. Fecit hoc quidē Iudae perdendi studio, & odio Christi, quo Sacerdotes quoq; et Scribas antea in rabiē illam impijssimā adduxerat. Sed dū paucos perdere conatur, plures seruat: imò (ut in prima salutis promissione habetur) dum in cautius in Christi calcaneum ruit, ut homine perdat, quem ille induerat, proprium caput ictui illi fatali subijcit, quo totū conculcari, et regnū eius euerti debebat. Est hoc memorabile et multa admiratione dignissimū opus diuinae prouidentiae, qua non bonis modò Angelis uerumetiā malis utitur ad ea perficienda, quae gloriae Dei & hominū saluti seruiunt. Et huius generis multa quotidie fiunt, ut Regnum Iesu Christi furiosis & impijs illorum machinationibus promoueatur, qui in eius excidiū conspirauerunt. Ita uero nõ solum in medio inimicorū suorum ille dominatur et regnat, uerumetiam eorundē opera & ministerio multa perficit, quae uix alia ratione fieri posse uidebantur. Horum consideratio ut nos consolari debet, ne impiorū conatibus facile terreamur: ita moneat simul omnes homines, ne suis cupiditatibus, quibus illos Satan accendit, indulgeant. Nam ut Iudas illius furijs abreptus seipsum perdidit, dum Christum ulcisci uult: ita omnes illi sibijpsis exitium accersunt, qui diaboli suggestiones admittunt, & effrenes ruunt quò eos animi libido rapit.
units.tr: Now, however, one thing deserves special attention: that Satan, the ancient enemy of the human race and the sole common author of our ruin, furthered our redemption and salvation, and so became the minister of this very thing, when he inflamed Judas to betray Christ to his enemies. He did this indeed from a desire to destroy Judas and from hatred of Christ, to which he had earlier driven the priests and scribes into that most impious rage. But while he tries to destroy a few, he preserves many. Indeed, as is stated in the first promise of salvation, while he rushes too rashly against the heel of Christ, in order to destroy the man whom Christ had put on, he exposes his own head to that deadly blow by which he himself was to be trodden down and his kingdom overthrown. This is a memorable work of divine providence, and one most worthy of great admiration, by which God makes use not only of good angels but also of evil ones to accomplish those things which serve the glory of God and the salvation of men. Many things of this kind happen every day, so that the kingdom of Jesus Christ is advanced by the furious and impious machinations of those who conspired for its destruction. Thus indeed he not only reigns and rules in the midst of his enemies, but also by their work and ministry accomplishes many things which seemed scarcely able to be done in any other way. Consideration of these things ought to console us, so that we are not easily terrified by the attempts of the wicked. At the same time it warns all men not to indulge their lusts, by which Satan inflames them. For just as Judas, carried off by his fury, destroyed himself while he wished to avenge Christ, so all those who admit the devil's suggestions and rush headlong wherever the lust of their minds carries them bring ruin upon themselves.

units.la: Caeterum uideamus, ut causam hanc Iudas infelix egerit. Primū accedit ad principes Sacer- dotū & praefectos templi, & cum illis colloquitur. Quod ut faceret in causa fuit, quòd capitales Christi hostes esse iampridem intellexisset. Nec difficile fuit homine obscurum & prius plerisq; exosum propter doctrina Christi professionem, se ingerere in illorum colloquium, qui authoritate omnibus alijs præstabant. Nam ut nihil non audent impij, qui cum Dei timore pudorem quoq; omnem abijciunt: ita omnes facile admittūt, quorum operam ad veritatis oppressionem sibi utilem fore putant. Quæ causa est, quòd turpissimi transfugæ & patrij soli proditores apud Reges potentissimos in pretio sunt, quodq; Episcopos & Abbates, qui toti Spirituales dici volunt, non pudet cum gregarijs militibus aut quibuslibet aliis consilia sua conferre, quos omnia venalia habere nouerunt. Neq; dubium est iucundissimum Sacerdotibus istis fuisse aduentum Iudæ: quia facilem eius conficiendi rationem sponte ipsis offerebat, quod ipsis facta grave & periculosum videbatur. Nam ut Matthæus annotauit, non minori cum impudentia quam impietate illis dixit: Quid vultis mihi dare, & ego eum vobis tradam? Quasi diceret: Videor vos de illo comprehendendo solicitos esse, & populi ad tumultus proclivis furoribus terreri: sed solicitudine ista minime opus est, siquidem mea opera uti libeat, quam ego vobis offero, & mercede mediocri contentus remissam absq; periculo vobis effectā dabo. Dicite modo, quid nam daturi sitis, et quid præmij ex vobis sperare debeam. Quo loco quid potissimum admirer, uix video: Impudentiam ne aut impietatem cum scelerata acceptorū beneficiorum & dulcissimæ consuetudinis obliuione coniunctam. Quid enim impudentius fieri poterat, quàm se ad scelus immanissimum sponte offerre, quod communi consensu omnes homines detestantur? adeò ut ne ipsi quidem proditores proditionis insimulari velint, & plerunq; illis ipsis inuisi sint, qui ipsorū opera utuntur. Notum enim est illud Augusti Cæsaris de Rimetalco Thrace, qui ab Antonio ad ipsum transierat: Proditionem amo, proditorem uero ipsum nō laudo. Et Aurelianus Heraclemonem quendam, qui patriam Thyanam ipsi prodiderat, occidi iussit, dicens, se proditorē amare non posse. Quid, quod in iure ciuili proditoribus & transfugis summum (ut uocant) supplicium constituitur: ut nimirum uiui exurantur? Antiquitus ijdem equis alligari, & his in diuersas partes adactis crudeliter discerpi solebant. Hodie in quatuor partes dissecantur. Fuit ergo hic diabolicus quidam furor, qui Iudam impulit, ut tam immani impudentia se præberet ad prodendum Christum, à quo nulla unquam injuria læsus fuerat. Quàm uero cæca fuit illa rabies, qua agitatus ipsorū arbitrio permittit quid dandum esse putent? Et cum ipsos in re maximi momenti non admodum liberales uideret, non tamen pedem refert, sed triginta denarijs (quod precium nō excedit quatuor florenos Germanicos aut libras Gallicas sex) se conduci patitur ad facinus, quo nullum scelestius atq; atrocius sol uidit unquam. Est hoc horribile exemplum, quo docemur, quanta auaritiæ vis sit, & quàm uere olim Moses dixerit, muneribus sapientum quoq; oculos excæcari. Possent huius generis multa referri, sed quia quoti die fiunt, proh dolor, quæ istis fidem faciunt, veterum commemoratione nequaquam est opus. Etenim si uerum fateri libeat, hæc præcipua malorū omnium, quibus hic mundus exagitatur, causa est, quòd ista Iudæ quæstio, QVID DABITVR MIHI? ubiq; regnat. Auditur hæc inter eos qui ad rem publicā aspirant. Eadē tractatur inter iudices, aduocatos & causidicos. In sponsalibus quoq; primū locum obtinet. Et utinam non in Ecclesia quoque inter ministros subinde repeteretur. In Scholis certè ita obtinuit, ut si hanc mouentibus illarum præfectis atq; rectoribus satisfeceris, mox ex stupidissimis asinis, exebriosis porcis, ex canibus rixatoribus & turpissimis quibuscunq; bestijs Magistros & Doctores creari uidebis, Metamorphosi plus quam Ouidiana. Hinc ergo fit, ut probitas, fides, pietas procul à Republica & Ecclesia exulent, & passim ferè Christus quoq; aut prodatur, aut saltem negligatur, dum omnes non nisi suum commodum siue quæstum quærunt, &c.
units.tr: But let us see how that unhappy Judas carried out this business. First he goes to the chief priests and the officers of the temple and confers with them. He was moved to do this because he had long understood that they were Christ's mortal enemies. Nor was it difficult for a man who was obscure, and who had previously been hated by most people because he professed the teaching of Christ, to thrust himself into the company of those who excelled all others in authority. For just as the wicked dare anything, and cast off all shame along with the fear of God, so they readily admit all those whose service they think will be useful to them for suppressing the truth. This is why the most shameful deserters and traitors to their own country are held in high esteem by the most powerful kings, and why bishops and abbots, who wish to be called wholly spiritual, are not ashamed to confer their plans with common soldiers or with any others whom they know to be ready to sell everything. Nor is there any doubt that the coming of Judas was most welcome to those priests, because he freely offered them an easy way of carrying out what seemed to them difficult and dangerous. For, as Matthew notes, he spoke to them with no less shamelessness than impiety: "What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you?" As if he were saying: "I see that you are anxious about arresting him, and that you are afraid of the people, who are prone to tumults. But there is no need for such anxiety, if you are willing to use my services, which I offer you. Content with a modest reward, I will hand him over to you, a thing already done and free from danger. Only tell me what you are going to give, and what reward I may hope to receive from you." At this point I scarcely know what I should most wonder at: the shamelessness or the impiety, joined with a wicked forgetting of the benefits he had received and of the most pleasant familiarity. For what could be more shameless than to offer himself willingly for the most monstrous crime, one which all men with common consent detest? So much so that even traitors themselves do not wish to be charged with treachery, and are often hated by those very men who make use of their services. For that saying of Augustus Caesar about Rhymetalces the Thracian, who had gone over to him from Antony, is well known: "I love treachery, but I do not praise the traitor himself." And Aurelian ordered a certain Heraclemon, who had betrayed his native city of Thyana to him, to be put to death, saying that he could not love a traitor. What of the fact that in the civil law the highest punishment (as they call it) is set for traitors and deserters, namely that they be burnt alive? In ancient times they were accustomed to be tied to horses and cruelly torn apart as the horses were driven in different directions. Today they are cut into four parts. So it was a certain diabolical frenzy that drove Judas to show himself, with such monstrous shamelessness, ready to betray Christ, by whom he had never been wronged in any way. And how blind was that madness by which, driven by it, he left it to them to decide what they thought should be given him! And seeing that they were not very generous in a matter of the greatest moment, he nevertheless did not draw back, but allowed himself to be hired for thirty pieces of silver (a sum not exceeding four German florins or six French pounds) for a deed than which the sun has never seen anything more wicked and atrocious. This is a horrible example, by which we are taught how great is the power of avarice, and how truly Moses once said that the eyes even of the wise are blinded by gifts. Many examples of this kind could be related, but since they happen every day, alas, to those who make these things credible, there is by no means any need to recall the ancients. Indeed, if we are willing to speak the truth, this is the chief cause of all the evils by which this world is harassed: that this question of Judas, WHAT WILL BE GIVEN TO ME?, reigns everywhere. It is heard among those who aspire to public office. The same question is pursued among judges, advocates and pleaders. It holds the first place even in betrothals. And would that it were not repeated from time to time in the Church too, among ministers. In the schools, certainly, it has so prevailed that if you satisfy this question for those who preside over and govern them, you will soon see masters and teachers created out of the most stupid asses, drunken swine, quarrelsome dogs and all sorts of the most vile beasts, a metamorphosis more than Ovidian. Hence it comes about that uprightness, faithfulness and piety are banished far from the commonwealth and the Church, and everywhere Christ himself is either betrayed or at least neglected, while all men seek only their own advantage or gain, and so on.

units.la: Marcus Euangelista Sacerdotes audito Iuda gauisos esse scribit, & ipse postquā illi pecuniā se daturos esse pacti sunt, mox omnia dispicere cœpit, & opportunitatem quæsiuit, qua Dominum absq; publici motus periculo proderet. Solet enim auaritia & impietas alacres & industrios facere, & ut demus nullius laboris & studij pigere eos, qui aduersus veritatem conspirauerunt, cum fere ignauissimi sint & nimium frigidi, qui illius discipulos se profitentur. Priuatim quoque nihil non faciunt homines, ut cupiditatibus pessimis indulgeant, quibus nimium uidetur quicquid pro veritate & salute publica facere debet. In præsenti tamē obseruabis, gauisos quidem fuisse Sacerdotes, & Iudam quoq; sibi lucri exhilaratū tanta industria rem gessisse: sed gaudiū istud fuisse momentaneū, Iudæ uero alacritatem non multò post in desperationē desijsse. Qui enim nunc pretio iniquitatis proditorem conducunt, cuius opera Christum intercipiant, ijdem postea eiusdem resurrectione territi militū linguas redimere coguntur, ut illum furto sublatum esse mentiantur. Accidit hoc multis olim, qui Ecclesiam clesiam crudeliter persecuti sunt: & nostro seculo multos subito infelicissimos factos fuisse vidimus, qui ex piorum sanguine voluptatem coeperunt. Eadem est eorum fors, qui ex usuris, ex militia mercenaria, caedibus & rapinis ditescunt. Ut autem Christus Iesus unus idemque est semper, nec cuillis tyrannorum aut Satanae conatibus vinci vel opprimi potest: ita gaudio vero & aeterno recreabuntur, quotquot in illo constantes per huius vitae pericula atque miserias eluctantur, & in eo spem salutis omnem reponunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Mark the evangelist writes that the priests rejoiced when they heard about Judas, and he himself, once they had agreed to give him money, at once began to examine everything and sought an opportunity by which he might betray the Lord without danger of public disturbance. For greed and impiety usually make men eager and diligent, and (to put it plainly) those who have conspired against the truth are never sorry for any labour or pains, whereas those who profess themselves his disciples are for the most part very lazy and far too cold. Men also, in private life, do nothing that they would not do to indulge their worst desires, for whom whatever ought to be done for the truth and the public good seems to be too much. Yet in the present case you will observe that the priests did indeed rejoice, and that Judas, cheered by his gain, carried out the business with such diligence; but that joy was short-lived, and Judas's eagerness soon ended in despair. For those who now hire a betrayer for the price of wickedness, through whose work they may seize Christ, are afterwards terrified by his resurrection and are forced to buy off the soldiers' tongues, so that they may lie that he was stolen away. This happened long ago to many who cruelly persecuted the Church, and in our own age we have seen many who began to take pleasure in the blood of the godly suddenly become most unhappy. The same fate awaits those who grow rich by usury, by mercenary soldiering, by murders and by plunder. But as Christ Jesus is one and the same always, and cannot be conquered or overwhelmed by the attempts of tyrants or of Satan, so all who struggle on in him through the dangers and miseries of this life, and place in him all their hope of salvation, will be refreshed with true and eternal joy. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCII.
units.tr: HOMILY 192.

units.la: Venit autem dies azymorum, qua oportebat macari pascha. Et misit Petrum ac Ioannem, dicens: Proficiscimini parate nobis Pascha, ut vescamur. Ipsi vero dixerunt ei: Ubi vis paremus illud? At ille dixit eis: Ecce postquam introieritis in urbem, occurret vobis quidam aquae amphoram baiulans: sequimini eum in domum, in quam ingredietur, & dicite patrifamilias aedium: Dicit tibi magister, ubi est diversorium, ubi pascha cum discipulis meis edam? Tunc ipse ostendet vobis coenaculum magnum stratum: illic parate. Profecti autem invenerunt omnia prout dixerat eis: & paraverunt pascha.
units.tr: Then came the day of unleavened bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, "Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it." They asked him, "Where do you want us to prepare it?" He said to them, "Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters, and say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' He will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there." So they went and found everything just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

units.la: Quoniam Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, propter nos dirum & infame mortis supplicium subire voluit, ut huius merito peccata nostra expiaret, & nos ex morte aeterna redimeret: in eo summul diligentissimus fuit, ut scandala removeret, quae ex eius cruce & morte apud homines imperitos atque infirmos enasci poterant. Et huc pertinet, quod de omnibus, quae ipsi eventura erant, frequenter apud suos discipulos disseruit, & tunc quoque praeclara edidit divinae virtutis exempla, quando iam extreme humiliari atque deprimi debebat. Ex illis enim colligi potest, eum non hostium vi superatum aut extinctum, sed ideo mortuum fuisse, quia mori voluit: quod apud Ioannem his verbis testatur: Pater diligit me, quia ego pono animam meam, ut rursus sumam eam: Nemo tollit eam a me, sed ego pono eam a meipso: Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus sumendi eam. Idue rò huius loci narratio evidentissime probat, in qua ultimae Coenae praeparatio ita describitur, ut vel caecus videre possit, illum nihil horum latuisse, quae ipsi urbem ingresso eventura erant, & eundem simul in hominum mentes ius & imperium habuisse, ut pro sua voluntate illas inclinare & flectere potuerit. In quorum tractatione ita nobis versandum est, ut meminerimus, nos quoque voluntarios & spontaneos esse debere in iis ferendis, quae nobis a Deo imponuntur: animumque vero nobis addat, quod Christus, qui suo exemplo nobis praeiuit, nos quoque & omnia nostra novit, neque nobis quicquam fortuitum accidere, neque nos supra vires tentari patietur. Quia vero in hanc historiam multa in Marco nostro diximus, nunc pleraque breviter perstrinxisse sufficiet.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, Jesus Christ, chose to undergo for our sake the dreadful and shameful punishment of death, so that by its merit he might expiate our sins and redeem us from eternal death, he took great care above all to remove the stumbling-blocks that could arise among ignorant and weak people from his cross and death. To this belongs the fact that he often spoke to his disciples about all the things that were to happen to him, and that even then, when he was about to be brought very low and humbled, he gave outstanding examples of divine power. From these it can be gathered that he was not overcome and put to death by the force of his enemies, but died because he willed to die, as he bears witness in John with these words: "The Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again." The narrative of this passage also proves this most clearly, in which the preparation of the last supper is described in such a way that even a blind man could see that nothing that was to happen to him when he entered the city was hidden from him, and that at the same time he had authority and rule over men's minds, so that he could incline and turn them according to his will. In treating these things we must keep in mind that we too ought to be willing and spontaneous in bearing what God lays upon us; and it should encourage us that Christ, who went before us in his example, knows us and all our affairs, and will allow nothing to happen to us by chance, nor will he allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. But since we have said much about this history in our treatment of Mark, it will now suffice to touch briefly on most points.

units.la: Rursus autem a temporis paschalis notatione Lucas orditur, quia sub illo mysterium nostrae redemptionis latet, ut nuper est dictum. Venit (inquit) dies azymorum, qua oportebat macari pascha. Loquitur autem de prima die azymorum, qui apud Matthaeum diserte nominatur, & decimus quartus erat mensis primi (qui nostro Martio respondet) quo agnum paschalem macta re & edere Moses iusserat, sicuti in Exodi capite duodecimo est videre. Admonet ergo nos haec temporis consignatio, Christum in illo etiam Legem Patris sui observasse, quam Iudaeis suis traditionibus corruperant, cum epulum illud in sequentem diem transtulissent ob Sabbati religionem. Quod ideo monuimus, ut videas superuacaneas esse eorum disputationes, qui nodum in scirpo quaerentes, quaestionem movent, cur sua hac Coena Dominus Iudaeos anteuerterit. Cogitur isti ad nescio quae mysteria confugere, quae ex Thalmudicis cloacis magno studio eruere satagunt, & dum circa illa occupantur, praeclarum illud Christi exemplum non observant, qui procul relictis aliorum superstitionibus, ea die & hora pascha suum comedit, quam Deus in Lege constituerat. Et videtur hoc Lucas non omnino obscure innuere, quando ait: Venit autem dies azymorum qua oportebat macari pascha. Quasi diceret: Instabat iam vespera illa, quae primae diei azymorum initium erat (scimus enim Hebraeos diem a vespera inchoare contra Romanorum morem, qui Solis exortum diei initium faciunt) quando agnus ille paschalis ex Legis praescripto occidi & comedi debebat, ideoque illum Dominus absque mora parati curavit, nihil eos moratus, qui patrum superstitiones secuti secus faciebant.
units.tr: Again, Luke begins with the note of the time of the Passover, because the mystery of our redemption lies hidden in it, as was said a little while ago. "Then came," he says, "the day of unleavened bread, on which the Passover had to be sacrificed." He speaks of the first day of unleavened bread, which is expressly named in Matthew, and it was the fourteenth day of the first month (which corresponds to our March), on which Moses had commanded that the Passover lamb be slaughtered and eaten, as may be seen in Exodus chapter 12. This note of time therefore reminds us that Christ also observed in this the Law of his Father, which the Jews had corrupted by their traditions, when they had transferred that feast to the following day for the sake of the observance of the Sabbath. We mention this so that you may see how superfluous are the disputes of those who, seeking a knot in a rush, raise the question why the Lord anticipated the Jews in his own supper. They are forced to flee to I know not what mysteries, which they labour hard to dig out of the Talmudic sewers, and while they are busy with these things they do not observe that outstanding example of Christ, who, leaving far behind the superstitions of others, ate his Passover on the day and at the hour that God had appointed in the Law. Luke seems to hint at this not obscurely when he says, "Then came the day of unleavened bread, on which the Passover had to be sacrificed." As if he said: That evening was now at hand, which was the beginning of the first day of unleavened bread (for we know that the Hebrews begin the day from evening, contrary to the custom of the Romans, who make the rising of the sun the beginning of the day), when that Passover lamb had to be killed and eaten according to the prescription of the Law; and therefore the Lord arranged for it to be prepared without delay, not hindered by those who, following the superstitions of the fathers, acted otherwise.

units.la: Quo loco diligenter observari debet Christi exemplum, qui Sacramentis & ritibus in Lege traditis ita usus est, ut nihil eorum neglexerit, quæ à Patre mandata fuerunt. Nā & circuncisus est, & postea baptizatus quoq;, cùm neq; circuncisione neq; baptismo opus haberet. Dies ite festos diligenter coluit, & ad publica sacra non sine periculo Hierosolymā profectus est. Et nunc ne imminentis quidem mortis periculo terretur, quò minus Pascha celebret et loco et tempore, quæ diuinitus constituta erant. Quia enim hominem verù assumpserat, et nos à iugo ceremoniarum legalium liberare debebat, nihil eorum praetermisit, quæ & hominem & seruatorē humani generis decebant. Suo autem exemplo Sacramentorum & ministerij sacri contemptores arguit, in quorum numero non solum prophani illi censentur, qui cum Deo cœlos & inferos negant, aut saltem ridentur: verumetiā hypocritæ, qui ut gratiā Dei & Christi merito omnem nostrae salutis laudē uendicent, tam verbi praedicatione quam Sacramentorum usum pro superuacaneis & inutilibus habent, et ideo neq; ex se natos baptizari curant, neq; ipsi ad mensam Domini accedunt, adhæc à coetibus sacris prorsus abstinent, perinde ac sine precibus quidem ipsis opus sit. Gloriantur quidem illi fide sua, sed quàm parū adhuc profecerint, ex hoc uno facis apparet, quòd Dei verbum & statuta tam parui faciunt: ut iam nihil dicam de illorum superbia, qua aduersus fidissimos Dei cultores, imò aduersus Dei Filium efferuntur, qui omnes in his diligentissimi fuerunt. Neminem ergo talium hominum siue scurrilitas siue hypocrisis moueat: sed discant singuli gratis animis bonitatem Dei agnoscere, qui eiusmodi subsidijs nostrae imbecillitati subuenire voluit. Simul autē imitemur Christi exemplum, ne latum unguem discedamus ab ea formula doctrinæ et sacrorum, quam nobis Deus tradidit. Noluit ille propter Sacerdotū authoritatē aut receptum in populo Iudaico morem alio tempore pascha edere, quàm quo Deus iusserat. Quantò minus igitur illum ea neglexisse putabimus, quæ maioris erant momenti? Neque superuacaneam putabimus esse hanc diligentiam: quia nisi Dei ordo seruetur, ei adeò non placebimus, ut neq; exercitia illa sacra pro suis agnoscat. Docent hoc Prophetæ, qui & circuncisione & sacrificia cum templo reijciunt, eo quòd illis Iudæi non rite uterentur. Et Paulus Corinth. Cœnam Dominicam edere negabat, eò quòd à primæ institutionis formula, quam Christus nobis tradidit, recessissent. Quid ergo illum hodie dicturū putabimus, si baptismū tot exorcismis, tot gesticulationibus non minus ridiculis quàm inutilibus corruptum, adhæc oleo, sale & sputo fœdatum atq; pollutum cerneret? in Cœna uero locum successisse uideret Missam, quæ & nomen Cœnæ, & omne eius ritum una cum usu uero prorsus aboleuit? Aut num nostros ille probaret, qui fractionem panis ex illa sustulerunt, & primitiuæ Ecclesiæ simplicitatem ceremonijs inutilibus, luxu item & pompis fastuosis prophanant?
units.tr: At this point the example of Christ should be carefully observed, who so used the sacraments and rites handed down in the Law that he neglected none of those things which the Father had commanded. For he was both circumcised and afterwards also baptized, although he had need of neither circumcision nor baptism. He diligently kept the festal days, and went up to Jerusalem for the public sacred feasts not without danger. And now he is not terrified even by the danger of imminent death from celebrating the Passover in the place and at the time that had been divinely appointed. For since he had truly taken upon himself a man, and was to free us from the yoke of the legal ceremonies, he omitted nothing of those things which befitted both man and the Saviour of mankind. By his own example, however, he rebukes the despisers of the sacraments and of the sacred ministry. Among these are counted not only those profane persons who deny, or at least are mocked for denying, heaven and hell along with God, but also hypocrites, who, in order to claim for the grace of God and the merit of Christ all the praise of our salvation, regard both the preaching of the Word and the use of the sacraments as superfluous and useless; and therefore they take no care to have their children baptized, nor do they themselves come to the table of the Lord, and moreover they abstain altogether from the sacred assemblies, as though there were no need of prayers for them. Those people indeed boast of their faith, but how little they have advanced is clear from this one fact, that they make so little of the Word of God and its ordinances. I say nothing now of their pride, by which they rise up against the most faithful worshippers of God, indeed against the Son of God himself, who were all most diligent in these things. Therefore let neither the buffoonery nor the hypocrisy of such men move anyone; rather let each one learn to acknowledge with a grateful mind the goodness of God, who wished to help our weakness with such aids. At the same time let us imitate the example of Christ, and not depart a finger's breadth from that form of doctrine and of the sacred rites which God has delivered to us. He was unwilling, on account of the authority of the priests or the custom received among the Jewish people, to eat the Passover at any time other than that which God had commanded. How much less, then, shall we think that he neglected those things which were of greater weight? Nor shall we think this care superfluous, because unless the order of God is kept, he will not be so pleased with us as to acknowledge those sacred exercises as his own. The Prophets teach this, who reject both circumcision and sacrifices along with the temple, because the Jews did not use them rightly. And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, refused to call it the Lord's Supper, because they had departed from the form of the first institution, which Christ delivered to us. What, then, do we think he would say today, if he saw baptism corrupted by so many exorcisms and so many gestures no less ridiculous than useless, and moreover defiled and polluted with oil, salt and spittle? And if in the Supper he saw the Mass taking the place of the Supper, which has utterly abolished both the name of the Supper, and all its rite together with its true use? Or would he approve of ours, who have removed the breaking of bread from it, and profane the simplicity of the primitive Church with useless ceremonies, and likewise with luxury and showy pomps?

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus, qui ad epulū illud parandum in urbe mittit Petrum & Ioannē, dicens: Profecti parate nobis pascha, ut uescamur. His uero de loco interrogantibus, hunc non sine miraculo indicat. Vbi quærat aliquis, cur istos potius miserit, quàm Iudam, ad quem res ista ex officio pertinere uidebatur, cùm quæstor esset, hæc autē absq; impensis non possent fieri? At noluit posthac eius opera uti Dominus, quem turpem à fide secessione fecisse, & iam cum bostibus suis coniurauisse sciebat. Et suo exemplo docet, ne uel uerbi uel sacrorū mysteriorum dispensatio committatur hominibus indignis, qui fide abnegauerunt, & palam diaboli castra sequuntur. Tulit quidem hypocritā & furem Dominus, & eius ministerio hucusq; usus est, apostatam uero & transfugam siue proditorem ferre non potest, neq; dignum iudicat, per quem conuiuiū illud sacrum præparetur. Quod exemplum utinam obseruarent, qui ad uerbi ministerium quosuis temere admittunt, quorū fides multis dubia est, uel etiam eos, qui non obscuris indicijs sese produnt, quòd à fide alieni, & mysteriorū eius prorsus ignari sint. Intelligent isti olim magno suo malo, quid fit cum Ecclesia Dei ludere, & dilectam Iesu Christi sponsam uanissimis scurris, uel etiam impuris lenonibus committere. Quid uerò de illis dicemus, qui cùm fide in Christum profiteantur, totam tamen fidei atq; religionis causam insidiosis Pontificum Concilijs subijciunt, ut hi de illa pronuntient, qui hostiles animos iam pridē publicè declarauerunt? Meminerint omnes isti, Ecclesiarum et religionis causam apud Deū maioris momenti esse, quàm quæ perfunctoriè tractari, aut perfide hominibus ineptis uel malis committi debeat.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ, who sends Peter and John into the city to prepare that feast, saying, "Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it." When they asked him where, he showed them the place, not without a miracle. Someone may ask why he sent these men rather than Judas, to whom this business seemed to belong by right of office, since he was the treasurer, and these things could not be done without expense. But the Lord did not wish to use his services from then on, since he knew that Judas had shamefully withdrawn from the faith and had already conspired with his enemies. And by his own example he teaches that the dispensing of neither the Word nor the sacred mysteries should be entrusted to unworthy men, who have denied the faith and openly follow the camp of the devil. Indeed the Lord endured a hypocrite and a thief, and made use of his ministry up to that point; but he cannot bear an apostate and deserter, or a traitor, nor does he judge him worthy to be the one through whom that sacred banquet is prepared. Would that those who rashly admit to the ministry of the Word just anyone would observe this example, men whose faith is doubtful to many, or even those who betray by not obscure signs that they are estranged from the faith and wholly ignorant of its mysteries. These men will learn to their great cost, someday, what it means to trifle with the Church of God, and to hand over the beloved bride of Jesus Christ to the most empty buffoons, or even to impure pimps. But what shall we say of those who, while they profess faith in Christ, nevertheless subject the whole cause of the faith and of religion to the deceitful councils of the Pontiffs, so that these men may pronounce concerning it, men who have long since openly declared their hostile spirits? Let all such men remember that the cause of the Churches and of religion is of greater weight before God than that it should be handled carelessly, or be committed faithlessly to foolish or wicked men.

units.la: Viderunt hoc Apostoli, qui ut alibi in eiusmodi negotijs grauiter & diligenter egerunt, ita hic quoq; nō temere ruunt ad id, quod ipsis mandabatur. Sciebant quidem rem sanctam præcipi, & totā urbem epulo huic esse destinatam: ne quid tamen peccent, de loco aut diuersorio quæstionem mouent aliquantò diligentius: Vbi uis (inquiunt) paremus illud? Est hoc non contemnendū obedientiæ uera exem-ra exem. ræ exemplum, qua in primis opus est in ijs, quæ ad Dei cultu faciunt. Nam colí quidem vult Deus, at cultu pro nostro arbitrio institui non vult, sed ut ab ipso præscriptam formulam sequamur præcipit. Ideo repræhenduntur in historia sacra, qui in excelsis sacrificabant, & Prophetæ palàm eos damnant, qui Deum humanis traditionibus colere audent. Nec est, quod ignorantiæ aliquis prætexat. Nam ut suam voluntatem nobis Deus abunde reuelauit, ita si quid nos adhuc latet, id quoq; manifestabitur, siquidem in illius mente & sensu inuestigando seduli fuerimus. Gaudet enim nostro studio Deus, & Christi promissio est: Quærite & inuenietis. Cui illud Apostoli consentit: Si cui deest sapientia, petat ab eo qui dat, Deo nimirū, qui dat omnibus benignè, nec exprobrat, & dabitur ei, Iacob. 1.
units.tr: The Apostles saw this. As elsewhere, in matters of this kind they acted seriously and carefully, and so here too they did not rush blindly into what had been entrusted to them. They knew that a holy thing was being commanded and that the whole city had been set aside for this feast. Yet, so as not to go wrong, they raised the question of the place and lodging with some care: "Where do you want us to prepare it?" This is a true example of obedience, which is especially needed in whatever pertains to the worship of God. For God wishes to be worshipped, but he does not wish worship to be devised at our own discretion; he commands us to follow the form he himself has prescribed. That is why, in sacred history, those who sacrificed on the high places are rebuked, and the Prophets openly condemn those who dare to worship God with human traditions. Nor may anyone plead ignorance as an excuse. For just as God has abundantly revealed his will to us, so if anything is still hidden from us, it too will be made manifest, provided we are diligent in searching out his mind and meaning. God delights in our zeal, and Christ's promise stands: "Seek, and you will find" (Matt. 7). The Apostle agrees: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him" (James 1).

units.la: Facit ad huius promissionis confirmationē præsens historia. Nec enim discipulos de loco quaeren res reijcit Christus, sed illum (ut paulò ante diximus) cum miraculo indicat, ut ad eius iussa capessenda sint alacriores. Ecce (inquit) postquam introieritis in urbem, occurret vobis quida aquæ amphoram baiulans, sequimini eum in domū usq; in quam ingreditur, & dicite patrifamilias, &c. Concurrunt hoc loco duo prorsus diuersa, uel potius contraria, Christi nimirum paupertas, & eiusdē diuina uirtus siue potentia, qua omnibus imperat. Paupertatis enim est, quod domo propria caret. At quid de domo dico, quando ipse fatetur, se non habere quò caput reclinet, & proinde auiculis quoq; & vulpibus esse egentiorem? Et qui nunc in domū alienam diuertit, prius Bethlehemi in stabulo alieno natus, & propter loci incommoditatem in præsepi depositus fuit. Hoc ut sui ergo nos amoris documentum est euidentissimum: ita impiam & nulla uenia dignam mundi huius ingratitudinem arguit, qui & olim suo creatori & redemptori locum negauit, & hodie eundē passim excludit. Potuit saltem olim sub duro Romanorum imperio stabulum inuenire, in quo nasceretur Dei Filius. Potuit in sanguinaria Hierosolymorū urbe hospitium impetrare, in quo cum suis discipulis agnum paschalem ederet, & Cœnam suam mysticā instituerct. At quot urbes, quot regna & populos (de ijs loquor qui illius nomen profitentur) ostendere poteris hodie, in quibus Euangelio eius omnis locus negatur, et ubi Ecclesia, quæ illius corpus est, adeo non patent stabula aut hospitia qualiacunq;, ut ne in syluis quidē tuti sint, qui in illius nomine coeuniunt? Non debet tamen ista ingratitudo atq; crudelitas aliquem offendere. Nā ut hic in extrema egestate uirtutis diuinæ argumentum æ… dit Christus, quo se omnium Dominum esse probat, dum procul absens quæ gerantur uidet, & simul in hominū animis operatur & agit, ut ipsum quantúmuis inuisum principibus tempore cōmodissimo exciperent: ita multò magis hodie ex cœlis omnia intuetur, & in omnium uoluntates ius habet atq; imperium, ut uel inuiti obtemperent eius mandatis, aut saltem nihil axsint aduersus eos, quorum ministerio ipse amplius uti vult. Idem etiam suis in huius vitæ peregrinatione laborantibus, nihil unquā defieri patietur. Curemus modò, ne quid ille in nobis nostra professione indignum uideat, & discipulos hosce imitemur, qui etsi eos multa absterrere poterant, aut saltē moram aliquā ipsis inijcere, mox tamen obediunt, & obedientiæ suæ fructū referunt uberrimū. Nam profecti omnia inueniunt, sicuti ille prædixerat, neq; aliquid obstitit, quò minus exequerentur id quod in mandatis acceperant. Quapropter hoc exemplo confirmati accingamur nos quoq; ad opus Domini, qui piis conatibus nunquā deerit, et suo spiritu reget, ut nostræ vitæ curriculū emensi in cœlesti Hierosolyma omnia ea inueniamus, quæ ille pollicitus est, et quæ suo sanguine nobis meruit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternū. Amen.
units.tr: The present history supports the confirmation of this promise. Christ does not refuse the disciples information about the place; rather, as we said a little earlier, he points it out with a miracle, so that they will take up his commands more eagerly. "Behold," he says, "after you have entered the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters, and say to the master of the house, etc." Two things wholly different, or rather opposite, meet here: Christ's poverty, and his divine power or might, by which he rules over all things. For it belongs to poverty not to have a house of its own. But why speak of a house, when he himself confesses that he has nowhere to lay his head, and so is poorer even than the birds and the foxes? And he who now lodges in another man's house was earlier born in a borrowed stable at Bethlehem and, because of the unsuitability of the place, laid in a manger. This is the clearest proof of his love for us, but it also shows up the impious and utterly unpardonable ingratitude of this world, which once denied room to its Creator and Redeemer and today shuts him out everywhere. At least under the harsh Roman rule a stable could be found in which the Son of God might be born. In the bloodthirsty city of Jerusalem he could obtain a guest-room in which he ate the Passover lamb with his disciples and instituted his mystical Supper. But how many cities, how many kingdoms and peoples (I speak of those who profess his name) could you point to today in which every place is denied to his Gospel, and where the Church, which is his body, is so far from having stables or lodgings of any kind that those who gather in his name are not even safe in the woods? Yet this ingratitude and cruelty should not disturb anyone. For just as here, in utmost poverty, Christ gives a proof of divine power by which he shows himself to be Lord of all, seeing from afar what is happening and at the same time working and acting in men's hearts, so that they received him at the most opportune time, though he was hated by the rulers, so much more today he looks down on all things from heaven and has right and rule over the wills of all, so that even the unwilling obey his commands, or at least they can do nothing against those whose ministry he wishes to use further. He will also never allow anything to be lacking to his people who labour on the pilgrimage of this life. We need only take care that he sees nothing unworthy of our profession in us, and imitate these disciples, who, though many things could have frightened them away or at least put some delay in their way, obeyed at once and reaped the most abundant fruit of their obedience. For having set out, they found everything just as he had foretold, and nothing stood in the way of their carrying out what they had received in command. Therefore, strengthened by this example, let us too set about the work of the Lord, who will never fail pious endeavours and will guide us by his Spirit, so that, having run the course of our life, we may find in the heavenly Jerusalem all those things which he has promised and which he has merited for us by his blood. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIII.

units.la: Et cum adesset tempus illud, discubuit, & duodecim Apostoli cum eo. Et dixit eis: Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha vesci vobiscum, antequam ego patiar. Dico enim vobis, me non amplius comesturum ex eo, quò usq; compleatur in Regno Dei. Et accepto poculo, cū gratias egisset, dixit: Accipite hoc, & partimini vobisipsis. Dico enim vobis, me non bibiturum ex fructu vitis, usq; quò Regnum Dei venerit.
units.tr: And when the hour had come, he sat down, and the twelve apostles with him. And he said to them, "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you, I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." And when he had taken the cup and given thanks, he said, "Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I say to you, I will not drink from the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes."

units.la: Lvcas Euāgelista passionis ac mortis Dominicæ historiā ab epulo Paschali exorditur, quod potstremū fuit Iesu Christi, priusquam moreretur, in terris hisce conuiuiū. Ideo autē illud præmittitur, quia fructū mortis Christi adumbrat, & hunc docet esse agnum illum Dei, qui tollit peccatum. mundi: simul uero Cœnam mysticam illustrat, quam ille paschatis loco substituit in suæ mortis com memorationem. Quia autem mos & ritus epuli illius veteris vulgo notissimus fuit, & quæ ad eius cognitionem pertinent, ex Mose peti possunt, nō multum in illo immorantur Euangelistæ, sed paucis annotant, Christū illud cum suis discipulis comedisse, ut hanc etiā Legis partē impleret, & suo exemplo Sacramentorum usum nobis cōmendaret, sicuti in proximo sermone diximus. In præsenti tamen Lucas primum actum Cœnæ illius describit, quo aliqua continentur, quæ non parum faciunt ad fidei & vitæ nostræ institutionem.
units.tr: Luke the evangelist begins the account of the Lord's passion and death with the Passover meal, which was the last feast Jesus Christ shared on earth before he died. He places this first because it foreshadows the fruit of Christ's death, and teaches that he is that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. At the same time it sets out the mystical Supper, which he put in the place of the Passover, in remembrance of his death. Since the custom and rite of that ancient feast were very well known to the people, and what pertains to understanding it can be drawn from Moses, the evangelists do not dwell on it at length. They note briefly that Christ ate it with his disciples, so that he might fulfil this part of the Law too, and by his example commend to us the use of the sacraments, as we said in the previous sermon. In the present passage, however, Luke first describes the act of that Supper, which contains several things that contribute not a little to the instruction of our faith and life.

units.la: Primum, quos in hoc epulo sacro conviuas Christus habuerit, indicatur. Cum adesset (inquit) tempus illud (quod nimirū huic rei diuinitus erat constitutū) discubuit, & duodecim Apostoli cū eo. Qui vero & quales isti fuerint tunc temporis, Euangelistæ passim docent. Fuit in illis certè magna rerum diuinarum & mysteriorum Regni Christi ignorantia, quod terrenū & victorijs atq; diuitijs siue potentia clarū fore somniabant, & sibipsis in eo opes atq; honores pollicebatur. Pariebat error iste æmulationē, qua alius supra aliū eminere cupiebat. Hinc lites oriebantur de primatu, quas non multò post in ipsa Cœna ab illis instauratas fuisse suo loco audiemus. Et hæc quidē vitia omnibus communia fuerunt. Petrus autē istis confidentia coniunxerat, qua & condiscipulos suos satis superbè contemptit, et Christo ipsum admonenti sese contumaciter nimis oppositit. Accessit his Iudas, quē Satan iā totum occupauerat, & qui cum Sacerdotū principibus cōspiratione factā omnē eius prodendi occasionē soli citè captabat: quem denique malitia incurabili in exitium ruere, Christus non poterat ignorare. Et hi quidē in Cœna hac sanctissima & maximorū mysteriorū plena conuiuæ fuerunt Filij Dei. Quem uero iftorū ille exclusit? quem reiecit? cui uel agni paschalis esum, uel sui corporis & sanguinis symbola negauit? Nihil certè huius ab Euangelistis traditur. Vnde nos colligimus, nimiū temerarios esse eos, qui multos à Cœnæ communione arcent, quorū malitia nō ita nota est, & de quorum conuersione nemo adhuc desperare potest. Præterexunt illi disciplinā, sine qua Ecclesiæ consistere nō possint. Atqui eandē nos quoq; necessaria esse dicimus, nō autē possumus videre qua ratione Cœna Dominica in fine aut usum diuersum conuerti debeat, ut separationis & exclusionis ab Ecclesia organum fiat, quam Christus instituit, ut Ecclesiæ colligendæ & conseruandæ seruiat, adeoq; unitatis Ecclesiasticæ vinculū sit. Dicunt illi, Sacramenta prophanari & euacuari, si indigni admittantur, adhæc iftorū communione siue societate alijs quoq; exitiale fieri, qui per illam in unū cum ipsis corpus coalescant. At ego neutrū istorum fieri dico. Nam qui primum illud affirmant, ij eadē opera Christum Cœnā suam prophanauisse & euacuasse dicent, quando Iudā ad illam admisit. Obijciunt illi scelus illius nō fuisse adhuc manifestū. Quo ore autē hoc dicunt, quando & Christus illud probè noverat, & hoc ipsum ille discipulis durante adhuc isto epulo indicauit? Vel num eos solos indignos hac mensa dicemus, qui in sceleribus celandis nimiū inepti sunt, impunè interim ad hanc uementibus hypocritis, qui quidus simulare aut dissimulare didicerunt? Quod si Christo licuit Iudā admittere, quem maximi scandali authorē ea ipsa hora fore sciebat, & qui non multò post abiecta et calcata fide, tā anima quàm corpore periturus erat: quæ ratio obstabit quò minus Ecclesiarū ministri eos admittant, quorū scelera nota quidē sunt, ipsi uerò ea ipsa actione pœnitentiā spondent, quoq; ad Ecclesiam redire & Christum uerbis & factis suis prædicare cupiant? Quod uero alios simul omnes, qui cum talibus ad Domini mensam accedunt, eorundem scelerum participes fieri nōnulli dicunt, nimis temerarium est, ne quid grauius dicam. Nec enim (ut sæpe aliās diximus) hīc scelerum communio agitur, sed Sacramentorum, quæ gratiæ suæ sigilla Deus esse voluit, & quibus simul eiusdem fidei unitas adumbratur, & quasi vinculo uisibili obstringitur. Cùmuero hypocritæ & pœnitere nescij fide careant, symbolis quidem externis communicare possunt, at cum pijs in unum corpus coalescere nō possunt, ut neq; hi cum illis uniuntur, nisi quoad symbola, quæ ipsis quidem salutis sigilla, impijs uero iustæ damnationis testimonia sunt. Non est ergo quod nobis periculum fingamus, ubi reuera nullum est. Caueri quidem anxie debet Sacramentorum prophanatio, at simul cauendum est, ne dum illam fugimus inconsulti- us, infirmorum conscientias uulneremus, aut dissidiorum materiam ex eo faciamus, quo concordia debebat foueri. Et cum Christi præceptum sit ne temere iudicemus, nemo sibi ea potestate sumere debet absq; singulari Dei uocatione, ut in aliorū cōscientias penetrare, & pro suo arbitrio ab Ecclesiæ communione aliquos excludere aut ad hāc admittere uelit. Sufficiat unicuiq; si Sacramenta secundū Christi institutione rectè administrari uideat, & suæ fidei sibi bene sit cōscius, alios uero qui fidē profitentur. fitentur Dei iudicio permittat, moneat autē ex Christianæ charitatis officio eos, quos suæ professioni minus respōdere intellexerit. Fecerūt hoc olim sanctissimi Dei cultores. Dauid certè in Psalmis que ritur, se à tabernaculi & sacrorū societate excludi, cùm ea tunc præ aliis fruerētur Saulis coniurati, quorum impietatē & perfidiam idem accusat. Prophetæ etiam abusum sacrorum & sui seculi mores acerrimè reprehendunt, ijdē tamē neminem unquam à templi communione excluserunt, multò minus autem ipsi à sacris illis abstinuerunt, ne cum aliorum sceleribus communicarent. Quid de Christo dicemus, qui ut hic ad mensam suam tot tamq; grauibus uitijs laborantes admisit, ita eodē baptismo cum promiscua populi turba baptizari voluit, in qua plerosq; impios hypocritas & incurabiles esse sciebat? Apostolis quoq; satis fuit, si qui fidē in Christū profitebantur, neq; illos unquā imperiosum illud alienarum conscientiarum scrutinium instituisse legimus. Paulus equidē cùm illi res esset cum Corinthiorum Ecclesia, in qua pleriq; moribus corruptissimis viuebat, & Cœna ipsa nō minus impiè quàm turpiter abutebantur, nihil huius monuit, sed satis illi uisum est præcepisse, & unusquisq; seipsum probet, ne de mensa Domini indignè edat aut bibat. Sufficiat ergo ista nobis quoq;, ne dum præposterè ac nimiæ curiositati indulgemus, turbarū atq; scismatum in Ecclesia simus authores. Interim minimè patrocinamur impuris canibus & porcis, qui si prophano cum cōtemptu piarum admonitionum ad sacra hæc mysteria ruant, procul dubio Deum ultorē sentient, qui suæ bonitatis sigilla & Ecclesiasticæ unitatis tesseras ab ipsis impunè calcari & prophanari non sinet.
units.tr: First, the guests whom Christ had at this sacred meal are indicated. "When the hour had come" (he says), which had certainly been appointed by God for this purpose, "he sat down, and the twelve apostles with him." Who these men were and what they were like at that time, the evangelists teach throughout. In them there was certainly great ignorance of the divine things and mysteries of Christ's kingdom. They dreamed that it would be earthly and famous for victories, riches and power, and they promised themselves honours and wealth in it. This error bred rivalry, by which each wanted to rise above the others. Hence arose disputes about primacy, which, as we will hear in its place, were renewed by them not long after, during this very Supper. These faults were common to them all. Peter, however, had joined to them a confidence by which he disdained his fellow disciples quite haughtily, and he set himself too stubbornly against Christ when Christ admonished him. Judas was added to these, whom Satan had already wholly taken over, and who, having made a plot with the chief priests, eagerly sought every opportunity of betraying him. Christ could not fail to know that this man, with his incurable malice, was rushing to his ruin. These then were the sons of God who sat at this most holy Supper, full of the greatest mysteries. But whom among these did he exclude? Whom did he reject? To whom did he deny the eating of the paschal lamb, or the signs of his body and blood? Certainly nothing of this is handed down by the evangelists. From this we gather that those are far too rash who keep many from communion in the Supper, whose wickedness is not so well known, and about whose conversion no one can yet despair. They overlook discipline, without which the Church cannot stand. Yet we too say that it is necessary, but we cannot see by what reasoning the Lord's Supper, which Christ instituted to serve the gathering and preserving of the Church, and so to be the bond of ecclesiastical unity, should be turned to a different use at the end, becoming an instrument of separation and exclusion from the Church. They say that the sacraments are profaned and made empty if the unworthy are admitted, and that fellowship with such men is deadly for others too, who through it would grow into one body with them. But I say that neither of these follows. For those who affirm the first point will by the same token say that Christ profaned and emptied his Supper when he admitted Judas to it. They object that his crime was not yet manifest. But with what face do they say this, when Christ knew it perfectly well, and he himself pointed it out to the disciples while the meal was still going on? Or shall we say that only those are unworthy of this table who are too clumsy at hiding their sins, while hypocrites, who have learned to pretend or to conceal, approach it with impunity? But if Christ was permitted to admit Judas, whom he knew would be the author of the greatest scandal at that very hour, and who would soon perish, soul and body, after casting off and trampling underfoot his faith, what reason will prevent the ministers of the Churches from admitting those whose wickedness is indeed known, but who by that very act promise repentance, and desire to return to the Church and to proclaim Christ by their words and deeds? As for some saying that all others who come to the Lord's table with such people become sharers in their sins, this is far too rash, to put it no more harshly. For (as we have often said elsewhere) what is at stake here is not a communion of sins but of sacraments, which God willed to be the seals of his grace, and by which the unity of the same faith is also portrayed and as it were bound by a visible bond. Hypocrites and those who know not repentance lack faith, so they can share in the outward signs, but they cannot grow into one body with the godly; nor are these united with those, except as regards the signs, which are indeed seals of salvation for the godly, but for the ungodly are testimonies of just condemnation. There is therefore no need for us to invent a danger where in truth there is none. Certainly the profanation of the sacraments must be guarded against with anxious care, but at the same time we must take care that, while we flee it too unwisely, we do not wound the consciences of the weak, or make out of it a matter of dissension where concord ought to be fostered. And since Christ commanded us not to judge rashly, no one ought to assume that power for himself without a special calling from God, so as to penetrate into the consciences of others and, at his own discretion, wish to exclude some from communion in the Church or admit others to it. It is enough for each person to see that the sacraments are rightly administered according to Christ's institution, and to be well aware of his own faith; and as for others who profess the faith, let him leave them to the judgment of God, yet admonish, out of the duty of Christian charity, those whom he perceives to be less fitting for their profession. The most holy worshippers of God did this in former times. David certainly complains in the Psalms that he was excluded from the tabernacle and the fellowship of the holy things, while Saul's conspirators then enjoyed them above others, whose impiety and treachery he himself accuses. The prophets too sharply rebuke the abuse of the sacred rites and the morals of their age, yet they never excluded anyone from communion in the temple, much less did they themselves abstain from those holy things, lest they share in the sins of others. What shall we say of Christ, who admitted to his table so many men labouring under such grave vices, and likewise willed to be baptized with the mixed crowd of the people, among whom he knew there were many impious hypocrites and incurable ones? It was also enough for the apostles that those who professed faith in Christ were accepted, and we read that they never instituted that domineering scrutiny of the consciences of others. Indeed, Paul, when he had to deal with the Church of the Corinthians, among whom many lived in most corrupt morals, and who abused the Supper itself no less impiously than shamefully, said nothing of this. It seemed enough to him to command that "let each one examine himself, so that he does not eat or drink unworthily from the Lord's table." Let this then suffice for us too, so that, while we do not indulge in misplaced and excessive curiosity, we do not become the authors of tumults and schisms in the Church. Meanwhile, we by no means defend impure dogs and swine, who, if they rush to these holy mysteries with profane contempt for pious admonitions, will without doubt feel God as avenger, who will not allow the seals of his goodness and the tokens of ecclesiastical unity to be trampled and profaned by them with impunity.

units.la: Sed ad loci propositi tractatione redeamus, quo quid primū fecerit Christus narratur, postquam cum discipulis discubuit. Oratione uerò eiusmodi instituit: Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha uesci uobiscum, antequā ego patiar: Dico enim uobis me nō amplius comesturū ex eo, quò usq; compleatur in Regno Dei. Quibus uerbis tria dicit. Primò de morte sua cōcionatur, & fatetur iam adesse tempus illud præfinitum, quo ipsum extrema quæq; pati oporteat. Id uerò illū cum sæpe aliàs, tū ante biduum quoq; fecisse Matthæus scribit. Fecit id præcipuè propter discipulos, quos aduersus scandalū crucis præmuniri oportuit, ne tā duro certamini succumberent, quo fidem ipsorū tentanda fore sciebat. Si mul tamen suo exemplo nos docet, ut quemadmodum ipse in mortis suæ meditatione assiduus fuit, & frequenter de ea cum discipulis disserit: ita nos quoq; in nostræ conditionis mortalis consideratione multū uersemur, ut magis instructi & armati simus aduersus eius terrores, quādo illa fores nostras pulsauerit. Errant in eo multi turpissimè, qui ne uitæ huius voluptates sibijpsis amaras faciant, omnem mortis mentione deuitant, & hanc ne ab alijs quidē inijci uolunt. Ridiculi planè homines, qui de ea meta nolunt uerba fieri, ad quā dies noctesq; cōtendunt, uel ad quā temporis uehiculo feruntur, quod ipsis uel inuitis uel saltē non cogitantibus, aut etiam dormientibus, perpetuo cursu pergit. Quis non rideat militem, qui cùm in castris agat, nihil tamen de hostis aduentu, de classico aut pugna audire uelit? Atqui uita quoq; nostra militia est, & inter hostes nostros mors numeratur, cum qua uelimus nolimus aliquando nos congredi oportet. Est enim hæc uia omnis terræ: & succumbūt quidē omnes homines in isto certamine, quoad corpus & huius sæculi uitam, cui semel finem imponi necesse est: nō uincuntur autē pij, qui tunc demū triumphant, quando animæ corporis huius uinculis solutæ in cælis uiuunt, corpora autem sub spe beatæ resurrectionis quiescūt. Quod qui probè intelligūt, ijs mortis cogitatio non terribilis, sed salutaris: non amara, sed iucunda est. Quia enim se mortales esse cogitant, non possunt huius uitæ illecebris animos suos addicere: sed uitam omnem ita instituunt, ut olim in Dei conspectu comparere possint: Idem quia sibi in cælis patriam & hæreditatē præparatam esse norunt, cupiunt omnino dissolui, ut cum Christo uiuant, quem ut unicum suæ salutis authorem supra omnia diligunt. Comprehendit ergo hæc consideratio non postremam sapientiæ partem, quæ & huius uitæ regulam certā præscribit, & cœlestium bonorum fidutia animum inter pericula & aduersa uacillantem recreat atq; suffulcit. Ideo sapientissimus ille mortalium Solomon dicebat: Melius est ingredi domum luctus aut funebrem, quàm domum cōuiuij: quia illic cernitur finis omnium hominum, & uiuens siue superstes id reponit in corde suo. Eccle. 7.
units.tr: But let us return to the treatment of the passage before us, where we are told what Christ first did after he had reclined with his disciples. He began with these words: "I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that I will not eat of it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." In these words he says three things. First, he preaches about his death, and confesses that the appointed time has now come, when he must suffer the final extremities. Matthew writes that he had said this often before, and also two days earlier. He did so chiefly for the sake of the disciples, who had to be armed against the scandal of the cross, so that they would not give way in such a hard struggle, by which he knew their faith would be tested. At the same time, by his own example he teaches us that, just as he himself was constant in meditating on his death and often discussed it with his disciples, so we too should dwell much on the consideration of our mortal condition, so that we may be better taught and armed against its terrors when death knocks at our doors. Many people err shamefully in this: to keep the pleasures of this life from turning bitter for themselves, they avoid all mention of death and do not want it even raised by others. They are plainly ridiculous people, who do not want to speak of that goal toward which they strive day and night, or toward which they are carried by the vehicle of time, which moves on in unending course whether they are unwilling, or do not think of it, or even are asleep. Who would not laugh at a soldier who, while he is in camp, does not want to hear anything about the enemy's approach, the trumpet call, or the battle? Yet our life too is a warfare, and death is counted among our enemies, and with it we must at some point come to grips, whether we like it or not. For this is the way of all the earth: all men indeed succumb in this contest, as far as the body and this life of the age are concerned, to which an end must once be set. But the godly are not conquered; they triumph then, when their souls, freed from the bonds of the body, live in heaven, while their bodies rest in the hope of a blessed resurrection. Those who understand this rightly find the thought of death not terrifying but salutary, not bitter but pleasant. For since they think of themselves as mortal, they cannot devote their minds to the allurements of this life, but order their whole life so that they may one day appear in the sight of God. And since they know that a homeland and inheritance are prepared for them in heaven, they desire above all to be dissolved, so that they may live with Christ, whom they love above all things as the sole author of their salvation. This consideration, therefore, comprises no small part of wisdom: it prescribes a sure rule for this life, and by confidence in heavenly goods it refreshes and sustains a mind that wavers amid dangers and adversities. Therefore that wisest of mortals, Solomon, said: "It is better to go into the house of mourning or of funeral than into the house of feasting, for there is seen the end of all men, and the living, or the survivor, lays it to heart." Eccles. 7.

units.la: Alterū, quod hic Christus facit, est, quod ardentissimū nostræ salutis desiderium profitetur. Desiderio (inquit) desideraui hoc pascha uesci uobiscū. Diserte autē de illo pascha te loquitur, quod tunc agebatur, ut ab alijs, quæ prius celebrauerat, iştud distinguat. Quid uerò hoc habuit præ alijs expetendū? Non aliud certè quàm horam illam æterno Dei decreto præfinitā, qua ipse in morte tradi, & hu mani generis redemptionem perficere debuit. Atqui mortis memoriam propter dirū illud & infame crucis supplicium illi, ut homini uero & nostrae infirmitati obnoxio, aliquando acerbissimam fuisse constat. Apud Ioannē certè illius recordatione commotus ait: Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater cōserua me ab hac hora. Et infra ipsum prae animi angustia sudauisse audiemus, sudo remq; eius non uulgarem, sed sanguineum fuisse. Vicit tamen omnes alios affectus amor ille immensus, quo nos complexus est, & qui tam ardens salutis nostrae desiderium excitauit, ut illā mortis suae merito redimere cuperet, & huius horā auidè expectaret. Et quid aliud faceret, qui alibi hūc cibum suum esse ait, ut faciat uoluntatem Patris sui, id est, ut quàm plurimos saluos faciat? De hoc Christi amore atq; desiderio Paulus dicit: Filius Dei dilexit me, tradidit semetipsum pro me. Meretur autem hoc multam & diligentem considerationem. Hinc enim dulcissima & efficacissima cōsolatio peti potest, quae sola aduersus cōscientiae tentationes nobis potest sufficere. Solet has Satā grauissimas excitare, & ferè eiusmodi cogitationes animis nostris inserit. Quid tu infelix porrò speres, qui quantus quantus es, peccator es, & propterea morte aeterna dignus? Num uero Deū propter te iustitia suae immemorem fore putas, quò minus te suā sententia, ceu fulmine, ad inferos praecipitem det? At in Filio Dei tibi fiduciam repositam esse dices: Stulte, num ille salutis tuae maiorem curam, quàm tu ipse habeat? Quid uero in te est, quo istud mereris? aut quid ex te sperare potest ille, qui sibi solus ad omnia sufficit, neq; tuo ministerio siue officio opus habet? Haec & multa alia similia astutus ille uete rator potest suggerere. Quibus nō aliud scutū fortius opponi poterit, quàm Dei bonitas, quae in hisce Christi uerbis euidentissimè elucet. Ita enim ille dilexit nos, ut Filium suum unigenitum aeterno decreto praedestinauerit, ut pro nobis homo factus nos mortis suae merito redimeret. Ipse uero non Patri solum obediens fuit, uerumetiam tanto nostri more accensus fuit, ut ardentissimo cum desiderio diem illum expectarit, quo operi huic tam salutari tamq; necessario manum admouere debuit. Impossibile ergo fuerit, te maiori salutis desiderio ardere, quàm ipse Dei Filius ardeat. Quis uero obsta bit, quò minus ille uoti sui compos fiat? Num Satan ex manibus eius rapiet eos, quos ipse pro suis agnoscit, & quos sanguinis sui pretio sibi acquisiuit? Invitat ille expansis brachijs omnes, qui laborāt & onerati sunt. Idè alta uoce ad se uenire iubet eos, qui uitam aeternam sitiunt. Audiamus ergo uo-cantem, obtemperemus inuitanti, & saluae erunt res nostrae. Nec enim periculum est, ne eos reiiciat, qui ipsius uerbo confisi ad ipsum ueniunt. Non minus autem nostri nos officij admonet ista consideratio, quod duplex est. Primò enim docet nos, ut ipsi quoq; non minori salutis publicae desiderio ardeamus, & toti in hoc simus, ut quàm plurimi ad Christū conuertantur, & in illo salui fiant. Est hoc officium Deo gratissimum, qui non alia re perinde ut hominum salute delectatur. Ideo Apostolus di cebat: Fratres, si quis inter uos aberrauerit à ueritate, & conuerterit eum quispiam, sciat quòd qui auerterit peccatorem ab errore uiae suae, seruabit animam à morte, & obteget multitudinem peccatorum. E contra non aliud atrocius scelus est, quàm illi scandalum aut perditionis causam praebuis-fe, pro quo Dei Filius mortem diram & acerbam subire dignatus est. Constat certè ab illius amore alienissimos esse, quos nulla salutis fraternae cura tangit, & qui infinita hominum millia facilè sinūt perire, modò ipsis bene sit. Deinde nostrae etiā salutis studio nos flagrare conuenit, & proinde curare ne tanto pretio redempti, in exitium nostrū relabamur. Turpe enim fuerit nos interea stertere aut frigere, dum Dei Filius propter nos tanto desiderio uritur. Est ergo hoc Christi distū dignissimum: quod nunquam non nobis in mentem ueniat, imò quod ipsi nobis subinde occinamus, quoties aut salu tis nostrae stem in dubium uocari, aut nos huius saeculi illecebris insecari sentimus, ut nostri officij minus recordemur. Illud enim unum, si probè expendatur, sidem nostram confirmare, & carnis desi deria praua restinguere poterit.
units.tr: The second thing Christ does here is that he professes his most ardent desire for our salvation. "I have earnestly desired," he says, "to eat this Passover with you." He clearly speaks of that particular Passover which was then being celebrated, so as to distinguish it from the others he had previously observed. But what did this one have above others to be desired? Certainly nothing other than that hour, appointed by the eternal decree of God, in which he was to be delivered up to death and accomplish the redemption of the human race. Yet it is clear that the memory of death, on account of the dreadful and infamous punishment of the cross, was at times most bitter to him, as to a true man subject to our weakness. In John, indeed, moved by the recollection of it, he says: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour." And below we hear that he sweated from the anguish of his mind, and that his sweat was not ordinary, but like blood. Yet that immense love, by which he embraced us, overcame all other feelings, and it stirred up so ardent a desire for our salvation that he wished to redeem us by the merit of his death, and eagerly awaited its hour. And what else would he do, who elsewhere says that his food is to do the will of his Father, that is, to save as many as possible? Of this love and desire of Christ Paul says: "The Son of God loved me and gave himself for me." This deserves much careful consideration. For from it can be drawn a most sweet and effective consolation, which alone can suffice for us against the temptations of conscience. Satan is accustomed to stir these up most severely, and he almost always plants thoughts of this kind in our minds: "What, you wretch, can you hope for, you who, whoever you are, are a sinner and therefore worthy of eternal death? Do you think God will be forgetful of his justice, so as not to cast you down to hell with his sentence like a thunderbolt? But you will say that your confidence is placed in the Son of God. Fool, does he have a greater care for your salvation than you yourself? But what is there in you by which you deserve this? Or what can he hope for from you, who is sufficient for himself in all things and has no need of your service or duty?" These and many other similar things that crafty old deceiver can suggest. Against them no stronger shield can be opposed than the goodness of God, which shines most clearly in these words of Christ. For he so loved us that he predestined his only begotten Son by eternal decree, so that, made man for us, he might redeem us by the merit of his death.
