Moreover, he himself was not only obedient to the Father, but was so inflamed with love for us that he awaited with most ardent desire that day on which he had to set his hand to this work, so salutary and so necessary. It is therefore impossible that you should burn with a greater desire for salvation than the Son of God himself burns. And who will stand in the way, so that he should not attain his desire? Will Satan snatch from his hands those whom he acknowledges as his own, and whom he has acquired for himself at the price of his blood? He invites all who labour and are burdened, with arms outstretched. He bids with a loud voice those who thirst for eternal life to come to him. Let us then hear him calling, let us obey him inviting, and our affairs will be safe. For there is no danger that he will reject those who come to him trusting in his word. Moreover, this consideration reminds us also of our duty, which is twofold. For first, it teaches us that we too should burn with no less desire for the public salvation, and be wholly intent that as many as possible may be converted to Christ and be saved in him. This duty is most pleasing to God, who delights in nothing so much as in the salvation of men. Therefore the Apostle said: "Brethren, if anyone among you has strayed from the truth, and someone turns him back, let him know that whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins." On the contrary, there is no more atrocious crime than to have given a stumbling-block or cause of perdition to one for whom the Son of God deigned to undergo a dreadful and bitter death. It is certain that those are most alien to his love who are not moved by any care for their brother's salvation, and who easily allow thousands of men to perish, provided that they themselves are well. Next, it is fitting that we also burn with zeal for our own salvation, and therefore take care lest, having been redeemed at so great a price, we fall back into our own destruction. For it would be shameful for us meanwhile to snore or grow cold, while the Son of God burns with such desire on account of us. This saying of Christ is therefore most worthy: it should never fail to come to mind, nay, we should sing it to ourselves again and again, whenever we feel either that our salvation is called into doubt or that we are being assailed by the allurements of this age, so that we forget our duty less. For this one thing, if it is weighed carefully, will be able both to confirm our faith and to quench depraved desires of the flesh.

units.la: Tertiū in Christi uerbis est, quod de epuli paschalis abrogatione cōcionatur, & hac sui illius desi derij causā adducit, cui humani generis redēptio inclusa est. Id uero singulari cū grauitate enūtiat. Dico enim uobis, me nō amplius comesturū ex eo, quo usq; cōpleatur in Regno Dei. Scimus autē per Regnū Dei ipsam redemptionē humani generis intelligi, & ideo huius quoq; prædicatione Euangelii Regni dici. Quoad uero Paschatis impletione, satis cōstat, hac in morte Christi esse factā qui pascha nostrū (ut Paulus inquit) immolat° est pro nobis, & uerus ille agnus Dei est, cuius sanguis nos tue-tur, ne quid in nos iuris habeat Angel° ille uastator, qui animas hominū perditas cupit. Quāuis uero in prasenti praesenti de solo paschate sermo sit, sub illo tamen omnia alia ueteris testamenti sacrificia cum uni-uersis ceremonijs Legalibus siue Mosaicis comprehenduntur. Itaque uerborum Christi sensus est: Instat iam tempus humanae redemptionis, & ideo ego huius Cenae horam auidè expectaui, ut hoc uo-biscum Pascha postremum agerem, nunquam epulum istud repetiturus, donec reipsa impletum, & Regnum Dei instauratum fuerit. Unde tamen nemo colligere debet, Iudaicum pascha à Christo re-petitum esse, aut idem à nobis porrò celebrari debere. Est enim locutio haec ei similis: Sede à dextris meis, DONEC ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Qua non hoc uult dicere Deus, quòd Filium post subactos hostes è throno diuinae maiestatis deturbari oporteat: sed quòd diuinam uirtu-tem palàm declaraturus sit aduersus omnes hostes, donec mortem quoq; ipsam (quam Apostolus no-uissimum hostem uocat) aboleuerit, adeò ut non reliquus sit alius, contra quem manu uictrici uta-tur. Quid uerò post hac aliud fiat, quàm quòd ipse aeternum regnabit, & omnibus eius aduersarijs deuictis atque ad aeternos inferorum cruciatus detrusis, Deus iam sit omnia in omnibus, sicuti idem Apostolus loquitur? Ad eundem modum, se posthac pascha comesturum negat, ut quousque impleatur in Regno Dei. At quia hoc erecto & restituto, nullus neque paschati neque alijs ceremonijs locus erit amplius, reliquum est, ut Christum non de ueteri illa umbra, sed ipsa ueritate loqui dicamus, quae nouum illud pascha nobis exhibuit & festum perpetuum, quod per omnes uitae nostrae dies extendi-tur, & quod aeternae ueritatis atq; syncerități peragi debere Paulus in priori ad Corinthios Cap. quinto docet. Facit ergo ad huius loci expositionem, quod apud Danielem de Christo dicitur, quòd ipse sacrificium & oblationem in dimidio hebdomadis ultimae abrogaturus sit. Coepit enim hoc fieri, quando in Iordane baptizatus & publico Patris testimonio commendatus est, quòd ipse sit Filius ille dilectus, in quo solo ille placatus sit. Quibus uerbis non obscurè significabatur, nullam porrò alio-rum sacrificiorum rationem fore Deo, sed in uno Christo omnes acquiescere debere. Quod uerò tunc coepit, postea in eius morte impletum atq; perfectum fuit, quod ueli scissio in ipso puncto mortis domi-nicæ facta euidentissimè docuit. Pascha autem sempiternum olim in caelis celebrabimus, quando ad Christum collecti cum eo gaudijs aeternis fruemur. Quo etiam referri debet, quod apud Matthaeum de poculo nouo dicit, quod bibiturus sit nobiscum in Regno Patris sui. Non debet autem toto hoc lo-co ofcitanter negligi, quod de legalium ceremoniarū abrogatione tam expressè loquitur. Quia enim typi aut figurae erant eorum, quae suo tempore in Christo debuerunt impleri, æquum, uel potius necesse fuit illas aboleri, cùm tempus illud perfectionis (ut Paulus ad Hebraeos dicit) aduenisset. Nam ut-bris manentibus dubia fuisset lux, quàm nobis Christus attulit. Nō temere ergo factum putabimus, quòd Apostoli tanta uehementia aduersus illos pugnarunt, qui circuncisionem & alia Legis exer-citia Christianis obtrudere conabantur. Nā initiò publica concilij uerè Apostolici authoritate con-uicti atq; repressi sunt, ut Lucas in Actis tradit. At cùm quidam ne sic quidem quiescerent, Paulus multis Epistolis docet, per ipsos totam Euangelij doctrinam corrumpi, Christi meritum euacuari, & hunc prorsus inutilem reddi. Quia enim, ut ex Daniele modò monuimus, per Messiam sacrificia & oblationes ueteres aboleri debuerunt, hunc nobis exhibitum esse negent oportet, quotquot illa ad huc retineri aut reduci debere contendunt. Quòd si uerò ueteres ritus antiquari oportuit, nimium imprudentes & temerarij sunt, qui nouos à ueteribus illis non multum diuersos hodie introducunt. Horum certè audaciae debemus, quòd Christianae religionis simplicitas per saecula aliquot superstitio-nibus partim Iudaicis partim gentilitijs obscurata, uel potius obruta atq; sepulta latuit.
units.tr: The third point in Christ's words concerns the abolition of the Passover meal. He speaks of it and gives as the reason for his longing the redemption of the human race, which is contained in it. He declares this with singular seriousness: "For I tell you, I will not eat of it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." We know that by the kingdom of God is meant the redemption of the human race itself, and so it is also called the kingdom of the gospel, which is preached. As for the fulfilment of the Passover, it is quite clear that it was accomplished in the death of Christ, who, as Paul says, "was sacrificed for us as our Passover," and who is the true Lamb of God, whose blood protects us so that the destroying angel, who seeks the lost souls of men, has no right over us. Although in the present passage he speaks only of the Passover, all the other sacrifices of the Old Testament, with all the legal or Mosaic ceremonies, are included under it. So the sense of Christ's words is this: "The time of human redemption is now at hand, and therefore I have eagerly awaited this hour of the Supper, so that I might celebrate this last Passover with you, never to repeat this feast until it has been truly fulfilled and the kingdom of God restored." Yet no one should conclude from this that the Jewish Passover was then repeated by Christ, or that it ought to be celebrated again by us. For this way of speaking is like that in "Sit at my right hand, UNTIL I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." God does not mean by this that the Son must be cast down from the throne of the divine majesty after his enemies have been subdued; he means that he will openly display his divine power against all enemies until he has also destroyed death itself (which the Apostle calls the last enemy), so that no other remains against whom he must use his victorious hand. What then will follow, except that he will reign eternally, and, all his adversaries having been conquered and thrust down into the eternal torments of hell, God will be "all in all," as the same Apostle says? In the same way, Christ says he will not eat the Passover again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. But since, when that kingdom is raised up and restored, there will be no place any longer either for the Passover or for the other ceremonies, we must say that Christ is speaking not of that old shadow but of the truth itself, which has given us that new Passover and perpetual feast, which extends through all the days of our life, and which Paul teaches in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter five, must be kept with the sincerity and truth of God. What relates to the explanation of this passage, then, is what is said of Christ in Daniel, that he would abolish sacrifice and oblation in the middle of the last week. For this began to happen when he was baptized in the Jordan and commended by the public testimony of the Father, that he is that beloved Son in whom alone God is well pleased. By these words it was plainly signified that henceforth there would be no other manner of sacrifice acceptable to God, but that all should rest in Christ alone. What began then was afterwards fulfilled and completed in his death, as the tearing of the veil at the very moment of the Lord's death most clearly showed. We shall celebrate an everlasting Passover in heaven at some time, when, gathered to Christ, we shall enjoy eternal joys with him. To this also should be referred what he says in Matthew about the new cup, that he will drink it with us in the kingdom of his Father. In this whole passage we should not carelessly pass over the fact that he speaks so plainly about the abolition of the legal ceremonies. For since these were types or figures of things that were to be fulfilled in Christ at their proper time, it was fitting, or rather necessary, that they be abolished, when that time of perfection (as Paul says to the Hebrews) had arrived. For if the shadows had remained, the light that Christ brought us would have been doubtful. We shall not think it rash that the Apostles fought so vehemently against those who tried to force circumcision and the other practices of the Law upon Christians. For at first they were convicted and restrained by the public authority of the apostolic council, as Luke relates in Acts. But when some would not be quiet even then, Paul shows in many letters that through them the whole doctrine of the gospel was corrupted, the merit of Christ emptied out, and he himself made utterly useless. For since, as we have just noted from Daniel, the old sacrifices and oblations were to be abolished through the Messiah, all who maintain that those things must still be retained or brought back must deny that he has been given to us. And if the old rites had to be abolished, those are excessively imprudent and rash who today introduce new ones that are not much different from those old ones. Certainly we owe it to the audacity of such men that the simplicity of the Christian religion, for some centuries obscured, or rather overwhelmed and buried, by superstitions partly Jewish and partly pagan, lay hidden.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, qua ipsius Cenae initiū describitur his uerbis: Et accepto pocu-lo cū gratias egisset, dixit: Accipite hoc, & partimini uobis ipsis. Ergo à gratiarū actione epulū hoc exorsus est Dominus, quod illū ali às quoq; facere solitum fuisse, ex alijs locis euidentissimè apparet. In praesenti autem, quia non vulgare, sed solenne & sacrum conuiuium agebatur, ritum quoq; solen-nem & in sacris epulis usitatum obseruat. Solebat enim ille, qui sacris praerat, accepto poculo, quod illi salutis aut salutationis dicebant, conceptis atq; solennibus uerbis gratias agere Deo. Exemplum huius mortis in Samuelis historia habetur, ubi puellae quaedam Sauli dicunt, Samuelē ascendere an-teipsum, ut epulum publicum, quod ex gratulatorijs uictimis eius loci ciues instruxerant, consecret: nec enim populum comesturū quicquam priusquam hoc fiat. Ad eundē morem Dauid quoq; allusit in Psalmo 116. dicens: Quam gratiam referam Domino pro illis omnibus, quae in me contulit, beneficijs, Calicem salutum tollam, & nomen Domini inuocabo. Idest, in conuiuio gratulatorio calice accepto & subleuato publicè toti Ecclesiae testabor, me illius ope fuisse seruatum. Quod Paulus etiam obseruauit, quando poculum Coenae Dominicae, poculum benedictionis nominat. Id uero Christus discipulos inter se partiri iubet, & eo omnes ad gratias Deo agendas excitat. Et rursus mortis suae mentionem facit, ut hanc simul atque eius fructum illis fidelius commendet. Sic enim ait: Dico enim uobis me non bibiturum ex fructu uitis, usquequo Regnum Dei uenerit. Quod ab illo veritissime dictum fuisse constat, quando haec illi Coena ultima fuit, postquam mox captus & occisus, Regnum Dei inter homines instaurauit. Quod autem hoc loco Christus fecit, & quod olim ueteres in suis conuiuiis facitarunt, hoc ipsum nobis quoque faciendum esse cogitemus, ne unquam absque gratiarum actione ad mensam accedamus. Quia enim Deus est qui panem producit, quo cor hominis confortatur, & uinum creat, quo laeti reddimur, qui deniq; pecoribus & feris pabulum praebet, constat nos Dei hospites siue conuiuas esse quoties edimus aut bibimus. Exigit ergo a nobis naturae lex, ut tanto beneficiori & nutritio grati simus, qui omnes huius mundi partes in nobis alendis atque uestiendis occupatas habet. Et qui istud serio cogitant, ij donis illius recte & sobrie utuntur, quae ratio est, quod Paulus per gratiarum actionem omnes cibos nobis sanctificari dicit. Nec enim haec a fide abesse potest, quae sola tam nos quam omnia quae facimus, Deo grata & accepta facit. Est ergo cum scelere & impietate coniuncta eorum ingratitudo, qui porcorum instar ad mensam ruunt, & de solo uentre implendo aut farciendo soliciti, unde cibos atque alimenta acceperint, ne cogitant quidem. Est hoc ingens peccatum, si nihil praeterea accedat: eoque grauius est, quod brutorum animalium exemplo arguitur, quae nutritios suos agnoscunt, & his gratiam aliquam referunt. Nascitur hinc cum luxu & intemperantia coniunctus donorum Dei abusus, ut uentri & gulae seruiant, quae aduita huius sustentationem accepimus. Quid uero non designat ebrietas? Rationis usum extinguit, mentem alienat & aufert, pudorem abstergit, bilem accendit, linguam ad conuitia, manus ad pugnam acuit & armat, libidini fomenta ministrat, rem domesticam dissipat & egestatem parit, cuius impatientia multi exagitati tumultuantur & turbas dant ipsi etiam Reipub. periculosas: denique nullum scelus tam atrox, tam turpe, tam periculosum est, quod non committi soleat ab illis, qui uino nimio obruti cum ratione pudorem quoque amiserunt. Exempla in historijs cum sacris tum prophanis passim occurrunt, & in primis huc pertinent minae Prophetarum, qui extrema quaeq; ebriosis denuntiant. Fugiamus ergo atq; detestemur pestem tam foedam & noxiam: quod tunc demum cum fructu fiet, si Deum bonorum omnium largitorem gratis animis agnoscamus. Tanta enim est bonitatis ac beneficentiae eius in omnibus mundi partibus sese exerentis suauitas, ut non possint no illius amore accendi, & in eius laudes totis animi ac corporis uiribus erumpere, quicunq; illam propius consideauerint. Quod si uero bonam gratiam Deo debemus pro temporarijs & corporalibus beneficijs, quanto maior eidem debebitur, quod Filium suum unigenitum, Iesum Christum, pro nobis in morte tradidit, ut peccata nostra expiaret, & suo corpore atq; sanguine nos alat & recreet ad vitam aeternam? Excitet nos ista rum consideratio, ut sicuti ipse desiderauit postremum hoc pascha cum discipulis comedere: ita nos omnibus reliquis in hoc simus, ut cū illo in coelis beato illo aeternae immortalitatis nectare recreemur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The last part of this passage remains, in which the beginning of the Supper itself is described in these words: "And when he had taken the cup and given thanks, he said, Take this and divide it among yourselves." So the Lord began this meal with thanksgiving, which he is shown from other places to have been accustomed to do. Here, because this was not an ordinary meal but a solemn and sacred feast, he also observes the solemn rite used in sacred meals. For the one who presided over the sacred rites, taking up the cup, which they called the cup of salvation or of greeting, used to give thanks to God in set and solemn words. An example of this custom is found in the history of Samuel, where some girls say to Saul that Samuel is going up ahead of them to bless the public feast, which the citizens of that place had prepared from the thank-offerings, for the people would not eat anything until this was done. David also alluded to this same custom in Psalm 116, saying: "What shall I render to the Lord for all the benefits he has bestowed on me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord." That is, at a festive banquet, having taken up and raised the cup, I will publicly testify to the whole Church that I was saved by his help. Paul also observed this when he called the cup of the Lord's Supper the cup of blessing. Christ, indeed, orders the disciples to share it among themselves, and by it he stirs them all to give thanks to God. And again he mentions his death, so that he may more faithfully commend to them both it and its fruit. For he says: "For I tell you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes." It is clear that he spoke most truthfully, since this was his last supper, after which he was soon seized and killed, and afterwards restored the kingdom of God among men. What Christ did here, and what the ancients in their feasts used to do, let us also consider that we ourselves should do, so that we never approach the table without giving thanks. For since it is God who brings forth bread, by which the heart of man is strengthened, and creates wine, by which we are made glad, and who finally provides food for cattle and wild beasts, it is clear that we are God's guests, or rather his dinner companions, whenever we eat or drink. Therefore the law of nature requires us to be grateful for so great a benefit and nourishment, which occupies all parts of this world in feeding and clothing us. And those who seriously consider this use God's gifts rightly and soberly; this is why Paul says that all foods are sanctified to us through thanksgiving. For this cannot be apart from faith, which alone makes us, and all that we do, pleasing and acceptable to God. Therefore the ingratitude of those is joined with wickedness and impiety, who rush to the table like swine, anxious only to fill or stuff the belly, and do not even think about where they received their food and sustenance. This is a great sin in itself, and it is all the more grievous because it is condemned by the example of brute animals, which recognize those who nourish them and return some thanks to them. From this arises an abuse of God's gifts, joined with luxury and intemperance, so that men serve the belly and the gullet, which we receive for the sustenance of this life. And what does drunkenness not bring about? It extinguishes the use of reason, alienates and takes away the mind, wipes away shame, inflames bile, sharpens and arms the tongue for insults and the hands for fighting, supplies fuel to lust, squanders household goods and brings forth poverty; men driven mad by this impatience riot and cause tumults even dangerous to the commonwealth. In short, there is no crime so atrocious, so shameful, so dangerous, that it is not commonly committed by those who, overwhelmed by too much wine, have lost shame together with reason. Examples occur everywhere in histories, both sacred and profane, and especially the threats of the prophets, who announce the worst punishments to drunkards. Let us therefore flee and detest a plague so foul and harmful; this will be done with profit only if we acknowledge God, the giver of all good things, with grateful hearts. For the sweetness of his goodness and beneficence, displayed in every part of the world, is so great that all who consider it closely cannot but be kindled with love for him and break out with all the strength of their soul and body into his praise. But if we owe God thanks for temporal and bodily benefits, how much greater thanks must be owed to him because he gave up his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, for us in death, to expiate our sins, and to nourish and refresh us with his body and blood unto eternal life? Let the consideration of these things stir us, so that just as he himself desired to eat this last Passover with his disciples, we too may take care to be refreshed with him in heaven by that blessed nectar of eternal immortality. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIV.

units.la: Et accepto pane, cum gratias egisset, fregit, & dedit eis dicens: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: hoc facite in mei recordationem. Similiter & poculū dedit eis, postquam coenasset dicens: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine, qui pro vobis effunditur.
units.tr: And when he had taken bread and given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying: "This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me." In the same way he also gave them the cup after supper, saying: "This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is shed for you."

units.la: Multis quidem & praeclaris argumentis Dei Filius ab initio statim sui in carnem aduentus amorem & beneuolentiam suam, qua humanum genus prosequitur, declarauit, hoc ipsum uere tunc omnium luculentissime praestitit, quando fatalis illa hora appropinquabat, qua pro mundi peccatis mori & seipsum in ara crucis Patri offerre debuit. Nam etsi pro humanæ naturæ infirmitate mortem horruerit, eandem tamen magno desiderio expetiauit, quòd per hanc publicæ omnium saluti consulere cuperet. Adhæc non tam de suis rebus solicitus fuit, quàm de discipulis, quos (quòd eos infirmiores & rudes nimium esse sciret) præceptis & admonitionibus saluberrimis instruxit, ut ad propositum certamen alacriores descenderent. Veruntamen ne illis solis consuleret, Cœnam mysticam quoq; instituit, quæ totum nostræ redemptionis negotium non solum adumbrat, verumetiam obsignat, eiusq; memoriam continet iucundam, quæ in Ecclesijs perpetuò celebrari & retineri debet. Quia autem de illa alibi prolixè diximus, nunc summa rerum capita perstrinxisse sufficiat.
units.tr: The Son of God, from the very beginning of his coming in the flesh, showed his love and goodwill toward the human race, which he embraces, by many notable proofs. He showed it most clearly of all when that fateful hour drew near, the hour in which he was to die for the sins of the world and offer himself on the altar of the cross to the Father. For although, because of the weakness of human nature, he shrank from death, he nevertheless desired it with great longing, because through it he wished to provide for the salvation of all. Moreover, he was less anxious about his own affairs than about his disciples. Knowing that they were too weak and untrained, he instructed them with the most wholesome precepts and admonitions, so that they might enter the coming contest more eagerly. Yet, so that he would not care for them alone, he also instituted the mystical Supper. This not only foreshadows the whole business of our redemption but also seals it, and it holds a pleasant memory of it, which ought to be celebrated and kept up constantly in the churches. Since we have spoken at length about it elsewhere, it is enough here to touch on the main heads of the matter.

units.la: Primum inter hæc est, ut quid illud sit uideamus, de quo in præsenti agitur. Vulgo quidem Cœnam Dominicam dicunt, & ita eam Paulus in priori ad Corinth. vocat. Causa nominis istius est, quòd illam Christus Dominus tempore vespertino, uel potius incipiente iam nocte instituit, postquam epulum paschale cum discipulis comedisset, de quo nuper est dictum. Ex eo igitur nomen retinuit, ut morti eius memoriam efficacius nobis commendet, etiamsi nunc pro Christianæ libertatis iure maturino tempore peragi soleat. Ne quis autem Cœnam hanc vulgarem esse arbitretur, Christi verba diligentius obseruare oportet & expendere, quæ nō obscurè docebunt, mysterium altius sub actione ista uili & contempta in speciem subesse. Nam primum ut quod ipse tunc fecit, nos quoq; faciamus iubet, & bis dicit: Hoc facite in mei recordationem. De pane autem loquens ait: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro uobis traditur. Et de poculo: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine, qui pro uobis effunditur. Quæ verba apud Marcum & Matthæum adhunc modum enuntiantur: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est Noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur. Ex iis ergo inter se collatis definitione Cœnæ eiusmodi colligere licebit: Est actio sacra ab ipso Christo instituta, in qua ex eius mandato panem & uinum inter nos distribuimus atq; sumimus, in recordationem mortis eius, in qua corpus suum pro nobis tradidit, & sanguine suum pro nobis effudit, ut Nouum testamentum compleret ratumq; faceret. Actione esse dico Cœnam, quod in omnibus aliis quoq; Sacramentis obseruari debet, & ea ad hoc genus pertinere sciamus. Etenim si illa omnia ex ordine consideres, actione ea constare uidebis, adeò ut si illa cessset, ipsa quoq; non sint. Quis enim Circuncisionem esse dixerit, in qua nulla sit præputij resectio? Num item sacrificium esse poterit, ubi nihil sacrificatur? Num baptismus ubi nemo baptizatur aut tingitur? Ita neq; Cœna erit, si nemo edat aut bibat. Est hoc propter eos obseruandum, qui per Sacramentum nuda symbola intelligunt, & aquam siue panem & uinum Sacramenta dicunt, etiamsi nemo illis utatur. Quæ opinio superstitionem peperit, ut symbola adorentur, aut saltem ipsis tribuatur, quod non illorum proprie est, sed ad totam actionem pertinet. Deinde author Cœnæ Christus indicatur, qui illam nobis instituit. Materia sunt panis & uinum, Christi verbo in eum usum consecrata, nonut in corpus & sanguinem eius transubstantientur, sed ut ueri corporis & sanguinis, quæ ille pro nobis tradidit, symbola sint. Causa finalis & usus, ut ista inter nos distribuamus atq; sumamus in gratam recordationem mortis Christi. Et ne recordatio hæc otiosa & inutilis sit, mortis suæ fructum diserte explicat, quādo corpus suum pro nobis traditum & sanguinem suum pro nobis, siue pro multis, id est, pro tota credentium multitudine fusum esse, & in eo Nouum illud testamentum contineri dicit. Quod uerò testamentum illud Nouum sit, Paulus in Epistola ad Hebræos ex Ieremia docet, per quem Iudæis nouum fœdus siue testamentum pollicetur, cuius summam his uerbis comprehendit: Ego ero Deus eorum, & ipsi erunt mihi populus: & propitius ero iniquitatibus eorum, & peccatorū ipsorum non amplius recordabor. Nouum uerò dicitur hoc testamentum, etiamsi idem prorsus sit cum ueteri, quod olim cum Abrahamo fecerat Deus, quia post multiplicem Iudaicæ gentis defectionem atq; perfidiam denuo instauratum fuit: quod item populum nouū ex gentibus adoptauit Deus, antiquatis simul (ut nuper Christus promisit) ceremonijs Mosaicis, in quarum locum noua Sacramenta successerunt, uirtute maiora (ut D. Augustinus inquit) utilitate meliora, actu faciliora, numero pauciora: quorum tamen idem usus est, qui olim ueterum fuit. Porrò testamentum hoc nouum in suo sanguine confirmare Christus ait, quia cum mortem testatoris intercedere oporteret, Deus autem mori non posset, ipse qui æternus est Dei Filius & Patri coessentialis, in assumpta humanitate mortuus est, ut nobis secundum testamentum illud, ad Regnum Dei & cœlestium bonorum hereditatem aditus pateret. Ergo finis & usus Coenae Dominicae praecipuus est, memoria siue recordatio mortis Christi, cuius merito nos ex peccatis et horum poenis, morte aeterna, redempti sumus. Non quidem recordatio otiosa aut frigida, qualis esse solet rerum nihil ad nos pertinentium, sed quae cum fide coniuncta, ipsum Christum & in hoc salutem omnem apprehendit, adeo ut per illum pascamur & seruemur ad uitam aeternam. Adhaec obsignatur hic nobis redemptionis per Christum factae beneficium, ut quod de Circuncisione olim Paulus dixit, eam Abrahamo datam fuisse sigillum iustitiae fidei, multo uerius de Coena possit dici, in ea nobis pignus & sigillum totius redemptionis nostrae certissimum & infallibile exhiberi. Ex isto fine Coenae alij dependent, qui proprie ex illo deriuantur. Primo enim fide in Christum profitemur, quando nos eius morte & sanguine testamur esse redemptos. Deinde est hoc externum uinculum, quo in unum corpus constringimur sub uno capite Christo. Praeterea non uno modo officijad monemur, quod est, ne sacris alienis communicemus, ut innocentiae et sanctitati studeamus, libertatem Christi sanguine partam constanter tueamur, et charitate colamus mutua. Est ergo Coena Domini officina quaedam operosissima, in qua omnis loci ac ordinis homines inueniunt quod agat, quae deniq; stimulos quoq; adhibet, quibus ad officium faciendum excitemur. Prodest aut principale hunc Coenae fine atq; usum cum ijs, quae illi proprie cohaerent, probe obseruare, ne eorum commenta admittamus, qui ex illa quiduis pro suo arbitrio fingunt. Alij enim in ea Christu pro peccatis viuorum atq; mortuorum offerri aiunt. Alij uiaticu ex illa fabricat, quo animae sustententur, ut purgatorij ignis ardores facilius ferant. Sunt qui corpus quoq; istis symbolis ad resurrectione pasci cogendant. Pleriq; pro corporali Christi praesentia litigant, quasi hanc ille sub symbolis istis sanciuerit. Qui errorut cu Papatu iam surgere exortus est, cum antea toti uetustati ignotus fuerit: ita superstitiones peperit plurimas, quibus meritum Filij Dei euacuatur, & hodie contentionu fere omnium causa est, quae Ecclesia in partes distrahunt magno cum multorum scandalo, qui uel resiliunt a fide, uel retinentur quo minus ad eam accedant. At quid obsecro huius dixit Christus, ex quo errores isti, quos recitauimus, elici possint?
units.tr: The first thing to see is what that is of which we are now speaking. Commonly it is called the Lord's Supper, and Paul calls it that in his first Epistle to the Corinthians. The reason for the name is that Christ the Lord instituted it in the evening, or rather when night was already coming on, after he had eaten the Passover meal with his disciples, which we mentioned just now. He therefore kept the name so that he might commend the memory of his death to us more effectively, even though, by the right of Christian liberty, it is now customarily celebrated in the morning. But lest anyone think this Supper to be an ordinary thing, we must observe and weigh carefully the words of Christ, which will teach without obscurity that a deeper mystery lies beneath this humble and despised action. For first he commands us to do what he himself then did, and he says it twice: "Do this in remembrance of me." Speaking of the bread, he says: "This is my body, which is given for you." And of the cup: "This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is shed for you." In Mark and Matthew these words are phrased thus: "This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many." From these passages, compared with one another, we may gather the following definition of such a Supper: it is a sacred action instituted by Christ himself, in which, at his command, we distribute among ourselves and take bread and wine, in remembrance of his death, in which he gave his body for us and poured out his blood for us, so as to complete and ratify the New Testament. I call the Supper an action, as must be observed in all the other sacraments as well, and we should know that they belong to this kind. Indeed, if you consider all of them in order, you will see that they consist of an action, so much so that if the action ceased, they too would not exist. Who would say that circumcision is circumcision where there is no removal of the foreskin? Likewise, can there be a sacrifice where nothing is sacrificed? Or baptism where no one is baptized or dipped? So there will be no Supper if no one eats or drinks. This must be observed on account of those who understand the sacrament to be bare signs, and who call water, or bread and wine, sacraments even when no one uses them. This opinion has given rise to superstition, so that the signs are worshipped, or at least given what does not belong to them properly but to the whole action. Next, the author of the Supper is named as Christ, who instituted it for us. The matter is bread and wine, consecrated for this use by the word of Christ, not so that they are transubstantiated into his body and blood, but so that they are signs of the true body and blood which he gave for us. The final cause and use is that we distribute and take these among ourselves in grateful remembrance of the death of Christ. And lest this remembrance be idle and useless, he plainly sets out the fruit of his death, when he says that his body was given for us and his blood shed for us, or for many, that is, for the whole multitude of believers, and that the New Testament is contained in it. What that New Testament is, Paul teaches in his Epistle to the Hebrews from Jeremiah, through whom God promises the Jews a new covenant or testament, whose sum he comprehends in these words: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people; and I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more." This testament is called new, even though it is altogether the same as the old one which God once made with Abraham, because after the many defections and faithlessness of the Jewish nation it was renewed again. It is also new because God adopted a new people from the Gentiles, the Mosaic ceremonies being at the same time abolished (as Christ recently promised), and in their place new sacraments have succeeded, greater in power (as Saint Augustine says), better in usefulness, easier in practice, and fewer in number. Yet their use is the same as that of the ancient sacraments. Furthermore, Christ says that he confirmed this New Testament in his own blood, because the death of the testator had to intervene, and God could not die. Therefore he who is the eternal Son of God, co-essential with the Father, died in the humanity he had assumed, so that, according to that testament, a way might lie open to us to the Kingdom of God and the inheritance of heavenly goods. The chief end and use of the Lord's Supper, then, is the memory or remembrance of the death of Christ, by whose merit we have been redeemed from sins, and from their penalty, eternal death. It is not an idle or cold remembrance, such as is usually had of things that have nothing to do with us, but one joined with faith, which lays hold of Christ himself and all salvation in him, so that we are fed and preserved through him to eternal life. Moreover, here is sealed to us the benefit of redemption made through Christ. What Paul once said of circumcision, that it was given to Abraham as a seal of the righteousness of faith, can much more truly be said of the Supper: in it is offered to us, as a pledge and seal, the most certain and infallible assurance of our whole redemption. Other things depend on this end of the Supper, and they are derived from it properly. First, by it we profess our faith in Christ, when we testify that we have been redeemed by his death and blood. Second, it is an external bond by which we are bound together into one body under one head, Christ. Besides, it reminds us of duties in more than one way: that we should not communicate in strange rites, that we should strive for innocence and holiness, that we should constantly guard the liberty won by the blood of Christ, and that we should cherish mutual love. The Lord's Supper is therefore a most busy workshop, in which men of every place and rank find something to do, and which also supplies goads by which we are stirred up to perform our duty. It is profitable to observe carefully this principal end and use of the Supper, together with those things which properly cohere with it, so that we do not admit the inventions of those who make of it whatever they please. For some say that in it Christ is offered for the sins of the living and the dead. Others make of it a viaticum, by which souls are sustained, so that they may more easily bear the burning of the fire of purgatory. There are those who even contend that the body is fed by these signs unto the resurrection. Most dispute about the corporal presence of Christ, as if he had ratified this presence under these signs. This error, which has arisen together with the Papacy, was entirely unknown to antiquity before. It has given rise to very many superstitions, by which the merit of the Son of God is emptied out. Today it is almost the cause of all the contentions which tear the Church into parties, to the great scandal of many, who either fall away from the faith or are held back from coming to it. But what, I beg you, did Christ say of this from which those errors which we have recited could be drawn?

units.la: Scio quidem aduersarios nostros nobis uerba Christi obijcere, qui dixerit: Hoc est corpus meum, &c & in his Tropum omnè negare, eo quod uerbu substantiuu, EST, hunc prorsus excludat. Quasi uero non infinitae locutiones in Scripturis inueniantur, in quibus idem uerbum habetur, etiamsi parabolica sint quae illic dicuntur. Ioseph certe Pharaonis somniu interpretas ait: Septe uaccae pingues sunt septem anni, & septem spicae bonae item sunt septem anni. Et Christus cum de semine locutus esset, quod sulcis mandatur, tande parabola exponens, dicit: Semé est Verbu Dei. Et de seipso idem dicit: Ego sum ostium, ego sum uitis uera, ego sum uia, &c. quae omnia figurate ab eo dicta esse notius est, quam ut demonstrari oporteat. Clamant illi, alia esse horu uerborum ratione, quia ista iam in mortem abitu rus & testamentu conditurus dixerit. At ego nego hanc temporis circunstantia ad Tropum excludendum sufficere. Et quid respondebut illi, si Christu cum iam morti magis uicinus esset, & in re nō minus seria Tropicis locutionibus usum esse ostendero? Nonne admonte Oliuarū in summo agone constitutus clamauit: Pater si uis, transfer poculu hoc a me? Quis in poculi uocabulo, quo crucis supplicium denotat, Tropu nō agnoscit? Quid quod ia expiraturus alta uoce dicit: Pater, in manus tuas depono spiritu meum? In quibus uerbis si Tropu nullu uelimus agnoscere, necesse erit, ut cu Anthropomorphitis Deu fingamus, qui humana forma constet, et pedes atq; manus habeat. Nihil ergo dicut qui hoc praetextu fucu facere conantur imperitioribus, quod haec postrema Christi uerba sint, & proinde non aliter quam secundum litera accipi debeant. Quin potius in totius actionis huius argumentum respicere nos conuenit, & mox patebit, de Sacramento hic agi, et proinde locutiones quoq; istas esse Sacramentales, quarum proprium est, ut signa rei signatae nomina accipiant, quod alibi per Circuncisionis, epuli paschalis, sacrificiorum, arcae & Baptismi exempla demonstrauimus. Nec ulla ratio probabilis apparet, quae nos in Coenae uerbis ab usitata locutionum eiusmodi interpretatione discedere cogat: quin potius multa sunt, quae nos monent, ut illa per Tropum exponantur.
units.tr: I know that our opponents throw the words of Christ back at us, when he said, "This is my body," and so on, and they deny that any trope is present in them, because the substantive verb IS excludes it altogether. As if innumerable expressions were not found in Scripture where the same verb occurs, even when what is said there is parabolic. Joseph, for instance, interpreting Pharaoh's dream, says: "The seven fat cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are likewise seven years." And when Christ had spoken of the seed that is sown in furrows, at last explaining the parable he says: "The seed is the Word of God." And of himself he says the same: "I am the door, I am the true vine, I am the way," and so on. That all these things were said by him figuratively is too well known to need proof. They cry out that these words have a different character, because he spoke them as one about to depart to death and about to make his testament. But I deny that this circumstance of time is enough to exclude a trope. And what would they answer if I show that Christ, when he was already closer to death, and in a matter no less serious, used tropical expressions? Did he not, placed in the great contest on the Mount of Olives, cry out: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me"? Who does not recognise a trope in the word cup, by which he denotes the punishment of the cross? What of the fact that, about to expire, he says with a loud voice: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit"? If we were unwilling to recognise any trope in these words, we would be obliged, with the Anthropomorphites, to imagine a God who has human form and has feet and hands. Those who attempt to deceive the unlearned by this pretext therefore say nothing when they claim that these are Christ's last words and so must be taken no other way than according to the letter. Rather, we ought to look to the argument of the whole action, and it will soon be clear that a sacrament is being treated here, and therefore that these expressions too are sacramental, the property of which is that the signs take the names of the things signified. We have shown this elsewhere by the examples of circumcision, the paschal feast, the sacrifices, the ark and baptism. Nor does any probable reason appear that compels us to depart in the words of the Supper from the customary interpretation of expressions of this kind. On the contrary, there are many things that warn us to explain them by a trope.

units.la: Inter quae non postremum censeri debet quod ex illis ipsis uerbis petitur argumentum. Nam si rigido sensu secundum literam accipi deberent, uel si a sensu litterali discedere nefas esset, nullam procul dubio in illis diuersitate admisissent Euangelistae, sed ijsdem syllabis ea nobis descripsissent. Atqui neque ijsdem uocabulis neque ijsdem syllabis in illis recitandis usi sunt, & aliqui nonnulla omiserunt, quae ab alijs ponuntur. Ergo non tam το ρητον quam uerborum illorum sensum spectandum esse. dum esse putarunt. Quod ut manifestius fit, illos inter se conferemus. Apud Marcum & Matthaeum de pane dicitur: Hoc est corpus meum. His Lucas addit: Quod pro nobis traditur. Hanc ipsam uerò particulam Paulus aliter exprimit, dicens: Quod pro nobis frangitur. Atqui corpus Christi neq; fractum esse, neq; frangi debuisse, Ioannes multis testatur. Itaq; frangendi uerbum Paulus per Metonymiam posuit, & de corpore dixit, quod in eius symbolo fieri solet, quando in Cœna frangitur panis, & distribuitur. In poculi uerbis manifestior est diuersitas. Matthaeus enim illa sic refert: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est Noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in peccatorum remissionem. Marcus idem plane dicit, omittit tamen quod de peccatorum remissione ille adiecit. Adde quod uterq; hoc loco subijcit, quod Lucas Christum in initio epuli Paschalis dixisse scribit, cùm ille accepto poculo solenniter benediceret: Dico enim vobis, me non bibiturum de fructu vitis, usquequo Regnum Dei venerit. Idem Christi verba de poculo sic exprimit: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine, qui pro vobis effunditur. En de poculo, non de vino loquitur, in qua locutione Metonymia est manifestissima. Deinde poculum hoc sive vinum non suum sanguinem, sed Nouum testamentum esse dicit, quod in suo sanguine ratum fit atq; impleatur. Vbi rursus effectum aut fructus sanguinis pro ipso sanguine ponitur. Quid ergo hic dicemus? Clamabimus ne, verba esse expressa, nuda, simplicia, rotunda, quae non aliter quam sonent accipi debeant, & in quibus sensum altiorem inquirere nefas sit? Id uero dicere non finit Euangelistarum authoritas, qui illa alij aliter reddiderunt. Num uero aliquos ex illis memoria lapsos esse dicemus? At hoc dicendo uniuersam Iesu Christi historiam in dubium uocabimus. Num igitur falsarios esse nociferabimur, qui Christum mendacij arguere & testamentum Filij Dei violare ausi fuerint? quibus conuitijs nos hodie aduersarij nostri proscindunt. Id dicant, qui cum pietate rationem quoq; & pudorem omnem exuerunt. Quid ergo reliquum est, quàm ut in illa diuersitate Spiritus sancti consilium agnoscamus, qui cùm lites olim circa hanc causam exorituras non potuerit ignorare, ista sic conscribi voluit, ut cogeremur animos à litera verborum & symbolis panis & vini altius in meditationem mortis Christi euehere, & huius fructum atq; effectum considerare, qui per illorum usum legitimum nobis obsignatur? Quod si uero Euangelistis licuit ex Spiritus consilio ita loqui & scribere, quis bonus obsecro nobis vitio vertat, si eum sensum verborum Christi proferamus, quem Euangelistae nobis tradiderunt?
units.tr: Among these, the argument taken from the words themselves ought not to be counted least. For if they had to be taken in a rigid sense according to the letter, or if it were wrong to depart from the literal sense, the Evangelists would undoubtedly not have admitted any difference among them, but would have described them for us in the same syllables. But in fact they did not use the same words or the same syllables in reciting them, and some omitted things that others include. Therefore we must look not so much to the [τὸ ῥητόν] letter as to the sense of those words, which they judged ought to be considered. To make this clearer, let us compare them with one another. In Mark and Matthew it is said of the bread: "This is my body." Luke adds: "which is given for you." But Paul expresses this very phrase differently, saying: "which is broken for you." Yet John testifies at length that the body of Christ was neither broken nor ought to have been broken. Therefore Paul used the verb "to break" by metonymy, and spoke of the body in terms of what is usually done with its sign, when in the Supper the bread is broken and distributed. The difference is more evident in the words about the cup. For Matthew reports them thus: "This is my blood, which is of the New Testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins." Mark says the same thing plainly, but omits what Matthew added about the remission of sins. Add that both of them, at this point, subjoin what Luke writes that Christ said at the beginning of the paschal feast, when, taking the cup, he solemnly blessed it: "For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes." Luke also expresses Christ's words about the cup thus: "This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Behold, he speaks of the cup, not of the wine, a figure of speech in which metonymy is most evident. Then he says that this cup, or wine, is not his blood but the New Testament, which is ratified and fulfilled in his blood. Here again the effect or fruit of the blood is put for the blood itself. What then shall we say here? Shall we cry out that the words are express, bare, simple, plain, which ought to be taken no other way than they sound, and in which it is wrong to seek a higher sense? The authority of the Evangelists does not allow us to say that, since they rendered these words differently. Shall we say that some of them slipped in memory? But by saying this we would call the whole history of Jesus Christ into doubt. Shall we then proclaim that those who dared to convict Christ of lying and to violate the testament of the Son of God are forgers? With such reproaches our opponents today tear us apart. Let those say this who have cast off with piety also reason and all shame. What remains, then, except that in this difference we acknowledge the counsel of the Holy Spirit, who, since he could not have been ignorant that disputes about this matter would arise, willed these things to be written so that we would be compelled to raise our minds from the letter of the words and the signs of bread and wine to a higher meditation on the death of Christ, and to consider its fruit and effect, which is sealed to us through the lawful use of those signs? But if the Evangelists were permitted by the counsel of the Spirit to speak and write in this way, who, I ask, good sir, would find fault with us if we set forth the sense of Christ's words that the Evangelists have handed down to us?

units.la: Accusant nos multi, quòd noui dogmatis authores simus, & Berengarij errore iam olim damna rum postliminio reuocemus. Id uero dicunt, qui aut ueteres atq; Orthodoxos patres nunquam legerunt, aut praeiudicio suo fascinati eas modo ex illorum scriptis locutiones excerpunt, quibus illi interdum ad Christi exemplum usi sunt, ut Cœnae mysticae dignitate populo commendarent, nō ut carnale eius praesentiam aut Cyclopica χρεοφαγίαν in mysterio hoc saluberrimo statuerent. Quod illorum libri lucu lentissimè testantur, in quibus diserè docent, non ipsissimū Christi corpus, sed eius symbolum siue figurā in Cœna nobis exhiberi. Tertullianus certè aduersus Marcionē de veritate corporis Christi disputās, inter alia hoc argumento utitur. Christus acceptū panē & distributū discipulis corpus suū illum fecit, Hoc est corpus meum dicendo, id est, FIGVRA CORPORIS MEI. Figura autē nō fuisset, nisi veritatis esset corpus. Cæterùm uacua res, quod est phantasma, corpus capere non posset. Idem aduersus eundem Marcionē lib.1. pane corpus Christi repraesentari dicit, quo uerbo D. Hieronymus quoq; in suis Comentarijs in Matthaeū usus est. D. Ambrosius item praecipuum in Cœna esse dicit, memoriā redemptionis nostrae, neq; praesentiā corporalis mentionē facit, quādo priorem Pauli ad Corinth. interpretatur. Et mox clarius mentē suam exponēs, subijcit: Quia enim morte Domini liberati sumus, huius rei memores in edēdo & potando, carnē & sanguinē, quae pro nobis oblata sunt, SIGNIFICAMVS. Rursus ibidē de Testamento differens, scribit: Testamentū ergo sanguine constitutū est, quia beneficij diuini sanguis testis est: in cuius TYPVM nos calicem MYSTICVM sanguinis ad tuitionē corporis & animae nostrae percipimus. Ex D. Augustino infinita huius generis testimonia producere possemus, sed sufficiat quod cōtra Adimantū Manichaei discipulum Cap.12. tale habetur: Nō dubitauit Dominus dicere, Hoc est corpus meum, cùm SIGNVM daret corporis sui. Quis uerò unquā inter ueteres inuētus fuit, qui patribus istis propter hasce uerborum Christi interpretationes litem moueri t, cùm in alijs dogmatibus crebrae inter illos cōtentiones exortae sint? Fuit ergo haec communis Ecclesiae doctrina, quā & nos hodie profitemur, neq; nos eius sententiae pudere potest, quam & corporis Christi veritas, & eiusdem incarnationis præcipua causa & ipsius Cœnæ finis proprius confirmant (ut alibi copiosius à nobis demonstratum est) & quam tot Martyres cum veteres tum recentiores etiam hisce nouissimis temporibus sanguine suo roborauerunt. Neq; eorum calumnias multum moramur, qui nos inania symbola habere, & Christum ipsum à Cœna sua excludere aiunt. Cur enim inania aut inutilia symbola dicantur, quæ uera et irrefragabilia redemptionis nostræ sigilla sunt, et id fidelissimè præstat, cuius ergò illa Christus instituit? Quomodo autem à Cœna sua Christum excludimus, qui actionem hanc prosus inutilem nobis fore fatemur, nisi illum uera fide apprehensum in illam adferamus? Vtinam uero omnes de eo potius soliciti essent, ut Christum intra animos suos agentem haberent, quàm ut præsentiam eius corporalem in pane assererent. Quis enim illius in pane usus fuerit, quando neq; anima hominis cibo corporeo ali, neq; Christus qui panis ille vitæ est, ore corporis percipi aut dentibus manducari potest? Num uerò illud Pauli ignoramus: Regnum Dei non est cibus & potus, sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto?
units.tr: Many accuse us of being the authors of a new doctrine, and of bringing back, by a kind of postliminy, the errors of Berengar long since condemned. But those who say this have either never read the ancient and orthodox Fathers, or, bewitched by their own prejudice, pick out only those expressions from their writings which those Fathers sometimes used, following the example of Christ, to commend to the people the dignity of the mystical Supper, and not to establish a carnal presence of him, or a Cyclopean eating of flesh [χρεοφαγία] in this most wholesome mystery. Their books bear clear witness to this, in which they plainly teach that it is not the very body of Christ itself, but its symbol or figure, that is exhibited to us in the Supper. Tertullian, certainly, when disputing against Marcion concerning the truth of the body of Christ, uses among other arguments this one: Christ, taking the bread and distributing it to the disciples, made it his body, saying, "This is my body," that is, "THE FIGURE OF MY BODY." But it would not have been a figure unless it were the body of the truth. Otherwise an empty thing, which is a phantasm, could not hold a body. The same Tertullian, against the same Marcion, book 1, says that the body of Christ is represented by the bread, a word which Saint Jerome also used in his Commentaries on Matthew. Saint Ambrose likewise says that the chief thing in the Supper is the memory of our redemption, and he makes no mention of a bodily presence when he expounds the former epistle of Paul to the Corinthians. And presently, explaining his mind more clearly, he adds: "For since we have been freed by the death of the Lord, remembering this in eating and drinking, we SIGNIFY the flesh and blood which were offered for us." Again, in the same place, discussing the Testament, he writes: "The testament therefore was established in blood, because the blood is the witness of the divine benefit; and in its TYPE we receive the MYSTICAL cup of blood for the preservation of our body and soul." From Saint Augustine we could bring forward endless testimonies of this kind, but it is enough that in Against Adimantus, the disciple of Manichaeus, chapter 12, the following is found: "The Lord did not hesitate to say, 'This is my body,' when he gave the SIGN of his body." But who was ever found among the ancients who stirred up a quarrel against these Fathers on account of these interpretations of Christ's words, when among other doctrines there have been frequent contentions among them? This, then, was the common doctrine of the Church, which we too profess today; nor can we be ashamed of that opinion, which both the truth of the body of Christ and the chief cause of his incarnation and the proper end of the Supper itself confirm (as we have shown more fully elsewhere), and which so many martyres, both ancient and more recent, even in these latest times, have strengthened with their blood. Nor do we much dwell on the calumnies of those who say that we hold empty symbols and exclude Christ himself from his own Supper. For why should the symbols be called empty or useless, when they are true and irrefutable seals of our redemption, and perform most faithfully that for whose sake Christ instituted them? And how do we exclude Christ from his own Supper, when we confess that the action would be altogether useless to us unless we bring him into it, apprehended by true faith? Would that all men were rather anxious about this, that they might have Christ acting within their souls, than that they assert his bodily presence in the bread. For what use would there be of him in the bread, when neither the soul of man is nourished by corporeal food, nor can Christ, who is that bread of life, be received by the mouth of the body or chewed by the teeth? Surely we do not forget that saying of Paul: "The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit"?

units.la: Ritus & ordo Cœnæ. Quia uerò in Ecclesia Paulus omnia decenter & certo ordine fieri uult, quo ritu ac ordine Cœnam suam discipulis Christus tradiderit, uidendum est. Nam in eo etiam à multis peccatur, qui mysteria tanta uel negligentius tractant, uelut authoritate aliquâ ipsis concilient, ea alieno & asciticio fuco, idest, ceremoniis ex suo cerebro conflictis, & apparatu superbo magis quàm sancto exornant. At Christus simplicitati, sobrietati & temperantiæ studuit consultò, ut nos in res ipsas potius, quàm in ea quæ sub sensus cadunt intentos esse doceret. Conuenit enim cum discipulis ut pascha perageret, & ideò cœtum hunc sacrum fuisse constat. Inter cœnandum de sua morte & redemptione humani generis, deq; hominis Christiani officio diligenter & prolixè concionatus est. Inde panè & uinû accepit, quæ ut apud omnes gentes concordiæ & unitatis symbola fuerunt semper: ita huic negotio optimè conueniunt, quia totum mortis eius fructum adumbrant, & ipsum docent panem atq; potum illum uiuificum esse, quo nos aduitam æternam pasci atq; seruari oporteat. Panè cum gratiarum actione acceptum fregit, & fractum discipulis distribuit di serte iubens, ut illum accipiant et edant. Eadem ratione & ritu poculû quoq; ijsdem porrexit, & peculiari mandato præcepit, ut ex illo omnes bibât. Nimirum quòd non posset ignorare illorum audaciâ, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus sacrilega impietate calicè sacrum ex Cœna abstulerunt laicis. Quia autè bis interea dixit, Hoc facite in mei recordationè, utiq; suo exemplo nobis præire voluit, neq; nos in huius mysterij actione quicquâ aliud facere debemus, quàm quod illum fecisse constat. Hic ergo Cœnæ ritus & ordo est optimus, ut in cœtu sacro habeatur cum publica gratiarû actione, ut hæc concio sacra præcedat, qua hominû mentes ad percipienda hæc mysteria excitentur: ut præter panem & uinâ nulla alia adhibeantur symbola: ut panis frangatur in Ecclesiæ conspectu, unum quoq; in poculû infundatur: ut minister, qui Christiu ces obit, illa singulis exhibeat, ipsi uerò manibus suis eadè accipiant, edant & bibant. Quoad supel-lectilem sacrâ, non dubium est, Christum, qui à luxu & ambitione alienissimus fuit, hìc quoq; modum nequaquam excessisse. Sufficiat ergo nobis etiam, ut munda sint omnia, splendorem uerò sumptuosum & qui ostentationi potius quàm pietati seruit, iis relinquamus, qui religionem quæstu & externo ornatu metiuntur. Etenim quæ Veteris Ecclesiæ frugalitas in uasis sacris & mysteriorum omnium dispensatione fuerit, omnes norunt, qui historias & patrum scripta uel obiter inspexère. Nec est, quod illa alicui sordeat. Vt enim auro non commendantur quæ auro non emuntur (ut Ambrosius ait) ita ritus iste Cœnæ, quæ nobis Christus tradidit, sub vili specie mysteria maxima et salluberrima celat, quorû consideratio nobis non minus necessaria quàm utilis atque iucunda est. Testatur enim Christû nostrû esse, et cũ bonis suis omnibus ex æquo ad omnes pertinere, qui sacra hæc symbola cum fide percipiût. Ideò nos peccatores esse admonet, & pœnitentiæ seruit, quãdo panis fractione testamur nos ex eorû numero esse, quorû peccata mortis eius merito expiari oportuit. Similiter fidè nobis commendat, quæ sola os illud est, quo piorû animæ Christo uescuntur. Adhæc charitatis officium adumbrat, cuius præcipuû opus est, ut singuli alijs quoq; Christû propinent, & quoscunq; possunt in eiusdem salutis societate attrahant. Hæc & alia huius generis, quæ alibi fusius exposuimus, si cui sordent, eâ quòd ornatu & ceremoniis theatricis non commendentur, næ ille animum prodit iniquissimum meriti atq; beneficiorum Christi æstimatorem, & dignus est, qui in Antichristi sordibus computrescat, qui Deum suum Mayzim auro & argento colere solet, sicuti de illo Daniel olim uaticinatus est. Restat ut de officio fidelium quædam dicamus, quo eos in Cœna hac mystica quàm maximè fungi decet. Admonet de illo Christus, dicens: Hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Qua voce non otiosam & perfunctoriam mortis Christi memoriam, sed cum fide & gratiarum actione coniunctam intelligi, supra diximus. Et quia circa hanc finis & cardo Cœnæ præcipuus versatur, Paulus verba ista diligentius explicans, ait: quotiescunq; ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annuntiate, donec venerit. Mortis vocabulo omnia comprehenduntur, quæ Dei Filius pro nobis fecit aut passus est. Nam ut mori posset, carnem mortalem illam assumere oportuit, ut ita per mortem suam aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est Diabolum. Attamen non satis erat eum mori, nisi morte deucta simul cœlos nobis aperiret, qui propter peccatum nobis clausi erant. Quare resurrectione etiam opus erat & ascensione in cœlos, de quibus suo loco dicetur. Hæc omnia in præsenti Christus comprehendit, quando Cœnam hanc ad sui recordationem peragere iubet. Simul autem gratiarum actionem & solennem beneficiorum suorum prædicationē nobis commendat, quam proprium hominis Christiani officium esse, uetustissimi quiq; scriptores testantur. Quia enim ad suum cultum Deus hominem condidit, huius gloria nobis ante omnia curæ esse debet. Ea autem non alio officio magis prouehitur atq; illustratur, quàm publica operum et beneficiorum eius commemoratione. Ideò hanc passim sanctiuouent, & id sacrificium Deo gratissimum esse Dauid testatur, & quidem acceptius multò, quàm si quis illi bouem cornibus & ungulis præstantem offerat. Et huc illud Petri referri debet, qui nos Dei peculium factos esse scribit, ut eius virtutes prædicemus, qui nos uocauit ex tenebris in admirabilem suam lucem. Quamuis autem hoc perpetuum sit hominis Christiani officium, in quo omnes etiam uitæ nostræ actiones occupatas esse conuenit, hic tamen solennis gratiarum actio commendatur, cuius usus & meditatio nos ad faciendum officium magis extimulet. Quæ causa est, quòd ea pij uehementer delectantur, & cùm suæ infirmitatis sibi ipsis probè sint conscij, minimè superuacaneum esse putant hoc Cœnæ mysticæ exercitium, sed eo quandocunque possunt, magna cum alacritate utuntur. Quia uerò ijdem intelligunt, Deum non à quouis laudari uelle, neque omnes ad prædicandum eius uirtutes esse idoneos, seipsos (quod Paulus monuit) diligenter probant siue examinant, ne uel hypocritica & falsa nominis Christiani professione, uel scelerata professionis istius prophanatione Dei oculos offendant. De quibus cùm alibi plura dixerimus, breuius nunc eadem perstrinxisse sufficiat. Discant singuli dilectionem Dei plus quàm paternam agnoscere, qui Filium suum Iesum Christum pro nobis in mortem tradidit. Simul autem huius bonitatem & ardentissimum nostræ salutis studium agnoscant, qui redemptionis nostræ per ipsum factæ memoriam perpetuam sacro hoc & solenni epulo consecrare dignatus est. Ad id ergo accedamus uera fide instructi, ut sicuti ore nostro sacratissima hæc corporis & sanguinis eius symbola accipimus: ita per illam ipsum Christum apprehendamus, & per illum pascamur atq; recreemur ad uitam æternam. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The rite and order of the Supper. Since Paul wants everything in the Church done decently and in good order, we must consider in what rite and order Christ handed over his Supper to the disciples. Many people sin here, by handling such great mysteries carelessly, or by trying to recommend them with some authority of their own, dressing them up with a borrowed and artificial coloring, that is, with ceremonies devised from their own brains and with a proud display rather than a holy one. But Christ deliberately aimed at simplicity, sobriety and moderation, so that he might teach us to attend to the things themselves rather than to what falls under the senses. He came together with his disciples to celebrate the Passover, and it is clear that this was a holy assembly. During the meal he preached carefully and at length about his own death, the redemption of mankind and the duty of a Christian. Then he took bread and wine, which have always been symbols of concord and unity among all nations, and so they suit this matter very well, since they foreshadow the whole fruit of his death and teach that the bread and drink are life-giving, by which we ought to be fed and preserved for eternal life. He took the bread with thanksgiving, broke it, and distributed it to the disciples, commanding them clearly to take and eat it. In the same way and with the same rite he also handed the cup to them, and by a special command ordered that all should drink from it. Clearly he knew of the boldness of those who in these latter times, in sacrilegious impiety, have taken the sacred cup away from the laity in the Supper. And because he said twice in the meantime, "Do this in remembrance of me," he certainly wanted to go before us by his example, and we ought to do nothing in the action of this mystery other than what it is clear he did. So this is the best rite and order of the Supper: that it be held in a sacred assembly with public thanksgiving; that a holy sermon precede it, by which the minds of men are stirred to receive these mysteries; that no other symbols be used besides bread and wine; that the bread be broken in the sight of the Church and the wine likewise poured into one cup; and that the minister who performs the Lord's office give these to each person, while they themselves take, eat and drink with their own hands. As for the sacred furnishings, there is no doubt that Christ, who was most remote from luxury and ambition, did not exceed due measure here either. It is enough for us, then, that all things be clean, and let us leave sumptuous splendor, which serves display rather than piety, to those who measure religion by profit and external ornament. For everyone who has glanced even briefly at the histories and the writings of the Fathers knows what the frugality of the Ancient Church was in its sacred vessels and in the administration of all the mysteries. Nor is there any reason for anyone to scorn it. For as things that are not bought with gold are not commended by gold (as Ambrose says), so this rite of the Supper which Christ handed down to us hides the greatest and most healthful mysteries under a cheap appearance, and the consideration of these is no less necessary and useful and pleasant for us. For it testifies that Christ is ours, and that with all his goods he belongs equally to all who receive these sacred symbols in faith. Hence it admonishes us that we are sinners and serves repentance, when by the breaking of the bread we bear witness that we are of the number of those whose sins had to be expiated by the merit of his death. Likewise it commends faith to us, which alone is the mouth by which the souls of the godly feed on Christ. Besides this it foreshadows the duty of love, whose principal work is that each person should also offer Christ to others and draw as many as they can into the fellowship of the same salvation. If anyone scorns these and other things of this kind, which we have set out more fully elsewhere, because they are not commended by theatrical ornament and ceremonies, he betrays a mind most unjust in valuing the merit and benefits of Christ, and he deserves to rot in the filth of Antichrist, who is accustomed to worship his god Mayzim with gold and silver, as Daniel once prophesied concerning him. It remains that we say something about the duty of the faithful, which it is most fitting that they perform in this mystical Supper. Christ admonishes them about it, saying: "Do this in remembrance of me." By this word, as we said above, is understood not an idle and perfunctory remembrance of Christ's death, but one joined with faith and thanksgiving. And because the chief aim and hinge of the Supper turns on this, Paul, explaining these words more carefully, says: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." By the word death are comprehended all the things which the Son of God did or suffered for us. For in order to be able to die, he had to assume that mortal flesh, so that by his death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil. Yet it was not enough for him to die, unless, having overcome death, he also opened for us the heavens, which had been closed to us on account of sin. Therefore there was also need of resurrection and of ascension into heaven, which will be spoken of in its place. Christ comprehends all these things in the present command, when he bids us celebrate this Supper in remembrance of him. At the same time he commends to us thanksgiving and the solemn proclamation of his benefits, which the most ancient writers all testify is the proper duty of a Christian. For since God made man for his own worship, the glory of God ought above all to be our care. Now this glory is advanced and made illustrious by no duty more than by the public commemoration of his works and benefits. Therefore the Scriptures everywhere sanctify this, and David testifies that such a sacrifice is most pleasing to God, and far more acceptable than if someone offered him an ox excelling in horns and hooves. And to this should be referred that saying of Peter, who writes that we have been made a people of God's own possession, so that we may proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light. Although this is the continual duty of a Christian, in which all the actions of our life ought to be engaged, yet here a solemn thanksgiving is commended, whose practice and meditation may spur us more to perform the duty. This is why the godly take great delight in it, and since they are well aware of their own weakness, they think this exercise of the mystical Supper is by no means superfluous, but use it whenever they can with great eagerness. But since they understand that God does not wish to be praised by just anyone, and that not all are fit to proclaim his virtues, they diligently prove or examine themselves (as Paul warned), lest they offend God's eyes either by a hypocritical and false profession of the Christian name, or by a wicked profanation of that profession. Since we have said more about these matters elsewhere, it is enough now to have touched on them briefly. Let each person learn to recognize the love of God, which is more than paternal, who handed over his Son Jesus Christ to death for us. At the same time let them acknowledge his goodness and his most ardent zeal for our salvation, who has deigned to consecrate in this sacred and solemn feast a perpetual memory of the redemption made for us through him. Let us therefore approach it instructed in true faith, so that just as we receive these most sacred symbols of his body and blood with our mouth, so through them we may lay hold of Christ himself, and be fed and refreshed by him to eternal life. To him be blessing, honor, glory and power forever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCV.
units.tr: Homily 195.

units.la: Veruntamen ecce manus eius qui me prodit, mecum est in mensa. Et Filius quidem hominis, prout definitum est, vadit: veruntamen væ homini illi, per quem proditur. Tunc ipsi cœperunt mutuò quærere inter se, quis nam esset ex ipsis qui hoc facturus esset. Orta est autē etiam contentio inter eos, quis eorum videretur esse maior. Ipse verò dixit eis: Reges gentium dominantur eis: & qui potestatem habent in eas, benefici vocantur: vos autem non ita. Sed qui maximus est inter vos, sit sicut qui minimus est: & qui princeps est, sicut qui ministrat.
units.tr: "But behold, the hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table. And truly the Son of man goeth, as it was determined: but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed." Then they began to enquire among themselves which of them it was that should do this. And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. And he said unto them: "The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve."

units.la: Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, in ultima Cœna, non solùm de sua morte & eius fructu multis disseruit (ut Ioannes Euangelista testatur) uerumeriam huius memoriam solenni ritu commendaut, Cœna nimirum mystica, quam ad nouissimum usq; illius aduentum in Ecclesia perpetuò retineri & exerceri debere. Paulus in priori ad Corinthios diserte docet. Est ea redemptionis nostræ & salutis in illo exhibitæ certissimum sigillum, nosque simul de omnibus admonet, quæ in toto salutis negotio nobis obseruatu & factu necessaria sunt. Quia uero ad illam cum duodecim discipu-lis discubuit, quos multis uitijs obnoxios fuisse constat, & inter quos Iudas quoq; numeratur, scelera-tissimus proditor, nō immeritō aliquis miretur, quid cum hoc simul & cum illis factum sit, quidq; ho-die etiam fieri debeat, si quando in externam Ecclesiæ societatem et sacrorum communionem irre-punt homines fraudulenti, aut etiam flagitijs infames? Commodè ergo nouam narrationem Lucas subijcit, qua exponit, quid cum Iuda fecerit Christus, qui deuoto ad omnem impietatē animo in pro-prium exitium ruebat, quid item cum reliquis discipulis, quos adhuc curabiles esse nouerat. Estq; tra-ctatio haec multis nominibus consideratu dignissima, ut Christi exemplum secuti, neq; indulgentia ni-mia scandalis patrocinemur, quibus Ecclesiæ ordo atque disciplina turbatur: neq; nimia seueritate aut importuno rigore eos abstterreamus, qui institutione & consolatione opus habent.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, at the last Supper, not only discoursed at length about his death and its fruit (as John the Evangelist testifies), but also commended the memory of it by a solemn rite, namely the mystical Supper, which he willed should be constantly retained and celebrated in the Church until his final coming. Paul teaches this plainly in his first letter to the Corinthians. It is the most certain seal of our redemption and of the salvation exhibited in him, and it reminds us at the same time of all the things that are necessary for us to observe and do in the whole business of salvation. But since he reclined at that table with the twelve disciples, who are known to have been liable to many faults, and among whom Judas, a most wicked traitor, was also counted, one may not unreasonably wonder what was done with him and with them, and what ought to be done today as well, if at any time deceitful men, or men infamous for their crimes, creep into the external fellowship of the Church and the communion of the sacred rites. Luke therefore fittingly adds a new narrative, in which he sets out what Christ did with Judas, who was rushing to his own destruction with a mind devoted to every impiety, and likewise what he did with the other disciples, whom he knew could still be healed. And this account is most worthy of consideration for many reasons, so that, following Christ's example, we neither lend our support to scandals by excessive indulgence, by which the order and discipline of the Church is thrown into confusion, nor frighten away by excessive severity or unseasonable rigour those who need instruction and comfort.

units.la: Et primò quidē Iudam ille aggreditur, in qua parte Lucas breuior est, quòd eam ab alijs copio-sius descriptā esse sciret. Ioannes actionis huius occasionē annotauit, nimirū quòd spiritu turbatus dixerit, uel potius testatus sit: Amen dico uobis, quòdunus ex uobis prodet me. Quā animi turbatio nem nostèr quoq; nō omnino dissimulat, quando narratione hanc cum Cœnæ institutione coniungens, illum quasi ex abrupto dixisse scribit. Veruntamē ecce manus eius qui me prodit, mecū est in mensa. Vbi nemini mirum uideri debet, Christum toto animo turbatū fuisse, quando & uerum hominē no-strisq; infirmitatibus (solo peccato excepto) obnoxium fuisse scimus, et nunc multiplex dolendi causa fuit, qua animus tam paternæ gloriæ quàm humanæ salutis studio flagrans non poterat non commo-ueri. Nam ut nihil dicamus de atrocissimi supplicij recordatione, quæ alibi eum conturbauit, dolo-rem illi mouit detestabilis ingratitudo Iudæ, qua is sibi exitiū accersebat. Qui enim toto animo com-motus fuit, quando populum instar ouium absq; pastore uagari uidebat, procul dubio discipuli dome-stici interitum sine gemitu uidere non potuit. Qui item alibi scandalorum authoribus uæ illud hor-rendum denuntiauit, non potuit non turbari, quando scandalum, quo nullum unquā in orbe scelera-tius uisum fuit, ex sua familia (ut sic loquar) enasciturū esse cogitabat. Debet autē diligenter obser-uari in Christo hæc animi turbatio, ut discamus, quàm illi displiceant homines nequam & hypocri-tæ, quibus lusus est Sacramentis eius abuti et publica scandala præbere ecclesijs. Imitemur præterea nos quoq; illius exemplum. Nisi enim turbemur aliorum impietate & nequitia, per quos religionem prophanari, & Ecclesiam offendi cernimus, satis constat nos à Christi Spiritu nimis esse alienos.
units.tr: And first he addresses Judas, and in this part Luke is briefer, because he knew it had been described more fully by the others. John noted the occasion of this action, namely that Jesus, troubled in spirit, said, or rather bore witness: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." Luke does not wholly conceal this disturbance of mind either, when he links the narrative with the institution of the Supper and writes that he spoke as if abruptly: "But behold, the hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table." Here no one should think it strange that Christ was troubled in his whole soul, since we know he was a true man, subject to our infirmities (sin alone excepted), and there was now a manifold cause for grief, so that a soul burning with zeal both for his Father's glory and for human salvation could not but be moved. For, to say nothing of the remembrance of the most atrocious suffering, which troubled him elsewhere, the detestable ingratitude of Judas, by which he was bringing ruin upon himself, caused him pain. For he who was moved in his whole being when he saw the people wandering like sheep without a shepherd, certainly could not see the destruction of a domestic disciple without groaning. Likewise he who elsewhere pronounced that terrible woe upon the authors of scandals could not but be disturbed, when he foresaw that a scandal, of a kind never seen in the world more wicked, was about to arise, as I may put it, from his own household. This disturbance of mind in Christ ought to be carefully observed, so that we may learn how much wicked men and hypocrites displease him, those who make sport of his sacraments and give public scandal to the churches. Moreover, let us also imitate his example.
