For unless we are troubled by the impiety and wickedness of others, through whom we see religion profaned and the Church offended, it is quite clear that we are too far removed from the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum etsi iustissimā doloris causam haberet, & optimo iure posset in Iudā uerbis acerbiori-bus inuehi, sic tamen cum illo agit, ut adhuc eius saluti atq; honori consultum cupiat. Primùm enim in genere scelus perstringit, ne Iudas hoc illū latere putaret: Vnus (inquit) ex uobis prodet me. Vel Manus eius qui me prodit, mecum est in mensa. Deinde quia illum minus cōmoueri sciebat, propius ferit, & simul perfidiæ istius atrocitatē exprimit (ut Marcus annotauit) dicēs: Vnus ex duodecim, qui intingit mecum in catinum. Quò etiam facit, quod apud Ioannem Dauidis testimoniū de simili perfidia conquerentis adducit: Qui edit mecum panē, suffulit aduersus me calcaneum suum. Tertiò quia nec sic quidem aliquid proficiebat apud contumacē et obstinatæ nequitiæ hominē, excusationē o-mnē ei adimit: & quia tales, cùm Deũ prorsus ludibrio habeant, sub eius tamen prouidentia scelerū suorū latibula quærunt, magna cū grauitate pronuntiat: Filius quidē hominis, prout definitū est, ua dit: Veruntamē uæ homini illi, per quē proditur. Ita nimirū admonens, Deum, qui rerū euentus suæ prouidentiæ decretis cōprehendit, et impiorū quoq; prauis conatibus ad suorū operū executionē bene utitur, simul illis pænas cōstituisse, quibus eorū impietas puniatur. Postremò, cum discipulis tãti sce-leris atrocitate attonitis, & quis nam proditor ille esset interrogantibus, ipse etiam Iudas (ut apud Matth.habetur) num se illū esse diceret, quærere auderet, apertius illum arguit, dicens: Tu dixisti. Et mox (ut Ioannes narrat) adiecit: Quod facis, fac citò. Non quidē iubens aut hortans, ut concep-tū animo facinus exequi pergeret: sed potius suo illū, ut merebatur, arbitrio permittens, ut quando incurabilis erat, protinus inde facesseret, ut impietatis suæ mēsura impleta, tandē digna illi præmia reportaret. Sunt ergo hæc indignantis uerba, quibus parentes boni interdum filios rebelles et incura-biles abs se reijciunt, utpote indignos quibus cum porrò altercentur. Et sensit intra animū suum Iu-das diuinæ comminationis uim. Mox enim foras se proripuit, ut illis se coniungeret, cum quibus an-tea aduersus Christum conspirauerat. Quia tamen discipulorum tanta fuit stupiditas, ut nihil huius intelligerent, intelligerent, Ioanni prius rem apertius indicauit, cui offa intincta & Iudæ tradita proditore quasi digito ostendit, nimirū ut per illum postea alij discipuli de toto isto negotio edocerentur. Est autem tota hæc tractatio admodum memorabilis, eò quòd multa contineat, quorum cognitio nobis hodie etiam non tam utilis quàm necessaria est.
units.tr: Yet although he had a most just cause for grief, and might rightly have assailed Judas in harsher words, he nevertheless deals with him in such a way as to wish his salvation and honour still to be consulted. For first he touches on the crime in general terms, lest Judas should think it hidden from him: "One of you," he says, "shall betray me," or "The hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table." Then, since he knew that Judas was less moved by this, he strikes closer and at the same time expresses the atrocity of that treachery (as Mark noted), saying: "One of the twelve, who dippeth with me in the dish." To this also belongs what he brings forward from David in John, where David complains of a similar treachery: "He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me." Thirdly, because even so he accomplished nothing with a stubborn and obstinate man of wickedness, he takes away from him every excuse; and because such men, though they utterly mock God, nevertheless seek hiding places for their crimes under his providence, he declares with great solemnity: "Truly the Son of man goeth, as it was determined; but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed." In this way he plainly admonishes that God, who comprehends the outcomes of events by the decrees of his providence, and who also makes good use of the wicked endeavours of the impious for carrying out his works, has at the same time appointed punishments by which their impiety is to be punished. Finally, when the disciples, astonished at the atrocity of so great a crime, asked who that traitor was, Judas himself (as is found in Matthew) dared to ask whether it was he, and Jesus more openly convicted him, saying: "Thou hast said it." And presently (as John relates) he added: "What thou doest, do quickly." He did not indeed command or urge him to proceed to carry out the crime he had conceived in his mind, but rather, leaving him to his own decision, as he deserved, since he was incurable, bade him at once to depart, so that, the measure of his impiety being filled, he might at last receive the rewards due to him. These, then, are the words of one indignant, by which good parents sometimes cast off rebellious and incurable sons from themselves, as unworthy that they should further be contended with. And Judas perceived within his own mind the force of the divine threat. For presently he rushed out, so that he might join those with whom he had previously conspired against Christ. Yet because the disciples were so dull that they understood none of this, so that they understood none of this, he first indicated the matter more plainly to John, to whom he showed by a sign, as it were with a finger, the morsel dipped and handed to Judas the traitor, namely so that through him the other disciples might afterwards be taught about the whole affair. This whole discussion is indeed most memorable, because it contains many things, the knowledge of which is not only useful but even necessary for us today.

units.la: Primò enim docet in Christi exemplo, quæ Ecclesiæ & fidelium omnium conditio sit in terris. Habent illi (ut alibi admonemur) hostes apertos undiq;, cùm ea mundi natura sit siue ingenium, ut neq; lucem veritatis neq; eos ferre possit, qui eam fouent atq; sequuntur. Sed plus periculi à domesticis atq; occultis inimicis imminet, qui ut minus caueri possunt, ita miris artibus & incredibili astutia sese insinuant, ut ne tunc quidem facile deprehendantur, quando cū apertis hostibus consilia sua conferunt, & nihil nō in Ecclesiæ perniciem moliuntur. Tales enim Moses habuit inter Israelitas, quorum gratia opes & honores Ægypti reliquerat. Tales fuerunt, de quibus Dauid in Psalmis non uno loco conqueritur. Paulus quoq; falsorum fratrum sæpe mentionem facit. Neminem ergo hominum nostri sæculi perfidia offendat. Scimus enim quid Christus de nouissimis temporibus dixerit: Filius hominis cum uenerit, num reperturus est fidem in terra? Et cùm ne Christi quidem mensa immunis fuerit, quò minus ad eam Iudas proditor accesserit, quid obsecro nos sperabimus, quibus aliorū arcana prorsus ignota & occulta sunt? Interim meminerimus, nobis perpetuò uigilandum esse, ne qui incautos proditorijs suis artibus circumueniant, & non tam nos quàm totam religionis causam in periculum adducant. Quò pertinet, quod alibi Dominus à suis prudentiam serpentinam requirit.
units.tr: First of all, it teaches from Christ's example what the condition of the Church and of all the faithful is on earth. They have (as we are admonished elsewhere) open enemies on every side, since the nature or disposition of the world is such that it can bear neither the light of truth nor those who cherish and follow it. But greater danger threatens from domestic and hidden enemies, who, the less they can be guarded against, insinuate themselves by wonderful arts and incredible cunning, so that they are not easily detected even when they confer their plans with open enemies and devise nothing that does not tend to the ruin of the Church. For Moses had such men among the Israelites, for whose sake he had left the wealth and honours of Egypt. Such were those about whom David complains in the Psalms in more than one place. Paul too often makes mention of false brethren. Let no one be offended, then, by the treachery of men of our age. For we know what Christ said about the last times: "When the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" And since not even Christ's own table was free of it, so that Judas the traitor was not kept from approaching it, what, I beg you, shall we hope for, to whom the secrets of others are altogether unknown and hidden? Meanwhile let us remember that we must always be on our guard, lest they circumvent the unwary with their treacherous arts, and bring into danger not only us but the whole cause of religion. To this belongs what the Lord elsewhere requires of his people: serpentine prudence.

units.la: Secundò idem hic suo exemplo nos admonet, quid fieri debeat cum hominibus flagitiosis, siue illi hostes occulti siue aperti sint. Est hæc doctrina admodū necessaria. Alij enim dum zelū gloriæ Dei prætexunt, nihil nō sibi in tales licere putant, & ita priuatæ vindictæ cupiditatē exaturare student. Alij uerò ut ignauiā suam excusent, charitatis prætextu utuntur, & sua indulgetia impios præfratiores & audaciores reddunt. At legē charitatis Christus suo exemplo interpretatur, dū Iudæ proditori minimè parcit, neq; scelus illius extenuat, saluti autē eius consulere studet, & quoad eius fieri potest, cauet, ne quæ turba aut tumultuosior contentio inter discipulos oriatur. Hac igitur ratione nos etiā uti conuenit, ut primò meminerimus, nō debere quenquā conniuere ad eorū scelera, in quos ei alii quid iuris est & imperij. Nec est quod uel amicitiam uel charitatem prætexamus, quando præcipuum amici officium & proprium charitatis Christianæ opus est, hominem in peccato suo periturū ab interitu reuocare. Etenim cùm hæc utilitas ex inimicis captari possit (ut Philosophi docuerunt) quòd illorū cōuitijs aut calūnijs docemur, quid in nostris moribus corrigi & emendari debeat, ab amici ueri & fidelis officio procul aberit, qui sua indulgetia nobis author est, ut deteriores fiamus, aut saltē in uitijs nostris perseueremus. Secūda autē cura sit, ut saluti & honori illorū cōsulere studeamus, ne nobis admonitionibus infames fiant, aut etiā magis exasperetur, qui corrigi debebat. Quapropter etsi publica scelera quæ iā multis alijs scandalo fuerūt, publicè corripi & reprehendi debeant, occulta tamē prudenter tegi & dissimulari debent, ne & eorū famam lædamus, quorū amicos nos esse profitemur, & multis alijs scandalum obijciamus, qui prius nihil huius suspicabantur. Peccant in eo multi hodie, qui simul importunis suis correptionibus sæpe maximorū dissidiorū authores sunt, dū ea in lucē proferunt, quæ melius latebant. Hic ergo locū habeat illud Salomonis, quo charitas multitudinē peccatorum operire dicitur. Quòd si autē aliquid desperata & incurabili malitia in apertū scelus & exitiū ruunt, eos tunc liberius & apertius non arguere modò, sed procul arcere & à nostro consortio repellere conuenit, quò minor sit exempli eorū authoritas, cæteri uerò timore concipiant. Interea autem si quid illi cōtra nos hostile moliantur, ad diuinæ prouidentiæ asylum nos confugere tutissimum fuerit. Illic enim discemus, neq; nobis aliquid fortuitum accidere posse, quod non dudum præuiderit Deus, qui suos non supra uires tentari patitur, neq; impunè laturos esse suam impietatem eos, qui efreni piarum admonitionum contemptu aduersus ipsum Deum insurgunt.
units.tr: Second, the same passage teaches by example what ought to be done with wicked men, whether they are open enemies or hidden ones. This teaching is very necessary. Some people, pretending zeal for the glory of God, think they may do anything to such men, and so they use this pretext to satisfy their desire for private revenge. Others, to excuse their own idleness, appeal to charity, and by their indulgence make the impious bolder and more shameless. But Christ interprets the law of charity by his own example: he does not spare Judas the traitor, nor does he play down his crime, yet he takes care for Judas's salvation and, as far as he can, guards against any tumult or sharper quarrel arising among the disciples. We too should act on this principle, and first remember that we must not connive at the crimes of those over whom we have no right or authority. Nor should we pretend that friendship or charity requires it, since the chief duty of a friend and the proper work of Christian charity is to call back from ruin a man who is perishing in his sin. For although, as the philosophers taught, we can profit even from enemies, since their reproaches and slanders teach us what in our conduct must be corrected and amended, far from the duty of a true and faithful friend is the one who, by his indulgence, is the cause of our becoming worse, or at least of our persisting in our faults. The second concern should be to take care for the welfare and reputation of those who need correction, so that they do not become infamous through our admonitions, or so that the one who ought to be corrected is not exasperated all the more. Therefore, although public crimes, which have already been a scandal to many others, ought to be rebuked and reproved publicly, hidden sins should be prudently covered and passed over, lest we injure the reputation of those whose friends we profess to be, and lest we put a stumbling block before many others who had previously suspected nothing of the kind. Many people today sin in this respect: with their importunate rebukes they are often the authors of the greatest quarrels, while they bring into the light things that were better hidden. Here, then, the saying of Solomon applies, that charity covers a multitude of sins. But if men, through desperate and incurable wickedness, rush into open crime and destruction, then it is fitting not only to rebuke them more freely and openly, but to keep them far off and to banish them from our fellowship, so that the authority of their example may be less, and so that the others may be struck with fear. Meanwhile, if such men plot anything hostile against us, it will be safest for us to flee to the refuge of divine providence. For there we shall learn that nothing can happen to us by chance which God has not long foreseen, the God who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond their strength, and that those who rise up against God himself, with unbridled contempt for pious admonitions, will not bear their impiety with impunity.

units.la: Tertiò de nostri ingenij socordia nos admonet discipulorum stupor qui (ut alij Euangelistæ testantur) Christi uerbis perterrefacti sese mutuò inspiciunt & quærunt quis nā ille sit, qui tantū facinus designare audeat? Quasi uerò aliquod scelus tā atrox & immane sit, quod nō possit in unūquenq; cadere si suā gratiā ipsi subducat Deus? Quàm multa autē in semetipsis singuli deprehendere potuissent, quæ eos monerēt, ut de sua potius salute soliciti esset quā in aliorū corda atq; arcana inquirerēt? Sed est uitium hoc omnibus ex carnis ingenio innatū, ut cùm in genere scelera arguuntur, alij alios inspiciant & suspectos habeant, nulli autem ferè in semetipsos descendant, & sui cordis affectus scrutentur. Quæ causa est, quòd ex sacris concionibus pauci meliores discedunt. Cur enim his moueantur, qui de quouis alio, quàm de ipsis agi putant? Est tamen laude dignus discipulorum dolor, quem illos ex tam tetri flagitij relatione concepisse alij Euangelistæ narrant. Est enim hoc filiorū Dei in genium, ut & huius gloriam ex animo quærant, et quorumuis aliorum saluti consultū cupiant. Non possunt ergo non dolere & ingemiscere, si quid audient siue audiunt, quo Dei gloria obscuratur, & multorum salus impeditur. Discimus igitur hoc loco de illis iudicare, qui omnia fuscā deq; ferunt, modò ipsi pro sua libidine pessimis suis cupiditatibus indulgere possint. Et hæc quidem dicta sint in actionem, quam cum Iuda, perdito & desperato proditore, Christus instituit.
units.tr: Third, the amazement of the disciples admonishes us about the dullness of our own minds. As the other Evangelists testify, they were terrified by Christ's words, looked at one another, and asked who it was that would dare to point to such a crime. As if any crime were so atrocious and monstrous that it could not fall upon any one of us, if God withdrew his grace from him! How many things might each of them have found in himself, which should have warned him to be anxious rather about his own salvation than to search into the hearts and secrets of others? But this fault is innate in all people from the nature of the flesh: when crimes are condemned in general, each looks at the others and regards them with suspicion, yet almost no one descends into himself and examines the affections of his own heart. This is why few people leave the sacred sermons better than they came. For why should they be moved by what they think is said of someone else and not of themselves? Nevertheless, the disciples' grief, which the other Evangelists report that they felt on hearing of so foul a crime, deserves praise. For it is the mark of the sons of God to seek the glory of God sincerely and to desire the salvation of all others. Therefore they could not help grieving and groaning if they heard, or were to hear, anything by which the glory of God was obscured and the salvation of many was hindered. Here, then, we learn to judge those who interpret everything in the worst light, as long as they themselves can indulge their own lusts and their worst desires. But let these things be said by way of application to the action that Christ undertook with Judas, the desperate and abandoned traitor.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad reliquos undecim discipulos, qui & ipsi non vulgariter peccarunt, ut simul uideamus quid cum illis sit actum. Quo loco illorum peccatum Lucas præmittit his uerbis: Orta est autem etiam contentio inter eos, quis eorū uideretur esse maior. Ergo contentionem ueterem de primatu instaurauerunt, in qua multiplex peccatum concurrit. Primo enim non excusabilis negligentiæ argumentum est, quòd eorum tam facilè tamq; citò obliti sunt, quæ de hac causa iam non semel illis Christus dixerat, & quæ apud Matth. cap. 18. atque 20. prolixè describuntur. Coniuncta est negligentiæ huic aliqua species ingratitudinis, cùm tristi illa mortis Christi mentione non aliter afficiantur, quàm quòd de suis rebus contentionem instituunt. Vbi enim zelus gloriæ Dei, quo toti ardere debebant? Vbi de Christo bene merendi studium, cuius beneficentiam toties erant experti? Quò item consuetudinis illius dulcissimæ desiderium recessit, quod olim Petrus professus dicebat: Domine, quò ibimus? tu uerba uitæ æternæ habes. Quid uero illud est, quod & hoc & memoriam beneficiorum eius reflinxit? Cæcus ambitionis affectus, & insanū præ aliis eminendi studium. Quod cùm per se reprehensionem mereatur grauissimam, auget tamen crimen hoc, quòd qui fratres & condiscipuli erant, iam se inuicem contemnunt, & charitatis immemores inter se altercantur, quod absque æmulatione, inuidia, odio, simultate & ira fieri non potuit: quæ omnia hominibus Christianis indignissima sunt. Sunt enim (ut Paulus ad Galatas scribit) opera carnis, quam mortificare debent, quicunque Deo in spiritu & ueritate seruire uolunt. Est hoc magnum argumentum nostræ corruptionis, quo item docetur quanta sit humani ingenij tarditas in percipiendis Regni Dei mysterijs. Hi enim illi sunt, quos mundos dicit Christus, & quos è toto hominum genere selegerat, ut relictis terrenis omnibus ad cælestē Regnum aspirarent, & eius pomœria per uniuersum orbem terrarum extenderent. Attamen regnum carnale somniant, utq; in illo excellere possint, nō magna cura tanguntur eorum, quæ de eius indignissima morte & condiscipuli impijssimo conatu dici audiuerant. Est autem hoc commune fere omnibus hominibus uitium, quòd aut omnino negligunt religionē, aut sub huius prætextu sua quærunt. Quæ causa est, quod eorum facile obliuiscuntur quæ audiunt, & tunc sese turpissimos præbent, quando ingenua & forti constantia in primis opus erat. Prodest autem hoc discipulorum exemplum aduersus eos obseruare, qui Regni Dei & salutis nostræ mysteria humanæ rationis acumine inuestigari posse arbitrantur, & qui postquam unam aut alteram de Christo concionem audiuerunt, quasi ad summum fidei & omnis scientiæ fastigium ascenderint, omnem præterea institutionem, adhæc admonitiones quoque omnes, ceu superuacaneas, contemnunt. Atqui nunquam ita proficimus, quin carnis reliquiæ maneant, cum quibus perpetuò pugnandum est, ut Paulus proprio exemplo docet. Accedit huic domestico malo Satā, qui nouis quotidie cuniculis animos nostros subire solet, si quo modo fidem nostram euertere queat. Quare perpetuo studio opus est illis, qui salutis & fidei naufragium nolunt facere.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the remaining eleven disciples, who also sinned not a little, so that we may see together what was done with them. At this point Luke introduces their sin with these words: "And there was also a contention among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest." So they renewed the old dispute about primacy, in which many sins come together. First, it is a proof of a neglect that cannot be excused that they so easily and so quickly forgot what Christ had said about this very matter more than once, and which is described at length in Matt. 18 and 20. Some kind of ingratitude is joined to this negligence, since they were not moved by the sad mention of Christ's death in any other way than by starting a contention about their own affairs. Where was the zeal for God's glory, with which they ought to have been wholly on fire? Where was the desire to deserve well of Christ, whose kindness they had so often experienced? And where has the longing for that most sweet fellowship gone, which Peter once professed, saying: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life"? What is it, then, that has wiped out both this and the memory of his benefits? A blind affection for ambition, and a mad desire to stand out above others. Although this alone deserves the gravest rebuke, the crime is made worse by the fact that they, who were brothers and fellow disciples, now despise one another and, forgetful of charity, quarrel among themselves, which could not happen without rivalry, envy, hatred, enmity and anger, all of which are most unworthy of Christians. For these are (as Paul writes to the Galatians) "works of the flesh," which all who wish to serve God in spirit and truth must mortify. This is a great proof of our corruption, and it also shows how slow the human mind is to grasp the mysteries of the kingdom of God. For these are the very men whom Christ calls clean, and whom he had chosen out of the whole human race, so that, leaving all earthly things, they might aspire to the heavenly kingdom and extend its boundaries throughout the whole world. Yet they dream of a carnal kingdom, and, so that they might excel in it, they are not greatly moved by what they had heard about his most unworthy death and the most impious attempt of a fellow disciple. Now this fault is almost common to all people: either they neglect religion altogether, or they seek their own interests under its pretext. This is why they easily forget what they hear, and show themselves most shameful just when a frank and brave constancy is most needed. It is useful, however, to observe this example of the disciples against those who think that the mysteries of the kingdom of God and of our salvation can be investigated by the keenness of human reason, and who, after hearing one or two sermons about Christ, think they have climbed to the summit of faith and all knowledge, and so despise all further instruction and, indeed, all admonitions as superfluous. Yet we never make such progress that the remnants of the flesh do not remain, with which we must always struggle, as Paul teaches by his own example. Added to this domestic evil is Satan, who is accustomed to creep into our minds daily by new tunnels, if somehow he can overturn our faith. Therefore, those who do not wish to suffer shipwreck of their salvation and faith need constant diligence.

units.la: Porrò uideamus, quid cum istis egerit Dominus. Merebantur quidem acerrimam reprehensionem propter uitia, quæ (ut diximus) plurima & grauissima in uno hoc facto concurrebant. Quia tamē communi, qui tunc inter Iudæos regnabat, errore decepti, nō malitia peccabant, nec aduersus ipsum aliquid hostiliter moliebantur, amicè eos instituit, & quæ nam Regni sui conditio sit, quodque ipsorum in illo officium futurum sit docet. Eius ergo mansuetudinis exemplum nobis exhibet, quam in illo Isaias prædicauit, quod linum fumigans non extinguat, neq; calamum quassatum conterat. Extant huius generis multa alia in sacris literis, quæ ut infirmos consolantur, ita omnes eos, qui Ecclesiarum gubernacula moderantur, admonent, ut ipsi quoq; similí bonitate atq; indulgentia utan-tur erga peccatores: ne nimia seueritate in desperationem eos conijciant, de quorum poenitentia ad-huc spes bona esse potest. Admonet de eo nos Paulus Apostolus, ad Romanos scribens: Debemus nos, qui firmi sumus, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, neq; nobis ipsis indulgere, id est, non nostris asse-ctibus morem gerere: qui ferè caeca aemulatione accensos ad nimium rigorem transfuersos abripiunt. Peccant in eo multi hodie, qui quasi Draconis leges (quas aliqui sanguine scriptas olim dicebat) ac-ceperint, peccata omnia capitalia faciunt, & temerarijs condemnationibus atq; excommunicationi-bus in desperationē conijciunt, aut saltē hostes faciunt eos, qui si commodius tractarentur, facile in via-m reduci poterant. Quis verò medicū probauerit, qui in quouis morbo pharmaca vehementissima adhibeat, aut quàm primùm aliquod membrū male affectum viderit, mox serras, ustiones & cauteria proferat? Quanto magis conscientiarum ratio haberi debet, ne quae consolatione & doctrina opus habent, durioribus minis aut correptione importuna territae succumbant? Proderit ergo non solum quid factū sit uidere, sed qua occasione & quo animo quidq; fiat expendere, nec statim desperare de ijs, qui adhuc lucifieri posse uidentur. Porrò quoad Christi actionem cum discipulis istis, hoc ordine procedit. Primū inter principes siue magistratus huius saeculi & Apostolos distinguit. Deinde sui ipsos admonet officij. Postremò praemium pollicetur, quo ipsorum labores compensare uelit.
units.tr: Let us now see what the Lord did with these men. They deserved the sharpest rebuke for their faults, which (as we have said) were many and very grave and all came together in this one act. Yet because they were deceived by the error common among the Jews at that time, they sinned out of ignorance rather than malice, and they were not plotting anything hostile against him. So he taught them kindly, and showed them what the nature of his kingdom is and what their duty in it would be. In this he gives us an example of the gentleness that Isaiah foretold of him, that he will not quench the smoking flax nor break the bruised reed. Many other passages of this kind are found in Holy Scripture. They comfort the weak, and they also admonish all who govern the churches to use the same kindness and indulgence towards sinners, so that they do not drive them into despair by excessive severity when there may still be good hope of their repentance. Paul the Apostle gives us this admonition in writing to the Romans: "We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves," that is, not to gratify our own feelings, which, driven by an almost blind zeal, carry off those inflamed with them into excessive rigour. Many today sin in this respect. They act as if they had received the laws of Draco, which some said were written in blood, and they treat every offence as a capital crime. By rash condemnations and excommunications they drive people into despair, or at least make enemies of those who, if they were handled more gently, could easily have been brought back to the way. But who would approve of a physician who applied the most violent medicines to every illness, or who, as soon as he saw any limb diseased, at once brought out saws, cautery irons and burning instruments? How much more regard should be had for consciences, so that those who need consolation and teaching may not give way, terrified by harsher threats or untimely reproof! It will therefore be useful not only to see what has been done, but to weigh the occasion and the spirit in which each thing is done, and not to despair at once of those who seem still capable of being brought to the light. Now as to Christ's dealing with these disciples, he proceeds in this order. First he distinguishes between the princes, or magistrates, of this age and the Apostles. Then he admonishes them of their own office. Lastly he promises a reward by which he is willing to recompense their labours.

units.la: Quoad primū, sepe iam diximus, discipulos cum vulgo Iudaeorum ex Prophetarum oraculis per peram intellectis. Regnū terrenū somniauisse, in quo ipsi dignitatibus donati supra omnes alios ex-cellerent. Et quia Christi regnū per omnes gentes vsq; ad extremos fines orbis terrarū Prophetae ex-tendunt, & Isaias perituros dicit omnes eos, qui illi seruire detrectauerint, illi omnia alia regna cef-satura putabant, ut Christo soli locus esset. Ut ergo isti errori medeatur, ait: Reges gentium domi-nantur eis, & qui potestatem habent in eas, benefici uocantur. Vos autem non ita. Quorum uerbo-rum sensus est: Vos quidem regnū somniatis, & uos in eorum locum putatis successuros esse, qui nunc gentibus hinc inde imperant. Sed multū fallimini hac uestra persuasione. Nam quoad politiam, mi-nimè turbabitur mundi huius facies, & manebunt omnino reges, qui gentibus dominentur, & quos alij pro suis tutoribus & benefactoribus agnoscant: Vos autem adeo non innaderis illorum regna, ut nihil prorsus cum illis commune habituri sitis. Vobis enim non regnū, sed ministerium: non principatus, sed obsequium destinatum est, ut omnium aliorum serui sitis atq; ministri. Imò quo quis plu-ribus seruierit, eo altiorem in uestro ordine gradum merebitur.
units.tr: As to the first point, we have often said already that the disciples, along with the common people of the Jews, had dreamed, from a wrongly understood reading of the oracles of the Prophets, of an earthly kingdom in which they, endowed with dignities, would excel all others. And since the Prophets extend Christ's kingdom through all nations to the farthest ends of the earth, and Isaiah says that all who refuse to serve him will perish, they supposed that all other kingdoms would be destroyed so that Christ alone might have a place. To correct this error, then, he says: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not so." The sense of these words is this: "You indeed dream of a kingdom, and you think that you will succeed to the places of those who now rule the nations here and there. But you are greatly mistaken in this belief. For as to the civil order, the face of this world will by no means be disturbed; there will still be kings who rule the peoples, and whom others acknowledge as their protectors and benefactors. You, however, will not so much invade their kingdoms that you will have anything at all in common with them. For you are destined not for a kingdom but for a ministry, not for dominion but for service, so that you may be the servants and ministers of all others. Indeed, the more people a man serves, the higher the rank he will earn in your order."

units.la: Est autem hoc loco diligenter obseruandum, Christum neque magistratus abolere, neque regi-bus aut principibus quod suum est eripere: sicuti neque oeconomiam, neque coniugium, aut alia Dei instituta turbat. Timent hoc saepe reges, quibus Episcopi & Monachi persuadent, potestatem suam ipsis minimè saluam fore, si Christum & Euangelium eius admittant. Sed est is Herodis er-ror, qui cùm nouum Iudaeorum regem natum esse audiret, ut regno suo consuleret, ipsum extinctum voluit, & eò crudelitatis deuenit, ut puellos Bethlehemiticos exemplo inaudito iugulari curarer. Et utinam hodie multi non similí truculentia in suae fidei creditum populum grassarentur, dum Euangelij praecones regnis suis insidiari arbitrantur, qui de nulla alia re minus cogitant. Fateor tamen huius mali culpam non minima ex parte in phanaticis quibusdam haerere, qui religionis & libertatis Christianae praetextu abutuntur, ut ordinem politicum turbent, & indignum esse di-cunt, hominem Christianum gladio armatum esse, quo alios suae professionis homines coerceat. Nam in Psalmis Christo populum spontaneum tribui dicunt, qui voluntariam ipsi obedien-tiam praestet, neque ui aliqua cogi opus habeat. Addunt & illa Isaiae: Concident gladios suos in ligones, & lanceas suas in falces: Nec feret gens contra gentem gladium, neque porrò bellis assue-scent. Item: Commorabitur lupus cum agno, pardus cum haedo accubabit, similiter iuuencus, leo & pecus saginatum simul erunt, & puer paruus ducet ea, Vacca & ursus pascentur, simulque accuba-bunt catuli eorū, &c. Item: Non afficient malis neq; uastabunt per omne montem meum sanctū, quia plena erit terra scientia Domini, &c. Ex his & similibus locis colligunt illi, magistratu atque iudi-cijs minimè opus fore inter homines Christianos, inter quos nullus locus sit iniurijs aut damnis, quibus impij se mutuò afficere consueuerunt. Sed falluntur omnes isti bifariàm. Primò quòd promi-sue ad omnes Christiani nominis professores extendunt, quod non nisi de vere pijs & in Christo renatis debet intelligi. Deinde, quod Ecclesiam fingunt eiusmodi, quae quoad externum statum, solis pijs constet: nec observant illud Christi, qui Euangelium reti magno confert, quo non solum pisces boni & sani, uerumetiam putres attrahuntur. Ecclesiam item agro confert, in quo semente facta hostis Satan zizania sua spargere soleat. Deniq; no uident, Prophetas sub parabolis eiusmodi eam pacem & tranquilitatem piorum describere, quae in coelis demum fruentur: ad huius saeculi autem conditionem pertinere quae de cruce Christus concionatur, & quod Paulus ait: Omnes qui uolent pie uiuere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem patientur. Et rursus: Per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi in Regnum Dei. Neminem ergo istorum hominum intemperies mouere debet, qui ut rempub. turbant, ita nostro tempore multas Ecclesias in extremum discrimen adduxerunt: multas omnino dissiparunt. Et sufficiat pijs, quod Christus Regnum suum ex hoc mundo esse negat, unde colligitur, illum neque mundi huius regna neq; ordinem politicum euertere.
units.tr: Here, however, it must be carefully noted that Christ neither abolishes magistrates nor takes from kings and princes what is theirs, just as he does not disturb household management, marriage, or the other institutions of God. Kings often fear this, because bishops and monks persuade them that their power will not be safe if they admit Christ and his Gospel. But this is the error of Herod, who, when he heard that a new king of the Jews had been born, wished to put him to death in order to protect his own kingdom, and fell into such cruelty that he had the boys of Bethlehem slaughtered, an unheard-of act. And would that today many did not rage with a similar savagery against the people entrusted to their faith, while they think that the preachers of the Gospel are plotting against their kingdoms, when they are thinking of nothing less. I confess, however, that the blame for this evil lies, in no small part, with certain fanatics, who use the pretext of religion and Christian liberty to disturb the political order, and who say that it is unworthy for a Christian man to be armed with a sword by which to restrain other men of his own profession. For they say that in the Psalms a willing people is given to Christ, which renders him voluntary obedience and has no need to be compelled by any force. They add also those words of Isaiah: "They shall beat their swords into mattocks, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Likewise: "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid, and the calf and the lion and the fatling together, and a little child shall lead them. The cow and the bear shall feed, and their young ones shall lie down together," and so on. Likewise: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord," and so on. From these and similar passages they conclude that there will be no need of magistrates or judgements among Christian men, among whom there is no place for the injuries and losses with which the wicked are accustomed to harm one another. But all these men are mistaken in two ways. First, because they extend these promises indiscriminately to all who profess the Christian name, whereas they ought to be understood only of those who are truly godly and reborn in Christ. Second, because they imagine a Church of such a kind that, as to its outward condition, it consists only of the godly, and they do not observe that saying of Christ, who compares the Gospel to a great net, by which not only good and sound fish but also rotten ones are drawn in. He also compares the Church to a field, in which, once the seed is sown, the enemy Satan is accustomed to scatter his tares. Finally, they do not see that the Prophets, under parables of this kind, describe the peace and tranquillity of the godly, which they will enjoy at last in heaven, whereas what Christ preaches about the cross, and what Paul says, that "all who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution," and again, "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God," pertains to the condition of this age. Therefore let the intemperance of these men not move anyone, for they disturb the commonwealth, and, as in our own time, they have brought many churches into the utmost peril, and indeed have scattered many of them altogether. And it is enough for the godly that Christ denies that his kingdom is of this world, from which it is gathered that he neither overturns the kingdoms of this world nor the political order.

units.la: At non minus principes uiri & qui magistratum gerunt, diligenter obseruare debent, quid illis in praesenti Christus tribuat. Primo illos gentibus dominari dicit. Id uero no de violento aut tyrannico imperio, sed de legitima potestate debet intelligi, qua illos Deus armauit. Quo illud Pauli pertinet, qui potestate nulla esse ait, quam quae ex Deo sit. Et notum est illud Prophetae: Deus iudicia tua Regi da. Dominantur ergo Reges, no quod quiduis pro sua libidine agendi ius habeat, sed quod Deus in illum gradu eos euexit, ut sua authoritate & legitimo imperio alios cohineat, ne pax publica turbetur. Colligit ex eo Paulus, eos qui magistratui resistunt, ordinationi Dei resistere, & proinde huic obtemperandum esse, no solum supplicium metu, uerumetiam propter conscientiam, ne ipsius Dei ira prouocemus, cuius multa dira & tristia exempla iam inde ab origine mundi edita sunt in eos, qui seditionibus temerarijs reipub. turbauerunt. Simul autem dominandi uerbum principes officij admonet, ut nimirum se Dominos esse meminerint, & proinde no languescant neq; frigeant in munere sibi commisso, & ne indulgentia nimia, aut etiam uitae dissolutioris exemplo, authoritatem suam prostituant. Si enim patrem familias non decent mores, qui in pueris aut seruulis facile excusantur: multo minus eos qui in repub. patrum loco sunt, omnia ea decent, quae in priuatis hominibus aliqua ratione excusari possunt. Et cum omne scandalum turpe & pernitiosum sit, nullum turpius & pernitiosius est illo, quod ex ijs nascitur, qui toti populo uirtutis exemplar esse debebant. Inexcusabilis autem est illorum ignauia, qui seipsos exarmant ea potestate et authoritate, qua illos Deus donauit. Sunt enim illi instar trunci illius, quem ranis a Ioue regem datum, & ab illis ludibrio habitum fuisse Aesopus olim fabulatus est, quod in illo nihil uiderent regia maiestate & seueritate dignum.
units.tr: But no less must princes and those who hold the magistracy carefully observe what Christ grants them in the present. First, he says that they lord it over the nations. This must be understood not of violent or tyrannical rule but of lawful power, with which God has armed them. To this belongs the saying of Paul, that there is no power except that which is from God. And the words of the Prophet are well known: "Give your judgements to the king, O God." Kings therefore lord it not because they have a right to do whatever they please, but because God has raised them to that rank, so that by their authority and lawful rule they may restrain others and public peace may not be disturbed. From this Paul concludes that those who resist the magistrate resist the ordinance of God, and that therefore he must be obeyed, not only from fear of punishment but also for conscience' sake, lest we provoke the very wrath of God, whose many dreadful and sad examples have been set forth from the beginning of the world against those who have disturbed the commonwealth by rash seditions. At the same time, by the word "lord it," he reminds princes of their office, so that they may remember that they are lords, and therefore may not grow slack or cold in the duty committed to them, and may not, through excessive indulgence or through an example of loose living, prostitute their authority. For if the morals that are easily excused in children or servants do not befit the head of a household, much less do those who stand in the place of fathers in the commonwealth fit all those things that can in some way be excused in private persons. And since every scandal is shameful and pernicious, none is more shameful and pernicious than that which arises from those who ought to be the model of virtue for the whole people. Moreover, the sloth of those is inexcusable who disarm themselves of that power and authority with which God has endowed them. For they are like that log which, as Aesop long ago told in a fable, was given by Jove as a king to the frogs, and which they mocked, because they saw nothing in it worthy of royal majesty or sternness.

units.la: Ne tamen haec in tyrannidem aut crudelitatem degeneret, simul alterius etiam membri meminerint principes, quo eos beneficos dici Christus ait. Constat enim hunc uetustissimum titulum esse, quo etiam unus ex Ptolemaeorum numero praecipue delectatus est, ut se Euergenten dici uellet. Nec alius illos magis decet. Quia enim in eum finem a Deo instituti sunt, ut publicam pacem tueantur, & ut quisque priuatim sub illis ius suum obtinere possit, merito ita dicuntur. Et hinc factum uidetur, ut quotquot passim inter gentes unquam praefuerunt, eiusmodi nominibus usi sint, quae subditis consolationi potius quam terrori essent. Aegyptij certe olim Pharaonum nomine suos appellabant, quae nox uindicem significat: eo quod principum sit populum suum uindicare & tueri, ne aliquorum uel tyrannide uel auaritia opprimatur. Graecis in usu fuit (ut apud Homerum est uidere) quod reges suos ποιμένας λαῶν: id est, pastores populorum dicerent. Latini Reges a regendo uocarunt, ut in re militari Duces a ducendo, & Imperatores ab imperando, quo uerbo legitima & iusta aliquid mandandi potestas denotatur. Et quamuis postea Imperatores pleraque libidinose & tyrannice facerent, pleriq; tamen Patres patriae dici uoluerunt, quae dignitas illis omnium maxima esse uisa est. Nostris temporibus nihil frequentius est titulo Clementiae & Gratiae, quibus ita delectantur principes, ut parum fit Clementissimos dicere, nisi ipsam Clementiam & gratiam itidem ingemines. Maiores nostri Reges Künig dixerunt a sciendo, quod scientia & sapientia instructos esse oportet eos, qui alicui genti cum utilitate & laude imperare uolunt. Vetustissimus etiam diadematum atque sceptrorum usus est, quibus ceu proprijs regni insignibus gaudent, ut admoneantur, ipsos tunc demum Reges uerosfore, si uirtutum omni genere coronati sint, & iudicia iusta atque recta proferant, si denique omnia ad iustitiae & publicae pacis regulam dirigant. Et ideo Poetae reges per sceptrum suum iurantes inducit, nimirum quòd hoc suæ potestatis sacratissimum symbolum esse sentirent. Quæ omnia si probè expendant quicunq; rempub. administrāt, ij procul dubio benefici erunt, tamen ut ipsorum potestas alicui grauis sit, ut potius toti populo nihil utilius, nihil iucundius, nihil denique magis necessarium possit excogitari. Hi enim ut subditorum corpora & fortunas tuentur, ita religionis etiam patroni sunt, ut illos Ecclesiæ nutritios merito appellaueris.
units.tr: Yet lest these things degenerate into tyranny or cruelty, rulers should also keep in mind the other member, by which Christ says they are called beneficent. For this is admittedly a very ancient title, one which even one of the Ptolemies took special delight in, wishing to be called Euergetes. No other title suits them better. For since they were appointed by God to this end, that they should protect public peace and that each person may be able to maintain his own right under them, they are rightly so called. And from this it seems to have come about that all who have ever ruled among the nations, wherever they were, used names that would be a comfort to their subjects rather than a terror. The Egyptians of old certainly called their Pharaohs by a name meaning "defender," since it is the prince's duty to defend and protect his people, lest they be oppressed by the tyranny or greed of any. Among the Greeks it was the custom (as one can see in Homer) to call their kings "shepherds of the peoples" [ποιμένας λαῶν]. The Latins called kings reges from regere, to rule, as in military affairs leaders are called duces from ducere, to lead, and commanders imperatores from imperare, to command, a word which denotes a lawful and just power of giving orders. And although afterwards the emperors did many things in a lustful and tyrannical manner, many of them nevertheless wished to be called Fathers of the Fatherland, a dignity which seemed to them the greatest of all. In our own times nothing is more common than the titles of Clemency and Grace, which rulers delight in so much that it is hardly enough to call them most clement unless they also repeat "clemency" and "grace" themselves. Our forefathers called kings Künig from sciendo, knowing, because those who wish to rule a people with profit and praise must be furnished with knowledge and wisdom. The use of diadems and sceptres is also very ancient, and rulers rejoice in them as the proper insignia of their kingdom, so that they may be reminded that they will be true kings only if they are crowned with every kind of virtue, and if they pronounce just and right judgments, and finally if they direct everything by the rule of justice and public peace. And for this reason the poets introduce kings swearing by their sceptre, no doubt because they felt it to be the most sacred symbol of their power. If all who administer the commonwealth weigh these things carefully, they will undoubtedly be beneficent; yet their power should not be burdensome to anyone, but rather nothing more useful, nothing more pleasant, and in short nothing more necessary could be devised for the whole people. For just as they protect the bodies and fortunes of their subjects, so they are also patrons of religion, so that you may rightly call them nursing fathers of the Church.

units.la: Sed alterum quoq; responsionis Christi caput consideremus, quo de Apostolorum officio ille concio natur, & id duobus membris comprehendit. Primum est: Vos autem non sic. Paucis verbis prohibet, ne sub ecclesiastici muneris prætextu in rempub. dominium affectent, neue etiam in ijs, quæ vulgo spiritualia dicuntur, more Regum imperare velint. Qua de re Petrus in ultimo Cap. Epistolæ suæ prioris grauem admonitionem contexit. Quo loco tamen minimè dissimulandum est, inter reipub. præsides & uerbi administros arctissima communione esse debere; ut hi quidem illos per Dei verbum regant, illi autem hos sua authoritate defendant. Docuit hoc Deus, quando in suo populo duos germanos fratres ipse constituit, ut penes unum Reipub. cura esset, alter uero doctrinæ & sacris uacaret. Saulis quoque imperium Israelitis utilissimum fuit, quoad ipse Samuelem audiuit ex Dei verbo sibi præscribentem quid facto opus esset. Sic Dauide Gad & Nathan, Prophetæ, familiarissimi fuerunt, & Ioas Rex Iudæ in Iehoiada Sacerdote præsidium fortissimum habuit, idem uero infelicissimè perijt, postquā eiusdem filium Zachariam crudeliter occidit, & absq; Dei verbo regnare uoluit. Isaias quoque Ezechiæ fidelem operam contulit, Manasses uero pessimè cessit, quòd & illum & alios Prophetas è medio sustulisset. Interim doctores curare decet, ne principum familiaritate & bonitate pro suo affectu abutantur, & ea occasione nouum in Ecclesia imperium sibi uendicent, aut in ditione alienam manus suas extendant. Etsi enim inter duos istos ordines coniunctio animorum firmissima esse debeat, distincta tamen sunt horum munera, & sic Deus ipse constituit: primò quidem quia unus non potest utrique sufficere (quod in Mosis & Apostolorum exemplis euidentissimè cernitur) partim uero ne doctores sibi ius sumant aliquid in Ecclesia statuendi pro sua libidine. Quod optimi & sanctissimi quique Reges sic obseruarunt, ut non semel ipsos Sacerdotes in ordinem redegerint, si eos uel exorbitare, uel in suo officio negligentiores esse uiderunt. Est ergo intolerabilis Pontificum tyrannis, qui religionis curam ad magistratum nihil pertinere aiunt, & sacrilegæ audaciæ eos accusant, qui ipsis cessantibus ad reformationem abusuum & ueræ doctrinæ instaurationem manum admouent: at idem sibi licere uolunt, ut ipsis quoq; principibus superbè imperent.
units.tr: But let us also consider the second head of Christ's reply, in which he speaks of the office of the Apostles, and comprises it in two members. The first is: But you are not so. In a few words he forbids them, under the pretext of the ecclesiastical office, to aim at dominion over the commonwealth, or to wish to rule in those things which are commonly called spiritual, in the manner of kings. Peter, at the end of the last chapter of his first epistle, has woven a grave admonition on this matter. Yet in this place it must by no means be concealed that there ought to be a very close fellowship between the governors of the commonwealth and the ministers of the Word; so that the former indeed rule the latter by the Word of God, while the latter defend the former by their authority. God taught this when among his own people he appointed two brothers, so that the care of the commonwealth rested with one, while the other devoted himself to teaching and the sacred things. The rule of Saul also was most useful to the Israelites, as long as he listened to Samuel prescribing to him from the Word of God what needed to be done. So Gad and Nathan, prophets, were most intimate with David, and Joash king of Judah had a very strong support in Jehoiada the priest; but the same Joash perished most wretchedly, after he cruelly killed Jehoiada's son Zechariah and wished to reign without the Word of God. Isaiah also gave faithful service to Hezekiah, but Manasseh fared very badly, because he had removed both him and the other prophets out of the way. Meanwhile teachers ought to take care that they do not abuse the familiarity and kindness of princes for their own affection, and on that occasion claim for themselves a new dominion in the Church, or extend their hands into another's domain. For although the joining of minds between these two orders ought to be most firm, their offices are nevertheless distinct, and God himself so appointed: first indeed because one cannot suffice for both (which is most clearly seen in the examples of Moses and the Apostles), and partly so that teachers do not arrogate to themselves a right to decide anything in the Church at their own pleasure. The best and most holy kings have observed this, so that more than once they brought the priests themselves back into order, when they saw them either going beyond their bounds or being too negligent in their office. Therefore the tyranny of the Pontiffs is intolerable, who say that the care of religion has nothing to do with the magistrate, and accuse of sacrilegious audacity those who, while they themselves are idle, put their hand to the reform of abuses and the restoration of true doctrine; yet they wish to be allowed the same right of domineering proudly over the princes themselves.

units.la: Altero membro Apostolorum munus definit, dicens: Sed qui maximus est inter uos, sit sicut qui minimus est, & qui princeps est, sicut qui ministrat. Exponuntur hæc clarius apud Matthæum, quando contentione simili propter ambitiosam filiorum Zebedæi postulationem exorta, discipulis dicit: Quicunq; uoluerit inter uos magnus fieri, sit uester minister: & quicunque uoluerit inter uos primus esse, sit uester seruus. Quibus uerbis illos non dominio sed ministerio destinat, et ex seruorum officio argumentum petit, quo illis molestiam & quibusuis seruiendi studium commendat. Constat enim inter seruos eum excellere, qui plurimum laborat, & ad rei domesticæ curam plus alijs confert. Quia ergo uos (inquit Christus) ego meos & Ecclesiæ meæ seruos feci, huc ego omnium præstantissimum iudicabo, qui se minimum putauerit, adeoq; qui reliquis omnibus uoluntarium seruitium præstiterit. Unde ita colligitur, in Christi leges peccare eos, quicunq; sub ministerij ecclesiastici prætextu alijs dominari uolunt, quos pro conseruis suis debebant agnoscere. Solomon olim terra contremiscere dicebat sub seruo, qui imperat. Quis ergo dubitet, totam rerum naturam, adeoq; ipsos cælestes spiritus exhorrescere, quādo eos sibi in Regno Christi imperium uendicare uident, qui ne serui quidem dici merentur, cū nihil eorum præstent, quæ ille à seruis suis requirit? Nemo tamen putauerit seruilem pusillanimitatem hic præcipi, qua doctores sese omnium libidini subijciant, & indulgentiores æquo illis turpiter blandiantur, quos arguere & reprehendere debebat. Quin potius in docendo magnanimitate opus est, ut (quod Paulus dicebat) experimentum præbeant Christi in ipsis loquentis. Ea autem magnanimitas humilitate & charitate temperari debet, ut omnibus constet, eos omnia facere ut aliorum saluti consulant, non ut suam potestatem ostentent, aut alicui insolentius dominentur. Faciunt huc Prophetarum & Apostolorum exempla, quæ si imitentur ministri, nō poterunt aberrare, Sed plura de hac re in sequenti Sermone dicentur. Nūc quod præcipuum huius loci caput est probè teneamus, ut debita seueritate coerceantur qui aduersus Deum & verbum eius hostiliter insurgunt: pia autem lenitate foueantur & in viam revocentur, quos adhuc tractabiliores & curabiles esse videmus. Cura deniq; fit, ut quàm plurimos Iesu Christo adducamus, qui fidis suis ministris optata æternæ felicitatis præmia retribuet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: With the second member he defines the office of the Apostles, saying: But whoever is greatest among you, let him be as the least, and he who is chief as he who serves. These things are set out more clearly in Matthew, where, a similar contention having arisen over the ambitious request of the sons of Zebedee, he says to the disciples: Whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant. By these words he appoints them not to lordship but to ministry, and from the office of servants he draws an argument by which he commends to them toil and a willingness to serve anyone whatsoever. For it is agreed that among servants he excels who labors most and contributes more than the others to the care of the household. Therefore, since (says Christ) I have made you my servants and servants of my Church, I shall judge him most outstanding of all who thinks himself least, and indeed who renders voluntary service to all the rest. From this it is concluded that those sin against the laws of Christ who, under the pretext of the ecclesiastical ministry, wish to lord it over others, whom they ought to acknowledge as their fellow servants. Solomon used to say that the earth trembles under a servant who rules. Who then can doubt that the whole of nature, and indeed the heavenly spirits themselves, shudder when they see those claiming dominion for themselves in the kingdom of Christ, who do not even deserve to be called servants, since they perform none of those things which he requires from his servants? Yet no one should suppose that a servile timidity is enjoined here, by which teachers subject themselves to the whim of everyone and shamefully flatter with excessive indulgence those whom they ought to rebuke and reprove. Rather, magnanimity is needed in teaching, so that (as Paul said) they may give proof of Christ speaking in them. Yet this magnanimity must be tempered by humility and charity, so that it is evident to all that they do everything to promote the salvation of others, not to display their own power or to domineer over anyone too insolently. The examples of the Prophets and Apostles bear on this, and if the ministers imitate them they will not be able to go astray. But more on this matter will be said in the following sermon. Now let us hold firmly to what is the chief point of this passage: that those who rise up hostilely against God and his Word are to be restrained with the severity that is due, while those whom we see still more tractable and curable are to be cherished with pious gentleness and brought back into the way. Finally, let there be care that we bring as many as possible to Jesus Christ, who will repay his faithful ministers with the desired rewards of eternal happiness. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCVI.

units.la: Nam uter maior est? qui accumbit, an qui ministrat? nonne qui accumbit? At ego sum in medio vestrum vt qui ministrat. Vos porrò estis qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis: & ego vobis pacisco, prout pactus est mihi Pater meus, regnū: Ut edatis & bibatis in mensa mea in regno meo, et sedeatis super thronos iudicantes duo decim tribus Israelis.
units.tr: For which is greater? He who sits at table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at table? But I am among you as one who serves. You are those who have continued with me in my trials. And I appoint to you a kingdom, as my Father has appointed one to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

units.la: ON temere à Sapiente illo dictum est, Principium peccati, superbia. Ut enim hac peccauerunt primi parentes: ita nobis etiam hæc præcipua peccandi causa est, quod nō contenti sorte nostra, ambitiosè aspiramus ad altiora, & tunc quoq; gloriam huius sæculi quærimus, quando toti videmur nos Deo consecrauisse. Exemplū huius vitij memorabile in Apostolis proponitur: qui cùm omnibus suis relictis hucusq; Christo comites indiuulsi adhæsissent, tamen regni terreni spe decepti, de hoc potius quàm de regno eius cœlesti propagando cogitarunt. Et tantas in illis vires habuit ex ambitione enata æmulatio, ut qui eiusdē magistri discipuli, & eiusdem Patris filij erant, odiosas inter se de primatu contentiones excitarent. Quas licet non semel iam antea Christus nō sine graui reprehensione repressisset, eandē tamē lite in ultima Cœna instaurauerunt: et tunc quidē, quādo ille de sua morte cōcionatus, eiusdē memoriā solenne instituerat, et inter hæc indignū et immane Iudæ proditoris facinus detexerat. Elucet autem in tanta discipulorum imbecillitate admirabilis & plus quàm paterna Christi bonitas, qui cùm optimo iure illos grauissimè corripere, imò ut suo cōsortio indignos reijcere posset, amicè tamē eos instituit, adhæc consolationibus dulcissimis et magnificis promissionibus spem eorum in posterum quoq; confirmat, ne unquam tam turpis delicti conscientia superati desperarent.
units.tr: It was not without reason that the wise man said, "The beginning of sin is pride." Our first parents sinned in this way, and for us too this is the chief cause of sin: not content with our lot, we aspire ambitiously to higher things, and we seek the glory of this world even when we seem wholly consecrated to God. A memorable example of this vice is set before us in the Apostles. Although they had left everything and had clung to Christ as companions without wavering, they were nonetheless deceived by hopes of an earthly kingdom, and thought more about this than about spreading his heavenly kingdom. Such was the power that ambition gave to the rivalry among them that disciples of the same Master and sons of the same Father stirred up hateful disputes among themselves about primacy. Christ had already more than once checked these quarrels, and not without serious rebuke, yet they renewed the same strife at the last Supper, at the very time when he had preached about his death and instituted its solemn memorial, and when he had also revealed the unworthy and monstrous crime of Judas the traitor. Yet in the midst of such weakness of the disciples there shines forth the admirable goodness of Christ, more than fatherly. Although he could justly have rebuked them most severely, indeed could have cast them out as unworthy of his fellowship, he instructed them in a friendly way, and by the sweetest consolations and magnificent promises he also strengthened their hope for the future, so that they should never despair because of the consciousness of so shameful a fault.

units.la: Et primò quidem ipsorum functionem à Regum aut principum conditione distinguens, eos Ecclesiæ suæ ministerio destinatos esse docuit. Ex eo autem colligit, illum demum alijs præstantiorem fore, qui quam plurimis seruierit. Debet autē hinc generalis doctrina peti, quæ ad omnis loci & ordinis homines extendatur, ne ex suæ conditionis aut donorum præstantia superbiendi occasionem arripiant. Ut enim Deus natura beneficus est: ita nos donis suis ita uti uult, ut aliorum commodis seruiant. Sic magistratum quidem authoritate, gloria & potestate armauit: sed in eum finem, ut Reipub. seruiat, & unumquemque tueatur, ut suo iure uti possit. Sic maritus uxorem excellit dignitate, sed ut huic consulat & eam aduersus omnem uim iniustam defendat. Similiter heri seruos existimatione multùm superant: sed si rem propius consideres, nemo magis seruit quàm herus, cui totius domus cura incumbit, & qui uilissimis quoq; mancipijs prospicere cogitur. Neq; alia est donorum Dei ratio, siue de animi, siue de corporis aut fortunæ bonis loquamur. Ideo enim sapientia & rerum cognitione multi donantur, ut imprudentiores consilio iuuent. Ideo corporis uiribus multi excellunt, ut infirmiores subleuent. Ideo pacem & otium multis largitur Deus, ut exules & egenos ipsi suscipiant. Ideo quidam diuitijs amplissimis abundant, ut pauperibus asyli & præsidij loco sint. Peccant igitur uehementer in Dei leges & providentiæ eius statuta, qui dona ista sibi solis uendicant, adeò ut iniuriam sibi fieri arbitrentur, si quid officij ab illis requiratur. Habet illi quidem rationes suas, quibus sese apud homines excusent, sed nunquam illas admittet Deus, qui olim dispensationis suæ rationem longè seuerius ab illis requiret.
units.tr: First, by distinguishing their office from the condition of kings or princes, he taught that they were destined for the ministry of his Church. From this he infers that the one who serves the greater number is the one who will at last be the more excellent of the others. From this a general doctrine should be drawn, extending to men of every place and rank, so that they do not seize on the excellence of their condition or gifts as an occasion for pride. For just as God is by nature beneficent, so he wills that we use his gifts in such a way that they serve the advantage of others. Thus he has armed the magistrate with authority, glory and power, but to this end, that he may serve the commonwealth and protect each one, so that each may be able to enjoy his right. So the husband excels his wife in dignity, but in order that he may care for her and defend her against every unjust violence. Likewise masters far surpass their slaves in standing, but if you consider the matter more closely, no one serves more than the master, on whom the care of the whole household lies, and who is obliged to provide even for the most lowly servants. Nor is the reason for God's gifts any different, whether we speak of goods of the mind, of the body, or of fortune. For many are given wisdom and knowledge so that they may help the less prudent with counsel. Many excel in bodily strength so that they may support the weaker. God grants peace and leisure to many so that they may themselves receive exiles and the needy. Some abound in very great riches so that they may serve as a refuge and protection for the poor. Those therefore sin grievously against God's laws and the statutes of his providence who claim these gifts for themselves alone, to the point of thinking they are wronged if any duty is required of them. They have their reasons by which they excuse themselves before men, but God, who will one day require an account of his stewardship far more strictly from them, will never accept those reasons.

units.la: Sequitur aliud argumentum ab Ecclesiæ dignitate desumptum, quod cum Interrogatione ponit, ut animos eorum magis feriat. Nam uter (inquit) maior est? qui accumbit, an qui ministrat? Nonne qui accubit? Vt istitur tota argumentatio simili ex communi hominum consuetudine petito, & est huiusmodi: Qui accumbunt, eorum maior est quàm ad mensam ministrantiū dignitas: Ecclesia autem est, quæ accumbit, & cibo æterno atq; cœlesti saturetur, nos autem huius cibi administri estis. Ergo illa nobis maior atq; excellentior est, ut absurdum fuerit, nos in illa primatu affectare, aut in illam dominari velle. Idem enim perinde est, ac si quis seruus sibi in herum ius sumat atq; imperium. Atqui Græcus ille Comicus dicebat: λυπεῖ με δ' ἐλθ, μὴ ζον οἰκέτης φρονῶν; id est, Molestus mihi seruus est, qui altius famulo sapit. Quis ergo eum ferre possit, qui supra herum quoq; sese extollit? Est autem hoc loco non ofcitanter nobis obseruanda Ecclesiæ dignitas, cuius felicitatem cum alibi nuptiali festo Spiritus sanctus coferat, rectè hanc Christus in præsenti sponsam facit, cui accumbenti Apostoli ministrent. At si illius ministri sunt hi, quos ipse Dei Filius ex toto mundo elegit; ut eos amicorum loco haberet, quanto magis eidem omnia alia, quæ in mundo sunt, debent seruire? Rectè ergo Paulus Corinthijs dicebat: Omnia vestra sunt; siue Paulus, siue Apollos, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue vita, siue mors, siue præsentia, siue futura, omnia (inquam) vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei. Possent ista infinitis exemplis demonstrari. Propter Ecclesiam enim regna conseruari & perdi, omnium seculorum historiæ docent: in quibus uidemus floruisse regna, quæ illi hospitium amicum præbuerunt, eadem uero funditus corruisse, quàm primum illam hostiliter sunt aggressa. Ægypto certè per Iosephum immensa beneficia contulit Deus, cum illic Ecclesiæ suæ domicilium pararet. At post quam Pharao ueterum beneficiorum oblitus illam opprimere cæpit, sibijpsi & regno suo exitium accersiuit. Babylonem quoq; gloria & potentia in immensum creuisse scimus; quando Nabuchodonosor & Evilmerodach Dei populum sub illis propter peccata captiuum humanius tractauerunt: Balthazar uero, qui tam Deo quàm Ecclesiæ eius superbe ac crudeliter insultabat; cum regno illo uere aureo (ut apud Danielem dicitur) miserè periit. Idem Persarum regibus accidit, qui à Cyri pietate degenerarunt, qui Iudæos ab exilio Babylonico liberauerat, ut ueri Dei cultum instaurarent. In Græcorum quoq; regibus aut Alexandri Magni successoribus, similia exempla sunt edita. At quid de regnis dicimus, quando totam hanc mundi fabricam propter Ecclesiam conditam esse constat, & propter hanc quoq; citius periturā esse, ne qui nouissimorum temporum turbis atq; calamitatibus victi in fide succumbant? Notum est enim illud Christi: Propter electos decurtabuntur dies illi. Superat tamen hæc omnia, quod æternus Dei Filius huic sponsæ suæ seruire dignatus est, & hodie etiam adhuc seruit: Nam ut illam sanguine suo pretioso abluit; ita etiamnum eam proprio corpore & sanguine alit & seruat, cuius liberationis testimonium atq; sigillum nobis in Cœna sua mystica exhibet. Et ideo eam in præsenti per accumbentis parabolam describit. Tractamus ista paulo fusius, quia de duobus nos admonent, quæ cognitu & obseruatu non tam utilia quàm necessaria sunt. Primo enim qui Ecclesiæ membra per fidem facti sunt, discant in nullo hominū gloriandum esse, sed in solo Christo; quem ut sponsum suum amare & solum obseruare debent. Semper ergo illud Apostolicū in animo uersent: Pretio empti estis, ne fitis serui hominū. Si enim nosipsos abnegare debemus, multò minus in aliorū uerba nos iurare conuenit; ne fidem Christo debitam ulla ex parte uiolemus. Et huc pertinet, quod in Psalmo Ecclesiæ dicitur: Audi filia, & vide, & inclina aurem tuam: obliuiscere populi tui & domus patris tui: Concupiscit Rex formam tuam: quia ipse est Dominus tuus, ipsum adorabis. Deinde omnes etiam Ecclesiæ ministros hic locus officij admonet: quod est, ut sponsam hanc soli Christo ad ducant, uirginem puram & castam, ut Paulus loquitur. Quo Ioannes Baptista respiciens discipulos cæca gloriæ ipsius æmulatione turbatis dicebat: Vos ipsi mihi testes estis, quod dixerim: Non sum ego ille Christus sed missus sum ante illum. Qui habet sponsam sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi, qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter uocem sponsi: hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est. At quia simul ministris, qui mensæ seruiunt, conferuntur, simul sui muneris esse meminerint, ut Ecclesiæ cibū suum apponant: ipsum uidelicet Christum, qui est panis ille uitæ, & qui solus animas saturat atq; seruat ad uitam æternam. Et huc pertinent, quæ cap.12: de seruo aut œconomo Christi dicta sunt.
units.tr: There follows another argument, drawn from the dignity of the Church, which he puts in the form of a question, so that it may strike their minds more forcibly. "For which is greater," he says, "he who sits at table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits?" The whole argument proceeds in this way, from a comparison taken from common human custom, and it runs as follows: those who sit at table have a greater dignity than those who serve at the table. But the Church is the one who sits and is filled with the eternal and heavenly food, while we are the ministers of this food. Therefore the Church is greater and more excellent than we are, so that it would be absurd for us to aspire to primacy over her or to wish to lord it over her. For this is exactly as if a slave were to claim for himself the right and power of a master. Indeed that Greek comic poet said: "λυπεῖ με δ' ἐλθὼν μὴ ζῶν οἰκέτης φρονῶν" [It is annoying to me when a slave thinks above his station]; that is, "A slave who thinks more highly of himself than a servant is a nuisance to me." Who then could bear one who raises himself above his master too? Here we must not carelessly observe the dignity of the Church, whose happiness the Holy Spirit elsewhere compares to a wedding feast; rightly, then, Christ makes her here the bride, to whom the Apostles minister as she sits at table. But if these men, whom the Son of God himself chose from the whole world, are her ministers, so that he might regard them as friends, how much more must all other things in the world serve her? Rightly then Paul said to the Corinthians: "All things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come, all things, I say, are yours; and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." These things could be shown by countless examples. The histories of all ages teach that kingdoms are preserved or destroyed on account of the Church. In them we see that those kingdoms flourished which offered friendly hospitality to her, while those which attacked her with hostility were utterly overthrown as soon as they did so. Certainly God bestowed immense benefits on Egypt through Joseph, when he was preparing a home there for his Church. But after Pharaoh, forgetting the earlier benefits, began to oppress her, he brought destruction upon himself and his kingdom. We also know that Babylon grew immeasurably in glory and power, when Nebuchadnezzar and Evil-merodach treated the people of God, captive there because of their sins, rather humanely; but Belshazzar, who insulted both God and his Church proudly and cruelly, perished wretchedly along with that kingdom, truly golden (as it is called in Daniel). The same happened to the kings of the Persians, who degenerated from the piety of Cyrus, who had freed the Jews from the Babylonian exile so that they might restore the worship of the true God. Similar examples are also recorded among the kings of the Greeks, or the successors of Alexander the Great. But why speak of kingdoms, when it is established that the whole fabric of the world was made for the sake of the Church, and that it too will perish all the sooner for her sake, so that those overcome by the troubles and calamities of the last times may not fail in faith? For that saying of Christ is well known: "For the sake of the elect those days will be shortened." Yet above all these things stands the fact that the eternal Son of God has deigned to serve this bride of his, and still serves her today. For as he cleansed her with his precious blood, so even now he nourishes and preserves her with his own body and blood, and in his mystical Supper he gives us the testimony and seal of this deliverance. And therefore he describes her in the present passage through the parable of one reclining at table. We treat these matters at some length, because they remind us of two things which are not so much useful to know and observe as necessary. First, those who have become members of the Church through faith should learn that they must glory in no man, but in Christ alone, whom they ought to love as their Bridegroom and to serve alone. Let them therefore always keep in mind that Apostolic word: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men." For if we ought to deny ourselves, much less should we swear by the words of others, lest we violate in any way the faith owed to Christ. To this also belongs what is said in the Psalm to the Church: "Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house. The King desires your beauty, for he is your Lord, and you shall worship him." Second, this passage reminds all ministers of the Church of their duty: that they should lead this bride to Christ alone, a pure and chaste virgin, as Paul puts it. John the Baptist had this in view when he said to his disciples, who were troubled by a blind rivalry for his own glory: "You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. This joy of mine is therefore complete." But because ministers are compared here to those who serve at table, let them remember at the same time that it is their office to set before the Church her food, namely Christ himself, who is that bread of life, and who alone satisfies souls and preserves them to eternal life. To this also belong the things said in chapter 12 about the servant or steward of Christ.

units.la: Restat tertium argumentū, quo discipulorum ambitionem Dominus refrenat, proprio nimirum exemplo eos arguens. At ego sum (inquit) in medio uestrū, ut qui ministrat. Habent uerba ista non obscuram exprobrationis speciem. Quasi diceret: Atqui miror, unde hæc ambitio in animos uestros ir repserit, quæ odiosas hasce rixas & contentiones subinde instaurat. Num uero in me aliquid huius unquam deprehendistis? Ego certè sub censu nasci uolui, & ipso mei natalis momento humilitatem & subiectionem testatus sum. Ego ne regnū in hisce terris affectare uiderer, aut alicui tumultuandi
units.tr: There remains a third argument by which the Lord restrains the disciples' ambition, namely by rebuking them with his own example. "But I am among you," he says, "as one who serves." These words carry no obscure appearance of reproach. It is as if he said: "I wonder where this ambition has crept into your minds, which keeps stirring up these hateful quarrels and contentions. Have you ever detected anything of this in me? I certainly chose to be born in humble circumstances, and at the very moment of my birth I bore witness to humility and submission. Did I ever seem to aspire to a kingdom in this world, or give anyone occasion for tumult?

units.la: Psalm. 45.
units.tr: Psalm. 45.

units.la: Ioan. 3.
units.tr: Ioan. 3.

units.la: Proprio exemplo Christus hu militatem sud det. ansam darem, ipse censum persolui: et de eo interrogatus, ius suum Caesari disertis verbis asserui. Et quamuis uos mihi discipulos domesticos delegerim, nihil tamen unquam feci pro imperio: quin potius uester minister factus sum, & talis etiamnum in medio uestrum uersor. Quin ergo sopito illo ambitioso contentionis spiritu, meum exemplum imitamini? Haec (inquam) & quaecunq; alia in hanc sententiam dici poterant, Christus paucis hisce verbis comprehendit. Et ne verbis nudis agere uideretur, mox nouum exemplum subiecit, cuius nunquam obliuisci possent. Nam ut Ioannes scribit, à mensa surrexit, & linteo succinctus discipulorum pedes abluit, hanc simul sui facti interpretationem inferens: Vos uocatis me, Magister ac Domine, & recte dicitis: sum enim. Si ergo ego lauî pedes uestros, dominus & magister, uos quoq; debetis inuicem alij aliorum pedes lauare. Et hoc illud regnum atq; imperium est, quod discipulis suis ad huius seculi potentiâ aspirantibus Christus destinauit. Ipsi uero deinceps istorum memores, nihil unquam sibi insolentius arrogauerunt: imo ne ferre quidem potuerunt, ut aliqui pio etiâ zelo de ipsis magnificentius aequo sentirent, sicuti in Petri & Ioannis, Pauli & Barnabae exemplis cernitur, quae Actor. cap. 3. & 14. describuntur. Paulus certè Corinthijs nimijs suorum doctorum admiratoribus scribebat: Sic nos aestimet homo, ut seruos Christi, &c. 1. Cor. 4.
units.tr: Christ teaches humility by his own example. I paid the tax myself, and when questioned about it I plainly asserted my right to Caesar's dues. And although I chose you as my intimate disciples, I never used my position to command, but rather I have made myself your servant, and I still live among you in that manner. Why then, putting aside that ambitious spirit of contention, do you not imitate my example?" I say this, and whatever else could be said to the same effect, Christ comprehended in these few words. And so that he should not seem to be teaching by bare words alone, he soon added a new example which they could never forget. For, as John writes, he rose from the table, girded himself with a towel, and washed the disciples' feet, adding at the same time the explanation of his act: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If then I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another's feet." This is the kingdom and rule that Christ appointed for his disciples, who aspired to the power of this world.
