Indeed, mindful of this afterwards, they never claimed anything more arrogant for themselves; rather, they could not even bear it when some, out of pious zeal, thought of them more highly than was fitting, as can be seen in the examples of Peter and John, and of Paul and Barnabas, described in Acts chapters 3 and 14. Paul certainly wrote to the Corinthians, who were too great admirers of their teachers: "Let a man so regard us as servants of Christ," etc. 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: Porrò quaeratur hic aliquis, Vnde ergo suum regnum habeant Romani Pontifices, qui Apostolorum successores se esse dicunt, et patrimonium Petri iactant, quod per multas terras longè lateq; extenditur? Est quaestio haec digna & necessaria cognitu. Nam uerbo Dei ista pugnat, & Petro dictum aiunt: Pascite oues meas. Item: Tibi dabo claues Regni caelorum, &c. At haec non soli Petro dicta esse, & salsissimum esse, quod illi de cathedra Petri Romae posita fabulantur, alibi abunde demonstratum est. Habent tamen propugnatores & defensores multos & graues, multi etiam tyrannidis illius diuturnitate & successibus atq; uictoriis illorum offenduntur. Sed facile patebit huius causae ueritas, si ueterum Prophetarum et Apostolorum uaticinia cum illorum historijs conferamus. Apud Danielem quatuor Monarchiarum successio per quatuor animalia describitur, quae ex mari uentis perturbato prodibat. Quarta bestia, cuius nomen nullum extat, conferetur, & hanc Romanam esse notius est, quàm ut demonstrari debeat. Tribuuntur illi decem cornua, quae tam in regna diuersa distrahenda esse portendunt. Inter illa enascitur cornu paruum, quod tribus cornibus deiectis & depressis creuit, quod quoq; grandia loquebatur, & imperiu sibi in omnia cum diuina tum humana uendicas bellu mouebat sanctis.
units.tr: Here someone may well ask: whence then do the Roman Pontiffs have their kingdom? They say they are the successors of the Apostles, and they boast of the patrimony of Peter, which extends far and wide over many lands. This question is worthy and necessary to be understood. For it is opposed to the Word of God, and they claim that to Peter was said: "Feed my sheep." Likewise: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," etc. But that these things were not said to Peter alone, and that the fable they tell about a chair of Peter set up at Rome is utterly absurd, has been abundantly demonstrated elsewhere. Nevertheless they have many and serious defenders, and many are offended by the long duration, successes and victories of that tyranny. Yet the truth of this cause will easily be made plain if we compare the prophecies of the ancient Prophets and Apostles with their histories. In Daniel the succession of four monarchies is described through four beasts which came up out of the sea, stirred by the winds. The fourth beast, whose name is not given, is to be identified, and that it is Roman is too well known to need demonstration. It is given ten horns, which portend that the empire is to be split into many different kingdoms. Among them there springs up a little horn, which grew after three of the horns were torn out and crushed; it also spoke great things, claimed dominion over all things both divine and human, and made war on the saints.

units.la: Conueniunt his quae Paulus in posteriori ad Thessal. de magno illo Christi aduersario uaticinatur fore nimirum, ut defectio fiat, & tunc reueletur homo ille sceleratus, filius (inquam) perditionis, qui se opponat atq; efferat aduersus omne quod dicitur Deus aut numen. Quibus cum si historias Romani Imperij conferas, & ea quae in hoc Pontifices gesserunt, mox ut haec impleta sint uidebis. Defectionis enim causam siue occasionem dedit prima Constantinus Magnus, qui sedem Imperij Byzantij transtulit, quae ab illo Constantinopolis nomen accepit. Ea enim Imperium uehementer labefactatu fuisse constat, cum ueteres familiae una cum opibus in Thraciam transferrentur, & peregrinis gentibus ostium aperiretur inuadendi Italiam et Romam ipsam uastandi, à qua Deus sanguine Martyrum suorum requirere statuerat. Ab eo igitur tempore Imperium diuisum est, ut alter quidem Imperator in Oriente, alter in Occidente regnare diceretur. Ceperunt tunc emergere decem cornua, id est, plures gentes & regna, in quae Imperij potentia distracta est, & quae paulò post ipsi Romae exitio fuerunt. Nam sub annum Domini CCCCX. Honorio Imperante Franci Treuiros occuparunt, euocati à Senatore quodam, cuius uxorem Lucius Praeses Romanus constupraverat, & inde in Belgicam & Celticam progressi Regnum constituerunt in Gallia duce Varamundo, qui primus illorum Rex nominatur. Et eodem tempore Gotti quoq; arma mouerunt. Cum enim horum auxilijs Theodosius contra Maximum & Eugenium bellum feliciter gessisset, & iisdem ob rem bene gestam stipendia constituisset, Arcadius autem et Honorius illa nollent pendere, eos contra se prouocauerunt, ut magnis copijs in Italiam moverent, & Stiliconis perfidia, qui in die Paschatis eos ex improuiso aggressus erat, magis irritati, Romam toto biennio obsessam tandem coeperunt duce Alarico. Factum id anno Christi CCCCXIII. Coepit ergo tunc foedissima Imperij dilaceratio, & Francorum atque Gottorum exemplis alij quoque populi audaciores facti similia tentarunt. Genfericus enim qui cum Vandalis in Africa confederat, ab Eudoxia, quae Valentiniani III. uxor fuerat, & quam Maximus illo occiso sibi duxerat, euocatus similiter urbem rapit & diripit, atq; Eudoxiam cum Imperij insignibus in Africam transfert: anno Domini CCCCCLIX. Vix autem elapsis annis sedecim anno nimirum incarnati Filij Dei CCCCLXXV. Odoacer Rufianus siue Herulus Orestem, qui filium suum, Augustulum nomine, exercitus fauore adiutus Imperatorem fecerat, ad Ticinum prælio uicit, ubi robur Italiæ prorsus extinctum est. Augustulus abiecta purpura profugit, urbem Odoacer triumphans ingreditur, seq; Romæ & Italiæ Regem dicit. Et hic finis fuit Imperij in Italia. Nam etsi Imperatores eò suos duces & præfectos sæpe mitterent, nullus tamen illic uerè regnare aut gentes, quæ illam subinde inuadebant, prorsus expellere potuit. Nam Iustiniani tempore Gotti duce Totila Romam obsederunt, & non audente ad illam appropinquare Bellisario, quem Imperator eò miserat, illam tandem captam ferro & flamma horribiliter uastarunt: quod factum esse scribitur anno humanæ salutis DXLVI. Et quamuis Totila digresso urbem Bellisarius reciperet, atq; nonnihil instaurasset, tamen triennio post eam Totilæ redeunti rursus occupandam relinquit.
units.tr: These agree with what Paul prophesies in his second letter to the Thessalonians about that great adversary of Christ: namely, that a falling away will happen, and then that wicked man, the son of perdition, will be revealed, who opposes and exalts himself against everything that is called God or object of worship. If you compare with these prophecies the histories of the Roman Empire, and what the Pontiffs have done in this matter, you will see at once that they have been fulfilled. The first to give the cause or occasion of the defection was Constantine the Great, who transferred the seat of empire to Byzantium, which from him received the name Constantinople. For it is well established that the Empire was greatly weakened then, when the ancient families were transferred together with their wealth into Thrace, and a door was opened for foreign peoples to invade Italy and lay waste Rome itself, for which God had determined to require the blood of his martyrs. From that time therefore the Empire was divided, so that one emperor was said to reign in the East and another in the West. Then the ten horns began to emerge, that is, several peoples and kingdoms into which the power of the Empire was torn, and which shortly afterwards brought about the ruin of Rome itself. For in the year of the Lord 410, under Honorius, the Franks occupied Trier, summoned by a certain senator whose wife the Roman governor Lucius had debauched; and from there, advancing into Belgica and Celtica, they established a kingdom in Gaul under their leader Varamund, who is named the first of their kings. At the same time the Goths also took up arms. For when Theodosius, with their help, had successfully waged war against Maximus and Eugenius, and had assigned them pay for that well-fought campaign, Arcadius and Honorius were unwilling to pay it; so they provoked them into moving against themselves with great forces into Italy. Further irritated by the treachery of Stilicho, who attacked them unexpectedly on Easter day, they at last besieged Rome for two whole years under their leader Alaric. This happened in the year of Christ 413. Then the most shameful dismemberment of the Empire began, and other peoples, made bolder by the examples of the Franks and Goths, attempted similar things. For Genseric, who had allied himself with the Vandals in Africa, was summoned by Eudoxia, who had been the wife of Valentinian III and whom Maximus had taken to himself after killing her husband; he likewise seized and plundered the city, and carried Eudoxia with the insignia of empire into Africa, in the year of the Lord 455. Scarcely sixteen years had passed when, in the year 475 of the incarnate Son of God, Odoacer the Rugian or Herulian defeated Orestes in battle at Ticinum. Orestes had made his son, named Augustulus, emperor, aided by the favour of the army; and there the strength of Italy was utterly extinguished. Augustulus, casting off the purple, fled; Odoacer entered the city in triumph and called himself King of Rome and Italy. And this was the end of the Empire in Italy. For although the emperors often sent their generals and prefects there, none of them truly reigned there, nor could any of them wholly expel the peoples who from time to time invaded it. For in the time of Justinian the Goths under their leader Totila besieged Rome, and when Belisarius, whom the emperor had sent there, did not dare to approach it, they at last took it and horribly laid it waste with sword and fire. This is written as having happened in the year of human salvation 546. And although Belisarius recovered the city after Totila had withdrawn, and somewhat restored it, nevertheless three years later he left it to be occupied again when Totila returned.

units.la: Inter istas turbas et regnorum, quæ ex Romani Imperij dilaceratione exortæ erant, collisiones, emersit paruum illud cornu, de quo Daniel scribit: Episcoporum uidelicet Romanorum potentia, qui hucusq; uiles & maxima ex parte Martyres Christi fuerant, tunc autem in urbe lacera & Italia omnibus præsidijs nudata regnum sibi uendicare cœperunt, dum Imperatores in Oriente aliis negotijs distinebantur. Et primum quidem de primatu in Ecclesia contentionem mouit regnante Mauritio Imp. Ioannes Constantinopolitanus Episcopus, cui se grauiter opposuit Gregorius Magnus, qui tunc Romæ præsidebat. Non multò post tamen Bonifacius III. anno Christi DCVII. à Phoca impetrauit, ut Roma Ecclesiarum omnium caput, & Romanus Episcopus οἰκουμενικὸς, id est uniuersalis totius orbis ecclesiarum pastor diceretur. Fuit hæc quasi natiuitas parui illius cornu, quod paulatim crescendo uires itidem maiores acquisiuit. Hac enim occasione Romani Episcopi in Imperatores ipsos ius quoddam prætexere cœperunt. Itaq; cum Leo III. Imperator Constantinopolitanus diuino & sanctissimo edicto imagines e templis auferri mandauisset, Gregorius III. Papa ita adeò indignè tulit, ut fulmine excommunicationis Leonem feriret, & eidem per Italiam tributa solui prohiberet. Fuit ea res magnorum motuum causa. Rauennæ certè (ubi Iustinus antea propter Longobardos, qui in Italia sedes posuerant, Exarchatum instituerat ad coercendā horum uim atq; potentiam) seditione excitata Paulus Exarchus cæsus, & Imperatori Leoni omne in Italia imperiū abrogatū siue ablatum est: & ita unum cornu ex illis decem decussum siue excisum fuit. Factum hoc est anno ânato Filio Dei DCCXXIX. Visus fuerat contra Imperatorem Papa in primis Longobardorum auxilijs, quorum potentia tunc in Italia omnibus formidabilis erat. Sed fuit hæc nouarum turbarum causa. Longobardi enim, ut suum in Italia regnum stabilirent atq; propagarent, Rauennam & quæ Imperatores hucusq; ceu infelices bellorum Gotticorum et Vandalicorum reliquias, per Exarchos administrarunt, occupare cœperunt, et tandem Romam quoq; cinxerunt obsidione. Itaq; Gregorius, qui Imperatorem sibi propter multas grauesq; iniurias merito infensum esse sciebat, non illius, sed Pipini, qui Maior domus siue Magister equitū apud Francos erat, opē implorauit, qui in Italia ducto exercitu effecit, ut Longobardi obsidionem urbis soluerent. Fuit hoc officium tam gratum sanctis illis patribus, ut mirifico consilio & aestutia incredibili Pipinum Regem Francorū faceret Zacharias Papa, Hildericho Rege (quem illi stupidum & regno indignum dicebant) in monasterium detrusò: quod accidisse constat sub annum Domini DCCLI. Fuit hoc alterum cornu, quod uere humiliauit Papa, ut sui imperij fideliore defensorem haberet Pipinum. Retulit hic quoq; Pontifici gratia, & urbes quasdam Italiæ, quæ prius Imperatoris fuerant, Romanæ sedi donauit, & tunc terrarum & urbium domini fieri cœperunt Episcopi. Nondum tamen præda ista pacificè & tutò frui poterant, Longobardis subinde Romam & Italiam infestantibus, ut acceptas ab illis iniurias ulciscerentur: & fortassis metuebat, ne aliquando Græci quoq; Imperatores sua repeterent. Ideo nouū asylum comenti, Carolum Pipini Filium, qui postea Magnus dictus est, rursus aduersus Longobardos euocauerunt, qui hos magno prælio uicit, & Desiderium Regem cum uxore & liberis in Galliam misit, & regnū illorum, quod annos ducentos et quatuor in Italia tenuerant, prorsus aboleuit, anno Christi natị DCCLXXIII. Itaque tertium quoq; bestiæ illius cornu deiecit Papa, & eo facto potentiam suam uehementer auxit. Nam sublatis iam ex Italia impedimentis omnibus, ne quid Græci quoq; Imperatores moliri possent, imaginem ueteris bestiæ excogitauit, & Carolum Occidentis Imperatorem creauit, ut ad manum haberet principem potentem, cuius auxilio contra hostes quosuis defenderetur. Factum hoc est Anno ab incarnatione Filij Dei DCCCI. octavo Calendarum Ianuarij, in Basilica Petri, acclamante toto populo & clero Romano: CAROLO AVGVSTO, à Deo Coronato MAGNO & Pacifico IMPERATORI, VITA & VICTORIA. Ferebant hoc indignissimè Constantinopolitani principes: sed quid facerent, quando neque ipsis inter se probè convenieb at, & muliebri atque crudeli Irenes imperio premebantur, quae non ita pridem filium Leonem IIII. per insidias interceptum oculis simul atque vita spoliaverat? Quàm verò ista optimis quibusque displicuerint, in Francorum principibus est videre, qui cum Carolus Imperij legibus eos subijcere & ipsorum iura antiquare vellet, coitiones facere coeperunt, et iugum illud aperte detrectarunt. Denique Vasco, unus ex procerum Vasconum numero, cum supplementum in Hispaniam ducere iuberetur, ausus est multa in faciem Caroli contra Imperium illud novum dicere, & illud aliorum omnium nomine detrectare. Inter alia haec illum dixisse, historici perhibent: Franci in tanta nominis tui amplitudine maiestate{?}, nihil optamus aliud, quàm ut Franci simus qui fuimus. Armorum vocationem, si ultrò offerres, notari ignominia nos putaremus. Cur milites tuos, Regnū tuum, Franciam tuam, Imperij provinciam facere studes, Imperio{?} subijcere, rei uagae, (ut expertus ipse es) & profugae? ut cum more suo, quae fortunae ludibria sunt, circumagi, temereue excurrere coeperit, nobis aut iure seruiendum sit, aut iniuria dimicandum? Imperium enim in Francia sempiternum fore quis spondere ausit, quod ex Italia in Orientem, ex Oriente ad te, non nominis Francici charitate, sed uictoriarum felicitate revocatum sit? Neque animus fefellit optimum hunc & suae gentis amantissimum principem. Nam etiamsi Carolus Romanam sedem ex omni discrimine liberasset, & eius filius Ludouicus noua donatione facta ipsam quoque Romam cum omnibus circa eam terris, civitatibus, portubus & maritimis Hetruriae locis Pontifici tradidisset, non tamen sempiterna fuit apud illos homines tantorum beneficiorum memoria: sed cùm Francos in ipsis defendendis minus alacres postea uiderent, Ecclesiae defensionem unà cum Imperio ad Germanos transtulerunt, & tandem institutis Electoribus Septemuiris illud in ea gente stabiliuerunt ijs conditionibus, quae ut ipsis utiles, ita Germanis principibus molestias, labores, bella denique externa & ciuilia pepererunt, sicuti historici copiose testantur. Haec ergo Pontificiae tyrannidis initia fuere, et istis incrementis atque gradibus ad tantam potentiam ascenderunt, quae nunc Regibus quoque potentissimis formidolosa est. Habet enim cornu illud (sicuti Daniel narrat) oculos hominis, id est, ualet astutia, prudentia, rerum usu & artibus, quibus ea etiam conficiunt Pontifices, quae non unquam fieri posse uidebantur. Habet os loquens grandia, & ad latus Altissimi loquitur, quasi ad hoc ordinatus sit, & huius causam agat. Naturam Christi se esse dicit Pontifex, Petri & Pauli successorem, Sanctissimum patrem, cui plenum ius sit in coelum euehendi quos uult, aut ad inferos detrudendi omnes, qui ipsi minus probantur. Mutat ergo leges & tempora, & tam in diuinis quàm humanis pro suo arbitrio dispensat. Poterat haec multis demonstrari, nisi publicè omnibus nota essent. Sufficiat nunc monuisse, uel eo uno indicio istos homines argui, quòd cùm Apostolorum successores dici & haberi uelint, tanta tamen impudentia regnū in hoc seculo uendicant, neque ad se pertinere cogitant, quae Christus in praesenti Apostolis dicit. Defendunt illi causam suam Regum authoritate, & donationes iactant, quarum aliquae fabulosae sunt (ut quae Constantini Magni nomine palliatur) aliae per fraudem aut etiam uim apertam extortae. Sed ut nihil in illis fictitium, nihil uiolentum sit, nos tamen simpliciter dicimus, neque Regibus licuisse dare, neque Episcopis accipere ea, quae cum eo munere pugnant, cui ipsos Deus destinauit. Regum enim & principum est rempub. administrare, ius dicere, gentibus dominari: Ecclesiarum ministris dicitur: Vos autem non sic. Et generalis regula est: Unusquisque in sua uocatione maneat. Ista obseruent homines Christiani, neque magnificis Pontificum titulis aut eorundem immani iam{?} aliquot seculis confirmata potentia moueantur.
units.tr: Amid these upheavals and collisions of kingdoms, which arose from the break-up of the Roman Empire, that little horn of which Daniel writes appeared: namely, the power of the Roman bishops. Until then they had been humble and, for the most part, martyrs of Christ, but now, while the city and Italy lay torn apart and stripped of every defence, and while the emperors in the East were occupied with other business, they began to claim a kingdom for themselves. The first to stir up a dispute over primacy in the Church was John, bishop of Constantinople, in the reign of the Emperor Maurice; Gregory the Great, who then presided at Rome, opposed him strongly. Not long afterwards, however, in the year of Christ 607, Boniface III obtained from Phocas that Rome should be called the head of all churches and the Roman bishop "ecumenical" [οἰκουμενικὸς], that is, pastor of the churches of the whole world. This was, as it were, the birth of that little horn, which, growing gradually, also acquired greater strength. For on this occasion the Roman bishops began to claim a certain right over the emperors themselves. So when Leo III, emperor at Constantinople, ordered images to be removed from the churches by a divine and most holy edict, Gregory III took it so badly that he struck Leo with the thunderbolt of excommunication and forbade tribute to be paid to him in Italy. This was the cause of great disturbances. At Ravenna, certainly (where Justinian had earlier set up the Exarchate, to restrain the power and strength of the Lombards who had settled in Italy), a rebellion broke out, Exarch Paul was killed, and the empire of Emperor Leo in Italy was entirely abolished or taken away. Thus one of those ten horns was struck down and cut off. This happened in the year 729 after the Son of God was born. The Pope had seemed to act against the emperor chiefly by means of the help of the Lombards, whose power was then feared throughout Italy. But this was the cause of new troubles. For the Lombards, in order to establish and extend their kingdom in Italy, began to seize Ravenna and the other territories which the emperors, through the exarchs, had hitherto governed as the unhappy remnants of the Gothic and Vandal wars, and at last they surrounded Rome with a siege. Therefore Gregory, who knew that the emperor was justly hostile to him on account of many grave injuries, implored the aid not of the emperor but of Pepin, who was mayor of the palace, or master of the horse, among the Franks. Pepin led an army into Italy and made the Lombards lift the siege of the city. This service was so welcome to those holy fathers that Pope Zacharias, by a wonderfully clever plan and incredible cunning, made Pepin king of the Franks, and thrust King Childeric (whom they called stupid and unworthy of the kingdom) into a monastery; this is known to have happened around the year of the Lord 751. This was the second horn, which the Pope truly humbled, so that he might have Pepin as a more faithful defender of his power. Pepin also repaid the pontiff with gratitude, and gave to the Roman see certain cities of Italy which had previously belonged to the emperor; and then bishops began to become lords of lands and cities. Yet they could not yet enjoy this booty peacefully and safely, since the Lombards kept attacking Rome and Italy from time to time, to avenge the injuries they had received from them; and perhaps the Pope feared lest at some point the Greek emperors too should reclaim their property. So they called out again against the Lombards that new refuge of their schemes, Charles, son of Pepin, who was later called the Great. He defeated them in a great battle, sent King Desiderius with his wife and children into Gaul, and utterly abolished the kingdom of the Lombards, which had lasted for two hundred and four years in Italy, in the year of Christ's birth 773. Thus the Pope also cast down the third horn of that beast, and by this act greatly increased his power. For with all the obstacles removed from Italy, so that the Greek emperors could attempt nothing either, he devised an image of the old beast and created Charles emperor of the West, so that he might have at hand a powerful prince by whose help he would be defended against any enemies. This was done in the year from the incarnation of the Son of God 801, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the Basilica of St Peter, with the whole Roman people and clergy acclaiming: "To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the Great and Peaceful Emperor, life and victory." The princes of Constantinople took this very badly; but what could they do, since they did not even agree well among themselves, and were oppressed by the womanish and cruel rule of Irene, who had not long before deprived her son Leo IV of his eyes and his life by treachery? How much these things displeased all the better sort may be seen among the princes of the Franks, who, when Charles wished to subject them to the laws of the empire and abolish their ancient rights, began to form conspiracies and openly refused that yoke. At last Vascus, one of the chiefs of the Gascons, when he was ordered to lead reinforcements into Spain, dared to say many things to Charles's face against that new empire, and to reject it in the name of all the others. The historians report that among other things he said: "Franks, in such great renown of your name and majesty, we desire nothing else than to be the Franks we were. If you were to offer us a summons to arms, we would think it a disgrace. Why do you strive to make your soldiers, your kingdom, your France a province of the empire, and to subject it to an empire which is a wandering and fugitive thing (as you yourself have experienced)? For when, in its own manner, it begins to be turned about as a plaything of fortune and to rush about rashly, are we to be slaves to it by right, or fight against it by wrong? For who would dare to promise that the empire will last forever in France, when it has been brought from Italy to the East, and from the East to you, not by love of the Frankish name but by the good fortune of victories?" Nor did this best of princes, most devoted to his own people, miss the truth. For even though Charles had freed the Roman see from every danger, and his son Louis, by a new grant, had handed over to the Pope Rome itself with all the lands, cities, ports and maritime places of Etruria around it, nevertheless the memory of such great benefits did not last forever among those men. Later, when they saw the Franks less eager to defend them, they transferred the defence of the Church together with the empire to the Germans, and at last, by establishing the seven Electors, they fixed it in that nation on conditions which, while useful to themselves, brought troubles, labours and finally foreign and civil wars upon the German princes, as the historians attest at length. These, then, were the beginnings of papal tyranny, and by these increases and steps they rose to such power as is now frightening even to the most powerful kings. For that horn (as Daniel relates) has "eyes of a man," that is, it has cunning, prudence, experience of affairs and skills, by which the Popes also accomplish things that seemed never possible. It has "a mouth speaking great things," and it speaks "against the Most High," as if it were appointed for this purpose and pleaded this cause. The Pope says that he is the vicar of Christ, the successor of Peter and Paul, the most holy father, who has full right to raise to heaven whom he wishes, or to cast all whom he finds less pleasing down to hell. He therefore changes laws and times, and dispenses in divine and human matters according to his own judgement. These things could be shown by many examples, were they not known publicly to everyone. It is enough now to have noted that these men may be convicted by this one sign alone: although they wish to be called and considered successors of the Apostles, they claim a kingdom in this world with such impudence, and do not consider that those things which Christ says to the Apostles in the present passage pertain to them. They defend their cause by the authority of kings, and boast of donations, some of which are fabulous (such as the one falsely attributed to the name of Constantine the Great), others extorted by fraud or even open force. But even if nothing in those grants were fictitious or violent, we nevertheless say plainly that it was not lawful for kings to give, nor for bishops to receive, those things which are contrary to the office to which God has appointed them. For it belongs to kings and princes to administer the commonwealth, to dispense justice, and to rule over peoples; but of the ministers of the Churches it is said: "But it shall not be so among you" [Matth. 20.26]. And the general rule is: "Let each remain in his own calling" [1 Cor. 7.20]. Let Christian men observe these things, and let them not be moved by the grand titles of the Pontiffs, or by the power of these men, which for some centuries now has been strengthened by violence.

units.la: Caeterum tempus est, ut ad Christi uerba reuertamur, qui ne discipuli sui peccati conscientia territi succumberent, aut omni praemij spe abiecta in suo munere fierent negligentiores, amica & dulci consolatione animos eorum erigit atque confirmat. Partes eius sunt duae. Prima eorum fidem atque constantiam praedicat, quod magnum est ad uirtutem incitamentum, quo generosiores animi uehementius quàm ulla alia ratione mouentur. Dicit ergo: Vos porro estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis, &c. Quasi diceret: Etsi hic uester lapsus grauis sit, & acerrimam correptionem mereamini: nolim tamen vos de mea gratia & salute vestra desperare. Nec enim vestrae fidei ideo oblitus sum: quin memori mente teneo, quàm facilè meae vocationi assenseritis, & quòd aliis omnibus à me turpiter deficientibus, vos soli mecum perseveraveritis, idq; in omnis generis tentationibus, quae me in hunc usq; diem exercuerunt. Pergite modo in posterum quoq;, neq; vos fallet spes praemij amplissima, etiamsi nullum in terris hisce regnum vobis paratum sit. Est autem exemplum hoc Christi probè observandum, ne asperius & durius tractemus eos, qui aliquando non poenitenda fidei & pietatis suae argumenta praebuerunt. Possunt enim tales facilè in viam reduci, si commodè tractentur, & eorum quae recte fecerunt, aliquam rationem haberi videant. Sunt ergo nō satis prudentes, qui omnia delicta pro capitalibus ducunt, & eos qui semel lapsi sunt tantummodo pedibus conculcant, neq; eos resurgere patiuntur, dum spem quoq; melioris sortis omnem illis negant.
units.tr: Now it is time to return to the words of Christ, who, so that his disciples would not be broken by the awareness of their sin, or grow more careless in their office with all hope of reward cast aside, raises and strengthens their spirits with a friendly and sweet consolation. It has two parts. The first commends their faith and steadfastness, which is a great incitement to virtue, and by which noble minds are moved more powerfully than by any other means. So he says: "You are those who have continued with me in my trials," etc. As if he were saying: although your fall is serious and you deserve a very sharp rebuke, I would not have you despair of my grace and of your own salvation. For I have not forgotten your faith; I keep in a mindful heart how readily you assented to my calling, and how, while all the others shamefully deserted me, you alone persevered with me, and that in every kind of trial which has harassed me to this day. Only go on in the future too, and the very ample hope of reward will not deceive you, even though no kingdom is prepared for you in this earth. This example of Christ is to be carefully observed, so that we do not treat harshly and severely those who at some time have given proofs of their faith and piety that do not deserve regret. For such people can easily be brought back to the right way if they are treated kindly, and if they see some account taken of what they did rightly. Those therefore are not wise enough who regard every offence as a capital crime, who simply trample underfoot those who have once fallen, and do not allow them to rise again, while denying them any hope of a better lot.

units.la: Non temere autem Christus suarum tentationum meminit. Significantur ea voce omnis generis adversa, quibus ad diffidentiam & defectionem solicitamur, sive illa proprie ad corpus sive ad animam pertineant. Etenim omnibus, quae homini accidere possunt, illum obnoxium fuisse constat. Pauperatem certè & inopiam iam inde à pueris sustinuit, adeo ut non haberet, quo reclinaret caput suum. Fuit inopiae coniuncta ignominia, cum omnium probris petitus sit, & à propriis etiam cognatis contemptui habitus. Sedibus item incertis hinc inde oberrans passim adversarios invenit, qui insidiosis disputationibus illum vel irretire, vel populo simul & magnatibus exosum sive suspectum facere conati sunt. Taceo nunc fugas & persecutiones, quarum fine non potuit attingere, quoad in terris hisce vixit. Quia autem ille caput nostrum est, suo exemplo docuit, quae omnium credentium sors in hoc mundo semper futura sit. Nec enim (ut ipse ait) discipulus magistro praestat, neq; servus, & aequum est, ut Filio Dei conformes fiant quoad crucem & afflictiones, qui regni & gloriae coelestis haeredes cum illo esse cupiunt.
units.tr: Christ did not mention his trials without reason. By this word are signified every kind of adversity by which we are pressed toward distrust and desertion, whether these pertain properly to the body or to the soul. For it is established that he was subject to all the things that can befall a man. He certainly endured poverty and want from boyhood, so that he had nowhere to lay his head. Shame was joined to his want, since he was assailed with the insults of all and was despised even by his own kinsmen. Wandering about hither and thither with no settled dwelling, he everywhere met adversaries who tried either to entangle him in insidious disputations or to make him hateful or suspect to the people and the great men at the same time. I say nothing now of the flights and persecutions, from which he could not escape for as long as he lived on this earth. But because he is our head, he taught by his own example what the lot of all believers will always be in this world. For (as he himself says) "a disciple is not above his master, nor a servant above his lord," and it is fitting that those who desire to be heirs with him of the heavenly kingdom and glory should be made like the Son of God in cross and afflictions.

units.la: Simul autem Apostolorum exemplo admonemur, quid nos inter tot rerum discrimina facere conveniat. Commendantur eo nomine illi, quòd cum Christo permanserint. In eo igitur nobis quoque est annitendum. Nec enim afflictiones per se laudem merentur, neq; aliquem servare possunt, ut quae ex peccato originem ducunt, & pijs cum impijs atq; sceleratis communes sunt. Eadem autem exemplo & merito Christi sanctificantur, ut exercitia ad virtutem & salutem fiant. Hunc ergo nobis ducem proponamus, & illius vestigia vestigemur. Docet hoc ille, quando generalem illam Christianis omnibus regulam praescribit: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget seipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Itaq; prima nobis cura sit (quod Petrus etiam monet) ne quis ut homicida, aut fur, aut maleficus aut alienarum rerum inspector affligatur. Beatos enim ipse Christus pronuntiat eos, qui propter iustitiam persecutionem patiuntur. Deinde non moveant nos mundi huius illecebrae aut exemplum: sed constanter perseveremus in finem usq;, quantumvis tristia & horrenda sint, quae Satan obijcit: iucunda autem & suavia carni, quibus nos ad defectionem solicitat. Quòd si vero nos propter delicta nostra affligi contingat, tamen ne tunc quidem animus nobis concidat. Nam pro facinoro fis ideo Christus in publico supplicium loco pati voluit, ut meritum suum ad hos quoq; extenderet. Deniq; ita cum illo permaneamus, ut in eius solius merito universa nostrae salutis fiducia nobis reposita sit, neue meritum statuamus in ijs, quae ipsi patimur, ut superstitiosi solent, qui in corporali exercitatione spem omnem collocant. Quia enim huius seculi afflictiones nullo modo conferri possunt cum coelesti illa gloria, quae olim revelabitur, illis quoq; hanc mereri nemo potest. Et notum est illud Pauli dictum: Si tradam corpus meum ut comburar, non habeam autem charitatem, nihil iuvor.
units.tr: At the same time, we are admonished by the example of the apostles as to what it becomes us to do amid so many dangers. They are commended on this account, that they remained with Christ. In this, then, we too must strive. For afflictions do not in themselves deserve praise, nor can they save anyone, since they arise from sin and are common to the godly and to the wicked and criminal alike. But they are sanctified by the same example and merit of Christ, so that they become exercises toward virtue and salvation. Let us therefore set him before us as our leader, and let us follow in his footsteps. He teaches this when he prescribes that general rule for all Christians: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Therefore our first care should be (as Peter also warns) that no one suffers as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or a meddler in other people's affairs. For Christ himself pronounces blessed those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake. Then let not the allurements of this world or its example move us, but let us persevere steadfastly to the end, however grievous and dreadful are the things Satan sets before us, and however pleasant and sweet are the things by which he urges us, through the flesh, to defection. But if it happens that we are afflicted on account of our own offences, then let not our spirit even then fall into despair. For Christ wished to suffer punishment in a public place for the crimes of others, so that he might extend his merit to these also. Finally, let us so persevere with him that the whole confidence of our salvation is laid up in his merit alone, and let us not set up merit in what we ourselves suffer, as the superstitious do, who place all their hope in bodily exercise. For since the afflictions of this age can in no way be compared with that heavenly glory which will one day be revealed, no one can earn that glory by them either. And the saying of Paul is well known: "If I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing."

units.la: Altera parte praemium amplissimum discipulis Christus pollicetur. Et ego vobis pacisc or, prout pactus est mihi Pater, Regnum, &c. In Graeco est διαθήκη, quod de illis dici solet, qui testamenta condunt & legant cuiq; quod ex suis bonis ad illum redire volunt. Et conuenit ea vox iam morituro. Neq; obstat, quòd eadem de Patre utitur. Nam etiamsi hunc minime mortuum esse cōstet, idem tamen Filio Regnum haereditario iure destinavit, ut hoc & legitimum & perpetuum esse significaret. Ideo in Psalm. scribitur: Postula à me, daboq; gentes, ut sint haereditas tua. Facit aute multum ad salutis certitudinem, quod huius rationem omne Deus testamento complexus est, sicuti in epistola ad Hebraeos prolixè demonstratur. Nam si hominis testamentum authoritate legitima confirmatum nemo abrogat, quanto inviolabilior erit eius veritas, quo nos Deus per Filium suum Regni coelestis hæredes scripsit? Quod enim hic discipulis dicit, id postea (ut Ioan.17.cap.habetur) ad omnes exten-dit, qui illorum verbo aut prædicatione edocti in illum credunt. In præsenti autē Regni illius, quod pollicetur, gaudium atque maiestatem duobus capitibus comprehendit.
units.tr: In the second part, Christ promises the disciples a very ample reward. "And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me," etc. In the Greek it is διαθήκη [diathēkē], a word usually said of those who make wills and bequeath to each person some part of their goods that they wish to pass to him. And the word suits one who is about to die. Nor is it an obstacle that the same word is used of the Father. For although it is certain that he is by no means dead, he nevertheless destined the kingdom for the Son by hereditary right, to signify that this is both lawful and perpetual. So it is written in the Psalm: "Ask of me, and I shall give the nations for thine inheritance." It contributes much to the certainty of salvation that God has embraced this covenant in a testament, as is shown at length in the epistle to the Hebrews. For if no one annuls a man's testament confirmed by lawful authority, how much more inviolable will its truth be, by which God has named us heirs of the heavenly kingdom through his Son? For what he here says to the disciples, he afterwards extends (as is found in John 17) to all who, taught by their word or preaching, believe in him. Now he comprehends the joy and majesty of that kingdom which he promises under two heads.

units.la: Primum est: Vt edatis & bibatis in mensa mea, in regno meo. Non debet hoc carnis sensu ac-cipi, ne felicitatem alterius seculi in uentris gulǽ delitiis collocemus, ut impurus ille & infelix Mahumet, qui primus Saracenis & Turcis leges tulit. Nam ut cap.20. audiuimus, Angelis simi-les erimus, neq; cibo aut generatione ulla opus erit, ubi corruptio nullum locum habebit. Et Regnum Dei cibum aut potū esse negat Apostolus. Est ergo hæc figurata locutio à Regum moribus aut con-suetudine sumpta, qui mensa sua eos dignantur, quos amore summo cōpletuntur, & sui honoris par-ticipes uolunt facere. Et sensus est: ipsos cœlestis gaudij atq; felicitatis ipsi consortes atq; cohæredes fore. Ita ipse apud Ioannem exponit: Vado paraturus uobis locum, et cum abiero et parauero uobis locum, rursus ueniam, & assumam uos ad meipsum, ut ubi sum ego, & uos sitis. Et rursus: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, uolo ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum: ut spectent gloriam illam meam, quam de-disti mihi: quia dilexisti me ante iacta fundamenta mundi. Est hæc non minus uera & certa quàm magnifica promissio. Nam huius amplitudinem descripturus Propheta, Deum diligentibus ipsum ea præparauisse dicit, quæ neq; oculi, neq; aures mortales, neq; hominis animalis intellectus compræ-hendere possunt. Nec est quod quisquam in mora periculum esse uereatur. Nam ut Ioannis quinto cap.docet Christus, anima quam primum hinc migrat, ad sedes illas æternæ felicitatis colligitur, corpus autem in spe lætæ resurrectionis quiescit, in qua ipsum quoq; animæ suæ restitutum ab omni corruptione liberabitur, ut totus homo Regni illius delitiis atq; gloria fruatur, quod hic nobis Chri-stus promittit. Horum meditatione nosipsos consolemur in omnibus aduersis: neq; dubitemus fore diem illum retributionis, de quo supra etiam cap.21. locutus est.
units.tr: The first is: "That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom." This must not be understood in a carnal sense, lest we place the happiness of the other age in the pleasures of gluttony, as that impure and unhappy Mahomet did, who first gave laws to the Saracens and Turks. For, as we heard in chapter 20, we shall be like the angels, and there will be no need of food or procreation, where corruption will have no place. And the Apostle denies that the kingdom of God is food or drink. This, then, is a figurative expression taken from the customs and practice of kings, who deign to admit to their table those whom they love most and wish to make sharers of their honour. And the meaning is that they will be partners and co-heirs of heavenly joy and happiness. So he himself explains it in John: "I go to prepare a place for you, and if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you unto myself, that where I am, there ye may be also." And again: "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am, that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me, for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world." This promise is no less true and certain than it is magnificent. For the Prophet, describing its greatness, says that God has prepared for those who love him things which neither eye nor ear of mortals, nor the understanding of natural man, can comprehend. Nor should anyone fear danger from the delay. For as Christ teaches in John 5, the soul, as soon as it departs hence, is gathered into those seats of eternal happiness, while the body rests in the hope of a joyful resurrection, in which it too, restored to the soul and freed from all corruption, will enjoy in full the delights and glory of that kingdom which Christ here promises us. Let us console ourselves in all adversities by meditating on these things, and let us not doubt that the day of that retribution will come, of which he also spoke above in chapter 21.

units.la: Secundum huius promissionis caput est: Sedebitis super thronos iudicantes duodecim tribus Is-raelis. Idem apud Matth.cap.19. habetur. Dicitur autem hoc etiam figuratè. Nam si proprie loqui uelimus, omne iudicium Dei est. Is uero omne iudicium dedit Filio, & (ut Paulus Athenien-sibus concionatur) hunc definiuit, ut in magno illo die iudicet orbem terrarum. Dicuntur autem iudicare Apostoli primo propter uerbum, quod in toto mundo prædicauerunt: quia ex eo Christus iudicabit, secundum illud: Prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabi-tur: qui nō crediderit, condenabitur. Cui consentit, quod apud Ioan.dicit: Qui reijcit me, nec recipit uerba mea, habet qui condemnet ipsum: Sermo quē locutus sum, ille iudicabit eum in ultimo illo die. Faciunt hæc plurimum ad cōmendandam doctrinæ Apostolicæ siue Euangelij authoritatē. Nam ex nouissimi iudicij sententia salus & perditio hominis pendebit: neq; aliquis irritū facere poterit, quod tunc iudex ille pronuntiauerit. Illa autē non aliunde quàm ex Euangelio petetur, cuius certa atq; in-fallibilis ueritas tunc multis magno suo malo innotescet, qui nūc præcipua eius capita scurriliter ri-dent. Deinde iudicaturi dicuntur Apostoli duodecim tribus Israelis, quia suo exemplo Iudæis omnē excusationem ignorantiæ eripient: quo sensu Niniuitas & Regina Sabæ alibi eorundē iudices fore dicit. Debet autē hinc quoq; generalis admonitio peti, ne nobis aliquæ iustæ aut idoneæ excusationis prætextum fore putemus. Nam ut olim, ita hodie quoq; Dei uerbum omnibus prædicatur, & ubiq; locorū omnis generis et ordinis homines inueniuntur, qui illi credūt et respiscūt. Horum ergo exem-pla, etsi nihil aliud accederet, incredulis ac contumacibus damnandis sufficient. Iudicabit aulicos à Regum authoritate pendentes Moses, qui cum fratribus affligi maluit, quā aulæ delitijs frui. Iudi-cabūt diuites, qui pro Regno Dei nihil amittere uolunt, Abrahamus, Zachæus & similes, qui Deo uocante omnia sua reliquerunt. Iudicabit pauperes impatientes et murmuratores Lazarus: milites impios & crudeles, Cornelius Centurio: usurarios, publicani, qui olim ad Christum conuersi sunt: im-pudicas omnes, scorta, quæ olim peccatorū suorum ueniam cum acerbis lachrymis quæsierunt. Sed longum foret per omnes hominum ordines sermonē extendere, & tempus est, ut dicendi finem facia-mus. Sufficiat nunc tenuisse, inanes fore in illo die delitias, quas sibi hodie multi fingunt. Eos enim, qui tot testibus conuincuntur, et quos propria conscientia accusat, quæ mille testium loco est, nemo li-berauerit, præter Iesum Christū, qui ut iudex ueniet iustus ad puniendū impios, ita fidus aduocatus & nindex erit omniū, qui Euangelio eius fidem habuerunt, & ex illius semine renati uitā uixerunt Christiana professione dignam. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The second point of this promise is: "You shall sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." The same words occur in Matthew 19. This is said figuratively. If we want to speak strictly, all judgment belongs to God. Yet he has given all judgment to the Son, and (as Paul preaches to the Athenians) he has appointed him to judge the world on that great day. The apostles are said to judge first because of the word they preached throughout the whole world, since Christ will judge by that word, according to the saying: "Preach the gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned." In agreement with this is what John says: "He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who condemns him: the word I have spoken will judge him on the last day." These things greatly serve to commend the authority of the apostolic doctrine, or of the gospel. For the salvation or ruin of a man will depend on the sentence of the final judgment, and no one will be able to overturn what that judge then pronounces. But that sentence will be sought from nowhere else than the gospel, whose certain and infallible truth will then become known, to the great harm of many, who now mock its main points with buffoonery. Next, the apostles are said to judge the twelve tribes of Israel, because by their example they will strip the Jews of every excuse of ignorance; in this sense he elsewhere says that the Ninevites and the Queen of Sheba will be their judges too. Indeed a general warning should be drawn from this, lest we think there is any pretext of a just or fitting excuse left for us. For as in former times, so today too the word of God is preached to all, and in every place men of every kind and rank are found who believe it and repent. Therefore the examples of these, even if nothing else were added, will be enough to condemn unbelievers and the obstinate. Moses will judge courtiers who depend on the authority of kings, he who chose to be afflicted with his brothers rather than enjoy the delights of the court. The rich who are unwilling to lose anything for the kingdom of God will be judged by Abraham, by Zacchaeus, and by similar men, who at God's calling left all they had. Lazarus will judge the poor who are impatient and murmur; Cornelius the centurion will judge impious and cruel soldiers; the publicans who were once converted to Christ will judge usurers; and the harlots, who once sought pardon for their sins with bitter tears, will judge all the unchaste. But it would be too long to extend our discourse through all the ranks of men, and it is time to bring our speech to an end. It is enough for now to have shown that the pleasures which many today imagine for themselves will be empty on that day. For those who are convicted by so many witnesses, and whom their own conscience accuses, which is in place of a thousand witnesses, no one will set free except Jesus Christ, who, as the just judge, will come to punish the wicked, and who will be the faithful advocate and defender of all who have trusted in his gospel, and who, born again from its seed, have lived a life worthy of the Christian profession. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVII
units.tr: HOMILY CXCVII

units.la: Dixit etiam Dominus: Simõ, Simõ, ecce, Satanas expetiuit vos quos ventilaret sicut triticum. Sed ego rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Tu igitur aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Ipse vero dixit ei: Domine tecum paratus sum & ad carcerem & ad mortem proficisci. At ille dixit: Dico tibi Petre, non canet hodie gallus, priusquam ter neges me tibi notum esse.
units.tr: The Lord also said: "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to have you, that he may sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again at some time, strengthen your brothers." But he said to him: "Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death." And he said: "I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today before you have three times denied that you know me."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster, Iesus Christus, nuper fidem suorum discipulorum magnifice commendauit, & ijsdem praemium amplissimum promisit: fore nimirum dicens, ut non solum Regni sui caelestis gaudio atq; delitijs fruantur, verumetiam olim doctrina et exemplo suo iudicent eos, a quibus nunc contemnantur. At sciebat eos pro carnis vitiosa ingenio confidentiores esse, & proinde in hoc etiam seculo ad altiorem dignitatem aspirare, atq; (quod sanctissimis quibusq; frequenter accidere solet) circa res huius seculi magis quam par sit occupari. Itaq; ne quam haberent occasionem gloriandi, quae illos securiores faceret, nunc ceu fidus aliquis dux siue imperator de periculo ipsis imminente concionari incipit, deq; turpi defectione, seu dispersione & fuga, quam passuri erant, illos praemonet, quae omnia apud Matthaeum & Marcum plenius exponuntur, ubi propheta etiam Zachariae testimonio admonitionem hanc confirmat, ut magis illos excitet. Habet tamen Lucas nonnulla, quae illi non attigerunt, qui diligentius ea exponit, quae cum Petro sunt acta. Quia enim hic alijs feruentior atq; confidentior erat, ideo periculo magis vicinus, sermonem cum illo instituit, sic tamen ut periculu hoc omnibus commune fore ostendat. Continet autē hoc Christi exemplum generale doctrinam, nos tunc quoq; quando omnia optime constituta esse videntur, nostrae infirmitatis memores esse debere, & cogitare quam multis casibus atq; periculis simus obnoxij, quae evitare non liceat, nisi gratia sua nobis Deus adsit, & vel incautos inq; exitium ruentes ipse in via retineat, vel iam lapsos & prostratos rursus erigat atq; confirmet. Et huc illa Pauli admonitio referri debet: Qui sibi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Sed singulas huius loci partes ex ordine videamus.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, lately commended the faith of his disciples in splendid terms and promised them a very generous reward. He said, of course, that they would not only enjoy the joy and delights of his heavenly kingdom, but that one day they would also judge, by their teaching and example, those by whom they are now despised. But he knew that they, because of the sinful nature of the flesh, were too self-confident, and therefore even in this age aspired to higher dignity and (as frequently happens to the holiest people) were too much taken up with the affairs of this age, more than was fitting. So, lest they have an occasion for boasting that would make them more careless, he now begins, like a faithful leader or commander, to speak about the danger hanging over them, and warns them of the shameful defection, or scattering and flight, which they were about to suffer. All of this is set out more fully in Matthew and Mark, where the prophet Zechariah's testimony also confirms this warning, so as to rouse them more. Yet Luke has some things which those others did not touch on, since he sets out more carefully what happened with Peter. For because Peter was more fervent and self-confident than the others, he was closer to the danger, and so Christ holds the discourse with him, yet in such a way as to show that this danger would be common to all. Moreover, this example of Christ contains a general teaching: that we too, even when all things seem to be in the best order, should remember our weakness and consider how many chances and dangers we are exposed to, which cannot be avoided unless God is present with us by his grace, and either holds back on the way those who are heedless and rushing to ruin, or raises up and strengthens those who have already fallen and been laid low. To this should be referred Paul's admonition: "Let him who thinks he stands see that he does not fall." But let us examine the individual parts of this passage in order.

units.la: Primo periculum praesens illis indicat, quod ipsi ignorabant. Simon, Simon (inquit) ecce Satanas expetiuit vos, quos ventilaret sicut triticum. Quae verba sic pronuntiantur, ut animi affectum plane paternum, & de salute illorum solicitum exprimant: demonstrandi autem particula, ECCE, ad certitudinem facit, ne quid de praedictionis huius veritate dubitent. Et si cum illis, quae hucusq; dicta sunt, conferantur, hunc sensum continent: Vos quidem regnum terrenum & huius seculi dignitates atq; triumphos animo concepistis, cum ego vos ad regni mei administrationem in hoc mundo, deinde ad aeternae gloriae possessionem destinauerim. Imo quasi iam portum attigeritis, securi nihil cogitatis de certaminibus, quae vos manent. Atqui magna vos undiq; pericula circumstant, & vobis cum hoste omnium infestissimo res est: cum Satana nimirum, qui ut ab ipsa rerum origine optimis quibusq; insidias struxit, ita nunc vobis quoq; imminet, & hoc quam maxime cupit, ut vos ventilare possit instar tritici: ut nimirum periculorum instantium magnitudine territi dispergamini, relicto me, in quo uno omnis vita atq; salus habetur.
units.tr: First, he shows them the present danger, which they themselves did not know. "Simon, Simon," he says, "behold, Satan has demanded to have you, that he may sift you like wheat." These words are spoken in such a way as to express a plainly fatherly feeling, one anxious for their salvation. The particle of pointing, "behold", serves to make certain, so that they should have no doubt about the truth of this prediction. And if these words are compared with what has been said so far, they carry this sense: "You have indeed conceived in your minds an earthly kingdom, and the dignities and triumphs of this age, whereas I have appointed you to administer my kingdom in this world, and afterwards to possess eternal glory. Indeed, you think, as if you had already reached harbour, that you are safe and do not think about the struggles that await you. Yet great dangers surround you on every side, and you have to do with the most hostile enemy of all: namely Satan, who, as he has laid snares for the best men from the very beginning of things, so now also hangs over you, and desires above all to sift you like wheat; that is, to scatter you, terrified by the size of the dangers at hand, leaving me, in whom alone all life and salvation is found."

units.la: Delineatur autem nobis hoc loco, vel potius perspicue satis depingitur, quae fidelium atque piorum omnium in hisce terris sors sit atq; conditio. Sunt quidem illi triticum illud bonum, quod ad caelestia horrea olim colligi debet, sicuti Ioannes Baptista docet: sed priusquam id fiat, multis flagellis obnoxij sunt, quibus illos excuti & ventilari necesse est, ne cum infelicibus paleis huius mundi in ignem aeternum abijciantur. Et ut hoc illorum bono fieri permittit Deus: ita in ijsdem ventilandis & cribrandis admodum assiduus, adeoq; importunus plane est Satan, qui cum nihil perinde ut hominum intéritu sitiat quiescere non potest, sed (ut Petrus proprio periculo edoctus monuit) subinde instar rugentis Leonis oberrat, & quaerit quem devoret. Exempla ab ipsa rerum origine infinita edita sunt, quibus hanc suam rabiem declarauit. Huc enim tentatio illa pertinet, qua primos parentes astutis blanditijs & magnificis promissionibus circumuenit: ita vero eos non ventilauit modo, sed infelices extra paradisum quoq; eiecit. Et quod tunc facere coepit, postea irremisso studio facere perrexit, quādo ei pulo subinde insidiatus est, quē Deus sibi in peculiū delegerat, & ex quo promissus ille humani generis redemptor debebat nasci. Sed & priuatim singulis instat, ut in Iobi historia esset videre. Illic enim à Deo interrogatur unde nam venisset? respondet, se hinc indeuagatum esse, & terram omnem obambulauisse: nimirum ut aliquos uentilandi & à Dei consortio excutiendi occasionem inueniret. Et in primis memorabile est, quod Iobum suo arbitrio committi petit, quàmuis hunc à Deo pro amico singulari haberi, & ab eodem illius pietatem commendari audiret. Tanta est ueteratoris illius impro bitas atq; audacia. Quid Dauidi accciderit, omnes nouerunt: quem ipsum quoq; virum esse audiuerat secundum cor Dei, & cuius tot fortia facta uiderat. Tamen illum modò periculis assiduis, modò voluptatum illecebris, modò gloriæ studio & ambitione uentilare nunquam destitit. Idem nunc etiam Petro maximè imminet, ut hunc à Christo auellat, quem alijs discipulis hucusq; uiderat esse feruentiorem. Debent ista exempla nos excitare, et perpetuò vigilemus, ne nos incautos ex improuiso opprimat. Cui enim parcat ille, qui singulares Dei amicos aggredi ausus est olim, & qui ne ab ipso quidem Filio Dei abstinuit, cum eum carne vestitum inter homines viuere uideret?
units.tr: Here we are shown, or rather it is portrayed clearly enough, what the lot and condition of all the faithful and pious is in this earth. They are indeed that good wheat which must one day be gathered into the heavenly barns, as John the Baptist teaches. But before this happens they are exposed to many flails, by which they must be shaken and winnowed, lest they be cast into eternal fire along with the wretched chaff of this world. And while God permits this for their good, Satan is very busy and altogether unrelenting in winnowing and sifting them. Since he thirsts for nothing so much as the destruction of men, he cannot rest; but, as Peter, taught by his own peril, warns, he roams about from time to time like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Examples of his rage have been given without number from the very beginning of things. For to this belongs that temptation by which he deceived our first parents with crafty flattery and magnificent promises, and so not only sifted them but also cast the unhappy pair out of paradise. And what he began to do then, he afterwards continued to do with unabated zeal, whenever he lay in wait for the people whom God had chosen for his own possession, and from whom that promised Redeemer of mankind was to be born. But he also attacks individuals privately, as can be seen in the story of Job. There God asks him where he has come from; he replies that he has wandered about here and there and gone through the whole earth, obviously seeking an occasion to sift some and cast them out of fellowship with God. And especially memorable is the fact that he asks that Job be committed to his own will, although he heard that Job was held by God as a special friend, and that his piety was commended by God. So great is the wickedness and audacity of that old deceiver. What befell David, everyone knows: he had heard that David was a man after God's own heart, and had seen his many brave deeds. Yet he never ceased to sift him, now with constant dangers, now with the allurements of pleasures, now with the desire for glory and ambition. The same now bears most heavily on Peter, that he may tear him away from Christ, whom he had hitherto seen to be more fervent than the other disciples. These examples ought to rouse us, and we should be ever watchful, lest he suddenly overwhelm us when we are unprepared. For whom will he spare, who has dared to attack the special friends of God in former times, and who did not even hold back from the Son of God himself, when he saw him living among men clothed in flesh?

units.la: Interim simul consolationem ex hoc loco petamus, ne diaboli conatibus terreamur. Nam esset quidem impudens planè illius audacia, idem tamen ex femeipso nihil potest, & facilè uincitur ab ijs, qui animum uolunt attendere. Adde, quòd diuinæ prouidentiæ fræno continetur, ut non plus illi liceat, quàm Deus permittit, qui humani generis amantissimus nos supra uires tentari non finit. Cupiebat quidem improbus ille totis viribus Iobum perdere: Sed terminum certum illius conatibus Deus præscripsit, quem transgredi non fuit ausus. Ideò primùm quidem opes solas ei abstulit, deinde in solum corpus manum suam extendit, vitam verò aut animam ledere non potuit. Et quid nam contra homines ille posset, qui nisi ita Deo videatur, ne in porcos quidem ius habet & imperium? Non est ergo, quòd illius truculentia & nocendi cupiditate terreamur. Curemus modò ut triticum Domini simus, & sponte exuamus leues atq; infelices carnis nostræ paleas, neq; locum demus cupiditatibus illius aut mundi studijs. Accingamur autem ad certamen istud, & (ut Paulus ad Ephesios docet) induamus armaturam Dei, quam hic nobis in uerbo suo monstrat & offert. Huius partes sunt baltheus ueritatis, quo lumbos nostros constringi oportet, ne prauis cupiditatibus difluamus: thorax iustitiæ, quam nobis in Christo Deus donat: calcei Euangelij, quo pedes & uniuersa uitæ nostræ consuetudo muniuntur, ne quid ex mundo periculi patiamur: scutum fidei, quo omnia hostis illius tela, quantùmuis ardeant, facilè reflinguuntur: galea salutis, ipse nimirum Christus, qui & caput nostrum est, & solus nobis defendendis atq; seruandis sufficit. Accedit his gladius Spiritus, Verbum Dei scilicet, quod ut impiorum quoque cordacalidissimè penetrat, ita diabolum terret, qui suis fallacijs locum esse nullum videt, ubi illius fulgor micat. Quibus omnibus si preces ardentes & assiduæ accedant, iam in manibus nostris erit uictoria. Nam etiamsi pugnam improbus ille subinde instauret, & cum mundo ipsam quoq; mortem & inferos contra nos in aciem producat, uincemus tamen nos in eo, qui nos dilexit, neq; nos quisquam separare poterit à dilectione Dei, qua hic nos complexus est in Filio suo Christo Iesu. Quòd si uerò in publicis Ecclesiæ certaminibus multos excidere & à fide deficere uidebimus, neminem istorum defectio offendat. Sunt enim illi non triticum Domini, sed paleæ infelices, quas uentilatione ista excuti & eijci oportet, ut purgatior fiat illius area.
units.tr: Meanwhile, let us also take consolation from this passage, so that we are not terrified by the attempts of the devil. For his audacity is indeed utterly shameless, yet he can do nothing of himself, and is easily overcome by those who are willing to pay attention. Add to this that he is held in check by the bridle of divine providence, so that he is allowed no more than God permits; God, who loves mankind most tenderly, does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. That wicked one indeed desired with all his might to destroy Job; but God laid down a fixed limit to his attempts, which he did not dare to overstep. Therefore God first took away only his goods, then stretched out his hand against his body alone, but could not harm his life or soul. And what could he do against men, who, unless it pleases God, does not even have power and authority over pigs? There is therefore no reason for us to be frightened by his savagery and his desire to harm. Let us only take care that we are the Lord's wheat, and willingly cast off the light and wretched chaff of our flesh, and give no place to its desires or to the pursuits of the world. Let us gird ourselves for this struggle and (as Paul teaches to the Ephesians) put on the armour of God, which he here shows and offers us in his Word. Its parts are: the belt of truth, with which our loins must be girded, lest we be loosened by wicked desires; the breastplate of righteousness, which God gives us in Christ; the shoes of the gospel, with which our feet and the whole course of our life are protected, lest we suffer any harm from the world; the shield of faith, by which all the fiery darts of that enemy, however blazing, are easily quenched; and the helmet of salvation, namely Christ himself, who is also our head and alone is enough to defend and save us. To these is added the sword of the Spirit, that is, the Word of God, which pierces even the hearts of the wicked most keenly, and so terrifies the devil, who sees no place for his deceits where its brightness shines. If burning and constant prayers are added to all these, victory will already be in our hands. For even if that wicked one renews the battle from time to time, and brings forth against us, together with the world, death itself and hell, yet we shall conquer through him who loved us, and no one will be able to separate us from the love of God, with which he has embraced us in his Son Christ Jesus. But if we see many fall away and desert the faith in the public struggles of the Church, let no one's defection give offence. For they are not the Lord's wheat, but wretched chaff, which must be shaken out and cast away by this winnowing, so that the threshing floor may be made cleaner.

units.la: Facit ad huius consolationis confirmationem altera huius loci pars, qua opem suam Christus discipulis, & Petro quidem in primis, pollicetur, simulq; docet unde nos quoque illam sperare debeamus. Dicit enim: Sed ego rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Quod ergo non perijt Petrus, licet primùm cum alijs discipulis relicto Christo fugerit, deinde eundem abnegauerit etiam, hoc diuina gratia opus fuit, quaut sustentatus & mox in uiam reductus est. Quod autem in præsenti Dominus Petro dicit, hoc omnes pij ad se transferre debent: quia (ut nuper diximus) preces suas & æterni Regni promissionem illa postea ad omnes extendit, qui Apostolorum doctrinam admittunt, & ipsi fidunt. Præcipua ergo salutis fiducia in tentationum omnium certaminibus nobis in Christo uno reposita sit, qui ut hostem nostrum iam olim uicit, ita hodie adhuc pro nobis intercedit, & fidelis Pontificis officio fungitur, ut qui nostras infirmitates ipse in propria persona sustinuit, & proinde illis condolere potest. Ideo Paulus, quando salutis nostræ certitudinem aduersus tentationes quasuis afferere nosque in eius fiducia confirmare uult, hoc potissimum argumento utitur, dicens: Christus est, qui mortuus est: imò verò, qui etiam excitatus est: qui etiam est ad dexteram Dei: qui etiam postulat siue intercedit pro nobis. Et ex eo laetus & quasi epinicium canens infert: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Christi? &c. Confutant istā illorum errorem, qui intercessionis Christi immemores, Deus sibi ipsis aduocatos & intercessores fingunt. Quae enim ratio est, quae id fieri debere persuadeat, quando ipsos Apostolos illo intercessore opus habuisse audimus? Vidit hoc Ioannes, dilectus illé discipulus, qui ipse etiam nos adunum Iesum Christum remittit, & se cum illis coniungit, quorum ipse est aduocatus: Habemus (inquit) aduocatum, Iesum Christum, iustum, & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, &c. 1. Ioan. 2.
units.tr: The second part of this passage contributes to the strengthening of this comfort. In it Christ promises his help to the disciples, and to Peter first of all, and at the same time teaches us where we too ought to hope for it. For he says: "But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail" (Luke 22:32). That Peter did not perish, although at first he fled with the other disciples and leaving Christ, and then also denied him, was the work of divine grace, by which he was upheld and soon brought back onto the way. What the Lord says to Peter in this place, all the godly ought to apply to themselves, because, as we said just now, he afterwards extended his prayers and the promise of the eternal kingdom to all who accept the teaching of the Apostles and trust in it themselves. Our chief confidence of salvation in all the struggles of temptation therefore rests in Christ alone, who, as he has already conquered our enemy, so today still intercedes for us and performs the office of a faithful High Priest, so that he who himself bore our infirmities in his own person can therefore sympathise with them. Hence Paul, when he wishes to affirm the certainty of our salvation against any temptations and to confirm us in its trust, uses this argument above all, saying: "Christ is he who died; yes rather, who was also raised; who is also at the right hand of God; who also makes request, or intercedes, for us." And rejoicing in this, and singing as it were a song of triumph, he adds: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" etc. (Rom. 8:34, 35). This refutes the error of those who, forgetful of the intercession of Christ, invent for themselves advocates and intercessors with God. For what reason is there that could persuade us that this ought to be done, when we hear that the Apostles themselves had need of that intercessor? John saw this, that beloved disciple, who himself also sends us to the one Jesus Christ, and associates himself with those of whom he is the advocate: "We have," he says, "an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins," etc. (1 John 2:1).

units.la: Obiter etiam hoc loco admonemur, quid de fide sentire debeamus, qua nos seruari omnis Scriptura docet. Hanc donum Dei esse Apostolus dicit, nimirum ad illud Christi respiciens: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Neque aliter sentire aut loqui possumus, quādo res ipsa docet, hominem animalem suis illis naturalibus, facultatibus non percipere ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Etsi vero fide donati sumus, eadem tamen in nobis propter innatam & perpetuo carni inhaerentem vitiositatem interdum uacillat & labascit: utq; Sol interdum nubibus obductis absconditur: ita illius etiā splendor afflictionū aut aliarum tentationū nubilis saepe obscuratur, ut minus agnosci queat. Exempla huius infirmitatis in omnibus fere sanctis, quorum fides & pietas prae alijs commendatur, esse uidere. Sed omnium loco sufficere potest, quod in Petro proponitur. Nam etsi hic Christi amantissimus fuerit, et is eum amore singulari complexus sit, proq; eo quàm fidelissimè intercesserit apud Patrem, turpiter tamen lapsus est, & peculiari gratia Dei opus habuit. Quid ergo de nobis speremus, qui ut electus illis Christi discipulus nequaquam sumus conferendi: ita quotidie experimur, quàm deplorata sit nostrae carnis ad omne malum procliuitas? Certè quàm primùm suam manum Deus nobis subduxit, toti perijmus. Unde sequitur, salutē nostram omnem ex mera & gratuita Dei misericordia pendere, nimium uero stultos & confidentes esse, quotquot suis uiribus aut meritis aliquid tribuunt.
units.tr: In passing, in this place we are also admonished what we ought to think about faith, by which all Scripture teaches that we are saved. The Apostle says that this is the gift of God, plainly looking to that saying of Christ: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him" (John 6:44). Nor can we think or speak otherwise, since the matter itself teaches that the natural man does not perceive by his natural faculties the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14). Although indeed we have been given faith, yet that same faith in us, because of the vice innate in us and clinging perpetually to the flesh, sometimes wavers and totters; and just as the sun is sometimes hidden by clouds drawn across it, so its brightness is often obscured by the clouds of affliction or other temptations, so that it can less easily be recognised. We may see examples of this weakness in almost all the saints, whose faith and piety are commended above others. But in place of all of them, what is set forth in Peter may suffice. For although he was most loving to Christ, and Christ embraced him with singular love, and although he interceded for him with the Father as faithfully as possible, yet he fell shamefully and had need of a special grace of God. What then should we hope for ourselves, who are by no means to be compared with that chosen disciple of Christ, when we experience every day how deplorable is the proneness of our flesh to every evil? Certainly as soon as God withdraws his hand from us, we are utterly lost. Whence it follows that our whole salvation depends on the mere and free mercy of God, and that all who attribute anything to their own strength or merits are truly foolish and overconfident.

units.la: Sequitur tertia uerborum Christi pars, qua officij quoq; Petrum admonet, & simul eius honori atq; existimationi consulit, ne propter abnegationem factā postea ab alijs contemneretur. Ait enim: Tu igitur aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Ita uero illi spem facit certam, quod ex Apostolatus gradu ipsum nequaquā deijcere uelit. Et constat illum huic postea singulari quadam ratione & quasi examine peculiari facto restitutum fuisse: quod Ioannes sub finem historiae suae Euangelicae diligenter exponit. Estq; obseruanda diligenter haec Christi bonitas atq; moderatio, qua Petrum ita de suo lapsu admonet, ut simul tamē studiose eius existimationi caueat. Meminerint huius ij, quibus cum peccatoribus res est: ne uel omnem spem gratiae Dei illis negent, uel apud alios aliorum famam atq; existimationem in periculum adducant. Quod in primis cauendum est in illis, quos ipse Deus in gradum eminentiorem euexit, & quorum authoritas sine publico scandalo & functionis, quam sustinent, contemptu labefactari non potest. At hodie passim emergunt, qui in principes quoq; uiros ius sibi arrogant, neq; illis sufficit, si hi sese publicè & priuatim ab ipsis admoneri, adhaec corripi etiam pati antur (si ita necessitas iubeat) nisi ab Ecclesiae consortio etiam exclusos toti populo spectaculum faciant. Quid uero huius unquam Prophetae fecerunt? Num tale quid cum Dauide faciendū esse putauit Nathan? Certè abunde huic satisfecit, quando scelus suum aperte confessus est, & animi uere paenitentis dolorem indicijs non obscuris declarauit. Et Christus Petrū quoq; abnegatorē illico respexit, & eidem in suo coetu locum dederunt discipuli, neq; uoluerunt ut prius Scenicum spectaculum fieret. Sufficiat ergo nobis etiā quod Christo satis fuit, neq; nobis graue sit eum admittere & ferre, qui se & peccasse & nunc paenitentia duci fatetur. Nam si uere paeniteat, id certè Deo probabitur, quo austeriores nos esse minimè decet. Sin fallat, seipsum potius quā nos fallet, neq; id impune feret apud Deum, qui dolos & mendacium odisse solet.
units.tr: There follows the third part of Christ's words, in which he also admonishes Peter about his office and, at the same time, looks after his honour and reputation, lest because of his later denial he be despised by others. For he says: "And you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers." In this way he gives Peter a sure hope that he does not intend to cast him down from the rank of apostle. It is clear that Peter was afterwards restored to this rank in a special way and by a kind of particular examination, which John carefully explains at the end of his Gospel history. This goodness and moderation of Christ must be carefully observed: he admonishes Peter about his fall, yet at the same time takes careful thought for his reputation. Let those remember this who have to deal with sinners: they must neither deny all hope of God's grace to them, nor endanger the reputation and esteem of others before other people. This must be guarded against above all in those whom God himself has raised to a higher rank, and whose authority cannot be shaken without public scandal and contempt for the office they hold. Yet today there are everywhere people who claim for themselves a right over even principal men, and it is not enough for them if these men allow themselves to be admonished publicly and privately, and even to be rebuked (if necessity so requires), unless they make a spectacle for the whole people by excluding them from the fellowship of the Church. But what did any of the prophets ever do of this kind? Did Nathan think anything like this should be done with David? Certainly he fully satisfied him when David openly confessed his crime and showed, by unmistakable signs, the grief of a truly penitent mind. And Christ immediately looked back at Peter, the denier too, and the disciples gave him a place again in their company, and they did not want a theatrical spectacle to be made first. Let it therefore be enough for us that it was enough for Christ, and let it not be burdensome for us to admit and bear with one who confesses both that he has sinned and that he is now led by repentance. For if he truly repents, that will certainly be proved to God, and we ought least of all to be stricter than God. But if he is deceiving, he will deceive himself rather than us, and he will not go unpunished before God, who is wont to hate deceit and lying.

units.la: Porrò praecipuum huius loci caput est, quòd Petrum hortatur Dominus, ut suae integritati & dignitati restitutus confirmet fratres suos tam doctrina quā exemplo, ne qui uel in peccato perseuerent, ubi semel lapsi sunt, uel conscientiae terroribus superati de Dei gratia desperent. Est hoc aequissimum, ut qui Dei gratiam experti sunt, eiusdem alios quoq; participes reddere studeant. Et in hoc diligentissimi fuerunt omnes, quorum pietatem Spiritus sanctus in scripturis commendat. Etenim Dauid, ut scandalo mederetur quod toti populo dederat, peccatū suum publicè confessus est Psalmis aliquot, quibus simul immensam Dei bonitatē magnificè commendat, & ita hodie adhuc omnes eos co
units.tr: Moreover, the chief point of this passage is that the Lord exhorts Peter, restored to his integrity and dignity, to strengthen his brothers both by teaching and by example, so that those who have either persisted in sin once they have fallen, or who, overcome by terrors of conscience, despair of God's grace, may not do so. It is most fitting that those who have experienced God's grace should also strive to make others partakers of it. In this all were most diligent, whose piety the Holy Spirit commends in the Scriptures. For David, to remedy the scandal he had given to the whole people, publicly confessed his sin in several Psalms, in which at the same time he magnificently commends God's immense goodness; and so even today he consoles all those who

units.la: {a} Fidei nostrae confidentia. firmat qui se peccatis grauari sentiunt, atq; ijsdem uiam monstrat, qua cum Deo in gratiam redire possint. Idem Paulum fecisse constat, postquam ex crudelissimo Ecclesiae hoste Christi serus factus est.
