Passim enim Dei misericordiam praedicat, & sui exempli usum hunc esse docet, ut omnes intelligant, illius fores omnibus patere, qui ad ipsum ex animo conuertuntur. Huc enim pertinet, quod in priori ad Timoth. scribit: Fidus sermo & dignus quem modis omnibus amplectamur, quod Christus Iesus uenit in mundum, ut peccatores seruaret: QVORVM PRIMVS sum ego: Verum IDEO misertus est mei, ut in ME PRIMO ostenderet Iesus Christus omnem clementiam: VTES-SEM EXEMPLAR ijs, qui crediturj essent ipsi in uitam aeternam. Et hic proprius usus est peccatorum, quae olim a sanctis designata fuisse legimus: nimirum, non quod de illis propterea minus honorifice sentire debeamus, aut ex illis peccandi occasionem arripere, nostrisque celeribus patrocinari: sed potius ut in illis agnoscamus Dei misericordiam, & ex ea consolationem petamus aduersus tentationes, quibus nos ad desperationem Satan adigere studet: ut deniq; agnita nostrae naturae infirmitate aduersus huius insidias uigilemus, imitemur autē eorum poenitentiam, quos olim sua miseri-cordia Deus dignatus est. Estq; hoc nouum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quod ille peccatis quoque suorum tam feliciter uti solet, ut aliorum emendationi & confirmationi seruiant, adeoque ex nobis tunc gloriae & gratiae suae uasa facit, quando ira & ignominia aeterna digni eramus. Huius ergo tam benignae uoluntati omnes se fe per fidei obedientiam accommodent, & si quando peccauerunt, scandalum omne e medio tollere studeant, cuius fuerunt authores. Etenim inexcusabilis & aeternis supplicijs digna est illorum improbitas, qui cum Dei gratia se seruatos esse fateantur, sua tamen facinora iactant, & multis alijs ad ea designanda stimulos addunt, quibus poenitentia & innocentia Christianae exemplum esse debebant. Quae nequitia utinam non uulgaris esset inter senes, quos suorum flagitiorum commemoratio tunc quoq; oblectat, quando alterum pedem iam in Charontis cymba posuerunt. Qui cum id non faciant, quod hoc loco Christus Petro praecipit, non est quod ex eiusdem & aliorum similium exemplis consolationem sperent.
units.tr: {a} The confidence of our faith. feel themselves burdened by sins, and shows them the way by which they can return into favour with God. Paul is known to have done the same, after he became a late disciple of Christ, having been the cruellest enemy of the Church. For everywhere he proclaims God's mercy, and teaches that his own example is meant to show that everyone should understand that the gates of God stand open to all who turn to him from the heart. To this belongs what he writes in his first letter to Timothy: "Faithful is the saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all longsuffering, as a pattern to those who would believe on him to eternal life." This is the proper use of sins, which we read were once designated by the saints: not that we should think any the less honourably of them, or seize from them an occasion for sinning and quickly defend our own offences, but rather that in them we may acknowledge God's mercy and seek from it consolation against the temptations by which Satan strives to drive us to despair; so that, having finally recognised the weakness of our nature, we may be watchful against his snares, and imitate the repentance of those whom God once deigned to favour with his mercy. This is a new proof of divine goodness, that he is wont to use even the sins of his people so successfully that they serve the correction and strengthening of others; and so he makes vessels of his glory and grace out of us, when we were worthy of wrath and eternal shame. Therefore let all accommodate themselves to this kindly will of God by obedience of faith, and if they have ever sinned, let them strive to remove from the midst every scandal of which they were the authors. For the wickedness of those is inexcusable and worthy of eternal punishments, who, while they confess that they have been saved by God's grace, nevertheless boast of their crimes and add goads for many others to pursue them, when by repentance and Christian innocence they ought to be an example. Would that this wickedness were not common among old men, whom the recollection of their own shameful deeds delights even then, when they have already put one foot into Charon's boat. Since they do not do what Christ here commands Peter, there is no reason for them to hope for consolation from his example and that of others like him.

units.la: Sed Petrum Domino respondentem audiamus: Domine, tecum paratus sum & ad carcerem & ad mortem proficisci. Magnifica sane promissio, sed non fallax modo, sed multis quoq; alijs erroribus atq; uitijs referta. Primum enim confidentior quam par fit, stolida praesumptione nihil non sibi tribuit. Deinde Christo contradicit temere, & eum tantum non mendacij arguit, quando se longe alium fore profitetur, quam ille dixerat. Adhaec cum commune omnibus periculum imminere audiuisset, ipse se ex illo eximens, seipsum alijs omnibus praefert: quod absq; illorum contemptu atq; ignominia fieri non poterat. Tam multa tamq; grauia peccata in hoc breui dicto cocurrunt, quae nos ideo obseruare decet, ut discamus quam foecundum malum sit confidentia. Quia enim hac aduersus Deum efferimur, nostro ille nos arbitrio permittit, quae causa est, ut nullum scelus tam graue aut absurdum sit, quod non desigenemus, nisi ille nos sua manu retineat. Docet hoc Christus Petri exemplo, cui respondet ad hunc modum: Dico tibi Petre, non canet hodie gallus, priusquam ter neges me tibi notum esse. Quasi diceret: Plus alijs te facturum esse promittis, ut qui neq; carceres neq; mortem mecum admre horreas: sed turpius quam alij cades, dum non contentus fuga, qua alij sibi consulent, tu insuper abnegabis me. Neq; id simpliciter, ut te meum discipulum esse modo neges, sed me tibi ne notum quidem esse iurabis, idq; non post longam moram. sed hac ipsa nocte facies, priusquam gallus primum cecinerit. Iduerò ipsi accidisse suo loco audiemus.
units.tr: But let us hear Peter answering the Lord: "Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death." A splendid promise indeed, but not only a false one; it is also full of many other errors and faults. For first, he is more confident than he ought to be, and with foolish presumption he ascribes everything to himself. Next, he rashly contradicts Christ, and very nearly accuses him of lying, when he declares that he will be quite different from what Christ had said. Besides, when he heard that a danger threatened all of them alike, he exempted himself from it and set himself above all the others, which could not be done without their contempt and disgrace. So many and such grave sins meet in this brief saying, and we ought to note them so that we may learn how fruitful an evil confidence is. For since we are puffed up with it against God, he leaves us to our own judgement, and so there is no crime so grave or absurd that we will not commit it, unless he holds us back with his own hand. Christ teaches this by the example of Peter, to whom he replies in this way: "I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today before you deny three times that you know me." As if he said: "You promise to do more than the others, since you shudder at going with me to prison or to death; but you will fall more shamefully than they, for not content with flight, by which the others will look to their own safety, you will moreover deny me. Nor will you deny merely that you are my disciple, but you will swear that you do not even know me; and you will do this not after a long delay, but this very night, before the cock first crows." We shall hear in its place how this came to pass for him.

units.la: { } Ingenium carnis.
units.tr: { } The nature of the flesh.

units.la: Adumbratur nobis hoc loco admodum eleganter & perspicuè carnis ingenium. Est haec natura gloriae & honorū appetens, quos etiam in rebus leuiculis & caducis, quaerere solet. Vt primum ergo se fide & Dei cognitione prae alijs donatam sentit, mox caeca persuasione fascinata nihil non sibi ipsi tribuit, seq; ad quaevis subeunda abunde instructam esse putat. Et uix aliud tam difficile est, quam non efferri donis spiritualibus. Exemplo nobis sunt Corinthij, quibus superbia ista non solum contentionum causa fuit, quibus Ecclesia ipsorum in partes distrahebatur, uerumetiam omne ordinem ecclesiasticum turbauit. Et qui illa semel turgere coeperunt, ij fere admonitiones nullas admittunt. At quando fides in periculo aliquo graviori declaranda est, turpiter labascunt, & ijs formidolosiores sunt, quos prius nimium insolenter contempserunt. Quae causa est, quod Deus fere multis ratio nibus eos humiliare solet, quos donis praeclarioribus instruit. Id in semetipso Paulus agnouit, quādo carni suæ aculeum datum, & à Satanæ Angelo colaphis cæsum, id est, variis tentationibus tam interni quàm externè incidentibus se exagitatum fuisse scribit, ne donorum & revelationum excellentia superbiret. Horum itaq; memores humiliter de nobis ipsis sentiamus, carnis verò præcipitem zelum habeamus suspectum, toti autem à Dei gratia pendeamus, qui ut per Filium suū Iesum Christum nos redemit, ita huic infirmos viribus quotidie novis armat & instruit, ut in eo possimus omnia: Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Here the nature of the flesh is set forth very elegantly and plainly. It is a nature that desires glory and honours, which it is accustomed to seek even in trifling and passing things. So when it first perceives that it has been given faith and the knowledge of God above others, straightway, bewitched by a blind persuasion, it ascribes everything to itself and thinks itself amply equipped for whatever must be endured. And there is scarcely anything as hard as not to be puffed up by spiritual gifts. The Corinthians are an example for us: this pride was not only the cause of the contentions by which their Church was torn into factions, but also threw the whole ecclesiastical order into confusion. And those who once began to swell with it hardly admit any admonitions at all. But when faith must be declared in some more serious danger, they waver shamefully, and they are more fearful than those whom they had previously despised too insolently. This is why God usually humbles, by many means, those whom he equips with more outstanding gifts. Paul recognised this in himself, when he writes that a thorn was given to his flesh and that he was struck with blows by the angel of Satan, that is, that he was harassed by various temptations falling upon him both inwardly and outwardly, lest he be puffed up by the excellence of his gifts and revelations. Therefore, mindful of these things, let us think humbly of ourselves, but let us regard the headlong zeal of the flesh with suspicion, and let us depend wholly on the grace of God, who, as he redeemed us through his Son Jesus Christ, so also arms and equips us, weak as we are, with fresh strength every day, that in him we may be able to do all things. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCVIII.

units.la: Et dixit illis: Quando misi vos absque crumena & pera, & soleis, numquid defuit vobis? Ipsi verò dixerunt: Nihil. Dixit ergo eis. At nunc qui crumenam habet, sumat eam, similiter & peram: & qui non habet, vendat pallium suum, & emat gladium. Dico enim vobis, adhuc oportere in me perfici scriptum illud: Et cum sceleratis numeratus est. Nam ea quæ de me scripta sunt, finem habent. At illi dixerunt: Domine, ecce duo gladij hic. Ipse verò dixit eis: Satis est.
units.tr: And he said to them: "When I sent you out without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?" They said: "Nothing." Then he said to them: "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has none, let him sell his cloak and buy a sword. For I tell you that this which is written must yet be fulfilled in me: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors.' For the things written about me have an end." And they said: "Lord, look, here are two swords." But he said to them: "It is enough."

units.la: Quemadmodum Christus Iesus, Dominus & redemptor noster discipulos, quos ipsi Pater dederat, toto eo tempore quo cum illis vixit, fidelissimè servavit: itaque tum instante iam mortis hora hinc migrare vellet, eosdem omnibus illis diligentissimè instruxit, quæ ipsis cognitu necessaria erant. Nam ut alia omittamus, quæ Ioannes prolixè describit, in illis quæ Lucas hucusque commemoravit, omnia ea continentur. Primo enim Regni sui ratione perspicuè tradidit, & ne quid in eo ab se alienum quærerent, docuit quod nā illud munus sit, ad quod ipsos destinarit. Deinde fidei & constantiæ ipsorum præmium amplissimum promisit, ut huius spe confirmati in posterum quoq; perseverent. Postremò ne promissione ista securiores facti in fiducias sibi à Satana structas minus observarent, qua & qualia ipsos pericula manerent prædicit. Et initiò quidem cum Petro egit, quem præ aliis confidentiorem, et proinde periculo etiam graviori obnoxium esse sciebat. At quod illi dixit, nunc aliis quoq; applicat, & adversus certamen, quod nunc præsoribus erat, duobus potissimum argumentis eos armat. Nam comparationem facit inter conditionem, quam hactenus satis lætam & felicem habuerant, et duriorem illam atq; periculosiorem, quam nunc erant subituri: & primò quidē quàm quietè hactenus vixerint, docet, ut huius memores in posterum minus dubitent de ipsius auxilio & protectione: deinde quā dura & gravia certamina ipsis appropinquent indicat, & in his quoq; ad protectionem divinam illos remittit.
units.tr: Just as Christ Jesus, our Lord and Redeemer, faithfully kept the disciples whom the Father had given him during all the time he lived with them, so, when the hour of death was now at hand and he was about to depart, he taught them most diligently all those things that were necessary for them to know. For, to leave aside other matters that John describes at length, all of these are contained in what Luke has recorded up to this point. First, he set out clearly the nature of his kingdom, and, lest they seek anything foreign to it, he taught what kind of office it was to which he had appointed them. Then he promised a most ample reward for their faith and steadfastness, so that, strengthened by the hope of it, they would persevere in the future as well. Finally, lest, made too secure by that promise, they should neglect the snares that Satan had laid for them, he foretold what dangers and what kind of dangers awaited them. And indeed he first dealt with Peter, whom he knew to be more confident than the others and therefore exposed to a more serious danger. But what he said to Peter he now applies to the others also, and he arms them against the conflict that was now at hand with two main arguments. For he makes a comparison between their condition, which until now they had found quite pleasant and happy, and the harder and more perilous condition they were now about to undergo. First, he shows how quietly they had lived until now, so that, mindful of this, they would in future doubt less about his help and protection. Then he points out how hard and grievous the struggles were that were approaching them, and in these too he sends them back to divine protection.

units.la: Primam partem à quæstione orditur, ut illos ipsos testes faciat eorum, quæ erat dicturus. Dicit enim: Quando misi vos absq; crumena & pera & soleis, numquid defuit vobis? Ita vero in mentem illis revocat quod Cap. 9. audiuimus. Illic enim cum ad prædicandū eos ablegaret, dixit illis: Nihil tollite ad iter, neq; virgas, neq; peram, neq; panē, neq; pecuniā, neq; binas tunicas habete. Apud Matthæu solearum quoq; aut calceorum fit mentio, quibus interdixerit illis. Sensus tamē est in præsenti: Meministis opinor, quales vos hactenus emiserim, nimirū omnibus ijs destitutos, quæ vulgus necessaria putat esse illis, qui aliquid negotij apud exteros volunt exequi. Scire tamen ex vobis velim, an aliquid tunc vobis defuerit? Respondent illi, sibi nihil prorsus defuisse. Ex eo autem vult colligant, minimè æquū fore aut honestum, si nunc ad periculi alicuius gravioris occursum ita cōsternentur, ut ab ipso secessionem faciant, cuius beneficentia atq; protectione tam luculento indicio perspexerint. Quin potius cogitent, ideo tam indulgenter abs se tractatos fuisse, ut paulatim assuefierent ad graviorarum discrimina, & nunc meritò ab ipsis alacritatem & constantiam in quovis periculo requiri. Et hic nobis etiam istius loci præcipuus usus esse debet, ut quoties fortuna lautiori fruimur & otio abundamus, meminerimus id non sine numine aut Dei prouidentia fieri, qui quòd nos adhuc infirmiores esse novit, lenius aut mollius tractat: non quidem, ut ex eo nobis perpetuū otium promittamus, sed ut interea præparemus nos ad quæuis adversa ferenda, eoq; constantiores atque fortiores simus, si quando illa immittuntur, quò diuturniorem Dei indulgentiam sumus experti. Est ergo turpis nimium multorum ingratitudo, qui quasi atrox ipsis iniuria fiat, adversus Deum ipsum murmurant & querelis iniquissimis omnia complent, quando otiū & quietem suā interturbari sentiunt. Atqui cogitare debebant, satis feriarum ipsis hucusq; datum fuisse, iam autē adesse tempus ut ipsi quoq; in arenam producti aliquando ædant militiæ Christianæ tyrocinium.
units.tr: He begins the first part with a question, so that they themselves may be witnesses of what he was about to say. For he says: "When I sent you out without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything?" Thus he brings back to their minds what we heard in chapter 9. For there, when he sent them out to preach, he said to them: "Take nothing for the journey, neither staves, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics." In Matthew there is also mention of sandals or shoes, which he forbade them. The sense, however, in the present passage is this: I think you remember what sort of men I sent you out as, namely stripped of all those things which the common crowd thinks necessary for those who want to carry out any business among strangers. Yet I want to ask you whether anything was lacking to you at that time. They answer that nothing at all had been lacking to them. From this he wants them to conclude that it would be by no means fitting or honourable if, now that some more serious danger meets them, they should be so dismayed as to withdraw from him, whose kindness and protection they had seen so clearly demonstrated. Rather, let them consider that they had been treated so leniently by him so that they might gradually become accustomed to greater dangers, and that it is now rightly required of them to show eagerness and steadfastness in any peril. And here, too, the particular use of this passage ought to be for us: whenever we enjoy a more comfortable fortune and abound in leisure, let us remember that this happens not without the divine will or the providence of God, who, knowing that we are still weaker, treats us more gently and softly. Not indeed so that we may promise ourselves from this a perpetual leisure, but so that meanwhile we may prepare ourselves to bear whatever adversities come, and be the more constant and brave if ever they are sent upon us, the longer we have experienced God's indulgence. Therefore the ingratitude of many is truly too shameful, who, as if some cruel injury were being done to them, murmur against God himself and fill everything with most unjust complaints whenever they feel their leisure and quiet disturbed. Yet they ought to have considered that enough holidays had been granted them until now, and that the time had now come when they too, led out into the arena, should at last display the apprenticeship of Christian warfare.

units.la: Simul autem debet ex hoc loco generalis doctrina atq; consolatio colligi, nihil unquam ijs defuturū esse, qui in Dei uocatione ambulant, & quā in ipsis impositum functionem fideliter obeunt. Nam quod in Apostolis factum est, quos in regione peregrina & in gente infesta Christus non sine miraculo sic aluit atq; seruauit, ut sibi nihil defuisse fateantur, hoc uniuersalibus promissionibus pollicetur omnibus illis, qui præcepta ipsius obseruant, & ipsi obediunt. Habentur illæ passim in Lege & Prophetis, & easdē Christus confirmat, apud Matthæū dicens: Quærite ante omnia Regnū Dei & iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia uobis adijcientur. Exemplis item pluribus promissiones istæ nō modo illustratæ, uerūmetiā ita confirmatæ sunt, ut de illis uel modica ex parte dubitare nefas sit. Iubetur Abrahamus subito exire ex natali solo, & domum patriam atq; gentem suam relinquere. Obtempe rat ille uocanti Domino, & quāmuis multa obstarent, quæ honeste, prudenter & non iniq;, aut immerito prætexi posse uidebantur, absq; mora tamen aditer accingitur, & tandē in infestissima Chananæorum gente (cuius pars non postrema Sodomæi & Gomorrhæi fuerunt) sedes sibi a Deo paratas esse intelligit. Vbi etiamsi primo fame dura exciperetur, quæ totam illam terram affligebat, et mox belli quoq; fortunam cogeretur subire, ita tamen eum seruauit Deus, ut ditissimes quoq; in ea gente facile uinceret, & ingentes opum thesauros possideret. Idē de eius filio Isaaco, de nepote Iacobo dicere possumus. Quid uero de Iosepho dicemus? Hic cum se non absq; Dei consilio a fratribus uenditus & in Ægyptum abductum esse intelligeret, seruitutem illam & exilium suam uocationem esse putauit, & hero suo quantumuis duro et ingrato fidelis fuit. Quare etiamsi ad tempus fortuna sibi aduersam sentiret, tamen postea ad summa dignitatem euectus totam gentem seruauit. Pertinet huc quod de filijs Israelis scribitur: qui cum Dei uocatione secuti ex Ægypto emigrauissent, totis annis 40. pane cœlitus demisso pasti sunt, & nihil eorū ipsis defuit, quæ ad uitā degendam sunt necessaria. Quod exemplū eo memorabilius est, quòd neq; ingratitudo & contumacia eorū obstitit, quo minus promissionem suā Deus ratam esse vellet, etiamsi illi quotidie mille mortes mererentur. Posset his Dauidis addi cum alijs innumeris, sed cum huius generis multa quotidie fiant publicè & priuatim, non opus est ueterū exemplorum commemorationi diutius insistere. Nos potius usum huius doctrinæ obseruemus, qui in duobus consistit. Primū institutioni seruit, & officij admonet omnis loci & ordinis homines, ne inopiæ aut egestatis metu ab officio suo discedant, sed à Deo sibi creditam stationē fideliter teneant. De hoc ergo cogitent Ecclesiarum ministri, ad quos præsens hoc Apostolorum exemplum pertinet, ut & Eliæ & aliarum qui eadem Dei liberalitate in hoc munere seruati sunt. At quia hodie multi non Dei uocationem expectant, sed uentris & opum studio ad Verbi ministerium rapiuntur, non mirum est, si nihil ipsis sufficiat, & Ecclesias subinde mutent, & prioribus relictis ad alias transeant, quando pinguioris stipendij spes offertur. Accomodent hanc quoq; doctrinam sibi qui rem pub. administrant, ad quos Moisis, Dauidis, Ezechiæ & similium exempla pertinent, qui cum Deo fideles fuerint, mirificè ab eo seruati sunt, etiamsi in suis hominibus parum aut nihil præsidij haberet. Et ne hæc ad uetus modo Testamentum pertinere putent, Constantinum quoque magnum habent & Theodosios, multosq; alios principes Christianos, quibus suam benedictionem Deus simili liberalitate contulit, cùm ipsi fideles essent suæ Ecclesiæ nutritij, quæ propria est principum uocatio. Debent horum in re domestica meminisse, qui numerosam familiam alunt, ne ut egestatem fugiant, ad impostauras, rapinas aut alias malas artes conuertantur, sed honesto labori & beneficentiæ studeāt, & procul dubio sentient Deum suæ promissioni non unquam defuturum esse. Deinde ad consolationem nostram hæc doctrina plurimum facit, si quando egestate & inopia nos premi sentimus, neq; aliqua in humanis spes fortis melioris affulget. Tunc enim cogitare nos decet, Deum hoc itauelle, qui etsi non superfluis bonis nos donat, tamen non omnino relinquet in se sperantes, & eidem facile esse, ut re quauis obuia suos alat atq; conseruet. Et huc illud Moisis referri debet, quo Christus etiam utitur: Non solo pane uiuit homo, sed omni uerbo quod exit ab ore Dei.
units.tr: At the same time, from this passage a general teaching and consolation should be drawn: that nothing will ever be lacking to those who walk in God's calling and faithfully perform the function laid upon them. For what happened with the Apostles, whom Christ, in a foreign region and among a hostile nation, nourished and preserved, not without a miracle, so that they confess nothing was lacking to them, this he promises by universal promises to all who keep his precepts and obey him. Such promises are found everywhere in the Law and the Prophets, and Christ himself confirms them, saying in Matthew: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." Many examples also not only illustrate these promises but confirm them so that it would be wrong to doubt them even slightly. Abraham is commanded suddenly to leave his native soil and to abandon his homeland and his people. He obeys the Lord calling him, and although many things stood in the way, which seemed to be able to be pleaded honourably, prudently, and not unjustly or undeservedly, he nevertheless sets out at once without delay, and at last understands that a dwelling place has been prepared for him by God among the most hostile nation of the Canaanites (of whom the Sodomites and Gomorrhites were no small part). There, even though at first he was met by a harsh famine, which afflicted that whole land, and was soon also compelled to undergo the fortune of war, God so preserved him that he easily prevailed even over the richest in that nation, and possessed vast treasures of wealth. The same we can say of his son Isaac and of his grandson Jacob. But what shall we say of Joseph? When he understood that he had been sold by his brothers, not without the counsel of God, and taken into Egypt, he thought that servitude and exile were his calling, and he was faithful to his master, however harsh and ungrateful. Therefore, even though for a time he felt fortune against him, afterwards he was raised to the highest dignity and preserved the whole nation. To this belongs what is written of the children of Israel: when, following God's call, they had gone out of Egypt, they were fed for forty years with bread sent down from heaven, and nothing that was necessary for living was lacking to them. This example is the more memorable because their ingratitude and stubbornness did not prevent God from wishing his promise to stand, even though they deserved a thousand deaths every day. These could be added to by David and by countless others, but since many such things happen daily, both publicly and privately, there is no need to dwell longer on the recounting of ancient examples. Rather let us observe the use of this teaching, which consists in two things. First, it serves for instruction and reminds men of every place and rank not to depart from their duty out of fear of want or poverty, but to hold faithfully the station entrusted to them by God. So let the ministers of the churches consider this, to whom this present example of the Apostles pertains, as also the examples of Elijah and of others who, by the same divine generosity, were preserved in this office. But since today many do not await God's calling, and are carried to the ministry of the Word by a zeal for their belly and for riches, it is no wonder if nothing suffices for them, and they change churches again and again, and, having left their former ones, pass over to others, whenever the hope of a fatter stipend is offered. Let those who administer public affairs also apply this teaching to themselves, to whom the examples of Moses, David, Hezekiah, and the like pertain: those who were faithful to God were wonderfully preserved by him, even though they had little or no help from their own people. And lest they think this pertains only to the Old Testament, they have Constantine the Great and the Theodosiuses, and many other Christian princes, to whom God gave his blessing with the same generosity, since they were faithful nurses of his Church, which is the proper calling of princes. Let those who support large households in their domestic affairs remember this, so that, in order to escape poverty, they may not turn to frauds, robberies, or other evil arts, but may devote themselves to honest labour and beneficence; and without doubt they will feel that God will never fail his promise. Second, this teaching does very much to console us if ever we feel ourselves pressed by want and poverty, and no strong hope of something better shines forth in human affairs. For then we ought to consider that God wills it so, who, although he does not give us superfluous goods, nevertheless will not wholly abandon those who hope in him, and that it is easy for him to nourish and preserve his people by any thing whatever that lies at hand. And to this the saying of Moses should be referred, which Christ also uses: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God."

units.la: Cæterum ad propositi loci tractationē redeamus. Pergit enim Dominus, & ne discipuli perpetuā pacē sibi pollicentes periculis improuisis offenderentur, quid illos porrò maneat, docet. Nam cum ijs quæ modò tractauimus, alteram huius argumenti partem connectens, ex opposito infert. At nunc qui crumenā habet, sumat eam, similiter & peram: & qui non habet, uendat pallium suum, & emat gladium: Quasi dicat: Hactenus quidem ea fuit uestra conditio, ut uobis neque commeatu, neque defensione armata opus fuerit, cum ego occultā uirtute hostes nostros cohibuerim, ne quid contra uos hostile tentarent, & quorumuis animos flexerim; ut uos excipere & liberaliter alere dignati sint. Nunc autem longè aliter res se habebunt, quando cum hominum animis tota etiam facies mundi mutata esse uideri poterit. Ergo quæ prius dedi præcepta pro eius temporis ratione, nunc locum amplius habere non possunt. Quin potius crumenas & peras & quicquid aliud aduitam tuendam opus est, sumite. Adhæc si cui pecunia desunt, is ne grauetur pallium uendere, ut gladium emat ad sui defensionem. At quid (inquis) audio? Iamne alia Christi mens est, quàm olim, quando dicebat: Ne resistatis malo, sed percutienti te in unam maxillam, obuerte & alteram? Iamne Apostolos gladio armare & hos pro se pugnare uoluit, ne à militibus & Pontificum seruis caperetur? Nequaquam ô bone: Sed potius (ut initio diximus) ad diuinam protectionem eos remittere uoluit: orationem autem illorum ingenio & moribus accommodat, ut reipsa discant, quàm stultè hucusque regnum terrenum, uictorias atq; triumphos de hostibus somniarint. Nam etiamsi de eo illos abunde iam monuisset, sciebat tamen animos ipsorum ab errore nondum liberatos esse: quod & rei euentus postea declarauit. Itaque nouam de hoc tractationem orditur, quam (ut quidam rectissimè obseruarunt) postea in horto demum absoluit, quando Petrum gladio pugnantem acriter reprehendit. Itaque in hunc finem & hoc sensu ista dicuntur: Video uos adhuc regni spe occupatos arma & gladios animo uersare. Sed agite, quando ita lubet, parate & instruite uos ad certamen. Iam enim instant pericula, quæ præsentem & acrem defensionem requirunt, & si unquam gladijs defendi uoluissem, id nunc facto opus esset. Sed uidebitis & reipsa experieminni, meum Regnum neque de hoc mundo esse, neque huius mundi armis defendi, &c. Habent ergo hæc Christi uerba Apositopesim, quæ (ut diximus) in horto supplebitur, ubi diserte docebit, ipsos à solius Patris auxilio debere pendere, & huius consilio atque decreto seipsos & causam hanc omnem pertinere. Sunt ergo ridiculi nimis, qui nodum in scirpo quærentes disputationem de usu gladij & defensione licita siue illicita instituunt, cùm potius de periculis imminentibus discipulos Christus præmonere, & simul docere uoluerit, fide & patientia opus fore, quando gladijs hîc nihil posset effici.
units.tr: But let us return to the treatment of the passage in hand. The Lord goes on, and lest the disciples, who were promising themselves perpetual peace, should be overtaken and offended by unforeseen dangers, he tells them what awaits them henceforth. Connecting this with what we have just discussed, he draws the other side of the argument as its opposite: "But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a wallet; and whoever has no sword, let him sell his cloak and buy one." As if he were saying: "Hitherto your condition has been such that you needed neither provisions nor armed defence, since I by a hidden power restrained our enemies, so that they could attempt nothing hostile against you, and I bent the minds of whomever I pleased, so that they deigned to receive you and generously support you. But now matters will stand quite differently, when the whole face of the world may appear to be changed along with men's minds. So the precepts I gave earlier, suited to that time, can no longer hold good. Rather, take purses and wallets and whatever else is needed for protecting your life. Moreover, if anyone lacks money, let him not hesitate to sell his cloak to buy a sword for his own defence." But what (you say) do I hear? Is Christ's mind now different from what it was once, when he said: "Resist not evil, but whoever strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also"? Does he now wish to arm the Apostles with swords and have them fight for him, so that they are not taken by soldiers and the servants of the high priests? By no means, good sir. Rather, as we said at the outset, he wishes to send them back to divine protection; yet he adapts his speech to their disposition and habits, so that they may learn by experience how foolishly until now they have dreamed of an earthly kingdom, of victories and triumphs over their enemies. For although he had already warned them about this at length, he knew that their minds were not yet freed from error, as the outcome of the event later made plain. Accordingly he begins a new treatment of this matter, which (as certain men have rightly observed) he finally completed afterwards in the garden, when he sharply rebuked Peter for fighting with the sword. So these words are spoken to this end and with this meaning: "I see that you are still occupied with hopes of the kingdom and turn over arms and swords in your minds. Well then, since it pleases you so, prepare and equip yourselves for the struggle. For dangers now press upon us, which demand a present and vigorous defence; and if ever I had wished to be defended by swords, it would be necessary now. But you will see and experience for yourselves that my kingdom is neither of this world, nor is it defended by the weapons of this world, etc." So these words of Christ contain an aposiopesis, which (as we have said) will be completed in the garden, where he will plainly teach that they must depend on the Father's help alone, and that they themselves and the whole cause pertain to his counsel and decree. Therefore those are far too ridiculous who, seeking a knot in a bulrush, set up a debate about the use of the sword and lawful or unlawful defence, when Christ rather meant to forewarn his disciples of the impending perils, and at the same time to teach that faith and patience would be needed, since nothing could be accomplished here by swords.

units.la: Facit ad huius sensus confirmationem, quòd ex æterno Patris decreto hæc fieri oportere, Prophetico testimonio probat, dum mox subiicit: Dico enim uobis, adhuc oportere in me perfici scriptum illud: Et cum sceleratis numeratus est. En hæc omnino fieri oportere testatur. Quis ergo illum discipulis serio mandauisse putet, ut aduersus Dei decretum arma sumant? Habet autem Emphasim particula ADHVC. Nam ea perinde utitur, ac si diceret: Multa quidem hucusque aduersa sustinui. Sub censu peregre ex Virgine paupercula natum uile præsepium excepit: Moxuitæ meæ insidiantem Herodem fugere coactus sum, quando nunquam genti nostræ amica Ægyptus mihi latebras præbuit. Inde reuersum ignobile Nazarethum suscepit, ubi duro manuum labore uictum mihi parauisque ad tempus illud, quo me Pater in publicum prodire, & munus illud obire uoluit, cui me destinauerat. Quod ut primum cœpi facere, quibus nō periculis & casibus exagitatus sum? Quoties insidijs Scribarum petitus? Quoties lapidibus immerentem Pharisæi obruere conati sunt? Ipsi denique mihi testes estis, quot labores, curas atq; sollicitudines sustinuerim. Et quid infelix Iudas aduersus me machinetur, paulò ante narraui. At nondum finis omnium apparet, quæ mihi ferenda Pater impossuit. Restat enim ut (quod Isaias prædixit) pro scelerato condemner, & in crucem suffixus non tam crudeli & diro quàm infami supplicio uitam hanc immortalem finiam. Reliqua, quæ de me scripta sunt, iam finem suum attigerunt. Quod uero reliquum est certamen, id adhuc mihi incumbit, & ut grauissimum erit, ita uos quoq; inuicta fidei constantia armatos esse oportebit, ne sub tanti scandali pondere succumbatis. Hic uerborum istorum sensus est, quibus Crucis scandalum remouere uoluit Dominus, idq; duobus argumentis: Primo quòd nihil fortuitum passurus sit, sed quòd hæc omnia ex Patris decreto fiant: Altero, quòd ita exigat nostræ salutis ratio, ut nimirum ipse pro scelerato damnetur, & morte sua, quam ipse innocens sustinere uelit, nostrorum scelerum noxam expiet, nosque cum Patre in gratiam reducat.
units.tr: What confirms this sense is that he proves by prophetic testimony that these things must happen according to the Father's eternal decree, when he immediately adds: "For I tell you that this scripture must yet be fulfilled in me: And he was numbered with the transgressors." Here he testifies that these things must altogether come to pass. Who then would think that he seriously commanded the disciples to take up arms against God's decree? The particle ADHUC (yet) gives emphasis. For he uses it as if he were saying: "Many hard things I have endured until now. Born at the census in a foreign land of a poor Virgin, I was received in a lowly manger. Soon after my birth I was forced to flee from Herod, who lay in wait for my life, since Egypt, never friendly to our nation, gave me a hiding place. Returning from there, I dwelt in obscure Nazareth, where I earned my living by hard manual labour and prepared myself for that time when the Father wished me to come forth in public and undertake the office for which he had destined me. As soon as I began to do this, by what dangers and mishaps was I not harassed? How often was I sought out by the plots of the scribes? How often did the Pharisees try to stone me though I had done no wrong? Finally, you yourselves are my witnesses how many labours, cares and anxieties I have endured. And what the unhappy Judas is plotting against me, I related a little while ago. But the end of all the things the Father has laid upon me does not yet appear. For it remains that (as Isaiah foretold) I be condemned as a criminal, and, nailed to the cross, end this immortal life by a punishment not so cruel and dreadful as it is infamous. The rest of what has been written about me has now reached its end. But what remains of the struggle still lies before me, and as it will be most grievous, so you too will need to be armed with unconquered constancy of faith, lest you succumb under the weight of so great a scandal." This is the sense of these words, by which the Lord wished to remove the scandal of the cross, and he did so by two arguments: first, that he will suffer nothing by chance, but that all these things happen by the Father's decree; second, that the reason of our salvation requires that he himself be condemned as a criminal, and that by his death, which he willingly endures though innocent, he should expiate the guilt of our sins and reconcile us with the Father.

units.la: Est autem hoc loco diligenter obseruandum, quòd ad scripturas discipulos suos Dominus remittit, ut ex his intelligant, se non aliud passurum esse, quàm quod ita fieri uelit Deus. Ita enim & seipsum pro assumpta humanitatis infirmitate consolari, et simul (ut diximus) illos aduersus scandalum praemunire voluit, quod ex morte sua ignominiosa enasciturum esse non ignorabat. Debemus autem nos exemplu eius imitari, ut quoties uel priuatim ipsi affligimur, uel publicos totius mundi motus & diras piorum persecutiones, exilia, tormenta, indignas mortes, adhæc Ecclesiarum dissipationes & excidia uidemus: non in hoc tam tristi spectaculo attonita mente hæreamus, sed oculos altius attollendo ea in mente renocemus, quæ in Scripturis habentur de nouissimi temporis conditione. Mox enim patebit, nihil hodie uel nobis uel alijs pijs accidere, de quo non aperta & perspicua extent sacrarum literarum oracula. Atqui Scripturam diuinitus inspiratam esse, & ipsissimum Dei Verbum esse constat. Vnde sequitur ista nobis quoq; non fortuitò accidere, sed ita Deo uisum esse, ut crucis amaritudo carnem ad huius mundi illecebras lasciuientem coerceat, & ut Filij sui socij facti in afflictionibus, cum eodem aliquando uiuamus atque regnemus. Hoc ut omne scandalum procul è medio tollit, ita consolatione dulcissima animos territos recreat, et cauet ne quid contra Deum dicamus nostra professione indignum. Mox enim sibi ipsi obijciet homo: Tu quis es, qui Deo litem moueas? Tune tibi ipsi melius consules, quàm is qui te creauit cùm nullus esses, & perditum Filij sui sanguine redemit? Tune tuam conditionem uis meliorem esse, quàm Domini & redemptoris tui fuerit? Simul ergo hic de Scripturæ Sanctæ præstantia, dignitate & usu nos locus iste admonet. Quis enim non eos libros admiretur & in pretio habeat, ad quos ipse Dei Filius iam mortem aditurus recurrere voluit, & ex quibus consolationè petijt, quæ et seipsum et discipulos suos confirmaret? Sufficiat hoc nobis aduersus canes Porphyrianos & porcos Iulianicos, qui aduersus sacras literas latrare & grunnire audent, eò quòd his multa continentur, quæ ipsorum cupiditatibus repugnant, neq; ipsorum intellectu comprehendi possunt. Non nobis, non nobis ô canes hi panes dati sunt: non nobis ô porci Acarnanij hæc fercula parata sunt: non gemmas curant galli Æsopici. Vos ergo ad Poëtarum prophanorum prostibula, ad philosophorum sterquilinia, ad fabulatorum lacunas remittimus. Illic ora uestra abluite, nares obesas pascite, et aures meretricias oblectate. Nobis modò Scripturas relinquite intactas, quæ Verbum illud Dei æternum continent, quod ut auro pretiosius, ita fauis melle stillantibus dulcius est.
units.tr: Now in this place we must carefully observe that the Lord sends his disciples back to the Scriptures, so that they may understand that he will suffer nothing other than what God wills should happen. For in this way he also comforted himself under the weakness of the humanity he had assumed, and at the same time (as we have said) wished to fortify them against the scandal which he knew would arise from his ignominious death. We too ought to imitate his example, so that whenever we are afflicted either privately, or see public upheavals throughout the world and the dreadful persecutions, exiles, tortures and unworthy deaths of the godly, and besides these the dispersions and ruin of the Churches, we should not cling to this sad spectacle with a stunned mind, but, lifting our eyes higher, recall to mind those things that are contained in the Scriptures concerning the condition of the last times. For soon it will become plain that nothing happens today either to us or to other godly people of which the clear and manifest oracles of the sacred letters do not stand forth. Yet it is agreed that Scripture is divinely inspired and is the very Word of God. Hence it follows that these things too do not happen to us by chance, but that it has so seemed good to God, so that the bitterness of the cross may restrain the flesh that wantons after the allurements of this world, and so that, made partners in his Son's afflictions, we may at some time live and reign with him. This, as it removes all scandal from the midst, so it refreshes frightened minds with the sweetest consolation, and it guards us against saying anything unworthy of our profession against God. For a man will presently object to himself: "Who are you, who would bring suit against God? Will you advise yourself better than he who created you when you were nothing, and redeemed you, lost, with the blood of his Son? Do you wish your condition to be better than that of your Lord and Redeemer?" So this place also reminds us of the excellence, dignity and use of Holy Scripture. For who would not admire and hold in esteem those books to which the Son of God himself chose to turn when about to face death, and from which he sought consolation to strengthen both himself and his disciples? Let this suffice for us against the Porphyrian dogs and the Julianic swine, who dare to bark and grunt against the sacred letters because many things are contained in them that oppose their desires and cannot be grasped by their understanding. These bread were not given to us, not to us, O dogs; these dishes were not prepared for us, O Acarnanian pigs; the Aesopian cocks do not care for gems. Therefore we send you back to the brothels of the profane poets, to the dunghills of the philosophers, to the pools of the fabulists. There wash your mouths, feed your bloated nostrils, and delight your harlot's ears. As for us, leave us the Scriptures untouched, which contain that eternal Word of God, which is more precious than gold and sweeter than honeycomb dripping from the comb.

units.la: Porrò discipulos Christi audire præstat, qui cùm illum de gladijs emendis verba facere audirent, illico respondent: Domine, ecce, duo gladij hic. Quibus verbis animos quidem ad Christi defensionem promptos & alacres testari volunt, simul uerò stupiditatè produnt, quam merito omnes cordati admirentur. Audiunt ita à Deo decretum esse, ut ille morte infami moriatur, & quidem publica authoritate damnatus. Quæ ergo stoliditas est Dei statuto gladios opponere velle, quasi his illius voluntas possit impediri? Et si omnino voluisset Christus armata manu defendi, quid obsecro profuissent gladij duo aduersus hostes eius, quos potentia & armis instructissimos esse non nesciebant? Sed ita suam stultitiam prodere solent, quotquot Regnum Christi ex carnis sensu metiuntur. Et mirum est, homines, qui natura à periculis abhorrent, in fidei & æternæ salutis causa plerunq; sua consilia, quæ periculorum plena sunt, tutissimis & saluberrimis Christi monitis præferre. Quod enim hic discipuli faciunt, hoc ipsum à multis hodie fieri consueuit. Iubet Dominus, ut in patientia nostra possideamus animas nostras, & idem per Prophetam clamat: In silentio & spe erit fortitudo vestra. At plerisq; hæc viuendi ratio displicet, qui tunc demum se Christianos esse arbitrantur, si populum ad seditiones concitent, bella suscipiant nò necessaria, aut alia huius generis conentur, quæ cum præsenti periculo coniuncta sunt. Ita uerò sibi ipsis malum accersunt, & ferè Ecclesias totas euertunt, quas alij pura ueritatis doctrina collegerunt, & suo sanguine confirmarunt, &c.
units.tr: Next, it is worth listening to Christ's disciples. When they heard him speak about buying swords, they immediately replied, "Lord, look, here are two swords." With these words they wish to show how ready and eager they are to defend Christ, but at the same time they reveal a stupidity that every sensible person rightly marvels at. They had heard that it had been decreed by God that he would die an infamous death, condemned by public authority. What foolishness is it, then, to want to oppose swords to God's decree, as if his will could be hindered by them? And even if Christ had wanted to be defended by an armed hand, what, I ask you, would two swords have achieved against his enemies, whom they knew to be most thoroughly equipped with power and arms? But this is how all those who measure Christ's kingdom by the sense of the flesh usually betray their folly. And it is remarkable that men who by nature shrink from dangers, in the cause of faith and eternal salvation, very often prefer their own plans, which are full of danger, to the safest and most wholesome admonitions of Christ. For what the disciples do here is what many today are wont to do. The Lord commands that in our patience we possess our souls, and through the Prophet he likewise cries, "In quietness and in hope shall be your strength." But this way of living displeases many, who think they are Christians only when they stir up the people to sedition, undertake unnecessary wars, or attempt other things of this kind that are bound up with present danger. In this way they bring evil upon themselves and almost overthrow whole churches, which others gathered by the pure doctrine of truth and confirmed with their own blood, etc.

units.la: Cæterùm Christus cognita discipulorum ignorantia, tractationem hanc uno uerbo abrumpit, cùm res in præsenti longiorem disputationè non admitteret. Dicit enim illis: Satis est: Quasi dicat: Video uos adhuc crassiores esse, ut ne nunc quidè id intelligatis, de quo uos toties admonui. Quia ergo apud uos uerbis & rationibus nihil proficitur, agite, sufficiùt iam ista, donec reipsa experiamini quid uelim. Ita uerò (quod supra diximus) tractationem istam suspendit in hortum usque, ubi cùm Petrus non minus infeliciter quàm temere pugnare instituisset, sibi dici audit: Converte gladium tuum in locum suum: omnes enim qui acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt. An putas quòd non possim nunc
units.tr: Moreover, Christ, perceiving the disciples' ignorance, cuts off this discussion with a single word, since the matter at hand did not admit of a longer dispute. For he says to them, "It is enough." As if he were saying: "I see that you are still too dull to understand even now what I have so often warned you about. Since nothing is gained among you by words and arguments, come, let these things suffice for now, until you learn in fact what I want." And so, as we said above, he postpones that discussion until the garden, where Peter, having begun to fight no less unhappily than rashly, hears himself told: "Put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword." Do you think that I cannot now

units.la: Discipuli gladios afferunt inepte.
units.tr: The disciples foolishly bring swords.

units.la: Christus armis non defenditur. nunc precari Patrem meum, qui præstet mihi plures quàm duodecim legiones Angelorum? Quo modo ergo implerentur Scripturæ, quæ sic oportere fieri dicũt? Ex his Christi verbis loci huius præsensus elici debet, quibus manifestè docet nõ se hoc velle, ut vel Petrus vel quisquam alius arma pro ipso capiat, & rationes adducit: Primam, quòd id per se non liceat, ut quisquam absq; Dei vocatione gladium sponte arripiat pro sui animi libidine. Et ad Legem illam vetustissimã alludit: Omnis qui sanguinem effuderit, eius sanguis fundetur. Alteram, quòd Angelis defensoribus posset uti, si vellet. Postremam, quòd obediendum sit voluntati Patris, quam in Scripturis revelatam habeamus. Unde colligimus, Regnum Christi nequaquam armis hominũ opus habere quibus defendatur, nec temere quenquam hoc prætextu debere arma sumere, nisi vocatione Dei peculiari id facere iubeatur. Scimus quidem Reges Ecclesiæ nutritios & propugnatores esse debere, et Deum horum opera sæpe feliciter illam defendisse, ut Davidis, Ezechiæ, Constantini, Theodosij & similium historiæ testantur. Quid verò hoc facit ad doctores, quorum longè alia est conditio? Quid ad homines privatos, qui quoad res externas magistratibus suis obedire, fidem verò & cultum Dei libera confessione, vitæ innocentia & (si ita opus sit) morte & sanguine suo debent tueri?
units.tr: Christ is not defended by arms. pray to my Father, who would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, which say that it must happen in this way? From these words of Christ the meaning of this passage ought to be drawn, in which he plainly teaches that he does not wish Peter or anyone else to take up arms on his behalf. He gives reasons: first, that it is not lawful in itself for anyone to snatch up the sword of his own accord, at the whim of his own mind, without a call from God; and he alludes to that most ancient law: "Whoever sheds blood, his blood shall be shed." Second, that he could use angels as defenders if he wished. Last, that the will of the Father must be obeyed, which we have revealed to us in the Scriptures. From this we gather that the kingdom of Christ by no means needs the arms of men to defend it, and that no one should rashly take up arms on this pretext, unless he is commanded to do so by a particular call of God. We indeed know that kings ought to be nurses and defenders of the Church, and that God has often defended it happily through their work, as the histories of David, Hezekiah, Constantine, Theodosius and others bear witness. But what does this have to do with teachers, whose condition is quite different? What does it have to do with private persons, who must obey their magistrates in external matters, but must defend the faith and the worship of God by free confession, by innocence of life, and, if need be, by their own death and blood?

units.la: Ex his apparet, quàm turpiter & quanto cum Christi ludibrio, huius loci authoritate olim abusus sit Bonifacius VIII. Pontifex, qui Canonē de Maioritate & obedientia condidit, qui in iure Pontificio inter Extravagantes numeratur: sic nimirũ non absq; numine dictos, cum extra omnes Christianæ doctrinæ limites vagentur, & Scripturas manifestè detorqueant. Summa Canonis est: Omnes quotquot sunt per totum orbem fideles, Romano Pontifici subesse debere, qui utriusq; gladij, spiritualis nimirum, & secularis, vel Ecclesiastici & politici potestatem habeat. Idque inter alias rationes ex Scripturis impiè detortis desumptas, etiã ex hoc loco demonstrare conatur, sic dices: In hac eiusq; potestate duos esse gladios, Spiritualem videlicet & Temporalem, Evangelicis dictis instruimur. Nam dicentibus Apostolis, Ecce gladij duo hîc, in Ecclesia scilicet, cum Apostoli loquerentur, non respondit Dominus, nimis esse, sed satis. Certè qui in potestate Petri temporalem gladium esse negat, male verbum attendit Domini proferentis: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam. Utrq; ergo est in potestate Ecclesiæ, Spiritualis scilicet gladius & Materialis: sed iis quidem pro Ecclesia, ille verò ab Ecclesia exercendus: ille Sacerdotis, is manu regum & militum: sed ad nutũ & patientiam Sacerdotis, &c. Quod autem verbis hisce docuit ille, reipsa non minus contumeliosè quàm insolenter exercuit adversus Albertum Romanorum Regem, cùm is per legatos suæ electionis & Imperij confirmationem ab illo postularet. Agebatur tunc annus à natali Christi MCCC. quando ambitiosus ille annum Iubilæum instauravit, reducta ex Iudaismo per Christum olim abrogato solennitate illa, quod nemo Pontificum ante illum facere ausus fuerat. Itaq; ut præsentibus legatis regijs penes se utriusq; gladij potestatem esse ostenderet, primo quidem eius solennitatis die in pontificalibus prodiens apostolicam benedictionē populo impertitus est: postero autem, habitu Imperiali & infula Cæsarea insignis, gladium ante se nudatũ iussit deferri, & ubi consedisset, alta voce dixit: Ecce duo gladij hîc. Quid verò est cũ Scripturis ludere ô fratres, si hoc non est? Primò enim adversus expressum Christi mandatũ, quo hîc ne Apostoli regna huius mundi invadat præcipitur, Imperatoriã quoq; potestatẽ sibi vendicat. Deinde Allegoriã fingit in verbis Christi, ab eius mente alienissimam. Adhæc locum hunc totũ detorquet, ut gladij usum afferat, ubi hunc Christus diserte damnat. Adde his, quòd ex gladio Spirituali, qui nõ alius est quàm Verbum Dei, iurisdictionem fabricat Ecclesiasticam, cui magistratus omnes, adeoq; Imperatorẽ ipsum subijcit. Deniq; hunc non serui modo et subditi, sed carnificis sui loco habet, quando hunc gladio non aliter quàm pro Sacerdotis nutu uti debere dicit. Et hi illi sunt, pro quibus hodie Reges & Imperatores pugnant, & in quorum gratiam seipsos suamq; authoritatem prostituunt, eos autem ferro & igne persequuntur, qui ipsos ex turpi illo Paparum seruitio vindicare student. Hæc item iam seculis aliquot turbarum omnium causa fuit, quibus infelix terrarum orbis exagitatus est, et hodie cum omnium fere regnorũ dissipatione exagitatur. At quãdo ita volunt infelices illi, nos Christi mente constanter teneamus, qui in Ecclesia sua ministros constituit, qui nõ alio quàm Spiritus gladio, id est Dei verbo pugnare debet adversus omnia, quæ contra hunc efferuntur. Idem ille magistratibus ius suum reliquit integrum, & horũ est populo ins dicere, verum Dei cultũ promovere, & huius studiosos sua authoritate tueri. Quod si faciant,
units.tr: From these things it is clear how shamefully, and to what great mockery of Christ, Boniface VIII, the Pontiff, once abused the authority of this passage, he who composed the canon On the Majority and Obedience, which is counted among the Extravagants in Pontifical law. Such things, indeed, are not said without the nod of the divine will, since they wander outside all the limits of Christian doctrine and plainly twist the Scriptures. The sum of the canon is this: all the faithful throughout the whole world ought to be subject to the Roman Pontiff, who has the power of both swords, namely spiritual and secular, or ecclesiastical and political. And among other arguments drawn impiously from twisted Scriptures, he tries to prove this also from this passage, speaking thus: "We are taught by the evangelical sayings that there are two swords in this power and authority, namely a spiritual and a temporal one. For when the Apostles said, 'Behold, here are two swords,' that is, in the Church, while the Apostles were speaking, the Lord did not answer, 'It is too much,' but 'It is enough.' Certainly he who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter has poorly attended to the word of the Lord when he said, 'Put your sword into its sheath.' Both therefore are in the power of the Church, the spiritual sword and the material one: but the former indeed is to be wielded for the Church, the latter by the Church; the former by the priest, the latter by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and sufferance of the priest," etc. But what he taught in these words, he practised in fact no less insolently than arrogantly against Albert, King of the Romans, when that man demanded from him, through his envoys, confirmation of his election and of his empire. It was then the year 1300 from the birth of Christ, when that ambitious man restored the Jubilee year, a solemnity that had been abrogated long before by Christ, having been brought back from Judaism, something no Pontiff before him had dared to do. And so, in order to show the royal envoys who were present that he held the power of both swords, on the first day of that solemnity he came forth in pontifical vestments and gave the apostolic blessing to the people. But on the following day, adorned with imperial dress and the Caesarean mitre, he ordered a naked sword to be carried before him, and when he had sat down, he said in a loud voice, "Behold, here are two swords." And what is this, brothers, if not playing with the Scriptures? For first, contrary to the express command of Christ, by which the Apostles are forbidden to invade the kingdoms of this world, he claims for himself imperial power as well. Then he invents an allegory in the words of Christ, most alien to his mind. Moreover, he twists this whole passage so as to bring in the use of the sword, where Christ plainly condemns it. Add to this that from the spiritual sword, which is nothing other than the Word of God, he fashions an ecclesiastical jurisdiction, to which he subjects all magistrates, and the Emperor himself. Finally, he treats the Emperor not merely as a servant and subject, but as his own executioner, when he says that the sword must be used only at the nod of the priest. And these are the men for whose sake kings and emperors fight today, and for whose favour they prostitute themselves and their authority, while they persecute with fire and sword those who strive to deliver them from that shameful servitude to the Popes. This also has been for several centuries the cause of all the disturbances by which the unhappy orb of the earth has been tormented, and today it is tormented with the destruction of almost all kingdoms. But since those unhappy men wish it so, let us hold constantly to the mind of Christ, who has appointed ministers in his Church, who ought to fight against everything that is raised up against it not with any other sword than the sword of the Spirit, that is, the Word of God. The same Christ left the magistrates their right intact, and it belongs to them to administer justice to the people, to promote the true worship of God, and to protect its zealous followers by their authority. If they do this,

units.la: Cotra Can. de Maior. et Obedient. licet pijs omnibus horum protectione legitimauti, quod Paulum non semel fecisse legimus, qui & manu armata sese defendi passus est, & ad Caesaris tribunal provocauit, quando praesides partim ignaues, partim sibi non satis aequos esse uidebat. Quod si autem omnes in suo munere cessent, neque apud homines defensio legitima inueniatur, a tumultibus tamen Christiani homines abstinere, nec alicui seditionum in Republica authores esse debent: sed patienter ferre quae Deus imponit. Hoc si fecerint, ij germani Iesu Christi discipuli atque imitatores sunt, quos & in hoc seculo ille seruabit, quoad ipsis utile ac salutare fuerit, & olim Regni sui caelestis cohaeredes faciet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Against the canon on superiors and obedience: although all the godly are lawfully protected by these, as we read that Paul did more than once, who allowed himself to be defended by armed men and appealed to Caesar's tribunal, when he saw that the governors were partly negligent and partly not fair enough to him. But if all of them shirk their duty, and no lawful defence is to be found among men, Christians must nevertheless abstain from tumults and must not be the authors of any sedition in the commonwealth, but must patiently bear what God lays upon them. If they do this, they are the true disciples and imitators of Jesus Christ, whom he will preserve in this age for as long as it is useful and salutary for them, and whom he will one day make heirs of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIX.

units.la: Et egressus profectus est ex more in montem Oliuarum, secuti sunt autem etiam eum discipuli eius. Cum vero peruenisset ad eum locum, dixit eis: Precamini, ne intretis in tentationem. Tum ipse auul-sus est ab eis quasi ad iactum lapidis, positisq; genibus precatus est, dicens: Pater, si vis, transfer poculum hoc a me, veruntamen non mea voluntas, sed tua fiat. Visus est autem ei Angelus e coelo, corroborans eum. Et ipse constitutus in angore, intentius orabat. Erat autem sudor eius quasi grumi sanguinis descendentes in terram. Et cum surrexisset a precatione, venisset ad discipulos, inuenit eos dormientes prae tristitia. Et dixit eis: Quid dormitis? Surgite & precamini ne intretis in tentationem.
units.tr: And he went out, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and his disciples also followed him. When he came to that place, he said to them: Pray, that you enter not into temptation. Then he himself was withdrawn from them about a stone's throw, and kneeling down he prayed, saying: Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me; nevertheless not my will, but yours be done. And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat was like drops of blood falling down upon the ground. And when he rose from prayer and came to the disciples, he found them sleeping for sorrow. And he said to them: Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray, lest you enter into temptation.

units.la: CHristus Iesus pro nobis passus est, non solum ut nos mortis suae merito redimeret, uerumetiam (sicut Petrus ait) ut nobis exemplo esset, cuius uestigia ipsi sequamur. Recte igitur Euangelistae diligentia singulari ex ordine omnia ea describunt, quae iam instante mortis hora fecit. inter quae primum locum obtinet Coena, quam cum discipulis suis ultimam habuit, & in qua cum ijsdem demultis disseruit, quae non minus nostrae quam illorum institutioni seruiunt. Sequitur nunc, ut omnibus quae ad illam pertinebat rite peractis ad montem Oliuarum exiuerit, ubi & captus est, & prius multa fecit, quae peculiarem consideratione merentur. Nunc ante omnia obseruari debet quod a Coena illa mystica, qua solennem mortis suae memoriam nobis commendauit, recta ad exequendam Patris sui voluntate progreditur, nec quo minus id faciat, per ea se patitur abstrahi, quae illic sibi euentura esse sciebat. Docemur hoc illius exemplo, quid nos facere deceat, quando in Coena illius nos eius discipulos publice professi sumus. Meditemur diligenter, quae Dei voluntas sit: nimirum ut nos totos ipsi consecremus, & peccato mortui vitam in illo niuamus nouam & nostra professione dignam: ut denique nos praeparemus ad quaevis ferenda, quae nobis ab illo imponuntur. Est ergo scelerata & execrabilis illorum lasciuia, qui ut olim gentes cum sacris suis ludos vel crudeles & sanguinarios, vel lasciuiae plenos coniungebant, ita ipsi ad pocula, ad stupra, ad usuras et quoduis aliud nequitiae genus reuertuntur. Sed accedamus ad huius loci expositionem, qui quatuor partibus constat. Prima locus indicatur, in quem Christus exiuit. Secunda, ut illic discipulos admonuerit de iis, quae tunc factu in primis necessaria erant. Tertia, quid ipse fecerit narratur. Quarta, quales se inter haec omnia gesserint discipuli.
units.tr: Christ Jesus suffered for us not only so that by the merit of his death he might redeem us, but also (as Peter says) so that he might be an example to us, whose footsteps we should follow. Rightly, therefore, the evangelists with singular care describe in order all that he did as the hour of his death drew near. Among these things the first place belongs to the Supper, which he held with his disciples as the last, and in which he discoursed at length with them on matters that serve our instruction no less than theirs. It follows now that, all things pertaining to the Supper having been duly completed, he went out to the Mount of Olives, where he was also taken, and where, before that, he did many things that deserve special consideration. Above all, it must be observed that from that mystical Supper, in which he commended to us the solemn memory of his death, he proceeds straight to carry out his Father's will, and does not allow himself to be drawn away from doing so by the things he knew would befall him there. We are taught by his example what it becomes us to do, since in his Supper we have publicly professed ourselves his disciples. Let us diligently consider what the will of God is: namely, that we consecrate ourselves wholly to him, and, dead to sin, live in him a new life worthy of our profession; and finally, that we prepare ourselves to bear whatever he lays upon us. Wicked and detestable, therefore, is the wantonness of those who, just as the Gentiles of old joined to their sacred rites games that were either cruel and bloody or full of lust, so themselves turn to drinking, debauchery, usury and every other kind of wickedness. But let us come to the exposition of this passage, which consists of four parts. First, the place is indicated to which Christ went out. Second, how he admonished the disciples about the things that were then especially necessary to be done. Third, what he himself did is related. Fourth, how the disciples conducted themselves amid all these things.

units.la: Quoad locum, fuit is ad montem Oliuarum. Matthaeus & Marcus Gethsemane dictum scribunt. Hieronymus in Commentariis in Isaiam a pinguedine aut fertilitate eum commendat, cui consentit quod Ioannes de horto annotauit, in quem Christus frequenter diuertit, adeo ut nec Iudae locus esset ignotus. Et Lucas in praesentia eum ex more illuc profectum esse scribit. Est-que hoc in primis memoratu dignum, quod & prius locum illum frequentauit, in quo se aliquando captum iri sciebat, & nunc in eundem sponte egreditur, cum tempus illud fatale instaret. Ex eo enim apparet, illum in mortis suae meditatione saepius versatum fuisse, ut se ad illam recte praepararet, & nunc volente se hostiu manibus tradidisse, ut ab ipsis captus ad mortem abriperetur. Nihil ergo illorum viribus tribui debet, quasi Sacerdotes tandem aduersus illum victoria potiti sint, quam diu quaefuerant. Mortuus enim est, quia sic Pater decreuerat, ipse uero illi obedire noluit. Ideo a-pud Ioannem dicebat: Nemo tollit animam meam à me, sed ego pono eam à meipso. Et Pilato suam potestatem superbius iactanti idem respondit: Non haberes potestatem aduersus me vllam, nisi tibi datum esset supernè. Id uero ad nostrae salutis certitudinem facit, & in conscientiae tentationibus effi cacissimè consolatur. Cur enim odio habeat Pater illè caelestis, quos Filii sui morte indigna redem-ptos esse voluit? Cur item Filius mortis suae meritum uolet irritum fieri? Aut cur nos ad se uenien-tes fastidiat, cùm ipse ad nos uenire, & seipsum pro nobis in morte tradere dignatus sit? Deinde no-stri etiam officij nos ille suo exemplo admonet. Est hoc, ut ipsi quoque frequentiores simus in mortis meditatione, neque imitemur delicatulos illos, qui eius ne mentionem quidem uolunt fieri, ne hac præsentis vitae gaudia ipsis interturbet. Ridiculi sanè homines, qui eius mentionē horrent, quod secum in sinu suo gestant, & quod uitari non potest, ut primum hora illa fatalis appropinquat. Est autem utilissima mortis consideratio: quia & scelerum illecebris obstat, & praemunit nos aduersus eius ter-rores, ne his unquam succumbamus. Facit denique, ut Christum imitati sponte obuiam eamus cruci, & alacri animo subeamus aduersa quaeuis, quibus nos Deus exerceri vult. Quid enim durum, quid intolerabile, quid insolens uideri potest illi, qui ad mortem quoque subeundâ iampridem se parauit, qua nihil terribilius est ijs, qui de hac non recte iudicare possunt? Et hic nos excitare debet discipulorum exemplum, qui etsi Christum mula in Caena de morte sua differentem audiuissent, & pro carnis infirmitate tristitiam & dolorem non paruum animo concepissent, tamen absque mora illum eò comitantur, neque eum nunc deserunt, quem miraculis florentem & in aliqua authoritate constitutum hucusque secuti fuerant. Si enim publico prouerbio notantur illi amici, qui in secundis adsunt, in aduersis autem nos derelinquunt: num eorum religionem aut cultum Christo probari posse putabi mus, qui dum pax multa & commodi priuatis spes sese offert, illo magnificè gloriantur, turpiter au tem deficiunt, quando eundem in membris suis periclitari uident?
units.tr: As to the place, it was the Mount of Olives. Matthew and Mark write that it was called Gethsemane. Jerome, in his Commentaries on Isaiah, commends it for its richness or fertility; this agrees with what John noted about the garden, to which Christ often resorted, so that not even the place was unknown to Judas. Luke writes that on this occasion he went there as was his custom. And this is especially worthy of note: he had frequented that place earlier, when he knew that he would one day be taken there, and now he goes out to it of his own accord, when that fatal time was at hand. For from this it appears that he had often been occupied in meditating on his death, so that he might prepare himself for it rightly; and that now, willingly, he handed himself over into the hands of enemies, so that, seized by them, he might be carried off to death. Nothing, therefore, should be attributed to their strength, as if the priests had at last gained the victory over him which they had long sought. For he died because the Father had so decreed, but he himself was unwilling to disobey him. Therefore in John he said: No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. And to Pilate, who boasted too proudly of his power, he gave the same answer: You would have no power at all against me unless it had been given you from above. This indeed contributes to the certainty of our salvation and most effectively consoles us in the temptations of conscience. For why should that heavenly Father hate those whom he willed to be redeemed by the unworthy death of his Son? Why should the Son likewise wish the merit of his death to be made void? Or why should he spurn us when we come to him, when he himself has deigned to come to us and to give himself up for us in death? Then, he also admonishes us by his example of our own duty. It is this: that we too should be more frequent in meditation on death, and not imitate those pampered people who do not even want mention of it made, lest it disturb the joys of this present life. Truly ridiculous men, who shudder at its mention, when they carry it in their bosom, and it cannot be avoided once that fatal hour approaches. But the consideration of death is most useful: it both stands in the way of the allurements of sin and fortifies us against its terrors, so that we never succumb to them. Finally, it makes us, imitating Christ, go willingly to meet the cross and bear with a cheerful mind whatever adversities God wills us to be exercised with. For what can seem hard, intolerable or strange to one who has long prepared himself to undergo even death, than which nothing is more terrible to those who cannot judge it rightly? And here the example of the disciples ought to rouse us. Although they had heard Christ speaking at the Supper about his death, and through the weakness of the flesh had conceived no small sadness and grief in their minds, nevertheless they accompany him thither without delay, and do not now desert him whom they had hitherto followed as one flourishing in miracles and invested with some authority. For if those friends are proverbially branded who stand by us in prosperity but abandon us in adversity, shall we think that the religion or worship of those can be approved before Christ who, while peace abounds and the hope of private advantage presents itself, boast of him magnificently, but shamefully fail when they see him endangered in his members?

units.la: Sequitur secunda pars, qua quid cum discipulis tunc egerit docetur. Quo loco Matthaeus & Marcus primo separationem inter illos factam esse scribunt. Nam alijs octo manere iussis, Petrum Iacobum & Ioannem assumpsit, cumque his aliquo usque progressus, expauescere & toto animo dis-erutiari coepit, & illis ipsis qui gloriae & maiestatis eius in clarificatione aliquando spectatores fue-rant, nunc dolorem & angustiam suam diserte fatetur, dicens: Tristis est ualde anima mea usque ad mortem. Et simul addit: Manete hic & vigilate. Item (quod in praesenti Lucas habet) Precami ni, ne intretis in tentationem. Tria ergo illu discipulis mandauisse audimus: Primum, ut maneant illic, ut ipse aliquantùm progressus possit commodius orare: Alterum, ut vigilent diligenter, ne ex improuiso opprimantur. Postremum, ne intrent in tentationem, id est, ne tentatione quam sua socor-dia accersant, turpiter vincantur. Et hac parte illis in mente reuocat, quod de Satanae insidijs pau-lò ante monuit. His autem generalis doctrina continetur, quod unumquenque nostrum facere conue niat, si quando duriora persecutionum certamina, aut quaecunque alia pericula imminent. Tunc enim ante omnia uidere oportet, ut in statione nobis credita maneamus, siue quis Ecclesiae minister sit, sine magistratum gerat, aut ad quodcunque aliud munus sit destinatus. Vt enim turpe fuerit nauclero, si uentis & fluctibus exortis ipse à clauo discedat: ita nunquam probari poterunt, qui tunc munus suum deserunt, quando ipsorum fides atque industria maximè requiritur. At hoc illud est, in quo ut plurimùm hodie peccatur, ideoque minus bene habent Ecclesia & Respublica. Veruntamen non sa tis fuerit locum occupare aut tenere, quem nobis Deus credidit, nisi attentissimè etiam vigilemus ad uersus Satanae insidias. Nam ut nuper dictum est, nunquam ille dormitat, & non hostes modo aper tos, verumetiam falsos fratres & propriam carnem nostram contra nos excitat, ut suis desiderijs nos infestet, & à Deo abstrahat. Nec quicquam tam difficile est, quàm illius artes deprehendere, quibus sese in animos quoque nostros insinuare solet. Imò etsi neruos omnes intendamus, nihil tamen contra illum ex nobis ipsis poterimus: & ideo studio nostro preces coniungere oportet, ut Deus im-probi illius audaciam frangere, mundi consilia & conatus dissipare, & carnem nostram infirmam Spiritu suo confirmare dignetur. Vtque preces nostrae efficaciores sint, certam de Dei bonitate fidu ciam concipere oportet, quae ut promissionibus eius nititur, ita exemplis infinitis augetur, quae Scrip-turas legentibus passim occurrunt.
units.tr: The second part follows, which teaches what he did with the disciples at that time. Here Matthew and Mark write that first a separation was made among them. For, bidding the other eight to remain, he took Peter, James and John, and having gone on with these a little way, he began to be astonished and to be utterly troubled in his whole mind; and he openly confesses his sorrow and anguish to those very men who had once been witnesses of his glory and majesty in its brightness, saying, "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death." And at the same time he adds, "Stay here and watch." Likewise (which Luke has at this point), "Pray, that you may not enter into temptation." We hear, therefore, that he gave three commands to the disciples: first, that they remain there, so that he himself might pray more conveniently after going on a little; second, that they watch diligently, lest they be overtaken unexpectedly; last, that they not enter into temptation, that is, that they not be shamefully overcome by a temptation which their own carelessness has brought on. And in this part he recalls to their minds what he had warned them of shortly before, concerning the snares of Satan. From these words a general teaching is drawn, which each of us ought to observe whenever harder struggles of persecution or any other dangers threaten. For then above all we must see that we remain at the post entrusted to us, whether someone is a minister of the Church, or bears the magistracy, or is appointed to any other office. For just as it would be shameful for a helmsman, if winds and waves arise, to leave the tiller himself, so those who then desert their office, when their faith and diligence are most required, can never be approved. But this is the very thing in which people for the most part sin today, and therefore the Church and the commonwealth fare the worse. Yet it will not be enough to occupy or hold the place which God has entrusted to us, unless we also watch most attentively against the snares of Satan. For, as was said recently, he never sleeps, and he stirs up against us not only open enemies but also false brethren and our own flesh, so as to harass us with its desires and draw us away from God. Nor is anything so difficult as to detect his arts, by which he is accustomed to insinuate himself even into our minds.
